plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Achilles is a mildew-resistant red gooseberry developed at England's East Malling Research Station, valued for pairing heavy, reliable cropping with much better resistance to American gooseberry mildew than older varieties like Leveller. The medium-large, smooth berries ripen to a deep pinkish-red with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor good for both fresh eating and cooking. Its upright, moderately vigorous bush is easier to manage and pick than sprawling heirloom types, making it a practical choice for smaller home orchards.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in fall in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun to partial shade; agarita grows naturally on rocky limestone hillsides and is extremely drought tolerant once established. Transplanting is best done in fall or early spring — avoid disturbing roots unnecessarily.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; agarita is a classic native Texas evergreen shrub with small, three-lobed, holly-like leaves (each with sharp spines) arranged in a distinctive trifoliate pattern — it looks like a small holly with fierce spines and makes an impenetrable wildlife barrier hedge. In spring it produces clusters of small, intensely fragrant yellow flowers, followed by brilliant red tart berries in late spring that are relished by birds and made by Texas foragers into highly prized jelly. The flavor is tart-sweet, similar to a currant. The berries ripen and fall quickly — traditionally harvested by spreading a tarp under the shrub and shaking the branches. Deer browse it rarely due to the spines. A tough, beautiful, and ecologically valuable native for difficult dry spots in zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Alachua is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) black muscadine bred by the University of Florida for Deep South and Florida growing conditions, and does not require a separate pollinator vine.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to maintain productive fruiting wood. Alachua is a University of Florida-released black muscadine bred and selected specifically for the low-chill, high-heat, high-humidity conditions of Florida and the Deep South, where it produces large, high-quality fruit reliably even in areas too warm for many Georgia- and Carolina-bred muscadine cultivars. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, bearing medium-to-large black fruit with good sweetness and flavor well suited to both fresh eating and processing. Its Florida-focused breeding makes it a particularly strong choice for muscadine growers in the warmest parts of the Gulf South, zone 7–10.

common_name: Alachua Southern Highbush Blueberry (Florida-Bred Low-Chill Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat; Alachua needs only about 300 chill hours, named for the north-central Florida county where the University of Florida breeding program that released it is based.
directions: Amend the planting bed to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines before setting out dormant bushes in winter, and mulch well to conserve moisture around the shallow root zone. Alachua is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for the state's mild winters, producing medium to large, firm, flavorful berries on a vigorous bush that ripens over a solid midseason window. Its very low chilling requirement makes it a dependable choice even after an unusually warm winter along the Gulf Coast, where higher-chill varieties can bloom poorly or fail to set fruit. Plant with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination and yield, fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain strong production.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Alapaha is an early-season University of Georgia rabbiteye named for the Alapaha River in south Georgia, bred for good fruit set and leaf-spot tolerance in humid climates.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Alapaha is an early-ripening rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Georgia and named for the Alapaha River region of south Georgia, bred to combine early harvest timing with better-than-average tolerance of Septoria and other leaf-spot diseases common in humid Gulf South summers. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and firm with good flavor for an early variety. Fruit set improves noticeably with a second rabbiteye cultivar planted nearby, since Alapaha is only partially self-fruitful. The upright, vigorous bush needs little training beyond removing old unproductive canes each winter. Mulch generously with pine bark or pine straw and avoid overhead irrigation late in the day to further reduce leaf-spot pressure in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February for best establishment. Alapaha is an early-season rabbiteye that ripens slightly ahead of mid-season varieties, extending the harvest window at the beginning of the season. Plant with Brightwell, Premier, or Climax for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun; Alapaha is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry selected for exceptional berry quality — the fruit is large, light blue, and has a dessert quality with a sweet-tart balance and crisp texture that earned it high consumer preference ratings in taste trials. Released in 2001, Alapaha is among the newer rabbiteye cultivars with improved fruit quality over the older varieties developed in the mid-20th century. It ripens early in the rabbiteye season (late May to mid-June in zone 8–9), overlapping with Premier and producing well with 300–400 chilling hours. The moderately vigorous, upright-to-spreading shrubs are productive and show reasonable resistance to late-season water stress.

common_name: Albion Strawberry (UC Davis Day-Neutral with Premium Flavor and Firm Flesh)
plant_note: Plant bare-root crowns in fall (October–November) in zone 9 for winter-spring production; Albion is a day-neutral variety and one of the most important in commercial California strawberry production. In zone 9, plant October–November, establish through winter, and harvest January–May. Day-neutral varieties flower continuously when temperatures are between 35–85°F, unlike June-bearers that require specific day length to initiate flowering. Albion was released by the University of California Davis in 2006 and is patented (Plant Patent PP16172). It has become one of the most widely grown commercial day-neutral varieties in California and across North America. In humid zone 9 conditions, angular leaf spot and other foliar diseases can be managed with good air circulation and preventive copper sprays.
directions: Plant crowns at soil level in full sun, well-amended soil. Pick fully red for best flavor. Albion Strawberry was released by the University of California Davis in 2006 (Plant Patent PP16172) by breeder Douglas Shaw and colleagues, and rapidly became one of the most commercially significant day-neutral strawberry varieties in North American production — widely planted in California's Watsonville and Salinas Valley commercial strawberry regions and increasingly adopted by home gardeners seeking premium-flavored everbearing varieties. The Albion name honors the historic English name for Great Britain, though the variety is entirely a California development. Albion's reputation among strawberry enthusiasts centers on its flavor: the combination of high sugar content, balanced acidity, and pronounced strawberry aroma places Albion consistently at or near the top in flavor comparisons among day-neutral varieties — closer to the flavor profile of heirloom or wild strawberries than most commercial types. The fruit is conical to long-conical in shape, medium to large, with uniformly bright red skin and firm, fully red flesh without the white center that characterizes lower-quality commercial strawberries. The firmness — significantly firmer than older varieties like Seascape — gives Albion good shipping quality for commercial growers and several days of excellent quality after harvest for home gardeners. Disease resistance is good: Albion shows strong resistance to Verticillium wilt and crown rot (Phytophthora cactorum), two of the most economically damaging strawberry diseases in California production systems.

common_name: Alexandria Alpine Strawberry (Heavy-Bearing Everbearing Woodland Strawberry)
plant_note: Start Alexandria's dust-fine seed indoors on the soil surface under light, since germination depends on light exposure and steady moisture at room temperature, then transplant the young clumps into rich, well-drained soil after the last frost.
directions: Start Alexandria's dust-fine seed indoors on the soil surface under light, since germination depends on light exposure and steady moisture at room temperature, then transplant the young clumps into rich, well-drained soil after the last frost. It performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, making it one of the more shade-adaptable strawberries for tucking beneath taller vegetables, shrubs, or fruit trees where full-sun beds are unavailable. Alexandria is valued among seed-grown alpine strawberries for its unusually heavy, extended production of small, intensely sweet, aromatic red berries with true wild-strawberry perfume. Because the runnerless plants stay in a tidy clump, they also work well as a low edible edging along a partly shaded path or border.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; space generously to allow for vigorous root-sprout spread and airflow between canes.
directions: Allegheny Blackberry is one of the most productive and widely distributed wild blackberries of eastern North America, growing in open fields, roadsides, forest edges, and disturbed ground from Nova Scotia south to Georgia. Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing plants 4 to 6 feet apart; plants spread rapidly by root sprouts and will form dense, wildlife-supporting thickets if not managed. White flowers appear in spring on stout, heavily prickled, arching second-year canes, followed by large, firm, sweet black drupes from June through July that rank among the finest-flavored of any native blackberry. After harvest, cut spent floricanes to the ground to encourage strong new primocanes; very cold-hardy plants will begin reliable production in their second full year.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil; Allstar is a mid-to-late season June-bearer (ripening about one week after Earliglow) developed by USDA and the University of Maryland for maximum yield, wide adaptability, and outstanding disease resistance — it produces among the largest-fruited berries of any June-bearing variety and is often recommended as the companion to Earliglow to extend the harvest season.
directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring; Allstar produces very large berries (among the largest of any June-bearer) with good flavor; the plants are vigorous and send out abundant runners; remove runners the first year to encourage crown establishment; plant Allstar alongside Earliglow to extend the June-bearing strawberry season by 1–2 weeks. Allstar is a USDA-bred June-bearing strawberry variety (released 1981) that has become one of the most widely planted commercial and home garden strawberries in the eastern United States, valued for its combination of high yields, large fruit size, and exceptional disease resistance. The berries are large — often significantly larger than Earliglow and most other June-bearers — with a conical shape, good firmness, and attractive glossy red color that makes them particularly well-suited for fresh market sales, U-pick operations, and home garden display. The flavor is sweet with moderate acidity — generally considered slightly less intensely flavored than Earliglow but still excellent for fresh eating, preserves, and pies. Allstar's greatest strength is its extremely broad disease resistance profile: it shows good to excellent resistance to red stele root rot, Verticillium wilt, and powdery mildew, making it a reliable producer even in challenging conditions. The combination of Earliglow (early) and Allstar (mid-late) is a classic recommendation from northeastern extension services for home gardeners who want a 2–3 week strawberry harvest window instead of a single concentrated crop. Vigorous runner production makes Allstar easy to propagate and maintain.

plant_note: Plant container-grown nursery stock or rooted cuttings in fall or spring into acidic, gritty, well-drained soil; this circumpolar alpine and arctic native resents heavy, poorly drained ground.
directions: Alpine bearberry is a low, mat-forming, deciduous dwarf shrub of arctic and alpine tundra across the Northern Hemisphere, with small, deeply veined leaves that turn brilliant red in autumn before dropping. It spreads slowly by trailing woody stems that root as they touch the ground, forming a dense evergreen-textured carpet well suited to rock gardens and cold-climate shaded groundcover plantings. Small urn-shaped white to pink flowers in late spring are followed by juicy black berries that ripen through red before turning glossy black; the fruit is edible raw but rather bitter and improves with cooking, and has traditionally been eaten by northern peoples with fat or fish. Site it in acidic, well-drained soil with some shade from hot afternoon sun, since it is adapted to short, cool growing seasons and struggles in warm, humid climates.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped nursery stock in fall or early spring; alpine currant tolerates deep shade and poor soil better than almost any other fruiting shrub.
directions: Alpine currant is an extremely tough, compact, mound-forming shrub long used for shade hedging in cold climates where few other woody plants tolerate dense shade and dry soil so well. Plant in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil; it is not particular about soil pH or fertility and shrugs off urban pollution and road salt. Inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear in spring, and female plants (this species is dioecious, so both sexes are needed for fruit) set small, glossy red currants in midsummer that are edible but tart and bland, used mainly by birds or for jelly rather than fresh eating. Prune after flowering to maintain a formal hedge shape, since it tolerates shearing extremely well and rarely needs spraying for pests.

plant_note: Start indoors early; seeds benefit from cold stratification.
directions: Alpine Regina is an everbearing woodland strawberry that produces small, intensely aromatic berries all season on tidy, runnerless clumps. Surface-sow the tiny seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, pressing them onto moist mix without covering, since light aids germination; a few weeks of cold stratification improves the sprouting rate. Transplant seedlings 8-12 inches apart in rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and some afternoon shade. Plants make an excellent edible border or container crop and often fruit the first year.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; seeds are very small and should be pressed onto the soil surface without covering.
directions: Alpine strawberries are compact, clumping, runner-free plants that produce small but intensely fragrant and flavored berries continuously from early summer through fall frost. Seeds are tiny and require light for germination — surface sow in trays and do not cover; keep moist at 65–75°F. Unlike garden strawberries, alpines form clumps rather than runners and are best propagated by division every 3–4 years or from seed. They are more shade-tolerant than hybrid strawberries, making them excellent for edging partially shaded paths. Harvest individual berries when fully red and aromatic.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally, into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; American barberry is the native, non-invasive Appalachian counterpart to the widely planted but ecologically problematic Japanese barberry.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; American barberry is a thorny, deciduous Appalachian native shrub with small, spine-tipped leaves, drooping clusters of small yellow flowers in late spring, and bright red, elongated berries that ripen in fall and persist into winter, providing food for birds when little else is available. It is a genuinely native, non-invasive alternative for gardeners who want the ornamental berry and thorny-hedge qualities of barberry without planting the widely naturalized and ecologically disruptive Japanese barberry. Because Berberis species can serve as an alternate host for wheat stem rust, avoid planting it in large numbers near commercial grain fields, a precaution that led to historic eradication programs targeting common barberry in agricultural regions. Otherwise easy to grow and largely trouble-free, it works well as an informal barrier hedge, wildlife planting, or specimen in a naturalistic border.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown specimens in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; plant two different cultivars near each other for reliable cross-pollination and heavy berry set.
directions: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun, planting two different cultivars for cross-pollination; American elderberry is a fast-growing native shrub of floodplains and woodland edges that produces large, flat-topped clusters of tiny, white, fragrant flowers in early summer followed by hanging clusters of small, dark-purple to black berries in late summer that are among the most nutritious and medicinally valued native fruits in North America — the basis of elderberry syrup, wine, pies, jams, and traditional immune-support preparations. Never eat raw elderberries in quantity (mildly toxic); cooking destroys the problematic compounds. The flowers are also edible and delicious battered and fried or infused into cordials. Excellent wildlife plant, supporting over 50 bird species. Named varieties 'Bob Gordon', 'Adams', and 'Nova' have larger berries and heavier yields.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; gooseberries may be illegal to plant in some US states where they are regulated as alternate hosts of white pine blister rust — check local regulations before planting.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun — American gooseberry is the native gooseberry of the northeastern US and Canada, one of the most productive edible native shrubs for cool-climate food gardens. The tart-sweet berries (ripening from green to reddish-purple in midsummer) are excellent for pies, jams, preserves, and fresh eating when fully ripe. The shrub tolerates partial shade better than most fruiting shrubs and produces reliably in conditions too shaded for currants and jostaberries. The stems bear short, sharp spines at the nodes; wear gloves when harvesting. American gooseberry is more resistant to powdery mildew than European gooseberry (R. uva-crispa), making it easier to grow in humid climates. Best in zones 3–7; does not perform well in hot, humid summers of zone 8 and south. Check state regulations on Ribes planting before ordering.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; at least two plants improve cross-pollination and fruit set.
directions: American highbush cranberry is a native Viburnum — not a true cranberry — bearing clusters of bright red, tart berries in fall that persist on the shrub into winter, providing critical food for wildlife during cold months. The berries have a distinct musky aroma when raw that largely disappears with cooking; they are high in pectin and excellent for jellies, sauces, and syrups as a cranberry substitute. Do not confuse with the European cranberrybush (V. opulus), which produces lower-quality, more bitter fruit. Prune out the oldest canes at the base every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and an open, multi-stemmed form.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; plant at least two shrubs for cross-pollination and better fruit set.
directions: Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, planting at least two shrubs to ensure cross-pollination; American highbush cranberry is not a true cranberry but a native viburnum that produces bright red, translucent, cranberry-sized berries in clusters from fall through winter that birds love and that can be made into preserves, sauces, and jellies with a flavor resembling true cranberries. The lacy white flower clusters in late spring are attractive, and the three-lobed leaves turn brilliant red-purple in fall. Plants are also important wildlife habitat shrubs for nesting birds. The native var. americanum is preferred over the European V. opulus (which escaped and has naturalized invasively in some areas).

plant_note: Set out rooted suckers or container-grown plants in spring once soil is workable, in poor, sandy, or saline soil in full sun; American silverberry needs no fertility amendment and spreads by root suckers, so site it where its colonizing habit can be contained away from cultivated beds.
directions: Set out rooted suckers or container plants in spring on poor, sandy, or saline ground where its vigorous, nitrogen-fixing roots and suckering habit can be left to spread without crowding cultivated beds. This silvery-leaved North American native tolerates conditions few other fruiting shrubs can, needing no supplemental fertility once established. Small, fragrant yellow flowers in early summer give way to silvery, mealy berries that ripen in fall and are used for jam, drying, and winter forage for birds. Unlike the related autumn olive and Russian olive, American silverberry is a true native across most of its range and behaves far less aggressively, making it a sound choice for windbreaks, erosion control, and reclamation plantings.

common_name: Amity Raspberry (Large Fall-Bearing Oregon Red Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or potted plants in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; as a fall-bearing (primocane) type, Amity can be mowed to the ground each winter for a single simplified fall crop.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost, in full sun, providing support for canes as they fill in. Amity was bred at Oregon State University as a fall-bearing (primocane) red raspberry, producing large, firm, richly flavored berries on the current season's new canes from late summer through fall, well after most summer-bearing varieties have finished. Because primocane types fruit on new growth, the entire planting can be mowed or cut to the ground each winter, radically simplifying pruning compared to summer-bearing varieties that require selective cane removal. This makes Amity a particularly low-maintenance choice for home gardeners wanting a single, reliable, high-quality fall raspberry crop without the more involved care summer-bearing brambles need.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Anna is a female cultivar and requires a male hardy kiwi vine (such as 'Meader' or a seedling male) within about 30–50 feet for pollination and fruit set. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola, since mature vines become heavy and vigorous.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, with a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor structure in place before planting. Anna is one of the most widely planted female hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) cultivars in North America, valued for its heavy, reliable production of smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruit that can be eaten whole, skin and all, unlike fuzzy supermarket kiwifruit. The fruit ripens in early fall with sweet, richly flavored, bright green flesh, and the vigorous vine is notably cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below what damages standard fuzzy kiwi (Actinidia deliciosa). As a dioecious cultivar, Anna requires a separate male hardy kiwi vine planted nearby for pollination — without one, the vine will grow and flower but set little to no fruit. A vigorous, productive choice for a well-supported arbor or fence line in zone 4–8.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Annapolis roots quickly and produces abundant runners for filling matted rows.
directions: Annapolis was bred at the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia and released in 1984 as an Earliglow-derived selection resistant to red stele root rot, giving northern growers an early cultivar for sites with a history of root disease. Fruit is medium-large, light red, and mildly sweet, ripening ahead of most other hardy June-bearers and extending the start of the home harvest season. The vigorous, freely runnering plants tolerate winters to zone 3 with only modest straw mulch protection. Because it fruits early, protect open blossoms from late spring frosts with row cover when a cold snap is forecast.

plant_note: Set canes early spring in a sheltered, sunny spot.
directions: 'Anne' produces exceptionally large, pale-yellow fall-bearing berries with a sweet, apricot-like flavor. Grow in rich, moisture-retentive soil and support the tall canes with a two-wire trellis to keep fruit off the ground. As a primocane variety it can be mown down each winter for a single autumn crop, simplifying pruning. The soft golden fruit does not ship well, making it an ideal home-garden and fresh-eating selection.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Apache is a thornless, erect blackberry that requires no trellis support, though a simple post-and-wire system improves fruit quality and harvest ease. In zone 9 Apache ripens June–July. Prune all fruited canes to the ground after harvest; tie new primocanes loosely to trellis wires.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Apache is a thornless erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas as part of their world-leading blackberry breeding program. It produces very large, firm, sweet-tart, jet-black berries — among the largest of any thornless blackberry variety at 1–1.5 inch length and 8–12 grams per berry. The erect habit allows Apache to be grown without trellis support, though light support improves the crop. The exceptional fruit size and good flavor make Apache a top choice for fresh eating, farmers' markets, and home preserving. In zone 9 Apache performs well and is resistant to the orange rust fungus that can devastate susceptible blackberry varieties in the humid Gulf South. The thornless canes make harvest much more pleasant and efficient than thorny types, and the erect habit means berries are not dragged through the mud on trailing varieties.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tissue-culture transplants in late winter or early spring; Apache is a biennial-caning plant (floricanes fruit in year two) so first full crop is the second season after planting. Space rows 6–8 feet apart for mechanized harvesting or 4–6 feet for home gardens. Chill hours required: approximately 300–500 hours below 45°F — suitable for zone 7–8 Gulf Coast winter conditions.
directions: Plant rooted canes or tissue-culture transplants in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil; prune floricanes to the ground after harvest to maintain plant vigor. Apache is a 2003 release from the University of Arkansas blackberry breeding program (the same program that produced Arapaho, Navaho, Kiowa, and Ouachita) and produces some of the largest blackberry fruits in commercial production — individual berries averaging 14–17 grams (roughly 3–4 times the size of a typical wild blackberry), with an excellent balance of sweetness and mild acidity that makes them outstanding for fresh eating. The thornless, erect canes (4–6 feet tall) require no support structures and are easy and pleasant to harvest without the scratches common to thorny types. Apache ripens in late July in Arkansas (later than Arapaho and Navaho), extending the fresh blackberry season into peak summer. The large, firm berries hold their quality well after harvest, giving Apache better shipping and shelf life than softer varieties — an advantage for market growers and home gardeners who want berries for preserving. Very productive when properly established, and the thornless, self-supporting habit makes it the most garden-friendly of the Arkansas blackberry releases.

plant_note: Plant in early spring for an erect, thornless hedge.
directions: 'Arapaho' is an early-ripening erect thornless blackberry with medium-large berries containing small, unobtrusive seeds. Its self-supporting canes need minimal trellising, making it well suited to compact plantings and home gardens. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and provide even moisture during the fruiting period for best size and flavor. Remove floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to five or six vigorous shoots per plant.

plant_note: Plant bare-root canes in late winter or early spring; in zone 9 plant December–March. Arapaho is erect-growing and needs only light tipping of new canes at 3–4 feet to encourage lateral branching for maximum fruiting wood — unlike trailing blackberries, no extensive trellis infrastructure is required. In zone 9 Arapaho requires only 400–500 chill hours, making it viable in most zone 9 areas. Fruiting occurs on second-year canes (floricanes); remove old canes to the ground after harvest each year.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Arapaho was the first thornless erect blackberry ever released, developed by the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program in 1993 — a significant milestone in blackberry cultivation that eliminated the primary obstacle to home garden blackberry growing for many people who found thorned blackberries impractical to pick and manage. The erect, self-supporting canes reach 5–7 feet and require only tipping (not a full trellis system) to remain manageable. The large, glossy, firm-yet-juicy berries with excellent sweet-tart flavor ripen in early June in zone 9, among the earliest erect blackberries. The firm texture allows berries to be picked and stored for several days without softening — an advantage for home gardeners who harvest on a schedule. Arapaho was succeeded by later thornless varieties (Apache, Natchez) with larger berries, but remains widely planted for its early ripening, good flavor, and reliable performance in zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant one male per 4–6 female vines after last frost; protect new shoots from cats, which are strongly attracted to kolomikta vines.
directions: Actinidia kolomikta is the hardiest kiwi species, tolerating temperatures to -40°F in zone 3, and is grown for its small (1 in), sweet, smooth-skinned fruits that ripen in late summer. The vine is ornamentally striking due to pink-and-white variegated foliage on male plants. It is dioecious and requires both male and female plants — one male per 4–6 females. Cats are intensely attracted to the plants and will damage young vines, so protect new plantings with wire cages. Prune each dormant season to maintain a framework of lateral arms on a sturdy arbor or fence.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring; extremely adaptable to wet or dry soils.
directions: Aronia is exceptionally hardy and tolerates wet, poorly drained soils, making it suitable for rain gardens. It is self-fruitful and rarely needs a pollinator, though yields improve with a second plant nearby. Prune by removing the oldest, thickest canes at the base every 3–4 years to encourage vigorous new growth and better light penetration. Harvest clusters in late summer when berries are very dark purple-black; the astringent flavor mellows after a light frost or processing.

common_name: Aunt Molly's Ground Cherry (Polish Heirloom Sweet Pineapple-Vanilla Husk Cherry)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Aunt Molly's is a sprawling plant (18–24 inches tall but spreading 3–4 feet) that benefits from some support or ample ground space. In zone 9, transplant March–April for production May through October or beyond. Ground cherries self-seed readily in zone 9 and may appear as volunteers in subsequent seasons without replanting. Harvest when the papery husk has turned tan-brown and dried, and the fruit inside has turned yellow-orange — fruits drop to the ground when fully ripe (hence the name 'ground cherry'). The papery husk protects the ripe fruit and allows it to store for several weeks longer than most fresh fruits; husked and refrigerated fruits keep 2–3 weeks.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest when the papery husk has browned and dried; ripe fruits drop to the ground. Aunt Molly's Ground Cherry is a Polish heirloom Physalis pruinosa — a member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) in the same genus as cape gooseberry (Physalis peruviana) but distinct in plant size (Physalis pruinosa is smaller and more compact than the large cape gooseberry) and fruit flavor profile. According to Seed Savers Exchange lore, the variety was brought from Poland by a gardener known as 'Aunt Molly' and preserved in American seed-saving collections, where it has been distributed and maintained as one of the finest flavored ground cherry varieties available. The fruits are small (0.5–0.75 inch), round, yellow-orange when ripe, enclosed in a papery tan husk (the inflated calyx) that the plant uses to enclose and protect the developing fruit. The flavor is the defining characteristic of Aunt Molly's and the reason it consistently receives the highest flavor ratings among ground cherry varieties in trial evaluations: a complex, intensely sweet flavor with distinct notes of pineapple, vanilla, and tropical fruit, sometimes described as tasting like a sweet tomato crossed with a pineapple. This flavor is more complex and concentrated than most Physalis pruinosa types. In zone 9, ground cherries thrive in the warm climate, producing prodigiously through summer and fall; established plants may behave almost as short-lived perennials in the mildest zone 9 locations, and self-seeding creates a supply of volunteer plants in subsequent seasons.

common_name: Aurora Blueberry (Very Late Season Northern Highbush Blueberry, Season-Extender Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.2), well-drained, organic-rich soil in full sun; Aurora is a Michigan State University-developed very late season northern highbush blueberry — ripening in late August to mid-September in Michigan and the Northeast, 4–6 weeks after early season varieties like Duke — the latest-ripening major highbush blueberry variety, allowing fresh blueberry harvest to extend well into September; plant with an early or mid-season variety for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in very acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil; maintain pH 4.5–5.2 with acid fertilizer; mulch with pine bark; Aurora ripens very late (late August through September) producing large, firm, light blue berries with outstanding flavor — considered by MSU researchers to have among the best flavor of any northern highbush variety; plant early-season varieties (Duke, Bluecrop) alongside for cross-pollination and a full-season harvest. Aurora blueberry is a Michigan State University-released variety (2003) that has become highly regarded among serious home blueberry growers and specialty producers for its combination of very late ripening season and exceptional berry quality. The variety was specifically developed as part of MSU's late-season breeding program aimed at extending the Michigan commercial blueberry season into September, reducing market glut during the peak July–August production and commanding higher prices for September-ripening fruit. Aurora ripens the latest of any major highbush blueberry variety — typically 4–6 weeks after early-season varieties like Duke and 2–3 weeks after Jersey (itself a late variety), making September fresh blueberries possible in zones 4–6 where frost would otherwise end the season. The berries are large to very large, firm (excellent handling and shelf life for a highbush variety), and have a notably good flavor — sweet, aromatic, and complex — that is consistently rated among the best of all highbush varieties in blind flavor tastings. The very firm texture also makes Aurora berries excellent for fresh eating (they snap satisfyingly rather than bursting), baking, and freezing. An excellent choice for home orchardists wanting to extend fresh blueberry season as late as possible into autumn.

common_name: Aurora Honeyberry (Late-Season University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Aurora is a late-flowering, late-ripening University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivar bred to avoid the spring frosts that can damage the earliest-blooming honeyberries, and needs a compatible late-blooming pollinizer planted nearby.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Aurora is self-infertile. Aurora was released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the leading haskap breeding program in North America, and is valued for its large, elongated berries with a sweet, well-balanced flavor closer to blueberry than the tart, sometimes bitter flavor of earlier haskap introductions. It blooms and ripens later than earlier-generation cultivars like 'Borealis', which helps the flowers dodge late spring frosts, and the fruit holds on the bush longer without dropping, extending the harvest window. Like other haskaps, Aurora is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures to -40F and flowers that survive down to about -8F, but it is poorly suited to hot, humid climates and performs best in short-season, cold-winter regions. Fruit is borne on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing branches for the first three to four years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Austin requires about 400–500 chill hours and needs a cross-pollinating companion such as Climax or Brightwell for good fruit set, since it is not self-fruitful.
directions: Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5–5.0 with peat moss or sulfur before planting; Austin is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Georgia breeding program, selected as an early-to-midseason ripening variety that fills the harvest window alongside Climax, extending the picking season before the midseason varieties come on. Berries are medium-large, light blue, and firm with good flavor, borne on vigorous, upright, productive bushes that establish quickly. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Austin is not self-fruitful and should be planted with at least one other compatible variety within about 50 feet for cross-pollination and full crops. Remove flower buds the first year or two after planting to direct the plant's energy into root and cane development rather than fruit; full production typically begins by year four. Mulch generously with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity, and irrigate consistently during fruit swell, since rabbiteye blueberries have shallow, fibrous roots that dry out quickly in Gulf Coast heat.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Austin needs roughly 500-550 chill hours and ripens early-to-mid season. Plant with another rabbiteye cultivar such as Climax or Premier for cross-pollination and a heavier set.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist. Austin is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry that ripens just after Climax in the early part of the season, producing medium-to-large, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor on a vigorous, upright bush. It extends the early harvest window when planted alongside Climax and Premier, and its dependable, heavy cropping habit combined with good disease tolerance has made it a standard early-season choice for Gulf South home orchards and u-pick plantings. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous new fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; Autumn Bliss fruits on current-season primocanes, so all canes can be mown to the ground each winter for simplified maintenance.
directions: Plant dormant canes in full sun in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, and cut all canes to the ground in late winter since fruit forms on the current season's growth. Bred at East Malling Research in England, Autumn Bliss was one of the first widely planted primocane (fall-bearing) raspberry cultivars and remains valued for ripening its crop earlier in the season than most other fall types, which is a real advantage in shorter-season gardens. The medium-to-large, dark red, conical berries have good flavor and hold reasonably well after picking, and the compact, sturdy canes often need little or no trellising. It can be more susceptible to certain cane diseases than newer primocane releases, so good air circulation and sanitation help keep it productive.

common_name: Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry (Brilliant Fall Color Multi-Season Native Tree)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Brilliance is prized for white spring flowers, edible summer berries, and outstanding orange-red fall color all on the same plant.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Autumn Brilliance is one of the most widely planted serviceberry cultivars for its exceptional multi-season interest: clouds of white flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge, sweet, blueberry-like edible fruit in early summer that birds also relish, and some of the most reliable, brilliant orange-red fall foliage color of any small flowering tree. It works well as a single or multi-trunked small specimen tree, a large shrub border, or a naturalized planting, and tolerates a range of soil conditions with minimal care once established. The berries can be harvested for fresh eating, baking, and preserves if picked before birds strip the tree, or left entirely for wildlife.

common_name: Autumn Magic Aronia (Compact Ornamental Black Chokeberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Magic is a compact black chokeberry selection bred as much for landscape use and fall color as for its edible fruit.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Magic is a compact black chokeberry cultivar selected primarily for landscape use, staying notably smaller and more rounded than seed-grown Aronia melanocarpa while still producing a good crop of glossy black, antioxidant-rich berries. The shrub is a genuine multi-season landscape plant: clusters of white flowers in spring, clean dark green summer foliage, and some of the most vivid red-purple fall color of any Aronia selection, making it a strong choice for a foundation planting or mixed border that also happens to produce useful fruit. Berries are highly astringent eaten raw and are best processed into juice, syrup, or dried additions to baked goods and trail mixes. The self-fertile, adaptable shrub tolerates wet or dry soils and both full sun and considerable shade, and needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems to stay dense and well-shaped.

plant_note: Plant in spring in any well-drained soil; autumn olive is highly invasive in the eastern U.S. — confirm it is legal in your state before planting.
directions: Autumn olive is a nitrogen-fixing Asian shrub with extremely high yields of small red-speckled berries that are rich in lycopene and have a sweet-tart flavor; it is among the most productive fruiting shrubs per acre in temperate climates. However, it is considered an invasive species across much of the eastern U.S. and is prohibited or discouraged in many states — verify legal status in your jurisdiction before planting. Named fruit-producing selections such as 'Garnet' or 'Red Wing' are more compact and productive than seedlings. Harvest by hand-stripping clusters in fall when berries are fully red; fruit quality improves after light frost.

common_name: Avonblue Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early Florida-Bred Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in strongly acidic, well-drained soil; Avonblue is largely self-fruitful with a low chill requirement near 400 hours, but yields improve with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar planted for cross-pollination.
directions: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in winter into acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) heavily amended with pine bark or peat moss, and mulch to keep the shallow root zone cool and evenly moist. Avonblue is one of the older University of Florida southern highbush releases and remains valued for its dependable early ripening, largely self-fruitful flowers, and tolerance of Florida's sandy, warm-winter growing conditions. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and mildly tart, produced on a moderately compact, rounded bush well suited to smaller home garden plantings. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water deeply during dry spells, and prune out old unproductive wood each winter to keep the bush renewing itself.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile, organically rich soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Bababerry is one of the very few raspberry cultivars bred specifically for low-chill, high-heat climates and needs afternoon shade protection in the hottest Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, organically rich soil in full sun with afternoon shade protection in hot climates, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool, since raspberries are naturally adapted to cooler regions and struggle with Gulf South summer heat. Bred in Louisiana specifically to fruit in low-chill, high-heat conditions where almost no other raspberry succeeds, Bababerry is an everbearing cultivar producing two crops a year — a smaller early-summer crop on floricanes and a heavier fall crop on primocanes — with medium red berries of good flavor. It represents one of the only realistic raspberry options for Gulf South gardeners determined to grow this normally cool-climate fruit, though yields and vigor remain modest compared to raspberries grown in their preferred cooler range. Cut spent floricanes to the ground after their early summer crop and manage primocanes for the fall crop, keeping the planting well watered and mulched through the hottest months.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or sulfur; Baldwin requires roughly 400–500 chill hours and is not self-fruitful, needing a cross-pollinating rabbiteye companion such as Tifblue, Climax, or Brightwell nearby for reliable fruit set.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive conditions rabbiteye blueberries need. Baldwin is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for ripening quite late in the season, extending the blueberry harvest well past earlier cultivars, with small to medium, firm, dark blue berries that hold their shape and flavor well, making them useful for fresh eating, freezing, and machine harvest alike. The plant is vigorous, productive, and well adapted to the acidic, sandy soils typical of the Gulf South, requiring a second compatible rabbiteye variety nearby for good cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: Baron Solemacher Alpine Strawberry (Runnerless German Heirloom)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, pressing the dust-fine seed onto the soil surface without covering since light aids germination.
directions: Baron Solemacher is a nineteenth-century German heirloom alpine strawberry prized for forming tidy, runnerless clumps rather than spreading by stolons, which makes it well suited to edging, containers, and small raised beds. Surface-sow the tiny seeds indoors and keep them consistently moist at 60-75F, since germination can be slow and uneven over several weeks. Transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade after the danger of frost has passed, and expect a light crop the first year with fuller production from year two onward. Plants bear small, intensely aromatic red berries from early summer into fall and are best increased by division every few years once established.

plant_note: Plant two or more named cultivars for cross-pollination in spring in sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil.
directions: Beach plum is a native Atlantic coastal shrub that thrives in sandy, salt-spray-exposed sites where few other fruits survive, making it invaluable for coastal and xeric gardens. The small (0.5–1 in), round fruits range from red to purple to blue at maturity in late summer and are traditionally used for preserves and jams on Cape Cod and Long Island. Plant at least two named cultivars such as 'Autumn' and 'Premier' for adequate cross-pollination, as seedlings are variable and often infertile. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape; heavy pruning reduces fruiting the following year.

plant_note: Plant runners or potted plants in spring in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; beach strawberry is naturally adapted to the dry, salty, sandy soils of coastal bluffs and beaches. Avoid rich soil or heavy fertilization, which produces excessive leafy growth and fewer fruits.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, infertile to average soil in full sun to light shade; beach strawberry is one of the two wild strawberry species that were crossed by French botanists in the 18th century to create the modern garden strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) — the other parent being the Virginian strawberry (F. virginiana). It is native to the Pacific coast of the Americas from Alaska to Chile, naturally growing on sandy bluffs, dunes, and coastal prairies where it tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor soil. The fruits are small by commercial standards but deeply aromatic and richly flavored compared to grocery store strawberries. The leathery, blue-green leaves are distinctly more salt- and drought-tolerant than those of garden strawberries. An excellent low-maintenance groundcover for sunny, dry, or coastal sites; spreads by runners to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; bear huckleberry grows naturally in acidic woodland understories and high-elevation forests of the southern Appalachians.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; bear huckleberry is a deciduous native shrub of the high-elevation Appalachian forests from North Carolina to Tennessee, naturally growing in the understory beneath oaks, hemlocks, and rhododendrons. The shiny black berries ripen in late summer and are eaten by bears (which explains the common name), black bears being primary dispersers in its mountain habitat. The berries are edible by humans as well — sweet and flavorful, similar to blueberries but with a distinctive tang. Like all huckleberries, the plant is challenging to cultivate outside its specific acidic, woodland conditions; it does not tolerate alkaline soil, dry soil, or full sun. Excellent for native woodland gardens in the southern mountains.

plant_note: Root stem tip cuttings in early fall or plant container-grown specimens in sharply drained, acidic, sandy or rocky, infertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; bearberry demands perfect drainage and acidic soil — it dies quickly in rich, moist, alkaline conditions.
directions: Root cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or gravelly, infertile soil in full sun to partial shade; bearberry (kinnikinnick) is a native, circumboreal evergreen groundcover that forms a tight, mat-forming carpet of small, shiny, paddle-shaped leaves with pink urn-shaped flowers in spring followed by bright red berries that ripen in fall and persist through winter, providing critical food for bears, grouse, foxes, deer, and songbirds. It is specifically adapted to barren, acid, infertile soils — adding fertilizer or organic matter kills it. Excellent for stabilizing slopes, covering dry banks under conifers, and in rock gardens. The berries are edible but mealy and very astringent when raw; historically used for medicinal tea and food in harsh conditions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in very well-drained, sandy or rocky, acidic soil; bearberry strongly resents wet, fertile conditions.
directions: Bearberry is a prostrate, evergreen groundcover native to circumpolar regions, widely used in northern and mountain landscapes for erosion control on dry, acidic, sandy slopes. The small red berries ripen in fall and persist through winter, providing important wildlife food for bears, grouse, and other species; they are mealy and bland fresh but edible when cooked or dried. Bearberry is best propagated from rooted stem cuttings as seed germination is notoriously slow and difficult. Once established, the plant is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free; avoid fertilizing or overwatering, which quickly kills it.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Beckyblue has a low chill requirement (around 350-400 hours), ripens early, and needs another low-chill rabbiteye such as Climax nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, in full sun with a compatible early-season pollinator nearby. Beckyblue is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry bred specifically for the low winter chill of the Deep South and Florida, ripening among the earliest of the rabbiteye cultivars and giving Gulf Coast growers a jump on the blueberry season. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and pleasantly mild-flavored, borne on a vigorous, spreading bush. Because it flowers early, plant it in a site with reasonable air drainage to reduce frost risk to the blooms in years with a late cold snap. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, mulch well to conserve moisture, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain strong early yields.

plant_note: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil, and prune out any wood older than three years each winter.
directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil, and prune out any wood older than three years each winter. Ben Alder is a late-season black currant from the Scottish Crop Research Institute's Ben breeding program, the same lineage that produced Ben Lomond, Ben Sarek, and Ben Nevis. It extends the black currant harvest window later into summer than most other Ben-series cultivars, bearing large, richly flavored berries on a vigorous, upright, cold-tolerant bush. Its late flowering helps it dodge spring frost damage that can cut yields in earlier-blooming currants, a useful trait in frost-prone regions.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn through early spring, burying the crown slightly deeper than it grew in the nursery to encourage strong new shoots from the base.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, setting the crown a couple of inches deeper than it sat in the pot to promote vigorous basal shoots. Bred in Scotland, Ben Connan is a compact black currant selection prized for combining a smaller, more garden-friendly bush size with very heavy yields of large, richly flavored berries, making it a popular choice where space is limited. It ripens earlier than many other black currant cultivars, giving a head start on the harvest season, and its dense, tidy growth habit needs less room between plants than older, larger currant varieties. Prune in the dormant season by removing about a quarter to a third of the oldest wood each year, since the best fruit forms on one- and two-year-old stems.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, peaty, moisture-retentive soil with access to irrigation; Ben Lear is an early-ripening cultivar, useful for home growers who want to harvest ahead of the main cranberry season.
directions: Ben Lear is an older, widely grown cranberry cultivar selected from a Wisconsin bog in the early 20th century, valued for its early ripening, large dark-red berries, and vigorous, easy-to-establish vines that make it a good choice for home bog beds where an early harvest is wanted. Flavor and color develop earlier in the season than in later-ripening cultivars like Stevens, though total yield per vine tends to run somewhat lower than the most productive modern releases. It requires the same demanding conditions as all cranberries: strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0-5.0), constant moisture, and a sandy-peat substrate that mimics its native bog habitat, along with a sand mulch layer to suppress weeds and support proper rooting. Vines take several years to establish before cropping heavily, but then perform reliably for decades. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once berries color fully and bounce when dropped, ahead of the main-season harvest of later cultivars.

plant_note: Plant bare-root bushes in autumn or early spring while dormant.
directions: 'Ben Lomond' is a heavy-cropping Scottish black currant with large, aromatic berries high in vitamin C, ideal for cordials and preserves. It flowers slightly late, giving some protection from spring frosts, and tolerates a range of soils if kept moist. Plant deeply, burying the crown a couple of inches, to encourage strong shoots from the base. Prune in late winter by removing about a third of the oldest wood, since fruit is borne best on one- and two-year-old stems.

common_name: Ben Nevis Black Currant (Heavy-Cropping Scottish Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root Ben Nevis bushes in early spring, several inches deeper than they grew in the nursery row to encourage a multi-stemmed base, into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in part shade to full sun.
directions: Plant dormant bare-root Ben Nevis bushes in early spring, several inches deeper than they grew in the nursery row to encourage a multi-stemmed base, into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in part shade to full sun. This Scottish-bred cultivar is prized on commercial currant farms for its heavy, reliable yields of large, glossy black berries that ripen a little later than older Ben-series varieties, which helps spread out the harvest window. The berries carry black currant's intense, tart, aromatic flavor and high vitamin C content, and are traditionally cooked into jams, cordials, and the French liqueur cassis rather than eaten fresh off the bush. Like other currants, Ben Nevis fruits well with several hours of daily shade, making it one of the more shade-tolerant fruiting shrubs for a partly wooded garden edge.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; can also be planted in fall. Ben Sarek is self-fertile and does not require a cross-pollinator. Plant 5–6 feet apart; the compact habit means Ben Sarek fits in smaller spaces than standard black currant varieties. Prune out wood older than 3 years annually to maintain productivity.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Ben Sarek is a compact black currant cultivar from the Scottish Crop Research Institute's 'Ben' series — the same breeding program that produced Ben Lomond and Ben Tirran. Ben Sarek is the most compact of the Ben series, growing only 3–4 feet tall while producing very heavy crops of large, dark, richly flavored black currant berries in July. The combination of compact size and exceptionally high productivity makes Ben Sarek the best choice for small gardens and urban growing situations where standard currant shrubs are too large. Black currants have a distinctive, intensely aromatic, bittersweet flavor — the basis for cassis liqueur and blackcurrant jam — that is unlike any other common fruit. The very high vitamin C content (more per ounce than almost any other fruit) and exceptionally high anthocyanin levels have made black currant products popular in European functional food and nutraceutical markets.

common_name: Ben Sarek Currant (Compact High-Yield Black Currant)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ben Sarek is a compact Scottish-bred black currant that fits small gardens and containers better than most currant cultivars.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Ben Sarek is a Scottish Crop Research Institute black currant bred for a naturally compact, dense habit that stays notably smaller than older black currant cultivars while still producing very heavy crops of large, richly flavored berries. Its compact size makes it one of the better black currant choices for small gardens and large containers, where a full-sized black currant bush would quickly outgrow the space. Berries are strongly aromatic and tart, best cooked into jam, syrup, cordial, and baked goods. Black currants fruit mainly on one-year-old wood, so remove the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the compact bush renewing itself with vigorous young growth.

common_name: Ben Tirran Black Currant (Late-Flowering Frost-Avoiding Scottish Black Currant)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool, moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Ben Tirran needs a long, cold winter chill period and is not a reliable choice for the Gulf Coast.
directions: Ben Tirran is a late-flowering, late-season release from the James Hutton Institute's black currant breeding program, bred so its blossoms open after the usual late-frost window, sharply cutting the risk of frost-damaged crops compared with earlier Ben-series currants. It forms a vigorous, compact bush carrying large, glossy black berries that ripen in late July into heavy, mechanically harvestable clusters with good resistance to powdery mildew and other common currant diseases. Because it needs a substantial cold winter chill to flower and fruit well, Ben Tirran is best suited to cold-winter regions and is unlikely to perform reliably in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens; northern growers should plant it with another black currant for cross-pollination. Harvest full clusters once berries turn glossy black and prune out about a third of the oldest wood each dormant season to keep the bush productive.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root bushes in early spring into acidic, moisture-retentive soil.
directions: Grow in full sun on well-drained, acidic soil and mulch with pine bark or sawdust to hold moisture around the shallow, fibrous root system. Berkeley is an older, widely planted mid-season highbush cultivar valued for large, firm, pale sky-blue berries with a mild, sweet flavor and good resistance to cracking. Its spreading, vigorous bushes are heavy and reliable producers over a long lifespan, and the plant also offers attractive orange-red fall foliage. Because it dislikes waterlogged soil, raised beds or amended rows are worthwhile on heavier ground.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Berry Blue is self-infertile and needs a compatible pollinizer such as Honey Bee or Aurora planted nearby for reliable fruit set.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Berry Blue is not reliably self-fertile. This is one of the earlier commercially available honeyberry cultivars in North America, forming a compact, tidy bush well suited to small gardens and mixed borders, with round-to-oval berries that ripen a bit later than the earliest University of Saskatchewan releases, helping spread out the harvest window when several cultivars are planted together. Flavor is tart with a mild blueberry-like undertone, better suited to jam, syrup, and baking than to fresh eating for most palates, though fully ripe fruit sweetens considerably. Berry Blue is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winters well below -30F, but struggles in hot, humid summer climates and is a poor match for zone 8-10 gardens. As with other haskaps, avoid heavy pruning in the first several years and then renew the oldest wood periodically to keep the bush productive.

common_name: Big Lifeberry Goji (Large-Fruited Compact Patio Goji)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring after frost danger; Big Lifeberry is a compact, breeding-program goji cultivar suited to smaller gardens and large containers as well as open ground.
directions: Plant in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0 in full sun; goji tolerates poor, alkaline soils where other fruiting shrubs struggle. Big Lifeberry is a modern breeding-program goji selection producing notably larger berries than seed-grown goji, on a more compact, better-branched plant that fruits at a younger age and fits large containers as well as garden beds. Its bushier, less sprawling habit than wild-type goji makes it easier to manage without the loose, arching growth typical of the species. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals; harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers rather than pulling on the fruit directly, since the sap can stain.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in early spring in strongly acidic, humus-rich, moist soil, ideally under light tree canopy.
directions: Bilberry is a low-growing European relative of blueberry that differs in producing berries singly rather than in clusters; the deep purple-red flesh (unlike blueberry's white flesh) stains heavily and has an intense, slightly tart flavor. It demands strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) with high organic matter and cool, moist conditions, making it challenging to grow in most American gardens but worth attempting in zones 3–7 under high shade or at elevation. Minimal pruning is needed; shear plants lightly every 3–4 years to rejuvenate. Harvest in mid- to late summer when berries are fully dark blue-black and tender.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February for best establishment. Biloxi requires only 150–200 chill hours, making it the best choice for the warmest parts of zone 9b and zone 10. Plant two or more southern highbush varieties for cross-pollination and maximum production. Acidify soil to pH 4.5–5.5 with sulfur if needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Biloxi is a very low-chill-hour southern highbush blueberry developed by USDA and Mississippi State University, requiring only 150–200 chill hours — among the lowest chilling requirements of any productive blueberry and making it suitable for the warmest areas of zone 9 and parts of zone 10. The medium-sized, light blue, firm berries ripen in April–May in zone 9 — among the earliest-ripening blueberries of the season — with a mild, sweet, and slightly tart flavor. The early ripening window allows Biloxi to produce before summer heat stresses the plant and before peak blueberry pressure from insects and birds. The vigorous, upright plant habit is well-adapted to Gulf Coast conditions. Biloxi was tested and released as a variety specifically suited to the Gulf South and Florida, giving it a track record of success in the climate conditions that characterize zone 9a and 9b.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Black Beauty is self-fertile and ripens over an extended late-summer window, so pick over successive weeks rather than in a single harvest.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Black Beauty is a University of Arkansas release bred specifically for fresh-market eating, producing very large, glossy black berries with a tender skin and mild, sweet flavor that is less musky than many older muscadine varieties. It is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, though nearby vines improve fruit set. Vigor is strong and disease resistance is good across the humid Gulf South. Because berries ripen unevenly over several weeks rather than all at once, plan on repeated picking passes through the harvest season for the best quality fruit.

common_name: Black Butte Blackberry (Oregon State Extra-Large-Fruited Bramble)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring, spacing 5-8 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart, and trellis the long trailing canes on a two-wire system typical of Pacific Northwest bramble production.
directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile soil and train the trailing, thorny canes onto a trellis, pruning out fruited floricanes each year after harvest to keep new primocanes productive. Black Butte was released by the Oregon State University blackberry breeding program in the 1980s and is best known among Pacific Northwest growers for producing exceptionally large fruit, with individual berries often noticeably bigger than those of Marionberry or most other trailing types. The berries ripen early in the trailing-blackberry season, are glossy black with good flavor, and their large size makes hand-picking notably faster than with smaller-fruited varieties. Because the canes are thorny and quite vigorous, Black Butte requires the same sturdy trellising and winter pruning used for other trailing blackberries grown in maritime climates.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in virtually any soil — moist or dry, acidic or neutral, clay or sand — in partial shade to full sun; black chokeberry is one of the most adaptable native shrubs in North America, thriving under conditions that defeat most other fruiting shrubs.
directions: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in virtually any soil — moist or dry, acidic or neutral, clay or sand — in partial shade to full sun; black chokeberry is one of the most adaptable native shrubs in North America, thriving under conditions that defeat most other fruiting shrubs. Aronia melanocarpa produces stunning clusters of small white flowers with prominent pink anthers in May, glossy, dark-green summer foliage, and massive clusters of small, dark-purple to near-black berries in August and September that persist into winter; the berries are extremely high in anthocyanins and antioxidants — among the highest recorded for any fruit — with an astringent, tart flavor excellent for juices, syrups, and wine. Fall foliage is a brilliant scarlet-red. The plant is essentially bulletproof once established, tolerating wet soils, clay, drought, and partial shade; it spreads by root suckers into dense thickets over time.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or dormant bare-root stock in early spring, burying the cutting deeper than other Ribes to encourage multiple basal shoots.
directions: Black currants fruit most heavily on one-year-old wood, so annual renewal pruning is critical: remove one-third of the oldest canes each late winter to stimulate vigorous new shoots. The berries have a strong, tannic flavor prized for jams and juices; harvest when the entire strig has turned glossy black. Choose blister-rust-resistant cultivars such as 'Consort' or 'Titania' where regulations permit. Verify local restrictions before planting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring and install a sturdy trellis at planting time; Black Diamond is a vigorous thornless trailing blackberry that needs generous wire spacing to accommodate its long canes.
directions: Black Diamond is a Washington State University thornless trailing blackberry developed as a machine-harvestable processing cultivar, prized for large, firm, jet-black berries with a mild, sweet flavor and good post-harvest storage compared to older trailing types. Vigorous, long canes require a sturdy multi-wire trellis; fan-train fruiting canes along the wires and cut them to the ground immediately after harvest, tying in the new season's primocanes to bear the following year's crop. Like other Pacific Northwest trailing blackberries, Black Diamond is bred for cool, dry summers and is more disease-prone in hot, humid climates, so growers in the Gulf South should give it full sun, excellent air drainage, and a well-drained raised bed to reduce fungal pressure.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; European black elderberry is the classic elderflower and elderberry species of English country-garden lore — grown for the intensely fragrant cream-white flower clusters used in elderflower cordial and champagne, and for the drooping clusters of small, jet-black berries used in elderberry syrup, wine, and preserves.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; prune hard in late winter to maintain shape and vigor. Sambucus nigra (black elderberry or European elder) is the classic European elder — a fast-growing, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub or small tree long cultivated for its remarkable botanical generosity: in late spring it produces large, flat-topped, highly fragrant clusters (corymbs) of tiny, cream-white flowers with a distinctive musky-lychee-pear elderflower fragrance; by late summer these transform into heavy, drooping clusters of small (1/4-inch), jet-black, glistening berries. Both flowers and berries are culinary staples in English and Scandinavian cooking: elderflower cordial (steeped flowers, sugar, lemon, citric acid) is one of England's most beloved summer drinks; elderflower 'champagne' (a lightly fermented drink) and elderflower fritters are summer traditions. The berries are made into elderberry syrup (rich in anthocyanins and vitamin C, widely sold as an immune-support supplement), elderberry wine, elderberry jam, and in Scandinavian juices (hyldebær saft). CAUTION: Raw flowers and berries contain mild cyanogenic glycosides — cook berries before eating in quantity; flower clusters are generally safe raw in cordials and wine but not in large raw amounts. The cultivar 'Sambuco' and 'Haschberg' are selected for large berry yields; 'Black Beauty' and 'Black Lace' are ornamental dark-leaved forms.

common_name: Black Fry Muscadine Grape (Dark-Skinned Sport of Classic Fry)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; not self-fertile and requires a self-fertile pollinizer variety such as Carlos or Cowart nearby for fruit set.
directions: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible self-fertile pollinizer variety nearby. Black Fry is a dark-skinned sport of the classic bronze Fry muscadine, retaining the same large fruit size and sweet flavor as its well-known parent while offering the deep black-purple skin some growers and markets specifically prefer over the bronze color. As with the original Fry, individual berries are notably large for a muscadine, and the vine is a strong, productive grower once established. Because it is not self-fertile, ensure a compatible pollinizer variety is planted within pollination range, and harvest as berries fully darken and detach easily with a gentle tug over an extended late-summer harvest window.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; black highbush blueberry is native to wet coastal-plain woodlands and pocosins and tolerates wetter soil than most cultivated blueberries.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; black highbush blueberry is native to wet coastal-plain woodlands and pocosins and tolerates wetter soil than most cultivated blueberries. Vaccinium fuscatum is a tall, southeastern coastal-plain native blueberry with small, urn-shaped white to pink flowers in spring followed by sweet, dark purple-black berries in summer that are edible and attractive to wildlife, growing naturally in the moist, acidic soils of pocosins, bay forests, and wet flatwoods from the Carolinas to the Gulf Coast. Its tolerance for consistently damp soil and light shade makes it a good choice for a rain garden, pond margin, or the moist, partly shaded portion of a mixed berry planting where standard rabbiteye or southern highbush blueberries would struggle. It benefits from a second blueberry species or cultivar nearby for improved pollination and fruit set, following the same acidic-soil culture as other Vaccinium.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in strongly acidic, sandy or rocky, well-drained soil; grows naturally in dry woodland edges and barrens.
