directions: Black huckleberry (Gaylussacia baccata) is a native eastern North American shrub distinct from Vaccinium huckleberries, bearing shiny blue-black berries in summer that differ from blueberries in having 10 large, hard seeds rather than many tiny seeds. Plants form slow-spreading colonies via rhizomes in dry, acidic soils (pH 4.0–5.0) and are extremely fire-adapted and long-lived. The berries have a rich, complex flavor prized for pies and preserves — often considered superior to blueberries by foragers. Difficult to cultivate commercially; best suited to naturalistic plantings in appropriate native habitat.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring before bud break, or divisions in fall; black raspberry tolerates partial shade better than red raspberry, making it valuable for forest edges and lightly shaded food gardens. The second-year canes (floricanes) bear fruit, so new plantings fruit in their second year.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; black raspberry is a native eastern North American cane fruit with intensely flavored, deep purple-black fruits that are prized above all other raspberries for their rich, complex flavor — more aromatic and concentrated than red or purple types. The canes are biennial, growing vegetatively the first year (primocanes) and fruiting in summer of the second year (floricanes), after which they die and should be cut out. New primocanes arise from the base annually. Unlike red raspberry, black raspberry spreads by tip-rooting: when the arching cane tips touch the ground in late summer, they root and form new plants. Harvest the hollow-centered fruits when they turn fully black — they release easily from the core. Excellent fresh, in preserves, syrup, and wine; also dried.

common_name: Black Satin Blackberry (Classic Thornless Semi-Erect Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Black Satin's sprawling canes need a sturdy trellis and regular tying through the season to keep the planting manageable.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the sprawling semi-erect canes onto a sturdy two-wire trellis. One of the earliest widely available thornless blackberry cultivars, introduced in the 1970s, Black Satin remains valued for its reliable, heavy production of large, glossy, firm black fruit with good flavor, ripening over a fairly long midsummer season. The semi-erect canes need more support and tying than fully upright modern cultivars, but the plant is vigorous, dependable, and tolerant of a range of soil conditions. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting productive and make room for new fruiting canes.

plant_note: Plant bare-root canes in early spring; trailing and semi-erect types need a trellis installed at planting.
directions: Blackberries fruit on second-year floricanes; remove all fruited canes at the base after harvest and thin new primocanes to 4–6 per hill. Erect types can be tip-pruned at 3–4 ft in midsummer to encourage lateral branching and larger yields. Harvest when berries are fully black, slightly soft, and the white core is not visible — they do not ripen further off the plant. Trailing cultivars require a T-trellis; thornless varieties are easier to manage but may be less cold-hardy.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; blackcap fruits on second-year canes, so tip-prune first-year primocanes in summer to encourage branching and next year's crop.
directions: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; blackcap fruits on second-year canes, so tip-prune first-year primocanes in summer to encourage branching and next year's crop. Rubus leucodermis is a western North American native bramble with arching, prickly canes coated in a whitish, waxy bloom, producing small white flowers in spring followed by dark purple-black, dome-shaped berries in early to midsummer that are tart, seedy, and excellent for jam, syrup, and baking. It tolerates lighter, drier soils and more shade than most cultivated raspberries, and its thicket-forming habit makes it useful for naturalized plantings, wildlife hedgerows, and erosion control on slopes as well as a home fruit patch. Remove spent floricanes after fruiting each year to keep the planting productive and manage its spreading habit.

common_name: Blake Kiwi (Compact Self-Fertile California Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
plant_note: Plant after last frost in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; self-fertile and does not require a separate male pollinizer vine.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training the vine onto a sturdy trellis or arbor. Blake was bred in California as a self-fertile fuzzy kiwifruit with a somewhat more compact, manageable growth habit than the very vigorous Hayward, making it a practical choice for home gardeners with limited space who still want to grow classic fuzzy-skinned kiwifruit without dedicating room to a separate non-fruiting male vine. Fruit is smaller than Hayward but has good flavor, and the self-fertile trait means a single plant can produce a crop, though yields improve somewhat with a nearby pollinizer if space allows. Prune annually during dormancy to manage vine growth and maintain productive fruiting wood, and provide sturdy, long-term support, since kiwi vines are heavy and long-lived.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring.
directions: 'Blanka' is a heavy-yielding white currant producing long trusses of large, translucent, mild-sweet berries that are less tart than red types. It is a robust, healthy bush that crops later in the season and holds its fruit well on the plant. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with partial shade in warm areas to avoid scorching the pale fruit. Prune to an open framework in winter and mulch annually to conserve moisture and feed the shallow roots.

common_name: Blue Belle Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Blue Belle is one of the original University of Saskatchewan haskap releases and needs a compatible pollinizer cultivar with overlapping bloom time planted nearby.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Blue Belle is self-infertile. Blue Belle was one of the founding quartet of haskap cultivars (alongside Berry Blue, Blue Bird, and Blue Moon) released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the introductions that brought large-fruited modern haskaps into wide North American cultivation. Berries are elongated, dusky blue, and sweet-tart with a flavor often compared to a cross between blueberry and raspberry, ripening two to three weeks ahead of standard blueberries in most climates. Like other haskaps, Blue Belle is exceptionally cold-hardy, surviving winter temperatures to -40F with flowers tolerating brief dips to about -8F, but it is not well suited to hot, humid summers and performs best in cooler, shorter-season climates. Fruit forms on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing branches for the first three to four years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep the shrub productive.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February. Blue Chip requires approximately 200–300 chill hours — a very low requirement making it suitable for zone 9b and warmer parts of zone 9a. Cross-pollinate with another low-chill variety. The dwarf, compact growth habit makes Blue Chip excellent for container growing and small landscapes.
directions: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Blue Chip is a low-chill-hour dwarf southern highbush blueberry selected for compact growth habit — typically reaching only 3–4 feet tall and wide, making it the most container-appropriate blueberry variety and an excellent choice for small gardens, patios, and raised beds where standard blueberries are too large. The moderate-sized, sweet, firm berries ripen in May–June in zone 9 with good flavor and production relative to the small plant size. Blue Chip's dwarf habit is not a compromise in productivity — the plant concentrates its energy into fruit production rather than excessive vegetative growth, and a mature container-grown Blue Chip in a large pot can produce 2–4 pounds of fruit annually. The ornamental value is also high: the spring white flower clusters, glossy summer foliage, and brilliant orange-to-red fall color make Blue Chip a true four-season specimen for containers and small gardens.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or softwood cuttings in early summer; plant in moist, fertile soil in a position sheltered from desiccating winds; blue elderberry tolerates more drought than eastern elderberry.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; blue elderberry is the western counterpart to eastern black elderberry, native from British Columbia to New Mexico, producing large flat-topped clusters (corymbs) of tiny white flowers followed by abundant powder-blue to nearly black fruits with a distinctive waxy blue bloom. The berries are somewhat sweeter and milder than eastern elderberry and were a major food plant for over 50 indigenous nations of the Pacific Coast and interior West — eaten fresh (ripe only), dried, made into jam, syrup, wine, and elderflower cordial. Like eastern elderberry, unripe or raw berries can cause nausea; cook before eating in quantity. An exceptional wildlife plant and one of the most productive native fruiting shrubs.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs or hardwood cuttings in late winter or spring in any moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; blue elderberry is far more drought and alkaline-soil tolerant than American elderberry (S. canadensis) and thrives in western conditions.
directions: Plant in any moist to well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade — blue elderberry is the western North American native elderberry, native from British Columbia to Baja California and east to the Rocky Mountains, producing large, flat-topped clusters of dark blue to blue-black berries with a distinctive waxy, blue-gray bloom (giving both plant and fruit their names). The berries are slightly sweeter than American elderberry (S. canadensis) and are used the same way — in jellies, juices, wines, elderflower cordial, and traditional medicine. Blue elderberry is significantly more drought-tolerant than American elderberry, adapts to alkaline soils, and grows in the dry, sunny conditions of western landscapes where the eastern species struggles. It is an important food and medicine plant in the traditions of dozens of western Native American nations. Plant where spreading by suckers is acceptable.

common_name: Blue Lake Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Purple Dooryard Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Blue Lake is a purple-fruited, Pierce's disease-resistant Florida bunch grape used for dooryard eating and juice or jelly, growing well on its own roots in most soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing good airflow through the canopy. Blue Lake is a purple Florida bunch grape carrying strong resistance to Pierce's disease, one of a small group of University of Florida-recommended cultivars able to shrug off the bacterial infection that limits most European wine grapes across the humid Gulf South. Unlike several of its Florida-bred counterparts, it typically grows well on its own roots and does not need grafting onto a resistant rootstock except in alkaline soils, simplifying establishment for home growers. Its purple berries are used both for fresh dooryard eating and for juice and jelly making, ripening in midsummer shortly after the earlier 'Stover' cultivar. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and maintain a preventive fungicide program to control the fungal fruit rots that are the main remaining disease threat in Florida's hot, humid summers.

common_name: Blue Moon Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Blue Moon is one of the original University of Saskatchewan haskap releases and needs a compatible pollinizer cultivar with overlapping bloom time planted nearby.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Blue Moon is self-infertile. Blue Moon was part of the founding quartet of haskap cultivars (alongside Berry Blue, Blue Belle, and Blue Bird) released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the introductions that established large-fruited modern haskaps in North American gardens and orchards. Berries are elongated, dusky blue, and sweet-tart with a flavor often described as a cross between blueberry and raspberry, ripening well ahead of standard blueberries and giving cold-climate gardeners one of the first fresh berry harvests of the season. Like other haskaps, Blue Moon is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures to -40F with flowers surviving brief dips to about -8F, but it performs poorly in hot, humid summers and is best suited to cooler, shorter-season climates. Fruit is borne on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning in the first three to four years to removing dead or crossing branches, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Bluebelle is a 1985 Florida-USDA rabbiteye release needing 450-500 chill hours, ripening mid-June through late July, and benefits from a second rabbiteye cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Bluebelle, released in 1985 through a joint Florida-USDA breeding effort, requires a moderate 450 to 500 chill hours and bears a long, productive mid-to-late-season crop stretching from mid-June through late July, extending the rabbiteye harvest window when planted alongside earlier cultivars. It is a vigorous, reliable, well-established variety with a long track record in Southern home orchards and commercial plantings alike. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid heavy late-season nitrogen, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production.

subcategory: Eastern Australian ornamental fringed-flower berry tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–11; Blueberry Ash (Fairy Petticoats, Pink Elaeo) is a beautiful, multi-season ornamental tree from eastern Australia — endemic to coastal rainforest margins of Queensland and New South Wales — producing profuse, distinctive, white or pale-pink, delicately fringed bell-shaped flowers in spring, followed by year-round clusters of brilliant blue-violet to cobalt-blue, blueberry-like drupes much loved by birds.
directions: Plant Elaeocarpus reticulatus in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment and in dry periods; mulch to maintain soil moisture and acidity; grows well in coastal gardens with some protection from strong wind. Blueberry Ash is one of the most ornamentally multi-season of all Australian native trees — providing year-round interest through its attractive, elliptical, fine-toothed leaves; the exquisite spring flowers (white or blush-pink, tiny fringed bells hanging in clusters, earning the nickname 'Fairy Petticoats'); and the persistent, brilliant cobalt-blue to blue-violet, blueberry-sized drupes that can be present on the tree year-round and are avidly consumed by parrots, doves, and other birds. The blue fruits are technically edible for humans but very astringent and are not eaten except in famine conditions; birds have no such reservation. Elaeocarpus reticulatus is a small to medium rainforest tree (20–40 feet in the wild) that adapts well to cultivation in garden situations, particularly in the humid, subtropical Gulf Coast climate. It makes an outstanding specimen, street tree, or privacy screen for zone 9–11 gardens; the year-round blue berries make it perhaps the most effective bird-attracting tree available for subtropical plantings.

plant_note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable.
directions: Bluecrop is a dependable northern highbush blueberry that yields large, mild, juicy berries in mid-season. Plant in acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending with peat or pine bark if needed, and mulch heavily to keep the shallow roots cool and moist. Give it full sun and consistent water, especially during fruit development. Prune out old canes each late winter to keep the bush productive, and plant a second highbush variety nearby to improve pollination and yields.

plant_note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark; the compact habit suits smaller garden beds and large containers.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Bluegold was bred at Michigan State University for a compact, dense, cold-hardy growth habit that fits well into smaller home garden beds and large containers where full-sized highbush varieties would quickly outgrow the space, while still producing a solid midseason crop of sweet, firm, light-blue berries. The naturally tidy shape needs less aggressive pruning to keep in bounds than many vigorous highbush cultivars, making it a practical choice for gardeners with limited room or those growing blueberries primarily as an ornamental edible landscape plant. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune lightly each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

plant_note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Bluejay was bred at Michigan State University for reliable cold hardiness and good resistance to several diseases that affect blueberries in humid climates, including some tolerance of mummy berry, producing firm, light-blue, mildly sweet berries in early to midseason on a vigorous, upright bush. The bush's tolerance for cold and its dependable, consistent production have made it a long-standing favorite for northern home orchards and commercial plantings alike, even as newer releases have entered the market. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter to maintain vigor, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; bog bilberry grows in subarctic and subalpine bogs and moist tundra and is the most cold-hardy edible Vaccinium available.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; bog bilberry absolutely requires constantly moist to wet, strongly acidic, poorly drained peaty or boggy soil and will not succeed in drier, neutral conditions. Vaccinium uliginosum is a circumboreal subarctic and subalpine species found in bogs, tundra, and moist mountain heaths across North America, Europe, and Asia — the hardiest of all Vaccinium, surviving temperatures to -60°F; it produces small, round, blue-black berries with a sweet, mild flavor and exceptionally high antioxidant content (higher than commercial blueberries). The berries are an important subsistence food for northern indigenous peoples and are used in jams, pies, and fresh eating. Best suited to cold, wet, acidic sites in zones 1–6 where it is invaluable for bog gardens and moist native plantings.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil, incorporating pine bark fines to boost organic matter and moisture retention.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil, incorporating pine bark fines to boost organic matter and moisture retention. Released by the University of Florida in 1985, Bonita is one of the earliest-ripening rabbiteye cultivars available, typically flowering and fruiting several weeks ahead of midseason types like Tifblue. It requires a compatible rabbiteye pollinator such as Climax or Beckyblue blooming at the same time to set a good crop, and while modern mid- and late-season rabbiteyes have generally surpassed it in overall yield, Bonita remains a useful choice for gardeners wanting the earliest possible rabbiteye harvest. The vigorous, spreading bush performs well across the humid Gulf South once established in properly acidified soil.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Boreal Beauty is self-infertile and needs a compatible University of Saskatchewan pollinizer, such as Boreal Blizzard, planted nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, since Boreal Beauty needs cross-pollination from another haskap cultivar to crop well. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program as part of its 'Boreal' series, Boreal Beauty ripens later than the earliest haskap introductions and produces firm, elongated, deep-blue berries bred to hold well on the bush without dropping, making it well suited to mechanical or delayed hand harvest. Like other haskaps, it is exceptionally cold-hardy and thrives in short, cool-summer growing seasons, but it is not well adapted to hot, humid climates. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood for the first several years, then shift to renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep the bush productive.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Boreal Blizzard is self-infertile and is often planted specifically as a compatible pollinizer for other University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivars such as Boreal Beauty.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, as Boreal Blizzard will not set a meaningful crop without a compatible pollinizer nearby. Part of the University of Saskatchewan's 'Boreal' haskap series, Boreal Blizzard produces a heavy crop of good-flavored blue berries and blooms at a time that makes it an effective pollen source for several other Saskatchewan-bred cultivars, so it is commonly planted in pairs specifically to boost yields in a mixed haskap planting. The upright, vigorous shrub is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating deep winter cold typical of the Canadian prairies, but struggles in hot, humid summer regions. Limit pruning to removing dead or crossing wood while the bush is young, then begin renewal pruning of older canes once the planting is established.

common_name: Borealis Honeyberry (Large-Fruited University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Borealis is one of the most widely planted University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivars, prized for large berry size, and needs a compatible early-blooming pollinizer such as 'Tundra' planted nearby for fruit set.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, since Borealis is self-infertile and needs cross-pollination to set fruit. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, Borealis produces some of the largest berries of any haskap cultivar, with a sweet-tart flavor often compared to a cross between blueberry and raspberry, and ripens in late spring, about two to three weeks before strawberries in most climates, making it one of the earliest fresh fruits of the season. Flowers open very early and tolerate temperatures down to about -8F, but a hard late freeze can still reduce fruit set, so plant in a site that avoids obvious frost pockets. Like other haskaps, Borealis is bred for cold-winter regions and struggles with root and crown health in hot, humid summers, so it is a poor fit for the Gulf Coast and performs best in short-season northern gardens. Minimal pruning is needed for the first four to five years beyond removing dead wood; thereafter remove one or two of the oldest, thickest canes annually to keep the shrub renewing itself.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; boulder raspberry grows naturally on rocky slopes, canyon walls, and foothills of the Colorado Front Range and Rocky Mountains. More drought-tolerant than fruiting raspberries and entirely thornless.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; boulder raspberry is one of the most beautiful ornamental native shrubs of the Rocky Mountain foothills — an entirely thornless, arching shrub with attractive, deeply lobed, maplelike leaves and stunning large (up to 2.5 inch), pure white, rose-like flowers in late spring. The species name 'deliciosus' was reportedly given because the flowers are so delightful, though the fruit (small, dry, sparse drupelets) is technically edible but far from impressive compared to other raspberries. The magnificent white flowers in May and June make boulder raspberry outstanding as a flowering ornamental in dry, rocky garden situations in zones 4–8. Completely thornless — unlike virtually all other Rubus — making it safe for high-traffic areas of the garden. The state flower of Colorado (not officially, but very emblematic of the Front Range foothills). Drought tolerant once established, appropriate for xeriscape plantings in the Rocky Mountain West.

common_name: Box Huckleberry (Long-Lived Evergreen Creeping Shade Shrub)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Box Huckleberry spreads very slowly by rhizomes to form a low, dense, evergreen groundcover, and established colonies are extremely long-lived.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, and mulch with pine needles or leaf litter to maintain acidity and moisture. Box Huckleberry is a rare, low, evergreen, boxwood-like shrub native to scattered sites in the eastern United States, forming slow-spreading clonal colonies that are among the longest-lived plant clones known, with some wild colonies estimated at over a thousand years old. Small, glossy, leathery evergreen leaves cover the low, dense mat of stems, and it bears small pink, bell-shaped spring flowers followed by sparse but edible, sweet, dark blue berries in summer, similar in flavor to other huckleberries though the plant fruits lightly in cultivation. Because it tolerates deep shade and stays low and evergreen year-round, it makes a distinctive, slow-growing woodland groundcover for shaded native gardens where few other fruiting shrubs will grow; give it consistent moisture and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizome mat once established.

common_name: Boyne Raspberry (Extreme Cold-Hardy Manitoba Red Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring; Boyne requires a long, cold winter chill and is best suited to northern gardens rather than warm, low-chill regions.
directions: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and provide a simple wire trellis for support. Developed at the Morden Research Station in Manitoba, Boyne is prized in the coldest raspberry-growing regions of North America for surviving harsh prairie winters with minimal cane dieback while still producing an early, heavy crop of medium-sized, firm, richly flavored red berries. As a floricane-fruiting cultivar it bears on second-year wood, so cut spent canes to the ground immediately after harvest and thin the following year's primocanes to keep the row open and productive. Its combination of hardiness and early ripening has made it a long-standing standard for home gardeners across the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies.

plant_note: Plant in early spring after frost danger passes; boysenberries are trailing types requiring a stout trellis.
directions: Boysenberries are vigorous trailing hybrids (blackberry x raspberry x loganberry lineage) that must be trained to a two- or three-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft. Cut all fruited canes to the ground after the summer harvest and tie new canes along the wires for next year's crop. Harvest when berries turn deep maroon-purple and have a rich, winey aroma. In zone 5–6 winters, remove canes from wires and lay them on the ground under mulch for protection.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; for the heaviest berry set, plant at least two Brandywine (or a compatible seedling) shrubs together for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant a second, genetically distinct viburnum nudum nearby to ensure heavy fruit set, since this species needs a compatible cross-pollinator. Brandywine is a Southeastern native shrub selected for its extraordinary berry display: clusters of pink berries that ripen through shades of rose and blue to a deep, glossy blue-black, often showing several colors on the same cluster at once, held above glossy, dark-green, disease-resistant foliage that turns burgundy-red in fall. It tolerates consistently wet soil better than most flowering shrubs, making it a strong choice for rain gardens, pond edges, and low, poorly drained spots where many shrubs struggle. The berries are an excellent food source for songbirds, who typically strip them soon after they ripen.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or rooted transplants January–March in zone 9; Brazos is specifically adapted to Texas and Gulf Coast soils and climate, including alkaline, calcareous soils where many varieties struggle. Space 4–5 feet apart to accommodate vigorous growth.
directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil in full sun; Brazos is a thorned, semi-erect blackberry developed by Texas A&M University and released in 1959 — for many decades it was the dominant commercial blackberry variety in Texas and the Gulf Coast South. Though newer thornless varieties have largely replaced it commercially, Brazos remains prized by home gardeners and farmers' market growers for its exceptional heat adaptation, flavor, and productivity on the alkaline soils that characterize much of central and south Texas. Berries are large, elongated, and very flavorful, ripening from late April through June in zone 9 — among the earliest major varieties. Unlike the University of Arkansas thornless releases (Natchez, Ouachita), Brazos tolerates alkaline soil pH (7.0–7.5) and calcareous caliche significantly better, making it the variety of choice for gardens on tight, rocky Hill Country soils or coastal prairie clay. Canes require trellising due to vigorous, semi-trailing growth. Wear heavy gloves when pruning. Remove fruited canes after harvest and select 4–5 of the strongest new canes per plant.

plant_note: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic soil during winter dormancy; Brightwell requires 400–500 chill hours and benefits from cross-pollination with Climax, Tifblue, or Premier. It is the most widely planted rabbiteye blueberry in the South due to its productivity, adaptability, and mechanical harvest suitability.
directions: Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark; Brightwell is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1983 that became the dominant commercial rabbiteye variety in the southeastern US for its outstanding combination of yield, adaptability, and suitability for mechanical harvesting on u-pick and commercial farms. Mid-season ripening (late June to July in zone 8–9) follows the early-ripening Climax and Premier, extending the harvest window. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, firm, with a dry scar and mild, sweet flavor that improves with heat — they tend to sweeten noticeably as they ripen fully over 2–3 weeks, making daily picking rewarding. The upright, vigorous plants are productive and show good disease tolerance under Gulf Coast conditions. As with all rabbiteye blueberries, plant at least two compatible varieties for cross-pollination. Mulch deeply with pine bark or wood chips; never use fresh hardwood mulch as it raises pH.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February for best establishment before summer heat. Brightwell blooms mid-season and cross-pollinates best with Premier, Tifblue, or Powderblue. Requires a companion pollinator planted within 50 feet for maximum berry production.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Brightwell is the most widely planted rabbiteye blueberry variety in the southeastern United States, valued for its consistent mid-season production, outstanding flavor, and broad adaptability across zone 6–9. The medium to large, light blue berries ripen in June–July in most Gulf Coast plantings and hold well on the bush, extending the harvest window over 4–6 weeks. Brightwell's moderate chilling requirement (350–400 hours below 45°F) suits it perfectly to zone 8–9 conditions where high-chill northern varieties fail. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain consistent moisture through summer, and fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) at bloom and again after harvest. Avoid lime applications, which raise soil pH above the acceptable range.

plant_note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Brigitta was bred in Australia and became internationally popular for its exceptionally firm, large, late-ripening berries with outstanding shelf life, holding quality in storage and transit better than most highbush varieties, a trait that has made it a favorite for both commercial growers and home gardeners wanting fruit that keeps well after picking. Ripening late in the season, it extends the harvest window when planted alongside earlier varieties, and the vigorous, upright bush is a reliable, heavy producer once established. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out old canes each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring in average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in average garden soil that stays reliably moist and prune out a few of the oldest canes each year to keep the upright, suckering shrub full and vigorous. Brilliantissima is a selection of native red chokeberry prized for its glossy, dark green summer foliage that turns brilliant scarlet in fall, paired with clusters of small white spring flowers and abundant bright red berries that persist into winter. The astringent fruit is not usually eaten fresh but is popular for jams, syrups, and wildlife forage, since birds tend to leave it until late in the season. It tolerates wet soil, drought, and a wide range of conditions, making it a tough, low-maintenance hedge or naturalized planting choice.

plant_note: Plant tip-rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; bristly dewberry is adapted to moist, shaded habitats — wetland margins, bog edges, and moist forest floors — unlike most blackberries that prefer dry, open conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; bristly dewberry is a trailing native bramble of moist, shaded, acidic habitats — sphagnum bog margins, moist pine flatwoods, wet woodland edges, and streambanks — producing small, rounded, black berries with a pleasant, mildly tart flavor. The semi-evergreen leaves have a distinctive leathery texture and glossy appearance. The plant is armed with tiny, bristle-like prickles (hence 'bristly') rather than the stout thorns of most blackberries. An important understory plant for moist, shaded, acidic native gardens where it provides both wildlife fruit value and ground cover function. Thrives in conditions too wet and shaded for most other fruiting plants.

common_name: Bristol Black Raspberry (Cornell Standard Black Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring; Bristol is a Cornell University release from the 1930s that remains one of the most widely grown black raspberries for home gardens for its large, glossy, firm fruit and vigorous, upright canes.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and tip-prune vigorous new canes in midsummer to encourage the lateral branching that carries next year's crop. Bristol was released by Cornell University in 1934 and quickly became a garden standard for its large, glossy-black, firm berries with rich, classic black raspberry flavor, produced in heavy clusters on strong, upright canes that need less support than sprawling types. It ripens in a concentrated midsummer window that makes for an efficient single harvest push, and the vigorous habit means a modest planting fills in and produces well within its second season. Watch for anthracnose in humid climates and provide good air circulation between hills; remove spent floricanes immediately after harvest to reduce disease pressure on the new canes.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Briteblue is a historic 1969 Georgia rabbiteye release, a sister selection to Delite and Bluebelle, needing another rabbiteye cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Briteblue, released in Georgia in 1969, is a sister selection to the well-known Delite and Bluebelle rabbiteye cultivars, valued for large, light-blue, firm berries with good flavor on a vigorous, upright bush, and has remained in cultivation for over half a century as a dependable mid-to-late-season producer for Southern home orchards. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid heavy late-season nitrogen, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in acidic, well-drained, pine-bark-amended soil; Britewell is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release bred for consistently heavy yields and needs a second mid-season rabbiteye cultivar nearby for good cross-pollination.
directions: Plant dormant or container bushes in winter in raised, sulfur-acidified beds where native soil is not already acidic, and keep a permanent layer of pine bark mulch over the root zone. Britewell is a University of Georgia rabbiteye selection valued by growers for consistently heavy, reliable cropping of firm, medium-blue berries with good flavor on a moderately vigorous, upright-spreading bush, ripening in the mid-season window alongside cultivars like Tifblue. Plant with a second mid-season rabbiteye for cross-pollination and fuller berry set, and feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest. Renewal-prune the oldest wood out each winter to keep young, productive canes coming and sustain the heavy yields the variety is known for.

plant_note: Plant rooted tip cuttings or bare-root canes in early spring and install a two-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft at the same time. Buckingham is thornless, unlike the original tayberry, which makes trellising and harvest considerably easier.
directions: Buckingham is a thornless Scottish-bred tayberry selection, carrying the same long, conical, deep purple-red berries and rich, sweet-tart raspberry-blackberry flavor as the original tayberry but on spineless canes that are much more pleasant to train, prune, and hand-pick. Fan-train the long trailing canes along wires, keeping the current season's primocanes separated from the fruiting floricanes to simplify post-harvest cleanup. Cut fruited canes to the ground immediately after harvest and tie the new canes onto the wires for next year's crop. In the cooler part of its range, detach canes from the trellis after leaf drop and cover with straw mulch or row cover for winter protection; in the humid Gulf South, prioritize good air circulation and a well-drained, elevated bed to reduce cane and fruit rot pressure.

plant_note: Plant one male plant for every 5–7 female plants in early spring; buffaloberry is wind-pollinated and both sexes must be within 50 ft.
directions: Silver buffaloberry is an extremely cold-hardy nitrogen-fixing shrub native to the Great Plains, valued for its bright red, tart berries that have historically been used by Indigenous peoples of North America for pemmican and sauces. It is dioecious and wind-pollinated, requiring male and female plants; purchase sexed plants, as seedlings cannot be sexed until flowering at 3–5 years. The thorny, silver-leaved plants thrive in alkaline, dry, or infertile soils where other fruits fail. Harvest by spreading a tarp and gently shaking or beating branches after a light frost, which softens the bitterness; berries are very tart raw but excellent cooked.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil, spacing plants generously to accommodate Cabot's vigorous, spreading growth habit.
directions: Cabot was released in 1998 from the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia and is grown for its unusually large, pale-red, glossy berries produced over a mid-season harvest window. Plants carry relatively few blossoms per crown but compensate with fruit size, and the cultivar shows good resistance to red stele root rot, a soilborne disease common in cool, humid strawberry ground. Its cold hardiness and vigor have made it popular with home growers throughout the Canadian Maritimes and the New England states. Thin runners regularly to keep berry size from declining as matted rows fill in.

common_name: Cabrillo Strawberry (UC Davis Day-Neutral Everbearing Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring for a day-neutral, everbearing crop that produces through the growing season rather than a single winter flush; Cabrillo is a UC Davis release bred to succeed older day-neutral varieties like Albion and Monterey, with strong yield across both winter and summer plantings.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Cabrillo is a day-neutral strawberry from the University of California, Davis breeding program, bred as an improvement on the widely grown Albion and Monterey cultivars, producing large, uniform berries with strong yield across multiple planting seasons rather than a single concentrated harvest. Because it is day-neutral, it can flower and fruit throughout the growing season rather than only during short winter days, giving Gulf South gardeners a longer strawberry season if grown as a spring-planted crop rather than the typical fall-planted short-day type. Maintain consistent drip irrigation, raised beds, and regular removal of runners to keep the plant's energy focused on fruit production.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart. Caddo is a compact, erect, thornless blackberry that fruits in the second year and needs only minimal trellising due to its shorter, sturdy canes.
directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun; Caddo is a more recent University of Arkansas thornless blackberry release, bred for a compact, upright plant habit that is noticeably shorter and tidier than older erect thornless cultivars, making it well suited to smaller home gardens and even large containers. It ripens early in the season, ahead of many other thornless varieties, with large, firm, glossy black, well-flavored berries. The compact habit reduces the need for trellising and makes hand harvest easier. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest few per plant to maintain good air circulation and fruit size.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted tip-cuttings in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; California blackberry grows naturally in moist coastal and foothill habitats — streambanks, woodland edges, and shaded ravines along the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to southern California. More shade and moisture tolerant than many blackberries.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted tip-cuttings in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; California blackberry is the native blackberry of the Pacific Coast — and one of the most historically significant berry plants in horticultural history, because it is one of the parent species of some of the world's most important hybrid blackberry cultivars. Rubus ursinus is a parent of the boysenberry (R. ursinus × loganberry), the loganberry (R. ursinus × red raspberry), and the marionberry (a complex hybrid involving R. ursinus) — three of the Pacific Northwest's most important blackberry cultivars. The small, intensely flavorful native blackberries (smaller than commercial blackberries but more aromatic and complex in flavor) are highly prized for fresh eating and making jams, pies, and wine. The plant is a sprawling, slender-caned, moderately thorny shrub that tolerates considerable shade — growing naturally in the moist shade of Douglas-fir forests and redwood groves along the Pacific Coast. The deeply lobed, compound leaves are attractive. An excellent native for wildlife gardens, edible landscapes, and shaded moist woodland edges in the Pacific Coast states.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a December–March crop; Camarosa is slightly later than Sweet Charlie but earlier than Chandler. It requires cool nights for best color and flavor development. Like all short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat as a winter annual planted each October.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Camarosa is a large-fruited, early-season strawberry developed by the University of California at Davis and released in 1992. For nearly a decade it was the most widely planted commercial strawberry in California and dominated early-season Florida production as well. The large, conical berries are dark red, very firm, and mildly sweet — excellent for shipping and processing but slightly less intensely flavored fresh than Sweet Charlie or Festival. Camarosa's principal strengths are its very high productivity, large and attractive berry appearance, and exceptional firmness that makes it the preferred variety for growers who need to ship or sell at farmers' markets where berries must look their best. In zone 9, Camarosa is planted October–November and harvested primarily in January–March. The plants are vigorous and productive but susceptible to powdery mildew and some soil-borne diseases — plant in raised beds with fresh soil or strawberry-specific fumigation. Maintain consistent drip irrigation to reduce disease and ensure uniform berry sizing.

common_name: Camellia Southern Highbush Blueberry (Mild-Flavored Productive Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat; Camellia needs about 300 chill hours, flowers early to midseason, and sets a heavier crop with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar planted nearby.
directions: Amend planting beds to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines before setting out dormant bushes in winter, and keep roots consistently moist with a thick mulch layer since southern highbush blueberries have shallow, fibrous root systems. Camellia is a University of Florida release known for very high, consistent yields of medium to large, firm, light-blue berries with a mild, low-acid flavor that many home growers find especially easy-eating fresh off the bush. The upright, vigorous plant tends to hold its crop well without excessive splitting in Gulf Coast humidity. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to renew fruiting wood, and fertilize lightly with an acid-forming blueberry fertilizer split between early spring and shortly after harvest.

plant_note: Plant plugs or bare-root transplants in fall for winter-spring production; in zone 9 plant September–November. Camino Real is a short-day variety that requires decreasing day length to initiate flower buds — plant in fall so shortening days trigger bud initiation before winter. In zone 9 this produces fruit from December through April. Camino Real has excellent heat tolerance for a June-bearing type, performing better than most strawberries through the warm Gulf Coast spring.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil with high organic matter; Camino Real is a University of California Davis-developed short-day strawberry cultivar selected for warm-winter California production and widely adapted to Gulf Coast and subtropical conditions. The large, firm, conical, deep red berries have outstanding fresh-eating flavor — a combination of sweetness, bright strawberry aroma, and moderate acidity that consistently ranks among the top cultivars in taste evaluations for warm-climate production. Firm berries have good shelf life after harvest (important for home gardeners who may not harvest daily), retaining quality for 3–5 days refrigerated without softening or loss of flavor. The plant shows good tolerance for common strawberry diseases including Phytophthora crown rot, which is important in humid Gulf Coast conditions where soil moisture management can be challenging. The variety performs best when planted in fall as a fresh transplant, fruiting through the cool season in zone 9 and producing its best-quality fruit in the cool winter months.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Canadian blackberry is naturally nearly thornless, unlike most wild brambles, making it easier to harvest and maintain.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Canadian blackberry is an Appalachian and northeastern native distinguished from most wild brambles by canes that are nearly or entirely without prickles, making harvest and pruning far more pleasant than with typical thorny wild blackberries. White flowers in late spring give way to large, sweet, juicy black fruit ripening in mid- to late summer, well suited to fresh eating, baking, and preserves. It tolerates more shade than many fruiting brambles, performing well at woodland edges and in partially shaded hedgerows where full-sun brambles struggle. Manage its spread by root suckers with an annual perimeter mowing or trenching, and remove spent floricanes after harvest each year to keep the patch productive and open.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Cape Fear is an early-ripening North Carolina State southern highbush release bred for low chill requirements, well suited to zone 8-9 Gulf South winters.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Cape Fear is a southern highbush blueberry released by North Carolina State University and selected for an early ripening window combined with a comparatively low chill requirement, which lets it set a full crop even after mild Gulf South winters that shortchange higher-chill northern highbush types. Fruit is medium-large, light blue, and firm with good classic highbush flavor. Cape Fear is only partially self-fruitful, so plant a second southern highbush or rabbiteye cultivar nearby to improve fruit set and berry size. Because southern highbush types have shallower, less drought-tolerant roots than rabbiteye, keep a thick layer of pine bark or pine straw mulch over the root zone and irrigate through dry spells, especially in the first two years after planting.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring.
directions: 'Captivator' is a nearly thornless American-type gooseberry producing sweet, teardrop-shaped reddish-purple berries that are pleasant for fresh eating. Its low thorn count and good mildew resistance make it one of the most user-friendly varieties for home gardeners. Grow in full sun to light shade in cool, moist, well-drained soil with a thick organic mulch. Prune lightly in winter to remove old and crowded wood, keeping the bush open and productive.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn to early spring in cool-summer climates; gooseberries perform poorly where summers are hot and humid and appreciate afternoon shade in warmer regions.
directions: Plant dormant, thorny bushes in fertile, well-drained soil in a spot with cool root conditions, mulching to conserve moisture and prune to an open framework to make harvest through the spines easier. Careless is a traditional English culinary gooseberry long grown for its heavy, reliable crops of large, pale green, thin-skinned berries that are quite tart when picked early for cooking but sweeten as they ripen toward translucent pale yellow-green, making it equally suited to pies, fools, and preserves or later fresh eating. The vigorous, somewhat spreading bush is one of the most widely planted gooseberry cultivars in British gardens and allotments. Prune in the dormant season to an open, airy shape to improve light penetration and reduce mildew pressure on the ripening fruit.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings late winter to early spring; Carlos is self-fertile and one of the most reliable muscadines for the Gulf South. It ripens mid-season (August–September in zone 9). Build a strong arbor or high-wire trellis to support vigorous vines.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5) in full sun; Carlos is a bronze-skinned muscadine developed by North Carolina State University and released in 1970, and remains one of the two or three most widely planted muscadines in the southeastern US because of its exceptional adaptability, consistent yields, and suitability for both fresh-eating and bronze muscadine wine production. The medium-sized, bronze-gold berries ripen uniformly in mid-season and have a mild, sweet musky flavor that is less pronounced than Scuppernong — making Carlos wines and juice more accessible to people new to muscadine flavors. Self-fertile, so it produces well as a single plant, though yields improve with a black muscadine variety nearby. Carlos is resistant to Pierce's disease, downy mildew, and other diseases that devastate European wine grapes in the humid South — no spray program is needed in most home garden settings. Prune in late winter, leaving only short spurs on permanent cordons. Harvest when berries slip from the cluster at a gentle tug.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in early spring as soon as ground can be worked.
directions: 'Caroline' is a vigorous fall-bearing red raspberry prized for large, intensely flavored fruit with high antioxidant content. Plant in full sun in fertile, slightly acidic soil and irrigate consistently during fruit development. Prune as a primocane type by cutting canes to the ground in late winter for one large fall harvest. Its heat tolerance makes it a strong choice for warmer parts of its range, though it benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring on a trellis in well-drained soil; Cascade Delight was bred for improved root rot resistance and can tolerate heavier soils better than older raspberry cultivars.
directions: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile soil and support the vigorous canes on a trellis, removing spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year. Released by Washington State University as an improvement on older Pacific Northwest cultivars like Meeker, Cascade Delight was specifically bred for resistance to Phytophthora root rot, a major limitation in wetter or heavier soils, while still producing large, firm, bright red conic berries with excellent flavor. It ripens slightly later than Meeker, extending the summer harvest window, and its firmer fruit holds up well for both fresh eating and shipping. Its improved disease resistance makes it a more forgiving choice than many older varieties for gardeners with imperfectly drained soil.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Centurion is a very late-ripening, cold-hardy rabbiteye that requires a cross-pollinating companion, since it is not self-fruitful.
directions: Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5–5.0 with peat moss or sulfur before planting; Centurion is a USDA-ARS-released rabbiteye blueberry prized as one of the latest-ripening varieties available, extending the harvest well past Tifblue into late July and into August in zone 8–9 and stretching the fresh-picking season for home growers and u-pick operations alike. It is also among the more cold-hardy rabbiteye selections, tolerating winter temperatures further north than many older varieties. Berries are small to medium, dark blue, firm, and flavorful, holding well on the bush without softening even in late-season heat. Plant with an early- or midseason variety such as Climax or Brightwell for cross-pollination, since rabbiteye blueberries including Centurion set little fruit without a compatible partner nearby. Established Centurion bushes are vigorous and heavy-bearing; renew a portion of the oldest canes each winter by cutting them to the ground to keep the bush productive and to encourage fresh, high-yielding new wood.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February. Centurion is a mid-to-late season rabbiteye variety that extends the harvest window into mid-July in zone 8–9 after early and mid-season varieties have finished. Plant with Premier, Climax, or Brightwell for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun; Centurion is a late-season rabbiteye blueberry that ripens in July in zone 8–9, extending the pick-your-own season after mid-season varieties like Brightwell have finished. The large, firm, dark blue berries have excellent flavor and shipping quality, and the upright, vigorous shrubs can reach 8–10 feet at maturity. Centurion requires approximately 400–500 chilling hours, making it suitable for zone 7–8b but less reliable in the mildest parts of zone 9a where chilling accumulation can be inconsistent. Plant as part of a multi-variety planting to achieve full-season harvest from late May through mid-July. The firm, large berries are particularly well-suited to fresh markets and U-pick operations where shelf life matters.

common_name: Chambourcin Grape (Disease-Resistant French-American Red Wine Grape)
plant_note: Set dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun in spring, choosing a site with a long frost-free season.
directions: Chambourcin is a French-American hybrid bred by Joannes Seyve that has become a signature red wine grape of Missouri, Pennsylvania, and other humid eastern growing regions because of its strong natural resistance to downy and powdery mildew. It is a late-ripening variety that needs a fairly long, warm growing season to fully mature, so it is less suited to the shortest-season northern climates than Minnesota-bred hybrids. The wine is deeply colored with soft tannins and fruity black-cherry and berry character, and can be produced in styles ranging from light and fruity to full-bodied and oak-aged. Canopy management to expose fruit clusters helps color and ripeness given its late harvest window.

common_name: Champanel Grape (Extremely Vigorous Pierce's Disease-Resistant Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring in well-drained to occasionally wet soil; Champanel is extremely vigorous and tolerates poor drainage and Pierce's disease pressure far better than most grapes, making it a strong choice for humid Gulf South sites where other grapes struggle.
directions: Plant in average to poorly drained soil in full sun on a strong arbor or high-wire trellis able to support very vigorous growth. Bred by Texas grape pioneer T. V. Munson in the late 1800s from a cross of the wild Vitis champinii with an American labrusca-type grape, Champanel is renowned for tolerating conditions that kill most grape vines outright, including heavy soil, occasional flooding, and Pierce's disease, a bacterial illness common in the humid South. The large, dark purple-black berries are tart and seedy, better suited to juice and jelly than fresh eating, but the vine's toughness makes it a dependable arbor and shade grape where other varieties fail. Prune to a permanent framework each winter to manage its rampant growth.

common_name: Chancellor Grape (Historic French-American Red Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun in early to mid spring.
directions: Chancellor, originally bred in France as Seibel 7053, was one of the most widely planted French-American red hybrids in the eastern United States through the mid-20th century, prized for its reliable productivity and moderate winter hardiness. The grape ripens midseason into loose clusters of blue-black berries that yield a soft, fruity red wine, historically used both as a varietal and as a blending grape to add color and body. It is more susceptible to bunch rot in wet years than the newer Minnesota-bred hybrids, so growers should prioritize good air circulation and timely fungicide applications during fruit set. Cane- or cordon-train on a vertical trellis and moderate crop loads to concentrate flavor in the smaller clusters.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root bushes in early spring into acidic, well-drained, organic-rich soil.
directions: Site bushes in full sun on acidic soil amended with peat or pine bark and mulch heavily to keep shallow roots cool and moist. Chandler is famous for producing some of the largest berries of any highbush blueberry, often nickel- to quarter-sized, with a mild, sweet flavor and a very long harvest window since ripe fruit holds well on the bush. Its extended ripening period spreads picking over several weeks rather than concentrating it into a short flush. Vigorous, upright canes benefit from a second pollinator variety nearby to improve fruit set and size.

plant_note: In zone 9, set dormant crowns or plugs October–November for January–March fruiting; Chandler is a short-day (June-bearing) strawberry that produces its primary crop when daylength is under 14 hours. The October–November planting in zone 9 triggers vegetative establishment before winter short days initiate flowering and fruit set.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in well-amended, raised beds or hill-and-furrow systems with good drainage; Chandler was released jointly by the California Strawberry Advisory Board and the USDA in 1983 and rapidly became the most widely planted commercial strawberry in the world. In California's Central Coast, it produces the majority of fresh market strawberries sold in the United States. In Florida and the Gulf Coast, it is the standard commercial season variety, planted October–November for harvest December–April. Chandler produces very large (1–2 oz), firm, bright red, conical berries with excellent sweet-acid flavor that remains consistent over an extended harvest season. The early-season production (December–January in zone 9) and large berry size made it the commercial benchmark. For home growers in zone 9, plant in raised beds with plastic mulch and drip irrigation; Chandler's vigor and large size reward careful management. Fruits can develop poorly in extreme heat — Chandler's season ends as temperatures rise above 80°F. Remove runners to keep plants productive. In zone 9, treat as an annual.

common_name: Charity Mahonia (Upright Fragrant Winter Flower Spikes)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Charity is a Slieve Donard hybrid bred for tall, upright, fragrant yellow winter flower spikes.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Charity, a classic Slieve Donard nursery hybrid of Mahonia japonica and Mahonia lonicera, bears tall, upright spikes of fragrant yellow flowers in late fall into winter, held above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage, followed by tart blue-black berries usable for jelly or wine. Its architectural form and off-season bloom give it strong winter garden value when little else is flowering. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart. Chattooga is a University of Arkansas erect thornless blackberry noted for ripening earlier in the season than most other thornless cultivars.
directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun; Chattooga is a University of Arkansas erect thornless blackberry release valued for ripening earlier in the season than most other thornless cultivars, extending the harvest window at the front end. It produces medium to large, firm, glossy black berries with good flavor on vigorous, upright canes that need only modest trellising support. Its early ripening makes it a useful companion to later-season thornless cultivars for a longer overall blackberry harvest. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest few per plant to maintain good air circulation and fruit size.

common_name: Chautauqua Gooseberry (Large Sweet English-Type Dessert Gooseberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement; more susceptible to American gooseberry mildew than hirtellum-type hybrids, so good air circulation matters.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, siting for good air circulation, and prune annually to an open center. Chautauqua is a large-fruited English-type dessert gooseberry, producing pale yellow-green berries considerably larger than most American-type varieties, with a rich, sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating out of hand rather than only cooking, a genuine treat among gooseberries where many varieties lean more tart. Because it descends primarily from European Ribes uva-crispa stock rather than the mildew-resistant American Ribes hirtellum lineage, it is more susceptible to American gooseberry mildew and benefits from a well-ventilated planting site and attentive pruning to reduce disease pressure. Harvest when berries reach full color and soften slightly for the sweetest dessert-quality fruit.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart. Fruiting occurs on second-year canes, typically May-June in zones 7-9.
directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5); Cherokee is one of the earliest University of Arkansas thornless blackberry releases, introduced in the early 1970s and long a standard against which newer thornless varieties are measured. Canes are erect and self-supporting, requiring only light trellising, and produce medium-to-large, firm, well-flavored black berries in a concentrated early-to-mid season harvest. Because it is an older release, Cherokee is generally less productive and somewhat more disease-prone than modern Arkansas thornless cultivars like Natchez or Ouachita, but its cold hardiness and long track record still make it a dependable choice. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 per plant to keep the planting productive.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in zone 8–11; Cherry of the Rio Grande is an attractive small fruiting tree native to southern Brazil and Uruguay — popular in South Texas and Gulf Coast gardens for its profuse crops of small, sweet-tart, deep purple-red fruits in spring and early summer, its tolerance of alkaline soils, and its handsome, semi-evergreen foliage.
directions: Plant Eugenia involucrata in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; once established it tolerates moderate drought, alkaline soils, and light frost to about 25°F; harvest fruits as they deepen to dark red-purple and become fully soft, as they drop quickly when ripe. Cherry of the Rio Grande is one of the most rewarding subtropical fruiting plants for Gulf Coast and South Texas gardens — it produces an early-season crop (April–June) of small, round to pear-shaped, dark red to almost black fruits on a handsome, densely branching shrub or small tree. The fruits have a sweet, rich, aromatic flavor with a pleasant cherry-like tang; they are eaten fresh, made into jams and jellies, or fermented into wine. A close relative of the more commonly known Pitanga (Surinam Cherry, Eugenia uniflora), but with a more refined, less resinous flavor. Hardy to about 25°F (zone 8 with some protection in zone 8a), and remarkably adaptable to the alkaline, often caliche soils of South Texas where many Eugenia species fail. Plants fruit at a young age and can bear two crops per year in warm climates. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape; the dense branching also makes it suitable as an informal hedge or screen.

plant_note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Chester ripens later in summer than most blackberry cultivars, extending the harvest season, and tolerates colder winters than many thornless types.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the vigorous semi-erect canes onto a sturdy trellis. Chester is one of the most widely planted thornless blackberry cultivars in North America, valued for a rare combination of good cold hardiness, strong resistance to cane blight and other diseases, and reliable production of large, firm, mild-flavored fruit that ripens later in summer than most cultivars, extending the blackberry harvest season. Its tolerance of colder winters than many thornless blackberries has made it a standard choice well beyond the Gulf South, though it performs well there too given adequate summer water. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to make room for the next season's fruiting canes.

common_name: Chickadee Blueberry (Very Early Large Low-Acid University of Florida Southern Highbush)
plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Chickadee is a very early, very low-chill University of Florida release bearing large, sweet, low-acid berries.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Chickadee is a University of Florida southern highbush release combining a very low chill requirement with unusually large, sweet, low-acid fruit, an appealing combination for fresh eating that also ripens very early in the season, giving Gulf South growers a jump on the blueberry harvest before summer heat and pest pressure build. As a southern highbush type it needs consistently moist, well-drained, highly acidic soil rather than the more forgiving conditions rabbiteye types tolerate. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old, unproductive wood each winter to maintain vigor and berry size.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart, and provide a two-wire trellis for the vigorous, thorny canes.
directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun and trellis the vigorous, thorny canes for support and easier harvest. Chickasaw is an older University of Arkansas blackberry release valued for its very large fruit size and vigorous, productive canes, ripening in the early-to-mid part of the season. Unlike the newer thornless Arkansas releases, Chickasaw retains thorns, so plant it where hand-picking around thorny canes is acceptable in exchange for its exceptionally large, firm, flavorful berries. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 canes per plant to sustain vigor and berry size in subsequent years.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Chilean guava is slow-growing and requires 2–3 years to produce a meaningful crop.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chilean guava is a compact, evergreen shrub with small, dark-green, aromatic leaves that produces masses of tiny, deep-pink to red berries with an intensely sweet, aromatic flavor reminiscent of strawberries and vanilla — reportedly Queen Victoria's favorite jam fruit. The plant makes an excellent evergreen hedge or foundation shrub in mild climates and tolerates light frost to about 12–15°F once established. Harvest berries in fall when they are fully ripe and very dark pink-red. Excellent for jams, jellies, and fresh eating. The closely related Ugni candollei (Chilean strawberry guava) is very similar with slightly different flavors.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 8–10; Chilean Myrtle is a small to medium evergreen shrub or tree native to the temperate rainforests of southern Chile and adjacent Argentina, grown for its extraordinarily beautiful, cinnamon-colored, smooth, exfoliating bark, profuse white flowers in summer, and round, black, edible berries with a sweet, aromatic, myrtle-like flavor.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Luma apiculata is adapted to the cool, moist, oceanic climate of Chilean Patagonia and performs best in mild, humid, coastal climates — avoid extreme summer heat and drought; mulch to maintain cool, moist root conditions. Luma apiculata (Chilean Myrtle, Arrayán, or Temu) is an evergreen shrub or small to medium tree native to the temperate rainforests of southern Chile (Araucania, Los Ríos, Los Lagos) and adjacent Neuquén in Argentina, growing in moist, sheltered valleys, forest edges, and riparian zones as an abundant component of the remarkable Southern Beech forests. The outstanding ornamental feature is the strikingly beautiful bark — smooth, exfoliating in large, irregular patches to reveal layers of cinnamon-orange, cream, and gray, producing a mottled, jewel-like trunk surface of extraordinary beauty, particularly on mature multi-stemmed specimens. Dense masses of small, white, 4-petaled flowers cover the plant in summer, followed by round, 1/4–1/3 inch, blackish-purple, aromatic, sweet, edible berries — the 'arrayán' fruit eaten by Chilean indigenous peoples and used for jams and fermented beverages. Luma apiculata is one of the most ornamentally desirable trees for mild-winter, cool-summer coastal gardens in zones 8b–10 and is widely planted in UK, Ireland, and the Pacific Northwest for its bark beauty.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese wolfberry spreads by roots and can become invasive in suitable soils — plant in a contained area or where spreading is acceptable.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade — Chinese wolfberry is similar to goji berry (L. barbarum) but more cold-hardy and shade-tolerant, producing red-orange elongated berries with the same sweet-astringent, tart-sweet flavor. In traditional Chinese medicine, the leaves (often cooked as a vegetable), young shoots, and berries are all used. The dried berries (gou qi zi) are a fundamental ingredient in Chinese tonic soups and herbal preparations, used for eye health and as a general tonic for centuries. Fresh berries are also edible and pleasant. The arching, thornless-to-spiny stems produce attractive light purple flowers in summer before the berries. Remarkably adaptable to difficult soils including alkaline, clay, and dry soils, and more shade-tolerant than most full-sun fruiting shrubs. Note that it spreads by roots and seeds; manage accordingly.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in very acidic, well-drained soil in full sun in early spring.
directions: Chippewa is a later University of Minnesota half-high release valued for combining a compact, 2- to 3-foot habit with unusually large berries for a half-high type and an early-to-midseason ripening window. It tolerates winter lows to roughly -30°F and performs reliably in zones where standard highbush blueberries suffer dieback, while still producing fruit with good sweetness and firm texture.
