Like other half-high cultivars it needs highly acidic soil, so growers should test pH and amend with elemental sulfur before planting if needed. Cross-pollinate with a second half-high or highbush cultivar to maximize berry size and yield.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter through early spring; in zone 8–9 plant February–March for maximum establishment. Choctaw is a thorny, erect variety that fruits early, typically late May to early June in the Gulf South — among the earliest-ripening named blackberries.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, acidic soil; Choctaw is an erect, thorny blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in 1980, one of the earliest-ripening blackberry varieties available and long valued in the mid-South and Gulf Coast for extending the harvest season ahead of later thornless varieties. The medium-sized berries are glossy black, firm, and exceptionally sweet with small seeds and outstanding flavor, considered by many Southern growers among the best-tasting of the University of Arkansas blackberry releases even decades after its introduction. The erect canes are self-supporting and highly productive, though the thorns require more careful handling at harvest and pruning than newer thornless varieties. Prune floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest; tip primocanes at about 36 inches in summer to encourage the lateral branches that carry the following year's crop. An excellent early-season partner for later-ripening varieties like Ouachita or Natchez to extend the blackberry harvest across the whole season. Zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement; well adapted to zones 3-7.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Clark is a Canadian-bred gooseberry hybrid selected for genuinely heavy, reliable production combined with good resistance to American gooseberry mildew, producing medium to large, red-pink berries with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor good for both fresh eating and cooking. The vigorous, productive bush has made it a favorite among home orchardists in colder regions who want dependable yields without the mildew management headaches that plague more disease-susceptible European heirloom varieties. Harvest when berries reach full color and slightly soften for the sweetest fresh eating, or pick a touch earlier and firmer for pies, jams, and fools where a tarter flavor is preferred.

plant_note: Plant 2-year-old container or bare-root plants in well-drained, very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) in winter or early spring; in zone 9 plant November–March during dormancy. Climax requires 400–500 chill hours and a cross-pollinator (Tifblue, Brightwell, or Premier) for best fruit set.
directions: Amend soil with peat moss, pine bark, or sulfur to achieve pH 4.5–5.5 before planting; rabbiteye blueberries like Climax will not thrive in neutral or alkaline soils. Climax is a rabbiteye blueberry (Vaccinium ashei) released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1974 and remains one of the most widely grown rabbiteye varieties in the Deep South because of its early season (it ripens in late May to early June in zone 8–9, the earliest of the major rabbiteye varieties), consistent productivity, and excellent fruit quality. Berries are medium-sized, light blue with a mild, sweet flavor and small dry scar. Plant in groups of 2–3 varieties for cross-pollination (rabbiteye blueberries are not self-fruitful). Remove flowers the first 2 years to direct energy into root establishment; full crops develop by year 3–4. Mulch 4–6 inches deep with pine bark or wood chips to maintain soil acidity and moisture. Climax is notably upright in growth habit and tolerates the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast well.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February for best root establishment before summer heat. Climax is an early-season rabbiteye that often ripens before Premier, making it the first choice for the earliest harvest in zone 8–9. Plant with Premier, Brightwell, or Tifblue for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Climax is one of the original rabbiteye blueberry cultivars released by the USDA and University of Georgia, selected for very early ripening — typically the first rabbiteye to color in a planting, beginning to ripen in late May in zone 8–9. The medium-sized, firm, light blue berries have good flavor but a somewhat thicker skin than later-season varieties; this firmness improves shipping quality. Climax's moderate chilling requirement (350–400 hours below 45°F) ensures reliable bloom in zone 8–9 without risk of late-season freeze damage. The upright, vigorous shrubs are productive and long-lived. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain acid fertilization with ammonium sulfate, and keep soil consistently moist through the production season.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in acidic, peaty, boggy or moist woodland soil; requires both male and female plants for fruit set.
directions: Cloudberry is a low-growing, rhizomatous Arctic-boreal species that requires cold winters, strongly acidic peat or sphagnum-rich soil (pH 3.5–5.0), and consistent moisture — it is exceptionally difficult to cultivate outside its native subarctic habitat. It is dioecious, so both male and female plants must be planted in proximity for fruit to set. The amber-golden berries are among the most highly prized wild fruits in Scandinavia and are used in traditional preserves; ripe berries are extremely soft and must be processed immediately. Not suited to continental climates south of USDA zone 5.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring; highly adaptable to dry, alkaline soils unlike most Ribes.
directions: Clove currant (Ribes odoratum, syn. R. aureum) is a tough, drought-tolerant native prairie shrub with intensely clove-spice-scented yellow spring flowers and glossy black berries in mid-summer. It tolerates alkaline, clay, or droughty soils far better than European currants, making it the best Ribes choice for the Great Plains and intermountain West. The berries range from mild to somewhat astringent depending on selection; look for named fruit-producing cultivars such as 'Crandall'. Prune by removing the oldest canes at the base every few years; the plant suckers moderately and can form a thicket if not managed. Verify state restrictions before planting.

plant_note: Plant rooted tip-layered cuttings or divisions in spring into moist, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; southern dewberry roots naturally wherever its trailing cane tips touch soil.
directions: Plant rooted tip cuttings in moist, well-drained sandy loam in full sun to light shade; southern dewberry is a low, trailing Gulf Coast and Southeastern native bramble that hugs the ground rather than growing upright, with slender, prickly canes that root wherever the tips touch soil. It is among the earliest brambles to flower, opening white blooms as early as late winter in the Deep South, followed by glossy black, sweet-tart drupes ready to pick weeks ahead of upright blackberries. Because canes trail and root freely, give it room to spread or confine it with a mowed border, and expect it to naturalize readily in sunny, sandy fields, roadsides, and open pine woods edges. After fruiting, cut back spent floricanes to tidy the patch and encourage vigorous new primocane growth for next year's crop.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring and install a sturdy trellis at planting time; Columbia Star is a vigorous thornless trailing blackberry that needs generous wire spacing to accommodate its long canes.
directions: Columbia Star is a USDA-Oregon State University thornless trailing blackberry bred for very large, firm, glossy-black berries with excellent, well-balanced sweet flavor, developed as a fresh-market improvement over older Pacific Northwest trailing cultivars like Marion. Canes are extremely vigorous and need a sturdy multi-wire trellis and generous plant spacing to manage their length. Train fruiting canes along the wires and remove them at ground level right after harvest, tying in the current season's new primocanes to bear next year's crop. Trailing blackberries of this type are bred primarily for the cool, dry summers of the Pacific Northwest and can struggle with fungal disease pressure in humid climates, so in the Gulf South prioritize excellent air circulation, full sun, and well-drained raised beds.

common_name: Columbus Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season Large-Fruited Southern Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Columbus is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release ripening late in the season with large, good-quality berries, extending the Southern blueberry harvest window. Plant with a different rabbiteye cultivar for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Columbus is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry that ripens late in the Southern blueberry season, extending fresh harvest well past most mid-season cultivars while still producing large, flavorful fruit on vigorous, productive bushes. Pairing Columbus with earlier-ripening cultivars like Austin, Alapaha, or Premier gives a Southern blueberry planting a long, staggered harvest from late spring through midsummer. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Columbus requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, lean soil in full sun; common barberry is very drought-tolerant once established but is an alternate host for wheat stem rust and is banned or restricted in some grain-producing states — check local regulations before planting.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean, alkaline to slightly acidic soil in full sun; common barberry is drought-tolerant and adaptable to poor soils but is an alternate host for wheat stem rust (Puccinia graminis) and is prohibited in many wheat-growing states — confirm legality before planting. Berberis vulgaris is a thorny, deciduous European shrub producing clusters of small, oval, bright-red berries (barberries) in fall with an intensely tart, citrusy, slightly astringent flavor rich in vitamin C; they are used in Persian cooking (zereshk polo — barberry rice pilaf) where they are a quintessential flavoring, and for making barberry jam, juice, wine, and candy throughout Europe and western Asia. The bright-yellow wood and bark contain berberine, a traditional medicinal compound. The berries are also an important food source for birds in winter.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; common manzanita is native to California's foothills and requires excellent drainage and dry summers — it will rot in humid, wet conditions.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in fall in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; manzanita absolutely requires excellent drainage and summer drought — it will not survive in humid climates or wet soils and is best suited to Mediterranean-climate gardens in California and similar dry-summer climates. Arctostaphylos manzanita is a large, beautiful, evergreen California native shrub or small tree with signature smooth, mahogany-red bark that peels to reveal bright, polished inner bark; it produces masses of urn-shaped, pink-white flowers beloved by hummingbirds and native bees in late winter through early spring, followed by small (1/3 inch), round, apple-like fruits (manzanita means "little apple" in Spanish) that ripen red to dark burgundy in summer. The edible fruits are tart and mealy, used by California Native Americans for making a refreshing cider-like beverage by soaking in water, and for making pinole (ground dried fruit). The exfoliating bark is one of the most beautiful features of any native western shrub.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Compactum holds its lower, denser form best out of hot afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade, and avoid the hottest afternoon sun, which can scorch the glossy, holly-like leaflets. Compactum is a dwarf selection of the Pacific Northwest native Oregon grape, staying under 3 feet tall and wide — roughly half the size of the species — while still producing the same fragrant, bright yellow spring flower clusters followed by dusty-blue, edible (if tart) berries beloved by songbirds, and the same spiny, holly-like evergreen foliage that turns purple-bronze in winter cold. Its smaller stature suits it to foundation plantings and shaded borders where full-size Oregon grape would eventually crowd the space. Prune only lightly, if at all, since its naturally compact habit needs little maintenance to stay tidy.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring once the ground can be worked, siting them along a fence or trellis in full sun.
directions: Grow this cold-hardy American grape on a two- or four-arm kniffin trellis, pruning heavily each winter to keep fruiting wood renewed and clusters well spaced. It produces the same deep blue-black, musky-sweet slip-skin berries prized in classic Concord grape juice and jelly, but without the seeds that fill traditional Concord fruit, making it far more pleasant for fresh eating. The vines share Concord's toughness and reliable heavy cropping in short-season northern climates, though clusters are typically a bit smaller and looser than the seeded parent. It is self-fruitful and widely adapted to home gardens outside hot, humid grape-growing regions.

common_name: Conquistador Grape (Disease-Resistant Black Juice and Jelly Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring in well-drained soil on a sturdy trellis; Conquistador carries strong Pierce's disease tolerance from its Munson-lineage breeding, making it a reliable choice for humid Gulf South vineyards and home arbors.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Developed from breeding lines descended from T. V. Munson's disease-resistant Texas grape stock, Conquistador produces vigorous vines with strong tolerance to Pierce's disease and other conditions that limit grape growing in hot, humid regions. The medium-sized black berries are tart and well suited to juice, jelly, and homemade wine rather than fresh eating out of hand. Because vines are vigorous and productive, prune firmly each winter to a permanent set of cordons and thin fruit clusters if growth becomes crowded, which improves air circulation and reduces fruit rot in humid weather.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; can also be planted in fall. Consort is self-fertile. This variety is specifically important in US states that allow Ribes cultivation but still recommend white pine blister rust-resistant cultivars. Prune out wood older than 3 years to maintain productivity. In zone 7 Consort performs reliably; zone 8 conditions may reduce dormancy needs.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Consort is a Canadian Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada black currant cultivar bred specifically for resistance to white pine blister rust (Cronartium ribicola) — a fungal disease that historically devastated currant and gooseberry plantings throughout much of North America and led to federal and state bans on Ribes species in the early 20th century. Consort's white pine blister rust resistance is an important practical attribute in regions where susceptible Ribes cultivars are still regulated or adjacent to white pine forests. The medium-sized, glossy, dark black berries ripen in July with the characteristic intensely aromatic, bittersweet black currant flavor valued for jams, cassis, juice, and wine. Consort grows as a vigorous, upright, productive shrub that is among the more cold-hardy black currant varieties, performing well throughout the northern US and Canada. The rust resistance trait means it can be grown where standard black currant cultivars are prohibited.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Consort was bred for resistance to white pine blister rust, which black currants can carry and spread to nearby white pines.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Consort is a Canadian-bred black currant developed specifically for resistance to white pine blister rust, a disease black currants can host and spread to nearby white pines, which historically got the crop restricted or banned in parts of North America. This resistance makes Consort a legal, low-risk choice for gardeners in areas where white pines grow nearby. Berries are the classic strong, aromatic black currant flavor, best used cooked into jam, syrup, and baked goods rather than eaten fresh, since raw black currants are quite tart and intense. Black currants fruit mainly on one-year-old wood, so prune out the oldest, least productive canes each dormant season and encourage a steady supply of vigorous young growth from the base.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Cowart is self-fertile and one of the earliest black muscadines to ripen (August in zone 9), making it the first black-skinned muscadine in the season. Excellent paired with Carlos or Fry for a mixed muscadine planting.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cowart is an early-ripening black muscadine developed by the Georgia Experiment Station (now UGA) and released in 1974. It is widely valued as a dual-purpose black muscadine: the large, jet-black berries (larger than Noble) are excellent for fresh eating with a rich, sweet, full-flavored muscadine taste, and also produce outstanding dark wine, juice, and jam. As one of the earliest-ripening black muscadines, Cowart extends the beginning of the black muscadine season and is frequently paired with Noble and other later-ripening varieties to spread harvest over a longer window. The thick skin makes berries more durable and longer-lasting after harvest than most muscadines. Cowart is self-fertile and requires no pollinizer, though yields increase with nearby compatible varieties. Disease resistance is excellent across the humid Gulf South. Harvest in late August when berries are fully black and slip freely from the stem with gentle pressure.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, peaty, moisture-retentive soil with access to irrigation.
directions: Cranberries require strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0), consistent moisture, and sandy-peat substrate — conditions that closely mimic their native bog habitat. A 3–4 in layer of coarse sand mulch helps suppress weeds and maintains the proper surface environment. The vines are slow to establish and typically take 3–4 years to produce a meaningful crop. Harvest in fall when berries turn deep red and bounce when dropped; home growers pick by hand rather than flooding.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Crandall is a clove currant selection notably more heat- and drought-tolerant than European black and red currants, making it one of the few currants that performs reasonably well in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Crandall is a selection of clove currant, a North American native species distinct from and considerably more heat- and drought-tolerant than the European black and red currants that struggle in hot summers, making it one of the more workable currant options for warmer zones. In spring it produces abundant, intensely spice-clove-scented yellow flowers that perfume the surrounding garden before setting large, sweet-tart black currants used fresh or in preserves. It is generally self-fertile though yields improve with a second plant nearby, and needs only routine removal of the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the shrub vigorous and productive.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Crandall is a clove currant selection that tolerates heat and humidity far better than European black and red currants, making it a realistic currant choice for Gulf South gardens.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Crandall is a selection of the American clove currant, native to the central United States and far more tolerant of heat and humidity than the European black and red currants that generally struggle south of zone 7. In spring, the bush covers itself in small, bright yellow flowers with an intense clove fragrance that perfumes the whole garden and draws early pollinators, followed in summer by large, sweet-tart black currants excellent for fresh eating as well as jam and preserves. Because it genuinely performs in warm climates, Crandall is one of the few currants a Gulf South gardener can grow successfully without fighting the plant's preference for cool summers. The naturally spreading, suckering habit forms an attractive informal hedge over time; prune out the oldest canes periodically to keep the planting vigorous and productive.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping blueberry is native to the southeastern coastal plain and needs consistently acidic soil, so avoid liming or planting near concrete foundations.
directions: Plant container stock in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping blueberry is native to the southeastern coastal plain and needs consistently acidic soil, so avoid liming or planting near concrete foundations. Vaccinium crassifolium is a trailing, mat-forming evergreen blueberry native to sandy pinelands and coastal areas of the Carolinas, with small, glossy, leathery leaves that take on bronze-red tones in cooler weather, pale pink urn-shaped flowers in spring, and small, sweet, edible blue-black berries in summer that both people and birds enjoy. It roots as it spreads to form a dense, low, evergreen carpet well suited to acidic-soil groundcover plantings, slopes, and the front of a native shrub border in Gulf South and coastal Southeast landscapes. Mulch with pine straw to maintain soil acidity and moisture, and avoid overhead irrigation with hard, alkaline water, which can gradually raise soil pH and reduce vigor.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil; excellent groundcover for dry, shaded slopes in western gardens.
directions: Creeping Oregon grape is a low-growing, mat-forming relative of upright Oregon grape, native to dry mountain forests and plains of western North America and exceptionally hardy once established. It spreads slowly by underground stems to form weed-suppressing colonies bearing clusters of blue-purple berries in summer that are sour but edible and rich in vitamin C. Like its taller relative, the berries are best used in jellies and syrups with added sweetener rather than eaten fresh. The plant requires no fertilizer and very little irrigation once established in appropriate rocky or sandy soil; excess moisture and fertility promote root rot.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping raspberry roots as it spreads along the ground and knits together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat within one to two growing seasons.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping raspberry roots as it spreads along the ground and knits together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat within one to two growing seasons. Rubus rolfei (long sold as Rubus calycinoides) is a low, mat-forming evergreen groundcover from Taiwan with small, crinkled, maple-like leaves that bronze in cool weather, tiny white flowers, and sparse, dull orange-red raspberry-like fruit that is edible but mild and seedy rather than flavorful. It is grown primarily as a tough, fast-spreading ornamental groundcover for slopes, walls, and container edges rather than for fruit production, tolerating foot traffic, heat, and a range of light conditions from partial shade to full sun. Shear back hard in late winter if growth becomes leggy, and take tip cuttings in summer to propagate new plants.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring to early summer; Creeping Raspberry roots readily wherever its trailing stems touch soil, so a single plant fills in as a dense mat within a season or two in partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun, spacing plants to knit together into a solid groundcover; established plantings tolerate light foot traffic and need only occasional shearing to keep them tidy. Creeping Raspberry is a low, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen trailing bramble native to Taiwan, grown chiefly as an ornamental groundcover for its glossy, crinkled, bronze-tinged leaves, small white flowers, and small orange-red, raspberry-like fruits produced in late summer that are edible, if mild and seedy, and readily eaten by birds. Its dense, mounding, self-rooting habit makes it useful for covering slopes, edging shaded beds, or spilling over walls in areas too shady for turfgrass, and unlike upright brambles it stays low and thornless-feeling underfoot. Cut back hard in late winter every few years to renew growth and prevent the center of the planting from thinning out.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring against a trellis or arbor in full sun.
directions: Train young vines onto a permanent support system and prune annually in dormancy, since fruit forms on the current season's growth from one-year-old canes. Crimson Seedless bears elongated, crisp, pink-to-red berries with a mild, sweet flavor on large, well-filled clusters that ripen late in the season. It is a late-season companion to earlier seedless grapes, extending the fresh-eating harvest into fall, and tends to color best where nights cool down as the fruit matures. Like most vinifera grapes it prefers a long, warm growing season and struggles in areas with high humidity and fungal disease pressure.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Croatan is one of the earliest North Carolina State highbush releases bred with low chill hours in mind, making it one of the more reliable highbush-type blueberries for zone 8-9 gardens.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Croatan is a historic North Carolina State University highbush blueberry release from the 1950s, bred specifically to bring highbush fruit quality to areas with milder winters than the traditional northern highbush belt, and it remains one of the lower-chill highbush options that can crop reasonably well in zone 8-9. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, firm, and sweet with the classic highbush flavor that many gardeners prefer over rabbiteye. Croatan is partially self-fruitful but produces heavier, larger-berried crops with a second southern highbush or rabbiteye cultivar blooming nearby. The compact, rounded bush needs consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil to perform well in Gulf South clay, so raised beds or heavily amended planting holes give the best results. Prune out the oldest wood each winter to keep the bush renewing itself.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, peaty, or sandy well-drained soil; thrives in cool, northern or high-altitude climates.
directions: Crowberry is a low, mat-forming evergreen shrub of arctic and subarctic bogs, heathlands, and tundra, requiring strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) and cool summer temperatures to thrive. The glossy black berries ripen in late summer and persist into winter under snow, remaining palatable after freezing — they are a critical subsistence food for northern Indigenous peoples and a major food source for migratory birds. Propagate by semi-hardwood cuttings taken in mid-summer; the plant rarely sets fruit in warm, humid climates. Minimal maintenance is needed once established as a groundcover in appropriate cold, northern gardens.

common_name: Cumberland Black Raspberry (Classic Heirloom Black Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring; Cumberland is an early-1900s heirloom black raspberry still grown today for its large, firm, richly flavored berries on tall, vigorous canes.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and give the tall, arching canes a simple wire support or tip-prune them at knee height in summer to keep the planting manageable. Cumberland is one of the oldest black raspberry cultivars still in commerce, long valued for unusually large, firm, deep-black berries with an intense, old-fashioned flavor well suited to jam, pie, and syrup making. The vigorous canes root at the tips wherever they touch soil, which is a fast way to propagate new plants but also means unchecked plantings will spread beyond their bed if canes aren't tipped back or trained. Remove spent floricanes after the midsummer harvest and thin to the sturdiest canes each spring for the best fruit size the following year.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil, and cover with straw mulch before the ground freezes to protect crowns through severe winters.
directions: Cyclone is a June-bearing strawberry noted for reliable survival to zone 3, making it a long-time favorite for home gardens across Minnesota, the Dakotas, and other regions with severe winters. Its concentrated harvest window is short compared to many cultivars, typically lasting about ten days, so plan for prompt picking and processing once the medium-to-large, bright red berries begin to ripen. Flavor is sweet and full-bodied, suiting fresh eating as well as freezing and preserving. Because the bulk of the crop ripens quickly, staggering plantings of an earlier and later cultivar alongside Cyclone can extend the overall harvest season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root plants in early spring in acidic, moist, sandy soil; Dangleberry requires the same acidic conditions (pH 4.5–5.5) as blueberries and thrives in the partial shade of longleaf pine and mixed pine-oak forests. In zone 9, plant in morning sun with afternoon shade. Like other huckleberries, it spreads by underground stolons and forms slowly expanding colonies. Very difficult to propagate from seed (requires cold stratification); purchase nursery stock.
directions: Plant in acidic, moist, sandy or organic soil in partial to full shade; Dangleberry tolerates and indeed thrives under open pine forest canopies where acid soil and dappled light create its native habitat. Gaylussacia frondosa is a native deciduous shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, found in longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods, and sandy pine-oak barrens from Maine to the Gulf Coast — a classic component of the native understory throughout zone 7–9. The small blue-black berries, ripe July–August, are sweet, distinctly resinous in flavor, and historically among the most prized wild fruits gathered by indigenous peoples and early settlers throughout the Southeast — often preferred over blueberries for their more complex flavor when made into jams, pies, and preserves. Dangleberry is closely related to the Black Huckleberry (G. baccata) but tends to be taller, more open in habit, and more shade-tolerant. The plant spreads by underground stolons to form loose colonies that provide excellent wildlife habitat — birds, black bears, and small mammals rely heavily on huckleberry fruits. In zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes with acidic, sandy soil, it is an outstanding native understory berry for shaded woodland gardens where blueberries struggle in too much shade.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Darlene is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine that sets crops reliably without a pollinator. In zone 9 it ripens in August–September. The balanced, sweet fruit and self-fertile habit make it an excellent single-vine option for small gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Darlene is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) bronze muscadine released by the University of Georgia for home garden and commercial production, valued for combining good fresh-eating fruit quality with the self-fertility that allows a single vine to produce a full crop. The medium to large, bronze-gold fruits have a sweet, mild, pleasant muscadine flavor with less of the strong musky note that some consumers find overpowering in older varieties. The tender skin and mild, sweet flavor make Darlene one of the more approachable fresh-eating muscadines for people new to the variety. The self-fertile habit is particularly valuable for home gardeners who have space for only one vine; unlike female-flowered varieties that require a separate pollinator, Darlene sets fruit reliably on its own. In zone 9 the vigorous vine grows readily in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers and produces consistently.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in early to mid-spring, spacing 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart on a support wire; fruiting occurs on second-year canes, ripening mid-to-late season.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and train the vigorous, self-supporting canes onto a wire trellis to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. Darrow was developed by USDA breeders and released in the late 1950s, named in honor of the noted small-fruit breeder George M. Darrow, and it was bred specifically for cold hardiness beyond what most erect blackberries of the era could tolerate. The berries are large, firm, glossy black, and tart-sweet, produced in heavy clusters over a mid-to-late season harvest window that extends the bramble season after earlier varieties finish. Its thorny, upright canes and strong winter hardiness have kept it in cultivation as a dependable choice for northern growers who need a blackberry that survives cold winters without cane dieback.

common_name: Darrow Blueberry (Evergreen Blueberry, Native Florida Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; Vaccinium darrowii is native to scrub, flatwoods, and dry pinelands of Florida and southeastern Georgia and is adapted to the sandy, acidic, well-drained soils of the coastal plain — it requires more acidic soil than commercial blueberry types.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich, sandy to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun; amend with peat moss or pine bark to increase acidity; mulch heavily with pine straw. Vaccinium darrowii (Darrow blueberry or evergreen blueberry) is a native Florida and southeast Georgia blueberry species — one of several native blueberries of the southeastern coastal plain — producing small, 1/4-inch, intensely flavored, blue-black berries in April–May with an extraordinarily rich, sweet-tart blueberry flavor that many consider superior to commercial cultivars. The small, semi-evergreen to evergreen, blue-green leaves are among the smallest of any blueberry species; the white, urn-shaped flowers in February–March are especially important for native bee pollinators emerging early. This species is a parent of several southern highbush blueberry cultivars (including 'Sharpblue,' 'Gulf Coast,' and 'O'Neal') bred for low-chill southern climates. Darrow blueberry is extremely low-maintenance in native soils — requiring no supplemental irrigation once established and producing reliably in the conditions of the coastal plain with minimal care. It is rarely available commercially but is outstanding as a native wildlife plant — birds and small mammals consume the berries eagerly.

plant_note: Set dormant crowns in early spring with the crown level to the soil surface in raised beds or well-drained rows, since Darselect performs best where soggy roots and standing water are not a concern.
directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring at soil level in fertile, well-drained ground, and mulch with straw to keep the large fruit clean and off the soil surface. Darselect was bred in France in the 1990s and quickly became a leading commercial and market-garden variety across western Europe before gaining a following among Mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest growers in North America. The berries are notably large, elongated-conical, and deep glossy red, with dense, firm flesh and a rich, well-balanced sweet flavor that holds up better in storage than many other June-bearing types. It ripens midseason and is often favored by growers who sell at farmers markets because the fruit's size and firmness make for an especially attractive display basket.

common_name: Daytona Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Pink Dooryard Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Daytona, released by the University of Florida in the early 1980s, is a pink-fruited bunch grape bred for home dooryard use with strong tolerance to Pierce's disease and downy mildew.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy. Daytona was released in the early 1980s from the University of Florida's bunch grape breeding program and is grown chiefly as a home dooryard grape, valued for its pink-blushed fruit and for standing up to Pierce's disease and downy mildew far better than European wine grapes in Florida's hot, humid climate. It does remain somewhat susceptible to anthracnose, ripe rot, black rot, and powdery mildew, so an ongoing fungicide program through the growing season is worthwhile even on a resistant cultivar like this one. Fruit is best suited to fresh eating off the vine rather than commercial wine or juice production. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and reduce disease pressure in humid weather.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; best suited to woodland edge plantings in its native Southeast.
directions: Deerberry is a native eastern North American Vaccinium species bearing clusters of small, blue-green to purple berries that ripen in midsummer with a flavor ranging from tart to mildly sweet depending on provenance and growing conditions. Unlike most blueberries, the flowers have exserted stamens (protruding well beyond the petals), giving them a distinctive open, star-shaped appearance that attracts native bees. The plant is very drought-tolerant once established and naturalizes well in dry, acidic woodland margins. Berries are edible fresh or cooked but have variable palatability; select superior-tasting wild ecotypes or named cultivars when available.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Delight is self-fertile and ripens early to mid-season, making it a reliable anchor variety for a home muscadine planting.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Delight is a long-established North Carolina State University bronze muscadine cultivar known for consistent production of medium-sized, sweet, thin-skinned bronze berries with good flavor for fresh eating, well ahead of the peak-season bronze varieties like Fry. Vines are vigorous and reliably productive, and the early-to-mid-season ripening window makes Delight useful for extending the start of the bronze muscadine harvest when paired with later cultivars. It is self-fertile and needs no separate pollinizer, though yield improves with additional muscadine varieties nearby. As with other muscadines, it shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases and Pierce's disease that limit bunch grape production in the humid Gulf South, needing minimal spray input once established. Harvest as berries color fully and detach easily from the stem; train vines to a sturdy two-wire trellis and prune annually in winter to keep fruiting wood renewed.

plant_note: Plant dormant container plants in winter to early spring in very acidic, well-drained soil; Delite ripens mid-to-late season and needs a second rabbiteye cultivar such as Tifblue or Climax nearby for cross-pollination and full berry size.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur well before planting; Delite is a USDA-ARS rabbiteye blueberry released from the small fruit research station at Poplarville, Mississippi, and prized among Gulf South gardeners for having the sweetest, lowest-acid flavor of the classic mid-century rabbiteye releases. Berries are medium-sized, dull blue, and ripen over a fairly long mid-to-late season window, making Delite a good choice for spreading out the fresh-eating harvest rather than a single heavy flush. Plants are vigorous and productive but need a compatible rabbiteye pollinator within about 50 feet, since Delite sets poorly on its own. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system from Gulf Coast summer heat, and avoid phosphorus-heavy fertilizers that blueberries tolerate poorly.

common_name: Delite Rabbiteye Blueberry (Extra-Sweet Midseason Southern Blueberry)
plant_note: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter into acidic, well-drained soil worked with pine bark or peat, and mulch well since rabbiteye blueberries root shallowly.
directions: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter into acidic, well-drained soil worked with pine bark or peat, and mulch well since rabbiteye blueberries root shallowly. Delite is an older University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for producing some of the sweetest fruit of any rabbiteye cultivar, with medium to large, light blue berries that ripen midseason. Like other rabbiteyes it needs cross-pollination from a second rabbiteye variety blooming at the same time to set a full crop, and its moderate chill requirement fits well within the zone 7-9 range common along the northern Gulf Coast. The upright, moderately vigorous bushes are long-lived and low-maintenance once established in properly acidified soil.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Dixie is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine that sets crops without a pollinator vine. In zone 9 it ripens September–October. The large, dark fruit and self-fertile habit make it an excellent standalone planting for gardeners with space for a single muscadine vine.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Dixie is a large, dark-skinned muscadine released by the University of Georgia, producing very large, round, dark purple to black berries with a sweet, rich flavor and thin, relatively tender skin that makes fresh eating more comfortable than older tough-skinned muscadine varieties. As a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) cultivar, Dixie sets heavy crops reliably without a pollinator vine — a significant practical advantage for home gardeners. The late-season ripening (September–October in zone 9) extends the fresh muscadine harvest into fall when most other fresh fruit has finished. The vigorous vines are productive once established and show good resistance to the common muscadine diseases including black rot and angular leaf spot that can be problems in the humid Gulf South. Dixie pairs well with Triumph (bronze) for a complementary planting that provides both dark and bronze-skinned muscadines from the same trellis system.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Doreen is self-fertile and a very late-season muscadine ripening in September–October in zone 9, the last of the major commercial varieties to ripen. This late ripening extends the muscadine harvest season and makes Doreen valuable for bronze wine blending.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Doreen is a bronze muscadine released by Mississippi State University in 1979 and named for a long-serving clerical employee at the university's experiment station. It is the most widely used late-season bronze muscadine, valued by commercial growers and home winemakers for extending the harvest season past Carlos and Scuppernong into late September and October. Yields are among the highest of any self-fertile bronze variety, making Doreen important for commercial production where volume matters. Berries are medium-sized, bronze-tan at maturity with a pleasant, mild muscadine flavor and good sugar content that makes excellent late-season wine. The plants are very vigorous and productive with strong disease resistance. Doreen is often planted in combination with Carlos to extend the bronze muscadine season from mid-August through October and to provide a range of flavors for blending. Prune heavily each winter; leave only short spurs on permanent cordon arms.

common_name: Dorman Red Raspberry (Heat-Tolerant Deep South Trailing Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil and train the long trailing canes onto a wire trellis, since Dorman Red does not stand upright like northern raspberries.
directions: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun and trellis the long, trailing canes on a two-wire support, since this variety sprawls rather than growing upright. Selected in the Deep South specifically to withstand summer heat that kills most raspberry cultivars outright, Dorman Red is one of the few raspberries that reliably fruits in zone 8-9 gardens where standard northern types decline within a year or two. It produces a single crop in late spring on second-year canes, with medium-sized, tart-sweet red berries that are excellent for preserves as well as fresh eating. Prune out spent floricanes immediately after harvest to make room for the current season's new growth, and keep roots mulched to buffer summer soil heat.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Downing is a nineteenth-century American heirloom gooseberry still widely grown for its reliable production and good mildew resistance.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Downing is a nineteenth-century American gooseberry, a Houghton seedling introduced in the 1850s and still one of the most widely planted heirloom gooseberries because of its reliable production, vigorous growth, and good resistance to powdery mildew compared with many European gooseberry cultivars. Berries are medium-sized, pale green, and tart, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, picked slightly underripe for cooking or left to fully ripen for a milder, sweeter fresh-eating berry. The self-fertile bush needs no separate pollinator and bears reliably from a young age. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the thorny bush productive and open enough for easy harvest, and site with some afternoon shade in hot climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides.

common_name: Doyle's Thornless Blackberry (Vigorous Trailing Thornless Bramble)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 10 feet apart to accommodate exceptionally vigorous, sprawling growth, and provide a sturdy trellis from the start.
directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil and train the long, trailing, thornless canes onto a sturdy multi-wire trellis, since this cultivar's vigor can overwhelm a light support structure within a couple of seasons. Doyle's Thornless was developed and patented by an amateur grower in Illinois and marketed directly to home gardeners rather than released through a university breeding program, and it became known for extremely heavy per-plant yields once established, with growers regularly reporting a single mature plant can produce many gallons of fruit. The berries are medium-to-large, sweet-tart, and hold their shape well for fresh eating, freezing, or preserving, ripening over an extended midseason window. It is self-fertile, though many growers plant more than one to maximize the already generous yields typical of the variety.

plant_note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Draper was released by Michigan State University in the 2000s and quickly became popular for producing exceptionally firm, crack-resistant, light-blue berries that hold their quality remarkably well after picking, a trait originally valued for mechanical harvesting but equally useful for home gardeners who want berries that keep well in the refrigerator. Ripening early to midseason on a vigorous, upright, productive bush, Draper combines good flavor with the kind of fruit durability that makes picking and storing a whole harvest far more forgiving than with softer-fruited varieties. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out old canes each winter, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, acidic, lean soil (pH 4.5–5.5) in partial shade; dryland blueberry is one of the few blueberry species that tolerates dry shade and lean, rocky, or sandy acidic woodland conditions where standard highbush blueberry would fail.
directions: Plant in dry to well-drained, acidic, sandy or rocky soil in partial shade or dappled woodland light; dryland blueberry is a compact native Vaccinium of eastern US woodlands and acidic ridge tops that earns its common name from its exceptional tolerance of dry, lean, acidic conditions — it is among the most drought-tolerant blueberries in cultivation. The white to pink bell-shaped flowers in spring are followed by small, intensely sweet blue-black berries in midsummer that are prized for fresh eating and bird fodder. Excellent fall color in shades of orange, red, and burgundy. Unlike highbush cultivars, no irrigation or supplemental fertilizer is needed once established in appropriate soil. Plant several individuals for cross-pollination and heavier berry crops. An underused native for dry, shaded slopes and woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant in spring in acidic soil; add sulfur or peat if needed.
directions: 'Duke' is a highly reliable early-season northern highbush blueberry with firm, mild-flavored berries that ripen over a concentrated window. It blooms late but ripens early, helping it dodge spring frosts while still producing an early harvest. Plant in full sun in acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, amending heavily with peat moss and mulching with pine bark. Provide consistent moisture, avoid lime, and prune out weak twiggy growth each late winter to maintain vigor.

common_name: Dumbarton Oaks Hardy Kiwi (Historic Vigorous Kiwiberry Vine)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola; Dumbarton Oaks is a female cultivar and requires a male hardy kiwi vine such as 'Meader' within about 30–50 feet for pollination and fruit set.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, with a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor in place before planting; Dumbarton Oaks is one of the older named hardy kiwi selections in American cultivation, long associated with the historic ornamental gardens of the Dumbarton Oaks estate in Washington, D.C., and maintained since among hardy fruit collectors and specialty nurseries as a vigorous, reliably productive female vine. Like other Actinidia arguta cultivars it produces smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruit that is eaten whole without peeling, with a sweet, complex flavor often compared to a cross between kiwi and green grape. As a dioecious cultivar it requires a separate male hardy kiwi vine planted nearby for pollination, since it will flower but set little fruit on its own. The vine is notably cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below what damages fuzzy kiwi, and grows vigorously once established, so provide a very sturdy, permanent support structure from the start.

plant_note: Divide rhizomatous colonies in spring or plant container stock in strongly acidic, sandy, well-drained to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf huckleberry is native to the dry, sandy, acidic pine flatwoods and coastal plain scrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf huckleberry is a low-growing, colony-forming native shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain longleaf pine ecosystem, spreading by rhizomes across the forest floor of dry, sandy pine flatwoods and scrub habitats. The small, black to deep blue-black berries are edible and flavorful — similar in taste to other huckleberries but produced on a very low-growing plant. The sticky, gland-dotted leaves are a distinctive feature. In the garden, it makes an excellent low, spreading ground cover for dry, sandy, sunny, acidic sites in zone 9a where few plants thrive. It is fire-adapted and rebounds strongly after prescribed burns in its natural habitat. An underused native ground cover for longleaf pine ecosystem restoration and dry, acidic, native plant gardens.

plant_note: Plant bare-root crowns or runner plants in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; in zones 3–8 plant March–April. Earliglow performs best where reliable cold winters supply the chilling hours needed for strong flowering — in zones 9–10 day-neutral varieties (Albion, Seascape) are better choices due to lower chilling requirements. Pinch all flowers in year 1 to direct energy into runner and crown development for maximum year 2 harvest. Plant in a matted-row or hill system 12–18 inches apart.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil with excellent moisture retention — strawberries are shallow-rooted and require consistent moisture; Earliglow is widely regarded by strawberry enthusiasts as one of the finest-flavored June-bearing varieties available, producing medium-sized, conical, deep-red berries with intense, aromatic, old-fashioned strawberry flavor uncommon in modern commercial varieties bred for shipping durability rather than taste. Earliglow is the earliest of all June-bearing strawberries — the first variety to ripen each season, typically one to two weeks ahead of mid-season types — and the red color extends through the flesh to the center (no white core), reflecting the full flavor development. The intense, sweet-tart, richly aromatic flavor is most comparable to wild strawberries and old heirloom varieties rather than the large but bland commercial berries in grocery stores. Earliglow produces most reliably in zones 3–8 where winter chilling is adequate; gardeners in the Gulf South should choose day-neutral types instead.

common_name: Earliglow Strawberry (Early June-Bearing, Disease-Resistant Eastern Strawberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; Earliglow is one of the earliest-ripening June-bearing strawberry varieties — it lives up to its name by producing ripe berries a week or more before most other varieties, which is a significant advantage in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic states where a late spring freeze can damage later-ripening crops while Earliglow has already fruited.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in early spring in full sun in well-prepared, well-drained soil; Earliglow is a June-bearing type (single concentrated crop in late spring) that produces abundant runners for establishing new beds; remove blossoms in the first year to encourage plant establishment for a heavier crop in year 2; mulch with straw over winter. Earliglow is a USDA-developed June-bearing strawberry variety released in 1975 that became one of the most important and widely planted commercial and home garden strawberries in the eastern United States for its combination of early ripening, excellent flavor, and disease resistance. The early ripening characteristic is particularly valuable in northeastern gardens (zones 4–7) where late spring frosts are a constant concern for berry production — Earliglow matures and is harvested before most other varieties even turn red, providing insurance against frost damage to developing fruits. The berries are medium-sized, glossy red, with a characteristic conical shape and excellent fresh flavor — consistently rated among the best-tasting June-bearing varieties by university extension trials for their balance of sweetness and acidity. Earliglow has exceptional disease resistance compared to many older varieties, showing good resistance to red stele root rot (Phytophthora fragariae) and Verticillium wilt — two of the most damaging strawberry diseases in cool, wet eastern growing conditions. The combination of early harvest, great flavor, and disease resistance made Earliglow the dominant strawberry variety in the Mid-Atlantic states for decades, and it remains one of the most-planted varieties in the region.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.
directions: Early Black is one of the oldest named cranberry cultivars still in cultivation, first selected from wild New England bogs in the mid-1800s and long favored in Massachusetts cranberry growing for its small, very dark, deeply colored fruit and dependable early ripening. Its early harvest window makes it useful in shorter-season northern locations where later-ripening cultivars like Pilgrim may not fully color before frost. Vines are relatively compact and cold hardy, tolerating the harsh winter conditions of traditional New England bogs with proper winter flooding or sanding. As with all cranberries, success depends on maintaining strongly acidic soil, a continuous water source, and a sandy-peat rooting layer.

common_name: Early Fry Muscadine Grape (Early-Ripening Sport of Classic Fry)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; not self-fertile and requires a self-fertile pollinizer variety such as Carlos or Cowart nearby for fruit set.
directions: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible self-fertile pollinizer variety nearby. Early Fry is a sport of the classic bronze Fry muscadine selected specifically for ripening earlier in the season than the standard variety, giving growers a jump on the muscadine harvest while retaining the same large fruit size and rich, sweet flavor that made the original Fry so popular across the South. The earlier ripening window can also help the crop finish before the heaviest late-summer pest and disease pressure builds, a practical advantage in humid Gulf Coast growing conditions. Harvest as berries fully color and detach easily from the stem with a gentle tug, and expect the harvest window to open somewhat ahead of standard Fry plantings.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or bare-root shrubs in early spring into well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; eastern prickly gooseberry is a woodland-understory native found growing wild in rocky deciduous forest across the eastern US and tolerates deeper shade than most fruiting shrubs.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; eastern prickly gooseberry is a native woodland shrub found scattered through rocky, deciduous forest understory from the Appalachians west to the Great Plains, distinguished from cultivated gooseberries by its densely bristly, spine-covered fruit and its genuine tolerance of significant shade, making it one of the few fruiting shrubs suited to a true woodland edible garden. Small, greenish, bell-shaped flowers in spring give way by midsummer to round, purplish-brown berries covered in soft prickly bristles that are removed by rubbing before eating; the tart-sweet pulp is used in preserves and pies much like other gooseberries once the spines are dealt with. It spreads slowly by suckers to form a loose thicket at a woodland edge, providing cover and fruit for wildlife as well as the gardener, and needs little care beyond removing the oldest canes every few years to keep new growth productive.

common_name: Ebony King Dewberry (Heirloom Self-Fruitful Southern Dewberry)
plant_note: Plant rooted tip cuttings or crowns in late winter to early spring on a low trellis; Ebony King was historically favored over other heirloom dewberries because a single planting sets a full crop without a separate pollinator variety nearby.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and train the trailing, thorny canes onto a low wire trellis to keep fruit clean and easy to pick. Ebony King is an early twentieth-century Southern dewberry selection once popular from Texas through the Gulf South for its dependable, self-fruitful cropping and glossy black, firm, sweet-tart berries that ripen ahead of blackberry season. It largely fell out of commercial favor as upright, easier-to-manage blackberry cultivars became available, but it remains a hardy, low-input option for gardeners wanting the distinctive early-season flavor of a true dewberry. Cut fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes onto the trellis for the following year's crop.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring; at least two cultivars within 60 ft improve cross-pollination and yields.
directions: Elderberries are fast-growing shrubs that fruit on current-season wood arising from two-year-old stems; cut one-third of the oldest canes to the ground each late winter to keep the planting vigorous. Plant two or more cultivars for cross-pollination — solo plantings produce far fewer berries. Harvest entire umbels (flat-topped clusters) in late summer when at least 95% of berries in a cluster are dark purple-black. Raw berries and green plant parts contain cyanogenic glycosides; always cook berries before eating.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart; fruiting begins on second-year canes, ripening in the mid-season window.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and cut new canes back after their first season to encourage strong lateral branching for the following year's crop. Eldorado was discovered as a chance seedling in Ohio in the early twentieth century and went on to become one of the most widely planted home-garden blackberries in the eastern and midwestern United States for much of the century, valued above all for its reliable cold hardiness and productivity without needing a second variety for pollination. The berries are medium-sized, glossy black, sweet, and nearly seedless-tasting compared to many older thorny types, ripening over a fairly long midseason picking window. Eldorado's erect, self-supporting thorny canes tolerate harsh winters better than many later thornless introductions, which is why it persisted in northern gardens long after flashier commercial varieties came and went.

plant_note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Elliott is prized above all for ripening later than almost any other highbush blueberry, extending the home harvest well into fall after earlier varieties have finished, with firm, small to medium, light-blue berries that start out fairly tart and develop better sweetness the longer they are left to fully color on the bush. The very late ripening window also means the crop largely escapes the peak pressure of many early-season pests and diseases. The vigorous, upright bush stores its fruit well both on the plant and after picking, making Elliott a valuable addition alongside early- and midseason varieties for gardeners wanting the longest possible blueberry season. Give full sun and consistent moisture, prune out old canes each winter, and plant with a second highbush variety for best pollination.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.0–5.5) soil in full sun to partial shade. Elliott's Blueberry is one of the most heat-tolerant native blueberries and performs well in the humid, warm conditions of zones 6–9 in the southeastern coastal plain.
directions: Elliott's Blueberry is one of the most valuable native blueberries for the warm, humid southeastern coastal plain, native to the moist to dry, acidic, sandy soils of pocosins, pine flatwoods, bay swamp edges, and woodland margins from North Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, where it grows in association with other ericaceous plants on acidic, well-drained soils. A vigorous, upright to arching shrub that can reach 8–12 feet in favorable conditions, it produces an abundance of small, sweet, dark blue berries in spring (April–May, depending on location) that ripen earlier than most highbush blueberries and are highly palatable to wildlife and humans alike. One of the most heat- and humidity-tolerant of the native blueberries, it is an excellent choice for the Gulf Coast region where northern highbush varieties struggle; it requires consistently acidic, well-drained soil and benefits from cross-pollination with other Vaccinium species. Plant multiple shrubs for cross-pollination and heavier fruiting; mulch with pine bark or pine needles to maintain soil acidity.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Encore is a late-season floricane (summer-bearing) raspberry that ripens its primary crop in late summer — later than most summer varieties. In zone 9 summer raspberries struggle with heat; Encore is best suited to zone 9a where cooler conditions at elevation or in coastal areas allow successful production. Provide mulch and afternoon shade in zone 9 to reduce heat stress.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Encore is a Cornell University late-season summer raspberry producing very large, conical, firm, dark red berries in the last 2–3 weeks of the summer raspberry season — ripening after most other summer varieties have finished, significantly extending the fresh raspberry harvest into mid-to-late summer. The very large berry size (larger than most summer varieties) and excellent sweet-tart flavor with complex aromatic notes make Encore the highest-quality of the late-season summer raspberry types. In zone 9 summer raspberries face significant challenges from heat — raspberries are most productive in zones 6–7 with cool summers — but in the cooler parts of zone 9a, along the coast, or at modest elevation, Encore can produce a satisfying late-season crop. The late-season ripening of Encore avoids the hottest weeks of summer, giving it better zone 9 performance than earlier varieties. Provide consistent irrigation and mulching to maintain the cool root zone conditions raspberries require.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; European hackberry is an extremely adaptable, drought-tolerant, and long-lived tree excellent for difficult urban and dry landscape sites.
directions: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in any well-drained, alkaline to acidic, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; European hackberry is remarkably adaptable to poor, dry, rocky soils, alkaline conditions, and urban pollution. Celtis australis is a long-lived (500+ year), medium to large tree of the Mediterranean basin and southern Europe, producing small (1/3 inch), round fruits that turn from yellow to orange to dark-purple-black when fully ripe in autumn, with a sweet, date-like flavor and a single large seed; the fruits were widely eaten by Mediterranean peoples since antiquity (the "lotus" fruit referenced by Homer that caused forgetfulness, though the identity of Homer's lotus is debated). The tree's beautiful, long-petioled, rough-textured leaves, tolerance of drought and heat, and picturesque form make it an excellent ornamental in zones 7–11; it is one of the best shade trees for very hot, dry, alkaline landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped specimens in well-drained, acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; mountain ash performs poorly in hot, dry climates — it is best suited to zones 3–6.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; European mountain ash is a graceful ornamental tree with pinnate, ash-like leaves that delivers three seasons of interest — clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring, abundant bright orange-red berry clusters from late summer through winter, and orange-red fall foliage. The profuse berries are eaten by waxwings, robins, thrushes, and other songbirds so eagerly that trees can be stripped within days of peak ripeness. The berries are edible to humans but contain parasorbic acid when raw (causing nausea) and must be cooked or frozen to destroy this compound; cooked berries make excellent jelly with a tart, cranberry-like flavor. Prefers cool, moist climates and does not perform well south of zone 6.

plant_note: Plant bare-root canes in early spring; primocane-fruiting types can yield a fall crop in their first year.
directions: Primocane-fruiting (everbearing) raspberries bear on the top portion of first-year canes in fall, then on lower portions the following summer if left. For the simplest management, mow all canes to the ground each late winter and enjoy a single fall crop on new primocanes — this eliminates disease buildup and minimizes pruning. Harvest from late summer through first frost when berries release easily from the plug. Consistent moisture during fruit development prevents crumbling.

plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun with well-drained soil.
directions: This everbearing mulberry yields sweet, plump berries over a long season on a compact, shrubby tree that is easy to manage. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates a range of conditions and is quite drought resistant once established. Prune in winter to keep it at a pickable height and to open the canopy. The fruit ripens over many weeks, so harvest regularly and expect birds to compete for the crop. Note that ripe berries stain, so site it away from patios and walkways.

plant_note: Set out crowns in early spring with the crown level at the soil surface.
directions: This everbearing 'Delizz' strawberry produces flushes of fruit from summer through the first frost rather than a single early crop. Plant crowns so the growing point sits right at the soil line, since burying it invites rot and planting too high dries out the roots. Grow in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist while berries are forming. It performs well in containers, hanging baskets, and beds. Pinch off early flowers on new plants to build strong roots before letting them fruit.

common_name: Evergreen Blueberry (Darrow's Blueberry, Lowbush Evergreen Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or amended soil; Darrow's Blueberry requires the same acidic conditions as other blueberries. Plant 2–3 varieties for cross-pollination. In zone 9, it requires only 100–200 chill hours, making it one of the few blueberries that reliably flowers and fruits even in warm Gulf Coast winters.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy or amended soil in full sun to partial shade; in hot zone 9 climates, afternoon shade improves fruit quality. Vaccinium darrowii (Darrow's Blueberry or Evergreen Blueberry) is a native, low-growing blueberry species from the coastal plain flatwoods and sandhills of the Southeast, ranging from South Carolina through Florida to Louisiana. It is unique among native blueberries for being semi-evergreen to fully evergreen — retaining most of its small, bluish-gray leaves through mild winters — and for requiring very few chill hours (100–200 hours below 45°F), making it one of the most reliable blueberries for warm zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where the commonly-planted Rabbiteye types (Vaccinium ashei) may not receive enough cold in mild years. Vaccinium darrowii is also an important breeding parent used by blueberry breeders at the University of Florida and USDA to develop the Southern Highbush blueberry series — its drought tolerance, evergreen foliage, and minimal chill requirement were bred into commercial cultivars. The wild species produces small but sweet, intensely flavored berries that are beloved by wildlife. It tolerates the high heat, humidity, and wet-dry cycles of Gulf Coast flatwoods better than most northern blueberry species.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; tolerates deep shade and is also grown as an ornamental landscape shrub.
directions: Evergreen huckleberry is a slow-growing Pacific Coast native prized both as an ornamental evergreen shrub and as a source of small, sweet-tart black berries that ripen from October through January — one of the few edible fruits to ripen in the Pacific Northwest winter. Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5 with pine bark or sawdust mulch. The plant is extremely slow to establish from container stock and may take 5–7 years for significant fruit production. Florists prize the glossy foliage as a cut green; pruning for floral use also serves to shape the shrub.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; once established, evergreen sumac requires virtually no supplemental water and will decline in heavy, poorly drained soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky or gravelly, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen sumac is one of the finest drought-tolerant evergreen shrubs for dry Southwest and Texas Hill Country landscapes, holding its glossy, leathery dark-green leaves through winter and providing year-round structure. Small creamy-white flowers bloom in late summer and attract bees and other pollinators, followed by dense clusters of deep-red, slightly sticky fruits that are documented as a food source for over 100 bird species including mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and Montezuma quail. It thrives on neglect once established and is an excellent choice for wildlife gardens, slopes, or as a large screening hedge. Avoid overwatering and heavy soils, which are the primary causes of decline.

plant_note: Set crowns in early spring at soil level so the growing point is neither buried nor exposed; Eversweet is day-neutral and fruits continuously through the first season rather than waiting for the following spring.
directions: Plant crowns in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing about a foot apart in raised beds or containers, and keep evenly moist with drip irrigation and a straw mulch to keep developing berries clean. Eversweet is a day-neutral strawberry bred for a longer, more consistently sweet fruiting season than many other everbearing types, producing a steady supply of medium, richly flavored berries from late spring through fall rather than concentrating fruit into one or two flushes. Pinch off the first flush of blossoms for a few weeks after planting to help young plants establish a strong root system before letting them fruit continuously. Renew the planting every two to three years as yields decline, and watch for the same pests and diseases common to other strawberries, including spider mites and gray mold in humid weather.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Excel is an early-ripening University of Georgia rabbiteye release with a relatively low chill requirement that suits Gulf South winters. Plant with Climax or another early rabbiteye for cross-pollination.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or sulfur several months before planting; Excel is an early-season rabbiteye blueberry from the University of Georgia breeding program, selected to open the harvest window ahead of standard mid-season varieties while still carrying good rabbiteye vigor and heat tolerance. Berries are medium to large, light blue, and firm, with a mild sweet-tart flavor typical of early rabbiteyes. Excel's relatively low chill requirement makes it reliable in zone 8-9 Gulf South winters that sometimes shortchange higher-chill northern varieties. It is not self-fruitful, so interplant with Climax or another early-blooming rabbiteye within about 50 feet for good fruit set and larger berries. Mulch with pine bark to keep roots cool and moist, and skip lime and phosphorus fertilizers, which blueberries handle poorly.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes early spring before growth begins.
directions: 'Fall Gold' is an extra-hardy everbearing yellow raspberry that produces very sweet amber berries on both first- and second-year canes. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil amended with organic matter and keep evenly moist.
