It bears a summer crop on overwintered canes and a fall crop on new primocanes; leave floricanes standing for two harvests or mow for one large fall picking. Suckers freely, so contain the planting with regular removal of wandering shoots.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; farkleberry is a native deciduous to semi-evergreen blueberry relative — the largest and most drought-tolerant Vaccinium in the Southeast — producing small, dark-blue to black, edible but astringent berries that are best dried or used in cooking rather than eaten fresh.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established, requiring no irrigation in the Southeast. Vaccinium arboreum (farkleberry or sparkleberry) is the largest native Vaccinium in the southeastern United States — a multi-stemmed, deciduous to semi-evergreen large shrub or small tree reaching 6–15 feet with smooth, reddish-brown exfoliating bark that is ornamentally attractive year-round. It is native to the dry, acidic soils of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, piedmont, and lower Appalachians, tolerating drought, sandy soils, and poor fertility far better than cultivated highbush blueberries. The small (1/4 inch), dark blue-black berries are technically edible, but are mealy, seedy, and quite astringent when eaten fresh — quite different from cultivated blueberries. They are far better suited to drying (they were used extensively by southeastern Native Americans as a dried fruit), cooking into jams and pies, or fermenting. Birds and wildlife consume the abundant fruit crops enthusiastically. As a garden plant, farkleberry is an underused native with beautiful four-season interest: white urn-shaped flowers in spring, glossy foliage in summer, brilliant red-orange fall color, and attractive bark in winter.

common_name: Farthing Southern Highbush Blueberry (High-Yield Midseason Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark; Farthing has a low chill requirement of roughly 300-350 hours and its heavy bloom benefits from a second midseason southern highbush cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and fuller berry set.
directions: Plant container-grown or dormant bare-root bushes in winter into raised, sulfur-amended beds if native soil is not already strongly acidic, and mulch with pine bark to conserve moisture through summer heat. Farthing is a University of Florida southern highbush release valued by Gulf Coast growers for its exceptionally heavy, reliable yields of medium-large, firm, light-blue berries with a mild, well-balanced flavor on a vigorous, upright bush. It ripens over a fairly long midseason window, which spreads out the harvest and makes it a strong choice for home orchards wanting an extended picking period. Feed lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and after harvest, and renewal-prune out the oldest wood each winter to sustain the heavy fruit set.

plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Favorite is a Black Spanish (Lenoir) seedling selection valued across the Gulf South for its strong tolerance of Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease that limits most European wine grapes in the region.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, providing good air circulation to reduce fungal disease pressure. Favorite is a seedling selection of Black Spanish (Lenoir), one of the historic Gulf Coast grape varieties long grown for its exceptional tolerance to Pierce's disease, a bacterial infection spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European wine grapes within a few years in the warm, humid South. It produces blue-black, juicy berries used for both fresh eating and home winemaking, ripening reliably where Vitis vinifera varieties fail. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and airflow through the canopy.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns October–November in zone 9 for harvest December–April; Festival is a mid-to-late season short-day variety that extends the Gulf Coast strawberry harvest past the early-season varieties. It is the recommended variety for Florida's commercial strawberry production in the Plant City/Hillsborough County region.
directions: Plant dormant crowns or plugs with crown at soil level in well-drained, raised beds or hills in full sun; Festival is a mid-to-late-season short-day strawberry released cooperatively by the USDA and University of Florida in 2000 that has become the dominant commercial strawberry variety in Florida's Hillsborough County, the largest strawberry-producing county east of the Mississippi River. Festival was developed to balance production timing with Chandler and extend the Gulf Coast season; it begins producing 2–3 weeks after Sweet Charlie and Chandler and continues fruiting longer into the spring. Berries are medium to large, very attractive, firm, bright red, with good sweet flavor and an excellent fresh appearance that makes them the standard for appearance at retail and export markets. Festival's disease resistance to anthracnose (Colletotrichum acutatum) is significantly better than Chandler, making it more reliable in warm, humid conditions where anthracnose crown rot can devastate the crop. An excellent choice for Gulf Coast home gardens and commercial growers where the extended season and disease tolerance are priorities.

plant_note: Plant softwood cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich acidic soil; provide a sturdy trellis or arbor — the twining vine reaches 20–30 ft.
directions: Schisandra chinensis is a vigorous deciduous twining vine native to northeastern China and Russia, bearing pendant clusters of small, brilliant red berries in late summer whose juice is famously described as simultaneously sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent — hence the common name wu wei zi ('five flavor fruit'). The plant is predominantly dioecious, so plant at least one male and one female vine for fruit production, though some cultivars bear perfect flowers. Train on a trellis, pergola, or fence with afternoon shade; the vine prefers cool, moist, slightly acidic woodland conditions. Prune to control size after fruiting; berries are used medicinally and in herbal preparations worldwide.

plant_note: Transplant rooted runner segments into cool, moist, acidic duff-rich soil under a closed forest canopy in spring.
directions: Grow as a low trailing groundcover in cool, consistently moist, acidic soil under dense conifer or mixed forest shade, replicating its native old-growth Pacific Northwest habitat. Thin trailing stems root at the nodes and spread slowly across mossy duff, bearing small three-to-five-lobed strawberry-like leaves. Solitary white flowers give way to small raspberry-red aggregate fruits prized by foragers but rarely produced in cultivation outside cool, humid coastal climates. Avoid heat, drought, and disturbed or compacted soil, which the species will not tolerate.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, or set out plugs in fall in mild climates; Flavorfest is a USDA-ARS release bred for outstanding fresh-eating flavor and good disease resistance in a mid-to-late June-bearing strawberry.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown right at soil level in full sun in well-drained, well-prepared soil, and remove the first flush of blossoms in a spring-planted bed's first weeks to push energy into establishment. Flavorfest was released by the USDA in the mid-2010s from the Beltsville breeding program specifically to combine excellent, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor with good resistance to common foliar diseases and better tolerance of a range of soil conditions than many older June-bearing varieties. The large, firm, glossy red berries ripen in a mid-to-late June-bearing window and hold their flavor and size well through the peak of the harvest rather than tapering off in smaller, less flavorful late fruit. Renovate the bed after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to maintain a productive planting for several years, and mulch with straw over winter in colder parts of its range.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February. Flordablue requires only 150–200 chill hours and is one of the earliest-ripening blueberries in the southeast. It benefits from cross-pollination with another low-chill variety like Sharpblue or Biloxi. Soil pH of 4.5–5.5 is essential — amend with elemental sulfur well in advance of planting if pH is too high.
directions: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Flordablue is a very low-chill-hour southern highbush blueberry developed by the University of Florida, requiring only 150–200 chill hours — one of the standard blueberry varieties for zone 9 and zone 10 gardens where inadequate winter chilling prevents northern varieties from producing. The medium-sized, firm, dark blue berries ripen in March–May in zone 9, among the very earliest blueberries of the season. Flordablue produces reliably in the mild winters of north-central and north Florida and the Gulf Coast, where more northerly varieties like Bluecrop or Blueray would fail to receive adequate winter chill. The flavor is mild, sweet, and pleasant — not as intensely flavorful as northern highbush varieties grown in their optimal cool climates, but very acceptable for fresh eating and processing. As a University of Florida release, it has an extensive track record of performance in Gulf Coast conditions.

plant_note: Plant transplants (plugs) in fall for winter-spring production; in zone 9 plant September–November. Florida Beauty is a day-neutral strawberry that fruits without a specific photoperiod requirement, allowing production throughout the cool season in zone 9 — from approximately November through April. Set plants with the crown at soil level (not buried, not too high). In zone 9 strawberries perform as cool-season annuals planted fresh each fall; the summer heat ends production and most gardeners replace plants each season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with high organic matter content; Florida Beauty is a University of Florida-developed day-neutral strawberry cultivar specifically bred for warm-winter production in zones 8–10, where traditional June-bearing strawberries from northern breeding programs produce poorly or fail entirely. The 'day-neutral' characteristic allows Florida Beauty to initiate flower buds and set fruit based on temperature rather than day length, enabling continuous fruit production throughout zone 9's cool season (November–April) regardless of the photoperiod. The medium-to-large, glossy, red fruits have excellent flavor — sweet with the bright strawberry character that distinguishes the best fresh-market strawberries from commercial long-distance shipping varieties. Florida Beauty was developed for performance in Florida, Gulf Coast, and similar warm-winter climates where most northern strawberry varieties fail to produce adequate fruit, making it one of the most appropriate strawberry choices for zone 9 home gardens.

common_name: Florida Radiance Strawberry (UF/IFAS Gulf-Latitude Short-Day Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Florida Radiance is a University of Florida IFAS release that became a dominant short-day strawberry across Florida and Gulf-latitude winter production regions worldwide.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Florida Radiance is a University of Florida IFAS-bred short-day strawberry that became one of the most widely planted cultivars in Florida and similar Gulf-latitude winter production regions, prized for its combination of early, high yield and good flavor in warm winter climates unsuited to many Northern-bred strawberry varieties. The bright red, well-formed berries perform reliably through a Gulf South winter growing season. As with other short-day strawberries in zone 9, plant fresh crowns each fall and treat as a winter annual, harvesting from winter into spring before the plants decline in summer heat. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce disease pressure common in humid Gulf Coast conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist to moderately wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Florida Serviceberry tolerates wet, sandy coastal plain soils where other serviceberries may struggle, and is smaller and more compact than Downy Serviceberry, making it a better fit for smaller gardens.
directions: Florida Serviceberry is a native shrub of moist to wet, sandy coastal plain habitats from Virginia south to Florida, producing clusters of small white flowers in late winter to early spring — among the first native flowers to open each year — that provide a critical early nectar and pollen source for emerging native bees and butterflies at a time when little else is blooming. The sweet, dark blue-purple berries that follow in late spring and early summer have a mild flavor reminiscent of blueberries and are avidly consumed by mockingbirds, catbirds, Baltimore orioles, cedar waxwings, and over 40 other bird species during the critical spring migration feeding period. The smaller, more compact stature compared to the familiar Downy Serviceberry makes Florida Serviceberry well suited to smaller gardens and naturalized plantings in the coastal plain Southeast. Plant in moist to moderately wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Florida Serviceberry tolerates the wet, sandy, coastal plain soils that can challenge other native fruit shrubs.

common_name: Florida127 Strawberry (Sweet Sensation, UF/IFAS Winter Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Florida127 (marketed as Sweet Sensation) is a University of Florida IFAS release bred at the Gulf Coast Research and Education Center specifically for Central Florida and Gulf-latitude winter production.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Florida127, sold under the brand name Sweet Sensation, was bred at the University of Florida's Gulf Coast Research and Education Center specifically for the mild winters of Central Florida and similar Gulf-latitude climates. It produces larger fruit and higher yield than the earlier Florida Radiance release, along with a longer shelf life and sweeter flavor that has made it popular with both commercial growers and home gardeners in the region. Like other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, planting fresh crowns each fall for harvest through winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce disease pressure in humid Gulf Coast conditions.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, keeping the crown at soil level in full sun and well-drained, humus-rich soil.
directions: Fort Laramie was bred at the University of Wyoming for extreme winter hardiness and continues to be one of the most cold-tolerant everbearing strawberry cultivars available, surviving open winters in zone 3 with minimal mulch protection. Plants produce a moderate spring flush followed by a lighter but steady crop through summer and into fall, with medium, firm, bright-red berries of good dessert quality. Because it tolerates cold so well, it is a reliable choice for northern Plains and mountain-region gardeners where many everbearing varieties struggle to overwinter. Remove blossoms for the first several weeks after spring planting to encourage strong root and crown establishment before fruiting begins.

common_name: Fredonia Gooseberry (American-Type Dark Red Disease-Resistant Gooseberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement; well adapted to zones 3-7.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Fredonia is an American-type gooseberry, bred from the same disease-resistant Ribes hirtellum lineage used in many modern hardy gooseberry releases, producing dark red, sweet-tart berries with good flavor and much better tolerance of American gooseberry mildew than older European heirloom varieties. The compact, manageable bush fits well into smaller home gardens, and its reliable, moderate productivity makes it a practical choice for growers who want a straightforward, low-fuss gooseberry without extensive mildew management. Harvest when berries reach full color and slightly soften for fresh eating, or pick a bit earlier for cooking and preserving, since gooseberries hold well on the bush at multiple ripeness stages.

common_name: Frontenac Grape (Cold-Hardy Riparia-Derived Red Wine Grape)
plant_note: Set dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun in early spring; space rows to allow good airflow.
directions: Frontenac was released by the University of Minnesota from a Landot 4511 by Vitis riparia cross, and its riparia parentage gives it exceptional hardiness to roughly -35°F, making it a mainstay for upper-Midwest and Canadian vineyards. The vine is vigorous, productive, and reliably winter-hardy without hilling, but the fruit carries very high natural acidity that typically needs to be balanced through deacidification or blending during winemaking. Berries are small, black, and produce a deep ruby wine with cherry and dried-cranberry character; the foliage also colors attractively red-purple in autumn. Prune to a bilateral cordon or cane system and thin fruit clusters in high-vigor years to concentrate flavor.

common_name: Fronteras Strawberry (Crown Rot and Mildew-Resistant Short-Day Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Fronteras is a UC Davis release documented with resistance to Macrophomina crown rot, an emerging major strawberry disease, plus moderate resistance to powdery mildew, Verticillium wilt, and Phytophthora crown rot.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Fronteras is a short-day strawberry from the University of California, Davis breeding program with a documented, unusually broad disease-resistance package, including resistance to Macrophomina crown rot, an emerging soil-borne disease that has become a significant problem in strawberry production, plus moderate resistance to powdery mildew, Verticillium wilt, and Phytophthora crown rot. This combination of resistances makes it a strong choice for gardeners whose beds have struggled with soil-borne disease in previous strawberry plantings. Like other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, planting fresh crowns each fall for harvest through winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds for the best results.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; IMPORTANT: Fry is NOT self-fertile and requires a self-fertile pollinizer (Carlos, Noble, Cowart) within 50 feet for fruit set. Without cross-pollination, Fry produces little to no fruit. Mid-season ripening (August–September in zone 9).
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun alongside a self-fertile pollinizer variety; Fry is a bronze muscadine developed by the Georgia Experiment Station and released in 1972, consistently regarded as the best fresh-eating muscadine available — the benchmark for table-quality muscadine grapes. The berries are extraordinarily large (up to 1.5 inches in diameter, one of the largest of any muscadine), bronze-gold at maturity with a beautiful appearance, excellent mild-sweet flavor, and thinner skin than most muscadines, making fresh eating more pleasant. Fry's principal limitation is its lack of self-fertility: it will produce essentially no fruit without a compatible self-fertile pollinizer planted within range. This has made it less popular commercially where single-variety plantings are common, but in home gardens where a pollinator is easily added, Fry is unmatched for fresh table quality. The vines are vigorous, productive once pollinated, and disease-resistant. Harvest when berries are fully bronze-gold and yield to gentle pressure.

common_name: Fry Seedless Muscadine Grape (Seedless Sport of Classic Fry)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; self-fertile, unlike the seeded parent Fry variety, so a single vine can produce fruit.
directions: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun. Fry Seedless is a seedless sport of the classic bronze Fry muscadine, retaining the same large size and sweet, richly flavored fruit that made the original Fry a Southern favorite, but without the large seeds most muscadines carry, making it more convenient for fresh eating. As is typical of seedless muscadine selections, individual berries run somewhat smaller than the seeded parent variety, a common tradeoff in muscadine breeding, but the flavor and eating quality remain excellent. Unlike seeded Fry, which requires a separate pollinizer, Fry Seedless is self-fertile, simplifying planting for gardeners who want just one or two vines. Harvest as berries fully color and detach easily with a gentle tug, typically over an extended late-summer season.

plant_note: Plant after last frost in spring; requires a long frost-free season of 200–240 days for fruit to mature.
directions: Fuzzy kiwi (the standard grocery-store kiwifruit) requires a long, warm growing season and is best suited to zones 7–9 with at least 200 frost-free days. Like hardy kiwi, it is dioecious and requires male and female plants — one male pollinates up to 8 females. Train vines on a T-bar or pergola trellis and prune hard each dormant season to manage the vigorous growth. Harvest in late fall before hard frost when the seeds have turned black and the flesh is tender; fruit ripens off the vine.

plant_note: Set out plugs or bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun on well-drained, raised beds; Galletta is a North Carolina State University day-neutral release bred for good flavor and consistent production through the warm Southeastern growing season.
directions: Plant on raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and pinch off the first several weeks of flowers on spring-set plants to build a stronger root system before letting the crop set. Galletta is a day-neutral strawberry from the North Carolina State University breeding program, selected to keep flowering and fruiting through summer heat rather than pausing like traditional June-bearers, which gives a longer, more spread-out harvest from spring through fall in the Southeast. Berries are firm, glossy, and well flavored, holding up better to summer warmth than many older day-neutral varieties bred for cooler California conditions. Keep plants consistently watered through hot spells, since day-neutral types are actively fruiting during the stress of summer, and refresh the planting every year or two as vigor declines.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Geneva is a female cultivar developed at Cornell's Geneva, New York research station and requires a male hardy kiwi vine within pollinating range for fruit set. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola for the vigorous vine.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a permanent, sturdy support structure. Geneva is a female hardy kiwi cultivar selected and released by Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural research station, bred for excellent fruit quality, good productivity, and reliable cold hardiness suited to northern growing conditions. The smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruit ripens in fall with sweet, tangy flavor typical of hardy kiwi, eaten whole without peeling, and the vine's Cornell breeding gives it dependable performance and disease tolerance in the humid Northeast, translating well to other regions with cold winters. As with all Actinidia arguta, Geneva is dioecious and needs a separate male vine planted nearby to ensure pollination and fruit set. A well-vetted, university-tested choice for a hardy kiwi arbor in zone 4–8.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Georgiagem is a 1986 Georgia rabbiteye release, needing another rabbiteye cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and full fruit set.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Georgiagem, released by the University of Georgia in 1986, produces a vigorous, productive bush bearing medium-to-large, well-flavored berries on a plant that has proven well adapted to the heat and humidity of the Deep South growing season. It fills a useful spot in the rabbiteye ripening sequence for growers building an extended harvest by combining early, mid, and late cultivars. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid heavy late-season nitrogen, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall in full sun; performs best where summers stay cool, struggling in regions with high heat and humidity.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall in full sun; this cultivar performs best where summers stay cool, struggling in regions with high heat and humidity. Gloire des Sablons is a distinctive French heirloom currant whose berries ripen with a marbled pink-and-cream streaked skin, midway in both color and sweetness between typical red and white currants. It is grown as much for its unusual coloring as for its genuinely good eating quality, being milder and less acidic than most red-fruited types. The self-fertile bush is vigorous, producing long, well-filled strigs in midsummer, and responds well to the same renewal pruning favored by other Ribes rubrum cultivars.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; mulch over winter in the coldest parts of its range.
directions: Glooscap is a 1983 release from the Kentville breeding program in Nova Scotia, bred from a cross of Micmac and Bounty, and remains valued decades later for its exceptional winter hardiness and heavy mid-season yields. The medium-sized berries separate cleanly from the cap at harvest, a trait that makes hulling for jam and preserves noticeably faster than with many dessert-type cultivars. Its toughness has made it a long-standing recommendation for cold-climate gardens from Newfoundland to the northern Plains. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to sustain productivity in following years.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring after frost danger; goji tolerates alkaline soils and drought once established.
directions: Goji berries are highly adaptable, tolerating poor, alkaline soils where other fruits fail, but perform best in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0. The arching, slightly thorny canes can be left as a shrub or trained to a central leader with a stake. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals. Harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers — ripe fruits are bright red-orange, soft, and drop easily (avoid touching them, as the sap stains).

plant_note: Plant bare-root canes in early spring; most golden raspberries are primocane-fruiting and will yield a fall crop in their first year.
directions: Golden raspberries are yellow-fruited mutations of red raspberry cultivars, most commonly primocane-fruiting (everbearing) types such as 'Anne' or 'Fall Gold', with exceptionally sweet, mild flavor and low acidity. Manage as you would a primocane-fruiting red raspberry: for the simplest system, mow all canes to the ground each late winter and allow new primocanes to grow and fruit in fall. For a two-crop system, retain canes over winter to produce a summer crop on floricanes. Harvest when berries turn fully golden-yellow and release easily; they are more fragile than red types and should be processed quickly.

common_name: Golden Shadows Pagoda Dogwood (Variegated Rainbow Pagoda Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Golden Shadows keeps its brightest chartreuse-gold variegation and is least prone to leaf scorch when given morning sun and afternoon shade, unlike the more sun-tolerant green species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Golden Shadows is a variegated sport of native pagoda dogwood selected for leaves edged in bright golden-yellow around a green center, a combination that brightens through the season and glows in the dappled light of a woodland-edge planting. It retains the species' distinctive tiered, horizontal branching habit — the source of its 'pagoda' name — along with small, flat-topped clusters of white spring flowers and blue-black summer berries relished by songbirds, but it stays noticeably smaller and shrubbier than the green species, usually 8-12 feet tall. Like the species it is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker, so avoid trunk injuries, provide good air circulation, and keep it out of hot, reflected-sun locations where the variegated leaf margins scorch.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring; fall planting works well in milder zones.
directions: Gooseberries tolerate partial shade better than most fruits and prefer cool, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0–6.5. Prune to an open-vase structure each late winter, removing canes older than 3 years and any crossing branches to reduce disease pressure. Pick berries early for cooking (when green and firm) or allow them to ripen to red, yellow, or white for fresh eating. Note: check local regulations, as Ribes species are restricted in some U.S. states due to white pine blister rust.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring before bud break in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; hawthorn gooseberry is a North American native gooseberry species that tolerates more shade and moisture than European gooseberry cultivars and is resistant to white pine blister rust.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; provide consistent moisture during fruit development. Ribes hirtellum (hawthorn gooseberry or Appalachian gooseberry) is a native North American gooseberry species found naturally in cool, moist woodlands, bog margins, and rocky slopes from Labrador to Missouri — the most widespread of the native American gooseberries and a parent of many modern gooseberry cultivars. The shrubs are compact and moderately thorny, producing clusters of small, 1/2-inch, green to red-purple, translucent fruits in June–July with the characteristic sweet-tart gooseberry flavor excellent for preserves, pies, fools, wines, and chutneys. Unlike European gooseberry cultivars (Ribes uva-crispa), which often struggle with mildew in humid eastern North American summers, R. hirtellum and its native cultivar hybrids have better disease resistance in humid climates. An important distinction: Ribes species (gooseberries and currants) can serve as alternate hosts for white pine blister rust; planting within 1,000 feet of white pine stands is regulated or prohibited in some states — check local regulations. In zone 9, gooseberry requires deep mulching and consistent moisture and is marginal at the southern edge of its range; best in cooler climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in very well-drained, sandy, acidic soil; gopher apple has a very deep taproot system and resents transplanting — plant young container stock and avoid disturbing once established.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy, infertile, acidic soil in full sun — gopher apple is native to the xeric scrub and dry pinelands of the southeastern coastal plain and is exceptionally drought-tolerant, thriving on soils too poor and dry for most plants. The small, low-growing shrub produces white apple-like edible fruits about 1 inch long that are sweet and mild when fully ripe, eaten by gopher tortoises (for which the plant is named), bears, deer, and other wildlife. A critically important food source for gopher tortoises in Florida. Spreads slowly via an extensive root system; once established, this tough native is essentially maintenance-free. Excellent for butterfly gardens and native scrub restorations in the deep South.

plant_note: Plant in early spring; goumi is partially self-fertile but yields improve with cross-pollination from a second plant.
directions: Goumi is a nitrogen-fixing shrub from East Asia that produces abundant small, cherry-red, speckled fruits with a sweet-tart flavor reminiscent of cherry. It is remarkably drought-tolerant once established and fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, making it a valued plant in permaculture systems. Prune lightly after fruiting to shape the plant and encourage denser branching; heavy pruning stimulates excessive vegetative growth at the expense of fruit. Harvest when berries are fully red and slightly soft — ripe fruits have little to no astringency and taste excellent fresh or dried.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; goumi berry is an East Asian nitrogen-fixing shrub producing elongated, cherry-red berries with silver speckles — sweet-tart and lycopene-rich — that ripen in late spring to early summer, several weeks ahead of most other berries; the roots fix nitrogen through Frankia bacterial symbiosis, improving soil fertility over time.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; extremely adaptable — drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and fixes nitrogen. Elaeagnus multiflora (goumi berry or natsugumi) is a deciduous shrub from China and Japan producing one of the earliest ripening berry crops in the edible landscape — the elongated, cherry-red, silver-speckled fruits ripen in late May to June (in zone 6–7), several weeks before blueberries or raspberries, filling a gap in the fresh fruit calendar. The fruits are tart-sweet, somewhat astringent when slightly underripe, with a pleasant fresh berry flavor when fully red; they are rich in lycopene (higher concentration than tomatoes), vitamins A, C, and E, and flavonoids. Unlike its aggressive invasive relative autumn olive (E. umbellata), goumi is not considered invasive in most regions — it produces less seed, spreads less aggressively, and is widely grown in permaculture and food forest systems. The roots fix atmospheric nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis, making goumi a valuable soil-building companion plant in the food forest understory layer. The attractive silvery-green foliage and small, fragrant, creamy-yellow flowers in spring are also ornamentally pleasing.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Granny Val is self-fertile and ripens mid-to-late season, producing very large black berries prized for fresh eating.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Granny Val is a Mississippi State University muscadine release bred for exceptionally large, glossy black berries with a good balance of sweetness and the classic musky muscadine flavor, ranking among the largest-fruited black muscadine cultivars available for home gardens. The large berry size makes it a favorite for fresh eating and an eye-catching addition to a mixed muscadine planting, and vines are vigorous and reliably productive once established on a sturdy trellis. Granny Val is self-fertile and does not need a separate pollinizer, though nearby compatible varieties tend to improve overall yield. As with other muscadines, it shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases and Pierce's disease that make bunch grapes difficult to grow in the humid Gulf South, needing minimal spray input. Harvest as berries turn fully black and detach easily from the stem, and prune annually each winter to renew fruiting wood and keep the vigorous vine in bounds.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown stock in spring after last frost; provide a fence, trellis, or shrub edge for the twining stems to climb, and site in well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hotter climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade, providing a sturdy trellis, fence, or shrub for support; Grape Honeysuckle is a non-invasive native alternative to the notorious Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica) that offers nearly all the same wildlife value — tubular yellow flowers for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees in June–July, followed by clusters of red berries consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and other songbirds in fall — without any of the aggressive, smothering growth habit that makes Japanese honeysuckle a serious ecological threat. One of its most distinctive features is its perfoliate leaves, where paired leaves fuse at the base so the stem appears to pass directly through a single disk-shaped leaf, giving the foliage a sculptural, unusual appearance. It is substantially more cold-hardy than most ornamental honeysuckle vines, thriving in zones 3–8, and is well-suited to the upper Midwest and Great Plains where few ornamental vines are fully reliable. Established vines are drought-tolerant once rooted.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in moist to wet, acidic soil along streambanks, pond edges, or other consistently moist sites in full to partial sun; gray alder establishes vigorously in wet conditions and should not be planted in dry or well-drained garden soil where it will struggle.
directions: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in moist to wet, acidic soil along streambanks, pond edges, or other consistently moist sites in full to partial sun; gray alder establishes vigorously in wet conditions and should be sited where roots will have reliable access to subsurface moisture or periodic flooding. Alnus incana is a fast-growing native tree of northern North America, prized for its ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis with Frankia bacteria and to stabilize eroding streambanks with its dense, fibrous root system; male catkins emerge in early spring before the leaves, providing an important pollen source for early-flying native bees. The persistent small woody cones that remain through winter supply seeds to goldfinches, siskins, and redpolls, and the bark and foliage support a rich diversity of Lepidoptera larvae including many specialist moth species of northern forests.

plant_note: Plant rooted runners or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; green strawberry is a slow spreader that forms small, tight clumps rather than the aggressive runners of F. vesca.
directions: Plant rooted runners or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; green strawberry spreads much more slowly than wood strawberry (F. vesca) and forms compact, slowly spreading clumps rather than long-running stolons. Fragaria viridis is a European native wild strawberry distinguished from the more common F. vesca by its fruits, which remain green even when fully ripe (turning creamy-white to slightly pinkish), and by its distinctively sweet, pineapple-like aroma that some find even more delicious than common wild strawberries. The berries are small (under 1/2 inch) but pack an extraordinary fragrance and flavor; they do not separate cleanly from the calyx when picked (unlike F. vesca) and are best eaten fresh directly from the plant. An excellent collector's plant and conversation piece in the fruit garden, though not productive enough for large-scale harvest.

plant_note: Transplant starts after all frost danger has passed; start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost.
directions: Ground cherries are grown as warm-season annuals in most climates; start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of frost has passed. The bushy plants produce prolific small fruits enclosed in papery husks and often sprawl without support — a tomato cage or light staking helps. Harvest when the papery husk has dried to tan-brown and the golden berry inside detaches easily. Fallen fruits left in their husks on the ground remain fresh for several weeks.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained, disease-free soil; avoid replanting into ground that has previously grown strawberries.
directions: Guardian was developed through the Rutgers-USDA strawberry breeding program and was widely planted across the eastern United States for its strong resistance to red stele and verticillium wilt, two soilborne diseases that historically limited strawberry production in humid climates. Plants are vigorous with a spreading habit, producing large, firm, conical berries with good flavor for fresh eating and preserving. Guardian remains a useful choice for gardeners in older strawberry ground or areas with a history of root disease pressure. Mulch with straw over winter in colder zones and renew beds every three to four years as yields decline with plant age.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in extremely acidic, well-drained soil; Gulf Coast requires 200–300 chill hours, lower than rabbiteye varieties but slightly higher than Sharpblue. Excellent choice for zone 8–9 gardens on the Gulf Coast. Plant with O'Neal, Sharpblue, or Emerald for cross-pollination.
directions: Prepare acidic soil to pH 4.5–5.0 before planting; Gulf Coast is a Southern highbush blueberry developed jointly by the USDA and the University of Florida and released in 1987, specifically bred for the lower-chill coastal regions of the Gulf South including Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and the Florida panhandle. It requires 200–300 chill hours and produces reliable crops where northern highbush varieties fail to fruit. Berries are medium-large, blue, firm, with a dry scar and good sweet flavor that develops best with warm, sunny ripening conditions. The plant has a naturally spreading habit and is fairly tolerant of the heavy clay soils found in coastal areas if drainage is adequate — raised beds work excellently. Gulf Coast is also noted for tolerance of the wet winters common on the Gulf Coast, as long as roots are not waterlogged for extended periods. An excellent variety to pair with Climax rabbiteye blueberry to extend season: Gulf Coast ripens 2–3 weeks before Climax begins.

common_name: Gulfcoast Southern Highbush Blueberry (Original Low-Chill Florida Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat; Gulfcoast needs only about 300 chill hours, ripens early, and yields best with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in raised beds or native soil amended to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines, setting out dormant bushes in winter and mulching well to protect the shallow root system from summer heat. Gulfcoast was among the first University of Florida southern highbush releases bred specifically for the state's mild winters, and it remains a reliable, vigorous producer of medium, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor on an upright, spreading bush. Its very low chilling requirement makes it dependable even after unusually warm winters along the Gulf Coast, where many northern blueberry varieties fail to set fruit. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water during dry spells to support fruit sizing, and prune out old wood each winter to keep the planting productive.

plant_note: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in early spring in very acidic soil; half-high types excel in zones 3–5 where standard highbush varieties suffer winter dieback.
directions: Half-high blueberries are crosses between highbush and lowbush species, combining the large-berry quality of highbush with the extreme cold hardiness of lowbush — cultivars such as 'Northblue', 'Northcountry', and 'Polaris' survive to -35°F when snow-covered. Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.0 and mulch heavily with pine bark or sawdust. Cross-pollination between two compatible cultivars improves berry size and total yield. Pruning is minimal for the first five years; thereafter remove the thickest, oldest canes each late winter to encourage fresh productive wood.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; self-fertile, so a single vine can produce fruit.
directions: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun. Hall is a self-fertile bronze muscadine producing medium to large, sweet, flavorful fruit on a vigorous, productive vine with good disease resistance, making it a practical, low-fuss choice for home gardeners who want reliable production from a single vine without needing to plant a separate pollinizer. The self-fertile trait, shared by a growing number of modern muscadine releases, has made varieties like Hall increasingly popular for smaller home gardens where space for multiple vines is limited. Harvest as berries fully color and detach easily from the stem with a gentle tug, typically over an extended ripening window from late summer into early fall.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger; provide a very sturdy trellis or pergola capable of holding hundreds of pounds of vine.
directions: Hardy kiwi vines are dioecious — plant one male vine for every 6–8 female vines or choose a self-fertile cultivar such as 'Issai'. The vines can take 4–7 years to bear fruit but become very productive once established, requiring a pergola or heavy-gauge trellis rated to hold at least 200 lbs. Prune to a permanent framework of main arms and renewal spurs each late winter, cutting lateral shoots back to 2–4 buds. Harvest when smooth, grape-sized fruits yield slightly to pressure and taste sweet.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in early spring into moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in fertile, evenly moist soil and prune out the oldest stems each dormant season to keep the multi-stemmed shrub productive, since fruit forms on both new and one-year-old wood. Haschberg is a European black elderberry selection widely grown across Central Europe for its heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries used in juice, syrup, and wine production. It produces broad, flat flower heads of creamy white blooms in early summer that are themselves used for cordials, followed by large, drooping fruit clusters in late summer. It is vigorous and consistently productive, and benefits from a second elderberry cultivar nearby for improved pollination and yield.

plant_note: Plant two compatible cultivars (cross-pollination required) in spring in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 2–7; Haskap (Honeyberry, Blue Honeysuckle) is an exceptionally cold-hardy edible honeysuckle shrub from the boreal forests of Siberia, Japan, and northern North America — one of the first fruits to ripen in spring, producing elongated, dark blue-purple berries with complex blueberry-raspberry-elderberry flavor used fresh, frozen, and in jams.
directions: Plant Haskap in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; always plant two or more compatible cultivars for cross-pollination; water regularly during establishment and fruit development; berries ripen 2–3 weeks before strawberries and should be harvested promptly. Lonicera caerulea var. edulis and its cultivated selections (Honeyberry or Haskap) represent one of the hardiest edible shrubs in cultivation — tolerating temperatures to -40°F or below in adapted varieties, and withstanding late spring frosts during bloom thanks to early-season cold-hardiness of the flowers. Two compatible cultivars are essential for reliable fruiting, as the species is largely self-incompatible; many named Canadian and Japanese breeding program selections are available for pairing. The elongated, dark blue-black berries are nutritionally similar to blueberries but with a distinctly more complex flavor — sweet-tart with blueberry, raspberry, and elderberry undertones and a pleasant tartness. The shrubs are extremely long-lived (50+ years), begin bearing in year 2–3 after planting, and require minimal pruning beyond removing deadwood. Excellent for northern gardens where blueberries struggle, and the extremely early ripening season makes them valuable for extending the fresh-fruit season.

plant_note: Plant after last frost in spring; requires a long frost-free season of 200–240 days to ripen fruit. Hayward is the dominant commercial fuzzy kiwi cultivar worldwide — the standard grocery-store kiwi — and is self-sterile, so a male pollinator vine must be planted nearby for fruit set.
directions: Hayward is the classic commercial fuzzy kiwifruit cultivar behind nearly every kiwi sold in grocery stores, prized for its large size, bright green flesh, and well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. Like all fuzzy kiwi it needs a long, warm growing season and is best suited to zones 7–9 with at least 200 frost-free days; it is dioecious, so a compatible male vine (roughly one male for every 6–8 female vines) must be planted nearby for pollination, since Hayward itself is a female-fruiting cultivar. Train vines on a sturdy T-bar or pergola trellis and prune hard each winter to control the vigorous growth and keep fruiting wood renewed. Harvest in late fall before hard frost once the seeds have turned black, and finish ripening the firm fruit indoors at room temperature.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in wet to moist soil along stream banks, pond margins, or low wet areas; hazel alder tolerates periodic flooding and establishes quickly when planted in consistently wet ground.
directions: Plant in consistently wet, moist-to-saturated soil along stream edges, pond margins, or low wet areas in full sun to partial shade; hazel alder is a multi-stemmed native shrub or small tree that thrives where few plants can, colonizing eroded stream banks and stabilizing them with a dense fibrous root system. Like other alders it hosts nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria in root nodules, enriching surrounding soil and supporting the broader riparian plant community. Reddish-purple male catkins emerge as early as February before any leaves appear, providing critical early-season pollen for queen bumblebees and other overwintered insects. The persistent woody seed cones persist through winter and are eaten by redpolls, goldfinches, and other seed-eating birds.

plant_note: Set rooted cuttings in spring into moist, fertile soil at the base of a sturdy fence, arbor, or large tree; plant in a location that receives at least a few hours of direct sun to encourage fruiting, and water well through the first growing season.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into moist, organically rich soil at the base of a large, sturdy support structure, watering thoroughly and mulching to retain moisture through the first growing season while the root system establishes. Heartleaf peppervine is a vigorous deciduous vine native to floodplain forests and bottomland thickets of the southeastern US, recognized by its broad, bold, heart-shaped leaves and the showy clusters of small berries that ripen from green through turquoise to blue-black in fall, providing an important food source for mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and other songbirds. This large-scale native vine is well suited to covering fences, large arbors, and the trunks of substantial trees in moist, lowland sites where vigorous growth is desired and space is not limiting. Once established on fertile, consistently moist soil, it requires no supplemental care and will cover its support structure rapidly; direct new growth as needed to keep the vine on its intended structure.

common_name: Herbemont Grape (Historic 1800s South Carolina Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Herbemont is a historic early-1800s South Carolina wine grape still valued today for its strong Pierce's disease tolerance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the canopy. Herbemont is a historic wine grape dating to the early 1800s in South Carolina, one of the older American hybrid grapes still valued today for its strong tolerance of Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection that has limited European wine grape production across the humid South for two centuries. It produces small, dark, sweet-tart berries used historically and still today for wine, offering a taste of the region's viticultural history along with genuine disease resilience that many modern hybrids still aim to match. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and airflow.

plant_note: Set dormant canes early spring while soil is workable, before bud break.
directions: Plant 'Heritage' canes in well-drained loam enriched with compost, spacing them 2-3 feet apart in rows. This reliable everbearing (primocane) variety fruits on first-year canes in late summer and again the following early summer. For a single heavy fall crop, mow all canes to the ground each late winter. Provide a trellis or T-post support and keep beds mulched to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Higgins is a female-flowered (pistillate) variety that requires a perfect-flowered pollinator vine nearby. Plant within 50 feet of Ison, Triumph, or another perfect-flowered variety. In zone 9 Higgins ripens in August–September. The very large fruit size makes it one of the most impressive muscadines at the market and fresh-eating table.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil and provide a pollinator vine; Higgins is a Georgia Experiment Station-released muscadine variety renowned for producing fruits of extraordinary size — large white (bronze-skinned) muscadines reaching 1.5–2 inches in diameter, among the very largest in the muscadine world. The large, pale bronze-gold fruits have a sweet, rich, floral muscadine flavor and a tender skin that makes fresh eating considerably more pleasant than older tough-skinned varieties. Higgins is primarily a fresh-eating variety; the impressive fruit size creates visual impact at farmers' markets and U-pick operations. As a female-flowered (pistillate) variety, Higgins requires a perfect-flowered pollinator nearby — without cross-pollination the vine sets little or no fruit. Plant alongside Ison, Triumph, or another self-fertile muscadine for reliable production. In zone 9 the long, warm summer provides ideal conditions for the large fruits to develop to their full potential size.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container stock in early spring once soil is workable; fall planting is possible in zones 6–8.
directions: Blueberries require acidic soil with a pH of 4.5–5.5; amend with elemental sulfur and use acidic mulch such as pine bark or wood chips 3–4 in deep. Plant at least two cultivars for cross-pollination and better fruit set. Prune out old canes older than 6 years at the base each late winter to stimulate productive new wood. Harvest when berries turn deep blue and detach with minimal resistance, typically 7–10 days after color change.

common_name: Himbo Top Raspberry (Productive Swiss Fall-Bearing Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or potted plants in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; as a fall-bearing type, Himbo Top can be mowed to the ground each winter for simplified pruning.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost, in full sun, and provide support for the tall, productive canes. Himbo Top was bred in Switzerland (its name drawn from the German word for raspberry, 'Himbeere') as a fall-bearing red raspberry, and it has become popular with commercial growers and home gardeners alike for combining very heavy yields with large, firm, well-flavored berries that hold their shape and quality well after picking. Producing fruit on current-season canes from late summer into fall, it can be managed with the simple annual mow-down pruning typical of primocane raspberries, making it a practical, high-yielding choice for gardeners who want strong production without complex cane management. Pick regularly during the fall fruiting window, since the heavy-bearing canes can set fruit faster than a light picking schedule can keep up with.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool-summer climates in fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; gooseberries perform poorly in hot, humid summer climates and need afternoon shade and reliable soil moisture where summers are warm.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are cool; mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune to an open framework each winter to ease harvest among the thorny stems. Hinnomaki Red is a Finnish-bred gooseberry cultivar prized for combining reliable productivity, good mildew resistance, and outstanding fruit quality — the medium-sized berries ripen from green to a deep red-burgundy with a rich, sweet-tart flavor considered among the best of any gooseberry for fresh eating out of hand, as well as excellent for pies, jams, and fools. The compact, upright bush is more manageable and less sprawling than many older gooseberry varieties, and its Nordic breeding gives it strong cold hardiness alongside dependable disease resistance in cool, humid summer climates. Best suited to northern gardens with cool summers; in hot, humid zones the plant struggles with heat stress and powdery mildew regardless of afternoon shade. Zone 3–7.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring.
directions: 'Hinnonmaki Red' is a hardy Finnish gooseberry with dark-red, aromatic berries that are tart when green for cooking and sweet when fully ripe for dessert. It shows good mildew resistance and thrives in cool, moist conditions. Grow in full sun to partial shade in rich, well-drained soil and mulch to keep the roots cool. Prune to an open-centered bush in winter, removing crossing and low branches, and wear gloves when harvesting the thorny stems.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool and pruning to an open vase shape each winter for easier harvest among the thorns. Hinnonmaki Yellow is the golden-fruited counterpart to the widely grown Hinnonmaki Red, bred in Finland from the same mildew-tolerant lineage and sharing its compact, upright, spiny habit. The translucent amber berries ripen a little later than the red form and carry a milder, honeyed sweetness many gardeners prefer straight off the bush, while both hold up well cooked into pies and preserves. Best suited to cool-summer climates, since heat and humidity bring on powdery mildew and fruit stress.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; hoary blueberry grows naturally at higher elevations in the southern Appalachians in moist acidic forest understory and open heath balds.
directions: Plant in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; hoary blueberry is a native Appalachian species of high-elevation heath and forest understory communities, distinguished by its distinctly hairy (hoary) twigs and leaf undersides — the fine hairs give new growth and undersides a grayish, woolly appearance. The plant is closely related to rabbiteye blueberry but adapted to cooler, higher-elevation sites. The blue-black berries are edible and well-flavored. In the garden, it performs well in moist, acidic shade conditions that suit other ericaceous plants like rhododendron and mountain laurel. An excellent native for the acid woodland garden in zones 5–8.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade to partial sun; hobblebush requires consistently moist conditions and cool summer temperatures and performs poorly in sites with hot, dry summers or direct afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade, allowing generous spacing for the broad, arching form; hobblebush requires cool summer temperatures and consistent moisture, and is best suited to northern gardens or high-elevation sites where summer heat is moderate. Viburnum lantanoides produces large, heart-shaped leaves on low-arching branches that root where they contact the ground — the source of the name 'hobblebush,' as the rooted stems can trip unwary woodland walkers — and bears flat-topped clusters of showy white flowers in April and May followed by berries that ripen from red to black and attract thrushes, cedar waxwings, and other wildlife. Fall foliage color is among the most dramatic of any native shrub, turning rich crimson to claret-red in September, making hobblebush a multi-season standout for shaded northern woodland gardens.

plant_note: Set dormant bare-root crowns into well-worked, well-drained soil in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, positioning the crown right at the soil surface so it is neither buried nor left exposed.
directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring with the crown level with the soil surface, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and pinch off the first season's blossoms so the plants put their energy into establishing strong roots and crowns before fruiting heavily the following year. Honeoye was bred at Cornell University's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station and released in the late 1970s, and it became a mainstay June-bearing variety across the colder parts of the Northeast, upper Midwest, and eastern Canada because of its outstanding winter hardiness and dependable, concentrated early-season crop. The berries are large, glossy bright red, and firm, with a bold, tangy-sweet flavor that many growers describe as more assertive than milder modern varieties, and the plants send out runners vigorously to fill in a matted row within a season or two. Honeoye ripens early to midseason and is frequently planted alongside later-fruiting varieties to stretch the harvest window in home gardens and pick-your-own plantings.

plant_note: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; include at least one Honey Bee or comparable pollinizer whenever planting fruiting haskap cultivars.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and include at least one Honey Bee or comparable pollinizer whenever planting fruiting haskap cultivars, since nearly all commercial haskaps are self-infertile. Honey Bee is a University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivar bred primarily as a universal pollinizer rather than for its own fruit production, chosen for heavy, well-timed flowering that overlaps with most other haskap cultivars' bloom windows. Its berries are edible and pleasantly flavored but smaller and less abundant than dedicated fruiting cultivars like Borealis or Aurora, so it is typically planted as roughly one bush in five or six. The bush is extremely cold-hardy and easy to grow, tolerating the same conditions preferred by other haskaps.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; plant at least two different cultivars for cross-pollination, as most cultivars are self-infertile.
directions: Plant two or more different cultivars for cross-pollination in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–7.0) in full sun; honeyberry is an edible-fruited honeysuckle native to boreal regions of Russia, Japan, and Canada that produces sweet-tart blue berries resembling elongated blueberries in late spring — the first fresh fruit of the season in cold climates. Plants tolerate temperatures to -40°F and the flowers survive spring frosts to -8°F. Fruit is borne on second-year wood, so avoid heavy pruning in the first three years. Cultivars 'Tundra', 'Indigo Gem', and 'Borealis' are among the most productive for North American gardens.

plant_note: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in early spring for cross-pollination; haskap blooms very early and needs a matching early-blooming partner.
directions: Honeyberries are among the earliest fruits to ripen — often 2–3 weeks before strawberries — and flowers can survive temperatures as low as -4°F, making them ideal for short-season climates. Two compatible cultivars from the same breeding group must be planted for cross-pollination. Minimal pruning is needed for the first 5 years; thereafter, remove a few of the oldest, thickest canes annually to renew. Harvest when berries are entirely blue-purple inside (cut one open to check), as color alone can be misleading.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container stock in early spring; give Honeywood extra room compared to compact cultivars, as it grows into a large, vigorous, upright shrub.
directions: Honeywood is a Saskatchewan-origin saskatoon selection known for its vigorous, upright growth habit and reliable heavy fruit set even on younger plants. The dark purple-blue berries have the classic sweet, nutty saskatoon flavor and hold well on the bush for a staggered harvest. Plant in full sun with good drainage; because the shrub grows tall and dense, allow generous spacing in a hedgerow planting and prune out older canes periodically to maintain vigor and light penetration. It is a common choice in commercial U-pick saskatoon plantings across the Canadian Prairies for its dependable productivity.

common_name: Hull Thornless Blackberry (USDA Semi-Erect Thornless Bramble)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 4-6 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart, and trellis the semi-erect canes since they arch and sprawl without support.
directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile soil and tie the semi-erect, arching canes to a two-wire trellis to keep fruit clusters accessible and off the ground. Hull Thornless was developed by USDA-ARS breeders at Beltsville, Maryland and released in the early 1980s as part of a program aimed at combining the thornless trait with better cold tolerance and fruit quality than earlier thornless releases. The berries are medium-to-large, glossy black, and notably sweeter than many of its thornless predecessors, ripening over a fairly long midseason window with good yields once the semi-erect canes are established. Because it tolerates cooler winters better than many thornless trailing types, Hull Thornless became a popular home-garden choice for growers who wanted thornless canes without moving to a warmer climate zone.

common_name: Illini Hardy Blackberry (Extreme Cold-Hardy Erect Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early to mid-spring after the coldest weather has passed; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, ripening mid-to-late season.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5). Illini Hardy is an erect, thorny blackberry developed at the University of Illinois specifically for reliable cane survival in cold northern winters where most blackberry varieties suffer significant winterkill, tolerating temperatures well below zero without winter cane protection. Berries are medium-sized, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening mid-to-late season with good yields once established. Because the canes are self-supporting and very cold-tolerant, Illini Hardy is a dependable choice for northern growers who want blackberries without the trellising and winter mulching that tender varieties require. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest 6-8 per plant to keep the planting productive and manageable.

common_name: Improved Rugen Alpine Strawberry (Everbearing German Woodland Strawberry)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; press the fine seed onto a moist starting mix and keep uncovered.
directions: Improved Rugen is a German alpine strawberry selection named for the Baltic island of Ruegen, valued for producing larger-than-typical fruit on plants that send out only a few short runners, so it stays tidier than wild seedling strawberries while still filling in a bed over time. Sow indoors in late winter, surface-sowing the dust-like seed and keeping it consistently moist under bright light. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, siting plants where they get a half day of sun; established clumps flower and fruit continuously from late spring into fall. Harvest the aromatic red berries as they ripen, since they soften quickly and do not hold well once picked.

plant_note: Plant after the last frost in full sun with a trellis or fence; Incense is a USDA hybrid combining the cold hardiness of native maypop with a more tropical relative for larger, more fragrant flowers, and the roots survive winter to resprout each spring in zone 6–9.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy trellis or fence for climbing; Incense is a USDA hybrid passionflower combining native maypop (Passiflora incarnata) with the more tender South American Passiflora cincinnata, bred to combine maypop's reliable cold-hardiness with larger, showier, more intensely fragrant deep-purple flowers than the straight native species. Like maypop, the vine dies back to the ground in winter through much of its hardiness range and resprouts vigorously from the roots in late spring — do not disturb or remove the crown before new growth appears, as it can be slow to emerge. Flowers are followed by egg-sized, aromatic fruit with sweet-tart pulp similar to tropical passionfruit, though fruit set is often lighter than the straight maypop species; plant more than one vine to improve cross-pollination and fruiting. Incense is also an important larval host plant for Gulf fritillary and variegated fritillary butterflies, adding pollinator-garden value beyond its fruit and ornamental flowers.

plant_note: Plant bare-root in fall or early spring; seed requires 60–90 days cold-moist stratification for germination; plant male and female shrubs for reliable fruiting as plants are dioecious.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Indian plum is a Pacific Northwest native deciduous shrub prized for being one of the earliest-blooming woody plants — small clusters of fragrant white flowers appear in February or March before leaves emerge, often while snow is still on the ground, providing an invaluable nectar source for early bees and hummingbirds. Small oval drupes (like tiny olives) ripen to blue-black with a single large stone; the flavor is astringent and bitter raw but palatable to birds and was eaten sparingly by many Native peoples. An excellent choice for wildlife habitat gardens, riparian buffers, and native plant landscapes in the Pacific Northwest and northern California.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Indigo Gem is self-infertile and needs a compatible pollinizer such as Indigo Treat or Berry Blue planted nearby, ideally a different cultivar series flowering at the same time.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Indigo Gem sets almost no fruit alone. Bred at the University of Saskatchewan from Russian breeding stock, Indigo Gem is one of the earliest widely planted North American haskap cultivars, valued for its productive, compact bush and elongated, deep-blue berries with a tart, slightly grape-like flavor closer to the wild species than the sweeter modern releases. It is among the earliest fruits to ripen each year, often ahead of strawberries, which makes it a useful season-opener but also puts its early flowers at some frost risk in variable spring weather. Like all haskaps, it is extremely cold-hardy but performs poorly in hot, humid summers, so it is best suited to northern gardens and short-season climates rather than the Gulf South. Fruit forms on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning in the first few years to dead or crossing branches before starting renewal pruning of older canes.

plant_note: Plant in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil; self-infertile, so interplant with a different overlapping-bloom cultivar such as Indigo Gem or Aurora.
directions: Plant in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and interplant with a different, overlapping-bloom cultivar such as Indigo Gem or Aurora for reliable pollination and fruit set, since this cultivar is self-infertile. Indigo Treat is a midseason haskap from the University of Saskatchewan breeding program, selected for a sweeter, less tart flavor than earlier releases like Indigo Gem, with large, elongated, deep-blue berries. The upright, extremely cold-hardy bush breaks dormancy early, so late spring frosts during bloom are the main risk to cropping rather than winter cold itself. Expect fruit to ripen a week or two after the earliest haskap cultivars.

plant_note: Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; pair with a similarly timed pollinizer such as Aurora or Borealis for adequate cross-pollination.
directions: Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and provide consistent moisture during fruit development for the best size and flavor. Indigo Yum is one of the later-flowering cultivars in the University of Saskatchewan's Indigo series of haskaps, bred for a milder, sweeter flavor than earlier Indigo-series releases. Because its bloom period does not fully overlap with the earliest Indigo cultivars, it should be paired with a similarly timed pollinizer, such as Aurora or Borealis, to ensure adequate cross-pollination and fruit set. The compact, productive bush produces large, oblong blue berries with thin, tender skin well suited to fresh eating, jams, and baking.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring.
directions: 'Invicta' is a heavy-cropping green culinary gooseberry with outstanding resistance to American gooseberry mildew. The vigorous, spreading, and notably spiny bush yields large pale-green berries excellent for pies, jams, and preserves. Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil and space generously for airflow. Prune to an open goblet each winter to ease harvest among the sharp thorns and shorten leading shoots to encourage fruiting spurs.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Ison is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine that does not require a pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis or pergola; the vigorous vines can spread 20–30 feet. In zone 9 Ison ripens in late August–September. Prune heavily in late winter to encourage productive new growth.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ison is one of the most widely planted muscadine varieties in the Southeast, selected by Ison's Nursery in Georgia for its combination of very large, sweet, black-bronze-skinned fruits and self-fertility — the perfect-flowered habit means a single Ison vine sets full crops without requiring a separate pollinator vine. The large, round to slightly oval fruits ripen to deep bronze-black with a rich, sweet, complex muscadine flavor and relatively low tannin compared to older varieties. Ison is used for fresh eating, juice, wine, and muscadine jelly, where the large fruit size and good juice content are advantageous. The vine is vigorous and productive once established, with crops of 30–60 pounds per mature vine in good growing conditions. Unlike some muscadine varieties that have a thick, tough skin, Ison's skin is more tender and the slip-skin characteristic less pronounced, making fresh eating more pleasant.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Issai is the only commonly available self-fertile Actinidia arguta cultivar, producing fruit without a separate male vine — an important practical advantage for gardeners with space for only one vine. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola; Issai is less vigorous than most hardy kiwi vines but still requires substantial support. In zone 9 it ripens in September–October.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Issai is a Japanese-selected cultivar of hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) notable for being reliably self-fertile — unlike the species, which requires separate male and female vines for fruit production, Issai is a self-pollinating selection that sets fruit as a single plant. The small, smooth-skinned, grape-sized kiwiberry fruits ripen in September–October to a dark green with a delicate strawberry-kiwi flavor — eaten whole without peeling, unlike fuzzy kiwis (Actinidia deliciosa) that require peeling. Hardy kiwi fruits are considerably smaller than supermarket fuzzy kiwis but have a thin, edible skin and a sweet, complex, tropical flavor. Issai is less vigorous than most Actinidia arguta plants — a compact 15–20 foot climber rather than the 40+ foot sprawl of standard hardy kiwi — making it more manageable in garden settings. In zone 9 the vines experience mild winters and may have reduced dormancy; provide some shading in the hottest zones.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; James is one of the oldest named muscadine selections still in commerce, a large-fruited bronze cultivar that needs a pollinator variety nearby since it produces only female flowers.
