Build a strong arbor or high-wire trellis to support vigorous vines.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis, and plant a self-fertile muscadine variety nearby for pollination, since James produces only female flowers. James is one of the oldest named muscadine selections still widely grown, a historic bronze cultivar prized for very large, sweet berries with the classic musky muscadine flavor, harvested for generations across the Deep South for fresh eating, jelly, and wine. Its long track record in Southern gardens speaks to its reliability and adaptability across a range of soils and conditions. Like other muscadines it resists Pierce's disease and the major fungal diseases of the humid South without a spray program. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Japanese Mahonia is the parent species behind the popular x media hybrids, valued for pendant, lemon-scented winter flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Japanese Mahonia bears bold, holly-like, pinnately compound evergreen foliage and, in late fall through winter, pendant racemes of small, lemon-scented yellow flowers that are among the earliest nectar sources for winter-active pollinators, followed by tart, dusty-blue-black berries that can be used for jelly. Its architectural foliage and off-season bloom give it strong winter garden value when little else is flowering. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes, since it needs little routine shaping.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container canes in spring on a trellis in well-drained soil; note that Japanese wineberry is invasive in parts of the eastern U.S. — check local regulations before planting.
directions: Japanese wineberry is an Asian Rubus species with distinctive red glandular-hairy canes that are ornamentally attractive year-round. It fruits on floricanes in mid-to-late summer, bearing translucent orange-red to deep ruby berries enclosed in a sticky calyx that opens at ripeness — a feature that helps distinguish ripe from unripe fruit and reduces bird predation. Cut all fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and thin primocanes to 4–6 per hill for next year's crop. The species naturalizes aggressively in disturbed areas in the eastern U.S. and is considered invasive in several states; confirm legality before planting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; Jeanne is self-fertile and its strong powdery mildew resistance makes it a low-maintenance choice for home plantings.
directions: Jeanne is a modern American-European hybrid gooseberry released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service, bred for high resistance to powdery mildew and other fungal diseases that commonly trouble older gooseberry cultivars. It produces medium-sized, deep maroon-red fruit with a full, sweet flavor considered an improvement over many traditional cultivars, ripening later in the season than most. The compact 2-3 foot bush bears reliably without a pollinator and is especially well suited to the Pacific Northwest and other cool, temperate climates.

plant_note: Plant after last frost in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; unlike Hayward, Jenny is self-fertile and does not require a separate male pollinizer vine.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training the vigorous vine onto a sturdy trellis or arbor system able to support its weight for decades. Jenny is a self-fertile fuzzy kiwifruit selection, a genuine practical advantage over the classic Hayward variety, which requires a separate non-fruiting male vine purely for pollination — Jenny produces a crop from a single plant, making it a far more space-efficient choice for smaller home gardens that can't accommodate two full-sized kiwi vines. Fruit is somewhat smaller than Hayward and yields are generally lighter without a dedicated pollinizer nearby, but a nearby male vine (of Jenny or another compatible variety) will still improve fruit set and size if space allows. Prune annually in the dormant season to control the vine's naturally vigorous, sprawling growth and keep fruiting wood productive.

common_name: Jersey Blueberry (Classic Northern Highbush Blueberry, New Jersey Standard Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.2), well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Jersey requires cross-pollination — plant with a compatible highbush variety such as Bluecrop, Duke, or Blueray for reliable fruit set and heavier yields; Jersey is a late-season highbush variety ripening in August in most of the Northeast, extending the fresh blueberry season after early and mid-season varieties have finished.
directions: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat moss or pine bark; maintain soil pH at 4.5–5.2 for healthy growth and production; mulch heavily with pine bark or acid wood chips; fertilize with ammonium sulfate in early spring; Jersey ripens in August (late season) producing large, firm, light blue berries with a mild, sweet flavor and excellent storage quality. Jersey blueberry is one of the oldest and most historically important highbush blueberry varieties in American commercial and home garden production — developed by Frederick Coville at the USDA Beltsville Agricultural Research Center in 1928 from deliberate crosses with wild Vaccinium corymbosum selections from the Atlantic coastal plain. Jersey was one of the first named highbush blueberry varieties released and became the cornerstone of the New Jersey commercial blueberry industry (the first commercial blueberry industry in the United States), for which it was specifically developed. For several decades, Jersey was essentially THE commercial highbush blueberry of the American East Coast, dominating production in New Jersey, Michigan, and the other blueberry-producing states before the development of newer varieties with earlier ripening or larger fruit. Despite its age (nearly 100 years of commercial production), Jersey remains popular for several reasons: its late-season ripening (August) extends the fresh blueberry window after most other varieties have finished, its very large, firm, light blue berries store and ship exceptionally well (better than softer-berried varieties), and its mild, sweet flavor is reliable and consistent. Jersey is considered somewhat milder in flavor than Bluecrop or Elliott but produces reliably in a wide range of conditions.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Jewel black raspberry is more heat-tolerant than red raspberry but still struggles in the hottest zone 9 summers. It is best suited to zone 9a or the cooler parts of zone 9b. The floricane crop ripens May–June in zone 9, ahead of peak summer heat, making June the primary harvest window.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Jewel is a Cornell University-released black raspberry (Rubus occidentalis) — an entirely distinct species from red raspberries with a different flavor, deeper color, and more intense aromatic character. Black raspberries produce jet-black, hollow drupes with an intensely rich, complex, wine-like flavor that differs dramatically from the lighter, brighter flavor of red raspberries — the dark color indicates very high anthocyanin content, among the highest of any commonly grown berry. Black raspberry flavor is described as a deep, earthy, complex fruitiness with more tannin and less overt sweetness than red raspberries, making them outstanding for jams, pies, syrup, black raspberry ice cream (a regional specialty in the Ohio River Valley), and liqueurs. Jewel is the leading commercial black raspberry variety, selected for large, firm fruits and good resistance to anthracnose disease. In zone 9 the June ripening precedes peak summer heat, making black raspberry production more feasible than red raspberry in warm climates.

common_name: Jewel Strawberry (Mid-Season June-Bearer, Premier New York Strawberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring as soon as soil is workable; Jewel is a Cornell University-developed mid-season June-bearing strawberry that has become the dominant commercial strawberry in New York State and is widely grown throughout the Northeast for its exceptional large-fruited, highly flavorful berries and outstanding performance in humid northeastern growing conditions.
directions: Plant in early spring; Jewel is a high-yielding, large-fruited mid-season June-bearer that peaks about 5–7 days after Earliglow; berries have excellent fresh flavor and store and process better than many June-bearers; remove flowers the first year; the plants are vigorous and winter-hardy in zones 3–7 with straw mulch. Jewel strawberry is a Cornell University-developed variety (released 1985) that became the dominant commercial and farm-stand strawberry in New York State and one of the most important strawberries in the northeastern United States. Cornell's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva bred Jewel specifically for northeastern growing conditions — the humid, cool summers and reliable winter cold of New York — and the variety's success reflects that targeted development: it performs exceptionally in zones 4–7 humid northeastern conditions where some varieties from drier or warmer climates show reduced vigor or disease problems. The berries are large to very large, consistently well-shaped, dark red throughout with outstanding fresh flavor — considered by many northeastern tasters to combine the best attributes of Earliglow flavor with Allstar size. Jewel is noted for holding flavor and firmness well across a range of weather conditions, producing consistently good berries even in the hot, humid spells that sometimes degrade the quality of other varieties during ripening. It is vigorous enough to be productive for 3–4 years in a well-managed bed, somewhat longer than many modern varieties. The standard strawberry at many northeastern U-pick farms and roadside stands.

common_name: Joan J Raspberry (Thornless Primocane Everbearing Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Joan J fruits on primocanes (first-year canes), so it can be mown to the ground each winter for simplified maintenance.
directions: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring, and mow or cut all canes to the ground each winter for the simplest maintenance approach, since Joan J bears fruit on the current year's primocanes rather than needing overwintered floricanes. This thornless, everbearing raspberry produces a large early-summer crop plus a second flush in fall, with smooth, spine-free canes that make picking and pruning far more pleasant than thorny raspberry cultivars. It is notably vigorous and disease-resistant, producing large, firm, richly flavored berries over an extended harvest window. Support canes with a simple two-wire trellis if grown for the full season rather than mown annually, and harvest when berries pull cleanly from the plug with no resistance.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; pair Jogranda with Jostine or another jostaberry cultivar for best cross-pollination and fruit set.
directions: Jogranda was released in 1985 by German breeder Rudolph Bauer as a follow-up to the original Josta jostaberry, selected for violet-black berries that run noticeably larger than Josta's and ripen two to three weeks later, which stretches the jostaberry picking season into midsummer. The spreading, slightly drooping canes benefit from light staking or a simple wire support as the heavy fruit clusters develop, and the thornless growth habit keeps harvest and pruning far less prickly than picking true gooseberries. Flavor is tangy and full-bodied, closer to black currant than gooseberry, and the fruit holds up well for jam, syrup, and home winemaking. Jogranda crops most heavily when planted with Jostine or another jostaberry for cross-pollination, and like other jostaberries it tolerates Gulf Coast heat better than straight black currants provided it gets consistent moisture and some afternoon shade.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. John produces heavier crops when cross-pollinated with Adams or another elderberry variety. In zone 9 it flowers in May–June and produces ripe berries in July–August. John is a vigorous spreader by root suckers in moist soils; mow around the planting to control spread.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained to periodically wet soil; John is a named American elderberry cultivar selected at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva as part of the New York State elderberry improvement program — the same program that produced the widely-grown Adams cultivar. John was selected as a pollinator companion for Adams, producing profuse flowers slightly earlier than Adams to ensure cross-pollination during the Adams flowering period. The vigorous, upright shrub produces large, flattened flower corymbs (elderflower clusters) with abundant small white flowers in early summer, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer. John is particularly valued in mixed elderberry plantings where it improves Adams yields through cross-pollination; the two varieties are the most common pairing in eastern American elderberry plantings. In zone 9 both elderberry flowers and berries are produced abundantly in favorable moist conditions.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container bushes in fall or late winter in cool, moisture-retentive soil; this early-season Dutch cultivar benefits from a site sheltered from late spring frost during bloom.
directions: Jonkheer van Tets is a classic early-ripening red currant valued for its long, uniform strigs of bright red, tart-sweet berries that ripen ahead of most other red currant cultivars, extending the harvest window when grown alongside later types like Rovada or Red Lake. It sets fruit heavily and reliably, but the early bloom period makes it vulnerable to late spring frosts, so a site with some air drainage or light overhead protection during flowering helps secure the crop. Grow in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, and prune out the oldest third of the wood each dormant season on an open, vase-shaped framework to maintain fruiting vigor. It performs best in regions with cool summers and struggles in hot, humid climates.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 8 plant January–March. Josephine is a fall-bearing (primocane) raspberry that in zone 8 begins ripening its fall primocane crop in late August–September. For a single large fall crop, mow all canes to the ground in late winter; for two crops per season, leave floricanes for an early summer crop followed by the fall primocane harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Josephine is a Cornell University fall-bearing (primocane) raspberry selected for exceptional fruit quality — widely considered to have the finest flavor of any fall-bearing raspberry released by the Cornell small fruit breeding program, with very large, conical, bright red berries and a sweet, complex, intensely raspberry-flavored aroma and taste that rivals the best summer-bearing varieties. The primocane-fruiting habit provides a late-season crop in August–October from first-year canes, avoiding the May–June crowded harvest season when many other soft fruits are also ripe. The berries are soft and best for fresh eating or immediate processing — Josephine is not a commercial shipping variety, but for home garden fresh eating it represents the highest quality among fall-bearing raspberries. The vigorous, productive canes grow 4–6 feet tall and the plants are reliably productive once established, returning annually from the root system.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; Josta is self-fertile and its thornless canes make it easier to manage than either gooseberry parent.
directions: Josta is the original jostaberry, released in 1977 by German breeder Rudolph Bauer after crossing black currant and gooseberry lines and doubling the chromosome count to stabilize a fertile hybrid; its name blends the German words for black currant (Johannisbeere) and gooseberry (Stachelbeere). Vigorous, thornless canes carry glossy, purple-black berries larger than a black currant but smaller than a gooseberry, with a mild, sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating, jam, and juice, and the plant shows strong natural resistance to the powdery mildew and leaf-spot diseases that trouble many gooseberries. Josta is more heat-tolerant than most true black currants, though it still fruits best with reliably moist soil and some afternoon shade in hot Gulf Coast summers. Prune out the oldest third of canes each dormant season to keep the naturally spreading, arching bush productive and open to light and air.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container stock in fall or late winter in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; jostaberry needs cool winters and struggles in the Deep South's mild, humid climate, performing best in the upper South and cooler regions.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and mulch to keep roots cool, since this hybrid inherits its cool-climate preference from both currant and gooseberry parents. Jostaberry is a thornless hybrid bred in Germany from a cross of blackcurrant and gooseberry, combining the vigor and disease resistance of both parents into a productive, easy-care shrub that bears large, smooth, dark purple-black berries with a flavor described as a cross between the two — richer and less tart than gooseberry, milder and less musky than blackcurrant. The thornless canes make picking far easier than with true gooseberries, and the shrub is notably resistant to the powdery mildew and rust diseases that trouble many currants and gooseberries. It performs best in regions with cold winters and mild summers, generally struggling with the heat, humidity, and mild winters of the Deep South, so it suits cooler parts of the transition zone and the upper South far better than true Gulf Coast gardens. Prune out the oldest third of canes each winter to encourage strong new fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; pair with Jogranda for best cross-pollination, and its thornless canes make maintenance easier than gooseberry parents.
directions: Jostine is a thornless, disease-resistant jostaberry cultivar prized for its compact growth habit, making it well suited to small gardens or container culture. It produces medium-to-large, deep violet berries with a complex, tart-forward flavor that ripens slightly later than the original Josta cultivar, extending the harvest into midsummer. Fruit holds well on the bush after ripening, giving growers a longer picking window for fresh eating, jams, and pies.

plant_note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Jubilee was bred in North Carolina and ripens early to midseason, producing large, firm, sweet, light-blue berries on a vigorous, productive bush well suited to warmer Southern growing conditions where lower-chill varieties are needed. The good heat tolerance for a highbush type makes it a solid choice for extending highbush blueberry production into milder climates than many Northern-bred varieties can handle. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune out the oldest canes each winter to maintain vigor, and plant alongside a second highbush variety to improve pollination and yield.

common_name: Keecrisp Blueberry (Crisp-Textured Mid-Late University of Florida Southern Highbush)
plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Keecrisp, a University of Florida cross of Sweetcrisp and Indigocrisp, ripens mid-to-late season and needs somewhat more winter chill than the earliest UF releases, best suited to the cooler edge of zone 8-9.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Keecrisp, a University of Florida cross between the earlier Sweetcrisp and Indigocrisp releases, inherits the notably crisp, firm texture that distinguishes the Crisp lineage from the softer flesh typical of most blueberries, giving the fruit excellent fresh-eating snap and good holding quality on the bush. It ripens mid-to-late season and carries a somewhat higher chill requirement than the earliest, lowest-chill UF releases, performing best in the cooler pockets of zone 8b-9a rather than the very mildest coastal winters. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Ken's Red is a female cultivar and requires a male hardy kiwi vine within pollinating range for fruit set. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola, since mature vines are vigorous and heavy once fruiting.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor. Ken's Red is a female hardy kiwi cultivar originating in New Zealand, distinguished from most other Actinidia arguta selections by its attractive reddish-purple fruit skin and red-blushed flesh near the skin, in addition to the sweet, tangy flavor typical of hardy kiwi. The smooth skin means the small, grape-sized fruit can be eaten whole without peeling, and its distinctive red coloring makes it a visually striking choice for a home fruit planting or farmers-market crop. Like all Actinidia arguta, it is dioecious and needs a separate male vine nearby to ensure good pollination and a full fruit set. A flavorful, ornamental option for gardeners who want something visually distinct from standard green-fleshed hardy kiwi, zone 4–8.

common_name: Kent Elderberry (Early-Ripening Nova Scotia American Elderberry Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in late winter to early spring (February-April in zone 9) in moist, fertile soil; pair with Adams, York, or another cultivar for cross-pollination and heavier fruit set.
directions: Kent was selected at the Kentville Research Station in Nova Scotia from Adams-derived American elderberry stock and is best known for ripening its clusters 10-14 days ahead of Adams or York, giving growers an earlier start to the harvest window. Flat-topped cymes of small white flowers appear in late spring, followed by dense, drooping clusters of small, very sweet black berries that hold their flavor well whether used fresh-cooked, dried, or pressed into juice and syrup. In Gulf Coast heat, site Kent where afternoon shade or consistent soil moisture is available, since it was bred for a cooler maritime climate and benefits from extra irrigation during peak summer; plant it alongside a second American elderberry cultivar to ensure good pollination. Manage root suckers each season to keep the planting contained, and prune out the oldest canes in late winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: Kestrel Blueberry (Very Early Low-Chill University of Florida Southern Highbush)
plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Kestrel is a University of Florida southern highbush release ripening very early, in April, bred for the low winter chill of the Deep South.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Kestrel is a southern highbush blueberry bred at the University of Florida specifically for the low winter chill of north and central Florida and the Gulf Coast, ripening its fruit very early, typically by April, well ahead of most other blueberry types, allowing home growers to harvest before the summer heat sets in and before many pest and disease pressures build. As a southern highbush type, it needs consistently moist, well-drained, highly acidic soil rather than the more forgiving conditions rabbiteye types tolerate. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old, unproductive wood each winter to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; Killarney was bred for extreme cold hardiness and needs no special winter protection in most northern gardens.
directions: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing rows to allow good air movement through the thicket. Killarney was released by the University of Manitoba specifically for prairie and northern climates and remains one of the most cold-hardy red raspberry cultivars available, reliably surviving winters that would damage many modern varieties. It bears a single summer crop of medium-sized, bright red, firmly textured berries with classic sweet-tart raspberry flavor on floricanes, so spent canes should be cut to the ground after harvest. Its toughness makes it a dependable choice for short-season gardens where more tender cultivars struggle.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter through early spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Kiowa is thorned, so wear heavy gloves during planting and all subsequent pruning. Space 4 feet apart in rows.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; Kiowa is a thorned, erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 1996 as part of the same breeding program that produced Natchez and Ouachita. It is distinguished principally by its extraordinary berry size — among the largest of any blackberry variety, often exceeding 10–14 grams per fruit — and its exceptionally long harvest season that can extend 6–8 weeks through June and July in zone 8–9. Flavor is sweet and complex. The upright, thorned canes are self-supporting and vigorous, producing heavily. Kiowa shows good adaptability to the South and mid-South, performing well in humid, hot climates where some varieties decline. The principal trade-off is the thorns — unavoidable when harvesting and pruning — but many growers consider this worthwhile for the combination of size, yield, and long season. Prune fruited floricanes to ground level after the last berries are harvested; tip primocanes at 36–42 inches in summer to promote lateral branching.

plant_note: Plant after last frost with a very sturdy pergola or trellis; self-fertile cultivars such as 'Issai' are suitable for single-plant planting.
directions: Kiwiberry is a compact-fruited selection of hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) grown specifically for smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruits that are eaten whole without peeling — they have the same flavor as standard kiwifruit but ripen 3–4 weeks earlier. Self-fertile cultivars such as 'Issai' and 'Ken's Red' allow single-plant production, but yields are higher when a male pollenizer is present. The extremely vigorous vines require a heavy-gauge trellis or pergola capable of bearing hundreds of pounds of vine and fruit; prune hard each dormant season to renewal spurs. Harvest when fruits yield to gentle pressure and taste sweet with no starchiness.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Koralle is self-fertile and, like other lingonberry cultivars, can produce two crops per year — a smaller summer crop and a larger fall crop.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions. Koralle is a classic Dutch-bred lingonberry cultivar, one of the earliest widely distributed named lingonberry selections and still valued for its heavy, reliable fruit production and vigorous, dense, low-growing habit. The glossy evergreen foliage forms an attractive year-round groundcover, topped with clusters of small white to pale pink bell-shaped spring flowers followed by bright red, tart berries used in Scandinavian-style jams, sauces, and preserves. Because lingonberries thrive in acidic soil and tolerate shade better than most fruiting shrubs, Koralle makes an excellent edible groundcover planted beneath blueberries, azaleas, or pines where soil is already acidic. Shear plants back lightly every few years to rejuvenate growth and maintain a dense, productive mat.

plant_note: Grow on a trellis or in a bounded bed in full sun; canes root readily where tips touch soil, so manage spread to keep the planting contained.
directions: Grow on a trellis or in a bounded bed in full sun, and prune out spent floricanes after harvest to keep the stand productive and accessible. Rubus coreanus, known in Korea as bokbunja, is a wild bramble species long harvested and increasingly field-cultivated for its firm, tart berries, most famously fermented into the traditional Korean fruit wine of the same name. The fruit ripens from red to a deep blackish-red, smaller and firmer than typical black raspberries, with a distinctly tart flavor valued in beverages, preserves, and traditional Korean herbal use. Plants form dense, arching, thorny thickets similar to black raspberry and root readily from cane tips that touch the soil, making propagation easy but also requiring management to keep the planting contained.

subcategory: East Asian compact edible mulberry shrub-tree
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after last frost in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 5–9; Korean Mulberry (Morus australis) is a compact, multi-stemmed mulberry native to Korea, Japan, China, and the Himalayas — smaller than White or Red Mulberry — bearing abundant small to medium, very sweet, juicy black-purple mulberries relished by birds and people, and with a long history of use in East Asian traditional medicine.
directions: Plant Morus australis in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment, then reduce as the plant is drought-tolerant once established; prune in winter to shape and control size; harvest berries as they ripen and turn deep purple-black, as they stain readily. Korean Mulberry is the smallest-growing of the commonly cultivated mulberry species — typically maturing as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree 5–15 feet tall — making it better suited to smaller gardens than the more vigorous White Mulberry (Morus alba) or American Red Mulberry (Morus rubra). The abundant small to medium berries are very sweet and richly flavored, ripening over several weeks in early to midsummer; birds are strongly attracted to fruiting trees so netting may be needed for a full harvest. In East Asian traditional medicine systems, the berries (sang shen), leaves (sang ye), bark (sang bai pi), and twigs (sang zhi) are all used in herbal preparations for treating conditions ranging from hypertension and diabetes to tinnitus and gray hair. The leaves are used for silkworm (Bombyx mori) cultivation like other mulberry species. Compact enough for container growing in large pots; prune annually to maintain size and maximize fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns or rooted tip cuttings in early spring along a trellis in full sun.
directions: Train the long, trailing canes onto a wire trellis and thin out spent floricanes after harvest to keep the planting productive and easy to pick. Kotata is a vigorous trailing blackberry developed for the Pacific Northwest that produces large, firm, glossy black berries with a rich, tart-sweet flavor well suited to both fresh eating and processing into jams and baked goods. It ripens in mid-summer with good yields on second-year canes and holds up well to shipping compared to older trailing types. The canes carry thorns, so gloves and careful trellis training make harvest and maintenance easier.

plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Krewer is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for ripening late in the season, extending the fresh blueberry harvest window well past most other Southern cultivars. Plant with Brightwell, Premier, or Climax for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Krewer is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry selected for its notably late ripening window, extending the fresh Southern blueberry harvest into midsummer after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, a valuable trait for home gardeners and market growers wanting to spread out the harvest season. The vigorous, productive bushes bear medium to large berries with good flavor and firmness. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Krewer requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other, choosing early- and mid-season partners to spread bloom timing and further extend the overall harvest. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: La Crescent Grape (Cold-Hardy Aromatic White Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a trellis in full sun with well-drained soil.
directions: La Crescent is a University of Minnesota-bred white wine grape prized for its intensely aromatic fruit, with apricot, citrus, and honeysuckle notes reminiscent of Muscat and Riesling. It shares the extreme cold-hardiness of its Minnesota-bred siblings, tolerating winter lows near -30°F, but ripens its fruit with very high sugar and high acid simultaneously, which winemakers use to produce off-dry or dessert-style wines. The compact clusters are prone to bunch rot in wet years, so growers benefit from leaf pulling around the fruit zone to improve airflow and sun exposure. Vigorous shoot growth means canopy management and cluster thinning are needed to avoid overcropping thin canes.

common_name: Lake Emerald Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Florida Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil, spacing vines a bit wider than most bunch grapes to accommodate its vigor; Lake Emerald is a light-green, Pierce's disease-resistant Florida bunch grape developed by the University of Florida for wine and juice production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing extra space between vines since Lake Emerald is a vigorous grower recommended for wider row spacing than most other Florida bunch grapes. Developed by the University of Florida's bunch grape breeding program at Leesburg, it is prized for strong resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by leafhoppers that has historically limited grape growing across the humid Gulf South, and it does not require grafting onto a resistant rootstock except in soils with a naturally high pH. It produces light green, juicy berries used mainly for wine and juice or jelly rather than fresh eating, ripening in midsummer just after the purple 'Blue Lake' cultivar. As with other Florida bunch grapes, a preventive fungicide spray program through the growing season is important to control the fungal fruit rots that thrive in hot, humid weather, and vines should be pruned hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons.

common_name: Lane Muscadine Grape (Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)
plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Lane is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) black muscadine released by the University of Georgia and does not require a separate pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis and prune heavily each winter.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Lane is a modern University of Georgia muscadine release valued for its very large, glossy black berries with a thinner, more tender skin than many older black muscadines, along with sweet, richly flavored flesh well suited to fresh eating. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, ripening in the mid-to-late season, and its improved skin quality and berry size have made it a popular choice for both home gardens and u-pick plantings across the Gulf South. Keep vines well watered during fruit development for the best berry size, and thin overcrowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid weather.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Late Fry is self-fertile and, true to its name, ripens near the very end of the muscadine season, extending harvest well past earlier black varieties like Cowart.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Late Fry is a University of Arkansas release bred as a black-fruited counterpart to the popular bronze variety Fry, producing very large, glossy black berries with the same thin skin and high sugar content that made Fry a favorite for fresh eating. It is self-fertile and ripens late in the season, filling out the tail end of the muscadine harvest after earlier black varieties are finished. Vigor and disease resistance are good across the humid Gulf South. Because it is one of the last muscadines to ripen, protect ripening clusters from birds and other wildlife, which concentrate on the few varieties still fruiting late in the season.

common_name: Latham Raspberry (Classic Cold-Hardy Heirloom Red Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Latham needs a substantial winter chill and performs best in cold-winter regions rather than the Gulf South.
directions: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and support rows with a simple two-wire trellis. Released by the University of Minnesota in the 1920s, Latham became one of the most widely planted red raspberries in the northern United States for decades because of its exceptional winter hardiness and reliable, heavy midsummer crop of firm, bright red berries with classic tart-sweet raspberry flavor. It is a floricane-fruiting type, bearing on second-year canes, so remove spent canes to the ground right after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest 4-6 per foot of row. Modern cultivars have surpassed it in disease resistance, but Latham remains valued in cold climates for its toughness and long track record.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Laurel-Leaved Currant is an unusual evergreen currant bearing pendulous, sweetly fragrant greenish-cream flowers in late winter, followed by small edible fruit on pollinated female plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to mostly shade or high overhead shade, and shelter from harsh winter wind. Laurel-Leaved Currant is unusual among currants for being evergreen, holding leathery, glossy, laurel-like leaves year-round, and for flowering in the depths of winter, producing hanging clusters of small, sweetly fragrant, greenish-cream flowers from January into March that are a valuable early nectar source for the first bees of the season. Plants are dioecious, so both a male and a female are needed for the female to set its small, edible red-to-black currants, which ripen in early summer and can be used like other currants once fully colored. It is an easy, low-maintenance shrub for the shaded winter garden, valued as much for its fragrance and evergreen structure as for its fruit. Prune only lightly, right after flowering, to remove damaged wood and maintain shape.

common_name: Leatherleaf Mahonia (Chinese Mahonia, Leatherleaf Oregon Grape)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall in well-drained, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; leatherleaf mahonia is one of the toughest shade shrubs and tolerates dry shade under trees once established. The spiny leaflets make handling difficult — wear gloves.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; leatherleaf mahonia is a bold architectural evergreen shrub with some of the most striking foliage in the shade garden — stiff, upright canes bearing enormous compound leaves (18–24 inches) of dark, holly-like leaflets with viciously spiny edges that create a dramatic tropical effect in the deepest shade. Fragrant yellow flowers appear in winter in drooping grape-like clusters, followed by powdery blue-purple berries in spring that are edible (tart, used for jelly and wine). It is one of the few large shrubs that truly thrives in deep, dry shade — an outstanding barrier plant and shade specimen. NOTE: Mahonia bealei is listed as invasive in several southeastern states including Texas and Georgia — check local invasive species lists before planting; the native alternative Mahonia trifoliolata (agarita) is an excellent substitute in Texas.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or sulfur; Legacy requires roughly 400–500 chill hours, moderate for a highbush type, and benefits from a second highbush or southern highbush cultivar nearby for the best fruit set.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.5 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch well to maintain the moist, acidic soil conditions blueberries require. Legacy is a USDA release bred from a cross between northern highbush and southern highbush parentage, giving it unusually broad climate adaptability — it performs well from the upper South through much of the Gulf region, bridging the gap between cultivars suited only to cold winters and those needing very low chill. The semi-evergreen bush produces heavy crops of firm, sweet, richly flavored medium-sized berries over a fairly long mid-to-late season, and its vigorous, upright growth habit makes it easy to manage and harvest. Its adaptability and reliable production have made it one of the more versatile blueberry cultivars for gardeners uncertain whether a northern or southern highbush type suits their exact climate. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with productive new wood.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; Leikora is a female fruiting cultivar requiring a male pollinator such as 'Pollmix' or 'Hergo-M' within 50–100 feet for fruit set. One male plant can pollinate 6–8 female plants. Sea buckthorn tolerates poor, sandy, gravelly soils — it is one of the most nutrient-poor-soil-tolerant fruiting shrubs due to its nitrogen-fixing root nodules. Avoid planting in wet or clay soils.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-fertile soil — sandy, rocky, and coastal soils are ideal; Leikora is a German-selected female sea buckthorn cultivar bred for commercial berry production, selected at the Bundesanstalt für Züchtungsforschung as one of the heaviest-bearing named female cultivars with large, bright orange-yellow berries that ripen in August–September in dense clusters along the stems. Sea buckthorn berries contain extraordinary concentrations of vitamin C (up to 15 times that of oranges), vitamin E, carotenoids, and omega-7 fatty acids — the nutritional profile has driven substantial commercial interest in sea buckthorn juice, oil capsules, and skincare products. The tart, acidic, tropical-citrus flavor of the fresh berries makes them challenging to eat raw but outstanding processed into juice (often blended with apple or honey to moderate acidity), jam, wine, and dietary supplements. Leikora is a thorny, nitrogen-fixing, drought-tolerant shrub adapted to harsh, exposed sites where few other fruiting plants survive.

common_name: Lemony Lace Elderberry (Golden Cutleaf Ornamental Elderberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; give Lemony Lace some afternoon shade in hot climates, where its bright gold foliage is prone to scorch in full, reflected summer sun.
directions: Lemony Lace is a compact, rounded ornamental elderberry selected for finely dissected, lacy, bright chartreuse-gold foliage held on contrasting near-black stems, a dramatic color and texture combination for a mixed border or foundation planting. Flat clusters of pinkish-white flowers appear in late spring, followed by small red berries that, like other red elderberries, are mildly toxic raw and should be cooked before any culinary use, or simply left for birds. It stays noticeably smaller and denser than wild red elderberry, needs only light shaping after bloom, and performs best where summers are not extremely hot and humid, since foliage color and vigor decline in the most intense Deep South heat.

plant_note: Plant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into fertile, well-manured soil; prune to an open framework since heavily laden branches tend to arch under the crop's weight.
directions: Plant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into fertile, well-manured soil, since Leveller needs steady moisture to size its fruit. This Victorian-era English dessert gooseberry, first raised in the 1850s, is still grown for its very large, pale yellow-green, thin-skinned berries with an exceptionally rich, sweet flavor once fully ripe. It is a vigorous, somewhat spreading bush that is more prone to American gooseberry mildew than modern disease-resistant releases, so good airflow matters in humid climates. Best reserved for dedicated fruit growers in cool-summer regions willing to manage its mildew susceptibility for the sake of exceptional flavor.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early to midsummer, or plant rooted container stock in spring; site at forest margins or on structures with dappled light, as this species naturally inhabits the woodland edge rather than open, exposed positions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, loamy to rocky soil in part shade to full sun along a trellis, fence, or forest edge; Limber Honeysuckle is a native twining vine found across northern and central North America from Quebec to British Columbia and south into the Ozarks and Appalachians, scrambling up shrubs and small trees along forest margins where it is an important nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds during their spring and early-summer residency. The flowers range from orange-yellow to red and appear in May–June in clustered whorls at the stem tips, followed by translucent red to orange berries in late summer that are eaten by thrushes, vireos, and other woodland songbirds. Like Lonicera prolifera, it has perfoliate leaves near the stem tips where the uppermost pair of leaves fuse into a disk, though in this species the leaves beneath the flower clusters are typically distinctly bluish-green. It is non-invasive and well-behaved in the garden, rarely exceeding 15 feet, making it one of the best native vine choices for small to medium trellises in northern gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted plugs or divisions in early spring in acidic, well-drained soil; also useful as a groundcover under acid-loving shrubs.
directions: Lingonberries require acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) and perform well as an ornamental groundcover in zones 2–7. They produce two crops per year — a smaller crop in midsummer and a larger one in fall. Minimal pruning is needed; shear plants to 3–4 in every few years to rejuvenate. Harvest when berries are deep red and slightly tart; they store well refrigerated and are traditionally used in Scandinavian preserves and sauces.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sandy to rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; locustberry is frost-tender and native to the pine rockland and coastal habitats of extreme South Florida and the Keys.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sandy to rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; locustberry is frost-tender and native to the pine rockland and coastal habitats of extreme South Florida and the Keys. Small, glossy, leathery leaves and delicate clusters of small flowers that open pink and fade to yellow give this native shrub extended seasonal interest, followed by small red berries that ripen to nearly black and are eaten by birds, while the foliage serves as a larval host plant for several native butterfly species. Highly tolerant of poor, rocky limestone soil, salt exposure, and drought once established, it is a valuable, low-maintenance shrub for a South Florida native landscape, coastal planting, or pollinator garden, requiring essentially no irrigation or fertilizer beyond its first year. Prune lightly to shape if a more formal habit is wanted, though it naturally maintains an attractive, open form without regular pruning.

plant_note: Plant rooted tip cuttings in early spring after last frost; provide a sturdy T-trellis at planting since canes reach 8–10 ft.
directions: Loganberry, a natural hybrid of blackberry and raspberry discovered in California in the 1880s, produces long, dark red, tart berries that are excellent for jams and wine. Train the vigorous trailing canes on a two- or three-wire trellis, weaving new primocanes along the wires during the growing season. After the summer harvest, cut all floricanes that bore fruit to the ground and secure the new primocanes in their place. The thornless 'LY59' strain is preferred for home gardens; in borderline zones, lay canes down and mulch after leaf drop.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in early spring in very acidic, well-drained soil.
directions: Lowbush blueberries require strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) and spread by underground rhizomes to form colonies. Manage in a two-year cycle: mow or burn half the planting to the ground each year so alternating sections produce a full crop annually. Harvest in midsummer when berries are deep blue-purple and sweet. Drought-tolerant once established, but irrigation during fruit fill improves berry size.

plant_note: Plant rooted tip-layered cuttings or crowns in late winter to early spring on a low two-wire trellis; Lucretia ripens several weeks ahead of upright blackberries, extending the bramble harvest into late spring before summer heat sets in.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy loam and train the sprawling, thorny canes onto a low trellis or wire to keep the large fruit off the ground. Lucretia is one of the oldest named dewberry cultivars still grown in the South, prized in Texas and the Gulf region in the early twentieth century for producing unusually large, glossy, sweet-tart fruit far earlier in the season than blackberries. Because dewberries flower and ripen so early, protect blossoms from late cold snaps and expect a short, intense harvest window rather than the extended cropping of modern blackberry cultivars. Cut spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to keep the sprawling planting from becoming an unmanageable thicket.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in late winter to early spring; in zone 7–9 plant December–February. Magnolia is self-fertile and does not require a separate male pollinator — unlike many muscadine varieties that carry only pistillate (female) flowers, Magnolia has perfect flowers (both male and female). Space vines 10–15 feet apart on a trellis system; the 4-arm Kniffin system is standard for muscadines in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Magnolia is a USDA-developed self-fertile bronze muscadine grape, bearing medium to large bronze-to-copper-colored fruits with a mild, sweet flavor and thin, tender skin — one of the more elegant-tasting muscadine varieties for fresh eating, without the strongly musky, foxy character of older selections. The perfect-flowered Magnolia vine can pollinate female-only varieties like Carlos and Fry planted nearby, making it doubly useful as a multi-variety vineyard anchor. Fruits ripen in late August to September in most zone 8–9 plantings, later than some early-season varieties. The vines are vigorous and productive, typically yielding 15–20 pounds per vine at maturity. Train on a 4-wire trellis system, prune back to 2–3 buds per spur in late winter, and fertilize lightly in early spring.

plant_note: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; maqui is dioecious — plant both male and female shrubs for fruit production, or purchase self-fertile cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; maqui berry is a Chilean native shrub prized for its small, intensely purple-black berries with the highest reported anthocyanin content of any known berry — significantly higher than acai, blueberries, or pomegranates, giving it extraordinary antioxidant properties. The berries have a pleasant sweet-tart flavor with herbal overtones; they are eaten fresh, made into juice, jams, and wine, and used extensively in Mapuche traditional medicine. It grows naturally in the coastal and Andean ranges of Chile and Argentina, tolerating mild frost, and adapts to a Mediterranean climate with dry summers. An emerging superfood crop with increasing commercial cultivation in Chile.

common_name: Mara des Bois Strawberry (French Day-Neutral Wild-Flavored Hybrid)
plant_note: Set dormant crowns in early spring with the crown at soil level, and pinch off blossoms for the first several weeks after planting to help day-neutral plants establish before they begin their extended fruiting cycle.
directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring in loose, well-drained soil, and remove flowers for the first few weeks to allow the compact, day-neutral plants to establish a strong root system before continuous fruiting begins through summer and into fall. Mara des Bois was developed in France in the early 1990s by combining garden strawberry lines with genetics from the wild alpine strawberry, giving it a fruity, perfumed aroma reminiscent of wild strawberries that sets it apart from typical supermarket varieties. The berries are small to medium, soft, and highly aromatic rather than large and firm, which makes them a favorite of chefs and farmers-market growers but less suited to long-distance shipping. Because it is day-neutral, Mara des Bois produces a steady trickle of fruit from late spring through fall frost rather than one concentrated June crop.

plant_note: Plant in early spring once soil is workable; elderberries fruit best with a second variety nearby for pollination.
directions: Marge is a prolific European elderberry prized for heavy yields of dark berries used in syrups, jams, and wine. Plant in full sun in moist, fertile soil and keep it well watered, as elderberries are shallow-rooted and thirsty. Fruit set improves dramatically with a second, different elderberry variety planted nearby for cross-pollination. Prune out the oldest canes each late winter to keep the plant vigorous and productive. Always cook the berries before eating, since raw fruit and other plant parts can cause stomach upset.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or tip-rooted canes in early spring as soon as soil is workable, with a T-trellis capable of handling 8-ft canes installed at the same time.
directions: Marionberry is a trailing blackberry hybrid (Chehalem x Olallie) developed by Oregon State University and is the most widely grown blackberry in the Pacific Northwest, prized for its deep, complex, slightly tart flavor. The thorny, vigorous canes must be trained along a two-wire trellis; weave new primocanes along the lower wire during the summer and tie them to the upper wire the following spring. After the mid-summer harvest, remove all fruited floricanes at the base and train the new primocanes into their place. Marionberries are sensitive to freezes below about 10°F; in colder areas, protect canes over winter.

common_name: Marquette Grape (Extreme Cold-Hardy Red Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun once soil is workable.
directions: Marquette is a University of Minnesota-bred red wine grape descended in part from Pinot Noir, valued for surviving winter lows near -30°F with only minor cane damage. Vines are vigorous and require an early, thorough trellis training program along with cluster thinning to manage heavy fruit set. The grapes produce a deeply colored, medium-bodied red wine with notes of black cherry, black pepper, and spice, and the variety shows good resistance to downy mildew though it can be prone to black rot in humid seasons. Site vines with good air circulation and avoid low frost pockets to protect the early-breaking buds from late spring freezes.

common_name: Mars Seedless Grape (Cold-Hardy Disease-Resistant Blue Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring in well-drained soil; Mars is self-fertile, compact, and well suited to a small arbor, patio trellis, or single-wire fence rather than a full commercial vineyard trellis.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Bred at the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in the 1970s, Mars combines good disease resistance with genuinely seedless, blue-black berries and a sweet, fruity, slip-skin flavor reminiscent of Concord but milder. Its compact vine habit and strong resistance to common grape diseases make it far easier to grow without a heavy spray program than European wine grapes, especially in humid climates. Prune hard each winter to a few renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation.

plant_note: Set out dormant nursery stock in early spring in full sun, spacing plants for eventual clump width.
directions: Martin produces some of the largest berries among the older Alberta-origin saskatoon selections, with a vigorous upright growth habit that suits both hedgerow and orchard-row plantings. Fruit clusters ripen fairly uniformly, making a single hand-harvest practical for home growers. Established plants sucker readily, so allow room for the clump to widen over time.

common_name: Matua Kiwi (Male Pollinizer for Fuzzy Kiwifruit)
plant_note: Plant after last frost in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis; a male-only vine grown purely to pollinate nearby female fuzzy kiwi vines such as Hayward and does not itself produce fruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, training the vine onto a sturdy trellis positioned to pollinate nearby female fuzzy kiwi vines. Matua is a New Zealand-bred male fuzzy kiwi selection grown exclusively to provide pollen for female vines like Hayward, which cannot set fruit without a compatible male nearby, since kiwifruit plants are dioecious with separate male and female vines. Matua blooms relatively early and vigorously, and one male vine can typically pollinate several female vines when well positioned within the planting, making efficient use of garden space for the non-fruiting pollinizer. Because Matua itself never produces fruit, prune it primarily to encourage abundant flower production and to keep its size manageable relative to the fruiting female vines it supports.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or container canes in spring into rich, well-drained soil at a partially shaded forest edge or under high canopy; this bramble suckers readily, and new canes lifted with roots attached transplant more reliably than seed.
directions: This slender, nearly thornless bramble stays compact and shrubby rather than sprawling, and it holds its foliage through mild winters where hardy, making it useful as a shade-tolerant edge planting under fruit trees or along a woodland path. It flowers and fruits nearly continuously in warm climates, producing small, soft, sweet-tart red raspberries that are eaten fresh, though they are more delicate and less productive per cane than temperate raspberries. Give it half-day shade and evenly moist soil, and thin out older canes each year to keep new fruiting wood coming. It offers gardeners in humid subtropical and tropical shade gardens a genuine raspberry-family fruit where classic raspberries fail from heat stress.

plant_note: Plant after last frost in full sun with a trellis or fence; roots are cold-hardy to zone 6 and re-sprout from the roots each spring.
directions: Maypop (Passiflora incarnata) is a North American native passionflower that is cold-hardy to zone 6, distinguishing it clearly from the tropical Passiflora edulis (passionfruit). The ornamental lavender flowers are stunning and the egg-sized yellow-green fruits have sweet, aromatic pulp similar to tropical passionfruit. Plants die back to the roots in zone 6–7 winters and re-sprout vigorously in late spring — do not remove the crown before new growth appears. Plant cross-pollinators nearby (more than one plant) for reliable fruit set. Harvest when fruits turn yellowish-green and fall or detach easily.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.
directions: McFarlin originated in Massachusetts in the 1870s and became the dominant commercial cranberry cultivar across the Pacific Northwest and Wisconsin bogs for much of the twentieth century before being largely replaced by Stevens. It produces large, firm, dark-red berries with good storage quality and was historically one of the parent cultivars used to breed Stevens. Vines are vigorous and productive but somewhat more susceptible to false blossom disease than newer cultivars, so growers should watch for leafhopper vectors and remove infected plants promptly. It remains of interest to home growers and heirloom collectors for its historical significance and reliable regional performance in cooler bog climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in early spring; McKenzie is self-fertile and tolerates wet or heavy soils better than most fruiting shrubs, making it a good choice for low-lying or clay sites.
directions: McKenzie is a North Dakota-selected black chokeberry valued for its taller, more vigorous growth and heavy annual fruit set compared to more compact aronia cultivars. The glossy black berries ripen in late summer and are extremely high in anthocyanins, making them popular for juice, syrup, and jam production despite their astringent raw flavor. Plant in full sun for the best fruit yield and fall color; the species tolerates poor, wet, or compacted soils that would stress most other fruiting shrubs, and it needs little more than occasional thinning of old canes to stay productive. Its exceptional cold hardiness suits it well to short-season northern climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Meader is a male cultivar grown solely to pollinate female hardy kiwi vines (such as Anna, Geneva, or Ken's Red) — it produces no fruit itself. One male vine can pollinate several female vines within about 30–50 feet.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a sturdy permanent trellis; site centrally within pollinating distance of the female vines it is meant to serve. Meader is a male hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) cultivar selected by Professor Elwyn Meader at the University of New Hampshire, prized specifically for its exceptional cold hardiness — among the most cold-tolerant hardy kiwi selections available, able to survive winter conditions that damage or kill less hardy male cultivars. As a male vine, it produces abundant flowers but no fruit; its sole purpose in the garden is to provide pollen for nearby female cultivars, and because Actinidia arguta is dioecious, at least one male vine is essential wherever female vines are grown for fruit. Its outstanding hardiness makes it the standard pollinator choice for northern hardy kiwi plantings, ensuring the pollinator survives winters that a female cultivar chosen for fruit quality alone might not, zone 3–8.

common_name: Meadowlark Blueberry (Ultra-Early Low-Chill Southern Highbush Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container bushes in winter into acidic, well-drained soil enriched with pine bark fines, and mulch to protect the shallow root system.
directions: Plant dormant bare-root or container bushes in winter into acidic, well-drained soil enriched with pine bark fines, and mulch to protect the shallow root system. Meadowlark is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for only about 200 chill hours, so it reliably leafs, blooms, and ripens even after unusually mild Gulf Coast winters that leave higher-chill cultivars sparse. It is one of the earliest-ripening blueberries available, often ready well ahead of standard rabbiteye types, though it benefits from a second early low-chill cultivar nearby for best pollination. Prune out old canes each winter and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring to keep plants vigorous.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring in deep, well-drained soil and support the long canes on a trellis; Meeker is a floricane type that fruits on second-year wood.
directions: Plant dormant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and train the canes to a two-wire trellis, since the long, productive canes bend heavily under a full crop. Meeker is the classic Pacific Northwest commercial red raspberry, bred at Washington State University and long the dominant processing variety in Washington and Oregon, valued for its consistently large, firm, bright red conic berries with excellent flavor for both fresh eating and freezing. It fruits on floricanes, so remove spent canes to the ground after harvest each year and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest shoots. It performs best where summers are mild and winters are not severely cold, and can be prone to root rot in poorly drained soils.

common_name: Merton Thornless Blackberry (Historic English Thornless Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container stock in early spring on a sturdy trellis; the semi-trailing, thornless canes need tying in through the season since they do not stand upright on their own.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the vigorous, semi-trailing canes onto a two-wire trellis, tying in new growth through the growing season. Bred in England from a thornless mutation, Merton Thornless was one of the first commercially grown thornless blackberry cultivars and became the parent of many later thornless releases, including some of the early Arkansas breeding lines. Fruit is medium-sized, glossy black, and moderately firm with a classic tart-sweet blackberry flavor, ripening in mid-to-late summer. Prune out spent floricanes to the ground after harvest and select the strongest new canes to retie for the following season.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown stock in spring in moist to well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican elderberry establishes rapidly and may produce its first berry clusters within one to two years of planting. Hardwood cuttings taken in winter root reliably in moist potting mix or directly in the ground. For heaviest fruit set, plant at least two individuals of different seed origins to encourage cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moderately moist soil; Mexican elderberry is more drought-tolerant than eastern common elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) once established and adapts well to the neutral to alkaline soils of the Southwest, California foothills, and the intermountain West. Sambucus mexicana (syn. Sambucus nigra subsp. cerulea) is the native elderberry of California, the Southwest, and the Pacific Northwest mountains, forming a large, fast-growing, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with massive, flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) of creamy-white blossoms in late spring that are irresistible to native bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects. The flowers are followed by heavy drooping clusters of small, powdery-blue to blue-black berries in late summer — excellent for elderberry syrup, jelly, wine, and traditional medicine. CAUTION: cook berries before eating; raw berries, bark, and leaves contain cyanogenic glycosides. An outstanding wildlife plant — the berries are consumed by dozens of bird species including waxwings, robins, and thrushes.

common_name: MidSouth Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Mississippi Bunch Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; MidSouth, released by Mississippi State University in 1981 from decades-old USDA breeding work in Meridian, Mississippi, is a self-fertile, highly Pierce's disease-tolerant bunch grape long grown across the Deep South mainly for jelly and juice.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the moderately vigorous canopy. MidSouth was released by Mississippi State University in 1981, tracing back to USDA breeding work begun in the late 1930s at the Meridian, Mississippi field station, and it remains valued today for its exceptional tolerance of Pierce's disease across Mississippi, Louisiana, and neighboring Gulf South states. Its self-fertile vines produce clusters of dark blue-purple berries covered in a heavy waxy bloom that ripen in late July to mid-August in the southern part of its range, with a rich, sweet-tart flavor carrying a hint of raspberry; the seeded, slip-skin berries are best suited to jelly and juice rather than fresh table use. The vine is more susceptible to fungal disease and root-knot nematodes than to Pierce's disease itself, so a regular fungicide program and nematode-aware site selection help keep plantings productive. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons to keep cluster and berry size from declining.

plant_note: Set out rooted semi-hardwood cuttings or nursery liners in spring after frost danger passes, in sandy, humus-rich, well-drained soil with light afternoon shade in hot climates; midyim tolerates only light, brief frost, so grow it in a movable container at the cold edge of its range.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery liners in spring in sandy, humus-rich, well-drained soil, giving light afternoon shade where summers run hot. This low, spreading Australian bush-food shrub produces small white flowers followed by white, red-freckled berries with a spicy, blueberry-like flavor over a long summer-to-fall season, forming a durable, drought-tolerant edible groundcover once its roots are established. It has almost no frost tolerance, so treat it as a container plant that can be moved under cover anywhere winter lows dip much below freezing. A light shearing after each fruiting flush keeps the mat dense and encourages the next round of flowers.

common_name: Mignonette Alpine Strawberry (French Everbearing Woodland Strawberry)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; surface-sow and do not cover, as the tiny seeds need light to germinate.
directions: Mignonette is a compact French heirloom alpine strawberry, considered an improved selection of the old Reine des Vallees type, grown for its dainty pointed red berries and rich woodland-strawberry perfume rather than for size or yield. Plants form neat, semi-evergreen mounds without runners and often produce a light crop the first season from an early indoor sowing. Grow in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; it tolerates partial shade but sets more fruit with several hours of direct sun. Because the berries are small, soft, and quick to perfume a whole bowl, they are best used fresh for snacking, garnishing desserts, or infusing drinks rather than for preserving.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in the dappled shade of maritime hammocks or coastal woodland edges; establish with regular water the first season, then reduce.
directions: A sprawling, semi-woody vine-shrub of Florida and Gulf Coast maritime hammocks, milkberry produces small fragrant white tubular flowers followed by glossy white berries that persist through much of the year and are relished by birds. It scrambles over neighboring shrubs or can be kept as a loose mounding groundcover shrub with occasional pruning. Grow in partial shade to filtered sun in humus-rich, well-drained soil typical of coastal hammock understories, and provide some wind protection when young since it is not a true front-dune plant. Its salt and drought tolerance once established make it useful as a naturalizing understory shrub in restored maritime forest plantings.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), fertile soil in part shade; miracle berry is a West African rain forest understory shrub that requires acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist conditions similar to blueberries — it cannot tolerate alkaline water or soil and performs best in acidic, non-chlorinated water.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in part shade; water with rainwater or filtered water — chlorinated tap water and alkaline water damage the plant. Synsepalum dulcificum (miracle berry or miracle fruit) is a West African evergreen shrub that produces the most remarkable edible berry in the botanical world: small (1-inch), red, olive-shaped berries containing a glycoprotein called miraculin, which temporarily binds to sour taste receptors on the tongue and causes sour, acidic foods to taste intensely sweet for 30–60 minutes after eating a single berry. The berries themselves have virtually no sugar content and a bland flavor — the effect is entirely on taste perception, not on the food itself. After eating a miracle berry, lemons taste like lemon candy, vinegar tastes sweet, sour cream becomes sweet cream, and Tabasco sauce tastes like hot doughnut glaze. Miracle berry parties (where participants eat the berry and sample unusual flavor combinations) have become a culinary novelty. The plant is native to West African rain forest understory and requires the same acidic, humus-rich, moist, part-shade conditions as blueberries — it is extremely pH-sensitive and will decline rapidly in alkaline soil or water. In zone 10–12, it can be grown outdoors; in zone 8–9, best in a pot brought indoors in winter.

common_name: Miss Blanc Grape (Mississippi-Bred White Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Miss Blanc, released by Mississippi State University in 1982, is a white, Pierce's disease-tolerant grape bred for Gulf South wine and juice production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the canopy. Miss Blanc was released by Mississippi State University in 1982, bred by USDA researcher N.H. Loomis specifically for Pierce's disease tolerance, and produces white grapes well suited to wine and juice production across the Gulf South where the disease limits most traditional wine grape choices. Its interspecific hybrid parentage gives it the disease resistance needed to thrive in the region's warm, humid growing conditions without the heavy spray program European wine grapes require. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and reduce fungal disease risk.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or bare-root shrubs in early spring into moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Missouri gooseberry tolerates more shade than most fruiting shrubs and is naturally found along woodland edges and fencerows.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Missouri gooseberry is a thorny, arching Midwestern and Great Plains native shrub found wild along woodland edges, fencerows, and thickets, tolerating more shade than most fruiting berries while still producing a reliable crop. Small, greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers in early spring give way to smooth, purple-black berries by early summer that are tart-sweet and excellent fresh once fully ripe, or cooked into pies, jams, and preserves while still slightly underripe and firmer. It is notably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than European gooseberry cultivars, and its wide native range makes it naturally adapted to variable continental climates from hot summers to severe winters. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to renew vigor, and watch for the sharp spines at each leaf node when harvesting or pruning.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall; mock strawberry is extremely adaptable and will colonize partial to full shade under trees where few groundcovers thrive. It spreads by runners similar to regular strawberry and can cover large areas quickly.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained to moderately moist, average soil — mock strawberry is one of the most shade-tolerant edible groundcovers available for difficult spots under trees. It spreads vigorously by runners, forming a dense weed-suppressing carpet of trifoliate leaves studded with small yellow flowers from spring through fall followed by round, bright red berries. The fruits are edible and safe but mild and nearly tasteless compared to true strawberries — they lack the complex aroma that makes true strawberry irresistible. They are best used in jams or flavored beverages rather than eaten fresh.
