The plant does well in lawn edges, woodland paths, and shaded slopes where it outcompetes many weeds while providing interest through yellow flowers and bright fruit. May naturalize aggressively; divide to control spread.

common_name: Monterey Strawberry (Day-Neutral UC Davis Heavy-Fruiting Strawberry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or plugs in fall (September–November in zone 9) for winter establishment and spring through fall harvest; Monterey is a day-neutral variety that produces fruit continuously throughout the growing season rather than in a single concentrated June crop. In zone 9, plant October–November for harvest beginning March–April and continuing until heat stops production in June, then resuming when temperatures cool in September–October. Beds typically remain productive for 2–3 seasons before renewal.
directions: Plant bare-root or plugs in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil; mulch with straw to maintain moisture and keep fruit off the soil. Monterey is a day-neutral strawberry developed by the University of California at Davis and released in 2009 by plant breeders Douglas Shaw and Kirk Larson — a variety bred to combine the high-productivity and large berry size of California commercial strawberries with the continuous-production advantage of day-neutral types. Day-neutral strawberries (unlike traditional June-bearing types) produce fruit throughout the growing season regardless of day length — triggered to bloom and fruit by temperature rather than day length. This gives Monterey a very long harvest window in zone 8–10, where it can produce from early spring through late fall with a summer break during the hottest months. The berries are large (1–1.5 inch diameter), firm, and very flavorful — significantly more aromatic and sweet than many commercial varieties, though with the large size that makes them visually attractive. Monterey was developed for California coast conditions (mild summers, year-round production) and performs exceptionally well in Gulf Coast fall and spring conditions that mimic coastal California temperatures.

common_name: Montgomery Rabbiteye Blueberry (Vigorous Mid-Season Southern Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Montgomery is a vigorous, productive rabbiteye blueberry cultivar bred for reliable mid-season production and good fruit quality in Southern growing conditions. Plant with a different rabbiteye cultivar for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Montgomery is a vigorous rabbiteye blueberry cultivar developed for Southern growing conditions, producing a reliable mid-season crop of medium to large, firm berries with good flavor. The bushes are notably vigorous and productive, establishing quickly and bearing well once mature, making Montgomery a dependable choice for filling out a mid-season harvest window alongside earlier and later rabbiteye selections. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, it requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rhizome divisions in spring into acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil under the broken canopy of conifers or tall deciduous trees; wild seed germinates poorly, so divisions or nursery plants establish far more reliably.
directions: Mountain huckleberry naturally colonizes the filtered light beneath conifer forests in the Pacific Northwest and Rockies, so give it acidic soil, steady moisture, and the dappled shade of nearby trees rather than open, exposed sun. Established plants spread slowly by underground rhizomes and reward patience with intensely flavored, dark purple berries in late summer that are considered by many foragers to be the finest of all the huckleberries for pies, jam, and eating fresh. It is notoriously slow to establish from nursery stock, so plant it where it can be left undisturbed for years. This is a true forest-floor crop, offering a genuinely shade-adapted alternative to sun-loving blueberries.

plant_note: Take hardwood cuttings in late winter or softwood cuttings in early summer and root in well-drained propagation mix; plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun — multicaulis mulberry is vigorous and begins fruiting within two to three years of establishment.
directions: Propagate from hardwood cuttings taken in late winter and root in a well-drained propagation mix under plastic film, or take semi-softwood cuttings in early summer; plant rooted cuttings out in spring after the last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Multicaulis mulberry is a vigorous, large-leaved variety of white mulberry selected in China for its enormous leaves — up to 12 inches long — that historically supported the silk industry; in the food garden it channels that same vigor into abundant, sweet white to pale-pink berries that ripen weeks ahead of most mulberries. The tree tolerates a wide range of soils including clay, heat, and urban conditions, and once established is drought-resilient while performing best with consistent moisture during fruiting. Harvest berries over several weeks as they ripen unevenly, spreading a sheet beneath the canopy and shaking branches gently to collect ripe fruit.

common_name: Munger Black Raspberry (Historic Commercial Black Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring; Munger was, for most of the 20th century, the dominant black raspberry cultivar grown for commercial canning and freezing and remains a reliable, vigorous choice for the home patch.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and tip-prune new canes at about 24-30 inches during the summer to force branching, since black raspberries fruit on lateral shoots off last year's canes rather than on the cane tips. Munger was selected in the late 1800s and went on to become the backbone of the commercial black raspberry industry in Oregon and the Midwest for decades, prized for its productivity, vigor, and the deep, wine-dark, firm berries that hold up well to picking and processing. The flavor is intensely rich and slightly tart, excellent for jam, syrup, and baking, and the arching canes root readily wherever an unpruned tip touches soil, so stake or tip-prune to keep the planting from wandering. Remove spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to the strongest four or five per hill each spring.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy, coastal soil in full sun to part shade; muntries is a low-growing, ground-hugging Australian native groundcover shrub from the coastal heathlands and mallee scrub of South Australia and western Victoria — producing small, round, green to purple-red berries with an apple-spice flavor four times higher in antioxidants than blueberries by weight.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly, coastal-type soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established; avoid clay or poorly drained soils. Kunzea pomifera (muntries, emu apple, or native cranberry) is a prostrate, ground-hugging Australian native shrub from the coastal heathlands, mallee scrub, and sand dunes of South Australia and western Victoria — one of the most remarkable and underappreciated Australian native food plants. The plant spreads slowly as a low (6–18 inch), dense, aromatic groundcover with tiny, dark-green leaves and small white bottlebrush-like flowers, eventually producing clusters of small (1/4–1/2 inch), round berries that ripen from green to red-purple in late summer. The berries have a unique, complex, sweet-spicy flavor combining apple, cinnamon, and a subtle eucalyptus note — quite unlike any other berry. Nutritionally, muntries are exceptional: ORAC (antioxidant) values four times higher than blueberries by weight, with high vitamin C, flavonoids, and polyphenols. Aboriginal Australians historically ate muntries extensively as a major food source across the southern Australian coast. In the modern Australian native food industry, muntries are used in jams, sauces, ice creams, and gourmet berry products, and are increasingly available from specialty nurseries. As a garden plant, muntries serves as an excellent low-maintenance native groundcover that also produces an edible crop.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in early spring; use self-fertile cultivars or plant one male ('bronze') vine per 4–6 female vines.
directions: Muscadine grapes are native to the southeastern U.S. and far more heat- and disease-resistant than European or labrusca types. Train to a single trunk with two permanent lateral cordons on a high-wire trellis at 5–6 ft; spur-prune cordons each dormant season to 2–3 bud spurs spaced 4–6 in apart. Many cultivars are not self-fertile, so check pollination requirements before purchasing. Harvest by shaking or hand-picking individual berries when they reach full color and slip easily from the skin.

plant_note: Plant runners or divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; musk strawberry is unique among strawberries in performing well in dappled or partial shade — a valuable trait for woodland or shaded garden situations where other strawberries fruit poorly.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; musk strawberry is a European native species and one of the most historically important cultivated strawberries before the modern hybrid garden strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) replaced it in the 19th century. The medium-sized fruits have an intense, musky-aromatic fragrance far more complex and perfumed than modern strawberry varieties — often described as combining strawberry with pineapple and rose. The plant uniquely tolerates partial shade, making it one of the few berry crops for understory or semi-shaded settings. Most cultivated plants are of a single sex (plants were traditionally vegetatively propagated), so both male and female plants must be obtained for fruiting. 'Capron Royal' and 'Profumata di Tortona' are heritage Italian cultivars. The berries are soft and must be eaten immediately after harvest.

plant_note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for Gulf Coast gardens; Mysore raspberry fruits primarily in cool weather — fall through spring — making it the ideal raspberry for zone 9–10 where temperate raspberries fail in summer heat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Mysore raspberry is the premier fruiting bramble for subtropical gardens — the only raspberry-type fruit that thrives and produces abundantly in zone 9–10 conditions where standard raspberries fail from summer heat and disease. Native to the hills of South Asia, it produces arching, thorny canes 5–8 feet tall with attractive silver-backed leaves and large clusters of small, dark-red to black berries with an intense raspberry flavor from October through April. Unlike temperate raspberries, it fruits on second-year canes (floricanes) but in a warm-climate evergreen pattern. Cut canes to the ground after fruiting; the plant regrows vigorously. It can be invasive outside cultivation where conditions suit it — avoid planting near natural areas.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted runners in spring in moist, acidic, peaty soil; requires cool summer temperatures and will not thrive where summers are hot.
directions: The nagoonberry (arctic raspberry) is a low-growing, rhizomatous Rubus native to Alaska, Scandinavia, and northern Russia, bearing small, deep rose-red berries in early summer that are considered among the finest-flavored wild berries in the boreal world — exceptionally fragrant, rich, and complex. Plants require cool, moist, acidic bog or tundra-edge conditions (pH 4.5–5.5) and cool summer temperatures; they will not survive heat and are rarely successful south of zone 5 except at high elevations. Propagate by dividing rhizomes in early spring. The Finnish-bred cultivar 'Mespi' (a nagoonberry x Arctic raspberry hybrid) shows improved yield and adaptability while retaining the outstanding flavor of the wild species.

plant_note: Plant two or more plants for cross-pollination in early spring; extremely adaptable to cold, dry, or alkaline sites.
directions: Nanking cherry is one of the hardiest fruiting shrubs available, reliably surviving temperatures below -40°F and tolerating poor, dry, or alkaline soils. The abundant small red cherries ripen in early summer and have a sweet, slightly tart flavor excellent for jams, juices, and fresh eating. Two or more plants are needed for cross-pollination; plants flower very early in spring and may need frost protection of blossoms in zones 3–4 during cold snaps. Prune after harvest to remove dead wood and open the canopy; the shrub is generally very healthy with minimal pest and disease problems.

plant_note: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; nannyberry is one of the most shade-tolerant native viburnums and grows naturally as a large shrub or small tree at the edges of moist woodlands and thickets.
directions: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; nannyberry is one of the most shade-tolerant native viburnums and grows naturally as a large shrub or small tree at the edges of moist woodlands and thickets. Viburnum lentago is a large native viburnum of the northeastern and central United States, producing shiny, deeply veined, finely toothed leaves and flat-topped clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring that are outstanding for native bees; the abundant, blue-black, berry-like drupes in fall and winter provide critical food for migrating and overwintering songbirds — particularly cedar waxwings, robins, and thrushes — and are also edible for humans, with a sweet, date-raisin flavor when fully ripe. The fall foliage turns rich wine-red to purplish-red; the plant often sends up suckers and gradually forms a thicket.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; Nantahala is a North Carolina State University release bred specifically for better heat and humidity tolerance than standard red raspberries, making it one of the more realistic red raspberry options for warm Southern gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool through summer heat, since red raspberries generally struggle south of the mountains. Nantahala was bred at North Carolina State University specifically to extend red raspberry production into warmer parts of the Southeast, combining better heat tolerance with good fruit size and quality than older Northern-bred varieties typically manage in Southern gardens. It bears its primary crop on second-year floricanes in early summer, ahead of the worst heat, and benefits from consistent irrigation and a site with some afternoon relief in the hottest zone 8-9 gardens. Even with its improved heat tolerance, red raspberry remains a marginal crop in the Deep South, so gardeners in zone 9 should treat it as an experiment best sited in the coolest, most sheltered spot available.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun in spring; natal plum is salt-tolerant and thrives in coastal conditions, making it ideal for Gulf Coast landscapes.
directions: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; natal plum is a South African native shrub with glossy, dark-green, oval leaves armed with forked spines, fragrant white flowers like large jasmine blooms, and cranberry-sized red to deep-crimson fruits that are among the finest edible berries available in zone 9–11 landscapes. The fruit has a rich, sweet, somewhat cranberry-like flavor and is excellent for jams, jellies, juices, and fresh eating. Plants bloom and fruit nearly year-round in frost-free climates. Salt-tolerant, drought-resistant, and excellent as a security hedge or coastal planting. Note: only the ripe red fruits are edible — all other plant parts including unripe fruits are toxic.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; in zone 9 February–March planting gives canes the longest establishment season. Space 3–4 feet apart in rows 8–10 feet apart. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, typically May–June in zones 8–9.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5); Natchez is a semi-erect, thornless blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 2007, widely considered one of the finest named varieties for the Gulf Coast and mid-South. It is the earliest-ripening major thornless variety, typically producing its first berries in late May to early June in zones 8–9 — a full 2–3 weeks before Ouachita and other Arkansas releases. Berries are very large (9–12 grams), elongated, jet-black, sweet, and aromatic with excellent fresh-eating quality. Yields are high, and the self-supporting semi-erect canes need only minimal trellising. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select 4–6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for next year's crop. Natchez is susceptible to double-blossom rosette disease in areas with high disease pressure; avoid overhead irrigation. In zone 9a, provide afternoon shade or plant on a north-facing slope to reduce heat stress during fruiting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown canes in late winter to early spring; in zone 9 plant December–February. Navaho is erect and self-supporting — tip new canes at 3–4 feet in midsummer to encourage branching and maximize fruiting wood the following year. Remove old canes to the ground after harvest. Chill hour requirement is approximately 400–500 hours (viable in most of zone 9). Navaho ripens in late June, about 2 weeks after Arapaho, providing a sequential harvest window when both varieties are planted.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Navaho is a thornless erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program and released in 1988. The large, glossy, jet-black berries are among the sweetest of any commercial blackberry variety — significantly sweeter than most thorned varieties and with a more balanced sweet-tart flavor than the extremely tart early-season varieties. The high sugar content and mild, pleasant flavor make Navaho berries exceptional for fresh eating without added sugar and for preserves where reduced sugar is desired. The thornless, erect habit makes harvesting unusually practical: no thorns to navigate and no extensive trellis infrastructure required. Navaho produces mid-to-late season, ripening in late June–July in zone 9, providing fruit after the earlier erect varieties have finished and extending the fresh blackberry season. The firm berries have good post-harvest shelf life, remaining harvestable for several days without softening if kept cool.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger eases.
directions: 'Navaho' is an erect, thornless blackberry that produces firm, very sweet berries with excellent shelf life on self-supporting canes. Because it grows upright it needs little or no trellising, though a single wire helps in windy sites. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and keep suckers thinned to maintain a manageable hedgerow. Prune out fruited floricanes each fall and tip new primocanes to encourage branching.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in early spring; in zone 8 plant February–March. Nero is self-fertile and does not require a cross-pollinator. The shrub is adaptable to a wide range of soils including poorly drained or wet sites where most fruiting shrubs fail. Nero suckers moderately and can form a small colony in suitable conditions — mow around the planting to control spread.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist soil — tolerates periodic wet feet better than most fruiting shrubs; Nero is a Czech-selected black chokeberry cultivar widely used in European commercial aronia production, selected for slightly more compact growth habit than Viking with comparable or superior berry yield relative to plant size. The medium to large, round, blue-black to jet-black berries ripen in late August–September with the characteristic high-tannin, astringent flavor of the species — intensely purple when juiced and among the highest known plant sources of anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins. Nero is the most widely grown aronia variety in European commercial production, where aronia juice and concentrate are major products. The compact, upright-to-rounded shrub fits well into mixed border plantings and provides four-season interest with spring flower clusters, glossy summer foliage, heavy late-summer berry crops, and outstanding fall color.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Nesbitt is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine and does not require a separate pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis or pergola; ripens mid-season, typically late August in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood on a two-wire trellis or arbor. Nesbitt is a University of Georgia-released muscadine selected for its combination of very large, deep purple-black fruit, vigorous productive vines, and reliable self-fertility, making it a popular home-garden choice that needs no separate pollinator vine. The fruit has a thin, tender skin for a muscadine, sweet juicy flesh, and good flavor for fresh eating, with fruit size among the largest of the widely grown self-fertile varieties. The vigorous vine bears heavily once established and holds its crop well, tolerating the humid, disease-prone conditions of Gulf South summers better than bunch grapes. A dependable, high-yielding choice for a home muscadine arbor in zone 7–9.

plant_note: Plant in spring; heat-tolerant dewberry-raspberry hybrid.
directions: The nessberry is an old dewberry-raspberry cross developed for the hot South, producing dark, wine-red berries with a sprightly flavor. Its trailing canes benefit from a low trellis and adapt well to heat and heavier soils where standard raspberries struggle. Plant in full sun in well-drained ground and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. Remove spent floricanes after the summer crop and train fresh primocanes for the following season.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Netzer performs reliably in the heat and humidity of Missouri and Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Netzer is a wild-selected Missouri ecotype of American elderberry that was carried into replicated University of Missouri and Missouri State University cultivar trials alongside Bob Gordon, Wyldewood, and Adams, where it consistently proved well adapted to hot, humid, southern-Midwest growing conditions. It bears the typical broad, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring followed by heavy sets of small, dark purple-black berries in mid- to late summer, and its native Ozark origin gives it good tolerance of the heat and humidity that stress northern-bred cultivars. Because it grows and fruits on a similar schedule to other American elderberry selections, Netzer cross-pollinates readily with cultivars such as Adams, Bob Gordon, or Wyldewood when planted in the same bed. Cut back the oldest canes each winter to renew fruiting wood, and control root suckers to prevent the planting from spreading into an unmanaged thicket.

common_name: New Hanover Southern Highbush Blueberry (Disease-Resistant Low-Chill NC State Release)
plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; New Hanover, a 2007 North Carolina State low-chill release, ripens mid-season (early-mid June) and shows good stem-blight and canker resistance.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. New Hanover, released by North Carolina State University in 2007, needs relatively little winter chill and ripens in early-to-mid June, offering a valuable combination of low-chill suitability for the Gulf South alongside notably good resistance to stem blight and canker, the fungal diseases that most often shorten the productive life of southern highbush blueberry bushes in humid climates. This disease tolerance makes it a lower-maintenance choice than many low-chill selections that trade hardiness for early ripening. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out any affected wood promptly despite its improved resistance.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Noble is self-fertile and mid-to-late season (September in zone 9). One of the best black muscadines for wine, juice, and jelly production due to its very high anthocyanin and resveratrol content.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Noble is a black-skinned muscadine released by North Carolina State University in 1971 and named for James Noble, an early muscadine researcher. It is the standard against which black muscadine wine varieties are measured: the deep purple-black berries are extraordinarily high in anthocyanins, resveratrol, and other polyphenols that give muscadine wine and juice its distinctive deep color and purported health benefits. Flavor is rich, musky, and complex — more intensely flavored than bronze varieties — producing deep-colored wine, juice, and jelly with earthy, berry notes. Fresh-eating quality is good but not as mild as bronze types; the thick skin and seeds are more pronounced. Noble is self-fertile and produces consistently high yields even as a single vine. Its exceptional disease resistance and adaptability make it one of the best black muscadines for the humid Gulf South. Harvest when berries are fully black and yield easily to gentle pressure.

common_name: Noir de Bourgogne Black Currant (Classic French Heirloom Black Currant)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this old French cultivar needs a real winter chill and struggles in Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Noir de Bourgogne is the historic black currant of Burgundy, France, long prized as the traditional base for cassis liqueur and still regarded by many growers as the benchmark for rich, aromatic black currant flavor. It is an early-season cultivar that carries long strigs of large, intensely flavored black berries with a distinctive musky-resinous aroma, and it is self-fertile though yields improve with a second cultivar nearby. Noir de Bourgogne is quite susceptible to powdery mildew and needs a substantial number of winter chill hours to flower and fruit well, so it is a poor match for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens and is better reserved for cold-winter regions. Where it is well adapted, prune out about a third of the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous, high-yielding young wood.

common_name: Nordic Raspberry (Extremely Cold-Hardy Minnesota Fall-Bearing Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or potted plants in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 3-7, as a fall-bearing type it can be mowed to the ground each winter.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost, in full sun. Nordic was bred at the University of Minnesota specifically for extreme cold hardiness, giving it a genuine advantage in the harshest northern growing regions where many other raspberry varieties suffer significant winter cane damage or fail outright. As a fall-bearing (primocane) type producing fruit on the current season's new canes, it can be cut entirely to the ground each winter, a simple, low-maintenance pruning approach well suited to gardeners in cold climates who want a reliable, straightforward raspberry crop without fussing over selective cane pruning. The compact, sturdy canes produce good yields of flavorful red berries from late summer into fall, right up until hard frost ends the season.

common_name: Northblue Blueberry (Half-High Cold-Hardy Highbush Blueberry, Northern Half-High)
plant_note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.2), well-drained, organic-rich soil in full sun; Northblue is a University of Minnesota-developed half-high blueberry variety with exceptional cold-hardiness (to -30°F or colder when established and mulched) specifically for zones 3–5 where standard highbush varieties suffer severe winter dieback; plant with Northcountry, Northsky, or Polaris for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.2) with excellent drainage; mulch with pine bark 3–4 inches deep to protect roots and maintain moisture; fertilize with acidifying fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) in spring; Northblue ripens mid-season (July in Minnesota and Wisconsin) producing large, dark blue berries with excellent highbush flavor — larger and better-flavored than lowbush but hardier than standard highbush. Northblue blueberry is one of the University of Minnesota-developed half-high blueberry varieties that transformed blueberry growing in zones 3–5 of the upper Midwest, making reliable blueberry production possible in climates where standard highbush varieties (which are typically hardy only to about -20°F with snow cover) suffered severe dieback or winter-killed entirely. The half-high blueberries were developed by crossing standard highbush Vaccinium corymbosum (for berry size and quality) with the ultra-cold-hardy native lowbush blueberry Vaccinium angustifolium (for hardiness) — and Northblue represents one of the earliest and most successful results of this breeding work. Northblue plants grow 2–3 feet tall — intermediate between lowbush (6–18 inches) and highbush (4–6 feet) — and produce large, dark blue berries with a distinctly better flavor and larger size than wild lowbush berries, closer to highbush quality. The combination of cold-hardiness to -35°F (with some snow cover and mulching), compact size, and genuinely good fruit quality (not just acceptable — actually good by highbush standards) makes Northblue one of the most important blueberry varieties for cold-climate gardeners. Cross-pollination with another half-high variety (Northcountry, Northsky, Polaris) is required for best fruit set.

common_name: Northcountry Blueberry (Half-High Minnesota Cold-Hardy Blueberry, Twin Cities Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.2), well-drained, organic-rich soil in full sun; Northcountry is a University of Minnesota half-high blueberry with extreme cold-hardiness (to -30°F) designed for zones 3–5; plant with Northblue, Northsky, or Polaris for cross-pollination; the compact plants (2–3 feet) are particularly suited to small gardens and landscaping in cold climates.
directions: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.2); mulch heavily; fertilize lightly with ammonium sulfate; Northcountry ripens slightly earlier than Northblue (late June to early July in Minnesota), making it valuable for extending the blueberry season from the beginning; berries are medium-sized, sky-blue, with a mild but pleasant flavor and good sweetness; the plants have attractive red-orange fall color. Northcountry blueberry is a companion half-high variety to Northblue from the same University of Minnesota breeding program, released together as a pair that complements Northblue's mid-season ripening with an earlier season (typically ripening 1–2 weeks before Northblue). The pairing of Northcountry (early) with Northblue (mid) or Northsky (late) is the standard recommendation from University of Minnesota Extension for home blueberry plantings in zones 3–5, providing a 3–4 week fresh blueberry season from one combined planting. The cross-pollination between these varieties also improves fruit set on both plants. Northcountry plants grow slightly more compact than Northblue (typically 24–36 inches rather than 36–48 inches), with a dense, mounded habit that makes them particularly attractive as landscape shrubs in addition to their edible fruit value. The berries are medium-sized (slightly smaller than Northblue), sky-blue in color, with a good sweet-mild flavor and good shelf life for a half-high variety. The extreme cold-hardiness — tested to -30°F with snow cover — and early ripening season make Northcountry one of the most important blueberry varieties for northern Minnesota, North Dakota, and other severe cold-climate gardening situations.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall after removing the waxy outer coating by rubbing in coarse sand or washing with a mild solvent, then allow natural cold stratification over winter; northern bayberry tolerates poor, sandy, acidic soil and salt spray, making it an outstanding native for coastal and disturbed sites.
directions: Sow seeds in fall after rubbing away the waxy seed coating, or provide a 60–90 day cold stratification period before spring sowing; northern bayberry grows naturally in coastal dunes, sandy thickets, and open woods from Newfoundland to North Carolina and thrives in lean, acidic, sandy or loamy soils with excellent drainage. This nitrogen-fixing native is highly tolerant of salt spray, wind, and drought, making it an exceptional choice for coastal landscapes and difficult sites where more refined shrubs fail. The aromatic, blue-gray waxy berries cluster tightly along the branches and persist into winter, historically rendered for bayberry candles; in the garden they provide excellent winter interest and food for birds such as yellow-rumped warblers. Northern bayberry spreads slowly by root suckers to form naturalistic colonies and requires both male and female plants for berry production.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in early spring into acidic, sandy to peaty, well-drained soil in full sun; northern blueberry is a dwarf, cold-hardy alpine and subarctic species native to exposed barrens, tundra, and mountain summits of northern New England and eastern Canada and needs excellent drainage plus reliably cold winters.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in early spring into acidic, sandy to peaty, well-drained soil in full sun; northern blueberry is a diminutive, mat-forming species native to windswept alpine barrens, coastal headlands, and subarctic tundra of northern New England, the Maritimes, and eastern Canada, where it hugs the ground to survive harsh, exposed conditions. Its small, sweet, powder-blue berries ripen in mid to late summer on a plant rarely taller than knee height, spreading slowly by rhizomes to form a low, dense groundcover on lean, acidic soil. Because it is adapted to a short, cool growing season and needs sustained winter cold to perform well, it is a specialty planting for far-northern or high-elevation gardens rather than a general-purpose landscape blueberry, and it will not thrive in hot, humid summer climates. Grow it as a rock-garden or barrens-style planting in sharply drained, lean, acidic soil, and avoid rich garden loam or added fertilizer, which favor weeds over this slow-growing native.

plant_note: Plant rooted tip cuttings in spring into dry, sandy or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; ideal as a low ground-covering berry plant for thin-soiled banks and barrens.
directions: Northern Dewberry is a low-trailing native of dry, open, sandy or rocky ground and thin-soiled barrens throughout eastern North America, distinguished from upright blackberries by its prostrate, creeping canes that root at the tips to form low, dense, ground-covering mats. Plant rooted tip cuttings in spring into dry, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing plants 2 to 3 feet apart; individual canes will trail and root freely to expand coverage over a wide area. White flowers appear in spring and ripen into sweet, black, aggregate drupes in late May to June, making Northern Dewberry one of the earliest-fruiting native brambles and a critical early-summer food source for bluebirds, mockingbirds, towhees, and box turtles. This species excels in sandy, infertile, full-sun sites where taller brambles and most garden fruits cannot survive, making it a uniquely useful edible ground cover for difficult dry spots.

plant_note: Set out bare-root or potted bushes in early spring once soil is workable, into strongly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark; Northland is exceptionally cold-hardy and well suited to zone 3-7 winters.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, amending generously with peat moss or pine bark fines, and mulch well to keep shallow roots cool and evenly moist. Northland was bred at Michigan State University by crossing highbush and lowbush blueberry species, resulting in a compact, spreading 'half-high' bush notable for extreme cold hardiness that lets it survive winters too harsh for standard highbush varieties. The medium-sized berries have good, classic sweet blueberry flavor and ripen reliably even in short northern growing seasons, and the naturally lower, denser habit makes the bush useful as an informal hedge or foundation planting in addition to its fruiting value. Give full sun and consistent moisture through fruit development, prune lightly each winter to remove the oldest wood, and plant with a second variety to improve pollination and yield.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root suckers/cuttings in early spring while dormant; Northline is self-fertile but sets a heavier crop with a second saskatoon cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Northline is a prairie-bred saskatoon selection valued for producing very large, sweet, almond-scented berries earlier in the season than many other named cultivars. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants to allow air movement and reduce foliar disease, and mulch to conserve moisture through establishment. It suckers moderately to form a multi-stemmed thicket over time, so remove wayward suckers if a tidier hedge form is wanted. The extreme cold hardiness of this cultivar makes it a staple of Canadian Prairie saskatoon orchards, where fruit is picked for fresh eating, pies, and preserves.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in very acidic, well-drained soil in full sun in early spring.
directions: Northsky is one of the most compact of the University of Minnesota half-high blueberries, growing only 10 to 18 inches tall, which makes it well suited to foundation plantings, containers, and rock-garden-style edible landscapes in severe-winter regions. It shares the extreme cold-hardiness of its half-high siblings, tolerating temperatures near -35°F when snow-covered, and ripens medium-sized, light-blue, sweet berries in mid- to late summer. Because the plant is so low-growing, mulching and consistent moisture are especially important to prevent root stress during dry spells. Plant alongside another half-high cultivar such as Northblue or Polaris to improve pollination and fruit set.

common_name: Norton Grape (Cynthiana, Flagship Ozark Native American Red Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Norton, also sold as Cynthiana, is a native American red wine grape with exceptional disease resistance, historically the flagship red wine grape of the Ozark and Missouri wine industry.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the vigorous canopy. Norton, also sold under the name Cynthiana, is a pure native American grape (Vitis aestivalis) with exceptional resistance to Pierce's disease, black rot, and other diseases that limit many other wine grapes across the humid South and lower Midwest, and it served historically as the flagship red wine grape of the Ozark and Missouri wine industry before Prohibition. It produces small, dark, high-acid berries that make deeply colored, full-bodied red wine, though the fruit is generally considered too tart and seedy for fresh eating. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, since Norton is a vigorous grower that needs regular canopy management to keep fruit quality high.

common_name: Nova Raspberry (Cold-Hardy Vigorous Canadian Red Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container stock in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nova was bred in Nova Scotia for exceptional winter hardiness and disease resistance.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a trellis or wire support to keep the vigorous canes upright. Bred in Nova Scotia, this summer-bearing red raspberry was selected for outstanding winter hardiness and strong resistance to common cane diseases, making it a reliable choice for gardeners in colder climates where less hardy cultivars struggle. It produces firm, medium-large, bright red berries with good flavor on tall, vigorous, spine-covered canes over a midsummer harvest season. Remove spent floricanes after fruiting and thin new canes each spring to maintain airflow and fruit quality.

plant_note: Plant canes in early spring while dormant.
directions: Nova is a hardy, disease-resistant red raspberry that stands up to harsh winters and yields firm, flavorful berries. Plant dormant canes in early spring in full sun and rich, well-drained soil, spacing them to allow airflow and easy picking. Provide a trellis or support to keep the fruiting canes upright. This summer-bearing type fruits on second-year canes, so remove spent floricanes after harvest while leaving new primocanes for next season. Mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Ochlockonee is a low-chill (about 400-450 hours), late-ripening rabbiteye that extends the harvest season and needs another rabbiteye cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist through the long southern summer. Ochlockonee is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry named for the Ochlockonee River in the Florida Panhandle, valued for ripening late in the season, after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, which lets home growers stretch fresh blueberry harvest into July. The vigorous, upright bush produces firm, medium-to-large, good-flavored berries in heavy clusters, and its low chill requirement makes it well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and remove old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full to partial sun; odorless bayberry is a coastal plain specialist that naturally inhabits wet pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bay swamps and performs best in consistently moist to seasonally wet conditions.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full to partial sun; odorless bayberry is a coastal plain specialist that naturally inhabits wet pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bay swamps and performs best in consistently moist to seasonally wet conditions. Myrica heterophylla is a semi-evergreen to evergreen native bayberry of the southeastern coastal plain, closely related to wax myrtle but lacking the characteristic aromatic fragrance; it produces similar small waxy berries that attract overwintering songbirds and provides dense cover in wet to moist habitats where few other shrubs thrive. This species is an excellent choice for rain gardens, wet swales, and pond margins in the Southeast, where its compact form and wildlife value make it a workhorse of native planting designs.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into fast-draining, mineral-rich, acidic soil in an open, sunny site.
directions: Grow this low, wiry-branched shrub in gritty, well-drained, acidic soil that mimics its native volcanic cinder habitat, and avoid rich garden soil or heavy watering that can encourage rot. Ohelo produces small, tart-sweet, cranberry-like berries in shades of red, yellow, or orange, borne alongside dainty urn-shaped pink or yellow flowers typical of the blueberry family. Native to high-elevation Hawaiian volcanic slopes, it tolerates poor, rocky ground and strong sun but is sensitive to wet, poorly drained conditions and to frost. The tangy fruit is traditionally used fresh or cooked into jams and sauces.

plant_note: Plant in spring in mild-winter regions; needs a long growing season.
directions: The olallieberry is a trailing blackberry hybrid (a cross involving loganberry and youngberry parentage) popular along the California coast for its rich, sweet-tart flavor. Its long, sprawling canes must be trained onto a trellis and are best separated by fruiting year for easier pruning. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with regular irrigation through the dry season. Prune out fruited canes after the early-summer harvest and tie in the new canes for next year.

common_name: Onslow Rabbiteye Blueberry (Vigorous Productive Southern Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Onslow is a North Carolina-released rabbiteye blueberry noted for strong vigor and heavy, reliable production. Plant with a different rabbiteye cultivar for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Onslow is a rabbiteye blueberry cultivar released for the Southeast, valued for exceptional plant vigor and consistently heavy production of medium to large, good-flavored berries. Its strong growth makes it well suited to establishing a productive planting relatively quickly, and it performs reliably across the range of soil conditions typical of Southern blueberry patches, provided the acidic, well-drained requirements common to all rabbiteye types are met. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Onslow requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: Optimus Blueberry (Machine-Harvest Early-Season Southern Highbush Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in well-drained, acidic soil amended with pine bark, spacing plants to allow good air circulation.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in winter in well-drained, acidic soil amended with pine bark, spacing plants to allow good air circulation. Optimus is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for a very low chilling requirement of roughly 150 to 200 hours, an early bloom period, and good natural leafing, all of which suit the mild, unpredictable winters of the Gulf Coast. The firm, round, medium-sized berries were selected with machine harvesting in mind, and the vigorous, disease-tolerant bushes have shown good field resistance to stem blight and Phytophthora root rot. Home growers get the benefit of a reliable, early-season crop on a tough plant that shrugs off the humid Southern growing season.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist.
directions: Plant dormant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Oregon Champion is a nineteenth-century American heirloom gooseberry long favored in the Pacific Northwest for combining decent mildew tolerance with the classic tartness of European-type gooseberries. The medium-sized, pale yellow-green berries have a smooth, faintly fuzzy skin and hold their tang well, making them as useful for pies and preserves as for fresh eating once fully ripe. The vigorous, spiny bush handles the region's cool, damp summers better than many English exhibition varieties.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; thrives in dry shade where few other fruiting shrubs succeed.
directions: Oregon grape is a native Pacific Northwest evergreen shrub with holly-like spiny leaves that produces clusters of tart, powder-blue berries in midsummer — one of the most shade- and drought-tolerant edible-fruiting shrubs available. The berries are too tart to eat fresh in quantity but are excellent for jellies, syrups, and wine when sweetened; they are high in berberine, a compound with traditional medicinal use. Plant in groups of three or more for best cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune by removing the oldest, leggiest canes at the base every few years to encourage compact, multi-stemmed growth.

common_name: Oregon Thornless Blackberry (Thornless Cutleaf Evergreen Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes on a sturdy trellis in early spring; the long trailing canes are vigorous and need firm tying and regular pruning to keep the planting contained.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and provide a strong trellis for the long, trailing, thornless canes, which are more vigorous than most upright blackberry cultivars. Oregon Thornless is a thornless sport of the cutleaf or 'Evergreen' blackberry, distinguished by deeply cut, fern-like leaflets that give the plant an almost ornamental appearance in addition to its fruit crop. Berries are medium-sized, firm, and tart, ripening late in the season and holding well on the vine after ripening. Because canes are highly vigorous and can root wherever tips touch soil, prune hard after harvest and keep tips off the ground to prevent the planting from spreading beyond its trellis.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; oriental photinia establishes readily and is quite drought-tolerant once rooted, but consistent moisture in the first season promotes faster establishment and stronger flowering the following spring.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; oriental photinia is adaptable to a range of soil types and is notably more disease-resistant than the commonly planted red-tipped photinia. Photinia villosa is a deciduous shrub or small tree from East Asia offering outstanding multi-season interest: flat clusters of small white flowers appear in spring, followed by persistent bright red berries that last well into winter, and the foliage turns a brilliant red-orange in autumn that rivals the best fall color of any shrub in the temperate garden. Birds, particularly thrushes and waxwings, relish the persistent berries through late winter, making this an excellent choice for a wildlife-supporting mixed shrub border.

common_name: Orlando Seedless Grape (First Pierce's Disease-Resistant Seedless Bunch Grape)
plant_note: Plant vines grafted onto 'Tampa' or 'Dog Ridge' rootstock in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Orlando Seedless was the first seedless bunch grape combining Pierce's disease resistance, released from the University of Florida's Leesburg breeding program.
directions: Plant grafted vines in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, since Orlando Seedless requires grafting onto 'Tampa' or 'Dog Ridge' rootstock for satisfactory growth and yield rather than growing on its own roots. Bred from interspecific crosses at the University of Florida's Agricultural Research Center in Leesburg, it was the first bunch grape to pair genuine seedlessness with resistance to Pierce's disease, the leafhopper-spread bacterial infection that devastated Florida's historic bunch grape industry. Its white, seedless fruit has good eating quality and fresh-market appeal, though the variety is notably more susceptible to anthracnose than other Florida-bred cultivars and can suffer berry shattering as clusters mature, so a consistent fungicide spray program from bud break onward is important. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to reduce disease pressure and improve berry size.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Osage is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry with a relatively compact habit compared to other erect varieties. In zone 9 it ripens in late May–June, one of the earlier erect thornless blackberries. Prune fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes on a two-wire trellis system.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Osage is a University of Arkansas-released thornless semi-erect blackberry selected for early ripening (among the first thornless erect blackberries to ripen in June in zone 9) and exceptional flavor — rated by Arkansas evaluators as the best-flavored of their thornless erect releases, with a rich, sweet, complex blackberry flavor and balanced sugar-to-acid ratio that surpasses the milder flavor of some other University of Arkansas varieties. The large berries are firm, glossy, and jet-black with excellent shelf life after harvest. The early ripening of Osage is a meaningful advantage in zone 9 where the blackberry harvest window can be shortened by early summer heat — getting the bulk of the crop in late May to mid-June avoids the worst of the heat. In zone 9 Osage is planted alongside mid-season varieties like Apache to extend the harvest over a longer period.

common_name: Osceola Blueberry (Southern Highbush Large-Berry Low-Chill Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in early spring in highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-amended, well-drained soil; blueberries require acidic conditions and will fail quickly in alkaline soils. In zone 9, Osceola requires only 150–200 chilling hours (hours below 45°F), making it reliable where northern varieties fail from insufficient winter chill. Plant 2 or more varieties for cross-pollination and improved yields. Osceola ripens May–June in zone 9. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain soil acidity.
directions: Plant in highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil; acidify if necessary with sulfur or peat moss. Mulch with pine bark or pine straw. Osceola is a southern highbush blueberry developed in Florida through the University of Florida breeding program — a hybrid of northern highbush (Vaccinium corymbosum) and the native southern rabbit-eye relative (Vaccinium darrowi) that produces a plant adapted to the warm, humid conditions and low chilling hours of the Gulf South. The challenge of growing blueberries in the Deep South is chilling requirement: most northern highbush varieties need 800–1,200 hours below 45°F per winter to break dormancy and fruit properly, a requirement never met in zone 8–10 winters where chilling hours typically run 150–400. Osceola and other southern highbush varieties were specifically bred for low chilling requirements (150–200 hours), allowing reliable fruiting in zone 8–10 where northern varieties fail. Osceola produces large, firm, high-quality berries with excellent flavor — among the largest of the southern highbush varieties — ripening mid-season (May–June in zone 9). It is one of the most widely planted commercial and home garden blueberries in Florida and along the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter through early spring; in zone 9 plant February–March for maximum establishment. Ouachita sets fruit in its second year, typically June in zone 8–9, slightly later than Natchez.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained acidic soil; Ouachita is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 2003 — one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in the mid-South and Gulf Coast because of its outstanding combination of productivity, fruit quality, and disease resistance. Berries are medium-large (7–9 grams), glossy black, firm, and mildly sweet with a pleasant balanced flavor and small seeds. Yields are among the highest of any named blackberry variety, and the plants show good resistance to orange rust and anthracnose — a meaningful advantage in the humid South. Canes are self-supporting but benefit from a simple T-trellis for row plantings. Prune floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest; thin primocanes to 4–6 per plant and tip at 36 inches in late summer to encourage lateral branching that will carry next year's fruit. Ouachita's mid-season ripening (about 2 weeks after Natchez) makes it an excellent partner variety for an extended harvest window.

plant_note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring into cool, acidic, consistently moist, humus-rich soil beneath spruce, hemlock, or other conifer canopy; this species tolerates deeper shade than most Vaccinium and is best started from nursery-propagated plants rather than seed.
directions: Native across the cool coniferous forests of Alaska, the Pacific Northwest, and northern Japan, this blueberry relative is remarkably tolerant of dense shade and thrives in the same acidic, mossy understory conditions that defeat most fruiting shrubs. Its pale pink spring flowers give way to soft blue berries by midsummer, among the earliest wild blueberries to ripen, with a mild sweet flavor traditionally gathered fresh or dried by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific coast and interior. Keep the soil consistently moist and acidic and avoid any lime or wood ash near the roots. For a genuinely shade-loving berry crop under established evergreens, this species outperforms almost any cultivated blueberry.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring in very acidic, well-drained soil; Ozarkblue needs roughly 800-900 chill hours yet still performs unusually well in warmer climates for a northern highbush type, making it one of the more heat-tolerant northern highbush blueberries available to southern growers.
directions: Plant in full sun in strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily to protect the shallow root system. Ozarkblue was developed by the University of Arkansas and stands out among northern highbush blueberries for its unusual heat tolerance and adaptability to warmer regions that would stress most other northern highbush cultivars, while still delivering the large size, firm texture, and excellent, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor the group is known for. It ripens late in the blueberry season, extending the harvest window when planted alongside earlier-ripening cultivars. Cross-pollination with a second highbush cultivar improves fruit set and size. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water deeply during dry spells, and prune out old canes each winter to keep the bush productive.

plant_note: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; pagoda dogwood is shade-tolerant and adaptable but is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker disease — provide good air circulation and avoid injuring the bark.
directions: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; pagoda dogwood is shade-tolerant and adaptable but is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker disease — provide good air circulation and avoid injuring the bark. Cornus alternifolia is the only native eastern dogwood with alternate (rather than opposite) leaves, and it produces one of the most distinctive and elegant branching patterns of any native tree — distinctly horizontal, tiered layers of branches that create a pagoda-like architectural silhouette outstanding in winter; its small, fragrant, flat-topped white flower clusters are followed by showy blue-black berries on red pedicels that are consumed by dozens of migrating bird species. Four-season interest: layered winter form, white spring flowers, summer fruit, and red-purple fall foliage.

common_name: Palmetto Southern Highbush Blueberry (University of Georgia Flavor-Standard Release)
plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Palmetto, a 2003 University of Georgia release, needs about 400-450 chill hours and ripens in early May, long regarded as a flavor benchmark among southern highbush cultivars.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Palmetto, released by the University of Georgia in 2003, needs a moderate 400 to 450 chill hours and ripens in early May, and has long been regarded by Southern blueberry growers as something of a flavor standard among southern highbush cultivars, prized for rich, well-balanced sweetness alongside a vigorous, productive, disease-tolerant bush. It performs reliably across a range of Gulf South soils and climates within its chill requirement, making it a dependable choice for home orchards seeking classic blueberry flavor. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain vigor and fruit quality.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in zones 9–11; in cooler zones grow in large containers and overwinter indoors.
directions: Passionfruit is a vigorous, tendril-climbing vine requiring a sturdy wire trellis or fence. Train the main stem vertically and allow lateral shoots to drape horizontally from the top — these laterals bear the flowers and fruit. Prune heavily after fruiting to rejuvenate the vine and maintain productive growth. Harvest when the fruit skin begins to wrinkle and the fruit falls or detaches easily; purple cultivars are generally more cold-tolerant than yellow types.

plant_note: Plant rooted vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun; Paulk is self-fertile and vigorous, so give it ample trellis space — it outgrows most older muscadine varieties.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and give the vine generous trellis space; Paulk is a self-fertile muscadine released by the University of Georgia breeding program and has quickly become popular for producing some of the largest berries of any muscadine cultivar, with glossy black-purple skin and a sweet, mild flavor good for fresh eating. Vines are notably vigorous and heavy-bearing, often needing more aggressive winter pruning than older varieties to keep the canopy in bounds and light penetrating to the fruiting spurs. Train young vines to a single trunk and permanent cordon along a wire, then prune all lateral growth back to short spurs each winter, since fruit forms on new shoots from that spur wood. Harvest from late summer into early fall as berries turn fully black and detach freely from the stem; because Paulk berries are large and thin-skinned relative to older varieties, pick promptly at ripeness to avoid splitting after rain.

common_name: Pearl Glam Beautyberry (Dark Purple Foliage Compact Beautyberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pearl Glam bears dark purple-black foliage year-round in addition to the classic vivid purple berry clusters.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; American beautyberry tolerates a wide range of conditions and needs little supplemental water once established. Pearl Glam bears striking dark purple-black foliage through the entire growing season, a departure from the plain green leaves of the straight species, paired in fall with the same eye-catching clusters of vivid purple berries that encircle the stems and persist after leaf drop, providing food for songbirds through winter. Its dark foliage color adds ornamental interest for months before the berry display even begins, and its more compact size fits smaller gardens than seedling-grown beautyberry. Prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth, since flowers and berries form on new wood.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Pearl River is an LSU AgCenter rabbiteye release bred for Louisiana's mild-winter, high-rainfall growing conditions and needs a second rabbiteye variety such as Climax or Brightwell nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or sulfur before planting; Pearl River is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the LSU AgCenter specifically for Gulf South dooryard and commercial plantings, selected for consistent production under Louisiana's mild winters and low-to-moderate chill hours. The medium-sized, light blue berries ripen mid-season and have a firm texture and mild, sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating and freezing. Plants are vigorous and moderately disease-tolerant, though they benefit from mulching with pine bark or pine straw to keep the shallow root system cool and moist. Not self-fruitful, so plant with at least one other rabbiteye cultivar within 50 feet for reliable cross-pollination and full-sized fruit. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself.

plant_note: Plant in early spring in full sun on well-drained ground; group two or more clumps for best cross-pollination and fruit set.
directions: Pembina was selected in North Dakota for its earlier ripening window compared to many prairie saskatoon cultivars, giving gardeners in short-season regions a head start on the harvest. The shrub forms a dense, rounded multi-stem clump with reliable annual bloom and good resistance to late spring frosts at flowering. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes each winter to keep fruiting wood vigorous.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; space generously, since Pennsylvania blackberry spreads by root sprouts into dense thickets if left unmanaged.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing generously to accommodate rapid spread by root sprouts; Pennsylvania blackberry is one of the most common and widespread wild blackberries of the eastern United States, forming stout, heavily armed, upright to arching canes in old fields, fencerows, and forest edges. White flowers open in late spring, followed by large, firm, sweet-tart black drupes that ripen over a long midsummer season and are excellent fresh or in preserves. Its vigorous, thicket-forming habit makes it valuable for wildlife cover and erosion control on a bank or hedgerow but requires regular management (cutting root suckers or mowing a defined perimeter) in a maintained garden setting to prevent it from spreading beyond its intended space. After harvest, remove spent second-year floricanes at ground level to make room for the current season's new primocanes, which will fruit the following year.

common_name: Perfection Red Currant (Classic American Heirloom Red Currant)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Perfection needs a solid winter chill and is a marginal choice at best for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Perfection is an early-twentieth-century American red currant selection, raised from a Fay's Prolific by Cherry cross, that has stayed in commerce for over a century because of its large, long, easy-to-strip clusters of bright red, tart berries. Bushes are vigorous and self-fertile, producing heavy crops on long strigs that make hand-picking faster than on many other red currant cultivars, and the fruit is well suited to jelly, syrup, and baking as well as fresh eating once fully ripe. Like most red currants, Perfection needs a meaningful number of winter chill hours and cool summer nights to perform well, so it should be treated as an experimental, likely underperforming choice in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast plantings rather than a dependable crop. Where climate allows, keep roots cool with mulch, prune out canes older than three years each winter, and pick full clusters rather than individual berries to preserve fruit quality.

common_name: Phoenix Tears Goji Berry (Compact High-Yield Goji Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring after frost danger; Phoenix Tears is a named goji selection bred for heavier fruit set and a more manageable habit than seed-grown goji.
directions: Plant in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0 in full sun; goji tolerates poor, alkaline soils where other fruiting shrubs struggle. Phoenix Tears is a named goji cultivar selected for heavy, reliable fruit production and elongated, bright red-orange berries with the tart-sweet flavor typical of the species, on arching, slightly thorny canes that can be left as a loose shrub or trained to a central leader with staking. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals for the following season. Harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers rather than pulling directly on the fruit, since the sap can stain skin and clothing.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.
directions: Pilgrim is a USDA-bred cranberry cultivar valued for producing some of the largest, deepest-red berries of any commonly grown cultivar, making it popular for fresh-market and specialty use. It ripens later in the season than Stevens, so it is best suited to regions with a long enough fall growing season to fully color before hard freezes. Vines are moderately vigorous with a somewhat more open growth habit than Stevens, requiring the same acidic, saturated bog conditions and coarse sand mulching used for other cranberry plantings. Established vines take three to four years to reach significant production but then bear reliably for many years with minimal maintenance beyond consistent moisture and acidic fertility.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Pineapple is a self-fertile bronze muscadine noted for a distinctive mild pineapple-like flavor note layered over the classic musky muscadine taste. Build a strong arbor or high-wire trellis to support vigorous vines.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. Pineapple is a self-fertile bronze muscadine grown by home gardeners and small vineyards for its distinctive flavor — a mild, sweet, tropical pineapple note layered over the classic musky muscadine taste, unusual enough among muscadine varieties to have earned the fruit its name. Being self-fertile, one vine sets a full crop without a second pollinator variety planted nearby, making it an easy choice for a single-vine home planting. As with other muscadines, it resists Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make European wine grapes difficult to grow in the humid South, so no regular spray program is needed. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest berries as they ripen and slip easily from the cluster.

plant_note: Plant bare-root crowns in early spring with crowns level at the soil surface; must be grown near standard red strawberries for adequate pollination.
directions: Pineberry is a white-fruited strawberry cultivar (largely derived from the South American species Fragaria chiloensis crossed with F. x ananassa) that produces pale cream-white berries with red achenes and a distinctive pineapple-like aroma when fully ripe. Pineberries have low self-fertility and require a red-fruiting strawberry variety planted nearby as a pollinator for adequate fruit set. Grow exactly as you would a june-bearing or everbearing strawberry, removing blossoms the first season to build root strength. Harvest when berries are white to pale pink with red seeds and give off a sweet pineapple fragrance.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring; grows well alongside red and white currants with identical cultural requirements.
directions: Pink currants are naturally occurring or selected mutations of red currant (Ribes rubrum) producing pale rose-pink to blush-colored berries that are milder and sweeter than the typical red forms — popular cultivars include 'Pink Champagne' and 'Gloire de Sablons'. Culture is identical to red currant: plant in cool, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0–6.5 and prune each late winter to retain 8–12 mixed-age canes, removing any older than 5 years. The translucent pink strigs are ornamentally striking and ripen slightly earlier than most red currants. Check state Ribes restrictions before ordering.

plant_note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil.
directions: 'Pink Lemonade' is an ornamental rabbiteye-type hybrid bearing translucent pink berries with a mild, sweet flavor that deepen in color as they ripen. It offers attractive white-pink spring blooms and fiery fall foliage in addition to novelty fruit. Grow in full sun in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5) kept evenly moist with a pine-bark or pine-needle mulch. Yields improve with a second blueberry variety nearby for cross-pollination; prune lightly after the third year to renew fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pixwell holds its berries away from the thorny stems on longer stalks, making harvest noticeably easier than many gooseberry cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in hot climates. Pixwell was bred specifically to make gooseberry picking less painful, holding its pale green, ripening-to-pink berries on longer stems that dangle clear of the thorny branches, unlike older cultivars whose fruit clusters tightly among the spines. The berries have the classic tart gooseberry flavor, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, and the plant is vigorous, cold-hardy, and self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive, and site with some afternoon shade in warmer climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Polana is a primocane (fall-bearing) raspberry that in zone 9 produces a fall crop on first-year canes in September–November — potentially the only practical raspberry crop in the warmest zone 9 areas, as the fall primocane season occurs during cooler fall temperatures. Mow or cut all canes to the ground in late winter for a single annual fall crop.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Polana is a Polish-bred, fall-bearing (primocane) raspberry producing its main crop on first-year canes in autumn — earlier than most other fall-bearing varieties, beginning to ripen in August–September in most climates. The earlier fall ripening is a significant advantage because it means more of the crop matures before winter freezes end the season in northern areas, and in zone 9 the earlier ripening of Polana compared to later fall-bearing types like Heritage means the crop starts before the hottest September weather. The firm, conical, dark red berries have excellent flavor — well-balanced sweet-tart with rich raspberry aroma. Polana is one of the most productive fall-bearing varieties per area; the compact, self-supporting primocane habit (no trellis needed) makes it practical for small gardens. In zone 9 fall raspberries are more reliably successful than summer varieties because the October ripening occurs in cooler conditions.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; Polka fruits on current-season primocanes and can be mown to the ground each winter or left partially unpruned for an added early summer crop.
directions: Plant dormant canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and mow all canes to the ground in late winter for the simplest management, since Polka is a primocane type that fruits reliably on first-year wood. Bred in Poland at the Brzezna research institute, Polka is a heavy-yielding fall raspberry known for large, firm, glossy conical berries with a pleasant sweet-tart flavor and good shelf life, making it popular with market growers as well as home gardeners. It ripens over a long fall window and holds up well to light rain without excessive fruit softening. Good air circulation and consistent moisture during fruiting help maximize berry size and reduce disease pressure.

plant_note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Ponca's upright, thornless canes need only a simple support and produce an unusually sweet, small-seeded berry prized for fresh eating.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the upright canes onto a simple two-wire trellis for support. Released by the University of Arkansas breeding program, Ponca is one of the newer thornless erect blackberry cultivars, notable for exceptionally high sugar content and small seed size that give it outstanding fresh-eating flavor compared to older, tarter cultivars. The compact, upright canes need less trellising than sprawling semi-erect types, and the plant produces a concentrated harvest over a relatively short picking window in early summer. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to make room for the canes that will fruit the following season.
