directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in extremely well-drained, lean soil — avoid summer irrigation once established; Toyon (California Holly, Christmas Berry) is a large, handsome, evergreen shrub native to California chaparral and oak woodland, producing spectacular clusters of brilliant red to orange-red berries in November–January — the traditional holiday decoration plant of coastal California and the plant thought to have inspired the name 'Hollywood.' The berries have a slightly bitter, astringent flavor when raw but become edible and pleasant when fully ripe and soft after frost or light cooking; indigenous Californians ate them roasted, fermented into cider, or dried. The white flower clusters in summer attract bees, and the winter berries support mockingbirds, waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds through the season when few other fruiting plants are active. Toyon is one of the most ornamentally rewarding California natives for gardens in the dry western zones and Mediterranean climates; its tolerance of the Gulf Coast requires excellent drainage and restrained irrigation.

common_name: Traminette Grape (Cornell-Bred Aromatic White Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root vines on a trellis in full sun once the ground can be worked in spring.
directions: Traminette was developed at Cornell University from a cross of Gewürztraminer with the French-American hybrid Joannes Seyve 23.416, combining Gewürztraminer's spicy floral aroma with much better cold tolerance and disease resistance than its vinifera parent. The vine buds out relatively late, which helps it dodge spring frosts, and it is widely planted across the mid-Atlantic, Midwest, and Northeast for its lychee, rose, and clove-scented white wine. It shows good resistance to powdery mildew and moderate resistance to bunch rot compared with straight vinifera cultivars, though crop loads should still be managed through cluster thinning for wine quality. Train on a vertical shoot-positioned trellis and prune to spurs or short canes for consistent yields.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns or plugs in early spring; Tribute is a day-neutral (everbearing) cultivar that flowers and fruits continuously through the growing season regardless of day length, rather than producing one concentrated June crop.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; remove the first flush of flowers after planting to strengthen the plant before letting it fruit. Tribute is a USDA-released day-neutral strawberry cultivar, valued for producing a steady, moderate harvest of medium-large, firm, well-flavored berries from late spring through fall rather than a single concentrated June crop, extending the home strawberry season significantly compared with traditional June-bearing types. It shows good resistance to several common strawberry diseases, including red stele and verticillium wilt, making it a dependable choice in a range of soil conditions. Because day-neutral types put continuous energy into fruiting rather than runner production, they produce fewer runners than June-bearers, and removing flowers for the first several weeks after planting helps establish a stronger root system for sustained production through the season.

plant_note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; provide a strong trellis.
directions: 'Triple Crown' is a thornless semi-erect blackberry famed for high yields of large, sweet, glossy-black fruit in mid to late summer. Train the vigorous canes onto a sturdy T-trellis and tip the primocanes at about four feet to promote fruiting laterals. Grow in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with consistent summer moisture during ripening. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to make room for next year's fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns or plugs in early spring; Tristar is a day-neutral (everbearing) cultivar that flowers and fruits continuously through the growing season, well suited to containers and small raised beds because of its compact habit.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; remove the first flush of flowers after planting to strengthen the plant before letting it fruit. Tristar is a USDA-released day-neutral strawberry cultivar bred alongside Tribute, valued for its compact, tidy plant habit and continuous production of small-to-medium, sweet, glossy red berries from late spring through fall, making it a favorite for hanging baskets, containers, and small raised beds where a sprawling June-bearer would be impractical. It shows good disease resistance for a day-neutral type, including tolerance to red stele root rot, and its everbearing habit means a small planting can supply a steady trickle of fresh berries all season rather than one large harvest. Pinch off runners as they form to keep the plant's energy focused on fruit production rather than spreading.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Triumph is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine that sets good crops without a pollinator but benefits from cross-pollination. In zone 9 it ripens in late August–September. Train on a sturdy trellis; the vigorous vines require heavy winter pruning to produce the next season's crop.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Triumph is a bronze-skinned (white) muscadine grape selected by the University of Georgia for large, sweet, bronze-gold fruits with an exceptionally sweet flavor and low acidity — one of the sweetest muscadine varieties available and a benchmark for fresh-eating quality among bronze muscadines. The large, round fruits (1–1.25 inches) ripen to a deep bronze-gold color and have a thin, tender skin with less of the tough slip-skin character that makes some muscadine varieties less appealing for fresh eating. The sweet, mild, slightly floral flavor with classic muscadine aromatic notes makes Triumph outstanding for fresh eating, and the golden color produces beautiful pale-gold juice and jelly. Triumph is a self-fertile (perfect-flowered) variety that sets crops reliably without a pollinator. In zone 9 the vine is vigorous and productive; provide generous spacing (20+ feet) for the mature vine's spread.

common_name: Tulameen Raspberry (Premium Late-Season British Columbia Raspberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring on a sturdy trellis; Tulameen has a long midsummer ripening window and canes benefit from support given the weight of the large fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil and support the tall canes on a two-wire trellis. Bred in British Columbia, Tulameen is a premium fresh-market red raspberry known for unusually large, firm, glossy berries with excellent sweet flavor and a notably long harvest window that extends well into late summer. It is a floricane-fruiting type, so remove spent canes to the ground after the season and thin new primocanes to the strongest shoots to maintain fruit size and quality. Because the canes are tall and heavily laden when fruiting, secure them well to the trellis to prevent wind and fruit-weight breakage.

plant_note: Plant bare-root canes in early spring on a trellis; tummelberry is more cold-hardy than tayberry and better suited to short-season northern gardens.
directions: The tummelberry is a Scottish-bred Rubus hybrid developed at the Scottish Crop Research Institute from a tayberry cross, selected specifically for greater cold hardiness and easier mechanical harvest than its parent. It produces large, dark red to maroon conical berries slightly smaller than tayberries in midsummer with a rich, aromatic flavor well suited to preserves, juices, and desserts. Train the long, semi-trailing canes on a two-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft, fruiting on second-year floricanes; cut all fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes for the following year. It is substantially hardier than tayberry and performs reliably in zones 4–5 with minimal winter protection.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Tundra is self-infertile and needs a compatible University of Saskatchewan pollinizer such as Borealis or Honey Bee planted nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Tundra will not set a worthwhile crop alone. Released by the University of Saskatchewan breeding program as a mid-to-late-season pollinizer partner for Borealis, Tundra bears firm, mild-flavored, elongated blue berries that hold their shape well and are less prone to splitting after rain than some earlier cultivars, making them good for both fresh eating and processing. The upright, vigorous bush is easy to hand-harvest and tends to crop reliably once established. Tundra is extremely cold-hardy, surviving winter lows well below -40F, but like all haskaps it performs poorly in hot, humid summer regions and is not recommended for the Gulf South. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood for the first several years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep production high.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart on a two-wire trellis. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, typically ripening early in the blackberry season.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Tupy is a vigorous, thorny, erect blackberry developed by the Brazilian agricultural research agency EMBRAPA from Arkansas breeding lines, and it has become one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in warm-climate regions of Latin America because of its exceptional heat tolerance and productivity under conditions too warm for many U.S.-bred varieties. Berries are large, glossy black, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening early in the season with a long harvest window and heavy yields. Because canes are thorny, plan for careful pruning and picking; remove fruited floricanes after harvest and tie in 4-6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for the following year. Tupy tolerates the intense heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast better than many thornless northern-bred varieties, making it a strong choice for zone 9-10 growers.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; a heavy straw mulch over winter is important in the coldest parts of its range.
directions: Veestar is an Ontario-bred June-bearer prized across the Canadian prairies and northern U.S. Midwest for combining very early ripening with exceptional winter hardiness. The first flush of berries is notably large and firm with bright red color and good flavor, though fruit size drops off quickly as the harvest continues, so the earliest picks give the best quality. Its vigor and productivity have kept it a standard recommendation for short-season, cold-winter gardens for decades. Apply a thick winter mulch and remove it gradually in spring to protect crowns from late freezes without delaying growth.

plant_note: Plant rooted cane tips in spring and train onto a wire trellis; cut out fruited canes after harvest and tie in new primocanes for the following season.
directions: Plant rooted cane tips in spring and train onto a wire trellis, cutting out fruited canes after harvest and tying in new primocanes for the following season. Veitchberry is an English hybrid bramble raised in the early twentieth century by the Veitch nursery dynasty, one of several blackberry-raspberry crosses developed in Britain around the same era as the loganberry. It produces large, dark purple-black, conical berries with an aromatic flavor closer to blackberry than raspberry, borne on long, vigorous, thorny trailing canes. It survives mainly in heritage fruit collections and specialist nurseries today, having been largely superseded by more disease-resistant modern hybrids.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted rhizome cuttings in early spring in strongly acidic, well-drained, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to light shade; velvetleaf blueberry is a cold-climate species that needs a genuinely cold winter and does not perform in hot-summer regions.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0), well-drained and sandy or peaty, in full sun to light shade; velvetleaf blueberry is a low, colony-forming native shrub of the boreal forest and northern Great Lakes and New England barrens, distinguished from the closely related lowbush blueberry by the fine, dense, velvety hairs covering its young twigs and the undersides of its light blue-green leaves — a texture you can feel by running a leaf between your fingers. It spreads by shallow rhizomes into loose colonies and, like other lowbush blueberries, is fire-adapted, resprouting vigorously from its roots after burning or hard mowing; commercial growers of Maine's wild blueberry barrens manage mixed stands of this species and Vaccinium angustifolium on a two-year burn-and-harvest cycle for the same reason. The small, powder-blue, sweet berries ripen in mid- to late summer and are borne most heavily on wood that grew the previous year, so avoid heavy pruning right before a harvest season. Foliage turns brilliant scarlet-red in fall. Plant at least two genetically distinct plants for reliable cross-pollination and best fruit set. This is strictly a cold-climate plant, thriving where winters are long and cold; it struggles and rarely fruits well south of its native range.

common_name: Venus Grape (Seedless Blue University of Arkansas Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil; Venus, bred by the University of Arkansas, is a seedless blue table grape with good disease resistance and a slip-skin, Concord-like flavor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy to help manage humidity-related fungal disease. Venus was bred by the University of Arkansas grape breeding program and produces genuinely seedless, blue-black berries with a slip-skin texture and sweet, richly fruity flavor reminiscent of Concord grapes, on a vine with good resistance to the common grape diseases that plague less resilient cultivars in humid climates. Its early to midseason ripening and reliable disease tolerance have made it a popular home-garden choice for gardeners wanting a seedless table grape without a heavy spray program. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Vernon ripens mid-season and needs another rabbiteye cultivar such as Climax or Tifblue nearby for cross-pollination and full fruit set.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Vernon is a mid-season rabbiteye blueberry bred for the Gulf South, producing an upright, vigorous, productive bush with firm, well-flavored, medium-to-large berries that hold well on the bush without excessive splitting in humid weather. It fills the harvest gap between early cultivars like Climax and later ones like Tifblue or Ochlockonee, giving home orchards a steadier, more extended supply of fresh fruit. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid high-nitrogen feeding late in the season, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or bare-root plants in early spring; in zone 8 plant February–March. Viking aronia is self-fertile and produces good crops without a cross-pollinator, though yields improve with another aronia variety nearby. The vigorous shrub tolerates wet, poorly drained soils that would kill most fruiting shrubs — a significant advantage in low-lying garden areas.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist or periodically wet soil; Viking is a Scandinavian-selected cultivar of black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) developed for maximum berry production, selected in Sweden for its very heavy crop load of large, dark purple-black berries on an upright, vigorous shrub. The berries ripen in late August–September and are among the most tannin-rich, astringent fruits in cultivation when eaten raw — the name 'chokeberry' derives from this mouth-puckering astringency. Processed into juice, syrup, wine, jam, or dried, the astringency mellows and the extraordinarily high anthocyanin and polyphenol content — among the highest of any commonly grown fruit — makes aronia products popular as nutritional supplements and functional foods. Viking is one of the highest-yielding aronia cultivars per area, producing 10–20 pounds per mature shrub. The shrub also provides excellent ornamental value with white flower clusters in spring and brilliant orange-to-red fall foliage.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Von is a thorny, trailing blackberry that requires a sturdy trellis or fence for support. It ripens earlier than most erect varieties — May–June in zone 9. Prune fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train the long, flexible primocanes on horizontal wires.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Von is a trailing (dewberry-type) blackberry selected by the University of Georgia specifically for the Gulf Coast and Deep South, with exceptional heat tolerance and disease resistance suited to the humid conditions of the lower South. Unlike the erect University of Arkansas varieties that were developed for upland conditions, Von was selected specifically for performance in the hot, humid, rainy conditions of coastal Georgia, the Florida panhandle, and Gulf Coast zone 9. The large, sweet, flavorful berries ripen in May–June in zone 9, earlier than most erect varieties. Von requires a trellis or fence to support its trailing, vining habit, but the trailing type has the advantage of naturally positioning the fruiting lateral branches where they receive maximum sun exposure. Disease resistance to orange rust and rosette disease is an important selection criterion in zone 9 where these diseases can be serious problems for susceptible trailing blackberry varieties.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in early spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; wax currant is a drought-tolerant Rocky Mountain and Great Basin native adapted to dry, rocky foothill and canyon slopes.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; wax currant is a compact, twiggy shrub with small, rounded, waxy-textured leaves and tubular, pale pink to whitish spring flowers that are visited by early-season bees and occasional hummingbirds. Small, bright red, glossy berries ripen in summer and are edible, though quite tart and seedy, generally best used cooked into jelly or syrup rather than eaten fresh out of hand. It is markedly more drought tolerant than most cultivated currants and gooseberries, thriving in the same dry, rocky, low-fertility soils found on sagebrush foothills and canyon slopes throughout its native range. Prune out the oldest stems periodically to renew productive wood, and avoid rich soil or frequent irrigation, both of which encourage lush, mildew-prone growth in this otherwise tough, low-maintenance native shrub.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; wax myrtle is highly adaptable and tolerates poor, sandy, wet, or salty soils, making it one of the most versatile native evergreens for the Southeast.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; wax myrtle is highly adaptable and tolerates poor, sandy, wet, or salty soils and thrives in coastal and inland settings alike. Myrica cerifera is a fast-growing, aromatic, nitrogen-fixing native evergreen shrub or small tree of the Southeast, valued for its densely branched form that provides excellent year-round cover, nesting habitat, and foraging sites for wildlife; the distinctive blue-gray, waxy-coated berries produced in dense clusters along the stems attract over 40 bird species including yellow-rumped warblers, tree swallows, and bluebirds. Plant in groupings to form evergreen screens or wildlife hedgerows, and allow the plant to grow to its natural multi-stemmed form for maximum habitat value.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement; well adapted to zones 3-7.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Welcome was developed in Canada from American gooseberry (Ribes hirtellum) stock, valued for combining good resistance to American gooseberry mildew — the disease that plagues many older European-type varieties — with reliable production of medium red berries carrying a pleasant, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. The upright, moderately vigorous bush is easier to manage and harvest than more sprawling heirloom types, and its cold hardiness suits it well to northern home gardens. Harvest when berries reach full color and slightly soften for fresh eating, or pick a bit earlier and firmer for pies, jams, and other cooked preparations where tartness is desired.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Welder is self-fertile and ripens in the mid-to-late season, and its Gulf Coast Texas origins make it especially well suited to hot, humid growing conditions along the coast.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Welder is a heritage Texas muscadine selection, originally found growing wild along the Texas Gulf Coast, long valued by home growers for its vigorous, reliably productive vines and dark bronze-to-purple berries with the strong, musky-sweet, classic muscadine flavor favored for fresh eating, jelly, and homemade wine. Its Gulf Coast origins give it excellent heat and humidity tolerance, and it has a long track record of thriving with minimal care in Texas and Louisiana home gardens where more refined modern cultivars can sometimes struggle. Welder is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinizer, though yields benefit from having other muscadine vines nearby. Like other muscadines, it shows strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make bunch grapes difficult in the humid South. Harvest as berries darken fully and detach easily from the stem with gentle pressure, and train the vigorous vine to a sturdy two-wire trellis with annual winter pruning.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; set the crown slightly below grade to encourage multiple basal shoots for a productive bush.
directions: Wellington XXX is a heritage English black currant cultivar dating to the early 20th century, still grown for its heavy, reliable yields of large, richly flavored, dark berries well suited to jams, syrups, and cordials. It is a vigorous, spreading bush that produces well even in cooler, shorter-season climates, and its mid-season ripening helps spread the harvest when grown with earlier or later black currant selections. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune out about a quarter of the oldest wood each winter to stimulate new fruiting canes, since black currants fruit best on one- and two-year-old growth. Watch for reduced vigor and yield in hot-summer regions, as this cultivar performs best where summers stay relatively cool.

common_name: Wentworth American Highbush Cranberry (Early-Ripening Fruit Selection)
plant_note: Set out a bare-root or container-grown Wentworth shrub in early spring into moist, well-drained soil, choosing a site with a half-day of shade if the location has hot afternoon sun.
directions: Set out a bare-root or container-grown Wentworth shrub in early spring into moist, well-drained soil, choosing a site with a half-day of shade if the location has hot afternoon sun, since this selection tolerates woodland-edge conditions better than many fruiting shrubs. Wentworth was selected for producing earlier-ripening, larger, better-flavored clusters of tart red berries than typical seedling highbush cranberries, though a second unrelated seedling nearby improves pollination and fruit set. The berries soften and mellow after a frost and cook down into a bright, tart preserve or sauce reminiscent of true cranberry, a useful substitute in regions where cranberry bogs are not practical. Its tolerance of part shade and reliable fruit set make Wentworth a good choice for a hedgerow or forest-garden edge planting where full sun is not available all day.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes from autumn to early spring; Whinham's Industry is notably tolerant of poor, heavy soils and partial shade compared with most other gooseberry cultivars.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, in full sun or light shade, and prune to an open vase shape each winter to ease harvesting among the thorny stems. A very old English cultivar dating to the mid-1800s, Whinham's Industry remains popular for its notable tolerance of poor, heavy, or shaded conditions where many other gooseberries struggle, along with strong resistance to American gooseberry mildew. Its medium-to-large, hairy-skinned berries ripen from green to a deep dusky red with a rich, sweet-tart flavor good for both dessert use and cooking. The vigorous, spreading habit and dependable heavy cropping have kept it a garden favorite for over a century.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 8–11; White Cross Berry is a drought-tolerant African savanna shrub or small tree with distinctive bicolor (green above, white/silver beneath) leaves bearing small, yellow star-shaped flowers and round, reddish-orange to dark-brown edible berries eaten across sub-Saharan Africa as a bush food and used medicinally.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, average to poor soil; Grewia bicolor is highly drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry and semi-arid conditions — once established it requires little or no supplemental water in warm arid and semi-arid climates. Grewia bicolor (White Cross Berry or Crossberry) is a thorny, much-branched shrub or small tree native to the dry, open savannas, bushveld, and semi-arid woodland of sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal east through Ethiopia and south through East Africa to South Africa and Mozambique — one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important shrubs of African savanna ecosystems. The distinctive bicolor leaves — deep green and glossy above, densely silver-white hairy and felted beneath — give the plant a shimmering two-tone appearance in the breeze. Small, 5-petaled, yellow or cream star-shaped flowers are borne prolifically from the leaf axils in summer, followed by round to oblong, 2–4-lobed berries — ripening from green through reddish-orange to dark brown or black — that are sweet-mucilaginous, edible raw or dried, and important bush food across the plant's range. The berries are browsed by elephants, giraffes, and many antelope species, and are eaten by indigenous peoples dried as a sweetener or fermented into beer. The roots and bark carry extensive traditional medicinal uses across sub-Saharan Africa for fevers, diarrhea, and sexually transmitted infections. An excellent drought-tolerant, wildlife-attracting shrub for hot, dry, sunny gardens in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring; white currants perform well trained as a cordon against a north- or east-facing wall.
directions: White currant is a yellow-fruited mutation of red currant sharing identical cultivation requirements: it fruits most heavily on spurs of two-year-old and older wood. The translucent, ivory-white berries are sweeter and milder than red currants and are prized for elegant fresh-eating and jellies. Prune each late winter to maintain 8–12 canes of mixed ages, removing canes older than 5 years. Harvest entire strigs when berries have turned fully translucent white-golden and taste sweet; check local Ribes restrictions before purchasing.

plant_note: Plant rooted hardwood cuttings or container shrubs in fall or very early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; white currant is the mildest-flavored of the currants, with translucent, pearl-like berries that are sweet enough to eat fresh.
directions: Plant rooted hardwood cuttings or container-grown shrubs in fall or very early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white currant fruits best with some afternoon shade in warm climates and benefits from a cross-pollinator though it is largely self-fertile. Ribes sativum in its white-fruited forms (often grouped with R. rubrum) produces distinctive, translucent, pearl-white to pale-pink berries with a milder, less tart flavor than red currants, making them more suitable for fresh eating and elegant as a garnish on desserts; they are excellent for jelly, wine, and as a decoration for cakes and pastries. White currant is one of the most attractive of all fruiting shrubs when in fruit — the translucent clusters catch the light beautifully. 'Blanka', 'Primus', and 'White Versailles' are classic cultivars available from specialty nurseries.

plant_note: Plant dormant hardwood-cutting-propagated bushes in fall into fertile soil in full sun to light shade; remove the oldest third of stems each winter to keep productive new wood coming.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall into fertile soil in full sun to light shade, removing the oldest third of stems each winter to keep productive new wood coming. White Imperial is a long-cultivated heirloom white currant prized as one of the sweetest and mildest of all currant varieties, with translucent, creamy-white berries pleasant enough to eat straight off the strig rather than only cooked into preserves. The upright, productive bush ripens long clusters in midsummer and is self-fertile, so a single bush sets a full crop. Its mild flavor and pale, attractive fruit make it popular for fresh eating, garnishing, and pale jellies where a less tart currant is wanted.

common_name: White Pearl Currant (Sweet Pale-Fruited Ornamental Currant)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring; White Pearl is a white-fruited currant, a color form of the red currant species, notable for milder, sweeter flavor than most red currants.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch); currants prefer cooler root zones and benefit from mulch. White Pearl is a white currant cultivar, a translucent, pale ivory-colored color form of the red currant species that lacks the anthocyanin pigment giving red currants their color, resulting in a noticeably milder, sweeter flavor with less tartness — a trait that makes white currants especially good for fresh eating out of hand rather than only for jelly and cooking. The long, drooping strigs of pearly, translucent berries are also strikingly ornamental against the green foliage. Self-fertile and productive, it fruits on spurs of older wood like other red-type currants, so prune to an open framework in winter and remove the oldest wood to maintain vigor. Net at ripening to protect fruit from birds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to average soil in zone 8–11; White Stinkwood is a large, graceful, fast-growing native shade tree of South Africa and eastern Africa, widely planted across the region as a street, park, and garden tree for its elegant, weeping form, light-filtering canopy, and excellent wildlife value — producing abundant small, yellow-orange to reddish drupes eaten by birds and small mammals.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to average soil; Celtis africana is drought tolerant once established, growing well in a wide range of soils including clay, rocky, and alkaline soils typical of the South African highveld and bushveld — water regularly only in the first year of establishment. Celtis africana (White Stinkwood, Witstinkhout) is a large, graceful, fast-growing deciduous to semi-evergreen tree native to the forests, river margins, and bush-margins of South Africa (particularly the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, and Mpumalanga) and extending north through East Africa. The English common name 'stinkwood' refers to the smell of freshly cut wood — the dried wood does not smell strongly and is actually a fine-grained, attractive timber used for furniture and flooring in South Africa (though far less valuable than the true 'Black Stinkwood,' Ocotea bullata). Celtis africana is one of South Africa's most popular garden shade trees: fast-growing, with an elegant, slightly weeping branch structure, fine-textured, lime-green foliage that provides deep shade, and outstanding wildlife value — the small, round, yellow-orange to red-black fruits are eagerly eaten by many fruit-eating birds including barbets, mousebirds, bulbuls, and starlings. The tree supports many butterfly species and is larval host plant for the Charaxes butterfly group.

plant_note: Transplant rooted runners in spring or fall; pin runner tips to moist soil and cut free when rooted. Easiest to establish from rooted plugs or runners rather than seed.
directions: Plant rooted runners in moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this native species is one parent of the cultivated strawberry and produces intensely flavorful small red fruits that surpass commercial strawberries in taste, though not in size. The plant spreads vigorously by runners to form a dense groundcover that suppresses weeds and tolerates moderate foot traffic. Fruits are borne in late spring through early summer; birds, chipmunks, and turtles compete for the harvest so a loose barrier net may be needed. Divide or thin the planting every 2–3 years by removing older central crowns and retaining the vigorous outer runners.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun; Wilder is an older American red currant cultivar valued for productivity and long, well-filled fruit clusters.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Wilder is an older American red currant cultivar long grown for its productivity and long, evenly filled clusters (strigs) of bright red, tart-sweet berries. It is self-fertile and bears reliably without a second bush for pollination, making it a practical single-plant choice for a small garden. Fruit is excellent for jelly, syrup, and baking, with the classic bright, tart currant flavor that mellows only somewhat with full ripeness. Because red currants fruit mainly on spurs of two- and three-year-old wood rather than new growth, prune to an open, vase-shaped framework each winter and remove any wood older than three years to keep the bush vigorous and productive. Net the bushes as fruit ripens, since birds are strongly drawn to currants.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; renewal-prune the oldest canes each winter to keep yields high.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, renewal-pruning the oldest canes each winter to keep yields high. Wilder is a vigorous early twentieth-century American red currant selected for its long, well-filled clusters of large, bright red berries and reliably heavy cropping. It is a workhorse jelly and juice currant, valued more for productivity and fruit size than for fresh eating, since the flavor stays tart even at full ripeness. Like other red currants it fruits on spurs of two- and three-year-old wood, and it is best grown in regions with cool summers and consistent moisture.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; Willamette is an Oregon State University release that became the backbone of Pacific Northwest commercial red raspberry production for decades and remains a dependable summer-bearing home garden variety.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil, and support the upright canes with a simple wire trellis to keep the heavy midseason crop off the ground. Willamette was released by Oregon State University and for much of the twentieth century was the standard red raspberry of the Pacific Northwest processing industry, valued for firm, richly flavored, deep-red berries that hold together well for freezing and canning as well as fresh eating. The floricanes bear a single concentrated crop in early-to-mid summer, and the plant's moderate vigor and reasonable disease tolerance made it a dependable choice for both commercial fields and home gardens for generations. It prefers the cooler summers of its native range and, like most red raspberries, is a more marginal performer in hot, humid climates, so give it the coolest, best-drained spot available outside the Pacific Northwest. Remove spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes each spring to the sturdiest four or five per foot of row.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement; very cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 3-7.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Willoughby was bred in Canada for genuine cold hardiness and good resistance to American gooseberry mildew, producing medium, deep red berries with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor good for fresh eating and cooking alike. The productive, reliable bush handles harsh northern winters better than many European-type gooseberries, making it a solid choice for cold-climate home orchards wanting good disease resistance without sacrificing fruit quality. Harvest when berries reach full color and slightly soften, and pick regularly through the ripening window, since gooseberries can be used both underripe and tart for cooking or fully ripe and sweet for fresh eating depending on preference.

plant_note: Sow cold-stratified seed in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; willow-leaved sea buckthorn is dioecious — plant at least one male per five or six females to ensure pollination and fruit production; it grows naturally along Himalayan river valleys and tolerates poor, gravelly, or stony soils.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil — willow-leaved sea buckthorn tolerates poor, gravelly, or stony ground and is highly drought-tolerant once established, making it a superb windbreak tree for cold, exposed sites. Cold-stratify seeds for 30–60 days before sowing in early spring, or sow fresh seed in fall for natural stratification. Because the species is dioecious, include at least one male tree for every five to six female trees to ensure reliable pollination and fruit set; the dense orange berry clusters ripen in late summer to autumn and are extraordinarily rich in vitamin C, carotenoids, and omega-7 fatty acids. Larger and more tree-like than common sea buckthorn (H. rhamnoides), it can reach 30 feet, providing significant shade and windbreak value while producing a heavy fruit crop.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February. Windsor requires 500–600 chill hours and is best suited for the colder areas of zone 9a where winter temperatures regularly provide adequate chilling. It is not recommended for zone 9b or warmer zones. Cross-pollination with another variety is beneficial for maximum yield.
directions: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Windsor is a southern highbush blueberry requiring 500–600 chill hours — more than the ultra-low-chill varieties like Flordablue and Biloxi, but still significantly less than northern varieties that require 800–1,200 hours. This intermediate chill requirement makes Windsor suitable for zone 9a where winters typically provide 500–700 chill hours but unsuitable for the warmer zone 9b areas. The advantage of Windsor's higher chill requirement is higher fruit quality — the berries are larger, firmer, darker, and more flavorful than very-low-chill varieties, with the rich, complex blueberry flavor that intensifies with more winter dormancy. Windsor was developed to provide the best possible fruit quality while still meeting the reduced chill requirements of the upper Gulf Coast. The midseason ripening (May–June in zone 9) follows the earliest varieties and provides an extended blueberry harvest season when planted alongside Biloxi or Flordablue.

plant_note: Plant grafted or own-rooted dormant vines in early spring on a well-drained slope with good air drainage.
directions: Wine grapes thrive in lean, well-drained soils with a pH of 5.5–6.5 and perform best on slopes with excellent air circulation to reduce disease pressure. Establish a vertical shoot positioning (VSP) trellis with catch wires at 4 and 5 ft above the cordon wire. Rigorous dormant pruning — leaving only 30–60 buds per vine depending on vigor — is essential for fruit quality. Harvest timing is cultivar- and use-specific; measure Brix (sugar) with a refractometer and monitor seed color and berry flavor.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or transplants in early spring; note that wineberry is invasive in much of the eastern U.S., so check local regulations before planting.
directions: Wineberry, native to Japan and China, produces small, brilliant red, jewel-like drupes with a sweet, delicate flavor; it is grown for fruit production in Asia and has naturalized extensively in the eastern U.S. and should be grown only in contained settings or where legal. The canes are covered in red glandular hairs and tip-root readily, so remove spent canes promptly and clear any rooted tips. Harvest when berries are uniformly bright red and detach easily from the sticky calyx — they do not ripen after picking and must be used within 1–2 days. Pruning follows the same floricane/primocane cycle as standard raspberries.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; mulch heavily with straw before the first hard freeze to protect crowns through harsh winters.
directions: Winona is an early-twentieth-century strawberry cultivar developed in Minnesota and grown for generations in northern home gardens for its exceptional cold hardiness and reliable annual June crop. The medium-sized berries are dark red, aromatic, and well suited to preserving, with a rich, old-fashioned strawberry flavor prized by heirloom growers. Vigorous runnering fills in matted rows quickly, making it well suited to the traditional matted-row growing system used across the northern Plains and upper Midwest. Because it predates most modern disease-resistant breeding, rotate planting sites and use certified disease-free stock to avoid buildup of soilborne pathogens.

common_name: Winter Sun Mahonia (Early-Flowering Glossy-Leaf Winter Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Winter Sun is a sister seedling to Charity, flowering earlier with glossy dark foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Winter Sun, a sister seedling to Charity, bears upright spikes of fragrant yellow flowers that open earlier in the fall-to-winter season than most Mahonia x media selections, held above glossy, dark green, holly-like evergreen foliage. Its earlier bloom timing extends the winter flowering window in the shade garden, providing an early nectar source before other Mahonia hybrids open. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes.

common_name: Winterthur Viburnum (Compact Possumhaw with Multi-Season Berry Color)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Winterthur is a compact possumhaw viburnum selection with berries that shift through pink, blue, and near-black as they ripen, all often visible on the same cluster at once.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; possumhaw viburnum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites, including rain gardens and pond margins. Winterthur is a compact selection of native possumhaw viburnum producing showy clusters of berries that pass through a striking sequence of pink, blue, and near-black as they ripen in late summer and fall, often displaying several colors on the same cluster at once, in addition to attractive burgundy-red fall foliage. Its smaller stature compared to the species fits typical residential borders better, and planting a second unrelated clone nearby improves the reliability and abundance of berry set.

common_name: Womack Blackberry (Texas A&M Heat-Tolerant Thorny Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart on a trellis. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, ripening in the main-season window in zones 8-9.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Womack is an erect, thorny blackberry released from the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program and bred specifically to withstand the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Texas and the western Gulf South. It produces medium to large, firm, sweet-tart berries with good flavor and holds up well to summer heat that causes softer varieties to decline in quality. As an older Texas A&M release, it is a dependable, disease-tolerant option where more modern thornless varieties struggle with heat stress. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select vigorous new primocanes to tie in for next year's crop; wear heavy gloves when working the thorny canes.

common_name: Woodard Rabbiteye Blueberry (Classic Large-Berried Southern Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Woodard needs a compatible rabbiteye pollinator such as Climax or Tifblue nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. One of the older, longer-established rabbiteye blueberry cultivars, Woodard is valued for its unusually large, soft-textured, mild-flavored berries that ripen in early-to-mid season, a bit ahead of many later rabbiteye types. The bushes are moderately vigorous and productive, though the soft fruit texture makes it better suited to fresh home use and processing than commercial shipping. Keep soil consistently moist through bloom and fruit development, and mulch well to conserve moisture and maintain the acidic soil conditions blueberries require.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil; worcesterberry is very thorny — wear heavy gloves when handling.
directions: The worcesterberry is a North American species of gooseberry (Ribes divaricatum) sometimes grown as a productive alternative to European gooseberries because it shows good resistance to powdery mildew and American gooseberry mildew. The small, dark purple-black berries resemble currants more than typical gooseberries and ripen in midsummer with a tart, rich flavor excellent for jams and pies. Prune to an open-vase structure each late winter, keeping 8–10 canes of mixed ages. Verify state restrictions on Ribes planting before ordering, as some states still restrict the genus.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Wyldewood produces heavier crops with cross-pollination from another elderberry variety nearby. In zone 9 it produces abundant flowers in May–June and ripe fruit clusters in July–August. Elderberries spread by root suckers in suitable conditions; manage spread with mowing around plantings.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil; Wyldewood is a named American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) cultivar developed from wild selections in Oklahoma by the Oklahoma State University extension program, selected for extraordinary production of large, dense berry clusters — corymbs up to 10–14 inches across with hundreds of small, dark purple-black berries per cluster. Wyldewood is considered one of the highest-yielding American elderberry cultivars, with mature plants producing 12–20 pounds or more of fruit clusters annually. The berries are used for elderberry syrup (widely used as an immune-support supplement), elderflower and elderberry liqueurs and wines, jams, pies, and lemonade. Raw elderberries contain very small amounts of cyanogenic compounds and should not be eaten raw in large quantities; cooking neutralizes these compounds. Wyldewood is specifically bred for Oklahoma and surrounding regions and performs excellently throughout zone 9 conditions.

common_name: Yadkin Southern Highbush Blueberry (Large-Fruited NC State Release)
plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Yadkin, a 1997 North Carolina State release, needs 500-600 chill hours and ripens late-mid season with large fruit and excellent soil adaptation.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Yadkin, released by North Carolina State University in 1997, needs a moderate 500 to 600 chill hours and ripens in the late-mid part of the season, bearing unusually large, flavorful berries on a bush noted for excellent adaptability across a range of soil types, from heavier clay-influenced ground to sandier sites, more forgiving than some southern highbush selections that demand near-perfect drainage. It suits the cooler edge of the Gulf South and areas just north of it where winter chill runs a bit higher than the mildest coastal zones. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain vigor.

common_name: Yellow Wonder Alpine Strawberry (Pale-Fruited Bird-Resistant Woodland Strawberry)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; the fine seed needs light and steady moisture to germinate.
directions: Yellow Wonder is a day-neutral alpine strawberry that ripens to a pale lemon-gold rather than red, a trait many gardeners value because birds are less likely to spot and peck the fruit before it can be picked. Plants form compact, runnerless clumps and flower and fruit continuously from summer into fall once established. Surface-sow seed indoors, keep evenly moist, and transplant seedlings into rich, well-drained soil in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates. The soft, sweet, low-acid berries have a pineapple-tinged wild-strawberry flavor and bruise easily, so pick and use them promptly rather than storing.

scientific_name: Rubus caesius x idaeus x ursinus hybrid
plant_note: Plant bare-root canes in spring on a sturdy two- or three-wire trellis; youngberry is a trailing type requiring support and grows best in warm, humid climates.
directions: The youngberry is a dewberry hybrid developed in Louisiana in the early 1900s by B.M. Young, producing very large, dark maroon-purple berries with a high juice content and sweet-tart flavor excellent for wine, juice, and pies. Culture is similar to boysenberry: train long, trailing canes on a T-trellis at 3 and 5 ft, fruiting on second-year floricanes; after harvest, cut all fruited canes to the ground and tie new primocanes in their place. The plants are less cold-hardy than standard blackberries and benefit from cane protection or mulching in zone 6 winters. Harvest when berries turn uniformly dark purple-black and release easily from the plug.

common_name: 4010 Forage Pea (Spring Field Pea Cover Crop)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in late summer for a fall cover; 4010 is a widely grown, tall, leafy field pea bred for quick biomass rather than seed harvest, commonly paired with oats as a companion cover crop.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed at a fairly high rate as soon as the ground can be worked in early spring, since 4010 peas germinate well in cool, moist soil but are not as winter-hardy as Austrian winter pea. Growers commonly mix it with spring oats, which give the tall, weak-stemmed vines something to climb and lean on, producing a combined stand that suppresses weeds quickly and can be mowed or grazed for forage or turned under as green manure. As a legume it fixes a meaningful amount of nitrogen for a following crop, and its rapid, dense early growth makes it a popular short-window cover between a spring vegetable harvest and a summer planting.

common_name: AU Early Cover Hairy Vetch (Early-Flowering Southern Hairy Vetch)
plant_note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover crop; AU Early Cover, an Auburn University-bred hairy vetch selection, flowers earlier than common hairy vetch, letting Deep South growers terminate and plant into it sooner ahead of a warm-season crop.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed in early fall onto a well-prepared bed, inoculating with the proper rhizobium if the field has not grown vetch recently. AU Early Cover was selected for earlier flowering than standard hairy vetch, which allows it to reach peak nitrogen-fixing biomass and be mowed or rolled down several weeks sooner than later-flowering vetch strains, an important advantage for growers on tight spring planting schedules in the Gulf South. Like other hairy vetches its scrambling vines climb over themselves and any companion cereal, forming a thick nitrogen-rich mulch that suppresses weeds and feeds the following crop as it breaks down.

common_name: AU Golden Sunn Hemp (Day-Neutral Seed-Producing Sunn Hemp)
plant_note: Broadcast or drill into warm soil after last frost; AU Golden flowers earlier than standard sunn hemp and can mature a viable seed crop even in the temperate Southeast.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed into warm, well-drained soil once temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, since this fast-growing tropical legume stalls in cool weather. AU Golden was bred at Auburn University from day-neutral sunn hemp germplasm specifically so growers as far north as Alabama and Georgia can save their own seed each year, unlike the older Tropic Sun cultivar, which needs short autumn days to flower and rarely sets viable seed on the mainland. Its early, abundant flowering also makes it a strong late-summer pollinator resource before it is mowed or crimped for nitrogen-rich, quickly decomposing biomass. Terminate at first bloom for maximum soil-building value, or let a portion go to seed to build up your own low-cost regional seed supply.

common_name: AU Merit Hairy Vetch (Early-Flowering High-Biomass Hairy Vetch)
plant_note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover crop; AU Merit, bred at Auburn University, flowers roughly two weeks earlier than common hairy vetch and produces more biomass, letting it be terminated sooner ahead of a spring crop.
directions: Broadcast or drill inoculated seed into a prepared seedbed in fall, providing a companion cereal grain such as rye or wheat as a scrambling support for the vining growth if a mixed planting is wanted. AU Merit was bred at Auburn University to flower roughly two weeks earlier than common hairy vetch strains while producing greater overall biomass, letting growers terminate the cover crop and fix substantial nitrogen (often 100 lb or more per acre) sooner ahead of a spring vegetable planting than standard hairy vetch allows. Its sprawling, viny growth forms a dense, weed-suppressing mat over winter. Terminate by mowing or rolling at or just after flowering, since vetch left to set seed can become a volunteer weed in following crops.

common_name: AU Robin Crimson Clover (Early-Maturing Reseeding Crimson Clover)
plant_note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover crop; AU Robin, bred at Auburn University, matures and flowers earlier than common crimson clover and reseeds itself reliably, making it well suited to the Gulf South's mild winters.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a prepared seedbed in fall, raking lightly to ensure good seed-to-soil contact. AU Robin was bred at Auburn University specifically for the Gulf South, flowering and setting seed earlier than common crimson clover strains, which allows it to complete its life cycle and reseed itself reliably even where a following summer crop needs the ground relatively early. Its brilliant crimson flower spikes provide excellent early-season pollinator forage in addition to nitrogen fixation and weed suppression. Because it reseeds so readily, a single planting can establish a self-sustaining crimson clover cover crop rotation in a bed over successive years if allowed to set seed before termination.

common_name: AU Sunrise Crimson Clover (Early-Blooming Reseeding Crimson Clover)
plant_note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring legume cover crop; AU Sunrise, released jointly by Auburn University and the USDA NRCS Jimmy Carter Plant Materials Center, blooms up to two weeks earlier than AU Robin and three weeks earlier than Dixie at lower latitudes.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a prepared seedbed in fall so plants can establish before the first hard freeze, then overwinter as a low rosette before resuming vigorous growth in late winter. AU Sunrise was specifically selected for very early flowering, which lets it complete seed set and reseed itself well ahead of the date a following summer crop needs the ground, an advantage over standard crimson clover strains that mature later in the Gulf South's mild winters. Its brilliant crimson flower spikes open earlier than almost any other winter annual legume, providing a critical early nectar source for emerging native bees while the plant fixes nitrogen and suppresses winter weeds. Because it reseeds so reliably, a single planting can sustain a self-renewing crimson clover stand across several seasons if allowed to shatter seed before termination.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Abyssinian crambe is a fast-growing brassica oilseed grown as a short, single-season summer annual rather than an overwintering cover.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed about a half-inch deep into a firm, well-drained seedbed in early spring once frost danger has passed for seedlings, keeping the surface evenly moist until the stand is up. Crambe abyssinica is an Ethiopian-origin brassica relative of cabbage and mustard grown almost entirely for its small round seeds, which are unusually rich in erucic acid and pressed for industrial lubricants, nylon precursors, and biodiesel rather than food use. It bolts quickly to a branching, waist-high plant topped with small white flowers, then sets seed pods within about three months, making it a useful short-cycle cash or rotation crop between vegetable plantings. Mow and incorporate residue after seed harvest, or terminate at early flowering as a green manure, since like other brassicas its glucosinolate-rich tissue offers some biofumigant suppression of soilborne pathogens when tilled in fresh.

common_name: Ace Forage Cowpea (Small-Seeded Texas Wildlife and Cover Crop Cowpea)
plant_note: Drill or broadcast into warm soil from mid-spring through early summer once frost danger has passed and soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Ace is a small-seeded forage cowpea bred by the Texas A&M AgriLife Research Forage Legume Breeding Program specifically for wildlife plots, cover cropping, and legume hay, released in 2018. Its smaller seed gives more seed per pound than older varieties like Iron and Clay, allowing lower seeding rates while still producing heavy biomass on sandy, low-rainfall soils. It blooms later in the season than comparable varieties, reaching first flower in late summer with seed maturing by mid-fall, which helps it avoid early frost kill in more northern parts of its range. Left to mature, a portion of its seed germinates quickly after ripening while the remainder germinates over the following months, giving stands some ability to reseed themselves.

plant_note: Sow in early spring around the last frost date, or in late summer 6–8 weeks before first frost to allow fall establishment.
directions: Inoculate seed with Medicago-specific rhizobium and broadcast at 15–20 lb per acre (about 1/4 oz per 100 sq ft), raking seed to 1/4 in depth into a firm, well-prepared seedbed with pH 6.5–7.0. Alfalfa fixes 100–200 lb of nitrogen per acre per year once established and deep taproots (up to 6 ft) break hardpan and mine subsoil minerals. Terminate by mowing at early bloom stage — typically every 30–40 days in summer — before the first killing frost; turning it under releases a large pulse of nitrogen. In perennial plantings, allow one cutting to go to seed to rejuvenate the stand every two or three years.

common_name: Alice White Clover (Large-Leaved Grazing and Cover Clover)
plant_note: Broadcast in spring or late summer onto a firm, weed-free seedbed; Alice establishes into a persistent, spreading perennial stand suited to pasture, orchard understory, or living mulch.
directions: Broadcast inoculated seed at a light rate onto a firm, weed-free seedbed no more than 1/4 inch deep. Alice is a large-leaved white clover bred in New Zealand for vigorous stolon spread and strong regrowth after grazing or mowing, giving it more bulk and ground coverage than common Dutch white clover while remaining lower-growing than giant ladino types. Its aggressive stoloniferous habit lets it fill bare patches quickly, making it a reliable nitrogen-fixing living mulch between perennial crop rows or a component in long-term pasture and cover mixes. Mow periodically to prevent taller companion plants from shading it out, and expect the stand to persist and spread for several years once established.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained to seasonally wet, alkaline to neutral, clay-loam to sandy loam, lean to average soil in full sun; alkali sacaton is the most alkaline- and salt-tolerant of the native southwestern bunchgrasses, growing on saline flats, alkali playas, and seasonally flooded bottomlands where most grasses cannot survive.
directions: Direct sow in spring in well-drained to seasonally wet, alkaline to neutral, clay-loam to sandy loam, lean to average soil in full sun; alkali sacaton is one of the most ecologically important and visually striking native grasses of the arid and semi-arid Southwest — a large, coarse bunchgrass producing massive, open, airy panicles (up to 20 inches long) of extraordinarily fine-textured, wind-trembling seed clusters that light up golden in morning and evening light. The enormous panicle creates one of the most beautiful seed head effects of any native grass — a luminous, cloud-like mass of fine-branched flower stalks hovering above the blue-green foliage in summer. The primary ecological niche is alkaline, saline, and seasonally flooded low-lying sites — alkali flats, salt meadows, river floodplains, and irrigation-influenced soils — where its exceptional tolerance for salt and alkali makes it the dominant or sole grass. An outstanding ornamental grass for challenging alkaline soils of the arid West. Very fast-germinating and establishing from seed. Related to prairie dropseed (S. heterolepis) but much larger.

plant_note: Broadcast seed in early spring as soon as soils can be worked, or frost-seed in late winter; alsike clover is one of the few clovers that establishes well in wet, acidic, or poorly drained soils where red and white clover fail. Inoculate seed with Rhizobium leguminosarum trifolii.
directions: Broadcast seed at 6–8 lbs per acre in early spring in full sun onto a firm, moist seedbed; alsike clover tolerates wet, poorly drained, and moderately acidic soils (pH as low as 5.5) where red clover and white clover fail to persist, making it the preferred clover for heavy-clay, low-lying, or seasonally flooded areas. Trifolium hybridum produces erect to ascending stems with smooth trifoliate leaves and distinctive pink-and-white bicolor flower heads that are exceptionally attractive to honeybees and are considered one of the best bee plants among the clovers; it is a natural hybrid species named for its intermediate characteristics between red and white clover. It is shorter-lived than red clover in persistently dry soils but outperforms all other clovers on wet, cold, or acidic ground. Fixes 80–160 lbs N/acre and is widely used in cool, wet northern and Pacific Northwest cover crop mixes.

common_name: Alyceclover (Warm-Season Forage and Cover Crop Legume)
plant_note: Broadcast or drill into warm, well-prepared soil after all frost danger has passed; alyceclover establishes slowly at first but grows vigorously once soil and air are warm, and it tolerates the wet, poorly drained, low-fertility soils common along the Gulf Coast better than most other summer legumes.
directions: Broadcast seed inoculated with the appropriate rhizobium at a shallow depth into a firm, warm seedbed in full sun; alyceclover is a warm-season annual legume long used across the Gulf South as summer forage, hay, and a nitrogen-fixing cover crop on soils too wet, acidic, or infertile for cowpeas or soybeans. It forms a dense, leafy, upright stand that suppresses weeds, tolerates close grazing or repeated mowing by regrowing from lower nodes, and fixes meaningful nitrogen for the crop that follows. Because it is frost-tender and slow to establish in cool soil, wait until soil has fully warmed before sowing, and expect a full, weed-suppressing stand within six to eight weeks under good moisture. Mow or graze before heavy frost, or terminate and incorporate the residue three to four weeks ahead of the next planting to let the nitrogen-rich foliage break down.

common_name: Amclo Arrowleaf Clover (Early-Maturing Dark-Seeded Arrowleaf Clover)
plant_note: Broadcast or drill in fall on well-drained soil; Amclo is an early-maturing arrowleaf clover cultivar, one of the original dark-seeded selections alongside Yuchi and Meechee that founded the modern arrowleaf breeding lines.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a well-prepared, well-drained bed in early fall and lightly cover, since arrowleaf clover establishes slowly at first but grows rapidly once cool weather sets in. Amclo is an early-maturing arrowleaf clover cultivar with dark, hard seed, developed as part of the same breeding work that produced Yuchi and Meechee, and its earlier flowering makes it a useful choice for pairing with later cultivars to extend bloom and nitrogen-fixing coverage across the spring. Its tall, upright stems topped with pinkish-white flower heads distinguish it in a mixed planting from lower-growing clovers, and it reseeds well on well-drained upland soils when allowed to flower before termination. Mow or graze before the plants become too woody and fibrous, since arrowleaf clover forage quality declines as it approaches full maturity.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; scarify seeds lightly for more uniform germination. Inoculate with Aeschynomene-specific Bradyrhizobium inoculant for nitrogen fixation in soils where the plant has not grown before.
directions: A native annual legume of moist, open, disturbed habitats, roadsides, and wet meadows in the southeastern US and throughout tropical America, producing delicate, sensitive pinnate leaves and clusters of small yellow, brownish-red-veined pea flowers from summer through fall. The jointed seed pods break apart at the segments at maturity — a characteristic trait that gives the plant the common name 'joint-vetch' — and the seeds are relished by mourning doves, quail, and other seed-eating birds, making this an excellent wildlife food plot legume for warm climates. Direct sow after last frost in moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; inoculate with Aeschynomene-specific Bradyrhizobium to maximize nitrogen fixation in new planting sites. It tolerates periodic flooding and is well adapted to the wet, disturbed margins of ponds and seasonal wet areas throughout zones 7-11.

plant_note: Sow 2–6 weeks before first fall frost; germinates and establishes faster than perennial ryegrass and can be interseeded into standing late-season crops.
directions: Broadcast seed at 20–25 lb per acre (about 1/2 oz per 100 sq ft) onto a prepared surface and rake to 1/4 in depth; annual ryegrass has one of the fastest establishment rates of all cool-season grasses, providing rapid erosion control and weed suppression. The dense, fibrous root system scavenges residual nitrogen effectively, locking it up over winter to prevent leaching. Terminate in early spring before it joints and sets seed — once headed, it becomes very difficult to kill without herbicide or repeated tillage. Mow to 2–3 in and till, or use a roller-crimper at boot stage for no-till termination; allow residue 2–3 weeks to break down before planting.

plant_note: Broadcast seed onto a firm seedbed in fall into average, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; sourclover is a fast, self-reseeding winter annual legume more compact than biennial yellow and white sweetclover.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, weed-suppressed seedbed in average, well-drained soil in full sun; sourclover is a fast-growing winter annual legume with small, bright yellow, sweetly fragrant flowers on slender spikes, related to but shorter-lived and less woody than the biennial yellow and white sweetclovers grown for forage and honey production. It fixes nitrogen efficiently over a single growing season, germinating with fall rains and completing its life cycle by late spring, making it well suited to rotation ahead of a summer cash crop without the multi-year commitment of biennial sweetclovers. It is notably tolerant of alkaline and saline soils where many other cover crop legumes struggle, and it self-seeds reliably once introduced to a compatible site. Mow or incorporate at early flowering for maximum green manure value, since the coumarin compounds that give sweetclovers their characteristic scent can taint hay if not properly cured.

common_name: Appin Turnip (Fast-Maturing Multi-Graze Forage Turnip Cover Crop)
plant_note: Sow in late summer, by roughly six weeks before the average first fall frost, for reliable winterkill and fast establishment.
directions: Broadcast or drill the fine seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer, since Appin establishes fast and can be ready for a first grazing or mowing in under two months. Bred as a multi-cut forage turnip, Appin produces a long, carrot-shaped root rather than a broad bulb, along with abundant regrowth after cutting, so it can be grazed or mowed more than once before winter. It reliably winterkills in colder zones when sown early enough, leaving decomposing roots and residue that add organic matter and open channels in the topsoil ahead of a spring planting. Where winters are mild enough that it survives, mow or graze before flowering to prevent it from setting seed.

common_name: Argentine Bahiagrass (Broad-Leaved Low-Maintenance Pasture and Lawn Grass)
plant_note: Seed or sod in late spring through summer once soil is warm; Argentine bahiagrass has broader, darker green leaves than Pensacola bahiagrass and is more commonly used for lawns rather than pasture and roadside plantings.
directions: Seed or sod in late spring through summer once soil is consistently warm, in average to poor, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun. Argentine bahiagrass bears broader, darker green leaf blades than the more common Pensacola bahiagrass, giving it a coarser but more lawn-like appearance, and is widely used for low-maintenance home lawns, roadsides, and erosion control across the Gulf South where its deep, extensive root system provides excellent drought tolerance once established. It requires little fertilizer and tolerates poor, sandy soils that stress most other turf grasses, though its tall, wiry seed heads need frequent mowing to keep a tidy appearance. Mow regularly through the growing season, and expect it to go dormant and brown after the first hard frost.

common_name: Aroostook Winter Rye (Cold-Hardy Standard Cover Crop Cereal Rye)
plant_note: Sow in fall through early winter; Aroostook, developed in Maine, is a widely used cover crop cereal rye valued as a dependable, cold-hardy standard for winter cover and spring weed suppression.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed into a prepared seedbed in fall, as late as early winter in mild climates since cereal rye germinates in cold soil better than almost any other cover crop grain. Aroostook, developed in Maine, is considered a gold-standard cover crop cereal rye cultivar, valued for outstanding cold hardiness, rapid fall establishment, and a dense root system that suppresses weeds and prevents erosion through winter. In spring it produces allelopathic compounds as it decomposes that further suppress weed germination in the following crop, a widely used benefit in no-till and reduced-till vegetable systems. Mow and terminate before the rye sets seed, typically at or just after flowering, since mature rye can be difficult to kill and may become a volunteer weed if allowed to seed.

plant_note: Sow in fall in mild-winter regions for late-season biomass and nitrogen.
directions: Inoculate with clover rhizobia and broadcast at about 0.2-0.3 lb per 1,000 sq ft onto a firm seedbed, covering no deeper than 0.25 inch. Arrowleaf clover is a reseeding annual legume of the southern United States that produces high biomass and fixes nitrogen well into late spring. It is later maturing than crimson clover, extending the window of living cover and pollinator bloom. Terminate by mowing at early to mid bloom, then incorporate or leave residue as mulch. Allowing a portion to set seed lets the stand reseed naturally for the following season.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill in fall; in zone 9 sow October–November. Australian Winter Pea is cold-hardy to about 10–15°F once established and is one of the most reliable cool-season leguminous cover crops for the Gulf South — it establishes in fall, grows slowly through winter, and produces a large flush of biomass in late winter and early spring before being terminated ahead of the spring garden. Inoculate with hairy vetch-type Rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Terminate by mowing or rolling when pods begin to form.
directions: Broadcast 40–80 lbs per acre (or 2–3 oz per 100 sq ft) into prepared soil in fall; Australian Winter Pea (Lathyrus hirsutus) is a vining, annual cool-season legume used as a winter cover crop and green manure throughout the Deep South, Gulf Coast, and mid-South. It is one of the few leguminous cover crops that establishes reliably in Gulf Coast fall conditions, tolerating the warm early-fall temperatures that prevent hairy vetch from establishing and the occasional winter cold snaps that kill crimson clover. The sprawling, twining vines produce a dense, weed-suppressing mat through winter and a large flush of nitrogen-rich biomass in late winter–early spring. When inoculated with the correct Rhizobium strain, it fixes 50–100 lbs of nitrogen per acre. Australian Winter Pea is sometimes called hairy vetchling or Caley pea; it is not edible and should not be confused with edible garden peas. Terminate by mowing or rolling 3–4 weeks before the next crop to allow residue to decompose and release nitrogen.

plant_note: Sow in early fall, often mixed with a cereal, so vines establish before frost.
directions: Inoculate seed with pea-vetch rhizobia and drill at 1.5-2 inches deep or broadcast at about 2-4 lb per 1,000 sq ft into a firm seedbed. Austrian winter pea is a viny legume that fixes substantial nitrogen and is frequently sown with cereal rye or oats for support and biomass. It overwinters in mild climates and resumes vigorous vining growth in spring. Terminate by mowing or crimping at early flowering when nitrogen fixation peaks, then incorporate or leave as mulch. The residue releases nitrogen quickly, benefiting a following heavy-feeding vegetable crop.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill after all frost danger has passed into warm soil in full sun; bahiagrass germinates slowly and unevenly, and stands often take a full season to fully establish, but once rooted it forms a durable, low-maintenance, deep-rooted sod that persists for years.
directions: Broadcast seed at 15–20 lb/acre into warm, well-prepared soil in full sun; slow to establish but exceptionally drought-tolerant, low-input, and persistent once rooted, thanks to a deep, extensive root system. Bahiagrass is a warm-season perennial grass widely planted across the Gulf South and Southeast as a durable pasture, hay, and erosion-control grass, particularly valued on poor, sandy, or infertile soils where few other forage grasses perform reliably. Its deep, tough root system makes it one of the most drought-resistant pasture grasses available in the region, and its low fertility requirements and tolerance of close, continuous grazing have made it a standard choice for Gulf Coast livestock pasture for decades. The characteristic seed heads, forked into a distinctive V or Y shape, are a recognizable feature of bahiagrass pastures throughout summer and fall. A tough, low-maintenance, long-lived grass for Gulf South pasture, roadside, or erosion-control plantings, zone 7–10.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before frost; balansa clover is exceptionally flood- and waterlogging-tolerant, making it ideal for wet, low-lying spots.
directions: Broadcast tiny seed at 2–4 lb/acre (due to its small seed size) onto a firm, moist seedbed; balansa clover establishes quickly and tolerates prolonged waterlogging that would kill crimson or Persian clover.
