Leucaena leucocephala (leadtree or wild tamarind) is a Central American tropical legume tree of extraordinary importance in global tropical agriculture — ranked among the most useful trees in the world for nitrogen fixation (fixing up to 500 lbs of nitrogen per acre per year), fast biomass production for green manure, livestock fodder, fuel wood, and erosion control in tropical agroforestry systems across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. It grows extraordinarily fast (to 15–20 feet in a year) in poor, dry soils and is highly drought-tolerant once established. Young leaves, seeds, and pods are edible as a vegetable in some cuisines; however, a toxic alkaloid (mimosine) limits consumption quantities. The tree is listed as invasive in Florida and Hawaii where it crowds out native vegetation in disturbed areas. In tropical agricultural systems, its nitrogen-fixing capacity and drought tolerance make it a key component of alley cropping systems and organic farming in the humid tropics.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy, neutral to slightly alkaline, low-fertility soil in full sun; scarify seed lightly and inoculate with medic-type Rhizobium before sowing; little burr medic self-seeds prolifically in suitable conditions and can maintain itself without reseeding in dryland farming systems.
directions: Direct sow in fall in dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy, neutral to slightly alkaline, low-fertility soil in full sun; scarify seed lightly and inoculate with medic-type Rhizobium before sowing; little burr medic self-seeds prolifically in suitable conditions and can maintain itself without reseeding in dryland farming systems. Medicago minima is a prostrate, hairy annual medic native to dry, disturbed, sandy soils of the Mediterranean region and widely naturalized throughout the dryland regions of the world; it produces tiny, yellow, pea-like flowers and distinctive spiny, coiled seed pods with hooked spines (burrs) that aid in seed dispersal, and fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium root nodules in poor, thin, sandy soils where clover and alfalfa struggle. It is particularly useful as a self-reseeding annual cover crop in dryland farming systems, sandy coastal gardens, and dry herb garden paths where its low, prostrate habit and nitrogen-fixing ability improve soil fertility with minimal water input.

common_name: Louisiana S-1 White Clover (Heat- and Drought-Tolerant Gulf South White Clover)
plant_note: Sow in fall for overwintering cover, or late winter in mild Gulf Coast climates; Louisiana S-1 was selected by the LSU AgCenter specifically for better heat and drought tolerance than common ladino white clover strains.
directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a firm, prepared bed in fall and rake lightly so the small seed makes good soil contact. Louisiana S-1 is an intermediate-type white clover developed by the LSU AgCenter to outlast common ladino clover through the long, humid summers and periodic drought typical of the Gulf South, while still flowering steadily through the growing season to support pollinators. It spreads readily by stolons to form a dense living mulch beneath fruit trees, in orchard rows, or overseeded into warm-season pasture grasses, fixing nitrogen that benefits neighboring plantings. Where summers turn hot and dry it reliably persists and reseeds better than northern-bred white clover cultivars, making it a dependable long-term groundcover rather than a one-season planting.

plant_note: Broadcast seed onto a firm seedbed in fall, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; low hop clover germinates with fall rains, overwinters as a low rosette, and completes its life cycle by late spring.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, weed-suppressed seedbed in average, well-drained soil in full sun; low hop clover is a small, low-growing annual clover with tiny, bright yellow, hop-like flower heads that dry to a distinctive papery brown as seed matures. It fixes modest nitrogen while providing quick, dense soil cover and light forage value, and its low, spreading habit makes it a good short-season nurse cover between vegetable plantings or in orchard row middles. Because it completes its life cycle quickly, it fits well into a rotation ahead of a warm-season cash crop, either tilled in green for maximum nitrogen contribution or left to mature and self-seed for a returning stand. It tolerates lean, sandy, or compacted soils where richer clovers may fail to establish reliably.

common_name: Lutana Cicer Milkvetch (Rhizomatous Perennial Range and Cover Crop Legume)
plant_note: Direct-sow scarified, properly inoculated seed in early spring into lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; requires a Rhizobium strain specific to cicer milkvetch, distinct from common pea or bean inoculants.
directions: Direct-sow scarified, properly inoculated seed into a lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline seedbed in early spring, since cicer milkvetch requires a specific Rhizobium strain rather than the common pea or bean inoculants. Lutana, released from Bridger, Montana plant materials work, was selected for early spring growth, fast recovery after cutting, and vigorous rhizome spread, making it one of the most widely planted cicer milkvetch cultivars for range seeding and long-term cover. Establishment is slow the first year while the plant builds its rhizome system, but stands become dense and highly productive by the second or third season and can persist for a decade or more without reseeding. Because it spreads aggressively underground, give it dedicated space away from less competitive companion species.

plant_note: Sow in late summer 6–10 weeks before first fall frost, or in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Mammoth is a single-cut, late-maturing type of red clover that produces the largest plant mass and highest nitrogen fixation of the standard red clovers.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 10–12 lbs per acre (1 lb per 1,000 sq ft) onto a firm, weed-free seedbed; inoculate with clover rhizobia for reliable nitrogen fixation in new ground. Mammoth Red Clover is a large, late-maturing single-cut type that produces more biomass per planting than standard medium red clover, reaching 3–4 feet in height and fixing 80–200 lbs of nitrogen per acre when properly inoculated; it is best terminated at early bloom for maximum nitrogen availability to the following crop. The large, showy magenta flower heads are outstanding for pollinators — a diverse range of native bees, bumble bees, and honey bees work the blooms heavily. In the South, sow in fall as a winter annual that overwinters, blooms in spring, and is terminated before summer cash crops go in.

common_name: Mancan Buckwheat (Large-Seeded Canadian Cover Crop Buckwheat)
plant_note: Sow anytime after last frost in warm, frost-free weather; a fast-establishing large-seeded selection that flowers in five to six weeks.
directions: Broadcast seed about half an inch deep into warm, workable soil any time after the last frost, since Mancan germinates within days and quickly forms a dense weed-smothering canopy. Developed in Canada, Mancan is a large-seeded selection with bigger leaves and thicker stems than older buckwheat varieties, giving it slightly greater biomass and a more robust stand for soil building and pollinator forage. Mow or till it under at first bloom, roughly five to six weeks after sowing, before seed sets, since buckwheat reseeds readily and can become a volunteer weed if left to mature. Because it breaks down quickly, it can be followed by a fall crop within two to three weeks of incorporation.

plant_note: Broadcast onto cold, newly workable soil as early in spring as the ground can be tilled, since this is among the most cold-tolerant sweetclovers.
directions: Broadcast onto cold, newly workable soil as early in spring as the ground can be tilled, since this is among the most cold-tolerant sweetclovers, long used as a green manure across Manchuria, Siberia, and northern China. Grow it as a short annual plow-down crop or let it stand a second season biennially for maximum root and nitrogen-fixing benefit before turning it under. As with other sweetclovers, avoid feeding moldy or improperly cured hay, because damaged foliage develops coumarin compounds that convert to a livestock-toxic anticoagulant.

plant_note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) when soil temperature is consistently above 65F; Manilagrass spreads more slowly than Empire or other Zoysia japonica cultivars, so plugging on a tight grid or laying full sod gives the fastest usable lawn.
directions: Install sod or plugs in spring through midsummer, keeping consistently moist during establishment, then mow at 1-2 inches with a sharp reel or rotary mower. Manilagrass is a fine-bladed, dense, dark-green zoysia species distinct from the broader-leaved Zoysia japonica used in cultivars like Empire, prized specifically for tolerating more shade than almost any other warm-season turfgrass while still forming a lush, carpet-like, golf-green-quality lawn in full sun. It spreads by both rhizomes and stolons but fills in more slowly than japonica-type zoysia, so patience during establishment pays off with a notably fine, plush texture once mature. Like other zoysias, it goes dormant and straw-colored after the first hard frost and greens back up in spring, and its dense growth habit resists weed encroachment once established. Watch for thatch buildup over time and dethatch periodically; avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which encourages thatch and disease pressure more than it improves this naturally slow, dense-growing grass.

common_name: Manor Buckwheat (Large-Seeded Canadian Cover Crop Buckwheat)
plant_note: Broadcast or drill into warm soil after all frost danger has passed, since Manor is killed by the lightest freeze.
directions: Manor was released by Agriculture Canada in the 1970s and became the dominant large-seeded buckwheat grown across the Northeast and Canadian prairies through the 1990s, prized for the bold seed size millers want for whole groats and soba flour. Drill or broadcast into a warm, well-worked seedbed once soil has warmed in late spring, then roll or shallow-harrow to firm the seedbed for even emergence. Its rapid, dense canopy smothers summer weeds within a few weeks and can be mowed or turned under at first bloom to build organic matter ahead of a fall crop. Because it carries no frost tolerance, time fall plow-down before the first killing freeze to avoid losing the stand outright.

subcategory: Southern African drought-tolerant edible tuber legume
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or in warm soil in full sun in sandy, well-drained, nutrient-poor soil in zone 9–12; Marama Bean (Morama Bean, Gemsbok Bean) is a perennial, tuberous-rooted wild legume from the Kalahari and Namib desert regions of Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa — a trailing vine developing an enormous edible storage tuber (sometimes reaching 100 kg in old plants) and producing flat woody pods with 2–3 large seeds with outstanding nutritional content: 30–35% protein and 40% fat, comparable to soybeans and peanuts combined.
directions: Direct sow Marama Bean in sandy, well-drained, nutrient-poor soil in full sun after last frost or year-round in zone 10–12; minimal fertilization needed; plants develop a large taproot tuber — do not disturb; harvest seeds when pods dry; water only during establishment. Tylosema esculentum is one of the most nutritionally remarkable wild legumes known — its seeds contain approximately 30–35% protein and 38–40% fat, making them nutritionally comparable to combining soybean and peanut in a single seed. For the San (Bushman) and other indigenous peoples of the Kalahari, marama beans have been a critical dry-season protein and fat source for thousands of years — seeds are boiled, roasted, or ground into a nutritious paste or flour, and the seeds can also be roasted to produce a beverage resembling coffee. The massive underground tuber (technically a massive swollen hypocotyl) accumulates water and carbohydrates over decades — older plants may develop tubers weighing 50–100 kg — and the water-rich flesh has historically provided emergency moisture in the desert. The trailing stems and attractive round leaves grow across sandy desert soils and fix nitrogen through root nodules. Under cultivation in well-drained, sunny garden conditions in zone 9–12, marama bean provides a drought-tolerant ground cover and nitrogen fixer while producing protein-rich seeds. Of serious interest to researchers as a potential drought-tolerant protein crop for arid regions facing food insecurity.

plant_note: Direct-sow from spring through midsummer for late-season grazing or cover, since Maris Kestrel is a short, leafy type bred for a long growing window.
directions: Maris Kestrel is a short-stemmed, high leaf-to-stem forage kale bred for excellent digestibility and cold tolerance, widely used to extend the grazing season into winter and as a wildlife food plot planting. Broadcast or drill into a firm, fertile seedbed from spring into midsummer, since the crop needs a long window before it reaches grazing readiness in late fall or winter. Its compact stature and lodging-resistant stems keep leaves off the ground and palatable even after hard frosts sweeten the foliage. Where used strictly as a cover crop, mow or graze off before bolting the following spring to prevent volunteer reseeding.

common_name: Marshall Annual Ryegrass (Georgia-Bred Cold-Tolerant Italian Ryegrass)
plant_note: Drill or broadcast in early fall for winter cover, or in early spring where summers stay cool; this cultivar is more winter-hardy and later-maturing than common annual ryegrass.
directions: Broadcast or drill into a prepared or no-till seedbed in early fall for a dense, fibrous-rooted winter cover that scavenges leftover nitrogen and improves soil tilth. Marshall is an older, widely grown Georgia-developed selection valued for better winter survival and later spring maturity than common annual ryegrass, giving a longer window of grazing or biomass production before it heads out. Terminate by mowing, herbicide, or crimping before seed set in spring to avoid it becoming a weedy volunteer in the following crop. Its extensive fibrous root system is particularly effective at reducing soil compaction and erosion on row-crop ground over winter.

common_name: Maton Cereal Rye (Texas-Bred Winter Cover & Grazing Rye)
plant_note: Drill seed in fall while soil is still workable, allowing several weeks of growth before the first hard freeze.
directions: Maton is a Texas A&M-developed cereal rye selected for strong early fall growth, winter hardiness, and grazing recovery, making it popular as both a forage rye and a soil-building cover crop across the southern Plains. It tolerates close, repeated grazing or mowing better than many rye types, regrowing from the crown to provide extended winter and early-spring ground cover. Left unmowed, it produces heavy biomass and a dense root mat that suppresses weeds and scavenges residual nitrogen ahead of summer planting. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or tillage before seed set to prevent volunteer regrowth.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill in fall on well-drained soil; Meechee matures later than Yuchi, extending flowering and nitrogen fixation deeper into late spring.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a well-prepared, well-drained bed in early fall and lightly cover, since arrowleaf clover seedlings establish slowly but grow rapidly once cool, moist weather sets in. Meechee is a later-maturing arrowleaf clover cultivar than the widely planted Yuchi, flowering and fixing nitrogen further into late spring before it finally sets seed, which lengthens the pollinator forage and cover window in a mixed winter-annual planting. Its tall, upright growth and arrow-shaped leaves distinguish it in the field from crimson or white clover stands, and it reseeds readily on well-drained soils when allowed to flower before termination. Pair it with an earlier arrowleaf cultivar or crimson clover in a blend to spread bloom time and grazing or green-manure availability across more of the spring.

common_name: Melrose Austrian Winter Pea (Ascochyta-Tolerant Winter-Hardy Forage Pea)
plant_note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early to mid-fall so vines establish before hard freezes; Melrose overwinters as a low rosette and resumes vigorous vining growth in spring.
directions: Melrose is a purple-flowered, indeterminate Austrian winter pea that ranks among the most winter-hardy field pea cultivars evaluated in southeastern variety trials, holding its own alongside Granger and Commonwinter through hard winters. Its long, sprawling vines produce heavier dry-matter yields than the older common Austrian winter and Fenn types, and it carries useful tolerance to Ascochyta blight, a common foliar disease of overwintering peas. Drill seed into a firm, fertile fall seedbed at a depth that ensures good soil contact, since the large seeds need consistent moisture to establish before cold weather sets in. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it pairs well in mixes with cereal rye or oats, using the grass as a trellis for its climbing tendrils while it fixes nitrogen for the following cash crop.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, sandy or loamy, lean soil in full sun; mesa dropseed grows naturally on dry, open desert mesas, sandy plains, and desert grassland of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran deserts and Great Basin transition zones. Extremely heat and drought tolerant — requires no supplemental irrigation in appropriate climates.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, sandy or loamy, lean soil in full sun; mesa dropseed is a medium-sized warm-season bunchgrass of desert mesas and sandy desert grasslands from the Texas Panhandle and New Mexico through Arizona and into the Great Basin — one of the characteristic dropseed grasses (Sporobolus) of the hot, dry southwestern lowlands. The airy, open, finely branched panicles are ornamental and distinctive. 'Dropseed' refers to the characteristic of the genus where the tiny, shiny seeds fall (drop) as soon as they are ripe, spreading quickly around the parent plant. An important forage grass for pronghorn, desert mule deer, and livestock on desert ranges. One of the better grasses for very hot, dry, sandy desert-grassland restoration planting mixes across the Southwest. Related to prairie dropseed (S. heterolepis, of the northern prairies) but adapted to much hotter, drier conditions. Fast-germinating and establishing from seed in appropriate warm, dry conditions.

common_name: Meyer Zoysia Grass (Classic Cold-Hardy Standard Zoysia Cultivar)
plant_note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently warm; Meyer is the classic, longtime-standard medium-textured zoysia cultivar, valued for cold hardiness but notably slow to fill in from plugs.
directions: Install plugs or sod in spring through midsummer and irrigate frequently until roots knit in, then mow at 1 to 2 inches. Meyer has been the benchmark medium-textured Zoysia japonica cultivar for decades, valued for good cold hardiness that extends its usable range further north than many zoysia selections, along with dense, wear-tolerant, weed-suppressing turf once fully established. Its main drawback, slow establishment from plugs, has led many growers to prefer newer, faster-filling cultivars like El Toro, though Meyer remains widely available and reliable. It handles moderate shade better than bermudagrass and goes dormant and straw-colored after the first hard frost, greening back reliably each spring. Avoid excess nitrogen and mowing too low, both of which stress zoysia turf.

plant_note: Overseed into an existing lawn or bare soil in spring or early fall; microclover was bred specifically as a small-leaved, low-flowering white clover for blending into turfgrass, staying inconspicuous under mowing instead of forming the tall, showy clumps of standard Dutch white clover.
directions: Overseed thinly into an existing lawn (after aerating or dethatching for better seed-to-soil contact) or scatter over bare soil in spring or early fall, keeping the surface moist until it sprouts. Microclover was selected specifically for lawn blends, with much smaller leaves and far fewer flowers than ordinary white clover, so it fills in bare and thin patches, fixes nitrogen for companion turfgrass, and stays green through drought while remaining low and unobtrusive under regular mowing rather than dominating the lawn's look. It tolerates close mowing better than standard clover and spreads by creeping stolons to knit together a resilient, low-input lawn that needs less fertilizer and less water than turfgrass alone. Because it fixes its own nitrogen, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization, which favors grass over clover and can thin out the clover component over time.

plant_note: Broadcast fine seed onto a well-prepared warm seedbed after last frost, or plant as a border strip around a cereal crop; it establishes slowly and benefits from weed-free conditions in its first weeks.
directions: Plant as a border or intercrop around maize and sorghum in a push-pull companion planting system; the sticky, aromatic foliage releases volatile terpenes that repel stemborer moths and confuse aphids, pushing them away from the cash crop while also attracting natural enemies of pests. It is sometimes used as a trap-crop border for ticks in pastures, since the sticky hairs physically entangle and kill tick larvae. Mow or graze periodically to keep it from becoming rank, and note it can naturalize in frost-free climates, so site it where spread is acceptable.

common_name: Moxie Teff (Fast-Growing Forage and Cover Crop Teff Grass)
plant_note: Surface-sow the fine seed after the last frost into a firm, warm seedbed; Moxie is a forage teff cultivar bred for rapid regrowth after cutting or grazing.
directions: Mix the tiny seed with sand or dry fertilizer for even broadcasting, then roll or cultipack to press it into firm contact with a warm, moist seedbed, since Moxie germinates poorly if seed is buried deep. As a forage-type teff selection, Moxie establishes a fine, fibrous root mat quickly, tolerates both short-term drought and periodic wet soil better than most warm-season grasses, and regrows readily after mowing, making it useful for filling a short summer gap between cash crops with repeated cuttings of biomass. Terminate by mowing before seed set to prevent volunteers, or simply let an early fall frost kill the stand.

common_name: Mt. Barker Subterranean Clover (Classic Self-Burying Reseeding Clover)
plant_note: Sow in fall for a winter annual cover crop; Mt. Barker is a classic, widely grown subterranean clover cultivar named for its unusual habit of burying its own seed pods at the soil surface after flowering, giving it excellent self-reseeding reliability.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, prepared seedbed in fall, raking lightly for good seed-to-soil contact. Mt. Barker is one of the oldest and most widely grown cultivars of subterranean clover, a low-growing winter annual legume that, true to its name, buries its own developing seed pods just below the soil surface after flowering, protecting the seed and making the stand exceptionally reliable at reseeding itself year after year without replanting. Its dense, mat-forming growth suppresses winter weeds effectively and fixes nitrogen for a following crop, while its low stature makes it useful as a living mulch under fruit trees, in orchard alleys, or between vegetable rows. The plant naturally dies back in late spring as temperatures rise, leaving a nitrogen-rich mulch and buried seed ready to germinate again the following fall.

plant_note: Broadcast onto a firm seedbed in fall; Nangeela flowers and sets seed later in spring than Mt. Barker or Dalkeith, extending its living-mulch and nitrogen-fixing window.
directions: Broadcast seed over a firm, moist bed in early fall and rake lightly, since good seed-to-soil contact is essential for even establishment. Nangeela is a later-flowering subterranean clover cultivar than the classic Mt. Barker and Dalkeith types, staying green and actively fixing nitrogen further into spring before it burrows and buries its own seed pods just below the soil surface for reliable self-reseeding. Its dense, low, mat-forming growth makes it a durable living mulch under fruit trees and in orchard alleys, tolerating light foot traffic and mowing far better than upright clovers. Choose Nangeela over earlier subterranean clover cultivars where a longer spring cover window is wanted before the stand naturally dies back with rising temperatures.

common_name: Napier Grass (Elephant Grass, Uganda Grass, Merker Grass)
plant_note: Plant stem cuttings (sections with 2–3 nodes) horizontally or at an angle in moist soil after soil warms to 65°F; napier grass is a tropical perennial killed by hard frost but grows with extraordinary vigor in zones 9–11, producing 20–40 tons of dry biomass per acre per year and forming dense stands that exclude all weeds — the single most productive warm-season biomass plant available for tropical and subtropical climates.
directions: Plant stem cuttings 3–4 inches deep at 2–3 foot spacing; napier grass establishes rapidly and reaches cutting height of 3–5 feet within 60–90 days; cut or chop-and-drop as green mulch every 6–8 weeks during growing season to maintain tender regrowth and prevent woodiness; use as chop-and-drop mulch for tropical garden beds or incorporate as green manure. Napier grass (Pennisetum purpureum) is arguably the most productive tropical biomass grass in the world — a C4 perennial native to sub-Saharan Africa (the Napier Valley region of Kenya) that has been planted throughout the humid tropics for fodder, green manure, and more recently as a dedicated biomass energy crop. Under optimal tropical conditions it can produce more than 40 tons of dry biomass per acre per year — a yield surpassed by few plants on earth — while requiring minimal inputs once established. In zone 9a and the Gulf Coast, Napier grass performs as a vigorous warm-season perennial from spring through late fall, dying back after the first frost but typically regrowing from established root crowns unless soil temperatures drop below about 20°F for extended periods. It is used in permaculture and tropical market gardens as a chop-and-drop biomass plant: the tall stems are cut every 6–8 weeks and the chopped material laid as mulch or incorporated as high-carbon green manure. The dense, fibrous root system accumulates significant organic matter in the soil over multiple seasons. New dwarf varieties ('Mott' dwarf napier) are available for smaller gardens. Note: classified as potentially invasive in Hawaii and Florida — check local guidelines before planting near natural areas.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Narbon vetch is a larger-seeded, more upright winter annual vetch than hairy or common vetch, historically grown as both a cover crop and a grain legume for livestock feed.
directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun in fall; Narbon vetch is a sturdy, semi-upright Mediterranean winter annual legume with broader leaflets and larger seeds than hairy or common vetch, historically grown as a dual-purpose cover crop and grain legume for livestock feed in parts of the Mediterranean and Middle East. It fixes substantial nitrogen over the winter growing season, and its more upright habit produces less tangled, easier-to-manage biomass than sprawling hairy vetch when grown as a standalone cover rather than with a grass companion. Pale blue-violet flowers appear in spring, followed by pods of relatively large, flattened seed that can be harvested for use as a rotational grain legume in addition to its soil-building role. Terminate by mowing or crimping at early flowering for maximum green manure value, or allow pods to mature if seed harvest is the goal.

common_name: Narrow-Leaf Lupin (Blue Lupin, Australian Sweet Lupin)
plant_note: In zones 7–9 sow in fall 4–8 weeks before first frost; in zones 3–6 sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; narrow-leaf lupin is more frost-hardy than white lupin (tolerates -10°C) and better adapted to sandy, acidic soils (pH 4.5–7.0) where white lupin and most legumes fail; the most important grain lupin species in Australia, where it transformed dryland wheat farming as a rotation crop.
directions: Broadcast or drill at 60–100 lbs per acre (1.5–2.5 lbs per 1000 sq ft); inoculate with Bradyrhizobium lupini Group G specifically matched to this species; narrow-leaf lupin is more drought-tolerant than white lupin once established and is excellent for poor sandy soils; terminate at early bloom by mowing and incorporating to release 80–140 lbs N/acre. Narrow-leaf lupin (Lupinus angustifolius) is the dominant commercial grain lupin species in Australia, where it was transformed by the breeding work of John Gladstones at the University of Western Australia into a major crop that revolutionized dryland wheat farming — the introduction of sweet, low-alkaloid varieties in the 1960s and 1970s enabled farmers in western Australia to use lupins as a grain legume rotation crop, building soil fertility in the highly acidic, phosphorus-deficient sands of the Australian wheat belt. Australia now produces the majority of the world's grain lupins, with Lupinus angustifolius representing 95% of production. As a cover crop in American gardens and small farms, narrow-leaf lupin excels in the same difficult conditions: acidic, sandy, infertile soils where clovers, vetch, and peas struggle to establish. It fixes 80–140 lbs N/acre with proper inoculation, produces substantial biomass, and its deep taproot improves soil structure. The flowers are blue to pale violet-blue on erect stems — attractive enough to serve double duty as an ornamental.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill in early spring or late summer into moist, fine-textured to heavy soil in full sun; narrow-leaf trefoil tolerates seasonally wet, saline, and alkaline soils better than most forage legumes.
directions: Broadcast or drill in early spring or late summer into moist, fine-textured to heavy soil in full sun; narrow-leaf trefoil tolerates seasonally wet, saline, and alkaline soils better than most forage legumes. A finer-stemmed, more prostrate relative of birdsfoot trefoil, it forms a low, spreading mat of narrow leaflets and small yellow pea-like flowers that fix nitrogen and provide non-bloating, palatable grazing for livestock without the bloat risk of clover. It persists in seasonally flooded pastures, saline lowlands, and heavy clay soils where alfalfa and clover struggle, making it a useful forage and cover legume for difficult, poorly drained ground. Once established it tolerates close, frequent grazing and self-seeds to maintain a persistent stand with minimal reseeding.

common_name: Neches White Clover (Early-Flowering Texas A&M White Clover)
plant_note: Sow in fall or late winter; Neches, released by Texas A&M AgriLife Research at Overton, flowers earlier than Durana and carries noticeably larger leaves, giving it a fast start as a nitrogen-fixing groundcover in Gulf South pastures and orchard alleys.
directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in fall and rake lightly to press it into good contact with the soil. Neches was bred at the Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center in Overton from a synthetic cross of pest-resistant USDA breeding lines and East Texas ecotypes, and it reaches full bloom noticeably earlier in spring than older intermediate white clovers, with leaves roughly a fifth larger than Durana. Its early flowering makes it a strong nectar source for pollinators before summer heat arrives, while its creeping stolons knit together a dense, low mat that suppresses winter weeds and fixes nitrogen for a following warm-season planting. Mow occasionally to keep the stand vigorous and prevent taller companion grasses or weeds from shading it out.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to early fall for a cool-season cover, or in early spring; Nemat was selected for biofumigant and trap-crop activity against root-knot nematodes and is more drought-tolerant than mustard covers, making it useful on lighter, drier soils.
directions: Broadcast seed at 8-12 lb per acre onto a raked, well-drained seedbed and keep evenly moist until the fast-germinating seedlings emerge. Nemat's rapid, spicy-scented foliage draws root-knot nematode juveniles into its roots, where the plant acts as a poor host and interrupts the nematode life cycle, while glucosinolates released from mowed, incorporated tissue add further biofumigant suppression of soilborne pathogens. Terminate by mowing and tilling in at early flowering, before pods form, to prevent volunteer reseeding into the following crop. Avoid rotating directly into other brassica vegetables the same season.

plant_note: Broadcast fine seed on a firm, weed-free seedbed after last frost and rake in lightly, no more than 1/4 inch deep; niger's small, oil-rich achenes are the main ingredient of commercial 'nyjer' finch seed and the plant also serves as a quick-establishing pollinator and wildlife food plot cover.
directions: Broadcast fine seed onto a firm, weed-suppressed seedbed and rake in shallowly, since niger germinates and establishes fast enough on its own to out-compete most warm-season weeds. Plants form a branching, sunflower-family stalk topped with small yellow composite flowers that are heavily worked by bees and other pollinators through late summer, followed by tiny black seeds prized by finches and other seed-eating birds. Mow or roll at flowering to terminate as a soil-building green manure, or let seed heads dry fully on the stalk before combining or hand-stripping if growing for birdseed. Because it is frost-tender and shallow-rooted, niger is best used as a fast summer-only cover between spring and fall cash crops rather than for winter soil protection.

plant_note: Sow from early spring through summer; Nitro is a fast, Peruvian-type annual alfalfa bred to be terminated the same season rather than grown as a persistent perennial forage stand.
directions: Broadcast or drill inoculated seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed no more than 1/2 inch deep. Nitro is a Peruvian-type annual alfalfa selected specifically for rapid, single-season green-manure use rather than the multi-year persistence of standard perennial alfalfa hay types, producing a tall, fast-growing stand and abundant nitrogen-rich biomass within about two to three months. Because it lacks strong winter hardiness compared to perennial cultivars, it winterkills reliably in cold climates, simplifying termination without herbicide or tillage. Mow or till under at bud-to-early-bloom stage for the greatest nitrogen contribution, and expect a vigorous regrowth flush if only partially cut before final incorporation.

common_name: Nitro Radish (Nitrogen-Scavenging Forage Radish Cover Crop)
plant_note: Sow 6-10 weeks before first frost; Nitro is a forage radish cultivar bred for rapid fall growth and aggressive nitrogen scavenging, capturing residual soil nitrogen in its foliage and root before winter leaching losses occur.
directions: Broadcast seed about 1/2 inch deep in late summer to early fall; Nitro is a forage radish cultivar bred for exceptionally fast fall growth and strong nitrogen-scavenging ability, rapidly taking up residual soil nitrogen left over from a previous crop's fertilization before fall and winter rains can leach it below the root zone. The large taproot also breaks through compacted soil layers, improving structure and water infiltration for the following crop. In zones cold enough for a hard freeze, the roots die and rot in place over winter, releasing the captured nitrogen back into the topsoil in plant-available form as they decompose, timed to benefit a spring-planted crop. In milder zones where the radish survives, mow before it flowers and sets seed to prevent it becoming a volunteer weed in the following crop.

common_name: Norcen Birdsfoot Trefoil (Cold-Hardy Pasture & Cover Legume)
plant_note: Sow shallowly into a firm seedbed in spring, using fresh or scarified seed inoculated with the correct Rhizobium strain.
directions: Norcen is a cold-hardy birdsfoot trefoil cultivar selected for improved winter survival in northern climates, grown as a long-lived perennial forage and cover legume on soils too wet, acidic, or infertile for alfalfa. Establishment is slow compared with clovers, so mow occasionally the first season to control weed competition while seedlings develop their root systems. Once established, its non-bloating foliage and deep taproot make it valuable for grazing, erosion control, and nitrogen-building cover on marginal ground for several years. It tolerates poorly drained or low-pH soils better than most other forage legumes.

plant_note: Sow early spring or late summer for a quick cool-season cover.
directions: Broadcast oat seed over worked soil in early spring or six to eight weeks before your first fall frost and rake in about half an inch. Fast, dense growth shades out weeds and its fibrous roots hold soil against erosion and winter rains. In cold zones the crop reliably winter-kills, leaving a soft mulch that is easy to plant into come spring. It also builds plenty of organic matter when turned under while still green.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before first fall frost; oats winter-kill below about 10°F, leaving a ready-to-plant mat of residue in spring without tillage.
directions: Broadcast seed at 50–80 lb per acre (about 1 oz per 30 sq ft) and rake to 1/2 in depth; oats establish quickly and produce substantial biomass before being killed by hard freezes. Their winter-killed residue lies flat as a weed-suppressing mulch that is easy to plant or transplant through in spring without additional termination work. Often mixed with field peas or hairy vetch to add nitrogen to the primarily carbonaceous grass residue. In mild-winter regions (zones 8–9), oats may overwinter and require mowing to terminate before spring planting.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill 6–10 weeks before the first fall frost into a well-prepared seedbed; oilseed radish grows quickly and, in USDA zone 5 and colder, reliably winter-kills, leaving surface residue and a decomposing root channel by spring.
directions: Broadcast seed at 8–12 lb/acre and lightly incorporate into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; oilseed radish germinates and grows rapidly, producing a vigorous rosette of large leaves over a long, thick taproot. Bred as a fast-biomass, high-glucosinolate type within the same species as tillage/forage radish, it is especially valued for biofumigation — as the roots and residue break down, they release natural sulfur compounds that can suppress certain soilborne pathogens and nematodes, in addition to the physical benefits of a deep taproot that fractures compacted soil layers and scavenges leachable nitrogen before winter. In mild-winter climates the rosette can survive and bolt in spring; mow before flowering to prevent an unwanted seed bank. The decomposing roots produce a strong sulfurous smell for a week or two after a hard freeze — this is normal and passes as residue breaks down.

plant_note: Sow six to eight weeks before frost so plants form a strong rosette to overwinter.
directions: Broadcast at about 0.25-0.5 lb per 1,000 sq ft and rake to cover 0.25-0.5 inch deep in a firm seedbed. Winter-type oilseed rape develops a deep taproot that breaks up compacted subsoil and scavenges nitrogen and sulfur. Overwintering plants bolt and flower in spring, providing early forage for pollinators if allowed to bloom. Terminate by mowing at early flowering before pods set, then incorporate the residue with tillage. Allow two to three weeks of breakdown before planting the following crop to avoid nitrogen tie-up.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 6–8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to partial shade; orchardgrass tolerates more shade than most pasture grasses, giving it its name from traditional use in the dappled light of orchard alleys.
directions: Drill seed 1/4–1/2 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to partial shade; establishes quickly and tolerates more shade than nearly any other common pasture or cover crop grass, a trait reflected in its name from long use as groundcover beneath orchard trees. Orchardgrass is a deep-rooted, long-lived, cool-season bunchgrass widely used across temperate North America as a high-quality hay and pasture grass, valued for its rapid spring growth, good regrowth after cutting or grazing, and reasonable drought tolerance once its root system is established. As a cover crop, it forms a dense, persistent sod useful for erosion control on slopes and waterways, and its shade tolerance makes it one of the few grasses well suited to groundcover beneath widely spaced fruit or nut trees, where full-sun grasses like bermudagrass or bahiagrass struggle. A versatile, shade-tolerant perennial grass for pasture, hay, or orchard-floor groundcover, zone 3–8.

common_name: Osceola White Clover (Ladino-Type Summer-Persistent White Clover)
plant_note: Frost-seed in late winter or broadcast in early spring onto a firm, weed-free seedbed; can also be sown in early fall in warmer zones for winter establishment.
directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed and rake lightly, since the tiny seed germinates best within the top quarter inch of soil. Osceola was bred at the University of Florida as an intermediate ladino-type white clover with notably better summer persistence in hot, humid conditions than standard Louisiana-type white clovers, making it well suited to Southeastern gardens and pastures. It spreads by surface stolons to form a dense, mowable, nitrogen-fixing groundcover that tolerates regular foot traffic and light grazing. Mow periodically to keep it from being shaded out by taller companion plants, or let it flower to support pollinators.

common_name: Pacific Gold Mustard (High-Glucosinolate Biofumigant Cover Crop)
plant_note: Sow in early fall for a fall-to-winter cover, or as early as soil can be worked in spring; Pacific Gold was bred specifically for elevated glucosinolate content, giving it a stronger biofumigant effect against soilborne pathogens and nematodes than standard mustard cover crops.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, well-prepared seedbed and rake to a shallow quarter-inch depth; Pacific Gold germinates quickly in cool soil and grows into a tall, vigorous stand that suppresses weeds through competition. It was selected specifically for high glucosinolate content in its leaf and stem tissue, which breaks down into biofumigant isothiocyanate compounds when the plant is chopped and immediately incorporated at early flowering, giving a stronger suppressive effect on soilborne pathogens, weed seeds, and some plant-parasitic nematodes than standard mustard cover crops. For the strongest biofumigation effect, mow and till in within minutes to trap the volatile compounds in the soil, then irrigate and cover with plastic tarp for one to two weeks. Terminate before seed set, since mustard reseeds readily and can become a weed if allowed to mature.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill seed into warm, moist, well-drained soil in full sun well after last frost; palisade grass is a tropical species that needs consistently warm soil to germinate and establishes best during the height of summer heat.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed into warm, moist, well-drained soil in full sun well after last frost; palisade grass is a tropical species that needs consistently warm soil to germinate and establishes best during the height of summer heat. This robust, tufted to shortly rhizomatous tropical forage grass produces abundant, leafy growth and deep, extensive roots that make it highly productive on acidic, low-fertility soils where many other forage grasses fail, and it is among the most widely planted pasture grasses across the tropics. It tolerates heavy grazing pressure and recovers rapidly, while its deep root system provides excellent erosion control on sloped or degraded pasture land. It is frost-sensitive and behaves as an annual outside consistently frost-free climates, going dormant or dying back with the first freeze.

common_name: Palmetto St. Augustine Grass (Shade-Tolerant Semi-Dwarf Lawn Grass)
plant_note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) when soil temperature is consistently above 70°F; Palmetto is a semi-dwarf St. Augustine cultivar selected for better shade tolerance and a finer, denser texture than older cultivars like Floratam, making it the preferred choice for the tree-shaded residential lots common throughout the Gulf South.
directions: Install sod or plugs in spring through midsummer, keeping consistently moist for four to six weeks during establishment, then mow at 2.5–3.5 inches. Palmetto is a semi-dwarf St. Augustine grass cultivar bred specifically for improved shade tolerance and a finer leaf texture than the older, more sun-demanding Floratam cultivar, making it the standard recommendation for Gulf South lawns with significant tree canopy where straight species or Floratam would thin out. It also shows good cold tolerance for a St. Augustine selection and a slower vertical growth rate, meaning less frequent mowing than more vigorous cultivars. Like all St. Augustine grass it spreads by above-ground stolons and establishes readily from sod or plugs, filling in bare spots within a season under good conditions. Watch for chinch bugs, a major pest of St. Augustine throughout the Gulf South, and gray leaf spot fungal disease in hot, humid, overwatered conditions — water deeply but infrequently rather than daily light sprinkling to reduce disease pressure.

plant_note: Scarify seeds and direct sow in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; panicled tick trefoil grows naturally in dry to moderately moist open woodlands, woodland edges, and old fields throughout eastern North America.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun at woodland edges and in naturalized plantings; panicled tick trefoil is one of the most important native wildflower legumes of the eastern woodland edge — a tall, erect perennial with trifoliate leaves and loose, elongated panicles of small pink to lavender pea flowers in late summer. The plant is critically important as a host plant for Eastern tailed-blue, silver-spotted skipper, and several other butterfly and moth species that are specialists of native legumes. The jointed seed pods break into small, sticky segments (the 'ticks' that give the genus its name) and cling tenaciously to clothing and animal fur — an effective dispersal strategy that makes some people view the plant as a nuisance. In naturalistic gardens and wildlife corridors, it is an outstanding wildflower that seeds itself through open, lightly shaded areas without becoming aggressive in well-maintained beds.

common_name: Pasja Hybrid Forage Brassica (Turnip-Rape Cover Crop Hybrid)
plant_note: Drill or broadcast in late summer for a fast-growing fall cover crop, or sow in early spring; Pasja is a turnip × rape hybrid bred specifically for rapid leafy growth and quick regrowth after cutting or grazing.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer, since Pasja germinates quickly and reaches a leafy, grazable or mowable stage in as little as seven to eight weeks, faster than either straight turnips or straight forage rape. As a hybrid between forage turnip and forage rape, it combines the rapid regrowth of turnip with the leafiness of rape, tolerating repeated cutting or grazing better than most other cover crop brassicas while still building a modest taproot that helps break up compacted soil. Its abundant, tender foliage breaks down rapidly once winterkilled or incorporated, releasing nutrients quickly ahead of a following crop, and it can be interseeded with cereal rye or clover to extend fall groundcover.

plant_note: Sow after last frost in warm soil; the most heat- and drought-tolerant warm-season cover grass, thriving in Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed 1/2 in deep into warm soil; pearl millet germinates and establishes faster than sorghum-sudangrass in sandy, low-fertility soils. It produces large amounts of biomass for smothering weeds and building organic matter, and tolerate short dry spells without wilting like corn or sorghum can. Mow or terminate before seed heads mature to prevent unwanted reseeding. Mix with cowpeas for a combined nitrogen-fixing and biomass cover.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–6 weeks after last frost in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; pearl millet is the world's most drought-tolerant cereal grain — it thrives where maize, sorghum, and other grains fail — and is an outstanding summer cover crop for hot, dry, sandy soil in zone 7–12 where it grows to 6–8 feet, fixes atmospheric carbon, suppresses weeds, and improves soil structure.
directions: Direct sow at 10–20 lbs per acre in warm, well-drained, lean soil in full sun; mow or incorporate when 50–60% heading for maximum biomass. Cenchrus americanus (pearl millet or bajra, formerly Pennisetum glaucum) is the world's most drought-tolerant cereal grain crop — an ancient African cultigen domesticated in the Sahel region over 3,000 years ago and now the primary staple grain for hundreds of millions of people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Pearl millet thrives under extremely high temperatures (up to 110°F), very low and erratic rainfall (8–20 inches annually), and highly infertile, sandy soils — growing successfully where maize, sorghum, and virtually any other grain crop cannot produce. The grain (bajra in India, the primary use) is ground into flour for flatbreads (bajra roti) and porridges; the nutritional profile is excellent (higher in protein, iron, and zinc than maize or sorghum). As a cover crop in zone 7–12, pearl millet is outstanding for hot, dry, sandy, infertile soils where most summer cover crops fail — it grows to 6–8 feet rapidly, produces enormous biomass to incorporate as organic matter, suppresses weeds completely, and requires essentially no inputs. It is also an important wildlife food and game food-plot crop for white-tailed deer, quail, and dove.

common_name: Pensacola Bahia Grass (Gulf South Drought-Tolerant Lawn and Pasture Grass)
plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed at 5–10 lbs/1000 sq ft in late spring when soil is consistently above 65°F; scratch seed into soil with a rake or slit-seeder for good soil contact. Pensacola Bahia germinates slowly (2–4 weeks) and establishes slowly — expect a full season before a complete stand develops. In zone 9, seed April–June for establishment by fall. Pensacola Bahia goes semi-dormant and may brown during cold winters but recovers reliably in spring.
directions: Sow scarified seed at 5–10 lbs per 1,000 sq ft after last frost when soil is warm; keep moist during the slow 2–4 week germination period. Pensacola Bahia is the standard low-maintenance lawn and pasture grass for the Gulf South coastal plain — a cultivar of bahia grass (Paspalum notatum) selected for improved cold tolerance, germination, and lawn quality over the common 'Argentine' type. Bahia grass is unique among Gulf South turf grasses for its extraordinary drought and heat tolerance combined with extremely low input requirements: it grows vigorously in poor, sandy, acidic soils with minimal fertilization, outcompetes many weeds once established, and maintains reasonable appearance through Gulf South summers with little supplemental irrigation. The deep, extensive root system (roots reach 6–8 feet deep) explains the drought tolerance — the roots access soil moisture well below what shallow-rooted turf grasses can reach. Pensacola is a narrower-leaf, more attractive form than common bahia grass, making it more acceptable for residential lawn use while retaining the toughness of the species. The grass is a fixture throughout Florida, coastal Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, where it covers millions of acres of utility areas, roadsides, pastures, and low-maintenance residential lawns.

common_name: Peredovik Sunflower (Russian Oilseed Sunflower, Standard Wildlife and Food Plot Variety)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in zone 9 (April–May), or midsummer (July) for a fall crop. Peredovik produces single-headed sunflowers on tall, upright stems (5–7 feet) with seed heads 6–8 inches in diameter packed with small, oilseed-type black or black-striped seeds. The small oilseed-type seed (smaller than confection sunflower varieties) is higher in oil content than large-seeded types, making it particularly attractive to songbirds, doves, and deer. Plant at higher density than confection sunflowers (6–8 inch spacing) to maximize seed heads per acre in food plot applications. Peredovik can be direct-harvested for bird feed or left standing as a wildlife food source. In zone 9's warm climate, Peredovik thrives with excellent drought tolerance once established — well-suited to dry summer conditions without irrigation.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 6–12 inches for maximum seed heads. Leave standing for wildlife or harvest heads when seeds are dry and firm. Peredovik is a Russian oilseed sunflower variety that was introduced to North America from the Soviet Union and became the standard oilseed sunflower for both commercial oilseed production and wildlife food plot planting across the United States. The name Peredovik (meaning 'leader' or 'front-runner' in Russian) reflects the variety's status in Soviet agricultural programs where sunflower was a major oilseed crop for domestic vegetable oil production. Peredovik produces the small, dark (black or black-and-gray-striped) seeds characteristic of oilseed sunflowers — smaller than confection-type sunflower seeds grown for direct human consumption, but with a higher percentage of oil per seed, a thin shell that wildlife and songbirds can crack easily, and a nutrient density that makes them preferred by many seed-eating birds over larger-seeded confection types. The variety's value for wildlife habitat and food plot management in the Gulf South and across the US has made it by far the most commonly planted sunflower variety in food plot and wildlife habitat seed mixes. For zone 9 gardeners interested in supporting native bird populations, Peredovik planted in a sunny corner of the garden or in a dedicated wildlife patch provides enormous nutritional value to mourning doves, goldfinches, house finches, northern cardinals, and many migratory sparrow species during fall migration. The plants also provide insect habitat and the tall stalks support overwintering insects beneficial for garden pest control.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; perennial horsegram is an East African legume used as a drought-tolerant, perennial tropical pasture cover crop in Queensland, Australia and across Africa and Southeast Asia — it excels in low-rainfall, infertile, acidic conditions where other tropical legumes cannot establish.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarify seed or soak 24 hours before planting. Macrotyloma axillare (perennial horsegram or axillaris) is an East African legume that has been widely adopted as a drought-tolerant, perennial tropical pasture cover crop in Queensland, Australia, where it was introduced and extensively trialed as a low-maintenance, nitrogen-fixing component of improved subtropical pastures. The cultivar 'Archer' was selected in Australia for superior persistence, drought tolerance, and productivity in dry subtropical conditions. Unlike annual tropical cover crops, perennial horsegram persists in the soil from one season to the next, regrowth from the root crown after dry-season dormancy — providing a permanent nitrogen-fixing cover without annual replanting costs. It is notably tolerant of acid, infertile, low-phosphorus soils where other legumes fail to establish. The plant produces twining stems with small trifoliate leaves and inconspicuous cream-colored flowers. In zone 9–12 gardens, it is an excellent choice for permanent cover under fruit trees on lean, acidic soil, where it builds fertility year by year without intervention.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sprigs in late spring once soil is warm; establishment is slow the first season but the stand fills in by year 2.
directions: Plant rhizome sections 2–3 in deep in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; perennial peanut tolerates poor, acidic soils typical of Gulf Coast landscapes. Establishment is slow the first year but the low, dense mat fixes nitrogen and crowds out weeds without mowing once established. It can be used as a lawn alternative, orchard under-planting, or living mulch in vegetable corridors. In zones 8–9 the top may freeze back in hard winters but the rhizomes resprout reliably from below ground.

common_name: Perennial Peanut (Pinto Peanut, Rhizoma Perennial Peanut, Ornamental Peanut)
plant_note: Plant sprigs (vegetative divisions) or sod plugs in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Arachis pintoi is one of the most popular and proven low-maintenance groundcovers for zone 8b-11, especially throughout Florida and the Gulf Coast where it has been widely used for decades as lawn alternative, median strip groundcover, and landscape cover. Spreads by rhizomes and stolons; mow occasionally to keep tidy. Drought-tolerant once established. Fixes nitrogen from the air, improving soil over time. The small yellow peanut-shaped flowers are decorative. Suppresses weeds effectively in established beds.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil — Perennial Peanut is one of the most adaptable and low-maintenance groundcovers for Gulf Coast zone 8b-11, establishing in a wide range of soil types and requiring minimal inputs once established. Arachis pintoi is a stoloniferous, mat-forming, perennial legume native to Brazil and Bolivia in the Fabaceae family, introduced to Florida and the Gulf Coast in the 1930s and now one of the most widely used ornamental groundcovers in the region. The plant produces a dense, attractive, low mat of 4-leaflet compound leaves (like a clover leaf) from creeping stolons and rhizomes, and throughout the warm months produces small (0.5-inch), bright golden-yellow, peanut-shaped flowers at the tips of short upright stems. As a legume, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis with Rhizobium bacteria, improving soil fertility over time — making it doubly valuable as both an ornamental groundcover and a nitrogen-contributing cover crop when incorporated into garden beds. The plant spreads steadily but is not considered invasive. In zone 8b-9, established plants die back to the roots in hard freezes but regrow vigorously in spring. A true perennial in zone 9b-11, requiring no replanting. One of the finest groundcovers for hot, humid Gulf Coast landscapes. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to early fall; perennial ryegrass establishes fastest of all cool-season grasses and forms dense sod for erosion control.
directions: Broadcast seed at 20–30 lb/acre and rake lightly to 1/4 in depth; perennial ryegrass germinates in 5–7 days at optimal temperatures and establishes the fastest ground cover of any cool-season grass, making it excellent for emergency erosion control or orchard middles. It can be used as a short-rotation annual cover in cold winters (zones 3–5) or managed as a persistent sod in mild climates. Terminate before planting vegetables by aggressive mowing followed by solarization or herbicide; perennial ryegrass regrows readily from crowns and requires thorough kill. Mix with red or white clover for a nitrogen-fixing living mulch under fruit trees.

common_name: Perennial Soybean (Glycine, Soja Bean, Wight's Perennial Soybean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun in any well-drained soil with good air circulation; Neonotonia wightii is a vigorously climbing, twining vine that needs support or space to sprawl — control by mowing before seed set to prevent unwanted spread. It is a prolific nitrogen fixer when properly inoculated with appropriate Bradyrhizobium strains. In zone 9, the tops are killed by frost but root crowns often survive and resprout in spring. Use as a summer biomass crop mowed into garden beds before fall planting, or as a trellis cover crop to fix nitrogen while creating summer shade. Check local invasive status.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil with support for climbing — Perennial Soybean is a vigorous, twining vine that grows rapidly in warm conditions and fixes large quantities of atmospheric nitrogen, making it one of the most productive leguminous cover crops for zone 9-12. Neonotonia wightii (formerly Glycine wightii, Glycine javanica) is a perennial, twining legume vine native to sub-Saharan Africa in the Fabaceae family — the same tribe (Phaseoleae) and general lineage as the commercial soybean (Glycine max), hence the common name 'Perennial Soybean,' though not directly edible as a food crop. The plant produces trifoliate leaves on twining stems that climb vigorously over other vegetation, fences, and trellises, and produces small (0.25-inch), lavender-purple flowers in axillary racemes through the warm months — the flowers attracting bees and small pollinators. As a legume, it forms root nodules with nitrogen-fixing Bradyrhizobium bacteria, fixing significant quantities of atmospheric nitrogen. Neonotonia wightii has been extensively used in tropical and subtropical agriculture as a high-biomass forage crop (the foliage is highly nutritious for livestock) and as a cover crop and living mulch in commercial plantations (coffee, citrus, macadamia) throughout the tropics to fix nitrogen and suppress weeds. In zone 9 home gardens, it is best used as a summer biomass-building cover to improve soil before mowing and incorporating before fall vegetable planting. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Broadcast seed at 8–12 pounds per acre in late summer or early fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Persian clover is winter-hardy to about 20°F, making it a useful winter annual in zones 7–9 where it overwinters and provides early spring nitrogen to following crops.
directions: Broadcast seed in late summer or early fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Persian clover is a Mediterranean annual clover widely used as a winter cover crop in mild-winter zones 7–9 where it establishes in fall, overwinters successfully, and produces a significant nitrogen-fixing spring flush before being incorporated as a green manure ahead of warm-season transplants. The distinctive pink-to-purple flowers open in the distinctive 'upside down' (resupinate) orientation that gives the species its name and common name. It is considered one of the best annual clovers for the winter-cover-crop niche in Gulf Coast and southeastern gardens — more productive and earlier-maturing than many other clovers in mild winters. Mow or till under at early flowering to maximize nitrogen release to following crops. Excellent as a nurse crop for cool-season vegetables.

plant_note: Sow 2–6 weeks before last spring frost, or in early fall in mild climates; flowers arrive in about 6 weeks and are among the best for attracting bees.
directions: Broadcast tiny seed at 3–5 lb per acre (a light dusting per 100 sq ft) on the surface of a firm, moist seedbed without covering, as seed needs light to germinate; rake in very lightly if birds are a problem. Phacelia establishes quickly in cool soil, outcompeting many weeds with dense, ferny foliage that also conserves soil moisture. The blue-purple flowers are exceptional for beneficial insects and bees — allow partial bloom before mowing to maximize pollinator benefit. Terminate by mowing just as the last flowers fade; it decomposes rapidly and leaves no allelopathic residue.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in warm soil after last frost in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; phasey bean germinates readily without scarification and establishes quickly in warm, humid conditions — ideal for summer cover cropping in the Gulf South.
directions: Phasey bean is a fast-growing tropical American legume that has become one of the most widely used summer cover crops in Hawaii and the Gulf Coast, valued for its rapid establishment, vigorous nitrogen fixation, heat and humidity tolerance, and ability to grow as a self-reseeding annual in frost-free areas of zone 9–11. The plant produces small, attractive red-purple flowers on erect, trifoliate-leaved stems throughout summer, with long, slender seed pods containing multiple seeds; it naturally reseeds in zone 9 and south, making it a long-term self-perpetuating cover crop in orchards, landscape beds, and permanent native plantings. As a legume, it inoculates easily with cowpea rhizobia and fixes 50–80 pounds of nitrogen per acre; its moderate height keeps it manageable as an understory cover beneath small fruit trees and shrub rows. Used extensively in no-till and reduced-tillage systems as a living mulch terminated by mowing in fall before cool-season crops are established.

common_name: Piper Sudangrass (Fine-Stemmed True Sudangrass Cover Crop)
plant_note: Sow after last frost once soil is reliably above 65°F; this true sudangrass establishes and tillers faster than taller sorghum-sudangrass hybrids and regrows vigorously after mowing.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed about 1 in deep into warm soil once temperatures are reliably above 65°F, since this true sudangrass (rather than a taller sorghum-sudangrass hybrid) germinates and tillers quickly in summer heat. Piper is valued for fine, quick-curing stems, lower prussic-acid risk than many sudangrass types, and resistance to leaf blight and anthracnose, and it regrows vigorously after mowing or grazing. Mow at 3-4 feet to encourage tillering and additional biomass before a final termination cut, and allow a few weeks for the fibrous residue to break down before direct-seeding a follow-up crop. Its deep, fibrous root system breaks up compacted soil and scavenges leftover nitrogen between summer plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, sandy or loamy, lean soil in full sun; plains lovegrass grows naturally in dry, open grasslands, sandy plains, and rocky desert slopes of the Southern Plains and Southwest. Excellent as an ornamental grass for hot, dry, full-sun locations.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, sandy or loamy, lean soil in full sun; plains lovegrass is a medium-sized, warm-season native bunchgrass of the Southern Plains and Chihuahuan Desert transition zone, producing delicate, extremely fine-textured, open, and airy panicles of tiny flowers and seeds from mid-summer through fall. The seed panicles create a misty, diaphanous effect — a haze of fine purple-pink to silvery seed heads floating above the grass clumps. The 'lovegrass' common name (shared by many Eragrostis species) references the delicate, romantic quality of the seed heads. Provides important food for doves, sparrows, and other seed-eating birds through fall and winter. Distinguished from the non-native weeping lovegrass (E. curvula) by its native origin, finer texture, and less weeping, more upright form. An excellent native ornamental grass for hot, dry, full-sun gardens and naturalistic prairie plantings in the southern plains states and Southwest.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after soil warms (68°F+) in moist to wet, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to loamy soil in full sun; prickly sesban (dhaincha) is one of the most important green manure and cover crop plants of tropical and subtropical rice farming systems — extraordinarily fast-growing (up to 1 inch per day), nitrogen-fixing (80–120 lbs N/acre), and tolerant of waterlogged, flooded, and saline soils that most cover crops cannot handle.
directions: Broadcast or drill at 20–30 lbs/acre in full sun in moist to waterlogged conditions; incorporate or chop-and-drop before seed set to prevent naturalization; do not allow to seed down in sensitive wetland areas. Sesbania bispinosa (prickly sesban or dhaincha) is one of the most important green manure and cover crop species in tropical Asian rice farming systems — a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing annual legume widely used across India, Bangladesh, Thailand, and the Philippines as a pre-rice or in-rice green manure crop. The plant's growth speed is remarkable: under warm, wet conditions it can add over an inch of height per day, reaching 4–8 feet in just 60–75 days from seeding. Its nitrogen fixation is similarly impressive, with reported values of 80–120 lbs of N per acre in a single growing cycle — equivalent to substantial synthetic fertilizer applications. Prickly sesban is uniquely adapted to waterlogged and flooded conditions that most cover crops cannot tolerate — making it the standard choice for pre-flooding cover crops in paddy rice systems, where it can be grown, then incorporated into the field before flooding for transplanted rice. It also tolerates moderately saline soils better than most legumes. The 'prickly' in the name refers to spines on the seed pods. In zone 8–12, dhaincha is an excellent summer cover crop for warm, moist gardens; cut before flowering to use as a soil amendment.

common_name: Puna II Forage Chicory (Improved Grazing & Cover Crop Chicory)
plant_note: Sow into a firm, weed-free seedbed in spring or late summer; seed is small and needs shallow, even coverage.
directions: Puna II is an improved New Zealand-bred forage chicory selected for high leaf yield, deep taproot vigor, and better persistence than older forage chicory types, and it is widely seeded into pasture and cover crop mixes for its mineral-rich, high-protein foliage. The deep taproot scavenges nutrients from well below the topsoil and helps fracture compacted ground, while the crown persists for several seasons if mowed or grazed rather than allowed to bolt and set seed. It pairs well in mixes with clovers and plantain for extended grazing or living-mulch cover in vegetable rotations. Mow periodically to prevent flowering if long-term persistence rather than reseeding is the goal.

common_name: Purple Bounty Hairy Vetch (Early-Flowering Winter-Hardy Hairy Vetch)
plant_note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early to mid-fall so plants establish before hard frost; Purple Bounty flowers roughly two weeks earlier than common hairy vetch, letting growers roll-crimp or mow-terminate it sooner ahead of a warm-season crop.
directions: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early to mid-fall so plants establish before hard frost; Purple Bounty was bred at the USDA-ARS Beltsville lab specifically for reliable winter survival as far north as upstate New York, filling a gap left by hairy vetch types adapted mainly to the mid-Atlantic and South. It flowers roughly two weeks earlier than common hairy vetch, which lets growers roll-crimp or mow-terminate it sooner ahead of a warm-season crop without sacrificing nitrogen contribution. Inoculate seed with the appropriate Rhizobium leguminosarum strain before planting, and mix with winter rye or wheat for structural support and easier mechanical termination.

common_name: Purple Prosperity Hairy Vetch (Early-Flowering Organic No-Till Hairy Vetch)
plant_note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early fall so plants establish before winter; Purple Prosperity flowers earlier than common hairy vetch, timing well with roller-crimper termination ahead of a no-till cash crop.
directions: Purple Prosperity was bred jointly by USDA-ARS, the Rodale Institute, and agricultural experiment stations at Penn State and Cornell between 1998 and 2005 to combine early flowering with reliable winter survival for organic no-till systems in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic. It matched or exceeded the winter hardiness of the earlier southern-bred AU Early Cover across a decade of multi-state trials, a rare combination since early-flowering vetches often sacrifice cold tolerance. Sow inoculated seed into a well-prepared fall seedbed, ideally mixed with a cereal grain that gives the sprawling vines something to climb. Because it reaches full bloom notably earlier than standard hairy vetch, it can be terminated with a roller-crimper and no-till planted into soon enough to fit an earlier warm-season crop into the same field.

common_name: Purple Tephrosia (Wild Indigo, Fish Poison Plant, Wild Hog Weed)
plant_note: Direct sow in full sun in any lean, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; Tephrosia purpurea is a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing, drought-tolerant shrubby legume native to tropical Asia, widely naturalized throughout the Gulf Coast and Caribbean, and an important larval host plant for the Ceraunus Blue butterfly (Hemiargus ceraunus) throughout zone 9-12. It grows naturally in disturbed, sandy, open ground and establishes rapidly in poor soils. The small pink to purple flowers are produced prolifically from spring through fall. CAUTION: Tephrosia purpurea contains rotenone and related toxins and is poisonous to fish and mildly toxic to mammals if consumed in quantity — do not plant near fish ponds or allow livestock to graze.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any lean, well-drained, sandy soil — Purple Tephrosia establishes readily in poor, disturbed, sandy soils and is one of the most drought-tolerant and ecologically valuable small legumes for zone 9-12, functioning as a nitrogen fixer, butterfly larval host, and pollinator plant simultaneously. Tephrosia purpurea is a low, spreading, semi-woody annual to short-lived perennial shrub in the Fabaceae family (tribe Millettieae) native to tropical Asia, Africa, and Australia, now naturalized throughout the Caribbean, Florida, and the Gulf Coast in open, disturbed, sunny habitats. The plant produces upright to spreading stems bearing pinnately compound leaves of 9–17 pairs of narrow, oblong, gray-green leaflets, and through the warm months produces numerous small (0.3–0.5 inch) pink to rosy-purple typical legume flowers in axillary and terminal racemes — modest individually but produced in sufficient quantity to provide a continuous, soft display through the growing season. As a legume, Tephrosia purpurea fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis and improves sandy, depleted soils over time. Its ecological role as a larval host plant for the Ceraunus Blue butterfly (Hemiargus ceraunus) throughout south Florida and the Caribbean makes it particularly valuable for butterfly gardens in zone 9b-12, where this small, brilliant blue butterfly seeks out Tephrosia for egg-laying. The plant also contains rotenone-related compounds that were historically used as a fish poison and mild insecticide — do not plant near fish ponds.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; purple three-awn grows naturally in hot, dry, open desert grassland, rocky slopes, and sandy plains throughout the Southwest and Southern Plains. Very drought tolerant — essentially no supplemental irrigation needed after establishment in appropriate climates.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; purple three-awn is the most widespread of the Aristida (three-awn) grasses of the western half of North America — a small to medium-sized warm-season bunchgrass named for the three awns (bristle-like extensions) on each seed that give the panicle its distinctive appearance. The purple-tinted seed heads in summer and fall are ornamental in mass plantings, creating a haze of fine purple-red color over large areas of desert grassland. An important native grass of the Chihuahuan Desert grassland, Sonoran Desert margins, and Southern Plains, often occurring in disturbed, degraded, or overgrazed soils where more palatable native grasses have been lost. Despite its common occurrence in disturbed sites, it is a valuable native for erosion control on dry, rocky, sandy slopes where more demanding species are difficult to establish. Three-awn grass seeds have been problematic for livestock and dogs — the sharp, twisted awns can penetrate skin and cause injury.

plant_note: Sow in fall in mild-winter regions; it is less cold hardy than hairy vetch.
directions: Inoculate with vetch-pea rhizobia and broadcast at about 1-2 lb per 1,000 sq ft, raking to cover 1 inch deep. Purple vetch is a fast-growing annual legume best suited to mild-winter climates where it fixes nitrogen through the cool season. It climbs readily, so pairing it with a cereal companion improves standability and biomass. Terminate by mowing or crimping at early bloom before viable seed forms to prevent weedy volunteers. Incorporate the succulent residue or leave it as a nitrogen-rich mulch two to three weeks before planting.

plant_note: Broadcast seed onto a firm seedbed in fall into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; rabbit's-foot clover tolerates poor, dry, acidic sand better than almost any other cover crop clover.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, weed-suppressed seedbed in lean, sandy soil in full sun; rabbit's-foot clover is named for its soft, fuzzy, elongated flower heads covered in fine silky hairs that resemble a small rabbit's foot, appearing pale pink to grayish over a long spring and early summer bloom. It is exceptionally tolerant of poor, droughty, acidic sand and other marginal soils where most other cover crop legumes fail to thrive, making it a useful stabilizing and nitrogen-fixing option for sandy, low-fertility ground. The soft, ornamental flower heads are sometimes used in dried arrangements, adding minor secondary value beyond its cover cropping role. Mow or till in at flowering for green manure, or allow seed to mature and shatter for a self-sustaining stand on suitable sandy sites.

common_name: Raleigh St. Augustine Grass (Cold-Hardy Piedmont-Adapted Lawn Grass)
plant_note: Establish from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently above 70°F; Raleigh was bred at North Carolina State University specifically for cold hardiness, allowing St. Augustine lawns further north and inland than heat-bred cultivars like Floratam tolerate.
directions: Install sod or plugs in spring through midsummer, water consistently through establishment, and mow at 3-4 inches, never scalping since St. Augustine cannot regrow from cut-back stem tissue.
