plant_note: Sow after soil is thoroughly warm; White Wonder is a taller, more drought-hardy foxtail millet strain than Golden German, grown mainly for hay and summer biomass.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed shallowly into warm soil once the heat of summer has settled in. White Wonder grows taller and coarser-stemmed than Golden German foxtail millet and tolerates drought stress notably better, which makes it a dependable choice for filling a hot, dry summer fallow window when other cover crops struggle to establish. Its vigorous, upright growth quickly shades out competing weeds and produces substantial biomass for mowing and incorporation, though the coarser stem makes it somewhat less palatable than finer-stemmed millet types if grazed. Mow before seed set to prevent reseeding, then let frost terminate the stand.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; best suited to Gulf Coast and tropical zones 8-11 where long frost-free summers allow full maturity.
directions: Direct sow in warm, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil after the last frost date when soil temperature is consistently above 70 degrees F, covering seed to about one-half inch depth. Wild bushbean establishes quickly and produces upright racemes of striking dark purple-red pea flowers from summer through fall, followed by long, narrow, cylindrical seed pods; the vigorous growth and prolific nitrogen fixation make it a valued green manure and livestock forage crop in Gulf Coast organic farming systems. It is much less cold-tolerant than hairy vetch and will not survive frost, so it must be turned under before the first fall freeze or allowed to reseed naturally in frost-free areas. Inoculate with appropriate cowpea-type Rhizobium for maximum nitrogen fixation on first plantings in new ground.

common_name: Willamette Common Vetch (Pacific Northwest-Bred Winter Annual Vetch)
plant_note: Sow inoculated seed 4-8 weeks before first fall frost; Willamette is a common vetch cultivar developed in Oregon's Willamette Valley for winter cover cropping and grass-seed rotations.
directions: Inoculate seed with the correct Rhizobium strain before drilling or broadcasting it into a fall seedbed, then lightly cover, since Willamette establishes best with good seed-to-soil contact ahead of cool, wet weather. Developed in Oregon's Willamette Valley, this common vetch cultivar was selected for a lower proportion of hard, dormant seed than older vetch lines, giving it more uniform germination and reducing the volunteer-weed risk it can pose in following grass-seed or grain crops. It fixes a substantial amount of nitrogen over winter and spring, growing a sprawling, tendrilled vine that benefits from a cereal companion like rye or oats for physical support. Mow or terminate at early bloom, before pods begin to swell, to release nitrogen quickly and avoid reseeding.

common_name: Winfred Forage Brassica (Kale-Turnip Hybrid Cover Crop)
plant_note: Drill or broadcast in late summer for fall through early-winter growth; Winfred combines a kale parent's leafiness with a turnip parent's fast establishment and regrowth after cutting.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer, since fine brassica seed needs only light covering to establish quickly. Winfred is a cross between forage kale and forage turnip, producing an unusually leafy plant with a modest bulb-like root, and it retains far more cold tolerance than pure forage rape, staying green and grazable even after hard freezes into the low teens. It regrows vigorously after mowing or grazing, supporting two to four cuttings across a single fall-to-winter season, and can be paired with cereal rye or clover for a mixed cover that adds nitrogen scavenging along with weed suppression. Because it holds its quality later into winter than most brassica covers, it is a good choice where a longer window of grazable or mowable green cover is wanted before spring planting.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast in early fall on sandy, dry, or calcareous soils. Best suited to Mediterranean-climate regions with mild, wet winters and dry summers.
directions: Drill seed 1-2 inches deep in early fall at 40-60 lbs per acre, preferably inoculating with the appropriate Rhizobium strain if wing pea has not been grown in the field before. The distinctive winged stems form a low, interlocking canopy that suppresses winter weeds effectively. Allow the stand to fix nitrogen through the winter and terminate in spring before full seed set. Wing pea performs best where drainage is good; avoid waterlogged or heavy clay soils.

common_name: Winsor Royal Buckwheat (Large-Seeded Cover Crop Buckwheat)
plant_note: Sow after soil has warmed and frost risk has passed; this diploid large-seeded type establishes and canopies quickly in warm conditions.
directions: Winsor Royal is a large-seeded diploid buckwheat released by the Winsor Grain Company of Minneapolis in 1982 and grown for its bold, market-acceptable seed alongside a lower test weight than modern hybrid types. Broadcast or drill shallowly into a warm, firm seedbed after frost danger has ended, since seedlings emerge within days but are easily killed by cold soil or frost. The crop forms a dense, fast-closing canopy that shades out weeds and provides a strong nectar source for pollinators through its extended bloom period. Mow or disk under at early flowering for a quick-building green manure, or let a later planting stand into fall as a short-season smother crop ahead of a cover crop rotation.

plant_note: Plant in early to mid fall so plants establish crowns before winter dormancy.
directions: Drill or broadcast at 2-3 lb per 1,000 sq ft about 1 inch deep into a firm, well-drained seedbed. Winter barley tolerates drought and saline soils better than other cereals and releases allelopathic compounds that suppress weeds. It is less cold hardy than rye or wheat, so it performs best in USDA zones 6 and warmer. Terminate in spring by mowing or crimping at the boot stage before pollen shed, then incorporate or leave as mulch. Barley residue breaks down faster than rye, allowing earlier planting of the succeeding crop.

plant_note: Sow from 6 weeks before to just after first frost; the most cold-hardy cover crop, germinating in near-freezing soil.
directions: Broadcast seed at about 1/2 in depth in fall; it germinates in cold soil when little else will. It scavenges leftover nitrogen and smothers weeds over winter, then puts on fast spring growth. Mow and turn under 2–3 weeks before planting, as its residue briefly suppresses small seeds.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast 4-6 weeks before hard freeze so plants tiller before dormancy.
directions: Sow at 60-120 lb per acre or about 2 lb per 1,000 sq ft, drilling 1-1.5 inches deep or broadcasting onto a firm, moist seedbed. Winter wheat overwinters as a rosette, resumes growth in spring, and scavenges residual soil nitrogen while suppressing weeds. It is easier to terminate than cereal rye, making it a good choice for gardeners. Terminate in spring by mowing at the boot to early-flowering stage, then incorporate with tillage or crimp and leave residue as mulch. Allow two to three weeks of decomposition before planting the following crop.

common_name: Wonderleaf Pearl Millet (Leafy Hybrid Forage and Cover Crop Millet)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is reliably warm; Wonderleaf is a leafy hybrid pearl millet bred for grazing and green-chop as well as summer soil cover.
directions: Broadcast or drill into warm, moist soil after the danger of frost has passed, since pearl millet germinates poorly in cold ground. Wonderleaf was bred as a leafier, more grazing-tolerant hybrid than grain-type pearl millets, regrowing vigorously after mowing or grazing while still building a dense summer canopy that shades out weeds and protects bare soil during the hottest part of the season. It is markedly more drought tolerant than sudangrass or corn and, unlike sorghum-sudangrass, carries no prussic acid risk, making it a safer choice where livestock may graze regrowth. Mow or graze before seed heads mature to keep the stand productive, and let frost terminate the planting at season's end.

plant_note: Broadcast onto a firm seedbed in fall; Woogenellup is one of the most widely grown subterranean clover cultivars in the southeastern Coastal Plain, adapted from southern Texas to Florida and comparatively tolerant of iron-deficiency chlorosis.
directions: Broadcast seed over a firm, moist bed in early fall and rake lightly, since good seed-to-soil contact is essential for even establishment. Woogenellup is a widely planted Australian-bred subterranean clover cultivar that has proven well adapted to the southeastern Coastal Plain from southern Texas through Florida, and it shows comparatively good tolerance of iron-deficiency chlorosis relative to many other subterranean clover cultivars, though it can still show symptoms on high-pH calcareous soils. Like other subterranean clovers, it buries its own seed pods just below the soil surface after flowering, which lets a stand reseed itself reliably without replanting in most years. Its dense, low, mat-forming growth makes an excellent living mulch and winter weed suppressor under fruit trees or in orchard alleys, dying back naturally as temperatures rise in late spring.

plant_note: Sow in early fall; it matures earlier than common hairy vetch.
directions: Inoculate seed and drill or broadcast at about 1-2 lb per 1,000 sq ft, covering to 1 inch deep in a firm seedbed. Woolly pod vetch is an early-maturing relative of hairy vetch that fixes nitrogen and produces dense sprawling growth. Its earlier flowering makes it easier to terminate ahead of spring planting than standard hairy vetch. Mow or roller-crimp at early bloom for effective no-till kill, then plant into the residue mat. Because it can reseed, terminate before pods harden to limit volunteers in future crops.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; no scarification is typically necessary but nicking hard seeds speeds germination. Incorporate as green manure before seed set to prevent self-seeding and protect livestock.
directions: A tropical annual legume covered in soft, spreading hairs, with trifoliate leaves and short racemes of small yellow pea flowers followed by distinctively woolly, inflated seed pods that rattle when ripe; naturalized widely across the southeastern US coastal plain in disturbed, open, moist to dry ground. Direct sow after last frost in warm, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil — it tolerates low-fertility sandy soils well and fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis. As a warm-season cover crop in tropical and subtropical gardens and fields, it establishes readily from seed with little input and builds organic matter effectively when tilled under as green manure. Like all Crotalaria species, the seeds contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids toxic to livestock and humans — always incorporate before seed set and keep animals away from flowering or seeding plants.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill in early fall beneath orchards or vineyards, or into stubble after summer harvest. Widely adapted to California's Central Valley and coastal valleys as a low-input winter cover.
directions: Sow at 30-50 lbs per acre by broadcasting into a rough seedbed or drilling 1-1.5 inches deep in early fall, inoculating seed with a pea-vetch Rhizobium strain for maximum nitrogen fixation. Woollypod vetch establishes a thick, vining canopy over winter that outcompetes annual weeds and protects bare soil from erosion in California's rainy season. Mow or roll the stand in spring at early to full bloom to release fixed nitrogen and create a surface mulch that conserves moisture ahead of summer crops. This species handles dry spells better than hairy vetch, making it a reliable choice for drier dryland and low-rainfall irrigated systems.

common_name: Wrens Abruzzi Rye (Early-Maturing Southern Winter Cereal Rye)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall; Wrens Abruzzi is one of the most widely grown cereal rye cover crop cultivars in the South, valued for earlier fall growth and earlier spring maturity than many other rye varieties, letting it be terminated and the ground replanted sooner.
directions: Broadcast seed at 100-120 lbs/acre (1.5-2 lbs/1000 sq ft) in fall; mow or roll-crimp before spring vegetable planting. Wrens Abruzzi is one of the most popular and widely available cereal rye cover crop cultivars in the southeastern United States, selected for vigorous fall establishment and notably earlier spring maturity than many other rye varieties, which lets growers terminate it and get the following crop planted sooner in spring. Like other cereal ryes, it germinates in cool soil down to the mid-30s Fahrenheit and grows steadily through winter, providing substantial biomass, deep rooting that improves soil structure, effective weed suppression, and erosion control on fallow ground during the cool season. Its dense root system scavenges and holds nitrogen that would otherwise leach away over winter, releasing it back to the soil as the residue breaks down after termination. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or incorporation two to three weeks before planting the following crop to allow residue to begin breaking down and to avoid allelopathic effects on small-seeded crops planted too soon after termination.

common_name: Yellow Lupin (European Yellow Lupin, Gelbe Lupine)
plant_note: Sow in spring as soon as soil can be worked in zones 3–7; or in early fall in zones 7–9; yellow lupin is the most acid-tolerant of the grain lupins (grows well at pH 4.5–6.5) and the most cold-hardy, tolerating frost to -12°C in the vegetative stage; its primary use in European agriculture is as a green manure and forage crop on the lightest, most acidic, most infertile sandy soils where few other crops succeed.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed at 80–120 lbs per acre into light, acidic, sandy soils with good drainage; yellow lupin is uniquely adapted to pH 4.5–6.5 soils where white and narrow-leaf lupins struggle; inoculate with Bradyrhizobium lupini Group A; the aromatic yellow flowers attract bees; terminate at early bloom when biomass is maximum and nitrogen content is highest. Yellow lupin (Lupinus luteus) is the most cold-hardy and most acid-tolerant of the three main grain lupin species, native to the Mediterranean coastal regions of Portugal, Spain, and Morocco, where it grows on the poorest, most acidic, driest sandy soils. In European agriculture, particularly in Germany, Poland, and the Baltic states, yellow lupin has been grown for centuries as the standard green manure crop for reclaiming heathlands and sandy 'bad lands' — soils so acid, infertile, and droughty that even rye struggles. The species' extraordinary tolerance of acid conditions (pH 4.5 being optimal, with acceptable performance to pH 4.0) makes it uniquely valuable for the poorest sandy soils in the American Southeast and Pacific Northwest where soil pH is challenging. The seeds of traditional varieties are very high in bitter alkaloids (even more so than white lupin) and require special sweet cultivars for food use; in Germany sweet-lupin breeding in the early 20th century produced commercial yellow lupin varieties that have been grown as animal feed. As a cover crop, yellow lupin fixes 80–130 lbs N/acre and produces enough biomass to significantly improve soil organic matter on very poor soils. The distinctive fragrant yellow flowers are genuinely attractive in bloom.

common_name: Yellow Serradella / Bird's-foot Trefoil Cover Crop
plant_note: Sow in fall as temperatures begin to drop. Like serradella, yellow serradella requires inoculation with a specific Ornithopus rhizobium strain for effective nitrogen fixation. Broadcast onto a prepared, weed-free seedbed and lightly incorporate or roll to ensure good seed-to-soil contact.
directions: Direct sow yellow serradella in fall at 8-12 lb per acre into sandy or loamy, well-drained soils with a pH of 5.0-7.0, using rhizobium-inoculated seed for reliable nitrogen fixation. It is slightly better adapted to neutral to mildly acidic soils than common serradella, making it a useful choice for a broader range of Mediterranean-climate growing conditions. The compressed, segmented pods shatter and reseed readily at maturity, so allow pods to ripen fully before mowing if natural reseeding is desired for the following season. Terminate by mowing or incorporating before pod shatter to prevent volunteer problems ahead of summer cash crops.

plant_note: Direct-sow in early spring or late summer; behaves like white sweet clover but is slightly shorter and prefers drier soils.
directions: Scarify hard-coated seed before sowing to improve germination, and inoculate with Sinorhizobium meliloti for reliable nitrogen fixation in new plantings. Broadcast at 10–12 lb/acre and press lightly into a firm seedbed; yellow sweet clover is more drought-tolerant than most clovers and establishes well on thin, calcareous soils. It overwinters as a rosette and bolts to bloom in spring of the second year; terminate at early bud for maximum N contribution. Allow 3–4 weeks between incorporation and planting to let allelopathic coumarin compounds dissipate.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill seed in fall on well-drained soil; Yuchi is the original widely commercialized arrowleaf clover cultivar, prized for tall growth, late spring flowering, and strong reseeding in Gulf South pastures and cover-crop rotations.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a well-prepared, well-drained bed in early fall and lightly cover, since arrowleaf clover seedlings are slow to establish but grow rapidly once cool, moist weather arrives. Yuchi grows much taller than crimson or white clover, standing well above competing winter weeds, and continues flowering later into late spring than most other winter annual clovers, extending the nitrogen-fixing and pollinator-forage window. Its arrow-shaped leaves and dense stands make it a long-standing standard for Deep South winter cover cropping, and it reseeds itself readily on well-drained soils if allowed to flower and set seed before termination.

common_name: Zeon Zoysia Grass (Fine-Bladed Shade-Tolerant Zoysia Cultivar)
plant_note: Establish only from sod or plugs (not seed) once soil is consistently above 65°F; Zeon is a fine-textured Zoysia matrella cultivar selected for notably better shade tolerance than bermudagrass and finer leaf texture than broader-bladed Zoysia japonica cultivars like Empire.
directions: Set plugs or sod closer together than coarser zoysia cultivars, 6-12 inches apart, since Zeon spreads more slowly and benefits from denser initial coverage; keep evenly moist through the first growing season. Zeon was selected and released by a Texas turfgrass producer for its unusually fine, soft leaf blade and strong performance in partial shade, making it a popular choice for lawns with filtered tree cover where bermudagrass thins out. It tolerates close mowing to a putting-green-like height, holds color well into cooler weather, and needs relatively little fertilizer or water once established, though it goes tan-brown with the first hard frost. Dethatch periodically since dense zoysia growth builds thatch over time, and avoid scalping, which slows recovery.

plant_note: Broadcast seed onto bare ground between rows or under trees in fall; Zorro fescue is a fine, low-growing, self-reseeding annual grass favored as living mulch in orchards and vineyards where it competes strongly against weeds without needing repeated mowing.
directions: Broadcast the fine seed over a lightly cultivated surface in fall and press it in with a roller or light raking, since Zorro fescue needs only shallow coverage to establish before winter rains. It germinates quickly, forms a dense, low mat of narrow leaves through winter and early spring, and reseeds itself so effectively that a single fall planting can persist as a cover for several seasons in a row. Growers value it in row middles and under perennial crops because its dense, shallow root mat suppresses weed germination and reduces erosion and dust without competing heavily for water once it dries down and goes dormant in early summer.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; 3D African daisy flowers best in cool weather and can stall or go semi-dormant during peak summer heat.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; 3D African daisy flowers best in cool weather and can stall or go semi-dormant during peak summer heat. Uniquely textured, semi-double flowers combine a ring of flat, colorful outer petals with a raised, spoon-shaped or quilled inner row, giving each bloom a layered, three-dimensional effect quite different from the flat, single daisy form of standard osteospermum. Its compact, mounding habit and long bloom season in cool spring and fall weather make it a popular container and border plant, particularly valued in mild-winter climates where it can be treated as a short-lived perennial rather than a single-season annual. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, provide excellent drainage, and expect reduced flowering during the hottest, most humid weeks of summer.

common_name: A Shropshire Lad Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since A Shropshire Lad is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber against a wall, fence, or pillar.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1996 and named for the A. E. Housman poetry collection, A Shropshire Lad carries large, softly cupped, warm peachy-pink blooms with a light, fruity fragrance, on long, arching canes that can reach 8-10 feet or more when trained as a climber, or be kept pruned as a large freestanding shrub. Its vigor and long, flexible canes make it a favorite for growing over an arch or pergola, and it repeat-blooms well from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Aaron Caladium (Large White Sun-Tolerant Strap-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Aaron is one of the most sun-tolerant caladium varieties — it tolerates 3–5 hours of direct morning sun without bleaching or burning, expanding its usefulness to lightly shaded positions.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Aaron is one of the oldest, most commercially important, and most reliably grown white caladium varieties — a large strap-leaf type producing elongated, lance-to-heart-shaped leaves with near-white to cream-white leaf surfaces and contrasting green margins, creating a clean, elegant, white-and-green color combination that is among the most versatile in shade garden design. Unlike many white caladiums that require deep shade, Aaron's strap-leaf form and leaf cuticle characteristics give it exceptional sun tolerance — Aaron can be planted in positions receiving 3–5 hours of direct morning sun without the bleaching, edge-burn, or leaf collapse that afflicts most large-leaved white fancy caladiums. This higher sun tolerance makes Aaron useful in transition zones between full shade and partial sun where white color is desired but deep-shade caladiums would stretch and underperform. The white coloration brightens dark shade positions dramatically and creates an elegant effect in formal garden beds, containers, and mass plantings along shaded foundations. Aaron remains one of the most widely produced commercial caladium varieties because of its reliable performance, good tuber production, vigorous growth, and consistent white color. In zone 9, Aaron produces its best growth and color during the warm season from May through October. Combine with 'Burning Heart' for bold red-and-white contrast in shade beds.

common_name: Aaron's Beard (Creeping St. John's Wort, Rose of Sharon Groundcover)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Aaron's beard spreads by underground rhizomes to form a dense, weed-smothering mat and tolerates the dry, root-filled soil under trees better than most flowering groundcovers.
directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath trees or on a bank too difficult to mow; Aaron's beard is a low, semi-evergreen, trailing sub-shrub grown for large, bright golden-yellow flowers with a prominent burst of long stamens that open through summer over blue-green foliage. It spreads steadily by underground rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing mat, tolerating dry shade, root competition, and poor soil better than nearly any other flowering groundcover, which makes it a workhorse for stabilizing shaded slopes and banks where mowing is impractical. Because it spreads assertively, give it a contained space, such as a bank bordered by pavement or a bed edged with a mowing strip, rather than a small formal border where its vigor would be unwelcome. Shear old plantings back close to the ground in late winter every few years to rejuvenate growth and keep flowering strong.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to early fall directly into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, setting the rhizome shallowly with its top at or just below the soil surface.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or early fall directly into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, setting the rhizome shallowly with its top at or barely below the surface in partial shade to full sun. Iris nelsonii, called the Abbeville iris, is a naturally occurring Louisiana iris species found historically in only a handful of roadside ditches near Abbeville, Louisiana, believed to have arisen from natural crossing among copper iris, giant blue iris, and zigzag iris. Its branched flower stalks carry brick-red to deep maroon-red blooms held above sword-shaped foliage in mid-spring, attracting bumblebees and swallowtail butterflies. Because wild populations are so geographically limited, growing nursery-propagated plants in a wet Gulf Coast rain garden or pond margin adds a flower color unmatched by any other native iris while easing pressure on the rare wild colonies.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture keeps the deeply cupped leaves from flattening out in Gulf South heat.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this award-winning cultivar produces exceptionally thick, heavily corrugated blue-green leaves that cup so deeply they will genuinely hold a puddle of water or a scoop of birdseed after a rain, a distinctive trait its name describes literally. The dense, mounded clump has excellent substance and slug resistance for a blue hosta, since blue-leaved cultivars are often thinner-leaved and more vulnerable. Near-white flowers appear on stout scapes in early to midsummer, held mostly within or just above the foliage. Divide in early spring only when necessary, since this cultivar is slow to reach full size and resents frequent disturbance; established clumps make an outstanding textural anchor for a shaded border.

common_name: Abraham Darby Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun in rich, well-drained soil; Abraham Darby is a vigorous grower that can be kept as a large rounded shrub with regular pruning or allowed to reach 10-12 feet as a short climber against a wall or pillar in warm Southern gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, compost-enriched soil and feed regularly through the growing season to support this heavy-blooming rose's vigorous repeat flowering. Bred by David Austin and named for the ironworks pioneer, Abraham Darby was introduced in 1985 and bears very large, deeply cupped blooms that open in warm blends of apricot, peach, and pink with a rich, fruity fragrance often compared to ripe peaches. Its vigorous, somewhat arching growth habit and strong disease resistance in humid conditions make it a dependable performer across the Gulf South, where it is frequently grown as a large shrub in a mixed border or trained up a pillar or low wall for extra height. Deadhead spent blooms through the season and prune hard in late winter to keep the shrub shapely and productive.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in virtually any soil in shade; Abraham-Isaac-Jacob is extraordinarily adaptable and will succeed in dry shade, wet shade, heavy clay, or sandy soil — conditions that defeat most shade groundcovers. It is slow to establish in the first year but spreads reliably thereafter by underground rhizomes.
directions: Plant in virtually any moist to dry soil in full to part shade; Abraham-Isaac-Jacob is a robust, large-leafed borage-family perennial from Turkey and the Caucasus that has earned a dedicated following among shade gardeners for one exceptional quality: it will cover dry shade under large deciduous trees where almost nothing else grows, spreading steadily by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat of enormous, rough-textured, heart-shaped leaves reaching 12–18 inches across on mature plants. In very early spring — February or March — clusters of small, intensely blue, reflexed flowers emerge on bare stems before the foliage appears, giving the unusual appearance of flowers seemingly floating above bare ground. The common name 'Abraham-Isaac-Jacob' describes the three-color pattern of the buds (purple), open flowers (blue), and spent flowers (pink), all visible simultaneously on the nodding flower cluster, similar to Pulmonaria. After flowering, the bold, tropical-looking foliage expands to dominate and cool the ground beneath trees for the rest of the season. An outstanding solution for the most difficult dry-shade situations.

common_name: Abu Hassan Tulip (Mahogany-Red Triumph Tulip Edged Bright Yellow)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Abu Hassan is a Triumph-class tulip with mahogany-red petals edged in bright yellow, blooming midseason.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Abu Hassan, a Triumph-class tulip, bears rich mahogany-red petals crisply edged in bright golden yellow, a warm, autumnal bicolor combination blooming in midseason on sturdy, medium-height stems typical of the versatile Triumph group. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring after all frost danger has passed, in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. In zones 8–9, Abyssinian Banana must be treated as a large annual or overwintered indoors; dig and pot the plant before frost and store in a frost-free location.
directions: Abyssinian Banana is the most dramatic of the ornamental bananas, native to the highland forests of Ethiopia and East Africa and grown worldwide as a bold tropical accent plant for its colossal size and the extraordinary visual impact of its enormous leaves — reaching up to 10 feet long with striking red midribs on deep green blades — that create an instant tropical atmosphere wherever they are planted. Unlike true bananas (Musa species), Abyssinian Banana is monocarpic, meaning each trunk (pseudostem) flowers once after 3–10 years and then dies; unlike rhizomatous bananas it does not produce pups from the base, and in Ethiopia the starchy corm and pseudostem are fermented to produce enset (a culturally crucial food for over 20 million people) rather than relying on the fruit for food. In zones 9b–11 it persists as a perennial; in zones 8–9 it is typically grown as an impressive annual or dug and stored frost-free for the winter. Provide the richest, most moisture-retentive soil available, regular fertilization, and full sun for maximum leaf size.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. Impatiens walleriana is susceptible to impatiens downy mildew (IDM), which has devastated impatiens plantings across North America since 2011 — if IDM has been a problem in your area, consider New Guinea impatiens or SunPatiens (Impatiens hawkeri types) instead, which are resistant to IDM. The Accent series has demonstrated good performance when planted in well-drained conditions with good air circulation. Do not overhead water.
directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Accent Red Impatiens is part of the Accent series of Impatiens walleriana — the standard, traditional shade-flowering annual that has been the top-selling bedding plant in North America for decades due to its unmatched ability to produce continuous, vivid color in deep shade conditions where virtually no other flowering annual will bloom adequately. The compact, mounded habit, brilliant scarlet-red flowers, and vigorous production without deadheading made the Accent series the industry benchmark for impatiens performance. Impatiens walleriana (busy Lizzie) is the defining shade bedding plant for beds under trees, north-facing foundations, and deeply shaded borders — its natural woodland origin (East African highlands) gives it genuine shade tolerance rather than the partial-shade preference of most 'shade plants'. The continuous, prolific bloom and brilliant color saturation in true shade conditions remains a standard that few plants can match.

common_name: Accolade Elm (Vigorous Disease-Resistant Hybrid Shade Tree)
scientific_name: Ulmus davidiana var. japonica × Ulmus wilsoniana 'Morton'
plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in a wide range of soils in full sun; Accolade, introduced by the Morton Arboretum, is an Asian-species hybrid rather than an American elm selection and carries excellent, broad resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where the tree quickly develops a dense, vase-to-rounded canopy of glossy, dark green foliage. Accolade is a hybrid of two Asian elm species introduced by the Morton Arboretum, prized for combining rapid growth, strong urban tolerance, and outstanding resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle, two of the biggest threats to elms in cultivation. Unlike American elm selections it does not aim to replicate the classic broad vase silhouette exactly, instead forming a somewhat more upright, uniform shade tree well suited to streets, parking areas, and residential landscapes where a fast-growing, trouble-free canopy tree is wanted. It tolerates heat, drought once established, and a range of soil types, and needs only routine formative pruning in its early years to develop strong branch structure.

common_name: Ace of Hearts Redbud (Compact Round-Leaf Dwarf Redbud)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Ace of Hearts stays notably smaller and denser than standard redbud, making it a good fit for small yards and foundation plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where its small mature size and dense canopy can be appreciated up close. Ace of Hearts is a dwarf, compact selection of eastern redbud, reaching roughly half the size of the species, with small, glossy, heart-shaped leaves packed tightly along the branches and a rounded, tidy habit that needs little pruning to stay in bounds. Like other redbuds it flowers on bare wood in early spring with a dense flush of small rosy-pink pea-like blooms before the leaves emerge, followed by clean, deep-green summer foliage that holds its glossy texture better in heat than the species form. Its small stature makes it well suited to foundation plantings, patios, and smaller residential landscapes where a full-sized redbud would quickly outgrow the space.

common_name: Acoma Crape Myrtle (Weeping White Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Acoma's gracefully weeping branch habit spreads wider than it grows tall, so allow ample lateral space when siting it.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Acoma is a distinctive weeping, semi-dwarf National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle with pure white flower clusters produced from summer into fall on gracefully arching branches, a growth habit unusual among crape myrtles that gives it strong specimen and accent value. Like its sibling cultivars it shows good resistance to powdery mildew and develops attractive mottled, exfoliating bark with maturity. Its spreading, weeping form makes it well suited as a small specimen tree, container planting, or bank cover where the arching branches can be shown off. Remove root suckers and prune only lightly to shape rather than heavily topping the plant.

common_name: Actaea Daffodil (Fragrant White Poet's Daffodil with Red-Rimmed Eye)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; Actaea is a poeticus-type daffodil, among the latest and most fragrant daffodils to bloom, with a small red-rimmed yellow eye.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Actaea bears flat, pure white petals surrounding a small, flat, yellow cup edged in a fine red rim, the classic Poet's Narcissus form, opening late in the daffodil season with an intense, sweet fragrance considered among the finest of any daffodil. Poeticus types like Actaea have a long garden history and naturalize well in meadows and orchards. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; acuminate epimedium spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover. It is one of the largest-flowered epimediums and produces unusually long, graceful flower spurs.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; acuminate epimedium is a Chinese species prized among epimedium collectors for its exceptionally long, elegant flower spurs — among the longest of any epimedium species — which give the flowers a dramatic, almost exotic appearance in the spring garden. The flowers come in combinations of white, purple, and pale violet with contrasting inner petals, and the unusually long curved spurs trail beneath like the limbs of a spider or a shuttlecock in flight. The foliage is semi-evergreen, with new leaves emerging with attractive bronze-red tints in spring before maturing to glossy green. More shade-tolerant than many epimediums and reliably drought-tolerant once established under trees. A superb epimedium species for the woodland garden and difficult dry-shade conditions.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Adagio is the most popular dwarf miscanthus selection and is particularly well-suited to smaller residential gardens where the full-size maiden grass cultivars would overwhelm the space.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Adagio is a compact dwarf miscanthus cultivar reaching only 3–4 feet — roughly half the size of standard maiden grass — making it one of the few miscanthus cultivars truly appropriate for small gardens, residential foundation plantings, and mixed borders without dominating surrounding plants. The narrow, fine-textured, silvery-green blades have a thin white midrib, giving the plant a delicate, refined appearance that belies its toughness and heat tolerance. In late summer, Adagio produces proportionally large, showy, silver-pink plumes that appear at about the height of the foliage mass, creating a beautiful late-season display that lasts well into winter. The compact size and early bloom time (earlier than most miscanthus — often blooming in late August in zone 9) make Adagio one of the most ornamentally productive miscanthus selections for the Gulf South, where the late-blooming miscanthus often do not flower before the first frost. Fall color transitions through golden-yellow. Excellent for mass planting, specimen use, or as a soft backdrop for autumn-blooming perennials. Cut back to 6 inches in February in zone 9 before new growth begins.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or pups (rooted offsets) in spring in well-drained, sandy to gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; Adam's Needle is the most cold-hardy and widely adaptable yucca native to the eastern United States, thriving across a remarkably broad range from zone 4 through zone 11 and performing in a wider range of climates than any other commonly grown yucca.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry soil in full sun; avoid clay soils or any location where water collects; once established, Adam's Needle is extremely drought-tolerant and virtually care-free; remove spent flower stalks after blooming; propagate from pups that form at the base of mature rosettes. Adam's Needle (Yucca filamentosa) is the most widespread and commonly grown yucca in American horticulture — native to the sandy coastal plains and dry inland areas of the southeastern United States from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Mississippi — and the standard garden yucca against which other species are compared. The species is named for its most distinctive leaf characteristic: along each leaf margin run numerous fine, thread-like fibers (filaments) that curl loosely and peel away from the leaf edge, giving the plant a distinctive fringe of white curling threads that is unique among commonly grown yuccas and easily visible in the field. The rosette of stiff, blue-green, sword-shaped leaves (2–3 feet long) grows slowly for 3–5 years before sending up a spectacular 4–8 foot flower spike bearing dozens to hundreds of nodding, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers with a sweet fragrance — one of the most dramatic summer flowering events in the native plant garden. The yucca moth (Tegeticula yuccasella) is the sole pollinator, with a mutualistic relationship unique in the plant-pollinator world: female yucca moths deliberately pack pollen onto the yucca stigma, then lay eggs in the ovary, and the larvae feed on some of the developing seeds — leaving enough viable seeds for yucca reproduction. Named cultivars include 'Color Guard' (yellow-striped leaves) and 'Bright Edge' (gold-margined leaves).

common_name: Admiral Semmes Azalea (Golden-Orange Southern Heritage Native Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container stock in fall or late winter in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial sun.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection, mulching well to keep roots cool. Admiral Semmes is a long-cultivated Southern heritage selection of native azalea grown for its fragrant, golden-orange flowers that open in a heavy spring flush on a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed shrub well adapted to Deep South heat and humidity. As with other native deciduous azaleas, its strong fragrance and heat tolerance have kept it in cultivation among Southern native-plant collectors even as flashier Asian evergreen azalea hybrids have dominated the broader nursery trade. Site it at a woodland edge or beneath high pine or hardwood canopy, and keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, since deciduous azaleas resent both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: Adolphe Audusson Camellia (Deep Red Camellia japonica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Adolphe Audusson is one of the most vigorous japonica cultivars and can become a large shrub or small tree over many years in zone 9 — allow adequate space at planting.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Adolphe Audusson is a classic, vigorous Camellia japonica cultivar valued for one of the deepest, richest red flower colors available in japonica camellias — a vivid blood-red to deep crimson-red in large, semi-double flowers with a prominent central cluster of golden-yellow stamens that creates a striking color contrast. The bold, saturated red flower color and large flower size make it one of the most eye-catching camellia selections for winter color in the shaded garden. Introduced in France in 1877 and still widely grown, Adolphe Audusson is a vigorous grower that develops into a large shrub or small tree in zone 9 conditions, with upright growth to 7–14 feet and dense, dark-green, glossy evergreen foliage. It blooms in mid-season (December through February in zone 9), with peak bloom typically in January. The bold red flower color provides exceptional cut-flower value — the flowers last well in arrangements. 'Adolphe Audusson Variegated' is a sport with red flowers marked with white streaks and spots; 'Adolphe Audusson Special' has darker red, more formal double flowers. Maintain consistent moisture and acidic soil; apply sulfur-based acidifying fertilizer if soil pH drifts above 6.5.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, rocky or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; tolerates caliche and desert soils well.
directions: Adonis Blazingstar is a slender, much-branched native perennial of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and adjacent Mexico, growing on dry, rocky, calcareous or sandy desert hills and open slopes in the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert regions. Unlike its white-flowered Great Plains relatives, it produces numerous bright yellow to orange-yellow, 5-petaled flowers 1 to 1.5 inches across on airy, much-forked stems, blooming freely from spring through fall and opening in the afternoon and evening hours rather than strictly at night. The lighter, daytime-accessible blooms attract a broader range of native bees and butterfly visitors than the nocturnal Mentzelia species, making it a highly productive pollinator plant across a long season. Direct sow in fall in extremely lean, rocky or sandy, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; an outstanding xeriscape perennial for Texas Hill Country and Chihuahuan Desert native gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; dislikes root disturbance from transplanting.
directions: 'African Bride' bears dramatic white blooms with contrasting near-black centers atop airy, threadlike foliage. Direct sow in place because love-in-a-mist resents transplanting once its taproot forms. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and thin seedlings for good airflow. After flowering, papery, dark-tinged seed pods develop that are excellent in fresh and dried arrangements. It self-sows readily, returning year after year in the garden.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in fall; African cornflag is a vigorous naturalizer in zones 8b–10, spreading freely by cormlets to form large colonies on slopes and roadsides. In zone 8 it may need light mulch protection in cold winters. Plant in areas where spread is welcome or where colonies can be naturalized.
directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; African cornflag is a vigorous South African corm in the iris family producing upright, sword-like fans of pleated, bright-green leaves and, in late winter and early spring (January–March), strongly arching flowering spikes bearing numerous, bright orange-red to scarlet tubular flowers that are powerfully attractive to hummingbirds and sunbirds. The flowers are curved and tubular — adapted for long-billed bird pollinators — and appear in great abundance on established colonies. It naturalizes freely in zones 8b–11 by producing abundant cormlets, spreading on sunny hillsides and roadsides in California, the Gulf Coast, and other warm-winter climates to form spectacular stands of winter-to-spring color. The variety 'Duckitt's Yellow' produces clear yellow flowers and is more restrained in spread. Outstanding for naturalizing on difficult slopes, sunny banks, and low-maintenance areas where a self-sustaining winter color display is desired.

plant_note: Plant tubers just below the soil surface in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade; African cyclamen flowers in autumn before or with the leaves and goes summer dormant. It is similar to C. hederifolium but larger in all parts — larger tuber, larger leaves, larger flowers — and slightly less cold-hardy. In zone 9 it can remain in the ground year-round; protect the tuber from hard frost in colder zones. The large tubers can reach 12 inches across in very old plants.
directions: Plant tubers near the soil surface in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part to full shade; African cyclamen is essentially a larger, more tender version of the familiar C. hederifolium — producing in autumn (September–November) before or with the leaves, pink to deep rose-pink, reflexed-petaled cyclamen flowers of the typical shuttlecock form, fragrant, and the characteristic ivy-shaped, attractively marbled and silver-patterned leaves that follow and persist through winter and spring before the plant goes summer dormant. What distinguishes C. africanum is scale: the flowers are larger than those of C. hederifolium, the marbled, silver-zoned leaves are larger, and the tubers of old plants can reach extraordinary dimensions — dinner plate-sized, flat-topped, brownish-gray corms that have been in the ground for decades and represent some of the most massive of all hardy bulbs. Native to the woodlands and scrubland of Algeria and Tunisia, it is marginally less cold-hardy than C. hederifolium, thriving in zones 8–11 and making it an outstanding candidate for the Gulf Coast and California shade garden where C. hederifolium can be inconsistent. Outstanding under the dry shade of large trees in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost as plants tolerate light frost.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained germination mix; seedlings grow quickly and should be potted on before becoming root-bound. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil as soon as the risk of hard frost has passed; osteospermum thrives in cool weather and slows during peak summer heat. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continuous bloom and pinch stem tips to promote branching early in the season. In zones 9–11 it may survive as a short-lived perennial; take stem cuttings in late summer to perpetuate favorite selections.

common_name: African Daisy (Freeway Daisy, Trailing African Daisy)
plant_note: Plant container transplants in spring or fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; trailing African daisy is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and is one of the most successful perennial groundcovers for sunny, dry slopes and roadside banks in California and the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; trailing African daisy establishes best in fall or early spring and becomes drought-tolerant once rooted. Osteospermum fruticosum (trailing African daisy or freeway daisy) is a sprawling, mat-forming perennial producing cheerful white, lavender, or purple ray flowers (1.5–2 inches across) with blue-purple disk centers in enormous profusion from fall through spring, with some blooms year-round in mild climates; blooming peaks in late winter and spring when the mat literally disappears under flowers. This South African native was heavily planted along California freeways beginning in the 1960s, giving rise to its common name 'freeway daisy'; it is now widely naturalized in coastal California. In zones 9–11, it performs as a perennial groundcover for hot, sunny, dry slopes, road banks, and xeric garden borders where its trailing stems quickly form a weed-suppressing mat. It does not tolerate frost below about 25°F but rebounds rapidly from light damage. Shear or mow hard after the main bloom flush to encourage compact regrowth and repeat bloom.

common_name: African False Lily of the Valley (Little White Soldiers)
plant_note: Divide offset bulblets or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade in spring; African false lily of the valley thrives in conditions of consistent shade and moisture that simulate its forest-floor native habitat. It goes semi-dormant in winter with reduced watering but is never fully deciduous in mild climates. Excellent for deep shade where bulbs that need more light would fail.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; African false lily of the valley is a South African forest-floor bulb prized for two qualities — its shade tolerance (making it one of the few true bulbs that thrives in deep shade) and the attractive dark-spotted pattern of its leaves (the species epithet maculata means 'spotted'). The broadly oval, smooth, dark-green leaves are irregularly decorated with darker green to bronze-purple spots and blotches that give each leaf a painted, dappled quality reminiscent of certain Pulmonaria or Arum species. In late spring through summer it produces dense, upright racemes of small, white, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers similar in form to lily of the valley but upright rather than pendant. The small, crowded, bright-white flowers create a cheerful, clean display. It spreads by producing numerous small offset bulblets, quickly forming a tight, spreading colony in favorable conditions. An outstanding choice for zones 9–11 where a shade-tolerant, spotted-leaved, white-flowering bulb groundcover is needed under dense tree canopy.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; African feather grass spreads by rhizome and can become aggressive in favorable, moist conditions, so site it where spread is acceptable or contain the roots.
directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; African feather grass spreads by rhizome and can become aggressive in favorable, moist conditions, so site it where spread is acceptable or contain the roots. Narrow, upright foliage sends up tall, slender, densely bristled flower spikes in late summer that stand stiffly upright rather than nodding, aging from green to a pale straw-buff that catches low light beautifully and persists well into winter for cut and dried arrangements. Native to South Africa, it is a bolder, more upright counterpart to the more familiar dwarf fountain grass, useful for adding height and strong vertical structure at the back of a border or in a large container. Cut the clump back hard in late winter before new growth begins, and divide or contain the spreading rhizomes to keep it from crowding neighboring plants.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil of average fertility in full sun to partial shade; African fern pine tolerates heat, drought once established, and urban conditions, and is commonly clipped as a hedge or espalier as well as grown as a specimen tree.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil of average fertility in full sun to partial shade, watering regularly the first year and then only occasionally once roots are established, since this East African conifer handles heat and drought far better than most needled evergreens. Fine, narrow, willowy leaves give the tree a soft, weeping texture unlike the stiff scale foliage of junipers and cypresses commonly used for the same purposes, and it responds well to shearing, which makes it a popular clipped hedge, screen, or espalier as well as an unclipped specimen tree in mild climates. It is widely planted as a street and parking-lot tree in California and the Southwest for its tolerance of reflected heat, compacted soil, and irregular irrigation, but is damaged by hard freezes and is only reliable outdoors in nearly frost-free zones.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost in a warm, sunny spot.
directions: Sow African flake daisy directly after the last frost, barely covering the seed in a sunny, well-drained bed. These cheerful yellow blooms with purple centers open on compact, fine-foliaged plants that shrug off heat and drought. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the display going through the warm months. Perfect for water-wise borders and containers, it asks for little more than sun and sharp drainage.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; African iris blooms most profusely in full sun but tolerates partial shade well. Avoid deadheading spent flower stalks — the branching stems continue to produce new flower buds from the same stalk for months.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; African iris is one of the most practical and reliable perennials for zone 8–11 landscapes, earning its common name 'fortnight lily' because it blooms in cycles roughly every two weeks throughout the warm season. The elegant white flowers with yellow and purple markings closely resemble true iris flowers but are produced on branching stalks that continue reblooming without deadheading — the spent blooms drop cleanly without the need for any grooming. The clumping, strap-like, evergreen leaves provide bold, attractive foliage year-round. It is exceptionally drought, heat, salt, and poor-soil tolerant once established, performing equally well in coastal and inland gardens. Divide congested clumps every 4–5 years in spring. A closely related species, Dietes bicolor (yellow African iris), produces pale yellow flowers with purple spots and is similarly adaptable. An outstanding low-maintenance perennial for mass plantings, borders, and water-wise landscapes.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; agapanthus blooms most freely when root-bound and when the bulb-like roots can see some light — avoid deep planting and unnecessary disturbance, as established clumps bloom most reliably when left undivided.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; African lily is a South African evergreen perennial that has become one of the most widely planted flowering perennials in warm-climate gardens worldwide — producing large, round, elegant, spherical flower heads of 20–40 individual, tubular, funnel-shaped, bright blue to violet-blue or white flowers on strong, upright, 2–4-foot stems above broad rosettes of glossy, strap-shaped, dark-green, evergreen leaves, blooming in summer (June–August). The spherical blue flower heads are among the most refined and beautifully structured of any summer-blooming perennial and associate superbly with white and yellow flowers. Agapanthus praecox (syn. A. orientalis) is the largest and most common species in cultivation, forming substantial clumps that flower most freely when moderately crowded and root-bound; excessive division reduces flowering. Tolerates partial shade, clay soil, coastal salt spray, and moderate drought once established. The deciduous species (A. campanulatus, A. caulescens) are hardier (to zone 6) but less evergreen; A. praecox is evergreen but limited to zone 8–12.

common_name: African Lily (Blue Lily of the Nile, Agapanthus)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; agapanthus is one of the best-performing perennials for Gulf Coast summer gardens — heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant once established, and producing a stunning display of blue or white trumpet flowers in July–September.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; bloom is best after mild crowding — do not divide too frequently. Agapanthus africanus (African blue lily or lily of the Nile) is a classic South African perennial that has become one of the most widely grown ornamental plants in warm, Mediterranean, and subtropical climates worldwide — producing bold clumps of long, strap-shaped, arching, dark-green evergreen leaves topped by tall (18–36 inch) stems bearing large, spherical umbels of 20–50 tubular, blue-violet to white flowers in July–September. The flower heads, 4–8 inches across and resembling a blue fireworks burst, are a stunning feature in summer borders when most other perennials have passed their peak. Agapanthus is remarkably adaptable once established — tolerating heat, drought, poor soils, and coastal salt spray — and practically maintenance-free. Flower color ranges from deep violet-blue through pale lavender to pure white; the blue forms are the most commonly grown. The plant is also outstanding as a container subject, performing reliably when somewhat pot-bound. CAUTION: All parts are mildly toxic if ingested; sap may irritate skin.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; African mahogany grows naturally in the Sahel and savanna belt of West Africa in seasonally dry, tropical conditions and is more drought-tolerant than the American mahoganies once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 10–12; African mahogany is a West African timber and shade tree in the Meliaceae family (same family as American mahogany), widely planted in tropical and subtropical regions for shade and timber. The pinnate compound leaves create a dense canopy that provides excellent shade. The reddish-brown wood is harder than West Indian mahogany but less prized in fine furniture; it is extensively used in flooring, general construction, and plywood production in Africa. In south Florida, African mahogany is widely planted as a fast-growing street and shade tree, developing a large, spreading crown that provides dense summer shade. More salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant than American mahogany and faster-growing, making it practical for large-scale urban tree planting in zone 10 coastal Florida.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; sow no earlier than 6 weeks before last frost, as large-seeded transplants tend to become rootbound quickly.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; sow no earlier than 6 weeks before last frost, as large-seeded transplants tend to become rootbound quickly. Tagetes erecta is the tall, large-flowered marigold with enormous double pompom flower heads 3–4 inches across in brilliant yellow, orange, and cream — sacred to the goddess Xochiquetzal in Aztec culture and still used extensively in Mexican Day of the Dead (Día de Muertos) festivals, where millions of flowers are harvested annually. The petals are edible and have a mild, spicy, slightly citrusy flavor; dried petals are used to color butter, cheese, and poultry feed (providing the beta-carotene that gives egg yolks their golden color in commercial farming). It is the most important commercial cut marigold species; choose large transplant sizes in spring as they establish quickly.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–June. Polly performs best as a container plant in zone 9, where it can be moved indoors during the rare cold snaps. In the warmest zone 9 areas it may survive as an in-ground perennial in a sheltered, heavily mulched location. Provide very bright indirect light or early morning sun with afternoon shade — direct summer sun bleaches and burns the dramatic dark leaves. Maintain high humidity (mist frequently or place on a humidity tray). In zone 9's warm, humid summers, Polly can be grown outdoors in deep shade for the summer season.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic, consistently moist but well-aerated soil — Alocasia require moisture but are sensitive to root rot in poorly drained or overly wet conditions; African Mask Alocasia (Polly) is a compact cultivar of Alocasia x amazonica, an Aroid hybrid of unknown tropical Southeast Asian species parentage, producing dramatically dark, arrow-shaped to elongated, deeply lobed leaves with prominent, contrasting, chalk-white primary and secondary veins against near-black to deep forest-green leaf surfaces. The high-contrast white vein pattern on the dark leaf — which does indeed have an unsettling resemblance to decorative African masks — is one of the most striking and dramatic foliage effects possible in a houseplant or shade garden specimen. The 'Polly' selection is a more compact form (18–24 inches) than the larger-growing Alocasia x amazonica species, making it more practical for container use and indoor cultivation. Each leaf is simultaneously a botanical and artistic object — the precise geometry of the veining pattern and the glossy, slightly undulating dark green leaf surface create an effect that is more designed than any human art and more dramatic than almost any other commonly grown plant.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; African milk barrel needs excellent drainage and full sun to develop its best form and spine color.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; African milk barrel needs excellent drainage and full sun to develop its best form and spine color. Thick, ribbed, barrel-shaped, blue-gray stems armed with formidable dark spines closely resemble a true barrel cactus despite being an entirely unrelated South African euphorbia, slowly clustering into a small cluster of columnar stems over years of growth. All parts exude a caustic, irritating milky latex sap when cut, so handle with gloves and eye protection during any pruning or repotting, and keep well away from children and pets. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact, well-spined growth, and protect from any frost.

common_name: African Milk Tree (Cathedral Cactus, Friendship Cactus)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings (allow the cut end to callus for several days before potting, since the latex sap otherwise inhibits rooting) or plant container specimens in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright light with some direct sun; African milk tree has no frost tolerance and is grown outdoors year-round only in zone 10-11, elsewhere as a container houseplant. CAUTION: the milky latex sap is a severe skin and eye irritant — wear gloves and eye protection when handling or pruning.
directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun, in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only after the soil has dried out. African milk tree is a fast-growing, cactus-like succulent shrub from Central Africa with tall, upright, triangular, ridged stems edged in small paired thorns and tiny leaves along the ridges; the widely sold 'Rubra' form has deep burgundy-red coloring that intensifies in strong light. Stems branch readily from the base and from pruning cuts, quickly producing a dense, candelabra-like clump that can eventually reach several feet tall indoors. Handle only with gloves and eye protection, since like other Euphorbias it exudes a milky latex sap when cut that is a potent skin and eye irritant and toxic if ingested; keep well away from children and pets. Repot every couple of years into fresh, fast-draining mix and prune to control height, using the resulting cuttings to propagate new plants after a callusing period.

common_name: African Queen Lily (Fragrant Apricot-Orange Trumpet Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; African Queen is a classic trumpet lily with purple-flushed buds opening into large fragrant apricot blooms.
directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, keeping the base of the plant shaded with mulch or companion plants. African Queen is a classic trumpet lily bearing large, intensely fragrant, apricot-orange trumpets that open from dramatic purple-flushed buds on tall, sturdy stems, a rich warm color and powerful scent that has made it a long-standing favorite for both garden borders and cut-flower use. Trumpet lilies tend to be more vigorous and tolerant of a range of soils than many Oriental hybrids. Leave the foliage in place after bloom until it yellows naturally, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in full sun in well-drained, fertile, deep soil; African Rosewood is a large, deciduous West African savanna tree of great commercial and ecological importance — its heartwood is one of the most internationally traded and threatened tropical timbers, prized for furniture and instruments — and it bears brilliant yellow pea-family flowers in terminal clusters before leaf-out in the dry season.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil; Pterocarpus erinaceus is a drought-adapted savanna tree that requires excellent drainage and tolerates seasonal dry periods — avoid waterlogged sites and heavy clay soils. Pterocarpus erinaceus (African Rosewood, Vène, or Kosso) is a large, deciduous legume tree native to the open savanna, guinea woodland, and dry forest zones of West Africa from Senegal east through the Sudan-Sahel zone to Ethiopia, a member of the Fabaceae family and one of the continent's most economically significant and critically over-exploited timber trees. The heartwood is dense, durable, deep reddish-brown to rose-red with interlocked grain — superficially resembling Asian rosewoods (Dalbergia spp.) — and has been the subject of massive illegal logging and export particularly to China and East Asia in the 21st century for furniture manufacture, resulting in international CITES trade regulation. Before logging, trees produce spectacular, dense, terminal clusters of deep-yellow pea-family flowers in the dry season on leafless branches. The tree is a critical component of the West African parkland agroforestry system where it is retained in farmers' fields for shade, nitrogen fixation, fodder, and traditional medicine (the red-staining bark gum is used medicinally across West Africa). A valuable shade and nitrogen-fixing tree for tropical agroforestry systems where large specimens can be grown sustainably.

common_name: African Trumpet Tree (Magnificent Fernandoa, Yellow African Trumpet)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Fernandoa magnifica is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 10-11 outdoor planting. The tree is relatively fast-growing and can begin blooming within 3–5 years from seed. The enormous clusters of large yellow-orange trumpet flowers make it one of the most impressive African ornamental trees for tropical landscapes. Semi-deciduous — it briefly drops leaves before the main spring bloom. Drought-tolerant once established on well-drained soil.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — African Trumpet Tree is drought-tolerant once established and grows vigorously in the well-drained, sandy soils of tropical coastal landscapes. Fernandoa magnifica is a medium-sized, semi-deciduous flowering tree from eastern tropical Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Zimbabwe) in the Bignoniaceae family, belonging to the same remarkable family that gave horticulture Jacaranda, Tabebuia, Catalpa, and Bignonia. The tree produces large, pinnately compound leaves and bears its flowers in massive, terminal, many-flowered panicles at the tips of the branches: each individual flower is a large (2–3 inch), funnel to broadly trumpet-shaped bloom in vivid yellow-orange to orange, with five spreading, frilled petal lobes and a slightly darker orange interior. When a Fernandoa magnifica flowers — typically in spring, often producing the display on leafless or partially leafless branches — the sheer density and size of the flower clusters is extraordinary, covering the branch tips in orange-yellow bloom. The species is a significant ornamental tree in tropical East African gardens and in tropical botanical collections worldwide, considered one of the finest flowering trees of the African continent in terms of bloom impact. Underused in zone 10-11 US tropical landscapes compared to its merit.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun in spring; African tulip tree grows very rapidly — often reaching 20 feet within a few years of planting — and begins producing flowers within 3–5 years from seed. It is considered invasive in Hawaii, parts of Florida, and many Pacific Island nations where it has escaped cultivation and displaced native vegetation in disturbed forest areas.
directions: Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; African tulip tree (fountain tree, fireball) is a large, fast-growing West African tropical tree of the bignonia family (Bignoniaceae) that produces one of the most spectacular and instantly recognizable flower displays of any tropical tree — large, upright, cup-shaped, terminal clusters of 10–20 large, flared, bright scarlet-orange to crimson flowers with yellow-edged petals are produced at the branch tips year-round in zone 10–12 tropical climates, creating a constant flaming-red display from a distance. The flower buds hold water — a trait used by children in the native range who squeeze the buds to squirt water — and are visited by sunbirds and bats as pollinators. The tree grows rapidly to 40–50 feet with a dense, spreading canopy, making it an effective but large shade tree. It has become invasive in Hawaii, Pacific island nations, and parts of tropical Florida, where it spreads aggressively by wind-borne seeds into disturbed forest areas — check local regulations before planting.

plant_note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix or water; African violets propagate easily from leaf cuttings with petiole attached, inserted into moist mix at 45 degrees — new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4–8 weeks. In zone 11–12 they can grow outdoors in deep shade and high humidity.
directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix: African violet is the world's most popular flowering houseplant, grown by millions indoors for its rosettes of soft, velvety, dark green leaves and year-round clusters of flowers in purple, violet, lavender, pink, white, and bicolor combinations. The keys to success are bright indirect light (east or north window in summer; south or west in winter), bottom-watering or careful top-watering that avoids wetting the crown and leaves, and consistently moist but not waterlogged, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) potting mix with good aeration. Feed every 4 weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets. The genus was recently reclassified from Saintpaulia to Streptocarpus; thousands of named cultivars are available through the African Violet Society of America.

plant_note: Tie or wire rhizome divisions onto submerged wood or rock rather than burying them in substrate; site in shaded, slow-moving water such as a bog garden margin, pond edge, or paludarium in a warm, frost-free spot.
directions: Attach the creeping rhizome to submerged wood, rock, or a mesh mount rather than planting it directly in soil, since burying the rhizome causes it to rot. Site in shallow, shaded, slow-moving fresh water in a warm, frost-free spot, or keep it as a partly submerged bog and aquarium plant elsewhere. Its deeply cut, glossy, leathery dark green fronds hold up well underwater or in constantly saturated soil, making it a durable choice for the shaded edge of a water feature, rain garden pool, or paludarium.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; African wild iris is remarkably drought-tolerant once established but benefits from regular watering during the first growing season — do not cut the flower stalks after blooming, as the same stalks rebloom for multiple years, and removing them sacrifices future flowering.
directions: Plant rhizomes or container specimens in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; African wild iris is a South African rhizomatous perennial of the iris family (Iridaceae) that is one of the most reliable, long-lived, and drought-tolerant evergreen perennials for Gulf Coast and warm-climate gardens, producing large, white, six-petaled flowers 3–4 inches across with bright-yellow and blue-violet marks at the petal bases on tall, branching, flat, fan-like stems from spring through early summer and intermittently at other seasons. The plant's most unusual feature is that it reblooms on the same persistent flower stems for multiple years — so the stems should never be removed after blooming, as the following season's flowers emerge from the same stalk. The fans of sword-shaped, dark-green, evergreen leaves are ornamental year-round and the plant spreads slowly into large, weed-suppressing clumps. Extremely adaptable to heat, drought, alkaline soil, and coastal conditions; an outstanding low-maintenance evergreen perennial for zone 8–11 public and residential landscapes, often seen lining roads and medians throughout the Gulf South.
