plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; agave-leaf sea holly is evergreen in mild winters and forms an impressive, large rosette of leaves that requires substantial space. The flower stems are summer-produced on previous year's growth, and the spent stems should be cut back after seeding. More cold-tolerant than expected for an Argentine species.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; agave-leaf sea holly is a large-scale Argentine eryngium that earns its common name through its remarkable foliage — the basal leaves are broad, strap-shaped, toothed along the margin with spine-tipped teeth, and arranged in a bold rosette that closely resembles a medium-sized agave in form and architecture. This agave-like rosette, in glossy, bright green, provides architectural structure throughout the year. In summer, tall, branching flower scapes emerge from the center carrying numerous small, pale-green to whitish, typical eryngium flower heads (each a rounded bur of spiky bracts above a domed disc) — smaller and less colorful than the metallic-blue European sea hollies but collectively impressive for their number and the height of the scapes. The whole plant creates a bold, architectural structure in the garden — a rosette of agave-like leaves at ground level sending up flowering stalks to 5–6 feet. Outstanding as an architectural specimen or back-of-border plant in drought-tolerant, Mediterranean-climate, or prairie-style gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Sow dust-fine seed on the surface of moist starting mix without covering — light is essential for germination. Ageratum produces fluffy, powder-puff blooms that attract butterflies and beneficial insects. Shear plants back lightly when flowering slows or plants become leggy to promote a fresh flush of bloom. Consistent moisture is important, as dry conditions cause the plants to stop flowering.

common_name: Agnes Galt Hibiscus (Historic Hawaiian Deep Pink Tropical Hibiscus)
plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Agnes Galt is a historic Hawaiian-bred tropical hibiscus cultivar prized for its vigorous, reliable bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Agnes Galt is a historic Hawaiian-bred tropical hibiscus bearing large, single, deep pink flowers in great abundance on a vigorous, upright shrub, a cultivar that helped shape the classic look of tropical hibiscus in mid-20th-century Hawaiian and Gulf Coast gardens. Its reliable, heavy flowering and tough constitution have kept it in cultivation for decades even as flashier modern hybrids have come and gone. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season.

common_name: Aimee Gardenia (Very Large Flower Exhibition Gardenia from Louisiana)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) soil in partial shade; 'Aimee Yoshiba' produces some of the largest gardenia flowers available — flowers can reach 4–5 inches across, making individual blooms among the most spectacular of any gardenia.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade protection; Aimee (also known as 'Aimee Yoshiba') is a Louisiana-associated gardenia cultivar producing some of the largest flowers of any commonly grown Gardenia jasminoides — individual blooms reaching 4–5 inches across with many rows of creamy white, wavy, overlapping petals that create a full, formal double flower of extraordinary refinement. The flowers open creamy white and age to a warm ivory-yellow, with the same intense, classic gardenia fragrance that has made gardenias the most beloved fragrant landscape shrub in the American South. 'Aimee' grows as a vigorous, upright-spreading shrub to 5–7 feet in typical Gulf South gardens, larger and more open in habit than compact cultivars like 'Radicans' or 'Chuck Hayes'. The spring bloom (April–June) is the primary season, often with sporadic rebloom in fall if conditions are favorable. As with all Gardenia jasminoides, 'Aimee' requires strongly acidic soil for healthy growth — iron chlorosis (yellowing leaves with green veins) is the primary symptom of insufficient acidity, corrected with sulfur soil acidification and acid-forming fertilizers. The large flower size and outstanding fragrance make 'Aimee' the preferred gardenia for cut flower use, where a single bloom can fragrance a room for several days.

common_name: Ajax Rain Lily (Classic Straw-Yellow-Fading-White Hybrid Rain Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ajax, a classic hybrid of Zephyranthes candida and Z. citrina, bears straw-yellow flowers that fade to white, flushing into bloom after summer rains.
directions: Plant bulbs 1 to 2 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ajax is a classic, long-cultivated hybrid rain lily, a cross of Zephyranthes candida and Z. citrina, bearing crocus-like flowers that open a warm straw-yellow and gradually fade toward white as they age, giving a two-toned effect across a single flush of bloom. Like other rain lilies, it flowers in sudden, reliable flushes triggered by a good soaking rain after a dry spell, particularly through the warm months, making a naturalized planting appear to bloom almost overnight. It is hardy and drought-tolerant once established, multiplying gradually by bulb offsets to form an increasing clump or drift at the border edge, along a walkway, or naturalized in a lawn area that isn't mowed too closely. Essentially carefree once planted, needing no regular care beyond occasional division of crowded clumps.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to part shade; ajuga is one of the most reliable and ornamental groundcovers for shaded areas under trees and along shaded borders, spreading by stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; space 12–18 inches apart and allow to spread. Ajuga reptans (bugleweed or carpet bugleweed) is one of the most widely grown and adaptable shade groundcovers in temperate gardens — a European native that spreads by horizontal stolons to form a dense, 4-to-6-inch-tall, weed-suppressing carpet of rosettes, producing spectacular spikes of small, tubular, blue-violet (or pink, white, or cream in cultivars) flowers in April–May that are important early-season nectar sources for native bees and bumble bees. The foliage is the primary season-long attraction: many cultivars offer striking leaf colors from dark bronze-purple ('Catlin's Giant,' 'Burgundy Glow') to variegated cream and pink ('Burgundy Glow') to metallic chocolate ('Black Scallop'). Ajuga thrives in the difficult dry-shade conditions under large trees where other groundcovers struggle. It is essentially maintenance-free once established, spreading moderately (not invasively) by stolons. In zone 9, it performs best in shade with consistent moisture and may go partially dormant in the hottest, driest summers; crown rot can occur in hot, humid conditions — ensure good air circulation.

common_name: Akila Purple Osteospermum (Self-Branching Seed African Daisy)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost as plants tolerate light frost. Akila is a seed-grown osteospermum series bred to branch and flower heavily on its own without pinching, unlike older seed strains that needed more grooming to fill out.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in well-drained germination mix, then transplant into full sun in well-drained soil once the worst frost risk has passed, since young plants tolerate light frost. Akila Purple is a seed-grown African daisy bred to branch and flower heavily right out of the pack without the pinching or grooming that older seed-raised osteospermum varieties needed to fill out into a full, floriferous plant, giving growers a vegetative-quality, uniform show from seed. The rich purple, daisy-form flowers with dark centers open on a compact, well-branched mound that performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons and slows during peak summer heat, similar to other osteospermums. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the display tidy and encourage continued bloom; in zone 9-11 gardens it can persist as a short-lived perennial, especially with a light summer trim to keep it from stretching in the heat.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, humus-rich, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade; Alabama azalea is a shallow-rooted woodland plant that requires well-drained, acidic soil and cannot tolerate alkaline, compacted, or waterlogged conditions.
directions: Alabama azalea is a rare native deciduous azalea endemic to the limestone cedar glades and sandy, acidic woodlands of central Alabama and adjacent states — one of the most sweetly fragrant of all native azaleas, its white to creamy-white flowers with yellow-orange blotches emit a delicate, spicy-sweet fragrance reminiscent of lemony honey that fills the woodland in spring. It blooms in April after the piedmont azalea but before leaves emerge, producing large, showy clusters of flowers at a time when the garden's background is still relatively bare. Alabama azalea is adapted to the warm, humid climate of the upper Gulf Coastal Plain, tolerating zone 9 summers better than most native azaleas of eastern North America — an important advantage for Gulf Coast native gardens where heat and humidity defeat many Rhododendron species. In acidic woodland gardens and under tall pines, plant in combination with native groundcovers like Carex, Pachysandra procumbens, and native ferns for an authentic Alabama woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, average to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; Alabama croton is a rare, disjunct native shrub of a few Alabama river-bluff counties and a separate Texas Hill Country population, and is notably drought-tolerant once established on well-drained slopes.
directions: Plant container shrubs in well-drained, average to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun. Alabama croton is a distinctive deciduous native shrub known from only a handful of dolomite bluff sites in central Alabama and a separate disjunct population in the Texas Hill Country, prized in cultivation for its silvery, metallic-scaled leaf undersides that shimmer in a breeze and its coppery orange-bronze fall color, which often persists as attractive winter foliage before finally dropping. Small, inconspicuous yellowish flowers appear in early spring, but the plant's real value is architectural and textural, forming a multi-stemmed, upright thicket useful as a specimen or informal screen. Its native rocky-bluff habitat makes it genuinely drought-tolerant and adaptable to lean, well-drained soils once established, an unusual trait among native shade shrubs, though it still benefits from watering through its first year or two. A rewarding, low-maintenance rarity for a native plant collector's garden.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, rocky or loamy soil in partial shade. Alabama Snow-Wreath is a critically rare Alabama endemic and should only be sourced from nurseries that propagate their own cuttings.
directions: Alabama Snow-Wreath is one of the rarest native shrubs in North America, a monotypic genus (the only species in its genus) restricted in the wild to a handful of limestone bluffs and rocky river slopes in northwestern Alabama and a very few widely scattered natural populations in other southeastern states. In April and May it produces a cloud of unusual, feathery, white, petal-less flowers — the 'petals' are entirely absent, and the display comes entirely from numerous long white stamens — giving the shrub an airy, ethereal appearance reminiscent of its common name. An adaptable plant in cultivation that grows well in partial shade in a wide range of soils from dry and rocky to moderately moist, Alabama Snow-Wreath is easy to propagate from cuttings and is increasingly available from specialty native plant nurseries. Never collect from wild populations — purchase only from nurseries that propagate their own plants from cultivated stock.

common_name: Alabama Sunrise Heucherella (Bright Gold-to-Red Seasonal Color-Change Heucherella)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alabama Sunrise changes color dramatically through the season, emerging bright gold in spring and deepening toward orange-red as temperatures cool in fall.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, with mulch to keep roots cool. Alabama Sunrise is a heucherella cultivar grown chiefly for its dramatic seasonal color transformation, unfurling bright gold-yellow leaves with red veining in spring that gradually shift toward warm orange and finally deep red-bronze tones as the weather cools in fall, giving the planting a constantly changing look through the growing season. Like other heucherella it spreads gradually to form a groundcover-like patch, combining the colorful foliage of heuchera with the vigorous habit of foamflower, and produces modest sprays of small white flowers in late spring that are secondary to its foliage display. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Alabama Sunset Coleus (Classic Orange-Red Heirloom Sun Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Alabama Sunset is a classic heirloom coleus cultivar with warm orange-red leaves veined in maroon and edged in chartreuse, a longtime favorite sun-tolerant selection for bold summer foliage color.
directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Alabama Sunset is a classic, long-popular coleus cultivar bearing warm orange-red leaves marked with darker maroon veining and a bright chartreuse-green edge, a fiery, autumnal color combination that has kept it a garden favorite for decades. It tolerates considerably more direct sun than traditional shade coleus, making it a versatile choice for both sunny mixed borders and shadier spots, though the richest, most saturated coloring develops with some protection from the most intense afternoon sun in zone 9. The vigorous, upright, well-branched plants provide season-long color without relying on flowers, which should be pinched off as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage. Pinch growing tips periodically through the season to maintain a dense, bushy habit and prevent the plant from becoming leggy.

plant_note: Start indoors; cold-moist stratification improves germination.
directions: 'Alan's Pride' is a first-year-flowering coneflower with unusual zesty lime-green blooms on graceful 2-foot stems. Start seed indoors and give it a period of cold-moist stratification to break dormancy and improve germination. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil where it becomes drought tolerant once established. The blooms draw bees and butterflies, and leaving seed heads standing feeds finches into fall and winter. Divide clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the marbled white variegation on Alaska's leaves is genetically stable and shows from the seedling stage on, making it easy to spot in a mixed planting.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; rich soil pushes leafy growth at the expense of bloom. Alaska is a classic compact, mounding nasturtium grown as much for its striking foliage as its flowers, with round leaves heavily marbled and streaked in creamy white over green, giving the plant strong ornamental value even before it flowers. It produces the same bright mix of cream, yellow, orange, and red single blooms typical of nasturtiums, and the variegated leaves make an especially attractive edible garnish alongside the peppery flowers. Its compact habit suits containers, edging, and small beds, and plants bloom continuously from early summer through frost with minimal care.

plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow after frost; needs light to germinate.
directions: 'Alaska' is a classic, long-lived Shasta daisy bearing large 3-inch white flowers with sunny yellow centers from summer into fall. Press seed onto the surface since it needs light to germinate, and keep it evenly moist until sprouts appear. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil for the sturdiest, most floriferous plants. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering, and the long stems make excellent cut flowers. Divide clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow after danger of frost; resents transplanting.
directions: 'Alaska' nasturtium stands out for its cream-and-green marbled foliage that stays showy even between the bright, edible flowers. Direct sow the large seeds where they are to grow, as nasturtiums dislike having their roots disturbed. Grow in full sun to part shade in lean soil, since overly rich ground produces leaves at the expense of blooms. Both the peppery flowers and leaves are edible and make a colorful garnish. This compact, bushy type is well suited to containers and bed edges.

common_name: Alba Chinese Wisteria (Fragrant White-Flowered Chinese Wisteria)
plant_note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; this white-flowered form of Chinese wisteria opens its blooms all at once for a dramatic display.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a very sturdy support structure built to carry the mature vine's considerable weight. This white-flowered form of Chinese wisteria bears dense, fragrant racemes that open nearly simultaneously along the vine before the leaves fully emerge, in the classic Chinese wisteria style, creating a striking curtain of white bloom rather than the more staggered, trailing display typical of Japanese wisteria. It twines counterclockwise, opposite the direction of Japanese wisteria, and grows vigorously, requiring firm pruning both in summer to control rampant growth and in late winter to shape and encourage flower bud formation. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity and plan for a genuinely large, long-term structure to support it.

plant_note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Alba is a white-flowered form of Japanese wisteria grown for its long, fragrant racemes.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a very sturdy support structure built to carry the mature vine's considerable weight. Alba bears long, pendulous racemes of pure white, intensely fragrant flowers in spring, offering a softer, more luminous alternative to the classic violet-blue wisteria for a moon garden, evening seating area, or pairing with darker-flowered companions. Like other Japanese wisteria it twines clockwise and grows vigorously, requiring firm summer pruning of rampant new growth and a shaping late-winter prune to encourage flower buds rather than rampant vegetative growth. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity and plan for a genuinely large, long-term structure to support it.

common_name: Alba Luxurians Clematis (White with Green-Tipped Petals Viticella Clematis)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Alba Luxurians is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Alba Luxurians bears nodding white flowers, each petal tip touched with soft green and often twisted into an irregular, informal shape, a subtle novelty coloring distinct from the solid white typical of most white clematis. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter, avoiding the guesswork of pruning old-wood types. Its abundant, quirky flowers bloom over a long midsummer season.

plant_note: Transplant in spring near a trellis or fence in full sun; like the species, this white-flowered form spreads by root suckers and tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity with ease.
directions: Plant along a fence, arbor, or trellis in full sun to light shade in ordinary garden soil, giving the vigorous vine plenty of vertical room to climb by tendril. This pure-white-flowered selection of the native maypop produces the same intricate, fringed blossoms as the wild form but without the usual purple banding, and still serves as the essential host plant for gulf fritillary and zebra longwing caterpillars. Bees and other pollinators visit the large flowers freely, and edible yellow-green fruit follows in late summer. Once established it spreads by root suckers and tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic drought better than almost any other flowering vine on the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is an unusual white-berried nandina selection with lighter green foliage than the species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Alba bears the same upright, cane-like habit and airy, compound foliage typical of nandina, but with lighter green summer color that turns bronze rather than red in cold weather, and clusters of unusual creamy-white berries in fall and winter that persist well into the following spring, a striking departure from the familiar red-berried species. Its upright canes and winter berry display make it a good architectural accent or informal screen. Prune out the oldest canes at ground level occasionally to keep the clump renewing itself with fresh growth.

common_name: Alba Plena Camellia (White Formal Double Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Alba Plena is one of the earliest-blooming japonica camellias — November through January in zone 9 — so site away from frost pockets where early-season cold snaps could damage open flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Alba Plena is one of the oldest and most historically significant Camellia japonica cultivars in cultivation — an early-season white camellia with perfectly formed, large, formal double flowers in pure white with tightly spiraled, overlapping petals arranged in a geometrically precise rosette pattern of extraordinary elegance. The pure white flowers are exceptional for formal garden compositions, white-themed borders, and cut-flower use — few winter-blooming plants can rival the pristine beauty of fully open Alba Plena flowers. In zone 9, it blooms from November through January, making it one of the earliest reliable winter blooms in the Southern garden. The vigorous, upright growth to 5–12 feet produces dense, glossy dark-green foliage that provides excellent year-round screening and foundation value. Alba Plena was introduced to Western cultivation from China in 1792 and has been grown in Southern American gardens since the early nineteenth century — one of the most historically long-cultivated garden plants in the South. Early bloom season means open flowers may occasionally be damaged by hard frosts in zone 9 winters; siting under the canopy of overhead trees provides some protection. Maintain acidic soil pH with periodic applications of acidic fertilizer and deep organic mulch.

common_name: Alba Semi-Plena Rose (White Semi-Double Historic Alba Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba Semi-plena is one of the oldest garden roses still cultivated, historically grown for attar of roses production.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba roses tolerate more shade than most roses, a legacy of their origin as tough, adaptable garden plants. One of the oldest identifiable garden roses still in commerce, Alba Semi-plena bears fragrant, semi-double white flowers with prominent golden stamens against distinctive gray-green foliage, and was historically cultivated in quantity for attar of roses and rosewater production, most famously in Bulgaria's Rose Valley. Like other Albas it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, followed by an attractive display of orange-red hips in fall. It is exceptionally disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Alba White Bleeding Heart (Pure White Old-Fashioned Bleeding Heart)
plant_note: Divide and replant dormant crowns in early spring or fall, handling the brittle roots carefully and setting them just below the soil surface.
directions: Plant in cool, fertile, humus-rich soil that drains well but never fully dries out, choosing a site with dappled morning light and shelter from hot afternoon sun. Expect the lush, chartreuse-green foliage and arching flower stems to die back and go fully dormant by midsummer, so mark its location and interplant with later-emerging perennials to fill the gap. Rows of pure white, heart-shaped flowers dangle from gracefully arching stems in mid-spring, offering a crisper alternative to the classic pink-and-white species. It remains a dependable, long-lived focal point for shaded borders and woodland gardens despite its brief above-ground season.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is the standard white-flowered form of eastern redbud, a naturally occurring color variant of the straight species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is the classic white-flowered form of eastern redbud, a naturally occurring color break from the typical rosy-pink to lavender bloom of the wild species, covering bare branches in clean white pea-family flowers in early spring before the heart-shaped green leaves emerge. It provides a softer, more understated spring display than pink or magenta redbud cultivars and pairs especially well with purple-leafed selections like Forest Pansy planted nearby for contrast. Growth habit, size, and cultural needs match the straight species — a small, adaptable native tree well suited to the dappled light of a woodland edge or understory planting, tolerating partial shade better than many flowering trees, though bloom is most abundant with several hours of direct sun. As with all redbuds, plant in well-drained soil, since the roots are prone to rot in heavy, wet sites, and avoid disturbing the root system once established, since redbud transplants best when young and container-grown.

plant_note: Divide offshoots or pot up nursery starts in spring into a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss, perlite, and coarse sand; keep the medium evenly moist with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and give a cooler, slightly drier rest over winter — never use tap water or ordinary garden soil.
directions: Albany pitcher plant is the sole member of the family Cephalotaceae and is found only in a small area of boggy, sandy heathland near Albany in southwestern Western Australia, where a winter-wet, summer-dry Mediterranean climate shapes a plant quite different from tropical Nepenthes despite the similar-looking traps. Its low rosettes produce small, ribbed, moccasin-shaped pitchers with a toothed peristome and a hinged lid that keeps rain from diluting the digestive fluid inside. Unlike true tropical Nepenthes, it prefers cooler growing conditions and a drier winter rest, tolerating brief light chills that would harm a Nepenthes, though it still cannot survive a hard freeze and should be grown in a container or cool greenhouse outside its narrow native climate zone. Pot it in a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss, perlite, and coarse sand, water only with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater, and never fertilize the soil, since this slow-growing carnivore obtains its nutrients from trapped insects rather than the roots.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola; introduced in 1921, Albertine is a once-blooming rambler prized for its intense fragrance.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola. Introduced in France in 1921, Albertine produces an overwhelming single flush of double, coppery salmon-pink blooms each early summer, carrying an intense, sweet fragrance that made it one of the most beloved ramblers of the 20th century for training over cottage doorways and arbors. Reddish young canes and glossy foliage add interest even between the single, dramatic bloom period. Prune only to control size or remove dead and crossing wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring as new growth begins in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; growth is slow the first two seasons.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and cut the whole clump back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Albostriata bears arching, bamboo-like blades striped in crisp white over green, a slightly more vigorous and sun-tolerant variegated selection than the golden 'Aureola', with white-and-green coloring that reads as cooler and brighter in deep shade than gold-variegated cultivars. Its cascading, fountain-like habit works equally well as a woodland-edge groundcover, container specimen, or textural companion to hostas and ferns. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 4–5 years as growth increases.

common_name: Albostriata Lily of the Valley (Striped-Leaf Lily of the Valley)
plant_note: Plant dormant pips (rhizome divisions) in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Albostriata spreads by rhizome as vigorously as the plain species, so confine it with a buried barrier or edging where a contained planting is wanted.
directions: Plant dormant pips (rhizome divisions) in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Albostriata spreads by rhizome as vigorously as the plain species, so confine it with a buried barrier or edging where a contained planting is wanted. Each broad, glossy leaf is finely pin-striped in creamy white from base to tip, a variegation that holds well through the season and reads as a shimmer of light across a shaded bed even before the classic sprays of small, nodding, intensely fragrant white bells open in mid-spring. It naturalizes readily into a dense, weed-smothering carpet in the deep, dry shade under trees where few flowering groundcovers thrive, but every part of the plant, including the small red berries, is toxic if ingested, so site it away from children's play areas or vegetable beds. Division is rarely needed and mainly done to control spread or share pips.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Alcazar is a 1910 French-bred bearded iris that was hugely influential as a parent plant in early 20th-century breeding.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Introduced in France in 1910, Alcazar was one of the first tall bearded irises to combine real height and vigor with rich bicolor coloring — pale violet standards over deeper purple-blue falls — and its influence runs through the pedigree of countless later cultivars. It remains a tough, floriferous heirloom in its own right, multiplying readily into large clumps that need dividing only every three to four years to stay vigorous. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage, since standing water around the rhizomes quickly leads to rot.

common_name: Alcazar Red Hot Poker (Vivid Orange-Red Kniphofia)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; good drainage is critical, especially in winter, since red hot poker rots in waterlogged conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; good drainage is critical year-round but especially in winter, when standing moisture around the crown quickly causes rot. Alcazar bears dense, torch-like flower spikes in a vivid, saturated orange-red that holds its intense color from bud through the full bloom period, rather than shifting through the red-to-yellow gradient typical of many red hot poker cultivars, held on sturdy stems above grassy, arching foliage from summer into fall. The tubular flowers are a favorite of hummingbirds, which visit reliably through the bloom season. In colder parts of its range, tie the leaves together over the crown and mulch deeply before the first hard freeze to protect the growing point, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering declines.

plant_note: Plant in spring once ground is workable. Best established in consistently moist to wet soil; boggy sites are ideal. This dioecious shrub requires both male and female plants for berry production.
directions: Plant in partial shade in reliably moist to boggy soil, mimicking its natural habitat along streambanks and in swampy woods. Dig a hole at least twice the width of the root ball and amend heavy clay with organic matter to improve moisture retention. Water deeply and consistently through the first two growing seasons to establish a strong root system. Berries attract birds in fall; plant at least one male and one female for fruit set.

plant_note: Sow in fall so the plumed, twisted-tail seeds overwinter and cold-stratify naturally, into well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; established plants tolerate severe drought, wind, and poor, shallow soil.
directions: Plant on a dry, rocky, well-drained slope or bank in full sun; alderleaf mountain mahogany is a tough, long-lived Rocky Mountain and Intermountain West foothill shrub with small, wedge-shaped, deeply veined leaves resembling alder foliage, evergreen to semi-evergreen depending on winter severity. Small, inconspicuous flowers in spring give way to the plant's real ornamental feature: clusters of feathery, silvery, corkscrew-tailed seed plumes that catch afternoon light through summer and fall, giving the whole shrub a soft, smoky appearance from a distance. Extremely drought and cold tolerant once its deep root system is established, it is browsed by deer and elk in the wild and provides valuable winter forage and cover for wildlife. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood, and the shrub is essentially maintenance-free in the lean, rocky soils it prefers.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Aleppo pine is a Mediterranean dryland pine adapted to hot, dry, alkaline conditions and thin limestone or sandy soils. One of the most drought-tolerant pines for hot, dry climates in zones 8–10.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Aleppo pine is the most drought-tolerant and widely distributed pine of the Mediterranean Basin, covering rocky, thin limestone and sandy soils around the sea from Spain to Turkey. In California and the Southwest US, it has been planted for over a century as a tough, drought-tolerant pine for hot, dry, alkaline conditions where most other pines fail. The light gray-green to blue-green paired needles and the open, slightly irregular crown give it a soft, Mediterranean character. Old trees develop a picturesque, wind-sculpted silhouette with distinctive sinuous, upswept branches. The small, asymmetric, orange-brown cones are persistent and add winter interest. Well-suited to the dry, alkaline conditions of California's interior valleys, the Southwest, and the alkaline calcareous soils of the Hill Country and Edwards Plateau of Texas.

common_name: Alexander's Great Brunnera (Giant Silver Heartleaf Brunnera)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alexander's Great is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction from an exceptionally large-leaved seedling found by Belarusian plantsman Alexander Zukeivich, producing markedly bigger silvered leaves than the widely grown Jack Frost.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alexander's Great is a giant-leaved brunnera selection bred to outsize the popular Jack Frost cultivar, with broad, heart-shaped leaves heavily overlaid in reflective silver and traced with contrasting green veining, brightening a dark shade bed on a bolder scale than standard brunnera. In spring, sprays of small azure-blue forget-me-not flowers rise above the emerging foliage before the leaves reach full size. Like other brunnera, it needs consistent moisture and will scorch in dry soil or hot afternoon sun, so mulch well and provide reliable shade in a Gulf South summer. It is propagated only by division, since named brunnera cultivars do not come true from seed.

common_name: Alexandrina Magnolia (Classic Large Pink-Purple Saucer Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Alexandrina is among the earliest-blooming saucer magnolia cultivars, so a sheltered site away from cold pockets helps protect the flowers from late frost damage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Alexandrina is one of the oldest and most widely planted saucer magnolia cultivars, producing large, goblet-shaped flowers in rich rose-purple on the outside and creamy white within, opening on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge. Its early bloom timing gives an unmistakable, showy spring display but also leaves the flowers vulnerable to browning from a late hard freeze, a common risk for early-flowering saucer magnolias, so siting away from low frost pockets helps. The tree grows into a broad, multi-stemmed small tree or large shrub with minimal pruning needs beyond removing dead or crossing wood, and established trees are otherwise low-maintenance and long-lived landscape specimens.

common_name: Alfred de Dalmas Moss Rose (Repeat-Blooming Pale Pink Moss Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Alfred de Dalmas, also sold as Mousseline, is a compact, repeat-blooming moss rose.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Alfred de Dalmas, also sold under the name Mousseline, bears soft pale pink, cupped, double blooms lightly touched with moss on the sepals, opening on a compact, well-behaved shrub that fits a smaller garden more readily than many taller moss roses. It reliably repeats bloom through the season rather than flowering just once, an unusual and valuable trait for the moss rose class. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after each bloom flush.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained soil under dry shade; this Algerian species is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and thrives beneath the root canopy of large trees where few other groundcovers survive.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry soil in full to partial shade, where its glossy, bronze-tinted heart-shaped leaves form a weed-suppressing mat through vigorous rhizomatous spread. Bright yellow flowers emerge in early spring before the foliage hardens, offering one of the earliest color displays in the shaded garden. Unlike most epimediums, E. perralderianum is semi-evergreen and retains attractive foliage well into winter, especially in milder parts of its hardiness range. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to showcase the spring flower display; once established, this species is among the most drought- and root-competition-tolerant of all groundcovers.

common_name: Algerian Ivy (Canary Island Ivy, Canariensis Ivy)
plant_note: Root cuttings or plant container transplants in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Algerian ivy is more heat and drought tolerant than English ivy and a better choice for zone 8–10 Gulf Coast shade gardens. It can also be grown as a trailing vine for containers.
directions: Plant cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Algerian ivy is the superior ivy for Gulf Coast zone 7–10 gardens — larger-leaved, more heat tolerant, and more drought tolerant than English ivy, making it better suited to the summer conditions of the Gulf South. The leaves are 3–8 inches across, rich glossy green (sometimes with a reddish tint in winter), and distinctly larger than the familiar English ivy. The variegated form 'Gloire de Marengo' has silvery gray-green leaves with creamy white margins and is one of the most beautiful of all shade vines. Like English ivy it can climb by aerial roots and spreads vigorously as a groundcover, but has a less aggressive spreading habit than English ivy and is less likely to invade natural areas. Still, plant with care and keep away from forest edges.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alice is a large-growing cultivar — allow 6–8 feet in all directions at planting time to avoid future overcrowding.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alice oakleaf hydrangea is an outstanding cultivar selected and named for Alice Recknagel Ireys, a distinguished American landscape architect, by Michael Dirr at the University of Georgia — the plant's finest characteristics reflecting the horticultural standards of its namesake. Alice produces exceptionally large, upright panicle flower clusters — sometimes reaching 14 inches long — that are among the biggest of any oakleaf hydrangea cultivar, creating a spectacular mid-May to June display in zone 9 gardens. The individual flowers open pure white and age gradually to a beautiful soft rose-pink, creating clusters that simultaneously show white and pink tones. The foliage is large, bold, and deeply lobed with the characteristic oak-leaf silhouette, turning rich burgundy-red in autumn in zone 9. Alice grows vigorously to 6–10 feet tall and equally wide, making it an outstanding large-scale specimen, naturalizing under trees, or massing for a bold woodland effect. The peeling cinnamon-brown bark is ornamental in winter. Alice received the Award of Garden Merit from the Royal Horticultural Society, confirming its outstanding ornamental performance.

common_name: Alice du Pont Mandevilla (Classic Vigorous Pink Mandevilla)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm, training the twining vine onto a trellis, arbor, or fence; Alice du Pont is one of the oldest and most vigorous mandevilla cultivars, producing large, clear pink, trumpet-shaped flowers over glossy foliage.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a trellis, arbor, or other support able to accommodate a vigorous twining vine. Alice du Pont is a long-established classic mandevilla cultivar, valued for producing large, glossy, deep green leaves and abundant clear pink, trumpet-shaped flowers continuously from late spring through fall, with a naturally vigorous, fast-climbing habit compared to some of the more compact modern mandevilla series. It thrives in the heat and humidity of a Gulf South summer, needing only regular water and monthly fertilizing during active growth. In zone 9a it typically dies back after a hard freeze but often regrows from the roots in a mild winter; in colder zones it is best grown as a container plant brought indoors or treated as an annual.

common_name: Alister Stella Gray Rose (Yellow-to-Cream Climbing Noisette)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a trellis, fence, or arbor for the climbing canes; Alister Stella Gray, introduced in 1894, is a fragrant climbing Noisette well suited to Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Plant at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun, and tie in canes as they extend. Alister Stella Gray, introduced in 1894, bears small, high-centered, richly fragrant flowers that open golden-yellow and fade attractively to cream as they age, often showing several shades at once within a single cluster. It repeats reliably through the growing season on a moderately vigorous climber well suited to a large trellis, pillar, or fence, and like other Noisettes it tolerates Southern heat and humidity with good disease resistance. Train canes horizontally to encourage more flowering side shoots, and prune lightly after the main flush to maintain shape.

common_name: All Gold Forest Grass (Golden Japanese Hakone Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; All Gold develops vivid chartreuse-yellow color in bright partial shade — deep shade causes the foliage to revert toward green, while direct sun scorches the delicate leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; All Gold is the all-golden form of the celebrated Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra) — a graceful, slow-growing, clump-forming grass producing cascading, arching, narrow leaves in a warm chartreuse-yellow to golden color that creates a luminous glow effect in the shade garden. The warm golden color of All Gold is even more vivid than the striped 'Aureola' cultivar — because all the leaf tissue is chartreuse-gold rather than striped, the overall color effect is bolder and more uniform. The gently cascading, arching habit creates the effect of flowing water tumbling down a slope, making Japanese forest grass one of the most graceful and unique ornamental plants available for the partial-shade garden. All Gold is slow to establish but gradually forms expanding clumps that become increasingly impressive with each year. The warm gold color lights up dark shade garden corners and combines beautifully with the cool blue of hostas and the burgundy tones of Japanese painted ferns and heucheras. In zone 9, All Gold performs in bright indirect shade — on the north or east side of structures, under high-canopied pines, or at the edge of tree canopies where filtered light predominates. Consistent moisture and humus-rich, acidic soil are essential; the plant will not tolerate drought or alkaline clay without amendment.

common_name: All Gold Hakonechloa (Solid Gold Japanese Forest Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; All Gold colors most brightly with a little morning sun but scorches in hot afternoon sun, and it spreads slowly, so patience is needed for the clump to reach full size.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, which scorches the bright foliage. All Gold is a solid-colored selection of Japanese forest grass bearing slender, gracefully arching, entirely bright chartreuse-gold blades that form a soft, cascading mound, glowing especially brightly in dappled light. Unlike running bamboo-relatives, Hakonechloa is a slow-spreading, well-behaved clumping grass that never becomes invasive, making it a safe, elegant choice for edging a shaded path, spilling over a container, or planting beneath larger shrubs. Its fine texture and luminous color pair beautifully with dark-leafed heuchera, hosta, and ferns. Cut back dried foliage in late winter before new shoots emerge, and be patient, since Hakonechloa is slow to establish and may take two to three seasons to reach its full spread.

common_name: All Summer Beauty Hydrangea (Reliable Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; All Summer Beauty is an older reblooming bigleaf hydrangea, flowering reliably on new wood even after a hard winter cuts back old stems.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun and drying wind. All Summer Beauty is an older bigleaf hydrangea cultivar valued for setting flower buds reliably on new wood, so it continues to bloom through summer even in years when a late freeze damages old stems and buds, a problem that leaves many other mopheads bloomless for a season. Its large, rounded mophead flower clusters shift from blue to pink depending on soil pH, blue in acidic soil and pink in more alkaline soil, and can be nudged toward blue with aluminum sulfate or toward pink with garden lime. Water deeply during dry spells, since bigleaf hydrangea wilts readily in heat, and prune only lightly right after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

common_name: Allee Lacebark Elm (Texas A&M Drought-Tolerant Shade Tree)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Allee was selected by Texas A&M for its uniform vase-shaped form, striking exfoliating bark, and excellent heat and drought tolerance for southern shade tree use.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Allee is a lacebark elm cultivar selected and introduced by Texas A&M University for its uniform, vase-shaped growth habit, resembling the classic silhouette of American elm without the vulnerability to Dutch elm disease that devastated that species. Its most striking feature is the beautifully mottled, exfoliating bark in patches of gray, green, orange, and brown that develops as the tree matures, giving significant year-round ornamental interest even in winter. It is highly tolerant of heat, drought, and the alkaline, compacted soils common in urban and suburban Southern landscapes, requiring only routine structural pruning while young to establish strong branch angles for a long-lived, storm-resistant shade tree.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in wet to moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; allegheny monkey flower grows in standing shallow water and saturated soils along stream banks, pond margins, and wet meadows. Seeds are tiny — surface sow without covering.
directions: Surface sow on moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil at pond margins, stream banks, and rain garden edges in partial shade to full sun; allegheny monkey flower is a native perennial of wet streambanks and pond edges across most of eastern North America, producing bright lavender-blue tubular flowers with distinctive two-lobed lips that give the plant a fanciful face resembling a grinning monkey — the whimsical origin of the common name shared across the Mimulus genus. The square stems are typical of the mint family to which it belongs. It grows in standing water up to 2 inches deep and in perpetually saturated soils at pond edges, making it excellent for naturalistic water garden margins. An important nectar plant for bumblebees and hummingbirds. Blooms from early summer into fall with consistent moisture. Self-sows freely along muddy stream banks. Excellent for naturalizing wet sites where its spreading colonies create a vivid blue summer display.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; Allegheny spurge is slower to spread than Japanese pachysandra but far more beautiful, with ornamentally mottled foliage.
directions: Plant divisions or container specimens in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Allegheny spurge is the native North American alternative to the ubiquitous Japanese pachysandra, producing semi-evergreen to evergreen mats of large, attractively silver-mottled leaves that are significantly more ornamental than the plain green of P. terminalis. The lightly fragrant, white to pink flower spikes emerge at ground level in early spring before the new leaves expand, adding a subtle bonus to the elegant foliage. It spreads more slowly than its Japanese counterpart but colonizes effectively over 3–5 years in suitable conditions. Extremely useful for naturalizing dry to moist, heavily shaded areas in zone 4–9 gardens, including the Gulf South where it handles summer heat better than expected for a woodland native.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring and plant in lean, sharply drained rocky soil; new divisions establish quickly.
directions: Allegheny stonecrop, also called wild live-forever, is an Appalachian native succulent found on rocky outcrops and thin mountain soils from Pennsylvania south to North Carolina, typically at moderate to high elevation. Unlike the low mat-forming stonecrops, it grows as an upright clump of fleshy, blue-green, toothed leaves reaching a foot or more, topped in late summer and early fall by flattened clusters of pale pink to white star-shaped flowers. The late bloom period makes it a valuable native nectar source for bumblebees and other pollinators building up reserves before winter, as well as migrating monarchs passing through the mountains. Grow it in lean, sharply drained, rocky soil in full sun to light shade; established clumps are extremely drought tolerant and need little care beyond occasional dividing to keep them vigorous.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Alley Cat colors best and resists leaf scorch with some afternoon shade, since its cream-and-white variegated leaves are more prone to sunburn than solid green redbud foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil sited with some relief from the hottest afternoon sun, which helps the variegated foliage hold its pattern instead of scorching at the leaf margins. Alley Cat is a variegated redbud selection bearing heart-shaped leaves heavily splashed and streaked in cream and white over green, giving the canopy a bright, almost frosted look through the growing season, and it produces the species' typical rosy-pink, pea-like flowers on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge. It grows as a smaller, slower tree than the straight species, staying more compact and tidy, which suits it well to a specimen spot in a shaded courtyard or woodland-edge planting where the bright foliage can be appreciated up close. Plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites, and prune only to remove dead, crossing, or reverted all-green branches, since variegated shoots can occasionally revert and should be cut out to keep the tree true to type.

subcategory: Gulf Coast native marginal aquatic perennial
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in full sun to partial shade in shallow water or permanently wet soil in zone 8–12; Alligator Flag (Fire-Flag) is a tall, dramatic, native marginal aquatic perennial found throughout the Gulf Coast, Caribbean, and tropical Americas — producing bold, canna-like foliage on tall stems reaching 6–8 feet and loose, zig-zagging racemes of small violet-purple flowers beloved by ruby-throated hummingbirds.
directions: Plant Thalia geniculata rhizome divisions in moist to wet soil or in the shallow margins of ponds in full sun to partial shade; space plants 3–5 feet apart and allow to form clumps; divide every 2–3 years to maintain vigor and spread to new areas. Alligator Flag is one of the most striking native marginal aquatics of the Gulf Coast and is an important wildlife plant throughout its natural range from the southeastern United States through the Caribbean and Central America into South America. The bold, upright, canna-like leaves create a dramatic vertical accent at the water's edge; the tall, arching, zigzag-jointed flower stalks bear small but intricate violet-blue flowers that are a magnet for hummingbirds throughout the warm season. In Gulf Coast gardens (zone 8–10), Alligator Flag can become a large, clump-forming colony in bog gardens, pond margins, and low wet areas; the foliage dies back to the rhizome after frost in zone 8–9 but re-emerges reliably in spring. Seeds develop in nutlet-like capsules and are relished by waterfowl. An excellent choice for naturalizing wet swales, retention pond edges, and rain gardens throughout the coastal South.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; alligator juniper is highly drought tolerant once established, growing naturally on dry, rocky mountain slopes and canyon walls of the Southwest at 4,500–8,000 feet elevation.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; alligator juniper is unmistakable — the only juniper with distinctive, deeply checkered, rectangular bark plates that perfectly resemble the textured, scaly skin of an alligator, making it one of the most easily identified conifers in the field. Native to the rocky, dry mountain slopes of southeastern Arizona, New Mexico, western Texas, and northern Mexico (the sky island mountain ranges and the Sierra Madre foothills) at mid-to-high elevations. One of the longer-lived junipers, with ancient specimens estimated at 500–1,000 years old. The blue-glaucous, berry-like seed cones are larger than most junipers. One of the drought-toughest conifers for the desert Southwest and Chihuahuan Desert transition zone — an excellent landscape tree for hot, dry, rocky sites where nearly nothing else survives. The dramatic bark texture makes it one of the most distinctive ornamental trees for dry southwestern landscapes.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in wet, acidic, mucky to sandy, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade near a water feature or in a rain garden; Alligator Lily requires consistently wet to waterlogged soil and will not tolerate drought. Divide bulb clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.
directions: Alligator Lily is a Florida endemic spider-lily found in wet flatwoods, freshwater marshes, and wet prairie margins of south and central Florida, producing elegant white flowers with reflexed petals and a distinctive fringed central cup (corona) characteristic of the Hymenocallis genus. Rare in cultivation despite being well suited to wet gardens, pond margins, and water features, Alligator Lily is a true South Florida native restricted to the peninsula and not found naturally anywhere else in the world. Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in wet, acidic, mucky to sandy, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade near a water feature or rain garden; established clumps multiply steadily through bulb offsets to form impressive colonies in appropriate wet conditions. Alligator Lily is intolerant of drought and requires consistently moist to wet soil — it performs best in natural pond margins, wet flatwood restoration plantings, and South Florida water gardens.

plant_note: Surface sow; needs light to germinate.
directions: This pastel blend of sweet alyssum forms low, spreading mounds smothered in tiny, honey-scented flowers. Sow on the soil surface and press in gently, since the seed needs light to sprout, and keep it moist until established. Grow in full sun to part shade along borders, in rock gardens, or cascading from containers. The fragrant blooms attract beneficial pollinators throughout the cool season. Shear plants back lightly if they slow in summer heat to encourage a fresh flush of bloom.

common_name: Alma Potschke Aster (Hot Pink New England Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Alma Potschke is a New England aster selection prized for its unusually vivid, glowing rose-pink flowers rather than the species' typical purple.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Alma Potschke is a long-popular New England aster cultivar named for the German nurserywoman who discovered it as a sport, valued for its intensely saturated, glowing rose-pink daisy flowers with yellow centers that stand out from the more common purple-flowered forms of the species. It blooms heavily from late summer into fall, providing critical late-season nectar for monarch butterflies staging for migration as well as bees and other pollinators when few other perennials are still flowering. Plants can become tall and somewhat floppy by bloom time; pinching stems back by a third in early summer encourages bushier, more self-supporting growth and delays flowering slightly. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and control its spreading habit.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into lean, acidic, sharply drained gravelly soil in a cold, sunny, wind-exposed site.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into lean, acidic, sharply drained gravelly soil in a cold, sunny, wind-exposed site, replicating the arctic and alpine tundra it occupies from Greenland and Arctic Canada south to isolated New England summits above treeline. Formerly classified in its own genus as Loiseleuria procumbens, it forms a tight, woody, prostrate mat scarcely a few inches tall, studded with tiny pink, bell-shaped flowers in late spring that provide early forage for high-elevation pollinators. It is exceptionally cold-hardy but demands the cool roots, sharp drainage, and short growing season of true alpine conditions, making it a specialty plant for troughs and scree gardens rather than conventional landscaping.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring or early fall; plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where this compact species spreads gradually to form a low, weed-suppressing edging.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; alpine barrenwort is a compact European species native to mountain woodlands of Italy and the western Balkans, valued as a low, long-lived edging or small-scale groundcover where taller epimediums would be out of scale. Wiry stems bear compound, heart-shaped leaflets on delicate stalks, and in spring carry loose racemes of small, unusual bicolor flowers with dull red sepals set off by contrasting yellow petals. It is one of the parent species behind many popular garden hybrid epimediums, but the true species itself remains an underused, tough, drought-tolerant choice for tucking along the front of a shaded bed or path. As with other epimediums, cut back old foliage in late winter so the modest flowers are not hidden.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and the roots shaded, letting the fine stems twine over a low fence, shrub, or wire support.
directions: Plant this cold-hardy species with its roots cool and shaded, ideally at the base of a low fence, wall, or open shrub for the wiry stems to scramble through. It is among the earliest clematis to bloom, opening nodding, lantern-shaped blue-purple to pink flowers on bare stems before most other vines have leafed out, followed by fluffy seed heads. Since it flowers on the previous year's growth, prune only lightly right after flowering to remove dead wood, never cutting it back hard. Its small scale and dainty flowers suit rock gardens, low trellises, or mixed borders where a larger clematis would be too much.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; alpine columbine is a compact, high-elevation species from the European Alps and resents hot, soggy lowland conditions.
directions: Direct sow in fall to allow winter cold to stratify the seed for spring germination, or start indoors after a period of cold, moist stratification, pressing seed lightly onto the soil surface without deep covering. Alpine columbine is a compact, high-elevation species from the European Alps, producing large, nodding, blue to violet-blue flowers with short, hooked spurs held above finely divided blue-green foliage, generally shorter and more richly colored than common garden columbines. It prefers full sun in cool, mountain-like climates but appreciates afternoon shade and sharply drained soil where summers are warm, since it resents the soggy, poorly drained conditions typical of lowland gardens. Like other columbines it is short-lived but self-seeds readily where happy, and seedlings may cross with other Aquilegia species growing nearby.

plant_note: Divide established mats or set out nursery starts in spring into sharply drained, lean soil; division is more dependable than seed, which needs cold stratification and germinates slowly.
directions: Divide established mats or set out nursery starts in spring into sharply drained, lean soil, since this alpine cushions poorly in heavy or wet ground. It forms a dense evergreen mat of small leathery leaves studded with unusual powder-blue globe flowers in late spring, making it a good filler between flagstones or on a sunny scree slope. Seed can be sown but needs several weeks of cold stratification and germinates slowly and unevenly, so division of an existing clump is the more dependable route.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring or plant divisions in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; alpine rock cress is one of the finest early-spring rock garden plants, covering itself in pure-white (or pink in cultivars) flowers before most other plants have emerged.
directions: Sow direct in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, or plant divisions in spring or fall; alpine rock cress requires excellent drainage — plants will rot in wet or waterlogged soil especially in winter. Arabis alpina is a mat-forming European alpine perennial in the mustard family, producing rosettes of grayish-green, slightly hairy leaves and in early spring covering itself completely in pure-white, 4-petaled flowers in dense racemes that create a solid mat of white from March through May — one of the most reliable and spectacular early-spring groundcovers for rock gardens, walls, and sunny banks. The pink-flowered cultivar 'Rosea' and semi-double 'Flore Pleno' are popular alternatives; all are excellent for spilling over walls and between rocks. Shear lightly after blooming to keep compact and encourage fresh growth.

plant_note: Divide established clumps carefully in early fall after flowering, ensuring each section has healthy roots and a rosette of leaves. Replant immediately in a gritty, humus-rich, well-drained mix in a cool, lightly shaded position such as a trough or rock garden. Protect from winter wet with a pane of glass rather than mulch, which can cause crown rot.
directions: Alpine snowbell demands excellent drainage and cool, consistently moist conditions; plant in a trough, raised bed, or rock garden crevice filled with a mix of gritty sand, pea gravel, and leaf mold. Choose a position with morning sun and afternoon shade, or dappled light, to replicate its high-altitude habitat. Divide established clumps after flowering in fall to propagate, handling the shallow roots with care and replanting immediately. Winter wet is the primary threat to survival — shelter plants with a pane of glass over winter if prolonged wet spells are typical in your climate.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; alpine wallflower is a perennial species from the Iberian Peninsula that is longer-lived than common wallflower (E. cheiri) in well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant rooted tip cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to slightly neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; alpine wallflower requires excellent drainage and is best propagated from cuttings annually as it tends to become woody and die out in the center after 2–3 years. Erysimum linifolium is a Spanish native perennial wallflower with narrow, linear, gray-green leaves (giving it the name "flat-leaved") and produces a long, extended succession of fragrant, lavender-purple to mauve flowers in terminal clusters from spring through summer; it blooms for several months if the spent flower clusters are regularly removed. The cultivar 'Bowles' Mauve' (formerly attributed to this species but now considered a complex hybrid) is one of the longest-blooming of all perennial wallflowers, flowering nearly year-round in mild climates and making it one of the most popular of all perennial wallflowers in UK gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in moist to consistently moist, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or rocky subalpine soil in partial shade to full sun; alpine wintergreen requires cool summer temperatures and strongly acidic conditions and is best suited to Pacific Northwest, Rocky Mountain, and upper Midwest gardens.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, peaty or sandy-rocky subalpine soil in partial shade to full sun; alpine wintergreen requires cool summer temperatures and good winter snow cover to perform at its best. Gaultheria humifusa is a mat-forming, evergreen sub-shrub of rocky subalpine and alpine slopes throughout the western mountains of North America from Alaska to California and New Mexico, producing a dense, low carpet of tiny, rounded, dark-green, slightly aromatic leaves — similar to the familiar eastern G. procumbens but much lower-growing — with small white urn-shaped flowers tucked among the leaves in summer, followed by small red, mildly wintergreen-flavored berries in late summer and fall. It is a superb groundcover for acidic rock gardens, alpine gardens, and under rhododendrons or conifers in cool-climate gardens. The berries are attractive to birds and safe for human consumption in small quantities. Not suitable for warm-climate gardens — it requires cold winters and mild summers.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Alta is a narrow, tightly columnar southern magnolia bred for improved cold hardiness and small-space use.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Alta bears the classic large, creamy-white, lemon-scented southern magnolia blooms and glossy evergreen foliage on an unusually narrow, densely branched, columnar form that fits tight side yards, screens, and formal allees where a full-spreading southern magnolia would be too wide. Its improved cold hardiness compared to many older cultivars extends its usable range further north than the species is typically recommended. Water deeply during establishment, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune only to remove dead or damaged wood, since magnolias need little routine pruning.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade along stream banks or at the margins of ponds; golden saxifrage requires consistent moisture and will not tolerate drought.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; alternate-leaved golden saxifrage forms dense, low, spreading mats along stream banks, seeps, and woodland spring margins and requires consistently high moisture — it will not survive drought. Chrysosplenium alternifolium is a diminutive, 3–6-inch-tall European and Asian native groundcover in the saxifrage family with small, rounded, kidney-shaped, toothed leaves and clusters of tiny, chartreuse-yellow to golden flowers surrounded by brightly colored, leaf-like bracts in early spring, creating a cheerful carpet of yellow-green along shaded, wet stream margins. It is uncommon in cultivation but is increasingly sought by shade and water garden enthusiasts for its ability to create a lush, moss-like carpet in the wettest, shadiest spots where other groundcovers fail; in North America it occurs natively in the far north.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Altona is a vigorous older German cultivar known for exceptionally sturdy flower stems.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Altona bears large, rounded mophead blooms in carmine-rose in alkaline soil, shifting to true blue in acidic soil, on notably sturdy stems that hold the heavy flower heads upright through wind and rain better than many older mophead cultivars. Its vigorous, reliable growth and dependable, long-lasting blooms have kept it in commerce since its introduction in Germany decades ago. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot Southern climates to prevent wilting.

common_name: Alumia Vanilla Cream Marigold (Large Anemone-Type Soft Yellow Marigold)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, or direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Alumia Vanilla Cream is a vigorous, early-flowering French marigold bred for large, densely double, anemone-form flowers in a soft, unusual lemon-cream color.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost, or transplant started seedlings, into well-drained soil in full sun. Alumia Vanilla Cream is a French marigold bred for unusually large, fully double, anemone-form flowers in a soft, creamy lemon-yellow that stands apart from the typical bright orange and gold of most marigolds, opening early and continuing vigorously through the season on a well-branched, uniform plant. Its large flower size and gentle color make it useful as a softer accent in mixed plantings that would clash with brighter marigold tones. Marigolds tolerate poor, lean soil and bloom best without heavy fertilizer, which favors foliage over flowers; deadhead spent blooms to keep the display tidy and encourage continued flowering, and water at the base rather than overhead to help avoid the powdery mildew and botrytis that can affect dense marigold plantings in humid weather.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or water, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich potting mix in partial shade; aluminum plant prefers consistently moist but never waterlogged soil — it is sensitive to drought (leaves collapse quickly) but equally sensitive to root rot in compacted or consistently wet media.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; aluminum plant is a Vietnamese shade perennial of the nettle family (Urticaceae) — one of the most easily grown and most instantly recognizable small tropical foliage plants — whose oval, quilted, dark-green leaves are distinctively marked with four elevated, raised, silver-white, metallic panels between the leaf veins that catch light and create a three-dimensional, embossed, hammered-aluminum effect on the leaf surface. The silver patterning is so striking and consistent that the plant is immediately recognizable even at a distance. It grows as a compact, bushy, somewhat succulent-stemmed mound and is among the most tolerant of lower indoor light levels of any tropical foliage plant, thriving in bright-shade to moderate-shade conditions where many other variegated plants would lose their markings. As an outdoor plant in zone 10–12, it forms a low mounding groundcover in shade gardens. Tip-pinch regularly to maintain compact, bushy growth — plants left unpinched become tall and lanky within a few months. Propagates trivially easily from stem cuttings rooted in water.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Always Summer produces new flower flushes over a longer window than older gardenia cultivars, so regular feeding through the growing season supports the extended bloom.
directions: Always Summer is a reblooming gardenia bred to flower repeatedly from late spring well into fall rather than concentrating bloom into one or two flushes, giving a much longer season of the classic waxy white, intensely fragrant flowers than older gardenia cultivars provide. It holds a compact, rounded, well-branched habit with glossy dark-green foliage and, like other modern reblooming gardenias, benefits from regular feeding with an acid-forming fertilizer through the growing season to fuel the repeated flower flushes. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, strongly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and watch for the yellowing (chlorotic) foliage that signals insufficiently acidic soil, correcting with sulfur or an acidifying fertilizer as needed.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall with the neck and top half of the bulb above soil level in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 8–10 amaryllis naturalize in the ground and bloom reliably each winter-spring without the 6–8 week dry rest period required for potted indoor forcing.
directions: Plant bulbs with the top half exposed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; amaryllis (correctly Hippeastrum) is one of the most spectacularly beautiful of all bulbous plants, producing massive trumpet-shaped flowers 6–8 inches across in brilliant red, pink, white, coral, salmon, or bicolor striped patterns on hollow, leafless stalks 18–24 inches tall. In zone 8–10 amaryllis naturalizes beautifully in the garden, blooming each January through April without any special treatment — simply plant the bulbs in fall, fertilize lightly in fall and early spring, and allow the foliage to die back naturally each summer.
