Gulf Coast gardens are famous for spectacular outdoor amaryllis displays along entry walks and in foundation plantings. The large clumps multiply year by year to create a more impressive display. Indoor forcing in pots requires a 6–8 week dry rest period at cool temperatures before returning to warmth and water.

common_name: Amas Bearded Iris (Historic Near-Species Violet-Blue Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Amas is a historic near-species tall bearded iris collected in Turkey in the early 20th century and heavily used in early hybridizing programs.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Amas is a historic near-species bearded iris collected in Turkey in the early 1900s, its soft violet-blue flowers with a light, sweet fragrance closer in character to the wild species that gave rise to modern tall bearded hybrids. Breeders leaned on it heavily in the early 20th century for its vigor, fragrance, and reliable rebloom, and it remains a tough, easy-to-grow garden plant in its own right, spreading steadily by rhizome offsets. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep the rhizomes in full sun with sharp drainage to avoid rot.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; needs light and cool soil.
directions: 'Amazing Grey' produces one-of-a-kind crepe-paper blooms in smoky lavender-grey tones, bred over many years from the Mother of Pearl blend. Scatter the tiny seed on the surface in early spring or fall, as it needs light and cool soil to germinate, and do not cover it. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil where it is quite drought tolerant. Because it resents transplanting, always direct sow where it is to bloom. Let some flowers form seed pods and it will happily self-sow for future seasons.

plant_note: Plant bulb offsets in spring into rich, humus-heavy, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Amazon lily is a true tropical understory plant that scorches in direct sun and is best grown in a shaded bed or large container in all but the mildest frost-free climates.
directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Amazon lily is a South American rainforest understory bulb with broad, glossy, dark green leaves and clusters of large, fragrant, pure white, daffodil-like flowers that can appear more than once a year in warm, humid conditions rather than on a single fixed bloom schedule. It genuinely requires shade, humidity, and consistent moisture to thrive, making it a poor fit for typical sunny bulb borders but an excellent choice for a shaded lanai, greenhouse, or humid understory planting in the tropics. Outside true frost-free zones, grow it as a container specimen that summers outdoors in shade and moves to a warm, bright indoor spot before any hint of frost, since even light chilling can damage or kill the bulb. Repot or divide crowded clumps only when flowering declines, as Amazon lily blooms best when slightly pot-bound.

common_name: Amazon Lily (Eucharis Lily, White Amazon Lily, Madonna Lily of the Tropics)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil or potting mix; Amazon Lily cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 50°F. Unlike most bulbs, it prefers consistent moisture year-round and only needs a brief 4–6 week dry spell to trigger blooming. Grow in groupings for best display — single bulbs rarely bloom as freely as established clumps. In zone 9, container culture allows flexibility. Keep the bulb top at soil level. Propagate by separating offsets. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Amazon Lily is one of the best bulbs for shaded positions in zone 10-11 outdoor tropical gardens, producing its most beautiful and abundant flowers in the bright filtered shade under large trees. Eucharis amazonica (formerly and sometimes still listed as E. grandiflora) is a large-bulbed, evergreen geophyte from the humid tropical forests of Colombia, Peru, and Bolivia in the Amaryllidaceae family, producing some of the most beautiful and fragrant flowers available from a shade-tolerant tropical bulb. The flowers are pendant, large (3–4 inch), pure white, 6-petaled, with a prominent green and white central corona surrounded by six outward-spreading tepals — the combination of pendulous form, snowy white color, and green-tinged central cup creates a flower of exceptional elegance. The fragrance is intensely sweet, jasmine-like, and far-carrying. Flowers are produced in clusters of 3–6 at the top of tall scapes, typically in spring and fall after a brief dry rest period, and the blooming of an established clump with multiple simultaneous flower spikes is one of the finest flower displays available from a shade garden bulb. The large, broad, glossy, dark-green leaves (12–16 inches long) are attractive in themselves year-round. Amazon Lily is used as a cut flower and for lei making throughout the Pacific. All parts are toxic.

common_name: Amazonian Zebra Plant (Chantinii Bromeliad, Zebra Aechmea)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, frost-free patio container; Amazonian Zebra Plant is one of the more cold-sensitive bromeliads and suffers damage below 45°F, so bring containers indoors well before frost outside zone 10-11. Pot in a coarse, fast-draining orchid-bark mix and keep the central cup topped off with rainwater or distilled water. Divide and pot up rooted offsets (pups) once they reach roughly one-third the size of the parent.
directions: Provide bright, filtered light — more light than most tank bromeliads tolerate is needed to bring out the bold banding, but direct midday sun will scorch the leaves, so an east-facing window or high-canopy shade outdoors is ideal. Aechmea chantinii is a large epiphytic bromeliad from the Amazon basin of Peru, Brazil, Colombia, and Ecuador, prized for broad, arching leaves marked with alternating horizontal bands of silver-gray and deep green that give the plant its 'zebra' common name; leaf margins carry small dark spines, so site it away from foot traffic. After several years of growth the rosette sends up a dramatic, multi-tiered flower spike of red-orange bracts holding small yellow-and-red flowers, followed by long-lasting berries. Keep the central water-holding cup flushed with fresh water every few weeks to prevent stagnation, and expect the mother rosette to die back naturally after flowering as pups take over.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Amber Gem is part of the Winter Jewels breeding series, with warm amber-gold flowers blooming in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist while the plant establishes. Amber Gem is part of the acclaimed Winter Jewels hellebore breeding series, producing rounded, outward-facing flowers in warm amber, apricot, and honey tones often accented with darker veining or a subtle picotee edge, held above leathery, evergreen, deeply divided foliage. Like other Lenten roses it blooms very early, often pushing through late-season snow or hard frost, providing reliable color in the shade garden when little else is flowering. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to showcase the flowers at their best, and site it away from areas where pets or children graze, since all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Amber Jubilee Ninebark (Multicolor Orange-Gold-Red Foliage Ninebark)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in any well-drained to moist, acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; multicolor foliage effect is strongest in full sun.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; ninebark is an exceptionally tough native shrub tolerating clay, poor soil, and drought once established. Amber Jubilee stands apart from the many purple- and burgundy-leaved ninebark cultivars by cycling through a distinct multicolor foliage display: new growth emerges bright orange-gold, matures through yellow-green, and finishes deep burgundy-red by fall, often showing several of these colors on the same plant at once. Its vigorous, upright habit and season-long shifting color make it a strong focal point in a mixed shrub border. Exfoliating bark on older stems adds winter texture; prune out the oldest stems at the base every 2–3 years to keep growth vigorous and colorful.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; tolerates dry shade under trees once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Amber Queen produces sprays of warm amber-orange flowers with a coppery cast in spring, an unusual warm tone distinct from the more common yellow, white, and pink epimedium flower colors, held above heart-shaped leaves that emerge bronze-tinted and mature to green. Its clump-forming habit spreads gradually into a dense, weed-suppressing patch useful for underplanting trees and shrubs in a woodland garden. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh and show off the spring flowers.

common_name: Amber Waves Coral Bells (Ruffled Amber-Gold Foliage Heuchera)
plant_note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Amber Waves holds its ruffled amber-gold foliage color best out of the hottest afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; some morning sun deepens the amber-gold foliage color while afternoon shade prevents scorch and fading in hot climates. Amber Waves bears ruffled, wavy-edged leaves in a warm amber-gold that holds color through the growing season, forming a dense mound topped in early summer by airy, wiry stems of tiny white flowers that attract hummingbirds and pollinators. Its bright, ruffled foliage provides season-long color in a shaded border even when not in bloom. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and remove old, tattered leaves in late winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; American alumroot is an adaptable native groundcover and the progenitor of many modern coral bell cultivars.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; American alumroot adapts to a wide range of soil conditions including rocky slopes and is more tolerant of dry shade than many shade perennials. Heuchera americana is the wild-type species native to eastern North American rocky woods, slopes, and woodland borders from Ontario to Georgia; it produces mounded clumps of rounded, shallowly lobed, marbled or plain green leaves with attractive silver veining and metallic overtones that are the primary ornamental feature, while the slender, wiry scapes bearing tiny, inconspicuous, greenish-white flowers in late spring are secondary. The species is the primary parent of the huge number of foliage heuchera cultivars now available, though many of these are complex hybrids; the wild type is a fine native plant in its own right for naturalizing in shaded woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in average to sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; American barren strawberry is the native eastern North American counterpart to the more commonly sold Eurasian Waldsteinia ternata, and is preferred for native plant and pollinator-focused shade plantings.
directions: Plant divisions in average, well-drained, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; American barren strawberry is a low, mat-forming native perennial found naturally in dry to moist deciduous woods and rocky slopes from the Appalachians north into New England and the upper Midwest, spreading slowly by short rhizomes to form an evergreen to semi-evergreen carpet of glossy, three-lobed, strawberry-like leaves. Bright yellow, five-petaled flowers appear in mid-spring just above the foliage, followed by small dry seed heads rather than a fleshy fruit — despite the common name, it produces no edible berry. It is slower to spread and less aggressive than its Eurasian relative, making it a good choice for naturalizing under native hardwoods without overwhelming companion woodland wildflowers. Once established it needs little care and tolerates the dry, root-filled soil typical of a mature shade garden; supplemental water is only necessary during the first growing season or in prolonged drought.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in mild-winter climates for the strongest plants and earliest bloom, or in early spring where winters are severe, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; American basket flower self-seeds readily once established.
directions: Sow directly in average, well-drained soil in full sun; tolerates heat and drought well once established and rarely needs supplemental fertility. Centaurea americana (American basket flower) is a tall, statuesque native prairie annual of Texas and the south-central United States, producing large, showy, thistle-like flower heads in shades of soft pink to lavender, each bloom cupped by a distinctive ring of straw-colored, papery bracts that form a woven, basket-like structure beneath the petals — the source of its common name. The flowers are exceptionally attractive to bees, butterflies, and other pollinators, and the tall, airy stems make an excellent, long-lasting cut flower. As a reseeding annual, it readily returns year after year once established in a sunny bed or meadow planting, providing reliable summer height and color with essentially no maintenance. An easy, dramatic native for a sunny cutting garden or naturalized wildflower planting, typically grown as an annual across zone 4–9.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; seeds germinate readily in warm soil without pre-treatment.
directions: American Basketflower is a showy native annual of prairies and roadsides across the south-central United States, producing large (3–4 in), lavender-pink, fragrant flower heads with an intricate basketwork of papery bracts beneath each bloom from June through August. Despite its common name and thistle-like appearance, it is not a true thistle and bears no sharp spines, making it safe to handle and ideal for mixed wildflower meadows and pollinator gardens. Sow seeds directly into lean, well-drained soil in full sun at or just after last frost; plants establish quickly and bloom within 60–90 days, requiring no irrigation once roots are established in typical prairie or roadside soils. The fragrant flowers are exceptional for native bees, butterflies, and goldfinches, which relish the seeds as they ripen in late summer.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; American basketflower germinates in cool soil and is best sown in fall in Gulf Coast gardens, where it overwinters as a basal rosette and blooms profusely in late spring before summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — American basketflower is a spectacular, large-flowered native annual of the Texas and Gulf Coast prairies, producing showy, 3–4 inch, thistle-like flower heads in shades of rose-pink to lavender-pink (and rarely white) with an intricate woven 'basket' of straw-colored bracts beneath the blooms — giving rise to the common name. Despite its thistle-like appearance, it is entirely spineless and easy to handle. The large, bright flower heads are superb for cutting and drying, and are heavily visited by bumblebees, honeybees, and monarch butterflies. It is one of the showiest and most easily grown native annuals for the southern prairie garden, blooming from May to July in a single, spectacular season and then self-sowing to return the following year. Outstanding in masses in wildflower meadows alongside Indian blanket, black-eyed Susan, and coneflowers.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; basswood performs best in rich, moist, slightly alkaline conditions and is more tolerant of chalk soils than most native trees.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; American basswood is one of the most important honey trees in North America — when the intensely fragrant cream-yellow flowers open in June and July, beekeepers consider it the single most important nectar flow of the year, producing linden honey renowned for its delicate, flowery flavor. The fragrance of a flowering basswood in a neighborhood can be detected at a distance of several blocks. The large, heart-shaped leaves, distinctive bract-winged fruiting clusters, and tall, straight trunk make it a notable landscape specimen. Young leaves are edible in spring salads; the inner bark (bast) is one of the best natural fibers for cordage in North America and was extensively used by Native Americans. Tolerates partial shade well, making it suitable for understory planting in very large gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; American beautyberry establishes readily and grows quickly, typically reaching 4–6 feet in its first few seasons. Softwood cuttings taken in summer root easily under intermittent mist.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil; American beautyberry tolerates a wide range of soil types and performs well in woodland edges, shade gardens, and naturalistic borders. Callicarpa americana is a deciduous native shrub of the southeastern United States and one of the most visually arresting plants in the native landscape — in late summer and fall it is covered in tight, globe-shaped clusters of vivid magenta to violet-purple berries arranged in rings directly along the arching stems, creating a spectacle unlike any other shrub. The berries persist well after leaf drop and provide outstanding late-season food for mockingbirds, robins, catbirds, and other wildlife. Prune hard in late winter (to within 6–12 inches of the ground) to encourage vigorous new growth and the heaviest berry production, as berries form on new wood; without pruning the shrub can become leggy over time.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; American bittersweet requires both male and female plants for fruit production — plant at least one male per 3–5 females, or select self-fertile cultivars. Do NOT plant Oriental bittersweet (Celastrus orbiculatus), which is invasive — verify you have the native species from a reputable native plant nursery.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; American bittersweet is a native deciduous twining vine prized for its spectacular fall and winter fruit display — clusters of small, round capsules that split open in autumn to reveal brilliant orange-red arils (fleshy seed coverings), creating a vivid orange-and-red effect that persists on the vine through winter and is widely used in dried arrangements and holiday decoration. The small, greenish-yellow flowers in early summer are inconspicuous but attract small native bees. The fruit is a critical winter food source for many songbirds including bluebirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and mockingbirds, which eat the arils while dispersing the seeds. American bittersweet is increasingly rare in wild populations because Oriental bittersweet (C. orbiculatus), an invasive Asian relative, has displaced it across much of the East — purchase only from reputable native plant nurseries and verify the species. Female plants require a nearby male for fruit set. An outstanding native vine for trellises, fences, and naturalistic settings where its wildlife value can be fully expressed.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist to moist-well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. American Bladdernut is excellent for naturalizing moist, shaded areas where few other large shrubs will grow.
directions: American Bladdernut is a large, multi-stemmed native shrub, native to moist, rich deciduous forest understories, streambanks, and floodplain edges throughout eastern North America from Quebec to Florida and west to Kansas, forming thickets in the shade of oaks, maples, and ashes where few other ornamental shrubs survive. In April and May it produces drooping clusters of small, white, bell-shaped flowers attractive to native bees; these are followed in summer by the plant's most distinctive feature — inflated, papery, three-chambered seed pods resembling small green Chinese lanterns that persist into fall and rattle audibly in the breeze, turning tan and remaining decorative into winter. The opposite, trifoliate leaves resemble those of box elder and turn yellow in fall. An underutilized native shrub for difficult shaded, moist sites — excellent for naturalizing under large trees where maintaining lawn is impossible.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving the twining fronds a low trellis, shrub, or fence to climb; only ever use nursery-propagated stock, since wild populations have been historically depleted by over-collection and the species is legally protected in several states.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, with a low support for the twining fronds to climb; never allow the soil to dry out, and avoid disturbing the shallow root system once established. Lygodium palmatum (American climbing fern, or Hartford fern) is a true botanical rarity — the only cold-hardy climbing fern native to North America, found in scattered acidic bogs, moist woodland edges, and stream banks from New England south through the Appalachians. Unlike typical ferns, its fronds do not simply arch from a central crown but instead twine and climb over shrubs and low vegetation, sometimes reaching several feet, giving it a vining habit unique among hardy ferns. Historically over-collected for Victorian-era flower arranging (a practice that led to some of the first plant protection laws in the United States, enacted in Connecticut specifically to protect this species), it remains uncommon in cultivation and should only be sourced as nursery-propagated stock. A genuine botanical curiosity for a consistently moist, acidic, partly shaded woodland garden in zone 5–8.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into rich, well-drained woodland soil; cold stratification over winter is required for germination, and plants will spend many years as a rosette before ever flowering.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall into deep, humus-rich woodland soil at a site that will not be disturbed for many years, as plants spend a decade or more building a large basal rosette before sending up their dramatic flowering stalk. Lightly cover seed and allow winter cold to provide necessary stratification; germination is slow and uneven, so patience is essential. Select the planting location carefully, since American Columbo develops a deep root system and resents transplanting at any stage. After the plant finally flowers and sets seed, it will die, so allow seed to mature and scatter for future generations.

common_name: American Dawn Dahlia (Large Coral-Pink Dinnerplate Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; American Dawn is a large informal decorative dahlia bearing bold coral-pink blooms with a soft golden blush at the center, a popular large-flowered garden and cut-flower variety. Stake plants early since the heavy blooms on tall stems require support.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. American Dawn is a large informal decorative dahlia producing bold, coral-pink blooms 8-9 inches across, with petals that soften toward a warm golden-peach glow near the center, giving the flower noticeable depth and dimension compared to single-toned varieties. The tall, vigorous plants produce continuously from midsummer through the first hard frost with regular deadheading, and the large, sturdy-stemmed blooms make excellent cut flowers. In zone 9, provide afternoon shade or expect some fading of the coral coloring during the most intense summer heat, with the richest color typically appearing in spring and fall. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, deep soil in full sun to partial shade. Select disease-resistant cultivars ('Valley Forge', 'Princeton', 'New Harmony') to reduce susceptibility to Dutch Elm Disease; choose open sites with good air circulation.
directions: American Elm was for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries the most important street and shade tree in eastern North America, the classic 'cathedral' tree whose interlocking vase-shaped canopies arched over village streets from New England to the Great Plains in an iconic display of American civic beauty — until Dutch Elm Disease (Ophiostoma ulmi), introduced from Europe in the 1930s, devastated the species throughout most of its natural range and removed it from the American streetscape within a few decades. Today, disease-resistant cultivars ('Valley Forge', 'Princeton', 'New Harmony') have restored American Elm to viability in the landscape and are the preferred planting choice for new trees; these cultivars maintain the original graceful, vase-shaped habit that made the species so beloved, with resistance to DED ranging from moderate to strong. American Elm is adaptable to a wide range of soils from wet bottomlands to dry uplands and tolerates urban conditions, road salt, compaction, and air pollution better than most native trees. Plant disease-resistant cultivars in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil; provide adequate space for the wide-spreading mature canopy.

plant_note: Float plants on still to slow-moving water surfaces in a pond, tub garden, or container water garden; American frogbit spreads rapidly by runners and can cover a water surface in warm weather. Native throughout the eastern US, it is non-invasive in its natural range.
directions: Float plants on the surface of still to slow-moving water in partial shade to full sun; American frogbit is a native floating aquatic that forms dense mats of rounded, slightly spongy, heart-shaped leaves on still pond surfaces and sluggish backwaters across the eastern US from the Gulf to the Great Lakes. The small, three-petaled white flowers with yellow centers bob at the water surface in summer. The plant provides critical nursery habitat for fish fry, frogs, and aquatic invertebrates under its floating mat, creating a shelter zone that significantly increases pond biodiversity. As a floating plant with dangling roots that absorb nutrients directly from the water, it is highly effective for improving water clarity and reducing algae by competing for dissolved nutrients. Unlike the invasive European frogbit (Hydrocharis morsus-ranae), American frogbit is native to the region and appropriate for naturalistic ponds and water gardens in the eastern US.

common_name: American Gold Rush Rudbeckia (Disease-Resistant Fuzzy-Leaved Black-Eyed Susan)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; American Gold Rush was named Perennial Plant of the Year for its outstanding resistance to Septoria leaf spot, a common fungal disease that disfigures many black-eyed Susan cultivars in humid climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. American Gold Rush was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year for its exceptional resistance to Septoria leaf spot and other fungal diseases that commonly disfigure black-eyed Susan foliage in hot, humid climates, staying attractive through the entire growing season where older cultivars decline. It produces abundant golden-yellow flowers with a distinctive dark red-brown ring around the central cone, held above narrow, softly fuzzy, silver-green foliage that adds textural interest even before bloom. It is drought-tolerant once established, blooms over a long summer season, and provides valuable seed for goldfinches if spent flower heads are left standing into winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring directly into saturated, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along a streambank, seep, or bog garden; this tiny native mat-former needs constantly wet soil and will not persist in average garden conditions.
directions: Plant divisions in spring directly into saturated, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along a streambank, seep, or bog garden; this tiny native mat-former needs constantly wet soil and will not persist in average garden conditions. Chrysosplenium americanum is a diminutive eastern North American wildflower found carpeting shaded seeps, spring runs, and streamside mud from the Great Lakes and Northeast south through the Appalachian Mountains, forming loose, creeping mats of small, rounded, opposite leaves studded in early spring with inconspicuous but ecologically valuable yellow-green flowers that draw small early-season pollinators. It naturalizes readily in a shaded bog garden, rain garden margin, or the muddy edge of a garden pond, filling gaps between sedges and ferns where few other groundcovers will grow in standing wet soil. Because it spreads by shallow, brittle stems that root as they creep, established patches are easily divided and moved in spring to extend the planting along a wet shaded edge.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, slightly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; American holly is dioecious — plant at least one male within 50 feet of female trees for berry production. Most named female cultivars are sold with a recommended male pollinizer.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; American holly is the native evergreen tree holly of the eastern US, producing the classic red-berried, spiny-leaved holly that symbolizes the Christmas season. It grows naturally from Massachusetts to Florida and west to Texas, often in moist, slightly shaded woodland conditions along the coastal plain and Piedmont. The red berries (persistent through winter on female trees when a male pollinizer is present) are consumed by dozens of bird species, providing critical winter food for robins, cedar waxwings, and mockingbirds. It tolerates partial shade and performs remarkably well in zone 8–9 heat, making it one of the best native evergreen screening or specimen trees for the Gulf Coast garden. Hundreds of named cultivars exist — look for 'Fosteri' (compact), 'Savannah' (heavy fruiting, zone 7–9), and 'East Palatka' (Gulf Coast adapted).

plant_note: Plant small container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall in well-drained, moist to dry soil; hop hornbeam establishes slowly and resents transplanting of large specimens — start with young nursery stock.
directions: American hop hornbeam is a small to medium understory tree of exceptional adaptability, tolerating everything from deep dry shade under mature oaks to moist bottomland edges — one of the finest native trees for difficult shaded sites where larger trees struggle. Its common name refers to the distinctive hop-like fruiting clusters that hang from branches in summer and fall, providing important food for ruffed grouse, wild turkey, northern bobwhite, and numerous songbirds and small mammals. The wood is extraordinarily hard and dense — historically used for tool handles and fence posts and known as 'ironwood' — and the pale, finely ridged gray bark provides year-round ornamental interest. Grow as a specimen or in groupings beneath taller oaks, hickories, and maples to create a multi-layered native woodland garden; it thrives with minimal care once established and is largely pest and disease free.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in early spring or late fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; transplants well from container stock but resents root disturbance once established.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; American hornbeam (also called musclewood or blue beech) is one of the finest small native understory trees, growing naturally in the deep shade of bottomland forests and stream banks across eastern North America. The distinctive smooth, gray, sinewy bark with ridge-like muscle-like sinews makes it an outstanding specimen year-round. Delicate hop-like seed clusters in fall provide food for many finch and songbird species. Outstanding golden-orange to orange-red fall color. It grows slowly — 10–12 inches per year — but is very long lived. One of the few small trees genuinely suited to planting in deep shade under large oaks or maples. Excellent for naturalistic woodland gardens and native plant landscapes.

plant_note: Sow seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or cold-stratify for 60–90 days before spring sowing; division of established clumps in early spring is the most reliable propagation method.
directions: Sow seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or divide established clumps in early spring, planting in moist but well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to dappled woodland light; American ipecac is an airy native perennial closely related to Gillenia trifoliata, producing clouds of small white five-petaled star flowers on reddish branching stems in late spring to early summer, followed by attractive reddish seed capsules. The foliage turns orange-red in fall and the persistent reddish calyces add winter interest. An excellent naturalistic garden plant that blends beautifully with hostas, ferns, and other shade-tolerant companions, and makes a delicate cut flower.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; needs light and cool soil.
directions: 'American Legion', the classic Flanders or corn poppy, opens brilliant scarlet-red single blooms that famously symbolize remembrance. Scatter the fine seed over prepared soil in early spring or fall and leave it uncovered, since light aids germination. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil where it thrives with little care. Direct sow where it is to grow because the seedlings dislike being moved. Allow spent flowers to set seed and this heirloom will naturalize and reseed for years.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola; introduced in 1902, American Pillar is a vigorous once-blooming rambler.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola. Introduced in 1902, American Pillar produces a spectacular single summer flush of large, single, deep pink flowers each marked with a bold white eye at the center, borne in such profusion that a mature plant in full bloom is hard to miss from a distance. Its vigorous growth and near-total lack of fragrance are typical of this class, but the sheer scale of the once-yearly floral display has kept it a garden favorite for well over a century. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

plant_note: Sow seeds in moist, fertile, well-drained to average soil in full sun to part shade; pokeweed establishes from seed and spreads readily by bird-dispersed seeds. CAUTION: all parts of this plant are toxic to humans and livestock — the roots, berries, and seeds especially so. Wear gloves when handling the plant. Despite being a dangerous plant to ingest, it is extremely valuable as a wildlife plant and is best managed in a wilder area of the garden.
directions: Sow seeds in moist, fertile, well-drained to average soil in full sun to part shade; American pokeweed is a large, dramatic native perennial of eastern North America with striking ornamental qualities — brilliant magenta-pink hollow stems, large tropical-looking leaves, long white flower racemes, and most notably the clusters of deep purple-black, shiny berries in late summer and fall that are among the most important food sources for migrating thrushes, mockingbirds, woodpeckers, and other fall-migrating birds that disperse the seeds widely. Despite being a generous wildlife resource, the entire plant — especially the roots, berries, and seeds — is dangerously toxic to humans and livestock, containing phytolaccatoxin and phytolaccigenin that cause severe gastrointestinal symptoms. The magenta pigment in the berries (pokeweed ink) was historically used to write documents, including some drafts of the US Declaration of Independence. The young spring shoots (poke sallet) have been boiled and eaten in Appalachian tradition after multiple changes of water to reduce toxins, but this practice is risky and not recommended. Best established in naturalized areas.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring as new growth begins to emerge; site at the edge of a pond, stream, or boggy area where soil remains consistently wet.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full shade in wet to permanently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil — stream margins, pond edges, and boggy woodland clearings are ideal. Divide large clumps in early spring by splitting the fibrous root mass with a sharp spade; replant divisions promptly and water heavily to prevent them from drying out before new roots establish. The spectacular rusty-brown fertile fronds emerge among the sterile fronds in late spring, providing striking late-season interest before the whole plant turns golden in autumn. Established clumps are very long-lived and develop substantial crowns; avoid moving or splitting unnecessarily once they are settled.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring after scarifying seeds (nick or sand the hard seed coat) in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; American senna is an impressive native perennial with bold foliage and prolific yellow flowers.
directions: Scarify seeds by nicking the hard seed coat with a file or soaking overnight in hot water, then direct sow in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; American senna is a vigorous grower once established. Senna hebecarpa is a large, bold native perennial of eastern North American moist woodlands and thickets growing to 4–6 feet tall, with large, pinnately compound leaves and clusters of bright yellow, 5-petaled flowers in late summer followed by flat, oblong seed pods eaten by birds; it is the larval food plant of the cloudless sulphur butterfly (Phoebis sennae), the sleepy orange butterfly, and several other sulphur species. The dramatic tropical foliage and prolific golden flowers make it a standout at the back of native plant borders and in naturalized wildlife gardens; it spreads slowly by rhizomes to form clumps.

common_name: American Skunk Cabbage / Yellow Skunk Cabbage
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring directly into boggy soil or shallow water margins; keep roots continuously moist and never allow to dry out during establishment.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring into saturated boggy soil or at the shallow margins of a pond, keeping the crown at or just below the waterline. Choose a site with dappled light or morning sun and afternoon shade, as the massive leaves can scorch in intense direct sun. Bright yellow spathes emerge from late winter onward before the foliage, providing important early-season color; the mild skunk odor fades quickly in open air. This slow-maturing native is a long-term landscape investment — allow several years for plants to settle and produce their full, architectural leaf canopy.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; American smoke tree grows naturally on rocky, alkaline, limestone-based, shallow soils in the Ozarks, Edwards Plateau, and southern Appalachians. Dislikes heavy, wet, fertile soils — lean, dry, well-drained conditions produce the best fall color.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; American smoke tree is the native North American species of smoke tree — rarer, larger, and considered by many horticulturists to be superior to the European smoke tree (Cotinus coggygria) for fall color. The large, oval, blue-green leaves turn extraordinary shades of orange, scarlet, and burgundy in autumn, rivaling the best maples for fall color brilliance. Named 'chittamwood' in the Ozarks, where it grows on rocky, limestone outcrops and cedar glades. The smoke-like display in summer (from the fluffy, hair-like styles remaining after flowering) is less showy than the European species but still attractive. Extremely drought-tolerant on dry, rocky, alkaline soils. Much less commonly grown than European smoke tree, despite its superior fall color — an underused native ornamental tree that deserves wider planting in appropriate dry, rocky, well-drained garden settings across the eastern US.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist to consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; American snowbell is native to streambanks, wet woodland margins, and boggy lowlands of the eastern and southeastern United States and performs best where roots can access reliable moisture throughout the growing season. It tolerates periodic brief flooding and is an excellent choice for rain gardens and shaded streamside plantings. Seed requires 3 months of cold moist stratification; container transplants establish more reliably.
directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil; American snowbell is a refined and underappreciated native shrub of eastern North America, bearing in May and June an elegant display of nodding, white, reflexed-petaled flowers with conspicuous bright-yellow stamens — the blossoms hang in short racemes beneath the arching stems, reminiscent of a smaller, shrubby version of the ornamental Japanese snowbell (Styrax japonicus) but entirely native and better adapted to wet sites. Styrax americanus is a multi-stemmed, loosely branched shrub native to moist, low-lying woodland margins, floodplain forests, and streambanks from Virginia to Florida and west to Missouri, making it an ideal choice for rain gardens, bioswales, and the moist edges of naturalistic woodland gardens where many other shrubs fail. The clean, elliptic leaves emerge fresh green in spring and offer a pleasant backdrop to the delicate flowers; fall color is a quiet soft yellow. A superb native alternative to non-native snowbell species for gardeners seeking an authentically regional plant with quiet seasonal beauty, exceptional ecological value for native bees, and reliable performance in wet or seasonally flooded sites.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in early fall; American spikenard is a bold, large perennial that requires ample space — allow 4–5 feet in every direction for a mature clump.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; American spikenard is a large, architectural native perennial of rich eastern forests that provides bold textural presence where scale plants are needed — the enormous, compound leaves with multiple pairs of leaflets can span 5 feet across, creating a tropical-looking foliage mass in the shade garden. Clusters of small, greenish-white flowers appear in midsummer on branched panicles, followed by clusters of dark reddish-purple to black berries that birds relish. The aromatic roots have a history of culinary and medicinal use in indigenous traditions and have been used as a flavoring similar to sarsaparilla. Dies to the ground in winter. Excellent as a bold accent in large-scale woodland garden compositions and native plant restorations.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral alluvial or bottomland soil in full sun. American Sycamore grows best in deep, moist, fertile soils near water and becomes a massive tree that requires ample space; do not plant near structures, sewer lines, or small yards.
directions: American Sycamore is one of the largest deciduous trees in North America — with trunk diameters commonly reaching 6–8 feet and old specimens exceeding 10 feet in diameter — native to the moist, rich alluvial soils of river bottoms, floodplains, and stream terraces throughout eastern North America from Maine to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas, where its massive, gleaming white upper trunk (revealed as the outer gray-brown bark sheds in large patches) makes it visible from great distances and impossible to mistake for any other native tree. The distinctive mottled, ivory-white, cream, and gray trunk bark is among the most ornamental features of any North American tree, and the large, maple-like leaves create deep, cooling shade in summer; the spherical, golf-ball-sized seed heads hang through winter and are consumed by a variety of birds including American goldfinches. Wood ducks, chimney swifts, and other cavity-nesting species prize the large hollow cavities that develop in old sycamores. Plant in deep, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil near water features, streams, or in large park settings; it is not appropriate for typical residential lots given its ultimately massive size.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into a prepared site in well-drained to moderately moist soil in full to partial sun; American vetch readily self-sows once established and can also be sown in early spring, though fall sowing allows cold stratification to improve germination rates the following spring.
directions: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into well-drained to moderately moist soil in a sunny to partially shaded meadow or woodland edge; nick or lightly sand the seed coat before sowing to improve germination, and inoculate seed with an appropriate rhizobium inoculant to activate nitrogen fixation from the first season. Vicia americana is a perennial scrambling vine native to meadows, prairies, roadsides, and open woodlands across most of North America, producing clusters of 4–9 purple-blue pea-like flowers from April through July that attract native bees and bumblebees while fixing atmospheric nitrogen into the soil through root nodules. It is an important larval host for the Gray Hairstreak butterfly and several other Lepidoptera, and its lightweight tendrils allow it to weave through grasses and low shrubs without smothering neighbors, making it an excellent addition to naturalistic meadow plantings.

plant_note: Divide established mats of rhizomes in spring or fall and press the rhizomes firmly onto the surface of rocky outcrops, walls, or peaty substrates in shade; American wall fern is naturally epiphytic — it grows on bare rock surfaces, ledges, and tree bark rather than in deep soil. Tuck the rhizomes into moss or humus in rock crevices and keep moist until established. It does not grow well in ordinary garden soil.
directions: Plant in rocky, mossy, or peaty substrates on ledges, walls, or rock surfaces in full to part shade; American wall fern is a charming, small, leathery native fern that grows naturally on shaded rock outcrops, cliff ledges, boulders, and the bark of old trees — always on surfaces rather than in deep soil. It is one of the few truly epiphytic temperate ferns and forms spreading mats of narrow, once-pinnate, deep-green fronds from long, creeping surface rhizomes. The fronds are evergreen in mild climates and semi-evergreen where winters are colder, providing year-round interest on shaded rock surfaces where little else can grow. An invaluable fern for the rock garden, stone wall, or any shaded, rocky feature where its unique habitat preference can be accommodated. It grows very slowly but forms charming, permanent mats once established in suitable conditions. Native throughout northeastern North America south to the Appalachians, it is the eastern counterpart of the western licorice fern (Polypodium glycyrrhiza).

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring and plant divisions in shallow water (0–6 inches deep) or at the water's edge in full sun to partial shade. American Water-Willow spreads by rhizomes to form dense colonies and is best established from divisions of existing clumps in wet, acidic, sandy or mucky streamside soil.
directions: American Water-Willow is a native aquatic and emergent perennial of clean streams, river margins, and shallow lake edges across eastern North America, where its rhizomatous colonies form dense mats of willow-like leaves in the current, catching and filtering silt while stabilizing stream banks. The bicolored white and violet flowers are produced prolifically from late spring through summer and are outstanding nectar sources for native bumblebees, hummingbirds, and sphinx moths visiting the shallow water's edge. Plant divisions in spring in shallow water (0–6 inches) or at the water's edge in full sun to partial shade; American Water-Willow spreads readily by rhizomes to form dense, erosion-controlling colonies and is an exceptional native plant for water garden edges, stream bank stabilization, and rain garden overflow zones where periodic flooding occurs. The dense underwater stems also provide important spawning and refuge habitat for small fish.

plant_note: Plant container vines in spring near a very strong support; purchase named cultivars like 'Amethyst Falls' or 'Blue Moon' for reliable blooming from an early age rather than seed-grown plants.
directions: Plant container-grown named cultivars near a very strong trellis, pergola, or fence in full sun to partial shade; unlike the invasive Asian wisterias (W. sinensis, W. floribunda), native American wisteria is well-behaved, will not escape into natural areas, and responds to pruning. The fragrant lilac-purple flower clusters appear in late spring, with good repeat bloom through summer on named cultivars. Prune twice yearly — once after the main spring bloom and again in late winter — to maintain size and encourage blooming spurs. American wisteria is naturally found in moist lowlands and swamps and tolerates wetter conditions than Asian species; do not confuse with the highly invasive Japanese and Chinese wisterias.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile loamy soil in full sun to partial shade. Yellowwood is a long-lived, low-maintenance native shade tree that does not bloom every year — heavy flowering is often biennial or triggered by summer drought stress.
directions: American Yellowwood is a superb native shade tree, native to rich, well-drained limestone bluffs, rocky slopes, and bottomland forest edges in the mid-South from North Carolina and Kentucky south to Alabama and west to Oklahoma, producing in May and June the most spectacular flowering display of any native shade tree — long, pendulous clusters of fragrant, white, pea-like flowers resembling wisteria that drape the wide-spreading canopy in a breathtaking display. The smooth, light gray bark resembles beech bark and is ornamental year-round; the bright green, pinnately compound leaves turn yellow in fall; and the wood at the heartwood core is bright yellow — hence the common name. Yellowwood blooms on alternate years or following stress, but the wait is always worth it. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; it adapts to a wide range of conditions once established and is a long-lived, virtually pest-free tree.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; astilbe wilts quickly in dry soil and needs reliable moisture through the growing season.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; astilbe wilts quickly in dry soil and needs reliable moisture through the growing season. Feathery, plume-like flower spikes in rich lavender-purple rise above deeply cut, fern-textured, bronze-tinged green foliage in early to midsummer, one of the older Arends hybrid astilbe cultivars still valued for its unusual purple flower color among the more common pinks, reds, and whites of the genus. Its plush, plume-like flower texture and reliable performance in consistently moist shade make it a classic choice for a woodland border, pond margin, or rain garden alongside hostas and ferns. Keep soil consistently moist through summer, top-dress with compost each spring, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a sturdy trellis, pergola, or arbor that can support the eventual weight of a mature vine — wisteria vines become very heavy over decades.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support structure; Amethyst Falls is the most popular and most widely planted cultivar of Wisteria frutescens — the American native wisteria — offering all the beauty of classic wisteria with critically better behavior in the garden. Asian wisterias (W. sinensis and W. floribunda) are considered invasive in many Eastern and Gulf South states and can escape cultivation into natural areas; American wisteria (W. frutescens) is a well-behaved native that produces similar, lightly fragrant, lavender-to-violet flower racemes without the invasive spreading of its Asian cousins. Amethyst Falls was selected for early bloom age (typically flowering in its second or third year, compared to 5–10 years for species wisteria), repeat blooming through summer after the main spring flush, and shorter flower racemes (4–6 inches) that are proportionally appropriate for smaller garden structures. The flowers are fragrant but less intensely so than Asian wisterias. In zone 9, Amethyst Falls blooms reliably from April through June with lighter repeat bloom flushes through summer. The vigorous twining habit quickly covers an arbor, pergola, or fence and the compound, dark-green deciduous foliage provides summer shade after bloom. Prune after bloom to control size; established plants tolerate hard pruning.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix without covering — browallia needs light to germinate — at 70–75°F; start 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to shaded beds after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix without covering, as browallia needs light to germinate; maintain 70–75°F soil temperature and expect germination in 2–3 weeks. Transplant after last frost into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial to full shade — it is one of the few true shade-loving annuals that blooms reliably without any direct sun, making it invaluable for north-facing beds, shaded patios, and hanging baskets under tree canopy. Pinch stems once or twice to encourage branching and a fuller mound of blue, violet, or white trumpet-shaped flowers, which bloom continuously from early summer until frost. Keep the soil consistently moist and water at the base to avoid fungal leaf spots.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Amethyst Glow is part of the Winter Jewels breeding series, with deep purple double flowers blooming in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist while the plant establishes. Amethyst Glow is part of the acclaimed Winter Jewels hellebore breeding series, producing rounded, outward-facing, fully double flowers in a deep, glowing amethyst-purple, densely packed with extra petaloids for a full, rose-like appearance, held above leathery, evergreen, deeply divided foliage. Like other Lenten roses it blooms very early, often pushing through late-season snow or hard frost, providing reliable color in the shade garden when little else is flowering. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to showcase the flowers at their best, and site it away from areas where pets or children graze, since all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Amethyst Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dark Purple-Red Reblooming Oakleaf)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Amethyst is grown for flower panicles that age to an unusually deep purple-red compared with the pink or rose tones of most other oakleaf hydrangea cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun. Amethyst is an oakleaf hydrangea selected for flower panicles that mature to a deep, saturated purple-red unusually dark for the species, extending the multi-season color display well beyond the typical white-to-pink progression of most oakleaf cultivars. The bold, deeply lobed foliage turns rich burgundy and orange in fall, and the exfoliating cinnamon bark adds winter interest once leaves drop. Prune, if needed, right after flowering, since flower buds for the following year set on the current season's growth by late summer, and avoid cutting back in fall, winter, or spring, which removes next year's bloom.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or late fall directly in very well-drained soil in full sun; Eryngium amethystinum is tap-rooted and resents transplanting — direct seeding or planting small container plants while young gives the best results. Established plants are very drought-tolerant and should not be moved.
directions: Sow seeds in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; amethyst sea holly is a European native producing the most intensely colored blue-violet flowers of any Eryngium, with small, egg-shaped thistle-like flower heads surrounded by prominent, spiky, metallic amethyst-violet bracts that color the entire upper portion of the plant in shimmering blue-purple from July through September. The metallic blue color is extraordinary — simultaneously blue, violet, and silver depending on the light angle. As with all sea hollies, the tap-rooted plants are extremely drought-tolerant and thrive in hot, dry, gravelly, or alkaline soils where they need no irrigation once established. Bees and butterflies mob the flowers throughout the long bloom season. The dried flower heads retain their metallic color and are excellent for everlasting flower arrangements. Combines beautifully with ornamental grasses, yarrows, and silvery-leafed plants.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–April. Amistad is a large salvia reaching 4–5 feet tall in zone 9 — allow ample space in the back of borders. It blooms from late spring through frost without deadheading, producing successive flushes of deep violet-purple flowers that are reliably the most intensely colored purple-violet available among summer sages. In zone 9 it may survive as a short-lived perennial in sheltered locations, though it often behaves as an annual. Take cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors as insurance.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Amistad Salvia blooms best without excessive fertilization; Amistad (Spanish for 'friendship') is a salvia hybrid raised by the late Argentine plantsman Hector Cattan, believed to be a cross involving Salvia guaranitica and Salvia gesneriiflora, producing large (4–5 foot), upright, extremely floriferous plants with deep violet-purple flowers of exceptional saturation — one of the most intensely colored blue-purple flowers available among summer-blooming plants of any kind. The tubular violet flowers with contrasting dark calyces are a premier hummingbird and swallowtail butterfly nectar source that attracts pollinators from significant distances. The color is genuinely impressive: a pure, saturated, gem-like violet that maintains its intensity through summer heat without fading, providing a bold, reliable color presence in the back of sunny borders from late spring through frost. Zone 9 gardeners in the Gulf South have embraced Amistad as one of the best large warm-season salvias available — its combination of size, intense color, heat tolerance, and continuous bloom fills the critical role of a dominant back-of-border plant through the entire summer season.

plant_note: Plant container specimens or offset pups in spring in very well-drained, rocky soil; amole is one of the most compact and easiest agaves for residential gardens — the relatively small size and lack of dangerous terminal spines make it more garden-friendly than many other agaves.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, rocky to gravelly, alkaline to neutral desert soil; amole (Agave schottii) is a compact, clustering agave native to the mountain slopes of Arizona and Sonora, distinctive for its narrow, linear leaves that lack the typical dangerous terminal spine of most agaves — making it one of the most garden-safe agaves for pathways and mixed plantings. The leaves have fine serrations along the margins but no sharp tip. Historically important to the Tohono O'odham people who used the saponin-rich leaves as soap (amole is the Spanish word for a soap plant) and harvested the roasted heart as food. Forms attractive dense rosettes that slowly spread by offsets; the tall flower spike appears after several years and is covered in fragrant yellow flowers. An excellent small-scale agave for dry gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Amur daylily is among the most cold-hardy species in the genus and blooms notably early, often the first daylily to flower in the garden each year.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and water well through the first season to establish. Native to the Russian Far East, Korea, Japan, and northern China, Hemerocallis middendorffii is a wild species daylily bearing clusters of fragrant, rich orange-yellow flowers held tightly atop relatively short, sturdy scapes well ahead of most modern daylily cultivars, typically opening in late spring to early summer. Its compact, clumping habit, cold hardiness, and early bloom time make it a useful species for extending the daylily season and for breeding programs, and it has been an important parent in the development of many early-flowering hybrid daylilies. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering, and expect the plant to seed itself modestly in favorable conditions since it is a true species rather than a sterile hybrid.

plant_note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; this is among the hardiest and most cold-tolerant Arisaema species, native to cool temperate forests of northeastern Asia.
directions: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Arisaema amurense is native to the cold forests of Manchuria, Korea, and the Russian Far East, giving it exceptional winter hardiness compared with many other jack-in-the-pulpit species, and it produces a green-and-white-striped spathe above deeply divided, five- to seven-part leaflets in mid-spring, followed by a spike of bright red berries in fall. Its cold tolerance makes it a good choice for northern woodland gardens where more tender Arisaema species struggle, and the fall berry display extends its season of interest well past bloom time.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Amur maackia tolerates a wide range of soil conditions including clay and is notably pH-adaptable for a legume. As a nitrogen-fixing tree, it improves soil fertility over time and requires little or no supplemental fertilizer once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Amur maackia is a genuinely underappreciated small to medium deciduous tree from the forests of northeastern China and Manchuria, valued primarily for blooming in July and August when almost no other trees are flowering — producing upright, dense racemes of small, white pea flowers with a delicate blue cast that are mildly fragrant and attractive to bees and other pollinators. The tree is a legume and fixes atmospheric nitrogen, gradually improving soil fertility. The foliage emerges in spring with a distinctive silvery-blue sheen as leaves unfurl (a reliable spring identification feature) and matures to dark glossy green through summer. The copper-brown, peeling bark on older specimens is ornamental year-round. Highly adaptable to urban conditions, clay soils, drought, and air pollution, and one of the hardiest flowering trees available (to zone 3). Closely related to Cladrastis (yellowwood) and with a similar leguminous form. An excellent, pest-resistant, four-season small street or garden tree that remains widely unknown outside specialist circles.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, dry, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; Anacacho orchid tree grows naturally on rocky limestone slopes and canyon walls of the Anacacho Mountains of southwest Texas and adjacent Mexico, adapted to thin, calcareous, dry soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; Anacacho orchid tree is a rare Texas native of rocky limestone canyon walls in the Anacacho Mountains of Kinney County, Texas — one of the most beautiful small native shrubs or small trees of the southwestern US. The flower display in spring is extraordinary for such a xeric plant — profuse, pure white, five-petaled, orchid-like flowers (the characteristic two-lobed leaf shape of all Bauhinia gives the entire genus the appearance of orchid plants) cover the shrub from tip to base. Unlike the tropical orchid trees widely planted in south Florida (B. purpurea, B. variegata), this species is hardy to about 15°F and adapted to dry, rocky, calcareous soils — making it far more practical for the Hill Country and Edwards Plateau. The characteristic bilobed leaf (like two fused circles) is distinctive and attractive. A rare and outstanding native ornamental.

common_name: Anastasia Chrysanthemum (Spider-Form Mum with Long Curling Petals)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Anastasia is a spider-form mum with long, curling ray florets, grown commercially in pink, bronze, lavender, white, and green.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; spider mums generally need more sun and staking support than compact garden mum types. Anastasia bears large, dramatic spider-form flowers with long, narrow, curling ray florets that give the bloom a fireworks-like, wispy appearance, sold commercially in pink, bronze, lavender, white, and green color forms and grown chiefly for cutting rather than garden display. Stake plants to support the tall stems and heavy flower heads, and disbud side buds if larger, showier terminal blooms are the goal.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in zone 6–9; Anceps Bamboo is a moderate-sized, cold-hardy, clumping or slowly spreading bamboo native to the Himalayan foothills of northwestern India (Simla Hills), producing slender, arching culms and fine-textured foliage in graceful, informal clumps — among the most shade-tolerant of the Yushania bamboos and suitable for woodland and partial-shade garden settings.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Yushania anceps spreads slowly by rhizomes but is not aggressively invasive — monitor spread and contain if desired with light trenching; excellent for woodland garden positions with filtered light. Yushania anceps (Anceps Bamboo or Indian Mountain Bamboo) is a medium-sized, clumping-to-slowly-spreading bamboo in the Yushania genus native to the temperate Himalayan foothills of northwestern India — particularly the Simla Hills (Himachal Pradesh) at elevations of 5,000–9,000 feet — where it grows in open montane forests, forest clearings, and hillside thickets. The culms are slender (0.5–1.5 inch diameter, 5–12 feet tall), gracefully arching, and clothed with numerous, fine, lance-shaped leaves that give the plant a delicate, soft-textured appearance. Yushania anceps occupies an intermediate growth category: more spreading than the strictly clumping Fargesia species but far less aggressive than most Phyllostachys runners — making it useful where a bamboo ground-cover effect is desired with controlled spread. It is among the more shade-tolerant of the Yushania group and performs well in light woodland or partial-shade garden positions. Hardier than many bamboos, tolerating temperatures well below zone 6 minimums when established in well-drained soil. An excellent, graceful bamboo for large-scale naturalistic or woodland garden settings.

plant_note: Root cuttings in late spring or plant after last frost; Andean sage grows as a tender perennial in zones 9–11 and can be overwintered indoors as a container plant in colder climates. It prefers well-drained, fertile soil and benefits from light fertilization during the growing season.
directions: Root cuttings in warm conditions and transplant to well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; Andean sage is one of the most extraordinary and unusual plants in the genus, producing a stark color contrast that stops visitors in their tracks: the flowers are an unusually deep, near-black navy-indigo color, emerging from large, pale jade-green calyces that make the dark flowers appear to float against a pale background — the visual effect is dramatic and completely unlike any other sage. The sticky, apple-scented foliage has white undersides and slightly viscid texture. Native to the Andean cloud forests of Peru, it blooms from late summer through fall and is reliably perennial in frost-free zones 9–11. The dark flowers and pale calyces are highly attractive to hummingbirds and make an excellent contrast with silver, gold, or pink companion plants.

plant_note: Site divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil along shaded streambanks or seepage slopes.
directions: Site divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil along shaded streambanks or seepage slopes, the moist montane forest settings where this Pacific Northwest native fern is naturally found from British Columbia into Oregon. Unusual among sword ferns, mature plants often produce small bulblets near the frond tips that can be pegged down to root and propagate new plants, a distinctive trait worth watching for. Its large, once-pinnate evergreen fronds make it a good companion for lady fern and deer fern in cool, damp woodland plantings.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into sun; Anemone clematis is an exceptionally vigorous, large climber and needs a sturdy, spacious support such as a large arbor, pergola, or fence.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to partial shade on a large, sturdy support; Anemone clematis is one of the most vigorous of all clematis species, capable of quickly covering an arbor, pergola, or fence with a dense curtain of growth and, in mid to late spring, an overwhelming flush of four-petaled, anemone-like flowers in white or soft pink, often fragrant, produced in such profusion that the entire vine can appear smothered in bloom for several weeks. It flowers on the previous year's growth, so it belongs to the group of clematis that should be pruned, if needed, immediately after flowering rather than in late winter — pruning in winter removes the wood that would have flowered that spring. Because of its size and vigor, give it ample space and a support strong enough to bear its eventual weight; it is not well suited to small trellises or delicate structures. Once established it is a tough, long-lived, relatively low-maintenance vine, though it prefers cooler summers and can struggle with the most intense Gulf Coast heat and humidity.

common_name: Angel Cheeks Peony (Fragrant Bomb-Type Soft Blush Pink)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Angel Cheeks is a fragrant bomb-type double peony in soft blush pink.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Angel Cheeks bears large, tightly domed bomb-form flowers in soft, gentle blush pink with a sweet fragrance, the rounded petaloid center rising from a ring of broader outer guard petals in the classic bomb form. Its soft color and fragrance make it a favorite for cutting and for scenting a spring garden. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist perlite year-round; in zones 10–11 grow as an outdoor perennial shrub; in colder zones grow as a houseplant or move outdoors to shaded spots in summer.
directions: Root stem cuttings with at least two nodes in water or moist perlite — they root reliably within 2–3 weeks. Angel wing begonias are cane-stemmed begonias grown for their large, wing-shaped leaves (often spotted white on dark green surfaces) and pendulous clusters of coral-red to pink flowers that appear repeatedly from spring through fall. Unlike tuberous or wax begonias, they grow as shrubby upright plants 2–4 feet tall and are true perennials in frost-free climates. They prefer bright indirect light and well-drained potting mix kept evenly moist. Repot when roots fill the container; pinch tips to control height and encourage bushiness. Remove spent flower clusters to maintain a tidy appearance.

common_name: Angel Wings Caladium (Linden's Caladium, White Vein Caladium, Xanthosoma Lindenii)
plant_note: Plant tubers 1–2 inches deep in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Caladium lindenii (also placed in Xanthosoma as X. lindenii) produces large, dramatic leaves in deep forest-green with strongly contrasting brilliant white veins forming a bold, graphic pattern — the primary midrib and major lateral veins are white to silvery-white, standing out vividly against the dark green blade. A different plant from the common hybrid caladiums (C. × hortulanum) — larger-leaved and producing more permanent, year-round foliage in zone 10-12 warm conditions. Protect from temperatures below 55°F; store tubers in warm conditions through winter in zone 9. CAUTION: toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Angel Wings Caladium is one of the most boldly patterned shade ornamentals available, producing large leaves with a striking, graphic pattern of brilliant white veins on deep green that is immediately eye-catching even in low-light conditions. Caladium lindenii (treated by some authorities as Xanthosoma lindenii) is a perennial, tuberous aroid in the Araceae family native to Colombia and Ecuador — distinct from the common hybrid caladiums (Caladium × hortulanum) grown from tubers as seasonal ornamentals, as C. lindenii is a larger, more permanent-growing species adapted to year-round cultivation in zone 10-12. The plant produces erect petioles bearing large (12–18 inch), broadly ovate to arrowhead-shaped leaf blades in deep, dark, forest-green. The most striking feature is the venation: the primary midrib and major lateral veins are a vivid, brilliant white to ivory-white, several millimeters wide, forming a bold geometric pattern across the dark green leaf surface — the pattern is so strongly contrasting that each leaf appears to have been painted with bright white brushstrokes against the dark ground. The white-on-dark pattern maximizes light reflection in the low-light conditions of its tropical forest floor habitat. In zone 10-12 outdoor gardens, it can be planted in deeply shaded positions as a permanent, boldly architectural shade groundcover or accent. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

plant_note: Divide established corms carefully in late spring when just barely in growth, or plant container-grown plants in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; dierama establishes slowly and resents disturbance — newly divided plants may take 2-3 years to flower. Plants grown from seed take 3-5 years to bloom. Give well-drained but consistently moist soil; dierama dislikes both drought and waterlogging.
