directions: Plant in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; angel's fishing rod produces some of the most gracefully beautiful flowers of any garden bulb — long, arching, wiry, thread-like stems that sway and dance in the slightest breeze, each stem bearing small, pendant, bell-shaped flowers in rose-pink, magenta, purple, or deep wine-red that hang from the arching tips like fishing lines. The stems are extremely slender and flexible, arising 4-7 feet above a clump of evergreen, rush-like, narrow leaves, and the combination of movement in the breeze and the pendant, jewel-like flowers creates an effect of extraordinary lightness and grace. The plant grows from corms that slowly multiply to form clumps, and established specimens are long-lived and imposing. Native to the mountain grasslands of South Africa (the Drakensberg and surrounding highlands), it requires deep, fertile, well-drained but consistently moist soil. It resents disturbance and establishes slowly but, once settled, is a magnificent garden presence. Best near water features where its reflection adds to the effect.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in part shade to full sun; angel's tears needs excellent drainage and dislikes wet conditions, especially in summer dormancy. It is native to the rocky, thin soils of the Iberian Peninsula. Established plants self-seed freely in suitable well-drained conditions. The triandrus group of hybrid daffodils ('Thalia', 'Ice Wings') derives from this species.
directions: Plant small bulbs in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, gritty soil in part shade to full sun; angel's tears is a miniature daffodil species from Spain and Portugal named for its distinctive flower form — the small, nodding, pure-white to cream-white flowers (1–3 per stem, held at a drooping angle as if bowing) each have reflexed outer petals that sweep backward as in a cyclamen flower, and a small, neat, rounded cup at the center, the whole creating an impression of shy, nodding delicacy that gives rise to the common name. The backward-swept petals and nodding, pendant pose are completely distinctive among commonly grown daffodils; no hybrid can quite replicate the graceful, tearful quality of the species. The flowers appear in early spring, usually before the garden daffodils are fully open, in masses of 1–3 nodding, cream-white flowers per stem. It naturalizes slowly but steadily in very well-drained, rocky or sandy garden soils, building colonies of the quiet, nodding white flowers under light-canopy trees in early spring. The parentage of the important Triandrus hybrid daffodil group — including the beloved white 'Thalia' and 'Ice Wings' — making this species the direct ancestor of some of the finest daffodils in cultivation.

plant_note: Plant rooted hardwood cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; angel's trumpets are heavy feeders and heavy drinkers — they require frequent watering and regular fertilization to produce the large, lush growth and abundant blooms they are capable of. All parts of the plant are highly toxic — do not grow where children or pets may ingest any part.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; angel's trumpet is among the most spectacular flowering plants in temperate-tropical horticulture, producing enormous (10–20 inch) pendulous trumpet-shaped flowers in white, yellow, peach, pink, or salmon that hang gracefully downward and fill the air with an intoxicating fragrance, particularly in the evening and night. With adequate water and nutrition, a well-established plant can produce 50–100 blooms simultaneously at peak season. Brugmansia is distinguished from Datura by its pendulous (not erect) flowers and woody, tree-like habit. All parts of the plant are extremely toxic — containing tropane alkaloids including scopolamine, atropine, and hyoscyamine — and should never be grown where children or pets may contact or ingest any part. In zone 8 it may die back in hard winters but regrows from established roots; in zone 9–11 it is evergreen and can be trained as a small tree. Propagate from 12-inch hardwood cuttings placed directly in moist soil.

common_name: Angel's Trumpet (White Angel's Trumpet, Moonflower Tree, Toé)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun to partial shade with consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Brugmansia suaveolens grows rapidly in zone 9 and can reach 8–15 feet in one season. In zone 9a, plants may be killed to the ground by hard frost but resprout vigorously from the root crown in spring. In zone 9b-10, it grows as a large evergreen shrub or small tree. Feed regularly with a balanced fertilizer during the growing season for maximum flower production. Propagate from stem cuttings. CAUTION: All parts are extremely toxic — wear gloves when handling.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Angel's Trumpet grows most vigorously and flowers most heavily in full sun with adequate moisture and fertilization, but appreciates afternoon shade in zone 9 to prevent wilting of the large leaves during peak summer heat. Brugmansia suaveolens is a large, fast-growing soft-stemmed shrub or small tree from the Atlantic rainforest of Brazil in the Solanaceae family, extinct in the wild but widely cultivated throughout the tropical and subtropical world. The plant produces some of the largest and most dramatically beautiful flowers in the plant kingdom: enormous pendulous trumpets 12–18 inches long hanging downward in a cascade of pristine white (in the species) or in various shades of pink, yellow, orange, and peach in cultivars. The flowers are intensely and penetratingly fragrant, especially at dusk and through the night — a sweet, heavy, tropical perfume that carries for remarkable distances on still evenings. In zone 9, a well-established Angel's Trumpet in full bloom may carry dozens to over a hundred simultaneous flowers — a spectacular display. The plant was a sacred ceremonial and medicinal plant to indigenous peoples throughout South and Central America. EXTREME CAUTION: All parts of all Brugmansia species — flowers, leaves, seeds, roots, sap — contain potent tropane alkaloids (hyoscine, hyoscyamine, atropine) causing severe anticholinergic toxicity in humans and animals; fatalities have been recorded.

plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Angelface was bred for larger flowers and a more compact, uniform habit than seed-grown angelonia, and it thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf South summers when most other bedding annuals fade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, and expect vigorous, heat-proof performance right through the hottest, most humid stretch of summer when many bedding plants stall. Angelface is a vegetatively propagated angelonia series bred for notably larger, snapdragon-like flower spikes and a denser, more uniform mounding habit than older seed-grown angelonia, blooming continuously from spring through frost in shades of blue, purple, pink, and white without deadheading. Its exceptional heat and humidity tolerance, along with resistance to the diseases that trouble many summer annuals in wet conditions, has made it one of the most reliable performers for Gulf South beds, borders, and containers through the peak of summer. Pinch young plants once to encourage bushier growth, and feed regularly through the season to sustain the heavy bloom.

common_name: Angelina Sedum (Glowing Gold Needle-Leaf Groundcover Stonecrop)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Angelina spreads quickly into a dense, low mat and roots readily from broken stem pieces, making it easy to propagate and fill in bare, dry, sunny spots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun. Angelina is one of the most widely planted groundcover sedums, forming a dense, low, spreading mat of needle-like, bright chartreuse-gold foliage that takes on warm orange-red tones in cold weather, giving strong seasonal color change in a low-maintenance planting. It spreads quickly by rooting along its trailing stems, making it useful for covering dry slopes, edging pathways, spilling over retaining walls, or filling gaps between pavers, and broken stem pieces root readily wherever they touch soil. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and needs essentially no supplemental care beyond occasional trimming to keep it within bounds.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Angelique blooms late in the tulip season with large, ruffled, peony-like double flowers on stems that may need some shelter from wind given the heavy flower heads.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from strong wind, since the large double flower heads can be heavy. Angelique is one of the most romantic and widely loved tulip cultivars, producing soft blush-pink, densely ruffled, peony-like double blooms that look more like a garden rose than a typical tulip, often with subtle deeper pink and cream streaking. It flowers late in the tulip season and is a favorite for both garden display and cut-flower arrangements, prized for its unusually long vase life among tulips. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Start seeds on the surface of a moist, fine-textured germination mix at 70–75°F; seeds need light to germinate so do not cover. Transplant into full sun after last frost, spacing 12–18 in apart in well-drained soil enriched with compost. Angelonia is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and rarely needs deadheading, as spent florets drop cleanly. Pinch stem tips early to encourage branching and a fuller plant shape.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring at the base of a trellis, shrub, or tree that will support the vine's twining growth; sow seeds 1 inch deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade and keep the area consistently moist until germination.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in spring at the base of a fence, trellis, or woody shrub in partial shade with moist, humus-rich soil, providing a support structure immediately so the twining stems can climb as they emerge. Anglepod milkvine is a native perennial of southeastern US woodlands, thicket edges, and streamside clearings, producing star-shaped, greenish-white flowers in the milkweed family that are followed by distinctively angled, warty seed pods splitting to release silky-plumed seeds in late summer. As a member of the milkweed family, it serves as a larval host plant for monarch butterflies and queen butterflies alongside true milkweeds, making it a valuable addition to wildlife gardens in shaded or woodland-edge sites where common milkweed does not thrive. The vine dies back to a perennial rootstock each winter and re-emerges reliably in spring; avoid disturbing the root zone once plants are established.

plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper or soak in hot water before sowing directly in warm soil after last frost; in zone 9, this can be treated as a fast-growing warm-season annual that self-seeds in frost-free winters. Grows best in lean, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, even sandy soil in full sun in frost-free or warm winter climates; anil indigo is a tropical American shrub historically cultivated as one of the primary sources of natural indigo dye — the leaves are harvested and fermented in water to extract the blue pigment indigotin, which was the world's most important natural blue dye before synthetic indigo was developed in the 1880s. It naturalized throughout the warm coastal Southeast after Spanish and French colonial plantations, and still grows spontaneously in disturbed areas of Florida and the Gulf Coast. In zone 9, it often behaves as a self-seeding annual or short-lived perennial; in zone 10 and warmer it is a true woody perennial. The small pink-lavender flowers in drooping racemes bloom repeatedly. Yields the same dye compound as the Asian species I. tinctoria.

common_name: Anise Sage (Black and Blue Sage, Brazilian Sage)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Salvia guaranitica is reliably perennial in zone 7–11 from tuberous roots that overwinter underground — established clumps grow larger and more floriferous each year.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; anise sage is one of the finest hummingbird plants for Gulf Coast gardens — the cultivar 'Black and Blue' in particular is prized for its deep, vivid cobalt-blue flowers held in glossy black calyces, producing a stunning color combination that is a magnet for rubythroated hummingbirds from summer through frost. The large, heart-shaped leaves are aromatic when crushed. In zone 7–11 it grows as a perennial from tuberous roots, with top growth dying back after frost and resprouts from established tubers in spring, often growing 4–5 feet tall and wide by midsummer. It spreads by underground stolons to form a substantial colony over time. Cut plants to the ground in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth. Other cultivars include 'Costa Rica Blue' (deeper blue, cooler tones) and 'Argentine Skies' (pale sky-blue).

common_name: Ann Chowning Louisiana Iris (Historic White Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in early fall in humus-rich, constantly moist soil so roots establish before the spring bloom flush; this classic white-flowered selection is part of the historic Chowning breeding line of Louisiana irises.
directions: Set rhizomes just below the soil surface in a bog bed, rain garden, or pond margin with rich organic soil, since Louisiana irises perform best with abundant moisture during spring growth. Ann Chowning produces clean white blooms with a bright yellow signal in mid-spring and is prized for naturalizing in the wet, humid conditions typical of Gulf Coast gardens. Feed lightly in late winter as growth resumes, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor. Reduce watering somewhat in the dormant summer period if grown outside standing water.

common_name: Ann Dasch Siberian Iris (Mottled Light Blue-Purple over Solid Deeper Blue-Purple)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ann Dasch bears mottled light blue-purple standards over solid deeper blue-purple falls, blooming midseason to late.
directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ann Dasch bears mottled light blue-purple standards over solid, deeper blue-purple falls, a subtly two-toned pattern that blooms midseason to late, extending the Siberian iris flowering window later than many earlier-blooming cultivars, over narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Ann Folkard Hardy Geranium (Magenta Black-Eyed Trailing Cranesbill)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ann Folkard has an unusually sprawling, trailing habit compared to most mounding hardy geranium cultivars, useful for scrambling through companion plants.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in hot climates. Ann Folkard is a distinctive hardy geranium with a long, sprawling, trailing habit rather than the tidy mound of most cultivars, sending out long stems that scramble through and over neighboring plants, studded with vivid magenta flowers marked by a bold black center from late spring through summer. Its foliage emerges chartreuse-yellow in spring, especially in a sunnier position, gradually greening as the season progresses, adding a second layer of color interest beyond the flowers. Its scrambling habit makes it useful for weaving through shrub borders or draping over a wall, though it can be cut back hard if it spreads further than wanted. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Ann magnolia blooms later than star magnolia, helping its flowers dodge late spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering magnolias.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Ann magnolia blooms later than star magnolia, helping its flowers dodge late spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering magnolias. One of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later, frost-dodging bloom, it produces rich reddish-purple, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact, shrubby, multi-stemmed plant well suited to smaller gardens where full-sized magnolia trees would be too large. Its later flowering window, roughly two to four weeks after star magnolia, gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts, which often blacken and ruin the flowers of earlier-blooming cultivars. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally, since magnolias generally need little pruning beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

plant_note: Plant container-grown hellebores in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February. Hellebores prefer consistent growing locations and resent transplanting — choose the final planting site carefully, as established plants bloom better when left undisturbed for years. In zone 9 hellebores perform best in deep shade under deciduous trees where they receive winter sun (when leaves are off the tree) and summer shade (protecting from intense heat). Mulch heavily to maintain cool, moist root conditions in summer. Anna's Red flowers December–March in zone 9, providing winter garden interest when almost nothing else blooms.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral, consistently moist soil — hellebores require cool root conditions and good drainage to prevent crown rot; Anna's Red is a named Lenten rose hybrid (Helleborus x hybridus) selected for its deep, rich, plum-red to burgundy-red nodding flowers that appear in the depths of winter — blooming December through March in zone 9 when virtually nothing else in the garden is flowering. Hellebores are among the most valuable shade garden plants precisely for their timing: the large, nodding, cup-shaped flowers open during the coldest, darkest weeks of the growing year, providing garden interest and early pollinator forage for bumblebees venturing out on warm winter days. The evergreen, leathery, deeply cut dark green leaves provide year-round structure in shade gardens even when plants are not in bloom. Anna's Red, like other Helleborus x hybridus selections, is the result of hybridization work that intensified and diversified the color range of Lenten roses far beyond the limited pink-purple range of the wild species. The nodding flower habit (flowers face downward) is traditional for hellebores and requires getting low to the ground to fully appreciate the beautiful interior of the flower — a charming quirk that makes hellebore viewing an intimate garden experience.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Annabelle performs well in morning sun with afternoon shade in zone 9 — full sun in the Gulf South causes wilting and bleaching, while deep shade reduces flower production.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Annabelle is the most famous and most widely planted smooth hydrangea cultivar — a native American species selected for its exceptionally large, pure-white, snowball-like flower heads that can reach 12 inches or more in diameter and weigh enough to bend the stems dramatically in rain. Annabelle was selected from a specimen found growing wild near Anna, Illinois, and has been in continuous cultivation since the 1960s. The extraordinarily large, spherical flower heads in brilliant white are one of the great spectacles of the summer garden in shade — there is almost nothing else that produces flower heads of this size in partial to full shade. Annabelle blooms on new wood, meaning it can be cut back hard each spring (to 12 inches) and will still flower the same season — unlike old-wood bloomers that lose flowers if cut incorrectly. This makes it nearly foolproof: any pruning approach that removes old stems in late winter produces abundant bloom. In zone 9, Annabelle blooms from May through July and handles summer heat in partial shade better than Hydrangea macrophylla. The flowers dry beautifully on the plant, transitioning from fresh white to paper-white to soft tan as they age through summer into fall. Divide or transplant in fall after dormancy.

plant_note: Succession sow every few weeks for continuous bloom.
directions: Sow annual candytuft directly in early spring, making successive sowings every few weeks for a long season of bloom. The flat clusters of white, pink, and purple flowers are fragrant and attract bees and butterflies. Grow in full sun and average well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to prevent crowding. Shear plants after flowering to keep them tidy and encourage a second flush.

plant_note: Sow directly; resents transplanting due to taproot.
directions: Direct sow annual mallow after the last frost, as it forms a taproot and resents transplanting. The large satiny hibiscus-like blooms in shades of pink and white appear all summer on bushy plants. Provide full sun and moderately fertile, well-drained soil, spacing generously for good air circulation. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and deadhead to keep the display fresh.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; transplant is also possible starting 6–8 weeks early indoors.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 in deep and cover lightly, as darkness can aid germination. Annual phlox prefers cool growing conditions and puts on its best show in spring and early summer. Deadhead spent clusters regularly to prevent seed set and keep flowers coming. In hot climates, plants may slow in midsummer heat; cut back and they will often rebloom as temperatures cool in fall.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has completely passed.
directions: Sow seed on the surface of moist starting mix, barely pressing in, as light aids germination. Grow on under bright light to prevent tall, weak seedlings before transplanting. Remove spent spikes at their base to encourage a continuous succession of new flower stems. Annual salvia blooms from early summer until the first hard frost.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring onto sandy or shelly ground in full sun near the salt line; this small annual succulent completes its life cycle in one warm season and readily reseeds itself on bare, salty ground each year.
directions: Scatter seed directly onto sandy or shelly, saline soil in full sun and keep lightly moist only until seedlings establish; this small, fleshy-leaved annual is the shorter-lived cousin of the more familiar trailing sea purslane and naturally colonizes the upper edges of salt flats, brackish pond margins, and open sandy beach soil along the Gulf. Its thick reddish stems and tiny pink flowers form a low mat that tolerates salinity most garden plants cannot survive, so it earns a place at the salty, sun-baked fringe of a coastal planting bed where nothing else will grow. Because it is a true annual, expect it to complete its cycle and drop seed within a single hot Gulf Coast summer, then return the following year from that seed bank.

plant_note: Direct sow onto bare, salty mud or sand at the marsh-upland border after the danger of frost has passed; this species self-seeds readily once established.
directions: This slender, succulent-leaved annual colonizes bare salt pans, marsh borders, and the upper edge of salt marshes where salinity is too high for most other plants, turning reddish-purple in fall as it sets seed. Sow directly onto disturbed saline soil in full sun; it needs no irrigation beyond natural rainfall and actually performs best on the driest, saltiest microsites in a planting. Because it is a true annual, expect it to die back each winter and reseed the following spring in undisturbed soil. Use it as a pioneer species on newly created or restored marsh edges alongside glasswort and saltwort, where its fibrous roots help hold bare salt-flat soil before perennial cordgrass fills in.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 in deep in moist starting mix; refrigerate seeds for 5–7 days before sowing to improve germination rates. Transplant after the last frost date into well-drained soil, as verbena is very susceptible to root rot in wet conditions. Shear plants back by one-third in midsummer if they become leggy to stimulate a fresh flush of bloom. Verbena thrives in heat and is drought tolerant once established.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant only when nights are consistently above 55°F.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in warm, moist starting mix and maintain soil temperature above 75°F for best germination. Annual vinca is self-cleaning and requires no deadheading, shedding spent blooms on its own. It excels in summer heat and humidity and is highly drought tolerant. Avoid planting in cold or wet soil, as chilling causes the foliage to yellow and growth to stall.

plant_note: Direct sow at last frost in dry, lean, well-drained sandy or rocky soil in full sun; self-sows reliably in open disturbed ground.
directions: Annual Wild Buckwheat is a strongly upright native annual of dry, open prairies, roadsides, and rocky or sandy plains throughout the Great Plains and south-central US. It produces dense, woolly-white, branching flower clusters of tiny white to cream-white flowers from July through October on stout stems with white-hairy, oblong basal leaves. The dense flower heads and seeds are outstanding food sources for goldfinches, sparrows, and native bees. Direct sow in spring in dry, lean, well-drained sandy or rocky soil in full sun — this species self-sows reliably and thrives in disturbed ground with minimal care.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun; antelope horns has a large taproot that makes it drought tolerant once established but very difficult to transplant — direct sowing in its permanent location is strongly preferred.
directions: Direct sow in fall in rocky, alkaline, or sandy, well-drained, dry soil in full sun — antelope horns is the iconic native milkweed of the Texas Hill Country, southern prairies, and Chihuahuan Desert, producing clusters of unusual, intricate flowers with green-white petals reflexed back to expose greenish-maroon hoods, giving the flower cluster an otherworldly appearance. The large, broad, horizontally spreading leaves are gray-green and waxy; the paired seed pods curve upward like antelope horns, full of silky-plumed seeds in late summer. It is one of the most important early-season monarch butterfly host and nectar plants in Texas, as it emerges and blooms in spring before other milkweeds are available during the critical spring migration period. Antelope horns is a deep-rooted perennial of great drought tolerance and longevity — once established in adapted caliche, limestone gravel, or dry clay it requires virtually no care or supplemental water and lives for decades.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; antelope horns milkweed develops a deep taproot and strongly resents transplanting — select a permanent location and sow in place, allowing seeds to cold-stratify naturally over winter for spring germination.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy, loamy, or gravelly soil in full sun; antelope horns milkweed develops a deep, fleshy taproot early in life and is extremely difficult to transplant successfully — choose a permanent site from the start and sow seeds in place, pressing them lightly into the soil surface. Asclepias asperula is a low, spreading native milkweed of the Southwest and Gulf Coast from Kansas and Oklahoma south through Texas and into New Mexico, growing in dry prairies, rocky hillsides, and open roadsides; it produces clusters of distinctive greenish-white flowers with purple to maroon markings from April through June, held at or just above the sprawling, rough-textured foliage — the curved, horn-like follicle pods that split to release silky-plumed seeds inspired the common name. It is one of the earliest-blooming milkweeds in its range and is a critical early-season host plant for monarch butterfly larvae and an important nectar source for migrating monarchs in spring; queen butterflies also use it as a larval host. Once established in appropriate lean, dry conditions, antelope horns milkweed is exceptionally drought-tolerant, long-lived, and essentially maintenance-free — avoid rich soils or regular irrigation, which will shorten its life.

common_name: Antenna Orchid (Trigger Orchid, Scorpion Orchid, Antennifera Restrepia)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered light in small pots of fine bark or sphagnum moss-bark mix in a cool to intermediate location; Restrepia antennifera is a cool-growing orchid from high-altitude Colombian cloud forests (5,000–9,000 feet) that prefers cooler temperatures (day 65–75°F, night 50–60°F). Excellent terrarium orchid — the small size and preference for high humidity (70%+) make it ideal for enclosed humid conditions. The leaves produce plantlets (keikis) at the leaf tips that can be detached and rooted. Blooms sequentially through most of the year. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered light in cool, humid conditions — Antenna Orchid is a miniature cloud forest orchid that grows most happily in the cool, high-humidity conditions of a terrarium or cool shaded porch and will decline in hot, dry summer conditions. Restrepia antennifera is a tiny, sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to the high-altitude cloud forests of Colombia and Venezuela in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most popular miniature orchids for terrarium culture for the extraordinary appearance of its flowers. The plant is very small — barely 4–8 inches tall — with a single, broadly oval, thick, leathery leaf per stem. But the flowers produced from the leaf base are visually extraordinary: the two lateral sepals are broad, fused along their inner margins into a single, deflexed 'synsepal' structure in yellow-orange to orange-red with contrasting purple-red veining and spotting — forming the lower visible portion of the flower. The two upper petals are highly modified into extremely long, thin, thread-like structures terminating in slightly thickened, warty, club-shaped tips — the 'antennae' that give the plant its common name and that wave gently in air movement. The lip is small and attached to the moveable column in a trigger mechanism related to pollinator deception. Restrepia antennifera produces flowers sequentially from the same leaf nodes, providing months of bloom from a small plant. An outstanding miniature orchid for terrarium culture. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Anthony Waterer blooms on new wood — shear to 6–8 inches in late winter or very early spring to stimulate maximum new growth and flower production.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Anthony Waterer is the classic carmine-rose Japanese spiraea cultivar — one of the oldest and most widely grown selections of Spiraea japonica, introduced before 1884 and still among the most popular compact summer-blooming shrubs in American horticulture. The flat-topped, 3–4 inch flower clusters are a rich carmine-rose to deep rose-pink color from June through August (in zone 7–8), with peak bloom lasting 4–6 weeks followed by scattered repeat bloom if sheared lightly after the first flush. As with all Japanese spiraea cultivars, Anthony Waterer blooms on new wood — shear the entire plant hard to 6–8 inches in late winter or very early spring to stimulate vigorous new growth and produce the densest possible flower coverage. An established plant that is not sheared becomes leggy and produces fewer flowers; annual hard pruning is the most important maintenance practice for this species. Anthony Waterer grows to 3–4 feet tall and wide with a neat, rounded, mounding form that requires virtually no pruning to maintain shape beyond the annual renewal shearing. The new growth often emerges with distinctive cream and pink variegation, maturing to green. The plant is exceptionally adaptable — tolerating clay soil, heat, drought, and urban conditions throughout zone 9.

plant_note: Plant in very well-drained, chunky, humus-rich, acidic epiphytic mix (orchid bark, perlite, and peat) in bright indirect light or deep shade; anthurium roots require excellent air circulation and will rot in dense, waterlogged soil. Keep roots slightly elevated if possible for best drainage.
directions: Plant in chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix in bright indirect light to deep shade — anthurium produces some of the most striking and long-lasting of all tropical flowers, with waxy, heart-shaped spathes in red, pink, white, coral, or burgundy surrounding a contrasting spadix, each spathe remaining attractive for 2–3 months. It is one of the most popular tropical houseplants worldwide and the most important cut flower in Hawaii's floriculture industry. As a garden plant in zone 10–12, it thrives in the deep shade of trees and covered patios, exactly where little else grows. The glossy, dark green leaves are themselves ornamental. It is sensitive to direct sun (which burns the leaves), overwatering, and temperatures below 55°F. In zone 9a it is an outstanding container plant for shaded patios, wintering indoors. Keep soil moderately moist and fertilize lightly every 6 weeks.

plant_note: Sow feathery-tailed seed in fall or set out nursery plants in fall to early spring into very well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Apache plume is native to dry washes and mesas of the desert Southwest and Great Basin.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Apache plume is a semi-evergreen Southwestern native shrub with small, deeply lobed leaves and a long, nearly continuous bloom of single, white, rose-like flowers from spring through fall. Each flower is followed by a distinctive cluster of pinkish, feathery, plumed seed tails that persist alongside the next flush of blooms, giving the shrub a two-toned, constantly changing appearance of white flowers and dusty-pink plumes at the same time. It is exceptionally drought, heat, and cold tolerant once established, thriving in the same lean, fast-draining, low-fertility soils that support native sagebrush and juniper communities. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain an open, airy form, and avoid rich soil or frequent irrigation, which produces lanky, less floriferous growth.

common_name: Apeldoorn Tulip (Classic Large Red Darwin Hybrid Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Apeldoorn is one of the most widely planted Darwin hybrid tulips, known for large flowers on sturdy, tall stems that hold up well to wind and rain.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Apeldoorn is a classic Darwin hybrid tulip, a group bred for extra-large flowers on strong, tall stems, producing bright, clear scarlet-red blooms that have made it one of the most commercially planted tulip cultivars in the world for mass displays and cut flowers. Darwin hybrids like Apeldoorn also tend to perennialize somewhat better than many other tulip types in climates with adequate winter chill, though in mild-winter zone 8-9 gardens they are still usually most reliable treated as a fresh fall planting.

common_name: Aphrodite Rose of Sharon (Deep Pink Red-Eyed Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Aphrodite bears large, single, deep rose-pink flowers with a prominent dark red eye at the center, a bold, saturated color combination that reads clearly from a distance, blooming heavily from midsummer into fall. It is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection, setting little seed compared to old-fashioned rose of sharon and avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with seed-grown plants, while remaining a tough, heat- and humidity-tolerant shrub. It requires little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and encourage the current season's flowering wood.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; the apothecary rose is one of the oldest roses in continuous cultivation, historically grown for medicinal and culinary petal use.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the apothecary rose is a compact, suckering, semi-double, deep pink to crimson rose grown in European monastery and apothecary gardens for centuries for its intensely fragrant petals, historically dried for medicinal preparations, potpourri, and rosewater, and famous as the heraldic Red Rose of Lancaster. It blooms once in late spring in a heavy, richly perfumed flush, followed by small orange-red hips that add fall interest if left unpruned. Own-root plants sucker readily to form a dense thicket over time, which can be an asset for an informal hedge or a nuisance in a tightly maintained border, so plan its placement with that spreading habit in mind. It is remarkably disease-resistant and cold-hardy compared to modern hybrid roses, needing only routine deadwood removal after its single bloom flush rather than the intensive spraying and pruning modern roses often require.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring into moist, rocky, slightly acidic soil in a partial-shade woodland setting; firm seed lightly into surface as light aids germination.
directions: Campanula divaricata is a delicate native bellflower of the Appalachian Mountains and upper Piedmont, producing airy, branching stems covered in tiny (1/3-inch), nodding, pale lavender-blue bells from July through September that are excellent for long-season color in shaded rock gardens. It grows in moist to dry rocky woodland slopes and cliff bases in slightly acidic soil. Bees and butterflies work the flowers for nectar. Self-seeds moderately without becoming invasive; combine with ferns, coral bells, and native gingers for a layered shade garden.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; Appalachian bugbane has a very restricted natural range in shaded gorges and moist ravines in the central Appalachians (TN, NC, KY, AL) and is a rare but stunning native for large shaded gardens.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, deep, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Appalachian bugbane (formerly Cimicifuga rubifolia) has a very restricted natural range in shaded gorges, moist ravines, and rich mesic slopes in Tennessee, North Carolina, Kentucky, and Alabama, making it one of the rarest and most conservation-significant native garden plants. It is closely related to the widely grown Actaea racemosa (black cohosh) and produces similar dramatic, arching, bottle-brush spikes of tiny white flowers on stems 4–6 feet tall in late summer and fall above bold, compound foliage, but is distinguished by its leaf shape — the leaflets are broader and more coarsely toothed, resembling those of a raspberry, hence the species name rubifolia. It is a magnificent specimen plant for large, shaded native gardens; purchase only nursery-propagated stock and never collect from the wild, as natural populations are small and threatened. Long-lived and deer-resistant once established.

plant_note: Plant rhizome/corm divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland or meadow soil in partial shade to full sun; Appalachian bunchflower grows naturally in rich mountain woodlands and moist mountain meadows and tolerates more shade than M. virginicum.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Appalachian bunchflower (Melanthium hybridum) is closely related to Virginia bunchflower (M. virginicum) but differs in growing primarily in rich, moist Appalachian mountain woodlands and forest margins rather than coastal plain wet meadows, and in bearing leaves that are somewhat wider and more variable — the name 'hybridum' reflects the morphological variability of the species rather than hybrid origin. It produces the same stately, grass-clump form and tall summer flowering stems 3–5 feet tall topped with large panicles of cream-to-greenish-white flowers that age purple, providing a dramatic vertical accent in the shaded native garden. Less commercially available than M. virginicum but worth seeking from Appalachian native plant nurseries for its superior shade tolerance and ornamental appeal in forested garden settings. All parts are toxic; handle with gloves.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Appalachian Red is grown for its unusually vivid magenta-red spring flower color, a distinct break from the softer pink-lavender of the straight species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Appalachian Red is a North Carolina State University introduction selected for exceptionally vivid, deep magenta-red flowers that bloom on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, standing out sharply from the softer pink-lavender tones of the wild species and from the more common purple-leafed and pink-flowered cultivars already popular in the nursery trade. Green, heart-shaped summer foliage and a classic small-tree vase shape follow the spring flower display, with attractive yellow fall color. Like other redbuds it is a valuable, adaptable native flowering tree for the understory or edge of a woodland garden, tolerating a good range of soil types as long as drainage is adequate, since redbud roots are susceptible to rot in wet, poorly drained sites. It performs well as a specimen tree, in a mixed native shrub-and-tree border, or naturalized at a woodland edge where its striking bloom color provides one of the most vivid early-spring accents in a partly shaded Southern garden.

common_name: Appalachian Rosinweed (Cumberland Plateau Endemic Large-Leaf Silphium)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Appalachian Rosinweed is a Cumberland Plateau (Kentucky, Tennessee) endemic with large basal leaves, rarely seen in cultivation outside its native region.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to light partial shade; established plants tolerate drought well thanks to a deep taproot typical of the genus. Appalachian Rosinweed is a regional endemic restricted to the Cumberland Plateau of Kentucky and Tennessee, bearing large, coarse basal leaves and tall flowering stalks topped with bright yellow, sunflower-like composite blooms in summer, a rarely cultivated species that offers valuable genetic and regional diversity for native plant gardens within its home range. Like other Silphium species, its flowers draw specialist bees and other pollinators, and the seed heads that follow feed goldfinches and other birds. It is exceptionally long-lived and low-maintenance once established, resenting transplant once the taproot is set.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Appalachian sedge is slow to establish but very long-lived once settled — allow 1–2 growing seasons for full establishment and spreading. It naturalizes readily from seed in suitable conditions, forming expanding clumps that can eventually replace turf grass in shaded areas. In zone 9 it performs as a reliable, low-growing, semi-evergreen to evergreen ground cover. Unlike many sedges that require moist soil, Appalachian sedge tolerates dry shade under mature trees — one of its most valuable practical attributes.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained to dry, moderately fertile to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Appalachian sedge is native to dry woodland habitats and tolerates the difficult conditions of dry shade under mature trees; Appalachian sedge is a fine-textured, low-growing native sedge endemic to the Appalachian region and extending through the Gulf South, providing an ecologically appropriate, low-maintenance alternative to lawn grass or imported ground covers in shaded landscapes. The narrow, arching, bright green to yellow-green leaves form a low, graceful, grass-like mound 6–10 inches high that spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding to form a naturalistic, weed-suppressing ground cover under trees. As a native species adapted to the woodland understory of the Southeastern United States, Appalachian sedge supports native invertebrates and serves as a host plant for several native skipper butterflies, contributing ecological function along with aesthetic value. Unlike turf grass, Appalachian sedge requires no mowing, very little fertilization, and tolerates the dry shade and root competition under mature trees that eliminates conventional lawn alternatives — its primary competitive advantage as a practical garden plant. The low-growing, flowing texture provides a natural woodland floor aesthetic compatible with native shade tree and shrub plantings.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Appalachian Spring is the most disease-resistant Cornus florida cultivar — specifically selected for resistance to dogwood anthracnose (Discula destructiva), the devastating fungal disease that has killed millions of dogwood trees in the eastern US.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Appalachian Spring is the most significant disease-resistant flowering dogwood cultivar ever introduced — selected from wild dogwood populations in the Appalachian Mountains specifically for its outstanding resistance to dogwood anthracnose (Discula destructiva), the fungal disease that since the 1970s has killed millions of wild dogwood trees across the eastern United States and continues to devastate unresistant trees in humid forest conditions. Dogwood anthracnose causes branch dieback, water-soaked lesions, and can kill an entire tree within 2–3 years of infection — it is the primary reason dogwood populations have declined so dramatically in eastern American forests. Appalachian Spring was selected by the US National Arboretum through a program specifically aimed at finding anthracnose-resistant genotypes among surviving wild populations where the disease had been established for decades. The flower display is classic white Cornus florida — large, four-bracted, pure white flowers in March through April — combined with the full suite of ornamental qualities: excellent fall red color, attractive horizontal branching, and fall red berries for wildlife. In zone 9, Appalachian Spring performs similarly to other Cornus florida cultivars but offers insurance against the anthracnose that has become more of a concern in humid Gulf South conditions.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions very carefully in fall in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, undisturbed forest soil in deep shade; Appalachian twayblade depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi for establishment and is essentially impossible to grow without these fungal partners present in the native soil. Only plant in existing undisturbed woodland with intact organic duff layer.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, undisturbed woodland soil in deep shade with an intact organic duff layer; Appalachian twayblade is a diminutive native terrestrial orchid of cool, shaded, moist forest floors in the Appalachians and adjacent regions. The plant is distinguished by a single pair of opposite, rounded leaves (hence 'twayblade' — two-blade) at the base of a slender stem bearing tiny greenish flowers. Like all native terrestrial orchids, it depends entirely on specific soil fungi (mycorrhizae) for survival and cannot be successfully grown in sterilized or amended potting soil. The plant's best use in the landscape is simply protecting existing populations in undisturbed woodland rather than attempting cultivation. Listed in some states as a species of conservation concern due to woodland habitat loss. Grow only from ethically sourced, nursery-propagated stock.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist shade; cold stratification over winter improves germination. Plants bloom in their second year.
directions: Appendaged Waterleaf is a native biennial or short-lived perennial of the waterleaf family, found in moist, shaded deciduous woodlands and rich floodplain forests across the eastern and central United States. In its first year it produces a rosette of large, pinnately lobed, soft-hairy leaves often decorated with pale whitish mottling; in the second year it sends up branched stems topped with rounded clusters of tubular, pale lavender to white flowers with conspicuously long-exserted stamens that give the blooms a feathery, soft appearance in spring. Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, and allow the colony to self-sow for a self-sustaining planting. It is an underused native for shaded wild gardens and woodland restoration plantings in zones 3-8.

common_name: Apple Blossom Amaryllis (Soft Pink-and-White Bicolor Amaryllis)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Apple Blossom is one of the best-selling amaryllis cultivars, bearing soft pink-and-white bicolor flowers, and naturalizes in the ground as a permanent perennial in zone 8-10 gardens.
directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Apple Blossom is one of the most widely sold amaryllis cultivars, prized for large, softly blushed pink-and-white bicolor blooms that read as delicate and romantic compared with the bolder solid reds and whites of many other cultivars, produced on tall, sturdy stalks in spring. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, where it naturalizes and multiplies over the years into an increasingly impressive clump. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after bloom rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb for next year's flowers, and it can also be forced into bloom indoors as a classic holiday container amaryllis by planting with about a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix.

common_name: Apple Blossom Caladium (Pale Pink-and-White Speckled Fancy Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; plant an inch or two deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Apple Blossom bears pale pink-and-white leaves finely speckled with darker pink.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Apple Blossom bears large, heart-shaped leaves in a delicate pale pink-and-white blend finely speckled with deeper pink, edged in green, a softer, more pastel-toned fancy-leaf caladium than the bold reds many gardeners associate with the genus. It provides months of reliable, low-maintenance color in shaded beds, borders, and containers without needing flowers, pairing especially well with ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Apple Blossom Camellia (Soft Pink-and-White Bicolor Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Apple Blossom is a classic, long-grown japonica selection valued for its delicate two-tone flowers on an easy-care, adaptable shrub.
directions: Apple Blossom is a long-cultivated camellia japonica prized for its semi-double flowers, which open a soft blush pink toward the petal edges fading to nearly white at the center, giving a delicate two-tone effect reminiscent of a spring apple blossom. It blooms in mid-to-late winter through early spring on a medium-sized, upright, well-branched evergreen shrub with the same glossy dark foliage typical of camellia japonica, providing color in the landscape during a season when little else is flowering. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly to shape only right after flowering, since next season's buds set over the following summer.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring or fall; in zone 9 gardens bulbs can stay in the ground year-round and be left undisturbed to bulk up into flowering clumps.
directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; where winters stay above the mid-20s the bulbs can remain in the ground year-round without lifting. Appleblossom is a long-grown, old-fashioned amaryllis cultivar passed hand-to-hand through Southern gardens, prized for its soft blush-pink petals brushed with white toward the center — gentler and more romantic than the bold reds of many modern hybrids. Each stout stem carries several large trumpet blooms in mid-to-late spring, appearing before or alongside the strap-shaped foliage, and established clumps flower more heavily each year if left undisturbed. Divide only when a clump becomes crowded, replanting offsets right away since the bulbs resent being stored dry out of soil for long.

common_name: Applecourt Japanese Painted Fern (Crested Painted Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring once new growth is visible; Applecourt is a crested selection of Japanese painted fern, chosen for frond tips that split into decorative fan-like crests in addition to the species' typical silver, green, and burgundy coloring.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade; Applecourt is a crested selection of Japanese painted fern, meaning the tips of the fronds and pinnae split into small, decorative fan-shaped crests, giving the plant a more ornate texture than the straight species while retaining its signature silver, green, and burgundy frond coloring. The best color develops with some morning light, but foliage will fade or scorch in afternoon sun. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to keep the planting vigorous and to share starts. Remove spent fronds in late winter before new fiddleheads emerge, and protect newly planted divisions from slugs, which are drawn to the tender new growth.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost; prefers cool growing conditions.
directions: Sow Apricot Beauty calendula a quarter inch deep around the last frost, as cool soil suits germination. This heirloom pot marigold bears soft semi-double blooms in apricot, peach, and pale-gold tones on tidy plants. The edible, medicinal petals are lovely in salads and herbal preparations. Deadhead often to extend bloom, and expect a fresh flush as autumn cools.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors 4 weeks early.
directions: 'Apricotta' is an award-winning cosmos with soft apricot-pink blooms centered in yellow on tall, sturdy stems ideal for cutting. Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors about a month early, barely covering the seed. Grow in full sun in average to lean soil, as rich ground produces foliage rather than flowers. It is drought tolerant once established and blooms prolifically from midsummer to frost. Deadhead or cut regularly to keep the plants flowering and to attract bees and butterflies.

common_name: April Dawn Camellia (Cold-Hardy Variegated Ackerman Hybrid Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; April Dawn was bred for cold hardiness and blooms later than most japonica camellias, avoiding much of the flower bud damage from late-winter freezes common in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) in partial shade, and mulch well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Bred by Dr. William Ackerman at the U.S. National Arboretum as part of his cold-hardy camellia breeding program crossing Camellia japonica with the hardier C. oleifera, April Dawn produces large, formal double blooms of white heavily streaked and marbled with pink, opening in late winter to early spring on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its late bloom timing and improved cold hardiness compared to standard japonica camellias make it more reliable in the northern Gulf South and in years with a late hard freeze, since fewer flower buds are lost to cold damage. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape, and avoid heavy pruning in fall, which removes the developing flower buds.

common_name: April Snow Camellia (Cold-Hardy White Ackerman Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; April Snow is part of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy camellia breeding program at the U.S. National Arboretum, selected for reliable flowering and better winter hardiness than typical Camellia japonica.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and mulch well to protect shallow roots. April Snow is one of the cold-hardy camellia introductions from Dr. William Ackerman's breeding program at the U.S. National Arboretum, developed to extend reliable camellia flowering into colder parts of the Southeast and mid-Atlantic than standard Camellia japonica cultivars can tolerate. It produces medium, formal double white flowers in early spring on a dense, rounded evergreen shrub, with glossy dark green foliage that provides structure and screening year-round even when not in bloom. Feed lightly with an acid-forming azalea-camellia fertilizer after flowering and again in early summer, and avoid heavy pruning except to shape, since camellias set next year's flower buds on the current season's growth. In Gulf Coast gardens, afternoon shade helps protect the flowers and foliage from scorch during hot spells.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; aquatic milkweed grows naturally in swamp forests, streambanks, and floodplain margins across the Gulf Coastal Plain. In zone 9, it may remain semi-evergreen in mild winters.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; aquatic milkweed is the only native milkweed in North America adapted to the forested swamp conditions of the Gulf Coastal Plain — growing naturally in the shade of bottomland forests, swamp edges, and along bayous and sluggish streams from Florida to Texas and north to Illinois. Unlike most milkweeds that demand dry, sunny conditions, this species thrives in wet, partially shaded sites where it provides monarch butterfly larval habitat in habitats otherwise lacking milkweed. The tiny white flowers in rounded clusters are delicate and fragrant. As a monarch host plant, it is critically important because it blooms in two seasons — spring and fall — aligning with monarch migration and breeding in the Gulf South. An outstanding zone 9a milkweed for shaded, wet areas and streamside gardens where no other milkweed will thrive.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost; in zones below 10, grow in containers and bring indoors before first frost.
directions: Root cuttings in moist sand/perlite mix in summer heat or plant container specimens in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Arabian jasmine is the national flower of the Philippines and the primary source of the jasmine scent used in perfumes and jasmine tea — the double-flowered form 'Grand Duke of Tuscany' is especially fragrant, with blooms that intensify their perfume at night. Plants bloom intermittently throughout the warm season and can be trained as vines on a trellis or grown as shrubs. Fertilize monthly during active growth with a balanced fertilizer. In zone 9 grow against a warm south-facing wall and protect from hard freezes; in zone 8 and colder grow in containers. Harvest flowers in the morning for the strongest fragrance.

plant_note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost once the soil has warmed.
directions: Arabian Night is a long-grown decorative dahlia whose densely packed, velvety petals open deep maroon and darken toward near-black as blooms mature, especially in cooler weather. The medium-sized flowers hold their color well as cut stems, and the sturdy plant habit generally needs only light staking. Pinch the central growing tip early in the season to encourage branching, and cut or deadhead spent blooms often to keep the plant flowering into fall. Its old-fashioned, near-black decorative form makes it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting deep, moody color without the size or staking demands of a dinnerplate variety.

common_name: Arabian Star of Bethlehem (Black-Centered Star Flower)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Arabian star of Bethlehem grows in late winter through spring, blooms in late spring, then goes summer dormant. In zones 7b–10 it can remain in the ground through summer dormancy with withheld water; lift and store dry in colder zones. An excellent cut flower with long vase life.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Arabian star of Bethlehem is one of the most distinctive and fragrant spring-blooming bulbs — a Mediterranean and North African native producing in late spring (May–June), tall, upright scapes bearing a raceme of large (2 inch), pure-white, six-petaled, cup-shaped flowers each with a dramatic, prominent, dark, blue-black to jet-black ovary at the center — a shining black jewel at the heart of each snow-white flower creating a startling, bold contrast of white and black that gives the blooms an immediately recognizable and distinctive appearance unlike any other common spring bulb. The fragrance is sweet and noticeable, particularly in the evening. The flowers are excellent cut flowers with exceptional vase life of 2–3 weeks, making this a valuable bulb for cutting gardens. The large, broad, strap-shaped leaves are present from autumn through late spring, then die back in summer dormancy. Outstanding in zones 7b–10 where it can remain in the ground as a perennial; in zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens it naturalizes effectively. A superb, slightly unusual spring-flowering bulb for the cutting garden.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings after all frost danger has passed into well-drained, full-sun soil.
directions: Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer and root them in a well-draining mix before transplanting to a permanent site in spring. This fast-growing coastal shrub thrives in sandy, poor soils and tolerates salt spray, making it ideal for seaside gardens in warm zones. The aromatic gray-green trifoliate leaves and purple flower spikes appear through summer and have long been used in Asian herbal traditions for their fragrant essential oils. In borderline zones 8-9, plant against a south-facing wall and mulch the base heavily to protect the crown through cold snaps.

common_name: Arapaho Crape Myrtle (True Red Upright Crape Myrtle with Dark Fall Foliage)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Arapaho is a later U.S. National Arboretum release bred for improved true-red flower color and mildew resistance on a tall, upright tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Arapaho is a later U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series release bred to improve on earlier red-flowered crape myrtles, combining true, vivid red summer flowers with strong resistance to powdery mildew and dark maroon-red fall foliage color that extends the tree's seasonal interest well past bloom time. The tall, upright habit suits it to specimen or street tree use in larger Gulf South landscapes. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

plant_note: Transplant into warm soil after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Archangel was bred for unusually large individual flowers and a well-branched, self-cleaning habit that holds up through the peak heat and humidity of a Gulf South summer.
directions: Archangel produces spikes of unusually large, snapdragon-like flowers along upright, well-branched stems, a bolder-flowered selection than many older angelonia strains, and is largely self-cleaning, dropping spent blooms without leaving behind unsightly dead flowers. Like other angelonia it thrives in the heat and humidity that wilt many summer annuals, blooming continuously from late spring through the first frost with minimal deadheading required. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, water regularly during establishment, and expect strong drought tolerance once the plant is rooted in, making it a reliable performer for Gulf South summer beds and containers.

common_name: Archduke Charles Rose (Color-Changing Antique China Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Archduke Charles is an antique China rose introduced around 1837, valued in Gulf South gardens for blooms that darken from pink to deep crimson as they age and for the class's characteristic heat and disease tolerance.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing plants 3-3.5 feet apart. Introduced around 1837, Archduke Charles is a classic China rose whose fully double blooms open pale pink at the petal edges with deep rose-red centers, then darken dramatically toward crimson-purple as they age in warm weather, so a single well-established bush can show several bloom colors simultaneously. Like other China roses it flowers almost without pause from spring through the first hard frost and carries strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, thriving in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South with minimal spray input. The rounded, bushy shrub works well massed, in mixed borders, or as an informal low hedge. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or weak wood; hard pruning is unnecessary and reduces flowering, since China roses bloom continuously on both old and new growth.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and replant immediately in wet, cold-climate shade. Well-suited to northern and high-elevation gardens where other groundcovers struggle.
directions: Establish divisions in spring in deep shade or heavy shade with consistently wet or waterlogged soil. This native species thrives at the margins of cold streams, bogs, and seeps in northern gardens. It spreads at a moderate pace by rhizomes, forming dense weed-suppressing colonies useful for stabilizing moist, shaded banks. Far less aggressive than its European relative, it makes a manageable groundcover for cold-climate woodland gardens.

common_name: Arctic Fox Rose Foxglove (AAS-Winning First-Year-Blooming Rose-Pink Foxglove)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost for bloom the same year; Arctic Fox Rose is an AAS-winning selection bred for unusually uniform, early first-season flowering compared to older foxglove strains.
directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil, starting seed early indoors under lights for the most reliable first-season bloom. Arctic Fox Rose is an All-America Selections winner bred for exceptional uniformity and speed to flower, opening dense, upright spikes of clear rose-pink, outward-facing bells with a maroon-speckled white throat several weeks earlier and more evenly than older foxglove strains. Its sturdy, well-branched habit holds up better in wind and rain than taller heirloom foxglove, making it useful in mixed borders and large containers as well as traditional cottage-garden plantings. Deadheading the main spike after bloom often prompts a flush of smaller side spikes, extending the display into summer. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas frequented by children or pets and wear gloves when handling the foliage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a cold, sunny site with reliable winter snow cover.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a cold, sunny site, replicating the circumpolar arctic tundra of Alaska, Arctic Canada, and Greenland where it forms dense evergreen hummocks. Its stems are clothed in tightly overlapping, four-ranked scale leaves that give the shoots a distinctive square cross-section, and nodding white bell flowers open on slender red stalks in summer. Extremely cold-hardy but slow-growing and intolerant of heat, it belongs strictly in far-northern or high-elevation native and rock gardens with cool summers and a reliable winter snow cover.

common_name: Areca Palm (Butterfly Palm, Golden Cane Palm, Madagascar Palm)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Areca Palm is frost-sensitive (damaged below 32°F) and should be planted in zone 10-11 for outdoor landscape use, or grown in large containers in zone 9. In zone 9, use as a large container specimen on the patio from spring through fall, moving to a greenhouse or heated space in winter. Areca Palm is chlorine-sensitive — use filtered or collected rainwater in hard water areas, and avoid over-fertilizing with fluoride-containing formulations.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Areca Palm prefers consistently moist conditions and will develop yellowing fronds (potassium deficiency) in the alkaline soils common across the Gulf Coast — acidify soil with sulfur and use palm-formulated fertilizer containing micronutrients. Dypsis lutescens (formerly Chrysalidocarpus lutescens) is the most widely sold palm in the US nursery trade and one of the most commonly planted landscape palms in zone 10-11 Florida, Texas, and Gulf South landscapes — the graceful, arching, feathery fronds on cane-like yellow-green stems form magnificent multi-stemmed clumps reaching 15–25 feet. The yellow-green color of the stems (giving 'Golden Cane Palm' its name) and the softly arching frond tips that sway in the slightest breeze create an exceptionally elegant tropical effect. Native to Madagascar, where it is now endangered in the wild due to habitat loss, Areca Palm has become one of the world's most cultivated ornamental palms. The NASA Clean Air Study ranked it as one of the best air-purifying plants, removing xylene, toluene, and formaldehyde from indoor air. Non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring 2–3 inches deep in full sun in well-drained, gritty to loamy soil in zone 7–10; Argentine Rain Lily is a summer-blooming South American bulb from the grasslands of Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil — producing beautiful, large (for the genus), nodding, funnel-shaped, rose-pink flowers on 12-inch stems within days of a soaking summer rain, with each flower held at a characteristic 45-degree angle that distinguishes Habranthus from Zephyranthes.
directions: Plant Habranthus robustus bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; bulbs perform best with a dry dormant period in late spring followed by a good soaking (simulating monsoon rains) to trigger flowering; clumps multiply over time and bloom most profusely when slightly crowded. Argentine Rain Lily is the largest-flowered and most robust species in the Habranthus genus — a group of summer-rain-triggered bulbs closely related to Zephyranthes but distinguished by the characteristic nodding, angled flower posture (held at roughly 45 degrees) rather than upright. Flowers emerge in impressive flushes within 24–72 hours of a summer downpour, creating a breathtaking display: 3–4 inch, rose-pink to pale-pink funnel-shaped flowers with a golden-yellow center, held on slender stems above narrow, rush-like leaves. Exceptionally easy to grow and reliably perennial throughout zone 7–10, including the Gulf Coast where summer rains naturally trigger perfect bloom cycles. Bulbs naturalize readily in lawn edges, rock gardens, and raised beds; they naturalize particularly well in Texas and the Gulf South where the summer rain/dry pattern matches their native South American prairie climate. Divide crowded clumps every 3–4 years and replant offsets to spread.

common_name: Argentine Skies Salvia (Pale Sky-Blue Anise Sage)
plant_note: Plant container plants after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Argentine Skies is a pale-flowered form of anise sage, cooler in tone than the popular Black and Blue cultivar.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Argentine Skies bears pale, powdery sky-blue flowers with pale green calyces, a much softer, cooler-toned selection of anise sage than the deep cobalt-and-black-calyx Black and Blue cultivar, useful for pastel garden schemes or as a gentler backdrop for bolder companions. Like other anise sage it grows from tuberous roots, dying back after frost and resprouting in spring, and spreads by underground stolons into a substantial colony over time. Cut plants to the ground in late winter and it will resprout vigorously, drawing hummingbirds from summer through frost.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Argentine trumpet vine tolerates partial shade more successfully than most Bignonia family vines and produces acceptable flower display in the filtered light of open tree canopy — one of the better shade-tolerant flowering vines for zone 8–11.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Argentine trumpet vine (lavender trumpet vine) is a South American evergreen or semi-evergreen vine of the bignonia family that produces clusters of large, flared, trumpet-shaped, soft-lavender to pale-lilac and white flowers with violet-purple striping and veining on the throat in spring (April–May) and intermittently through the year, creating a refined and graceful floral display above its dense, glossy, dark-green, tendril-climbing foliage. The soft, delicate lavender-lilac color and the large, attractive, trumpet flower form give it a more elegant and less brash appearance than orange or red trumpet vines. It is notably more shade-tolerant than most Bignoniaceae vines and can bloom acceptably in partial-shade positions — a valuable attribute for the shadier garden where most large flowering vines fail. Hardy to approximately 20°F in zone 8, it is one of the more cold-tolerant of the tropical trumpet vine family. Excellent trained on arbors, fences, and large trellises in zone 8–11. May be invasive in some warm, moist climates — monitor for naturalization near natural areas.

common_name: Argentine Trumpet Vine (Garrocha Tecoma, Red Esperanza)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Tecoma garrocha is cold-hardy to zone 7-8 (20–25°F) — more cold-tolerant than T. stans. It grows as a large sprawling shrub or small tree in zone 9. The long, tubular flowers are outstanding hummingbird attractants. Prune by one-third in late winter to shape and stimulate new flowering stems. Can be trained as a small tree with staking. The orange-red flower color is somewhat different from yellow-flowered T. stans, offering a warmer-toned alternative. Propagate from stem cuttings or seed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Tecoma garrocha grows most vigorously in full sun and will produce fewer flowers and become leggy in shade. Tecoma garrocha is a large, fast-growing, semi-deciduous shrub or small tree native to Argentina and Bolivia in the Bignoniaceae family, closely related to the commonly grown Yellow Bells (T. stans) but with distinctly orange-red to coral-red tubular flowers rather than yellow — a color difference with significant ornamental consequence.
