Prune by removing the oldest canes at ground level each year to keep the planting full from top to bottom rather than shearing, which leaves bare lower stems.

common_name: Aureola Hakone Grass (Golden Japanese Forest Grass)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Aureola's golden-yellow variegation fades to green in deep shade — partial shade with 2–4 hours of dappled light produces the brightest color while preventing leaf scorch.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Aureola is the most widely grown and celebrated variegated selection of Hakonechloa macra — Japanese forest grass — a graceful, slow-spreading, clump-forming grass producing cascading, arching blades variegated with creamy yellow to bright golden-yellow longitudinal stripes on a green background, creating one of the most luminous and elegant shade-garden ground covers available. The soft, cascading habit of the blades, with each tuft flowing gently in even the slightest breeze, creates a fluid, calming motion in the garden that no other shade grass rivals. Aureola was named Perennial Plant of the Year 2009 and consistently ranks among the most highly regarded shade plants in American horticulture. The golden variegation brightens shaded areas where color is difficult to achieve — planted with dark hostas, dark-leafed heucheras, or deep green ferns, Aureola creates outstanding luminous contrast. In zone 9, it grows as a deciduous to semi-evergreen perennial that may struggle in the hottest, driest summer conditions; provide consistent moisture, deep shade, and organic mulch. The blades turn rich orange-red in fall, adding seasonal interest. Slow to establish but long-lived once mature.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring as new growth begins in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; growth is slow the first two seasons, so avoid overcrowding young plants.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and cut the whole clump back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Aureola is the most widely grown Japanese forest grass cultivar, its cascading, arching, bamboo-like blades brightly striped in gold and green, lighting up dark corners of the shade garden with a luminous, almost glowing effect, especially where dappled light catches the foliage. The color intensifies in cooler weather and takes on pink-bronze tints in fall before going dormant for winter. Its slow-spreading, mounding habit works equally well as a woodland-edge groundcover, container specimen, or textural companion to hostas, ferns, and heuchera. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 4–5 years as growth increases.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in part shade to full shade; Aureomaculata is fully evergreen and perennial in zone 7b–10, requiring minimal care once established. Avoid sites with reflected afternoon sun as this causes leaf scorch; deep shade under live oaks or magnolias is ideal in zone 9.
directions: Plant in part shade to full shade in moist, rich, well-drained soil; the Aureomaculata cultivar of farfugium is the celebrated leopard plant, named for the dramatic random yellow-to-white spots splashed across the large, round, glossy green leaves — each plant is uniquely patterned, no two exactly alike. The bold, irregular spotting creates a striking tropical effect in shade gardens, contrasting dramatically with the plain green foliage of surrounding shade plants. Like the species, Aureomaculata thrives in the heat and humidity of zone 8–9 shade gardens where the more common Ligularia dentata fails — it is fully heat-tolerant once established in shade and requires only consistent moisture to perform well year-round. Bright yellow daisy flowers appear November–January, providing rare winter color. The spotted foliage is best appreciated at mid-range distances; plant where it can be viewed from garden paths.

common_name: Aureomarginata Winter Daphne (Gold-Margined Fragrant Evergreen Daphne)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade; Aureomarginata bears gold-margined variegated foliage and is noted as hardier and more garden-reliable than the plain green form of winter daphne, with intensely fragrant late-winter flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade, taking special care to avoid wet feet, since daphne is notoriously intolerant of poor drainage. Aureomarginata bears the same rounded, evergreen foliage as plain winter daphne but each leaf is neatly edged in gold, adding year-round color and interest beyond the famously fragrant bloom period, and nurserymen and gardeners widely consider it hardier and more reliable in cultivation than the plain green species form, which can be temperamental. Clusters of small, waxy, pink-flushed white flowers open in late winter to very early spring, releasing an intensely sweet fragrance that carries a remarkable distance for the size of the bloom, making it a prized shrub to site near an entry, path, or window. Avoid disturbing the roots once planted, and resist the urge to over-fertilize or overwater, since daphne performs best in lean, well-drained conditions with minimal interference.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Aureovariegata sedge is a classic, long-cultivated clumper that neither runs nor self-sows aggressively.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Aureovariegata sedge is a classic, long-cultivated clumper that neither runs nor self-sows aggressively. Arching, evergreen leaves are striped with a soft golden-yellow center bordered in green, a warmer, more golden variegation pattern than the white-edged sedge cultivars more commonly sold, brightening shaded ground with a sunny glow even on overcast days. One of the older gold-variegated Japanese sedge selections still in cultivation, it forms a neat, fountain-shaped mound useful as a border edger, container filler, or small-scale groundcover under high-canopy shade trees. Comb out old foliage by hand in late winter rather than shearing, and divide congested clumps in spring only when the center begins to thin.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty, humus-enriched soil in partial to full shade in spring; auriculas prefer cool conditions and excellent drainage — heavy, wet soil in summer is fatal.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, gritty, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-enriched soil in partial to full shade; auricula (mountain cowslip) is a European alpine primrose that has been cultivated for centuries as a specialist exhibition plant, with growers producing flowers of extraordinary complexity — perfectly circular, velvet-textured petals in yellow, red, blue-gray, maroon, and white, many with intricate patterns of contrasting colors and a distinctive white or yellow central 'paste' (meal) that coats the center of the flower like powdered sugar. It requires excellent drainage (rot easily in soggy soil), cool temperatures, and consistent moisture. The thick, fleshy, powder-coated (farinose) leaves are distinctive. A heritage plant with centuries of breeding history, prized by specialists in the UK but underused in American gardens. Best in cool climates; struggles in hot, humid summers south of zone 7.

common_name: Aurora Fernleaf Bleeding Heart (White-Flowered Summer-Persistent Dicentra)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Aurora bears pure white flowers over blue-green ferny foliage and, kept moist, stays in active growth through summer rather than going dormant like common bleeding heart.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, spacing 12 to 18 inches apart. Aurora bears pure white, dangling, heart-shaped flowers held above finely dissected, blue-green ferny foliage, a clean white counterpart to the pink-flowered wild form of Western Bleeding Heart, and if kept consistently moist through summer it remains in active growth and continues flowering intermittently rather than going summer-dormant the way common bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis) does. It spreads gently by rhizomes and self-sowing to form an attractive groundcover colony in cool, moist, shaded sites, working well under conifers and deciduous trees alongside ferns and other woodland perennials. In hot climates it may still go dormant in summer heat but reliably re-emerges in fall or the following spring. Divide in early spring to increase plantings.

common_name: Aurora Zinnia (Two-Tone Vintage-Palette Blooms with Contrasting Centers)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Aurora bears two-tone, vintage-toned blooms with contrasting centers, a modern cut-flower breeding introduction.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches. Aurora bears large, two-tone blooms in soft, vintage-inspired color combinations with a contrasting center, a subtler, more nuanced palette than solid-colored zinnia cultivars, popular among floral designers seeking muted, antique-toned bouquets. Plants bloom heavily from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading or harvesting to encourage continuous production. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

common_name: Australia Canna (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Red-Flowered Canna)
plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Australia is grown chiefly for its striking near-black glossy foliage, which holds its dark color best in full sun.
directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun, feeding monthly during the growing season for the best foliage color and flowering. Australia is a dramatic canna cultivar grown primarily for its glossy, deep maroon-black leaves, among the darkest of any commonly available canna, which serve as a bold foil for its clear red summer flowers and for brighter-colored companion plants nearby. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder that wants consistent moisture but sharp drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground through zone 9 and warmer, expanding into a larger clump each year that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones the rhizomes can be lifted after the first frost kills the foliage and stored dry over winter.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring once temperatures are reliably warm in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Australian tree fern is frost-tender and needs protection or container culture with winter shelter outside zones 9b and warmer.
directions: Plant container stock in spring once temperatures are reliably warm in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Australian tree fern is frost-tender and needs protection or container culture with winter shelter outside zones 9b and warmer. Cyathea cooperi is a fast-growing, dramatic tree fern from Australia with a slender, fibrous trunk topped by a crown of large, lacy, arching fronds up to 10 feet long, creating an instant tropical, prehistoric look in a shaded courtyard or lush understory planting. It is one of the fastest-growing tree ferns in cultivation, adding a foot or more of trunk height annually under good conditions, but its speed comes with a need for consistent moisture and high humidity, since the trunk itself absorbs water. In marginal zones, wrap the fibrous trunk with burlap or frost cloth ahead of hard freezes, or grow it in a large container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Australian violet spreads vigorously by stolons and runners to form a dense, grass-excluding ground cover mat in cool, moist, shaded conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Australian violet is a low-growing, spreading violet from the moist, shaded woodlands and gullies of southeastern Australia, producing attractive, kidney-shaped leaves and small, charming violet flowers with white-and-purple markings that bloom nearly year-round in mild climates. It spreads by horizontal stolons to form a dense, low, weed-suppressing mat that makes an excellent ground cover under trees in shade. In zone 9a, it thrives as an evergreen ground cover in moist, shaded areas such as under live oaks and camellias, where it provides continuous year-round ground cover and periodic bloom. It tolerates foot traffic better than most shade ground covers. A popular ground cover in Australian gardens, it has become a favorite for shade gardeners across the Gulf South.

common_name: Australian Wax Plant (Common Wax Flower, Hoya australis)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket or trained vine on a trellis in bright indirect to partial shade; Hoya australis can tolerate brief temperatures to 35°F if the soil is dry — its Australian origin makes it more cold-tolerant than most Hoyas. In zone 9b-10, it can be grown outdoors in a sheltered spot. As with all Hoyas, never remove old flower stalks (peduncles) — new flower clusters emerge from the same peduncle each season. Allow to become slightly pot-bound before repotting. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light to partial shade — Hoya australis blooms most freely in bright indirect to gentle morning sun and will produce few flowers in shade, but performs well as a trailing houseplant even in moderate light. Hoya australis is a vigorous, twining, semi-succulent epiphytic vine native to eastern Australia (Queensland and New South Wales), one of the few Hoyas from the Australian continent rather than Southeast Asia, and one of the most cold-tolerant commonly grown Hoya species. The plant produces long, trailing stems of paired, broadly oval to slightly rounded, fleshy, glossy, dark-green leaves that are thicker and more succulent than most commonly grown Hoyas. In summer (its natural Southern Hemisphere flowering season, now extended to warm months in cultivation), Hoya australis produces large, globe-shaped umbels of 20–40 individual star-shaped flowers — pure white with a faint pink-red corona — with an intensely sweet, musky, almost spicy fragrance that is among the most powerful of any Hoya species. The combination of vigorous growth, good cold tolerance (relative to other Hoyas), reliable blooming, and powerful fragrance makes Hoya australis one of the most recommended starter Hoyas and a valuable addition to zone 9 shaded container and patio displays. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Austrian copper rose is exceptionally cold hardy and is the historic source of true yellow and orange coloring in modern rose breeding.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Austrian copper rose is a tough, exceptionally cold-hardy species rose bearing single, brilliant orange-red flowers with a bright yellow reverse that gives an unusual two-toned, flame-like effect in the garden, especially striking en masse or against dark foliage. It blooms in a single, intense flush in late spring and was historically the key source of true yellow pigment introduced into modern rose breeding lines, since most older roses could produce only white, pink, or red tones. The species carries a distinctive, somewhat unpleasant scent noted in its species name (foetida means foul-smelling in Latin), most noticeable up close rather than at a distance. It tolerates poor, dry soil and harsh winter cold better than most other old garden roses, making it a good choice for a tough, low-input hedge or specimen in a cold, challenging site, requiring only removal of dead wood after its single spring bloom.

common_name: Autograph Tree (Pitch Apple, Balsam Apple, Florida Clusia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Autograph Tree is extremely salt-tolerant and grows vigorously in coastal Gulf Coast conditions including salt spray, sandy soils, and high humidity. In zone 9a it is frost-sensitive (damaged below 32°F) and should be planted in sheltered locations or used as a large container specimen. In zone 9b–11, it is a reliable evergreen landscape shrub or small tree. The thick leaves are so firm that initials scratched into them remain permanently visible — hence 'Autograph Tree.'
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in sandy, rocky, or average well-drained soil; Autograph Tree is exceptionally drought- and salt-tolerant once established, making it one of the premier coastal shrubs for zone 10–11 Gulf Coast and South Florida landscapes. Clusia rosea is a tropical tree from the Caribbean and tropical Americas that has become one of the most widely planted landscape shrubs in South Florida, the Keys, and coastal South Texas for its bold, glossy, ovate, extremely thick, leathery dark-green leaves and tolerance of the most challenging coastal growing conditions. The leaves' remarkable rigidity — they feel like synthetic material — allows text or drawings scratched with a nail or key to remain permanently etched as the leaf expands and matures, making it a natural curiosity and the source of the common name 'Autograph Tree.' In late summer, the plant produces attractive cup-shaped white to rose-pink flowers followed by fleshy green fruits that split open to reveal red seeds — both attractive to birds. Clusia rosea develops aerial roots that eventually reach the ground, giving mature specimens a striking strangler-fig appearance. The milky white latex sap was historically used as a boat caulk ('pitch') by Caribbean peoples — hence the name 'Pitch Apple.' A large, fast-growing hedge or specimen plant for zone 10–11.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost when soil is warm.
directions: Direct sow Autumn Beauty sunflowers an inch deep after the last frost, spacing them a foot or more apart for their branching habit. Each plant sends up multiple stems glowing in gold, bronze, orange, and burgundy, reaching five to seven feet tall from midsummer into fall. Their pollen-rich faces draw bees and butterflies, and the blooms make long-lasting cut flowers. Stake in windy sites and leave a few heads to ripen for the birds.

common_name: Autumn Blaze Maple (Fast-Growing Hybrid Freeman Maple)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Autumn Blaze is a hybrid of silver and red maple combining the fast growth of silver maple with the stronger wood and fall color of red maple.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Autumn Blaze is a hybrid cross between silver maple and red maple, bred to combine the rapid growth rate of silver maple with the sturdier branch structure and reliable orange-red fall color of red maple, avoiding the weak, storm-prone wood that has made straight silver maple less popular as a landscape tree. It grows into a dense, oval-to-rounded shade tree relatively quickly compared to most large shade trees, making it a popular choice where gardeners want a mature-looking canopy sooner rather than later. It is adaptable to a range of soils and tolerates urban conditions reasonably well, though like its silver maple parent it can have somewhat brittle wood in ice or heavy wind, and should be kept away from underground utilities and pavement given its vigorous surface roots.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Autumn Bride is a selection of the native species Heuchera villosa and is notably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than most Heuchera cultivars, making it one of the best-performing coral bells for the deep shade and muggy summers of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; established clumps tolerate summer drought and heavy shade far better than most Heuchera hybrids. Autumn Bride is a selection of Heuchera villosa, the heat- and humidity-adapted native alumroot of the southern Appalachians and Gulf South uplands, chosen for its large, softly fuzzy, chartreuse-green leaves and — most notably — its late bloom time. While most coral bells flower in late spring, Autumn Bride sends up tall, airy, 18–24 inch spikes of small creamy-white flowers in late summer and early fall, right when few other shade perennials are blooming, making it a valuable late nectar source for native bees. Its species-level heat and humidity tolerance make it dramatically more reliable in deep, humid Gulf South shade than the many showy-leaved Heuchera hybrids that decline in southern summers. Excellent massed as a shade groundcover or woodland-edge border plant in zone 4–9.

common_name: Autumn Cattleya (Crimson Cattleya, Ruby Orchid, Purple Queen Orchid)
plant_note: Grow in slatted orchid pots or baskets with coarse bark media in bright indirect to direct morning sun; Cattleya labiata needs bright light (bright indirect to filtered sun) to bloom reliably and will not flower in dim conditions. Cannot tolerate frost — minimum 50°F. In zone 9, grow year-round on a bright, sheltered porch or indoors at a south or east window. Natural blooming occurs in fall (September–November in the Northern Hemisphere). A summer rest with reduced watering (not complete drought) encourages flower spike development. Repot every 2–3 years. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light — Cattleya labiata requires more light than most houseplants but less than most outdoor ornamentals; bright filtered sun or a south-facing window with light curtain is ideal. Cattleya labiata is a spectacular epiphytic orchid endemic to a restricted range in northeastern Brazil (Pernambuco, Alagoas, and adjacent states), discovered by William Swainson and introduced to cultivation in England in 1818. The first flowers opened at William Cattley's greenhouse in Barnet in 1824, causing a sensation — the large (5–8 inch), wavy, deep lavender-purple flowers with a ruffled, velvety, deep magenta-crimson lip were unlike anything previously seen in European horticulture. The plant was named Cattleya labiata in Cattley's honor, and the entire genus was named for him. Cattleya labiata became the parent of thousands of hybrid orchids over the following two centuries — the traditional 'corsage orchid' of the 20th century is a Cattleya hybrid, and C. labiata's influence runs through the vast majority of the large-flowered Cattleya orchid hybrids still popular today. The fall-blooming season (September–November in the Northern Hemisphere) gives the plant its common name 'Autumn Cattleya.' The flowers are waxy, intensely fragrant, and extraordinarily beautiful. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; autumn cherry blooms in October–November and again in spring, and the cultivar 'Autumnalis' is widely planted for its remarkable ability to produce flowers in warm fall weather as well as the main spring flush.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; autumn cherry is a Japanese species celebrated as the parent of the cultivar 'Autumnalis', which holds the exceptional distinction of producing semi-double, pale pink flowers twice — in October-November when temperatures drop in fall, and again in early spring. In mild winters, the fall flowering can continue sporadically through winter into spring, providing flowers for weeks or months. The weeping forms (var. pendula) create graceful, cascading silhouettes, and 'Autumnalis Rosea' has deeper pink, semi-double flowers. More cold-hardy than many ornamental cherries and longer-lived than double-flowering varieties. A cherished ornamental for fall-winter garden interest, providing color at a time when almost no other flowering trees are in bloom. Less vigorous than Yoshino cherry but more refined.

plant_note: Plant corms in late summer or early fall, 3–4 inches deep, before they bloom spontaneously out of the soil without any leaves — corms planted in August will often flower in September without any soil; they produce their large, strap-like leaves in spring and go dormant by summer.
directions: Plant corms in late summer 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; autumn crocus corms will sometimes flower spontaneously without any soil if left unplanted — plant promptly after purchase. Colchicum autumnale, called autumn crocus or naked ladies for the way its large, goblet-shaped, lilac-pink flowers emerge from bare ground in September–October without any foliage (the leaves appear separately in spring and then die back by summer), is one of the most reliably magical spectacles of the fall garden — a carpet of delicate crocus-like flowers appearing suddenly from empty-looking soil. All parts of the plant are toxic (it contains colchicine, used medicinally) and should not be confused with true crocuses, which are safe. Naturalize under deciduous shrubs or in lawns where it can be left undisturbed; the foliage must not be cut until it yellows naturally in late spring.

plant_note: Plant dry tubers in late summer to early fall with the flat, rough side up about 1 inch below the soil surface in sharply drained soil; autumn cyclamen goes completely dormant in summer — plant where summer moisture will be naturally absent or where they will be sheltered from summer rain by tree canopy.
directions: Plant tubers in late summer in sharply drained, gritty, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees in shade to part shade; autumn cyclamen is a Mediterranean woodland bulb that produces charming swept-back flowers in pink, rose, or white at the most unexpected moment — emerging directly from bare earth in September and October before any leaves appear, carpeting dry shade beneath oaks and conifers with cheerful color just as the garden winds down. After flowering, the strikingly attractive silver-patterned, ivy-shaped leaves emerge and persist through winter and spring, creating a beautiful ground-level tapestry. The plant disappears completely in summer when it requires dry dormancy. It naturalizes freely from self-sown seed, expanding gradually into carpets under trees where little else will grow. Tubers slowly enlarge to saucer-size over decades and become long-lived garden heirlooms.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in sharply drained soil in late summer; sternbergia flowers best in dry, baked conditions after a warm, dry summer — plant on slopes, raised beds, or at the base of south-facing walls where summer drainage is excellent. Bulbs resent being disturbed once established and should be left undivided for years.
directions: Plant bulbs in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; autumn daffodil (Sternbergia lutea) produces bright, clear-yellow crocus-like flowers in September and October from bare soil before the narrow, glossy, dark-green leaves emerge — making it look remarkably like a yellow crocus but actually a member of the amaryllis family. Native to the Mediterranean and Middle East, where it grows in rocky limestone soils and olive groves, it thrives in dry, alkaline conditions that mimic its native habitat. The flowers appear after summer drought breaks with the first autumn rains, a Mediterranean timing cue; in humid climates, plant in very well-drained raised beds and avoid summer irrigation. Foliage persists through winter and disappears in late spring. An excellent companion to autumn crocus in the fall bulb garden.

common_name: Autumn Damask Rose (Rare Repeat-Flowering Fragrant Pink Damask)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Autumn Damask is the rare repeat-flowering damask rose, blooming again lightly in fall.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Autumn Damask is historically remarkable as one of the very few old European roses capable of a genuine, if lighter, second bloom in fall, a trait most old garden rose classes lack entirely, bearing loosely double, clear pink, intensely fragrant flowers in both flushes. Its ancient origins and repeat-blooming trait made it an important ancestor in the eventual development of modern repeat-flowering rose classes. Deadhead the spring flush to encourage the fall repeat, and prune lightly in late winter to shape.

common_name: Autumn Embers Encore Azalea (Deep Red Reblooming Compact Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Autumn Embers is a compact, deep red-flowered selection from the reblooming Encore azalea series, flowering in spring and again in summer and fall.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with protection from harsh afternoon sun in the hottest part of zone 9. Autumn Embers is a compact-growing selection within the Encore reblooming azalea series, producing deep, rich red double flowers in the main spring flush and then again through summer and fall, giving significantly more color over the season than traditional once-blooming azaleas of similar size. Its smaller mature size compared to many Encore cultivars fits foundation plantings and smaller borders where a full-sized azalea would outgrow the space. Water deeply during dry spells, especially before the later bloom flushes, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom to avoid removing the buds destined for later color.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; autumn fern is one of the most adaptable shade ferns, tolerating summer heat, humidity, and periodic drought better than most species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; autumn fern is outstanding for its spectacular copper-red to orange new fronds that emerge in spring and again in late summer — the intense metallic color fades to lustrous, glossy dark green as fronds mature, giving the plant two distinct seasons of visual interest. It is one of the most heat-tolerant and adaptable shade ferns, performing well across much of the eastern U.S. including the Gulf South where many ferns struggle. Evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild winters; the old fronds can be cut to the ground in late winter to make way for the spectacular spring flush of colored new growth. Tolerates dry shade better than most ferns once established.

common_name: Autumn Fire Sedum (Improved Deep Pink-to-Bronze Stonecrop)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; like Autumn Joy, Autumn Fire declines in rich, wet soil, so lean, well-drained conditions give the sturdiest, most upright stems.
directions: Autumn Fire is an improved sport of the classic Autumn Joy sedum, selected for sturdier, less floppy stems and larger, more richly colored flower heads that hold up better through the season, particularly in humid climates where the original Autumn Joy sometimes splays open. Succulent, blue-green foliage emerges in spring, builds into broccoli-like flower buds by midsummer, opens dusty pink in late summer, and deepens through rose and finally rust-bronze by fall, with the dried seedheads persisting attractively into winter. Extremely drought-tolerant once established thanks to its water-storing succulent tissue, it thrives in the same lean, sharply drained, full-sun conditions as its parent and should not be planted where regular irrigation keeps the soil consistently moist, which encourages weak, sprawling growth. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in spring.

common_name: Autumn Frost Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Gold Margin)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Autumn Frost keeps the strongest blue cast on its center in deeper shade, while the gold margin brightens with a little morning sun.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with some morning sun to bring out the brightest color contrast between the blue-green center and gold margin. Autumn Frost is a sport in the Frances Williams lineage of hostas, bearing thick, heavily corrugated, frosty blue-green leaves edged in a wide, irregular band of creamy gold that deepens as the season progresses, giving the clump a rich, layered color display from spring through fall. Near-white flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Its heavy leaf substance provides good resistance to slug damage compared to thinner-leaved hostas, and the bold, dual-tone foliage makes it an effective focal point or specimen in a shaded border. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring as new growth emerges.

common_name: Autumn Gold Ginkgo (Seedless Male Ginkgo with Golden Fall Color)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Autumn Gold is a grafted male cultivar selected for a uniform, broadly pyramidal habit and reliable golden fall color, and being male it never produces the malodorous, messy fruit of female ginkgo trees.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, and water regularly through the first two to three seasons to help the young tree establish, since mature ginkgo are exceptionally tough and drought-, pollution-, and pest-tolerant once rooted in. Autumn Gold is a grafted, male-only selection of ginkgo prized for its symmetrical, broadly pyramidal form and its dependable, uniform display of clear golden-yellow fan-shaped leaves each fall, often dropping in a dramatic, near-simultaneous leaf fall over a day or two once peak color is reached. Because it is propagated from a male tree, Autumn Gold never produces the notoriously foul-smelling, messy fruit that female ginkgo trees bear, making it a far better choice than a seed-grown tree of unknown sex for street tree plantings, lawns, or anywhere fallen fruit would be a nuisance. Ginkgo is one of the most resilient shade trees available, tolerating urban pollution, compacted soil, heat, and periods of drought with ease, and it is essentially free of serious insect and disease problems. Little pruning is needed beyond removing any dead or crossing branches while the tree is young.

common_name: Autumn Gold Swamp Sunflower (Rich Golden-Yellow Compact Native Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Autumn Gold is a compact swamp sunflower selection with rich golden-yellow flowers, more self-supporting than the tall species.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Autumn Gold produces the deep, rich golden-yellow, daisy-form flowers with dark centers typical of swamp sunflower, blooming heavily from September into November when few other perennials are at peak display, but on a more compact, self-supporting plant than the species, which can reach six to ten feet and flop without staking. Its shorter stature suits a mid-border position and reduces maintenance while retaining the full fall color impact. Highly attractive to migrating monarch butterflies, native bees, and seed-eating birds. Divide every three to four years in spring to prevent center die-out in mature clumps.

common_name: Autumn Jazz Arrowwood Viburnum (Uniform Reliable Fall-Color Native Viburnum)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Jazz, a Chicagoland Grows selection of native arrowwood viburnum, bears a dense, uniform habit and reliable red-orange to yellow fall color, with blue-black berries that are heavily favored by birds.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; native arrowwood viburnum tolerates a wide range of soils and light conditions. Autumn Jazz, a Chicagoland Grows introduction, is a selection of native arrowwood viburnum bred for a dense, uniform, rounded habit and unusually reliable fall foliage color, turning a consistent blend of red-orange to burgundy each autumn rather than the more variable coloring typical of seedling-grown arrowwood. Flat clusters of white spring flowers give way to blue-black berries in fall that are heavily favored by migrating and overwintering songbirds, making it a valuable native wildlife planting as well as an ornamental hedge or screen. It requires minimal maintenance once established and tolerates urban conditions, clay soil, and periodic drought well. Prune right after flowering if shaping is needed.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Autumn Joy declines in rich, wet soil — excessive fertility and moisture cause floppy stems and reduced flowering; plant in lean, well-drained conditions for the most compact, upright habit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Autumn Joy (the trade name for Hylotelephium telephium 'Herbstfreude', a hybrid of German origin) is one of the most widely planted and most beloved perennials in American horticulture — valued for its exceptionally long season of ornamental interest that spans from the emergence of the succulent, blue-green, glaucous foliage in spring through the broccoli-like flower bud stage in summer, peak bloom in late summer, and the distinctive russet-bronze dried seedhead stage in fall and winter that persists ornamentally into December. The flower clusters open dusty-pink in late August, deepen to rose-salmon through September, and then to brick-red to mahogany in October — a three-month color progression from a single set of flower heads. The dried, rust-colored seedheads persist attractively through winter and are outstanding in dried arrangements. Autumn Joy is extraordinarily adaptable — it thrives in sand, clay (if not waterlogged), drought, heat, coastal salt spray, and alkaline conditions that would challenge most perennials. In zone 9, the heat and humidity of the Gulf South are the primary challenges: Autumn Joy performs well but requires sharply drained soil and should not be planted where summer irrigation keeps soil consistently moist. The succulent stems and leaves store water efficiently, making established plants remarkably drought-tolerant. Divide every 3–4 years in spring as clumps enlarge.

common_name: Autumn Leaves Heuchera (Heat-Tolerant Color-Changing Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Autumn Leaves was bred by Terra Nova Nurseries from heat- and humidity-tolerant parentage (Heuchera villosa x americana), making it a stronger performer in hot, humid Gulf South summers than many coral bells cultivars.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Autumn Leaves is a coral bells cultivar bred from heat- and humidity-tolerant Heuchera villosa parentage, giving it noticeably better resilience through hot, muggy Southern summers than many of the more delicate purple-leaved cultivars. Its foliage shifts through the season, emerging warm red in spring, mellowing to taupe-bronze through summer, then flaring back to ruby-red in fall, giving it seasonal interest beyond a single static leaf color. Small cream flower spikes appear in late spring but are secondary to the changing foliage display. Give it consistent moisture through the hottest months and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Autumn Minaret Daylily (Tall Late-Season Yellow Daylily)
plant_note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Autumn Minaret's tall flower scapes benefit from a sheltered spot away from strong wind, though the plant itself is otherwise easy-care and long-lived.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving the tall scapes room at the back of a border where their height won't shade shorter neighbors. Bred by Dr. A. B. Stout at the New York Botanical Garden and introduced in 1951, Autumn Minaret sends up remarkably tall, slender flower scapes to 5–6 feet topped with clusters of small, star-shaped, soft golden-yellow blooms with a light spicy fragrance, opening notably late in the season when most daylilies have finished for the year. Its height and late bloom time make it a distinctive vertical accent and a valuable extension of the daylily season into late summer and early fall, when garden color is often waning. Established clumps are long-lived and rarely require division more than once every five or more years.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in moist to dry, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; autumn moor grass is one of the few ornamental grasses that genuinely performs well in dry shade — a rare and valuable quality for challenging landscape situations.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to dry, well-drained soil; autumn moor grass establishes readily and begins producing attractive flower spikes in its first season. Sesleria autumnalis is a compact, fine-textured European moor grass that is one of the most valuable ornamental grasses for difficult garden situations: it is genuinely shade-tolerant, performing well in both partial and dappled shade, it is drought-tolerant once established, and it blooms in late summer and fall when most ornamental grasses are already looking tired — the chartreuse to cream, bottlebrush-like flower spikes emerge in August through October above bright green, arching foliage that stays attractive nearly year-round. The low, mounding habit (12–18 inches) makes it ideal for edging, mass planting under trees, or mixing with shade perennials such as hostas and heucheras.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in spring; autumn pineapple lily blooms in late summer through fall (August–October) and goes dormant for winter. In zones 7–8 mulch heavily after the first frost. In zones 6 and colder lift bulbs after frost and store dry and frost-free for the winter.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; autumn pineapple lily is one of the most compact and garden-practical pineapple lily species — a smaller plant than E. comosa or E. pallidiflora that blooms in the late summer and autumn period (August through October), extending the pineapple lily season beyond the summer-blooming species into the transition to fall. The characteristic pineapple lily flower arrangement is retained — a dense, cylindrical spike of individual star-shaped flowers topped by a rosette of leaf-like bracts creating the silhouette that inspires the pineapple common name — but on a more compact plant 12–18 inches tall in pure white to cream-white or greenish-white. The autumn bloom timing is particularly valuable in the late-season border. Like all pineapple lilies, it is strongly fragrant — each individual floret lightly sweet, the whole spike pleasantly aromatic in warm weather — and the succulent, broadly strap-shaped basal leaves are attractive throughout the growing season. Outstanding in containers, where the pot can be moved indoors when frost threatens.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; autumn sage is one of the finest and most hummingbird-attractive natives for zone 7–10 gardens.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; autumn sage is a compact, woody-based native of Texas and the Mexican mountains that blooms nearly year-round in mild climates — producing clusters of tubular flowers in brilliant red, cherry-pink, coral, salmon, or white that are magnets for ruby-throated hummingbirds and butterflies from spring through late fall. It tolerates extreme drought, summer heat, and alkaline rocky soil with negligible care. Cut back by one-half in late winter to promote dense, floriferous new growth. Among the most reliably ornamental and wildlife-valuable natives for dry Texas and Gulf Coast landscapes. Named varieties include 'Furman's Red' (large, intense red), 'Raspberry Royal', 'Cold Hardy Pink', and 'Wild Thing'.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike its moisture-loving spring and summer relatives, Autumn Snowflake wants a drier summer dormancy and is an old Southern pass-along bulb that persists for decades at abandoned homesites with no care.
directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in late summer. Autumn Snowflake is a diminutive fall-blooming bulb, sending up thread-like stems bearing one or two small, nodding, bell-shaped white flowers delicately flushed with pink at the base, often appearing before or alongside the grassy foliage in late summer to early fall — a welcome bit of bloom when little else in the bulb garden is active. It is smaller and daintier than its better-known spring and summer snowflake relatives, and unlike those moisture-loving cousins it actually prefers a drier summer rest, making it well suited to a sunny, well-drained border or rock garden rather than a damp woodland setting. Once established it slowly multiplies by offset bulbs and self-seeding, and like many old Southern pass-along bulbs it needs no supplemental water or feeding to keep returning each fall for years.

common_name: Autumn Sun Toad Lily (Large White Spotted Late-Blooming Shade Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Autumn Sun has better sun tolerance than most toad lilies — it performs in positions with morning sun provided afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture are maintained.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Autumn Sun is a hybrid toad lily valued for its relatively upright habit, large white-and-purple spotted flowers, and better adaptability to sun and heat than pure Tricyrtis hirta selections. The intricate orchid-like flowers — white with distinctive purple spotting arranged in patterns across the petals and a prominent central column — bloom in late summer and fall (August–October in zone 9) at a time when most shade perennials have finished flowering, providing valuable late-season interest in shade positions that are bare of bloom by August. The flowers appear in the leaf axils along the arching to upright stems, creating a succession of bloom that extends over 4–6 weeks rather than a single flush. Tricyrtis 'Autumn Sun' produces broader, more strappy foliage than T. hirta and has slightly greater tolerance for warmer conditions — an advantage at the warm end of its range (zone 9) where summer heat can stress less adapted toad lily selections. In zone 9, toad lilies perform best in deep, consistently moist shade under canopy trees where summer temperatures are moderated; the fall blooming period occurs as temperatures cool toward the optimal range. Divide established clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor. An outstanding choice for naturalizing in moist, shaded garden positions where late-season bloom is a priority.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Avalanche is a pre-1885 multiflora tazetta that has naturalized in mild-winter Southern gardens for generations.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Avalanche is a historic tazetta daffodil, recorded since before 1885, that carries an unusually heavy load of blooms on each stem — often a dozen or more small, fragrant white flowers with pale yellow cups clustered together, opening over a long season in late winter. Like other tazetta types it needs little winter chill and perennializes reliably in the Gulf South, multiplying steadily into large naturalized drifts when left undisturbed. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back completely before removing it so the bulbs can store enough energy for next year's heavy bloom.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, gravelly or loamy, humus-rich alpine or subalpine soil in partial shade; avalanche lily is a specialist of high-elevation subalpine meadows and avalanche tracks in the Cascades and Olympics, blooming as snowfields recede in early summer. Very difficult to transplant from the wild; obtain nursery-grown plants only.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, gravelly or loamy, humus-rich alpine or subalpine soil in partial shade; avalanche lily is one of the iconic wildflowers of the Pacific Northwest high country — pure white, reflexed-petaled flowers with yellow anthers that emerge through melting snowfields in early summer immediately after the snow retreats in Cascade and Olympic subalpine meadows. The sight of thousands of avalanche lilies blooming across a retreating snowfield at Mt. Rainier or the Olympics is one of the most spectacular wildflower displays in North America. Notoriously difficult to grow in lowland gardens, as it requires the very specific combination of cold winters, cool summers, and well-drained subalpine soils it evolved in. Best suited to rock gardens in the mountains; in lowland gardens, the cool, moist conditions of the Pacific Northwest coast give the best chance of success. Obtain only nursery-propagated corms; the species is protected in national parks.

plant_note: Plant in full sun with even moisture; tolerates damp clay soils and light shade but struggles where summers are consistently hot and humid.
directions: Plant in full sun with even moisture, though it tolerates damp clay soils and light shade. Avalanche carries a crisp white central stripe down each narrow green leaf blade, the reverse variegation pattern of the more common Overdam, and holds its color and upright habit through summer heat better than many variegated grasses. It forms a neat, sterile clump that sends up slender flower stems in early summer, opening pinkish-green and maturing to a warm wheat color that stands through winter. Because it does not set viable seed, Avalanche stays contained rather than self-sowing, making it a tidy, well-mannered choice for formal borders and mass plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; geum requires good drainage to prevent crown rot in winter and performs best with afternoon shade in hot summer climates.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in zone 4–7; avens (geum) produces brilliant bowl-shaped flowers in warm shades of scarlet, orange, apricot, and yellow in late spring and early summer above a neat mound of hairy, strawberry-like basal foliage. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to prolong the bloom period and encourage a repeat flush in late summer. In hot climates protect from afternoon sun and ensure consistent moisture — plants struggle and may die back in sustained summer heat above 85°F. Divide congested clumps in early fall every 2–3 years; popular garden hybrids such as 'Mrs. J. Bradshaw' (scarlet) and 'Lady Stratheden' (yellow) are easily found at nurseries.

common_name: Avondale Chinese Redbud (Intense Rose-Purple Compact Redbud)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Avondale stays more compact and shrubby than the species and is notably more shade-tolerant than Eastern redbud, making it well suited to smaller gardens and understory positions.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the multi-stemmed shrub room to develop its dense, rounded form. Avondale is a New Zealand selection of Chinese redbud prized for producing the most intensely colored bloom of any redbud in general cultivation, with deep rose-purple to magenta pea flowers packed so densely along every branch, twig, and even the older trunk wood that the bare stems all but disappear under the spring flower display. Its naturally compact, shrubby habit stays smaller and tidier than the species, and its greater shade tolerance compared with Eastern redbud makes it a strong choice for a woodland-edge planting, foundation bed, or small-garden specimen where its eye-level bloom show can be appreciated up close. Large, glossy heart-shaped leaves follow the flowers and turn clear yellow in fall; prune only to remove dead or crossing wood right after bloom.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Awabuki is cold-sensitive below zone 8 — plant in a protected location in zone 8, or choose the more cold-hardy V. odoratissimum (standard sweet viburnum) instead.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Awabuki is the most attractive and most dramatic viburnum for Gulf Coast zone 8–10 landscapes — a vigorous, large-growing evergreen shrub or small tree producing enormous, glossy, dark-green leaves with an extraordinary mirror-like surface sheen that catches and reflects light unlike any other commonly grown landscape shrub. The leaves (4–8 inches long) have such a pronounced, lacquered surface gloss that the plant appears polished — the deep, wet-looking gloss is so intense it almost looks artificial. This exceptional foliage texture makes Awabuki a striking specimen plant and creates a more architectural, tropical effect than standard sweet viburnum. White, fragrant flower clusters (panicles) appear in spring, followed by small red berries that age to black and attract birds. The fast, vigorous growth makes Awabuki excellent for rapid screening and privacy hedges — it can grow 3–4 feet per year in zone 9 with adequate water and fertilizer. Awabuki is more cold-sensitive than standard sweet viburnum (V. odoratissimum) and can suffer significant damage in zone 8 during severe winters; zone 9 coastal gardens are ideal. Prune after spring bloom to control size — Awabuki tolerates heavy pruning and can be maintained as a formal hedge.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; a native wetland sedge ideal for rain gardens, pond edges, stream banks, and consistently moist shaded spots where most plants struggle.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in consistently wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; awl-fruited sedge tolerates prolonged standing water and is an excellent choice for the lowest and wettest spots in rain gardens, bioswales, and naturalized wet areas. Carex stipata is a robust native sedge found throughout eastern North America in wet forests, swamps, and stream banks, producing coarse, upright, bright green, W-shaped stems (the distinctive spongy stem cross-section identifies many Carex species) 2–3 feet tall with prominent, straw-colored to brownish flower and fruit spikes in early summer; the awl-shaped perigynia (seed coverings) give it a spiky, somewhat bristly appearance at fruit set. Plant in masses for effective erosion control on wet slopes and stream banks; it provides important cover and seed for waterfowl and songbirds.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Ayesha is instantly recognizable for its unusual cupped, hooded petals that resemble a lilac cluster rather than a typical hydrangea floret.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Ayesha is one of the most distinctive hydrangea cultivars in cultivation, its individual florets cupped and curled inward so tightly that a full flower head looks remarkably like a cluster of lilac blooms rather than the flat-petaled florets typical of the species, in shades of lilac-mauve to soft blue depending on soil pH. Beyond its unusual form, some gardeners report a faint sweet fragrance from the blooms, a rare trait in mophead hydrangeas. It blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates to keep blooms from wilting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Aztec Grass develops the most vivid cream striping in partial shade — full sun may bleach the variegation to white and stress the fine-textured foliage in Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Aztec Grass is a fine-textured, cream-variegated liriope cultivar — producing very narrow, grass-like leaves with cream to ivory-white longitudinal striping on a green base. The very narrow leaf texture (narrower than standard liriope cultivars) gives plantings a soft, grass-like appearance that differs from the bold strap-leaf texture of Big Blue or Gold Band, creating a finer, more delicate groundcover effect appropriate for intimate garden spaces and detailed plantings. The cream-white variegation on the narrow leaves creates a bright, light-reflective effect in shade conditions — useful for illuminating dark areas under tree canopies or alongside dark hardscape features. Aztec Grass forms compact clumping mounds rather than aggressive spreading, making it appropriate for defined groundcover areas and edging applications. In summer, small lavender to pale purple flower spikes appear above the foliage, followed by black berries. Like all liriopes, Aztec Grass is remarkably adaptable in zone 9 — tolerating heat, drought, shade, and the root competition of mature trees. The fine texture makes it an effective underplanting beneath high-canopied specimens where bolder groundcovers would compete visually. Shear to 3 inches in late winter to remove old foliage before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep and 6–8 inches apart after the last frost in well-drained, sandy, moderately fertile soil in full sun; allow bulbs to dry completely before each winter in zones 7 and colder by lifting and storing in a cool, dry place.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep after the last frost in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; the Aztec lily (Jacobean lily) produces one of the most exotic and striking flowers in the bulb world — a deep, velvety crimson bloom resembling a Tudor rose or an orchid, with three upward-pointing petals and three downward-curving petals surrounding yellow-tipped stamens, emerging on a leafless stem before or with the strap leaves. Each bulb produces 1–2 flowers in spring. After bloom, allow the foliage to ripen completely before cutting it back. In zones 8–11, leave bulbs in the ground year-round in well-drained soil; in colder zones dig and store dry over winter at 50–60°F.

common_name: Aztec Sunset Zinnia (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Double Bicolor Cream-Gold-Rust)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Aztec Sunset, a Fleuroselect Gold Medal winner, bears double bicolor blooms in cream, gold, rust, and red on dwarf bushy plants.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 8-12 inches. Aztec Sunset, a Fleuroselect Gold Medal winner in the Mexican zinnia species, bears small, double blooms blending cream, gold, rust, and red in a warm, autumnal color mix on a dwarf, densely branching, bushy plant, distinct from the larger single blooms of many Zinnia haageana selections. Its compact size and heavy, prolific flowering make it excellent for edging, containers, and mass plantings. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, dry to average, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; pinch stems in spring and early summer to promote bushy, self-supporting growth — unpinched plants flop in late summer.
directions: Direct sow in fall in dry, well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun and pinch the growing tips two or three times from spring through July to produce a bushier plant that does not require staking; azure blue sage is a native North American prairie sage that produces some of the deepest, truest sky-blue flowers in the autumn garden on plants that reach 3–5 feet, blooming from late summer through frost when most other flowers are winding down. The intense blue color makes it exceptional in combination with yellow and orange fall-blooming plants. It is highly drought-tolerant, long-lived in dry soils, and beloved by bumblebees, honeybees, and migrating monarch butterflies. Cut back hard in early spring before new growth begins.

plant_note: Divide tuberous roots in early spring or fall, or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Azure monkshood resents dry conditions and performs best in cool, moist positions with partial shade from afternoon sun. Do not move established plants unnecessarily — they resent disturbance. ALL PARTS ARE EXTREMELY TOXIC if ingested or if sap contacts broken skin.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; azure monkshood is the most valuable of the autumn-blooming monkshoods, native to central China and blooming in September and October when deep blue flowers are precious — its large, dense spikes of rich violet-blue, hooded flowers ('monks' hoods') are among the last major perennial flowers of the season, providing an anchor of rich cool color in the autumn garden when most perennials have finished. The flowers are architecturally bold and distinctive in shape — each with the characteristic helmet-shaped hood that protects the nectar and is adapted for pollination by bumblebees, the only insects strong enough to push into the hooded flower. The deep, glossy, dark-green, deeply lobed foliage is attractive throughout the growing season before the late bloom. The cultivar 'Arendsii' produces particularly large, luminous dark-blue flowers. EXTREME CAUTION: all parts of all monkshoods contain aconitine, one of the most potent plant toxins known — wear gloves when handling and keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; baboon flower grows through the cool season and blooms in spring, then goes dormant in summer. In zone 8–10 with dry summers, the corms can be left in the ground permanently. In wetter climates, lift and store dry through summer. The common name comes from baboons in South Africa digging and eating the corms.
directions: Plant corms in fall in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; baboon flower is a charming South African spring bulb from the Cape Floristic Region, producing pleated, fan-like foliage and dense spikes of bright, vivid flowers in a wide range of colors — violet, purple, blue, pink, red, cream, and white — in late winter to spring. The flowers are fragrant in many varieties, with a light, sweet scent. The common name derives from baboons digging and eating the corms in their native South Africa (hence 'babiana' from 'baboon'). Growing on a Mediterranean bulb cycle — fall planting, cool season growth, spring bloom, summer dormancy — it naturalizes well in California, the Gulf Coast, and similar mild, dry-summer climates. The dense, ribbed, pleated leaves are distinctive. Different color forms are available as mixed-color bulb packages or separately. Lovely for late winter and early spring color when few bulbs are blooming, combining beautifully with freesias, ixia, and sparaxis from the same season.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zones 8–11 sow in fall for winter and spring bloom — nemophila performs best in cool weather and declines in summer heat.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool, moist soil in partial shade; baby blue eyes is a California native annual that produces cheerful sky-blue flowers with white centers on low spreading mounds of delicate ferny foliage from early spring through early summer. It is an excellent cool-season companion for spring bulbs and woodland edges where dappled shade keeps plants cool. In Gulf Coast and mild-winter gardens, fall sowing produces a carpet of blue flowers from November through March. Plants die back in summer heat and self-sow lightly to naturalize in suitable sites. Regular moisture during dry spells is the key to prolonging the bloom season.

common_name: Baby Doll Lotus (Dwarf White Bowl Lotus)
plant_note: Plant the tuber horizontally just beneath the soil surface in a wide, shallow container of heavy clay loam, then set the pot so 2 to 4 inches of water covers the soil in a sunny, warm, wind-sheltered spot.
directions: Lay the tuber horizontally just under the soil surface in a wide, shallow tub of heavy clay loam, being careful not to break the growing tip, then top the container with two to four inches of water in a warm, sheltered, sunny spot. This is one of the smallest lotus cultivars available, staying compact enough for a half-barrel or large tub rather than requiring a full-sized pond. It produces small, creamy-white single blooms held on short stems above rounded blue-green leaves once the water has warmed in early summer, continuing intermittently into fall. Its dwarf scale makes it a popular choice for patio water gardens and for gardeners wanting to try lotus culture without dedicating a large pond to it.

common_name: Baby Gem Boxwood (Compact Slow-Growing Dwarf Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Baby Gem is a compact, slow-growing Japanese boxwood selection that requires less frequent shearing than most boxwood cultivars to hold a small, tidy form, making it useful for low edging and small-scale formal plantings.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun with afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9. Baby Gem is a compact, naturally slow-growing boxwood selected to hold a small, dense, rounded shape with minimal pruning, making it an efficient choice for low edging, knot gardens, and small formal accents where a full-sized boxwood cultivar would quickly outgrow the space and require constant shearing. Its fine-textured, glossy, light-to-medium green foliage stays dense from the ground up, and the plant's naturally compact habit reduces the maintenance burden common to boxwood hedging. It tolerates Gulf South heat and humidity reasonably well with afternoon shade and sharp drainage, since boxwood roots are highly susceptible to root rot in wet soil. Watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest, treating with a systemic insecticide if infestation becomes heavy. Light shearing once or twice a season, if any, is usually sufficient to maintain its naturally tidy form.

common_name: Baby Moon Daffodil (Miniature Fragrant Late Yellow Jonquil)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; Baby Moon is a miniature, late-blooming, fragrant jonquilla daffodil well suited to naturalizing in warm climates.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Baby Moon bears small, clear yellow, sweetly fragrant flowers on very short stems, blooming later than most daffodils in a miniature jonquilla form that fits neatly into rock gardens, containers, and the front of a border. As a jonquilla-type it tends to naturalize and perennialize especially well in mild-winter climates like the Gulf South, where many large trumpet daffodils fail to return reliably. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

plant_note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in warm, moist medium or in water; baby rubber plant is very easy to propagate and is one of the most forgiving houseplants for indoor culture. It tolerates occasional underwatering (its thick leaves store moisture) and low light, but resents overwatering — allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings. In zones 10–12 it grows outdoors as a shade-loving groundcover or border plant.
directions: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in filtered shade outdoors in zones 10–12; baby rubber plant is one of the most reliably successful and forgiving houseplants in cultivation — a Central and South American tropical native producing thick, rounded, deeply glossy, dark-green leaves on compact, upright to spreading stems that create a neat, controlled, lush mound of tropical foliage in indoor environments. The fleshy, somewhat succulent leaves store moisture and allow the plant to tolerate periods of drought far better than most non-succulent houseplants, making it an excellent choice for occasional-waterers and forgetful gardeners. It thrives in the low-to-medium indirect light typical of indoor environments and in the higher humidity of kitchens and bathrooms. Variegated cultivars are widely available, including 'Variegata' (cream and green marbled leaves), making the genus among the most popular of all houseplant groups. In tropical zones it grows as a semi-succulent shade groundcover. Easy to propagate from stem cuttings placed directly in moist potting mix. It is closely related to the ornamental pepper family (Piperaceae) and its genus contains over 1,000 species.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; baby sage blooms most heavily from summer through fall, and a hard cut-back in late winter promotes vigorous new growth.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; baby sage is a compact, woody-based subshrub native to Mexico and Arizona that is one of the finest ornamental sages for Gulf Coast and Southwest gardens, producing small, blackcurrant-scented leaves and racemes of two-lipped flowers in brilliant cherry-red, ruby, pink, or the famous bicolor pattern of 'Hot Lips' (red upper lip, white lower lip that reverts to pure red in heat). Blooms nearly year-round in mild climates, from late spring through frost. Hummingbirds visit the flowers constantly. Cut back to 6–12 inches above ground in late winter to promote vigorous new growth. Extremely drought-resistant once established. 'Hot Lips' is the most widely grown selection; 'Cerro Potosi' (true cherry-red) is a classic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or small pots in spring in partial to full shade in consistently moist, well-drained soil; Baby Tears spreads rapidly by creeping stems to form a dense carpet and can become invasive in moist, shaded garden beds in zone 9. In zone 9a, it may be killed back by hard frost but resprouts from the roots in spring; in zone 9b-10 it is evergreen year-round. Excellent for filling between stepping stones in shaded paths, in terrariums, and as a living groundcover in containers beneath shade trees.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; Baby Tears cannot tolerate drought and will brown and die rapidly if the soil dries out, but equally cannot tolerate waterlogged conditions — the ideal is consistently moist soil that never dries or stands in water. Soleirolia soleirolii is a tiny, delicate, creeping perennial native to the islands of Corsica, Sardinia, and surrounding western Mediterranean, producing a dense, bright green to chartreuse, mossy carpet of minute, round, 1/4-inch leaves on thread-like, branching stems that root at every node. The effect of a well-established planting is an unbroken, emerald velvet carpet that perfectly covers soil, fills gaps between paving stones, and softens harsh edges in shaded garden spaces. The plant spreads steadily by its rooting stems to fill available space; once established in suitable moist, shaded conditions it requires no care other than occasional trimming at the edges. Baby Tears is one of the finest plants for creating a fresh, lush, mossy effect in shaded terrarium and vivarium plantings where it thrives in the humid enclosure. Also available in gold ('Aurea') and silver variegated ('Variegata') forms.

common_name: Baby Tut Papyrus (Compact Miniature Egyptian Papyrus)
plant_note: Grow in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy garden soil so the crown sits at or just below the water's surface, or in a small container kept constantly saturated; Baby Tut is the most compact of the dwarf papyrus selections, well suited to small water features and tabletop containers.
directions: Set potted divisions into a submerged aquatic container of heavy garden soil with the crown at or just below the waterline, or grow it in a small pot kept constantly saturated in a saucer of water. Baby Tut is the smallest of the dwarf Egyptian papyrus selections, forming a tidy clump of slender stems only a foot or so tall topped with miniature mop-like tufts, making it practical for a small tabletop water garden, the shallow margin of a compact pond, or a mixed container where full-sized papyrus would overwhelm the planting. Its diminutive scale doesn't reduce its need for constant moisture, since papyrus in any size still wants its roots sitting in water or fully saturated soil at all times to thrive. Outside its hardy range, grow it as a warm-season annual or bring the pot indoors for winter, keeping it in a water-filled saucer on a bright windowsill.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil; baby's breath requires very well-drained soil and full sun and will not tolerate heavy, acidic, or wet conditions. Amend acid soils with lime before planting.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; baby's breath produces enormous clouds of tiny white or pale pink flowers on airy, branching stems from early to midsummer that are indispensable as a filler in fresh and dried flower arrangements. The delicate, misty appearance belies a tough, long-lived perennial that thrives in poor, dry, alkaline soil where many plants fail. Cutting stems regularly for arrangements encourages continuous blooming. For drying, harvest stems when flowers are fully open and hang upside-down in bundles. The cultivar 'Bristol Fairy' (double-flowered) is the most widely grown; 'Perfecta' has especially large double flowers. Best suited to zones 3–7; may be short-lived in humid hot climates.

common_name: BabyWing White Begonia (Compact Orchid-Flowered Interspecific Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade or sun; BabyWing White is a compact interspecific hybrid begonia bearing large, orchid-like white flowers on a tidy 12-15 inch plant.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade or sun, watering to keep soil evenly moist without becoming soggy. BabyWing White, an interspecific hybrid bred by PanAmerican Seed, bears unusually large, pure white, orchid-like flowers held above glossy dark green foliage on a compact, well-branched plant, a smaller-scale growth habit than the taller Whopper and Dragon Wing hybrid begonias in the same interspecific group. It blooms nonstop from planting through frost with no deadheading required, holding up well to summer heat and humidity, and performs equally well in a shaded bed, a partly sunny border, or a container. It is essentially maintenance-free once established, needing only regular watering during dry spells; treat as an annual outside its tender perennial zone range.

common_name: Babylon Bronze Dahlia (Giant Copper-Bronze Dinner-Plate Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; stake tall plants at planting time since the giant blooms are heavy.
directions: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost, and stake plants at planting time since the massive flower heads weigh down the stems in wind and rain. Part of the Babylon series of giant dinner-plate dahlias, Babylon Bronze produces flowers up to 10 inches across in warm copper-bronze and burnt-orange tones that deepen toward the center, making a bold, dramatic statement in the back of a cutting garden or mixed border. Pinch the growing tip early to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant, and disbud surrounding side buds if the largest possible single blooms are the goal. In zones colder than 8, lift tubers after the first light frost blackens the foliage and store in a cool, dry, frost-free place over winter.

plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Babylon is one of the largest-flowered crocosmia cultivars available, with individual blooms notably bigger than most named selections.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Babylon produces some of the largest individual flowers in the genus, bearing arching sprays of bold orange-red, trumpet-shaped blooms considerably bigger than most named crocosmia cultivars, held above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer. Its outsized flowers make a strong architectural statement in the border and are a favorite of hummingbirds, as well as an excellent long-lasting cut flower.
