Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; seeds germinate in cool soil and young plants are frost hardy. For fall bloom, sow again in late summer.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/4 in deep in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked. Bachelor buttons resent transplanting due to a taproot and grow best when started in place. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong blooming, or allow a few to set seed for natural reseeding. Plants decline in summer heat; a second sowing in late summer yields a flush of fall bloom in cool climates.

common_name: Bachelor's Button Blue Boy (Classic Deep Blue Annual Cornflower)
plant_note: Direct sow in place (bachelor's button does not transplant well); sow in fall for zone 9 winter and spring bloom — seeds germinate readily in cool, moist soil and seedlings tolerate hard frost. In zone 9, sow September–November for bloom January–April. Bachelor's button also responds well to succession sowing every 3 weeks for extended bloom. The brilliant blue color of 'Blue Boy' is among the truest, deepest blues available in garden annuals — a rarer and more saturated blue than most flowers that claim to be blue.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface or barely covered in fall in zone 9; thin to 8–12 inches. Bachelor's Button 'Blue Boy' (also called Cornflower) is a classic annual flower producing deeply pigmented, true-blue, button-shaped double flowers on slender, upright, gray-green stems — one of the few annual flowers that achieves a genuinely vivid blue rather than the bluish-purple that most 'blue' flowers actually are. The deep ultramarine-blue of 'Blue Boy' is the defining color of the species and one of the most sought-after flower colors in gardening. Bachelor's buttons are among the most carefree, self-maintaining annuals in the cool-season garden: they germinate readily in cool, even cold soil; tolerate hard frost; grow without special care in lean soil; and self-seed prolifically to return year after year without replanting. The common name 'Cornflower' reflects the plant's European origin as a weed of grain fields (corn in the British sense, meaning wheat) where the blue flowers appeared among cereal crops — a cultural and agricultural history that makes bachelor's buttons a significant plant in European folk traditions. The flowers make excellent fresh and dried cut flowers, the blue color lasting well when dried.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness; seed needs darkness and cool to germinate.
directions: 'Back to Black' bears compact plants covered in tiny three-quarter-inch flowers of the deepest purple, so dark they appear jet black. Start seed indoors in darkness at cool temperatures, since viola seed germinates best without light. Grow in full sun to part shade, taking advantage of the cool weather of spring and fall when violas perform best. Use it as a spring bulb cover or for fall color once summer annuals fade. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and the flowers are edible for garnishing.

common_name: Bahama Senna (Chapman's Senna, Mexican Senna, Coastal Senna)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in full sun in well-drained, sandy to rocky, alkaline to neutral soil; Senna mexicana var. chapmanii (Chapman's Senna) is the native Florida variety — found naturally in pine rocklands and coastal hammocks of Miami-Dade County and the Florida Keys. It is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 9b-12. Exceptionally drought and salt tolerant. The bright yellow flowers are a major nectar source and Senna species in general are the exclusive larval hosts for Cloudless Sulphur (Phoebis sennae) and Sleepy Orange (Eurema nicippe) butterfly caterpillars. Propagate from seed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy, rocky, or alkaline soil — Bahama Senna is exceptionally drought and salt-tolerant once established and thrives in the challenging coastal and limestone rock conditions of South Florida where many other ornamental shrubs struggle. Senna mexicana is a compact, evergreen to semi-evergreen shrubby Senna native to the Caribbean (Bahamas, Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola) and southern Florida (Chapman's Senna / var. chapmanii, endemic to Miami-Dade County and the Keys) in the Fabaceae family. The plant produces pinnately compound leaves of 4–6 pairs of oval, gray-green leaflets and produces clusters of bright golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers at the branch tips through the warm months and intermittently year-round in zone 10-12. The flowers are followed by flattened, dark-brown seed pods. Bahama Senna is one of the most important butterfly host plants available for zone 9b-12 gardens: Senna species are the exclusive larval host plants for two of the most abundant and beautiful Florida butterflies — the large, brilliant yellow Cloudless Sulphur (Phoebis sennae) and the Sleepy Orange (Eurema nicippe) — both of which lay their eggs exclusively on Senna foliage and whose caterpillars feed on the leaves. A landscape with established Senna mexicana will be host to these butterflies throughout the warm months. An outstanding, low-maintenance native flowering shrub for coastal zone 9b-12 gardens. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Bahama Wild Coffee is a frost-tender native shade shrub suited to zones 9b–11 and an excellent understory plant under live oaks and tropical hardwoods in south Florida landscapes.
directions: Bahama Wild Coffee is a compact native evergreen shrub, native to the coastal hammocks and tropical hardwood forests of south Florida, the Keys, the Bahamas, and the Caribbean, where it grows as a common understory shrub beneath larger canopy trees in partial to full shade. Similar to Wild Coffee (Psychotria nervosa) but with smaller, shinier, privet-like leaves (hence the species epithet ligustrifolia, meaning privet-leaved), it produces small white flowers year-round that attract native bees and butterflies, followed by clusters of red berries that turn black and are avidly consumed by migratory warblers, thrushes, and robins in fall and winter. An outstanding native shade shrub for zone 9b–11 landscapes where its shade tolerance, modest size, year-round bloom, and exceptional wildlife value make it a versatile foundation plant, hedge component, or understory specimen. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; established plants tolerate brief drought but prefer consistent moisture.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil temperatures are consistently above 65°F; rake seed lightly into the top quarter inch of soil and keep the seedbed moist until germination, then reduce watering as the sward fills in.
directions: Broadcast seed at 5–10 lb per 1,000 sq ft after the last frost once soil is reliably warm, lightly raking it into the top quarter inch and rolling the seedbed to ensure good seed-to-soil contact. Bahia grass is the dominant turf and pasture grass of Florida and the Gulf Coast, prized for its exceptional drought tolerance and ability to thrive in the poor, sandy, acidic soils where other grasses fail. Once established, deep rhizomes and a dense root system allow it to survive extended dry periods with little or no supplemental irrigation, making it highly cost-effective for large lawns, roadsides, and pastures. Mow regularly to 3–4 inches to suppress the tall, forked seed stalks that emerge quickly in summer; no fertilizer is required on most native Gulf Coast soils.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bailey Compact is a smaller-growing selection of American cranberrybush viburnum.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Bailey Compact is a smaller-growing selection of the native American cranberrybush, bearing flat clusters of white spring flowers followed by bright red, tart, cranberry-like fruit that persists into winter and draws birds, all on a shrub considerably more compact than the straight species. Its manageable size fits foundation plantings and smaller landscapes better than full-size cranberrybush viburnum, while still producing a good crop of ornamental and wildlife-friendly fruit. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

plant_note: Plant this South American wax palm in full sun on well-drained soil in late spring, giving it wide open space to develop its stout gray trunk and stiff, waxy-blue crown.
directions: Plant this South American wax palm in full sun on well-drained soil in late spring, giving it wide open space to develop its stout gray trunk and stiff, waxy-blue palmate crown over many years. It tolerates seasonal flooding as well as periods of drought once its deep root system is established, making it useful in low-lying Gulf Coast landscapes. Space it well away from walkways since older leaf bases can be sharply toothed. Use it as a slow, long-lived specimen or avenue palm where a bold silvery silhouette is wanted.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in very well-drained, lean, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral desert soil in full sun; Baja fairy duster is a desert plant that requires excellent drainage and is damaged at temperatures below 28°F. In zone 9 it dies back in hard winters but resprouts vigorously from established roots. Supplemental watering every 2–3 weeks in summer promotes repeat blooming.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Baja fairy duster is a desert shrub native to the Baja California peninsula and Sonoran Desert that produces clouds of brilliant, brushy, red powder-puff flowers consisting almost entirely of long, bright-red stamens with no conspicuous petals — a classic desert flower form that has evolved specifically for hummingbird pollination. It blooms heavily in spring and fall with sporadic flowers between, providing critical nectar for migrating and resident hummingbirds during the desert seasons when few other plants are in bloom. The fine, bipinnate, semi-evergreen foliage has a soft, feathery texture. More cold-sensitive than the pink fairy duster (Calliandra eriophylla, which is already well-known in Arizona desert gardens), it is best suited to the warmer deserts and coastal warm-winter climates of zones 9b–11. Outstanding combined with desert willow (Chilopsis linearis), autumn sage (Salvia greggii), and other hummingbird-attracting desert plants.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; this fast-growing Mexican sage benefits from a full growing season to reach flowering size before fall bloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Baja fireworks sage grows quickly into a large, upright shrub with soft, velvety, gray-green leaves and dense spikes of rich rose-magenta to fuchsia flowers that open over an extended fall display, often continuing until the first hard frost. Its rapid growth rate and heavy fall bloom make it a favorite for adding late-season color and hummingbird activity when many other perennials have finished flowering. Give it full sun for the most compact, floriferous growth, though it also performs well with afternoon shade in the hottest climates. Cut the woody framework back hard after a killing frost and mulch the crown, since new growth from the base each spring produces the strongest, most floriferous stems for the coming season.

plant_note: Direct sow on bare, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in fall; scarify or soak seeds to break seed coat dormancy before sowing into desert wildflower beds or native mixes.
directions: Bajada Lupine is one of the smallest native annual lupines in North America, forming low, dense clusters of tiny palmate leaves and producing small but charming spikes of lavender to bicolored blue-and-white flowers across sandy bajadas, desert flats, and gravelly washes of the Mojave and Sonoran deserts in winter and early spring. It is a cheerful and common participant in California desert superbloom events and mixes well with other small desert annuals such as desert bluebell and desert gold poppy. Sow seeds in fall directly onto bare, dry, sandy or gravelly, freely draining soil in full sun; scarify or soak seeds overnight before planting to speed germination. This species self-sows readily in suitable conditions and is widely available through California native seed suppliers for use in native and desert wildflower mixes.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Baker's anthurium is a compact epiphyte well suited to a hanging basket or mounted display.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Baker's anthurium is a compact epiphyte well suited to a hanging basket or mounted display. Long, narrow, leathery, strap-shaped leaves radiate outward from a short stem in a fountain-like rosette, quite different from the broad heart-shaped leaves of the florist's anthurium, and mature plants produce small greenish spathes followed by decorative clusters of bright orange-red berries that persist for months. Native to Central American cloud forests, where it grows as an epiphyte on tree branches, it appreciates the same loose, fast-draining, orchid-bark-based mix and bright, filtered light as other epiphytic anthuriums. Water when the mix approaches dryness, maintain high humidity, and avoid dense, water-retentive potting soil that encourages root rot.

subcategory: Gulf Coast native deciduous conifer swamp tree
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root transplants in early spring in full sun in moist to wet, acid, well-drained to seasonally flooded soil in zone 4–11; Bald Cypress is the quintessential tree of the Gulf Coast and Deep South — native from Delaware to Texas in lowland swamps, river floodplains, and bayou margins — producing graceful, feathery, deciduous foliage that turns brilliant orange-russet in fall, and distinctive 'cypress knees' (pneumatophores) when growing in standing water.
directions: Plant Taxodium distichum in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil — it tolerates standing water, drought once established, alkaline soils, and urban conditions, making it one of the most adaptable large trees in its range; young trees benefit from regular watering for the first 1–2 years, after which they become remarkably tough and self-sufficient. Bald Cypress is among the most iconic trees of the American South — the defining image of Gulf Coast bayous, cypress swamps, and river floodplains — yet it is equally at home in ordinary garden soil and among the most pest- and disease-resistant of all large deciduous trees. Growing 50–70 feet tall with a buttressed base, strongly vertical form, and spectacular fine-textured, feathery foliage, it provides outstanding summer shade and brilliant fall color (unusual for a tree this adapted to tropical Gulf Coast conditions). The famous 'knees' — woody projections from roots that emerge above the waterline — appear primarily in flooded conditions and are thought to provide oxygen to waterlogged roots. Ancient specimens exceed 600 years old; the Montezuma Cypress (Taxodium mucronatum) of Mexico is related and evergreen. Bald Cypress is an ideal large specimen tree for rain gardens, pond edges, low-lying areas, and urban street plantings where other trees fail.

common_name: Baldcypress (Iconic Gulf South Deciduous Conifer, Adaptable from Wetlands to Upland Sites)
plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in early spring; Baldcypress (Taxodium distichum) is one of the most adaptable, long-lived, and ecologically important native trees of the Gulf South and southeastern United States. Despite its association with swamps and bayous — where it produces the famous knees (pneumatophores) that rise above the water surface — Baldcypress grows well in average well-drained garden soils without any standing water, and is significantly more drought-tolerant than its wetland reputation suggests once established. In zone 9, Baldcypress is fully hardy and thrives without special care. The tree is deciduous, losing its soft, ferny needles each fall in a display of russet-orange to cinnamon-red fall color — one of the few conifers with brilliant fall color. The distinctive flat-topped, feathery foliage, pyramidal young form that develops a broad, spreading crown with age, and fluted buttressed trunk at maturity make Baldcypress one of the most architecturally distinctive trees in the American South.
directions: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in spring. Mulch well and water in establishment year. Adaptable to wet or well-drained sites. Baldcypress (Taxodium distichum) is among the most ecologically significant and historically important trees of the American South — a tree so deeply associated with the Gulf South landscape that it appears in literature, art, photography, and the cultural imagination of the region as a symbol of the bayous, swamps, and river bottoms that characterize Louisiana, Mississippi, and coastal Texas and Florida. The species' outstanding longevity (trees over 1,000 years old have been documented, and ancient specimens in swamps date to several thousand years) and the extraordinary buttressed trunks and pneumatophore knees of trees growing in standing water make ancient Baldcypress groves among the most dramatic natural features of the Gulf South. Baldcypress is also one of the most valuable and prized timber species in North American history — the naturally durable, rot-resistant wood (due to cypressene, a natural preservative compound in the heartwood) was used for everything from coffins and cisterns to boat building and historic structures throughout the Southeast, and old-growth cypress timber salvaged from ancient swamps or river bottoms remains highly prized. For home landscapes, Baldcypress provides exceptional value: fast growth in youth (2–3 feet per year in good conditions), extreme long-term durability, stunning fall color (unusual in a conifer), adaptability to wet or dry sites, excellent wildlife value (ducks, wading birds, and many other species use cypress swamps), and a unique, irreplaceable aesthetic that connects home gardens to the Gulf South landscape tradition.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; baldhip rose is one of the few native roses that thrives in woodland shade rather than full sun.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; baldhip rose is one of the few native roses that thrives in woodland shade rather than full sun. Small, delicate, single pink flowers open in late spring on slender, sparsely thorned canes with fine, fern-like compound leaves, followed by small orange-red rose hips that characteristically drop their sepals early, leaving a smooth, 'bald' hip that gives the species its common name. Native to coniferous forest understories along the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to California, it is unusual among wild roses for genuinely thriving in shade, making it a valuable native shrub for a woodland garden where sun-loving roses would fail to flower. It needs little care beyond occasional thinning of old canes and provides good wildlife cover and berries for birds through fall and winter.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into prepared soil, lightly pressing into the surface and allowing winter cold to stratify seeds naturally for spring germination.
directions: Sow seeds in fall directly into well-drained, gritty soil in a partially shaded location, pressing them lightly into the surface without covering, as light assists germination. The deeply lobed, glossy dark-green leaves emerge in spring, and established plants will send up impressive 4- to 5-foot spikes of white and purple hooded flowers in summer. Balkan bear's breech spreads more slowly than Acanthus mollis and is notably more cold-hardy, making it a better choice for gardens in zones 5 and 6. Once established, it tolerates drought and dry shade but dislikes waterlogged soils, especially in winter.

plant_note: Attach individual rosettes or clumps to tree branches or mounts using monofilament; Ball Moss naturally seeds itself and colonizes tree bark, utility wires, and fences through wind-dispersed seeds. No soil or watering required once established — it is a true atmospheric bromeliad.
directions: Ball Moss is a native atmospheric bromeliad, native to the southeastern United States, Central America, South America, and the Caribbean, growing as an epiphyte on tree branches, utility wires, and even bare rock and fences in zones 8–11 — the silver-gray, ball-shaped clusters of recurved, scale-covered leaves are a familiar sight on live oaks and other trees throughout the Gulf Coast, Texas, and Florida. Often confused with Spanish moss (Tillandsia usneoides), Ball Moss grows in compact, round clusters rather than draping curtains, and is similarly harmless to its host tree — it uses the tree only for support and draws no nutrients from it, absorbing water and minerals entirely from the air and rain through its silvery trichome-covered leaves. Tiny, inconspicuous lavender flowers appear on slender stalks in late summer, followed by elongated seed capsules that split to release seeds attached to silky hairs (like dandelion seeds) that carry them on the wind to new hosts. Ball Moss requires no care, no soil, and no watering — simply attach a clump to rough bark in a bright location and allow it to grow and self-seed.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost; calendula prefers cool weather.
directions: Sow Ball's Orange calendula a quarter inch deep around your last frost date, as it germinates best in cool soil. This heirloom pot marigold bears fully double, brilliant orange blooms on sturdy stems, both edible and prized for herbal salves. Deadhead regularly to prolong flowering, and pick petals for teas or garnishes. It reseeds happily and often gives a second flush as temperatures cool in fall.

common_name: Ballerina Zinnia (Soft Pastel-Pink Blend Fully Double Blooms)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Ballerina bears a soft pastel-pink blend of large, fully double blooms, a modern cut-flower breeding introduction.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches. Ballerina bears large, fully double blooms in a soft blend of pastel-pink tones, a gentler color palette than the bold primary colors of many classic zinnia cultivars, well suited to romantic or wedding-themed cutting gardens. Plants bloom heavily from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading or harvesting to encourage continuous production. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow outdoors in early spring; blooms appear the second year from seed.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, just barely covering them, since light aids germination; thin or transplant to 12–18 in spacing. Balloon flowers are late to emerge in spring — mark their location to avoid accidentally digging the fleshy taproot. Deadhead spent flowers to extend the blooming period through summer, and avoid dividing since the taproot resents disturbance. Plants are long-lived and improve in beauty over many years with minimal care.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; balm-leaved archangel is considerably clumping and non-invasive compared to the spreading deadnettle (L. purpureum) and yellow archangel (L. galeobdolon) — it stays in a well-behaved, gradually expanding clump and is not a runner or aggressive spreader.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; balm-leaved archangel is a Southern European woodland perennial dead-nettle (Lamiaceae) that is considerably more refined and better-behaved than its commonly grown relatives — it produces a clump-forming, upright, non-spreading, bushy habit (unlike the invasively spreading yellow archangel) with large, broadly oval, prominently veined, soft-hairy, dark-green, nettle-like leaves (resembling Melissa officinalis in both leaf form and texture) and in late spring produces whorls of large, two-lipped, rich deep-pink to rosy-magenta flowers considerably larger and more showy than the typical small-flowered deadnettles. The combination of large, attractive, deep-rose flowers in a shade-tolerant, non-invasive, clumping perennial is unusual and valuable. It dies back after summer dormancy in hot climates but regrows in fall. Goes dormant in summer heat. Semi-evergreen in mild winters. Excellent as a refined spring-blooming shade perennial for zone 4–9 woodland gardens where non-invasive groundcovers are needed.

common_name: Balmy Pink Bee Balm (Dwarf Non-Flopping Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Balmy Pink is a dwarf bee balm bred with sturdy, non-flopping stems and good powdery mildew resistance, a compact, tidy option for a Gulf South pollinator border.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Balmy Pink is a dwarf bee balm cultivar noted for sturdy, upright stems that resist the flopping common in taller Monarda varieties, along with good resistance to the powdery mildew that often disfigures bee balm foliage in humid summer conditions. It bears the classic shaggy, tubular pink flowers over a compact, tidy mound that suits a smaller border or container planting. Its dwarf habit and disease resistance make it easier to keep looking attractive through a full Gulf South growing season than many heirloom bee balm types. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and provide good air circulation to further reduce mildew pressure.

common_name: Balmy Purple Beebalm (Compact Mildew-Resistant Bee Balm)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing good air circulation.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing good air circulation between plants to reduce powdery mildew. Balmy Purple is part of a compact bee balm series bred for a dense, tidy, mildew-resistant habit far smaller than traditional bee balm, staying under 18 inches while still producing the same tubular purple flower heads that hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies rely on through summer. Its small scale fits border edges and mixed containers where full-size bee balm would be too large, while its improved disease resistance keeps foliage cleaner through humid summers than many older Monarda didyma cultivars. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and airflow.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; balsam fir grows naturally in cold, moist coniferous and mixed forests of the Northeast, requiring cool, moist conditions — it does not tolerate heat or dry soils. Best for zones 3–5.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; balsam fir is the Christmas tree of the Northeast — the sweet, clean, resinous fragrance of balsam fir needles is the quintessential Christmas scent, and the tree holds its needles exceptionally well after cutting. The species forms the upper forest zone of the Appalachians from New England to the peaks of the Smoky Mountains, and the classic boreal forest landscape of northern Canada. Balsam sap collected from bark blisters was historically used as a waterproof cement, medicinally as a wound treatment, and in optical instruments as 'Canada balsam' for mounting microscope slides. The flat needles with their two distinct white stomatal bands (underside) are characteristic of firs. Short-lived in the landscape (40–70 years) compared to other conifers, and best in the cool, moist conditions of the upper Midwest and New England.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in late winter to early spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; balsam poplar grows naturally along stream banks, lake shores, and wet floodplains in boreal forests across Canada and the northern US. Very fast growing but needs moist soil.
directions: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun along water features, floodplains, and wet areas; balsam poplar is the most widespread tree of the boreal forest, forming groves along rivers and lake shores from Alaska to Newfoundland. Its common name 'balm of Gilead' reflects the intensely sweet, balsamic fragrance of the opening buds in spring — one of the most distinctive and beloved spring fragrances of the northern forest. The sticky, resinous buds have been used in traditional medicine as a cough remedy and wound herb, and the bud resin has been used by bees (as propolis) and by indigenous peoples as a wound plaster. A very fast-growing, large tree requiring moist to wet soil and ample space. The female trees produce cottony seed fluff that can be messy; male cuttings are often preferred for planting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Bambino alocasia's compact, dwarf size makes it well suited to a windowsill or small container display.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Bambino alocasia's compact, dwarf size makes it well suited to a windowsill or small container display. Small, narrow, dark green, arrow-shaped leaves with pale silvery-green veining grow on a naturally dwarf, compact hybrid that stays well under a foot and a half tall even at maturity, offering the same striking arrow-shaped alocasia silhouette as larger relatives on a scale appropriate for a small pot or tabletop display. Its manageable size makes it one of the more practical alocasia choices for a limited indoor growing space, a terrarium-adjacent shelf, or a mixed shade container where full-sized elephant ears would quickly overwhelm the display. Provide consistent warmth and high humidity, protect from direct sun which scorches the leaves, and allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; bamboo muhly is native to Arizona, New Mexico, and Mexico and tolerates both drought and light shade, making it versatile for difficult spots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; bamboo muhly is a large, feathery ornamental grass that is often mistaken for young bamboo at first glance — the numerous, fine, arching stems bear tiny delicate leaves and produce an airy, light-filtering visual effect remarkably similar to a small bamboo clump but without the invasive spreading habit. It grows naturally in rocky canyon bottoms and streamside slopes in the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Desert region, where it tolerates both drought and periodic flooding. Unlike most ornamental grasses that are grown primarily for fall plumes, bamboo muhly is grown mainly for its outstanding texture and motion — a billowing cloud of delicate stems that moves with the slightest breeze. It tolerates light shade and makes a superb screen or specimen. Cut back to 12 inches in late winter.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Bamboo palm is one of the most cold-sensitive chamaedorea palms — protect from temperatures below 32°F, which can cause significant damage to the foliage and growing points.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Bamboo palm is a multi-stemmed, clumping, shade-tolerant tropical palm native to Mexico and Central America — producing slender, cane-like stems with narrow, pinnately divided, deep-green fronds that create a lush, tropical, bamboo-like effect in shade gardens and interiors. The slender stems, dense clustering habit, and finely divided fronds make it one of the most elegant tropical palms for shaded outdoor gardens in zone 10–12 and one of the finest indoor palms for zone 9 and colder regions. As a landscape plant in zone 10, Bamboo palm creates outstanding screening, privacy hedges, and tropical atmosphere in partial to full shade under trees and near buildings. The palm is exceptionally tolerant of low light — one of the most shade-tolerant palms in cultivation — and maintains attractive appearance in conditions too dark for most other landscape plants. In zone 9, it can be grown outdoors with protection from cold snaps and is excellent as a large container plant moved indoors during winter. It adapts well to indoor conditions — moderate light, regular watering, and good drainage produce vigorous indoor specimens. Provide regular balanced fertilizer during the growing season; avoid over-fertilizing, which can cause salt buildup in container culture.

common_name: Banana Boat Sedge (Golden Variegated Broadleaf Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions in moist to consistently wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Banana Boat is a slow-creeping, rhizomatous broadleaf sedge with wide, bright yellow leaves that scorch quickly in direct sun.
directions: Plant in moist to consistently wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, avoiding direct sun which quickly scorches the bright foliage. Banana Boat is a broad-leaved sedge unlike the fine-bladed carex most gardeners picture, producing wide, softly arching, glowing yellow leaves with a thin green edge that lend a bold, almost tropical texture to deeply shaded beds under trees and along shaded stream banks. It spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing patch rather than a tight clump, filling gaps between hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials over two or three seasons. It tolerates periodically wet soil better than most sedges, making it a useful choice for shaded low spots, and needs little care beyond removing winter-damaged foliage in early spring.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Banana Custard bears soft, creamy-yellow flowers, a gentler tone than the brighter gold of the wild mullein species.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since this rot-prone perennial declines quickly in heavy, wet soil. Banana Custard produces dense spikes of soft, creamy-yellow flowers with contrasting purple-mauve stamens over gray-green, felted foliage, a gentler, more muted tone than the brighter gold of common wild mullein. Its soft color blends easily into cottage-style plantings alongside pastel companions without dominating the color scheme. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage continued bloom over a long season from late spring into summer, and expect this hybrid mullein to be relatively short-lived, benefiting from occasional replacement or self-sown seedlings to maintain the planting over the years.

plant_note: Rest the cluster of banana-shaped storage tubers on top of the aquarium substrate rather than burying it, with only fine root hairs anchored below; burying the tubers causes them to rot.
directions: Native to spring-fed rivers and calm lakes of the southeastern United States, this small aquatic gets its common name from the cluster of banana-shaped tuberous roots it produces, which stores energy and anchors the plant without needing to be buried in substrate. Grown fully submersed in freshwater aquaria, it produces rounded, olive-green lily-pad-like leaves on long petioles under medium aquarium lighting; if left unpruned, leaves will reach the surface and float, so trim tall petioles regularly to keep the plant as a mid-ground species. It does not require CO2 injection but grows more vigorously with it. Propagate by dividing offshoot tuber clusters away from the main plant once they have their own leaves and roots.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in midsummer under mist or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; banana shrub is slow-growing but extremely long-lived and low-maintenance once established — it should not be heavily pruned as this removes the flowering wood and reduces the fragrant display.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; banana shrub (formerly Michelia figo, now reclassified as Magnolia figo) is a Chinese evergreen magnolia relative that has been a classic southern garden shrub for over a century — prized not for showy flowers but for the intensely, exotically sweet, banana-custard-like fragrance of its small, creamy-yellow, purple-edged, tulip-shaped flowers that are produced in abundance from spring through fall amid the dense, glossy, dark-green, leathery leaves. The flowers are small but individually so powerfully fragrant — a single established shrub can perfume an entire garden — that they are worth seeking out close up, where the heavy, tropical sweetness creates an extraordinary sensory experience disproportionate to the flower's size. Banana shrub grows as a dense, compact, slow-growing, rounded evergreen shrub with a formal, refined habit and requires minimal care. It tolerates partial shade well and is one of the most versatile and dependable fragrant shrubs for zone 7–11, performing reliably for decades with little attention. 'Port Wine' (deep-burgundy purple flowers with stronger fragrance) is an outstanding cultivar.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; banana shrub is a classic Deep South garden plant, reliably perennial in zones 7–10 and producing its delightfully banana-scented flowers in spring and summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; banana shrub is a classic evergreen shrub of the South, related to magnolias and producing small, creamy-yellow flowers edged in maroon-purple that emit an intense fragrance reminiscent of ripe bananas — particularly potent in warm, humid air. The fragrance carries considerable distance and can be detected from many feet away when the plant is in full bloom in spring and early summer. The evergreen foliage is attractive year-round. This plant has been grown in Southern gardens for well over a century and is among the most beloved fragrant shrubs for the warm-climate garden. In zone 9a it is a reliable, low-maintenance garden anchor that thrives with minimal care once established. A few individual flowers in a small vase can fill a room with fragrance.

plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil, unlike most crocus which prefer drier sites.
directions: Set corms 3-4 inches deep and about 3-4 inches apart in humus-rich soil that holds more moisture than a typical crocus bed, in light woodland shade or a partially shaded border. Unusual among crocuses for its lilac-lavender, iris-like flowers with three enlarged, deeply fringed inner petals, it blooms in autumn alongside its narrow grass-like leaves rather than before them. It is well suited to naturalizing at the edge of woodland gardens or beneath deciduous shrubs where soil stays cool and slightly damp. Established clumps slowly form drifts and provide a distinctive late-season nectar source for pollinators.

common_name: Bandana Lantana (Compact Mounding Landscape Lantana Series)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Bandana was bred for a compact, uniform mounding habit that stays tidier than older seed-grown lantana, making it well suited to mass plantings and containers as well as beds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, and avoid overwatering, since lantana is highly drought-tolerant once established and prone to root problems in soggy soil. Bandana is a vegetatively propagated landscape lantana series bred for a compact, dense, mounding habit and a wide range of vivid multicolor flower clusters that shift shades as they age, blooming nonstop from spring through frost and drawing butterflies heavily throughout the season. Its uniform size and tidy growth make it more predictable for mass landscape plantings than older seed-grown lantana cultivars, which can vary in vigor and habit, while retaining the same outstanding heat and drought tolerance the species is known for. In the coldest parts of its hardiness range it dies to the ground in winter and returns from the roots in spring; further north it is grown as a summer annual.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–11; Bangalow Palm is a fast-growing, elegant, slender-trunked rainforest palm native to the subtropical and tropical east coast of Australia (Queensland and New South Wales) — one of the most planted landscape palms in subtropical Australia, California, and similar warm climates for its graceful, tropical appearance, purple-lavender flower clusters, and red ornamental fruits.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Bangalow Palm establishes rapidly and grows relatively fast for a palm — water deeply and regularly in establishment and fertilize with slow-release palm fertilizer containing magnesium; does not tolerate salt spray or cold below 28°F. Archontophoenix cunninghamiana (Bangalow Palm, Piccabeen Palm, or King Palm) is a tall, slender-trunked, elegant feather palm native to the rainforest gullies, creek banks, and rainforest margins of coastal Queensland and New South Wales in eastern Australia, one of the most widely planted and popular landscape palms in subtropical Australia, Hawaii, California, South Florida, and warm Mediterranean climates worldwide. The palm is renowned for its extreme elegance: a straight, smooth, ring-marked trunk supporting a neat, compact crown of arching, pinnate fronds of deep green. In summer, spectacular pendant inflorescences emerge from below the crown shaft — large, branching clusters of small purple-to-lavender flowers that develop into masses of round, bright-red fruits. Bangalow Palms grow at a moderate pace in ideal conditions, reaching mature height of 40–50 feet, and are highly tolerant of partial shade — often planted beneath established tree canopy where many palms struggle — as well as full sun once established. Naturalized and occasionally invasive in parts of Hawaii where it colonizes moist valleys; check local invasive lists.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; banjine is native to the coastal heaths and scrubs of southwestern Western Australia where it receives high rainfall but excellent drainage. It blooms in spring, producing dense, rounded heads of rich rose-pink tubular flowers. It does not tolerate root disturbance well — plant in final position without repotting. Sensitive to overwatering and poor drainage.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; banjine (or rice flower) is a neat, compact, mounding Australian shrub from the coastal heathlands of southwestern Western Australia — producing in spring dense, rounded terminal clusters of many small, tubular, four-petaled flowers in a rich, warm, rosy-pink to deep pink, each small flower head about an inch across and the clusters collectively covering the plant in an abundant pink display. The common name 'rice flower' comes from the appearance of the dense, rounded, tightly packed flower clusters resembling a cluster of tiny rice grains dipped in pink. The compact, neat, naturally mounding growth habit and glossy, small, dark-green leaves provide attractive structure year-round, and the plant maintains a tidy, ornamental character without significant pruning. It is in the Thymelaeaceae family (the same family as daphne), and like daphne, it has a reputation for sensitivity to site conditions — it resents transplanting, requires excellent drainage, and is unforgiving of waterlogged conditions. In the right position in zones 9–11 Mediterranean-climate or warm coastal gardens, however, it is a rewarding, long-lived, compact ornamental shrub.

common_name: Bantel's Sensation Snake Plant (Narrow White-Striped Sansevieria)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Bantel's Sensation bears narrow leaves with fine, vertical white-and-green striping, a more delicate look than common snake plant cultivars.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix. Bantel's Sensation forms slender, stiffly upright leaves finely striped in white and dark green, a more delicate, refined texture than the broader, more heavily mottled foliage of common snake plant cultivars, giving it a distinctive vertical, grass-like presence. Like other snake plants it tolerates low light, infrequent watering, and general neglect exceptionally well, making it one of the most forgiving houseplants available, and older leaves may occasionally revert to plain green, which should be removed at the base to keep the clump true to type. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent.

common_name: Barataria Louisiana Iris (Bright Rose-Pink Midseason Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Barataria, named for the Louisiana bay and historic pirate stronghold, bears bright rose-pink flowers in midseason.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Barataria, named for the historic Louisiana bay and bayou region south of New Orleans, bears bright, clear rose-pink flowers on a well-branched plant blooming in midseason, adding a vivid pink note to the Louisiana iris color range that runs heavily toward blues and purples. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Plant bulb offsets with the neck at or just above soil level into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Barbados lily is the wild species behind many hybrid amaryllis and naturalizes readily and persistently in Gulf Coast and Florida gardens.
directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Barbados lily is a wild, naturalized amaryllis species long established around old homesteads and cemeteries throughout the Gulf South and Florida, sending up tall, leafless stalks topped with two to four trumpet-shaped, orange-red flowers in spring, smaller and more numerous per stalk than showy hybrid amaryllis. Strap-like leaves follow the flowers and persist through summer before dying back for a winter dormancy in cooler parts of its range, though it stays evergreen in essentially frost-free gardens. It is tougher and considerably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than most florist hybrid amaryllis, multiplying steadily by offsets into substantial naturalized clumps that can persist and rebloom for decades with virtually no care. Leave clumps undisturbed for the best flowering, dividing only when a planting becomes overcrowded and bloom noticeably declines.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy prairie soil in full sun; Barbara buttons is a native prairie perennial of the Texas and Oklahoma coastal prairie that is essentially unknown in horticulture despite its charming flowers and adaptability to lean soils — it is an excellent wildflower for prairie-style gardens in the Gulf South.
directions: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Barbara buttons self-seeds modestly in suitable prairie conditions. Marshallia caespitosa (Barbara buttons or white prairie marshallia) is a small, delightful native prairie perennial found in dry, rocky, and sandy prairies from Texas and Oklahoma east to Tennessee — one of the least-known and most charming small wildflowers of the southern prairies. The plant produces low, tufted rosettes of narrow, spatula-shaped leaves and slender, 8-to-20-inch, leafless flower stems each topped with a single, globular, 1-to-1.5-inch flower head composed entirely of white, tubular disc florets (no ray florets) — resembling a small, white, powder-puff button with elongated, protruding style branches giving a fringe-like texture. The effect is unexpectedly refined and delicate for a prairie plant. Barbara buttons blooms in late spring (April–June) in zone 9 and is a quiet, elegant presence in prairie-style wildflower gardens. The flowers attract native bees and small butterflies. A genuinely underused native perennial deserving wider cultivation in southeastern prairies and dry, sunny garden borders.

common_name: Barbara Karst Bougainvillea (Classic Magenta-Red Everblooming Tropical Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average soil in full sun; bougainvilleas bloom most prolifically under slight water and fertilizer stress — avoid overwatering and excessive nitrogen which promote vegetative growth at the expense of flowering.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Barbara Karst is one of the most popular and widely planted bougainvillea cultivars for Gulf South gardens — a vigorous, large-scale vine producing brilliant magenta-red to cerise-red bracts (the showy colored structures surrounding the inconspicuous true flowers) through most of the year in frost-free conditions. In zone 9, Barbara Karst blooms most heavily in spring and fall when temperatures moderate; in winter (November–February) the vine may defoliate partially during cold spells and bloom is reduced. The brilliant magenta-red bract color is one of the most vivid in the warm-climate garden palette and creates an unmistakable tropical visual impact when the vine is in full bloom. Bougainvilleas bloom most prolifically under slight stress — dry-down periods between waterings, lean soil without excessive nitrogen, and root constriction (slightly root-bound in containers) all promote flower production over vegetative growth. This counterintuitive cultural requirement (bloom more when stressed) is the most important management principle for bougainvillea. The thorny stems require careful placement away from pedestrian areas. In zone 9, Barbara Karst may be killed to the ground by severe freezes but returns from the roots; cover with frost cloth during freezes below 28°F. Outstanding trained on walls, fences, and pergolas where the massive bloom display can be appreciated.

common_name: Barbara Mitchell Daylily (Award-Winning Pale Pink Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this cultivar is one of the most extensively propagated daylilies in commerce.
directions: Hybridized by Franklin and Curt Hardy and awarded the Stout Silver Medal in 1993, Barbara Mitchell bears large, heavily ruffled, pale pastel-pink blooms with a deeper pink watermark eye that hold up beautifully in heat and humidity. Grow it in enriched, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every few years to sustain heavy flowering. Because of its exceptional flower substance, vigor, and near-universal garden performance, it became one of the best-selling and most widely tissue-cultured daylily cultivars of its era, and it remains a standard-bearer for the modern pink daylily class.

common_name: Baron Girod de l'Ain Rose (Red Petals Edged White Hybrid Perpetual)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this 1897 Hybrid Perpetual sport is known for its distinctive white-picotee-edged red petals.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. A sport discovered in 1897, Baron Girod de l'Ain bears large, fragrant, deep red double blooms each irregularly edged in a crisp band of white, a striking picotee effect that makes every flower distinct and has kept the cultivar sought after by old-rose collectors ever since. Like other Hybrid Perpetuals it blooms mainly in a strong spring flush with some sporadic repeat later in the season. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering canes.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–11; Baronii Palm is a graceful, clustering, shade-adapted palm endemic to the rainforests of eastern and northwestern Madagascar — producing multiple slender canes topped by elegant arching fronds — one of the more cold-tolerant Dypsis species from Madagascar's highlands, performing well in zone 9 with protection.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Dypsis baronii is a clustering palm that produces new stems (suckers) from the base — more drought tolerant than many Dypsis species due to its highland Madagascar origin; water moderately and apply palm fertilizer twice yearly. Dypsis baronii (Baronii Palm or Madagascar Bamboo Palm) is a multi-stemmed, clustering palm endemic to Madagascar — one of the most palm-diverse countries on Earth, with over 170 endemic palm species — native to the humid forests of eastern and northwestern Madagascar at moderate elevations. The genus Dypsis (formerly split into Chrysalidocarpus and several other genera) is the largest palm genus in Madagascar. Dypsis baronii produces multiple slender, bamboo-like stems (1–2 inch diameter) in dense clusters, topped by graceful, arching, pinnate fronds with slightly arching, feathery leaflets — creating an elegant, clumping effect. Among the more cold-hardy Dypsis species available, it has performed in zone 9b with some protection in California and Gulf Coast gardens. The clustering habit and moderate size make it suitable for smaller gardens than the more commonly planted Areca Palm (Dypsis lutescens). Excellent as a privacy screen, garden accent, or container specimen in zone 9–11 subtropical gardens.

common_name: Baronne Prevost Rose (Extremely Hardy Antique Hybrid Perpetual)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Baronne Prevost, introduced in 1842, is an extremely cold-hardy Hybrid Perpetual rose that also performs well in warm Southern gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Baronne Prevost, introduced in 1842, is one of the earliest Hybrid Perpetual roses and remains prized for its extreme hardiness and large, deep rose-pink, flat, quartered blooms densely packed with petals in the old-fashioned style, carrying a strong classic rose fragrance. Its wide climate tolerance, from cold northern winters to hot Southern summers, has kept it a mainstay of heirloom rose collections for over 180 years. It blooms in a strong spring flush with some repeat through summer and fall, and benefits from richer soil and more regular feeding than tougher China or Tea roses. Prune moderately in late winter to shape and remove old wood, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage additional flowering.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in spring; barren strawberry is among the most tolerant and low-maintenance shade groundcovers for dry, difficult conditions under trees where grass will not grow.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; barren strawberry is a Central European native that superficially resembles a strawberry plant but produces no edible fruit — it is grown as an extremely tough, low-growing, semi-evergreen groundcover that spreads steadily by stolons to form dense, uniform mats of three-part, strawberry-like, glossy leaves that remain attractive through winter. Small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers appear in early spring before most other perennials emerge. It tolerates drier soil conditions than most shade groundcovers, making it exceptionally useful under dense, dry-rooted trees like Norway maples and Norway spruce where few other plants survive. Essentially maintenance-free once established — no deadheading, no division required for years. An underused, genuinely excellent shade groundcover that deserves wider planting. Also useful on dry slopes and as lawn replacement under trees in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; epimediums tolerate dry shade under established trees better than almost any other perennial groundcover. Do not disturb established plantings unnecessarily — they improve dramatically over years.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; epimedium (barrenwort, bishop's hat) is arguably the most underused and underrated of all shade groundcovers — a slowly spreading, low-maintenance perennial that tolerates dry shade under established tree roots better than any other herbaceous perennial. The attractive, heart-shaped leaflets are often mottled with red or bronze when young, and the dainty four-petaled flowers resembling tiny hats or butterflies in yellow, pink, white, red, or bicolor appear in spring. E. x versicolor 'Sulphureum' has pale yellow flowers and reliably semi-evergreen foliage in mild winters. Once established, epimediums are nearly drought proof and essentially pest-free. Cut old foliage to the ground in late winter before new growth begins to showcase the spring flowers. A plant that rewards patience — increasingly impressive each year after establishment.

common_name: Barrett Browning Daffodil (Early White-and-Orange Small-Cup Daffodil)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; Barrett Browning is an early-blooming small-cup daffodil with a strong white-and-orange contrast.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Barrett Browning bears crisp white petals surrounding a small, frilled orange-red cup, a bold contrast held on sturdy stems that open among the earliest daffodils each spring. Its early bloom timing and reliable performance have kept it a garden favorite for mass plantings and naturalizing. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

common_name: Bartered Bride Joe Pye Weed (White-Flowered Spotted Joe-Pye Weed)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Bartered Bride is a white-flowered sport of spotted Joe-Pye weed discovered at the Chicago Botanic Garden, otherwise similar in scale and habit to the species.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Bartered Bride is a striking white-flowered selection of spotted Joe-Pye weed, discovered as a naturally occurring color break and named for its unusual pure white, domed flower clusters that stand out against the green foliage rather than the mauve-pink typical of the species. It reaches the same imposing size as wild spotted Joe-Pye weed and draws the same heavy traffic from swallowtails, monarchs, and countless bees during its late-summer bloom, making it a good way to add color contrast to a large pollinator planting, rain garden, or pond edge without losing habitat value. Give it plenty of room and reliably moist soil, since it will decline quickly in dry conditions, and divide clumps in spring every several years if a larger planting is desired. Leave seed heads standing into winter for visual interest and songbird forage.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring onto the surface of moist, sandy or peaty soil; seeds are tiny and light-dependent for germination — do not cover, and keep the seedbed consistently moist until plants are established.
directions: Bartram's Rosegentian is a Florida endemic perennial found in wet flatwoods, moist savannas, and seepage slopes, making it one of the largest-flowered members of its genus with vivid rose-pink blooms up to 1.5 inches across appearing in summer and fall. It requires consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soils in full sun — conditions that mimic its natural flatwoods habitat — and will not tolerate prolonged drought or alkaline garden soils. Sow seeds on the surface of moist, lean growing media in spring without covering, as the fine seeds require light for germination; transplant young seedlings carefully once they reach an inch tall, as the taproot is sensitive to disturbance. This species is an important component of Florida flatwoods wildflower restorations and is a significant nectar source for native bees and butterflies during its long summer-to-fall bloom period.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Bartzella is an intersectional (Itoh) hybrid, crossing herbaceous peony with tree peony parentage, bearing enormous, semi-double to double, clear lemon-yellow flowers with a faint red flare at the base of each petal and a light citrus fragrance. Unlike most herbaceous peonies its strong, woody-based stems hold the huge blooms upright without staking, and its foliage stays clean and attractive well after bloom into fall. Itoh hybrids tolerate more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight Paeonia lactiflora cultivars, performing reliably into zone 9 with some afternoon shade, and die back to the ground each winter like an herbaceous peony rather than persisting as a woody shrub.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown specimens in spring into very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in bright light with some direct sun; Euphorbia obesa is dioecious (separate male and female plants), and since it is a slow-growing, vulnerable South African species, only purchase nursery-propagated plants rather than wild-collected material.
directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun, in very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix, watering sparingly and only once the soil has dried out completely. Baseball plant is a slow-growing South African succulent whose nearly spherical, leafless, ribbed stem is patterned with alternating bands of green and grayish-purple that closely mimic the stitching of a baseball, an appearance that has made it a favorite novelty succulent for collectors and windowsill growers alike. Unlike spiny cacti, it is entirely unarmed but still exudes a caustic milky latex when cut or damaged, so handle with care and wash off any sap contacting skin immediately. Its extremely slow growth means offsets and new plants are usually grown from seed rather than cuttings, and mature plants eventually elongate slightly from the classic ball shape as they age. Give excellent drainage above all else, since overwatering and cool, wet conditions are by far the most common causes of rot in cultivation.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; basket plant spreads by long, arching stolons tipped with plantlets, similar in habit to a spider plant.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; basket plant spreads by long, arching stolons tipped with plantlets, similar in habit to a spider plant. Thick, succulent, strap-shaped leaves form a dense central rosette from which long, wiry stolons arch outward, each tipped with a small rosette of new plantlets that root readily wherever they touch soil, an offsetting habit reminiscent of the familiar spider plant and giving rise to its common name from the many hanging 'baskets' of plantlets a mature specimen produces. Occasionally producing small, fragrant white flowers on tall stalks, it is grown chiefly for its easy-care foliage and prolific plantlet production, making it simple to propagate and share. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, provide bright indirect light, and separate rooted plantlets to propagate new plants or refresh an aging specimen.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to clay soil in full sun to partial shade; bastard oak is adapted to the limestone soils and rocky, alkaline, well-drained upland sites of the Edwards Plateau and Gulf Coast prairies, where it grows in conditions that exclude most other oaks.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to clay, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — bastard oak (Quercus sinuata) is a medium to large deciduous white oak of the limestone-dominated Edwards Plateau, Cross Timbers, and Gulf Coast prairies of Texas and adjacent states, notable for its distinctive leaves with deep, rounded, scalloped lobes unlike any other Texas oak. It grows on rocky limestone hillsides and in deep clay draws, tolerating both the thin, alkaline, rocky soils of the Hill Country and the heavy black clay soils of the Blackland Prairie with equal adaptability. The tree is moderately fast-growing for an oak, long-lived, and provides outstanding shade and wildlife value (acorns in the white oak group ripen in one season and are highly palatable to deer and wildlife). An underutilized oak for the challenging alkaline, clay, and limestone soils of central and south Texas garden sites where other oaks perform poorly.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Bat Face Cuphea is grown as a tender perennial in zones 9–11 — it may survive mild zone 9 winters in sheltered locations, behaving as a perennial in warmer areas and a warm-season annual in colder areas of zone 9. Prune lightly in late winter to encourage fresh growth and abundant new flowering. In zone 9 it thrives in the hottest summer months and blooms continuously from spring through frost, becoming more floriferous as heat increases.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — cuphea is drought-tolerant once established and blooms better in lean soil than in rich, consistently moist conditions; Bat Face is a cuphea cultivar with one of the most distinctively shaped and visually memorable flowers in the ornamental plant world — each small, 0.5-inch tubular flower is deep crimson-red with two spreading, rounded purple petals at the tip that create an unmistakable bat face impression when viewed from the front, complete with the suggestion of eyes, nose, and ears in the petal arrangement. The bat face appearance is not accidental or fanciful — the distinctive petal structure is genuinely face-like in a way that is immediately recognized by most observers, making Bat Face cuphea the most conversation-starting small plant in the summer garden. The hummingbird-attractive tubular flower structure, combined with continuous bloom from spring through frost and excellent heat tolerance, makes Bat Face an outstanding zone 9 summer performer. The moderate spreading, bushy habit covers itself in hundreds of the tiny bat-face flowers simultaneously during peak bloom, creating an effect that is both charming and genuinely unusual in the summer garden.

common_name: Bat Flower (Black Bat Flower, Cat's Whiskers)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in deep shade to partial shade; bat flower is one of the few tropical ornamentals that genuinely prefers deep shade — direct sun scorches the leaves rapidly. In zone 9 it needs frost protection; grow in a container that can be brought indoors, or mulch heavily and hope for mild winters. High humidity is essential.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in deep to partial shade with high humidity; bat flower produces one of the most extraordinary flowers in the plant kingdom — the inflorescence consists of two large, dark purple-black wing-like bracts (resembling a bat in flight), a cluster of maroon-purple flowers in the center, and up to 28 long, thread-like purple whiskers (bracteoles) hanging down 12–28 inches, giving the flower a ghostly, otherworldly appearance. Native to the forest floor of tropical Southeast Asia from southern China to Malaysia, it requires warm, humid, shaded conditions and is intolerant of direct sun, drought, or temperature below 50°F. In zone 10–12 it is a reliable outdoor perennial shade plant; in zone 9 it is best grown in a container as a specimen that can be overwintered inside. The large, glossy leaves are attractive year-round even when not in flower, and the plants bloom from late spring through autumn.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; bat-faced cuphea is one of the most continuously blooming and hummingbird-attractive annuals available for Gulf South summer gardens.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; bat-faced cuphea (bat's wing cuphea) is a Mexican native grown for its unique and vivid flowers — small, tubular, with brilliant red petals at the base and a pair of purple-red, rounded, ear-like upper petals that give each flower the uncanny appearance of a tiny bat's face, displayed in dense clusters from late spring until frost. The flowers are irresistible to ruby-throated hummingbirds. Plants bloom essentially nonstop in warm weather with no deadheading required. Extremely heat-tolerant and productive in Gulf Coast summer conditions when most cool-season annuals have declined. In zones 9–11 it overwinters as a semi-woody subshrub; in cooler climates grow as a long-season annual. 'Georgia Scarlet' is a popular selection.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep and 6 inches apart in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; bath asparagus tolerates partial shade and does well at the edges of deciduous woodland. In regions where it is edible, the unopened flower spikes may be harvested in May before the flowers open and cooked like asparagus — the remaining stems will still flower normally.
directions: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for May-June bloom; bath asparagus (Pyrenean star-of-Bethlehem) is a tall, stately, and distinctly unusual ornithogalum producing elegant 12-24 inch upright spikes of numerous small, pale greenish-yellow, star-shaped flowers that open progressively from the base upward through late spring — the overall effect is airy and quietly striking in the border or at a woodland edge. This species is notably edible: the young, tightly furled flower spikes are traditionally harvested before the flowers open, bundled, and boiled or steamed like asparagus, a practice so ingrained in the English city of Bath that the plant acquired its most familiar common name. Native to Mediterranean scrub and grassy slopes and naturalized across parts of southern England and western Europe, it is well adapted to dry summer dormancy and low-maintenance cultivation. It slowly increases by offsets to form modest clumps and rarely becomes invasive. An unusual dual-purpose plant equally at home in the ornamental border and the edible garden.

common_name: Bath's Pink Dianthus (Heat-Tolerant Southern Groundcover Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; cheddar pinks cultivars are among the most drought- and heat-tolerant perennials available, thriving in lean, rocky, or sandy soils where richer soil causes rot.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Bath's Pink was discovered and named by a Georgia gardener and has become one of the most reliable cheddar pink selections for hot, humid Southern gardens, forming a dense, low mat of fine, silvery-blue foliage topped in spring with abundant fragrant, soft pink, fringed flowers. It shows notably better heat and humidity tolerance than many other dianthus cultivars, an important quality for gardeners south of the plant's more typical cooler range, and it thrives in the same lean, sharply drained, rocky-to-sandy soil that other cheddar pinks require. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

common_name: Batik Bearded Iris (Striking Purple-and-White Streaked Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Batik is a striking and unusual bearded iris cultivar named for its irregular, brushed and streaked pattern of deep purple over a white ground, giving each ruffled flower a hand-dyed, painterly look unlike the more uniform color patterns of most bearded iris. Its bold, unmistakable appearance has made it a long-standing favorite for gardeners wanting a conversation-piece iris that stands out in a mixed spring border. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans to keep the clump vigorous and floriferous.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Bauer's grevillea is notable among grevilleas for being one of the few species that tolerates partial shade — most grevilleas are strictly full-sun plants. It forms a compact, spreading, ground-hugging mound and blooms most heavily in spring but flowers sporadically year-round. No phosphorus fertilizer — fatal to Proteaceae. Named for the Austrian botanical artist Franz Bauer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Bauer's grevillea is a compact, spreading, relatively low-growing Australian grevillea — native to the rocky, somewhat shaded forest margins and valley floor habitats of New South Wales — that stands apart from many grevillea species in its greater shade tolerance, making it one of the few Proteaceae useful for planting in the dappled shade or semi-shade of woodland margins and north-facing hillsides. The flowers are in the typical grevillea 'toothbrush' or clustered style — dense clusters of small, curved, tubular red to pink-red flowers with projecting, hooked styles that create the characteristic grevillea flower cluster — produced in greatest abundance in spring but appearing sporadically through the year in favorable mild-winter climates. The foliage is small, dark green, and finely textured, creating a compact, spreading, mat-like mound that works well as a low-maintenance groundcover shrub in the right conditions. Like all Proteaceae, it requires lean soil and absolutely no phosphorus fertilizer. Named for Franz Bauer, the celebrated Austrian botanical artist at Kew whose extraordinary illustrations documented the new Australian flora in the early 19th century.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant nursery starts in spring into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun in essentially frost-free coastal sites; bay cedar is a pantropical strand shrub found along the immediate coastline from South Florida through the Caribbean and Gulf.
directions: Plant in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun along the immediate coastline; bay cedar is a dense, rounded, salt-tolerant strand shrub with soft, narrow, yellow-green leaves clustered toward branch tips and small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers produced nearly continuously in warm weather. It forms a natural windbreak hedge along tropical and subtropical shorelines, tolerating direct salt spray, poor sandy soil, and drought that would quickly kill most ornamental shrubs, and it requires essentially no irrigation once established. Small, dry, corky fruit follow the flowers and float on ocean currents to colonize new shoreline, the same strategy used by many other strand-zone pioneer species. Because it is strictly frost-tender, grow it only in true frost-free coastal gardens or as a large container specimen brought under cover elsewhere; light trimming after major growth flushes keeps the naturally rounded form dense.

common_name: Bayou Sunbeam Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Yellow Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.
directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade.
