plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun; Bermuda Palmetto is the only palm species native to Bermuda and tolerates salt spray and coastal wind exceptionally well.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun; once established, Bermuda Palmetto tolerates drought, salt spray, and coastal wind exceptionally well, reflecting its origin on the exposed, storm-battered island it's named for. It is the only palm species native to Bermuda and one of only a handful of true island-endemic palms in the Atlantic, bearing large, stiff, fan-shaped fronds on a stout trunk topped with the persistent leaf-base 'boot' pattern typical of the genus. Slow-growing and long-lived, it makes an excellent coastal landscape specimen where salt tolerance is essential, and needs little care once established beyond occasional removal of old fronds.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Berry Awesome is a Summerific series cultivar with large lavender-pink flowers and dusty blue-green foliage, an unusual soft color palette among typically bold-colored hardy hibiscus cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Berry Awesome bears large, 8-9 inch, soft lavender-pink flowers with a deep rose-red eye, held against distinctive dusty, blue-green foliage that sets it apart from the more common dark-purple or plain-green-leaved hardy hibiscus cultivars. The softer, cooler color palette makes it a versatile choice for pairing with a wider range of companion plants than the bold reds and hot pinks typical of many hardy hibiscus. It blooms in a steady succession of huge flowers from midsummer into fall, each lasting a single day but replaced continuously. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown. It is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil, though Japanese beetles can damage foliage and flowers where present.

common_name: Berry Dazzle Crapemyrtle (Dwarf Mildew-Resistant Fuchsia-Pink Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Berry Dazzle is a true dwarf crapemyrtle, staying about 4 feet tall, bred with powdery mildew resistance and fuchsia-pink blooms, well suited to a small Gulf Coast bed or container.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Berry Dazzle is a genuine dwarf crapemyrtle, staying about 4 feet tall and wide, bred with resistance to powdery mildew so its foliage stays clean through the humidity of a Gulf South summer while producing a heavy show of fuchsia-pink blooms. Its compact size makes it well suited to small foundation plantings, mixed borders, or large containers where a tree-form crapemyrtle would be far too large. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through summer and fall. Because of its naturally compact habit, Berry Dazzle needs little pruning beyond removing dead or damaged wood in late winter.

common_name: Berry Nice Winterberry Holly (Large-Fruited Female Winterberry)
plant_note: Plant female shrubs alongside a compatible male pollinator such as Jim Dandy in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; Berry Nice bears unusually large, bright red berries on a vigorous, well-branched shrub.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, and site a compatible male pollinator such as Jim Dandy within pollinating range, since winterberry is dioecious and female plants need a male nearby to set fruit. Berry Nice bears notably large, bright red berries in heavy clusters along the bare branches after leaf drop, standing out in size compared to many other winterberry cultivars, on a vigorous, well-branched shrub with good density. Its oversized, showy fruit provides strong winter interest and a reliable food source for overwintering songbirds. Prune only lightly and only after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Berry Smoothie Heuchera (Pink-Purple Raspberry Coral Bell)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; in zone 9, heucheras benefit from afternoon shade protection — the bright foliage colors fade and the plants decline in intense afternoon sun combined with Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Berry Smoothie is one of the most vividly colored heuchera introductions — producing large, rounded, ruffled leaves in a rich, warm raspberry-pink to deep rose-pink color that is more saturated and vivid than the softer peachy tones of 'Georgia Peach' and the cooler tones of 'Caramel'. The warm raspberry-pink foliage creates a strong color focal point in the partial-shade garden with a boldness that few other heucheras match. The metallic, slightly reflective surface of the leaves catches available light in shade conditions, making Berry Smoothie one of the brightest and most visible heucheras in low-light situations. The color typically deepens to burgundy-raspberry in cooler fall and winter temperatures and lightens slightly in the summer heat. In early summer, small, airy white flower sprays rise above the foliage on slender scapes — delicate accents to the dominant foliage display. Heuchera hybrids like Berry Smoothie are essential partial-shade perennials for zone 9 gardens — they provide multi-season foliage color in areas where most other plants offer only green. Divide heucheras every 3–4 years in early spring when the crown becomes too elevated above the soil surface and performance declines. In zone 9, plant in the shadiest locations available, with consistent moisture and excellent drainage.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Berry Swirl is part of the Winter Jewels breeding series, with double, raspberry-pink swirled flowers blooming in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist while the plant establishes. Berry Swirl is part of the acclaimed Winter Jewels hellebore breeding series, producing full, ruffled double flowers in swirling raspberry-pink and cream tones that give each bloom a distinctive marbled, painterly appearance, held above leathery, evergreen, deeply divided foliage. Like other Lenten roses it blooms very early, often through late-season snow or hard frost, providing reliable color in the shade garden when little else is flowering. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to best showcase the flowers, and site it away from areas where pets or children graze, since all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Berry White Hydrangea (Large White-to-Rose-Red Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Berry White bears large, dense flower panicles on strong stems that hold up without flopping even as color deepens and the panicles gain weight.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Berry White produces large, dense, conical flower panicles that open pure white in midsummer and gradually flush to a deep rose-red as they mature into fall, giving a full season of two-toned color on the same shrub as older and newer flowers open at different rates along each panicle. Its sturdy, well-branched stems support the heavy flower heads upright through summer storms far better than older seedling-grown panicle hydrangeas. Like other H. paniculata cultivars it blooms reliably on new wood, so prune hard in late winter to a low framework to encourage vigorous new growth and maximize the size and color of the following summer's panicles.

common_name: Bertram Anderson Lungwort (Narrow Silver-Spotted Blue-Flowered Pulmonaria)
plant_note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Bertram Anderson bears narrow, heavily silver-spotted leaves and vivid blue spring flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture prevents the leaves from wilting or scorching in summer heat. Bertram Anderson bears narrow, elongated leaves heavily marked with silver spots, a finer-textured look than many broader-leaved lungwort cultivars, topped in early spring by clusters of vivid blue flowers that open from pink-tinged buds. Its narrow foliage habit and strong flower color have kept it a long-standing favorite among Pulmonaria collectors. Cut back tattered summer foliage to encourage a fresh flush of clean new leaves, and divide congested clumps in fall.

common_name: Betberg Solomon's Seal (Bronze-Emerging Spring Foliage Solomon's Seal)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Betberg emerges deep bronze-purple in spring before greening up, a foliage-color trait distinct from the plain-green and variegated Solomon's Seal cultivars already common in cultivation.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, though it performs best and lasts longest in partial to full shade in warm climates. Betberg is prized for its striking spring emergence, when the arching stems and paired leaves unfurl a deep, glossy bronze-purple before gradually shifting to the typical fresh green through late spring, a distinctive seasonal color display not seen in the plain-green or white-edged Solomon's Seal cultivars more commonly grown. Small, dangling, white, bell-shaped flowers hang in pairs from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by blue-black berries in fall. It is an easy, long-lived, essentially carefree woodland perennial, spreading slowly by rhizomes to form an increasingly graceful colony, and combines beautifully with ferns, hostas, and hellebores. Cut stems back to the ground after they yellow in fall.

common_name: Betty Anne Voss Azalea (Salmon-Pink Double Robin Hill Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Betty Anne Voss is a Robin Hill azalea prized for large, hose-in-hose double blooms and a spreading habit.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Betty Anne Voss bears large, hose-in-hose double blooms in soft salmon-pink on a wide-spreading, low-mounding Robin Hill azalea, a breeding group developed for cold hardiness and large flower size on a more compact plant than Southern Indica types. Its spreading habit works well massed as a groundcover-like planting under high shade or as an underplanting for taller shrubs and trees. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Betty Bowring is the classic white-flowered brunnera, a break from the blue forget-me-not flowers typical of the species.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, keeping the root zone evenly moist through summer since foliage wilts quickly in dry conditions or hot sun. Betty Bowring bears plain green, rough-textured, heart-shaped leaves without the silver patterning of many newer brunnera cultivars, but is instead grown for its airy sprays of small, pure white flowers in spring, a striking contrast to the sky-blue, forget-me-not-like blooms typical of the species. The bright white flowers stand out well against dark green foliage and pair nicely with other shade-garden whites such as astilbe or Solomon's seal. In the Deep South, give this selection its coolest, shadiest spot and supplemental water during summer heat, since brunnera generally performs best where nights stay relatively cool.

common_name: Betty Corning Clematis (Fragrant Pale Lavender Bell Clematis)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Betty Corning blooms on new growth, so it can be pruned back hard each late winter.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Betty Corning, discovered as a chance seedling in a New York garden in the 1930s, bears delicate, nodding, bell-shaped flowers in soft pale lavender with gently recurved petal tips and a light, sweet fragrance, blooming over an unusually long season from early summer well into fall. Its refined, understated flowers and fragrance set it apart from the bolder, flatter blooms of large-flowered hybrid clematis, and because it flowers on new growth it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing bloom, a more forgiving pruning regime than many older clematis cultivars require.

common_name: Betty Magnolia (Little Girl Series Late-Blooming Reddish-Purple Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Betty is a compact 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolia from the U.S. National Arboretum, bred to bloom later than star and saucer magnolias to help avoid late-frost flower damage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Betty is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, producing large, fragrant, deep reddish-purple, multi-petaled, tulip-shaped flowers with a paler interior on a compact, multi-stemmed tree small enough for a modest-sized yard. Like its sibling Jane, its key advantage is later bloom timing than star and saucer magnolias, helping the flowers dodge the late spring freezes that often damage earlier-blooming magnolias, and it sometimes produces a light rebloom later in the season as well. Give it a sheltered spot with consistent moisture and avoid heavy pruning, since magnolias generally need little routine shaping beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Betty Sheffield Camellia (Iconic White Picotee-Edged Camellia japonica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Betty Sheffield is one of the most iconic Southern camellia families, known for its large white flowers streaked and edged in red or pink.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Betty Sheffield is one of the most celebrated Camellia japonica cultivars in Southern gardening, producing huge, formal to semi-double blooms in white edged and streaked with red or pink in an ever-varying, unpredictable picotee pattern that has made it a favorite exhibition flower for generations. The large, upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in mid to late winter and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its dramatic flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Betty Woods Daylily (Ruffled Double Gold Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Betty Woods holds its double form and gold color well in Gulf South heat and reliably rebounds after summer flushes of bloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Betty Woods is a long-popular double daylily, producing consistently full, ruffled, cream-to-gold blooms with a green throat that hold their double form far more reliably in heat and humidity than many other double cultivars, which is why it remains a garden and hybridizing standard decades after its introduction. It is a strong, vigorous rebloomer over a long summer season and increases quickly into full, floriferous clumps. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring. Its dependable doubling and heat tolerance make it one of the better double daylilies for Gulf Coast gardens, where many double-flowered cultivars revert to single form under stress.

common_name: Beverly Sills Bearded Iris (Award-Winning Coral-Pink Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Named for the opera singer and introduced in 1979, Beverly Sills is one of the most decorated bearded iris cultivars ever released, winning both the American Iris Society's Award of Merit and its top honor, the Dykes Medal, for its ruffled, coral-pink flowers with a bright tangerine beard on tall, well-branched stems. Its clear, luminous color and vigorous, floriferous habit have kept it a garden and show standard for decades. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; seeds germinate in late winter to early spring.
directions: Bexar Clover is a small native annual of dry, rocky, calcareous, or sandy open ground in Texas and adjacent south-central states, blooming from March through May with compact, globe-shaped cream-white to pale pink flower heads. Sow seeds directly in fall into lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; no soil amendment is needed, and fertility encourages weeds at the expense of this clover. An ecologically valuable species that supports specialist native bee communities in the south-central US, it self-sows freely and naturalizes reliably in open, disturbed ground with minimal competition.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bicknell's sedge is a prairie and savanna native that adapts to average garden soil once established.
directions: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bicknell's sedge is a prairie and savanna native that adapts to average garden soil once established. Clumps of narrow, medium-green foliage send up wiry stems in late spring topped with plump, oval, straw-colored seed heads tinged coppery-brown at maturity, giving the plant strong textural interest well beyond its bloom period. Native to tallgrass prairies, savannas, and open woodland edges across the central and eastern United States, it combines well with prairie wildflowers and grasses in a naturalistic planting or rain garden and provides seed for songbirds through fall and winter. It tolerates both the dry conditions of prairie plantings and the light shade of savanna edges, needing no supplemental water once its root system is established.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright indirect light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; bicolor ox tongue tolerates lower light than most succulents and rots in overly wet or dense soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright indirect light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; bicolor ox tongue tolerates lower light than most succulents and rots in overly wet or dense soil. Thick, tongue-shaped, dark green leaves marked with irregular pale green to white bands and spots are arranged in two opposite rows in juvenile plants before spiraling in maturity, and tall, arching flower stalks bear clusters of small, pink-and-green, pouch-shaped flowers that give the genus its stomach-referencing name. Native to South Africa, it tolerates the lower, indirect light of a shaded windowsill or porch better than most succulents, making it a good choice for spots too dim for cacti or echeverias but still too bright and dry for typical foliage houseplants. Water only when the soil is fully dry and divide offsets from the base to propagate.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil or potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; bidens blooms almost immediately from transplant and continues until frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; bidens (Apache beggartick, golden goddess) is a trailing, fine-textured annual from the arid Mexican highlands that produces a continuous, self-cleaning display of bright golden-yellow, five-petaled daisy-like flowers against the ferny, deeply divided foliage from late spring until frost. The fine texture and trailing habit make it ideal for softening container arrangements and hanging baskets, where it weaves through and around companion plants. Extremely heat-tolerant, drought-resistant once established, and nearly indestructible in containers. Occasionally self-sows in mild climates. 'Goldmarie', 'Peter's Gold Carpet', and 'Golden Goddess' are popular compact selections. Excellent as a combination trailer with salvia, vinca, and zinnias.

common_name: Big Bang Chinese Ground Orchid (Large-Flowered Vigorous Bletilla)
plant_note: Plant dormant pseudobulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring after last frost; Big Bang is a vigorous Bletilla selection with unusually large magenta-pink flowers and a heavier bloom count than the species.
directions: Plant pseudobulbs 2-3 inches deep in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade. Big Bang bears notably large, showy magenta-pink flowers on upright spikes in April to May before the pleated, strap-like foliage reaches full height, with a heavier flower count per spike and bigger individual blooms than the standard species, making a bolder statement in a shaded border. Clumps expand slowly over years; never dig out the entire clump, instead taking divisions from the perimeter while leaving the main clump undisturbed. Provide a light mulch in the coldest parts of its range, and avoid waterlogged soils, which cause pseudobulb rot.

common_name: Big Begonia (Large-Scale Landscape Wax Begonia Series)
plant_note: Plant purchased transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; the Big series was bred for unusually large, vigorous plants and flowers compared to traditional smaller wax begonias, making a bold impact in beds and large containers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun with adequate moisture. The Big begonia series was bred to scale up the classic wax begonia into a much larger, more substantial landscape plant, with glossy leaves and abundant flower clusters in white, pink, or red covering a mounding plant considerably bigger than traditional bedding wax begonias. Its larger size and heat tolerance make it a strong choice for mass plantings, large containers, and borders where a bigger, bolder begonia display is wanted, and it tolerates more direct sun than many begonias provided soil moisture stays consistent. It is largely self-cleaning and needs little maintenance beyond routine watering and fertilizing through the growing season.

common_name: Big Ben Peony (Full Double Deep Maroon-Red Late-Season Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Big Ben is a full double peony in deep maroon-red, a vigorous late-season bloomer.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Big Ben bears large, full double flowers in deep, dramatic maroon-red, blooming late in the peony season, which extends the flowering window into a period when many earlier peonies have finished. Its dark, saturated color and vigorous, robust plant make it a strong anchor for the back of a peony border. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into dry, sandy or calcareous, well-drained soil; lightly scarify seeds before sowing to improve germination rates and encourage spring bloom.
directions: The tallest of the Texas bluebonnets, Big Bend Bluebonnet is a native of dry, rocky and sandy desert washes in the Trans-Pecos and Big Bend region of far west Texas, producing dramatic upright spikes of deep blue lupine flowers on stems reaching 4 feet or more in March and April. Direct sow seeds in fall on bare, sandy or rocky, freely draining soil in full sun; lightly scarify or nick seed coats before planting to break dormancy and speed germination. This species thrives in dry, low-humidity climates and is not suited to the humid eastern portions of Texas, performing best in calcareous, well-drained soils of the Hill Country and Trans-Pecos. It does not transplant well and self-sows reliably in suitable desert garden and xeriscape conditions once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Big Blue is the most widely planted clumping liriope cultivar and establishes readily in a very wide range of conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Big Blue is the most commonly grown clumping liriope cultivar — a robust, grass-like perennial ground cover forming dense clumps of arching, dark-green, strap-like leaves about one-half inch wide, topped by erect spikes of dark violet-purple flowers in late summer followed by shiny black berries in fall. It is the workhorse of shade ground covers across much of the South and Gulf Coast, performing reliably under trees, on slopes, and in any location where turf grass fails due to insufficient light. Big Blue is notably more vigorous than the species and maintains its dark color better through the extremes of Gulf Coast summers. The clumping (non-spreading) habit means it stays where planted without becoming invasive, unlike the running lilyturf species. In zone 9, liriope stays green year-round as a fully evergreen ground cover. Mow or cut back to 3–4 inches in late winter (January–February in zone 9) before new growth emerges to remove worn winter foliage and stimulate a fresh flush of clean leaves. Excellent under live oaks, pines, and other established trees where few ground covers survive.

common_name: Big Blue Lilyturf (Border Lilyturf, Muscari Liriope)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to full sun; Big Blue lilyturf is the clumping (non-spreading) species of liriope — one of the most widely used shade groundcovers in the American South, with upright to arching, dark-green, grass-like foliage, summer spikes of purple flowers, and persistent black berries — virtually indestructible once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to full sun; shear to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Liriope muscari (big blue lilyturf or border lilyturf) is one of the most widely planted and reliably performing shade groundcovers and border plants in the American South and Gulf Coast — a clumping (not spreading) species distinct from creeping lilyturf (L. spicata). The plant produces dense, arching clumps of dark-green, grass-like evergreen leaves 12–18 inches long, topped in summer with upright spikes of small, purple to violet flower clusters resembling grape hyacinth (muscari — hence 'muscari' in the name) rising above the foliage. The flowers are followed by persistent, shiny, black berry-like fruits that provide additional ornamental interest through fall and winter and are eaten by birds. Named cultivars are numerous and widely available: 'Big Blue' (classic standard); 'Monroe White' (white flowers); 'Gold Band' (yellow-striped leaves); 'Silvery Sunproof' (cream-striped, more sun-tolerant). Liriope muscari is extraordinarily adaptable in the Gulf South: it tolerates deep shade, drought, poor soils, salt spray, and competition from tree roots — performing where few other groundcovers survive. Shear clumps to the ground in late winter (use a lawnmower) to remove tattered old foliage before fresh new growth emerges in spring.

common_name: Big Blue Sea Holly (Large-Flowered Steel-Blue Eryngium)
plant_note: Transplant divisions or started plants in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Big Blue is a selection of flat sea holly chosen for extra-large, intensely steel-blue flower heads and bracts.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, even sandy or rocky soil in full sun; rich, moist soil produces floppy, short-lived growth in this drought-loving perennial. Big Blue bears branching stems topped with thistle-like, metallic steel-blue flower heads surrounded by spiny, equally blue bracts from midsummer into fall, larger and more intensely colored than the species, and the whole plant takes on a silvery-blue cast that makes it a striking accent among softer-textured perennials and grasses. Established plants develop a long taproot that makes them extremely drought-tolerant but resentful of transplanting or division, so site it thoughtfully the first time. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers heavily, and the dried flower heads hold their color well for cutting and winter arrangements; leave some stems standing through winter for texture and seed for goldfinches.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring on a firm seedbed once soil temperatures reach 65°F; press seed into the soil surface without deep coverage, as big bluestem needs warmth and light contact to germinate well.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a weed-suppressed, firm seedbed in full sun after the last frost, pressing seed lightly into the surface and keeping the area moist for the first three to four weeks until seedlings emerge. Plants establish slowly in the first season, sending energy into deep roots rather than top growth, so avoid mowing below six inches and withhold fertilizer entirely. By the second and third year, clumps reach their full height of four to eight feet, bearing the distinctive three-branched turkey-foot seed head in August and September. Cut plants back to four to six inches in late winter before new growth begins, and expect spectacular copper-bronze fall color each autumn.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of prepared, weed-free soil in spring; big bluestem seed germinates best with good soil contact. Alternatively, cold-stratify seed for 30 days before spring sowing to improve germination rate.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average, dry soil in full sun; big bluestem is the dominant grass of the tallgrass prairie, once covering hundreds of millions of acres from Manitoba to Texas, and is a cornerstone native grass for prairie restorations, meadow gardens, and large-scale naturalized plantings. The blue-green foliage turns brilliant orange-copper-burgundy in fall and holds through winter as attractive standing tan straw. The distinctive three-parted seed heads — resembling turkey feet in silhouette — are architectural and wildlife-valuable. Deep roots (up to 10 feet) make it exceptional for erosion control and sequestering carbon. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; never needs irrigation or fertilizer in average to dry soil. Cut back to 6 inches in early spring before new growth begins.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly brackish to fresh, sandy or clay soil in full sun; big cordgrass grows naturally along tidal freshwater river margins, freshwater marshes, and the brackish upper zones of estuaries. It spreads by strong rhizomes to form dense colonies.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to brackish, sandy to clay soil in full sun at pond margins, tidal freshwater marshes, and streambanks; big cordgrass is the largest of the native cordgrasses, producing bold, coarse, erect culms to 6–10 feet in height that create an impressive, wetland structural element. Growing naturally along tidal rivers, upper brackish marshes, and freshwater wetland edges from the Atlantic to the Gulf Coast, it tolerates occasional salinity but thrives equally well in fresh water. The large, comb-like seed heads in late summer and fall are distinctive and provide abundant seeds for marsh birds including secretive rails. The dense, vigorous rhizomes are highly effective for shoreline stabilization and marsh restoration along tidal rivers and freshwater margins. A bold, architectural statement plant for large pond edges, wetland gardens, and stream bank stabilization in zones 5–10.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Big Daddy's heavy, deeply puckered leaves are among the most slug-resistant of any large hosta, making it excellent for gardens where slug pressure is high.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Big Daddy is a prized large hosta selected from H. sieboldiana known for exceptionally large, deeply cupped and heavily puckered, powder-blue leaves that hold their blue color well into summer. The thick, waxy leaf texture is among the most slug-resistant available in a large hosta, making it the preferred choice for gardeners who struggle with slug damage. The cupped leaf surface collects dew and light rain, giving the crown water directly. Pale lavender to nearly white flowers appear in midsummer and are attractive though secondary to the bold foliage. Big Daddy is a steady grower that requires 3 years to reach its best appearance but is extremely long-lived. Mulch with 2–3 inches of wood chips to keep roots cool and moist; consistent moisture is essential for maintaining leaf quality and preventing edge browning in warm weather.

common_name: Big Duck Gold Marigold (AAS-Winning Huge Golden-Yellow Compact Marigold)
plant_note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or sow directly once soil warms; Big Duck Gold, an AAS winner, bears huge 3-inch golden-yellow blooms on compact 15-inch plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors for a head start or sow directly after frost danger passes, barely covering them. Big Duck Gold, an All-America Selections winner, bears exceptionally large, three-inch, fully double golden-yellow blooms on a notably compact fifteen-inch plant, an unusual combination of large flower size and short stature among African marigold cultivars. Plant in full sun where the strong scent helps deter garden pests, making it a classic vegetable-garden companion. Deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming all summer and pinch young plants to encourage branching.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (in zone 8–10) or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; big quaking grass is a cool-season annual that germinates in fall, overwinters, and sets ornamental seed heads in spring before dying with summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in fall (in the South) or spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; big quaking grass is a cool-season annual from the Mediterranean region grown for its remarkably ornamental, large, heart-shaped, pendant spikelets that tremble and dance in the slightest breeze — earning it the common name and making it one of the most charming ornamental grasses for cut flower arrangements, dried flower crafts, and naturalistic garden borders. The spikelets begin green and ripen through shades of gold and tan. In zone 9a, it thrives as a fall-sown annual that blooms in spring before dying in summer heat. Self-sows to naturalize in appropriate conditions. The dried seed heads retain their ornamental value indefinitely when cut before fully ripe. A beloved cottage garden and cutting garden grass for spring arrangements.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained conifer forest soil in partial to full shade; big rattlesnake plantain is the western counterpart to the eastern G. pubescens and requires the same mycorrhizal-associated, acidic, needle-mulched forest soil conditions — purchase nursery-propagated stock only.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained conifer forest soil in partial to full shade near established conifers, never in conventional garden beds; big rattlesnake plantain needs mycorrhizal fungal associations to thrive long-term. Goodyera oblongifolia is the Pacific Northwest and western counterpart to the eastern G. pubescens, producing a larger and bolder basal rosette of dark green, oval leaves 2–3 inches long with a single prominent silver-white central stripe (rather than the dense white netting of G. pubescens) that makes the evergreen foliage striking and distinctive year-round on the forest floor. In late summer it produces a leafy stem 8–15 inches tall bearing a spike of small white orchid flowers on one to three sides of the stem. It is the most common and garden-tolerant native orchid of the Pacific coast forest understory, suitable for naturalistic planting in moist, shaded conifer gardens from northern California to British Columbia. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants.

plant_note: Set out transplants after frost danger passes in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike smaller wax begonias, the Big series tolerates more direct sun without scorching.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing plants 14–18 inches apart to fill in as a bold, season-long bedding display. Big Red is part of a landscape begonia series bred for scale, producing much larger leaves and flowers than traditional wax begonias on plants that reach 18–24 inches, with glossy bronze-green foliage and clusters of bright red flowers produced continuously from planting until frost. Its larger size and heat tolerance make it a strong mass-planting choice for beds and borders in Gulf South summer heat, where it keeps flowering with minimal deadheading required. It requires no pinching to stay full and holds up better to summer downpours than smaller, more delicate bedding begonias.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; big red sage grows naturally on rocky limestone outcrops and cliff faces of the Edwards Plateau in central Texas and is adapted to dry, thin, calcareous soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; big red sage is a rare and distinctive Texas endemic of the Edwards Plateau, where it grows on exposed limestone outcrops, ledges, and thin, rocky calcareous soils in areas of central Texas. The flowers are among the largest of any native Salvia — rich scarlet-crimson tubes nearly 1.5 inches long on tall, erect spikes — making it one of the most spectacular fall-blooming salvias in cultivation and an exceptional hummingbird attractor. The common name 'penstemonoides' (penstemon-like) refers to the form of the flower, which somewhat resembles a penstemon in shape. A rare plant in the wild with a limited natural range, it has gained popularity in native plant horticulture as a stunning, drought-tolerant hummingbird and butterfly plant for zone 7–10 dry gardens. Thrives in alkaline limestone soils typical of the Texas Hill Country.

common_name: Big Rose Begonia (Large Green-Leaf Rose-Pink Landscape Begonia)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade to filtered sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Big Rose is part of a landscape begonia series bred for large size and heat tolerance.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in well-drained, fertile soil. Big Rose bears large clusters of clear rose-pink flowers over glossy green foliage on a vigorous, well-branched plant considerably larger than standard wax begonias, making it efficient for filling beds, borders, and large containers with continuous summer color. It tolerates more heat and sun than many shade begonias, provided soil moisture stays consistent, and needs no deadheading to keep flowering steadily from planting until frost. Its scale and vigor suit it well to mass landscape plantings where a big visual impact is the goal.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out plugs after the soil has warmed in late spring, choosing a low spot or floodplain-type site where the deep roots can access subsurface moisture.
directions: Direct sow or plant plugs in late spring once soil has warmed, siting in full sun in a low-lying or seasonally moist spot such as a swale, arroyo edge, or floodplain; established clumps then tolerate long dry spells thanks to deep roots. Avoid deep planting of seed, since it germinates best from a shallow covering. This robust bunchgrass of the American Southwest forms one of the largest native grass clumps in the region, sending up tall, fine-textured blue-green foliage topped by large plumed seed heads in late summer, and it is valued for erosion control, wildlife habitat, and bold vertical structure in xeric and native plant gardens.

plant_note: Plant seeds immediately upon collection (they lose viability quickly) or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; big-leaf mahogany requires frost-free conditions and grows naturally in tropical and subtropical forests of Central and South America.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–12; big-leaf mahogany is the commercial mahogany of global trade — the source of almost all mahogany lumber in furniture, cabinets, boats, and fine woodwork worldwide. Native to tropical forests of Central and South America from Mexico to Brazil, it produces spectacular large, compound leaves up to 12 inches long that unfurl pink-bronze before maturing to glossy dark green. The enormous seed pods hang from the canopy and split to release winged seeds. The species is now protected under CITES Appendix II due to severe overharvesting, with few large trees remaining in accessible forests. In zone 10 Florida, it grows as a large ornamental shade tree, widely planted in Miami-Dade parks and neighborhoods. Planting contributes to conservation of this critically important and over-exploited tropical timber species.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; bigleaf aster spreads robustly by rhizomes to form a dense groundcover colony — ideal for shaded slopes where erosion control and low-maintenance ground coverage are desired.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade, amended with leaf mold or compost to support the large, coarse foliage that distinguishes this species from all other native asters; bigleaf aster produces the largest basal leaves of any native aster — broad, rough-textured, and heart-shaped, often 4–6 inches across — which emerge as a dense, low rosette in spring and suppress weeds effectively before the 1–2 foot flowering stems rise in late summer, bearing pale lavender to white daisy flowers with yellow centers from August through September. It spreads vigorously by stout rhizomes to form extensive groundcover colonies on shaded slopes and woodland floors and is an excellent, low-maintenance native alternative to invasive groundcovers in areas of dense tree shade and moderate moisture. Divide every 3–4 years to rejuvenate colonies and share divisions; the bold foliage provides strong textural contrast alongside ferns, trilliums, and other fine-leaved woodland plants.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, amended soil; in zones 8–10, fall planting is preferred. Dig a wide, shallow hole — 2x the width of the root ball — and set the plant at the same depth it grew in the container.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in morning sun with afternoon shade; bigleaf hydrangeas are the classic summer-blooming shrubs with large mophead or lacecap flower clusters in blue, pink, or white. Flower color depends on soil pH — blue in acidic soil (pH below 5.5) and pink in alkaline soil (pH above 6.5); to maintain blue, add aluminum sulfate and maintain pH below 6.0. In the South (zones 8–9) afternoon shade is essential to prevent wilting and maintain flower quality. Old-wood bloomers (most classic varieties) should be pruned only immediately after flowering — never in fall, as this removes next year's buds. Reblooming types such as 'Endless Summer' bloom on both old and new wood, making them more reliable after hard winters.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade; ligularia wilts dramatically in dry conditions or afternoon heat — it requires consistent moisture and shade from afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade; ligularia is a bold-textured Asian shade perennial valued for its very large, rounded, kidney-shaped leaves and clusters of bright orange-yellow daisy-like flowers on tall stems in midsummer — providing rare, vibrant color in the shaded garden at a time when most shade plants have finished blooming. The large, purple-backed leaves on named cultivars like 'Desdemona' and 'Othello' are dramatically ornamental even out of bloom. However, ligularia is extremely sensitive to heat and dry air — the large leaves wilt badly in full afternoon sun or dry conditions, recovering at night but looking stressed through the day. It requires consistently moist to boggy soil and cool shade to look its best. Best suited to cool-summer climates (zone 4–7) or consistently moist, shaded stream banks in zone 8. An outstanding plant for boggy shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; bigleaf magnolia requires protection from strong winds, which shred the enormous leaves. Partial afternoon shade is important in zones 7–8.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil sheltered from strong winds in partial shade; bigleaf magnolia holds the distinction of producing the largest simple leaves of any native tree in North America — up to 32 inches long and 12 inches wide — and the combination of these extraordinary leaves with the enormous, intensely fragrant white flowers (up to 16 inches across) makes this one of the most spectacular ornamental trees in the world. The cream-white flowers in late spring to early summer have a distinctive sweet fragrance detectable from considerable distance. It grows naturally as a rare understory tree in moist, protected ravines and hollows of the South Appalachians and Gulf States. Site it in a protected, partly shaded location away from wind — the huge leaves shred easily in exposed sites. The rose-pink fruiting cones in fall are ornamental and provide food for birds.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall after cold stratification (or plant naturally in fall for natural stratification) in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; bigleaf maple grows naturally in moist, coastal forests and stream banks of the Pacific Northwest and is the largest maple in western North America.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; bigleaf maple is the dominant large deciduous tree of moist Pacific Northwest forests, producing the largest leaves of any North American maple — up to 12 inches wide with 5 deep lobes. The massive leaves produce an extraordinary large-textured canopy unlike any other temperate tree. In Pacific Northwest old-growth forests, bigleaf maple trunks and limbs are often draped in thick carpets of mosses, ferns, and licorice fern, creating some of the most magical, fairy-tale forest scenes in North America. Long, pendulous clusters of small, fragrant yellow-green flowers attract early-season pollinators. The paired samaras are large, forming a unique, U-shaped pair. Fall color is golden-yellow to bright orange. The sap can be processed into maple syrup, though production is lower than sugar maple.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade. Bigleaf Snowbell is most spectacular when planted where its pendant white flowers can be viewed from below, such as on a slope above a path or at the edge of a raised bed.
directions: Bigleaf Snowbell is a beautiful native understory shrub or small tree, native to the moist, rich deciduous forests of the southeastern United States from Virginia and Tennessee south to Florida and west to Louisiana, where it grows as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree 6–12 feet tall in the shade of larger hardwoods and pines along stream terraces and ravine slopes. In May and June it produces cascading racemes of fragrant, pure white, bell-shaped flowers with conspicuous yellow stamens that cover the branches in a spectacular display and attract native bees; the flowers are best appreciated from below, where the full pendant clusters are visible against the dark canopy. The large, soft-textured leaves (up to 5 inches long) give the plant its common name and create an attractive bold texture in the shade garden. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and protect from drought; it is more adaptable to heat and humidity than Japanese snowbell (Styrax japonicus) and is a superior choice for southeastern gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; bigroot geranium tolerates dry shade better than almost any other groundcover and spreads steadily by surface-running rhizomes.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial to full shade; bigroot geranium is arguably the best dry-shade groundcover for temperate gardens, producing a dense, weed-suppressing mat of aromatic, lobed leaves that color beautifully in fall, and producing magenta-pink to white flowers in late spring to early summer. It is one of very few ornamentals that thrives in the challenging dry shade under mature maples and beeches where little else will grow. The sticky, scented foliage is deer-resistant. Semi-evergreen in mild winters. Surface rhizomes spread steadily without becoming invasive. Divide in spring or fall to expand plantings. The aromatic leaves were historically used as a geranium oil source in the perfume industry.

plant_note: Plant rooted suckers or cuttings in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bigtooth aspen is the eastern counterpart to quaking aspen, more common on drier, sandier soils in the Northeast and Great Lakes region. It also spreads by root suckers to form clonal colonies.
directions: Plant root suckers or cuttings in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bigtooth aspen is distinguished from quaking aspen by its larger, more coarsely toothed leaves with larger, irregular, rounded teeth (reflecting the name 'grandidentata' — large-toothed). More common on sandy, dry soils and mixed hardwood-aspen forests of the Northeast and Great Lakes region. Like quaking aspen, it spreads clonally by root suckers to form groves, and the flat petioles cause the leaves to tremble in the breeze. The bark is greenish-white to cream-colored, somewhat less white than quaking aspen. Fall color is a warm golden-yellow. The bigtooth aspen grove supports important habitat structure — the trees are fast-growing pioneer species that provide early succession habitat for nesting birds and beaver activity. Excellent for naturalistic, large-scale native woodland restoration in appropriate cool climates.

common_name: Bill MacKenzie Clematis (Golden Bell Tangutica Clematis)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots shaded, then let the twining vine climb a fence, arbor, or large shrub in full sun.
directions: Give this vigorous clematis a large support to scramble over and keep its roots cool with mulch or low companion plants while the top growth reaches into full sun. Nodding, bell-shaped, bright yellow flowers with thick waxy petals appear from midsummer well into fall, followed by fluffy silvery seed heads that extend garden interest into winter. Because it flowers on new wood, cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter to keep it dense and floriferous rather than bare-legged. It is one of the toughest and most vigorous of the small-flowered clematis, tolerant of poor soil once established.

plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light on a moss pole or bark support with chunky, well-draining aroid mix; the striking orange-yellow petioles are the most distinctive identifying feature of this species and develop best color in bright indirect light. Keep consistently moist but not waterlogged — allow the top inch to dry before re-watering. The long, lance-shaped leaves require vertical space. Tolerates humidity levels from 50–80%. Propagate from stem cuttings. A relatively fast grower among collector philodendrons. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-aerated, chunky potting mix with a climbing support — Billie's Philodendron is a hemi-epiphytic climber that grows most vigorously and produces its largest, most dramatic leaves when ascending a moss pole or other support. Philodendron billietiae is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to French Guiana, Suriname, and northern Brazil in the Araceae family, named in honor of Frieda Billiet, a Belgian botanist who collected the type specimen. The plant is distinguished in the Philodendron genus by two immediately striking characteristics: its long, bright orange to orange-yellow petioles, and its narrowly elongated, lance-shaped leaves with distinctly wavy or undulate margins — a leaf shape quite different from the broad, cordate leaves typical of many popular philodendrons. The petioles are a vivid, warm orange-yellow that contrasts brilliantly with the glossy, dark green leaf blade — the orange petioles visible from a distance and making the plant immediately recognizable among a collection of philodendrons. The leaves are large (18–36 inches on mature plants), elongated-lanceolate, with gently rippled margins and a leathery, glossy dark green texture. The mid-rib is pale yellow-green against the dark surface. A popular and relatively fast-growing collector's philodendron valued for its unique petiole color and leaf form. All parts toxic.

common_name: Biloxi Crape Myrtle (Light Pink Vigorous Gulf Coast Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Biloxi grows quickly into a medium-to-large tree and performs especially well in the humid Gulf Coast climate for which it is named.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Biloxi is a vigorous, medium-to-large National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle named for the Mississippi Gulf Coast city, producing clear light pink flower clusters over a long summer bloom season on a fast-growing, upright tree. It shows strong resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem for older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars in the humid Gulf South, and develops attractively mottled, exfoliating cinnamon-and-gray bark as it matures. Fall foliage takes on orange to red tones before dropping. Remove root suckers as they appear and prune selectively to remove crossing or dead branches rather than heavily topping the tree, which spoils its natural vase-shaped form.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Biokovo spreads steadily by rhizome to form a dense weed-suppressing mat and tolerates dry shade better than most flowering groundcovers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, and water regularly the first season while the rhizomes spread and knit the planting into a solid mat. Biokovo is a hybrid cranesbill named for a mountain range in Croatia, forming a low, dense, semi-evergreen carpet of aromatic, lobed leaves that turn attractive orange-red tones in fall, topped in late spring by a heavy flush of small, white flowers delicately blushed with pink at the base of each petal. It is among the most reliable and low-maintenance flowering groundcovers available, tolerating dry shade, poor soil, heat, and drought far better than most perennials grown for groundcover use, and it resists deer and rabbit browsing thanks to its scented foliage. An occasional light shearing after bloom keeps the mat tidy, but otherwise it needs no regular care beyond dividing overgrown patches every several years to control spread or propagate new plantings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; birchleaf spirea is a tough, adaptable native tolerant of a range of soil conditions.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; birchleaf spirea is a tough, adaptable native tolerant of a range of soil conditions. Rounded, toothed leaves resembling those of a birch tree cover a low, mounding native shrub topped with flat clusters of small white flowers in late spring and early summer, followed by reliable orange-red fall foliage color, native to open woods and rocky slopes across northern and western North America. Its compact, tidy, mounding habit and tolerance of a range of soils and light conditions make it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a native shrub border, foundation planting, or mass planting where a smaller-scale flowering shrub is wanted. Prune lightly after flowering to shape if needed, and expect minimal pest or disease problems from this tough, adaptable native species.

subcategory: Pacific island sticky-seeded shade coastal tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in zone 10–12; Bird Catcher Tree (Para Para) is a large-leaved tropical tree native to Pacific islands from New Zealand to Hawaii, Australia, Southeast Asia, and East Africa — famous for its extremely sticky, narrow, club-shaped fruits that trap small birds, insects, and lizards, sometimes fatally — and grown ornamentally for its bold, tropical, large-leaved foliage in shaded or semi-shaded positions.
directions: Plant Pisonia umbellifera in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; young trees prefer some protection from the hottest afternoon sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees are fairly drought-tolerant; the sticky fruits should be considered when siting — place away from areas frequented by small birds and do not plant near bird feeders. Bird Catcher Tree is one of the more ecologically unusual trees of Pacific island forests — its narrow, club-shaped fruits are covered in an extremely sticky, clear resin that adheres to anything that brushes against it, and small birds investigating the fruit clusters can become fatally entangled. This macabre adaptation has made it a subject of scientific and popular fascination: in some Pacific island seabird colonies (particularly on Heron Island, Australia), large numbers of migratory petrels and shearwaters are trapped each breeding season. Despite its sinister seed-dispersal strategy, the Bird Catcher Tree is a handsome ornamental with very large, glossy, paddle-shaped leaves creating a bold tropical texture in the shade garden; it performs well as a specimen or screen in zone 10–12. The variegated form ('Variegata') with green and cream-white blotched leaves is particularly attractive and widely grown as an ornamental across tropical and subtropical regions.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a sheltered, frost-free location or in containers moved indoors during cold spells. In zone 9 grow in a protected, deep-shade spot or use as a container plant on a shaded porch. The broad, undivided fronds are unlike typical fern foliage and provide a bold, tropical texture in shade gardens.
directions: Grow in bright to moderate shade in well-draining, humus-rich soil or a loose bark-based potting mix; bird nest fern grows as an epiphyte in nature, perching on tree trunks with its roots in accumulated leaf litter. The glossy, strap-like fronds emerge from a central rosette and can reach 4 feet long in ideal conditions. Avoid pouring water into the central cup where new fronds emerge, as this encourages rot; water the root zone and allow the mix to approach dryness between waterings. Fertilize monthly during the growing season with a dilute balanced fertilizer. This fern is excellent in bathrooms and covered patios where humidity is naturally higher.

subcategory: iconic orange-blue crane-flower South African perennial
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rhizome divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bird of paradise is a slow-growing perennial from the Eastern Cape of South Africa requiring patience — container-grown transplants typically take 2–4 years to reach first flowering, and seed-grown plants 5–7 years. Once established, plants are drought-tolerant and long-lived, blooming continuously for decades. Overcrowded clumps flower best — do not divide unnecessarily. Full sun is essential for flowering; part shade produces foliage but few flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bird of paradise is one of the most internationally recognized flowering plants in horticulture — the floral emblem of Los Angeles, a staple of tropical-theme gardens worldwide, and one of the most distinctive and immediately identifiable flowers produced by any plant. The flowers emerge from a horizontal, boat-shaped, green-purple spathe (the 'beak' of the 'bird') on a tall, stiff scape held above the large, oval, paddle-shaped, blue-green leaves on long petioles. The flower itself consists of three vivid, saturated-orange sepals arranged in a fan and three blue-purple petals — two fused into a pointed, arrow-shaped structure that projects forward — the overall composition creating an unmistakable resemblance to the head and crest of a tropical bird, complete with orange 'crown' and blue 'beak'. The flower's elaborate structure is adapted for pollination by sunbirds in its native South Africa: the weight of the bird on the blue petal structure exposes the pollen-covered anthers that dust the bird's feet. Native to the coastal and riverine scrub of the Eastern Cape of South Africa, it grows in full sun, lean, well-drained soil, and tolerates considerable drought when established. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a reliable, long-lived, repeating-bloom perennial that produces its extraordinary flowers throughout the year when mature.

common_name: Bird's Beak Oncidium (Bird's Mouth Orchid, Dove Orchid, Pink Oncidium)
plant_note: Grow in a small pot with fine to medium bark or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun; Oncidium ornithorhynchum blooms in fall and winter on long, arching, much-branched racemes that can reach 24 inches and carry 100–200 small flowers in rose-pink to lilac-lavender — the entire inflorescence is extraordinarily floriferous and the fragrance (a sweet, vanilla-baby-powder scent) is among the most pleasant of any orchid. A cool-to-intermediate grower that appreciates nighttime temperatures of 55–62°F in fall to trigger blooming. Protect from frost. One of the best fall-blooming orchids for zone 9-11 outdoor culture. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light in fine to medium bark or on a mount — Bird's Beak Oncidium grows most vigorously in intermediate conditions and produces its most spectacular, multi-branched bloom spikes when given cool, dry fall nights that trigger the inflorescence development. Oncidium ornithorhynchum is a compact, sympodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Costa Rica, and Colombia — one of the most free-flowering and fragrant of the many smaller Oncidium species, widely grown by orchid enthusiasts for the extraordinary fall flower display and remarkable fragrance. The plant is small and compact — oval, slightly flattened pseudobulbs 2–3 inches tall with 2–3 soft, narrow leaves. In fall and early winter, multiple flower spikes emerge from the base of the pseudobulbs and branch repeatedly to produce long, arching, pendant racemes bearing 50–200 small (0.5-inch) flowers in rose-pink to lilac-lavender, with a small, distinctly shaped lip that gives the species name ornithorhynchum (Greek: 'bird's beak'). The sheer flower quantity on a well-grown, established plant creates a cascade of soft pink-lavender that is exceptional among small orchids. The fragrance is the plant's other outstanding quality: intensely sweet, warm, and pleasant — commonly described as resembling vanilla, baby powder, or sweet clover — produced throughout the day and most concentrated in warm morning conditions. An outstanding fall-blooming orchid for zone 9-12. Non-toxic.

common_name: Bird's Nest Anthurium (Hookeri Anthurium, Lance-Leaf Bird's Nest)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, shaded patio container, or in zone 10-11 outdoor shade gardens; Anthurium hookeri is more tolerant of lower humidity, lower light, and temperature fluctuation than most collector anthuriums, making it a good choice for beginners in the genus. In zone 9b-10 in deep shade, it can be grown as an outdoor tropical groundcover or specimen. Provide moist, well-drained, humus-rich growing medium. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in moderate to deep shade in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or potting medium; Bird's Nest Anthurium is one of the most adaptable and shade-tolerant of the large Anthurium species, tolerating the reduced light and humidity of typical indoor environments better than most of its relatives. Anthurium hookeri is a large epiphytic to terrestrial anthurium from the forests of Trinidad, the Lesser Antilles, Guyana, and northeastern South America, growing in a distinctive bird's nest rosette form — the large, broadly elongated, glossy, dark-green leaves (12–24 inches long) radiate outward in a vase or funnel shape similar to Asplenium nidus, the Bird's Nest Fern, and for the same functional reason: the funnel shape channels rain and falling debris toward the plant's root zone, efficiently gathering nutrients and moisture. The leaves are thick, leathery, glossy, and a rich dark emerald-green with deeply impressed veins. Unlike the demanding velvet anthuriums, A. hookeri tolerates moderate indoor conditions, lower humidity, and even some neglect while remaining attractive. It produces typical anthurium flowers (green-white spathe and spadix) that, when pollinated, develop into small, purple, globose berries along the spadix. An excellent large specimen foliage plant for zone 9 shaded indoor and outdoor spaces. All parts toxic.

common_name: Bird's Nest Bromeliad (Blushing Nidularium, Innocentii Bromeliad)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or in a shaded, frost-free container garden in zone 10-11; Bird's Nest Bromeliad is a rainforest-floor species with essentially no cold or frost tolerance. Pot in a loose, well-draining, humus-rich bark-and-peat mix that mimics the leaf litter it grows in naturally, and keep humidity elevated. Divide and pot up rooted offsets once they have formed several of their own leaves.
directions: Grow in medium to deep, filtered shade — Nidularium innocentii is a true forest-floor understory plant and is more shade-tolerant than most tank bromeliads, with strong light bleaching or browning the leaves. Native to the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, it forms a dense, low rosette of glossy, dark green to purplish-bronze strap leaves; at flowering time the innermost leaves flush bright red, cradling small white to lavender flowers nestled deep at the center like eggs in a nest, which gives the genus its common name. It is closely related to Neoregelia but is distinguished botanically by its floral bracts, which form a tight, layered structure around the flowers rather than lying flat. Keep the central cup filled with rainwater or distilled water and grow it on the moist side, since this species comes from consistently humid rainforest floors rather than drier epiphytic niches.

common_name: Bird's Nest Fern (Nest Fern, Spleenwort Bird's Nest)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, shaded patio container, or in zone 9b-11 shade garden; Bird's Nest Fern cannot tolerate frost but is one of the more cold-tolerant large tropical ferns, surviving brief temperatures to 32°F if the rhizome is protected. In zone 9-11, plant outdoors in deeply shaded spots with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — outstanding under large trees or in north-facing shaded beds. Avoid getting water into the center rosette cup where it can cause rotting. Do not use neem or oil sprays on the fronds which cause browning.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil or potting mix; Bird's Nest Fern is one of the most shade-tolerant and adaptable of all large ferns, thriving in the deep, dry shade under large trees where most ferns would fail. Asplenium nidus is a large epiphytic fern native to tropical Asia, eastern Australia, and the Pacific Islands that grows naturally anchored to the bark of large trees, its roots drawing moisture and nutrients from accumulated organic matter. The frond pattern is unlike typical ferns: broad, undivided, strap-like, bright-green, glossy fronds up to 4 feet long arch outward from a central rosette in a shape that perfectly mimics a bird's nest — the dense, brown, fibrous mass of old frond bases at the center closely resembles the construction of a large bird's nest, giving the plant its common name. The fronds have an attractive central black midrib. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, Bird's Nest Fern is one of the finest large-scale shade plants for tropical effect, combining bold architectural form, glossy tropical foliage, and shade tolerance that allows it to thrive under oak trees. It also makes a striking large houseplant for bright-to-moderate indoor light.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Bird's Nest snake plant's compact rosette habit makes it well suited to a small pot, dish garden, or tabletop planting.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Bird's Nest snake plant's compact rosette habit makes it well suited to a small pot, dish garden, or tabletop planting. Broad, dark green leaves banded with lighter gray-green markings spiral outward from a central point into a low, dense, bird's-nest-like rosette rarely more than a foot across, a dwarf, clumping sport of the classic upright snake plant discovered in the 1940s. Its diminutive size and slow growth make it an easy, long-lived houseplant for a windowsill, desk, or terrarium-style dish garden, tolerating the same range of low light and infrequent watering that makes larger snake plants so forgiving. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Bird's Nest spruce is extremely slow-growing and well suited to foundation plantings and rock gardens where a large conifer would be inappropriate.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Bird's Nest spruce is extremely slow-growing and well suited to foundation plantings and rock gardens where a large conifer would be inappropriate. Dense, dark green needles cover a wide, flat-topped, mounding shrub with a distinctive central depression that gives the plant its common name, resembling a nest sunk into the top of the mound as the outer branches grow slightly taller than the congested center. One of the most popular dwarf Norway spruce cultivars, it grows only two to three inches per year, remaining a manageable, tidy specimen for foundation plantings, rock gardens, and mixed conifer beds for decades without pruning. It tolerates a range of soils and light conditions better than many dwarf conifers and needs only occasional watering during establishment and drought.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun for a late winter to spring bloom; self-sows prolifically where happy.
directions: Bird's-eye Gilia is a charming California native annual wildflower bearing masses of small, tubular, violet-purple flowers marked with a ring of deep purple and a yellow-orange throat — the three-toned pattern gives the species both its common name and its epithet tricolor. It is native to the dry, open grasslands and oak woodland clearings of California's Central Valley and Coast Ranges, where it blooms from February through May. Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; seeds require cool, moist conditions to germinate and will sprout through winter rains to bloom in late winter and spring. Bird's-eye Gilia self-sows prolifically in open, sunny, California-native garden beds and makes an excellent companion for California poppies and native clarkia.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or divisions in fall in very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or rocky, dry, poor soil in full sun to partial shade; birdfoot violet will not thrive in clay, wet, or fertile soils — it requires the conditions of the sandy pine barrens and dry rocky glades in which it is native.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy or rocky, dry, poor soil in full sun to partial shade — birdfoot violet is one of the most beautiful of all native violets, with the largest and most vividly colored flowers of the eastern species — 1 inch lavender to pale violet or bicolored (the classic bicolor form has dark upper petals and pale lower petals with an orange eye). The deeply divided, multi-lobed leaves closely resemble a bird's foot, giving the plant its common name. Unlike most violets that thrive in moist, rich soil, birdfoot violet is strictly a plant of dry, poor, acidic, sandy, or rocky soils — pine barrens, sandstone outcrops, and dry, open glades where soil fertility is minimal. It will languish and die in clay or rich soil. An outstanding and distinctive native for sandy, acidic rock gardens and dry native plant gardens in zones 3–8; a specialist larval host for several native fritillary butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early.
directions: 'Birdhouse' produces hard-shelled gourds that, once cured, can last for decades and be carved, painted, or drilled like wood for countless craft projects. Direct sow after frost in warm soil or start indoors a few weeks early, giving the vigorous vines plenty of room to sprawl or a sturdy trellis to climb. Grow in full sun in rich, well-drained soil with steady moisture through the long season. Allow the gourds to fully mature and dry on the vine, then cure them in a dry, airy spot for several months before crafting.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Birkin philodendron is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as an indoor plant.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Birkin philodendron is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as an indoor plant. A spontaneous mutation of the hybrid 'Rojo Congo,' this compact, non-climbing philodendron produces glossy, dark green leaves finely pinstriped with creamy white to pale yellow veins that grow more pronounced as each leaf matures, giving the plant a crisp, sharply patterned look distinct from other variegated philodendrons. Its neat, upright, self-heading rosette habit and modest size make it well suited to a tabletop or shelf as much as a floor specimen, needing no staking or climbing support. Allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings and avoid direct sun, which fades the variegation and can scorch the leaves.

common_name: Bishop of Auckland Dahlia (Dark Red Single Bloom over Near-Black Foliage)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Bishop of Auckland, part of the popular Bishop series, bears single dark red blooms held above near-black, bronze-purple foliage.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up. Bishop of Auckland, part of the celebrated Bishop series that began with the classic Bishop of Llandaff, bears simple, single, dark blood-red blooms with a ring of golden stamens at the center, held above dramatic near-black, deeply cut, bronze-purple foliage that provides ornamental value even before flowering begins. The single, open flower form makes it especially attractive to bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds compared to fully double dahlia types. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep flowers coming, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Bishop of Llandaff Dahlia (Dark Bronze-Foliage Scarlet-Flowered Peony Dahlia Classic)
