As a European wetland-edge native, it tolerates a range of light conditions from full sun to partial shade, making it a versatile choice for the damp, dappled-light edges of a woodland pond or rain garden. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow winter cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Black Snakeroot is a native woodland member of the carrot family with distinctive round, bristly seed heads.
directions: Plant in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, similar to the woodland conditions where it grows wild across eastern and central North America. Black Snakeroot bears small, greenish-white flower clusters in late spring on branching stems above deeply divided, palmate leaves, followed by distinctive round, bur-like seed heads covered in hooked bristles that catch on fur and clothing to disperse. Despite the common name it has no confirmed effect on snakebite; the name reflects historical folk use rather than proven medicinal value. It self-sows readily in a woodland garden and provides early-season nectar for small native bees and flies before many showier woodland wildflowers bloom.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; black spruce is adapted to boggy, poorly drained, acidic soils of northern bogs and swamps where few other conifers grow. Extremely cold-hardy — one of the few trees that survives the transition zone to arctic tundra.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; black spruce is the dominant tree of the boreal bog landscape of northern North America — growing across Canada and the northern US in cold, acidic, waterlogged bogs and muskeg where its shallow root system tolerates the poorly oxygenated, saturated soils that exclude most other conifers. A slow-growing, narrow, densely crowned spruce with distinctive clusters of persistent old cones that remain on the tree for years, giving branches a 'beaded' appearance. The needles are short and dark blue-green. Important for wildlife, providing nesting habitat for many boreal birds. The inner bark was used by Indigenous peoples for food and medicine. A key species for northern bog and wetland ecological plantings, rain garden wet zones, and permaculture systems in cold climates. The dwarf cultivar 'Nana' (12–18 inches tall) is used in rock gardens and container plantings.

common_name: Black Star Calla Lily (Deep Purple-Black with Darker Throat)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Black Star bears some of the darkest, near-black flowers available among colored calla lily hybrids.
directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where hot afternoon sun will not scorch the foliage. Black Star bears dramatic, deep purple-black spathes with an even darker throat, one of the most intensely dark colors bred into calla lily hybrids, creating a moody, dramatic accent in a border or container planting. Narrow, glossy green leaves rise through summer before the plant goes dormant in fall. In zones 8-10 it can be left dry in the ground through a mild winter, while in colder climates the rhizomes should be lifted and stored dry like dahlia tubers. Reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall to encourage the plant into its natural dormant period.

common_name: Black Star Gladiolus (Deep Wine-Red Edged Near-Black)
plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season. Black Star bears deep, dark wine-red flowers edged in near-black burgundy.
directions: Black Star bears deep, dark wine-red flowers edged in near-black burgundy, among the darkest colors available in gladiolus, making a dramatic accent in a cutting garden or as a striking cut flower paired with brighter companions. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; needs light and cool soil.
directions: 'Black Swan' bears intricate, finely cut semi-double blossoms as dark as cabernet on graceful, curved stems. Scatter the tiny seed on the soil surface in early spring or fall, leaving it uncovered since light and cool temperatures aid germination. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil where it is drought tolerant. Sow it along a frequented path or in a large container where its 3-to-5-inch blooms can be admired up close. Direct sow only, as poppies resent root disturbance, and let it self-sow for future years.

common_name: Black Taffeta Heuchera (Ruffled Near-Black Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; dark foliage color holds best out of intense afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Black Taffeta produces large, heavily ruffled and puckered leaves in an intense near-black purple with a glossy, almost metallic sheen, one of the darkest and most texturally dramatic heuchera cultivars available, holding its deep color through the growing season better than many dark-leaved heucheras that fade to bronze in summer heat. Its bold, ruffled texture and near-black color create a striking anchor point when paired with chartreuse hostas, silver-leaved brunnera, or bright-flowered shade perennials. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

common_name: Black Truffle Cardinal Flower (Near-Black Spring Foliage Scarlet Lobelia)
plant_note: Plant transplants in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Black Truffle emerges with near-black spring foliage that ages to maroon, bearing the classic scarlet cardinal flower blooms.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, at a pond margin, rain garden, or any low spot that stays reliably damp. Black Truffle is a patented cardinal flower selection prized for its striking near-black spring foliage, which gradually ages to a rich deep maroon through summer, providing months of dramatic foliage color in addition to the tall, brilliant scarlet flower spikes that draw hummingbirds heavily from mid to late summer. Its dark leaves make an especially strong contrast against the vivid red blooms, more dramatic than the plain green foliage of the straight species. Cardinal flower is naturally short-lived but self-sows and can be divided to maintain a planting; keep soil consistently moist, since it does not tolerate drought.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; black tupelo develops a deep taproot and transplants best when young — avoid moving established trees.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately wet, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; black tupelo (also called blackgum or sourgum) is widely regarded as one of the finest native trees for fall color in the eastern United States, turning brilliant scarlet — sometimes the first tree in the landscape to color in early autumn — weeks before most other species. It is remarkably adaptable, growing naturally in both swampy bottomlands and dry upland ridges, and tolerates periodic flooding as well as moderate drought once established. The small blue-black fruits ripening in September are among the most intensely sought wildlife foods of the season, consumed by at least 36 bird species including wood thrushes, robins, cedar waxwings, and wood ducks. Plant while young as the deep taproot makes transplanting difficult once trees exceed 3 inches in trunk diameter.

common_name: Black Velvet Alocasia (Little Queen Alocasia, Black Velvet Elephant Ear)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to low-light conditions in well-drained, slightly gritty, aerated potting mix; Alocasia reginula needs better drainage than many aroids — root rot in soggy media is the most common cause of decline. Allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. This jewel alocasia stays small (12–18 inches) and is suited to smaller containers. Maintain warm temperatures (65–85°F) and moderate humidity. Propagate by separating offsets (corms) from the parent rhizome. All parts toxic if ingested — calcium oxalate crystals.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-drained, aerated soil — Black Velvet Alocasia is a compact 'jewel' alocasia that performs best in the bright, diffuse light of a shaded indoor or sheltered outdoor position and will not tolerate direct sun, which scorches the velvety leaf surface. Alocasia reginula is a small, rhizomatous aroid native to Borneo (Sabah, Malaysia) in the Araceae family, one of the most coveted of the so-called 'jewel alocasias' — a group of compact, ornamental Alocasia species prized for extraordinary foliar texture and color rather than dramatic size. The leaves are the defining feature: heart-shaped to sagittate, thick, and covered in a dense, velvety, blue-black to dark charcoal-green surface with a distinctive texture resembling crushed velvet — the velvet quality results from tightly packed, densely hairy papillae covering the leaf epidermis. The veins are silver-white to pale silver, creating a bold, contrasting pattern of silver lines on the near-black velvet surface — a combination of texture and color contrast unlike almost any other aroid. The undersides are a deep maroon-purple. The plant remains compact (under 18 inches), making it ideal for terrariums, small containers, and sheltered shaded spots in zone 11-12 tropical gardens. All parts toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; resents transplanting.
directions: 'Black Velvet' bears glamorous, ruby-black edible flowers that add drama to salads, cheese plates, and garden beds alike. Direct sow the large seeds where they are to grow, since nasturtiums dislike root disturbance. Grow in full sun to part shade in lean soil, as overly rich ground yields foliage instead of flowers. Both the peppery flowers and leaves are edible. Its compact, bushy form suits containers, borders, and bed edges, blooming from summer to frost.

common_name: Black Velvet Petunia (Near-Black Deep Purple Petunia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Black Velvet was one of the first petunias bred to reach a genuinely near-black flower color.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Black Velvet bears deep, velvety, near-black flowers with a soft matte texture, a dramatic, moody color rare among bedding annuals that makes it a favorite for designers looking to add contrast or a Gothic touch to a mixed container or border. Its rich color reads best against pale or bright companions like white, chartreuse, or silver-leaved plants rather than getting lost among other dark hues. Deadhead regularly or shear back by half in midsummer if growth becomes leggy, which prompts fresh, bushier regrowth and renewed bloom through fall.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants or root hardwood cuttings (12–18 inch stem sections planted directly in moist soil) in early spring. Black Willow establishes exceptionally rapidly and begins producing root anchorage within weeks; it is the preferred native species for immediate streambank and erosion control in moist to wet sites.
directions: Black Willow is the largest native willow in North America and the most important native tree for the immediate stabilization of eroding streambanks, native to the moist to wet, sandy and gravelly alluvial soils of rivers, streams, and floodplains throughout eastern North America from New Brunswick to Florida and west to Montana and New Mexico. Its aggressive, fast-establishing root system grips unstable bank soil within weeks of planting, and hardwood cuttings root readily when simply pushed into moist streambank soil in early spring — making it the fastest and cheapest native solution for stream restoration and bank protection. The pendulous, narrow, lance-shaped leaves create a graceful, weeping appearance over water; catkins appear in early spring, providing one of the season's earliest pollen sources for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Black Willow is short-lived (40–60 years) and prone to branch breakage in ice and wind storms, but its rapid establishment and wildlife value (woodpecker habitat, caterpillar host plant) make it an invaluable native pioneer for wet, disturbed sites where quick establishment is the priority.

common_name: Black and Bloom Salvia (Bigger, Bolder Hummingbird Sage)
plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts after last frost in humus-rich, evenly moist soil; this selection outperforms the older 'Black and Blue' with larger flowers and near-black stems and calyces.
directions: Site in full sun to light afternoon shade with consistently moist, fertile soil for the strongest bloom and darkest calyx color; this cultivar was bred for improved vigor and larger deep-cobalt flowers compared with the classic 'Black and Blue'. It spreads by rhizomes to form a dense clump and is one of the top hummingbird plants for late summer into fall in Gulf Coast gardens. In zone 8 the top growth is killed by hard freezes but the roots reliably resprout in spring under a thick mulch layer; further south it stays evergreen.

common_name: Black and Blue Sage (Deep Cobalt Hummingbird Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Black and Blue dies back to the ground in zone 8 freezes but returns vigorously from tuberous roots in spring — in zone 9, the tuberous roots typically survive mild winters without protection.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade after the last frost date; Black and Blue is widely considered the finest hummingbird salvia in cultivation — producing large (1.5–2 inch), tubular, deep cobalt-blue flowers in whorled spikes above the dark foliage, with uniquely dark, nearly black calyces that create a dramatic two-tone contrast between the vivid blue corolla and the black tube. The specific combination of long tubular flowers, deep cobalt color, and black calyces is visually extraordinary — a flower color depth and richness not commonly seen in North American garden perennials. Hummingbirds are drawn irresistibly to Black and Blue — the deeply tubular flower is perfectly suited to hummingbird feeding and a well-established colony in bloom will have multiple hummingbirds visiting constantly from late spring through frost. The plant grows 3–5 feet with a robust, upright habit that provides excellent height and structure in the mid-to-back border from spring through frost. In zone 9, Black and Blue blooms from late May through hard frost — a 6-month blooming season that makes it one of the finest long-blooming tender perennials for Gulf South gardens. The tuberous roots store energy through mild winters and resprout vigorously in spring. Pair with orange Hamelia patens or red Justicia fulvicoma for a hummingbird-garden color combination of outstanding effectiveness.

common_name: Black and Blue Salvia (Deep Cobalt-Blue Hummingbird Sage with Black Calyces)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Black and Blue spreads by underground rhizomes to form a gradually expanding colony — a desirable quality for naturalizing in large plantings but plant where spreading can be accommodated or managed.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Black and Blue is one of the most spectacular hummingbird plants available for Gulf South gardens — Salvia guaranitica 'Black and Blue' produces large (2-inch), deep cobalt-blue to ultramarine-blue tubular flowers with contrasting jet-black calyces that frame each flower, creating a vivid blue-and-black color combination that is more intensely blue than almost any other commonly grown summer perennial. The flower color is genuinely deep, pure blue — not the blue-purple of most blue flowers — making Black and Blue one of the most useful plants for achieving true blue in warm-climate garden compositions. The black calyces that remain after the flowers drop maintain the ornamental display and create the impression of more flowers than are actually present. Ruby-throated hummingbirds find this salvia irresistible — the large, deep-blue flowers produce abundant nectar and the flower size is ideal for hummingbird bill geometry. The plants grow vigorously to 3–5 feet and spread by underground rhizomes, gradually naturalizing in suitable conditions. In zone 9, Black and Blue is a semi-evergreen perennial that may be damaged by hard freezes but returns from the rhizomes in spring with mulch protection. Cut back to 12 inches in late winter to encourage fresh, vigorous regrowth.

common_name: Black-Eyed Stella Daylily (Compact Gold Daylily with Maroon Eyezone)
plant_note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; like other Stella-line daylilies, Black-Eyed Stella is fast to establish and forgiving of average garden conditions.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and remove spent scapes at the base regularly to encourage the near-continuous flush of bloom. Black-Eyed Stella is a compact sport in the Stella d'Oro family, producing the same golden-yellow, ruffled flowers but marked with a distinct maroon-red eyezone encircling the throat, giving each bloom noticeably more contrast and depth than the solid-colored original. It shares the same reliable, extended bloom season from late spring through fall, tough constitution, and low, mounding habit that made Stella d'Oro a landscape standard, making it a good choice for gardeners who want the eyezone detail of larger daylily cultivars in a compact, everblooming plant. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in early spring on prepared soil surface in full sun — seeds need light and should not be covered; alternatively sow in fall for natural cold stratification and vigorous spring germination. Transplants started indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost bloom the same year.
directions: Direct-sow seeds on prepared soil surface in full sun in early spring or fall, pressing lightly without covering as seeds need light for germination; black-eyed Susan is one of the most reliably beautiful and adaptable native wildflowers of eastern and central North America, blooming with golden-yellow daisy-like flowers with distinctive dark chocolate-brown centers from midsummer through frost. It thrives in lean, dry to moderately fertile, well-drained soil and deteriorates in rich, wet conditions — never amend the soil with heavy fertilizers. A short-lived perennial that self-seeds freely to perpetuate naturally; leave seed heads standing through winter as they are a critical food source for goldfinches and other songbirds. Excellent as a cut flower and as a native companion for grasses and other prairie perennials.

common_name: Black-Eyed Susan Vine (Thunbergia Annual Tropical Climbing Vine)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; soak seeds overnight in warm water before starting to improve germination. In zone 9, transplant March–April and plant in a location with trellis or support to climb. Black-Eyed Susan Vine is a perennial in zone 10–11 (frost-free) but grown as an annual in zone 9 where it blooms prolifically from late spring through fall. Excellent in hanging baskets where the vining branches cascade attractively, and on small trellises and fence posts.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost at 65–70°F; transplant to a trellis or support after last frost. Black-Eyed Susan Vine (not related to the native perennial Rudbeckia) is a fast-growing African tropical vine with a twining habit that quickly covers a small trellis, fence section, or mailbox post with dense foliage and continuous bloom. The distinctive 1–1.5 inch flowers have five flattened petals in a circular arrangement around a dark purple-black or white center tube — the dark center among the orange or yellow petals creating the characteristic 'black-eyed' appearance that gives the vine its common name. Colors range across orange, yellow, white, and salmon, with the classic orange-with-black-center the most recognizable form. Black-Eyed Susan Vine is particularly valuable in the Gulf South for its heat and humidity tolerance — it blooms continuously through hot summers when many other annual vines fade or slow down. The vine is well-scaled for residential use: reaching 5–8 feet rather than the 20–30 feet of aggressive vines like trumpet creeper, making it appropriate for small gardens, fences, and containers with a tomato cage for support.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring wedged into crevices of limestone or other calcareous rock in partial shade to full shade; black-stemmed spleenwort grows in nature in the crevices of shaded limestone cliffs and canyon walls and does best when planted into the joints of a limestone rock wall or rock garden rather than in open soil.
directions: Plant divisions in spring by wedging them into crevices of limestone or calcareous rock in partial to full shade; black-stemmed spleenwort grows naturally in the shaded joints of limestone and dolomite cliffs throughout the southeastern and south-central US and is best established directly in rock crevices rather than in open soil. Asplenium resiliens is a small, tufted evergreen fern with shiny, dark-brown to black stipes (stems) — the feature that gives it its common name — and once-pinnate, 4–10 inch fronds with rounded, alternate pinnae with slightly toothed margins. It is a limestone specialist very similar to the ebony spleenwort (A. platyneuron) but smaller and more heat-tolerant, native to shaded limestone outcrops and canyon walls from Virginia to Arizona. An excellent fern for a shaded limestone rock wall or naturalistic limestone garden, where it will establish in crevices and require essentially no maintenance once settled.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; black-edged sedge grows in dry to moderately moist, sandy or rocky, acidic soils in woodland settings across the southeastern US. One of the better sedges for dry-shade conditions.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, sandy or rocky, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; black-edged sedge is a low-growing, clump-forming native sedge of the southeastern piedmont and Coastal Plain, growing in the dry shade of upland oak and pine woodlands where few other grasses or sedges survive. The common and scientific names (nigromarginata = black-margined) refer to the dark margins of the scales in the fruiting spikes, a useful identification feature. This is one of the most genuinely drought-tolerant and shade-tolerant sedges available for difficult dry-shade conditions — a garden situation where moisture-loving sedges like carex appalachica, laxiflora, and platyphylla would struggle. The plant stays very low and compact, spreading slowly into small colonies without becoming aggressive. An excellent ground layer plant for dry, shaded, wooded areas in zone 9a.

plant_note: Start indoors; stratification aids germination.
directions: Blackberry lily is actually a member of the iris family, bearing orange, red-spotted flowers followed by clusters of glossy black seeds resembling blackberries. Start seed indoors, as a period of cold stratification improves germination. Grow in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil with its fanned, sword-like foliage adding structure to the border. The tall, clean stems make excellent cut flowers, and the seed heads are prized for dried arrangements. It self-sows and returns reliably as a short-lived perennial.

common_name: Blackberry Wine Corydalis (Deep Wine-Purple Long-Blooming Shade Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blackberry Wine bears deep wine-purple tubular flowers over blue-green ferny foliage through much of the growing season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; consistent moisture, especially in summer heat, keeps the plant flowering well. Blackberry Wine bears clusters of deep wine-purple, spurred, tubular flowers held above finely cut, blue-green, ferny foliage, blooming over an unusually long stretch of the growing season from spring into fall rather than the brief spring show typical of many woodland Corydalis species. Its long bloom period and soft, airy foliage texture make it a valuable filler among hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials. Divide congested clumps in spring, and keep soil from drying out during summer to sustain continued flowering.

plant_note: Plant transplants in spring after last frost in zone 9; established plants are drought-tolerant and semi-evergreen. Blackfoot Daisy requires sharp drainage — it will rot in heavy clay or wet soils. Add coarse gravel or decomposed granite to heavy soils before planting. In zone 9, plants may go semi-dormant in the hottest summer weeks and resume blooming as temperatures cool.
directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; excellent drainage is non-negotiable — Blackfoot Daisy (Melampodium leucanthum) will not survive in clay soils that stay wet after rain. Melampodium leucanthum is a small, mounding native perennial that blooms nearly year-round in zone 8–10, covering itself with perfectly formed white daisies with yellow centers, each approximately 1 inch across. It is native to the semi-arid limestone hills of Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, where it grows in thin, rocky, alkaline soils in full sun with minimal rainfall. In zone 9 gardens, Blackfoot Daisy is an exceptional xeriscape and rock garden plant that requires no supplemental irrigation once established and no deadheading — spent flowers simply fall cleanly from the plant. The honey-scented flowers attract small native bees, skippers, and butterflies throughout the growing season. Plants are remarkably long-lived in the right conditions, forming expanding mounds of fine-textured gray-green foliage that are attractive even when not in bloom. Trim back hard in late summer to encourage fresh growth and extended fall blooming. Note: the annual Melampodium paludosum (Medallion Flower) is a distinct tropical species from the same genus but with different cultural requirements.

common_name: Blackhawks Big Bluestem (Deep Purple-Black Native Prairie Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Blackhawks develops unusually deep purple-black foliage color by midsummer, intensifying further into fall, unlike the blue-green typical of the wild species.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun. Blackhawks is a striking big bluestem selection that develops deep, glossy purple-black foliage color as the season progresses, intensifying further with cool fall weather, a dramatic departure from the blue-green summer color of the wild species, topped by the characteristic turkey-foot-shaped seed heads in late summer that give big bluestem its folk name. Like the straight species it is a tall, structural native grass well suited to the back of a border, a naturalized meadow, or a mass planting, tolerating a wide range of soil conditions from moist to fairly dry once established. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges to keep it tidy and vigorous.

common_name: Blackie Sweet Potato Vine (Deep Purple-Black Ornamental Sweet Potato Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Blackie' produces the most intense dark-purple coloring in full sun — plants in shade become more green-purple and lose the dramatic near-black color that is the primary ornamental feature.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Blackie Sweet Potato Vine is a cultivar of ornamental sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) selected for its deep purple-black to near-black leaf color — the most dramatic dark foliage of any commonly grown ornamental annual, producing a cascade of deeply lobed, star-shaped leaves in a color so dark it reads as nearly black in high contrast compositions with chartreuse or white companions. The purple-black color is produced by extremely high anthocyanin concentrations in the leaf tissue — the same pigment chemistry that makes purple basil, dark caladiums, and black elephant ear dark, but at an intensity that produces the closest approach to true black available in an annual foliage plant. 'Blackie' is one of the most vigorous ornamental sweet potato vines, spreading 4–8 feet during the Gulf South growing season to create a dense, ground-covering mat of dark foliage. The vine is one of the most effective design tools for creating contrast in mixed container plantings and annual border compositions: the deep purple-black creates dramatic negative space against which brighter flowers and lighter foliage appear to glow. In zone 9, Blackie grows as a warm-season annual, though the storage tubers sometimes survive mild winters in protected positions. Outstanding paired with 'Margarita' (chartreuse sweet potato vine), 'Diamond Frost' euphorbia, or bright orange and yellow tropical flowers.

plant_note: Plant only young, nursery-grown container plants in fall in dry, sandy, rocky, or acidic, very well-drained soil in full sun; blackjack oak is extremely difficult to transplant from the wild due to its deep taproot and thrives in the poorest, most droughty soils available.
directions: Blackjack oak is the signature tree of dry, sandy, impoverished 'blackjack' soils across the southeastern United States — its distinctive club-shaped, three-lobed leaves with a broad, rounded top and narrow base are immediately recognizable, and the tree is virtually impossible to establish in rich or moist soils, thriving only in the driest, poorest, most acidic conditions that prevent most trees from growing. Often found alongside post oak in the 'Cross Timbers' forest of Oklahoma and Texas, blackjack oak commonly forms dense, almost impenetrable thickets on sandy, infertile ridges that are habitat for some of the most specialized dry-land wildlife communities in the South. Despite its demanding site requirements, blackjack oak is a highly valuable wildlife tree: its small acorns are consumed by wild turkey, whitetail deer, and at least 30 species of birds, and the crooked, gnarled dead snags are prime nesting habitat for cavity-nesting birds. In landscapes with genuinely poor, dry, acidic, sandy soils, it is one of the most reliable native trees for creating a self-sustaining, wildlife-rich oak woodland.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants in fall into lean, sandy or gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun, ideally against a dry wash or rocky slope similar to its native Mojave and Sonoran Desert habitat.
directions: Set out container-grown plants in fall into lean, sandy or gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun, ideally against a dry wash or rocky slope similar to its native Mojave and Sonoran Desert habitat. Bladder sage produces small tubular violet-and-white flowers favored by hummingbirds and native bees, followed by its namesake inflated, papery seed capsules that persist and rattle through summer, adding ornamental interest after bloom. It is a wiry, intricately branched shrub that is nearly leafless in dry periods, an adaptation that makes it extremely drought tolerant once established. Avoid summer irrigation and heavy soils, which quickly cause root rot in this true desert specialist.

common_name: Blanc Double de Coubert Rose (Fragrant Pure White Rugosa Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; Blanc Double de Coubert is a fragrant white rugosa rose noted for its papery, crepe-textured petals.
directions: Plant in average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; rugosa roses excel in poor, dry, or coastal soils that would stress most other roses. Blanc Double de Coubert bears large, loosely double, pure white blooms with a papery, crepe-like petal texture and a strong, sweet fragrance, opening against the rugged, deeply veined rugosa foliage that stays clean and disease-free through the season. The vigorous shrub is exceptionally cold-hardy and salt-tolerant, useful for coastal plantings and difficult, sandy sites. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since rugosas bloom on both old and new growth and resent hard pruning.

common_name: Blanche Ferry Sweet Pea (Pink-and-White Bicolor Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Blanche Ferry, introduced in 1889, is a compact-vined heirloom with distinctive rose-pink-and-white bicolor flowers.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Introduced in 1889 and named for the daughter of the D.M. Ferry seed company's founder, Blanche Ferry bears richly fragrant, bicolor flowers with rose-pink standards and white to pale pink wings, on a somewhat shorter, bushier vine than many other heirloom sweet peas of its era. It remains a favorite among heirloom flower gardeners for its strong scent and old-fashioned charm. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost date, or sow directly in spring; blanket flower is short-lived (often 2–4 years) in humid climates with heavy soil — sharp drainage is critical to longevity. Deadhead regularly to prolong the extended bloom season. The plant often self-sows, producing seedlings that may vary from the parent.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; blanket flower is a North American prairie hybrid producing some of the most vivid and eye-catching daisy flowers in horticulture — large (3–4 inch), wheel-like blooms in the most intense combinations of red, orange, gold, and yellow, with the traditional pattern showing scarlet-red ray petals broadly tipped in rich golden-yellow and a dark, burgundy-red central disk, creating a warm-toned, richly colored flower that earns the name 'blanket flower' from its resemblance to the bold geometric patterns of Native American blankets. The bloom season is extraordinarily long — from early summer through hard frost — with regular deadheading maintaining a near-continuous display. Drought-tolerant and heat-loving, it thrives in the exact difficult conditions (poor soil, heat, dry spells) that exhaust other perennials, making it outstanding for low-maintenance sunny borders. Modern cultivars include the compact 'Goblin' (12 inches), 'Fanfare' (tubular petals), and 'Arizona Sun' (deep red with gold tips). Short-lived in clay or humid conditions — excellent drainage is the key to perenniality.

plant_note: Press seed onto the surface after frost; light aids germination.
directions: Press blanket flower seed onto firmed soil around the last frost, leaving it uncovered since light speeds germination. This heat-loving wildflower blazes with red, orange, and yellow daisy-like blooms all summer, thriving in sandy, lean soils where other plants sulk. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant and a magnet for bees and butterflies. Deadhead for continuous color, or leave a few heads to self-sow next season.

common_name: Blaze Climbing Rose (Improved Blaze Scarlet Climber)
plant_note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring or fall against a fence, mailbox post, or arbor in full sun; Blaze is an easy, forgiving climber for Gulf South gardens, tolerating average soil and less fastidious care than many modern climbing roses.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil against a sturdy support, and tie the vigorous canes in as they grow since Blaze climbs by producing long stems that must be trained rather than by twining on its own. Introduced in 1932 and improved with a stronger repeat-blooming selection released in the 1950s, Blaze became one of the most widely planted climbing roses in mid-20th-century America for its clusters of bright, semi-double scarlet-red blooms produced in a heavy spring flush with continued bloom through summer. It is exceptionally vigorous and forgiving, tolerating a wide range of soils and light care while still covering a fence or arbor with reliable color, which explains its enduring popularity in older Southern gardens. Prune out the oldest canes every couple of years at the base to keep the plant renewing itself with vigorous new growth.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; blazingstar has sticky leaves that trap insects — handle with care. It does not transplant well and should always be sown in place. The flowers open in the afternoon and early evening, releasing their fragrance for moth pollinators as dusk approaches.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Lindley's blazingstar is one of California's most beautiful native annual wildflowers — producing large (2–3 inch), golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers of exceptional saturation and brilliance, each with a prominent central boss of numerous golden stamens that gives the flower a sunburst quality on a par with the finest rose. The flowers open in the afternoon (remaining closed during morning hours) and emit a rich, warm, vanilla-honey fragrance at dusk that attracts hawkmoths and other night-flying pollinators. The leaves and stems are covered with tiny, barbed hairs that stick to clothing and trap small insects — an adaptation shared with the genus. Native to dry, rocky, sandy habitats in the California Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills, it thrives in lean, well-drained soils where competing vegetation is sparse. In the garden, mass sowings create a brilliant field of golden flowers in spring and early summer, particularly in gravel gardens and dry native plant meadows. The evening-opening, fragrant flowers make it an exceptional plant for any area where an outdoor seating space or evening garden can capture the dusk fragrance.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root crowns or container plants in early spring in rich, evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; bleeding heart thrives under deciduous trees where it receives spring sun before the leaf canopy closes, then retreats into summer dormancy as conditions dry.
directions: Plant bare-root crowns or container stock in early spring in rich, evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; set roots 1 inch deep and water thoroughly to establish. Lamprocapnos spectabilis (formerly Dicentra spectabilis) is the quintessential cottage-garden shade perennial, producing arching, 18-to-24-inch stems hung with perfectly heart-shaped, rosy-pink flowers with protruding white inner petals from mid-spring to early summer — the effect of a string of dangling lockets over blue-green, deeply cut foliage has made it one of the most beloved shade-garden plants for over two centuries. Plants go summer-dormant once heat arrives in June or July (earlier in the South), so interplant with hostas, ferns, or astilbes to fill the gap; the dying foliage of bleeding heart can look messy, so grow neighboring plants close enough to cover it naturally. The cultivar 'Gold Heart' has vivid gold foliage for extra shade-garden brightness; 'Alba' has pure white flowers. Hardy in zones 3–9, though in zones 8–9 it blooms earlier (February–April) and goes dormant faster — treat as a spring ephemeral.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; bleeding heart vine performs best in bright filtered shade and struggles in hot, direct afternoon sun in zone 9. It is particularly effective as a patio container plant that can be moved to protection in colder zones.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; bleeding heart vine is one of the most exquisitely beautiful flowering vines available for shaded tropical and subtropical gardens, producing pendant clusters of flowers that are truly bicolored — the white, inflated, papery calyx (the balloon-like outer part) encloses a brilliant red corolla with protruding red stamens, creating a striking red-and-white contrast that gives the plant its common name. After the red corollas drop, the white calyces persist for weeks and gradually turn pinkish-purple, extending the display. This semi-twining vine blooms most heavily in spring and again in fall and prefers the bright, filtered shade of a pergola or porch where the flowers can be enjoyed up close. In zone 9a it needs winter protection or overwintering indoors; it thrives outdoors year-round only in frost-free areas. Keep it slightly root-bound in containers for best bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun at pond edges, marshy ground, or rain gardens; blister sedge tolerates seasonal flooding and shallow standing water.
directions: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun at pond edges, marshy ground, or rain gardens; blister sedge tolerates seasonal flooding and shallow standing water. Narrow, arching green leaves form loosely spreading clumps from which upright stems rise in early summer, tipped with distinctive, inflated, papery seed capsules that swell like tiny balloons and give the plant both its common name and a striking textural accent. Widespread in marshes, wet meadows, and pond margins across temperate North America, it spreads gradually by rhizome in consistently saturated soil, making it a useful component of a naturalized wetland or bioswale planting alongside blue flag iris and pickerelweed. It provides cover and seed for marsh birds and requires no maintenance beyond cutting back old growth in late winter.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Blonde Ambition tolerates poor, dry, and alkaline soils and needs no supplemental fertilization once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Blonde Ambition is a Plant Select introduction (discovered and named by Colorado horticulturist Dan Johnson) selected from the native shortgrass-prairie species blue grama for its unusually large, showy, horizontally held chartreuse-to-golden seed heads, which resemble tiny eyelashes or flags lined up along the flowering stems from midsummer through fall. The fine-textured, blue-green foliage forms a low, dense mound, while the flowering stems rise well above it, and the straw-gold seed heads persist through winter, providing months of texture and movement along with seed for birds. It is exceptionally heat and drought tolerant once established, reflecting its origin as a dominant grass of the shortgrass prairies of the Great Plains and American Southwest, and needs minimal irrigation, no fertilization, and no winter protection. Cut the previous season's growth back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges to keep the clump tidy.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; gold foliage color holds best out of the hottest afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Blondie produces bright, warm golden-blonde foliage with a slight ruffled texture, one of the brighter and more consistently colored gold heucheras available, holding its warm tone through the season better than many gold cultivars that fade to chartreuse in shade or bleach out in strong sun. In early summer it sends up airy, wiry stems of small white flowers above the foliage that draw hummingbirds and pollinators. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

plant_note: Divide offset pups or plant container-grown specimens in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; blood banana is grown for its striking foliage rather than for edible fruit, which is small and full of hard seeds.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; blood banana is an ornamental selection of the wild seed banana grown for its dramatic broad, blue-green leaves heavily splashed and streaked with maroon-red blotches, with pseudostems that carry the same deep burgundy mottling. It is smaller and more manageable than fruiting dessert bananas, reaching 5 to 8 feet, making it a good fit for mixed tropical borders and large containers where a full-sized banana would overwhelm the space. Small, seedy, essentially inedible fruit may form after flowering, so grow it strictly as a bold foliage and texture plant rather than for any edible crop. In zone 9 the top growth is killed by frost most winters, but a thick mulch over the root zone helps the rhizome resprout vigorously once the soil warms in spring; where winters are colder, dig and store rhizomes indoors or grow in a large container that can be moved under cover.

plant_note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface (neck at or slightly below soil level) in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; blood lily blooms most reliably in partial shade with consistent moisture and warmth — drought stress causes the bulb to go dormant prematurely without blooming.
directions: Plant bulbs just below soil surface in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; blood lily (fireball lily, powder puff lily) is an African tropical bulb that produces one of the most spectacular and unexpected flower displays of any shade-tolerant bulb — a single large, smooth, spherical, perfectly round, 4–6-inch-diameter ball composed entirely of several hundred individual small, bright scarlet to orange-red, star-shaped flowers with prominent, projecting, golden-tipped stamens, rising on a stout, purple-mottled stem directly from the soil before or simultaneously with the emerging leaf growth. The ball-like flower head has a precise, geometric, almost artificial perfection that makes it appear more like a designed object than a natural flower. It blooms in spring to early summer, then produces a large rosette of broad, soft, tropical-looking leaves that persist through the growing season before dying back in winter. Unlike the related Haemanthus, Scadoxus multiflorus does not tolerate complete drought dormancy and performs best with some moisture year-round. A dramatic and relatively easily grown shade garden bulb for zone 9–12 tropical and subtropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; blood lily flowers appear in late summer to early autumn BEFORE the leaves emerge (the leaves follow and are present through winter and spring), then the plant goes summer dormant and leafless — a hysteranthous (flowers before leaves) flowering pattern unique within its family. Keep completely dry in summer. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant bulbs (neck exposed) in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; blood lily is a botanical curiosity as much as a garden beauty — a South African Cape bulb that flowers before its leaves appear, sending up in late summer and early autumn (August–October) a fat, stout, dark-red to spotted stem only 4–8 inches tall topped by a dense, hemispherical to globular brush of hundreds of tiny, brilliant scarlet-red flowers with long, projecting red stamens — creating the unmistakable silhouette of a bright-red shaving brush of very large dimensions, as thick and dense as a pom-pom. The flower head remains decorative for several weeks. After flowering, two (rarely three) large, broad, thick, tongue-like, glossy-green leaves emerge and persist through winter and spring before dying back in summer dormancy. The dramatic, shaving-brush flower form — wholly unlike any other bulb flower — is immediately recognizable and memorable. Native to the rocky, sandy, dry slopes and scrubland of the Western Cape, it thrives in the Mediterranean-climate conditions of zones 9–11 in the garden. In humid-summer climates container culture with controlled summer dryness is recommended.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Blood Tip develops its darkest red tips with bright light and cool weather.
directions: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Blood Tip develops its darkest red tips with bright light and cool weather. Pale green rosettes are dramatically tipped in deep blood-red at each leaf point, a striking two-tone color combination that intensifies in cooler weather and bright light, forming a spreading mat of tightly packed rosettes typical of hens-and-chicks. Extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, it multiplies readily by offsets to form an expanding colony, making it a colorful, low-maintenance choice for a rock garden, green roof, or trough planting. Water only occasionally, and separate offsets to propagate or fill bare patches as individual rosettes flower once and die, leaving the surrounding colony to continue.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blood of China is an old, historic camellia cultivar valued for its dependable, vivid red winter bloom.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blood of China is an old, historic camellia cultivar valued for its dependable, vivid red winter bloom. One of the oldest camellia cultivars still commonly grown, dating to the early nineteenth century, it produces semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a vivid, saturated blood-red that opens over a long bloom season from fall through winter on a vigorous, upright shrub with glossy, deep green foliage. Its long history in Southern gardens and reliable, generous flowering have kept it in cultivation for two centuries, and it remains a benchmark red camellia against which newer introductions are still compared by collectors. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid overhead watering which can spot the flowers, and prune lightly after flowering finishes to shape if needed.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; blood-red cranesbill is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and performs well in alkaline, rocky soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade; blood-red cranesbill forms a low, compact mound of deeply dissected, dark-green leaves covered in bright magenta-crimson flowers from late spring through summer — with repeat bloom after shearing — and then turns brilliant orange-red in fall, making it a three-season performer. It is unusually drought-tolerant and lime-tolerant for a geranium, thriving in rocky banks, wall crevices, and gravelly soils where most plants struggle. Shear plants by half in midsummer after the main bloom flush to prompt fresh growth and a second round of flowers in late summer. 'Album' (white) and 'Striatum' (pale pink with pink veins) are classic selections. Long-lived and requires essentially no maintenance.

common_name: Bloodgood Japanese Maple (Red Upright Japanese Maple)
plant_note: Plant container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial shade; in zone 9, afternoon shade is essential to prevent leaf scorch — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal for Bloodgood in hot-summer climates.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, humus-rich soil in dappled to partial shade; Bloodgood is the single most widely planted and most reliable upright red-leafed Japanese maple cultivar in American horticulture — selected for excellent dark reddish-purple leaf retention through summer (resisting the tendency of many red-leaf maples to fade to greenish-bronze in summer heat), attractive upright-spreading form reaching 12–18 feet, and reliable deep scarlet-red fall color. The five-lobed, deeply cut leaves emerge rich reddish-purple in spring and hold good color through the growing season with adequate moisture and afternoon shade. Bloodgood's vertical-upright branching pattern creates an elegant, architecturally refined form that provides seasonal interest year-round — spring leaf emergence, summer purple foliage, scarlet fall color, and attractive branching structure in winter. In zone 9, Bloodgood requires careful siting with afternoon shade, moist but well-drained soil, and protection from hot dry winds to prevent summer leaf scorch. It performs reliably as a landscape tree in zone 9 with correct placement — east-facing exposures or locations under tall trees providing dappled afternoon shade are ideal. Consistent moisture during summer heat stress periods is the key to success in zone 9. The reddish-purple bark on young stems adds winter interest.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in water or moist perlite and plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost; bloodleaf develops its most intense coloration in bright indirect light to partial shade — deep shade reduces color intensity while full hot sun can scorch the leaves.
directions: Root stem-tip cuttings in water or moist perlite and plant in moist, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost; bloodleaf (beefsteak plant) is a South American native grown for its spectacular, glowing crimson to deep wine-red foliage — the leaves are broadly notched and suffused with vivid red-pink pigmentation that makes the plant appear to glow in the summer border and container garden. It is used as a vivid foliage accent and is excellent for creating high-contrast combinations with yellow, orange, and white-flowered companions. Pinch growing tips regularly to maintain a compact, bushy form and prevent leggy growth. Root cuttings in water in autumn before frost to overwinter indoors as a houseplant; plants can grow for several years in warm indoor conditions. In zones 10–12 it persists as a tender perennial sub-shrub. An irreplaceable element of Victorian-era bedding designs, now enjoying renewed popularity in mixed container arrangements.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds need cold winter stratification and germinate in early spring — sow fresh seed immediately after harvest as viability drops rapidly when dry.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds need cold winter stratification and germinate in early spring — fresh seed sown immediately after harvest in late spring also works well as seeds lose viability quickly when dry. Bloodroot is a spring ephemeral native to eastern North American deciduous forests; it emerges very early in spring, often while snow still lingers, with a large, deeply lobed, blue-green leaf wrapped around a single bud that unfurls into a brilliant, pure-white flower with 8–12 petals and a golden center lasting only a day or two but spectacularly beautiful. The thick rhizome exudes bright red-orange latex sap when cut (giving rise to its common name) and the plant goes completely dormant by early summer; pair with hostas or ferns to fill the void. Plant has toxic sap; handle rhizomes with gloves.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes in fall or early spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; bloodroot thrives in the margins of ponds, streams, and bogs, and requires consistently moist to wet conditions that simulate its natural South African fynbos wetland habitat. It is not drought-tolerant. The rhizomes and roots bleed a vivid blood-red to orange-red latex when cut, responsible for the common name.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; bloodroot (not to be confused with the North American woodland wildflower Sanguinaria canadensis, also called bloodroot) is a tall, impressive South African wetland perennial producing large, pleated, sword-shaped, bright-green, fan-like leaves of distinctive form and in spring (October through January in the Southern Hemisphere, April through June in cultivation), tall, branching panicles of vivid, bright-yellow, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers carried well above the leaf fans. The flowers are produced in such abundance on the tall, airy panicle that a large, established clump in full bloom is an impressive sight — masses of golden-yellow flowers floating above the architectural pleated foliage. The common name refers to the vivid blood-red to orange-red latex that bleeds from any cut surface of the red-pigmented rhizomes — a distinctive characteristic of the genus. It is a naturally marshy-edge plant of the South African Cape fynbos wetlands and requires consistently moist to wet conditions, making it ideal for the margins of garden ponds and bog gardens in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets or nursery divisions in spring into very well-drained, sandy or gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this hybrid does not come true from seed and is propagated only by division of its basal offsets.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy or gritty soil in full sun, giving light afternoon shade in the hottest inland climates to preserve leaf color; 'Bloodspot' is one of the earliest and best-known intergeneric hybrids between Manfreda maculosa and Agave macroacantha, combining the soft, pliable, spineless (or nearly spineless) leaves of manfreda with the vigor and rosette form of agave. Its broad, gray-green leaves are heavily speckled with maroon-red spots that intensify with bright light and cooler temperatures, and unlike true century-plant agaves it is polycarpic, meaning the rosette does not die after flowering. Mangaves are notably faster-growing and more cold-tolerant than many pure agave species, and 'Bloodspot' in particular has become a staple of Texas and Gulf Coast xeriscape design for its dramatic color and reliable garden performance in well-drained beds and containers alike. Good air circulation and sharp drainage are essential, since rot rather than cold is the most common cause of failure.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts in spring into a light, acidic mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark; keep the medium moist year-round with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide bright, humid conditions — never use tap water or ordinary garden soil.
directions: Bloody pitcher plant takes its name from the deep blood-red to maroon coloring of its tubular pitchers, and comes from montane forests of Peninsular Malaysia and Sumatra, where it grows as an epiphytic and terrestrial vine. It is a vigorous, free-pitchering species that adapts well to intermediate greenhouse or windowsill conditions and is considered one of the easier highland Nepenthes to flower and propagate from cuttings. Pot it in a light, acidic, low-nutrient medium of sphagnum moss and orchid bark, and irrigate only with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater, since tap water minerals build up in the potting mix and burn the roots. Give it bright, indirect light and steady humidity, and never fertilize the soil directly.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Bloom-A-Thon azaleas rebloom continuously from spring through fall rather than in a few discrete flushes, and tolerate more sun than most traditional azaleas.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, though this series tolerates considerably more direct sun than older azalea types once established. Bloom-A-Thon is a breeding series developed as an alternative to the Encore line, valued for a more continuous rebloom pattern through the growing season rather than distinct spring, summer, and fall flushes, along with a naturally more compact, mounded habit that needs little pruning to stay tidy. Cultivars are available across a range of flower colors including hot pink, lavender, red, and white, all sharing strong heat tolerance and repeat flowering suited to long Gulf South growing seasons. Water deeply during dry spells to support the extended bloom cycle, and prune lightly right after the heaviest spring flush to shape the plant without removing developing buds for later color.

common_name: Bloom-A-Thon Hot Pink Azalea (Reblooming Compact Vivid Pink Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Bloom-A-Thon Hot Pink reblooms continuously from spring through fall rather than in a few discrete flushes and tolerates more sun than most traditional azaleas.
directions: Bloom-A-Thon Hot Pink carries vivid, saturated hot-pink flowers on a compact, naturally mounded shrub, part of a breeding series developed as an alternative to the Encore line with a more continuously repeating bloom pattern through the growing season rather than distinct spring, summer, and fall flushes. Its tidy habit needs little pruning to stay in shape, and like other Bloom-A-Thon selections it tolerates considerably more direct sun than older azalea types once established, extending its usefulness beyond the deep shade typically required for reliable azalea bloom. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, water deeply during dry spells to support the extended bloom cycle, and prune lightly right after the heaviest spring flush to avoid removing developing buds for later color.

common_name: Bloom-A-Thon Lavender Azalea (Reblooming Compact Lavender-Purple Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Bloom-A-Thon Lavender reblooms continuously from spring through fall rather than in a few discrete flushes and tolerates more sun than most traditional azaleas.
directions: Bloom-A-Thon Lavender carries soft lavender-purple flowers on a compact, naturally mounded shrub, offering a cooler-toned option within the Bloom-A-Thon series that pairs easily with pinks, blues, and white companion plantings. Like its siblings in the line it reblooms nearly continuously through the growing season rather than flowering only in short flushes, and its tidy habit needs little pruning to hold shape. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, water deeply during dry spells to support the extended bloom cycle, and prune lightly right after the heaviest spring flush to avoid removing developing buds for later color.

common_name: Bloom-A-Thon White Azalea (Reblooming Compact White Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Bloom-A-Thon White reblooms continuously from spring through fall rather than in a few discrete flushes and tolerates more sun than most traditional azaleas.
directions: Bloom-A-Thon White carries clean, pure white flowers on a compact, naturally mounded shrub, providing a versatile neutral that brightens a shaded bed and pairs with virtually any other color in a mixed planting. It shares the series' hallmark near-continuous rebloom through the growing season rather than a few short flushes, and its tidy habit needs little pruning to hold shape. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, water deeply during dry spells to support the extended bloom cycle, and prune lightly right after the heaviest spring flush to avoid removing developing buds for later color.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; BloomStruck is an Endless Summer series hydrangea bred for improved heat and sun tolerance, sturdier red-tinted stems, and better disease resistance than older reblooming cultivars.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; BloomStruck tolerates more direct sun than most bigleaf hydrangeas, though afternoon shade is still beneficial in the hottest Gulf South summers. Part of the Endless Summer series, BloomStruck was bred for improved heat tolerance, sturdier dark red-purple stems, and better resistance to powdery mildew than older reblooming hydrangea cultivars, along with vivid rose-pink to purple mophead flowers that shift with soil pH. It flowers on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year, so a late spring frost that damages old buds does not prevent a strong summer and fall rebloom. Flower color ranges from blue-purple in acidic soil to rose-pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

common_name: Bloomerang Lilac (Reblooming Dwarf Lilac with Spring and Summer Flushes)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; deadhead the heavy spring flush promptly to encourage the intermittent summer and fall rebloom this series is bred for.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and deadhead spent spring flower clusters promptly to redirect energy into the intermittent summer rebloom this series was bred to produce. Bloomerang, developed by Proven Winners, was among the first lilacs marketed specifically for reblooming, opening a full flush of fragrant purple-lavender flowers in spring like a standard lilac and then continuing to produce scattered new blooms on current-season wood through summer and into fall. Its compact, rounded habit fits smaller gardens and foundation plantings better than large old-fashioned lilac shrubs, and it shares the family's need for a real winter chill and good air circulation to perform and stay free of powdery mildew. Light monthly feeding and consistent moisture through summer support the extended rebloom cycle better than the sparser feeding a once-blooming lilac needs.

plant_note: Plant offsets in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to sandy, dry soil in full sun; blue agave is cold hardy to approximately 23–28°F when established in sharply-drained soil and performs well in zone 9 with a degree of winter protection for young plants.
directions: Plant offsets in well-drained, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun — blue agave is the world-famous Mexican highland succulent that is the sole legal source of tequila, cultivated in vast plantations in the Jalisco region of Mexico where it requires 7–10 years to mature before the piña (heart) is harvested for distillation. As an ornamental landscape plant it is spectacularly bold: rigid, channeled, blue-gray leaves up to 5 feet long with very sharp terminal spines form enormous symmetrical rosettes that make striking architectural focal points. After 7–12 years of growth, a single 20-foot flower spike is produced; the plant dies afterward but produces numerous offsets. Outstanding for dramatic, statement-making specimens in dry, hot, zone 9–11 landscapes, tropical-style gardens, and as a large container plant. The 'Weber Azul' variety is the tequila industry standard and the most commonly available cultivar in nursery trade.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; Blue Angel is a giant that requires generous spacing — allow at least 5 feet in each direction — and takes 4–5 years to achieve its spectacular full size.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade; Blue Angel is a giant hosta of the first rank — at maturity forming a massive mound of enormous, deeply veined, glaucous powder-blue to blue-gray leaves that can measure 18 inches long by 14 inches wide. The overall clump reaches 3–4 feet tall and 5–6 feet wide in ideal conditions, making it one of the largest blue hostas in cultivation. The extremely thick, waxy leaf cuticle provides exceptional slug resistance and helps maintain the characteristic blue color through summer, as the waxy bloom reflects blue wavelengths while absorbing others. Near-white, lightly fragrant flowers appear in midsummer on tall, attractive scapes. In zone 8–9, consistent moisture and deep shade are essential to maintain leaf quality through summer; a large, deep mulch layer helps keep roots cool. A single established clump is a spectacular focal point in any shade garden.

plant_note: Set out young trees in fall on dry limestone slopes or upland alkaline soils; shows somewhat greater tolerance to emerald ash borer than other native ashes.
directions: Set out young trees in fall on dry limestone slopes or upland alkaline soils, where its distinctive four-angled, winged young twigs and thick corky bark set it apart from other native ashes. This species shows somewhat greater tolerance to emerald ash borer than other North American ashes, making it a more resilient choice for restoration and specimen plantings where ash trees are otherwise declining. Its dense, rounded canopy provides good shade for dry, calcareous sites that few large shade trees can handle. Historically its inner bark sap was boiled down to produce a blue dye, giving the species its common name.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or set out nursery transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; growth from seed to a landscape-sized barrel is slow, typically many years.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; native to the arid hills of Hidalgo state in central Mexico, this compact barrel cactus is prized for its smooth, powdery blue-gray to gray-green stem and neat rows of golden-yellow spines that contrast sharply against the body color. Unlike many solitary barrel cacti, mature specimens readily offset from the base to form multi-headed clumps over time, adding to its sculptural appeal in xeriscape and container design. A ring of bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers appears at the crown in mid-to-late summer, followed by small yellow fruit. It tolerates brief cold snaps into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit but is more cold-sensitive than the classic golden barrel (Echinocactus grusonii), so in zones 8b-9 it should be sited in a warm, sheltered, south-facing microclimate with protection from prolonged winter wet.

common_name: Blue Boa Agastache (Large-Flowered Deep Violet-Blue Hyssop)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Blue Boa was bred for unusually large flower spikes and a deeper violet-blue color than most garden agastache hybrids.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, and avoid low spots where water collects over winter. Blue Boa produces unusually large, dense spikes of deep violet-blue flowers over aromatic, mint-scented foliage from midsummer through fall, giving it more visual weight in the border than many finer-textured agastache cultivars. The abundant nectar-rich flowers draw hummingbirds, bumble bees, and butterflies steadily through the long bloom season, and the sturdy upright stems hold up well without staking. Once established it tolerates heat and dry spells with ease, though it performs best with excellent soil drainage year-round.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; needs darkness to germinate.
directions: 'Blue Boy' dazzles with true sky-blue flowers that are wonderful massed and practically care-free thanks to their drought tolerance. Direct sow in early spring or fall, covering the seed since bachelor's button needs darkness to germinate. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil. The flowers can be used fresh or dried, and the edible petals make a colorful garnish. Deadhead to extend bloom, and it will self-sow to return the following season.

common_name: Blue Butterfly Bush (Sky Flower Clerodendrum, Uganda Clerodendrum)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs after last frost in partial shade to full sun; in zone 9, Blue Butterfly Bush performs best in morning sun with afternoon shade protection in summer. It blooms most profusely in spring and fall when temperatures are moderate. In zone 9a, it will freeze back to the roots in hard winters but resprouts vigorously; in zone 9b-10 it is semi-evergreen to evergreen. Prune back hard after each major bloom flush to stimulate repeat flowering. Can also be grown in a large container.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Blue Butterfly Bush adapts to most soils and responds well to regular fertilization and moderate watering during active growth periods. Clerodendrum ugandense (now sometimes reclassified as Rotheca myricoides) is a large shrub from the highlands of East Africa — Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania — producing one of the most charming and distinctive small flowers in the tropical plant world. Each individual flower consists of four pale blue petals spreading like wings and a single deep violet-blue lower petal curving downward, creating the unmistakable silhouette of a small blue butterfly perched on the stem. The flowers are borne in loose, airy panicles at the branch tips throughout the warm season in zone 9, with the most spectacular flushes in spring and fall. The overall effect of a plant in full bloom — dozens of tiny sky-blue butterflies hovering in clusters at every stem tip — is extraordinary and unlike any other flowering shrub available in zone 9. Blue Butterfly Bush is a fast grower that responds well to hard pruning, which stimulates vigorous new growth and repeat blooming cycles. Excellent as a container specimen on a sunny to partly-shaded patio.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; blue butterfly moraea flowers in autumn (September–November in the Southern Hemisphere, blooming in autumn/early winter in cultivation in the Northern Hemisphere) unlike the spring-blooming pavonia moraeas. It is a summer-rainfall South African species — not a Cape winter-rainfall species — and therefore more tolerant of summer moisture than many other moraeas. The flowers last only a single day but are produced in succession.
directions: Plant corms in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; blue butterfly moraea is notable for two unusual characteristics: it flowers in autumn rather than spring (unlike most iris-family South African plants), and the flowers are a vivid, clear, mid-to-deep blue — a color that is striking in any plant but particularly valuable in the autumn flower season when pure-blue flowers are rare. The individual blooms are typical moraea form — three large outer falls with a yellow, black, and white 'nectar guide' marking at the base, three smaller inner standards, all in clear blue-violet to mid-blue — and each lasts only a single day, but the corm produces multiple flowering stems and each stem multiple flowers in succession over several weeks of autumn bloom. The tall, branching, airy flowering stems rise well above the single, cylindrical, grass-like leaf. It is a summer-rainfall grassland species from the Drakensberg foothills and eastern South Africa, giving it better tolerance of summer rain than the Cape winter-rainfall species, and making it more practical for the zone 9 Gulf Coast autumn garden where rainfall continues through summer and fall. An exceptional autumn blue for zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in spring in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; blue butterwort is one of the most common and easily grown native butterworts of Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine savannas.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade. Blue butterwort forms a low rosette of pale green, sticky-glandular leaves that trap small insects, and in spring sends up striking, pale blue-violet flowers with a darker throat on wiry stalks well above the foliage, among the showiest of the native Gulf Coast butterworts. It grows abundantly in wet pine flatwoods and savannas from the Carolinas to Louisiana and is considered one of the easiest butterworts to cultivate, tolerating a broader range of moisture and light than many carnivorous plants as long as the soil stays consistently acidic and nutrient-poor.
