Grow in pure rain water or distilled water in the tray method and never fertilize; combine with sundews and pitcher plants for an authentic, low-maintenance Gulf Coast bog garden display.

plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partly to fully shaded site, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system from summer heat. Blue Cadet forms a low, dense mound of small, rounded, blue-green leaves and produces abundant lavender flowers on short scapes in mid to late summer. Introduced by Paul Aden in the 1970s, it remains a popular compact edging and groundcover hosta for shaded borders.

common_name: Blue Cascade Distylium (Spreading Groundcover Evergreen Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Blue Cascade spreads wider than it grows tall, making it useful as a large-scale evergreen groundcover on slopes or under high tree canopy where mowing is impractical.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, spacing plants to allow the low, wide-spreading branches to knit together into a dense evergreen groundcover over a couple of seasons. Blue Cascade is a low, mounding, ground-hugging distylium selection with fine-textured, blue-green foliage that cascades over walls, banks, and slopes, sharing the parent species' resistance to leaf spot, scale, and deer browsing along with tolerance for both wet and dry, sunny and shaded sites. Its width-over-height habit makes it a durable substitute for juniper or low spreading yew in Gulf South landscapes, where those traditional groundcover shrubs often struggle with heat, humidity, and root rot. Requires little to no pruning beyond removing an occasional wayward branch to keep the mounded outline tidy.

common_name: Blue Cathedral Bells Cup and Saucer Vine
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks early; needs warmth to germinate.
directions: Also called monastery bells, this fast-growing vine bears 2-inch cup-shaped flowers that open pale green and mature to violet purple. Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost in warmth, standing the flat seeds on edge in the soil. Grow in full sun to part shade near arbors, fences, or trellises where it quickly forms a fragrant privacy screen. Pinch back the tips to encourage branching and more blooms. It flowers from summer until frost and is grown as an annual outside frost-free zones.

common_name: Blue Chalk Sticks (Blue Senecio, Senecio mandraliscae)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; Blue Chalk Sticks spreads vigorously by stem rooting and becomes an effective ground cover in sunny, well-drained areas of zone 9–12 landscapes.
directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Blue Chalk Sticks is a spreading South African succulent ground cover producing dense clusters of narrow, cylindrical, powder-blue to blue-gray leaves in a distinctive chalk-blue color that provides unique cool-toned contrast in warm-palette Southern landscapes. The intensely blue-gray coloring makes it one of the most visually striking ground covers for sunny, dry gardens and one of the few plants that provides true blue-gray color at the ground level. Stems sprawl and root as they spread, forming a low (12–18 inch tall), dense mat that suppresses weeds and requires virtually no maintenance once established in appropriate conditions. Small white daisy-like flowers appear in summer; the flowers are ornamentally insignificant but produce viable seed. Blue Chalk Sticks is deer-resistant, heat-tolerant, and extraordinarily drought-tolerant once established, making it ideal for xeric, water-wise landscaping in zone 9–12. Propagates very easily from stem cuttings pressed into moist gritty soil. Note: the sap can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals (like most Senecio species).

plant_note: Set out shrubs in spring after soil warms.
directions: 'Blue Chiffon' Rose of Sharon is a deciduous flowering shrub with large, double, lacy blue flowers borne from summer through fall. Plant in spring in full sun to light shade in average, well-drained soil, giving it room to reach its mature size. Water regularly the first year to establish, after which it becomes fairly low-maintenance and tolerant of heat. Prune in late winter or early spring to shape the shrub and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. The long bloom season and hardiness make it a reliable summer backbone for borders and hedges.

common_name: Blue Chip Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Sterile Compact Buddleja)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new flowering growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth. Blue Chip was one of the first true dwarf butterfly bush cultivars introduced, staying under 3 feet tall and wide — a fraction of the size of older Buddleja davidii selections — while still producing lavender-blue flower spikes continuously from summer through frost. Its compact, mounding, sterile habit fits containers, small borders, and mass plantings where full-size butterfly bush would need constant hard pruning to control, and it draws butterflies and hummingbirds heavily despite its small stature. It tolerates heat and drought well once established, needing little care beyond the annual cutback.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in full to partial shade; blue cohosh is slow to establish but extremely long-lived once settled and is best left undisturbed after the first season.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in full to partial shade; blue cohosh is slow to establish but extremely long-lived once settled, and is best left undisturbed after the first season. Caulophyllum thalictroides is an elegant eastern North American native woodland perennial that emerges with a striking blue-green color in spring, bearing large, deeply compound leaves resembling meadow rue that give the plant a delicate, airy texture; small, inconspicuous yellowish-green to purplish flowers appear in early spring before the leaves fully expand, followed by ornamental clusters of deep blue, berry-like seeds (actually exposed ovules, not true fruits) in late summer and fall that persist well into winter. The plant has significant ethnobotanical history but all parts are toxic — do not ingest. Use it as an elegant foliage accent in shaded native plant gardens and woodland borders.

plant_note: Sow in spring or fall; seeds benefit from cold stratification.
directions: Sow blue columbine in fall or after cold-stratifying the seed, pressing it onto the surface since light helps it sprout. This hardy perennial wildflower nods with delicate blue-and-white spurred blooms that lure hummingbirds and bees in late spring. It appreciates partial shade and consistent moisture, making it a graceful choice for woodland edges and containers. Leave seed heads to self-sow, as plants are relatively short-lived but readily replace themselves.

plant_note: Divide the fleshy-rooted clumps in early spring or fall and replant into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in a cool, lightly shaded spot, keeping the crown just below the soil surface.
directions: Divide the fleshy-rooted clumps in early spring or fall and replant into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in a cool, lightly shaded spot, keeping the crown just below the soil surface. Loose racemes of vivid, true-blue, tubular flowers rise above finely divided, blue-green foliage from mid-spring into early summer, offering one of the purest blue tones available among shade perennials. The plant tends to go semi-dormant in hot, humid weather, so it performs best where summers stay relatively cool and the soil never dries out completely. Pair it with hostas, ferns, or other later-emerging perennials that can fill in as it fades back after flowering.

plant_note: Plant small divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in early fall; blue corydalis goes dormant in summer and benefits from companions that fill in the gap — site with hostas or ferns that expand as corydalis fades.
directions: Plant small divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; blue corydalis is a Chinese native considered by many plantspeople to be the finest and most desirable small shade perennial introduced in the last thirty years — its ferny, deeply divided, blue-green leaves emerge in late winter and spring bearing a prolonged display of slender, tubular, vivid sky-blue to turquoise flowers from April through June. The flower color is uniquely intense and clear — a pure, vibrant blue-turquoise that is extraordinarily rare in shade garden perennials. The plant goes fully dormant in summer (essentially disappears after June heat arrives) and can be interplanted with summer-expanding companions to fill the void. Hardy to zone 5 but struggles in persistent summer heat and humidity in the Deep South. 'Blue Panda', 'China Blue', and 'Pere David' are celebrated cultivars. An absolutely must-have shade garden plant for cool to moderate climate gardeners.

plant_note: Direct sow on dry, sandy, or gravelly soil in full sun after the last frost; blue curls germinates readily in warm soil but requires excellent drainage and low soil fertility — it thrives in barren, open patches where it has little competition from grass.
directions: Blue curls is a native annual wildflower of pine barrens, dry sandy clearings, and open woodland paths across the eastern United States — tiny but dazzling when in bloom, bearing intricate blue to violet flowers with dramatically long, arching stamens (the 'curls') that give the plant its evocative name and distinguish it from all other wildflowers in the landscape. The strongly aromatic foliage has a pungent, camphor-like scent similar to basil and other members of the mint family; blue curls has historically been used as an insect repellent and minor herbal remedy. It is one of the most important native annual wildflowers for supporting specialist bees in dry, sandy, barren habitats — bombylius flies and small native bees are primary pollinators. Direct sow on disturbed sandy soil in full sun; it thrives in poor, dry conditions and competition-free open ground where few other plants grow well, self-seeding from late summer through fall to return the following year.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (or very early spring) into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; blue curls is a Texas native winter annual that germinates with fall rains and blooms in early spring, self-sowing readily once established.
directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; blue curls is a fast-growing Texas and northern Mexico native winter annual, producing tightly coiled, fiddlehead-like flower clusters that slowly unfurl to reveal small, densely packed, violet-blue flowers with prominent stamens, opening from late winter into spring on branching, slightly sticky-hairy stems. It is one of the earliest and most reliable spring nectar sources for native bees on the southern Great Plains and Texas Hill Country, often blooming alongside bluebonnets in a naturalistic wildflower planting. Sow seed in fall to take advantage of cool-season germination and root growth, since spring-sown plants bloom later and less vigorously; established plantings self-seed freely in favorable dry, sunny conditions, returning reliably each year without replanting.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Blue Curls echeveria holds its powdery blue color and tight rosette form best in bright light.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Blue Curls echeveria holds its powdery blue color and tight rosette form best in bright light. Thick, powdery, silvery-blue leaves curl gently backward at the tips, forming a loose, spreading rosette that offsets readily to form small clusters, and the popular 'Topsy Turvy' selection of this species curls its leaves even more dramatically. Native to dry hillsides in northeastern Mexico, it is easy to grow and propagate, tolerating a range of light conditions though coloring and form are best in bright light, making it a versatile addition to a succulent dish garden or xeriscape container arrangement. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves to protect the delicate powdery bloom, and separate offsets to propagate.

plant_note: Grow in full sun on lean, gritty, fast-draining soil, mimicking the rocky Eastern Cape slopes it comes from and avoiding winter soil moisture buildup.
directions: Grow this South African cycad in full sun on lean, gritty, fast-draining soil, mimicking the rocky Eastern Cape slopes it comes from and avoiding any winter soil moisture buildup. Its rigid, powder-blue leaflets held in a tight symmetrical crown make it a striking accent for xeriscape and Mediterranean-style gardens where color contrast against green foliage is wanted. It is extremely slow-growing and drought-tolerant once established, needing only occasional deep watering through the hottest months. Protect it from prolonged freezes below the upper 20s F, as it is hardier than tropical cycads but not reliably cold-hardy.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Stokesia requires excellent drainage and will not tolerate wet soil, particularly during winter — heavy clay soils must be amended with grit and organic matter for adequate drainage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Blue Danube is the classic Stoke's aster cultivar — one of the most reliable and widely planted named selections of Stokesia laevis, an attractive native wildflower of the southeastern United States ranging from South Carolina to Louisiana. The large (3–4 inch), lavender-blue to periwinkle-blue flowers have the distinctive multi-petaled, fringed structure of stokesia — each flower head resembles a very large cornflower (Centaurea) with deeply cut, fringe-edged blue petals radiating from a lighter-colored center. The clear blue to lavender-blue flower color is exceptional in the summer border and combines beautifully with yellow, white, and orange companions. Blue Danube typically blooms from June through August in zone 9, with the first flush being the heaviest. Stoke's aster is native to the pine savannas and flatwoods of the Deep South and is perfectly adapted to the heat, humidity, and sandy soils of the Gulf Coastal Plain — one of the most underused native perennials for zone 9 full-sun gardens. It is reliably perennial in zone 9, forming expanding clumps that can be divided every 3–4 years. Exceptional drought tolerance once established; deer-resistant.

plant_note: Plant cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; blue dawn flower is frost-sensitive (killed to the ground by frost but often returning from roots in zone 8-9) and grows as a vigorous perennial in frost-free zone 9-11. Can become invasive in warm coastal climates. Listed as invasive in Hawaii and Florida.
directions: Plant cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; blue dawn flower (blue morning glory) is one of the most spectacularly beautiful ornamental vines for warm climates — producing abundant 3–4 inch diameter, vivid violet-blue to deep blue-purple morning glory flowers (changing color slightly through the day from bright blue in morning to blue-purple by afternoon) from spring through fall on a vigorous, twining vine that can grow 10–15 feet or more in a season. Unlike many morning glories, this is a perennial vine (in zones 9–11) that builds a woody base and becomes more vigorous each year. Spreads by self-seeding abundantly and can be invasive in warm coastal and subtropical climates — listed as invasive in Hawaii and Florida. A magnificent flowering vine for trellises, fences, and arbors in zones 8–11 where its aggressive nature can be managed. The vivid blue is particularly rare and striking among flowering vines. Hummingbirds visit the flowers.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential — blue daze rots in moist, heavy soil. In zone 9–11 it acts as a perennial.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun after last frost; blue daze is one of the most beloved summer annuals in Gulf Coast gardens, producing a continuous cascade of brilliant sky-blue flowers from spring through frost over trailing stems of soft silver-green leaves. It behaves as a perennial groundcover in zone 9–10, spreading to form a low, drought-tolerant mat of near-constant bloom through the summer months when most plants struggle with heat. The blue flower color is exceptionally vivid under southern summer sun. Excellent in containers, hanging baskets, rock gardens, or as a front-of-border annual where summer heat and excellent drainage are provided. Propagate by rooted stem cuttings in fall to maintain plants through winter in zone 9+.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring after the last frost in constantly moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in deep to partial shade; blue deinanthe emerges late and its soft new growth can be damaged by a late freeze, so wait until frost danger has fully passed.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring after the last frost in constantly moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in deep to partial shade; blue deinanthe emerges late and its soft new growth can be damaged by a late freeze, so wait until frost danger has fully passed. Deinanthe caerulea is a rare Chinese woodland perennial in the hydrangea family, forming a slowly spreading clump of broad, quilted, dark green leaves topped in mid to late summer by nodding, waxy, violet-blue flowers held just above the foliage. It is a connoisseur's shade plant for consistently moist, cool woodland gardens, resenting both summer drought and waterlogged winter soil, and performs best where summers stay relatively mild. Mulch heavily to conserve soil moisture and protect the shallow rhizomes over winter; established clumps are slow to increase and are best left undisturbed for several years between divisions.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall 3 inches deep in full sun in well-drained, lean, dry to summer-dry soil in zone 7–10; Blue Dicks is among the most abundant and widespread of all California wildflowers — carpeting grasslands, chaparral hillsides, and oak savannas from Oregon to Baja California and east to Utah and Arizona — with dense, rounded clusters of small, bright blue-purple to lavender flowers held on long, wiry, leafless stems from late winter through spring, one of the most reliable wildflowers in the California native palette.
directions: Plant Dichelostemma capitatum corms in fall 3 inches deep in any well-drained, lean soil in full sun; they thrive in rocky, clay, or sandy soils as long as drainage is good; provide minimal water in winter and spring (natural rainfall is usually sufficient), then dry completely in summer; corms multiply readily into large colonies. Blue Dicks is one of the most quintessentially Californian of all spring wildflowers — a familiar sight on roadsides, hillsides, and open grasslands throughout the state where it blooms in abundance from February through May. The small, bright blue-purple to lavender, tubular flowers are packed into tight, round clusters (capitulum) at the top of tall, slender, wiry stems that sway gracefully in the breeze — creating a beautiful, airy effect when naturalized in masses. The corms were a major starchy food source for many California Indigenous peoples — eaten raw, roasted in the coals, or boiled; they have a slightly sweet, nutty flavor and were an important caloric staple. Blue Dicks is one of the easier California native corms to grow outside California and adapts to a wider range of summer conditions than many species; in humid summer climates, plant in raised beds or well-drained slopes to ensure good summer drainage. An essential component of California native wildflower meadows and oak savanna restoration plantings.

common_name: Blue Diddley Chaste Tree (Compact Lavender-Blue Dwarf Vitex)
plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Diddley is a Proven Winners compact chaste tree, staying 3-6 feet tall, giving a smaller-scale alternative to full-sized vitex for a Gulf Coast bed or border.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Diddley is a compact chaste tree selection, staying 3-6 feet tall, considerably smaller than the classic 10-20 foot vitex species, making it easier to fit into a residential foundation planting or mixed border. It produces the same fragrant, gray-green foliage and lavender-blue flower spikes as larger vitex selections, blooming from summer into fall and tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil well once established. Its smaller stature means it needs less aggressive pruning than full-sized vitex; simply cut back lightly in late winter to encourage fresh growth and maintain a tidy shape.

common_name: Blue Ensign Pulmonaria (Solid Green Vivid Blue-Flowered Lungwort)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Blue Ensign is an Award of Garden Merit-winning lungwort valued for its unusually vivid, deep cobalt-blue flowers, among the most intensely colored of any pulmonaria cultivar, held above plain, unspotted green leaves rather than the silver-mottled foliage typical of most lungwort cultivars. Its early spring bloom, opening before many companion shade perennials leaf out, provides an important nectar source for emerging bumblebees, and its solid green leaves offer a plainer foliage backdrop that lets the striking blue flowers stand out. Divide congested clumps in early fall every few years to maintain vigor and flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or start indoors with 4–6 weeks of cold stratification; Baptisia is slow to establish but extremely long-lived — a well-placed plant improves for decades and is one of the finest native perennials available.
directions: Sow seed in fall directly in prepared ground or stratify cold for 4–6 weeks before indoor sowing; seedlings establish slowly — expect little the first year and a full plant by year 3 — but once established Baptisia is virtually indestructible, drought-tolerant, and long-lived for decades. Blue false indigo is a magnificent eastern North American native prairie and woodland-edge perennial, producing upright 3–4 foot clumps of blue-green foliage and stunning spikes of deep violet-blue pea flowers in late spring that are among the showiest of all native flowers; the inflated dark seed pods that follow are ornamental into winter and beloved by flower arrangers. Tolerates poor, dry, rocky soils and light shade but flowers most abundantly in full to partial sun; once established, do not move or divide as it resents disturbance.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; division every 2–3 years maintains the intense blue color.
directions: Plant in full sun and very well-drained, lean to average soil; blue fescue is a cool-season grass that goes semi-dormant in the heat of summer and performs best in cool, dry climates. The tight, spiky mounds of intensely silvery-blue foliage are striking as edging or mass plantings; tan flower spikes appear in early summer. Divide every 2–3 years in early spring, discarding the dead center and replanting the vigorous outer portions — this maintains the best blue coloration. Avoid heavy, wet clay soils and humid conditions which promote crown rot.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil at pond or stream margins; keep the rhizome at the soil surface, not buried. Blooms best in full sun but tolerates partial shade.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions at the soil surface in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; blue flag iris is the quintessential native wetland iris of the northeastern and central US and Canada, growing in marshes, bogs, wet meadows, and streambanks with bold violet-blue flowers veined with white and yellow in late spring. It is native across a vast range from Labrador to Virginia, making it more cold-hardy than the similar southern blue flag (I. virginica). The flowers provide nectar for specialist long-tongued native bees and bumblebees. Plant at the margin of a water garden, in a rain garden, or in any consistently moist location. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested. The rhizomes spread slowly to form handsome colonies; divide every 4–5 years in fall to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in partial shade; blue flax lily tolerates full sun in cooler climates but requires afternoon shade in zone 9-11 heat.
directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in partial shade; blue flax lily tolerates full sun in cooler climates but requires afternoon shade in zone 9-11 heat. Dianella caerulea is an outstanding, low-maintenance evergreen perennial from eastern Australia with arching, strap-like, dark-green leaves and airy panicles of small, blue-purple, six-petaled flowers on slender stems in spring and summer, followed by distinctive, bright, electric-blue to indigo berries in fall and winter that are one of the most striking ornamental fruit colors in the plant world; the berries persist attractively for months. It forms handsome, slowly expanding clumps and is an outstanding drought-tolerant, shade-tolerant groundcover for warm-climate gardens in zones 8-11, where it is used extensively as a border edging and under-tree groundcover. Very deer-resistant.

common_name: Blue Fortune Agastache (Long-Blooming Lavender-Blue Anise Hyssop Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Fortune requires excellent drainage — it is one of the few commonly grown ornamental perennials that truly suffers in heavy clay soil or standing water, making raised beds and amended beds essential in clay-heavy Gulf South soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Blue Fortune is an interspecific hybrid agastache (Agastache foeniculum x A. rugosa) combining the anise fragrance and lavender-blue color of anise hyssop with improved heat and humidity tolerance from the Korean mint parent. The long, cylindrical flower spikes in soft lavender-blue to violet-blue bloom from summer through fall, creating an extended pollinator resource that attracts hummingbirds, monarch butterflies, swallowtails, bumble bees, and numerous native bee species in large numbers. The anise-mint fragrance of crushed leaves is pleasant and fresh — the foliage is edible and can be used as an anise-flavored herb for teas, desserts, and salads. Blue Fortune is more persistent in zone 8-10 than straight Agastache foeniculum, making it one of the more reliable agastache options for Gulf South gardens where high summer humidity and heat can challenge the genus. The upright, stiffly branching habit and lavender-blue flower color make Blue Fortune an outstanding companion for warm-orange and yellow fall-blooming perennials — Rudbeckia, Helenium, Salvia greggii — where the cool blue provides complementary contrast to warm fall colors. Excellent drainage is the most critical cultural requirement — plants in poorly drained clay soils are short-lived regardless of other conditions.

common_name: Blue Fox Tail Orchid (Sky-Blue Rhynchostylis, Celestial Orchid, Blue-Lipped Rhynchostylis)
plant_note: Grow in a slatted basket with coarse bark or bare-rooted in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun with good air circulation; Rhynchostylis coelestis is a small, compact vandaceous orchid from Thailand and Vietnam that produces erect to arching, dense cylindrical racemes of small (0.5-inch) white flowers heavily spotted and the lip colored in vivid sky-blue to violet-blue — making it one of the very few orchids with true blue coloring. Blooms summer to fall. More compact and easier to manage than the larger R. gigantea. Intermediate to warm growing. Good air circulation is important. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun in a slatted basket with good air circulation — Blue Fox Tail Orchid grows most vigorously in bright, well-ventilated, warm conditions and produces its distinctive blue-tinged flower spikes most freely in summer to fall with appropriate light and temperature. Rhynchostylis coelestis is a compact, monopodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Thailand and Vietnam, a member of the small genus Rhynchostylis in the tribe Vandeae — closely related to Vanda and Aerides and sharing their strap-leaved, monopodial growth habit and preference for bright light and good air circulation. The plant is compact — rarely exceeding 10–18 inches in height — with leathery, strap-shaped, dark-green leaves in two ranks. In summer and fall, erect to arching, dense, cylindrical racemes 6–10 inches long emerge from the leaf axils, packed with small (0.5-inch) flowers that create the plant's exceptional ornamental quality: the flowers are white to pale blue-tinted at the petal tips, but the lip (the enlarged front petal) is a vivid, saturated sky-blue to violet-blue — a true blue flower color unusual in orchids and in plants generally. The blue lip contrasts dramatically with the white to spotted white flower body, creating a jewel-box quality in the dense, rounded raceme. Rhynchostylis coelestis has contributed its blue color to many hybrid Vanda and vandaceous orchids. The species epithet coelestis means 'sky-colored' in Latin, directly referencing the blue flowers. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or stem cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; blue ginger requires warm temperatures and high humidity to thrive — it does not tolerate cold, dry, or windy conditions. In zone 9 it dies back to the ground after frost but reliably regrows from rhizomes in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; blue ginger is one of the most treasured and sought-after shade plants for tropical and subtropical gardens, producing dense terminal clusters of intensely deep royal-blue flowers — the rich, saturated blue is among the most vivid blues in tropical horticulture — on upright, bamboo-like stems with spirally arranged, glossy, broad leaves. The flowers appear in late summer and fall, at exactly the time when blue is most welcome in the garden palette. Despite the name, it is not a true ginger (Zingiberaceae) but belongs to the spiderwort family. It grows most luxuriantly in warm, sheltered, brightly shaded spots — beneath a pergola, porch, or canopy tree — in zones 9–12. In zone 9a it dies back completely after frost, but established rhizomes regrow reliably each spring and the plant typically blooms in its first year of regrowth. A true collector's plant and one of the best shade perennials available for the Gulf Coast garden.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, poor to average, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; blue globe onion self-seeds and naturalizes freely in well-drained, sunny conditions and often produces bulbils (small bulbs in the flower head) for easy propagation.
directions: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, poor to average, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; blue globe onion is a delicate and graceful allium from Siberia and Central Asia that produces perfectly round, cornflower-blue flower globes about 1–1.5 inches in diameter in late spring to early summer — the only ornamental allium with a true clear blue flower color (most others range from purple to violet). The slim, grass-like leaves are inconspicuous. It naturalizes freely by self-seeding and bulbil production in well-drained soils and is a charming component of rock gardens, gravel gardens, and wild-style meadow plantings where it can spread at will. Excellent for filling spaces between rocks and in gravel mulch.

common_name: Blue Glow Agave (Compact Hybrid Agave with Glowing Leaf Margins)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil in full sun; Blue Glow is a compact hybrid agave that stays smaller and better-behaved than Agave americana, without the sharp terminal spines of many agave species.
directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; agave requires perfect drainage and will rot quickly in heavy clay or wet sites. Blue Glow is a hybrid agave prized for its compact, symmetrical rosette of smooth, blue-green leaves edged in a thin, glowing gold-and-red margin that appears almost illuminated when backlit by low sun, an effect that has made it one of the most popular ornamental agave hybrids for modern xeric and container design. Unlike many agave species it lacks the vicious terminal spine, making it safer to site near paths and seating areas. It needs essentially no supplemental water once established beyond occasional deep soaking during extended drought, and its smaller mature size fits containers and smaller garden beds better than large agave species.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost, or sow in late summer for fall and spring germination; blue grama requires well-drained to dry soil and establishes slowly, reaching full size in its second or third year.
directions: Sow seed in well-drained to dry soil in full sun; blue grama is one of the most drought-tolerant native grasses of the short-grass prairie, once covering vast areas of the central and western United States. Its most distinctive feature is the unusual curved seed heads, shaped like sideways combs or eyelashes that stand on stiff wiry stems and sway in the breeze from midsummer through fall. It forms a fine-textured, low, blue-green turf in natural settings and is increasingly used as a lawn substitute in arid and semi-arid climates that require dramatically reduced water use. In garden settings it mixes beautifully with wildflowers and is highly resistant to deer browsing. Leave seed heads standing through winter for maximum ornamental value.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil warms.
directions: Blue grama is a native prairie grass and the most heat- and drought-tolerant of the native bunchgrasses. Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, in full sun and well-drained soil. Its distinctive seed heads project horizontally like eyelashes, turning golden brown and sometimes red as they curl and dry in fall. The feathery foliage forms a tidy clump ideal for xeriscapes, meadows, and naturalized plantings. Once established it needs little water and thrives with minimal care.

common_name: Blue Hawaii Elephant Ear (Steel-Blue Metallic Colocasia with Dark Stems)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring after the last frost in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Blue Hawaii's metallic blue-green leaf color intensifies with more light — partial sun (3–4 hours direct) combined with consistently moist soil produces the best color development.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Blue Hawaii is one of the most striking ornamental Colocasia cultivars for Gulf South gardens — producing large, heart-shaped leaves in a remarkable steel-blue to turquoise-blue metallic color with contrasting purple-black stems and dark veining that creates an unusual, jewel-like combination found in very few other garden plants. The metallic blue-green leaf color — a quality that changes slightly with light intensity, becoming more intensely blue in partial sun and more green in deep shade — develops from the waxy, blue-tinted cuticle on the leaf surface and is unlike the green, chartreuse, or black coloration of other commonly grown elephant ear cultivars. Blue Hawaii is more compact than 'Black Magic' or the standard green taro, typically reaching 3–5 feet in garden conditions — a more manageable scale for mixed border use while still providing bold tropical impact. The combination of the metallic blue leaf color and dark stems creates an extraordinary tropical accent that pairs beautifully with golden-leaved companions (gold-leaved hostas, Golden Japanese forest grass) and with vivid orange or red flowering plants where the blue foliage provides striking complementary contrast. In zone 9, Blue Hawaii is perennial, dying back in cold winters and returning reliably from persistent tuberous roots in spring. Consistent moisture — supplemental irrigation during dry periods — is important for maintaining leaf quality and the best metallic color.

common_name: Blue Hawaii Taro (Blue-Green Foliage Purple-Stemmed Variegated Elephant Ear)
plant_note: Plant tubers or container plants after the last frost in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Blue Hawaii requires consistent moisture and performs well in pond margins, bog gardens, and low areas with consistent water — drought causes leaf stress and color loss significantly faster than in standard green-leaved colocasia.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Blue Hawaii is a distinctive Colocasia esculenta cultivar producing medium-to-large, heart-shaped leaves in a rich blue-green to teal-green color with prominent darker veining and a contrasting deep purple-black stem coloration — the combination of blue-green leaf blades with dark purple stems creating a striking two-toned visual effect unlike the plain green of standard taro or the pure black of 'Black Magic'. The blue-green leaf color is unusual among elephant ear cultivars and gives 'Blue Hawaii' a cool-toned, almost metallic appearance in the garden that contrasts effectively with warm orange, yellow, or hot-pink tropical companions. The dark purple stems extend the ornamental interest — particularly visible when the large leaves move in a breeze, revealing the colorful stem as a secondary design element. Blue Hawaii is an outstanding tropical water garden and bog garden plant: like all Colocasia esculenta, it grows naturally in moist to seasonally flooded conditions and performs best in perpetually moist or wet soil, tolerating standing water at the margins of ponds and water features. In Gulf South zone 9, Blue Hawaii grows as a perennial with heavy winter mulching, returning vigorously each spring; in zone 10–11, it is evergreen. The tropical effect of an established clump at a water garden edge — combining the large blue-green leaves, dark stems, and reflected light from the water — is genuinely impressive and unique in the landscape.

common_name: Blue Heaven Little Bluestem (Upright Steel-Blue Native Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Blue Heaven is a sturdy, upright selection of native little bluestem with strong steel-blue summer foliage that turns rich mahogany-orange in fall without flopping open like many wild-type plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; little bluestem thrives in poor, rocky, clay, or sandy soil and performs poorly if overfed. Blue Heaven produces strongly upright, steel-blue foliage through summer that transforms into a warm mahogany-orange-red in fall, holding its color and structural form through much of winter, when the fluffy silver seed heads also catch low light beautifully. Its sturdier, more upright habit compared to the straight species resists the flopping that can affect wild little bluestem in rich soil, making it a reliable choice for a naturalistic border or meadow planting. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and provides valuable habitat and seed for birds; cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Blue Heron is a Fringed-class tulip with violet-purple flowers and a finely fringed petal edge, blooming late in the season.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Blue Heron bears rich violet-purple flowers with a finely crystalline-fringed petal edge distinctive to the Fringed tulip class, blooming late in the tulip season for an extended spring bulb display when paired with earlier-blooming cultivars. Its cool, deep purple tone provides strong contrast against yellow, orange, or white companion tulips. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, alkaline to slightly acidic, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; blue hesper palm is cold-hardy to approximately 12–15°F when established and requires excellent drainage — it will not tolerate wet or waterlogged soils.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — blue hesper palm is arguably the most ornamentally striking palm in the world for dry climates, producing enormous, rigid, deeply divided, silvery powder-blue fan fronds up to 6 feet across on a stout, solitary trunk that grows very slowly to 30–40 feet. Native to Baja California and northwest Mexico, it is one of the most cold-tolerant fan palms for dry-climate gardens, hardy to approximately 15°F once established, and thriving in the hot, dry conditions of zone 9–11 Southwest and Gulf Coast. The spectacular 15–20 foot long creamy-yellow flower stalks that extend dramatically beyond the crown are among the most dramatic flowering events of any palm. Extremely drought tolerant once established — planted in well-drained soil, it requires virtually no supplemental irrigation in warm, dry regions. Growth is very slow (6–12 inches per year), so purchase the largest specimen the budget allows.

common_name: Blue Hill Salvia (Blauhugel Sky-Blue Meadow Sage)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Blue Hill is distinguished from other meadow sage cultivars by its true, clear sky-blue flower color rather than the violet-blue or purple-blue tones common in the group.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean garden soil in full sun, spacing plants so the upright clumps can fill in without crowding. Blue Hill sends up dense, slender spikes of small, clear sky-blue flowers over aromatic, wrinkled gray-green foliage in late spring to early summer, and shearing the spent spikes back by about half typically brings on a second, lighter flush later in the season. The clear blue color reads differently in the border than the more common violet-blue meadow sage cultivars, making it a useful companion for pink, yellow, or white-flowered neighbors, and the tubular flowers are readily visited by bees and occasional hummingbirds throughout the bloom period.

common_name: Blue Horizon Ageratum (Tall AAS-Winning Cut-Flower Ageratum)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Blue Horizon is an AAS-winning tall ageratum, growing much taller than typical bedding ageratum, making it useful as a cut flower rather than only a low edging plant.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after the last frost. Blue Horizon was an All-America Selections winner recognized for breaking from the typical low, mounding ageratum habit, growing to two and a half feet tall with long, sturdy stems that make it genuinely useful as a cut flower, unlike most ageratum bred only for low bedding and edging use. It produces the same fuzzy, powder-puff clusters of soft lavender-blue flowers over a long summer season, drawing butterflies, and holds up well in arrangements. Deadheading spent flower clusters encourages continued bloom, and the plant tolerates heat well, though consistent moisture keeps it flowering most vigorously.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; blue hosta is notably more heat tolerant than most blue-leafed hosta cultivars and seeds relatively true — seedlings often produce good, deep-green to slightly glaucous plants.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade — blue hosta (Hosta ventricosa) is a large, vigorous species from eastern Asia notable for producing some of the deepest, most attractive purple-lavender flowers in the genus — tall, attractive scapes of deep violet bell-shaped flowers in midsummer that are significantly more ornamental than the pale flowers of most hostas. The large, rounded, dark green to slightly glaucous leaves form a lush, mounded clump 2–3 feet tall and 3–4 feet wide. It is also one of the more heat-tolerant hosta species, performing well in zone 8–9 in consistently moist, deeply shaded conditions where many hybrid cultivars decline. Unlike most hostas, it seeds true from open-pollinated seeds, making it easy to naturalize in appropriate shaded conditions. The cultivar 'Aureomarginata' (golden-edged blue hosta) adds variegated interest with a gold to cream margin on the dark leaves.

common_name: Blue Ice Amsonia (Compact Early-Blooming Blue Star)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Blue Ice is a compact amsonia hybrid, staying under 15 inches tall while producing especially dense clusters of periwinkle-blue, star-shaped flowers in mid-spring — a deeper, more saturated blue and a longer bloom period than many taller amsonia species. Its small, tidy, mounding habit fits border edges and rock gardens where full-size Amsonia tabernaemontana or A. hubrichtii would be too large, and like other amsonias it is deer-resistant, drought-tolerant once established, and essentially pest-free. No staking or division is needed; the foliage remains an attractive fine texture through summer with good fall color in cooler climates.

common_name: Blue Ivory Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Creamy White Margin)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Ivory holds its blue-green leaf color best in deeper shade, since direct sun fades the waxy blue cast and can scorch the pale margins.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, avoiding direct afternoon sun, which fades the blue-green leaf color and can scorch the creamy margins. Blue Ivory is a medium-sized hosta cultivar with thick, heart-shaped, deeply veined blue-green leaves edged in a wide, irregular band of creamy white to ivory that brightens as the season progresses, creating strong two-tone contrast in a shaded border. Near-white flowers appear on scapes held above the foliage in summer. The heavy substance of its leaves makes it more slug-resistant than many thinner-leaved hosta cultivars, and its bold variegation reads well from a distance, making it a good choice for brightening a dark corner of the shade garden. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring as new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall (October–November in zone 9); in zone 9 pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6–8 weeks before planting — hyacinths require a cold period for proper flower stalk development that zone 9 winters do not reliably provide. Plant chilled bulbs 4–6 inches deep in December or January after refrigerator treatment. In zone 9 treat hyacinths as annual spring bulbs; the bulbs rarely produce flowering-quality bloom in subsequent years without repeat chilling. The intense, sweet fragrance of hyacinth flowers is among the most powerful and recognized of any spring bulb — a single stem in a small room perfumes the entire space. Blue Jacket produces deep navy-blue to violet-blue flowers in dense, tightly packed spikes — one of the deepest blue colors among commonly grown hyacinth cultivars.
directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs in partial sun to full sun — morning sun with afternoon shade in zone 9 helps the flowers last longer before heat damage — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist soil with excellent drainage to prevent bulb rot; Blue Jacket Hyacinth is one of the premier deep blue-purple hyacinth cultivars, producing the intensely fragrant, densely packed flower spikes that define the classic hyacinth form — each spike carrying 30–40 individual, waxy, star-shaped florets in a deep navy-blue to violet-blue color that represents the most saturated blue available in this flower type. The extraordinary fragrance of hyacinth is one of the defining scents of spring gardening — a heavy, sweet, powdery-floral perfume that is immediately recognizable and has inspired perfumers for centuries. Individual flower spikes last 1–2 weeks in the garden and can be brought indoors as cut flowers where the fragrance transforms a room. For zone 9 gardeners, pre-chilled hyacinth bulbs planted in December–January provide a spectacular late-winter flowering display (February–March) in containers, border pots, and garden beds — one of the most reliable ways to bring the intense color and fragrance of hyacinth into the Gulf South spring garden.

plant_note: Sow in place; needs darkness to germinate, cover seed.
directions: Sow blue lace flower directly where it is to grow, covering seed completely since it needs darkness to germinate. The powder-blue umbels resemble a colored Queen Anne's lace and are cherished by florists for airy arrangements. Provide full sun, well-drained soil, and support for the slender stems in exposed sites. Keep evenly moist during establishment and stagger sowings for a longer cutting season.

common_name: Blue Lady Hellebore (Classic Slate-Blue Lenten Rose)
plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Lady is an older, well-established hellebore selection with slate-blue to purple-gray single flowers blooming in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist while the plant establishes. Blue Lady is a long-cultivated hellebore selection valued for its unusual slate-blue to smoky purple-gray single flowers, a cooler and more muted tone than the pinks, reds, and whites more commonly seen in Lenten rose selections, held above leathery, evergreen, deeply divided foliage. Like other Lenten roses it blooms very early, often through late-season snow or hard frost, providing reliable color in the shade garden when little else is flowering. Its subdued, smoky coloring pairs especially well with silver-leaved companions like brunnera or lamium in a woodland border. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to showcase the flowers, and site it away from areas where pets or children graze, since all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring in full sun in 6–18 inches of water, in aquatic pots with heavy clay loam and slow-release aquatic fertilizer tablets in zone 9–12; Blue Lotus (Blue Water Lily of the Nile) is a stunning tropical aquatic from Egypt, the Nile Basin, and East Africa — sacred in ancient Egyptian religion and art — bearing beautiful, sky-blue to pale-lavender, star-shaped, fragrant flowers that open in the morning on floating pads in full sun above still or gently moving water.
directions: Plant tubers in aquatic containers with heavy clay loam (no potting mix — it floats) and aquatic fertilizer tablets, submerged 6–18 inches deep in full sun; Nymphaea caerulea requires warm water (above 65°F) and full sun (minimum 6 hours) to bloom — overwinter tubers indoors in cold climates or treat as an annual. Nymphaea caerulea (Blue Lotus, Blue Water Lily, or Egyptian Blue Lotus) is a tropical, day-blooming aquatic water lily native to the Nile River and associated waterways of Egypt, Sudan, and East Africa, one of the most historically and culturally significant flowers in human civilization. The Blue Lotus was the sacred flower of ancient Egypt — appearing in thousands of tomb paintings, bas reliefs, hieroglyphics, and temple carvings across 3,000+ years of Egyptian religious art, where it symbolized the sun, rebirth, and creation. The flower is botanically distinctive: sky-blue to lavender-blue, star-shaped, with a yellow center and a delicate, sweet, tea-like fragrance. It blooms in the morning sun and closes in the afternoon. Nymphaea caerulea was used in ancient Egyptian ritual and festival use — the flowers were floated in water, worn as garlands, and appear to have been used in traditional pharmacological preparations for their mildly psychoactive aporphine alkaloid content. In modern warm-climate pond gardening (zone 9–12), the Blue Lotus is one of the most beautiful and historical of all aquatic ornamentals, growing vigorously in full-sun ponds and water features. Store tubers above 55°F indoors over winter in colder climates.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile, loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; blue Louisiana iris tolerates slightly drier conditions than other Louisiana irises and blooms later in the season, making it valuable for extending the iris bloom season in Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun — the zigzag iris is one of the parent species of the spectacular Louisiana iris hybrid group, producing large, rich blue-purple flowers on distinctively zigzag stems that hold the blooms close to the foliage in late spring. It is native to the wet bottomlands, swampy thickets, and stream margins of the Lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf Coast, where it grows in moister, shadier conditions than most other Louisiana iris species. The flowers have the classic Louisiana iris form — broad, spreading falls with a yellow signal patch and narrow, upright standards — in deep blue-violet that is stunning in mass plantings along pond edges and in rain gardens. It is one of the more cold-hardy Louisiana iris species, tolerating zone 6 winter cold well. An essential component of any wetland or rain garden featuring native iris species.

plant_note: Divide established clumps immediately after flowering in spring or in early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in shade; blue lungwort does not tolerate dry shade or drought. Unlike the common spotted lungwort (P. saccharata), this species has unspotted, plain-green, narrow leaves and is considered to have the most intensely blue flowers of any Pulmonaria.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; blue lungwort is considered the finest species for flower color, producing the most intensely and purely cobalt-blue flowers of any Pulmonaria — a richer, deeper blue than the usually mauve-blue of common lungwort and superior in color purity to most named hybrids. The characteristic color-change from red-pink in bud to brilliant sky-blue as the flower opens is most dramatic in this species and gives mixed-color clusters a unique bicolor effect in early spring before any other shade perennials have emerged. Unlike the familiar spotted lungwort (P. saccharata) and its many hybrids, the leaves of P. angustifolia are plain, unspotted, medium-green, and narrower, making it distinctly different in appearance throughout the growing season. It forms a compact, low groundcover of attractive foliage that persists through summer into fall in moist shade conditions. Combined with early daffodils and hellebores, it creates one of the most effective early-spring shade-garden combinations.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring inside a sunken barrier or root-pruning edge, since this grass spreads aggressively by rhizomes and can become a garden thug or escape into wild dune and coastal habitat if left uncontained.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and sandy, well-drained soil, and install a sunken root barrier or grow it in a large buried container, since this grass spreads quickly by aggressive rhizomes and is considered a weedy escapee in some coastal and dune habitats in the northern United States. Once established it tolerates poor, sandy, salt-exposed soil and needs little supplemental water, which is why it is traditionally used for stabilizing dunes and banks. Wide, strikingly powder-blue blades form an upright, spreading colony topped by tan wheat-like flower spikes in summer, giving strong color contrast in coastal gardens when its spread is kept in check.

common_name: Blue Maid Holly (Compact Female Meserve Hybrid Blue Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Maid is female and needs a compatible male pollinator such as Blue Prince planted nearby to set its red berries.
directions: Blue Maid carries the blue-green, glossy, spiny foliage typical of the Meserve hybrid hollies on a somewhat more compact plant than Blue Princess, with a dense, well-branched habit suited to a smaller hedge or foundation planting. Once pollinated by a compatible male such as Blue Prince blooming nearby, it produces a heavy crop of bright red berries that persist through winter and provide food for birds. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter before new spring growth begins, since Meserve hollies generally hold their form well with minimal shaping.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or root stem cuttings in late summer for overwintering; blue marguerite blooms most freely in cool weather and may slow down in the hottest midsummer weeks. It is perennial in zones 9–11 where it can persist for several years as a small, sub-shrubby plant; in colder zones treat as a tender annual. Deadhead regularly to prolong bloom.
directions: Start seeds early indoors or plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; blue marguerite is a South African native producing one of the most reliably cheerful and saturated sky-blue daisy flowers available in cool-season gardening — a compact, bushy, small shrubby plant covered from spring through summer (and in mild climates through winter and fall) with 1–1.5 inch daisy flowers in clear, true, vivid sky-blue with a small golden-yellow central disc. The specific blue is particularly valuable in horticulture — a clean, medium blue that photographs accurately and provides a reliable complementary contrast to orange, yellow, and golden flowers in mixed plantings. It performs best in cool to moderate temperatures and may reduce flowering in the hottest midsummer weeks in humid climates. Blue marguerite is particularly valuable in the Gulf Coast and mild Pacific Coast winter gardens, where it blooms prolifically through fall and mild winters. Variegated-leaf cultivars ('Variegata') are also available. Outstanding in containers, where it can be overwintered indoors in cold climates and moved outdoors in summer.

common_name: Blue Mediterranean Fan Palm (Silvery-Blue Atlas Mountain Fan Palm)
subcategory: cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Mediterranean Fan Palm is a striking silvery-blue-leaved variety from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, generally more cold hardy than the green species form of Mediterranean fan palm.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun. Blue Mediterranean Fan Palm is a striking silvery-blue-leaved form of Mediterranean fan palm originating from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, offering the same clumping, multi-trunked, drought-tolerant habit as the green species but with the added ornamental value of powder-blue fronds that stand out dramatically against darker landscape plantings. It is often noted as somewhat more cold hardy than the plain green form, and like the species it is highly drought-tolerant once established and tolerates poor, sandy, or coastal soils. Water regularly the first year to establish, then only during extended dry spells, and remove old fronds as they brown to keep the clumping crown tidy.

common_name: Blue Mist Dwarf Fothergilla (Blue-Foliage Bottlebrush Witch Alder)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Blue Mist' keeps its best steel-blue foliage color with some afternoon shade in hot Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter and avoid letting the root zone dry out, since this dwarf witch alder relative struggles in poor, compacted ground. 'Blue Mist' is prized for its distinctive blue-gray summer foliage, a striking departure from the plain green leaves of the species, set off in early spring by small, fragrant, white bottlebrush-shaped flower spikes that open before the leaves emerge and draw in early bees. In fall the blue-toned leaves shift into a mix of orange, red, and yellow for a second season of strong color. This compact, slow-growing selection stays under 3 feet and works well massed at a woodland edge or foundation planting, and it has a track record of good garden performance recognized with a Pennsylvania Horticultural Society Gold Medal Award.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in late spring or plant container-grown shrubs in spring; cut caryopteris back hard to 4–6 inches in early spring to maintain compact form and maximize flowering — it blooms on new wood produced each season. In zones 5–6 it may die back to the ground but resprouts vigorously from the roots.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; blue mist shrub is a compact, late-summer flowering shrub that fills a critical role in the garden: just as most spring and summer shrubs have finished blooming, caryopteris erupts in August through October in dense clusters of small, intense china-blue to violet flowers covering the tops of the aromatic gray-green stems. The blue color is unusually saturated and clean, closer to true blue than almost any other hardy shrub. Bumblebees, honeybees, and other pollinators mob the flowers throughout the extended bloom period. The plant has a pleasant minty-sage fragrance when the foliage is brushed. It thrives in hot, dry, full-sun conditions with excellent drainage and poor soil — conditions that kill many other shrubs. 'Dark Knight' and 'Longwood Blue' are outstanding cultivars with deep blue-violet flowers. Caryopteris is outstanding combined with ornamental grasses and late perennials like sedums and asters.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; blue mistflower spreads aggressively by rhizomes in moist, fertile conditions and should be sited where its spreading habit can be accommodated.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; blue mistflower (hardy ageratum) is a native eastern North American perennial that blooms in late summer to fall — precisely when the shade garden most needs color — producing frothy, powder-blue to lavender flower heads in large flat-topped clusters that closely resemble annual ageratum and are magnets for migrating monarch butterflies, painted ladies, and dozens of native bee species. It spreads vigorously by rhizomes in moist, fertile soil and is best used in naturalistic plantings, rain gardens, and woodland edges where its colonizing habit is a virtue. Unlike many fall-blooming natives, it tolerates considerable shade. Excellent for the critical late-season pollinator support corridor in southeastern and Gulf South gardens.

plant_note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Moon requires a very sturdy trellis, pergola, or arbor that can support the mature vine weight — wisteria vines become extremely heavy over time.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support structure; Blue Moon is the most outstanding American wisteria cultivar available — a selection of Wisteria macrostachya (Kentucky wisteria, native to the central United States) that combines the non-invasive native wisteria's better behavior with several remarkable additional qualities: exceptional cold hardiness (to -40°F, reliably hardy to zone 3 — far hardier than any Asian wisteria), spectacular long racemes (8–12 inches) of silvery-blue-lavender fragrant flowers, and most remarkably, repeat blooming — producing a main spring flower flush in May followed by two or more additional bloom flushes in summer, a quality almost completely absent in single-blooming wisteria. The ability to bloom multiple times per season gives Blue Moon a greatly extended flowering season (May through August) compared to the single brief bloom of Asian wisteria. Like all W. macrostachya selections, Blue Moon is well-behaved — it does not spread invasively into natural areas as Asian wisterias do. In zone 9, it blooms most reliably with adequate chill hours (zone 9a); the floral display is exceptional in zones 3–8. Established vines bloom at a younger age than Asian wisteria and require less time to become established performers.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Blue Moon Woodland Phlox spreads slowly by stolons to form loose, semi-evergreen mats in partially shaded areas. Bloom time is April–May in zone 9 — a valuable window when shade garden color options are limited. After blooming, trim plants lightly to maintain neat foliage and stimulate fresh growth. In zone 9 plants may benefit from afternoon shade protection during the hottest summer months; provide consistent moisture to prevent summer dormancy. The notched petals distinguish this species from garden phlox (P. paniculata).
directions: Plant in partial shade to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Blue Moon Woodland Phlox is a genuine shade perennial, growing naturally in the dappled shade of deciduous forest understories; Blue Moon is a cultivar of Wild Blue Phlox (Phlox divaricata), a native eastern North American woodland perennial that provides one of the most delicate and refined spring floral displays available for shaded garden situations. The loose clusters of fragrant, lavender-blue to violet-blue flowers appear in April–May on semi-upright, slightly sticky, hairy stems above the semi-evergreen foliage — the combination of color, fragrance, and delicacy creating a wildflower charm that is difficult to match with non-native spring shade perennials. Blue Moon was selected for deeper, more saturated blue-violet color than typical wild-collected P. divaricata, which tends toward pale lavender — the named cultivar's richer color provides more visual impact in shaded settings where color intensity is often difficult to achieve. As a native species adapted to eastern North American woodland conditions, Wild Blue Phlox in zone 9 provides early spring color in the specific shaded, woodland-edge conditions where it evolved — under deciduous oaks, in the partial shade of north-facing slopes, and in the sheltered pockets that mimic its natural forest understory habitat.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; blue moor grass tolerates poor, rocky, and calcareous soils better than richer garden ground.
directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; blue moor grass tolerates poor, rocky, and calcareous soils better than richer garden ground. Fine, narrow, evergreen leaves are blue-green on top and glossy dark green beneath, forming a low, dense, neat tuft that stays attractive through winter in mild climates, with small, dark, bottlebrush-like flower spikes appearing in early spring before most other grasses have even begun growing. Native to limestone grasslands and rocky slopes across Europe, it is a well-behaved, non-invasive clumper ideal for edging a border, rock garden, or dry shade under high canopy, tolerating both sun and part shade better than most true grasses. It needs little care beyond an occasional comb-out of old foliage and rarely requires division.

common_name: Blue Mouse Ears Hosta (Miniature Thick-Leaved Blue Hosta)
plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Mouse Ears is a true miniature hosta, staying tiny for years, which makes it a favorite for rock gardens, troughs, and the front edge of a shade border.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Blue Mouse Ears won the American Hosta Growers Association Hosta of the Year award and remains one of the most popular miniature hosta cultivars, forming a tight, slow-spreading mound of thick, rounded, powdery blue-green leaves that keep their color and substance better through summer heat than many thinner-leaved hostas. Its small size and unusually slug-resistant, thick foliage make it a favorite for containers, rock gardens, and the front of a shaded border where larger hostas would be out of scale. Lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer. It divides easily but slowly, so mature clumps take a few years to bulk up enough to split.

common_name: Blue Muffin Viburnum (Compact Native Arrowwood with Heavy Blue Berries)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Muffin is a compact arrowwood viburnum selected for unusually heavy production of vivid blue berries, and planting a second unrelated arrowwood clone nearby improves fruit set.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally with a different arrowwood viburnum clone nearby to improve cross-pollination and berry set. Blue Muffin is a compact selection of native arrowwood viburnum bred specifically for heavy, reliable production of vivid, deep blue berries in fall, a standout food source for birds and a striking ornamental display against the shrub's red-purple fall foliage. Its smaller mature size compared to the wild species fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and hedgerows where a full-sized arrowwood would need more room. It is highly adaptable to a range of soil conditions from dry to moist and needs only occasional structural pruning to maintain shape.

common_name: Blue My Mind Evolvulus (True-Blue Trailing Dwarf Morning Glory)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after the last frost in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential, as with all evolvulus, and Blue My Mind was bred for a more vigorous, floriferous habit than older blue daze selections. In zone 9–11 it behaves as a perennial.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun, and take care not to overwater, since evolvulus rots quickly in heavy, moisture-retentive soil. Blue My Mind is a vigorous, heavy-flowering selection of dwarf morning glory prized for its unusually true, vivid sky-blue flowers, a color rare among heat-tolerant summer annuals, produced in enormous numbers over small, silvery-green, fuzzy foliage on low, trailing stems from spring through frost. It performs best in hot, dry conditions and is an excellent choice for containers, hanging baskets, rock gardens, and the front of a sunny border where its intense blue color can be appreciated up close. In zones 9–11 it persists as a woody-based perennial in a protected, well-drained site; elsewhere it is grown as a warm-season annual, propagated by cuttings taken before frost.

subcategory: Chilean rare true-blue tuberous climbing nasturtium
plant_note: Plant tubers in fall 2–3 inches deep in full sun to partial shade in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, sandy or rocky soil in zone 8–10; Blue Nasturtium is an exceptionally rare Chilean tuberous vine — one of the very few true-blue flowering vines in cultivation — native to rocky, dry hillsides and coastal scrub in Chile where it climbs through shrubs during the cool wet winter season and dies back to its tuberous root in dry summers, bearing small but exquisitely beautiful deep-blue to violet-blue flowers contrasting with white-eyed centers.
directions: Plant Tropaeolum azureum tubers in fall in extremely well-drained, lean, sandy or rocky soil in partial to full sun; the plant grows in cool, wet winters and requires dry summers — absolutely no summer water is essential for tuber persistence; in mild-winter climates (zone 9–10), it grows over winter and early spring as a delicate, wispy vine. Blue Nasturtium is one of the most coveted of all rare bulb collectors' plants — a Chilean vine that produces an abundance of small (3/4 inch) but perfectly formed, intense violet-blue flowers with a characteristic white eye at the center, on delicate, twining stems. True blue is exceptionally rare in flowering plants generally and almost unknown in the Tropaeolum genus (all other nasturtiums produce orange, yellow, red, or pink flowers) — making T. azureum a uniquely prized rarity. Native to the coastal and foothill scrub of central Chile, it grows during the Mediterranean climate winter (cool, moist) and goes completely dormant in the hot, dry Chilean summer; cultivation outside Chile requires closely replicating this regime — autumn planting, winter/spring growth and flowering, then complete summer dryness from June through October. In zone 9 (Gulf Coast), its cool-season growth habit suits the mild winters well and the hot, dry summer dormancy period aligns with the climate; the main challenge is ensuring summer dryness — grow in containers or under an overhang to protect from summer rain.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in well-drained, dry to average, rocky or clay, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; blue oak is highly adapted to the dry, hot summer conditions of California foothill woodlands and is extremely drought-tolerant once established. Do not irrigate in summer after the first year.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, dry, rocky to clay, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; blue oak is named for the distinctive bluish or glaucous hue of its deeply lobed, somewhat wavy leaves, which is an adaptation to intense summer sun and drought. It is the dominant oak of the California foothills, forming extensive blue oak woodlands on dry, rocky slopes at 200–3500 feet elevation throughout the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills. The tree is semi-deciduous — losing leaves early in summer drought and regaining them with fall rains in addition to the standard spring flush. The relatively sweet acorns were a food staple for numerous California indigenous cultures. Extraordinarily drought and heat tolerant — the blue oak's ability to survive summers with essentially no water after establishment is exceptional among deciduous trees. A landmark species for ecological restoration of California foothill habitats.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or divide established clumps in spring or fall in very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil; blue oat grass is a cool-season grass that suffers in hot, humid summers — in zones 7–9 it may go semi-dormant in summer and is best planted in a location with afternoon shade and excellent drainage to discourage crown rot.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil in full sun; blue oat grass is one of the most dramatically colored ornamental grasses available, producing a tight, arching mound of steely blue-gray, semi-evergreen foliage as intensely glaucous as any blue-leafed hosta or blue spruce. The narrow, stiff, steel-blue leaves emerge fresh in cool spring weather and catch low-angle light magnificently. In early summer, tall, arching flower spikes resembling oat grains emerge in a paler tan color that gradually dries and persists attractively into fall. It is native to the rocky, calcareous mountains of southern France and northwestern Spain and requires excellent drainage to survive — clay or moist soils lead to crown rot within a few seasons. Superb as a specimen or repeated accent in gravel gardens, xeriscape plantings, and as a blue foliage contrast to golden or red-leafed plants.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; blue palo verde is extremely drought tolerant once established (essentially zero supplemental water in Sonoran Desert gardens after 2–3 years). Frost-sensitive in youth but tolerates brief temperatures to 15°F when mature.
