directions: Plant scarified seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; blue palo verde is the state tree of Arizona and the signature large tree of the Sonoran Desert — a spectacularly beautiful, low-branched, naturally multi-stemmed small tree whose entire trunk, branches, and even branchlets are photosynthetically active and bright blue-green ('palo verde' = green stick in Spanish). The trunk synthesizes chlorophyll, allowing the tree to photosynthesize even when it drops its tiny leaves during drought. In spring, the tree produces a breathtaking, completely enveloping display of brilliant yellow flowers that cover every branch tip, creating one of the most spectacular natural flowering events in North American desert landscapes. The edible seeds (large, protein-rich) were a staple food for the Tohono O'odham and other desert peoples. Extremely drought tolerant and fast-growing for the desert. The flat seed pods are also edible when young and green. An essential native for Sonoran Desert gardens, xeriscape, and low-water landscape plantings in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant divisions in late winter or very early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Panda is a cool-season plant in zone 8-9 — plant early enough to allow bloom before summer heat arrives, as the plant goes dormant in hot weather and re-emerges in fall.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Panda is a named selection of Corydalis flexuosa — a Chinese woodland species — producing clusters of unusually vivid, true gentian-blue tubular flowers with a distinctive white eye, mounted on delicate, ferny, blue-green foliage that creates a lacy, fine-textured effect in the spring shade garden. The electric gentian-blue flower color is genuinely rare among herbaceous plants — few perennials produce flowers in this particular clear, saturated blue — making Blue Panda uniquely valuable in the spring shade palette. In zone 9, Blue Panda behaves as a cool-season shade perennial: it emerges in late winter, blooms from March through May, goes dormant as summer heat arrives, and re-emerges in fall for a secondary growth period. This summer dormancy is completely normal and the plant reliably re-emerges the following season. Plant among summer-growing companions (hostas, ferns, astilbes) whose foliage will cover the empty space during summer dormancy. The ferny foliage and the brilliant blue flowers combine beautifully with spring bulbs, hellebores, and other early-season shade companions. In zone 9's warmest locations, summer dormancy may be extended and survival requires excellent drainage to prevent rhizome rot.

common_name: Blue Paradise Garden Phlox (Fragrant Lavender-Blue Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing at least 18 inches apart for air circulation.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation. Blue Paradise bears large, strongly fragrant flower clusters in a cool lavender-blue that appears deeper blue-violet in the cooler light of morning and evening, one of the closest approaches to true blue in the garden phlox palette, each flower centered with a small magenta-red eye. It blooms over a long season from midsummer into fall and is a strong draw for butterflies, hummingbirds, and evening pollinators drawn by its fragrance. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor and airflow, which helps manage the powdery mildew that affects garden phlox in humid climates.

common_name: Blue Pearl Crocus (Pale Silvery-Blue Species Crocus)
plant_note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Blue Pearl is an early species crocus with a distinctive bronze-yellow base color on the outer petals.
directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; good drainage prevents corm rot during the dormant summer months. Blue Pearl opens pale, silvery blue-lavender flowers with a bronzy-yellow base and a bright orange-yellow throat, the outer petals often showing a subtle bronze flush that gives the flower extra depth compared to solid-colored crocus cultivars. Blooming among the earliest crocus of the year, it works well massed in a rock garden, naturalized in a lawn, or tucked along a border edge where its small scale can be appreciated up close. Allow the grass-like foliage to die back naturally after flowering before mowing over naturalized plantings, and clumps will slowly multiply by cormlets to fill in over the years without needing regular division.

plant_note: Start indoors; surface sow, needs light to germinate.
directions: 'Blue Planet' is a tall ageratum whose fuzzy, long-lasting blue flowers look like tiny explosions and shine in gardens, containers, and bouquets. Start seed indoors and surface sow, since the seed needs light to germinate. Grow in full sun to part shade in rich, well-drained soil kept evenly moist. Unlike many ageratums, this variety branches freely without pinching and flowers prolifically. It pairs beautifully with white flowers and blooms from summer to frost.

plant_note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; H. ventricosa is one of the more heat-tolerant hosta species, performing adequately through zone 9 where most large-leaved hostas struggle in summer heat.
directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; H. ventricosa grows well in deeper shade than many hostas and is one of the heat-tolerant species that performs more reliably in warm-climate zones 7–9. Hosta ventricosa is a large-growing species with very glossy, deep-green, broadly ovate to heart-shaped leaves 8–12 inches long with prominently impressed veins that give the leaves a quilted appearance; unlike most large hostas the leaves are glossy rather than glaucous (waxy). The striking deep-violet to violet-purple flowers are among the most colorful of any hosta species, blooming in July–August on tall scapes that stand well above the leaf mound — they are attractive both fresh and as dried stems. The cultivar 'Aureomaculata' has yellow-centered leaves in spring that turn all green by summer; 'Aureomarginated' has yellow-margined leaves. H. ventricosa produces viable seed that germinates readily — one of the few hosta species that breeds relatively true from seed.

plant_note: Plant after the soil has warmed in late spring — ceratostigma emerges late and can be mistaken for dead if planted too early. Space 12–18 inches apart to allow for spreading.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade; blue plumbago is a low-growing groundcover that delivers brilliant cobalt-blue flowers from August through first frost — some of the most intensely colored blue flowers of any autumn-blooming plant. As temperatures drop in fall the foliage transforms to vivid crimson-bronze, creating a striking display alongside the continuing blue flowers. Plants emerge very late in spring, so mark their location and do not disturb. Once established, ceratostigma spreads steadily by underground runners to form a weed-smothering mat and tolerates moderate drought. Shear to the ground in early spring to encourage fresh, dense growth.

common_name: Blue Plumbago (Sky Blue Everblooming Gulf South Shrub for Sunny Borders and Hedges)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Plumbago auriculata is one of the most widely used landscape shrubs in zone 9-11 Gulf South and Florida — it is frequently used as a large-scale mass planting or informal hedge where its fast growth and long bloom season create maximum visual impact.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Plumbago is one of the most valued and widely planted flowering shrubs for Gulf South landscapes — an evergreen to semi-evergreen South African native that produces clusters of small, five-petaled, sky blue to pale periwinkle-blue flowers nearly continuously from spring through frost in zone 9, creating one of the most sustained flowering displays of any commonly grown landscape shrub. The sky blue flower color is genuinely unusual in the warm-season landscape palette and is particularly valuable as a cooling contrast to the warm orange, yellow, and red tropicals that dominate Gulf South summer gardens. The slightly sticky calyx is a minor nuisance (small pets and children can find seeds sticking to fur or clothing) but not a significant garden problem. Plumbago is fast-growing, drought-tolerant once established, salt-spray tolerant for coastal plantings, and adapts to a wide range of soil types including the poor sandy soils common along the Gulf Coast. In zone 9, the tops are often damaged or killed by hard freezes but plants return quickly from the roots in spring, producing new growth and beginning bloom by late spring. The fast regrowth after frost damage makes Plumbago one of the most resilient landscape shrubs for zone 8b–9 gardens. Cassius blue butterflies use Plumbago as their primary larval host plant — an important ecological function that makes Plumbago doubly valuable in Gulf South butterfly gardens.

common_name: Blue Point Juniper (Pyramidal Blue-Green Screening Conifer)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Point tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soils better than many blue conifers, making it one of the most widely planted screening junipers in the South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Blue Point is one of the most widely planted landscape junipers, forming a dense, neatly pyramidal cone of soft, silvery blue-green foliage that requires minimal pruning to keep its naturally tidy shape. Its predictable, formal habit makes it a favorite for foundation plantings, entryway accents, and mass screening, and it tolerates heat and drought once established far better than it tolerates poorly drained, soggy soil. Give it full sun and good air circulation to reduce the risk of fungal blights common to junipers in humid climates, and shear lightly if a more formal shape is desired, though the naturally symmetrical form rarely needs heavy correction.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun after last frost; blue porter weed blooms nearly year-round in frost-free climates and is one of the most important butterfly and hummingbird plants in the Gulf South.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; blue porter weed is a native Florida and Caribbean plant that produces long, slender spikes of tiny deep-blue to violet flowers that open a few at a time along the spike and are accessible to butterflies and hummingbirds that probe each floret in sequence — making it one of the most reliable butterfly attractors in Gulf Coast butterfly gardens, blooming nearly continuously through the warm season and year-round in frost-free zones. It naturalizes along roadsides and disturbed areas in south Florida. Plants are drought-tolerant once established and thrive in sandy, well-drained soil. Pinch growing tips to encourage bushier growth. Cut back hard if frost-damaged in zone 9.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9–11 it naturalizes as a self-sowing perennial subshrub.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun after temperatures warm; blue porterweed is a star butterfly plant of the tropical Gulf Coast, producing long slender spikes with intense blue-purple flowers that open progressively up the spike from the base throughout summer and fall. The flowers are critically important for gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and monarch butterflies; hummingbirds also visit the spikes regularly. In zone 9–10 it naturalizes as a weedy self-sowing subshrub in disturbed, sandy areas — appropriate for a wild, naturalistic butterfly garden but not a formal border. The common name 'porterweed' comes from the dark, beer-like color of the steeped leaves historically used as a beverage. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage additional blooming.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Prince is a male pollinator cultivar and produces no berries itself but is needed nearby for female Blue Girl or Blue Princess holly to fruit.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Prince is a male pollinator cultivar and produces no berries itself but is needed nearby for female Blue Girl or Blue Princess holly to fruit. Small, spiny, glossy, blue-green leaves cover a dense, compact, exceptionally cold-hardy holly bred by crossing English and evergreen Japanese holly species, holding its rich blue-green color and dense form through harsh winters that damage many other broadleaf evergreen hollies. As the male counterpart in the popular Blue-series holly pairing, it produces no berries of its own but is essential for pollinating nearby female Blue Princess or Blue Girl hollies, which cannot set their showy red berries without a male plant within pollination range. Plant one male for every three to five female Blue-series hollies, shear lightly to maintain shape if a formal hedge is wanted, and provide the same acidic, well-drained soil other hollies prefer.

common_name: Blue Princess Holly (Meserve Hybrid Blue Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; plant a male pollinator such as 'Blue Prince' nearby, since Blue Princess is female and needs a compatible male to set berries.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant a compatible male pollinator such as 'Blue Prince' within about 30–40 feet, since this female cultivar needs cross-pollination to produce its signature berries. Blue Princess is one of the most widely planted Meserve hybrid hollies, its glossy, spiny, blue-green leaves and heavy crop of bright red winter berries combining the cold-hardiness of Ilex rugosa with the refined, lustrous foliage of English holly, making it more reliably cold-tolerant than English holly alone. Its dense, pyramidal, evergreen form works well as a specimen, foundation planting, or informal hedge, with the winter berry display providing strong seasonal interest and food for birds. Prune, if needed, in late winter before new spring growth begins.

common_name: Blue Princess Verbena (Texas Superstar Trailing Verbena)
plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Blue Princess is a Texas Superstar release selected for outstanding heat tolerance combined with better cold tolerance than many trailing verbenas, extending its usable range.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Blue Princess is a Texas Superstar-designated trailing verbena selected specifically for reliable performance across the wide swing between brutal summer heat and occasional hard freezes typical of Texas and the Gulf South, blooming in dense, lavender-blue clusters almost continuously from spring through frost. Its vigorous trailing habit makes it well suited to retaining walls, hanging baskets, and the tops of raised beds where it can spill over the edge, and it holds up to humidity better than many older verbena selections, showing good resistance to the powdery mildew that often disfigures verbena in a humid Southern summer. It is drought tolerant once established and benefits from an occasional shearing back by a third to keep growth dense and encourage a fresh flush of bloom.

common_name: Blue Puffball Chaste Tree (True Dwarf Leaf Spot-Resistant Vitex)
plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Puffball is a true dwarf chaste tree, staying only about 3 by 4 feet, bred with leaf spot resistance and well suited to a small Gulf Coast garden or large container where a full-sized vitex would be too large.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Puffball is a genuine dwarf chaste tree, staying about 3 feet tall and 4 feet wide, a fraction of the size of the straight species, and bred with resistance to leaf spot that keeps its fragrant, gray-green foliage looking clean through a humid Gulf South summer. It produces the same lavender-blue flower spikes as full-sized vitex selections on a compact, rounded form suited to small beds, foundation plantings, or large containers. It blooms on new growth through summer into fall and tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil well once established. Cutting back lightly in late winter encourages fresh growth and continued heavy flowering.

common_name: Blue Ripple Sweet Pea (Blue-Flaked White Spencer Sweet Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Blue Ripple is a ruffled Spencer-type sweet pea with a distinctive flaked and striped petal pattern.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Blue Ripple bears large, ruffled, Spencer-type flowers on a white ground flecked and striped with blue-violet, an unusual broken-color pattern that gives every bloom a distinctive, painterly look and makes for eye-catching cut arrangements. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows the vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

common_name: Blue River II Hardy Hibiscus (Large White Dinner-Plate Hibiscus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost, or plant nursery divisions, in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Blue River II is a Dr. Harold Winters hybrid bred for enormous pure-white flowers on a cold-hardy perennial that dies back to the ground each winter and re-emerges late in spring.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Blue River II is a classic hardy hibiscus hybrid bred by Dr. Harold Winters, producing enormous, pure-white, dinner-plate-size flowers — often 8 to 10 inches across, among the largest flowers of any hardy garden perennial — over a mounding plant with maple-like green foliage. Unlike tropical hibiscus, it is fully cold-hardy and dies back completely to the ground each winter, re-emerging quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown before new growth appears. It thrives in reliably moist to wet soil and tolerates boggy conditions better than most perennials, making it a strong choice for a rain garden or pond margin as well as a well-watered border. Individual flowers last only a day, but a mature plant produces a long, heavy succession of blooms from mid- to late summer. Cut the dead stalks to the ground in late winter before new growth begins.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Blue Rug juniper tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and rots in wet, poorly drained ground.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Blue Rug juniper tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and rots in wet, poorly drained ground. Trailing, ground-hugging branches are densely clothed in intensely silvery-blue, needle-like foliage that lies nearly flat against the soil, spreading widely to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat rarely more than a few inches tall, one of the lowest and bluest of all groundcover junipers. Its low, spreading habit and rich blue color make it an excellent choice for cascading over a retaining wall, covering a dry sunny bank, or filling in between larger shrubs in a xeriscape planting, requiring no mowing or shearing to maintain its form. Water regularly during the first year to establish, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and avoid overhead watering that keeps the dense foliage wet, which encourages fungal disease.

common_name: Blue Sage (Eranthemum, Directweed, Blue Sage Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in partial to full shade in spring; Eranthemum pulchellum performs best in its Gulf Coast winter bloom cycle when established before summer. It blooms primarily in winter (December–March in zone 9-10) when its vivid blue flowers provide critical late-season color. Mulch the base heavily in zone 9a to protect roots from hard frost; plants may freeze to the ground but resprout from protected roots.
directions: Plant in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; Eranthemum pulchellum is one of the few shrubs that produces its best blooms in shade and actually prefers protection from direct afternoon sun in zone 9. Eranthemum pulchellum (Blue Sage or Directweed) is a small tropical shrub from India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia in the Acanthaceae family, notable for producing its vibrant, true-blue flowers during the cool season — December through March in zone 9 — at a time when blue-flowered plants are exceptionally rare. The individual flowers are small (1/2 inch) but borne in numerous terminal spike clusters that cover the plant in a haze of brilliant sky-blue to deep blue color, providing exceptional winter interest in the Gulf South garden. The deep green, quilted foliage is attractive year-round and the plant tolerates the dry shade under oak trees that defeats most other flowering ornamentals. Eranthemum performs remarkably well as a container specimen on shaded patios and porches, bringing winter blue-flower color to spaces that otherwise have no flowering plants. In zone 9a it may freeze to the ground in hard winters but typically resprouts. Prune hard in early spring after the main bloom flush to encourage bushy new growth.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring in lean, rocky, fast-draining soil in full sun after the last hard freeze.
directions: Blue sage is a rounded, silvery-leaved subshrub native to rocky slopes and pinyon-juniper woodlands of the Mojave Desert transition zone in Southern California, Nevada, and Arizona at elevations between roughly 4,000 and 8,000 feet, which gives it unusual cold hardiness for a desert sage. Its dense, felted foliage releases a strong, resinous fragrance when brushed, and from midsummer into fall it produces spikes of rose-purple bracts surrounding smaller violet-blue flowers that draw hummingbirds, bumblebees, and native carpenter bees. Because seed set is sparse and germination unreliable in cultivation, propagation is almost always by stem cuttings taken in late spring or fall. Give it gravelly, alkaline soil with sharp drainage and withhold summer water once established, as root rot in humid or heavy soils is its main limiting factor.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost at 70–75°F; do not cover seeds as they need light for germination. Transplant after last frost in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil.
directions: Start seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost at 70–75°F without covering — blue salvia needs light to germinate — and transplant after last frost in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. It blooms continuously from early summer through frost with upright spikes of small violet-blue flowers above neat, mealy-textured foliage that butterflies and hummingbirds visit steadily throughout the season. In zone 8–11 it is a short-lived perennial; in cooler climates it is treated as a warm-season annual but is one of the longest-blooming and most heat-tolerant blue flowers available for the summer garden. Deadhead or shear lightly to prevent setting seed and extend the bloom season; 'Victoria Blue' and 'Henry Duelberg' are popular cultivars for zone 8–9 gardens.

common_name: Blue Satin Rose of Sharon (Azurri Blue Satin, Large Blue-Purple Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Blue Satin bears some of the largest flowers of any rose of sharon cultivar, single blooms up to 5 inches across in a rich blue-purple with a small red eye at the center, opening from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, well-branched shrub. Its bold flower size and saturated color make it a strong summer focal point in a mixed border or informal hedge, and like other modern rose of sharon selections it sets relatively little seed compared to old-fashioned, seed-grown althea. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established, needing little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning.

subcategory: tall blue-flowered South African iris relative
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; blue sceptre is a larger, more robust species than the commonly grown A. ecklonii — forming substantial, bold clumps of iris-like sword-leaves and producing in late spring and summer tall, branching spikes of small but intensely blue flowers. The individual flowers last only one day but are produced in rapid succession from clustered, wiry buds. It self-sows freely in mild-climate gardens in suitable conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; blue sceptre is the largest and most impressive Aristea species — a South African iris-family perennial of the Western Cape fynbos that forms substantial architectural clumps of erect, sword-shaped, bright-green iris leaves 3–4 feet tall and in late spring through summer produces tall, branching, candelabra-like flowering scapes carrying dense clusters of small, vivid, saturated, sky-blue to gentian-blue, six-petaled flowers that are individually ephemeral (lasting one day) but collectively produced in rapid succession so that a plant in full bloom carries numerous bright-blue flowers simultaneously. The clear, pure, deep blue of the flowers — a typical aristea characteristic — is a distinctive and beautiful color in the summer perennial border, and at the scale of A. capitata with its tall scapes, the blue is deployed in an architectural structure of considerable presence. It thrives in the semi-shade of woodland margins and dry shade of large shrubs in zone 9 Gulf Coast conditions. Once established it self-sows modestly in suitable moist-to-dry shade garden soils.

plant_note: Divide established clumps or plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; blue sedge spreads slowly by rhizomes and can be used as a groundcover under trees where it gradually fills in. It tolerates both dry shade and moist shade as well as alkaline soils — one of the most adaptable of all sedges.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil from full shade to full sun; blue sedge is a low-growing, rhizomatous spreading sedge native to Europe and northern Africa with attractive steel-blue to blue-green, semi-evergreen foliage that spreads gently into a fine-textured, low groundcover. Unlike many ornamental sedges that require consistent moisture, Carex flacca tolerates dry shade under trees quite well and even succeeds on thin chalk soils — making it far more adaptable than most shade groundcovers. The 'Blue Zinger' cultivar is a compact, intensely blue selection excellent as a groundcover or front-of-border edging. It looks particularly effective planted in large drifts under light-canopy trees where the blue foliage creates a cool, restful effect. Mow or shear lightly in early spring to remove old foliage and encourage fresh new growth.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in warm, moist potting mix or plant container specimens near a strong trellis, fence, or arbor in full sun after last frost; blue sky vine grows aggressively and requires substantial support — it can cover a large pergola in a single season.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens against a strong pergola, fence, or arbor in full sun; blue sky vine is one of the most spectacular flowering vines for Gulf Coast landscapes, producing pendant clusters of enormous sky-blue trumpet flowers 3 inches across from summer through fall on vigorous vines that can grow 20–30 feet in a single season. The large, heart-shaped leaves and cascading flower clusters create an exotic tropical effect. In zone 9 plants die back after frost but regrow from the roots in spring; in zone 10–11 they are evergreen and bloom nearly year-round. Plants can become invasive in tropical areas; monitor spread. The species is sterile and does not set seed, so spreading occurs only by root suckering and vegetative growth.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential to prevent crown rot.
directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; wet or heavy ground causes rot far more readily than this sedum is bothered by drought. Blue Spruce is a low, trailing sedum with fine, needle-like, powdery blue foliage that closely mimics a miniature conifer, spreading into a dense, textural mat topped with clusters of star-shaped yellow flowers in summer. Its low, spreading habit and cool blue color make it an effective groundcover for rock gardens, gravel gardens, and the edges of raised beds, spilling attractively over rock walls or container edges. It spreads readily but is easy to control by simply pulling or trimming back trailing stems; divide congested patches in spring to renew vigor or propagate new plantings.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; cold-moist stratification over winter significantly improves spring germination. Container transplants may be planted in spring or fall.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall or plant container transplants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; blue star is a stunning native perennial of eastern streambanks and woodland edges, producing clouds of small, pale-blue star-shaped flowers in late spring above willowy, fresh-green foliage. The foliage is attractive all season and turns brilliant golden-yellow in fall, giving the plant a remarkable three-season display. Established plants are long-lived, drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially pest-free — a nearly perfect low-maintenance perennial. It grows slowly to a substantial clump over several years; dividing is not necessary and the plant should be left undisturbed once established. An exceptional combination plant for partial shade alongside hostas, ferns, and native woodland wildflowers.

plant_note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions after the last frost into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; press the roots in firmly and keep evenly moist while the creeping stems knit together, which typically takes one full growing season for a solid mat.
directions: Plant starter plugs in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, or full sun where summers are cool and soil stays consistently moist; blue star creeper forms a dense, ankle-high mat of tiny round bright-green leaves studded from late spring through summer with pale blue, five-pointed star-shaped flowers only a fraction of an inch across. It roots as it spreads, filling gaps between stepping stones and pavers and tolerating light foot traffic once established, which makes it a popular substitute for turf in small shaded paths and between patio stones. It does not tolerate drought or foot traffic as well as some steppable thymes, so keep the soil from drying out during hot weather and avoid heavy or repeated trampling. Foliage stays evergreen in mild-winter climates and dies back to the crown where winters are cold, returning reliably from the roots in spring. Trim back periodically to keep it from climbing into neighboring low plants.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil or in a container with orchid-type epiphytic potting mix; blue star fern often grows as an epiphyte on the rough bark of cabbage palms and oak trees in the wild. It tolerates both wet and dry conditions remarkably well for a fern.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained to moderately dry soil in partial to full shade; blue star fern (golden polypody) is one of the most striking native ferns of the Gulf Coast and Florida, producing large, deeply lobed, silvery blue-green fronds with a distinctive blue-gray cast unusual in ferns — the fronds can reach 3 feet long and create a bold, sculptural effect in the shade garden. It is one of the few ferns that grows naturally as an epiphyte on the rough, furrowed bark of cabbage palms (Sabal palmetto) and live oaks in coastal Florida and the Gulf states, where it wedges into bark crevices and grows without soil, sustained by rainfall and humidity. In garden cultivation it is more drought tolerant than most ferns, making it valuable for drier shaded spots. The orange-yellow round sori on the frond undersides are an attractive feature. An outstanding large, architectural fern for zone 8–12 shade gardens.

common_name: Blue Star Juniper (Dwarf Silvery-Blue Mounding Juniper)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; like other junipers, Blue Star will not tolerate wet feet and needs sharp drainage.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Star will not tolerate soggy or heavy clay soil and needs sharp drainage to avoid root and crown rot. This dwarf, mounding juniper produces dense, star-shaped sprays of intensely silvery-blue, prickly foliage on a slow-growing, irregular mound that stays small for many years, making it a mainstay of rock gardens, foundation plantings, and mixed conifer borders where a low, textural, blue-toned accent is wanted. Its fine, dense form needs little to no pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward branch, and it is extremely low-maintenance and drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor, rocky soil that would stress most other shrubs. Deer generally avoid it, and it holds its blue color year-round in mild climates.

plant_note: Divide clumps or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; blue stars self-seeds freely in suitable climates and can spread into a loose, naturalistic colony — deadhead after the main flush to reduce self-seeding if self-propagation is not desired in formal garden settings.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; blue stars is a South African evergreen perennial of the iris family (Iridaceae) that produces loose, branching stems bearing numerous small, intensely bright, sky-blue to violet-blue, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers — each individual flower is short-lived (opening in the morning and closing by afternoon) but the plant produces a continuous succession of fresh blooms throughout the warm season, creating a sustained display of clear blue that is one of the few true blues available in warm-climate gardens. The narrow, grass-like, dark-green, evergreen leaves form a compact, fine-textured, clump-forming basal rosette from which the flowering stems arise. Blue stars performs acceptably in partial shade conditions, which distinguishes it from many other blue-flowered perennials that require full sun. It self-seeds freely in moist climates and can naturalize into loose colonies in suitable conditions. An underused and valuable source of true-blue flower color for warm-climate shade and partial-shade gardens in zone 9–11.

common_name: Blue Tango Bromeliad (Pink Bract with Blue-Tipped Flower Spike)
plant_note: Grow in containers or protected shade in zone 10-11, or as a houseplant elsewhere; Blue Tango Aechmea has no frost tolerance. It bears a bold hot-pink bract topped by small blue-tipped flowers on a branched spike.
directions: Give bright, filtered light or partial shade; Aechmea bromeliads scorch in direct hot sun but need good light to flower and hold their best color. Blue Tango produces a dramatic, long-lasting hot-pink branched bract topped with small blue-tipped flowers that fade to pink as they age, held well above the broad, silver-banded, arching leaves in a classic urn-shaped rosette. Like other Aechmea it flowers only once per rosette, after which offsets, or pups, form at the base and can be separated and repotted once they reach about a third the size of the parent. Keep the central cup topped with water, and grow in a loose, fast-draining bromeliad or orchid mix rather than heavy garden soil.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; soak seed first.
directions: Butterfly pea is a vigorous tropical climber with velvety, vivid blue blooms prized as a natural dye and for herbal tea. Soak the seed overnight and direct sow after frost in warm soil, providing a trellis for the twining vines to climb. Grow in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil kept evenly moist through the warm season. It flowers best in heat and attracts pollinators as it winds up its supports. Outside frost-free zones grow it as an annual or in a container to overwinter indoors.

common_name: Blue Trailing Achimenes (Long-Flowered Hot Water Plant)
plant_note: Start dormant scaly rhizomes shallowly in moist, warm potting mix in early to mid spring; growth is slow to emerge and stalls in cool soil below roughly 70°F, hence the 'hot water plant' nickname referring to the warm water once traditionally used to break dormancy. Grown as a warm-season houseplant or basket plant, dormant and dry over winter.
directions: The classic wild species behind many modern Achimenes hybrids, valued for its abundant violet-blue, flared, tubular flowers held just above soft, slightly hairy, toothed leaves on lax, semi-trailing stems. Grow in bright, indirect light with some protection from hot midday sun, and pot in a light, humus-rich mix that stays evenly moist through the growing season without becoming waterlogged. High humidity keeps the foliage lush; dry air can cause leaf edges to brown. As the flowering season winds down in fall, gradually withhold water and let the top growth die back, then store the small scaly rhizomes dry and cool until repotting the following spring.

common_name: Blue Vanda (Autumn Vanda, Tessellated Blue Orchid)
plant_note: Mount on a slab or hang bare-root in a slatted teak basket with little or no medium so the thick silver aerial roots have maximum air exposure; Vanda coerulea comes from cooler mid-elevation hills of Assam, Myanmar, and Thailand with a distinct cool, dry winter, and is more temperature-tolerant than most Vandas but still needs very bright light and daily root wetting followed by rapid drying to thrive. Source only nursery-propagated plants, as wild collection helped make this species one of the first orchids protected under international trade law.
directions: Provide very bright light — more than most Phalaenopsis or Cattleya tolerate — with strong air movement around the roots, since Vanda coerulea is a monopodial, leafless-root epiphyte that depends on frequent wetting and thorough drying rather than a bark potting mix. This is the famous "Blue Vanda" of the Khasi Hills, historically significant as one of the first orchids to display true blue-violet pigment, with a distinctive checkered (tessellated) pattern across the 4-inch flowers borne on upright racemes in fall. Water or mist the aerial roots daily in warm weather and let them dry within a few hours; humidity should stay high but standing moisture on the roots invites rot. Vanda coerulea is the parent species behind the great majority of blue-flowered Vanda hybrids in cultivation today, including the classic Vanda 'Rothschildiana.'

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or start indoors and transplant in spring into moist to wet, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; blue vervain thrives in rain gardens, pond margins, wet meadows, and roadside ditches.
directions: Direct sow fresh seed in fall in moist to wet, average soil in full sun to partial shade, pressing seeds onto the soil surface; blue vervain is a native North American wetland perennial that produces dense candelabra-like clusters of tiny violet-blue flowers from midsummer through early fall on branching, square stems to 5 feet tall. The sequential upward blooming pattern along each spike creates a dynamic appearance as blooms progress over several weeks. It is an important nectar source for native bees and the seeds are eaten by songbirds, especially sparrows and finches, in winter. Excellent for rain gardens, bioswales, and wet meadow plantings where soil stays reliably moist. Self-sows freely in wet conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks early.
directions: 'Blue Victory' offers a long season of deep violet-blue flower spikes on compact 20-inch plants that look stunning massed or in containers. Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil where it performs well even in hot, humid climates and is fairly drought tolerant once established. It makes an excellent cut or dried flower and attracts bees and hummingbirds. Deadhead spent spikes to keep the plants blooming through the season.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled light; blue walking iris is tender below 28°F but resprouts from established clumps in zone 9 after light freezes. In zone 8 treat as a large container plant and overwinter indoors.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to filtered light — blue walking iris is one of the most dramatically beautiful foliage and flowering plants for the shaded Gulf Coast garden, producing bold, fan-shaped clumps of upright, iris-like leaves 3–4 feet tall. The large, intricately patterned blue-purple flowers — each 3–4 inches across with white and golden markings — open from plantlets produced at the tips of flower stems; when these plantlets become heavy enough, the stem bends to the ground and the offset roots to start a new plant nearby, 'walking' the clump gradually across the garden. The flowers last only a single day but appear in succession over several weeks in late spring and early summer. An outstanding large-scale accent or specimen plant for the shaded side of buildings, under oaks, and in tropical-style garden compositions in zone 9–11. Grow in containers in cooler zones.

plant_note: Scarify seed with sandpaper and soak 24 hours before sowing; direct sow in fall for natural stratification and spring germination. Transplant potted plants in spring. Plants are slow to establish and should not be divided or moved once sited.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor, even dry soil in full sun; blue wild indigo is a long-lived native prairie perennial that forms a substantial, rounded, blue-green shrub-like clump bearing stunning spikes of true-indigo-blue pea flowers in May, followed by interesting inflated, rattling seedpods that persist through winter. It is a larval host plant for several native butterfly and moth species. Choose its permanent location carefully — blue wild indigo has a deep taproot and strongly resists transplanting once established, but plants can persist for 50+ years with no maintenance. Initially slow to establish (3 years to a full-sized clump), but thereafter essentially indestructible and extremely drought-tolerant. A specimen plant that will outlast the gardener.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Wonder fan flower is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and blooms continuously through summer.
directions: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Wonder fan flower is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and blooms continuously through summer. Distinctive, one-sided, fan-shaped flowers in vivid violet-blue cover trailing stems nearly continuously from early summer through frost, needing no deadheading to maintain a nonstop flower display, making this a classic, reliable choice for a hanging basket or container that cascades attractively over an edge. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives through the hottest, most humid part of summer when many other trailing annuals decline, tolerating dry spells with minimal wilting. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and expect vigorous, trouble-free growth through the entire warm season without deadheading.

common_name: Blue Wonder Toad Lily (Compact Heavy Shade-Tolerant Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Blue Wonder is a compact toad lily hybrid noted for good tolerance of heavy shade, useful for the darkest corners of a woodland bed where many flowering perennials fail.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Blue Wonder is a compact toad lily hybrid bearing creamy white to powder-blue flowers heavily speckled with blue-purple spots, blooming from September into frost when most of the shade garden has finished flowering for the season. Its notably good tolerance of heavy shade makes it a useful choice for the darker, more enclosed corners of a woodland garden where many flowering shade perennials struggle to bloom well. The compact, upright habit fits neatly into a mixed shade border without sprawling. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch with leaf litter, and divide congested clumps in spring if flowering begins to decline.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or divide existing plants in early spring; plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — blue wood aster is the most shade-tolerant of the native asters and grows naturally in the dim understory of mature deciduous forests.
directions: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or divide existing plants in early spring; plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — blue wood aster is the most shade-tolerant of the native asters and grows naturally in the dim understory of mature deciduous forests. Symphyotrichum cordifolium is invaluable as one of very few native plants that blooms with full vigor in deep shade from September through October, producing 1/2-inch, star-shaped, lavender-blue to violet-blue flowers by the thousands on freely branching stems when shade-garden foliage plants have lost their interest. In autumn it creates a breathtaking display of blue beneath the yellow fall leaves of maples and beeches; it is a critical nectar source for late-season migrating monarchs and native bees in woodland settings where other asters cannot grow. The plant self-seeds and gradually naturalizes into stunning woodland colonies.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, woodland soil in shade; blue wood sedge establishes more readily from fall-planted divisions which give the roots time to establish before summer heat. The blue-green foliage is evergreen in zones 7-9.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; blue wood sedge is prized for its distinctly blue-green to glaucous foliage — a true blue-tinged color unusual among groundcover plants — that remains evergreen in the warm winters of zones 7–9 and provides striking color contrast against darker green ferns, hostas, and woodland perennials. It is a southeastern Coastal Plain and Piedmont native that tolerates the humid heat of zone 8–9 far better than many northern sedges, making it a premium choice for Southern shade gardens. The low, arching clumps spread slowly by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat. Essentially maintenance-free once established in appropriate moist, shaded soil. The glaucous leaf coloration is most intense in deeper shade.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or early fall and replant at the same depth in well-drained to moist woodland soil in partial to full shade. Space 12-15 inches apart to create a weed-suppressing groundcover carpet within 2-3 growing seasons.
directions: Blue Wood Sedge is a refined native sedge with distinctive blue-green arching foliage that forms slowly spreading colonies, making it an outstanding low-maintenance groundcover for shaded sites. It is notably tolerant of dry shade once established — one of the most challenging garden conditions — and thrives beneath the root competition of mature oaks, maples, and other large deciduous trees. The fine-textured foliage contrasts beautifully with broad-leaved shade plants such as hostas, wild ginger, and trilliums in naturalistic woodland plantings. Mow or cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges to keep plantings looking fresh.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Yucca is cold-hardy but needs sharp drainage above all else and rots in wet, poorly drained soil.
directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Yucca is cold-hardy but needs sharp drainage above all else and rots in wet, poorly drained soil. Rigid, powder-blue leaves radiate in a dense, symmetrical rosette atop a slow-growing, thickening trunk that eventually branches, giving mature specimens a striking, tree-like silhouette prized in desert landscape design, topped periodically with a tall spike of creamy white, bell-shaped flowers. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert of Mexico and far west Texas, it is one of the more cold-hardy trunk-forming yuccas available, combining strong architectural form with reliable performance in a xeriscape or rock garden. Water only occasionally once established, and plant on a slope or raised bed in heavier soils to guarantee the sharp drainage this species demands.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Blue Zinger sedge tolerates a wide range of light and moisture conditions — from dry shade to moist, sunny locations — making it one of the most versatile ground cover plants available. In zone 9 it performs as a reliable evergreen perennial, maintaining its distinctive blue-gray foliage through the year. The blue coloration is most vivid in spring and fall; summer heat may slightly mute the blue intensity. Division every 3–4 years in spring maintains vigor. An excellent choice for replacing lawn grass in dry-shade areas under trees.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Blue Zinger sedge tolerates a remarkably wide range of conditions from dry shade to moist full sun; Blue Zinger is a cultivar of Carex flacca (glaucous sedge or blue sedge), a European sedge species selected for its intensely blue-gray foliage — one of the few genuinely blue-toned ground cover plants for shaded and partially shaded garden areas. The thin, arching, blue-gray leaves form a low, dense, slowly spreading mat that provides an elegant, fine-textured alternative to conventional grass lawn in shaded areas where turf grass fails. Unlike many ornamental grasses and sedges, Blue Zinger tolerates shade well while also performing adequately in full sun — a genuine dual-exposure tolerance that makes it broadly useful across garden microclimates. The distinctive blue-gray foliage color provides a neutral, cooling visual counterpoint to green and gold foliage plants in shade garden combinations, and functions as a living mulch that suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and prevents soil erosion on shaded slopes. As an evergreen perennial, Blue Zinger provides year-round ground coverage in zone 9 with minimal maintenance once established.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; needs light to germinate.
directions: 'Blue and Breezy' perennial flax opens charming 1-inch sky-blue flowers each dawn on airy, arching stems, with fresh blooms replacing the day-old ones each morning. Surface sow where plants are to grow, pressing the seed in lightly since it needs light to germinate. Grow in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil where it shrugs off heat, drought, cold, and poor ground. Its constant color and fine texture suit meadows, borders, and naturalized areas. It self-sows readily to fill in over time.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; blue-eyed Mary spreads steadily by stolons and self-sows moderately in suitable shaded conditions, gradually colonizing the floor of the shade garden.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; blue-eyed Mary (creeping navelwort) is a southern European native that spreads steadily to form low, loose mats of heart-shaped, bright-green leaves and covers itself with an extraordinary display of vivid, azure-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers in early spring — the flowers are notably larger and more intensely blue than true forget-me-nots, making this one of the finest shade plants for early-spring blue flower color. The semi-evergreen foliage provides year-round groundcover and the plant multiplies gradually by runners and self-sowing to colonize the woodland floor without becoming invasive. Excellent for naturalizing under deciduous trees alongside spring bulbs, hostas, ferns, and bleeding heart. 'Alba' (pure white) and 'Grandiflora' (larger flowers) are attractive cultivar selections. Combines especially well with yellow-flowered Epimedium for complementary color contrast.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring or fall in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; blue-head gilia is a cool-season annual that performs best before summer heat and declines in hot weather. It self-sows freely in appropriate conditions. Sow in broad drifts for the best display — individual plants are not very showy but masses create a beautiful blue haze.
directions: Direct sow seeds in cool weather in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; blue-head gilia is a California and Pacific Northwest native annual prized as one of the finest and most easily grown native annual bee plants — producing branching, wiry, finely-dissected-leaved stems topped by dense, round flower heads (like a spherical blue thimble) composed of many tiny, tubular, sky-blue to pale blue-violet florets packed tightly together in a tight ball. The spherical flower heads, carried on branching stems above the fine-textured foliage, create an airy, blue-haze effect in mass plantings reminiscent of meadow wildflower fields. It is exceptionally attractive to native bees — particularly small native bees, sweat bees, and mining bees — making it one of the highest-ranked native annual plants for supporting native bee populations. The fine texture of the foliage and the airy, branching habit combine with the unusual spherical, blue thimble flower heads to create a wildflower that is distinctive and ornamental without being showy. Outstanding in native plant meadow mixes, cutting gardens, and any sunny position where a bee-supporting blue annual is desired for spring through early summer.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination, or plant container-grown divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; blue-eyed grass naturalizes readily by self-seeding in suitable moist, open conditions.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant container divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; blue-eyed grass is a charming native member of the iris family that looks like a delicate grass but produces a continuous succession of tiny, six-petaled, bright violet-blue flowers with a yellow center from late spring through summer in a cheerful, prolific display. The flat, grass-like foliage is neat and attractive at all times. It naturalizes readily in moist meadow, prairie, and lawn-edge conditions by self-seeding to form soft, spreading colonies over time. Excellent at the front of a border, in rock gardens, along stream banks, and scattered through a native lawn mix. Highly attractive to small native bees and hoverflies. The related S. bermudiana (Bermuda blue-eyed grass) is similar but slightly more tolerant of dry conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; blue-eyed Mary is a self-sowing woodland annual that requires a period of cold, moist stratification over winter to germinate the following spring.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; blue-eyed Mary is a self-sowing woodland annual that requires a period of cold, moist stratification over winter to germinate the following spring. Collinsia verna is a delicate eastern North American native wildflower that carpets rich floodplain and cove forests in mid-spring with two-toned flowers — a white upper lip and vivid blue lower lip — held in tiered whorls up slender stems, blooming alongside Virginia bluebells and trout lily. It completes its life cycle quickly, flowering, setting seed, and dying back by early summer, so it is best naturalized in a woodland garden where it can self-sow into open patches of leaf litter year after year rather than planted as a permanent bedding annual. Avoid heavy mulch that would prevent the tiny seeds from reaching bare soil, and let plants stand until seed has fully dispersed before any cleanup.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting in spring; cold-moist stratify for 4-6 weeks before sowing to improve germination rates.
directions: Blue-flowered Eryngo is a standout native perennial prized for its deep blue to violet-blue, thistle-like flower heads surrounded by ornamental spiny blue bracts that appear in late summer and fall. It is native to the wet, acidic flatwoods, savannas, and bog margins of the southeastern United States, and demands moist to wet, sandy or peaty, acidic soil in full sun to perform well. Start seeds with a period of cold-moist stratification to improve germination, and transplant young plants in spring after they have developed a sturdy root system. Plants are slow to establish but long-lived once settled, and their vivid late-season blooms are highly attractive to bees, butterflies, and other pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall or start by division in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; blue-stemmed goldenrod is one of the very few goldenrods that blooms reliably in shade, making it irreplaceable for the shaded fall garden.
directions: Grow in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — blue-stemmed goldenrod is one of the most valuable native goldenrods for woodland and shaded gardens, distinguished by its distinctive blue-green to purple-blue stems and its genuine shade tolerance in a genus that is almost entirely full-sun. The small golden flower clusters emerge from the leaf axils along the upper portion of the arching stems in September and October, creating a wreath-like effect (explaining the alternate common name 'wreath goldenrod'). It grows naturally in moist, rich woodland understories throughout the eastern US and is well-adapted to the dry shade under large trees where most goldenrods cannot survive. An outstanding plant for bringing late-season native pollinator value into the shaded garden when almost no other native plants are blooming. The seeds provide fall food for native sparrows and other seed-eating birds.

plant_note: Transplant small divisions with intact rhizomes in early fall in cool, moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade under conifers or northern hardwoods; bluebead lily requires strongly acidic conditions (pH 4.5–5.5) and cool summer temperatures and will not persist in warm, dry, or alkaline sites.
directions: Transplant small divisions in early fall in cool, moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade under conifers or northern hardwoods; bluebead lily (corn lily) is a native perennial of cool northern and montane forests from Newfoundland south through the Appalachians, producing broad, glossy, lily-like basal leaves and erect stems bearing small, greenish-yellow, lily-of-the-valley-like flowers in late spring, followed by the ornamental feature for which it is named: clusters of intensely vivid, metallic, deep-cobalt-blue berries in late summer that are among the most striking fruit colors found in any hardy native plant. The berries are toxic but visually extraordinary. Requires specifically cool summer temperatures, strongly acidic soil, and consistent moisture — it cannot persist in zones warmer than 6 or in alkaline or dry conditions. Best naturalized in acidic woodland gardens in the northeastern US and upper Midwest alongside trilliums, trout lilies, and Canada mayflower.

plant_note: Grown from a potted shrub or cutting; plant after frost danger passes.
directions: The Blueberry Pie butterfly bush produces dense clusters of deep blue-violet, sweetly fragrant blooms that draw butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds all summer. This vigorous flowering shrub is easy to grow and provides months of pollinator activity in the sunny border. Plant a potted shrub in full sun with well-drained soil and water moderately until established. Deadhead spent flower spikes to prolong bloom and prune hard in early spring to keep the plant compact and full of new flowering wood.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Bluebird is a selection of native smooth aster valued for good mildew resistance and upright habit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Bluebird bears abundant blue-violet, daisy-form flowers with a golden center on tall, upright, sturdy stems clothed in smooth, blue-green foliage that stays notably clean and mildew-free compared to many garden asters. As a selection of a widespread North American native, it tolerates a range of soils and needs little care beyond staking in very rich soil where growth may be lush. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bluebird mountain hydrangea is more cold-hardy and reliably reblooms after a hard pruning better than many bigleaf hydrangeas.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bluebird mountain hydrangea is more cold-hardy and reliably reblooms after a hard pruning better than many bigleaf hydrangeas. Delicate, lacecap flower heads ring a center of small, fertile blue (or pink in alkaline soil) flowers with a fringe of larger, showier sterile florets, a more refined, airy bloom than the tight mophead clusters of standard bigleaf hydrangea, on a compact, well-branched shrub with narrower, more textured leaves. As a mountain hydrangea it tolerates more cold and sun than typical bigleaf hydrangeas and blooms on both old and some new wood, making it more forgiving of pruning mistakes and late spring frosts that can eliminate the year's flowers on old-wood-only cultivars. Amend soil pH to control flower color — more acidic soil produces blue tones, more alkaline soil produces pink — and mulch well to keep roots cool and moist through summer.

common_name: Bluebird Rose of Sharon (Clear Blue-Violet Red-Eyed Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Bluebird is an older, long-cultivated rose of sharon and, unlike the sterile National Arboretum triploid introductions, can self-seed, so remove spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bluebird is a widely grown, older rose of sharon selection carrying clear blue-violet, single flowers with a small red eye at the center, considered one of the truest blue tones available among rose of sharon cultivars, blooming heavily from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. It is tough and easy to grow in average garden soil, tolerating heat and humidity well, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from semi-hardwood cuttings in fall to allow root establishment through the rainy season, into well-drained, average to lean, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants need little to no summer water.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and water only to establish, since summer irrigation on settled soil is the leading cause of root rot and premature death in this famously drought-adapted shrub. Blueblossom ceanothus is one of the showiest California native shrubs, producing a spectacular late-winter to spring display of dense, powder-blue to deep cobalt flower clusters that smother the glossy, dark evergreen foliage and draw enormous numbers of native bees. It grows quickly, often 2 to 3 feet a year while young, reaching large shrub or small multi-trunked tree size along the coast, and works well as an informal hedge, slope stabilizer, or specimen where its rapid early growth and long-term drought tolerance can be put to use. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since old wood does not resprout reliably, and avoid heavy pruning into bare wood.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; scarify seed to aid germination.
directions: The Texas bluebonnet is a cherished heirloom lupine that carpets roadsides and meadows with spikes of blue spring flowers. Scarify the hard seed coat and direct sow in fall for the strongest spring display, since the seedlings resent transplanting. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil where it tolerates drought. Plant it in mass for the most captivating effect in naturalized wildflower areas. Allow pods to ripen and it will self-sow to return year after year.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into lean, well-drained soil among established native grasses; close proximity to host grass roots is essential for successful germination and growth.
directions: Bluehearts is a striking native annual hemi-parasite of southeastern coastal plain pine savannas, attaching to the roots of nearby native grasses to obtain additional water and nutrients while still photosynthesizing on its own — for garden success, direct sow seeds into an area already colonized by native warm-season grasses such as little bluestem, wiregrass, or broomsedge, as plants cannot establish without host root contact. Slender, rough-textured stems rise from a basal rosette and bear erect spikes of vivid violet-blue tubular flowers from summer through fall, making Bluehearts one of the most visually stunning of all southeastern savanna wildflowers. It thrives in lean, sandy, or gravelly soils in full sun and does not tolerate shade, competition from dense vegetation, or artificially enriched garden soils. Once sown into a native grass planting, it often self-seeds in subsequent years, gradually becoming a reliable component of a savanna-style wildflower garden.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun. Bluejack Oak demands xeric, nutrient-poor conditions and will not tolerate clay, excessive moisture, or shading from taller vegetation.
directions: Bluejack Oak is a distinctive native tree of sandhills, xeric upland forest, and fire-maintained scrub across the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Texas, immediately recognizable among oaks by its blue-gray, paddle-shaped leaves with pale, hairy undersides that give the small tree a frosted, silvery appearance unlike any other eastern oak. Adapted to the driest, most nutrient-poor sandy soils of the coastal plain, Bluejack Oak is extremely drought-tolerant and fire-resilient, regenerating rapidly from its extensive root system after low-intensity fires that historically maintained the sandhills where it is one of the dominant trees. The small acorns ripen in fall and are a critical food source for white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, small mammals, and Florida Scrub-Jays in dry upland communities where larger mast-producing oaks may be absent. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun — Bluejack Oak will not tolerate clay, excess moisture, or shade.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for cold stratification and spring germination, or direct sow in early spring; bluestem goldenrod is one of the very few native goldenrods that thrives in significant shade, making it invaluable for shaded pollinator gardens.
directions: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination, or provide 4–6 weeks of cold stratification before spring sowing; bluestem goldenrod grows in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil and is among the most shade-tolerant of all goldenrods. Solidago caesia is an eastern North American native goldenrod of deciduous forest interiors and edges producing slender, arching, bluish-green stems bearing clusters of small, bright-yellow flowers nestled in the leaf axils along the arching stem length (not in a large terminal plume like most goldenrods) from late summer through fall, creating an elegant, arching spray of yellow that is invaluable for late-season pollinator support in shaded gardens. Unlike most goldenrods that require full sun, bluestem goldenrod is specifically adapted to woodland shade and is an outstanding choice for the transition zone between sunny and shaded garden areas; it is an excellent companion for native wood asters, great Solomon's seal, and native ferns.

plant_note: Surface sow (light required for germination) in moist, slightly acidic soil; the plant self-sows to naturalize in moss gardens, lawn alternatives, and moist, shaded rock gardens.
directions: Scatter seed on moist, acidic soil in partial shade in early spring; this diminutive native wildflower carpets lawns, mossy banks, and lightly shaded meadows with pale blue four-petaled flowers in spring, creating an effect like scattered stars across a green sky. It naturally grows in thin, slightly moist, acidic soil of lawns and forest edges and is a wonderful component of a native lawn alternative. Allow it to go to seed after flowering to maintain the colony. The plant tolerates light foot traffic and can naturalize into an existing lawn if mowing is delayed until it sets seed in late spring. Does not perform well in heavy clay or alkaline soil.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; bluff oak is a white oak group species of bluffs, rocky slopes, and dry uplands of the lower Piedmont and Gulf Coastal Plain. It is closely related to Durand oak and often confused with it in the field.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; bluff oak is a medium to large white-oak group oak of the lower Piedmont and Gulf Coastal Plain, naturally growing on rocky bluffs, dry slopes, and upland sites from North Carolina to Georgia and Alabama. The leaves are variable but typically club-shaped with rounded lobes, resembling a smaller or more graceful white oak leaf. Like all white-oak group oaks, the sweet acorns ripen in a single season and are immediately germinated by squirrels and blue jays. The tree provides important acorn mast for wildlife and supports the full suite of moth and butterfly caterpillars that depend on native oaks. Relatively uncommon in cultivation and underused compared to its relatives, bluff oak is a dependable, drought-tolerant native for dry, upland settings in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in dry to moist, well-drained, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; blunt-lobed woodsia is the most drought-tolerant native eastern fern and an excellent choice for dry, rocky shaded slopes and walls.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown plants in spring in dry to moist, rocky, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; blunt-lobed woodsia establishes readily and is among the most drought-tolerant of all native ferns, making it uniquely valuable for challenging dry, rocky, shaded garden situations. Woodsia obtusa is a delicate-looking but tough native fern widely distributed across eastern North America from Canada to the Gulf states, producing compact, 8–18 inch, slightly hairy, light green fronds that are twice-pinnate with distinctive blunt-tipped (obtuse) lobes from which it takes its name; unlike most ferns it thrives in well-drained, even dry, rocky, alkaline soil such as limestone ledges and rocky woods. An excellent candidate for rock gardens, shaded dry walls, and naturalized areas under trees where soil is shallow or competitive. Semi-evergreen in mild winters.

common_name: Blush Loropetalum (Dwarf Soft Pink Chinese Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Blush is a dwarf loropetalum selection with soft pink flowers and green-tinged burgundy foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Blush forms a dense, compact mound bearing soft, gentle pink, fringe-petaled flowers over foliage that leans more green than the deep burgundy typical of many loropetalum cultivars, giving it a softer overall look for gardens wanting a subtler color than the bold magenta-and-purple selections common in the trade. Its dwarf habit suits foundation plantings and low borders without the need for constant pruning to control size. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

common_name: Blush Noisette Rose (The Founding Noisette Rose)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Blush Noisette is the founding rose of the Noisette class, bred in Charleston, South Carolina in the early 1810s and one of the very few rose classes to originate in North America.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Blush Noisette is historically significant as the original rose of the Noisette class, raised from seed in Charleston, South Carolina around 1811-1817 by rice planter John Champneys and further developed by nurseryman Philippe Noisette, making it one of the very few major rose classes bred in North America. It produces large clusters of small, soft pink, sweetly fragrant blooms in nearly continuous flushes through the growing season, on a vigorous, arching shrub that can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a modest climber. Noisette roses remain some of the best-adapted roses for the heat and humidity of the Deep South, and Blush Noisette needs little more than a sunny site and occasional shaping to perform for decades.

common_name: Blush Pink Loropetalum (Soft Pink Compact Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Blush Pink is a compact loropetalum with softer green-tinted foliage and pale pink fringe flowers, a gentler look than the deep-purple cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; good drainage is essential, since waterlogged soils cause rapid root rot. Blush Pink offers a softer look within the loropetalum family, with green-tinted foliage rather than the deep purple-red of most popular cultivars, paired with soft pale pink fringe flowers in spring and intermittently through summer and fall, giving a gentler, more pastel effect useful for blending with green-foliage companions. Its compact, mounding habit fits foundation plantings and shrub borders without requiring constant shearing to control size. Loropetalums are among the most heat- and humidity-tolerant ornamental shrubs for the Gulf South and are largely free of serious pest and disease problems; no pruning is required, but plants respond well to light shaping immediately after the main spring bloom.

common_name: Blush Pink Nandina (Soft Pink New-Growth Compact Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; new-growth color is most vivid with several hours of direct sun, while afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in the hottest part of the Gulf South summer.
directions: Blush Pink is a dwarf, mounding nandina selected for new foliage that emerges soft candy-pink before maturing to green, giving a softer, pastel-toned flush of color than the red new growth typical of most dwarf nandina cultivars. Its compact, dense habit fits foundation plantings and mixed containers, and the plant is sterile, producing no berries and avoiding the self-seeding that has made standard nandina an invasive problem in parts of the Southeast.
