Asplenium bradleyi (Bradley's spleenwort) is a small, charming native fern found on shaded sandstone and acidic rock outcroppings from Pennsylvania through the Appalachians to Alabama and Arkansas — one of the few ferns naturally adapted to the sharply drained, stressful conditions of vertical rock surfaces. It is a hybrid species (A. montanum × A. platyneuron) producing semi-evergreen, once-pinnate fronds 4–8 inches long with a distinctive dark-brown to nearly black midrib (rachis) contrasting with medium-green leaflets — giving the frond a two-toned, elegant appearance. While rarely available in general nurseries, it is grown by fern specialists and is an outstanding subject for naturalistic rock gardens, shaded stone walls, and terrarium-style displays. The dark midrib trait comes from its ebony spleenwort parent (A. platyneuron). Best planted in fall or early spring; protect from full exposure until established in its rocky pocket.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; brain cactus needs excellent drainage and its thin, wavy ribs are prone to sunburn if moved into intense sun too quickly.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; brain cactus needs excellent drainage and its thin, wavy ribs are prone to sunburn if moved into intense sun too quickly. Numerous thin, tightly packed, undulating ribs wind around a rounded body in a convoluted, folded pattern that closely resembles a brain, an unusual and instantly recognizable form among globe cacti, topped with delicate, pale pink to lavender flowers with a darker central stripe in spring. Native to central Mexico, it is a popular novelty cactus for its bizarre, sculptural rib pattern, and its relatively small size makes it well suited to a windowsill collection or mixed cactus dish garden. Water only when the soil is fully dry, acclimate gradually to strong direct sun to avoid scorching the thin ribs, and protect from frost.

common_name: Brakelights Red Yucca (Compact Deep-Red Hesperaloe Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; its compact, uniform habit makes it ideal for mass planting along walkways, medians, and small residential beds where the straight species would be too large.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun, spacing plants for a tidy, uniform mass planting since 'Brakelights' is a selected dwarf sport of red yucca that stays roughly half the size of the species. It forms a dense rosette of narrow, fibrous-edged, blue-green leaves and produces shorter, more compact flower spikes packed with intensely deep red-orange tubular blooms nearly continuously from spring through fall, making it one of the most reliable long-season hummingbird plants for hot climates. Like the species it is extraordinarily heat and drought tolerant, deer resistant, and unfussy about soil as long as drainage is sharp, but its smaller, denser form fits parking lot islands, foundation plantings, and small residential xeriscapes where the taller straight species would overwhelm the space. Being a patented selection, it is propagated only by division rather than seed, ensuring uniform color and size.

common_name: Branford Beauty Fern (Vigorous Silver-Painted Hybrid Lady Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Branford Beauty is a sterile hybrid between Japanese painted fern and lady fern, combining painted fern's silvery coloring with lady fern's larger size and greater vigor and heat tolerance.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Branford Beauty is a sterile hybrid between Japanese painted fern (Athyrium niponicum) and the native lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina), combining the silvery-gray frond coloring and reddish stems inherited from its painted fern parent with the larger stature, greater vigor, and improved heat tolerance of lady fern. The result is a more substantial, faster-growing plant than a typical Japanese painted fern, better able to hold up through Gulf South summer heat and humidity while retaining much of the ornamental silver coloring that makes painted ferns so popular. Fronds emerge silvery-gray with burgundy-red stems in spring, filling out into an attractive, arching clump that provides season-long texture in the shade garden. As a sterile hybrid, it does not set spores and spread by itself, making it a well-behaved choice for mixed shade plantings alongside hostas, heucheras, and other ferns. Cut back old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants to allow the creeping rhizomes room to knit together into a colony over several seasons.
directions: 'Branford Rambler' is a stoloniferous hybrid between lady fern and Japanese painted fern that spreads gently by creeping rhizomes to knit together an expanding groundcover, rather than staying in a tight clump like its sibling selection 'Branford Beauty'. Upright, deciduous fronds reach about two feet tall, their fresh green blades set off by dark maroon-red stipes that echo the coloring of Japanese painted fern without the silvery variegation. It performs best in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and is deer resistant, making it a dependable choice for massing under trees or along a shaded path. Allow room for it to ramble, or use it as a filler between larger specimen ferns and hostas where a slowly spreading textural carpet is wanted.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain above 60°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and bring indoors when temperatures approach 50°F. Brasil Philodendron grows as a trailing or climbing vine, extending several feet in a single season when well-grown. Stem cuttings root easily in water or moist potting mix, making propagation simple. Outdoors on a shaded porch or pergola in zone 9, the warm summer humidity promotes rapid growth and large, vivid leaves. In zone 10–11 it can be grown as a permanent outdoor shade plant in protected locations.
directions: Plant in bright indirect light to shade — never in direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil; Brasil is a variegated cultivar of Heartleaf Philodendron (Philodendron hederaceum) producing the familiar heart-shaped leaves of the parent species in a striking bicolor pattern — each leaf displays a central zone of chartreuse to bright yellow-green contrasting with the dark forest green of the leaf margins, with the boundary between the two tones being irregular and painterly rather than a precise stripe. The color pattern creates a vivid, spontaneous, almost abstract effect that gives Brasil philodendron a more artful and dynamic quality than regularly striped or symmetrically patterned foliage plants. The trailing, vining habit makes Brasil excellent for hanging baskets, the edges of containers, and as a trailing accent on shaded shelves and pedestals — the long stems cascading over the container edges to create a flowing, lush effect. Heartleaf Philodendron in general is one of the most genuinely shade- and low-light-tolerant trailing plants available, surviving in conditions where most other ornamental plants decline, making Brasil one of the most practically useful shade container plants for zone 9 covered patios and indoor situations.

plant_note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; brass buttons spreads by creeping rhizomes to knit into a solid carpet within a season or two under consistent moisture.
directions: Plant divisions or starter plugs in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; brass buttons is a low, mat-forming New Zealand groundcover with finely divided, fern-like bronze-green foliage that spreads by creeping rhizomes to form a dense, textural carpet — a favorite substitute for turf in small shaded paths, between stepping stones, and as a soft, non-mowed filler around larger plants. Tiny, button-like yellow-green flowers appear in summer but are inconspicuous against the foliage, which is the main ornamental feature. It tolerates light foot traffic once established and stays low without mowing. Keep the soil from drying out for extended periods, since it thins in prolonged drought, and give it some afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the foliage from scorching. Divide congested patches in spring to fill in bare spots or start new plantings elsewhere.

Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Braun's holly fern needs more consistent moisture and cooler conditions than Japanese holly fern and is best in northern zones and high-elevation gardens. Polystichum braunii is a beautiful, semi-evergreen to evergreen native fern of cool, moist hardwood and mixed forests of eastern North America, Europe, and Asia; its elegant, narrowly lanceolate fronds are densely covered in silvery-white scales when unfurling in spring, creating a striking pewter effect, and the mature fronds are lustrous, deep green with neatly doubly-pinnate, spiny-tipped pinnae giving it the holly-fern look shared by the genus. It is an outstanding choice for shaded rock gardens, cool woodland borders, and naturalizing under conifers in zones 3–7.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile potting mix or garden soil in shade to part shade; Brazilian coleus is a trailing South African plectranthus with distinctive, velvety, rounded, dark-green leaves traced with silver veins on the upper surface and purple on the underside — one of the most beautiful foliage plants for shade containers and hanging baskets.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in shade to part shade; water when the top inch of soil dries. Plectranthus oertendahlii (Brazilian coleus or silver spurflower) is a trailing South African succulent-stemmed perennial in the mint family (Lamiaceae), native to the shaded, moist forest floors of KwaZulu-Natal province in South Africa. Despite the common name 'Brazilian coleus,' it is entirely South African in origin — the misnomer likely arises from its use as a tropical shade plant in Brazilian gardens. The plant produces distinctively beautiful, rounded, scalloped-edged leaves (1–2 inches across) with a velvety texture, dark-green with prominently traced, pale-silver veins on the upper surface and a rich purple-burgundy on the underside — one of the most attractive foliage patterns in the plectranthus family. It produces spikes of small, white to pale-lavender flowers but is grown primarily for foliage. As a shade container and hanging basket plant, P. oertendahlii is outstanding — the trailing stems and beautiful leaf patterning make it an eye-catching specimen. It also works beautifully as a shade terrarium subject and as an indoor plant in low-light situations. The cultivar 'Uvongo' has particularly striking leaf markings.

common_name: Brazilian Joseph Coat (Purple Calico Plant, Bloodleaf Joyweed)
plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or purchased transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Brazilian joyweed roots easily from cuttings placed in moist soil or water, making propagation trivially simple for overwintering or expanding plantings.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun (for deepest foliage color) to part shade; tip-prune regularly to maintain bushy, compact growth and prevent legginess. Alternanthera brasiliana (Brazilian Joseph coat) is a fast-growing tropical tender perennial or warm-season annual grown for its spectacular deep-purple to burgundy-purple, bronze, and maroon foliage — among the most richly colored of all foliage annuals. The narrow, lance-shaped to spatula-shaped leaves are a uniform deep burgundy-purple above and lighter purple below; the color is most intense in full sun. Like other alternantheras, it is used extensively as an edging or carpet-bedding plant in formal annual color schemes, and its rich foliage color creates outstanding contrast against chartreuse, gold, or white flowering annuals. Brazilian joyweed grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and provides consistent foliage color from spring through frost without the need for regular deadheading. In zone 9–10, it often survives mild winters and resprouts from roots; take stem cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors in colder zones.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, lean to average, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in zone 7–10; Brazilian Needle Palm is among the most cold-hardy of all South American palms — native to the campos of southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina, tolerating temperatures to 12–18°F when established — with stiff, blue-green fan fronds and a distinctive trunk covered in persistent, matted fiber and needle-like spines.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to average soil; Trithrinax brasiliensis is drought tolerant and adapted to poor, dry grassland soils of the South American campos — requires excellent drainage; water regularly only in establishment, then minimal supplemental water needed in appropriate climates. Trithrinax brasiliensis (Brazilian Needle Palm or Spiny Trunk Palm) is an attractive, slow-growing fan palm native to the subtropical campos (savanna grasslands) of Rio Grande do Sul in southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina, one of the most cold-tolerant fan palms available from South America. The trunk is distinctive: covered in a dense mat of persistent leaf-base fibers and needle-like spines up to several inches long that give it a rough, armored texture. The stiff, flat fan fronds — divided into narrow segments — have a blue-green to silvery-green color that contrasts beautifully with the dark trunk. Cold hardiness is the plant's outstanding horticultural characteristic: established specimens survive temperatures of 12–18°F (zone 7b–8a) when planted in well-drained soils, making it one of the very few ornamental palms suitable for garden conditions in zone 7. Drought tolerant once established. A valuable, unusual cold-hardy palm for large landscape gardens in the South and Southwest United States where an extremely exotic, palm-like accent plant is desired in zone 7 or warmer climates.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, organically rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade after last frost; Brazilian plume flower blooms most heavily in late summer to fall and again in spring in frost-free climates.
directions: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial to full shade; Brazilian plume flower is a South American native soft-wooded shrub that delivers one of the most spectacular flower displays possible in a shaded landscape — dense, upright, plume-like clusters of tubular rose-pink to deep magenta flowers from late summer through frost, and again in spring. The large, oval, dark-green leaves are handsome throughout the year. Hummingbirds visit the flowers repeatedly. Requires consistent moisture and resents drought; water deeply during hot, dry spells. Cut back by one-half to two-thirds in early spring to promote vigorous, floriferous new growth. In zone 9 it may be killed to the ground by hard frost but re-sprouts from the base; mulch heavily in winter.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Brazilian red cloak is a fast-growing tropical shrub best treated as a large container specimen or root-hardy perennial outside true frost-free zones.
directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Brazilian red cloak is a bold, fast-growing tropical shrub grown for its striking upright flower spikes, in which large, deep red-maroon bracts overlap like shingles and part to reveal pure white, tubular flowers, creating a strong color contrast that blooms heavily from late summer into winter in frost-free climates. Large, glossy, dark green leaves give the shrub a lush, substantial presence even between flowering flushes, quickly filling out a tropical border or privacy planting where winters stay mild. It grows rapidly and can become leggy without regular pinching or a hard pruning in early spring, which encourages the dense, well-branched form that shows off the flower spikes best. Where frost is a risk, grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter, or mulch heavily and expect it to die back and resprout from the roots after a light freeze.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, moist soil in zone 9–11; Brazilian Skyflower is a compact, rounded shrub from the scrubby savannas and forest edges of Brazil — smaller and more cold-hardy than the common Pigeon Berry (Duranta erecta) — producing abundant sprays of small, violet-blue to lavender flowers in dense, narrow racemes throughout the warm season, followed by yellow-orange berry clusters, and making an excellent low hedge or border shrub for warm gardens.
directions: Plant Duranta stenostachya in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; prune after flowering to maintain compact shape; more cold-hardy than Duranta erecta, tolerating light frost to about 28°F. CAUTION: the berries are toxic to humans and pets. Brazilian Skyflower is a close relative of the widely grown Pigeon Berry (Duranta erecta) but with a distinctly different character: where D. erecta is a large, sprawling, vigorous shrub or small tree reaching 15 feet, D. stenostachya stays compact and rounded at 3–6 feet, making it much more manageable in typical garden situations. The flower spikes are narrower and more erect than D. erecta's cascading clusters, giving a slightly different visual effect; the violet-blue to lavender flower color is similar. Originally from the cerrado and forest-savanna transitions of interior Brazil, it is adapted to the seasonal drought and lean soils of tropical savannas — making it more drought-tolerant than D. erecta once established. The compact form makes it an excellent choice for informal hedges, mixed shrub borders, and foundation plantings in zone 9–11 gardens. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit the flowers just as reliably as they visit D. erecta. The yellow-orange berry clusters are ornamental through winter and much appreciated by mockingbirds and thrushes — but should not be eaten by people or pets.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Brazilian tree fern forms a dramatic architectural accent with new fronds emerging in coppery-red before maturing to dark green.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Brazilian tree fern develops a short, scaly trunk over time and produces striking architectural fronds up to 3 feet long with a distinctive ladder-like arrangement of leaflets. New croziers and expanding fronds emerge in vivid copper to red tones before maturing to dark, glossy green. The contrast between the dark mature fronds and the red new growth is especially dramatic in spring. It thrives in sheltered, humid, shaded positions in zones 8b-11, excellent at the base of a building wall or among large tropical perennials in a sheltered courtyard garden.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into a sunny location; thin seedlings to allow ample room for the tall, branching stems to develop.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in a sunny, open site and thin to 18-24 inches apart; plants grow quickly into tall, stiff-stemmed clumps that need no staking in most conditions. From summer through frost, the candelabra-like branching spikes carry masses of tiny purple-violet flowers that are outstanding butterfly magnets, particularly for skippers, painted ladies, and swallowtails. Cut plants back by half after the first flowering flush to encourage a second wave of bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding. This naturalized South American species self-sows prolifically and can spread widely in open, sunny sites across the Southeast, so site it where volunteer seedlings can be tolerated or remove spent flower heads to manage spread.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks early; darkness aids germination.
directions: Brazilian vervain, also called tall or purpletop verbena, sends up airy wands of rose-violet to lavender blooms atop tall, slender stems. Start seed indoors six to eight weeks early, covering it since darkness aids germination. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil where it tolerates drought once established. Its see-through height creates a light, floating layer of color in the border and is a magnet for butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds. It reseeds readily as a welcome volunteer and is grown as an annual where winters are cold.

plant_note: Anchor unweighted cuttings loosely in pea gravel or plant in submerged pots of heavy garden soil capped with sand, then lower into 1-3 ft of water once temperatures warm.
directions: Plant bunched, weighted stem cuttings directly into submerged containers of heavy loam topped with pea gravel to keep them anchored; new roots form quickly from the stem nodes. This fast-growing submerged oxygenator competes with algae for nutrients and shelters fish fry, but it spreads aggressively and is regulated or banned as invasive in some states, so confine it to contained water features and never release it into natural waterways. Thin regularly by pulling out handfuls of stems, and overwinter tender specimens indoors in cold climates since hard freezes kill top growth to the crown.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade after frost; Brazilian yellow sage blooms most heavily in fall and winter in frost-free climates and performs best in consistent moisture with partial-shade protection from intense afternoon sun, which causes leaf scorch.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Brazilian yellow sage (yellow jacobinia, golden justicia, golden plume) is a Central American tropical shrub of the family Acanthaceae that produces dense, upright, cone-shaped spikes of bright-yellow, tubular, two-lipped flowers in the fall and winter months — at a time when yellow-flowering shade plants are exceptionally rare. The golden-yellow flower spikes, clustered densely at the tips of the arching stems, provide a vivid autumn-to-winter color display in the warm-climate garden that is nearly unmatched among partial-shade flowering shrubs. The large, soft, oval, velvety-hairy leaves are attractive and provide bold foliage texture in the shade garden. Like other shade-tolerant members of the Acanthaceae, it performs remarkably well in the dappled light of open tree canopies — one of few large-growing shade-tolerant shrubs that produce ornamental spikes of flowers rather than solitary tubular flowers. In zone 9 it freezes to the ground but regrows vigorously in spring. Cut back after flowering to encourage compact regrowth.

plant_note: Direct sow in very early spring or fall; seeds germinate in cool soil and seedlings tolerate frost.
directions: Surface sow by scattering seed on bare ground and pressing lightly without covering, as light aids germination. Breadseed poppies resent root disturbance and must be sown in place. Thin to 6–12 in when seedlings are 2 in tall. The ornamental seedpods are striking after petals drop and are valuable dried; harvest when the cap at the top turns from green to tan.

common_name: Break Out Dahlia (Blended Pink-Cream-Yellow Dinnerplate Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Break Out is a large AA-size dinnerplate dahlia with blended pink, cream, and soft yellow petals, a favorite for cut-flower growers.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants at planting time since the massive flowers can topple stems in wind. Break Out bears huge, informal decorative blooms blending soft pink, cream, and pale yellow tones within each flower, a subtle, ever-shifting color combination that has made it a favorite among specialty cut-flower growers for its unusual, painterly palette. Disbud side buds to concentrate energy into fewer, larger blooms if maximum flower size is the goal, or leave them for more numerous, slightly smaller flowers. Deadhead spent blooms regularly, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; breath of heaven requires excellent drainage — it declines quickly in wet, heavy, or poorly-drained soils. Do not over-fertilize; rich soils reduce flowering and shorten plant life. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain compact shape. The aromatic foliage releases a sweet citrus-like scent when touched. Not tolerant of salt spray.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; breath of heaven is a South African Cape fynbos shrub prized for two complementary qualities: the fine, soft, needle-like, heather-like aromatic foliage that releases a sweet citrus-like scent when brushed or touched — earning the common name 'breath of heaven' — and the winter to early spring flowering, when the entire shrub becomes covered in hundreds of tiny, five-petaled, pink to white-pink flowers so numerous and so densely covering the fine, feathery foliage that the plant appears dusted with confetti, giving the alternative common name 'confetti bush'. The flower display in late winter and early spring, when the fine-textured shrub is smothered in small, clear-pink flowers against the bright-green, aromatic, needle-like foliage, is one of the most cheerful winter garden displays available in zone 9 landscapes. The aromatic foliage is attractive year-round and the light, fine texture provides a delicate contrast to bolder neighboring plants. It demands excellent drainage — the primary requirement for success — and lean soils. A valued landscape shrub in California and in Gulf Coast Mediterranean-style gardens.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Breathless euphorbia is a compact, mounding selection bred for a fuller, denser habit than the similar Diamond Frost cultivar.
directions: Plant transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Breathless euphorbia is a compact, mounding selection bred for a fuller, denser habit than the similar Diamond Frost cultivar. Countless tiny, star-shaped white flowers cover a dense, airy mound of fine-textured foliage nearly continuously through the growing season, creating a soft, baby's-breath-like cloud of white that serves as an excellent filler between bolder, more colorful companions in a mixed container or border. More compact and densely mounding than the popular Diamond Frost cultivar, it needs little deadheading or maintenance to maintain its nonstop flower display through summer heat and humidity. Water when the top inch of soil dries, avoid overwatering which can lead to root rot, and note that the milky sap can irritate skin, so wear gloves when handling or pruning.

common_name: Brenthurst Tropical Sage (Pink Bicolor Salvia coccinea)
plant_note: Transplant after all danger of frost once soil has warmed; this reseeding tropical sage selection thrives in the long hot summers of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Transplant into well-drained beds in full sun to light shade, spacing plants a foot or so apart to let the branching stems fill out over the season. This soft-pink-and-white bicolor selection of the Gulf Coast native tropical sage blooms nonstop from late spring until frost and is a magnet for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees. It tolerates heat, humidity, and brief drought far better than most bedding salvias, and readily self-sows to return the following year. Use it in cottage borders or pollinator plantings where its pastel spikes contrast nicely with the more common red-flowered forms.

common_name: Bressingham Ruby Bergenia (Ruby-Red Winter Foliage Pigsqueak)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring just below soil level with the crown at the surface, in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, and remove tattered older leaves by pulling them sharply downward to snap them free from the rhizome. Bred at England's Bressingham Gardens and long a garden standard, Bressingham Ruby bears deep magenta-rose flower clusters on red stems in early spring above large, rounded, leathery leaves that turn an intense ruby-red through fall and winter, among the deepest winter color of any bergenia cultivar. Its bold, glossy foliage provides year-round structure and texture at the front of shaded borders and along shaded walkways, and it tolerates drier soil once established better than many other bergenias. Divide crowded clumps every 4–5 years in spring by cutting through the woody, surface-creeping rhizomes.

plant_note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; unlike deciduous Plumeria rubra, Bridal Bouquet is evergreen in frost-free climates and blooms nearly year-round, with distinctive elongated, fiddle-shaped leaves quite different from typical plumeria foliage.
directions: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Plumeria pudica, commonly sold as Bridal Bouquet, is a distinctive species with elongated, glossy, dark green, fiddle- or spoon-shaped leaves entirely different from the broad, oval leaves of standard Plumeria rubra hybrids, giving it a unique tropical texture even when not in bloom. Unlike most plumeria, it is evergreen and nearly ever-blooming in frost-free conditions, producing clusters of pure white flowers with a soft yellow throat and a mild, pleasant fragrance almost continuously rather than in a single seasonal flush. It also branches and fills out more readily than many plumeria, forming a fuller, bushier plant at a younger age. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors before temperatures drop into the 40s, since it tolerates cold poorly even compared to other plumeria, and reduce water in winter if kept in a cooler spot. Outdoors in frost-free zones it makes an excellent low-maintenance flowering hedge or specimen.

common_name: Bridal Veil Astilbe (Classic White Arendsii Astilbe)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Bridal Veil requires consistently moist soil and does not tolerate prolonged drought, so mulch heavily and irrigate through dry spells, especially in zone 9 summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Bridal Veil is one of the classic Georg Arends astilbe hybrids, producing airy, arching plumes of pure white flowers in early summer above finely cut, glossy green compound foliage, a graceful contrast to the deeper reds and pinks of many other astilbe cultivars. Like other astilbes it thrives in the consistently moist, humus-rich, shaded conditions found near streams, ponds, and under trees, and struggles if allowed to dry out, especially through zone 9 summer heat where deep shade and heavy mulch are important for success. The dried seed plumes remain attractive for weeks after bloom, and dividing the clump every three to four years in early spring keeps it vigorous.

common_name: Bridal Wreath Spiraea (Plena Old Fashioned Bridal Wreath)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Spiraea prunifolia blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering to preserve next year's flower buds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Spiraea prunifolia, the Bridal Wreath Spiraea, is one of the oldest ornamental shrubs in continuous cultivation in American gardens — grown since the early nineteenth century for its exceptional late winter to early spring flower display of small, perfectly double, white, button-like flowers arranged in dense rows along each long, slender, arching branch before any foliage appears. The distinctive flower arrangement on the bare stems is unlike any other spiraea: dozens of small, round, double flowers line up in rows along the branch length from base to tip, covering the entire structure with a lacy white effect. The fully double, non-fading white flowers persist longer than single-flowered types. Unlike the more common Vanhoutte spiraea (S. × vanhouttei), Spiraea prunifolia has glossy, deep-green, relatively small leaves that turn attractive orange-red to burgundy in fall — providing outstanding fall color that S. × vanhouttei lacks. Spiraea prunifolia grows somewhat more upright than Vanhoutte (5–7 feet tall, wider than tall) with a graceful arching form. In zone 9, it blooms in late February through March — one of the earliest spring-blooming shrubs in the landscape. Like Vanhoutte, it must be pruned only immediately after flowering; pruning in fall or winter removes the old-wood flower buds essential for the spring display.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or pups in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Bright Edge is a variegated selection of native Adam's needle yucca with bold gold margins along each blue-green leaf, the reverse pattern from the central-striped Color Guard cultivar.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun to partial shade. Bright Edge is a variegated form of the native Adam's needle yucca, each stiff, sword-shaped, evergreen leaf edged in a bright golden-yellow margin around a blue-green center, providing bold architectural color in the landscape year-round in addition to the tall summer spikes of white, bell-shaped flowers. Like the species it is extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and adaptable to poor, sandy, or coastal soils once established, needing almost no supplemental water or care. It slowly forms offsets (pups) at the base that can be separated to propagate new plants, and old flower stalks can be cut down after the blooms fade.

common_name: Bright Eyes Phlox (Pink-with-Red-Eye Tall Garden Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; plant in groupings of 3–5 plants for the best garden effect — a single Bright Eyes plant is less impressive than a cluster, which creates the large mass of color characteristic of traditional phlox borders.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Bright Eyes is a classic tall garden phlox cultivar producing large, rounded flower heads in soft pink with a distinctive dark crimson-red eye at the center of each five-petaled flower — the bicolor pink-and-red pattern creating a vibrant, cheerful flower that has been a garden favorite since the early twentieth century. The large, domed panicles (8–12 inches across) are sweetly fragrant and produced on upright stems 30–42 inches tall in July through September. The contrasting eye pattern gives each individual flower an appealing depth and complexity that pure-color phlox cultivars lack. The fragrance is one of the most pleasant in the summer garden. As with all Phlox paniculata cultivars, powdery mildew can be a problem in humid climates — Bright Eyes is somewhat susceptible, so provide excellent air circulation (wide spacing, no overhead watering) and treat preventively with sulfur or neem oil sprays if mildew is a recurring problem. Deadheading the central panicle when it fades promotes side-shoot flowering and extends the season. In zone 9, tall phlox is treated as a short-lived perennial — it grows most reliably in zone 4–8 and may decline after 1–2 seasons in the intense summer heat of zone 9.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: 'Bright Lights' is a vibrant sulphur cosmos blend with bold 2.5-inch flowers in warm oranges, golds, and reds from midsummer to first frost. Direct sow after the last frost once soil is warm, barely covering the seed. Grow in full sun in average to lean soil, since rich ground favors foliage over flowers, and it is drought tolerant once established. Butterflies and hummingbirds flock to the nectar-rich blooms, making it superb for wildflower and naturalized areas. Deadhead or cut regularly to keep flowers coming.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost; thrives in heat and poor soil.
directions: Direct sow Bright Lights cosmos after the last frost, barely covering the seed in a sunny, well-drained spot. This heat- and drought-tolerant heirloom produces semi-double blooms in glowing shades of gold, orange, and scarlet that keep coming until frost. Lean soil actually encourages more flowers and less floppy growth, so hold back on fertilizer. Deadhead or cut for bouquets to fuel a nonstop pollinator show.

common_name: Brilliance Autumn Fern (Vividly Colored Copper-Red Shield Fern)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial to full shade; Brilliance is more heat-tolerant than many shade ferns and performs reliably in zone 9 under the canopy of tall pines or in north-facing positions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Brilliance is a cultivar of the autumn fern (Dryopteris erythrosora) selected for more vivid and saturated copper-red new frond color than the standard species — a significant improvement since the species itself is already one of the most ornamentally striking ferns available for the shade garden due to its unusual two-season color effect. The new fronds emerge in spring (and again with each flush of new growth through the growing season) in a vivid copper-red to burnt-orange color that is unlike any other hardy shade fern — completely different from the standard green of most fern species and creating a dramatic color contrast against adjacent green-foliaged shade plants. As the fronds mature they transition through orange-bronze to a glossy, rich, deep-green that provides excellent foliage texture for the rest of the season. Brilliance intensifies this color sequence beyond the species — the spring copper-red is more vivid and the contrast between new and mature fronds more dramatic. The plant is semi-evergreen to evergreen in zone 9, maintaining attractive fronds through mild winters with only light frost damage. The evergreen or semi-evergreen quality in zone 9 provides winter landscape interest that fully deciduous ferns cannot. Unlike many cool-climate shade ferns that struggle in Gulf South heat, Dryopteris erythrosora tolerates summer humidity and heat reliably in zone 9.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; needs light and cool soil.
directions: 'Brilliant' oriental poppy is a majestic perennial with intense red 4-inch blooms that make a spectacular focal point in spring and early summer. Surface sow the fine seed in early spring or fall, leaving it uncovered since it needs light and cool soil to germinate. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and direct sow where it is to grow because it resents having its taproot disturbed. The foliage dies back after flowering, so pair it with later perennials to fill the gap. Pair its red blooms with yellow, gold, purple, or blue for striking contrast.

common_name: Brilliant Red Tropical Hibiscus (Classic Large Single Red Hibiscus rosa-sinensis)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Brilliant is one of the most continuously free-blooming tropical hibiscus varieties in Gulf South summer heat — even in August when other hibiscus varieties have reduced bloom, Brilliant typically maintains good flower production.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Brilliant is one of the classic large-single tropical hibiscus cultivars — a time-tested variety producing very large (5–6 inch), brilliant solid-red, single flowers with the typical flared, five-petaled hibiscus form and prominent staminal column. The pure, intense red of 'Brilliant' — without the pink undertones of some red hibiscus or the orange overtones of others — is the quintessential tropical hibiscus red that defines the color archetype. Individual flowers last one day but are produced in continuous succession throughout the warm season on well-fertilized, adequately watered plants — a mature hibiscus in peak condition can produce 20–40 open flowers daily. Hibiscus rosa-sinensis is the national flower of Malaysia and a widely revered cultural symbol across Southeast Asia and the Pacific — Brilliant's classic single-red form is the type most closely associated with this symbolic status. In zone 9, Brilliant grows as a large perennial shrub in protected locations but may be severely damaged or killed by hard freezes — container-grown specimens provide the flexibility to overwinter indoors during cold spells. The continuous bloom, vivid color, and hummingbird attraction make Brilliant one of the most effective tropical accent plants for Gulf South summer container displays and protected courtyard gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Brilliant is an older showy-stonecrop cultivar and a parent of the widely grown Autumn Joy hybrid group.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Brilliant forms tidy, upright clumps of pale gray-green succulent foliage topped from late summer into fall by broad, flat clusters of vivid rose-pink flowers that are noticeably brighter and clearer in color than the muddier tones of many later hybrids. Its sturdy stems stand well without staking and its flowers draw heavy bee and butterfly traffic right as many other perennials are winding down for the season. Leave the dried flower heads standing through winter for structure and wildlife cover, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep them vigorous.

plant_note: In desert gardens, sow on the soil surface after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm; seeds germinate rapidly after warm rains.
directions: Bristly Nama is a tiny, prostrate native annual that forms dense, bristly mats of narrow, hairy leaves completely blanketed with small, vibrant purple to magenta-purple, funnel-shaped flowers from spring through fall following desert rains. It is native to sandy flats, dry washes, and open disturbed ground in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and adjacent Mexico, where it is one of the most cheerful and reliable wildflowers of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran deserts after monsoon events. Scatter seed on bare, dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun with no soil preparation needed — it thrives in lean conditions that would challenge most plants. It is an excellent low-growing native annual for desert garden edges, dry sandy slopes, and any hot, arid problem area where conventional plants fail.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; ligularia wilts dramatically in dry soil or hot afternoon sun and needs reliable moisture and shade to look its best.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; ligularia wilts dramatically in dry soil or hot afternoon sun and needs reliable moisture and shade to look its best. Large, rounded, deeply glossy purple-black leaves provide bold, dramatic foliage color from spring through fall, topped in mid- to late summer by bright orange-yellow, daisy-like flower clusters that create a striking contrast against the near-black leaves. One of the most popular dark-leaved ligularia cultivars for its combination of season-long foliage color and reliable summer bloom, it makes a bold accent for a shaded, consistently moist border or pond-edge planting where its water needs can be easily met. Keep soil constantly moist, since ligularia wilts visibly within hours of drying out even in shade, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or plant nursery starts into very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; brittlebush is one of the most common and recognizable low desert shrubs, blanketing hillsides in gold each spring.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; brittlebush is a rounded, silvery-leaved desert shrub whose felted, gray-white foliage reflects intense sun and reduces water loss, and it is one of the most visually dominant plants of the Sonoran Desert, covering hillsides in a haze of bright yellow, daisy-like flowers on tall, leafless stalks each spring. The dried, resinous stems were historically burned as incense by Spanish missions and Native peoples, giving the plant one of its alternate common names, incienso. Fast-growing and short-lived compared to many desert shrubs, it typically declines after five to ten years but self-sows readily in disturbed, sunny, well-drained soil to replace itself. Prune out dead or woody stems in fall to encourage fresh growth, and avoid rich soil or regular irrigation, both of which shorten its already modest lifespan.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; broad beech fern spreads by shallow rhizomes to form loose, airy colonies that are attractive when naturalized under deciduous trees in moist, slightly shaded woodland settings.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; broad beech fern spreads rhizomatously to naturalize into a loose, open colony under trees. Phegopteris hexagonoptera is a native deciduous fern of eastern North American moist woodlands, producing wide, triangular fronds 15–24 inches long on slender stems — the distinctive triangular shape with the lowest pair of leaflets widely angled outward ('hexagonal' refers to the six-sided shape of the frond) makes it easy to identify among other native ferns. It is delicate in appearance but robust in growth, naturalizing readily in moist, shaded settings under deciduous trees to create an airy, fine-textured ground cover. The light green, somewhat thin fronds have a fresh, springtime appearance throughout the season and die back cleanly to the ground in fall.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil, including dry, poor, or rooty ground, in partial to full shade; broad-leaved butcher's broom spreads slowly by rhizomes and, unlike the common spiny butcher's broom, has soft, unarmed foliage safe to handle.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil, tolerant of dry, poor, or root-filled ground, in partial to full shade; broad-leaved butcher's broom is an unusual evergreen shade shrub whose apparent 'leaves' are actually flattened, leaf-like stems called cladodes, broader and softer than those of the common spiny butcher's broom (Ruscus aculeatus), and — unlike that spiny relative — pleasant and safe to handle. Tiny greenish flowers appear directly on the surface of the cladodes in late winter, and on female plants pollinated by a nearby male, these are followed by bright red berries that persist attractively through much of the year. It tolerates deep, dry shade under mature trees better than almost any broadleaf shrub, spreading slowly by rhizomes into a low, dense, glossy-textured colony that needs essentially no maintenance once established. A useful, unusual evergreen for the most difficult dry shade in a woodland or shade garden, valued by flower arrangers for its long-lasting cut foliage.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions inside a buried rhizome barrier in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this running bamboo spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes and needs physical containment in any garden setting.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions inside a buried rhizome barrier in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this running bamboo spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes and needs physical containment in any garden setting. Thick, upright canes carry unusually broad, glossy, deep-green leaves up to a foot long that bleach an attractive straw color at the margins in winter, giving the clump a bold, coarse, tropical texture unlike typical fine-leaved bamboos. It is one of the most shade-tolerant bamboos available and colonizes dry shade, deep shade under trees, and difficult slopes where turf and most groundcovers fail, making it useful for erosion control or as a dense screen in problem shaded sites — but only where its spread can be fully contained. Cut old canes to the ground in late winter to refresh the clump and control height.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall immediately after collection for natural warm-then-cold stratification over winter; seeds require a period of warm followed by cold moist stratification to break dormancy, and germination may be slow and uneven over the first spring and into the second year — patience is essential.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall as soon as it is collected, as broad-leaved linden requires a sequential warm then cold stratification period to break its compound dormancy; germination is slow and may extend into the second spring, so mark the planting site carefully and keep it weed-free. Plant in deep, fertile, moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, where the tree will develop a stately, broadly domed crown reaching 60 feet or more at maturity. In early summer the tree produces hanging clusters of fragrant creamy-yellow flowers along winged bracts that attract bees in enormous numbers — broad-leaved linden is considered one of the most important bee-forage trees in European temperate forestry and produces a prized light honey. Harvest flower clusters when fully open but before they begin to brown and dry them quickly in a warm, airy space; the dried flowers (tilleul) brew into a delicate, mildly sedative herbal tea with a long tradition in French and central European folk medicine.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; broad-leaved toad lily blooms earlier in summer than most Tricyrtis species and its arching stems benefit from the support of nearby ferns or shrubs.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; broad-leaved toad lily blooms earlier in summer than most Tricyrtis species and its arching stems benefit from the support of nearby ferns or shrubs. Tricyrtis latifolia is an East Asian woodland species with broad, glossy, clasping leaves along arching stems, topped and lined along the upper leaf axils with clusters of pale yellow flowers heavily speckled with purple-brown spots in early to midsummer, earlier than most other toad lilies bloom. Its early flowering extends the toad lily season in a shaded border, pairing well with later-blooming Tricyrtis hirta selections for a longer overall display. Give it consistent moisture and rich soil, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of wet, muck, or saturated soil in partial shade to full sun; soft rush requires light for germination — do not cover seed. Alternatively, plant divisions in spring. Grows naturally in marshes, pond edges, wet meadows, and roadside ditches throughout North America.
directions: Plant in wet to saturated, mucky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun at the edges of ponds, streams, and rain gardens; soft rush is one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important wetland plants in the world, native throughout North America, Europe, and Asia. The cylindrical, medium-green stems are leafless — photosynthesis occurs through the stem surface — and the small, brown flower clusters emerge from the side of each stem near the tip. The stems were historically used for basket weaving, rush matting, tallow-soaked rush lights, and chair seat weaving — uses that persist in traditional crafts today. In the garden, soft rush is an essential component of constructed wetlands, bioswales, and naturalistic pond margins, providing year-round architectural interest with its vertical, cylindrical stems and supporting numerous wetland invertebrates and nesting birds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; broadleaf stonecrop tolerates both rocky outcrop conditions and light shade better than many sun-loving sedums.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; broadleaf stonecrop tolerates both rocky outcrop conditions and light shade better than many sun-loving sedums. Flat, powdery, blue-gray to silvery rosettes, often blushed purple-red in bright light, spread into a dense, low mat studded with bright yellow, star-shaped flower clusters in late spring, native to rock outcrops, cliffs, and thin forest soils along the Pacific Coast from California to British Columbia. Its natural tolerance for both sun and partial shade sets it apart from many other native sedums, making it a versatile groundcover for a rock garden, green roof planting, or the thin soil at the base of established trees. Water only occasionally once established, and divide congested mats to propagate or refresh an aging planting.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring in dry to moist, calcium-rich, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; broadleaf woodland sedge is adapted to rocky, calcareous (limestone-derived) forest floors and also grows in more neutral upland forests throughout its range.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; broadleaf woodland sedge is one of the most distinctive native shade sedges of the eastern United States, notable for its unusually wide, almost ribbon-like leaf blades that are significantly broader than other shade sedges — an immediately recognizable trait at close range. The foliage is an attractive blue-green to glaucous color, adding a cool, pale note to the shade garden. It grows naturally on rocky, calcium-rich forest floors associated with limestone or calcareous soils in rich mesic woodlands. Extremely shade tolerant and drought resistant once established — a rare combination that makes it an outstanding low-maintenance groundcover under dense mature tree canopies where both shade and summer drought are challenging. Excellent with other dry-shade natives like wild ginger and Solomon's seal.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring or early fall while soil is workable.
directions: Set this narrow, columnar juniper in full sun and well-drained soil; it tolerates poor, dry, and rocky ground once established. Space plants at least 5 feet apart when used as a screen so the slender pyramidal form fills in without crowding. Water regularly the first year to establish deep roots, then reduce watering as it becomes quite drought-tolerant. Its dense evergreen foliage holds green year-round, making it a reliable windbreak or accent needing almost no pruning.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; soak seed to speed germination.
directions: 'Broken Colors' four o'clock delights with mottled and bicolored tubular flowers in shifting shades, no two blooms alike, carrying a lilac-and-jasmine fragrance. Soak the large seed to speed germination and direct sow after the last frost in full sun to part shade. Grow in average, well-drained soil with moderate water. The flowers open in the late afternoon and evening, perfuming the garden, and attract hawk moths and hummingbirds. In cold zones the plants form tubers that can be dug and stored, or grown fresh from seed each year.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full to partial shade; brome-like sedge grows naturally in wooded swamps and wet depressions and is useful for stabilizing consistently soggy, shaded ground.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; brome-like sedge is a native wetland woodland sedge with fine, grass-like, arching foliage forming loose tufts, naturally found in wooded swamps, seasonally flooded depressions, and the muddy margins of woodland streams. It tolerates standing water for extended periods and thrives in the kind of consistently soggy, shaded ground where lawn grass and many perennials fail outright, making it useful for stabilizing soil at the edge of a rain garden basin, drainage swale, or low spot in a wooded yard. Established plantings spread modestly and need little care beyond reliable moisture. It provides valuable habitat and forage for wetland wildlife while requiring no fertilizer, mowing, or other routine maintenance once settled.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil under high open-canopy shade, mimicking its native New Zealand beech-forest floor habitat.
directions: Unlike its more sun-exposed relative Astelia chathamica, this species grows naturally as a true forest-floor plant beneath New Zealand native canopy and is genuinely happy in full shade. Bronze-to-olive, finely nerved arching foliage forms a graceful fountain-shaped clump that pairs well with ferns and hostas in a shaded woodland bed. Keep soil consistently moist but well drained, and mulch the crown in colder parts of its range to protect it from hard freezes.

common_name: Bronze Beauty Ajuga (Classic Glossy Coppery-Bronze Bugleweed)
plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile soil in full shade to part shade; Bronze Beauty is a classic ajuga selection with glossy, coppery-bronze foliage and blue flower spikes, distinct from tricolor and near-black ajuga cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to part shade; ajuga is one of the most reliable and ornamental groundcovers for shaded areas under trees and along shaded borders. Bronze Beauty is a classic, long-cultivated ajuga selection bearing glossy, rounded leaves in a rich, uniform coppery-bronze, a simpler, more solid-colored counterpart to the mottled tricolor and near-black ajuga cultivars more recently introduced, topped in spring by short spikes of deep blue flowers. It spreads by stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat that tolerates foot traffic reasonably well and thrives in the dry shade beneath established trees where turf grass struggles. Divide and thin congested patches every few years to maintain vigor and prevent crown rot in overly wet or crowded conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in rich, humusy, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give regular water through summer to keep the glossy evergreen foliage from scorching, and cut back old flower spikes in late summer.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in rich, humusy, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give regular water through summer to keep the glossy evergreen foliage from scorching, and cut back old flower spikes in late summer. Beesia deltophylla is a Chinese woodland evergreen forming a slowly spreading clump of glossy, deltoid, heart-shaped leaves that emerge with a distinct bronze cast before deepening to rich glossy green, topped in mid to late spring by slender spires of small white flowers held well above the foliage. Its lustrous, weather-resistant leaves make it a handsome year-round groundcover or path edging in a shaded garden, pairing well with hellebores, hardy ferns, and other Asian woodland perennials that share its preference for humus-rich, evenly moist soil. It is deer resistant and largely untroubled by pests, needing only an annual mulch and division every several years once clumps become congested.

common_name: Bronze Elegance Chrysanthemum (Hardy Warm-Bronze Button Mum)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Bronze Elegance is a hardy button-type garden chrysanthemum long grown as a genuinely perennial fall-blooming mum rather than a disposable florist pot mum.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to encourage bushy, well-budded growth rather than tall, floppy stems. Bronze Elegance bears small, densely packed button flowers in a warm, coppery bronze that pairs naturally with the oranges and golds of the autumn garden, opening over a long stretch from early to mid fall. As a true garden-hardy chrysanthemum it returns reliably for years and slowly bulks up into a substantial clump, unlike short-lived florist mums bred purely for pot sales. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and floriferous.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Bronze Peacock arose as a tissue-culture mutation of Rodgersia pinnata 'Ideal' and has the darkest foliage of any rodgersia cultivar, though it needs more shade and moisture in the Gulf South than in cooler climates to avoid leaf scorch.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, along a pond edge or in a damp woodland bed; Bronze Peacock is grown primarily for its foliage, producing large, glossy, deeply bronze-brown palmate leaves that are the darkest of any rodgersia cultivar available, standing out dramatically against greener shade-garden companions. In summer it sends up plumes of small pink flowers above the foliage, similar to an astilbe, but the bronze leaves remain the main attraction through the season. It needs reliably moist, even boggy soil to perform well and will scorch or wilt in dry conditions, so a spot near a water feature or low, damp corner of the garden suits it best. In hot Southern climates give it more shade than the mostly-sun exposure it tolerates further north, since intense summer sun combined with humidity stress can damage the foliage.

plant_note: Start indoors; surface sow, needs light to germinate.
directions: 'Bronze Queen' brings warm, smoky bronze-toned trumpet flowers and a captivating evening fragrance to borders and cottage gardens. Start seed indoors and surface sow, pressing it in lightly since the fine seed needs light to germinate. Grow in full sun to part shade in rich, well-drained soil kept evenly moist. The elegant blooms perfume the garden in the evening and attract pollinators and hummingbirds. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the plants blooming through the warm season.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Rodgersia podophylla has the most striking bronze spring foliage coloring of all the rodgersias and is best sited where the morning sun or a dappled canopy reveals this emerging bronze coloring — deep full shade suppresses the bronze tones.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; bronze shield rodgersia is a Japanese and Korean shade perennial with the most architecturally dramatic foliage of all the rodgersias — the large, hand-shaped, palmate leaves with five to nine toothed, glossy leaflets open in spring in a vivid bronze to copper-brown coloring, gradually transitioning through the season to bright green, then returning to bronze, copper, and red tints in autumn. The bronze coloring intensifies in spring and fall when the plant receives some sunlight; deep shade suppresses the coloring but the large, architectural foliage remains handsome throughout. Tall, creamy-white, astilbe-like flower plumes are produced in midsummer well above the foliage. Rodgersia podophylla forms slowly spreading colonies by thick, creeping rhizomes and is best suited to permanently moist, partly shaded positions beside water, in wet woodland gardens, or in rain gardens where the rhizomes can spread unimpeded. The large-scale combination of bold architectural foliage and tall summer flowers makes it one of the most impressive large shade garden perennials available.

common_name: Bronzeschleier Tufted Hair Grass (Bronze-Tinted Flower Panicles)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Bronzeschleier bears bronze-tinted flower panicles rising above a dark green foliage mound.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; tufted hair grass tolerates more shade than most ornamental grasses, an unusual and valuable trait in the genus. Bronzeschleier, German for 'bronze veil,' sends up an airy haze of flower panicles tinted warm bronze rather than the pure gold of related cultivars, rising above a tidy mound of dark green, fine-textured foliage for a subtler, warmer-toned display. Its shade tolerance and delicate flower display make it a good choice for a woodland-edge border or partly shaded mixed planting. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.

plant_note: Surface-sow seed in fall directly onto moist, calcareous, sandy or mucky soil at the water's edge without covering (seed requires light for germination); brook lobelia seed is tiny and needs moisture and cold stratification to germinate reliably — fall sowing in a permanently moist spot along a stream bank, limestone seep, or pond margin allows natural stratification and spring germination; do not allow the seedbed to dry out at any point.
directions: Plant in consistently wet, calcareous to neutral, sandy or peaty soil in partial sun to light shade; brook lobelia is a small, delicate native perennial of limestone fens, calcareous seeps, wet meadows, and stream banks across boreal and northern North America from Newfoundland to British Columbia south to New Jersey and the Great Lakes region — it inhabits some of the most specialized and ecologically sensitive wetland habitats on the continent, particularly calcium-rich fens and spring seeps where few other wildflowers can compete. Despite its diminutive stature of 6–12 inches, it is an exquisite plant when in bloom from June through August, producing a loose raceme of sky-blue, two-lipped flowers on wiry, leafy stems that emerge from a basal rosette of small, spoon-shaped leaves; the flowers are structurally identical to the more familiar great blue lobelia (L. siphilitica) but in miniature, with the same characteristic slit in the upper petals and protruding anther column. Lobelia kalmii is named in honor of Pehr Kalm, the Finnish-Swedish botanist and student of Linnaeus who traveled extensively in North America from 1748 to 1751 and collected many of the specimens that became the basis for Linnaeus's descriptions of North American plants; it is one of the most cold-hardy lobelias, surviving the deep winters of USDA Zone 2. It is best suited to naturalistic wet garden settings such as bog gardens, wet meadow margins, and the edges of naturalistic ponds and streams where it can colonize moist, calcareous soils with minimal competition, and is smaller and more refined in appearance than either L. siphilitica or L. cardinalis.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; brook saxifrage grows naturally along shaded, cool mountain stream banks and spray zones of waterfalls in the southern Appalachians, requiring consistent moisture and cool root temperatures.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, cool, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade alongside streams, water features, and seepy areas; brook saxifrage is an Appalachian endemic of shaded mountain stream banks, spray zones, and seepage areas in the southern Appalachian Mountains, where it grows in constantly moist, cool, shaded conditions near running water. The deeply palmately lobed, maplelike leaves resemble small monkshood (Aconitum) leaves — giving the species its epithet — and are attractive throughout the growing season. Loose panicles of small white flowers rise above the foliage in early summer. Requires consistent soil moisture and will not tolerate drought or heat; in zone 7 and warmer, site in the deepest, coolest shade available with consistent moisture from a water feature or seep. Excellent for naturalistic stream-side or water garden plantings in mountain gardens and cool-climate shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; brook wakerobin is the smallest North American trillium and is best grown in a raised bed, trough, or rock garden where drainage and scale can be closely managed.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; brook wakerobin is the smallest North American trillium and is best grown in a raised bed, trough, or rock garden where drainage and scale can be closely managed. Trillium rivale is a diminutive, highly prized Pacific Northwest species native to streamside seeps in the Siskiyou Mountains, producing tiny mottled or plain green leaves and delicate white to pale pink flowers, often finely speckled with purple-red spots, in early spring. Its jewel-like scale and refined flower make it one of the most sought-after trilliums among alpine and woodland plant collectors, though it demands sharper drainage than most trilliums while still needing consistent moisture during the growing season — a balance best achieved in a raised, gritty, humus-amended bed. Source stock only from reputable nurseries propagating from seed or division, never from wild-collected plants, since natural populations are limited and slow to recover from collection.

common_name: Brookside Hardy Geranium (Clear Blue Finely Cut Cranesbill)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Brookside bears very finely dissected, almost fern-like foliage and clear sky-blue flowers over a long summer season.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in hot climates. Brookside produces clear, true sky-blue flowers with a small white eye over finely cut, almost lacy, fern-like foliage that gives the whole plant a soft, airy texture different from the coarser leaves of many hardy geranium cultivars. It flowers over a long season from late spring into summer, with a light shearing after the first flush encouraging repeat bloom and fresh foliage. Its billowing, slightly sprawling habit works well tumbling over the edge of a border or path, and it combines nicely with yellow- or chartreuse-foliaged companions for color contrast. It tolerates heat and some drought once established, and dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring keeps the plant vigorous.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into lean, acidic, excessively well-drained sandy soil in full sun; use only nursery-propagated plants since natural populations are globally rare.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into lean, acidic, excessively well-drained sandy soil in full sun, reproducing the coastal heathlands and pine barrens from Newfoundland to New Jersey where this rare, fire-adapted shrub grows alongside bearberry and lowbush blueberry. Its needle-like evergreen foliage and inconspicuous, wind-pollinated flowers in earliest spring give it a heath-like texture that fills a distinct niche in a dry, sandy native planting. Because natural populations are globally rare and disturbance-dependent, use only nursery-propagated plants and avoid rich or moisture-retentive soils that this dune and barrens specialist will not tolerate.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in poor, dry, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; broomsedge thrives in neglected, nutrient-poor conditions that most plants cannot tolerate — it is a pioneer species that colonizes disturbed soils and old fields and should not be planted in fertile garden beds where it will be outcompeted.
directions: Broomsedge bluestem is one of the most common and ecologically important native grasses of the American South — the first grass to colonize old fields, roadsides, and disturbed land, where its upright copper-bronze clumps create the characteristic tawny winter landscape of fallow farmland across the Gulf Coastal Plain and Piedmont. While often dismissed as a 'weed grass' in agricultural contexts because it indicates overgrazed or impoverished soil, broomsedge provides critical winter habitat: the dry, papery clumps shelter overwintering quail coveys, song sparrows, and small mammals, and its seeds are consumed by field sparrows, grasshopper sparrows, and many other birds through fall and winter. In ecological restoration and native meadow projects, broomsedge functions as a pioneer species that stabilizes disturbed soils and builds organic matter as a precursor to diverse plant communities; it also provides excellent visual interest in naturalized areas where its orange-copper fall and winter color creates a warm, burnished landscape texture. Combine with native wildflowers like goldenrods, asters, and ironweeds in dry, sunny meadow restorations.

plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Brother Stefan is a giant-class hosta needing significant room to reach full size over several seasons.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing generous room since this is a giant-class hosta that takes several years to reach its full mature spread. Brother Stefan bears huge, heavily corrugated, bright chartreuse-gold leaves that brighten a shaded bed and hold their color well into summer before mellowing slightly, with pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer providing a secondary, minor season of interest. Its large scale makes it an effective anchor or focal specimen in a woodland or shade border, best given room to spread without crowding from smaller companions. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on the tender new growth in spring, and expect the plant to need several growing seasons before it reaches its full impressive size.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to part shade; brown boronia is notoriously difficult to cultivate successfully outside its native coastal heathland habitat — demanding perfect drainage, cool root conditions, and the precise soil chemistry of Western Australian coastal peat-sand. Grafted plants on Correa rootstocks improve reliability. Short-lived (5–8 years) but produces intense fragrance. Worth attempting for its unparalleled scent. The flower extract has been used commercially in perfumery.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to part shade; brown boronia is legendary among Australian garden enthusiasts for producing one of the most intensely beautiful, complex, and powerful floral fragrances of any plant in the world — a rich, warm, spicy-floral scent with fruity undertones that has been compared to a combination of roses, sweet peas, and anise, extraordinarily powerful from a single small shrub and impossible to ignore in the garden. The fragrance of Boronia megastigma is considered by perfumers and garden writers to be among the finest natural plant scents, and commercial extraction of boronia fragrance compounds has been used in perfumery for over a century. The flowers themselves are small, pendant, four-petaled, in a distinctive two-tone coloring: dark, brownish-red to mahogany on the outside (giving the common name 'brown boronia') with bright yellow-green on the inside, hanging in clusters from the fine, dark-green, needle-leaved branches in spring. The visual effect is quiet and understated — but the fragrance transforms every garden space within range. Notoriously demanding in cultivation outside its native coastal peat heaths of Western Australia, but the reward of its fragrance for those who succeed is without peer.

common_name: Brown's Anthurium (Giant Velvet Leaf Anthurium, Large-Veined Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow in deep to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky aroid mix; Anthurium brownii is a very large velvet anthurium from Costa Rica and Colombia with leaves that can reach 36–48 inches in mature specimens — among the most imposing of the ornamental velvet anthuriums in terms of leaf size. The dark, blue-green to forest-green leaves have a noticeable velvety texture from surface papillae and the primary veins are paler, creating a subtle lighter-on-dark pattern. A slow-growing but very long-lived specimen plant for tropical shade gardens. Requires warm (above 60°F), humid conditions. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in deep shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, chunky aroid mix with consistently warm temperatures and high humidity — Brown's Anthurium is one of the most impressively large of the velvet anthurium species, eventually producing immense leaves in warm, stable conditions that rival A. regale in scale.
