Anthurium brownii is a climbing, hemiepiphytic anthurium in the Araceae family native to Costa Rica, Panama, and northwestern Colombia — a member of the section Cardiolonchium (velvet anthuriums) alongside A. crystallinum, A. regale, A. magnificum, and A. warocqueanum. Named in honor of N.E. Brown, a botanist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. The plant produces large, broadly cordate (heart-shaped) leaves that can reach 36–48 inches or more in well-established, mature specimens — placing it among the largest-leaved of the velvet anthuriums. The leaf surface is dark, saturated forest-green to blue-green, with a distinctly matte, velvety texture from the papillate (bumped) epidermal surface characteristic of the section. The primary veins (midrib and main lateral veins) are paler — silvery-green to yellowish-green — creating a moderately contrasting pattern of lighter veins on the dark ground that is less dramatically high-contrast than A. regale or A. magnificum but elegant in the subdued, refined manner appropriate to deep-shade foliage. A magnificent, slow-growing specimen plant for tropical shade gardens and large-scale interior spaces. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost date or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier for bloom the first season.
directions: Press seeds onto moist soil surface or cover very lightly; they need light to germinate and germinate readily in 7–14 days. Unlike Rudbeckia hirta, R. triloba is a true biennial-to-short-lived-perennial that produces abundant small golden-yellow flowers with a dark center from midsummer through hard frost. Plant in full sun to partial shade in average garden soil; plants self-sow prolifically and naturalize easily in meadow and prairie plantings. Deadhead some stems to extend the season and let others set seed to perpetuate the colony.

common_name: Brozzonii Magnolia (Very Large Nearly-White Late-Blooming Saucer Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Brozzonii is a late-blooming saucer magnolia cultivar whose delayed flowering helps its enormous blooms dodge late frost damage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Brozzonii produces some of the largest flowers of any saucer magnolia cultivar, goblet-shaped and nearly white with only a faint pink flush at the base, opening on bare branches before the leaves emerge. It blooms noticeably later than 'Alexandrina' and most other saucer magnolias, a valuable trait that lets its flowers largely escape the late hard freezes that regularly damage earlier-opening cultivars. The tree grows into a broad, multi-stemmed small tree with minimal pruning needs beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Brunette performs best in cool to moderate summer conditions and is most reliably perennial in zones 4–7; in zone 8, site in the coolest, most shaded location available with consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Brunette (formerly classified as Cimicifuga simplex 'Brunette') is one of the most spectacular and coveted dark-leaved shade perennials — producing deeply divided, compound leaves in a rich, deep brownish-purple to nearly black color that creates an extraordinary dark foliage mass in the shade garden unmatched by any other commonly available hardy perennial. The dramatic dark foliage emerges in spring as deep bronze-purple, deepens to near-black through summer, and provides four months of bold foliage texture before the tall, wand-like flower racemes (4–6 feet) of pure white to pinkish-white fragrant flowers appear in fall. The combination of the dark foliage and white flowers creates an extraordinary contrast — the white flowers appearing to glow above the near-black leaf mass. The flowers are fragrant, adding an unexpected sensory dimension to this primarily foliage-focused plant. Brunette performs best in zones 3–7 where summer temperatures are moderate; zone 8 gardeners can succeed with careful siting in the shadiest, coolest, most consistently moist positions available. In zone 9, Brunette is a challenging plant that may succeed in very sheltered positions with heavy shade and consistent irrigation but is not reliably perennial in the Gulf South heat without these specific conditions.

common_name: Brympton Red Dianthus (Heritage Deep Red Garden Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Brympton Red is an RHS-listed heritage garden pink with deep red flowers.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Brympton Red, a Royal Horticultural Society-listed heritage garden pink, bears deep, solid red flowers with the strong clove fragrance typical of the best garden pinks, opening over compact, evergreen blue-green foliage. Its rich, saturated color and heirloom pedigree make it a strong choice for a historic or cottage-garden border. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or late summer in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Buchanan's sage is damaged below about 25 degrees F and is best suited to zones 8-10. In zone 7 it can survive mild winters in sheltered positions. The flowers are very large for a salvia — 2 inches or more — and appear primarily in summer through fall. Hummingbirds are strongly attracted to the deep color and nectar.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; Buchanan's sage is a Mexican native producing some of the darkest, most intensely colored flowers in the genus — the very large, 2-inch tubular flowers are a deep, rich, ruby-magenta to dark cherry-red with a distinctive velvety sheen and a texture from the dense hairs on both corolla and calyx that makes the flowers appear almost jewel-like. Unusually large for a salvia flower, the individual blooms are arranged in open, airy clusters on upright stems from summer through frost. The rich, dark color is highly attractive to hummingbirds. As a compact perennial subshrub, it stays below 2-2.5 feet and is suitable for the front or middle of a sunny or partly shaded border in zones 8-10, or as a container specimen overwintered indoors in colder zones. Relatively rare compared to the common salvias but highly valued by gardeners who know it for its unusually large, darkly colored flowers.

common_name: Bucket Orchid (Large Helmet Orchid, Macrantha Coryanthes)
plant_note: Grow in a large, open slatted basket with coarse bark — Coryanthes macrantha produces pendant flower spikes that must emerge through the bottom of the basket; solid pots prevent blooming. High humidity (70–80%+) is essential. Water daily in active growth; reduce slightly in winter. Requires warm temperatures (65–85°F) year-round. The extraordinary 'bucket' mechanism requires no action by the grower — flowers self-function to trap and release bees for pollination, but in cultivation outside the orchid's native range, hand-pollination with a toothpick is needed for seed set. An advanced collector's orchid requiring attention to its specific cultural needs.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to shade in a large open slatted basket with high humidity — Bucket Orchid is a demanding, specialized orchid best suited to advanced collectors with greenhouse or high-humidity conditions. Coryanthes macrantha is an epiphytic orchid native to Venezuela, Colombia, Trinidad, and Tobago in the Orchidaceae family, belonging to one of the most scientifically celebrated genera in all of botany for possessing what may be the most elaborate and sophisticated pollination mechanism in the plant kingdom. The lip of the Coryanthes flower is modified into an actual functioning bucket structure: a water-collecting, cup-shaped depression at the base of the complex lip assembly, which fills with a liquid secreted by the two glands above it. Male orchid bees (Eulaema, Eufriesea species) are attracted to the flower by an irresistible fragrance compound that the bees collect for use in mating displays. While gathering this compound from the front of the flower, male bees invariably slip and fall into the liquid-filled bucket. The bee cannot fly in the wet liquid and must crawl along the inner bucket surface toward the only exit — a narrow tube-shaped passage at one end — where it must squeeze past the column, collecting pollinia on its back in the process. When the same bee visits another Coryanthes flower and falls into its bucket and crawls out, the pollinia are precisely deposited on the stigma. The entire mechanism has the precision of engineered machinery. One of the most remarkable evolutionary achievements in nature, now available for cultivation by dedicated orchid enthusiasts.

plant_note: Root calloused stem segments in spring in sharply draining cactus mix, watering only lightly until new growth confirms establishment.
directions: Root calloused stem segments in spring in sharply draining cactus mix, watering only lightly until new growth confirms establishment. Buckhorn cholla branches into an open, antler-like silhouette with tan to golden spines and produces bronze-orange or yellow flowers in late spring followed by spiny fruit. It is a structural focal point for desert landscapes and mixes well with palo verde or creosote as companion plantings. Keep it well back from paths, since the spiny joints detach easily and are painful to remove.

plant_note: Plant young, nursery-grown trees in fall in well-drained, limestone-based, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Buckley's oak is a calcicole (limestone lover) native to the Edwards Plateau and Cross Timbers — avoid clay, poorly drained, or highly acidic soils.
directions: Buckley's oak (also called Texas red oak) is a native tree of the limestone hills and rocky canyons of the Texas Hill Country, Edwards Plateau, and Cross Timbers region — the most important red-oak-type tree for autumn color in central Texas. In October and November, its deeply lobed leaves turn brilliant shades of orange-red, red, and scarlet — spectacular fall color unusual for the semi-arid Texas Hill Country where most oaks turn only dull brown or rust. Because it grows naturally on the shallow, rocky limestone soils and caliche of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau, it is better adapted to alkaline soils than most other red oaks in its group; it is one of the few native oaks that will tolerate the alkaline, calcium-rich soils common across central Texas that cause iron chlorosis in acid-adapted species. The medium-sized acorns are consumed by white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and scrub-jays, and the tree provides important larval host resources for hundreds of native Lepidoptera. Excellent choice for limestone-soil native landscapes in central Texas and the Oklahoma Cross Timbers.

plant_note: Plant in wet to moist, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; buckwheat tree is a wetland obligate native to pond margins, bogs, and bottomland swamps of the Gulf Coast Coastal Plain — keep roots consistently wet.
directions: Buckwheat tree is an evergreen native shrub or small tree of the Gulf Coastal Plain, forming dense thickets in bogs, bay swamps, and along black-water stream margins from South Carolina to eastern Texas — a dominant species in some Gulf Coast wetland plant communities known as 'titi bays.' In early spring, dense racemes of fragrant white to pinkish flowers smother the branches before the leaves fully emerge, providing critical early-season nectar for native bees, including honeybees, which produce a distinctively flavored 'titi honey' prized by beekeepers. The distinctive buckwheat-shaped winged fruits ripen in summer and persist into fall, giving the tree its common name. Grow at the margins of rain gardens, constructed wetlands, or low-lying acidic areas where the soil stays moist to wet — it forms a naturalistic thicket that provides excellent wildlife cover and spring pollinator support.

plant_note: Plant cuttings or container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, rich soil in partial shade to full sun; buckwheat vine grows naturally in moist to wet, alluvial, bottomland forests and swamp margins of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in naturalized settings along stream margins, pond edges, and moist woodland borders; buckwheat vine is a native vine of the southeastern US in the knotweed (Polygonaceae) family, producing distinctive, unusual fruit structures — each seed is enclosed in a winged, membranous structure resembling a miniature winged seed that aids wind dispersal, giving the plant an unusual ornamental quality in fruit. The white to cream flower clusters in summer attract bees and butterflies. In moist, shaded bottomland settings it can twine vigorously through shrubs and small trees, providing textural interest at the forest margin. An unusual and underappreciated native vine for naturalistic, moist woodland garden designs in zone 9a.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring; when grown in the ground with ample water and nutrients, the internodes stay long and the plant grows tall and straight — the characteristic swollen 'buddha belly' internodes develop when the plant is stressed by container culture, drought, or root restriction. Grow in a large pot or restrict roots for the ornamental belly effect.
directions: Plant in fertile soil in full sun in zones 8–12; Buddha belly bamboo is a clumping tropical bamboo from southern China celebrated for its unique ability to produce dramatically swollen, compressed internodes when grown under stress — in restricted containers, drought conditions, or with root confinement. These short, bulging internodes resemble the rounded belly of a laughing Buddha statue, making individual culms highly ornamental and used in the crafting of Buddha belly canes sold in craft stores. In the open garden with adequate water and nutrients, the plant grows tall and straight with normal internodes; the 'belly' effect requires deliberate stress through container culture or root restriction. A non-invasive clumping bamboo that stays within its allotted space, making it safer for garden use than running species.

common_name: Buddha Camellia (Giant Loose Peony-Form Rose-Red Reticulata Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Buddha is a historic Chinese reticulata camellia noted for producing some of the largest flowers of any camellia.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind. Buddha bears enormous, loose peony-form, rose-red blooms that can reach 7 inches across, among the largest flowers of any camellia, on an open, somewhat sprawling shrub that benefits from staking or support to keep the heavy blooms from weighing branches to the ground. Its sheer flower size makes it a dramatic specimen and exhibition camellia, blooming in mid-to-late winter into spring. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

common_name: Buddy Purple Gomphrena (Dwarf Purple Globe Amaranth)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Buddy Purple is a dwarf, compact gomphrena bred for uniform edging and bedding use.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; gomphrena thrives in heat and shrugs off drought once established. Buddy Purple is a compact selection of globe amaranth bearing small, clover-like, rich purple flower heads in dense abundance on tidy, uniform mounds, making it a reliable choice for edging, mass bedding, and containers where taller gomphrena would sprawl. The papery flower heads hold their color for months in the garden and dry beautifully for everlasting arrangements when cut and hung upside down. It blooms non-stop from early summer through frost with no deadheading required and needs little beyond occasional watering during extended dry spells.

common_name: Buff Beauty Hybrid Musk Rose (Fragrant Apricot-Buff Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Buff Beauty is a fragrant, apricot-buff hybrid musk shrub rose that tolerates a bit of shade.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hybrid musk roses tolerate more shade than most rose classes, blooming reasonably well with just a half-day of direct sun. Buff Beauty bears large clusters of double, warm apricot-buff blooms that soften as they age, with a strong, musky-sweet fragrance and coppery new foliage that adds color even before the flowers open. The lax, spreading shrub repeats bloom well through the growing season and can be trained as a short climber against a wall or fence for extra height. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through summer to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Buff Beauty Rose (Apricot-Buff Hybrid Musk Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Buff Beauty is a 1939 English hybrid musk rose valued for warm apricot-buff clustered blooms, strong fragrance, and better tolerance of part shade than most roses.
directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 4-6 feet apart to allow for its broad, spreading habit. Bred by Ann Bentall and introduced in England in 1939, Buff Beauty is a hybrid musk rose bearing large clusters of warm apricot-buff, fully double blooms with a strong, sweet musk fragrance, aging to a soft cream as they open. As a hybrid musk, it is more shade-tolerant than most roses, flowering respectably with as little as four to five hours of direct sun, which makes it useful in gardens where a fully open, all-day-sun spot isn't available. The lax, arching canes can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber against a wall or fence, and the plant blooms in flushes from late spring through fall with good resistance to blackspot. Prune back by about a third in late winter if grown as a shrub, or simply thin out old wood if trained as a climber, since Buff Beauty flowers on both old and new growth.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in early spring.
directions: Buffalo Clover is a native annual or biennial clover of dry to moderately moist, open, disturbed ground throughout the eastern and central US, historically associated with bison grazing lands and open forest clearings. It produces showy bicolored flower heads — creamy-white banner petals contrasting with pink to red wing petals — making it among the most ornamental of the native US clovers, blooming in spring and early summer. Direct sow in fall into average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; it tolerates moderate soil fertility and self-sows in open, disturbed ground, providing nectar for bumblebees and small native bees.

common_name: Buffalo Gal Rugosa Rose (Low, Spreading Pink Ground Cover Rugosa Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; Buffalo Gal is a low, spreading rugosa hybrid useful as a tough, drought-tolerant ground cover.
directions: Plant in average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; the low, wide-spreading habit makes it useful as a tough, drought-tolerant flowering ground cover on slopes or in difficult sandy sites. Buffalo Gal bears single to semi-double, deep pink blooms with a light fragrance in repeated flushes through the growing season, on a low, dense, rugosa-type shrub that inherits the parent species' outstanding disease resistance and salt tolerance. Its spreading form works well cascading over a low wall or covering a sunny bank. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood and maintain shape, since rugosa-type roses resent hard pruning.

plant_note: Install plugs or sod in spring once soil has warmed to at least 60°F; space plugs 12–18 inches apart and water consistently through the first season to establish deep roots.
directions: Install plugs or sod sections in spring into well-drained, full-sun soil, spacing plugs 12–18 inches apart; plugs will spread via stolons to fill gaps within one to two growing seasons. Once established, this fine-bladed native grass of the Great Plains requires minimal irrigation, surviving and thriving on natural rainfall across most of its range, though an occasional deep watering during extended drought maintains better color and density. Mow once or twice per season to 3–4 inches if a tidy appearance is desired, or leave unmowed for a naturalistic, soft-textured meadow effect; the blue-green foliage turns a warm straw color during winter dormancy and greens up reliably each spring. Avoid heavy foot traffic during dormancy and do not over-fertilize, as excess nitrogen encourages weeds and diminishes the natural competitive advantage of this adapted native.

plant_note: Sow after last frost once soil consistently warms to 65°F; use cold-treated (stratified) seed for better germination. Plugs and sod are faster than seed for establishing.
directions: Sow cold-treated seed in full sun after soil warms to 65°F in lean, clay to loam, alkaline to neutral soil; buffalograss is the most drought-tolerant of the true lawn grasses, the historical turf of the Great Plains that once covered millions of acres, and it requires one-tenth the water of Kentucky bluegrass. The soft, curly, blue-green blades stay short (3–5 inches) without mowing and go dormant tan in winter. It establishes slowly from seed (use plugs or sod for faster coverage) and will not tolerate acidic soil, heavy shade, or heavy foot traffic. It is dioecious — plant a mix of male and female seed or use non-seeding cultivars for a tidier appearance.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; bugbane grows slowly but becomes very long-lived once established — choose the permanent site with care.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; bugbane (formerly Cimicifuga) is one of the finest tall shade perennials, producing elegant, towering wands of tiny, fragrant white to cream flowers in late summer and fall, rising 4–7 feet above bold, deeply divided compound leaves. Dark-leaved selections like 'Brunette' (chocolate-purple foliage) and 'Hillside Black Beauty' provide dramatic contrast against lighter companions throughout the season. Plants are extremely long-lived and resent transplanting once established — grow in the same spot for decades. The subtle, sweet fragrance of the flowers carries on the evening air. Divide very carefully in early spring only when absolutely necessary.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted runners in spring or fall; plants spread by stolons and will fill in quickly — space 6–12 inches apart for coverage within one growing season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, though ajuga tolerates more sun in cooler climates; it spreads by surface stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing carpet topped by spikes of blue-violet flowers in spring. The low, rosette foliage comes in a range of colors from deep burgundy-bronze ('Caitlin's Giant', 'Burgundy Glow') to chocolate-purple, making it one of the most ornamentally versatile shade groundcovers. In hot, humid climates, crown rot can strike dense stands — improve air circulation by thinning plants if rot appears. Mow lightly after flowering to remove old spikes and encourage a tidier rosette. Spreads aggressively; install edging to keep it out of lawns.

plant_note: Mount on bark, driftwood, or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; bulb air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering.
directions: Mount on bark, driftwood, or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; bulb air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering. A distinctive, bulbous, onion-like base of tightly curled, silvery-green, twisting leaves gives this small epiphyte an almost octopus-like or squid-like appearance unlike the straighter, more open forms of many other air plants, with a spike of small violet flowers emerging from bright red bracts when mature. Native to Central American and Caribbean forests, where it grows perched on tree branches absorbing moisture and nutrients through specialized leaf scales, it thrives with a thorough soak or misting two to three times a week followed by good air circulation to dry the base and prevent rot. Provide bright, filtered light rather than direct sun, and remove the mother plant's offsets (pups) once they reach about half the parent's size to propagate.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to average soil in full sun; bulbine is extremely drought-tolerant once established and actually declines with excessive watering — in the Gulf South, it performs best in raised beds, rock gardens, and other well-drained positions where it receives no supplemental irrigation after the first growing season.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained to dry, sandy to average soil in full sun; bulbine is a South African succulent perennial that has earned a devoted following in Gulf Coast and Southwestern gardens for its exceptional combination of long-season ornamental interest and rock-bottom water requirements — it grows as a spreading, mounding clump of narrow, soft, succulent, grayish-green leaves and through most of the warm season produces slender, upright stems topped with elongated, loose racemes of small, bright-yellow to orange-yellow, six-petaled flowers with distinctive, fluffy, yellow-and-orange, brush-like stamen tufts that are the genus's trademark feature. 'Hallmark' is the most widely sold selection, with warm-orange flowers. The plant blooms nearly continuously from spring through fall and is virtually maintenance-free once established. It is extremely drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and adaptable to poor, sandy soils, making it one of the most useful and underplanted perennials for xeriscape and low-water Gulf Coast gardens in zone 9–12. Light frosts may damage the foliage but established plants typically recover quickly.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, rocky, humus-rich, circumneutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; bulblet bladder fern naturally colonizes mossy rocks and cliff faces and benefits from a gritty, well-drained substrate even while needing consistent moisture.
directions: Cystopteris bulbifera is a delicate, deciduous native fern of eastern North American rocky, moist, shaded woodlands and cliff faces, producing finely dissected, lacy, narrowly triangular fronds on long, pale-pink to rosy stipes that arch gracefully and often drape over rocky outcrops; its most distinctive feature is the small, pea-sized bulblets that form on the undersides of fronds, especially near the midrib, which drop to the ground and develop into new plants, giving the colony a gently self-spreading character over time. It prefers moist, humus-rich, rocky soils with good drainage and a circumneutral to slightly alkaline pH — often found on limestone cliffs and talus slopes — and is an excellent choice for shaded rock gardens, crevice walls, and naturalizing over boulders in zones 3–8. Its extraordinarily delicate, lacy texture contrasts beautifully with bold-leafed shade plants such as hostas and large-leafed trilliums. In warm weather the fronds may go summer-dormant if conditions become dry; consistent moisture extends the growing season.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered sun in fall; bulbous adder's-tongue is the smallest and earliest-emerging of the Gulf Coast adder's-tongue ferns, common in damp lawns, moist pastures, and open sandy woods from the Carolinas to Texas.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered sun in fall; bulbous adder's-tongue is the tiniest member of its genus in the region, its single small, rounded, undivided blade barely an inch or two tall arising each winter from a small underground bulb-like stem, with a short fertile spike beside it bearing a row of spore cases. It appears briefly in the cool, wet season in damp lawns, moist sandy pastures, and open pine woods across the Gulf and South Atlantic coastal plain, then withers away by late spring, making it easy to overlook among grass and low groundcover. Like other adder's-tongues it relies on a long-term underground mycorrhizal relationship, so newly planted crowns take time to settle in and should not be disturbed once sited. Best suited to a damp, lightly shaded corner of a native lawn alternative or woodland-edge planting where its brief winter appearance can be enjoyed up close.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, rocky, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; bullgrass is native to rocky limestone canyons, slopes, and dry woodlands of the Chihuahuan Desert region and is highly adapted to hot, dry, alkaline conditions — it is one of the best native grasses for rocky, well-drained sites in the Texas Hill Country and western Texas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky to sandy, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; once established, bullgrass requires no supplemental irrigation. Muhlenbergia emersleyi (bullgrass or bull muhly) is a large, robust, clump-forming native grass of the Chihuahuan Desert and trans-Pecos Texas — one of the largest muhly grasses, producing dense, fountain-like clumps of coarse, flat, dark-green leaves 18–36 inches long and towering, feathery, purple-tinged flower plumes 4–6 feet tall in late summer and fall. While the related Gulf muhly (M. capillaris) is more widely known for its cloud of fine-textured, pink-purple fall plumes, bullgrass is larger-growing and adapted to drier, more alkaline, rocky conditions of the Trans-Pecos and Edwards Plateau. The large, showy plumes are effective in the autumn landscape for 4–6 weeks. The clumps are long-lived and provide year-round structural interest with their bold, arching leaf texture. Like all muhly grasses, bullgrass requires excellent drainage and lean soil — rich, wet soil causes it to flop and rot. An outstanding grass for hot, dry, rocky, western Texas-style landscapes.

common_name: Bullseye Mountain Laurel (White Flowers with Bold Maroon Ring Pattern)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Bullseye bears white flowers marked with a bold, distinct maroon ring pattern, one of the most strikingly patterned mountain laurel cultivars.
directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Bullseye bears white flowers marked with a bold, wide maroon ring encircling the inner petal surface, an especially strong, graphic patterning that stands out even from a distance, opening on the classic gnarled, sculptural evergreen shrub habit typical of the species. Its striking pattern makes it a strong specimen or woodland-border accent. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Transplant small clumps with intact rootball in moist, very acidic, humus-rich, cool soil in full shade in spring; bunchberry demands cold winters, cool summers, very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5), and consistent moisture — it fails rapidly in warm, dry, or alkaline conditions.
directions: Transplant clumps with rootball intact in moist, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, cool soil in full to partial shade in spring; bunchberry is a native boreal ground-layer plant that forms a carpet of tidy, four-leaved rosettes with four white bracts surrounding a central cluster of tiny flowers in late spring — structurally miniature versions of flowering dogwood flowers — followed by clusters of brilliant red berries in late summer that attract birds and are edible to humans (mild, mealy). It is one of the finest shade groundcovers in cold, acidic woodland gardens but is extremely particular about its requirements: cool summer temperatures, very acidic conditions, moist but not waterlogged soil, and at least a few months of hard winter cold. Spreads slowly by rhizomes in ideal conditions.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring or early fall in part shade to full sun, spacing closely if used as a lawn substitute or ground cover.
directions: Plant plugs or divisions in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil, choosing part shade in hot climates or full sun where summers are cooler and moisture is reliable. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to knit together into a fine-textured groundcover and tolerates occasional mowing, making it a low-maintenance substitute for turf in small areas. The narrow, powder-blue foliage forms dense, mounding tufts a few inches tall, giving borders, pathway edges, and shady lawn alternatives a cool blue color note through the growing season.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; bunny ears cactus is spineless but covered in fine, easily detached glochids that irritate skin, so handle with thick gloves or folded paper.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; bunny ears cactus is spineless but covered in fine, easily detached glochids that irritate skin, so handle with thick gloves or folded paper. Flattened, rounded, pale green pads studded with regularly spaced tufts of tiny golden-yellow glochids give the plant a charming polka-dot pattern, and new pads branch off in pairs from the top of older ones, loosely resembling a bunny's ears as the plant matures into a many-padded clump. Despite lacking true spines, the fine, barbed glochids detach at the slightest touch and embed painfully in skin, so this cactus is best displayed out of reach of curious hands, pets, and passing foot traffic. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide full sun for compact, well-spaced pad growth, and remove and root fallen pads to propagate.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors 6 weeks early.
directions: Bunny tails forms an upright fountain of charming, fluffy flower heads as soft as a real bunny's tail. Direct sow after frost or start indoors about six weeks early, in full sun to part shade. Grow in average, well-drained soil where it becomes very drought tolerant once established. It is easy to grow and excellent for the cutting garden, adding whimsy and texture wherever it is planted. The plumes dry beautifully for lasting arrangements and can be harvested before they fully mature.

plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; bupleurum tolerates light frost and performs best as a cool-season crop, bolting and losing quality in sustained summer heat.
directions: Sow in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun, thinning to 6-9 inches apart; bupleurum is a florist's staple grown not for showy petals but for its airy sprays of tiny, chartreuse-green flowers surrounded by leaf-like bracts of the same acid-green color, which pair with nearly any other cut flower and hold their fresh color for one to two weeks in a vase. The upright, branching stems and slender blue-green foliage add a light, textural, greenery-like presence to bouquets and arrangements without competing with bolder blooms. Like many cool-season umbellifers it bolts and declines in the heat of summer, so succession sow every three to four weeks in spring for a steady cutting supply, and expect a second flush from a fall sowing in mild climates. Harvest when most of the flower clusters on a stem have opened for the longest vase life.

plant_note: Plant young trees in fall in deep, moist to dry, well-drained to clay soil in full sun; bur oak is extraordinarily adaptable to a wide range of soils including alkaline clay but develops best in deep, moist, well-drained loam — plant small as the deep taproot resists transplanting.
directions: Bur oak is the most majestic and long-lived of all North American oaks — individual trees commonly live 400–600 years and may exceed 1,000 years on favorable sites, developing massive, deeply furrowed, corky trunks and broad, spreading crowns of great character and presence. The acorns are the largest produced by any North American oak, each nearly half-enclosed in a distinctive fringed, mossy cup that gives the species its alternate name 'mossycup oak' — these large, low-tannin acorns were the most important food item for many plains tribes, who harvested and processed them into flour. Bur oak's extraordinary drought resistance — the result of a massive taproot that may penetrate 14 feet in the first year — made it the tree that historically crossed the prairie/forest boundary into the Great Plains, creating the legendary prairie grove ecosystems that supported bison herds. Like all oaks, it supports hundreds of native Lepidoptera species as host plants and its acorn crops feed deer, turkeys, bears, woodpeckers, and dozens of other wildlife species. A tree to plant for future generations.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Burford is self-fruitful and produces abundant berries without a male pollinizer — a distinct advantage over most other landscape hollies.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Burford holly is one of the most commonly planted landscape hollies in the South — a large, dense, rounded to broadly mounding shrub reaching 8–15 feet tall with exceptionally glossy, dark-green foliage and notably reduced spines compared to the species (most leaves have only a single terminal spine rather than the species' four-five-spined leaves). This reduced spininess makes Burford far easier to work around than typical Chinese hollies. The outstanding feature that separates Burford from all other landscape hollies is its self-fruitfulness: female plants set abundant, large, bright-red berries every year without any male pollinizer plant nearby — a critical advantage in residential settings where only one plant will be grown. The red berries ripen in fall and typically persist through winter. Burford is adaptable to a wide range of soils and extremely heat-tolerant, performing reliably in Gulf Coast zone 9 without the summer stress that affects some hollies. A dwarf form ('Dwarf Burford Holly', Ilex cornuta 'Burfordii Nana') reaches 3–4 feet and is suitable for foundation plantings and low hedges. Prune in late winter or spring after berries have served their wildlife purpose.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; surface sow, needs light.
directions: Burgundy amaranth makes a dramatic backdrop in the flower garden with towering deep-red plumes and a bold presence in arrangements. Surface sow after the last frost in warm soil, pressing the fine seed in lightly since it needs light to germinate. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil where it tolerates heat and drought. About 105 days after sowing, beige, protein-rich grain forms in the plumes and can be cooked like rice. The tender young leaves are also edible cooked like spinach, and the plumes dry well for crafts.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; like other Gaillardia, Burgundy is short-lived in heavy, wet soil, so sharp drainage matters more than fertility for long-term survival.
directions: Burgundy is an older, long-grown Gaillardia selection valued for its unusually solid, deep wine-red ray petals, lacking the yellow tips typical of most blanket flower cultivars, which gives it a richer, more uniform color for a border or cutting garden. Like other Gaillardia x grandiflora selections it produces a long succession of single, daisy-form flowers with a domed central cone from late spring through fall, drawing bees and butterflies throughout the season, and its native prairie parentage gives it strong heat and drought tolerance. Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, and deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom, or leave some heads to set seed if self-sown volunteers are welcome in the bed.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs 8–12 inches apart in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Burgundy Glow develops its best tricolor coloration in partial shade with some morning sun — in deep shade the foliage may revert toward plain green.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Burgundy Glow is the most striking variegated ajuga cultivar — a tricolor selection producing leaves in a complex combination of green, creamy white, and deep burgundy-pink to rose-red in irregular patches and blotches across each leaf. The variable, irregular color pattern gives each leaf a unique, painterly appearance, and the overall effect of a mass planting is one of the most dramatic and colorful ground covers available for partial to full shade conditions. The tricolor foliage provides year-round ornamental interest — particularly striking in late winter and spring when the color is most intense — and combines beautifully with solid-foliage companions like hostas, ferns, and dark-leafed heucheras. In spring, short spikes of blue flowers add additional color above the tricolor carpet. The spreading, stoloniferous habit fills in to create a dense mat at 4–6 inches tall. Like all ajugas, Burgundy Glow spreads by runners and may eventually send shoots into adjacent lawn areas — edging the planting area with a physical root barrier or regular edge-trimming keeps the colony contained. Crown rot can affect ajuga in hot, humid conditions with poor air circulation; adequate spacing and well-drained soil prevent this problem in zone 9.

common_name: Burgundy Lace Japanese Painted Fern (Wine-Red Silver Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in partial to full shade; Japanese painted ferns develop their most vivid color in bright indirect light — deep shade reduces color intensity, while any direct sun bleaches and scorches the fronds.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Burgundy Lace is among the most dramatically colored Japanese painted fern cultivars — producing fronds with deep wine-red to burgundy coloration most intense along the midrib and central portions of each frond, contrasting with a pewter-silver overlay on the pinnae and a darker burgundy-green at the margins. The three-color combination of silver, wine-red, and dark green creates an extraordinary foliage texture effect that has no equivalent among hardy shade ferns. Like all Japanese painted ferns, Burgundy Lace is a deciduous fern that emerges in spring with its most vivid color, maintains ornamental interest through summer in the shade garden, and dies back to the ground with frost. The arching, triangular fronds emerge with maximum color intensity in spring, then mellow slightly through summer while retaining their distinctive coloration. Japanese painted ferns are the most popular ornamental ferns in American shade gardens — widely used in the partial-shade perennial border combined with hostas, astilbes, and shade-tolerant groundcovers. In zone 9, Japanese painted ferns perform well in deep shade with consistent moisture and mulched, humus-rich soil; they tolerate the Gulf South summer heat better than most cool-climate ferns when summer sun is excluded. Divide in spring every 3–4 years as clumps enlarge.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Burgundy Lace is a fringed-type tulip with fine, crystalline petal edges rather than the deep ruffling of parrot tulips.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Burgundy Lace bears deep wine-red petals edged with a fine, crystalline fringe that catches the light like frost along each margin, a more delicate effect than the heavy ruffling of parrot-type tulips while still adding real textural interest to the bloom. Its rich, dark color and refined fringed edge make it a striking cut flower and a good companion for pale or white tulips in mixed plantings. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil. Cultivar selection matters greatly—dwarf types top out at 3 feet while standard forms can reach 10 feet or more, so choose based on available space.
directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil with a pH between 5.0 and 6.5, incorporating sulfur or acidifying fertilizer if your native soil is alkaline. Burgundy loropetalum establishes readily in Gulf Coast landscapes and rewards minimal pruning with its best natural form—avoid heavy shearing, which reduces flowering and distorts the graceful branching habit. Magenta-pink fringe flowers appear most heavily in late winter and spring, but sporadic bloom continues throughout the warm months. Mulch the root zone to conserve moisture and maintain the soil acidity this plant prefers.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Burkwood viburnum blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Burkwood viburnum is a hybrid between Korean spice viburnum and service viburnum, combining the intense, spicy-sweet fragrance of its Korean parent with more vigorous growth, glossier foliage, and better heat tolerance, opening rounded clusters of pink buds that fade to white in early to mid spring. Its foliage is semi-evergreen in milder climates, holding dark green leaves through much of winter before dropping, and turning attractive burgundy-red in fall where it does go fully deciduous. The rounded, multi-stemmed shrub makes an excellent specimen near an entrance or window where its fragrance can be appreciated, or massed as a flowering screen. Prune lightly immediately after bloom to maintain shape, since later pruning removes the following year's flower buds.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, groundcover, or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Burle Marx philodendron spreads by short rhizomes into a low, clumping groundcover rather than climbing.
directions: Grow as a houseplant, groundcover, or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Burle Marx philodendron spreads by short rhizomes into a low, clumping groundcover rather than climbing. Named for the celebrated Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx, this hybrid produces glossy, elongated, arrow-shaped leaves on a compact, spreading plant that forms a dense, low groundcover in a shaded tropical bed in frost-free climates, or an easy-care rosette in a container further north. Its rhizomatous, non-vining habit makes it useful for filling in beneath larger shade plants or trailing gently over a container's edge, needing no staking or climbing support to look full. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, divide the spreading rhizome to propagate or control size, and protect from any frost.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average, loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun to partial shade; burning bush is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions. NOTE: Burning bush is listed as invasive in many eastern and midwestern US states and should NOT be planted where native forest borders are present — it self-sows abundantly and displaces native vegetation.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average, loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun to partial shade; burning bush is one of the most widely planted ornamental shrubs in North America — famous for its extraordinary, blazing, neon-scarlet to crimson fall color, one of the most brilliant autumn displays of any deciduous shrub. The distinctive corky, wing-like ridges on the stems ('winged' euonymus) are immediately distinctive and attractive year-round. Extremely adaptable — tolerating a wide range of soils, light conditions, and drought. However, burning bush has escaped cultivation and naturalized in forests throughout the eastern and midwestern US, where it displaces native understory vegetation. Listed as invasive in Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and other states — banned from sale in some states. Native plant alternatives with comparable fall color include: native highbush blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) and black gum (Nyssa sylvatica). If planting, choose a dwarf, compact cultivar ('Compactus') away from natural areas and remove the small orange-red berries before birds can disperse the seeds.

common_name: Burning Heart Caladium (Vivid Scarlet-Red Center Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Burning Heart's vivid scarlet coloration is most intense in bright partial shade — deep shade may cause the red to soften toward pink-orange.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Burning Heart is one of the most vivid and boldly colored red caladiums available — a large fancy-leaf type producing heart-shaped leaves with a dramatic, burning-scarlet to crimson-red center that bleeds and radiates outward from the main veins, creating a fiery effect set against wide, fresh-green margins that frame and intensify the red center by contrast. The intensity of the red in Burning Heart is exceptional among caladiums — a true scarlet rather than the pink or rose tones of many nominally 'red' caladium varieties — creating one of the most vivid color contrasts in the shade garden plant palette. As a large fancy-leaf type, Burning Heart produces the classic large, glossy, heart-shaped leaves reaching 12–18 inches on vigorous plants in optimal conditions. In zone 9, Burning Heart performs reliably through the warm season (May–October), producing the best leaf size and most intense color in the June–August peak heat period when warm soil and air temperatures stimulate maximum growth. The vivid red coloration is outstanding in mass plantings against green groundcovers, as a focal point in mixed shade containers, or combined with the bold white leaves of 'Aaron' or 'Candidum' for maximum red-and-white contrast. Maintain consistent moisture and mulch to stabilize soil temperature and prevent drought stress that causes leaf burn.

plant_note: Establish from fresh seed or a nursery-grown offset in a well-drained bed with light shade to full sun; water regularly the first year to establish, then rely on natural rainfall except during extended drought.
directions: Establish this Australian cycad from fresh seed or a nursery-grown offset in a well-drained bed with light shade to full sun, since it tolerates surprisingly cool winters for a cycad once its root system is settled. Its dense rosette of long, arching, dark green pinnate leaves makes a strong architectural mass planting or understory accent beneath high-canopy trees. Water regularly the first year to establish, then let it rely on natural rainfall except during extended drought. It is exceptionally slow-growing, so plan for it as a long-term structural feature rather than a fast-filling accent.

common_name: Burro's Tail (Donkey Tail, Lamb's Tail Sedum, Burro's Tail Sedum)
plant_note: Plant in a hanging basket or cascading container in bright indirect light to full morning sun with very fast-draining succulent mix; Burro's Tail is best grown in a hanging basket where its cascading stems (reaching 2–3 feet) display beautifully without the leaves getting dislodged by foot traffic. The plump, blue-green leaves fall off at the slightest touch — handle minimally and place in a location where it won't be brushed. Detached leaves will root on dry succulent mix. In zone 9, grow as a patio or indoor container plant; bring indoors when temperatures drop below 40°F.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light to direct morning sun in very fast-draining succulent or cactus potting mix; the most important cultural requirement for Burro's Tail is excellent drainage — saturated soil causes rapid root rot. Sedum morganianum is a succulent native to southern Mexico (Veracruz and Oaxaca states) that is among the most popular and distinctive trailing succulent plants for hanging baskets and cascading container arrangements worldwide. The plant produces long, pendant stems densely covered in overlapping, swollen, teardrop-shaped, blue-green to gray-green leaves that create the appearance of a thick, plump rope or braided tail — hence both common names. Well-established specimens in large baskets can develop stems 24–36 inches long, forming a striking curtain of silvery-green fleshy leaves that moves with air currents. In late spring and early summer, small, pendant, rose-pink to red star-shaped flowers appear at the stem tips. The notable fragility of the leaves — which drop at the slightest touch, creating a carpet beneath the plant that must be swept regularly or will root as a natural propagation mechanism — requires placing the plant in a protected, low-traffic location. In zone 9 and cooler, it is strictly a container and indoor plant.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs rooted from semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or early spring into well-drained, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on the coast or partial shade inland; bush anemone is naturally rare in the wild but adapts well to cultivated garden conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun along the coast or partial shade in hotter inland gardens, watering occasionally through the first two summers to establish a deep root system; bush anemone is a naturally rare California endemic, restricted in the wild to a handful of Sierra Nevada foothill canyons, yet it performs reliably in cultivation across a wide range of climates. Glossy, leathery, dark evergreen leaves set off large, fragrant, pure white, anemone-like flowers with prominent golden stamens in late spring to early summer, creating a striking display against the deep green foliage. Once established it tolerates considerable summer drought, though it looks and blooms best with an occasional deep soak during the driest months rather than complete neglect. Prune lightly after flowering to shape and remove any winter-damaged wood, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions or transplants in fall in dry to average, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; bush honeysuckle is extremely adaptable to dry, rocky, or poor soils and is one of the most shade and drought tolerant of all native flowering shrubs.
directions: Bush honeysuckle (Diervilla) is an easy-to-grow native flowering shrub of eastern North American rocky woods and dry slopes, producing small but cheerful, tubular yellow flowers in summer that turn orange-red as they age, providing an attractive bicolored display on the same plant; the compact habit and beautiful foliage that turns brilliant orange-red in fall add to its landscape value through three seasons. Despite sharing the 'honeysuckle' common name with the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica), Diervilla is a completely different and well-behaved native genus that poses no invasive risk and is in fact declining in parts of its range due to habitat loss. It spreads slowly by underground stolons to form colonies — useful for erosion control on shaded, dry slopes where few other shrubs perform reliably — and tolerates dry shade better than almost any other flowering native shrub, including spots under shallow-rooted maples and in the dry, poor shade near building foundations. Hummingbirds and native bumblebees visit the flowers, and the autumn foliage provides late-season color in woodland garden situations.

common_name: Bush Lily (Natal Lily, Kaffir Lily, Clivia)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in shade to part shade; Clivia miniata is one of the finest shade-tolerant ornamental bulb plants in the world — thriving in dense shade under trees where few other ornamentals flower — producing spectacular umbels of 12–20 brilliant orange to yellow, lily-like flowers in spring; the large, strappy evergreen leaves provide year-round structure in the shade garden; CAUTION: All parts are toxic.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in shade to part shade; Clivia dislikes direct hot sun — shade under trees is ideal; allow to become pot-bound for best flowering; CAUTION: All parts are toxic. Clivia miniata (bush lily, Natal lily, or Kaffir lily) is one of the most spectacular and reliable shade-flowering ornamental plants available — a South African native from the shaded forest understory of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape that has become a treasured garden plant worldwide. Unlike most ornamental bulbs that demand full sun, clivia thrives in deep shade — exactly the kind of dense shade under large trees where most plants struggle or fail — producing bold, strappy, arching, evergreen leaves (12–18 inches long, dark-green, leathery) that provide attractive year-round structure, and then in late winter to spring, spectacular upright stems bearing umbels of 12–20 large (2–3 inch), tubular, lily-like flowers in brilliant orange with yellow throats, or in cultivated forms, pale-yellow, cream, orange-red, and rare green-flowered varieties. The flowers are followed by clusters of large, round, red to orange berries that persist decoratively for months. Clivia has become one of the most prized and collected ornamental plants in Japan and China, where exceptional yellow and rare variegated-leaf forms command extraordinary prices. All parts of the plant are toxic; do not eat.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bush poppy does not transplant well and should be established from small container plants with minimal root disturbance. Seed germination requires smoke treatment or scarification. Established plants resent supplemental summer irrigation. Cut back by one-third after flowering to maintain compact shape.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bush poppy is a California chaparral native that produces a uniquely beautiful combination — narrow, gray-green, willow-like, glaucous leaves on an arching shrub and, from spring through summer, large (2–3 inch), bright golden-yellow, four-petaled poppy flowers that open to a pure, clear, unornamented yellow of exceptional purity against the glaucous foliage. The simple, clean flower form — each petal a perfect, softly-textured quarter-circle of yellow — combined with the silver-blue foliage creates an effect of cool, refined beauty appropriate to the dry, sunny California garden. It is native to chaparral slopes throughout the California coast ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills, growing on dry, rocky, lean soils in full sun and requiring no summer irrigation once established. Seed germination in the wild is triggered by the heat and chemicals of chaparral fires. In the garden, fire-adapted plants like this one can be started from cuttings or from smoke-treated seed. Outstanding for drought-tolerant California native plantings where it provides yellow flowers and silvery foliage contrast.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix without covering — bush violet needs light to germinate — at 70–75°F; start 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to shaded beds after all danger of frost has passed. It self-sows readily once established, so later plantings often need no help.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix without covering, as bush violet needs light to germinate; maintain 70–75°F soil temperature and expect germination in 2–3 weeks. Transplant after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to partial sun — this old-fashioned cottage-garden species is taller and more upright than the compact hybrid Browallia speciosa sold in bedding packs, with a looser, willowy habit topped by five-lobed violet-blue flowers with a small white eye, blooming continuously from early summer to frost. Unlike the hybrid, bush violet comes true from its own seed and self-sows readily once established, so a single planting often returns for years in beds where it is happy. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching and a fuller shape, and keep soil evenly moist; it wilts visibly when dry but recovers quickly once watered. Good for cutting and for filling gaps in shaded borders through the heat of summer.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall in a site with room for a slow-growing specimen conifer.
directions: This slow-growing spruce features weeping, lace-like branches clothed in soft blue-green needles for an elegant textured specimen. Plant in full sun and cool, moist, well-drained soil; it appreciates protection from harsh, drying winds. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, especially while young, as Engelmann spruce dislikes prolonged drought. Little pruning is needed beyond removing damaged branches, letting the graceful cascading habit develop naturally.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bushy aster tolerates both moist and moderately dry conditions and adapts well to a range of garden soils, from meadow edges to lightly shaded borders.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pinch or shear by a third in early summer to encourage a bushier, more floriferous, self-supporting habit. Symphyotrichum dumosum (bushy aster, or rice button aster) is a native perennial of meadows, open woodland edges, and roadsides across the eastern United States, forming a dense, twiggy, well-branched mound covered from late summer into fall with an abundance of small, numerous, pale lavender to white, yellow-centered flowers — the profusion of small blooms, densely packed like rice grains along the stems, gives rise to the 'rice button' common name. Its adaptability to both sun and partial shade, and to a range of soil moisture levels, makes it one of the more versatile native asters for different garden situations, and the late, long-lasting bloom period provides valuable nectar for native bees and migrating butterflies when few other plants are still flowering. A reliable, easy native for the middle or front of a sunny to lightly shaded fall border, zone 4–8.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or spring in moist to wet, well-drained to poorly drained soil in full sun; bushy bluestem thrives in the wet, sunny conditions along pond margins, drainage ditches, and seasonal wet depressions of the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Bushy bluestem is one of the most attractive native grasses for moist to wet, sunny sites in the Gulf Coastal Plain — in fall, the tops of the upright stems explode into distinctive fluffy, silvery white seed heads that give the grass a spectacular cotton-like appearance unlike any other native grass, making it highly ornamental for fall and winter interest in the garden and landscape. Found naturally in wet flatwoods, swales, pond margins, and roadside ditches throughout the Gulf South and southeastern coastal plain, it grows in exactly the sunny, wet conditions that are often difficult to plant — making it a superb choice for rain gardens, detention ponds, seasonal depressions, and moist bioswales in zone 6–10 landscapes. Like other bluestems, its seed heads provide food for grassland birds through winter, and the dense clumps offer nesting and escape cover for small mammals and ground-nesting birds. Its tolerance of periodic flooding and standing water makes it one of the most reliable native grasses for wet, sunny sites where little else will establish.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial to full shade in spring; butcher's broom is one of the most shade and drought-tolerant shrubs for difficult, deeply shaded, dry conditions.
directions: Plant divisions or container specimens in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial to full shade; butcher's broom is a Mediterranean native evergreen subshrub that fills a nearly unique niche — it thrives in the deep, dry shade under mature evergreens and dense broadleaf trees where almost no other ornamental plant survives, producing stiff, spine-tipped, dark-green cladodes (flattened stem segments that function as leaves) with tiny greenish-white flowers in midwinter followed by ornamental bright-red berries (on female plants only, requiring a male in proximity) that persist through winter. The plant is extremely drought-tolerant and salt-resistant once established. The stiff, prickly branches were historically used to sweep butcher's blocks. An invaluable plant for the most challenging dry-shade conditions in zone 7–9 gardens.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes or divisions in spring or early fall with the crown just below the soil surface.
directions: This Siberian iris opens bicolor blooms of soft butter-yellow falls and crisp white standards atop slender, grassy foliage. Plant in full sun to light shade in moist, humus-rich soil; it tolerates wetter ground better than bearded iris. Keep evenly watered during the spring bloom period and divide clumps every few years to maintain vigor. It is low-maintenance and reliably hardy, spreading into graceful clumps that make excellent border and waterside plantings.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost, or purchase transplants; in zone 9, plant in spring for summer and fall bloom in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; melampodium is one of the most heat-tolerant and carefree yellow-flowering annuals for Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting or direct sow in warm soil; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; no deadheading needed. Melampodium paludosum (butter daisy or melampodium) is a Central American native annual producing cheerful, 1.5-inch, bright-yellow daisy flowers with a yellow center continuously from late spring through hard frost on neat, mounded, self-cleaning plants that require no deadheading — spent flowers drop cleanly. This combination of bright, warm color, non-stop bloom, compact mounding habit, heat tolerance, and carefree nature makes melampodium one of the top summer annuals for hot, humid Gulf Coast gardens, where it outperforms many other yellow-flowering annuals. It is outstanding as an edging plant, in masses for summer color beds, and in containers. Unlike many yellow daisies, it is resistant to spider mites and maintains clean, disease-free foliage through the summer heat. The 'Medallion' and 'Derby' series are the most widely planted; 'Lemon Delight' has lighter, lemon-yellow flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Siberian iris tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and needs no rhizome exposure at planting.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Siberian iris tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and needs no rhizome exposure at planting. Crisp white falls contrast sharply with clear butter-yellow standards, a clean two-tone combination that has made this one of the most enduringly popular Siberian iris cultivars since its introduction decades ago, blooming above narrow, grass-like foliage that stays attractive well after flowering finishes. Unlike bearded iris, Siberian iris grows from a fibrous root system rather than a rhizome, tolerates moist to average soil without rotting, and is essentially pest- and disease-free, making it one of the lowest-maintenance perennials for a sunny border or pond-adjacent planting. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in early spring or fall, and cut foliage back in late fall or early spring before new growth begins.

plant_note: Scarify seeds lightly and sow directly in spring; germination is fast in warm soil. In zone 8, start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost passes.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil; Buttercup Bush is drought-tolerant once established and thrives on neglect in sandy or rocky soils where other shrubs struggle. The cheerful golden-yellow flowers bloom for an extended season from summer into fall, providing reliable late-season forage for native bees and other pollinators. In zone 8, hard freezes will kill the top growth to the ground, but the plant reliably resprouts from its root system in spring. Cut frosted stems back to the crown in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and a tidy shrub form.

plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Buttercup is a classic clear-yellow crocosmia, a color less common than the reds and oranges typical of the genus.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Buttercup bears arching, one-sided sprays of clear, bright yellow, tubular flowers above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer, a cheerful, sunny color that stands apart from the more common red and orange crocosmia cultivars. Its flowers draw hummingbirds and make good cut flowers, holding well in a vase. Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection, and give it consistently moist, well-drained soil for the best flowering display.

common_name: Buttercup Tree (Poro Poro, Rose Silk Cotton)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Buttercup tree is a Central American tropical deciduous tree producing one of the most spectacular floral displays in the tropical world — large (3–4 inch), brilliant-yellow, poppy-like flowers with silky yellow petals appearing on bare, leafless branches in the dry season — similar in effect to yellow silk floss tree or yellow jacaranda.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; the tree naturally defoliates in a dry season to bloom. Cochlospermum vitifolium (buttercup tree or poro poro) is a Mexican and Central American tropical deciduous tree that creates one of the most dramatic dry-season flowering displays in the tropical world. The tree is deciduous in response to drought or cooler temperatures: as it drops its large, deeply-lobed, vine-like leaves (the species name 'vitifolium' means 'grape-leaved,' referring to the leaf shape), the bare branches produce large (3–4 inch across), brilliant golden-yellow flowers with five silky, crinkled petals and prominent yellow stamens — like enormous buttercups or golden poppies — covering the entire leafless tree in a blaze of yellow. The effect is similar to a yellow Tabebuia or yellow jacaranda — a complete crown of golden flowers on bare branches — spectacularly showy. The tree is fast-growing, drought-tolerant, and appropriate for tropical dry landscapes; it can actually flower more prolifically with a dry season. Fluffy, cotton-like seed fibers in the large seed capsules provide the name 'silk cotton.' Bark fibers have traditional uses in rope and textile making in Mexico. An exceptional and underused ornamental for zone 10–12 tropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; winter hazels are best in sheltered positions where late frosts will not damage the early blooms. Propagate by softwood cuttings in early summer.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade with shelter from late-season frosts; buttercup winter hazel is the smallest and most refined of the Corylopsis species, producing delicate, drooping racemes of pale yellow, primrose-scented flowers in late winter or very early spring — among the earliest ornamental shrubs to bloom, often appearing in late February or March alongside snowdrops and before forsythia. The small flowers are each shaped like a tiny cowslip, nodding in clusters on bare winter stems. The heart-shaped, finely toothed leaves emerge bronze-green after flowering and mature to fresh green with fine veining. More compact than other winter hazels, it is well suited to smaller gardens and shaded woodland edges where its subtle, early charm can be appreciated up close. Site in a sheltered spot to protect blooms from late freezes.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or fall; set crowns just 1 in below soil level in full sun to light afternoon shade.
directions: Plant fans with the crown about 1 in deep, spreading roots outward over a small mound of soil in the hole, and water thoroughly after planting. Buttered Popcorn is a classic, reliable, heavy-blooming daylily with rounded, ruffled, rich golden-yellow flowers with a lightly ruffled edge, produced in abundance over a long midseason bloom period on well-branched scapes with high bud count. Its dependable vigor, strong scapes, and clear, cheerful color have kept it a garden standard for mass plantings and mixed borders for decades. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines, and remove spent scapes after all buds open to keep the planting tidy.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Buttered Rum heucherella colors best with a few hours of morning sun and consistent moisture.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Buttered Rum heucherella colors best with a few hours of morning sun and consistent moisture. Large, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves emerge amber-orange in spring and deepen to rich caramel-brown through summer, with contrasting pale pink flower spikes rising above the foliage in late spring. A cross between heuchera and tiarella, it combines the bold leaf shape of tiarella with heuchera's tougher constitution and more compact, non-stoloniferous habit, making it a well-behaved clumping groundcover rather than a spreader. Use it to edge a shaded path or brighten the front of a woodland border, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; established plants tolerate brief dry spells and coastal salt exposure better than most ferns.
directions: Butterfield's holly fern is a rare selection of Japanese holly fern distinguished by long, arching, glossy dark-green fronds with unusually deep, sharply serrated leaflet margins, giving the whole clump a jagged, textural look unlike the smoother-edged species. Like the straight species, it is remarkably tolerant of heat, salt spray, and dry shade once established, making it one of the toughest broadleaf evergreen ferns for difficult sites along the Gulf Coast. Site it in part to full shade in well-drained soil, where its stiff, leathery fronds resist wind damage and provide months of structural evergreen interest with minimal upkeep. Use it as a specimen near entries and shaded patios where its distinctive serrated foliage can be appreciated up close.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, acidic soil.
directions: Japanese iris produces large, flat, ruffled blooms whose delicate petals resemble butterflies taking flight in late spring and summer. Plant in full sun to part shade in rich, acidic soil that stays consistently moist; it thrives at pond edges and in rain gardens. Never let the soil dry out during the growing season, and avoid lime. Divide congested clumps in early fall and remove spent flower stalks to keep plantings tidy.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in partial shade with well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil; Hippeastrum papilio is evergreen — it does not go dormant and should not be allowed to dry out completely between waterings. Unlike most Hippeastrum species and hybrids that require a dry dormancy period to rebloom, H. papilio can bloom multiple times per year in good conditions without a rest period. Plant bulbs with the top third above soil level. In zone 9, container culture provides flexibility. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in partial shade to bright indirect light — Butterfly Amaryllis is significantly more shade-tolerant than most Hippeastrum species and hybrids, and actually performs better in partial shade than full sun in zone 9.
