Hippeastrum papilio is a truly unusual species within the large Hippeastrum genus — one of the most distinct and ornamentally striking species, native to a limited area of southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina states) in the Amaryllidaceae family. The flowers are the defining feature: large (6–8 inch), 6-petaled, pale green to yellow-white with bold, dark red-maroon to burgundy veining and striping on each petal, creating a pattern of vivid dark streaks on a pale background that strongly resembles a butterfly's wing — a resemblance that inspired the species name 'papilio' (Latin for butterfly). Unlike the brightly colored, cultivated Hippeastrum hybrids that go fully dormant in winter, H. papilio is an evergreen species that maintains its strap-like leaves year-round and can bloom multiple times per year without a dormancy period. The flowers appear in clusters of 2–4 at the top of tall scapes. The species has become an important parent in Hippeastrum hybridization, contributing its evergreen quality and unusual striped coloring to offspring. All parts are toxic due to lycorine and other alkaloids.

plant_note: Chilling the seed briefly before sowing improves this dwarf delphinium's germination.
directions: Start these dwarf delphiniums indoors several weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil cool since they germinate best below 65F. This heat-tolerant blend blooms the first year in shades of marine blue, light blue, soft rose, and white, making it well suited to small spaces and the front of cottage borders. Provide rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture, and give plants afternoon shade in hot climates. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage a second flush of bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 8–9 plant September–March. Butterfly Blue blooms most freely in spring and fall with a summer lull in zone 9's heat — deadhead spent blooms consistently to extend the flowering season. Shear back by one-third after each main flush of bloom to stimulate fresh foliage and new flower buds. In zone 9 the plant may decline in summer heat — treat it as a cool-season perennial, planting in fall for winter-spring display.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, gritty soil — pincushion flowers fail in heavy, wet soils and thrive in rocky or sandy garden conditions; Butterfly Blue is an All-America Selections award-winning perennial pincushion flower that earned widespread recognition for its almost continuous bloom cycle and unique medium blue-lavender flower color that is genuinely uncommon in the full-sun perennial palette. The delicate, dome-shaped flower heads with divided petals radiating around a pin-cushion center bloom on long, wiry, branching stems that create an airy, wildflower effect different from the solid masses of most garden perennials. The long, thin stems make Butterfly Blue outstanding for cutting, and the soft lavender-blue color works with almost any companion planting palette. As a pollinator plant, Butterfly Blue is exceptionally effective — butterflies, bees, and beneficial insects are strongly attracted to the accessible, nectar-rich flowers. The plant performs best in well-drained, slightly alkaline conditions that mirror its Mediterranean-European homeland origins.

common_name: Butterfly Deep Red Pentas (Heat-Proof Red Star-Cluster Hummingbird Plant)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pentas is one of the few red-flowering annuals that reliably attracts hummingbirds — the tubular, star-shaped flower clusters are perfectly sized for hummingbird feeding and are visited throughout the bloom season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Butterfly Deep Red is a Pentas lanceolata cultivar in the Butterfly series — producing dense, rounded clusters of tubular, star-shaped flowers in deep, rich red throughout the warm season. Pentas (star cluster) is one of the most valuable warm-season annuals for Gulf South butterfly and hummingbird gardens: the flower clusters are a concentrated nectar resource attracting monarch butterflies, gulf fritillaries, zebra longwings, sulphurs, hummingbirds, and numerous other pollinators in a steady stream through the long Gulf South summer. The deep red of 'Butterfly Deep Red' is particularly effective at attracting hummingbirds, which strongly prefer red tubular flowers. Pentas blooms without pause from planting through frost in zone 9, maintaining vigorous flower production through the brutal Gulf South August heat that reduces or stops flowering in many other summer annuals — one of the few ornamentals that looks better in August than in June. The Butterfly series was bred specifically for compact habit, continuous bloom, and heat tolerance, making it more reliable in Gulf South conditions than older, taller pentas varieties. In zone 10-12, Pentas grows as a perennial subshrub; in zone 9, it is a warm-season annual that may self-sow in sheltered, mild winters. Plant in masses for maximum visual impact and to create a substantial nectar resource for migrating monarchs in late summer and fall.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; butterfly ginger is invasive in Florida, Hawaii, and parts of the Gulf Coast — consider this before planting and do not plant near natural areas. Container planting prevents spread.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; butterfly ginger is among the most intensely fragrant of all flowering plants — the pure white, butterfly-shaped flowers in summer and fall fill the garden with a heady sweet fragrance that carries 20–30 feet in still evening air. It is the national flower of Cuba and is widely grown throughout the tropics for its extraordinary perfume, used to scent garlands and leis. The tall, handsome reed-like stems 4–6 feet tall with broad, lance-shaped leaves make it an imposing accent or screening plant in shaded areas. In zone 8–9 the foliage dies back in winter but the roots resprout reliably from established rhizomes. Note that this species is listed as invasive in Florida, Hawaii, and the Pacific islands — plant responsibly, do not plant near waterways or natural areas, and contain the rhizomes if needed.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; butterfly gladiolus is a summer-rainfall species from the Drakensberg foothills and eastern South Africa that tolerates summer moisture well, unlike the Cape winter-rainfall gladioli. It spreads aggressively by stolons in favorable conditions. Flowers July–September (Northern Hemisphere). The unusual grayish-green-yellow-and-purple bicolor flower is unlike any other gladiolus and has been used extensively in breeding for unusual color forms.
directions: Plant corms in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; butterfly gladiolus is the most distinctively unusual-colored of the commonly available species gladioli — producing in late summer (July–September) tall spikes of flowers in a complex, subtle, difficult-to-describe combination of grayish-green to yellowish-green outer coloring overlaid and mottled with purple-violet inside — the whole flower an intriguing, unusual, somewhat somber mixture of muddy green-yellow and purple that is unlike any other color in the gladiolus genus and perfectly captures the muted, mysterious 'butterfly' quality that inspired the common name. The flowers are substantial and well-formed, the spikes tall and elegant, and the overall effect in a planting scheme is a striking departure from the clear, saturated colors of most gladioli into the unusual territory of complex, multi-toned, gray-green-and-purple harmony. It spreads aggressively by underground stolons, building large colonies in suitable moist, fertile conditions — a vigorous and persistent perennial rather than a tender annual-treated corm. The interesting color has made it valuable in gladiolus breeding for unusual, bicolor, and broken-color forms. Outstanding for sophisticated color-aware planting schemes in zones 7–10.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring; butterfly iris spreads by stolons to form large colonies and is excellent as a groundcover in shaded spots where grasses will not grow.
directions: Divide rhizomes in spring or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; butterfly iris (Japanese iris, fan iris) is a shade-tolerant, spreading Japanese iris that forms broad, fan-shaped clumps of flat, evergreen, sword-like leaves and produces a profusion of delicate, orchid-like, lavender-blue flowers with distinctive ruffled, fringed petals marked with yellow and white — the frilled, butterfly wing-like petals give the flower an unusually refined, delicate quality that differs from the more boldly structured bearded and Louisiana irises. It is one of the most shade-tolerant of all irises, thriving in partial shade under high trees where bearded irises would fail to bloom. The spreading, stoloniferous rhizomes create dense, weed-suppressing groundcover colonies in moist, partially shaded spots. 'Ledger's Variety' and 'Uwaduraku' are notable cultivars. Excellent for naturalized woodland edge plantings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Butterfly Japanese maple needs protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, which scorch its variegated leaves.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Butterfly Japanese maple needs protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, which scorch its variegated leaves. Small, delicate, blue-green leaves are irregularly margined in creamy white, often blushed pink on new growth, giving the airy, upright canopy a light, fluttering appearance that inspired the cultivar's name, on a naturally narrow, columnar form well suited to a smaller garden or container where wider-spreading maples would be too large. Its fine-textured, variegated foliage provides season-long interest, turning soft yellow-pink in fall, and its upright habit makes it a good vertical accent for a shaded border or Japanese-style garden without the footprint of broader cultivars. Site out of hot afternoon sun and strong wind, which quickly scorch the delicate variegated leaf margins, and water during dry spells, especially for the first few years after planting.

common_name: Butterfly Kisses Coneflower (Dwarf Double Pink Pompom Coneflower)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Butterfly Kisses is a dwarf double-flowered coneflower well suited to containers and small borders.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Butterfly Kisses bears fragrant, fully double, rose-pink pompom blooms on a compact, dwarf plant considerably shorter than most coneflower cultivars, fitting neatly into containers, small borders, or the front of a bed where taller coneflowers would overwhelm the space. It blooms over a long summer season and tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead for continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Butterfly Laelia (Christmas Orchid, Mexican Laelia, Two-Keeled Laelia)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork or rough bark, or in a clay pot with very coarse bark or rock chips — Laelia anceps comes from seasonally dry, high-elevation rocky cliffs and oak forests in Mexico and requires excellent drainage and a dry rest in summer after blooming to trigger its characteristic winter bloom in December–January. In zone 9, it is one of the most reliably outdoor-grown Mexican orchids, tolerating brief temperatures to 28°F when the pseudobulbs and medium are dry. High light (bright indirect to partial direct sun) and excellent air circulation are essential. Bloom spikes emerge in fall; flowers open December–January just in time for the holidays. Fragrant in warm conditions.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct light mounted on bark or in a clay pot with very coarse drainage medium — Butterfly Laelia demands outstanding drainage and air circulation around its roots and performs best with a pronounced dry-warm rest period in the summer months following bloom. Laelia anceps is a sympodial, epiphytic to lithophytic orchid native to Mexico (Oaxaca, Veracruz, Chiapas, Hidalgo) and Honduras in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most cold-tolerant, widely cultivated, and historically important of the Mexican Laelia species and a cornerstone of classic orchid hybridizing. The plant produces cylindrical to spindle-shaped pseudobulbs 3–5 inches tall, each topped with 1–2 stiff, dark-green, leathery, strap-shaped leaves. In late fall, an exceptionally long (to 3 feet) arching flower spike emerges from the apex of the mature pseudobulb, bearing 3–5 (occasionally to 9) large flowers at its tip. Each flower is 3–4 inches across, in shades of soft rose-pink to pale lavender-pink, with a prominent, trumpet-shaped, three-lobed lip in deeper rose to magenta-purple with a white to cream base — the combination giving the flower a dignified, formal beauty that made Laelia anceps one of the most cherished orchid species in Victorian-era collections. Blooming reliably in December and January, the 'Christmas Orchid' provides a display of tropical elegance at a season when few other orchids flower. Fragrant on warm, sunny days. One of the finest Mexican orchids for zone 9–11 outdoor culture on protected, frost-free porches or trees. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, lean, sandy or rocky soil in zone 6–10; keep completely dry from midsummer through fall; Butterfly Mariposa Lily is one of California's most spectacular native bulbs — native to chaparral, oak woodland, and mountain meadows — bearing large, upright, cup-shaped flowers in white to cream, yellow, or deep purple with distinctive butterfly-like markings at the petal bases and a contrasting band of color above the nectary.
directions: Plant Calochortus venustus bulbs in fall in extremely well-drained, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; provide regular water in late winter and spring during active growth, then withhold all water from late spring/early summer through fall to replicate the California dry-summer climate — summer moisture is the primary cause of bulb failure outside California. Butterfly Mariposa Lily is one of the most variable and beautiful of all Calochortus — a large genus of exclusively Western North American native bulbs that has been called 'the lilies that ate California.' The cup-shaped flowers can be white, cream, yellow, deep wine-purple, or lavender, nearly always with bold, dark, butterfly-like blotches at the petal bases in contrasting colors — the effect is like a stained-glass window in miniature. In California gardens with dry summers, they are straightforward bulbs for naturalizing in grassland gardens, among coastal scrub, and on sunny embankments; outside California, success requires excellent drainage and rigorous summer drought. Grow in containers that can be moved under a porch roof in summer, or in raised beds under an overhang. Resist the urge to water in summer — it mimics their native dry-summer climate. Multiplies by offsets and self-sows in suitable conditions.

plant_note: Fall sow or cold-stratify 30 days before spring planting.
directions: Sow butterfly milkweed in fall or cold-stratify the seed for about a month before a spring sowing to break dormancy. This native perennial forms compact, bushy clumps crowned with vivid orange flower clusters that are a critical nectar and host resource for Monarchs. Its deep taproot makes it drought-tolerant but slow to establish and best left undisturbed once planted. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and avoid rich, wet soils.

plant_note: Mount on a slab or pot loosely in a small amount of coarse bark in a small pot, since Psychopsis papilio dislikes having its roots disturbed and produces a single, persistent flower spike that should never be cut off after blooming — it continues to branch and re-flower from the same spike for years.
directions: Grow in bright, filtered light similar to a Cattleya, with warm, humid, well-ventilated conditions and consistent moisture that never becomes stagnant around the single, flattened pseudobulb. Native to Trinidad, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, Psychopsis papilio produces one striking flower at a time atop a tall, wiry, continuously elongating spike — long, twisting, mahogany-and-yellow sepals and petals held above a smaller lip create an uncanny resemblance to a butterfly or moth in flight, a display that can recur intermittently for years from the same spike. The mottled, purplish-green, paddle-shaped leaf is also distinctive and ornamental in its own right. Keep the bark or moss mix lightly moist at all times and avoid letting the roots dry out completely, since this species lacks the substantial water-storing pseudobulbs of many other epiphytic orchids.

common_name: Butterfly Pink Pentas (Heat-Proof Soft-Pink Star Cluster Hummingbird Annual)
plant_note: Plant container transplants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; the soft pink color of Butterfly Pink is more versatile in mixed planting combinations than the deep red — it complements both warm and cool color companions in summer borders.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Butterfly Pink is a soft rose-pink to warm-pink cultivar in the Butterfly series of Pentas lanceolata — producing the same rounded star-cluster flower heads and outstanding heat tolerance as the series, in a color that is more softly toned than the vivid deep red of 'Butterfly Deep Red'. The warm soft-pink color is among the most versatile for mixed summer combinations: it complements orange and yellow tropicals without the color clash that can occur with cool pink, works well with deep purple companions (sweet potato vine, Purple Queen Bougainvillea), and creates elegant pastels when combined with white and lavender. Like all Pentas, Butterfly Pink is a butterfly and hummingbird magnet throughout its extended bloom season — the nectar-rich star-shaped flower clusters are visited by swallowtails, monarchs, gulf fritillaries, skippers, and other pollinators in large numbers. The heat performance in Gulf South summer conditions is outstanding — one of the primary ornamental assets of the genus. In zone 10-12, Pentas grows as a perennial subshrub. In zone 9, it functions as a warm-season annual that may self-sow in sheltered conditions. Mass planting in 12-18 inch grids creates the most effective nectar resource for migrating monarchs passing through the Gulf South in September–October.

plant_note: Scarify or nick the hard seed coat and soak overnight before sowing indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil after last frost. In zone 9–11 it is semi-evergreen and may be planted year-round.
directions: Nick the hard seed coat, soak seeds overnight, then start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in well-drained potting mix at 70–80°F; transplant after last frost in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in zone 9–11. Butterfly senna produces masses of bright golden-yellow flowers from fall through early winter on arching branches with compound, ferny foliage — one of the showiest fall-blooming shrubs for Gulf Coast and South Florida landscapes. It is a critical host plant for cloudless sulphur butterfly larvae, and the adult butterflies nectar heavily on the bright flowers. Growth is fast and may require pruning to maintain shape; cut back hard in early spring before new growth begins to keep the plant compact. The related Senna alata (candlestick plant) blooms in candle-like spikes and is equally effective in zone 9–11.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seeds for 4–6 weeks in the refrigerator, then start indoors; or direct sow in fall for natural stratification and spring emergence.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds by mixing with moist sand in a sealed bag and refrigerating for 30 days before sowing at soil surface — seeds need light and should not be covered. Butterfly weed has a deep taproot that makes it drought tolerant once established but very sensitive to transplanting; direct sowing or using deep individual cells causes the least disturbance. First-year plants rarely bloom, investing energy into root development; blooms appear reliably from the second year onward in vivid orange clusters that are among the most attractive nectar sources for monarchs and other butterflies. Leave seedheads through winter to self-sow and feed birds.

common_name: Butterfly Wings Camellia (Ruffled Twisted-Petal Deep Pink Reticulata Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Butterfly Wings is named for its distinctively ruffled, twisted reticulata camellia petals.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind. Butterfly Wings is named for its deep pink, semi-double blooms with distinctively ruffled, twisted petals that catch and flutter in a breeze, an unusual texture among reticulata camellias that mostly show smoother, more even petal forms. It grows into an upright, vigorous shrub with the bold, leathery foliage typical of the species, blooming in mid-to-late winter into spring. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes; nasturtiums resent transplanting.
directions: Sow the large seeds directly where plants are to grow once the soil has warmed, planting about half an inch deep. These compact plants show warm butterscotch flowers that are edible and add a peppery bite to salads and garnishes. Avoid overly rich soil, which pushes foliage at the expense of blooms, and let plants dry slightly between waterings. Their tidy habit makes them ideal for containers and the front of a border.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, rich, disturbed soil in full sun to partial shade; butterweed is a native winter annual/biennial that germinates in fall, overwinters as a rosette, and blooms in early spring, then dies back after setting seed for the year.
directions: Plant in moist, rich, disturbed soil in full sun to partial shade; butterweed is a native winter annual to biennial wildflower common in floodplains, ditches, wet fields, and disturbed bottomland soil across the eastern and central United States, where it forms bright, unmissable sheets of golden-yellow daisy flowers in early spring before most other plants have greened up. It germinates in fall, overwinters as a low rosette of glossy, deeply lobed leaves, then bolts and blooms in March and April, providing an important, abundant early-season nectar source for the first bees and other pollinators active in spring. After flowering and setting abundant seed, plants die back completely by early summer, so it works best worked into a naturalized wet meadow, floodplain planting, or the damp margin of a rain garden rather than a tidy, controlled bed, since it self-seeds prolifically and can be locally weedy in the moist, disturbed soil it favors. Note that butterweed contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids and is toxic if ingested by livestock, so avoid planting it in or near grazed pasture.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich, moderately moist soil in partial to deep shade; button fern is unusually drought tolerant for a fern and prefers somewhat drier, rockier conditions than most shade ferns — it will not tolerate waterlogged soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich, moderately moist soil in partial to deep shade — button fern from New Zealand is one of the most charming and distinctive small ferns in cultivation, producing graceful, arching, dark-stemmed fronds lined with small, round, button-like leaflets (pinnae) that give it a uniquely textured, decorative appearance quite unlike typical ferns. It is substantially more drought tolerant than most ferns, preferring rocky or well-drained, humus-rich soils rather than the constantly wet conditions needed by many shade ferns. This makes it an excellent choice for shaded container gardens, terrariums, hanging baskets, and rocky shade garden pockets where soil dries between waterings. It grows well as a houseplant in moderate to bright indirect light. In the Gulf Coast and South, it is hardy to around 25°F and grows outdoors year-round in zone 8–11 in partial to deep shade under trees and on north-facing banks.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or rooted cuttings in spring or fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; buttonbush is one of the very few woody shrubs that can grow with its roots submerged in standing water and thrives in areas that flood seasonally.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring or fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; buttonbush is an essential native shrub for wet, seasonally flooded, or permanently moist sites — pond margins, rain gardens, wet swales, and creek banks where it thrives in conditions that eliminate every other large shrub. The spherical, white, pincushion-like flower heads appear in midsummer and are one of the finest native pollinator plants available, attracting an extraordinary diversity of native bees, bumblebees, skippers, and swallowtail butterflies that few other native plants can match. The round, persistent seed heads provide winter food for waterfowl and songbirds. An outstanding choice for rain garden perimeters, bioswales, and naturalized wet areas in zone 5–10 landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Buttons stays notably low and dense, making it a good choice for edging, foundation plantings, or containers where full-sized gardenias would outgrow the space.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest climates. Buttons is a compact, low-growing gardenia cultivar that produces an abundance of small, single, star-shaped white flowers rather than the large double blooms of classic gardenia varieties, and while individual flowers are smaller, plants bloom so heavily that the effect is a dense, sweetly fragrant flush of white against small, glossy dark-green leaves. Its dwarf, dense habit makes it well suited to low borders, container growing, and small-space gardens where standard gardenias would need frequent pruning to control size. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer during the growing season, keep soil consistently moist but well-drained, and watch for the whitefly and scale issues common to gardenias in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained to brackish, sandy or rocky coastal soil in full sun. Buttonwood is highly salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant once established, making it an excellent choice for coastal landscaping in Zone 9b–11. It is not technically a mangrove but grows in the upland fringe of mangrove forests.
directions: Buttonwood is a native coastal tree or large shrub of the upper tidal fringe and coastal upland that transitions from saltwater to terrestrial habitats, growing at the landward edge of mangrove forests along both coasts of Florida, the Florida Keys, and throughout the Caribbean. Though often grouped with mangroves in coastal conservation contexts, Buttonwood is not a true mangrove but a member of the Combretaceae family that grows in the mangrove associates zone and shares the extreme salt tolerance that characterizes its habitat. The small, button-like seed heads that give it its common name are distinctive; the dense, slow-growing wood is exceptionally hard and was historically used for fuel, charcoal production, and as a building material. Highly salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant, and wind-resistant once established, Buttonwood is an excellent native landscaping choice for coastal South Florida homeowners seeking an attractive, low-maintenance native tree or large hedge plant for Zone 9b–11.

plant_note: Plant in partial shade to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–11; Byfield Fern (Bowenia spectabilis) is a small, unusual cycad endemic to the rainforests of central Queensland, Australia — unique among cycads for having bipinnate (twice-divided) fronds that give it a distinctly fern-like appearance — growing from a subterranean stem and producing a low, spreading crown of graceful, glossy, deeply divided fronds in the shade.
directions: Plant Bowenia spectabilis in humus-rich, moist, freely draining, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; protect from frost, direct sun, and poorly drained soil — the underground stem rots readily in waterlogged conditions; fertilize lightly in spring with a slow-release cycad formulation containing trace elements. Caution: all parts are highly toxic — seeds, leaves, and stems contain harmful cycasin glycosides — keep away from children, pets, and livestock. Byfield Fern is botanically extraordinary — one of only two species in the Bowenia genus, and the only cycad genus with bipinnate fronds, where the leaflets are themselves further divided, creating a lacy, fern-like texture that is quite unlike the stiff, pinnate fronds typical of all other cycads. The plant grows from a fully subterranean, tuberous stem that barely shows above ground, producing fronds directly from the underground caudex; mature plants slowly produce offset stems underground. In its native Queensland rainforest understory, it grows in deep shade on well-drained slopes, perfectly suited to cultivation under the canopy of large trees in frost-free subtropical gardens. A rare and coveted plant in specialist collections for its uniquely fine-textured, graceful foliage and compact size.

plant_note: Plant corms 4-6 inches deep in late summer, well before the leafless flower spikes push up in early autumn.
directions: Plant the large corms 4-6 inches deep and roughly 6-9 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil during late summer dormancy, choosing a spot that gets sun to light shade. Each corm produces an unusually high number of crocus-like lilac-pink blooms that open directly from the soil without foliage, followed the next spring by large cabbage-like leaves that must be left to die back naturally. It is one of the most floriferous colchicums and naturalizes readily in turf, borders, or woodland edges for a burst of unexpected fall color. Because the foliage and corms are toxic, keep it away from areas where pets or livestock graze.

plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in fall for spring flowering; Byzantine gladiolus is a spring-blooming, fully hardy species planted in fall — completely different timing and hardiness from the tender summer gladiolus. In zones 6-9 the corms overwinter in the ground and naturalize freely, multiplying by offsets. Excellent drainage is essential; corms rot in wet soils.
directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun in fall; Byzantine gladiolus is a world apart from the tender, summer-blooming garden gladiolus — it is planted in fall, blooms in late spring (May-June), and is fully cold-hardy to zone 5, naturalizing in well-drained conditions without any annual lifting or replanting. The flowers are a vivid, intense magenta-pink with paler centers — an unusual, saturated fuchsia-magenta color carried elegantly on graceful, arching stems with up to 20 florets per spike. The plant increases freely by cormlets to form naturalized colonies in appropriate soils, creating large drifts of spring color over time. Native to the western Mediterranean — Spain, North Africa, Turkey — it has been grown in European gardens since the 17th century and has naturalized on the Channel Islands and other mild Atlantic locations. A revelation for gardeners accustomed to lifting tender gladiolus annually; this species is trouble-free perennial. Combines beautifully with blue Camassia and late tulips for spring plantings.

common_name: C.M. Wilson Camellia (Light Pink Anemone-Form Camellia japonica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; C.M. Wilson is a classic Southern camellia bearing soft pink anemone-to-peony-form flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. C.M. Wilson bears large, soft light-pink blooms in an anemone to loose peony form, with a mass of small petaloids at the center surrounded by broader outer petals, a classic old Southern camellia form that has remained popular for generations. The vigorous, upright evergreen shrub blooms over a long midseason window and provides dense, glossy year-round structure. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cabaret is a large maiden grass selection with unusually broad blades and a wide creamy-white central stripe.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; maiden grass tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden conditions well once established. Cabaret bears unusually broad blades for a Miscanthus cultivar, each striped with a wide creamy-white center bordered by green margins, giving the large, fountain-shaped clump a bold, luminous presence in the landscape, topped by coppery-pink plumes in late summer that age to silvery-tan. Its large mature size makes it a strong specimen or screening plant where a bold textural statement is wanted. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or field-dug trees in spring in any well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to alkaline, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; cabbage palm transplants remarkably well even as a large tree and quickly re-establishes its root system. Remove all fronds at transplanting to reduce transpiration stress.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade — cabbage palm, the state tree of Florida and South Carolina, is the most cold-hardy of all the large, single-trunk native palms and the defining tree of the southeastern coastal plain from the Carolinas through Florida and around the Gulf Coast. The arching, blue-green fronds make it instantly recognizable as the symbol of the South. It is remarkably adaptable — tolerating salt spray, flooding, drought, alkaline soil, and hurricane-force winds (the flexible trunk bends dramatically but rarely breaks). White flower clusters in summer attract pollinators; the small black fruits feed dozens of bird species and are an important food source for cedar waxwings, fish crows, and raccoons. The growing bud ('heart of palm' or 'swamp cabbage') is edible but harvesting kills the tree. It transplants unusually well even when large, as shown by the millions of palms transplanted annually in Florida landscaping.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cabbage rose has a lax, arching habit and benefits from support or informal training against a fence or trellis.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cabbage rose is a complex old hybrid renowned for its extremely full, densely packed, globular flowers with dozens of tightly overlapping petals arranged in the swirling, layered form that made it the favorite subject of Dutch and French flower painters for centuries, most famously Pierre-Joseph Redouté. Its rich, classic old-rose fragrance is nearly as celebrated as its form, and the petals are used in the same rosewater and rose-oil traditions as damask rose, particularly in the historic Provence perfume industry that gave the plant one of its common names. Flowering occurs in a single generous flush in late spring, on a lax, somewhat floppy shrub that looks best trained loosely against a support or allowed to arch naturally among other cottage garden plants. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape, since it blooms on old wood and heavy dormant-season pruning removes the coming season's flowers.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 8–11; Cabbage Tree Palm is the only palm native to the Australian mainland east of the Great Dividing Range — a tall, stately, single-trunked fan palm from Queensland and New South Wales coastal rainforests and wet lowland forests, producing a large crown of deeply divided, glossy, green fan fronds and adapting well to cooler subtropical and warm-temperate climates.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Livistona australis tolerates periods of seasonal flooding and performs well in consistently moist soils — maintain soil moisture with mulch and water deeply; provide wind protection when young. Livistona australis (Cabbage Tree Palm or Australian Fan Palm) is a tall, elegant, single-trunked fan palm native to the wet coastal lowlands, rainforest margins, and swampy lowland forests of Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria — the only palm naturally occurring in southeastern Australia and one of the most cold-tolerant of all Livistona species. The trunk grows slowly and steadily over many years, eventually reaching 60–100 feet, topped by a large, rounded, dense crown of deeply divided, pendulous, glossy, bright-green circular fan fronds. The common name 'Cabbage Tree Palm' references the edible growing tip (the 'cabbage' or heart of palm) which was eaten by indigenous Australians and early settlers — though removing the growing tip kills the palm. Livistona australis is a popular landscape palm across Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, the Mediterranean, and warm subtropical regions of North America for its elegant form, tolerance of coastal conditions, and cold hardiness — one of the few large fan palms surviving brief freezing temperatures when established. Excellent specimen palm for large landscapes in zone 8b–11.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; zinnias grow quickly in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in a warm, sunny bed, or start indoors a few weeks earlier. This blend produces some of the largest zinnias available, with rolled, quill-like petals four to six inches across in pink, white, red, orange, and yellow. Space plants for good airflow to reduce powdery mildew and water at the base rather than overhead. Cut blooms frequently for bouquets to keep the plants flowering until frost.

plant_note: Start indoors for earlier bloom; tubers can be lifted and stored over winter.
directions: Start seed indoors about a month before the last frost, then transplant into rich, well-drained soil after the weather settles. This blend produces tall, sturdy plants with narrow, elongated petals in peach, yellow, and deep maroon, and blooms up to six inches across make excellent cut flowers. Stake taller plants and deadhead often to keep them blooming into fall. In colder zones, dig and store the tubers over winter to replant the following spring.

common_name: Cactus Flowered Zinnia (Twisted-Petal Heirloom Cut Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil, or start indoors 4 weeks early for an earlier bloom; zinnias thrive in the heat of a Gulf Coast summer and bloom continuously until frost.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Cactus Flowered zinnia is a classic heirloom strain distinguished by long, narrow, twisted and rolled petals that curl and quill like a cactus-flowered dahlia, giving the large, four- to five-inch blooms a shaggy, dramatic texture very different from flat-petaled standard zinnias. The tall, sturdy plants bloom in a vivid mix of reds, oranges, pinks, and yellows from early summer through frost, and the unusual petal form makes them a standout in cutting gardens and mixed bouquets. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the plant flowering, and water at the base rather than overhead to help avoid the powdery mildew that zinnias are prone to in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; cactus pelargonium is summer-dormant and deciduous — losing all its leaves in summer and requiring bone-dry conditions during this dormancy. It grows and flowers in winter and spring. The succulent, woody stems are covered with persistent sharp spines derived from hardened leaf bases — giving the 'cactus' appearance. Not suited to humid-summer climates without container management.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; cactus pelargonium is one of the most botanically unusual and structurally distinctive pelargoniums — a winter-growing, summer-dormant succulent pelargonium from the dry, rocky, winter-rainfall areas of the southern Cape and Little Karoo, producing thick, fleshy, gray-green, branching succulent stems that are covered with persistent, sharp, cactus-like thorns derived from the hardened bases of fallen leaf stalks. During winter and spring, the stem nodes produce deeply-lobed, kidney-shaped or heart-shaped, gray-green leaves, and from the leaf axils emerge umbels of small, attractive white-to-pale-pink flowers with deep maroon-purple blotches on the upper petals — a distinctive small bicolor pattern against the white base. In summer, the leaves fall and the plant enters complete dormancy as a leafless, spiny, gray-green succulent stem — almost indistinguishable from a small cactus. The combination of the cactus-like spiny dormant structure in summer and the fresh-leaved, flowering winter plant is completely distinctive and unlike any other commonly grown pelargonium. Outstanding as a curiosity and conversation piece in the succulent or Mediterranean garden.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun to partial shade; Caddo maple is a heat and drought tolerant selection of sugar maple from the Wichita Mountains of Oklahoma, significantly more adaptable to the conditions of the southern plains than northeastern sugar maple provenances.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun to partial shade; Caddo maple is a naturally heat-tolerant and drought-adapted selection of sugar maple (Acer saccharum) collected from the Caddo-Kiowa country of the Wichita Mountains in southwestern Oklahoma — the southern edge of the species' native range. Plants grown from seed collected at this southerly provenance are significantly better adapted to the summer heat and periodic drought of the southern plains and lower Midwest than sugar maples sourced from Pennsylvania or Vermont nurseries. The fall color is the brilliant red, orange, and yellow typical of sugar maple. Used in street tree trials in Kansas and Oklahoma where its heat tolerance has proven superior to northern-sourced maples. The best available choice when a true sugar maple is desired for gardens in zones 6–8 in the transition-zone South.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Caerulea bears semi-double, sky-blue flowers rather than the single flowers of the species, on tall spikes well suited to a moist meadow or border planting.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; camassia tolerates seasonally wet spring soil better than most bulbs but appreciates drier conditions during its summer dormancy. Caerulea bears tall, upright spikes of semi-double, clear sky-blue, star-shaped flowers in late spring, fuller and showier than the single flowers of the wild species, rising well above strappy, grass-like foliage. Native in form to wet meadows of the Pacific Northwest, it naturalizes readily in a moist border or meadow planting and combines beautifully with late tulips and ornamental grasses. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to recharge the bulb, and established clumps need little care beyond occasional division if flowering declines after many years.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Caesar weed is a tropical annual that self-sows freely in zone 9 and can become weedy in disturbed areas. The fibrous stems have commercial fiber potential.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Caesar weed is a pantropical annual or short-lived perennial mallow widely distributed in disturbed habitats throughout the tropics and naturalized in the Gulf South. The lobed leaves and small, pink, hibiscus-like flowers are moderately attractive, and the plant provides useful wildlife habitat — the burr-like fruits attach to animal fur for seed dispersal. The fibrous stems produce a strong bast fiber historically used like jute in rope and coarse textile manufacture in parts of Africa and Asia. More notable as a botanical curiosity and fiber plant than as a primary garden ornamental; useful in wildlife gardens where its fruits provide seed food and the stems provide habitat. The plant is non-native but is naturalized throughout the Gulf South.

common_name: Caesar's Brother Siberian Iris (Classic Deep Violet-Blue Iris)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; unlike bearded iris, Siberian iris rhizomes are planted a couple of inches below the soil surface and tolerate wetter soil and less division over time.
directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Introduced in the 1930s, Caesar's Brother is one of the longest-lived and most widely planted Siberian iris cultivars, producing tall, elegant, deep violet-blue-purple flowers over narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Cafe au Lait Rose Dahlia (Blush-Pink Sport of Cafe au Lait)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Cafe au Lait Rose is a blush-pink sport of the famously popular Cafe au Lait dahlia, widely grown for wedding bouquets.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants at planting time since the massive flowers can topple stems in wind. Cafe au Lait Rose, a blush-pink sport of the enormously popular Cafe au Lait dahlia, bears huge, softly ruffled dinnerplate blooms in delicate dusty rose tones, sharing its parent's dreamy, romantic color palette that has made both cultivars favorites for wedding and event florists. Disbud side buds to concentrate energy into fewer, larger blooms if maximum flower size is the goal. Deadhead spent blooms regularly, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Café au Lait Dahlia (Giant Peach-Cream Decorative Dahlia, Most Photographed Variety)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep after last frost; Café au Lait is a formal decorative dahlia type producing very large (8–12 inch) blooms on tall (4–5 foot) plants. Stake plants early — the heavy blooms on long stems require support. In zone 9, plant March–April for summer-fall bloom; the warm Gulf Coast summers can cause some bloom reduction in peak July–August heat, with best flowering in June and September–November. Pinch the growing tip when 12–18 inches tall to encourage multiple blooms per plant. The peach-cream-blush coloring is most defined in cool fall weather; summer heat can cause the coloring to wash out slightly to a paler cream.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately. Pinch growing tip when 12 inches tall. Café au Lait is arguably the most widely photographed and socially media-documented dahlia variety of the modern era — a formal decorative dahlia with dinner-plate-sized blooms (8–12 inches diameter) in the distinctive warm blush-peach-cream-coffee coloring that gives the variety its French café name. The color is not easily described in conventional color terms: it is a complex, warm-toned mixture of cream, peachy-buff, blush pink, and very light coffee-tan that shifts perceptibly across the bloom from center to edge and changes character in different lighting — appearing more coral-peachy in warm golden afternoon light and more cream-pink in cooler morning light. This complex, warm-neutral coloring has made Café au Lait the most popular dahlia in the wedding flower industry and in the aesthetic sensibility of social-media garden photography, where its warm, muted tones photograph beautifully and complement the neutral color palettes favored in contemporary interior and event design. As a garden plant, Café au Lait is physically impressive — the enormous blooms on 4–5 foot plants are genuinely spectacular from late summer through fall — with the added utility of being one of the most spectacular and long-lasting cut flowers available, vase life extending 7–10 days when cut in the morning at the proper maturity stage.

plant_note: Plant tubers after all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed.
directions: This prolific dahlia shifts through the season from vivid pink and purple to a smoky mauve, giving weeks of color changes on strong stems. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost, and pinch the growing tip early to encourage bushy, branching growth. Stake or corral tall plants and cut blooms often to keep flowers coming. In zones colder than 8, lift and store the tubers in a cool, dry place over winter.

plant_note: Plant tubers after all frost danger passes and soil is reliably above 70°F; cold soil causes rot.
directions: Set tubers knobby-side up, 2 in deep in rich, moist, well-drained soil; for a head start, pot tubers indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost date in a warm (75–80°F) location. Caladiums are prized for spectacular heart-shaped foliage in combinations of red, pink, white, and green rather than for their flowers. They excel in shady spots where little else provides vibrant color and thrive in humid conditions. In fall, before temperatures drop below 50°F, dig tubers, allow to cure for 2 weeks, and store in dry vermiculite at 60–65°F.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, peat or coir-based, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5) soil in deep shade to bright indirect light; calathea is sensitive to fluoride, chlorine, and salt in water — use rainwater or filtered water for best results. Never expose to direct sun, which bleaches and burns the foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, peat-based, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect shade; calatheas are among the most spectacularly decorative foliage plants in the world, producing large, rounded or lance-shaped leaves with intricate patterns of dark green, silvery green, and cream in bold graphic patterns that look almost painted. C. orbifolia in particular produces enormous round leaves with elegant silver stripes. The foliage of most calatheas moves with the light — leaves rise in the evening and lower in the morning in a circadian rhythm that gives the related marantas their name 'prayer plants.' In zone 10–12 calatheas thrive as outdoor shade garden plants under tree canopy; in zone 9a they are outstanding patio container plants in bright, indirect shade. They require consistently moist (but never waterlogged) soil, high humidity, and protection from drafts and direct sun.

plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Caldwell Pink is a 'found rose' rescued from an old Texas homestead by rose rustlers, and its polyantha vigor and disease resistance make it one of the toughest small shrub roses for the humid Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart for a dense flowering hedge or mass planting. Caldwell Pink is a 'found rose' — a once-common variety that fell out of the nursery trade but survived for decades at an old homesite before being rediscovered, propagated, and named by Texas rose rustlers for the town of Caldwell, Texas, where it was found. It produces a profusion of small, fully double, medium-pink pompon blooms in dense clusters nearly continuously from spring through fall, on a compact, well-branched polyantha shrub. It is extremely disease-resistant and largely free of the blackspot and mildew problems that plague many modern roses in humid climates, needing no spraying and very little care beyond an annual light shaping. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and heat, making Caldwell Pink one of the most reliable low-maintenance flowering shrubs for Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in cool soil; young plants tolerate frost and prefer cool weather.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in cool, well-drained soil in early spring. Calendula prefers cool weather and will slow or stop blooming when summer heat arrives, often rebounding in fall. Deadhead consistently to prevent seed set and extend the blooming period. The ray petals are edible and can be used as a garnish or in salads.

plant_note: Direct sow on bare soil in fall for spring germination; seeds benefit from cold stratification; calico aster also spreads readily by self-seeding and can be transplanted as container divisions in spring or fall.
directions: Calico aster is one of the most wildlife-valuable of all native asters, producing enormous quantities of tiny white flowers with magenta-to-purple centers arranged in sprays along horizontal branches — the 'calico' name aptly describes the two-tone disk flowers that change color as they age from yellow to red-purple, creating a patchwork effect. This species is distinguished from similar asters by its tolerance of dry to moist shade under tree canopy, making it one of the few native asters that genuinely thrives in partial woodland shade rather than requiring full sun. Over 70 species of specialist native bees use it as a critical late-season pollen source, and the seeds feed dozens of sparrow, junco, and finch species through fall and winter. Plant in woodland edges, naturalized areas, and native hedgerows where the naturalistic branching form and prolific flowering provide a long season of wildlife habitat.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Calico Hearts is a slow-growing miniature that needs sharp drainage and careful, infrequent watering.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Calico Hearts is a slow-growing miniature that needs sharp drainage and careful, infrequent watering. Plump, rounded, heart-shaped leaves in olive-green are speckled with irregular reddish-brown or purple blotches, a distinctive mottled, calico-like pattern that gives this small South African succulent its common name and makes it a favorite for collectors seeking unusual leaf patterning on a manageable, windowsill-friendly scale. Slow-growing and clump-forming over time, it offsets gradually from the base and is easily propagated from individual leaves that root readily when allowed to callus before placing on soil. Water sparingly and only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light, and propagate from leaf or stem cuttings.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; calico plant produces its most vivid and complex foliage colors in bright light — in deep shade the colors fade significantly toward green.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant transplants in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; calico plant (Joseph's coat alternanthera, party time plant) is a tropical South American annual grown entirely for its brilliantly colored, small foliage — the tiny, densely-packed leaves are produced in vivid combinations of red, orange, yellow, chartreuse, pink, bronze, and variously multicolored patterns depending on cultivar, creating a remarkably intense and permanent color effect that serves a similar role to coleus in partially shaded garden settings. It is used primarily as a low edging plant, knot garden element, and mosaic bedding plant where its compact, clipping-tolerant growth and intense color can be used to create formal patterns. In full sun the colors are most vivid; partial shade produces acceptable but somewhat more muted tones. Clipping to maintain compact shape is recommended. 'Red Threads' (fine-textured red), 'Yellow Fine Leaf', and 'Party Time' (pink and red) are popular selections. Frost-tender; treated as annual north of zone 9.

common_name: Calidora Alocasia (Heat- and Sun-Tolerant Upright Glossy Elephant Ear)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Calidora is notably heat- and sun-tolerant for the Alocasia genus.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun. Calidora produces large, upright, glossy medium-green leaves on a robust, fast-growing plant, standing out among Alocasia hybrids for its notable heat and sun tolerance, allowing it to thrive in more exposed Gulf South conditions than most alocasias, which typically need protected shade. Its bold, glossy foliage and vigorous habit make it a strong architectural specimen for a tropical-themed border or large container. Protect from cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit, which causes the plant to go dormant or suffer dieback.

common_name: California Alocasia (Cold-Hardy Heavily Textured Elephant Ear)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; California bears large, heavily textured green leaves and is more cold-hardy than many Alocasia selections.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. California bears large, heavily textured, deeply veined green leaves on a robust plant selected for improved cold hardiness and resistance to common Alocasia pests compared to many other selections in the genus, making it a more forgiving choice for gardeners at the cooler edge of Alocasia range. Its bold, textured foliage provides strong architectural presence in a shaded tropical-themed border or large container. Protect from direct hot sun, which scorches the leaves, and mulch heavily over winter in the coolest parts of its range.

plant_note: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, gravelly to rocky, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; California barrel cactus needs sharp drainage and full desert sun, and rots quickly in wet or heavy soil.
directions: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, gravelly to rocky, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; California barrel cactus needs sharp drainage and full desert sun, and rots quickly in wet or heavy soil. Thick, ribbed, cylindrical stems densely armed with long, curved, colorful spines ranging from yellow to red slowly grow into an iconic barrel shape over many decades, topped in summer with a ring of yellow to orange flowers followed by small yellow fruit, a familiar and long-lived architectural presence across the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts. Extremely slow-growing and long-lived, individual plants can live over a century in the wild, making a mature specimen a significant, irreplaceable landscape investment best sourced from nursery-propagated stock rather than wild-collected plants, which are protected in many areas. Water only occasionally once established, provide maximum sun and heat, and never allow the base to sit in standing water, which quickly causes fatal rot.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in well-drained, slightly acidic, dry to average, deep soil in full sun; California black oak grows on drier slopes and ridges at 2000–8000 feet elevation throughout the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges. The large, deeply lobed leaves turn gold and russet in fall.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; California black oak is the largest and most widely distributed of the California red-group oaks, growing from the Oregon border to Baja California in the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges at mid-elevations. The deeply lobed, bristle-tipped leaves (characteristic of the red oak group) are large and bold — up to 8 inches long — turning brilliant gold, orange, and russet in fall for some of the finest fall color of any California native. The large, nutritious acorns were a dietary staple of numerous Sierran indigenous cultures including the Miwok and Paiute, providing a high-calorie starch food after leaching of bitter tannins. California black oak is an important food source for Steller's jays, band-tailed pigeons, acorn woodpeckers, mule deer, and black bears in mountain habitats. A magnificent landscape tree for large-scale California and Pacific Northwest plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil; seeds germinate best in darkness, so cover lightly.
directions: Direct sow this heirloom in early spring or fall in mild climates, covering the seed since it needs darkness to sprout. Also called desert bluebells, it shrugs off cold and drought and rewards a large sowing with upward-facing, luminous blue chalices. Give it lean, well-drained soil and full sun, and avoid overwatering once established. It reseeds readily and is a favorite of bees.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall so winter rains establish seedlings, or plant nursery starts in fall to early spring, into lean, very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; California buckwheat is a foundational chaparral and coastal sage scrub shrub prized above nearly any other plant for the sheer volume and diversity of native bees, wasps, and butterflies its flowers support. Narrow, gray-green, needle-like leaves cluster along woody stems below rounded umbels of tiny white to pink flowers that bloom from late spring through fall and dry to attractive rust-brown seed heads that persist through winter and add off-season texture. It thrives on neglect once established, needing no summer irrigation and often declining if watered on the same schedule as lawns or border perennials nearby. Leave the dried flower heads standing through winter for seed-eating birds and structural interest, then lightly shape in late winter before spring growth resumes.

subcategory: native marginal aquatic tall bulrush reed
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in full sun in wet soil or shallow water (up to 12 inches deep) in zone 7–11; California Bulrush (Totora) is a tall, stout, round-stemmed native sedge found from the Pacific Coast through Central and South America — forming impressive stands of bright-green, round, rush-like stems reaching 6–10 feet that provide critical nesting, foraging, and cover habitat for wetland wildlife, and historically used by indigenous peoples for food, weaving, boat-building, and thatching.
directions: Plant Schoenoplectus californicus divisions in wet soil, pond margins, or in water up to 12 inches deep in full sun; plants spread by rhizomes to form large colonies — contain in aquatic pots for small ponds, or allow to naturalize in wildlife gardens; cut stems to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. California Bulrush (formerly Scirpus californicus, also called Totora in South America) is one of the most important wetland plants of the Western Hemisphere — forming the dominant vegetation in freshwater marshes, pond margins, and estuaries from California and the Gulf Coast through Central and South America, including the famous floating reed islands of Lake Titicaca in Peru and Bolivia, where indigenous Uros people have built entire communities on platforms woven from Totora stems for centuries. The tall, cylindrical, bright-green stems are strongly ornamental in the water garden and provide exceptional value for wildlife: dense stands shelter nesting red-winged blackbirds, provide cover for waterfowl and marsh wrens, and support aquatic invertebrates vital to fish and amphibian populations. The seeds are eaten by ducks and other waterfowl. A fast-growing, vigorous species that establishes rapidly in disturbed wetlands and along pond banks, making it useful for erosion control and wetland restoration as well as ornamental use.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out transplants in fall so roots establish over the mild coastal winter ahead of the spring bloom flush.
directions: California bush sunflower is a fast-growing, soft-leaved subshrub of coastal sage scrub from Santa Barbara south into Baja California, producing a mounded flush of golden-yellow daisy flowers with dark centers from late winter through early summer, sometimes reblooming after rain. It is among the most reliable nectar and pollen sources for native bees and butterflies during California's late-winter bloom gap, when few other perennials are flowering, and it also provides cover and seed for birds. Plants are naturally short-lived, typically fading after five to eight years, but cutting stems back hard by half after the main bloom keeps growth dense and extends vigor, and it roots readily from cuttings if replacements are needed. It thrives in poor, rocky, or clay soils with excellent drainage and needs no irrigation once established, though a hard freeze below the mid-20s F will damage or kill top growth.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in California's mild climate. Adaptable from coastal fog to dry inland slopes; performs best with a summer dry period once established. Avoid sites with prolonged hard freezes.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this adaptable shrub tolerates clay, sand, and loam equally well once established. Water regularly for the first two summers to help roots reach deep moisture, then taper to infrequent irrigation or rely on winter rainfall alone. The berries ripen from green through red to near-black, providing a long season of color and food for birds. Lightly tip-prune after fruiting to maintain a tidy shape if desired, or allow to grow into a large screening shrub.

subcategory: native American fan palm with filamentous leaves
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; California fan palm is the only palm native to western North America — growing wild at desert oases in the Colorado Desert of California and Baja California where underground water reaches the surface. More cold-hardy than W. robusta (to about 15°F) and substantially stockier in trunk, growing more slowly to a large, massively trunked specimen. The leaf segments have characteristic thread-like white filaments along their margins. A defining plant of California desert oasis landscapes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; California fan palm is the only palm species native to the wild landscapes of western North America — a native of the oasis springs and seeps of the Colorado Desert of California and adjacent Baja California, where it forms the iconic oasis groves in which the combination of towering, massively trunked palms and the lush green contrast of palm fronds against the arid desert landscape represents one of the most dramatic plant-landscape compositions in North American horticulture. The trunk of mature California fan palms is massively, impressively stocky — much wider in diameter than the slender W. robusta — developing over decades and centuries into a thick-waisted, gray-tan column of considerable girth that supports the characteristic large, circular, gray-green fan leaves. The leaf segments carry distinctive thin, white, thread-like filaments along the margins — the 'filifera' (thread-bearing) of the species name — that shimmer in breeze and sun. The full-sized crown of large, wavy-ribbed, circular fan leaves surrounded by the characteristic hanging skirt of persistent dead fronds creates the quintessential California desert-oasis palm silhouette. More cold-hardy than W. robusta (surviving to approximately 15°F) and longer-lived, developing over centuries into ancient, massive specimens of extraordinary character in suitable landscapes. The defining palm of California and the warm desert Southwest.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in fall in shade; California fawn lily requires a cool, moist growing season (spring) and summer dormancy — do not water or disturb after the foliage dies back in summer. It takes 3–5 years from a corm to reach blooming size and may take 2 years to establish after transplanting. Do not allow corms to dry out between purchase and planting.
directions: Plant corms in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full to part shade; California fawn lily is a beautiful native wildflower of the Pacific Coast ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills, producing two broad, glossy, mottled leaves (the mottling in dark and light green gives the appearance of a fawn's spots — hence 'fawn lily') and in March through May one to three reflexed, lily-like flowers of pure white to cream-white with yellow centers and gracefully swept-back petals that curve fully back like a Turk's cap, each nodding on an arching stem above the paired mottled leaves. The combination of the beautifully mottled foliage and the elegant, reflexed white flowers creates a plant of extraordinary refinement in the woodland garden. Like all erythroniums it is a spring ephemeral — disappearing completely by early summer. The cultivar 'White Beauty' is a vigorous, large-flowered selection widely available and one of the finest white flowers of the spring shade garden. It forms offsets slowly to create small but beautiful colonies over years.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown plants in fall in lean, very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; California fuchsia requires excellent drainage and no summer irrigation once established — it evolved in the Mediterranean climate of California where summer drought is the norm. Cut back hard to 6 inches in late winter to stimulate vigorous new growth for the next bloom cycle. Previously classified as Zauschneria californica.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; California fuchsia (formerly Zauschneria californica) is a California and Baja California native that produces one of the most spectacular late-season, drought-tolerant flowering displays of any western plant — a spreading, somewhat shrubby perennial with small, gray-green to silvery-hairy leaves that from August through November is completely covered in brilliant, intense, scarlet-orange to cardinal-red, tubular flowers, each 1–1.5 inches long and perfectly shaped for hummingbird pollination. The timing of the bloom — late summer through autumn — coincides exactly with the southward migration of the rufous, Anna's, and Allen's hummingbirds along the Pacific Coast, making California fuchsia one of the most important late-season hummingbird nectar sources in the western United States. It thrives in the dry, lean, Mediterranean-climate conditions of its native chaparral and coastal scrub habitat and actually resents summer watering once established. The cultivar 'Everett's Choice' and 'Catalina' are particularly vigorous and floriferous. Outstanding for California native gardens, drought-tolerant western landscaping, and any sunny, lean, dry position where a brilliant late-season display is desired.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow California Giants zinnias a quarter inch deep after the last frost once soil is reliably warm. This classic heirloom produces massive four-to-six-inch double blooms in a rainbow of colors on tall, sturdy stems ideal for cutting. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, and cut or deadhead often to keep flowers coming until frost. Give good airflow to limit powdery mildew, and enjoy the constant parade of butterflies.

common_name: California Gold Bougainvillea (Golden-Orange Vigorous Tropical Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; California Gold produces vivid golden-orange papery bracts on a vigorous, thorny climbing vine that needs a sturdy support and thrives on somewhat neglectful, dry conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun on a strong, permanent trellis, arbor, or wall, since mature vines become heavy and woody over time. California Gold produces masses of vivid golden-orange papery bracts, the true flowers being the small white blooms tucked inside, covering the vigorous, thorny vine through the warm season, especially heavily when the plant is kept on the dry, slightly stressed side, since bougainvillea blooms more prolifically with somewhat restricted water and root space than when pampered. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and is one of the more cold-hardy bougainvillea colors for the warmer parts of zone 9, though hard freezes will still cause dieback that regrows from the roots in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on bare, moist to seasonally wet soil; will self-sow and return reliably in suitable conditions.
directions: California Goldfields is a tiny native annual that forms legendary carpets of solid golden-yellow across vernal pools, coastal grasslands, and valley floors in spring, and is one of the principal wildflowers of California superbloom events in years with ample rainfall. Scatter seed in fall on bare, moist to seasonally wet, clay-heavy or sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, pressing seed lightly into the surface without covering. Plants self-sow prolifically and will re-establish year after year where conditions suit them, requiring no supplemental irrigation once the rains begin. This low-growing annual works beautifully as a groundcover in California native gardens or meadow plantings alongside other vernal pool species.

plant_note: Install plugs on close spacing in spring or fall so rhizomes can knit together into a lawn-like sward; water regularly until established, then reduce as the planting fills in.
directions: Install plugs or divisions on tight spacing in spring or fall in full sun to light shade and well-drained soil, watering consistently until the rhizomes spread and knit together into a solid patch. Once established it needs little supplemental water and can be mowed occasionally to maintain a tidy, lawn-like appearance, or left unmowed for a soft meadow look. This California native sedge spreads by rhizomes to form a fine-bladed, gray-green sward that is increasingly used as a low-water alternative to traditional turf lawns, on slopes, and in coastal and native plant gardens.

plant_note: Sow seed in fall to allow cool, moist winter conditions to break dormancy naturally; fall planting mimics the grass's native germination cycle and produces stronger first-year plants.
directions: Sow seed in fall on rocky or fast-draining soil in partial shade, particularly under native oaks or chaparral shrubs where summer soil moisture is minimal. Scratch seed lightly into the surface and allow winter rains to do most of the watering; supplemental irrigation in the first spring helps seedlings size up before summer dormancy. Plants go partially or fully dormant in summer heat, so site them where the dried foliage will be screened by surrounding plants. Once established, clumps self-sow modestly and can be divided in early fall to expand a planting.

subcategory: California native chaparral perennial pollinator wildflower
plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; California milkweed benefits from natural winter chilling and rainfall to break seed dormancy, then goes summer-dormant after flowering in its native chaparral and foothill habitat.
directions: Sow seed in fall so winter rain and cold can naturally break dormancy, in lean, rocky or sandy soil with excellent drainage and full sun; this species is native to dry chaparral, foothill, and coastal sage scrub habitats of California and goes dormant in summer after its distinctive deep maroon-purple flowers fade. The thick, woolly gray-green leaves and unusually dark flower color set it apart from most other milkweed species, and it requires very little supplemental water once established, making it well suited to Mediterranean-climate native gardens. Like other milkweeds it serves as a larval host plant for monarch butterflies and provides nectar for a range of native bees during its spring bloom.

plant_note: Set out a container-grown, cutting-propagated plant in fall so it can root in before the rainy season, giving it a trellis, fence, or shrub to twine up; seed germination is notoriously unreliable so propagation is primarily by cuttings.
directions: Set out a container-grown, cutting-propagated plant in fall so it can root in before the rainy season, giving it a trellis, fence, or shrub to twine up and part shade in hot inland gardens (it tolerates more sun near the coast).
