directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; cape honeysuckle is a South African evergreen scrambling shrub-vine that is one of the most reliable and versatile hummingbird plants for Gulf Coast and southwestern zone 9–11 gardens, producing clusters of long, tubular, brilliant scarlet-orange to orange-red, honeysuckle-like flowers in flushes from fall through spring — at the opposite end of the warm season from most summer-blooming hummingbird plants — when migrating and wintering hummingbirds most need reliable nectar sources. It grows as a large, lax, sprawling shrub or a climbing vine if given support, and can be trained against walls, over fences, or left to sprawl as a groundcover on banks. Tolerates partial shade (blooming acceptably in open tree canopy), drought, heat, poor soil, and alkaline conditions once established. In zone 9 it may freeze back in hard winters but recovers quickly from established roots. 'Aurea' (clear-yellow flowers, more refined in habit) is an attractive alternative to the standard orange form. Excellent as a slope cover, espaliered vine, and sprawling hedge.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; cape honeysuckle is extremely adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and is virtually foolproof in warm climates. Train the scrambling stems onto a support structure early — the plant does not twine or cling on its own and must be tied.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — poor, sandy, alkaline, and rocky soils are all acceptable; cape honeysuckle is not a true honeysuckle but a South African scrambling shrub that produces clusters of brilliant orange-red tubular flowers almost continuously from late fall through spring in zone 9 — filling the garden with color exactly when other flowering plants are dormant. It is extraordinary as a hummingbird and butterfly plant. The plant does not twine or cling like a vine but scrambles vigorously through other shrubs or must be tied to a trellis or fence; alternatively it makes an excellent sprawling groundcover on slopes or a large informal mound-shaped specimen shrub. A yellow-orange cultivar ('Aurea') is also available. Cape honeysuckle withstands heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil with ease once established and grows rapidly in warm weather. In zone 8 it may suffer significant frost damage but recovers vigorously from roots in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool spring soil; blooms open in response to sunshine.
directions: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained soil and full sun, where the flowers can enjoy plenty of light. The daisy-like blooms in orange, yellow, white, and salmon open when hit by the sun to reveal a dark, purple-ringed center that bees and butterflies love. Provide lean soil and let plants dry between waterings, as they tolerate drought well. Deadhead to prolong the display through the cooler part of the season.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring (or early fall) in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Nerine bowdenii is the most cold-hardy nerine species — hardy to zone 7 in well-drained soil — producing spectacular clusters of bright-pink, strap-petaled, spidery flowers on bare stems in autumn (September–November), after most other bulbs have finished; flowers appear before or with the strap-shaped leaves; naturalizes readily in mild climates.
directions: Plant bulbs with the tip just at or slightly above soil level in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; do not disturb once established; water sparingly in summer dormancy. Nerine bowdenii (Cape nerine or Bowden lily) is the most cold-hardy species in the Nerine genus — a South African native bulb from the mountains of the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal — and one of the most spectacular bulbs for fall flowering in zone 7–10. The plant produces striking, 2-foot bare stems topped with large umbels (6–8 flowers per head) of bright, vivid pink, reflexed, strap-petaled flowers with distinctively wavy, crinkled petal margins — a uniquely spidery, exotic appearance unlike any other fall bulb. The flowers appear in September through November, after the bulb's strappy, strap-shaped leaves have died back for summer — blooming from apparently bare ground, then producing the strap-like leaves after or alongside the flowers. N. bowdenii naturalizes readily into permanent clumps that increase over years and flower more prolifically as they become established. The bulbs bloom best when slightly crowded and resent disturbance. Unlike its tender relative Nerine sarniensis (Guernsey lily), N. bowdenii is hardy in zone 7 with good drainage and a sheltered position. A classic autumn bulb for the Mediterranean-climate and mild-winter garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger passes in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; plumbago establishes quickly and begins blooming within one growing season. In zone 8 it may die back to the ground in hard freezes but regrows vigorously from the roots in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; cape plumbago is one of the most beloved and widely used flowering shrubs of Gulf Coast landscapes, producing continuous clusters of sky-blue to powder-blue flowers from spring through the first frost — a color rarely achieved by other summer-blooming shrubs in the heat. The arching, semi-scandent stems naturally mound and sprawl, making it ideal for slopes, large containers, espalier on fences, or informal hedges. It is remarkably drought tolerant once established and thrives in the heat and humidity of zone 9. A white cultivar ('Alba') is also widely available. Prune back by one-third in early spring to encourage fresh, dense regrowth and a compact habit; in zone 9 it remains evergreen year-round. An outstanding long-season butterfly and bee plant, particularly attractive to swallowtail butterflies.

common_name: Cape Primrose (Nodding Violet, Trailing Cape Primrose, Saxicolous Streptocarpus)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-draining, peat-based or coir-based potting mix; Streptocarpus saxorum is particularly susceptible to root rot — use a fast-draining mix and allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings. It thrives in hanging baskets or cascading over the edge of containers. Prefers moderate temperatures (60–80°F) and avoids extreme summer heat. Blooms nearly continuously in good conditions. Propagate from leaf cuttings or stem tip cuttings. Excellent on a bright, cool, shaded porch in zone 9 from spring through fall, with winter indoors.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-draining, porous potting mix — Cape Primrose produces its best bloom in bright indirect light and will fail in dim positions while being scorched by any direct sun exposure. Streptocarpus saxorum is a compact, trailing to semi-prostrate perennial native to Tanzania (and the broader East African highlands) in the Gesneriaceae family, one of approximately 155 Streptocarpus species and one of the most delicate and graceful of the trailing gesneriads for container and hanging basket culture. The plant produces trailing stems of small (0.75–1 inch), round, velvety, mid-green leaves with a softly hairy texture. From among the leaves, delicate, thin flower stalks emerge throughout the growing season carrying one or two pale lavender to soft lilac flowers at the tip — each flower a small (1-inch), tubular, slightly two-lipped bloom with a white throat and five spreading rounded lobes, borne on long, arching pedicels that nod gracefully in the slightest air movement. The overall effect of multiple cascading stems with dozens of nodding lavender flowers is charming, elegant, and refined. S. saxorum's relatively compact form, continuous bloom habit, and tolerance of lower light levels than many flowering plants make it an excellent choice for shaded porches, indoor bright-window positions, and cool, sheltered shade gardens in warm climates. Often grown as a houseplant at the boundary between indoor and outdoor culture. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Divide established clumps or set out nursery starts in spring, planting at the same depth they were growing and watering in well to establish the fine root system.
directions: Plant divisions or containerized starts in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil, siting in full sun to light shade; this South African restio tolerates both boggy soil near water features and moderate garden watering once established. It resents hard freezes and is best reserved for mild coastal or Mediterranean-climate gardens. The wiry, jointed, dark-green stems grow in dense upright clumps that resemble a rush or horsetail and bear small brown flower clusters near the stem tips in summer, giving strong vertical texture near ponds, in modern plantings, or as a textural accent among succulents and grasses.

plant_note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; never use fertilized potting mix, garden soil, or tap water, all of which harm this plant.
directions: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; never use fertilized potting mix, garden soil, or tap water, all of which harm this plant. Long, narrow, strap-shaped leaves are covered in reddish, sticky, glandular tentacles that glisten with dewy droplets and slowly curl around any small insect unlucky enough to land and become trapped, one of the easiest and most forgiving carnivorous plants for beginners due to its tolerance of average humidity and simple care requirements compared to fussier carnivorous species. Native to nutrient-poor, seasonally wet fynbos habitat in South Africa's Cape region, it self-sows readily under good growing conditions, producing abundant fine seed and volunteer seedlings, and blooms with small pink flowers on tall stalks well above the sticky leaves. Keep the growing medium constantly moist with pure water, provide bright light for the best dew production, and feed occasionally with small insects if grown indoors away from a natural insect supply.

common_name: Cape York Lily (Aussie Plume, Native Turmeric)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to dappled shade; Cape York lily is an Australian rainforest curcuma adapted to warm, humid shade conditions and produces a stunning, upright plume of white, pink, or lilac-purple bracts in summer — one of the most ornamental of all gingers.
directions: Plant rhizome sections 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; allow rhizomes to dry and go dormant in winter. Curcuma australasica (Cape York lily or Aussie plume) is an Australian native curcuma — one of very few curcuma species native outside of South and Southeast Asia — found in the rainforests of Cape York Peninsula in far north Queensland. It produces attractive, broadly lance-shaped, medium-green leaves and upright, compact flower 'cones' 10–14 inches tall composed of overlapping, overlapping, boat-shaped bracts in white, pink-tipped white, or lilac-purple, with tiny, cream-yellow true flowers emerging between the bracts. The Australian origin gives it slightly different cultural requirements from Asian curcumas — it prefers the seasonal rhythm of a wet summer and dry winter characteristic of tropical Queensland. As a cut flower, the inflorescences last 2–3 weeks in a vase. In zone 9–12 shade gardens, it thrives in the same conditions as other gingers: moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in dappled shade. A lovely, rarely-grown species for ginger collectors and tropical garden enthusiasts.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early fall or plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; Cappadocian navelwort performs best in dappled or half shade with consistent moisture. The cultivar Cherry Ingram has slightly larger, more intensely blue flowers; Starry Eyes has distinctive blue-and-white bicolor petals. It is more long-lived than the spring-flowering O. verna.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; Cappadocian navelwort is a low-growing shade perennial from Turkey producing small, perfect, pure sky-blue flowers with a white eye — identical in form to forget-me-not flowers but more intensely colored, longer-blooming, and on a more reliably perennial plant. The flowers appear in early to mid spring in loose sprays above neat mounds of dark-green, heart-shaped, somewhat hairy leaves and have a particularly clear, clean blue that is outstanding in the shade garden. Unlike the more common spring navelwort (O. verna), which dies back and goes dormant in summer, O. cappadocica is reliably evergreen or semi-evergreen and maintains its attractive foliage through the growing season as a groundcover. The cultivar Cherry Ingram is the most floriferous selection; Starry Eyes has bicolored flowers with a blue center and white picotee edge to the petals — a genuinely beautiful and unusual flower form. An outstanding companion for hellebores, epimediums, and ferns in the woodland garden.

plant_note: Surface sow, as the seed needs light; Cappuccino blooms the first year from an early start, producing warm mahogany-brown flowers ringed in gold, a distinctive departure from the solid yellow of the classic wild black-eyed Susan.
directions: Surface sow in well-drained, average soil in full sun, since the fine seed needs light to germinate well. Cappuccino produces richly colored flowers with a warm mahogany-brown center zone bordered by a bright golden-yellow edge, a striking bicolor combination that stands out among the many solid-yellow black-eyed Susan cultivars available. Grown as a short-lived perennial or reseeding annual depending on climate, it blooms heavily from summer into fall and makes an excellent cut flower, drawing bees and butterflies throughout its bloom period. Deadheading spent flowers extends the bloom season, and leaving a few seed heads to mature late in the season allows it to self-sow for the following year.

common_name: Captain Rawes Camellia (Original 1820s Rose-Pink Reticulata Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Captain Rawes was the first Camellia reticulata introduced to Britain in the 1820s from Yunnan, China.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind since reticulata camellias are less cold-hardy than japonica types. Captain Rawes was the first reticulata camellia brought to the West from Yunnan, China in the 1820s, and it remains prized for large, semi-double, rose-pink blooms up to 5-6 inches across on an upright shrub or small tree with distinctively large, matte, leathery leaves that set the species apart from japonica and sasanqua camellias. It grows more openly and slowly than japonica types and blooms in mid-to-late winter into spring. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

common_name: Captain Romance Calla Lily (Deep Red-Pink Captain Series)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Captain Romance is part of the vigorous, large-flowered Captain series of colored calla lily hybrids.
directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where hot afternoon sun will not scorch the foliage. Captain Romance bears large, richly colored deep red-pink spathes on a vigorous plant, part of the widely grown Captain series of colored calla lily hybrids bred for strong stems, generous bloom, and reliable garden and cut-flower performance. Narrow, glossy green leaves rise from the rhizome through summer before the plant goes dormant in fall. In zones 8-10 it can be left dry in the ground through a mild winter, while in colder climates the rhizomes should be lifted and stored dry like dahlia tubers. Reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall to encourage dormancy.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Caradonna is prized for its nearly black flower stems, which contrast dramatically with the violet-blue flowers and remain ornamental even after the petals fade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Caradonna is one of the most widely planted hardy salvias, valued for its slender, nearly black flower stems topped with dense spikes of rich violet-blue flowers that create a striking two-tone vertical accent through the front and middle of a sunny border. Shearing the plant back by about half after the first flush of bloom encourages a strong second and sometimes third round of flowers into late summer. It is drought-tolerant once established, rarely bothered by deer or rabbits, and draws bees and hummingbirds throughout its long bloom season; in hot, humid zone 9 summers it may decline and is best treated as a shorter-lived perennial refreshed every few years.

common_name: Carajuru (Chica Vine, Blood Vine, Bejuco de Indio)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in late spring on a strong trellis or arbor in full sun to partial shade; Fridericia chica (formerly Bignonia chica, Arrabidaea chica) is a vigorous tropical vine suited to zone 10-11 outdoor culture. It grows rapidly and blooms profusely in the warm months with clusters of rosy-pink to magenta trumpet flowers. The leaves have been used for millennia as a source of a red-orange to brick-red natural dye ('chica' dye) by indigenous peoples of the Amazon Basin for body painting and ceremonial use. The dye color comes from the carotenoid pigment bixin. Propagate from cuttings.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Carajuru blooms most prolifically in full sun and produces attractive foliage display in partial shade. Fridericia chica (formerly Arrabidaea chica, Bignonia chica) is a vigorous, woody, tendril-climbing vine native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and tropical South America (Peru, Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela) in the Bignoniaceae family — one of the most historically significant ornamental plants of the tropical Americas for a quality beyond its ornamental flower display: its leaves yield 'carajuru' or 'chica,' a brilliant red-orange to brick-red natural dye that has been used by indigenous peoples of the Amazon Basin for body decoration, face painting, textile dyeing, and ceremonial preparation for thousands of years, and that remains in use today. The vine produces clusters of attractive, rosy-pink to magenta-pink, 1.5-inch, tubular trumpet flowers with five spreading petal lobes, produced through the warm months and attracting hummingbirds. The compound leaves (2 leaflets + tendril) contain the carotenoid pigment bixin and related compounds responsible for the red dye — the same class of compound that gives annatto its orange color. Beyond its ethnobotanical significance, F. chica is a fast-growing, flowering tropical vine with genuine ornamental value in zone 10-12 warm garden conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Caramel bears unusual soft apricot-caramel flowers that deepen slightly toward the center, a warmer, more muted tone than the bright golden-yellow typical of most coreopsis cultivars, held above a compact, tidy mound of narrow foliage. It flowers heavily from early summer into fall and draws bees and small pollinators, tolerating heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first flush of bloom to encourage a fresh round of flowers and keep the habit tidy; divide congested clumps every few years in spring if the center begins to thin.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Caramel is a heat-tolerant Heuchera villosa selection that holds its color and vigor better than many Heuchera americana hybrids in Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, with some morning sun to develop the richest color; Caramel is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction bred from heat-tolerant Heuchera villosa parentage, producing rounded, ruffled leaves that emerge apricot-orange and mature to a warm amber-caramel with rosy undertones, deepening further as nights cool in fall. The villosa heritage gives Caramel notably better tolerance of Gulf South heat and humidity than many hosta-and-heuchera-border classics, which can struggle or rot in a wet zone 9 summer. Small white flowers appear on wiry stems in early summer but are secondary to the foliage display. Give it consistent moisture without waterlogging, since good drainage matters more than rich soil for keeping the crown from rotting. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 3-4 years, and remove tattered old leaves in late winter to make way for fresh spring growth.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Caramel shows better heat tolerance than many dark-leafed heucheras and performs reasonably well in zone 8–9 with afternoon shade and consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Caramel heuchera is one of the most warm-toned and visually distinctive Heuchera x villosa hybrids, producing large, maple-shaped leaves in a glowing amber-to-caramel color that is brightest in spring when leaves first unfurl and in fall when cooler temperatures intensify the coloring. This cultivar has H. villosa parentage that makes it significantly more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many modern heuchera hybrids — an important quality for Southern and Gulf Coast gardens where most coral bells struggle in summer. The loose mound of large, peach-to-caramel leaves acts as a bold ground-level accent that combines exceptionally well with blue-green hostas, blue-leafed ferns, and dark-colored astilbes. Small pinkish flowers appear on wiry scapes in summer. Divide every 3 years when the crown heaves, replanting the youngest outer rosettes at proper soil depth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring when soil is warm; Cardboard Palm grows slowly — a single new set of leaves per year is normal. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. In zone 9a, protect from extended hard freezes; the foliage may brown below 25°F but established plants typically resprout from the crown. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — keep away from children and pets.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, sandy or gritty soil; Cardboard Palm is extremely drought-tolerant once established and will rot in wet, poorly-drained conditions. Zamia furfuracea is a cycad (an ancient gymnosperm, not a true palm) native to the coastal sand dunes and scrub of Veracruz, Mexico. It is one of the most widely planted landscape cycads in Gulf Coast and Florida gardens, prized for its symmetrical rosette of tough, leathery, dark olive-green fronds with broad, felt-covered leaflets that have the exact texture and appearance of corrugated cardboard — the characteristic that gives the plant its common name. The extremely slow growth rate (one complete flush of new leaves per year), prehistoric architectural form, and rugged adaptability to dry, poor, salt-exposed coastal soils make it an ideal low-maintenance specimen for zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes. Cardboard Palm is an excellent partial-shade plant under mature trees where other ornamentals fail — its deep-green leaves brighten shaded spots and it tolerates the root competition and dry shade of live oak canopies. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic to humans, dogs, and cats — the seeds and starchy trunk contain macrozamin and other cycasin compounds that cause liver failure.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; a western North American native perennial with brilliant scarlet flowers that are outstanding for hummingbirds and are held on long sticky stems — the catchfly characteristics give it a distinctive tactile quality in the garden.
directions: Direct sow in spring, or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost risk has passed; cardinal catchfly prefers dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and is drought-tolerant once established. Silene laciniata is a native wildflower of the Pacific Coast ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills, producing long-stemmed, brilliant scarlet flowers with fringed (lacinate) petals on sticky, 12–36 inch stems from spring through fall; the vivid red flowers are a magnet for hummingbirds and are among the most spectacular of all native red wildflowers. It is more heat- and drought-tolerant than many Silene species and is suitable for dry woodland edges, rocky slopes, and naturalized gardens in the western US and in the drier parts of the Southeast. The sticky stems deter crawling insects from reaching the flowers.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed before sowing to speed germination; provide a trellis.
directions: Nick and soak the hard seeds overnight, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis, pole, or fence. This vigorous vine climbs six to twelve feet and carries deep-red, white-throated flowers that hummingbirds and pollinators adore, along with delicate fern-like foliage. Give it full sun and steady moisture through the growing season. Provide sturdy support early, as the twining stems grow quickly once warm weather arrives.

common_name: Cardinal Creeper (Red Morning Glory, Hybrid Cypress Vine)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in full sun after last frost in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil; cardinal creeper is a vigorous annual hybrid vine (cross between Ipomoea quamoclit and I. coccinea) combining the finely divided, feathery foliage of cypress vine with slightly larger, cardinal-red, star-shaped flowers; extremely fast-growing, blooms summer through frost, and attracts hummingbirds prolifically.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms; nick or soak seeds 24 hours before planting; the vine grows quickly to 6–15 feet with minimal care. Ipomoea x multifida (cardinal creeper or cardinal vine) is a naturally occurring hybrid between cypress vine (I. quamoclit) and red morning glory (I. coccinea) — combining the most appealing ornamental features of both parents. From cypress vine, it inherits the deeply pinnately cut, feathery, bright-green foliage that creates an extraordinarily delicate, lacy texture. From red morning glory, it inherits slightly larger, more robust flowers (3/4–1 inch across) of the same intense cardinal-red as its parents. The result is a vigorous, fast-growing, annual ornamental vine that covers trellises, fences, and arbors with a curtain of delicate, feathery foliage and an abundance of small, brilliant-red, star-shaped tubular flowers from summer through fall. The flowers are irresistible to hummingbirds, which visit constantly throughout the day. The vine self-sows readily in warm climates and can be treated as a perennial in zone 9–10. A classic hummingbird garden plant that requires almost no care once established on a trellis.

plant_note: Surface-sow seed (do not cover — seed needs light to germinate) indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; seed requires light and warmth to germinate. Transplant to the garden after frost danger passes, placing in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near water features, rain gardens, or boggy areas; cardinal flower produces brilliant scarlet flower spikes from midsummer into fall that are the premier nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds in eastern North America. The intensity of the red is almost unmatched in the native plant palette. Plants are short-lived perennials that self-seed freely — allow some seedlings to remain to perpetuate the colony, as individual plants typically live only 2–3 years. Division of offsets (basal rosettes) in early fall also maintains the planting. Plants tolerate standing water and thrive along stream banks and pond edges. The great blue lobelia (Lobelia siphilitica) is a closely related blue-flowered species equally valuable for pollinators.

plant_note: Start dormant tubers in shallow trays of barely moist mix in late winter to early spring, tuber crown just at the soil surface. Sold and grown as a potted houseplant; goes dormant and can be stored dry over winter like other tuberous sinningias.
directions: A tuberous, shrubby gesneriad grown for its clusters of brilliant red-orange tubular flowers held above velvety, silver-haired foliage, formerly classified in the genus Rechsteineria. Give it bright indirect light — a lightly shaded east or south window works well — and pot in a loose, well-drained mix, since the tuber rots quickly in wet, heavy soil. Water thoroughly and let the top of the mix dry before watering again, and stop watering once foliage yellows in fall so the tuber can rest dry and cool through winter. Its hairy leaves and stems make it prone to water-spotting, so water at the soil line rather than overhead and keep it away from cold drafts.

common_name: Cardinal de Richelieu Rose (Deep Purple-Violet Gallica Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinal de Richelieu is a classic 19th-century Gallica rose, blooming once in a single heavy spring flush like other old Gallicas.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinal de Richelieu tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough 19th-century Gallica. Introduced in France in the 1840s, it bears richly fragrant, fully double flowers that open deep magenta-crimson and age to a striking dark purple-violet, among the darkest colors found in old garden roses, set against dense, relatively thornless, arching canes and matte green foliage. Like other Gallicas it blooms just once, in a spectacular, heavily perfumed flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season, so it suits a mixed shrub border or dedicated old-rose garden better than a spot where repeat bloom is expected. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering rather than the intensive spray programs modern roses often require.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–12; Cardinal's Guard (Firespike) is a large, shade-tolerant tropical shrub from the Caribbean and Central America — naturalized in South Florida and widely grown throughout Gulf Coast gardens — bearing spectacular, tall, brilliant-red, erect flower spikes of small, waxy, tubular flowers in fall and winter that create an extraordinary display in the shade garden and are magnets for hummingbirds during fall migration.
directions: Plant Odontonema tubaeforme in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment and through summer; cut back hard in late winter (before new growth emerges) to encourage compact, bushy growth and prevent woodiness; propagate easily from stem cuttings. Cardinal's Guard is one of the most valuable shade-garden flowering shrubs for the Gulf Coast — its spectacular scarlet-red flower spikes in fall and winter create color in shaded spots at a season when most other plants have stopped blooming, and the flowers are an important fuel stop for hummingbirds during fall migration. The plant performs remarkably well in the partial shade of large trees, where most other fall-blooming shrubs fail to flower well; in deep shade, it will grow vegetatively but reduces flowering. In zone 9, it dies back to the ground after hard frost and re-emerges from the roots in spring, re-establishing quickly to bloom again by October–November. In zone 10–12, it grows as a substantial, multi-stemmed shrub year-round. The tall, elegant flower spikes with their waxy, bright-red individual flowers are also excellent cut flowers. An indispensable plant for Gulf Coast butterfly and hummingbird gardens.

common_name: Carefree Beauty Rose (Cold-Hardy Own-Root Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Carefree Beauty was bred by Iowa State University professor Griffith Buck as part of a program developing own-root, winter-hardy, disease-resistant roses that need no spraying or winter protection, and it performs equally well across a wide climate range from the northern Midwest to the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Bred by Dr. Griffith Buck at Iowa State University and introduced in 1977, Carefree Beauty is one of the best-known results of his decades-long program to develop tough, own-root roses that survive harsh Midwestern winters without protection and resist disease without spraying — goals that happen to also produce excellent performance in the hot, humid Gulf South. It bears large, semi-double, clear pink blooms with a light fragrance in generous flushes from late spring through fall, followed by an abundant crop of showy orange-red hips that provide fall and winter interest and feed birds. The vigorous, upright shrub shows strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew and needs minimal care once established. Prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood, and leave some hips on the plant through fall for ornamental and wildlife value.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings (wear gloves — milky latex is an irritant) or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade after frost; Caribbean copper plant grows fastest and colors most intensely in full sun; partial shade produces somewhat less vivid coloring but is acceptable.
directions: Root stem cuttings (caution — wear gloves, latex is a skin and eye irritant) or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; Caribbean copper plant is a tropical American shrub or small tree grown entirely for its spectacular, deep-mahogany to wine-red, rounded foliage — the constantly produced, oval, alternate leaves emerge in brilliant coppery-red and mature to deep burgundy-maroon, maintaining their rich coloring throughout the season. In the tropical garden it provides a bold, jewel-toned color anchor that contrasts dramatically with lime-green foliage (aralia, euphorbia tirucalli 'Sticks on Fire'), silver-gray plants, and orange-flowered tropical perennials. It is fast-growing to 10–15 feet in tropical climates, functioning as a screening shrub or specimen small tree; in cooler zones 9 gardens it may be damaged by hard frost but resprouts from the roots. Insignificant yellowish flowers. All parts contain toxic, milky latex — handle with gloves and avoid eye contact. Excellent as a bold color contrast in mixed tropical borders.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck just above the soil surface in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Caribbean spider lily is native to the islands of the Caribbean and produces large, white, spider-like flowers with the characteristic Hymenocallis 'cup and strap' form — a central funnel-cup connecting the bases of long, narrow, spreading, strap-like perianth segments. It is strongly fragrant in the evening. In zone 9 it remains in the ground as a perennial; bring indoors in winter in colder zones.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Caribbean spider lily is a bold, tropical Hymenocallis species from the Caribbean islands — producing in summer umbels of large, pure-white, powerfully fragrant, spider-lily flowers in the distinctive Hymenocallis form: a central, flared funnel-cup at the heart of the flower, from the margins of which radiate six long, narrow, reflexed, strap-like perianth segments creating the signature spider-lily silhouette of a central cup surrounded by long, radiating white streamers. Each flower in the 3–8 flower umbel spans 6–8 inches across; a mature clump in bloom is a striking tropical display. The fragrance is very strong and sweet, most intense in the evening, carrying through the summer garden air. The broad, bright-green, strap-shaped, glossy leaves form handsome clumps even when not in flower — providing bold, tropical-looking foliage throughout the summer. It thrives in the warm, humid summer conditions of zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens in partial shade, where it naturalizes into ever-larger, more floriferous clumps over time. Outstanding combined with other bold, tropical-looking shade plants — cannas, elephant ears, gingers — for a lush, tropical summer border.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; caricature plant is excellent in partial shade where other tropical foliage plants such as coleus and impatiens also perform well.
directions: Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade; caricature plant is a tropical shrub from New Guinea and the Pacific Islands that is grown entirely for its extraordinary variegated foliage — large, shiny, oval leaves boldly streaked, blotched, and suffused with yellow, cream, rose-pink, or purple-red markings on a dark-green background, with the irregular patterning suggesting (to imaginative observers) the exaggerated features of cartoon faces or caricatures, giving the plant its common name. The color intensity and pattern of the leaf markings vary with the amount of light — plants in brighter partial shade develop the most vivid contrasts, while plants in deeper shade become more uniformly green. Small, tubular, purplish-red flowers appear occasionally on mature plants in tropical conditions but are secondary to the foliage display. Widely grown as a houseplant and greenhouse specimen in cool climates; in zone 10–12 it functions as a year-round outdoor foliage shrub of considerable ornamental impact.

common_name: Carillon Japanese Snowbell (Weeping White-Flowered Snowbell Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or large shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Carillon is a weeping, pendulous-form Japanese snowbell suited to smaller gardens, and does not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally as an understory planting beneath high-canopy shade; Japanese snowbell is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Carillon grows in a distinctly weeping, pendulous form, its cascading branches hung with white, bell-shaped flowers in late spring to early summer, forming a broad, shrubby mound rather than the upright tree shape typical of the species. Its smaller, weeping habit suits a spot where a full-sized snowbell tree would be too large, such as near a patio or at the front of a shaded border. Mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches.

plant_note: Plant offsets or leaf cuttings in spring into very well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright to moderate shade; unlike most succulents, Gasteria naturally grows understory in rock crevices and scrubby thicket shade and scorches in unfiltered afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright to moderate shade; carinated gasteria is a South African succulent adapted to grow under bushes and in rocky crevices, and it genuinely prefers protection from direct, intense sun, unlike the vast majority of succulents grown in full exposure. Thick, tongue-shaped, dark green leaves are often patterned with rough, wart-like tubercles or pale spots and are arranged in a low, two-ranked or spiraling rosette that stays compact for years. Slender, arching flower stalks bear pendant, gasteria-shaped (stomach-shaped) orange-pink tubular flowers over an extended bloom season, drawing hummingbirds and sunbirds in its native range. It offsets readily at the base and can also be propagated from individual leaf cuttings allowed to callus before rooting, making it easy to share and multiply as a durable, low-light houseplant or shaded container succulent.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter through spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Carissa is one of the most compact and slow-growing Chinese holly cultivars — maintaining a mounded form of 3–4 feet without frequent pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Carissa is a compact, slow-growing Chinese holly (Ilex cornuta) cultivar with a distinctive characteristic that sets it apart from all other Chinese holly cultivars: its leaves have only a single terminal spine rather than the multiple sharp spines of standard Chinese holly. This makes Carissa the most maintenance-friendly and user-safe holly cultivar for residential settings — plants around walkways, children's play areas, and high-traffic zones where the multiple sharp spines of Rotunda, Burford, and other Chinese holly types would create hazards. The deep, lustrous, dark-green foliage is more elongated and less glossy than some Chinese holly types but still attractive and evergreen year-round. Carissa is a female clone and requires a nearby male Chinese holly for berry production — when pollinated, it produces attractive red berries. The compact, naturally mounded habit (3–4 feet) requires minimal pruning to maintain in typical landscape situations. Extremely tough — tolerating clay soil, drought once established, heat, and partial shade without significant performance loss. Essentially pest-free, deer-resistant, and pollution-tolerant, making it practical for urban and suburban foundation plantings.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Carlton is widely regarded as one of the very best daffodils for naturalizing and perennializing in the low-chill winters of the South, multiplying into large drifts over the years where many other daffodils decline.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Carlton bears large, soft yellow flowers with a slightly darker trumpet in a classic large-cup form, and has earned a reputation as one of the single best-performing daffodils for naturalizing across the South, reliably returning and multiplying into substantial drifts for decades with essentially no care, unlike many Northern-bred daffodils that dwindle after a year or two in mild-winter climates. Its fragrant flowers open in early to midspring and are excellent both left in the garden and cut for indoor arrangements. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding, tying, or cutting it, since the leaves recharge the bulb for next year's flowers, and divide congested clumps every several years after foliage yellows if bloom quality declines.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–12 weeks before fall planting (August–September in zone 9) in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; carnations are outstanding cool-season flowers in zone 9, blooming prolifically from winter through spring before summer heat stops them — treat as a winter annual in zone 9.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–12 weeks before transplanting; plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Dianthus caryophyllus (carnation or clove pink) is the florist's carnation — one of the world's most commercially important cut flowers, comprising billions of stems in the global cut flower trade annually alongside roses and chrysanthemums. The classic double-flowered, fringed-petal blooms in red, pink, white, yellow, orange, purple, and bicolor shades have been cultivated for over 2,000 years; the spicy-sweet, clove-like fragrance of old-fashioned varieties is one of the most beloved flower scents. Modern commercial carnations are often scentless but long-lasting; old-fashioned cottage garden varieties retain the characteristic clove fragrance. Carnations are also edible flowers — the petals (with the bitter white base removed) are sweet and mildly spicy, used to flavor wines, liqueurs (Chartreuse), and desserts; they are the traditional garnish for some Spanish and Greek dishes. In zone 9, carnations are outstanding winter-spring bloomers; plant in fall for a February–May flower season. Standard (tall) types need staking; compact border carnations are self-supporting.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.
directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Carnegie is a long-standing, dependable pure white hyacinth cultivar, its dense spike of waxy florets opening clean white with none of the pink or cream undertones some white hyacinths show, and carrying the same powerful, sweet fragrance typical of the species. Its versatile, neutral color makes it easy to combine with any other spring bulb, and it has remained a florist and bulb-forcing standard for decades. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled hyacinth bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since the bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for good flowering in subsequent years without repeat chilling.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Carnival's cream-variegated foliage brightens in partial shade — full afternoon sun in zone 9 may bleach the cream margins to white and scorch the leaf tips.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Carnival is a variegated liriope cultivar with cream to creamy-white longitudinal striping on dark-green, strap-like leaves — forming compact, mounding clumps of distinctive two-tone foliage that brightens shade garden areas with the cream-on-green contrast effect common to effective shade variegated plants. Carnival's pink to rose-pink flower spikes (a warmer, pinker color than the purple-violet of most liriope cultivars) rise above the variegated foliage in summer and create an attractive three-color combination of cream-striped green leaves, pink flower spikes, and eventually blue-black berries in fall. The pink flowers rather than typical purple flowers are Carnival's most distinctive attribute among variegated liriope selections — the flower color combines with the cream foliage variegation to create a lighter, airier, more pastel effect than dark-purple-flowered types. Like all liriopes, Carnival is adaptable and low-maintenance in zone 9 — tolerating heat, drought, shade, and root competition from trees while remaining evergreen through mild Gulf South winters. The variegated foliage is most effective when mass-planted in sizeable groupings where the light-reflective cream-and-green texture creates a visual effect visible from a distance. Shear to 3 inches in late winter to remove old foliage before new spring growth emerges.

common_name: Carnivorous Bromeliad (Lantern Bromeliad, Berterone's Catopsis, Tank Trap Bromeliad)
plant_note: Grow mounted on bark or cork, or in a small pot with bromeliad bark mix, in partial shade with good air circulation; Catopsis berteroniana is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 10-12 outdoor culture or protected porch/indoor culture in zone 9. Keep the central tank (cup) filled with rainwater or distilled water — the waxy, pale yellow-white powdery coating on the inner tank walls may trap insects that slide in and drown, contributing to the plant's nutrition. Clean the tank occasionally to remove debris. Propagate from offsets.
directions: Grow in partial shade to bright indirect light in bromeliad bark medium or mounted on bark — Carnivorous Bromeliad performs best in the dappled light of a shaded outdoor position or bright indoor location with good air circulation. Catopsis berteroniana is a small to medium-sized epiphytic bromeliad native to southern Florida (where it is endangered), the Caribbean, Central America, and South America in the Bromeliaceae family, noteworthy as the only bromeliad species with a convincing scientific case for genuine carnivory. The evidence, documented in ecological studies, is based on a distinctive combination of features not found in other bromeliads: the smooth, very steeply angled inner walls of the central tank are coated with an unusual white, powdery, waxy substance (trichomes) that reflects UV light — attracting insects — while simultaneously making the walls so slippery that trapped insects cannot escape. The drowned insects accumulate in the tank and are thought to be digested by the plant's absorptive trichomes. While not as definitively carnivorous as Sarracenia or Nepenthes, the adaptation appears functional. The plant itself is attractive: pale yellow-green to whitish foliage forms an open, lantern-like rosette. It produces a tall, erect inflorescence with small, white to yellow flowers. An unusual and scientifically interesting collector's bromeliad.

common_name: Carol Mackie Daphne (Variegated Fragrant Pink-Flowered Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Carol Mackie bears cream-margined variegated leaves and intensely fragrant pale pink spring flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun; Daphne resents disturbance once established, so choose a permanent site and avoid transplanting. Carol Mackie bears blue-green leaves crisply edged in creamy white through the growing season, brightening the shrub even out of bloom, and in mid-spring produces clusters of small, intensely fragrant pale pink flowers that perfume the surrounding garden. Its compact, rounded habit and season-long variegated foliage make it a favorite specimen near an entry or path where its fragrance can be enjoyed up close. Avoid heavy pruning and wet feet, both of which Daphne tolerates poorly; all parts are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina allspice blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates significant shade and is one of the few large flowering shrubs that performs well in light to moderate shade.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina allspice blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates significant shade and is one of the few large flowering shrubs that performs well in light to moderate shade. Calycanthus floridus is a deciduous native shrub of the southeastern United States with a rounded, spreading habit and remarkable, deeply fragrant, strap-petaled flowers with brick-red to burgundy petals that resemble no other flower in the garden; blooming from late spring through summer, the flowers have a complex, spicy-sweet scent compared variously to strawberries, banana, and pineapple, and the aromatic quality extends to the crushed leaves and bark. The plant suckers gently from the base over time and can be used as an informal hedge, woodland shrub border specimen, or under-planted beneath large trees; it is completely carefree once established in zones 4–9.

plant_note: Plant young container-grown trees in fall in wet, poorly drained, seasonally flooded soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina ash is a small wetland tree of swamps, sloughs, and pond margins across the Gulf Coastal Plain and tolerates prolonged standing water.
directions: Plant young container-grown trees in fall in wet to seasonally flooded, poorly drained soil in full sun to partial shade, since Carolina ash naturally roots in cypress-tupelo swamps, sloughs, and pond margins where standing water lingers for much of the year. It stays small compared to other native ashes, usually developing a multi-trunked, shrubby to small-tree form with glossy compound leaves, and its inflated, corky-winged seed pods float on floodwater to disperse, giving the tree its 'pop ash' nickname. Inconspicuous spring flowers provide early nectar for native bees before the leaves fully emerge, and the seeds are eaten by waterfowl and other wetland wildlife. It is a dependable small shade tree for the wettest corners of a Gulf Coast landscape, including pond edges, rain garden basins, and low spots that hold water after heavy rain.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained to moist, acidic, sandy or loamy soil; Carolina bayberry tolerates poor, infertile, wet, and acidic conditions where most shrubs fail. Cold-stratify seeds for 3 months before sowing.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, acidic, sandy or poor soil in full sun; Carolina bayberry is a southeastern native shrub closely related to but distinct from the wax myrtle (Morella cerifera) — it is more compact and cold-hardy, with narrower leaves and slightly smaller, waxy gray berries on the female plants. Like all bayberries, only female plants produce berries, and one male is needed per 4–6 females for berry set. The fragrant, waxy berries were historically used to make bayberry candles, soap, and as a flavoring. The aromatic foliage is evergreen to semi-evergreen, releasing a pleasant spicy-resinous scent when crushed. Excellent for dry, infertile, sandy, acidic sites, roadsides, and coastal landscapes in zones 5–9 where it fixes nitrogen through root associations and requires virtually no care once established.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina bogmint grows naturally in the same wet pine savannas and seepage bogs as pitcher plants along the South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida Panhandle coastal plain.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade. Carolina bogmint is a showy member of the mint family native to wet pine savannas and seepage bogs of the South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida Panhandle coastal plain, producing dense, rounded heads of pink-purple, two-lipped flowers in summer that stand out against the low, grassy texture of a typical bog garden planting. It grows in the same nutrient-poor, consistently wet, acidic ground favored by pitcher plants and orchids, making it a natural companion plant that adds late-summer color once the spring pitcher plant flowers have faded. Keep the soil constantly moist to wet and avoid fertilizing, since like its bog neighbors it is adapted to low-nutrient conditions and rich garden soil favors weeds over this specialized wetland native. Established clumps slowly spread by rhizome in a favorable bog garden setting.

common_name: Carolina Buckthorn (Native Understory Tree with Red-to-Black Fruit)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Carolina Buckthorn is a native understory tree found across the southeastern and south-central US, including Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas, and Alabama, and is unrelated to the invasive European buckthorns.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it as an understory or woodland-edge tree where it naturally occurs. Carolina Buckthorn is a native small tree or large shrub found across the southeastern and south-central United States, valued for its clusters of small berries that ripen through a striking progression of colors from red to dark purple-black over summer, providing an extended food source for birds and other wildlife as different berries in the same cluster ripen at different rates. Its glossy, deep green foliage and neat, rounded form make it a good choice for naturalized plantings, woodland gardens, and wildlife landscaping, and unlike the invasive European buckthorns it is a well-behaved native that does not spread aggressively. It tolerates a range of soil types and light conditions once established and needs little maintenance beyond occasional shaping if a more tree-like form is wanted.

plant_note: Scarify seeds or soak overnight before sowing in moist, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Carolina bush pea is a legume that fixes nitrogen and improves poor soil. It develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established — site carefully. Plants are very long-lived and clumps expand slowly over many years.
directions: Sow scarified seeds in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Carolina bush pea is a tall, upright native legume of the southern Appalachians producing striking, dense spikes of bright yellow pea flowers in May and June that strongly resemble lupines — it is one of the few native alternatives to lupines for the middle South where lupines fail in summer heat. The clover-like, three-parted leaves are attractive through the season and the whole plant, including the hairy leaves and stems, has a pleasingly robust, textural quality. After flowering, the inflated seed pods are ornamental. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it thrives in lean, infertile soil where other ornamentals struggle. It is extremely long-lived — plants may persist for 25 or more years without division or disturbance — and forms impressive clumps of increasing magnificence. The common name 'Aaron's Rod' refers to the tall, upright flowering spikes. Excellent as a lupine substitute for gardens in the mid-South where genuine lupines perform poorly in summer heat.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, loamy to sandy-loam soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants tolerate drought and moderate clay. All parts of Carolina Cherry Laurel contain hydrogen cyanide compounds — never eat leaves, bark, or seeds.
directions: Carolina Cherry Laurel is an evergreen native tree or large shrub of the coastal plain and piedmont from North Carolina to central Florida and west to Texas, where it grows at forest edges, in disturbed sites, and along stream banks in full sun to partial shade. The glossy, lance-shaped evergreen leaves, fragrant white flower clusters in early spring, and dense branching habit make it one of the most popular native plants for hedges, privacy screens, and naturalized windbreaks in the Southeast, especially in Zones 8–10 where it grows vigorously year-round. Clusters of glossy black drupes ripen in fall and winter and are eagerly consumed by mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, robins, and other fruit-eating birds, though all parts of the plant contain hydrogen cyanide compounds and must never be eaten by humans or livestock. Plant in well-drained, loamy to sandy-loam soil in full sun for best flowering and fruiting; established plants tolerate extended drought, moderate clay, and salt spray in coastal settings.

plant_note: Scatter seeds directly in fall into thin, dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; germination occurs naturally in late winter.
directions: Carolina Clover is a delicate, small native annual of dry, open, thin-soiled, and disturbed ground throughout the southeastern US, producing characteristic trifoliate leaves and tiny white to pale pink flower heads in spring — one of the few truly native Trifolium species in the region. Sow directly in fall into thin, dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; it thrives on neglect and competes poorly in rich, heavily mulched beds. An important early spring nectar source for bumble bees, mason bees, and small native bee species, it self-sows prolifically and works well naturalized in thin-soiled areas, native meadow plots, or low-maintenance lawn areas as an ecologically superior alternative to non-native clovers.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring around the last frost date onto bare, dry, sandy or disturbed soil; seeds need light to germinate so press firmly onto the surface without covering.
directions: Carolina Desert-chicory is a native annual or biennial of the chicory family, found on dry, sandy, open ground, old fields, and disturbed areas throughout the southeastern and south-central United States. Plants produce hollow, milky-sapped stems rising from a basal rosette of pinnately lobed leaves, topped with large, showy, pale yellow flower heads up to 2 inches across from spring through early summer, followed by fluffy, dandelion-like seed heads that scatter readily on the wind. Grow in poor, dry, sandy, or rocky soil in full sun — fertile or clay soils encourage leafy growth at the expense of flowering, and this species thrives on neglect and minimal moisture once established. Self-sows dependably in open, disturbed ground and serves as an early, important nectar source for native bees, particularly small Hylaeus species active in early spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in a partially to fully shaded location; cold stratification over winter improves germination the following spring.
directions: Carolina Elephantfoot is a native aster-family perennial bearing large, rough-hairy, spatula-shaped basal leaves and wiry, branching stems that carry clusters of small, fuzzy, lavender-pink composite flower heads from late summer into fall. It thrives in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, making it well suited to woodland gardens and shaded native plantings where few other natives will bloom. Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall and allow winter cold to break dormancy naturally; transplants are slow to establish and direct sowing is strongly preferred. Once settled, plants self-seed modestly and gradually colonize, providing late-season forage for native pollinators in otherwise dim corners of the landscape.

plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper or nick the seed coat before sowing, then direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination. Carolina False Lupine develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting — sow seeds in a permanent, well-drained site. Can also be sown in early spring after last frost.
directions: Scarify seeds with sandpaper to break dormancy, then direct sow in fall or early spring into well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Carolina False Lupine develops a deep taproot early and should be sown in its permanent location rather than transplanted. This southeastern native perennial produces bright yellow, upright pea-flower spikes in April–May that closely resemble lupine blooms, making it an outstanding lupine substitute for the hot, humid climates of the Piedmont and Appalachian foothills where true lupines struggle. Unlike lupines, Thermopsis villosa is genuinely heat and humidity tolerant, thrives in the Southeast, and is long-lived once established, slowly spreading by rhizomes to form an impressive clump. It fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules and requires little to no fertilization.

common_name: Carolina Fanwort (Feathery Native Submerged Oxygenating Pond Plant)
plant_note: Plant weighted bunches or rooted stems directly in the pond, fully submerged, in full sun to partial shade after last frost; Carolina Fanwort is a classic feathery, fine-textured submerged oxygenator native to the southeastern US, helping keep pond water clear.
directions: Plant weighted bunches of cuttings or rooted stems directly in the pond substrate or a submerged planting basket, fully underwater, in full sun to partial shade. Carolina Fanwort is a native submerged aquatic with finely divided, feathery, fan-shaped underwater foliage in soft green to reddish-bronze tones, growing entirely below the surface aside from small floating leaves and tiny white to pale purple flowers that occasionally reach the surface in summer. As a submerged oxygenator, it helps maintain healthy pond water quality by absorbing excess nutrients that would otherwise fuel algae growth and by releasing oxygen into the water, benefiting fish and other pond life, while its dense underwater growth provides cover for fry and other small aquatic creatures. It grows vigorously in nutrient-rich water and may need periodic thinning to prevent it from overtaking a smaller pond.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky soil in partial shade; Carolina hemlock grows naturally on rocky, exposed ridges and cliffs in the southern Appalachians — more tolerant of dry, rocky, exposed conditions than eastern hemlock but still requiring cool, humid, acidic conditions.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky soil in partial shade; Carolina hemlock is a rare native conifer with a highly restricted range — endemic to the rocky ridges, cliff faces, and exposed rocky outcrops of the Blue Ridge Mountains in Virginia, the Carolinas, Georgia, and Tennessee, where it grows on sites too steep, rocky, and exposed for eastern hemlock. Distinguished from eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) by its more open, irregular, rugged appearance, needles that radiate in all directions around the branchlet (rather than lying flat in two rows), and slightly larger cones. The narrow, rocky, clifftop habitat makes it more tolerant of drier, more exposed conditions than eastern hemlock. Like eastern hemlock, it is severely threatened by hemlock woolly adelgid (Adelges tsugae) — a devastating introduced pest responsible for the death of hemlocks across the eastern US. Valuable ornamental specimen tree for its bold texture and rugged appearance, preferred by some gardeners over eastern hemlock for its more irregular, natural form.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Carolina Holly is dioecious — plant one male for every 2–3 females within 50 feet for reliable berry production. Seeds require double stratification and are slow to germinate.
directions: Carolina Holly is a native deciduous holly of the coastal plain and lower piedmont from the Carolinas south to Florida and west to Texas, growing as a large shrub or small tree at forest edges, hammock borders, and along stream banks in partial shade to full sun. The small but vivid red to orange-red berries, held in clusters along the bare winter branches after leaf drop, are an important food source for robins, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, hermit thrushes, and other fruit-eating birds during fall migration and winter. Like all native hollies, Carolina Holly is dioecious — both male and female plants are required within pollinator range for berry production — and its modest size compared to American Holly makes it suitable for smaller gardens where the larger species may overwhelm the space. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants tolerate moderate drought and require little maintenance.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall near a trellis, fence, or arbor for the vine to climb.
directions: This evergreen vine covers fences, trellises, and arbors with fragrant, bright yellow trumpet blooms in late winter to early spring. Plant in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil and provide sturdy support for the twining stems. Water regularly while establishing, then it tolerates moderate drought once mature. Note that all parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so site it away from areas frequented by pets and children; prune lightly after flowering to control size.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in late spring or plant container-grown specimens on a trellis, fence, or through shrubs in moist, well-drained, average, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Carolina jessamine is the state flower of South Carolina and one of the finest native vines for the Southeast.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens on a trellis, fence, arbor, or mailbox post in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Carolina jessamine is an evergreen, twining native vine that produces a spectacular display of bright, golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped, sweetly fragrant flowers in late winter to early spring — often the first vine to bloom, sometimes as early as January in zone 9. The glossy, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves are handsome year-round. The vine grows vigorously to 10–20 feet and can be allowed to cascade down banks, scramble through shrubs, or climb structures. All parts of the plant are highly toxic — do not confuse with true jasmines and never allow children to put flowers in their mouths. Valuable early-spring nectar source for native bees and hummingbirds returning from winter.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Carolina laurelcherry is native to the coastal plain from North Carolina through Florida and Texas and is one of the most widely used native evergreen screening plants for Gulf Coast gardens — extremely fast-growing and adaptable.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Carolina laurelcherry is fast-growing and can be pruned as a formal hedge or allowed to grow as a multi-stemmed small tree. Prunus caroliniana (Carolina laurelcherry or cherry laurel) is one of the most useful and fastest-growing native evergreen plants for Gulf Coast privacy screens, hedges, and windbreaks — a glossy-leaved, fast-growing shrub or small tree native to the coastal plain from North Carolina through Florida and Texas, producing small clusters of fragrant white flowers in spring followed by small, black, cherry-like fruits (the 'mockingbird berry' that Northern Mockingbirds consume voraciously). The dense, lustrous, dark-green, lanceolate leaves give it a formal, refined appearance well-suited to clipped hedges and screens; it grows 2–3 feet per year when young and can form a dense privacy screen within 3–4 years. CAUTION: The leaves, seeds, and stems contain amygdalin (prussic acid precursor) and are toxic if ingested in quantity — the mature black fruits are consumed safely by birds but should not be ingested by people. Carolina laurelcherry also volunteers prolifically from bird-dispersed seeds in the Gulf South; it can become weedy in natural areas near plantings.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in fall in dry to moist, well-drained, slightly acidic sandy or loamy soil in light partial shade to full sun; Carolina lily is native to open pine woods and sandy woodland edges and performs best with excellent drainage and some protection from the hottest afternoon sun in zone 8-9.
directions: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in fall in dry to moist, well-drained, slightly acidic sandy or loamy soil in light partial shade to full sun; Carolina lily is native to open pine woods and sandy woodland edges and performs best with excellent drainage and some protection from the hottest afternoon sun in zone 8-9. Lilium michauxi is the southeastern native counterpart to the better-known Turk's cap lily (L. superbum), producing 2-4 foot stems bearing one to several pendant, strongly reflexed orange flowers with prominent red spots and recurved petals from June through July; the flowers are visited by large native bees and sphinx moths and the plant grows naturally in the sandy, acidic soils of longleaf pine flatwoods and open upland woods throughout the Southeast. Unlike many lilies, it is adapted to summer heat and humidity and tolerates zone 8-9 conditions; plant it in a well-drained, partially shaded spot in a native woodland garden where it will slowly increase by bulb offsets.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), sandy to loamy, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Carolina lily is a dry-land lily adapted to the sandy, well-drained, acidic soils of southeastern pine forests — unlike most lilies, it does not tolerate wet or poorly-drained conditions.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade — Carolina lily is the southeastern counterpart to Canada lily and the most drought-tolerant of our native lilies, adapted to the dry, sandy, acidic soils of longleaf pine and oak-hickory forests from the mid-Atlantic through the Deep South. It produces nodding, orange to red, strongly reflexed (turkscap-type) flowers with dark spots and a prominent yellow center in July–August on stems with attractive whorled leaves. The flowers are intensely sought by ruby-throated hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies. Unlike most lilies, it thrives in the sandy, well-drained, dry-summer conditions of southeastern pine flatwoods and is one of the few native lilies suited to zone 8–9 heat and drought. Outstanding for naturalizing under pines in the coastal South. Endangered by habitat loss; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

plant_note: Surface sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; southern lobelia naturally occurs in moist to wet bottomland forest understories and shaded stream margins and requires consistent moisture to thrive.
directions: Lobelia amoena is a native lobelia of moist, shaded lowland forests and swamp edges from North Carolina to Florida and west to Mississippi, producing tall racemes of bright blue to blue-violet flowers from August through October in habitats where many other flowering perennials cannot survive; it is less commonly cultivated than L. cardinalis or L. siphilitica but is increasingly appreciated as an outstanding shade-tolerant, moist-soil native for the lower South. The brilliant blue flowers on 3–4 foot stems are outstanding for hummingbirds and large bees; the plant gradually spreads by short rhizomes. Surface sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, keeping seeds on the soil surface as light aids germination.

common_name: Carolina Midnight Loropetalum (Near-Black Purple Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina Midnight holds its darkest foliage color in full sun and grows vigorously enough to need an annual shaping to control size in smaller beds.
directions: Carolina Midnight is a vigorous, large-growing loropetalum selected for exceptionally dark, near-black purple foliage that holds its intensity through the growing season better than many purple-leaf loropetalum cultivars, which tend to fade toward green in summer heat. Frilly, spidery, deep magenta-pink flowers stand out sharply against the near-black leaves in a heavy spring flush, with lighter rebloom into fall. Its large mature size makes it best suited to a screen, background planting, or small tree form rather than a tight foundation bed; like other loropetalum it tolerates heat, humidity, and normal garden soil well as long as drainage is adequate, and should be pruned, if needed, right after the spring bloom to avoid cutting off the next flush of flower buds.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost in average to moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; seeds benefit from a brief 2–4 week cold-moist stratification before sowing to improve germination rates. Site at woodland edges or along naturalistic fences where twining stems can climb through adjacent shrubs.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade at a woodland edge or naturalistic fence where slender twining stems can climb through shrubs or simple supports. Carolina Milkvine is a softly hairy, heart-leaved native perennial in the milkweed family (Apocynaceae), producing small, star-shaped, dull brownish-purple flowers in summer that are followed by spindle-shaped seed pods splitting open to release seeds with silky white plumes. Like other milkweeds it exudes latex sap when cut and supports generalist milkweed bugs and potentially monarch butterflies as a larval host plant. It is an underused native vine well suited to naturalistic woodland garden settings where it weaves through existing shrubs without smothering them.

common_name: Carolina Moonlight Baptisia (Yellow-Flowered Hybrid False Indigo)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents being moved once established, so choose its planting site carefully.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since the deep taproot resents transplanting once established. Carolina Moonlight is one of the earliest and still most popular hybrid baptisia cultivars, producing tall spikes of soft, clear yellow flowers in late spring above blue-green foliage, followed by ornamental dark seed pods that persist into fall and rattle attractively in the wind. Like all baptisias it is exceptionally long-lived, drought-tolerant, and essentially pest-free once established, functioning almost like a flowering shrub in the perennial border despite dying back to the ground each winter. It needs no division and improves in floral display for many years, so give it its full mature spread from the start.
