plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring just as growth emerges, or take stem cuttings in early summer; Carolina phlox is best propagated vegetatively by division or cuttings rather than seed, as seedlings may not come true to type and take 2 years to reach bloom — divide every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent center die-out.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina phlox is a superior native alternative to the widely grown garden phlox (Phlox paniculata), closely resembling it in flower form and color but distinguished by its thicker, glossier, lanceolate leaves and significantly better resistance to powdery mildew — the common epithet 'thick-leaf phlox' reflects the noticeably more substantial leaf texture that imparts this disease resistance. Native to the southeastern United States from North Carolina to Georgia and westward, it produces dense, domed panicles of fragrant, five-petaled flowers in bright pink to purple-pink from June through August, providing critical mid-summer nectar for swallowtail butterflies, sphinx moths, and ruby-throated hummingbirds. It performs best in partial shade with adequate moisture and good air circulation, which further reduces mildew pressure; plant in groups of three or more for visual impact and divide clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor, as older clumps tend to become woody in the center. Carolina phlox is an excellent candidate for the mid-border of native perennial gardens and woodland edge plantings, where its upright habit and long summer bloom period fill the gap between spring and late-summer wildflowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to shade; Carolina ponysfoot establishes quickly in warm soil and spreads by creeping stems that root at each node — a naturally aggressive but low-growing groundcover that fills in open spots under trees.
directions: Seed or plant in moist, sandy to average soil in any light from full sun to deep shade in zones 7–11; Carolina ponysfoot is a native warm-season groundcover of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain and one of the most shade-tolerant groundcovers available for the South. The small, round to kidney-shaped leaves on creeping stems form a dense, soft carpet that stays under 3 inches tall and tolerates moderate foot traffic. In zone 9, it persists year-round as a semi-evergreen groundcover. It is frequently encountered as a native 'weed' in lawns in the Southeast where it is actually beneficial — a naturally occurring alternative to introduced groundcovers that requires no irrigation once established. The tiny greenish flowers are inconspicuous. Often sown as a grass substitute under large trees where grass will not grow.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, sandy peat in full sun to partial shade; Carolina redroot spreads by its namesake bright red-orange rhizomes through the same fire-maintained pine savanna wetlands that support pitcher plants along the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant divisions in wet to saturated, acidic, sandy peat in full sun to partial shade; Carolina redroot forms a fan of woolly, gray-green, sword-shaped leaves and sends up branched flower stalks in summer bearing small, fuzzy, cream-to-yellow flowers with a distinctive woolly texture, but the plant's real signature lies underground, where the thick, spreading rhizomes are a vivid blood-red-orange, historically used by Native peoples and early settlers as a dye and medicinal plant. It grows through the same fire-maintained, nutrient-poor pine savanna wetlands as pitcher plants and orchids along the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, spreading steadily by rhizome to form colonies in consistently wet, sunny, acidic ground. In a home bog garden it adds bold vertical foliage contrast to the low rosettes of sundews and butterworts, and divisions establish readily as long as the soil never dries out.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Carolina rhododendron is more drought tolerant than most rhododendrons but still requires consistently moist, acidic soil — mulch heavily to maintain moisture and protect shallow roots.
directions: Carolina rhododendron is one of the most compact and garden-worthy of all native North American rhododendrons — a small-leaved, dense, evergreen shrub from the high-elevation heath balds and rocky slopes of the southern Appalachians that produces masses of rose-pink to white flower clusters in April and May that can cover the entire plant in bloom. It is notably more heat-tolerant, drought-adaptable, and pest-resistant than the large-leaved rhododendrons (R. maximum and R. catawbiense) and adapts to typical garden conditions more readily; its compact size (2–6 feet) makes it appropriate for small-space native gardens and foundation plantings where large rhododendrons would overwhelm the space. The tiny, dark-spotted dots (puncta) on the leaf undersides give it the alternate name 'punctatum' and help identify it in the field; the small, leathery evergreen leaves roll upward in cold temperatures as a water-conservation mechanism, creating a distinctive winter appearance. One of the best native rhododendrons for shaded rockeries, acidic slopes, and native woodland gardens in the mid-Atlantic and upper South.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; full sun is essential for best flowering and disease resistance.
directions: Carolina Rose is a slender, drought-tolerant native of dry open woods, meadows, and roadsides throughout eastern North America, thriving in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soils where more vigorous shrubs struggle. Plant rooted cuttings or suckers in spring into a sunny, open site, spacing plants 3 to 5 feet apart to allow air circulation and natural colony spread. In June, the arching stems bear fragrant, single, pale to deep pink flowers about 1.5 to 2 inches across, followed by small, persistent red rose hips that feed mockingbirds, thrushes, and waxwings well into winter. No spraying or heavy pruning is needed; simply remove dead wood in late winter and allow the plant to spread slowly by suckers into an informal, wildlife-friendly thicket.

common_name: Carolina Sapphire Cypress (Fast-Growing Silvery-Blue Arizona Cypress)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Carolina Sapphire is a fast-growing Arizona cypress selection prized for striking silvery-blue foliage and a citrusy fragrance, but it requires excellent drainage and struggles in heavy, poorly drained Gulf Coast clay.
directions: Plant in full sun in sharply well-drained soil, avoiding heavy clay or any site prone to standing water. Carolina Sapphire is a fast-growing selection of Arizona cypress discovered as a chance seedling in North Carolina, valued for its striking, silvery-blue, finely textured foliage that is among the bluest of any hardy conifer, and for crushed foliage that releases a pleasant citrus-and-mint fragrance. It grows quickly into a dense, broadly pyramidal tree, making it useful as a fast screen or specimen where its color provides strong contrast against green-foliaged evergreens. Unlike the heat- and humidity-tolerant native eastern red cedar, Arizona cypress is adapted to drier climates and is notably intolerant of wet feet, so good drainage is essential; in the heavy clay and high humidity typical of much of the Gulf Coast, root and foliage diseases such as cypress canker and root rot can shorten its lifespan, and it performs best on a raised bed, slope, or sandy, well-drained site. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant and need little supplemental water once roots are established. Prune, if needed, in late winter to maintain shape; avoid overhead irrigation, which increases disease pressure on the foliage.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Carolina silverbell is one of the finest native small trees for understory planting under tall deciduous trees.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly to moderately acidic soil in partial to dappled shade; Carolina silverbell performs best in the cool, moist conditions of forest understory and does not tolerate drought or heavy clay well. Halesia carolina (syn. H. tetraptera) is a beautiful native small tree of the southern Appalachians producing cascading clusters of pure-white, bell-shaped, 4-petaled flowers covering the bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, creating a breathtaking floral display; the flowers are followed by ornamental, 4-winged, tan seed pods that persist through fall. One of the most spectacular spring-flowering native trees of the Southeast, excellent as a specimen or in mass plantings along woodland paths; the flowers are particularly lovely when viewed from below against a blue sky. Outstanding companion for dogwood, redbud, and rhododendron.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Carolina Silverbell thrives as an understory tree beneath taller oaks, beeches, and tulip poplars. Choose a sheltered site with protection from afternoon sun and drying winds in zone 9's climate. Seed requires warm-cold double dormancy stratification (90 days warm + 90 days cold) before germinating; buy nursery stock for best results. Flowers appear before or with the leaves in spring — the effect is spectacular.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade under the canopy of taller trees; Carolina Silverbell is at its absolute best as a woodland understory tree receiving dappled light rather than direct afternoon sun. Halesia tetraptera (also listed as H. carolina) is a native deciduous tree of the Southern Appalachians and Piedmont, with populations extending to the Gulf Coastal Plain of Louisiana and Mississippi, where it grows in moist ravines, bottomland hardwood forests, and shaded creek banks. In April–May (earlier in zone 9), the branches are literally covered with pendant clusters of pure white, four-petaled bell-shaped flowers just before the leaves emerge — the display earned it the common name 'Snowdrop Tree,' as the dangling white bells cascade along every branch with the appearance of snowflakes frozen in time. The flowers are followed by winged, four-ridged fruits (the source of the species name 'tetraptera,' meaning four-winged) that persist into winter and are eaten by wood ducks, wild turkeys, and songbirds. The tree grows relatively quickly for an understory species — 12–15 feet in 10 years in good conditions — with a naturally attractive multi-stem or single-trunk form, attractive exfoliating bark on mature specimens, and clear yellow fall color. In zone 9 Gulf Coast woodland gardens, Carolina Silverbell provides spring floral interest under large live oaks where most ornamentals fail.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring 4–6 inches deep in moist to wet, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Carolina spider lily grows naturally along stream banks, lake margins, and moist to seasonally flooded woodland openings of the southeastern US.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist to wet, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Carolina spider lily is a native southeastern bulb of moist to wet streambanks and lake margins, producing spectacular clusters of pure white, fragrant flowers in summer with the characteristic long, spidery tepals and central cup ('corona') that gives all Hymenocallis the common name 'spider lily'. The large, strap-like leaves are attractive before, during, and after flowering. The flowers are intensely fragrant, particularly in the evening when they attract large sphinx moths as pollinators. This is one of the most widely grown native spiderlilies for garden use, suitable for rain gardens, pond margins, and wet woodland edges. More cold-hardy than some Hymenocallis species, thriving in zones 6–10.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in a shaded woodland bed so that winter cold provides the stratification needed for spring germination; Carolina spring beauty is a spring ephemeral that goes completely dormant by late spring, so mark planting locations carefully. Combine with later-emerging shade perennials like ferns or wild ginger to maintain interest after the foliage vanishes.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade under deciduous trees; seeds require cold, moist stratification and will germinate in early spring before the tree canopy leafs out. Claytonia caroliniana is a delicate spring ephemeral of rich hardwood forests in eastern North America, closely related to Virginia spring beauty (C. virginica) but distinguished by its broader, oval leaves; it produces loose racemes of white to pale pink flowers with darker pink veins in early spring, providing one of the earliest nectar sources for queen bumblebees and early native bees emerging from overwintering. The plant grows from a small, deep-seated corm and goes completely dormant by late May or June; the corms are edible and have a mild, chestnut-like flavor, though wild plants should never be harvested. Plant densely in drifts of 25 or more for best visual impact on the spring woodland floor.

common_name: Carolina Wild Indigo (Grayhairy Wild Indigo, Coastal Plain Baptisia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot; Carolina Wild Indigo is a narrow Coastal Plain and Sandhills endemic (Virginia to Georgia) with gray-hairy foliage and cream to pale yellow flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean to average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Carolina Wild Indigo is a regional Coastal Plain and Sandhills endemic, native from Virginia to Georgia, distinguished from the more widely grown Baptisia species by its distinctly gray-hairy, silvery-toned foliage and its cream to pale yellow spring flowers held on a shorter, more compact plant than white or blue wild indigo. Following bloom, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest, and the plant serves as a larval host for several native butterfly species while its flowers draw bumblebees, among the few pollinators strong enough to trip the flower's mechanism. It is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free once established. Avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants; simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, average to sandy, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are drought-tolerant and require little supplemental care in zones 7–10.
directions: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, average to sandy, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are drought-tolerant and require little supplemental care in zones 7–10. Carolina wild petunia is a slender-stemmed native perennial with opposite, oblong leaves and a succession of lavender-blue, funnel-shaped flowers 1.5 inches across from spring through fall; individual flowers last only one day but are produced continuously over a long season. It is a specialist host and nectar plant for the common buckeye butterfly and the Malachite butterfly in southern Texas and Florida. The plant self-seeds moderately and gradually naturalizes into open, sandy, or rocky woodland edges and roadsides; in zone 9–10 it persists as a semi-woody subshrub.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; plants establish a basal rosette the first year and flower in late spring of the second year.
directions: Carolina Woollywhite is a native biennial or short-lived perennial in the aster family, native to dry, sandy, open ground, pine barrens, and roadsides from the Carolinas to Florida and Texas. In its first year it forms a basal rosette of deeply pinnate, fern-like leaves covered in soft white woolly hair; in its second year it sends up branched, upright stems 2 to 4 feet tall topped with open, corymb-like clusters of small white to cream composite flowers in late spring. Grow in dry, lean, sandy, acidic soil in full sun — rich or heavy soils will cause it to decline; it is quite drought-tolerant once established. Allow plants to set seed freely, as self-sowing is the primary means of maintaining a colony; the small seeds are a food source for sparrows and finches in native garden plantings.

common_name: Carolyn Whorton Caladium (Classic Rose-Pink Large Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Carolyn Whorton is a vigorous, large-tuber-producing variety that improves with successive seasons as tubers increase in size.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Carolyn Whorton is one of the most classic and beloved large fancy-leaf caladium varieties — a vigorous, large-leaved type producing heart-shaped leaves with a rose-pink to warm-pink center that radiates from the primary veins outward across the leaf, set against fresh-green margins with occasional splashes and spots of pink extending into the green zone. The warm, medium-pink tone of Carolyn Whorton differs from the cool pink-lavender of 'Pink Symphony' and the very pale shell-pink of some pastel types — it has a clear, warm, rose-pink quality that reads well at a distance in shade border plantings and has a friendly, cottage-garden quality distinct from the bold drama of red varieties. Carolyn Whorton is a vigorous, proven performer that produces large numbers of daughter tubers over successive seasons, making it one of the best caladiums for naturalizing a permanent in-ground planting in zone 9 where tubers overwinter reliably. Combine Carolyn Whorton with white caladiums ('Aaron', 'Candidum') for a soft pink-and-white romantic effect, or with green-and-white companions (white impatiens, white begonias) to highlight the pink tones. The large leaf size and warm pink coloration make this variety outstanding for massing under trees and in shaded foundation plantings where continuous warm-season color is desired from May through October.

plant_note: Plant in full sun to light shade in consistently moist, well-drained, fertile soil, ideally grouped in triple or clustered plantings; has essentially no frost tolerance so confine to the very warmest zone 10-11 landscapes.
directions: Plant this fast-growing Australian feather palm in full sun to light shade in consistently moist, well-drained, fertile soil, ideally grouped in triple or clustered plantings the way it is traditionally used in South Florida landscapes. Its smooth green crownshaft, arching fronds, and rapid growth rate make it one of the quickest ways to establish a tropical canopy effect near patios and pools. Feed regularly with a palm-specific fertilizer to prevent potassium deficiency, a common issue in fast-growing feather palms. It has essentially no frost tolerance, so it is best confined to the very warmest zone 10-11 landscapes.

plant_note: Surface sow around the last frost; light aids germination.
directions: Sprinkle Carpet of Snow alyssum onto firmed soil around the last frost and press in without covering, as light aids germination. This low, spreading heirloom carpets beds and container edges with masses of tiny, honey-scented white flowers. It draws in bees and beneficial insects and blooms from spring into fall, pausing only in extreme heat. Shear lightly if it flags mid-season to spark a fresh flush of bloom.

common_name: Carter's Sunburst Camellia (Striped Pale-Pink Exhibition-Form Japonica Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; Carter's Sunburst is an outstanding exhibition camellia and one of the most distinctive for its striped, spotted, and suffused pink-on-pale-pink flower coloring that sets it apart from solid-color camellias.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; Carter's Sunburst is one of the most immediately recognizable Camellia japonica cultivars — producing large, semi-double to peony-form flowers in pale pink to soft blush with overlaid deep pink stripes, streaks, and blotches distributed across the petals in patterns that are never exactly the same flower-to-flower. The striped and spotted flower coloring is distinctive enough that Carter's Sunburst is among the most frequently identified camellias by home gardeners and garden visitors — the unpredictable pink-on-pale-pink pattern creates visual complexity that solid-color camellias cannot match. The flowers are large (typically 4–5 inches across), combining good exhibition size with the informal charm of variegated coloring. Carter's Sunburst is a mid-season bloomer (typically February–March in zone 9), flowering after the earliest camellias and before the latest, filling a useful mid-winter bloom window. The plant grows as a medium-to-large, dense, upright evergreen shrub with the characteristically glossy, dark-green camellia foliage that provides attractive year-round structure. In zone 9, Carter's Sunburst is a reliable perennial landscape shrub requiring primarily acidic soil, consistent moisture, and protection from afternoon sun that can bleach the pale-pink flower color. An outstanding specimen plant near garden entrances where the distinctive striped flowers can be seen closely.

common_name: Casa Blanca Oriental Lily (Giant Pure White Fragrant Cut-Flower Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall (November–December) in zone 9 for late spring to early summer bloom; orient bulbs pointed end up, 5–6 inches deep, and give afternoon shade where summer sun is intense. In zone 9's warm winters, lift and refrigerate bulbs for about 8 weeks at 34–40°F before fall replanting to sustain vigorous bloom in future years.
directions: Plant bulbs 5–6 inches deep in fall with the pointed end up, and mulch over the planting area to moderate soil temperature and conserve moisture. Casa Blanca is one of the most widely grown Oriental hybrid lilies in the world, producing enormous, pure white, outward-facing flowers 8–10 inches across with gently recurved petals and prominent rust-orange anthers, held on tall, sturdy stems that make it a favorite for both garden borders and cut-flower arrangements. Its intense, sweet fragrance is among the strongest of any lily, capable of scenting an entire room or garden area from a single planting, and the flawless white blooms pair elegantly with almost any color scheme. Stake taller stems in windy sites to protect the heavy flower heads, and remove spent blooms before they set seed to redirect energy back into the bulb for next year's display.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery-grown container stock in fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil along a streambank, seep, or shaded slope.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery-grown container stock in fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil along a streambank, seep, or shaded slope, mimicking the subalpine forest openings and avalanche chutes of the Cascades and northern Rockies where it grows wild. Unlike most rhododendrons, its cream-white flowers open along the stem below the newest leaves rather than in a terminal truss, giving it a distinctive, informal look in a woodland or native shrub border. It struggles in hot, humid summers and is best reserved for cool-climate gardens with reliable moisture and good air movement.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a cool, partly sunny site.
directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring into consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a cool, partly sunny site, recreating the snowmelt-fed subalpine meadows of the Cascade and Olympic Mountains where it forms low, spreading mats. Bell-shaped pink flowers appear in early summer followed by sweet, powder-blue berries considered among the best-flavored of the wild huckleberries and are eagerly sought by birds, bears, and foragers alike. It resents summer drought and heat, so it performs best in cool-climate gardens or high-elevation native plantings with reliable soil moisture.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable; Cascade Creeper spreads readily by stolons to form a dense groundcover, useful for covering shaded ground quickly.
directions: Tuck divisions into moist, well-drained woodland soil enriched with compost, and water regularly the first season while the spreading stolons take hold. Cascade Creeper is a vigorous, fast-spreading foamflower selection bred to knit together into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover more quickly than clump-forming Tiarella cultivars, with lobed, maple-like green leaves that take on burgundy tones in cooler weather. Fluffy spikes of white to pale pink star-shaped flowers rise above the foliage in spring, drawing early pollinators to the shade garden. Because of its spreading habit, it is especially useful for covering a shaded slope, filling in under trees, or edging a woodland path, though it is more assertive than compact clumping Tiarella selections and needs more room to roam. Established plantings tolerate some dry shade once rooted in, though consistent moisture keeps the groundcover densest and most attractive.

common_name: Cascade Falls Bald Cypress (Weeping Groundcover-Form Bald Cypress)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; stake and train a leader early if a taller cascading specimen is wanted, since left alone it hugs the ground.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, staking the central leader while young and tying it upward if a tall, cascading fountain form is the goal; left untrained, the branches sprawl outward and downward into a low, undulating mound. Cascade Falls is a strongly weeping selection of the native bald cypress, its soft, ferny, blue-green foliage draping in dense curtains that turn coppery rust before dropping for winter, making it a dramatic choice for spilling over a retaining wall, bank, or large container. Like the species it tolerates both swampy, seasonally flooded sites and ordinary well-drained garden soil, and develops the same distinctive rounded knees when grown in consistently wet ground. Prune out any vigorous upright shoots that revert toward the species' normal pyramidal habit to keep the weeping character intact.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to dry soil in partial to full shade; Cascade Oregon grape is more shade-tolerant and lower-growing than M. aquifolium, making it a better choice for dense forest understory shade and the dry shade under conifers.
directions: Plant in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Cascade Oregon grape is more drought and shade tolerant than the better-known tall Oregon grape (M. aquifolium) and is superior for naturalizing as a ground cover in dry, shaded forest settings under conifers or other dense trees. Mahonia nervosa is a low-growing western native evergreen shrub 12–24 inches tall with long, pinnate, holly-like leaves with many narrow leaflets, clusters of yellow flowers in early spring before many other shade shrubs bloom, and blue-black berries that are loved by birds and used to make preserves and a tart beverage in the Pacific Northwest. The evergreen foliage turns wine-red to bronze in winter, providing year-round interest. An excellent, underused evergreen ground cover for the Pacific Northwest and adaptable dry-shade situations in western gardens; deer resistant.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in rich, moist, acidic soil.
directions: Cascade Spice bears large, ruffled Japanese iris blooms in rich purple and white for a bold late-spring to summer display. Site in full sun to part shade in acidic, humus-rich soil kept consistently moist, ideal at the edge of a pond or in a rain garden. Do not allow the soil to dry out during active growth, and avoid alkaline amendments. Deadhead spent stalks and divide crowded clumps in fall to sustain strong flowering.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface sow the tiny seed, which needs light.
directions: Sow the fine seed on the surface indoors several weeks before the last frost, as it requires light to germinate. This trailing blend spills over hanging baskets and container edges with blooms of blue, blue with a white eye, lilac, red, ruby, and white. Keep it consistently moist and provide afternoon shade where summers are hot. A light midseason shearing renews the display and keeps plants full.

common_name: Cassata Daffodil (White with Frilled Yellow-to-White Split Cup)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; Cassata is a Division 11 split-corona daffodil with a white perianth and a frilled, flattened yellow-to-white split cup that opens flat against the petals.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom rather than cutting or braiding it. Cassata, a Division 11 split-corona (butterfly or collar) daffodil, bears a clean white perianth behind a frilled, flattened cup that starts golden yellow and fades toward white, the corona split into segments that lie open against the petals rather than forming the typical cup or trumpet shape, giving the flower an orchid-like or camellia-like appearance unlike any other daffodil division. It blooms in midseason and is completely deer- and rodent-resistant.

plant_note: Divide and plant in spring into full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil, spacing clumps far enough apart to show off the fountain-like habit.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and moist, well-drained soil; this cultivar tolerates brief drought once established but produces the fullest flower display with regular moisture. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter to make way for fresh growth. Narrow green blades arch outward in a fountain shape and turn gold, orange, and burgundy in fall, while bottlebrush-like tan-to-copper flower spikes appear earlier in the season than on the straight species, extending the display into winter as tawny seed heads.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep shade to partial shade; space 18–24 inches apart and water regularly until established.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep shade to partial shade; cast iron plant thrives in conditions that defeat nearly every other ornamental, including dense root competition under established trees, poor drainage, and near-zero indoor light. The broad, glossy, deep-green strap leaves grow slowly but are extraordinarily long-lived and require almost no maintenance beyond the occasional removal of damaged foliage. Water sparingly once established — the rhizomes store moisture and rot in permanently waterlogged soil — and fertilize lightly once or twice per year with a balanced slow-release fertilizer. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 5–10 years to maintain vigor.

subcategory: Tropical ornamental and industrial oil plant
plant_note: WARNING: ALL parts of Ricinus communis are EXTREMELY TOXIC — the seeds contain ricin, one of the most potent naturally occurring toxins known. Keep away from children and livestock; wear gloves when handling seeds and wash hands thoroughly. Plant seeds directly outdoors after last frost in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average soil; Castor Bean is a fast-growing tropical ornamental with extraordinarily large, bold, star-shaped leaves in green, bronze, or deep red — one of the most dramatic foliage plants available for large seasonal tropical landscape displays.
directions: SAFETY WARNING: All parts of Ricinus communis — especially seeds — are extremely toxic due to ricin content; never plant where children or livestock have access; wear gloves when handling seeds and pods and wash hands immediately after contact. Direct sow 2 large seeds 1–2 inches deep in full sun after last frost in well-drained, fertile, loamy soil; thin to the strongest seedling. Ricinus communis (Castor Bean or Castor Oil Plant) is a fast-growing, large, tropical perennial or annual shrub in the Euphorbiaceae family native to the eastern tropical African highlands and horn of Africa, now naturalized throughout tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. As a landscape ornamental, Castor Bean is unsurpassed for bold, tropical foliage effect: the huge, deeply-lobed, star-shaped leaves — reaching 1–3 feet across — come in deep bronze, dark red-maroon, or bright green depending on cultivar, held on long stalks atop rapidly growing plants that can reach 6–15 feet in a single season. The industrial importance is enormous: castor oil (cold-pressed from the seeds after ricin deactivation) is one of the most commercially important specialty vegetable oils — valued as a lubricant, biodiesel feedstock, cosmetic emollient, nylon-11 precursor, and traditional purgative medicine. The seeds contain ricin — a biological toxin in the RIP (ribosome-inactivating protein) class — one of the most acutely toxic natural substances known; as few as 4–8 seeds can be lethal to an adult if chewed. All handling of seeds and seed pods should be done with gloves.

plant_note: Divide root masses or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; cat's claw vine is very aggressive and is considered invasive in Texas, Florida, California, and many warm-climate regions worldwide — research local invasive status before planting and avoid sites adjacent to natural areas where escaped plants could spread into native vegetation.
directions: Divide root masses or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; cat's claw vine (cat's claw creeper, yellow trumpet vine) is a Mexican and Caribbean deciduous to semi-evergreen vine of the bignonia family (Bignoniaceae) that clings to walls, trees, fences, and masonry with remarkable tenacity through specialized, three-pronged, claw-like tendrils at the leaf tips — the claws can grip and penetrate the most vertical, smooth surfaces and provide virtually no-effort climbing capability. In spring, before or as the new leaves emerge, the vine produces a profusion of large, bright-yellow, funnel-shaped, trumpet flowers in spectacular abundance covering the entire plant. The vine is extraordinarily tough, drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and adaptable, and recovers quickly from hard freezes that kill it back to the large, persistent underground root system. It is, however, aggressively invasive in many warm-climate regions, spreading by seeds and underground tubers into natural areas and difficult to eradicate once established. An impactful, low-care vine for contained, fence-line, and masonry situations in zone 8–11 where its invasive spread can be managed.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cat's Meow is a more compact, tidier-habited sport of the popular Walker's Low catmint, fitting smaller borders and edging.
directions: Plant in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; catmint rots quickly in wet, heavy soil over winter, so good drainage matters more than fertility. Cat's Meow arose as a more compact, upright, and floriferous sport of the widely grown Walker's Low, covering itself in short spikes of lavender-blue flowers over gray-green, aromatic foliage from late spring through summer, with a shearing after the first flush reliably triggering a strong second bloom into fall. Its tighter, rounder habit holds up better without flopping than older, looser catmints, making it useful for edging paths and border fronts where Walker's Low would sprawl too wide. Extremely drought-tolerant once established and generally ignored by deer and rabbits, it needs only an annual spring cutback to remove old growth before new shoots emerge.

common_name: Cat's Pajamas Catmint (Compact Early-Blooming Dwarf Catmint)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, average soil in full sun; Cat's Pajamas is a compact, densely mounding catmint bred to stay tidy without the sprawling, floppy habit common in larger catmint cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, average soil in full sun, spacing plants so the dense, rounded mounds can fill in without overlapping. Cat's Pajamas produces abundant short spikes of lavender-blue flowers over fine, gray-green aromatic foliage beginning in late spring, holding its compact, tidy form through the season far better than taller, more sprawling catmint cultivars. The dense flowering habit and small stature suit edging, rock gardens, and containers where a full-size catmint would quickly overwhelm the space. Bees visit the abundant flowers steadily through the bloom period, and shearing lightly after the first flush encourages continued flowering into summer.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Catalina California fuchsia is a larger, more vigorous selection that spreads readily once established and tolerates heat and drought well.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Catalina California fuchsia is a larger, more vigorous selection that spreads readily once established and tolerates heat and drought well. Soft, gray-green, felted foliage sets off masses of vivid red-orange, tubular flowers from late summer into fall, a season when few other California natives are still blooming, making it an important late-season nectar source for migrating hummingbirds preparing for their journey south. This robust selection, originating from Catalina Island populations, grows larger and spreads more vigorously by rhizome than many other California fuchsia cultivars, useful for covering a dry slope or bank where a spreading groundcover is wanted. It needs no supplemental water once established and benefits from being cut back hard in late winter to remove old growth before the next season's flush.

common_name: Catalina Torenia (Heat-Tolerant Trailing Wishbone Flower Series)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Catalina is a heat-tolerant, trailing torenia series bred to perform well in hot, humid summer conditions where many shade annuals decline.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade. Catalina torenia produces abundant, snapdragon-like flowers in shades of blue, purple, pink, and yellow, each marked with a distinctive dark throat, on a trailing, spreading plant well suited to hanging baskets, containers, and shaded bedding displays. Unlike older torenia varieties that can struggle and decline in peak summer heat, the Catalina series was specifically bred for improved heat tolerance, keeping up strong bloom through the hottest, most humid part of the Gulf South growing season. It thrives in the same moist, shaded conditions that suit impatiens and begonias, and benefits from regular fertilizing and consistent moisture to sustain its nonstop flowering.

common_name: Catawba Crape Myrtle (Deep Purple Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Catawba is a medium-sized National Arboretum crape myrtle reaching 10–15 feet — allow adequate space at planting and never top-prune.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Catawba is a National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle producing one of the deepest, richest purple flower colors available in crape myrtles — a vivid, true violet-purple that holds color through the heat of the Gulf South summer without fading to pink or lavender. Purple is among the rarest and most sought-after crape myrtle flower colors — most purple-claiming cultivars prove to be lavender, mauve, or reddish-purple — but Catawba's color is among the most reliably true purple in cultivation. The flowers are produced in large, compact clusters from June through September in zone 9, covering a medium-sized multi-trunked tree to 10–15 feet with vivid purple bloom. Fall foliage transitions to attractive orange-red. The exfoliating bark develops an attractive mottled pattern of gray and tan with age. Like other National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles, Catawba shows good resistance to powdery mildew. Its medium size makes it appropriate for the majority of residential landscapes where the large tree-form Natchez and Muskogee would eventually overwhelm the space. Catawba is an excellent choice for the gardener who wants a distinctive crape myrtle that stands apart from the dominant pink and red cultivars. Never top or severely prune — proper pruning removes only dead and crossing branches.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; like other baptisias it develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting, so choose the permanent site with care. This species is native to dry, sandy coastal plain woods and pine flatwoods of the Southeast.
directions: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; catbells is an unusual and distinctive Southeastern coastal plain native wild indigo, immediately recognizable by its perfoliate leaves — round, disk-like blue-green foliage that appears to be pierced through the middle by the stem, giving the sprawling, low-growing plant a striking, almost succulent architectural texture unlike any other Baptisia species. In late spring it produces small clusters of bright yellow pea-family flowers scattered along the trailing stems, followed by the inflated seed pods typical of the genus. Native to dry, sandy pine flatwoods and scrub habitats from the Carolinas through Georgia and into the Florida panhandle, it thrives in lean, well-drained, sandy soil and full sun, tolerating drought and poor fertility better than richer garden perennials. Like all baptisias it fixes nitrogen, is deer-resistant, and develops a deep, tough taproot that makes established plants essentially permanent but impossible to transplant successfully — sow seed directly where the plant is meant to grow.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained to dry, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; catbrier spreads by both seed and underground rhizomes to form dense, thorny thickets that provide important nesting cover and berry food for wildlife in dry woodland and edge habitats.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun for wildlife habitat restoration; catbrier is a common native greenbrier of dry woodlands and woodland edges throughout eastern North America, distinguished from other Smilax by the glaucous (blue-white) coloring on the underside of the leaves. Like all greenbriers, it is an armed, scrambling vine with stout, curved thorns and tendrils, climbing through shrubs and into tree canopy. The blue-black berries that persist through winter are critically important food for numerous thrushes, mockingbirds, and other fruit-eating birds. Dense catbrier thickets provide nesting cover for ground-nesting birds including bobwhite quail and wild turkey. The young shoots in spring are edible, resembling asparagus in flavor, and have been used as a spring vegetable by indigenous peoples and early settlers. The starchy underground tubers can be processed into a flour-like starch. Primarily a wildlife planting rather than a garden ornamental.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring in dry, rocky, alkaline, or sandy soil in full sun; catclaw acacia develops a deep taproot quickly and is extremely drought tolerant once established — not suitable for moist, clay, or frequently irrigated soils.
directions: Catclaw acacia — nicknamed 'wait-a-minute bush' because its small, curved, cat-claw-like thorns snag clothing and skin, halting passage — is a native shrub to medium tree of dry washes, rocky slopes, and desert grasslands from south Texas to California and south into Mexico. Despite its formidable armament, catclaw acacia is one of the most important native bee plants in the Chihuahuan Desert and south Texas, producing abundant cream-colored, cylindrical flower spikes in spring that support hundreds of native bee species and are the source of a prized honey; it is considered the single most important native honey plant in the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts by commercial beekeepers. The long, flat seed pods ripen in summer and fall and are consumed by deer, javelinas, and large-seeded birds; the dense, thorny structure of established shrubs creates impenetrable wildlife brush habitat essential for quail, roadrunners, and nesting songbirds throughout south Texas. Best suited to xeric native plantings, dry washes, and wildlife habitat gardens where its thorny nature is an asset rather than a liability.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to average, well-drained soil in full sun; catclaw mimosa has long, fleshy taproots that make transplanting difficult — direct sow in permanent locations and scarify seeds with hot water or sandpaper before planting for best germination.
directions: Catclaw mimosa is a native scrambling perennial of dry prairies, rocky glades, and open woodlands in the south-central United States, armed with small, recurved prickles that catch on clothing and slow passage through its loose, sprawling stems — the 'catclaw' refers to these hook-shaped thorns, while 'sensitive briar' describes the leaves that fold instantly when touched, a characteristic shared with many Mimosa species. Pink, globe-shaped, pompom-like flower heads appear from May through August and are vigorously worked by native bumblebees and smaller bees for pollen; as a legume, it fixes nitrogen through root nodules and helps improve soil in dry, impoverished areas. Its spreading, semi-prostrate habit and prickles make it most appropriate for naturalized areas, dry meadow restorations, and native prairie gardens where its sprawling character can provide ground-level interest and soil improvement without maintenance; it is drought-tolerant to an extreme degree once established on deep, sandy or rocky soil.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall, setting them 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in full shade before hard frost.
directions: Trillium catesbaei is a distinctive southeastern native trillium that sets itself apart from the upright-flowered species by bearing a single, nodding, pink to rose-red flower with strongly recurved petals beneath the three-leaved whorl in April and May, giving it an unusually graceful, pendant appearance. It grows naturally in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soils in the Piedmont and mountain foothills from North Carolina and Georgia to Alabama, tolerating the warmer zone 8–9 summers better than most northern trilliums. Purchase only nursery-propagated divisions — wild populations are declining due to habitat loss and poaching. Pairs beautifully with ferns, wild ginger, and bloodroot in a shaded native garden.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall with the nose just below the soil surface into deep, moist, humus-rich soil, and mulch heavily since flowering-size bulbs take several years to build up before blooming.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall with the nose just below the soil surface into deep, moist, humus-rich soil, and mulch heavily since flowering-size bulbs take several years to build up before blooming. Native to shaded, moist mountain forests in central China, it needs the same cool, reliably damp woodland conditions as its larger relative Cardiocrinum giganteum and resents drying out or heavy midday sun. After several seasons of building a rosette of broad, heart-shaped leaves, a tall flowering stem finally emerges bearing pendant, trumpet-shaped white flowers streaked with maroon inside the throat in summer. The parent bulb dies after flowering but leaves offset bulbs behind, so a patch renews itself over time in an undisturbed shaded corner of the garden.

common_name: Cathedral Live Oak (Pyramidal Strong-Leader Live Oak Selection)
plant_note: Plant container trees in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, deep soil in full sun; Cathedral is a live oak selection bred for a strong central leader and pyramidal-to-ovoid form, a better street and urban tree shape than the wide-spreading straight species.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, deep soil in full sun; live oak tolerates a wide range of soils including compacted urban sites once established. Cathedral was selected specifically for a strong central leader and a more pyramidal-to-ovoid canopy shape than the enormous, wide-spreading form typical of straight-species Southern live oak, making it far better suited to street plantings, medians, and smaller urban and suburban lots where the species' eventual 60-100 foot spread would be impractical. It retains the same tough, evergreen, wind- and salt-tolerant character that makes live oak the iconic Gulf Coast landscape tree. Water deeply during establishment, and prune minimally to develop good branch structure while the tree is young.

plant_note: Separate rosette offsets from established clumps in spring and pot in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; cathedral window haworthia grows naturally tucked among rocks in dappled shade in South Africa's Eastern Cape, so it wants bright indirect light rather than direct sun, making it one of the easier soft-leaved succulents for an east- or north-facing windowsill.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a shallow pot of gritty, fast-draining cactus mix, and let the soil dry out between waterings. Haworthia cymbiformis forms a low, dense rosette of plump, pale-green, boat-shaped leaves whose translucent, rounded tips act as tiny windows, letting light reach photosynthetic tissue deeper in the leaf when the plant is naturally half-buried in sandy soil in the wild. It offsets readily around the base, quickly forming a tight cluster of rosettes that can be divided every couple of years to make new plants. Unlike hard-leaved zebra-type haworthias, its leaves are soft, glossy, and nearly translucent along the margins, and the whole rosette plumps or wrinkles noticeably to signal watering needs. It tolerates lower light than almost any other succulent, making it a reliable choice for a bright bathroom or office desk as well as a classic windowsill spot, and it sends up thin, wiry stems of small white summer flowers that are easily trimmed off if not wanted.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; daylilies tolerate a wide range of soil conditions and need little care once established.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; daylilies tolerate a wide range of soil conditions and need little care once established. Large, elegantly ruffled flowers open in a soft, dusty lavender-orchid shade with a subtle deeper eyezone and a lightly ruffled gold edge, a refined pastel color combination that has made this classic mid-twentieth-century cultivar a long-standing favorite among daylily collectors and a parent behind many later lavender and purple-toned daylily hybrids. Reliable and easy-growing like other daylilies, it thrives in average garden soil with minimal care, tolerating heat, drought, and a range of soil types once established, and each flower lasts only a single day but is followed by a long succession of new blooms through its flowering season. Deadhead spent flowers and remove old bloom stalks after flowering finishes, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Catherine Woodbury Daylily (Classic Fragrant Lavender-Pink Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Catherine Woodbury is an older, historically important cultivar credited with introducing true pink and lavender tones into modern daylily breeding.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Introduced in 1967, Catherine Woodbury was a groundbreaking cultivar in daylily breeding history, prized for its soft, clear lavender-pink flowers with a chartreuse-green throat and gentle fragrance at a time when most daylilies were shades of orange, yellow, or red. It remains a garden favorite for its refined color and pleasant scent, blooming in a single flush during early-to-mid summer rather than the extended rebloom of more modern reblooming cultivars. Daylilies are otherwise easygoing, thriving in average soil with routine watering, and clumps can be divided every three to four years in spring or fall to control size and maintain vigorous bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade; Catlin's Giant produces significantly larger leaves than standard ajuga cultivars — individual leaves can reach 4–6 inches long, creating a bolder, more dramatic groundcover effect.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade; Catlin's Giant is the large-leaved ajuga cultivar — producing individual leaves 3–6 inches long (two to three times the size of standard ajuga cultivars) in a rich, glossy, mahogany-bronze to purplish-bronze color that creates a dramatically bolder groundcover effect than any other bugleweed selection. The large, rounded, glossy leaves with their deep bronze coloration create a texture and visual weight that reads from a greater distance than fine-leaved types — making it effective as a visible groundcover under trees and in areas where it will be seen from across the garden. In spring, upright spikes of blue-violet flowers rise 6–8 inches above the large bronze foliage — the blue against bronze combination is visually striking and attracts bees and other pollinators. Catlin's Giant spreads by surface stolons to form an expanding mat but is slightly slower to fill in than smaller-leaved cultivars because fewer stolons are produced per unit area. The large leaves provide excellent weed suppression once established, creating dense coverage that blocks light to weed seeds below. In zone 9, ajuga is semi-evergreen to evergreen through mild winters. Catlin's Giant may show heat stress in the peak of Gulf South summer — plant in locations with afternoon shade and consistent moisture to help it through the most intense heat periods.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; catmint spreads into mounds and works well as a low groundcover or edging plant along pathways and borders.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; catmint forms attractive soft mounds of grey-green, aromatic foliage smothered in lavender-blue flower spikes from late spring through early summer, and again in fall after cutting back. It is one of the most reliable, long-blooming, and drought-tolerant perennials for the sunny border, thriving in poor dry soils where other plants fail. Shear the entire plant by one-half after the first flush of bloom fades — typically in early July — and within 3–4 weeks a full second flush of flowers will appear and continue into fall. Note that catmint, like catnip (N. cataria), can attract intense interest from cats; 'Walker's Low' and 'Six Hills Giant' are popular landscape cultivars.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade; cattail sedge grows naturally in bottomland woods and along pond and stream margins and is named for its distinctive thick, cattail-like seed spikes.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; cattail sedge is a distinctive native of bottomland woods, pond margins, and shaded stream edges, named for its thick, cylindrical seed spikes that resemble a miniature cattail flower head — an unusual and easily identifiable feature among native sedges. The arching, medium-green foliage forms a loose clump that fits naturally at the shaded edge of a pond or rain garden alongside true cattails, sedges, and other wetland natives. It tolerates periodic flooding and needs consistently moist to wet soil to perform its best, making it a poor choice for a typical dry border but a strong one for a shaded water's-edge planting. Established clumps require little maintenance beyond reliable moisture.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Cattleya bears large plumes of bright orchid pink named for its resemblance to the orchid genus.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial to full shade, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat. Cattleya produces tall, upright stems topped with large, feathery panicles of vivid orchid-pink flowers that open above new foliage tinged reddish-bronze before maturing to dark green, giving the plant strong color from both flowers and emerging leaves. It is one of the taller arendsii selections and makes a bold vertical accent toward the back of a shaded border or along a woodland path edge. Because it is listed as reliable into zone 9 by some growers, it is a reasonable astilbe to trial in a Gulf Coast garden provided it gets deep afternoon shade and never dries out during the hottest months.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately wet soil in part shade; Caucasian comfrey spreads vigorously by rhizomes and should be given adequate space or planted where spreading is welcome, such as under trees or in a naturalized shade garden. It can be used as a dynamic accumulator like other comfreys, but is grown primarily for its ornamental sky-blue flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Caucasian comfrey is the most ornamental of all the comfrey species, producing intensely azure-blue to sky-blue, nodding, tubular flowers in arching clusters — distinctly different from the murky purple-pink of common comfrey (Symphytum officinale) and the cream flowers of creeping comfrey (S. grandiflorum). The brilliant, clear blue of the flowers from April to June is exceptional in the partly shaded garden and approaches the blue of gentian and pulmonaria. Like all comfreys, it spreads vigorously by rhizomes to form a substantial colony, which makes it excellent as a large-scale groundcover under trees and shrubs, but means it should be planted where it has room to expand. The large, rough, hairy leaves are typical of the genus and effectively suppress weeds once established. Native to moist, fertile slopes and streambanks of the Caucasus mountains, it is cold-hardy to zone 4 and tolerates woodland conditions well.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Caucasian pincushion flower requires alkaline to neutral soil (pH 6.5–7.5) — acidic soils cause poor performance and early death. It is longer-lived in cool climates (zones 3–6) than in hot, humid conditions and may require division every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. Deadhead continuously for a long blooming season from summer through frost.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Caucasian pincushion flower is a classic cottage-garden perennial from the Caucasus Mountains producing lavender-blue to soft violet, 2–3 inch, pincushion-like flower heads on long, wiry stems from midsummer through fall — each flower head composed of a central dome of tubular disc florets surrounded by a ring of enlarged, ruffled outer florets in soft lavender to lilac-blue to near-white, held 18–24 inches high on slender stems that sway gracefully in garden breezes, making them exceptional as long-stemmed cut flowers. The very long vase life and delicate, informal character of the flowers has made this one of the premier cottage-garden and cutting-garden perennials since the Victorian era, appearing in countless English cottage-garden paintings alongside sweet peas and roses. Requires alkaline to neutral soil — plants in acid conditions perform poorly and decline. Cultivars include 'Clive Greaves' (medium lavender-blue, one of the oldest named forms still widely sold), 'Miss Willmott' (white), and 'Perfecta' (lavender-blue, frilled florets).

plant_note: Plant cuttings or divisions in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Caucasian stonecrop is highly adaptable and drought tolerant, spreading by creeping stems that root at the nodes to quickly cover dry, rocky, or sandy ground.
directions: Plant cuttings or divisions in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Caucasian stonecrop (Dragon's Blood stonecrop in its red-leaved cultivars) is one of the most widely used low succulent groundcovers in temperate gardens — a mat-forming Eurasian sedum with flat, slightly scalloped, fleshy leaves that may be dark green or burgundy-red depending on cultivar, and flat-topped clusters of rose-pink to bright pink flowers in midsummer. The cultivar 'Dragon's Blood' with its deep purplish-red foliage is one of the best-selling groundcover plants in the nursery trade. 'Tricolor' has green, pink, and white variegated leaves. Spreads quickly by creeping stems rooting at nodes to cover slopes, rock walls, and dry banks. Hardy, reliable, and virtually pest-free. One of the most important species for green roof plantings, slope stabilization, and dry, hot, sunny groundcover situations where conventional plants fail.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or fall in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; shear back by half after flowering to keep plants compact. Arabis caucasica is drought-tolerant and excellent for dry, sunny walls and rock garden situations. It may become invasive in some regions by self-sowing — deadhead to prevent excessive spread.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Caucasus rock cress is a classic spring rock garden plant producing dense mats of soft, gray-green, woolly-textured leaves and, in April through May, a profusion of pure-white, four-petaled flowers in flat-topped clusters that completely cover the mat and cascade over walls in a clean, fresh display of early-spring white. The grayish, soft-hairy leaf texture is attractive even out of flower, providing a silvery quality in the rock garden year-round. It is among the earliest herbaceous plants to flower in spring and is traditionally combined with purple aubrieta and golden Aurinia saxatilis (basket of gold) to create the classic British spring rock garden color combination of purple, white, and gold. Double-flowered ('Flore Pleno') and pink-flowered ('Pink Pearl') cultivars are available. Variegated-foliage forms have cream-edged leaves and are ornamental year-round.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, several inches deep, in humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs where the plant will get bright spring light before the canopy leafs out.
directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, several inches deep, in humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs where the plant will get bright spring light before the canopy leafs out. This close cousin of the more common Corydalis solida is a true spring ephemeral, pushing up ferny gray-green foliage and dense spikes of purple, pink, or occasionally white flowers in earliest spring before vanishing completely by early summer. Its hollow, chambered tuber distinguishes it from solid-tubered relatives, and it slowly naturalizes into loose colonies in cool woodland gardens. Avoid disturbing the site in summer since the plant is dormant and invisible underground.

common_name: Cecil Houdyshel Crinum (Classic Soft Pink Fragrant Crinum Lily)
plant_note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Cecil Houdyshel is one of the most reliably free-flowering crinum cultivars, often reblooming several times through the growing season.
directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Cecil Houdyshel produces abundant clusters of soft pink, sweetly fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers on tall scapes above strap-like evergreen foliage, and is known among crinum enthusiasts for blooming repeatedly through the warm season rather than in just a single flush, giving more overall color than many other crinum cultivars. Like other crinums it is extremely long-lived and low-maintenance once established, tolerating heat, humidity, and a range of soils, and it rarely if ever needs division since the bulbs bloom best when left undisturbed for many years.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring; the climbing form of Cecile Brunner is extremely vigorous and needs a large, sturdy support, while the original bush form stays much smaller and suits a mixed border.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Introduced in 1881 and universally known as the Sweetheart Rose, Cecile Brunner produces small, perfectly formed, high-centered buds in soft pale pink that open to dainty, lightly fragrant blooms, traditionally favored for boutonnieres and small posies because of their miniature, exquisite shape. It exists in both a compact bush form suited to a border and a famously vigorous climbing sport that can scramble thirty feet or more into a tree if left unchecked, so gardeners should choose the form that fits their space. It is a tough, easy rose with good disease resistance and needs only routine pruning to control its size, particularly for the climbing form.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to alkaline, deep soil in full sun. Cedar Elm tolerates alkaline limestone soils, compaction, drought, and urban conditions better than most other elms and is the preferred native elm for landscapes in central and south Texas.
directions: Cedar Elm is the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant of the native elms, native to the river bottoms, limestone floodplains, and upland limestone woods of Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Louisiana, where it frequently grows adjacent to cedar (Juniperus species) — hence its common name. Its most distinctive habit is bloom timing: unlike all other North American elms that bloom in late winter before leaf-out, Cedar Elm blooms in late summer and fall (August–October), producing tiny, inconspicuous flowers followed by small, papery, winged seeds; this unusual timing means it can be confused with a disease-stricken elm (sparse fall foliage is normal, not worrying). A tough, adaptable native shade tree that tolerates the alkaline limestone soils, compaction, and summer heat of Texas landscapes with exceptional resilience, Cedar Elm is one of the most widely recommended native shade trees for central and south Texas gardens. Grow in full sun in any well-drained to moist soil; it adapts readily to both alkaline limestone and acidic sandy soils.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container transplants in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in partial shade; cedar sage is one of the few native salvias that genuinely prefers shade and is found growing naturally under cedar (Juniperus) and oak woodlands in central Texas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; cedar sage is a compact, low-growing native perennial of the limestone woodlands of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau — one of the very few native salvias that grows naturally in shade under Ashe juniper (cedar) and live oak canopies, making it exceptionally valuable for shaded Texas gardens. The small, rounded, hairy leaves are fragrant, and the brilliant red tubular flowers are produced on short spikes from spring through fall in shade conditions where few other flowering plants thrive. It is a critical hummingbird food plant. The plant stays compact and low (12–18 inches), spreads slowly by underground stolons, and requires almost no maintenance in well-drained shaded sites. Combine with turk's cap and inland sea oats for a beautiful dry shade planting.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or loamy, average to lean soil in full sun; Cedar of Lebanon grows naturally on well-drained limestone slopes of the mountains of Lebanon, Turkey, and Syria. It tolerates drought and lean soils but requires excellent drainage — wet, heavy soils cause rapid decline.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; Cedar of Lebanon is the most historically and culturally significant conifer in the world — the tree of the ancient Middle East, used to build King Solomon's Temple, Noah's Ark in the Midrash, and the fleets of the Phoenician traders. A young tree is non-descript, but old trees (100+ years) develop the flat, table-top, broadly spreading crown with massive horizontal limb tiers that is instantly recognizable — the form that appears on the flag of Lebanon. The cedar forests of Lebanon were already depleted by ancient times; only a few groves of ancient trees survive today on the slopes of the Cedars of God reserve. Plant in a very large, permanent space — old trees develop a majestic, wide-spreading crown wider than they are tall. More drought and alkaline-soil tolerant than deodar cedar. Cold-hardy to zone 5.

common_name: Cedric Morris Poppy (Large Pale Mauve-Pink Oriental Poppy)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Oriental poppies go dormant and disappear entirely in summer, so mark the spot to avoid disturbing the dormant crown.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Oriental poppies resent wet, heavy soil and summer humidity, so good drainage is essential. Named for the British plantsman and painter Cedric Morris who raised it, this cultivar bears exceptionally large, pale mauve-pink flowers with a prominent dark eye, a soft, painterly color that has made it a favorite among garden designers looking for a gentler alternative to the typical fiery Oriental poppy palette. Like other Oriental poppies it dies back to dormancy through summer heat before re-emerging with fresh foliage in fall, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown. It performs best in climates with cooler summers and struggles in the humid, hot conditions of the Deep South.

plant_note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Celadine is a plumeria cultivar with soft yellow-and-white flowers and a strong, sweet fragrance, a popular choice among collectors for its reliable bloom and classic coloring.
directions: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Celadine is a plumeria cultivar bearing soft, creamy yellow flowers brightening toward a deeper yellow throat and edged in white, a gentle color combination carrying the strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance the genus is famous for. It is a reliable, free-flowering cultivar favored by plumeria collectors for its consistent bloom production through the warm season. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to prevent stem rot. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes. Excellent drainage is essential year-round.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification; the plant self-sows reliably and will naturalize once established, filling a shaded bed with bright spring color.
directions: Direct sow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall; celandine poppy produces stunning bright yellow four-petaled flowers in early spring, making it one of the most brilliant color plants for the shade garden before the tree canopy closes. The plants bloom for several weeks in spring, then go partially dormant in summer heat but re-emerge in fall for additional sporadic flowering in cool climates. The bright orange sap from cut stems has traditional medicinal uses but is toxic and a skin irritant. Once established, it self-sows abundantly to naturalize throughout a shaded bed, so site carefully if you don't want it to spread. Combine with Virginia bluebells and trilliums for a classic spring shade display.

common_name: Celine Forestier Rose (Pale Yellow Climbing Noisette Rose)
plant_note: Plant own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or fence; Celine Forestier is a fragrant, repeat-blooming, pale yellow climbing Noisette rose well suited to the Gulf South heat.
directions: Plant own-root stock in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or fence. Celine Forestier bears pale lemon-yellow, quartered double blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening in flushes nearly continuously through the warm season on a vigorous climbing Noisette that, like other roses in its class, thrives on the heat and humidity of the Gulf South that stresses many modern climbers. Its soft color and repeat bloom make it a graceful choice for an arbor, porch post, or fence. Prune lightly after each bloom flush and train canes horizontally along the support to maximize flowering side shoots.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant only after soil is warm, as cold temperatures cause stunted plants.
directions: Sow seed on the surface of moist starting mix and lightly press in — seed needs light and warmth to germinate. Do not rush transplanting into cold soil, as chilling causes plants to stall and go prematurely to seed. Deadhead spent plumes on crested and feathered types to extend the display. Celosia makes an excellent dried flower; harvest spikes just as they reach full color.

common_name: Celsiana Rose (Semi-Double Light Pink Fragrant Damask)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Celsiana bears semi-double, light pink blooms with a graceful, informal form and strong fragrance.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Celsiana bears large, semi-double, soft light-pink blooms with translucent, papery petals and prominent golden stamens, opening in a graceful, informal, loosely cupped form with a strong, classic damask fragrance considered among the best of the class. Like most damask roses it blooms in a single strong flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to fall, setting the rhizome shallow with its top just at or barely below the soil surface in well-drained soil in full sun; Cemetery Iris is a sterile, ancient bearded iris spread entirely by hand-me-down rhizome division, which is exactly how it reached the countless Southern graveyards and homesites where it still blooms every spring with no care at all.
directions: Plant rhizomes shallow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Cemetery Iris earns its common name from its long association with old Southern graveyards, where it was traditionally planted at gravesites for its clean white, faintly fragrant blooms and because, once established, it needs no attention whatsoever and will outlive the person who planted it by generations. It is an ancient, sterile bearded iris hybrid believed to have spread out of the Mediterranean along old trade and pilgrimage routes centuries ago, reproducing only by rhizome offsets, so every planting traces back to a division from an older clump. It blooms for a few weeks in mid-spring on sturdy stems above gray-green fans of foliage, tolerates poor, dry soil far better than modern bearded iris hybrids, and is essentially immune to the fungal rot that plagues iris grown in humid, poorly drained ground.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in extremely well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; cenizo is adapted to the caliche and limestone soils of the Chihuahuan Desert and Edwards Plateau and will decline rapidly in rich, moist, or poorly drained soils. Never amend the planting hole with organic matter.
directions: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline soil; cenizo is the iconic native shrub of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau and one of the most drought tolerant and xeric shrubs in the South — its silver, feltlike leaves reflect heat and reduce water loss, allowing it to thrive in the hottest, driest conditions where other shrubs fail. The lavender-purple tubular flowers burst open in response to humidity — most dramatically in the 24–48 hours before a summer rain — giving it the folk name 'barometer bush.' Bloom cycles repeat with each moisture event from summer through fall, covering the entire silver shrub in purple. Cultivars include 'Green Cloud' (dark green leaves, rich purple flowers), 'White Cloud' (white flowers), and 'Compact' (dense, 3–4-foot habit).
