Never overwater or fertilize — excess moisture is the primary killer. Outstanding for xeric, native, and wildlife gardens in zones 8–11.

common_name: Centennial Star Magnolia (Arnold Arboretum Pure White Star Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped plants in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Centennial was released by the Arnold Arboretum in 1972 to mark its hundredth anniversary.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Centennial, introduced by the Arnold Arboretum in 1972 for its hundredth anniversary, bears pure white, fragrant, star-shaped flowers with 28 to 33 narrow tepals per bloom, a notably high petal count that gives an exceptionally full, showy floral display in late winter to early spring before the leaves emerge. It grows a bit more vigorously and upright than many other star magnolia selections, developing into a small tree over time rather than staying strictly shrubby. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost in warm, well-drained soil.
directions: Center Court is an elegant creamy-white dahlia that blooms nonstop all season and produces tubers reliably, making it a great choice for beginners. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed. Pinch young plants to promote branching and cut flowers regularly to prolong blooming. In cold-winter regions, dig and store the tubers indoors after the first frost blackens the foliage.

common_name: Center Glow Ninebark (Glowing Bicolor Foliage Ninebark)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Center Glow's two-tone leaf coloring is most vivid in full sun and fades toward a more uniform green-purple in shadier spots.
directions: Center Glow is a large, vigorous ninebark selected for unusual bicolor foliage: new leaves emerge with wine-purple margins surrounding a glowing chartreuse-to-orange center, an effect most pronounced on fresh spring and summer growth before the whole leaf gradually deepens toward purple with age, giving the shrub a constantly shifting, luminous look through the season. Clusters of small white-to-pink flowers in late spring draw pollinators, followed by reddish seed capsules and, once leaves drop, attractive exfoliating bark for winter interest. Like other ninebarks it is exceptionally tolerant of clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding, and needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems at the base to stay full and vigorous.

common_name: Center Stage Red Crapemyrtle (Black-Foliage Cerise-Red Compact Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Center Stage Red is a Proven Winners ColorChoice crapemyrtle bred by Spring Meadow Nursery for disease resistance and near-black foliage that dramatically sets off its cerise-red blooms, on a compact 10-12 foot form.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Center Stage Red bears near-black foliage that provides dramatic, season-long contrast to its clusters of vivid cerise-red flowers, standing out from the many crapemyrtle series bred primarily for flower color alone. Bred for good disease resistance, it holds its foliage well through a humid Gulf South summer, and its compact 10-12 foot mature size fits more readily into a residential landscape than older, larger crapemyrtle varieties. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood, preserving the plant's natural vase-shaped form.

common_name: Center Stripe Agave (Thorn Crested Agave, Variegated Agave)
plant_note: Plant pups or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Agave lophantha (also classified as Agave univittata by some authorities) is a Texas native agave of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos regions, notable for a distinctive light-green to pale central stripe running down the center of each dark green leaf — one of the most ornamental markings of any native agave.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky or sandy soil; Center Stripe Agave tolerates partial shade better than most agaves and is useful as an understory plant under open-canopy trees where full-sun agaves would struggle; it offsets moderately and forms attractive clumps over time; terminal spines are very sharp — site away from foot traffic. Center Stripe Agave is a small to medium agave native to the limestone hills and rocky slopes of the Edwards Plateau, Rio Grande Plains, and Trans-Pecos regions of Texas, where it grows in dry, shallow, rocky soils in full sun to dappled shade under live oaks and junipers. The species is readily identified by its namesake characteristic: each dark green leaf bears a distinctive lighter central stripe (yellow-green to pale green) running from base to near the tip — a coloration that gives the plant exceptional visual interest even among other agaves and makes it one of the most ornamental small agaves for garden use. The leaves also have prominent teeth along the margins and a stout, dark terminal spine, creating a 'thorn-crested' silhouette that is characteristic of the species. Plants form rosettes of 1–2 feet in diameter and height, producing pups readily to eventually form multi-rosette clumps. Unlike the massive Century Plant or Whale Tongue Agave, Center Stripe Agave is appropriately sized for small gardens, containers, and mixed plantings where a bold accent is needed without dominating the space. Cold-hardy to about 5°F, tolerates alkaline soils, and adapts to a wide range of well-drained site conditions throughout zone 9a and the Gulf South.

common_name: Center of Attention Distylium (Upright Burgundy New-Growth Evergreen Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Center of Attention grows taller and more upright than most distylium cultivars, making it useful as a screen or informal hedge without frequent pruning.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow the upright, vase-shaped form to develop into a screen or informal hedge without crowding. Center of Attention is a First Editions distylium selection with a notably taller, more upright habit than typical mounding distylium cultivars, producing burgundy-red new growth that matures to glossy dark green, along with small maroon flowers along the stems in late winter. Like other distylium, it shares the species' rare tolerance for both full sun and full shade, wet or dry soils, and strong resistance to the pests and diseases that trouble many broadleaf evergreens in humid Gulf South summers, along with being seldom browsed by deer. Its taller, narrower form makes it particularly useful as a living privacy screen or vertical accent where a low, spreading distylium would be the wrong shape, and it needs only occasional shaping to maintain its natural upright form.

common_name: Centipede Grass (Low-Maintenance Gulf South Lawn Grass)
plant_note: Seed (0.25–0.5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft), sprig, or plug in late spring when soil is above 65°F; centipede grass grows slowly and requires patience during establishment (1–2 full growing seasons for complete coverage from seed), but once established requires minimal inputs. DO NOT over-fertilize — centipede grass is adapted to infertile, acidic soils and excessive nitrogen causes iron chlorosis, scalping, and rapid decline.
directions: Seed or plug in late spring; mow at 1.5–2 inches and fertilize minimally — no more than 1 lb nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft per year. Centipede grass is the low-maintenance lawn grass of the Southeast, occupying an important niche as the grass for homeowners who want an attractive lawn with minimal fertilization, mowing, and irrigation requirements. Native to China and Southeast Asia, centipede grass was introduced to the US in 1916 and spread across the Gulf Coastal Plain states where its preference for acidic soils, low fertility tolerance, moderate shade adaptation, and low water requirements suited the conditions of the pine-forested South. Centipede produces a medium-textured, light to medium green, dense sward that grows slowly enough to require mowing only every 10–14 days. The most critical management consideration is restraint: centipede grass is notoriously susceptible to 'centipede decline' caused by over-fertilization (especially excess nitrogen and phosphorus), high pH (above 6.5), and over-irrigation — it evolved in infertile acidic soils and heavy maintenance inputs push it out of its ecological comfort zone. The ideal centipede lawn receives one application of 15-0-15 or similar fertilizer per year at 0.5–1.0 lb nitrogen per 1,000 sq ft, minimal phosphorus, maintained soil pH of 5.5–6.0, and supplemental irrigation only during drought. 'TifBlair' is the most cold-hardy cultivar; 'Hammock' and 'Tennessee Hardy' are excellent regional selections.

common_name: Century Celosia (Tall Vigorous Plumed Cutting Celosia Series)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Century is a tall, vigorous plumed celosia series bred for long, sturdy stems well suited to cutting, unlike shorter bedding-type celosia.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes. Century is a tall-growing plumed celosia series bred specifically for the cut-flower trade, producing long, sturdy stems topped by dense, feathery flame-shaped plumes in vivid gold, orange, red, and pink that hold their color and form exceptionally well both fresh and dried. Its greater height compared to compact bedding celosia varieties makes it far more practical for cutting gardens and floral arrangements, and the plants tolerate heat and humidity well through a long summer bloom season. Harvest stems for fresh use anytime, or cut for drying once the plumes are fully colored and hang upside down in a dry, dark, well-ventilated spot.

plant_note: Plant pups (offsets from the mother rosette) or container-grown plants in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; agave requires perfect drainage above all else — it will rot quickly in clay soil or where water pools. Plant slightly above grade to improve drainage.
directions: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, lean, rocky or sandy soil — perfect drainage is the only critical requirement; century plant is one of the most dramatic and architectural plants available for hot, dry landscapes and can survive on rainfall alone in appropriate climates once established. The large blue-gray rosette of thick, succulent leaves with sharp terminal spines and hooked marginal teeth grows slowly over 10–30 years before producing a single towering flower stalk (15–30 feet tall) laden with thousands of yellow flowers — then the main rosette dies, leaving behind offsets (pups) that perpetuate the clump. The juice of the leaf base was fermented by indigenous peoples of Mexico to make pulque; the young flower stalk was roasted and eaten as a sweet vegetable. Despite the name 'century plant,' blooming typically occurs after 10–30 years, not 100. Outstanding as a bold specimen and accent plant for xeric landscapes; handle with caution due to the sharp terminal spine which can cause serious injury.

common_name: Cerise Queen Yarrow (Cherry-Pink Cottage Garden Yarrow)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, surface-sowing since yarrow seed needs light to germinate, or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Cerise Queen tolerates poor, dry soil and needs no fertilizer to thrive.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; rich soil or too much water leads to floppy, weak-stemmed growth in this drought-tough native selection. Cerise Queen is a compact, long-blooming yarrow cultivar bearing flat-topped clusters of small, cherry-pink to cerise flowers with paler pink centers above finely dissected, aromatic, fern-like gray-green foliage, blooming from early summer well into fall if deadheaded. Like the wild species, it thrives on neglect, tolerating poor soil, heat, humidity, and drought once established, and its nectar-rich flower clusters draw a steady stream of butterflies and other pollinators while resisting deer and rabbits. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring or fall to keep the planting vigorous and to control its naturally spreading habit.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; in zone 8b–9 the plant is usually killed back to the crown by hard freezes but regrows from the roots once the soil warms.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ceylon leadwort is a sprawling, semi-scandent subshrub found through the tropics and subtropics of Asia and Africa that bears loose spikes of small white flowers with a slender green calyx, blooming most heavily where it gets some relief from the hottest afternoon sun. It spreads slowly by root suckers to form an informal, arching mound and works well tucked under high tree canopy or along a shaded fence line where fewer flowering shrubs perform. It is drought tolerant once established and needs little care beyond an annual cutback in late winter to control size and encourage fresh flowering growth; wear gloves when handling cut stems, since the sap can irritate sensitive skin.

plant_note: Start indoors early since these carnations are slow to reach bloom.
directions: Start seed indoors well before the last frost, as this blend is slow to reach flowering. Chabaud carnations bear fragrant, clove-scented double blooms in scarlet, purple, pink, white, yellow, and bicolors atop blue-green foliage, one flower per stem for excellent cutting. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil and even moisture. Deadhead and pinch early to build sturdy, well-branched plants.

plant_note: Start indoors well before the last frost; slow to reach bloom.
directions: Start Chabaud carnations indoors eight to ten weeks before the last frost, covering seed lightly, then harden off and transplant after frost danger passes. This heirloom Dianthus bears fragrant, fully double blooms in a rich mix of colors prized for cut arrangements. Give it full sun, well-drained soil, and support the tall flower stems. Deadhead to prolong the display, and in mild zones it will return as a short-lived perennial.

plant_note: Break off a mature joint with tongs in spring, let the cut end callus for one to two weeks in a dry shaded spot, then set it a few inches into fast-draining soil and withhold water until roots form.
directions: Break off a mature joint (segment) with tongs in spring, let the cut end callus for one to two weeks in a dry shaded spot, then set it a few inches into fast-draining soil and withhold water until roots form. This Sonoran Desert native forms a small silvery-spined tree with pendulous chains of fruit that persist year-round, making it a dramatic accent or barrier planting. Handle with heavy gloves and long tools, since the barbed joints detach at the slightest touch and are notoriously difficult to remove from skin or fabric. Give it full sun and a spot away from foot traffic and pets.

common_name: Chalice Vine (Cup of Gold, Hawaiian Wedding Flower)
plant_note: Root woody cuttings in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic, rich soil in full sun; chalice vine is slow to establish but eventually forms a massive, woody-stemmed vine requiring a very large, sturdy support. Bloom is best on established plants and often increases when the plant experiences mild drought stress in late summer-fall.
directions: Plant in fertile, rich, well-drained soil in full sun; chalice vine is one of the most spectacular large-flowering plants in the world, producing enormous chalice-shaped flowers 8–10 inches across in golden yellow with purple veins and a powerful, tropical, coconut-like fragrance, strongest at night. The massive, woody vines with large, glossy evergreen leaves can eventually cover a large wall, pergola, or building. It is one of the showiest of all tropical vines for zone 10–11 landscapes and a traditional feature of California and Florida coastal gardens. Established plants are surprisingly drought tolerant. Bloom is typically heaviest in late winter through spring and again in fall. Caution: all parts of this plant, including the nectar, are highly toxic — the active alkaloids can cause severe poisoning. Do not plant where children, pets, or livestock can access the plant.

plant_note: Plant offsets or nursery starts in fall so roots establish before winter rains, setting the crown slightly proud of the soil surface to prevent rot.
directions: Plant on a rocky slope, rock wall, or raised bed with sharp drainage, tucking the base into gravel or crevices so winter rain sheds away from the crown. Water sparingly during the growing season and keep completely dry through the summer dormancy that follows its spring bloom. The thick, chalky-white leaves form a striking rosette that reflects heat and rarely needs supplemental water once established. Its coral-pink flower stalks rise above the foliage in late spring, drawing hummingbirds to coastal and inland rock gardens.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; chalk maple performs better in zone 7–9 summer heat than sugar maple, Japanese maple, or most other ornamental maples.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; chalk maple is a small-to-medium native understory maple of the Southeast Appalachians and Piedmont, closely related to sugar maple but significantly more heat-and-drought-tolerant and better suited to the zone 7–9 garden than its more famous relative. The common name comes from the distinctive light-colored, chalky-white to pale gray bark. The 3–5 lobed leaves turn magnificent shades of yellow, orange, and scarlet in fall — one of the best native maples for fall color in the South. It grows naturally as an understory tree on rocky slopes and bluffs with well-drained, calcareous soils. An outstanding and underused native small tree for shaded gardens in the Southeast where sugar maple and Japanese maple both struggle with the heat and humidity.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in lean, well-drained, sandy or loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; chalky bluestem is an excellent Gulf Coastal Plain grass for sunny, dry to moderately moist sites in zones 7–10.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; chalky bluestem is a native grass of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, closely related to big bluestem (A. gerardii) and broomsedge (A. virginicus) but distinct in the powdery, chalky-white bloom (waxy coating) that covers the stems and upper leaf sheaths, giving the plant a cool, glaucous appearance that sets it apart in the landscape. Like broomsedge, the foliage turns warm shades of bronze and copper in fall, providing excellent winter interest in the ornamental garden. The fine, fluffy seed heads in fall are attractive and provide seeds for numerous sparrows and other small birds. A reliable grass for dry, sunny spots in the Gulf South where it grows naturally in open pine flatwoods, old fields, and sandy roadsides. Combines beautifully with muhly grass, native wildflowers, and yuccas in low-maintenance Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors or plant container stock after last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; champaca is frost-tender and suitable for zones 10–12 outdoors. In zone 9 it may survive in warm, sheltered microclimates or be grown as a large container specimen.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; champaca is a large tropical tree from the eastern Himalayas and Southeast Asia that produces some of the most intensely fragrant flowers in the botanical world — the golden-orange, magnolia-like blooms have a complex, fruity-floral-spicy scent used in 'Joy' by Jean Patou (once called the world's most expensive perfume) and numerous other fine fragrances. The flowers are sacred in Hindu and Buddhist traditions and used extensively as temple offerings across South and Southeast Asia. In India, garlands of champaca flowers are worn in the hair. The essential oil, extracted by enfleurage or solvent extraction, is extraordinarily expensive. In the home garden in zone 9, grow as a large container specimen moved indoors in winter, where even a few flowers will perfume an entire room.

common_name: Champagne Elegance Bearded Iris (Reblooming Soft Beige-Pink Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Champagne Elegance is a widely grown reblooming bearded iris known for a second flush of bloom in fall.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Champagne Elegance bears soft, blended beige-pink standards and falls with a warm, glowing quality that reads almost peach in some light, and it is one of the most dependable reblooming bearded iris cultivars available, often producing a second flush of flowers in late summer or fall in addition to its main spring bloom. Its gentle, warm coloring pairs easily with almost any companion planting. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep the rhizomes in full sun with sharp drainage to avoid rot; light feeding after each bloom cycle helps support reliable reblooming.

common_name: Champaka (Joy Perfume Tree, Yellow Champak, Magnolia champaca)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Champaka grows rapidly in zone 9b-11 and typically begins flowering at 3–5 years from seed. In zone 9a, container culture allows winter protection — large containers can be moved to a greenhouse or enclosed space. In zone 9b-10, plant against a south-facing wall for warmth and frost protection. The intensely fragrant flowers are used for garlands, perfumery, and religious offerings throughout South and Southeast Asia.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — Champaka grows most vigorously in full sun but benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Magnolia champaca (formerly Michelia champaca) is a large, fast-growing evergreen tree from the Himalayan foothills of India and Southeast Asia in the Magnoliaceae family, cultivated throughout the tropical world for one of the most celebrated flower fragrances in perfumery. The small (2–3 inch), creamy-white to golden-yellow flowers are produced in extraordinary abundance from spring through fall on established trees — typically dozens to hundreds of flowers open simultaneously — and release a fragrance variously described as combining orange blossom, ylang ylang, jasmine, and spice in a complex, penetrating, euphoric composition. Jean Patou's 'Joy' perfume (once the world's most expensive perfume per ounce) was built substantially around champaka absolute. In South and Southeast Asia, the flowers are woven into garlands for religious offerings in Hindu and Buddhist temples and worn as hair adornments at weddings and festivals. The flowers are among the most revered in Asian botanical culture. In zone 9-10 Gulf Coast landscapes, Champaka is a fast-growing ornamental tree that blooms for months and fills garden spaces with its remarkable fragrance.

common_name: Champneys' Pink Cluster Rose (Original Noisette Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall at the base of a support for its climbing habit; Champneys' Pink Cluster was bred around 1811 by John Champneys of Charleston, South Carolina, and is the founding rose of the entire Noisette class — the only class of roses developed in North America — making it historically significant as well as well adapted to Gulf South heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil at the base of a fence, arbor, or trellis, allowing 4-6 feet for its spreading, semi-climbing habit. Bred around 1811 by rice planter John Champneys of Charleston, South Carolina, by crossing the musk rose with an early China rose, Champneys' Pink Cluster became the founding parent of the Noisette class — the only major class of roses developed in North America — after cuttings were shared with a Charleston nurseryman named Philippe Noisette, who sent seedlings on to his brother in Paris. It bears large, loose clusters of small, semi-double, soft pink, fragrant blooms in repeated flushes from spring through fall on long, lax canes best trained on a support. As an early hybrid between a China rose and a musk rose, it carries strong heat tolerance and repeat bloom, traits that were unusual in roses available in Europe at the time and that make it well suited to the modern Gulf South garden. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to shape and remove spent wood, training new canes onto the support as they grow.

common_name: Chandleri Elegans Camellia (Antique Anemone-Form Pink Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Chandleri Elegans is one of the oldest camellia cultivars still in general cultivation, introduced in England around 1831, with large anemone-form rose-pink flowers centered by a dense cluster of small petaloids.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Chandleri Elegans, introduced in England around 1831, is one of the oldest camellia cultivars still widely grown, prized for large, anemone-form flowers with a ring of broad, rose-pink outer petals surrounding a dense central cluster of smaller, irregular petaloids, a distinctive form quite different from the neat, layered rows of formal-double camellias. Occasional flowers show attractive white mottling or streaking. Its long cultivation history and reliable performance have kept it a fixture in historic and heritage camellia gardens across the South for nearly two centuries. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it flowers in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chansonette has a spreading, cascading habit well suited to hanging baskets, banks, and low walls.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Chansonette is a sasanqua camellia grown for its deep rose-pink, peony-form double flowers and its distinctive low, spreading, cascading growth habit, which sets it apart from the more upright sasanqua cultivars and makes it especially useful trained over a low wall, planted on a bank, or grown in a large hanging container. It blooms heavily in fall, offering reliable color when few other shrubs are flowering, and like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica cultivars. Prune only lightly to shape after flowering, since flower buds set later in the growing season.

plant_note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. Chantilly performs best under the cool temperatures and short days of fall, winter, or early spring cut-flower production.
directions: Surface-sow the fine seed indoors under bright light 12-16 weeks before the intended transplant date, since snapdragon seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered. Chantilly is a cut-flower snapdragon series distinguished by open-faced blooms that stay flat rather than closing into the pinched 'dragon mouth' of traditional types, a form florists favor for its softer look in arrangements. It performs best under the cool temperatures and short days of fall, winter, or early spring production rather than the heat of summer, and can be grown either as a single tall stem or pinched for multiple cutting stems. Available in shades from bright white and cream-yellow to salmon, bronze, and deep purple, it is best suited to mild-winter or high-tunnel cut-flower operations.

common_name: Chaparral Yucca (Our Lord's Candle, Spanish Bayonet)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring into sharply drained, rocky or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; site well away from paths, as the rigid, needle-tipped leaves are sharp enough to puncture skin.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, rocky to sandy soil in full sun and withhold supplemental irrigation once established; this chaparral and coastal-sage native from California and Baja California forms a dense, silvery-blue-green rosette of narrow, rigid, needle-tipped leaves that stays low and tidy for years before sending up its signature bloom spike. The plant is monocarpic, meaning each individual rosette flowers only once, in its case producing a dramatic 6-12 foot pole-like spike crowded with hundreds of creamy-white, purple-tinged, fragrant bell flowers over a period of weeks in late spring, after which that rosette dies; some populations (formerly classed as subsp. percursa) offset from the base and persist as clumps, while the typical form is usually solitary. Because of the years-long buildup to a single spectacular bloom, it is prized in xeriscape and rock-garden design as a long-term architectural accent rather than a repeat-flowering perennial. It tolerates poor, rocky soils and extended drought better than almost any other landscape yucca relative but resents heavy clay and wet winter feet.

common_name: Chapel Hill Gold Lantana (Cold-Hardy Sterile Gold Lantana)
plant_note: Set out nursery transplants after the last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; Chapel Hill Gold is a North Carolina State University release bred for cold hardiness well beyond most lantana as well as sterility, so it does not set the viable seed that lets ordinary lantana escape into natural areas.
directions: Plant nursery starts after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Chapel Hill Gold is a landscape lantana bred at North Carolina State University for two traits at once — root hardiness well into zone 7b, letting it return reliably as a herbaceous perennial in much colder winters than most lantana can survive, and functional sterility, meaning it produces few to no viable seeds and so does not spread into surrounding natural areas the way common seed-producing lantana cultivars can. It covers itself from late spring through frost in rounded clusters of clear golden-yellow flowers that are a magnet for butterflies and other pollinators. Once established it is highly drought tolerant and needs little supplemental water. In zone 9, expect the top growth to die back to the ground after a hard freeze; cut the dead stems back close to the ground in late winter and new growth will resprout from the crown in spring. Avoid overwatering and rich soil, both of which encourage leggy growth at the expense of flowering.

common_name: Chapel Hill Yellow Lantana (Cold-Hardy Yellow Native Selection)
plant_note: Plant container plants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; more cold-hardy than most lantana cultivars, often returning reliably from the roots after mild winters.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Chapel Hill Yellow was selected by the North Carolina Botanical Garden for improved cold hardiness compared to typical lantana cultivars, regularly surviving winters as a root-hardy perennial in areas where less hardy selections are killed outright, while producing clusters of clear golden-yellow flowers continuously from late spring through frost. Its vigorous, upright growth and heavy, long-lasting bloom make it a strong butterfly and pollinator plant for a sunny border in regions at the colder edge of lantana's usual perennial range. It tolerates heat, humidity, and drought with ease once established; cut back hard in late winter after the coldest weather passes to remove winter-damaged growth and promote vigorous new flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in dry, sandy, strongly acidic soil in full sun; Chapman's blazing star is a Coastal Plain endemic growing in dry, sandy pine flatwoods and scrub in Florida and the immediately surrounding states. It requires the xeric, nutrient-poor conditions of the longleaf pine ecosystem.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Chapman's blazing star is a Florida-centered Coastal Plain endemic of dry sandy pine flatwoods and scrub habitats, one of the most drought-tolerant blazing stars adapted to the extreme xeric soils of the longleaf pine ecosystem. The vivid rose-purple flower spikes in summer are as ornamentally attractive as those of the more widely grown liatris species and especially valuable in zone 9a gardens where many temperate liatris species struggle in summer heat. The flowers are critically important late-summer and fall nectar sources for monarch butterflies and numerous native bees in the Gulf South. Plant in dry, infertile, sandy soils in naturalistic pine flatwoods or xeric native plant gardens.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun; Chapman's butterwort grows in shallow standing water of Florida panhandle and Gulf Coast flatwoods bogs, tolerating wetter conditions than most butterworts.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun. Chapman's butterwort forms a flat, ground-hugging rosette of pale yellow-green, sticky leaves that press directly against the soil surface, an adaptation to the shallow standing water of the wet Florida panhandle and Alabama flatwoods bogs where it grows, often with the rosette partly submerged during the wettest months. Striking violet-pink flowers on slender stalks appear in spring, held well above the low foliage, and the sticky leaf surface traps and digests small insects the same as other butterworts. It tolerates wetter, more consistently saturated conditions than most Pinguicula species, making it a good match for the lowest, wettest spot in a home bog garden alongside pitcher plants. Grow in pure rain water or distilled water and never fertilize, since both tap water minerals and ordinary garden fertility are fatal to butterworts over time.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist but well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; Chapman's rhododendron is a rare Florida Panhandle endemic best purchased only as nursery-propagated stock from growers who cultivate it responsibly, never wild-collected.
directions: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist but well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; Chapman's rhododendron is a rare Florida Panhandle endemic best purchased only as nursery-propagated stock from growers who cultivate it responsibly, never wild-collected. Rhododendron chapmanii is a federally listed endangered evergreen shrub found only in a handful of sandhill and scrub sites in the Florida Panhandle and southwest Georgia, with small, leathery leaves and clusters of rose-pink, funnel-shaped flowers in early to mid-spring. Unlike most rhododendrons, it is naturally adapted to sharply drained, sandy soil and considerable sun exposure, making it more drought-tolerant than typical evergreen rhododendrons and a good candidate for a well-drained Gulf Coast native garden. Growing this rare species in cultivation from nursery-propagated stock helps support conservation of the species by reducing pressure on its few remaining wild populations, so buy only from reputable native-plant nurseries with documented cultivated origin.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chardonnay Pearls' gold foliage holds its brightest color with a few hours of direct sun but benefits from afternoon shade in peak Gulf South summer heat to prevent scorch.
directions: Chardonnay Pearls is a slender deutzia selected for bright chartreuse-gold foliage that lights up a shaded border through the growing season, topped in mid-to-late spring by small, pearl-like white flower buds that open into star-shaped white blooms, giving the shrub a two-tone gold-and-white display. Its low, mounded, well-behaved habit fits foundation plantings and mixed borders where a compact flowering shrub with season-long foliage color is wanted, unlike plain-green deutzia cultivars that offer interest only during the spring bloom window. It tolerates partial shade better than many golden-leaved shrubs while still coloring and flowering well, and needs only light pruning right after bloom to keep a tidy, rounded shape.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall (September–November in zone 9); fall planting allows root establishment before the spring bloom season. Charjoy's Jan is a registered Louisiana iris cultivar from the Charjoy series developed by hybridizer Charles Chapman. Louisiana iris rhizomes should be planted at or just below soil surface — do not bury deep. In zone 9 plants bloom in April–May; in the fall before bloom, fertilize with a slow-release fertilizer formulated for acidic-soil plants. The moist to wet, acidic soil conditions of the Gulf South coastal plain are ideal — Louisiana irises grow naturally in bayous, swamp margins, and wet meadows.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, very acidic to slightly acidic, fertile soil — Louisiana irises thrive in the acid, wet soils that characterize the Gulf South coastal plain; Charjoy's Jan is a registered cultivar in the Louisiana iris series developed by Charles Chapman, producing the large, flat, fleur-de-lis-form flowers characteristic of the Louisiana iris hybrids (Iris x louisiana) — a complex group combining genetics from five native Gulf Coast iris species that together account for the extraordinary color range and form variation available in Louisiana iris breeding. Louisiana irises are among the most adapted irises for the Gulf South climate — heat tolerant through zone 9, fully cold hardy to zone 4, and thriving in the moist to wet, acidic soil conditions that are common across the Gulf Coast where bearded iris, Japanese iris, and Siberian iris perform poorly. The April–May bloom time fills a critical spring window when the large, brightly colored iris flowers are at their most dramatic — creating one of the finest native wildflower displays available for zone 9 water garden edges, bayou margins, and moist border plantings. Louisiana iris culture is supported by the Society for Louisiana Irises, a dedicated organization that maintains registration, hybridization, and evaluation of the hundreds of cultivars available.

common_name: Charles Darwin Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Charles Darwin's large, heavy blooms benefit from a sturdy, well-branched framework and occasional support after heavy rain.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001, Charles Darwin bears very large, deeply cupped blooms in a distinctive mustard-bronze to old-gold color that deepens as the flower ages, with a strong tea fragrance, on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its unusual bronze-gold tones set it apart from the more common clear yellows and pinks in the English rose palette, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Charles de Meurville Water Lily (Classic Marliac Large Wine-Red Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun; Charles de Meurville, a classic Marliac introduction, bears exceptionally large, deep wine-red to burgundy flowers on a vigorous plant.
directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun, allowing plenty of room for this vigorous cultivar to spread. Charles de Meurville is a classic French Marliac-bred hardy water lily producing exceptionally large, deep wine-red to burgundy star-shaped flowers with a subtle fragrance, among the largest and darkest-colored blooms of any hardy water lily cultivar, held above vigorous, spreading foliage that can quickly fill a good-sized pond. Its long history and dramatic bloom color have kept it a favorite for gardeners wanting a bold, dark accent in a water garden. Divide rhizomes every two to three years when they crowd their container, and feed during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets pushed into the soil for the best bloom.

common_name: Charles de Mills Rose (Deep Crimson-Purple Flat-Flowered Gallica)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Charles de Mills is a Gallica rose of uncertain but early origin, blooming once in a single heavy spring flush.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Charles de Mills tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough Gallica of uncertain but early origin. Its very full, densely packed double flowers open a rich crimson-purple and open remarkably flat with a neatly quartered, almost geometric center, considered by many collectors one of the most perfectly formed blooms of any old garden rose, carrying a strong, classic old-rose fragrance. Like other Gallicas it blooms just once, in a spectacular flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow where plants are to grow, as flax resents transplanting.
directions: Direct sow in early spring where plants will grow, since flax does not transplant well. This easy, low-maintenance blend produces showy flowers on delicate stems that dance in the breeze and draw pollinators. It tolerates hot, dry conditions once established, so water sparingly. Allow some plants to go to seed for reseeding and successive bloom.

common_name: Charming Beauty Gladiolus (Soft Pink with White Throat)
plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season. Charming Beauty bears soft pink flowers with a contrasting white throat.
directions: Charming Beauty bears soft, clear pink flowers with a bright white throat, a gentle, classic gladiolus color combination that fits nearly any bouquet or garden color scheme. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; chaste tree demands excellent drainage and thrives in hot, dry conditions that defeat many ornamentals.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; chaste tree is a fast-growing, multi-stemmed deciduous large shrub or small tree with deeply fragrant, spicy gray-green palmately compound leaves — a strong, pleasant sage-and-lavender scent — and tall, upright spikes of lavender-blue flowers from summer through fall that make it one of the most valuable summer-blooming ornamentals for hot, dry climates. It blooms profusely on new growth; cutting back hard in late winter to 12–18 inches above ground produces vigorous new shoots and the best flower display. The dried fruits were historically used as a spice and medicinal herb (the name 'chaste tree' refers to its historical use to reduce libido). 'Shoal Creek' (large, deep blue spikes) and 'Abbeville Blue' are outstanding selections.

plant_note: Often grown as a biennial; sow in spring or fall for bloom the next year.
directions: Sow in spring or fall in a sunny, sheltered spot, as this classic biennial typically flowers the second year. Chater's Double, developed in the 1880s, produces tall spires of ruffly double blooms in golden-yellow, rose, maroon, salmon-pink, scarlet, and white over a long bloom period. Stake the tall stalks in windy sites and water at the base to reduce rust. Let some flowers set seed, as hollyhocks reseed reliably.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled or part shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind and hard freezes.
directions: This dramatic New Zealand perennial forms a broad clump of arching, silvery-scaled sword-shaped leaves that catch light beautifully in a woodland-edge or coastal border. It tolerates full sun in cool, humid climates but colors and performs best with afternoon shade in warmer zones, where leaf scorch can occur. Inconspicuous flowers are followed by orange berries on female plants when a male is nearby. Give it sharp drainage, since soggy winter soil is its main limiting factor outside mild coastal gardens.

subcategory: evergreen coastal perennial with giant glossy leaves
plant_note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in part shade with protection from hot midday sun and drying wind, ideally in a cool, humid coastal microclimate.
directions: This striking perennial from New Zealand's remote Chatham Islands produces bold, glossy, ribbed leaves the size of dinner plates topped by dense rounded clusters of vivid blue flowers in late spring. It is notoriously fussy outside cool, humid, maritime climates, demanding constant moisture, rich organic soil, and reliable shade from intense sun. Gardeners in the Pacific Northwest and similar mild coastal zones have the best luck; inland heat and drought quickly cause collapse. Grow it as a specimen in a sheltered shade bed with generous mulch and steady irrigation.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chattahoochee requires consistent moisture and good organic content in the soil — it does not tolerate drought or heavy clay without amendment.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Chattahoochee phlox is widely considered the finest Phlox divaricata cultivar — a selection originally found growing wild near the Chattahoochee River in Florida, distinguished by its exceptionally clear, lavender-blue to periwinkle-blue flowers with a distinctive deep purple eye at the center of each five-petaled flower. This characteristic purple-eyed blue-lavender color combination is one of the most beautiful in the spring garden, and a mass planting of Chattahoochee phlox in partial shade creates a carpet of color in April through May in zone 9 that rivals any other spring-blooming perennial. The fragrant flowers attract early butterflies and pollinators. After blooming, the semi-evergreen foliage maintains a neat, ground-covering mat through the growing season — Phlox divaricata spreads by stolons and self-seeding to gradually naturalize beneath trees and shrubs. In zone 9, morning sun with afternoon shade is the ideal exposure — the flowers open most fully with some direct light but the plant needs protection from the intense afternoon sun and heat that causes rapid decline. Shear lightly after bloom to neaten and encourage compact new growth. Excellent for woodland gardens, native plant landscapes, and naturalized areas under deciduous shade trees.

plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally, growing tip up, in heavy clay soil without added organic matter, in a wide, shallow, undrained container submerged just a few inches below the water surface in full sun; Chawan Basu is one of the classic dwarf bowl lotus cultivars for small container water gardens.
directions: Chawan Basu, whose name translates roughly to teacup lotus, is one of the most popular dwarf bowl lotus cultivars for small-scale water gardening, staying compact enough to bloom well in a half-barrel or large glazed bowl rather than needing a full pond. Its single flowers open white with a soft pink blush concentrated at the petal tips, held above the rounded, blue-green, umbrella-like leaves typical of lotus, and it flowers repeatedly through the warm season once established. Feed with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets during the growing season, and in zones with hard winter freezes, move the container to a frost-free space or sink it below the ice line for winter protection, since lotus tubers are more cold-sensitive than most hardy water lilies.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall promptly; they dry out quickly.
directions: Plant checkered fritillary bulbs in fall as soon as possible, since the delicate bulbs dry out quickly, setting them about four inches deep. The nodding bell flowers display a distinctive checkerboard pattern in purple or white in mid-spring. It prefers moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade and naturalizes well in damp meadows and woodland edges. Handle the fragile bulbs gently at planting and let foliage die back to ensure return.

plant_note: Move small divisions along with a generous scoop of their native soil into acidic, humus-rich ground beneath pines or mixed hardwoods, disturbing the root zone as little as possible to protect the fungal partners the plant depends on.
directions: Move small divisions along with a generous scoop of their native soil into acidic, humus-rich ground beneath pines or mixed hardwoods, disturbing the root zone as little as possible to protect the fungal partners the plant depends on. Its low rosette of dark green leaves is netted with fine silvery-white veining and stays attractive through winter, while a slender spike of small, white, hooded flowers appears in summer. Because it relies on an intact mycorrhizal relationship, this native orchid rarely thrives if transplanted into ordinary garden soil, so it is best grown as a foliage accent in an undisturbed woodland setting rather than a typical perennial bed. Its patterned leaves make it a subtle but rewarding groundcover for collectors of native shade flora.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; cheddar pinks are among the most drought and heat tolerant of all Dianthus species — they are exceptional in alkaline, rocky, or sandy soils where other perennials fail.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun — cheddar pinks are native to the limestone gorges of Cheddar, England and are among the most drought-tolerant and heat-resistant perennial dianthus available, forming compact, mat-like mounds of very narrow, blue-gray, evergreen foliage tipped with intensely fragrant, deep rose-pink to cerise flowers in late spring. The rich clove fragrance is as strong as cottage pinks but the plant is smaller, tidier, and notably more heat and alkaline-soil tolerant. The Perennial Plant Association named it Perennial Plant of the Year in 2015. Superb for rock gardens, dry walls, gravel gardens, and edging in alkaline or sandy soils where drainage is excellent. Shear lightly after bloom to maintain compact mounds and often promotes a second flush of bloom in fall. Very long-lived in appropriate conditions; clumps may persist for decades.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring after temperatures are consistently above 60°F in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; chenille plant roots easily and establishes quickly in warm weather. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage dense, bushy growth and maximum flower production.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; chenille plant is one of the most unusually beautiful tropical flowering plants, producing long, pendulous, fuzzy catkin-like flower spikes in brilliant crimson-red that dangle like fluffy chenille tassels 12–18 inches long — an unmistakable and astonishing floral display unlike anything else in the garden. The flowers are produced nearly year-round in frost-free zones. It thrives in the warm, humid conditions of zone 10–12 and is used as a summer annual or large container plant in cooler zones; in zone 9 it may be grown as a seasonal annual or overwintered in a greenhouse. Bright filtered light or morning sun produces the most flowers while preventing leaf scorch in the afternoon heat. Regular watering and monthly fertilization during the growing season keeps the plant vigorous and blooming well. Propagate from 6-inch stem cuttings in late spring.

common_name: Cherokee Brave Dogwood (Deep Red Flowering Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Cherokee Brave requires excellent drainage and partial shade in zone 9 — morning sun with afternoon shade prevents the leaf scorch and stress that shortens the life of dogwoods in the Gulf South's intense summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Cherokee Brave is the finest red-flowering dogwood cultivar — a selection with deep rosy-red to crimson-red bracts that are noticeably darker and more intensely colored than older red dogwood cultivars like 'Cherokee Chief.' The deep, saturated crimson-red bracts create one of the most spectacular spring flowering displays available for the partial-shade Southeast garden in March through April. Like the native species, Cherokee Brave is an understory tree — it evolved growing beneath the canopy of larger hardwoods in the forest edge, making it one of the finest specimens for sites that receive morning sun and afternoon shade. This understory adaptation is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the intense afternoon sun and summer heat stress full-sun dogwoods. The spring floral display is followed by attractive horizontal branching with dark-green summer foliage and excellent red fall color. Glossy red berries in fall provide bird food. In zone 9, dogwoods perform best in the northern portions and in protected, afternoon-shaded positions — mulch heavily around the root zone to maintain cool, moist soil. The striking contrast between the dark red bracts and white-centered bracts creates a bicolor effect that distinguishes Cherokee Brave from solid-red cultivars.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Cherokee Brave opens deep pink spring blooms with reddish new foliage, followed by red fall color and berries that attract birds. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, siting it in part shade or where it gets afternoon protection in hot regions. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, as dogwoods are shallow-rooted and dislike drought. This selection shows improved resistance to powdery mildew; prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered spot with dappled light in warm climates.
directions: Cherokee Chief bears rich rosy-red bracts in spring on graceful horizontal branches, with glossy foliage that turns red in autumn. Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and give it part shade or afternoon protection where summers are hot. Maintain even soil moisture with mulch, since the shallow roots suffer in dry conditions. Prune sparingly right after bloom to shape the canopy and remove any damaged wood.

common_name: Cherokee Crape Myrtle (Red-Flowered Dwarf-to-Medium Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cherokee is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's earlier Native American tribe-named crape myrtle releases, a Lagerstroemia indica selection predating the mildew-resistant indica x fauriei hybrids like Natchez.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours direct sun); Cherokee is a bright red-flowering crape myrtle from the U.S. National Arboretum's early tribe-named breeding series, producing dense clusters of vivid red crepe-textured flowers through the heat of summer on a dwarf-to-medium multi-stemmed shrub. Being a straight Lagerstroemia indica selection rather than one of the later indica x fauriei hybrids, it carries more susceptibility to powdery mildew than mildew-resistant selections like Natchez or Tuscarora, so give it full sun and good air circulation to minimize disease pressure. Its more compact size compared to the largest crape myrtle cultivars makes it a fit for smaller landscapes or foundation plantings where a full-size tree form would be too large. As with all crape myrtles, never top or hard-prune the main framework — a practice sometimes called 'crepe murder' — since it ruins the natural vase-shaped form permanently; instead prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or crowded twiggy growth.

common_name: Cherokee Daybreak Flowering Dogwood (White-Edged Variegated Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Cherokee Daybreak bears creamy-white-edged variegated foliage along with white flower bracts.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; understory planting beneath high, open tree canopy mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. Cherokee Daybreak bears green leaves edged in creamy white through the growing season, brightening the canopy from a distance, and pairs the variegation with a heavy spring display of white flower bracts and rich pink-to-deep-red fall color. Its bright, variegated foliage gives it strong ornamental value even when not in bloom. Water during dry spells, especially the first two years, and avoid deep planting or heavy mulch piled against the trunk.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in dappled light with cool, moist, acidic soil.
directions: Cherokee Princess is prized for its heavy set of large, pure-white spring bracts and a well-branched, rounded form. Plant in moist, acidic, organically rich soil in part shade, protecting it from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind. Mulch to keep the shallow root system cool and consistently moist. Enjoy red fall foliage and berries that feed birds; prune only lightly after flowering to maintain the tidy structure.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring or fall; Cherokee Rose establishes readily and grows vigorously in zone 7–9. The canes are extremely thorny and reach 15–20 feet — site at the back of borders, on fences, or as a naturalized hedge where the thorns provide security. Once established it requires virtually no maintenance.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Cherokee rose is a large, vigorous climbing rose native to China that naturalized across the Deep South and is now Georgia's state flower. The single, 3–4 inch white flowers with prominent golden stamens are produced in extraordinary abundance in March–April, covering the long canes with a spectacular display that has made this rose a Southern garden tradition for over two centuries. The hips that follow are large, pear-shaped, red, and persist through winter — they are extremely high in vitamin C and were historically made into rosehip syrup and tea. The evergreen to semi-evergreen foliage is attractive year-round and the thorny canes form impenetrable barriers that deter deer and intruders. Requires almost no care once established; thrives on neglect.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in shade; Cherokee sedge grows naturally in low, moist woodland bottomlands and creek margins of the southeastern Coastal Plain and requires consistent moisture to perform well.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Cherokee sedge is a taller, more vigorous shade sedge native to the moist bottomland forests and creek banks of the southeastern US, from North Carolina west to Texas. The arching, strap-like dark green blades are among the boldest of any native carex species and create a lush, tropical-looking groundcover in moist, shaded bottomland gardens. Unlike many sedges, it tolerates periodic flooding and will grow happily at the wet edge of a pond or stream bank in shade. Particularly valuable for filling wet, low, shaded areas under large trees near water features. Spreads moderately by short rhizomes to form colonies. Provides important habitat structure for ground-nesting birds and small mammals in wet woodland settings.

common_name: Cherokee Sunset Flowering Dogwood (Variegated Pink-Bracted Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Cherokee Sunset bears variegated pink, green, and yellow foliage along with pink bracts.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; understory planting beneath high, open tree canopy mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. Cherokee Sunset bears striking variegated foliage in shades of pink, green, and cream through the growing season, turning deep purple-red in fall, complementing a spring display of pink flower bracts and paired with the good mildew and anthracnose resistance bred into the Cherokee series of dogwood cultivars. Its combination of colorful foliage and floral display gives it two strong seasons of interest beyond the standard white or pink dogwood bloom alone. Water during dry spells, especially the first two years, and avoid deep planting or heavy mulch piled against the trunk.

common_name: Cherokee Sunset Rudbeckia (AAS-Winning Double Bronze-Gold Black-Eyed Susan)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Cherokee Sunset is an All-America Selections winner producing double and semi-double flowers in a warm mix of bronze, mahogany, and gold tones.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Cherokee Sunset is an All-America Selections winner bred from black-eyed Susan for unusually full, double and semi-double flowers in a rich mix of bronze, mahogany, rust, and gold tones, a striking departure from the single golden-yellow blooms of the straight species. It flowers heavily from summer through fall on sturdy, well-branched plants, providing long-lasting cut flowers and reliable garden color while tolerating Gulf South heat and drought once established. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the display going, and though it is usually grown as a warm-season annual or short-lived biennial, plants may self-seed and return in favorable spots.

common_name: Cherry Berry Hosta (Miniature White-Centered Hosta with Red Petioles)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cherry Berry is a miniature hosta with white-centered green leaves and bright red petioles and flower scapes, an unusual color trait for the genus.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Cherry Berry is a diminutive miniature hosta bearing small, white-centered green leaves, but its standout trait is the bright cherry-red coloring of its petioles and flower scapes, an unusual and eye-catching feature rare among hosta cultivars. Its tiny mature size fits containers, rock gardens, and the front edge of a shaded border. Divide clumps every four to five years in spring if increased numbers are wanted, since the compact habit means division is rarely necessary for plant health.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Cherry Blossom is part of the Winter Jewels breeding series, with soft pale pink single flowers blooming in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist while the plant establishes. Cherry Blossom is part of the acclaimed Winter Jewels hellebore breeding series, producing rounded, outward-facing, single flowers in soft, blush pink reminiscent of its namesake tree blossoms, held above leathery, evergreen, deeply divided foliage. Like other Lenten roses it blooms very early, often pushing through late-season snow or hard frost, providing reliable color in the shade garden when little else is flowering. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to showcase the flowers at their best, and site it away from areas where pets or children graze, since all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Cherry Bounce Louisiana Iris (Historic Cherry-Red Award-Winning Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Cherry Bounce, bred by Louisiana iris pioneer Ira Nelson, won the DeBaillon Award in 1951 for its clear cherry-red flowers.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Cherry Bounce, bred by Louisiana iris pioneer Ira Nelson at the University of Southwestern Louisiana and honored with the Society for Louisiana Irises' DeBaillon Award in 1951, bears clear, bright cherry-red flowers that helped establish red as a viable Louisiana iris color in an era when the class was still dominated by blues and purples. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Surface sow, as the seed needs light; blooms the first year from an early start.
directions: Start indoors and surface sow, since the seed needs light to germinate and benefits from an early start to bloom the first year. Cherry Brandy bears three-to-four-inch maroon-red velvet petals around a dark chocolate center for a rich, luxurious look. Grow in full sun with average, well-drained soil and moderate water. Deadhead to extend the bloom and cut stems freely for long-lasting arrangements.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks early; surface sow for light.
directions: Surface sow this unique deep-red rudbeckia indoors eight weeks before the last frost, as light aids germination. Cherry Brandy produces rich burgundy daisies with dark centers, prized as long-lasting cut flowers. Transplant to full sun and average well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Deadhead regularly to keep new blooms coming, and treat it as an annual though it may overwinter in mild zones.

plant_note: Sow in darkness, as phlox seed germinates best when covered.
directions: Start seed indoors and cover it, since annual phlox germinates best in darkness. Cherry Caramel offers unusual creamy-beige flowers with dark cherry centers that make dreamy, fragrant cut flowers and draw pollinators and hummingbirds. Grow in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil and even moisture. Bloom may pause in intense summer heat and renew as cooler weather returns, so keep plants deadheaded.

common_name: Cherry Choco Latte Hibiscus (White with Pink Veining and Chocolate Foliage)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Cherry Choco Latte is a Summerific series cultivar with huge white flowers veined deep pink around a large red eye, over dark chocolate-tinged foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Cherry Choco Latte bears enormous, 8-9 inch white flowers intricately veined in deep pink radiating from a large red eye, held against dark, chocolate-tinged foliage that adds moody contrast beneath the pale blooms. It flowers in a steady succession of huge blooms from midsummer into fall, each lasting a single day but replaced continuously by new buds. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown, and watch for Japanese beetle damage on foliage and flowers where present.

common_name: Cherry Dazzle Crapemyrtle (Very Compact Cherry-Red Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Cherry Dazzle is part of the Razzle Dazzle series of true dwarf crape myrtles bred for compact, mounded landscape use.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Cherry Dazzle is a true dwarf crape myrtle from the Razzle Dazzle series, staying under 3 feet tall even at maturity, and bears vivid cherry-red flower clusters from summer into fall on a dense, mounded shrub that needs no pruning to control size, unlike full-size crape myrtles that are often cut back hard each winter. Its compact scale suits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where a full-size crape myrtle would quickly outgrow the space. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Cherry Hearts Epimedium (Heart-Shaped Leaf Cherry-Red Barrenwort)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Cherry Hearts is named for its distinctly heart-shaped leaflets, which emerge tinged in red-bronze in spring before maturing to green, paired with sprays of bright cherry-red flowers with white-tipped spurs held on wiry stems above the foliage. Its compact size and distinctive leaf shape make it a good choice for the front of a shaded border or a woodland rock garden where its detail can be appreciated up close. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh and show off the spring display.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer to fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; cherry laurel is among the very few broadleaf evergreens that thrives in dense shade, making it a standard understory hedge and screening plant in maritime and Pacific Northwest climates. Leaves and seeds contain cyanogenic compounds and are toxic if eaten.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial to full shade; cherry laurel is a vigorous, broad-spreading, broadleaf evergreen shrub native to southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia, grown for its large, glossy, deep-green leaves and upright spikes of small, fragrant white flowers in mid-spring, followed by cherry-like fruits that ripen from red to glossy black. Few other evergreen shrubs of comparable size tolerate the deep, dry shade cast by mature trees as well as cherry laurel does, which has made it a staple hedge, screening, and foundation plant throughout the maritime Pacific Northwest and the British Isles for generations. Compact cultivars such as 'Otto Luyken' and 'Zabeliana' stay low and spreading for foundation use, while 'Schipkaensis' (Schip laurel) is notably more cold hardy for zone 6 gardens. Because it self-seeds readily in the deep shade it favors, cherry laurel has naturalized aggressively in woodlands in parts of the Pacific Northwest and the United Kingdom, so spent flower spikes should be sheared off before fruit ripens in gardens near wild or natural areas, and all plant parts other than the ripe fruit pulp should be kept away from children and grazing animals.

common_name: Cherry Queen Spider Flower (Deep Cherry-Red Heirloom Cleome)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Cherry Queen is part of the classic Queen series of spider flower and self-sows readily once established.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Cherry Queen is the deep cherry-red to magenta-pink member of the classic Queen series of spider flower, its large, airy flower heads carrying the same long, spidery stamens as its Rose Queen and White Queen relatives but in a richer, more saturated color that reads boldly from a distance. Like other cleomes it shrugs off Gulf South summer heat that stalls out cooler-season annuals, growing vigorously through July and August and blooming continuously from the top of each elongating stem until frost. The slightly sticky, aromatic foliage is typical of the species, and established plantings self-sow freely, though volunteer seedlings may show some color drift toward pink or white over successive generations. An excellent nectar source for hummingbirds, butterflies, and sphinx moths.

plant_note: Direct sow the large seeds after frost; they resent root disturbance.
directions: Direct sow the large, pebble-like seeds after frost about half an inch deep, an easy task for young gardeners. Cherry Rose Jewel bears bright, peppery, edible blossoms and rounded leaves that make elegant additions to salads and appetizer plates. Keep soil lean rather than rich to encourage flowers over foliage, and water moderately. Nasturtiums are known to deter some garden pests while attracting pollinators.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: This bigleaf hydrangea produces color-shifting blooms that mature to rich cherry-red tones from spring into fall on a compact, rounded shrub. Plant in part shade with morning sun and afternoon protection in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil. Water deeply and regularly, especially in heat, and mulch to conserve moisture. It blooms on both old and new wood, so prune only to remove dead stems in early spring for the most reliable flowering.

common_name: Cherrybark Oak (Swamp Red Oak, Elliott's Oak)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in rich, moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic, deep, well-drained bottomland or bluff soil in full sun; cherrybark oak is native to the rich, well-drained ridges and terraces above flood lines in bottomland hardwood forests — it does NOT tolerate prolonged flooding.
directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic bottomland or bluff soil in full sun; cherrybark oak is generally regarded as one of the finest and most beautiful of all North American oaks — a majestic timber tree reaching 80–120 feet with a straight, clear trunk and distinctive shaggy, plated bark reminiscent of black cherry (hence the name). The deeply lobed, very large leaves have outstanding scarlet to orange-red fall color. The abundant small acorns are a critical food source for deer, turkeys, wood ducks, and squirrels. Unlike many red-group oaks, cherrybark oak is intolerant of flooding and requires the rich, well-drained ridges and terraces of bottomland hardwood forests — the 'cherrybark ridges' of bottomland forest. It is the fastest-growing of the large southern oaks (4–5 feet per year when young) and develops into an impressively large, long-lived specimen tree.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Chesapeake, a U.S. National Arboretum hybrid (Viburnum utile x carlesii), bears glossy, semi-evergreen foliage and fragrant pink-budded white flowers, with good shade tolerance for a flowering viburnum.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Chesapeake tolerates more shade than most flowering viburnums while still blooming reliably. Bred at the U.S. National Arboretum from a cross of Viburnum utile and V. carlesii, Chesapeake combines the glossy, semi-evergreen foliage and refined habit of one parent with the intensely fragrant, pink-budded white flower clusters of the other, opening in mid-spring and perfuming the surrounding garden with a sweet, spicy scent. In milder winters it holds much of its foliage into the cold season, providing more structure and screening value than fully deciduous viburnums. It requires little routine care beyond an occasional shaping prune right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood. A versatile shrub for a shaded foundation planting, woodland edge, or fragrance garden near a path or entry.

plant_note: Plant young trees in fall on well-drained, rocky or sandy slopes where this ridge-loving oak naturally thrives, since it tolerates drought and poor soil far better than bottomland oaks.
directions: Plant young trees in fall on well-drained, rocky or sandy slopes where this ridge-loving oak naturally thrives, since it tolerates drought and poor soil far better than bottomland oaks. Its thick, deeply furrowed bark and coarse, chestnut-like leaves give strong winter and textural interest in naturalized or restoration plantings. Because it resists rot and drought stress once established, it is an excellent long-lived specimen for dry hillsides, ridgetops, and low-maintenance shade areas. Acorns are relatively large, low in tannin, and readily eaten by wildlife.
