plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; chestnut rose is unusually disease-resistant and tolerates heat and humidity well compared to many old garden rose species.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; chestnut rose is unusually disease-resistant and tolerates heat and humidity well compared to many old garden rose species. Fine, ferny, glossy foliage and attractive, peeling, cinnamon-colored bark give this Chinese species rose year-round ornamental appeal beyond its clear pink, single to semi-double summer flowers, which are followed by distinctive, spiny, chestnut-bur-like orange-red hips that give the species both its common name and a striking, unusual fall and winter feature unlike the smooth hips of most roses. Notably resistant to black spot and other common rose diseases that plague many garden roses in humid climates, it is an easy, low-spray option for a Gulf South or humid-climate garden where disease pressure on roses is often severe. The edible, vitamin-C-rich hips are also used in some regions for jams, jellies, and traditional preparations. Prune minimally, mainly to remove old or damaged canes, since it flowers on both old and new wood.

common_name: Cheyenne Crape Myrtle (Semi-Dwarf True Red Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Cheyenne's compact size and true red flower color make it a popular choice for smaller foundation plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Cheyenne is valued among National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles for its true, vivid red flower color, a shade less common among crape myrtle cultivars than the many available pinks, lavenders, and whites. The compact, semi-dwarf size fits foundation plantings and smaller landscapes better than the large tree-form crape myrtles, and it shows good resistance to powdery mildew typical of the National Arboretum breeding program. Fall foliage takes on attractive orange-red tones. Remove root suckers and prune lightly to remove dead or crossing branches rather than heavily topping the plant.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Cheyenne Sky reliably colors red earlier in the season than most switchgrass cultivars, often showing color by early summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Cheyenne Sky is a compact selection of the native prairie grass switchgrass, bred to stay a tidy 30-36 inches tall with a strongly upright, non-flopping habit that makes it well suited to smaller garden beds and container plantings where the straight species (which can reach 5-6 feet) is too large. Its most distinctive feature is early, reliable color change: the blue-green summer foliage begins flushing wine-red from the tips down by early to midsummer, well ahead of most other switchgrass cultivars that do not color until fall, giving it a much longer season of ornamental interest. Airy, pink-tinged seed head panicles appear above the foliage in late summer, adding movement and texture and providing winter forage for birds. As a switchgrass cultivar it retains the deep, fibrous root system and drought tolerance of the wild species, requires no supplemental fertilization in average soils, and adapts to both dry upland sites and periodically moist low spots. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Cheyenne Spirit is unusual among Echinacea cultivars in producing true-to-color seed — seeds collected from Cheyenne Spirit plants will produce seedlings with the same range of colors as the parent generation, making seed saving practical. In zone 9 coneflowers are at their best in spring (March–May) and fall (September–October), often going semi-dormant in the peak of summer heat. Provide excellent drainage — Echinacea tolerates drought but is susceptible to root rot in consistently wet soil. Allow some seed heads to mature for winter bird interest (goldfinches especially prize Echinacea seeds).
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Cheyenne Spirit Echinacea demands excellent drainage and thrives in the dry, sunny conditions that replicate its native prairie habitat; Cheyenne Spirit is an All-America Selections award-winning Echinacea hybrid that was groundbreaking at its release for producing a true mixed-color coneflower that could be grown from seed — an unusual achievement among modern Echinacea hybrids, most of which are sterile or produce off-color seedlings. The seed-grown mix produces coneflowers in an unexpectedly wide range of colors including red, orange, yellow, cream, white, and purple — colors across almost the entire warm and cool spectrum — creating a naturalistic wildflower planting of varied, harmonious color from a single seed packet. Each individual plant produces flowers in one consistent color throughout its life, making the mixed effect something that develops across the planting rather than within individual plants. The combination of genuine native-area adaptation (Echinacea purpurea is native across much of the Eastern and Central US), exceptional bee and butterfly value, drought tolerance, and the genuine mixed-color seed innovation that allows informal, naturalistic planting without purchasing multiple named cultivars makes Cheyenne Spirit one of the most useful single Echinacea varieties for zone 9 pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface (light needed for germination — do not bury seeds) or plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cheyenne Spirit can be grown from seed with good germination rates, producing first-year flowers in the spring-to-fall flowering window.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cheyenne Spirit is the 2013 All-America Selections Flower Award winner — a seed-grown echinacea with outstanding, wide-range flower color variability that produces a multi-color meadow effect from a single seed packet. Individual plants flower in shades ranging from deep red, orange, yellow, cream, and white to coral, rose, and purple — a spectrum of colors that, when multiple plants are grown together, creates a dynamic, painterly mix reminiscent of a wildflower meadow. Unlike named clonal varieties with fixed colors, Cheyenne Spirit's color variability is part of its appeal, ensuring a naturalistic, mixed-color planting effect. The flowers have the classic Echinacea form — broad, flat petals surrounding a prominent, spiny, coppery-orange central cone — and are produced from June through October in zone 9. Cheyenne Spirit is one of the few echinacea cultivars that reliably flowers in the first growing season from seed, making it useful for quick establishment of pollinator gardens. The diverse color range means each planting is unique. Outstanding for meadow-style gardens, naturalistic borders, and any situation where a dynamic, multi-color late-summer to fall display is desired.

common_name: Chianti Sunflower (Deep Burgundy-Red Branching Pollen-Free Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed, spacing plants to allow branching, or succession sow every 2-3 weeks for continuous blooms.
directions: Sow directly in full sun after the soil has warmed, giving plants 12-18 inches of space so their side branches can develop fully. Chianti is prized for its unusually dark, wine-red petals that read almost black-red in bright light, a striking departure from the orange-reds of most branching sunflower cultivars. Because it branches freely, a single plant produces many flowers in succession over several weeks rather than one big bloom all at once, extending the cutting season from one sowing. The pollen-free flowers stay tidy in mixed bouquets and won't shed onto tablecloths, and deadheading spent blooms encourages the plant to keep producing new side shoots into fall.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into well-drained, average, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chiapas sage roots to the ground in hard freezes but reliably resprouts from the base in zone 8–9 gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chiapas sage is a compact, mounding Mexican salvia with small, glossy, dark green leaves and slender spikes of vivid magenta-pink flowers produced almost continuously from spring through the first hard frost, with the heaviest flush in fall. Its dense, tidy habit and long bloom season make it a reliable filler for borders and large containers, and hummingbirds visit it steadily throughout the warm months. In zone 8, expect the top growth to die back in a hard freeze, with new shoots emerging from the crown once the soil warms in spring; a layer of mulch over the root zone improves winter survival at the cold edge of its range. Cut plants back by about a third in late winter to encourage bushy new growth and the season's heaviest bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Chicago Apache requires full sun to develop and hold its intense scarlet-red coloring — in shade or partial shade the flower color is significantly less vivid and bloom production decreases.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Chicago Apache is widely regarded as one of the finest scarlet-red daylilies — a mid-season bloomer producing large (5-inch), velvety, brilliant scarlet-red flowers with a small yellow throat on 26–28 inch scapes. The intense glowing red color holds through the heat of summer without significant fading, a difficulty with many red and orange daylilies. It was introduced by James Marsh of the famous 'Chicago' hybridizing program and was awarded the Stout Silver Medal in 1986. The large, well-formed flowers make it an outstanding specimen plant or mass-planting accent in the full-sun border. Though it does not rebloom as prolifically as miniature varieties, it produces abundant scapes over a 3–4 week main bloom season. The red color is striking when planted alongside white or pale-yellow companions. Divide every 3–4 years when center growth becomes congested.

plant_note: Divide and transplant bare-root fans in spring or late summer, spreading roots out in a shallow planting hole with the crown just below the soil surface.
directions: Plant bare-root fans in spring in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, keeping the crown at or just below grade to encourage strong fan development. Mulch lightly to conserve moisture and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigorous bloom. Chicago Fire, part of the long-running Chicago series of daylilies, bears intensely saturated red-orange blooms with a darker throat that seem to glow in the summer border. It is a heat-tolerant, vigorous grower valued for its bold, fiery color that stands out even from a distance.

common_name: Chicago Lustre Arrowwood Viburnum (Glossy Disease-Resistant Heavy-Fruiting Native Viburnum)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chicago Lustre bears glossy, dark green, disease-resistant foliage and heavier-than-typical fruit set, providing abundant food for birds.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; native arrowwood viburnum tolerates a wide range of soils and light conditions. Chicago Lustre is a selection of native arrowwood viburnum prized for its glossy, lustrous, dark green foliage that shows good resistance to the leaf spot diseases that can trouble arrowwood in humid climates, and for producing a heavier fruit set than the species, yielding abundant blue-black berries in fall that are an important food source for migrating and overwintering songbirds. Flat clusters of white flowers open in late spring, drawing pollinators before the berries develop. It grows into a large, dense, multi-stemmed screening shrub with minimal maintenance once established, tolerating clay soil, urban conditions, and periodic drought. Prune right after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Chief Mix Celosia (Large-Plumed Bedding Cockscomb Series)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Chief is a classic large-plumed bedding celosia series bred for uniform, sturdy, weather-resistant flower heads.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes. Chief Mix is a long-standing large-plumed celosia series prized for producing exceptionally big, dense, flame-shaped plumes in a full range of gold, orange, red, pink, and purple on uniform, well-branched plants that hold up well to summer rain and wind. It thrives in heat and blooms steadily from early summer through frost with minimal deadheading, making it a reliable bedding and cutting plant for the hottest part of the garden. Plumes hold their vivid color extremely well when cut fresh or dried, hung upside down in a cool, dark, well-ventilated spot.

plant_note: Start indoors in warmth; celosia needs steady heat to grow well.
directions: Start seed indoors in warm conditions a few weeks before the last frost and transplant only after the soil is warm. Red Flame forms compact, uniform cockscomb heads made of countless tiny flowers in waves of deep red that last a long time in the garden or vase. Give it full sun, warmth, and well-drained soil for the best color. Harvest stems for fresh or dried arrangements as the heads reach full size.

plant_note: Plant in spring in very well-drained, dry, calcareous or rocky soil in full sun. Avoid any soil amendment with organic matter; this plant demands lean, dry conditions to thrive and bloom freely.
directions: Chihuahuan Globe Mallow is a compact, velvety-soft native mallow shrub of the Chihuahuan Desert and adjacent Texas Hill Country, its stems and leaves coated in dense, silky white hairs that give the plant a striking silver-gray appearance year-round. From summer through fall it produces cheerful, bright yellow, five-petaled mallow flowers about 1-1.5 inches across, the golden blooms providing a vivid contrast against the silver foliage. Plant in very dry, poor, calcareous or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; wet or clay-heavy soils quickly lead to root rot, so excellent drainage is non-negotiable. Once established it requires minimal supplemental irrigation and is an outstanding choice for Texas xeriscape designs, Chihuahuan Desert gardens, and other arid Southwest landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Chihuahuan sage is the most compact and finely textured of the Leucophyllum species and tends to have a naturally rounded habit that rarely needs pruning — ideal for formal low hedges in zone 8–11 landscapes.
directions: Plant in spring or early fall in extremely well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Leucophyllum species suffer in waterlogged or heavily amended acidic soils and must have excellent drainage to thrive. Chihuahuan sage (L. laevigatum) is the most compact and finely textured of the native Texas sage species, with smooth, small, grey-green leaves and a naturally mounded, nearly spherical habit that makes it one of the most refined-looking drought-tolerant shrubs for formal and informal use in hot, dry landscapes; like all Leucophyllum, it responds to humidity and soil moisture by bursting into bloom with masses of small, lavender to purple tubular flowers — a phenomenon known as 'barometer bush' behavior because blooming is triggered by summer monsoon rains. Essentially maintenance-free once established and highly tolerant of alkaline caliche soils.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date in well-drained soil, or start indoors a few weeks earlier where summers are short.
directions: Sow shallowly in lean, fast-draining soil, since rich or waterlogged ground leads to soft growth and fewer flowers. Once seedlings are established, water only moderately, as this coastal native prefers to dry out between waterings and holds up well to salt spray and heat. Low, trailing plants form a dense mat of succulent foliage smothered in funnel-shaped blue flowers with white and yellow throats that resemble small morning glories, opening fresh each day through summer and making a striking edging, groundcover, or spiller for containers and hanging baskets.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Chilean glory flower grows rapidly from seed and begins blooming within 3–4 months. In zones 8–10 it is perennial above or below ground; in colder zones grow as an annual. It climbs by tendrils to 8–15 feet and requires a trellis, fence, or shrub to support it.
directions: Start seeds indoors early and train on a trellis in full sun; Chilean glory flower is a vigorous tendril-climbing vine from Chile and Peru producing masses of small (1 inch), tubular flowers in brilliant orange-red to scarlet (with yellow and orange-yellow forms also available) in long racemes from summer through the first hard frost — an extended, prolific bloom display on a fast-growing vine that reaches 8–15 feet. The small, bright flowers resemble a more refined version of Eccremocarpus, with the tubular shape irresistible to hummingbirds during migration. It climbs using leaf tendrils over trellises, fences, shrubs, and netting with remarkable speed. In zones 8–10 the roots may survive winter to resprout; in colder climates treat as an annual started from seed each spring. A good combination vine with purple-flowered plants such as Cobaea scandens or morning glory, where the orange-red flowers create striking complementary color.

common_name: Chilean Hard Fern (Large Bronze-Emerging Colony-Forming Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade; Chilean Hard Fern is a large, colony-forming South American species with thick, leathery, crinkle-edged fronds that emerge bronze-orange before maturing to deep green.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade, and give it room, since this is one of the largest and boldest of the hardy Blechnum ferns. Chilean Hard Fern spreads by creeping rhizomes to form substantial colonies of thick, leathery, ladder-like fronds with distinctively crinkled margins, the new growth emerging a striking bronze-orange before maturing to deep glossy green, creating dramatic textural and color contrast in the shaded border or woodland edge. Its much larger scale and colonizing habit set it apart from the smaller, tighter clumps formed by Deer Fern and other Blechnum species already common in cultivation. Keep soil consistently moist, since it does not tolerate drought, and mulch generously to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature through summer heat.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Chilean jasmine is more cold-hardy than the commonly sold tropical Mandevilla cultivars — surviving to zone 7b with root mulching, where it dies back to the ground and regrows. It blooms in summer, producing clusters of large, pure-white, funnel-shaped, intensely fragrant flowers. All parts are milky-sapped and toxic if ingested. Provide a sturdy climbing structure.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Chilean jasmine is the most cold-hardy and most fragrant of the mandevilla vines — significantly more cold-tolerant than the showy tropical Mandevilla sanderi hybrids commonly sold in summer, surviving reliably to zone 7b and making it a viable perennial vine for gardens far colder than those where tropical mandevillas must be overwintered indoors. The flowers are produced in summer in loose clusters of 3–5, each flower a large (2–3 inch), pure-white, funnel-shaped, five-petaled blossom with a slightly twisted, windmill-like arrangement of the petals and a powerfully sweet, intense fragrance that is often compared to jasmine but with a richer, more complex depth than most jasmines — one of the most fragrant summer-climbing vines available for temperate gardens. It twines vigorously and can reach 15–20 feet on a sturdy support over several seasons. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it performs as an outstanding, reliable perennial climber with an extended summer bloom season. The white flowers and sweet fragrance make it ideal for placement near porches, pergolas, and garden seating areas.

plant_note: Plant tubers in fall 2–3 inches deep in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 7–9; provide complete dry summer dormancy; Chilean Nasturtium is a slender, twining, tuberous vine from the mountain scrublands of Chile and Argentina — producing abundant, small (3/4-inch), five-petaled, bright-orange to reddish-orange flowers with a short spur over a long cool growing season — one of the smaller and more cold-hardy of the tuberous Tropaeolum species.
directions: Plant Tropaeolum ciliatum tubers in fall in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil; grows through winter and spring in cool, moist conditions; provide a fine trellis, net, or shrub for the slender stems to twine through; withhold all water from June through September (summer drought essential for tuber persistence). Chilean Nasturtium is a delicate, slender, twining vine — more refined in scale than the common garden nasturtium — with small, rounded, peltate leaves and a continuous production of small, five-petaled, bright-orange to brick-red flowers from winter through spring. The vine climbs by twisting petioles (leaf stalks) rather than tendrils, winding gracefully through supporting plants or netting. Native to the scrubby, rocky hillsides of central and southern Chile and adjacent Argentina, it follows the Mediterranean climate pattern: growing in cool, moist winters and dying back completely to its small tuberous root in summer. Like all tuberous Tropaeolum, summer drought is an absolute requirement — even a small amount of summer water can cause the tubers to rot. In zone 7–8, the tubers are adequately cold-hardy in the ground (below frost penetration depth) with good drainage. A charming companion for other winter-growing plants like Oxalis, Ixia, and other Chilean bulbs that share its growing-season preferences.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in very well-drained, gritty to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Chilean oxalis is native to the rocky, high-altitude Andes of Chile and Argentina — a rock garden plant requiring excellent drainage, poor-to-lean soil, and a dry, cool winter dormancy. It tolerates significant frost when well-drained (to zone 5). The deeply folded, silver-gray, many-leafleted foliage is as ornamental as the flowers.
directions: Plant small bulbs in very well-drained, gritty to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Chilean oxalis is the most ornamental and most widely grown of the Andean oxalis species in cultivation, prized for its extraordinary foliage as much as its flowers. The leaves are composed of numerous (up to 22) small, deeply folded, pleated, gray-green to silver-blue-gray leaflets that fold downward in the classic oxalis sleep-movement at night and in cold, opening in sun to reveal the pleated, accordion-fold texture of each individual leaflet — the whole leaf a marvel of geometrically precise botanical engineering in soft silver-gray. In late spring the compact mounds of silver foliage are covered with large (relative to plant size), satiny, clear pink to deep pink or lilac-pink, five-petaled flowers with slightly darker veining. Native to the high-altitude, gravelly Andes slopes where drainage is excellent and winters dry and cold, it thrives in well-drained rock garden conditions in zones 5–9, where the combination of silver foliage and clear pink flowers in a compact, tidy mound makes it one of the finest rock garden plants available from South America.

plant_note: Plant against a sturdy wall, fence, or pergola in spring, tying in new growth as it develops since it climbs by leaning rather than by tendrils or twining.
directions: All parts other than the flowers should be treated as inedible, since this is a relative of the potato — grow it strictly as an ornamental screen. Plant this fast-growing, semi-woody scrambler against a sturdy wall, fence, or pergola in spring, tying in new growth as it develops since it climbs by leaning rather than by tendrils or twining. Large, fragrant clusters of blue-purple, star-shaped flowers with bright yellow centers open from summer into autumn and continue even in a partly shaded position, though bloom is somewhat fuller with a few hours of direct sun. Cut back hard in early spring where winters are borderline, since it often regrows vigorously from the base after cold damage.

common_name: Chili Pepper Coleus (Narrow Serrated Burgundy-and-Lime Sun Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Chili Pepper, part of the FlameThrower series, bears narrow, serrated leaves variegated dark burgundy and lime green, bred for full sun to part shade and very late flowering.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; the FlameThrower series was bred specifically for strong sun tolerance. Chili Pepper bears narrow, finely serrated leaves splashed with dark burgundy and lime green in a striking bicolor pattern, forming an upright, well-branched plant that holds its vivid color through summer heat better than many older coleus cultivars. Like other FlameThrower selections it flowers very late in the season, keeping the foliage display uninterrupted for months. Water regularly during establishment and pinch growing tips occasionally to maintain a full, bushy habit.

common_name: Chimborazo Dahlia (Vivid Orange-Red Collarette with Golden Collar)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Chimborazo is a collarette dahlia with vivid orange-red outer ray florets and a contrasting golden-yellow collar.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. Chimborazo bears a single ring of vivid orange-red outer ray florets surrounding a contrasting golden-yellow inner collar, a bold, fiery color combination distinctive to the collarette class, and its open, single-layer form leaves the flower's center accessible to bees and other pollinators. Its bright, warm coloring makes it a strong accent in a sunny cutting garden or mixed border. Deadhead spent blooms regularly, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 in deep in moist starting mix at 65–70°F. Rotate planting locations each year, as China asters are prone to Fusarium wilt when grown in the same soil repeatedly. Avoid overhead watering and ensure good air circulation to reduce disease pressure. Harvest cut flowers when petals are just beginning to open fully for maximum vase life.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors; succession sow for prolonged bloom.
directions: An old-fashioned single-flowered China aster blend in cool reds, pinks, purples, and white for midsummer color. Sow seed directly after frost or start indoors, barely covering the seed. Plant toward the back of the bed where the two-to-three-foot stems provide height and long-lasting cut flowers. Deadhead spent blooms and rotate planting sites each year to reduce aster wilt.

common_name: China Boy Holly (Compact Male Meserve Hybrid Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; China Boy is the standard male pollinator for China Girl and other female Meserve hollies blooming at the same time, and does not itself produce berries.
directions: China Boy is the male counterpart bred alongside China Girl in the Meserve holly line, sharing the same compact, dense, glossy dark-green, spiny foliage but producing no berries of its own, since only female holly plants fruit. Its main garden role is as a reliable pollinator planted within about 30-40 feet of China Girl or other compatible female Meserve hollies to ensure a heavy berry set on the female plants, though it is also a handsome, fully ornamental evergreen shrub in its own right for a hedge or foundation planting. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter before new growth begins.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; China fir tolerates summer heat and humidity better than most true firs, making it a substitute conifer for warm-temperate gardens where Abies species struggle.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring, spacing them well back from structures in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water regularly through the first two seasons while roots establish. China fir forms a broad pyramidal tree with stiff, glossy, dark green needles borne in dense whorled tiers, and old bark exfoliates in long reddish-brown strips that add winter interest. Unlike many needled conifers it resprouts vigorously from cut stumps and tolerates the humid summers of the southeastern United States, where it is grown as a large screening or specimen tree rather than the timber crop it forms across much of China. Lower branches often decline with age and can be limbed up to reveal the trunk on mature specimens.

common_name: China Girl Holly (Compact Female Meserve Hybrid Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; China Girl is female and needs a male pollinator such as China Boy planted nearby to set its red berries.
directions: China Girl is a compact, self-branching Meserve hybrid holly with glossy, spiny, dark green leaves and, once pollinated, a reliably heavy crop of bright red winter berries, making it a popular and dependable evergreen shrub for foundation plantings, hedges, and mixed borders. It is more heat-tolerant than some other blue holly selections, an advantage in warmer regions where straight Meserve hollies can struggle, but as a female cultivar it needs a male pollinator such as China Boy blooming nearby to fruit well. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter before new growth begins.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into the garden 2–4 weeks before last frost, as plants tolerate light frost.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in well-drained germination mix; seedlings grow quickly and can be transplanted while still small. Plant in full sun in well-drained, neutral-to-slightly-alkaline soil; heavy clay and overwet conditions lead to crown rot. Deadhead spent flowers continuously to prevent early seed set and extend the blooming season well into summer. Plants often decline in intense summer heat but may rebloom in fall if sheared back and kept watered.

common_name: China Town Tulip (Pink-Cream Viridiflora Tulip with Variegated Foliage)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; China Town is a Viridiflora-class tulip with soft pink-and-cream flowers marked by a green flame, and unusually also bears variegated foliage.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. China Town bears soft pink-and-cream petals streaked down the center with a feathered flame of green, the distinctive partial-green coloring that defines the Viridiflora group, and unusually for a tulip, the foliage itself is also variegated with cream-white margins, giving this cultivar ornamental interest even before the flowers open. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; chinaberry is naturalizing throughout the US Gulf South and is considered invasive in many areas. Avoid planting near natural areas — it spreads prolifically by bird-dispersed seeds. The berries are toxic to humans and most mammals.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun, with awareness of invasive potential; chinaberry is an Asian deciduous tree widely naturalized across the US Gulf South, Caribbean, and tropics worldwide. The fragrant, lilac-purple flower clusters in spring are highly ornamental and have given the tree the names 'Persian lilac' and 'pride of India.' The clusters of small, yellow berries that persist through winter are striking ornamentally but are toxic to humans, dogs, and livestock (though consumed by birds, which distribute the seeds widely). The tree is drought and heat tolerant, fast-growing, and adaptable to almost any well-drained soil — characteristics that, combined with prolific bird-dispersed seeding, make it invasive in many parts of the South. Used in agroforestry in tropical countries for natural insecticide compounds (azadirachtin relatives from the same Meliaceae family as neem). Caution: do not plant near natural areas.

common_name: Chinaberry Tree (Bead Tree, Pride of India)
plant_note: Plant container stock or direct sow seeds in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; chinaberry grows extremely rapidly (5–10 feet per year) and is widely naturalized across the Gulf South — be aware it is invasive in some states.
directions: Plant in any well-drained, moist to dry soil in full sun; chinaberry grows in almost any condition and requires minimal care — it is extremely fast-growing. CAUTION: Invasive in the southeastern United States — verify local regulations before planting. Melia azedarach (chinaberry or bead tree) is an Asian tree that has naturalized across the entire Gulf Coastal Plain and has been a fixture of southern rural landscapes for generations, valued for its extraordinary fast growth (5–10 feet per year), deep, cooling shade, and clusters of fragrant, lilac-purple flowers in April–May that make it one of the most ornamentally beautiful trees in bloom despite its weedy reputation. The clusters of small, round, yellow-white berries persist into winter and are eagerly consumed by American Robins and other fruit-eating birds, which has facilitated its spread. CAUTION: The berries are toxic to humans (causing gastrointestinal distress) and especially to pigs; all parts of the plant contain triterpenoids and limonoids. Chinaberry is listed as invasive in Florida, Georgia, and much of the Gulf South. Historically important as a fast-growing 'pioneer tree' for farmstead windbreaks and shade, and the hard berries have been used for rosary beads and crafts (giving it the 'bead tree' name).

common_name: Chindo Viburnum (Award-Winning Large Evergreen Screening Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Chindo grows quickly into a dense, large evergreen screen or small tree and is more cold-hardy than the species type, extending its range further north.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Chindo is a selected, more cold-hardy form of sweet viburnum that earned a Gold Medal Award from the Georgia Botanical Garden for its outstanding performance as a large, fast-growing evergreen screen. It has bold, glossy, deep green leaves considerably larger than most viburnums, white spring flower clusters, and showy red fruit that matures to black, all on a dense shrub that quickly reaches privacy-hedge size or can be limbed up into a small multi-trunked tree. It tolerates heat and humidity very well, making it a Gulf South landscape staple for fast screening, and needs only occasional shaping to control size in a smaller garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring or fall when the soil is cool and moist; Astilbe chinensis is more drought-tolerant and summer-heat-tolerant than most astilbes, making it a better performer in gardens south of zone 6 where the classic A. x arendsii hybrids often struggle.
directions: Plant in partial shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil — Astilbe chinensis tolerates more sun and drier conditions than most astilbes but performs best with afternoon shade and reliable moisture. The finely cut, fern-like foliage is attractive throughout the growing season and the plume-like flower spikes in mauve-pink to rosy-purple bloom later in summer than most astilbes, extending the shade garden's color season. After flowering, the dried seed heads persist attractively into winter and provide texture and wildlife food. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor — as the center of the clump dies out, division is needed to rejuvenate it. Unlike many moisture-loving shade plants, established plants have fair tolerance for summer dry spells.

common_name: Chinese Chaste Tree (Monk's Pepper, Negundo Chastetree, Five-Leaf Chaste Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun to partial shade; Chinese Chaste Tree grows vigorously in zone 9 humid conditions and benefits from hard pruning each spring to maintain a bushy, floriferous habit — left unpruned it becomes a large, somewhat leggy multi-stemmed tree. More cold-hardy than the common Chaste Tree (V. agnus-castus) and better adapted to humid, hot climates. Self-seeds prolifically in moist conditions — considered mildly invasive in some Southeast Asian countries.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; Chinese Chaste Tree is drought-tolerant once established and adapts broadly to soil types including clay and alkaline calcareous soils prevalent across the Gulf South. Vitex negundo is a large aromatic shrub or small tree from tropical and subtropical Asia (India, China, Southeast Asia) that is one of the most widely-used medicinal plants in Asian botanical medicine traditions — the berries (used as a spice in China), leaves, and roots are employed for numerous traditional remedies and the berries are considered a substitute for black pepper (hence 'Monk's Pepper'). In zone 9 Gulf Coast and Southern gardens, it is grown primarily as an ornamental for its fragrant, silver-gray, divided foliage and long summer flower spikes of small, lavender-blue, tubular flowers that attract bees, butterflies, and other pollinators in profusion from June through September. The pleasantly aromatic, camphor-like foliage repels some insect pests. Chinese Chaste Tree is closely related to the common American Chaste Tree (V. agnus-castus) but produces more narrowly divided leaves (often 5–7 leaflets rather than 5), adapts better to Southeast Asian humid conditions, and is reportedly somewhat more drought-tolerant. Hard pruning to 12 inches each February keeps the plant vigorous and maximizes flower production.

plant_note: Propagate by dividing offsets that form around the base of the rosette, or by rooting individual leaves in moist mix as with African violets. Grown indoors year-round as a compact houseplant or terrarium plant.
directions: A rosette-forming gesneriad from southern China grown much like an African violet, with thick, quilted leaves marked by a silvery sheen along the veins and clusters of small, pale yellow tubular flowers rising just above the foliage. Grow in bright, indirect light or under fluorescent or LED plant lights, since direct sun bleaches the patterned leaves. Pot in a light, fast-draining mix in a shallow container that matches the rosette's modest root system, and water from the base or around the crown to avoid rot at the center of the rosette. Its compact size makes it well suited to a windowsill collection or a covered terrarium, where the extra humidity keeps the leaf margins from browning.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Chinese climbing hydrangea is slow to establish (2–3 years before significant growth), but once established it becomes a long-lived, vigorous vine. It clings using aerial rootlets.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese climbing hydrangea is closely related to Japanese climbing hydrangea (Schizophragma hydrangeoides) but considered by many to be the more ornamentally impressive species, producing even larger, more spectacular flowerheads with broad, pure white sterile bracts that completely surround the central fertile flowers. The individual lacecap-like flower clusters can exceed 12 inches across. It clings to trees, walls, and trellises using aerial rootlets — no support structures needed. Like its relatives, it is slow to establish but becomes a spectacular, long-lived climber that requires no pruning to maintain. An outstanding shade vine for large masonry walls, mature trees, and shaded pergolas in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in spring in woodland soil; this species emerges very late in the season and needs a long growing period to build up the large tuber required for flowering. Mark the planting site carefully.
directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Chinese cobra lily is among the most dramatic of all woodland aroids, producing a tall purple-striped green spathe with a conspicuously long, whip-like appendix that extends 12-18 inches beyond the spathe opening, giving the plant an exotic, otherworldly appearance. The large leaf, divided into many radiating leaflets, creates a spectacular tropical effect. In its native habitat in the Himalayan foothills and mountain forests of central China, it grows in moist mountain ravines and forest understory at 4,000-9,000 feet elevation. In cultivation, the large tubers gradually produce offsets that can be separated after several years. The species performs best in the Pacific Northwest, Upper South, and mild-winter regions of zones 7-10.

plant_note: Plant acorns in fall immediately after collection or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Chinese cork oak develops a deep taproot and is highly drought tolerant once established. More cold-hardy than the European cork oak (Q. suber).
directions: Plant acorns in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Chinese cork oak is the Asian counterpart of the European cork oak (Quercus suber) — and in many ways a superior ornamental and more cold-hardy version of its famous cousin. Native across a huge range in Japan, Korea, and China, it develops a similarly distinctive thick, deeply furrowed, corky bark, but is deciduous (the European cork oak is evergreen) and considerably hardier to cold, surviving to zone 5 compared to zone 7-8 for cork oak. The chesnut-like toothed leaves are attractive and larger than the European cork oak's leaves. The acorns are covered almost entirely by the shaggy, bristly, elongated acorn cup scales — one of the most distinctive acorn features of any oak. An excellent ornamental for large gardens in zones 5–9 where the dramatic corky bark texture and bold silhouette are desired. More versatile climatically than cork oak but rarely grown in North America.

common_name: Chinese Cymbidium (Sin Mui Orchid, Chinese New Year Orchid, Dark Cymbidium)
plant_note: Grow in a medium pot with fine to medium bark or peat-based orchid mix in partial to full shade with cool fall temperatures; Cymbidium sinense is the most important and widely cultivated of the 'Chinese' or 'Oriental' cymbidiums — small-flowered, highly fragrant species that have been cultivated in China and Japan for over 2,000 years for their elegant, thin-petaled flowers and intense, elusive fragrance. Unlike the large-flowered hybrid cymbidiums, C. sinense produces smaller (1.5-inch), darker flowers in maroon, red-brown, or greenish-brown with a white lip. Cool fall nights (50–58°F) are essential to trigger blooming. Hardy to zone 8 with protection. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in a medium pot with fine to medium bark or humus-rich terrestrial orchid mix — Chinese Cymbidium grows most successfully when given cool fall temperatures (50–58°F nights) to trigger blooming and tolerates considerably more shade than the large-flowered hybrid cymbidiums used in the cut flower trade. Cymbidium sinense is a terrestrial to semi-epiphytic, sympodial orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to southern China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan (Ryukyu Islands), Vietnam, and India (Assam) — the most significant species in the group of 'Oriental' or 'Chinese' cymbidiums that have been cultivated in China and Japan for more than 2,000 years, centuries before the development of the large-flowered hybrids that now dominate Western horticulture. The Chinese, Japanese, and Korean horticultural traditions around C. sinense and its relatives (the 'koran' or Chinese orchid culture) emphasize the subtle fragrance, elegant simplicity, and venerable cultural associations of these species over the bold colors of hybrid cymbidiums. The plant produces strap-like, dark-green, arching leaves 24–30 inches long and, in winter, erect flower spikes bearing 10–20 small (1.5-inch) flowers in maroon, red-brown to dark wine-red, or greenish-brown with a white, red-spotted lip. The fragrance is the defining quality: elusive, refined, and distinct — described as 'subtle orchid fragrance' or a soft, spicy-sweet floral scent, most perceptible close-up in cool morning conditions. The 'Chinese New Year' connection references the winter to early spring bloom timing. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; like Sempervivum, the individual rosette flowers once and dies after producing a cone-shaped bloom spike, but offset rosettes continue the colony.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese dunce cap forms tight, powdery blue-gray rosettes of fleshy, pointed leaves that closely resemble hens-and-chicks, spreading steadily by short runners that produce new offset rosettes around the mother plant. Its common name comes from the unusual conical flower spike that rises from a mature rosette in late summer to fall, densely packed with small white to pale pink star-shaped flowers, after which that individual rosette dies back, much like the related Sempervivum. Because offsets continually replace spent rosettes, the overall clump persists and slowly expands for years despite the monocarpic habit of any single rosette. It is easy to grow in rock gardens, trough plantings, and shallow containers, tolerating more shade than most true sedums while still requiring the sharp drainage typical of the succulent family.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or divide basal offshoots and plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile potting mix in bright indirect light to deep shade; Chinese evergreen is among the most low-light-tolerant foliage plants available — dark green cultivars survive in quite dim conditions, while variegated or colored cultivars require more light to maintain their pattern.
directions: Root stem cuttings or divide offshoots in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile potting mix in bright indirect light to deep shade; Chinese evergreen is one of the most tolerant and adaptable of all tropical foliage plants, suited to interior conditions of very low light intensity that defeat most other tropical houseplants. The lance-shaped to elliptic leaves are produced in erect rosettes and may be plain dark green, or variegated in combinations of silver-gray, light-green, white, cream, pink, red, and orange depending on cultivar — modern breeding has produced cultivars in a remarkably broad color range. The plant tolerates irregular watering, low humidity, and dim fluorescent light with less decline than virtually any other ornamental plant, making it a staple of interior plantscaping in offices, shopping malls, and shaded building lobbies. It is one of several plants demonstrated in NASA clean-air studies to filter certain indoor air pollutants. 'Silver Queen' (silver-green), 'Emerald Beauty' (dark-green), 'Red Siam' (deep red-edged), and 'Super White' are widely grown selections. All parts toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese evergreen oak is one of the most ornamental and adaptable evergreen oaks for zones 7–9, with excellent heat and humidity tolerance and a refined, upright form. More shade-tolerant than most oaks.
directions: Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese evergreen oak is a handsome, moderate-sized evergreen oak native to China, Japan, and Korea, producing long, narrow, slightly wavy-margined, glossy dark green evergreen leaves with distinctive reddish-bronze new growth — creating a refined, almost tropical appearance more reminiscent of a Southern Magnolia relative than a typical oak. One of the most ornamental and well-behaved evergreen oaks for humid subtropical gardens in zones 7–9, more tolerant of the heat and humidity of the Southeast than many evergreen oaks from the Mediterranean. The slender leaves and upright, oval crown make it suitable for smaller garden spaces where live oak would be too massive. Produces small, elongated acorns. Increasingly available at specialty nurseries and becoming recognized as an excellent evergreen street and garden tree for the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; clumps spread gradually by rhizome into arching, bamboo-like stands and benefit from a spring topdressing of compost.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; clumps spread gradually by rhizome into arching, bamboo-like stands and benefit from a spring topdressing of compost. Disporum longistylum is a Chinese woodland perennial grown for its upright then gracefully arching stems clothed in narrow, evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves that emerge deep purple-black in early spring before maturing to green, with small, nodding, creamy white bell flowers appearing at the stem tips just as new growth unfurls. The widely grown selection 'Night Heron' is especially prized for its near-black spring stems and foliage and has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Site it where its architectural, cane-like stems can be appreciated against a dark backdrop in a shaded border, and divide congested clumps in early spring if flowering declines.

subcategory: drooping-tipped fan palm for subtropical landscapes
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese fan palm is distinguished among fan palms by the characteristic drooping, pendulous tips of the leaf segments that give mature leaves a graceful, arching, fountain-like silhouette — the source of the alternative common name 'fountain palm'. It grows slowly to 30–40 feet over many decades. Young plants are more shade-tolerant than most palms. Hardy to about 22°F when established in zone 8b-9 Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese fan palm is one of the most graceful and most distinctively silhouetted of all the commonly grown subtropical fan palms — native to southern China and the Ryukyu Islands of Japan (where it also naturalizes), producing over decades a single, stout, gray-brown trunk of considerable character topped with a large, rounded crown of circular fan leaves. What makes the Chinese fan palm immediately recognizable is the characteristic behavior of the leaf segments at their tips: unlike the stiff, erect, uniformly divided segments of Washington palms and other common fan palms, the outer portions of each Livistona chinensis leaf segment droop downward in a pendulous, graceful arc — so that the leaf as a whole has a beautifully arching, layered, fountain-like silhouette where the central part of the fan is held stiffly and the leaf tips fall gracefully downward. This pendulous-tip character gives the palm its alternative common name 'fountain palm' and makes a mature specimen — a substantial gray trunk with a full crown of large, arching, droop-tipped fan leaves — one of the most graceful and easily recognizable palm silhouettes in the subtropical landscape. Slow-growing and long-lived. Young plants show good shade tolerance, making them useful for shaded positions where fast growth is not required. A classic zone 9 Gulf Coast landscape palm of considerable elegance.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; can also sow in fall in mild winter climates.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in early spring directly where they are to grow; cover seeds lightly as they germinate better in darkness. The clusters of tiny, intensely blue flowers resemble true forget-me-nots but bloom for a much longer period — from late spring well into summer. Shear plants back by one-third after the first main flush to encourage a second wave of bloom. Plants self-sow freely; allow some seeds to drop for naturalised succession planting in subsequent years.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; transplant to part shade after frosts. Chinese foxglove self-sows modestly in mild climates and is short-lived but reseeds to maintain a colony. In zones 8–9 it often overwinters as a basal rosette and reblooms the following year.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant to moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Chinese foxglove is an elegant short-lived perennial from China producing a basal rosette of deeply lobed, somewhat sticky, aromatic leaves and upright stems bearing a succession of large (2-inch), tubular, rose-pink to rose-purple flowers with yellow, spotted throats — extremely similar to foxglove in form but in warm, rosy-purple tones rather than the usual foxglove purples and whites. The flowers appear over a long season from late spring through midsummer and are attractive to bees. A related species, R. glutinosa, provides di huang — one of the most important herbs in traditional Chinese medicine, used for thousands of years to treat blood-deficiency conditions. R. elata is the ornamental species, valued for its shade tolerance, its foxglove-like effect in the garden, and its combination of interesting, textured foliage with refined, warm-colored flowers in situations where foxglove itself would prefer cooler conditions.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the last frost, or in fall in zones 8–9; loropetalum establishes quickly in warm soil and rewards with rapid growth during the first growing season with adequate moisture.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; loropetalum is one of the most popular landscape shrubs for the Gulf Coast and Southeast, prized for its burgundy to purple-bronze foliage that holds color year-round and its showy fringe-like flowers in spring and sporadically through the year. The purple-leaved forms ('Plum Delight', 'Burgundy', 'Purple Diamond') are especially striking contrasted against green neighbors. It tolerates summer heat and humidity better than most ornamental shrubs. Prune immediately after the main spring flowering to shape; do not shear into tight balls — this destroys the natural graceful arching habit and removes flowering wood. Apply a slow-release, acid-forming fertilizer in early spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese fringetree is adaptable to a wide range of soils including heavier clay if drainage is reasonable. It is more heat and drought-tolerant than the native white fringetree, making it an excellent choice for the South.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese fringetree rivals the native white fringetree in spectacular spring flower display, producing dense, drooping clusters of slender, white, four-petaled flowers that cover the entire tree in a frothy, fragrant cloud of white in May and June, giving the tree the appearance of being draped in snow. The flowers are both fragrant and profuse enough to be visible from a great distance. Male trees tend to produce heavier floral displays than females; female trees produce attractive clusters of dark blue-black berries beloved by birds in late summer and fall. Compared to the native Chionanthus virginicus, the Chinese species blooms slightly later, is notably more heat-tolerant and adaptable in zone 8–9, and has a tidier rounded habit. The large, glossy, leathery leaves are attractive all summer and the gray, furrowed bark is interesting in winter.

plant_note: Plant dormant pseudobulbs 2–3 inches deep in spring after last frost; established clumps can be divided in early spring or fall. In zone 7–9 Chinese ground orchid is reliably perennial, dying back to the ground in winter and re-emerging each spring to bloom in April–May before the foliage fully expands.
directions: Plant pseudobulbs 2–3 inches deep in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade; Chinese ground orchid is one of the very few true hardy orchids suitable for temperate garden conditions, producing charming magenta-pink to white flowers on upright spikes in April–May before the pleated, strap-like foliage reaches full height. It is one of the most effective shade garden plants for adding color in spring when few other shade perennials are in bloom. Clumps expand slowly over years — never dig out the entire clump; instead take divisions from the perimeter while leaving the main clump undisturbed. Provide a light mulch in zone 5–6 winters; in zone 7–9 plants are generally fully hardy without protection. Avoid waterlogged soils, which cause pseudobulb rot.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in shade; this rhizomatous spreader naturalizes slowly to form a colony under trees. Keep well-watered through summer heat — wilting is a reliable drought indicator. Hardy to zone 7 with light mulch protection.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; Chinese hardy impatiens is one of the finest perennial groundcovers for deep shade, native to forested mountain slopes of Sichuan province in China and completely unlike the annual impatiens of traditional bedding plant use. Its dark, narrow, lance-shaped leaves carry a broad, silver-white central stripe along the midrib that brightens the shaded garden floor even in very low light — a near-luminous quality making it exceptional for animating dark corners under large trees. In autumn it produces small, hooded, pale-yellow flowers characteristic of wild impatiens, an attractive but modest secondary feature to the season-long foliage display. It spreads by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing carpet in shaded spaces where little else thrives, and is hardy to zone 7 with light winter mulch. Evergreen or semi-evergreen in mild winters. A highly refined, patterned alternative to hostas for the woodland garden, combining well with ferns, heucheras, and other shade perennials.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; Chinese hat plant requires warm temperatures and blooms most heavily in fall and winter in frost-free climates.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chinese hat plant is a Himalayan shrub grown for its uniquely structured flowers — each blossom has an expanded, saucer-shaped orange-red calyx (the 'hat') surrounding a smaller tubular corolla, giving each flower the appearance of a Chinese mandarin's hat. The flowers appear in arching terminal clusters from fall through spring in frost-free climates when hummingbirds and sunbirds seek them out. The plant is drought-tolerant and blooms most prolifically during cooler, drier periods. Prune hard after bloom to rejuvenate and shape. In zone 9 protect from frost or grow in large containers.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; in zone 9–10 Chinese hibiscus can be grown as a large, long-lived landscape shrub with winter protection. Mulch heavily around the base in fall in zone 9; established trunks resprout even if top growth is killed.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — Chinese hibiscus is the quintessential tropical flowering shrub, producing the largest and most spectacular flowers of any landscape shrub: blooms 4–8 inches or more across in virtually every color of the rainbow — red, pink, orange, yellow, white, lavender, and complex multi-toned combinations — blooming from spring through frost in zone 9 and nearly year-round in zone 10–12. Flowers last only a single day but the plant produces so many buds that the display is constant. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom; apply slow-release fertilizer every 4–6 weeks during the growing season. In zone 9, mulch heavily in fall and expect some stem dieback in hard winters, but established plants resprout reliably from the base. Essential for the tropical-theme summer garden in any zone as a magnificent container plant moved outdoors in summer.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun in spring or fall; Chinese holly tolerates heat, drought, and clay soils far better than English holly and is the primary holly of choice for Gulf Coast and southeastern landscapes.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese holly is the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant of all the landscape hollies — an essential, tough, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub for Gulf Coast and southeastern landscapes that tolerates summer heat, poor soil, clay, drought, and partial shade far better than English holly (I. aquifolium). The leaves are rectangular with four characteristic spiny corners, giving them a distinctive, blocky appearance different from other hollies. Most cultivars set heavy crops of large, brilliant red berries without a pollinator tree. 'Burfordii' (single terminal spine, heavy berries, classic selection), 'Needlepoint' (narrow, single-spined leaf, columnar form), 'Dazzler' (heavy berry producer), and 'Rotunda' (compact, dwarf, no berries) are widely grown selections. Remarkably tough and long-lived once established in the landscape.

plant_note: Scarify seeds by soaking in near-boiling water for 24 hours before sowing to break dormancy and improve germination rates.
directions: Soak seeds in hot water and allow them to cool overnight before sowing directly into prepared ground in spring after frost danger has passed. Plant seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained soil and keep evenly moist until germination occurs. Transplant seedlings to their permanent location while still small, as the taproot establishes quickly and resents disturbance. Allow generous spacing to accommodate the wide canopy this tree develops at maturity.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; in mild-winter zones sow in fall for spring bloom. Collinsia resents transplanting and always performs best from direct sowing.
directions: Scatter seed on the soil surface and press lightly; Chinese houses germinates readily in cool weather and does not transplant well. The two-lipped flowers in white and purple are arranged in diminishing whorls up the stem like tiers of a pagoda, giving the plant its whimsical common name. It is a California native annual adapted to partially shaded woodland edges and performs beautifully as a spring-flowering groundcover under deciduous shrubs or in dappled shade. Plants self-sow to naturalize in suitable sites. In warm climates it completes its cycle quickly; in zone 9–11 a fall sowing and a late-winter sowing extend the season of bloom.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chinese ixora is considerably more shade-tolerant than the common tropical ixora (Ixora coccinea) and performs in the dappled light of open tree canopy where the red-flowered species would cease blooming.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chinese ixora is an East Asian evergreen shrub of the coffee family (Rubiaceae) closely related to the common tropical ixora (I. coccinea) but producing its characteristic, dense, rounded, terminal clusters of small, tubular flowers in a soft-pink to rose-pink or white color rather than the vivid red-orange of the common species. The flowers are produced continuously from spring through fall, with some intermittent bloom at other seasons in frost-free climates, creating a long-season display of soft-pink color that is more easily incorporated into refined garden color schemes than the intense red-orange of common ixora. Chinese ixora is notably more shade-tolerant than its common relative, blooming acceptably in partial shade conditions — making it one of the few continuously-blooming flowering shrubs useful in shaded positions in zone 9–12. Like all ixoras, it requires strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) for best performance; alkaline soil causes interveinal chlorosis. It is more cold-hardy than I. coccinea, surviving temperatures to approximately 28°F in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in spring; emergence is very late (late May to June in most climates), so mark the location to avoid disturbing the tubers while they are dormant.
directions: Plant tubers in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade in a sheltered spot; this Chinese species is one of the most beautiful of all the jack-in-the-pulpit relatives, producing a pristine white striped spathe with delicate pink-to-green striping that emerges in early summer from the still-bare soil. The large, divided, umbrella-like leaves unfurl after the flower and remain attractive until late summer. Unlike most arisaemas, the tubers are relatively easy to grow and the plant does well in enriched woodland garden soil with reliable summer moisture. It goes completely dormant by late summer and must be marked to avoid digging the tubers accidentally. Hardy to zone 6 with good drainage and mulching; outstanding in dappled shade beneath maples and oaks.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or loamy, dry to average soil in full sun; Chinese juniper is very drought tolerant and adapts to poor, dry, alkaline soils — making it one of the most widely used landscape junipers in the US. Avoid wet, poorly drained conditions.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or loamy, dry to average soil in full sun; Chinese juniper is the most important juniper species in horticulture — the parent of an enormous number of hybrid and cultivated varieties that dominate commercial landscape planting across North America. Cultivars range from flat-spreading groundcovers (Pfitzer junipers, Juniperus x pfitzeriana, are crosses with J. sabina) to columnar accent trees and compact mound forms. The species itself varies from a large, upright tree form to spreading shrub forms. The iconic 'Blue Point' (pyramidal), 'Torulosa' (irregular, Hollywood juniper), 'Kaizuka' (spreading-irregular), 'Blue Vase', 'Old Gold', and 'Sea Green' are all widely planted cultivars or hybrids involving this species. Exceptionally tolerant of dry, poor, alkaline soils, heat, and cold — the workhorse conifer of American commercial landscaping.

plant_note: Chilling seed before sowing improves germination; spreads by runners.
directions: Start seed indoors well before the last frost, ideally after a brief cold period to improve germination. Also called winter cherry, this hardy perennial forms papery orange husks prized for dried arrangements and fall decor. Grow in full sun to part shade with average soil, giving it room since it spreads by underground runners and can be aggressive. Harvest the lanterns once they turn bright orange and hang them to dry.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese lantern abutilon grows into a tall, upright shrub and benefits from occasional pinching to stay bushy rather than leggy.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese lantern abutilon grows into a tall, upright, somewhat leggy shrub with maple-like leaves and pendant, bell-shaped flowers in orange with distinctive dark red veining, the coloring that earned it the nickname candy corn plant among collectors. It blooms over a long season, often nearly year-round in essentially frost-free gardens, and is a reliable, easy-care source of hummingbird nectar with minimal pest or disease trouble. Pinch young plants regularly to encourage branching, since unpinched stems tend to grow tall and sparse rather than full and floriferous. Where winters bring hard freezes, expect significant dieback, with recovery from the roots likely if mulched; alternatively, grow it in a large container that can be moved to a sheltered spot for winter protection.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give it a sheltered spot out of harsh winter wind at the colder end of its range, since the evergreen foliage can be damaged by exposure in hard freezes.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath high, open tree canopy; Chinese leatherleaf mahonia is a tall, architectural evergreen shrub with long, upright canes topped by whorls of narrow, spiny-toothed, leathery leaflets, giving it a bold, almost tropical silhouette unlike the lower, mounding mahonias more commonly grown. In late fall into early winter it produces dramatic upright racemes of bright yellow, faintly fragrant flowers held above the foliage like candelabra, opening earlier than most other mahonias and providing valuable nectar for pollinators and hummingbirds during the coldest, leanest part of the year; blue-black, grape-like berries follow and are relished by birds. Its strongly vertical, sculptural habit makes it a striking accent for the back of a shaded border or a shady courtyard corner rather than a foundation planting. It is the parent, along with M. japonica, of the popular hybrid Mahonia x media selections such as 'Charity' and 'Winter Sun'. Prune out the oldest canes at ground level after flowering if the clump becomes leggy, to encourage fresh basal growth.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Chinese mahonia is more shade-tolerant and less cold-hardy than Oregon grape (M. aquifolium).
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Chinese mahonia is a more refined, less aggressive alternative to Oregon grape (M. aquifolium) for warm-climate shade gardens, producing an upright, narrow form with elegant pinnate leaves bearing multiple narrow, deeply toothed, dark-green, glossy leaflets and dense clusters of fragrant yellow flowers in fall followed by small, blueberry-like, powdery-blue fruits. It is specifically more shade-tolerant and heat-tolerant than the popular Oregon grape. The evergreen foliage provides year-round structure in the darkest parts of the shade garden. Valuable for winter interest with both flowers and persistent fruits. Excellent in formal shaded landscapes and Japanese-inspired gardens.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; unlike the North American mayapple, Chinese mayapple is evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild climates and does not go dormant by midsummer.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; unlike the North American mayapple, Chinese mayapple is evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild climates and does not go dormant by midsummer. Podophyllum pleianthum is a bold Asian relative of the familiar native mayapple, with large, glossy, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves held on sturdy stems and clusters of dark maroon-red, drooping flowers hidden beneath the foliage in spring, followed by large orange-red fruit. Its substantial, architectural leaves and persistent foliage make it a striking textural specimen for a shaded border or woodland garden, holding interest through more of the season than the spring-ephemeral American species. Give it rich, evenly moist soil and protection from harsh winter wind at the cooler end of its range, and divide the slowly spreading rhizome in fall to propagate.

common_name: Chinese Money Plant (UFO Plant, Pancake Plant, Missionary Plant)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in zone 9; Chinese Money Plant cannot tolerate frost and must be kept above 50°F. It adapts well to indoor conditions with bright indirect light. Rotate the pot quarterly to prevent the plant from leaning toward the light source. The plant produces offsets (pups) at the base and on stems — remove these with roots and pot separately to propagate. Allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings to prevent root rot.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light — Chinese Money Plant does best near a bright window but not in direct sun, which scorches the round leaves; it also tolerates somewhat lower light than most popular foliage plants. Pilea peperomioides is a small, compact, upright houseplant native to Yunnan province in southern China, first collected in 1906 and brought to Europe by Norwegian missionary Agnar Espegren in 1946 — who shared cuttings with friends and neighbors so prolifically that the plant spread throughout Scandinavia as a houseplant decades before it became formally described and commercially available in the rest of the world, earning the nickname 'Missionary Plant.' The plant is immediately recognizable by its extraordinary round, peltate leaves (the stem attaches to the center of the underside of the leaf, not the edge) in a bright, glossy, medium-green — each leaf resembling a small green pancake or shield on a thin stem. Multiple leaves on long, flexible petioles radiate from a central upright stem, creating a distinctive, architectural form unlike any other common houseplant. In recent years, Chinese Money Plant has become one of the most sought-after houseplants globally, widely shared between plant enthusiasts as pups (offsets) because it freely produces new plantlets at the base and along stems. It is non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Chinese parasol tree is fast-growing and self-sows abundantly — seedlings are common in warm-climate gardens and the tree can become invasive in the southeastern US. Remove unwanted seedlings while small.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Chinese parasol tree (fenghuang tree or phoenix tree in Chinese, critical in Chinese mythology as the only tree on which the mythical fenghuang/phoenix would perch) is a fast-growing deciduous tree from China and Japan with extraordinary ornamental character — the smooth, bright gray-green bark is distinctive and attractive year-round, the enormous 3–5 lobed, maple-like leaves (up to 12 inches wide) create a bold, tropical appearance, and the unusual fruits (split open as boatlike follicles with edible seeds attached to the margins) are unlike any other temperate tree fruit. The seeds have a mild flavor and are eaten roasted in China. Widely planted across the southeastern US and has naturalized in many areas. The botanical family Malvaceae places it with hibiscus, cotton, and cacao. Beautiful spring flower spikes of greenish-yellow flowers. The pale gray bark is particularly attractive in winter, glowing almost white against a dark background. A dramatic, fast-growing ornamental but aggressive self-sower.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Chinese photinia requires good air circulation — do not plant against walls or in crowded situations where poor air circulation promotes Entomosporium leaf spot disease.
