directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun with good air circulation; Chinese photinia is the large-growing photinia species that serves as the parent of the more commonly planted Fraser photinia (Photinia × fraseri) — a robust, large evergreen shrub or small tree growing 10–25 feet tall with broad, leathery, serrated, glossy dark-green leaves and dramatic new-growth red coloration when young foliage first emerges in spring. The new growth displays the vivid red coloration characteristic of all photinias — a flush of bright red new leaves that contrasts dramatically with the existing dark-green foliage in spring and provides several weeks of striking seasonal color. Chinese photinia is more cold-hardy than Fraser photinia and grows substantially larger, functioning as a true screening tree or large specimen shrub rather than just a foundation shrub. It is notably more resistant to Entomosporium leaf spot disease (the fungal disease that disfigures many Fraser photinias) than its hybrid offspring. White flower clusters in spring are followed by red berries that attract birds. The tall, screening habit makes Chinese photinia valuable for privacy screens and large property divisions — it can reach tree proportions over decades. Provide excellent drainage and good air circulation to minimize leaf spot.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese pistache tolerates drought, alkaline soil, clay, and reflected heat — making it one of the most adaptable shade trees for Gulf Coast urban conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese pistache is widely regarded as the single best fall-color deciduous shade tree for the Gulf South — one of the very few trees that reliably produces brilliant orange, scarlet, and red fall color in zone 9, where autumn temperatures are too mild for most fall-color trees to perform. While maples, oaks, and sweetgums produce muted or inconsistent fall color in zone 9, Chinese pistache reliably transitions to vivid orange-red in late October through November even with the mild, late arrival of cool nights in the Gulf Coast region. The tree grows 30–40 feet tall with a broad, rounded canopy that provides excellent shade, and it is well-suited to the challenging conditions common in Gulf Coast urban landscapes — clay soils, alkaline soil pH, extended summer drought, reflected heat from pavement, and periodic wet periods all fail to deter established Chinese pistache. Female trees produce ornamental clusters of small red berries that transition to blue-purple in winter and are attractive to birds. Trees are dioecious (separate male and female trees); most nursery trees are grafted males selected for form, or named females. Exceptionally low-maintenance once established — no serious pest or disease problems affect Chinese pistache in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, average to fertile soil in zone 6–9; Chinese Pistachio is a highly adaptable, medium to large deciduous shade tree native to China, grown primarily for its outstanding, brilliant, reliable autumn color — reds, oranges, and yellows — in climates where Japanese Maples struggle; one of the best autumn-color street and shade trees for the hot-summer, mild-winter South and Southern Plains.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor, alkaline-tolerant soil; Pistacia chinensis is drought tolerant once established and adaptable to clay, calcareous, and compacted soils — an ideal street and parking-lot tree for hot, dry southern climates where few trees provide reliable autumn color. Pistacia chinensis (Chinese Pistachio) is a large, handsome, deciduous tree native to the mountains and valleys of central and western China (Sichuan, Hubei, Shaanxi), a member of the same genus as the edible pistachio nut (P. vera) and closely related to the mastic tree (P. lentiscus). Its primary ornamental value is its outstanding, consistent, brilliant autumn foliage — turning vivid combinations of red, orange, scarlet, and yellow that rival New England maples in color intensity, but dependably in climates from zone 6 through zone 9 including the Deep South, Gulf Coast, and Texas where true maples produce disappointing autumn color. The tree is extremely tough and adaptable: drought tolerant once established, alkaline soil-tolerant, heat-resistant, relatively pest- and disease-free, and tolerant of urban pollution and compacted soils. Small, blue-black drupes on female trees (pistachio-like but not edible commercially) are attractive to songbirds. Chinese Pistachio has become one of the recommended utility and street trees for Texas, Oklahoma, and the Gulf States precisely because of its reliable autumn color and toughness under extreme summer heat and drought.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese plumbago blooms in late summer and fall — pruning stems back in spring to just above the first new growth encourages bushier habit and better flowering.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese plumbago is a shrubby, deciduous perennial from western China producing clusters of brilliant, clear-blue, five-petaled flowers from midsummer through fall — one of the best sources of true blue color in the late-season garden. The vivid cerulean-blue flowers are distinguished from hardy plumbago (C. plumbaginoides) by the upright shrubby form and slightly larger flowers. In autumn, the dark green foliage turns brilliant burgundy-red simultaneously with the last flush of flowers, creating an exceptional combination of blue flowers and red foliage. Hardy to zone 6, it dies back to the ground in cold winters and re-sprouts from the roots. In zone 9, it may remain evergreen in mild winters. Combines beautifully with ornamental grasses and late-season yellow wildflowers in fall gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese redbud is notably more shade-tolerant than Eastern redbud and adapts well to understory positions. The cultivar 'Avondale' has the most intensely colored, nearly purple-rose flowers and is one of the most spectacular spring-flowering woody plants available in small sizes.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese redbud is a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree from central China that produces an extraordinary spring flowering display on bare branches in early spring — densely packed, vibrant rosy-purple pea flowers covering every branch, twig, and even directly on older wood (cauliflory) before a single leaf emerges. The intensity of the floral display is arguably greater than Eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis) because the flowers are deeper in color (deeper rose to violet-magenta) and the shrubby habit places them at eye level where the bloom can be most appreciated. The cultivar 'Avondale' (from New Zealand) is considered among the finest woody ornamentals in cultivation, with unusually intense, deep rose-purple flowers. Chinese redbud is more shade-tolerant and more compact than Eastern redbud, making it more manageable in smaller gardens and better suited to underplanting in partial shade. The heart-shaped leaves are large and glossy, turning yellow in fall. Long-lived, disease-resistant, and exceptionally showy in spring.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to light shade, allowing generous space since this is one of the largest-growing viburnums; prune immediately after bloom since flowers form on old wood.
directions: Chinese snowball viburnum produces some of the largest flower clusters of any hardy landscape shrub, with sterile snowball-shaped heads 6 to 8 inches across opening lime-green in mid-spring before maturing to pure white. Because the flowers are sterile, the plant sets no fruit, trading wildlife berries for weeks of striking bloom display. It grows into a large, rounded, semi-evergreen shrub in the Gulf South (fully deciduous in colder zones) and works best as a specimen or large screening plant where its considerable mature size is an asset rather than a problem. Give it room, water it well while establishing, and resist heavy pruning except right after flowering.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chinese stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chinese stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance. Smooth, flaking, multicolored bark in patches of gray, tan, and cinnamon provides outstanding winter interest, complemented by white, camellia-like summer flowers with prominent yellow-orange stamens and rich orange-red fall foliage color, giving this small ornamental tree four full seasons of garden interest. Related to camellias and prized among collectors for its combination of showy summer flowers, exfoliating bark, and vivid fall color on a manageable small-tree scale, it makes an outstanding specimen for a shaded woodland garden or Asian-style planting. Provide consistent moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, mulch well to keep roots cool, and avoid disturbing the root zone once established, since stewartias transplant and establish slowly.

common_name: Chinese Sweet Box (Compact Fragrant Winter-Flowering Sarcococca)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Chinese Sweet Box, native to Jiangxi, China, is a distinct Sarcococca species from the more commonly grown S. hookeriana, forming a compact, rounded mound of glossy evergreen foliage with fragrant midwinter flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it performs best in low light and can struggle in strong sun. Chinese Sweet Box, native to Jiangxi Province, China, and genuinely distinct from the widely planted Sarcococca hookeriana, forms a compact, rounded mound of glossy, deep-green, evergreen foliage that provides reliable year-round structure in the shaded garden, producing small, inconspicuous but powerfully sweet-scented white flowers in the depths of winter that perfume the surrounding air, followed by small black berries. Its dense, tidy habit and shade tolerance make it a valuable evergreen filler beneath trees, along shaded foundations, or as a low informal hedge where winter fragrance near a path or entry is wanted. Water during dry spells and prune lightly after flowering only if needed to maintain shape; otherwise it requires very little maintenance.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese sweetshrub is less cold-hardy and less fragrant than the American Calycanthus floridus but bears much larger, showier flowers, and benefits from some wind and afternoon-sun protection.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some shelter from strong wind and the hottest afternoon sun; Chinese sweetshrub is a striking relative of the familiar American Carolina allspice, bearing much larger flowers — broad, white-to-blush, waterlily-like blooms with a yellow-streaked interior — in late spring, a dramatic step up in size and showiness from the smaller maroon flowers of the American species, though with only a light fragrance rather than the American plant's strong spicy scent. Glossy, deep-green, oval leaves turn a clear yellow in fall. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than American Carolina allspice and appreciates a sheltered woodland-edge position rather than full, exposed sun. A choice, uncommon specimen shrub for a partly shaded border, valued more for the size and elegance of its individual flowers than for fragrance. Prune only lightly after flowering to shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial shade; Chinese sweetspire is evergreen in zones 7–10 (losing some leaves in colder parts of its range) and prefers partial shade, tolerating more shade than Virginia sweetspire. More heat and drought tolerant than Virginia sweetspire.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial shade; Chinese sweetspire is the Asian counterpart of Virginia sweetspire (Itea virginica) — a graceful, slightly larger evergreen shrub from the forests and stream banks of central and southern China, with similar (but somewhat larger and more leathery) glossy green leaves and long, fragrant, white flower spikes in summer. More heat- and drought-tolerant than Virginia sweetspire, and evergreen in zone 7–10 rather than deciduous. The long (4–6 inch), slender, fragrant white flower spikes are produced in summer and have a pleasant, sweet scent. Fall color in mild climates is less spectacular than Virginia sweetspire (which turns brilliant red), remaining more greenish-yellow in warmer zones. A refined, shade-tolerant evergreen shrub for the mild, humid Gulf Coast and similar climates where an elegant partial-shade shrub with fragrant summer flowers is desired. Less commonly grown than Virginia sweetspire but valuable for its additional heat-tolerance and evergreen quality in the South.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese sycopsis is an uncommon Hamamelidaceae relative that blooms in late winter and provides year-round interest with its holly-like evergreen foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese sycopsis is an uncommon and underused member of the witch-hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) from central China, providing year-round ornamental interest through its dense, holly-like evergreen foliage of dark, glossy, spiny-margined leaves. The late-winter flowers — small, yellowish, without petals — are unspectacular individually but appear in late January or February before most woody plants show any sign of life, providing early-season pollen for queen bumblebees. The compact, dense growth habit makes it an excellent formal evergreen screening shrub or hedging plant. More shade-tolerant than most Hamamelidaceae relatives and particularly well adapted to the woodland garden in zones 7–9. Rarely available in US nurseries but worth seeking from specialist growers for a distinctive, refined addition to the winter garden.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring or plant tuberous roots 3–4 inches deep after last frost; Incarvillea is tap-rooted and resents transplanting — sow direct or in deep pots that can be transplanted without root disturbance. The fleshy roots store energy through winter but are not frost-hardy in poorly drained or wet soils; mulch heavily in zones 5–6.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Chinese trumpet flower is one of the most exotic-looking hardy perennials for temperate gardens, producing large, vivid rose-pink to magenta, trumpet-shaped flowers that look exactly like tropical bignonia or mandevilla — 2–3 inch wide tubular blooms in brilliant color — on compact plants with attractive, pinnately compound leaves. The combination of tropical flower size and shape with genuine hardiness to zone 5 is remarkable. Plants emerge late in spring (mark their location to avoid disturbing the dormant roots) and produce a concentrated flush of flowers in June, after which the plant rests. It requires excellent drainage through winter to prevent root rot. I. mairei is a more compact, earlier-blooming species; I. olgae is taller with smaller, profuse pink flowers excellent for cutting.

common_name: Chinese Trumpet Vine (Chinese Trumpet Creeper, Grandiflora Trumpet Vine)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a very sturdy trellis, fence, pergola, or arbor in full sun to partial shade; Campsis grandiflora grows vigorously and produces vines too heavy for lightweight supports. Unlike C. radicans, C. grandiflora generally does not self-adhere to surfaces and requires tying to its support. It blooms on new wood — prune in late winter before growth begins for maximum bloom. In zone 9, it blooms from summer through fall. A significant hummingbird plant. Less aggressively spreading by root suckers than C. radicans.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Chinese Trumpet Vine blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates and even benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat, extending the blooming season. Campsis grandiflora is a vigorous, deciduous, woody climbing vine native to China and Japan in the Bignoniaceae family, closely related to the American Trumpet Vine (Campsis radicans) but producing flowers roughly twice the size — 3–4 inches across rather than the 2-inch flowers of its American relative. The large, trumpet-shaped flowers are borne in terminal clusters of 6–12, in vivid shades of orange-red with a salmon-orange interior tube — somewhat less intensely red than C. radicans and more orange-apricot in tone. The flowers bloom from mid-summer through fall in successive flushes and are extraordinary hummingbird attractants. Unlike C. radicans, which clings to surfaces via aerial holdfast roots, C. grandiflora generally lacks strong self-clinging ability and requires tying to support structures — a quality that makes it more controllable in small garden spaces. The intergeneric hybrid Campsis × tagliabuana 'Madame Galen' (C. radicans × C. grandiflora) combines the best features of both parents and is one of the most widely planted trumpet vines in US gardens. Zone 7–9 hardiness makes C. grandiflora a better Gulf Coast choice than the more cold-hardy but aggressively spreading C. radicans.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy or sandy loam soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese tulip poplar grows naturally in the moist subtropical and warm-temperate mountain forests of central and southern China, at elevations of 1,500–5,500 feet, in humid conditions with adequate summer rainfall.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy or sandy loam soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese tulip poplar is the Asian counterpart of the American tulip poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera) — the only two species in the genus, separated by millions of miles of ocean yet producing very similar leaves and flowers. The leaves are distinctively more deeply notched (2 lobes per side rather than 1 in North American tulip poplar) and slightly smaller, giving a more intricate, finely cut appearance. The flowers are smaller and greener than the North American species' bold orange-and-yellow flowers, but share the same tulip-like form. Chinese tulip poplar grows more slowly and at a smaller ultimate size than American tulip poplar, making it more appropriate for gardens of moderate size. More tolerant of heat and humidity than North American tulip poplar in zones 7–9. Of great botanical interest as a 'living fossil' — a relict of the ancient flora of the Northern Hemisphere from the Cretaceous period, now restricted to two isolated populations on opposite sides of the Pacific Ocean.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Chinese Virginia creeper is one of the most shade-tolerant ornamental vines and is particularly effective as a self-clinging shade vine on north and east-facing walls.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Chinese Virginia creeper is a shade-adapted relative of the American Virginia creeper (P. quinquefolia), notable for its strikingly beautiful foliage — the dark green leaves are marked with silver-white veining along the main veins, creating a distinctive, elegant variegated effect. The velvety texture of the leaves enhances this decorative quality. In shade, the silver veining is most pronounced; in full sun, the plant is less attractive and the variegation less distinct. The vine clings to walls, fences, and tree trunks using adhesive tendrils. In fall, the leaves turn rich red-orange even in shade — unusual for a variegated plant. An outstanding shade vine for covering north-facing masonry walls where few other vines perform well.

common_name: Chinese Wild Ginger (Evergreen Silver-Mottled Shade Groundcover Ginger)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Asarum splendens spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a gradually expanding groundcover — plant 8–12 inches apart and allow 2–3 seasons for plants to fill in and create a solid mat.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Asarum splendens (Chinese wild ginger) is a superior species for Gulf South shade gardens because it is more heat-tolerant than the American native wild gingers (A. canadense, A. shuttleworthii) while providing the same excellent groundcover qualities — producing broad, heart-shaped, evergreen leaves with a dramatic silver-and-dark-green mottled pattern that creates one of the most ornamental groundcover displays available for full-shade positions. The silver mottling covers 50–70% of each leaf surface in irregular patterns, creating a luminous, almost metallic quality that reflects available light in dim shade positions and brightens dark garden areas that most groundcovers occupy without visual distinction. The genus name Asarum refers to the small, inconspicuous, brown-purple flowers produced at or below soil level in spring — they are hidden by the foliage but botanically characteristic. The ground-hugging habit (6–10 inches) and slow rhizomatous spread make Chinese wild ginger an outstanding groundcover for defined garden areas — it does not spread aggressively out of control but gradually fills a planting space over several seasons. More tolerant of zone 9 summer heat than American wild gingers, making it the preferred Asarum for Gulf South gardens. Outstanding under camellias, azaleas, and other shade-casting shrubs where it fills bare soil with ornamental year-round foliage.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Chinese winter hazel benefits from a sheltered position to protect early blooms from late frosts. Grows to a larger multi-stemmed shrub than dwarf winter hazel.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese winter hazel is a large, multi-stemmed shrub native to mountain forests of central China, producing long, pendulous racemes of soft yellow flowers with a light, sweet fragrance in late winter or very early spring before the leaves emerge. Each drooping chain of 15–20 small flowers resembles a string of yellow bells, and a well-established shrub in full bloom creates a spectacular curtain of pale gold in the February garden. The large, boldly veined, heart-shaped leaves that follow are attractive through summer, turning yellow in fall. One of the more cold-tolerant Corylopsis species, surviving reliably to zone 6 and worth trying in sheltered zone 5 microclimates. The variety var. calvescens 'Spring Purple' has purple-flushed new growth; 'Wisley Red' has red-tinged new leaves and calyces.

plant_note: Plant grafted or layered plants (NOT seedlings) in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese wisteria requires a very strong, permanent support — the vines can reach 100 lbs per linear foot on mature, established plants. INVASIVE: Chinese wisteria is a Category I invasive pest plant in the southeastern United States, escaping cultivation and smothering native forest understories. Consider the non-invasive native alternatives Wisteria frutescens or W. macrostachya instead.
directions: Plant grafted plants in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun with very strong permanent support; Chinese wisteria is one of the most spectacular flowering vines in temperate gardening — in full bloom in April and May the plant is covered with cascading, pendulous clusters (racemes) of fragrant, violet-purple flowers up to 12 inches long that open all at once in a breathtaking floral display. The fragrance is sweet and pervasive. However, Chinese wisteria is classified as an invasive exotic pest plant throughout the southeastern United States, where it has escaped cultivation to smother trees and native forest understory in a manner similar to kudzu. It twines clockwise (Japanese wisteria, W. floribunda, twines counterclockwise). The vines become massive with age — potentially requiring structural reinforcement of pergolas and arbors. For gardeners seeking wisteria bloom without ecological risk, the native American wisterias (Wisteria frutescens, W. macrostachya) offer similar floral display with smaller racemes and WITHOUT the invasive risk. Confirm wisteria regulations in your state before planting Chinese or Japanese wisteria.

plant_note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese witch hazel dislikes wet, waterlogged soil or heavy clay — ensure adequate drainage; it is the most cold-hardy of the Chinese witch hazels and reliable in zones 5–8.
directions: Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese witch hazel dislikes wet, waterlogged soil or heavy clay — ensure adequate drainage; it is the most cold-hardy of the Chinese witch hazels and reliable in zones 5–8. Hamamelis mollis is the best of the Chinese witch hazels and one of the finest winter-blooming shrubs for temperate gardens; it produces exceptionally large, softly golden-yellow, strap-petaled flowers with an extraordinarily rich, spicy-sweet fragrance — one of the finest natural perfumes of any flowering plant — on bare stems in January and February when the garden is otherwise dormant. The large, soft, round leaves turn butter-yellow to orange-yellow in fall before dropping; and the plant has a distinctive, broadly spreading, vase-shaped form. The cultivar 'Pallida' (pale sulfur-yellow) and 'Goldcrest' (deep golden yellow with red centers) are among the finest selections.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese witchhazel is slow to establish and resents root disturbance — container plants are far more reliable than bare-root. Grafted plants are also available and bloom sooner.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese witchhazel is one of the most fragrant of the witchhazels, producing its spidery yellow to orange flowers in the dead of winter (January through February) with an intensely sweet, warm, spicy scent that carries remarkable distances on cold air. The flowers are frost-resistant and remain attractive even after mild snow and ice events. Chinese witchhazel (H. mollis) is a primary parent of the popular Hamamelis x intermedia hybrids that dominate nursery trade — including 'Arnold Promise' (yellow), 'Jelena' (orange), and 'Diane' (coppery-red). The large, rounded leaves turn a clear golden-yellow in fall. Slow to establish but very long-lived and low-maintenance once settled.

subcategory: South African long-lasting cut flower bulb
plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; chinkerinchee grows through the cool season and blooms in late spring. In zone 9–10 it naturalizes; in cooler zones, lift after the foliage dies and store dry through summer. It is widely grown as a commercial cut flower crop in South Africa and exported worldwide for its exceptional vase life.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; chinkerinchee is a South African Cape bulb famous in the cut flower trade for the extraordinary vase life of its flowers — blooms can last 3–4 weeks in a vase, making it one of the longest-lasting cut flowers available. The dense, conical spikes of pure-white, star-shaped flowers with dark centers are produced in late spring on upright, 18–24 inch stems. The flowers open progressively from bottom to top over several weeks, extending the display period. The vernacular name 'chinkerinchee' comes from the sound the dry stem makes when rubbed against itself in a breeze. It is a major South African agricultural export, with bulbs wrapped in newspaper and shipped around the world because of their unusual longevity out of water during transport. The flowers are also attractive in the garden or naturalized in zone 9–10, forming colonies where the dry summer dormancy can be accommodated.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Chocoholic bears bronze-purple foliage and mauve-pink bottlebrush flowers that fade to white, a distinct bloom color from the white-flowered dark-leaved bugbane cultivars already common in cultivation.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, deep, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Chocoholic, a seedling selection of the popular dark-leaved 'Brunette', bears the same rich bronze-purple, deeply cut foliage but is distinguished by its flower color, opening mauve-pink rather than pure white and gradually fading toward white as the tall, fragrant bottlebrush spikes age in late summer and early fall, a subtle but distinctive departure from other dark bugbane cultivars. The dark foliage glows in dappled shade and provides months of textural contrast against nearby hostas and ferns before the late-season flower spikes extend the display well past when most shade perennials have finished blooming. Performs best in cooler climates; in the warmth of zone 8, provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture. Divide in spring only when necessary, since established clumps resent disturbance.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow Chocolate Cherry sunflowers an inch deep after the last frost, spacing them to allow for their branching habit. Each plant carries multiple five-to-eight-inch blooms in deep burgundy-to-black petals around dark chocolate centers on six-to-seven-foot stems. They make dramatic, pollen-rich cut flowers that keep coming through summer and fall. Cut regularly to encourage more side blooms and leave a few for the pollinators.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; space 6–8 inches apart for ground cover use — Chocolate Chip fills in quickly through stolons and will create a dense mat within 1–2 seasons.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Chocolate Chip is one of the most distinctive and smallest ajuga cultivars — an extremely compact, low-growing selection reaching only 2–4 inches in height (less than half the height of standard ajuga cultivars) with tiny, dark chocolate-brown to bronze-purple leaves that form a miniature, very dense, tight mat of foliage. The diminutive scale makes Chocolate Chip useful in situations where even standard dwarf ajuga would be too tall — between stepping stones, in tight rock garden crevices, as a living carpet under small specimens, and in the smallest garden spaces. In spring, short, upright spikes of blue-violet flowers appear, providing seasonal nectar for early bees and pollinators. The spreading, stoloniferous habit fills in quickly — Chocolate Chip will cover 6–12 inches within the first season of planting and gradually expand to a continuous mat. Unlike some larger ajuga cultivars that can spread aggressively into lawn areas, Chocolate Chip's fine texture and compact stature make it more containable. The dark bronze-purple leaf color provides year-round ornamental interest — the darkest and most interesting foliage color of any common ajuga cultivar. Excellent under ornamental trees, in woodland paths, and as a living ground cover between stepping stones.

common_name: Chocolate Chips Manfreda (Wavy-Leaf Mottled Manfreda Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in part shade to full sun; light afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps preserve the deep chocolate-maroon leaf mottling.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in part shade to full sun, where its low rosette of soft, undulating, gray-green leaves heavily blotched with dark chocolate-maroon spots forms a striking groundcover-scale accent along the front of a xeric bed. In summer it sends up a tall, slender, branching spike of small, greenish-brown, tubular flowers with a sweet, spicy fragrance that intensifies at dusk, attracting hawk moths and hummingbirds much like its wild manfreda relatives. Selected and introduced by a Texas specialty nursery, this cultivar has become a favored parent in mangave breeding programs for its distinctive spotting and soft, non-spiny leaf texture, and it works equally well massed as a small-scale xeric groundcover or grown as a specimen in raised beds and containers. Sharp drainage is essential since, like other manfredas, it is prone to rot in heavy or poorly drained soil.

common_name: Chocolate Cosmos (Black Cosmos, Mexican Chocolate Flower)
plant_note: Plant tubers or container-grown divisions after last frost when soil is warm; chocolate cosmos is extinct in the wild and all plants in cultivation are vegetatively propagated clones — it sets no viable seed; in zones 8–11 it can overwinter as a tuberous root; in colder zones treat as a tender tuber (like dahlia) to be dug and stored indoors over winter or grow as an annual from purchased tubers each spring.
directions: Plant tubers 2 inches deep after last frost in a sunny, well-drained bed; chocolate cosmos prefers fertile, moist but well-drained soil and blooms from midsummer through fall; in zones 7–8, mulch heavily over the tuberous roots in fall for overwintering; in zone 9a the tubers typically survive mild winters without lifting; deadhead spent flowers to encourage continuous bloom. Chocolate cosmos (Cosmos atrosanguineus) is one of the most remarkable plants in horticulture for a single characteristic: the dark maroon to near-black velvet flowers have a genuine, unmistakable fragrance of chocolate — specifically, warm dark chocolate or cocoa — that intensifies in the warmth of the afternoon sun and is most perceptible when you hold the flower close to your face or on warm, still days. The scent is caused by compounds including methyl salicylate and related aromatic chemicals in the flower's oils that happen to share chemical similarities with compounds in cocoa. The flower itself is also visually extraordinary: a flat, velvety, 1–1.5 inch daisy-form flower in the deepest burgundy-brown to near-black, with a darker central disc and a rich, velvety texture that catches light beautifully. Native to Mexico (Morelos state) where it was collected and described in 1861, Cosmos atrosanguineus is now considered extinct in the wild — the species exists only in cultivation, where all plants are vegetatively propagated clones descended from a small number of original specimens. Since it cannot set seed (all plants are genetically identical and clonal), it must be propagated from cuttings, tuberous root divisions, or tissue culture. It is a genuinely extraordinary garden plant for its combination of visual drama and unique fragrance.

common_name: Chocolate Covered Cherry Coleus (Seed-Grown Shade Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Chocolate Covered Cherry is a seed-grown coleus with rosy pink-and-mahogany foliage edged in crisp green, bred to hold its rich color well in shaded to partly shaded beds and containers.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Chocolate Covered Cherry is a seed-grown coleus bearing rosy pink and deep mahogany foliage with a crisp chartreuse-green margin, a rich color combination that reads well from a distance in a shaded bed or mixed container. It performs best out of direct, intense afternoon sun, holding its most saturated color in dappled or partial shade rather than full exposure. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into fuller, more colorful foliage rather than seed production. Pinch growing tips periodically through the season to encourage a dense, well-branched habit and prevent legginess.

common_name: Chocolate Drop Coleus (Compact Deep Chocolate-Maroon Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Chocolate Drop is a compact ColorBlaze series coleus with small, deep chocolate-maroon leaves on a dense, mounding plant well suited to containers.
directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Chocolate Drop stays notably compact for a ColorBlaze series coleus, bearing small, deep chocolate-maroon leaves on a dense, tightly mounding plant that fits containers, edging, and small-scale plantings where larger coleus cultivars would sprawl. Its rich, dark, near-solid coloring provides a strong contrast foil for brighter flowers and foliage nearby. Water regularly during establishment and pinch growing tips occasionally to maintain a full, bushy habit; flowers late in the season like other ColorBlaze selections.

plant_note: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil; drought tolerant once established.
directions: Direct sow in spring in lean, well-drained soil and full sun, where the plants thrive with minimal fuss. Native to the dry southwestern U.S., this hardy heirloom, also called chocolate daisy, gives off a genuine chocolate fragrance strongest in the morning and late afternoon. Plant it along walkways or patios where visitors can catch the scent, and water sparingly once established. Deadhead to encourage repeat bloom through the season.

common_name: Chocolate Mint Coleus (Dark Bronze Foliage with Green Edge)
plant_note: Plant transplants or rooted cuttings after all frost danger has passed in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chocolate Mint pairs deep chocolate-brown foliage with a fresh mint-green edge.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, adjusting light exposure to what the growing conditions allow, since coleus color intensifies in brighter light but the plant scorches in the harshest afternoon sun. Chocolate Mint carries rich, deep chocolate-brown leaves rimmed in a crisp mint-green edge, a striking color combination that reads almost like a painted leaf and provides months of reliable foliage color from spring through frost. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushy, well-branched growth, and remove flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage rather than seed production.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed before sowing; provide a trellis for the vines.
directions: Nick and soak the seeds, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis, arbor, or fence. This Japanese morning glory carries large, four-to-five-inch, rosy-chocolate blooms above attractive green-and-white variegated foliage. Give it full sun and moderate water, and avoid overly rich soil that favors leaves over flowers. Provide sturdy support early since the vines climb quickly in warm weather.

common_name: Chocolate Ruffles Heuchera (Chocolate Ruffles Coral Bells)
plant_note: Set divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial shade, since strong afternoon sun can scorch its large leaves.
directions: Set divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial shade, since strong afternoon sun can scorch its large leaves. This heavily ruffled Heuchera villosa-type hybrid produces broad, deeply savoyed foliage in rich milk-chocolate brown, held above the soil in a loose mound, with airy white flower spikes rising well above the leaves in summer. Its villosa parentage gives it noticeably better heat and humidity tolerance than many glossier heuchera hybrids, making it a good performer in warm-summer regions like the Gulf South. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the crown vigorous.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in shade to dappled shade; Chocolate Shogun was bred by Japanese astilbe breeder Nagasaki Teruhisa and tolerates somewhat more sun than most astilbe cultivars provided soil moisture stays consistent.
directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade to dappled shade; Chocolate Shogun stands out among astilbe cultivars for its glossy, deeply serrated, chocolate-bronze foliage, which provides rich color contrast in the shade garden even before the plumes appear. In summer it sends up airy, feathery plumes blushed white to soft pink above the dark foliage. Astilbe does not tolerate drought and will brown and decline quickly without steady moisture, so mulch well and water regularly through the growing season, especially in a hot, humid Gulf South summer. Leave the dried plumes standing through fall and winter for ornamental interest, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; germinates readily in warm, moist soil.
directions: Melochia corchorifolia is a fast-growing tropical annual in the mallow family with soft, hairy, ovate leaves and clusters of small purple-pink flowers that attract small native bees throughout the warm season. Native to tropical Asia and Africa, it has naturalized across moist, disturbed habitats of the southeastern US, Gulf Coast, and Caribbean, including roadsides, wet ditches, and waste ground. Direct sow seeds after last frost into full sun; the plant establishes quickly in moist soil and tolerates moderate heat and humidity well. Stems have historically been used as a bast fiber similar to jute in parts of its native range.

common_name: Chocolate White Snakeroot (Dark-Leaved Native Woodland Selection)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Chocolate is a dark-foliaged selection of the native white snakeroot, valued as much for its purple-bronze leaves as for its late-season flowers.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this selection tolerates deep shade and dry soil once established better than most dark-foliaged perennials, which are more often bred for sun. Chocolate carries rich, glossy, purple-bronze foliage through the growing season, deepest in color with some morning sun, then tops out in late summer to fall with airy, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers that draw a heavy late-season crush of bees and butterflies when few other shade plants are blooming. It self-seeds readily, and while the straight species is a valuable native, all parts of white snakeroot are toxic to livestock and were historically responsible for fatal 'milk sickness' in humans who drank milk from cows that had grazed it, so keep it out of pastures and away from grazing animals. Deadhead spent flower heads if self-seeding becomes excessive, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years.

common_name: Choctaw Crape Myrtle (Large-Flowered Bright Pink Indian-Series Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Choctaw is a tall U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series crape myrtle noted for very large flower clusters and among the best mildew resistance in the series.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, allowing ample room for this tall, tree-form cultivar to reach its mature size. Choctaw is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, prized for its clear bright pink flowers borne in exceptionally large clusters, among the largest of any crape myrtle cultivar, on a tall tree reaching up to 30 feet with age. It ranks among the most mildew-resistant cultivars in the Indian series, an important trait in the humid Gulf South, and develops attractive exfoliating bark for winter interest. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Chorus Line Daylily (Ruffled Pink with Rose Eyezone)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Chorus Line won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal for its distinctive pink flowers with a contrasting rose-pink eyezone and picotee edge.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Chorus Line earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal, its highest honor, for ruffled, pale pink flowers marked with a distinct rose-pink eyezone and a matching picotee edge along the ruffled petals, a crisp, defined pattern that stands out among softer, unpatterned pink daylily cultivars. It blooms heavily on well-branched scapes above a vigorous, quickly multiplying clump. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering through the bloom season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and flower count.

plant_note: Root 2–3 segment stem tip cuttings in well-drained cactus mix or perlite; Christmas cactus needs bright indirect light indoors and benefits from a summer vacation outdoors in a shaded location. To induce blooming in November–December, expose to cool temperatures (50–55°F) and 12–14 hours of darkness for 4–6 weeks in fall. Move to brighter, warmer conditions once buds form.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light indoors in well-drained cactus mix; Christmas cactus is one of the most widely grown houseplants in the world, a Brazilian forest epiphyte that blooms in winter — producing vivid tubular flowers in red, pink, white, coral, or purple at the stem tips in November through January, timed perfectly for the holiday season. The flat, segmented, spineless green 'leaves' are actually stems (phylloclades). Unlike desert cacti, Christmas cactus is a forest epiphyte from cloud forests and requires more moisture, organic matter, and indirect light than most cacti. Blooming is triggered by shortening day length and cool temperatures in fall — a dark garage or cool room for 4–6 weeks in October initiates the bud set. The plant is long-lived: specimens can be passed down through generations and grow for 30–50+ years. 'Christmas cactus' versus 'Thanksgiving cactus' (S. truncata) are often confused — the Thanksgiving cactus has pointed segment margins and blooms in November, while the Christmas cactus has rounded margins and blooms in December. Both are commonly sold under the same name.

common_name: Christmas Carol Hellebore (Fragrant White Christmas Rose)
plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall in humus-rich, well-drained shade; Christmas Carol is a Helleborus niger selection bred for exceptionally early, long-lasting bloom and a light, sweet fragrance unusual among hellebores, often flowering by the actual Christmas holiday in mild climates.
directions: Plant with the crown at soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun. Christmas Carol is a Helleborus niger (Christmas rose) cultivar bred for an especially heavy bud count, extra-long bloom season, and a light, pleasant fragrance rare among hellebores, most of which have little to no scent. Pure white, saucer-shaped flowers with a central boss of golden stamens open from late fall into winter and often continue into early spring, aging to a soft pink blush as they mature, held above dark, leathery, evergreen foliage. Like other Christmas roses, it is more particular about drainage and consistent moisture than the tougher Lenten rose (H. x hybridus) and appreciates a spot that doesn't dry out or stay soggy. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to show off the flowers and reduce leaf spot disease, and top-dress annually with compost, since hellebores are heavy feeders that reward rich soil with a bigger bloom display.

common_name: Christmas Cheer Azalea (Very Early-Blooming Red Kurume Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Christmas Cheer is one of the earliest-blooming landscape azaleas, often flowering well before most other Kurume and Southern Indica cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Christmas Cheer is a compact Kurume-type azalea grown widely in Southern landscapes for its unusually early spring bloom, often opening its bright red to red-pink, hose-in-hose flowers well ahead of most other azalea cultivars and giving an early jolt of color to the late-winter garden. Its dense, mounding, evergreen habit suits foundation plantings, borders, and mass plantings where reliable early color is wanted. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.

plant_note: Take pencil-thin stem cuttings in spring, cure the cut ends for a week or more, then plant shallowly in gritty, well-drained soil and hold off watering until roots establish.
directions: Take pencil-thin stem cuttings in spring, cure the cut ends for a week or more, then plant shallowly in gritty, well-drained soil and hold off watering until roots establish. This slender, sparsely spined cholla often hides beneath nurse shrubs and becomes most visible in winter when it is studded with bright red, cherry-like fruit that can persist for months. It tolerates more cold than most chollas and works well tucked into rock gardens or native hedgerows where its winter color stands out against gray desert foliage.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in a sheltered, shaded spot; tolerates transplanting well.
directions: Set crowns just below soil level in well-drained but moisture-retentive soil amended with leaf mold or compost. This native fern stays evergreen through winter in zones 6 and warmer, making it valuable for year-round ground cover under deciduous trees. Once established it tolerates moderate drought better than most ferns, though it prefers steady moisture through summer. Old fronds flatten to the ground in winter but remain green; remove them in early spring to allow unobstructed emergence of the new season's fronds.

common_name: Christmas Gift Amaryllis (Classic Pure White Holiday Amaryllis)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Christmas Gift is a classic pure white amaryllis long popular as a forced holiday container bulb.
directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Christmas Gift bears large, pure white flowers with a faint green throat, a clean, classic color that has made it one of the most popular amaryllis cultivars for forcing into bloom around the winter holidays, though it performs equally well as a garden or naturalized bulb in zone 8-10. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, multiplying into an increasingly full clump over the years. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb, and for container forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix for traditional winter bloom indoors.

common_name: Christmas Heliconia (Holiday Heliconia, Narrow Heliconia, Angusta Heliconia)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Heliconia angusta is one of the more shade-tolerant and cold-tolerant heliconias, growing naturally as a forest understory plant and surviving temperatures to 28–30°F with rhizome protection in zone 9. In the Northern Hemisphere it blooms November–January ('Christmas Heliconia'). Divide clumps every 3–4 years. Excellent as a long-lasting cut flower (2–3 weeks). Propagate by dividing rhizomes.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Christmas Heliconia is one of the most shade-tolerant of the commonly grown heliconias, naturally adapted to forest understory conditions and producing reliable bloom even in relatively dim positions in zone 9-11 shade gardens. Heliconia angusta is a compact, clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to Brazil, Bolivia, and Peru in the Heliconiaceae family, one of the smaller-growing heliconias and one of the most valuable for several reasons: its relatively compact size (3–6 feet, more manageable than the massive H. bihai or H. caribaea), its notable shade tolerance, its moderate cold tolerance for a heliconia (surviving zone 9 winters), and its bloom season — in the Northern Hemisphere, H. angusta produces its striking inflorescences from November through January, coinciding with the Christmas holiday season and earning the affectionate name 'Christmas Heliconia.' The erect inflorescences bear bright red, narrow, keeled bracts alternating along the stem in the classic heliconia 'lobster claw' pattern, with small white to pale yellow flowers emerging from within each bract. The narrow bracts (the 'angusta' — narrow) give the inflorescence a slimmer, more elegant silhouette compared to broader-bracted species. An excellent choice for zone 9 shade gardens where larger, less cold-tolerant heliconias cannot be reliably grown.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; Christmas Orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; Christmas Orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11. Named for French botanist Jerome Triana and designated the national flower of Colombia, this classic large-flowered cattleya species produces broad, ruffled, fragrant lavender-pink petals surrounding a deep magenta-and-gold throat, blooming naturally in December in its high-elevation Colombian Andes habitat and giving the plant its common English name. A cooler-growing cattleya than many tropical lowland relatives, reflecting its native mountain cloud-forest habitat, it appreciates a distinct temperature drop at night and does not thrive in constant hot, humid lowland warmth. Water when the bark mix approaches dryness, provide bright light with some direct morning sun for reliable flowering, and give the plant a cooler night temperature if possible to encourage its natural winter bloom cycle.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Christmas Palm (Manila Palm, Adonidia Palm) is the most widely planted small landscape palm in Florida, the Caribbean, and tropical gardens worldwide — a compact, fast-growing, elegant Philippine native that produces brilliant clusters of shiny-red fruits ripening at Christmas time, making it one of the most recognizable and beloved ornamental palms in subtropical landscapes.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Veitchia merrillii is fast-growing for a palm and relatively tolerant of brief dry periods once established — fertilize with palm-specific slow-release fertilizer containing magnesium and potassium twice per year; very sensitive to cold below 32°F. Veitchia merrillii (Christmas Palm, Manila Palm, or Adonidia Palm, syn. Adonidia merrillii) is a slender, elegant, single-trunked feather palm native to the tropical forests of the Philippine archipelago, and unquestionably the single most planted small ornamental palm in South Florida, the Caribbean, and tropical landscape gardens worldwide. The appeal is immediate: a compact, tidy, self-cleaning, fast-growing palm that matures at 10–25 feet — ideal for residential lots — with a smooth, prominently ringed trunk, a well-defined crown shaft, and gracefully arching, bright-green pinnate fronds. The most distinctive seasonal feature is the clusters of brilliant, scarlet-red to crimson fruits that ripen in November through December, cascading beneath the crown in spectacular holiday-colored display that gave the palm its name. Veitchia merrillii adapts to a wide range of well-drained soils including South Florida's alkaline limestone, tolerates salt spray better than many palms, and grows well in full sun with regular irrigation. Susceptible to Lethal Yellowing disease in Florida; choose resistant 'Maypan' hybrids or treat prophylactically with oxytetracycline injections in endemic areas.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens or fresh divisions in early fall in moist, alkaline to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Christmas rose requires 2–3 years to establish and bloom freely.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally on a slope or raised position where winter drainage is reliable; Christmas rose produces pristine white flowers in midwinter to early spring, often blooming through snow, when scarcely any other garden plant shows color. Unlike most garden plants, helleborus niger prefers neutral to slightly alkaline soil — work lime into acidic beds before planting. Do not divide established plants unnecessarily, as they resent disturbance and take 1–2 seasons to recover. Remove old foliage in late fall to reduce fungal issues and allow a clear view of the winter blooms.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens after last frost in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; in zone 9 and south, Christmas senna is perennial and shrubby — in zone 8 it often freezes back but regrows from the roots; avoid heavy clay and wet soils.
directions: Christmas senna is a semi-evergreen, fast-growing tropical shrub from the Caribbean and Central America that earns its common name by producing showy clusters of bright canary-yellow flowers from October through December and into winter — blooming abundantly when most other landscape plants have shut down for the season. It is one of the most important larval host plants for cloudless sulphur butterflies and orange-barred sulphur butterflies, with adults laying eggs on the foliage throughout the warm months and caterpillars consuming the leaves until the plant is bare, then quickly regrowing — a cycle that makes Christmas senna an outstanding butterfly garden plant. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, it grows rapidly to form a large, billowing shrub that can be cut back hard in late winter to maintain a manageable size and stimulate vigorous new growth; it tolerates poor, sandy soils and drought once established, making it low-maintenance in suitable climates. Note: it can naturalize and spread by seed in zone 9b–11 — monitor and remove seedlings in ecologically sensitive areas.

common_name: Christmas Tree Hosta (Dark Green Center with Irregular White Margin)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil. Christmas Tree bears dark green leaf centers with irregular, crisp white margins.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partly to fully shaded site, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Christmas Tree bears dark green leaf centers bordered by irregular, crisp white margins, a classic high-contrast variegation pattern that brightens a shaded planting throughout the growing season. It produces lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer. Mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system from summer heat, and divide congested clumps every several years in spring.

common_name: Christmas Tree Liriope (Cone-Shaped White-and-Lavender Flower Spikes)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Christmas Tree liriope is named for its distinctively cone-shaped flower spikes, wider at the base and tapering to a point.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; established clumps tolerate considerable drought and root competition from trees once settled in. Christmas Tree liriope forms tidy clumps of strappy, dark green, evergreen foliage and is named for its unusual flower spikes, which flare wider at the base and taper to a point in a distinct conical shape reminiscent of a small evergreen tree, opening white at the base and shading to soft lavender toward the tip in late summer. It makes a durable, low-maintenance edging or mass planting for shaded borders and pathways, spreading slowly into solid clumps rather than running aggressively. Shear or mow the foliage back hard in late winter before new growth emerges to remove tattered old leaves and keep the planting looking fresh for the coming season.

common_name: Chromatella Water Lily (Classic Marliac Hardy Yellow Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun; Chromatella, introduced by the historic Latour-Marliac nursery in the late 1800s, is one of the oldest and most widely grown hardy yellow water lily cultivars.
directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun. Chromatella was introduced by the historic French Latour-Marliac water lily nursery in the late 1800s and remains one of the most historically significant and widely sold hardy yellow water lily cultivars, producing star-shaped, canary-yellow flowers over attractively mottled, purple-blotched green foliage. Its long track record of reliable performance across a wide range of climates has kept it a standard recommendation for water gardens more than a century after its introduction. Divide rhizomes every two to three years when they crowd their container, and feed during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets pushed into the soil for the best bloom.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chrysler Imperial is an AARS 1953 winner bred by Walter Lammerts and, like many classic hybrid teas, benefits from a preventative fungicide program in humid climates.
directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chrysler Imperial is a classic hybrid tea rose, an All-America Rose Selections winner in 1953, celebrated for its large, velvety, deep-crimson double flowers and an intense, old-rose fragrance that earned it the James Alexander Gamble Fragrance Medal in 1965 — one of the highest honors in rose fragrance. Its rich color and heavy scent made it a mid-century garden and florist standard, and it remains a favorite where classic hybrid tea form and strong perfume matter more than the disease resistance of modern landscape roses. As with most older hybrid teas, expect to manage black spot and powdery mildew with a regular preventative spray program in humid, rainy climates. Prune hard in late winter, feed monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to keep the repeat-flowering cycle going.

common_name: Chuck Hayes Gardenia (Cold-Hardy Reblooming Double-White Gardenia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) soil in partial shade; gardenias are notoriously pH-sensitive — yellow leaves (chlorosis) in established plants is the primary symptom of insufficient soil acidity; acidify with sulfur and use fertilizers formulated for acid-loving plants.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade; Chuck Hayes is a standout gardenia cultivar selected for two key improvements over standard Gardenia jasminoides: superior cold-hardiness (zone 7 reliable, versus zone 8 for most gardenias) and a rebloom tendency that produces flowers in both spring and fall rather than the single spring-only bloom flush of the species. Named for the North Carolina gardener who selected and propagated it, Chuck Hayes represents a significant horticultural improvement that extends gardenia culture northward and provides a longer bloom season throughout the Southeast. The flowers are classic double-white gardenia — the iconic, deeply fragrant, creamy white multi-petaled blooms that represent the pinnacle of floral fragrance in the American garden — produced in April–June and again in September–October in favorable conditions. The compact, rounded habit (3–5 feet) is more manageable than standard gardenia, fitting typical residential border spacing without crowding. The cold-hardiness improvement makes Chuck Hayes the preferred choice for zone 7b-8a gardeners who have lost standard gardenias in severe winters, and provides additional security for zone 9 gardeners in the rare extreme cold events that affect the Gulf South. Gardenias require consistent moisture and strongly acidic soil — iron chlorosis from insufficiently acidic soil is the most common cultural problem.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring into very well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; chuparosa is a Sonoran and Mojave Desert wash-dweller adapted to intense heat, drought, and poor soil.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; chuparosa is a sprawling, nearly leafless desert shrub of the American Southwest with slender gray-green stems that carry out most of the plant's photosynthesis, an adaptation to extreme drought and heat in its native washes and rocky desert flats. Tubular, bright red-orange flowers, rich in nectar, are produced heavily in late winter and spring and again after summer rains, and are one of the most reliable early-season hummingbird nectar sources in the low desert, giving the plant its Spanish common name meaning 'hummingbird sipper.' It tolerates reflected heat, poor rocky soil, and long dry spells that would kill most other flowering shrubs, needing supplemental water only to establish and during the driest extended stretches. Prune out dead or frost-damaged wood in spring, since plants may drop leaves or die back partially in a hard freeze but generally resprout well from older wood.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; church steeple lily is a tropical West African species adapted to shade and moisture — growing naturally in the humid, shaded understory of tropical West African forests. In zones 9b–11 it grows well outdoors in part shade year-round; in zone 9a it benefits from protection or a sheltered, south-facing position. The common name 'church steeple lily' refers to the tall, slender, pointed buds before opening. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; church steeple lily is a shade-loving tropical West African crinum — one of the few crinum species that prefers shade rather than sun — producing in summer and autumn umbels of 6–10 pure-white, long-tubed, strongly fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers with very long perianth tubes that taper to a point in bud before opening (the 'church steeple' shape that gives the common name). The opened flowers are pure white with a very slender tube and spreading lobes, sweetly fragrant in the evening, and elegant rather than bold in character — a refined white tropical lily for the shade garden. Native to the humid, shaded understory of West and Central African tropical forests from Senegal to Uganda, it evolved for consistent shade and moisture, making it an invaluable crinum for the zone 9–11 tropical shade garden where few other large summer-flowering bulbs with genuine shade tolerance are available. Combined with clivias, drimiopsis, and other shade-tolerant South African and tropical bulbs, it provides an extended season of white fragrant flowers in the deep shade garden. The dark-green, broad strap-shaped leaves are handsome throughout the year.

common_name: Cigar Calathea (Pampano, Cuban Cigar Plant, Wax Calathea)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in late spring in partial shade to full sun with consistently moist, rich, well-drained soil; Calathea lutea is one of the largest and most robust calatheas, reaching 6–10 feet tall — provide ample space. In zone 9, it grows as a large-leaf accent with rhizomes surviving mild winters under heavy mulch. The large paddle-shaped leaves are used to wrap food in tropical cuisine (similar to banana leaves). The white, powdery wax coating on the leaf undersides is characteristic. Propagate by rhizome division.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, organically rich, well-draining soil — Cigar Calathea grows vigorously in partial shade but also tolerates full sun in moist soils, and produces its largest leaves with adequate moisture and warmth. Calathea lutea is a large, clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America in the Marantaceae family — one of the largest-growing calatheas, reaching 6–10 feet in height, and one of the most useful and dramatic as a landscape accent in tropical and subtropical gardens. The leaves are enormous (up to 5–6 feet long, 18–24 inches wide), paddle-shaped, borne on tall, erect petioles, and characterized by a distinctive white, powdery, waxy bloom (pruinose coating) on the undersides that gives the leaf a two-tone appearance — bright green above, silvery-white below. The inflorescences that give the plant its common name 'Cigar Calathea' are compact, cylindrical, waxy yellow-green structures resembling a half-smoked cigar, emerging from near the base of the plant. The large leaves have been traditionally used throughout the Caribbean and Central America for wrapping food (particularly tamales), for thatching in Cuba ('pampano'), and as natural platters. In zone 9-11 gardens, Cigar Calathea creates an instant tropical landscape statement with its enormous leaves.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost, or propagate by stem cuttings; plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; cigar flower is an outstanding hummingbird plant for Gulf Coast gardens and produces non-stop blooms through the hot, humid summer.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; trim lightly after main bloom flushes to maintain compact habit. Cuphea ignea (cigar flower) is a Mexican native tender perennial grown as a warm-season annual in most climates, producing an endless succession of tubular, bright orange-red flowers 1 inch long with a distinctive black and white tip that gives each flower the appearance of a tiny lit cigar — the most descriptive common name in horticulture. The flowers bloom non-stop from late spring through frost on bushy, compact plants with dark-green, lance-shaped leaves; hummingbirds visit the tubular flowers avidly, making cigar plant one of the best hummingbird plants for hot-summer gardens. In zone 9–10, it frequently survives mild winters and grows as a perennial, becoming substantially larger and more prolific than annual specimens. The related Cuphea hyssopifolia (Mexican heather, dwarf cigar plant) has much smaller, lilac-purple flowers and more compact habit. Cigar plant's heat tolerance, disease resistance, and near-constant bloom make it outstanding for massed planting in zone 9 gardens.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost at 70–75°F or take stem cuttings from overwintered plants; transplant after all frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil. In zone 9–12 plant container specimens directly into the landscape.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost or root stem cuttings from overwintered plants, then transplant after all frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; cigar plant is a compact, free-flowering tropical with striking narrow tubular flowers in bright red tipped in dark purple and white — strongly resembling tiny lit cigars, complete with a 'ash' tip — that hummingbirds visit continuously from spring through frost. It blooms without pause throughout the summer heat, making it exceptional for containers, borders, and hanging baskets where continuous color is needed. In zone 9–12 it is a perennial sub-shrub; in other climates treat as a warm-season annual or overwinter cuttings indoors. The related Cuphea hyssopifolia (false heather) is smaller with tiny lavender flowers and equally heat-tolerant.

common_name: Cilician Cyclamen (Autumn-Winter-Flowering Pale Pink Hardy Cyclamen)
plant_note: Plant tubers in late summer to fall, shallowly, in gritty, well-drained soil in dry shade under trees; Cilician Cyclamen bears smaller, pale-pink flowers with a deeper-pink nose and neatly patterned leaves, blooming in autumn into winter, later than Cyclamen hederifolium.
directions: Plant tubers shallowly, just below the soil surface, in late summer to fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in dry shade beneath trees, where the summer dormancy period stays relatively dry. Cilician Cyclamen, native to mountainous woodland in southern Turkey, bears dainty, pale pink flowers with a deeper pink blotch at the nose in autumn into early winter, blooming somewhat later in the season than the more commonly grown Cyclamen hederifolium, above neat, attractively patterned silver-and-green leaves that persist through winter before going dormant in late spring. It thrives in the same dry shade under mature trees that defeats most other perennials, self-sows gently over time to form a colony, and needs no supplemental water once dormant for summer. Avoid overhead watering during dormancy, since the tubers are prone to rot in consistently wet soil.

common_name: Cinderella Swamp Milkweed (Deep Rose-Pink Native Milkweed Selection)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (seeds need 30-day cold stratification) or cold-stratify indoors and start in late winter; Cinderella is a selection of native swamp milkweed chosen for larger flower clusters in a deeper rose-pink than the wild species, tolerating wet soil where many milkweeds struggle.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Cinderella is a selection of native swamp milkweed bred for larger, showier clusters of deep rose-pink flowers than the wild species, while retaining swamp milkweed's essential value as a monarch butterfly host plant and its unusual tolerance of consistently wet soil, where common milkweed and butterfly weed both struggle. Flowers bloom over a long season from early to late summer and draw monarchs, swallowtails, and bumblebees in heavy numbers. Unlike some milkweed species, it does not spread aggressively by rhizome and stays in well-behaved clumps, making it one of the easiest milkweeds to place in a mixed border, rain garden, or pond margin without it taking over. Leave seedpods standing through fall and winter for wildlife interest and natural reseeding, or deadhead spent flowers to prevent excess self-sowing. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Divide established crowns in early spring or plant container-grown plants in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in shade to part shade; cinnamon fern is a wetland and streamside plant that tolerates standing water briefly but prefers reliably moist, never-dry conditions. It grows naturally in swamps, bogs, moist woods, and streambanks and is the most heat-tolerant of the osmunda ferns.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to part shade; cinnamon fern is one of the most beautiful and distinctive native ferns, providing a remarkable two-season display: in spring, the emerging croziers (fiddleheads) are densely covered with cinnamon-brown wooly hairs — giving the fern its name — and the separate, upright, cinnamon-colored fertile fronds that bear the spores arise from the center of the clump like brown candles, producing a distinctive spring silhouette. The fertile fronds are produced before the vegetative fronds and persist through the growing season, turning from green to rich, warm brown as the spores ripen. The vegetative fronds are large, arching, and medium-green, forming vase-shaped clumps of considerable scale and presence in the shade garden. Native throughout eastern North America from Canada to Florida, it is the most heat-tolerant of the large osmunda ferns and grows in zone 10 in Florida's swamps. The woolly fiddlehead hairs have historically been harvested as potting medium for orchids. Forms long-lived, increasingly large crowns that are landmarks in moist shaded gardens.

common_name: Cinnamon Girl Distylium (Bronze New-Growth Evergreen Shade Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to full shade; distylium is exceptionally adaptable to both light levels and soil moisture once established.
