directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to full shade — distylium is one of the most adaptable evergreen shrubs available, thriving in nearly any light level and tolerating both drought and occasional wet soil once established. Cinnamon Girl produces new growth flushed a warm coppery bronze-red before maturing to lustrous dark green, giving season-long color contrast on a dense, mounding, wider-than-tall shrub that functions as a low-maintenance, deer-resistant alternative to boxwood or Indian hawthorn. Small, inconspicuous red flowers appear in late winter but are not the plant's main ornamental feature. It requires little pruning to hold its naturally tidy, rounded form, and tolerates heat, humidity, and both sun and shade with equal ease, making it a versatile foundation or mass-planting shrub across a wide range of garden conditions.

plant_note: Set out nursery plants in spring; roses are grown from grafted or rooted stock, not seed.
directions: Plant this compact shrub rose in spring in a sunny, well-drained bed, spacing plants for good airflow. Cinnamon Hearts forms tidy mounds topped with clusters of fragrant cherry-red blooms from spring into fall. Water deeply and regularly during the first season to establish roots, then keep soil evenly moist. Prune lightly in late winter and remove spent blooms to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Cinnamon Orchid (Aromatic Lycaste, Yellow Lycaste, Spice Orchid)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in bark-based medium in a clay or wooden container; Lycaste aromatica is deciduous — it sheds its large leaves in winter after a dry rest period, and this dry period (reducing water in fall as growth slows) is essential for triggering the spring bloom. Flowers emerge on short stems directly from the leafless pseudobulbs in spring before new growth starts. The cinnamon-spice fragrance is powerful and carries. Tolerates temperatures to 45–50°F briefly — one of the more cold-tolerant Lycaste species. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in well-draining bark medium — Cinnamon Orchid needs good light for pseudobulb development and to fuel the next year's bloom, but should be protected from intense direct midday sun that scorches the large, broad leaves. Lycaste aromatica is a deciduous, sympodial epiphytic orchid native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador in the Orchidaceae family, grown for flowers with one of the most immediately recognizable and pleasant fragrances of any commonly cultivated orchid — a clean, warm, distinctly cinnamon-spice fragrance that smells precisely of ground cinnamon sticks with a hint of honey, and that carries powerfully several feet from the plant on warm days. The plant produces conical, angular pseudobulbs with 2–3 large, broad, pleated leaves (18–24 inches) that drop in fall. From the leafless pseudobulbs in spring, numerous short flower spikes emerge simultaneously — a well-established plant may produce 15–25 or more individual spikes at once, each carrying a single, 2-inch, upward-facing flower in clear, bright canary-yellow to golden-yellow with a small, darker orange lip. The display of dozens of fragrant yellow flowers simultaneously emerging from leafless pseudobulbs in a mass burst of spring bloom is one of the most memorable of any sympodial orchid. A forgiving and adaptable orchid that tolerates cooler temperatures than many tropical species. Non-toxic.

common_name: Cinnamon-Scented Hoya (Lacunosa Hoya, Porcelain Flower, Trough Wax Plant)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio hanging basket in zone 9; Hoya lacunosa cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It is one of the more prolific bloomers in the genus, producing its intensely cinnamon-scented flower clusters frequently throughout the warm months with minimal coaxing. Allow to become slightly pot-bound before repotting. Never remove old flower stalks (peduncles) — new clusters are produced from the same peduncle each season. Propagate from stem cuttings in moist potting mix or perlite. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Hoya lacunosa blooms most freely in bright indirect light and will produce few flowers in dim conditions, but it is one of the more adaptable Hoyas and can tolerate lower light without the decline that affects less robust species. Hoya lacunosa is a compact, trailing to twining epiphytic vine from South and Southeast Asia (India, Malaysia, Thailand, Java, Borneo, Sumatra) in the family Apocynaceae, producing smaller leaves than most Hoyas — elliptical, dark-green, waxy, with a distinctive pitted or trough-marked surface texture (the specific epithet 'lacunosa' means 'marked with pits or troughs'). The primary ornamental appeal is the flowers: small, waxy, white to cream, star-shaped flowers with a yellow or pale center, arranged in tight, globe-shaped umbels of 15–30 individual florets, produced at the tips of the characteristic persistent flower stalks (peduncles). The flowers produce an intense, sweet, spicy fragrance often described as pure cinnamon or warm vanilla-cinnamon — far more pronounced than the subtle fragrance of most other commonly grown Hoyas. The fragrance is most intense in the evening and on warm days, filling a room with a pleasant bakery-like scent whenever a cluster is in bloom. Hoya lacunosa is considered one of the easiest and most rewarding Hoyas for beginners, blooming freely with minimal care. Non-toxic to pets.

common_name: Cirrus Mealycup Sage (Silvery-White Foliage and Flower Spikes)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Cirrus bears silvery-white flower spikes and foliage, a striking counterpart to the more common blue and purple mealycup sage selections.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Cirrus bears luminous silvery-white flower spikes over soft, gray-green foliage, a bright, cool-toned counterpart to the more common blue and purple mealycup sage selections, useful for a moon garden or as a calming break between more vividly colored companion plants. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it flowers continuously from summer through fall with minimal deadheading, drawing bees and butterflies throughout its long bloom season. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage continued bloom, and treat as a perennial in zones 8-10 or a heat-loving annual further north.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or early fall by splitting the root mass with two forks back-to-back; citron daylily establishes quickly and multiplies steadily. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade. Being an evening-blooming species, site it where it can be enjoyed from patios or windows in the evening hours when the fragrance is most apparent.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; citron daylily is a Chinese species daylily that differs from the common hybrid daylilies in two remarkable ways — it blooms in the evening and at night (opening after 5 pm and lasting through the following morning before closing) and its flowers are strongly fragrant, with a sweet, lemony scent that carries through the garden on summer evenings. The flowers are pale, clear, lemon-yellow — more delicate and refined in color than most hybrid daylilies — and appear from July onward, later than most daylilies and filling the summer sequence. The plants form large, arching clumps of strap-like foliage reaching 3–4 feet, with the slender flower scapes rising well above the leaves and bearing multiple buds that open successively over an extended period. As a parent of many early daylily hybrids, it contributed both fragrance and late-season bloom genetics to the daylily breeding program. For evening garden use — gardens intended to be enjoyed after work hours — it is uniquely valuable for fragrance after sunset when hybrid daylilies have closed.

common_name: Citronella Crocosmia (Lemon-Yellow with Dark Eye Montbretia)
plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Citronella bears lemon-yellow flowers marked with a small dark central eye, a distinctive pattern within the genus.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Citronella bears arching, one-sided sprays of clear lemon-yellow, tubular flowers, each marked with a small contrasting dark eye at the throat, above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer, a subtly patterned twist on the classic yellow crocosmia color. Hummingbirds visit the flowers reliably, and cut stems hold up well in arrangements. Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection, and provide consistently moist, well-drained soil for the best display.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Citronelle's bright chartreuse-yellow color is most vivid in some morning sun with afternoon shade, since heavy shade dulls the color toward green.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade with some morning sun to bring out the brightest foliage color. Citronelle is one of the most vividly colored yellow-leaved heuchera cultivars, producing a dense mound of glowing chartreuse-yellow leaves that light up a shaded border and pair strikingly with dark-leaved companions like Caramel or Obsidian heuchera, purple-leaved heucherella, or blue hostas. Small, airy sprays of pale flowers rise on wiry stems above the foliage in early summer, though the plant is grown primarily for its foliage color rather than its blooms. Divide the clump every few years in spring as the center begins to heave or thin, replanting vigorous outer sections.

common_name: City of Haarlem Hyacinth (Soft Primrose-Yellow Hyacinth)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.
directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. City of Haarlem is one of the few widely available yellow hyacinths, its densely packed spike opening a soft, creamy primrose-yellow that is a genuinely unusual color in the hyacinth palette, carrying the same intense, sweet fragrance typical of the species. Its pale color pairs beautifully with blue or purple hyacinths and early daffodils in a mixed spring bulb display. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled hyacinth bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since the bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for good flowering in subsequent years without repeat chilling.

common_name: City of Portland Canna (Classic Salmon-Pink Heirloom Canna)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; divide every few years to prevent overcrowding.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun. A garden favorite for more than a century, this heirloom canna produces abundant upright panicles of rich salmon-pink flowers with a yellow throat and fine yellow petal edging, held well above lush mid-green paddle-shaped foliage. It is a reliable, vigorous bloomer from midsummer through fall and tolerates heat and humidity better than many newer hybrids, making it a dependable choice for large containers or tropical-style borders. Established clumps benefit from division every few years to prevent overcrowding and maintain strong flowering.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cityline is a compact bigleaf hydrangea series bred for a dense, tidy, rounded habit and strong stems that hold up large mophead blooms without flopping, well suited to smaller gardens and container culture.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Cityline is a series of compact bigleaf hydrangeas, named for individual cities, bred for a dense, rounded, well-proportioned habit that stays under 3 feet and holds its large mophead blooms upright on strong stems rather than flopping under the flower weight, a common problem with older, taller hydrangea cultivars. Its compact size makes it especially well suited to foundation plantings, small gardens, and large containers where a full-sized hydrangea would be too large. Individual cultivars within the series bloom in shades from blue and purple to pink and red depending on soil pH, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, adjustable with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune lightly if needed, since bloom occurs primarily on old wood formed the previous season and heavy pruning removes next year's flower buds.

common_name: Clair de Lune Dahlia (Classic Primrose-Yellow Collarette Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Clair de Lune is a classic collarette dahlia with pale primrose-yellow outer petals and a creamy-white inner collar.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. Clair de Lune, a classic and widely grown collarette dahlia, bears a single ring of soft primrose-yellow outer petals surrounding a ruffled, contrasting creamy-white inner collar, the layered two-tone structure distinctive to the collarette class and highly attractive to bees and other pollinators, unlike the fully double forms that hide their centers. Its open, airy form and gentle color have made it a longtime garden favorite. Deadhead spent blooms regularly, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Claire Austin Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since Claire Austin is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber or kept pruned as a large shrub.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing support if training the vigorous canes upright as a short climber. Introduced by David Austin in 2007 and named for his daughter-in-law, Claire Austin carries large, cupped, pale creamy-white to soft lemon blooms that fade toward pure white as they open, with a strong myrrh fragrance that intensifies on warm days. Its vigorous, somewhat lax growth habit allows it to be trained against a fence or pillar for extra height, or kept as a large freestanding shrub with regular pruning, and it repeat-blooms well from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Claire Grace Beebalm (Mildew-Resistant Wild Bergamot Selection)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Claire Grace is a Mt. Cuba Center-recommended selection of native wild bergamot chosen for superior powdery mildew resistance and strong pollinator appeal compared to the straight species.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing good air circulation between plants. Claire Grace is a selection of native wild bergamot (Monarda fistulosa) chosen for improved resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures most bee balm cultivars by midsummer in humid climates, while retaining the lavender-pink flowers and strong, sweet-mint fragrance that make wild bergamot such a magnet for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. It tends to be more heat- and drought-tolerant than the red-flowered Monarda didyma cultivars, reflecting its origin from a species native to drier prairie and meadow habitat across much of North America. Established clumps bloom over a long season from early to midsummer and spread gradually by rhizome to form an expanding colony, so give it room or plan to divide every few years to keep it in bounds. Cut plants back by half in late spring if a more compact, later-blooming plant is desired, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and airflow, which further reduces mildew pressure.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; clammy locust grows naturally on rocky slopes, forest edges, and disturbed areas in the southern Appalachians and Piedmont. Like other locust species, it fixes nitrogen and improves lean soils.
directions: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; clammy locust is the ornamentally superior native locust of the southern Appalachians, producing large, elegant clusters of rose-pink (not white like black locust) flowers that are among the most beautiful of any native North American tree in spring. The species name 'viscosa' and common name 'clammy locust' refer to the distinctive sticky, clammy glands on the leaf stalks, branchlets, and seed pods that make the plant sticky to the touch. More compact than black locust and less aggressive in spreading — a significant advantage in the garden. Nitrogen-fixing, drought-tolerant once established, and tolerant of lean, poor soils where other trees struggle. The pink flowers make it a far better ornamental specimen than black locust for garden use. Spreads by root suckers like other locusts but less aggressively. An underused native ornamental small tree.

common_name: Clamshell Orchid (Cockleshell Orchid, Black Orchid, Florida Native Clamshell)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark or in a slatted basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun; Prosthechea cochleata is a Florida native orchid that grows naturally on mangroves, buttonwood, and live oak trees in coastal hammocks. Water regularly in active growth; reduce in winter. This species blooms almost continuously in warm conditions — individual flower spikes open a succession of flowers over many months. Wild Florida plants are protected — purchase only nursery-propagated stock. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light mounted on bark or in a slatted basket — Clamshell Orchid grows most vigorously with good air circulation and bright, filtered light similar to the dappled canopy light in its native Florida coastal hammock habitat. Prosthechea cochleata (formerly Epidendrum cochleatum) is an epiphytic orchid native to Florida (from Hillsborough and Volusia counties southward to the Keys), the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, and northern South America in the Orchidaceae family, holding the distinction of being the national flower of Belize. The flower is immediately and unmistakably distinctive: unlike almost any other orchid, the flower is oriented upside down — the broadly shell-shaped (cochleate), dark purple to nearly black, deeply ribbed lip is at the TOP of the flower (not at the bottom as in most orchids), with the narrow, greenish-cream, twisted petals and sepals hanging downward below it like tentacles or a fringe. The visual impression is of a dark-purple clamshell or scallop shell with wispy tentacles — completely unlike any other common orchid flower. A further remarkable quality is that in warm conditions, Prosthechea cochleata blooms almost continuously — each spike continues opening new flowers over many months, making it one of the most persistent-blooming of any orchid species. A Florida native of distinctive character. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–March or September–November. Clara Curtis is among the most vigorous and spreading of the Chrysanthemum x rubellum species — divide clumps every 2–3 years to prevent crowding and maintain vigor. Pinch stem tips in spring and early summer to promote bushy, compact growth and abundant flowering; unpinched plants tend toward tall, floppy stems. In zone 9 it blooms September–November, providing fall color when most summer perennials are exhausted. The light fragrance of the daisy-like flowers is more pleasant than the sharp, camphor scent of many chrysanthemums.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Clara Curtis blooms equally well in partial shade, where the flower colors tend to be slightly richer and more saturated than in full sun conditions; Clara Curtis is a Chrysanthemum x rubellum species hybrid producing large (2–3 inch), single, daisy-form flowers in a warm soft pink to rose-pink color — distinctly different in both growth habit and flower form from the tight, pompom-flowered, potted mums of the florist trade. While florist mums are typically short-lived perennials requiring frequent replacement in Southern gardens, Clara Curtis is a genuinely robust, long-lived, spreading perennial that increases steadily in size over years, producing freely spreading clumps covered in the clear pink single daisy flowers from September through November. The single-flower form is more graceful and more naturalistically attractive than double mums, and the clear warm pink color works beautifully with the yellows, oranges, and burgundies of the fall palette. As a source of fall color in the perennial garden at a season when most summer plants are past peak, Clara Curtis is an irreplaceable addition to zone 9 gardens — blooming into November when frosts have begun and most summer color has ended.

common_name: Clara Indian Hawthorn (Compact White-Flowered Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Clara produces pure white flowers and a naturally compact, tidy habit that needs little pruning to stay in bounds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates partial shade with somewhat reduced flowering. Clara is a compact Indian hawthorn selection valued for its clean white flower clusters in spring, a crisper look than the pink tones of most other cultivars, held against the same leathery, dark green, disease-resistant foliage typical of the species. Its naturally tidy, rounded size fits foundation plantings and low borders without the size Majestic Beauty or other larger selections eventually reach. Like other Indian hawthorns it is outstanding for coastal Gulf gardens, tolerating salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil, and needs only a light shaping prune right after spring bloom.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets (pups) in spring in gritty, mineral, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; claret cup is among the most cold-hardy of all North American cacti, tolerating winter lows well below 0°F where soil stays dry.
directions: Plant rooted offsets in a raised bed, berm, or crevice garden of coarse gravel, decomposed granite, or mineral scree in full sun, keeping soil dry through winter to prevent rot; unlike most cacti, claret cup survives severe cold as long as its roots stay dry and unfrozen-wet. Clumps of cylindrical, spine-covered stems slowly multiply into mounds of 20 or more heads, topped in mid- to late spring by brilliant scarlet-red, cup-shaped flowers that are among the showiest of any hardy cactus and are a favored early-season hummingbird nectar source. Water sparingly only during active spring and summer growth and withhold water entirely from late fall through winter. Established clumps are essentially indestructible in the right drainage and are outstanding for rock gardens, dry berms, and desert-style xeriscape plantings from the high plains through the Southwest.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost while soil is still cool; succession sow every 3 weeks for extended bloom.
directions: Direct sow on the soil surface or barely cover; seeds germinate best at cool soil temperatures and seedlings dislike transplanting. Thin ruthlessly to 9–12 in because overcrowded plants bloom poorly and are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Clarkia thrives on neglect in poor, well-drained soil — fertilizing too heavily causes lush foliage at the expense of flowers. Plants naturally set seed and die when summer heat arrives; in mild-winter climates, sow in fall for late-winter to spring bloom.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring on moist to wet sandy or loamy soil; clasping coneflower is a prolific self-seeder and will return annually once established in the garden — scatter seed in moist areas after last frost for summer bloom.
directions: Clasping coneflower is a native annual of moist prairies, roadsides, and disturbed fields across the south-central United States, named for its distinctive stem-clasping leaves that wrap around the stalk — it stands apart from other coneflowers by producing a single, upright, daisy-like yellow flower with a long, domed, dark brown cone on each branching stem, giving it a resemblance to a miniature black-eyed Susan on a taller, more upright plant. It is one of the most reliable warm-season annuals for the Gulf Coast and lower South, germinating quickly in warm weather and blooming in as little as 8–10 weeks from seed — its tolerance for summer heat and humidity makes it far more dependable than many other coneflowers in zone 8–9 gardens. In meadow plantings and naturalized areas, it self-seeds prolifically and gradually forms dense colonies that provide continuous summer-to-fall bloom with zero maintenance. Excellent companion for Gulf Coast natives like prairie verbena, standing cypress, and annual gaillardia in dry, sunny native meadow designs.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; clasping milkweed grows in dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, open habitats — prairies, savannas, and open pine woodlands. It is named for its broad leaves that clasp the stem at the base.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun in prairie, savanna, or open woodland garden settings; clasping milkweed is a striking native with unusually large, broad, blue-green leaves that wrap around the stem — the 'clasping' or 'amplexicaul' leaf base is the most distinctive feature. The rounded, rosy-pink to purple-pink flower heads in late spring to early summer are produced at the stem tips and have a subtle, sweet fragrance. The species is common in dry, sandy grasslands and open pine woodlands across the eastern US and is an important monarch caterpillar host plant. Clasping milkweed develops a deep taproot that makes it difficult to transplant — direct sow or plant very young plants without disturbing the root. An outstanding native for dry, open prairie gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky or loamy soil in partial to full shade; clasping twisted-stalk is a plant of cool, moist, boreal and mountain forests from Alaska and Canada south through the Rocky Mountains and northern Appalachians, requiring consistently cool, moist, shaded conditions.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky or loamy soil in partial to full shade; clasping twisted-stalk is the larger and more widespread of the two North American twisted-stalk species, growing from Alaska and Canada through mountain forests south to California, Arizona, New Mexico, and the Appalachians. The leaves are heart-shaped, with the base clasping the stem (hence 'clasping' and the species name 'amplexifolius'), creating an attractive, layered, overlapping arrangement along the arching, multiple-branched stems. The small, cream-white to greenish-white flowers hang from twisted pedicels in the leaf axils in early summer, followed by oval red berries that smell and taste mildly of cucumber (earning the common name 'cucumber root'). The berries were eaten raw and cooked by Indigenous peoples across the range. Young shoots can be eaten like asparagus. A larger and more imposing woodland plant than rosy twisted-stalk, more tolerant of a wider elevation range and making a bold statement in woodland garden settings.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, replanting immediately in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade. Handle rhizomes gently as they are slow to re-establish after disturbance.
directions: Clasping Twistedstalk is a graceful native woodland perennial notable for its distinctively zigzagging stems and oval clasping leaves that create an architectural layered effect in the shade garden. Small white to pale pink bell-shaped flowers hang beneath the leaves on twisted pedicels in late spring, giving way to showy red berries in late summer and fall that are relished by thrushes and other forest birds. It thrives in cool, moist, humus-rich soil under a canopy of deciduous trees and performs best where summers are cool. Amend planting areas generously with leaf mold or composted bark and maintain even moisture throughout the growing season.

common_name: Class Act Hosta (Corrugated Creamy-White Center with Dark Green Margin)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil. Class Act bears dark green margins framing heavily corrugated, creamy-white leaf centers.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partly to fully shaded site, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Class Act bears heavily corrugated, deeply textured leaves with creamy-white centers bordered by dark green margins, the pronounced puckering giving the foliage a bold, three-dimensional quality distinct from smoother-leaved hosta cultivars. It produces lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer. Mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system from summer heat, and divide congested clumps every several years in spring.

common_name: Claudia Wannamaker Southern Magnolia (Fast-Growing Pyramidal Southern Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Claudia Wannamaker is a fast-growing, densely pyramidal southern magnolia selected in South Carolina, widely planted across the Deep South.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Claudia Wannamaker, selected in South Carolina, bears the classic large, creamy-white, lemon-scented southern magnolia blooms on a notably fast-growing, densely pyramidal tree with glossy, deep green leaves and attractive rusty-brown leaf undersides, making it one of the most widely planted southern magnolia cultivars across the Deep South for its reliable, uniform growth habit. Water deeply during establishment, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune only to remove dead or damaged wood, since magnolias need little routine pruning.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Clementine bears vivid apricot-orange flowers, a warmer tone than most garden mullein hybrids.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than fertility, since rich, wet soil leads to rot and weak growth. Clementine bears dense spikes of vivid apricot-orange flowers, each centered with contrasting purple-mauve stamens, over gray-green, felted foliage that adds textural interest even before bloom. Its warm color makes a striking companion to blue-flowered perennials like salvia or catmint in a sunny border. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage continued bloom over a long summer season, and expect this hybrid mullein to be relatively short-lived, often performing best as a biennial or short-lived perennial that benefits from occasional replacement or self-sown replacements.

plant_note: Direct sow at or 2 weeks before last frost; cold stratification of seed for 7 days in the refrigerator improves germination.
directions: Press seed lightly onto the soil surface with barely 1/8 in of cover — light aids germination. Cleome self-sows prolifically and can become weedy; deadhead to limit reseeding if preferred. The tall, airy flower heads open from the base upward over several weeks, providing an extended season of bloom. Handle plants with care as stems bear small spines and the foliage has a musky scent.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Cleopatra is a vigorous, upright grower that can be maintained as a formal hedge or clipped into a topiary form — prune immediately after the bloom season ends to avoid removing next season's flower buds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Cleopatra is a vigorous, upright Camellia sasanqua cultivar producing single to semi-double, rose-pink to deep-pink flowers with prominent golden-yellow stamens from October through December in zone 9. The medium-pink flower color is clear and saturated — a classic, feminine camellia pink that combines well with white-flowering companions, silver-foliage plants, and the dark evergreen foliage of camellias and hollies in the fall garden. Cleopatra is one of the more sun-tolerant sasanqua camellias, performing well in 4–6 hours of direct sun that would stress most japonica camellias, and it is more vigorous and faster-growing than many sasanqua selections. The upright, dense, somewhat narrow-columnar habit (6–12 feet tall, somewhat narrower than its height) makes it useful for screening and hedge applications where height is needed in a limited horizontal space. As with all sasanqua camellias, the fall flowers are mildly fragrant — pleasant but not overwhelming. Cleopatra was one of the foundational sasanqua cultivars widely planted across the Gulf South in the mid-twentieth century and remains a reliable, proven performer for zone 9 camellia gardens. Fertilize with azalea-camellia acidic fertilizer in spring and early fall.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in warm, fertile, moist soil in full sun; Cleopatra is a genetically unstable novelty canna that produces an unpredictable mix of solid green and maroon leaves, and yellow, red, and mixed-color flowers, sometimes all on the same plant.
directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in warm, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun. Cleopatra is a genuinely unusual novelty canna known for genetic instability that causes individual leaves to emerge solid green or solid maroon in unpredictable patches on the same plant, paired with flowers that can be solid yellow, solid red, or streaked and spotted with both colors, sometimes even on the same flower stalk, making every plant a bit of a surprise from season to season. This chimeric, ever-changing display has made it a favorite conversation piece among collectors and canna enthusiasts despite, or because of, its unpredictability. Like other cannas it thrives with generous water and rich soil, tolerating boggy conditions at a pond edge. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter; in zone 8-10 gardens it can typically be left in the ground with heavy winter mulch.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in spring in very well-drained, sunny conditions; Cleveland sage requires excellent drainage and dislikes summer irrigation — it is truly a dry-climate plant that thrives on neglect.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Cleveland sage is a California native aromatic shrub with one of the strongest and most complex sage fragrances in the genus — deeply resinous, herbaceous, and intensely medicinal. The gray-green, deeply textured leaves are used as a culinary sage substitute (particularly appropriate with poultry and game) and were traditionally used by Kumeyaay and other indigenous peoples for ceremonial smudging. It blooms profusely in spring with whorls of lavender-blue flowers on tall spikes that are outstanding for hummingbirds and native bees. In summer-dry Mediterranean climates and warm dry gardens, it is one of the best ornamental shrubs available — extremely drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and low-maintenance once established.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to moderately acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; cleyera is very cold hardy once established but prefers protection from harsh winter winds and reflected heat from walls. It is a slow-growing, long-lived shrub that rarely needs pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly to moderately acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — cleyera is one of the most refined and underused evergreen shrubs for southern shade gardens, producing elegant, glossy, dark green leaves with reddish new growth on a naturally pyramidal to oval form. The small, creamy-white, fragrant flowers in spring are followed by dark red to black berries that attract birds; the plant is sacred in Shinto tradition in Japan, where it is planted at shrines. Cleyera is an outstanding foundation plant, informal hedge, or large specimen for the shaded, acidic, humus-rich conditions under tall pines and oaks throughout zone 7–9. It grows more slowly than many companion plants (camellias, gardenias) but eventually becomes a large, refined, long-lived shrub requiring almost no maintenance beyond an occasional light shaping. Excellent companion plant for camellias and azaleas in woodland garden compositions.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall into rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, matching the limestone canyons and rocky slopes of the Southwest and southern Rockies where cliff fendlerbush grows wild.
directions: Plant container stock in fall into rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, matching the limestone canyons and rocky slopes of the Southwest and southern Rockies where cliff fendlerbush grows wild. In late spring it produces an abundant flush of four-petaled, white to pale-pink, sweetly fragrant flowers resembling mock orange blossoms, drawing native bees, hawk moths, and hummingbirds to an otherwise sparse rocky landscape. It is highly drought- and cold-tolerant once established and needs no supplemental irrigation, making it well suited to xeriscape and native rock-garden plantings. Deer tend to browse it lightly, and its dense, twiggy branching provides good cover for small birds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; cliff penstemon is adapted to rocky cliff faces and needs sharp drainage, ideally planted at an angle or in a rock wall crevice.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; cliff penstemon is adapted to rocky cliff faces and needs sharp drainage, ideally planted at an angle or in a rock wall crevice. Small, rounded, blue-gray leaves form a dense, trailing mat that cascades over rock, studded in late spring and early summer with large, vivid magenta-pink flowers disproportionately showy for its low, ground-hugging scale, native to rocky cliffs and outcrops in the Cascade and Siskiyou mountain ranges. Its naturally cliff-dwelling habit makes it an outstanding choice for a rock wall, crevice garden, or steeply sloped scree bed where its trailing stems can drape over an edge, tolerating thin, rocky, nutrient-poor soil that would stress richer garden plants. Water sparingly once established, plant at an angle or on a slope to shed excess moisture from the crown, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil.

plant_note: Divide and plant rosettes in spring into thin, sharply drained soil over rock or a crevice garden gap.
directions: Cliff stonecrop is a rock-outcrop specialist native to the central Appalachians of West Virginia, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina, where it clings to shaded sandstone, shale, and limestone ledges with a southern exposure. Rosettes of waxy, glaucous blue-gray leaves form low, spreading colonies that remain evergreen through winter, tinting purplish in cold weather. Clusters of small white flowers open on short stems in late spring, providing nectar for small bees and other pollinating insects before most summer perennials have started blooming. Site plants in a crevice garden, dry stone wall, or thin gravelly soil over rock with light to partial shade, avoiding rich or waterlogged sites where the shallow roots quickly rot.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring 3–4 inches deep in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in zone 8–10; Climbing Alstroemeria is a vigorous tuberous climbing vine from the misty Andean cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador — related to Alstroemeria but distinctly different in its twining, climbing habit — producing large, pendant, trumpet-shaped flowers in brilliant orange to red-orange with yellow interiors spotted with brown-purple, held in generous clusters at the ends of long, scrambling stems.
directions: Plant Bomarea multiflora tubers in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; provide support for the twining stems to climb; keep consistently moist through the growing season; in zone 8–9, mulch heavily in winter to protect the tubers from frost. Climbing Alstroemeria is a genus of tuberous, climbing vines closely related to the familiar Alstroemeria (Peruvian Lily) of florists, but with a distinctly different growth habit — the stems twine and scramble through surrounding vegetation to heights of 3–6 feet, decorated with alternate, bright-green, resupinate (twisted) leaves. The large flower clusters at the stem tips bear 10–30 individual pendant, tubular flowers in brilliant orange to deep red-orange (B. multiflora is one of the most vivid-colored species) with a contrasting yellow interior and brown-purple speckling. The genus Bomarea comprises some 120 species throughout the Andes and tropical Americas — an undeservedly neglected group that most temperate gardeners have never encountered despite the extraordinary floral display. Native to the cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador at elevations of 6,000–10,000 feet, B. multiflora prefers cool to mild temperatures — making it better suited to the mild climates of the Pacific Coast and zone 8–9 Southeast than strictly tropical conditions. Hummingbirds are the primary pollinators in its native range.

plant_note: Set out grafted or own-root plants in spring or fall against a trellis, arbor, or pillar in full sun with good air circulation; Climbing America repeats reliably through the Gulf South growing season but benefits from a preventive disease program or an airy site in humid summers.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil against a sturdy support, training canes as horizontally as possible along the structure to promote flowering side shoots along the entire length of the plant. Discovered as a climbing sport of the 1976 All-America Rose Selections winner 'America', Climbing America carries the same warm coral-orange to salmon-pink, high-centered hybrid-tea-shaped blooms and rich spicy fragrance as its parent but on long, vigorous climbing canes that reach well up a trellis or arbor. It flowers in a strong spring flush with continued repeat bloom through summer and fall, making it a long-season source of color and cut flowers for a sunny fence line or entry arbor. Remove old, unproductive wood each winter to keep new flowering canes coming.

plant_note: Plant near a fence, shrub, or trellis in moist to wet, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; stems scramble and sprawl through surrounding vegetation rather than twining — provide sturdy support or allow it to clamber through a native shrub border.
directions: Climbing aster is the only vining aster native to North America, an extraordinary scrambling perennial from the Gulf Coastal Plain and Florida that clambers 6–15 feet through shrubs and fences to display enormous masses of small, lavender-to-pink flowers with yellow centers in late fall, often blooming well into December in zone 8 and 9 gardens. Because it flowers so late in the season — October through December in the Deep South — climbing aster serves as a critical last nectar source for late-migrating monarchs and queens, sulphur butterflies, and overwintering native bees that remain active through early winter in the Gulf Coast region. Plant it where it can scramble through a wax myrtle, yaupon holly, or native shrub border; its somewhat weedy scrambling stems are hidden by surrounding plants while the spectacular late-autumn bloom is the garden's last big show before frost. Cut back hard in late winter to control spread and encourage vigorous new stems for next season's bloom.

common_name: Climbing Bird's Nest Fern (Common Microsorum, Crocodile Fern, Wart Fern)
plant_note: Grow in shade as a houseplant, on a bark mount, or in zone 9b-11 outdoor shade gardens; Microsorum punctatum is more cold-tolerant than Asplenium nidus and can survive brief temperatures to 32°F if the rhizome is protected with mulch. In zone 9-10, plant outdoors in deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil under trees. The plant naturally creeps and climbs surfaces with its surface-creeping rhizomes — allow it to grow up mossy tree trunks or walls for the most natural appearance. Propagate by dividing rhizome sections with attached fronds.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or potting medium; Climbing Bird's Nest Fern is highly adaptable and among the most shade-tolerant of the large structural ferns for zone 9 Gulf Coast outdoor shade gardens and indoor use. Microsorum punctatum (also known as Phymatosorus punctatus) is a widespread, variable epiphytic to terrestrial fern distributed across tropical Africa, Asia, the Pacific Islands, and Australia, growing naturally in forest understories, on mossy tree trunks, and on rock faces. The plant produces long, strap-like, undivided fronds of various sizes (depending on cultivar and conditions) — from 12 to 36 inches — in bright to medium green, with the characteristic small, round, orange-brown sori (spore clusters) scattered across the frond undersurface in a dotted pattern that can be visible from above in strong light. Some forms have attractively crested or wavy frond margins. A popular cultivar, 'Grandiceps,' has strongly crested frond tips. The rhizome creeps across surfaces, attaching and climbing — in zone 9-10 outdoor shade gardens it naturally climbs the trunks of large oaks and palms, eventually producing an impressive colony of ferns ascending tree trunks. More cold-tolerant than Bird's Nest Fern (Asplenium nidus), making it preferable for zone 9 outdoor planting. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; climbing bleeding heart is a biennial that germinates in late spring, forms a basal rosette in its first year, then climbs and blooms in its second year. It self-sows freely in moist, shaded conditions and can be treated as a self-perpetuating annual colony once established.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade at the base of a trellis, fence, or scrambling support; climbing bleeding heart is a unique native biennial vine of moist, rocky, shaded slopes and forest margins in the Appalachians and northeastern North America. The lacy, glaucous blue-green foliage is extremely finely divided and feathery, resembling the leaves of bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos/Dicentra) or corydalis, and the plant climbs by means of clinging petioles to reach 6–10 feet. The small, nodding, tubular flowers — white to pale pink — are produced in summer of the second year in clusters from the leaf axils, resembling tiny bleeding hearts. Self-sows freely in appropriate conditions to form a naturalized colony. An unusual and beautiful native vine for shaded woodland trellises and shrub edges, little known in cultivation.

plant_note: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, organically rich soil in partial to full shade near a trellis, fence, or tree; climbing dogbane is a bottomland native that tolerates brief flooding and performs best in the shade of bottomland hardwood forests along Gulf Coast waterways.
directions: Climbing dogbane is a rare native alternative to the widely planted Confederate jasmine (Trachelospermum jasminoides), naturally found in the moist bottomland forests, swamp margins, and stream banks of the Gulf Coast from Virginia to Texas — it is the only species in its genus native to North America. Unlike its Asian relative, climbing dogbane adapts to shaded conditions under bottomland oaks and cypress, making it one of the few woody ornamental vines that will thrive in genuine shade; it produces clusters of small, fragrant, yellowish-white five-petaled flowers in early summer that are visited by native bees and butterflies. The milky latex sap makes it unpalatable to deer, and the plant is host to several specialist milkweed butterflies and moths in the family Apocynaceae. While less commonly available commercially than Confederate jasmine, climbing dogbane is worth seeking out from native plant nurseries for shaded trellises, arbors, and woodland garden structures where a fragrant, native evergreen vine is needed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; climbing fetterbush grows naturally in Gulf South cypress and blackgum swamps and needs the same acidic, wet conditions in cultivation.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; climbing fetterbush is an unusual native Gulf South evergreen shrub with small, glossy, dark-green leaves and clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers similar to its relative Pieris japonica, but famous for a remarkable habit in the wild — in its native cypress and blackgum swamps, it grows as a true climber, sending stems up underneath the loose, fibrous bark of the host tree, invisible except where leafy branchlets emerge through cracks in the bark many feet up the trunk. In ordinary garden cultivation without a suitable host tree, it instead grows as a low, sprawling, spreading shrub, still worthwhile for its evergreen foliage and flowers in a wet, shaded native plant garden. It needs the same reliably moist, acidic soil as its swampy origin and struggles if allowed to dry out. A conversation-piece native shrub for a bog garden or swamp-margin planting within its narrow Gulf South range.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, moist to moderately dry soil with support for the tendrils in zone 8–10; Climbing Gazania is a scandent shrub or climbing perennial from the high-altitude shrub zones and forest edges of the Andes in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru — bearing large (3–4 inch), brilliant orange-red, daisy-like flowers with gold-yellow centers at the stem tips on plants that climb by modified leaf tendrils through surrounding shrubs — a uniquely beautiful, little-known Andean ornamental.
directions: Plant Mutisia clematis in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide shrubs, netting, or a trellis for the modified leaf tendrils to grip; keep evenly moist in the growing season; protect from hard frost below 25°F; propagate from stem cuttings in late spring. Climbing Gazania (Mutisia) is one of the most remarkable genera in the Asteraceae (daisy) family — unlike virtually all other members of the daisy family which are herbaceous or non-climbing, Mutisia species are climbing, tendril-bearing, woody-stemmed scandent shrubs that scramble through Andean cloud forest and shrub margins by means of modified leaf extensions acting as tendrils. The large, solitary daisy-like flowers — brilliant orange-red in M. clematis with a golden-yellow center disc — are produced repeatedly at the stem tips and are genuinely spectacular on close inspection, resembling a large, elegant gerbera daisy held by a climbing vine. The approximately 60 Mutisia species are distributed along the length of the Andes from Venezuela to Patagonia; most are challenging to cultivate but M. clematis is considered one of the more tractable in mild climates. A genuinely unusual and conversation-worthy plant for mild, coastal garden climates in zone 8–10 where cool temperatures, consistent moisture, and good drainage can be provided.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; climbing gloxinia grows rapidly and begins blooming in summer. It climbs by twining leaf petioles and needs a trellis, mesh, or shrub for support. In zones 9–10 it may overwinter as a perennial; in colder climates grow as an annual from seed or overwinter cutting-rooted plants indoors.
directions: Start seeds early indoors and train on a trellis or other support in full sun to part shade; climbing gloxinia is a Mexican native vine producing large (2–3 inch), softly tubular, trumpet-shaped flowers in clear, warm rose-pink to soft magenta — a flower form and color closely resembling gloxinia (Sinningia), hence the common name, on a freely climbing vine 6–10 feet long. The hairy, somewhat gloxinia-like leaves contribute to the resemblance. The flowers are abundant from summer through fall and the whole plant has a pleasant, cottage-garden quality — softly colored, generous with bloom, and adaptable to growing up fences, trellises, tripods, and into shrubs. Previously classified as Asarina erubescens, it belongs to the snapdragon family and shares some visual qualities with that family. 'Magic Dragon' is a widely available seed strain in the nursery trade. An excellent companion to softer-colored annual and tender perennial vines on a mixed-planting trellis or fence.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist, rich soil near a trellis or at the margin of a pond, stream, or rain garden; climbing hemp weed is a fast-growing perennial vine in zones 8 and warmer, dies back after hard frost but returns reliably from the roots in Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Climbing hemp weed is a vigorous native twining vine of the aster family (Asteraceae), native to wetland margins, pond edges, freshwater tidal marshes, and moist thickets across the Gulf Coastal Plain and eastern United States — despite being little-known in cultivation, it is one of the highest-value native vines for late-season pollinators. Dense clusters of small, fluffy white to pinkish flowers cover the vine from late summer through fall and are magnets for migrating monarchs and a remarkable diversity of native specialist bees; it is among the most important native late-season nectar sources in Gulf Coast wetland habitats. The vine climbs and twines quickly in warm seasons, making it useful for rapidly covering trellises, fences, and chain-link at the edges of rain gardens, constructed wetlands, and moist riparian restoration plantings. In zone 9 and south it remains semi-evergreen; in zone 8 it freezes to the ground but returns vigorously from the roots each spring.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; climbing hydrangea is very slow to establish — it may appear not to grow for the first 2–3 years while developing its root system. After establishment it grows steadily and becomes long-lived and self-sustaining. It climbs by aerial rootlets and requires no additional support on rough surfaces like brick, stone, or wood.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade to part shade; climbing hydrangea is among the most valuable vines for shaded positions — one of the few vigorous, ornamental climbers that succeeds and blooms in substantial shade. It clings to walls, tree trunks, and structures by tiny adhesive aerial rootlets without damaging sound mortar and masonry. In June and July, established plants produce large, flat-topped flower heads (lace-caps) up to 10 inches across — creamy white with ornamental sterile flowers surrounding a center of tiny, fertile flowers — in breathtaking abundance that is one of the showiest June spectacles possible on a shaded wall. The bark on mature stems exfoliates in thin, cinnamon-red sheets, creating beautiful winter interest. The broadly oval, glossy leaves turn bright yellow in fall. Native to Japan and Korea, it is slow to begin growing after planting (famously described as 'the first year it sleeps, the second year it creeps, the third year it leaps') but is exceptionally long-lived and essentially maintenance-free once established on a suitable structure.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall against a sturdy wall, fence, or large tree it can cling to.
directions: This vigorous woody vine climbs walls and trees by aerial rootlets, covering surfaces with heart-shaped leaves and fragrant, lacy white blooms in late spring. Plant in part shade to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; it also tolerates morning sun with steady moisture. Be patient, as it is slow to establish but grows rapidly once settled, eventually reaching great heights. Provide strong support and prune after flowering only to control size.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; climbing hydrangea vine is a streamside and swamp-forest plant in nature and requires consistent soil moisture. It climbs by aerial rootlets and establishes well on tree trunks, rough stone, and brick without additional support.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in part to full shade; climbing hydrangea vine is a native eastern North American alternative to the Asian climbing hydrangea (H. anomala subsp. petiolaris), found naturally in moist forests and swamp edges from Virginia to Florida and Louisiana. It climbs trees, walls, and structures by clinging aerial rootlets, and in late spring produces clusters of small, sweet-fragrant, white flowers without the large sterile bracts of the Asian species — more modest but very sweetly scented and genuinely attractive to pollinators. The leaves are glossy, dark-green, and semi-evergreen to evergreen in zones 7–9, making it useful for year-round coverage of shaded surfaces. It tolerates deeper shade than most vines and is one of the few self-clinging climbers native to the southeastern US. Outstanding for climbing shaded tree trunks, stone walls, and other structures in moist, shaded southern gardens where Asian vines perform poorly. Supports the ecology of the forest system it comes from — its berries are eaten by several bird species.

plant_note: Direct sow at last frost in moist, open, well-drained soil in full sun; seeds can also be fall-sown to overwinter in the ground for natural cold stratification and earlier spring germination. Give plants a sturdy fence or trellis to climb — this is a vigorous grower and will quickly cover available support. Best suited to wildlife garden settings where free spreading is acceptable.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun along a fence, trellis, or through a sturdy shrub; Climbing Milkweed (also called Honeyvine) is a vigorous twining native perennial in the milkweed subfamily, producing smooth, heart-shaped leaves and dense clusters of small, sweetly honey-fragrant white flowers from July through September that are outstanding nectar sources for monarch butterflies and many native bees. It is native to moist, open, disturbed ground, fencerows, and thicket edges throughout the eastern and central US, and produces classic milkweed seed pods that split to release plume-tailed seeds. Climbing Milkweed can spread aggressively from both seed and rhizomes in favorable conditions and is best suited to naturalistic or wildlife garden settings where its habit of covering fences and scrambling through shrubs is welcome rather than a problem.

common_name: Climbing Pinkie Rose (Thornless Southern Heirloom Climber)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall against a fence, arbor, or mailbox post in full sun to partial shade; Climbing Pinkie is one of the most shade-tolerant and disease-resistant climbers available, tolerating a few hours less sun than most roses while still flowering well.
directions: Plant against a fence, arbor, or trellis in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained soil, and tie the long, nearly thornless, arching canes to their support as they grow. Discovered in 1952 as a climbing sport of the 1928 polyantha rose 'Pinkie', this heirloom produces large clusters of small, semi-double, clear rose-pink blooms in an overwhelming flush each spring with lighter sporadic rebloom through summer and fall. Its near-total lack of thorns, outstanding resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, and tolerance of poor soil and partial shade have made it a beloved pass-along rose throughout the Deep South for generations, often found scrambling over old fences and porches with no spray program at all. Prune immediately after the main spring bloom to shape and remove old wood, since next year's flowers form on canes grown this season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and set out on a trellis, fence, or lattice in partial shade to full sun after frost; climbing snapdragon climbs by twisting its leaf stalks (petioles) around thin supports and is one of the few climbing annuals that flowers well in partial shade.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and set out on a trellis, lattice, or fence in partial shade after frost; climbing snapdragon is a Mexican native annual vine that climbs by twisting its leaf stalks around thin supports, covering itself with snapdragon-like, tubular, two-lipped flowers of rosy purple, lavender, pink, or white from summer until frost. The triangular, softly hairy, ivy-shaped leaves and twining, scandent growth create a soft, romantic effect on trellises, fences, and mailbox posts. It is notably more shade-tolerant than most annual vines and is one of the few that blooms freely in filtered shade — valuable for shaded pergolas, north-facing fences, and areas receiving only 4–5 hours of direct sun. Hummingbirds are attracted to the tubular flowers. 'Bride's White', 'Mystic Pink', and 'Violet Purple' are the most widely available color selections. In zones 9–11, the plant may overwinter as a short-lived perennial.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; climbing snapdragon is a tender perennial from Spain and southwestern Europe typically grown as an annual in North America; it climbs by its petioles and drapes beautifully over walls, containers, and hanging baskets.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 60–70°F; transplant after last frost into partial shade to sun in moist, well-drained soil; climbing snapdragon (Asarina procumbens) is a charming, soft-hairy, trailing vine-like plant native to rocky cliff faces and limestone walls in northeastern Spain, producing snapdragon-like pale yellow flowers with cream-yellow throats throughout the summer. The self-clinging petioles allow it to scramble over rough surfaces and through other plants; it is especially beautiful draping over stone walls, tucked into rock garden crevices, or spilling from containers and hanging baskets. In zone 7–10 it is perennial and can be propagated from cuttings; in colder zones grow as an annual. Distinguished from the related climbing snapdragons (Lophospermum) by its pale yellow flowers rather than pink or red.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; this slow-establishing evergreen vine rewards patience with years of low-maintenance coverage once mature.
directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; this slow-establishing evergreen vine rewards patience with years of low-maintenance coverage once mature. Glossy, leathery, evergreen leaves cling self-sufficiently to a wall, tree trunk, or fence by aerial roots much like climbing hydrangea, producing frothy, creamy-white clusters of small flowers in late summer when few other climbing shrubs are blooming. Native to forests of China, it is slower to establish than more vigorous climbing vines, often taking several years before it begins climbing in earnest, but once established requires little maintenance and holds its evergreen foliage through mild winters better than deciduous climbing hydrangea relatives. Provide consistent moisture during establishment, be patient during the slow early years of growth, and site on a shaded wall or trunk where its self-clinging roots can attach.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; climbing ylang ylang is a tropical Indian and Southeast Asian climbing shrub in the custard apple family with intensely fragrant, yellow-green flowers with the characteristic ylang ylang perfume — the scent is extraordinarily powerful at night and the flowers are used in traditional Indian garland-making.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; provide a strong trellis or allow to scramble through a supporting tree. Artabotrys hexapetalus (climbing ylang ylang or manorangini) is a tropical Indian and Southeast Asian climbing shrub in the custard apple family (Annonaceae) that climbs by means of distinctive hooked, curved peduncles (flower stalks) that become woody and hook-like as the flower develops — anchoring the plant to supporting branches without true tendrils or twining. The plant produces small, pale yellow-green to yellow flowers in clusters, with six tepals (three outer, three inner) — the flowers have an extraordinarily powerful, sweet, heady fragrance almost identical to true ylang ylang (Cananga odorata) — intensely sweet, floral, slightly fruity — and are among the most powerfully fragrant flowers in the tropical garden. The scent intensifies dramatically at night, making this plant outstanding for outdoor seating areas in the tropics. In South India, the flowers are used in temple garlands, hair decorations, and in traditional perfume making — the essential oil extracted from the flowers is used in Ayurvedic preparations and in the perfume industry as a low-cost ylang ylang substitute. A remarkable and underused tropical fragrance plant for zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant in spring once all frost risk has passed and soil has warmed. Choose a sturdy trellis, fence, or tree to support the hooked stems, and site in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil. Mulch generously around the base to retain moisture through the warm growing season.
directions: Take semi-hardwood cuttings 4-6 inches long in late spring or summer, remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and insert into a warm, humid propagation environment with bottom heat near 80°F. Once well rooted, harden off and transplant to a permanent location with robust support, as the vine climbs by means of strong hooked stems that anchor to host structures. Water consistently during establishment, then reduce frequency once the plant is settled; mature plants tolerate brief dry spells but flower most profusely with regular irrigation and monthly balanced fertilization from spring through fall. Prune lightly after each flush of bloom to encourage branching and additional flowering, and position near seating areas or windows to take full advantage of the powerful ylang-ylang fragrance that intensifies in the evening.

plant_note: Plant offsets in well-drained, organically rich soil in full shade to bright indirect light; pot-bound clumps bloom more freely so resist dividing unless necessary.
directions: Plant offsets or container plants in well-drained, organically enriched soil in full shade to bright indirect light, keeping the fleshy roots slightly pot-bound to encourage flowering; clivia produces clusters of brilliant orange or yellow trumpet flowers on tall scapes in late winter to spring when given a 6-week cool, dry rest period (50–55°F) in autumn. Water regularly during active growth but reduce watering sharply in fall to trigger the rest period that promotes next season's bloom. In zone 9 and cooler, grow in containers and bring indoors before frost. Divide large clumps after flowering by severing rooted offsets with a clean knife and allowing cuts to callus before repotting.

common_name: Clog Plant (Guppy Plant, Goldfish Plant, Pouch Flower)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket or trailing container in bright indirect light to partial shade; Clog Plant cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It blooms most freely with a brief, dry, slightly cool rest period (6–8 weeks at 55–60°F with reduced watering) in fall before resuming regular care in winter-spring for peak bloom. Propagate from stem-tip cuttings in moist mix. Use a fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix. Water thoroughly and allow to approach dryness between waterings — the thick stems store water and are susceptible to rot in heavy media.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade as a hanging basket or trailing container plant — Clog Plant flowers most prolifically in bright indirect light (a bright east or north window) and will produce few flowers in dim conditions. Nematanthus gregarius (formerly Hypocyrta radicans and various other synonyms) is a trailing, semi-succulent epiphytic vine from the coastal Atlantic Forest of Brazil in the Gesneriaceae family, closely related to Columnea and Aeschynanthus. The common names — 'Clog Plant,' 'Pouch Flower,' 'Guppy Plant' — all refer to the distinctive shape of the flowers: small (half an inch to an inch), bright orange to orange-red, balloon-shaped or pouch-shaped with a small, pinched opening at one end, the overall silhouette remarkably resembling a tiny Dutch wooden clog, a bloated tropical fish, or a miniature water balloon. The flowers emerge from the leaf axils along the trailing stems in succession throughout the warm months, often blanketing an established hanging basket in dozens of the tiny orange pouches simultaneously. The stems are clothed in small, fleshy, shiny, dark-green, opposite leaves that have a bright, glossy quality. Clog Plant is one of the most rewarding of the trailing gesneriads for indoor hanging baskets — reliably blooming for months once established in appropriate conditions. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into moist, humus-rich soil; cold stratification over winter dramatically improves germination rates the following spring.
directions: Scatter seed onto moist, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded site in early fall, barely covering with a thin layer of fine soil or leaf mold. Natural winter cold breaks seed dormancy; do not attempt to rush germination with artificial heat. Plants require consistent moisture and will decline in dry or compacted soils, so amend planting beds with compost before sowing. Expect slow establishment over the first two seasons before plants begin reliable late-summer bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta clausa spreads aggressively by stolons compared to most hostas, quickly colonizing large areas in appropriate conditions. Excellent as a shade groundcover for difficult areas.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta clausa is one of the most unusual hostas — a Korean species named for its cleistogamous (closed) flowers that never open fully, staying closed and self-pollinating without releasing pollen or allowing cross-pollination. This botanical curiosity means the flowers, while attractive in bud, never display the characteristic open, funnel-shaped hosta flower. The species compensates with an unusually aggressive spreading habit for a hosta — it sends out stolons to colonize large areas, making it one of the best groundcover hostas for naturalizing in shade gardens. The dark green, medium-sized leaves are attractive and conventional in appearance despite the botanical curiosity of the closed flowers. An excellent choice where spreading shade groundcover is desired without the aggressive nature of English ivy.

common_name: Cloud 9 Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming Compact White Flowering Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, organically rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates; dogwoods are shallow-rooted and need consistent moisture, especially while establishing.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, siting it in morning sun with afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Cloud 9 is a compact, exceptionally heavy-flowering flowering dogwood selection, producing such a dense covering of large, pure white bracts each spring that the tree can appear almost solid white, an especially prolific bloom that has made it one of the most popular white dogwood cultivars in nursery production. Its smaller, more compact mature size than the species also suits it to smaller residential landscapes. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, since dogwoods are shallow-rooted and stressed by drought; prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering, and watch for powdery mildew and dogwood borer in humid climates.

common_name: Cloud Nine Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming White Flowering Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Cloud Nine is particularly valued for its prolific blooming even at an early age — often flowering in the first or second year after planting, earlier than many dogwood cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Cloud Nine is one of the most widely admired white flowering dogwood cultivars — selected for its unusually profuse bloom (the bracts cover the tree so densely at peak bloom that the branches are nearly invisible), its somewhat horizontally spreading branch structure that creates a wider than tall profile, and its ability to bloom as a young tree in its first or second year rather than requiring 5–7 years before flowering as is common with seedling-grown trees. The large, overlapping, pure-white bracts (each slightly overlapping the adjacent bract, creating a solid canopy of white) cover the entire tree at peak bloom in March through April in zone 9 — the flowering display has been described as looking like the tree is covered in white clouds, giving the cultivar its name. The wider-than-tall spreading form gives Cloud Nine a distinctive silhouette even when not in flower — an elegant horizontal branching pattern that is attractive year-round. Excellent red to maroon fall foliage color and red berries for wildlife follow the spring bloom. In zone 9, plant in morning sun and afternoon shade on the north or east side of structures to minimize summer heat stress on this understory native.

common_name: Cloud Nine Switchgrass (Tall Airy Blue-Green Native Switchgrass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Cloud Nine is one of the tallest switchgrass cultivars, valued for its billowy, airy flower panicles that create a soft, cloud-like effect above the blue-green foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun; adaptable to clay, wet, and dry soils. Cloud Nine is one of the tallest switchgrass selections commonly grown, producing upright, blue-green foliage topped by unusually large, airy, cloud-like flower panicles in late summer that catch the light beautifully and persist as attractive tan seed heads through winter. Its height and strong vertical presence make it an excellent back-of-border screen or specimen planting, and like other switchgrass cultivars it tolerates a wide range of soil conditions, drought, and periodic flooding with ease. Cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges to keep the clump tidy and vigorous.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant transplants March–May. Torenia fournieri is one of the few annual flowers that genuinely tolerates and performs well in partial to full shade — making it an invaluable substitute for impatiens in shaded situations. Clown Rose is a compact selection in the Clown series bred for uniform growth, compact habit (8–12 inches), and excellent heat tolerance — an improvement over older, leggier torenia selections that declined in zone 9 summer heat. In zone 9 torenia performs most reliably in spring and fall in full shade; summer heat may reduce flowering but the plant recovers when temperatures moderate. Self-seeds modestly in zone 9, providing some volunteer reseeding.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil — Torenia is one of the few annual flowers that genuinely performs in full shade, making it invaluable for deep-shade situations where most flowering annuals cannot maintain blooming; Clown Rose Torenia is a compact selection of Wishbone Flower (Torenia fournieri), a shade-tolerant tropical annual from Vietnam producing an unusual, bicolor, tubular-to-open flower in rose-pink with a deeper rose-pink lower lip and a bright yellow center spot — a color combination that is vivid and cheerful in the low-light conditions of deep shade where these flowers are most practical. The common name 'Wishbone Flower' comes from the two curved stamens that are fused at the tips inside the flower, forming a wishbone shape visible when the flower is examined closely.
