Torenia's genuine shade tolerance — it requires shade in hot climates and will bleach and decline in direct sun — makes it one of a very small group of annual flowers that can deliver consistent, colorful bloom in the deep shade under trees, on north-facing walls, and in covered garden structures where no direct sun reaches. In zone 9, where summer shade garden color is particularly difficult to maintain, Torenia provides one of the most reliable warm-season flowering options for genuinely shaded situations from spring through early fall.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Clubbed Sedum forms tight, dense rosettes and rots quickly in wet or dense soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Clubbed Sedum forms tight, dense rosettes and rots quickly in wet or dense soil. Thick, club-shaped, powdery blue-gray leaves are densely packed into tight, compact rosettes that offset readily to form a spreading mat, blushing soft pink at the tips in bright light and producing small white star-shaped flowers on short stalks in spring. Native to rocky slopes in Mexico, it forms an unusually neat, symmetrical rosette compared to many trailing sedums, making it a favorite for succulent arrangements and rock garden pockets where its tidy form can be appreciated. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves to protect the powdery coating, and provide bright light for the tightest, best-colored rosettes.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in late summer in a hot, dry, sun-baked site that mimics its Mediterranean habitat.
directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in late summer in a hot, sharply drained bed against a south-facing wall or rock garden slope, since this species needs a thorough summer baking to flower well. Large crocus-shaped, bright golden-yellow blooms appear directly from bare soil in autumn, usually just ahead of or alongside the narrow gray-green leaves. It is a choice bulb for a dry Mediterranean-style border, gravel garden, or bulb frame where winter wet can be avoided. Established clumps are best left undisturbed for years, as sternbergias resent frequent lifting and division.

plant_note: Surface-sow; seed needs light to germinate. Established clumps spread steadily by rhizome and can also be divided in spring or fall.
directions: Surface-sow seed in fall or early spring, pressing it lightly into well-drained, fertile soil without covering, since light aids germination; established clumps can also be divided in spring or fall. Clustered bellflower produces dense, rounded clusters of upward-facing violet-purple bells packed tightly at the stem tips, a habit distinctive enough to have earned it the old common name Danesblood, and it spreads steadily by rhizome to form a substantial patch over a few seasons. Give it full sun to light afternoon shade and average, well-drained soil; it is more vigorous and spreading than most clump-forming bellflowers, so site it where its wandering habit is welcome or divide it regularly to keep it in bounds. Deadhead spent flower clusters to prolong bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost directly into soil already occupied by native warm-season grasses; hemi-parasitic roots require close proximity to host plants for establishment.
directions: Clustered False Foxglove is a native annual hemi-parasite of the southeastern coastal plain, found in pine savannas and flatwoods where it attaches to the roots of nearby warm-season grasses to supplement its own photosynthesis; sow seeds directly among established native grasses such as wiregrass or broomsedge, as plants will fail to thrive in bare soil without host root contact. Its crowded, fascicled (clustered) leaf arrangement gives the stems a distinctively bushy, fine-textured appearance, setting it apart from other Agalinis species. From late summer through fall, it produces abundant rosy-pink trumpet flowers that attract native bees and support specialist pollinators in southeastern savanna restorations. Scatter seeds on the soil surface among host grasses at last frost and avoid transplanting, as disturbed roots disrupt the critical host-parasite connection.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall, or direct sow seed in fall for natural cold stratification; clustered mountain mint spreads moderately by rhizomes and self-seeds in average to moist soils — it is less aggressively spreading than some Pycnanthemum species and is generally well-behaved in garden settings while still forming useful colonies over time.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; clustered mountain mint is widely regarded as the most ornamentally distinguished of all native Pycnanthemum species, set apart from the more common P. tenuifolium and P. virginianum by its large, broad, silvery-white bracts that surround the dense, clustered flower heads and persist long after the small white flowers fade — from midsummer onward the upper portions of the plant take on a striking silver-white frosted appearance that is exceptionally showy and provides weeks of ornamental interest. It is one of the single most valuable native plants for pollinators in eastern North America: studies at the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center have recorded over 60 species of native bees visiting a single planting, along with dozens of butterfly species, making it a keystone resource in any pollinator garden or native meadow planting. The foliage is strongly mint-scented when crushed and deer-resistant; the plant spreads moderately by rhizomes to form a useful, weed-suppressing colony in average to moist garden soils and tolerates partial shade better than most other mountain mints. Clustered mountain mint is a premier native plant choice for rain gardens, stream edges, moist meadow margins, and any garden situation with consistently adequate moisture and partial to full sun.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or scarify and cold stratify seeds for 60 days before spring sowing. Clustered poppy mallow has a deep taproot and transplants poorly — direct seeding in the final location is strongly preferred.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; clustered poppy mallow is a Midwestern prairie native related to the more commonly grown wine-cup (C. involucrata), producing the same vivid magenta-wine to deep purple-red, cup-shaped flowers but with a more upright, clustered growth habit rather than the sprawling form of wine-cup. The flowers are produced in clustered groups near the stem tips from early summer through fall. Like all Callirhoe, it develops a deep taproot that stores carbohydrates and enables the plant to survive drought and fire — making it extremely persistent in lean, dry, well-drained conditions once established. Decline occurs in rich, moist soils. An outstanding drought-tolerant native for dry prairie and meadow gardens where its brilliant color stands out against grasses and other drought-tolerant wildflowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry, lean, sandy or gravelly soil; adapted to California's dry-season blooming cycle.
directions: Clustered Tarweed is a glandular-sticky, resinous native annual of dry, open, disturbed ground, roadsides, and grassland edges in southern California's coastal sage scrub and chaparral zones, bearing tightly clustered heads of small, yellow, 5-rayed composite flowers from summer through early fall on slender, branching, rough-textured stems. It is an ecological specialist of California's summer-dry Mediterranean climate, germinating with spring warmth and blooming through the long rainless months when it serves as a critical late-season pollen and nectar source for native bees. Direct sow in spring after last frost in dry, lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun, pressing seed lightly to the surface; no supplemental irrigation is needed or desired after plants are established. This species is best suited to gardens within its native southern California range where summer drought and heat drive its bloom cycle.

subcategory: shade-tolerant clustering palm with bipinnate fishtail leaves
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; clustering fishtail palm is unique among commonly grown palms in having bipinnate (twice-divided) leaves — the individual leaflets are further divided into irregular, jagged, triangular to wedge-shaped segments with ragged tips that resemble fish tails. The clustering habit (multiple stems per clump) means individual stems can die after flowering without killing the whole plant. In zone 9 it requires a protected, warm microclimate; in zone 10-11 it thrives. Shade tolerant.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; clustering fishtail palm is botanically unique among the commonly grown palms in producing bipinnate leaves — leaves that are divided not once (as in all other feather palms, where a central rachis carries rows of leaflets) but twice, the primary leaflets themselves being further divided into multiple secondary segments. These secondary segments are irregular, asymmetrical, wedge-shaped to triangular, with a jagged, torn, irregular margin at the wide outer tip that closely resembles the tail of a fish — hence the common name 'fishtail palm'. The overall textural effect of the bipinnate, fishtail-segmented leaf is unlike any other palm — a complex, slightly disheveled, fern-like yet bold tropical texture that catches light differently from all directions and creates an immediately distinctive, unusual palm silhouette. The clustering habit (the palm grows as a clump of multiple individual stems) is equally important: because individual caryota stems are monocarpic (they flower from top to bottom over several years and then die), the clustering species maintains the clump indefinitely as new stems continuously replace old ones — unlike monocarpic single-trunk species. More shade-tolerant than most large palms. The sap and fruits of Caryota species contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic to skin and mucous membranes — avoid contact with fruit pulp.

common_name: Clyde Redmond Louisiana Iris (Classic Deep Blue Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Clyde Redmond is a widely grown, classic Louisiana iris cultivar producing large, richly colored deep blue-violet flowers in mid-spring, a color long considered one of the standards against which other blue Louisiana iris cultivars are judged. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape where many other perennials would struggle. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist to dry, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy, well-drained soil in partial shade; coast azalea is one of the most drought-tolerant of all native azaleas once established and thrives in the sandy, acidic coastal plain soils of the Atlantic Seaboard.
directions: Coast azalea is a compact, stoloniferous native azalea of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain's sandy pine barrens and oak scrublands — producing one of the most intensely fragrant flowers of any native azalea, with white to pale pink blooms that emit a strong, sweet vanilla-clove fragrance in April and May before the leaves fully expand. Unlike most native azaleas that form upright, single-stemmed shrubs, coast azalea spreads slowly by underground stolons (horizontal stems) to form broad, low colonies — a growth habit that makes it one of the finest native azaleas for use as a naturalized groundcover or mass planting under open pinelands and dry oak canopy. Its compact, low stature (rarely over 4 feet) and tolerance of dry, sandy, nutrient-poor acidic soils make it more versatile in the landscape than taller species; it is also more heat-tolerant than northern azaleas and performs reliably in the upper Gulf Coastal Plain. Several hybrid azaleas have been developed from this species for their fragrance and compact habit.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; coast banksia is salt- and wind-tolerant and one of the hardiest banksias, surviving brief temperatures to 23°F (zone 8). Like all Proteaceae, it is severely damaged or killed by standard fertilizers with phosphate. Excellent drainage is essential.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic soil in full sun; coast banksia is one of the most adaptable and cold-hardy Australian banksias, a coastal tree of eastern Australia growing 10–30 feet with distinctive pale-green leaves that are dark green above and silvery-white below — creating a two-toned effect as leaves move in the wind. The characteristic cylindrical banksia flower spikes (4–6 inches long) are produced primarily in autumn and winter in soft, pale-yellow, and are among the richest natural nectar sources of any flowering tree — overwhelming in the volume and concentration of the nectar they produce. This makes them critical wildlife habitat for honeyeaters, lorikeets, bats, and a vast array of insects including native bees. The hardened, woody seed cones that follow the flowers can persist on the branch for years before opening to release seeds in response to fire (a key ecological adaptation). One of the most cold-tolerant banksias and the best starting species for gardens in zones 8b–11 seeking Australian native character.

plant_note: Sow seed indoors in late winter on sterile cactus mix, then transplant outdoors in spring once temperatures stay reliably mild; best near the coast or in a protected microclimate inland.
directions: Sow seed indoors in late winter on sterile cactus mix, then transplant outdoors in spring once temperatures stay reliably mild. Native to coastal bluffs and mesas of San Diego County and northern Baja California, this compact, barrel-shaped cactus bears yellow-green flowers that often have a reddish throat, blooming in late winter to early spring. It is one of the more cold-sensitive barrel cacti and does best near the coast or in a protected microclimate inland. Plant it in decomposed granite or sandy soil for the sharp drainage it needs to avoid rot.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into constantly moist, humus-rich soil along a shaded streambank or seep, where the plant will self-sow into congenial damp crevices.
directions: Coast boykinia is a Pacific coastal native found along redwood-shaded streambanks, seeps, and damp rock outcrops from California to British Columbia, forming clumps of rounded, shallowly lobed, maple-like leaves topped by loose, airy panicles of small white, star-shaped flowers in late spring and early summer. It requires constant moisture and cool root conditions to perform well and will scorch or go dormant early if soil dries out, making it ideal for the wet, shaded margins of a woodland stream, pond, or rain garden. Established clumps slowly spread by rhizome and self-sow into nearby damp crevices; combine with sword fern, redwood sorrel, and wild ginger for an authentic Pacific Northwest streamside planting. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile to average soil; Coast Coral Tree is a spectacular South African native and one of the most widely planted street trees of Southern California, capable of brief light frosts in zone 8–9, and produces masses of brilliant red-orange flowers on bare thorny branches in late winter and spring before the feathery trifoliate leaves emerge.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Erythrina caffra is drought tolerant once established — water deeply and infrequently during summer in Mediterranean and subtropical climates and rely on winter rainfall in coastal California conditions; avoid heavy clay with poor drainage. Erythrina caffra (Coast Coral Tree or South African Coral Tree) is a large, semi-deciduous tree native to the coastal forests and river margins of Eastern South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape) that has become one of the defining ornamental trees of the Southern California street landscape, the official city tree of Los Angeles. Trees lose most of their leaves in late winter and simultaneously burst into spectacular bloom — the dense, columnar racemes of bright coral-red to orange pea-family flowers covering the bare, spiny branches from January through March create an unforgettable winter floral display unmatched by almost any other tree in temperate gardens. The flowers are rich in nectar and attract hummingbirds, lorikeets, and sunbirds across its global planted range. Erythrina caffra is more cold-hardy than the related E. variegata — tolerating brief periods near 25°F when established in well-drained soil — which has made it the standard large coral tree for zone 8b–9 California and Southeastern gardens. A nitrogen-fixer that enriches surrounding soil; useful for large spaces, street medians, and parks.

plant_note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall directly where the tree is to grow, since the long taproot resents transplanting once established.
directions: Coast Live Oak is the iconic evergreen oak of California's coastal ranges, forming a broad, dense, often wider-than-tall canopy of stiff, holly-like leaves over a massive, gnarled trunk. It is a keystone species of California oak woodland, supporting acorn woodpeckers, scrub jays, and dozens of other wildlife species, and is famously intolerant of summer irrigation, which encourages fatal Phytophthora root disease. Give it lean, well-drained soil and withhold water beneath the drip line once established, and it will live for centuries with essentially no care. Its slow growth and enormous mature size reward gardeners planting for the long term rather than quick shade.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, moisture-retentive, fertile loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; coast redwood grows naturally in the fog belt of the California and Oregon coast where summer fog provides constant atmospheric moisture. It grows best in moist, cool, deep soils.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, moisture-retentive, fertile loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; coast redwood is the world's tallest living tree — the tallest known individual (Hyperion in Redwood National Park) reaches 380 feet. Native to the fog belt of the California and Oregon coast, coast redwood is uniquely adapted to harvest water from fog directly through its needles, supplementing root-absorbed water in the dry California summer. Remarkably fast-growing for such a large tree — growth of 3–5 feet per year is common in ideal conditions in zones 8–10. Distinct from giant sequoia in being taller but much slimmer, with flat needles arranged in two ranks (like yew), and in its ability to sprout vigorously from the base after cutting or fire. Widely planted in California, the Pacific Northwest, and milder parts of the world (Ireland, New Zealand, the UK). Cutting-propagated plants from named selections are more reliable for garden planting than seed-grown trees.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained sandy soil in part shade; Coastal Azalea is a low, suckering native deciduous azalea of the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, naturally forming spreading colonies in sandy pine woods rather than a single upright shrub.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, humus-rich, acidic, sandy soil in part shade, mimicking the open pine woodland and coastal plain scrub where it grows wild. Coastal Azalea is one of the lowest-growing of the native deciduous azaleas, spreading by root suckers into loose colonies rather than staying as a single tidy shrub, which makes it useful as a woodland-edge groundcover or naturalized drift rather than a formal specimen. Its fragrant white to pale pink flowers, sometimes with a yellow blotch, open in mid-spring before or with the emerging foliage and carry a sweet, clove-like scent that carries well on the breeze. Unlike many native azaleas that prefer consistently moist streambank soil, Coastal Azalea tolerates drier, sandier conditions once established, reflecting its native habitat on the coastal plain, though it still benefits from a thick mulch layer and supplemental water during dry spells. Prune only to remove dead wood, since it needs little shaping to look at home in a naturalistic planting.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial to full shade. Coastal Doghobble is one of the most shade-tolerant native broadleaf evergreen shrubs available for southeastern gardens and can thrive under dense tree canopy where few other shrubs persist.
directions: Coastal Doghobble is a graceful, arching, broadleaf evergreen native shrub, native to moist, acidic, shaded streambanks, ravine slopes, and moist, sandy forest understories of the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Mississippi, where its arching stems weave through the understory to form dense, impenetrable thickets — hence the 'doghobble' name, as hunting dogs became entangled in the arching stems. In April and May it produces racemes of small, white, urn-shaped flowers along the undersides of the arching branches, followed by attractive dark green, leathery, lance-shaped leaves that turn burgundy-red to bronze in winter, providing excellent cold-season color in the shade garden. One of the most shade-tolerant native broadleaf evergreen shrubs available, Coastal Doghobble thrives under dense tree canopy where azaleas and camellias struggle; provide consistently moist, acidic soil and avoid alkaline conditions or prolonged drought.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before sowing in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.
directions: Coastal Indigo is a low, spreading native perennial with attractive silvery-hairy, pinnate foliage and clusters of brilliant rose-pink to coral-red pea flowers that continue from spring through fall, making it one of the longest-blooming native legumes of the southeastern coastal plain. It is native to dry, sandy, open ground, pine flatwoods, and roadsides from Georgia to Texas, and is notably more ground-hugging and spreading than most other Indigofera species. Scarify seeds before sowing in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; amending or over-irrigating the soil will cause decline. An underused, exceptionally long-blooming native perennial for sandy, full-sun Gulf Coast gardens in zones 7 through 10, drought-tolerant once established.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic, peaty or sandy soil; inkberry requires acidic conditions (pH 4.5–6.0) and is one of the most adaptable native shrubs for wet, seasonally flooded sites. Plant both male and female plants for berry production.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; inkberry is a versatile native evergreen holly of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain with glossy dark green leaves and small black berries that provide essential winter food for over 35 bird species including bluebirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and hermit thrushes. Unlike many hollies, inkberry tolerates wet, seasonally flooded sites and even some saltwater intrusion, making it ideal for rain gardens, bioswales, and poorly drained sites where most shrubs fail. Numerous compact cultivars have been developed for landscape use, including 'Compacta' (3–4 ft), 'Shamrock' (3–4 ft, very cold hardy), and 'Nigra' (4–6 ft with good fruiting). Both male and female plants are needed for berry production; one male ('Nordic' or 'Strongbox') pollinates several females.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full to partial sun along the coastal plain; coastal Joe-Pye weed is more compact than inland species and thrives in the moist, acidic soils of Atlantic and Gulf coastal lowlands.
directions: Coastal Joe-Pye weed is the compact, coastal-adapted Joe-Pye species of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, typically shorter and more restrained than its inland relatives (hollow Joe-Pye and spotted Joe-Pye) while producing equally beautiful, rounded, domed flower clusters of dusty pink to light purple that smother the plant in late summer and fall. Its compact size (3–5 feet) makes it more appropriate than the 6–8 foot inland species for typical garden borders, perennial beds, and rain gardens where the giant inland Joe-Pye weeds would overwhelm surrounding plants. Like all Joe-Pye weeds, it is a specialist butterfly plant — tiger swallowtails, monarchs, and large skippers congregate on the flower heads in late summer with impressive regularity — and an important late-season nectar source for native bees preparing for winter. It is naturally adapted to the acidic, sandy, moderately moist soils of coastal flatwoods, wet savannas, and streamside thickets of the Gulf Coast Coastal Plain, making it an ideal choice for naturalized woodland-edge gardens in the Deep South.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coastal jugflower requires excellent drainage and lean, low-phosphorus soil — like all Proteaceae, phosphorus fertilizer is lethal. It is native to the coastal sand dunes and heaths of southwestern Western Australia. The primary ornamental value is the extraordinarily fine, soft, silver-gray, silky-textured foliage — the name 'sericeus' means 'silky'. The small, tubular, red flowers in spring are secondary to the foliage in ornamental value.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coastal jugflower is grown almost exclusively for its foliage — one of the finest-textured, most silvery-soft, most ethereally beautiful of all Australian native shrub foliages. The leaves are divided into multiple, extremely fine, thread-like silver-gray segments covered in silky, lustrous, silver hairs that catch light from every angle and create an overall impression of a plant made from fine, soft, silver-gray floss — a shimmering, luminous, soft-silver cloud of extraordinary fine texture. Each leaf has multiple, feathery, thread-like lobes covered in the lustrous, silky hairs of the species name 'sericeus'. The whole shrub creates a medium-to-large mound of incomparably fine, silver-gray, soft-textured foliage that provides year-round textural and color contrast with nearby bold-leaved or dark-leaved plants. In spring it produces small, tubular, red flowers in the leaf axils — pleasant but not the primary ornamental point. Native to the coastal sand dunes and heathlands of southwestern Western Australia where its silver, reflective foliage may reduce water loss and reflect intense sunlight. Outstanding as a silver foliage specimen or contrast plant in zone 9 Mediterranean-climate gardens requiring excellent drainage and lean soil.

plant_note: Surface-sow in fall onto dry, sandy, nutrient-poor soil in full sun, pressing seed in but leaving it exposed to light since it is a light-dependent germinator that should not be buried deeply.
directions: Surface-sow in fall onto dry, sandy, nutrient-poor soil in full sun, pressing seed in but leaving it exposed to light since it needs light to germinate; established plants spread gently by rhizome to form loose colonies. Despite the common name it is not a true Solidago but a close goldenrod relative with narrow, resinous, aromatic leaves and flat-topped clusters of small gold flowers from late summer into fall. It is an exceptional late-season nectar source for migrating monarchs, native bees, and beneficial wasps, and thrives on the dry sandy ridges and pine barrens of the coastal plain where richer-soil goldenrods struggle. Deadhead spent flower heads if self-seeding is not wanted, as it can colonize open sandy sites readily.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial sun to full sun; coastal plain joe-pye weed tolerates periodic standing water and is ideal for rain gardens, bog margins, and low wet areas that challenge most perennials.
directions: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial sun to full sun; coastal plain joe-pye weed tolerates periodic standing water and is ideal for rain gardens, bog margins, and low wet areas that challenge most perennials. Eutrochium dubium is a shorter and more compact species than the common E. purpureum, typically reaching 4–5 feet with distinctive whorled leaves in sets of three rather than four, and large, rounded, mauve-pink flower clusters from July through September that are among the best pollinator resources in the late-summer native garden, drawing monarch butterflies, swallowtails, and dozens of native bee species. It is native to Atlantic coastal plain wet meadows and swamps from Maine to Florida and is particularly well adapted to the heat and humidity of the Southeast.

common_name: Coastal Plain St. John's-Wort (Atlantic St. John's-Wort)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; this species grows naturally in seasonally flooded pine savannas, wet flatwoods, and pond edges across the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to light shade, mimicking the seasonally flooded pine flatwoods and pond margins where it grows wild. This small, upright, semi-evergreen shrub has fine, needle-like leaves and produces a summer-long succession of bright yellow flowers with a prominent tuft of stamens at each branch tip, attracting native bees and other small pollinators. It tolerates standing water for extended periods yet also handles the seasonal dry-down typical of Gulf Coast wet pinelands, making it a resilient choice for the fluctuating water levels of a rain garden or pond-edge planting. Use it as a filler shrub among taller wetland trees or massed along a ditch or bioswale where few other woody plants can establish.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in dry to moderately moist, strongly acidic, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun. Coastal Plain Staggerbush is adapted to the xeric, fire-maintained scrub and flatwood habitats of the Florida peninsula and requires excellent drainage — it will not tolerate clay, wet soils, or alkaline conditions.
directions: Coastal Plain Staggerbush is a native evergreen shrub endemic to the dry, sandy, fire-maintained scrub and flatwood habitats of the Florida peninsula, where its dense, leathery-leaved growth and small white to pink urn-shaped flowers in spring make it a characteristic component of the open, sunny, infertile sand communities dominated by oaks and palmettos. Adapted to the same xeric conditions as Florida Rosemary, Scrub Hickory, and other Florida scrub specialists, Coastal Plain Staggerbush requires excellent drainage and periodic low-intensity fire to maintain the open, competitive-free conditions it requires. Like other Lyonia species, the foliage contains grayanotoxins and is toxic to livestock if consumed. Plant in dry, strongly acidic, sandy, well-drained, infertile soil in full sun — Coastal Plain Staggerbush thrives in the nutrient-poor, fire-managed conditions of its native habitat and requires no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established.

plant_note: Take hardwood cuttings 8–12 inches long in late winter before bud break and insert directly into moist soil at the water's edge in full sun; rooting is rapid and reliable. Coastal Plain Willow establishes quickly from cuttings and can also be established by planting dormant rooted stems directly in saturated soil.
directions: Coastal Plain Willow is the most abundant native willow of the coastal plain wetlands, stream banks, tidal margins, and disturbed wet soils from Virginia south through Florida and west to Texas and the Caribbean, forming dense multi-stemmed thickets that provide critical cover and nesting habitat for waterfowl, shorebirds, and muskrats. Like all willows, it produces copious pollen and nectar in early spring that are among the first resources available to emerging queen bumblebees, native sweat bees, and early butterflies; the foliage hosts the caterpillars of Viceroy, Mourning Cloak, and numerous native moths. Propagate easily from hardwood cuttings taken in late winter before bud break, inserting 8–12 inch stems into moist, wet soil in full sun; rooting is rapid, establishment reliable, and fallen branches that contact moist soil root naturally. Coastal Plain Willow spreads aggressively by root suckers in wet areas and is best used in large, naturalized riparian settings where its vigorous growth habit is an asset.

plant_note: Direct sow or root stem cuttings in spring into loose, dry, sandy soil in full sun; the trailing stems root wherever they touch sand, so a small planting spreads into a full groundcover mat within a season.
directions: Plant into loose, dry, sandy soil in full sun and avoid overwatering, which quickly rots this short-lived dune perennial; coastal ragweed forms a low, bushy, deeply lobed mat that roots at the stem nodes as it spreads, making it useful for stabilizing loose sand on a beachfront lot or open coastal bed where little else will take hold. It thrives in the intense heat, salt spray, and drought of a Gulf Coast summer and needs essentially no supplemental care once rooted in appropriate sandy ground. Because it produces abundant wind-borne pollen, site it away from patios, windows, and other areas where people spend time outdoors, and reserve it for dune stabilization or the far edges of the landscape rather than near the house.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with necks at soil surface in moist to well-drained, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zone 8–11; Coastal Spider Lily is a robust, salt-tolerant native bulb of the coastal scrubs, shell mounds, and beach margins of Florida and the Caribbean — producing large, spectacular, pure-white, intensely fragrant spider lily flowers on tall stems throughout summer — among the most salt-tolerant and coastal-adapted of all native Florida bulbs.
directions: Plant bulbs with necks at or just above soil surface in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Hymenocallis latifolia is tolerant of coastal conditions — salt spray, limestone soils, and periodic drought once established — an excellent native bulb for coastal gardens and sandy, alkaline-soil landscapes in zone 8–11. Hymenocallis latifolia (Coastal Spider Lily or Perfumed Spider Lily) is a large, robust, bulbous perennial native to the coastal scrubs, hammocks, rocky pinelands, shell mounds, and beach margin habitats of southern Florida, the Florida Keys, and the Caribbean islands. The large, pure-white, intensely fragrant flowers — the characteristic Hymenocallis 'spider lily' form, with long, narrow, recurving petals surrounding a central, funnel-shaped corona with projecting stamens — are produced in umbels of 3–12 on tall, stout scapes, blooming in summer and fall. The fragrance is extraordinary — sweet, powerful, and vanilla-spice-like — and strongest in the evening, attracting hawk moths and nocturnal pollinators. Hymenocallis latifolia is distinguished from the freshwater-adapted H. littoralis by its preference for well-drained, coastal, limestone, and sandy soils rather than wet or flooded conditions, making it more versatile for typical garden settings. It shows excellent tolerance of salt spray, alkaline limestone soils, and sandy coastal substrates — making it outstanding for coastal Florida, Gulf Coast, and Caribbean garden planting where many bulbs fail.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery plugs in spring into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this low mat-forming verbena roots at the nodes as it creeps, so a few starter plants fill in quickly along a sunny coastal bed edge.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or plugs into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this Florida dune native forms a dense, glossy mat of toothed foliage studded with deep pink to lavender flower clusters that bloom nearly year-round in mild Gulf Coast winters. Once its roots reach moisture reserves it needs no supplemental irrigation and shrugs off salt spray and blowing sand, making it a good choice for stabilizing loose soil along a sunny walkway or coastal border. The nectar-rich blooms draw bees, butterflies, and moths through the long warm season, and the trailing stems can be trimmed back hard in late winter to keep growth tidy.

plant_note: Establish divisions in fall on rocky, well-drained slopes or open woodland in filtered shade.
directions: Establish divisions in fall on rocky, well-drained slopes or open woodland in filtered shade, the dry chaparral-edge and oak-woodland habitat this California and Oregon native occupies in the wild. It is the most drought-tolerant western Dryopteris, holding its leathery, twice-pinnate evergreen fronds through the long dry season with little irrigation once roots are established. Use it as a durable filler in dry-shade native plantings where more moisture-demanding wood ferns would struggle.

plant_note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed in spring into deep, dry, infertile sand; this coastal-plain wildflower is built for droughty, excessively drained dunes and scrub and will rot in average garden soil.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed in spring into deep, dry, infertile sand — this coastal-plain wildflower is built for droughty, excessively drained dunes and scrub and will rot in average garden soil. Its wiry stems carry bright yellow, ball-like flower heads made of distinctive papery, honeycomb-textured bracts from summer through fall, attracting a steady stream of small native bees, skippers, and beneficial wasps. It reseeds readily on bare sandy ground and is a favorite of coastal restoration plantings in Florida and along the Gulf shore. Give it full, unobstructed sun and avoid mulch or irrigation once established, since both encourage fungal problems.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to average, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; cobaea penstemon is a calcicole (limestone lover) that absolutely requires sharp drainage and does not tolerate clay or wet soils — excellent for rock gardens and dry limestone slopes.
directions: Cobaea penstemon bears the largest flowers of any native American penstemon — its tubular, inflated blooms in shades of lavender to pale purple (occasionally white) with purple guidelines are two inches or more across, giving a tropical richness that seems almost too spectacular for a native of dry limestone prairies. Native to the rocky, alkaline prairies and cedar glades of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and Missouri, it is one of the premier spring-blooming wildflowers of the southern Great Plains, with flower spikes rising from handsome rosettes of glossy, evergreen leaves in April and May. Bumblebees force their way into the large floral tubes to reach nectar, and the plant is an outstanding spring pollinator plant in dry, sunny native gardens. Sharp drainage on limestone or alkaline sandy soil is non-negotiable for this species in cultivation — it thrives in raised beds, rock gardens, and dry stone walls where water runs away quickly; it dies from root rot in typical garden soils with any tendency toward moisture retention.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in a container of live sphagnum moss and coarse sand kept constantly wet with cool, mineral-free water; site where roots stay cool and the pitchers get bright light, ideally with running or seeping water through the pot.
directions: Grow only nursery-propagated stock in a bog container or pond-edge planting of live sphagnum moss, perlite, and sand, watered exclusively with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water since it is sensitive to minerals and fertilizer. Its distinctive tubular, hooded pitchers resemble a rearing cobra and are veined with translucent patches that lure and trap insects for the plant's nutrition. Unlike most Sarracenia, it needs consistently cool root temperatures, so situating the pot where cold water can trickle through or keeping it partly shaded from hot afternoon sun helps it thrive. It is a striking, conversation-starting addition to a shaded bog garden or the cool margin of a water feature.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; cobweb houseleek needs sharp drainage and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil.
directions: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; cobweb houseleek needs sharp drainage and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil. Small, tight rosettes of fleshy, pointed leaves are laced across the tips with fine, white, web-like filaments that give the impression of a spider's cobweb draped over each rosette, an unmistakable and much-loved trait among the many hens-and-chicks species and cultivars. Extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant, native to rocky alpine slopes across the mountains of Europe, it forms an expanding mat of tightly packed rosettes that multiply readily by offsets, making it a classic, easy-care choice for a rock garden, stone wall crevice, or trough planting. Water only occasionally once established, and separate offsets to propagate or fill in bare patches, since each individual rosette is monocarpic and dies after flowering, leaving surrounding offsets to continue the colony.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in warm (75–80°F), well-drained seed-starting mix, do not overwater; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm, spacing 9–12 inches in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in warm (75–80°F), well-drained seed-starting mix, do not overwater; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm, spacing 9–12 inches in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Celosia argentea encompasses the plumed celosia (var. plumosa) with feathery flame-shaped flower heads and the brain-like crested cockscomb (var. cristata), both of which come in brilliant, jewel-toned shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and cream; the flower heads are outstanding dried everlastings and fresh cut flowers. In tropical and subtropical Africa, the leaves and young shoots are an important leafy vegetable (known as "soko" in Nigeria and "quélites" in parts of Mexico), eaten boiled or added to soups and stews; the plant is nutritious and fast-growing. Very heat-tolerant and long-blooming; an excellent zone 9–11 annual.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 2–4 weeks before last frost in peat pots to minimize transplant shock; celosia dislikes root disturbance. Direct sow outdoors after soil warms to 70°F. In zone 9, start in March for spring planting or in August for fall color.
directions: Start in peat pots indoors or direct sow after soil warms to 70°F in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Celosia argentea var. cristata (cockscomb) is the most dramatically formed of the celosias, producing a single, large, brain-like, fan-shaped, fasciated (abnormally flattened and broadened) flower head that can reach 4–6 inches wide in deep crimson, scarlet, orange, yellow, pink, or cream — the odd, velvet-textured, convoluted crest is one of the most unusual flower forms in cultivation and has been grown in gardens since ancient times in Asia, where it is used as a temple offering plant. Cockscomb thrives in hot, humid conditions and is outstanding in Gulf South gardens from late spring through frost; it is heat-tolerant and drought-resistant once established. Dwarf types ('Chief' series, 'Jewel Box' series) grow 6–10 inches with proportionally large flower heads; tall types can reach 18–24 inches. All celosias make exceptional dried flowers — harvest the crests before the first frost and hang upside down to dry; they hold color for months.

common_name: Cockspur Coral Tree (Ceibo, Cry Baby Tree, Fireman's Cap)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost; in zone 9, Cockspur Coral Tree dies back to the ground or trunk in cold winters but resprouts vigorously each spring and often blooms in the same year after being cut back. In zone 10-11 it is an evergreen or semi-deciduous tree; in zone 9 it behaves as a large die-back perennial. The thorny stems require care — wear heavy gloves when pruning. Seeds are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Cockspur Coral Tree is quite drought-tolerant once established and tolerates a wide range of soils including sand and alkaline conditions. Erythrina crista-galli (Cockspur Coral Tree or Ceibo) is the national tree and national flower of both Argentina and Uruguay — its spectacular, intense red flowers are also depicted in the coat of arms of Argentina. The flowers are large (2–2.5 inches), waxy, brilliant red, and clustered into drooping racemes at the branch tips in spring and summer; the characteristic 'crista-galli' (rooster's crest) refers to the hooded shape of the large standard petal. In warm climates the tree blooms March–June and again in fall, attracting hummingbirds, orioles, and numerous other nectar-feeding birds. In zone 9, the plant dies back to the root system after hard frost each winter and regrows to 5–8 feet by the following summer, blooming on new wood — acting effectively as a large, spectacular die-back perennial. In zone 10-11 it grows into a 30-foot tree with massive flowering displays. The thorny branches and trunks are a defensive characteristic; all parts of the plant are toxic if consumed. 'Compacta' is a dwarf cultivar reaching 6–8 feet suitable for smaller gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in average, well-drained to moist, adaptable soil in full sun to partial shade; cockspur hawthorn is extremely adaptable to a wide range of soils and moisture conditions and is one of the most drought-tolerant and pollution-tolerant of all native hawthorns.
directions: Cockspur hawthorn is a native small tree or large shrub of the eastern United States named for its long, curved thorns (3–4 inches) that resemble a rooster's spur and made it one of the most effective barrier hedges historically used to create impenetrable property boundaries before barbed wire. Its extremely wide, horizontal branching creates a distinctive, picturesque silhouette that provides year-round interest: white flower clusters in May, glossy red fruits persisting through winter, and spectacular scarlet-to-orange fall foliage color. As a wildlife tree, it is exceptional: the long-persistent red fruits are consumed by cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, robins, and bluebirds through winter when other food is scarce; the dense, thorny structure provides the safest possible nesting habitat for catbirds, thrashers, and wood thrushes. A thornless cultivar ('Inermis') is available for locations where the formidable thorns would be a hazard, providing all the wildlife and ornamental benefits of the species without the thorns.

common_name: Coco Magnolia / Dwarf White Jade Orchid
plant_note: Plant in spring in a sheltered spot with bright filtered light or morning sun and afternoon shade. Magnolia coco prefers moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil and performs exceptionally well in large containers, which allow the root zone to be protected during unusual cold spells in zone 9.
directions: Take semi-hardwood cuttings in late spring or early summer, wound the base lightly, apply rooting hormone, and root under intermittent mist or inside a humidity tent at 75-80°F with bright indirect light. Transplant rooted cuttings into organically enriched, well-drained soil and avoid heavy clay or sites prone to waterlogging, as Magnolia coco is sensitive to root rot. Unlike most magnolias that bloom in a single dramatic flush, this compact species produces its nodding, creamy-white, intensely sweet-scented flowers from spring through fall, making it especially rewarding near a patio, entryway, or courtyard window. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and midsummer, and deadhead spent flowers to keep the plant tidy and encourage the next wave of bloom.

common_name: Coco Yellow Marigold (Uniform Compact Bright Yellow African Marigold)
plant_note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or sow directly once soil warms; Coco Yellow, part of the Coco African-type series, bears uniform compact plants with bright yellow double blooms.
directions: Start seeds indoors for a head start or sow directly after frost danger passes, barely covering them. Coco Yellow, part of the compact, uniform Coco African-type marigold series, bears bright yellow, fully double blooms on a tidy, dwarf plant well suited to edging, containers, and mass bedding where the larger, taller African marigold cultivars would be out of scale. Plant in full sun where the strong scent helps deter garden pests. Deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming all summer.

common_name: Coconut Lime Coneflower (Double Green-and-White Pompom Echinacea)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Coconut Lime produces fully double, pompom-like flowers combining a creamy white outer ring of petals with a raised, shaggy lime-green center, an unusual double form and color combination quite different from the simple single daisy flowers of the wild species. Its novel double form makes it a strong focal point in a mixed border and a good cut flower, though like other double coneflower cultivars it can be somewhat shorter-lived than the straight species and benefits from sharp drainage, particularly through humid summers. It still draws some pollinators, though double flowers generally offer less accessible pollen and nectar than single-flowered coneflower types.

common_name: Coconut Orchid (Thin-Leaved Maxillaria, Red Coconut Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark or in a basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light; Maxillaria tenuifolia is tolerant of a wider range of conditions than many epiphytic orchids and adapts well to intermediate indoor or shaded porch culture. Water regularly during active growth; reduce watering in winter but do not allow to desiccate completely. The coconut fragrance of the flowers is strongest on warm, sunny days and carries several feet from the plant. Blooms spring–summer. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in coarse bark medium or mounted on cork — Coconut Orchid needs good light to bloom reliably but benefits from protection from the most intense direct summer sun that can scorch the thin leaves. Maxillaria tenuifolia is a small, creeping, sympodial epiphytic orchid native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most beloved small orchids in the collector world for a single, unforgettable characteristic: the flowers smell exactly, unmistakably, and powerfully of fresh coconut — a sweet, creamy, tropical fragrance that seems impossible from a small orchid flower but is real and carries several feet from the plant on warm days. The plant itself is modest in stature: a creeping mass of small, oval-to-egg-shaped pseudobulbs each producing a single, narrow (the 'tenuifolia' — thin-leaved), grass-like leaf 8–14 inches long. In spring and early summer, individual flowers emerge one per pseudobulb on very short stems from among the leaves — each flower 1–1.5 inches across, dark red to maroon-red with cream to yellow spotting on the lip, the overall coloration somewhat dark and modest in contrast to the extraordinary fragrance. A container or mounted specimen in full coconut bloom is one of the most pleasant aromatic experiences available from a tropical orchid. Non-toxic.

common_name: Coconut Sundae Dianthus (White with Red-Pink Center, Repeat-Blooming)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Coconut Sundae, part of the Scent First series, bears white petals with a vivid red-pink center on a repeat-blooming fragrant double pink.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Coconut Sundae, part of the Scent First breeding series, bears double flowers in crisp white with a vivid red-pink eye at the center, a bold bicolor combination on a fragrant, repeat-blooming plant bred to flower over a longer season than many older dianthus cultivars. Its extended bloom period and strong clove scent make it a strong performer for a sunny border or container. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and encourage continued rebloom.

common_name: Codsall Pink Deutzia (Fully Double Pink-Flushed Rough Deutzia)
plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Codsall Pink bears fully double, pink-flushed flowers, unlike the single-flowered species and the white 'Pride of Rochester' already common in cultivation.
directions: Root cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; deutzia blooms on old wood and should be pruned right after flowering by thinning the oldest, flowered stems to the ground to maintain vigor and density. Codsall Pink bears fully double flowers, each with an extra ruffle of petals flushed rose-pink on the outer surface and paler within, in dense, upright panicles covering the arching branches in late spring and early summer, a richer, showier bloom than the single white flowers of the species or the semi-double 'Pride of Rochester'. It tolerates partial shade acceptably and, like other deutzias, develops attractive exfoliating warm-brown bark on older stems that adds winter interest once the leaves have dropped. An easy, trouble-free, long-lived deciduous shrub for the mixed border.

plant_note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 8–9 plant March–April. Coffee Cups is evergreen and root-hardy in zone 8b–11; in zone 8a and colder, mulch heavily to protect tubers over winter. Prefers partial shade to shade in zone 9 where afternoon sun can scorch the large leaves; full sun is acceptable if consistent moisture is maintained.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9; Coffee Cups is a distinctive Colocasia esculenta cultivar whose large, bright green leaves develop strongly upturned margins as they mature, forming a pronounced cup or bowl shape that collects and holds rainwater — creating a living water feature that attracts wildlife and provides a dramatic focal point in the garden. The cupped leaves can hold several cups of water at a time, glinting and shimmering in dappled light; the effect is most pronounced on leaves of 18 inches or larger diameter. Unlike many dramatic elephant ear varieties, Coffee Cups performs well in partial to deep shade with consistent moisture, making it one of the most useful large-leaf shade plants for zone 8–9 gardens. The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every 2–3 years to control spread. Provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions, as the plant grows naturally along streamsides and in boggy areas.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring before new growth begins, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Colchis barrenwort is one of the most drought-tolerant and vigorous of all epimediums and is the parent of the widely grown E. × versicolor hybrids — it performs admirably in the dry shade of competitive tree roots where most shade groundcovers fail.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Colchis barrenwort is a Caucasian (Georgian and Iranian) epimedium species recognized as one of the most vigorous, drought-tolerant, and adaptable of the garden epimediums — it forms a steadily spreading, dense, weed-suppressing mat of compound, heart-shaped, spiny-edged, leathery, semi-evergreen leaves that are bronzed on emergence in spring before maturing to glossy, dark green. In spring, airy sprays of small, clear-yellow, four-petaled, spurred flowers — quite different from the long-spurred flowers of E. grandiflorum — rise just above the foliage. The species is one parent of E. × versicolor 'Sulphureum', the most commonly grown yellow epimedium. Colchis barrenwort is exceptional in its ability to spread and provide effective weed suppression in the dry shade under mature deciduous and coniferous trees. The previous season's foliage persists as an attractive bronze groundcover through winter before being replaced by spring growth. Among the very best plants for dry, difficult shade in zone 4–8.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in moist seed-starting mix; do not cover seeds as they require light to germinate. Pinch flower spikes as they form to maintain foliage color and density. In zone 9–11 coleus may be grown as a perennial with winter protection.
directions: Start seeds indoors or root cuttings easily in water; coleus is one of the most versatile and vividly colored foliage plants for shade and part-shade gardens, producing spectacular leaves in virtually every color combination imaginable — red, burgundy, orange, yellow, lime, pink, purple, bronze, and intricate multicolored patterns and textures. Modern sun-tolerant hybrids extend its use to full sun, but traditional coleus is happiest with morning sun and afternoon shade or dappled light under trees, where its colors often intensify beautifully. It is a workhorse of summer container gardening and shade bedding. Pinch the small flower spikes that develop in late summer to maintain bushy growth and color; once allowed to flower and set seed, foliage quality declines. In zone 9–11 old plants often survive mild winters and resprout in spring; take cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors in colder zones.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; foliage color change is most vivid with some direct light.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun. Color Flash is grown primarily for its unusual foliage, which shifts through the season from green to purple to burgundy-red as summer progresses, an ongoing color transition that few other astilbe cultivars offer, topped by soft pink flower plumes in summer that are almost secondary to the changing leaf color. Its dynamic, ever-shifting foliage provides months of interest beyond the relatively brief flowering period typical of most astilbes. Consistent moisture is essential — astilbes wilt and scorch quickly in dry shade; divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor, and mulch well to conserve soil moisture through summer heat.

common_name: Color Guard Yucca (Variegated Gold-Striped Adam's Needle)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or pups in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Color Guard is a variegated selection of native Adam's needle yucca, with a bold central gold stripe on each leaf that provides year-round color even without flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun to partial shade. Color Guard is a striking variegated form of the native Adam's needle yucca, with each sword-shaped, evergreen leaf marked by a broad creamy-yellow central stripe bordered in blue-green, giving strong architectural color to the garden year-round rather than only during its tall summer flower spike of white bell-shaped blooms. Like the species it is extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and adaptable to poor soils once established, needing almost no supplemental care. It slowly produces offsets (pups) at the base that can be separated to propagate new plants, and spent flower stalks can be cut down after bloom.

common_name: ColorBlaze Kingswood Torch Coleus (Tall Striped Shade Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Kingswood Torch is a Proven Winners ColorBlaze coleus bred for a tall, upright habit and striking striped foliage, performing best with morning sun and afternoon shade in a hot Gulf South summer.
directions: Plant in partial sun to full shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix, giving it morning sun and afternoon shade for the best performance in a hot climate; Kingswood Torch is a tall, vigorous coleus in the Proven Winners ColorBlaze series, bearing burgundy foliage boldly striped with chartreuse and cherry-red down the center of each leaf, creating a flame-like effect that gives the cultivar its name. Its upright, three-foot habit makes it a strong thriller plant for the back of a shaded container or border rather than a low edging plant. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy in foliage production, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage fuller branching and prevent the tall stems from becoming leggy.

plant_note: Start indoors and surface sow, as light aids germination; transplant to well-drained soil.
directions: A hardy, drought-tolerant perennial yarrow blend with feathery foliage and flat flower clusters in red, rose, pink, yellow, and white. Surface sow seed indoors and press it in without covering, since light aids germination. Transplant to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where it needs little water once established. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and cut flowers for fresh or dried arrangements.

plant_note: Start transplants after 4 weeks cold-moist stratification (or direct sow in fall), in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Colorado blue columbine tolerates more sun in cool mountain climates but requires afternoon shade in zone 6–8 heat.
directions: Start transplants after 4 weeks cold-moist stratification (or direct sow in fall), in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Colorado blue columbine tolerates more sun in cool mountain climates but requires afternoon shade in zone 6–8 heat. Aquilegia caerulea is the Colorado state flower and one of the most beautiful native columbines, with large flowers (2–3 inches) of clear, sky-blue sepals and pure-white, flat petals with long, straight blue spurs — a bicolor combination of exceptional purity; it grows naturally in mountain meadows and open forests from Wyoming to New Mexico at elevations of 6,000–11,500 feet and blooms in June–August. It is shorter-lived than some columbines (typically 3–5 years) but self-seeds freely to maintain the colony; remove spent flowers only partially to allow sufficient seed to set. The long spurs are adapted to hawkmoth pollination, and it is an important nectar source for several sphinx moth species.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall with plenty of room for the broad pyramidal form.
directions: This iconic conifer forms a stately pyramid of silvery-blue needles, serving as a striking specimen or windbreak. Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained soil and give it space, as mature trees grow large. Water regularly while young to establish deep roots, then it tolerates cold and moderate drought well. Avoid crowding to reduce needle-cast and canker problems, and prune only to remove dead or damaged branches.

common_name: Colorado Water Lily (Changeable Apricot-Pink Hardy Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant the tuber in an aquatic basket of heavy loam topped with gravel and submerge so the crown sits 8 to 18 inches below the surface in a sunny, calm spot.
directions: Position the tuber in a container of heavy garden soil topped with gravel and lower it into the pond so the crown rests eight to eighteen inches below the water surface in full sun. This hardy changeable-type lily is prized for flowers that open a warm salmon-apricot and gradually deepen to a coppery pink as they age, giving multiple color tones on the plant at once. The lightly tea-scented blooms are held just above mottled bronze-green pads from late spring through fall. Its moderate spread makes it a good fit for mid-sized backyard ponds where a color-shifting bloom is wanted without overwhelming the water surface.

common_name: Colorific Louisiana Iris (White-Lavender Standards over Ruffled Purple Falls)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Colorific bears white standards flushed pale lavender over ruffled medium reddish-purple falls with a yellow line crest.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Colorific bears a striking bicolor pattern, white standards lightly flushed pale lavender rising above ruffled, medium reddish-purple falls marked with a bright yellow line crest at the signal, a lively two-tone contrast within a single bloom. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

subcategory: Pacific Northwest native nodding tiger lily
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4–6 inches deep in full sun to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 4–9; Columbia Tiger Lily is the iconic native lily of the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to California — producing tall, elegant stems bearing numerous nodding, brilliant-orange, Turk's Cap-style flowers with maroon spots — growing naturally in open woodland margins, meadows, and forest clearings, and historically an important food plant for many Pacific Northwest Indigenous peoples.
directions: Plant Lilium columbianum bulbs 4–6 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; provide consistent moisture through the growing season and avoid waterlogged conditions; mulch with leaf mold to keep roots cool; allow foliage to die back naturally after flowering. Columbia Tiger Lily is one of the most graceful and naturally beautiful of all North American native lilies — a hallmark wildflower of Pacific Northwest meadows, forest openings, and stream-side clearings that blooms in midsummer with dozens of brilliant orange, reflexed flowers spotted with maroon on each tall stem. The lily grows naturally in the transitional zone between open meadow and forest edge, preferring the soil moisture of forest proximity with the light of open areas — conditions replicated in the dappled shade of garden woodland margins. Many Pacific Northwest Indigenous groups — including the Chinook, Quileute, Klallam, and Quinault — ate the bulbs, roasted or boiled, as a significant starchy food source; the bulbs have a pleasantly mild, slightly bitter flavor similar to other edible lilies. An excellent plant for naturalizing in Pacific Northwest native gardens; it self-sows in suitable conditions and multiplies by bulb offsets to form larger colonies over time. Combines beautifully with Camas, Red Columbine, and native ferns.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or cold-stratify seeds indoors for 3–4 weeks before spring sowing.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface and provide 3–4 weeks of cold stratification (fall sowing outdoors achieves this naturally) to break dormancy. Columbines bloom most freely in their second and third years and are prolific self-seeders that will hybridize freely, creating a constantly shifting mix of colors. Leafminer damage creates white tunnels in the foliage but rarely threatens plant health; remove affected leaves and dispose of them. Plants are short-lived perennials (3–5 years) but the colony self-perpetuates readily through self-seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall for cold stratification and spring germination, or start indoors in late winter with 4–6 weeks of cold stratification at 35–40°F followed by germination at 60–70°F; transplant to moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall for cold stratification and spring germination, or start indoors in late winter with 4–6 weeks of cold stratification at 35–40°F followed by germination at 60–70°F; transplant to moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost. Thalictrum aquilegiifolium is one of the most beautiful and easily grown European meadow rues; its finely divided, blue-green foliage resembles columbine or maidenhair fern in texture and produces tall, airy stems in early to mid-summer bearing large, fluffy, lavender-purple to white flower clusters composed of prominent stamens rather than petals — a delicate, cloud-like effect outstanding at the back of a shaded border. In full sun it can wilt during heat waves; partial shade improves performance and longevity, especially in the South; it is excellent with hostas, astilbe, and bleeding heart in moist woodland garden borders.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; columbine meadow rue will tolerate full sun if soil remains consistently moist but looks most refined in the dappled shade of an open woodland garden.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; columbine meadow rue will tolerate full sun if soil remains consistently moist but looks most refined in the dappled shade of an open woodland garden. Thalictrum aquilegifolium is arguably the most beautiful of the meadow rues, with large, glaucous, blue-green leaves so similar in shape to columbine (Aquilegia) that the plant appears to be a columbine when not in flower; in late spring and early summer it produces large, fluffy, globe-shaped panicles of tiny flowers in lilac-purple, rose, or white (var. album) formed entirely of prominent stamens without petals, giving the flower heads an unusually light, powder-puff texture. It makes an outstanding companion for hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials and is long-lived and essentially care-free once established.

plant_note: Surface sow, as the seed needs light; stock thrives in cool weather.
directions: Start seed indoors and surface sow, since stock germinates best with light, then transplant while the weather is still cool. This blend forms upright, single-stemmed columns of fully double, clove-scented blooms excellent for bouquets and drying. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and even moisture, and set plants out early because stock dislikes summer heat. It performs especially well in containers and cool spring gardens.

common_name: Comanche Crape Myrtle (Coral-Pink Mildew-Resistant Indian-Series Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Comanche is a 1978 U.S. National Arboretum release from the Indian-series breeding program valued for coral-pink flowers and good mildew resistance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Comanche is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, an interspecific hybrid of Lagerstroemia indica and Lagerstroemia fauriei released in 1978 for improved powdery mildew resistance over older all-indica cultivars, bearing large clusters of coral-pink flowers through summer on a medium-to-large tree. Like other Indian-series crape myrtles it develops attractive exfoliating bark and good fall foliage color, adding multi-season interest beyond the summer bloom. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Comanche Water Lily (Changeable Peach-to-Copper Hardy Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun; Comanche is a classic changeable-color Marliac-type water lily, its flower color shifting noticeably over the several days each bloom is open.
directions: Comanche is a classic changeable hardy water lily, opening a warm peachy-apricot on its first day and deepening through copper-orange to a rich burnt-red-orange by the final day of bloom, giving a single planting a constantly shifting color display over its bloom cycle. The cupped flowers are held over mottled, purple-flecked green foliage typical of the older Marliac-bred hardy water lily lines. Divide rhizomes every two to three years when they crowd their container, and feed during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets pushed into the soil for the strongest, most reliable bloom.

plant_note: Plant in spring once soils have warmed in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun. In zones 7-8 provide a light mulch over the root crown in winter for added protection.
directions: Comfortroot is a native Hibiscus of wet longleaf pine flatwoods, bogs, and seasonal wetlands along the southeastern coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida, bearing cream-white to pale yellow flowers with a striking dark maroon eye from July through September. Its deeply lobed, palmate leaves give it a distinctive texture among native mallows, and its smaller stature compared to showier rose mallows makes it useful in tighter planting schemes. Grow in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, nutrient-poor soil in full sun, mimicking the conditions of its native longleaf pine savanna habitat. An excellent, low-maintenance native for Gulf Coast landscapes, rain gardens, and longleaf pine ecosystem restorations where most ornamentals would struggle.

common_name: Command Performance Peony (Full Double Vivid Coral-Pink)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Command Performance is a full double peony in vivid coral-pink with a strong upright habit.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Command Performance bears large, full double flowers in vivid, saturated coral-pink on an especially strong, upright plant that holds its heavy blooms well without excessive flopping, an advantage over some floppier double peony cultivars. Its bright color and sturdy habit have made it a reliable choice for both garden display and cutting. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Commander Hay Hens and Chicks (Large Purple-Centered Sempervivum)
plant_note: Plant offsets in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun.
directions: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun, and remove faded rosettes after they bloom and die to keep the mat tidy. Commander Hay is one of the older, best-known large-rosette sempervivum cultivars, an Award of Garden Merit winner with broad, deep maroon-purple centers shading out to bright green leaf tips, giving mature clumps a striking two-toned, almost metallic look. Its bigger-than-average 4–5 inch rosettes make it a strong single-specimen focal point in rock gardens and alpine troughs, not just a filler groundcover, while it still spreads readily by offsets over time. Like all sempervivums it needs sharp drainage and full sun to hold its best color and dense form, fading and stretching in shade.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seed for several weeks, then direct-sow shallowly in spring; division of established rhizome clumps is an easier, faster route.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun or light shade, giving it room to spread by rhizome since it forms colonies over time. Small, bell-shaped white to greenish flower clusters appear in early to midsummer and are disproportionately attractive to pollinators for their size, drawing large numbers of native bees, honeybees, and butterflies, including many that get their tongues briefly trapped by the flower's sticky pollen mechanism. The milky latex sap and reddish stems distinguish it from true hemp, and the plant was historically used by Indigenous peoples for its strong bast fibers. Because it spreads assertively once established, it is best placed in a naturalized meadow or pollinator patch rather than a small formal bed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; common bamboo is one of the most widely distributed bamboos in the tropics and subtropics but is frost-tender and only reliably hardy in the warmest parts of zone 9 and up.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with room for a large, dense clump, since this tropical timber bamboo forms tall, thick culms and does not run aggressively the way many temperate bamboos do.
