directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving some afternoon shade in the hottest climates to preserve the best leaf coloring. Cooperi is one of the oldest and most distinctive tropical hibiscus cultivars, grown as much for its narrow, pointed leaves splashed in green, cream, and pink as for its single scarlet-red flowers, giving the shrub year-round ornamental interest even between bloom flushes. The variegation is often most vivid on new growth and in brighter light, fading somewhat in deep shade. Prune to shape and remove any reverted solid-green shoots, which grow more vigorously than the variegated growth and can overtake the plant if left unchecked; feed with a slow-release fertilizer through the growing season for the best color and bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cootamundra wattle is fast-growing and may bloom in 2–3 years from seed. It is short-lived (10–15 years) but spectacular during its prime years. In zone 9 it can be grown as a large shrub or small tree reaching 15–20 feet. Seed coats require nicking or brief boiling water treatment before sowing. In southern and eastern Australia it is listed as invasive outside its native range. All plant parts are potential allergens.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cootamundra wattle is one of the most widely grown and most spectacular of the Australian wattles — a fast-growing, relatively short-lived (10–15 year) small tree or large shrub of exceptional beauty in late winter and early spring when the entire tree is covered in a cloud of hundreds of tiny, intensely fragrant, bright golden-yellow, spherical flower pom-poms against a foil of finely divided, beautiful, silver-blue to blue-gray, twice-pinnate foliage. The silver-blue leaf color and golden-yellow flowers in combination create a vivid contrast of cool silver and warm gold that is one of the most striking color combinations in all of winter horticulture, and a tree in full bloom — the silvery foliage invisible beneath a total coating of brilliant, fragrant, golden-yellow — represents one of the most theatrical winter spectacles in zone 9 gardens. The flowers are intensely fragrant, the sweet, honey-like scent carrying for considerable distances in calm winter air. Fast-growing, drought-tolerant once established, and relatively inexpensive to purchase — making it one of the most rewarding, high-impact winter-flowering investments in the zone 9 garden. Short-lived but worth replanting.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; beech resents root disturbance and compacted soil, so choose a permanent site with plenty of room to grow.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade, choosing a permanent location since beech roots are shallow and easily damaged by digging or soil compaction nearby. Copper Beech is a classic purple-leaved selection of European beech, prized for foliage that emerges deep purple-bronze in spring and generally holds a rich copper-purple color through summer before turning bronze-gold in fall, providing dramatic color contrast as a specimen or shade tree. It grows into a large, dense, majestic tree with smooth gray bark that stays attractive through winter, and its lower branches sweep gracefully toward the ground if left unpruned, though it can also be limbed up for a more traditional shade-tree form. It is a slow to moderate grower that rewards patience with great longevity, but it needs a real winter chill and struggles with the heat and humidity of the Deep South, performing best in cooler temperate climates well outside zone 9.

common_name: Copper Canyon Daisy (Mountain Marigold, Lemmon's Marigold)
plant_note: Root tip cuttings easily in spring or plant container-grown transplants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; copper canyon daisy is native to Copper Canyon (Barranca del Cobre) in Mexico and is drought tolerant once established. Prune by one-third after bloom flushes to maintain compact shape.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; copper canyon daisy is one of the finest large perennial flowering shrubs for zone 8–11 gardens — a sprawling, aromatic shrub covered in masses of small, bright golden-yellow daisy flowers in fall and winter (and sometimes spring) when very little else is blooming. The deeply divided, fernlike leaves are pungently aromatic (a strong citrus-mint-marigold scent that is powerfully deer repellent) and retain an attractive gray-green color through much of the year. It is outstanding for fall color, butterfly attraction, and combining with blue salvias or purple ageratum for a stunning gold-and-purple fall combination. Prune back by one-third after each bloom flush to keep the plant compact; an unpruned shrub can spread to 6 feet or more. In zone 8, top growth may be killed by hard freezes but roots resprout reliably.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Copper Frost holds its silvery overlay best out of hot afternoon sun.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Copper Frost holds its silvery overlay best out of hot afternoon sun. Deeply cut, coppery-orange leaves are brushed with a metallic silver overlay along the veins, deepening in tone through the cooler months and providing striking color contrast against greener shade companions. Airy, wiry stems carry small creamy-white flowers above the foliage in late spring, drawing in early bumblebees. Clumping and slow to spread, it holds a tidy shape for years without becoming invasive, making it a reliable choice for edging shaded beds, container plantings, or the front of a woodland border; divide only when the crown becomes congested, typically after three to four years.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to early fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; fall planting allows roots to establish before winter.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; copper iris is the only native American iris with brick-red to burnt-orange-copper flowers — a unique and striking color that no other wild iris can match. It grows naturally in swamps, bayou margins, and bottomland forests of the lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf Coast, where it tolerates periodic inundation. The plant is one of the parent species of the spectacular Louisiana iris hybrids and contributes their warm red-copper-orange color range to hybrid cultivars. Plant at pond margins, in consistently wet rain garden areas, or in soil that stays moist throughout the growing season. It spreads by rhizome into colonies and can be divided in late summer to expand plantings.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; copper lily is native to the dry, grassy prairies and roadsides of the Gulf Coast and performs best with a summer dry period followed by rainfall to trigger flowering.
directions: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — copper lily is a charming, small-bulbed rain lily native to the coastal prairies and grassy roadsides of southeastern Texas and Louisiana, producing star-shaped, copper-pink to rosy-pink flowers on short scapes in late summer and fall following rain events. Like all rain lilies, the flowers appear seemingly overnight after summer storms or irrigation, lasting 2–3 days before fading, with successive flushes following each rain. The narrow, rush-like leaves are nearly evergreen in zone 9–10 and die back in hard freezes. It naturalizes freely in well-drained, open soils, spreading by both offsets and seed to form dense, floriferous colonies in lawn-edge plantings, rock gardens, and sunny to lightly shaded perennial borders. An outstanding low-maintenance bulb for the Gulf Coast that requires no irrigation once established in well-adapted soils.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Aeonium decorum branches freely and forms a dense, multi-rosette mound over time.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Aeonium decorum branches freely and forms a dense, multi-rosette mound over time. Small to medium rosettes of pale green leaves edged in fine reddish cilia branch freely from woody stems, quickly forming a dense, bushy mound of dozens of small pinwheel-shaped rosettes, and popular variegated selections add cream and pink striping to the already attractive foliage. Its compact size and freely branching habit make it one of the easier aeoniums to grow into a full, well-shaped specimen relatively quickly compared to slower, less-branching relatives. Water occasionally through the cooler growing season, reduce watering during summer semi-dormancy, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix at 70–80°F and transplant after all frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil in zone 10–12, or use as an annual container specimen in colder climates.
directions: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix at 70–80°F and transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; copper plant is a bold tropical foliage shrub whose large, oval, copper-bronze to reddish-burgundy leaves streaked with pink, orange, and green provide unmatched color intensity in summer beds and containers. In full sun the leaf coloration is most vibrant — partial shade produces larger but less intensely colored leaves. Plants grow rapidly to 4–6 feet in a warm season, making them excellent privacy screens and bold border backdrops in zone 10–12. Fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer for the best leaf color and take cuttings in late summer before frost to overwinter rooted plants indoors; in frost-free zone 10–12 it is a year-round landscape shrub.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; copper rain lily blooms in late summer following rain events, similarly to zephyranthes rain lilies, producing distinctive funnel-shaped flowers held at an angle (not fully upright) in warm coppery-orange to reddish-orange on the outer surfaces, yellow inside. It naturalizes freely by seed in the Gulf Coast region and can become a pleasant garden colonizer in lawns and dry borders.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; copper rain lily is a South American Habranthus species that has naturalized across the Gulf Coast states from Texas to Florida and distinguished itself from the white zephyranthes rain lilies by its warm, coppery-orange to burnt-orange and yellow flower color — a unique warm-toned rain lily that fills a color niche (orange-copper funnel flowers) that no other commonly grown species covers. The flowers are held at a distinctive 45-degree angle (Habranthus, meaning 'graceful flower', characteristically tilts its flowers rather than holding them erect like Zephyranthes), giving each stem a graceful, nodding poise rather than the stiffly upright stance of Zephyranthes. The outer surfaces of the tepals are a warm reddish-copper to coppery-orange; the inner faces are yellow, creating a bicolor effect when viewed from below. Like its zephyranthes relatives, it flowers in flushes following summer rain events, producing masses of small, coppery blooms simultaneously across a naturalized planting. It self-seeds freely in Gulf Coast conditions and can colonize dry lawns and open garden areas without supplemental care. A delightful, self-sustaining small bulb for naturalistic and lawn-edge plantings.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Copper Spoons develops its richest metallic bronze color in bright, direct light.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Copper Spoons develops its richest metallic bronze color in bright, direct light. Thick, rounded, spoon-shaped leaves are coated in a dense, felted, rusty-copper fuzz on their new growth, aging to a more silvery-bronze tone, giving this Madagascar shrub a warm, metallic sheen unlike almost any other commonly grown succulent, produced on a substantial woody-based shrub that can eventually reach shoulder height or taller. Small yellow flowers appear occasionally but the plant is grown chiefly for its striking coppery foliage color, which intensifies with age and bright sun exposure. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide maximum bright light for the deepest copper coloring, and prune to shape as the shrub matures.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; copperleaf is a bold tropical foliage plant that provides outstanding summer color in zone 9 gardens where it is grown as a summer annual or tender perennial.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; copperleaf holds its most vivid foliage colors in full sun — in shade the color becomes less intense. Acalypha wilkesiana (copperleaf or Jacob's coat) is a tropical Pacific Island shrub grown worldwide as a tropical foliage plant for its spectacularly colorful, large (3–5 inch), copper-red, bronze, maroon, red-orange, yellow, or multicolor variegated leaves in an enormous range of named cultivars — each leaf is often a mosaic of two or three colors in irregular patterns or in distinct margins. The effect in mass plantings is bold and tropical, creating intense color impact that few other foliage plants can match in summer heat. Common cultivar groups include 'Mosaica' (rich coppery-red), 'Marginata' (green leaves with copper-red margins), 'Musaica' (orange to bronze), and 'Tricolor' (red, pink, and green). In zones 9–12, copperleaf grows as a perennial shrub; in colder zones, root cuttings in fall and overwinter indoors. It thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity and is essentially pest-free in those conditions, making it one of the best choices for low-maintenance tropical-themed summer color.

common_name: Coppertina Ninebark (Copper-Orange New Growth Foliage Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Coppertina emerges bright coppery-orange in spring, deepening to burgundy-red as the foliage matures through summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Coppertina stands out among dark-leaved ninebarks for its color-shifting foliage, emerging a vivid coppery-orange in spring before deepening to a rich burgundy-red through summer, a warmer tone than the near-black purple of Diabolo, with clusters of small white-to-pink flowers in late spring followed by reddish seed capsules and exfoliating bark for winter interest. Full sun brings out the most vivid color contrast between new and mature growth, while shadier sites mute the effect. It tolerates a wide range of soil conditions and needs only occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems at the base each year to keep the shrub full and encourage the brightest new copper growth.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; like other distylium cultivars, Coppertone is remarkably adaptable to both wet and dry sites and to sun or shade once established.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it as a low-maintenance evergreen hedge, foundation shrub, or mass planting where deer pressure is a concern, since distylium is rarely browsed. Coppertone is a First Editions selection of distylium prized for its striking bronze-copper new growth in spring, which matures to glossy dark green, giving the shrub a two-toned seasonal display on a mounding, medium-sized evergreen frame, with small maroon-red flowers appearing inconspicuously along the stems in late winter. It shares the exceptional adaptability of the species — thriving in full sun or full shade, wet or dry soil, and resisting the leaf spot and scale problems that trouble many broadleaf evergreens in humid Gulf South summers. Requires only occasional shaping, as its naturally dense, mounded form rarely needs hard pruning.

plant_note: Take stem cuttings in spring, callus the cut ends for two to three days, then set into gritty succulent mix and water lightly until roots form.
directions: Plant in well-drained containers or rock gardens with full sun exposure to develop its signature copper-orange coloring, which fades to yellow-green in shade. Allow the soil to dry completely between waterings and protect the plant from frost, bringing containers indoors where winters are cold. The fleshy, pointed leaves form loose rosettes on trailing stems that cascade attractively over pot edges and low walls. Clusters of small white star-shaped flowers appear on tall stalks above the foliage in late winter or spring.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; coppery mesemb is widely used along roadsides and highway slopes for erosion control because of its rapid, dense spread.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; coppery mesemb forms a dense, fast-spreading mat of gray-green, cylindrical succulent leaves studded with copper-orange to salmon flowers with a yellow center, opening in bright sun over a long spring to summer bloom season. Its rapid growth and deep, soil-binding root system make it one of the most widely planted groundcovers for erosion control on dry highway embankments, freeway slopes, and other large, difficult-to-irrigate sites. It tolerates poor, sandy, and saline soil with ease, needing supplemental water only to establish a new planting, after which mature mats are essentially self-sufficient on rainfall alone in mild coastal climates. Being frost-tender, it is best reserved for essentially frost-free gardens or replanted annually from cuttings where hard freezes are likely.

common_name: Cora Cascade Vinca (Trailing Disease-Resistant Annual Vinca)
plant_note: Transplant out after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, ideally two to three weeks after the last frost; Cora Cascade is a trailing habit selection bred for the same aerial and soil-borne disease resistance as the upright Cora series.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil or containers in full sun after the soil has warmed, since cool, wet conditions invite the root and stem rot that vinca is otherwise notably prone to. Cora Cascade brings the upright Cora series' breakthrough resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight and root rot to a low, trailing habit suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and groundcover use, spilling over container edges in a dense mound of glossy foliage covered in flat, five-petaled blooms from late spring through the first frost. It shrugs off heat, humidity, and drought once established, needing far less water than the disease-prone open-pollinated vincas of decades past, and rarely requires deadheading since spent flowers are self-cleaning. Avoid overhead watering and overly rich, waterlogged soil, both of which undercut its main advantage over older vinca types.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Cora series annual vinca has superior disease resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight — a serious fungal disease of annual vinca (Catharanthus) in hot, humid conditions like zone 9's summer — making it significantly more reliable in the Gulf South than older vinca varieties. In zone 9 annual vinca is one of the most heat-tolerant and long-blooming summer bedding plants available; Cora Cherry thrives in the hottest, most humid summer weeks when most other annuals decline. The plant is self-cleaning — old flowers drop off without deadheading, keeping the plant tidy throughout the season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — annual vinca thrives in heat and performs poorly in cool, wet, or poorly drained conditions; Cora Cherry is an All-America Selections award-winning annual vinca (Catharanthus roseus) from the Cora series, producing vivid, deep cherry-red, five-petaled flowers with a contrasting white eye that bloom continuously from planting until frost without deadheading. Annual vinca (technically not a true vinca but sharing the common name due to similar flower appearance) is among the top performers for hot, humid summer bedding in zone 9 — it genuinely thrives in tropical heat and actually improves in flowering intensity as temperatures rise. The Cora series was specifically bred for resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight, a fungal disease that devastates vinca plantings in humid summer conditions typical of the Gulf South; this disease resistance makes Cora dramatically more reliable than older annual vinca varieties in zone 9. The intense cherry-red flowers and the plant's exceptional summer performance make Cora Cherry one of the best red bedding annuals available for Gulf Coast summer gardens where heat and humidity challenge most alternatives.

common_name: Cora Louise Itoh Peony (White Lavender-Flared Intersectional Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Cora Louise bears large, semi-double, near-white flowers brushed with fine violet-purple flares near the center around a boss of gold stamens, a refined, orchid-like combination on a compact, densely branched plant that rarely needs staking. Like other Itoh hybrids it blooms over a longer season than herbaceous peonies because a single stout stem carries multiple buds that open in sequence, and the clean, deeply lobed foliage holds up well through summer heat and humidity. It tolerates more heat and a broader soil pH range than traditional herbaceous peony cultivars, making it a good choice for gardeners at the warmer edge of the peony-growing range who still get enough winter chill to trigger reliable bloom.

common_name: Cora Orchid Vinca (Disease-Resistant Lavender-Orchid Annual Vinca)
plant_note: Transplant into warm soil a week or two after the last frost once nights stay reliably above 60°F; like other Cora selections, Cora Orchid resists the Phytophthora and Aerial Blight diseases that devastate older vinca strains in hot, humid, rainy Gulf South summers.
directions: Cora Orchid carries soft lavender-orchid flowers with the same rounded, five-petaled form as other vinca, standing out among the more common white, pink, and red vinca shades for its cool, unusual pastel tone. It shares the Cora series' strong resistance to soilborne and foliar blight diseases that plague older heirloom vinca strains in wet, humid weather, making it dramatically more reliable in Gulf South plantings that see frequent summer rain. Once established it is remarkably heat- and drought-tolerant, blooming continuously from late spring through the first frost with essentially no deadheading, and its toughness has made the Cora series a standard choice for low-maintenance municipal and home landscape plantings across the Deep South.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Cora is a vegetatively propagated vinca series from Syngenta Flowers — one of the highest-performing Catharanthus series for heat, humidity, and Phytophthora blight resistance. The Cora series is widely used in commercial landscaping and public plantings throughout the Gulf South precisely because of its superior disease resistance and longer season performance compared to seed-grown vinca series. Cora Strawberry produces vivid strawberry-red to rose-red flowers with a white central eye on plants with notably glossy, dark green foliage — the glossy foliage being a distinguishing trait of the Cora series that provides additional ornamental value between flower cycles.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent moisture during establishment — Cora Strawberry Vinca is extremely heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant once established, requiring minimal water and no deadheading to maintain continuous bloom; Cora Strawberry Vinca is a premium, vegetatively propagated Catharanthus roseus cultivar producing vivid strawberry-red flowers with a white central eye on compact, well-branched, glossy-leaved plants — one of the highest-rated commercial vinca series for disease resistance, heat performance, and season-long ornamental quality in the Gulf South landscape. The Cora series distinguishes itself from seed-grown vinca series through consistently higher resistance to Phytophthora crown rot — the primary disease that limits annual vinca performance in humid zone 9 conditions — and through the notably glossy, dark green foliage that remains attractive throughout the season regardless of flowering intensity. Catharanthus roseus (annual vinca, Madagascar periwinkle) is the quintessential Gulf South summer annual — heat-thriving, drought-tolerant, self-cleaning, and maintaining its bloom display through the peak summer conditions of July–September that challenge most other annual species. The vivid strawberry-red with white eye of Cora Strawberry provides one of the most visually energetic bicolor combinations available in the vinca color range — the strawberry-red and white creating a lively, high-contrast display effective in both formal mass planting and mixed container compositions.

common_name: Cora Stubbs Peony (Japanese-Form Rose-Pink with Pink-and-Cream Center)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cora Stubbs is a Japanese-form peony with rose-pink outer petals and pink-and-cream staminodes.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cora Stubbs bears a Japanese-form flower, a ring of broad, rose-pink guard petals surrounding a dense center of narrower staminodes blended pink and cream, a softer, more textured center than the vivid contrast of Gay Paree, and highly attractive to bees since the flower's structure remains more open than a fully double bloom. Its refined color combination has made it a popular choice among peony collectors. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Cora Vinca (Disease-Resistant Heat-Tolerant Annual Vinca Series)
plant_note: Transplant into warm soil a week or two after the last frost once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Cora thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South summer and is one of the few bedding annuals that shrugs off Phytophthora blight in wet soil.
directions: Transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid overhead irrigation late in the day since even this disease-resistant series performs best with good air movement around the crown. Cora was bred specifically for strong resistance to Phytophthora and Aerial Blight, the soilborne and foliar diseases that devastate older annual vinca plantings in hot, humid, rainy summers, making it dramatically more reliable than heirloom vinca strains in Gulf Coast beds and highway medians. Once established it is remarkably drought- and heat-tolerant, blooming continuously from late spring through the first frost with almost no deadheading or maintenance required. Its toughness and disease resistance have made it a standard choice for low-input municipal and commercial plantings as well as home landscapes across the Deep South.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; coral aloe is the most cold-tolerant flat-leafed aloe and tolerates brief freezes to 25°F. It requires less water than most garden plants but is killed by prolonged wet soil. One of the finest aloes for mild-climate gardens as it is spineless (safe for children), ornamental, and produces outstanding hummingbird-attracting flowers.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; coral aloe is widely considered one of the finest landscape aloes for mild-climate gardens — a flat-growing, rosette-forming South African species completely lacking the teeth and spines that make most aloes difficult to handle. The broad, smooth, glaucous blue-gray to gray-green leaves with thin, pinkish margins are attractive all year, taking on warm peach-apricot tones in cool weather. In winter to spring, dramatic branched flower spikes arise carrying clusters of vivid coral-red to orange tubular flowers that attract hummingbirds in numbers throughout the winter and early spring, providing a critical nectar source when little else is in bloom. Coral aloe spreads slowly by offsets to form impressive colonies and is an outstanding, child-safe alternative to spiny aloes in gardens frequented by children. Its lack of spines, glaucous foliage, spectacular winter flowers, and hummingbird attraction make it arguably the most garden-worthy of the commonly available aloes.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with protection from hot afternoon sun.
directions: Prized for its glowing coral-red winter bark, this Japanese maple also offers soft green spring foliage that shifts to golden-yellow in fall. Plant in part shade with rich, moist, well-drained soil, protecting it from drying wind and intense afternoon sun that can scorch leaves. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist. Prune minimally in late winter to reveal the colorful stems and maintain the graceful branching form.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 8 the stems freeze to the ground in hard winters but resprout vigorously from the deep, heat-tolerant root system each spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; coral bean is one of the most striking native shrubs of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, producing brilliant scarlet tubular flowers in long spikes in spring before the leaves emerge — they are among the most important hummingbird nectar plants in the Southeast. In fall the pods split open to reveal vivid coral-red seeds that are highly ornamental but extremely toxic if swallowed. The stems bear recurved spines that deter browsing; the plant dies to the ground in hard freezes in zone 7–8 but regrows rapidly from an established root crown. It tolerates partial shade, sandy soil, drought, and salt spray — making it an outstanding native plant for difficult spots in Gulf Coast gardens. The red seeds were traditionally used as ornamentation and have important Native American cultural uses.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface sow as seeds need light to germinate — do not cover.
directions: Press seeds onto the surface of a moist germination medium — do not cover, as light is required for germination; transplant to a humus-rich, well-drained site after last frost. Grown primarily for their spectacular mound-forming foliage in shades of burgundy, copper, lime, silver, and purple, heucheras also produce airy wands of tiny flowers beloved by hummingbirds. Divide every 3–4 years in early spring to rejuvenate the woody crowns; reset divisions with the crown at soil level. Most modern hybrids tolerate more sun with adequate moisture but prefer afternoon shade in hot climates.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; coral bells is the species whose brilliant red flowers gave rise to the name and most early flower-heuchera hybrids.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; coral bells from the Southwest requires excellent drainage and is less tolerant of heavy clay or wet soils than eastern heuchera species. Heuchera sanguinea is a native of the Rocky Mountains and northern Mexico and is the species whose brilliant, bell-shaped, red to coral-red flowers on tall, wiry scapes gave rise to the common name "coral bells"; it produces rounded, scalloped, dark-green leaves with light-silver marbling and bears 12–18-inch flowering stems in late spring and early summer that are exceptional as cut flowers and irresistible to hummingbirds. Unlike the foliage heucheras derived from H. americana and H. villosa, H. sanguinea is grown primarily for its flower show; the named cultivars 'Firefly', 'Splendens', and 'White Cloud' are classic garden selections, and many modern landscape heucheras carry its flower genes.

common_name: Coral Bells Azalea (Classic Coral-Pink Masses-of-Bloom Kurume Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Kurume azaleas perform best in morning sun with afternoon shade protection in Gulf South climates — afternoon shade reduces heat and drought stress during the critical summer period.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Coral Bells is a classic Kurume azalea cultivar — one of the Japanese Kurume (city of origin, Kurume, Japan) hybrids that are among the most widely planted azaleas in the American South, characterized by small, glossy leaves, compact mounding habit, and spring flowering so profuse that the foliage can be completely obscured by flowers. The spring bloom display of 'Coral Bells' — masses of small, hose-in-hose (double) to single, coral-pink to warm rose-pink flowers covering the entire plant simultaneously — is one of the quintessential signs of Gulf South spring alongside dogwood and wisteria. The hose-in-hose flower form (one flower nestled inside another, giving the appearance of a double flower with extra petals) is characteristic of many Kurume cultivars and adds ornamental complexity to each individual flower. In zone 9, Kurume azaleas perform as reliable evergreen foundation and landscape shrubs that require only occasional pruning after bloom to maintain their compact, mounded habit. The small, glossy, dark-green leaves provide attractive year-round structure. Strongly acidic, humus-rich soil and consistent moisture are the most critical requirements — chlorosis from insufficient acidity is the most common cultural problem, corrected by soil acidification with sulfur and acid-forming fertilizers.

common_name: Coral Berry Ardisia (Christmas Berry, Hen's Eyes, Marlberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in partial to deep shade under established trees; Ardisia crenata thrives in the dry, root-competitive shade beneath mature live oaks and other large trees where most ornamentals fail. In zone 9a, plants may freeze to the ground in hard winters but resprout from the crown in spring. INVASIVE NOTE: Ardisia crenata is listed as invasive in Florida, Texas, and other Gulf Coast states where birds disperse seeds into natural areas — do not plant near forests, wetlands, or parks. Legally restricted in some counties.
directions: Plant in partial to deep shade in any well-drained soil — Coral Berry Ardisia is one of the most shade- and drought-tolerant small shrubs available, performing in conditions of deep dry shade under large oaks that defeat nearly all other ornamentals. Ardisia crenata (also listed as A. crispa) is a small, upright evergreen shrub from India, Southeast Asia, and Japan in the Primulaceae family that produces one of the most striking winter ornamental displays in zone 9 gardens: during November–February, pendulous clusters of bright coral-red to vivid scarlet round berries the size of small pearls hang in dramatic arching sprays below the dark, glossy, wavy-edged, evergreen leaves. The berries persist on the plant for months, and fully loaded plants in December–January are extraordinarily ornamental. The plant blooms in summer with small, inconspicuous white to pinkish flowers that are followed by the developing berries. White-berried ('Alba') and pink-berried forms are available. CAUTION: Classified as invasive in Florida, Texas, Louisiana, Georgia, and other Gulf and Southeast states — birds devour the berries and disperse seeds freely into natural areas where the plant displaces native understory species. Remove berries before they fall if planting in areas with access to natural lands.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after the last frost in a location with partial shade; mulch the root zone to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature.
directions: Carolina Snailseed is a twining woody vine native to woodland edges, thickets, and fencerows across the southeastern United States. It produces small, heart-shaped to kidney-shaped leaves and inconspicuous greenish flowers on female plants in summer, followed by dense clusters of brilliant red berries in fall that persist into winter and provide important food for mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and hermit thrushes. Grow in average to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; it tolerates a range of soil conditions once established. Note that the berries, while highly attractive to wildlife, are toxic to humans — plant where children will not have unsupervised access to the fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained soil in full sun; twinspur flowers best in cool weather and benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained soil in full sun; twinspur flowers best in cool weather and benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Slender, wiry stems carry a profusion of small, coral-pink, spurred flowers over a long cool-season bloom period, more heat-tolerant and longer-lived as a perennial than many other diascia species and hybrids, native to South African mountain grasslands. It performs best in climates with mild summers or as a cool-season bedding plant further south, where the intense heat of a Gulf South or Deep South summer typically causes it to decline, making it better suited to spring and fall display than year-round performance in hot climates. Deadhead and shear lightly to encourage continued bloom, provide consistent moisture, and treat as a cool-season annual in hot-summer climates.

common_name: Coral Carpet Sedum (Fine-Textured Bronze-Red Groundcover Stonecrop)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Coral Carpet forms an extremely low, fine-textured mat that colors bronze-red in full sun and cool weather, greening somewhat in shade or high summer heat.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, even gravelly soil in full sun; this creeping stonecrop is one of the lowest-growing groundcover sedums available, forming a dense carpet barely two to three inches tall studded with tiny, bead-like leaves that shift from bronze-green in summer to a richer coral-red in full sun and cool weather. Clusters of small white starry flowers appear in early summer, but the fine, mossy foliage texture is the main draw, making it useful for planting between stepping stones, along the edges of dry rock gardens, or as a low-water lawn substitute on a small scale. It tolerates foot traffic better than most sedums but resents standing water and heavy, poorly drained soil, which quickly cause rot. It requires no fertilizing and spreads readily from small broken-off pieces that root wherever they touch soil, so division and propagation are essentially effortless.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and give plants room to reach their full 3-foot spread without crowding. Bred by Sam Wissing and introduced in 1964, Coral Charm opens a vivid coral-orange and fades gracefully through peach to soft cream-pink as each large, semi-double flower ages, so a single plant can show several shades at once during peak bloom. It is an early-season bloomer with strong, upright stems that rarely need staking, and it has become one of the most widely planted of the coral-toned peonies for its vigor and reliable performance. Full sun and excellent drainage are essential; wet feet in winter are more likely than heat to kill an established peony.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or small container plants in spring once the soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; roots readily from stem cuttings and is rarely propagated from seed in cultivation.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or small container plants in spring once the soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; coral creeper spreads by rooting stems as it grows, forming a low, dense mat useful as a border edging or filler beneath larger shrubs and trees. Salmon-pink to coral-red tubular flowers appear in flushes almost year-round in frost-free climates, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds, and the semi-glossy foliage stays attractive in light shade where many flowering groundcovers thin out. It is easy to propagate and quick to fill in a bed, but is strictly tropical and tender, dying back or dying out in any real frost.

plant_note: Transplant container-grown plants in spring into well-drained soil, spacing closely to form a continuous low groundcover.
directions: Set plants in full sun with good drainage, watering deeply during establishment and only occasionally afterward thanks to the shrub's compact, drought-tolerant root system. A light shearing in late winter keeps the low mound shape neat and stimulates fresh bloom cycles. Semi-double coral-orange flowers with hints of yellow at the base cover the small, dense mounds of foliage from late spring through frost, a hallmark of the Drift series bred for continuous bloom and reduced disease susceptibility compared to older groundcover roses. It works well cascading over walls or spilling from raised beds and containers.

plant_note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface in fall in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; coral drops grows, flowers, and goes dormant on the Cape winter-rainfall schedule — emerging in autumn, flowering in late winter and spring, then going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer. The name 'bulbifera' refers to the bulbils produced in the leaf axils, a common propagation strategy of Cape bulbs.
directions: Plant bulbs near the soil surface in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; coral drops is one of the most colorful of the Lachenalia species — producing the characteristic two strap-shaped, often purple-spotted, somewhat succulent leaves and in late winter through spring (February–April in cultivation), dense, upright, bottlebrush-like racemes of pendant, tubular bells in a striking combination of coral-red to orange-red at the top of each tube fading through yellow to greenish-yellow at the tube base — a three-toned color scheme of warm coral, yellow, and green that is visually complex and beautiful. The bright, tricolor flower tubes are surrounded by slightly smaller outer perianth segments. It produces small bulbils in the leaf axils that fall and generate new plants when conditions are suitable — an efficient natural propagation strategy adapted to the Cape fynbos. Outstanding for container culture in zones 8–11, where the pot can be kept dry in summer. One of the most colorful and largest-flowered of the commonly grown lachenalias.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; coral fountain establishes quickly and roots readily from stem cuttings. It is outstanding cascading over walls, planted at the top of raised beds, or in hanging baskets where the arching stems can drape downward.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; coral fountain (firecracker plant) is a uniquely textural and continuously blooming tropical perennial with masses of thin, arching, rush-like green stems cascading in a weeping habit, studded nearly year-round with small, tubular, coral-red flowers that hummingbirds visit with enthusiasm. The stems have virtually no leaves — the photosynthesis occurs in the green stems themselves, giving the plant an unusual, airy, almost fern-like texture when not in bloom that is strikingly different from any other flowering plant. It is exceptionally drought, heat, and salt tolerant once established and performs at its best cascading over retaining walls, spilling from large containers, or planted in raised beds where the arching, weeping habit shows to best effect. In zone 9 it may suffer frost damage to stems but typically regrows from established roots. A yellow-flowered form is also available. One of the most reliable and continuously blooming hummingbird plants for Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Surface sow into warm soil, as the fine seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Surface sow into warm soil after frost, since the small seed needs light to germinate. Coral Fountain produces dramatic pendulous tassels in shades of coral that dry beautifully for everlasting arrangements, wreaths, and crafts. Grow in full sun with average soil and moderate water for the fullest tassels. Harvest stems as the flowers reach full color and hang them to dry.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coral gum is from the dry, hot interior goldfields region of Western Australia — requiring hot, dry conditions and excellent drainage. It blooms over a very long period (spring through summer, often year-round in warm climates) producing the distinctive coral-red to pink, ribbed, lantern-shaped buds and flowers. More reliable in hot, dry, inland Mediterranean climates than in humid coastal conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coral gum is one of the most colorful and most reliably floriferous of all ornamental eucalyptus — a small to medium-sized mallee or tree from the hot, arid goldfields of the Western Australian interior that produces over a very long season (often effectively year-round in warm climates) a succession of distinctive, beautiful coral-red to bright-pink flowers. The flower buds are themselves highly ornamental: angular, ribbed, lantern-shaped, coral-red to pink caps of distinctive sculptural form that remain on the tree in developing clusters for weeks before the cap falls and the dense, pink-red stamen clusters expand. The flowers, when open, are large clusters of vivid coral-red to rosy-pink, crimson-tipped stamens against the gray-green foliage — a rich, warm-pink to coral-red that is among the most vivid flower colors produced by any Australian tree. The combination of long bloom season, ornamental bud form, vivid flower color, and compact size (15–25 feet) makes it one of the best ornamental eucalyptus for the zone 9 garden. Native to the hot, dry goldfields of WA — a landscape of red soils, sparse desert vegetation, and blazing summer heat — it is thoroughly adapted to the hot, dry conditions of zone 9 summers.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring near a trellis, fence, or other support; stems twine and will climb 10–15 feet.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis or fence; unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle this native species is well-behaved and will not escape into natural areas. The long, tubular scarlet-to-coral flowers bloom heavily in spring and continue sporadically through fall, providing the long-tube nectar that ruby-throated hummingbirds require. Prune in late winter or just after the main spring flush to shape the vine and remove dead wood. In the deep South it is semi-evergreen and may retain foliage through mild winters; in colder zones it loses leaves but regrows vigorously from the base in spring.

subcategory: landscape shrub rose, Knock Out series
plant_note: Transplant container-grown plants in spring once frost danger has passed, spacing to allow good air movement around the mature shrub.
directions: Set plants in full sun with well-drained, fertile soil, watering consistently the first year to establish a deep root system. An occasional light pruning in late winter maintains a compact, well-branched shape and promotes vigorous new flowering wood. Single, coral-orange blooms with a lighter reverse open in flushes from late spring through fall on this compact member of the Knock Out series, bred for strong disease resistance and minimal care. The warm coral tone stands out among the more common red and pink Knock Out selections, and plants rebloom reliably without deadheading.

common_name: Coral Magic Crape Myrtle (Color-Changing Coral-to-Orange Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container plants in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Coral Magic is a compact, shrub-form crape myrtle whose flower color shifts from coral-orange to deeper red-orange as blooms age, giving a multi-toned display.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Coral Magic is part of a compact, shrub-sized series of crape myrtles bred for smaller landscapes, foundation plantings, and large containers, bearing clusters of vivid coral-orange flowers that deepen toward red-orange as they age, so a single truss shows several tones at once through the long summer bloom season. Its naturally rounded, dense habit needs little to no pruning to maintain shape, unlike full-size crape myrtles that are often disfigured by improper topping, and it shares the improved powdery mildew resistance of modern breeding. Water regularly the first season to establish a deep root system; established plants are drought-tolerant and need only occasional deep watering through summer.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Coral Nymph is a distinctive bicolor selection of the native tropical sage with salmon-pink and white two-toned flowers, more delicate in appearance than standard red S. coccinea and outstanding in heat-tolerant garden designs for the Gulf Coast and Deep South.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into well-drained, moderately fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade. Coral Nymph is a bicolor-flowered cultivar of the native American Salvia coccinea (tropical sage), producing distinctive two-toned flowers with salmon-coral upper lips and soft white lower lips on the same spikes — a gentler, more pastel coloration than the vivid red of the species that combines well with soft-colored perennial plantings. Like all S. coccinea cultivars, it is heat- and humidity-tolerant in the extreme, blooming continuously through Gulf Coast and Southern summers without deadheading, and self-seeds prolifically so that a single planting effectively perpetuates itself. Outstanding for hummingbird and butterfly gardens; annual in most zones but naturalized and perennial in zone 9–11.

common_name: Coral Nymph Salvia (Bicolor Coral and White Tropical Sage)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Coral Nymph self-seeds freely in zone 9 — mark seedling locations to preserve self-sown plants that often bloom earlier and more prolifically than transplants.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Coral Nymph is the most distinctive color form of Salvia coccinea (tropical sage or scarlet sage) — producing flowers with a rich salmon-coral upper lip (hood) and a creamy-white lower lip in a distinctive bicolor combination that creates a softer, more complex color effect than the pure red or pure white solid-colored forms. The 18–30 inch upright plants produce slender, whorled flower spikes continuously from late spring through hard frost (and year-round in frost-free zone 9 winters). Salvia coccinea is a Gulf South native — naturally occurring in coastal woods and disturbed areas from the Carolinas to Florida and Texas — making Coral Nymph perfectly adapted to Gulf South heat, humidity, and summer conditions. Unlike many salvias that are sensitive to Gulf South summer heat, S. coccinea thrives through the hottest months and actually intensifies its bloom production in late summer and fall. Coral Nymph self-seeds freely in zone 9 gardens, creating a self-maintaining annual colony that renews itself without replanting. Hummingbirds, sphinx moths, and several butterfly species visit the tubular flowers throughout the long bloom season. The partial-shade tolerance is a practical advantage for gardeners who want color in less-than-full-sun areas — Coral Nymph blooms acceptably in 3–4 hours of direct sun per day.

common_name: Coral Plant (Coral Physic Nut, Multifid Jatropha, Physic Nut)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs after last frost in full sun with well-drained soil; Coral Plant grows rapidly in warm conditions and can reach 10 feet in zone 9-10. In zone 9a, it freezes to the ground or roots in cold winters but resprouts vigorously in spring; in zone 9b-10 it is a reliable semi-evergreen shrub. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are highly toxic — the seeds in particular contain curcin and ricin-like toxins and are potentially lethal if consumed by children or pets. The milky sap is also irritating.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Coral Plant is drought-tolerant and thrives in the poor, well-drained soils of zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes, tolerating the summer heat and periodic drought that challenges many tropical ornamentals. Jatropha multifida is a large, architectural shrub or small tree from tropical America (Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean) grown throughout the subtropical world for its striking combination of deeply lobed, palm-like leaves and vivid coral-red to scarlet flowers. The foliage is dramatically ornamental: large (up to 15 inches across), deeply cut into 7–11 finger-like lobes reminiscent of a Cannabis or Ricinus leaf, on long, flexible petioles that give the plant a bold, tropical sculptural quality. The flowers are borne in flat-topped clusters of tiny, brilliant coral-red, star-shaped blooms that appear prolifically at the branch tips throughout the warm season, attracting butterflies and occasionally hummingbirds. The interesting three-lobed fruit capsules that follow contain large seeds that, while potentially useful as a biofuel crop in some tropical production systems, are highly toxic and should not be consumed. In zone 9, Coral Plant is a fast-growing tropical accent that provides months of flowering interest and bold architectural foliage through the summer and fall.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; coral plant is a fast-growing, drought-tolerant tropical perennial that produces its best growth and blooms in warm, sunny conditions, yet also tolerates more shade than most flowering shrubs.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; coral plant is drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms more heavily under mild drought stress. Russelia equisetiformis (coral plant or firecracker fern) is a Mexican native producing a dense, weeping, fountain-like mound of slender, rush-like, bright-green to gray-green photosynthetic stems (reduced leaves — hence the species name 'equisetiformis,' meaning 'horsetail-like') hung with hundreds of slender, 1-inch, bright-red tubular flowers from spring through frost. The effect is of an almost waterfall-like cascade of green stems and red flowers — one of the most graceful and romantic ornamental shrubs for tropical and subtropical gardens. Ruby-throated hummingbirds and butterflies visit the tubular flowers extensively. Coral plant is exceptionally heat, drought, and salt-tolerant once established, performing well in coastal gardens, under dry overhangs, and in containers on sunny patios. In zone 9, it dies back in hard freezes but resprouts reliably from roots; in zone 10–12, it is an evergreen perennial. It roots quickly from stem cuttings and can be propagated freely for mass plantings.

common_name: Coral Sunset Peony (Semi-Double Fading Coral-Peach to Cream)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Coral Sunset opens coral-peach and fades to soft cream, an unusual warm color rare among peony cultivars.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Coral Sunset bears semi-double flowers that open a warm coral-peach and gradually fade to soft cream as they mature, an unusual warm color rare among peony cultivars that are more typically found in shades of pink, red, and white. Its distinctive coloring has made it one of the most sought-after and widely imitated peony introductions of its era. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Plant tubers or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; coral vine is fast-growing and can cover a fence or trellis in a single season. The tuberous roots store carbohydrates and allow rapid regrowth from the base after frost damage in zone 7–8.
directions: Plant tubers in well-drained soil in full sun on a fence, trellis, or arbor; coral vine is one of the most beloved and reliable vining plants of the Gulf South — a fast-growing, drought-tolerant vine from Mexico that covers itself in sprays of small heart-shaped pink to magenta flowers in summer through frost, creating a solid curtain of pink that is irresistible to bees, particularly bumble bees and honeybees. The vine climbs by tendrils and can reach 20–30 feet when established. In zone 7–9 the tops die back in hard frost but established tuberous roots resprout vigorously each spring, often growing 10–15 feet in a single season. The flowers and tubers are edible (tubers roasted like sweet potatoes in Mexico). A white-flowered form ('Album') is less vigorous but charming. A fixture in traditional Gulf South gardens for generations.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors a few weeks earlier for a head start. Coral Zinnia carries four-to-five-inch blooms in sun-kissed coral on sturdy stems that are ideal for cutting and beloved by butterflies. Space plants for good airflow and water at the base to limit powdery mildew. Cut or deadhead often to keep the plants blooming until frost.

plant_note: Divide established suckers or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to alkaline, average to poor soil in partial to full shade in spring; coralberry is the most shade and drought tolerant of the native fruiting shrubs and excels in the deep dry shade under dense tree canopy.
directions: Divide suckers or plant container specimens in well-drained to dry, average to poor soil in partial to full shade; coralberry (Indian currant, buckbrush) is one of the most valuable and underused native shrubs for the most difficult landscape challenge: dry, deep shade under dense tree canopy where most plants refuse to grow. Coralberry not only survives in these conditions but thrives, spreading steadily by suckers to form colonies of arching, wiry stems bearing small, oval, bluish-green leaves and dense clusters of small, coral-pink to rosy-red berries that persist through winter — important food for bobwhite, pheasant, grouse, cedar waxwings, and other wildlife. Unlike most native shrubs, it tolerates alkaline soil, clay, and root competition from established trees. Its stoloniferous spreading habit makes it excellent for erosion control on shaded slopes and embankments. The cultivar 'Foliis Variegatis' has yellow-variegated leaves that are effective in lightening dark shade. Often overlooked by gardeners in favor of showier shrubs, it is irreplaceable for solving the deep-dry-shade problem.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost in warm, well-drained soil and stake tall plants.
directions: Coralie blends the most perfect blush and pink shades, pairing beautifully with other soft-toned flowers in the cutting garden. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil after the ground warms. Because the plant grows tall, provide sturdy staking or support unless you are cutting frequently. Pinch early for branching, cut often to keep blooms coming, and lift tubers to store indoors over winter in cold zones.

plant_note: Plant bulbils or rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade under beech or other deciduous trees; coralroot rarely sets seed (it relies primarily on bulbil propagation) — collect the small, dark, rice-grain-sized bulbils from the leaf axils and plant immediately, or allow them to fall naturally and naturalize. Spring ephemeral: mark locations before the foliage disappears in summer.
directions: Plant bulbils in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full shade under beech or similar large deciduous trees; coralroot is a fascinating and unusual European spring woodland plant, historically classified as Dentaria bulbifera, that reproduces primarily by dropping tiny, dark, oval bulbils from the axils of the pinnate leaves rather than by seed — a vegetative propagation strategy adapted to the deep shade of beech forest floors where seed germination is unreliable. The plant produces handsome, pinnately-divided leaves with narrow leaflets and, in April and May, slender stems bearing loose clusters of pale-pink to lilac-pink, four-petaled flowers. The distinctive bulbils are clearly visible as small, dark, rice-like structures clustered at the base of each leaf through the spring season. Rarely found in cultivation despite its quiet charm; it is a true ancient-woodland indicator species in Britain and Europe, appearing almost exclusively in woodland with unbroken centuries of continuity. Outstanding for the specialist woodland garden under large, established beeches and other canopy trees where its preferred alkaline leaf-mold soil accumulates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; cordyline tolerates wind, coastal salt spray, and brief frosts to about 14°F, making it well suited to zone 8–11 coastal and subtropical landscapes.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; cordyline creates striking architectural focal points with its long sword-like leaves radiating from a central trunk in green, burgundy, bronze, or pink depending on cultivar. Tolerant of wind, coastal salt spray, and brief frosts down to about 14°F, it thrives in zone 8–11 landscapes where it adds unmistakable tropical structure as a specimen, backdrop, or container plant. Growth is moderately fast in warm climates where it can eventually reach 15–20 feet; strip older lower leaves as they dry to maintain the clean, palm-like trunk. Water regularly until established, then reduce to occasional deep watering as it is quite drought-tolerant once roots are set.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost date; seeds tolerate light frost and germinate best in cool soil.
directions: Sow seed on the soil surface and tamp lightly; good drainage is essential since coreopsis rots in wet soil over winter. Deadhead regularly to keep the bright yellow flowers coming all summer. Shear plants back by half after the first flush to encourage compact regrowth and a second bloom. Divide clumps every 2–3 years in spring to prevent the center from dying out.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; cork-stemmed passionflower is native to the tropical Americas and naturalized throughout the Gulf South, where it grows in disturbed habitats, forest margins, and coastal thickets.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; cork-stemmed passionflower is a compact, small-flowered passionflower with distinctively corky, ridged stems that distinguish it from other species. The tiny greenish-white to cream flowers are inconspicuous but produce small, dark purple to black berries that are important food for white-eyed vireos, gray catbirds, and other frugivorous birds. Most significantly, it is an essential larval host plant for multiple Gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and Julia heliconian butterfly species — its small, tri-lobed leaves are consumed voraciously by caterpillars. In zone 9a, it is a reliable perennial vine that provides critical butterfly habitat with almost no maintenance.

plant_note: Divide clumps or plant nursery starts in spring directly into consistently moist to boggy soil or a shallow-water container feature.
directions: Divide an established clump or plant a nursery start in spring into consistently wet soil or a submerged pot at the edge of a pond, siting it in full sun to part shade where it will not dry out. Keep the roots saturated throughout the growing season, since this rush struggles wherever soil is allowed to dry between waterings. Its leafless, medium-green stems twist and coil into tight corkscrews, creating a distinctive sculptural accent in bog gardens, water features, and containers, and the curled stems are often cut for use in floral arrangements.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in wet to moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun. Corkwood is a rare species that should only be sourced from specialty native plant nurseries; it is listed as threatened or of conservation concern in most states where it occurs.
directions: Corkwood is one of the rarest and most botanically unusual native shrubs in North America — a monotypic genus (Leitneriaceae family) with no close relatives among living plants, native to the tidal swamps, brackish marshes, and wet bottomlands of scattered, disjunct localities in Georgia, Florida, Texas, Arkansas, and Missouri, where it forms thickets in periodically flooded, organic soils. Its most remarkable characteristic is its wood, which is lighter than cork — making it the least dense wood of any known North American woody plant — and the plant occupies a phylogenetically isolated position in the evolutionary tree of flowering plants. Catkin-like male and female flowers appear on separate plants in spring before the leaves emerge. Despite its rarity, Corkwood is adaptable to a range of wet to moist soil conditions in partial shade to full sun and is occasionally available from specialty native plant nurseries; plant male and female specimens together for seed production. Listed as threatened in several states and on NatureServe's watch list.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in spring in warm, humid conditions. Choose a site with partial shade and moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; Polyalthia suberosa naturally grows as an understory shrub and performs best with some protection from intense afternoon sun in zone 10-11 tropical gardens.
directions: Sow fresh seed at a depth of 0.5 inch in moist, well-drained potting mix and maintain temperatures above 72°F to achieve germination within 2-4 weeks; allow seedlings to reach 6-8 inches before transplanting to a permanent understory or semi-shaded garden position. Corky bark polyalthia establishes most successfully in organically enriched, consistently moist soil with good drainage, and benefits from a layer of organic mulch to retain moisture and suppress weeds during the first growing season. Once established, this unusual custard-apple family shrub requires minimal maintenance; its small cream to yellow-green flowers attract pollinators and are followed by small black fruits that draw birds, adding wildlife interest to tropical garden compositions. The deeply furrowed, corky gray-brown bark develops distinctive textural character with age, making it a conversation piece as a specimen shrub or informal screen in zone 10-11 tropical and subtropical gardens.

common_name: Corn Cockle (Old-Fashioned Rose-Purple Cool-Season Annual from Grain Fields)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (zone 9: September–November) or early spring where winters are cold; Corn Cockle does not transplant well and is best sown directly where it will grow. In zone 9, fall sowing produces the most robust plants and best flowering (February–April). The plant self-seeds reliably once established and will return each year from dropped seed without further planting. Seeds and all plant parts are toxic if ingested — do not plant where children or animals may eat them. The common name reflects the plant's original habitat as a weed of European cereal (corn) fields, where the purple flowers appeared among wheat and barley.
directions: Scatter seeds on prepared soil in fall or early spring; press in without covering deeply. Corn Cockle does not transplant well — sow in situ. Do not ingest seeds or plant material. Corn Cockle (Agrostemma githago) is a strikingly beautiful old-fashioned annual flower from the pink family (Caryophyllaceae) — a naturalized European wildflower (native to the Mediterranean region) that was once common in grain fields across Europe and Britain as a weed among cereal crops, where the large rose-purple flowers nodding on tall, slender, silvery-hairy stems created a dramatic and romantic visual effect in the spring grain fields. The flowers are 2–3 inches across, with five rounded petals in rose-purple to deep pink with a pale throat and distinctive darker veining and a ring of small dark spots at the base of each petal — a pattern of elegant complexity that makes individual flowers as beautiful when examined closely as the whole plant is from a distance. The long, narrow, silvery-hairy sepals that extend beyond the petals give the unopened buds a distinctive appearance and add texture to flower arrangements. Corn Cockle was once widespread as a grain field weed in Britain and Europe but has declined drastically due to herbicide use and improved grain seed cleaning, making it now more common as a cultivated garden plant than as a wild species — a poignant reversal for a once-ubiquitous wildflower. The seeds are poisonous (containing saponins called agrostemmic acid/githagin) — a significant historical concern when grain contaminated with corn cockle seeds was milled into flour, causing 'githagism' poisoning.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in zones 8–10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies. Ixia requires a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; corn lily produces slender, wiry, grass-like stems bearing clusters of star-shaped flowers in luminous shades of white, yellow, pink, orange, red, and blue-green with contrasting dark eyes in late spring. Individual plants are airy and delicate — plant in generous clusters of 25 or more for maximum visual effect. The flowers close in cloudy weather and open fully only in bright sunlight. After bloom, allow foliage to die down completely before removing it; in climates with wet summers, lift corms and store dry until fall. Naturalize readily in well-drained, dry-summer California gardens. Excellent cut flower with long vase life.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade near permanent water; corn lily is a wetland and moist-meadow plant of mountain streams and high-elevation meadows — ALL PARTS ARE EXTREMELY TOXIC.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; corn lily requires consistently moist to wet conditions and is a plant of high-elevation mountain meadows, stream banks, and seepy slopes in western North America. Veratrum californicum is a dramatic, large native perennial closely related to eastern false hellebore (V. viride) producing equally spectacular, tightly pleated, corn-like leaves up to 12 inches wide on stems reaching 3–6 feet tall in early spring, and dense, white-flowered panicles in mid-summer; it differs from V. viride primarily in its white (not greenish-yellow) flowers and western North American range. ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE AMONG THE MOST TOXIC OF ANY NATIVE NORTH AMERICAN PLANT — especially the roots, which have caused fatal poisoning in livestock and have dramatic teratogenic effects on developing lambs if consumed by pregnant ewes early in pregnancy. Grow only in areas inaccessible to livestock, children, and pets.

common_name: Corn Marigold (Field Chrysanthemum, Yellow Oxeye, Segetum Daisy)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 4 weeks before last frost, or in fall in mild climates; corn marigold is a cool-season annual that blooms best in spring and early summer before heat arrives; it is closely related to garland chrysanthemum (Glebionis coronaria) but grown for its ornamental bright yellow daisy flowers rather than for edible greens.
directions: Direct sow on the surface or very shallowly in a weed-free seedbed; thin to 6–10 inches; no fertilization needed — corn marigold blooms best in poor to moderately fertile soil; deadhead spent blooms to extend the season; it self-sows reliably where happy. Corn marigold (Glebionis segetum) is a European and Mediterranean wildflower annual that was once so abundant in grain fields across England, northern Europe, and western Asia that it was considered a serious weed of cultivation — its cheerful bright yellow daisy flowers turning entire wheat and barley fields golden. The common name 'corn marigold' reflects this agricultural history: 'corn' in the old English usage means any small grain (wheat, barley, rye, oats), not maize, and the yellow flowers among the green grain stalks were a familiar sight in pre-herbicide farming landscapes. Despite its weedy past in traditional agriculture, corn marigold has become valued as a garden and wildflower annual for its prolific, long-lasting yellow blooms, its tolerance of poor, dry soils, and its value to pollinators including bees and hoverflies that visit the flowers freely throughout the cool-season bloom period. It is closely related to garland chrysanthemum (Glebionis coronaria) — the Asian edible chrysanthemum greens vegetable — but has narrower, more divided leaves and is grown strictly for ornament. In meadow and wildflower seed mixes for European-style plantings, corn marigold is a standard component for its reliable germination, fast bloom, and cheerful long-season color. The cut flowers are excellent and long-lasting.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and bring indoors before temperatures approach 45°F. Massangeana corn plant is sensitive to fluoride and boron in tap water, which causes leaf tip and edge burn — use filtered water, rainwater, or allow tap water to sit uncovered overnight to dissipate chlorine. In zone 10–11 it can be grown as a permanent landscape tree reaching 15–20 feet. Outdoors in zone 9's summer humidity, the plant grows more rapidly than indoors. The fragrant white to cream flower spikes that appear on mature plants have an intense, sweet fragrance noticeable across a significant distance.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light — never in direct sun, which bleaches and burns the variegated leaves — in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil; allow soil to dry slightly between waterings; Massangeana is the classic variegated corn plant dracaena, producing wide, strap-like leaves with a broad bright yellow to lime-green central stripe on a dark green background — the most distinctive and widely recognized leaf pattern of any tropical foliage plant in the American market. The large leaves (up to 3 feet long and 4 inches wide) are produced in rosettes at the tips of the thick, upright, cane-like stem — a growth form that naturally produces the same architectural, palm-tree-like effect whether grown as a 2-foot houseplant or a 15-foot landscape tree in tropical zones. Corn plant is among the very best shade and low-light tropical foliage plants for zone 9 outdoor display — its tolerance of low light conditions, relative drought tolerance, and ability to go without watering for extended periods makes it practical as an outdoor container specimen on covered patios and porches where access to the plant for watering may be irregular. The plant's ability to shed its lower leaves and expose the attractive, bamboo-like stem as it grows creates an evolving form over years that becomes increasingly interesting as the plant matures.

common_name: Corn Plant Dracaena (Mass Cane, Fortune Plant)
