Cupcake is an unusual cosmos selection in which the outer petals fuse along their edges into a shallow cup or chalice shape, resembling a fluted cupcake wrapper around the central boss of gold stamens, a distinctly different form from the flat, open-faced blooms of typical cosmos. It flowers over a long season atop tall stems held above finely cut, ferny foliage, and its unusual shape makes it a conversation piece in cutting gardens and pollinator borders alike. The plants rarely need staking despite their height and continue blooming into fall with regular deadheading.

common_name: Cupcake Zinnia (Ruffled Semi-Double Bicolor Cut-Flower Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Cupcake is a semi-double, scabiosa-flowered zinnia mix known for frilly, ruffled center petals in contrasting bicolor combinations, producing unusually textured blooms distinct from flat-petaled zinnia types.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 9-12 inches. Cupcake is a scabiosa-flowered zinnia mix with a distinctive ruffled, cushion-like center of small, tightly packed petals surrounded by a single or semi-double outer ring of larger petals, giving each bloom an unusual layered, textured look often compared to a frosted cupcake. Colors run through mixed pastels and bicolors, with many blooms showing contrasting tones between the outer ring and the ruffled center. Plants are tall and productive, blooming continuously from midsummer through frost with regular deadheading or harvesting, and the unusual flower form makes Cupcake a popular novelty addition to cutting gardens and mixed bouquets alongside more traditional single- and double-flowered zinnia types. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

common_name: Cupid Peperomia (Creeping Peperomia, False Philodendron Peperomia)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in well-draining, perlite-enriched potting mix; Peperomia scandens can be grown as a hanging basket plant, a vining plant on a small trellis, or a groundcover on a shaded patio. Allow the top inch to dry between waterings. The variegated form ('Variegata') has cream-margined leaves and is the most commonly available; the solid green form is less common. Prefers temperatures above 60°F. Propagate from stem cuttings. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in well-draining potting mix — Cupid Peperomia is tolerant of lower light conditions than many other houseplants but produces its most attractive, full growth in bright indirect conditions. Peperomia scandens is a trailing to climbing peperomia native to Mexico, Central America, and northern South America in the Piperaceae family, one of the most widely grown of the larger-leaved peperomias for its attractive trailing habit and appealing heart-shaped foliage. The plant produces long, somewhat fleshy, scandent (vining/climbing) stems with broadly heart-shaped to broadly oval, light to medium-green, slightly glossy, succulent-textured leaves 1.5–2.5 inches long. The most commonly sold form is 'Variegata,' which has the same heart-shaped leaves but with irregular, cream to ivory margins and variegation on the green background — a soft, attractive cream-and-green combination that has made this form popular as a trailing houseplant and basket specimen. The plant's trailing stems can reach 2–4 feet in length, making it effective in hanging baskets and on shelves where the vines can drape. It can also be trained up a small trellis or moss pole, where it produces an attractive, light-textured, climbing display. The common name 'False Philodendron Peperomia' reflects the Philodendron-like appearance of the heart-shaped leaves. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in well-drained, poor to average, dry soil in full sun 4–6 weeks before last frost; cupid's dart is short-lived in heavy or moist soils but self-sows to perpetuate itself in sandy, dry, well-drained conditions.
directions: Direct sow in dry, well-drained, poor soil in full sun; cupid's dart produces lavender-blue, papery, cornflower-like flowers on long wiry stems from early summer through fall, borne above clumps of long, narrow, grayish-green leaves. The semi-papery flowers hold their color beautifully when dried and were historically used in love potions (hence the common name). Plants are short-lived perennials in heavy, wet soils but persist for years in lean, sandy conditions and self-sow reliably. An excellent, low-maintenance border plant for dry, sunny sites that pair beautifully with ornamental grasses, eryngium, and phlomis. Divide in early spring or collect seed annually in humid climates where plants are short-lived.

common_name: Curcuma (Siam Tulip, Hidden Lily, Thai Tulip)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; curcumas emerge from dormancy late (May–June), so patience is required. In zone 8–9 mulch heavily in fall and the rhizomes typically overwinter successfully in the ground.
directions: Plant rhizomes 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Curcuma alismatifolia (Siam tulip) is one of the most striking ornamental gingers, producing elegant upright flower spikes in late summer with a cone of showy bracts in pink, purple, or white, resembling a large tulip — hence the name. The broad, tropical foliage and exotic inflorescences make curcumas outstanding cut flowers and exceptional accent plants in the shaded summer border. They emerge late in spring from dormancy (don't panic and dig them — wait until June), grow and flower through summer, then die back to the ground in fall. The ornamental Curcumas differ from culinary turmeric (C. longa) but the two are closely related; several curcuma species have both edible and ornamental value.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring into rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil on exposed, sunny sites; this slow-growing, long-lived evergreen tolerates shallow, rocky soils where little else grows.
directions: Plant container stock in fall or early spring into rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil on exposed, sunny sites, since curl-leaf mountain mahogany is a slow-growing, long-lived evergreen native to dry foothills and mountain slopes throughout the Intermountain West. Its inconspicuous spring flowers are wind-pollinated, but the shrub's dense evergreen cover and abundant, twisted-plumed seed heads make it critical winter browse and cover for mule deer, bighorn sheep, and small birds. It is remarkably drought- and cold-hardy once established, tolerating shallow, rocky soils where little else will grow, and needs essentially no irrigation after the first two seasons. Growth is slow, so choose the planting site carefully, as this long-lived shrub can persist for centuries.

common_name: Curly Fries Hosta (Miniature Gold Hosta with Wavy Twisted Leaves)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Curly Fries develops its brightest gold color with a few hours of morning sun and holds up well as an edging plant or container specimen given its small mature size.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving a little morning sun for the brightest gold color on this novelty miniature. Curly Fries is a small, distinctive hosta cultivar with narrow, wavy, twisted gold leaves that curl and ripple along their length, giving the clump a texture unlike almost any other hosta and living up to its playful name. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer, but the foliage is the main attraction, forming a dense, low mound well suited to the front of a shaded border, a rock garden, or a container where its unusual form can be appreciated up close. Its small size makes it a good choice for gardeners with limited space who still want a distinctive gold hosta. Divide clumps every four to five years in spring if increased numbers are wanted, since the compact habit means division is rarely necessary for plant health.

common_name: Curly Locks Hosta (Wavy Gold-Centered Narrow-Leaf Hosta)
plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Curly Locks is a sport of Praying Hands with the same narrow, upright leaf form but with wavy, twisted margins and a bright gold leaf center.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, with a little morning sun to bring out the brightest gold coloring in the leaf centers. Curly Locks arose as a sport of the narrow-leaf novelty hosta Praying Hands and keeps its parent's distinctive upright, folded leaf form while adding wavy, twisted margins and a strong gold center against dark green edges, giving the clump an even more sculptural, textural look. The narrow, vertical habit makes it stand out sharply against broad-leaved hosta neighbors and works well as a specimen in a container or at the front of a shaded border. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years and watch for slugs on the tender emerging growth.

plant_note: Sow seed shallowly on prepared, firm seedbed once soil temperatures consistently exceed 65°F; stolon-grown transplants establish considerably faster than seed.
directions: Broadcast seed lightly over a firm, weed-suppressed seedbed in late spring, pressing seed into the soil surface rather than covering deeply, as germination requires light and warmth. Keep the seedbed moist for three to four weeks until seedlings are visible, then transition to infrequent deep watering to encourage deep rooting. Once established, this grass spreads by stolons to fill gaps and form a cohesive turf that tolerates heavy foot traffic and prolonged drought. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization, which promotes weedy competition over the grass itself.

plant_note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Curly Slim air plant curls its leaves tighter when kept on the drier side and relaxes them when well hydrated, so drying thoroughly between waterings encourages its signature curl.
directions: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Curly Slim air plant curls its leaves tighter when kept on the drier side and relaxes them when well hydrated, so drying thoroughly between waterings encourages its signature curl. Broad, bulbous leaves twist and curl dramatically into loose ringlets, giving this popular air plant a whimsical, almost cartoonish silhouette that has made it one of the most recognizable and widely sold tillandsia species, with a tall spike of pink bracts and violet-blue flowers appearing at maturity. Native to seasonally dry forests from Mexico to Central America, it naturally sheds moisture quickly between the infrequent rains of its dry-season habitat, and its curl relaxes noticeably after a good soak before tightening again as it dries. Soak thoroughly once or twice a week and shake off excess water from the curled leaf bases, where trapped moisture is the most common cause of rot.

plant_note: Direct-sow after the soil warms in spring into lean, well-drained soil; seed needs light contact, so press in rather than bury.
directions: Sow into poor, dry, sunny soil where richer conditions would cause it to flop, and thin seedlings to give each plant room to branch. Curlycup gumweed gets its name from the sticky white resin that coats the tightly curled green bracts beneath each bright yellow bloom, and it flowers heavily from midsummer into fall when many other prairie natives have finished. That late, resinous bloom makes it an important late-season nectar source for a wide range of bees, including many specialist and long-tongued species, as well as small butterflies. It tolerates drought, poor soil, and roadside conditions extremely well, and often behaves as a short-lived perennial that reseeds itself into disturbed ground.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket, or mount on a slab, in bright, indirect light in a loose, fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Curtis's hoya is a small, slow-growing miniature best suited to a small pot, terrarium, or mounted display.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket, or mount on a slab, in bright, indirect light in a loose, fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Curtis's hoya is a small, slow-growing miniature best suited to a small pot, terrarium, or mounted display. Tiny, thick, silver-speckled, heart-shaped leaves lie closely along thin, wiry, creeping stems that root as they spread, forming a dense, low mat or a delicate curtain when allowed to trail from a small hanging pot. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it is among the smallest and slowest-growing hoya species commonly cultivated, making it well suited to windowsill, terrarium, or miniature garden displays where larger hoyas would be out of scale. Let the potting mix dry between waterings, provide bright filtered light for the best leaf speckling, and avoid overpotting this slow-growing miniature in too large a container.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; curve-flowered sage is drought-tolerant once established and prone to rot in heavy, poorly drained, or overly moist soil.
directions: Plant transplants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; curve-flowered sage is drought-tolerant once established and prone to rot in heavy, poorly drained, or overly moist soil. Slender stems carry narrow leaves and elegant, gracefully curved, deep magenta-rose tubular flowers held in loose spikes through a long summer and fall bloom season, an understated but reliably prolific bloomer that draws hummingbirds throughout its flowering period. Native to dry, rocky slopes in Mexico, it is well adapted to lean, fast-draining soil and tolerates drought once established, making it a good candidate for a xeriscape border or gravel garden where richer, moisture-retentive soil would encourage rot. Water sparingly once established, cut back in late winter to remove any frost-damaged growth, and provide full sun for the best flowering.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; cushion aloe scorches in direct hot sun and rots in dense or constantly wet soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; cushion aloe scorches in direct hot sun and rots in dense or constantly wet soil. Plump, translucent-tipped leaves are densely packed into tight, low rosettes, with the swollen, window-like leaf tips allowing light to filter down into the plant's interior, an adaptation shared with several small haworthias native to rocky crevices in South Africa where the rest of the plant hides below ground level for protection from intense sun. Its small, clustering rosettes spread slowly by offsets into a dense mat, making it well suited to a shallow succulent dish garden, terrarium-adjacent display, or windowsill collection where its unusual translucent leaf tips can be appreciated up close. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light, and separate offsets to propagate or refresh a crowded pot.

plant_note: Sow in fall to allow seeds to naturally stratify; germination is often slow and benefits from the full cold period.
directions: Cusp Blazing Star is a drought-tolerant native of Texas, Oklahoma, and New Mexico prairies and cedar brakes, producing slender stems densely clad with narrow, pointed leaves topped by vivid lavender-purple flower spikes in late summer. It is an excellent choice for hot, dry south-central gardens where many other Liatris species struggle, offering outstanding ornamental value with almost no supplemental irrigation once established. Direct sow seeds in fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, as this species does not tolerate wet or heavy clay conditions. Plants bloom most prolifically when grown in poor to moderately fertile soil and left undisturbed to develop their deep corms over several seasons.

common_name: Custard Candy Daylily (Cream-Yellow Ruffled Daylily with Rose Eye)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Custard Candy is a popular reblooming daylily cultivar with creamy pale-yellow flowers marked by a rose-pink eye zone and matching ruffled edge, a soft companion to bolder-colored daylily cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Custard Candy bears soft, creamy pale-yellow flowers accented with a rose-pink eye zone and a matching ruffled picotee edge, a gentle, pastel color combination that pairs well with the bolder reds, purples, and oranges of many other daylily cultivars in a mixed border. It reblooms readily over a long season from early to late summer, producing a steady supply of flowers, and is exceptionally easy to grow, tolerating a wide range of soil types and requiring little care beyond routine watering. The reliable, floriferous performance and soft coloring have made it a popular choice for both dedicated daylily collectors and casual gardeners. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost for fast, easy germination.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors for an earlier display. As the name promises, cutting these old-fashioned two-to-two-and-a-half-inch blooms makes the plants flower more, producing continuously until fall frost. Space for airflow and water at the base to limit powdery mildew. Cut stems often to fill bouquets and keep the plants covered in blooms.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in moist to wet, rich soil in partial shade to full sun; cutleaf coneflower spreads aggressively by rhizomes in moist conditions and should be sited where it has room to naturalize — divide clumps every 2–3 years.
directions: Cutleaf coneflower is the tallest of all North American coneflowers — commonly reaching 6–8 feet or more in moist, rich soil — producing long-stalked, deeply lobed leaves with a coarse, tropical texture and airy sprays of bright yellow, drooping-petaled flowers with a distinctive greenish-yellow dome from July through September. Unlike most other coneflowers that require full sun and dry to average soils, cutleaf coneflower thrives in partial shade in moist bottomland conditions, making it invaluable for the sunny-to-shaded edges of rain gardens, stream banks, and moist woodland borders where a tall, dramatic native perennial is needed. The double-flowered heirloom cultivar 'Hortensia' (Golden Glow) has been grown in American gardens since the 1890s and still persists in old homesteads across the South, where it spreads freely by rhizomes through shaded gardens. It spreads vigorously and can be invasive in small spaces — site it where it can naturalize freely in large native beds or along stream margins.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade in fall, when this species' evergreen sterile frond emerges; like other grapeferns it depends on soil mycorrhizae and is slow to establish from division.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade in fall, since this fern's single, finely divided, lacy sterile frond emerges in autumn and stays green through winter before withering the following summer, an unusual schedule opposite most ferns. A separate beaded fertile spike, when present, rises alongside the sterile blade in late summer or fall and releases spores that depend on a long, hidden underground partnership with soil fungi before a new plant appears, so division and transplant success is slow and unpredictable. It grows scattered through open deciduous woods, old fields, and woodland edges across much of the eastern and southeastern United States, more often noticed for its handsome winter foliage than for size, since mature plants rarely exceed ten inches. Treat it as a patient, long-term addition to a shaded woodland floor rather than a fast-establishing groundcover, and avoid disturbing the soil around planted crowns.

plant_note: Direct-sow into lean, gritty, well-drained soil after the soil warms; established plants tolerate poor, rocky ground.
directions: Sow into fast-draining, lean soil in full sun and avoid rich beds or heavy irrigation, which shorten this drought-adapted plant's life; it thrives on neglect in gravelly or sandy sites across the western Great Plains and Southwest. From late summer into fall it produces abundant yellow, aster-like daisies over finely divided, spine-tipped foliage, blooming at a time when many other nectar sources have dried up. The late flowers draw numerous native bees, honeybees, and migrating butterflies, making it a useful addition to a xeriscape or rock garden pollinator planting. It behaves as a short-lived perennial or subshrub, often reseeding to persist in the same general area.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; the compact cultivar 'Crispa' is lower and more spreading (18 inches tall, 3–4 feet wide) than the straight species and is the preferred selection for groundcover use. Branches root where they touch the ground, increasing spread.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; cutleaf stephanandra is a graceful, arching Japanese shrub in the rose family producing elegantly divided, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves with a refined, lacy texture that gives it its common name. In spring it produces clusters of small, white star-shaped flowers along the arching branches, attractive but secondary to the exceptional foliage. In autumn the leaves turn orange, red, and purple before dropping. The compact cultivar 'Crispa' is particularly valuable as a groundcover — growing only 18 inches tall while spreading 3–4 feet wide, with crimped, finely cut leaves that form a thick, weed-suppressing mat in shade. Branches that touch the ground root themselves (layering), helping the plant colonize large areas under trees where grass and other groundcovers fail. Among the finest shade-tolerant ornamental shrubs for the difficult zone between trees and planting beds, providing excellent weed suppression and year-round ground cover.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in deep shade under deciduous trees. Cutleaf Toothwort goes completely dormant by late spring — mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant rhizomes during summer garden work.
directions: Cutleaf Toothwort is a native spring ephemeral of moist, rich, deciduous woodlands across eastern North America, producing clusters of small white to pale pink flowers on 6–15 inch stems in early to mid-spring, shortly before the forest canopy closes and blocks the light that spring ephemerals depend on. The deeply cut, three-parted leaves with their toothlike lobes give the plant its common name and are an identification feature distinguishing it from the similar Slender Toothwort; the leaves appear in early spring, the plant flowers, sets seed, and retreats entirely underground by early summer, remaining dormant until the following winter. A member of the mustard family, the rhizomes have a mild, peppery, horseradish-like flavor and were eaten raw by various Native American peoples. Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in deep shade; Cutleaf Toothwort self-seeds freely in hospitable woodland gardens and gradually colonizes the forest floor.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the deeply and sharply lobed foliage will slowly knit together into a dense groundcover mat.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the deeply and sharply lobed foliage will slowly knit together into a dense groundcover mat. Cutting Edge is named for its distinctively jagged, almost fern-like leaf margins, marked with a bold dark maroon central zone that intensifies in cooler weather, and is topped by fluffy white to pale pink bottlebrush flower spikes in mid-spring. Like other modern tiarella introductions it spreads gently by stolons rather than aggressively, making it well suited to woodland edges and shaded rock gardens. Keep soil consistently moist, since foliage can scorch during dry spells in too much sun.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3 inches apart in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moisture-retentive soil in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; narcissus cyclamineus is one of the earliest-blooming daffodil species and performs best in a sheltered position in partial shade with reliably moist, leafy soil — woodland edges, moist grass, and light shade under deciduous trees are ideal. Avoid hot, dry, or exposed sites.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in fall for early spring bloom; Narcissus cyclamineus is one of the most distinctive and botanically fascinating of all daffodil species — a diminutive, early-blooming miniature whose most striking feature is its strongly reflexed perianth segments, swept sharply backward like the petals of a cyclamen flower, exposing a disproportionately long, narrow, tubular golden trumpet and giving the flower a dynamic, wind-blown appearance unlike any other narcissus. It is one of the earliest daffodils to bloom, often flowering in late February or early March before many larger daffodils have emerged. This species is the parent of many of the most beloved small daffodil hybrids, including 'Tête-à-tête', 'February Gold', and 'Jack Snipe', and it naturalizes beautifully in moist grass and light woodland shade, increasing steadily over time to form cheerful early-spring colonies. Native to northwest Spain and Portugal, it is less tolerant of dry summer conditions than most daffodils and performs best where the soil retains some moisture year-round.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or start transplants after cold stratification in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately dry, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cylindric blazing star demands exceptionally sharp drainage and will rot in wet, clay soils.
directions: Direct sow in fall or start transplants after cold stratification in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately dry, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cylindric blazing star demands exceptionally sharp drainage and will rot in wet, clay soils. Liatris cylindracea is the smallest and most delicate-looking liatris, native to dry, open, rocky prairies and limestone glades of the Great Lakes region and northeastern prairies; it produces small, cylindrical (rather than spherical) flower heads in bright rose-purple from July through August on slender stems, blooming from the top down in the characteristic liatris fashion. An outstanding choice for dry rock gardens, gravel borders, and xeriscape gardens in the northern portion of its range; it is important for specialist native bees and migrating monarch butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in dry, rocky, sandy, or gravelly, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring. Cylindrical Blazingstar is among the most drought-tolerant of all blazingstars and specifically adapted to calcareous or gravelly prairie and alvar soils.
directions: Cylindrical Blazingstar is a compact, drought-tolerant native perennial of dry prairies, rocky outcrops, calcareous alvars, and gravelly open woodlands of the Great Lakes region and Midwest, producing spikes of few, widely spaced, cylindrical purple flower heads on stiff, slender stems in July and August that are prized for cut flowers and dried arrangements as well as for their wildlife value. Notably more drought-tolerant than most blazingstars and specifically adapted to thin, rocky, calcareous or gravelly soils of limestone outcrops and dry prairie remnants, Cylindrical Blazingstar is an outstanding choice for rock gardens, xeriscapes, and dry native plant gardens across the northern United States. The compact size and long vase life of the cut flowers make it one of the most popular Liatris species among native plant enthusiasts and cut flower gardeners. Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in rocky, sandy, or gravelly, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; established corms are extremely long-lived and slowly form clumps.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded-to-sunny patio container in bright indirect to full sun in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; cylindrical snake plant is extremely drought-tolerant and far more likely to be killed by overwatering than neglect.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded-to-sunny patio container in bright indirect to full sun in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; cylindrical snake plant is extremely drought-tolerant and far more likely to be killed by overwatering than neglect. Thick, rigid, cylindrical leaves rise straight up from the base like a cluster of gray-green spears banded with faint darker striping, a striking architectural silhouette very different from the flat-leaved snake plants more commonly grown, and the leaves are sometimes braided together for a novelty potted specimen. Native to dry, rocky regions of Angola and the Congo, it stores water in its succulent leaves and tolerates weeks of neglect, low light, and irregular watering, making it one of the toughest and most forgiving houseplants available. Water only when the soil is completely dry, provide as much bright light as possible for the fastest growth, and avoid cold drafts below the mid-50s Fahrenheit.

plant_note: Nick or soak seeds overnight in warm water before direct sowing after last frost in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; cypress vine self-seeds prolifically in warm climates and can become invasive — deadhead if naturalization is not desired.
directions: Nick or soak seeds overnight in warm water before direct sowing after last frost in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; cypress vine self-seeds prolifically in warm climates and can become invasive — deadhead if naturalization is not desired. Ipomoea quamoclit is a delicate, fast-growing annual vine from tropical America with extraordinarily fine, feathery, deeply pinnate leaves resembling cypress foliage and a long succession of small (1-inch), brilliant scarlet, star-shaped flowers with a white eye from summer through frost that are irresistible to ruby-throated hummingbirds. In zone 9–10 it self-seeds vigorously and can naturalize along fences and into disturbed areas; it has been listed as invasive in some southeastern states, so monitor seedling spread and remove volunteers if they escape the garden area. An outstanding container or trellis plant for attracting hummingbirds.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; allow ample space — D.D. Blanchard grows into a large, pyramidal tree 30–50 feet tall.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; D.D. Blanchard is one of the most magnificent Southern magnolia cultivars — distinguished by exceptionally dark, glossy, almost black-green upper leaf surfaces with a rich, coppery-orange to russet-brown underside that is among the most vivid and attractive of any Southern magnolia selection. The underside color is a significant ornamental feature: when a breeze stirs the branches, the leaves momentarily reveal their orange-bronze undersides, creating a shimmering two-tone effect that no other tree quite replicates. D.D. Blanchard is a large tree with a naturally pyramidal form, growing 30–50 feet tall with a 20–30 foot spread — a specimen tree with an imposing, stately presence appropriate for large residential landscapes and commercial settings. The giant, creamy-white, intensely fragrant flowers (8–12 inches across) bloom from May through July in zone 9, with intermittent bloom through summer. Like all Southern magnolia cultivars, D.D. Blanchard produces large, cone-like fruits with brilliant red seeds that are consumed by birds and wildlife. An outstanding selection for the Gulf South where the tree is most at home — performing magnificently in zone 8–10 heat and humidity.

common_name: Dad's Favourite Dianthus (Historic White Laced in Velvety Maroon)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Dad's Favourite is a historic Paisley/laced pink from the 1800s with white semi-double flowers laced in velvety maroon.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Dad's Favourite, a historic Paisley or laced garden pink dating to the 1800s, bears white, semi-double flowers intricately laced with velvety maroon, an elegant patterned bloom typical of the antique laced pink class prized by heritage garden collectors. Its long cultivation history and refined form have kept it a favorite among dianthus enthusiasts. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall, 4–8 weeks before the ground freezes, for spring bloom.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall at a depth of 3 times the bulb's height (typically 6–8 in) in well-drained soil with the pointed end up. Daffodils naturalize readily and multiply over time; deer and rodents avoid them because the bulbs are mildly toxic. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally — at least 6 weeks — so the bulb can store energy for next year's bloom. Divide congested clumps every 5–7 years when flowering diminishes.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring after last frost in lean, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; in zones 9–11 it self-sows as a short-lived perennial. Dahlberg daisy performs best in hot, dry conditions and declines in heat with excessive moisture. Excellent for filling cracks and edges in hot, dry, sunny spots.
directions: Sow in lean, well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; Dahlberg daisy is a Texas native annual (perennial in zones 9–11) producing exceptionally fine-textured, thread-like, aromatic foliage — almost needle-like and strongly fragrant when crushed — covered throughout the warm season with masses of tiny, bright golden-yellow daisy flowers, each only 1/2 inch across but produced in such uncountable profusion that the plant appears to be a cushion of living gold. The extremely fine foliage texture combined with the continuous small-scale flower display creates an effect unlike any other — a mounding, golden, aromatic, lacy confection that is outstanding for edging, filling containers, and naturalizing in hot, dry, sandy situations. A Texas Hill Country native, it thrives in the exact difficult conditions — poor, dry, alkaline, rocky soil in baking summer sun — that defeat most garden plants. Self-sows freely to maintain colonies in appropriate climates. The foliage releases a pleasant, chamomile-like herbal fragrance when brushed.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 60°F.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 in deep with the eye pointing up after the last frost when soil reaches 60°F; set a stake at planting time to avoid spearing the tuber later. Pinch the growing tip when plants are 12 in tall to encourage branching and more flowers. In zones below 8, dig tubers after the first killing frost, cure them for a week, then store in slightly damp peat at 40–50°F through winter. Disbudding side buds around the main bud produces exhibition-quality blooms.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; dahoon holly grows naturally in swamps, stream banks, and wet flatwoods and tolerates standing water and high water tables better than any other native holly except possumhaw. Plant male and female plants for berry production.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun — dahoon holly is one of the most beautiful and ecologically important native trees of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, growing naturally in the understory of bottomland swamps, cypress heads, wet pine flatwoods, and stream banks from Virginia to Texas. Female plants (a male nearby is needed for pollination) produce abundant clusters of small, brilliant red to orange-red berries that persist from fall through winter, providing critical food for robins, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and dozens of other fruit-eating birds during winter when food is scarce. The narrow, elliptic, dark evergreen leaves are attractive year-round. It tolerates flooding and wet soils better than almost any other tree in cultivation and is outstanding for rain gardens, wet low spots, pond margins, and other challenging wet sites in zone 7–11. An excellent winter-interest tree for the shaded, wet areas of Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Daikagura is a classic Japanese camellia cultivar producing very large, peony-form flowers boldly streaked and mottled in rose-red and white, one of the showiest variegated camellia forms.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Daikagura is a centuries-old Japanese camellia cultivar prized for exceptionally large, formal peony-form flowers, densely packed with irregularly waved and twisted petals boldly streaked and mottled in rose-red over a white background, a strikingly variegated pattern unique to each bloom. The dramatic size and coloring make individual flowers a focal point in the winter garden, and the plant's dense, glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage provides year-round structure. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it blooms in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9, when little else is in flower. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, which scorches the glossy leaves, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

plant_note: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, deep soil in full sun; daimyo oak grows naturally in mountain forests and forest edges of China, Korea, and Japan, producing the largest leaves of any oak — up to 18 inches long — that create a dramatic, bold-textured specimen effect in the landscape.
directions: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, deep soil in full sun; daimyo oak (emperor oak) is the boldest-textured oak in the world, producing enormous, deeply lobed, paddle-shaped leaves that can reach 18 inches long and 10 inches wide — the largest leaves of any temperate-zone oak, creating a strikingly coarse, tropical-looking canopy texture completely unlike the small-leaved English oak. Native to mountain forests of China, Korea, and Japan, it is a relatively small to medium oak suitable for residential gardens where its dramatic foliage creates a bold statement. The leaves turn bronze to red-brown in fall and often persist on the tree into early winter before dropping (marcescent). Relatively slow-growing compared to other oaks. The species is the host plant for the silkworm Antheraea yamamai (the Japanese oak silkworm) which produces golden 'tussah' silk. An outstanding specimen tree for gardens where dramatic large-leaved texture is desired.

common_name: Dainty Red and Yellow Lady's Purse
plant_note: Surface sow the fine seed, which needs light; keep cool and evenly moist.
directions: Surface sow the very fine seed indoors, since it needs light and cool conditions to germinate well. This compact, bushy plant produces one-to-two-inch inflated, slipper-shaped blooms in sunny yellow marked with striking red blotches. It performs beautifully cascading from containers, hanging baskets, and garden edges. Keep it consistently moist, give it part shade in warm climates, and protect it from intense heat.

plant_note: Surface sow the fine seed, which needs light; keep cool and evenly moist.
directions: Surface sow the tiny seed indoors, giving it light and cool temperatures for reliable germination. This charming, compact plant bears one-to-two-inch slipper-shaped blooms in sunny yellow dusted with delicate red spots for a hand-painted effect. It shines in containers, hanging baskets, and along garden edges. Keep the soil evenly moist and provide part shade and protection from heat in warm regions.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Dakota Goldcharm is an especially compact, low-growing golden spirea bred for tight foundation plantings and edging.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun for the brightest foliage color; spirea tolerates poor soil and drought once established but flowers and colors up best with a half-day or more of direct sun. Dakota Goldcharm stays notably lower and tighter than most golden-leaved spirea cultivars, forming a dense, mounded dwarf shrub with bright chartreuse-gold foliage that takes on orange-red tints in cool spring and fall weather, topped by small clusters of pink flowers in late spring. Its diminutive size fits low borders, rock gardens, and mass plantings where taller spirea would overwhelm the scale of the design. Shear off spent flowers after the main bloom flush to tidy the mound, and cut the whole plant back hard every few years in late winter to keep growth dense and prevent the center from opening up.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Dakota prairie rose is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant, well adapted to harsh northern plains conditions.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Dakota prairie rose is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant, well adapted to harsh northern plains conditions. Fragrant, single pink flowers cover this low, suckering native shrub in early summer, followed by bright red hips that persist through winter as valuable food for birds and wildlife on the harsh, wind-swept northern Great Plains where it grows natively. Extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, it spreads slowly by root suckers into loose colonies that help stabilize prairie soil, making it a valuable, low-maintenance native shrub for a prairie restoration or naturalistic planting in cold, dry climates where more tender roses would not survive winter. It needs no fertilizer, spraying, or winter protection, dying back partially in severe cold and resprouting reliably each spring.

common_name: Dallas Blues Switchgrass (Extra-Wide-Blade Powder-Blue Native Switchgrass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Dallas Blues has unusually wide, powder-blue leaf blades compared to most switchgrass cultivars, giving it a bolder, more substantial texture in the border.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun; adaptable to clay, wet, and dry soils. Dallas Blues stands out among switchgrass cultivars for its unusually broad, powder-blue leaf blades, giving it a bolder, coarser texture than the fine-bladed straight species, topped in late summer by large, airy, pinkish flower panicles that age to a warm tan and persist through winter. Like other switchgrass cultivars it is a durable, low-maintenance native grass that tolerates heat, drought, and periodic flooding with equal ease, providing valuable structure, seed for birds, and habitat for beneficial insects. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Dalmatian Series Foxglove (Compact First-Year-Blooming Landscape Foxglove)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost, since Dalmatian needs a longer head start than some foxglove strains to reliably flower the first year; transplant out after frost danger has passed into partial shade.
directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil, and keep evenly moist through establishment since this compact series has a shallower root system than taller heirloom foxglove strains. Dalmatian is a vegetatively uniform, dwarf foxglove series bred specifically for landscape beds and containers, topping out under two feet with densely packed spikes of speckled, tubular bells in shades of purple, peach, rose, cream, and white that open reliably the first year from an early sowing. Its compact, self-supporting habit needs no staking and fits smaller garden spaces and mixed containers better than the taller old-fashioned biennial types. In mild climates plants sometimes persist as short-lived perennials or self-seed lightly, though named-series seedlings will not come true from self-sown seed. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so plant away from areas frequented by children or pets.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; damask rose is the classic perfume rose grown commercially in Bulgaria, Turkey, and Iran for attar of roses and rosewater distillation.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; damask rose is an ancient hybrid species prized above nearly any other rose for the depth and quality of its fragrance, the source of true attar of roses and rosewater produced commercially in the valleys of Bulgaria, Turkey, and Iran. Loosely double, pink to light red flowers open over a generous spring flush, and some strains rebloom lightly in fall, though the once-blooming forms remain the most commonly grown for fragrance and hip production. Petals are traditionally hand-harvested at dawn, when essential oil content peaks, for distillation, drying, or use in culinary rosewater and preserves. It grows into a tall, somewhat lax, arching shrub that benefits from light support or informal training, and like other old garden roses, it is generally more disease-resistant and needs less routine spraying than modern hybrid tea roses.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; damianita demands sharp drainage above all else and rots quickly in heavy clay or any soil that stays wet, especially through winter.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; among the most heat- and drought-tolerant native shrublets available, thriving in conditions that kill most perennials outright, but requires perfect drainage and struggles in humid, poorly drained gardens. Chrysactinia mexicana (damianita) is a small, rounded, woody-based evergreen shrublet native to the limestone hills and rocky slopes of the Trans-Pecos, west Texas, and northern Mexico, with fine, needle-like, resinous, aromatic foliage that releases a pungent, camphor-like scent when brushed or crushed. From spring through fall, and especially heavily after rain, the plant is smothered in small, bright golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers that draw bees and butterflies and make a vivid mounded splash of color against its dark, textured foliage. Its extreme drought and heat tolerance make it a staple of xeriscape and rock garden design across the drier parts of Texas and the Southwest, and it also tolerates the humidity of the Gulf South reasonably well provided the drainage is sharp. An excellent low-water accent plant for a sunny rock garden or gravel bed, zone 7–10.

common_name: Dance Ballerina Dance Siberian Iris (Award-Winning White Plicata over Lavender-Rose)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Dance Ballerina Dance won the Morgan-Wood Medal in 1989 for its near-white plicata standards over ruffled lavender-rose falls.
directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Dance Ballerina Dance, winner of the American Iris Society's Morgan-Wood Medal in 1989, bears near-white, delicately veined plicata-patterned standards rising above ruffled lavender-rose falls, an elegant two-tone combination that has made it one of the most acclaimed Siberian iris cultivars. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

plant_note: Plant small rhizomes 1–2 inches deep in spring after soil warms to 70°F in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; dancing ladies ginger dies back to the ground each winter in zones 8–9 but reliably re-emerges from the rhizome in spring. Excellent in containers, shade gardens, and as a companion to begonias, caladiums, and ferns.
directions: Plant small rhizomes 1–2 inches deep in spring after soil warms to 70°F in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Globba winitii is a charming, small Thai ginger producing arching, pendant inflorescences with decorative pink to purple bracts and tiny, vivid yellow flowers that dangle in a way that resembles a line of dancing figures, earning its delightful common name; it is one of the finest small gingers for shaded tropical and subtropical gardens. In late summer and fall the bracts are replaced by tiny bulbils that drop to the ground and produce new plants, gradually naturalizing the planting. Dancing ladies ginger dies back to the ground each winter in zones 8–9 but reliably re-emerges from the rhizome in spring. Excellent in containers, shade gardens, and as a companion to begonias, caladiums, and ferns.

common_name: Dancing Ladies Ginger (Nodding Globba, Marantina Globba, Jewel Globba)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Globba marantina cannot tolerate frost but is one of the hardier Globba species, surviving rhizome temperatures to approximately 28°F with heavy mulch in zone 9. The plant goes dormant in winter — leaves die back and rhizomes rest until spring warmth. Propagate by dividing rhizomes in spring or from bulbils (small round propagules) that form in the inflorescence instead of seeds. The arching flower stems need shade to produce their most vivid color.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Dancing Ladies Ginger is among the most shade-tolerant of the ornamental gingers and produces its most delicate and beautiful flower display in the filtered light under large trees. Globba marantina is a small, clump-forming, deciduous ginger native to Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Vietnam, Indonesia) in the family Zingiberaceae, one of approximately 100 Globba species now popular in the ornamental ginger world for their delicate, dancing flower display. The plant produces stems 18–36 inches tall of broad, soft, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive purple blush on the undersides. In summer and fall, arching flower stalks emerge from the leaf tips bearing loosely branched inflorescences of remarkable, pendant, dancing flowers: each individual flower is about an inch long with reflexed, purple-maroon to burgundy bracts and small yellow petals that hang and dangle from thin pedicels in the slightest air movement — the massed, dancing effect of dozens of tiny, pendant purple-and-yellow flowers on arching stems is the quality that earned the genus the name 'Dancing Ladies Ginger.' A distinctive feature of Globba is the replacement of most flowers by small, round, fleshy bulbils — mini-propagules that drop and sprout new plants, forming colonies over time. One of the finest shade-tolerant gingers for zone 9 Gulf Coast woodland gardens.

common_name: Dancing Lady Orchid (Golden Shower Orchid, Tiger Orchid, Sphacelatum)
plant_note: Grow in a slatted pot or basket with coarse bark media in bright indirect to filtered direct light; Oncidium sphacelatum is one of the more tolerant Oncidiums, adapting to a wider range of conditions than many spray orchids. In zone 9, it can grow on a shaded porch in a hanging basket from spring through fall, then moved indoors in winter. The plant blooms from pseudobulbs of the previous season — maintain 3+ mature pseudobulbs for reliable blooming. Water regularly while in growth, reduce in winter rest. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct morning sun — Dancing Lady Orchid produces its best blooms with 4–6 hours of bright filtered light and will not bloom reliably in dim indoor conditions. Oncidium sphacelatum is a large, clump-forming, sympodial epiphytic orchid native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Belize, Venezuela, and Colombia, widely distributed in highland tropical forests from sea level to 5,000+ feet. It is one of the largest commonly grown Oncidiums and produces some of the most spectacular spray-type orchid inflorescences available: long, arching, multi-branched panicles 3–5 feet in length carrying hundreds of individual flowers in vivid yellow and chestnut-brown — the small (half-inch to 1-inch) flowers have brown-barred petals and a dominant, bright yellow, flared lip that gives dancing lady orchids their name (the yellow lip resembles the skirt of a dancer twirling in a yellow dress with brown accents). A well-established plant in full bloom with 2–3 long, branching inflorescences simultaneously open is one of the most dramatic of all orchid displays. The plant is a prolific grower that divides readily, forming large clumps. Oncidium sphacelatum has been used extensively in producing the Oncidium intergeneric hybrids now widely sold as potted orchids. Non-toxic to pets.

common_name: Dancing Queen Hosta (Intensely Rippled Glossy Gold Foliage)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil. Dancing Queen, a sport of the popular Paul's Glory, bears intensely rippled, glossy gold foliage.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partly to fully shaded site, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Dancing Queen, a striking sport of the widely grown Paul's Glory, bears solid gold leaves with intensely rippled, glossy, undulating surfaces that catch the light beautifully, a bold, glowing color and texture combination for a shaded border. It produces lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer, though the glossy gold foliage is the primary ornamental feature. Mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system from summer heat.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, gritty soil to help them survive summer dormancy.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in a sunny, sharply drained spot, since this dwarf iris is prone to rot in soil that stays wet through summer dormancy. It opens bright egg-yolk yellow flowers with darker spotting on the falls, often before its four-sided grassy leaves fully lengthen, making it one of the very earliest bulbs to bloom alongside snowdrops and winter aconite. The blooms are small enough to enjoy up close in rock gardens, troughs, or the front of a raised bed. Bulbs frequently split into non-flowering offsets after the first year, so gardeners often replant fresh bulbs for reliable repeat bloom.

common_name: Danica Arborvitae (Very Dwarf Bright Green Globe Arborvitae)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Danica is a very dwarf, tightly globe-shaped Danish-bred arborvitae that stays compact for many years without pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Danica forms a very dwarf, perfectly rounded globe of dense, bright green, fine-textured foliage that turns a warm bronze-green in winter cold before greening back up in spring, staying naturally compact for many years without any pruning or shearing. Its small, tidy scale makes it especially useful for rock gardens, low borders, container plantings, and small foundation beds where even the smallest standard arborvitae would eventually outgrow the space. Like other arborvitae it prefers cooler climates with consistent moisture and can struggle in extreme summer heat and humidity, so afternoon shade helps where summers are hottest. Established plants need only occasional deep watering during drought and essentially no maintenance to keep their naturally neat form.

common_name: Danish Flag Poppy (Red Petals with White Cross Breadseed Poppy)
plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; needs light and cool soil to germinate.
directions: Scatter the tiny seed on the soil surface in early spring or fall, leaving it uncovered since light and cool temperatures aid germination; grow in full sun in well-drained soil, where it is drought tolerant once established. Danish Flag produces striking, brilliant scarlet-red single blooms marked with a bold white cross at the base of the petals, a distinctive pattern that gives the cultivar its name and makes it an instantly recognizable addition to a cottage or cutting garden. Direct sow only, since poppies resent root disturbance, and let plants self-sow for future years once established. The attractive seed pods that follow can be left to dry for arrangements, and all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Direct sow, as this ornamental carrot resents transplanting.
directions: Direct sow where plants are to grow, since this ornamental carrot dislikes root disturbance. Also called false Queen Anne's lace, Dara adds soft, airy, lacy umbels to the garden and to fresh or dried arrangements without the aggressiveness of the true species. It is fairly drought tolerant once established, so water moderately. Cut stems when the umbels are freshly open for the longest vase life.

common_name: Darcey Bussell Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Darcey Bussell's compact, bushy habit fits smaller borders and mixed plantings better than the larger, more sprawling English rose cultivars.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2006 and named for the celebrated British ballerina, Darcey Bussell produces deep crimson-red, fully double rosette flowers with a fruity, slightly musky fragrance on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub noticeably smaller and tidier than many older English rose cultivars. Its manageable size and rich, saturated color make it a strong choice for a smaller border or mixed planting where a full-size climbing English rose would be out of scale, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Darcy's sage is hardier than most scarlet salvias and can survive brief dips to about 20 degrees F when established. In zones 8-10 it grows as a long-lived perennial subshrub. Prune back by one-third in early spring to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Darcy's sage is a compact Mexican native from the Sierra Madre Oriental of Nuevo Leon and Coahuila producing an exceptionally long season of brilliant, clear scarlet-red flowers — a deeper, truer red than the salmon-to-pink range of most Salvia greggii cultivars — from spring through frost. The flowers are two-lipped and slightly larger than those of autumn sage, making it particularly effective for hummingbirds. Native to dry, rocky, limestone slopes at 8,000-10,000 feet elevation, it is adapted to hot, dry, alkaline conditions and proves drought-tolerant once established. It was recently discovered by plant explorers and introduced to cultivation in the 1990s, and its combination of true scarlet color, extended bloom season, and drought tolerance has made it a favorite in the heat-tolerant perennial border. Exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds throughout its very long bloom period from April through October in mild climates.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Fuchsia grows as a perennial woody shrub in zones 10–11 and as a season-long annual in zones 3–9. In zone 9 it often survives mild winters — cut back in early spring and the woody base regrows. Hanging baskets require daily watering in summer heat; afternoon shade prevents wilting. Spent flowers drop cleanly, so deadheading is not required for continued bloom.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil or high-quality potting mix in containers; Dark Eyes is one of the most recognizable and widely grown fuchsia cultivars, distinguished by its richly colored double flowers with vivid red-pink sepals spreading backward from a full, rounded, deep violet-purple corolla — a classic fuchsia color combination that is simultaneously jewel-toned and reminiscent of tropical birds in flight. The pendant flowers are borne continuously throughout the growing season on trailing to semi-upright stems that make Dark Eyes ideal for hanging baskets, window boxes, and elevated container positions where the downward-facing flowers are viewed at eye level or from below. Fuchsia flowers are among the most reliably shade-tolerant of all flowering annuals, performing in deep shade conditions where most flowering plants fail to bloom adequately. Hummingbirds are extremely attracted to fuchsia flowers and will visit frequently, making Dark Eyes a reliable hummingbird garden plant in any shaded position.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Dark Towers, a Plant Select introduction, is grown as much for its dark maroon-bronze foliage as for its pale pink tubular flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since penstemon is prone to crown rot in wet, heavy soil. Dark Towers, a Plant Select introduction, pairs tall spikes of pale pink, tubular flowers with striking dark maroon-bronze foliage that holds its color through the growing season, giving the plant strong ornamental value even between bloom flushes. It attracts hummingbirds and bees while in flower and tolerates heat and drought well once established, needing minimal supplemental water beyond the establishment period. Deadhead spent flower spikes to encourage additional bloom, and avoid overly rich soil or excess fertilizer, which produces weak, floppy growth in penstemon.

common_name: Dark Vader Pulmonaria (Deep Violet-Blue Silver-Spotted Lungwort)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dark Vader bears unusually dark violet-blue flowers over heavily silvered leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; good drainage combined with consistent moisture keeps the fleshy roots from rotting while preventing the leaves from scorching in a dry site. Dark Vader produces unusually deep violet-blue flowers, darker and more saturated than most lungwort cultivars, opening in early spring atop leaves that are heavily overlaid with silver spotting, giving the foliage striking presence well after the flowers fade for the rest of the season. Like other pulmonaria, it thrives in the moist, dappled shade of a woodland setting and pairs well with hostas, ferns, and other spring-flowering shade perennials such as hellebores and epimedium. Cut back tattered foliage after flowering if powdery mildew appears in humid summer weather, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in fall or early spring.

common_name: Dart's Gold Ninebark (Classic Golden-Yellow Foliage Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Dart's Gold is one of the original golden-foliage ninebark cultivars and can scorch in the hottest, most exposed full-sun sites without adequate soil moisture.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; some afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in hot climates while still keeping the foliage bright gold rather than fading to green. Dart's Gold is a longtime classic among golden-leaved shrubs, producing bright chartreuse-yellow foliage that holds its color through the growing season, contrasting well with dark-leaved companions like Diabolo ninebark or purple-leaved smokebush, and small clusters of white-to-pink flowers appear in late spring followed by reddish seed capsules. Mature stems develop the characteristic peeling, multi-layered bark that gives ninebark its common name, adding winter interest once the leaves drop. It tolerates a wide range of soil conditions, including clay and periodic flooding, and needs only occasional renewal pruning to remove old stems at the base and keep the shrub full.

common_name: Darwin's Orchid (Star of Bethlehem Orchid, Comet Orchid, Christmas Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark or in a slatted basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to filtered morning sun; Angraecum sesquipedale blooms in winter (November–January), triggered by seasonal temperature drops to 55–60°F at night — this natural temperature fluctuation is essential for inducing bloom. Protect from temperatures below 50°F. In zone 9, grow on a shaded porch in a basket from spring through early fall, then move inside to a bright, cool windowsill for the winter bloom period. Water regularly in growth; reduce slightly in winter. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle filtered light in a well-draining bark medium or mounted on cork — Darwin's Orchid grows best in bright, diffuse light similar to dappled forest canopy and will not bloom reliably in dim interior conditions. Angraecum sesquipedale is a large, monopodial epiphytic orchid endemic to Madagascar in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most historically significant plants in all of evolutionary biology — the subject of Charles Darwin's famous 1862 prediction. Examining dried herbarium specimens of A. sesquipedale with their extraordinary flower structure — large (5-inch), waxy, pure white, six-pointed, star-shaped flowers with a single, enormously elongated, thin, whip-like nectar spur hanging below the flower to a length of 11–13 inches — Darwin proposed in his book 'Fertilisation of Orchids' that somewhere in Madagascar, an undiscovered moth must exist with a proboscis long enough to reach the nectar at the base of the spur. Critics ridiculed the prediction. In 1903, 21 years after Darwin's death, a subspecies of the hawk moth Xanthopan morganii was discovered in Madagascar with a proboscis of exactly the predicted length — the confirmation of a prediction from evolutionary logic. The flowers are intensely fragrant at night, attracting their hawk moth pollinators. A large, impressive orchid with stunning winter flowers and extraordinary scientific heritage. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Davenport is a Fringed-class tulip with deep cherry-red blooms and fine crystalline fringe, blooming late in the season.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Davenport bears deep, rich cherry-red blooms with fine, crystalline fringe edging each petal, the delicate icy-textured margin distinctive to the Fringed tulip class, blooming late in the tulip season for an extended spring bulb display when paired with earlier-blooming cultivars. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; David Howard's dark bronze foliage holds its color best in full sun.
directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; David Howard's dark bronze foliage holds its color best in full sun. Rich, warm apricot-orange decorative flowers contrast beautifully against deep bronze-purple foliage, a striking two-tone combination that has made this compact, long-blooming cultivar one of the most popular dark-leaved dahlias for both borders and containers since its introduction decades ago. Its shorter, bushier habit compared to many taller dahlia cultivars makes it well suited to the middle of a border or a large container, where its dark foliage provides season-long color even between flushes of bloom. Stake if grown in a windy site, deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost blackens the foliage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space at least 18 inches apart — good air circulation is essential to minimize powdery mildew, the primary phlox disease in humid climates.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation; David was named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2002 and is widely considered the best white tall garden phlox cultivar ever introduced — selected by David Benner of New Hope, Pennsylvania, specifically for outstanding resistance to powdery mildew, the devastating fungal disease that disfigures most Phlox paniculata cultivars by midsummer in humid climates. Most phlox cultivars develop severe powdery mildew by July or August in the East and Gulf South — their leaves turn white with fungal coating that persists through the rest of the season. David's powdery mildew resistance is dramatically superior to older cultivars, maintaining clean, attractive dark-green foliage well into fall. The large, fragrant, pure white flower heads (panicles) are produced from July through September in zone 8, making it one of the finest long-season white perennials. The intensely fragrant flowers are outstanding for cutting and garden performance. In zone 9, tall garden phlox is not reliably perennial — it performs best as a short-lived perennial in zone 8 and colder. In zone 9's intense summer heat, phlox often declines, but with afternoon shade and consistent moisture it can be maintained for 2–3 years.

common_name: David Verity Cuphea (Prolific Orange-Red Tubular Hummingbird Annual for Summer Heat)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; David Verity is a sterile hybrid that does not set seed — propagated vegetatively by cuttings and sold only as container plants rather than seeds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; David Verity Cuphea is one of the most valuable and consistent hummingbird-attracting annuals for Gulf South summer gardens — a hybrid Cuphea (likely Cuphea ignea x C. llavea parentage) that produces an extraordinary abundance of small, tubular, bright orange-red flowers tipped with purple-black from spring through hard frost, creating a continuous nectar source that ruby-throated hummingbirds and butterflies find irresistible. The small, tubular flower form is precisely calibrated for hummingbird bill access — each flower produces concentrated nectar that makes these plants extremely effective hummingbird magnets in late summer and fall when migrating hummingbirds are actively fueling up for their Gulf of Mexico crossing. The flowers are produced so prolifically and continuously that established plants rarely appear to be between bloom flushes — the orange-red and black color combination creates a vivid display through the longest, hottest Gulf South summer days. 'David Verity' is sterile and propagated by cuttings, making it available only as nursery transplants. The compact, mounding to slightly spreading habit makes it excellent for container culture (where it can be overwintered as a tender perennial) and for summer border edge plantings. In zone 9, it grows as a warm-season annual from spring transplanting through first frost. In zone 10–12, it may survive winter as a subshrub. No deadheading required — spent flowers drop cleanly and new buds open continuously.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; plant at least one male and one female close together, since this species is dioecious and only pollinated females produce the ornamental berries.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, though established plants tolerate deeper shade under high tree canopy. David viburnum is a low, mounded evergreen shrub from western China valued for its leathery, deeply three-veined, glossy dark green leaves that hold their color through winter, forming a dense architectural groundcover unlike most deciduous viburnums grown for flowers or fall color. Flattened heads of small white flowers appear in late spring, and where a male plant grows nearby, female shrubs set clusters of long-lasting, metallic turquoise-blue berries that are one of the more unusual fruit colors in the shade garden. Its tidy, spreading habit suits it to massing along a shaded foundation, edging a woodland path, or filling a bed beneath taller understory trees.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; David's epimedium stays evergreen in mild winters and its bright yellow flowers show up especially well against the glossy, dark green, spiny-edged foliage.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; David's epimedium stays evergreen in mild winters and its bright yellow flowers show up especially well against the glossy, dark green, spiny-edged foliage. Epimedium davidii is a west-central Chinese species forming a low, evergreen clump of glossy, leathery, spine-toothed leaflets, with wiry stems carrying loose sprays of bright yellow, long-spurred flowers well above the foliage in mid-spring. Its clean evergreen foliage and vivid, clear yellow flower color make it a good choice for a shaded border or rock garden where year-round structure is valued alongside spring bloom. It spreads at a moderate, well-behaved pace by rhizome and is easy to grow under standard epimedium conditions, tolerating typical garden soil once established.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Davidson's penstemon is a high-alpine mat-forming species that needs sharp drainage and struggles with heat and humidity.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Davidson's penstemon is a high-alpine mat-forming species that needs sharp drainage and struggles with heat and humidity. Small, glossy, evergreen leaves form a dense, low, woody mat that hugs rocky ground closely, studded in early summer with large, vivid violet-blue, tubular flowers disproportionately showy for the plant's diminutive scale, native to high-elevation talus slopes and rocky ridges from the Cascades through the Sierra Nevada. Its tight, cushion-forming habit and tolerance of thin, rocky alpine soil make it a choice specimen for a trough garden, rock garden crevice, or alpine bed in a cool-summer climate, but it performs poorly in hot, humid regions far from its high-mountain origins. Water sparingly, provide sharp drainage above all else, and avoid any soil enrichment, which this lean-soil specialist does not need or tolerate.

plant_note: Plant a young tree in spring after the ground has thawed, in deep moist soil with room to grow large.
directions: Dawn redwood is a fast-growing deciduous conifer often called a living fossil, prized for feathery fern-like foliage that turns coppery orange before dropping in fall. Give it full sun and consistently moist, well-drained soil; it tolerates wet sites and even seasonal flooding better than most conifers. Choose a location with abundant vertical and horizontal space, as mature trees reach 70 to 100 feet with a broad conical form. Water deeply during establishment and through dry spells for the first few seasons. It needs no pruning to develop its naturally elegant shape.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; site it near a path or entry where its winter fragrance can be enjoyed on mild days.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, in a sheltered spot away from harsh winter wind that can brown open flowers. 'Dawn' is an upright, multi-stemmed hybrid selected at Bodnant Garden in Wales, prized for clusters of small, tubular, rose-pink buds that open to pale pink and release a strong, sweet fragrance intermittently from late fall through late winter, often on bare wood well before other shrubs stir. The dull, coarsely toothed leaves emerge bronze-tinted in spring and take on modest red tones in fall, but the plant's main season of interest is the depth of winter, when little else in the shaded border is in bloom. Renewal-prune older stems back to the base every few years after flowering to keep the shrub from becoming leggy at its base.

common_name: Dawn to Dusk Catmint (Pink-Flowered Giant Catmint)
