In zone 9, Diamond Head is reliably perennial, dying back in cold winters but returning from persistent tubers in spring. The compact habit makes it outstanding for mixed borders, container plantings, and defined landscape spaces where a controllable but dramatic dark tropical accent is desired.

common_name: Diamond Lake Hosta (Rounded Deep Blue Shadowland Series Hosta)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil. Diamond Lake, part of the Shadowland series, bears rounded, deep blue foliage on a medium-sized plant.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partly to fully shaded site, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Diamond Lake, part of the modern Shadowland breeding series, bears rounded, deeply blue-toned foliage with a smooth, waxy bloom that helps the color hold through the season better than many older blue hosta cultivars. It produces lavender flowers on scapes in summer. Mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system from summer heat, and divide congested clumps every several years in spring.

common_name: Diamond Mound Euphorbia (Compact Mounding Baby's Breath Euphorbia)
plant_note: Set out transplants after the last frost into full sun in well-drained soil; Diamond Mound holds a tighter, more rounded habit than the looser, airier Diamond Frost, making it useful as a filler in beds and containers without sprawling.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and avoid overwatering, since this euphorbia is more drought-tolerant than most bedding annuals and dislikes wet, soggy roots. Diamond Mound produces a dense cloud of tiny white flowers over fine-textured foliage almost continuously from spring through frost, giving beds and containers a soft, airy filler texture similar to baby's breath but on a heat-tolerant, low-maintenance annual. Its tighter, more compact mounding habit than the trailing Diamond Frost selection makes it useful as a well-behaved filler that does not spill over neighboring plants, while still needing no deadheading to keep flowering. Established plants tolerate heat and short dry spells well, and light, regular feeding keeps the fine bloom display dense through the growing season; the milky sap can irritate skin, so gloves are recommended when handling or pruning it.

common_name: Diamond Rouge Hydrangea (Deep Red Fall-Color Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Diamond Rouge is selected for panicles that mature to an unusually deep, saturated red rather than the more common pink.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Diamond Rouge opens creamy white in midsummer, then deepens through pink to an unusually saturated, dark rose-red by late summer and into fall, a richer, more intense red than most panicle hydrangea cultivars achieve, on sturdy, upright stems that support the dense conical panicles without staking. The strong color development is most pronounced with cooler night temperatures in late summer, so fall color tends to be more dramatic than midsummer color. Like other H. paniculata cultivars it blooms on new wood, so prune hard in late winter to a low, well-spaced framework of buds to encourage vigorous new growth and the largest, most colorful panicles.

common_name: Diamond Snow Euphorbia (Compact Heat-Tolerant White-Flowered Filler Annual)
plant_note: Set out transplants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Diamond Snow tolerates heat and humidity well, blooming continuously through the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after frost danger passes. Diamond Snow is a compact, mounding annual euphorbia bred as part of the popular Diamond series, producing a dense cloud of tiny white flowers above fine, airy foliage, creating a baby's-breath-like filler effect that softens and fills gaps between bolder-flowered plants in beds, borders, and mixed containers. The tighter, more compact habit compared to the larger Diamond Frost makes it especially well suited to smaller containers and tight planting spaces. It blooms continuously from spring through frost with minimal deadheading required, tolerates heat and drought well once established, and performs reliably in the intense heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer where many other fine-textured annuals falter. Water regularly while establishing, then reduce frequency, since the plant prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings.

common_name: Diamond Spire Gardenia (Narrow Columnar Fragrant Gardenia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Diamond Spire is a narrow, upright columnar gardenia cultivar bred for tight spaces where a standard rounded gardenia would be too wide, while still producing the classic fragrant double white flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest Gulf Coast gardens. Diamond Spire is a narrow, upright gardenia selection bred to give the intensely fragrant, double white summer flowers of a classic gardenia in a tight, columnar footprint suited to narrow side yards, foundation plantings, and vertical accents where a standard wide-spreading gardenia wouldn't fit. Glossy dark evergreen foliage clothes the upright stems from top to bottom, and the strongly perfumed blooms open over the summer, filling the surrounding air with the classic gardenia scent. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in spring and again in early summer, keep soil consistently moist but well drained, and watch for whitefly and sooty mold, common gardenia pests in humid climates. Prune only lightly right after flowering to maintain the narrow form.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in sandy, well-drained soil; plants form a rosette in the first year and bolt to flower in the second year, then self-sow to maintain the colony.
directions: Diamond-petal Evening Primrose is a tall, statuesque biennial native to sandy dunes, open disturbed ground, and dry plains of the Great Plains, forming a low, flat gray-green rosette in its first year and shooting up a leafy spike to 6 feet in its second year. The distinctive, large, clear yellow flowers have noticeably diamond- to rhombus-shaped petals 2-3 inches across and open in the evening, attracting hawk moths for pollination before closing by mid-morning. Direct sow in fall in sandy, lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow their architectural second-year form to develop. Plants self-sow reliably in open sandy ground, keeping a self-sustaining colony going year after year without replanting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; in zone 8–9 plant September–March. Diana Clare establishes best with consistent moisture during the first growing season. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in fall after foliage declines to maintain vigor. In zone 9 provide reliable shade and moisture to protect from summer heat; mulch heavily around the crown. The plant goes summer-dormant in heat — do not overwater dormant plants.
directions: Plant in full shade to light dappled shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Diana Clare is a highly awarded Pulmonaria cultivar from Terra Nova Nurseries, distinguished by its extraordinarily silver-splashed leaves — the foliage is so heavily overlaid with bright silver that individual leaves appear nearly entirely silver with just a hint of green remaining, creating one of the most dramatic foliage effects of any shade perennial. The plants bloom very early in spring (February–April) with vivid violet-blue to purple-red flowers (the classic lungwort two-tone pink-then-blue color shift as individual flowers age on the same plant) that are among the first nectar sources available to early pollinators including queen bumblebees emerging from winter dormancy. As the flowers fade the striking silver foliage takes over as the primary ornamental feature throughout summer and fall. Lungwort (Pulmonaria) is one of the most reliable low-maintenance shade groundcovers for the mid-Atlantic and Southeast, tolerating dry summer shade once established better than most shade perennials.

common_name: Diana Rose of Sharon (Sterile White Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood.
directions: Diana was introduced by the US National Arboretum as part of a breeding program aimed at improving on old-fashioned rose of sharon, and it remains one of the best white-flowered selections available. Its large, pure white, 4 to 5 inch flowers stay open later into the evening and remain open longer during the day than most rose of sharon cultivars, and as a sterile triploid it sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older althea. Bloom runs from midsummer into fall on new wood, giving a long season of clean white color when many other shrubs have finished flowering; site it as a summer anchor in a mixed border or informal hedge.

common_name: Diane Witch Hazel (Red-Flowered Winter Witch Hazel)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; witch hazel flower buds need real winter chill to open well, so bloom is most reliable in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 and can be sparse in mild winters.
directions: Diane is the most widely grown red-flowered witch hazel, producing clusters of narrow, spidery, ribbon-petaled flowers in a deep coppery red that opens in late winter while the shrub is still bare, one of the earliest and most distinctive flower displays of the gardening year. Its fall foliage color, orange to red-purple, is also considered among the best of the intermedia witch hazels, giving Diane strong two-season interest beyond the winter bloom. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since witch hazel resents both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: Diane's Gold Brunnera (Chartreuse-Gold Heartleaf Shade Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Diane's Gold holds its chartreuse-gold heart-shaped foliage color through the summer better than many gold-leaved perennials.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the bright foliage. Diane's Gold bears bold, heart-shaped, chartreuse-gold leaves that hold their bright color through the summer better than many gold-leaved shade perennials, topped in early spring by sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers before the foliage fully expands. Its glowing foliage color lights up a dark corner of the garden long after the spring flowers fade. Keep soil consistently moist, especially during summer heat, and divide congested clumps in early spring or fall.

plant_note: Broadcast seed in spring once soil has warmed, or plant plugs, into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; dichondra tolerates foot traffic and mowing far better than most shade groundcovers, making it a genuine turfgrass alternative for lawns under trees.
directions: Broadcast seed in spring once soil has warmed, or plant plugs, into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; dichondra tolerates foot traffic and mowing far better than most shade groundcovers, making it a genuine turfgrass alternative for lawns under trees. Dichondra micrantha is a low, mat-forming perennial with small, rounded, bright green, kidney-shaped leaves that has long been used across the warm-climate South and California as a fine-textured lawn substitute in shaded areas where turfgrass thins out, spreading by creeping stems that root at the nodes to knit into a dense, weed-suppressing carpet. It tolerates regular mowing to keep it low and neat, handles moderate foot traffic, and stays green through the warm season with regular water, though it goes off-color and semi-dormant with cold snaps in the cooler part of its range. It needs reasonably good drainage and a warm climate to thrive, struggling in prolonged freezes or waterlogged, poorly drained soil.

plant_note: Plant corms immediately after division in late summer or early fall, 3-4 inches deep, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; dimpled trout lily is the common southeastern trout lily of rich cove forests and floodplain woods from Georgia and the Carolinas into Alabama and Tennessee.
directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep immediately after division in late summer or early fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil under deciduous trees; do not allow corms to dry out before planting. Dimpled trout lily takes its name from the distinctly dimpled, umbilicate seed capsule that lies flat on the ground as it ripens, a reliable field mark separating it from the similar Erythronium americanum, which holds its capsule upright on an erect stalk; both share the same mottled, trout-spotted leaves and nodding, reflexed yellow flowers in late winter to early spring. It forms dense, slowly spreading colonies in rich southeastern cove forests and floodplain woods and makes an excellent naturalizing companion for trilliums, bloodroot, and other regional spring ephemerals. Like other trout lilies it disappears completely by late spring, so plant it where later-emerging ferns or hostas can take over the display.

common_name: Dinema (Twin Spur Orchid, Polybulbon Epidendrum, Caribbean Creeper)
plant_note: Grow mounted on bark or cork, or in a shallow basket with coarse bark; Dinema polybulbon is an excellent beginner orchid for outdoor culture in zone 9-11 — it is cold-tolerant, fast-growing, and produces its modest but pleasant fragrant flowers in late fall and winter. The creeping, spreading rhizomes quickly colonize the surface of a cork mount or flat bark piece. Water regularly in active growth; reduce slightly in winter. Tolerates temperatures briefly to 38–40°F. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow mounted on rough bark or cork in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light with moderate humidity — Dinema polybulbon is one of the most cold-tolerant small epiphytic orchids for zone 9-11 outdoor culture and adapts exceptionally well to outdoor mounted culture on a shaded, protected porch. Dinema polybulbon (formerly Epidendrum polybulbon) is a small, creeping, sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Belize, Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, and Puerto Rico in the Orchidaceae family — one of the cold-hardiest of the small, Caribbean-origin epiphytic orchids regularly available in the orchid trade. The plant spreads by creeping rhizomes that slowly colonize the surface of its mount, each section producing a very small, round to oblong pseudobulb topped with 2 narrow, stiff, dark-green leaves about 2–3 inches long. In late fall and winter, short flower spikes (2–3 inches) emerge from between the leaves, bearing 1–2 small (1-inch) flowers in yellow-white with yellow-orange stripes on the sepals and petals and a white to cream lip — modest in size but pleasantly fragrant on warm days. The plant's creeping, mat-forming growth habit, cold tolerance, and unfussy culture make it an excellent starter orchid for zone 9-11 collectors beginning outdoor epiphyte culture. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Dinner Plate aeonium forms a flat, single rosette and is monocarpic, dying after flowering once mature.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Dinner Plate aeonium forms a flat, single rosette and is monocarpic, dying after flowering once mature. Hundreds of small, tightly overlapping, fringed leaves arrange themselves into an almost perfectly flat, circular rosette that can reach nearly two feet across, an extraordinary geometric form unlike any other commonly grown succulent, densely covered in fine cilia along the leaf edges that catch the light. Like some other aeoniums it is monocarpic, meaning the rosette flowers once after several years of growth and then dies, so plan to take offsets or start new plants from seed before the parent completes its life cycle. Water occasionally, protect from intense midday sun which can scorch the flat rosette, and grow in a shallow container that showcases its unusual flattened form.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost; lift and store where not hardy.
directions: Plant dinnerplate dahlia tubers after the last frost, laying them horizontally about six inches deep with the eye facing up. These giant blooms can reach ten to twelve inches across and require staking at planting to support the tall stems. Grow in full sun and rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply once shoots emerge and pinching to promote branching. In cold climates lift and store the tubers in a frost-free place over winter.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade after frost; dipladenia performs best in consistently moist but well-drained soil — waterlogged roots cause yellowing and dieback, while drought stress causes bud drop and leaf loss.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; dipladenia (mandevilla, rocktrumpet) is a Brazilian tropical twining vine widely sold throughout the garden industry as a patio and container flowering plant for its large, trumpet-shaped, glossy-petaled flowers in vivid shades of red, deep-pink, rose-pink, and white, produced continuously throughout the warm season on new growth. It is one of the most extensively-sold container flowering vines in the American nursery trade, marketed under the names dipladenia (for the more compact, less-twining forms) and mandevilla (for the larger, more vigorous climbing forms). The glossy, deep-green, oval leaves and shining, varnished-looking flower petals give the plant a distinctive, tropical-polished appearance. As an outdoor perennial in zone 10–12 it grows vigorously on trellises and arbors; in cooler climates it is used as a summer annual or overwintered as a container plant indoors. The compact cultivars (sold as 'Dipladenia') are bushy and non-vining; the larger forms (sold as 'Mandevilla') climb to 10 feet or more. The plant exudes milky sap; wash hands after pruning.

common_name: Dipt in Wine Coleus (Burgundy-Lime Ruffled ColorBlaze Coleus)
plant_note: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in full sun to light shade with even moisture; pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushiness.
directions: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in full sun to light shade with even moisture. Part of the ColorBlaze series bred for garden performance in sun, this coleus carries small, pointed, serrated leaves in rich burgundy-wine with pink veining and a lime-green rim that can brighten to gold in strong sun. Its upright, well-branched habit fills out quickly and holds color intensity through summer heat better than many older shade-type coleus. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushiness and remove any flower spikes to keep foliage production strong.

common_name: Director George T. Moore Water Lily (Classic Fragrant Tropical Violet-Purple Day-Bloomer)
plant_note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after water has warmed well past last frost; Director George T. Moore, a classic 1941 Missouri Botanical Garden introduction, bears fragrant, star-shaped, violet-purple day-blooming flowers.
directions: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 12 to 18 inches deep in a full-sun pond, waiting until the water has warmed well above 70°F, since tropical water lilies are cold-sensitive and grow poorly if planted too early. Director George T. Moore, introduced in 1941 by the Missouri Botanical Garden and named for its longtime director, is a classic, long-cultivated tropical water lily bearing large, star-shaped flowers in a rich violet-purple with a sweet, distinctive fragrance, opening during the day above the water's surface on strong stems held well above the pads. It is a vigorous grower, producing abundant bloom through the warm season, and in zones below its perennial range is typically grown as a warm-season annual or overwintered indoors as a dormant tuber. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly through the growing season, remove spent flowers and yellowing pads, and divide congested tubers as needed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; disanthus is slow-growing and dislikes root disturbance — plant carefully and do not move. It requires reliably moist, acidic conditions similar to Japanese maples and kalmia, and grows naturally in moist mountain forests of Japan and central China.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil in part shade; disanthus is a monotypic genus in the witch-hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) — a single species from mountain forests of Japan and central China that is grown primarily as one of the elite autumn-coloring shrubs. The broadly rounded, heart-shaped leaves closely resemble those of Cercis (redbud) in shape, turning in autumn to some of the most spectacular colors achievable in a garden shrub: brilliant combinations of crimson, orange, purple, and claret, often with all colors simultaneously visible on a single leaf. In October, tiny, deep wine-purple flowers appear directly on the bare and falling-leaf branches — so small and dark that they are easily missed but distinctive and curious up close, with reflexed petals in pairs. A slow-growing, understated but ultimately magnificent shrub for the woodland garden with moist, acidic conditions, outstanding autumn color, and a refined year-round form. Often cited by plantsmen as one of the most desirable garden shrubs, despite remaining little-known outside specialist collections.

common_name: Disco Belle Hardy Hibiscus (Dwarf Large-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost or set out container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Disco Belle stays much shorter than older hardy hibiscus types, keeping its enormous flowers close to eye level rather than atop tall stems.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, and keep the root zone consistently damp through the growing season, since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant that wilts quickly if allowed to dry out. Disco Belle was bred as a dwarf, compact hardy hibiscus series reaching only 18–24 inches tall, far shorter than older hardy hibiscus types that commonly reach 4–6 feet, while still producing the same dinner-plate-sized, 8–10 inch flowers in shades of red, pink, and white, often with a contrasting red eye. The compact habit makes it useful for smaller borders, mass plantings, and containers where larger hardy hibiscus would be out of scale, and it dies back to the ground each winter, re-emerging reliably in late spring. Cut the dead stems back to a few inches above the ground in late winter before new growth begins.

plant_note: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, strongly to moderately acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full shade to part shade; discolor calanthe is a Japanese native terrestrial orchid and one of the hardiest of all cultivatable orchids, surviving winters to zone 5 when grown in protected, well-drained woodland conditions.
directions: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly to moderately acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), well-drained woodland soil in full shade; allow divisions to establish for a full season before expecting bloom. Calanthe discolor (discolor calanthe) is one of the hardiest and most gardener-friendly of all terrestrial orchids — a Japanese and East Asian species that can be grown as a perennial in the shade garden from zone 5 through zone 9, emerging in spring with attractive, pleated, semi-evergreen basal leaves and producing elegant, upright flower spikes 10–18 inches tall bearing 12–20 graceful, two-toned, purple-and-white orchid flowers in April–May. The contrast between the purplish-brown outer tepals and the pure-white lip (labellum) is striking and distinctive. Unlike epiphytic orchids (which grow in bark mixes), calanthes grow in humus-rich, acidic woodland soil and are treated much like hostas — planted in shaded beds, left to establish, and allowed to slowly clump up over years. In the shade garden, they bloom at an important transition period (April–May) before most summer shade perennials reach peak. C. discolor has been used extensively in breeding cold-hardy terrestrial orchid hybrids.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in zone 9–11; Wallichia disticha (Distichous Fishtail Palm) is a striking, unusual Himalayan palm with a unique flat, fan-like crown — all fronds held in a single plane, giving a two-dimensional silhouette — native to shaded forest margins from Nepal and northeastern India to southern China, and notable for being monocarpic (each stem flowers once, then dies, while the clump persists).
directions: Plant Wallichia disticha in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in bright partial shade, protecting from harsh afternoon sun and cold below 28°F; water regularly during establishment and provide a balanced slow-release palm fertilizer in spring and summer. The Distichous Fishtail Palm is one of the most architecturally distinctive of all palms — its unique flat crown, with all fronds arranged in a single vertical plane like pages in an open book (the meaning of 'distichous'), creates a dramatic, two-dimensional silhouette unlike any other palm species. Native to the moist, seasonally cool forests of the eastern Himalayas from Nepal through northeast India to southern China and Myanmar, it is adapted to partial shade and cooler conditions than most palms — making it useful in gardens where more tender palms fail. Wallichia disticha is monocarpic like most fishtail palms: each individual stem flowers and fruits once then dies, but the clump produces multiple stems and the overall plant persists. It is not as commonly cultivated as many other palms but is prized by collectors for its unusual form; it makes a spectacular specimen in zone 9–11 gardens in a sheltered, partially shaded position with reliable moisture.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; distylium is exceptional in its tolerance of both full sun and full shade with no significant change in growth quality — a rare characteristic among broadleaved evergreens.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Distylium racemosum is a Japanese evergreen shrub in the witch hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) that is gaining significant recognition as one of the most adaptable and low-maintenance broadleaved evergreens for zone 7–10 landscapes. It produces glossy, leathery, dark-green leaves on spreading, arching branches and bears unusual, petal-less winter flowers with prominent red stamens that emerge in February–March in zone 9, providing early-season color before most shrubs bloom. The strongly adaptable nature of distylium is its defining quality — it thrives in full sun to dense shade, in dry or moist soils, in clay or sandy soils, and in both acid and moderately alkaline pH ranges. This adaptability makes it invaluable for difficult landscape situations where few plants perform reliably. Named compact cultivars have made distylium increasingly available in the trade: 'Cinnamon Girl' (4–5 feet, copper-bronze new growth), 'Vintage Jade' (4 feet, spreading), and 'Coppertone' (2.5–3 feet, compact) are among the most widely sold selections. Distylium is completely free of serious pest and disease problems in zone 9, requires no deadheading or shaping, and is highly deer-resistant — a compelling combination for the low-maintenance Gulf South garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Distylium myricoides (sold as 'Vintage Jade' and related cultivars) has become one of the most popular new evergreen shrubs in the US Southeast for its compact habit, year-round glossy foliage, and exceptional heat and drought tolerance once established.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Distylium is a genus of evergreen shrubs and trees in the witch-hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) from China and Japan, emerging as one of the most important new landscape shrubs for the mid-South and Southeast. The species D. myricoides produces small, glossy, dark green leaves with a neat, compact, spreading habit and unusual winter-to-early-spring flowers — red stamens without petals that create a purplish-red haze across the plant in late winter. Exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established and resistant to deer browsing. Widely used in current Southeast US landscaping as a low-maintenance foundation plant; cultivars including 'Vintage Jade', 'Linebacker', and the Coppertone series are widely available. Thrives in part shade and full sun with minimal care. Disease and pest resistant.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost danger passes and soil warms.
directions: Diva is a tall, prolific dahlia producing rich plum blooms with exceptional vase life for a large flower. Set tubers about 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun once soil is warm, and wait to water heavily until growth appears. Because plants grow very tall, install sturdy stakes or a support cage early in the season. Cut or deadhead spent flowers frequently to prolong blooming into fall. Lift and store tubers over winter where the ground freezes.

common_name: Divisilobum Soft Shield Fern (Finely Dissected Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Divisilobum is a finely dissected soft shield fern selection with lacy, feathery, evergreen fronds.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Divisilobum is a soft shield fern selection with exceptionally finely cut, lacy, almost feathery fronds, among the most delicate-looking textures of any hardy evergreen fern, though the foliage is actually quite tough and weather-resistant. The arching, evergreen fronds hold their good looks through much of the winter in milder climates, providing structure and texture in the shade garden even in the off season. Its refined, dissected texture contrasts beautifully with the broad leaves of hostas or heucheras and pairs well with other ferns of contrasting form. More tolerant of dry shade than many ferns once established, though it still performs best with consistent moisture and a humus-rich soil that mimics its native woodland floor habitat. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter just before new growth (fiddleheads) emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years.

common_name: Dixie Deb Louisiana Iris (Classic Early Yellow Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Dixie Deb was one of the first widely popular clear yellow Louisiana iris cultivars and remains a garden standard for its dependable, floriferous performance and compact, early-blooming habit that often opens ahead of many other Louisiana iris cultivars in spring. Its long garden history and easy vigor have kept it in circulation among heirloom iris growers for decades. Keep the bed consistently damp through the growing season, top-dress with compost in early spring, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain strong bloom.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes and plant in fall or spring in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 6–10; Dixie Iris is the largest-flowered native iris of the Gulf Coast states — Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Florida Panhandle, and South Carolina — producing spectacular, large, blue-violet to red-purple flowers in spring at pond edges, drainage ditches, bayous, and moist meadows where it is tolerant of prolonged flooding and alkaline as well as acidic soils.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade — Iris hexagona is adapted to water-saturated soils and tolerates several weeks of complete flooding; excellent for rain gardens, pond margins, wet ditches, and boggy areas. Iris hexagona (Dixie Iris or Zigzag Iris) is a large-flowered, robust, native beardless iris indigenous to the coastal wetlands, bayous, river margins, brackish marshes, and wet prairie soils of the Gulf Coast states — Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina — and one of the most spectacular native wetland wildflowers of the Deep South. The large, showy flowers (3–4 inches across) are produced in spring in shades of deep blue-violet to rich red-purple, sometimes with yellow signals, held on sturdy, zigzag-branched stalks (hence one common name 'Zigzag Iris') above glossy, strap-like foliage reaching 3–4 feet. Iris hexagona is the dominant native parent species in the development of Louisiana Irises (Iris × louisiana hybrids) — the largest-flowered, most diverse, and most adaptable of all American native iris groups, created by hybridization with I. fulva, I. brevicaulis, and I. nelsonii. Unlike most garden irises, Dixie Iris thrives in wet, boggy, poorly drained, even flooded soils and tolerates wide pH variation. Excellent for Gulf Coast rain gardens, pond edges, and natural wet-area planting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Dixie wood fern is a naturally occurring, sterile hybrid between southern wood fern and log fern, larger and more vigorous than either parent.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Dixie wood fern is a naturally occurring, sterile hybrid between southern wood fern and log fern, larger and more vigorous than either parent. Dryopteris x australis forms a substantial, upright-arching clump of glossy, dark green, semi-evergreen fronds that hold up well through summer heat and humidity, making it one of the most reliable large ferns for southeastern gardens. Because it is a sterile hybrid it produces no viable spores and will not self-sow or become weedy, spreading only slowly by an expanding crown, which makes it a well-behaved choice for a shaded border or woodland garden where a bold, non-invasive fern is wanted. It tolerates heavier soil and more summer moisture than many ferns and needs little care beyond removing old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide only when clumps become overcrowded, since peonies otherwise thrive undisturbed for decades. Introduced in 1946, Do Tell is a Japanese-form peony with soft lavender-pink guard petals surrounding a full, ruffled center of narrow, cream-and-pink staminodes that give the bloom a frilly, two-toned appearance distinct from the fully double cultivars. It flowers in early-to-midseason on strong stems that generally stand up well without staking, and its lighter, more open form sheds rain better than heavy doubles. Like other lactiflora cultivars, it needs real winter cold to set buds and is best suited to zones 3–8.

plant_note: Plant by direct seed or division in spring in any sunny, well-drained soil; dog fennel is a robust, fast-growing perennial throughout the Gulf Coast and effectively self-seeds to return annually even where it is treated as an annual in colder zones — cut back hard in winter.
directions: Dog fennel is a ubiquitous native perennial of roadsides, old fields, and disturbed open areas throughout the Southeast, instantly recognizable by its thread-fine, feathery, intensely aromatic foliage — the camphor-like scent has historically made it a natural insect repellent, and bundles were placed in farm buildings and bedding to repel fleas and lice. Despite its weedy reputation in some circles, dog fennel is an ecologically important native: the clouds of tiny white flowers produced on 3–6 foot wiry stems in late fall are among the final nectar sources of the season for migrating monarchs and late-flying native bees in the Gulf Coast region, often blooming well into November in zone 9. The fine-textured, billowing foliage provides striking textural contrast in the naturalistic garden and is used by some designers as a feathery filler among coarser-leaved perennials. Cut back to a few inches in late winter; it regrows rapidly from the base and will reach full height by midsummer even in the Gulf South's hot climate.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), fertile soil in full shade to part shade; dog hobble is a native Appalachian understory shrub with long, arching branches and glossy, evergreen foliage that turns attractive burgundy-bronze in winter — one of the finest native shade shrubs for woodland gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in deep to part shade; mulch with pine bark or pine needles to maintain soil acidity. Leucothoe fontanesiana (dog hobble or drooping leucothoe) is an elegant native Appalachian understory shrub growing along shaded stream banks and moist forest floors from Virginia south to Georgia and Tennessee. The plant produces long (3–5 foot), gracefully arching stems clothed in glossy, lance-shaped, evergreen leaves — in summer a rich, dark green, transforming to dramatic shades of burgundy, bronze, and red-purple in winter (especially in cultivars like 'Rainbow' and 'Girard's Rainbow'). In late spring, drooping clusters of urn-shaped, white flowers (resembling lily-of-the-valley flowers) line the undersides of the arching branches — fragrant and attractive. Dog hobble earns its common name from the impenetrable tangles it forms along mountain creek banks, through which hunting dogs cannot easily pass. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form colonies. As a shade garden plant, Leucothoe fontanesiana provides outstanding year-round interest: spring flowers, summer foliage, and winter color in sites too acidic and shady for most other shrubs. The cultivar 'Scarletta' has especially vivid scarlet winter color.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root plants in early spring before leaf break. Cold stratify seeds for 90–180 days at 34–40°F before sowing if starting from seed.
directions: Plant in a sunny, open location with well-drained soil; Dog Rose tolerates poor, rocky, and chalky conditions and does not require amendment or fertilization. Take hardwood cuttings in late autumn or early winter, root them in sandy compost, and overwinter in a cold frame before transplanting the following spring. Once established, it is highly drought-tolerant and requires little supplemental watering. Prune out oldest canes after flowering to maintain an open framework and encourage vigorous new growth bearing the following season's blooms and hips.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial shade to shade; dogtooth violet goes completely summer-dormant and requires dry conditions during its summer rest. Naturalizes readily under deciduous trees in Europe and in North American woodland gardens.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; dogtooth violet is the European counterpart of the North American fawn lilies — a widespread Eurasian woodland spring ephemeral producing beautifully mottled brown-and-silver basal leaves and nodding, reflexed-petaled flowers in pink, white, lilac, or rose. The common name 'dogtooth violet' comes not from the flower but from the elongated, tooth-shaped corm. The mottled foliage is as attractive as the flowers. Plant in large drifts of 20 or more under deciduous trees for best effect — single corms are easily lost, but a naturalized colony creates a stunning spring display. Goes completely dormant by late spring; suitable for underplanting with summer-dormant perennials or in spots that go dry in summer. More widely available in North American commerce than the native Erythronium species, with many named cultivars in pink, rose, purple, and white.

common_name: Dolce Blackcurrant Heuchera (Deep Purple-Black Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dolce Blackcurrant is a Proven Winners introduction with deep purple-black foliage and a compact habit suited to shaded containers and small borders.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dolce Blackcurrant is a compact coral bells cultivar in the Proven Winners Dolce series, bearing glossy, ruffled leaves in a near-black deep purple that holds its intense color well through the season with some morning sun. Its dense, tidy mound stays small and neat without sprawling, making it especially useful for shaded container plantings, edging along a shade path, or as a dramatic dark accent tucked among chartreuse or silver-leaved companions in a mixed bed. Small pale flower spikes rise above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the rich, glossy leaf color. Provide consistent moisture and sharp drainage, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Dolce Heuchera (Compact Colorful Coral Bells Series)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Dolce heuchera develops its richest foliage color with some morning sun but needs protection from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the leaves in Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with morning sun for the best foliage color, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat. Dolce is a heuchera breeding series bred for compact, uniform habit and an especially wide range of rich, saturated foliage colors — from near-black and deep wine-purple to caramel, lime, and silvery-blue — that hold their color well through the growing season, topped by airy sprays of small pink to white flowers in late spring that attract hummingbirds. Its tidy, well-behaved clumps make it a reliable choice for the front of a shaded border, mass plantings, or containers, and the wide color range allows striking combinations when several Dolce selections are planted together. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, and remove tattered winter foliage in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Dolce Key Lime Pie Coral Bells (Chartreuse-Lime Foliage Heuchera)
plant_note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Dolce Key Lime Pie bears bright chartreuse-lime foliage with a contrasting red-purple leaf underside.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; some morning sun brightens the chartreuse foliage color while afternoon shade prevents scorch in hot climates. Dolce Key Lime Pie bears bright, glowing chartreuse-lime leaves with a contrasting deep red-purple reverse visible when the ruffled leaf edges curl, forming a dense mound topped in early summer by wiry stems of small white flowers that attract pollinators. Its vivid, citrus-bright color lights up a shaded border and pairs well with darker-leaved companion perennials. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and remove old, tattered leaves in late winter.

common_name: Dolce Licorice Heuchera (Near-Black Foliage Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Dolce Licorice is part of the Proven Winners Dolce series, grown for its near-black, glossy foliage that holds its dark color through the season better than many purple heucheras.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in the Gulf South to keep the foliage from bleaching. Dolce Licorice is part of the Proven Winners Dolce breeding series, selected for deep, glossy, near-black leaves with a ruffled edge that hold their dramatic color from spring through fall rather than fading to green in summer heat the way many dark-leaved heucheras do. Airy sprays of small white flowers rise above the foliage on wiry stems in early summer and draw in pollinators, though the foliage remains the main attraction. Its compact size suits container plantings, mixed shade borders, and edging, where the dark color makes a strong contrast against silver or chartreuse companions. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, resetting the crown at its original depth.

common_name: Dolce Peach Melba Heuchera (Warm Orange-Peach Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Dolce Peach Melba is a Proven Winners introduction with warm peach-orange foliage and a compact habit suited to shaded containers and small borders.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some morning sun to develop the richest color; Dolce Peach Melba is a compact coral bells cultivar in the Proven Winners Dolce series, bearing ruffled leaves that open warm peach-orange and shift toward rosy amber as they mature, giving the compact mound a shifting, multi-toned glow through the season. Its tidy, dense growth habit stays small and neat, making it especially useful for shaded container plantings, edging along a shade path, or as a warm-toned accent among cooler purple or green companions in a mixed border. Small pale flower spikes rise above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the warm leaf color. Provide consistent moisture and sharp drainage, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Dolce Silver Gumdrop Heuchera (Silvery-Purple Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dolce Silver Gumdrop is a Proven Winners introduction with a frosty silver overlay on deep purple leaves and a compact, tidy habit.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture and sharp drainage together matter more to coral bells than either factor alone, since heuchera crowns rot quickly in soggy, poorly drained sites. Dolce Silver Gumdrop bears ruffled, deep purple leaves overlaid with a frosty metallic-silver sheen that catches the light differently than the flatter purple tones of older heuchera cultivars, forming a dense, compact mound well suited to shaded containers and small border plantings. Small, pale flower spikes rise above the foliage in late spring, though the season-long foliage color is the main draw. Provide consistent moisture through summer heat, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the plant vigorous and well-shaped.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dolce Spearmint is a Proven Winners introduction with bright lime-green foliage and a compact habit suited to shaded containers and small borders.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dolce Spearmint is a compact coral bells cultivar in the Proven Winners Dolce series, bearing bright, glossy, lime-green to chartreuse leaves that brighten a shaded corner and provide strong contrast against darker-leaved companions like purple heucheras or bronze-leaved perennials. The dense, tidy mound stays small and neat, making it especially useful for shaded container plantings, edging along a shade path, or lighting up a dim spot in a mixed border. Small pale flower spikes rise above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the vivid leaf color. Provide consistent moisture and sharp drainage, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Dolce Wildberry Heuchera (Compact Glossy Purple Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dolce Wildberry is a Proven Winners introduction with a compact habit well suited to shaded containers, small borders, and edging.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dolce Wildberry is a compact coral bells cultivar in the Proven Winners Dolce series, bearing glossy, scalloped purple leaves with dark charcoal veining on a tidy, dense mound that stays neat without sprawling. Its small size makes it especially useful for shaded container plantings, edging along a shade path, or tucking into a mixed bed where a larger Heuchera would overwhelm its neighbors. Small pale flower spikes rise above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the rich, glossy leaf color. Provide consistent moisture and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Domino Coreopsis (Bicolor Red-Brown Center with Yellow Tips)
plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Domino bears bicolor flowers with a deep red-brown center zone and bright yellow petal tips, a bold ring pattern typical of plains coreopsis selections.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, lean, average soil in full sun; plains coreopsis tolerates poor, dry soils better than richer garden beds. Domino bears small, single flowers with a bold, contrasting pattern, a deep red-brown center ring surrounded by bright yellow tips, on a compact, airy plant that self-sows readily to naturalize a sunny meadow or wildflower planting. Its fine, uniform pattern makes it a strong choice for mass plantings and pollinator gardens. Deadhead to prolong bloom or allow seed heads to mature and drop for reseeding the following year.

common_name: Don Juan Rose (Velvet Red Climbing Rose)
plant_note: Set out grafted or own-root plants in spring or fall against a trellis, arbor, or pillar in full sun with good air circulation; Don Juan needs regular fungicide attention or careful site selection in humid Gulf South summers to keep blackspot in check, but rewards the effort with repeat flushes of classic red blooms.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil against a sturdy support, and train canes horizontally where possible to encourage more flowering side shoots along the length of the plant. Bred in Italy by Malandrone and introduced in 1958, Don Juan bears large, velvety, deep crimson-red blooms of classic high-centered hybrid-tea form carried on long stems, backed by a strong, sweet damask fragrance that makes it a favorite for cutting as well as climbing display. It repeat-blooms in flushes from late spring through fall and remains one of the most widely grown red climbing roses in American gardens for the richness of its color and scent, though it benefits from a preventive spray program or an airy site to manage blackspot in humid climates. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the plant vigorous and encourage strong new growth.

common_name: Don Quichotte Tulip (Vivid Cerise-Pink Triumph Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Don Quichotte is a Triumph-class tulip with vivid cerise-pink flowers, a good cultivar for forcing indoors as well as garden display.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Don Quichotte, a Triumph-class tulip, bears vivid, saturated cerise-pink flowers on sturdy, medium-height stems, blooming in midseason, and is noted as a particularly reliable cultivar for forcing into early bloom indoors in addition to standard garden and landscape display. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

common_name: Donation Camellia (Classic Pink Williamsii Hybrid Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Donation is one of the hardiest and most floriferous camellia hybrids and, unlike many camellias, sheds its own spent blooms cleanly instead of holding on to browned flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Donation is a Camellia x williamsii hybrid, a cross between C. japonica and the more cold- and sun-tolerant C. saluenensis, and it combines the best traits of both parents: a vigorous, upright, densely branched habit smothered in late winter to early spring with large, semi-double, clear orchid-pink flowers. It is widely regarded as one of the finest garden camellias ever raised, prized not only for its heavy, reliable bloom but also for cleanly dropping its faded flowers on its own, sparing gardeners the tedious deadheading that camellias with browning, persistent blooms require. It tolerates more sun and cooler conditions than many Camellia japonica cultivars, though afternoon shade still helps prevent leaf scorch in hot Gulf South summers, and it needs little pruning beyond light shaping right after bloom.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors, as the seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Surface sow the seed indoors several weeks before the last frost, since it needs light to sprout, and transplant after frost. Dondo White forms billowy clusters of fluffy, pure-white blooms on upright plants reaching twenty-four to thirty inches, adding vertical interest and texture to borders and containers. It flowers continuously from summer through frost. Grow in full sun with even moisture and deadhead to prolong the display.

common_name: Doris Dianthus (Salmon-Pink Fragrant Long-Blooming Border Carnation)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Doris is a long-blooming border carnation hybrid valued for its long flowering season.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Doris bears fully double, salmon-pink flowers with a darker rose-pink eye and the classic sweet clove fragrance of dianthus, opening over an unusually long season from late spring well into fall with regular deadheading. As a border carnation type it grows a bit taller and more upright than low, mat-forming cheddar pinks, making it useful as a middle-of-the-border filler as well as an edging plant. Shear lightly after the main flush and deadhead through summer to keep flowers coming.

common_name: Dorothy Eckford Sweet Pea (Classic Pure White Grandiflora Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Dorothy Eckford, introduced around 1901, was long considered the finest pure white sweet pea of its era.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Introduced around the turn of the 20th century and named for a member of the famous Eckford sweet pea breeding family, Dorothy Eckford bears large, richly fragrant, pure white flowers that were considered the finest white sweet pea of its time, on a vigorous, tall-climbing vine. Its clean color and strong scent have kept it a favorite heirloom for cutting gardens ever since. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

common_name: Dorothy Perkins Rose (Classic Rose-Pink Cluster-Flowered Rambler)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor; introduced in 1901, Dorothy Perkins was one of the most widely planted ramblers of the early 20th century.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor. Introduced in the United States in 1901, Dorothy Perkins produces enormous single-flush clusters of small, double, rose-pink flowers each summer, and became so widely planted in early 20th-century gardens that it remains one of the most historically iconic ramblers, though it is somewhat prone to powdery mildew compared to newer disease-resistant climbers. Its flexible, trailing canes make it well suited to training over an arch, pergola, or fence. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, fence, or pillar; Dortmund is a Kordesii-class climber bred for cold hardiness and repeat bloom.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, fence, or pillar for the climbing canes to be trained onto. Dortmund bears large, single, bright red flowers with a bold white eye at the center and a light fragrance, opening in dramatic clusters against glossy, disease-resistant dark green foliage, and unlike many older climbers it reliably repeats its bloom through summer rather than flowering just once. As a Kordesii-class rose bred from cold-hardy species stock, it tolerates harsher winters than many climbing roses. Tie new canes horizontally along the support as they grow, since horizontal training encourages more flowering side shoots than canes left to grow straight up.

plant_note: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; dotted blazing star is extraordinarily drought-tolerant, developing a deep corm-like root system that enables plants to survive extreme drought conditions. It grows slowly in early years as it develops its deep root system before investing in aerial growth. Established plants can live for 100 or more years in undisturbed prairie conditions.
directions: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; dotted blazing star is the most drought-tolerant blazing star species, native to the dry, sandy and gravelly prairies and rocky hillsides of the central Great Plains from Canada to Texas and New Mexico. It is distinguished from other liatris by its very narrow, almost needle-like leaves dotted with small, translucent oil glands (the punctata of the name) and its compact, lower stature compared to the common spike gayfeather. The purple flower spikes open from top to bottom in August and September — the characteristic reverse bloom order of all liatris — providing late-season color and an important nectar source for monarchs and other migrating butterflies. The deep corm-like root system enables plants to survive extreme drought and poor soils, and established plants can live for 100 or more years in undisturbed prairie conditions — one of the longest-lived prairie wildflowers. Slow to establish but extremely long-lived once settled.

plant_note: Surface sow into warm soil, as the fine seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Surface sow into warm soil after frost, since the fine seed needs light to germinate. These low-growing plants form a carpet of brilliantly colored, rose-like double flowers that open on sunny days through the heat of summer. Very drought tolerant, moss rose needs only occasional watering and thrives in dry banks and hot, reflected-heat spots. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil for the best flowering.

plant_note: Often grown as a biennial; sow in spring or summer for bloom the next year.
directions: Sow in spring or summer, since this short-lived perennial is usually grown as a biennial that blooms its second year. Double Blend forms large clusters of edible, double flowers in many colors that rank among the longest-lasting cut flowers. In the garden the sweet, spicy-scented blooms draw butterflies and bees, and the mild clove-flavored petals garnish salads. Grow in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil and even moisture.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or very early spring while dormant, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Double Bloodroot is sterile and spreads only slowly by rhizome, never by seed, so start with nursery-propagated divisions rather than expecting it to naturalize on its own.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees; let the foliage die back naturally in early summer as the plant goes dormant, and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizomes. Sanguinaria canadensis 'Multiplex' is a showy double-flowered form of the native spring ephemeral bloodroot, bearing fully doubled, camellia-like white blooms with dozens of narrow petals in place of the single flower's simple eight to twelve petals. Because the flower is sterile and produces no seed, it never triggers the rapid petal drop that ends the single form's bloom within a day or two of opening — the double flowers instead persist attractively for one to two weeks, a significant advantage for garden display. Like the species, each striking, blue-green, deeply lobed leaf wraps protectively around its flower stem as it emerges in earliest spring; the cut rhizome exudes the characteristic red-orange sap that gives the plant its common name. A prized, long-lived heirloom woodland perennial for a shaded native garden, zone 3–8.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in very well-drained, dry, sandy to gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral, poor soil in full sun; double bubble mint is native to rock ledges and dry slopes in the Chihuahuan Desert region and must have excellent drainage — wet soils are lethal.
directions: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in very well-drained, dry, sandy to gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral, poor soil in full sun; double bubble mint is native to rock ledges and dry slopes in the Chihuahuan Desert region and must have excellent drainage — wet soils are lethal. Agastache cana is a compact, long-blooming agastache native to the Chihuahuan Desert mountains of western Texas and southern New Mexico, producing narrow, intensely bubble-gum-and-licorice-scented leaves (the origin of its common name 'Double Bubble Mint') and dense, fluffy, 6–8 inch spikes of rose-pink to dark-pink tubular flowers from midsummer through hard frost that are exceptional hummingbird and bumblebee forage. It is among the most drought-tolerant and heat-adapted of all Agastache species; deer-resistant, essentially disease-free, and outstanding for rock gardens, dry borders, and xeriscape designs in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into lean soil and full sun.
directions: Direct sow after frost in average-to-lean soil and full sun, since rich ground limits flowering. Double Click produces a profusion of mostly double, some semi-double, chrysanthemum-like blooms in pink, white, and carmine red. Once established it is easy to care for and drought tolerant, so water sparingly. Deadhead or cut for bouquets to prolong bloom, and let a few flowers set seed to reseed.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August for fall bloom. Double Click series cosmos blooms 75–90 days from seed — longer than single-flowered cosmos. The double flowers have significantly longer vase life than single cosmos; harvest as buds begin to open for 7–10 days of cut flower enjoyment. In zone 9 successive sowings 4–6 weeks apart through spring extend the productive season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral soil — cosmos performs best in poor soil and actually blooms less when over-fertilized; Double Click Cranberry is a semi-double to fully double-flowered cosmos variety in a vivid deep cranberry-magenta color — an unusual form for a species (Cosmos bipinnatus) that is normally only available in single-petaled form. The Double Click series from PanAmerican Seed was developed specifically to introduce double-flowered forms to the cosmos genus, creating lush, full, pompom-like flower heads that look more like a small chrysanthemum or dahlia than the familiar daisy form of standard cosmos. The deep cranberry color paired with the full, multi-petaled form makes Double Click Cranberry one of the most distinctive cosmos varieties for cut flower production and ornamental garden use. Like all cosmos, it is extremely heat-tolerant and drought-resistant once established — a remarkable low-maintenance annual that produces continuously from first bloom until frost.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Double Delight is an AARS 1977 winner bred by Swim & Ellis and benefits from preventative fungicide application and consistent feeding in humid climates.
directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Double Delight is a landmark hybrid tea rose, an All-America Rose Selections winner in 1977, celebrated for its striking bicolor blooms — creamy white petals that develop a vivid strawberry-red edge that deepens with sun exposure and age, so a single bush shows blooms in varying stages of color at once. Its heavy, intense, spicy-sweet fragrance is considered among the finest of modern roses, making it a favorite for cutting as well as garden display. Like many hybrid teas from this era, it needs a regular preventative fungicide program in humid, disease-prone climates to keep the foliage healthy through summer. Prune hard in late winter, feed with rose fertilizer monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Double Dragon Amaryllis (Fully Double Red-and-White Amaryllis)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Double Dragon bears fully double, ruffled red-and-white flowers with an unusually high petal count, resembling a peony more than a typical amaryllis.
directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Double Dragon bears fully double, ruffled blooms in bold red streaked and edged with white, with an unusually high petal count that gives each flower a full, peony-like form rather than the simple six-petaled star typical of most amaryllis cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, naturalizing and multiplying into an increasingly full clump over the years. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb, and for container forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix for traditional winter bloom indoors.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; double flowering plum blooms in early spring before the leaves. Prune immediately after flowering to encourage vigorous new growth. The double-flowered cultivar 'Multiplex' is most widely available.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; double flowering plum is a Chinese shrub producing double-flowered, rosy-pink blooms so profusely that stems are completely hidden under flowers in very early spring. The popular cultivar 'Multiplex' has fully double, deep rose-pink flowers with a ruffled, peony-like form. This is one of the most spectacularly spring-flowering woody plants for cold climates — reliably cold-hardy to zone 3 with outstanding early season color. Often confused with double flowering almond (Prunus glandulosa) in the garden trade; both are excellent ornamental spring shrubs. The flowers appear before leaves, making the bare-stem flower display especially dramatic. Prune hard immediately after bloom to maintain compact shape and maximize next year's flowering. Short-lived (10–20 years) but easy to propagate from cuttings.

common_name: Double Japanese Arrowhead (Old World Fully Double White-Flowered Arrowhead)
plant_note: Plant tubers or divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after last frost; this Old World arrowhead species bears fully double white flowers, distinct from the single-flowered native arrowhead species.
directions: Plant tubers or divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun. This Old World arrowhead, native across Europe and Asia, is grown in cultivation almost exclusively in its fully double form, bearing showy, pompom-like white flowers with many extra petal segments in place of the simple three-petaled bloom of the wild species, a distinctly more ornamental flower than the native North American Sagittaria species more commonly planted. Its arrow-shaped leaves rise above the water on sturdy stems, providing vertical accent and cover for pond wildlife at the margin. It spreads by tubers to form a colony over time; divide and thin every few years to control spread and maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Double Knock Out Rose (Double Red Knock Out Rose)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours direct sun); Double Knock Out has the same exceptional disease resistance, heat tolerance, and low-maintenance requirements as the original Knock Out.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Double Knock Out rose is the most popular cultivar in the Knock Out series and is now the best-selling landscape rose in America — a double-flowered sport of the original Knock Out selected for its lush, fully double, deep-red to cherry-red flowers that more closely resemble a traditional garden rose than the single-petaled original. While the original Knock Out has 5 petals in the typical wild-rose single form, Double Knock Out produces 18–25 petals in a cupped, decorative double form that most gardeners associate with 'real' roses. This additional petal count gives the flowers a fuller, more luxurious appearance while maintaining essentially all the disease resistance, repeat bloom, and low-maintenance characteristics of the parent. Double Knock Out blooms from spring until hard frost in zone 9, self-cleaning without deadheading, and requires only one annual pruning in late winter (February in zone 9) cutting the plant back to 12–18 inches. Like the original, it shows exceptional black spot resistance — a critical trait in the humid Gulf Coast climate where most roses require weekly fungicide programs. The deep-red flower color is consistent through the season without fading. Numerous Knock Out series siblings exist: Pink Knock Out, Pink Double Knock Out, Sunny Knock Out (yellow), Rainbow Knock Out (coral-pink), and others.

plant_note: Set out the shrub after danger of hard frost; it is a woody deciduous shrub, not typically grown from seed for this cultivar.
directions: Plant this double-flowered althea in full sun with well-drained soil, spacing shrubs 5-8 feet apart to allow their broad upright habit room to mature. It blooms late summer into fall on the current season's growth, so prune in late winter or early spring to shape and encourage flowering wood. Water regularly the first two seasons until the roots establish, after which it tolerates heat and short dry spells. The full, layered pink blooms are sterile, so this cultivar reseeds far less than single-flowered forms.

common_name: Double Play Big Bang Spirea (Bright Gold Reblooming Spirea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; best foliage color develops in full sun, and deadheading the first flush of flowers encourages the summer rebloom that gives this series its name.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun; spirea tolerates poor soil and drought once established but colors up and flowers best with a full day of sun. Double Play Big Bang produces some of the brightest gold foliage in the reblooming Double Play spirea series, holding vivid yellow color through summer heat better than many older golden spirea cultivars, and topped by rounded clusters of pink flowers that appear in a heavy spring flush with continued rebloom through summer, especially with deadheading. Its compact, rounded habit fits foundation plantings, low borders, and mixed shrub beds without the sprawling size of older spirea varieties. Shear off spent flower clusters after the first bloom flush to encourage continued summer flowering, and cut the whole shrub back by up to a third every few years in late winter to renew dense, vigorous growth.

common_name: Double Play Candy Corn Spirea (Orange-Red New Growth Reblooming Spirea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Candy Corn is grown chiefly for its multicolor spring foliage, which opens bright orange-red and matures through yellow to lime-green on the same branch.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun for the strongest foliage color contrast. Double Play Candy Corn is grown primarily for its striking multicolor new growth, which emerges a vivid orange-red at the branch tips and matures backward through yellow to lime-green, giving each stem a gradient effect reminiscent of its namesake candy, with small clusters of pink flowers in late spring adding a secondary season of interest. New flushes of colorful growth continue to appear through the growing season, especially after a light shearing, keeping the color display going well past spring. Its compact, mounded habit suits low borders and foundation plantings, and cutting the whole shrub back hard every few years in late winter keeps growth dense and encourages the most vivid new color.

common_name: Double Play Gold Spirea (Reblooming Gold-Foliage Compact Spirea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; best foliage color develops in full sun, and deadheading the first flush of flowers encourages the summer rebloom that gives this series its name.
directions: Double Play Gold is a compact, part of Proven Winners' reblooming Double Play spirea series, valued for bright gold foliage that emerges with orange-red tints in spring and holds its color through summer, topped by rounded clusters of pink flowers. Unlike older spirea cultivars that bloom in one spring flush, Double Play selections rebloom through summer, especially if the spent flower clusters are sheared off after the first round fades, giving a longer season of both foliage and flower interest from a low, tidy mound. It is extremely tough and low-maintenance, tolerating drought, heat, and poor soil once established, and a single light shearing after the first bloom flush is usually all the pruning it needs.

common_name: Double Play Painted Lady Spirea (Blue-Green Foliage Pink-Flowered Reblooming Spirea)
scientific_name: Spiraea japonica 'Painted Lady' (Double Play Painted Lady)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; deadheading the first flush of flowers encourages the summer rebloom that gives the Double Play series its name.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun; spirea tolerates poor soil and drought once established but flowers most reliably with a full day of direct sun. Double Play Painted Lady carries cool blue-green foliage rather than the gold or orange-red tones of other Double Play series members, providing a calmer backdrop for its clusters of rich pink flowers, which open in a heavy spring flush and continue reblooming through summer, especially when spent clusters are sheared off promptly. Its compact, rounded form fits foundation plantings and mixed borders where a reliable, long-blooming small shrub is needed without a bold foliage-color statement. Cut the whole shrub back by up to a third every few years in late winter to keep growth dense and renew vigorous flowering wood.

common_name: Double Play Spirea (Reblooming Compact Spirea Series)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; deadhead the first flush of flowers to encourage a stronger rebloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear off the first round of spent flowers to prompt a stronger summer rebloom.
