plant_note: Start indoors and set out after frost; grown as an annual in cold climates.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant to full sun once weather settles. This florist favorite produces cheerful golden globe blooms on tall wiry stems that are prized in fresh and dried arrangements. The tough plants tolerate drought, heat, and heavy or poor soil, so avoid overwatering. Harvest stems when the orbs are fully colored and hang upside down to dry for long-lasting decor.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early fall; drumstick primrose requires consistently moist soil during its spring growing season and appreciates light mulch — it goes semi-dormant in summer heat and benefits from drier conditions then.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; drumstick primrose is an unusual and distinctive Himalayan spring primrose that differs from all other primroses in its flower arrangement — rather than flat clusters or single flowers, it produces perfectly spherical, drumstick-like, ball-shaped flower heads on upright stalks, densely packed with small, purple, lilac, pink, rose-red, or white flowers that bloom in early to mid-spring, often pushing through the last snow of the season. The bold, spherical flower heads create a strong visual statement quite different from the low, spreading flower clusters of common primroses, and the contrast of the round, upright flowers with the rosette of large, coarsely toothed, wrinkled leaves creates an architectural quality. One of the most cold-hardy of all ornamental primroses (to zone 2) and effective in large drifts under deciduous trees where snow melt provides the moisture conditions it needs. 'Alba' (white), 'Grandiflora' (large purple heads), and 'Ruby' (deep red) are standard cultivars.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds after last frost in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; drumstick sesbania grows naturally in wet ditches, pond margins, and seasonally flooded roadsides across the Gulf Coastal Plain. Scarify seed coat by soaking 24 hours in hot water before sowing.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun along pond edges, wet roadside ditches, and seasonally flooded areas; drumstick sesbania is a native Gulf Coast fast-growing shrubby annual to short-lived perennial — one of the most vigorous nitrogen-fixing native legumes of the wetland margins and wet roadsides of the Gulf South. The bright yellow flowers in summer are highly attractive to native bees, especially large bees and carpenter bees. The long, distinctive seed pods rattle when shaken — a characteristic of the genus that gives one of its common names. A native plant valued for quick erosion control and soil improvement on wet, disturbed sites. Note: seeds and foliage are toxic to livestock; do not plant in pasture settings. Native to the Gulf Coastal Plain from Florida to Texas.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Drunkard's Dream is an epiphytic forest cactus and needs the same airy, orchid-bark-based mix and irregular watering as other jungle cacti.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Drunkard's Dream is an epiphytic forest cactus and needs the same airy, orchid-bark-based mix and irregular watering as other jungle cacti. Slender, jointed, bottle- or club-shaped stem segments branch repeatedly into an oddly whimsical, top-heavy tangle that gives the plant its playful common name, with small, bright yellow-orange, bell-shaped flowers appearing at the stem tips in late winter and spring. Native to the humid Brazilian rainforest canopy, where it grows perched on tree branches rather than rooted in soil, it prefers bright, filtered light rather than the intense direct sun of desert cacti and appreciates higher humidity than most succulents. Its arching, branching stems make it a natural fit for a hanging basket, and it is propagated easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus before potting.

common_name: Duc de Rohan Azalea (Antique Salmon-Orange Southern Indica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Duc de Rohan is an antique Southern Indica azalea long grown in old Gulf South gardens for its warm salmon-orange bloom color.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, allowing plenty of room for the mature shrub's spread. Duc de Rohan is an antique Southern Indica azalea cultivar that has been grown in old Gulf South gardens for generations, valued for its warm, unusual salmon-orange flowers that stand apart from the more common pinks, reds, and whites of other Southern Indica cultivars. The large, evergreen shrub produces its heaviest bloom in a single dramatic spring flush and provides dense structural greenery the rest of the year. Water deeply while establishing and during dry spells, and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for the following spring form soon after bloom ends.

plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Ducher is an 1869 French China rose noted for being one of the hardiest and most cold-tolerant of the China class, while still carrying the class's excellent heat and humidity tolerance for the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1869, Ducher is a compact China rose bearing clusters of fragrant, fully double, creamy-white blooms tinged with pale pink at the center, set against small, dark, glossy foliage. It is considered one of the most cold-hardy roses in the China class, extending its usefulness slightly beyond the warmest zones where most Chinas thrive, while still carrying their signature nonstop bloom cycle and strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew in humid climates. The compact, rounded shrub suits borders, low hedges, and container culture. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood; deadhead spent blooms to encourage the next flush, though the plant reblooms readily even without deadheading.

common_name: Duchess Blue and White Torenia (Compact Bicolor Wishbone Flower)
plant_note: Start seed indoors and transplant after the last frost; performs well massed under trees or in shaded container plantings.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant after the last frost. Duchess is a newer, extra-compact torenia series bred for a tidy mounded habit and heavy bud set, an improvement in uniformity over older wishbone flower strains. Duchess Blue and White produces crisp, two-tone violet-blue and white tubular flowers with the characteristic fused wishbone-shaped stamens, held just above neat foliage. It handles heat and humidity better than many older torenia selections and works well massed under trees or in shaded container plantings where few flowering annuals thrive.

common_name: Duchess of Albany Clematis (Pink Tulip Texas Clematis)
plant_note: Set out in spring with the crown planted a couple of inches deep and the roots shaded, allowing the slender stems to twine up a trellis, obelisk, or fence in full sun.
directions: Grow this heritage cultivar of the Texas native clematis on a narrow support such as an obelisk or wire trellis, keeping its roots cool and shaded beneath low plantings. From midsummer into fall it produces slender, tulip-shaped, deep pink flowers with a candy-striped reverse that nod outward from the wiry stems rather than facing up, a distinctive habit inherited from its Texas parent species. Because it blooms on new growth, cut the vine back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter to renew vigor. It is more heat- and drought-tolerant than many large-flowered clematis, making it a good choice for warmer gardens.

common_name: Duchess of Edinburgh Chrysanthemum (Semi-Double Bright Red with Yellow Eye)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Duchess of Edinburgh bears semi-double, bright red flowers with a yellow eye.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil. Duchess of Edinburgh bears semi-double flowers in bright, warm red with a contrasting yellow center eye, giving the open flower form a two-tone effect uncommon among the more solid-colored garden mum cultivars. Pinch stem tips in spring and early summer to promote bushy, compact growth, since unpinched plants tend toward tall, floppy stems. Divide clumps every two to three years to prevent crowding and maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant deeply with the crown below soil level and shade the roots with mulch or low companion plants, allowing the vine to climb into full sun above.
directions: Dating to 1876, this antique clematis produces fully double, pure white rosette-shaped flowers with a light green tint that carry a fresh, sweet fragrance rare among large-flowered clematis. It flowers earliest in the season on old wood, so prune lightly right after the first flush to shape the vine and encourage a smaller repeat bloom on new growth later in summer. Give it fertile, well-drained soil and a sturdy support such as a trellis or pergola post. Because its doubled flowers can be sparse in cooler climates, siting it in a warm, sheltered spot improves flower quality.

common_name: Duchess of Portland Rose (Original Namesake Portland Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Duchess of Portland is the original namesake rose of the entire Portland class, bearing bright crimson-scarlet semi-double flowers.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Duchess of Portland is the original rose that gave its name to the entire Portland class of old garden roses, bearing bright, clear crimson-scarlet, semi-double flowers held close against the foliage on short stems, a distinctive tight, ruffled foliage collar just beneath each bloom being a hallmark trait of the class it founded. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a hallmark advantage of the Portland class over many once-blooming old garden rose types. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Duchesse de Brabant Rose (Cupped Antique Tea Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Duchesse de Brabant is an 1857 tea rose famously worn as a boutonniere by Theodore Roosevelt and prized in Deep South gardens for its cupped, silky pink blooms and outstanding heat tolerance.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1857, Duchesse de Brabant bears silky, cupped, shell-pink blooms with a light, fruity tea fragrance, held on a bushy, rounded shrub with soft blue-green foliage. President Theodore Roosevelt reportedly wore its blooms as a boutonniere, and the rose has remained a favorite of Southern gardens ever since for its dependable, near-continuous bloom and excellent tolerance of heat and humidity. It shows good resistance to blackspot compared with modern hybrid teas and asks for little beyond routine watering once established. The nodding, cupped flower form and soft coloring make it a favorite for cutting and for cottage-style borders. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; avoid hard pruning, which delays and reduces bloom.

common_name: Duchesse de Nemours Peony (Fragrant Double White Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake or ring the strong stems before the heavy, fragrant blooms open. Bred in France in 1856 and still a benchmark white peony, Duchesse de Nemours opens creamy-yellow at the bud and matures to pure white with a strong, sweet lemon-tinged fragrance, on stems that hold up well to wind and rain compared to many older doubles. It is an early- to mid-season bloomer that forces well as a cut flower, often chosen by florists and wedding growers for its reliability and scent. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or spring in humus-rich, acidic, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade with protection from afternoon sun; established colonies spread gently by rhizome and tolerate summer dry shade once rooted in.
directions: Plant divisions in fall or spring in humus-rich, acidic, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade with protection from afternoon sun; established colonies spread gently by rhizome and tolerate summer dry shade once rooted in. Vancouveria hexandra is a deciduous native of moist coastal and montane forests from Washington through northern California, forming loose colonies of wiry, dark stems bearing delicate, apple-green leaves divided into small heart-shaped leaflets, with airy clusters of tiny white flowers held above the foliage on thread-like stalks in late spring. Its common name refers to the reflexed, backward-swept petals that give each miniature flower an inside-out appearance, and its finely divided foliage adds fine texture beneath native shrubs and conifers where it functions as a well-mannered, non-aggressive groundcover. Unlike its evergreen relative Vancouveria planipetala, this species dies back in winter, so leave the previous year's dried foliage in place until new growth resumes in spring.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in rich, moisture-retentive soil beneath redwoods, oaks, or other coastal forest canopy.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in rich, moisture-retentive soil beneath redwoods, oaks, or other coastal forest canopy, since this California endemic naturally forms the lush fern understory of Coast Range mixed-evergreen woodlands. The broadly triangular, bipinnate fronds are a brighter, softer green than most sword ferns and arch gracefully from a slowly expanding crown, giving a fuller, lacier look than western sword fern. It is an excellent structural anchor for shaded native gardens that receive regular winter rain and light summer watering.

common_name: Duet Variegated Beautyberry (First Stable Variegated White-Berried Beautyberry)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Duet, a 2006 US National Arboretum and Tennessee Tech release, is the first stable variegated-foliage beautyberry, bearing white-margined leaves and white berries that feed songbirds through winter.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Duet, released in 2006 through a collaboration between the U.S. National Arboretum and Tennessee Tech University, was the first stable variegated-foliage beautyberry introduced to cultivation, bearing leaves crisply edged in white that provide season-long ornamental interest well before the berries even form, on the same arching, graceful branches typical of purple beautyberry. In fall, the plant produces clusters of pure white berries along the stems rather than the more familiar violet-purple, a striking, luminous display against the variegated foliage, and those berries persist into winter as a valuable food source for mockingbirds, robins, and other songbirds. It performs best with a hard pruning in late winter, since it flowers and fruits on new growth, encouraging vigorous new stems each season. An outstanding dual-purpose foliage-and-fruit shrub for the wildlife or mixed border.

common_name: Duke Gardens Plum Yew (Compact Spreading Japanese Plum Yew)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; give it room to spread wide rather than tall, since this selection stays low and mounding rather than upright.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial to full shade, and water regularly the first year until established. This selection is a low, dense, wide-spreading form of Japanese plum yew, distinct from the upright species in habit, making it an excellent evergreen groundcover or foundation planting for deep shade where few other conifers perform. Like the species it tolerates heavy shade, root competition from mature trees, and heat and humidity far better than true yews, and it is not browsed by deer. Its dark, glossy, soft needles hold their color through winter, giving year-round structure to a shaded bed.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, very acidic, sandy, low-nutrient soil in full sun to partial shade; dull meadow beauty grows naturally in wet longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods seeps, and pitcher plant bogs of the southeastern Coastal Plain. It requires acidic, nutrient-poor, moist sandy conditions to thrive.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy, low-nutrient soil in full sun to partial shade; dull meadow beauty is a taller, more robust native Rhexia of the southeastern longleaf pine savanna ecosystem, producing clusters of pale rose-pink to nearly white four-petaled flowers with the distinctive curved yellow anthers typical of all Rhexia species. It grows in a narrower ecological range than Maryland meadow beauty, primarily in the wet flatwoods and pitcher plant bogs of the lower Coastal Plain from North Carolina to Louisiana. Like all meadow beauties, it is pollinated primarily by buzz-pollinating bumblebees that vibrate the anthers at the precise frequency to release pollen. The characteristic jug-shaped, urn-necked seed capsule is ornamental in autumn. Requires the exact conditions of its longleaf pine savanna habitat — very acidic, moist, sandy, and nutrient-poor — making it a specialist plant for bog gardens and wet pine savanna restorations.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix at 70–80°F in bright indirect light to deep shade; in zones 10–12 plant outdoors in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Root stem cuttings by laying cut sections horizontally on moist potting mix or inserting upright sections in perlite and peat at 70–80°F; dieffenbachia grows vigorously in deep shade and tolerates the low-light conditions of interior spaces that defeat most ornamental plants, producing large paddle-shaped leaves strikingly patterned in cream, white, and various shades of green. Outdoors in zones 10–12, use in mass plantings under trees or along shaded foundations where its bold tropical texture creates lush contrast. All parts contain calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense burning and temporary loss of speech if chewed — keep away from children and pets, and wear gloves when cutting. Flush soil occasionally to prevent fertilizer salt buildup.

common_name: Dumbcane (Leopard Lily, Tropic Snow Dieffenbachia, Giant Dumbcane)
plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Dieffenbachia amoena is one of the largest Dieffenbachia species, producing bold canes 4–6 feet tall with large (18–24 inch) leaves in deep green with irregular cream to white markings along the midrib and veins. One of the most tolerant large shade plants for low-light indoor and outdoor shaded positions. Water moderately, allowing the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. CAUTION: all Dieffenbachia parts are toxic if ingested — the calcium oxalate crystals and protein-digesting enzymes cause temporary but severe swelling of the mouth and throat ('dumb,' unable to speak, hence the common name). Keep away from children and pets.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained soil — Dumbcane is one of the most shade-tolerant, bold-textured, large-leaved ornamental plants for low-light interior and shaded outdoor positions, and one of the most widely grown tropical ornamentals in the world for this reason. Dieffenbachia amoena is a large, upright, cane-forming perennial aroid in the Araceae family native to tropical America (Colombia, Brazil, Central America) — one of the larger and more robust species in the genus Dieffenbachia, which comprises approximately 60 species of tropical aroids grown widely as ornamental foliage plants throughout the world. The plant produces thick, semi-woody canes 4–6 feet tall clothed in large, broadly elliptic to ovate leaves 18–24 inches long. The leaves are the ornamental feature: deep, lustrous, forest-green with irregular stripes, blotches, and feathering of cream to white along and between the primary veins — creating a boldly variegated pattern of dark and light across the large leaf surface. The plant is extraordinarily tolerant of low light, irregular watering, and indoor conditions, making it one of the classic large interior foliage plants of offices, lobbies, and shaded indoor spaces worldwide, and a permanent outdoor specimen in zone 10-12 landscapes. The common name 'Dumbcane' refers to the toxic effects of chewing on the plant: the calcium oxalate crystals and proteolytic enzymes cause immediate, severe swelling of the mouth and throat that temporarily renders the victim unable to speak. CAUTION: severely toxic if ingested — keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Plant in spring in moist soil with room for a large shade tree.
directions: Dura Heat is a river birch selection with creamy exfoliating bark and strong tolerance of summer heat and humidity. Plant it in full sun to part shade in moist, slightly acidic soil; it thrives in wet spots where other trees struggle. Water deeply during establishment and dry spells to prevent leaf drop. Its resistance to bronze birch borer makes it a durable landscape and shade tree. Prune only in summer or fall, since birches bleed heavily if cut in late winter or early spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring before new growth starts; river birch transplants best when young. In zone 8–9 plant October–February for establishment before summer heat. Dura-Heat is notably more heat and drought tolerant than standard river birch and shows better heat resistance than Heritage birch in the hottest parts of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically flooded soil; Dura-Heat is a heat-tolerant selection of native river birch (Betula nigra) selected at the University of Alabama for superior performance in the hot, humid summers of zone 7–9. The exfoliating, creamy-to-salmon bark that peels in papery sheets is the tree's primary ornamental feature, providing year-round interest — the effect is most dramatic on multi-trunk specimens. Unlike most birches, which require cool summers, Dura-Heat thrives in zone 9's climate and tolerates temporary flooding, making it valuable along streams, ponds, and in rain gardens. Fall color is a modest yellow. The tree is relatively fast-growing (2–3 feet per year when young) and provides dappled shade suitable for understory plantings.

common_name: Dural White Butterfly Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Pure White Australian-Bred Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Dural White Butterfly, bred in Australia, bears ruffled, pure white flowers on a vigorous, floriferous plant.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Dural White Butterfly, bred by Australian hybridizer John Taylor, bears large, ruffled, pure white flowers on a vigorous, heavily branched plant that produces an especially generous bloom count, making it one of the most widely grown white Louisiana iris cultivars worldwide. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: Durango Marigold (Early-Flowering Compact French Marigold Series)
plant_note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors a few weeks early for earlier bloom; Durango is an early-flowering, weather-tolerant French marigold series with large flowers relative to its compact plant size.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Durango is a popular French marigold series known for flowering earlier from seed than many older marigold types, producing unusually large, fully double flowers in gold, orange, and red bicolor tones on a compact, weather-resistant plant that holds up well in rain and wind. It performs reliably through summer heat and needs only routine deadheading to keep flowering strongly. Like other marigolds it is drought-tolerant once established and its pungent foliage is generally left alone by deer and rabbits, making it a dependable bedding and container annual.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in warm, fertile, moist soil in full sun; Durban is grown primarily for its vividly striped pink, orange, and bronze foliage, among the most colorful ornamental-leaf cannas in the trade.
directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in warm, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun. Durban is grown chiefly for its dramatic foliage, with broad leaves striped in shifting bands of hot pink, orange, and bronze that provide season-long color even between the plant's orange flower spikes, making it one of the showiest foliage cannas available for tropical-look Gulf South landscaping and large container plantings. Like other cannas it thrives with generous water and rich soil, tolerating even boggy conditions at a pond edge. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage; in zone 8-10 gardens it can typically be left in the ground with a heavy mulch layer for winter protection.

common_name: Dusky Challenger Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Deep Purple Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and sharply drained soil.
directions: Hybridized by Schreiner's Iris Gardens and awarded the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1992, Dusky Challenger is a towering tall bearded iris with velvety, near-black deep purple blooms and exceptional bud count and branching. Grow it in full sun with lean, well-drained soil, planting rhizomes shallowly so the tops are not buried, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years. It is widely regarded as one of the most influential and best-selling dark bearded iris cultivars ever released, and it remains a parent behind many modern black-toned iris introductions.

common_name: Dusky Coral Pea (Running Postman Coral Pea)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; dusky coral pea is a fast-growing, vigorous vine or trailing groundcover suitable for difficult, sunny, dry banks and slopes where few other flowering vines would survive. It blooms mainly in spring but sporadically year-round in mild climates. The dense, trailing stems with large, three-parted, dark-green leaves provide excellent soil erosion control. Very tolerant of coastal exposure and poor soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; dusky coral pea is a robust, vigorous, trailing or twining Australian native legume from the coastal scrub and dry forests of eastern Australia — producing in spring a succession of the distinctive Kennedia flower form: a typical sweet-pea-family flower with a broad, curved, deep dusky-red to dark coral-red to brick-red standard petal and smaller, darker, often almost blood-red wing and keel petals, the whole flower a rich, warm, dusky-red combination. The flowers are borne in clusters of 2–4 in the leaf axils, scattered throughout the vine over the spring bloom period. The plant itself is vigorous and fast-growing — potentially reaching considerable size as a vine or sprawling, mounding groundcover — with large, trifoliate, deep-green, somewhat coarse-textured leaves. Excellent for covering difficult, dry, sunny, rocky banks and slopes where its drought tolerance, fast growth, and nitrogen-fixing root nodules make it both ornamental and functionally valuable. The trailing stems root where they contact soil, spreading into an increasingly dense groundcover. An excellent, low-maintenance, soil-stabilizing ornamental for zone 9 coastal and inland slopes.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost risk passes.
directions: Surface-sow tiny seeds on moist germination mix and provide light at 65–75°F; germination is slow and uneven over 10–14 days. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; excellent salt and drought tolerance makes this ideal for coastal and hot dry sites. The silvery white, felted foliage is the ornamental feature — pinch off yellow flower buds when they appear to keep plants neat and maintain vigorous leaf growth. In zones 8–11 dusty miller overwinters as a short-lived perennial.

common_name: Dutch Chocolate Baptisia (Decadence Series Bronze-Flowered False Indigo)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Dutch Chocolate is part of the compact Decadence breeding series, bred to fit smaller garden spaces than the tall, sprawling wild Baptisia species while keeping the plant's legendary toughness and longevity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Dutch Chocolate is a compact hybrid selection from the Decadence breeding series, developed to bring Baptisia's celebrated toughness, long lifespan, and pollinator appeal into a smaller, tidier plant better suited to modern garden borders than the tall, wide-spreading straight species. In late spring it produces dense spikes of unusual smoky maroon-brown flowers with a subtle chocolate cast, followed by ornamental dark seed pods that persist into fall. Like all baptisias it develops a deep taproot and resents being moved once established, so choose its planting site carefully; established plants are extremely drought-tolerant, essentially pest-free, and improve for many years without needing division.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall in drifts for best effect.
directions: Plant Dutch crocus corms in fall three to four inches deep in well-drained soil, setting them in generous drifts. The large goblet-shaped flowers in purple, white, and yellow open in early spring for bees emerging from winter. Grow in full sun to light shade and avoid summer irrigation while corms are dormant. Let the grassy foliage ripen fully, and the corms will multiply into showy colonies over time.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall, 4–6 in deep; in zones 5–6 apply a winter mulch for protection.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–6 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Dutch iris bloom in late spring to early summer and are superb cut flowers with a vase life of 7–10 days. The large falls and standards come in shades of blue, purple, yellow, white, and bicolor. After bloom, allow foliage to die back naturally; in warm, humid climates the bulbs may rot in summer — lift and store dry in a cool place if this occurs. Replant in early fall and incorporate grit into heavy clay soils to improve drainage.

common_name: Dutch Master Daffodil (Classic Golden-Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; Dutch Master is a classic large trumpet daffodil, one of the earliest and most vigorous golden-yellow trumpet cultivars in commerce.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Dutch Master bears the classic large, solid golden-yellow trumpet form most people picture when they think of a daffodil, opening early in the spring season on sturdy stems that hold up well to wind and rain. Its vigor and reliability have made it one of the most widely planted trumpet daffodils for mass naturalizing in lawns, orchards, and woodland edges. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

plant_note: Plant small corms (clusters of rice-grain-sized cormlets) 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Dutchman's Breeches is a spring ephemeral that disappears by early summer — plant it where summer perennials or ferns will fill the void it leaves behind.
directions: Plant cormlets (clusters of small, rice-grain-like corms) 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; in spring the delicate foliage emerges early and the flowers appear, then the entire plant disappears underground by early June. Dutchman's Breeches (Dicentra cucullaria) is one of the most charming and distinctive of all native spring ephemerals — small, pale-green, finely divided leaves emerge in earliest spring alongside arching stems bearing 4–10 waxy, white, heart-shaped flowers with two inflated spurs that form a distinctive pantaloon or 'breeches' shape pointing upward, as if a tiny pair of trousers hung to dry on a line. The flowers are one of the first spring forest wildflowers and are pollinated primarily by long-tongued bumblebee queens that can reach the nectar at the tips of the spurs. By June the plant is dormant and invisible underground. Outstanding companion to Virginia bluebells, trout lily, bloodroot, and other spring ephemerals in moist woodland gardens; all parts toxic if eaten.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil.
directions: Dwarf Alberta spruce is a slow-growing conifer forming a naturally dense, cone-shaped pyramid of soft green needles, ideal for small gardens and containers. Plant it in full sun and well-drained soil, avoiding hot, reflective spots that can scorch the fine foliage. Provide good air circulation to reduce spider mite pressure, and rinse the foliage periodically in dry weather. Water consistently, as its shallow roots dry out quickly in pots. It rarely needs pruning thanks to its tidy, formal habit.

plant_note: Tie or glue the rhizome to driftwood, lava rock, or other hardscape with cotton thread or cyanoacrylate gel until roots attach naturally, typically within 3-6 weeks; do not bury the rhizome in substrate, as this causes rot.
directions: Grown fully submersed in freshwater aquaria attached to hardscape rather than planted in substrate; the tough, dark-green, arrowhead-shaped leaves and rhizome are highly resistant to algae fouling and grazing by herbivorous fish, making this one of the most forgiving true aquatic plants sold in the hobby. It thrives under low to medium aquarium lighting and does not require CO2 injection, though growth accelerates modestly with supplemental CO2 and liquid fertilizer. Native to slow, shaded forest streams of West Africa (Cameroon), it tolerates a wide range of water hardness and a pH of roughly 6.0-7.5. Propagate by dividing the horizontal rhizome into sections with at least two to three leaves and re-attaching each piece to new hardscape.

plant_note: Plant young transplants in spring into acidic, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full to partial sun.
directions: Plant young transplants in spring into acidic, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full to partial sun, matching the boreal barrens, subalpine meadows, and lakeshores across its wide transcontinental range from Alaska to New England. This low, tufted shrub bears small white-to-pink flowers in late spring followed by sweet, dark blue berries relished by grouse, songbirds, and small mammals. Its compact, mat-forming habit makes it a good choice for a sunny native rock garden or as a groundcover at the front of an acidic border.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; like Burford holly, Dwarf Burford is self-fertile and sets fruit without a male pollinator — a major advantage over hollies requiring cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Dwarf Burford Holly is a compact sport of Burford holly (Ilex cornuta 'Burfordii') that inherits most of the parent's excellent landscape traits — self-fertile heavy red berry production, single-spine leaves, glossy dark-green foliage, and outstanding deer resistance — in a much more restrained package reaching only 3–5 feet tall and wide, compared to the large-shrub to small-tree dimensions of standard Burford holly. The compact size makes Dwarf Burford exceptionally versatile for foundation plantings, low hedges, mass planting as ground cover, and container culture in situations where the full-size Burford would quickly become oversized and require heavy pruning. Like all Chinese hollies, Dwarf Burford produces the characteristic single prominent terminal spine rather than the ring of spines of American holly, making it somewhat less hazardous to plant near walkways and play areas. The heavy red berry crop matures in October–November and persists through winter, providing striking red accent color against the dark-green foliage. Extremely tough and adaptable — tolerates clay, alkaline soil, drought, and heat once established. One of the best small evergreen shrubs for the Gulf Coast region.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall, root stem cuttings, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; shear catmint back by one-third to one-half immediately after the first main flush of flowers fades to promote a second flush of bloom in late summer — this deadheading and shearing is the primary cultural key to prolonging the blooming season.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf catmint is a low-growing Caucasian perennial that forms billowing, soft mounds of small, gray-green, aromatic, toothed, hairy leaves and produces dense, continuous spikes of small, tubular, lavender-blue to violet flowers in late spring and early summer, creating one of the most attractive and bee-friendly edging plants available for the perennial border. The soft, hazy, silver-gray foliage and lavender-blue flower combination creates a classic cottage garden look that is attractive even out of flower. Bumblebees and honeybees work catmint flowers with unusual intensity. If sheared back by half after the first main flush fades in early summer, it produces a second flush of bloom in August–September. Drought-tolerant and long-lived. The named cultivar 'Walker's Low' (despite its misleading name, reaches 18–24 inches) is the most widely planted selection for its extra-vigorous, large-flowered display. Distinguished from the larger Nepeta x faassenii by being the true species and setting viable seed.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in wet soil in shallow standing water up to 6 inches deep or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf cattail spreads by rhizome and is best confined to a submerged container in a small or formal pond.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in wet soil in shallow standing water up to 6 inches deep or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf cattail spreads by rhizome and is best confined to a submerged container in a small or formal pond. Narrow, grass-like leaves rise to a modest two feet, far shorter than the towering native common cattail, topped in summer by small, plump, rounded brown flower spikes that give the same classic cattail silhouette in a scale appropriate for a small water garden or container pond. Its compact size and much less aggressive spread compared to standard cattails make it one of the few cattails suitable for a residential-scale pond without quickly overwhelming the space, though it still spreads steadily by rhizome if left unconfined in open soil. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to control spread and maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant divisions of the rhizomatous clump in spring after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; musella is cold-hardy to zone 7 when mulched and re-sprouts from the underground rhizome after hard freezes kill the above-ground pseudostems.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in spring; the dwarf Chinese yellow banana is a cold-hardier alternative to ornamental bananas, forming compact clumps of paddle-shaped, blue-green leaves and producing a spectacular, long-lasting, waxy yellow flower head resembling an enormous lotus blossom from atop the pseudostem after 2–3 years of growth. Unlike most bananas, the inflorescence can last for months rather than weeks, and the plant is monocarpic — the main stem dies after flowering but produces offset pups around the base that will flower in future years. Mulch the rhizome base heavily in zone 7 over winter; the pseudostems may freeze but the roots reliably re-sprout. Excellent focal-point specimen plant for tropical-themed gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in dry, sandy or gravelly, well-drained, acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Dwarf Chinkapin Oak produces sweet acorns with very low tannin content — one of the most palatable native acorns for wildlife and humans. The rhizomatous root system spreads to form colonies in appropriate conditions.
directions: Dwarf Chinkapin Oak is a colony-forming native shrub oak of dry, rocky, sandy, or calcareous upland soils across the eastern United States from New England to Texas, spreading by underground rhizomes to form dense thickets in acid barrens, shale outcrops, dry prairies, and other open, infertile habitats. Though modest in stature at 3–8 feet, it produces large, sweet, low-tannin acorns with coarsely toothed chestnut-like leaves, and the acorns were historically harvested and eaten raw — without the leaching required for most other acorns — by Native Americans across its range; they remain among the best-tasting acorns of any North American oak. Spreading steadily by rhizomes to form wildlife thickets, Dwarf Chinkapin Oak provides year-round habitat value: dense nesting cover, summer leaf-litter decomposition, and a reliable annual fall acorn crop for turkeys, deer, squirrels, and many bird species. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in dry, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; no supplemental irrigation needed once established in xeric conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade in spring; dwarf comfrey spreads moderately by rhizomes and self-sowing, forming dense weed-suppressing mats in shaded conditions — divide every few years to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; dwarf comfrey is a low-growing Caucasian relative of common comfrey (S. officinale) grown as an ornamental groundcover — the broad, hairy, dark-green, elliptic leaves form a dense, effective weed-suppressing mat that persists through winter in mild climates, and in early spring pendulous clusters of small, tubular, creamy-yellow to pale-blue flowers dangle from arching stems before nearly any other perennial emerges. The plant spreads by rhizomes and self-sowing at a moderate, manageable pace. Much less aggressive than common comfrey. The cultivar 'Hidcote Blue' (blue-lavender flowers) and 'Hidcote Pink' are improved ornamental selections more widely grown than the straight species. Excellent as a companion to hostas, ferns, and epimediums in dry to moderately moist shade where uniform groundcover is needed. Tolerates drier soil than most comfrey species.

common_name: Dwarf Creeping Gardenia (Miniature Gardenia, Radicans Gardenia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Radicans is more shade-tolerant than standard gardenias and performs well with 3–4 hours of morning sun followed by afternoon shade, avoiding the leaf scorch that can occur in intense afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Radicans is a low-growing, spreading dwarf form of the common gardenia that stays 12–18 inches tall while spreading 3–4 feet wide, creating a compact, flowing ground cover or low shrub form with all the fragrance and ornamental qualities of its larger relatives in a much more manageable size. The small, double, white flowers (about 1 inch across) are produced abundantly in late spring and summer and carry the same intensely sweet, classic gardenia fragrance as the standard-size plants, making this one of the most fragrant plants available for a low-growing ground cover position. The glossy, dark-green, narrow foliage is evergreen in zone 9 and attractive year-round. Radicans is effective as a ground cover under trees with partial shade, along shaded walkway edges, cascading over retaining walls, and in containers where its low, spreading habit can be displayed. It requires the same acidic, humus-rich, moist soil that all gardenias prefer and is sensitive to soil pH above 6.5 — yellowing foliage (chlorosis) in zone 9 is often a sign of pH too high or iron deficiency in alkaline soils. Excellent for zone 9 where the mild winters allow it to thrive and bloom reliably year after year.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions just at or slightly above the soil surface in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; do not plant too deeply or the rhizome will rot.
directions: Plant rhizomes just at the soil surface in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; dwarf crested iris is one of the most charming native shade wildflowers, carpeting the woodland floor with colonies of pale lavender-blue iris flowers marked with white and yellow crests in early spring before the tree canopy fully opens. It grows naturally on wooded slopes, creek banks, and woodland paths across the eastern US. The low-growing, grass-like foliage spreads quickly by shallow rhizome to form dense, weed-suppressing mats — an excellent living mulch under trees. Plant where you can enjoy the flowers up close. The plant goes semi-dormant in summer heat but greens up in fall. Divide crowded colonies in late summer or early fall. The white form 'Alba' is occasionally available.

common_name: Dwarf Firebush (Compact Native Hummingbird Shrub for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Dwarf Firebush flowers on new growth — cut back hard (to 6–12 inches) in late winter each year to promote vigorous new growth and the most prolific flowering.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Dwarf Firebush ('Compacta') is a compact cultivar of the native Hamelia patens (firebush), a Florida and Gulf Coast native shrub that is one of the most outstanding hummingbird and butterfly plants for subtropical gardens — producing dense clusters of tubular, orange-red to coral-red flowers continuously from late spring through fall on a more compact, manageable 3–4 foot plant compared to the 6–10 foot of the full-sized species. The combination of orange-red tubular flowers (ideal for hummingbirds), black-purple berries (eaten by songbirds), reddish new growth, and reliable heat/drought performance makes Dwarf Firebush one of the finest all-around wildlife shrubs for zone 9 landscapes. Ruby-throated hummingbirds visit constantly during migration (March–May and July–October) and resident Gulf South hummingbirds use it throughout the warm season. Gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and numerous other butterfly species nectar on the flowers regularly. In zone 9, Dwarf Firebush may be killed to the ground by hard freezes but returns vigorously from the roots in spring — treat as a perennial subshrub and cut back to 6 inches in late February to promote fresh growth. In protected locations and zone 9b, the plant may remain evergreen through mild winters. The compact habit makes it proportionate for residential gardens where the full species would be too large.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade to full sun. Dwarf Fothergilla performs best in consistently moist, acidic soil — avoid alkaline or poorly drained locations.
directions: Dwarf Fothergilla is one of the finest native shrubs for four-season interest in the southeastern garden, native to wet pine savannas, pocosins, and moist, acidic coastal plain habitats from North Carolina to Alabama, producing fragrant, white, bottlebrush-like flower spikes of pure white stamens in March and April before the leaves emerge — among the most beautiful of all native spring-blooming shrubs. The broadly ovate, blue-green summer leaves are attractive in their own right; they turn to exceptional shades of crimson, orange, and yellow in fall, often with all three colors on a single leaf. Easy to grow in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, Dwarf Fothergilla is compact enough for small gardens and is valuable as a foundation planting, border accent, or naturalized understory shrub. Provide acidic, consistently moist soil and avoid alkaline conditions, which cause chlorosis.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; dwarf goat's beard is considerably more tolerant of dry shade than the larger Aruncus dioicus and performs acceptably in drier woodland conditions where the larger species would decline.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; dwarf goat's beard is a diminutive Korean species that provides all the ornamental qualities of the full-sized goat's beard (Aruncus dioicus) in a compact, groundcover-scale package suitable for smaller gardens and shaded edging — the finely divided, fernlike, bright-green, delicate leaves form a tidy, low, cushion-shaped mound, and the plant produces small but charming, feathery, white flower plumes in late spring to early summer. The foliage is among the finest-textured of any shade perennial and creates a delicate, lacey effect in the shade border. After the flowers fade, the seed heads turn russet-brown and remain ornamental through late summer. In autumn the leaves develop attractive yellow-orange coloring. A refined, tidy, and well-behaved shade perennial — it does not self-seed aggressively and remains in a controlled clump. Excellent as a low groundcover under deciduous trees, in rock garden shaded pockets, and at the front of shaded borders. More drought-tolerant than the species once established.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown container trees in fall in rocky, dry, well-drained, alkaline or acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf hackberry is among the most stress-tolerant of all native trees, thriving on exposed limestone outcrops and dry rocky ridges where few trees survive.
directions: Dwarf hackberry is a small native tree of rocky limestone glades, cedar barrens, dry cliffs, and open woodland edges across the eastern and central United States — the most compact and stress-tolerant of the native hackberries, growing slowly into a rounded shrub or small tree on exposed, droughty sites where little else establishes. Like larger hackberries, it is one of the most important wildlife trees for native butterflies: the larvae of hackberry emperor, tawny emperor, and American snout butterflies feed exclusively on hackberry foliage, making all Celtis species invaluable host plants for these specialist butterflies. Its small, orange-to-dark-purple berries ripen in fall and are consumed by at least 48 species of birds — it is one of the top bird-attracting fruiting native trees for fall migrants. Its tolerance of rocky, alkaline, shallow limestone soils and exposed cliff-face conditions makes it ideal for dry stone walls, rocky native plantings, and limestone-soil landscapes where conventional trees fail to thrive.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early fall and replant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in deep shade; divisions establish slowly and resent disturbance, so choose the planting site carefully before establishing.
directions: Plant Hexastylis naniflora in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil under dense deciduous or mixed forest canopy, replicating the Blue Ridge foothill conditions where it is endemic to the Carolinas and Georgia. The small, heart-shaped leathery leaves form a tight, slowly-spreading evergreen mat that provides year-round groundcover even in deep shade. Tiny urn-shaped flowers hide at soil level in late winter and early spring, pollinated by fungus gnats and ground-crawling insects. Because this is a rare species of conservation concern, always source plants from reputable native plant nurseries rather than collected specimens.

common_name: Dwarf Himalayan Sweet Box (Low Spreading Deep-Shade Fragrant Groundcover Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to deep shade; this low, dense, spreading dwarf sweet box works as a groundcover for deep dry shade, bearing tiny, intensely fragrant winter flowers and black fruit.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to deep shade, where it tolerates conditions few other evergreen shrubs will grow in, including dry shade once established. This dwarf, low-growing form of Himalayan sweet box spreads gradually by suckering rhizomes into a dense, glossy-leaved evergreen groundcover only knee-high or shorter, useful for massing beneath trees or along a shaded foundation where a taller shrub would be unwelcome. Tiny, inconspicuous white flowers hidden among the leaves in midwinter release a surprisingly powerful, sweet fragrance that carries well beyond the plant itself, followed by small black berries. It requires very little maintenance once established and tolerates deep shade, root competition, and periods of drought better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen. Water during extended dry spells the first year or two while roots establish.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil.
directions: Dwarf Hinoki cypress is a slow-growing evergreen with rich green, fan-shaped sprays of foliage that form a graceful, sculptural pyramid. Plant it in full sun to light shade in moist but well-drained soil, avoiding soggy sites that cause root rot. It appreciates shelter from harsh drying winter winds, which can brown the foliage. Water regularly during establishment and in droughts, then it becomes fairly self-sufficient. Little pruning is needed, and its naturally elegant layered form makes it a favorite for rock gardens and containers.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; dwarf honey bush is smaller and somewhat more frost-tolerant than Melianthus major. Cut back to the ground after frost — it resprouts vigorously from the base. Handling the foliage releases an unpleasant, pungent odor; gloves recommended.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun to part shade; dwarf honey bush is the compact species of the South African Melianthus genus — producing the same striking blue-gray, serrated, pinnate foliage as its larger relative M. major but in a more restrained size (2–5 feet) suitable for mixed borders and smaller gardens. The foliage has the distinctive, sharply toothed, almost claw-like leaflet margins of the genus and the same beautiful glaucous blue-gray color that reads as near-exotic in the garden. Dark maroon to brick-red tubular flowers appear on upright spikes in late winter and spring, producing copious nectar that earned the genus its common name — in South Africa, the flowers drip with honey-like nectar attractive to sunbirds and hummingbirds. The bruised foliage has an unpleasant odor (described variously as peanut butter or something less pleasant), so site away from paths or wear gloves when handling. Cuts back to the ground in cold winters in zones 8–9 and resprouts reliably.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial to full shade, ideally in a container or pond-margin planter with a barrier; dwarf horsetail spreads by rhizome and, like all Equisetum, can become difficult to control if planted directly in garden soil.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial to full shade, ideally in a container or pond-margin planter with a barrier; dwarf horsetail spreads by rhizome and, like all Equisetum, can become difficult to control if planted directly in garden soil. Equisetum scirpoides is a diminutive, wiry, evergreen relative of the larger common horsetail, forming a low tangle of thread-thin, curling, dark green segmented stems that give it a fine, almost mossy texture quite different from its taller, coarser relatives. Its small scale and tolerance of constant moisture and shade make it useful in a bog garden, container water feature, or the shaded edge of a pond where its curling stems provide unusual year-round textural interest. Confine it firmly, since even the dwarf species spreads steadily by rhizome, and it will colonize any consistently damp soil it can reach.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta minor is one of the smallest true hosta species, forming tiny clumps suitable for the front of shaded borders, woodland rock gardens, and path edges where its petite scale is an advantage.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta minor is a Korean dwarf hosta species — one of the smallest hostas in the wild, producing tiny, oval, dark green leaves with distinctive wavy margins and very small clumps appropriate for the scale of rock garden features, shaded path edges, and the front of woodland borders. The flowers are tall relative to the leaf mound, producing lavender to purple flower scapes that rise above the foliage in attractive proportions. A plant of rock ledges and cliff margins in the mountains of Korea. As the parent or ancestor of many modern miniature and small hosta cultivars, understanding this species illuminates the full range of hosta diversity. Useful for trough gardens, small shaded terracotta pots, and other situations where the massive clumps of standard landscape hostas would be too large.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy, humus-rich, dry to moist soil in partial shade; dwarf iris requires excellent drainage and strongly acidic soil — it will not tolerate clay, wet, or neutral to alkaline conditions.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in very well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade; dwarf iris is one of the smallest and most charming native irises of the eastern US, producing miniature (2–3 inch) violet-blue flowers with yellow signals on stems only 3–5 inches tall in early spring — often the first iris to bloom, along with hepatica and spring beauty. It grows naturally in dry, acidic, sandy soils of open pine woodlands and dry, rocky woodland edges from Virginia to Georgia, in conditions very different from the moist requirements of most native irises. The leaves are narrow and grasslike. It spreads slowly by slender rhizomes to form a low colony. Excellent for naturalizing in acidic, dry-shaded rock gardens or under pines in the Southeast — one of the few dwarf irises suited to zone 8–9 conditions.

common_name: Dwarf Jamaican Heliconia (Firebird Heliconia, Stricta Heliconia)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring when soil temperature reaches 65°F+ in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Heliconia stricta grows best in the dappled light of tropical-style beds and shaded ornamental borders. In zone 9, the rhizomes survive mild winters underground — mulch heavily in zone 9a to protect roots from hard frost. The 'Dwarf Jamaican' and 'Firebird' cultivars are among the most compact and zone-9-tolerant selections. Divide clumps every 3–4 years. The upright, scarlet to orange-red bracts are excellent for tropical cut flower arrangements.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Heliconia stricta grows and blooms best with morning sun and afternoon shade in zone 9's intense climate, where full-day sun combined with heat and dryness can stress the large paddle-shaped leaves. Heliconia stricta is one of the most widely grown and zone-adaptable of the heliconias, a species from the tropical forests of Central and South America and the Caribbean (Trinidad, Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil) that has given rise to numerous popular garden cultivars. The plant produces the characteristic banana-like paddle foliage on tall upright stems, topped by the distinctive erect, boat-shaped bracts: in the species and most cultivars, the bracts are waxy, bright scarlet to orange-red, arranged in an upright raceme and persist for weeks as cut flowers or on the plant. Popular named cultivars include 'Dwarf Jamaican' (compact form with red-orange bracts), 'Firebird' (vivid orange-red bracts), and 'Sharonii' (scarlet bracts with green tips). Heliconia stricta is significantly more compact than the giant species (H. bihai, H. caribaea) that can exceed 15 feet, making it practical for residential zone 9 tropical garden beds. The flowers are excellent hummingbird attractants. In zone 9a, rhizomes usually survive mild winters with heavy mulch protection.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; dwarf Japanese garden juniper tolerates drought and poor soil once established and rots in wet, poorly drained ground.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; dwarf Japanese garden juniper tolerates drought and poor soil once established and rots in wet, poorly drained ground. Dense, soft-textured, blue-green needle foliage covers stiffly horizontal branches that layer over one another as the plant spreads, forming a low, textured, wave-like mound popular both as a durable groundcover and as classic material for outdoor bonsai and rock garden specimens. Its tight, compact branching and slightly mounded (rather than flat) habit compared to other groundcover junipers gives it more three-dimensional texture, useful for softening the edge of a rock garden, retaining wall, or foundation planting. Water regularly during the first year, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and shear lightly if a more formal, tighter mound is wanted.

plant_note: Divide and transplant nursery-propagated rhizome clumps in fall into gritty, humus-rich, near-neutral soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged; purchase only propagated stock, since this federally threatened Great Lakes endemic must never be dug from the wild.
directions: Divide and transplant nursery-propagated rhizome clumps in fall into gritty, humus-rich, near-neutral soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, mimicking the thin soils over limestone gravel along Great Lakes shorelines where this species is endemic. This diminutive iris spreads slowly into a dense groundcover and produces pale blue-violet flowers in mid-spring that are an early nectar source for queen bumblebees and other emerging native bees. Because it is federally listed as threatened, purchase only from nurseries selling propagated stock and never dig from wild populations. It makes an excellent choice for a shaded to partly sunny rock garden or shoreline restoration planting in the upper Midwest and Great Lakes basin.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally, into humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees; all parts of this plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where children or pets graze on plants.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees; dwarf larkspur is a true spring ephemeral woodland wildflower that emerges, blooms, sets seed, and goes fully dormant within about two months each spring, disappearing completely by early summer well before the tree canopy closes. Deeply cut, delicate foliage sends up short spikes of vivid blue to violet-blue (occasionally white) spurred flowers in early to mid spring, blooming alongside other woodland ephemerals like trillium and bloodroot in undisturbed forest understory. Because the plant vanishes completely by summer, mark its location to avoid accidentally disturbing the dormant roots, and interplant with later-emerging ferns or hostas that fill the same space once the larkspur has gone dormant. All parts are toxic if eaten, a trait shared with cultivated larkspurs and delphiniums, so avoid planting where livestock, pets, or small children might be tempted to sample the foliage.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall, pressing 1–2 inches deep in dry, sandy, strongly acidic soil in full sun; dwarf live oak spreads primarily by underground rhizomes to form dense thickets in dry, sandy longleaf pine flatwoods and coastal scrub of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; dwarf live oak is a running, rhizomatous scrub oak of the longleaf pine flatwoods and coastal scrub habitats of the southeastern Coastal Plain. Unlike typical upright oaks, this species stays very low (usually under 3 feet) and spreads by underground rhizomes to form dense, thicket-like colonies — a fire-adapted growth form that allows it to re-sprout vigorously after ground fires in its native longleaf pine savanna habitat. The small, evergreen leaves are typical of live oaks. The acorns provide food for bobwhite quail, wild turkey, deer, and numerous other wildlife. An outstanding native for stabilizing dry, sandy soils and creating dense, low wildlife cover in the longleaf pine ecosystem. Its low habit makes it useful as a large-scale native ground cover in dry, sandy, sunny sites.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out after all frost danger passes.
directions: This compact dahlia mix grows to about eighteen inches, making it ideal for containers, borders, and small-space gardens. Start seeds indoors under bright light six weeks before the last frost, then move plants outdoors once nights stay warm. The cheerful single blooms come in reds, pinks, yellows, and whites and draw bees and butterflies through summer. Deadhead regularly for continuous color, and in cold zones lift and store the tubers over winter.

plant_note: Start indoors well ahead of last frost; seeds need light to germinate.
directions: This dwarf petunia blend stays compact and covers itself in trumpet-shaped flowers in red, purple, blue, and white. Surface-sow the tiny seeds on moist mix and press them in without covering, since they need light to sprout, and start them indoors a couple months before planting out. Grow in full sun in containers, borders, or hanging baskets and feed regularly for nonstop bloom. Pinch back leggy stems and deadhead to keep the plants tidy and flowering.

plant_note: Sow in cool soil in early spring; soaking seeds overnight aids germination.
directions: This naturally compact sweet pea mix keeps the classic fragrance without needing a tall trellis, so it suits containers and small beds. Soak seeds overnight and sow in cool early-spring soil, since sweet peas love chilly starts and dislike summer heat. Provide steady moisture and a sunny spot, and pick blooms often to prolong the flowering season. A short bit of twiggy support or a low fence helps the bushy vines stay upright.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring or fall in part shade to full shade; dwarf mondo grass establishes slowly but requires virtually no care once established. In zone 7–10 it is fully evergreen through winter and thrives year-round with minimal irrigation in shaded sites. Divisions spaced 4–6 inches apart will fill in to a continuous mat in 2–3 years.
directions: Plant divisions or plugs 4–6 inches apart in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade; dwarf mondo grass (Ophiopogon japonicus 'Nanus') is a miniature selection of standard mondo grass, growing only 2–4 inches tall compared to the 6–12 inch standard form, creating a fine-textured lawn-like effect in shaded areas where turfgrass cannot grow. It is one of the most popular shade groundcovers in the Gulf Coast South, used extensively under large live oaks, in Japanese-style gardens, between stepping stones, and along shaded pathways. The plant is nearly indestructible in zone 7–10 once established — it tolerates dry shade, occasional flooding, and foot traffic, and maintains its attractive dark green foliage year-round without mowing or fertilization. Small, pale lavender flowers appear in summer, followed by dark blue berries, but the foliage is the principal attraction.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost (or under glass 4 weeks before) in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, poor to average, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; dwarf morning glory does not like to be transplanted — direct sow where it is to grow and thin to 9–12 inches.
directions: Direct sow after last frost (or under glass 4 weeks before) in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, poor to average, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; dwarf morning glory does not like to be transplanted — direct sow where it is to grow and thin to 9–12 inches. Convolvulus tricolor is a bushy, non-climbing annual with satiny, funnel-shaped flowers uniquely marked with three concentric bands of color — vivid blue on the outside, white in the middle, and golden-yellow at the center with a white eye — that remain open all day (unlike true morning glories, which close by afternoon). This unusual all-day flowering habit makes it more practical for busy gardeners and for areas where morning shade would close a true morning glory. It is compact and bushy rather than vining and makes an outstanding front-of-border or container plant for hot, dry positions; flowers attract small native bees and hoverflies.

subcategory: shade-tolerant Gulf Coast native understory palm
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to full sun; dwarf palmetto is the most cold-hardy and most shade-tolerant of the native American palms — growing wild as an understory plant in moist bottomland forests and swamp margins from North Carolina through Florida and along the entire Gulf Coast to Texas. Unlike most palms it thrives in deep shade and standing water conditions. Usually trunkless or with a very short subterranean trunk, the blue-green fan leaves emerging directly from ground level. Moves poorly from landscape — always use container-grown plants.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to full sun; dwarf palmetto is one of the most ecologically important and most garden-useful native palms of the American Southeast — a component of the moist bottomland forests, river floodplains, and swamp margins from North Carolina and Tennessee south through Florida and west along the entire Gulf Coast to eastern Texas. Unlike the overwhelming majority of palms, which require full sun and good drainage, dwarf palmetto is a genuine understory plant adapted to deep shade, periodic flooding, and poorly drained, humus-rich bottomland soils — the quintessential 'shade palm' of the Gulf Coast. It grows naturally in dense shade under the canopy of live oaks, bald cypress, magnolias, and bottomland hardwoods, forming colonies of rosette-like clusters of blue-green to gray-green fan-shaped leaves (costapalmate — intermediate between fan and feather palm) emerging at or very near ground level from a short, often completely subterranean trunk. The blue-green leaf color, the bold fan-leaf texture, and the tropical character of the mature colony create a lush, subtropical understory effect under shade trees that no other cold-hardy plant replicates. Cold-hardy to well below 0°F in established plants. Outstanding as an understory palm beneath live oaks and other shade trees in Gulf Coast zone 7–11 gardens, especially in low, moist sites where drainage-sensitive palms would fail.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in permanently moist to shallow-water conditions in full sun to partial shade; dwarf papyrus is a miniature African papyrus well-suited to container water gardens, small ponds, and indoor/outdoor aquatic settings. Remove offsets regularly to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in permanently moist to shallow-water soil or grow in a pot sitting in water in full sun to partial shade; dwarf papyrus is a diminutive South African relative of the famous Nile papyrus (Cyperus papyrus), growing to only 18–30 inches — compact enough for container water gardens, bird baths, and small aquatic pots that full-sized papyrus would overwhelm. The characteristic papyrus umbel of thread-like rays topped with tiny flower clusters is present in miniature, giving the same architectural, firework-display appearance as giant papyrus on a much more manageable scale. In zone 9a, it can be grown outdoors year-round in a frost-protected microclimate or as a container plant moved indoors in winter. Excellent for small-space water gardens, tabletop ponds, and indoor aquatic gardens. Propagates readily by division and by floating the spent flower heads in water — the ray tips root to produce new plantlets.

plant_note: Plant small divisions or rooted sprigs in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; dwarf pennywort roots readily at every leaf node and spreads quickly in warm, damp conditions, so a small planting fills in fast.
directions: Plant small rooted sprigs into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; dwarf pennywort is a very low, fast-spreading creeper with tiny, round, scalloped, bright-green leaves on thread-like stems that root at each node as they travel, quickly knitting into a lush green carpet in damp, shaded ground. It is useful as a soft filler around container edges, along shaded shady bed margins that stay damp, or at the moist border of a water feature, and is also grown submersed or emersed in aquariums and paludariums as an easy, fast-growing accent plant. It spreads aggressively wherever moisture and shade both stay high, so give it a contained spot or a location where its spread is wanted rather than a tidy formal bed; it is far less vigorous, and can struggle, in drier or sunnier conditions. In frost-free to nearly frost-free climates it stays evergreen; farther north within its range it dies back in winter and returns from the roots in spring.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sowing into very well-drained, rocky, alkaline, calcareous soil in full sun.
directions: Dwarf Prairie Clover is one of the smallest Dalea species, forming low, spreading mats of woody prostrate stems clothed in tiny, resin-dotted pinnate leaves and producing small, dense spikes of bright pink to rose-purple flowers from spring through summer. Native to the dry Chihuahuan Desert and south Texas plains, it is among the most heat- and drought-adapted of the prairie clovers and must have extremely well-drained, rocky, alkaline, calcareous soil in full sun to thrive. Scarify seeds before fall sowing and avoid any supplemental irrigation once plants are established. Its prostrate, mat-forming habit makes it especially useful for dry rock gardens, xeriscape plantings, and rocky calcareous slope stabilization throughout zones 6-10.

plant_note: Plant small divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic conifer forest soil in partial to full shade; dwarf rattlesnake plantain requires specific mycorrhizal fungal associations and will not establish in conventional garden beds — plant in undisturbed woodland soil under conifers, and purchase only nursery-propagated stock.
directions: Plant small nursery-propagated divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic conifer woodland soil in full to partial shade; dwarf rattlesnake plantain requires specific mycorrhizal fungal associations and must be planted in undisturbed, needle-mulched acidic woodland soil near established conifers. Goodyera repens is the smallest and most delicate of the native rattlesnake plantains, a circumboreal terrestrial orchid of conifer and boreal forests throughout the Northern Hemisphere, with a basal rosette of tiny (1–2 inch), dark-green leaves intricately patterned with a silver-white central stripe and lateral veins — giving the plant the appearance of a miniature jewel orchid or snake skin. In late summer it produces a slender spike of tiny, fragrant, white orchid flowers. It is a jewel of the woodland floor and one of the most suitable native orchids for garden culture, as it tolerates being transplanted better than most terrestrial orchids when moved with its surrounding soil intact. Never collect from the wild; purchase nursery-propagated stock only.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; needs a dry summer baking.
directions: Plant dwarf reticulated iris bulbs in fall about four inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil and full sun. The jewel-toned blue and purple flowers with contrasting markings bloom in late winter before most other bulbs. It needs a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well in subsequent years, so avoid irrigated beds. Plant it at the front of borders or in rock gardens where its early flowers can be admired up close.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into dry, sandy or rocky, calcareous to slightly acidic well-drained soil.
