Echeveria propagates readily from leaf cuttings (leaves gently twisted off and left to callus, then placed on moist gritty soil), stem cuttings, and offsets (chicks) produced by the mother hen rosette. In humid Gulf Coast climates, Echeveria should be planted in raised beds or containers with excellent drainage; humidity-tolerant species like E. peacockii, E. imbricata, and E. runyonii perform better in coastal gardens than the most sensitive species. Outstanding as container specimens, in rock gardens, and in xeric landscape designs.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 16–20 weeks before desired outdoor transplant date; in zone 9 start seeds July–August for fall transplanting (September–October) for winter bloom, or start October–November for February–March transplanting for spring bloom. Lisianthus seed is extremely fine and often comes pelleted for easier handling — do not bury, as light is required for germination. The long lead time from seed to bloom (150–200 days) makes lisianthus one of the longest-season annuals. The Echo series is one of the most reliable lisianthus series for garden performance — bred for heat tolerance and resistance to botrytis. In zone 9 lisianthus blooms November–April; it declines in summer heat and is grown as a cool-season crop.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–7.5) soil with consistent moisture — Lisianthus is unusual among cut flower crops in preferring near-neutral or slightly alkaline soil conditions rather than the acidic soil preferred by most floriculture crops; Echo Blue Lisianthus is a leading commercial lisianthus cultivar producing the double, ruffled, blue-to-blue-violet flowers that represent one of the most elegant and sophisticated floral presentations available from any annual cut flower crop — the multiple layers of tissue-thin, ruffled petals and the rich blue color combining to create a flower that resembles a combination of a rose and a poppy in blue. Lisianthus (Eustoma grandiflorum) is a native wildflower of the US prairies and southern states that has been developed into one of the most valuable commercial cut flower crops in the world — the cut stems lasting 1–3 weeks in a vase, making them among the longest-lasting of all cut flowers. The blue-to-purple color range of Echo Blue is particularly valuable in cut flower work where true blue flowers are rare and high-value. For zone 9 gardeners growing lisianthus as a cool-season annual (November–April), the long growing time required is rewarded with one of the most sophisticated and beautiful cut flower crops available from any home garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Eco Lacquered Spider' spreads quickly by wiry, above-ground stolons and roots readily wherever a node touches moist soil, filling in as a dense groundcover within a season or two.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled woodland light; this selection tolerates more sun in cooler climates if kept consistently watered. 'Eco Lacquered Spider' was selected and introduced by plantsman Don Jacobs of Eco Gardens in Georgia for its glossy, dark green, bronze-tinged foliage and unusually vigorous, far-reaching stolons that radiate out from the crown like spider legs, rooting as they go to knit together a dense, weed-suppressing mat faster than the species. Cheerful five-petaled bright yellow daisy flowers appear in flushes from mid-spring through early summer with sporadic rebloom into fall. It is an excellent low-maintenance native groundcover for shaded slopes, woodland-garden edges, and beneath deciduous shrubs, and provides early-season pollen and nectar for small native bees.

common_name: Ecuador Velvet Philodendron (Verrucosum Philodendron, Velvet-Leaf Philodendron)
plant_note: Grow on a moss pole or bark support in bright indirect light with chunky, well-drained aroid mix; Philodendron verrucosum is a climbing, hemi-epiphytic species that grows best when its aerial roots have something to attach to. Maintain consistently moist but not saturated media and high humidity (60–80%+) — this species naturally grows in humid cloud forest environments. Cooler nighttime temperatures (60–65°F) can intensify the golden venation on the leaves. Propagate from stem cuttings with a node. All parts toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in chunky, well-aerated potting mix with a climbing support — Ecuador Velvet Philodendron climbs vigorously and produces progressively larger leaves as it ascends a moss pole or bark surface. Philodendron verrucosum is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid from the cloud forests of Ecuador, Colombia, Peru, and Costa Rica in the Araceae family, widely considered one of the most beautiful velvet-leaved philodendrons in the collector trade and globally sought by tropical plant enthusiasts. The leaves are large (up to 18–24 inches on established climbing stems), broadly cordate (heart-shaped), and covered in a dense, velvety, dark forest-green surface with a distinctive iridescent sheen and a bold pattern of yellow-gold to pale gold primary and secondary veins that stand out brilliantly against the dark velvet background. The petioles are clothed in fine, bristly hairs (the 'verrucose' quality — warty or bumpy) in shades of yellow-green to pinkish. The undersides of the leaves are deep maroon-red to burgundy — a rich color contrast visible whenever the leaves catch air movement. The leaf texture, venation pattern, and color combination make P. verrucosum one of the most photographed and desired philodendrons in modern tropical plant collecting. All parts toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

common_name: Ed Murray Daylily (Classic Near-Black Red Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ed Murray, introduced in 1978, remains a benchmark near-black red daylily grown for its dark color and reliable rebloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ed Murray, introduced in 1978, remains one of the most widely grown near-black red daylilies decades after its release, prized for its rich, deep red petals that read almost black in certain light, set off by a small chartreuse-green throat. Its dark, dramatic color and dependable, floriferous performance have kept it a benchmark against which other dark red daylilies are still measured. Like other daylilies it grows easily in average soil with routine watering, tolerates heat well, and mature clumps can be divided every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and increase the planting.

common_name: Eden Climbing Rose (Pierre de Ronsard Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in a sunny spot with rich, well-drained soil, spacing them well from walls or fences to allow air movement, and tie the canes to a support as they grow.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, tying the long canes to a fence, pillar, or arbor as they extend since this rose does not climb on its own. Large, cupped, old-fashioned-style blooms open cream at the center and blush to soft pink toward the outer petals, opening in flushes from late spring through fall with a light fragrance. It is noted for glossy, disease-resistant foliage that holds up well through summer heat and humidity compared to many older climbers. Prune lightly after the first flush to shape the plant and remove spent blooms, saving harder structural pruning for late winter dormancy.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost — seeds are extremely fine and should be pressed onto the soil surface without covering; transplant after last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost, pressing the dust-fine seed onto moist surface-sown seed mix without covering — seeds need light to germinate; grow on in a bright window until after last frost, then transplant to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade for best summer longevity. Edging lobelia is a South African native producing masses of small, two-lipped flowers in intense sky-blue, violet, white, or magenta-rose in a continuous cascade from spring through early summer, then again in fall after summer heat abates and it is typically sheared back. The plant blooms most prolifically in cool weather and fades in peak summer heat; afternoon shade significantly extends its performance in hot summer climates. Popular for container edges, hanging baskets, and formal bed borders. 'Crystal Palace' (deep blue, bronze foliage), 'Cobalt Blue', and 'White Lady' are classic selections.

common_name: Edith Bogue Magnolia (Cold-Hardy Upright Southern Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Edith Bogue has a narrower, more upright form than most Southern magnolia cultivars — a significant advantage in smaller spaces.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Edith Bogue is the most cold-hardy Southern magnolia cultivar available for routine landscape use — surviving temperatures as low as -10°F and reliably winter-hardy in zone 5 where no other Southern magnolia cultivar can be grown. The cultivar originated from a tree planted by Edith Bogue in Montclair, New Jersey, that survived severe winters that killed all other Southern magnolia selections in the area. This exceptional cold hardiness expands the range of the magnificent Southern magnolia northward into climate zones previously inaccessible to the species. Beyond cold hardiness, Edith Bogue has a distinctly narrower, more columnar to pyramidal habit than most Southern magnolia cultivars — a significant advantage in residential landscapes where the typical broad, spreading form of standard Southern magnolias would require too much space. The upright form makes Edith Bogue appropriate for tighter spaces along buildings, driveways, and in urban settings. The glossy, dark-green leaves with a lighter underside and the classic creamy-white, deeply fragrant flowers (8–12 inches across) are characteristic of the species. In zone 9, it performs superbly — the superior cold hardiness is not needed in the Gulf South, but the narrow habit is a consistent advantage.

common_name: Edith Wolford Bearded Iris (Blue-and-Gold Bicolor Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Edith Wolford is a multiple-award-winning bearded iris known for its striking two-toned blue-and-gold blooms.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Edith Wolford is one of the most honored bearded iris cultivars of the late 20th century, winning the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal, and is prized for its striking bicolor blooms combining soft butter-yellow standards (upper petals) with deep violet-blue falls (lower petals), a color combination that stands out strongly in the spring border. The tall, sturdy stems hold up well in wind and rain, and the clump multiplies at a good pace, benefiting from division every three to four years after bloom to keep it vigorous. Good drainage is essential, since soggy soil quickly leads to rhizome rot.

common_name: Edulis Superba Peony (Early Fragrant Rose-Pink Double Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; dating to 1824, Edulis Superba is one of the oldest peony cultivars still widely grown.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Dating to 1824 and still in commerce two centuries later, Edulis Superba is one of the oldest peony cultivars widely grown today, opening rose-pink double blooms with a sweet, old-fashioned fragrance early in the peony season, often in time for Memorial Day in much of its range, which made it a traditional favorite for cutting for that occasion. Its long garden history is a testament to reliable vigor and dependable bloom rather than novelty, and established clumps can persist and flower for generations with minimal care. Divide only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may take a year or two to resume full bloom after transplanting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Edward Goucher blooms continuously from spring through frost, producing successive flushes of the lavender-pink tubular flowers that are distinctly more colorful than white-flowered Abelia x grandiflora. Prune lightly after the first spring flowering flush to maintain shape and stimulate reblooming; avoid heavy pruning that removes flowering wood. In zone 9 this abelia is nearly evergreen, losing only a portion of its leaves in the coldest winters. It tolerates pruning into a formal hedge but looks best when allowed to develop its naturally graceful, arching habit.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Edward Goucher Abelia is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most freely in full to partial sun; Edward Goucher is a hybrid abelia cross between Abelia x grandiflora and Abelia schumannii, producing a medium-sized (4–5 foot), gracefully arching shrub with distinctly more colorful flowers than standard white-flowered abelia — the small, tubular flowers are lavender-pink to lilac-pink, creating a softer, more distinctly colored floral display that continues from late spring through frost. The semi-evergreen to nearly evergreen foliage has a refined, fine texture, and the new growth emerges with a bronze-red tint that transitions to dark green — adding foliage color interest beyond the continuous flower display. Abelia in general is one of the most butterfly-attractive landscape shrubs available in zone 9, and Edward Goucher's colored flowers enhance this quality — the lavender-pink flowers are particularly attractive to swallowtails, skippers, and sulphurs throughout the long bloom season. The combination of zone 9 adaptability, long bloom season, drought tolerance once established, and the graceful natural habit has made Edward Goucher one of the most classic and enduringly popular landscape shrubs for Gulf South gardens since its introduction.

common_name: Egyptian Papyrus (Nile Grass, Paper Reed, Papyrus Sedge)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in shallow water (0–12 inches deep) or in constantly wet, boggy soil at the pond's edge in full sun to partial shade; Cyperus papyrus grows vigorously in zone 9 humid conditions and spreads by thick rhizomes. In zone 9a, the tops die back in hard frosts but rhizomes survive if the root zone stays above freezing — mulch heavily or maintain in water that doesn't freeze solid. Divide clumps every 2–3 years. Excellent in containers set in decorative water bowls or water features.
directions: Plant in shallow water, boggy pond margins, or constantly wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Egyptian Papyrus requires reliably moist to wet conditions and will decline rapidly if allowed to dry out. Cyperus papyrus is the famous tall sedge of the Nile Delta — the same plant used by ancient Egyptians to produce papyrus paper, one of the earliest writing materials, by splitting and layering the inner pith of the tall stems. In zone 9 Gulf Coast water gardens, it creates an extraordinary tropical effect: triangular, bright green stems rise 5–10 feet tall topped by enormous, spherical, light and airy umbels of thin radiating bracts tipped with tiny flower clusters — the silhouette of a giant, architectural feather duster or sparkler held at the top of a pole. Multiple stems from a single clump sway gracefully in breezes, creating constant motion. The plant also produces smaller stem-tip cuttings that can be inserted upside-down in water to produce offsets (whip propagation). In the humid Gulf Coast climate, Egyptian Papyrus grows with exceptional vigor in water gardens, pond margins, rain gardens, and boggy corners of the landscape. It is naturalized in parts of the Gulf Coast and Florida where escaped plants colonize canal banks and wetland margins.

common_name: El Desperado Daylily (Yellow Daylily with Red Watermark Eye)
plant_note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; El Desperado is a vigorous, heavy-budded tetraploid daylily that establishes readily and clumps up quickly under good garden conditions.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and provide consistent moisture through the bloom season for the largest, cleanest flowers. Bred by Bill Munson and introduced in 1990, El Desperado bears large, wide-petaled golden-yellow blooms marked with a bold, deep red-maroon watermark eye radiating up each petal from a green throat, a striking color combination that helped it win the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2001. Its high bud count and strong branching produce a long, dependable bloom season, and the tetraploid vigor gives it thick, substantial petals that hold up well in Gulf South heat and humidity. Deadhead spent scapes and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to maintain strong flowering.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; shelter from strong wind, which can shred the large, soft leaflets.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside a pond, stream, or other reliably damp spot, since this rodgersia struggles wherever soil dries out for extended periods. Elderleaf rodgersia is a Chinese woodland species named for its pinnately compound leaves, which closely resemble those of an elderberry shrub rather than the palmately lobed foliage typical of most other rodgersia species, giving it a distinct, refined texture in the bog or shade garden. In midsummer, wiry flower stems rise well above the foliage mound carrying loose, feathery, creamy-white plumes reminiscent of a large astilbe. Mulch generously to retain soil moisture through summer, and divide congested clumps in early spring only when vigor declines, since rodgersias resent frequent disturbance.

plant_note: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; largely deer-resistant and low-maintenance once established, like its parent Karl Foerster.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. A golden-variegated sport of the industry-standard Karl Foerster, Eldorado was discovered by growers in Washington State and shares its parent's strictly upright, non-flopping habit while adding a bright yellow stripe down the center of each narrow green leaf. Slender purplish flower spikes rise above the foliage in midsummer and mature to a rich wheat tone that persists through winter, reaching up to 5-6 feet in bloom. As a sterile hybrid it produces no viable seed, so it spreads only by slowly expanding clump and poses no self-seeding concerns.

common_name: Eleanor Taber Indian Hawthorn (Deep Pink-Flowered Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Eleanor Taber is valued for its deep rose-pink flowers, showier than the paler pink or white of many Indian hawthorn selections.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates partial shade with somewhat reduced flowering. Eleanor Taber is a long-popular Indian hawthorn selection prized for its especially deep, rich rose-pink flower clusters in spring, a stronger color than the softer pinks and whites typical of the species, set against the same leathery, dark green, disease-resistant foliage. Like other Indian hawthorn selections it is outstanding for coastal Gulf landscapes, tolerating salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil with ease, and needs only a light shaping prune right after spring bloom to keep its naturally tidy, rounded form. Good air circulation helps reduce Entomosporium leaf spot, the main disease concern for Indian hawthorn in humid climates.

common_name: Eleanor Tabor Indian Hawthorn (Deep Pink Compact Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Eleanor Tabor bears an unusually heavy flush of deep pink flowers each spring, richer in color than many Indian hawthorn cultivars, on a dense, rounded shrub with glossy, leathery, disease-resistant evergreen foliage followed by small blue-black berries that draw birds. Its bold spring color and dependable form make it a strong choice for foundation plantings, low hedges, and coastal landscape beds. Like other Indian hawthorn cultivars, it tolerates salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils well; provide good air circulation between plants to help minimize leaf spot disease in humid climates.

common_name: Electra Heuchera (Gold Foliage with Red Veins Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; the bright gold color holds best out of the hottest afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates to keep the bright foliage color from fading. Electra is a Terra Nova Nurseries heuchera grown for its striking bright gold to chartreuse leaves overlaid with a network of contrasting deep-red veins, a color combination that stands out sharply among green- and purple-leaved shade perennials. In early summer it sends up airy, wiry stems of small white flowers above the foliage that attract hummingbirds and beneficial pollinators. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting divisions slightly deeper than their original position since the crown tends to lift out of the soil over time.

plant_note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; the bright chartreuse color holds best with some direct light but scorches in hot afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, and pinch flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant bushy and foliage-focused. Electric Lime is a Proven Winners coleus grown for its nearly solid, glowing chartreuse-lime leaves, one of the brightest foliage colors available for shade plantings and a strong contrast plant against dark-leaved companions like purple heuchera or bronze begonias. It tolerates more sun than many coleus cultivars without scorching, provided soil moisture stays consistent, but still performs best out of the hottest afternoon sun in Gulf South summers. Pinch tips regularly through the season to keep plants full and compact, and take cuttings before frost to overwinter indoors.

common_name: Electric Lime Heuchera (Chartreuse Ruffled Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Electric Lime is a bright chartreuse-foliaged coral bells selection that lights up shaded borders and combines especially well with dark-leaved companions.
directions: Grow in evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, protecting from hot midday sun which can bleach the vivid foliage color. Electric Lime forms a dense, ruffled mound of glossy, lime-to-chartreuse leaves with fine red venation radiating from the center, providing strong color contrast against purple-leaved heucheras, dark hostas, or black mondo grass. Slender flower spikes bearing small white to pale pink bells appear in early summer above the foliage, attracting hummingbirds and small pollinators. Like most Heuchera cultivars it resents heavy, wet clay, so amend planting sites with compost or grit, and divide clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous new growth.

plant_note: Sow in cool soil before the last frost; in mild climates sow in fall for winter and spring bloom.
directions: Soak seed overnight and sow in cool soil several weeks before the last frost, or in fall where winters are mild. This blend offers mildly scented, long-stemmed cut-flower cultivars that flower in the short days of winter and cool spring. Provide a trellis, keep roots cool and evenly moist, and harvest often to extend the bloom period. Parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil before the last frost for spring and early summer bloom.
directions: Soak the seed overnight and sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost beside a sturdy trellis. This striking variety bursts with large ruffled blooms in electric magenta-red and a powerful sweet perfume, carrying three to four flowers per long, sturdy stem. Keep roots cool and consistently moist, and cut frequently for vase-worthy bouquets that hold well. Parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from children and pets.

common_name: Elegans Camellia (Chandleri Elegans, Pink Anemone-Form Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Elegans has a spreading, somewhat horizontal habit — allow 6–8 feet of space on all sides at planting to accommodate its eventual spread.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Elegans is one of the oldest and most historically celebrated Camellia japonica cultivars in American horticulture — introduced by English nurseryman Alfred Chandler in 1831 and still one of the finest camellias for landscape and specimen use nearly two centuries later. The large, anemone-form flowers display a distinctive structure with five large, broad outer guard petals in deep rose-pink to shell-pink surrounding a central boss of densely packed, smaller, petaloid stamens (petaloids) in the same pink color — creating a unique, shaggy, high-centered flower form quite different from the flat formal doubles or simple singles of other camellias. The large flowers — up to 4 inches across — are exceptionally showy and produced in mid-season (December through March in zone 9). The shrub develops a characteristically spreading, somewhat horizontal habit that is distinctive from the more upright growth of most japonica camellias, eventually reaching 5–10 feet tall and 6–10 feet wide. 'Elegans Champagne' is a sport with white petals and yellow petaloids; 'Elegans Supreme' has ruffled pink petals. Provide morning sun and afternoon shade in zone 9, consistent moisture, and acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil.

plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Elegans develops its best glaucous blue-gray color and largest leaf size in partial to full shade — direct sun bleaches the blue tones to yellow-green and scorches the large leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Elegans is one of the most magnificent large-leaved hostas ever selected — a cultivar of Hosta sieboldiana (the blue siebold hosta) that produces exceptionally large (up to 18 inches long, 14 inches wide), heavily corrugated, intensely glaucous blue-gray leaves arranged in a massive, layered, bowl-shaped mound. The intense blue-gray color, the deeply puckered and corrugated leaf surface that catches shadows and creates dramatic texture, and the sheer scale of a mature plant (2–3 feet tall, 4–6 feet wide after several years) make Elegans one of the most impressive foliage plants available for the shade garden — a bold focal point that commands attention from any distance. In summer, pale lavender-white flowers appear on sturdy scapes above the foliage — modest flowers, but a pleasant accent to the dominant foliage display. Elegans grows slowly but steadily, becoming more magnificent each year; a 10-year-old plant in ideal conditions can reach 5–6 feet in diameter. In zone 9, hostas perform well in deep shade with consistent moisture and mulched soil — the combination of shade, moisture, and mulch moderates soil temperature enough to maintain the hosta through the Gulf South summer. Divide in early spring every 5–8 years when clumps become crowded or vigor declines.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Elegantissima is a variegated boxwood cultivar grown for its cream-edged foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with some direct sun, which helps preserve the variegation better than deep shade. Elegantissima bears small, rounded leaves narrowly edged in creamy white, giving the whole shrub a soft, luminous appearance quite different from the solid green of most boxwood, and it holds this variegation year-round on a compact, rounded shrub. It grows a bit slower than solid-green boxwood cultivars and is a good choice for adding brightness to a shady foundation planting or mixed border. Shear lightly once or twice a season to maintain a tidy form.

common_name: Elena Elephant Ear (Buttery Chartreuse with Purple Veins)
plant_note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Elena bears buttery-yellow to chartreuse leaves with purple veining and white-to-purple petioles, coloring brightest in full sun.
directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun for the brightest color, though it also performs well with some afternoon shade in the hottest part of zone 9. Elena bears luminous buttery-yellow to chartreuse leaves marked with fine purple veining, held on striking white-to-purple petioles that provide additional color contrast against the bright foliage. Its sun-tolerant, glowing color makes it a strong focal point in a bog garden, pond edge, or large container where a bright accent is wanted. The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every two to three years to control spread, and keep soil consistently wet.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; Elephant Bush tolerates brief temperatures to about 28–30°F when established and dry, making it useful for zone 9b–12 landscapes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun to light shade; Portulacaria afra (Elephant Bush, Dwarf Jade, or Spekboom in Afrikaans) is a South African succulent shrub and small tree that is both one of the most ecologically important plants on earth and one of the most practical ornamental succulents for warm, dry landscapes. In its native South Africa's Eastern Cape, spekboom forms vast thicket ecosystems and is one of the most efficient carbon-sequestering plants known — Kruger National Park estimates that spekboom thicket sequesters 4–10 times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforest. As a garden plant, Elephant Bush is valued for its ease of care, attractive small rounded succulent leaves (resembling jade plant Crassula ovata but faster-growing and more heat-tolerant), and its edible, pleasantly sour leaves used in South African salads and stews. The shrubs grow rapidly in warm conditions (up to 3 feet per year in zones 10–12), are extraordinarily drought-tolerant once established, and root easily from stem cuttings. The leaves are eaten by elephants (hence 'Elephant Bush'), baboons, and other wildlife in the wild. Excellent as a low-water landscape shrub, large container specimen, or informal hedge in zone 9b–12; root cuttings easily to propagate. The similar-looking variegated form (leaves edged in cream) is widely grown as a decorative specimen.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; elephant ear begonia requires good air circulation to prevent fungal issues — in humid climates, overhead watering should be avoided and plants should be spaced to allow air movement around the hairy leaves, which can trap moisture if too crowded.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; elephant ear begonia (Begonia scharffii, syn. B. haageana) is one of the largest and most architecturally impressive of the shrub begonias — it grows with a stout, upright, branching, cane-like habit reaching 3–5 feet, with enormous, asymmetric, heart-shaped leaves that can reach 12 inches or more in length, rich olive-green on the upper surface and vivid deep-red on the undersides, with both surfaces covered with soft, silvery-white hairs that give the foliage a luminous, textured quality in low light. Large, pendant clusters of white to pale-pink flowers with prominent yellow stamens are produced at branch tips throughout the warm season. The hairy, large-leaved, red-backed foliage and the bold shrubby habit combine to make it a commanding specimen in shaded gardens, large containers, and conservatories. It tolerates lower humidity better than most shade-growing tropical plants and is one of the easier large begonias to grow as an overwintering indoor houseplant in cool climates. An outstanding architectural shade specimen for zone 10–12 outdoor gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock or scarified, soaked seeds in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; Guanacaste is the national tree of Costa Rica and one of the most impressive shade trees of Central America — it is fast-growing and drought-tolerant once established but requires protection from frost below 30°F.
directions: Scarify seeds with sandpaper and soak overnight before sowing; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun; provide frost protection when young. Enterolobium cyclocarpum (Guanacaste or elephant ear tree) is one of the most massive and magnificent tropical shade trees of Central America — the national tree of Costa Rica — growing to an enormous size with a broadly spreading crown reaching 80–100 feet in diameter that provides extraordinary shade. The common name 'elephant ear tree' comes from the distinctive, flat, dark-brown, ear-shaped seed pods 2–4 inches across that resemble a stylized elephant ear. The tree produces fluffy, white, powder-puff flowers followed by distinctive coiled pods containing 6–15 seeds surrounded by edible, sweet, pulpy flesh used in traditional beverages in Costa Rica. The seeds are high in protein and have been used as animal feed. The wood is valuable for furniture and construction throughout Central America. In zone 10–12 gardens with no frost risk, the tree is a spectacular choice for large-scale tropical landscaping where its enormous size can be accommodated; it grows fast (to 15–20 feet in 3–4 years) and eventually dominates the landscape.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; elephant foot is a native woodland understory perennial of the Gulf Coastal Plain and eastern US that thrives in the dappled shade of pine and hardwood forests — an important nectar plant for native butterflies that is rarely available in nurseries but easy to grow from seed in shaded spots.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; thin to 12 inches and allow to self-seed. Elephantopus tomentosus (elephant foot or tobacco weed) is a native perennial wildflower of eastern North American woodlands and the Gulf Coastal Plain — common in the pine and hardwood forest understory from Virginia through Florida and Texas but rarely cultivated, despite being a genuinely useful and attractive shade-garden native. The plant produces a basal rosette of large (6–10 inch), broadly oval, hairy, slightly crinkled leaves (the 'elephant foot' shape that gives it its name) and branching flower stalks 18–30 inches tall in late summer–fall bearing small, lavender-purple, composite flower heads loosely clustered at the branch tips. The flowers, while individually small, are produced in loose, graceful clusters and are strongly attractive to native bees and skippers. A long-lived, easily self-seeding perennial for woodland and shade-garden naturalization, elephant foot is an excellent native companion for ferns, coral bells, and other shade plants in Gulf Coast understory gardens. Essentially maintenance-free in suitable conditions.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2–4 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; Amorphophallus bulbifer is distinguished from A. konjac by producing small aerial bulbils (tiny tubers) in the axils of its leaf divisions — these bulbils fall and self-propagate, making this species the easiest amorphophallus to multiply in the garden.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; elephant foot yam is an Indian tropical aroid that produces a brief, dramatic, pink-green and mottled spathe over a dark, club-shaped spadix in spring (with a mild carrion odor for one day), then emerges with one or two enormous, intricately divided, single compound leaves — each leaf rising from a single upright stem on a dramatically patterned, mottled, snake-skin-like, gray-green and brown-spotted petiole, spreading the leaflets of a single deeply compound leaf into an elegant, tropical umbrella form reaching 2–4 feet across. The most distinctive feature distinguishing A. bulbifer from other amorphophallus is the production of small, brown, edible aerial bulbils (tiny tubers, about the size of large marbles) that form in the leaf axils at the junction of the leaflets — these bulbils drop and self-propagate freely in suitable warm, shaded conditions. More cold-tolerant than the similar A. konjac in zone 7. An outstanding, easily grown, and self-multiplying shade garden aroid for tropical and warm temperate gardens.

common_name: Elephant Head Amaranth (Dramatic Drooping Ornamental Grain Amaranth)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil; this tall, heat-loving amaranth thrives in the long, hot Gulf Coast summer and needs a full season to develop its massive seed head.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, thinning seedlings to their final spacing since they resent transplanting once established. Elephant Head amaranth is grown for its dramatic, thick, deeply lobed, drooping seed head, which curves and folds over itself in a shape strikingly reminiscent of an elephant's trunk or head, colored in deep wine-red to maroon and reaching well over a foot long on a robust, statuesque plant. Beyond its striking presence as a garden and dried-flower accent, it is a true grain amaranth: the abundant small seeds are edible and nutritious, traditionally harvested and ground much like other grain amaranths, and the young leaves are edible as a cooked green as well. Stake in exposed, windy sites, since the heavy seed head can weigh the stalk over, and harvest for drying once the head has fully colored and the seed inside begins to feel firm.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry to moderately moist, sandy, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; elephant's foot grows naturally in dry to moist, sandy, open pine flatwoods and woodland edges of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; elephant's foot is a distinctive native of the southeastern Coastal Plain, named for its unusually large, rough, basal leaves that spread flat along the ground like the wrinkled feet of an elephant. The plant sends up tall, branched stems in summer topped with small, composite lavender-purple flower heads enclosed in leaf-like bracts — an unusual and ornamentally distinctive inflorescence structure. The flowers attract numerous small bees and butterflies. A shade-tolerant native that provides interest in dry, sandy, partial-shade conditions of pine flatwoods and open woodland gardens in zone 9a. A native plant that is extremely common as a 'weed' but underappreciated as an ornamental.

common_name: Elf Mountain Laurel (Dwarf Pale Pink Compact Selection)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Elf is a true dwarf mountain laurel selection with pale pink buds opening to near-white flowers, well suited to small gardens.
directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Elf stays notably compact and dwarf for a mountain laurel, reaching only three to four feet at maturity with proportionally smaller leaves and flowers, bearing pale pink buds that open to near-white blooms. Its small stature makes it one of the few mountain laurel cultivars practical for a foundation planting or smaller garden bed. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Elfin Creeping Fig (Miniature Tiny-Leaved Terrarium and Topiary Vine)
plant_note: Grow indoors year-round in bright, indirect light and high humidity, or move outdoors after the last frost into shade; Elfin's dwarf, dense growth and tiny quarter-inch leaves make it a favorite for terrariums, fairy gardens, and topiary forms.
directions: Grow in bright, indirect light with consistently moist, well-drained soil and high humidity, misting regularly or using a pebble tray if grown indoors where air is dry. Elfin is a dwarf sport of climbing fig selected for tiny, densely packed quarter-inch leaves and slow, compact growth that stays low and creeping rather than developing the larger juvenile leaves and vigorous climbing habit of standard creeping fig, making it especially well suited to terrariums, dish gardens, fairy gardens, and small topiary forms trained over wire frames. Its fine texture and tight growth habit also make it useful as a miniature groundcover in shaded outdoor containers in warm climates. Trim regularly to maintain shape and density, and protect it from direct sun and cold, both of which stress the fine foliage; outside zone 9's mildest microclimates it is best treated as a houseplant or brought in over winter.

common_name: Elijah Blue Fescue (Compact Intense-Blue Ornamental Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Elijah Blue is the most widely sold blue fescue cultivar, selected for a more compact habit and more intense, consistent blue color than the straight species.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean to average soil; Elijah Blue is the standard nursery-trade blue fescue cultivar, selected for tight, uniform, intensely silvery-blue mounds of needle-fine foliage that hold their color and neat habit more reliably than seed-grown plants of the straight species. It is a cool-season grass that grows most vigorously in spring and fall and can go semi-dormant or look ragged during the peak heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer, so give it the best possible drainage and avoid heavy, wet clay, which promotes crown rot far faster than drought stress does. Slender tan flower spikes rise just above the foliage in early summer. Divide clumps every two to three years in early spring, discarding the woody, browned-out center and replanting the vigorous outer sections, which keeps the blue color and tight mounding habit at its best. Excellent as edging, in rock gardens, or massed as a low, textural groundcover in a sunny, well-drained bed.

common_name: Elizabeth Clematis Montana (Vigorous Fragrant Pale Pink Spring Clematis)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Elizabeth is an extremely vigorous spring-blooming Clematis montana selection needing a very sturdy, large support.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a large, sturdy support such as a pergola, fence, or mature tree. Elizabeth produces an overwhelming single spring flush of small, soft pink, vanilla-scented flowers covering the entire vine, one of the most vigorous Clematis montana selections available and capable of climbing 20 feet or more in ideal conditions. It flowers on the previous year's growth, so prune only right after bloom to control size, never in winter or spring, which would remove the coming display. Its enormous mature size makes it best suited to a large property where it can cover a substantial structure rather than a small garden bed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Elizabeth magnolia was the first yellow-flowered magnolia hybrid widely introduced to the nursery trade.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Elizabeth magnolia was the first yellow-flowered magnolia hybrid widely introduced to the nursery trade. Bred at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and released in the 1970s, this landmark hybrid was the first widely available magnolia with soft, primrose-yellow flowers, a color previously unseen in cultivated magnolias, opening on bare branches in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge, with a light, sweet lemon fragrance. Its introduction opened the door to the many yellow-flowered magnolia hybrids bred since, and it remains a garden favorite for its unusual color, upright pyramidal form, and good resistance to the late-frost damage that plagues some earlier-blooming white magnolias. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally, removing only damaged or crossing branches as needed.

common_name: Elizabeth Oliver Foamflower (Double Pale Pink Native Foamflower)
plant_note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Elizabeth Oliver bears unusual double, pale pink flowers on a native foamflower selection that spreads to form a groundcover.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, the same woodland conditions the native species favors. Elizabeth Oliver bears unusual double, pale pink flower spikes in spring above lobed, softly hairy leaves that often take on bronze-red tones in cooler weather, spreading gently by stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing native groundcover over time. Its double flower form is a rare trait among foamflower cultivars, giving a fuller, more textured bloom than the typical single-flowered species. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch with leaf litter or shredded bark to mimic its native forest-floor habitat.

common_name: Elizabeth Salter Daylily (Stout Medal Ruffled Pink Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Elizabeth Salter won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal for its large, heavily ruffled pink blooms.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Elizabeth Salter earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal, its highest honor, for large, heavily ruffled, clear pink flowers with a lightly gold-edged throat, held on tall, well-branched scapes above a vigorous, floriferous clump. Its clean, saturated pink and generous ruffling have made it a benchmark pink daylily and a popular parent in modern hybridizing programs. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering through the bloom season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and flower count.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist to occasionally boggy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.
directions: Juncus patens 'Elk Blue' is a selection of the Pacific Coast native gray rush chosen for its especially strong steel-blue foliage color, forming tight, upright, evergreen tufts of narrow round stems that hold their color better than the straight species through summer heat. It tolerates both boggy, saturated soil at a pond edge and ordinary garden moisture once established, and unlike many wetland rushes it also handles brief dry spells, making it a flexible choice for rain gardens or the damp partial shade beneath open-canopy trees. Its stiff, architectural, blue-gray vertical form provides useful textural and color contrast against broad-leaved shade perennials such as hostas and heucheras. Cut back hard in late winter every few years to remove old, browning stems and rejuvenate the clump.

common_name: Ellamae Agapanthus (Large Blue Lily of the Nile)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Ellamae is a large-growing agapanthus that benefits from ample space to form broad clumps — allow 24–30 inches between plants at planting, and resist dividing until the clump is truly overcrowded and bloom quality declines.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Ellamae is a robust, large-growing agapanthus cultivar that is one of the most widely grown and best-performing selections for warm-climate gardens — producing large, arching clumps of wide, strap-like, dark-green evergreen leaves from which tall (4–5 foot) flowering scapes rise in summer, each bearing large, dense globular heads of deep blue-purple, trumpet-shaped flowers. The large flower heads are spectacular in mass plantings and outstanding as cut flowers — lasting well in arrangements. Ellamae is more cold-hardy than many agapanthus, tolerating brief freezes to about 10–15°F, and it thrives in zone 7–11 as a reliable perennial where it forms ever-expanding clumps over the years. In zone 9, Ellamae blooms from June through August in full sun, with the season extending into September in partial shade. The large, stately habit — with foliage clumps reaching 2–3 feet and flower scapes rising to 4–5 feet — gives it a sculptural, architectural quality exceptional for creating bold masses along fences, walls, and drives. Extremely drought-tolerant once established. Divide only when clumps become overcrowded — large, mature clumps produce the most spectacular flower displays.

common_name: Ellen Bosanquet Crinum (Classic Wine-Red Fragrant Crinum Lily)
plant_note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Ellen Bosanquet is one of the most celebrated crinum cultivars for its rich, deep wine-red, fragrant flowers.
directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Ellen Bosanquet is widely regarded as one of the finest crinum lily cultivars ever introduced, producing large clusters of intensely fragrant, deep wine-red, trumpet-shaped flowers held on tall, sturdy scapes above strap-like evergreen foliage. Once established, the massive bulb persists and multiplies for decades with essentially no care, making it a classic pass-along plant of old Southern gardens and cemeteries. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil conditions with ease, and division is rarely necessary, since crinum bulbs actually bloom best when left undisturbed and slightly crowded.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall. Elliott's Aster is naturally adapted to wet, seasonally flooded soils in coastal plain habitats from zone 7b–10 and tolerates both extended wet periods and seasonal drought once established. In zone 9 it blooms prolifically in October–November, one of the latest natives to flower, providing nectar at a critical time for migrating monarch butterflies.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained to periodically wet soil; Elliott's Aster is a native fall-blooming aster of the Southeastern Coastal Plain and Gulf Coast, producing spectacular masses of lavender to purple daisy flowers with yellow centers on 3–5 foot stems in October–November — among the latest native wildflowers to bloom in zone 9. The prolific late-season bloom covers the plant in hundreds of small flowers and provides critical nectar for migrating monarchs, native bees, and late-season pollinators when other nectar sources have shut down. Elliott's Aster is naturally adapted to the wet, poorly drained soils of coastal plain habitats, including wet edges of ponds, drainage ditches, and low spots in the landscape where most other ornamentals struggle. It tolerates brief flooding and heavy clay soils far better than most native asters. Cut back to 6 inches in late winter before new growth emerges; divide crowded clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Elliott's bluestem is a warm-season native grass that establishes quickly from seed and is well-adapted to the nutrient-poor, sandy soils of the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Elliott's bluestem is a native warm-season grass of the southeastern Coastal Plain, prairies, and longleaf pine savannas, producing upright clumps of blue-green foliage that turn copper to reddish-bronze in fall — among the finest native grasses for fall and winter color in zone 8–10. The feathery seed heads emerge in late summer, catch the light, and provide winter bird food. It is notably tolerant of the nutrient-poor, well-drained, sandy soils that characterize much of the Gulf Coastal Plain — a quality that makes it excellent for low-maintenance naturalized plantings, coastal restoration, and xeric landscape areas. It performs best in lean soils; rich, amended soil causes excessive growth and floppy stems. An outstanding component of native plant gardens, butterfly gardens, and longleaf pine understory plantings throughout zone 8–10.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into moist, acidic soil; seeds require cold-moist stratification over winter and will germinate the following spring — do not cover seeds, as light aids germination.
directions: Elliott's Gentian is a native perennial of southeastern wet savannas, pitcher plant bogs, and seepage slopes, producing some of the most intensely colored violet-blue tubular flowers of any eastern wildflower during September through November — often the very last wildflower blooming before hard frost. It is genuinely difficult to cultivate and requires close replication of its native habitat: consistently moist to wet, highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), nutrient-poor, sandy or peaty soil in partial sun, as well as the presence of specific mycorrhizal fungal associates in the soil that the plant depends on for long-term survival. Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall without covering them, as they need cold stratification and light for germination; expect very slow seedling growth, with plants typically requiring two or more years to reach blooming size. This species is best established from seed directly into a naturalistic savanna or bog restoration rather than in a conventional garden setting, as transplanting is difficult and container-grown specimens rarely persist without their native fungal partners.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun in spring; Elliott's lovegrass is tolerant of heat, drought, and salt spray, making it ideal for coastal and hot, dry southern landscapes.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, sandy to loamy, poor to average soil in full sun; Elliott's lovegrass (blue lovegrass) is a native southeastern US ornamental grass with unusually attractive blue-gray to silver-blue foliage — the narrow, arching leaves have a distinctly glaucous quality that is rare among warm-season grasses and provides cool, silvery-blue contrast in the summer landscape. Open, delicate panicles of tiny, silvery-purple spikelets appear in summer and fall, creating a misty, translucent effect when backlit. The plant is highly adaptable to the difficult coastal and sandy soils of the Gulf South, tolerating salt spray, drought, and poor soil conditions with negligible care. A natural choice for low-water, native-plant, and coastal landscape designs in zones 7–10. Does not become as weedy as some lovegrass species.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Pyrola species are notoriously difficult to transplant successfully because of a dependence on specific soil mycorrhizal fungi, so purchase only nursery-grown stock and disturb roots as little as possible.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in full to partial shade, and avoid disturbing the roots more than necessary, since this species relies on a close relationship with soil fungi that makes it slow to establish after transplanting. Elliptic Shinleaf forms a low evergreen rosette of glossy, elliptical leaves from which a slender flowering stalk rises in summer, bearing a loose spike of nodding, waxy, greenish-white flowers with a sweet fragrance and a distinctive curved style. It spreads slowly by rhizomes in the deep leaf litter of rich, undisturbed forest floors, making it best suited to an established woodland garden rather than a young or heavily amended bed. Leave fallen leaves in place as mulch to maintain the organic, fungus-rich soil layer it depends on.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; elm-leaved goldenrod is one of the most shade-tolerant goldenrods in the eastern US, blooming reliably in the conditions of an open woodland understory.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, humus-rich to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — elm-leaved goldenrod is an eastern North American native recognized by its leaves, which closely resemble elm leaves with strongly toothed, slightly rough-textured blades on short petioles. It grows naturally in moist, open woodland and woodland edges, making it one of a small number of goldenrods genuinely adapted to shaded conditions. The arching, one-sided (secund) racemes of small golden flowers appear in late summer through fall in shaded locations where most goldenrods cannot bloom. Like blue-stemmed goldenrod, it fills an important ecological niche by providing late-season nectar and pollen in shaded settings where pollinators searching for fall resources would otherwise find nothing. Spreads by rhizome to form a colony. An excellent native goldenrod for adding late-season ecological value to the woodland garden.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; compact enough for containers.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost about an inch deep in full sun, spacing 8-12 inches apart. This blend of shorter, branching sunflowers includes classic single forms and multi-petaled pom-pom types that draw pollinators and make cheery bouquets. Their compact, drought-tolerant habit suits containers, borders, and small gardens. Water regularly while young and deadhead to keep new blooms coming.

common_name: Emarginate Dimerandra (Pink Rock Orchid, Dimerandra, Caribbean Rock Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on rough bark or cork, or in a small slatted basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun; Dimerandra emarginata is a relatively cold-tolerant epiphytic orchid from lowland tropical areas of the Caribbean and Central America, adapting to zone 9b-12 in warm, protected outdoor positions. It blooms throughout the warm months in zone 9-10 with cheerful small pink flowers. Water regularly in active growth; reduce in winter. The compact, reed-like growth habit makes it easy to mount and display. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light mounted on bark or in a small slatted basket — Emarginate Dimerandra thrives in the open-air conditions of a shaded outdoor porch in zone 9b-12 and benefits from excellent air circulation around its root zone. Dimerandra emarginata is a compact, reed-stemmed, sympodial epiphytic orchid native to the Caribbean (Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico), Mexico, and Central America in the Orchidaceae family, a member of the large and diverse Epidendreae tribe closely related to Epidendrum. The plant produces slender, cane-like pseudostems 10–20 inches tall from clustered, small pseudobulb bases, each cane clothed in overlapping, narrow, distichous (two-ranked) leaves. Through the warm months, terminal flowers emerge from the upper leaf axils — each flower small (0.75–1 inch), in a cheerful, clear rose-pink to cerise pink with a broad lip. While not a dramatic specimen, Dimerandra emarginata is a free-flowering, easy-care, cold-tolerant epiphytic orchid whose continuous summer bloom of fresh pink flowers on reed-like stems makes it an pleasant garden companion for zone 9-11 outdoor orchid collections. Its relative cold-tolerance (withstanding brief dips to 35–38°F on protected porches) makes it one of the epiphytic orchids most likely to succeed in zone 9 outdoor culture. Non-toxic.

common_name: Ember's Wish Salvia (Salmon-Red Australian Hybrid Sage)
plant_note: Set out nursery starts after frost danger has passed in well-drained, amended beds or large containers; Ember's Wish is an Australian-bred hybrid sage, a sister selection to Wendy's Wish with warm salmon-red flowers.
directions: Give it full sun and good drainage; Ember's Wish tolerates heat and humidity better than many salvias and blooms nearly nonstop through the hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season. A sister selection to the popular Wendy's Wish, it bears warm salmon-red flowers with contrasting dark calyces on sprawling, arching stems, offering a warmer color option within the same vigorous, free-flowering hybrid group prized by hummingbirds and butterflies. Cut back hard in late winter to renew growth, and take softwood cuttings in fall as insurance since plants can be short-lived in wet winter soils. In colder zone 8 pockets treat as a root-hardy perennial and mulch the crown heavily.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; check local invasive species listings before planting near natural woodland areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; brightest gold variegation develops with a few hours of direct sun. Emerald 'n Gold is a compact, colorful euonymus cultivar with glossy green leaves broadly edged in bright golden-yellow, taking on a pink-red blush through winter cold that adds a second color phase beyond the summer gold-and-green look. Like other euonymus fortunei cultivars, it grows as a low, spreading mound if unsupported or climbs given a wall or trellis, making it a versatile, bright accent for foundation plantings, low borders, or trained against a fence. It tolerates drought, poor soil, and air pollution well, but watch for euonymus scale and treat promptly if it appears.

common_name: Emerald Blue Creeping Phlox (Sky-Blue Moss Phlox)
plant_note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Emerald Blue performs best in sharply drained, lean soil — rich, moist soil promotes lush foliage growth at the expense of flowering and increases susceptibility to crown rot.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Emerald Blue is the standard sky-blue cultivar of Phlox subulata (moss phlox or creeping phlox) — a low, mat-forming native perennial that in early spring (March–April in zone 7–8) produces such a profusion of lavender-blue flowers that the entire plant is obscured under a carpet of blooms. The color of Emerald Blue is a clear, mid-blue lavender — lighter and more purely blue than purple cultivars like 'Red Wings' and 'Scarlet Flame', creating a soft, cool, sky-blue effect that photographs beautifully and reads as a gentle blue sweep across rockeries, slopes, and garden borders. The very dense, needle-like, evergreen foliage forms a tight, weed-suppressing mat year-round; after the brief but spectacular spring bloom, the plant remains attractive as a low, fine-textured, deep-green groundcover through summer, fall, and winter. Creeping phlox is outstanding for slopes, embankments, and rock gardens where its spreading mat anchors soil and outcompetes weeds. Shear lightly after bloom (to 2–3 inches) to encourage dense new growth and a more compact habit. In zone 9, creeping phlox blooms in late February through March — very early in the Gulf South spring — and then serves as an unobtrusive fine-textured groundcover through the warm season. Sharp drainage is the single most critical requirement.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; check local invasive species listings before planting near natural woodland areas, since the species can escape cultivation in parts of the eastern US.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; more compact and better-behaved as a mounding shrub than as an aggressive climber compared to the plain species. Emerald Gaiety is a longtime favorite variegated euonymus cultivar, its glossy, oval, dark-green leaves crisply edged in white, turning a soft pink-tinged blush in cold winter weather for added seasonal interest. It grows as a low, mounding shrub when unsupported or will climb given a wall or trellis to attach to, making it flexible as a foundation shrub, low hedge, or wall cover. It is tough and adaptable, tolerating drought, poor soil, and air pollution, but is susceptible to euonymus scale, so monitor closely and treat promptly if scale insects appear.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil, spacing for a hedge if desired.
directions: Emerald Green arborvitae is a narrow, upright evergreen with dense sprays of bright green foliage, widely planted in rows for privacy screens and hedges. Plant in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil, spacing plants roughly 2 to 4 feet apart for a solid living wall. Water regularly during the first two seasons to establish deep roots and prevent winter browning. It holds its color and slender form well without shearing, though it can be trimmed lightly. Protect young plants from heavy snow load and browsing deer.

common_name: Emerald Knight Fringe Tree (Fruitless Male Native Fringe Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Emerald Knight is a male (fruitless) native fringe tree selection with an upright, dense habit.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; native fringe tree tolerates a wide range of soils once established and is a tough, low-maintenance small flowering tree for the Southeast. Emerald Knight is a male selection of the native fringe tree bred for an upright, dense habit and glossy dark-green foliage, and being male it sets no fruit, avoiding the dropped-fruit litter of female or seed-grown plants while still producing the species' signature cloud of fragrant, fringe-like white flowers in mid-spring. Its denser, more structured form than typical seedling fringe trees suits it well to formal plantings or as a specimen near a patio. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood, since fringe tree needs little routine pruning.

common_name: Emerald Mist Brunnera (Green-Silver Mottled Siberian Bugloss)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Emerald Mist has softly mottled green-and-silver leaves rather than the fully silvered leaves of some brunnera selections.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, keeping soil evenly moist through summer since foliage can wilt or scorch in dry conditions or hot sun. Emerald Mist bears heart-shaped leaves softly mottled and misted with silver over a green base, a more subtle, watercolor-like variegation than the boldly silvered leaves of some other brunnera cultivars, giving it a softer, more textural look in the shade border. Airy sprays of small, bright blue, forget-me-not-like flowers appear in early spring above the foliage. Its gentler variegation pairs well with both bold and fine-textured companions, from hostas to ferns to heucheras, without competing for attention the way a fully silver-leaved selection might. Established clumps rarely need division and self-seed only sparingly compared to the plain species.

common_name: Emerald Pagoda Japanese Snowbell (Large-Flowered Vigorous Snowbell Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Emerald Pagoda bears unusually large white flowers and thicker, more vigorous foliage than the species, and does not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally as an understory tree beneath high-canopy shade; Japanese snowbell is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Emerald Pagoda bears noticeably larger, pure white, pendant, bell-shaped flowers than the species type, held above thicker, glossier, more substantial foliage on a more vigorous, upright-growing tree that establishes faster than many other snowbell selections. Its larger flowers and stronger growth make it a good choice where a bolder, quicker-maturing specimen is wanted. Mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches.

common_name: Emerald Ripple Peperomia (Ripple Peperomia, Green Ripple Pepper)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant in zone 9; Emerald Ripple Peperomia is not frost-tolerant and must be grown in containers brought indoors when temperatures approach 50°F. It tolerates low light better than most ornamental foliage plants and is an excellent choice for dim indoor spaces. Small pot size is important — root rot from overwatering in oversized pots is the most common failure. Allow soil to dry partially between waterings. Variegated forms ('Variegata', 'Silver Ripple') are equally easy to grow.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to low light in well-drained, peat-based or peat-free potting mix; Emerald Ripple Peperomia is one of the most tolerant of all foliage houseplants for low-light conditions, surviving in dim offices, north windows, and interior rooms that are challenging for most ornamentals. Peperomia caperata is a small, compact, rosette-forming tropical from Brazil in the pepper family (Piperaceae), prized for its deeply puckered, corrugated, heart-shaped leaves whose heavily textured surface creates a striking contrast of dark emerald green in the ridges and pale silver-green in the valleys — a tactile as well as visual interest that makes it one of the most distinctive small foliage plants available. The plant stays small (under 10 inches) indefinitely, making it ideal for terrariums, dish gardens, windowsill collections, and small decorative containers. In late summer and fall, the plant produces interesting, narrow, white rat-tail-like flower spikes — unusual in appearance but not particularly showy. Numerous cultivars exist including 'Rosso' (dark green above, intense red-purple below), 'Variegata' (cream-edged leaves), and 'Silver Ripple' (silver-gray textured leaves). All are easy to grow and safe for pets and children.

common_name: Emerald Snow Loropetalum (Cold-Hardy White-Flowered Green Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Emerald Snow was bred for improved cold hardiness compared to older white-flowered loropetalum selections, making it more reliable in the northern part of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Emerald Snow is a white-flowered Loropetalum chinense selection that departs from the more familiar burgundy-leaved, pink-flowered loropetalum cultivars, instead pairing clean green evergreen foliage with abundant, fringe-petaled white flowers in spring and scattered rebloom later in the season. Bred for improved winter hardiness relative to older white-flowered selections, it holds up well through colder snaps common in the northern Gulf South while retaining the vigorous, adaptable growth habit typical of the species. Its all-green foliage makes it a versatile companion for gardens that already feature plenty of burgundy loropetalum, offering contrast and a softer, more traditional look for a hedge, foundation planting, or mixed border. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

common_name: Emerald Vine (Jade Satin Pothos, Amydrium, Green Galaxy)
plant_note: Grow on a moss pole or tree support in bright indirect light in well-draining, chunky aroid mix; Amydrium medium climbs vigorously and requires a support to develop its most attractive, large adult foliage — without a support, it trails and the leaves remain smaller. Allow the top inch to dry between waterings. Maintain moderate humidity. Propagate from stem cuttings. As the plant matures on its support, the leaves develop perforations similar to Monstera. Often sold under the incorrect trade name 'Jade Satin Pothos.' All parts toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light on a moss pole or tree support — Emerald Vine is a vigorous climber that produces distinctly larger, more attractive leaves when ascending a support compared to when trailing, and should be provided with a tall support for best ornamental effect. Amydrium medium is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Vietnam, Philippines, Borneo) in the Araceae family — a relatively recently recognized genus in the aroid trade, where it is commonly misidentified as a Pothos or Scindapsus species and sold under the trade name 'Jade Satin Pothos.' The plant produces climbing stems with large (8–16 inches), oval to broadly heart-shaped, leathery, deeply glossy leaves in an exceptionally rich, dark emerald-green — the glossy surface of A. medium leaves has a depth and intensity of color that has made it popular in the tropical plant collecting community. In juvenile stage, the leaves are solid, undivided, and simple; as the plant matures and climbs, the leaves develop windows (perforations) scattered across the blade surface, adding visual interest. The intense, varnished-looking green surface combined with the developing perforations on adult leaves makes Amydrium medium one of the most ornamentally appealing of the lesser-known climbing aroids. All parts toxic.

common_name: Emily Brontë Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Emily Brontë blooms in generous flushes and benefits from regular deadheading to sustain repeat flowering through the season.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2018 and named for the author of Wuthering Heights, Emily Brontë bears warm pink, rosette-shaped flowers with a fresh tea fragrance, on a healthy, well-branched, medium-sized shrub bred for improved disease resistance over older English rose cultivars. It flowers in generous flushes from late spring through frost, and its manageable size and clean foliage make it a reliable choice for a mixed border where a compact, classic-form English rose is wanted.

common_name: Emily Bruner Holly (Large Red-Berried Hybrid Holly)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Emily Bruner requires a male pollinator (James Swan or other Ilex × koehneana male) nearby for heavy berry production.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Emily Bruner is one of the finest large-statured evergreen holly trees for the Gulf South — a hybrid between Ilex latifolia (lusterleaf holly) and Ilex aquifolium (English holly) that combines the large, deep-green, dramatically lustrous leaves of the former with the heavy red berry production and classic holly appearance of the latter. The large, glossy, finely spined leaves (3–4 inches long) create an exceptionally handsome texture — more coarse and more dramatic than American holly (Ilex opaca) and much bolder and glossier than Chinese holly (Ilex cornuta). The tree grows into a broad, pyramidal to oval form reaching 10–25 feet tall with heavy, persistent red berry clusters that develop after cross-pollination from a male plant (James Swan is the recommended male pollinator for Emily Bruner). The massive red berry clusters that develop in October through December are among the most spectacular berry displays of any landscape holly — birds consume the berries through winter. Emily Bruner is excellent as a specimen tree, screening plant, or large accent in mixed shrub borders. The outstanding year-round appearance and heavy berry production make it one of the finest alternatives to American holly for large-scale landscape use in zone 9.

common_name: Emily McKenzie Crocosmia (Orange-Red Bicolor with Dark Throat)
