plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Emily McKenzie is a classic older crocosmia cultivar producing burnt-orange flowers each marked with a bold, dark mahogany-red blotch at the base of each petal, a distinctive bicolor eye pattern unlike the solid-color flowers of many other crocosmia cultivars, held on arching sprays above bold, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer. The tubular flowers are a strong draw for hummingbirds and also make good, long-lasting cut flowers. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time; mulch over the corms for winter protection in the colder part of its range.

common_name: Emory Paul Dahlia (Giant Orchid-Lavender Dinnerplate Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep after soil has warmed; set a sturdy stake or cage at planting time to support the heavy flower heads.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep after soil has warmed, setting a sturdy stake or cage at planting time to support the heavy flower heads. One of the largest-flowered dinnerplate dahlias grown, Emory Paul produces full, formal double blooms in orchid-lavender to fuchsia-pink that can reach 10–14 inches across under good culture. Like other giant dinnerplate types it blooms from midsummer to first frost and performs best with consistent moisture and monthly feeding. Dig and store tubers after frost in all but the mildest climates.

plant_note: Scarify the hard seed coat lightly and direct sow into lean, well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Emory's globemallow blooms opportunistically after rain and can flower nearly year-round in mild desert winters.
directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; Emory's globemallow is an upright, gray-felted Sonoran Desert native with soft, velvety, three-lobed leaves and abundant, cup-shaped, orange to salmon flowers arranged in loose spikes that appear opportunistically after rain, sometimes flowering multiple times a year in response to seasonal moisture rather than on a strict calendar. It is a fast-growing, short-lived perennial that self-sows readily in disturbed, sunny, well-drained soil, quickly recolonizing bare ground after fire or grading and providing a reliable, low-water source of color and pollinator forage. Fine hairs covering the foliage can be mildly irritating to skin and eyes for sensitive individuals, so handle with care when pruning or clearing spent growth. Cut plants back hard after a bloom flush fades to encourage fresh growth and renewed flowering with the next rain event.

common_name: Emperor I Japanese Maple (Late-Leafing Frost-Resistant Red Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Emperor I leafs out later in spring than most red Japanese maple cultivars, avoiding damage from late frosts.
directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Emperor I holds deep reddish-purple foliage color through the growing season better than many older red Japanese maple cultivars, and its notably late spring leaf-out — about two weeks behind most red-leaf cultivars — protects the new growth from the late frosts that can damage earlier-leafing maples. Its upright, well-branched form makes it a strong choice for a small specimen tree in a partly shaded border or as an accent near a patio, and its heat tolerance has made it a popular choice for warmer zones where some red Japanese maples scorch. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Emperor of China Chrysanthemum (Fully Double Silvery-Pink Quilled Petals)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Emperor of China is a fully double, silvery-pink, quilled-petal heirloom chrysanthemum on a tall 3-4 foot plant.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil. Emperor of China, a long-cultivated heirloom, bears fully double flowers with narrow, quilled, silvery-pink petals on a tall, vigorous plant that also produces attractive bronze-red fall foliage color, a distinctive dual-season interest rare among garden mums. Pinch stem tips in spring and early summer to promote bushy, compact growth, since unpinched plants tend toward tall, floppy stems. Divide clumps every two to three years to prevent crowding and maintain vigor.

common_name: Empire Kousa Dogwood (Compact Upright Rutgers Kousa Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Empire is a Rutgers-bred kousa dogwood with a compact, upright habit and reliably heavy flowering.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Empire, bred at Rutgers University, grows in a compact, upright form narrower than the species, making it a good fit for smaller landscapes or where space is limited, while still producing a heavy, reliable early-summer display of white bracts. Its tidy habit requires less pruning to maintain a neat form than more spreading kousa dogwood cultivars. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade; Empress is noted for producing the largest flowers of any common toad lily cultivar, on an upright clump well suited to a shaded border's mid-height layer.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade; Empress bears extra-large, wide-opening, spidery flowers up to an inch and a half across, white with deep purple-red spotting, noticeably larger than most other toad lily cultivars and striking enough to draw close inspection. It flowers in late summer into fall on an upright, thirty-inch clump, providing fresh color in the shade garden as most other perennials are winding down. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native woodland floor conditions, and divide congested clumps in spring if flowering begins to decline. Combine with hostas, ferns, and other fall-interest shade perennials for a layered woodland display.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, very humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; Empress Wu is the largest known hosta and requires enormous spacing — allow 6–7 feet in each direction — taking 5+ years to reach full impressive size.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, very humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade; Empress Wu holds the distinction of being the largest named hosta cultivar in existence, with individual leaves measuring up to 18 inches long by 15 inches wide on petioles that themselves can reach 24 inches — the overall plant forms a magnificent mound 3–4 feet tall and 5–7 feet wide after 5+ years of establishment. The large, dark olive-green, heavily textured, deeply veined leaves are outstanding. Pale lavender flowers are produced on tall scapes in midsummer. This hosta is a commitment — it requires years of patience before reaching its full potential — but the result is arguably the most impressive deciduous perennial a shade garden can display. Consistent moisture, deep organic mulch, and protection from afternoon heat in zone 7–8 are essential; in zone 9 it is marginal and benefits from cooling in the hottest months. Empress Wu does not divide easily for several years after planting.

common_name: Empress of India Nasturtium (Dark Red Blue-Green Foliage Nasturtium)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Empress of India is a classic heirloom nasturtium prized for deep crimson-red flowers held above distinctive blue-green foliage, a striking color combination unlike the more common orange-flowered, green-leaved types.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of flowers. Empress of India is a beloved heirloom nasturtium dating to the Victorian era, valued for its striking combination of deep, velvety crimson-red flowers set against distinctive blue-green, rounded leaves, a more refined and dramatic look than the typical bright orange-and-green nasturtium. Both the peppery flowers and leaves are edible, adding a colorful, spicy accent to salads, and the compact, mounding habit suits containers, edging, and small garden spaces. It blooms continuously through the growing season with essentially no care beyond occasional watering during dry spells, and self-seeds readily if seed pods are left to mature.

common_name: Enchantment Lily (Classic Upright Orange-Red Spotted Asiatic Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Enchantment, introduced in the 1940s, remains one of the most widely planted Asiatic lily cultivars ever released.
directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, keeping the base of the plant shaded with mulch or companion plants. Introduced in the mid-20th century, Enchantment bears upright, unscented, bright orange-red blooms heavily spotted with maroon toward the throat, and its ease of growth, vigorous multiplying habit, and reliable early-summer bloom made it one of the best-selling lily cultivars of all time, still widely grown today. Its sturdy, upright flower form needs no staking under normal conditions. Leave the foliage in place after bloom until it yellows naturally, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers.

common_name: Encore Autumn Amethyst Azalea (Reblooming Purple-Lavender Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Autumn Amethyst is a compact, mounding Encore variety well suited to foundation plantings, mixed borders, and large containers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4-6 hours of direct sun for the strongest rebloom; Encore Autumn Amethyst produces semi-double, rich purple-lavender flowers in a heavy spring flush and then again in smaller bursts through summer and fall. The compact, dense, mounding habit fits neatly into foundation plantings and smaller garden beds without the need for frequent pruning. As with other Encore azaleas, more direct sun than traditional spring-only azaleas need is required for dependable fall rebloom, so avoid deep, all-day shade. Water deeply during dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer after the spring bloom flush to support the later rebloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Belle Azalea (Reblooming Soft Pink Orchid-Form Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom. Autumn Belle bears soft, orchid-pink flowers with an unusually narrow, twisted petal form that gives each bloom a delicate, spidery appearance distinct from the broader, more rounded flowers of most other Encore azaleas, in a heavy spring flush with recurring bloom in summer and fall. Its compact habit suits foundation plantings, borders, and containers where a smaller-scale reblooming azalea is wanted. Like all Encore azaleas, it needs more direct sun than traditional azaleas for dependable fall rebloom. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush to support subsequent bloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Bonfire Azalea (Compact Reblooming Red-Orange Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Autumn Bonfire is one of the more compact Encore varieties, well suited to small beds, foundation plantings, and containers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4-6 hours of direct sun for the most reliable rebloom. Encore Autumn Bonfire is a compact, dense reblooming azalea bearing vivid red-orange flowers in a heavy spring flush and then intermittently again through summer and fall, giving three seasons of color from one small shrub. Its tight, mounding habit keeps it well proportioned for foundation plantings, small courtyard gardens, and large containers without regular pruning. Like other Encore azaleas it needs more direct sun than traditional spring-only azaleas to rebloom well, so avoid deep shade sites. Keep the shallow root zone consistently moist with mulch, and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer after the spring bloom flush to support later flowering.

common_name: Encore Autumn Bravo Azalea (Reblooming White Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Autumn Bravo is one of the few pure white reblooming azaleas, making it valuable for formal gardens, white-themed borders, and mixed plantings where strong colors are used and a white accent is needed.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Bravo is the standard white-flowered Encore azalea cultivar — producing pure white, semi-double flowers with a light touch of pink at the petal edges in spring and again in substantial summer and fall bloom flushes. White-flowered reblooming azaleas are less common than pink, red, and purple reblooming selections, making Autumn Bravo particularly valuable for garden designs that require a white azalea with the extended bloom season of the Encore series. The pure white flowers provide maximum contrast with deep green foliage and make outstanding companions for dark-purple or deep-red flowering companions like Autumn Royalty or Autumn Fire. Autumn Bravo grows as a compact, well-rounded shrub to 2.5–3.5 feet tall and wide, suitable for mixed shrub borders, foundation plantings, and large containers. It shows the Encore series' characteristic requirement for more sun than traditional azaleas — at least 4 hours of direct sun is necessary to achieve reliable summer and fall rebloom. In deep shade, spring bloom may be adequate but fall rebloom will be sparse. The semi-evergreen foliage holds well through zone 9 winters.

common_name: Encore Autumn Carnation Azalea (Reblooming Ruffled Double Pink Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom. Autumn Carnation produces full, ruffled, double pink flowers whose densely layered petals resemble a carnation bloom, a fuller, more elaborate flower form than the single or semi-double flowers of many other azaleas, opening in a heavy spring flush with recurring bloom in summer and fall. Its showy, frilly flowers make it a strong specimen or accent plant in a mixed shrub border. Like all Encore azaleas, it needs more direct sun than traditional azaleas for dependable fall rebloom. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush to support subsequent bloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Chiffon Azalea (Reblooming Light-Pink Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Autumn Chiffon is one of the most compact Encore varieties and is excellent for smaller planting spaces and container use.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Chiffon is a refined, compact reblooming azalea producing medium-sized, single, very light pink to blush-pink flowers in spring and again in summer and fall — the palest and most delicate flower color in the common Encore azalea lineup, with petals so light they appear nearly white in bright sun. The softly colored flowers create a particularly elegant effect in combination with deep green foliage and make Autumn Chiffon one of the most useful Encore selections for sophisticated color schemes where pastel blends are desired. The compact habit stays 2–3 feet tall and wide, fitting neatly into smaller foundation plantings, mixed shrub borders, and large containers. Like all Encore azaleas, it requires more direct sun than traditional azaleas for reliable fall rebloom — a minimum of 4 hours and ideally 5–6 hours of daily direct sun produces the best fall bloom quality. The semi-evergreen foliage holds through zone 9 winters with minimal damage. Fertilize with an azalea-specific acidic fertilizer immediately after the spring bloom to support subsequent reblooming.

common_name: Encore Autumn Coral Azalea (Reblooming Large Coral-Pink Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom. Autumn Coral produces large, semi-double flowers in a bright coral-pink on a vigorous, larger-growing shrub than many other Encore selections, opening in a heavy spring flush with recurring bloom in summer and fall. Its bold flower size and saturated coral color make it a strong focal point in a mixed shrub border or foundation planting where a larger reblooming azalea fits the space. Like all Encore azaleas, it needs more direct sun than traditional azaleas for dependable fall rebloom. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush to support subsequent bloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Debutante Azalea (Reblooming Orchid-Pink Double Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom. Autumn Debutante was one of the original Encore azalea introductions, producing full, double, orchid-pink flowers in a heavy spring flush with recurring bloom in summer and fall — a soft, romantic color and ruffled double form that has made it one of the most enduringly popular cultivars in the Encore line since its release. Its compact, rounded habit suits foundation plantings, borders, and large containers. Like all Encore azaleas, it needs more direct sun than traditional azaleas for dependable fall rebloom. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush to support subsequent bloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Fire Azalea (Reblooming Red Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Autumn Fire is a compact Encore variety well-suited to smaller spaces, foundation plantings, and containers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom; Encore Autumn Fire is a compact reblooming azalea producing vivid, clear red single flowers in spring and again in summer and fall — one of the few dependably red reblooming azaleas available, as red pigmentation in azaleas can be difficult to achieve with good rebloom habit. The flowers are produced prolifically in spring and recur reliably in summer and fall flushes, making Autumn Fire a standout accent plant for three-season color. The compact habit (24–36 inches tall and wide) fits it well for foundation plantings, borders, and mixed shrub beds where the larger-growing traditional azaleas would overgrow the space. Like all Encore azaleas, it requires more sun than traditional azaleas for reliable fall rebloom — plant where it receives at least half a day of direct sun. The compact size also makes it suitable for large containers. In zone 9 the semi-evergreen foliage typically holds well through winter. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring bloom flush to support subsequent rebloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Ivory Azalea (Reblooming White Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom. Autumn Ivory produces clean, pure white, single to semi-double flowers in a heavy spring flush with recurring bloom in summer and fall, one of the few dependably white-flowered cultivars in the reblooming Encore line. Its crisp white color makes it a versatile companion for the many pink-, red-, and purple-flowered Encore selections, brightening shaded borders and pairing well with darker-foliaged shrubs. Like all Encore azaleas, it needs more direct sun than traditional azaleas for dependable fall rebloom. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush to support subsequent bloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Monarch Azalea (Reblooming Lavender-Pink Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade (4–6 hours of sun is ideal for rebloom — more sun than traditional azaleas require); Autumn Monarch is one of the larger-growing Encore varieties and benefits from 4–6 hours of direct morning sun to produce the best fall bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Monarch is one of the leading cultivars in the revolutionary Encore Azalea series — a breakthrough group of reblooming landscape azaleas that bloom in spring AND again in summer and fall, dramatically extending azalea interest beyond the traditional single spring flush. Autumn Monarch produces large (2.5–3-inch), semi-double, lavender-pink flowers in a spring bloom followed by repeated summer and fall flushes that persist until frost. The Encore series was developed by plant breeder Robert E. Lee (Plant Development Services) over 15 years by crossing traditional azaleas with the naturally reblooming Rhododendron oldhamii from Taiwan. Encore varieties require more sun than traditional azaleas — 4–6 hours of direct sun daily maximizes fall rebloom; in deep shade the spring bloom may be adequate but fall rebloom is sparse. Autumn Monarch is one of the larger Encore cultivars, reaching 3.5–5 feet. Fertilize immediately after spring bloom with an azalea-specific acidic fertilizer to support fall rebloom.

common_name: Encore Autumn Moonlight Azalea (Reblooming White Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4-6 hours of direct sun; like other Encore varieties, Autumn Moonlight needs more direct light than traditional spring-only azaleas to rebloom dependably in summer and fall.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with several hours of direct sun for the strongest rebloom; Encore Autumn Moonlight bears large, single, pure white flowers with a soft chartreuse-yellow blotch in the throat, opening in a heavy spring flush and then again in lighter bursts through summer and into fall. Its bright white bloom reads especially well in shaded or evening gardens, where it lights up the understory against darker-leaved companions. As with other Encore azaleas, avoid deep, all-day shade, since inadequate light reduces the summer and fall rebloom cycles that distinguish this series from traditional once-blooming azaleas. Water deeply during dry spells, mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and moist, and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer after the spring flush to support later reblooming.

common_name: Encore Autumn Princess Azalea (Reblooming Pink-and-White Bicolor Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom. Autumn Princess bears large, semi-double flowers in soft pink edged with a thin band of white, a delicate bicolor pattern that gives each bloom a hand-painted look, opening in a heavy spring flush with recurring bloom in summer and fall. Its refined, layered flower color makes it a standout among the Encore line's many solid-colored cultivars. Like all Encore azaleas, it needs more direct sun than traditional azaleas for dependable fall rebloom. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush to support subsequent bloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Royalty Azalea (Reblooming Purple Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Autumn Royalty is widely considered one of the best-performing Encore azaleas for rebloom quantity and flower color intensity.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Royalty is one of the most popular and widely recommended Encore azalea cultivars — a medium-sized reblooming shrub producing large (2.5–3-inch), bright purple to violet-purple single flowers in spring with reliable and abundant rebloom through summer and fall. The purple-violet flower color is distinctive and unusual among commonly available landscape azaleas, which tend toward pink, red, and white; Autumn Royalty fills an important color range in the landscape palette. It is widely regarded as one of the strongest reblooming Encore varieties, producing substantial fall flushes when given adequate sun. The medium, upright-rounded habit reaches 3–4 feet and fits foundation plantings and mixed borders without overwhelming adjacent plants. Like all Encore azaleas, performance in fall bloom is directly linked to sun exposure — plants receiving less than 4 hours of direct sun may bloom adequately in spring but produce sparse fall color. Amend planting area with pine bark and acidifying fertilizer to maintain the required pH 4.5–6.0 range, especially in alkaline Gulf Coast soils.

common_name: Encore Autumn Sangria Azalea (Reblooming Bicolor Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Autumn Sangria is a vigorous-growing Encore variety that may need occasional pruning immediately after the spring bloom to maintain a tidy size.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Sangria is a distinctive reblooming azalea with flowers in a beautiful, wine-rose to deep rosy-pink color with a lighter center — a rich, saturated color with the warmth of burgundy and the brightness of pink combined in a tone reminiscent of the wine it is named for. This vibrant color is more intense and warm-toned than the cooler lilac-purple of Autumn Royalty or the clear red of Autumn Fire, making it a good companion for rose, salmon, and warm-toned plantings. Autumn Sangria is a medium-large Encore selection, growing 3–4 feet tall and wide with vigorous habit. The spring bloom is particularly heavy, followed by reliable summer and fall rebloom flushes when given adequate sun. In zone 9, Autumn Sangria typically begins its spring bloom in mid-March and continues in flushes through November. The semi-evergreen foliage is attractive and holds well through zone 9 winters. Apply a layer of pine bark mulch 2–3 inches deep to protect the shallow root system from temperature extremes and moisture loss during summer heat.

common_name: Encore Autumn Sunburst Azalea (Reblooming Coral-Pink Semi-Dwarf Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom; a compact selection well-suited to smaller spaces and containers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom. Autumn Sunburst is a semi-dwarf Encore azalea producing bright coral-pink flowers with a ruffled edge in a heavy spring flush and recurring bloom in summer and fall, on a smaller-growing plant than many other Encore selections. Its compact size fits foundation plantings, small borders, and large containers where full-size azaleas would eventually crowd the space. Like all Encore azaleas, it needs more direct sun than traditional azaleas for dependable fall rebloom. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush to support subsequent bloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Sunset Azalea (Reblooming Orange-Red Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun for reliable rebloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom. Autumn Sunset bears warm orange-red flowers with a coral cast, a fiery color that stands apart from the pinks, purples, and whites more common among Encore azaleas, in a heavy spring flush with recurring bloom in summer and fall. Its warm-toned flowers pair well with yellow- and gold-foliaged companion shrubs and add a distinct color note to a mixed azalea planting. Like all Encore azaleas, it needs more direct sun than traditional azaleas for dependable fall rebloom. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring flush to support subsequent bloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Twist Azalea (Reblooming Pink-and-White Bicolor Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Autumn Twist is grown for its striped, bicolor blooms and benefits from the same sun exposure other Encore azaleas need to rebloom well.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4-6 hours of direct sun to support strong repeat bloom. Encore Autumn Twist is notable among reblooming azaleas for its striped, swirled pink-and-white flowers, with individual blossoms and even individual plants varying in the exact pattern and proportion of color, giving each shrub an informal, painterly look in the landscape. It flowers heavily in spring and produces smaller rebloom flushes through summer and into fall, provided it gets enough direct sun. Water deeply during dry periods, keep a layer of mulch over the shallow, fibrous root system, and feed with an acid-forming fertilizer after the spring bloom to encourage continued flowering later in the season.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Encore azaleas rebloom in summer and fall in addition to their main spring flush, unlike most traditional azaleas that flower only once.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, protecting plants from harsh afternoon sun in the hottest part of zone 9 summers. The Encore breeding series, developed in Louisiana beginning in the 1990s, was a breakthrough because it combined the classic look of Southern azaleas with genuine repeat blooming, flowering not just in the traditional spring flush but again in summer and often into fall, greatly extending the color season of a plant long associated with a single brief burst of spring bloom. Dozens of named Encore cultivars are now available across a wide range of flower colors and mature sizes, all sharing the reblooming trait and reasonably good heat tolerance for the Gulf South. Water deeply during dry spells, especially heading into the summer and fall bloom flushes, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom to shape without removing the buds that will produce later color.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in rich, moist soil with afternoon shade.
directions: Endless Summer is a reblooming bigleaf hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, producing large mophead blooms from spring through fall. Plant it in morning sun with afternoon shade in rich, consistently moist soil, and mulch to keep roots cool. Flower color shifts with soil chemistry: acidic soil yields blue blooms while alkaline soil produces pink, so amend accordingly. Because it blooms on new growth too, light pruning is forgiving, though it rebounds best with minimal cutting. Keep it well watered, as wilting in heat is common.

plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun; EnduraScape was bred specifically for improved resistance to powdery mildew, the disease that most commonly ends the season early for older verbena cultivars in humid Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, and avoid overhead watering where possible, since good air circulation further reduces the already-low mildew risk on this series. EnduraScape is a landscape verbena series bred for outstanding heat and humidity tolerance combined with strong resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that commonly disfigures and shortens the bloom season of older verbena cultivars in the hot, humid Gulf South. It forms a dense, fast-spreading, low mat covered in clusters of small flowers continuously from spring through frost, holding up to summer heat with minimal fading or dieback compared to less disease-resistant verbena types. Its vigorous, weed-suppressing spread and low-maintenance disease resistance make it well suited to mass plantings, slopes, and hot, sunny beds where reliable, long-season color is the priority.

common_name: Enduring Summer Crapemyrtle (True Dwarf Reblooming Disease-Resistant Series)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Enduring Summer is a true dwarf crapemyrtle series, staying only 4-5 feet tall, bred with leaf-spot and powdery mildew resistance and a strong reblooming habit for a small Gulf Coast bed or container.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Enduring Summer is a true dwarf crapemyrtle series that stays a compact 4-5 feet tall, far smaller than the tree-form crapemyrtles that dominate most Gulf South landscapes, making it a good fit for small beds, foundation plantings, or large containers. It is bred with resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew and reblooms steadily through summer, especially if spent flower clusters are removed. Like other modern crapemyrtle introductions, it should be pruned lightly to remove only dead or crossing wood rather than subjected to the severe topping sometimes called 'crape murder,' which sacrifices natural form and delays bloom.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist to average, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Engelmann spruce grows naturally at high elevations (6,000–12,000 feet) in the Rocky Mountains and requires cool, moist conditions — it does not tolerate heat, drought, or alkaline soils well.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist to average, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Engelmann spruce is the dominant conifer of the subalpine Rocky Mountain forests — the tree that defines the timberline forest from Colorado to British Columbia, often co-occurring with subalpine fir (Abies lasiocarpa) in the classic subalpine parkland just below treeline. The blue-gray to dark blue-green needles are sharp (typical of all spruces) and the crown is narrowly conical with pendulous lower branches. Engelmann spruce wood is valued as a tonewood for acoustic guitar tops, violin tops, and piano soundboards — the finest-grained specimens produce some of the best tonewood available. More cold-tolerant than Colorado blue spruce but generally less drought-tolerant. Best in cool, high-elevation or northern garden sites in zones 2–6 where the cool, moist conditions of its natural habitat can be approximated.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall so winter cold moist-stratifies the seed naturally, into well-drained, dry to average, limestone-based or clay-loam soil in full sun; Engelmann's daisy is a deep-taprooted Great Plains prairie native adapted to heavy soils and periodic drought.
directions: Direct sow in fall into well-drained clay-loam or limestone soil in full sun, allowing winter cold to break seed dormancy naturally; a deep, thick taproot makes established plants extremely drought tolerant but hard to transplant, so site it where it can stay long term. Coarse, deeply lobed, rough-textured basal leaves send up branching flower stalks topped with cheerful yellow daisy-like blooms from spring through early summer, and again after fall rains, that are heavily visited by native bees and small butterflies. Foliage dies back somewhat in peak summer heat and regrows with cooler fall weather, so avoid judging plants on midsummer appearance alone. A true low-input, tough tallgrass and shortgrass prairie perennial, it is an excellent choice for naturalistic prairie restorations, pollinator meadows, and dry, unirrigated beds across the southern Great Plains.

plant_note: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Engelmann's hedgehog cactus needs sharp drainage and thrives in desert heat once established.
directions: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Engelmann's hedgehog cactus needs sharp drainage and thrives in desert heat once established. Clustering, cylindrical stems densely armed with long, colorful spines in shades of tan, gray, and reddish-brown eventually form substantial multi-stemmed mounds, bursting into a spectacular flush of large, vivid magenta-pink flowers each spring that rank among the showiest blooms of any Southwest desert cactus. Native to the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts, it is a familiar sight in rocky washes and desert flats across the Southwest, forming impressive colonies over many decades of slow growth. Water only occasionally once established, provide full sun and sharp drainage, and be patient, since this long-lived species grows slowly but rewards years of minimal care with an increasingly spectacular spring flower display.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline limestone-based soil in full sun; Engelmann's sage is endemic to the limestone hills of the Edwards Plateau in central Texas and naturally adapted to alkaline, rocky, shallow soils with excellent drainage. It performs poorly in heavy, moist, or acidic soils.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Engelmann's sage is a rare, endemic Texas Hill Country salvia found naturally only on the limestone hills and canyons of the Edwards Plateau in central Texas. It produces dense spikes of vivid violet-blue to blue-purple flowers with white markings from spring through fall, blooming particularly heavily after rains — a characteristic adaptation to seasonal rainfall patterns. The plant forms a compact, drought-hardy subshrub with small, gray-green, aromatic, woolly-textured leaves that are pleasant-scented when brushed. More compact and refined in habit than many salvias and exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established in well-drained soil. It is not widely known outside Texas native plant circles but is an outstanding, drought-tolerant perennial for zone 7–10 gardens with alkaline soil — a category that includes much of the Texas Hill Country, where it can be grown as a true perennial.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; this selection has smaller, finer leaves than typical Virginia creeper and clings tightly to masonry and wood.
directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; this selection has smaller, finer leaves than typical Virginia creeper and clings tightly to masonry and wood. A finer-textured, smaller-leaved selection of the native Virginia creeper, it clings tightly to brick, stone, and wood surfaces with adhesive tendril discs, covering walls and structures densely with palmate, five-lobed leaves that turn a brilliant scarlet-red in fall, one of the showiest native fall foliage displays of any vine. Extremely tough and adaptable, tolerating poor soil, drought, shade, and urban pollution, it provides valuable dark blue berries for birds in fall and is a larval host plant for several native moth species. Prune as needed to keep growth away from windows, gutters, and shingles, since the adhesive tendrils can damage some building surfaces and are difficult to remove once attached.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees; English bluebells naturalize readily over years to form dense, sweeping drifts and should be planted where the foliage can die back undisturbed through spring.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees; English bluebells are the iconic spring flower of British woodlands, producing drooping, one-sided racemes of deeply fragrant, nodding, narrow-petaled, violet-blue bell-shaped flowers on arching stems in mid-spring that form breathtaking sweeping drifts when naturalized under a deciduous canopy. They reliably self-seed and naturalize to create ever-expanding colonies that need no routine care. The foliage dies back by midsummer. Note: do not confuse with the Spanish bluebell (H. hispanica) which is more robust, upright, and less fragrant — Spanish bluebells hybridize with English bluebells and the hybrid is outcompeting the native in the UK. True H. non-scripta droops distinctly to one side and has a sweet, distinctive fragrance.

common_name: English Edging Boxwood (True Dwarf Boxwood, Dwarf English Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade; Suffruticosa is highly susceptible to boxwood blight — do not plant near existing boxwood plantings where blight has been detected, and avoid planting in humid, poorly drained locations that favor disease.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade with some direct sun; Suffruticosa is the true dwarf English boxwood — the cultivar used for centuries in European formal knot gardens and low hedges, producing extremely dense, slow-growing, fine-textured, bright-green foliage mounds that clip beautifully into precise geometric forms. The very slow growth (6–9 inches per decade) and naturally tidy, globe-shaped habit make Suffruticosa the traditional edging boxwood for formal herb gardens, parterre gardens, and low border edging — a role it has filled in European gardens since at least the seventeenth century. The sweet, resinous fragrance of the foliage is the quintessential boxwood scent, associated with formal gardens throughout the Western garden tradition. However, Suffruticosa is highly susceptible to boxwood blight, the devastating fungal disease (Calonectria pseudonaviculata) that has been spreading across the Eastern United States since 2011 and can kill entire boxwood plantings within a season. For new plantings in areas where boxwood blight is present, disease-resistant Korean boxwood cultivars (Winter Gem, Green Velvet, Green Mountain) are strongly recommended over English boxwood. Where boxwood blight is not a current concern, Suffruticosa remains an outstanding traditional garden plant requiring precise siting in well-drained, aerated soil with good air circulation.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; English holly tolerates deep shade for foliage growth but sets its heaviest crop of berries with at least a few hours of direct or bright filtered sun, and requires a male pollinator nearby for female plants to fruit.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to filtered sun; English holly is the classic broadleaf evergreen of Christmas wreaths and greenery, native to western and southern Europe, bearing stiff, glossy, spine-edged dark green leaves and, on pollinated female plants, abundant bright red berries that persist through winter and feed thrushes, waxwings, and other birds when little else is available. It is dioecious, so a male cultivar such as 'Blue Prince' or 'J.C. van Tol' (a self-fertile selection) must be planted within pollinator range of a female such as 'Blue Princess' or 'Argentea Marginata' for reliable fruit set. As a large, pyramidal shrub or small tree it makes an outstanding dense screen, windbreak, or specimen for shaded woodland-edge gardens, and it withstands shearing well if a more formal hedge is wanted. In the Pacific Northwest, English holly has escaped cultivation and is classified as an invasive species in forest understories, so gardeners in that region should choose non-invasive native or sterile cultivars instead, or deadhead berries before birds can disperse the seed.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container transplants in fall in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; English ivy is widely adaptable but can be invasive outside cultivated areas — do not plant near forests, natural areas, or unmanaged land. In zone 9a it may struggle in summer heat and drought.
directions: Plant cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; English ivy is the classic, most widely used shade groundcover in temperate gardens — the glossy, lobed, evergreen leaves in many different sizes and variegations (solid green, silver-variegated, gold-variegated, small-leaved, large-leaved) create a dense, weed-suppressing carpet under trees. It climbs structures by aerial rootlets and has been used for centuries to cover buildings, walls, and slopes. However, English ivy is invasive in many parts of the United States east of the Rockies, smothering native understory plants and climbing trees — where naturalized, it can eventually kill large trees by girdling. Plant only in maintained, contained situations and remove regularly from any areas where it might spread to natural woodland. In zone 9a summer heat and humidity can reduce vigor; the heat-tolerant 'Needlepoint' and small-leaved varieties perform better in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average loamy soil in full sun; English oak is widely adaptable to a range of soil types and is tolerant of clay and somewhat wet conditions, unlike many oaks. Grows more slowly than American red oak but lives for centuries.
directions: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep fertile to average loamy soil in full sun; English oak is the archetypal oak of European culture — the 'royal oak,' the great forest tree of England, the sacred tree of the Celts — producing the classic, deeply lobed oak leaf and small, elongated acorns held on distinctive long stalks (peduncles, giving the alternate common name 'pedunculate oak'). English oak has been planted throughout North America in parks, estates, and arboreta for centuries, developing into magnificent specimens in suitable climates. It is more tolerant of clay soils and seasonal wetness than most American oaks. The acorns are consumed by squirrels, jays, deer, and other wildlife. Many cultivated varieties exist, including the fastigiate (columnar) 'Fastigiata' or 'Skyrocket' forms widely used in street tree plantings. A very long-lived tree — English oaks commonly reach 500–800 years of age, and individual trees are counted among the oldest living things in Europe.

plant_note: Start seeds 12–14 weeks before desired transplant date by pressing them onto the surface of moist mix without covering, then cold-stratifying at 35–40°F for 3–4 weeks before moving to 50–60°F bright light; transplant into partial shade in fall or very early spring.
directions: Start seeds at cool temperatures (50–60°F) in moist seed-starting mix with seeds pressed on the surface; germination requires light and cool stratification, so refrigerate freshly sown trays at 35–40°F for three weeks before moving to a bright, cool location. Transplant into partially shaded, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; primroses bloom prolifically in the cool dappled light under deciduous trees where spring sun reaches before the canopy leafs out. In zone 4–6 they are fully hardy perennials that return reliably each spring; in zone 7–8 treat them as cool-season annuals that perform best from fall through late spring and then go semi-dormant in summer heat. Divide overcrowded clumps in early fall every 2–3 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; English Roseum is a tough, adaptable, cold-hardy rhododendron widely used in commercial and municipal landscaping.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; English Roseum is a tough, adaptable, cold-hardy rhododendron widely used in commercial and municipal landscaping. Full, rounded trusses of clear pink flowers open in late spring above large, glossy, dark evergreen leaves on a dense, vigorous, well-branched shrub valued for its exceptional toughness and adaptability across a wide range of climates and soil conditions. One of the most commonly planted landscape rhododendrons in North America due to its reliability, heat and cold tolerance, and resistance to common rhododendron problems, it is a dependable choice for foundation plantings, mass plantings, and shaded borders where a fussier hybrid might struggle. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

plant_note: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting in late summer and set established transplants into the garden in fall for spring bloom; wallflowers are biennials that overwinter as leafy rosettes and bloom profusely in mid-spring. In zone 8–10 a fall-planted transplant may bloom the same winter-spring season.
directions: Start seeds in late summer in well-drained seed mix and set transplants into the garden in fall in full sun in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil; wallflowers overwinter as leafy rosettes and burst into bloom in mid-spring with intensely fragrant four-petaled flowers in gold, orange, crimson, cream, and burgundy — one of the richest scents in the spring garden. Excellent drainage is non-negotiable; they rot quickly in wet, heavy soils. In zone 8–10 they can behave as short-lived perennials or nearly year-round bloomers in cool seasons. Pull plants after flowering and replace with summer annuals, or allow them to self-seed; volunteer seedlings will often appear but may not come true to the parent cultivar's color.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; English yew is one of the very few conifers that thrives in deep shade and tolerates heavy pruning for hedging or topiary. All parts except the fleshy red aril contain toxic taxine alkaloids and must be kept away from children and livestock.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; English yew is a long-lived, slow-growing evergreen conifer native to Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, prized in cultivation for dense, dark-green, needled foliage that holds its color and density in deep shade where almost no other conifer will grow. Left unpruned it slowly develops into a broad, spreading small tree, but it tolerates repeated, severe shearing better than almost any other woody plant and has been the classic subject of formal hedges and topiary in shaded European gardens for centuries. Female plants produce small, bright red, fleshy arils in fall that are the only non-toxic part of the plant — the needles, bark, wood, and seed within the aril all contain taxine alkaloids that are dangerous if ingested by people, pets, or livestock. Established plants are extremely drought- and pollution-tolerant once rooted in and require little care beyond an annual shearing if a formal shape is desired.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, or start indoors a few weeks early, spacing plants about a foot apart. This unusual heirloom bears 3-4 inch chartreuse-green edible blooms that are striking in the garden and on the plate. Heat-loving and productive, it flowers endlessly until frost when regularly cut and deadheaded. Water at the base and space for airflow to reduce powdery mildew.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in any well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; once established, epimedium is remarkably drought tolerant and can thrive in the dry root zone under large trees.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; epimedium is among the most valuable groundcovers for difficult dry shade — one of the few plants that genuinely thrives in the dry, root-filled zone under mature maples, beeches, and other large shade trees where almost nothing else survives. The heart-shaped, often evergreen or semi-evergreen leaves are attractive year-round, turn bronze in winter, and the small but intricate crimson and pink bicolored flowers in early spring are delightful at close range before most shade perennials emerge. It spreads slowly but persistently by rhizome to form a dense, tidy, weed-suppressing mat. Shear back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge. The genus contains dozens of outstanding species and cultivars; E. × rubrum is one of the most widely available and adaptable.

common_name: Erebus Longwood Water Canna (True Aquatic Coral-Pink Submerged-Culture Canna)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after last frost; Erebus, bred at Longwood Gardens specifically for true aquatic, submerged culture, bears coral-pink flowers over blue-green striped foliage.
directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun, once all frost danger has passed. Erebus is one of a small group of true aquatic water cannas bred at Longwood Gardens specifically to thrive with their crowns and lower stems submerged, unlike ordinary garden canna, which will rot if kept constantly wet at the root. It bears clear coral-pink flowers above handsome, blue-green foliage marked with subtle striping, adding bold tropical texture and color to the pond margin through the warm season. In zones below its perennial range, lift and store the rhizome indoors over winter like standard canna. Divide congested clumps in spring as new growth begins.

plant_note: Let a harvested pad callus for a week in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end an inch into very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in late spring; erect pricklypear tolerates salt spray and sandy coastal soil better than most garden plants.
directions: Plant a callused pad in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; erect pricklypear is a taller, more upright-growing native pricklypear of Gulf and Atlantic coastal dunes and sandy scrub, forming a shrubby, multi-jointed clump 2 to 4 feet high. Bright yellow, sometimes red-throated flowers open in late spring and early summer, followed by reddish-purple, edible fruit (tunas) enjoyed fresh, juiced, or made into jelly once the glochids are carefully removed or burned off. It handles salt spray, sandy soil, and coastal wind better than almost any other flowering succulent, making it valuable for beachfront xeriscape and dune stabilization plantings. Handle pads and fruit with heavy gloves and tongs to avoid the fine, easily embedded glochids, and site it away from foot traffic areas.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Erlicheer is a fully double tazetta daffodil with a low chilling requirement, making it one of the few double-flowered narcissus that reliably rebloom and naturalize in mild Gulf South winters instead of blind out after a year or two.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Erlicheer is a fragrant, fully double tazetta daffodil bearing clusters of creamy white, ruffled blooms flecked with pale yellow, closer in form to a small gardenia than a typical trumpet daffodil. Most double daffodils need more winter chill than the Deep South provides and gradually decline into blind, non-flowering foliage after a season or two, but Erlicheer's tazetta parentage gives it the same low chilling requirement as Grand Primo and paperwhites, letting it rebloom and slowly naturalize where fancier doubles fail. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom rather than cutting or braiding it, and leave clumps undisturbed to bulk up for a few years before dividing.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ermine canna's compact size suits it to container culture and smaller borders where full-sized cannas would overwhelm the space.
directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ermine canna's compact size suits it to container culture and smaller borders where full-sized cannas would overwhelm the space. A long-cultivated dwarf canna selection, it produces clean, fresh green foliage and clusters of creamy white flowers held well above the leaves from summer through fall, offering a softer, more subtle color option than the bright reds, oranges, and yellows typical of most cannas. Its compact habit makes it a good choice for the middle of a mixed border, a large container, or the edge of a pond planting where taller cannas would need to be set further back. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring, and mulch heavily or lift rhizomes for winter storage outside zones 8-11.

plant_note: Plant in spring with the crown set a couple of inches below the soil surface and the base shaded, giving the vine a sturdy fence, pergola, or large shrub to climb into full sun.
directions: Plant with the roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs a trellis, arbor, or fence in full sun, watering regularly during dry spells to keep flowering strong. This long-blooming, vigorous cultivar produces large, glowing magenta-red flowers with contrasting golden anthers from midsummer through early fall, one of the most reliable and free-flowering of the older large-flowered hybrids. Because it blooms on both old and new wood, it only needs light shaping in late winter rather than a hard cutback, so leave the framework mostly intact when pruning. Its strong constitution and heat tolerance make it a dependable choice for covering fences and arbors quickly.

common_name: Escarboucle Water Lily (Classic Marliac Crimson-Red Hardy Water Lily)
plant_note: Set the rhizome horizontally in a wide planting basket of heavy garden soil capped with gravel, then lower the container so the crown rests 12 to 24 inches beneath the water surface in full sun.
directions: Anchor the rhizome in a wide aquatic basket of heavy loam topped with gravel, then submerge the container so the crown sits one to two feet below the surface in full sun. This vigorous, century-old French hybrid from the Latour-Marliac nursery produces large, brilliant crimson-red flowers with prominent golden stamens that stay open even in partly shaded or cooler water where many other lilies close early. Bloom runs from early summer into fall, and the dark green pads spread generously, so it suits medium to large ponds better than small container water gardens. It is widely regarded as one of the most reliable and free-flowering red hardy water lilies available.

plant_note: Plant in shallow, very well-drained, peat-based, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect shade; rex begonias have shallow root systems and perform best in wide, shallow containers rather than deep pots.
directions: Plant in shallow, very well-drained, peat-based soil in bright indirect shade, keeping the soil evenly moist but never soggy, since the rhizome rots quickly in wet conditions. Escargot is one of the most recognizable rex begonia cultivars, its rounded leaves marked with a bold, concentric silver-and-green spiral radiating from a dark center in a pattern that closely resembles a snail's shell, giving the plant its name. Like other rex begonias, it is grown almost entirely for its dramatic foliage rather than its small, inconspicuous flowers, and makes an outstanding container specimen for shaded porches and patios where the spiral pattern can be appreciated up close. Divide congested rhizomes in spring, or root individual leaf cuttings in moist peat to propagate new plants.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March–May. Escargot performs best as a container plant that can be moved indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F — maintaining it as an indoor-outdoor plant allows the spiral foliage to be appreciated year-round. Rex begonias prefer high humidity (above 50%), making zone 9's humid summer climate well-suited to outdoor summer use in deep shade. Avoid wetting the leaves — water at the soil level only to prevent powdery mildew and leaf spotting. Do not overwater — allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings.
directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil — Rex begonias are moisture-sensitive in both directions, suffering from both drought and standing water; Escargot is one of the most famous and distinctive Rex begonia cultivars, producing leaves whose silvery-green surface is marked with a dramatic spiral pattern — the leaf base curls around itself in a tight coil before unfurling, creating a permanent snail-shell spiral pattern on each leaf that gives the variety its name. The silver-green leaf surface with darker green spiral accents and red-purple undersides creates a truly extraordinary visual effect unlike any other commonly grown plant. Rex begonias (Begonia rex-cultorum) are cultivated entirely for their extraordinarily varied and complex leaf patterns rather than their flowers — the small, insignificant flowers are typically removed to redirect energy into foliage production. Escargot is considered one of the most architectural and conversation-starting plants in the shade garden precisely because the spiral leaf pattern is so unexpected and perfect that it appears designed rather than grown. In zone 9 it excels as an outdoor container plant for deep shade areas during the warm months, then transitions easily indoors as a houseplant for cooler periods.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season. Espresso bears deep, earthy reddish-brown and maroon blooms, an unusual dark gladiolus color.
directions: Espresso bears deep, unusual reddish-brown to maroon blooms, an earthy, near-chocolate color rare among gladiolus cultivars that are more typically found in bright pinks, reds, and yellows, making it a distinctive choice for moody or autumnal cut-flower arrangements. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

plant_note: Start indoors and set out after frost; surface-sow as light aids germination.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, pressing it onto the surface since light aids germination, and transplant once frost danger passes. This blend produces upright architectural spikes of red, purple, white, and Fleuroselect gold-medal coral that bloom nonstop and draw butterflies and other pollinators. Give it full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil. Deadhead faded spikes to keep the color coming through the season.

common_name: Estella Rijnveld Tulip (Red-and-White Feathered Parrot Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from wind; parrot tulips have fringed, twisted petals that can be damaged by heavy rain or wind.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from strong wind and heavy rain. Estella Rijnveld is one of the most theatrical parrot tulips, its large, deeply ruffled and twisted petals boldly feathered and flamed in vivid red and pure white, giving each bloom the look of a hand-painted flower rather than anything subtle or restrained. It makes a dramatic late-spring statement in the border and an equally striking, long-lasting cut flower. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

common_name: Etoile Rose Clematis (Nodding Cerise-Pink Bell-Form Texas Clematis)
plant_note: Set out in spring with the crown planted a couple of inches deep and the roots shaded, allowing the slender stems to twine up a trellis, obelisk, or fence in full sun; Etoile Rose is a Texensis-type clematis with nodding, semi-double cerise-pink bell flowers.
directions: Grow this Texensis-type clematis on a narrow support such as an obelisk or wire trellis, keeping its roots cool and shaded beneath low plantings. From summer into early autumn it produces nodding, bell-shaped, semi-double flowers in vivid cerise-pink with recurved petal tips, a fuller, more textured bloom than the simple tulip-shaped flowers typical of most Texas clematis hybrids. Because it blooms on new growth, cut the vine back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter to renew vigor. It is more heat- and drought-tolerant than many large-flowered clematis, making it a good choice for warmer gardens.

common_name: Etoile Violette Clematis (Deep Violet-Purple Viticella Clematis)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Etoile Violette is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Etoile Violette produces a profusion of small, deep violet-purple flowers with contrasting yellow-cream stamens over a long midsummer season, on a vigorous vine well suited to scrambling through roses or large shrubs where it adds a long-lasting second wave of color. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter, avoiding the guesswork of pruning old-wood types. Its abundant, small-scale flowers and easy care have made it a favorite among gardeners looking for a low-maintenance, high-performing clematis.

plant_note: Set out container plants in spring against a fence, arbor, or trellis in full sun to light shade, watering well until established in well-drained soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil next to a fence, arbor, or pergola so the twining stems have something sturdy to climb, and water regularly the first season while roots establish. Clusters of tubular, richly fragrant cream to pale yellow flowers open in late spring and early summer, gradually deepening to orange as they age, and are followed by small red berries that draw songbirds. It is a vigorous, semi-evergreen to deciduous climber that tolerates heat, dry spells, and poor soil once established, making it useful for covering a large structure quickly. Prune after flowering to keep it in bounds, since it can grow rampantly in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface-sow and provide light, then set out after frost as a foliage annual.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, leaving it uncovered on the surface where light and cool nights encourage germination. Grown for its fragrant, frosty blue-green rounded foliage, Silver Drop makes long-lasting filler for fresh and dried arrangements. Transplant to full sun after frost and pinch to encourage bushy, well-branched stems. Harvest foliage once stems are firm and cure it upright or hang to dry.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or fall and set crowns just below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil under deciduous cover; fresh seed has deep double dormancy and can take 18–24 months to germinate even with cold-moist stratification, so division is the practical propagation method.
directions: Divide established clumps in early spring or fall and set crowns just below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil under deciduous cover. This European relative of American baneberries and black cohosh produces feathery compound foliage and small white bottlebrush flower spikes in late spring, followed by glossy black berries that are showy but toxic if eaten, so it is grown strictly as an ornamental or wildlife plant rather than an edible. It prefers cool, shaded, humusy sites such as beech or hazel woodland and resents drying out during summer. Established plants are long-lived and slowly clump-forming rather than aggressive spreaders.

common_name: European Chain Fern / Climbing Chain Fern
plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in a sheltered, shaded position with consistently moist to wet soil; protect from hard frost in the first winter.
directions: Plant in deep shade in rich, permanently moist to wet soil, such as along a stream bank or at the base of a shaded wall where moisture naturally accumulates. Set the crown at soil level and water thoroughly at planting, then maintain consistent moisture throughout the growing season — this fern will not tolerate drying out. The long arching fronds benefit from shelter from wind, which can damage the tips before they harden. Watch for bulbils forming at the frond tips in late summer; peg them gently to the soil surface and they will root and produce new plantlets, a simple way to propagate this impressive fern.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; European columbine is a classic cottage garden perennial that thrives in partial shade and self-seeds freely, creating naturalized drifts in shaded borders and woodland edges over time.
directions: Sow seeds in fall directly where plants are to grow, pressing lightly onto the soil surface and allowing winter cold to stratify the seeds for spring germination; European columbine self-seeds readily and does not need to be replanted each year once established. Aquilegia vulgaris is the classic European columbine of cottage gardens and woodland edges, a well-loved perennial with delicate blue-green, clover-like compound leaves and nodding, spurless or short-spurred flowers in shades of blue-violet, purple, white, and pink from late spring through early summer; unlike many North American columbines with long spurs, the European species tends toward shorter spurs and double flowers in garden varieties. The 'Nora Barlow' cultivar with doubled, pompom flowers in red, pink, and white is particularly well-known. Columbines self-seed generously and will hybridize freely among themselves; seedlings may vary in color. Short-lived perennials (2–4 years) that renew themselves by seeding.

plant_note: Plant corms just below the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade; unlike other hardy cyclamen that require dry summer dormancy, C. purpurascens remains in leaf year-round and should receive moisture through summer as well as winter. It establishes slowly from corms but is very long-lived once settled.
directions: Plant corms in shade in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; European cyclamen is uniquely distinct from the other two commonly grown hardy cyclamen species (C. hederifolium and C. coum) in two important ways — it is the only hardy cyclamen that blooms in summer (July and August) rather than autumn or winter, and it is the only one that does not require a dry summer dormancy period, remaining in leaf and active year-round. The flowers are sweetly fragrant (unlike most hardy cyclamen), in shades of pale to deep rose-pink, with the typical reflexed, swept-back petals of the genus. The rounded, dark-green leaves are beautifully marbled with silver patterns and are never lost — the plant is essentially evergreen. Native to the shaded limestone woodlands of the Alps and Apennines in central Europe, it requires cool, moist, slightly alkaline conditions under deciduous trees. Slower to establish and rarer in cultivation than C. hederifolium, but uniquely valuable for its summer bloom, fragrance, and year-round leaf retention.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; European hophornbeam is remarkably drought tolerant and limestone-adapted, growing naturally on dry, rocky, calcareous soils in mountain forests of southern Europe where summer drought is common.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; European hophornbeam is a refined, small-to-medium deciduous tree of dry, rocky, calcareous mountain forests from southern Europe through Turkey and the Caucasus — closely related to the American hophornbeam (Ostrya virginiana) but slightly smaller and more drought-adapted. The distinctive fruiting clusters of papery, bladder-like inflated husks enclosing each nutlet hang in loose, pendulous clusters resembling hops (Humulus lupulus) — one of the most distinctive and ornamental fruiting features of any deciduous tree. The finely toothed, birch-like leaves turn gold in autumn. The wood is exceptionally hard and dense. More drought-tolerant than most other deciduous trees, making it an excellent choice for dry, alkaline, rocky garden soils in full sun or light shade. The hop-like fruiting clusters are attractive from summer through winter. An underused but beautiful ornamental tree for dry, chalky, or limestone-based soils where larger trees struggle.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, fertile to average, loamy or clay loam soil in full sun to partial shade; European hornbeam is remarkably adaptable to a wide range of soil types, tolerating heavy clay soils and moderately wet or dry conditions.
directions: Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, fertile to average, loamy or clay loam soil in full sun to partial shade; European hornbeam is one of the most important and widely planted trees in the European formal garden tradition — valued both as a large specimen tree and as one of the premier hedging and pleaching trees, because its dense, twiggy branching retains dead tan leaves through the winter (marcescence) just like beech, creating a solid, opaque winter hedge. The wood is extraordinarily hard and tough — 'hornbeam' literally means 'hard tree' — historically used for making cogwheels, tool handles, and cutting boards. The oval leaves turn gold in autumn. The fruiting catkins with their distinctive three-lobed involucres (leafy bracts around each nut) are attractive. Exceptionally pollution-tolerant and adaptable to urban conditions. The cultivar 'Fastigiata' (columnar hornbeam) is one of the premier street trees in European cities. An excellent hedge, screen, and formal pleached allee tree for gardens with the space for its imposing mature size.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after cold stratification in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; European larch is one of the fastest-growing conifers in European forestry, particularly in the mountains. It requires full sun and good drainage but is tolerant of cold, snow, and wind.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; European larch is the dominant conifer of the Alps, Carpathians, and Sudeten mountains — the classic 'golden mountain' tree whose needles turn brilliant gold in October above the treeline, creating the famous autumn color displays in the Swiss and Austrian Alps.
