A fast-growing, long-lived, graceful tree producing the characteristic clustered needles on spur shoots of all larches — soft, light green in spring, deepening to rich green in summer, then golden-yellow in fall. The small, oval cones are among the most attractive of any conifer. Widely used in British and European forestry and ornamental planting. The weeping cultivar 'Pendula' is a dramatic, cascading accent tree. More adaptable to garden conditions than western larch, growing in a wider range of well-drained soils in zones 2–7.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes; eyes no deeper than 1–2 in below soil surface. European peony is the old-world species behind many historic double cultivars and blooms earlier than the more commonly grown Paeonia lactiflora.
directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall, 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, setting the pink eyes no more than 1–2 inches below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. European peony is the old-world species behind many historic garden doubles, blooming earlier in spring than the more commonly grown Chinese peony and forming a more compact, rounded clump with deeply cut, dark green leaves. The classic double crimson cultivar 'Rubra Plena' has been passed down in gardens for centuries and remains one of the earliest and longest-lived peonies still commonly grown. Like all peonies it resents being planted too deep or divided too often, and mature clumps can remain productive and largely trouble-free for decades with only an annual fall cleanup of the foliage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained to moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to clay soil in shade to full sun; European grey sedge is one of the best groundcover sedges for dry shade — thriving in the dry, dense shade of live oaks and other large trees where few other plants survive — and naturalizing readily into low-maintenance sweeps of arching, fine-textured, deep-green foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile soil in shade to partial shade; drought-tolerant once established in shade; mow or shear in late winter to refresh foliage before spring growth. Carex divulsa (European grey sedge or field sedge) is a clumping evergreen sedge native to the grasslands, roadsides, and dry woodlands of Europe and the Mediterranean region — but now naturalized across much of California, the Pacific Northwest, and parts of the Southeast, where it has been widely adopted in sustainable landscaping for its outstanding performance as a drought-tolerant, shade-tolerant groundcover. In dry shade — the notoriously difficult zone under established live oaks, magnolias, and other large tree canopies where irrigation is restricted and root competition is intense — grey sedge stands out as one of the most reliable and beautiful options: it forms dense, arching, fine-textured mounds of deep-green, grass-like foliage that remain attractive year-round with minimal care. It spreads slowly by seed and division to form a low-maintenance sweep. Unlike turf grass, grey sedge requires no mowing (though shearing in late winter refreshes its appearance), no fertilizer, and little water once established. The thin, arching leaf blades and graceful fountain form give a naturalistic, prairie-edge aesthetic. It is the backbone of California's 'dry shade garden' design movement, used extensively under native oaks in drought-tolerant home landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to lean, rocky, loamy, or sandy soil in full sun; European smoke tree is very drought-tolerant once established and actually produces more vibrant foliage color and a better 'smoke' display in lean, slightly stressed, well-drained to dry soils than in rich, moist, fertile conditions.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to lean, rocky, loamy, or sandy soil in full sun; European smoke tree is one of the most widely grown and loved ornamental shrubs in temperate gardens — famous for the extraordinary summer display of its tiny flowers, which are followed by large, loose panicles of fine, hair-like, pinkish-purple styles (the fuzzy threads remaining after the petals fall), creating the effect of a misty 'smoke cloud' surrounding the entire shrub in summer. The purple-leaved cultivars ('Royal Purple', 'Grace', 'Velvet Cloak') are among the most popular shrubs in the garden center trade — the deep wine-purple foliage contrasting with the ethereal pink-purple smoke creates a striking effect through the entire growing season. Fall color in the purple forms is spectacular: scarlet to orange-crimson. Native to southern Europe and central Asia. Extremely adaptable — tolerating dry, lean, rocky, alkaline soils where other flowering shrubs struggle. The purple-leaved forms are ubiquitous in modern garden design for their dramatic foliage season-long effect.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; European snowball bush is an old-fashioned, sterile-flowered cultivar that produces no fruit.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; European snowball bush is an old-fashioned, sterile-flowered cultivar that produces no fruit. This long-cultivated heirloom shrub bears large, perfectly round clusters of pure white flowers in late spring, opening lime-green and aging to snowy white, giving the shrub the appearance of being covered in dozens of large snowballs at peak bloom, a classic pass-along plant of old Southern and Midwestern gardens for generations. Because every flower in the cluster is sterile (unlike the fertile lacecap flowers of the wild species), it produces no berries, trading wildlife food value for a much showier, fuller flower display. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's flowers; watch for aphids, which favor the tender new growth of this species.

plant_note: Plant acorns (which take two years to mature) in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; European turkey oak is one of the fastest-growing oaks and adapts to poor, dry soils where other oaks fail. Common name refers to Turkey (the country) where it is widespread, not the bird.
directions: Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; European turkey oak is a fast-growing, large deciduous oak native to southern Europe and western Asia, named for its abundance in Turkey (not the bird). It produces deeply and variably lobed, bristle-tipped leaves with variable shape, and its most distinctive feature is the acorn cup covered in long, outward-curling, mossy-looking scales — creating some of the most ornamental acorn cups in the genus. The acorns require two full growing seasons to mature, a characteristic of the red oak group. A tough, adaptable tree for poor, dry soils where English oak would fail, commonly used in Europe for woodland planting on difficult sandy or chalk soils. The fall color is variable — yellows and bronzes. Note that in the southeastern US the name 'turkey oak' refers to the native Quercus laevis, an entirely different species.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; European wild ginger is slower to establish than native Asarum canadense but has glossier, more ornamental leaves and is more tolerant of hot, dry shade.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — European wild ginger is a low, slowly spreading shade groundcover with extraordinarily glossy, deep green, kidney-shaped leaves that remain evergreen through winter in zones 5–8, creating a lustrous, polished carpet under trees and shrubs. The leaves are significantly glossier and more ornamental than native wild ginger (A. canadense), which is deciduous. Small, brownish-purple, three-lobed flowers appear hidden at ground level in spring. It spreads slowly and politely by rhizome, creating a refined, weed-suppressing mat in appropriate conditions. It tolerates dry shade better than the native species once established. Unlike native Asarum, the European species does not host certain specialist insects, but its ornamental value is superior. An outstanding foliage plant for shaded woodland gardens in zones 4–8.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; European wood sedge is a graceful, arching, loosely clumping sedge that naturalizes beautifully in shaded woodland gardens and tolerates deep shade better than most sedges.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; European wood sedge tolerates deep shade remarkably well and makes an elegant, naturalizing ground layer under trees. Carex sylvatica is a fine-textured European sedge that grows in loose, arching clumps 12–24 inches tall with bright green, very narrow leaves that cascade gracefully and slender, nodding, green flower spikes in early summer; it naturalizes slowly by self-seeding under deciduous trees and makes a beautiful, fine-textured woodland ground cover that contrasts well with broad-leaved shade plants like hostas, hellebores, and astilbe. More tolerant of dry shade than many sedges once established, and adaptable to a range of soil types from heavy clay to sandy loam. Largely ignored by deer and rabbit.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained soil in full sun; euryops is nearly always propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.
directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil, spacing plants 24–36 inches apart, and shear lightly after each bloom flush to keep the rounded mound tidy and dense. Native to South Africa, euryops daisy is a fine-textured, silvery-gray-leaved shrub that produces bright golden-yellow, 2-inch daisy flowers almost continuously in mild climates, with the heaviest flush in fall through spring and lighter bloom through summer heat. It is highly drought- and salt-tolerant once established, making it a mainstay of Gulf Coast and coastal landscaping, and is largely untroubled by pests or disease as long as drainage is sharp — soggy soil is its main weakness. Hardy as a perennial shrub only in zones 9–11; further north it is grown as a container plant brought indoors before frost or replaced annually as a warm-season bedding plant.

common_name: Eva Cullum Phlox (Clear Pink Red-Eyed Garden Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space at least 18 inches apart for good air circulation, since Eva Cullum has better mildew resistance than most older pink phlox but still benefits from open airflow.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Eva Cullum produces large, fragrant flower heads in a clear, true pink centered with a small red eye, a crisp combination that holds its color well through the heat of summer without fading or muddying. It is noted among tall garden phlox cultivars for above-average resistance to powdery mildew, staying cleaner and more attractive into fall than many older pink selections, though it still benefits from full sun and generous spacing. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings, which typically revert to a muddy magenta rather than coming true to the parent's clear pink.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in well-drained, limestone-based or average soil in full sun to partial shade; Eve's necklace tolerates both dry limestone soils and the partial shade of a woodland edge.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in well-drained, limestone-based or average soil in full sun to partial shade; Eve's necklace tolerates both dry limestone soils and the partial shade of a woodland edge. This small, graceful understory tree native to limestone woodlands and stream edges across Texas, Oklahoma, and Louisiana produces drooping clusters of fragrant, pale pink to rose flowers in mid-spring, followed by distinctive black seed pods constricted between the seeds like a string of beads, giving the tree its common name. Compound, locust-like foliage casts light, dappled shade, and the tree's small mature size makes it a good choice for planting under power lines or in a smaller landscape where a full-sized shade tree would be too large. It is drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established, needing only occasional shaping in its early years to develop a strong branch structure.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; also sow in fall in zones 8–10 for winter bloom; evening stock closes its flowers during the day — plant near windows, patios, or pathways where fragrance is appreciated at dusk.
directions: Direct sow on the soil surface or barely covered in early spring in cool, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; evening stock is grown almost entirely for its intense, sweet, clove-like fragrance that fills the air at dusk and into the night when the small pale purple to white flowers open. Unlike the showy daytime stocks (Matthiola incana), evening stock has modest flowers that close and appear wilted by day — plant it where fragrance matters more than visual impact: beside paths, under windows, or in containers near sitting areas. An outstanding companion to evening gardens, moon gardens, or any planting designed for after-dark enjoyment. Sow in succession every 3–4 weeks for continuous fragrance.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost about an inch deep in full sun, thinning to 12-18 inches apart. This branching heirloom bears 4-6 inch sunset-hued blooms with dark centers in many rich tones on one plant, over a long bloom period that keeps vases full and pollinators fed. Because it branches, cut stems regularly to encourage more flowers. Water while establishing and stake tall stalks in windy locations.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil with afternoon shade.
directions: Ever After Ruby is a reblooming azalea that produces vivid ruby-red flowers in spring and again from summer into fall. Plant it in dappled or partial shade in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch to protect the shallow roots. Keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since azaleas resent both drought and soggy feet. Shear lightly right after the spring flush to encourage a fuller shape and stronger repeat bloom. Feed with an acid-loving-plant fertilizer in spring.

common_name: Ever Red Loropetalum (Dwarf Mounding Red-Leaf Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Ever Red's naturally dwarf, mounding habit needs little to no pruning to hold a tidy shape in a small bed or foundation planting.
directions: Ever Red is a dwarf, densely mounding loropetalum selection that holds a compact size well below the larger, more vigorous fringe flower cultivars, making it a practical choice for small foundation beds where standard loropetalum quickly becomes too large. Its small leaves emerge burgundy-red and hold that deep color better through summer heat than many red-leaf loropetalum selections, set off by frilly, spidery magenta-pink flowers concentrated in spring with lighter scattered rebloom later in the season. Like other loropetalum it is easygoing in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and full sun to partial shade, needing only an occasional light shaping right after the main spring bloom to stay tidy.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade; Evercream, part of the Evercolor sedge series, bears narrow leaves margined in bright creamy white over dark green centers.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. Evercream, part of the Proven Winners Evercolor sedge series, forms a neat, arching mound of narrow, dark green leaves crisply margined in creamy white, holding its bright variegation and evergreen foliage through the growing season and into winter in milder zones. Its fine texture and bright edging make it a strong companion for hostas, ferns, and heucheras at the front of a shaded border, or as a container specimen. Trim back tattered foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Everest carries crisp white-margined leaves year-round and colors best out of direct afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Everest is an evergreen Japanese sedge cultivar with narrow, gracefully arching leaves striped in bright white along the margins and deep green down the center, giving a crisp, frosty look that reads well from a distance in a shaded bed. It tolerates some gentle morning sun but colors up best and resists leaf scorch when protected from hot afternoon exposure, making it a dependable choice for the deeper, cooler shade under trees and on the north side of buildings. Deer generally leave it alone, and it needs little more than an early-spring grooming to remove tired winter foliage before new growth emerges. Its slowly spreading habit works well as a repeated accent along a shaded path or massed as a fine-textured groundcover.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; a few hours of morning sun deepens the gold stripe without scorching the foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and comb out dead blades by hand each spring rather than shearing, since cutting the evergreen foliage back hard can leave the clump looking ragged for weeks. Evergold forms a neat, arching mound of narrow, grass-like leaves with a broad creamy-gold stripe down the center of each dark-green blade, brightening shaded borders and container plantings year-round in mild climates where the foliage stays evergreen through winter. Its compact, well-behaved habit and season-long color make it one of the most reliable variegated sedges for edging shaded paths and underplanting shrubs. Divide congested clumps in spring every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and clean color.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; evergold sedge provides persistent chartreuse-yellow-and-green foliage that brightens dark shaded corners year-round.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; evergold sedge is one of the most popular shade foliage plants in cultivation, producing dense, arching clumps of narrow leaves with a bright yellow-gold central stripe and dark green edges that glow with captured light even in deep shade. The evergreen foliage provides color through winter and is at its most vibrant in spring, making it an invaluable element in shade gardens for pairing with purple-leaved heucheras, blue hostas, and dark-leaved shrubs. Virtually maintenance-free beyond removing the oldest leaves in early spring. Tolerates clay soil and periodic drought once established. Excellent in containers and as a graceful edging plant along shaded paths.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or fall, or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; candytuft blooms on the previous year's growth — shear back by one-third immediately after flowering to keep plants compact and promote dense new growth for next year's bloom. It dislikes hot, humid summer conditions and performs best in cool climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen candytuft is one of the standard spring-blooming edging and rock garden perennials of temperate gardens — a low, spreading, semi-woody subshrub producing dense, flat-topped clusters of brilliant pure-white flowers from March through May that completely cover the plant and provide one of the most reliable and pristine spring displays available. The flowers are produced in such abundance that the dark-green, narrow, glossy, evergreen foliage is invisible beneath the white bloom. After flowering, light shearing maintains compact, dense growth. It is evergreen through winter (retaining its dark-green leaves), adding ground-level interest even when not in flower. Outstanding for edging paths and borders, cascading over low walls, filling rock garden pockets, and providing a spring carpet in full sun. The cultivar 'Snowflake' is a superior form with larger flower heads and particularly dense, rounded flower clusters.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; evergreen climbing hydrangea is less cold-hardy than the deciduous climbing hydrangea and benefits from a sheltered site.
directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; evergreen climbing hydrangea is less cold-hardy than the deciduous climbing hydrangea and benefits from a sheltered site. Glossy, leathery, evergreen leaves cover a self-clinging vine that attaches to walls, trellises, and tree trunks by aerial roots much like its more familiar deciduous relative, producing flat, lacecap clusters of small fertile flowers surrounded by larger, showy white sterile florets in summer. Native to cloud forests of Mexico and Central America, it holds its foliage year-round in mild climates, providing continuous coverage on a north-facing wall or shaded fence unlike the winter-bare deciduous climbing hydrangea. Provide a sturdy support for the self-clinging stems, keep soil consistently moist, and mulch well to protect roots in the colder parts of its hardiness range.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or plant container-grown plants in fall or winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full shade to part shade; evergreen currant is native to the understory of Coast Live Oak woodland and is adapted to summer-dry conditions under tree canopy. It requires excellent drainage and may struggle in wet clay soils. Established plants need no supplemental water in summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; evergreen currant is one of the finest California native groundcovers for dry shade under oaks and other native trees — a low, spreading shrub from Santa Catalina and Anacapa islands and the adjacent mainland coast that thrives in the same summer-dry, shaded conditions as Coast Live Oak woodland where few other plants succeed. The rounded, dark-green, leathery leaves have an appealing, aromatic, resinous fragrance when crushed. In late winter and early spring it produces small clusters of tiny, deep-wine-red to rose-pink flowers that are disproportionately attractive to hummingbirds for their size. The plant requires essentially no summer water once established and actually resents summer irrigation, making it outstanding for planting beneath oaks where summer watering risks fatal Phytophthora infections of the oaks. An essential plant for California native gardens and water-wise landscapes requiring shade coverage without summer irrigation.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Evergreen Giant is more heat- and sun-tolerant than most liriopes and can be used in brighter positions than smaller cultivars while still performing well in shade.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Evergreen Giant is a distinctively large-growing liriope cultivar that reaches 18–24 inches tall — nearly twice the height of standard Big Blue — with correspondingly wide, bold, arching leaves that give it a dramatically different presence in the landscape. Where standard liriope reads as a fine-textured edge plant or ground cover, Evergreen Giant has the bold, architectural quality of a small ornamental grass and can serve as a substitute for clumping ornamental grasses in shade or semi-shade situations where grasses typically fail. The white to pale lavender flower spikes are produced reliably above the foliage in late summer. Evergreen Giant is particularly well-adapted to zone 9 heat and humidity, maintaining better summer appearance than some of the smaller liriope cultivars that can look worn by August in the Deep South. It is also somewhat more drought-tolerant than smaller cultivars once established, performing adequately in drier spots under established tree canopies. Cut back to 4–6 inches in late winter (January in zone 9) before new growth begins to refresh the foliage. Outstanding mass-planted as a bold, low-maintenance ground cover under trees, along driveways, or on slopes.

plant_note: Divide and transplant clumps into humus-rich, well-drained shade soil in spring after new growth begins.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind. New wiry black-stemmed fronds emerge bronze-pink in spring and mature to blue-green, persisting through winter in milder climates. Top-dress annually with leaf mold or compost and keep evenly moist but never waterlogged. Old tattered fronds can be cut back in late winter before new growth flushes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; evergreen mock orange is less cold-hardy than northern mock orange species and best suited to zones 7-9.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; evergreen mock orange is less cold-hardy than northern mock orange species and best suited to zones 7-9. Fragrant, creamy white, single flowers open along arching, semi-scrambling branches in late spring, carrying the classic sweet orange-blossom scent typical of the genus, on a Mexican native species that holds its glossy foliage semi-evergreen through mild winters in warmer zones where deciduous mock orange relatives lose their leaves. Its sprawling, somewhat vine-like habit makes it useful for training against a wall or trellis as much as a freestanding shrub, and its milder climate tolerance broadens the range of conditions where fragrant mock orange bloom can be enjoyed. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, and provide some winter protection at the colder edge of its hardiness range.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil in shade; evergreen Solomon's seal is one of the best low-maintenance shade perennials for zones 6–9, combining a beautiful arching habit with year-round foliage in mild winters.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; evergreen Solomon's seal is a Chinese relative of Polygonatum with remarkable ornamental virtues — unlike the deciduous native Solomon's seals, this species retains its lustrous, dark green, arching foliage through winter in zones 7–9, providing year-round structure in the shade garden. The small, white, nodding bell flowers in late spring have a sweet fragrance and the plant spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form an attractive, weed-suppressing groundcover. The combination of shade tolerance, evergreen habit, and adaptability to the heat and humidity of zone 8–9 makes it particularly valuable for Southern shade gardens where deciduous perennials disappear for half the year. Spreads slowly and does not become aggressive.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen wisteria is a Chinese legume vine suited for zones 8–10, where it retains its leaves year-round unlike deciduous wisterias.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen wisteria is a Chinese legume vine in the same family as wisteria, producing dark, wine-purple to reddish-purple flower clusters from midsummer through fall — a very different bloom time from the spring-flowering true wisterias. The pinnate leaves are glossy and retain their attractive appearance year-round in mild climates. Compared to the aggressive true wisterias, Millettia reticulata is more restrained and less invasive, making it somewhat more manageable in the garden. The deep purple to burgundy flower clusters have a spicy, grapelike fragrance. An excellent vine for providing summer-through-fall fragrant flowering interest on arbors and pergolas in zone 9a gardens, where it is reliably perennial.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Everillo emerges lime-green and matures to a bright, glowing chartreuse-gold, holding its color through the season better than many variegated sedges.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Everillo is a striking sedge cultivar that emerges bright lime-green in spring and matures into a glowing chartreuse-gold that holds its vivid color through summer and into fall, brightening dark corners of the shade garden without needing flowers. Its fine-textured, arching, grass-like form provides an excellent textural contrast to broad-leaved hostas, ferns, and heucheras, and it tolerates both consistently moist soil and brief dry spells once established. It is evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild climates and needs only an occasional combing-out of old foliage in early spring to keep it looking fresh.

common_name: Eversheen Sedge (Fine Yellow-Green Striped Evergreen Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade; Eversheen, part of the Evercolor sedge series alongside Evercream and Everillo, bears fine yellow-green striped foliage.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. Eversheen, part of the Proven Winners Evercolor sedge series, forms a neat, arching mound of fine-textured foliage striped in yellow-green, holding its bright color and evergreen habit through the growing season and into winter in milder zones. Its fine texture and luminous color make it a strong companion for hostas, ferns, and heucheras at the front of a shaded border, or as a container specimen. Trim back tattered foliage in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; excellent drainage is essential.
directions: Evolution Emerald Ice is a low, drought-tolerant sedum grown as a groundcover, offering fresh green succulent foliage and pink summer blooms that draw pollinators. Plant it in full sun in gritty, sharply drained soil, since wet or heavy ground causes rot. Once established it thrives on neglect and needs little supplemental water. Shear back lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and tidy. Divide clumps in spring every few years to expand your planting or renew vigor.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Evolution mealycup sage grows taller than most bedding-type salvia farinacea selections, useful for the middle or back of a border.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Evolution mealycup sage grows taller than most bedding-type salvia farinacea selections, useful for the middle or back of a border. Tall, sturdy spikes of rich violet-blue flowers with a soft, powdery-white bloom on the calyxes rise well above the narrow gray-green foliage, giving this selection a bolder, more upright presence than the shorter bedding types typically used at the front of a border. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it flowers continuously from summer through fall with minimal deadheading, drawing bees and butterflies throughout its long bloom season, and holds up well as a cut flower. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage continued bloom, and treat as a perennial in zones 8-10 or a heat-loving annual further north.

common_name: Excalibur Pulmonaria (Silver-Leaf Lungwort with Narrow Green Edge)
plant_note: Divide and transplant in early spring or right after flowering, planting crowns at the same depth they were growing previously.
directions: Plant in cool, humus-rich soil that stays consistently moist, choosing a site sheltered from harsh afternoon sun that can scorch the silvered leaves. Mulch to keep roots cool and shear back tattered foliage after flowering to encourage a fresh, cleaner-looking rosette for the rest of the season. The lance-shaped leaves are almost entirely silver with just a thin green margin, giving it one of the brightest foliage displays in the genus, while clusters of funnel-shaped flowers open pink and mature to blue in early spring. It brightens dim corners of the shade garden nearly year-round and pairs well with hostas and ferns.

common_name: Excelsior Hybrid Foxglove (Classic Outward-Facing Mixed-Color Strain)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors or sow directly in late summer for fall transplanting; in zone 9 foxglove is grown as a winter annual or biennial, with plants established in fall blooming the following spring. Excelsior is the classic older foxglove strain, distinguished by densely packed, outward- and upward-facing florets held all the way around the spike rather than hanging to one side.
directions: Plant in partial shade — filtered light under tall trees suits it well — in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil; Excelsior Hybrids is the long-standing classic foxglove seed strain, bred to hold its tubular, spotted flowers evenly all the way around the spike in an outward- and upward-facing arrangement rather than the one-sided, downward-hanging habit of the older wild-type foxglove, giving a fuller, more dramatic bloom spike viewed from any angle. Flowers come in a mix of purple, pink, cream, and white, each with distinctive dark spotting inside the throat that guides pollinating bumblebees to the nectar. As a true biennial, plants form a low rosette of foliage in year one and send up the tall flowering spike in year two, though fall-sown plants in mild-winter zones can bloom the following spring; it self-seeds readily where happy, so a planting can sustain itself with new rosettes appearing each year once established. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where children or pets might sample the foliage or flowers, and wear gloves when handling.

common_name: Exotic Star Amaryllis (White with Green Throat and Pink Star Pattern)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Exotic Star bears white flowers with a green throat and faint pink star-shaped veining radiating through each petal.
directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Exotic Star bears large, softly colored white flowers touched with a green throat and faint pink star-shaped veining that radiates outward through each petal, a more subtle, refined color pattern than the bold solid reds of many popular amaryllis cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, naturalizing and multiplying into an increasingly full clump over the years. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb, and for container forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix for traditional winter bloom indoors.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Exquisite bears extra-large double blooms ranging from magenta to soft rose on tall 2-4 foot plants.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches. Exquisite bears extra-large, fully double blooms ranging from rich magenta to soft dusty rose across the same planting, giving a naturally varied palette of related pink-purple tones on tall, vigorous stems reaching two to four feet, excellent for cutting. Plants bloom heavily from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading or harvesting to encourage continuous production. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

common_name: Eyelash Begonia (Tiger Begonia, Miniature Begonia, Bowerae)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded terrarium plant in zone 9; Begonia bowerae is one of the smallest and most manageable rhizomatous begonias, fitting perfectly in a 4–6 inch pot or as a terrarium specimen. It cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. Grow in a wide, shallow container to accommodate horizontal rhizome spread. Keep the rhizome at the soil surface. Allow the top half-inch of growing medium to dry between waterings. Excellent for terrariums, dish gardens, and windowsill collections. Propagate from leaf-petiole cuttings.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Eyelash Begonia flowers most freely in bright indirect light (a north or bright east window) and will survive in lower light but produce fewer blooms. Begonia bowerae is a small rhizomatous begonia native to the mountains of Chiapas, Mexico, one of the most charming and widely-grown of the many miniature and compact begonias popular with houseplant collectors. The plant produces a low, spreading rosette of small (2–3 inch), bright emerald-green leaves with a distinctive chocolate-brown to dark maroon edge blotching — a 'tiger' pattern of irregular dark markings around the leaf margins that gives the species its alternative common name 'Tiger Begonia.' The leaf margins are fringed with distinctive white hairs or eyelash-like cilia that stand out against the green leaf surface — the feature that inspired the most widely-used common name 'Eyelash Begonia.' In late winter and spring, the plant produces airy sprays of pale pink to white flowers on long, thin stems well above the foliage — delicate, wispy, and charming in contrast to the bolder leaf display. Begonia bowerae has been used extensively in breeding to produce hybrid miniature begonias (the 'Tiger' hybrids and related compact rhizomatous types). It is one of the easiest begonias for windowsill and terrarium culture, forgiving, compact, and ornamental year-round.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained acidic soil in partial to full shade; this rare species is restricted to the Savannah River drainage in Georgia, South Carolina, and adjacent North Carolina and should only be sourced from licensed nurseries propagating their own stock.
directions: Faded Trillium is a rare and geographically restricted sessile trillium endemic to the Savannah River drainage in the Piedmont and upper Coastal Plain of Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina, growing in moist, rich deciduous hardwood forests over well-drained, loamy soils. Its pale yellow to cream-colored sessile flowers are smaller and less showy than many trilliums — giving the species its common name — but the silvery-mottled leaves are attractive throughout the spring season. Classified as a species of conservation concern, this trillium should never be collected from wild populations; it is occasionally propagated by specialty native plant nurseries. Plant rhizome divisions in fall in deep, humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil in the shade of deciduous trees, allowing the plants to emerge and bloom in spring before the canopy leafs out fully.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fairy bells spread steadily by rhizomes and are ideal for naturalizing as a shade groundcover under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade, spacing 12–18 inches apart; fairy bells is an elegant woodland perennial whose arching stems bear alternate, lance-shaped leaves and hang small creamy-white bell-shaped flowers at each tip in mid-spring, followed by glossy black berries that ripen in late summer. The variegated form 'Variegatum' with white-edged leaves is especially striking in deep shade. Plants spread slowly but steadily by rhizomes to form a refined groundcover that tolerates dry shade under established deciduous trees once established. Divide in early spring every 4–5 years to propagate and share; plants need little other maintenance.

common_name: Fairy Blush Camellia (Small-Flowered Pale Pink Compact Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Fairy Blush's fine texture and compact size suit it to a smaller bed, low hedge, or mass planting where a large camellia would be out of scale.
directions: Fairy Blush produces an abundance of small, single, pale pink flowers with a delicate blush deepening toward the petal edges, held above fine-textured, small, glossy evergreen leaves quite different from the larger, coarser foliage of many camellia cultivars. Its dainty flower form and dense, twiggy growth make it useful as a low informal hedge or mass planting where the sheer quantity of small blooms creates a soft haze of color through the bloom season. Like other camellias it needs consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and a layer of mulch to protect its shallow roots; prune, if needed, only lightly right after flowering to avoid removing next season's buds.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil before or around the last frost; it dislikes summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in cool soil around the last frost, barely covering the fine seed. Fairy Bouquet is a charming blend of dainty three-quarter-inch snapdragon-like blooms in bright colors above airy foliage, also known as toadflax. It makes a colorful mass planting, container filler, or border edging and attracts pollinators. It prefers cool weather, so sow early and provide even moisture before summer heat arrives.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fairy crassula tolerates more shade than most succulents and spreads readily into a groundcover mat.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fairy crassula tolerates more shade than most succulents and spreads readily into a groundcover mat. Rounded, spotted, olive-green leaves cover a low, spreading succulent that tolerates considerably more shade than most crassula species, spreading by both creeping stems and tiny plantlets that form on airy flower stalks and drop to root nearby, quickly filling in as a low-maintenance groundcover under trees or along a shaded border edge. Its shade tolerance and easy, spreading habit make it a useful succulent groundcover option for the dry shade beneath established trees where few other succulents would survive. Water only occasionally, since it tolerates and even prefers drier shade conditions, and divide or thin the spreading mat as needed to control size.

plant_note: Direct-sow scarified seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to rocky, poor soil in full sun in spring; fairy duster is intolerant of clay, wet, or rich soil — it thrives in the harshest, driest, most alkaline desert and rocky foothill conditions and declines quickly in moist, fertile, or amended garden soil.
directions: Sow scarified seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to rocky, poor soil in full sun; fairy duster is a low-growing native Sonoran and Chihuahuan Desert shrub in the pea family (Fabaceae) — one of the most charming and ecologically valuable small flowering shrubs of the desert Southwest — producing masses of powder-puff-like flower heads composed entirely of long, filamentous, pink-white to deep-pink stamens that give the plant its evocative common name. The silky, feathery flower clusters appear in late winter through spring, just as desert wildflowers peak, and provide an exceptionally early nectar source for emerging queen hummingbirds, sphinx moths, and native bees. The delicate, twice-pinnate, tiny-leafleted, gray-green foliage is drought-deciduous (dropped in extreme drought) and creates a fine, airy texture. Fairy duster grows naturally on dry, rocky, desert foothill slopes and bajadas and demands perfectly drained, lean, rocky soil — it fails in amended or moist garden soil. Its cold-hardiness to approximately 10°F makes it the most cold-adapted of the calliandras, suitable through zone 7. An excellent xeriscape shrub for dry Southwest gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained woodland soil in zone 4–8; Fairy Lanterns (Hooker's Fairy Bells) is a graceful, rhizomatous woodland perennial native to the shaded coniferous and mixed forests of the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to central California — producing arching, leafy stems and pairs of small, nodding, cream-colored bells and bright-red-orange berries that glow like lanterns in the understory shade.
directions: Plant Prosartes hookeri in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade under conifers or deciduous trees; mulch with leaf mold or bark to maintain cool, moist, acidic conditions; the plant spreads slowly from rhizomes to form attractive colonies — divide every 3–4 years if desired. Fairy Lanterns is a beautiful native woodland perennial of the Pacific Coast forests — closely related to and often still listed as Disporum hookeri — forming elegant clumps of arching, leafy stems that emerge in early spring and bear pairs of small, narrow, nodding, creamy-white bell-flowers at the branch tips. The common name comes from the brilliant red-orange berries that follow the flowers in late summer, glowing like tiny lanterns in the deep forest shade. The plant grows naturally in the humus-rich, acidic, perpetually moist soil of Pacific Coast conifer forests alongside Trillium, Oxalis, and ferns; in cultivation it prefers analogous conditions — reliable moisture, acidic soil, and overhead canopy shade. A refined and overlooked native plant that deserves wider use in Pacific Northwest woodland gardens and shady borders; it pairs beautifully with native ferns, bleeding heart (Dicentra formosa), and wild ginger (Asarum caudatum). The berries are not considered edible for humans but are taken by thrushes and other woodland birds.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial shade; fairy wand is dioecious — plant in groups of 3–5 to ensure both male and female plants are present for seed production.
directions: Chamaelirium luteum is an elegant and architecturally distinct native perennial of eastern North American deciduous forests and woodland margins, producing a basal rosette of smooth, spatula-shaped, deep-green leaves from which arise wand-like flowering stems in spring — male plants bearing slender, arching, horizontal spikes of tiny white flowers, female plants bearing stouter, upright white spikes that eventually bear seed capsules — giving the two sexes a strikingly different appearance. It grows in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to light shade from New England to Florida, and the species name luteum (yellow) refers to the yellow-green coloration of the rhizome, called "devil's bit" by herbalists because the tip appears bitten off. Plant in groups of 3–5 to ensure male and female plants are present for pollination and seed set. The plant is slow to establish but extremely long-lived and very deer-resistant.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; fairy washboard tolerates lower light than sun-loving succulents and scorches in direct hot sun.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; fairy washboard tolerates lower light than sun-loving succulents and scorches in direct hot sun. Thick, dark green triangular leaves are ridged with raised, corrugated, washboard-like horizontal ribs, an intricate textured pattern that spirals up the tightly packed rosette and gives the plant its distinctive common name. Native to rocky grasslands in South Africa, it is a slow-growing, clustering species well suited to a succulent dish garden or windowsill collection where its unusual ribbed texture is easy to appreciate up close. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light to avoid scorching, and separate offsets from the base to propagate.

common_name: Fall Muhly (Purple Muhly, Deer Grass Muhly)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; fall muhly is drought-adapted and performs best in lean soils without supplemental irrigation once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; fall muhly is a western and southwestern native grass closely related to Gulf muhly and pink muhly grass, producing somewhat coarser, denser clumps of deep-green foliage and vivid purple, airy seed plumes in fall — the purple color is more intense and held longer than some other muhly species. It is an outstanding grass for hot, dry, rocky garden conditions in zone 7–10, thriving in the rocky limestone and caliche soils of central Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona where many ornamental grasses struggle. The fall color display — masses of burgundy-purple plumes catching the fall light — is one of the most beautiful seasonal displays available in a drought-tolerant native grass. Excellent for xeriscape, parking lot medians, rocky slopes, and any location that receives reflected heat from pavement. Cut back to 6–8 inches in late winter before new growth begins. Combines beautifully with fall-blooming natives like asters, salvias, and fall-blooming sedums.

common_name: Fallen City Caladium (Dark Green Fancy-Leaf with Deep Red Speckling)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Fallen City bears dark green fancy-leaf foliage heavily speckled with deep red splotches, best in partial shade.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Fallen City bears dark green fancy-leaf foliage heavily speckled and splotched with deep red across the leaf surface, a bold, richly patterned combination that stands apart from the more uniform coloring of many fancy-leaf caladium cultivars. It provides months of reliable, low-maintenance color in shaded beds, borders, and containers without needing flowers, pairing especially well with ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Falling Waters Bald Cypress (Weeping-Form Bald Cypress)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Falling Waters is a distinctive weeping selection of bald cypress usually trained onto a central leader to create a dramatic cascading specimen tree.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and stake or train the leader when young if a taller cascading form is wanted, since the weeping branches otherwise spread along the ground. Falling Waters is a striking weeping cultivar of the native bald cypress, its soft, ferny, blue-green deciduous foliage draping in cascading curtains from the branches rather than the upright, pyramidal form typical of the species, turning warm rust-orange in fall before dropping. It thrives in the same wide range of conditions as the wild species, from swampy, seasonally flooded ground to ordinary well-drained garden soil, making it a distinctive specimen tree for a pond edge, rain garden, or prominent lawn feature. Once established it needs little routine care beyond occasional watering during extended drought and removal of any reverted upright growth to preserve the weeping habit.

plant_note: Plant bulb or container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic soil in zone 5–9; False Aloe is a low-growing native perennial of the eastern and central United States from New York south to Florida and west to Kansas, producing rosettes of narrow, dark-green, purple-spotted succulent-like leaves and tall, slender flower spikes of tubular, greenish-yellow, intensely fragrant flowers in summer — hummingbird and hawk moth magnet.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; Manfreda virginica is highly drought and heat tolerant once established — requires excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water; it is native to rocky outcrops, cedar glades, and dry woodland edges across its range. Manfreda virginica (False Aloe, American Aloe, or Rattlesnake Master) is a low-growing, clumping, bulbous perennial in the Asparagaceae family (closely related to Agave) native to the eastern and central United States from Maryland and Pennsylvania south through the Appalachians and Piedmont to Florida and west through Missouri, Oklahoma, and Kansas. The plant forms loose, ground-level rosettes of narrow, strap-like, semi-succulent, gray-green or dark-green leaves often beautifully marked with purple-red spots and blotches — giving a mottled appearance sometimes compared to a rattlesnake's scales. In summer, a tall, slender, unbranched flower spike emerges from the center of the rosette reaching 2–5 feet, topped with 10–30 tubular, greenish-yellow to brownish flowers that open in the evening and are intensely, sweetly fragrant — powerful enough to perfume a large garden area at dusk. The flowers are excellent hawk moth (Sphingidae) and hummingbird attractors. Unlike agave, Manfreda virginica is not monocarpic — it blooms annually without dying. An outstanding native accent plant for dry, sunny to partly shaded positions in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall or early spring in deep, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; false anemone is native to cool, moist mountain forests in Japan and struggles where summers are hot and humid, so give it the coolest, most sheltered shade position available.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in fall or early spring in deep, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; false anemone is native to cool, moist mountain forests in Japan and struggles where summers are hot and humid, so give it the coolest, most sheltered shade position available. Anemonopsis macrophylla forms an elegant clump of deeply divided, anemone-like leaves and sends up branched stems of nodding, waxy, lilac to mauve, cup-shaped flowers with contrasting darker purple stamens in mid to late summer. It is one of the most coveted specialty woodland perennials among shade-garden collectors for its refined texture and unusual bloom color, though it is notoriously slow to establish and intolerant of drought, root disturbance, or heavy clay. Site it in a permanently cool, humus-rich pocket alongside hostas and ferns, keep the root zone mulched year-round, and avoid dividing established clumps except to propagate, since plants may sulk for a season or two afterward.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings under mist or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich, freely draining soil in partial to full shade after frost; false aralia is sensitive to overwatering and root rot — use a freely draining potting mix and allow the top inch to dry between waterings, especially in cooler conditions where the plant's water uptake is reduced.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; false aralia (spider aralia) is a New Caledonian tropical tree in the ginseng family (Araliaceae, now reclassified to Plerandra elegantissima from Schefflera elegantissima) with one of the most dramatic and phase-changing foliage sequences of any tropical plant — juvenile plants (the form most commonly sold as a houseplant) produce long, narrow, deeply serrated, copper-bronze to dark blackish-brown, almost spider-like leaflets radiating from each leaf stalk like the fingers of a dark, elaborately toothed hand, creating an extraordinarily refined and dramatic appearance quite unlike any common houseplant. As the plant matures and reaches tree size, the leaf form transitions dramatically to large, broad, rounded, glossy-green leaflets similar to a large Schefflera, losing the juvenile spider form. In the landscape it becomes a substantial tree to 20 feet. The juvenile, spider-like foliage form is the primary ornamental feature and is best maintained by keeping the plant in a container where root restriction prevents rapid maturation. An exceptional architectural accent for shaded tropical patios and zone 10–12 shade gardens.

plant_note: Scarify seeds and direct-sow in fall in full sun in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; germination is improved by cold-moist stratification. Once established, false blue indigo forms a long-lived, deep-rooted clump that should not be disturbed or moved.
directions: Scarify seeds by nicking or rubbing with sandpaper, then direct-sow in fall in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; false blue indigo is slow to establish but extremely long-lived once rooted — it may take 2–3 years to reach blooming size but plants can survive in the same spot for decades without needing division. The blue-green clover-like foliage is attractive all season; in late spring dramatic spikes of indigo-blue pea-like flowers appear, followed by inflated black seed pods that are decorative through winter and rattle in the breeze. A deep taproot makes it impossible to transplant once established, so siting is permanent. Outstanding as a drought-tolerant native prairie perennial; it is also a host plant for Wild Indigo Duskywing, Hoary Edge, and Orange Sulphur butterfly larvae.

plant_note: Fall direct sowing mimics natural seed dispersal and provides the cold stratification needed for reliable spring germination.
directions: False Boneset is a tough, drought-tolerant prairie and meadow perennial native to central and eastern North America, bearing clusters of creamy white flower heads from late summer into fall when many other wildflowers have finished blooming. It is especially valued as a critical late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies and native bees fueling up before migration or overwintering. Sow seeds directly in fall into dry, well-drained soils in full sun; this species tolerates poor, rocky, or clay soils and actually performs best without supplemental fertilization. Once established, False Boneset is long-lived, self-seeds moderately, and integrates well into naturalistic prairie plantings and pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; false bugbane is native to seepage slopes and streambanks and performs best in a consistently moist, boggy spot such as a rain garden or the edge of a shaded pond.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; false bugbane is native to seepage slopes and streambanks and performs best in a consistently moist, boggy spot such as a rain garden or the edge of a shaded pond. Trautvetteria caroliniensis is an eastern and western North American native with large, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves and airy clusters of fluffy white flowers made up of showy stamens rather than petals, blooming in late spring to early summer above the bold foliage. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form a colony in consistently damp shade, providing a coarse, textural contrast to ferns and fine-leaved sedges along a shaded stream bank or wet woodland garden. Give it constant moisture — it does not tolerate summer drought — and full to partial shade, since foliage scorches quickly in hot sun or dry soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; false goat's beard is the only native North American astilbe species and is more tolerant of summer heat than the Asian-origin hybrid astilbes commonly sold in nurseries.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade — this is the only native US species in the astilbe family and is a magnificent plant for moist, shaded spots in the mid-Atlantic and Appalachian region. The large, pinnately compound leaves are coarser-textured than hybrid astilbes, and the creamy white to yellowish flower plumes in late spring and early summer can reach 4–6 feet tall — among the tallest of any shade perennial. Excellent at the back of a shaded border or naturalized in moist woodland gardens alongside ferns, hostas, and trilliums. More heat tolerant than hybrid garden astilbes and better adapted to the variable rainfall of the Southeast. The dried plumes persist attractively into fall and winter. Unlike the rhizomatous spreading of some astilbes, this species forms upright, gradually expanding clumps.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring as soil becomes workable, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Astilbe biternata is the only astilbe native to North America and establishes best with consistent moisture during its first season.
directions: Plant crown divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial shade, with the crown set just at or slightly below the soil surface. Astilbe biternata is the only species of astilbe native to North America, occurring naturally in the moist, rich coves and wooded slopes of the southern Appalachians, where it produces bold, bi- to tri-ternate foliage and large, creamy-white plume flowers from June to July — far larger and more architectural than most Asian astilbes. Keep evenly moist throughout the growing season; drought causes premature browning of leaf margins and reduces flowering. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor, as older crowns can die out at the center.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; false hellebore emerges very early in spring and is a bold architectural plant, but all parts are extremely toxic — never allow contact with eyes, mouth, or open wounds.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade near streams, bogs, and moist woodland; false hellebore requires consistently high moisture and is best in permanently wet or seepy sites. Veratrum viride is one of the most dramatic and bold-textured native wildflowers of eastern North American and Pacific Northwest mountain forests; it emerges very early in spring as spectacular, tightly pleated, corn-like leaves that unfurl to produce a towering, 3–6-foot-tall stem bearing large, plume-like panicles of small, yellowish-green, star-shaped flowers in mid-summer. The dramatic tropical appearance belies the plant's extreme cold-hardiness and cold-zone nativity; it is outstanding for bold foliage effect in moist, shaded woodland gardens. ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE EXTREMELY TOXIC — among the most poisonous native plants in North America, causing severe neurological symptoms if ingested. Handle with gloves and keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in deep, cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in full to partial shade; Deinanthe bifida is a rare Japanese woodland perennial that requires protection from afternoon sun and drying winds, and rewards patient cultivation with unusual nodding flowers and bold textured foliage.
directions: Plant divisions in cool, deep, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in full shade, enriched with leaf mold or compost; Deinanthe bifida is a rare and prized collector's plant in the hydrangea family (Hydrangeaceae), native to the shaded mountain woodlands of Japan, where it produces bold, deeply textured, wrinkled leaves and nodding, cupped white to pale-blue flowers in summer that are unlike any other shade perennial in appearance. It requires consistent moisture and cool root conditions — mulch heavily to maintain soil temperature and moisture through summer. Protect from deer and slugs, and avoid disturbing established clumps, which resent division and are slow to re-establish.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or scarify and cold-stratify seeds before spring planting.
directions: Scarify seeds and cold-stratify for 4–6 weeks before spring sowing, or direct sow in fall to let natural winter conditions break dormancy. Baptisia is a slow-starting plant — expect minimal bloom for the first 2–3 years, but once established, the clump requires virtually no care and lives for decades. The indigo-blue lupine-like flower spikes appear in late spring and are followed by attractive, inflated seedpods that rattle in the wind. Do not attempt to transplant established plants, as the deep taproot does not tolerate disturbance.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in any moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; false indigo is extremely adaptable to difficult wet, flooded, or droughty conditions once established and can be used for streambank stabilization.
directions: Plant in any moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; false indigo is a large, airy native shrub with pinnately compound leaves and 3–6 inch spikes of unusual dark purple-violet flowers with bright orange anthers in early summer — a striking color combination. It blooms at a time when few other shrubs are flowering, providing important early nectar for native bees and the southern dogface butterfly, whose caterpillars feed exclusively on the plant. It is one of the most adaptable native shrubs for wet, poorly drained soils, riverbanks, and flood-prone areas, tolerating temporary inundation and spreading to stabilize streambanks. After the flowers, clusters of resin-dotted seed pods remain through winter. Prune back by one-third after flowering to maintain a compact form. Despite its common name it has no connection to true indigo (Indigofera).

plant_note: Plant softwood or semi-hardwood cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, organically rich soil at streambanks, pond edges, or low-lying areas prone to seasonal flooding.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade along streambanks, pond margins, and low-lying areas subject to periodic flooding; false indigo bush is a fast-growing, wide-ranging native shrub found from Ontario to Florida and west to the Great Plains, producing striking 3–6 inch racemes of deep purple flowers with bright orange anthers that create a vivid two-tone contrast in late spring — one of the most visually dramatic native shrubs in flower. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it actively improves soil fertility and is an excellent anchor species for riparian restoration and streambank erosion control projects. The fine-textured, pinnately compound foliage remains attractive through the season, and the plant tolerates brief inundation that would kill most shrubs. Bees — especially bumble bees and native leafcutter bees — heavily visit the flowers. In rich, moist conditions it can sucker to form large colonies, which is desirable for mass plantings and erosion control; remove suckers to keep it shrub-sized in garden settings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; false lily of the valley spreads slowly and politely by rhizome, unlike the aggressive true lily of the valley it resembles.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; false lily of the valley spreads slowly and politely by rhizome, unlike the aggressive true lily of the valley it resembles. Glossy, evergreen, strap-shaped leaves form a low, tidy rosette from which short spikes of small, star-shaped, fragrant white flowers rise in mid-spring, giving it a passing resemblance to lily of the valley without that plant's toxicity concerns or runaway spread. Native to moist woodland understories in central China, it holds its foliage year-round in mild climates, making it a useful evergreen edger or small-scale groundcover under shrubs and trees where a well-behaved companion to hellebores and hostas is wanted. It resents hot, dry conditions, so keep soil consistently moist and mulch to conserve moisture through summer.

plant_note: Divide clumps or set out nursery plugs in spring into consistently moist to wet, rich soil along pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens; unlike true nettles, its leaves carry no stinging hairs.
directions: Divide clumps or set out nursery plugs in spring into consistently moist to wet, rich soil along pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens; unlike true nettles, its leaves carry no stinging hairs, so it is safe to handle and site near paths. It quietly colonizes damp shade by rhizome and inconspicuous green flower spikes, functioning more as habitat infrastructure than a showpiece. Because it lacks the toxic aphids and chemistry of true stinging nettle, gardeners plant it as a safe host for Red Admiral, Eastern Comma, and Question Mark caterpillars, all of which will readily switch to it where wild nettle is scarce.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed immediately after harvest in late spring directly into the garden; seed requires warm-then-cold double dormancy and will not germinate until the second spring after a double stratification period. Alternatively sow in fall outdoors and allow to stratify naturally over winter for spring germination.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade under deciduous trees or in a shaded rock garden; false rue anemone is a charming and delicate small European woodland perennial in the buttercup family, closely related to the North American native Enemion (with which it was once synonymous), producing a profusion of small five-petaled white flowers on thread-fine stems from March through May before going fully dormant by early summer. The lacy, blue-green, thrice-divided leaves closely resemble those of meadow rue (Thalictrum) and rue anemone (Thalictrum thalictroides), making it a beautiful companion for both in the spring woodland garden. It spreads slowly by self-sowing to form loose, delicate colonies and is especially effective planted in drifts in shaded rock garden crevices, at the base of stone walls, or along woodland paths. A refined and uncommon plant that rewards the collector of shade perennials with its elegant early-spring display.

plant_note: Plant divisions or fresh seeds in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; false rue anemone is a delicate spring ephemeral of moist, rich deciduous forest floors in the eastern and central US, naturalized by spreading tuberous roots into modest patches.
directions: Plant fresh seeds or small tuber divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; false rue anemone is a delicate native spring ephemeral of rich, moist deciduous forest floors across the eastern and central US, producing small, compound leaves very similar to rue anemone (Thalictrum thalictroides) — the two species are similar enough that false rue anemone was long classified with Isopyrum. The small, white, five-petaled, star-shaped flowers are produced in early spring in great profusion on the small, branched plants. Despite the modest size, a naturalized colony provides a lovely, delicate spring display in deep shade where few other plants bloom. The plant is gone by late spring. Spreads slowly by tuberous roots and self-sowing. Easy to overlook if not in flower — pairs well with trilliums, wild ginger, and other spring wildflowers for a rich woodland spring garden composition.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; false rue anemone is a spring ephemeral that goes dormant by early summer — it is one of the most delicate and beautiful of all native spring woodland wildflowers.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; false rue anemone goes dormant by early summer and is a spring ephemeral that should be planted with later-emerging shade plants to cover the gap. Isopyrum biternatum is a delicate, diminutive native spring ephemeral of midwestern and southern floodplain forests, closely resembling rue anemone (Anemonella thalictroides) with its finely divided, ternate, glaucous leaves and white, star-shaped, 5-petaled flowers on hair-fine stems in early spring; unlike rue anemone (eastern), false rue anemone is primarily a midwestern species found in rich bottomland forests from Ontario to Georgia and Kansas. It forms small colonies from fibrous roots in humus-rich, moist soil and is a charming, difficult-to-find native wildflower for collectors of spring woodland plants.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; false sarsaparilla is a vigorous twining vine or sprawling shrub that blooms in late winter and early spring (July–September in Australia; January–April in zone 9) when little else is flowering. Several selections are available: 'Happy Wanderer' (vigorous vine with deep purple flowers), 'Mini Haha' (compact shrub form), white-flowered and pink-flowered forms. Tolerates moderate drought once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; false sarsaparilla is one of the most widely grown and adaptable Australian native ornamentals outside its homeland — a vigorous twining vine or sprawling groundcover shrub that produces in late winter and early spring a spectacular, prolific display of small but densely clustered, typical sweet pea-family flowers in vivid, rich, deep purple-violet with a distinctive small, contrasting, white-and-yellow mark at the center of each standard petal. The flowers are borne in long, pendant or arching racemes of 20–40 individual blossoms, and a plant in full late-winter bloom — covered in masses of deep-purple flower racemes against the dark, leathery, lance-shaped evergreen leaves — is a very striking sight in the winter-spring garden. The bloom period (late winter to early spring) provides vivid purple color at a time when the garden most needs it, and the flowers are attractive to honeyeating birds and bees. The form 'Happy Wanderer' is among the most commonly available and most vigorous cultivars. Tolerates considerable neglect once established, making it an ideal low-maintenance vine for fences, banks, and ground-covering in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant offsets or direct sow seeds in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, infertile, neutral to alkaline, coastal soil in full sun. False Sisal produces offsets (pups) freely around the base of the rosette — these are the most reliable propagation method. It is monocarpic, blooming once after 10–20 years then dying, but the offsets ensure colony persistence.
directions: False Sisal is a native agave of the coastal scrub, pine rocklands, and coastal dune communities of southern Florida and the Caribbean, producing a dramatic, architectural rosette of long, sword-like, blue-green leaves armed with sharp terminal spines and marginal teeth. Like all agaves, False Sisal is monocarpic — the main rosette blooms once after 10–20 years, sending up a spectacular branched flower stalk reaching 15–25 feet tall bearing thousands of pale yellow flowers that attract a spectacular diversity of moths, bats, and native bees, before the main rosette dies. However, the plant compensates by freely producing offsets (pups) around its base for years before flowering, ensuring colony persistence. Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, infertile, neutral to slightly alkaline coastal soil in full sun; False Sisal is highly drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established but cannot tolerate frost, clay, or persistently wet conditions.

common_name: False Solomon Seal (Feathery False Lily of the Valley)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring before new growth in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in part shade to full shade; false Solomon seal spreads slowly by rhizome to form colonies in suitable conditions, providing outstanding woodland texture and wildlife value.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; mulch with leaf litter to maintain the woodland conditions the plant prefers.
