Maianthemum racemosum (false Solomon seal or Solomon plume, formerly Smilacina racemosa) is one of the most beautiful and important native woodland wildflowers of eastern North America — a rhizomatous perennial producing graceful, arching, unbranched stems 18–36 inches tall with broad, prominently parallel-veined leaves arranged alternately, and ending in a feathery, branching plume of tiny, creamy-white, fragrant flowers in April–May — superficially resembling Solomon seal (Polygonatum biflorum) in stem and leaf but distinguished by the terminal flower cluster rather than axillary flowers. The flowers are followed by attractive clusters of small, green-spotted berries ripening to ruby-red in late summer, which are edible (somewhat bitter-sweet) but more important as bird food for migratory thrushes and other fruit-eating birds. The plant provides bold, tropical-looking foliage texture in shaded woodland gardens, making an excellent companion for ferns, trilliums, and hostas. It is largely maintenance-free in suitable cool woodland conditions but struggles in hot, dry zones without consistent moisture.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; false Solomon's seal spreads slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies and is best left undisturbed once established.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; false Solomon's seal spreads slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies and is best left undisturbed once established. Maianthemum racemosum (formerly Smilacina racemosa) is one of the most beautiful and versatile native woodland wildflowers of eastern North America; it produces arching stems bearing large, parallel-veined, oval leaves arranged alternately in a pattern nearly identical to true Solomon's seal (Polygonatum), but unlike Solomon's seal it bears showy, frothy plumes of tiny, fragrant, white flowers at the stem tips in late spring — one of the most ornamental flowering effects in the spring shade garden — followed by clusters of ruby-red berries in late summer that are mildly edible when fully ripe but somewhat cathartic. It is an outstanding, all-season shade perennial with interest from spring flowers through red fall berries and golden fall foliage.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost date or start indoors 4–6 weeks earlier for bloom the first season.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in the garden or start indoors; unlike true perennial rudbeckia, heliopsis often blooms robustly in its first season from an early start. Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil; plants tolerate heat and short dry periods better than helenium. Deadhead regularly throughout summer to keep the golden-yellow, semi-double or double flowers coming continuously from July through September. Divide clumps every 3 years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and prevent the center from dying out.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in cool, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; false violet is native to cool northern and montane forests and struggles in hot, dry, or heavy clay conditions further south.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in cool, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; false violet is native to cool northern and montane forests and struggles in hot, dry, or heavy clay conditions further south. Dalibarda repens is a diminutive, creeping woodland groundcover with rounded, violet-like, evergreen leaves and two kinds of small white flowers — showy open blooms that rarely set seed and inconspicuous self-pollinating blooms low on the plant that do — followed by small dry, raspberry-like fruit. It forms a low, dense mat in consistently cool, moist, acidic woodland soil and is best used as a specialty groundcover in a shaded rock garden or native plant collection rather than a large-scale planting, since it spreads slowly and resents disturbance. Keep the soil evenly moist with a leaf-litter mulch and avoid summer drought stress, which quickly causes the shallow-rooted mats to decline.

common_name: Falstaff Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Falstaff's very dark flower color is most intense in cooler weather and can bleach somewhat in the hottest, most intense summer sun.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1999 and named for the Shakespearean character, Falstaff carries deep velvety crimson-purple blooms that darken further as they age, one of the darkest flower colors among English roses, with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous, arching shrub. Its dramatic, saturated color makes a bold accent in a mixed border, especially paired with lighter pastel companions, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fan aloe needs excellent drainage and is one of the more distinctively shaped aloes, developing a branching, tree-like form.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fan aloe needs excellent drainage and is one of the more distinctively shaped aloes, developing a branching, tree-like form. Flat, gray-green leaves arrange themselves in two neat, opposite ranks along each branch tip, forming a striking, hand-fan-shaped rosette unlike the typical spiral leaf arrangement of most other aloes, on a slow-growing, branching, shrub-to-small-tree form topped with orange-red flower spikes in late winter. Native to a very limited range in South Africa's Western Cape mountains, it is a highly prized specimen among aloe collectors for its unique fan-shaped growth habit and slow, tree-like branching structure that takes many years to develop. Water only occasionally once established, provide bright light with some protection from the most intense afternoon sun, and be patient with its slow, architecturally rewarding growth.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown rooted rhizome sections in acidic, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil under open pine or oak canopy in spring; fan clubmoss forms a mycorrhizal partnership with soil fungi and colonies transplanted from the wild rarely establish, so treat it as a slow, long-term planting from certified nursery stock.
directions: Plant nursery-grown rooted rhizome sections in acidic, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil under open pine or oak canopy in spring; fan clubmoss forms a mycorrhizal partnership with soil fungi and colonies transplanted from the wild rarely establish, so treat it as a slow, long-term planting from certified nursery stock. Long, horizontal above-ground runners send up flattened, fan-shaped, evergreen branches that closely resemble a miniature cedar seedling, gradually knitting together into broad woodland-floor colonies once established. It is the clubmoss most often cut for holiday greenery ('running cedar') in the eastern and southeastern United States, and heavy wild harvesting has made established colonies increasingly scarce, so cultivated plantings help take pressure off native stands. Once rooted it tolerates the light, dappled shade and dry-to-average duff of upland pine-oak woods with little care.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; fan flower tolerates coastal salt spray, heat, and humidity far better than most annuals, making it ideal for Gulf Coast container gardens.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; fan flower is an Australian native that produces an almost continuous cascade of distinctive fan-shaped flowers in lavender-blue, purple, white, or pink — each flower has five petals arranged like an open hand or fan, all on one side (the upper half of the flower is missing, giving it a uniquely asymmetric appearance). It trails attractively from hanging baskets and container edges and tolerates heat, humidity, coastal conditions, and mild drought significantly better than most summer annuals. Self-cleaning (no deadheading required). One of the most heat-tolerant lavender-blue-flowered annuals for Gulf South summer gardens. 'Blue Wonder' and 'Surdiva Blue' are excellent long-blooming selections.

common_name: Fan Scarlet Cardinal Flower (Compact Early-Blooming Seed Strain)
plant_note: Surface-sow seed (do not cover) indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Fan Scarlet is a compact, early-blooming seed strain of cardinal flower bred for uniform first-year flowering from seed.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near water features, rain gardens, or boggy areas. Fan Scarlet was bred as a compact, uniform seed strain that reliably flowers the first year from seed and blooms earlier in the season than typical straight-species cardinal flower, producing the same brilliant scarlet flower spikes prized as the premier nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds, on a plant scaled for containers and smaller garden beds. Plants are short-lived perennials that self-seed freely; allow some seedlings to remain to perpetuate the colony, as individual plants typically live only two to three years.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fanal requires consistently moist soil — it will not tolerate prolonged drought, and in zone 9 summer heat the crown should be mulched deeply and irrigation provided during dry periods.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fanal is one of the most widely grown and celebrated astilbe cultivars — a Georg Arends hybrid producing deep blood-red to garnet-red plume-like flower spikes in early summer above a mound of attractive, bronzy-green, finely cut compound foliage. The dark red flower color of Fanal is among the deepest and most saturated in the astilbe genus — a vivid crimson-red that provides maximum color impact in the shaded border when paired with white, pale pink, or silver-foliage companions. The dark, bronzy-tinted foliage is ornamental even when the plant is not in bloom. Astilbes are among the finest shade-garden perennials for moist, humus-rich soils — they thrive in conditions that challenge most plants: deep shade, wet spots near streams and ponds, and the damp cool environments under trees. In zone 9, astilbes require careful siting in deep shade with consistently moist soil and good organic matter to succeed through the summer heat — they are not as reliable in zone 9 as in zone 5–7. Mulch heavily to keep the crown cool and moist. The dried flower plumes remain attractive for weeks after bloom and provide winter garden interest. Divide every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Fancy Frills Tulip (White Fringed Tulip Feathered Pink)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Fancy Frills is a Fringed-class tulip with white petals feathered pink at the edges, blooming late in the season.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Fancy Frills bears white petals delicately feathered with pink at the edges, each petal margin finely crystalline-fringed in the distinctive texture of the Fringed tulip class, blooming late in the tulip season for an extended spring bulb display when paired with earlier-blooming cultivars. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Plant tubers (bulbs) in spring after soil warms to 65°F or above in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; fancy leaf caladiums are among the most spectacular foliage plants for shaded summer gardens in zone 9 and thrive in the hot, humid Gulf Coast summer when planted in shade.
directions: Plant tubers 2 inches deep with the knobby side up in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade after soil warms above 65°F; keep consistently moist. Caladium bicolor (fancy leaf caladium) is among the most dazzling shade plants for Gulf Coast gardens — a Brazilian tropical producing enormous, arrow-shaped, paper-thin leaves 6–18 inches long in spectacular combinations of white, pink, red, rose, and green in hundreds of named cultivars, with intricate patterns including bold veining, freckling, splashing, and marbling that make each leaf look individually hand-painted. The leaves are entirely the spectacle — the small flowers that occasionally appear should be removed to direct energy to foliage. Caladiums thrive in the hot, humid shade that challenges most other plants: full shade under live oaks, dappled light under large canopy trees, and shaded patios are ideal. They go dormant and the tubers can be left in the ground in zones 9–12 through mild winters, or dug and stored at 55–60°F. The 'Strap Leaf' (Caladium picturatum) types have narrower leaves; 'Sun Tolerant' cultivars can handle morning sun. A defining seasonal plant for the humid Gulf South shade garden.

plant_note: Plant tubers 1–2 inches deep, knobby side up, after soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 this is typically March–May. Tubers can be left in ground year-round in zones 9–11 with winter mulch, or lifted after frost kills foliage and stored above 60°F for replanting.
directions: Caladiums are the quintessential tropical shade plant, producing large, paper-thin leaves in spectacular combinations of red, pink, white, and green that brighten dark beds and containers through the summer heat. Plant tubers shallowly in loose, humus-rich, well-drained soil under trees or on the north side of structures where they receive bright indirect light or dappled morning sun; direct afternoon sun bleaches and scorches the leaves. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged — the tubers rot readily in standing water. In zone 9 the long warm season produces lush foliage from May through October; reduce watering as leaves yellow in fall and allow tubers to go dormant in place with a layer of mulch.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out transplants in spring into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; in zone 9, Fanfare can also be started in late summer for fall establishment and bloom the following year.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Fanfare won an All-America Selections award in 2005 for its distinctive flower form, in which the base of each ray petal fuses into a narrow, trumpet-like tube before flaring open at the tip, giving the red-orange, yellow-tipped blooms a ruffled, almost fringed look that sets it apart from the flat-petaled species and standard hybrid cultivars. The unusual petal shape does not reduce pollinator appeal, and bees and butterflies visit it as readily as ordinary blanket flower. It flowers over a long season from late spring through fall on a compact, mounding plant that rarely needs staking. As with all Gaillardia, sharp drainage is the single most important factor for survival through humid Gulf Coast summers and wet winters.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing at least 18 inches apart for air circulation; Fanick's Phlox was discovered thriving in a San Antonio, Texas, nursery where standard garden phlox cultivars had failed, and it is one of the few tall garden phlox selections that reliably survives as a true perennial through Gulf South summer heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation. Fanick's Phlox was discovered as a chance seedling at Fanick's Garden Center in San Antonio, Texas, where it persisted and thrived for years despite the intense summer heat that typically causes garden phlox (Phlox paniculata) to decline or succumb to powdery mildew within a season or two in the South. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension trials confirmed its outstanding heat tolerance and disease resistance relative to standard garden phlox cultivars, and it was subsequently promoted as one of the few tall phlox reliably perennial in zone 8-9 gardens. It produces large, fragrant clusters of soft lavender-pink flowers from early summer into fall, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds, on sturdy, upright stems that hold up well without staking. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in early spring to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent flower heads to prolong bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding.

common_name: Fannie Munson Caladium (Classic Large Rose-Pink Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fannie Munson produces large, heavy tubers over successive seasons — in zone 9, leave tubers in ground over winter with a layer of mulch protection.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fannie Munson is one of the most enduring and widely sold large fancy-leaf caladium varieties — a classic pink caladium with large, heart-shaped leaves bearing deep rose-pink to warm-pink centers and veining that radiates from the leaf center, semi-translucent whitish areas between veins that create a luminous, stained-glass effect, and fresh-green margins that frame and contrast the vivid pink interior pattern. The distinctive leaf pattern of Fannie Munson — the combination of deep rose-pink veins, translucent pink-white intervein areas, and the green margin — creates one of the most elegant and recognizable fancy-leaf caladium appearances, more detailed and complex than solid-colored types and more structured than randomly mottled varieties. Fannie Munson has remained in continuous commercial production for many decades because of its reliable performance, vigorous tuber production, excellent leaf quality, and universally appealing soft-pink color scheme. In zone 9, Fannie Munson is outstanding through the entire warm season (May–October), the tubers increasing in size year over year when allowed to overwinter in-ground with protective mulch. The warm-pink coloration pairs beautifully with pure white companions (white impatiens, 'Aaron' or 'Candidum' caladiums, white-flowered begonias) for a soft romantic effect, or with burgundy-to-dark-foliage companions for high contrast.

common_name: Fantasy Crape Myrtle (Tall White-Flowered Fauriei Selection with Cinnamon Bark)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fantasy is a pure Lagerstroemia fauriei selection, rather than an indica hybrid, grown mainly for its outstanding cinnamon exfoliating bark and very large mature size.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, siting this large, tree-form selection where it has ample room to grow into a substantial shade tree. Fantasy is a selection of Lagerstroemia fauriei, the Japanese species behind the mildew resistance and exfoliating bark of the modern Indian-series hybrids, grown less for its relatively modest white flower clusters than for its own outstanding qualities: smooth, richly colored cinnamon bark that peels in large sheets, and a fast-growing habit that can reach 30 to 40 feet, among the tallest of any crape myrtle. It is essentially free of powdery mildew, a trait inherited from its Lagerstroemia fauriei parentage. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural form; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter as the tree matures into a fine specimen or shade tree.

common_name: Fantasy Pink Morn Petunia (Compact Pink-and-White Milliflora Petunia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Fantasy Pink Morn is a compact milliflora-type petunia bred for tidy, uniform bedding and container use.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Fantasy Pink Morn belongs to the milliflora class of petunia, bred for smaller, more numerous flowers on compact, densely branched plants rather than the fewer, larger blooms of grandiflora types, opening soft pink petals with a white star at the center in great profusion. Its tidy, uniform habit makes it especially well suited to edging, window boxes, and mixed containers where a large-flowered petunia would look coarse. It requires little deadheading to stay tidy and floriferous through the summer, and responds well to a midsummer shearing if growth becomes sparse in peak heat.

common_name: Fantin-Latour Rose (Soft Pink Cupped Centifolia Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Fantin-Latour is a Centifolia-type rose named for the French painter famous for his rose still lifes.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Fantin-Latour tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough old garden rose. Named for the French painter Henri Fantin-Latour, celebrated for his luminous rose still-life paintings, this Centifolia-type rose bears very full, softly cupped, soft pink double blooms with a light, sweet fragrance on a graceful, arching, relatively tall shrub. Like other old Centifolia types it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow in place; tolerates poor dry soil well.
directions: Direct sow this western native in early spring, barely covering the small seed. Farewell to spring produces spikes of ruffled pink to lavender flowers on slender upright stems that make good cut flowers. It prefers lean, dry soil and full sun, blooming as spring transitions into summer. Avoid overwatering and fertilizing, which reduce flowering, and let plants self-sow for future displays.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in part shade to full shade; farfugium establishes readily in moist, shaded locations. In zone 7b–10 it is fully evergreen through winter and thrives year-round. The bold, leathery foliage provides a dramatic tropical effect throughout the growing season; flowers appear in fall to winter.
directions: Plant in part shade to full shade in moist, rich, well-drained soil; farfugium (sometimes called leopard plant) is one of the finest and most underused shade perennials for Southern gardens, producing large, round, leathery, glossy green leaves up to 12 inches across on long petioles — creating a bold, tropical-looking accent in shaded beds where most other perennials look tired. Unlike its cousin Ligularia dentata, farfugium tolerates the heat and humidity of zone 8–9 summers without wilting, making it far better suited to Gulf Coast gardens. Bright yellow daisy flowers appear in November–December, providing rare winter color in shade beds. The standard species has plain green leaves; the cultivar 'Aureomaculata' (leopard plant) features dramatic yellow spots on the foliage. Divide crowded clumps every 3–4 years in early spring; the plant is virtually maintenance-free beyond occasional watering during dry periods.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Farges' barrenwort forms a slowly spreading clump with red-mottled new growth and delicate pink to white spring flowers.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where the plant can build a slowly expanding clump over several seasons. Epimedium fargesii is a west-central Chinese species with narrow, spiny-margined leaflets that emerge mottled with red-bronze tones before maturing to green, complemented by loose sprays of small pink-to-white, long-spurred flowers in spring. Its refined foliage texture and subtle flower color suit a shaded woodland or rock garden setting where it can be viewed up close, and it combines well with hellebores and hardy ferns as a long-lived, low-maintenance groundcover.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Farges' jack-in-the-pulpit is one of the more adaptable and easy-to-grow Chinese Arisaema species, tolerating a wider range of garden conditions than some of its relatives.
directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Farges' jack-in-the-pulpit is one of the more adaptable and easy-to-grow Chinese Arisaema species, tolerating a wider range of garden conditions than some of its relatives. Arisaema fargesii is a Chinese woodland aroid with broad, three-parted, glossy dark green leaflets often marked with a paler central vein, and a green-and-white striped hooded flower with a distinctive drooping, tongue-like appendage in mid-spring, followed by a spike of red berries in fall. Its relatively easygoing nature and handsome, boldly patterned leaves make it a good entry point into growing Arisaema for gardeners new to the genus, thriving in the same conditions favored by hosta and ferns. As with all Arisaema, the berries and sap contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals, so keep the attractive fall fruit away from pets and children.

plant_note: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; also does well started from seed for bedding use, since Fascination breeds fairly true.
directions: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost, spacing plants 12–18 inches apart for a compact bedding effect. An Award of Garden Merit winner, Fascination is a dwarf, bushy dahlia grown as much for its dark bronze-purple, finely cut foliage as for its semi-double, bright pink flowers with a lighter pink collar, produced prolifically from midsummer through frost. Its compact habit needs no staking and no pinching, making it far lower-maintenance than tall dinner-plate types, and its dark foliage adds season-long contrast in mixed containers and border edges even between flushes of bloom. In zones colder than 8, lift tubers after the first light frost blackens the foliage and store in a cool, dry, frost-free place over winter.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; Fascinator prayer plant wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; Fascinator prayer plant wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11. Oval leaves are patterned with bold reddish-pink veins radiating from the midrib over a rich green background, a striking color combination that intensifies with bright indirect light, and like all prayer plants the leaves fold upward at night and unfurl again each morning in a distinctive daily rhythm. Native to the humid forest floor of Brazil, it thrives in the higher humidity of a bathroom, kitchen, or terrarium-adjacent setting and struggles in dry indoor air, often developing crispy leaf edges without a humidifier or regular misting. Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged, avoid tap water high in fluoride or chlorine if leaf tips brown, and divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and renew vigor.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Fashion is a Glenn Dale Hybrid that tolerates more cold than Southern Indian Hybrids — hardy to zone 6 — while still performing excellently in zone 9 heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Fashion is one of the classic Glenn Dale Hybrid azaleas — a group developed by USDA plant breeder Benjamin Yeo Morrison at the Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station in Maryland from the 1930s through the 1950s to extend azalea hardiness beyond the frost-tender Southern Indian Hybrids while maintaining large flowers and good landscape habit. Fashion produces distinctive, hose-in-hose (flower-within-a-flower) double flowers in a warm salmon-coral to orange-salmon tone — a color combination unusual among landscape azaleas, where pink, purple, and red predominate. The hose-in-hose flower form gives each bloom a doubled, full appearance that is particularly attractive and distinctive. Plants grow vigorously to 4–6 feet in zone 9, with a broad, mounded to spreading habit and semi-evergreen to evergreen foliage. Fashion blooms in mid-spring and is a single-season bloomer (unlike the Encore rebloomers), but the distinctive flower color and form make it a valued addition to the azalea collection. The Glenn Dale Hybrids as a group are underused in modern landscapes compared to the heavily marketed Encore series; Fashion represents a classic selection worth preserving.

plant_note: Plant divisions or transplants in spring in full sun and hot, dry, well-drained soil; avoid wet winter sites.
directions: This selection of pink muhly grass was chosen specifically for flowering roughly three weeks earlier than the straight species, so the trademark haze of cotton-candy-pink plumes appears in late summer rather than fall, extending the display before cool weather arrives. Fine, wiry blue-green foliage forms a tidy mound that stays neat all season and needs no staking or deadheading. Gardeners in regions with shorter autumns choose 'Fast Forward' over standard pink muhly so the bloom show has time to develop before frost cuts it short. It thrives in hot, lean, well-drained soil and resents winter wet, so raised beds or sandy sites suit it best.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fastigiata is one of the older, classic narrow upright boxwood selections, used for generations in formal European-style gardens.
directions: Fastigiata is a long-established, classic narrow upright boxwood cultivar, its name referring to the fastigiate, columnar branching habit that has made it a staple of formal European-style garden design for generations, typically used in matched pairs or rows to frame an entry, path, or formal parterre. Its dense, deep green, small-leaved foliage gives the same year-round structure as other boxwood cultivars while holding a taller, narrower profile than rounded forms. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; light shearing in late winter or after the spring flush maintains a crisp, formal outline.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost, or direct sow in warm soil.
directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow in warm soil, spacing plants about a foot apart. Fata Morgana offers soft, ruffled pincushion blooms in shades of peach and apricot on slender stems, lovely in borders, cottage gardens, and bouquets. Deadhead and cut regularly to keep the long-lasting flowers coming and to draw pollinators. Give it full sun and well-drained soil.

plant_note: Start from seed after the last frost or set out nursery divisions in spring so plants establish a strong root system before their first winter.
directions: Fatal Attraction stands apart from ordinary purple coneflower by pairing rich magenta-purple ray petals with near-black stems and calyxes, giving the whole plant a dramatic two-tone silhouette even before the dark orange-brown cone opens. Grow it in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; overly rich or wet ground softens the stem color and can shorten the clump's lifespan. Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering into late summer, or leave the last flush standing so the spiny seed heads feed goldfinches through winter. The strong dark stems make this cultivar a favorite for cut-flower gardeners who want contrast without relying on unusual petal color alone.

common_name: Father Hugo Rose (Golden Rose of China)
subcategory: species shrub rose, early spring bloomer
plant_note: Set container or bare-root plants in early spring in well-drained soil, spacing widely to accommodate the shrub's fountain-like mature form.
directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation and well-drained soil, watering deeply while roots establish and then relying mostly on natural rainfall. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since blooms form on the previous year's growth. This is one of the earliest roses to flower each year, covering its arching, fern-like foliage with pale yellow single blooms in mid-spring before most other roses have even leafed out. Small dark hips follow in fall, and the fine-textured foliage gives the shrub an airy, graceful habit distinct from typical garden roses.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Fatshedera is a bigeneric hybrid between Fatsia japonica and English ivy and inherits a sprawling, semi-vining habit that benefits from staking or a support if grown upright.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind. This unusual bigeneric cross between Fatsia japonica and English ivy was first raised in France in 1912 and combines the bold, glossy, lobed foliage of Fatsia with a looser, semi-climbing habit inherited from its ivy parent. Left unstaked it sprawls and roots where it touches soil, making a good shade groundcover or informal hedge, or it can be tied to a support for a more upright accent. It tolerates deep shade better than most broadleaf evergreens, is easy from cuttings, and needs only an occasional light pruning to control its size.

common_name: Fatsia (Japanese Fatsia, Japanese Aralia, Glossy-Leaf Paper Plant)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; fatsia is exceptionally shade tolerant and actually performs better in deep shade than in full sun, where the large leaves can bleach and burn in heat.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fatsia is one of the most dramatic and tropical-looking shade shrubs for zone 7–11 gardens, producing enormous, glossy, deeply lobed leaves 12–18 inches across on bold, multi-stemmed plants that create an instant tropical feel in the darkest garden corners. The leaves hold their rich, dark green color year-round and are remarkably resistant to wind damage. Clusters of small white ball-shaped flowers appear in fall, followed by black berries. It is one of the most shade-tolerant large shrubs available and thrives under the dense canopy of live oaks and other large trees where most plants fail. The variegated form ('Variegata') has attractive white-edged leaves. Equally at home as an outdoor landscape shrub in zone 7–11 and as a bold container plant for covered patios and atriums.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors a few weeks early.
directions: Direct sow after frost or start indoors 4-6 weeks early, spacing compact plants 8-10 inches apart. These single-row-petaled French marigolds make pollen easy for bees to reach, and their tidy, full habit shines at the front of a bed or tucked among vegetables. They grow and flower quickly with continuous blooms from spring to frost. Deadhead for tidiness and prolonged flowering, and water at the base.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Faxon yucca is a slow-growing Trans-Pecos native that eventually forms a stout, tree-like trunk over many years.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; Faxon yucca is a large, dramatic, tree-forming yucca of the Chihuahuan Desert and Trans-Pecos region, with stiff, dagger-like blue-green leaves crowded at the tips of one or more thick, woody trunks that develop slowly over decades of growth. A massive, densely packed flower spike of creamy white, waxy bell-shaped blooms rises several feet above the foliage in spring, one of the showiest floral displays of any cold-hardy desert plant. It is extremely drought and heat tolerant once established and tolerates winter cold well beyond what its desert origin suggests, needing only sharp drainage and full sun to thrive for many decades as a slow-growing architectural specimen. Give it plenty of room from walkways, since the rigid, spine-tipped leaves can cause painful puncture injuries on contact.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil or start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; feather celosia is a distinct form of celosia from the cockscomb (cristata) type, producing upright, feathery, silky plume-like flower heads in brilliant shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and purple that are among the most striking warm-season bedding and cut flowers for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface after last frost (they need some light for germination); thin to 6–12 inches depending on variety size. Celosia argentea var. plumosa (feather or plume celosia) is one of the three main celosia types — the others being the brain/cockscomb cristata form and the wheat-spike spicata form — distinguished by its upright, tapering, silky, feathery plume-like flower heads that resemble ostrich feathers or soft velvet flames in brilliant, saturated colors. The plumosa types are among the most brilliantly colored warm-season annuals available for bedding, cut flower, and container gardens; flowers are extraordinarily heat-tolerant, blooming continuously through Gulf Coast and Southern summers that defeat most other annuals. Colors range from deepest crimson red through orange, gold, peach, pink, and creamy white. Fresh flowers have a unique velvety texture; dried flowers hold their color well for wreaths and dried arrangements. The foliage and flowers of all celosia types are edible (used as vegetables in parts of Africa where Celosia argentea is an important leaf vegetable) and highly nutritious.

common_name: Feather Falls Carex (Fine-Textured Weeping Green Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Feather Falls forms a dense, gracefully weeping mound of fine, bright green foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Feather Falls forms a dense, fountain-like mound of very fine, bright green, thread-like foliage that cascades gracefully over its edges, functioning almost like a miniature ornamental grass in shaded spots where true grasses struggle to perform. Its fine texture provides an excellent contrast to bold, broad-leaved shade perennials like hostas and heucheras, and works especially well spilling over the edge of a raised bed, container, or low wall. It tolerates both consistently moist soil and brief dry spells once established and is evergreen to semi-evergreen in milder climates, needing only an occasional light combing-out of tired old foliage in early spring to stay looking fresh.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring; 'Karl Foerster' is sterile and must be propagated by division.
directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in average, moisture-retentive soil; 'Karl Foerster' feather reed grass is one of the most reliable and widely adapted ornamental grasses, tolerating clay soil, humidity, and cold winters that defeat many others. Strongly upright, narrow clumps emerge early in spring with feathery bronze-pink plumes appearing in early summer that fade to wheat-gold and persist through winter. Cut back to 4–6 in in late winter or early spring before new growth begins. Divide every 4–5 years in spring when the center begins to die out.

plant_note: Plant bulbs or corms in fall 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; situate in a woodland margin or meadow edge with consistent moisture.
directions: Stenanthium gramineum is a striking native bulbous perennial of the eastern United States and Appalachian foothills, producing a basal clump of long, grass-like, channeled leaves and an impressive flowering stem 3–6 feet tall topped with a dramatic, loose, feathery panicle of hundreds of tiny white to greenish-white or purplish-tinged star-shaped flowers from July through September — one of the tallest and most dramatic native wildflowers for moist shade gardens. It occurs naturally in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to acidic soils in open woods, meadow margins, and along stream banks in partial shade to full sun; plant bulbs in fall 2–3 inches deep. The tall flower spikes sway gracefully in summer breezes and provide important late-season nectar for pollinators including native bees and butterflies. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade in spring; rodgersia requires reliably moist to boggy soil and will not perform well if allowed to dry out — a mulched site near a stream, pond, or rain garden is ideal.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade; featherleaf rodgersia (elder-leafed rodgersia) is a Chinese shade perennial of exceptional character, producing some of the most bold and handsome foliage of any shade garden plant — the large, pinnately divided leaves with five to nine leaflets resemble an oversized elderberry leaf and are arranged in striking rosettes that expand from reddish-bronze emerging buds in spring to large, deep-green, prominently veined, leathery-textured plates that color to rich bronze, copper, and burgundy tones in autumn. In early to mid-summer the plant sends up tall, branching, astilbe-like flower plumes of tiny, pink to creamy-white, starry flowers well above the foliage. The cultivar 'Superba' with deep-pink flowers and bronze-flushed foliage is among the most widely grown, and 'Chocolate Wing' (dark-chocolate-red spring and fall foliage) is exceptional. Rodgersia requires consistently moist to wet soil and dislikes drought — it is ideal beside water features and in wet shade gardens where it can eventually colonize large areas with its slowly spreading rhizomes.

plant_note: Nick or soak scarified seed and direct sow in spring into rocky or caliche soil in full sun once the ground has warmed.
directions: Featherplume is a small, wiry-branched, nitrogen-fixing legume shrub of limestone hills, caliche flats, and rocky canyons across the Chihuahuan Desert from West Texas and southern New Mexico into northern Mexico. Its bicolor pea flowers, magenta fading to cream, open in flushes from spring through fall after rain and are followed by silky, feather-tipped seed plumes that catch the light and give the plant both its common name and extended ornamental interest into winter. It is a larval host for several native skipper butterflies and its flowers draw a steady stream of small native bees. Once rooted it is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant, needs no fertilizer thanks to its nitrogen-fixing nodules, and rarely requires pruning beyond an occasional shaping after the main spring bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; February daphne resents root disturbance and transplants poorly once established, so choose its permanent site carefully from the start.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial shade and leave it undisturbed once sited, since daphnes resent root disturbance; February daphne is a small deciduous shrub cherished for its very early, intensely fragrant, rosy-purple to pink flowers that wreathe the bare stems in late winter, often opening while snow is still on the ground and well before almost anything else in the garden. Flowers give way to bright red berries in summer, and the plant is compact and upright, fitting neatly into a shaded shrub border or entry planting where the winter fragrance can be enjoyed at close range. It performs best in cooler summer climates with a real winter chill and can be short-lived or stressed in prolonged summer heat and humidity. Every part of the plant, especially the berries and sap, is toxic if ingested and the sap can irritate skin, so site it away from children and pets who might be tempted by the colorful fruit, and wear gloves when pruning. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and avoid disturbing the root zone once planted.

common_name: February Gold Daffodil (Early-Blooming Miniature Cyclamineus Daffodil)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; February Gold is one of the earliest daffodils to bloom, often flowering in late winter well ahead of most other cultivars, giving an early splash of color in the shade garden's dormant season.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. February Gold is a Cyclamineus-type daffodil, recognizable by its swept-back petals and long trumpet that give the flower a distinctive windblown look, and it is prized above all for being one of the very earliest daffodils to bloom, often opening its golden-yellow flowers in late winter well before most other cultivars have even emerged. Its smaller, more graceful proportions compared to large trumpet types make it a good fit for naturalizing under deciduous trees and shrubs, where it gets adequate sun before the canopy leafs out. It multiplies reliably in climates with sufficient winter chill and, like all daffodils, is completely resistant to deer and rodents.

common_name: Felicia Hybrid Musk Rose (Fragrant Silvery-Pink Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Felicia is a fragrant, silvery-pink hybrid musk shrub rose that tolerates a bit of shade.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hybrid musk roses tolerate more shade than most rose classes, blooming reasonably well with just a half-day of direct sun. Felicia bears large clusters of double, silvery-pink blooms with soft salmon undertones and a strong, musky-sweet fragrance, opening on a dense, well-rounded shrub considered one of the most reliably floriferous hybrid musks. It repeats bloom well through the growing season and works equally well as a freestanding shrub or informal flowering hedge. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through summer to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Felicite Parmentier Rose (Pale Flesh-Pink Fragrant Alba Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; introduced in France in 1834, Felicite Parmentier is a compact Alba rose valued for its neat, dense habit.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba roses tolerate more shade than most roses, a legacy of their origin as tough, adaptable garden plants. Introduced in France in 1834, Felicite Parmentier bears very full, quartered, pale flesh-pink double blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening from deeper pink buds on a notably compact, dense shrub, more manageable in size than many taller Alba roses. Like other Albas it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season, and it is exceptionally disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Felix Crousse Peony (Classic Ruby-Red Double Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring.
directions: Plant divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil, and avoid mulching too heavily over the crown since burial deeper than two inches inhibits flowering. Provide grow-through support early in spring growth to keep the heavy blooms upright through summer storms. Dating to 1881, Felix Crousse is a long-established French heirloom prized for its intensely fragrant, ruby-red double flowers with a faint silvery sheen on the outer petals. Its midseason bloom time and dependable vigor have made it a mainstay of cut-flower and cottage-garden peony collections for generations.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; felt bush is a large-growing Madagascar succulent shrub that needs excellent drainage and tolerates full sun once acclimated.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; felt bush is a large-growing Madagascar succulent shrub that needs excellent drainage and tolerates full sun once acclimated. Large, undulating, triangular leaves are covered in a dense, brown-gray, velvety felt of fine hairs, giving the foliage a soft, suede-like texture and grayish color that is dramatically different from the smooth, glossy leaves of most kalanchoes, with the cultivar 'Fang' developing curious tooth-like growths on the leaf undersides. Left to grow, it becomes a substantial architectural shrub well over head height in frost-free gardens, or a striking large container specimen elsewhere, contrasting bold, felted texture against finer-leaved succulent companions. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact, well-textured growth, and protect from any frost.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in very well-drained, lean, calcareous or sandy soil in full sun; plants resent wet feet and thrive in rock gardens and dry prairie restorations.
directions: Fendler's Bladderpod (formerly Lesquerella fendleri) is a compact, cushion-forming native perennial in the mustard family, native to dry, calcareous, rocky, or sandy open ground across Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and adjacent states. In early spring — often before almost any other wildflower has opened — it covers itself in bright yellow, 4-petaled mustard flowers held just above a silver-gray mat of densely hairy, spatulate basal leaves; the flowers are followed by round, inflated, bladder-like seed pods that persist ornamentally on the plant. These early blooms are a critical first nectar source for native mining bees, mason bees, and other native pollinators emerging in late winter and early spring when forage is scarce. Grow in very well-drained, lean, calcareous or sandy soil in full sun; Fendler's Bladderpod is an excellent and underused native for rock gardens, dry native prairie mixes, and xeriscape plantings across the southern Great Plains.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade; Fendler's meadow rue grows naturally in open to lightly shaded canyon slopes, aspen groves, and montane meadow edges of the southern Rockies and Great Basin.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade; Fendler's meadow rue is the native meadow rue of the southern Rocky Mountains and Great Basin, growing in aspen groves, canyon-side scrub, and montane meadow margins. Like other meadow rues, it produces elegant, compound, blue-green, maidenhair-fern-like foliage — the primary ornamental feature — and loose panicles of small, wind-pollinated flowers. Fendler's meadow rue is dioecious (separate male and female plants), with the male plants having the showier flowers due to the dangling, yellow-green stamens. Notably more drought-tolerant than its eastern relatives, adapted to the drier conditions of the Rocky Mountain West. The finely textured, glaucous foliage provides excellent texture contrast in dry, shaded or dappled garden sites. A useful native for rock gardens, aspen-garden companion plantings, and dry shade under western native trees.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall or transplant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; fern-leaf corydalis is nearly evergreen in mild climates, providing attractive ferny foliage year-round. It self-sows freely in suitable moist, shaded conditions. Unlike the blue and yellow perennial corydalis species, this one blooms in spring and early summer, producing dense, upright racemes of golden-yellow tubular flowers above the fine, fern-like leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; fern-leaf corydalis is a Chinese woodland corydalis that provides two distinct garden qualities in one compact plant: extraordinary foliage and good spring flowers. The foliage is the main attraction — finely divided, multi-pinnate, lacy leaves of extreme delicacy, closely resembling the fronds of certain ferns or the foliage of fine ferny rock garden plants, in a soft, bronze-tinted green that deepens to bronzy-red in cooler weather and is nearly evergreen in mild climates, providing attractive winter presence in the shade garden. Against this cloud of delicate ferny foliage, dense, upright, cylindrical racemes of small, spurred, golden-yellow tubular flowers appear in spring and early summer — the soft yellow blooms contrasting warmly with the bronze-green fronds. It self-sows freely in cool, moist, shaded conditions, establishing naturalized colonies in suitable woodland garden soil. The combination of fern-like texture, bronze-green color, near-evergreen presence, and yellow spring flowers makes it an unusually versatile and attractive shade groundcover plant for zones 5–8.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; fern-leaf philodendron climbs readily and develops its most deeply divided leaves when given vertical support.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; fern-leaf philodendron climbs readily and develops its most deeply divided leaves when given vertical support. Mature leaves are cut into numerous narrow, finger-like segments radiating from a central point, giving the plant a delicate, feathery, fern-like texture that sets it dramatically apart from the broad, solid leaves typical of most philodendrons, with new leaves unfurling a coppery bronze before deepening to green. Native to Brazilian rainforests, it climbs steadily up a moss pole or trellis, and taller, more mature plants produce progressively larger and more finely divided leaves than young specimens. Keep humidity high, provide bright indirect light, and allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings to prevent root rot.

plant_note: Set out container-grown fernbush in fall or early spring into lean, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun.
directions: Set out container-grown fernbush in fall or early spring into lean, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun, where it establishes as a tough, aromatic shrub with finely dissected, fern-like foliage native to the dry mountains and mesas of the Great Basin and interior West. Plants produce airy spires of small white, rose-like flowers from midsummer into fall, well after most Great Basin shrubs have finished blooming, making it a valuable late-season nectar source for native bees and butterflies at elevation. Fernbush is exceptionally cold- and drought-tolerant, thriving in the same lean soils as sagebrush and pinyon-juniper, and needs no supplemental water once rooted in. Light shaping after bloom keeps the naturally rounded form tidy.

common_name: Ferncliff Copper Dahlia (Warm Burnt Copper-Orange Dinnerplate Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Ferncliff Copper is a large formal decorative dinnerplate dahlia in warm burnt copper-orange tones.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants at planting time since the massive flowers can topple stems in wind. Ferncliff Copper bears huge, formal decorative blooms with neatly overlapping petals in a warm, burnished copper-orange, a rich autumnal color that stands out among the more common reds, pinks, and yellows of the dinnerplate class. Disbud side buds to concentrate energy into fewer, larger blooms if maximum flower size is the goal. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep new flowers coming, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in spring in full sun and moist, well-drained soil.
directions: German-bred and more compact than many maiden grass selections, 'Ferner Osten' forms a tidy fountain of narrow green leaves with a fine central white rib that gives the clump a light, airy movement. Deep red plumes open above the foliage in late summer, aging to pink and then silver as they persist into winter, and the leaf blades turn a coppery orange in fall. Choose this cultivar over larger Miscanthus selections where a smaller footprint is needed but the same feathery winter interest is still wanted. Cut the whole clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Fernleaf Bamboo (Chinese Goddess Bamboo, Tiny Fern Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; this dwarf form stays small enough for large containers and border edges.
directions: This is the smallest commonly grown Bambusa multiplex cultivar, with tiny, fern-like leaves clustered densely along wiry culms, giving the whole plant a soft, feathery texture unlike any other clumping bamboo. It stays under 8 feet and forms a tight, non-invasive clump, making it a favorite for foundation plantings, tight side yards, and large patio pots in warm climates. Provide dappled shade in the hottest part of the day, especially inland, since foliage can scorch in full Gulf Coast summer sun. Thin out old culms occasionally at the base to maintain its naturally graceful, mounding form.

plant_note: Direct sow near established oaks in spring in well-drained, dry to average, slightly acidic, lean, open or rocky woodland soil in partial shade to full sun; fernleaf false foxglove is an annual hemiparasite that self-sows near oak roots in open, dry oak barrens, pine-oak woods, and acidic shale barrens.
directions: Direct sow near established oaks in spring in well-drained, dry to average, slightly acidic, lean soil in partial shade to full sun; fernleaf false foxglove is an annual or short-lived perennial hemiparasite of dry oak barrens, pine-oak woodlands, and acidic shale barrens of the eastern US, producing deeply pinnately dissected, fern-like foliage (giving the plant its common name) and clusters of bright yellow, tubular two-lipped flowers in summer. The extremely finely cut leaves are among the most distinctive and attractive of any Aureolaria species, making the plant recognizable even without flowers. Like all Aureolaria, it taps the roots of nearby oaks for supplemental water and nutrients; unlike the perennial species, it completes its cycle in a single season and perpetuates by self-sowing. More tolerant of dry, sunny, open conditions than the perennial Aureolaria species. A specialist plant of high ecological value in oak barrens conservation and restoration.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Fernleaf Full Moon maple prefers cooler, more sheltered conditions than sun-tolerant Japanese maple cultivars.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Fernleaf Full Moon maple prefers cooler, more sheltered conditions than sun-tolerant Japanese maple cultivars. Deeply and finely dissected leaves, cut almost to the leaf base into slender, fern-like lobes, give this full moon maple relative a distinctly soft, feathery texture unlike the more classic star-shaped leaf of Japanese maple, turning an extraordinary blend of orange, red, and burgundy in fall that is often considered among the best of any maple's autumn display. Native to Japanese mountain forests, it is more cold-hardy but less heat-tolerant than many Japanese maple cultivars, performing best in cooler climates with protection from strong afternoon sun and wind. Provide consistent moisture and dappled shade, avoid hot, dry, or windy sites that stress the delicate foliage, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; fernleaf peony is a steppe species that resents heavy, wet clay.
directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall, 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, setting the eyes no more than 1–2 inches below the soil surface in lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Fernleaf peony is instantly recognizable by its finely dissected, almost feathery foliage that looks more like a carrot top or fennel plant than a typical peony leaf, topped in mid-spring by single or double, deep blood-red cupped flowers held just above the foliage on notably shorter stems than most garden peonies. Native to the steppes of southeastern Europe and the Caucasus, it prefers sharper drainage and leaner soil than the modern Chinese hybrid peonies and resents heavy, wet clay. The foliage remains attractive as a fine-textured accent through much of the growing season even after the brief but showy early bloom has passed.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring and set the divisions into cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in dappled or full shade.
directions: Divide established clumps in spring and set the divisions into cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in dappled or full shade. Finely dissected, fern-like foliage emerges bronze-purple in cool spring weather and gradually mellows toward green as temperatures rise, while loose clusters of small pink to lavender flowers appear above the leaves in spring. Its low, mounding habit and colorful new growth make it a useful edging or front-of-border plant in a shaded woodland bed, especially paired with contrasting gold or chartreuse foliage nearby. Like many Corydalis species it prefers consistent moisture and cool summers, and it can decline in prolonged heat and humidity.

common_name: Festiva Maxima Peony (Classic Fragrant White Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with the pink eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; planting too deep is the most common reason this and other peonies fail to bloom. Introduced in 1851, Festiva Maxima is one of the oldest and most widely planted peony cultivars still in commerce, prized for its huge, extremely fragrant, double white flowers flecked with crimson at the petal centers, opening earlier than most peony cultivars. Set out grow-through peony rings or stakes in spring before the heavy flowers weigh the stems down, especially after rain. It requires a real winter chill to set buds and is not reliable south of zone 8; expect little bloom the first year or two while the clump establishes, with plants living and flowering for decades once mature.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade; scoliopus is a California coastal woodland specialist requiring cool, shaded, consistently moist conditions similar to its native redwood forest habitat.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade; scoliopus must have consistently moist, cool conditions and summer-dry stress will cause premature dormancy or death. Scoliopus bigelovii is one of California's most unusual native woodland perennials, producing mottled strap-like leaves in winter and bearing small brownish-purple veined flowers with a fetid odor from January through March, attracting fungus gnats for pollination. It is native to cool, moist, shaded canyons and redwood forest understories along the California coast and goes dormant by late spring.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, rich, well-drained alluvial soil in partial to full shade; this Louisiana endemic grows naturally on the low hardwood ridges and terraces bordering the Atchafalaya Basin and appreciates the same seasonally damp, leaf-litter-covered ground.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, rich, well-drained alluvial soil in partial to full shade; this Louisiana endemic grows naturally on the low hardwood ridges and terraces bordering the Atchafalaya Basin and appreciates the same seasonally damp, leaf-litter-covered ground. Its broad, heavily silver-mottled leaves and sessile maroon-to-yellow-green flowers closely resemble those of Trillium cuneatum, but the common name refers to the faint carrion scent the flowers give off to draw in the small flies and beetles that pollinate them. Extremely restricted in the wild to a handful of south Louisiana parishes, it is best sourced only from nurseries growing seed-propagated stock, and makes a conversation-starting addition to a shaded native bed already hosting spider lilies or Louisiana iris. Once established the clump slowly bulks up by offsets and needs little more than an annual leaf-mold top-dressing and protection from summer waterlogging.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; fetterbush requires very acidic, waterlogged conditions and will not thrive in neutral or alkaline soil.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; fetterbush is a native evergreen shrub of pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bog margins across the coastal South, producing glossy, leathery, sharply ribbed leaves (the midrib runs parallel to the leaf margin — a key identification feature) and small pink to white urn-shaped flowers in early spring that are critically important for native mining bees and early bumblebee queens. The plant naturally grows in waterlogged, very acidic soil and is adapted to conditions that are difficult for most other plants. An outstanding native plant for bog gardens, wet acid borders, and naturally moist sandy soils in the Southeast. All parts are toxic to livestock and humans if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; fever tree grows naturally at the edges of swamps, pocosin bogs, and moist woodlands in the southeastern coastal plain. It requires consistent soil moisture and performs poorly in dry soils or full sun, making it an ideal plant for moist shade or rain garden settings.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade; fever tree is one of the rarest and most unusual native shrubs of the southeastern coastal plain, found naturally only in a narrow band of swampy pocosins and wet pine savannas in coastal Georgia and the Carolinas. In the coffee family (Rubiaceae), it is related to gardenias and quinine trees — and indeed the bark was historically used as a quinine substitute to treat malaria (hence 'fever tree'). In early summer, the plant produces clusters of small, tubular, rose-to-magenta flowers, each surrounded by spectacular, greatly enlarged, rose-pink to rosy-red sepals (calyx lobes) that resemble large pink bracts or petals and create a showy, ornamental display far larger than the flowers themselves — similar in strategy to dogwood bracts. The large, tropical-looking leaves give the shrub a bold texture unusual among native plants. A conservation-significant plant that also makes an outstanding specimen for moist shaded gardens in zones 7–9, appreciating conditions similar to native azaleas.

plant_note: Divide established clumps or plant container-grown plants in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil; fiber optic grass thrives in boggy conditions or at the water's edge and can be grown as an aquatic in shallow water (up to 2 inches deep). Keep consistently moist — it does not tolerate drought.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; fiber optic grass is a charming miniature rush-like plant producing dense mounds of very fine, thread-like, bright-green foliage tipped with tiny white to pale brownish flower spikelets that catch the light like the tip of a fiber optic strand — hence the common name. The effect is distinctly whimsical and appealing. It is excellent as a container plant for water features, terrariums, and bog gardens, thriving in consistently wet conditions at pond or stream edges, in water gardens, and as a houseplant in very bright light. In zones 8–11 it grows as a reliable evergreen perennial in wet conditions. Its compact, fine-textured form contrasts beautifully with broad-leafed aquatic plants and it makes an unusual cascading element in container plantings or hanging baskets where moisture is maintained.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist medium, or air-layer branches; fiddle-leaf fig is sensitive to being moved — choose a permanent location with bright, indirect light and consistent conditions. Direct sun causes leaf scorch, deep shade causes poor growth and dropping. Water when the top 2 inches of soil are dry and ensure good drainage to prevent root rot.
directions: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in filtered shade outdoors in zones 10–12; fiddle-leaf fig has become one of the most widely grown and immediately recognizable indoor trees of the early 21st century, prized for its enormous, deeply wavy-edged, violin-shaped leaves (12–18 inches long) in rich, dark, glossy green that create an unmistakably tropical and architecturally dramatic statement in interior spaces. Native to the lowland tropical rainforests of West Africa, it grows as a large tree to 50 feet in its native habitat. As a houseplant it requires bright, indirect light (a few feet from a south or west window), consistent watering (allowing the top 2 inches to dry between waterings), and avoidance of both overwatering (the primary cause of root rot and leaf drop) and cold drafts. It dislikes being moved and may drop leaves in response to environmental changes. In zones 10–12 it can be grown outdoors as a specimen tree in partial shade. Cleaning the large leaves with a damp cloth maintains their glossy appearance and maximizes light absorption.

common_name: Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron (Horsehead Philodendron, Panda Plant, Panduraeforme)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Philodendron bipennifolium cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. A moss pole or climbing support is beneficial — the leaves grow progressively larger as the plant climbs. Grow in a well-draining, aroid potting mix. Allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Propagate from single-node stem cuttings in water or moist media. The leaf shape varies greatly between juvenile and mature forms. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron produces its most dramatic and largest leaves with consistent bright indirect light and a climbing support, but adapts to lower light conditions without serious decline. Philodendron bipennifolium (formerly classified as P. panduraeforme, a name still commonly used in horticultural trade) is a climbing philodendron native to Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru in the family Araceae. The common names 'Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron' and 'Horsehead Philodendron' both refer to the distinctive shape of the adult leaves — a broad, slightly elongated outline with two distinctive basal lobes and a characteristic narrowing in the middle that creates a violin or fiddle silhouette, or, from another angle, a horse's head profile. The leaves are glossy, bright to dark-green, leathery, and held on long petioles that give the plant an open, airy structure. In the juvenile form, the leaves are much smaller and simpler; the characteristic fiddle shape develops progressively as the plant matures. As a rapidly growing, adaptable climbing philodendron with an unusual and attractive leaf form, P. bipennifolium has long been popular in cultivation and has been used in breeding the modern 'Philodendron Florida' hybrid series. All parts contain calcium oxalate and are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Fiddleleaf Morning Glory (White Beach Morning Glory)
plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed, or set out rooted cuttings, after the last frost into loose, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; this trailing dune vine tolerates salt spray, wind, and shifting sand better than almost any other flowering ground cover.
directions: Direct sow scarified seed or root stem cuttings after the last frost in loose, well-drained sandy soil in full sun, watering only to establish since the vine is adapted to droughty dune sand. Fiddleleaf morning glory sends out long, prostrate, fleshy stems lined with distinctive lobed, fiddle-shaped leaves and opens white, funnel-shaped flowers with a soft yellow throat through the warm months. It is a close coastal relative of the pink-flowered railroad vine, and its network of trailing stems and deep roots make it an effective, low-growing sand stabilizer for beachfront and other extremely sandy, salt-exposed Gulf Coast sites. Because it spreads by rooting at the nodes, it also works well cascading over a hot, dry retaining wall or bank where little else will grow.

plant_note: Press seed lightly into bare, well-drained soil in spring, or plant rooted stolon offsets for faster establishment.
directions: Press seed lightly into bare, well-drained soil in spring, or plant rooted stolon offsets for faster establishment on dry lawns, prairies, or rocky openings. Silvery basal foliage forms a dense mat that spreads by runners into a durable low groundcover, topped in mid-spring by clusters of small whitish-pink flowers on separate male and female plants. It is the primary larval host for the American Lady butterfly and offers early pollen to small native bees at a time when few other flowers are open. Once established it needs almost no supplemental water or fertilizer and tolerates foot traffic and poor soil better than turfgrass.

plant_note: Install plugs eight to twelve inches apart in spring or fall; because it spreads by rhizomes it can be assertive in richer, moist soil, so give it a contained area.
directions: Install plugs eight to twelve inches apart in spring or fall; this rhizomatous North American native sedge spreads steadily to knit into a fine-textured, no-mow lawn substitute that can also be mowed occasionally to two or three inches for a tidier look. It tolerates a wider range of soil moisture than most meadow sedges, handling both summer drought and periodic heavier watering, which makes it versatile for converting turf areas in mixed-use yards. Because it spreads by rhizomes it can be assertive in richer, moist soil, so give it a contained area or expect to edge it back from adjoining beds.

plant_note: Direct-sow in fall so seed overwinters and stratifies naturally, or moist-cold stratify seed 30 days before an early-spring sowing.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in fall or cold-stratify before a spring sowing, into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the plant forms a basal rosette its first year and sends up a tall flowering stalk the following season before setting seed. Field thistle is one of the least aggressive native thistles, staying put in a clump rather than spreading like weedy introduced thistles, and its large pink-purple blooms are a magnet for bumblebees, swallowtails, fritillaries, and migrating hummingbirds. Leave the finished flower heads standing into fall so goldfinches can strip the down and seed. Give it room at the back of a meadow planting since the silvery, spine-edged foliage and flower stalks get tall by late summer.

common_name: Fielder's White Azalea (Heavy-Blooming Pure White Southern Indica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Fielder's White is a classic Southern Indica azalea grown across the Deep South for its exceptionally heavy pure white spring bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving the large mature shrub adequate room to spread. Fielder's White is a Southern Indica azalea long favored in Deep South gardens for the sheer density of its pure white spring flowers, which can cover the entire shrub so thoroughly that little foliage shows through during peak bloom. Its large, vigorous, evergreen habit makes it well suited to hedges, screens, and estate-scale plantings where a dramatic white spring display is wanted. Water deeply during establishment and dry spells, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; nasturtiums resent transplanting.
directions: Direct sow the large seed about half an inch deep after frost, since nasturtiums dislike root disturbance from transplanting. Fiesta Blend brings spicy edible flowers in orange, yellow, and orange-peach bicolors that brighten hanging baskets, containers, and garden walls. Both the peppery blossoms and leaves are edible and prized in salads. Grow in lean soil and go easy on fertilizer, as rich soil favors foliage over flowers.

common_name: Fiesta Hibiscus (Orange-Yellow with Red Veining Tropical Hibiscus)
