plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Fiesta is a vividly colored tropical hibiscus cultivar with striking red veining over an orange-yellow base.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Fiesta carries large, single flowers in a fiery blend of orange and yellow overlaid with bold red veining radiating out from the throat, a vivid, sunset-toned combination that lives up to its festive name and stands out even among the wide color range typical of tropical hibiscus. Flowers last only a single day, as with all hibiscus, but a well-grown plant produces a steady flush of new buds for continuous color from spring through frost in warm climates. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–May. Fiesta del Sol is a compact selection (2–3 feet) of Mexican Sunflower — dramatically smaller than the standard species (5–6 feet), making it practical for mixed borders and small garden spaces where the standard type would overwhelm surrounding plants. The compact size was the primary selection criterion for this All-America Selections winner. Despite the smaller size, Fiesta del Sol produces the same vivid orange flowers as the standard type, beginning to bloom earlier from seed (55–70 days vs 80–90 days for taller selections). Self-seeding occurs in warm conditions; allow a few plants to go to seed in zone 9 for volunteer seedlings in subsequent seasons.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Fiesta del Sol Tithonia thrives in the heat and lean conditions that reduce the excessive vegetative growth and delayed flowering of overfertilized plants; Fiesta del Sol is an All-America Selections award-winning compact cultivar of Mexican Sunflower (Tithonia rotundifolia), bred specifically to reduce the scale of this Mexican native from its typical 5–6 foot height to a more garden-friendly 2–3 feet while retaining the vivid, large (3–4 inch), brilliant orange-scarlet flowers and the exceptional heat, humidity, and drought tolerance that make Tithonia outstanding for zone 9 summer gardens. The vivid orange-scarlet flowers are among the most intensely colored of all summer annuals — a warm, saturated orange that is particularly effective in late-summer and fall garden compositions with purple, blue, and cream companions. Tithonia is one of the premier butterfly and pollinator plants available — the large, nectar-rich flowers attract swallowtails, fritillaries, monarchs, and large sulphur butterflies in significant numbers throughout the bloom season. The drought tolerance and heat performance of Tithonia in the peak of Gulf South summer (July–September) when many annuals struggle to maintain quality makes it one of the most reliable high-color, high-pollinator-value summer plants available for zone 9.

plant_note: Sow directly in the garden in spring after the last frost, or start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; fig-leaved hollyhock is biennial, forming a leaf rosette the first year and sending up tall flowering spikes in the second — sow in successive years to ensure bloom every season.
directions: Sow seed directly in the garden after the last frost in spring, pressing seed shallowly into the surface of fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; fig-leaved hollyhock is a biennial that spends its first season as a ground-level rosette of deeply lobed, fig-shaped leaves before sending up tall flowering spikes the following summer. To maintain a continuous display, sow seed each year so that first-year rosettes and second-year blooming plants are always present side by side in the border. The single flowers in warm shades of yellow, apricot, orange, and pink open in succession from the base of the spike upward through midsummer, and the plant's naturally tough constitution makes it notably more resistant to hollyhock rust (Phragmidium malvacearum) than the common A. rosea. After the main spike sets seed in late summer, cut it back to encourage side shoots that may reflower before frost, and allow some seed to fall and self-sow for the following year's plants.

plant_note: Plant once nighttime temperatures stay reliably warm, in soil that drains well but does not dry out completely between waterings; reserve for the most frost-protected zone 10-11 sites.
directions: Plant this Pacific-island fan palm in full sun to light shade once nighttime temperatures stay reliably warm, in soil that drains well but does not dry out completely between waterings. Its nearly perfect circular fronds on a slender, ringed trunk make it one of the most refined specimen palms for courtyards and poolside plantings in the warmest zone 10-11 pockets. Feed lightly but regularly through the growing season since it is a moderately heavy feeder for a palm of its size. It has essentially no cold tolerance, so reserve it for the most frost-protected coastal or Florida sites.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Filamentosa is a fine-textured nandina selection with unusually narrow, thread-like leaflets.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, where the best orange-red fall and winter color develops. Filamentosa bears unusually narrow, thread-fine leaflets that give the entire shrub a soft, lacy, almost fern-like texture very different from the broader-leaved standard nandina, turning warm orange-red in cold weather. Its fine texture makes an interesting contrast planting alongside bolder-leaved shrubs and perennials. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs little routine care beyond occasional thinning of old canes.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or fall; set crowns just 1 in below soil level in full sun to light afternoon shade.
directions: Plant fans with the crown about 1 in deep, spreading roots outward over a small mound of soil in the hole, and water thoroughly after planting. Final Touch earns its name as one of the latest-blooming daylily cultivars widely grown, opening its ruffled, near-white flowers with a faint yellow-green throat well after most other daylilies have finished for the season, extending the daylily display into late summer. Planting it alongside early- and midseason cultivars stretches the overall daylily bloom season by several extra weeks in the garden. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines, and remove spent scapes after all buds open to keep the planting tidy.

common_name: Fine Wine Weigela (Compact Dark-Purple-Foliage Weigela with Rose-Pink Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; foliage color and bloom are both best with at least six hours of direct sun, though the shrub tolerates part shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and prune lightly right after the main spring flush to shape the compact mound without removing next year's buds. Fine Wine is a dwarf sport of the popular dark-leaved Wine and Roses weigela, bred smaller still for tight spaces, foundation plantings, and mixed containers, with narrow, deep burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season and clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds. Its compact, mounded habit needs little pruning to stay tidy, and the dark foliage provides season-long color contrast in a border even between bloom flushes. Established plants are drought-tolerant and largely trouble-free, needing only an occasional renewal cut to the oldest wood to keep growth vigorous.

plant_note: Broadcast seed onto bare, well-drained soil in fall so plants can form a branching rosette before flowering in spring.
directions: Broadcast seed onto bare, well-drained soil in fall so plants can form a branching rosette before producing masses of small yellow daisies in spring, often carpeting sandy Texas fields alongside bluebonnets and other winter annuals. Unlike its perennial relative Tetraneuris scaposa, this species is a true annual that reseeds itself each year given open, undisturbed ground. It is a reliable early nectar and pollen source for small native bees and beneficial flies emerging in late winter and early spring across Texas prairies. Keep it in lean, dry soil, since fertile or overwatered beds crowd this low, fine-textured wildflower out.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; finger poppy mallow grows naturally in dry, open prairies and rocky, calcareous outcrops of the south-central US from Texas to Kansas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, dry to moderately moist, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; finger poppy mallow is a distinctive perennial winecup with deeply cut, finger-like leaf lobes that give it its common name — the narrow, finger-like divisions distinguish it from other Callirhoe species. The vivid magenta-red, cup-shaped flowers are typical of the genus. It grows naturally in dry, calcareous prairies and rocky outcrops from Texas to Kansas, tolerating alkaline soils and summer drought well once the deep taproot is established. Like all Callirhoe, it develops a large, fleshy, turnip-like taproot that stores water and nutrients, making established plants very long-lived and drought resistant. An excellent native for xeric, prairie-style gardens and calcareous soil landscapes in the south-central US.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable, setting crowns level with the surrounding soil.
directions: Tuck divisions into moist, well-drained woodland soil enriched with compost, and water regularly the first season while the spreading stolons take hold. Once established it tolerates the dry shade at the base of trees better than many foamflowers as long as it isn't left to dry out for extended periods. Its narrow, finger-like leaf lobes radiate outward like a painted hand and darken to deep burgundy along the veins in fall and winter, complementing the fluffy white-pink spring flower spikes. The fine-textured foliage contrasts nicely with bolder hostas and ferns in a shaded border.

common_name: Fingers Anthurium (Cut-Leaf Anthurium, Radiating Finger Anthurium, Mexican Finger Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky aroid mix; Anthurium pedatoradiatum produces leaves that are deeply and narrowly divided into 9–11 fingerlike segments radiating from a central point — an unusual, dramatically different leaf form from the typical heart-shaped anthurium leaf. The overall leaf can reach 18–24 inches across in mature plants, making it a bold architectural statement in shaded spaces. More tolerant of intermediate conditions than many velvet anthuriums. Keep warm (above 55°F) and moderately moist. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil — Fingers Anthurium is one of the most structurally unusual of the ornamental anthuriums, producing leaves that are dramatically divided into narrow, spreading, fingerlike segments rather than the entire (undivided) heart-shaped or arrow-shaped form typical of the genus. Anthurium pedatoradiatum is a climbing, hemiepiphytic anthurium in the Araceae family native to southern Mexico (Chiapas, Tabasco, Veracruz) and Central America, one of a handful of Anthurium species that produce leaves divided into multiple narrow lobes or segments (a condition called pedatifid or palmatifid division). The plant produces leaves that are deeply divided into 9–11 narrow, lanceolate to oblong segments (lobes) radiating from a central point in the pattern for which the species name pedatoradiatum ('radiating fingers') was given — the individual segments smooth, dark green, and spreading outward from the center like the fingers of an outspread hand. In juvenile plants, the leaves begin simple and heart-shaped, transitioning to the deeply divided adult form as the plant matures and climbs. Fully adult leaves in well-established plants can reach 18–24 inches across, producing a dramatic, palm-like or philodendron-selloum-like silhouette in a shaded garden. The unusual leaf division makes this one of the most architecturally distinctive anthuriums for interior and shaded tropical garden design. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

common_name: Fire Alarm Heuchera (Terra Nova Red Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Fire Alarm is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction bred for consistently bright red foliage color, which holds best with reliable moisture and some protection from the hottest afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Fire Alarm is a Terra Nova Nurseries coral bells selection prized for leathery leaves that emerge bright fire-engine red and deepen to a rich brown-red through summer before flaring back to vivid red in fall, giving the plant strong color interest across three seasons. Tiny cream flowers rise on wiry stems above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the striking leaf color that is the main draw. Give it consistent moisture, especially if grown with any direct afternoon sun, since drought stress dulls the leaf color and can scorch the foliage. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and share plants.

common_name: Fire Dance Red Hot Poker (Dwarf Red-Orange Kniphofia)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Fire Dance is a dwarf red hot poker with an extended bloom season compared to older, single-flush cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; good drainage is critical year-round, since red hot poker rots in waterlogged soil. Fire Dance produces compact torch-like spikes opening bright red in bud and aging to orange, creating the classic two-toned effect on a dwarf, sturdy plant that blooms repeatedly over an extended season from early summer well into fall, longer than many older red hot poker cultivars that flower in a single flush. Its compact size fits smaller borders and mass plantings, and the tubular flowers draw hummingbirds reliably throughout the long bloom period. In colder parts of its range, tie the grassy foliage together over the crown and mulch deeply before the first hard freeze, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering declines.

common_name: Fire Island Hosta (Chartreuse Hosta with Red Petioles)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fire Island develops its brightest gold leaf color and most vivid red petioles and stems with some morning sun, though it tolerates deeper shade with a more muted, greener leaf color.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving morning sun or bright dappled light for the best color contrast between foliage and stems. Fire Island is a compact, fast-growing hosta cultivar with smooth, chartreuse-to-gold leaves that turn a more vivid yellow-green as they mature through the season, set off dramatically by bright red-purple petioles and scapes that intensify in cooler weather and with more light exposure. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes above the foliage in mid to late summer. Its compact size and striking color combination make it an excellent edging or container hosta, and its vigorous, fast-multiplying habit means clumps fill in quickly compared to slower-growing hosta cultivars. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, and watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fire Light was bred for exceptionally strong, sturdy stems that hold its large flower clusters upright without flopping, even after heavy rain.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Fire Light was bred specifically to solve the floppy-stem problem common in many panicle hydrangea cultivars, holding its large, dense, white flower clusters proudly upright even as they age and turn deep red-pink in late summer and fall. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood, so a hard renewal pruning in late winter does not sacrifice the season's flowers. It tolerates more sun and less consistent moisture than mophead hydrangeas once established, and the sturdy stems make it a good choice for a mixed border where less rigid hydrangea cultivars tend to sprawl after rain.

common_name: Fire Light Tidbit Hydrangea (Miniature Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Fire Light Tidbit is the smallest selection in the Fire Light panicle hydrangea line, well suited to a container or the front of a mixed border.
directions: Fire Light Tidbit is a true miniature panicle hydrangea, staying under 2-3 feet tall while still producing the same sturdy-stemmed, upright white flower panicles that age to deep pink-red typical of the larger Fire Light selections. Its diminutive size makes it one of the few panicle hydrangeas practical for a large container, small foundation bed, or the front edge of a border, without sacrificing the reliable, strong-stemmed flower display the series is known for. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter, since it blooms on new wood and tolerates a hard cutback without losing the coming season's flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, average to rocky, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; fire pink self-sows freely and is best treated as a short-lived perennial that renews by seedlings.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, average to rocky, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fire pink is a native Eastern North American wildflower that produces some of the most vivid scarlet-red flowers in the spring garden, with deeply notched five-petaled blooms on sticky-stemmed plants that hummingbirds visit eagerly from April through June. Plants are short-lived (2–3 years) but self-sow freely in suitable conditions and maintain colonies in rocky woodland edges, dry slopes, and shaded roadsides. Plant in groups for the best visual impact; individual plants are sparse in habit. Combine with native ferns, wild columbine, and foamflower for a diverse native understory planting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Fire Spinner ice plant needs sharp drainage and is more cold-hardy than many other ice plant species.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Fire Spinner ice plant needs sharp drainage and is more cold-hardy than many other ice plant species. Small, fleshy, needle-like leaves cover a low, spreading mat smothered from late spring through fall in vivid, glistening, daisy-like flowers with a bold two-tone pattern of orange-red centers fading to purple-pink tips, a striking bicolor bloom that catches and reflects light with the characteristic 'icy' sheen the genus is named for. A Plant Select-introduced hybrid recognized for exceptional cold hardiness compared to most Delosperma species, it thrives in a xeriscape border, rock garden, or hot, dry parking strip planting with minimal supplemental water once established. Water only occasionally, shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested mats to propagate or refresh an aging planting.

common_name: Fire and Ice Hosta (White-Centered Green-Margin Hosta)
plant_note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; Fire and Ice is a sport with a bold white-centered leaf and a narrow, irregular dark-green margin, one of the most widely sold variegated hostas.
directions: Plant in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade, avoiding direct hot afternoon sun which can scorch the white center. Fire and Ice is one of the most dramatic and widely grown variegated hostas, with narrow, pointed leaves dominated by a bold, nearly pure-white center bordered by a thin, irregular dark-green margin — the strong color contrast makes it a standout accent or edging plant even from a distance. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in mid- to late summer. Because so much of the leaf lacks chlorophyll, it grows a bit more slowly and stays smaller than solid-green hostas of similar parentage, and it benefits from consistent moisture and protection from slugs, which tend to target the softer white tissue. A dependable, high-contrast choice for brightening a dark shade bed.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, spacing tall plants about a foot apart for airflow. Fireball Blend delivers intense 4-5 inch blooms that are stunning at the back of a bed or planted in mass. The long-lasting flowers hold well both on the plant and in the vase, so cut and deadhead often to keep them coming until frost. Water at the base and space generously to limit powdery mildew.

plant_note: Plant outdoors as a groundcover in zone 10-11, or grow in shallow pots/hanging baskets elsewhere; Fireball Bromeliad has no frost tolerance and is damaged below 35°F. In warm-winter landscapes it is widely used as a mass-planted color bed under tree canopies, since it spreads quickly into a dense, self-repeating carpet as pups root beside the parent rosette. Divide and reset overcrowded clumps every 1-2 years to keep individual rosettes tight and well colored.
directions: Give bright, filtered light or a few hours of gentle morning sun — Fireball colors up brightest red with more light exposure, while deep shade fades the rosette toward green. Neoregelia 'Fireball' is a compact hybrid bromeliad, one of the most widely planted dwarf Neoregelia cultivars in Florida and Gulf Coast landscaping, forming a tight, flat rosette only a few inches across that turns a saturated wine-red to fire-engine red as it matures. It is grown almost entirely for its intense, long-lasting foliage color rather than its small, inconspicuous violet flowers, which are tucked low in the central water-holding cup and barely rise above the leaves. Because each rosette is small and shallow-rooted, it thrives tucked into rock gardens, tree crotches, mixed containers, or as a dense edging planting, and established colonies self-propagate readily from offsets. Keep the tiny central cup topped with water and avoid heavy fertilizer, which encourages green, less colorful growth.

common_name: Fireball Hardy Hibiscus (Purple-Foliage Velvety Red-Flowered Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Fireball is a patented hardy hibiscus selection from a 40-year Fleming breeding program, notable for dark purple, maple-like foliage that provides striking contrast to its velvety red flowers all season, not just at bloom time.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer since hardy hibiscus wilts quickly in dry conditions. Fireball stands apart from most hardy hibiscus cultivars for its dark purple, deeply lobed, maple-like foliage, which provides season-long color contrast rather than the plain green leaves typical of the genus, and the compact plant produces velvety red, 10-inch flowers from midsummer into fall. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location and be patient rather than assuming it has died. The striking foliage makes it valuable as a bold accent even between bloom flushes, and it is generally pest-free and undemanding given consistently moist, fertile soil.

common_name: Firebush (Scarlet Bush, Hummingbird Bush, Mexican Firebush)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring after last frost; firebush establishes quickly and begins flowering within the first summer. In zone 9–10, firebush is perennial and grows to 6–12 feet, often dying back to the ground after hard freezes but regenerating vigorously from the root crown. In zone 8, it performs as an annual or a returning perennial depending on winter severity. Established plants require minimal supplemental irrigation except during severe drought.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil of any quality — firebush thrives in poor, sandy, low-fertility conditions and performs well without supplemental fertilization once established. Firebush (Hamelia patens) is one of the highest-value native flowering shrubs for wildlife-friendly Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes — a Florida native and tropical American species that produces tubular, bright orange-to-red flowers in dense, clustered cymes from early summer continuously through the first frost, creating one of the longest-lasting flowering displays of any shrub in the region. The relentless summer bloom makes firebush a magnet for hummingbirds, butterflies (especially Gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and swallowtails), and native bees throughout the growing season; the small, dark purple-black berries that follow the flowers are eaten by mockingbirds, cardinals, and other berry-eating birds, making firebush valuable at multiple levels of the food web. Unlike many nectar plants, firebush blooms heavily in partial shade as well as full sun, making it one of the few flowering shrubs that reliably attracts hummingbirds in partially shaded sites. The foliage is medium green to bronze-tinged (more colorful cultivars like 'Compacta' exist) with a whorled leaf arrangement that gives the plant a distinctive tropical texture. Firebush is extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, grows rapidly in poor soils, and requires essentially no care beyond occasional pruning to shape — an ideal low-maintenance native for zone 9 wildlife gardens.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in warm, moist perlite/peat mix or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost; crossandra blooms nearly year-round in warm, humid, frost-free conditions.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to partial shade; crossandra is an Indian native grown for its salmon-orange to coral-red flowers borne in four-sided spikes nearly year-round in warm, frost-free conditions, making it one of the most continuously blooming ornamentals for shaded areas in tropical and subtropical landscapes. Plants prefer consistent warmth and humidity — they struggle when temperatures drop below 55°F and require protection from direct afternoon sun in hot climates. In the Gulf South grow as a container plant, bringing indoors in winter. Fertilize monthly during active growth. The flowers make excellent leis in Hawaii.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost with a month of cold-moist stratification, or set out nursery divisions in spring, into very well-drained, dry, gravelly or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; firecracker penstemon is one of the earliest and most reliable hummingbird plants of the desert Southwest, sending up spikes of narrow, tubular, brilliant scarlet-red flowers in early to mid spring, often before most other perennials have begun growth. Evergreen to semi-evergreen basal rosettes of blue-green leaves persist through winter, giving structure to the border even out of bloom. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and largely deer resistant, needing little more than good drainage and full sun to perform reliably for years. Deadhead spent flower spikes to tidy the plant, and avoid heavy summer irrigation or rich, moisture-retentive soil, both of which lead to crown rot in this desert-adapted species.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or container plants in well-drained, average-fertility soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; firecracker plant blooms most heavily in full sun and produces flowers nearly year-round in frost-free climates.
directions: Root stem cuttings easily in moist sand or perlite, or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; firecracker plant produces arching, rush-like, nearly leafless stems covered in tubular scarlet-red flowers that are among the most effective hummingbird and butterfly attractors in Gulf Coast landscapes, blooming almost continuously from spring through fall and year-round in frost-free zones. The plant forms a graceful, weeping mound that drapes beautifully over walls, slopes, and containers. Extremely drought-tolerant once established. Cut back hard in late winter if frost-damaged to encourage fresh growth; plants recover quickly. Coral and yellow-flowered selections are also available.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or small container vines in spring after frost danger has passed, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun with a trellis, obelisk, or fence to twine on.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or small container vines in spring after frost danger has passed, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun with a trellis, obelisk, or fence to twine on. Firecracker vine is named for its small, tubular, two-toned red-and-yellow flowers that resemble tiny lit firecrackers and appear in a near-continuous flush from spring through fall. It is a modestly sized, well-mannered twining vine rather than a rampant grower, making it a good choice for containers, hanging baskets, or a small trellis on a porch or patio in warm climates. Where winters bring hard frost it is usually grown as a container plant brought indoors, or replanted annually.

plant_note: Nick seed and direct sow after frost.
directions: Nick the seed coat and direct sow firecracker vine after the last frost in warm soil. This twining morning glory relative bears small scarlet trumpet flowers with yellow throats that draw hummingbirds. Provide a fence or trellis in full sun and average soil, and it will climb quickly through summer. Deadheading is unnecessary, but remove faded flowers if you wish to limit self-seeding.

plant_note: Root 3–4 inch stem tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light mix, then transplant into a hanging basket once rooted. Best started in spring or early summer so plants establish before winter's lower light. Grown year-round as a houseplant.
directions: An epiphytic trailing gesneriad best grown in a hanging basket filled with a chunky, fast-draining mix of peat, perlite, and orchid bark, mimicking its native life on tree branches in Central and South American rainforests. Give it bright, indirect light — an east window or a few feet back from a south window — and let the mix dry slightly between waterings, since the fleshy leaves store some moisture and resent constant sogginess. Small white to pale pink tubular flowers appear singly along the trailing stems nearly year-round, followed by round orange-red berries that persist for weeks and give the plant its common name. Regular light misting or a nearby humidity tray helps replicate the moist air of its native habitat and keeps the small, glossy leaves from crisping at the edges.

common_name: Firefly Climbing Hydrangea (Gold-Edged Variegated Foliage Climbing Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree; Firefly is a gold-edged variegated selection of climbing hydrangea.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree trunk the vine can cling to with its aerial rootlets. Firefly bears the same white lacecap flowers and peeling cinnamon bark as the species climbing hydrangea, with leaves edged in bright gold that catch the light against a shaded wall or fence even when the plant isn't in bloom. Like other climbing hydrangeas it establishes slowly for the first several years before growing vigorously once rooted in. Prune after flowering only to control size or remove wayward growth, since it needs minimal routine pruning once established.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil.
directions: Firefly is a compact bush honeysuckle prized for its glowing amber-to-gold foliage and small yellow flowers borne over a long season. Adaptable and tough, it grows in full sun to part shade and tolerates poor, dry, or rocky soils once established. Its dense habit and spreading roots make it useful for erosion control on slopes and banks. Prune in late winter or early spring to renew and control size, since it blooms on new wood. The nectar-rich flowers attract bees and other pollinators.

common_name: Fireglow Japanese Maple (Translucent Red Upright Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; backlit siting (with the sun behind the tree in early morning or late afternoon) shows off the translucent quality of the leaves.
directions: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun. Fireglow is a compact, upright, non-dissected Japanese maple cultivar prized for foliage that glows a translucent red-orange when backlit by low morning or evening sun, a quality that gives the cultivar its name, deepening to a rich maroon-red in shadier light through summer before a bright red fall display. Its smaller, more rounded five-lobed leaves and tidy, upright habit make it a good choice where a smaller-scale specimen tree is needed near a patio, entry, or Japanese-style garden. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Fireland Yarrow (Orange-Red Fading to Gold Yarrow)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Fireland opens fiery orange-red and ages through gold, giving a warm multicolor display on the same plant.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; excellent drainage matters more than fertility, since rich, wet soil leads to weak, floppy growth and crown rot. Fireland produces flat-topped clusters of flowers that open a vivid orange-red and age gracefully through amber to gold, giving a warm, multicolor tapestry effect across the plant as older and newer flowers open at different stages, held on sturdy stems above aromatic, finely cut gray-green foliage. It blooms from early summer into fall, especially with regular deadheading of spent flower heads, and its strong stems resist the flopping that troubles some taller yarrow cultivars. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it thrives in lean, sharply drained soil and benefits from division every two to three years in spring to maintain vigorous, dense growth.

plant_note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Firepot is a waterlily-form dahlia with a compact habit well suited to smaller borders and containers.
directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Firepot is a waterlily-form dahlia with a compact habit well suited to smaller borders and containers. Flat, broad petals arranged in shallow, overlapping layers give this cultivar the distinctive waterlily flower form, colored in glowing shades of orange and gold that flicker like flame, a softer, less densely petaled bloom shape than fully double decorative or ball dahlias that shows off individual petals more clearly. Its compact size compared to many taller dahlia cultivars makes it a good choice for a smaller border or large container where towering dinner-plate dahlias would be out of scale. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost blackens the foliage.

common_name: Firepower Nandina (Compact Brilliant-Red Winter-Color Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Firepower's most dramatic color display occurs in full sun with cold winter temperatures — the combination of sun exposure and cold triggers the most vivid scarlet-red foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Firepower is a compact, mounded dwarf nandina selection producing some of the most vivid fall and winter foliage color available in any compact evergreen shrub — the fine-textured, compound foliage transitions from lime-green in summer through orange to brilliant scarlet-red in fall and winter, with the most intense red occurring during and after the coldest periods. The bright red winter color of 'Firepower' is significantly more intense than the reddish tones of most other nandina cultivars, making it particularly outstanding in winter landscapes when few other evergreen shrubs provide warm color. In Gulf South winters (mild in zone 9), the red coloration is variable — coldest winters produce the best red; mild winters produce more orange and red-orange. The compact, naturally rounded habit (2–3 feet) requires minimal pruning and maintains its shape without shearing, making Firepower one of the most truly low-maintenance landscape shrubs for Gulf South foundation plantings, parking lot islands, and mass plantings. The fine bamboo-textured foliage creates an appealing contrast with bold-leaved plants. 'Firepower' does not produce berries (it is functionally sterile), eliminating the concern about nandina berry toxicity to birds that has arisen in some regions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after temperatures are reliably above 50°F; firespike establishes rapidly in warm, humid weather in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade. It can also be planted in fall in zone 9–10 and will establish over winter with reduced watering.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; firespike is one of the most valuable shade plants for Gulf Coast gardens, producing tall, dramatic spikes of brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers from late summer through frost — at exactly the time when ruby-throated hummingbirds are fueling up for migration, making it one of the premier hummingbird plants of the Southeast. Unlike most flowering plants, firespike performs best in bright shade to partial shade and actually blooms more reliably away from direct afternoon sun in the heat of zone 9. The large, glossy, deep-green leaves provide bold tropical texture throughout the season. Cut back by half in early spring to encourage dense branching and more flower spikes; in zone 8 it may die back to the ground in hard freezes but regrows from the roots reliably. Propagates easily from stem cuttings taken in summer.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; firespike is one of the finest partial-shade hummingbird plants for the Gulf Coast — it blooms most heavily in fall (September–December), providing critical nectar for migrating ruby-throated hummingbirds when few other hummingbird plants are in flower.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; firespike is a Central American tropical shrub of the Acanthaceae family that provides one of the finest fall-season hummingbird plant experiences available to Gulf Coast gardeners — from September through December, when most summer-blooming hummingbird plants have finished, firespike erupts into long, upright, brilliant scarlet-red, tubular flower spikes at the tips of each stem, creating a mass of vivid red color at exactly the time when migrating ruby-throated hummingbirds are moving through the Gulf Coast on their southward migration and actively seeking high-calorie nectar sources. The plants bloom prolifically in fall and the flowering continues until frost kills the stems; in zone 9 the roots survive and regrow reliably in spring, and in zone 10–12 firespike is a permanent, multi-season evergreen perennial. It tolerates partial shade — one of its most valuable attributes — blooming acceptably in the dappled shade of open tree canopies where most hummingbird plants would fail to flower. The glossy, dark-green, oval leaves are attractive year-round. An absolutely essential plant for Gulf Coast wildlife gardens.

common_name: Firestick Plant (Pencil Cactus, Milk Bush, Naked Lady)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown specimens in spring in full sun in any very well-drained soil; Firestick Plant cannot survive frost and should be grown in containers in zone 9 that are brought indoors before frost. In zone 10-11, plant outdoors in a sunny, dry location. CRITICAL CAUTION: The abundant milky white latex sap is one of the most severe plant irritants known — contact with eyes can cause temporary to permanent blindness. Wear heavy gloves, eye protection, and long sleeves whenever working with this plant. Keep away from children and pets.
directions: Plant in full sun in any very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Firestick Plant is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives with minimal water in hot, sunny conditions — overwatering or poor drainage causes rapid decline and root rot. Euphorbia tirucalli is a large, succulent shrub or small tree native to tropical East Africa (Madagascar, Mozambique, Tanzania) and widely distributed throughout the tropics as a traditional living fence plant, medicinal species, and petroleum-substitute biofuel candidate. The plant consists almost entirely of dense, tangled masses of smooth, pencil-thick, green cylindrical stems with virtually no leaves — the stems perform photosynthesis directly. The 'Sticks on Fire' cultivar (the 'Firestick' form) produces young stem tips in vivid orange, yellow, and red — most intensely colored in full sun and cool weather — creating the appearance of a bush on fire. The effect in winter months when the color intensifies is extraordinary. CRITICAL WARNING: The abundant milky white latex sap that immediately flows from any cut or broken stem is a potent toxin and irritant — it can cause severe skin blistering, is extremely dangerous if it contacts the eyes (potentially causing permanent damage or blindness), and is toxic if ingested. Handle with heavy protective equipment only.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; pyracantha requires full sun for best berry production — plants in shade produce fewer fruits.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade; firethorn is an evergreen thorny shrub that earns its place in the landscape through a spectacular fall and winter display of clustered, brilliant orange, red, or yellow berries that cover the shrub in such abundance they literally hide the foliage — providing one of the most eye-catching ornamental fruit displays available in temperate gardens. White flower clusters in spring attract bees. Excellent as an espalier against a wall or fence, as a barrier hedge (the thorns are fierce), or as a freestanding specimen. Cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds flock to the berries. 'Mohave' (orange-red, disease-resistant), 'Lalandei' (orange, vigorous), and 'Teton' (yellow-orange, upright) are widely grown. Berries are mildly toxic to humans; do not eat.

plant_note: Surface-sow in early spring on bare, disturbed soil in full sun; seed needs light and cool temperatures to germinate.
directions: Scatter seed onto bare mineral soil in full sun and press in without covering, since it is adapted to colonize open, disturbed ground such as burned areas, clearings, and roadsides. Fireweed sends up tall spires of bright magenta-pink flowers from bottom to top over several weeks in mid- to late summer, and is one of the most valuable late-season nectar plants for bumblebees and honeybees across its wide northern range. It spreads by rhizome and readily self-seeds via wind-borne fluffy seed, so it is best given its own bed or a naturalized area rather than a tidy border. Give it room to roam; once established it forms dramatic drifts of color that keep blooming as many other perennials fade.

common_name: Firewitch Dianthus (Perennial Plant of the Year Magenta Cheddar Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; cheddar pinks cultivars are among the most drought- and heat-tolerant perennials available, thriving in lean, rocky, or sandy soils where richer soil causes rot.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Firewitch was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 2006, prized for its dense, low mat of needle-like, silvery-blue evergreen foliage that stays attractive year-round, covered in spring by an abundance of fragrant, clove-scented, vivid magenta-pink flowers. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, rocky, or sandy soil where richer, moister conditions actually shorten its life, making it an excellent choice for a rock garden, dry border edge, or the gaps between paving stones. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat tidy and encourage denser growth, and avoid heavy mulch or rich soil that can cause crown rot.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens after last frost in partial shade to full sun; Fireworks Clerodendrum blooms primarily in late winter to early spring (December–March in zone 9) when it produces its most spectacular floral display. In zone 9a it freezes to the roots in hard winters but resprouts vigorously in spring; in zone 9b-10 it is evergreen. The plant spreads by root suckers and can colonize a large area over time — manage by removing suckers or installing a root barrier. The dark burgundy undersides of the leaves are as ornamental as the flowers.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Fireworks Clerodendrum is a vigorous grower that can reach 6–15 feet quickly in zone 9-11, making it best suited for large spaces or where a bold statement is desired. Clerodendrum quadriloculare is a large tropical shrub or small tree native to the Philippines, Sulawesi, and New Guinea, widely grown in tropical and subtropical landscapes for its spectacular winter-to-spring floral display: large, domed to rounded panicles up to 12 inches across of individual tubular flowers, each with a long pink-to-deep-rose tube opening into 5 white to pale pink star-shaped petal lobes that spread flat — the overall effect of hundreds of these flowers clustered together in a dome against the dark foliage is precisely that of an exploding fireworks burst, earning the common name. The large leaves have a distinctive two-toned appearance — dark, glossy bronze-green above and deep burgundy-purple below — making the foliage ornamental even when the plant is not in bloom. Blooming primarily December–March in zone 9, the plant provides floral color at a time when relatively few tropical shrubs are in bloom. The suckering habit can be used to create a large informal screen or hedge; remove excess suckers to maintain a single-stemmed specimen form.

common_name: Fireworks Fountain Grass (Variegated Pink-Burgundy Ornamental Grass)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants after last frost in full sun and very well-drained soil; this cultivar does not come true from seed and is propagated by division. Fireworks is more strikingly variegated but generally less vigorous than plain purple fountain grass.
directions: Plant after last frost in full sun and very well-drained soil; Fireworks fountain grass is a striking variegated cultivar with slender, arching blades striped in hot pink, burgundy, and creamy white over a dark red-purple base — considerably showier and more colorful than plain purple fountain grass ('Rubrum'), making it a strong accent or container centerpiece plant through the heat of summer. It thrives in full sun and dry-to-average soil once established, tolerating heat and drought well but requiring consistent moisture during the first few weeks after transplanting. Like other Pennisetum setaceum selections it is grown as a warm-season annual outside of zone 9–11, or can be overwintered as a houseplant in a bright spot after cutting back before the first frost. In frost-free climates it can persist as a short-lived perennial and self-seed; remove spent flower plumes before seed set if naturalizing is a concern in warmer zones. Divide congested clumps in spring if grown as a perennial.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Fireworks Goldenrod spreads steadily by underground rhizomes — divide every 2–3 years when clumps become crowded. Unlike taller goldenrod species, Fireworks remains compact and does not flop without support. The arching, fountain-like flowering stems reach 3–4 feet in the August–October bloom season — timing that fills the critical late-summer to fall gap in the native perennial garden. Goldenrod does NOT cause hay fever — the airborne pollen responsible for fall allergies comes from ragweed (Ambrosia) which blooms simultaneously. Goldenrod's heavy, sticky pollen is designed for bee transport, not wind dispersal.
directions: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Fireworks Goldenrod adapts to a wide range of soil conditions and is drought tolerant once established; Fireworks is a cultivar of Wrinkle-Leaf Goldenrod (Solidago rugosa), selected for its distinctive, highly ornamental, arching flower plumes — the yellow flower branches radiate outward and downward from the main stem in a pattern that genuinely resembles an exploding firework, creating one of the most architecturally interesting flower forms available among native fall perennials. Unlike the more common Canada Goldenrod (S. canadensis) with its straight, upright flower plumes, Fireworks' arching, fountain-like sprays create a different kind of visual movement in the fall garden — the gentle arching heavy with tiny yellow flowers creating a horizontal spray pattern that photographs beautifully and provides an interesting contrast to the upright forms of fall asters and ironweeds. Goldenrod is arguably the most important late-season pollinator plant in the Eastern US — supporting more than 100 bee species (including specialist bees that only use goldenrod) as both a nectar and pollen source during September and October when insects are building winter energy reserves. As a native species throughout the Gulf South, Solidago rugosa 'Fireworks' supports the local beneficial insect community with zero cultivation investment after establishment.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Fireworks Gomphrena is genuinely heat-loving — it grows slowly in cool spring conditions and then rapidly accelerates in summer heat. In zone 9 this annual thrives in the same conditions (intense heat, high humidity) that defeat many ornamentals, blooming prolifically from planting until frost. The distinctive starburst flower structure with long protruding pink bracts and yellow tips makes Fireworks instantly recognizable among gomphrena. Plants are self-cleaning and do not require deadheading to bloom continuously.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil — gomphrena thrives in poor soil and blooms less when over-fertilized; Fireworks is an All-America Selections award-winning annual from an unusual wild species (Gomphrena pulchella) rather than the standard globe amaranth (G. globosa). Unlike the familiar round, button-shaped flowers of common gomphrena, Fireworks produces an entirely different structure: a long, cylindrical head with protruding hot-pink bracts tipped with yellow, creating an effect that genuinely resembles a small exploding firework from a distance — one of the most distinctive and unusual flower forms among heat-tolerant annuals. The tall, branching plant (2–3 feet) produces dozens of the unusual starburst flowers continuously through the entire summer and fall season without deadheading, making it both highly ornamental and nearly zero-maintenance once established. As one of the best annual flowers for zone 9's summer conditions — extreme heat, humidity, and occasional drought — Fireworks fills a critical role in the garden when most cool-season annuals have long since given up.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting, or direct sow after last frost in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fireworks Gomphrena is among the most heat-tolerant summer annuals — it thrives in the brutal Gulf South August heat that collapses most other summer annuals.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Fireworks Gomphrena is an All-America Selections award-winning annual producing one of the most distinctive and arresting flower forms available in a summer annual — elongated, branching, multi-headed inflorescences with deep magenta-pink to fuchsia base flowers tipped with bright golden-yellow, creating a visual resemblance to exploding fireworks that gives the variety its name. Unlike the compact, ball-shaped flower heads of standard Gomphrena globosa, 'Fireworks' produces taller, more branched stems with elongated floral structures that create an airy, open texture radically different from the round button flowers of globe amaranth. The plants bloom from summer through frost with no deadheading required — the spent flower heads dry naturally on the plant, providing additional ornamental interest and wildlife seed value in the fall garden. Fireworks Gomphrena is one of the most reliable Gulf South summer annuals for sustained performance in brutal heat: where impatiens, petunias, and other summer annuals collapse in July-August humidity and heat, Fireworks continues to bloom without interruption. Butterfly gardens benefit greatly from this variety — monarch butterflies, skippers, and gulf fritillaries visit the flowers prolifically. The upright, open habit works well as a background annual in mixed beds and as a cut flower with exceptional vase life.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March–May. Rex begonias perform best with high humidity and consistent warmth, making zone 9's humid summer climate ideal for outdoor summer use in deep shade. Keep consistently moist but not waterlogged; water at soil level, not on leaves. Bring indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F. The large, colorful leaves are at their most vivid in spring and fall — summer heat and dry conditions may slightly mute the color intensity.
directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil — Rex begonias require consistent moisture and high humidity while being extremely sensitive to waterlogged soil; Fireworks is a large-leafed Rex begonia cultivar with a dramatically colorful, multi-zone leaf pattern that has become one of the most popular Rex begonia cultivars for its spectacular foliage display. The very large, asymmetrical leaves (12+ inches across) display multiple distinct color zones: the central area is deep silver-purple to lavender, surrounded by a contrasting zone of deep burgundy-red, then another ring of metallic silver, and finally dark green margins — creating a concentric ring pattern of contrasting colors that genuinely resembles the radial burst of a firework when viewed from above. The Rex begonia group (Begonia rex-cultorum) represents one of the most extraordinary examples of deliberate ornamental foliage development in horticulture — the plant is grown exclusively for its extraordinary leaf appearance, with the flowers considered insignificant compared to the foliage. Fireworks pushes the Rex begonia form to an extreme of color variety and leaf size that is genuinely difficult to believe in a living plant, making it one of the most conversation-provoking houseplants or shade container plants available.

common_name: Fireworks Solomon's Seal (Gold-Striped Variegated Solomon's Seal)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fireworks is a Japanese selection with cream-and-yellow striped leaf margins and red-tinted stems, more vigorous with a few hours of morning sun.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, siting it where a few hours of gentle morning sun can reach the arching stems for best variegation and vigor. Fireworks bears egg-shaped green leaves brightly flecked and streaked with creamy white and yellow along red-tinted stems, with the coloring intensifying into a fuller white-edged margin as the clump matures, and small white bell-shaped flowers dangle beneath the arching stems in spring. It spreads by rhizome into a broad, slowly expanding colony that can reach a yard across within several years, faster and showier than the plain species. Give it consistent moisture and a woodland-style leaf mulch, and expect strong performance through Gulf Coast summers, since Polygonatum in general tolerates zone 9 heat far better than many other variegated shade perennials.

common_name: First Arrival Itoh Peony (Large Lavender-Pink Semi-Double)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; First Arrival is one of the earliest-released Itoh hybrids, bearing large lavender-pink semi-double blooms.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. First Arrival, one of the earliest Itoh (intersectional) hybrids ever released, bears large, semi-double flowers in soft lavender-pink with a ring of golden stamens visible at the open center, combining the strong stems and repeat-flowering tendency of Itoh hybrids with a classic soft peony color. Its early introduction and reliable performance helped establish Itoh hybrids as a mainstream peony class distinct from herbaceous and tree types. Unlike tree peonies, Itoh hybrids die back to the ground each winter like herbaceous types, and their sturdy stems hold up blooms without staking.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; First Frost is a sport of Halcyon hosta and shares its parent's notably good heat tolerance among blue-leafed hostas.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; First Frost hosta is a sport of the much-loved 'Halcyon' cultivar, maintaining the parent's clear blue-gray leaf color while adding a broad, creamy-white to yellow margin that brightens and lightens in the shade garden. Named the American Hosta Growers Association Hosta of the Year in 2010, it represents an outstanding example of selecting from sports — the natural mutations that appear spontaneously on existing cultivars. The leaves are medium-sized, broadly ovate, and held more upright than many hostas, creating an attractive vase-like silhouette. Light lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in midsummer. Like Halcyon, First Frost has better heat tolerance than most blue hostas and performs reasonably well in zone 8–9 when given consistent moisture and deep shade. The blue-gray center contrasting with the cream-to-yellow margin creates a sophisticated two-tone effect that combines beautifully with chartreuse-leaved companions.

common_name: First Lady Flowering Dogwood (Yellow-Variegated Fall-Color Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; First Lady bears yellow-variegated foliage that turns red and maroon in autumn.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; understory planting beneath high, open tree canopy mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. First Lady bears foliage marked with bright yellow variegation through spring and summer, transitioning to vivid red and maroon fall color, giving the tree strong ornamental value well beyond its white spring flower bract display. Its bright variegated leaves stand out against darker-foliaged plantings and make it a good specimen or focal accent. Water during dry spells, especially the first two years, and avoid deep planting or heavy mulch piled against the trunk.

common_name: First Lady Marigold (AAS-Winning Sunny Yellow Double Marigold)
plant_note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or sow directly once soil warms; First Lady, an AAS winner, bears sunny yellow double blooms to 3.5 inches across on 20-inch plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors for a head start or sow directly after frost danger passes, barely covering them. First Lady, an All-America Selections winner, bears large, fully double, bright sunny-yellow blooms up to three and a half inches across on sturdy, uniform 20-inch plants, one of the earliest-blooming African marigold cultivars to reach flowering size from seed. Plant in full sun where the strong scent helps deter garden pests, making it a classic vegetable-garden companion. Deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming all summer and pinch young plants to encourage branching.

common_name: First Light Swamp Sunflower (Compact Early-Blooming Native Fall Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; First Light is a compact, earlier-blooming swamp sunflower selection well suited to a mid-size border position.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. First Light stays notably more compact than the straight species, generally under four feet, and begins blooming somewhat earlier in the fall season, extending the golden-yellow, daisy-form flower display that swamp sunflower is known for. Its shorter stature makes it more self-supporting than the tall, sometimes floppy species and fits a mid-border position where the species' six-to-ten-foot height would be impractical. Highly attractive to migrating monarch butterflies, native bees, and seed-eating birds during the critical late-season nectar window before frost. Divide every three to four years in spring to prevent center die-out in mature clumps.

subcategory: Pacific Island coastal ornamental poisonous tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, sandy or loamy, slightly acidic to neutral coastal soil in zone 10–12; Fish Poison Tree (Box Fruit, Sea Putat) is a large, ornamental coastal tree native to the beaches and coastal mangroves of the Indo-Pacific region from East Africa through South and Southeast Asia to tropical Australia and the Pacific Islands — bearing spectacular, nocturnal, white to pink-tipped, powder-puff flowers with prominent stamens, followed by distinctive, square-ridged, woody fruits that float in seawater — historically important as a fish stupefier and source of toxic compounds used across the Pacific for traditional fishing.
directions: Plant Barringtonia asiatica in moist, well-drained, sandy coastal soil in full sun; highly tolerant of salt spray and sandy soils; water regularly during establishment; the flowers open at night and fall by morning — best appreciated in the evening. CAUTION: all parts contain toxic saponins and other compounds; seeds and bark were used traditionally across the Pacific to stun fish in tidal pools for harvesting — do not consume. Fish Poison Tree is one of the most architecturally striking coastal trees of the Indo-Pacific — the large (4–6 inch), pompon-like flowers with their dramatic pink-tipped white stamen bundles open at dusk and are gone by morning, attracting nocturnal bats, moths, and hawk moths as pollinators. The fruits are equally distinctive: large (golf ball to baseball sized), square-ridged, four-winged, corky structures that float in seawater and are ocean-dispersed throughout the Indo-Pacific — one of the most remarkable examples of ocean-dispersal in flowering plants. Throughout Oceania, the toxic seed extracts were used for fishing: pounded seeds thrown into tidal pools or reef systems stunned or killed fish within minutes, allowing easy collection. The bark and leaves also have documented traditional medicinal uses across the Pacific Islands for skin conditions and headaches. A magnificent ornamental for sheltered coastal sites in zone 10–12 with evening-opening flowers that create a magical night-garden effect.

common_name: Fishbone Cactus (Ric Rac Cactus, Zig-Zag Cactus)
plant_note: Root stem-segment cuttings in spring or summer after allowing the cut end to callus for a day or two, then set in a fast-draining orchid-bark-based cactus mix in bright indirect light; this epiphyte grows naturally on trees and rocks in Mexican cloud forests and resents both direct sun and soggy roots.
directions: Grow in a well-drained, chunky orchid-bark or cactus potting mix in bright indirect light, never full sun, which quickly scorches the flattened stems. The strongly toothed, zig-zagging stem margins that give this jungle cactus its common name are a striking year-round feature, and in fall mature plants produce large, fragrant, pale pink to white flowers that open at night along the notches of the stems. As an epiphyte from tropical Mexican forest canopies, it prefers higher humidity and more regular moisture than desert cacti, though the top inch of mix should still dry between waterings to prevent stem rot. It is superb in a hanging basket or on a high shelf where its cascading stems can trail freely.

common_name: Fishbone Prayer Plant (Herringbone Plant, Calathea Burle Marx)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant in zone 9; Fishbone Prayer Plant requires warmth, high humidity (50–70%), and consistently moist conditions. Water with filtered, distilled, or rainwater — tap water fluoride causes leaf tip browning. Propagate by rhizome division in spring. Leaves fold upward at night and open horizontally during the day (nyctinasty). More tolerant of lower light and less humidity than many Calathea species, making it a good choice for beginners in the prayer plant group.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Fishbone Prayer Plant maintains its attractive markings best with consistent bright indirect light but tolerates somewhat lower light than many of its relatives. Ctenanthe burle-marxii is a prayer plant (Marantaceae family) from coastal Brazil, named in honor of Roberto Burle Marx (1909–1994), the legendary Brazilian landscape architect and plant collector who transformed tropical garden design. The plant produces spreading rosettes of oval leaves with a distinctive herringbone or fishbone pattern: the ground color is pale gray-green to silver, crossed by darker olive-green bars or chevrons running parallel from the midrib to the leaf edges — a pattern that gives alternate common names 'Fishbone Plant' or 'Herringbone Plant.' The undersides of the leaves are deep magenta-purple. Unlike many of its relatives in the Marantaceae (notably Calathea species), Ctenanthe burle-marxii is generally regarded as more forgiving and adaptable to typical home growing conditions, particularly in its tolerance of lower humidity. It spreads by rhizomes to form a dense, attractive groundcover in zone 11 outdoor shade plantings. Non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; fishhook barrel cactus is native to the rocky desert slopes of the Sonoran Desert in Arizona and Mexico and is one of the most cold-hardy large barrel cacti — tolerating temperatures to 15°F when established in well-drained soil.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established plants require no supplemental irrigation in most dry climates. Ferocactus wislizeni (fishhook barrel cactus) is one of the most architecturally bold native cacti of the Sonoran Desert — a large, cylindrical cactus reaching 4–6 feet tall and 18–30 inches in diameter, bearing dramatic, heavy, hooked central spines up to 3 inches long (the 'fishhook' that gives it its name) in red, yellow, or reddish-brown surrounded by flat, cross-banded lateral spines in a striking radial pattern around each areole. In late summer–fall, the plant produces rings of orange to yellow flowers at the crown — a reliable late-season bloomer when the desert has little else flowering. The bright-yellow, waxy, pineapple-shaped fruits persist long after the flowers and are eaten by many desert animals. A characteristic name: the central spine curves like a fishhook and was used by Indigenous peoples for that purpose. Famous for 'leaning south' — mature barrel cacti in Arizona often lean toward the southwest, apparently tracking the sun. An outstanding specimen plant for hot, dry, alkaline gardens.

common_name: Fishnet Stockings Coleus (Netted Chartreuse-and-Green Veined Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Fishnet Stockings is a coleus cultivar with bright chartreuse leaves overlaid by a fine, dark green net-like vein pattern, giving the foliage a distinctive lace or netted texture unlike solid-colored coleus varieties.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Fishnet Stockings is a distinctively patterned coleus cultivar whose bright chartreuse-green leaves are overlaid with a fine, dark green network of veins, giving the foliage a netted or lace-like texture that reads as a pattern rather than a solid color from a distance. This intricate veining makes it a striking textural accent in mixed containers and shaded beds, standing out clearly next to solid-colored or broadly variegated coleus companions. Like most coleus, it prefers some protection from the harshest midday sun in zone 9, developing its clearest patterning with morning sun and afternoon shade. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy focused on foliage production, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage a fuller, more compact, well-branched habit.

common_name: Five Fingers Vine (Arrow-Leaf Syngonium, Jamaica Arrowhead, Five-Lobed Syngonium)
plant_note: Grow in partial shade to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or as a container plant; Syngonium auritum is one of the native Florida species of Syngonium, found naturally in Collier and Monroe Counties as an epiphytic climber on trees in subtropical hammocks — making it distinct from the common houseplant Syngonium podophyllum (which is South American). The leaves are adult-form from an early age in favorable conditions, becoming large (12–18 inches) and distinctively divided into 3–5 spreading, finger-like lobes — very different from the simple arrowhead-shaped juvenile leaves of most Syngonium. Protect from frost in zone 9. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or as an epiphytic climber on a rough bark surface — Five Fingers Vine is one of the largest-leaved and most ornamentally striking of the Syngonium species in its adult form and is also notable for being the only Syngonium species native to Florida. Syngonium auritum is a climbing, hemiepiphytic perennial aroid in the Araceae family native to Jamaica, Cuba, the Caribbean, and southern Florida (Collier and Monroe Counties in hammock forests) — a member of the same genus as the common houseplant arrowhead vine (S. podophyllum) but considerably larger-leaved in mature form and with a distinctly different leaf shape. The plant climbs by adhesive aerial roots and, in juvenile form, produces simple, arrow-shaped leaves typical of Syngonium. As the plant matures and climbs higher, the leaves transition dramatically to the adult form: large (12–18 inches), deeply divided into 3–5 (occasionally more) spreading, broadly elliptic lobes, giving the leaf the appearance of a large, flattened hand with outstretched fingers — the 'five fingers' of the common name. The leaf surface is dark, lustrous, deep green. In southern Florida hammock forests, Syngonium auritum climbs naturally up tree trunks and over understory vegetation, its large adult leaves capturing light in the forest understory. A significant climber for shaded tropical patios and zone 10-12 outdoor landscapes. CAUTION: toxic to pets and irritating to skin from calcium oxalate.

common_name: Five Holes Plant (Standleyana Monstera, Cobra Plant, Albo Monstera)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in well-draining, porous aroid mix with a climbing support; Monstera standleyana is a small, fast-growing climbing monstera that adapts well to hanging baskets or moss poles. The popular 'Albo Variegata' form has irregular cream-white to white variegation on the glossy green leaves — maintain bright indirect light to preserve variegation (dim conditions reduce variegation). Allow top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Propagate from stem cuttings. All parts toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in aerated, well-draining potting mix with support for climbing — Five Holes Plant is a small-leaved, fast-growing Monstera that produces a dense, attractive climbing display and adapts well to both support climbing and hanging basket culture. Monstera standleyana is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, and Ecuador in the Araceae family, one of the smaller-leaved Monstera species commonly grown in tropical plant collections — in contrast to the large, fenestrated (hole-bearing) foliage of M. deliciosa, M. standleyana produces smaller, oval, glossy, deep-green leaves 4–8 inches long with no holes or fenestrations even at maturity, but with a high-gloss, lacquered surface quality and compact, vigorous growth habit that has made it popular in miniature tropical gardens and as a climbing vine. The plant's name in the trade — 'Five Holes Plant' — actually refers to a different, less-common Monstera species (M. obliqua) and has been misapplied; M. standleyana itself does not develop holes. The most widely grown form is 'Albo Variegata' — a variegated cultivar with irregular cream-white to white blotching, streaking, and patterning overlaid on the glossy green leaf — one of the most sought-after Monstera variegates in the collector market. M. standleyana 'Albo' has commanded exceptionally high prices in the tropical plant hobby. All parts toxic.

common_name: Five-Ribbed Gongora (Quinquerib Gongora, Punch Orchid, Incense Orchid)
plant_note: Grow in an open slat basket or mounted on cork — like Stanhopea, Gongora produces pendant (downward-hanging) flower racemes that must emerge from the bottom of the container; a solid pot prevents blooming. Use coarse bark or mount without medium. Bright indirect to filtered direct light. Water regularly in active growth; reduce in winter. Blooms in summer with cascading pendant spikes of fragrant flowers. Fast-growing and free-blooming once established. Protect from temperatures below 50°F. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in an open-bottom slatted basket or mounted on cork in bright indirect to filtered direct light — Five-Ribbed Gongora produces its pendant flower spikes downward through the basket medium and cannot bloom in a solid container. Gongora quinquenervis is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid with a wide natural range from Mexico through Central America to Peru, Bolivia, Brazil, and Venezuela in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most ornamentally rewarding of the pendant-blooming orchids for several reasons: it is fast-growing, free-blooming (producing multiple long pendant racemes per pseudobulb annually), and produces its flower display more persistently than the typically brief-flowering Stanhopeas. The plant forms dense clusters of ribbed, angular pseudobulbs each with 2 broad, pleated leaves. In summer, multiple flower spikes (6–18 inches) emerge from the base of the pseudobulbs and cascade downward in long, graceful arcs bearing 15–30 flowers each — the individual flowers are about 1 inch across, highly complex in shape (insect-mimic form with the column modified to match Eulaema bee proportions), typically in yellow-orange to tawny-orange with reddish-brown spots and a contorted, complex lip. The flowers emit a warm, sweet, incense-like to honey-anise fragrance used by Eulaema male bees to attract females. A cascade of multiple pendant Gongora spikes in summer bloom is a graceful and unusually beautiful display. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown vines in spring; akebia is semi-evergreen in mild climates and fully deciduous in cold climates. It twines and needs a strong trellis, arbor, or fence. Note: akebia can be invasive in some eastern US states — check local regulations and monitor spread; it naturalizes readily from fallen fruits.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil of average to rich fertility in part shade to full sun; five-leaf akebia is an elegant, twining Asian vine producing delicate, compound leaves with five rounded blue-green leaflets that persist through winter in mild climates, plus unusual, intensely vanilla-chocolate-scented maroon-purple and pale-pink flowers in early spring — the female flowers are larger and darker purple, the male flowers smaller and rose-pink, and both appear together on the same plant before the leaves fully emerge. Two different plants must be present for the interesting, sausage-shaped, gray-purple fruits to develop — edible but bland, with a mild, slightly sweet flesh.
