The vine is vigorous and tolerates shade better than most flowering vines. In mild climates, akebia can spread aggressively through bird-dispersed seeds and should be monitored; select sterile cultivars or remove fruits if invasiveness is a concern in your region.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in California and mild-winter gardens; seeds germinate through winter and bloom in early spring.
directions: Five-spot is a cheerful California native annual with trailing stems and white, bowl-shaped flowers, each petal tipped with a bold violet-purple spot that inspired the common name. It is native to moist valley floors and shaded woodland edges in California's coastal ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills. Sow seed in fall directly into moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to filtered sun, pressing seeds lightly into the surface without covering. It pairs beautifully with California poppies and baby blue eyes, and self-sows reliably in cool, moist conditions to return each spring.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost, barely covering the seed, and thin plants to 12-18 inches apart. Fizzy White is a show-stopper with 2.5-4 inch semi-double pure white blooms of pleated, zigzag-edged petals around fluffy tufted centers. This heat-loving annual attracts butterflies and other pollinators and makes an airy cut flower. Grow in lean soil with modest water, since rich, wet conditions favor foliage over flowers; deadhead to prolong bloom.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; flame acanthus is native to the limestone hills and brushlands of south-central Texas and northeastern Mexico and is extremely drought tolerant and heat tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; flame acanthus (hummingbird bush) earns its name with brilliant orange-red tubular flowers that literally glow like flames and attract hummingbirds from the moment the plants begin blooming in late spring through fall. It is a tough, deciduous or semi-evergreen native shrub of the Texas brush country that thrives in rocky alkaline soil, extreme heat, and drought conditions that would wilt most plants. The orange-scarlet flowers are produced in profusion from spring through frost, providing hummingbirds with a nearly continuous nectar source. It is deer resistant and rabbit resistant. The plant dies to the ground in hard freezes in zone 7–8 but resprouts vigorously from established root systems. An essential and easy plant for the wildlife-friendly Gulf Coast garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in dappled shade; does not tolerate transplanting well once established — site carefully.
directions: Plant in moist, deeply acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade from taller deciduous trees; flame azalea is the most spectacular of the native deciduous azaleas, producing brilliant orange, red, and yellow flowers (often in multiple hues on the same plant) in late spring that blaze against the emerging green foliage at the peak of the Appalachian wildflower season. The flower display can range from pale yellow to deep orange-red depending on the individual plant's genetics — purchase in bloom to get the color you want. Plant with the crown above soil level and mulch lightly with pine bark or oak leaves to maintain acidity. Prune only lightly after bloom to shape.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Flame bears a warm orange-red bicolor spathe, deeper toward the base and lighter toward the tip.
directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where hot afternoon sun will not scorch the foliage. Flame bears a warm bicolor spathe shading from deep fiery orange-red at the base to a lighter orange at the tip, evoking its namesake, on narrow, glossy green foliage that rises through summer before the plant goes dormant in fall. Its hot color makes a striking accent in a warm-toned border alongside cannas, dahlias, and other bold summer bulbs. In zones 8-10 it can be left dry in the ground through a mild winter, while in colder climates the rhizomes should be lifted and stored dry like dahlia tubers. Reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall to encourage the plant into its natural dormant period.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; flame freesia grows through the cool season and blooms in spring in a Mediterranean cycle. In zone 8–10 it naturalizes as a perennial; in zone 7 and colder, lift corms after foliage dies and store dry through summer. It performs similarly to freesia in culture but is more heat-tolerant.
directions: Plant corms in fall in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; flame freesia is a South African corm related to ixia and freesia, producing upright stems of 8–12 brilliantly-colored, cup-shaped flowers in vivid shades of orange, red, or pink-salmon — the intense warm-orange forms being particularly striking and giving rise to the common name 'flame freesia.' The fan-like arrangement of narrow, sword-shaped leaves is typical of the iris family and attractive before bloom. Growing on a Mediterranean cycle (fall planting, cool-season growth, spring bloom, summer dormancy), flame freesia naturalizes easily in well-drained Mediterranean and Gulf Coast gardens where the soil dries in summer. The brilliant warm colors make it outstanding for combining with blue or purple spring-blooming companions. It is more tolerant of heat and humidity than many South African bulbs, adapting well to the Gulf Coast climate where it grows and blooms from late spring.

common_name: Flame Grass (Fall-Coloring Red-Orange Miscanthus Ornamental Grass)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; Flame Grass is earlier-blooming than most Miscanthus cultivars — it flowers in August in the Gulf South, providing fall interest beginning in late summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; Flame Grass is the most dramatically fall-coloring Miscanthus cultivar — a relatively compact (3–5 foot) selection of maiden grass that transforms in fall from the typical blue-green summer foliage to brilliant orange-red, then fiery orange and red, mimicking the fall color display of deciduous trees in climates where such displays are uncommon. In zone 9 the fall color develops in October–November as temperatures cool, creating a warm-season grass display just as most other perennial flowers are winding down. Flame Grass is earlier-blooming than most miscanthus cultivars (August–September), producing the characteristic feathery white-silver flower plumes above the fall-coloring foliage. At the warm edge of its range (zone 9), Flame Grass performs best with some afternoon shade protection during peak summer heat and reliable moisture — the intensity of fall color may be slightly less than in cooler climates where the full color transformation is triggered by sharper temperature swings. The compact size (3–5 feet vs. 6–8 feet for standard maiden grass selections) makes Flame Grass proportionate for typical residential borders. Cut to 6 inches in late winter before new growth begins. Outstanding in naturalistic plantings where the fall color transition provides a dramatic seasonal focal point.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; the rhizomes prefer cool soil — keep them shaded even when the top growth reaches into the sun; in hot summers the plant may go dormant.
directions: Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; the rhizomes prefer cool soil — keep them shaded even when the top growth reaches into the sun; in hot summers the plant may go dormant. Tropaeolum speciosum is the spectacular perennial climbing nasturtium from the cool, moist forests of Chile, producing long, twining stems with small, deeply lobed, bright-green leaves and a seemingly endless succession of vivid scarlet-red, spurred nasturtium flowers followed by striking, blue-black berries surrounded by bright red sepals from summer through early fall. It is famously beautiful scrambling through dark evergreen shrubs like yew or rhododendron in cool, moist British gardens, but is challenging in hot climates — it requires cool soil, consistent moisture, and partial shade and goes dormant in heat. A collector's plant for the cool, moist garden.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Flame bears unusual double pink flowers on an upright tree that sets very few seed pods.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Flame bears unusual double, rosy-pink flowers that create a fuller, more ruffled bloom than the typical single-flowered redbud, opening on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, and it produces very few seed pods, an advantage for gardeners who find the abundant pods of standard redbuds messy. The upright tree carries the classic heart-shaped summer foliage and yellow fall color typical of the species. Redbud roots are susceptible to rot in wet, poorly drained sites, so ensure adequate drainage, and prune minimally beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil with room for a small tree.
directions: Flame Thrower is a redbud selection celebrated for multicolored foliage that emerges burgundy and matures through orange and yellow to green, plus rosy-red spring flowers on bare branches. Plant it in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil, giving the best color in a spot with some sun. Water regularly during the first couple of seasons to establish its roots. Prune lightly after flowering only to shape or remove dead wood. The early blooms are a valuable nectar source for pollinators.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun in spring; flame vine blooms most abundantly in winter and early spring following a dry rest period — maintain moderately dry soil from October through December to trigger the most prolific flowering display.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; flame vine (golden shower vine, orange trumpet vine) is a South American evergreen tropical vine of the bignonia family that creates one of the most spectacular mass-flowering displays of any vine in the tropical and subtropical garden — in winter and early spring (December–March in the Gulf South), the entire vine, which can cover a fence, wall, or support structure for 30 feet or more, becomes completely blanketed from end to end with thousands of long, tubular, brilliantly vivid orange-red to flame-orange flowers arranged in dense, rounded clusters, transforming the entire structure into a cascade of blazing orange that is visible from great distances. The winter flowering season is particularly valuable in zone 9–12 winter gardens when few other vines or shrubs produce color. It is a vigorous grower that requires strong support and substantial space. In zone 9 it may be killed back by hard freezes but typically resprouts vigorously from established roots. Excellent on large arbors, fences, trellises, and covering walls where its spectacular winter display can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Flame Vine (Mexican Flame Vine, Orange Glow Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun; flame vine establishes quickly and blooms prolifically in warm weather; it may freeze to the ground in zone 8–9 winters but typically resprouts from the roots in spring.
directions: Root cuttings in moist potting mix and plant after last frost in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; provide a strong fence, arbor, or trellis to support the fast-growing vines, which can reach 10–20 feet; flame vine produces an almost continuous cascade of small, brilliant orange, daisy-like flowers with yellow centers that make it one of the most visually stunning vines for frost-free gardens and one of the top nectar sources for butterflies and hummingbirds in the Gulf South. In frost-free zones it blooms year-round; in zone 9 it blooms spring through fall and may freeze back in cold winters. Nearly maintenance-free once established, tolerating heat, coastal conditions, and drought once rooted. Excellent for screening fences, covering arbors, and cascading over walls.

plant_note: Root stolon cuttings easily in moist potting mix; flame violet requires warm temperatures (above 60°F night minimum), high humidity, and consistent moisture — it will not tolerate cold, dry air, or drought. In zone 10–12 it can be grown outdoors in deep shade as a groundcover.
directions: Root stolon cuttings in moist potting mix and grow in bright indirect light to deep shade with high humidity — flame violet is a spectacular tropical groundcover from South America, closely related to the African violet, producing velvety, elliptic leaves with bronzy-copper, silver, and green iridescent patterns (the 'peacock' coloration) and brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers with yellow throats throughout the warm season. The plant spreads by long, slender stolons that root wherever they contact moist soil, quickly filling a hanging basket or ground space in tropical garden conditions. It is a superb houseplant, terrarium plant, and outdoor shade groundcover in zone 10–12, thriving in the warm, humid, deeply-shaded conditions under tropical trees and structures where few other flowering plants succeed. The foliage alone is outstanding; the brilliant flowers are a bonus. Dozens of cultivars offer variations in leaf pattern (silver-veined, pale green, bronze) and flower color (pink, orange, white, lavender).

common_name: Flamenco Red Hot Poker (Mixed Yellow-Orange-Red Seed Strain)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost danger has passed; Flamenco is a mixed-color seed strain producing a range of yellow, orange, and red-flowered plants.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 inch deep and keep evenly moist at 65-75°F until germination, then plant in well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Flamenco is a mixed seed strain producing a colorful range of torch-like flower spikes across a planting, from clear yellow through orange to red, with many individual spikes showing the classic two-toned gradient as florets open from the base upward, all held on sturdy stems above grassy, arching foliage. The tubular flowers draw hummingbirds reliably through the summer and fall bloom season. Because it is grown from seed, individual plants vary in exact color, giving informal drifts extra visual variety. In colder parts of its range, tie foliage together and mulch deeply over the crown before the first hard freeze to protect the growing point.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full sun; flaming glorybower is a tropical West African vine that blooms most prolifically in bright, indirect light or part shade conditions in warm, humid climates.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; provide trellis or arbor support. Clerodendrum splendens (flaming glorybower) is a spectacular West African tropical vine producing dense, terminal clusters of brilliant scarlet-red, tubular flowers with prominent protruding stamens in large, rounded cymes that blaze against the dark, glossy, heart-shaped leaves — one of the most intensely colored flowering tropical vines available. Unlike the better-known bleeding heart vine (C. thomsoniae, with red and white flowers), C. splendens produces entirely scarlet flowers in even larger clusters and is a more vigorous climber. It blooms primarily in winter and spring in zone 10–12 — a welcome season when few tropical vines flower. The plant is an outstanding container plant and can be grown on a warm patio or sunroom in zone 9, brought outdoors in summer and protected in winter. Hummingbirds and butterflies are strongly attracted to the scarlet flower clusters. The vine roots easily from stem cuttings in warm, moist conditions.

common_name: Flaming Parrot Tulip (Yellow-and-Red Streaked Parrot Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from wind; parrot tulips have fringed, twisted petals that can be damaged by heavy rain or wind.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from strong wind and heavy rain. Flaming Parrot carries large, ruffled, canary-yellow petals streaked and flamed with vivid red, the flame pattern intensifying as each bloom matures, giving the flower a fiery, dynamic look that changes over its bloom life. Its tall stems and bold, large-scale flowers make it an eye-catching addition to a late-spring border or cutting garden. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

common_name: Flaming Sword Bromeliad (Vriesea splendens, Flaming Vriesea)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 9; Vriesea splendens cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. Keep the central tank filled with filtered or rainwater; flush monthly to prevent stagnation. Grow in a well-draining bark and perlite mix. Unlike many bromeliads, Flaming Sword appreciates somewhat higher humidity (50%+) for best appearance. The flame-red flower spike persists for 2–4 months before declining. After blooming, collect and pot the pups that emerge at the base. Non-toxic to pets and children.
directions: Grow in moderate to bright indirect shade — Flaming Sword Bromeliad is one of the most shade-adapted bromeliads, thriving in the dim conditions of its native deep-forest habitat and maintaining beautiful banded foliage year-round indoors without direct sunlight. Vriesea splendens is a tank bromeliad native to Trinidad, Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, and Brazil in the tropical Americas, one of the most spectacularly ornamental of the bromeliad genera in terms of both foliage and flower spike. The broad, arching leaves are dark green decorated with irregular horizontal bands and blotches of dark maroon to purple-black, creating a dramatic striped effect that makes the plant attractive even when not in flower. At bloom time, a tall, flattened, sword-shaped flower spike emerges from the central cup — vivid scarlet to orange-red, perfectly flattened (like a broad sword blade), with small yellow tubular flowers emerging from the bract margins at night. The combination of the bold banded foliage and the flaming-red sword spike creates one of the most striking single-plant displays in indoor horticulture. The bract spike remains ornamentally vivid for 2–4 months — among the longest-lasting flower displays of any indoor plant. Extensively hybridized with related Vriesea species to produce hybrids with varied bract colors, sizes, and foliage patterns. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Start indoors and set out after frost, or direct sow in warm soil.
directions: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow in warm soil, spacing plants about a foot apart. This wheat celosia adds a vertical element with rosy-pink, soft, textured flower spikes that invite a touch and shine in beds and large containers. It loves heat and full sun and makes an excellent fresh or dried cut flower. Water evenly and harvest spikes for drying when fully colored.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, coarse, airy, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) epiphytic potting mix in bright indirect light to dappled shade; anthurium grows as an epiphyte in the wild and requires excellent aeration and drainage around the roots — heavy, compacted potting media causes rapid root rot.
directions: Plant in coarse, airy, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) epiphytic potting mix (orchid bark, perlite, and peat works well) in bright indirect light; allow the top inch of growing medium to dry between waterings. Anthurium andraeanum (flamingo flower) is the classic potted tropical plant with extraordinary, long-lasting blooms — a Colombian and Ecuadorian native producing the most distinctive flower structure in tropical horticulture: a glossy, heart-shaped, waxy 'spathe' (modified leaf) 3–5 inches across in red, pink, white, orange, purple, or bicolor — often described as looking plastic or lacquered — from which a finger-like yellow to white 'spadix' protrudes; the spathe and spadix together resemble a stylized flamingo or a hand with a pointed finger. Individual blooms last 2–3 months on the plant and 2–4 weeks as cut flowers. In zones 10–12, anthurium grows as a perennial landscape plant in shade; in colder zones, it is grown as a houseplant or shaded greenhouse plant. CAUTION: All parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested; sap may irritate skin.

common_name: Flamingo Flower (Pigtail Plant, Flamingo Lily, Scarlet Flamingo)
plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky aroid mix; Anthurium scherzerianum is a compact, free-flowering anthurium from the cloud forests of Costa Rica and Guatemala that produces waxy, brilliantly colored spathes in red, orange, or pink throughout the year, paired with a distinctively coiled, corkscrew-spiral orange spadix — the 'pigtail' that distinguishes it from the flat-spadixed A. andraeanum. Very compact (12–18 inches), it is one of the best anthuriums for shaded patio containers in zone 10-12. Water moderately, allowing slight drying between watering. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, chunky aroid mix — Flamingo Flower is one of the most free-flowering and adaptable of the anthurium species for shaded indoor and outdoor ornamental use, producing its brilliantly colored waxy spathes through most of the year in warm, bright-shaded conditions. Anthurium scherzerianum is a compact, clumping, epiphytic anthurium in the Araceae family native to the cloud forests of Costa Rica and Guatemala, and the smaller of the two most commonly cultivated ornamental anthurium species (the other being the larger, flat-spadixed A. andraeanum). The plant is immediately distinguished by its distinctive inflorescence: a waxy, shield-shaped spathe 2–3 inches across in vivid scarlet-red (also available in pink, salmon, orange, and white forms) paired with a uniquely coiled, spiral, corkscrew-curled spadix in orange-yellow — the 'pigtail' that gives the plant one of its common names and distinguishes it from all other commonly grown anthuriums. The compact size (12–18 inches in height and spread), continuous blooming habit, and tolerance of lower light levels make A. scherzerianum one of the ideal anthurium species for shaded patio containers, interior plants, and protected outdoor positions in zone 10-12. The waxy spathes are extremely long-lasting — individual inflorescences remain fresh and ornamental for 6–10 weeks on the plant. Produces flowers continuously in warm conditions, with multiple spathes at different stages of development simultaneously. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

common_name: Flamingo Maiden Grass (Fine-Textured Soft-Pink Plume Miscanthus)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Flamingo bears fine-textured foliage and graceful, drooping soft-pink flower plumes that fade to white.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; maiden grass tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden conditions well once established. Flamingo bears fine, narrow blades on a graceful, arching clump, topped in late summer by unusually soft, drooping plumes that open a warm pink before gradually fading to creamy white, a softer and more colorful flower display than the typical silvery Miscanthus plume. Its fine texture and cascading flower form add movement and softness to a mixed border or specimen planting. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; flannel bush is extremely drought-tolerant and native to dry slopes and chaparral — it is killed by summer irrigation or waterlogged soils. Establish without supplemental watering beyond what is needed for the first one to two summers and then cease irrigation entirely. All plant parts cause skin, eye, and respiratory irritation from tiny barbed hairs.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, dry soil in full sun with NO summer irrigation once established; flannel bush is one of California's most spectacular native shrubs, covering itself in large (1.5–2.5 inch), saucer-shaped, intensely golden-yellow flowers from April through June — on a mature specimen the display of hundreds of golden flowers against the dark, lobed, flannel-textured, gray-green leaves is one of the showiest spectacles in the native California garden. The flowers technically lack petals; the bright-yellow 'petals' are enlarged, petal-like sepals. Named for the distinctive, flannel-soft texture of the leaves and stems, which are densely covered with stellate hairs. The plant strongly prefers lean, well-drained, dry soils and dry summers — conditions that suit California native planting schemes and water-wise gardens, but make it difficult in climates with summer rainfall. The hybrid 'Ken Taylor' (F. californicum x F. mexicanum) is the most commonly cultivated, offering extra-large flowers over an extended season. CAUTION: the fine hairs are a serious skin and eye irritant — wear gloves and eye protection when pruning.

plant_note: Sow direct in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost, or in fall for spring germination; scarify or soak seed 24 hours before sowing to soften the hard seed coat and improve germination speed.
directions: Sow scarified or soaked seed 1 inch deep in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis, fence, or shrub margin for the tendrils to grip; flat pea is a tough European perennial vine that climbs to 4–6 feet by summer and produces clusters of small pink and magenta-crimson flowers with distinctive winged stems from which the common name derives. Unlike the annual sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus), it has no fragrance, but is far more persistent — once established it returns reliably each spring and spreads gradually by seed. It is drought-tolerant and will grow in poor, thin soils where little else climbs, making it valuable on dry banks, hedgerow margins, and informal screens. Cut stems back to the ground in late fall to remove old growth and prevent untidy sprawl.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; flat-topped white aster grows naturally in moist open woods, shrubby wetland edges, and acidic bog margins across eastern North America. It spreads by rhizomes to form expanding colonies in appropriate moist, acidic conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; flat-topped white aster is a distinctive tall native of moist, acidic habitats across eastern North America, immediately recognizable by its flat-topped, wide-spreading flower clusters (corymbs) in which dozens of white-rayed flowers are held in one broad horizontal plane rather than the branching or arching arrangement of most asters. This creates an unusually airy, table-like floral display at the top of sturdy, leafy stems in late summer and fall. The flat flower surface is an ideal landing platform for large swallowtail butterflies, bumblebees, and numerous native bee species that would struggle on the branching flower heads of other asters. Grows naturally in moist, open woodlands, wetland margins, and shrubby bog edges — preferring partial shade and consistent moisture. An excellent back-of-border or woodland-edge plant for moist sites where its architectural form provides height and late-season interest.

plant_note: Plant container vines near a very sturdy support structure in spring; like the species, Flava is vigorous, heavy, and spreads by root suckers, so control spread promptly by mowing or digging out suckers.
directions: Plant near a very sturdy fence, masonry wall, pergola, or large tree in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil. Flava is a yellow-flowered selection of the native trumpet vine, replacing the species' typical orange-red trumpet flowers with clear, bright golden-yellow blooms from June through September, while retaining the same vigorous, aerial-root climbing habit and importance as hummingbird forage. Like the straight species, it is extremely vigorous, spreading by root suckers and capable of quickly covering — or overwhelming — a support structure, so it needs a genuinely sturdy structure and regular control of suckers around the base. The sap can cause skin irritation in some people; wear gloves when pruning or handling the vine.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; flax-leaf tulip is a Central Asian species from the arid mountains of Tajikistan and Uzbekistan that requires hot, dry summer dormancy to persist reliably. It naturalizes in lean, very well-drained, sunny conditions where summer is dry, but rots in wet summers. The narrow, gray-green, wavy-edged leaves are distinctive; the brilliant scarlet-red flowers with a small black-and-yellow center basal blotch are among the most vivid of any wild tulip.
directions: Plant bulbs in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; flax-leaf tulip is among the most intensely, brilliantly colored of all wild tulip species — producing in mid-spring (April–May) small but spectacularly vivid, glossy, signal-red to brilliant scarlet-vermillion, bowl-shaped flowers with a distinctive small, sharp-edged black basal blotch edged with yellow at the center of each petal, creating a sparkling tricolor of scarlet, black, and yellow within each flower. The narrow, wavy-edged, gray-green leaves (giving the species epithet 'linifolia' = 'flax-leaved') are held close to the ground in an attractive, somewhat sprawling rosette around the short stem. Native to the rocky, arid, mountain steppes of Central Asia — Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and adjacent regions — it evolved for hot, dry summers and is one of the better naturalizing wild tulips in dry, lean, sunny garden conditions, returning reliably year after year where summer drainage is good. Combined with T. tarda (yellow), T. praestans (orange-red), or T. clusiana (pink-and-white) in a wild tulip rock garden, it provides the most brilliant red in the palette. A parent of some compact hybrid tulips.

common_name: Flirt Nandina (Dwarf Compact Red-Tipped Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; new growth color is most vivid with several hours of direct sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 18–24 inches apart for a low mass planting or border edge. Flirt is a dwarf, mounding nandina bred to stay compact without the tall, leggy cane growth of larger nandina cultivars, producing new foliage that emerges bright red and matures to green through summer before returning to deep red-burgundy in fall and winter cold. Its small size and dense, tidy habit fit foundation plantings, mixed containers, and border edges where full-size nandina would need constant cutting back, and it is sterile, producing no berries and therefore no risk of the self-seeding that has made standard nandina invasive in parts of the Southeast. Little pruning is needed beyond removing occasional damaged stems.

common_name: Flore Pleno Double Snowdrop (Layered-Petal Double-Flowered Snowdrop)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Flore Pleno bears a fully double flower with multiple layered inner petals, a historic and long-cultivated form distinct from the single-flowered species.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees where they receive good light before the canopy leafs out. Flore Pleno, a centuries-old sport of the common snowdrop first recorded in the 1700s, bears a charmingly full, double flower packed with numerous small, ruffled inner petal segments in place of the simple three-part bloom of the wild species, opening in late winter to very early spring as one of the first flowers of the year. It naturalizes gradually into drifts under favorable conditions, multiplying by offset bulbs, and is best left undisturbed once established, dividing and replanting clumps only while still in leaf ('in the green'), immediately after flowering while the foliage is still active, for best transplant success. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Florida anise is a reliable, low-maintenance native shrub for shaded, acidic woodland conditions in the Gulf South.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Florida anise is a southeastern native evergreen shrub that is one of the very best shade-tolerant shrubs for Gulf Coast and Southeast landscapes, producing handsome, lance-shaped, glossy dark-green leaves that release a strong anise-star fragrance when bruised or crushed. Unusual dark maroon-red, multi-petaled starfish-like flowers appear in spring and sporadically through the year. All parts of the plant are poisonous and should not be confused with the edible Asian star anise (Illicium verum). Provides excellent year-round screening in shaded areas and is notably deer-resistant due to its aromatic foliage. Tolerates wet soils seasonally.

common_name: Florida Anise Shrub (Spicy-Scented Native Shade Shrub with Dark Red Spring Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial to deep shade; Florida Anise Shrub is not related to culinary anise and is toxic — the pleasant anise-like fragrance from the crushed leaves comes from anethole compounds, but the plant contains toxic substances and should never be used in cooking or herbal preparations.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial to deep shade; Florida Anise Shrub (Illicium floridanum) is a native Gulf South evergreen shrub of extraordinary shade tolerance and distinctive character — tolerating deep shade under magnolias and live oaks while producing one of the most unusual spring flower displays of any native shrub: dark red, multi-petaled, starry flowers with narrow, strap-shaped petals arranged in a loose, spidery pattern, appearing in April–May with a pleasant but faint sweet-spicy fragrance. The large, glossy, dark-green leaves are the plant's dominant feature through most of the year — broader and more tropical-looking than most native shrubs — and when crushed or bruised they release a strong, pleasant anise-spice fragrance from volatile oils, giving the plant its common name. The fragrance is from anethole compounds similar to those in culinary anise, but Florida anise shrub is toxic and must never be confused with star anise or used in food preparation. Florida Anise Shrub grows naturally in moist, shaded ravines and creek banks in the Florida panhandle and along the Gulf Coastal plain from Florida to Louisiana — it is the quintessential native Gulf South shade shrub, evolved under the same dense-canopy conditions that dominate Gulf South residential landscapes. The fast growth rate allows it to reach privacy-screen heights quickly, and the dense, branching evergreen habit creates an impenetrable visual screen. An outstanding native hedge shrub for shaded property edges. All parts are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Florida anise is one of the finest native evergreen shrubs for deep shade in the Gulf South and grows naturally along shaded stream banks in Florida and adjacent states.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Florida anise is one of the finest native evergreen shrubs for deep shade in the Gulf South and grows naturally along shaded stream banks in Florida and adjacent states. Illicium floridanum is a large, evergreen native shrub or small tree with glossy, dark-green, elliptic leaves 3–6 inches long that are remarkably aromatic when bruised, smelling strongly of anise or licorice; in mid- to late spring it produces unusual, star-shaped, maroon-red to burgundy flowers with numerous strap-like petals that are fascinating if not conventionally beautiful, and the flowers are followed by star-shaped seed capsules similar to (but not the same as) culinary star anise. It forms a naturally dense, multi-stemmed shrub that is excellent for hedges, screens, and foundation plantings in shaded sites in zones 7–10; all parts of the plant are toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; keep the crown at or above soil level and mulch to maintain moisture and acidity.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Florida azalea is one of the earliest and most fragrant of the native deciduous azaleas, producing clusters of brilliant golden-yellow to orange-yellow tubular flowers with exserted stamens in early spring before or with the emerging leaves. The fragrance is intensely sweet and carries far in the still spring air. It is native to the wooded ravines and stream banks of the Florida Panhandle, south Georgia, and Alabama and is one of the best native azaleas for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens, tolerating the heat and humidity better than northern species. Plant as a foundation shrub, in a native garden, or massed along a woodland edge. Prune only immediately after bloom if needed; never shear. The color is exceptionally vivid when purchased in bloom.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Florida Beauty philodendron holds its cream-and-green variegation best with consistent bright indirect light.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Florida Beauty philodendron holds its cream-and-green variegation best with consistent bright indirect light. Deeply lobed, uniquely shaped leaves are heavily splashed and speckled in cream, yellow, and pale green over a darker green base, no two leaves patterned quite alike, on a climbing hybrid vine believed to descend from Philodendron pedatum crossed with a variegated relative. Its unusual, deeply cut leaf shape combined with bold, splashy variegation makes it a sought-after specimen for collectors, and it climbs readily up a moss pole to produce larger, more dramatically lobed and patterned leaves as it matures. Prune out any leaves that revert to solid green to keep the plant's energy focused on variegated growth, and rotate the pot for even light exposure.

plant_note: Plant divisions or dormant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; Florida bellwort spreads slowly by rhizomes into a loose colony and is best left undisturbed once established beneath a deciduous canopy.
directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath hardwood canopy; Florida bellwort is a warm-climate specialist restricted to rich wooded bluffs, ravine slopes, and floodplain forests of the Florida panhandle, southern Georgia, and southern Alabama, ranging much farther south than most other Uvularia species. It produces the same nodding, twisted, pale yellow bell-shaped flowers typical of the genus in early to mid-spring, held above perfoliate leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, followed by attractive three-angled seed capsules. Clumps spread gradually by short rhizomes to form loose colonies over years rather than aggressively covering ground, making it well suited to a shaded native plant collection or woodland garden that mimics the calcareous bluff forests of the Deep South. It combines beautifully with trilliums, wild ginger, and other spring-flowering shade natives that share its habitat.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into sandy, acidic soil in full sun; seeds require no cold stratification in Florida's mild winters and will germinate with seasonal rainfall.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall into lean, dry, sandy, and acidic soil in full sun, pressing lightly onto the surface without burial; in Florida's mild climate, seeds germinate with cool-season rainfall and establish their corms over the first growing season. This Florida-endemic blazing star produces slender, wispy spikes of small rose-purple flower heads on thin, upright stems from late September through November, making it one of the latest-blooming native wildflowers available for Gulf Coast gardens. It is critically important as a late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and native bees when little else is in bloom. Plants are extremely drought-tolerant once established but will decline and rot in heavy clay or consistently wet soil.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in pure sandy, well-drained, infertile, acidic soil in full sun; Florida Blazingstar is a Florida endemic best suited to xeric scrub and flatwoods conditions. The small corms are slow to establish but persistent once settled in appropriate soil.
directions: Florida Blazingstar is a small native perennial endemic to the sandy scrub, sandhill, and dry flatwood communities of the Florida peninsula, producing slender spikes of small, pinkish-purple flower heads in fall that provide a vital late-season nectar source for native bees, skippers, and migrating monarchs in one of the most imperiled native plant communities in the United States. Adapted to the infertile, extremely well-drained, white-sand soils of Florida's ancient scrub ridges, this compact blazingstar forms tight clumps from persistent corms in habitats that most other plants cannot tolerate. Like other Florida scrub plants, it depends on periodic, low-intensity fire to maintain the open, sunny conditions it requires. Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in pure, infertile, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; established plants require no supplemental irrigation or fertilization in appropriate xeric conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry, lean, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Florida bluestem is adapted to the droughty, nutrient-poor sandy soils of pine flatwoods and sandhills in the Florida peninsula and adjacent Gulf Coast states.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, lean, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Florida bluestem is an endemic of Florida and the immediate Gulf Coast region, growing in dry, open pine flatwoods and longleaf pine sandhills where its deep root system accesses subsoil moisture during droughts. Taller than most bluestems, the plant produces attractive, arching, blue-green foliage in summer that transitions to warm copper and bronze tones in fall, creating a bold vertical element in the landscape. The fluffy, silvery-white seed heads wave attractively in the breeze and provide food for native sparrows and grassland birds. An outstanding native grass for dry, sandy, acidic soils of the Gulf South where it is ecologically appropriate and naturally sustainable. Excellent in restoration plantings of longleaf pine ecosystems and in low-maintenance landscapes on sandy soils where other grasses fail from drought.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; Florida boxwood grows naturally in the understory of tropical and subtropical hardwood hammocks of extreme south Florida and the Keys, tolerating the dense shade of the hammock canopy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, moderately fertile soil in partial to full shade; Florida boxwood is a native evergreen shrub of the tropical hardwood hammock understory in south Florida and the Keys, bearing small, shiny, leathery leaves that superficially resemble true boxwood (Buxus), hence the common name. Though unrelated to northern boxwood, it serves a similar function as a shade-tolerant, small-leaved, evergreen understory shrub that can be sheared into hedges and formal shapes. Small orange-red to red fruits provide food for tropical birds. One of the few native south Florida shrubs genuinely adapted to deep shade within the hammock canopy, making it valuable for shaded landscape settings in zone 10. An important but little-known native for ecologically appropriate south Florida landscaping.

common_name: Florida Butterfly Orchid (Tampa Butterfly Orchid, Florida Encyclia)
plant_note: Mount on rough-barked wood or cork, or grow in a slatted basket with coarse bark; the Florida Butterfly Orchid grows naturally on live oak, bald cypress, buttonwood, and slash pine trees in southern Florida and performs best when its roots can cling to rough bark surfaces. Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun. Water regularly in active growth (spring–fall); reduce watering in winter dry rest. The fragrant flowers appear in summer. Wild plants are protected — only purchase from reputable nurseries that propagate legally. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow mounted on bark or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to filtered direct morning sun — Florida Butterfly Orchid grows most vigorously when its roots adhere to rough bark surfaces with excellent air circulation, mimicking its natural epiphytic habitat on Florida hardwood hammock trees. Encyclia tampensis is a small to medium epiphytic orchid native to Florida (Brevard County south through the Keys) and the Bahamas in the Orchidaceae family — the state wildflower of Florida, one of the most important and distinctive native orchids of the Sunshine State. The plant produces round to egg-shaped pseudobulbs with 2–3 narrow, leathery, dark-green leaves and, in summer, branched flower spikes bearing 5–45 small (1.5-inch) flowers. Each flower has narrow, greenish-bronze sepals and petals that frame a prominent, broad, white to pale lavender lip with a striking purple blotch or striping — the flower's color pattern of upright, narrow, insect-like dark-colored petals surrounding a prominent, pale, broad lip led to the common name 'Butterfly Orchid.' The flowers emit a pleasant, honey-like to spicy fragrance, strongest on warm mornings. Encyclia tampensis is the most frequently found native orchid in Florida's remaining hammock and cypress forests. Wild plants are protected by Florida law — all cultivated plants must derive from legally propagated nursery stock. An excellent native orchid for outdoor cultivation in zone 9b-12. Non-toxic.

common_name: Florida Cardinal Caladium (Vivid Red All-Red Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Florida Cardinal was developed at the University of Florida and is one of the finest red caladiums for heat and humidity tolerance.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Florida Cardinal is a University of Florida breeding introduction — a vivid red caladium with predominantly red leaf coloration (deep rose-red to cardinal-red center) transitioning to narrow green margins, creating a boldly red-dominated leaf effect that is one of the most vivid pure-red caladiums available. The nearly solid red leaf, with red dominant over most of the surface and only a narrow green border at the margin, creates a strong, high-contrast visual impact in shade garden plantings where the vivid red stands out dramatically against the typical green-dominated background. Florida Cardinal was selected by University of Florida breeders for superior heat and humidity tolerance — attributes particularly relevant for Gulf South gardeners who grow caladiums through the intense summer conditions of zone 9. Caladiums are among the few ornamentals that actually perform better in heat and high humidity than in cool conditions — the tropical conditions of the Gulf South summer suit them ideally. In zone 9, Florida Cardinal grows from late April through October with essentially no special care beyond moisture and shade. Mass plantings of Florida Cardinal under trees or in shaded foundation beds create a carpet of vivid red that transforms the appearance of the shade garden from late spring through fall. The tubers increase each year and can be divided in spring to multiply planting material.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy to sandy-loam soil in full sun; Florida Cherry Palm is highly drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established but is cold-sensitive and restricted to frost-free Zone 10–11 landscapes. Fresh seeds germinate in 2–6 months in warm, moist, well-drained medium.
directions: Florida Cherry Palm — also called Buccaneer Palm — is one of the rarest native palms in the continental United States, known from only a handful of natural populations in the Florida Keys, while more widespread through the Caribbean and the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico. The trunk is distinctively swollen in the middle and tapered at both ends, giving the palm a unique hourglass or belly-shaped profile not found in any other palm native to Florida; the small, round, cherry-sized fruits ripen from green through yellow to bright red and are edible, eaten fresh or used in Caribbean countries to make a cherry liqueur. Extremely drought-tolerant and highly salt-tolerant once established, Florida Cherry Palm is among the toughest ornamental palms for Zone 10–11 coastal and xeric landscapes. Plant fresh seeds in warm, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; germination takes 2–6 months and young plants grow slowly before accelerating in their preferred warm, sunny, frost-free conditions.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants in spring with roots shaded by mulch or low neighboring plants; prune only lightly and just after flowering.
directions: Set out container-grown plants in spring with roots shaded by mulch or low neighboring plants while the twining petioles climb a trellis or shrub toward filtered light. Creamy white to pale green flowers with a striking dark maroon-purple stamen cluster appear on the previous year's wood in late spring and summer, so prune only lightly and just after flowering to avoid cutting off next year's display. It is a more compact, semi-woody grower than many large-flowered hybrids, making it well suited to a shaded container or small trellis near a patio. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, especially through its first growing season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Florida Clover Ash is a rare native restricted to Miami-Dade pine rocklands and is best suited to frost-free Zone 10–11 South Florida landscapes. It is available from specialty native plant nurseries.
directions: Florida Clover Ash — also called West Indian Clover Ash — is a native member of the Melastomataceae (melastome) family, found in the United States only in the pine rocklands and tropical hardwood hammocks of Miami-Dade County, Florida, where it is listed as critically imperiled. The lance-shaped, three-veined leaves are glossy and attractive; clusters of small white to pale pink flowers appear in spring and summer and are followed by dark purple-black berries eaten by birds including the White-crowned Pigeon. An ornamental and ecologically significant native shrub of the highly threatened South Florida pine rockland community — one of the most endangered ecosystems in the United States — Florida Clover Ash deserves wider cultivation in Zone 10–11 South Florida native plant gardens. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are drought-tolerant in the rocky, thin soils of its native pine rockland habitat.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moist soil in partial shade to full sun in zone 7–11; Florida Coontie is the only cycad native to the continental United States — a small, slow-growing, drought-tolerant landscape groundcover native to Florida and the Caribbean, critically important as the SOLE larval food plant of the Florida Atala butterfly (Eumaeus atala), a species nearly extirpated by over-collection of Coontie for starch; now widely planted for Atala butterfly conservation.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Zamia integrifolia is extremely drought tolerant once established — the large underground starch-storing caudex enables survival through months-long droughts; avoid overwatering or clay soil with poor drainage. Zamia integrifolia (Florida Coontie, Comptie, or Florida Arrowroot) is the only cycad species native to the continental United States, occurring naturally in scrub, pine flatwoods, coastal hammocks, and rocklands of peninsular Florida, the Florida Keys, and parts of the Caribbean. The plant is a small, compact, low-growing cycad — virtually stemless, with glossy, dark-green, finely divided pinnate fronds emerging from a buried or partly exposed starchy underground caudex — forming attractive, groundcover-size clumps 1–3 feet tall. The starchy caudex was extensively processed by indigenous Floridian peoples (Timucua, Seminole) and later by European settlers as 'Florida arrowroot' — a nutritious, starch-flour used for bread, porridge, and starch products, driving commercial Coontie starch factories in early 20th-century Florida until over-harvesting nearly extirpated the plant from the wild. Today, Florida Coontie is critically important as the only larval food plant of the Florida Atala butterfly (Eumaeus atala), a spectacular iridescent blue butterfly nearly lost when Coontie populations collapsed; its recovery depends directly on Coontie restoration. An outstanding, low-maintenance native landscape plant for Florida gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall or late winter in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial sun; Florida flame azalea is native to Gulf South ravines and stream bluffs and resents heavy, poorly drained clay — mound or amend planting sites on wet sites.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection; mulch well to keep roots cool and never let the root zone dry out completely in the first two seasons. Rhododendron austrinum is a deciduous native azalea of the Gulf Coastal Plain — from the Florida panhandle and south Georgia west into Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana — prized as one of the most fragrant of all native azaleas. In early to mid-spring, before or as the leaves emerge, the shrub is smothered in large trusses of intensely honeysuckle-scented flowers ranging from clear yellow through orange to deep gold-orange, drawing in early spring pollinators including native bees and swallowtail butterflies. It naturally colonizes the dappled shade of bluffs, ravines, and stream banks under a high pine and hardwood canopy. Excellent as a specimen or in a woodland-edge shrub border in the Gulf South, where it is far better adapted to summer heat and humidity than most Asian azalea hybrids. Zone 7–9.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in spring after the last frost into moist, well-drained soil; in zone 8, mulch the root zone heavily in winter as tops may die back but roots typically survive.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade, setting the crown at or just below the soil surface and watering deeply to establish. Florida gama grass is a compact relative of eastern gamagrass suited to the understory and margins of Florida hammocks, flatwoods, and wet prairie edges, and it performs well in garden beds with consistent moisture. Apply a two- to three-inch layer of mulch around the base to conserve soil moisture and protect the crown in the cooler end of its range. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and expand the planting.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in sandy, well-drained, infertile, acidic soil in full sun. Florida Goldenrod is a Florida endemic best suited to xeric scrub, sandhill, and flatwoods habitats; it does not thrive in clay, amended, or waterlogged soils. Established plants spread slowly by short rhizomes.
directions: Florida Goldenrod is a native perennial endemic to the sandy, xeric scrub, sandhill, and flatwoods habitats of the Florida peninsula, producing bright yellow flower spikes in fall that provide critical late-season nectar for native bees, monarch butterflies, and numerous other pollinators in the imperiled Florida scrub ecosystem. Distinctly compact compared to most goldenrods, with a more open, arching inflorescence suited to the sparse, sunny, sandy conditions of Florida's ancient scrub communities where many competing plants cannot grow. Like the other specialized plants of Florida's scrub, Florida Goldenrod depends on periodic, low-intensity fire to maintain the open, well-lit conditions it requires. Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in sandy, infertile, acidic, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; established plants are virtually maintenance-free and very drought-tolerant once the root system is established.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall in moist, acidic, organically rich soil in partial to full shade; mulch well to retain moisture and protect the fibrous root system — avoid dry or alkaline soils.
directions: Florida leucothoe is an upright, arching, semi-evergreen to evergreen native shrub that thrives beneath pines and oaks in moist, acidic, sandy or loamy soils — one of the Southeast's most graceful shade-garden shrubs, seldom seen in commerce despite its outstanding ornamental qualities. In spring, fragrant clusters of small white, urn-shaped flowers hang along the arching branches, feeding native bees; glossy, poplar-shaped leaves persist through winter in the Deep South. Plants form loose colonies via underground runners, providing excellent erosion control on shaded slopes and stream banks in the Gulf Coastal Plain from South Carolina to Florida and Mississippi. Grow in consistently moist soil away from drought and reflected heat; pair with native azaleas, swamp roses, and Syngonium for a woodland understory that supports diverse wildlife.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), well-drained to moderately wet soil in part shade to full shade; Florida leucothoe thrives in moist woodland edges, stream banks, and shaded sites where its arching, fountain-like form creates an elegant understory effect.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to moderately acidic, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; Florida leucothoe thrives in moist, shaded woodland gardens alongside ferns, azaleas, and hostas. Agarista populifolia (Florida leucothoe or tall leucothoe) is a large, arching, semi-evergreen to evergreen native shrub forming an elegant fountain of gracefully nodding branches clothed in lustrous, dark-green, alternate, lance-shaped to ovate leaves; small, white, urn-shaped, sweetly fragrant flowers are produced in pendulous clusters in April–May, covering the branches in a frothy, white-flowered curtain. The overall effect is remarkably elegant for a native shrub, combining refined foliage, fragrant flowers, and an architectural arching form that makes it one of the finest native screening and understory shrubs for the Deep South. Florida leucothoe is found wild in moist woodland ravines and bottomlands from South Carolina to northern Florida and is especially well-adapted to warm, humid, acidic-soil gardens in zones 7–9. Though often confused with the common drooping leucothoe (Leucothoe fontanesiana), Florida leucothoe is substantially larger, more heat-tolerant, and better adapted to zone 8–9 gardens.

plant_note: Surface sow in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial sun; Florida lobelia is a warm-season perennial adapted to the subtropical Gulf Coast climate and performs best where summer heat and humidity are consistently high — it is less cold-tolerant than most native lobelias and needs protection from hard freezes in zone 8.
directions: Lobelia floridana is a Florida and Gulf Coast endemic found in moist to wet flatwoods, swamp margins, and roadside ditches, where it produces blue flowers on branching stems in the fall — a critical bloom period for late-migrating pollinators and hummingbirds along the Gulf Coast flyway. It often behaves as a short-lived perennial, freely self-seeding in moist, disturbed soils to perpetuate itself in a favorable site; in warmer zones it may persist for several years without replanting. Surface sow in spring in consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in a site that stays wet through the summer growing season, and allow plants to set seed before cutting back to encourage naturalization.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Florida maidenhair fern grows naturally on shaded limestone outcrops and the bases of limestone walls and tree roots in Florida hammocks and the Caribbean, requiring good drainage and slightly alkaline to neutral (not acidic) conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade — Florida maidenhair fern is native to Florida hammock forests and limestone outcrops throughout Florida, the Caribbean, and tropical America, closely resembling the popular houseplant maidenhair (A. raddianum) but more cold and heat tolerant and uniquely adapted to the limestone-influenced, neutral to slightly alkaline soils of Florida garden settings. The fronds are more robust and somewhat less fragile than A. raddianum, making it more suitable as an outdoor landscape plant in zone 9–11. New fronds emerge with a lovely pinkish-bronze color that matures to bright green, creating a multicolored effect on established clumps. It is excellent for shaded patio containers, covered porches, and shaded garden beds with neutral to slightly alkaline limestone soils, where it provides an elegant, lacey texture. Unlike A. raddianum, it tolerates the outdoor humidity and heat of zone 9–10 without the constant intensive care needed by its more tropical relative.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida maple is significantly more heat, drought, and alkaline-soil tolerant than the northern sugar maple (Acer saccharum) and is the maple of choice for Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade — Florida maple is the southern adaptation of the sugar maple group, a medium-sized native tree of limestone bluffs, rich upland woods, and creek bottoms throughout the Southeast, providing outstanding fall color (orange, scarlet, and gold) in zone 7–9 where the northern sugar maple fails in summer heat. The distinctive 3-lobed leaves are smaller than those of northern sugar maple; trees are compact, multi-season ornamental trees with smooth gray bark, golden spring flower clusters, and the classic maple winged seeds (samaras) in spring. Florida maple tolerates the heat and soil alkalinity of zone 8–9 gardens significantly better than northern sugar maple cultivars and is the appropriate choice for fall color, shade, and wildlife value in Gulf Coast landscapes. Trees yield a small quantity of sap that can be made into a light maple syrup in the brief late-winter cold spells of zone 7–8.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained to moist, average to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida mistflower is more drought-tolerant than the common blue mistflower (C. coelestinum) and performs well in dry, sandy Gulf Coast soils.
directions: Florida mistflower is a Gulf Coast native closely related to but distinct from the common blue mistflower (Conoclinium coelestinum), with deeply dissected, pinnately cut leaves that give it a finer, lacier texture — the species name 'dissectum' refers to these divided leaves. It grows naturally in dry to mesic pine flatwoods, scrub oak habitat, and open sandy uplands of the Gulf Coastal Plain from Texas to Florida, making it more drought-tolerant and better adapted to the dry, sandy soils common across the region than its close relative. The vivid electric-blue flower clusters appear in fall and provide a spectacular nectar source for monarchs making their southward migration through the Gulf Coast; it is one of the most important native fall-blooming perennials for the Texas-to-Florida monarch flight corridor. Its compact, finer-textured form and better drought tolerance compared to C. coelestinum make it ideal for dry-soil native gardens, rock gardens, and xeric restoration plantings in the coastal Southeast.

plant_note: Plant tubers after all frost danger has passed when soil temperature is consistently above 65°F; in zone 9 plant April–June. Florida Moonlight is a sun-tolerant caladium variety — it handles 4–6 hours of direct sun better than most caladiums, making it usable in brighter locations than typical deep-shade caladiums, though it performs best with afternoon shade protection. In zone 9 caladium tubers can remain in the ground year-round in the warmest areas; in cooler zone 9 locations dig and store tubers after the foliage dies back in fall. The white leaves actually brighten shaded areas dramatically, making Florida Moonlight one of the best choices for illuminating dark garden corners.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil rich in organic matter — caladiums are woodland tropical plants that require the consistent moisture and filtered light of their forest-floor habitat; Florida Moonlight is a strap-leaf caladium variety producing medium-sized, lance-shaped leaves that are an exceptional, nearly pure white with thin, barely visible veins and delicate green leaf margins — one of the brightest and most luminous white caladiums available, producing a striking glow-in-the-shade effect that makes shaded areas appear lit from within. White caladiums like Florida Moonlight are specifically valued for their ability to brighten and visually enlarge dark garden areas — the reflective white leaves catch and amplify whatever ambient light reaches the shade garden, creating an appearance of much more light than is actually present. Florida Moonlight is also one of the more sun-tolerant caladiums, accepting 4–6 hours of direct morning sun with good moisture — making it more versatile than shade-only varieties for partially shaded transitional garden areas. In zone 9's hot summers, the combination of tropical heat tolerance and shade preference makes Florida Moonlight one of the most practical ornamental plants for the deep shade under mature trees where few other plants thrive.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Florida paspalum is a native perennial bunch grass of moist to dry open habitats throughout the southeastern Coastal Plain, including pine flatwoods, woodland edges, and moist roadsides.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Florida paspalum is one of the largest-statured native Paspalum species of the southeastern Coastal Plain, forming an erect, robust bunch grass with broad, flat leaves and characteristic two-ranked seed spikes. The plant grows naturally in pine flatwoods, open woodland edges, and moist prairies throughout the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain. As a native grass, it provides structural habitat for grassland birds, the seeds feed numerous ground-foraging birds, and the dense growth supports native insects. In the garden, it functions as a medium-to-large native bunch grass for moist, sunny, naturalistic plantings in zone 9a where it is perennial without irrigation. Good companion for native wildflowers in a longleaf pine ecosystem-style garden design.

plant_note: Transplant in spring after seeds have been cold-stratified for 4-6 weeks; plant into dry, acidic, sandy soil in full sun — avoid clay or amended garden soils.
directions: Florida Phlox is a Florida-endemic native perennial of dry, sandy, acidic pine flatwoods, sandhills, and scrub habitats, bearing clusters of lavender-pink to pale lavender 5-petaled flowers in spring atop narrow, stiff, slightly glandular-hairy stems. It is highly adapted to the extremely infertile, droughty, and acidic sandy soils characteristic of longleaf pine ecosystems where few other flowering perennials can survive, making it an exceptional choice for Florida native gardens and longleaf pine restoration plantings. Cold-stratify seeds for 4-6 weeks before sowing, then start indoors and transplant into dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun in spring. Avoid amended or enriched soils, clay, and any consistent moisture — this species demands conditions that mimic its native scrub habitat to thrive long-term.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, sandy or rocky soil in full sun to partial shade. Florida Privet tolerates salt spray, drought, and alkaline soil, making it ideal for coastal landscapes in zones 8b–11 where other native shrubs struggle.
directions: Florida Privet is a tough, adaptable native shrub, native to coastal hammocks, scrub, and beach margins of south Florida, the Keys, and the Caribbean, where it grows in thin, well-drained, sandy or rocky soils under the influence of salt spray and periodic drought. Related to the ornamental privets used in hedges but native to the Southeast, it produces tiny yellow-green flowers in very early spring (sometimes as early as January) that are among the first nectar sources of the year for native bees, followed by small, dark blue to black oval berries that are important food for migrants and resident birds. An excellent native hedge, screen, or windbreak plant for coastal zones 9–11 where it tolerates salt, alkaline soil, drought, and occasional flooding; male and female plants are needed for berry production, so plant a group for wildlife benefit. Prune as needed for shaping — it is fast-growing and responds well to trimming.

common_name: Florida Red Ruffles Caladium (Ruffled-Margin Red Strap-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Florida Red Ruffles is a University of Florida caladium introduction — bred specifically for Gulf Coast conditions and performance.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Florida Red Ruffles is a University of Florida caladium introduction distinguished by a remarkable leaf characteristic rarely found in other caladiums: distinctly ruffled, wavy, frilled leaf margins that give the foliage a crinkled, textured appearance unlike the smooth-edged leaves of most standard fancy and strap-leaf caladiums. The combination of the crimson-red to scarlet-red strap-leaf coloration and the unusually ruffled margins creates a more textured, ornamental leaf quality than any smooth-leaved red caladium — the frilling adds visual depth and interest that makes Florida Red Ruffles exceptional in close-up container plantings and detailed garden borders where the leaf texture can be appreciated. The strap-leaf form (narrower, more elongated leaves than fancy-leaf types) and compact habit produce a finer texture than large fancy-leaf varieties, making Florida Red Ruffles proportionate for small-scale applications. The ruffled margin trait is genetically stable and consistent across the crop — every leaf shows the characteristic crimping. Florida Red Ruffles performs well in the Gulf South heat and humidity for which it was bred, and the tubers overwinter successfully in-ground in zone 9b with mulch protection. Combine with smooth-leaved companions to highlight the textural contrast of the ruffled margins.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in very well-drained, highly acidic (pH 3.5–5.5), dry, sandy soil in full sun. Florida Rosemary requires the harsh, fire-maintained, nutrient-poor scrub conditions to which it is adapted; it will decline in rich, moist, or shaded conditions.
directions: Florida Rosemary is one of the most ecologically fascinating native shrubs in North America — a dominant species of the imperiled Florida scrub habitat, native to the ancient, white sand ridges of the Florida peninsula where it creates one of the strangest visual phenomena in American botany: "Florida rosemary rings," circular patches of bare white sand 3–20 feet in diameter surrounding each plant, kept barren by allelopathic chemicals (terpenes and phenolics) that the plant releases through its roots to prevent competing plants from establishing. Not a true rosemary (Rosmarinus), it bears superficial resemblance to the culinary herb with its needle-like, aromatic, evergreen leaves densely arranged on erect stems, but is a monotypic genus in the heath family (Ericaceae). Small red-orange flowers in fall are followed by tiny berries consumed by Florida scrub-jays, gopher tortoises, and other scrub species. Grow in the driest, most infertile, most acidic sand you can provide in full sun; it is intolerant of irrigation, rich soil, shade, or the weed-suppressive conditions that most ornamental plants require.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun. Florida Royal Palm performs best in moist, humid conditions and benefits from regular irrigation and fertilization during the growing season; it is intolerant of frost below 30°F.
directions: Florida Royal Palm is the most stately and formal of the native Florida palms, endemic to the wet, subtropical forests and swamp edges of the Everglades and extreme southern Florida, where it rises with a dramatically smooth, grayish-green, ringed trunk topped by a brilliant emerald-green crownshaft and an arching crown of long, gracefully curving feather-leaf fronds — a silhouette that defines the classical tropical landscape aesthetic. Once widely planted along formal avenues and boulevards in south Florida and Cuba (where the related Roystonea regia has the same role), Florida Royal Palm is a protected native species in Florida and an important component of Everglades ecosystem restoration. The white to purple flowers attract native bees, and the small olive-like fruits feed a wide variety of native birds and are an important food for the threatened Florida manatee in flooded situations. Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 10–11; fertilize regularly with a palm-specific fertilizer to prevent nutrient deficiencies.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in spring into moist to moderately dry soil in partial to full shade; space plugs 9–15 inches apart to allow the mat-forming habit to knit together as a low-maintenance groundcover.
directions: Plant divisions in spring into well-drained to moderately moist soil beneath oaks, pines, or other high-canopy trees, spacing plugs 9–15 inches apart and watering in thoroughly to settle the roots. Florida sedge is an evergreen, fine-textured native of the southeastern coastal plain that spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a dense, low-maintenance mat just four to ten inches tall, making it one of the best native alternatives to turfgrass in shaded Florida and Gulf Coast landscapes. Once established, it requires little supplemental irrigation and no fertilizer, thriving in the naturally lean, acidic soils found under longleaf pine and live oak canopies. Mow or shear lightly once a year in late winter if a tidier appearance is desired, then allow fresh foliage to flush before the growing season begins.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Florida Sunshine is a Louisiana Super Plants selection, a chartreuse-gold foliage sport of the Florida-native anise shrub, brightening further to yellow in fall and colder weather.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Florida Sunshine is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated selection of the Florida native anise shrub, grown almost entirely for its brilliant chartreuse-to-gold evergreen foliage, which glows in a shaded bed year-round and intensifies to a deeper yellow with cooler fall and winter temperatures — an unusually reliable, low-maintenance way to add sustained bright color to deep shade where flowering plants often struggle. Crushed leaves release the same anise-like fragrance as the straight species. Its narrow, upright growth habit makes it useful as a bright vertical accent or informal screen in a shaded border, contrasting well against dark-green companions like azaleas, camellias, or hollies.
