It tolerates a range of shade levels and adapts to both moist and average garden soil once established, needing little more than routine watering during dry spells and an occasional light shaping if a more formal look is wanted.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring (necks at soil level) in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zone 7–11; Florida Swamp Lily is a spectacular, large-flowered, native Crinum bulb indigenous to the wetlands, swamp margins, bayous, and river edges of the Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida — producing clusters of large, fragrant, white, spider-lily-like flowers all summer from enormous bulbs adapted to standing water and periodic flooding.
directions: Plant large bulbs with necks at or just below soil surface in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun — Florida Swamp Lily is adapted to saturated, flooded soils and should be placed at pond edges, in rain gardens, or in any consistently moist to wet position; never allow to dry out in summer. Crinum americanum (Florida Swamp Lily or American Swamp Lily) is a large, robustly growing, bulbous perennial native to the freshwater and slightly brackish marshes, swamp margins, bayou edges, and river shores of the Gulf Coastal Plain from Texas east through Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida — one of the most dramatic and handsome native wetland flowers of the southeastern United States. The large, clustered, white, fragrant, spider-lily-like flowers — each bloom with 6 long, narrow, straplike petals and long, projecting stamens — are produced in umbels of 3–9 on long, stout, hollow scapes reaching 2–4 feet, blooming repeatedly through summer and fall. The enormous, onion-like bulbs adapt remarkably well to standing water conditions — the plants naturally grow with their lower bulb sections submerged — and tolerate both freshwater and slight salinity. Crinum americanum is closely related to the widely planted C. asiaticum (Giant Crinum) but is native to the Americas and naturally cold-hardy through zone 7. An outstanding, floriferous, low-maintenance native plant for Gulf Coast wet gardens, pond margins, and rain gardens. Do not confuse with the invasive Crinum bulbispermum.

common_name: Florida Sweetheart Caladium (Compact Pink Strap-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Florida Sweetheart is a strap-leaf type with higher sun tolerance than standard fancy-leaved types.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to partial sun; Florida Sweetheart is a University of Florida strap-leaf caladium introduction — a compact variety producing narrower, more elongated, lance-shaped leaves (strap-leaf habit) in rose-pink to medium pink coloration with green margins, creating a soft, delicate pink effect quite different from the bold, large-patterned fancy-leaved types. The smaller leaf size and narrower shape of strap-leaf caladiums create a finer, more graceful texture in mass plantings — particularly effective in edging applications, container gardens, and detailed plantings where the standard 18–24 inch fancy types would be too large in scale. Florida Sweetheart's soft pink coloration creates a romantic, cottage-garden effect in shade positions — the pink tones are effective paired with white companions (white impatiens, white caladiums like 'Candidum', white-flowered ajuga) or with contrasting deep purple foliage (dark heucheras, black ajuga). The higher sun tolerance of strap-leaf caladiums compared to standard fancy types allows Florida Sweetheart to be planted in positions receiving 3–4 hours of morning sun — expanding its usefulness to partially shaded locations that might bleach or damage large white-leaved types.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade. Florida Thatch Palm is slow-growing and does not tolerate frost — it is appropriate only for zones 10–11. Source only from nurseries to protect wild populations in the Florida Keys.
directions: Florida Thatch Palm is an elegant, slender native palm endemic to the coastal hammocks and rocky shorelines of the Florida Keys and extreme southern Florida, with a natural range extending through the Caribbean and Central America, where it grows in limestone soils near the coast and in coastal hammock understories. Its graceful crown of silvery-green fan-shaped fronds provides an authentically tropical appearance in zone 10–11 landscapes, and small white flowers in spring produce clusters of round white berries that are important food for Florida Keys birds, particularly white-crowned pigeons. Slow-growing, drought- and salt-tolerant once established, and tolerant of brief cold snaps to about 30°F, Florida Thatch Palm is an excellent specimen palm for small gardens or use as an understory palm beneath taller coconut or royal palms in south Florida landscapes. Wild populations are protected in Florida; always purchase nursery-grown plants.

plant_note: Set plants or direct-sow into wet, sandy or peaty soil in spring and keep the root zone from drying out through establishment.
directions: Unlike the common annual tickseeds, this fleshy-leaved Florida endemic is a true fall-blooming perennial best planted where soil stays consistently moist, such as pond margins, low prairies, and the damp edges of marshes. It is found statewide except the far northern Panhandle and supplies a critical late-season nectar source for bees and migrating butterflies after most Gulf Coast wildflowers have finished. Set plants or direct-sow into wet, sandy or peaty soil in spring and keep the root zone from drying out through establishment. Once rooted it spreads slowly to form dense colonies that tolerate periodic standing water.

plant_note: Plant conservation-sourced nursery transplants in spring in cool, moist, well-drained, rich, acidic, humus-rich soil on a north-facing or east-facing slope in deep to partial shade. Florida Torreya requires the cool, humid microclimate of a shaded ravine and will not survive in exposed, hot, or dry conditions. Obtain plants only from reputable conservation nurseries growing ex situ material.
directions: Florida Torreya — also called Stinking Cedar for its pungent, resinous foliage — is one of the most critically endangered trees on Earth, native to a handful of steep, moist ravines along the Apalachicola River in the Florida Panhandle and adjacent Georgia, where the cool, humid microclimate provides conditions unlike anywhere else in Florida. Once abundant in these ravine forests, the species was devastated by an unknown fungal disease beginning in the 1950s and is now functionally extinct in the wild, surviving only as root sprouts and in ex situ conservation plantings maintained by botanical gardens and the nonprofit Torreya Guardians. The plum-like seeds were roasted and eaten by the Creek Nation and early settlers, and the dense, aromatic wood was historically used for fence posts and fuel. Plant in cool, moist, well-drained, rich, acidic soil in deep shade on a north-facing slope; obtain plants only from conservation nurseries producing legally sourced stock, as wild collection is not permitted.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade, mimicking the leaf-litter-covered floor of a limestone hammock; never dig from the wild, since this species is protected in Florida.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in rich, humusy, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in deep to partial shade, and mulch with leaf litter to hold moisture as it would in its native hammock habitat. Only source plants from reputable native-plant nurseries, since this fern is a threatened Florida native and should never be collected from the wild. Over time it develops a short, upright trunk topped by a crown of broad, finely divided fronds, giving it a miniature tree-fern presence that is unusual among the ground ferns typically used in South Florida shade gardens.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring and plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Florida Wood Fern is adapted to the subtropical conditions of the Florida peninsula and Gulf Coast and is one of the most ornamental evergreen ferns for Zone 8b–10 shade gardens.
directions: Florida Wood Fern is a handsome evergreen native fern of the southeastern coastal plain, native to the moist, shaded understories of cypress swamps, bayheads, and bottomland hardwood forests from South Carolina to peninsular Florida, where it grows in the humid, warm-temperate and subtropical conditions of the lower coastal plain. Its dark, glossy, leathery fronds are fully evergreen in zones 9–11, making it one of the most attractive year-round ferns for warm-climate shade gardens, and its tolerance of briefly flooded conditions suits it to rain garden depressions and pond margins in partial shade. Closely related to Southern Wood Fern (Dryopteris ludoviciana) but adapted to the warmer, more subtropical conditions of the Florida peninsula, it is a better choice than its northern relative for zone 9b–10 landscapes. Divide clumps in spring and plant in deeply amended, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; mulch generously to maintain moisture.

plant_note: Plant conservation-sourced nursery transplants in spring in cool, moist, well-drained, rich, acidic soil in deep shade on a north- or east-facing slope. All parts except the red aril are extremely toxic — do not plant where children or livestock have access. Seeds require an extended warm-then-cold stratification of 12–18 months before germination.
directions: Florida Yew is an extremely rare and critically endangered native conifer restricted to fewer than two dozen sites in the moist, shaded ravines along the Apalachicola River in the Florida Panhandle, where it shares habitat with Florida Torreya in one of the most species-rich temperate forest communities in the southeastern United States. The small evergreen tree or large shrub produces fleshy, bright red arils surrounding a single hard seed in fall; the aril is the only non-toxic portion of the plant, as all other parts including the seeds, bark, and needles contain highly toxic taxine alkaloids that can be rapidly fatal to humans and livestock. Related to the yews exploited in the development of Taxol, a significant cancer chemotherapy drug, Florida Yew has declined catastrophically from unknown causes and numbers fewer than 250 remaining individuals in the wild. Plant conservation-sourced transplants in cool, moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade — this species is intolerant of direct sun, drought, heat, or compacted soils and demands the microclimate of a deeply shaded, cool ravine.

plant_note: Soak dried corms in water for 4 hours before planting; plant 2 inches deep with the pointed side down (or flat side down if unsure — they are forgiving). In zones 8–11, plant in fall for winter and spring blooms. In zones 4–7, plant in early spring for summer bloom.
directions: Plant soaked corms 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; florist anemone is one of the most prized cut flowers of the Mediterranean winter and spring, producing brilliant 2–3 inch poppy-like flowers in an exceptional range of colors — deep crimson, clear red, violet, pink, and white, all with dramatic black stamens in the center. The De Caen series (single) and St. Brigid series (semi-double) are the most popular cultivars for home cutting gardens. In Gulf Coast and Deep South gardens (zones 8‑9), plant corms in October or November for winter to spring blooms; temperatures above 75°F send plants into dormancy. The corms are inexpensive and can be planted in masses for a spectacular floral display.

plant_note: Sow seeds indoors 4–6 months before desired bloom time in cool conditions (60°F) in well-drained potting mix; cyclamen persicum is the species parent of all florist cyclamen, but the species type is smaller, more fragrant, and better adapted to outdoor garden conditions than the large-flowered hybrids sold as pot plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial to full shade in zones 9–11; florist cyclamen is the wild species behind all the large-flowered hybrid cyclamen sold as indoor pot plants, but the wild species type is smaller, more fragrant, and far more garden-worthy in Mediterranean and subtropical climates. It grows naturally in the rocky, shaded forests and scrublands of the eastern Mediterranean (Greece, Turkey, Lebanon), flowering in winter and spring during the rainy season and going dormant in summer drought. In zone 9–10, it can be grown as an outdoor perennial in shaded, well-drained beds — a revelation for gardeners accustomed to treating it as a disposable pot plant. The natural-type flowers are smaller than hybrid forms but intensely fragrant. Keep tubers dry in summer; resume irrigation in fall for winter bloom. Excellent in rock gardens, under trees, and in winter shade garden containers.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile succulent potting mix in bright indirect light to part shade; florist kalanchoe is a short-day plant — it requires 6+ weeks of days shorter than 12 hours to initiate flowering, which occurs naturally in fall/winter.
directions: Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral succulent potting mix in bright indirect light; allow to dry between waterings; provide 6+ weeks of short days (less than 12 hours) to induce re-flowering. Kalanchoe blossfeldiana (florist kalanchoe or Christmas kalanchoe) is one of the world's best-selling potted plants — a Madagascar succulent producing a compact mound of glossy, scallop-edged, fleshy, dark-green leaves and dense, upright clusters of long-lasting, 4-petaled flowers in red, orange, yellow, salmon, pink, white, and purple — flowers that remain fresh for 6–8 weeks or more on the plant. The plants are 'forced' into bloom by commercial growers by manipulating photoperiod (day length); at home, allowing plants to experience natural short days in fall and early winter will trigger re-blooming. In zones 10–12, kalanchoe can be grown outdoors in frost-free, well-drained locations as a tender perennial; in zone 9 and cooler, it is an outstanding houseplant and winter gift plant. After blooming, cut back flower stalks and reduce water; resume normal watering and fertilizing in spring. CAUTION: Toxic to cats and dogs.

plant_note: Start tubers indoors in shallow trays of moist peat or potting mix with the concave side up in late winter; Florist's Gloxinia is typically sold as potted flowering tubers in bloom and grown as a houseplant. After flowering, allow the plant to go dormant by reducing watering — the foliage will yellow and die back. Store dry tubers in peat moss at 55–60°F through winter, then restart in fresh potting mix in late winter. Seeds are extremely fine — do not cover, just surface-sow on moist mix under fluorescent lights. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Florist's Gloxinia flowers most prolifically in the bright indirect light of a north or east window and will refuse to bloom in dim conditions; direct sun scorches the large, velvety leaves. Sinningia speciosa is a tuberous gesneriad from the rainforests of southern Brazil, cultivated since the 1820s and now available in an extraordinary range of cultivars and hybrids that have transformed the originally modest native plant into one of the most spectacular of all indoor-blooming plants. The flower buds emerge directly from the center of the plant and open to large, flared, trumpet-shaped blooms 3–4 inches across in vivid colors including violet, purple, white, pink, red, and bicolored forms with spotted, frilled, or picotee edges — all with a velvety texture matching the large, soft, dark-green, hairy leaves that surround them. The combination of huge, velvety flowers in saturated colors and the compact rosette of lush foliage makes a well-grown Gloxinia in full bloom one of the most visually striking of all flowering houseplants. Modern hybrid varieties bloom more freely and over longer periods than the species, and can be regrown from tubers through multiple seasons. The name 'Gloxinia' commonly used in commerce is technically incorrect — true Gloxinia is a related but distinct genus; the florist plant is correctly Sinningia speciosa. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; succession sow for continuous cutting.
directions: Direct sow after frost in full sun, spacing closer at 6 inches for single stems or wider for branching plants. This florist mix blends apricot, lemon, peach, and gold shades from named cultivars, offering both single-stemmed and branching types for varied bouquets. Sow successively every couple weeks for a continuous cutting supply. Cut when the first petals lift and water evenly while establishing.

common_name: Floristan Liatris (Classic Tall Gayfeather for Cut Flowers and Pollinators)
plant_note: Plant corms in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Floristan is a classic, widely grown gayfeather cultivar bred for uniform, tall flower spikes prized in both pollinator gardens and the cut-flower trade.
directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Floristan is a classic, long-cultivated selection of native gayfeather bred for tall, uniform, densely packed spikes of fuzzy violet-purple flowers (a white-flowered 'Floristan White' counterpart is also available) that open from the top down, unusual among spike-flowering perennials, making a striking vertical accent in the border. Its reliable, uniform habit has made it a mainstay of the commercial cut-flower trade as well as home gardens, and the flowers are a strong draw for butterflies, bees, and other pollinators through their summer bloom season. Cut spent flower spikes for indoor arrangements or deadhead to tidy the plant, and divide congested clumps of corms every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; Floristan White is the white-flowered counterpart to the classic Floristan Violet gayfeather, sharing the same tall, uniform flower spikes.
directions: Plant corms in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding heavy, waterlogged ground that can rot the corms over winter. Floristan White is a long-cultivated selection of native dense blazing star bred for tall, densely packed, pure white bottlebrush spikes that open from the top down, an unusual flowering pattern among spike-forming perennials, and pairs naturally with its violet-flowered Floristan Violet sibling in cut-flower and pollinator plantings. Like the species, it draws heavy traffic from butterflies, bees, and other pollinators through its summer bloom season and provides seed for finches if spikes are left standing into fall. Its reliable, uniform habit and strong stems have made it a mainstay of the commercial cut-flower trade as well as the perennial border; divide congested corm clusters every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors (seeds need light) 6–8 weeks before last frost; do not cover seeds; transplant to well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost.
directions: Surface sow indoors (seeds need light) 6–8 weeks before last frost; do not cover seeds; transplant to well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost. Ageratum houstonianum is one of the few reliable blue-flowered annuals for summer borders, producing dense, rounded clusters of fuzzy, powder-blue to lilac-blue (and in cultivars, white and pink) flowers from early summer through frost; the blue forms are invaluable as a true-blue counterpoint to yellow and orange summer annuals and are excellent for creating blue-and-white formal bedding schemes. Tolerates partial shade better than most summer annuals, making it useful for bright, open shade situations; it is a good companion planting around cabbage and brassicas as a potential pest deterrent. The species can be mildly allelopathic and self-toxic in dense plantings.

subcategory: groundcover shrub rose, Flower Carpet series
plant_note: Transplant container-grown plants in spring into well-drained soil, spacing to let the wide-spreading mounds knit together into a solid groundcover.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, watering deeply through the first growing season to encourage roots to spread beneath the wide, low canopy. Once established, the vigorous, disease-resistant foliage needs little care beyond an annual cutback in late winter to renew growth. Small, bright pink semi-double flowers smother the spreading mounds almost continuously from late spring to frost, a signature trait of the original Flower Carpet introduction that popularized low-maintenance groundcover roses. Its dense habit suppresses weeds and works well on slopes, in mass plantings, or cascading over retaining walls.

common_name: Flower Record Crocus (Classic Large-Flowered Purple Dutch Crocus)
plant_note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Flower Record is a classic large-flowered Dutch crocus cultivar prized for its rich, uniform purple color.
directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Flower Record naturalizes well in a lawn or border and multiplies steadily by cormlets over the years. Large, goblet-shaped flowers open a rich, deep violet-purple with a subtle darker feathering at the base and a bright orange-yellow throat and stamens, a bold, saturated color that reads strongly even from a distance, making it one of the most widely planted large-flowered Dutch crocus cultivars for mass spring color. It opens wide in full sun each day and closes at night or in overcast weather to protect the pollen. Allow foliage to die back naturally before mowing over naturalized plantings, and divide congested clumps in summer dormancy if flowering begins to decline after many seasons.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; flowering almond blooms on old wood — prune immediately after flowering to promote vigorous new growth that will carry next year's flowers. Do not prune in fall or winter, which removes the flower buds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; flowering almond is a Chinese shrub long cultivated in Asian gardens, producing small, double-flowered blooms so densely that stems are buried in flowers from tip to base in early spring. The double pink cultivar 'Sinensis' and double white 'Alba Plena' are the most widely grown forms. Unlike most Prunus shrubs, flowering almond has little wildlife value (the double flowers limit pollinator access and fruit rarely sets) but provides exceptional ornamental impact in the spring garden. After flowering, the plant is an unremarkable medium deciduous shrub, so site it where it can be seen from a window during its brief but spectacular early spring bloom and is less conspicuous the rest of the year. Prune hard immediately after bloom to maintain a compact, floriferous shape.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; in the South, flowering dogwood requires afternoon shade protection and is significantly more stressed and disease-prone in full sun — understory conditions mimic its natural habitat.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to dappled shade — flowering dogwood is one of the most beloved native understory trees of the eastern US, producing its iconic four-bract 'flowers' (actually modified leaves surrounding tiny true flowers) in brilliant white or pink in early spring before the leaves emerge, covering the tiered, horizontal branches in a sheet of bloom visible through the forest from a distance. The leaves are followed by clusters of brilliant red berries in fall that feed migrating birds, and the foliage itself turns brilliant scarlet and purple in autumn. In the South, flowering dogwood is more susceptible to dogwood anthracnose fungal disease in hot, wet, poorly-aired conditions than in the North; plant in well-drained soil with good air circulation and avoid wetting foliage to reduce disease pressure. Zone 9 specimens benefit from afternoon shade and consistent moisture during summer heat.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost; in zones below 9, grow in containers and bring indoors before frost.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; flowering maple is not a true maple but a tropical shrub with maple-like leaves and pendant, bell-shaped flowers in yellow, orange, red, pink, or white that hang in clusters from arching branches and bloom almost continuously in frost-free climates. An excellent hummingbird and butterfly plant. Pinch growing tips monthly to keep plants bushy and floriferous. Feed monthly with a balanced fertilizer during active growth. Container-grown plants can be overwintered indoors in a bright, cool room; reduce watering in winter and resume normal care in spring. Bring containers outdoors after last frost.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring and plant 2-4 inches deep in a submerged pot of heavy loam set at the pond margin in up to 6 inches of standing water.
directions: Set rhizome divisions into containers of heavy garden soil and place them at the pond edge in shallow water, where the rush-like foliage sends up tall stalks topped with umbels of pink, three-petaled flowers in mid to late summer. It thrives in the same shallow marginal zone as pickerelweed and sagittaria and tolerates both standing water and periodic drying. Because it spreads by rhizome fragments and bulblets and is classified as a noxious aquatic weed in several US states and Canadian provinces, confine plantings to pots and check local regulations before adding it to a pond.

subcategory: native prairie and woodland edge perennial
plant_note: Direct-sow in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; flowering spurge develops a deep taproot and resists transplanting once established — site carefully. It thrives in lean, dry soils and drought conditions and will self-sow to establish a colony over time. Wear gloves when handling as the milky sap is a skin and eye irritant.
directions: Sow in lean, well-drained, dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; flowering spurge is a graceful, airy native perennial found in prairies, roadsides, and open woodlands from Ontario to Florida, producing clouds of tiny white flowers with bright-white petal-like bracts from June through September — the entire upper portion of the plant becomes a frothy white mist of bloom in summer. Its structural similarity to Baby's Breath (Gypsophila) in the garden is striking — the branching sprays of tiny white flowers have the same airy, cloud-like quality and fill a similar garden role, but as a long-lived native perennial adapted to dry, lean soils. The milky sap is caustic and was used medicinally by Native Americans. Flowering spurge is drought-tolerant, self-sowing, and an important late-season nectar source for butterflies including skippers, hairstreaks, and sulphurs that congregate on the flowers. The gray-green foliage turns reddish in fall. An outstanding filler plant for lean, dry soils in full sun.

plant_note: Press seeds onto moist seed-starting mix surface without covering — nicotiana seeds need light to germinate — at 65–75°F; start 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all danger of frost has passed in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Press seeds onto moist seed-starting mix surface in bright light without covering at 65–75°F — seeds need light for germination; start 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost danger passes in full sun to partial shade. Flowering tobacco produces an extended succession of tubular, star-shaped flowers in white, pink, lime-green, red, and crimson from early summer until frost, with the white-flowered forms releasing one of the most intensely sweet fragrances in the evening garden, attracting sphinx moths and hummingbirds after dark. Modern dwarf hybrids (Sensation series) are day-neutral and odorless; for fragrance seek out the species or older heirloom selections. It tolerates partial shade better than most summer annuals and self-seeds freely where happy.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds (nick or scarify seed coat for improved germination) or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in spring; senna establishes rapidly from seed and may bloom the first year from seed; it dies to the ground in zone 8 but rebounds vigorously from the root.
directions: Direct-sow scarified seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; flowery senna (Argentine senna) is a fast-growing South American shrub that provides one of the most spectacular late-summer and fall flower displays available in the Gulf Coast garden — smothered from late August through November in clusters of brilliant, clear-yellow, five-petaled flowers that glow with exceptional intensity as other summer plants fatigue. It is critically important as the larval host plant for the Cloudless Sulphur butterfly (Phoebis sennae) and the Sleepy Orange butterfly (Abaeis nicippe) — expect to find caterpillars feeding on the foliage throughout summer, which is a sign of success rather than a problem. The plant is fast-growing, drought-tolerant, and thrives in poor, dry soil — conditions that suit it for problem, hot, dry corners of the garden. In zone 8 it dies to the ground in winter but rebounds from the root to 6–8 feet by midsummer. Excellent screening plant for late-season butterfly gardens.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Fluffy Ruffles Boston fern wants higher humidity than average indoor air and benefits from regular misting.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Fluffy Ruffles Boston fern wants higher humidity than average indoor air and benefits from regular misting. This dense, compact sport of the classic Boston fern produces heavily divided, finely ruffled, densely overlapping fronds that give the whole plant a plush, feathery texture quite different from the longer, more open fronds of standard Boston fern, staying more compact and upright rather than trailing dramatically. Its bushier, less pendulous habit makes it a good choice for a tabletop or pedestal display as well as a hanging basket, and it shares the classic Boston fern's air-purifying reputation and easy care once its humidity needs are met. Keep the potting mix consistently moist, provide humidity through misting or a pebble tray, and trim any browned fronds at the base.

plant_note: Direct sow in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in a sunny location at or just after last frost.
directions: Trichostema brachiatum is a delicate, much-branched native annual of the mint family, closely related to the blue curls of the eastern US, producing small pale blue to lavender flowers on slender aromatic stems from midsummer through fall. It is native to dry, sandy or rocky open ground, cedar glades, and thin soils across the south-central and southeastern US, and performs best in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun with no summer irrigation. Direct sow in spring and thin to 6-9 inches apart; avoid rich or clay soils, which cause lanky growth and reduce flowering. An excellent choice for naturalistic rock gardens, prairie restorations, and dry native meadow plantings.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed, then direct sow after frost at the base of a support.
directions: Nick the hard seed coat and soak overnight, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis or fence. Flying Saucer bears 5-inch white blooms streaked with blue pinwheel stripes and occasional flecks, each flower slightly different, on vigorous vines to 10 feet. On cloudy days the flowers stay open all day, and the heart-shaped leaves lend a tropical look. Note that parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

common_name: Flying Saucers Morning Glory (Blue-and-White Marbled Morning Glory)
plant_note: Nick or soak seeds overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow after last frost; morning glories resent transplanting.
directions: Nick the seed coat with a file or soak overnight, then direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a trellis or fence. Flying Saucers produces large flowers marbled and striped in blue and white in an unpredictable, painterly pattern that varies from bloom to bloom, so no two flowers look quite the same, an appealing novelty on an otherwise typical fast-growing, twining vine. Like other Ipomoea tricolor types it opens fresh each dawn and closes by early afternoon, blooming most heavily as days shorten in late summer and fall. Deadhead spent flowers before seed set to prevent unwanted volunteers the following year, since morning glories self-sow readily in warm climates.

plant_note: Cold stratify seed 60–90 days before sowing; surface sow on moist mix under lights 6–8 weeks before spring for first-year transplants. Easier to propagate by dividing established clumps in early spring or fall.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; foam flower is a native Eastern North American woodland groundcover that spreads gently by stolons to form a weed-suppressing mat. The maple-leaf-shaped foliage is attractive all season and often develops bronze or reddish marbling in fall; in late spring, airy white flower spikes rise above the foliage for several weeks. Divide clumps every 2–3 years in early spring to maintain vigor. The plant is deer-resistant and extremely low-maintenance once established in a cool, shaded site with consistently moist soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; avoid planting too deeply — the crown should rest at soil level.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, mimicking its native habitat on the forest floor; foamflower produces mounded clumps of deeply lobed, often burgundy-marked foliage and sends up airy white flower spikes in mid-spring that give the plant its common name. Running forms spread by stolons to colonize an area; clump-forming varieties stay tighter. Modern cultivars (many under the Heucherella group when crossed with Heuchera) offer extraordinary foliage variation. Pair with ferns, hostas, and wild ginger for a classic woodland floor combination. Plants dislike summer drought — mulch to retain moisture and site in a spot with consistent moisture.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; Heucherella is a sterile bigeneric hybrid between Heuchera (coral bells) and Tiarella (foamflower) combining the bold, colorful foliage of heuchera with the spreading, ground-covering habit and foamy spring flowers of tiarella.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in part to full shade; mulch to maintain cool, moist roots. Heucherella tiarelloides (foamy bells or heucherella) is a sterile bigeneric hybrid between Heuchera (coral bells) and Tiarella (foamflower) — two closely related native North American shade perennials that cross naturally and have been extensively hybridized to produce a range of outstanding, foliage-forward shade perennials combining features of both parents. Heucherella plants produce the bold, often brilliantly colored and patterned foliage of heucheras (in purple, bronze, caramel, silver-and-green, lime green, and other combinations) combined with the ground-covering, stoloniferous spreading habit and foamy spring flower spikes of tiarella — an outstanding combination for shade gardening. Unlike their heuchera parents, many heucherella selections also show good heat tolerance. Modern named cultivars ('Sweet Tea,' 'Stoplight,' 'Tapestry,' 'Brass Lantern') offer striking foliage colors that change seasonally. In zone 9, heucherella performs best in shade with consistent moisture and protection from summer afternoon heat. An excellent companion for hostas, ferns, and astilbes in shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; foothill palo verde is the smaller, more drought-resistant palo verde of rocky Sonoran Desert slopes and bajadas. More cold-hardy than blue palo verde, surviving to about 10°F when established. Extremely slow-growing on the rocky, dry sites it prefers.
directions: Plant scarified seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; foothill palo verde (yellow palo verde) is the smaller, stouter, more spiny, and more drought-resistant companion of blue palo verde in the Sonoran Desert — where both species often grow together on rocky desert slopes, bajadas, and wash margins. Distinguished from blue palo verde by its shorter stature, more yellow-green (rather than blue-green) trunk and branches, more prominent spines, and pale yellow flowers (slightly paler than blue palo verde's bright yellow). Like blue palo verde, the green trunk is photosynthetically active, allowing drought survival after leaf drop. Slower growing than blue palo verde and eventually smaller, making it appropriate for smaller garden spaces. The seeds are also edible. Produces the iconic Sonoran Desert 'nurse plant' relationship with saguaro cactus — more saguaro seedlings establish and survive under the nurse canopy of palo verde and other desert shrubs than in open desert. An essential Sonoran Desert native for xeriscape plantings in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; foothill penstemon needs sharp drainage and struggles in heavy clay or overwatered garden soil.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; foothill penstemon needs sharp drainage and struggles in heavy clay or overwatered garden soil. Narrow, blue-green leaves set off tall spikes of vivid blue to violet-blue, tubular flowers held well above the foliage from late spring through summer, one of the most intensely blue-flowered of the California native penstemons and a strong draw for bees and hummingbirds. Native to dry, rocky foothill slopes and chaparral edges across California, it thrives on lean soil and minimal supplemental water once established, making it a good choice for a California native meadow, rock garden, or dry border. Cut back spent flower spikes to tidy the plant and may encourage a lighter rebloom, and avoid rich, moist soil or heavy mulch that can lead to crown rot.

plant_note: Plant container-grown palms in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; footstool palm is frost-tender and grown as an indoor or greenhouse palm outside zones 10-11.
directions: Plant container-grown palms in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; footstool palm is frost-tender and grown as an indoor or greenhouse palm outside zones 10-11. Distinctive round, pleated, fan-shaped leaves give this Southeast Asian palm both its common name and a soft, almost circular silhouette unlike the more angular fan shape of many other fan palms, with a slender trunk that grows quickly and gracefully upward once established. Popular as a young potted palm for interior spaces due to its attractive round leaf shape and relatively fast juvenile growth, it eventually becomes a substantial landscape tree in frost-free tropical climates far too large for typical indoor culture. Water when the top of the potting mix or soil begins to dry, provide bright indirect light or filtered outdoor shade, and protect from any frost, since the species has essentially no cold tolerance.

common_name: Forest Bell Bush (River Bells, Broad Mackaya)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in partial to full shade in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; Forest Bell Bush prefers the cool, shaded conditions of its native forest habitat and will scorch in full afternoon sun in zone 9. It blooms most heavily in winter to spring (December–March in zone 9), providing lavender flower color when the shade garden has little else in bloom. In zone 9a, hard freezes may kill top growth but established plants typically resprout from the crown in spring.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Forest Bell Bush is one of the finest shade-tolerant flowering shrubs for zone 9 Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes, providing beautiful lavender blooms in the cool season when most shade plants are not flowering. Mackaya bella is a glossy-leaved evergreen shrub native to the subtropical coastal forest and riverine bush of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, growing naturally in the shade of forest margins and along shaded stream banks — conditions that translate perfectly to zone 9 shaded garden beds. The attractive, large, dark-green, glossy leaves have attractive wavy margins and create an excellent textural backdrop year-round. In winter to spring, the plant produces delicate, tubular, 5-lobed flowers 2 inches long in pale lavender with darker veining — a distinctive, elegant color combination that is very different from the saturated purples of most tropical flowering shrubs. The flowers are produced in loose, airy terminal spikes over a period of 6–10 weeks. Forest Bell Bush is a monotypic genus (only one species in the genus Mackaya) in the Acanthaceae family, closely related to the Justicia and Eranthemum plants well-suited to Gulf Coast shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall with the top third above the soil surface in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; Veltheimia bracteata goes summer-dormant (June–August) and must be kept dry during this rest period — reduce watering significantly as foliage yellows and allow it to die back naturally before storage or dry pot rest. It resumes active growth in fall.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to part shade; forest lily is a South African bulb in the hyacinth family that thrives in the dappled shade conditions that defeat most flowering bulbs — producing handsome rosettes of large, glossy, wavy-edged leaves in autumn, then, in late winter and early spring (January–March), tall pinkish-mottled scapes topped with dense, drooping clusters of tubular flowers in warm rose-pink to coral-pink that closely resemble a soft-colored red-hot poker or kniphofia in miniature. The combination of shade tolerance, winter-to-spring bloom period, and attractive foliage through the cool season makes it uniquely valuable for shaded gardens in zones 9–11 where almost no other flowering bulb performs reliably in shade. After flowering it enters mandatory summer dormancy (June through August) and must be kept relatively dry during this period — a reversed dormancy cycle opposite to most northern temperate bulbs. Outstanding as a container specimen for a shaded patio and excellent for naturalizing under evergreen trees.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Forest Pansy does not transplant well when large — purchase and plant small container trees and disturb the root system as little as possible.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Forest Pansy is the most widely grown and recognized purple-leafed redbud cultivar — selected for its spectacular, rich purple to wine-red heart-shaped leaves that emerge in spring immediately after the rosy-pink flower display and persist with deep purple coloration through summer, transitioning to orange-red in fall. The stunning spring sequence begins with the bare branches covered in rosy-pink flowers in February–March in zone 9 (before the leaves emerge), followed immediately by the emergence of the deep wine-red heart-shaped leaves — a foliage display that maintains dramatic interest throughout the growing season. The purple leaf color is most intense in spring and early summer, gradually fading to greenish-purple through the hottest summer months, then reviving to orange-red in fall. Forest Pansy grows as a small multi-trunked or single-stemmed tree to 15–25 feet tall and wide, with an elegant horizontal branching pattern. It is more shade-tolerant than many ornamental trees, performing well with 4–6 hours of sun in the understory of larger trees, though leaf color is most vibrant in full sun. In zone 9, afternoon shade helps prevent summer leaf scorch. Plant in well-drained soil — redbud roots are highly susceptible to root rot in poorly drained, wet sites.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, woodland soil for natural cold stratification and spring germination; forest phacelia is a true shade-tolerant annual-biennial wildflower that naturalizes readily under deciduous trees, blooming in spring before the canopy leafs out and filling gaps in the woodland floor with lavender-blue flowers beloved by native bees.
directions: Scatter seeds in fall in moist, woodland soil under deciduous trees or in shaded beds; seeds need cold stratification and will germinate in early spring when temperatures warm. Forest phacelia is a native annual or biennial wildflower of eastern North American forests (Appalachian region south to Alabama) that is one of the rare shade-tolerant native annuals — it germinates and blooms in the dappled light of early spring before the tree canopy fills in, producing ferny, deeply divided, slightly hairy leaves and clusters of 5-petaled lavender-blue flowers with prominent violet stamens that are outstanding for early-season native bees, especially bumble bee queens just emerging from dormancy. It self-seeds reliably in suitable shaded, moist sites to form a self-sustaining colony. Not widely available commercially but worth seeking out from native plant nurseries; grows easily from fresh seed collected in summer.

common_name: Forever Red Heuchera (Season-Long Deep Red Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; deep color holds year-round with some winter chill.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates to keep the deep color from bleaching out. Forever Red is a Proven Winners heuchera bred to hold its rich, deep wine-red foliage color consistently from spring through winter, unlike many red- and purple-leaved heucheras that fade to green or bronze as the season progresses. Compact and dense, it forms a tidy mound well suited to border edges, rock gardens, and mixed containers, sending up small white flowers on wiry stems in early summer that draw hummingbirds and pollinators. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting divisions slightly deeper than their original position as the crown lifts over time.

common_name: Forget Me Anthurium (Forgetii, Silver Vein Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light with high humidity (60–80%); Anthurium forgetii is a compact collector's anthurium that performs well as a tabletop specimen. Use a chunky, well-aerated epiphytic mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil. Water thoroughly when the top layer dries. Propagate from stem cuttings with an aerial root or from seed. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Anthurium forgetii produces its best foliage with consistent bright indirect light and will slow considerably in dim conditions. Anthurium forgetii is a medium-sized velvet anthurium native to the department of Chocó in Colombia, closely related to Anthurium crystallinum and Anthurium magnificum but immediately distinguished by one uniquely diagnostic feature: unlike virtually every other commonly grown anthurium, the leaves of A. forgetii have no sinus — the two basal lobes of the otherwise heart-shaped leaf are pressed together or slightly overlapping, creating a completely closed, teardrop-shaped leaf base with no open notch. In all other respects, the leaves are classically beautiful: velvety, dark emerald-green, with bold, bright silver-white primary veins. The closed leaf base and generally more compact growth habit (compared to the giant velvet anthuriums like A. veitchii and A. warocqueanum) make A. forgetii a more practical choice for collectors with limited space. It produces the characteristic Anthurium flowers (green-white spathe and spadix) that are ornamentally inconsequential. Anthurium forgetii has become an important parent in hybrid anthurium breeding, contributing the closed-sinus trait to offspring. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to early fall so plants overwinter as rosettes and bloom in spring alongside tulips and daffodils.
directions: Scatter seeds on the soil surface or barely cover them; they germinate best in cool conditions and seedlings overwinter as low rosettes in mild climates. Forget-me-nots self-sow prolifically once established — let plants go to seed, then pull them after flowering to control spread. The sky-blue flowers are traditionally combined with spring bulbs in beds and create a charming filler under shrubs in partial shade. Remove spent plants when temperatures rise, as they become straggly and die back in summer heat.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; self-sows readily in the garden.
directions: Chinese forget-me-not produces soft clouds of tiny sky-blue flowers that suit borders and cottage plantings. Scatter seeds directly on prepared soil in early spring and press them in lightly, keeping the bed evenly moist until seedlings appear. This easy annual tolerates partial shade and often self-sows to return in following seasons. Cut a few stems for small bouquets, and shear lightly after the first flush to encourage more bloom.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; forked bluestem grows naturally in moist to wet pine flatwoods, seasonal wetland edges, and disturbed moist areas of the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; forked bluestem is a distinctive tall native grass of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, named for the unusually forked arrangement of its seed-bearing spikes — unlike most bluestems with single spikes, this species produces multiple racemes at the stem tips that fan out in a fan-like or V-forked pattern, creating a bird-foot effect at the top of each stem. The silky seed heads are covered in long, gossamer hairs that catch the light and shimmer silver-white in fall sun. It grows naturally in moist to wet pine flatwoods, the margins of bay swamps, and disturbed moist roadsides throughout the Gulf South, tolerating seasonal flooding better than most bluestems. The fall foliage turns orange-copper to burgundy, combining dramatically with the silver-white seed heads. An underused native grass for moist sites in zone 9a where it provides bold autumn color and distinctive textural interest.

common_name: Forked Felt Fern (Dry-Shade-Tolerant Arrow-Leaved Felted Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Forked Felt Fern bears simple, arrow-shaped, felted fronds rather than the lacy, dissected fronds of most garden ferns, and is notably tolerant of dry shade once established.
directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in partial to full shade; unlike most ferns, Forked Felt Fern tolerates and even prefers soil that dries between waterings, making it a valuable choice for dry shade under trees where few other ferns will thrive. Its fronds are simple and undivided rather than lacy, arrow- or hand-shaped and covered in a soft, silvery-tan felt of star-shaped hairs that gives the plant an unusual, almost succulent texture and helps it withstand drought, spreading slowly by creeping rhizomes to form a low mat or spilling attractively over rock edges and pot rims. It is easy to grow once sited correctly, needing little more than occasional water during extended dry spells, and works well in a woodland rock garden, on a shaded stone wall, or in a shallow container.

subcategory: wild-type cool-season larkspur for meadows and cutting
plant_note: Direct sow in fall a few weeks before the first hard frost, or as early as possible in spring, since seed needs a cool spell to germinate well.
directions: Scatter seed directly where plants are to grow, since larkspur taproots resist transplanting, and lightly rake it into loosened soil in fall or very early spring while the ground is still cool. Thin crowded seedlings once they emerge and let plants overwinter as small rosettes where hardy. Slender, branching stems carry loose spikes of small, spurred blue-violet flowers over finely cut, airy foliage, giving a wilder, more open look than the taller cultivated larkspurs and providing an easy self-seeding source of early cut flowers and pollinator forage for meadow-style plantings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown azaleas in fall (September–November in zone 9); fall planting allows root establishment before the spring bloom season. Azaleas demand acidic soil — pH 5.0–6.0 is ideal; test and amend before planting with elemental sulfur or peat moss if pH is too high. Do not plant deeply — the crown must be at or slightly above soil level. Formosa is one of the largest and most vigorous Southern Indica azalea cultivars, eventually reaching 8–10 feet tall and wide if unpruned. Prune immediately after spring bloom (before July) — later pruning removes developing flower buds. In zone 9 Formosa blooms February–April in a spectacular mass of large, vivid magenta-purple flowers that can cover the entire shrub.
directions: Plant in partial shade — filtered light under tall pines or high-branched deciduous trees is ideal; avoid deep shade or full afternoon sun — in well-drained, very acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil; Formosa is one of the defining large Southern Indica azalea cultivars, producing massive specimens with very large (3–4 inch), vivid reddish-purple to magenta-purple, single flowers in an overwhelming spring bloom display that, when a mature Formosa azalea is in full flower, can completely cover the shrub in a solid mass of vivid purple bloom — one of the most dramatic flowering displays available from any single shrub species in the Gulf South landscape. Southern Indica azaleas (Rhododendron indicum cultivars) are among the most important and historically significant landscape shrubs of the American South — thriving in the partial shade, acidic, well-drained conditions under the longleaf pine and mixed hardwood forests that characterize the Gulf Coast region, and producing their spring bloom display in February–April when the landscape is transitioning from winter to spring. The combination of dense evergreen foliage year-round, the spectacular spring bloom, and exceptional longevity (Formosa azaleas over 50–75 years old are common in old Gulf South gardens) makes this cultivar one of the most enduring and valuable ornamental shrubs for zone 7–10 partial shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Formosa grows very large and should be given ample space from structures and other plants — a mature specimen in zone 9 can reach 12–15 feet in all directions.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Formosa is one of the oldest and most vigorous Southern Indian Hybrid azaleas, a bold, large-growing shrub producing masses of large, vivid purple-magenta flowers — among the most intensely colored of all the common landscape azaleas — in a spectacular mid-spring display. In zone 9 Gulf Coast conditions where winter cold is limited, Formosa can reach remarkable dimensions: 12–15 feet tall and equally wide after decades in the landscape, forming massive, billowing specimen plants that stop traffic during bloom season. The bold magenta-purple color is unmistakable and highly visible from a distance, making it an outstanding landscape accent. Formosa has been grown in the American South since the early 20th century and anchors many older gardens across the Gulf Coast, often outliving the buildings they were planted near. It is semi-evergreen in zone 9, holding most of its large, glossy, dark-green leaves through mild winters. The vivid flower color is too bold to mass indiscriminately — use as a large-scale focal point or planted singly against an evergreen backdrop. Prune immediately after bloom; do NOT prune in fall or winter, which removes flower buds.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring; Formosa lily is remarkably fast from seed — flowering in as little as 90–120 days — making it one of the fastest seed-to-flower lilies available. In mild climates (zone 7+) it naturalizes as a short-lived perennial or self-sowing biennial. It is susceptible to lily mosaic virus carried by aphids; protect with aphid control or grow from fresh, disease-free seed each season.
directions: Sow seeds in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Formosa lily is a tall, slender, fragrant lily native to Taiwan that blooms in August through October — far later than most lilies — producing large (4–6 inch), pure-white, trumpet-shaped flowers with a rich, sweet fragrance on the exterior, with a yellow center fading to purple-streaked markings on the inside of the tube. It is one of the most fragrant lilies grown in gardens and one of the latest-blooming, providing essential late-season fragrance and large-scale floral impact when most lilies have long finished. Remarkably, it blooms from seed in 90–120 days — faster than almost any other lily — and self-sows readily in mild climates to maintain a permanent, naturalized colony. It is ideal for Gulf Coast and zone 8–10 gardens where summer heat and humidity defeat many bulb lilies. In zone 6–7 it performs as an annually-replanted bulb. The pure-white fall flowers are striking against the late summer garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to deep shade; Formosa toad lily is more heat tolerant than the Japanese toad lily (T. hirta) and is the toad lily species to choose for zone 7–9 gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to deep shade — Formosa toad lily is a shade garden gem from Taiwan, producing extraordinarily intricate, orchid-like flowers in September–November with white petals heavily spotted with purple-maroon and a bright yellow central structure, on arching stems with glossy, clasping leaves. Unlike most flowering plants, it blooms in the cooling days of fall precisely when the shade garden most needs color. It is more heat tolerant than the Japanese toad lily (T. hirta), making it the better species for zone 7–9 gardens where summer heat can stress T. hirta. The stolon-spreading habit allows it to naturalize over several years into expanding colonies in appropriate moist, shaded woodland conditions. The botanical intricacy of the individual flowers rewards close inspection — few shade perennials produce a more beautifully detailed flower. Outstanding in shaded borders alongside hostas, ferns, and autumn fern.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Formosan Wood Fern unfurls new fronds in a striking bright chartreuse-yellow that matures to deep green, and is notably tolerant of dry shade once established.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Formosan Wood Fern, native to Taiwan, unfurls its finely divided fronds in a striking bright chartreuse-yellow each spring, a vivid color unmatched by other Dryopteris in cultivation, before the fronds mature to a rich, glossy deep green for the rest of the season, creating an eye-catching two-tone effect in the shaded border as new growth continues to emerge through the year. It forms a tidy, slowly spreading clump and, once established, tolerates drier shade conditions better than many wood ferns, making it useful under established trees where soil moisture is inconsistent. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges to keep the clump looking fresh.

plant_note: Sow after frost; soaking hard seeds overnight speeds sprouting.
directions: Four o'clocks earn their name by opening fragrant, trumpet-shaped blooms in the late afternoon and evening in a lively mix of colors. Soak the hard seeds overnight and sow after frost in a warm, sunny spot where the fast-growing bushy plants can fill out. The evening flowers attract moths and hummingbirds, and the plants form tuberous roots that can be lifted and stored in cold regions. In mild zones they return each year and often self-sow.

plant_note: Divide established rhizomes in spring once new growth begins, replanting divisions 3 to 4 inches deep in rich, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade.
directions: In spring, once new shoots are visible at the base, lift and divide the thick rhizomes with a sharp spade, ensuring each division has at least one healthy growing point, and replant 3 to 4 inches deep in rich, humus-amended, consistently moist soil in partial shade. Hedychium forrestii produces bold, tropical-looking stems 4 to 6 feet tall topped with fragrant white flowers bearing striking red stamens in late summer, extending the season when many perennials are fading. In zone 7, apply a generous layer of mulch over the rhizomes in late fall after the foliage is cut back by frost, as the rhizomes are the most cold-sensitive part of the plant. Consistent moisture throughout the growing season is key to vigorous growth; divide clumps every 3 to 4 years to maintain vigor and increase your planting.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in fall or softwood cuttings in summer; plant container-grown shrubs in almost any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade. Forsythia blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering to preserve next year's buds. Hard pruning in late summer or fall removes next spring's flower buds.
directions: Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; forsythia is the most widely planted early-spring flowering shrub in the temperate world — a hybrid of two Asian species producing cascading arches of branches covered, before any leaves appear, with bright, clear-yellow flowers in late February through April, depending on location. The intensity of color — pure, saturated spring-yellow on bare branches against the still-dormant landscape — makes it one of the most visually arresting events of the early garden year. After the flowers fade, the arching branches clothe themselves in dark-green foliage that provides a pleasant, medium-textured hedge or background through summer. It is among the most cold-hardy, drought-tolerant, and adaptable flowering shrubs available — growing in clay, sand, poor soil, and partial shade without complaint. The cultivar 'Lynwood Gold' (also sold as 'Lynwood Variety') is the most widely planted, with an upright habit and consistently large, fully open flowers. 'Meadowlark' is exceptionally cold-hardy to zone 4. Pruning should be done only immediately after flowering.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; forsythia sage is a large plant that needs room — it can grow 6–8 feet tall in a single season. In zone 8a, cut to the ground in winter and mulch; roots are reliably hardy to at least 15°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; forsythia sage is a bold, large-growing Mexican salvia that produces masses of bright clear-yellow flowers in dense whorls up tall, square stems from October through frost — its bright yellow blooms at the same time forsythia blooms in spring create a striking parallel, giving rise to its common name. The plant is remarkable for its tremendous size — growing 5–8 feet tall in a single season — and for its late-season bloom when most other plants are finishing. The large, heart-shaped leaves are powerfully aromatic when bruised. It is an outstanding hummingbird plant in fall when migrating birds need energy. The stems die back after frost but resprout vigorously from established root crowns in spring. One of the finest large fall-blooming perennials for the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; introduced in 1923, Fortune is a historic large-cup daffodil that has remained popular for a full century.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Introduced in 1923, Fortune bears a clear yellow perianth surrounding a large, ruffled orange-red cup, a bold combination that helped make it one of the most influential and widely planted large-cup daffodils of the 20th century and a parent behind many later orange-cupped cultivars. Its century of continuous popularity is a testament to reliable, vigorous garden performance. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

plant_note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; Fortune's hosta is an adaptable, vigorous, medium-to-large hosta that tolerates a wider range of light conditions than many other hosta species.
directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; Fortune's hosta tolerates brief periods of morning sun better than most other hostas, making it adaptable to a wider range of garden positions. Hosta fortunei is a medium-to-large hosta species that was one of the first hostas popularized in Western gardens and has since given rise to an enormous range of named cultivars — particularly the classic variegated forms 'Albopicta' (green-margined yellow centers fading to all-green by midsummer), 'Aureomarginata' (yellow-margined green), and 'Albomarginata' (white-margined green). The species itself has smooth to slightly corrugated, gray-green to olive-green leaves 7–9 inches long, and lavender flowers in July–August. It is among the most widely planted and adaptable of the medium-large hostas and tolerates more sun and occasional drought stress than larger-leaved species, making it a reliable choice for beginner and experienced shade gardeners alike.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; established clumps spread gently to form a tidy colony.
directions: Fortune's chloranthus is a Chinese woodland perennial closely related to the smaller, more commonly grown Chloranthus japonicus, distinguished by taller stems, glossier whorled leaves, and showier, more elongated brush-like spikes of tiny, fragrant white flowers composed almost entirely of stamens rather than true petals. It spreads gradually by rhizome into a neat, weed-suppressing colony beneath deciduous trees and pairs well with hellebores, hostas, and ferns in a refined shaded border. Give it evenly moist, humus-rich soil and protection from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the foliage in warmer parts of its range. Clumps are rarely bothered by deer or serious pests and can be divided in early spring every few years to expand the planting.

common_name: Fortune's Double Yellow Rose (Antique Coppery-Orange Climber)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a warm, sheltered site and a fence or wall to climb; Fortune's Double Yellow, brought from China in 1845, blooms once heavily in spring and needs a mild winter climate to perform its best.
directions: Plant against a warm, sheltered wall, fence, or trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Fortune's Double Yellow, also called Beauty of Glazenwood, was introduced from a Chinese garden in 1845 and remains treasured for its unusual coppery orange-and-yellow semi-double blooms, a color combination unlike almost any other antique rose, opening from buds flushed crimson. It flowers in a single spectacular spring flush on a vigorous climbing plant, performing best in the mild winters of zone 7 and warmer where its tender growth is not cut back by hard freezes. Give it a warm, protected site such as a south-facing wall, and prune only lightly right after the spring bloom to preserve as much of the flowering wood as possible for next year.

Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fortune's holly fern is slightly more cold-hardy than Japanese holly fern (C. falcatum) and has more matte, less glossy pinnae with a broader, more rounded shape and a somewhat more erect frond habit. Cyrtomium fortunei is an evergreen Asian fern widely used in zones 6–10 as a bold-textured, low-maintenance shade groundcover; its broadly arching fronds have large, matte to semi-glossy, dark-green pinnae that are slightly less waxy than its close relative C. falcatum and give the plant a subtler, more refined texture that blends well with fine-textured shade companions like Japanese forest grass and creeping Jenny. It is highly deer-resistant, adaptable to clay and dry soil once established, and excellent as an underplanting beneath live oaks, magnolias, and camellias in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as the shoots emerge; division every 3–5 years maintains vigor. Fortune's hosta is one of the most adaptable and vigorous of the species hostas and tolerates a wider range of light and soil conditions than many cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fortune's hosta is one of the oldest and most influential species in hosta cultivation, first described in the 1880s by gardener and plant hunter Philip Franz von Siebold and named for plant hunter Robert Fortune. Modern research suggests it may be a naturally occurring hybrid of Japanese species, but it has been widely grown and hybridized for over 140 years. The medium-sized, heart-shaped, glossy dark green leaves are more tolerant of sun and heat than many larger-leaved hostas, and the plant is particularly vigorous and adaptable. Pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in midsummer attract hummingbirds. Dozens of named cultivars have been selected, including the popular 'Albomarginata' (cream-edged leaves) and 'Aureomarginata' (gold-edged leaves). More tolerant of Gulf Coast heat and humidity than many cultivated hostas.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Fortune's osmanthus is a hybrid between O. fragrans and O. heterophyllus, combining the exceptional fragrance of the first with the cold hardiness of the second.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Fortune's osmanthus is a hybrid evergreen shrub combining the most desirable traits of its two parents — the extraordinary apricot-peach fragrance of the tea olive (O. fragrans) with the improved cold hardiness and dense, attractive, spiny-leaved foliage of the holly osmanthus (O. heterophyllus). The tiny, cream-white flowers in fall produce the same intensely sweet, far-carrying fragrance as tea olive, perfuming the garden from a considerable distance. This hybrid is cold-hardy to about 0°F (USDA zone 7) compared to tea olive's zone 8 hardiness, making it the better choice for the colder end of the zone 7–9 range. An excellent, deer-resistant, relatively low-maintenance evergreen shrub for the partial-shade garden in zones 7–9.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Fortune's saxifrage blooms in autumn rather than spring, unlike most saxifrage species, providing late-season color in a shaded border.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Fortune's saxifrage blooms in autumn rather than spring, unlike most saxifrage species, providing late-season color in a shaded border. Saxifraga fortunei is an East Asian woodland species with glossy, rounded, sometimes bronze-tinted leaves forming a neat mound, sending up airy, branched sprays of small, asymmetrical white flowers with elongated lower petals in autumn, often continuing until the first hard frost. Its distinctive fall bloom time sets it apart from spring-flowering saxifrages and makes it a valuable late-season companion for toad lily and fall-blooming anemone in a shaded border. Give it consistent moisture and protection from harsh winter wind, and mulch lightly in colder parts of its range to protect the crown over winter.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Fortuniana is a vigorous once-blooming climber long used both as a Deep South and Florida garden rose in its own right and as the standard nematode-resistant rootstock for grafted roses in sandy Southern soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a fence, arbor, or other sturdy support to climb; Fortuniana is a vigorous, thornless-to-nearly-thornless rambling climber that produces a single spectacular flush of fragrant, fully double white flowers each spring, followed by handsome glossy foliage for the rest of the season. It is prized across Florida and the Gulf South both as a garden plant in its own right and as the region's standard rootstock for grafted roses, since its extensive, nematode-resistant root system lets grafted varieties thrive in the sandy, nematode-prone soils where own-root roses often struggle. Give it plenty of room to sprawl or climb, and prune immediately after its spring bloom rather than in winter, since flowers form on the previous year's growth.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Foster No. 2 is the female (berry-producing) form widely sold in commerce; Foster No. 1 is the male pollinizer form and should be planted nearby for best berry production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Foster holly is a hybrid of American holly (Ilex opaca) and Dahoon holly (Ilex cassine) selected from a population in Birmingham, Alabama, by E.E. Foster in 1954. It is one of the most widely planted landscape hollies in the South and is distinguished by a distinctly narrower, more columnar habit than most other hollies — making it ideal for tight spaces, narrow screens, and situations where a tall, slim evergreen accent is needed. The small, somewhat spiny, dark-green leaves and dense, narrow growth create a refined, formal appearance. Female plants (the widely sold 'Foster No. 2') produce abundant small red berries that ripen in fall and persist through winter, attracting birds. The narrow habit and attractive berries make Foster holly an outstanding street tree, screening plant between properties, and formal landscape accent. Male plants ('Foster No. 1') must be planted nearby for reliable berry production. Foster holly is notably adaptable to the Gulf Coastal Plain's humid, hot summers and performs well in zone 9 where it is widely used in formal residential and commercial landscapes.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 5–8; Fountain Bamboo is the most shade-tolerant clumping bamboo available for temperate gardens — a cold-hardy, non-invasive mountain bamboo native to Sichuan and Yunnan Province, China, producing slender, gracefully arching, deep-green to purple-tinted culms and fine-textured foliage in elegant fountain-like clumps ideal for woodland and shade garden settings.
directions: Plant in partial to deep shade with consistent moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun — Fargesia nitida is the premier shade-tolerant bamboo for woodland and north-facing garden positions; mulch heavily to maintain cool, moist root conditions. Fargesia nitida (Fountain Bamboo, Blue Fountain Bamboo, or Chinese Fountain Bamboo) is an elegant, slow-growing, non-invasive clumping bamboo native to the high montane forests and alpine meadow edges of Sichuan, Yunnan, and adjacent western Chinese mountains at elevations of 8,000–12,000 feet, where it is a primary food bamboo of the giant panda alongside F. murielae. In garden cultivation, F. nitida is recognized as the most shade-tolerant of all hardy bamboos available — thriving in deep shade positions where other bamboos refuse to grow — and is particularly valuable for woodland garden settings, shaded north-facing boundaries, and forest understory plantings. The slender culms (0.5–1 inch diameter, 4–12 feet tall) often develop attractive purple, red, or dark-tinted coloration in the nodes and internodes — particularly on new culms — contrasting beautifully with the fine, dark-green leaves. Like F. murielae, it is a monocarpic species (flowers once after decades and dies), and the current garden plants have 60–80+ years of growth before the next masting. Cold-hardy to zone 5; prefers cool summers and suffers in prolonged heat above 90°F.
