common_name: Fresh Look Red Celosia (AAS-Winning Compact Vivid-Red Cockscomb Celosia)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting or direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fresh Look Red is a crested (cockscomb) type celosia — the ruffled, velvety, brain-like flower heads are distinctive and maintain their vivid color through the entire warm season without fading.
directions: Transplant after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fresh Look Red is an All-America Selections award-winning celosia in the crested (cockscomb) type — producing the distinctive velvety, ruffled, brain-shaped flower heads in vivid crimson-red. The compact, uniform habit (12–18 inches) with large, well-developed flower heads makes Fresh Look Red more ornamental and practical for garden use than older cockscomb types that were often taller and less uniformly sized. The velvety texture of the crested flower head is unique in summer annuals — the crimped, corrugated surface catches light at different angles to create depth and luminosity in the vivid red color that plain-surfaced flowers cannot match. The color maintains its intensity through the entire warm season without bleaching or browning — one of the few truly summer-proof vivid-red annuals for Gulf South gardens where July–August heat causes many flowers to fade or develop heat-stress brown tones. The compact size and vivid color make Fresh Look Red outstanding for mixed container plantings, border edging, and mass plantings in full-sun summer beds. The flower heads dry well for winter arrangements, maintaining their deep red color for months when dried quickly in a warm, low-humidity location.

common_name: Fresh Look Yellow Celosia (AAS-Winning Bright Yellow Long-Season Cockscomb)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after the last frost, or direct sow after soil is consistently warm (75°F+); Fresh Look Yellow maintains its vibrant golden-yellow color throughout the season without fading, a trait that earned it AAS recognition over earlier yellow celosia selections that tended to fade to cream in heat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fresh Look Yellow is an All-America Selections winner in the cockscomb (cristata) type of Celosia argentea — producing rounded, brain-like, velvety crested flower heads in clear, vivid golden yellow that maintains its color throughout the long season without fading to cream or pale yellow as earlier yellow celosia varieties tended to do in Gulf South summer heat. The color consistency was the key improvement that earned the AAS award — a true, saturated golden-yellow that holds its intensity from first bloom through fall frost, providing a reliable color anchor in summer and fall mixed borders. The crested, velvety flower heads have a unique texture — velvet-soft, deeply convoluted, with a rich tactile quality that makes them as interesting to touch as to see — and the heads last for months on the plant without deadheading. Fresh Look Yellow is an outstanding cut flower and dried flower plant: the vivid yellow crested heads dry naturally on the stem without significant color loss, making them valuable for dried arrangements that last for months after harvest. Excellent in mixed summer combination plantings with deep blue salvias, orange lantana, and bronze foliage plants. In Gulf South zone 9, celosia can often be direct-seeded in warm soil for a late-summer crop when transplant-grown plants have passed peak.

common_name: Frida Hemple Caladium (Bold Solid-Red Classic Large Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Frida Hemple's solid-red coloration retains its intensity in bright partial shade but may fade to an orange-red in deep shade with insufficient light.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Frida Hemple (also sold as 'Freida Hemple') is one of the most boldly colored and commercially important red caladium varieties — a large fancy-leaf type producing classic heart-shaped leaves in a vivid, nearly solid crimson-red to scarlet-red coloration with only narrow green margins framing the predominantly red leaf surface. The almost entirely red leaf color — covering 80–90% of the leaf surface with no significant white or pink zones — creates a bolder, more saturated red display than varieties with mixed patterns, and makes Frida Hemple one of the most effective caladiums for massing in shade positions where pure, saturated red color is the design goal. The large leaf size (leaves can reach 12–16 inches on established plants) and vivid coloration make Frida Hemple outstanding in formal shade bed plantings, as a front-of-border accent, and in large container designs where the bold red needs to carry over distance. Frida Hemple has been a commercially important caladium cultivar for many decades — its reliable vigor, consistent color, and excellent tuber production have kept it in continuous commercial production. Combine with white companions ('Aaron', 'Candidum', white impatiens) for maximum red-and-white contrast, or with deep green groundcovers (creeping Jenny, carpet bugle) to intensify the red color by contrast. Consistent moisture throughout the warm season ensures largest leaf development.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a sheltered spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hotter inland zones. This slow-growing member of the tea family resents root disturbance, so site it carefully from the outset.
directions: Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil similar to what camellias prefer, keeping the pH between 5.0 and 6.5 and the root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged. The large, white, camellia-like flowers with showy yellow stamens open from autumn through winter, providing color when little else is blooming in the garden. Protect young plants from hard freezes with frost cloth, as established specimens tolerate brief dips to the upper teens but young transplants are more vulnerable. Minimal pruning is needed; remove only crossing or damaged branches in late spring after the main flush of bloom.

common_name: Fried Green Tomatoes Hosta (Large Corrugated Green Hosta)
plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fried Green Tomatoes is a large, vigorous hosta with glossy, deeply corrugated green leaves related to the popular Sum and Substance breeding line.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and give the clump plenty of room, since this is a large, spreading hosta that needs several seasons to reach full size. Fried Green Tomatoes produces broad, rounded, glossy medium-green leaves with heavy corrugation and slightly rippled margins, forming a substantial mounding clump that works well as a bold specimen or anchor plant in a shaded border. Pale lavender-white flowers appear on tall scapes in mid to late summer, though the leaves are the main attraction. Like other large-leaved hostas it tolerates a bit more sun than thin-leaved cultivars if the soil stays consistently moist, but performs best out of hot afternoon exposure in Southern gardens. Divide only when necessary, since large hostas resent frequent disturbance and take a season or two to recover their full size afterward.

plant_note: Root 2-3 inch stem tip cuttings in moist potting mix or terrarium substrate under high humidity; Friendship Plant roots quickly at warm temperatures (70-75°F) and benefits from frequent pinching to stay bushy rather than sprawling. Keep soil evenly moist but never soggy.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in humus-rich, well-draining potting mix, and keep humidity elevated — this Central and South American forest-floor species (Pilea involucrata) is a compact, spreading houseplant prized for its heavily quilted, deeply veined oval leaves, which are bronzy-green above with a metallic bronze-purple sheen and deep maroon-red beneath, arranged in a low, mounding habit that thickens with regular pinching. The 'Moon Valley' cultivar, the most widely sold selection, has even more pronounced, crinkled 'moonscape' texture and chartreuse-green coloring. Friendship Plant earns its common name from how readily cuttings root and get passed between gardeners; a single stem tip roots in days under warm, humid conditions. Pinch growing tips regularly to prevent legginess, and expect stems to become woody and less attractive after 1-2 years, at which point refreshing the plant from cuttings works better than trying to rejuvenate an old specimen. Excellent in terrariums, dish gardens, and humid bathrooms; it declines quickly in dry indoor air.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in rich, moist soil with afternoon shade.
directions: Frill Ride is a bigleaf hydrangea bearing bold mophead blooms with distinctive frilled petal edges in shades that shift with soil pH. Plant it in morning sun and afternoon shade in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool. Acidic soil pushes blooms toward blue while alkaline soil yields pink, so amend to steer the color you want. Prune just after flowering, since it blooms mainly on old wood. Water generously in heat to prevent the large leaves and flowers from wilting.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring. Fringe cups is a Pacific Northwest native perennial in the saxifrage family that forms semi-evergreen rosettes of rounded, softly hairy, heart-shaped leaves and sends up elegant, 18–30 inch racemes of small, urn-shaped flowers whose petals are deeply fringed, opening white and aging to pink and red, in spring and early summer. It spreads modestly by seed and rhizomes to naturalize into a graceful woodland groundcover that pairs beautifully with ferns, bleeding heart, and tiarella. Tolerates deep shade under conifers.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fringe cups self-seeds freely in moist shade conditions and may naturalize into a loose colony — deadhead spent flower spikes to reduce self-seeding in formal garden settings or allow to naturalize in woodland garden situations.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fringe cups is a Pacific Northwest and Western North American woodland perennial in the saxifrage family (Saxifragaceae) that is closely related to heucheras and tiarellas and shares their preference for partial to full woodland shade — it grows as a clump of basal, roundly heart-shaped, hairy, dark-green leaves (remarkably similar to Heuchera leaves) and in late spring produces tall, slender, upright flower stems to 24 inches, each bearing an elegant, elongated spike of small, nodding, greenish-white to cream, urn-shaped flowers with the petals elaborately fringed (cut into narrow, thread-like segments) at their margins — creating a delicate, lacey floral effect along the entire length of the spike. The flowers fade through white to pink to rose-red as they age, so a single spike carries multiple color stages simultaneously. The foliage rosettes are attractive year-round and are semi-evergreen in mild winters. Self-seeds freely in moist shade. A graceful, refined, and underused shade perennial for zone 5–9 woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in early spring in moist, shaded spots; fresh seed can be surface sown in fall for natural cold stratification. Tellima self-sows modestly and can establish small colonies over time.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; fringecups is a Pacific Northwest native woodland perennial in the saxifrage family closely related to heucheras and tiarellas. In spring it sends up slender wands of small, urn-shaped flowers with intricately fringed petals that open cream-white and age to rose-pink. The rounded, hairy, semi-evergreen leaves form a dense, attractive clump at the base. It blooms for an unusually long period of 6–8 weeks and performs well in the challenging dry shade of Douglas fir and redwood forests. A reliable, low-maintenance shade perennial that combines beautifully with ferns, native gingers, and bleeding heart.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; fringed bleeding heart remains in bloom from spring through fall in cool climates and does not go summer-dormant like the common bleeding heart.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fringed bleeding heart is a native Appalachian perennial that surpasses the common bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis) in most garden settings by blooming continuously from spring through hard frost in cool climates — the deeply ferny, blue-gray, dissected foliage is attractive all season and never goes summer-dormant. The dangling, heart-shaped, rose-pink flowers appear in loose, nodding clusters on arching stems. It tolerates more heat and summer drought than the common bleeding heart. Self-sows gently to maintain a naturalized presence in woodland gardens without becoming invasive. Excellent in combination with hostas, ferns, and astilbes for a year-round shade border. Hybrids such as 'King of Hearts' (compact, deep rose) and 'Luxuriant' (strong bloomer) often replace the straight species in commerce.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; or cold stratify seeds 60 days and sow indoors in late winter. Transplant to very well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to light shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed blue star is a native amsonia of the southeastern Coastal Plain sandhills and pine barrens, adapted to the infertile, droughty, acid soils of longleaf pine habitats where few ornamental perennials survive. The very fine, needle-like foliage is distinctive among amsonias — quite different from the broad leaves of A. tabernaemontana — and turns a glowing golden-yellow in fall, one of the best fall color displays of any low-maintenance perennial. The star-shaped blue flowers in spring are typical of the genus. It performs better in poor, dry, acidic soil than in rich garden conditions — improved soil and irrigation can cause floppy growth. An excellent, low-maintenance native for dry, sandy, acidic sites in the Southeast.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost, or plant transplants, into sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed catchfly is native to open pine savannas and sandy roadsides and prefers lean soil over rich garden beds.
directions: Direct sow after last frost, or plant transplants, into sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed catchfly is native to open pine savannas and sandy roadsides and prefers lean soil over rich garden beds. Slender, sticky-hairy stems bear narrow leaves and clusters of vivid red, deeply fringed, tubular flowers in late summer and fall, opening in the evening to attract nectaring sphinx moths and hummingbirds. Native to open longleaf pine woodlands and sandy prairies across the western Gulf coastal plain, it is a striking, little-known addition to a native pollinator garden that provides late-season color when few other wildflowers are still fresh. It self-sows in loose, sandy soil and needs no fertilizer, performing best in the same lean, well-drained conditions it favors in the wild.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade after frost; aristolochia fimbriata is low-growing and spreading — excellent as a small-scale groundcover or container spiller — and is a key host plant for Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly larvae.
directions: Direct-sow or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade; fringed dutchman's pipe is a compact, spreading, South American perennial grown primarily as a wildlife plant and groundcover for shaded areas — the handsome, heart-shaped leaves are distinctly patterned with silver-white veining against deep green, giving the plant attractive foliage interest independent of its flowers. Small, curved, pipe-shaped, lemon-scented flowers with finely fringed edges appear throughout the warm season, but the plant's greatest value is as a confirmed host plant for the Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor), a stunning iridescent-blue butterfly whose larvae feed exclusively on Aristolochia species. Unlike the larger, climbing Aristolochia macrophylla and A. tomentosa, A. fimbriata stays low and spreading, making it practical for smaller gardens, containers, and shaded garden edges. It is important to note that certain other non-native Aristolochia species (A. elegans, A. littoralis) are actually toxic to Pipevine Swallowtail larvae; A. fimbriata supports them safely. Semi-evergreen in mild winters.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, sandy or silty soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed gentian is a biennial that forms a rosette in its first year and blooms in late summer of its second. It requires moist, lean, calcareous or neutral soil and does not tolerate competition — it thrives in disturbed seep margins, wet meadow edges, and streambanks.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, sandy or silty soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed gentian is one of the most beautiful and coveted native wildflowers of northeastern North America, producing brilliant violet-blue, vase-shaped flowers with dramatically fringed petal margins in late summer and fall — the fringed edges of each petal lobe are deeply cut into hundreds of fine filaments, creating an extraordinarily ornate, lacey appearance unique among North American wildflowers. The plant is notoriously difficult to establish in gardens, requiring very specific conditions — moist, open, lean, near-neutral soils free of competition, such as seep margins, calcareous stream banks, and disturbed wet meadows. Once established in appropriate conditions it self-sows to maintain a colony. John Muir rhapsodized about encountering it in Wisconsin prairies. A specialist plant for wet, calcareous, open sites — immensely rewarding when conditions are right.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; fringed loosestrife spreads by rhizomes and seeds to form colonies in moist woodland edges, stream banks, and wet meadows. The cultivar 'Firecracker' has striking purple-bronze foliage.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun along stream banks, pond margins, rain gardens, and moist woodland edges; fringed loosestrife is a native North American species of the primrose family, producing starry, five-petaled, bright yellow flowers in midsummer that dangle from arching stems above broad, opposite leaves. The common name comes from the distinctive fringe of fine hairs on the leaf petioles. The cultivar 'Firecracker' has become popular in the ornamental trade for its striking, deep purple-bronze foliage that contrasts dramatically with the yellow flowers and adds unusual dark color to the moist shade garden throughout summer. Self-sows and spreads by rhizomes in appropriate moist conditions to form naturalistic colonies. Provides nectar for numerous small native bees and is a host plant for pollen-specialist bees of the genus Macropis.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall; fringed polygala requires moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained forest soil in deep shade and is notoriously difficult to establish from seed or transplant — it grows in association with specific mycorrhizal fungi. Best acquired as established container plants.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained, undisturbed forest soil in deep shade; fringed polygala is a tiny, jewel-like native groundcover of the cool, moist northern hardwood and mixed conifer forests of eastern North America. The small, rose-pink to magenta flowers have a unique, highly ornamental structure — the two wing-like lateral sepals and the fringed lower petal create a shape resembling a miniature orchid or a tiny winged fairy. The flowers are pollinated by large bumblebees that must be heavy enough to depress the flower's structure to reach the nectar. Two types of flowers are produced: the showy open flowers above ground and hidden cleistogamous flowers underground that self-pollinate without opening. A challenging but rewarding woodland plant for undisturbed, acidic, forest-floor conditions; does not tolerate root disturbance or soil compaction.

plant_note: Direct sow in wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; fringed sedge grows naturally along shaded stream banks and forested seeps and is one of the few native sedges adapted to deep woodland shade with standing water or continuously saturated soil.
directions: Plant in wet to consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade along stream banks, forested swamp edges, and shaded seeps; fringed sedge is one of the most shade-tolerant of the large native wetland sedges, growing naturally in the deep shade of forested bottomlands and streamside forests across eastern North America. Its most distinctive feature is the long, pendant female spikes — drooping catkins that hang loosely from arching stems, the scales tapering to delicate bristle tips (the 'fringe') — which create a graceful, weeping texture in the woodland garden. The clumps form slowly expanding, elegant tufts of medium-textured, grass-like foliage that remain attractive throughout the growing season. Excellent in rain gardens with overhead tree cover, shaded bioswales, and streamside restoration where full-sun sedges fail due to shade. The seeds are consumed by various marsh and woodland birds.

plant_note: Transplant rooted runners in early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage, ideally on a shaded slope or among rocks where water never stands.
directions: Transplant rooted runners in early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage, ideally on a shaded slope or among rocks where water never stands. Rounded, glossy, scalloped leaves take on bronze and red tones through winter, and in early spring wiry stems lift dainty, nodding, deeply fringed bells in shades of pink or white. This Japanese woodland native spreads slowly by creeping stems to form a low mat and is prized in shaded rock gardens for its combination of year-round foliage color and delicate spring flowers. It performs best where summers stay cool and moist, and it resists heavy clay or soil that dries out completely.

plant_note: Mount on bark or grow in a shallow, fast-draining orchid basket in bright, indirect to direct light; fringed star orchid needs strong light and good air movement to bloom, more sun than most cattleya-alliance relatives tolerate.
directions: Mount on bark or grow in a shallow, fast-draining orchid basket in bright, indirect to direct light; fringed star orchid needs strong light and good air movement to bloom, more sun than most cattleya-alliance relatives tolerate. Large, pale green to cream flowers are edged with an extraordinary, deeply fringed, lacy lip that looks almost hand-cut, opening with an intense, sweet fragrance most noticeable in the evening that has made this species one of the most important parents used in breeding fragrant hybrid cattleyas. Native to Central American dry forests where it grows exposed to strong light on tree branches, it needs considerably more direct sun than most orchids to flower well, along with excellent drainage and air movement around its roots to prevent rot. Mount on a slab or grow in a basket with minimal, very fast-draining medium, water thoroughly then allow to dry quickly, and provide the strongest light the plant will tolerate without leaf burn for reliable flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm in very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; in zones 9–11 plants may be started in late winter for earlier establishment. Avoid amended or rich soils — Fringed Twining Milkweed performs best in lean, xeric conditions that mimic its native desert habitat. Provide a low trellis or nearby shrub for the twining stems to climb.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Fringed Twining Milkweed is a drought-adapted native perennial milkweed vine of desert shrubland, washes, and roadsides from California to Texas in the southwestern US. It produces long, narrow to linear leaves and clusters of small, pale to rose-pink, star-shaped flowers with a distinctive fringed corona that bloom across a long summer season. Like true milkweeds it produces latex sap and classic spindle-shaped seed pods with plume-tailed, wind-dispersed seeds. It is a particularly important late-season milkweed resource for monarch butterflies on their fall migration routes through the Southwest, and should be kept dry and given excellent drainage to perform well — it declines quickly in heavy or poorly drained soils.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; fringeleaf coreopsis grows naturally in moist, open woodlands and woodland edges in the southeastern Coastal Plain and blooms in fall — one of the latest-blooming native coreopsis species.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; fringeleaf coreopsis is a fall-blooming native of the southeastern Coastal Plain, extending its bloom season later into the autumn than most coreopsis — a significant advantage in the garden where its bright yellow flowers provide critical fall color and nectar from September through November. The leaves are somewhat different from other coreopsis — broader, almost rounded, with slightly fringed or undulate margins that give the species its common name. It grows naturally in moist, open woodlands, forest edges, and the transition zones between flatwoods and upland habitats, tolerating partial shade better than sun-demanding coreopsis species. The extended fall blooming is exceptionally valuable for migrating monarch butterflies and late-season pollinators. Well-adapted to zone 9a conditions in moist, partially shaded garden situations.

plant_note: Best sown in fall for natural cold stratification over winter, or direct sow in early spring. Seeds may also be cold-stratified for 4–6 weeks in the refrigerator before spring sowing.
directions: Sow seeds in fall to allow natural cold stratification, or cold-stratify refrigerated seeds for 4–6 weeks before a spring direct sowing. Ruellia humilis is a low-growing native perennial that thrives in hot, dry conditions — it is excellent for road cuts, rock gardens, and dry slopes where many other plants struggle. The lavender-blue tubular flowers closely resemble petunias and appear throughout summer, providing nectar for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees. Note that this is the well-behaved native species and should not be confused with Ruellia simplex (Mexican Petunia), which is invasive in the Southeast; established plants spread modestly by self-seeding to form a colony.

plant_note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface in very well-drained, sandy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in fall; frizzle sizzle follows the Cape winter-rainfall growth cycle — growing and flowering in winter and spring, then going summer dormant. Keep dry in summer dormancy. Full sun maximizes the dramatic spiral leaf curling — shaded plants may produce less tightly curled foliage.
directions: Plant bulbs near the soil surface in very well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; frizzle sizzle is a South African Cape bulb that has attracted unusual attention from collectors and gardeners primarily for its extraordinary foliage — the leaves are not flat strap-like leaves but tightly spiral, corkscrew-curled, like a pig's tail or a phone cord, creating an immediately bizarre and eye-catching effect quite unlike any other commonly grown plant. The leaves, each spiraling through one to several complete rotations as they grow, create a tightly curled, wispy, almost spring-like cluster of spirals at ground level that is so unusual it reliably draws a second look from every observer. In late winter through spring it produces small, nodding, greenish-yellow to yellow, vanilla-fragrant flowers on short stems — pleasant but secondary to the extraordinary foliage. The spiral curling is a genuine botanical trait of the species rather than a cultivated mutation. It grows naturally in the sandy coastal heathlands of the Western Cape. Outstanding as a container plant where the unique spiral foliage can be examined closely and protected from summer rain during dormancy.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness; transplant while cool, or sow in late summer for fall and spring bloom.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before setting out, covering it since pansies germinate best in darkness, and transplant while weather is cool. Frizzle Sizzle Lemonberry features ruffled 2 to 2.5-inch tricolor blooms of lemon, deep burgundy, and berry-purple edges that intensify in cool spring temperatures. These low-growing edible flowers suit beds, borders, and containers. Deadhead to prolong blooming and provide even moisture, as they fade in summer heat.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or plugs in spring in any well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, moist to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; frogfruit is extremely adaptable and roots readily wherever stems contact moist soil, spreading quickly to fill in bare ground.
directions: Plant plugs or rooted cuttings in any well-drained, moist to dry soil in full sun to partial shade — frogfruit is a tough, trailing native groundcover of Gulf Coast roadsides, disturbed prairies, and open woodland margins, hugging the ground so tightly (1–3 inches tall) that it can be used as a low-maintenance lawn substitute or mowed path edge in full sun. Despite its modest appearance, it is one of the most ecologically important low-growing native plants in the South: the tiny white to pink flower heads bloom nearly year-round in warm climates and serve as a critical nectar source for many small native bees and flies, while the leaves are larval host plants for the Phaon crescent and common buckeye butterflies. It roots at stem nodes wherever it contacts moist soil, spreading rapidly to colonize bare areas but never invasively outcompeting other established plants. Heat, drought, and salt tolerant; extremely low-maintenance once established. Blooms are most prolific in spring and fall.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Frohnleiten is a vigorous, evergreen epimedium selection that spreads into a good-sized groundcover patch faster than many slower epimedium species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Frohnleiten is a vigorous, evergreen to semi-evergreen epimedium hybrid producing sprays of bright yellow flowers with reddish-bronze centers in spring, held just above heart-shaped leaves that emerge coppery-bronze and mature to leathery green, often taking on burgundy tones again in winter. It spreads at a good pace into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover, faster than many other epimedium species, making it useful for covering larger areas of dry shade under trees or shrubs. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, lean to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; frost aster is extremely adaptable and virtually impossible to kill once established — thriving in poor, dry soils of roadsides, old fields, dry woods edges, and disturbed areas. Requires no fertilization and self-sows abundantly.
directions: Direct sow in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, lean to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; frost aster is one of the most widespread, adaptable, and ecologically important native asters in North America — covering vast areas of old fields, roadsides, dry woodland edges, and disturbed areas from eastern Canada to Texas and Florida. The common name 'frost aster' refers to the pure white ray flowers (which remain white even as temperatures drop), the late blooming season (October through November, after the first frosts in northern areas), and the feathery, silvery-white seed plumes that linger through winter, creating a frosted effect in the garden. The 1/2-inch white flowers with yellow centers, produced in massive quantities on highly branched stems, are extraordinarily abundant and valuable as late-season nectar for monarch butterflies, native bees, and many other pollinators. One of the most important late-season nectar sources in eastern North America. Self-sows prolifically in lean soils. An essential native plant for dry old-field restorations and natural-style gardens seeking maximum wildlife value.

common_name: Frost Prince Camellia (Upright White Cold-Hardy Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Frost Prince is the upright-habit companion to the cascading Frost Princess cold-hardy camellia.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Frost Prince bears single white flowers with gold stamens on an upright, vigorous shrub, a cold-hardy hybrid bred as the upright counterpart to the cascading Frost Princess, both selected to extend camellia growing into colder climates than the species normally tolerates. It flowers in fall into early winter, providing color when little else is blooming. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

common_name: Frost Princess Camellia (Cascading Wavy-Petal White Cold-Hardy Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Frost Princess is a cold-hardy hybrid camellia with a graceful cascading habit and wavy-petaled white flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Frost Princess bears single, white flowers with distinctively wavy, irregular petal edges and prominent gold stamens on a graceful, cascading shrub, a cold-hardy hybrid bred to extend camellia growing into colder climates than the species normally tolerates. It flowers in fall into early winter, and its spreading, arching habit suits it to a slope, wall, or container where the cascading form can be appreciated. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

plant_note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot.
directions: Frost Proof is a cold-tolerant gardenia bearing intensely fragrant white flowers against glossy evergreen leaves, and it withstands cooler temperatures better than typical gardenias. Plant it in morning sun with afternoon shade in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. Keep watering consistent, as fluctuating moisture causes bud drop. Feed with an acid-loving-plant fertilizer during the growing season and prune lightly after the main bloom. Protect from harsh winter wind at the colder edge of its range.

common_name: Frosted Curls Carex (New Zealand Hair Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Frosted Curls forms a tousled mound of fine, curling, silvery pale-green foliage and tolerates shade well but is best kept out of deep, dense shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, though this New Zealand hair sedge also tolerates considerably more sun than most shade sedges provided moisture is adequate. Frosted Curls produces a loose, tumbling mound of very fine, hair-like leaves in a pale, frosted silvery-green that curls and twists at the tips, giving the whole clump a soft, textural, almost windswept look that pairs nicely with bolder-leaved shade perennials. It stays evergreen in mild climates and is useful at the front of a border, in containers, or cascading over a low wall where its curling texture can be seen up close. Comb out dead foliage in early spring and divide congested clumps every few years to keep the mound looking fresh; avoid deep, dense shade, which thins the plant and dulls its color.

common_name: Frosted Violet Heuchera (Silver-Frosted Purple Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Frosted Violet bears deep purple leaves overlaid with a silvery-white frosted sheen across the upper surface, a metallic, icy effect that shifts and shimmers with changing light, distinguishing it from the many solid-purple heuchera cultivars. Its cool, silvery-purple tone pairs well with pink- and white-flowered shade companions and provides striking contrast against gold hostas or chartreuse foliage. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Frostproof is notably more cold-hardy than standard gardenia cultivars, extending reliable gardenia culture further north than the species typically tolerates.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun. As its name suggests, Frostproof was selected specifically for improved cold hardiness compared to standard Gardenia jasminoides, tolerating colder winters with less dieback than most cultivars while still producing the classic, intensely fragrant, creamy white double flowers gardenias are grown for. Its compact, naturally dense habit also makes it a good choice for foundation plantings and smaller borders where a full-sized gardenia would grow too large. Consistent moisture and acidic soil are essential, since gardenias quickly develop yellow, chlorotic foliage in alkaline or poorly drained conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; frostweed grows naturally in moist woodland edges, creek bottoms, and open woods from the eastern US to Texas and tolerates considerable shade while still producing flowers.
directions: Sow seeds in fall or plant transplants in moist, partially shaded woodland-edge soil; frostweed is a tall, commanding native perennial wildflower that earns its evocative name from a remarkable winter phenomenon: when the first hard freeze strikes the green stems, the sap freezes and expands, splitting the bark and extruding curling ribbons and sheets of ice in fantastical flower-like formations called 'ice flowers' or 'frost flowers' that persist for hours after sunrise. This natural ice art is one of the most spectacular surprises in the winter garden. The plant itself produces masses of small white flowers beloved by butterflies — particularly migrating monarchs — from late summer through fall. It is an important nectar source at a critical migration season. Tolerates part shade and moist conditions, making it one of the few native tall perennials suited to moist woodland edges and rain gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Frosty Curls produces a dense, tousled mound of fine, silvery-green, thread-like blades that curl and twist at the tips, giving the whole plant a soft, frosted, almost woolly texture unlike the straighter blades of most sedges. Its pale, cool coloring and curling texture make it a distinctive accent for containers, rock gardens, and border edges where a soft, contrasting foil to bolder-leaved companions is wanted. Comb out dead blades by hand each spring to keep the evergreen foliage looking tidy, and divide congested clumps in spring every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate with spring warmth.
directions: Frying Pans is a diminutive California native annual closely related to the California poppy but considerably smaller, with finely dissected, blue-green foliage and tiny, bright yellow, 4-petaled flowers barely half an inch across that spread wide and flat — earning the whimsical common name from their resemblance to a miniature skillet. It is native to dry, rocky foothill grasslands and open chaparral in the Sacramento Valley and Sierra Nevada foothills, where it often grows in thin, gravelly soils with little competition. Direct sow in fall by scattering seed on dry, lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; like its relatives, it resents transplanting and performs best with no soil amendment. It self-sows freely and makes an excellent low-growing native filler for California dry-garden borders, rock gardens, and native meadow mixes.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or water, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; fuchsia begonia is more drought-tolerant than most begonias and performs better in lower-humidity environments — allow the top inch of soil to dry slightly between waterings to prevent root rot in the fibrous root system.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; fuchsia begonia is a Venezuelan shrubby begonia uniquely suited to milder and drier conditions than most tropical begonias — it produces a graceful, freely branching, shrubby habit reaching 2–4 feet with small, oval, glossy, bright-green, slightly toothed leaves and an abundance of pendant, fuchsia-like, coral-red to bright-pink flower clusters hanging on long, slender pedicels throughout the warm season and nearly year-round in frost-free climates. The delicate, drooping flower clusters have a jewel-like quality that closely resembles fuchsia flowers in their pendant form and rich coloring — hence the common name — but this plant is better adapted to warmth and partial shade than true fuchsias. It is the most drought-tolerant of the commonly grown shrub begonias, making it better suited to indoor conditions and gardens with inconsistent irrigation. An outstanding specimen in hanging baskets, tall containers, and sheltered outdoor shade gardens in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or plant container-grown plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean soil in full sun to part shade; fuchsia-flowering gooseberry requires summer dormancy and must not be watered after late spring. It is spiny and forms impenetrable thickets — an advantage as a barrier planting but a consideration near paths.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; fuchsia-flowering gooseberry is a California native coastal shrub producing one of the most spectacular winter-flowering displays of any western native plant — long, pendant, brilliant-red flowers (dangling on slender stalks in clusters of 1–4) from January through March that are, in form and color, almost identical to a fuchsia flower: deeply red, tubular, with projecting red stamens that extend beyond the tube. These winter-blooming flowers appear on nearly leafless or semi-leafless stems and are an overwhelmingly important resource for Anna's and Allen's hummingbirds during the period when almost no other nectar sources are available. The plant goes fully dormant in summer — browning its leaves and appearing dead, which is entirely normal. The thorny stems create an excellent barrier planting and wildlife shelter. A startlingly beautiful winter-blooming native shrub for California and Pacific Coast gardens in zones 8b–10.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun. Fudingzhu is a Chinese tea olive selection bred for exceptionally heavy, repeat bloom — flowering several times a year rather than the one or two main flushes typical of standard tea olive — filling the garden with the intensely sweet, apricot-like fragrance for which the species is prized over a much longer season. Its more compact growth rate compared to seed-grown tea olive makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller gardens where the species' eventual large size would be unwelcome. Plant it near a patio, walkway, or window where the fragrance can be enjoyed on its frequent bloom cycles; little pruning is needed beyond light shaping after flowering.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fuji cherry is among the earliest ornamental cherries to bloom, often flowering in February. Its compact size and early bloom date make it suitable for smaller gardens where large cherries would be too imposing.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fuji cherry is a Japanese alpine species from the slopes of Mount Fuji, characteristically small and shrubby compared to the large ornamental cherries, bearing small, finely cut, incised-margined leaves (incisa = cut) and a profusion of tiny white to pale pink flowers from February to March — among the earliest cherries to bloom. The small stature makes it appropriate for small garden spaces and courtyard gardens where full-sized cherries would be overwhelming. Good fall color in shades of orange and red provides a second season of interest. Important parent in breeding compact ornamental cherry cultivars, including the popular columnar 'Amanogawa' cherry. The widely planted Okame cherry (Prunus x incam 'Okame') is a cross between P. incisa and P. campanulata (Taiwan cherry).

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in bright light with some direct sun; Fukien tea has no frost tolerance and is grown outdoors year-round only in zone 10-11, elsewhere as a houseplant or patio plant brought in well before cold weather.
directions: Grow in bright light with a few hours of direct sun daily, in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil kept evenly moist but never waterlogged. Fukien tea is a small-leaved, rough-textured evergreen shrub from Southeast Asia that is one of the most popular subjects for indoor bonsai worldwide, prized for tiny, glossy, dark green leaves, naturally gnarled and easily shaped woody stems, and a long season of small white star-shaped flowers followed by tiny red berries that can appear almost year-round in good light. It is notoriously fussy about consistency: sudden changes in light, temperature, humidity, or watering routine often trigger leaf drop, so once a good spot near a bright window is found, avoid moving the plant and keep humidity elevated with regular misting or a pebble tray. Prune and wire young growth to develop bonsai form while the plant is actively growing in spring and summer, and repot every one to two years into fresh, fast-draining mix as roots fill the container.

common_name: Full Eclipse Louisiana Iris (Near-Black Award-Winning Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.
directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Full Eclipse is a modern award-winning Louisiana iris cultivar bred for exceptionally deep, near-black purple flowers that read as solid dark velvet even in strong light, a striking contrast when paired with the paler blues, whites, and yellows more typical of the class. As with other Louisiana iris, consistent moisture is the key to strong bloom, so it performs best at a pond edge, in a rain garden, or in a low spot that other perennials find too wet. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, replanting fans promptly since exposed rhizomes dry out and lose vigor quickly.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Full Moon produces some of the largest individual flowers of any coreopsis cultivar, broad, pale creamy-yellow blooms up to 3 inches across held well above a full, vigorous clump of narrow foliage, giving it a bolder presence in the border than the smaller-flowered threadleaf types. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall and draws bees and small pollinators, tolerating heat and humidity well once established. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring if the center begins to thin.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis.
directions: Nick and soak the seed overnight, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis or screen. This easy vine climbs with delicate ferny foliage and produces small tubular blooms that stay open all day and attract hummingbirds. Give it full sun and a support to twine up, watering while young until established. Most parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep it away from children and pets.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Furman's Red is among the most cold-hardy Salvia greggii selections, regularly surviving winters that damage or kill other autumn sage cultivars back to the ground.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and avoid overwatering, since this Texas native subshrub is highly susceptible to root rot in soggy or heavy clay conditions. Furman's Red is a superior autumn sage selection valued for its true, deep scarlet-red flowers and its exceptional cold hardiness, which allows it to survive winters in colder parts of its range that would set back other Salvia greggii cultivars. It blooms in continuous flushes from spring through hard frost, drawing hummingbirds throughout the growing season, and its compact, well-branched habit needs only an occasional hard cutback in late winter to stay dense and floriferous. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on lean soil and minimal supplemental water, making it a low-maintenance choice for xeriscape and pollinator gardens across the Gulf South.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; Furry Feather calathea wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; Furry Feather calathea wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11. Long, narrow, wavy-edged leaves are covered on both surfaces with a soft, velvety fuzz, deep green on top and rich burgundy-red beneath, a plush, tactile texture unlike the smoother, glossier leaves of most other calatheas. Native to the humid forest floor of Brazil, it shares the family's characteristic nyctinastic movement, folding its leaves upward at night and lowering them again by day, and it thrives in the higher humidity of a bathroom, kitchen, or grouped plant display. Provide a humidifier or regular misting to prevent the notoriously crispy leaf edges calatheas develop in dry indoor air, and use distilled or rain water if tap water causes browning.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or hardwood cuttings in late fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; deutzia blooms on old wood and should be pruned immediately after flowering by thinning the oldest, flowered stems to the ground to maintain vigor and density.
directions: Root cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; fuzzy deutzia is a Chinese and Japanese deciduous shrub that creates a spectacular late-spring and early-summer flowering display — the upright to arching branches become completely covered from tip to base with dense, upright panicles of white or pink-tinged, five-petaled flowers in late May to June, creating one of the fullest and most exuberant white-flowered shrub displays of the season. The name 'scabra' (rough) refers to the distinctive, rough, scurfy, sandpaper-textured surface of the ovate leaves, which distinguish it from the smooth-leaved species. 'Plena' with double, rose-flushed flowers, 'Pride of Rochester' with large, semi-double, white flowers with pink reverses, and 'Nikko' (dwarf, ground-cover habit) are the most widely planted cultivars. Tolerates partial shade acceptably. After a few years, the arching stems develop attractive, warm-brown, exfoliating bark that provides additional winter interest. An easy, trouble-free, and long-lived deciduous shrub that has been reliably ornamental in temperate gardens for well over a century.

common_name: G.G. Gerbing Azalea (Classic White Southern Indica Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; a white sport of Formosa, G.G. Gerbing grows to similar large dimensions and needs the same generous spacing.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; like other Southern Indian Hybrid azaleas, G.G. Gerbing is a large, vigorous shrub that resents root disturbance once established, so site it with its mature size in mind. A white-flowered sport of the classic 'Formosa' azalea discovered in Florida, G.G. Gerbing produces an overwhelming mid-spring flush of large, pure white, ruffled flowers with a faint chartreuse throat blotch that lights up shaded borders and woodland edges. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it can reach 8–12 feet tall and wide after decades, forming a dense, billowing evergreen mass that anchors older Southern landscapes much as its magenta parent does. Prune only immediately after the spring bloom finishes, since flower buds for next year set on the current season's growth soon after — pruning in fall or winter removes the coming spring's flowers.

common_name: GRANDE Amethyst Heuchera (Oversized Purple Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to light shade; GRANDE Amethyst is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction bred for an unusually large, spreading clump, tolerating more sun than most coral bells in trials while still performing best with afternoon shade in a hot Gulf South summer.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to light shade, giving it plenty of room to spread; GRANDE Amethyst is bred to form a dramatically oversized clump compared to standard coral bells, reaching up to three feet wide, with rich violet-purple foliage marked by bold black-purple veining that makes a strong groundcover-scale statement in a shade bed. Because of its larger size it also tolerates a bit more sun than most Heuchera cultivars, though the deepest color and best performance still come with reliable moisture and protection from the harshest afternoon sun. Small sprays of pale flowers rise above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the bold leaf color and scale. Divide only when necessary, since the plant's large-clump habit is part of its appeal.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall for cool climates; Galahad is a classic Pacific Giant delphinium strain bearing pure white flowers on tall, dense spikes.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, staking tall flower spikes to protect them from wind and summer storms. Galahad produces towering spikes densely packed with large, semi-double, pure white flowers with a subtle white 'bee' at the center, one of the cleanest, purest white strains in the classic Pacific Giant delphinium series, opening from the base of the spike upward over several weeks in early summer. Its clean color makes it an excellent companion for the darker blues and purples of other Pacific Giant strains such as King Arthur or Black Knight in a mixed planting. In warm climates it is typically grown as a cool-season annual or short-lived biennial since it declines quickly in summer heat and humidity. All parts are toxic if ingested. Cut spent flower spikes back hard after the first bloom flush to encourage a possible secondary round of flowering.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, very acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; purchase only from nursery-propagated sources — galax has been over-collected from the wild for the floral trade and is declining in many areas.
directions: Plant in moist, very acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; galax is one of the premier evergreen groundcovers for deep shade in acidic woodland gardens. The round, glossy, leathery leaves form a dense, weed-suppressing carpet that turns brilliant bronze-wine-red through fall and winter before returning to rich green in spring — providing bold, year-round color in the shade garden. The small white flowers on tall wands in late spring are attractive to bees. It grows naturally on the rocky, acidic woodland slopes of the Southern Appalachians, where it is sometimes called 'coltsfoot.' Galax leaves are highly prized in the floral industry and are heavily wild-harvested — purchase only nursery-propagated plants. Spreads slowly but persistently by rhizome to form colonies.

common_name: Galaxy Caladium (White with Vivid Red Spots Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Galaxy's white-and-red spotted pattern is most vivid in bright partial shade — deep shade may cause the red spots to fade toward pink.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Galaxy is a spotted fancy-leaf caladium producing white to cream-white heart-shaped leaves decorated with vivid red to crimson spots and splashes scattered across the leaf surface, creating a constellation-like pattern that gives the variety its evocative name. The contrasting pattern of vivid red spots on a white background creates one of the most visually energetic caladium patterns — the red-on-white spotted effect is immediately striking and distinctive, quite different from the veined or marbled patterns of most other caladium varieties. The irregular spot placement — no two leaves have identical pattern — contributes a spontaneous, natural quality to the display that complements both formal and informal garden styles. Galaxy adds a unique spotted pattern to mixed caladium plantings where it creates visual variety alongside the solid-colored, veined, and bicolor types. In zone 9, Galaxy performs reliably through the entire warm season (May–October) with tubers increasing in size year to year in-ground plantings. The white background and red spots create outstanding combinations with solid green groundcovers (mondo grass, liriope) and dark companions (black ajuga, dark heuchera) where the spotted pattern provides maximum contrast. Maintain consistent moisture and mulch to ensure the finest leaf quality.

common_name: Galaxy Magnolia (Deep Pink Late-Blooming Hybrid Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Galaxy blooms 2–3 weeks later than saucer magnolia, significantly reducing the risk of late frost damage to the large pink flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Galaxy is a USDA National Arboretum hybrid magnolia introduction — a cross between Magnolia liliiflora 'Nigra' (the dark-purple Japanese magnolia) and Magnolia sprengeri 'Diva' (the vivid pink Chinese magnolia) that combines the intense dark-pink to reddish-purple color and late bloom timing of the former with the large flower size and vigorous tree habit of the latter. The large, upright, tulip-shaped flowers (6–8 inches across when fully open) are deep rose-pink to reddish-pink on the exterior and lighter pink on the interior, produced in exceptional profusion on an upright, oval-to-pyramidal tree reaching 20–30 feet at maturity. The bloom timing — 2–3 weeks later than saucer magnolia (Magnolia × soulangeana) — is Galaxy's most practically important quality: in zone 6–7, late frosts frequently damage the flowers of earlier-blooming saucer magnolias; Galaxy's delayed bloom schedule moves past the most dangerous late-frost window. The upright habit and considerable height distinguish Galaxy from low-branching, spreading saucer magnolias — Galaxy has a more tree-like form appropriate for use as a street tree or in more formal landscape settings. In zone 9, Galaxy blooms in February–March with no frost risk, producing an exceptional flower display in warm winter conditions.

plant_note: Sow in cool soil before the last frost, or in fall in mild climates; seed benefits from chilling.
directions: Direct sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost, or in fall where winters are mild; chilling the seed improves germination. This memorable cut flower blooms from late spring into early summer in carmine, lilac, salmon, blue, pink, and white, adding height at the back of the bed. It reseeds readily and prefers cool conditions. Note that all parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so site it away from children and pets.

common_name: Gallery Art Deco Dahlia (Compact Bronze-Orange Patio Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost, or grow in a large container; Gallery Art Deco is part of the dwarf Gallery series bred specifically for compact borders and patio pots.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep in the garden or a large container; unlike tall border and cutting dahlias, Gallery series dahlias rarely need staking thanks to their naturally dwarf, sturdy habit. Gallery Art Deco carries fully double decorative blooms blending bronze, orange, and gold tones on a compact plant well suited to the front of a border, mixed container, or small bed where taller dahlias would overwhelm the space. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the long summer-to-frost flowering going, and feed lightly, since Gallery types are bred to stay short and heavy fertilizing can encourage floppy, oversized growth. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist to seasonally wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Galveston spider lily is endemic to the upper Texas Gulf Coast and adjacent Louisiana coastal marshes and wet prairies, where it grows in the brackish to freshwater marsh edges and seasonally flooded grasslands. It tolerates brief salinity and periodic flooding. The common name 'Alligator Lily' reflects its preferred wet, marshy habitat.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist to seasonally wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Galveston spider lily is a Gulf Coast endemic — one of the few flowering plants whose native range is centered specifically on the Texas Gulf Coast and its immediate vicinity, making it a plant of genuine regional botanical significance for gardeners in the greater Houston-Galveston-Beaumont area. It blooms in summer, producing pure-white, fragrant, spider lily flowers in the classic Hymenocallis form — a central funnel-cup with six long, reflexed, strap-like white perianth segments spreading outward — adapted to the hot, humid, occasionally flooded conditions of the Texas coastal prairie and marsh edges. This is one of the most locally appropriate native plants for zone 9a Gulf Coast landscapes incorporating wet or rain-garden features, coastal prairie restoration, and native plant gardens in the Galveston Bay region. The common name 'Alligator Lily' records the marshy alligator habitat where it naturally occurs. Growing a Galveston spider lily in a Houston-area garden is a form of ecological stewardship for a plant restricted to a limited coastal range.

plant_note: Set out young trees in fall on dry, rocky mountain slopes and mesas across the Intermountain West, where this drought-tolerant oak often forms colonial thickets from root sprouts.
directions: Set out young trees in fall on dry, rocky mountain slopes and mesas across the Intermountain West, where this drought-tolerant oak often forms dense colonial thickets from root sprouts. Its lobed, deciduous leaves turn russet-orange in fall, and its abundant acorns are an important food source for deer, black bear, and wild turkey. Gambel oak works well as a low-water specimen or naturalized thicket planting in xeriscape and wildfire-resilient landscaping in its native high-desert range. Once established it requires minimal irrigation and tolerates poor, rocky soils that few other oaks can handle.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; Ganges Primrose is a Southeast Asian Strobilanthes producing nearly continuous pale lavender-blue flowers on a shrubby, semi-sprawling plant — it performs in conditions similar to Persian Shield (S. dyerianus) but is grown primarily for flowers rather than foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; pinch to encourage bushiness and more prolific flowering. Strobilanthes isophyllus (Ganges primrose or India snapweed) is a shrubby, semi-sprawling tropical perennial from India and Southeast Asia in the acanthus family (Acanthaceae), producing a nearly continuous display of pale lavender-blue to soft violet, snapdragon-like (tubular, two-lipped) flowers from spring through fall in warm climates. The plant is grown primarily for its prolific flowering rather than its foliage — the leaves are glossy, lance-shaped, and dark green, attractive but not as dramatic as those of the related Persian Shield (S. dyerianus). Strobilanthes isophyllus tolerates a range of light conditions from bright indirect to quite deep shade, where it continues to flower more readily than many shade plants. In zone 9–12, it grows as a perennial; in colder climates, it makes an excellent container plant that can be overwintered indoors. The similar 'Gossip Girl' and 'Kimberley Blue' cultivars are sometimes attributed to this species or close relatives. A useful and underused shade-flowering perennial for warm, humid climates where few ornamentals bloom reliably in full shade.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost danger in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; garden balsam thrives in the heat and humidity of Southern summers and is one of the most reliable and colorful warm-season annuals for shade and partial-shade gardens in zones 8–11.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface or barely covered in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to part sun; thin to 10–18 inches. Impatiens balsamina (garden balsam) is an old-fashioned cottage-garden annual — among the first flowering plants brought from Asia to Europe in the 16th century — producing upright, fleshy stems densely clothed with double, camellia-like flowers 1–2 inches across tucked along the stem in pink, red, white, lilac, salmon, and bicolor. The mature seed pods explode and scatter seeds with light touch (giving rise to 'touch-me-not' and the genus name Impatiens), and plants self-seed freely in warm, moist gardens. Garden balsam is one of the best heat-tolerant, humid-climate alternatives to the common impatiens (I. walleriana, which succumbs to impatiens downy mildew in humid areas) — it thrives through Southern summers with vigor and color when many annual flowers struggle. The compact, double-flowered 'Tom Thumb' series is popular; the taller 'Camellia-flowered' types are favored for cutting.

plant_note: Divide established clumps after flowering in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade; Clivia gardenii produces narrower, darker leaves than C. miniata and nodding (pendant) rather than erect flowers. It is one of the rarer species in cultivation, growing naturally in the moist, shaded, low-altitude forests of KwaZulu-Natal. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; Garden Clivia differs from the commonly grown orange clivia (C. miniata) in producing distinctly different flowers — the individual blooms nod or are pendant (pointing downward or outward) rather than facing upward and outward as in C. miniata, creating a more quietly elegant, drooping display of funnel-shaped flowers in orange-red to yellow-red above the same broad, strap-shaped, deep-green evergreen leaves. The nodding flower form, while less spectacular than the bold C. miniata umbels, has a refined, somewhat mysterious quality — the pendant flowers dangling in clusters that must be lifted to be viewed. It is more shade-tolerant and moisture-loving than C. miniata in its natural habitat of humid, low-altitude KwaZulu-Natal forests near streams and in swampy ground. As a garden plant for zones 9–11, it provides the same outstanding shade-tolerance as C. miniata — evergreen foliage in deep shade, winter flowers — in a different and somewhat more collector-oriented flower form. Rarely seen in general horticulture; sought by clivia specialists.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring after temperatures are consistently above 60°F in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; crotons require consistent warmth and thrive in hot, humid, tropical weather. Cold below 50°F causes leaf drop. The milky sap is irritating — wear gloves when pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade — the most vibrant leaf coloration develops in brighter light; deep shade produces greener, less intensely colored foliage. Garden croton is one of the most spectacularly colorful foliage plants in tropical horticulture, with leathery leaves that combine vivid red, orange, yellow, green, and purple in patterns ranging from fine-speckled splashes to broad blotches, depending on the hundreds of named cultivars available. Hundreds of leaf shapes exist: broad and lobed, narrow and twisted, curled, or oak-leaf shaped. It thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast and Florida in full outdoor culture in zone 9–12. Mite infestations are the most common pest problem, particularly in dry conditions — maintain adequate soil moisture and mist foliage during droughts. Crotons drop leaves readily when moved, so establish carefully. An outstanding specimen and landscape plant for bold tropical color.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring, 2–6 weeks after the last frost, for fall bloom.
directions: Plant in spring into fertile, well-drained soil; pinch growing tips every 2–3 weeks from planting until midsummer (around July 4) to develop compact, well-branched plants with dozens of buds. Mums are short-day plants that begin flower bud formation as nights lengthen; stop pinching by midsummer to avoid disrupting this process. Mulch heavily after the first hard frost to improve winter hardiness in colder zones. Divide annually in spring to rejuvenate the planting and maintain plant vigor.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or division clumps in spring in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; pinch stem tips repeatedly through midsummer (until about July 15 in most zones) to encourage bushy growth and maximum flower bud development for fall bloom.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; pinch growing tips every 2–3 weeks from spring through mid-July to encourage branching and maximize fall bloom. Chrysanthemum morifolium is the garden mum — the standard fall-flowering perennial of American horticulture, producing a spectacular flush of daisy-like to button-like to pom-pom flowers in a huge range of colors (white, yellow, bronze, orange, red, pink, purple, lavender) in August–October depending on cultivar. Hardy garden mums are classified by flower form (single, decorative, cushion, pompon, spider, quill, and more) and blooming time (early, mid, late season). In zones 5–7 they are reliably perennial with some protection; in zones 8–9 they may be treated as warm-season annuals that bloom September–November and then decline, as summer heat interferes with vegetative development. Divide clumps every 2–3 years in spring to maintain vigor. The key cultural requirement is consistent pinching through summer — without it, plants develop long, ungainly stems with few flowers rather than the compact, floriferous mounds depicted in catalogs.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface-sow as light is needed, and set out after frost.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, pressing the tiny seed onto the surface since light is required for germination. Garden Party Blend produces large 3-inch ruffled floribunda blooms in abundance all season on mounding, upright plants that draw butterflies. Set out after frost in full sun in beds or containers around the patio. Deadhead and feed lightly to keep the colorful display going into fall.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, organically rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; space 18–24 inches apart with good air circulation to minimize powdery mildew problems.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart with excellent air circulation; garden phlox is a native Eastern North American perennial that produces large, rounded heads of fragrant flowers in pink, red, white, lavender, or bicolor shades from midsummer into fall — one of the best summer perennials for cutting. Powdery mildew is the primary challenge: thin stems to 5–7 per clump, water at the base only, and choose mildew-resistant cultivars such as 'David' (white) or 'Robert Poore' (purple). Deadhead faded flower heads to prevent seedlings that revert to magenta. Divide every 3 years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent the center of the clump from dying out.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; garden pinks can also be sown in fall for established plants that bloom freely in their first spring.
directions: Direct-sow seeds on the surface of well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun in early spring or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; garden pinks are among the most fragrant border perennials, producing spicy clove-scented single or double flowers in pink, red, white, and bicolor combinations in late spring and early summer above blue-grey grassy foliage. Excellent drainage is essential — they rot quickly in wet, heavy, or acidic soils. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage a second flush of bloom, and shear the entire plant by about one-third after the main flowering season to maintain a compact, tidy mound. Short-lived in humid climates but easily propagated by cuttings taken in summer or by division in early fall every 2–3 years.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil; blooms later in the season and generally taller than the more commonly grown Veronica spicata.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in average, well-drained soil in full sun in spring, spacing plants to allow good air circulation around the narrow, upright clumps. Garden speedwell produces long, slender leaves and tall, tapering spikes of violet-blue flowers from midsummer into early fall, blooming later and often taller than the more commonly grown Veronica spicata, making it a favored source of blue for late-season borders and cut-flower arrangements. It tolerates average garden soil and some drought once established but flowers most heavily with consistent moisture and a spring feeding.
