Deadhead spent spikes back to a lateral bud to extend bloom, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Garden Treasure Itoh Peony (Large Yellow Intersectional Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates; Itoh peonies tolerate the marginal chill of zone 8b–9 better than straight herbaceous cultivars.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Garden Treasure is one of the most widely grown Itoh (intersectional) peonies, producing an abundance of huge, semi-double golden-yellow blooms with a faint rose flare at the petal base over a long bloom period, since the woody-based, bushy plant carries many buds per stem that open in succession rather than all at once. Like other Itoh hybrids its sturdy stems support the heavy flowers without staking and the attractive, deeply cut foliage remains clean through summer and into fall, long after most herbaceous peonies have declined. It tolerates a wider soil pH range and more heat than traditional Paeonia lactiflora cultivars, making it one of the more forgiving peonies for the warmer edge of peony range, though reliable flowering still depends on some winter chilling.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost, or purchase transplants; garden verbena requires warm soil (above 60°F) to grow and bloom — transplant only after frost risk has fully passed. Deadhead regularly to extend bloom into summer; in zone 9–10 it blooms spring through winter with minimal care.
directions: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost, or plant purchased transplants in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately dry to moist soil in full sun — garden verbena is one of the most popular and versatile bedding plants in the world, available in a continuous spectrum from pure white through pink, salmon, red, scarlet, purple, lavender, and bicolor combinations, blooming prolifically from spring through fall. The trailing to mounding habit (depending on cultivar) makes it outstanding in containers, hanging baskets, window boxes, and as a low bedding plant. Modern disease-resistant series ('Superbena', 'Lascar', 'Obsession') provide significantly better powdery mildew resistance and longer bloom seasons than older varieties. In zone 9–11 garden verbena often overwinters and behaves as a short-lived perennial, providing bloom through winter; in zone 7–8 it is an annual. Remove spent flower clusters regularly to maintain maximum bloom production through summer.

common_name: Gardenview Scarlet Beebalm (Classic Tall Red Bee Balm)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Gardenview Scarlet is a classic tall red bee balm cultivar with better mildew tolerance and vigor than many older red selections, though it still benefits from good air circulation in humid Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Gardenview Scarlet is a long-established red bee balm cultivar valued for its large, vivid scarlet-red flower heads held on tall, sturdy stems, making it a reliable hummingbird and butterfly magnet for the summer border. It generally shows better vigor and somewhat improved mildew resistance compared to older heirloom red Monarda didyma selections, though like most red bee balms it still benefits from good air circulation, morning sun with some afternoon shade in the hottest climates, and consistent soil moisture to minimize powdery mildew in humid Gulf South summers. The aromatic, mint-scented foliage is typical of the genus, and the plant spreads by underground stolons to form an expanding colony over time. Divide every two to three years in early spring to control spread, renew vigor, and improve air circulation within the clump. Deadhead spent flower heads to tidy the planting, though the seed heads also provide some winter interest and food for finches if left standing.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade; rose daphne resents root disturbance and wet feet above all else, so choose its permanent site — ideally a rock garden or raised bed with excellent drainage — carefully from the start.
directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade, ideally on a slope or raised bed where water never stands around the roots; rose daphne is a low, mat-forming, evergreen shrub that in late spring smothers itself in small, intensely fragrant, rosy-pink flower clusters — one of the most powerfully scented small shrubs grown, easily perfuming an entire rock garden or path. It is a classic choice for alpine and rock gardens, where its trailing habit can drape attractively over stones. Good drainage is the single non-negotiable requirement for success; more rose daphnes are lost to wet, heavy soil than to cold, pests, or neglect. Like other daphnes, it resents being moved once established, so plant it in its permanent spot and avoid disturbing the root zone afterward. Mulch lightly with gravel rather than organic mulch to keep the crown dry.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a sturdy fence, trellis, or arbor as support. Garlic vine blooms most prolifically in fall and again in spring with intermittent bloom throughout the warm season; it flowers better in full sun but tolerates partial shade. Frost damages foliage in zone 9 but established plants typically resprout from the base.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with sturdy support for the vigorous vines; garlic vine (Mansoa alliacea) is a striking tropical vine from the Amazon basin producing clusters of lavender-purple to purple-pink, trumpet-shaped bignonia-family flowers in successive waves through the warm season, most heavily in fall and spring. Its common name comes from the pronounced garlic odor of the crushed leaves, stems, and flowers — a distinctive fragrance that has led to its use in traditional medicine in South America. The three-part leaves and decorative clusters of flowers make it an attractive flowering vine for tropical and subtropical screens and arbors; the vines climb vigorously and can cover a large fence or pergola quickly. It flowers most prolifically in full sun but tolerates partial shade and performs well in the humid heat of Gulf Coast zone 9–10 gardens. The unusual garlic fragrance is surprising and memorable in the garden.

common_name: Gateway Joe Pye Weed (Large Wine-Red-Stemmed Native Pollinator Perennial)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Gateway is a slightly more compact selection of spotted Joe Pye weed, still large but sturdier and less floppy than the wild species.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Gateway is a popular, slightly more compact selection of spotted Joe Pye weed, producing huge, domed clusters of dusty mauve-pink flowers atop sturdy, wine-red-tinged stems in late summer, a magnet for swallowtails, monarchs, and countless other butterflies and bees. Its large scale makes it an excellent back-of-border native for a pollinator garden, rain garden, or pond edge where soil stays reliably moist, and the dried seed heads provide winter interest and food for songbirds if left standing. It spreads slowly to form a substantial clump over time and can be divided in spring if a larger planting is wanted.

common_name: Gatsby Gal Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact White-to-Pink Blooming Selection)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gatsby Gal is a Proven Winners selection in the Gatsby series of oakleaf hydrangeas, chosen for a compact, well-proportioned habit that fits more easily into a residential landscape than the full-sized species.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gatsby Gal produces large, elongated flower panicles that open white in early summer and take on a soft pink blush as they age, on a more compact plant than the straight oakleaf hydrangea species, making it easier to fit into a foundation planting or shade border. Like all oakleaf hydrangeas, it is a Southeastern US native fully adapted to the heat, humidity, and clay soils of the Gulf South, developing excellent burgundy-red fall foliage and attractive peeling bark for winter interest. Requires little pruning; remove only dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since next year's blooms form on the current season's growth by late summer.

common_name: Gatsby Moon Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large Double-Flowered Oakleaf Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gatsby Moon is part of the Gatsby series bred for extra-large, heavily double flower panicles on a full-sized oakleaf hydrangea shrub.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving this full-sized cultivar plenty of room to reach its mature spread. Gatsby Moon is part of the Gatsby series of oakleaf hydrangeas bred for exceptionally large, densely double, pure white flower panicles that age to a soft pink, giving an especially showy, full-looking bloom compared with the single-flowered species. The bold, deeply lobed foliage turns outstanding shades of burgundy, orange, and purple in fall, and the exfoliating cinnamon bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering, since next year's flower buds form on the current season's growth by late summer, and avoid pruning in fall, winter, or spring, which removes the coming year's blooms.

common_name: Gatsby Pink Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large White-to-Deep-Pink Color-Shift Selection)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gatsby Pink is a Proven Winners oakleaf hydrangea noted for an especially dramatic color transformation, with large white blooms deepening to rich pink through the summer.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gatsby Pink produces large, showy flower panicles that open pure white in early summer and gradually deepen to a rich, saturated pink as they age through the season, giving an extended, ever-changing floral display. Its full-sized habit fits well in a woodland border or mass planting where its bold texture and multi-season interest can be appreciated. Like other oakleaf hydrangeas, it develops burgundy-red fall foliage and attractive cinnamon, peeling bark for winter interest, and is fully adapted to the heat, humidity, and clay soils of the Gulf South. Requires little pruning; remove only dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since next year's blooms form on the current season's growth.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in loose, well-drained germination mix; plants develop a deep taproot early so pot on before roots become crowded. Plant in full sun and lean, well-drained soil — gaura thrives on neglect and declines in fertile, wet conditions. The wand-like stems bearing butterfly-shaped white or pink flowers sway gracefully all season without deadheading. Cut plants back to 6 in after the first heavy bloom flush to encourage a tidy second flush through autumn.

common_name: Gay Butterflies Butterfly Weed (Mixed-Color Butterfly Milkweed Strain)
plant_note: Direct sow after danger of frost, or start indoors and transplant, into well-drained, average-to-lean soil in full sun; this open-pollinated seed strain of butterfly weed produces a mix of orange, yellow, and red-orange flowered plants from the same sowing.
directions: Sow in well-drained, lean-to-average soil in full sun; like the wild species, Gay Butterflies resents wet feet and rich, heavily amended soil and performs best where it is left largely undisturbed once established. This heirloom seed strain was selected to broaden the color range of straight butterfly weed, producing a mix of orange, gold, yellow, and red-orange umbels on the same deep, drought-tolerant taproot that makes the species so tough in poor, dry sites. It is a larval host for monarch caterpillars and a strong nectar draw for a wide range of butterflies, bees, and other pollinators through a long summer bloom season. Because the taproot resents transplanting once mature, direct-sow where plants are to remain or transplant only small, young seedlings, and expect variable bloom color to appear starting the second year.

common_name: Gay Paree Peony (Japanese-Form Rose-Pink with Ruffled Cream Center)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gay Paree is a Japanese-form peony with rose-pink guard petals surrounding a ruffled creamy-white center.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Gay Paree bears a striking Japanese-form flower, a single ring of broad, rose-pink guard petals surrounding a dense, ruffled mass of narrower creamy-white staminodes at the center, a lighter, more textured bloom than the fully double bomb form and highly attractive to bees since the flower's structure remains more open. Its two-tone contrast has made it one of the most recognizable and widely planted Japanese-form peonies. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep; they germinate readily at 65–75°F and grow quickly into compact transplants. Plant in sharply drained, even poor soil in the hottest, sunniest location available — gazania excels in sandy or gravelly beds where other plants fail. Flowers close at night and on overcast days, but modern hybrid varieties stay open longer than older types. Drought tolerance is excellent once established; overwatering and heavy clay soils are the most common causes of failure.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun, ideally with some shelter from hard freezes.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun, ideally with some shelter from hard freezes; Geiger tree is native to beach dunes and coastal hammocks of South Florida and the Caribbean and is exceptionally salt- and wind-tolerant, making it a signature small tree of Florida Keys and coastal landscaping. Clusters of crepe-textured, brilliant orange-red flowers appear nearly year-round in frost-free areas, followed by white, pear-shaped fruit that birds relish, while the large, rough, sandpapery leaves give the plant a distinctive tropical texture. It can be maintained as a large multi-trunked flowering shrub with occasional pruning or allowed to grow into a small canopy tree. Protect young plants from temperatures below the high 20s F, since it is one of the more cold-tender salt-tolerant natives available.

common_name: Gem Box Boxwood (Naturally Rounded No-Shear Dwarf Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Gem Box naturally holds a neat, rounded form without regular shearing, making it useful for low, formal-looking edging with far less pruning maintenance than traditional boxwood.
directions: Gem Box is a naturally compact, mounding boxwood hybrid bred to hold a tidy, rounded form on its own, essentially eliminating the frequent shearing that traditional boxwood hedging requires while still giving the same fine-textured, dense, dark-green formal look. It tolerates heat, cold, and a wide pH range better than many older boxwood cultivars and shows improved resistance to boxwood blight in independent trials, a significant advantage given how damaging that disease has become in Southern landscapes. Give it moist, well-drained soil and afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, watch for boxwood leafminer (the primary Southern boxwood pest), and expect to do little more than an occasional light touch-up shearing to keep its naturally neat habit looking crisp.

common_name: General Jacqueminot Rose (Fragrant Crimson Hybrid Perpetual)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; introduced in France in 1853, General Jacqueminot became one of the most influential red roses of the 19th century.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced in France in 1853, General Jacqueminot bears large, intensely fragrant, velvety crimson-red double blooms on a vigorous, upright shrub, and its rich color and powerful old-rose scent made it hugely influential as a parent behind countless later red roses, including many modern hybrid teas. It blooms mainly in a strong spring flush with some sporadic repeat later in the season, a typical pattern for Hybrid Perpetual roses bred before reliable everblooming traits were established. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering canes.

common_name: Generale Vicomtesse de Vibraye Hydrangea (Antique French Mophead)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this old French cultivar shifts reliably between clear pink and true blue depending on soil pH.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. One of the older named French mophead hydrangeas still grown, Generale Vicomtesse de Vibraye is prized for producing an especially clean, true color shift, opening a clear rose-pink in alkaline soil and a rich, saturated blue in acidic soil, making it a favorite for gardeners wanting to demonstrate or fine-tune the classic hydrangea pH effect. The rounded flower heads are medium-sized and produced in good quantity on a compact, well-branched shrub. It blooms on old wood, so limit pruning to right after flowering, and provide morning sun with afternoon shade in hot Southern climates to keep the blooms from wilting.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or divide established clumps in spring or fall; Geneva bugle does not spread by stolons (unlike the common Ajuga reptans) and is much less aggressive — it forms well-behaved clumps that spread slowly by seed and division rather than running stems. It prefers drier, poorer soils than A. reptans and is more tolerant of drought and exposed positions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Geneva bugle is the well-behaved, non-running relative of the familiar carpet bugleweed (Ajuga reptans) — forming neat, slowly spreading clumps rather than running by stolons, making it far better suited to controlled garden situations where A. reptans would become invasive. It is native to dry meadows, rocky grassland, and open woodland edges of central Europe, producing similar dense, upright spikes of brilliant deep-blue to violet-blue flowers in spring and early summer above rosettes of dark-green, obovate, slightly hairy leaves. Because it does not spread by creeping runners, it cannot carpet ground as rapidly as A. reptans, but its well-behaved habit, greater drought tolerance, and preference for lean, drier soils make it superior for dry gardens, rock gardens, and situations where invasive runners would be a problem. Excellent for naturalizing in short grass (allowed to grow through without mowing in spring), where the blue flower spikes provide a clean, early-summer wildflower display.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; gentian sage develops tuberous roots that can be lifted and stored frost-free like dahlias in zones colder than zone 8, or left in the ground where it is perennial. Tubers are often readily available and give a head start over seed. The cultivar 'Cambridge Blue' is a pale sky-blue form; 'Oxford Blue' is the deep cobalt blue of the species.
directions: Start indoors early or plant tubers in full sun after danger of frost passes; gentian sage produces one of the most intensely cobalt-blue flowers in horticulture — large, open-mouthed, hooded flowers of deep, saturated gentian-blue (hence the common name) appearing in pairs along upright stems from summer through frost, each bloom substantially larger than most salvias and in a blue so vivid it registers as startling in the summer border. The species color is deep cobalt-blue; the cultivar 'Cambridge Blue' produces a softer, cleaner, sky-blue that some find more elegant. Both are remarkable for the purity and intensity of the blue. A Mexican native, it develops tuberous roots and is perennial in zones 8–11, where it can form substantial, long-lived clumps. In colder climates it is treated as a tender perennial or grown from tubers started indoors and lifted after frost like dahlias. Outstanding combined with orange Hemerocallis, yellow Rudbeckia, or white flowers that will contrast with the cobalt blue.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Gentle Shepherd is a classic near-white daylily prized for its clear, pale color and ruffled form.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Gentle Shepherd bears large, ruffled, near-white blooms with a soft chartreuse-green throat, one of the palest and most consistently near-white daylilies available, opening on sturdy scapes above a full clump of arching foliage. Its light color makes it a favorite for moon gardens and evening viewing, where it glows in low light. Deadhead spent blooms daily for a tidy appearance, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigorous bloom.

plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. George Davison is an old, long-cultivated crocosmia selection bearing clear golden-yellow flowers on arching sprays above bold, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer, a cheerful, sunny color that stands apart from the more common orange and red crocosmia cultivars. Its more compact stature than taller crocosmia cultivars suits it to the front or middle of a mixed border, and the tubular flowers draw hummingbirds and make good cut flowers. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time.

common_name: George L. Taber Azalea (George Tabor Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; George L. Taber is a large-growing Southern Indian Hybrid azalea requiring excellent drainage and soil acidity — amend clay soils with pine bark and sulfur before planting.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade (morning sun, afternoon shade is ideal); George L. Taber is the quintessential Gulf Coast landscape azalea — a large-growing Southern Indian Hybrid producing enormous quantities of large (3–3.5-inch), pale orchid-pink to light lavender-pink flowers with a distinctive deeper purple-pink blotch on the upper petals in spring. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is among the most recognizable and widely planted spring-blooming shrubs, capable of reaching 8–10 feet tall and wide after decades in the landscape. The semi-evergreen foliage is medium-green and holds through zone 9 winters. George L. Taber was selected from open-pollinated seedlings in a Florida nursery and named after the Florida State nurseryman; it became one of the dominant landscape azaleas of the 20th-century South. It blooms mid-season with a spectacular display that lasts 2–3 weeks and is best appreciated when mass-planted or used as a large accent. Requires good drainage — plants in poor drainage develop root rot rapidly. Fertilize after bloom with an acid-forming fertilizer.

common_name: George Lindley Taber Azalea (Light Pink Darker-Blotched Southern Indica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; George Lindley Taber is a large, vigorous Southern Indica azalea and parent to the popular white-flowered sport Mrs. G. G. Gerbing.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light such as high pines or open hardwoods. George Lindley Taber bears large, light pink flowers with a darker pink blotch and edging, opening in a massive mid-spring flush on a big, vigorous Southern Indica shrub that can reach well over 8 feet with age, a scale typical of old Gulf South gardens where century-old specimens are still common. It is the parent plant behind the popular white-flowered sport Mrs. G. G. Gerbing, discovered as a branch mutation. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Georgetown Tea Rose (Found Texas Tea Rose)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Georgetown Tea is a Texas 'found rose,' rescued and named for the Central Texas town where it was rediscovered growing at an old homesite, similar in character to Duchesse de Brabant and Mrs. B.R. Cant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Georgetown Tea is a Texas 'found rose' rescued by rose rustlers from an old homestead near Georgetown, Texas, and — like most tea roses that have survived generations of Southern neglect — it is exceptionally heat-tolerant and disease-resistant. It produces large, fragrant, loosely double blooms in soft pink to apricot tones that open from long, elegant buds, flowering nearly continuously from spring through fall in a warm climate. Grown own-root, it regrows true to type from the base after cold damage or hard pruning, and it needs little more than full sun, decent drainage, and an occasional light shaping to perform reliably for decades, much as it has at the old homesite where it was found.

plant_note: Plant seeds or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean to average, loamy or rocky soil in full sun; Georgia aster requires lean, well-drained soils and full sun — it is naturally found on rocky, acidic, clay or sandy soils of xeric (dry) Piedmont forest openings, roadsides, and clearings. Rich, fertile soils cause lush growth that flops and reduces flowering.
directions: Plant seeds or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean to average, loamy or rocky soil in full sun; Georgia aster is a rare and beautiful native aster endemic to the southeastern US — restricted to a narrow range in the Piedmont of Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Alabama, where it grows in xeric, fire-maintained openings in longleaf and mixed-pine upland forest. One of the largest-flowered of the native asters, producing abundant showy clusters of violet-purple to lavender flowers with yellow centers in fall (October–November) — among the latest-blooming of all native asters and an exceptionally valuable late-season nectar source for migrating monarchs and native bees. Listed as a species of conservation concern due to habitat loss from fire suppression and development. An outstanding native pollinator plant for dry, acidic, lean soils in the southeastern Piedmont. Closely related to the New England aster but more heat-tolerant and better adapted to the warm, humid Southeast.

common_name: Georgia Blue Speedwell (Low Spreading Groundcover Veronica with Vivid Blue Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Georgia Blue spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, quickly forming a low mat useful for edging paths, rock gardens, and small-scale groundcover plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; good drainage is important, as this low groundcover speedwell dislikes standing water. Georgia Blue is a low, mat-forming veronica that spreads via trailing stems, producing a carpet of small bronze-green leaves smothered in early spring by masses of vivid gentian-blue flowers with tiny white eyes, one of the earliest and most eye-catching groundcover blooms of the season. Its dense, semi-evergreen foliage continues to provide low textural groundcover after the spring flower show fades, and light shearing after bloom keeps the mat tidy and can prompt sparse rebloom later in the season. It is well suited to rock gardens, path edges, and the front of borders where a low, spreading, easy-care perennial is needed, and established plantings tolerate both light foot traffic and short dry spells.

common_name: Georgia Charm Indian Hawthorn (Compact Rose-Pink Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Georgia Charm produces rose-pink flower clusters in spring above compact, dense, glossy evergreen foliage, followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds, on a tidy, rounded shrub sized for smaller foundation plantings and low hedges. Like other Indian hawthorn cultivars, it tolerates salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils well, making it a dependable choice for coastal Gulf Coast landscapes. Good air circulation between plants helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions; established plants need little care beyond occasional shaping.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Georgia Holly is dioecious and requires both male and female plants nearby for berry production. It is rare in cultivation but available from specialist native plant nurseries.
directions: Georgia Holly is a rare and regionally endemic native deciduous holly of the upper coastal plain and piedmont, found in a narrow range across Georgia, Alabama, and adjacent states, where it grows as a spreading shrub in the understory of moist, well-drained, sandy-loam upland forest. Distinctive among native hollies for its unusually long flower and fruit pedicels — the scientific epithet longipes means 'long-footed' — the bright red berries appear to float in space on their elongated stalks, making them more visible and accessible to birds than the closely bunched berries of many other holly species. A candidate for greater cultivation in the native plant garden, Georgia Holly is a multi-season ornamental shrub with small white spring flowers, deep green summer foliage, vivid fall berries, and clean branch structure in winter. Plant rooted cuttings in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; as with all native hollies, both male and female plants must be present for berry production.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Georgia lobelia is restricted in the wild to pocosins, bay swamps, and wet pine flatwoods of the Southeast and requires consistently moist to wet soil in the garden — excellent in rain gardens and at pond margins.
directions: Lobelia georgiana is an uncommon native lobelia of the southeastern coastal plain from North Carolina to Georgia and northern Florida, found in the wild primarily in pocosins, wet pine savannas, and the moist margins of bay swamps; it produces tall racemes of vibrant, deep blue-violet flowers from August through October that are visually similar to L. siphilitica but adapted to the acidic, consistently wet soils of coastal plain flatwoods habitats. It is rarely available from nurseries but is a valuable ecological garden plant for moist, partially shaded situations in zones 7–9 where it supports late-season migrating hummingbirds. Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil; do not allow to dry out at any point during the growing season.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in very well-drained, acidic, rocky, thin soil in full sun; Georgia oak is a rare endemic of granitic flatrocks and exposed rocky outcrops of the southern Appalachians and Piedmont, specializing in conditions with thin, excessively well-drained, acidic soil over granite.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in very well-drained, acidic, rocky, thin soil in full sun; Georgia oak is a rare, small-statured oak endemic to granitic flatrock outcrops and thin, rocky soils of the southern Appalachians and Georgia-Carolina Piedmont — one of the more restricted native oaks in the eastern United States, found primarily on Stone Mountain in Georgia, Hicks Knob in Georgia, and a few scattered Piedmont locations. It is a small tree or large shrub reaching 25–30 feet, with small, deeply lobed leaves that are smaller than most red oaks, turning a reliable, rich red-orange in fall. The compact size and superb fall color make it an outstanding specimen tree for rock gardens, rocky slopes, and smaller properties in zones 6–9 where space constraints prohibit larger oaks. A significant conservation plant with a very limited natural range.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; morning sun deepens the peach-pink color of the ruffled leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with some protection from intense afternoon sun; Georgia Peach is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction with large, heavily ruffled leaves that open peachy-orange and shift toward soft rose-pink as they mature, giving the clump a shifting, multi-toned color display through the season. The undersides of the leaves show a deep purple-red that peeks through as the ruffled margins curl, adding extra depth to the foliage color. Small cream-white flowers appear on wiry stems in late spring above the foliage mound. Give it sharp drainage and consistent soil moisture, since this heuchera dislikes both waterlogged crowns and prolonged drought. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 3-4 years to keep the planting vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Georgia Peach Heuchera (Georgia Peach Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Georgia Peach is a H. villosa hybrid and one of the most heat-tolerant coral bells available, making it a good choice for zone 8–9 gardens where most heucheras struggle through humid summers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Georgia Peach heuchera produces large, rounded, peach-to-apricot leaves with silvery overlay and a distinctive pinkish-rose tint that deepens in cool weather and brightens in warm spring sun. It is a Heuchera x villosa hybrid — the species native to humid southeastern mountains — which makes Georgia Peach significantly more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many northern-derived cultivars. This tolerance for southern summers is its defining advantage for Gulf Coast and zone 8–9 gardens. The leaves are notably large and thick with a soft texture characteristic of its villosa heritage. Pink flowers on wiry stems appear in early summer. It was selected as the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2016. Divide every 3–4 years when the crown heaves out of soil, maintaining proper planting depth when resetting divisions; a crown planted too shallowly or too deeply will decline.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated transplants in spring in dry to moist, well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun. Georgia Plume is critically rare in the wild and should only be sourced from specialty native plant nurseries; the species rarely produces viable seed and is most effectively propagated by root cuttings.
directions: Georgia Plume is one of the rarest and most endangered native shrubs in the United States, a monotypic genus (the only species in its family in North America) endemic to the Sandhills and longleaf pine region of Georgia, where fewer than 50 wild populations survive in dry, sandy, acidic longleaf pine savannas and turkey oak ridges. In July it produces spectacular terminal plumes of small white, four-petaled flowers in drooping clusters 6–12 inches long — an arresting display on a plant that looks unlike anything else in the native flora. The species rarely sets viable seed in the wild (likely due to the collapse of its pollinator community), and natural populations reproduce almost entirely by root sprouting; specialty native plant nurseries propagate it by root cuttings. Grow in dry to moist, well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in partial to full sun — it is intolerant of heavy, wet, or alkaline soils. Supporting cultivation of Georgia Plume in private gardens is an important conservation act.

common_name: Gerald Darby Iris (Purple-Stemmed Pond-Margin Hybrid Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or spring in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to light shade; Gerald Darby is a hybrid of Iris virginica and Iris versicolor grown as much for its purple-flushed stems and foliage as for its violet-blue flowers.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, at a pond margin, rain garden, or any low spot that stays reliably damp. Gerald Darby is a well-known hybrid between the native blue flag irises Iris virginica and Iris versicolor, valued not only for its violet-blue flowers in late spring but for the deep purple flush that colors its stems and the base of its foliage, adding ornamental interest well before and after the bloom period. Like its parent species it tolerates standing water at the pond's edge as well as ordinary garden soil that stays evenly moist, making it a versatile choice for a water garden or boggy border. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Gerald Derouen Louisiana Iris (Vivid Red Award-Winning Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.
directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Gerald Derouen is a Louisiana Cajun-bred cultivar prized for its clear, saturated velvety red flowers held on strong, well-branched stalks, and it remains one of the standard reds against which newer red Louisiana iris introductions are still compared. Like other Louisiana iris it performs best where its roots never fully dry out, making it an excellent choice at a pond edge, in a rain garden, or in a naturally low, poorly drained corner of the landscape. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, replanting fans with a few inches of rhizome promptly since the roots dry out quickly once exposed.

common_name: Geranium Daffodil (Fragrant White Tazetta with Orange-Red Cup)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; Geranium is a classic tazetta daffodil bearing multiple intensely fragrant flowers per stem, well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Geranium bears clusters of three to five white flowers per stem, each centered with a small, ruffled orange-red cup, carrying a powerful, sweet fragrance typical of tazetta daffodils and blooming reliably even in the mild winters of the Gulf South, where many large trumpet daffodils fail to naturalize. Its multi-flowered habit makes each stem a small bouquet in itself, excellent for cutting. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds vertically, pointed end down, barely covered, as they are sensitive to orientation; maintain 70–75°F for germination. Plant so the crown sits slightly above soil level to prevent crown rot, which is the most common cause of plant failure. Water at the base rather than overhead; gerberas prefer a dry-wet-dry cycle rather than constantly moist soil. Deadhead spent flowers by cutting the stem to the base to encourage continuous bloom from spring through fall in mild climates.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 10–12 weeks before setting out and transplant in cool weather into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; wear gloves when handling German primrose, since the leaf hairs contain primin, a compound that causes contact dermatitis in some people.
directions: Start seed indoors 10–12 weeks before setting out and transplant in cool weather into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; wear gloves when handling German primrose, since the leaf hairs contain primin, a compound that causes contact dermatitis in some people. Primula obconica is a Chinese species long grown as a cool-season flowering pot and bedding plant, with soft, rounded, hairy leaves and clusters of round-faced flowers in white, pink, red, salmon, and purple held above the foliage over a long cool-weather bloom period. It is grown as a winter or early-spring bedding and container plant in mild climates or as a greenhouse and indoor flowering plant further north, valued for its long bloom season and wide color range in shaded or filtered-light conditions. Because sensitive individuals can develop a skin rash from contact with the glandular hairs, primin-free modern cultivars are available and preferable for households with skin sensitivities or young children.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained soil after last frost; germander sage requires excellent drainage and lean soil — rich, moist soils cause weak, floppy growth and crown rot. It thrives in alkaline, rocky, caliche soils of Texas and the Southwest where it acts as an evergreen perennial to subshrub in zones 7–9.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; germander sage is a small evergreen to semi-evergreen subshrub from the dry mountains of Mexico producing small, rounded, silver-gray to blue-gray leaves on compact, arching stems and brilliant electric-blue flowers from spring through fall — the striking cerulean-blue color of the flowers is more vivid and saturated than almost any other hardy sage. Native to rocky, limestone soils of the Sierra Madre and Chihuahuan Desert foothills at 4,000–8,000 feet elevation, it is adapted to the alkaline, well-drained soils common in Texas, New Mexico, and the Gulf Coast region. It is one of the best low-water-use ornamental plants for Texas gardens: compact, deer-resistant, drought-tolerant, and in near-continuous bloom. Excellent in rock gardens, xeriscapes, and as a low edging plant.

common_name: Gerrie Hoek Dahlia (Heirloom Soft Salmon-Pink Waterlily Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Gerrie Hoek is a long-cultivated heirloom waterlily dahlia with soft salmon-pink, shallow cupped blooms resembling a water lily.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants in exposed sites to support the broad, flat blooms in wind. Gerrie Hoek, a long-cultivated heirloom, bears shallow, cupped, waterlily-form flowers in soft salmon-pink, the broad, gently overlapping petals creating a flatter, less densely layered bloom than decorative or ball dahlia types, resembling an actual water lily floating in a pond. Its old-fashioned charm and reliable performance have kept it popular with heirloom dahlia collectors for decades. Deadhead spent blooms regularly, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring or fall into amended, well-drained soil, setting the bud union at or just below grade in cold climates.
directions: Set plants where they receive at least six hours of direct sun and good air circulation to limit blackspot, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. This David Austin English rose produces large, intensely fragrant, old-fashioned rosette blooms in deep pink over repeated flushes from late spring through fall. Prune hard in late winter to encourage strong new flowering canes, and feed monthly through the growing season for the best repeat bloom. It can be grown as a bushy shrub or trained as a short climber against a wall or fence.

common_name: Gethsemane Moonlight Chrysanthemum (Semi-Double Primrose-Yellow, Rapidly Spreading)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Gethsemane Moonlight bears semi-double, primrose-yellow daisies on a rapidly spreading clump.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil. Gethsemane Moonlight bears semi-double, soft primrose-yellow daisy flowers on a plant that spreads notably faster and more vigorously than many other hardy mum cultivars, quickly filling in a naturalized area or informal border with cheerful late-season color. Divide clumps every two to three years to prevent crowding and control its enthusiastic spread, and pinch stem tips in spring and early summer to promote bushy, compact growth.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ghost fern establishes quickly and produces its distinctive silvery fronds from the first season, becoming more substantial each subsequent year.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ghost fern is a hybrid cross between the Japanese painted fern (Athyrium niponicum var. pictum) and the lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina), combining the silver-frosted, upright-arching habit of the lady fern with the metallic silver-to-pewter coloring of the painted fern. The fronds are broader and more erect than Japanese painted fern but retain the glowing, silvery-white overlay that gives the plant its ghostly name. It was the Perennial Plant Association Plant of the Year in 2012. Ghost fern grows upright and arching rather than lying flat, creating a more vertical accent in the shade garden than its Japanese painted fern parent. It is generally considered hardier and more vigorous than Japanese painted fern and tolerates a wider range of soil conditions. Pair it with dark-leafed hostas, pulmonaria, epimedium, or brunnera for outstanding silver-and-contrast combinations in deep shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant stem or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty, slightly alkaline to neutral succulent mix in full sun to part shade; ghost plant is one of the most cold-tolerant of the echeveria-type succulents, withstanding brief drops to 20°F when dry — and one of the easiest succulents to propagate from individual dropped leaves.
directions: Plant stem cuttings or individual leaves in very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in full sun to part shade; allow to dry between waterings. Graptopetalum paraguayense (ghost plant or mother of pearl plant) is a Mexican succulent closely related to echeverias — producing flat, open rosettes of thick, triangular, pointed leaves in a distinctive pale-blue, grey-lavender, or pinkish color (shifting with light levels and season) with a pearlescent, ghostly quality that gives the plant its evocative common name. The leaves are 2–3 inches long, arranged in a symmetric rosette, and have a chalky, powdery surface texture. Ghost plant is remarkable for its propagation ease — individual leaves dropped from the rosette readily produce new rosettes at the base, making it one of the simplest succulents to multiply. It also tends to trail over time, producing stems up to 12 inches long with rosettes at each node, making it excellent for hanging baskets or draping over rock walls. Ghost plant is significantly more cold-hardy than most succulents in the Crassulaceae family, surviving brief freezes to 20°F when the soil is dry — making it an excellent outdoor succulent for zone 7–11 rock gardens and raised beds.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; giant allium does not tolerate wet, waterlogged soils and the bulbs must be kept dry during summer dormancy — it is best where soils dry out after flowering. Plant in drifts of 5-9 bulbs for best ornamental impact.
directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; giant allium does not tolerate wet, waterlogged soils and the bulbs must be kept dry during summer dormancy — it is best where soils dry out after flowering. Allium giganteum is the largest of the ornamental alliums, producing massive, round, 5-6 inch diameter spherical flower heads of hundreds of small, rosy-purple to violet-purple star-shaped flowers on tall (3-5 foot), rigid stems in late May and June — one of the most architectural and spectacular effects in the early summer bulb garden. The dried seed heads retain their spherical shape beautifully for months after bloom and are outstanding in dried arrangements; they also provide seeds for finches and sparrows in fall and winter. Plant in drifts of 5-9 bulbs for best ornamental impact.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, fertile to average, deep loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; giant arborvitae is more adaptable to moisture and shade than eastern arborvitae (T. occidentalis). It grows in very moist conditions and tolerates temporary flooding.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, fertile to average, deep loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; giant arborvitae (western red cedar) is among the most significant trees in the cultures of the Pacific Northwest indigenous peoples — the canoe tree, the totem pole tree, the longhouse tree, whose rot-resistant red wood served as the primary building material across the coastal Northwest. Despite the common name 'western red cedar,' it is not a true cedar but a member of the Cupressaceae. It grows to over 200 feet tall with a massively buttressed base in the moist coastal rainforests from northern California to Alaska. The foliage has a distinctive pineapple-like fragrance when crushed. Widely planted as a fast-growing hedge and privacy screen in the Pacific Northwest. The cultivar 'Green Giant' (a Thuja plicata hybrid) is the most widely planted privacy screen tree in the eastern US.

plant_note: Plant tubers or divisions in late spring once water temperatures have warmed; place in the shallow margins of a pond or stream with 2 to 6 inches of water over the crown.
directions: Plant tubers or divided clumps into heavy loam or aquatic planting compost in a basket or directly into the muddy margins of a pond or water feature, with 2 to 6 inches of water covering the crown. Site in full sun for the best flowering — the large white three-petaled blooms appear in summer and are most prolific in warm, bright conditions. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigorous growth and encourage generous flowering. In zones below 8, lift and overwinter tubers in damp sand in a frost-free location, replanting the following spring once water temperatures exceed 65°F.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring or fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade to part shade; giant bellflower is one of the tallest and most imposing bellflowers and genuinely thrives in shade — native to the shaded, moist ravines and streamsides of northern Europe and western Asia. It self-sows freely in suitable conditions and may naturalize in woodland gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part to full shade; giant bellflower is the most shade-tolerant and one of the largest-flowered of the European bellflowers — a tall, imposing perennial native to shaded, moist, north-facing banks and woodland ravines from Scotland to Siberia, producing large, broadly-toothed, nettle-like leaves on stout stems up to 4–5 feet tall and in June–July, the most substantial, richest, most deeply colored flowers of any commonly grown bellflower. The individual flowers are large (1.5–2 inches), tubular, bell-shaped, and in the best forms a deeply saturated, rich violet-purple or near-cobalt blue — not the pale lavender of most campanulas but a genuinely strong, saturated, blue-purple. It is one of the few bellflowers that actively prefers shade, and in the garden it combines with hostas, ferns, astilbes, and woodland wildflowers as a tall, shaded-border perennial of real presence. The cultivar 'Brantwood' (rich violet-purple) and 'Gleaming' (pure white) are widely available. Self-sows in appropriate moist, shaded conditions to build a colony.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds or divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; giant blue cohosh blooms before the leaves are fully expanded (like trilliums and other spring woodland ephemerals), requiring rich, moist, undisturbed woodland conditions. Seeds require double dormancy — germination may take two seasons.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in deep to partial shade; giant blue cohosh is the larger of the two North American blue cohosh species, blooming slightly earlier in spring than common blue cohosh (C. thalictroides) and producing larger, more dramatic purplish-bronze flowers before the leaves expand — giving a ghostly, early-spring display in rich maple-basswood and beech-maple forest understories. The glaucous blue-green, compound foliage that follows is attractive throughout summer, and the brilliant blue, berry-like seeds (technically a fleshy seed coat — not a true berry) are ornamental in late summer. Like common blue cohosh, this species is toxic and has a history of dangerous misuse as an abortifacient. A beautiful native for deep woodland shade gardens with consistently moist, rich soil — particularly under large maples, beeches, or basswood where it grows naturally.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy to mucky soil in full sun to partial shade; giant blue iris naturally grows in salt-influenced freshwater and brackish marshes of coastal Louisiana and is uniquely tolerant of poor drainage, flooding, and coastal salt influence.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — giant blue iris is one of the showiest of all Louisiana iris species and one of the primary parents of Louisiana iris hybrids, endemic to the coastal freshwater and brackish marshes, swampy forests, and wet prairies of coastal Louisiana. Its flowers are spectacularly large (5–7 inches across) in clear blue to blue-purple on tall stems (3–5 feet) that tower above the robust, broad leaf fans, blooming in April–May in spectacular drifts. It is significantly more salt and flood tolerant than other Louisiana irises, thriving in the challenging conditions of coastal garden areas with periodic saltwater influence. The species is an important wetland stabilizer in its native coastal marsh habitat. In gardens, it is outstanding for pond margins, rain garden edges, and any wet, low spot that holds water seasonally. Louisiana iris hybrids derived from this species have expanded greatly on its already exceptional ornamental traits.

common_name: Giant Carrion Flower (Zulu Giant, Starfish Flower)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant divisions after the danger of frost has passed, in gritty, very well-drained soil in bright light with some afternoon shade; allow cuttings to callus for several days before setting in the rooting medium.
directions: Plant in gritty, very well-drained soil in bright light with light afternoon shade in the hottest climates; this South African succulent forms a low, spreading mat of soft, four-angled, toothed, cactus-like stems that root easily wherever they touch the ground. In late summer it produces some of the largest flowers of any succulent grown in gardens, up to 10-14 inches across, star-shaped, and covered in fine wrinkled maroon-and-cream banding that mimics rotting flesh both in appearance and in scent, a strategy that lures flies as pollinators rather than bees. It is more cold-sensitive than most desert succulents and needs winter protection or container culture outside of zone 9-11, and unlike true cacti it appreciates slightly more regular moisture during active summer growth followed by a dry winter rest. Its sprawling habit makes it a striking, talking-point groundcover for raised beds, rock gardens, and container plantings in warm-climate xeriscapes.

common_name: Giant Chain Fern (Western Chain Fern, Coast Chain Fern)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full shade to part shade; giant chain fern is one of the largest ferns native to North America, native to moist canyons and stream banks of the Pacific Coast from British Columbia south to Baja California, with fronds reaching 9 feet in optimal conditions — outstanding as a large-scale shade and water feature planting.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in deep to part shade; keep consistently moist — does not tolerate drought. Woodwardia fimbriata (giant chain fern or western chain fern) is the largest fern native to North America, growing in the moist, shaded canyons, redwood forests, and coastal creek sides of the Pacific Coast from southern British Columbia south through California to Baja California. In optimal conditions — constantly moist, deeply shaded, humus-rich — the bold, lance-shaped, once-pinnate fronds reach 4–9 feet in length, creating a dramatic, primordial atmosphere in shade gardens. The common name 'chain fern' refers to the chain-like pattern of elongated, linked sori (spore-bearing structures) visible on the underside of fertile fronds — a distinctive feature shared with the eastern Virginia chain fern (W. virginica). Giant chain fern is evergreen in mild climates, semi-evergreen in colder parts of its range. It is an excellent companion for other Pacific Coast woodland natives: sword fern (Polystichum munitum), redwood sorrel (Oxalis oregana), and trilliums. For large-scale shade, stream bank, and bog garden plantings where a dramatic, bold-textured fern is needed. Rarely available commercially but worth seeking from native plant nurseries.

plant_note: Propagate by gently separating rooted offsets in spring and setting them into fast-draining, rocky soil without burying the chalky rosette; never touch or hose off the powdery bloom, which protects the leaves from sun.
directions: Propagate by gently separating rooted offsets in spring and setting them into fast-draining, rocky soil without burying the chalky rosette, or start fresh seed in cool weather on the soil surface. This striking Baja California native carries the thickest natural white-chalk coating of any succulent, and that powdery bloom should never be touched or hosed off since it protects the leaves from intense sun. It goes dormant and can shrink in the heat of summer, so water sparingly during that period and increase moisture slightly during the cooler growing season. Site it on a slope or in a container where excess water drains away instantly from the crown.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring, pressing seed into firm moist soil; or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant. Giant coneflower can also be planted as a container plant in spring or fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; giant coneflower is the most dramatic member of the Rudbeckia genus, growing 5–8 feet tall and producing large, glaucous blue-green basal leaves that make a striking presence even before the flowers appear. The 3–4 inch yellow daisy flowers with prominent elongated dark brown cones are produced prolifically in summer on branching tall stems. The bold blue-green foliage is the plant's secret weapon — it is one of the few native perennials with truly blue-toned leaves, providing wonderful contrast with other summer perennials. Birds feed heavily on the seeds through fall and winter if left standing. A native of the south-central United States, it is especially well-adapted to Gulf Coast gardens.

common_name: Giant Dahlia Flowered Zinnia (Classic Large Double-Bloom Cutting Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 4 weeks early; give tall plants sturdy support in windy sites and full sun for the biggest blooms.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes. Giant Dahlia Flowered is one of the oldest and best-known zinnia strains, producing fully double, densely petaled blooms up to five or six inches across that closely resemble dahlia flowers, held on tall, sturdy stems that make them outstanding for cutting. The mixed strain covers a broad range of vivid colors from crimson and scarlet through orange, pink, purple, and cream, and a single row of plants can provide a long season of bouquet material from midsummer through frost. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching and more stems, deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, and water at the soil line rather than overhead, since wet foliage in humid weather invites powdery mildew.

plant_note: Plant in filtered sun to light shade and rich, well-drained soil, giving it room to eventually develop a tall, palm-like trunk; keep away from prolonged frost.
directions: Plant this Mexican cycad in a site with filtered sun to light shade and rich, well-drained soil, giving it room to eventually develop the tall, palm-like trunk that makes it one of the largest cycads grown in cultivation. Its glossy, arching, bright green pinnate fronds create a bold tropical statement near entries, courtyards, or as a specimen anchoring a large bed. It grows faster than most cycads with consistent moisture and fertilization but still takes many years to develop significant trunk height. Keep it away from prolonged frost, as it is less cold-hardy than Dioon edule but well suited to protected zone 9-10 landscapes.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; giant dogwood is best sited where its spectacular horizontal branching structure can be appreciated from a distance — avoid planting against structures where the distinctive horizontal form cannot be seen.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, average to fertile soil in partial shade; giant dogwood is an East Asian deciduous tree considered by many plantspeople to be the finest and most architecturally distinguished large dogwood species — it develops a uniquely spectacular, perfectly horizontal, tiered, layered branching structure in which each layer of branches extends in a flat, table-like plane from the central trunk, creating a dramatically architectural silhouette reminiscent of a cedar of Lebanon in miniature, but made entirely of horizontal, flat-planed foliage tiers. In early summer, the upper surfaces of all the horizontal branches become covered with flat, corymb-like clusters of small, creamy-white flowers (without the large bracts of C. kousa or C. florida). The oval, alternate leaves turn deep-red to burgundy in autumn, and small, round, blue-black fruits provide food for birds. The legendary cultivar 'Variegata' (Wedding Cake Tree), with leaves broadly and irregularly margined in cream-white on the horizontally tiered branches, is one of the most spectacular variegated trees in cultivation and is widely regarded as a masterpiece of the ornamental tree world.

plant_note: Sow seeds in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; giant echium is monocarpic, forming a large leafy rosette for 2-3 years before sending up a single massive flower spike and then dying. It self-sows prolifically and forms persistent colonies. It is damaged below 25 degrees F and is best suited to zones 9-11 or sheltered zones 8b locations. Keep protected from frost until the rosette is large and established.
directions: Sow seeds or plant container-grown rosettes in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; giant echium is one of the most spectacular biennial plants in existence, native to La Palma in the Canary Islands and producing, in its flowering year, a single enormous vertical tower of flowers reaching 8-15 feet in height — a solid column of densely packed, small, blue-violet flowers numbering in the tens of thousands on a single plant. The effect is unlike anything else in horticulture: a rigid, architectural spire of blue that attracts extraordinary concentrations of bumblebees, honeybees, and other pollinators for weeks. After flowering, the plant dies but sets abundant seed, maintaining self-sowing colonies in appropriate conditions. The bold, silver-hairy, strap-like rosette leaves in the juvenile stage are also attractive and architecturally impressive. In zones 9-11, giant echium has become an important ornamental plant in coastal California, parts of the Gulf Coast, and similarly mild climates. Closely related to E. wildpretii (Tower of Jewels, with red-pink flowers) and E. candicans (Pride of Madeira, branching shrub).

plant_note: Divide corms in spring when soil temperatures reach 65°F or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; giant elephant ear requires ample moisture and rich soil to produce its spectacular oversized foliage — drought stress immediately reduces leaf size.
directions: Divide corms in spring or plant container specimens in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; giant elephant ear is the largest-leaved of all the commonly grown elephant ears, producing individual leaves that can reach 5–6 feet long and nearly as wide on robust, upright petioles — each leaf is a single, immense, blue-green to pale-green paddle with a distinctive chalky, glaucous bloom on the upper surface. The effect of a mature clump, with 6–10 massive leaves arching outward like an exploding green fountain, is uniquely dramatic in the garden. Thrives in consistently moist to wet soil and at pond and stream margins. Goes fully dormant in winter but corms are cold-hardy to zone 8 when heavily mulched. The popular 'Thailand Giant' selection is selected for maximum leaf size. Distinct from Alocasia macrorrhiza and Colocasia esculenta — this species has the palest, most glaucous, most impressive foliage of the three. Excellent for tropical-look gardens in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant divisions or offsets in spring after temperatures are reliably above 65°F in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade to full sun; Alocasia macrorrhiza grows vigorously in warm, humid weather and produces new leaves rapidly in good conditions. In zone 9 it may die back to the ground after hard freezes but regrows from established rhizomes in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; giant elephant ear is one of the most dramatically bold-textured tropical plants available for zone 9–12 gardens, producing truly enormous, upward-pointing, arrow-shaped leaves — 2–4 feet long — on stout petioles that can reach 6–15 feet tall, creating an unmistakably tropical visual impact that transforms any landscape. Unlike the Colocasia elephant ears (which droop their leaves), Alocasia macrorrhiza holds its leaves upward and outward, creating a distinctive architectural silhouette. It thrives in the bright, filtered shade beneath large trees and palms in the hot, humid Gulf Coast climate, where high moisture, rich soil, and warmth produce the largest, most spectacular plants. The massive rhizomes are edible (raw parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals — must be cooked) and are used as a starchy vegetable in Pacific Island cuisine. Remove damaged leaves promptly and fertilize monthly during the growing season for best growth.

plant_note: Detach and pot the bulbils (small plantlets) that form on the parent plant in profusion before and after flowering, or transplant offsets (pups) from around the base; giant false agave is a monocarpic plant that flowers once after many years of vegetative growth, then dies — but it produces such enormous numbers of aerial bulbils on the flowering stalk that a single plant effectively seeds itself prolifically into the surrounding area.
directions: Detach aerial bulbils or transplant basal offsets in well-drained to dry, average to poor, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; giant false agave (Mauritius hemp, Cuban hemp) is a large, agave-like, rosette-forming succulent of tropical American origin in the asparagus family (Asparagaceae), grown in warm-climate gardens worldwide for its bold, architectural form — it produces a massive, trunk-less or short-trunked rosette of broad, sword-shaped, medium-green to gray-green leaves up to 8 feet long with finely toothed margins and a terminal spine, creating a large, impressive structural specimen. After many years of growth, the plant produces one enormous, tree-like, terminal flowering spike that can reach 25–30 feet in height, covered in thousands of greenish, fragrant flowers and subsequently masses of bulbils (miniature plantlets) that drop to the ground and root. After flowering the parent rosette dies, but the bulbils and any basal pups ensure continuity. 'Variegata' and 'Medio-picta' are cultivars with cream-striped or cream-centered leaves. An outstanding, bold, architectural specimen for large Gulf Coast and tropical gardens where scale and drama are desired.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; the outsized leaves of Giganteum make a bold, tropical-looking statement in a shaded bed or large container.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh sun that scorches the leaves. Giganteum is a large-scale variety of Farfugium japonicum, the Gulf Coast garden staple known as leopard plant, producing rounded, glossy, deep-green leaves considerably larger than the straight species — often close to a foot across on mature plants — giving it a bold, almost tropical presence in a shade bed. Clusters of small, daisy-like yellow flowers rise above the foliage on tall stems in fall. Its large scale makes it a strong focal point or specimen plant rather than a filler, and like other farfugium it tolerates deep shade and dense root competition under trees better than most broadleaf perennials.

plant_note: Plant in very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil in full sun; giant feather grass requires excellent drainage and dislikes waterlogged soils especially in winter. In zones 7–9 it grows as a semi-evergreen perennial and performs best in Mediterranean-style dry-summer gardens.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; giant feather grass is a spectacular large-scale ornamental grass from the Iberian Peninsula producing a semi-evergreen mound of narrow, arching, dark-green leaves from which arise in early summer enormously tall, delicate, transparent flower stalks — reaching 5–6 feet — bearing open, airy, glittering panicles of large golden oat-spikelets that catch and transmit sunlight with a shimmering, jewel-like quality unlike any other grass. The effect is breathtaking when backlit by morning or evening sun and the dried seed heads persist attractively through summer. Native to dry, limestone hillsides of Spain and Portugal, it is perfectly adapted to poor, well-drained, alkaline soils and thrives in drought conditions once established. It makes a spectacular specimen plant or repeated accent in the dry border, gravel garden, or Mediterranean-style planting where it provides transparent, see-through height without blocking the view.

common_name: Giant Flatsedge (Mexican Papyrus, New World Coastal Umbrella Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Giant Flatsedge, native from the Gulf Coast through the Caribbean and Latin America, is a New World relative of Egyptian papyrus, taller with smaller flower umbels.
directions: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun, or directly in a boggy, permanently wet spot. Giant Flatsedge, native from the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana through the Caribbean and much of Latin America, is the New World counterpart to Egyptian papyrus, producing tall, thick, triangular stems topped with a burst of thin, drooping bracts, though its individual flower umbels are smaller and more delicate than true Egyptian papyrus. Its imposing height and bold, architectural silhouette make it an excellent vertical accent and privacy screen at a Gulf Coast pond edge, and as a regional native it tolerates the area's heat, humidity, and seasonal flooding without complaint. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; giant fleece flower is a substantial plant requiring considerable space — allow 5–6 feet on all sides and site away from delicate smaller companions.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; giant fleece flower is a large, boldly impressive East Asian perennial that produces, from spring through autumn, an enormous vase-shaped clump of large, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves rising to 5–7 feet in height, crowned from late June through August by enormous, loose, feathery, billowing clouds of tiny, creamy-white flowers in large branching panicles that create an airy, frothy, white-mist effect on a massive scale — one of the most impressive flower mass displays possible in the perennial garden. Unlike the weedy Japanese knotweed (Reynoutria japonica), giant fleece flower behaves as a well-mannered, clumping, non-running perennial that does not spread beyond its designated space and requires no containment. The flower heads age through pinkish-buff to tan as they dry in place, extending the display through late summer and into fall. Cut the entire plant to the ground in late winter for the cleanest regrowth. An excellent background specimen for large herbaceous borders, beside water features, and in naturalistic settings.

subcategory: Mexican giant fiber and ornamental plant
plant_note: Plant container stock or bulbils in spring in full sun in very well-drained, lean to average, rocky to sandy soil in zone 9–11; Giant Furcraea is one of the largest of all monocarpic agave relatives — native to the dry tropical forests and thorny scrublands of Oaxaca, Guerrero, and Puebla, Mexico — forming an enormous rosette of arching, green, serrate-edged leaves reaching 8–15 feet across, before producing a colossal terminal flower spike of 30–50 feet bearing tens of thousands of small white flowers and then dying.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, alkaline-tolerant soil; Furcraea macdougalii requires excellent drainage and is highly drought tolerant once established — avoid clay, overwatering, or high-fertility soil; allow abundant room as the rosettes reach imposing dimensions. Furcraea macdougalii (Giant Furcraea or Huizache Morado) is one of the most dramatic and massive of all monocarpic succulent plants — a close relative of Agave in the Asparagaceae family native to the dry tropical deciduous forests and thornscrub of Oaxaca, Guerrero, and Puebla in southern Mexico. The enormous leaf rosettes — up to 10–15 feet across and 6–10 feet tall — are composed of long, arching, bright-green to gray-green, sword-shaped leaves with serrated-spined edges, giving the plant an imposing, architectural presence. Like all Furcraea species and most agaves, the plant is monocarpic: after growing for a decade or more, it produces a single, enormous terminal inflorescence — the flower spike of F. macdougalii is among the tallest of any succulent plant, reaching 30–50 feet — bearing tens of thousands of small, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers and thousands of vegetative bulbils (small plantlets) that can be collected and grown into new plants. After flowering and setting seed and bulbils, the mother plant dies, but the bulbils ensure abundant new plants. The leaf fibers were historically used for cordage, rope, and mat-making by indigenous peoples of Oaxaca.
