plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in zone 6–11; Giant Hesperaloe is a large, dramatic accent plant native to the limestone highlands of Coahuila and Tamaulipas, Mexico — forming massive, 5–8 foot rosettes of long, stiff, fiber-edged leaves and producing enormous flower spikes to 15 feet tall topped with white, lily-like flowers — larger and more cold-hardy than the common Red Yucca (H. parviflora).
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, alkaline-tolerant soil; Hesperaloe funifera requires excellent drainage and low fertility — it will rot in clay or wet conditions; once established, extremely drought tolerant with no supplemental water needed in western Texas, New Mexico, and similar arid climates. Hesperaloe funifera (Giant Hesperaloe or Giant Red Yucca) is a large, dramatic, rosette-forming succulent in the Asparagaceae family native to the limestone mountains and gravelly desert plains of Coahuila, Tamaulipas, and San Luis Potosí in northeastern Mexico, closely related to the better-known Red Yucca (Hesperaloe parviflora) but substantially larger in all respects. The leaf rosettes reach 5–7 feet tall and wide, with long, stiff, blue-green, linear leaves edged with white, thread-like fibers that peel away attractively. The flower spikes produced in late spring are spectacular: straight, branching stalks reaching 10–15 feet tall, covered in large, nodding, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers with pink or greenish tinges — larger, whiter, and more lily-like than the red-orange flowers of H. parviflora, and equally attractive to hummingbirds. Giant Hesperaloe is fully cold-hardy to zone 6b and extremely heat-tolerant — ideally suited to hot, alkaline, dry garden conditions from Texas and Oklahoma through New Mexico and Arizona. The leaves are also a traditional cordage fiber source used by indigenous peoples of northeastern Mexico.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a pond or stream margin in partial shade in spring; giant Himalayan cowslip needs permanently damp soil and will not tolerate summer drought.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently wet, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog garden in partial shade in spring. Primula florindae is the largest of the commonly grown primroses, native to boggy meadows of the Tibetan plateau, sending up tall stems topped with a drooping, fragrant cluster of bell-shaped, sulfur-yellow flowers dusted with a pale mealy coating in mid to late summer, later than most other primroses bloom. Its late bloom time and tall stature make it a valuable addition to a shaded bog garden or water feature, extending the primrose season and pairing well with astilbe, rodgersia, and Japanese primrose along a damp woodland edge.

plant_note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface in moist, deeply humus-rich, well-drained but moisture-retaining, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; giant Himalayan lily is monocarpic — the main bulb flowers once then dies, but produces offsets that will flower in 3–5 years. Plant in groups of bulbs of varying sizes to ensure annual flowering. Very deep, organic soil is essential — it grows naturally in cool, moist, humus-rich forest floors of the Himalayas and needs consistent moisture and shade.
directions: Plant bulbs near the soil surface in deeply humus-rich, moist, well-drained but moisture-retentive, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; giant Himalayan lily is possibly the most spectacular of all woodland bulbs — a monocarpic lily relative from the cool, moist, deep-shade forest floors of the Himalayas and western China that produces, after 4–7 years of vegetative growth, a towering flowering stem of almost incomprehensible scale: a stout, hollow scape up to 10–12 feet tall bearing in midsummer a succession of 15–20 large, white, outward-facing, funnel-shaped, strongly fragrant lily flowers, each marked with a deep wine-red to maroon streak down the inner throat — the whole structure an architectural titan of the summer shade garden, visible from considerable distance, unique in the garden world. After flowering and seeding, the main bulb dies, but it produces several offset bulblets that will grow for years before themselves flowering. A colony planted with offsets of varying sizes provides a succession of annual flowering stems. Despite its imposing stature, it demands the moist, cool, deeply organically-rich conditions of its Himalayan forest habitat — consistently moist soil, deep shade, and cool summers. Not suitable for hot, dry gardens. For appropriate cool, shaded, woodland gardens in zones 7–9, it represents one of the ultimate spectacles of the bulb world.

plant_note: Push stem cuttings 1-2 inches into nutrient-rich aquarium substrate, stripping lower leaves first so no foliage is buried; new roots form from the buried nodes within one to two weeks.
directions: A fast-growing background stem plant for freshwater planted aquaria, native to Southeast Asian wetlands, grown submersed with roots anchored in fine nutrient-rich substrate rather than garden soil. It performs well under medium aquarium lighting and appreciates root tab fertilizer plus liquid iron; CO2 injection is not required but produces noticeably denser, more compact growth and richer leaf color. Regularly pinch and replant the tops of tall stems to prevent the lower portions from becoming leggy and to propagate new plants. This species is the legal, non-restricted alternative to the federally listed noxious weed Hygrophila polysperma and is not itself a listed invasive or noxious species.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (October–November in zone 9) for winter establishment and spring bloom; larkspur requires cool soil (below 65°F) for good germination and does not transplant well. In zone 9 fall sowing is the correct approach — seeds sown in spring when soil is already warming germinate poorly and produce weak, short-lived plants that bolt quickly. The Giant Imperial series produces the largest and most densely flowered larkspur spikes in cultivation — each spike reaching 4–5 feet with densely packed, fully double flowers in colors including blue, pink, lavender, rose, and white. Plants are toxic if ingested. Self-seeds reliably in zone 9 to naturalize for subsequent seasons when plants are allowed to mature and set seed.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil with consistent cool-season moisture — larkspur germinates poorly when soil temperature exceeds 65°F; must be direct-sown in fall in zone 9 for proper spring bloom; Giant Imperial Larkspur is the premier large-flowered larkspur selection for garden and cut flower use, producing tall (4–5 foot), densely flowered spikes in the classic delphinium-like form — with fully double, spurred florets densely packed along the entire upper portion of each spike in blue, lavender, pink, rose, and white — creating one of the most visually impressive cool-season annual cut flower and garden border plants available. Annual larkspur (Consolida ajacis, formerly classified as Delphinium ajacis) is the annual equivalent of the perennial delphinium, providing the same tall spike form, clear blue and purple color range, and cottage garden character in a direct-sow annual that naturalizes readily through self-seeding in appropriate climates. In zone 9 larkspur grown from fall sowing blooms in March–May — providing one of the most impressive large-scale spring flower displays available from an annual, with the tall flower spikes creating strong vertical accents in the spring border and providing exceptional long-stemmed cut flowers. Allow plants to set seed before removing for naturalized self-seeding in subsequent years.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring or direct sow in fall in moist, moderately fertile to rich soil in full sun; giant inula requires substantial space and strong, deep, moist soil to achieve its maximum size and effect. It does not tolerate dry conditions well. A single established plant can spread over 4 feet and may require support in exposed, windy positions.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; giant inula earns its name — one of the most dramatically large and architecturally bold perennials in temperate gardens, producing enormous basal leaves that can exceed 3 feet in length and coarse, winged, branching stems reaching 6–10 feet in rich, moist conditions. In July and August these giant stems carry loose clusters of golden-yellow, spider-petaled daisy flowers (3–4 inches across, with very fine, thread-like ray petals similar to those of I. hookeri but on a vastly larger scale) that are individually beautiful but produce their greatest impact through the sheer dramatic scale of the plant bearing them. Native to the Caucasus region, it thrives in moist, fertile ground near water features, at the back of large, wide borders, and in any bold, naturalistic planting where its monumental scale is an asset rather than a problem. A single specimen in a choice position in a large garden creates an immediate focal point of extraordinary presence during its late-summer bloom period. Attracts bees and butterflies enthusiastically and provides seeds for birds. Not suitable for small gardens.

plant_note: Surface sow seed in fall in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; seeds require cold stratification so fall sowing or winter sowing is preferred. Giant ironweed naturalizes readily in moist soils and can be aggressive — allow 4–6 feet of space.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; giant ironweed is one of the most dramatic native wildflowers for the back of a large border or naturalized area, growing 5–10 feet tall with flat-topped clusters of intense royal purple flowers in late summer and fall that are irresistible to monarchs, painted ladies, giant swallowtails, and dozens of native bee species. The vivid purple color is one of the most saturated of any native wildflower. It grows naturally along stream banks, moist woodland edges, and roadside ditches throughout the eastern US and is one of the most reliable and showy native plants for late-season pollinator value. The tall stems and architectural seed heads provide winter interest and bird food. It spreads by rhizome in moist soil and should be given space or divided annually to control spread in the border.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give 'Gigantea' extra room compared with standard leopard plant, since its leaves grow considerably larger and the clump spreads wider at maturity.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give 'Gigantea' extra room compared with standard leopard plant, since its leaves grow considerably larger and the clump spreads wider at maturity. This selection of leopard plant produces dramatically oversized, glossy, rounded leaves nearly twice the size of the species, creating a bold, tropical-textured mass in a shaded border, bog garden, or large container where a strong architectural statement is wanted. Clusters of daisy-like yellow flowers rise above the foliage on tall stalks in fall, adding late-season color after most other shade perennials have finished blooming. Give it consistently moist soil, since the outsized leaves wilt dramatically in dry conditions, and protect from hard freezes and drying winter wind where marginally hardy.

common_name: Giant Leopard Plant (Bold Round-Leaf Deep-Shade Fall-Blooming Gulf South Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Farfugium performs best with consistent moisture — the large leaves can wilt dramatically in dry conditions before recovering overnight, but persistent drought causes leaf scorch and decline.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Giant Leopard Plant (Farfugium japonicum) is one of the most dramatic and valuable shade perennials for Gulf South gardens — a bold-textured, evergreen perennial producing very large (8–12 inch across), round to kidney-shaped, dark glossy green leaves on long stalks, creating a striking, tropical-looking effect in deep shade positions where most ornamentals struggle to survive let alone thrive. The leaves are among the largest of any commonly grown Gulf South shade perennial, providing a dramatic bold-texture contrast in planting combinations with fine-textured shade companions like ferns, mondo grass, and liriope. In fall (October–November in zone 9), Farfugium produces clusters of bright yellow, daisy-like flowers on tall stalks above the foliage — a welcome burst of color in the shade garden during a season when few other shade plants are flowering. This timing — fall bloom in deep shade — makes Farfugium essentially unique among commonly grown shade perennials and provides an important ornamental bonus beyond the year-round foliage display. Farfugium is particularly associated with Gulf South garden tradition and appears prominently in New Orleans and coastal Mississippi shade gardens. The plant is adaptable to a range of shade conditions, from bright indirect light to fairly deep shade under large trees, maintaining good leaf size and color across this range. Division of established clumps every 3–5 years maintains vigor and provides plants for expanding shade garden areas.

plant_note: Set transplants into a well-drained, mineral-rich carnivorous plant mix (equal parts perlite, sand, and peat) kept evenly moist with rain or distilled water; Mexican butterworts tolerate slightly richer, better-drained conditions than bog-dwelling sundews and pitcher plants.
directions: Set transplants into a well-drained, mineral-rich carnivorous plant mix (equal parts perlite, sand, and peat) kept evenly moist with rain or distilled water; Mexican butterworts tolerate slightly richer, better-drained conditions than bog-dwelling sundews and pitcher plants. Broad, flat, pale yellow-green leaves coated in a glistening, sticky film trap and slowly digest small insects that land on the leaf surface, one of the largest-leaved of the Mexican butterwort species, producing showy, tall-stemmed purple flowers in season that add ornamental value beyond the plant's carnivorous foliage. Native to limestone cliffs and seasonally moist rock outcrops in Mexico, it tolerates a brief dry season better than bog-dwelling carnivorous plants, going through a smaller, more compact winter rosette (a succulent, non-carnivorous form) during its natural dry dormant period. Reduce watering somewhat in winter to allow the natural dormant rosette to form, resume regular moist conditions in spring as new growth emerges, and provide bright, indirect light rather than harsh direct sun.

plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; giant montbretia establishes quickly and multiplies vigorously by corm offsets — divide every 3–4 years when clumps become crowded, as congested corms produce fewer and shorter flower stems.
directions: Divide corm chains or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; giant montbretia is the largest and boldest of the garden-grown crocosmia species — it produces much wider, strongly pleated, bright-green, sword-like, upward-arching leaves (considerably broader than those of common C. × crocosmiiflora hybrids) and in summer, tall, 3–4-foot arching stems carry dense, one-sided racemes of notably large, widely flared, horizontal, deep-orange to flame-orange flowers. Unlike the common montbretia hybrids whose flowers hang pendant or downward along the raceme, Crocosmia masoniorum holds its flowers horizontally or upward-facing, giving the raceme a more open and showy display effect with the flowers projecting prominently outward from the stem. The species is the parent of several important crocosmia cultivars, including the popular 'Lucifer'. It is less invasive than the common C. × crocosmiiflora forms that can spread aggressively. An excellent, bold, and architecturally striking perennial for summer color, cut flowers, and partial-shade borders in zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown crowns in spring in deep, rich, constantly moist to boggy soil in partial shade; giant gunnera needs a genuinely wet site — the margin of a pond or stream, or a bog garden basin kept saturated — and generous room to spread its enormous leaves.
directions: Plant in deep, rich, constantly moist to boggy soil in partial shade at a pond or stream margin, giving it as much room as a large shrub since a well-grown specimen produces enormous, coarsely lobed, rhubarb-like leaves that can reach five feet or more across on thick, prickly stalks. In summer it sends up bizarre, cone-shaped flower spikes from the base, followed by small orange-brown seed clusters, but the giant foliage is the real reason it is grown — few perennials create a bolder, more tropical-looking accent at the edge of a water feature or bog garden. It needs constant moisture and rich soil to reach full size and will scorch or stall in dry conditions. In the colder part of its hardiness range, protect the dormant crown over winter with a thick mulch of its own cut-back leaves or straw, since a hard freeze reaching the crown can kill the plant outright. Site it away from small paths, since the leaf stalks are covered in stiff prickles.

common_name: Giant Peace Lily (Large Spoon Flower, Cochlear Spathe Peace Lily, Mexican Peace Lily)
plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Spathiphyllum cochlearispathum is a much larger species than the common Peace Lily (S. wallisii / S. floribundum), reaching 4–5 feet in height with large, bold, glossy leaves up to 24 inches long and substantial white spathes. It makes a dramatic statement as a large foliage and flowering specimen for shaded tropical gardens in zone 10-12 or as a large interior specimen. Water consistently, allowing the top soil to partially dry between waterings. CAUTION: toxic to pets — calcium oxalate in all Spathiphyllum parts.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil — Giant Peace Lily thrives in the warm, consistently moist, deeply shaded conditions of a sheltered tropical garden or large interior space in zone 10-12, where its bold, large-leaved clumps and substantial white spathes make a far more dramatic statement than the compact common Peace Lily (S. wallisii). Spathiphyllum cochlearispathum is a large, clumping, rhizomatous perennial aroid in the Araceae family native to southern Mexico and Central America in the Orchidaceae family — one of the largest-growing species in the Spathiphyllum genus, which comprises approximately 40 species of tropical shade aroids widely grown as ornamental plants throughout the world under the collective common name 'Peace Lily.' The plant produces substantial clusters of upright, long-petioled, broad, glossy, dark-green, elliptic to lanceolate leaves 18–24 inches long on petioles 18–24 inches tall, creating a bold, architectural, large-leaved mound 4–5 feet tall and wide. Through the warm months, erect flower spikes emerge from the crown carrying the characteristic Spathiphyllum inflorescence: a large (4–6 inch), white, spoon-shaped spathe surrounding an erect, cylindrical, white to cream-green spadix. The flowers are modestly fragrant. Unlike the compact common Peace Lily grown as an interior plant, S. cochlearispathum in appropriate outdoor conditions creates a substantial, luxuriant tropical presence appropriate to large shaded gardens. CAUTION: toxic to pets if ingested.

common_name: Giant Pelican Flower (Brazilian Dutchman's Pipe, Calico Flower)
plant_note: Set out potted plants in spring once nights stay warm, giving the twining vine a sturdy arbor or wire support to climb; it needs consistent moisture and rich, well-drained soil to fuel its rapid growth.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil next to a strong trellis or arbor, watering deeply and regularly through the growing season since this vine is a heavy feeder that grows fast in warmth and humidity. It produces enormous, mottled maroon-and-cream pouch-shaped flowers with a long tail-like tip that give off a faint carrion scent to lure pollinating flies, blooming heavily from summer into fall. Where winters are too cold to leave it outdoors it can be grown in a large container and overwintered in a bright, frost-free space, and it also serves as a larval host plant for pipevine swallowtail butterflies. Prune in late winter to control size and encourage fresh flowering growth.

common_name: Giant Philodendron (Gigas Philodendron, Panama Velvet Philodendron)
plant_note: Grow on a large moss pole or tree support in bright indirect to filtered light with a chunky, free-draining aroid mix; Philodendron gigas is a vigorous climber that eventually produces leaves 3–4 feet long — allow adequate vertical and horizontal space. Juvenile leaves (the stage most commonly encountered in trade) are dark velvety olive-green with pale veins; adult leaves are enormous and more broadly ovate. Maintain consistently moist media and high humidity (60%+). Propagate from stem cuttings. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered light on a large climbing support — Giant Philodendron is a vigorous climbing species that increases its leaf size dramatically as it gains height, and produces its most impressive foliage when allowed to climb freely rather than trail or hang. Philodendron gigas is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid endemic to Panama in the Araceae family, named 'gigas' (Greek for giant) for the ultimate size of its adult leaves — one of the most impressive of the climbing philodendrons in terms of pure foliar scale. Juvenile plants produce velvety, dark olive-green to bronze-green, broadly cordate leaves 12–18 inches long with a rich, plush texture and pale yellowish-cream to yellow venation — the velvet texture and dark color combination being similar to the highly prized P. verrucosum. As the plant climbs and matures, leaves grow progressively larger and can ultimately reach 3–4 feet in length on established plants climbing large tree trunks in its native Panamanian rainforest. The transition from the compact, velvety juvenile phase (the form most commonly grown and sold) to the enormous adult phase makes P. gigas one of the most dramatic transformation experiences in tropical aroid horticulture. An exciting, fast-growing collector's philodendron with considerable impact even in juvenile stage. All parts toxic.

plant_note: Plant large bulbs 6–8 inches deep in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; giant pineapple lily produces very large, thick bulbs that take 2–3 years to reach peak flowering size. In zones 7–8 mulch heavily in winter. Lift bulbs in zone 6 and colder. Ideal planted in large containers where the tropical effect can be moved to shelter in winter.
directions: Plant large bulbs in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; giant pineapple lily is the largest species in the genus — producing the most impressive, most boldly architectural pineapple lily display available. The strap-shaped, broadly spreading, glossy-green basal leaves can reach 3 feet long and create a large, bold, tropical rosette before the flower scape emerges in midsummer. The flower scapes, reaching 3–4 feet, carry thick, substantial, densely flowered cylindrical spikes of greenish-white to cream-white, star-shaped flowers surmounted by the characteristic leafy bract rosette that creates the unmistakable pineapple silhouette — but at a scale substantially larger than any other species in the genus. The whole display is sweetly fragrant, the flowers attracting bees throughout their midsummer bloom period. In large containers on a terrace or in a prominent border position, a well-established clump of E. pallidiflora creates an architectural tropical effect that is difficult to match with any other bulbous plant in temperate climates. The subspecies subsp. pallidiflora is the most commonly grown; subsp. pole-evansii reaches even greater size.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting 2-3 inches deep with growing tip up; Giant Purple Wakerobin bears leaves dramatically marbled purple and silver with deep red flowers. Never dig from the wild.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2 to 3 inches deep with the growing tip pointed upward. Giant Purple Wakerobin, native to redwood and Douglas-fir forests of coastal Oregon and northern California, is grown as much for its dramatically marbled foliage as for its flowers, the broad leaves patterned in bold silver, gray-green, and purple-bronze mottling beneath an erect, deep maroon-red, sessile flower, among the showiest-foliaged trilliums in cultivation. Never dig plants from the wild, since trilliums take five to seven years to bloom from seed and wild populations are vulnerable to overcollection; purchase only nursery-propagated stock. It establishes slowly but rewards patience with a long-lived, increasingly showy woodland colony.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, spacing tall plants about a foot apart for good airflow. Giant Purple bears bright 4-6 inch blooms on long, sturdy stems that make excellent long-lasting cut flowers. It is heat tolerant and disease resistant, blooming endlessly until frost when cut and deadheaded. Water at the base and space generously to reduce powdery mildew.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; giant reed spreads aggressively by rhizome and is classified as invasive in many warm, wet regions including parts of the Gulf South — confine roots with a barrier or avoid planting near streams, ditches, or natural areas where it can escape into waterways.
directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun, ideally in a large, contained bed with a sturdy root barrier; giant reed is an enormous, bamboo-like ornamental grass capable of reaching 15–20 feet in a single season, historically valued for fast, dense screening, windbreaks, and erosion control on slopes and streambanks, with broad, blue-green, cane-like foliage and tall, plume-like flower heads in late summer and fall. Its extraordinary vigor is also its major drawback: giant reed spreads aggressively by thick underground rhizomes and readily escapes cultivation into wet ditches, streams, and floodplains across the warmer, wetter parts of the country, where it is classified as invasive and actively removed by land managers because it crowds out native riparian vegetation and increases wildfire fuel load when dry. Because of this, site it only where root spread can be fully contained — a large in-ground barrier, a bed surrounded by pavement, or a large container — and never plant it near natural waterways, wetlands, or unmanaged land. Cut old canes to the ground in late winter before new growth begins to keep plantings tidy.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; giant rush grows naturally in wet meadows, pond margins, and stream banks across Europe and western Asia. The cultivar 'Afro' has attractively spiraling and curling stems.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; giant rush is a robust Eurasian rush producing tall, blue-green, somewhat rigid, cylindrical stems in dense clumps at the margins of wet areas. The blue-green color of the stems is more pronounced and attractive than most rushes, lending a cool, architectural quality to pond edges and rain gardens. The cultivar 'Afro' is widely available in the ornamental trade for its amusing, naturally spiraling and corkscrew-curling stems that maintain their twisted form throughout the season. The small, brown, starry flower clusters appear in mid-stem in summer. More vigorous and taller than soft rush (J. effusus), making it better suited to larger water features and naturalizing in extensive wet areas. Provides winter structure and shelter for wetland wildlife.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; giant scabious requires considerable space for its full development — allow at least 4 feet on all sides for a mature, well-branched clump.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; giant scabious is a bold, architectural Caucasian perennial that grows to an impressive 6–8 feet in height on wiry, branching, much-divided stems bearing large, deeply lobed, dark-green leaves and a profusion of tall-stemmed, pale primrose-yellow, pincushion-type flowers (similar to but much larger than ornamental Scabiosa) from June through August — the flowers are particularly attractive to bumblebees and butterflies. The entire plant has an elegant, refined appearance despite its large scale, with the flowers appearing on slender, widely branching wiry stems that allow the border plants behind to remain visible. Excellent as a back-of-border specimen in large herbaceous borders, in naturalistic plantings with grasses and meadow perennials, and in cottage-style gardens. Does not require staking if grown in full sun; partial shade may require support. Long-lived and improves in floral display over years.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; giant sea kale develops a deep, fleshy taproot and deeply resents transplanting once established — site carefully, as the taproot can penetrate 3–4 feet into the soil.
directions: Plant divisions in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; giant sea kale (ornamental crambe, Caucasian sea kale) is one of the most impressively bold and architecturally dramatic perennials available for large-scale garden use — in spring it produces an enormous basal mound of massive, dark-blue-green, deeply lobed, cabbage-like leaves, then erupts in early summer into a huge, branching, cloud-like flower structure rising 4–6 feet and spreading nearly as wide, composed of millions of tiny, honey-fragrant, pure-white flowers arranged in a vast, airy, billowing dome that creates a gypsophila-on-a-giant-scale effect. The effect in full flower is one of the most impressive of any garden plant — a living fountain of white filling a space the size of a small car. After flowering the seed pods create an additional season of interest. Excellent as an extraordinary back-of-border specimen or as a focal point in large herbaceous gardens; requires considerable space. The fleshy taproot penetrates deeply and the plant resents disturbance once established.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade; giant sedge forms much larger, bolder clumps than most native sedges and needs reliable moisture, growing naturally in southeastern bottomland swamps and wet woods.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; giant sedge is a bold, architectural southeastern native, forming substantial arching clumps of broad, glossy, deep-green blades noticeably larger in scale than the fine-textured sedges typically used as lawn substitutes. It grows naturally in bottomland swamps and wet woods across the Gulf South and makes a strong structural accent or specimen clump at the edge of a pond, rain garden, or shaded wet spot, contrasting well with finer-textured ferns and grasses nearby. It needs consistently moist to wet soil to reach its full size and tolerates periodic flooding without issue. Established clumps require little maintenance beyond adequate moisture; cut back old foliage in late winter if it becomes tattered before new growth emerges in spring.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average, well-aerated loamy soil in full sun; giant sequoia requires excellent drainage and will not tolerate waterlogged soil or clay. Plant in a permanent site — moving established trees is extremely difficult.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average loamy soil in full sun; giant sequoia is the largest living thing on Earth by volume — the named individuals in Sequoia National Park include General Sherman (at 52,500 cubic feet the largest), General Grant, and many other titans. Native to a narrow band of the western Sierra Nevada of California at 4,000–8,000 feet elevation, where it grows in moist, deep soils fed by snowmelt. The reddish-brown, deeply furrowed, fire-resistant bark (up to 3 feet thick on old trees) is one of the tree's most distinctive features. Seeds are tiny (1/4 inch long) but grow surprisingly rapidly for such a massive tree. Young trees are surprisingly suitable for large-property planting in zones 5–8 where it can reach impressive size within decades. The round, egg-shaped cones are only 2–3 inches long — remarkably small for the world's largest tree. A deeply awe-inspiring species worthy of every large garden.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3 inches apart as early as possible in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; giant snowdrop is best planted 'in the green' (as actively growing transplants after flowering in late winter) rather than as dry bulbs, as dry bulbs establish more slowly and fail more often. If planting dry bulbs, do so immediately upon receipt and keep soil moist. Avoid planting in dry or exposed positions.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees and shrubs for January-March bloom; giant snowdrop is the most substantial and vigorous of the commonly grown snowdrops — larger in all its parts than the common snowdrop (G. nivalis), producing broader, glaucous blue-green leaves and larger, more pendant, teardrop-shaped white flowers with distinctive inner segments variably marked with green at both base and tip, creating a more boldly patterned flower than most other Galanthus species. It blooms from January through March depending on the season and location, often beginning as the earliest winter aconites open. Giant snowdrop is one of the best-performing shade bulbs available — it not only tolerates but actively prefers partial to full shade under deciduous trees, where it naturalizes freely by offsets and self-seeding to form expanding colonies, eventually creating the large naturalized drifts that are among the most admired sights of late-winter gardens. It is significantly more tolerant of drier summer conditions than G. nivalis and thus adapts well to the root-competitive, summer-dry conditions beneath established trees. For best establishment, plant 'in the green' (as growing plants) immediately after flowering.

plant_note: Mount on a large, sturdy board or basket lined with sphagnum moss in bright indirect light in partial shade; Giant staghorn eventually grows very large and heavy, so use a mounting surface and hanging hardware rated for substantial weight from the start.
directions: Mount on a large, sturdy board or hang in a heavy-duty basket in bright indirect light; Giant staghorn fern is an Australian epiphyte closely related to the common staghorn fern but distinguished by its massive size and its shield fronds, which overlap and fold upward around the crown to form a distinctive, cupped, antler-shaped nest rather than lying flat against the mount. Unlike the common staghorn, this species does not produce offset pups, so it can only be propagated from spores, making mature specimens slower to come by and more prized among collectors. Given years of growth, a single plant can eventually reach several feet across and weigh well over a hundred pounds, so choose a permanent mounting location and robust hardware from the outset. Soak or thoroughly water the root mass weekly, allowing it to drain fully between waterings, and never let it sit in standing water.

common_name: Giant Sunflower (Tall Wetland-Margin Native Perennial Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in moist to wet soil in full sun; Giant Sunflower is a tall (to 10 feet) native perennial sunflower of wet meadows and pond margins, blooming later than most native sunflower species.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, average soil in full sun, at a pond margin, rain garden, or damp low spot. Giant Sunflower is an imposing native perennial sunflower reaching up to 10 feet tall, bearing numerous smaller flower heads than the familiar annual sunflower but in much greater number, blooming later in the season, from late summer into fall, than most other native perennial sunflowers, extending the pollinator nectar season. Its height and colony-forming spread by rhizomes make it best suited to a large naturalized wetland-edge planting or rain garden rather than a small formal border. The abundant seed heads that follow are a valuable fall and winter food source for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to control spread and maintain vigor.

common_name: Giant Sword Fern (Macho Fern, Coarse Sword Fern, Florida Sword Fern)
plant_note: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Nephrolepis biserrata is the largest of the North American sword ferns, producing arching fronds 3–6 feet long that make a dramatic statement as a bold specimen or mass planting under trees. In zone 9, established plants cut back in freezes but regrow vigorously from the rhizomes in spring. Once established, this fern is remarkably drought tolerant for its size. Excellent for naturalizing under live oaks, palms, and other mature shade trees where its spreading, naturalistic clumps fill large areas with little care. A Florida native of genuine ecological value — larval host for fern-feeding insects. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Giant Sword Fern grows most luxuriantly in the dappled shade under large trees where it receives consistent moisture and protection from direct afternoon sun, though it also adapts to brighter light if kept adequately watered. Nephrolepis biserrata is a large, rhizomatous, evergreen fern native to South Florida, the Caribbean, Mexico, Central and South America, tropical Africa, Asia, and the Pacific Islands in the Nephrolepidaceae family — a member of the sword fern genus that includes the Boston Fern (N. exaltata) and Tuberous Sword Fern (N. cordifolia), but considerably larger than either. The plant produces dense, spreading colonies of upright to arching, pinnate fronds 3–6 feet long with dark-green, broadly oblong pinnae (leaflets) that are coarsely toothed (biserrate) along the margins — the texture is coarser and bolder than the common Boston Fern. In Florida, Nephrolepis biserrata grows naturally as both a terrestrial and epiphytic fern in wet hammocks, cypress swamps, and on the trunks of large trees, often forming large, dramatic, cascading masses. As a landscape plant, it is unmatched for dramatic effect in large, shaded areas — a single established clump can spread to 6 feet across, filling substantial areas under oaks and palms with a bold, green tropical texture. One of the finest bold-texture shade plants for zone 9b-12 Gulf Coast landscapes. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Divide offsets or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade after frost danger has passed; giant taro requires abundant moisture and fertilizer during the growing season and appreciates filtered light — protect from harsh afternoon sun which scorches the enormous leaves.
directions: Divide offsets or plant container specimens in consistently moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; giant taro is the tropical foliage plant of maximum dramatic impact — its enormous, upward-pointing, arrow-shaped leaves can reach 3–4 feet in length on petioles rising to 6–15 feet, creating an unmistakable, prehistoric, jungle-scale effect that no other plant in zone 8–12 gardening can match. The architectural, waxy, deep-green leaves with prominent white midribs create instant tropical drama in pools, patio gardens, and mixed tropical borders. It differs from Colocasia (taro) in that the leaves point upward and outward rather than drooping, and the petioles attach at the base of the leaf rather than near the center. In zone 8, top growth is killed by frost but the root mass often survives if mulched heavily; in zones 9–12 it is evergreen. Spreads by offshoots that can be divided. Corms are edible only after prolonged cooking (toxic raw). 'Variegata' (green and white-striped) and 'Borneo Giant' are selected forms.

plant_note: Plant fresh rhizome divisions or fresh seeds in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in shade; giant trillium requires two cold stratification periods (double dormancy) to germinate from seed and is slowest grown from division. Plant in deep shade with consistent organic matter.
directions: Plant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deeply organic woodland soil in deep shade under large-canopy trees; giant trillium is the western counterpart of the eastern large trilliums, native to moist redwood forests, mixed evergreen forests, and oak woodlands of the California Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills. The large, mottled, dark-marbled leaves — held in the characteristic trillium pattern of three at a node — are among the most distinctive spring ephemeral foliage in western North America, and the upright, sessile flowers range from white through deep red-maroon, with the maroon or dark red forms especially striking. The flowers are carrion-scented, attracting fly pollinators rather than bees. Like eastern trilliums, seeds require two years of stratification and plants require 5–7 years to reach flowering from seed. One of the most spectacular native wildflowers for deep woodland shade gardens in California and the Pacific Northwest.

common_name: Giant Upright Elephant Ear (Night-Scented Lily, Asian Taro)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring when soil temperature reaches 65°F+ in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil. Unlike most Colocasia elephant ears which prefer full sun and wet conditions, Alocasia odora thrives in partial to deep shade with moist but well-drained soil. In zone 9, the rhizomes survive mild winters; mulch heavily in zone 9a. Divide clumps every 3–4 years. The fragrant spathes appear in spring and early summer.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Alocasia odora is distinctly more shade-tolerant than most Colocasia elephant ears and performs best in the dappled light of woodland gardens, shaded borders, and understory plantings where its massive, upright, arching leaves create a dramatic tropical effect. Alocasia odora is a clumping tropical perennial from China, Japan, and Southeast Asia with bold, arrow-shaped leaves that can reach 3–4 feet long on upright petioles 3–5 feet tall — forming a bold, architecturally dramatic mass in the shade garden that evokes a tropical jungle. Unlike Colocasia whose leaf stems attach at the center of the leaf (peltate), Alocasia leaves attach at the notch — making it easy to tell the two genera apart. The common name 'Night-Scented Lily' refers to the fragrant greenish-white spathes (similar to calla lily flowers) produced in spring, which release a sweet, vanilla-like fragrance after dark. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, Alocasia odora is one of the finest large foliage plants for bringing tropical scale to shaded spots — under live oaks, in north-facing beds, or along shaded house walls — where conventional sun-loving plants would fail. In mild winters it remains evergreen; a hard freeze browns the foliage but the underground rhizomes survive to resprout vigorously.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting 2-3 inches deep with growing tip up; Giant White Wakerobin is a West Coast species bearing cream-white, sometimes pink-blushed flowers held tight against mottled leaves. Never dig from the wild.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2 to 3 inches deep with the growing tip pointed upward; established plants take several years to settle in but persist for decades once happy. Giant White Wakerobin, a West Coast species ranging from California to Washington, bears an unstalked (sessile) flower of cream-white petals, sometimes blushed pink with age, held erect and tight against a whorl of handsomely mottled gray-green and maroon leaves, a larger and often more richly marked plant than the familiar Eastern Trillium grandiflorum. Never dig plants from the wild, since trilliums take five to seven years to bloom from seed and wild populations are vulnerable to overcollection; purchase only nursery-propagated stock. It naturalizes slowly beneath deciduous trees alongside ferns and other woodland wildflowers.

plant_note: Attach offset pups to the rough bark of a host tree or mount on a piece of untreated wood using monofilament or cotton string; do not use wire or metal clips. Giant Wild Pine requires no soil, absorbing water and nutrients through its leaf scales — mist 2–3 times per week in warm months and once per week in winter.
directions: Giant Wild Pine is the largest native bromeliad in the continental United States, native to the cypress swamps, mangrove edges, and tropical hardwood hammocks of south Florida and the Florida Keys, where it grows as a true epiphyte on the branches of cypress, live oak, and other trees, absorbing all its water and nutrients from the air, rain, and debris through specialized scales (trichomes) on its leaves. Its dramatic tank-forming rosette of stiff, gray-green leaves holds a cup of water that serves as a vital micro-habitat for tree frogs, insects, and even small lizards; a tall, multi-colored flower spike of red and purple bracts emerges in spring, followed by the death of the main rosette and production of one or more offset pups that continue the plant's life. Listed as Threatened in Florida due to the invasion of the Mexican Bromeliad Weevil (Metamasius callizona), which has devastated wild populations, Giant Wild Pine is most effectively grown secured to the rough bark of a host tree in bright, indirect light with regular misting to replace the moisture it would receive from tropical rains and morning dew.

common_name: Giant Wild Pine (Swollen Tillandsia, Large Air Plant, Cardinal Air Plant)
plant_note: Wire or secure pups or seedlings to rough bark of a tree or mount on drift wood in bright indirect light; Tillandsia utriculata is the largest native Florida tillandsia, forming imposing rosettes 2–4 feet across on tree trunks in south Florida hammock and cypress forests. The plant is monocarpic — the main rosette blooms once (on a branched, 3–5 foot spike of white flowers) and then dies, but first produces several pups (offset rosettes) that will eventually bloom in their turn. Wild plants are protected in Florida. The Tillandsia utriculata weevil (Metamasius callizona) is an invasive pest that has devastated populations throughout south Florida — purchasing from reputable nurseries helps preserve wild genetic diversity. Zone 9-12. Non-toxic.
directions: Secure to rough tree bark or drift wood in bright indirect to partial direct light, misting or dunking in water 2–3 times weekly in summer, less in winter — Giant Wild Pine is best established by attaching young pups or seedlings to rough-barked substrate where they will slowly develop their root system and expand into impressive, architectural specimens. Tillandsia utriculata is a large, rosette-forming, epiphytic bromeliad in the Bromeliaceae family native to Florida (Charlotte to Dade Counties), the Caribbean, Mexico, and Central America — the largest Tillandsia species native to Florida and one of the most imposing of all native Florida epiphytes. The plant forms a broad, upright to arching, green to gray-green rosette 2–4 feet across of smooth, somewhat succulent, strap-shaped leaves that taper to a point. These broad, water-collecting leaves create a central cup that catches rainwater and organic debris, supporting a small aquatic community of tree frogs, insects, and microorganisms. When the rosette matures after several years of growth, it produces a spectacular, branched flower spike 3–5 feet tall bearing numerous small, white tubular flowers with a pleasant fragrance — a terminal bloom that exhausts the main rosette, which then dies. Before dying, the main plant produces 2–5 pups (offsets) from the base that will grow on to bloom in turn. Wild plants in Florida have been severely impacted by the invasive Mexican bromeliad weevil (Metamasius callizona), which has decimated populations throughout south Florida. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to morning sun.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun, mulching well to keep roots cool. One of the most celebrated Exbury hybrid deciduous azaleas, Gibraltar bears large, ruffled, brilliant orange flowers with a bold yellow-orange flare and a light fragrance, opening in vivid trusses that cover the shrub in mid to late spring and rank among the most eye-catching colors in the deciduous azalea group. Fall color adds a second season of interest, with the foliage turning shades of orange, red, and purple before dropping. Site it where the intense flower color has room to make a statement — as a woodland-edge specimen or backdrop to a shade border — and keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, since deciduous azaleas resent both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: Gilty Pleasure Toad Lily (Gold-Foliage Fall-Blooming Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gilty Pleasure is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction grown as much for its gold foliage as its flowers, giving season-long color in a shade bed rather than only at bloom time.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Gilty Pleasure stands apart from most toad lily cultivars for its gold foliage, which holds bright color through the growing season rather than staying plain green, providing a long season of interest well before the lavender-pink, deeply freckled, orchid-like flowers open in fall. The gold leaf color develops best with some morning light but stays attractive even in fairly deep shade. As with other Formosa toad lilies, it is more heat tolerant than the Japanese species, making it a good choice for zone 7-9 shade gardens. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch with leaf litter, and divide congested clumps in spring as needed to maintain vigor.

common_name: Ginger Wine Ninebark (Copper-to-Burgundy Foliage Compact Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Ginger Wine is a more compact ninebark than older cultivars like Diabolo, fitting smaller mixed borders and foundation plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Ginger Wine bears warm ginger-copper new growth that deepens toward burgundy-wine as leaves mature, giving a two-toned effect across the shrub through the growing season, on a more compact, rounded frame than older, larger-growing dark-leaved ninebark cultivars. Small clusters of white-to-pink flowers appear in late spring, followed by reddish seed capsules, and mature stems develop the characteristic exfoliating bark that adds winter interest. Full sun produces the richest foliage color. It needs only occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems at the base every year or two to keep the shrub full and vigorous.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Gingerland is a strap-leaved type caladium — the leaf shape is more elongated and narrower than standard heart-shaped fancy types, creating a different textural effect.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Gingerland is one of the most popular strap-leaf caladium cultivars — producing narrower, more elongated, lance-shaped leaves (rather than the broad heart shape of standard fancy caladiums) in a pattern of creamy-white with scattered red-crimson speckling and a green margin that creates a soft, delicate appearance quite different from the bold leaf patterns of large-leaved types. The strap-leaf form produces a more graceful, airy texture in mass plantings compared to the bold, overlapping effect of large fancy caladiums — Gingerland creates a lighter, more refined textural effect appropriate for intimate garden spaces and detailed planting designs. The fine red spotting on the white leaf surface becomes more vivid in brighter conditions, making Gingerland a versatile cultivar that can be used in bright indirect light to partial shade. Strap-leaf types like Gingerland typically tolerate somewhat more sun than standard fancy types and are often recommended for partial-sun locations (3–4 hours direct sun) where their coloration remains good without the bleaching that affects white-leaved fancy cultivars. In mixed caladium plantings, Gingerland's finer texture creates effective contrast with the large, bold leaves of 'Candidum', 'White Queen', or 'Red Flash'.

common_name: Ginko Craig Hosta (Small Narrow Green Leaves Edged in White)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil. Ginko Craig is a small, long-popular hosta with narrow, lance-shaped green leaves edged in crisp white.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partly to fully shaded site, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Ginko Craig, a long-established, widely grown small hosta, bears narrow, lance-shaped green leaves crisply edged in white, a fine-textured, dependable variegated selection that has remained popular for edging and mass planting for decades. It produces lavender flowers on scapes in summer. Mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system from summer heat, and divide congested clumps every several years in spring.

common_name: Gipsy Queen Clematis (Deep Velvety Purple Viticella-Type)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Gipsy Queen blooms on new growth, so it can be cut back hard each late winter, an easier pruning regime than early-flowering cultivars require.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis, arbor, or fence. Gipsy Queen bears richly saturated, velvety deep purple flowers with a subtle reddish sheen, blooming freely from midsummer into fall entirely on the current season's growth, which makes it one of the easiest clematis types to prune, since the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter without sacrificing any of the coming season's bloom. Its vigorous, free-flowering habit and deep, dramatic color make it a strong choice for covering a fence or arbor quickly each year. This forgiving pruning regime also makes it a good choice for gardeners new to growing clematis.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial sun; pearl bush blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering ends, never in fall or early spring, or blooms will be lost.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial sun; Girald's pearl bush is a large, arching Chinese ornamental shrub native to Shaanxi province that puts on one of the most spectacular spring flower displays of any cold-hardy deciduous shrub, smothering its long arching branches with racemes of pure white, 5-petaled flowers in mid-spring just as the leaves are emerging. The flower buds are distinctly round and pearl-like before opening — the origin of the common name. It is slightly larger and somewhat hardier than the related Exochorda racemosa and can ultimately reach 12–15 feet, so allow ample space in the landscape. Prune selectively for shape only immediately after bloom, as flower buds are set on the previous season's wood; deadwood can be removed at any time.

common_name: Girard's Rainbow Leucothoe (Pink-Copper New Growth Evergreen Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist, deeply acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Girard's Rainbow bears new growth in shades of pink, cream, and copper before maturing to green.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, deeply acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mimicking its native Appalachian stream-bank habitat. Girard's Rainbow emerges each spring in vivid tones of pink, cream, and copper before gradually maturing to glossy green, giving the arching, evergreen shrub a colorful, ever-changing foliage display on top of the fragrant white bell-shaped spring flowers typical of the species. Its variegated new growth makes it more ornamentally striking than the straight species, especially massed under rhododendrons or azaleas. All parts are toxic; spreads slowly by stolons to form a graceful, naturalistic colony.

plant_note: Plant dormant, nursery-propagated bare-root crowns in fall just below the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained but evenly moist woodland soil in partial shade.
directions: Cypripedium 'Gisela' is a garden hybrid (C. macranthos x C. flavum parentage) bred to combine the vigor and adaptability of Asian lady's slipper species with showier flower color, producing rose-pink to magenta pouched blooms with a paler lip in late spring above pleated, ribbed foliage. It is considerably easier to establish and grow on than most wild-collected Cypripedium species, tolerating garden conditions better while still preferring a cool, humus-rich woodland bed with dappled shade and consistent moisture during the growing season. Mulch lightly with leaf litter each fall to protect the shallow root system and replicate its native forest-floor habitat, and avoid disturbing established clumps, which slowly bulk up into multi-stemmed specimens over years. Site alongside ferns and hostas in a shaded border where its unusual pouch flowers become a spring focal point.

common_name: Gitts Perfection Dahlia (Formal Decorative Show Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; stake tall plants at planting time since the huge blooms are heavy.
directions: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost, staking plants early since the giant, formal blooms are heavy on the stem. A longtime favorite on the dahlia show bench, Gitts Perfection produces huge, perfectly formed, formal decorative blooms in soft lavender-pink with neatly overlapping, evenly spaced petals — the precise, symmetrical form that show judges look for in the formal decorative class. Pinch the growing tip early to build a well-branched plant, and disbud surrounding side buds to concentrate energy into fewer, larger, exhibition-quality blooms. In zones colder than 8, lift tubers after the first light frost blackens the foliage and store in a cool, dry, frost-free place over winter.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Glacier is a compact Kurume azalea bred for a dense, heavily flowered, pure white spring display.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Glacier is a compact Kurume-type azalea producing a dense, heavy flush of small, pure white, hose-in-hose flowers each spring, its tidy mounding habit and fine-textured evergreen foliage making it well suited to foundation plantings, borders, and mass plantings where a smaller-scale white azalea is wanted. Its full, floriferous bloom and manageable size have kept it a mainstay in Southern gardens alongside other classic Kurume selections. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, gravelly or rocky subalpine soil in partial shade; glacier lily grows in subalpine and alpine meadows from the Rockies through the Cascades, blooming immediately as snow melts. Challenging in lowland gardens; best in cool, high-elevation or north-facing slope sites.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, gravelly or rocky subalpine soil in partial shade; glacier lily is the yellow-flowered counterpart of the white avalanche lily, both species blooming immediately as snow retreats in Rocky Mountain and Cascade subalpine meadows. The brilliant golden-yellow, reflexed petals distinguish it from the white E. montanum. The unfussy, elegant flowers with their swept-back petals in clear yellow are among the most beautiful of the high mountain wildflowers. Grizzly bears dig the corms in large quantities in the Rockies and Yellowstone, making the species an important grizzly food source. Columbian ground squirrels also harvest the corms and seeds extensively. The plant's ecological associations in subalpine meadow ecosystems make it difficult to grow successfully in lowland gardens, but in appropriately cool, rocky, well-drained mountain garden settings it naturalizes to form striking colonies.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or plant nursery transplants in moist, neutral to slightly alkaline, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Glade Fern is often found naturally on moist limestone outcrops and in rich, calcareous woodland glades.
directions: Glade Fern is an unusual and distinctive native fern, native to the rich, moist, shaded glades, ravine floors, and calcareous woodland slopes of eastern North America from Quebec to Georgia and Tennessee, where it grows in the mineral-rich soils derived from limestone or dolomite that many ferns cannot tolerate. Unlike most ferns with finely divided pinnate fronds, Glade Fern produces long, strap-shaped, single-pinnate fronds with widely spaced, pointed pinnae that give it a loose, airy, elegant appearance quite different from the denser-textured wood ferns and lady ferns. A deciduous fern that dies back to the ground in fall and re-emerges in spring, it spreads slowly by short-creeping rhizomes to form loose colonies and is best used as a textural contrast plant among finer-textured shade ground covers. Grow in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil (pH 6.5–7.5) in partial to full shade; the preference for slightly alkaline conditions makes it a good companion to plants that enjoy limestone-derived soils.

plant_note: Divide established clumps and transplant in early spring before fronds fully unfurl; plant into moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Glade Fern is an elegant, upright native fern of moist, shaded rocky woodland glades, limestone bluffs, and humus-rich forest floors throughout eastern North America, producing erect once-pinnate fronds with long, narrow lance-shaped pinnae that give the plant an unusually slender, airy, almost grass-like silhouette among woodland ferns. This distinctive narrow texture makes it an outstanding contrast plant alongside broad-leaved shade perennials such as hosta, ligularia, and Solomon's seal in woodland and shade garden settings. Plant in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; amend heavy clay soils with leaf mold or compost before planting to ensure good drainage and aeration. Established plants tolerate brief summer dryness but perform best with consistent moisture and benefit from a mulch of shredded leaves to retain soil moisture through the growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of moist to wet, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; glade lobelia grows in bogs, seepage slopes, and wet pine flatwoods of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, peaty or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; glade lobelia is a native Gulf Coastal Plain lobelia of wet, acidic, bog-like habitats — seepage bogs, sphagnum seeps, and wet longleaf pine flatwoods — producing beautiful blue to blue-violet flower spikes in late summer through fall. It is named for its occurrence in the wet, open 'glades' (clearings) within longleaf pine flatwoods — the type of habitat that supports many of the most interesting plants of the Gulf South. The blue-violet flowers attract hummingbirds and numerous large native bees. Like other lobelias, it requires consistently moist to wet soil and performs best when never allowed to dry out. An outstanding native for bog gardens, rain gardens, and consistently moist, acidic, partially shaded settings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; glade mallow grows naturally in the rich, moist limestone glades and streambanks of the Upper Midwest and Appalachians. It is dioecious — plant male and female plants for seed production.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; glade mallow is the only member of its genus — a tall, coarse-textured native perennial that is monotypic in the family Malvaceae, producing broadly palmately lobed leaves and small white flowers in summer. It grows naturally in the calcium-rich limestone glades and moist streambanks of the upper Midwest and eastern mountains, making it an unusual choice for alkaline, moist garden conditions. The plant is dioecious (separate male and female plants required for seed), an unusual trait in the mallow family. A rare plant in both the wild and in cultivation, glade mallow is a distinctive native specimen for large, naturalistic gardens with moist, alkaline, calcareous soils. Its bold, textured foliage and architectural height (to 6 feet) provide strong summer presence in the native garden.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall (October–November in zone 9); in zone 9 ornamental alliums are not reliably perennial — the bulbs require cool winter temperatures for proper flower induction that zone 9 winters may not reliably provide. Plant fresh bulbs annually for best results, or provide 8–10 weeks of pre-chilling in the refrigerator before planting. Allium 'Gladiator' produces large (4-inch), round, violet-purple flower heads on tall (3–4 foot) stems in April–May in zone 9. The flowers are self-supporting and do not require staking. All Allium foliage has the characteristic onion-garlic scent when crushed. After flowering, the seed heads remain ornamental through summer, providing structural interest even after the flowers have dried.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Allium requires excellent drainage and is susceptible to bulb rot in wet, clay soils; Gladiator is one of the largest and most impressive ornamental Allium hybrids, producing large (4-inch), perfectly spherical, tightly packed flower heads composed of hundreds of small, star-shaped, violet-purple florets on tall (3–4 foot), self-supporting stems — creating one of the most dramatic and architecturally bold spring bulb flower forms available in ornamental gardening. The large, globe-shaped flower heads of Allium 'Gladiator' provide a completely different visual character than the low-growing, daisy-form or trumpet-form flowers that dominate the spring bulb season — the large, floating balls of violet-purple held well above the surrounding plants creating a structural, architectural element that works both in the mixed spring border and as a bold vertical accent in the landscape. The dried seed heads remaining after the flowers fade are fully as attractive as the fresh flowers — the structural, cage-like seed heads maintaining visual interest through summer when most spring bulbs have gone dormant. As a relative of edible onion and garlic, Allium foliage and flowers are completely deer-resistant — an important practical attribute for areas where deer browse regularly.

plant_note: Plant corms after the last frost; make successive plantings every 2 weeks through early summer for extended bloom.
directions: Plant corms 4–6 in deep in well-drained soil with the pointed end up after the last frost; succession plant every 2 weeks through midsummer for continuous cut flowers. Tall varieties need staking; a single bamboo cane tied loosely to the stem works well. In zones below 7, dig corms after frost blackens the foliage, dry for 2–3 weeks, remove offsets (cormels), and store at 35–45°F in mesh bags through winter. Harvest cut spikes when the lowest 2–3 buds show color for longest vase life.

common_name: Glamour Girl Garden Phlox (Mildew-Resistant Coral-Pink Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing generously for airflow; Glamour Girl is a Walters Gardens Garden Girls-series phlox bred for very good powdery mildew resistance, a major advantage over many older garden phlox in the humid Gulf South.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants generously for good air circulation; Glamour Girl bears large, domed clusters of hot coral-pink flowers held on dark purple stems, part of the Garden Girls series bred for very good powdery mildew resistance, the fungal disease that disfigures the foliage of many older tall garden phlox varieties in humid summer conditions. Its more compact, tidy habit than heirloom phlox cultivars fits well into a mixed perennial border. Deadhead the central flower cluster once it fades to encourage side-shoot rebloom, and avoid overhead watering to further reduce disease pressure. In zone 9, tall phlox is treated as a somewhat short-lived perennial and may decline after a couple of seasons in intense summer heat, so division and replanting every few years helps maintain vigor.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost date, or direct sow outdoors 2 weeks after last frost, in well-drained, average soil in full sun; globe amaranth thrives in heat and humidity and is one of the most reliable summer annuals for zone 8–11 where summer heat defeats most other annuals.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost date, or direct sow outdoors 2 weeks after last frost, in well-drained, average soil in full sun; globe amaranth thrives in heat and humidity and is one of the most reliable summer annuals for zone 8–11 where summer heat defeats most other annuals. Gomphrena globosa is a tropical annual grown for its papery, clover-like, globe-shaped flower heads in vivid magenta-purple, pink, white, and orange that bloom continuously from midsummer through frost with virtually no care; the flower heads retain their color perfectly when dried, making it one of the best everlasting annuals — simply hang upside down to dry for wreaths, arrangements, and crafts. The flowers are excellent for small native bees and bumblebees; the plant is extraordinarily heat-tolerant and largely pest- and disease-free. An outstanding plant for hot-summer gardens and zone 9–11 landscapes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or provide seeds with 8–10 weeks of cold stratification at 35–40°F before sowing in spring; globeflowers prefer consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
directions: Direct sow in fall or provide seeds with 8–10 weeks of cold stratification at 35–40°F before sowing in spring; globeflowers prefer consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade and are excellent in moist meadow, rain garden, and waterside plantings. Trollius europaeus is a beautiful European native perennial in the buttercup family producing palmately lobed, deeply cut foliage and glowing, lemon-to-golden-yellow, fully rounded, globe-shaped flowers 1–2 inches across in late spring and early summer; the incurved, petal-like sepals give the flower a distinctive, rounded shape unlike any other buttercup family member. Globeflowers perform best in cool, moist climates and partial shade, declining in heat and drought — they are outstanding in zones 3–6 but marginal in zone 7 and generally unsuited to the Deep South. Pair with marsh marigold and primulas for a spectacular cool-season waterside planting.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after cold stratification, or sow in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; globe sedge is common in moist to wet forested bottomlands and wet woodland margins across eastern North America.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in woodland gardens, rain gardens, and wet bottomland settings; globe sedge is a native eastern sedge recognized most easily by its striking perigynia — the inflated, balloon-like seed sacs that swell to a distinctive round shape, giving the plant the common name bladder sedge or globe sedge. Each fruiting head contains relatively few but very large, inflated perigynia that catch the eye and make this species easy to identify among woodland sedges. The plant grows naturally in wet to moist, shaded bottomlands, seepage slopes, and forested wetland margins throughout eastern North America. It is an important component of the woodland floor layer and provides seed food for wood ducks and other wetland birds. An excellent ground layer plant for moist, shaded native woodland gardens in zones 4–9.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or spring in very well-drained, poor to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; globe thistle develops a deep taproot and performs best in lean, dry conditions — rich or wet soils cause floppy growth and shorter life.
directions: Direct sow in poor, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; globe thistle produces perfectly spherical, metallic blue flower heads on branching, silvery-white stems with deeply lobed, thistle-like leaves from midsummer into fall, providing a bold architectural element and an exceptional magnet for bees and butterflies, especially bumblebees. Cut stems at three-quarter stage and hang upside down to dry — the round heads hold their color and shape for months in dried arrangements. Plants are drought-tolerant and long-lived in poor, dry soils but short-lived in heavy, wet clay. Divide or transplant only in early spring before roots become too deep; established plants resent disturbance.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; globeflower requires consistently moist soil and struggles in dry or hot conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing 12–18 inches apart; globeflower is a late-spring to early-summer perennial with nearly perfect spherical, clear-yellow to orange flowers on upright stems above deeply divided, dark-green foliage — imagine a large, wild-looking double buttercup. It thrives beside ponds, streams, and in bog gardens where the soil stays reliably moist, and performs particularly well in cool northern climates where summers are mild. In hotter zones (7+) it struggles and often declines by midsummer. Divide every 3–4 years in late summer after the foliage dies back. Modern hybrids of T. x cultorum offer orange, lemon-yellow, and cream flower colors and are more vigorous than the straight species.

plant_note: Plant large bulbs in fall for dramatic late-spring globes.
directions: Plant Globemaster allium bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Each stout stem produces a massive violet globe up to ten inches across that lasts for weeks and draws countless bees. Position the plants among perennials that hide the fading foliage, which yellows before the flowers finish. The dried seed heads make striking architectural accents in the garden or in arrangements.

common_name: Globosa Nana Japanese Cedar (Dwarf Globe Sugi)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Globosa Nana' forms a naturally rounded mound and needs little to no pruning to keep its shape.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their naturally rounded outline to develop without crowding. 'Globosa Nana' is one of the oldest and most popular dwarf Japanese cedar selections, forming a dense, symmetrical mound of soft, blue-green, slightly twisted needles that take on a plum-bronze cast in cold weather before greening up again in spring.
