Its predictable globe shape and slow growth make it a dependable anchor plant in mixed conifer gardens, foundation plantings, and Asian-style landscapes where a formal, low-maintenance mass is wanted without shearing.

common_name: Glorie van Heemstede Dahlia (Heirloom Canary-Yellow Waterlily Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Glorie van Heemstede is a long-cultivated heirloom waterlily dahlia bearing clear canary-yellow flat blooms.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants in exposed sites to support the broad, flat blooms in wind. Glorie van Heemstede, a classic Dutch heirloom, bears shallow, cupped, waterlily-form flowers in a clear, cheerful canary-yellow, the broad, gently overlapping petals creating a flatter bloom than decorative or ball dahlia types. Its old-fashioned charm and reliable, prolific bloom have kept it popular with heirloom dahlia collectors for decades. Deadhead spent blooms regularly, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Gloriosa Daisy (AAS-Winning Large-Flowered Black-Eyed Susan Annual)
plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost (seeds tolerate light frost) or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier for earlier blooms; Gloriosa Daisy is a short-lived perennial in zones 3–10 that blooms its first summer from seed. In zone 9, direct sow January–March for late spring blooms, or again in August–September for fall and winter blooms. Gloriosa Daisy self-seeds prolifically in favorable conditions, naturalizing in beds and meadows.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface (needs light for germination) 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Gloriosa Daisy is a cultivated selection of the native black-eyed susan (Rudbeckia hirta) that earned the first AAS Award given to a rudbeckia in 1957 — a selection that dramatically increased the flower size of the native species while maintaining the same robust, adaptable, heat-tolerant character. Standard R. hirta produces 2–3 inch flowers; Gloriosa Daisy produces flowers 4–6 inches in diameter, with the classic yellow daisy form (golden-yellow ray petals surrounding a dark brown, slightly cone-shaped central disk) scaled up to a presence visible from a distance. The flowers are sometimes semi-double and occur in solid yellow, bicolor yellow with a mahogany band at the center, solid orange, and mahogany-red forms, giving the planting a naturalistic wildflower quality. Gloriosa Daisy is a native-plant-adjacent choice for naturalistic gardens, meadow plantings, and xeric landscapes where it provides summer color with minimal supplemental irrigation. The plants attract bees, butterflies, and in fall the seed heads provide food for goldfinches and other birds. Self-seeding in place, Gloriosa Daisy can naturalize in a garden with benign neglect.

plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4 in deep after last frost; in zones 8+ can be planted in early spring once soil is 65°F.
directions: Plant the fragile, finger-shaped tubers horizontally 4 in deep, handling carefully to avoid snapping them; provide a trellis or support as the vine climbs by leaf-tip tendrils. The striking reflexed flowers in flame-red and yellow with wavy-edged petals are produced freely from midsummer into fall. All parts of the plant are highly toxic if ingested — site away from children and pets. In zones below 8, dig tubers after foliage dies, dry them, and store in dry peat moss at 50–60°F over winter.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant in zone 9; Philodendron gloriosum cannot tolerate temperatures below 60°F. Unlike most philodendrons that climb, P. gloriosum is a terrestrial crawler that spreads horizontally on its thick rhizome — plant in a wide, shallow container to accommodate this growth habit. Use a well-aerated potting mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil. Water thoroughly, then allow to slightly dry between waterings. All parts toxic if chewed.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Glorious Philodendron needs consistent bright indirect light for healthy growth and the maintenance of its velvety leaf texture, but will burn in direct sun. Philodendron gloriosum is a terrestrial (ground-crawling, not climbing) philodendron native to the humid tropical forests of Colombia, where it creeps along the forest floor on a thick, horizontal rhizome. Unlike the majority of popular philodendrons that climb by aerial roots, P. gloriosum spreads sideways — each new leaf is produced from a stem node extending along the surface of the growing medium, giving the plant a distinctly different and dramatic growth habit. The leaves are enormous when mature (up to 24–36 inches on well-grown specimens), heart-shaped, with a velvety, deep emerald-green surface crossed by bold white veins in a pattern that inspired the specific epithet 'gloriosum.' The velvety texture results from tiny papillae on the leaf surface that scatter light, creating the characteristic soft, matte sheen. Glorious Philodendron has become one of the most sought-after collector aroids internationally, valued for both its spectacular foliage and its unusual growth habit. All parts are mildly toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 3 in deep in fall; naturalize in lawns, rock gardens, or under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall, 3 in deep and 2–3 in apart, in any well-drained soil; glory-of-the-snow blooms very early, often pushing through snow in late winter to early spring. The vivid blue, star-shaped flowers with white centers naturalize freely by both offsets and self-seeding, forming large colonies over time. Plant in large drifts under deciduous trees where they receive full sun while leafless and will not be disturbed during summer dormancy. No special care is needed once established; bulbs rarely need dividing.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3 inches apart in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; glory-of-the-snow is one of the earliest-blooming hardy bulbs, emerging and often flowering through the last snows of late winter or very early spring. It self-seeds prolifically and naturalizes into large colonies under deciduous trees and in lawns, increasing dramatically over the years.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for very early spring bloom; glory-of-the-snow (Chionodoxa forbesii, often sold as C. luciliae) is among the most brilliant and freely naturalizing of all early spring bulbs — a small, tough, Turkish native that produces loose upright clusters of 6-12 star-shaped flowers in a vivid, saturated gentian-blue with a striking, pure white eye at the center, the white zone surrounded by the deep blue petals creating a precise, bold contrast. It blooms in early March, often pushing up through snow, making it one of the first vivid colors of the garden year. Native to mountain meadows and rocky open slopes in western Turkey, it is extraordinarily cold-hardy and sun-adaptable, performing especially well in the partial shade of deciduous trees where the spring light reaches the ground before leaf-out. It self-seeds with great freedom, forming large naturalized colonies that increase year after year without any attention, eventually carpeting large areas under trees with early spring color. The larger-flowered pink cultivar 'Pink Giant' and the compact, deep-blue C. sardensis are excellent companions.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; glossy abelia is among the longest-blooming shrubs in the Southeast, flowering from late spring through fall frost.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; glossy abelia is a semi-evergreen hybrid shrub that ranks among the most reliably long-blooming ornamentals for the Southeast and Gulf South, producing masses of small, funnel-shaped, white to blush-pink, pleasantly fragrant flowers continuously from late spring through hard frost — a bloom period of 5–6 months that few shrubs match. The small, glossy, bronze-tinged leaves are attractive year-round in mild climates. Hummingbirds and butterflies visit the flowers consistently. It is highly adaptable to soil conditions, tolerating heat, humidity, and urban pollution. Prune selectively in late winter to remove oldest canes and encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth. 'Kaleidoscope' (variegated yellow and green) and 'Confetti' (variegated pink-white) are popular selections.

common_name: Glossy Privet (Tree Privet, Evergreen Privet Tree)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; glossy privet grows into a substantial small evergreen tree if left unpruned and self-seeds aggressively — it is a documented invasive species in the Gulf South and should be sheared before flowering or replaced with a non-invasive alternative near natural areas.
directions: Plant in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; glossy privet is a large, fast-growing evergreen shrub or small tree with big, glossy, dark-green leaves and showy panicles of small white flowers in late spring, historically planted as a substantial screening hedge, street tree, or specimen for its handsome, dense evergreen canopy. Left unpruned it grows quickly into a 20–30 foot tree; sheared regularly it can be maintained as a tall, dense hedge or screen. The abundant, heavily fragrant flowers give way to prolific clusters of small blue-black berries that birds spread widely, and glossy privet has become a serious, well-documented invasive species across the Gulf South and much of the southeastern United States, forming dense stands in bottomland forests and disturbed woodland edges that displace native trees and shrubs. Because of this, it is best avoided in new plantings near natural areas — where a large-growing broadleaf evergreen screen is wanted, non-invasive alternatives like Podocarpus macrophyllus, Ilex, or Ternstroemia gymnanthera are strongly preferable.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; glossy sarcandra is a slow-growing East Asian forest understory shrub best purchased as an established plant rather than raised from seed.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath established trees or against a shaded wall; glossy sarcandra is an evergreen East Asian understory shrub grown for its glossy, deep-green, sharply toothed foliage and, most of all, for the clusters of small, bright orange-red berries that ripen in late fall and persist through winter, giving deep shade a spot of color when little else is blooming there. The tiny greenish flowers themselves are inconspicuous. Long used in traditional East Asian herbal medicine and prized in Japanese and Chinese flower arranging (ikebana) for its cut branches of glossy leaves and berries, it is grown ornamentally in the West mainly as an unusual, refined evergreen for the woodland shade garden. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native forest floor conditions; protect from hard freezes in the colder end of its hardiness range.

common_name: Glowing Embers Hydrangea (Deep Pink-to-Purple German Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Glowing Embers is a longstanding German-bred mophead hydrangea still considered a top performer for deep, saturated flower color.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun. Glowing Embers is a German-bred bigleaf hydrangea, roughly a half-century old, still regarded as one of the finest mopheads for deep, saturated flower color, ranging from rich pink in more alkaline soil to deep purple-red in strongly acidic soil, a shift managed with soil amendments if a specific shade is wanted. The large, rounded flower heads are held on a sturdy, well-branched, moderately compact shrub. Water deeply during dry spells to prevent wilting, and prune only lightly right after flowering, since flower buds for the following year form on the current season's growth by late summer.

plant_note: Surface-sow since light aids germination; as a biennial it flowers the second year.
directions: Surface-sow spring through midsummer since light aids germination, thinning plants to 12-18 inches. This sturdy biennial produces foliage the first year and tall spikes of extra-large gloxinia-like blooms the second year, and it self-sows readily for naturalized areas. It performs best in part shade with rich, moist, well-drained soil. Note that all parts of foxglove are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 sow March–May. Gnome Pink is one of the most compact gomphrena selections available — reaching only 6–9 inches with a spreading, mounding habit, producing globe-shaped, clover-like, rose-pink flowers on short stems. The papery, dry-textured flower heads are naturally long-lasting both on the plant and as dried flowers — maintaining their color and shape for months when cut and dried. In zone 9 gomphrena is one of the best-adapted heat-and-humidity-tolerant summer annuals available, actively thriving in conditions that reduce or stop flowering in many other annuals. The plants are essentially unaffected by zone 9 summer heat, continuing to produce abundant flowers through July–September when the heat discourages many annuals. Excellent for dried flower arrangements.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Gnome Pink Gomphrena thrives in heat and poor-to-moderate soil conditions and declines in overly fertile, wet situations; Gnome Pink is a dwarf compact selection of Globe Amaranth (Gomphrena globosa), producing the distinctive clover-like, rounded, papery flower heads in bright rose-pink at a miniature scale — just 6–9 inches tall — that makes it practical for edging, rock gardens, small containers, and front-of-border situations where taller gomphrena selections would be out of scale. The flower heads of gomphrena are composed of papery, everlasting bracts surrounding tiny true flowers — the bracts providing the color and texture that are both attractive in the garden and naturally suited to drying, as the papery texture means the flowers hold their color and form after cutting and air-drying without the wilting and discoloration that affects more conventional floral textures. Globe Amaranth is one of the most genuinely heat-adapted summer annuals for zone 9 — a tropical species from Central America and South Asia that actively grows and flowers through the hottest conditions zone 9 can produce, while also being drought tolerant after establishment, requiring minimal care, and providing continuous flower production through the entire summer growing season.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Gnu Again is a reblooming iris that flowers again in late summer or fall in climates with a long enough growing season.
directions: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Gnu Again is a reblooming iris that flowers again in late summer or fall in climates with a long enough growing season. Creamy yellow standards contrast with white falls delicately edged in the same soft yellow, a clean, cheerful color combination on a dependable, award-winning reblooming bearded iris that, given a sufficiently long and mild growing season, produces a second flush of bloom in late summer or fall beyond the typical single spring display. Reblooming iris cultivars generally need consistent moisture and a light feeding after the first spring bloom to support the energy demands of a second flowering cycle, performing best in climates with long, warm falls rather than an early hard frost. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, and keep rhizome tops exposed to sun to prevent rot.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; goat's beard is a large perennial that needs substantial space — allow 4–6 feet of spread at maturity.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving each plant a full 4–5 feet of space; goat's beard is a dramatic, native, large-scale shade perennial whose huge plumes of creamy-white feathery flowers in late spring to early summer rise on stems to 6 feet, mimicking an enormous astilbe or a white smoke tree. Male plants produce the showiest flower plumes; female plants bear smaller plumes and later develop attractive seed clusters. Foliage remains handsome through summer and fall. Excellent at woodland edges, along streams, or in naturalistic shade gardens where its scale can be fully appreciated. Divide only when absolutely necessary as established plants are extremely long-lived and resent disturbance.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; Goat's Horn Cactus needs excellent drainage and is slow-growing, taking several years to reach flowering size.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; Goat's Horn Cactus needs excellent drainage and is slow-growing, taking several years to reach flowering size. A rounded, ribbed, blue-gray body speckled with fine white wool is armed with dramatically long, curved, twisting dark spines that curl outward like a goat's horns, one of the most distinctively spined of all the star cactus species and a favorite of collectors for that ornamental spination alone. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert of northern Mexico, it produces large, funnel-shaped yellow flowers with a reddish throat once mature, but is grown by most collectors chiefly for its dramatic curling spines and silvery-blue, woolly-speckled body. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide strong direct sun for the best spine development and body color, and protect from frost and winter wet.

plant_note: Direct-sow scarified seeds in lean, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; goat's rue grows naturally in dry, sandy soils of pine barrens, open woodlands, and roadsides and thrives in lean conditions where most ornamentals fail. It is a nitrogen-fixer that improves soil fertility over time. The deep, rope-like roots (giving rise to 'Devil's Shoestring') make established plants drought-tolerant but resistant to transplanting.
directions: Direct-sow in lean, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; goat's rue is a low, spreading native legume with bicolored flowers in a striking combination — cream-white wings contrasting with a magenta-pink standard (the upper petal), creating a two-toned floral effect in clusters at the stem tips from May through July. The silky, pinnate leaves with soft, silvery hairs are attractive throughout the season. As a legume, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and naturally improves poor, sandy soils over time — a characteristic adaptation to the nutrient-poor pine barrens and sandhill habitats where it grows. The deep, twisted, rope-like roots (hence 'Devil's Shoestring') make mature plants drought-tolerant but difficult to transplant. It is the sole larval host plant for the Frosted Elfin butterfly (Callophrys irus), a declining species that depends entirely on goat's rue for caterpillar food. An outstanding choice for naturalistic dry gardens, sandy soils, and butterfly conservation plantings.

plant_note: Direct-sow in moist, average to fertile soil in full sun to part shade; INVASIVE WARNING: Galega officinalis is a listed noxious weed in Colorado, Montana, Washington, and other western US states and is prohibited from sale and planting in those states. It spreads by seed and rhizomes and has colonized moist roadsides and riparian areas in western mountain states. Verify local regulations before planting.
directions: Sow in moist, average soil in full sun to part shade — VERIFY LEGALITY: listed noxious weed in several western US states; Goat's rue is a European legume with considerable historical significance: it was used for centuries as a treatment for diabetes in European folk medicine, and in the 20th century, chemists isolated the compound galegine from its leaves — the study of galegine's guanidine chemistry directly led to the development of metformin, now the world's most widely prescribed diabetes medication. The plant itself produces attractive racemes of white, pink, or lilac pea flowers in early summer above pinnate foliage and is ornamental in bloom. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it improves soil fertility. However, it has become a significant invasive weed in riparian and moist disturbed areas of the western United States (listed as a noxious weed in Colorado, Montana, and Washington states). In areas where it is legal to grow, it is an interesting historical medicinal and ornamental plant.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface (needs light to germinate) in early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; goatsbeard is dioecious — plant multiple plants for the best display, as male plants produce slightly more dramatic flower plumes.
directions: Sow on the soil surface in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in early spring; goatsbeard is one of the most magnificent native shade perennials in North America, forming large, bold clumps of compound, ferny leaves topped in early to midsummer by massive, arching plumes of creamy-white flowers resembling a giant astilbe — earning it the common name. Male plants produce the showiest, most upright plumes; female plants produce somewhat more pendulous plumes followed by seed heads that dry attractively. It grows naturally in moist, rich woodland slopes and creek banks throughout the eastern US and Pacific Northwest, performing best in cool, moist, shaded conditions. An outstanding bold-textured plant for the large-scale woodland garden or shaded border, paired with hostas, ferns, and native wildflowers. Not suited to hot, dry climates; performs best in zone 3–7.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface (gaillardia needs light to germinate — do not cover), or plant container divisions in spring in lean, very well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Goblin must have excellent drainage and lean soil — in rich, moist soil plants become floppy and short-lived.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Goblin (also sold as 'Kobold') is the most popular and most widely planted compact gaillardia — a dwarf selection staying 12–14 inches tall, compared to the 24–30 inch standard blanket flower, with the same spectacular, vivid bicolor flowers: large, daisy-like blooms with rich red petals tipped bright golden-yellow surrounding a raised, textured, deep-red central button. The intense red-and-yellow bicolor pattern mimics the traditional woven patterns of Southwest Native American blankets, giving the plant its common name. Goblin blooms nearly continuously from late spring through hard fall frost in zone 9, requiring only light deadheading to remove spent flower heads and trigger continued production. It is extraordinarily drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant — performing exceptionally well in the dry, hot conditions of the Gulf South summer that stress many perennials. The compact habit makes Goblin appropriate for the front of borders, rock gardens, and containers where the standard blanket flower would be oversized. Outstanding for pollinator gardens — bees, butterflies, and native pollinators are strongly attracted. Gaillardia is actually a somewhat short-lived perennial in the Deep South and should be expected to decline after 2–3 years; it self-seeds readily and naturalistic populations maintain themselves indefinitely in well-drained soils.

common_name: Goblin Orchid (Trumpet Mormodes, Twisted-Column Orchid, Bugle Orchid)
plant_note: Grow in an open basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to partial direct light; Mormodes buccinator is a deciduous orchid — it sheds its leaves in fall as the pseudobulbs ripen and blooms from the leafless pseudobulbs in winter on pendant to arching spikes. A dry rest period in fall (reduce watering as leaves yellow) is important for triggering bloom. Resume watering as new growth starts in spring. The twisted, asymmetric flowers are pollinated by male orchid bees that are thrown off the trigger mechanism onto the bee's body in different positions depending on flower orientation, ensuring cross-pollination. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light in coarse bark medium in an open basket — Goblin Orchid grows most vigorously in good light with the open-basket culture that provides the root aeration appropriate to its natural epiphytic habitat in tropical deciduous forests. Mormodes buccinator is a deciduous, sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most scientifically fascinating of the New World orchids because of its uniquely asymmetric, twisted flowers and sophisticated pollination mechanism. The plant produces large, fusiform (spindle-shaped) pseudobulbs with several broad, pleated leaves that drop in fall. From the leafless pseudobulbs in winter, pendant to arching flower spikes emerge bearing 8–20 medium-sized flowers (1.5–2 inches) that are immediately remarkable for their twisted, asymmetric form: the column is rotated (twisted) to the right or left relative to the flower center, with the lip pointing to one side rather than forward or downward as in most orchids. This asymmetric column orientation — with the trigger mechanism in a different position in different flowers or between different plants — is related to the pollination system: male euglossine bees (orchid bees) that land on the trigger are catapulted by the spring-loaded mechanism onto their dorsal (right) or ventral (left) surface, depending on flower orientation, ensuring that pollinia from differently-oriented flowers are placed on different body positions of the bee — a mechanism designed to prevent self-pollination. Flowers vary from orange-yellow to brown-maroon. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Sow in place as soon as soil is workable; dislikes transplanting.
directions: Direct sow godetia into lean, well-drained soil in early spring, barely covering the fine seed. It resents rich soil and heavy feeding, which produce foliage at the expense of the satiny cup-shaped blooms. Thin seedlings to 8-12 inches and keep evenly moist until established, then water sparingly. Cool weather intensifies the pink and lavender flower colors, so it performs best in spring and early summer before extreme heat.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in spring in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun to partial shade; Godfrey's butterwort is a federally threatened species restricted to a few counties in the Florida panhandle, and wild collection is illegal.
directions: Plant only nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun to partial shade. Godfrey's butterwort is a federally threatened carnivorous plant known only from a handful of wet flatwoods and seepage bog sites in the Florida panhandle, closely related to blue butterwort but with pale violet flowers marked by a distinctive white-and-yellow throat, blooming in early spring above a low rosette of sticky, insect-trapping leaves. Because its entire wild range is so narrow and legally protected, it should be grown only from documented nursery propagation as a specialty addition to a Gulf Coast bog garden, never collected from the wild. Give it the same pure-water, no-fertilizer regimen required by all butterworts, and site it where consistent moisture and acidity can be reliably maintained year-round.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, giving this fern generous room since it dwarfs typical painted and lady ferns.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Godzilla is a robust hybrid lady fern, similar in parentage to other silver-frosted Athyrium hybrids but selected and named for its outsized stature, forming a much larger clump with broader, more upright fronds than typical Athyrium cultivars. It carries a silvery overlay on the fronds inherited from its Japanese painted fern parentage while showing far greater vigor and heat tolerance than straight painted fern. Use it as a bold textural anchor in a shade border where a standard-size Athyrium would be lost, pairing it with hostas and heucheras for scale contrast.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in rich, well-drained soil in deep shade during spring or early fall.
directions: Plant this selection in loose, humus-rich soil beneath trees where little else will grow, and water regularly the first season while the thick rootstock establishes. Growth is slow, so choose a permanent spot; established clumps need only an annual topdressing of compost and are otherwise nearly maintenance-free. Compared to the straight species, this cultivar produces much larger, broader, heavily arching evergreen leaves in a bold architectural rosette, with the same inconspicuous fall flowers hidden at the base and red berries that follow. Its oversized leathery foliage makes a striking specimen or focal point in a deep-shade woodland bed where dramatic texture is otherwise hard to come by.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Gold Band develops its most vivid gold marginal banding in partial shade — deep shade may reduce the brightness of the yellow striping, while full sun can scorch the delicate variegation.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Gold Band is the premier gold-variegated liriope cultivar — producing dark-green, strap-like leaves with a consistent, bright-gold to cream-yellow marginal band along each leaf edge that creates a vivid two-tone effect more striking than the narrower variegation of some other liriope cultivars. The wide, clear gold banding on each leaf creates a bright, luminous effect in the shade garden — gold variegated foliage naturally reflects more light than solid green, making Gold Band an effective way to brighten dark shade areas with ground-level illumination. In late summer and fall, erect spikes of deep purple-violet flowers rise above the foliage, followed by ornamental black berries that persist into winter. Gold Band forms clumping mounds rather than spreading aggressively, making it appropriate for defined planting areas and as a border edging. The gold-variegated foliage creates outstanding textural and color contrast when mass-planted under dark-stemmed trees or combined with solid-green groundcovers, dark-foliaged heucheras, or the blue-gray tones of hostas. In zone 9, liriope is essentially bulletproof — tolerating heat, drought, shade, clay, and neglect with minimal performance reduction. Gold Band is evergreen throughout zone 9, providing year-round groundcover value. Shear to 3 inches in late winter to remove old or frost-damaged foliage before new spring growth emerges.

common_name: Gold Banded Liriope (Bold Gold-Edged Variegated Lilyturf for Partial Shade)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Gold Banded maintains brighter, more vivid gold-yellow margins in partial shade — full sun fades the gold toward cream-yellow, while deep shade reduces the gold intensity further.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Gold Banded is a variegated liriope (lilyturf) cultivar producing the characteristic strap-shaped, grass-like leaves of Liriope muscari with an added golden-yellow to bright yellow longitudinal stripe along each leaf margin — a bolder, warmer variegation than the cream-white margins of the more common 'Variegata' liriope. The wide gold-yellow leaf margins (sometimes covering 30–40% of the leaf width) create a vibrant, luminous visual that brightens shaded positions with warm-color light rather than the cooler cream-white of standard variegated liriope. Gold Banded is fully compatible with all the same growing conditions as standard liriope: adaptable to a wide range of soil types (including clay), drought-tolerant once established, salt-spray tolerant for coastal positions, and reliable in the full range of Gulf South zone 8-10 conditions. The spike of small lavender-purple flowers in late summer (August–September) above the variegated foliage is attractive and provides late-season color. Black berries in fall are decorative and provide food for some bird species. The gold variegation makes Gold Banded an outstanding border accent for partial-shade edges, where the warm-gold margins create a bright linear effect that defines the border line against adjacent lawn or darker mulch areas.

common_name: Gold Bar Miscanthus (Dwarf Banded Zebra Grass)
plant_note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; divide clumps every few years to maintain vigor and banding intensity.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing clumps every few years to maintain vigor and banding intensity. Discovered as an open-pollinated seedling of the banded cultivar Strictus, Gold Bar carries the same horizontal creamy-yellow banding but on a shorter, denser, more rigidly upright plant with far more numerous bands per leaf blade, giving it a bolder striped look than its parent. Flowering later in the season than most maiden grasses, it produces coppery-bronze plumes above the compact clump in late fall in warmer zones. Its small stature relative to typical Miscanthus sinensis makes it useful as an accent or specimen in gardens too small for full-size zebra or porcupine grass.

common_name: Gold Carpet Heucherella (Low Spreading Gold Foliage Foamy Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gold Carpet spreads by stolons into a low, dense groundcover mat, spreading more actively than clump-forming heucherella cultivars.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture combined with good drainage keeps the shallow root system healthy. Gold Carpet spreads by stolons into a low, dense mat of bright chartreuse-gold, maple-like leaves, functioning as a true groundcover rather than the tidy mound habit typical of most heucherella cultivars, making it useful for filling in bare shaded ground beneath trees or along a woodland path. Small, airy white flower spikes appear above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the season-long carpet of golden leaves. Water regularly during summer heat, and divide or thin the spreading mat as needed to keep it within bounds or to propagate additional plants for other areas of the garden.

common_name: Gold Cone Juniper (Narrow Columnar Golden-Foliage Juniper)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; golden foliage color is strongest and growth stays tightest with full sun, while light shade fades the color and loosens the columnar habit.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, since this narrow columnar juniper is intolerant of wet feet and develops its brightest gold color and tightest form with maximum light. Gold Cone is a sport of common juniper selected for a strongly upright, slender columnar habit and soft golden-yellow new growth that mellows to yellow-green with age, making it a popular vertical accent for narrow beds, foundation corners, and formal plantings where space is tight. It needs essentially no pruning to hold its naturally tidy spire shape and tolerates drought, wind, and poor soil once established, though it performs best in climates with a real winter chill and can struggle with humid, mild-winter heat. Avoid overhead watering and crowding, which encourage the fungal blights that trouble junipers in humid regions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Gold Dust Aucuba is a female cultivar — plant a male aucuba nearby for the red berries that develop in fall and persist through winter. 'Variegata' is female; males include 'Mr. Goldstrike' and other Aucuba japonica male selections. Plant in consistent shade — sun causes unattractive yellowing and leaf scorch. Aucuba tolerates the heavy shade under large evergreen trees, along north-facing walls, and beneath dense canopies where most other shrubs fail. Excellent salt and pollution tolerance makes it useful in difficult urban situations.
directions: Plant in deep shade to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Gold Dust Aucuba is one of the most shade-tolerant large shrubs available, thriving in conditions where direct sunlight never reaches and where most ornamental shrubs slowly decline; Gold Dust is the classic variegated cultivar of Japanese Aucuba (Aucuba japonica), producing large, glossy, dark green leaves heavily speckled and splashed with bright gold and yellow markings — a bold, striking foliage pattern that provides strong ornamental interest in the deep shade conditions where the plant grows best. The gold-speckled leaves literally brighten dark shade garden areas, reflecting and amplifying available light in a way that creates a visual sense of brightness even under dense tree canopy. The combination of large, lustrous, gold-variegated foliage with the tolerance to thrive in genuinely deep shade — not just the 'partial shade' that many 'shade plants' actually require — makes Gold Dust Aucuba one of the most useful and irreplaceable shrubs for the specific problem of planting in dense shade under established trees, along north-facing walls, or in any situation where direct sunlight is effectively absent. Pollinated female plants produce clusters of bright red to scarlet berries that develop in fall and persist through winter, adding seasonal fruit color to the year-round foliage interest.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Gold Dust dracaena is one of the more shade-tolerant dracaenas, thriving in dimmer corners better than most foliage houseplants.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Gold Dust dracaena is one of the more shade-tolerant dracaenas, thriving in dimmer corners better than most foliage houseplants. Slender, wiry, bamboo-like canes carry pairs of glossy, dark green, oval leaves speckled with irregular creamy-yellow spots that resemble flecks of gold dust scattered across the foliage, an airy, open growth habit quite different from the dense rosettes of most other dracaenas. Native to West African forest understories, it tolerates lower light than almost any other commonly grown dracaena, making it a good choice for a north-facing window or interior office space with only moderate natural light. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, avoid overwatering, and prune leggy canes to encourage bushier branching.

common_name: Gold Edger Hosta (Small Gold Groundcover Hosta)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil.
directions: Space divisions closely in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to take advantage of Gold Edger's dense, mounding habit as an edging or groundcover plant. It tolerates more sun than many hostas, which helps deepen its golden leaf color. The small, rounded, chartreuse-gold leaves form a tidy low mound, with pale lavender flowers rising just above the foliage in summer. Introduced by Paul Aden, Gold Edger is a fast-multiplying, reliable cultivar long used for edging paths and shaded borders.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; gold fountains sedge holds its bright variegated color best out of direct hot afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; gold fountains sedge forms a neat, arching mound of slender leaves edged in bright gold, the variegation showing strongest in the cultivar 'Kaga-nishiki' widely sold under this common name. Its fine, fountain-like texture and bright color brighten shaded plantings without the maintenance and disease concerns of many flowering shade perennials, holding good color from spring through fall in climates with humid summers. Inconspicuous flower spikes appear in spring but are incidental to the foliage display that is the plant's main ornamental feature. It combines well at the front of a shade border with hostas, ferns, and heucheras, providing a fine-textured, brightly colored contrast to their broader leaves, and it divides easily every few years in spring if a planting needs to be expanded or rejuvenated.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring while soil is cool; in zone 9 plant September–February for establishment before summer heat. Gold Heart bleeding heart is spring-ephemeral — the plant emerges from dormancy in late winter or early spring, blooms in April–May, and then goes completely dormant as summer heat arrives, disappearing from the garden until the following spring. In zone 9 the summer dormancy occurs earlier and more completely than in cooler climates. Mark plant locations to avoid disturbing dormant roots. The golden foliage is most vivid in spring emergence; overplanting with summer annuals conceals the dormant gap.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil — bleeding hearts require consistent moisture and cool root zone conditions; Gold Heart is a cultivar of the classic bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis, formerly Dicentra spectabilis) selected for its exceptional golden-yellow foliage — brilliant warm gold in spring when it first emerges from dormancy — that provides a dramatic contrast to the arching, pendant, rosy-pink heart-shaped flowers unique to bleeding hearts. While standard bleeding heart has conventional green foliage, Gold Heart's golden leaves transform the plant into a dual-feature specimen: an ornamental foliage plant even before the flowers appear and a striking flower display when the long, arching stems are laden with pendant heart-shaped blooms in April–May. The flowers have a characteristic two-outer-petal-over-two-inner-petal structure creating the perfect heart silhouette with a protruding white tip — one of the most instantly recognizable and beloved flower forms in the temperate garden. Gold Heart performs well throughout zone 9 as a spring ephemeral but requires excellent drainage to prevent crown rot during summer dormancy in hot, humid conditions.

common_name: Gold Lycaste (Dowiana Lycaste, Costa Rica Lycaste, Golden-Lipped Orchid)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in bark-based medium in a clay or wood container; Lycaste dowiana requires a cool-dry winter rest (nights 50–60°F, reduced watering October–February) for spring blooming. Without cool nights, the plant vegetates but does not flower. The leaves drop in fall as the plant enters dormancy. Flowers emerge from leafless or new-growth pseudobulbs in late winter or spring. One of the most beautiful yellow-flowered Lycaste species, similar in culture to L. aromatica. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light in bark medium in a clay or wooden pot — Gold Lycaste performs best in cool, well-ventilated conditions and benefits from the temperature differential between day and night typical of intermediate orchid cultivation. Lycaste dowiana is a deciduous, sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to Costa Rica and Panama in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most ornamentally beautiful of the Lycaste species and particularly valued for its large, richly colored flowers in golden-yellow. The plant produces large, angular pseudobulbs with broad, pleated leaves (up to 24 inches long) that drop in fall as the plant prepares for its winter rest period. From the leafless pseudobulbs in late winter and spring, individual flower spikes emerge (multiple per pseudobulb on well-established plants), each carrying a single large (4–5 inch), long-lasting flower in brilliant golden-yellow with an intensely colored, orange-red to orange-maroon, three-lobed lip that provides a vivid color contrast against the warm yellow petals. The flowers are pleasantly fragrant, with a sweet, honey-like quality. As with most Lycaste species, L. dowiana has contributed to many of the large-flowered hybrid Lycaste and Lycaste alliance orchids popular in cultivation, contributing its yellow color and vigor to the hybrids. An elegant, free-flowering orchid for zone 9-11 collectors with cool winter conditions. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Gold Mound is evergreen and root-hardy in zone 9a with freeze protection; it may die back to the ground in hard freezes but recovers quickly from the roots in spring. Place in full sun for the most intense golden-yellow foliage — plants in shade develop a greenish tint and lose the characteristic gold coloration.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Gold Mound Duranta is a compact, golden-foliaged cultivar of the tropical Duranta that produces stunning chartreuse-to-golden-yellow leaves throughout the growing season, in dramatic contrast to the deep green foliage of surrounding plants. Unlike the standard blue-flowered Duranta erecta, Gold Mound rarely flowers or fruits, redirecting its energy into the vivid foliage display that makes it a premier landscape accent in zone 9–11. The compact, mounding habit (2–4 feet tall and wide) makes it far more manageable than the standard species, which can reach 15–20 feet without regular pruning. Gold Mound performs exceptionally well as a low border plant, foundation shrub, or container specimen in the Gulf Coast, where it provides year-round color in the landscape. The bright gold leaves intensify through summer heat, and the plant withstands the full force of Gulf Coast summers without wilting or losing color.

plant_note: Plant container plants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Gold Mound is a compact, low-mounding lantana selected for its dense, tidy habit and solid clusters of bright golden-yellow flowers produced almost continuously from late spring through frost, drawing butterflies heavily throughout the season. Its smaller, more restrained scale than tall lantana cultivars like Miss Huff fits foundation plantings, border edges, and mass plantings where a lower, more uniform mound is wanted. It tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and poor soil with ease once established; cut back hard in late winter after the coldest weather passes to remove any winter-damaged growth and encourage vigorous new flowering growth.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after flowering to keep the mounded habit tidy and encourage fresh golden new growth. Gold Mound forms a low, dense, rounded mound of bright yellow-gold foliage that holds its color through the growing season better than many gold-leaved spirea cultivars, accented by flat clusters of small pink flowers in early summer. Its compact, tidy habit and reliable color make it a popular choice for low borders, foundation edges, and mass plantings needing consistent, low-maintenance color. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, it tolerates poor soil and urban heat with minimal care.

plant_note: Sow indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or plant divisions in spring in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Gold Plate needs excellent drainage and resents heavy, wet clay.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun, staking in windy sites if needed to keep the tall stems upright, and cut flower heads for fresh or dried arrangements just as they fully open. Gold Plate is a classic straight-species selection of the Caucasus native Achillea filipendulina, distinguished from hybrid yarrows by its exceptionally large, flat, mustard-gold flower heads — often 5–6 inches across — held well above ferny, aromatic, gray-green foliage on sturdy stems. It is among the tallest garden yarrows, valued for the back of the border and for cutting gardens, and its dried flower heads hold color for months. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established; divide congested clumps every 2–3 years in spring to maintain vigor and flower size.

common_name: Gold Standard Hosta (Classic Gold-Centered Green-Margined Hosta)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gold Standard is one of the most widely planted variegated hosta cultivars, with leaves that emerge chartreuse-green and mature to a bright golden-yellow center edged in a contrasting dark green margin.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the brightest gold color. Gold Standard is one of the most enduringly popular variegated hosta cultivars, producing medium-to-large clumps of heart-shaped leaves that emerge chartreuse-green in spring and brighten through the season to a vivid golden-yellow center framed by a distinct, contrasting dark green margin, a striking color transformation that provides changing seasonal interest from a single planting. Pale lavender flowers rise above the foliage on tall scapes in mid-to-late summer. The gold coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic coloring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage, and apply iron phosphate bait around vulnerable new growth if damage appears.

plant_note: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Gold Star croton needs strong light to hold its bright yellow leaf speckling.
directions: Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Gold Star croton needs strong light to hold its bright yellow leaf speckling. Narrow, elongated, glossy green leaves are heavily speckled with bright golden-yellow spots that can nearly cover the leaf surface in strong light, one of the most vividly gold-toned of the many croton leaf-color selections and a striking accent among the deeper reds and oranges of other croton cultivars. Like other crotons it colors most intensely with abundant direct or bright indirect light, fading to duller green in low light, and it holds its foliage year-round in frost-free gardens or as a long-lived container and houseplant elsewhere. Water when the top inch of soil dries, protect from any frost, and wipe dust from the glossy leaves periodically to keep them looking their best.

common_name: Gold Star Esperanza (Cold-Hardy Compact Yellow Bells)
plant_note: Set out transplants after last frost in full sun in well-drained, lean, alkaline-tolerant soil; Gold Star was selected for improved cold hardiness and a more compact habit than standard yellow bells, allowing roots to survive winters as cold as zone 7b-8a where the species itself typically needs zone 8b or warmer to reliably return.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil after the danger of frost has passed. Gold Star is a selection of esperanza (yellow bells) chosen for a more cold-hardy root system and a more compact, better-branched habit than the standard species, which lets gardeners in zone 7b and 8a grow it as a reliable perennial that dies back to the ground and resprouts each spring, rather than needing to treat it as a tender annual or overwinter it indoors. It produces the same masses of bright golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped, hummingbird-attracting flowers from early summer through the first hard frost, but on a shrub that typically stays a more manageable 4-6 feet rather than the 8-12 feet the straight species can reach in zone 9-11. In milder zones it remains semi-evergreen; where winters kill the top growth, cut the dead stems back to the ground in late winter and the plant resprouts vigorously and blooms the same season. Prune to shape in early spring to encourage the most compact, floriferous growth.

common_name: Gold Thread Cypress (Threadleaf Golden False Cypress)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; the golden color develops best with several hours of direct sun daily.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, keeping soil evenly moist, especially while young, since this species is less drought-tolerant than junipers or pines. Gold Thread Cypress forms a loose, mounded to broadly pyramidal shrub of cascading, thread-like, bright golden-yellow foliage that provides strong, season-long color contrast against green-leaved shrubs and dark conifers, with the color often deepening to a coppery gold in winter cold. Its fine, weeping texture and bold color make it an effective specimen or focal point in a mixed shrub border or foundation planting. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or damaged branches; avoid shearing, which disrupts the natural cascading form.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; gold tree blooms spectacularly for 1–2 weeks before and just as the leaves emerge in late winter/early spring — the entire tree covered in brilliant golden-yellow trumpet flowers with no leaves visible. One of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–12; the gold tree (golden trumpet tree) produces one of the most spectacular flowering displays of any tree in the world — for 1–2 weeks in late winter or early spring, the entire tree is covered in blazing, golden-yellow trumpet flowers before a single leaf has emerged, creating a vision of solid gold visible from hundreds of feet away. The display lasts only 1–2 weeks and is immediately followed by the production of deeply cut, palmate compound leaves. The species is the national tree of Brazil and widely planted as a street and specimen tree throughout the tropics. Drought-tolerant once established, growing naturally in deciduous tropical dry forest. In south Florida (zone 10), it produces its spectacular bloom in February-March — one of the great floral spectacles of the Miami-Fort Lauderdale area.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or divide established plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; gold and silver chrysanthemum is valued primarily as a foliage plant and groundcover rather than for its flowers. The small, yellow button flowers appear very late — October-November — and may not fully open before frost in northern zones, but the foliage is ornamental from spring through fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; gold and silver chrysanthemum is grown primarily for its exceptionally beautiful foliage rather than its flowers — the deeply lobed, dark forest-green leaves are edged and outlined with a neat, precise border of bright, silvery-white hairs that precisely traces every contour of each leaf lobe and margin, creating the striking two-tone appearance that gives the plant its common name. The contrast between the dark green leaf surface and the precise silver edging is quite extraordinary, particularly in autumn when cooler temperatures intensify both the green and the silver tones. The plant forms a low, mounding, spreading groundcover that is drought-tolerant and adaptable to a range of soils once established. Small, mustard-yellow button flowers appear very late in October and November and may not fully develop before frost in zone 5-6 gardens, but in warmer zones the late bloom adds an additional seasonal interest. Native to coastal cliffs and rocky slopes of Japan, it thrives in well-drained conditions in full sun.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Goldband sedge is a well-behaved clumper that neither runs nor self-sows aggressively.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Goldband sedge is a well-behaved clumper that neither runs nor self-sows aggressively. Arching, grass-like leaves are edged in a bold golden-yellow band that brightens through the growing season and holds its color well into winter in mild climates, giving the evergreen clump year-round presence. It forms a neat, fountain-shaped mound that works equally well as a container centerpiece, a border edger, or massed as a groundcover under high-canopy shade trees where turf will not grow. Comb out old, tattered leaves by hand in late winter rather than shearing, and divide only when the center of the clump begins to thin.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification; seed requires 60–90 days of cold, moist conditions before spring germination. Division of established clumps in spring provides faster establishment.
directions: Sow cold-stratified seed in fall or early spring in moist, average to rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; this early-blooming native carrot-family plant produces flat-topped clusters of small yellow flowers in April–May, making it one of the earliest sources of pollen for native bees, beetles, and flies at a time when little else is blooming. It is also an important early host plant for black swallowtail butterflies, whose caterpillars feed on the ferny foliage. The plants are short-lived but self-sow reliably in suitable conditions. Excellent at the front of the native plant border or naturalized in a moist meadow.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; alternatively, cold-stratify seeds for 60–90 days in the refrigerator and direct sow in early spring — golden alexanders requires a cold moist period to break dormancy and germinates poorly without stratification.
directions: Direct sow in fall, or cold-stratify for 60–90 days and sow in spring, in moist to average, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; golden alexanders is one of the most shade-tolerant native wildflowers in the carrot family and is an excellent choice for lightly shaded or woodland-edge gardens with moist soil. Zizia aurea is a native North American perennial in the Apiaceae (carrot/parsley) family producing bright, golden-yellow, flat-topped umbels of tiny flowers in April through June — one of the earliest yellow-flowered natives to bloom, bridging the gap between spring bulbs and summer perennials; it is a critical early-season nectar source for native bees and an important larval host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly (Papilio polyxenes), whose caterpillars feed on the foliage. It tolerates partial shade and moist to periodically wet soils and naturalizes beautifully in rain gardens, woodland margins, and native plant meadows. Dark green, compound leaves remain attractive throughout the season after bloom.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; golden angel's trumpet produces large, pendant, golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers and is one of the most spectacular large-flowered tropical shrubs. CAUTION: All parts of all Brugmansia species are extremely toxic — do not plant where children or pets have unsupervised access.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; golden angel's trumpet is an Andean species producing enormous, pendant, trumpet-shaped flowers up to 12 inches long in soft golden-yellow, often with a rich, sweet, tropical fragrance strongest in the evening. A single well-grown plant can carry dozens of pendant blooms simultaneously, creating a spectacular tropical accent. Like all Brugmansia, all plant parts are dangerously toxic — containing tropane alkaloids (scopolamine, atropine) that cause hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, and potentially fatal poisoning. Never use any plant part medicinally without expert guidance. In zone 9, grow as a container plant moved indoors in winter or in a frost-protected location. Fertilize heavily with a balanced fertilizer every 2 weeks during the growing season to achieve maximum bloom production. The large, pendant flowers are adapted for pollination by large hawk moths.

common_name: Golden Angel's Trumpet (Large Pendulous Yellow-Trumpet Brugmansia Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; all parts of Brugmansia are toxic if ingested — plant away from children's play areas and avoid contact with sap; wash hands after pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Queen is a yellow-flowered Brugmansia (angel's trumpet) producing the spectacular large-scale tropical display characteristic of the genus — very large (10–14 inch), pendulous, trumpet-shaped flowers in warm golden-yellow hanging in clusters from the branch tips, releasing an extraordinary heavy fragrance particularly intense in the evening hours. The golden-yellow flower color of 'Golden Queen' is distinctly different from the white, peach, pink, and apricot tones of other angel's trumpet varieties — a warm, pure yellow that creates a dramatic tropical focal point in partial shade. In zone 9, Brugmansia grows as a large tropical shrub or small tree reaching 6–12 feet, blooming most heavily in spring and fall as temperatures moderate from summer extremes. The plant requires generous water and fertility to produce its finest flower display — large containers require daily watering in summer. All parts of Brugmansia are toxic if ingested and should be handled with caution; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. In zone 9b and 10, Golden Queen grows as a perennial. In zone 9a, frost may kill the top growth but the plant often returns from the roots with mulch protection; container-grown specimens can be moved indoors before frost. The spectacular flowers and fragrance make angel's trumpets one of the most dramatic ornamentals for Gulf South tropical garden designs.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Anniversary bears gold-and-green variegated foliage that turns purple-red in fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, which brings out the brightest gold variegation. Golden Anniversary bears leaves brightly marked in gold and green that shift to purple-red tones in fall, giving the shrub multi-season foliage interest beyond its clusters of small white summer flowers. Its bold variegation makes it a strong accent in a mixed border, especially paired with dark-foliaged companions for contrast. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs only light pruning after the main bloom flush to maintain shape.

common_name: Golden Anniversary Lamium (Gold-Edged Silver-Striped Dead Nettle)
plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Golden Anniversary bears green leaves broadly edged in gold with a silver center stripe, a brighter, warmer variegation than solid-silver Lamium cultivars, useful for lighting up deep shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun, which scorches the variegated foliage. Golden Anniversary bears distinctively three-toned leaves, a broad golden-yellow margin surrounding a central silvery stripe over green, a warmer, brighter variegation pattern than the solid-silver Lamium cultivars more commonly grown, paired with lavender-pink flowers from late spring into summer. The gold edging is especially effective at lighting up deep or dry shade beneath trees, where its glow reads clearly even in low light. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to encourage fresh growth, and divide congested patches in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Golden Apeldoorn Tulip (Golden-Yellow Darwin Hybrid with Black Base)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Golden Apeldoorn is a golden-yellow sport of the classic red Apeldoorn Darwin hybrid tulip, with a black basal blotch.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Golden Apeldoorn, a golden-yellow sport of the classic red Apeldoorn Darwin hybrid, bears large, clear yellow blooms marked with a contrasting black basal blotch at the center, on strong, tall stems typical of the Darwin hybrid group. Darwin hybrids like Golden Apeldoorn also tend to perennialize somewhat better than many other tulip types in climates with adequate winter chill, though in mild-winter zone 8-9 gardens they are still usually most reliable treated as a fresh fall planting.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Golden Ball Cactus is more tolerant of light shade than many columnar cacti but colors and flowers best in full sun.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Golden Ball Cactus is more tolerant of light shade than many columnar cacti but colors and flowers best in full sun. A densely ribbed, cylindrical cactus is entirely clothed in soft, glowing golden-yellow spines that catch the light and give the whole plant a warm, luminous glow, starting as a rounded ball and slowly elongating into a short column over many years, eventually producing bright yellow flowers near the crown once mature. Native to southern Brazil, it is slow-growing but very long-lived and low-maintenance, tolerating a wide range of indoor and outdoor conditions better than many spinier, more temperamental cacti. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide as much direct light as possible for the richest golden spine color, and protect from frost.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in fall or early spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; scarify seed for faster, more even germination if starting from seed.
directions: Plant container-grown stock in fall or early spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; this Trans-Pecos native thrives in exactly the hot, dry, alkaline conditions that defeat most flowering trees. Fragrant, powder-puff, golden-yellow flower balls cover the fine, mimosa-like bipinnate foliage in flushes from spring through fall, especially after summer rain, drawing bees and butterflies, and the plant is unarmed (thornless), unlike mesquite or acacia. It is usually grown as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small specimen tree and is extremely drought tolerant once established, needing supplemental water only the first year or two. Hard freezes can kill it to the ground, but it reliably resprouts from the root in spring.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; golden bamboo REQUIRES a bamboo root barrier (18-inch deep polypropylene sheet) before planting — it is a highly aggressive running bamboo that will invade neighboring properties and is invasive in many southeastern US states without containment.
directions: Plant ONLY within a contained area using an 18-inch deep root barrier in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; golden bamboo (also called fishpole bamboo for its use in making fishing poles) is the most widely planted and most problematic bamboo in the southeastern US — it has naturalized and become invasive along streams, roadsides, and disturbed areas from the Carolinas to Texas, outcompeting native vegetation. Despite its invasive potential, it remains widely sold and planted because of its fast growth, dense screening ability, and striking golden-yellow canes as they mature. The culms turn yellow-gold with age (green when young), and the distinctive swollen internodes near the base of young shoots are characteristic. If used, ALWAYS contain with a root barrier and remove rhizomes that escape under or through the barrier. Harvest young edible shoots when they emerge in spring. Listed as invasive in multiple southeastern states.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring into very well-drained, gritty, mineral soil in full sun; golden barrel cactus grows extremely slowly from seed, so nearly all garden specimens are purchased as nursery-grown plants rather than started at home.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, mineral soil in full sun; golden barrel cactus is one of the most recognizable and widely grown landscape cacti, forming a nearly perfect sphere ribbed with stiff, golden-yellow spines that intensify in color with strong sun exposure. Growth is famously slow, gaining only an inch or two of diameter per year even in ideal conditions, so a large specimen represents many years of growth and is valued accordingly in the nursery trade. A ring of small yellow flowers may appear atop mature specimens in summer once the plant reaches significant size, though many garden specimens never flower. Water only during the warm growing season and withhold water almost entirely in winter, since cold, wet soil is the primary cause of rot in this otherwise tough, long-lived desert species.

common_name: Golden Celebration Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Golden Celebration's large, heavy blooms benefit from a bit of afternoon shade in the hottest climates and a sturdy, well-branched framework to support the flower weight.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1992, Golden Celebration is one of the most celebrated of all English roses, bearing very large, deeply cupped, rich golden-yellow blooms with a strong, warm fragrance often compared to sauternes wine and tea, on a vigorous, arching shrub with glossy, disease-resistant foliage. Its combination of flower size, color saturation, and fragrance made it an instant classic, and it repeat-blooms generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading, tolerating heat better than many older yellow rose cultivars.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; golden chain tree grows naturally on alkaline limestone soils and tolerates chalky conditions better than most ornamental trees. The hybrid 'Vossii' produces the longest pendulous chains of flowers and sets fewer viable seeds than the species, reducing the risk of seed toxicity. ALL PARTS ARE HIGHLY TOXIC if ingested — keep away from children and pets.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; golden chain tree is one of the most spectacular of all spring-flowering trees, producing long, pendant racemes of brilliant, clear-yellow pea flowers up to 24 inches in length in May and June — so dense and vividly colored that the entire tree appears to drip with cascades of golden chains, from which the common name derives. The famous Laburnum Walk at Bodnant Garden in Wales — a 180-foot tunnel of intertwined laburnums, trained overhead to create a tunnel of golden chains — demonstrates the full theatrical potential of this tree. In smaller gardens, a single mature specimen in full bloom against a dark background or blue sky is extraordinary. Native to central Europe and tolerant of shallow, chalky soils and part shade. The hybrid 'Vossii' is the most commonly planted, with the longest flower chains. EXTREME CAUTION: all parts of the plant, especially the seed pods and seeds, contain cytisine (a toxic alkaloid similar to nicotine) and are highly poisonous — the plant should never be planted where children play.

plant_note: Divide and plant rhizomes in spring once water temperatures warm above 60°F, placing crowns in heavy loam or clay aquatic soil in containers submerged 6–12 inches below the water surface; golden club thrives in the still or slow-moving water of ponds, streams, and freshwater wetlands and is among the most shade-tolerant of native aquatic plants. Site in partial shade to full sun — it tolerates considerably more shade than most aquatics. Established clumps can be divided every 3–4 years in spring.
directions: Plant in still to slow-moving water 4–12 inches deep in heavy, nutrient-rich aquatic soil in partial shade to full sun; golden club is one of the most distinctive and visually striking native aquatic plants of eastern North America, producing in early spring — often while other plants are barely stirring — unusual upright flower spathes consisting of a slender, bright golden-yellow spadix on a pure-white stem, held above the water surface like a glowing torch that gives the plant its evocative common name. The large, oblong, blue-green leaves have a remarkably hydrophobic waxy surface coating that causes water to bead and roll off in glistening droplets, a phenomenon known as the lotus effect, making the foliage appear perpetually dry and silvery in wet conditions. Orontium aquaticum is tolerant of considerable shade compared to most aquatics — a valuable trait for water features beneath overhanging tree canopies where many emergent plants fail to perform — and spreads gradually by rhizome to form a handsome colony. A superb choice for naturalistic ponds, rain gardens with permanent water features, and native plant water gardens throughout zones 5–10.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall to allow natural cold-moist stratification and spring germination; alternatively, cold-stratify seed for 3–4 weeks at 40°F and sow in early spring. Golden columbine self-sows readily and a well-placed colony will naturalize and self-perpetuate over time.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Aquilegia chrysantha is a native columbine of the American Southwest — native to canyon walls, stream banks, and moist woodland edges in New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico — and is one of the most heat-tolerant and long-blooming of all columbines, producing exceptionally long-spurred, bright yellow flowers on 3–4 foot stems from late spring through summer, with the spurs significantly longer than those of most other columbine species. It is an outstanding hummingbird plant, and the extralong nectar spurs are specifically adapted to hummingbird pollination; both hummingbirds and sphinx moths visit the flowers avidly. More tolerant of heat and dry conditions than European columbines, it performs reliably into zone 9 in the West with afternoon shade. Allow to self-sow freely to build a naturalized colony; plants are short-lived perennials (3–5 years) that persist through abundant self-seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in well-drained, rocky, sandy, or disturbed lean soil in partial shade to full sun; golden corydalis is a winter annual to biennial that germinates in cool weather and blooms in spring through early summer. It self-sows readily in rocky, open, disturbed areas.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, rocky, sandy, or lean disturbed soil in partial shade to full sun; golden corydalis is a charming, finely dissected-leaved native annual of rocky, disturbed soils, stream gravel bars, talus slopes, and sandy open ground across a wide range of North America from Alaska to Texas. The bright, pure golden-yellow flowers are produced in dense terminal clusters on sprawling, succulent stems from spring through early summer. Common names 'scrambled eggs' aptly describes the tumbled, bright yellow flower clusters. Self-sows freely in rocky, open, disturbed garden areas to create naturalized colonies that persist indefinitely. One of the more widespread and adaptable native Corydalis species, tolerating a range of climates from boreal to semi-arid. Visited by bumblebees and long-tongued specialist bees that access the spurred flowers.

plant_note: Set out rooted stem cuttings or container plants into well-drained sandy soil in spring after frost danger passes; water in well and then taper off once roots establish.
directions: Native to the coastal strand and stabilized dunes of peninsular Florida, golden creeper forms a low, mounding evergreen mat with narrow succulent leaves and small yellow-green tubular flowers followed by orange-red fruit. It spreads by trailing stems that root as they touch sand, making it an effective low groundcover for binding dune soil without the height of sea oats or panic grass.
