Apply acidic camellia-azalea fertilizer in spring and early fall; maintain 3–4 inches of pine bark mulch at all times to protect the shallow root system.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (October–November in zone 9) for winter establishment and spring bloom; Clarkia amoena does not transplant well and must be direct-sown. Cool soil (50–65°F) is required for good germination. In zone 9 fall sowing is the appropriate approach — spring sowing in warming soil produces poor germination and short-lived, heat-stressed plants. Grace Pink produces large (2–3 inch), semi-double, satiny pink flowers with a slightly darker pink center zone — a classic, clear, pure pink that is effective in mixed cool-season plantings. Plants in zone 9 bloom February–April before summer heat arrives. Self-seeds modestly in zone 9 where soil conditions are appropriate. Godetia (Clarkia amoena) is native to the Pacific Coast of North America.
directions: Direct sow in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent cool-season moisture — Godetia germinates and grows best in cool conditions (50–65°F) and declines rapidly as summer heat arrives; Grace Pink Godetia is a compact selection of Farewell-to-Spring (Clarkia amoena), a Pacific Coast native wildflower producing satiny, semi-double, clear rose-pink flowers (2–3 inches) on upright stems in late winter and spring — one of the most elegantly textured cool-season annuals available, with a silky petal surface that catches and reflects light in a way that gives the flowers an unusual luminous quality. The satiny, slightly translucent texture of godetia petals is entirely different from the matte, paper-like texture of many other cool-season annuals, providing an unusual visual refinement that makes godetia flowers one of the most elegant and graceful cut flowers available from a direct-sow cool-season crop. The clear, pure pink of Grace Pink — without the purple or salmon undertones that characterize many pink annual flowers — works harmoniously with virtually any companion planting in the cool-season garden, from blue violas to white alyssum to yellow snapdragons. In zone 9 fall-sown godetia provides a distinctive and relatively under-used February–April bloom display that is more refined and elegant in character than the more commonly planted cool-season annuals.

common_name: Grace Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Grace's slightly nodding flower habit shows the blooms to good effect on a raised bed or slope where they can be viewed from below.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001, Grace bears warm apricot, deeply cupped rosette blooms with a light tea fragrance, on a vigorous, well-branched shrub whose slightly nodding flower habit distinguishes it from more upright-facing English rose cultivars. Its warm, glowing apricot tone pairs well with both cool blues and other warm-toned companions in a mixed border, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Grace Smokebush (Large-Leaved Purple Hybrid Smoke Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained to dry, average to lean soil in full sun; Grace is a hybrid between the European and American smoke trees, larger and more vigorous than typical Cotinus coggygria cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, average to lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this hybrid smoke tree tolerates rocky, sandy soils where many flowering shrubs struggle. Grace is a cross between the European smoke tree and the American smoke tree, combining larger, more translucent wine-purple leaves with a taller, more vigorous, tree-like habit than most Cotinus coggygria cultivars, and its summer display of airy, pink-tinged smoke-like flower panicles is correspondingly larger and showier. The purple foliage takes on brilliant scarlet-orange fall color before dropping, giving the plant a second season of strong ornamental interest. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, needing only an occasional thinning cut in late winter to maintain an open, well-shaped form; hard pruning each spring produces larger leaves but sacrifices the summer smoke display, so choose a pruning approach based on which effect matters more in a given planting.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to shallow-water conditions in full sun; graceful cattail is a smaller, more refined Eurasian cattail well-suited to smaller water gardens and ponds where the native broadleaf or narrowleaf cattail would be too large and vigorous.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to shallow-water conditions in full sun; graceful cattail is a Eurasian species intermediate in size between dwarf cattail (T. minima) and the common cattails, reaching only 3–5 feet — making it considerably more manageable for smaller water gardens. The brown seed heads are smaller and more graceful than those of common cattails, and the gap between male and female sections is more pronounced and consistent. While spreading by rhizomes as all cattails do, it is less aggressively spreading than broadleaf cattail. Provides excellent wildlife habitat at a human-garden scale: the seed cotton, young shoots, and pollen are all usable as described for other cattail species. A refined and underused alternative to native cattails for ornamental water gardens and small ponds where scale is important.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gracillimus performs best in full sun — in partial shade the arching form becomes loose and floppy, and fall color and flowering are reduced.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gracillimus is the classic maiden grass — the most refined and elegant Miscanthus sinensis cultivar, producing fine-textured, very narrow (1/4-inch wide), arching, medium-green leaves with a thin, white midrib that catches the sun and gives the planting a silver-glinting effect in breeze. The extremely fine leaf texture contrasts beautifully with bold-textured companions like hostas, rudbeckias, and coneflowers. Gracillimus grows into a large, gracefully arching fountain form (5–7 feet tall, 4–5 feet wide) that provides outstanding textural accent in the perennial border and a striking specimen effect when planted singly or in small groups. In late summer and fall, copper-red to bronze flower plumes rise above the foliage and dry to soft tan-gold, providing winter interest that persists until cut back in late winter. The seed heads are attractive to finches and other seed-eating birds. Note: Miscanthus sinensis can be invasive in some eastern states — check local invasive species guidance before planting near natural areas. In zone 9, Gracillimus is reliably perennial and may flower in late summer before cutting back in late winter. Cut to 6 inches in February before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Graffiti was bred for a compact, uniform, early-flowering habit better suited to bedding and container use than taller, later-blooming seed-grown pentas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, and expect a compact, floriferous plant that begins blooming quickly and continues nonstop through the hottest part of summer. Graffiti is a vegetatively propagated pentas series bred for a smaller, more uniform, earlier-flowering habit than older seed-grown pentas, producing dense clusters of small, star-shaped flowers in red, pink, lavender, or white that are outstanding at drawing butterflies and hummingbirds throughout the growing season. Its compact size makes it especially well suited to container plantings, small beds, and mass landscape use where a shorter, tidier plant is preferred over taller pentas selections. Deadheading is not required for continued bloom, and the plant tolerates heat and humidity with ease, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South pollinator gardens through summer's peak.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Graffiti pentas is grown as an annual in zones below 10 and as a short-lived perennial in zone 10–11 where light frosts are rare. Deadheading spent flower clusters encourages continuous bloom but is not strictly necessary — Graffiti series was selected for its tendency to bloom continuously without requiring deadheading. In zone 9 pentas thrives in the hottest summer weeks when most other flowering annuals decline, blooming most freely from June through October in intense heat.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Graffiti Red is an All-America Selections award-winning compact pentas (Egyptian star flower) from the Graffiti series — a heat-loving tropical annual producing dense, domed clusters of vivid red, five-petaled star-shaped flowers continuously from planting until frost. Pentas is genuinely tropical in its heat preferences, performing most vigorously in zone 9's intense summer months and essentially thriving in the conditions (high temperature, high humidity) that cause most cool-season annuals to fail. The five-petaled star flowers are a key butterfly, hummingbird, and skipper nectar source — the flat, open flower structure accessible to a wide range of pollinators and the brilliant red color attracting hummingbirds make Graffiti Red one of the most effective wildlife garden plants for the Gulf Coast summer. The compact Graffiti habit (12–18 inches vs. the sprawling 3+ feet of older pentas varieties) makes it suitable for container plantings, front-border use, and formal bedding where tidiness is required.

common_name: Graham Blandy Boxwood (Extremely Narrow Columnar Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Graham Blandy's extremely narrow form makes it useful in tight spaces where even standard columnar boxwood cultivars would be too wide.
directions: Graham Blandy is one of the narrowest columnar boxwood cultivars available, growing tall and slender in a tight, almost exclamation-point form that fits spaces too narrow for other upright boxwood selections, such as flanking a narrow gate or walkway. Its fine, deep green foliage provides the same year-round formal structure as other boxwood but in a distinctly vertical, space-saving silhouette that needs little pruning to maintain. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; because its narrow form relies on strong vertical growth, avoid heavy shearing that would disrupt its naturally columnar habit.

common_name: Graham Thomas Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Graham Thomas grows as a large, arching shrub in most gardens but can be trained as a short climber to 10-12 feet in warm climates, making it flexible for a border, hedge, or trellis.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood; where grown as a climber, tie the long canes horizontally along a fence or trellis to maximize side-shoot flowering. Bred by David Austin and introduced in 1983, Graham Thomas was named for the renowned English rosarian and combines the rich, deep golden-yellow, cupped-to-rosette blooms and strong tea fragrance of an old garden rose with the vigor and repeat-flowering habit of a modern shrub rose. It quickly became one of the best-selling English roses ever introduced and remains a benchmark yellow rose for its combination of color saturation, fragrance, and reliable rebloom from late spring through frost. It shows good disease resistance in humid climates when given full sun and adequate air movement.

common_name: Gran's Favourite Dianthus (White Laced Reddish-Purple Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Gran's Favourite bears white semi-double flowers heavily laced in reddish-purple, holder of an RHS Award of Garden Merit.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Gran's Favourite, a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit garden pink, bears semi-double white flowers intricately laced with a fine reddish-purple pattern radiating from the center, a refined old-fashioned look prized by dianthus collectors, carried on a compact, fragrant, blue-green foliage mound. It shows good heat tolerance for the class when grown in sharply drained, lean soil. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

plant_note: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to moderately moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; grand crinum requires ample room to develop — the mature bulb can reach 12 inches across and the leaf spread 5–6 feet. Avoid disturbing established clumps as transplanting sets the plant back significantly.
directions: Plant with the bulb neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained, moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; grand crinum lily is one of the most enduring and spectacular large-scale ornamental bulbs for coastal Gulf Coast landscapes, producing massive strap-like leaves and large, fragrant, spider-like clusters of white flowers with long, recurved petals and prominent red anthers on stout stems 2–3 feet tall — blooming repeatedly from spring through fall. A single well-established bulb produces a clump 4–5 feet wide with multiple bloom stalks simultaneously, creating a dramatic tropical effect. Crinum asiaticum is exceptionally salt tolerant — it is one of the few large ornamental plants that thrives in coastal beachfront conditions right to the edge of salt spray. It also tolerates periodic flooding and waterlogged soils remarkably well, making it valuable for low spots and wet areas where other plants struggle. Essentially indestructible once established; plants decades old are commonly found thriving without any maintenance in old Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Grand Duchess sorrel follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — growing and blooming in winter and spring, going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer. Several color forms are in cultivation — 'Grand Duchess White', 'Grand Duchess Lavender', 'Grand Duchess Pink' — all sold as selections of this species. The flowers are notably large for the genus, opening to 1.5–2 inches across.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Grand Duchess sorrel is among the most prolific and showy of all the winter-growing Cape oxalis — producing from winter through spring an extended succession of large (1.5–2 inch), flat-faced, funnel-shaped flowers in clear, vivid purple to rose-purple to lavender or white (depending on the selected form), each flower with a contrasting yellow center, rising above compact, clover-like, dark-green foliage in a continuous, profuse bloom display that can last 3–4 months of winter and early spring. The flowers are substantially larger than most Cape oxalis species, giving the plant a presence disproportionate to its small bulb size. It has been selected into named color forms ('Grand Duchess White', 'Grand Duchess Lavender', 'Grand Duchess Pink') sold in the bulb trade and widely grown in California and Mediterranean-climate gardens. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, it provides a bright, low-maintenance, winter-through-spring color display that requires almost no attention — plant the bulbs in fall, enjoy the flowers from winter through April, water withheld in summer. One of the most rewarding and easy-to-grow winter bulbs for warm-climate gardens.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11.
directions: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Fully double, camellia-like white flowers open in clusters from summer through fall, releasing the classic, powerfully sweet Arabian jasmine fragrance used to scent jasmine tea, with far more petals per flower than the simpler single or semi-double forms of the species, making this one of the most ornamentally prized jasmine cultivars for fragrance gardens. Its warmth-loving nature makes it a superb container plant that can be moved to a sheltered spot or brought indoors for winter outside the warmest zones, continuing to bloom under bright indoor light with adequate humidity. Water regularly, feed during the growing season to sustain the heavy, fragrant bloom, and prune after flowering to shape and encourage bushier growth.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, fertile, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; grand fir grows naturally in moist river valleys and lower mountain slopes of the Pacific Northwest and inland Rockies. Faster growing than most firs when provided adequate moisture.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, fertile, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; grand fir is the fastest-growing of the true firs (Abies) in the Pacific Northwest — capable of adding 2–3 feet per year in ideal moist, fertile conditions. The largest grand firs reach over 200 feet in the Cascade Range. The needles are distinctively arranged in two flat, horizontal ranks on each branchlet (like a comb), with the dark green upper surface contrasting with the two white stomatal bands on the undersides. When crushed, the needles produce a pleasant citrus-like fragrance. Grand fir is an important component of moist Douglas-fir and western hemlock forest communities at lower elevations. The Christmas tree industry occasionally uses grand fir, but the less-aromatic fragrance and shorter needle retention make it less preferred than noble fir and Fraser fir. An excellent fast-growing ornamental for large, moist landscape sites in zones 5–8.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Grand Monarque is an antebellum-era heirloom tazetta long grown as a Southern pass-along bulb alongside Grand Primo and paperwhites, sharing their low chilling requirement and reliable naturalizing habit.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Grand Monarque is a classic antebellum Southern heirloom tazetta, bearing clusters of fragrant, creamy white flowers with a pale lemon-yellow cup on each strong stem, blooming in mid to late winter ahead of most other daffodils. Like Grand Primo, its low chilling requirement makes it one of the most reliable narcissus for perennializing in mild Gulf South winters, and it has been passed hand to hand between Southern gardeners for generations, often found still blooming each year at old homesites long after the house and garden around it have vanished. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and once established, let the clumps multiply undisturbed for years before dividing.

common_name: Grand Primo Daffodil (Classic Fragrant Southern Heirloom Tazetta)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Grand Primo is a classic Southern heirloom tazetta daffodil that has naturalized into huge drifts around old homesites and cemeteries across the Deep South for well over a century.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Grand Primo is one of the classic Southern heirloom pass-along daffodils, a multi-flowered tazetta bearing clusters of fragrant, creamy white flowers with a pale lemon-yellow cup on each stem, blooming reliably each winter in old Deep South gardens, cemeteries, and abandoned homesites where it has naturalized into vast drifts over a century or more with zero care. Its low chilling requirement makes it one of the most dependable daffodils for perennializing in mild Gulf South winters, unlike many modern trumpet daffodils that need cold most Southern gardens cannot provide. Allow the foliage to die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and once established, simply leave the bulbs undisturbed to multiply on their own for years.

common_name: Grand Slam Camellia (Bright Red Peony-Form Camellia japonica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Grand Slam is a popular award-winning Camellia japonica cultivar valued for its large, vivid red, semi-double to peony-form flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Grand Slam is a widely grown Camellia japonica cultivar bearing large, bright, true red flowers in a loose semi-double to peony form packed with ruffled petals, one of the most vivid reds available among camellia cultivars and a longtime award winner on the camellia show circuit. The vigorous, upright evergreen shrub blooms in mid-season and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its striking winter flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Grandchild is an award-winning, double, reflexed mauve-pink chrysanthemum on a hardy bushy perennial.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil. Grandchild bears fully double, reflexed flowers in soft mauve-pink, the petals curving gracefully backward toward the stem in the classic reflexed form, on a hardy, bushy perennial that has earned recognition among garden mum enthusiasts for its reliable performance and refined bloom shape. Pinch stem tips in spring and early summer to promote bushy, compact growth, and divide clumps every two to three years to prevent crowding and maintain vigor.

common_name: Grandiflora Hydrangea (Hills of Snow, Historic Round White Smooth Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Grandiflora, known historically as Hills of Snow, is an older round-flowered smooth hydrangea selection predating Annabelle.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. Grandiflora, long known by the common name Hills of Snow, was one of the earliest selections of smooth hydrangea bred for large, rounded, all-sterile-floret flower heads, predating the now more famous Annabelle by several decades and helping establish the mophead-form smooth hydrangea as a garden staple. It blooms reliably on new growth each year regardless of winter cold. Cut stems back hard, to 12-18 inches, in late winter to encourage a fresh flush of sturdy flowering stems, since older, thinner stems tend to flop under the flower weight.

common_name: Grandma's Yellow Rose (Texas Superstar Found Heirloom Yellow Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Grandma's Yellow is a Texas Superstar 'found' rose — an old, disease-tough garden survivor identified and propagated by Texas rose experts rather than a modern commercial breeding program release.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Grandma's Yellow is a Texas Superstar-designated rose identified and propagated by Texas horticulturists as a tough, disease-resistant 'found' rose — a survivor discovered thriving in an old home landscape long after the original planting was forgotten, a hallmark of genuinely tough antique and found roses well adapted to Southern conditions. It produces deep golden-yellow, repeat-blooming flowers on a vigorous, disease-resistant shrub that needs far less spray intervention than most modern hybrid tea roses to stay healthy through a humid Gulf South growing season. Like other Texas Superstar-designated found roses, it rewards low-input, minimal-spray care once established — light pruning in late winter and routine watering during dry spells are usually all it needs to perform reliably for years.

plant_note: Nick and soak seeds, then direct sow once soil is warm.
directions: This beloved heirloom climbs quickly to produce large, velvety purple trumpets marked with a striking star-shaped center. Nick the hard seed coats and soak overnight, then sow directly against a trellis or fence once the soil is warm. Blooms open in the morning and feed pollinators, with heart-shaped foliage covering the support all season. Provide sturdy vertical structure, as vines can reach ten feet or more.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed, then direct sow after frost at the base of a support.
directions: Nick the seed coat and soak overnight, then direct sow after frost at the base of a fence or trellis. This dependable heirloom is a vigorous climber with deep purple blooms and heart-shaped leaves that cover supports, trail on the ground, or spill from baskets. It may self-sow, so remove spent flowers if you want to limit volunteers. Note that parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Install a trellis, arbor, or fence before planting. Plant in early spring in well-drained soil; keep roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into sunlight.
directions: Provide a sturdy support structure such as a trellis, fence, or pergola, and plant in well-drained, dry to average soil in partial shade — this native midwestern vine prefers its roots cool and shaded while its stems climb toward sunlight. Unlike invasive non-native honeysuckles, Grape Honeysuckle is well-behaved and will not spread aggressively or self-seed excessively. Water regularly for the first growing season to establish, then scale back irrigation; established vines are drought-tolerant and thrive with little intervention. The distinctive perfoliate leaves and tubular yellow to orange flowers are magnets for ruby-throated hummingbirds and native bees from late spring through midsummer.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall, 3–4 in deep; foliage emerges in fall and overwinters, so plant early enough for roots to establish.
directions: Plant small bulbs 3–4 in deep in any well-drained soil; foliage emerges in fall and overwinters as a low ground cover, with tight clusters of cobalt-blue, urn-shaped flowers appearing in early to mid-spring. Muscari naturalizes aggressively by offsets and self-seeding and can spread widely — site where this is desirable or divide clumps every few years in fall to control spread. Excellent planted beneath tulips and daffodils to create complementary color combinations. Deer and rodents generally leave them alone.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or water, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; grape ivy is adaptable to a wide range of conditions but requires protection from temperatures below 45°F, which cause leaf drop and defoliation — in zone 9, grow in protected positions against south-facing walls or as a container specimen moved indoors in winter.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; grape ivy is a Venezuelan tropical evergreen vine of the grape family (Vitaceae) that has been among the most widely grown and reliable shade-tolerant tropical foliage vines for over a century — it climbs by tendrils to form dense, leafy masses of three-parted (trifoliate), broadly rhombic (diamond-shaped, hence rhombifolia), glossy, dark-green leaves with prominent, rusty-brown, finely hairy undersides that give the plant an attractive textured quality when the foliage is disturbed. The lustrous, dark-green foliage, reliable shade tolerance, and easy cultivation make it an enduringly popular choice for covering shaded walls, trellises, and structures in tropical and subtropical gardens, and as a trailing vine in large containers and hanging baskets indoors or in sheltered outdoor positions. 'Ellen Danica' (oak-leaf grape ivy) has more deeply lobed, oak-leaf-like leaflets and is slightly more cold-sensitive. Outdoors in zone 10–12 it can reach 15 feet or more on suitable supports in shade conditions where most other vines would fail to thrive.

common_name: Grape Soda Coral Bells (Rounded Deep Purple-Red Heuchera)
plant_note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Grape Soda bears rounded, deep purple-red foliage that tolerates heavier shade than most Heuchera cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Grape Soda bears rounded, ruffled leaves in a deep, saturated purple-red that holds its rich color well in shadier sites than many other coral bells cultivars tolerate, forming a dense mound topped in early summer by wiry stems of small white flowers that attract pollinators. Its dark, glossy foliage provides strong color contrast against lighter-leaved shade companions like hostas and ferns. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and remove old, tattered leaves in late winter.

plant_note: Plant nursery starts after last frost into well-drained, average, fertile soil in full sun; grape-leaf flowering maple is a fast-growing Chilean shrub that prefers a Mediterranean-type climate with moderate humidity over intense heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average, fertile soil in full sun; grape-leaf flowering maple is a fast, large-growing Chilean shrub with soft, gray-green, grape-like leaves and an abundant spring display of large, saucer-shaped, mallow-like flowers in shades of lavender, blue-violet, or white, among the showiest blooms of any commonly grown abutilon. It grows quickly, often reaching full size within just a few years, making it useful for a fast privacy screen or a dramatic single-season specimen in mild-winter gardens. It performs best in climates with moderate summer humidity similar to its native Chilean range and can suffer more from prolonged intense heat and humidity than some of the more tropical abutilon species, so afternoon shade is worthwhile in the hottest, most humid parts of its zone range. Prune after flowering to control size and shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and protect the root zone with mulch through winter at the cooler edge of its hardiness.

common_name: Grapeleaf Anemone (Vigorous Pink Fall-Blooming Shade Tolerant Anemone)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Anemone tomentosa is more vigorous and spreading than Japanese anemone hybrids — plant where it has room to expand, or use physical root barriers to contain the spread.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Anemone tomentosa (Grapeleaf Anemone, sometimes listed as 'Robustissima') is a vigorous, spreading species of fall-blooming anemone from China — larger and more aggressive than the refined Japanese anemone hybrids but valued precisely for that vigor and excellent heat tolerance that makes it reliable at the warm edge of the Anemone range (zone 9). The large, lobed, grape-leaf-like foliage (giving the common name 'Grapeleaf Anemone') is bold and attractive in summer, followed by tall (3–4 foot) stalks of simple, cup-shaped, warm-pink flowers with bright yellow centers that bloom in August–October — providing valuable late-season color in shaded garden areas when most shade perennials have finished flowering. The fall bloom season and shade tolerance make Grapeleaf Anemone one of the relatively few plants that provide clear-colored flowers in partial shade through September and October in zone 9. The vigorous stoloniferous spread — more aggressive than Japanese anemone hybrids — is a practical consideration: plant in defined beds with physical edging or barriers, or in naturalistic settings where spreading is welcome. The spreading habit creates an effective groundcover under deciduous trees but can overtake smaller companions. More adaptable to clay soil than most anemones; tolerates periodic moisture variability better than the more refined hybrid types.

plant_note: Plant corms from nursery-propagated sources in spring in wet, acidic, peaty or sandy, nutrient-poor soil in full sun to partial shade; grass pink orchid requires an open, wet, acidic bog or seep environment with full sun to partial shade and nutrient-poor conditions.
directions: Grass pink orchid is one of the most common and widely distributed of all eastern North American bog orchids — a single grasslike leaf and an upright flower stem bearing up to 10 vivid magenta-pink flowers with a distinctive bearded lip appear in late spring and early summer in acidic, wet bogs, seepage slopes, pitcher plant savannas, and longleaf pine flatwoods across the Gulf Coastal Plain. Unlike most orchids, grass pink orchid grows from small, underground corms that can be purchased from specialist native plant nurseries and planted in appropriate bog garden conditions, making it more accessible than most native terrestrial orchids. The flowers practice deceptive pollination — the bearded yellow lip (which resembles a pollen-covered stamen to naive bees) flips downward when a bee lands, dropping the bee onto the actual pollen masses on the column below; bees learn quickly and return infrequently, so the plant depends on a steady supply of inexperienced native bees. An important component of Gulf Coast bog gardens when combined with pitcher plants (Sarracenia), sundews, and bog sedges in full-sun, wet, acidic soil.

subcategory: Australian botanical novelty with triggered pollination
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; grass trigger plant is native to the sandy, peaty, often seasonally moist soils of southeastern Australia. The trigger mechanism — the column (fused style and stamens) that snaps to deposit pollen on visiting insects — can be observed and reset by gently touching a flower; it will snap back within a few hours. The plant is partially insectivorous, secreting sticky glands on the stem that trap small insects.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; grass trigger plant is one of the most remarkable and botanically interesting of all commonly grown ornamental plants — a botanical curiosity on par with the Venus flytrap in its unusual adaptation. Each flower of Stylidium contains a 'trigger' — the column, a structure formed by the fusion of style and stamens — that is held under tension and, when touched by a visiting insect seeking nectar, snaps rapidly across the flower in a powerful, spring-like mechanism, depositing pollen onto the insect's body (or collecting pollen from a pollen-carrying visitor). This triggered snap is one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom — occurring in milliseconds — and can be reset: after firing, the column slowly resets to the cocked position over a few hours, ready to fire again. The flowers are small, pink to rose-pink, five-petaled, and produced in many-flowered racemes on stems above the narrow, grass-like (graminifolium = grass-leaved) basal leaf rosette in spring and early summer. Additionally, the glandular-sticky stem hairs trap small insects — contributing to the plant's partially insectivorous nutrition. A plant that combines attractive appearance with a genuinely dramatic and demonstrable botanical mechanism that can be shown to observers in the garden.

plant_note: Surface-sow seed onto consistently moist, calcium-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in fall so winter cold and moisture trigger germination the following spring; seed needs light and should not be buried.
directions: Surface-sow seed onto consistently moist, calcium-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in fall so winter cold and moisture trigger germination the following spring, since seed needs light and should not be buried. Despite its common name it is not a grass at all but a low perennial forb, producing single, five-petaled, cream-white flowers etched with delicate green veining atop wiry stems in late summer and fall — a period when few other wetland natives are still blooming. This late-season nectar makes it valuable for bees, flies, and other pollinators stocking up before winter, and it is a signature species of calcareous fens and wet, sedge-dominated meadows across the Appalachian and Great Lakes region. Site it in a permanently damp, mineral-rich seep or fen garden for best results.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; grass-leaf daylily stays notably compact and narrow-leaved compared with modern hybrids, making it useful for the front of a border or a smaller garden.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and keep evenly watered while the fans establish. Native across Siberia, northern China, Korea, and Japan, Hemerocallis minor is a dwarf wild species with fine, narrow, grass-like foliage and lightly fragrant, clear lemon-yellow flowers on slender scapes in early summer, considerably smaller in every dimension than modern hybrid daylilies. Its diminutive scale, cold hardiness, and long history in cultivation have made it a valued parent species in daylily breeding, particularly for miniature and dwarf hybrid lines. The tidy, non-spreading clumps rarely need division more than once every four or five years, and the fine-textured foliage remains attractive even when the plant isn't in bloom, unlike the coarser foliage of many large-flowered hybrids.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; grass-leaved ladies' tresses thrives in wet, open pine savannas, wet meadows, and roadside ditches of the coastal plain — purchase only nursery-propagated stock.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring in moist to wet, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; grass-leaved ladies' tresses grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods, open bogs, moist meadows, and roadside wet ditches throughout the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Texas, often in large populations. Spiranthes praecox is one of the more unusual ladies' tresses species, distinctive for its very narrow, grass-like basal leaves and its relatively early bloom time — the tightly spiraled, pure-white flower spikes appear from March through May, earlier than most other Spiranthes, making it an important early-season nectar source for native bees emerging in spring. It is much easier to cultivate than most native orchids as long as the soil remains consistently moist and acidic; plant at the margin of a rain garden, bog garden, or retention pond. Never collect from the wild; purchase nursery-propagated plants from reputable native plant nurseries.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; grass-leaved golden aster grows naturally in dry, sandy pine flatwoods and sandhills of the Coastal Plain from Virginia to Texas, where it is one of the most reliable and abundant wildflowers of the longleaf pine ecosystem.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; grass-leaved golden aster is one of the most characteristic and abundant native wildflowers of the longleaf pine flatwoods ecosystem, producing silvery, silky, grass-like leaves from a rosette and bright golden-yellow daisy flowers in late summer and fall. The silvery-gray leaf surfaces (from dense silky hairs) give the plant a distinctive shimmer in the sun that led to the common name 'silkgrass.' It is adapted to the challenging conditions of deep, white, nutrient-poor sand in full, hot summer sun — conditions that discourage most garden plants. The bright fall flowers are an important late-season nectar source for skippers, hairstreak butterflies, and native bees in the coastal plain. One of the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant native wildflowers for zone 9a sandy gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow on wet, sandy substrate or plant divisions in spring in shallow water or wet soil in partial shade to full sun; grassleaf arrowhead grows naturally in pond margins, slow streams, and other wet habitats with variable water levels.
directions: Plant in shallow water to consistently wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; grassleaf arrowhead is an aquatic native with unusual leaf variation — unlike the typical arrowhead-shaped leaves of most Sagittaria, this species produces narrow, grass-like leaves (particularly when submerged) that give it its common name. The plant adapts its leaf form to water depth: submerged leaves are very narrow and strap-like, emergent leaves may be broader and more typical of the genus. Small, three-petaled white flowers are produced on erect stems above the water. Provides food for waterfowl (the small corms are eaten by ducks) and habitat for small aquatic invertebrates. An adaptable native aquatic for constructed wetlands, bog gardens, and the shallow margins of ornamental ponds in zones 5–10.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil; keep consistently moist throughout establishment.
directions: A delicate native perennial of wet longleaf pine savannas, seepage bogs, and flatwood margins of the southeastern coastal plain, producing narrow, grass-like basal leaves and slender upright flowering stems topped with solitary, fluffy, pink to rose-lavender, powder-puff composite flower heads in late summer to fall. One of several Marshallia species endemic to southeastern US flatwoods and among the most visually charming of the group. Grow in moist to wet, sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor soil in full sun; avoid fertile or amended soils, which suppress flowering and favor rank vegetative growth. An excellent, underused native wildflower for wet garden edges and longleaf pine savanna restorations in zones 7-9.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions into consistently moist to saturated soil in spring; ideal for pond margins, rain gardens, and freshwater marsh edges rather than dry beds.
directions: This clump-forming rush grows through the Southeast in wet pine flatwoods, ditches, and the freshwater fringes of brackish marshes, producing wiry blue-green stems topped with small clustered brown flower heads in summer. Plant divisions into damp to saturated soil in full to partial sun; it tolerates both standing water and seasonal drying better than many rushes, making it forgiving in rain gardens and stormwater basins. It rarely needs division or maintenance once established and provides fine winter texture along pond edges. Combine it with pickerelweed and native sedges for a layered freshwater marsh planting that also offers cover for small wetland wildlife.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; gravel bottlebrush is native to the seasonally wet, sandy, gravelly soils of southwestern Western Australia — tolerating periodic waterlogging better than most Australian shrubs, which makes it more adaptable to the wet-summer Gulf Coast conditions of zone 9 than many Australian natives. It blooms in summer (November–February in Australia), providing summer bottlebrush interest. Outstanding for birds.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; gravel bottlebrush is a Western Australian shrub of the Myrtaceae family — related to the true bottlebrushes (Callistemon) and honeymrtles (Melaleuca) — that produces in summer vivid, spherical to rounded, bottlebrush-type flower heads of brilliant orange to orange-red composed of densely massed, projecting stamen bundles in warm, vivid orange, each flower head 2–3 inches across and the plant in full bloom covered in multiple such heads of intense orange. Unlike many Australian shrubs that are summer-dry and drought-tolerant, gravel bottlebrush is native to the seasonally wet, gravelly, sandy flats that experience periodic winter-spring flooding — and therefore tolerates summer moisture and periodic wet conditions significantly better than most Australian ornamentals. This moisture tolerance makes it more suitable for the humid-summer conditions of the zone 9 Gulf Coast than the strictly dry-climate Australian shrubs. The summer bloom timing provides vivid orange bottlebrush flowers in the summer garden season — a different and valuable window from the spring-blooming Australian genera. Outstanding for birds and bees.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; gray beardtongue is one of the most drought-tolerant native penstemons of the Appalachian region.
directions: Sow direct in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; gray beardtongue tolerates dry, rocky, thin soils better than most native penstemons and does not need rich soil to perform. Penstemon canescens is a native penstemon of the Appalachian region from Pennsylvania to Georgia, growing in dry, rocky woods, slopes, and ledges; it has grayish-hairy (canescent) leaves and produces loose, terminal racemes of tubular, lavender to pink-purple flowers with darker veining in late spring and early summer that are visited by native bumble bees, large carpenter bees, and hummingbirds. The soft gray foliage is ornamental even when not in bloom; it naturalizes in rocky, dry-slope native plant gardens and is excellent in combination with native grasses and drought-tolerant forbs.

plant_note: Set out young trees in spring on sandy, acidic, or poor soils where this tough pioneer species readily colonizes abandoned fields and roadsides.
directions: Set out young trees in spring on sandy, acidic, or poor soils where this tough pioneer species readily colonizes abandoned fields and roadsides. Its slender, chalky-white trunks with black triangular patches beneath each branch and its fine-textured, fluttering foliage give it strong ornamental value in multi-stem clumps. Gray birch tolerates poor drainage and infertile ground better than paper birch but is shorter-lived, typically thriving for only 30-50 years, making it best suited to naturalized or reclamation plantings rather than a long-term specimen. It requires little supplemental water once established, unlike its moisture-loving birch relatives.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall; very adaptable — tolerates clay, compaction, and a wide range of moisture levels once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to moderate shade; gray dogwood is one of the most wildlife-friendly native shrubs in the eastern US, producing clusters of white berries on distinctive red pedicels in late summer that attract catbirds, robins, thrushes, and over 90 other bird species. The shrub tolerates dry soil, compacted clay, and partial shade better than most native dogwoods. It spreads by root suckers to form dense thickets valuable for erosion control and wildlife corridors; remove suckers in spring if a more contained form is desired. Small white flower clusters in early summer are visited by numerous native bees and short-tongued pollinators.

plant_note: Scarify or hot-soak seeds before starting indoors; transplant in spring into dry, calcareous or sandy, lean, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Gray Globemallow is a robust, erect native perennial of dry, calcareous grasslands, rocky slopes, and roadsides in Texas and the southwestern United States, distinctive for its densely silver-gray woolly stems and broad, deeply lobed, gray-green leaves that remain ornamental even when the plant is not in flower. From spring through summer it produces upright spikes of salmon-orange to brick-red mallow flowers 1 inch across that are highly attractive to native bees and hummingbirds. Grow in dry, calcareous or well-drained sandy, lean soil in full sun; plants rot quickly in heavy, wet, or organically rich soils. Scarify or soak seeds in hot water before starting indoors, then transplant into the garden in spring — an outstanding xeriscape perennial for Texas Hill Country and southwestern gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, poor to average soil in full sun; gray goldenrod is the most drought-tolerant of the common eastern goldenrods, thriving in dry, sandy, and rocky soils where other goldenrods cannot establish.
directions: Sow seed in fall in well-drained, dry to average, poor to average soil in full sun — gray goldenrod is the most drought-tolerant of the common eastern North American goldenrods, taking its common name from the grayish, downy-hairy stems and leaves that help reduce water loss in its characteristic dry, open habitats: rocky outcrops, sandy barrens, dry roadsides, and dry open woodland edges throughout the eastern US and into the Great Plains. The one-sided arching racemes of golden yellow flowers curve gracefully toward the ground in late summer and fall, providing important late-season nectar for migrating monarch butterflies and a wide range of native bees. While not as showy as some taller goldenrods, gray goldenrod is invaluable for difficult dry, sandy, or rocky sites where creating a pollinator-supporting native planting is otherwise challenging. Historically used by Native American nations as a yellow dye plant.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade at cool higher elevations in the southern Appalachians; Gray's lily is one of the rarest and most beautiful native lilies, limited to a few counties in Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Gray's lily grows naturally in heath balds and moist meadows at 2,500–5,500 feet elevation in the southern Appalachians and prefers cool, moist, acidic conditions. Lilium grayi is one of the rarest and most beautiful native North American lilies, with a restricted natural range limited to a few counties in Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee; it produces small (1.5–2 inch), nodding, reddish-orange to scarlet, bell-shaped flowers with spots (less reflexed than the similar Carolina lily) on slender stems in early to mid-summer. Purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs — never wild-dug plants. It requires cool, acidic, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade and is challenging outside its native climate zone; it is best in cool, humid mountain gardens in the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in spring; Gray's sedge grows naturally in wet woodland edges and stream-side meadows and requires consistently moist to wet conditions — it will not thrive in dry soil.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Gray's sedge (morningstar sedge, mace sedge) is a native North American woodland sedge grown primarily for its extraordinarily ornamental seed heads — large, spiky, star-shaped, mace-like fruiting heads that look remarkably like medieval weapons, held on upright stems above the bright-green, arching foliage clumps from summer through early fall. The seed head is the plant's primary ornamental feature and is excellent for both fresh and dried flower arrangements. The plant provides attractive foliage mass in moist, shaded corners throughout the growing season. It grows naturally in wet woodland edges and floodplain forests and is most at home beside streams, ponds, and rain garden margins in partial shade. An excellent specimen plant for rain gardens, bioswales, and wet native plant gardens in zones 4–9.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; cold stratification for 30 days improves germination rate. Plants may bloom the first year from an early sowing.
directions: Sow in well-drained, average to poor, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; the gray-headed coneflower is a tall, drought-tolerant prairie native with drooping yellow petals reflexed away from a distinctive elongated gray-brown cone, giving it an unmistakable silhouette in the summer meadow. It blooms from midsummer through fall and spreads gently by self-seeding without becoming aggressive. The crushed foliage smells pleasantly of anise. An important pollen source for prairie bees and the seed is taken by goldfinches in fall. Mixes beautifully with other tall prairie plants like goldenrod and ironweed in naturalistic plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination, or sow in early spring directly on the soil surface as seeds need light to germinate; press seeds gently into the surface but do not cover.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall or early spring, pressing them lightly into contact with soil but not covering, as they require light for germination. Grayhead coneflower is one of the most graceful native prairie composites, with long drooping bright yellow petals reflexed sharply back from a distinctive tall oval gray-brown cone that releases an anise-like fragrance when rubbed — this upright cone distinguishes it clearly from the flatter cones of Rudbeckia. Plants bloom prolifically from July through September on branching 3–5 foot stems clothed in pinnately divided leaves, and they self-seed freely to naturalize into expanding colonies in prairie restorations and meadow gardens. Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established, grayhead coneflower thrives in poor, well-drained soils and is an important late-summer nectar source for bees and butterflies.

common_name: Graziella Miniature Maiden Grass (Narrow Early-Flowering Miscanthus)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Graziella is a compact, narrow-bladed maiden grass cultivar selected for earlier flowering than many other Miscanthus sinensis cultivars, giving reliable plume display even in shorter-season gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Graziella is a refined, narrow-leaved maiden grass cultivar valued for its tidy, upright, vase-shaped habit and notably early flowering compared to many other Miscanthus sinensis selections, sending up silvery-pink plumes by late summer that mature to a warm, silvery-tan and persist attractively through much of winter, adding movement and structure to the garden even in the dormant season. The fine, arching, dark-green foliage turns attractive gold and copper tones in fall before going dormant. Because it flowers earlier and reliably in a wide range of climates, it is a dependable choice where a longer, cooler growing season limits bloom on later-flowering miscanthus cultivars. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches above the ground in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and a tidy, upright form.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after cold stratification in very well-drained, rocky, lean, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, dolomitic or limestone-derived soil in full sun; Great Basin bristlecone pine grows naturally on exposed, rocky, dolomitic ridges at 9,000–11,500 feet elevation in the White Mountains and Great Basin ranges. Requires excellent drainage and lean, nutrient-poor soils — very fertile conditions cause early death.
directions: Plant seeds in spring in very well-drained, rocky, lean, slightly alkaline, dolomitic or sandy soil in full sun; Great Basin bristlecone pine is the world's oldest known living organism — individual trees in the White Mountains of California and the mountains of Nevada exceed 5,000 years of age. Methuselah, a named specimen in the White Mountains, is over 4,800 years old. The trees survive extreme conditions of thin dolomitic soil, blistering cold, intense UV radiation, and annual drought that kill competitors, and their resinous, dense wood resists decay for thousands of years after death. In garden culture, bristlecone pines are surprisingly adaptable to lower elevations if given lean, extremely well-drained soil and full sun; they grow very slowly (adding only a few inches per year), making them perfect long-term bonsai subjects or rock garden specimens. The distinctive bottle-brush branch tips (with dense needle clusters on spur shoots) and the distinctive bristly cones are unmistakable. A tree grown from seed will still be young in several human lifetimes.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost on the soil surface without covering (light improves germination); transplant to moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Great blue lobelia thrives at pond margins and rain garden edges.
directions: Start seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix under light 8 weeks before last frost; transplant to moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade at pond margins, stream banks, or rain garden edges where soil stays consistently wet. Great blue lobelia produces striking sky-blue flower spikes from late summer through fall that are magnets for hummingbirds and native bumblebees — the only pollinators strong enough to open the flower. It tolerates more shade and more moisture than most flowering perennials. Self-sows readily in moist sites to maintain persistent colonies. The closely related L. cardinalis (cardinal flower) has identical requirements but red flowers; growing them together creates a spectacular two-season hummingbird garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring on moist soil, or divide established clumps in early spring or fall; great burnet transplants easily from container-grown stock and establishes quickly in moist sites.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; great burnet is a stately perennial producing airy, branched stems topped with small oval heads of deep red to maroon flowers from midsummer through fall. The fine-cut blue-green compound leaves have the same cool, cucumber-like flavor as salad burnet (Sanguisorba minor) and can be used fresh in salads and drinks. Great burnet has become fashionable in contemporary naturalistic planting designs, where its tall airy flower stems weave beautifully through grasses and other meadow perennials. Japanese cultivars (S. obtusa, S. tenuifolia) with longer, more elegant flower spikes are widely used in hybrid plantings. Tolerates moist to occasionally wet soil.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4–6 inches deep in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; great camas is the tallest and showiest of the native camas species, with stately spikes of deep blue to cream flowers in late spring that were an important food source for many Native American peoples.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, organic, slightly acidic to neutral soil in a site that is wet in spring but dries out somewhat in summer; camassia naturalizes beautifully in moist meadows, pond edges, and wet woodland margins under deciduous trees. Great camas is the tallest camas species, native to wet meadows and forest openings of the Pacific Coast ranges from British Columbia to California, producing bold spikes 2–4 feet tall of star-shaped flowers in deep violet-blue to creamy white in May and June — one of the most spectacular of all spring bulbs for naturalizing in moist settings. The bulbs were a staple starchy food for many Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest; note that the poisonous Death Camas (Anticlea venenosum) resembles camas in leaf and grows in similar habitats — they are distinguished by flower color (death camas has creamy white flowers, edible camas has blue). Plant in large sweeps for maximum impact.

common_name: Great Expectations Hosta (Large Gold-Centered Blue-Margined Hosta)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Great Expectations was named Hosta of the Year in 1998 for its large, thick, corrugated leaves with a creamy gold center and irregular blue-green margin, one of the most dramatic large hosta cultivars available.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the best center color. Great Expectations was named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 1998, celebrated for its large, thick, heavily corrugated leaves with a broad, creamy-gold to chartreuse center bordered by an irregular, wavy blue-green margin, creating a bold, three-dimensional textural and color display in the shade garden. Pale lavender-white flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. As a sport of the popular blue hosta Sum and Substance, it inherits vigorous, substantial growth, forming a large, imposing clump over time that works well as a specimen or focal point. The gold coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic contrast. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

common_name: Great Maiden's Blush Rose (Soft Blush-Pink Fragrant Alba Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Great Maiden's Blush is a centuries-old Alba rose famed for its subtle color and tolerance of light shade.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba roses like Great Maiden's Blush tolerate more shade than most roses, a legacy of their origin as tough, adaptable garden plants long predating modern breeding. Recorded since at least the 15th century, it bears intensely fragrant, soft blush-pink double blooms against distinctive gray-green foliage, a refined color combination that has earned it poetic nicknames across the centuries. Like other Albas it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season, and it is exceptionally disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in fall; cold stratification over winter is essential for reliable germination the following spring. Fresh seed sown immediately after harvest also germinates well. Germination can be slow and uneven.
directions: Direct sow seed in fall into moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded woodland garden or border. The cold of winter naturally stratifies the seed, and germination occurs the following spring; patience is needed as emergence can be slow. Plants reach blooming size in the second or third year, producing their distinctive deep rose-pink pincushion flowers surrounded by decorative pointed bracts from late spring through midsummer. Deadheading prolongs the blooming season, and the plants will self-sow gently once established.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions or container stock in early spring before new growth emerges; seed requires complex double-dormancy stratification and takes 2 or more seasons to germinate — divisions are far more reliable.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; great merrybells is a graceful native woodland perennial that unfurls from tightly rolled shoots in early spring alongside bloodroot and trillium. The arching stems carry large, creamy-yellow pendant bell flowers at the tips — some of the most elegantly proportioned flowers in the native woodland plant palette. After flowering the stems straighten and support handsome, bright green leaves through summer. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a clump; it is not aggressive and pairs beautifully with Solomon's seal, ferns, and wild ginger in a shade garden. Provide consistent moisture and topdress with leaf compost each fall.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; great Solomon's seal is a bold, architectural species reaching 3–5 feet in height and requires ample space.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; great Solomon's seal requires generous spacing as it reaches 3–5 feet in height and spreads steadily to form large, impressive colonies over time. Polygonatum commutatum is the largest native eastern North American Solomon's seal, an impressive, bold-textured perennial with stout, strongly arching stems bearing large, oval, parallel-veined leaves and 2–8 pendant, greenish-white, tubular flowers per leaf node in late spring followed by dark blue-black berries in summer; the dramatic fall color is a rich, buttery yellow. It is one of the finest and most impressive native shade perennials for large-scale plantings under trees, along fence lines, and in naturalized woodland gardens; it combines well with ostrich ferns, hostas, and ligularia for a bold, tropical-looking shade planting.

common_name: Great Solomon's Seal (Giant Native Woodland Solomon's Seal)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in partial to full shade; plant rhizomes horizontally just below the soil surface, 2–3 inches deep; Great Solomon's Seal spreads slowly by rhizomes to form expanding colonies.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Great Solomon's Seal is the largest North American native Solomon's seal — a magnificent woodland plant producing arching stems 4–7 feet tall (significantly larger than the common Solomon's seal, P. biflorum, which reaches only 2–3 feet) hung with pairs of pendulous, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers in late spring, followed by ornamental blue-black berries relished by birds in fall. The large, boldly-oval, alternate leaves arranged along the gracefully arching stems create an architectural, tropical effect that is one of the most dramatic structure elements available for the native shade garden. The arching form and large leaves provide outstanding textural contrast with fine-textured groundcovers, ferns, and hostas in the shade border. Great Solomon's Seal spreads slowly by underground rhizomes to form expanding colonies that naturalize effectively under the canopy of deciduous trees, creating an increasingly impressive woodland garden planting over years. The native habitat of creek banks and moist woodland edges informs its garden requirements: consistent moisture and humus-rich, acidic soil are essential for the best performance, though established plants show reasonable drought tolerance once roots are deeply established. In zone 9, it thrives under tall pines and deciduous hardwoods where summer shade and organic leaf-litter soil accumulate.

common_name: Great Star Hydrangea (Starburst-Shaped Floret Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Great Star blooms on new wood, so prune hard in late winter to stimulate strong new growth and maximum flowering.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Great Star is unlike any other panicle hydrangea in flower form — instead of the usual small, densely packed florets, each individual sterile flower has four long, narrow, twisted petals radiating outward, giving the loose, airy flower panicles a distinctive spidery, starburst appearance rather than the typical dense cone shape. Blooming white in summer and often picking up pink tones as panicles age into fall, it makes an unusual textural accent among more conventional mophead and panicle hydrangeas. Like other H. paniculata cultivars it blooms on new wood, so prune hard in late winter to a low framework of buds for the strongest flowering; established plants are more sun- and drought-tolerant than bigleaf hydrangeas.

common_name: Great White Heron Japanese Iris (Large Pure White Iris)
plant_note: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade; Japanese iris are heavier water users than Siberian or bearded iris and perform best at a pond margin or in a bog-like bed that never fully dries out during the growing season.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade. Great White Heron produces exceptionally large, broad-petaled, pure white flowers characteristic of Japanese iris, flatter and showier than the more upright, narrower blooms of bearded or Siberian iris, on tall, elegant stems above sword-like foliage. Unlike most other iris types, Japanese iris demand consistently moist, acidic soil through the growing season and decline quickly if allowed to dry out, though they tolerate standing water for only brief periods rather than being true bog plants year-round; a pond margin or heavily irrigated bed suits them best. Divide clumps every three to four years in early fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

plant_note: Introduce tubers to calcareous or chalk-based soils in open woodland or grassland edges in early spring. Soil pH should ideally be neutral to alkaline; amend acidic soils with horticultural lime before planting. Keep the planting area free of aggressive grass competition, which can crowd out young plants before they establish.
directions: Select a site with calcareous, well-drained soil and partial shade from an open woodland canopy or tall hedgerow. This robust orchid performs best where thin, alkaline soils discourage competitive rank grasses and allow the orchid to access sunlight at ground level. The fragrant greenish-white flower spikes appear in late spring to early summer and attract long-tongued moths after dark. Maintain steady soil moisture through summer, and remove any encroaching vegetation each autumn to prevent smothering the basal leaf rosette that overwinters at ground level.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, slightly acidic, well-drained sandy or rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; greater coreopsis grows naturally in dry, open woodlands, woodland edges, and sandy barrens across the southeastern Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in dry, lean, slightly acidic, well-drained sandy or rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; greater coreopsis is a tall, robust native perennial of dry, open woodlands and woodland edges across the southeastern United States — a larger, more woodland-adapted alternative to the familiar lanceleaf and threadleaf coreopsis of full-sun meadow gardens. The plant produces bright yellow coreopsis flowers on tall, branching stems in summer, but distinguishes itself by thriving in the partial shade and dry, lean soil conditions of open forest understories where sun-demanding coreopsis decline. The paired (opposite) leaves often consist of three narrow, spreading lobes that can give the appearance of six leaves at each node. Excellent at the woodland edge where it bridges the gap between sun-garden coreopsis and shade-garden plants, blooming prolifically with just a few hours of direct sun. Seeds provide food for native birds in fall and winter.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or stem sections in spring or fall in any moist, well-drained soil in full shade to full sun; greater periwinkle is extraordinarily adaptable and establishes quickly from stem sections placed in moist soil. It spreads aggressively by arching stems that root at the nodes — contain with edging where spread must be controlled.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moderately moist soil in full shade to partial sun; greater periwinkle is a vigorous, trailing, evergreen groundcover with larger, glossier, darker green leaves than the more refined Vinca minor — it covers ground more aggressively and thrives in the heat and humidity of zones 7–11 where V. minor can struggle. Sky-blue, star-shaped, 1.5-inch flowers appear from early spring through summer. Particularly valuable in the hot Southeast and Gulf Coast where its heat tolerance far exceeds V. minor. The variegated form ('Variegata', with leaves edged in creamy white or yellow) provides striking year-round foliage interest in shaded spots. Be aware that V. major can be invasive in riparian zones and warm-climate areas where it spreads into native plant communities — do not plant near natural areas or waterways in warm climates. Excellent for covering slopes, under trees, and in difficult shaded areas in contained residential landscapes.

plant_note: Plant divisions in well-drained to moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; greater wood rush is one of the most tolerant groundcovers for deep shade, dry shade, and acid soil under conifers.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained to moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; greater wood rush forms spreading rosettes of broad, glossy, grass-like leaves with a distinctive fringe of white hairs along the margins, making it one of the most versatile shade groundcovers and one of the very few plants that tolerates the extreme dry shade and acidic conditions under large established conifers. Brown flower spikelets appear in early spring on stems above the foliage. The gold-variegated cultivar 'Aurea' provides year-round bright-gold foliage color even in deep shade and is especially effective along woodland paths. Spreads steadily by stolons; divide every 4–5 years to renew vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring or fall in shaded, moist to moderately dry sites; greater woodrush establishes slowly but once settled it is essentially permanent and requires no maintenance.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; greater woodrush is a broad-leaved, rush-like European woodlander that forms handsome, slowly expanding evergreen clumps of rich green foliage throughout the year. Unlike lawn grasses, it thrives in the deep dry shade under dense tree canopies. In spring it produces airy, branched clusters of tiny rusty-brown flowers on arching stems. The golden-leaved cultivar ‘Aurea’ brightens dark corners with vivid chartreuse-yellow winter foliage that fades to green in summer. It is one of the most effective and lowest-maintenance shade groundcovers for difficult dry shade, and the evergreen foliage provides year-round ground cover where deciduous plants leave a seasonal gap.

plant_note: Soak the small, irregular, dried tubers in water for 24 hours before planting — this step is essential, as dry Anemone blanda tubers absorb water very slowly and will establish poorly if planted without soaking; plant soaked tubers 2-3 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart with the concave (hollow) side facing up, in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, 4-8 weeks before first frost. Plant in large quantities for a naturalistic woodland effect and do not disturb established clumps.
directions: Soak tubers overnight, then plant 2-3 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in fall for very early spring bloom; Grecian windflower is one of the most valuable and versatile of all shade-tolerant spring bulbs — a low-growing, spreading, deciduous woodland tuber (technically a rhizome, not a true bulb) from the mountains of southeastern Europe and Turkey that produces daisy-like flowers 1-2 inches across in vivid blue, rich pink, or pure white with a bright yellow center, the petals reflexing in cold weather and closing at night, fully opening only when the sun reaches them. It blooms in March and April, carpeting the ground under deciduous trees and shrubs with jewel-like color at a time when little else is in flower. It is outstanding in deep or partial shade, naturalizing freely by both offset and self-seeding to form expanding colonies beneath trees where many other plants fail. Always soak the dried tubers for at least 12-24 hours before planting as they desiccate during storage and must be fully rehydrated to establish successfully.

plant_note: Plant tubers just below the soil surface with the flat root-side down in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty or rocky soil in full sun to part shade; Greek cyclamen is unusual among hardy cyclamen in tolerating full sun in Mediterranean climates and developing long, thick anchoring roots that contract deeply into the soil — in rocky cliff habitats it may be essentially un-extractable. It flowers in early autumn (September–October) before the leaves. The tuber base produces downward-pointing roots from the center and lower surfaces, unlike C. hederifolium which roots from the sides.
directions: Plant tubers in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Greek cyclamen is the most heat- and drought-tolerant of the autumn-flowering cyclamen species — native to the rocky limestone cliffs, stony garigue, and thin, dry, alkaline soils of Greece, Crete, Turkey, and Cyprus — and therefore an outstanding cyclamen for Mediterranean-climate and warm-winter gardens in zones 7–11 where conditions are too hot and dry for C. hederifolium to thrive consistently.
