plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry, sandy, acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Gulf bluestem is a coastal specialist growing in dry, sandy, coastal habitats from Texas to North Carolina. It is one of the most important native grasses for beach and dune stabilization on Gulf Coast shorelines.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun along coastal dunes, sandy beaches, and dry, exposed coastal garden settings; Gulf bluestem is a low-growing, creeping-rooted native bluestem of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, especially adapted to the harsh, salt-spray, wind-exposed, nutrient-poor sandy soils of coastal dunes and beach strands. Unlike upland bluestems that form upright bunches, this species has a more sprawling, prostrate habit with shorter culms and broad, glaucous blue-green leaves that withstand the physical stress of coastal exposure. The fine seed heads in fall provide food for coastal sparrows and other birds. An outstanding native for beach and dune gardens in zone 9a where it stabilizes sandy areas with minimal care. Spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form low, dense mats. More salt-tolerant than most native grasses and naturally resistant to wind and drought in coastal conditions.

common_name: Gulf Coast Muhly (Gulf Muhly, Gulf Hairgrass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container transplants in spring in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Gulf Coast muhly grows naturally in coastal flatwoods, pine savannas, and well-drained sandy areas from the Carolinas to Texas and tolerates both drought and brief flooding.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Gulf Coast muhly is one of the most spectacular native grasses of the southeastern coastal plain, producing dense tufts of fine, arching leaves topped with extraordinary clouds of pink-purple to reddish plumes in October–November — the fall bloom is breathtaking in mass plantings, creating a haze of color resembling smoke drifting over the landscape at sunset. It is the native counterpart to the widely planted inland pink muhly (M. capillaris) but is even better adapted to the sandy, humid Gulf Coast environment and more salt-tolerant. The fine-textured foliage is attractive throughout the growing season. Shear to 4–6 inches in late winter before new growth begins. An outstanding fall-blooming native for the Gulf Coast landscape.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination, or sow in early spring with cold stratification; Gulf Coast penstemon performs best in partial shade in the intense summer heat of zones 7–9 and appreciates afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Gulf Coast penstemon is a regionally native Texas and Louisiana species adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coastal Plain where most other penstemons struggle. It produces lavender-pink tubular flowers on erect spikes in spring that are excellent hummingbird and butterfly attractors. Unlike western penstemons that require perfect drainage and full sun, P. tenuis actually grows in moist, even temporarily wet soils and tolerates the heavy clay soils common in Gulf Coast gardens. It self-sows modestly and can establish small colonies. A critical native plant for Gulf Coast pollinator gardens that is still under-utilized.

common_name: Gulf Coast Phlox (Trailing Phlox, Pineleaf Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in late winter or early spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun to partial shade; excellent drainage is essential — Phlox nivalis will rot in heavy or wet soils, particularly during summer.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Phlox nivalis, the trailing phlox or pineleaf phlox, is a low-growing, mat-forming native phlox found naturally in the Coastal Plains and sandhills from Virginia through the Gulf Coast states — ideally adapted to the well-drained, lean, sandy pine-savanna soils of the Gulf South where most other ground covers struggle. In early spring (March–April in zone 9), the spreading mats of fine, needle-like evergreen foliage are covered with large (3/4 inch), five-petaled flowers in shades of pink, lavender-pink, or white, creating a stunning carpet of color before the heat of summer arrives. The flower display is brief but intensely colorful, and after bloom the tight, fine-textured evergreen mats remain attractive year-round as a weed-suppressing ground cover. Phlox nivalis is native to Gulf Coast longleaf pine savannas — it is particularly adapted to the combination of infertile, sandy, well-drained soil, full sun to dappled pine shade, and periodic drought that characterizes these ecosystems. Avoid heavy clay or consistently moist soil; excellent drainage is the key to success. A superb choice for rock gardens, sunny slopes, and lean sandy bank stabilization in zone 7–9.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container specimens in spring in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gulf Coast yucca grows naturally in the sandy coastal prairies and open pine flatwoods of eastern Texas and Louisiana and is extremely well adapted to the heat, humidity, and poor soils of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Plant offsets or container specimens in very well-drained, dry, sandy to loamy soil in full sun — Gulf Coast yucca is a stemless or short-stemmed native yucca endemic to the sandy coastal prairies and pine flatwoods of Louisiana and East Texas, forming low rosettes of long, flexible, dark blue-green leaves with softer, less-rigid tips than Spanish bayonet (Yucca aloifolia). Tall, upright flower stalks 3–6 feet emerge in early summer bearing large clusters of creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers that are the exclusive food source for the yucca moth (Tegeticula sp.), which simultaneously pollinates the flowers and lays its eggs in the ovary — one of the most specialized and obligate plant-pollinator relationships in nature. The relationship is so specific that Gulf Coast yucca will not set seed without its yucca moth pollinator. An excellent, low-maintenance native structural plant for sandy, poor soils, drought garden designs, and coastal prairie restoration.

common_name: Gulf Cockspur Grass / Michaux's Cup Grass
plant_note: Direct-sow seeds at the soil surface or barely covered in sandy or disturbed soil after the last frost date, in a location with full to partial sun and good drainage.
directions: Direct-sow seeds at or just below the surface of sandy, well-drained soil in full to partial sun after the last frost date, thinning seedlings to 12-18 inches apart once they reach 3-4 inches tall. This native grass of coastal plain disturbed habitats is well-adapted to low-fertility soils and requires no supplemental fertilizer, which would promote rank vegetative growth at the expense of seed production. Water lightly during establishment, then rely on natural rainfall once plants are 6-8 inches tall, as Gulf Cockspur Grass is tolerant of both brief drought and periodic flooding in its native habitat. Allow seed heads to mature fully on the plant before cutting for forage or wildlife use, as the seeds provide valuable food for ground-feeding birds in late summer and fall.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun in saline, alkaline, or brackish wet to seasonally flooded soils along Gulf Coast bay margins, salt flats, and transition zones; gulf cordgrass tolerates both salt and alkaline conditions that would kill most grasses.
directions: Gulf cordgrass (formerly Spartina spartinae) is a dominant warm-season perennial grass of Gulf Coast salt flats, tidal margins, and alkaline coastal prairies from Texas to Florida, forming dense monocultures that bridge the ecological transition zone between tidal salt marsh and upland prairie. Its stiff, round, sharply pointed leaf blades make it distinctive and somewhat prickly to handle, but the plant is invaluable for stabilizing saline, alkaline, or brackish coastal soils where few other plants establish — it has exceptional salt tolerance that exceeds most native coastal grasses. Historically, gulf cordgrass prairies were important feeding and nesting habitat for Attwater's prairie chickens and migratory shorebirds; coastal prairie bird species including horned larks, savannah sparrows, and sedge wrens use the dense stands for winter foraging. In Gulf Coast coastal restoration projects and living shoreline designs, gulf cordgrass is planted in the transition zone between smooth cordgrass tidal marsh and upland black needle rush or salt flat communities, where it reliably establishes and spreads via rhizomes.

common_name: Gulf Muhly (Pink Muhly Grass, Big Muhly)
plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry, sandy, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Gulf muhly grows naturally in dry, sandy longleaf pine flatwoods and savannas of the Gulf Coastal Plain, where it is an important component of the native bunchgrass community.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Gulf muhly is a larger-statured Muhlenbergia of the longleaf pine savanna ecosystem, producing robust bunchgrass clumps with the same misty, fine-textured pink to purplish seed heads in fall that make Muhlenbergia capillaris (pink muhly) so beloved in ornamental gardens. This species is adapted specifically to the dry, sandy, fire-maintained habitats of the Gulf Coastal Plain longleaf pine ecosystem and is somewhat larger and more heat-tolerant than M. capillaris. The dramatic fall cloud of pink seed heads catches low autumn sun beautifully. In zone 9a, Gulf muhly blooms reliably from September through November, providing late-season interest when most other ornamental grasses have already peaked. Fire-adapted and responds well to early spring burning or cutting back to the ground.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or divisions in spring in full sun in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Gulf muhly is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast and Southeast.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gulf muhly grass is spectacular in October and November when it erupts in an explosion of airy, rose-pink to magenta flower plumes that transform the plant into a translucent cloud of color, most dramatic in late afternoon backlighting when the plumes glow with an almost phosphorescent intensity. A clump-forming grass that stays tidy from spring through late summer when the flower display begins; it is one of the signature plants of fall Gulf Coast and Southeast landscapes. Very drought-tolerant once established and excellent for dry banks, medians, and low-water native gardens in zone 6–10. Cut back to 6 inches in late winter and divide every 3–4 years when clumps become congested.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in wet, moist to seasonally flooded, brackish or fresh, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; gulf paspalum is a wetland-obligate coastal grass that thrives in tidal marsh margins, freshwater-saltwater transition zones, and seasonally flooded Gulf Coast flats.
directions: Gulf paspalum is a native grass of Gulf Coast tidal marshes, freshwater-brackish ecotones, and moist coastal flats from Texas to Florida, commonly forming dense colonies in the transition zone between fresh and salt water that are among the most important habitat areas for mottled ducks, blue-winged teal, and other dabbling waterfowl in the western Gulf Coast. The grass produces single-spoked seed heads distinctive among Gulf Coast grasses that ripen in summer and fall and are heavily consumed by waterfowl; its dense, matting rhizomes stabilize the soft, saturated soils of tidal margins and help resist shoreline erosion from boat wake and tidal action. In coastal garden ponds, rain garden overflow areas, and constructed freshwater wetlands in zone 8–11, gulf paspalum provides low, dense, wildlife-friendly groundcover in the shallowest water zones; it tolerates both freshwater flooding and moderate salinity. A component of Gulf Coast wetland restoration seed mixes, it establishes quickly and provides immediate stabilization and wildlife value.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Gulf penstemon is one of the few penstemons adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast, where most other species struggle.
directions: Direct sow in fall or transplant plugs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — Gulf penstemon is a rare native treasure: one of only a handful of Penstemon species adapted to the humid, wet winters and brutally hot summers of the Gulf Coast region from eastern Texas to Louisiana and western Mississippi. In spring it produces tall, airy spikes of small, tubular lavender to violet-blue flowers with white-striped throats that are intensely attractive to native bees (particularly bumblebees) and ruby-throated hummingbirds. It blooms prolifically in March through May, then sets seed and dies back to a basal rosette through summer heat. Self-sows reliably to persist in the garden; it thrives in moist, slightly acidic soils of pine flatwoods and stream margins — conditions very different from the dry, alkaline soils preferred by most western penstemons. The species to choose for humid South garden penstemon trials.

common_name: Gulf Stream Nandina (Gulf Stream Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Gulf Stream develops the most vivid blue-green summer color and richest winter-red color with 4–6 hours of direct sun — in deep shade the summer foliage color is more muted green.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Gulf Stream is an outstanding mid-sized compact nandina cultivar that fills the gap between the very dwarf Firepower and the full-size species — reaching a tidy 30–42 inches with a dense, rounded, upright-mounding habit and exceptional seasonal foliage interest. The distinctive characteristic of Gulf Stream is its brilliant blue-green summer foliage — more intensely blue-colored than most nandinas — followed by outstanding orange to red to burgundy winter coloring. It is a semi-sterile selection that produces few berries, reducing the invasive spread concerns associated with the species. Gulf Stream was selected by the late nurseryman John Hampton Brinkley of Lewisville, North Carolina, and has been widely promoted by the National Arboretum as an outstanding landscape selection. The medium size, dense habit, and excellent foliage color make Gulf Stream appropriate for foundation plantings, mixed shrub borders, and mass plantings where neither the very dwarf Firepower nor the large standard species is appropriate. Like all nandinas, it is adaptable to a wide range of soils and light conditions, extremely drought-tolerant once established, and resistant to deer browsing.

plant_note: Set out the potted or bare-root shrub after hard frost; this named cultivar is grown from plants, not seed.
directions: Plant this shrub rose in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart for their rounded habit. Gumball Goody blooms from spring to fall in a candy mix of light pink, deep pink, and yellow on a compact, tidy plant well suited to borders and containers. Water deeply and regularly during establishment and the growing season, keeping foliage dry to limit disease. Prune in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, and deadhead to encourage repeat flushes.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings (which root very readily) or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; gumbo limbo is one of the easiest tropical trees to propagate — large fence posts and even entire trees can be transplanted and will root. It is highly salt, drought, and wind tolerant.
directions: Plant hardwood cuttings or container trees in well-drained, rocky, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; gumbo limbo is nicknamed the 'tourist tree' because its distinctive reddish, peeling bark resembles a sunburned tourist. The shiny, exfoliating, copper-red outer bark peels off in thin sheets to reveal smooth new bark beneath — one of the most ornamentally interesting barks of any South Florida native. The tree is remarkably tough: hurricane-resistant due to flexible limbs, very tolerant of salt spray and coastal conditions, and one of the few South Florida hammock trees that can be grown from large cuttings — even cut limbs several inches in diameter, stuck in moist soil, will root readily. The red, fleshy fruits are eaten by numerous subtropical birds. A cornerstone of South Florida coastal hammock forest and an outstanding landscape tree for zone 10 coastal settings.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Gumpo is a very low, spreading Satsuki azalea that blooms later in spring than most azaleas, extending the azalea display into early summer.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Gumpo is a classic dwarf Satsuki azalea from Japan, valued for its unusually low, spreading, groundcover-like habit and large flowers relative to its small size, blooming several weeks later in late spring than most other azaleas and extending the azalea season into early summer. Named forms are available in white, pink, and variegated pink-and-white flower colors, all sharing the same compact, mounding growth well suited to low borders, rock gardens, and container culture. Water deeply during dry spells and protect from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the foliage; prune lightly right after flowering to shape without removing next year's buds.

common_name: Gumpo Pink Azalea (Dwarf Low-Spreading Pink Satsuki Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Gumpo Pink is a dwarf, late-blooming Satsuki azalea popular for bonsai and low borders.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Gumpo Pink forms a very low, dense, spreading mound bearing large, soft pink flowers in late spring into early summer, blooming weeks after most other azalea groups have finished, which extends the azalea season in a Gulf South garden. Its low, ground-hugging habit makes it useful as an edging plant, rock garden specimen, or bonsai subject, distinct from the taller, more upright Kurume and Southern Indica types. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Gumpo White Azalea (Dwarf White Satsuki Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Gumpo White is a low, dwarf Satsuki azalea that blooms noticeably later than most spring azaleas, extending the azalea season into early summer.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Gumpo White is a dwarf Satsuki azalea forming a low, dense, wide-spreading mound smothered in large, pure white, ruffled flowers that open several weeks later than most Southern Indica and Kurume azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer, which makes it valuable for stretching the azalea display later into the season. Its low, compact habit and slow growth rate suit it especially well to foundation plantings, border edging, rock gardens, and container or bonsai culture, where its fine texture and heavy bloom show to best advantage. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds set soon after bloom ends on this later-flowering type.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in wet to moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; gynandrous sedge is characteristic of forested swamps, alder thickets, and the shaded margins of ponds and streams across eastern North America.
directions: Plant in wet to consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun at the shaded margins of water features, forested wetlands, and streambanks; gynandrous sedge is a tall, robust native sedge of eastern wetland forests, forming large, graceful clumps with broad, arching leaves and long, nodding spikes that droop elegantly at maturity. The nodding spike arrangement distinguishes it from many upright-spike sedges and makes it particularly graceful in moist garden settings. It grows naturally in the shade of forested swamps and alder carr communities, providing important nesting habitat for marsh birds and seed food for wood ducks and swamp sparrows. A strong architectural plant for the margin of a naturalistic pond or rain garden in partial shade where its height and drooping flower spikes make a striking statement.

common_name: Gypsy Lord Bearded Iris (Blue-and-Purple Bitone Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Gypsy Lord is a bitone bearded iris pairing lighter blue standards with deeper violet-purple falls.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Gypsy Lord bears lighter blue-violet standards over deeper, richer purple falls, a classic bitone color pattern on large, ruffled blooms held on tall, sturdy stems well above the fan of foliage. Its bold, saturated coloring and strong garden performance have kept it popular among bearded iris growers for mixed borders and cutting. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep the rhizomes in full sun with sharp drainage to avoid rot.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; H.F. Young blooms on old wood in late spring, so prune only lightly to remove dead or weak stems.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. H.F. Young bears large, clear mid-blue flowers with cream-colored stamens, a clean, true blue considered one of the finest of its color class among large-flowered clematis hybrids. Because it flowers mainly on old wood from the previous season, limit pruning to removing dead or damaged stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole plant back hard. Its reliable, large blooms and award-winning garden performance have kept it a long-standing favorite.

common_name: Habanero Coleus (Narrow Ruffled Spicy-Orange Sun Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Habanero, part of the FlameThrower series, bears narrow, ruffled, spicy-orange foliage on a plant bred for full sun to part shade and very late flowering.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; the FlameThrower series was bred specifically for strong sun tolerance. Habanero bears narrow, deeply ruffled, fiery orange leaves that live up to the series' spicy naming theme, forming an upright, well-branched plant that holds its vivid color through summer heat better than many older coleus cultivars. Like other FlameThrower selections it flowers very late in the season, keeping the foliage display uninterrupted for months. Water regularly during establishment and pinch growing tips occasionally to maintain a full, bushy habit.

plant_note: Plant rosette divisions or offsets in spring, wedged into shaded rock crevices or a gritty, humus-amended, sharply drained substrate in full shade; Haberlea rhodopensis is a remarkable resurrection plant from the Rhodope Mountains of Bulgaria and Greece that can survive complete desiccation and revive fully upon rewatering.
directions: Plant rosette offsets into shaded north- or east-facing rock crevices or in a very gritty, sharply drained mix of equal parts loam, coarse grit, and leaf mold, ensuring the crown sits above the soil line to prevent rot; Haberlea rhodopensis is one of very few vascular plants capable of surviving complete desiccation — a trait known as poikilochlorophylly — and will fully revive from a desiccated state when moisture returns. It produces compact rosettes of wrinkled, spoon-shaped leaves and bears clusters of pale lilac, tubular flowers on short stems in spring; excellent drainage is non-negotiable, as the crown rots in poorly drained or wet winter conditions. Once established, it requires minimal supplemental watering and thrives with the reflected cool humidity of a shaded stone face.

common_name: Habranthus (Copper Lily, Rain Lily, Upward-Facing Zephyr Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; habranthus is distinguished from Zephyranthes by its flowers, which are borne at an upward-angled rather than strictly upright orientation. Plant and then largely ignore — they naturalize and bloom after summer and fall rain events.
directions: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; habranthus (copper lily) is a summer-dormant rain lily that puts on a brief, intense show of large, bright pink trumpet flowers shortly after summer and fall rains, earning the name 'rain lily' for this reliable weather-triggered response. Unlike the straight-up flowers of Zephyranthes, habranthus flowers are borne at a jaunty upward angle, giving them a distinctive, graceful appearance. The flowers are 2–3 inches across, pale to deep rose-pink with a yellow base, and often striped. This species is more vigorous and larger-flowered than most rain lilies. In zone 7–10 the small bulbs naturalize freely to form expanding colonies in lawns and borders. A classic, low-maintenance companion to other Gulf South summer rain lilies (Zephyranthes) with which it can be mixed for a longer combined bloom season.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall into rich, humus-heavy woodland soil under deciduous trees; the deep taproot resents disturbance, so choose a permanent spot and be patient while the clump establishes.
directions: This diminutive European woodland perennial in the carrot family produces odd, charming chartreuse flowers ringed by leaf-like bracts in very early spring, often before the surrounding trees have leafed out, followed by neatly lobed dark-green leaves that persist as a low mound through summer. It is slow to bulk up from seed or division but extremely long-lived and undemanding once settled, forming a slowly expanding clump that needs almost no maintenance. Use it as a specimen at the front of a shaded border or rock garden alongside other early bloomers like hellebores or snowdrops; it resents hot, dry summers and is best suited to cool woodland conditions rather than the Deep South.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and water well until new growth appears.
directions: Grow in consistently moist, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and provide shelter from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the delicate cream leaf margins. Deep shade to part shade suits this cultivar well, and a summer mulch layer helps keep roots cool and moist. Heart-shaped green leaves are irregularly edged in creamy white, giving a softer, lacier look than solid-silver brunnera cultivars, and sprays of tiny sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the foliage in spring. It brightens deep shade beds nicely when paired with dark-leaved heucheras or ferns for contrast.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 9–11; Hainan Fan Palm is a small to medium, shade-tolerant, clustering fan palm endemic to the tropical rainforests of Hainan Island, China — producing dense clusters of slender stems topped by circular, deeply divided, bright-green fan fronds, and among the more cold-tolerant of tropical clustering fan palms.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Chuniophoenix hainanensis prefers the moist, shaded conditions of its native forest understory — protect from direct sun, cold below 26°F, and drought; mulch deeply to maintain cool, moist root zone. Chuniophoenix hainanensis (Hainan Fan Palm) is a small, clustering, forest-understory fan palm endemic to the tropical rainforests of Hainan Island, China — a biodiversity hotspot with numerous endemic species. The genus Chuniophoenix contains only two species, both endemic to southern China. The Hainan Fan Palm forms dense clusters of slender, reed-like stems topped by attractively divided circular fan fronds with individual segments hanging gracefully. Unlike most fan palms which prefer full sun, Chuniophoenix hainanensis is genuinely shade-adapted and performs best in partial to deep shade, reflecting its position as a forest understory specialist. The palm has gained attention from palm enthusiasts for its clustering habit, shade tolerance, moderate cold hardiness (surviving to zone 9a with protection), and compact size suitable for smaller garden spaces. Small, round, orange-red fruits appear periodically on female plants. Listed as Vulnerable in the wild due to habitat loss on Hainan; always purchase nursery-grown specimens.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; hairy alumroot is native to the rich woodlands and rock outcrops of the Appalachians and is better adapted to the humidity and summer heat of the mid-Atlantic and upper South than the Pacific Coast native species.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; hairy alumroot is native to the rich woodlands and rock outcrops of the Appalachians and is better adapted to the humidity and summer heat of the mid-Atlantic and upper South than the Pacific Coast native species. Heuchera pubescens is a distinctly hairy alumroot native to the central and southern Appalachian Mountain woodland zone, producing bold, shallowly lobed, softly hairy, medium-green leaves and taller-than-average panicles of small, whitish to greenish-pink flowers with hairy sepals and petals in late spring to early summer; it is a strong, reliable shade perennial for the East and mid-South that tolerates the heat and humidity of zone 7–8 better than many western heuchera cultivars. An excellent naturalizer for woodland gardens, it bridges the gap between showier garden hybrids and the purely ecological value of wild-collected plants.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; hairy alumroot is the most heat-and-humidity-tolerant native Heuchera species and outperforms H. americana and H. sanguinea cultivars in zone 7–9 summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; hairy alumroot is the native Heuchera of the Southern Appalachians and Ozarks and is significantly more tolerant of heat and humidity than other native Heuchera species — making it the top choice for shade gardens in zone 7–9 where summer temperatures are brutal. The large, maple-shaped leaves with dense soft hairs (giving a velvety texture) are handsome throughout the season, and small white flowers on 2–3 foot stems appear in late summer when little else in the shade garden is blooming. This species is the parent of many popular hybrid 'coral bells' cultivars, including 'Autumn Bride' (exceptionally heat-tolerant with large white flowers in fall). The foliage is semi-evergreen in zone 7–8 and provides attractive winter interest. Divide every 3–4 years as the crown heaves upward from the soil.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall onto the surface of moist, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded woodland edge or savanna margin, since seed needs a full season of cold exposure and light to break dormancy, or plant nursery-grown transplants in fall to skip the slow seedling stage.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall onto the surface of moist, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded woodland edge or savanna margin, since seed needs a full season of cold exposure and light to break dormancy, or plant nursery-grown transplants in fall to skip the slow seedling stage. This tall, downy-stemmed relative of the carrot family produces broad umbels of small greenish-white flowers in late summer, providing a late-season nectar source for wasps, flies, beetles, and native bees when few other woodland plants are blooming. It also serves as a larval host plant for black swallowtail butterflies, extending that species' host range into shadier habitats than the sun-loving carrot family usually occupies. Despite the species name it is not seriously dangerous to handle; the name references its resemblance to more toxic relatives, so simply avoid ingestion as with any wild member of this plant family.

plant_note: Start transplants after cold stratification or direct sow in fall in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun; hairy beardtongue adapts to more diverse conditions than most penstemons and is one of the easiest eastern species to establish.
directions: Start transplants after cold stratification or direct sow in fall in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun; hairy beardtongue adapts to more diverse conditions than most penstemons and is one of the easiest eastern species to establish. Penstemon hirsutus is the most adaptable and shade-tolerant of the eastern penstemons, native to dry to moist rocky soils, open woodlands, and forest edges across the northeastern and central United States; it produces sticky-hairy, soft stems and lavender to pale violet, tubular flowers with a prominent white palate (lower lip) in late spring to early summer, providing nectar for early queen bumblebees and the specialist Osmia penstemonorum bee. Unlike the dry-adapted western penstemons, it tolerates some shade and moderate moisture, making it more useful in the typical eastern garden; the dwarf variety 'Pygmaeus' is an outstanding rock garden plant.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; hairy Cape sorrel follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle, growing and flowering in winter and spring, then going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer. The name 'hirta' means hairy — the stems and leaves are covered with soft hairs. Many color forms exist — pink, red, lilac, purple — produced from the same bulb source. Best in containers in humid-summer climates where summer dormancy is difficult to manage in the ground.
directions: Plant small bulbs in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; hairy Cape sorrel is a Western Cape fynbos oxalis of sprawling, somewhat untidy growth habit — the stems spreading outward and upward from the central corm in a loose, branching, hairy-stemmed mound — that produces in winter and spring an extended succession of large (for the genus), funnel-shaped to wide open, five-petaled flowers in a remarkable diversity of colors across the wild population: deep pink, rose-magenta, clear lilac, purple-mauve, salmon-pink. The flowers are somewhat larger than typical small Cape oxalis species, and the combination of the hairy, somewhat glandular stems with the large, saturated-color flowers creates an impression of lush, somewhat tactile, cottage-garden charm. It is one of the variable Cape oxalis species — seed populations including multiple color forms — and selected forms with particularly vivid or unusual colors are sometimes sold in cultivation. For the zone 9 container or rock garden winter garden, it provides an extended period of cold-season color and interest during the months when the garden most needs it.

plant_note: Transplant into moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun after the last frost; do not allow the root zone to dry out during establishment.
directions: Start seeds indoors in a sandy, acidic mix in fall or winter and grow on for transplanting in spring into a moist to wet, sunny location with acidic, sandy or peaty soil that does not dry out in summer. Taller and more moisture-demanding than its relative Carphephorus corymbosus, this native perennial of wet longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods, and bog margins has hairy, upright stems, narrow rough leaves, and a loose, paniculate branching structure that produces fluffy, rose-purple composite flower clusters in late September and October. It is native to the coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and Texas and provides critically late-season nectar for monarch butterflies, native bees, and skippers in Gulf Coast gardens. Best performance comes from consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; plants will struggle in dry or alkaline conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in dry, rocky or sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral, infertile soil in full sun. Hairy Goldenrod is well-adapted to dry rock outcrops, ledges, and sandy open areas and is particularly drought-tolerant among goldenrods once established.
directions: Hairy Goldenrod is a compact native perennial of dry, rocky or sandy open areas, shale barrens, rocky outcrops, and infertile upland soils across the northeastern United States, recognizable among goldenrods by its densely hairy (hispid) stems and leaves that give the entire plant a soft, grayish appearance. The small clusters of bright yellow flowers are produced on short, compact stems from August through September and attract native bees, small butterflies, and other pollinators visiting rocky, dry habitats where fewer plant species grow. Distinguished from other goldenrods by its smaller stature, hairy texture, and preference for lean, rocky, dry soils, Hairy Goldenrod is an excellent native choice for rock gardens, dry slopes, sandy paths, and xeriscapes where most goldenrods would languish. Direct sow seeds in fall in dry, rocky or sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants are very drought-tolerant and require no supplemental irrigation or soil amendment.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; scarify or cold-stratify seeds to improve germination.
directions: Hairy Lespedeza is a robust, erect native perennial with stiffly hairy stems, large trifoliate leaves, and dense rounded clusters of white to cream-white pea flowers from August through October, making it one of the latest-blooming native legumes in the eastern US. It is native to dry, open woods, pine barrens, and acidic sandy or rocky soil throughout eastern North America, and its late flowers provide critical nectar for fall-flying native bees while the seeds are prime food for quail, turkey, and sparrows. Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, slightly acidic, well-drained soil, scarifying seeds beforehand to encourage germination. Plants are highly drought-tolerant once established and require minimal care in sandy or rocky garden soils.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; hairy lip fern thrives in exposed, dry, acidic rock outcrops and open woodland slopes and is among the most drought-tolerant eastern native ferns.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; hairy lip fern is among the most drought-tolerant of the eastern native ferns and thrives in exposed, dry, acidic rock outcrops, talus slopes, and open rocky woodland that would kill more shade-sensitive fern species. Cheilanthes lanosa is a small, tufted, evergreen fern of eastern North America distinctive for its densely hairy fronds — both the stipes and the undersides of the pinnae are covered in rust-colored hairs that give the plant a fuzzy, russet-brown appearance especially in dry conditions — a feature that reflects its adaptation to drought by reducing water loss. It grows naturally on dry, often south-facing, acidic sandstone, quartzite, and occasionally limestone outcrops from Connecticut to Georgia and westward, forming small, persistent colonies. An excellent fern for dry-shade rock gardens, open stone walls, and naturalistic xeric native plantings where its unusual texture and drought tolerance are assets.

plant_note: Install container-grown or bare-root plants in early spring on a rocky slope, bluff, or streambank site with sharp drainage, since this species naturally roots into shallow, gravelly soil pockets.
directions: Hairy mock orange is a compact deciduous shrub of rocky bluffs, river gorges, and moist ledges scattered through the central and southern Appalachians, distinguished from the more widespread Philadelphus inodorus by its fragrant, four-petaled white flowers and softly hairy young stems and leaf undersides. Clusters of sweetly scented blooms open in late spring and draw bumblebees, mason bees, and other early-summer pollinators to woodland edges where few other shrubs are yet flowering. It performs best on a lean, well-drained, slightly rocky slope with morning sun and afternoon shade, mimicking the cliff and ravine habitats where it grows wild. Renewal-prune the oldest canes to the ground every few years after flowering to keep the multi-stemmed form vigorous and floriferous.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to average, well-drained, acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy penstemon is exceptionally drought tolerant and performs well in rocky, poor, infertile soils where other plants struggle.
directions: Hairy penstemon is a widely adaptable native penstemon of rocky outcrops, dry meadows, open woodlands, and roadsides in the northeastern and north-central United States, producing spikes of pale violet to whitish, hairy-coated tubular flowers in late spring that are a critical food source for bumblebee queens emerging from winter dormancy and seeking early-season pollen and nectar. The plant is covered in fine hairs from the stems to the flower tubes — hence 'hirsutus' — giving it a soft, gray-green, velvety texture that is attractive in its own right; rosettes of glossy, toothed leaves persist year-round as a semi-evergreen groundcover in milder zones. It is one of the most drought tolerant and cold hardy of all eastern penstemons, adapting to virtually any dry, well-drained site in zones 3–8 with no supplemental irrigation once established; excellent for rock gardens, dry slopes, and hell-strip plantings in regions with cold, dry winters. Self-seeds moderately to form naturalized colonies in suitable rocky or sandy soils.

plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions after last frost in well-drained, average to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; hairy phlox benefits from light shearing after bloom to maintain a compact, dense mat and encourage reblooming in fall.
directions: Plant container plants or divisions after last frost in well-drained, average to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; hairy phlox benefits from light shearing after bloom to maintain a compact, dense mat and encourage reblooming in fall. Phlox amoena is a low-growing, mat-forming native phlox of dry, open woodlands, forest edges, and rocky barrens of the southeastern United States from Virginia to Florida and west to Tennessee; it produces small, hairy, semi-evergreen leaves and a profuse display of small, pink to magenta-pink, five-petaled flowers with a characteristic lobed petal shape in early spring, often providing one of the earliest color displays in the native perennial garden. It is an excellent, low-maintenance native groundcover for slopes, rock gardens, and dry to average woodland edges in zones 5–9; more heat-tolerant than creeping phlox (P. subulata) and a good choice for the humid South.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger has passed in consistently moist to wet soil. Nick or soak seeds in warm water overnight before sowing to improve germination speed and uniformity.
directions: Hairy Rose Mallow is a native perennial of river banks, wetland margins, and moist open habitats from Virginia to Florida and Texas, bearing enormous flowers 4-6 inches across in white to pale pink with a deep maroon eye from June through September. Its stout stems and broadly lobed leaves are covered in dense, soft, velvety hairs that distinguish it from the closely related Hibiscus moscheutos. Grow in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, rich soil in full sun; it is ideally suited for rain gardens, pond edges, and wetland restoration sites where the soil stays reliably moist or intermittently flooded. Plants die back to the ground each winter and re-emerge reliably in spring, growing quickly to flowering size by midsummer.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 2 to 4 weeks after last frost into moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded or partially shaded location; seeds require warm soil temperatures of 65 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit to germinate well.
directions: Sow seeds directly into moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded or woodland-edge location 2 to 4 weeks after the last frost, when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees Fahrenheit; barely cover seeds with fine soil and keep the area consistently moist until germination. Hairy Ruellia is best suited to partially shaded spots with reliably moist, fertile soil — stream banks, rain garden edges, and damp woodland borders closely mimic its native habitat in the southeastern US forests. Plants establish slowly in their first season but develop into upright, hairy-stemmed clumps that produce lavender-blue trumpet flowers from summer through early fall, drawing hummingbirds and sphinx moths. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom and reduce aggressive self-seeding; in frost-prone areas at the northern edge of its range, apply a light mulch over the crown in late fall to protect the root system through winter.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in dry to moist, slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; hairy skullcap grows naturally in dry to moist hardwood forest understories and tolerates a range of shade from partial to fairly deep — one of the more adaptable native skullcaps.
directions: Sow seed in fall in dry to moist, slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade — hairy skullcap is a native Scutellaria of eastern deciduous woodland, producing terminal clusters of blue-violet, 3/4-inch, two-lipped flowers on hairy stems 6–16 inches tall from late spring through early summer. The genus name comes from the small, helmet-shaped (scutellum) protrusion on the upper side of the calyx visible in fruit. Native bumblebees are the primary pollinators. Hairy skullcap grows naturally in dry to moist hardwood forest understories from New York south to Florida and west to the Midwest — one of the more shade-tolerant and drought-tolerant native skullcaps, able to perform in the challenging dry-shade conditions under mature deciduous trees. The basal and stem leaves are opposite and elliptic, distinctly hairy. An attractive and ecologically valuable small native for the shaded wildflower garden and native plant border.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full shade; hairy spicebush grows naturally in wet, shaded pocosins, bay swamps, and moist pine flatwoods of the Carolinas coastal plain. It is rarer and more restricted in distribution than common spicebush (L. benzoin).
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full shade in naturalistic woodland or wetland settings; hairy spicebush is a rare and threatened native shrub of the Carolinas coastal plain, naturally restricted to wet, shaded pocosins and bay swamps where it grows beneath pond pines and Atlantic white cedars. Like common spicebush (L. benzoin), the leaves, bark, and twigs are aromatic when crushed with a spicy, benzoin-like fragrance. The small yellow flowers appear on bare stems in very early spring, providing pollen for early-emerging native bees. A host plant for spicebush swallowtail butterfly (Papilio troilus) caterpillars, which use both Lindera species. More restricted to wet, acidic, shaded conditions than common spicebush and more appropriate for pocosin and bay swamp restoration. A rare plant with significant conservation value.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy spiderwort grows naturally in dry, rocky, open woodlands and rocky outcrops of the southeastern US.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; hairy spiderwort is a native southeastern spiderwort adapted to dry, rocky, open woodland conditions — more drought-tolerant and shade-tolerant than most tradescantias. The name reflects the long, conspicuous hairs on the stem (hirsuticaulis = hairy stem). The flowers are typically rose-pink to lavender-pink rather than the blue-violet of Ohio spiderwort, offering a different color palette. The characteristic three-petaled, ephemeral flowers open each morning and close by afternoon. As a relatively small, compact species growing in dry, rocky soils, it is useful in rock gardens and dry shade settings where larger, moisture-loving tradescantias would not thrive.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy sunflower grows naturally in dry to moderately moist, open and partially wooded habitats across the eastern and central US.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy sunflower is a stiffly hairy, rough-textured native perennial sunflower named for the dense, bristly hairs that cover the stems and leaves. It grows in a wide range of open to partially wooded habitats, tolerating more shade than most sunflowers while still blooming reliably. The bright yellow daisy flowers in late summer and fall are excellent late-season nectar sources for native bees and the seeds are consumed by goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. The rough, hairy foliage is notable deer-resistant compared to the smoother-leaved sunflower species. Spreads gradually by rhizomes to form modest colonies. A reliable, low-maintenance native sunflower for the back of a mixed border or at a woodland edge in zones 4–9.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; hairy toad lily is particularly valuable because it blooms in late summer and fall when few shade perennials are in flower.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart; hairy toad lily blooms from late August through October when the shade garden is otherwise winding down, producing arching stems lined with lance-shaped leaves and studded along their upper portions with intricately spotted, orchid-like white-and-purple flowers that genuinely resemble miniature tropical orchids. The species name 'hirta' refers to the soft hairs covering stems and leaves. Plants spread gently by rhizomes to form loose colonies over time. Divide in early spring every 3–4 years to increase plantings; division is best done before new growth emerges. The closely related T. formosana is similar but tolerates zones 5–9 and tends to run more aggressively.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy umbrella-sedge grows naturally in wet meadows, marsh edges, and ditches across the eastern and southeastern US.
directions: Direct sow or plant divisions into saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Hairy umbrella-sedge takes its common name from the soft, hairy sheaths clasping its stems and from the loose, umbrella-like clusters of small brownish flower spikelets held above the grass-like foliage in summer. It grows naturally in wet meadows, marsh margins, roadside ditches, and pond edges across the eastern and southeastern United States, tolerating both consistently saturated soil and brief shallow flooding. In a home rain garden or pond margin it adds fine, upright texture and a long season of subtle bloom, requiring little care beyond consistent moisture once established. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; hairy urospermum self-sows freely in lean, dry soils and can naturalize aggressively in favorable Mediterranean-climate conditions. It thrives in poor, dry, rocky soils and declines in rich, moist conditions. The flowers are short-lived individually but produced continuously through a long season.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; hairy urospermum is a Mediterranean coastal native of the chicory family producing a low rosette of deeply toothed, somewhat hairy, dandelion-like leaves and from spring through summer, a prolific and extended succession of substantial, clear, pale-primrose-yellow chicory-type flowers (1.5–2 inches across) on slender, branching stems. The flowers are produced continuously over several months rather than in a brief flush, and the clear, soft-yellow ray flowers with their slightly squared, five-notched tips have a clean, soft, naturalistic charm reminiscent of dandelion flowers but more refined in scale and arrangement. It thrives in poor, dry, rocky, and limestone soils of Mediterranean coastal scrub and roadsides — conditions that defeat most ornamentals — and is therefore useful in difficult, lean, dry positions in gardens in Mediterranean-climate zones. It self-sows freely in lean, open ground, building naturalized colonies that require no maintenance in appropriate conditions. An underused ornamental for gravel gardens, dry rocky banks, and naturalistic wildflower areas in zones 7–10.

plant_note: Plant container-grown cuttings in spring in very well-drained, dry, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy wicky is a specialist of dry, sandy, acidic soils in the longleaf pine ecosystem and will not tolerate moist or fertile conditions.
directions: Plant in dry, lean, sandy, strongly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy wicky is a diminutive evergreen shrub of the longleaf pine ecosystem of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, growing in the driest, most nutrient-poor, acidic white sands of pine scrub, sandhills, and dry pine flatwoods. Its characteristic small, hairy, needle-like leaves and low, spreading habit distinguish it from the large, showy mountain laurel (K. latifolia) of Appalachian forests. Despite its small stature, the flowers are disproportionately showy for the plant's size — the same distinctive cupped, saucer-like Kalmia blooms in bright pink with ten anthers tucked in pockets around the rim — produced in summer when few other shrubs bloom. An outstanding native for low-maintenance landscaping in dry, acidic sandy soils in zone 7–9 where mountain laurel would fail in summer heat.

plant_note: Transplant nursery-propagated stock in spring into dry, sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor, well-drained soil in full sun; scarify seeds before starting indoors.
directions: Hairy Wild Indigo is a federally endangered native wild indigo endemic to a small number of longleaf pine flatwoods sites in Brantley County, Georgia, with a total wild population numbering only in the hundreds of individuals. It produces densely hairy, gray-green foliage covered in distinctive spider-web-like (arachnoid) hairs and yellow pea flowers in spring, requiring dry, sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor, very well-drained soil in full sun — the same extreme conditions found in intact longleaf pine flatwoods. Obtain only nursery-propagated plants from reputable specialty native plant nurseries and transplant into the garden in spring, as seed-grown plants typically require two to three years to reach first bloom. Cultivating nursery stock of this species is a meaningful act of conservation for one of the rarest plants in the United States.

plant_note: Sow seed directly in autumn under deciduous trees; cold stratification over winter improves germination rates.
directions: Sow seed in autumn directly onto lightly raked, moist soil beneath deciduous trees, where natural leaf litter will provide cover and cold winter temperatures will stratify the seed for spring germination. This tall woodland grass prefers humus-rich, moist soil and will produce its most graceful nodding spikelets under moderate shade. Once established, it self-seeds freely in favorable conditions, creating naturalistic drifts without becoming invasive; simply remove unwanted seedlings while young if spread needs managing. Avoid fertilizing as excess nitrogen produces overly tall, floppy growth that loses the elegant, arching habit that makes this grass so ornamentally valuable.

plant_note: Divide clumps or set out plugs in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil, spacing plants to knit together into a low, textured groundcover over one or two seasons.
directions: Divide clumps or set out plugs in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil, spacing plants to knit together into a low, textured groundcover over one or two seasons. It occurs naturally in rich deciduous forests across eastern North America, tolerating deep shade and competition from tree roots better than most true grasses or sedges, and it spreads gradually by short rhizomes without becoming aggressive. Fine, grass-like leaves edged with soft white hairs form neat evergreen-to-semievergreen tufts, and small brownish flower clusters appear on wiry stems in mid-spring. Its fine texture and shade tolerance make it a useful low-maintenance filler between hostas, ferns, and other woodland perennials where turf grass will not grow.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; halberd-leaved rose mallow is a native perennial of floodplain forests, streambanks, and moist open areas throughout the eastern US, with large pink flowers and distinctive three-lobed, halberd-shaped leaves that distinguish it from other native Hibiscus species.
directions: Plant in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; halberd-leaved rose mallow is native to wet areas and thrives in rain gardens, pond margins, bioswales, and consistently moist borders. Hibiscus laevis is a native eastern US perennial hibiscus of floodplains, streambanks, and wet meadows, distinguished from the similar H. moscheutos by its distinctively halberd-shaped (like the medieval weapon — three-lobed with two lateral points) leaves and smooth stems (laevis = smooth); it produces large, showy, 5–6 inch pale pink flowers with deep red centers from midsummer through early fall, similar in scale and beauty to other native rose mallows. The plant dies to the ground in winter but re-emerges reliably from a woody crown in spring; it is particularly valuable as a native pollinator plant for large bees and hummingbirds in wet areas. Less commonly grown than H. moscheutos but equally beautiful and better suited to shaded, wet settings.

plant_note: Scarify or soak seeds for 24 hours before direct sowing at the soil surface or just below in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, wet to moist soil near pond margins, streambanks, or rain garden depressions. Halberd-leaf Rose Mallow self-sows readily in favorable wet conditions.
directions: Halberd-leaf Rose Mallow is a tall, dramatic native perennial, native to the streambanks, marshy shores, and wet meadow edges of eastern North America from New York to Florida and west to Nebraska and Oklahoma, producing a succession of large, showy, white to pink flowers with a dark red center from July through September on stems reaching 6 feet in wet soil. The deeply three-lobed, halberd-shaped leaves distinguish it from the more common Swamp Rose Mallow (Hibiscus moscheutos), and the flowers are slightly smaller but equally attractive to hummingbirds and large native bees such as carpenter bees, which are among the few insects strong enough to force their way into the blossom. A perennial that dies to the ground in winter and re-emerges reliably from a stout root crown in spring, Halberd-leaf Rose Mallow is excellent for naturalizing the wet margins of ponds, detention basins, and rain gardens where its moisture requirement is easily met. Sow scarified seeds in place in wet soil in early spring, or divide established clumps.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or divide established clumps in early spring. Halberd-leaved yellow violet grows naturally in rich, well-drained mesic woodland slopes, especially in association with oak-hickory and cove hardwood forests.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade on wooded slopes and in cove hardwood forests; halberd-leaved yellow violet is one of the more distinctive native woodland violets, named for the unusual shape of its leaves — triangular with two spreading basal lobes that resemble the blade of a medieval halberd. The foliage often displays attractive silver mottling along the veins, adding interest beyond the spring blooming period. Clear lemon-yellow flowers with purple veining appear in early spring, providing one of the earliest woodland floral displays. Unlike many forest violets, this species prefers well-drained, sloped woodland sites rather than moist bottomland conditions. An excellent groundcover for dry, shaded slopes in naturalistic woodland gardens where its spreading colonies create attractive spring ground-level interest before the tree canopy closes in.

plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Halcyon is medium-sized and fits well in mixed shade borders where it provides color contrast against green hostas, ferns, and heucheras. Divide every 3–4 years when clumps become overcrowded.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Halcyon is the most widely planted and best-known blue hosta, a cultivar from Eric Smith and raised by the Tardiana Group in England from crosses of Hosta sieboldiana elegans with other species, producing medium-sized (18–24 inch) clumps of thick, glaucous, distinctly heart-shaped leaves in a cool, slate-blue color that is more blue than any other commonly available hosta in most garden conditions. The blue color is created by a waxy coating on the leaf surface that is most intense in moderate to deep shade; sun exposure bleaches the coating and reduces the blue tone. Pale lavender flowers appear in summer on branching scapes above the foliage. Halcyon is extraordinarily slug-resistant due to its thick, heavily glaucous leaves — another major advantage over many hostas. A foundational plant for shade gardens that need cool contrast color against gold-leaf or green-variegated companions.

common_name: Halley's Comet Florida Anise (Large-Flowered Red Anise Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring or fall; Halley's Comet flowers more heavily than the wild species and benefits from consistent soil moisture during its spring bloom period.
directions: Halley's Comet is a selection of native Florida anise chosen for producing a much heavier crop of flowers than typical seedling plants, with numerous, larger, deep maroon-red, multi-petaled starfish-shaped blooms that open along the branches in spring. Like the species it forms a dense, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub with anise-scented foliage when bruised, thrives in the deep, acidic shade under pines and hardwoods that stumps many flowering shrubs, and is notably deer-resistant. Give it moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and shelter from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the leaves; all parts of the plant are toxic if eaten and it should not be confused with the culinary star anise, Illicium verum.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hameln blooms earliest of the common Pennisetum alopecuroides cultivars — typically beginning in late July in zone 9, which is an advantage over later-blooming forms that may not flower before the first frost in colder zones.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hameln is the most widely planted dwarf fountain grass cultivar — a compact selection of Pennisetum alopecuroides reaching 24–36 inches in both height and spread, making it the most garden-friendly size class of fountain grass for typical residential landscapes. The soft, arching, medium-green blades produce dense, mounding clumps from which upright flower scapes rise in summer, bearing the characteristic bottle-brush or fox-tail plumes in creamy white to slightly rosy-pink, aging to tan through fall and winter. Hameln is one of the earliest-blooming Pennisetum alopecuroides cultivars, typically beginning in late July in zone 9 — this early bloom is advantageous in zone 9 where the long growing season allows plants to reach maximum plume development. The dried seed heads and foliage provide exceptional winter interest, remaining attractive through February when the plant should be cut back to 4–6 inches. Unlike many fountain grass selections that self-seed aggressively, Hameln is considered relatively sterile or low-seeding — reducing invasive spread concerns. Outstanding for mass planting, border edging, and container culture. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; essentially pest-free.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in mid to late spring once soil has warmed, in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; wait until nighttime lows are reliably above 50F before planting out.
directions: Hammock fern forms a low, spreading colony of once-pinnate fronds that emerge a striking salmon-pink to coppery-rose before maturing to rich medium green, giving it seasonal color rarely seen among garden ferns. Native to hammocks and moist woodland understories from Mexico through the Caribbean and naturalized in Florida, it spreads by creeping rhizomes to form an attractive small-scale groundcover in consistently moist, humus-rich shade. In the Gulf Coast garden it performs best at the warmer end of its range, tolerating summer heat and humidity with ease but benefiting from heavy mulch or container culture where hard freezes threaten. Combine with other warm-climate ferns and broadleaf evergreens in a sheltered courtyard or shaded bed out of drying winter winds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained to moderately wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; hammock sweet azalea tolerates wet, shaded conditions better than most azaleas — it naturally grows in moist hammock forests and swamp margins.
directions: Hammock sweet azalea is a large, summer-blooming native azalea of the Gulf Coastal Plain — the most heat-tolerant and latest-blooming of all eastern native azaleas, producing fragrant clusters of tubular, white (occasionally pink-tinged) flowers with a clammy, sticky texture in July and August, when summer heat makes gardening difficult and most flowering shrubs have long since finished blooming. Its natural habitat is the moist, shaded understory of hardwood hammocks, bay swamps, and magnolia-dominated wet forests from Florida to Louisiana, making it the most shade- and moisture-tolerant of all Gulf Coast native azaleas. In Gulf Coast landscape gardens, it fills a critical niche as a large, fragrant, summer-flowering shade shrub for moist, acidic woodland conditions — pair with ferns, Louisiana irises, and swamp spider lily in moist, acid-soil shrub borders for a true Gulf Coast hammock garden. The late summer bloom time and fragrant flowers attract hummingbirds and giant native sphinx moths that are still active in summer heat.

plant_note: Pot divisions in a light, well-drained, humus-rich mix in partial to full shade with high ambient humidity; it is best grown in a terrarium, greenhouse, or shaded frost-free garden rather than open dry air.
directions: Pot in a light, humus-rich, well-drained mix and keep humidity elevated, since the thin fronds dry out quickly in open air. Provide partial to full shade year-round, as direct sun quickly bleaches and scorches the foliage. Its glossy, palmately lobed fronds fan out like slender fingers or spider legs on wiry dark stipes, giving it a distinctive silhouette that stands out in a shaded terrarium, greenhouse bench, or frost-free shade garden.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes with at least one growing point or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; hanging lobster claw requires rich, consistently moist soil and warm temperatures to flower — dry conditions, poor soil, or temperatures below 55°F cause the plant to go dormant and halt flowering.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; hanging lobster claw is the national flower of Bolivia and one of the most spectacular and instantly recognizable tropical flowers in the world — the inflorescence consists of a long, pendant, drooping flower stalk from which 8–20 red, orange, and yellow bracts hang vertically downward in a precisely alternating, pendant chain, each bract edged in vivid yellow and tipped in green, creating a brilliantly colored, dangling cascade that hangs like a living chandelier from beneath the enormous paddle-shaped leaves. The pendant, downward-hanging display (unusual among heliconias, most of which hold their bracts erect) makes it particularly spectacular when displayed at eye level or above, where the full cascade can be appreciated. Hummingbirds feed from the small, tubular flowers nestled within each bract. It grows best in partial shade with rich, moist soil. The cut inflorescences are among the most prized of all tropical cut flowers and last for weeks in a vase. An essential ornamental in zone 10–12 tropical gardens.

common_name: Hansa Rugosa Rose (Fragrant Reddish-Purple Rugosa Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; Hansa is an old, exceptionally cold-hardy, fragrant rugosa rose that tolerates poor, sandy, and coastal soils.
directions: Plant in average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; rugosa roses excel in poor, dry, or coastal soils that would stress most other roses. Hansa bears large, double, reddish-purple blooms with an intensely strong, clove-like fragrance, followed by large, showy orange-red hips that provide fall and winter interest and attract birds. The rugged, wrinkled-leaved shrub is exceptionally cold-hardy and disease-resistant, tolerating salt spray and poor soil better than nearly any other rose class. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since rugosas bloom on both old and new growth and resent hard pruning.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; established clumps tolerate both dry and periodically wet soil.
directions: One of the older red-tinged switchgrass selections, 'Hanse Herms' forms a narrow, upright clump of steel-blue foliage that reddens progressively through summer until it is a deep burgundy by fall. A cloud of fine pink-tinted flower panicles hovers above the foliage in late summer, and the colored blades remain attractive well into winter. Gardeners choose it over green-leaved switchgrass cultivars specifically for this season-long color shift from blue to wine-red. It tolerates heat, drought, and occasional wet soil once established, making it a low-fuss vertical accent or screen.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Happy Bean peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Happy Bean peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thick, curved, bean-shaped, semi-succulent leaves are densely packed along upright, fleshy stems in a distinctive pincushion arrangement, giving the plant a quirky, playful texture unlike the flatter or rounder leaves of most peperomia species. Native to dry rocky habitats in Peru, it stores water in its thick leaves and tolerates missed waterings far better than soggy soil, making it a good low-maintenance choice for a bright windowsill or succulent-style dish garden. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light to keep growth compact rather than stretched, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Happy Returns is a sister seedling to Stella d'Oro and shares its outstanding rebloom habit, compact size, and adaptability.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Happy Returns is a classic reblooming compact daylily producing slightly fragrant, soft lemon-yellow, ruffled 3-inch flowers continuously from early summer through fall. Bred as a Stella d'Oro companion with cooler, lighter yellow coloring that blends more subtly into the mixed border, it blooms at the same time and repeat-blooms reliably through the season. The soft lemon color complements blues, purples, and whites beautifully in perennial borders. Happy Returns is notably fragrant at dusk, a quality unusual in modern daylilies. Divide every 3–4 years when the center of the clump becomes woody and bloom declines. In zone 9 it begins blooming in April and continues through November with semi-evergreen foliage through mild Gulf Coast winters.

common_name: Happy Single Flame Dahlia (Fiery Orange-Red Single Bloom over Bronze Foliage)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Happy Single Flame, part of the Happy Single series, bears fiery orange-red single blooms over dark bronze foliage.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up. Happy Single Flame, part of the compact, garden-friendly Happy Single series, bears vivid, fiery orange-red single blooms with a ring of golden stamens at the center, held above dark bronze, finely cut foliage on a well-branched, floriferous plant scaled for containers and small borders. The single, open flower form makes it especially attractive to bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds compared to fully double dahlia types. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep flowers coming, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Happy Trails Portulaca (Vigorous Trailing Moss Rose Series)
plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Happy Trails is a vigorous trailing portulaca series bred for larger flowers and a more spreading habit than seed-grown moss rose, making it a strong container and hanging basket performer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; overly rich or consistently wet soil promotes rot and reduces flowering. Happy Trails is a vegetatively propagated portulaca series bred for a more vigorous, trailing habit and larger, brighter flowers than typical seed-grown moss rose, making it an excellent choice for hanging baskets and containers where its cascading stems can spill over the edge. Flowers open fully only in bright sun and close on cloudy days and in the evening, covering the succulent, fleshy foliage in bright color through the hottest, driest part of summer when many other annuals struggle. It needs very little water once established and is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant flowering annuals available for a Gulf South summer container.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall immediately after collection for natural cold stratification; or purchase dormant corms for fall planting in moist, rich, well-drained woodland soil in light shade.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in the dappled shade of deciduous trees; harbinger of spring is among the first native wildflowers to bloom in eastern North American woodlands, appearing as early as February or March with tiny clusters of white flowers with dark reddish-purple anthers — the 'salt and pepper' pattern that gives it its alternate name — often poking through melting snow before any other plants stir. A diminutive spring ephemeral with carrot-family affiliation; foliage emerges briefly with the flowers then disappears completely by late spring. Grows from a small corm and spreads slowly in colonies in moist, rich bottomland forests. A charming and historically significant plant for native woodland and early pollinator gardens.

common_name: Harbor Dwarf Nandina (Classic Spreading Groundcover Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Harbor Dwarf is one of the most shade-tolerant nandina selections and spreads gradually by underground rhizomes to form a dense, low groundcover.
directions: Harbor Dwarf is one of the longest-established and most reliable dwarf nandina cultivars, a low, spreading selection grown as a mass groundcover under trees, along foundations, and on slopes where its rhizomatous spread gradually knits together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat.
