plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in moist to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Nandina is one of the most adaptable ornamental shrubs for the Southeast and Gulf Coast, tolerating clay soil, drought, dense shade, and coastal conditions better than almost any comparable plant.
directions: Plant in virtually any well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to full shade; Nandina is one of the toughest and most site-adaptable ornamentals for Southern gardens, though it develops the best red fall and winter foliage color in full sun, and in heavy shade may remain more green year-round. Nandina domestica (heavenly bamboo — not a true bamboo) is an elegant, upright evergreen shrub native to China and Japan with fine-textured, pinnate (bamboo-like) foliage that emerges bronze-red in spring, turns green in summer, and becomes brilliant red to burgundy-red in fall and winter, especially in sun; large, pyramidal clusters of white flowers in May–June are followed by persistent clusters of bright-red berries that last through winter and provide exceptional wildlife value. The berries are relished by Cedar Waxwings and American Robins. Standard Nandina grows 4–6 feet tall; compact cultivars like 'Harbour Dwarf' (2–3 feet), 'Fire Power' (2 feet, intense red fall color), and 'Lemon Lime' (lime-green foliage) are popular. Note: Nandina berries are toxic to dogs and cats; berries may be invasive in some southeastern states — check local regulations.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed, then direct sow after frost at the base of a support.
directions: Nick the seed coat and soak overnight, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis or fence. This showy climber opens sky-blue flowers in the cool of morning that close in afternoon heat but stay open all day when cloudy or in fall. Give it full sun and a support to twine up, watering while young until established. Note that parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

common_name: Heavy Metal Switchgrass (Steel Blue Upright Switchgrass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Heavy Metal is adaptable to clay, wet, and dry soils — one of the most versatile native ornamental grasses for difficult sites.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Heavy Metal is the most celebrated upright switchgrass cultivar — named for its stiffly vertical, non-flopping growth habit and distinctive steel-blue summer foliage color, in contrast to the arching, floppy form of the switchgrass species and many other cultivars. The rigid, bolt-upright stems (4–5 feet tall) maintain their strict vertical form through all weather without flopping or spreading outward — a critical landscape quality that makes Heavy Metal outstanding for formal accent use, vertical punctuation in borders, and screening where a reliably upright column of foliage is desired. The summer foliage is an attractive steel-blue to blue-green color; in fall it transitions through yellow, orange, and burgundy for one of the finest fall color displays of any native grass. Pink seed heads wave in late summer breezes. Heavy Metal is a prairie native (Panicum virgatum) that is exceptionally adaptable — tolerating clay, periodic flooding, drought, and the full range of Gulf South conditions that challenge many ornamental grasses. The wildlife value is significant: the seeds are eaten by many songbirds, and switchgrass provides nesting habitat and overwintering cover for many native insects and small mammals. Cut to 4–6 inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge bamboo is a CLUMPING bamboo (Bambusa genus) with tight, non-invasive rhizomes — no root barrier needed. This is one of the most reliable non-invasive bamboos for warm climates, ideal for privacy screens and hedges.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge bamboo (and its many cultivars including the striped 'Alphonse Karr' with yellow culms streaked green) is one of the most widely planted bamboos in the southeastern US, Gulf Coast, and California — a clumping bamboo that does not spread invasively but grows into a graceful, dense clump of arching culms perfect for screens, hedges, and specimen plantings. Because it is Bambusa (a clumping bamboo genus), it does not send out long, invasive rhizomes like the Phyllostachys running bamboos — making it suitable for gardens where invasive spread is a concern. The dense, arching clumps provide excellent year-round visual screening. 'Alphonse Karr' with its yellow and green striped culms is one of the most popular ornamental bamboos in warm climates. Grows vigorously in the Gulf Coast and Florida.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge maple is exceptionally adaptable to poor soil, drought, pollution, and pruning, tolerating urban conditions better than most maples.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge maple is exceptionally adaptable to poor soil, drought, pollution, and pruning, tolerating urban conditions better than most maples. Small, rounded, dark green leaves with softly lobed margins cover a dense, tidy, small-to-medium tree that tolerates heavy pruning and shearing exceptionally well, making it a traditional European choice for clipped hedges and formal allees as much as a freestanding shade or street tree, turning a modest but pleasant yellow in fall. Native to Europe and western Asia, it is remarkably tolerant of poor, compacted, alkaline urban soils, drought, and air pollution, performing reliably in difficult street tree and parking lot planting sites where more particular maple species struggle. It needs little supplemental care once established beyond routine pruning if grown as a hedge, and its small mature size and dense branching make it a versatile shade tree for a smaller residential lot.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost about an inch deep in full sun, thinning to 12-18 inches apart. This heirloom mix blends the sunny yellows of Lemon Queen, warm tones of Autumn Beauty, and deep reds of Velvet Queen in 4-8 inch multi-branching blooms. Because the plants branch, cut stems regularly to encourage a long succession of flowers for bouquets and pollinators. Water while establishing and stake tall stalks in exposed sites.

common_name: Helen Campbell Cleome (Classic White Heirloom Spider Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost; the tall stature and mildly thorny stems are best sited toward the back of a border, away from foot traffic.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost; Helen Campbell is an early-20th-century heirloom selection prized for pure white, spidery flower clusters with long, whisker-like stamens that open progressively up tall flower spikes through summer. Unlike newer compact, spineless cleome cultivars, it retains the traditional tall stature and mildly thorny stems of old-fashioned spider flower, making it best sited toward the back of a border or away from foot traffic. Flowers release a musky fragrance most noticeable at dusk, drawing hawkmoths and hummingbirds, and the plant self-sows readily once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Helen Johnson bears unusual coppery apricot-rose flowers that shift subtly in tone as they age and as light changes through the day.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than fertility for this rot-prone perennial. Helen Johnson bears dense spikes of unusual coppery apricot-rose flowers, each centered with contrasting purple-mauve stamens, a subtle, shifting color that reads differently depending on the light and time of day, over gray-green, felted foliage. Its distinctive, muted coloring makes it a favorite for designers working with warm, earthy border palettes alongside heucheras, coral bells, and other coppery-toned companions. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage continued bloom, and expect this hybrid to be relatively short-lived, often performing best as a biennial or short-lived perennial refreshed by occasional self-sown seedlings.

common_name: Helene Rose of Sharon (White with Deep Red Veined Eye Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Helene is one of the original US National Arboretum rose of sharon introductions, prized for its crisp white-and-red flower contrast.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Helene bears crisp white, single flowers marked with a deep reddish-purple eye that radiates outward along the petal veins, a striking, high-contrast pattern distinct from the solid-eyed look of many other rose of sharon cultivars, blooming from midsummer into fall. Like its sibling introductions it is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection that sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older, seed-grown rose of sharon while remaining a tough, heat- and humidity-tolerant shrub. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and maximize flowering wood.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant only after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep; germination is slow (14–28 days) and benefits from bottom heat at 70–80°F consistently. Transplant into rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; heat brings out the intensely vanilla-scented, deep purple flower clusters. Pinch tips once or twice before transplanting to produce bushier plants with more flowering heads. In zones 10–11 heliotrope is a shrubby perennial; elsewhere take cuttings in late summer to overwinter prized fragrant selections indoors.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall in humus-rich, well-drained shade; transplanted divisions establish more reliably than seed.
directions: Plant with the crown at soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade — morning sun is tolerated, but afternoon sun causes leaf scorch. Hellebores bloom in late winter to early spring, often through snow, and the nodding flowers face downward; tipping the pot or planting on a slope allows a better view of the flower interior. Remove old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to improve air circulation and reduce leaf spot diseases. Hellebores self-sow freely, and seedlings from hybrid plants will vary; divide named selections in early spring to maintain specific colors.

plant_note: Scatter seeds on bare, dry, sandy soil in fall; do not cover, as light aids germination, and avoid compacted or moist ground.
directions: Heller's Cudweed is a southeastern native annual everlasting that produces upright stems densely clothed in white woolly hair, topped in spring with clusters of tiny composite flower heads bearing papery, straw-white bracts that hold their form when dried. The entire plant emits a pleasant, mild balsam-like fragrance when brushed or crushed, making it useful in dried arrangements as well as native habitat plantings. Like other cudweeds, it serves as a critical larval host plant for the American Painted Lady butterfly. Sow seeds on the surface of dry, lean, sandy, well-drained soil in fall and leave them undisturbed through winter; plants self-sow freely in open, sunny ground and need no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established.

plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Hellfire bears deep, saturated blood-red flowers, among the darkest reds available in the genus.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Hellfire produces arching, one-sided sprays of deep, saturated blood-red, tubular flowers, among the darkest, most intense reds available among named crocosmia cultivars, held above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer. Its dramatic color makes it a strong companion to the more famous Lucifer within a hot-colored border, and hummingbirds visit the flowers reliably through the bloom season. Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–October. Hello Yellow butterfly weed, like all Asclepias tuberosa, is late to emerge in spring — mark plant locations to avoid disturbing dormant roots. Do not transplant established plants as the deep taproot resists disturbance. Plants bloom in their second year from seed; container-grown plants may bloom the first season. In zone 9 butterfly weed is extremely drought-tolerant once established — one of the most drought-adapted native perennials for full-sun locations.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty, neutral to slightly acidic soil — butterfly weed must have excellent drainage and thrives in dry, hot conditions; Hello Yellow is a cultivar of native butterfly weed (Asclepias tuberosa) selected for its clear, bright, warm yellow flower clusters — a color variant of the standard vivid orange species that provides a softer, cooler yellow tone for garden designs where the species orange clashes with surrounding plants. Asclepias tuberosa is one of the most ecologically important native plants for monarch butterfly conservation — it is a host plant for monarch caterpillars and an important nectar source for adult monarchs, swallowtails, and other native pollinators. Unlike the common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca), butterfly weed does not spread aggressively and does not produce the milky latex sap, making it a much more garden-friendly choice that can be integrated into managed landscape plantings without concern for spreading. Hello Yellow's warm yellow flowers pair naturally with orange, bronze, and gold companion plants, creating summer combinations that reference prairie flower meadows where Asclepias tuberosa is naturally found growing alongside goldenrods, coneflowers, and grasses. Drought tolerance, native provenance, and wildlife value make it a cornerstone plant for responsible zone 9 landscapes.

common_name: Helvola Water Lily (Miniature Yellow Hardy Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged only 4-12 inches below the water surface in full sun; Helvola is one of the smallest hardy water lily cultivars and is well suited to a half-barrel, small tub, or shallow container garden rather than a deep pond.
directions: Helvola is among the smallest and most widely grown miniature hardy water lily cultivars, producing tiny, star-shaped, soft canary-yellow flowers only 2 inches across over small, mottled, purple-speckled leaves, on a plant scaled for a shallow tub, small container pond, or even a large decorative bowl rather than a full-sized pond. Its diminutive size makes lotus- and water-lily-growing accessible to gardeners without room for a large water feature, and it flowers freely through the warm season once established in shallow, undrained water. Divide rhizomes every couple of years as the small container becomes crowded, and feed during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets for the best bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in consistently moist to wet soil; keep soil evenly moist through the first growing season to establish deep roots.
directions: Henderson's Checker-mallow is a rare native Sidalcea of brackish marsh margins, tidal meadows, and wet coastal lowland habitats in the Pacific Northwest, primarily in Washington and Oregon, where it produces erect spikes of deep rose-pink mallow flowers in summer atop sturdy, upright stems. It is one of the most moisture-tolerant checker-mallows and thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, mucky or heavy soil in full sun — conditions that would be fatal to most ornamental perennials. Plant container-grown transplants in spring and keep soil wet through establishment; once rooted, plants form long-lived clumps that spread slowly by rhizomes and naturalize well in restored wetland settings. It is an important larval host for specialist pollinators in its native range and an excellent choice for rain gardens, wet borders, and Pacific Northwest wetland restoration plantings.

plant_note: Plant corms immediately after division in late summer or early fall, 3-4 inches deep, in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Henderson's fawn lily is native to open oak woodlands and rocky slopes of southwest Oregon and northern California and, unlike many Erythronium, wants sharper drainage and a summer-dry dormant period.
directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep immediately after division in late summer or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; give it a spot that dries out in summer, mimicking the Mediterranean-climate oak woodlands of southwest Oregon and northern California where it grows wild. Henderson's fawn lily is among the showiest western trout lilies, with heavily mottled leaves and one to several nodding, lilac to soft purple flowers marked with a dark maroon zone at the throat, blooming in March and April on slopes that are damp in winter and spring but bone-dry by early summer. Because it is adapted to that wet-winter, dry-summer rhythm rather than the consistently moist soil eastern woodland species prefer, it performs best in a rock garden, raised bed, or bulb frame with excellent drainage where summer irrigation can be withheld once the foliage yellows. Source corms only from nurseries propagating responsibly, since wild populations are localized and slow to recover from collection.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall onto moist, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded site; cold stratification over the Pacific Northwest winter provides the chill needed for spring germination.
directions: Sow fresh seed in early fall directly onto prepared soil in a lightly shaded, well-drained garden bed or open woodland edge, pressing seed into the surface without covering. The corms require a cold, moist winter period to germinate successfully, and seedlings typically emerge among the first wildflowers of the Pacific Northwest spring. Provide consistent moisture through the brief spring growing season, then withhold water as the foliage begins to yellow after flowering, mimicking the plant's natural summer-dry habitat. Once established, Henderson's Shooting Star will form expanding colonies and self-sow reliably under favorable conditions.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Henna is a trailing coleus cultivar with finely cut, lacy, copper-orange leaves edged in chartreuse-green, an unusual warm color combination well suited to hanging baskets and container edges.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Henna is a trailing coleus cultivar with finely dissected, lacy-textured leaves in a warm copper-orange center fading to a chartreuse-green edge, an unusual combination that reads as warm and glowing rather than the cooler purples and reds common among coleus. Its cascading, trailing habit makes it especially well suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and the edges of large containers, where it spills gracefully over the rim, and the fine, ferny leaf texture provides contrast against bolder, broad-leaved companion plants. Like most coleus, it performs best with some protection from the most intense midday sun in zone 9, coloring up most vividly with morning sun and afternoon shade. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage denser, bushier trailing growth.

common_name: Henon Bamboo (Giant Timber Form of Black Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; being a running bamboo it requires an 18-24 inch deep rhizome barrier to contain spread.
directions: Henon is a large-culm selection of black bamboo grown for timber-scale poles rather than dark color; unlike the straight species its mature culms stay green to grayish-green rather than turning black, and it grows considerably taller and thicker, making it the preferred choice where sturdy poles or a dramatic upright grove effect is wanted. It runs by rhizome like other Phyllostachys, so a physical barrier or regular trenching is essential to keep it from escaping into lawns or neighboring beds. Feed young groves with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer in spring to speed culm size increase over the first several growing seasons. Once established it tolerates heat, humidity, and occasional flooding, and thins naturally into a graceful, high-canopied grove if older culms are selectively removed.

common_name: Henri Martin Moss Rose (Vivid Crimson-Red Moss Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Henri Martin is a vigorous, arching moss rose with vivid crimson-red blooms.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Henri Martin bears loose, semi-double, vivid crimson-red blooms with a light, sweet fragrance, opening from lightly mossed buds on a vigorous, arching shrub that can be trained as a short climber against a fence or pillar. Like most moss roses it blooms just once, in a spectacular flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Henry Duelberg Sage (Perennial Native Blue Texas Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Henry Duelberg is a selection of the Texas native Salvia farinacea that is more reliably perennial in zone 9 than the standard Victoria Blue hybrid cultivars used as annuals in northern gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Henry Duelberg is a white-flowered selection of Salvia farinacea (mealy cup sage) — the Texas native blue sage that is the parent of the widely grown 'Victoria Blue' annual series, but Henry Duelberg itself is selected as a reliably perennial landscape form for zones 7–11 rather than an annual bedding plant. Wait — Henry Duelberg is actually a white-flowered form. Let me clarify: Henry Duelberg sage produces pure white flowers on silvery-mealy calyces on upright spikes, providing a clean white effect different from the blue-violet standard S. farinacea. The plant grows 2–3 feet tall with an upright, tidy habit and blooms from spring through frost with virtually no deadheading required. Like all S. farinacea selections, Henry Duelberg is highly attractive to butterflies and bees, and the mealy calyx texture persists ornamentally even after individual flowers have dropped, extending the effective display period. In zone 9, Henry Duelberg is reliably perennial — the woody crown overwinters even through moderate freezes and rebounds vigorously in spring. The plant self-seeds mildly, creating a self-maintaining colony without becoming weedy. Outstanding heat, drought, and humidity tolerance make Henry Duelberg one of the most durable and reliable perennial salvias for Gulf South conditions. A Texas native with exceptional local adaptation.

common_name: Henry Duelberg Salvia (Vigorous Native Texas Blue Mealy Sage Selection)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Henry Duelberg's exceptional drought tolerance once established makes it ideal for low-irrigation landscapes — water weekly for the first season, then only during extended drought.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Henry Duelberg is a superior selection of mealy blue sage (Salvia farinacea) — a Texas native wildflower — chosen for its outstanding garden performance: larger, more vigorous plant habit, more robust flower spike production, and excellent persistence compared to typical nursery-grown mealy sage seedlings. Named for Henry Duelberg, a San Antonio area rancher and plant enthusiast who grew this selection for years, the cultivar was popularized by plantsman Scott Ogden and represents one of the most valuable native perennial salvias for Gulf South gardens. The lavender-blue to rich violet-blue flower spikes — each 6–12 inches tall with densely packed whorls of small tubular flowers along white-farinose (mealy-powdery) stems — bloom from early spring through heavy frost, providing an extremely long ornamental season. The extended bloom, exceptional heat and drought tolerance, deer resistance, and powerful attraction to hummingbirds, monarchs, swallowtails, and native bees make Henry Duelberg Salvia one of the top performers for zone 8-10 pollinator gardens and xeriscape designs. In zone 9, established plants are essentially self-sustaining on rainfall alone after the first season. The fine-textured blue flower spikes combine well with coarser-textured native companions — Salvia greggii, Lantana, Gulf muhly — in low-maintenance native plant gardens.

common_name: Henry Eckford Sweet Pea (Vivid Orange-Scarlet Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Henry Eckford is named for the Scottish breeder who transformed sweet peas from small wild-type flowers into the large, colorful Grandiflora forms of the late 1800s.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Named for the Scottish nurseryman whose decades of breeding work founded the modern Grandiflora sweet pea, Henry Eckford bears vivid, richly fragrant, orange-scarlet flowers on a vigorous, tall-climbing vine, representative of the dramatically larger and more colorful sweet peas Eckford introduced starting in the 1880s. It remains a valued heirloom for gardeners tracing sweet pea breeding history as well as for its strong color and fragrance. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom.

common_name: Henry Eilers Rudbeckia (Quilled-Petal Native Sweet Coneflower)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Henry Eilers was discovered growing wild in an Illinois prairie remnant and is prized for its distinctive quilled, tubular petals.
directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun. Henry Eilers, discovered growing wild in an Illinois prairie remnant and named for the naturalist who found it, is a striking selection of native sweet coneflower with golden-yellow petals rolled into distinctive narrow quills rather than the typical flat ray form, giving each flower a spidery, unusual look quite different from other Rudbeckia. The tall, sturdy, well-branched plant bears fragrant, anise-scented foliage and blooms heavily from late summer into fall, providing valuable late-season nectar for pollinators and seed for goldfinches. It tolerates average to moist soil better than many drought-loving Rudbeckia species, making it a good fit for a rain garden edge as well as a standard border. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained to evenly moist soil in partial shade to full shade; Henry's anise is native to moist woodland ravines and shaded slopes of central China and demands protection from hot afternoon sun in zones 7–9 or foliage will scorch. Avoid low frost pockets where cold air pools; a sheltered courtyard or north-facing slope provides ideal conditions in the colder end of its range.
directions: Plant in partial shade to deep shade in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with excellent drainage; Henry's anise is one of the finest shade-tolerant broad-leaved evergreen shrubs for gardens in zones 7–9, offering year-round glossy, lance-shaped, deep-green foliage with a distinct anise fragrance when crushed — a characteristic shared with the closely related native Florida anise (Illicium floridanum). Illicium henryi produces charming, star-shaped flowers from spring through early summer in shades of rose-red to deep carmine-pink, with petals arranged in the distinctive multi-layered pattern characteristic of the genus; the flowers are subtly fragrant and appear among the glossy foliage over an extended season. An outstanding plant for shady courtyards, woodland borders, and foundation plantings where a refined, deer-resistant, evergreen structure is needed; it pairs beautifully with Japanese maples, camellias, and Hydrangea quercifolia in the shade garden. CAUTION: all parts are toxic if ingested — do not confuse with culinary star anise (Illicium verum).

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Henry's anise tree is the hardiest of the Chinese Illicium species and one of the few broad-leaved evergreen shrubs that thrives in deep shade in zones 6–9.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Henry's anise tree is a Chinese evergreen shrub or small tree prized for its ability to thrive in deep shade — one of the relatively few large-growing broad-leaved evergreens that performs well in the dense shade beneath mature trees where most broadleaf shrubs languish. The large, glossy, dark green, willow-like leaves are aromatic when crushed. The flowers are rosy red to deep pink, star-shaped, and appear in late spring — more showy than those of the native Florida anise (I. floridanum) but less fragrant. Named for Augustine Henry, the Irish plant explorer who collected extensively in China in the late 19th century. Somewhat hardier than Florida anise, tolerating temperatures to 0°F in a sheltered spot. An excellent large screening shrub for shaded gardens in the Southeast.

common_name: Henry's Garnet Virginia Sweetspire (Fall Color Shade Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Henry's Garnet tolerates wet, periodically flooded soils better than most landscape shrubs — it is excellent for rain gardens and moist, low-lying areas.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Henry's Garnet is the most widely grown and most celebrated Itea virginica cultivar — a superior selection chosen by Mary Henry of Gladwyne, Pennsylvania, for its outstanding combination of fragrant summer flowers, exceptional fall color, and adaptability to difficult growing conditions. In late June and July, the shrub produces 4–6 inch, drooping, bottlebrush-like clusters of small, fragrant white flowers that attract bees and butterflies. But Henry's Garnet's most remarkable attribute is its fall color — in September through November, the foliage transitions to vivid burgundy-red to deep garnet, one of the most reliable and intense fall color displays of any native shrub, maintained even in zone 9 where fall temperatures are mild. The fall color persists for 6–8 weeks — far longer than most fall-color shrubs. Henry's Garnet spreads by suckering to form a colony over years, making it effective as a mass planting for naturalizing, rain garden planting, and stream-bank erosion control. Unlike most fall-color shrubs that require full sun for good color development, Henry's Garnet develops excellent color even in partial shade — a notable advantage for shade gardens. The spreading habit and outstanding fall color with shade tolerance make it one of the finest native shrubs for zone 9.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 8-10 inches deep (the stem roots above the bulb, so depth is important) in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Henry's lily is unusual among true lilies in tolerating lime-rich soils and partial shade, making it useful in dappled light under trees where other lilies fail.
directions: Plant bulbs 8-10 inches deep (the stem roots above the bulb, so depth is important) in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Henry's lily is unusual among true lilies in tolerating lime-rich soils and partial shade, making it useful in dappled light under trees where other lilies fail. Lilium henryi was discovered in central China by Augustine Henry in 1888 and introduced to Western horticulture shortly after; it is a spectacular architectural lily, producing stout stems up to 8 feet tall in full vigor bearing large whorls of leaves and 20-30 pendant, Turk's-cap-type flowers of warm apricot-orange with dark spotting and reflexed petals in late July and August. The plant is vigorous, long-lived, disease-resistant, and increases slowly by bulb offsets; its unusual tolerance of chalk and alkaline soils makes it an outstanding choice for gardens on limestone where most lilies are difficult.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Henry's rodgersia has more finely cut, coppery-tinted foliage than other rodgersia species and benefits from a sheltered site out of drying wind.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Henry's rodgersia has more finely cut, coppery-tinted foliage than other rodgersia species and benefits from a sheltered site out of drying wind. Rodgersia henrici is a Chinese woodland species with deeply divided, palmately compound leaves emerging bronze-copper in spring before maturing to dark green, and airy, branched plumes of small creamy-white to pale pink, astilbe-like flowers held well above the foliage in summer. Its finely textured, coppery new growth distinguishes it from the coarser-leaved rodgersia species more commonly grown, adding another layer of foliage interest to a shaded bog garden or streamside planting. Give it constant moisture and rich soil, and protect the large, thin leaves from wind, which can tatter the foliage and dull its bronze coloring.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Henryi blooms on old wood in late spring with a possible light rebloom on new growth, so prune only lightly to remove dead or weak stems rather than cutting the vine back hard.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Henryi is one of the oldest and most classic large-flowered clematis cultivars, producing enormous, creamy white flowers with conspicuous chocolate-brown stamens that create a striking contrast against the pale petals. Because it flowers mainly on old wood from the previous season, heavy pruning removes the coming season's bloom, so gardeners should limit pruning to removing dead or damaged stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole plant back as with Jackmanii-type clematis. It has been a garden favorite for well over a century for its dependable, large-scale white flower display.

plant_note: Plant offsets (chicks) in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun; hens and chicks require virtually no soil depth and thrive in rock crevices, walls, and containers with minimal growing medium.
directions: Plant offsets ('chicks') in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun — they need almost no soil depth and anchor themselves quickly; hens and chicks are among the hardiest and most drought-tolerant succulents for cold-climate gardens, forming tight rosettes of fleshy, pointed leaves in an extraordinary range of colors from green to burgundy, purple, silver, and bicolor depending on cultivar. The 'hen' rosette blooms once (typically in year 2 or 3) with a dramatic starburst flower stalk, then dies, but leaves behind dozens of 'chicks' that fill the gap. Outstanding for rock gardens, green roofs, wall crevices, alpine troughs, dry stone walls, and containers; they thrive on negligence and rot immediately in wet, poorly drained conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in early spring in humus-rich, slightly alkaline soil; purchase only nursery-propagated plants as wild collection is unsustainable and transplants rarely survive.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil (unlike most woodland plants, hepatica prefers near-neutral to mildly basic soil from calcareous bedrock) in full to dappled shade. One of the earliest spring wildflowers in eastern North America, the cup-shaped flowers in shades of white, pink, and lavender open in late February–March before any leaves appear, emerging through snow on fuzzy, insulating stems. The leathery, three-lobed leaves that develop after flowering persist through winter and often have beautiful mottled markings. Extremely slow-growing from seed (3–5 years to bloom); purchase only from ethical native plant nurseries. May live for decades undisturbed.

common_name: Her Highness Louisiana Iris (Historic Pure White Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Her Highness, introduced in 1957, bears pure white flowers on a historic Louisiana iris cultivar.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Her Highness, introduced in 1957, bears clean, pure white flowers, an early representative of the white Louisiana iris class that helped pave the way for later white cultivars such as Dural White Butterfly. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; herald's trumpet is a very large, vigorous vine requiring substantial, permanent support — a mature plant can cover a large pergola or building wall 40–50 feet across. It blooms in spring (April–June), producing large clusters of enormous, white, fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers. In zone 9 it may be frost-damaged in hard winters but regrows from the roots. Requires consistent moisture during the growing season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; herald's trumpet is one of the most spectacular of all tropical and subtropical flowering vines — a native of the eastern Himalayan foothills and northern India that produces in spring (April through June) enormous, trumpet-shaped flowers of breathtaking scale: each individual flower is 4–5 inches long and 3–4 inches across at the opening, pure white, five-petaled, with a narrow tube flaring to a wide, rounded, slightly fragrant trumpet that resembles an Easter lily flower of exaggerated dimensions. These enormous white trumpet flowers are borne in large, clustered bunches of 6–20 at the ends of the stems, so that a mature vine in full spring bloom — covering a large pergola or two-story wall — presents hundreds of the enormous, pristine-white trumpets simultaneously in a display of singular tropical grandeur. The large, oval, glossy, dark-green leaves are bold and handsome year-round. The vine is very large-growing, reaching 30–50 feet on suitable permanent support, and is a decades-long commitment. In zone 9a it requires a warm, sheltered position and may suffer frost damage in severe winters but regrows. One of the ultimate ambitions of warm-climate gardeners — a vine you plant and tend for years to achieve an unforgettable eventual spectacle.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, alkaline to neutral woodland soil in full shade; ALL PARTS ARE TOXIC and should not be grown where children or pets have unsupervised access.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full shade, replicating its natural habitat of base-rich European deciduous woodland; herb Paris dislikes acidic conditions and resents disturbance. Paris quadrifolia is a singularly distinctive European woodland perennial producing an unbranched stem topped with a precise whorl of exactly four broad leaves and a single greenish-yellow flower in late spring, followed by a glossy black berry. The entire plant is poisonous (containing steroidal saponins) and should be handled with care; it is slow to multiply but an elegant collector's plant for shaded woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, moderately infertile, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to light shade. Hercules' Club spreads by root sprouts and can form thickets — site accordingly. Handle with care due to the large, sharp spines on trunk and branches.
directions: Hercules' Club is a large, dramatic native shrub or small tree of the coastal plain and piedmont of the southeastern United States, notorious for the massive, knobby, claw-like spines that stud the trunk and branches and make it instantly identifiable from a distance. A member of the citrus family (Rutaceae) and closely related to Sichuan pepper, the aromatic bark and leaves contain numbing, anesthetic compounds that were applied by many Native American peoples directly to sore gums and toothaches — earning it the folk name toothache tree — as well as used as a fish poison and in various medicinal preparations. A primary host plant for the giant swallowtail butterfly, one of the largest butterflies in North America, Hercules' Club is an outstanding native choice for wildlife gardens in the Southeast. Plant in well-drained, moderately infertile, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established, it spreads by root sprouts and benefits from open, sunny, naturalized settings.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or early spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Heritage is particularly suited to rain gardens, stream banks, and other moist sites where most trees struggle.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Heritage is the premier named cultivar of river birch — introduced by Earl Cully of Heritage Tree Nursery in Jacksonville, Illinois, and selected for outstanding bark exfoliation quality, larger leaf size, and superior heat tolerance compared to unselected species plants. The spectacular bark display is the tree's signature attribute: the outer bark exfoliates in large, curling, papery sheets throughout the year, revealing the inner bark in a complex palette of salmon-pink, cream, cinnamon-brown, and reddish-tan tones — a year-round ornamental effect that is one of the finest bark displays of any tree in cultivation. In winter when the tree is bare of leaves, the multi-trunked form with its layered, peeling, multi-colored bark is truly spectacular against a winter sky. Heritage is also one of the most heat-tolerant birches — unlike white or paper birch that decline in the heat of zone 7 and warmer, Heritage river birch thrives through zone 9 in moist to wet sites, making it the birch of choice for the Gulf South. It is highly resistant to bronze birch borer, which devastates most white birch species in the eastern United States. The naturally multi-trunked form and year-round bark display make Heritage an exceptional specimen and focal-point tree.

common_name: Heritage Rose (Classic David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Heritage is an older David Austin introduction and can be somewhat more susceptible to black spot than newer, disease-bred cultivars, so good air movement and routine care matter.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1984, Heritage is one of the most beloved and enduring early English roses, carrying soft shell-pink, cupped, shallowly rosetted blooms with a distinctive lemony myrrh fragrance that helped define the fragrance profile many gardeners now associate with English roses. Its graceful, arching, densely foliaged shrub and reliably repeat-blooming habit from late spring through frost have kept it in continuous cultivation for decades, and it remains a benchmark for softness of color and fragrance among pink English roses.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Herme is a classic, long-cultivated camellia cultivar with semi-double flowers variably marbled and striped in pink, rose, and white, no two quite alike.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light. Herme is a long-established, historic Camellia japonica cultivar with roots tracing back to Japan, producing semi-double flowers with an irregular, ever-varying marbled pattern of soft pink, deeper rose, and white, so that individual blooms on the same shrub display a range of patterning rather than an identical, uniform color. This unpredictable variegation has made it a favorite among camellia collectors for generations. It blooms in winter into early spring on an evergreen shrub with the same glossy, dark green foliage typical of the species, and benefits from consistent moisture, acidic soil, and protection from harsh afternoon sun.

common_name: Hermosa Rose (Clear Soft Pink Globular China-Bourbon Rose)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Hermosa, introduced in 1840, bears clear soft-pink, globular double blooms on a small, tidy China-Bourbon type bush.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Hermosa, introduced in France in 1840, bears clear, soft pink, globular double blooms with a light, sweet fragrance on a small, tidy, well-behaved bush blending traits of the China and Bourbon classes, flowering in flushes nearly continuously through the growing season. Its compact size and reliable, gentle color have made it a long-standing favorite for small gardens, edging, and container culture where larger old garden roses would be impractical. Prune lightly to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; it needs little other care once established.

common_name: Herrenhausen Soft Shield Fern (Finely Divided Golden-Green Lacy Fern)
plant_note: Plant container-grown ferns in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Herrenhausen bears finely divided, lacy golden-green fronds and tolerates more drought than most ferns once established.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; once established, this cultivar tolerates more drought than most ferns, though regular moisture keeps the fronds lushest. Herrenhausen forms an elegant, arching rosette of finely divided, lacy, golden-green fronds, a finer, more delicate texture than many other soft shield fern selections, holding its evergreen-to-semi-evergreen foliage through much of the winter in milder zones. Its refined, feathery texture makes it a graceful companion to bolder-leaved hostas and heucheras in a shaded border. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if needed.

common_name: Hershey Red Azalea (Compact Kurume-Type Red Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Hershey Red is a compact Kurume-type azalea long grown in Southern landscapes for its dependable, vivid red spring bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation, and mulch to protect the shallow root system. Hershey Red is a classic, compact Kurume-type landscape azalea grown for generations in Southern gardens for its dense, mounding habit and heavy spring flush of vivid, saturated red flowers that hold their color well without fading. Its smaller mature size compared with many Southern Indica azaleas makes it useful for foundation plantings, borders, and mass plantings in tighter spaces. Water deeply during dry spells and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for the following spring form soon after bloom ends and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Hetz Midget Arborvitae (Extremely Compact Dwarf Globe Arborvitae)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Hetz Midget is among the smallest and slowest-growing arborvitae cultivars available, often taking decades to reach even modest size.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Hetz Midget forms an extremely dense, tidy, naturally globe-shaped mound of fine, bright green, scale-like foliage, growing so slowly that it needs virtually no pruning or shearing to maintain its neat form over many years, making it a low-maintenance choice for rock gardens, foundation plantings, and small-space landscapes where a full-size arborvitae would quickly overwhelm. Its diminutive scale and dense texture also suit it well to mixed conifer collections and formal edging. Like other arborvitae it prefers cooler climates with consistent moisture and struggles in the extreme heat and humidity of the Deep South, so afternoon shade is helpful in warmer parts of its range. Established plants need only occasional deep watering during drought and essentially no shaping.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens or divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; heucherella is sterile and does not set seed — it propagates only by division and is sold exclusively as named clones.
directions: Plant container specimens or divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; heucherella is an intergeneric hybrid between Heuchera (alumroot) and Tiarella (foamflower) that combines the bold, colorful foliage of heuchera with the running, spreading habit and delicate flowers of tiarella. The result is a versatile, shade-tolerant perennial with large, deeply lobed, often intricately patterned or color-contrasted leaves — available in deep burgundy, caramel, chartreuse, and multi-tone combinations — and frothy white to pink flower spikes in spring. The sterile hybrid is generally more heat-tolerant and vigorous than tiarella and holds its ornamental foliage better through summer than many heuchera. Excellent as a shade groundcover, border edger, and container plant. 'Sweet Tea', 'Bridget Bloom', 'Stoplight', and 'Solar Eclipse' are outstanding named selections.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Hicks Yew is a naturally narrow, upright hybrid selected in the early 1900s at the Hicks Nurseries on Long Island and remains one of the most widely planted foundation and hedge shrubs in the northeastern and midwestern United States. All parts except the red aril flesh are toxic if eaten.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average garden soil in partial to full shade; Hicks Yew is a columnar hybrid between English yew (Taxus baccata) and Japanese yew (Taxus cuspidata) that combines the deep-shade tolerance of its parents with markedly better cold hardiness, making it one of the most dependable evergreen conifers for foundation planting, screening, and formal hedging as far north as USDA zone 4. Its naturally upright, multi-stemmed, vase-shaped habit needs little corrective pruning to stay narrow, though it accepts shearing readily for a tighter formal hedge. The dark, glossy, flattened needles hold their color through winter, and female plants set small red arils in fall that attract birds, though the seed inside the aril and every other part of the plant contain toxic taxine alkaloids. Unlike most evergreens, Hicks Yew performs equally well on the shaded north side of a building as it does in full sun, and it tolerates urban pollution and heavy clay so long as drainage is adequate.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Higasa is a Satsuki-type azalea that blooms later in the season than most Southern Indica and Kurume cultivars, and is a popular subject for bonsai as well as landscape use.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. Higasa is a Satsuki-type azalea prized for its unusually large, deep rose-pink flowers with a darker blotch, blooming later in late spring to early summer after most Southern Indica and Kurume azaleas have finished, which extends the overall azalea bloom season in the landscape. Satsuki azaleas like Higasa are also widely used in bonsai for their fine branching and responsiveness to training, though it performs equally well as an unpruned landscape shrub. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the current season's flush ends.

plant_note: Divide established clumps immediately after flowering or in early fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; High Contrast is a Terra Nova Nurseries selection, a seedling of 'Berries and Cream', bred for deer resistance and heavily ruffled, high-contrast foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; High Contrast bears ruffled, dark green leaves heavily overlaid with silver, giving strong visual contrast that stands out even from a distance in a shaded bed. Pink flower buds open and age to blue in early spring, appearing alongside the emerging foliage for a two-toned floral display typical of the genus. It is noted for good deer resistance, useful where browsing pressure limits shade-garden plant choices. Keep soil consistently moist, since lungworts decline quickly in dry shade, and divide congested clumps after flowering to maintain vigor.

common_name: High Fragrance Camellia (Exceptionally Fragrant Blush-Pink Hybrid Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; High Fragrance is a hybrid between C. japonica and C. lutchuensis — the C. lutchuensis parent contributes the fragrance that is absent in standard C. japonica varieties.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; High Fragrance is one of the most important fragrant camellia cultivars — a hybrid between Camellia japonica and the fragrant species C. lutchuensis that produces the elegant, refined flowers of japonica combined with a genuine sweet, jasmine-like fragrance that is absent from the vast majority of camellia varieties. Most camellia flowers, despite their beauty, are essentially scentless — the discovery that crossing with the fragrant C. lutchuensis could introduce lasting fragrance into hybrid offspring was a significant horticultural development. High Fragrance produces medium-sized, semi-double to peony-form flowers in soft blush-pink to white-with-pink tones in late winter to early spring — the same season as other camellias — with a sweet, clean fragrance detectable several feet from the plant under favorable conditions. The fragrance intensity is variable with temperature: warm, calm mornings amplify the scent; cold or windy conditions reduce it. The plant grows as a medium-sized, evergreen shrub with the characteristic glossy, dark-green camellia foliage. An outstanding choice for planting near entryways, patios, and garden seating areas where the fragrance can be appreciated. In zone 9, High Fragrance is a reliable perennial shrub that blooms most heavily in late January–March.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; High Hat camellia produces large, formal flowers on a compact, upright shrub.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; High Hat camellia produces large, formal flowers on a compact, upright shrub. Large, formal double flowers open a clear, soft pink with neatly overlapping, evenly arranged petals in a classic, symmetrical form long favored by camellia show exhibitors, blooming over a long winter and early spring season on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub. Its reliable, high-quality flower form and manageable, upright habit have made it a long-standing favorite among camellia collectors and show growers seeking dependable, exhibition-quality blooms without a sprawling mature size. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid overhead watering which can spot the delicate petals, and prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring; sweet peas thrive in cool weather.
directions: Nick or soak the hard seeds overnight to speed germination, then sow directly 1 inch deep in cool, moist, well-drained soil in early spring. This tall vining variety produces intensely fragrant cream flowers edged in lavender, so provide a trellis or netting 5 to 6 feet tall for support. Keep roots cool and evenly moist, and cut blooms frequently to prolong flowering. Plants fade in summer heat, so start them early where summers are hot.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after soil has warmed above 65°F in consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to a few hours of direct sun; feed lightly on a monthly schedule through summer.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after soil has warmed above 65°F in consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. A large, sun-tolerant fancy-leaf caladium whose broad, heart-shaped leaves show striking pink-to-cream variegation traced with darker venation, with the exact balance of pale and colored areas shifting noticeably with light exposure. It is one of the more vigorous sun-bred caladium selections, holding leaf size and color well in beds receiving several hours of direct sun, unlike older shade-only fancy-leaf varieties; give it monthly light feeding through summer for the boldest color display.

common_name: Highpoint Nuttall Oak (Fast-Growing Own-Root Nuttall Oak Selection)
plant_note: Plant container trees in fall or early spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Highpoint is a fast-growing, own-root Nuttall oak selection with a uniform oval crown and bronze-red new growth, tolerant of wet, clay bottomland soils.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Nuttall oak tolerates seasonal flooding and heavy clay far better than most oaks, making it a strong choice for bottomland and low-lying sites. Highpoint, patented as QNFTA, is a clonally propagated, own-root Nuttall oak selection valued for uniform, symmetrical oval crown development and attractive bronze-red new growth in spring, offering more predictable landscape performance than seedling-grown trees of variable form. It shares the species' brilliant red fall color, one of the best displays among Southern bottomland oaks. Water deeply during establishment, and prune minimally to develop good branch structure while the tree is young.

common_name: Highrise Live Oak (Narrow Columnar Live Oak for Tight Urban Sites)
plant_note: Plant container trees in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, deep soil in full sun; Highrise is a narrow, upright live oak selection reaching only about 25 feet wide versus 60-100 feet for the species, developed for tight urban sites.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, deep soil in full sun; live oak tolerates a wide range of soils including compacted urban sites once established. Highrise, patented as QVTIA, was bred specifically for an unusually narrow, upright canopy, spreading only about twenty-five feet wide compared to the sixty to one hundred foot spread of the straight species, making it one of the only live oak selections practical for street tree plantings, narrow medians, and other tight urban sites where a full-sized live oak canopy would conflict with buildings or utilities. It retains the same tough, evergreen, wind- and salt-tolerant character that makes live oak the iconic Gulf Coast landscape tree. Water deeply during establishment, and prune minimally to develop good branch structure while the tree is young.

common_name: Hightower Willow Oak (Uniform Pyramidal Clonal Willow Oak Selection)
plant_note: Plant container trees in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Hightower was the first clonally propagated willow oak cultivar, selected for a strong central leader and uniform pyramidal form.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun. Hightower, patented as QPSTA, was the first willow oak selection propagated clonally rather than from seed, chosen for a strong central leader and consistently uniform, pyramidal-to-oval canopy that gives far more predictable street and shade tree performance than the variable form typical of seedling-grown willow oaks. It shares the species' fine, narrow, willow-like leaves, fast growth rate, and adaptability to a range of soils that have made willow oak a widely planted Southern shade and street tree. Water deeply during establishment, and prune minimally to develop good branch structure while the tree is young.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; highveld protea is distinctly more cold-hardy than the Cape fynbos proteas — native to the summer-rainfall grasslands and rocky highveld of the Drakensberg and Mpumalanga at 4000–6000 feet elevation, where frosts are a regular feature. It tolerates harder frosts than P. repens or P. cynaroides (to zone 7b) and summer rainfall — making it more adaptable to non-Mediterranean climates. Like all Proteaceae, it requires excellent drainage and no phosphorus fertilizer.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; highveld protea is the most cold-tolerant widely available Protea species — the protea of the summer-rainfall highveld of South Africa, growing naturally at high altitude in the rocky grasslands and cliff faces of the Drakensberg, Mpumalanga, and Limpopo where hard frosts occur regularly in winter. This cold tolerance (to zone 7b) expands the Protea genus into gardens significantly colder than the Mediterranean-climate zones where most proteas are restricted. The flower heads are medium-sized, cup-shaped, white to creamy-white to pale pink, somewhat less flamboyant than the showier Cape species but still distinctively beautiful. It grows into a small tree with a characteristic, gnarled, fire-adapted trunk and gray, fire-resistant bark. Unlike the Cape fynbos proteas adapted to winter rainfall, P. caffra comes from a summer-rainfall climate — making it significantly more tolerant of summer humidity and rain, and suitable for a wider range of garden climates including the Gulf Coast and Southeast where summer dryness cannot be guaranteed. An important species for gardeners who want to grow true Protea in zones 7–9 outside the Mediterranean climate zone.

plant_note: Sow directly in fall onto dry, rocky, calcareous soil; winter cold stratification supports reliable spring emergence.
directions: An endemic Texas penstemon restricted to rocky limestone outcrops and cedar glade openings of the Edwards Plateau; direct sow in fall onto very well-drained, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun and allow winter cold to stratify seed naturally. The flowers are arranged in distinctive whorls of three at each stem node — a reliable identifying trait — and emerge in brilliant magenta-red to carmine in April through June, attracting hummingbirds. Thin established seedlings to 12-18 inches and provide no supplemental water after the first season. An underused, striking native penstemon for Texas limestone gardens and dry, sunny borders in zones 6-9.

common_name: Hillside Black Beauty Bugbane (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Snakeroot)
plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery stock in spring into deep, fertile, consistently moist soil, and stake tall flower spikes in exposed sites.
directions: Grow in rich, humus-laden soil that never dries out, since this large woodland perennial suffers quickly in drought or exposed, windy sites. Give it plenty of room at the back of the border and stake the tall bottlebrush flower spikes if the planting site is breezy. The deeply cut foliage emerges near-black and holds its dark purple color through the season better than many older bugbane cultivars, contrasting dramatically with the fragrant white flower spikes that open in late summer and early fall. Bees are drawn to the late-season blooms, and the dark foliage makes an excellent backdrop for lighter-colored shade perennials in front of it.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; Himalayan bergenia is a smaller, more compact species than the commonly grown B. cordifolia and better suited to small gardens or tight spaces. Divide every 3–4 years when clumps become congested and flower production decreases.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; Himalayan bergenia is a compact species from the mountainous regions of Afghanistan, Kashmir, and the Himalayas — smaller in leaf and overall stature than the familiar elephant ears bergenia (B. cordifolia) but sharing its essential character of thick, rounded, leathery, evergreen leaves that develop rich burgundy-red tones in winter cold. The early-spring flowers — appearing in March and April from pink-red flower stems that may even push through snow — are held in neat, rounded clusters of pure white to pale-pink, cup-shaped blooms, each sweetly fragrant (unlike B. cordifolia). The combination of compact size, fragrant white flowers, good winter color, and unusual origin from extreme Himalayan altitudes gives this species a distinctly different quality from the coarser B. cordifolia. A better choice for small shade gardens, containers, and woodland-edge situations where B. cordifolia would be too large. The cultivar 'Bach' is a hybrid derived in part from B. stracheyi with outstanding winter foliage color.

plant_note: Sow seeds indoors in late winter at cool temperatures (50–60°F) without heat; Himalayan blue poppy requires cool germination temperatures and is killed by heat above 75°F during germination. In the first year, remove any flower buds that form (preventing bloom) to allow the plant to build root strength — this greatly increases perennial persistence. It performs as a monocarpic perennial in hot climates, living 2–3 years.
directions: Start seeds at cool temperatures indoors and grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; Himalayan blue poppy produces flowers of a blue so pure and saturated that they are difficult to believe are real — large, clear sky-blue, silky-petaled flowers 3–4 inches across with golden stamens, carried in loose clusters on hairy stems in early summer. Native to the alpine meadows and open forests of Tibet, Bhutan, and Yunnan at 10,000–16,000 feet elevation, it requires cool summer temperatures to thrive and does not perform well in hot, humid climates. In the Pacific Northwest, Scotland, and the cooler parts of the northeastern US, it is a long-lived perennial; in hot-summer climates it tends toward monocarpic behavior — flowering spectacularly and declining. The key to perennial persistence is removing flower buds in year one to allow full root development. Requires consistently moist, cool, acidic conditions with afternoon shade. For many plantspeople, successfully establishing and flowering this plant is considered an achievement; for others in suitable climates it is surprisingly manageable.

plant_note: Surface-sow fresh seeds in late summer or fall, or cold-stratify for 4–6 weeks and sow indoors in late winter; Himalayan blue poppy requires cool, humid conditions (Pacific Northwest, Scotland, high-altitude gardens) and struggles in hot, dry summers. Plants die after setting seed if allowed to flower in their first year — remove flower buds the first season to build strong clumps. Requires acidic, humus-rich, constantly moist but well-drained soil.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade in cool, humid climates; the Himalayan blue poppy hybrid (M. betonicifolia x M. grandis) is one of the most coveted and difficult plants in temperate horticulture — producing the most impossibly, unreasonably beautiful blue flowers imaginable, enormous (4–5 inch), sky-blue to deep cerulean-blue saucer-shaped poppies with a central boss of golden stamens, held on tall, leafy stems in late spring and early summer. The blue is not merely blue — it is a saturated, luminous, impossible clear blue that appears almost artificially colored to first-time viewers. Achieving this in the garden requires cool, humid summers (the plant's native habitat is the cloud forests of the Himalayas at 10,000–14,000 feet), acidic and constantly moist but excellently drained soil, and the patience to prevent flowering for the first year. In suitable cool, moist climates (Seattle, Scotland, high-altitude gardens) it is achievable; in hot, dry, or alkaline conditions it invariably fails. The cultivars 'Slieve Donard' and 'Lingholm' ('Blue Ice') are vigorous and perennial rather than monocarpic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Himalayan fleeceflower spreads steadily by rhizomes to form a dense mat and tolerates the dry shade found under mature trees once established.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Himalayan fleeceflower forms a dense, weed-suppressing mat of lance-shaped leaves topped from midsummer into fall with upright, bottlebrush-like spikes of small pink flowers that age gradually to a deep russet-red, so a single planting shows two-tone color as older and newer spikes bloom side by side. Foliage takes on attractive bronze-red tones in fall and persists semi-evergreen into winter in milder climates. It spreads at a steady, moderate pace by rhizomes, tolerates dry shade under trees better than many groundcovers once established, and needs little maintenance beyond cutting back old flower spikes and foliage in late winter before new growth begins. A dependable, long-blooming groundcover for the front of a shaded border or beneath open shrubs.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Himalayan giant astilbe grows much larger than typical garden astilbe hybrids and needs significantly more space and moisture to reach full size.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Himalayan giant astilbe grows much larger than typical garden astilbe hybrids and needs significantly more space and moisture to reach full size. Astilbe rivularis is an imposing Himalayan and Chinese species dwarfing the familiar garden astilbe hybrids, with large, coarsely divided leaves and towering, airy, branched plumes of tiny greenish-white to pale pink flowers in summer that can reach shoulder height in ideal conditions. Its massive scale makes it a dramatic architectural specimen for a boggy, shaded streamside planting or the back of a large woodland border, standing out among smaller-scale shade perennials. It demands considerably more moisture than typical astilbe cultivars, thriving at a pond edge or in a rain garden where its roots never dry out, and struggles in drier garden conditions that ordinary astilbe would tolerate.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Himalayan hydrangea grows into a substantial large shrub to small tree over time and needs room to reach its mature size.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Himalayan hydrangea is a large, vigorous shrub to small tree from the Himalayan foothills, producing broad, flat lacecap flower clusters in creamy white in early summer, larger and often earlier-blooming than many familiar garden hydrangeas. As the shrub matures over several years, the bark begins to peel and flake in attractive cinnamon-brown patches, giving it worthwhile winter interest well beyond its bloom season — a feature few other hydrangeas offer. Its eventual large size makes it best suited to a woodland-edge planting, the back of a large shrub border, or as a specimen with high, filtered shade from taller trees, rather than a small foundation bed. It flowers on the current season's growth, so any pruning to control size or shape is best done in late winter before new growth begins, without sacrificing that year's bloom. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells, since hydrangeas wilt quickly when the soil dries out.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Himalayan indigo is drought-tolerant and thrives in lean conditions — avoid rich or wet soils that produce lush but floppy growth. In zone 5–6 it may die back to the ground in hard winters but resprouts vigorously from the base in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Himalayan indigo is a large, graceful, arching shrub or subshrub from the mountain forests and open slopes of the Himalayas, producing an extraordinary profusion of rose-pink to magenta-pink, tiny pea flowers in dense, pendulous racemes from June through September — covering the sweeping, arching branches so densely during the flowering peak that the individual branches are almost obscured by bloom. The elegant, pinnate foliage is soft-gray-green throughout the season, creating an attractive textural complement to the vivid flower clusters. As a legume, it fixes nitrogen and improves poor soils. Himalayan indigo is one of the finest long-blooming shrubs for full sun in temperate gardens — combining drought tolerance, extended bloom, attractive foliage, and a graceful weeping habit in a plant that is still relatively little-known outside specialist gardens. Prune hard to the ground or to 6 inches in late winter to maintain compact, vigorous, floriferous growth.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or early spring, just below the soil surface, in deep shade with consistent moisture; seed germination requires cold stratification and is extremely slow. Himalayan mayapple emerges earlier in spring than the American species and the foliage is more ornamental — deeply lobed with attractive purplish-brown mottling.
directions: Plant in deep, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; Himalayan mayapple is a collector's shade perennial prized for its deeply lobed, marbled leaves with intricate purplish brown and green mottling that emerge in spring with dramatic effect. The single white flower with a pink flush sits at the leaf junction and develops into an ovoid red fruit that is edible when fully ripe — the only edible part of the plant. All other parts contain potent podophyllotoxin, the basis of several cancer chemotherapy drugs, and are toxic. In cultivation P. hexandrum is generally grown as an ornamental curiosity rather than as a fruit plant. It forms spreading colonies in ideal conditions, going fully dormant in midsummer. Closely related to American mayapple (P. peltatum) but considerably more ornamental.

plant_note: Plant out in spring once the soil is workable and hard frosts are unlikely. In colder parts of its range (zones 7–8), choose a sheltered, south-facing wall or overhang to protect the woody base from freezing.
directions: Take softwood cuttings in late spring or early summer and root them in a moist, gritty mix in a shaded, humid environment; pot on once roots are established. Plant in a sheltered, partially shaded position in fertile, moisture-retentive but well-draining soil, and mulch the root zone deeply in autumn to protect the woody crown from winter cold in zones 7–8. Cut back top growth after frost kills it and allow the plant to re-sprout from the base in spring. Divide established clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and to propagate additional plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Hinckley's columbine is a Texas endemic of Brewster County in the Big Bend area and grows naturally in rocky limestone canyons with afternoon shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in partial shade in zones 7–9; Hinckley's columbine is a rare Texas endemic of Brewster County in the Big Bend region of the Chihuahuan Desert, one of the most remote and geologically dramatic counties in Texas.
