directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun — partial shade is preferred in zone 9 where the cool, moist, shaded conditions of the natural forest understory habitat are approximated under deciduous trees — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Indigo Blue Forget-Me-Not is a deep-colored selection of Woodland Forget-Me-Not (Myosotis sylvatica), producing the characteristic tiny, five-petaled, sky-to-indigo blue flowers with a small yellow eye in dense clusters on low, branching stems — creating a spreading mat of blue bloom that is one of the most universally recognized and beloved cool-season garden flowers. The characteristic tiny blue flowers of forget-me-not have been celebrated in poetry, art, and sentiment for centuries — the simple, vivid blue of the flowers carrying a disproportionate emotional resonance compared to the diminutive scale of individual blooms. As a woodland native, Myosotis sylvatica genuinely tolerates and prefers partial shade conditions — growing naturally beneath deciduous trees where it benefits from winter sun through bare branches and then spring dappled light through emerging leaves. In zone 9 forget-me-nots provide a solid carpet of blue in January–March, naturalizing through self-seeding in appropriate cool, moist, partially shaded sites to create an ever-expanding spring wildflower planting requiring no annual replanting.

common_name: Indigo Spires Sage (Long-Spiked Hybrid Indigo-Blue Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; Indigo Spires is a large, spreading plant that requires ample space — allow 3–4 feet in all directions and position at the back of the border where its 3–5 foot height does not overwhelm smaller plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun after the last frost date; Indigo Spires is one of the finest and most widely grown salvias for the Gulf South — a hybrid between Salvia farinacea and S. longispicata that produces exceptionally long (12–18 inch), spirally twisted flower spikes of deep indigo-violet flowers from late spring through hard frost. The extraordinarily long flower spikes are one of Indigo Spires' most visually distinctive features — the 12–18 inch wands of deep indigo flowers tower above the dark-green foliage in a spiraling, twisted arrangement that creates a unique textural effect unlike any other common garden salvia. Indigo Spires blooms virtually continuously from May through November in zone 9 — one of the longest blooming seasons of any perennial for the Gulf South. Deadheading or shearing back after each main bloom flush stimulates additional growth and prolongs peak appearance. The plant grows vigorously in zone 9 heat and humidity, requiring ample space for its eventual 3–5 foot height and spread. Deep blue-violet to indigo flower color is a scarce and prized quality in summer-blooming perennials — Indigo Spires provides this difficult color reliably through the hottest part of the Gulf South growing season when most blue-flowered plants cease blooming. Outstanding pollinator value — multiple bee and butterfly species visit constantly. Reliably perennial in zone 9.

common_name: Indigo Spires Salvia (Exceptionally Long Blue-Violet Spike Perennial Salvia Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Indigo Spires grows to 4–5 feet and should be placed toward the back of mixed borders; the elongating flower spikes continue growing throughout the season, eventually reaching 12–18 inches in length by fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Indigo Spires is a hybrid Salvia (S. farinacea x S. longispicata) producing one of the most spectacular and long-season blue-purple flower displays of any commonly grown perennial — tall, dense, deep blue-violet to indigo flower spikes that elongate continuously throughout the growing season, eventually reaching 12–18 inches in length by fall and creating a dramatic vertical blue accent that persists from late spring through hard frost in zone 9. The elongating spike behavior distinguishes Indigo Spires from most other salvias: rather than producing a flush of flowers and then declining or deadheading the spent portion, the spike continues adding new flowers at the growing tip while maintaining color lower down — a continuously expanding, self-renewing flower spike that becomes more impressive as the season progresses. The deep, rich indigo-blue color is more saturated and richer than standard Salvia farinacea cultivars — closer to a true indigo in the spectrum, creating a deeper, more intense blue effect in the summer border. Hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies visit the flowers extensively. Indigo Spires grows vigorously to 4–5 feet and spreads by underground rhizomes — it naturalizes readily in Gulf South zone 9 gardens, returning from the roots each spring after frost kills the tops and expanding the planting gradually over years. Cut back to 12 inches in late winter to encourage fresh, vigorous regrowth.

common_name: Indonesian Wax Ginger (Pineapple Ginger, Candle Ginger, Small Taper-Lip)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in spring in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Tapeinochilos ananassae cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It performs best in the warm, humid conditions of zone 10-11 and is best treated as a container plant in zone 9. The spectacular inflorescence emerges at the base of the plant or on separate short stems from the rhizome — place where it can be viewed from ground level. The waxy bracts are exceptionally long-lasting, both on the plant and as cut flowers (2–4 weeks vase life). Divide clumps every 3 years.
directions: Plant in partial shade with consistent moisture — Tapeinochilos ananassae grows best in dappled light with regular watering and performs poorly in full sun or dry conditions. Tapeinochilos ananassae is a rhizomatous tropical perennial from Australia (Queensland) and Papua New Guinea in the Costaceae family (closely related to the spiral gingers, Costus species), producing one of the most extraordinary inflorescences in the entire ginger order. The plant grows as a clump of upright, cane-like stems clothed in spirally-arranged, glossy, dark-green leaves similar to Costus. But the inflorescence is unlike anything else in cultivation: a dense, cylindrical to conical spike of hard, waxy, overlapping, brilliant scarlet-red bracts that build upon each other to create a form strikingly and precisely resembling a miniature red pineapple — complete with the scale-like bract pattern of the pineapple's exterior. From within each bract, small, tubular yellow flowers emerge in succession. The 'pineapple ginger' inflorescence is produced on separate short flowering stems that emerge from the rhizome at ground level, distinct from the leafy canes, making the fiery red pineapple spikes appear at the plant's base surrounded by the taller leafy canes — a dramatic tropical display. The waxy bracts are exceptionally long-lasting as cut flowers (up to a month in water), making Tapeinochilos ananassae important in the tropical cut flower industry.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Unlike Impatiens walleriana (common impatiens), New Guinea impatiens tolerate and actually perform well in partial sun to full sun conditions — they are not exclusively shade plants. The Infinity series was bred specifically for heat tolerance and disease resistance, including resistance to downy mildew (Plasmopara destructor) that devastated common impatiens plantings across North America in 2011–2014. In zone 9 the Infinity series blooms continuously from spring planting through frost with minimal care, making them one of the most reliable continuous-blooming annuals for the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in partial shade to partial sun (2–4 hours of direct sun) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil — Infinity New Guinea Impatiens performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade in zone 9's climate; Infinity is a New Guinea impatiens series from PanAmerican Seed that represents the modern generation of improved, heat-tolerant, disease-resistant New Guinea impatiens — a step change in reliability and performance over older New Guinea varieties that often struggled in the combination of heat, humidity, and downy mildew pressure that characterizes Gulf South summer conditions. New Guinea impatiens (Impatiens hawkeri), unlike the common bedding impatiens (I. walleriana), has significantly better heat tolerance and sun tolerance — growing and flowering satisfactorily in conditions that would cause common impatiens to collapse. The large, flat, single or semi-double flowers (3–4 inches across in some colors) in a wide range of solids and bicolors bloom continuously and prolifically without deadheading. For zone 9 gardeners frustrated by the decline of common impatiens in summer heat and the susceptibility to downy mildew, Infinity New Guinea impatiens provides a genuine, heat-adapted alternative for partial-shade color through the longest and hottest part of the growing season.

common_name: Inflated Air Plant (Balbis' Tillandsia, Spreading Air Plant, Northern Needleleaf)
plant_note: Wire to rough bark or mount on drift wood in bright indirect light; Tillandsia balbisiana is a medium-sized Florida native Tillandsia with a distinctive inflated, bulb-like pseudo-stem at the base, from which spreading, curved, gray-green leaves emerge. The inflated base gives the plant a characteristic shape unlike most other air plants. Monocarpic — blooms once on a branched spike with violet-blue flowers, then produces pups and dies. Mist or dunk in water 2–3 times weekly. More cold-tolerant than many Tillandsia species. Wild plants are protected in Florida. Zone 9-12. Non-toxic.
directions: Secure to rough bark, cork, or driftwood in bright indirect to partial direct light, misting or dunking regularly — Inflated Air Plant establishes readily on rough-barked surfaces and is one of the more distinctive Florida native tillandsias for its strongly inflated, pseudobulb-like base that sets it apart from the spreading, grass-like or funnel-forming shapes of other species. Tillandsia balbisiana is an epiphytic bromeliad in the Bromeliaceae family native to Florida (Charlotte to Monroe Counties), the Caribbean (Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico), Mexico, Central America, and northern South America — a common and adaptable Tillandsia species across the Gulf Coast and Caribbean regions. The plant is immediately recognizable by its strongly swollen, hollow pseudo-stem base (resembling a small bulb or flask) from which the leaves emerge in a rosette pattern — the base provides water storage and is an adaptation to the seasonally dry conditions of coastal hammock environments. The leaves are narrow, channeled, curved, gray-green to silver-gray from their dense trichome (scale) covering — the typical air plant leaf type that absorbs water and nutrients from rain and atmospheric moisture. When the plant matures, a branched flower spike emerges bearing coral-pink to red bracts and small, violet-blue flowers — a monocarpic bloom after which the rosette produces pups and dies. An excellent, distinctive native tillandsia for zone 9-12 outdoor air-plant collections. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry is one of the most adaptable native shrubs for wet, acidic conditions but also tolerates moderate drought once established.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun — inkberry is a native evergreen holly shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, growing naturally in bogs, pocosins, pine flatwoods, and moist woodland margins. It tolerates shade, wet soil, and flooding conditions that defeat most other shrubs. The small black berries in late summer and fall are consumed by dozens of bird species including wild turkeys, wood ducks, and bluebirds; bees (especially Melittidae oil-collecting bees) work the small white flowers in spring. It spreads steadily by suckering roots and can form dense, wildlife-shelter colonies over time. Named cultivars include 'Shamrock' (compact, mounding) and 'Densa' (dense form). An outstanding native evergreen for wet, acidic soils where Rhododendron and Kalmia cannot be grown. Plants are dioecious — both male and female plants are needed for berry production.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry tolerates wet, poorly drained sites and standing water better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen shrub, making it a strong choice for rain gardens and low, boggy spots. Plant both a male and a female cultivar nearby if berries are wanted, since the species is dioecious.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry is exceptionally tolerant of wet feet and periodic flooding, unusual among broadleaf evergreens, and also handles drier upland soils once established. Ilex glabra is a native evergreen holly of the wet pinelands, pocosins, and coastal plain wetlands of the eastern and Gulf Coast United States, valued in the landscape as a fine-textured, small-leaved, boxwood-like substitute that thrives in acidic, poorly drained soils where boxwood struggles. Small, inconspicuous white flowers in late spring give way, on female plants, to small black berries that persist into winter and are an important food source for songbirds. The dense, upright to rounded habit takes shearing well, making it a popular choice for a low hedge, foundation planting, or naturalistic screen in a partly shaded woodland-edge landscape. A tough, adaptable, wildlife-valuable native evergreen for difficult wet or acidic sites, zone 4–9.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger has passed. Requires sharp drainage and full sun; does not tolerate wet or poorly drained soils. Avoid transplanting once established, as this shrub develops a deep, fleshy taproot.
directions: Select a dry, rocky, or sandy site in full sun with excellent drainage — this prairie native will not persist in heavy or consistently moist soil. Scarify seeds with sandpaper and cold-stratify for 60 days before sowing, or propagate from softwood cuttings in early summer. Once established, this nitrogen-fixing shrub improves soil and needs little supplemental water. Clusters of small white flowers in late spring attract native bees and butterflies, making it a valuable addition to a wildlife garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; also easily started indoors 6 weeks before last frost. Self-sows abundantly once established — remove seedlings where not wanted.
directions: Direct sow in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; inland sea oats is one of the most valuable native ornamental grasses specifically because it thrives in deep shade — a condition that defeats virtually all other ornamental grasses. The flat, bamboo-like leaf blades form a graceful arching clump, but the showstopper is the hanging, oat-like seed clusters that emerge in summer, dangling from slender wiry branches, and persist into winter — turning from green to copper-tan to warm bronze, rattling pleasantly in the wind. It grows naturally along stream banks and in bottomland forests, giving it outstanding tolerance of both shade and periodic wet soils. Self-sows prolifically once established and can become weedy; deadhead if you want to limit spread. The seeds are relished by songbirds in fall.

plant_note: Grow as a shaded houseplant in a well-drained, moisture-retentive terrestrial orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Insigne slipper orchid is one of the more cold-tolerant paphiopedilum species and prefers cooler winter temperatures than tropical lowland orchids.
directions: Grow as a shaded houseplant in a well-drained, moisture-retentive terrestrial orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Insigne slipper orchid is one of the more cold-tolerant paphiopedilum species and prefers cooler winter temperatures than tropical lowland orchids. One of the original slipper orchid species that helped launch the popularity of the genus among Victorian-era orchid collectors, it produces a single striking flower per stem, with mottled coppery-green, twisted petals framing a large, glossy, pouch-shaped maroon-brown lip, the distinctive 'slipper' that gives the whole genus its common name. Native to cool, humid forests in the Himalayan foothills, it tolerates and even prefers cooler conditions than many tropical orchids, making it a good choice for a cooler room or unheated sunroom rather than a hot, humid greenhouse. Keep the mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, provide bright indirect light rather than direct sun, and repot every one to two years as the terrestrial mix breaks down.

common_name: Intensia Phlox (Vigorous Heat-Tolerant Fragrant Annual Phlox Series)
plant_note: Set out transplants after the last frost into full sun in well-drained soil; Intensia was bred from Phlox drummondii crosses for much better heat and drought tolerance than older annual phlox, holding up through the peak of Gulf South summer once established.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and water deeply but infrequently once established to encourage the deep rooting that gives this series its notable drought tolerance. Intensia is a vegetatively propagated annual phlox series bred for a dense, mounded, well-branched habit covered in clusters of fragrant, brightly colored flowers that bloom continuously from spring through frost without deadheading. Its markedly improved heat and drought tolerance compared to older seed-grown annual phlox, along with good resistance to powdery mildew, makes it a far more reliable choice for hot, humid Gulf South summers where traditional phlox often struggles and fades. The mounded habit and long bloom season suit it well to beds, borders, and mixed containers, and light, regular feeding keeps the dense flower display going through the growing season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Intenz bears vivid purple-red, slender wheat-type flower spikes on a heat-tolerant summer annual.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting, or direct sow after last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Intenz bears slender, upright, vividly saturated purple-red flower spikes in the narrow wheat-celosia form, opening on sturdy stems that hold up well as fresh or dried cut flowers, and blooms from summer through frost with heat tolerance that keeps it flowering through the hottest part of the Gulf South growing season. Its intense color and long, straight stems make it a strong performer in a cutting garden. Deadhead or cut spent stems to encourage continued branching and flowering, and expect some self-sowing if seed heads are left in place.

plant_note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall into well-drained foothill soil; young trees establish a deep taproot quickly and resent later transplanting.
directions: Interior Live Oak replaces Coast Live Oak in California's hot, dry inland valleys and Sierra Nevada foothills, where it forms dense woodlands alongside Blue Oak and Gray Pine on thin, rocky, summer-baked soils. Its glossy, convex, holly-shaped leaves curl slightly and reflect sunlight, an adaptation to the intense heat of its interior range, and mature trees develop a dark, dense, rounded canopy that provides critical shade and acorn forage for deer and birds in otherwise open foothill grassland. It is markedly more heat- and drought-tolerant than the coastal species and better suited to hot interior gardens with alkaline or decomposed-granite soils. Plant it where nothing else will thrive on a hot, dry slope and expect a long-lived, low-maintenance shade tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; intermediate fothergilla is a hybrid between F. gardenii and F. major and is best propagated by softwood cuttings. The cultivar 'Blue Shadow' is most widely available and prized for its intense blue-green summer foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; intermediate fothergilla is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between small fothergilla (F. gardenii) and large fothergilla (F. major), combining the best traits of both parents — the compact habit of the dwarf parent with the larger flower heads and superior fall color of the tall parent. The fragrant, bottlebrush-like white flowers emerge before the leaves in early spring, offering a spectacular display of creamy puffball blooms on bare stems. The summer foliage of the cultivar 'Blue Shadow' is an unusually intense blue-green — among the most striking blue tones of any deciduous shrub — before turning a fiery combination of red, orange, and yellow in fall. A superb specimen shrub for woodland gardens, foundation plantings, and native shrub borders in zones 4–8, combining especially well with azaleas, mountain laurels, and other acid-loving shrubs.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; intermediate periwinkle is less cold-hardy than V. minor (hardy to zone 4) or V. major (hardy to zone 6), surviving reliably in zones 7–9. It blooms in late autumn and winter when temperatures are mild, providing off-season color that the other periwinkles do not offer. It may naturalize in mild climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; intermediate periwinkle is a less well-known Mediterranean species that occupies a horticultural niche distinct from both of the commonly grown periwinkles (V. minor and V. major) in one key way — it blooms in autumn and winter rather than spring. From October through February in zones 8–10, it produces the characteristic five-petaled, pinwheel periwinkle flowers in pale, milky-white to palest lavender-white or soft blue-lavender, adding off-season color to the shade garden when almost nothing else is in bloom. The evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves are narrower and glossier than those of V. major, giving the plant a slightly finer texture. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a weed-suppressing groundcover in dry shade under trees — notably more drought-tolerant than V. minor in warm climates. The cultivar 'Wojo's Gem' has cream-variegated leaves with white margins and is particularly ornamental. A useful addition to the winter-interest shade garden in Gulf Coast and Mediterranean-climate gardens where mild winters allow its distinctive flowering season to be fully appreciated.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; interrupted fern thrives in consistently moist conditions and is particularly effective at pond edges, stream banks, and wet woodland areas. Avoid disturbing established specimens.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; interrupted fern is one of the most distinctive and easily recognized native ferns of eastern North America, named for its unique habit of placing spore-bearing fertile pinnae in the middle section of certain fronds — interrupting the green sterile pinnae above and below with brown fertile segments that drop early in the season, leaving characteristic gaps in the frond's silhouette. This genus (Osmunda) produces the fibrous 'osmunda fiber' root mass prized for centuries as a potting medium for orchids and epiphytes. Interrupted fern grows in moist, shaded conditions similar to cinnamon and royal ferns but tolerates slightly drier slopes within the moist woodland. The large vase-shaped crown makes a bold structural statement in the wet shade garden and the graceful fronds provide excellent textural contrast with broad-leaved hostas and astilbes.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Intrigue is grown primarily for its narrow, dark purple-bronze foliage, an unusual fine-textured leaf form quite different from the broad paddle-shaped leaves of most canna cultivars.
directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun. Intrigue is grown chiefly for its distinctive, narrow, deeply colored purple-bronze foliage, a finer-textured leaf shape than the broad, paddle-like leaves typical of most canna cultivars, giving it an almost banana-leaf-meets-grass appearance that stands out in a tropical-themed border. Smaller orange flowers appear above the foliage in summer, though the striking leaf color and texture remain the plant's primary ornamental draw. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

plant_note: Plant the potted rose in spring after hard frosts; sold as a live plant.
directions: Plant this floribunda rose in spring in a hole amended with compost, keeping the graft at soil level in colder zones. Clusters of richly fragrant purple-plum blooms appear from spring through fall on an elegant upright form, making a bold focal point. Provide full sun, well-drained soil, and consistent moisture, watering at the base to keep foliage dry. Prune in late winter to shape the plant and deadhead spent clusters to encourage repeat flowering.

common_name: Invincibelle Mini Mauvette Hydrangea (Dwarf Mauve-Pink Reblooming Smooth Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Invincibelle Mini Mauvette is a dwarf selection within the reblooming Invincibelle series, fitting small borders and containers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Invincibelle Mini Mauvette produces rounded flower heads in a soft mauve-pink on a notably dwarf, dense plant, the smallest in the reblooming Invincibelle series of native smooth hydrangeas, making it well suited to small borders, foundation plantings, and large containers where full-size smooth hydrangeas would be too large. It blooms on new growth from summer into fall, so it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers, and deadheading spent blooms encourages continued rebloom. This native species tolerates more sun and a wider range of soil conditions than bigleaf hydrangea, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for small-space gardens.

common_name: Invincibelle Ruby Hydrangea (Deep Pink-Red Reblooming Smooth Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Invincibelle Ruby bears some of the deepest, most saturated pink-red flower color in the Invincibelle smooth hydrangea series.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Invincibelle Ruby produces rounded flower heads that open a deep pink and mature to an unusually rich ruby-red, one of the darkest colors in the reblooming Invincibelle series of native smooth hydrangeas, on strong stems that hold the flower heads upright without flopping. It blooms on new growth from summer into fall, so unlike oakleaf and bigleaf hydrangeas, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers, and deadheading spent blooms encourages continued rebloom. This native species tolerates more sun and a wider range of soil conditions than bigleaf hydrangea, making it a reliable choice for borders and foundation plantings across a broad range of climates.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Invincibelle Spirit was the first pink-flowered selection of native smooth hydrangea, a species traditionally available only in white.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Invincibelle Spirit was a breakthrough introduction as the first pink-blooming cultivar of native smooth hydrangea (the species behind the classic white Annabelle), producing rounded clusters of soft pink flowers on a native plant traditionally available only in white. Like Annabelle, it blooms on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter and still flower reliably the same year, and it rebounds quickly from winter damage in colder zones. Its stems are somewhat sturdier than old Annabelle types but can still benefit from light staking in a very rainy, exposed site. It is a good pollinator plant and, being a native species selection, tends to be adaptable and low-maintenance across a range of soil conditions.

common_name: Invincible Hosta (Fragrant Glossy Green Vigorous Hosta)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Invincible is noted for exceptional vigor, slug resistance, and fragrant flowers relative to most hosta cultivars.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously. Invincible forms a dense, glossy, deep green mound noted for exceptional vigor and unusually good resistance to slug damage compared with most hosta cultivars, quickly forming a full, healthy clump. It produces abundant, sweetly fragrant, near-white flowers in mid to late summer, a stronger scent than typical hosta flowers, which are usually a secondary feature; here the fragrance adds real value to a shaded seating area or path edge planted nearby. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous, healthy growth.

common_name: Ionantha Air Plant (Blushing Bride Tillandsia, Sky Plant)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark, driftwood, wire, or shells in bright indirect to direct morning light; Ionantha Air Plant needs no soil whatsoever. Water by dunking in water for 20–30 minutes twice per week in warm months or misting heavily every 2–3 days. After watering, shake off excess water and allow to dry completely within 4 hours — sitting in stagnant water causes rot at the base. A good indirect air source prevents this. In zone 9, plants can grow outdoors year-round in protected spots and survive brief temperatures to 32°F dry. Produces offsets (pups) after blooming.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct morning sun — Ionantha Air Plant performs best with 3–4 hours of bright indirect or morning sun and will bleach and dry out in harsh full afternoon sun in zone 9. Tillandsia ionantha is a small, epiphytic bromeliad native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and northwestern Venezuela in the family Bromeliaceae, one of the approximately 650 species of Tillandsia and by far the most widely grown and sold air plant in the world. Like all tillandsias, it has no functional roots — the small roots serve only to anchor the plant to its substrate. All water and nutrients are absorbed through specialized scales on the leaf surfaces called trichomes. The plant forms a small, tight rosette of silvery-green, slightly recurved, stiff leaves about 2–3 inches across. Its most dramatic quality is its response to blooming: in spring (or when seasonal cues trigger reproduction), the inner leaves of the entire plant flush brilliant red to rose-magenta over a period of days before the small violet-purple tubular flowers emerge from the center — the entire plant glowing red for weeks. After flowering, the parent plant gradually produces 2–6 pups before declining. The combination of tiny size, no soil requirement, dramatic bloom-time color, and extreme adaptability has made T. ionantha the definitive entry point for air plant collecting.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors 6-8 weeks earlier for earlier bloom.
directions: Irish Eyes replaces the typical dark chocolate-brown cone of black-eyed Susan with a glowing lime-green center, so the golden-yellow ray petals appear to float around a genuinely green eye rather than a black one. Grown as a fast, reliable warm-season annual (or short-lived perennial in mild climates), it thrives in average to lean soil and full sun and tolerates heat and short dry spells better than most annual bedding flowers. Deadhead regularly to keep new buds coming through summer and into fall, and use it as a color-echo companion for other green-centered or lime-toned flowers in a cutting bed. Its unusual eye color makes it a conversation piece in mixed borders where standard Rudbeckia hirta is already common.

plant_note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Irish moss knits together into a solid moss-like mat over one growing season with consistent moisture, and struggles badly through hot, humid summers, so afternoon shade is important south of its cool-summer comfort zone.
directions: Plant small starter plugs in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; despite the common name, Irish moss is not a true moss but a mat-forming flowering perennial with tiny, bright-green, needle-like foliage that looks and feels remarkably moss-like underfoot, studded with small white star-shaped flowers in early summer. It is a favorite lawn substitute and filler between flagstones and pavers in cool, mild-summer climates, tolerating light foot traffic once the mat is established. It needs consistently moist soil and struggles in hot, humid, or drought-prone conditions — it thrives in the Pacific Northwest and similar cool-summer regions but performs poorly and often dies out over a hot, humid Gulf South summer, so treat it as a plant for a small, easily watered, part-shade nook rather than a large sunny expanse in warm climates. Water regularly during dry spells and avoid walking on it while newly planted.

plant_note: Set out nursery divisions in spring after frost danger has passed; this compact selection tolerates both average garden soil and periodic wet feet, unlike many border perennials.
directions: This University of Arkansas introduction forms a tidy, rounded mound of fine, threadlike foliage that looks almost like a dwarf conifer until it is topped with masses of small purple button flowers in late summer. Plant in full sun in well-drained to occasionally moist soil; it is far more compact and floriferous than the straight species and needs no staking. It is an outstanding late-season nectar source for butterflies, including migrating monarchs, and its fine texture makes it a good foil for bolder-leaved prairie companions. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Iron Butterfly Tiarella (Deeply Cut Dark-Centered Foamflower)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; forms a slowly spreading, non-invasive clump.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, mulching with leaf litter to keep roots cool and evenly moist. Iron Butterfly bears finely cut, almost fern-like or butterfly-shaped leaves marked with a bold, dark purple-black central blaze along the veins, a more deeply dissected leaf form than most foamflower cultivars, topped by fluffy spikes of white to pale pink star-shaped flowers in spring. Its fine texture and dark central marking make it a strong textural contrast to broader-leaved hostas and heucheras in a shaded planting, and foliage often takes on additional burgundy tones through fall, remaining semi-evergreen in milder climates. Divide congested clumps in spring or fall every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Iron Cross Begonia (Iron Cross Plant, Beefsteak Geranium)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant in zone 9; Iron Cross Begonia cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It is rhizomatous — grow in a wide, shallow container to allow horizontal rhizome spread. Keep the rhizome at soil level (do not bury it) and allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. High humidity (50–70%) improves appearance and prevents powdery mildew. Propagate from leaf cuttings or rhizome sections. Excellent for terrariums.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Iron Cross Begonia thrives in the bright, indirect light of a north or east window and will scorch in direct sun. Begonia masoniana is a rhizomatous begonia from China (Guangxi province) and South Vietnam with one of the most immediately recognizable leaf patterns in the houseplant world: the large, deeply textured, quilted, bright-green, heart-shaped leaves bear a bold, dark brown to blackish pattern at the center that precisely resembles a German Iron Cross or a four-pointed star within a circle — a marking that appears on every leaf with striking consistency and regularity. The textured, bumpy leaf surface — covered in fine hairs and raised blisters — adds a three-dimensional quality to the ornamental effect. Small, white to pale pink flowers appear in spring but are secondary to the dramatic foliage. Iron Cross Begonia prefers the warm, humid conditions of its subtropical native habitat and will maintain beautiful foliage year-round in appropriate indoor conditions. It is more tolerant of lower humidity than cane-type begonias but still benefits from supplemental humidity in dry indoor environments. The leaf pattern is so distinctive and consistent that it was originally thought to be a deliberate human selection, but it occurs naturally in the wild population.

plant_note: Plant small, scaly bulbs 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in spring after frost danger passes; iron cross oxalis goes dormant in winter and the bulbs can be left in the ground in zones 7–10. In colder zones, lift and store dry indoors. Bulbs multiply freely to form attractive clumps over the seasons.
directions: Plant scaly bulbs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; iron cross oxalis is one of the most cheerful and distinctive small bulbs available, producing four-parted, clover-like leaves in fresh green with a bold, chocolate-purple, cross-shaped zone in the center of each leaflet — the iron-cross pattern that gives it its common name and makes it instantly recognizable. The deep rose-pink to rose-red flowers appear in clusters above the foliage throughout summer, adding color from late spring until fall. A native of the Mexican highlands, it forms compact clumps that multiply steadily from the scaly bulblets and provide a weed-suppressing carpet through the warm season. The foliage folds closed in direct midday heat and at night (a characteristic of all oxalis), reopening in morning and evening light. In mild climates (zones 7–10) the bulbs overwinter in the ground to return dependably each spring. Excellent for container displays, rock gardens, and front-of-border edges where the boldly patterned foliage provides season-long textural interest.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seed, then start indoors; benefits from a chilling period.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds in the refrigerator for several weeks, then sow indoors or direct sow in fall for natural chilling. This swamp milkweed blend produces clusters of pink and rose blooms that are irresistible to monarch butterflies and hummingbirds. It grows best in consistently moist to wet soils such as near a pond or rain garden but adapts to average beds. As a host plant for monarch caterpillars, leave foliage intact and avoid pesticides to support the life cycle.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost, or direct sow in spring.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow in spring, barely covering it. Long, wiry stems carry pincushion blooms in white, lilac, and blue shades that are outstanding and long-lasting in bouquets. This tough, fairly drought-tolerant, hardy plant has few pests and blooms over an extended season. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, and cut or deadhead frequently to keep flowers coming.

common_name: Isabella Sprunt Rose (Antique Pale-Yellow Tea Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Isabella Sprunt is an 1855 sport of the antique Tea rose Safrano, valued for its clear pale-yellow blooms and near-continuous flowering in the Gulf South's long growing season.
directions: Plant own-root stock in full sun in well-drained soil, giving it room to grow into a loose, upright shrub. Isabella Sprunt arose as a sport of the antique Tea rose Safrano in 1855, keeping its parent's elegant pointed buds and light tea fragrance but opening to a clear, soft butter-yellow rather than Safrano's apricot-orange. Like other old Tea roses it thrives on heat and humidity that frustrate modern hybrid teas, blooming in flushes almost continuously from spring through the first hard frost with minimal spray or fertilizer input. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, since old Teas bloom best on a framework of older canes rather than after hard cutting back.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Isabellina shares the same tall, sturdy, long-stemmed habit as its Queeny Lime series relatives and is grown mainly as a cut flower for its unusual soft coloring.
directions: Sow seed a quarter inch deep after last frost in full sun and thin to 12-18 inches. Isabellina produces large, semi-double to double blooms in a soft, muted butter-yellow that ages toward cream, a subtle coloring prized by cut-flower growers for blending into pastel and neutral-toned bouquets alongside the similarly muted Queeny Lime series. Plants are tall and vigorous with strong stems well suited to cutting, blooming from midsummer through frost with regular harvesting or deadheading to keep new flowers coming. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the main disease risk for zinnias in humid climates, and stake in windy sites since the large flower heads can be top-heavy on tall stems.

common_name: Ispahan Rose (Clear Pink Long-Blooming Damask Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ispahan is a Damask rose of ancient Persian origin, notable for an unusually long bloom period among once-blooming old roses.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ispahan tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough, ancient Damask. Believed to date back centuries to Persia, Ispahan bears clear pink, intensely fragrant double blooms and, while it still flowers just once a year rather than truly repeating, its single bloom period runs unusually long, six weeks or more, considerably longer than most other once-blooming old garden roses. Like other Damasks it needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering rather than the intensive spray programs modern roses often require, and it is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Issai is a dwarf beautyberry that sets fruit reliably even as a young plant, unlike some beautyberries that need a few seasons to bear heavily.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Issai is a compact, dwarf beautyberry selection that reliably sets heavy clusters of bright violet-purple berries even on young plants, without needing the several-year establishment period some beautyberries require before fruiting well. Its small mature size makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and smaller gardens where the full-sized native American beautyberry would grow too large. It flowers and fruits on new wood, so cutting the shrub back hard to a foot or so from the ground each late winter encourages vigorous new growth and the heaviest berry production the following fall.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Italian arum is winter-active and produces foliage through the cold months, filling the off-season gap when most shade plants are dormant.
directions: Plant tubers in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Italian arum has an unusual reverse-season growth cycle — the large, glossy, dark-green, arrow-shaped leaves emerge in fall, display through winter with striking silver or gray-white marbling, and die back by early summer, then clusters of brilliant orange-red berries on bare stems persist through summer, providing the most visually arresting fruit display of any shade garden perennial. The unusual winter-foliage-summer-berry cycle makes it an invaluable complement to spring- and summer-growing companions. 'Marmoratum' has particularly vivid silver marbling. All plant parts are toxic — the berries are especially dangerous. Naturalizes slowly by self-seeding to form colonies in the deep, undisturbed shade of mature trees where few other plants perform.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun in early spring or fall; Italian bugloss is tap-rooted and resents transplanting once established, so direct seeding or planting very small container plants is preferable. Cut back hard after the first flush of bloom in June to encourage a second flowering in late summer. Short-lived in rich, wet soils; thrives in lean, well-drained conditions.
directions: Sow seeds in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Italian bugloss produces flowers of a true, pure, brilliant blue that is almost unmatched in the late-spring perennial garden — the open, five-petaled, white-eyed flowers are produced in large, branching clusters on tall, leafy stems and are among the most intensely blue of any hardy perennial. As a member of the borage family, it is exceptionally attractive to bees and butterflies throughout its long June-July bloom period, and cutting back the spent flower stalks after the first flush often promotes a secondary flush in late summer. The plant is coarse and hairy in texture — the broad, rough leaves and stems have bristly hairs that can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals — and the tap root makes division impractical, but these characteristics matter little given the breathtaking blue of the flowers. Best planted in the middle or back of a sunny border where the coarser foliage is hidden by neighboring plants. The cultivar Loddon Royalist is the most floriferous and most widely grown selection.

plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Italian gladiolus is a fully hardy, fall-planted, spring-blooming species that naturalizes readily in dry, sunny sites and does not need lifting in zones 7-10.
directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Italian gladiolus, like its close relative Byzantine gladiolus, is planted in autumn and blooms in late spring rather than following the tender-summer-gladiolus schedule most gardeners expect. Gladiolus italicus produces loose, one-sided spikes of up to twenty small, pinkish-purple flowers on wiry stems in May and June, and has long grown as a cornfield weed across the Mediterranean basin, where it is sometimes still called corn flag for its habit of springing up among grain crops. It is drought-tolerant once established and multiplies by offset cormlets to form informal drifts in gravelly or sandy, alkaline-leaning soils. Bees and other pollinators visit the flowers readily, and the plant combines well with other fall-planted hardy bulbs such as Byzantine gladiolus and species tulips in naturalistic, low-water spring plantings.

common_name: Italian White Sunflower (Cream-White Branching Beach Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Italian White is a branching, multi-flower type that produces dozens of blooms per plant over a long season, unlike single-stem types that produce one large flower. For cut flower production in zone 9, it can be sown in February–March for spring blooms and again in August–September for fall production. Helianthus debilis naturally tolerates coastal conditions including salt spray and sandy soils.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; Italian White grows well in poor, sandy, well-drained soils and requires minimal fertilization — excess nitrogen produces large plants with fewer flowers. Italian White Sunflower (Helianthus debilis rather than the common H. annuus) is a beloved heirloom cut flower sunflower producing a profusion of small (3–4 inch), cream-white to ivory-colored flowers with dark chocolate-brown to near-black centers — a color combination of remarkable elegance that is unlike any other annual sunflower. The pure cream-white petals surrounding a contrasting near-black center disk create a sophisticated, almost formal aesthetic that pairs beautifully with other cut flowers in arrangements where the standard yellow sunflower would be too assertive. Individual plants are heavily branching and produce 20–50 or more flowers per plant through the summer, providing a continuous supply of cut stems over several months. The species (H. debilis, the cucumberleaf or beach sunflower) is native to coastal dunes of the southeastern United States including Florida's Gulf Coast, giving it genuine native plant credentials for zone 8–10 gardeners and explaining its exceptional drought, heat, and sandy-soil tolerance. Italian White is also an outstanding pollinator plant — the accessible flower centers are visited heavily by bees, butterflies, and other beneficial insects throughout the bloom season. A versatile, beautiful, and genuinely useful heirloom annual for both cut flower production and pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun in well-drained, lean, dry to summer-dry soil in zone 6–10; Ithuriel's Spear is a striking California native corm — native to grasslands, chaparral, and woodland edges in the Central Valley foothills and Coast Ranges — bearing large, loose, open umbels of trumpet-shaped, vivid blue-violet to lavender flowers on tall, wiry stems in late spring and early summer, long after the narrow, strap-like leaves have died back completely.
directions: Plant Triteleia laxa corms in fall 3–4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; leaves emerge in winter and die back by late spring before the flowers appear — mark planting locations carefully; provide no summer water as summer drought is essential; corms naturalize readily and multiply by offsets over several years. Ithuriel's Spear takes its poetic name from John Milton's Paradise Lost, where the angel Ithuriel carries a spear that reveals true forms — a name given to this plant, perhaps, for its dramatic, spear-like, erect flower stems. The loosely arranged umbels of 6–18 trumpet-shaped flowers in vivid blue-violet to pale lavender (occasionally white) are among the most beautiful in the California native flora, appearing in late spring to early summer on tall, wiry, leafless stems at a time when many other spring wildflowers have finished blooming. The cultivar 'Queen Fabiola' is widely available in the trade and has particularly large, rich-violet flowers and reliable performance in cultivation. Unlike many California native bulbs, Triteleia laxa has proven adaptable to some garden irrigation in summer and has naturalized in gardens outside California — though best growth and persistence comes with dry summers. Excellent for cutting; flowers last well in the vase.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost in warm soil; lift and store over winter where it freezes.
directions: Ivanetti is a classic ball dahlia in deep burgundy-to-purple-black tones, a favorite for cutting thanks to its perfect globe form and strong stems. Plant tubers eye-up in full sun and well-drained soil after the last frost, watering only lightly until growth emerges. Pinch the growing tip early to encourage branching and more blooms, and deadhead through the season. In cold regions dig the tubers after the first frost and store them dry until spring.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 10–12; Ivory Cane Palm is a graceful, clustering palm native to the rainforests of Java, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula — one of the most ornamental of the tropical understory palms, producing multiple slender, ivory-white to yellowish-green canes topped by elegant, pinnate fronds with characteristic jaggered, fishtail-tipped leaflets — excellent for shaded tropical garden positions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Pinanga coronata is adapted to rainforest understory conditions and should be protected from direct sun, especially harsh afternoon sun, and from cold below 45°F — mulch deeply and maintain consistent moisture. Pinanga coronata (Ivory Cane Palm or Crowned Pinanga) is a multiple-stemmed, clumping palm in the large Pinanga genus native to the lowland and sub-montane rainforests of Java, Bali, Sumatra, and Peninsular Malaysia, where it is a common and characteristic element of the forest understory. The palm is distinguished by its attractive, ivory-white to pale-yellowish-green cane-like stems — slender (1–1.5 inch diameter), smooth, prominently ringed — arising in clusters to create an elegant, bamboo-like multi-stemmed effect topped by graceful, arching pinnate fronds with attractively jagged (praemorse) leaflet tips. The Pinanga genus contains hundreds of species from South and Southeast Asian rainforests, most of which share the characteristic of being shade-adapted understory palms growing beneath the closed canopy. Pinanga coronata is among the most widely cultivated Pinanga for tropical gardens in zone 10–12, valued for its manageable size, elegant multi-stemmed habit, and tolerance of deep shade. Small red to black fruits appear periodically in colorful clusters. An outstanding shade-tolerant, multi-stemmed palm for tropical garden understory positions.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring; this evergreen blooms very early in the season.
directions: Ivory Prince, a Lenten rose, is among the earliest perennials to bloom, opening upright creamy-white flowers flushed with rose and green in late winter to early spring. Its leathery evergreen foliage stays attractive year-round in partial to full shade. Plant in rich, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist while establishing. All parts are toxic if eaten, so site it away from areas where children or pets graze, and remove old leaves in late winter to showcase the blooms.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; ivory sedge is native to rocky, calcareous slopes and performs surprisingly well in dry shade under trees where few other ornamentals survive.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to rocky soil in partial to deep shade; ivory sedge is one of the finest native sedges for extremely challenging shade conditions — it grows naturally on shaded limestone bluffs and rocky slopes where deep shade and dry, rocky soils combine to exclude nearly all other plants. The very fine, delicate, bright-green, almost thread-like leaves form soft, airy tufts 6–12 inches tall that sway gracefully with the slightest air movement, creating a cloud-like texture unlike the bolder carex species. It is one of very few ornamental plants that genuinely tolerates deep dry shade under dense, shallow-rooted trees — a notoriously difficult garden situation. Unlike most sedges, it performs well in neutral to slightly alkaline soils and requires sharp drainage. The delicate texture makes it an outstanding companion to bold-leafed hostas and ferns in the shade border. Semi-evergreen to evergreen in most growing zones.

common_name: Ivy Leaf Morning Glory (Ivy Morning Glory)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost danger in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; nick or soak seeds for 12–24 hours to improve germination; ivy leaf morning glory self-seeds prolifically and can become invasive in warm climates — pull unwanted seedlings when small.
directions: Nick or file seeds and sow directly after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide a trellis or fence for the twining stems. Ipomoea hederacea (ivy leaf morning glory) is a native North American morning glory producing ivy-shaped, three-lobed leaves that immediately distinguish it from common morning glories with heart-shaped foliage; the 1.5-to-2-inch flowers are sky-blue to pale blue to violet with a white throat, appearing profusely from summer through frost. The ivy-shaped foliage is the key ornamental distinction — it creates a finer texture and more elegant twining pattern on fences and trellises than the typical morning glory. This species is native to the eastern US and tropics and naturalizes readily in disturbed soils, roadsides, and old fields; it self-seeds abundantly and can spread aggressively in the landscape. It is valuable as a wildlife plant — the flowers provide nectar for bumblebees and the seeds feed native sparrows and mourning doves through winter. Zone 9 and warmer: treat as a warm-season annual that self-seeds reliably.

common_name: Ixora (Flame of the Woods, Jungle Geranium)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; ixora is highly sensitive to alkaline soil and high pH — in alkaline or limestone soils, apply acidifying fertilizer and chelated micronutrients regularly to prevent the severe chlorosis that is the most common problem with this plant in the Southeast.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; ixora is one of the most popular tropical flowering shrubs in the world, producing dense, rounded clusters of small tubular flowers in brilliant shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and white nearly year-round in frost-free gardens and spring through fall in zone 9. The flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) are 3–4 inches across and attract butterflies throughout the bloom season. It is a slow-growing, compact shrub and one of the best choices for formal hedges and foundation plantings in tropical and subtropical landscapes. The main cultural challenge is soil pH: ixora demands strongly acidic conditions (pH 5.0–6.0) and in the alkaline limestone soils of Florida and the Gulf Coast, iron and manganese deficiencies cause chronic yellowing. Use acidifying fertilizer specially formulated for ixora and apply chelated iron if chlorosis appears. Avoid 'lollipop pruning' (shearing into balls) which reduces blooming — prune lightly by selectively removing branches.

common_name: J.C. Harvey Crinum (Vigorous Pale Pink Pass-Along Crinum Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; J.C. Harvey is a Crinum moorei x zeylanicum hybrid known above all for extreme vigor and toughness, making it a classic Southern pass-along plant.
directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the plant room to form a substantial clump over time. J.C. Harvey is a hybrid crinum lily bearing large, pale pink, fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers with darker reddish-pink buds atop tall stalks, but it is grown at least as much for its legendary vigor and toughness as for its bloom, having been passed hand to hand among Southern gardeners for generations as an almost indestructible landscape bulb. Established clumps tolerate drought, heat, and neglect once settled in, though they bloom best with regular moisture and feeding during the growing season. Crinums resent disturbance, so once planted, leave the clump undisturbed for years to reach full size and flowering potential, dividing only when significantly overcrowded.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to average soil in full sun in spring; jacaranda requires several years of establishment before blooming — trees grown from seed may take 7–10 years; grafted trees bloom much sooner. Frost kills the tops in zone 9 but established trees typically resprout from the base.
directions: Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun; jacaranda is a South American deciduous tree that is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world — in spring, before or as the leaves emerge, the entire tree becomes covered in masses of large, tubular, lavender-blue to violet-purple flowers arranged in billowing panicles that transform the canopy into a breathtaking cloud of blue-purple. The flowering display lasts 6–8 weeks and the fallen flowers carpet the ground beneath the tree in a second violet display. The finely divided, fern-like, bright-green, doubly-pinnate leaves are attractive through the growing season. Jacaranda is the definitive 'purple flowering tree' of warm-climate landscapes worldwide — seen lining streets in Los Angeles, Johannesburg, Sydney, and throughout zone 9–11 in the southern United States. It is frost-sensitive, with established trees tolerating brief dips to approximately 25°F in zone 9 — tops may be killed by hard freezes, but established root systems often resprout. Requires a dry season to flower most reliably. An iconic specimen tree for zone 9–11 gardens.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jack Frost cannot be grown from seed (it will not come true) and must be propagated from divisions taken in early spring or late summer.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jack Frost brunnera was the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2012 and remains the most celebrated and widely grown silver-foliage shade perennial available. The large, heart-shaped leaves are almost entirely covered with a brilliant, reflective silver overlay, with only the green primary veins visible — in the shade garden, the silver leaves appear to glow with an inner light and illuminate dark corners as effectively as white flowers. In spring, tiny azure-blue forget-me-not flowers appear on wiry stems above the silver foliage, creating a jewel-like spring display. The silvery foliage remains effective from emergence in spring through summer decline, brightening the shade border for months. Consistent moisture is the most critical requirement — Jack Frost scorches badly in dry conditions and in hot afternoon sun. In zone 8, afternoon shade, consistent watering, and mulching are required to maintain it through summer. It will not produce viable seeds.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jack Frost bears foliage margined in bright white, a variegated selection of Chinese privet grown as a tough, easy-care hedge or accent shrub.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Jack Frost bears leaves boldly margined in crisp white around a gray-green center, a striking variegated pattern that brightens a mixed border or hedge planting year-round, since the foliage is evergreen. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease and needs only occasional shearing to maintain a tidy shape as a hedge, screen, or specimen accent. Its bright, variegated foliage provides ornamental value distinct from solid-green privet hedging, working well as a lighter-colored backdrop for darker-leaved shrubs and perennials.

common_name: Jack Snipe Daffodil (Reflexed White-and-Yellow Cyclamineus Daffodil)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; Jack Snipe is an early, dwarf Cyclamineus-type daffodil with strongly swept-back petals.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Jack Snipe bears white petals swept sharply backward from a bright yellow trumpet, the characteristic wind-blown look of Narcissus cyclamineus hybrids, opening early in the season on short, sturdy stems well suited to rock gardens, containers, and the front of a border. Its compact size and early bloom make it a good companion to later, taller daffodils for an extended spring display. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

common_name: Jack of Diamonds Brunnera (Large Silver-Splashed Heartleaf Brunnera)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jack of Diamonds is a sport of Jack Frost with even larger leaves and bolder silver coloring, and like other named Brunnera cultivars must be propagated from divisions rather than seed to keep the pattern true.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Jack of Diamonds arose as a sport of the celebrated Jack Frost brunnera and is distinguished by noticeably larger leaves and an even bolder, more extensive silver overlay across the heart-shaped foliage, with only fine green veining showing through. In spring, sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the foliage on wiry stems, adding a soft blue counterpoint to the metallic silver leaves. Its large-scale foliage makes a bigger textural and visual statement in the shade border than Jack Frost, useful as a focal point or in bolder plantings alongside hostas and ferns. Consistent moisture is essential — brunnera foliage scorches quickly in dry soil or hot afternoon sun, and in zone 8 gardens it needs reliable afternoon shade and regular watering to look its best through summer. Divide clumps in early spring or late summer when they become crowded, since named cultivars do not come true from seed and must be propagated vegetatively.

common_name: Jack-in-the-Pulpit (Native Woodland Perennial with Iconic Hooded Spathe)
plant_note: Plant corms (the small, rounded, tuber-like structures) 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; Jack-in-the-Pulpit is a native woodland understory plant that requires deep shade and consistent moisture to thrive. In zone 9, plant fall or early spring in the shadiest, moistest areas of the garden with high organic matter soil. Plants emerge in spring, produce their distinctive hooded flower structure and foliage through summer, then go dormant by midsummer (the foliage dies back to the ground). The corms slowly enlarge over years; established large corms produce female flowers and clusters of red berries in fall. All parts are toxic if eaten raw due to calcium oxalate crystals.
directions: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade; keep consistently moist. Do not eat any part of the plant raw. Jack-in-the-Pulpit (Arisaema triphyllum) is among the most recognizable and beloved native wildflowers of the eastern United States — an araceous (Arum family) perennial widely distributed in moist woodland understories from Quebec to Florida and west to the Great Plains. The plant takes its common name from the distinctive reproductive structure: an erect, clublike spadix (Jack) standing inside a hooded, striped spathe (the Pulpit), a form so architecturally precise and recognizable that it has become iconic in American botanical illustration and nature education. The spathe's stripes typically alternate green-white or purple-brown-green, and the entire structure has a jewel-like elegance that makes Jack-in-the-Pulpit one of the most aesthetically sophisticated of native spring wildflowers. One of the most unusual biological characteristics of Arisaema triphyllum is its sexual flexibility: plants can change sex from year to year, typically producing male flowers when small and female flowers when the corm has accumulated sufficient energy reserves, making large, vigorous corms most likely to produce the red-berried fall clusters. The berries (clusters of brilliant red drupes that replace the spathe in fall) provide important fall food for wood thrushes and other migratory birds. Jack-in-the-Pulpit is an excellent choice for deep shade gardens where it naturalizes slowly in moist woodland conditions, providing spring interest in areas too dark for most flowering plants.

common_name: Jackanapes Crocosmia (Bicolor Red and Yellow Montbretia)
plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in full sun once soil has warmed after the last frost.
directions: Jackanapes is one of the most distinctive crocosmia cultivars grown, bred by Alan Bloom, with striking bicolor blooms of rich red-orange outer segments surrounding a bright golden-yellow center. The zigzag flower spikes are shorter and stiffer than many montbretia hybrids, making the clumps sturdy and less prone to flopping. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain the strongest color contrast. Its compact size and bold two-tone flowers make it a striking front-of-border accent or container specimen.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Jackie stays more compact than many mullein hybrids, fitting smaller borders and front-of-border placement.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since mullein rots readily in heavy, wet soil. Jackie produces compact spikes of soft peachy-pink flowers with contrasting purple-mauve stamens over gray-green, felted foliage, staying notably shorter and more compact than many mullein hybrids, which suits it to smaller borders, rock gardens, and the front of a sunny bed where taller mulleins would be out of scale. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting and encourage continued bloom over a long season from late spring into summer. Like other hybrid mulleins it tends to be relatively short-lived, so allowing some self-seeding or taking root cuttings helps maintain the planting over time.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jacklyn alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jacklyn alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Narrow, elongated, deeply lobed leaves with dramatically undulating, ruffled margins and prominent silvery-white venation give this hybrid a fine, sculptural texture unlike the broader, smoother leaves of most other commonly grown alocasias. Its slender, upright leaf form and eye-catching vein pattern make it a popular specimen among collectors seeking something more textured and refined than standard elephant ear shapes, well suited to a shaded plant grouping where its distinctive silhouette stands out. Provide consistent warmth and high humidity, protect from direct sun which scorches the leaves, and allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings to prevent rot at the rhizome.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the top grows in sun; Jackmanii is one of the oldest and most reliable large-flowered clematis cultivars, blooming on new growth so it can be pruned back hard each late winter.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool (mulch well or shade the base with low companion plants) while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis, fence, or other support. Introduced in England in 1862, Jackmanii is one of the most enduring and widely grown clematis cultivars ever bred, producing an abundance of large, velvety, deep purple flowers from early summer into fall. Because it flowers entirely on new growth, it belongs to the group of clematis that should be pruned hard, back to about a foot from the ground, in late winter, which keeps the vine vigorous and full of bloom rather than leggy and bare at the base. It is a tough, adaptable, long-lived vine that has introduced generations of gardeners to clematis.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Jackson brier is the most ornamental of the southeastern Smilax species with glossy, lance-shaped leaves and is commonly used in Southern floral arrangements as greenery — it has been shipped as 'smilax' by florists for over a century.
directions: Plant in spring in moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade against a trellis, fence, or tree for support; Smilax smallii climbs by tendrils and can reach 10–20 feet, providing dense evergreen coverage in shaded areas. Jackson brier is the most ornamental of the native southeastern Smilax species, producing long, lance-shaped, glossy dark green leaves on gracefully arching, somewhat thorny stems; it is the 'smilax' of traditional Southern floriculture — the garlands of small-leafed, shiny green vine used to decorate churches, ballrooms, and mantles throughout the South for weddings and holiday celebrations for well over 100 years. Small, greenish-white flowers in early spring are not showy but are fragrant, and small blue-black berries in fall are important food for mockingbirds, catbirds, and other wildlife. Valuable as a native evergreen shade vine in zone 7–10 landscapes.

common_name: Jacob Cline Bee Balm (Red Bee Balm, Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Jacob Cline spreads aggressively by underground stolons — divide every 2–3 years to prevent the colony from expanding beyond its intended area.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Jacob Cline is widely considered the finest red bee balm cultivar for hot, humid climates — selected for its exceptional resistance to powdery mildew, the primary problem that disfigures most Monarda didyma cultivars in Gulf South summer conditions. Most bee balm cultivars develop severe powdery mildew by midsummer in the humidity of the Gulf Coast — white, powdery coating on the foliage that disfigures the plant for the remainder of the season. Jacob Cline was selected from a large planting for the plants that remained cleanest through humid summers, resulting in dramatically superior mildew resistance compared to standard bee balm selections. The large, intense scarlet-red flower heads are exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds, which hover around the tubular flowers seeking nectar — Jacob Cline is one of the finest hummingbird plants available for partial-shade gardens in zone 9. It also attracts bees, swallowtails, and sphinx moths. The aromatic, mint-scented foliage is characteristic of the mint family. Jacob Cline spreads vigorously by underground runners and should be divided every 2–3 years in early spring to contain the colony and maintain plant vigor. In zone 9, it blooms from May through August.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; Jacob is among the earliest-blooming Christmas rose selections, often flowering in early winter.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist through establishment. Jacob is prized as one of the earliest Christmas rose selections to flower, often opening its large, rounded, pure white blooms with a faint pink blush by early winter — well ahead of the traditional Helleborus niger bloom time — giving gardeners a jump on winter color while most other perennials are dormant. The dark, leathery, evergreen foliage stays attractive year-round, providing structure between bloom seasons in a shaded border or woodland garden. Remove old, tattered leaves in late winter just before flowering to best display the blooms, and note that all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil for spring germination, or start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost after 4–6 weeks of cold stratification at 35–40°F. Transplant in early spring to partially shaded beds.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall or plant container divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; jacob's ladder forms an attractive clump of ladder-like, pinnately compound leaves topped in late spring and early summer with clusters of cup-shaped, lavender-blue flowers with prominent yellow-orange stamens that give the plant an elegant, airy presence in the shade garden. It performs best in cool to moderate climates (zone 3–7) with consistent moisture and afternoon shade; plants often go partially dormant in the heat of summer in warmer climates and may require some shade protection there. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early fall; it self-seeds modestly but not aggressively. The cultivar 'Brise d'Anjou' offers striking cream-variegated foliage that lights up shaded corners.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall or stratify and sow in early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jacob's ladder self-sows reliably in appropriate conditions and forms steadily expanding colonies over time.
