An absolutely essential plant for the shaded landscape in zones 6–9 where traditional yews fail.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog in partial shade in spring; Japanese primrose must have constant moisture and is best established beside permanent water features.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside streams, ponds, or bog gardens; Japanese primrose (candelabra primrose) is the most dramatic of all primroses, producing tall stems bearing multiple stacked whorls of flowers in crimson, pink, magenta, lilac, orange, or white from late spring through early summer — each successive whorl opens above the last in the classic candelabra arrangement that gives the primrose family one of its most spectacular forms. It self-sows freely in moist, suitable conditions to colonize streambanks and pond margins. Excellent combined with ostrich ferns, hostas, and astilbes in a cool, moist, partially shaded water-garden setting. Dies back completely in hot, dry summers; consistent moisture throughout the growing season is essential. 'Miller's Crimson', 'Postford White', and 'Valley Red' are classic cultivar selections.

common_name: Japanese Privet (Wax Leaf Privet, Wax Ligustrum)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil — Japanese privet is one of the most soil-adaptable landscape shrubs in zone 9, tolerating clay, sand, slightly alkaline, and compacted soils that stress most other plants. Full sun to partial shade are both acceptable.
directions: Plant in nearly any well-drained soil — Japanese privet is extraordinary in its adaptability, accepting clay, sand, alkaline soils, compacted urban soils, reflected heat, and neglect without significant decline — in full sun to partial shade; Japanese privet is the most widely planted hedge and screen shrub across the Gulf South, a vigorous, large-growing evergreen producing dense, glossy, waxy, dark-green leaves on stout stems that respond readily to shearing into formal hedges or can be allowed to grow into substantial multi-trunked small trees reaching 18 feet. White flower clusters in late spring have a distinctive, heavy fragrance that some find pleasant and others find objectionable; the flowers produce abundant blue-black berries in fall and winter that are consumed and spread by birds — a characteristic that has made ligustrum a serious invasive plant in natural areas across the Southeast and Gulf South. The berries are mildly toxic to humans and should be noted in gardens used by children. Despite its invasive potential, Japanese privet remains the dominant hedge plant in zone 9 residential and commercial landscapes due to its unmatched combination of heat tolerance, drought tolerance, adaptability, and fast growth. Alternatives for non-invasive hedging include Podocarpus macrophyllus, Ternstroemia gymnanthera, and Distylium.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; Japanese red pine grows naturally on dry, poor, rocky mountain slopes of Japan and Korea, adapting to lean, acidic, well-drained conditions. Avoid fertile, moist soils which cause excessive, rank growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; Japanese red pine (akamatsu, 'red pine') is celebrated in Japanese art and literature — the sinuous, red-barked old specimens on rocky mountain outcrops of Japan are among the most recognizable images in East Asian landscape painting. The orange-red, flaking bark on the upper trunk and branches is uniquely beautiful, deepening in color and contrast as the tree matures. The paired, soft, blue-green needles and naturally irregular, layered crown give the tree a relaxed, artistic quality that makes it the premier pine for Japanese-inspired landscape design. The cultivar 'Umbraculifera' (Tanyosho pine) is a dwarf, umbrella-shaped form widely used in Japanese gardens. The cultivar 'Oculus-Draconis' ('Dragon's Eye') has variegated needles with yellow bands. Somewhat susceptible to pine wilt nematode in the eastern US.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese roof iris is unusual among irises for genuinely thriving in partial shade, and was historically planted directly into thatched roofs in Japan, where it tolerated thin soil and part-day sun.
directions: Plant shallow rhizome divisions, barely covered, in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike most bearded and beardless irises, which demand full sun, Japanese roof iris flowers reliably in dappled shade, making it a rare shade-tolerant iris option. In late spring, the fans of broad, ribbed, glossy leaves send up flattened stems topped with large, flat-faced, lavender-blue flowers marked with a distinctive white and violet crested pattern on the falls, resembling a small Japanese iris (Iris ensata) in form though considerably more shade-adapted and drought-tolerant once established. Its historic use rooted directly into Japanese thatched roofs, where it survived on minimal soil and inconsistent moisture, speaks to its toughness and adaptability. An excellent, unusual choice for adding iris-type flowers to a partly shaded border or woodland-edge planting where full-sun irises would fail to bloom, zone 4–9.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial to full shade in spring; kerria is one of the most shade-tolerant flowering shrubs available, producing better bloom in partial shade than in full sun in hot climates.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial to full shade; Japanese rose is one of the most valuable flowering shrubs for shade — producing brilliant golden-yellow, rose-like flowers in early spring on gracefully arching, bright-green stems that are themselves ornamental through winter when the bark retains vivid chartreuse-green color. It spreads gradually by suckering to form colonies and is excellent for naturalizing in shaded areas, under trees, and on north-facing slopes where little else blooms. The double-flowered form 'Pleniflora' (pompom-like, globe-shaped flowers) is more commonly grown than the single species. 'Golden Guinea' (single flowers, larger) and 'Picta' (white-variegated leaves) are other notable cultivars. Bloom is most abundant in partial shade in hot-summer climates; full sun can bleach and shorten the flower display. Tolerates considerable root competition from trees.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Japanese sedge provides year-round evergreen foliage and tolerates a wide range of soil conditions including clay and dry shade.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Japanese sedge forms graceful, arching clumps of narrow, dark-green, evergreen leaves that provide year-round texture in shaded borders and woodland gardens where most ornamental grasses cannot thrive. The gold-variegated selections 'Gilt' and 'Fisher's Form' provide bright foliage contrast in deep shade that few other plants match. Plants are low-maintenance once established, requiring only the removal of tattered older leaves in early spring. Tolerates a wide range of soil conditions including clay, alkaline soil, and periodic dry spells once established. Divide in spring every 4–5 years if clumps become congested. Excellent as a shade groundcover in mass plantings.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring or fall; plant at least one male per several females for berry production.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; skimmia is a refined Japanese shrub with glossy, aromatic, evergreen leaves that provides three seasons of interest — fragrant white flower clusters in spring, persistent bright-red berries (on female plants) that remain decorative through winter, and handsome foliage year-round. It is one of the finest shade shrubs for dense-shade situations that defeat most flowering shrubs. The plant is dioecious — you need at least one male (often sold as Skimmia japonica 'Rubella' or 'Fragrans') for every three female plants to produce berries. Yellowing leaves indicate iron or manganese deficiency in alkaline soil; treat with chelated iron. Never allow plants to dry out — they wilt dramatically in drought.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese snowbell performs best with protection from hot afternoon sun in zones 7–8 and benefits from a sheltered position that protects flowers from late frosts, which can damage emerging buds. Amend heavy clay soils generously with compost to ensure good drainage and aeration. Seed requires 3 months of cold moist stratification and germinates slowly; nursery transplants are strongly recommended.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Japanese snowbell is one of the most elegant and refined small ornamental trees for the garden, producing in late May and June an extraordinary display of pendant, pure-white, bell-shaped flowers hanging in rows beneath the horizontal branching — creating a layered, wedding-cake silhouette when viewed from below that reveals the full beauty of its blooms. Styrax japonicus is a graceful multi-stemmed or lightly branched small tree with excellent horizontal structure and clean, fine-textured dark-green foliage that turns yellow to red in fall; the cultivars 'Pink Chimes' and 'Carillon' offer weeping forms and pink-flushed flowers for smaller gardens. It performs particularly well as an understory tree beneath high-canopy oaks, planted where afternoon shade protects it from drought stress — it is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Virtually pest- and disease-free, making it an outstanding choice for zones 5–8 gardens seeking a refined, low-maintenance flowering tree of exceptional beauty.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; arching stems emerge from creeping rhizomes and clumps expand steadily without becoming invasive, tolerating average garden soil once established.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; arching stems emerge from creeping rhizomes and clumps expand steadily without becoming invasive, tolerating average garden soil once established. Polygonatum falcatum is a Japanese woodland species producing gracefully arching stems lined with paired, glossy, pointed leaves and hung in late spring with small, cream, green-tipped, bell-shaped flowers dangling in pairs or trios along the underside of the stem. It is the parent of several popular variegated selections such as 'Nippon Sunbeam' and 'Silver Lining', but the green species itself makes a refined textural addition to a shaded border or woodland garden, contrasting well with broad-leaved hostas and ferns. Established clumps need little care beyond a yearly mulch of leaf compost and division every four to five years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs or root semi-hardwood cuttings in early summer; Japanese spirea transplants easily and establishes quickly in most soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese spirea is a tough, adaptable deciduous shrub that earns its place in the landscape through months of ornamental interest — colorful new foliage in spring (gold in 'Gold Flame', chartreuse in 'Gold Mound'), dense flat-topped clusters of pink to deep rose flowers in early summer, good fall color, and attractive twiggy winter form. Deadhead after first flowering and shear lightly to encourage a second flush of bloom. Hard rejuvenation pruning to 6–8 inches in early spring every 3–4 years keeps plants vigorous. Note that Japanese spirea is invasive in parts of the eastern United States; check local invasive plant lists and consider using native spiraea relatives (Physocarpus, Fothergilla) where appropriate.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant rooted divisions in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; space 6–9 inches apart and mulch well the first year to maintain moisture and suppress weeds until the plants fill in.
directions: Root stem cuttings or set out plugs in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing 6–9 inches apart; Japanese spurge is the classic deep-shade groundcover for the eastern United States, forming a dense, weed-suppressing mat of glossy, dark-green, whorled leaves that are evergreen year-round and tolerate the challenging dry shade under mature trees. White flower spikes appear in mid-spring, followed by the new growth flush. Requires acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) — plants yellowing in alkaline soil respond to acidifying fertilizer and sulfur applications. Once established it spreads steadily by underground stems and requires minimal care. Susceptible to pachysandra blight (Volutella) in humid climates; improve air circulation and avoid overhead irrigation.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring before new growth or in early fall; Primula sieboldii is winter-dormant and goes completely underground from July through February, so mark planting sites to avoid disturbing the invisible rhizomes.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Japanese star primrose is a refined shade garden perennial from Japan producing beautifully fringed or ruffled flowers in pink, lavender, white, and magenta in early spring — the delicate, often lacy petals give a completely different character from the simple round flowers of common primrose. The textured, crinkled leaves emerge in early spring alongside the flowers and persist through early summer, then the plant disappears completely below ground until the following spring. This summer dormancy makes it well-adapted to dry woodland conditions. The Japanese have cultivated hundreds of named cultivars ('sieboldii') for over 400 years as a refined collector's plant with extraordinary variety in flower form and color.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in acid, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with afternoon shade; stewartia transplants best when young and small and establishes slowly. It dislikes root disturbance and should be sited carefully as a permanent specimen. Requires consistent moisture and does not tolerate drought or compaction.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; Japanese stewartia is widely considered one of the finest four-season landscape trees available, earning distinction in every month of the year: brilliant white, camellia-like flowers with orange stamens bloom in June–July during the quiet gap between spring and late-summer bloomers; large, leathery leaves turn orange-red in fall; and the stunning exfoliating bark reveals a patchwork mosaic of gray, orange-brown, cream, and reddish-brown that makes it arguably the most beautiful bark of any deciduous tree in temperate horticulture. The pyramidal growth habit is elegant and requires little pruning. Trees grow slowly but steadily to 20–30 feet over many decades and are extremely long-lived. Unlike the native Stewartias (S. ovata, S. malacodendron), Japanese stewartia is considerably more cold-hardy and easier to establish in most garden conditions.

plant_note: Set rooted divisions six to ten inches apart in spring into well-drained soil; water regularly the first season to establish.
directions: Set rooted divisions six to ten inches apart in spring into well-drained soil; the small rounded succulent leaves form a dense low carpet that fills quickly between pavers and along path edges. It tolerates more shade than most stonecrops, making it useful where a sun-loving sedum would scorch, and small yellow star flowers appear in summer. Water regularly the first season to establish, after which it needs little beyond occasional deep watering during extended drought.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; Japanese tassel fern is one of the most elegant and refined shade ferns for the South, thriving in humid, warm-climate gardens and tolerating summer heat better than many Polystichum species.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; keep consistently moist but never waterlogged. Polystichum polyblepharum (Japanese tassel fern) is a distinguished East Asian evergreen fern prized among gardeners for the extraordinary beauty of its emerging fronds in spring — the new croziers (fiddleheads) are densely covered in golden, hair-like scales, giving the emerging fronds a luminous, tasseled appearance as if dusted with golden silk fibers, which is especially vivid when backlit. As the fronds unfurl, they mature to glossy, dark-green, bipinnate (twice-divided) fronds 18–24 inches long arranged in a graceful, arching vase-shaped rosette. Unlike many ferns that look tired by late summer, Japanese tassel fern maintains its polished, dark-green gloss through the heat of a zone 9 summer when planted in shade with consistent moisture. It is a slow-growing but extraordinarily refined plant for shaded borders, woodland gardens, and formal shade beds. The evergreen fronds provide year-round structure in the shade garden.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Ternstroemia is one of the few large evergreen shrubs that performs reliably in partial to full shade in zone 9 — a critical attribute where few options exist.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Ternstroemia gymnanthera is a slow-growing, refined evergreen shrub from Japan and China that has been widely sold in the Gulf South nursery trade under the name 'Cleyera' — though it is botanically distinct from true Cleyera japonica. It produces dense, oval, waxy, dark-green leaves (emerging with distinctive bronze to wine-red new growth) on neat, naturally well-shaped plants with excellent ornamental appeal throughout the year. Small, creamy-white, fragrant flowers appear in summer beneath the foliage, followed by orange-red berries. The combination of beautiful new-growth color and outstanding shade tolerance makes it a valuable alternative to Red Tip Photinia in shaded situations where photinia would fail from disease. Ternstroemia grows slowly and requires no pruning to maintain an attractive shape, ultimately reaching 5–8 feet in typical garden conditions. Unlike Photinia, it is essentially free of serious pest and disease problems in zone 9 — an important advantage in Gulf Coast conditions. It is also deer-resistant. The cultivar 'Burnished Gold' has chartreuse-gold variegated leaves; 'Big Bronze' has exceptionally large, deep-bronze new growth. An outstanding but underutilized alternative to photinia, nandina, and ligustrum in partial to full shade settings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in full sun in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Japanese tree lilac is exceptionally tolerant of urban conditions including air pollution, compacted soils, heat, and drought once established. The cultivar 'Ivory Silk' is the most widely planted, offering a more compact, uniform habit than the species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Japanese tree lilac is the tree-form lilac of North American streetscapes and public gardens, valued for its extraordinary cold hardiness (to zone 3), its tolerance of urban stress, and its massive, creamy-white flower panicles that appear in June — two to three weeks after common lilacs — providing lilac-family bloom when the familiar spring shrubs have long finished. The panicles can reach 12 inches long and are produced in great abundance, creating a white-cloud effect in early summer. The scent is distinctive — not the sweet, classic lilac fragrance but a heavier, privet-like quality that some find pleasant and others less so. The bark is attractive and cherry-like on mature specimens, reddish-brown and lightly exfoliating. Highly resistant to powdery mildew (a common problem on common lilacs) and largely trouble-free in the landscape. The cultivar 'Ivory Silk' is a compact, heavy-blooming selection that is the most commonly available.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moisture-retentive, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese umbrella pine is slow-growing and should be planted in a permanent site where it will have room to develop its distinctive layered form. Avoid alkaline soils or dry sites.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moisture-retentive, fertile to average soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese umbrella pine is among the most distinctive and beautiful conifers in cultivation — a botanical 'living fossil' with no close living relatives, placed in its own family (Sciadopityaceae). The leaves are unique: elongated, dark, lustrous, deep green 'needles' (actually modified stems called cladodes) arranged in tight whorls of 20–30 around each stem node, creating the umbrella-like appearance that gives the tree its common name. The effect is deeply sculptural — each horizontal branch tier holds a perfect whorl of glossy, umbrella-like foliage clusters. Very slow growing (6–12 inches per year), making it a long-lived architectural accent plant that takes decades to reach impressive size. The glossy foliage does not fade or bronze in winter. One of the most sought-after conifers by conifer collectors and garden designers for its uniquely dramatic and elegant silhouette.

plant_note: Set potted divisions or bare rhizomes into heavy garden soil in an aquatic planting basket, positioning the crown at or just below the water surface at a pond shelf or bog edge in spring; prefers full sun to light shade and steady standing water.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in heavy loam within a submerged aquatic container so the crown sits under one to two inches of water, or in permanently saturated soil at the pond margin. Give the plant full sun to light shade and avoid letting the container dry out during the growing season. In early summer it sends up violet-blue, flattened iris blooms with yellow throat markings above narrow, sword-shaped foliage, making it a graceful marginal accent distinct from the more aggressive yellow flag iris. It spreads slowly by rhizome and rarely self-sows aggressively, so it is a good choice where a well-behaved marginal iris is wanted.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants on a very strong support structure in spring; Japanese wisteria is vigorous and heavy — supports must be extremely sturdy. Prune twice yearly (summer and winter) to control size and encourage flowering. May take 3–7 years to bloom from seed or cutting.
directions: Plant on an extremely sturdy support structure in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Japanese wisteria is considered by many gardeners the most ornamental of the wisterias, producing extraordinarily long (up to 36 inches), pendant flower racemes in shades from white through lilac, violet, and purple — cascading down in waves of color in spring. The fragrance is sweet and pervasive. However, it is the most aggressive and potentially invasive of the wisterias in the American South (it is invasive in many southeastern states) — the native alternatives (W. frutescens, W. macrostachya) are strongly recommended for environmental responsibility. If growing Japanese wisteria, regular biannual pruning is essential to contain the plant and promote flowering. NOTE: all wisteria parts are toxic if ingested; the seeds particularly so.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese witch hazel grows naturally in the mountains of Honshu and Kyushu, Japan, where it flowers in late winter on the bare branches before leaves emerge. More heat-tolerant than Chinese witch hazel — a better choice for zones 7-8.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese witch hazel is one of the parents of the widely grown Hamamelis x intermedia hybrid witch hazels (crossed with Chinese witch hazel H. mollis) — producing some of the most widely planted late-winter-flowering shrubs in the world. The species itself produces yellow to yellow-orange, ribbon-like, spidery petals on bare branches in late winter, earlier than most witch hazels, with a pleasant sweet fragrance. More heat-tolerant than the Chinese species, making it a better choice for zone 7–8 gardens in the southeastern US. The outstanding fall color of yellow to orange-red makes it a four-season ornamental shrub. Parent of many named cultivars and interspecific hybrids including 'Arnold Promise' (yellow, very fragrant), 'Jelena' (copper-orange), and 'Diane' (red) — among the most celebrated winter-flowering shrubs in horticulture. Excellent as a woodland garden shrub flowering in the dormant season when nothing else is in bloom.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Anemone flaccida is a spreading Japanese woodland anemone that forms an attractive, slowly creeping carpet of deeply lobed, softly toothed, glossy green leaves beneath deciduous trees. In mid spring it bears open, five- to seven-petaled white to pale pink flowers with a central boss of yellow stamens, held just above the foliage in loose drifts. Unlike many spring ephemerals it retains attractive foliage well into summer in consistently moist shade before going dormant. It spreads gently by rhizome to naturalize into a low, weed-suppressing groundcover, making a graceful companion for hostas, ferns, and epimediums in a woodland setting.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Japanese wood poppy goes dormant by midsummer in hot climates, so interplant with later-emerging ferns or hostas to fill the gap it leaves behind.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Japanese wood poppy goes dormant by midsummer in hot climates, so interplant with later-emerging ferns or hostas to fill the gap it leaves behind. Hylomecon japonica is a poppy-family woodland ephemeral from Japan, Korea, and China closely resembling the North American celandine poppy, with soft, deeply divided, fern-like leaves and cheerful, four-petaled, bright yellow flowers held above the foliage in early to mid spring. It spreads gently by rhizome to form a loose colony in humus-rich woodland soil, making an attractive spring companion for trillium, bloodroot, and other woodland ephemerals before going summer-dormant. Give it consistent spring moisture while in growth and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizomes once established.

plant_note: Tie or glue the rhizome to driftwood or rock with cotton thread or cyanoacrylate gel until new roots grip the surface, usually within a month; never bury the rhizome in substrate, as this causes it to rot.
directions: An epiphytic fern of Southeast Asian streams, grown fully submersed in freshwater aquaria attached to hardscape rather than rooted in substrate; its tough, leathery, dark-green fronds resist grazing fish and algae buildup better than most soft-leaved aquatic plants. It tolerates low light well and does not need CO2 supplementation, making it a mainstay of low-tech planted tanks, though it also grows readily under medium to high light. Small plantlets frequently form along the leaf margins and can be removed and re-attached to new hardscape once they have a few small roots, or the rhizome itself can be cut into sections to propagate additional plants.

plant_note: Mount on sphagnum-covered boards or plant in hanging baskets in bright indirect light in partial shade; Java staghorn tolerates slightly drier conditions between waterings than most other staghorn species thanks to its finely divided, silvery, hair-covered fronds.
directions: Mount on sphagnum-covered boards or hang in a basket in bright indirect light; Java staghorn fern is an Indonesian epiphyte prized among collectors for its finely divided, drooping, silvery-gray fertile fronds covered in fine hairs (trichomes) that give the whole plant a soft, frosted appearance quite different from the broader, upright fronds of the common staghorn. Its upright, deeply lobed shield fronds clasp the mounting surface and gradually build up a nest of organic debris that feeds the plant, just as in other Platycerium species. The dense hair covering helps the fronds tolerate brief drying between waterings better than some relatives, but the plant still prefers regular soaking of its root mass followed by thorough drainage rather than constantly soggy conditions. It produces offset pups over time that can be separated and mounted individually once they have their own root system, making it easier to propagate at home than non-offsetting species like Platycerium superbum.

common_name: Javelin Forte Deep Rose Spanish Lavender
plant_note: Plant the live starter after frost danger passes; sold as a live plant.
directions: Plant this compact Spanish lavender in spring in lean, sharply drained soil after frost danger has passed. Deep rose-pink bracts crown purple flowers above classic silver-green foliage on a tidy, mounded plant ideal for containers and borders. Give it full sun, avoid heavy or wet soils, and water sparingly once established since it is drought-tolerant. Shear lightly after the main flush to keep the plant compact and encourage rebloom.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; bearded iris rots quickly if planted too deep or kept in soggy soil.
directions: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; bearded iris rots quickly if planted too deep or kept in soggy soil. Ruffled, richly textured flowers combine deep burgundy-purple standards with lighter, veined falls edged in a lace-like ruffle, a bold, dramatic bicolor combination typical of modern award-winning bearded iris breeding, blooming on tall, sturdy stems in late spring. Like other tall bearded iris, it thrives in lean to average soil with excellent drainage, needing full sun and no more than light fertilizing to bloom well, and multiplies steadily by rhizome division over several years. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, discarding the older central rhizomes and replanting only vigorous outer divisions, and keep the rhizome tops exposed to sun to prevent rot.

common_name: Jazz Hands Dwarf Pink Loropetalum (Compact Purple-Leaf Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the compact Jazz Hands series holds a tidy rounded shape naturally and needs little pruning beyond an occasional light shaping right after the spring bloom.
directions: Jazz Hands Dwarf Pink is a compact member of the Jazz Hands loropetalum series, bred to fit small beds and container plantings while still delivering the deep burgundy-purple foliage and ribbon-like, spidery pink flowers the species is known for. Its dense, well-branched, rounded habit stays smaller than most loropetalum cultivars, holding good foliage color through the season with a heavy spring flower flush and scattered rebloom later on. It shares the easy care of other loropetalum selections, tolerating normal garden soil, heat, and humidity as long as drainage is good, and needs only minimal shaping right after its main bloom period to stay neat.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Jazz Hands foamflower wants consistent moisture and struggles in dry shade.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Jazz Hands foamflower wants consistent moisture and struggles in dry shade. Bred from native eastern foamflower stock, this Terra Nova selection carries bold, deeply cut, maple-like leaves with a dark central shadow, held on sturdy stems above which fluffy, bottlebrush spikes of small starry pink-white flowers rise in mid-spring. Its clumping, non-stoloniferous habit keeps it tidy in a mixed border rather than spreading into a running mat like straight-species foamflower, and it is a good nectar source for early native bees. Combine with hostas, ferns, and heucheras for season-long textural contrast in a shaded bed, dividing crowded clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Plant in poor, rocky, or sandy well-drained soil in full sun; needs little supplemental water once established, well suited to xeriscaping.
directions: Plant in poor, rocky, or sandy well-drained soil in full sun, where it needs little supplemental water once established. Selected from the popular cultivar The Blues for its notably compact, non-flopping habit, Jazz forms a tight upright clump of narrow blue-green foliage that stays shorter and sturdier than most little bluestem selections. Purplish-bronze flower spikes appear in late summer, followed by fluffy silvery-white seed heads that persist into early winter and catch backlight beautifully. The blue-green blades shift to vivid red, orange, and purple tones with the first cool nights of fall, giving the plant strong multi-season interest in a smaller footprint, well suited to xeriscaping and small-space native plantings.

common_name: Jazzberry Jam Hardy Hibiscus (Fuchsia-Pink Compact Perennial Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Jazzberry Jam's compact, well-branched habit needs less staking than older, taller hardy hibiscus cultivars.
directions: Jazzberry Jam produces vivid fuchsia-pink, dinner-plate-sized flowers with a deeper red eye at the center, on a compact, sturdy, well-branched plant bred to stay shorter and less prone to flopping than older hardy hibiscus cultivars. Like other Hibiscus moscheutos selections it is naturally suited to wetland-edge conditions and needs consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to bloom well from midsummer into fall. It dies back completely to the ground each winter and is slow to re-emerge in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown, and expect vigorous, trouble-free regrowth each year given adequate water and sun.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Jean May is a popular exhibition-quality sasanqua camellia known for its double shell-pink flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Jean May is a popular sasanqua camellia grown for its full, double, soft shell-pink flowers, considered among the more refined and exhibition-worthy blooms in the sasanqua group, produced in a heavy fall flush on an upright, moderately vigorous evergreen shrub. It offers reliable, showy color in the landscape during a season when few other shrubs are flowering, and like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica cultivars, blooming well from partial shade into full sun. Prune only lightly to shape after flowering, since flower buds set later in the growing season.

common_name: Jean's Appalachian Snow Dogwood (Anthracnose-Resistant White Flowering Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Jean's Appalachian Snow was bred at the University of Tennessee specifically for resistance to anthracnose and powdery mildew, two diseases that have devastated flowering dogwoods across much of the humid South.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Jean's Appalachian Snow is a University of Tennessee-bred flowering dogwood selected specifically for resistance to dogwood anthracnose and powdery mildew, two fungal diseases that have killed or badly disfigured flowering dogwoods across much of the humid South in recent decades, making disease-resistant selections like this one an increasingly important choice over older, more vulnerable cultivars. It produces the classic large, pure white bracts in early spring on a naturally graceful, horizontally branched small tree, followed by good fall color and red berries that feed birds. As an understory species, it performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, mimicking its native woodland-edge habitat. Mulch heavily around the root zone to keep soil cool and moist through Gulf South summer heat.

common_name: Jeana Garden Phlox (Highly Mildew-Resistant Pollinator Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Jeana was discovered growing along a Tennessee riverbank and shows outstanding natural resistance to powdery mildew, the disease that disfigures most garden phlox by midsummer.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade with good air circulation. Found growing wild along the Harpeth River in Tennessee, Jeana has become one of the most celebrated garden phlox introductions of recent decades for its outstanding resistance to powdery mildew, a fungal disease that routinely turns the leaves of older phlox cultivars gray and unsightly by midsummer. It produces unusually large numbers of small, soft lavender-pink flowers packed into wide domed clusters over a long summer bloom season, and research trials have documented it as an exceptional magnet for butterflies, drawing more pollinator visits than most other phlox cultivars tested. Divide the clump every few years in spring to maintain vigor, and keep soil consistently moist for the best flowering.

common_name: Jeanne d'Arc Crocus (Classic Large-Flowered Pure White Dutch Crocus)
plant_note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Jeanne d'Arc is a classic large-flowered Dutch crocus cultivar that naturalizes well in lawns and borders.
directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Jeanne d'Arc naturalizes well in a lawn or border and multiplies steadily by cormlets over the years. Large, goblet-shaped, pure white flowers with faint violet feathering at the base and a bright orange-yellow throat open wide in full sun each early spring day, one of the longest-cultivated and most classic large-flowered Dutch crocus cultivars still widely grown today. Its clean white color makes it a versatile companion planted alongside purple or striped crocus cultivars for high-contrast spring drifts. Allow the grass-like foliage to die back naturally before mowing over a naturalized planting, and divide congested clumps during summer dormancy if flowering begins to decline after many years.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; 'Jeddeloh' develops a distinctive nest-like depression at the center of the plant as it ages and needs consistent moisture, never drying out completely.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a site sheltered from full afternoon sun and drying winds, and keep the root zone consistently moist since hemlocks do not tolerate drought. 'Jeddeloh' is a dwarf, mounding selection of eastern hemlock with fine, soft, dark green needles on branches that radiate outward and slightly downward, forming the shallow central depression that gives nest-form conifers their name. Its slow growth and low, spreading shape suit it to rock gardens, shaded foundation plantings, and mixed dwarf conifer collections rather than screening, and, like all eastern hemlocks, it should be monitored for hemlock woolly adelgid in regions where that pest is established.

common_name: Jeepers Creepers Tiarella (Deeply Cut Maroon-Centered Foamflower)
plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable, setting crowns level with the surrounding soil.
directions: Set divisions into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in spring or fall, spacing plants far enough apart to let their slow-creeping stolons knit together into a solid mat over a season or two. Keep the planting mulched with leaf mold to hold moisture and suppress weeds while the shallow roots establish. The deeply lobed leaves emerge green with a bold maroon-black central star that intensifies in cooler weather, and airy spikes of small white star-shaped flowers rise above the foliage in mid-spring. It makes an excellent evergreen-in-mild-climates edging or woodland groundcover beneath deciduous shade trees.

common_name: Jelena Witch Hazel (Copper-Orange Winter Witch Hazel)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; witch hazel flower buds need real winter chill to open well, so bloom is most reliable in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 and can be sparse in mild winters.
directions: Jelena is widely regarded as one of the finest copper-orange witch hazel cultivars, its spidery, ribbon-petaled flowers opening a warm burnt-orange with a reddish flush toward the base of each petal, glowing against bare winter branches when little else in the garden shows any color. It carries some of the best fall foliage of any witch hazel cultivar as well, turning shades of orange, red, and yellow that echo the winter flower color, giving it real two-season value in a shaded border. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since witch hazel resents both drought and waterlogged soil.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Jelly Bean Plant develops its best red tips in bright light and stays plain green in shade.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Jelly Bean Plant develops its best red tips in bright light and stays plain green in shade. Plump, cylindrical, blue-green leaves tipped in bright coral-red closely resemble a cluster of jelly beans, an appropriately whimsical common name for this easy, fast-growing Mexican sedum that branches and spreads readily along sprawling stems, eventually forming a substantial mound or trailing mass in a container or garden bed. One of the most widely grown and easily propagated sedums, it roots readily from stem or leaf cuttings and tolerates a range of conditions, making it a popular, low-maintenance choice for succulent arrangements and xeriscape plantings alike. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for the best red coloring, and propagate easily from cuttings.

common_name: Jellybean Plant (Pork and Beans, Sedum rubrotinctum)
plant_note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in dry, gritty mix after the last frost, letting cut ends callus for a few days before setting them in soil.
directions: Grow in shallow containers or as a groundcover in fast-draining succulent mix, watering only when the soil is fully dry and allowing bright sun to bring out the plant's best color. Individual leaves detach easily and root readily where they fall, so it spreads quickly along rock edges and container rims. Its plump, bean-shaped leaves turn from jade green to ruby red under strong light and cool temperatures, giving the plant its jellybean nickname. Small star-shaped yellow flowers appear on short stalks in spring above the trailing foliage.

common_name: Jersey Princess American Holly (Premier Rutgers Dense Heavy-Fruiting Native Holly)
plant_note: Plant container trees in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jersey Princess, a Rutgers University release, is a premier female selection of native American holly with dense pyramidal form and a heavy, long-persisting crop of red berries. Plant a compatible male pollinator within range for fruit set.
directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a compatible male American holly within range for pollination, since hollies are dioecious and only fertilized female plants produce berries. Jersey Princess, bred and released by Rutgers University, is widely regarded as one of the finest American holly cultivars available, forming a dense, uniform, classically pyramidal evergreen tree clothed in glossy, spiny dark green leaves and producing an exceptionally heavy crop of bright red berries that persist on the tree for months into winter, a long-lasting food source for cedar waxwings, robins, mockingbirds, and other birds during the leanest part of the year. Its dense, tidy habit needs less corrective pruning than many holly cultivars to look its best. An outstanding evergreen specimen, screen, or wildlife tree for a Southern landscape with acidic soil.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Jerusalem sage requires excellent drainage and dislikes wet soils especially in winter. It is damaged below about 10-15 degrees F and is best suited to zones 7-10. Hard-prune in spring to prevent legginess and maintain a compact shrub form.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Jerusalem sage is a robust, aromatic Mediterranean shrub producing some of the most distinctive and beautiful yellow flowers in the ornamental garden. The large, rounded leaves are covered in dense, soft, white-woolly hairs that give the entire plant a silvery-gray appearance and make it exceptionally drought-tolerant. In late spring and early summer, tall stems bear whorled clusters of vivid, brilliant-yellow tubular flowers arranged in stacked rings around the stem in tiers, giving a candelabra effect that is unique among flowering shrubs. The dried brown seed whorls persist attractively on the stems through winter and are ornamental in their own right. Native to rocky, dry hillsides throughout the eastern Mediterranean from Greece to Israel, it thrives in the hot, dry, alkaline conditions of Mediterranean-climate gardens, Gulf Coast landscapes, and dry borders where most ornamental shrubs would struggle. Combines beautifully with lavender, rosemary, and other silver-leafed Mediterranean plants.

plant_note: Plant container stock or scarified, soaked seeds in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Jerusalem thorn is extremely drought-tolerant once established and one of the fastest-growing native trees for hot, dry sites in the Southwest and Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; scarify seeds with sandpaper and soak overnight before sowing. Parkinsonia aculeata (Jerusalem thorn, palo verde, or retama) is a spectacular, fast-growing, native thorny tree of the Sonoran Desert and south Texas brushlands — one of the most drought-tolerant of all North American trees — producing cascading, bright-green, photosynthetic stems and flattened, grass-like leaf rachises (the true leaves are reduced to tiny leaflets that drop early) with a weeping, delicate, almost feathery texture. In spring and sporadically after rains, the tree is smothered in masses of bright-yellow, fragrant, pea-like flowers that are outstanding for bees and other native pollinators. The green stems photosynthesize year-round, even when leafless — an adaptation for the desert. Jerusalem thorn grows extremely fast (4–6 feet per year when young) and is one of the best trees for quickly establishing a windbreak, shade, or wildlife habitat in hot, dry, alkaline soils. Young plants are somewhat frost-tender; established trees survive brief drops to 15°F. The seed pods and green seeds are edible in traditional Indigenous and Mexican cuisines.

plant_note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil once soil has warmed after the last frost.
directions: Jescot Julie is an orchid-type dahlia with narrow, spoon-shaped petals that curl into tubes at the tip, giving each bloom a spiky, star-like look in shades of orange-bronze over a bright golden-yellow reverse. The two-toned effect is strongest in cooler fall weather, and the airy flower form contrasts with the dense doubles common among dinnerplate dahlias. Provide sturdy staking as it grows to full height, and cut regularly for bouquets, since it is a strong repeat bloomer once established. Its distinctive spoon-petal shape appeals to gardeners and flower arrangers looking for texture rather than the classic ball or decorative dahlia form.

common_name: Jesse's Song Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal White-and-Violet Plicata Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil.
directions: Bred by Bunny Williamson and awarded the Dykes Medal in 1990, Jesse's Song is a classic plicata-pattern tall bearded iris with crisp white petals stitched and stippled in violet-purple around the ruffled edges. Plant rhizomes shallowly in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid mulching directly over the rhizome to prevent rot. Its crisp bicolor patterning and strong garden vigor made it an enduringly popular exhibition and landscape cultivar, and it is still frequently recommended decades after its introduction as an entry point into collecting plicata-type bearded iris.

common_name: Jester Ornamental Pepper (Multicolor Upright Fruit Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Jester is a compact ornamental pepper bred for a heavy, colorful fruit display rather than culinary use, and does well in containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Jester is compact enough for containers and makes a colorful patio or border accent. It produces an abundance of small, upright, conical fruits that ripen through purple, cream, orange, and red, often showing several colors at once on a single densely branched, mounded plant covered almost entirely in fruit rather than foliage by late summer. Grown primarily for ornamental impact rather than flavor, though the small fruits are technically edible and quite hot; its dense, compact habit and heavy fruit set make it a strong seasonal color plant for beds, borders, and mixed containers through fall.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; jetbead tolerates deep shade and poor soil better than most flowering shrubs but self-sows readily, so deadhead spent flowers where volunteer seedlings are unwanted.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; jetbead tolerates deep shade and poor soil better than most flowering shrubs but self-sows readily, so deadhead spent flowers where volunteer seedlings are unwanted. Rhodotypos scandens is a tough, adaptable, deciduous shrub related to Kerria, with pleated, sharply toothed, opposite leaves and single, four-petaled white flowers in mid-spring followed by clusters of glossy, jet-black, pea-sized fruit that persist into winter and give the plant its common name. It is one of the most shade-tolerant flowering shrubs available, thriving in the deep, dry shade beneath mature trees where few other shrubs perform, and asks for essentially no maintenance once established beyond occasional renewal pruning. Because it seeds itself freely and can naturalize into nearby wooded areas in some regions, it is best used in a contained landscape bed rather than adjacent to natural woodland, with faded flowers removed before seed matures if spread is a concern.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jetfire is an early-blooming, cyclamineus-type daffodil that naturalizes readily and is one of the most reliable early-season daffodils.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jetfire is an early-blooming, cyclamineus-type daffodil that naturalizes readily and is one of the most reliable early-season daffodils. Bright golden-yellow petals sweep dramatically backward away from a long, strongly contrasting orange-red trumpet, a bold, swept-back flower form typical of the cyclamineus daffodil group, opening among the very earliest daffodils each spring on compact, sturdy stems well suited to a rock garden, container, or the front of a border. One of the most popular and widely planted small daffodil cultivars for its vivid bicolor contrast and reliable early bloom, it naturalizes readily into larger clumps and provides an early nectar source for the season's first bees. Let foliage die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer once dormant.

common_name: Jethro Tull Coreopsis (Fringed Spoon-Petaled Threadleaf Coreopsis)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Jethro Tull is a threadleaf coreopsis cultivar with distinctive fluted, spoon-shaped gold petals that give the flowers a fringed, textured look.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; threadleaf coreopsis thrives on soil too poor and dry for many other perennials. Jethro Tull produces bright golden-yellow flowers with distinctively fluted, spoon-shaped petals that curl slightly along their length, giving each bloom a fringed, three-dimensional texture unlike the flatter petals of most other coreopsis cultivars, held above fine, airy, thread-like foliage. It flowers heavily over a long summer season and tolerates heat and drought exceptionally well once established, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for the front of a sunny border or a mass planting. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first flush fades to encourage a fuller rebloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

common_name: Jetstream Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact Upright Oakleaf Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Jetstream stays more compact and upright than older, larger oakleaf hydrangea cultivars like Alice, fitting smaller foundation and border plantings.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Jetstream bears large, upright, cone-shaped white flower panicles that age to a soft pink over a more compact, tidy, upright shrub than older oakleaf hydrangea selections, fitting smaller foundation beds and mixed borders without sacrificing the bold, deeply lobed foliage and outstanding orange-red-purple fall color the species is known for. Its exfoliating, cinnamon-colored bark adds winter interest after leaves drop. As with other oakleaf hydrangeas, flower buds form on the previous year's wood, so prune only in the weeks immediately following bloom to avoid removing next year's flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost; dislikes root disturbance.
directions: Direct sow the large seeds 1/2 to 1 inch deep after the last frost, as nasturtiums resent transplanting. This compact jewel-toned blend makes an excellent edging plant and produces edible flowers and leaves with a peppery flavor for salads. Plants are fairly drought-tolerant and actually bloom best in lean soil, since rich soil favors foliage over flowers. Provide full sun to part shade, and grow in a sunny window for winter color indoors.

common_name: Jewel Mix Nasturtium (Classic Mixed-Color Compact Nasturtium)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Jewel Mix is a classic compact, mounding (non-vining) nasturtium blend producing a full range of warm flower colors from cream through gold, orange, and deep red.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; overly fertile soil produces lush leaves at the expense of flowers. Jewel Mix is one of the most classic and widely grown nasturtium blends, producing compact, bushy plants (rather than the long trailing vines of climbing types) covered in semi-double flowers spanning cream, yellow, gold, orange, salmon, and deep red, all with the same cheerful, informal charm nasturtiums are known for. Both flowers and round leaves are edible with a peppery, watercress-like bite, making them a popular addition to salads and as an edible garnish. The compact habit suits containers, edging, and small beds, and plants bloom continuously from early summer through frost with minimal care.

common_name: Jewel Orchid (Velvet Orchid, Red Jewel Orchid)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, terrarium specimen, or shaded patio plant in zone 9; Ludisia discolor cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Unlike most orchids, Jewel Orchid grows in regular well-draining potting mix (a peat-based or coir-based mix) rather than bark media — it is terrestrial, not epiphytic. Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged. High humidity (50–70%) improves leaf appearance and prevents tip browning. Propagate from stem cuttings placed in moist mix. The white flower spikes appear in late fall to winter. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in moderate to deep shade — Jewel Orchid is one of the most shade-tolerant orchids available and one of the very few plants that actually prefers low light, thriving in conditions where other ornamentals would refuse to survive. Ludisia discolor is a terrestrial orchid from the humid rainforest floors of South and Southeast Asia (India, China, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Philippines), belonging to the informal group called 'jewel orchids' (Goodyerinae tribe) that are grown primarily for their extraordinary foliage rather than their flowers. The leaves are velvety, creeping, dark maroon-green to nearly black on the upper surface, decorated with a network of precisely delineated veins in vivid rose-red or copper-gold that create a glittering, jewel-like pattern in any light, especially in the deep shade where the plant thrives naturally. In late fall to winter, tall spikes rise above the foliage bearing small, white, delicate flowers in loose racemes — charming but secondary to the leaf display. The plant is a low, creeping, semi-succulent terrestrial that spreads slowly by horizontal stems rooting at nodes. Ludisia discolor is the most widely available and easiest of the jewel orchids and is the recommended starting point for growers new to the group. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Sow direct at or just after last frost in moist, shaded soil; jewel weed self-seeds prolifically and will often naturalize in moist, shaded stream margins and woodland gardens with no intervention once established.
directions: Sow direct at last frost date in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; jewel weed self-seeds so abundantly that once established it will return year after year without intervention — it is best established by purchasing transplants or directing seeds into the garden in fall for spring germination. Impatiens capensis is a native North American annual wildflower of moist, shaded stream banks, woodland margins, and seeps; it produces succulent, blue-green stems bearing oval, toothed leaves and a profusion of small, orange-spotted, spurred flowers from mid-summer to frost that are intensely attractive to ruby-throated hummingbirds on their southward migration. The ripe seed pods explode forcefully when touched, dispersing seeds several feet (giving rise to "touch-me-not" and providing the genus name Impatiens). The juice of crushed stems is a traditional folk remedy for poison ivy rash and stinging nettle; while scientific evidence is limited, the plant often grows near both and is a useful companion to know.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring after the last hard frost in a sheltered, partially shaded site with humus-rich, reliably moist soil.
directions: Site in partial shade with protection from cold, drying winds, which can damage the emerging fronds that flush in striking shades of copper and burgundy-red in spring. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained but consistently moist soil, incorporating plenty of leaf mold or composted bark at planting to retain moisture and encourage robust growth. The single gem-like bulbil at each frond tip can be pegged to moist compost in late summer to propagate new plants; sever the frond once roots are established. Mulch generously each autumn with leaf mold to protect the crown and feed the soil as it breaks down.

common_name: Jeweled Shooting Star / Midland Shooting Star
plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall onto the surface of well-drained, gritty or rocky soil; natural cold stratification through winter is essential for reliable spring germination.
directions: Press fresh seed onto the surface of sharply drained, gritty soil in a partially shaded rock garden or limestone outcrop setting in fall, without covering deeply. Cold winter temperatures are required to break seed dormancy, and seedlings will begin to appear in early to mid-spring. Jeweled Shooting Star is adapted to very specific limestone habitats, so replicating those conditions with lean, alkaline, well-drained soil gives the best results. Allow the foliage to die back undisturbed in early summer as plants enter dormancy, and mark the site clearly to avoid accidental disturbance.

plant_note: Direct sow seed on the soil surface (seeds need light to germinate) in moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade just before last frost; jewelweed self-sows prolifically and typically establishes as a self-sustaining colony once introduced — no further planting is needed after the first year.
directions: Scatter seed on the surface of moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in early spring; jewelweed is a tall native annual of moist woodlands, stream banks, and swampy areas throughout most of North America — one of the few native annuals that thrives in deep shade and moist conditions. The orange, trumpet-shaped flowers are uniquely constructed with a curved spur and are the primary nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds in eastern North America during their southward fall migration. The ripe seed pods burst explosively when touched (hence 'touch-me-not'), flinging seeds up to 3–4 feet. Fresh crushed stems and leaves are widely used as a folk remedy to relieve the itch of poison ivy contact, with some evidence supporting anti-inflammatory compounds in the juice. Jewelweed is a powerful self-sower that naturalizes in moist, shaded areas and requires no care once established.

common_name: Jim Dandy Winterberry Holly (Early Male Pollinator Winterberry)
plant_note: Plant as a pollinator alongside compact early-blooming female cultivars such as Red Sprite; one Jim Dandy can pollinate several nearby females if bloom times overlap.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, matching this male selection's early bloom time to an early-flowering female cultivar to ensure the berry set gardeners actually grow winterberry for. Jim Dandy itself produces no berries since winterberry is dioecious, but it is a compact, floriferous pollen source that stays proportionate to dwarf female cultivars rather than overwhelming them the way a full-size male can. Its small white spring flowers are inconspicuous but essential to fruiting nearby females. Prune only lightly and only after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Joan Senior Daylily (Classic Near-White Award-Winning Daylily)
plant_note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Joan Senior holds its near-white color best with some afternoon shade in the hottest Gulf South summers, since intense heat can give the petals a faint yellow cast.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch below soil level in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, and water deeply through the first season to establish a strong root system. Bred by Bill Munson and introduced in 1977, Joan Senior bears large, ruffled, near-white flowers with a faint chartreuse-green throat that appear almost luminous in the garden, backed by a light, sweet fragrance uncommon among daylilies. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1994 and remains one of the most widely grown and admired near-white daylily cultivars for its clean color, heavy bud count, and dependable, extended rebloom from late spring into summer. Deadhead spent scapes to keep the planting tidy and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost after cold-stratifying for 4–6 weeks; transplant in spring.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds for 4–6 weeks in a moist medium in the refrigerator before sowing indoors; germination is improved but still irregular. Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; this native prairie plant tolerates occasional wet feet and dry spells once established. Cutting stems back by half in June (Chelsea chop) reduces ultimate height and prevents the need for staking without sacrificing the domed, mauve-pink flower clusters beloved by butterflies. Seedheads are ornamentally interesting into winter and provide food for goldfinches.

subcategory: Florida Keys endemic coastal native shrub
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to dry, rocky, alkaline, sandy coastal soil in zone 10–12; Joewood is a rare, slow-growing, evergreen shrub or small tree native exclusively to the Florida Keys and southernmost Miami-Dade County coastal hammocks — bearing fragrant, small, white, star-shaped flowers in clusters and distinctive, hard-wooded branches — an endemic Florida native of significant conservation concern that provides critical habitat value in coastal hammock ecosystems.
directions: Plant Jacquinia keyensis in rocky, alkaline, well-drained to dry, sandy coastal soil in full sun to partial shade; it is highly adapted to salt spray, thin rocky substrate, and periodic drought, making it an excellent choice for coastal restoration plantings and coastal hammock gardens in the Florida Keys and extreme South Florida; water sparingly once established. Joewood is one of the rarest and most regionally restricted native shrubs in the United States — found naturally only in the Florida Keys and the southern tip of Miami-Dade County, where it grows in coastal hammock communities on porous, alkaline, marl and coral rock soils just above the tidal zone. The species is classified as Threatened in Florida due to habitat loss from development, sea-level rise, and invasive plant competition. Small, leathery, spine-tipped leaves, fragrant white star-flowers produced repeatedly through warm months, and distinctive hard, contorted wood give Joewood a distinct, sculptural appearance suited to both naturalistic coastal plantings and cultivated low-maintenance coastal gardens. It provides nectar for native bees and butterflies and fruit for migratory birds. A slow-growing plant that rewards patience with exceptional performance in otherwise challenging coastal conditions. Sourcing from Florida-native nurseries propagated from local ecotypes is strongly recommended to support regional genetic conservation.

plant_note: Plant container stock in deep to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in zone 10–12; the Joey Palm (Johannesteijsmannia magnifica) is one of the most spectacular of all shade palms — endemic to the rainforest floors of Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo — producing among the largest undivided leaves of any palm, each enormous diamond-shaped frond reaching 10–15 feet long and 6–8 feet wide, in deep, humid forest shade.
directions: Grow Johannesteijsmannia magnifica in deep to bright indirect shade in moist, humus-rich, acidic, very well-drained soil with high organic matter; maintain consistently high humidity (80%+), protect from any direct sun (the large leaves scorch badly in direct light), and never allow the root zone to dry; in zone 10–12, this is a slow-growing but supremely architectural shade garden specimen. The Joey Palm is arguably the most spectacular of all ornamental understory palms for tropical gardens — producing magnificent, enormous, diamond- or rhombus-shaped, undivided fronds each ribbed with prominent veins on a stout petiole, creating a bold tropical statement in the shaded garden. It grows strictly as a forest floor specialist in its native Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo, never breaking into direct sun, and requires analogous conditions in cultivation: dense shade, high humidity, consistently moist soil, and warm temperatures above 50°F at all times. There are only four species in the Johannesteijsmannia genus — all endemic to Sundaland and all similar in their enormous, undivided fronds — with J. magnifica being the largest and most dramatic. All are threatened or endangered in the wild due to forest clearance. In zone 10–12, plant under the canopy of large trees or on the north or east side of a building where shade is assured; it makes an unrivaled specimen in tropical rain garden settings.

common_name: Joey Tomocik Water Lily (Vigorous Bright Yellow Heat-Tolerant Hardy Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun; Joey Tomocik is noted for continuing to bloom heavily through hot summer water temperatures that slow many other hardy water lily cultivars.
directions: Joey Tomocik is a vigorous hardy water lily bearing bright, clear yellow, star-shaped flowers held well above the water on strong stems, standing out from the more muted creamy-yellow tones of older yellow-flowered cultivars. It is particularly valued for continuing to flower heavily through the hottest stretch of summer, when the bloom of many other hardy water lilies slows or stalls, making it a strong performer for warm Gulf South ponds. Divide rhizomes every two to three years when they crowd their container, and feed during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets pushed into the soil for the best, most continuous bloom.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in deep shade in tropical climates (zone 11–12); Joey's Palm is a spectacular, nearly stemless, understory fan palm native to the lowland tropical rainforests of Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo, and Sumatra — one of the most extraordinary of all palms — producing enormous, undivided, diamond-shaped leaves up to 9 feet tall and 4 feet wide from what appears to be ground level, without a visible stem.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), consistently moist, well-drained soil in deep shade; Johannesteijsmannia altifrons requires high humidity (above 80%), constant warmth (above 65°F), and deep, forest-floor shade — it does not tolerate direct sun, cold, or any degree of drought; the large leaves shred in wind. Johannesteijsmannia altifrons (Joey's Palm, Daun Payung, or Umbrella Leaf Palm) is among the most extraordinary and visually striking plants in the entire palm family — a nearly acaulescent (essentially stemless) rain forest floor palm native to the lowland dipterocarp rainforests of Peninsular Malaysia, southern Thailand, Borneo, and Sumatra, whose defining characteristic is the production of enormous, undivided, diamond or leaf-shaped fronds — each up to 9 feet tall and 4 feet wide — that emerge directly from a short, near-underground stem, creating the appearance of enormous individual green 'sails' or parasols growing from the forest floor with no visible trunk. These massive, pleated, entire (undivided) fronds rival Victoria amazonica water lily pads as the largest leaves of any monocot. In the rainforest understory, the leaves form natural rain-collecting shelters used by various small animals. Johannesteijsmannia altifrons requires the most exacting tropical rainforest conditions of any commonly cultivated palm: deep shade, constant warmth, high humidity, consistent moisture, and strongly acidic soil — making it a challenging but spectacularly rewarding specimen for advanced tropical plant collectors in zone 11–12.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring near a trellis, fence, or other support; stems twine and will climb 10–15 feet.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis or fence; well-behaved and non-invasive, unlike Japanese honeysuckle. John Clayton is a yellow-flowered selection of native coral honeysuckle, discovered in Virginia and named for the 18th-century botanist, bearing long, tubular, clear yellow flowers instead of the species' typical scarlet-to-coral color, with a long bloom season from spring through fall and light rebloom. It provides the same long-tube nectar source ruby-throated hummingbirds rely on, while giving gardeners a color alternative to the more common red-flowered selections for pairing with other warm-toned plantings. Prune in late winter or just after a bloom flush to shape the vine and remove dead wood; semi-evergreen in mild Gulf South winters.

common_name: John Creech Sedum (Compact Scalloped-Leaf Groundcover Stonecrop)
plant_note: Plant cuttings or divisions in spring in very well-drained, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant cuttings or divisions in spring in very well-drained, dry to average, lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade. John Creech is a compact, tidy selection of Caucasian stonecrop, staying lower and more restrained than the vigorous straight species, forming a dense mat of small, scalloped, bright green leaves topped by clusters of star-shaped pink flowers in midsummer. Its smaller scale and less aggressive spread make it a better fit for rock gardens, container plantings, and small-space groundcover than more rampant sedum spurium cultivars, while still spreading readily enough to fill in bare, dry spots quickly. Extremely low-maintenance and drought-tolerant once established; propagate easily from stem cuttings that root at the leaf nodes.

common_name: John Fanick Phlox (Heat-and-Humidity-Tolerant San Antonio Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation; John Fanick, selected in San Antonio, Texas, is noted for exceptional heat and humidity tolerance and a long bloom season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation to help minimize powdery mildew, the primary phlox disease in humid climates. John Fanick was selected in San Antonio, Texas specifically for its outstanding tolerance of extreme summer heat and humidity, conditions that cause many other tall garden phlox cultivars to decline or succumb to mildew, making it one of the most dependable phlox choices for Gulf South and Texas gardens. It bears soft pink flowers with a darker pink eye in a long bloom season that stretches from early summer well into fall, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds throughout. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and airflow.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. John Nelson is a selected cleyera cultivar valued for denser branching and more compact, uniform growth than seed-grown plants, with the same glossy, oval, dark-green leaves that emerge bronze-red on new growth and small, fragrant, creamy flowers in summer followed by red berries. Its improved density makes it a stronger choice for screening and hedging than straight-species cleyera, while retaining the shade tolerance that makes the species valuable as an alternative to photinia or ligustrum in partly shaded Gulf Coast landscapes. It requires little pruning to hold an attractive form and is largely untroubled by pests or disease.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness; violas prefer cool spring and fall weather.
directions: Sow seed in darkness indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow in cool spring or fall weather. These charming purple, yellow, and white faces bloom prolifically and can poke up above light snow. Though perennial in zones 4-8, they are often grown as annuals since they falter in extended heat. Grow in part shade with moist soil, use them as spring bulb cover, and let them self-sow to return year after year.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Johnson's Blue is a classic, long-established hardy geranium hybrid with lavender-blue flowers, blooming mainly in a single strong spring flush.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Johnson's Blue, a long-standing classic hardy geranium hybrid dating to the mid-twentieth century, bears large, clear lavender-blue flowers over deeply lobed, attractive foliage, blooming mainly in a strong spring flush with lighter, sporadic rebloom later if deadheaded.
