Its sprawling, mounding habit weaves attractively through and under other perennials, and it has remained a garden favorite for decades despite the introduction of longer-blooming modern cultivars like Rozanne. In the heat of a zone 9 summer it appreciates afternoon shade and consistent moisture. Shear back hard after the main flush to encourage tidier, fresher growth and possible rebloom.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in pure, infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun. Jointweed is a Florida scrub and coastal plain endemic that requires the xeric, open conditions of its native sandy habitats and will not thrive in clay, amended, or irrigated garden soils.
directions: Jointweed is a delicate-looking native perennial of the sandy coastal plain scrub, sandhills, and open pine flatwoods of the southeastern United States, producing masses of tiny white to pink flowers on jointed, wiry stems from summer through fall that create a misty, cloud-like appearance and provide essential late-season nectar for monarch butterflies and many native bee species on the sandy scrub habitats where few other wildflowers bloom at the same time. A member of the buckwheat family, Jointweed is adapted to the infertile, white-sand soils of ancient Florida scrub ridges and coastal plain sandhills where it serves as a foundational component of the herbaceous layer. Like other Florida scrub plants, it benefits from periodic, low-intensity fire that removes competing vegetation and maintains the open, sunny conditions required. Direct sow seeds in fall in pure, infertile, sandy, acidic, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; established plants are long-lived and drought-tolerant once their root systems develop.

plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Jomanda is a compact, heavily branched ball dahlia that produces an unusually large number of blooms per plant, making it a favorite for cutting.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. Jomanda bears perfectly formed, tightly packed ball-shaped blooms in a bright, warm orange that hold their shape well both on the plant and in the vase, opening from an already generous branching habit that keeps new buds coming in steady succession all season. It is widely grown by cut-flower growers specifically for the sheer volume of usable stems it produces from a single tuber. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep new flowers coming, and stake plants in exposed sites since the dense flower heads can weigh down stems in wind. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Plant in fall; fragrant and good for warm climates.
directions: Plant jonquilla daffodil bulbs in fall about six inches deep in well-drained soil and full to partial sun. These fragrant narcissi carry several small golden flowers per stem and tolerate warmer climates better than most daffodils. They naturalize freely and are resistant to deer and rodents. Allow the grassy foliage to ripen fully before removal to build strong bulbs for next year.

common_name: Josef Lemper Hellebore (Vigorous Pure White Christmas Rose)
plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; Josef Lemper is a vigorous, floriferous Christmas rose selection that blooms earlier and more heavily than the straight species, often flowering around the winter holidays in mild climates.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist through establishment. Josef Lemper is a superior selection of the traditional Christmas rose, valued for producing more flowers per plant and blooming earlier and more reliably than older seed-grown Helleborus niger, often opening its large, pure white, saucer-shaped flowers around the winter holiday season in mild climates and continuing into late winter elsewhere. The dark, leathery, evergreen foliage stays attractive year-round, providing structure in the shade garden even between bloom seasons. Remove old, tattered leaves in late winter just before flowering to best display the blooms, and keep in mind that all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Joseph's Coat Amaranth (Multicolor Foliage Ornamental Amaranth)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Joseph's Coat is grown for its brilliantly multicolored foliage, splashed with red, gold, green, and bronze, rather than for showy flowers.
directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed. Joseph's Coat is grown chiefly as a dramatic foliage plant, its upper leaves splashed and blotched in vivid combinations of red, gold, orange, green, and bronze that intensify with heat and full sun, providing bold color through the entire summer without needing showy flowers. It makes a striking specimen or background planting in a hot, sunny border and tolerates drought and poor soil well once established. Young leaves of this species are also edible and used as a cooked green in parts of Asia and Africa, though the plant is most commonly grown in Western gardens purely for its colorful ornamental foliage.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants in spring with the crown a couple of inches deep and roots shaded, then train the twining stems onto a trellis or obelisk positioned so the top of the vine reaches full sun.
directions: Give this compact clematis a modest trellis or obelisk to climb, keeping the root zone shaded and moist while the top growth flowers in full sun to light shade. Its claim to fame is an unusually long-lasting, fully double flower packed with narrow rose-pink petals layered into a tight rosette, blooming from early summer and often repeating into fall as temperatures cool. Because it flowers on both old and new stems, it needs only a light tidy-up in late winter rather than hard pruning, so remove dead or weak growth and leave the rest. The dense, ruffled blooms make it a standout specimen for a container trellis or small garden support.

subcategory: spectacular large South African autumn bulb
plant_note: Plant large bulbs with the upper half exposed above the soil surface in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Josephine's lily flowers in late summer and autumn (March–April in South Africa; August–October in zone 9), producing flowers before the leaves emerge (hysteranthous). The spectacular candelabra flower head develops from a leafless scape. This is a very large bulb requiring patience — 4–7 years from seed to first flower. It is named for Empress Josephine of France, who grew it at Malmaison.
directions: Plant large bulbs (upper half exposed) in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Josephine's lily is one of the most spectacular of all South African bulbs — producing in late summer and early autumn a floral display of almost theatrical grandeur: a fat, stout, leafless scape emerging from the large, round-shouldered, papery-tunic bulb and rising to 24–36 inches, then expanding at the apex into an enormous, spherical, candelabra-like umbel of 20–40 or more individual flowers, each on its own radiating, arching pedicel, the whole structure spanning 24 inches or more across — a complete ball of brilliant, deep-pink to carmine-pink to salmon-red, narrowly tubular-funnel flowers with reflexing petal tips and projecting stamens, creating an unmistakable silhouette of a giant, pink fireworks burst frozen in botanical form. After the spectacular flower head, the strap-like leaves emerge and persist through winter and spring. The bulb is named for Empress Josephine Bonaparte, who cultivated it at Château de Malmaison from bulbs obtained from South Africa. A plant of exceptional scale, patience (4–7 years from seed or purchased offset to first flower), and spectacular reward for the zone 9 garden's most dramatic space.

plant_note: Plant small nursery-grown transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; growth is extremely slow, often only 1-3 inches a year, and container specimens establish far more reliably than direct seeding.
directions: Plant in lean, gravelly or sandy, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun and resist the urge to amend the planting hole or irrigate on a regular schedule; Joshua trees are adapted to the high-elevation Mojave Desert of California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah, where winter cold and summer drought are both part of the plant's natural rhythm. This unmistakable, multi-branched arborescent yucca is topped with rosettes of stiff, dagger-like blue-green leaves and can eventually reach 15-40 feet with a gnarled, candelabra-like silhouette that takes many decades to develop. Established trees are extremely drought tolerant and cold hardy into the single digits Fahrenheit, but they are notoriously slow-growing and intolerant of poor drainage, soggy soil, or excess summer humidity, which makes them best suited to arid inland gardens rather than the humid Gulf Coast. Like other yuccas, the creamy, waxy spring flower clusters depend on the yucca moth (Tegeticula synthetica) for pollination, and mature trees are a keystone habitat feature in their native range.

common_name: Journey's End Lily (Crimson-Pink White-Edged Oriental Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; Journey's End is a late-summer-blooming Oriental lily with large, richly colored, recurved blooms.
directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade, keeping the base of the plant shaded with mulch or companion plants. Journey's End bears large, strongly fragrant, recurved blooms in deep crimson-pink broadly edged in white with darker spotting toward the throat, opening late in the Oriental lily season to extend summer color into early fall. Its tall, sturdy stems make an excellent, long-lasting cut flower, though the intense fragrance can be overwhelming in a small enclosed room. Leave the foliage in place after bloom until it yellows naturally, since it recharges the bulb for next year's flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown rosettes in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; unlike hens-and-chicks, Jovibarba rosettes multiply by splitting the crown into new rosettes ('rollers') rather than by sending out offsets on runners.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun; Jovibarba is a close relative of Sempervivum (hens-and-chicks) commonly sold alongside it for rock gardens, troughs, and xeriscape plantings, but it multiplies in a genuinely different way — instead of producing new rosettes on runners like Sempervivum, mature Jovibarba rosettes split at the crown into several new rosettes, which loosen and can simply roll away from the mother plant to root nearby, giving rise to the common name 'rollers.' Rosettes are typically green to bronze, sometimes with reddish tips in strong sun, and form tight, low mats that spread slowly to cover gravel beds, rock crevices, and shallow containers. It is extremely drought-tolerant and cold-hardy once established, needing excellent drainage above all else — soggy soil, not cold, is what kills it. Like Sempervivum, individual rosettes are monocarpic, flowering once on a tall stalk and then dying, but the surrounding offsets carry the planting on indefinitely. Ideal for rock gardens, green roofs, and any lean, sharply drained, sunny spot where little else will thrive.

common_name: Jowey Winnie Dahlia (Tightly Quilled Cerise-Pink Ball Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Jowey Winnie is a miniature ball dahlia with tightly quilled cerise-pink globes on strong stems, excellent for cutting.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage bushier growth and more blooms. Jowey Winnie bears perfectly round, tightly quilled miniature ball flowers in vivid cerise-pink, held on strong, straight stems that hold their spherical shape well both on the plant and after cutting. Its compact bloom size and reliable form make it a favorite among exhibitors and cut-flower growers alike. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming through the season, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Jubilation is a Southern Living Plant Collection release bred for unusually large flowers on a more compact, cold-hardy plant than older gardenia cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade. Jubilation is a Southern Living Plant Collection gardenia bred for exceptionally large, fully double, intensely fragrant white flowers on a plant more compact and reliably cold-hardy than many older gardenia cultivars, making it a good fit for foundation plantings and smaller beds where a big gardenia bloom is still wanted. It flowers over a long season from late spring into summer, and its improved cold tolerance extends dependable gardenia culture a bit further north than older selections allow. Like all gardenias it is sensitive to soil pH, developing yellow, chlorotic leaves if the soil is not sufficiently acidic, so use an acid-forming fertilizer and keep soil consistently moist for the healthiest, most floriferous plant.

plant_note: Plant container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; avoid pruning until immediately after the spring bloom since flower buds form on old wood.
directions: Bred at the Arnold Arboretum from Viburnum carlesii x V. bitchiuense, Judd viburnum was developed to keep the intense, sweet fragrance of Korean spice viburnum while gaining better vigor and disease resistance. Pink buds open to fragrant white to pale-pink flower clusters in mid-spring, followed by red fruit that ripens to black and reddish-purple fall foliage. Its dense, rounded, symmetrical habit needs little pruning beyond the occasional light shaping right after flowering, making it a low-fuss choice for a fragrant foundation planting or mixed shrub border.

common_name: Jude the Obscure Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Jude the Obscure's large, heavy flowers benefit from a bit of afternoon shade in the hottest climates to extend their bloom life.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1995, Jude the Obscure carries large, deeply cupped, golden-yellow blooms that pale toward the outer petals as they mature, famous for one of the strongest and most distinctive fragrances of any English rose, a rich, fruity scent often described as fresh guava. Its full, heavy flowers can nod on their stems, especially after rain, and it is a somewhat lax, medium-sized shrub best sited where its fragrance can be enjoyed up close, repeat-blooming from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Judge Solomon Azalea (Bright Orange-Red Southern Indica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Judge Solomon was bred in Mobile, Alabama and remains a Deep South landscape standard for its bright, saturated bloom color.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. Judge Solomon is a classic Southern Indica azalea bred in Mobile, Alabama, one of the historic centers of azalea breeding in the Deep South, and is prized for its vivid orange-red flowers produced in an overwhelming spring flush on a large, vigorous, evergreen shrub. It has been a fixture of historic Gulf Coast azalea gardens and estate plantings for generations, valued for the sheer volume and intensity of its bloom. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for the following year set soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Judy Magnolia (Little Girl Series Reddish-Purple Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Judy is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred for later, frost-dodging bloom on a compact, upright plant.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Judy is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later bloom timing that helps the flowers dodge late spring frosts, producing reddish-purple, tulip-shaped blooms on a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed plant. Its later flowering window gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Julia Child is an AARS 2006 winner bred by Tom Carruth and noted for strong disease resistance for a floribunda, needing less spraying than many older rose varieties.
directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Julia Child is a floribunda rose named for the famous chef with the blessing of the Julia Child Foundation, an All-America Rose Selections winner in 2006 prized for its rich, buttery-gold, ruffled double flowers produced in generous clusters, along with a distinctive licorice-and-clove fragrance unlike most other roses. It is notably more disease-resistant than many older rose varieties, holding clean, glossy foliage with less spraying, which makes it a good choice for gardeners who want strong rose performance without a heavy maintenance program. The compact, well-branched, floriferous habit suits both mixed borders and mass plantings. Prune in late winter, feed with rose fertilizer through the growing season, and deadhead to encourage the next flush of the repeat bloom cycle.

common_name: Julia Rose Itoh Peony (Semi-Double Fading Red-Orange to Peach to Yellow)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Julia Rose is an Itoh (intersectional) hybrid whose semi-double blooms open deep red-orange and fade through peach to soft yellow.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Julia Rose, an Itoh (intersectional) hybrid combining traits of herbaceous and tree peonies, bears semi-double flowers that open a deep red-orange and gradually fade through peach to soft yellow as they age, giving a single planting a striking gradient of warm colors rarely seen in straight herbaceous peony cultivars. Itoh hybrids have sturdier stems that hold up blooms without staking and often rebloom lightly, along with better disease resistance than many lactiflora cultivars. Unlike tree peonies, Itoh hybrids die back to the ground each winter like herbaceous types.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall onto a firm, weed-free seedbed, pressing seed lightly into the soil surface rather than burying it deeply.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late fall onto a firm, weed-free seedbed, pressing seed lightly into the surface since it needs light to germinate. Choose a well-drained, low-fertility site in full sun; established plants tolerate drought and poor soils and resent heavy clay or overly rich beds. This compact, cool-season bunchgrass forms a fine-textured tuft of blue-green foliage topped by narrow, spike-like flower panicles in late spring, making it a good filler for short prairie plantings, rock gardens, and dry meadow borders. It goes semi-dormant in summer heat and looks best combined with other short natives rather than grown as a specimen.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; June displays the best color contrast in partial shade with some morning sun — deep shade causes the golden center to fade to chartreuse.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; June is one of the most celebrated hostas ever introduced — named the Hosta of the Year by the American Hosta Society in 2001 and consistently one of the top-ranked hostas for its spectacular golden-yellow to chartreuse center surrounded by a wide margin of deep blue-green to gray-blue, creating one of the most vivid and striking bicolor hosta foliage patterns available. Each leaf displays the centered gold with the blue-green margin in a broad, heart-shaped form that makes this medium-sized hosta (18–24 inches tall, 30–42 inches wide) one of the most beautiful foliage plants for the shade garden. 'June' is a sport of 'Halcyon' — the reverse of the parent's cool blue coloration — and the two combine beautifully to create complementary foliage effects. In partial shade, the gold center develops its richest, most saturated butter-gold color; in deep shade, it fades toward chartreuse. In zone 9, hostas prefer deep shade and consistent moisture — the intense summer heat stresses hostas more than in their preferred zone 3–7 range, and consistent irrigation with organic mulch is essential for success. June emerges in early spring with particularly attractive spring color and produces lavender flowers in mid-summer. Divide every 4–5 years in early spring.

common_name: Jungle Flame (Flame of the Woods, West Indian Jasmine)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moist, humus-rich, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), fertile soil in full sun to part shade; ixora is a cornerstone landscape shrub of South Florida, South Texas, and the Gulf Coast in zones 9–12, producing year-round clusters of vivid red, orange, pink, or yellow tubular flowers — one of the most continuously blooming tropical shrubs.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), humus-rich, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; acidify soil with sulfur if pH is above 6.0 — ixora is highly pH-sensitive and yellows rapidly in alkaline soil. Ixora coccinea (jungle flame or flame of the woods) is one of the most widely grown tropical landscape shrubs in South Florida, South Texas, Central America, and tropical Asia — prized for its dense, nearly year-round display of brilliant, dome-shaped flower clusters (corymbs) of small, tubular, four-petaled flowers in glowing shades of red, orange, salmon, pink, white, and yellow. Modern landscape cultivars include compact ('Nora Grant,' 'Super King,' 'Dwarf') and standard forms; the classic straight species produces vivid scarlet-red flowers. Ixora's critical cultural requirement is acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.0); in the alkaline soils common in coastal Florida and South Texas, plants develop interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between leaf veins due to iron and manganese deficiency) and decline unless soil is regularly acidified with sulfur or treated with chelated iron. The flowers are a nectar source for butterflies and hummingbirds; in traditional medicine (Ayurveda), various parts of the plant are used for a range of ailments. One of the most rewarding tropical shrubs where it is winter-hardy.

common_name: Justin Brouwers Boxwood (Small Dense Compact Rounded Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Justin Brouwers stays naturally small and dense, needing little pruning to hold its shape.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with some direct sun. Justin Brouwers forms a naturally dense, tidy, rounded mound of small, dark green leaves without heavy shearing, staying compact for many years and making it a low-maintenance choice for edging, small hedges, or foundation plantings where a naturally neat form is wanted. Its small mature size suits it to tight spaces where larger boxwood cultivars would quickly outgrow the site. Light shearing once a year keeps the form especially crisp, but is not strictly necessary.

common_name: Juul's Allstar Dahlia (Vivid Orange-Red Incurved Cactus Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Juul's Allstar bears vivid orange-red incurved cactus flowers with narrow, pointed, recurving petals.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake taller cactus dahlias to keep the narrow, spiky blooms upright in wind. Juul's Allstar bears vivid, saturated orange-red cactus-form flowers with narrow, pointed petals that recurve dramatically away from the center, one of the most vivid colors available in the incurved cactus class. Its spiky, sculptural flower form provides striking textural contrast to rounder decorative and ball dahlia types in a mixed cutting garden. Deadhead spent blooms regularly, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring with at least one growing bud, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade in spring; Kahili ginger tolerates more shade and cooler temperatures than most tropical gingers and is one of the best hedychiums for zone 7–10 gardens where some frost tolerance is needed.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; Kahili ginger is a Himalayan and Indian ginger species that produces some of the most fragrant and attractive flowers of any hedychium — in summer and early fall, dense, 12–18-inch cylindrical flower spikes emerge from the tips of the leafy pseudostems, covered with a succession of large, intensely sweet-scented, yellow flowers with prominent, vivid-red stamens and filaments that project well beyond the yellow petals, creating a striking red-and-yellow bicolor effect against the deep-green, lance-shaped, tropical foliage. The fragrance of Kahili ginger is one of the finest ginger scents — sweet, tropical, and penetrating — carried on the air for considerable distances from established plants. It is one of the hardiest of the ornamental hedychiums, tolerating frost to approximately 15–20°F in zone 7 when the rhizomes are mulched. Excellent in partial shade borders, beside water features, and in large containers moved indoors in winter in colder zones. Listed as invasive in Hawaii, where it has naturalized aggressively in wet forest areas.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Kaleidoscope is compact (2–3 feet) and rarely requires pruning to maintain its tidy mounding habit — remove any all-green reversion shoots immediately to prevent them from overwhelming the variegated growth. The seasonal color change is most dramatic: spring growth emerges golden-yellow, summer foliage is green-and-yellow variegated, and fall coloring turns the leaves orange, red, and burgundy before winter. In zone 9 this multi-season color display makes Kaleidoscope one of the most ornamentally valuable dwarf landscape shrubs available.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Kaleidoscope tolerates a wide range of conditions and is drought-tolerant once established; Kaleidoscope is a multi-season variegated abelia cultivar that earned recognition through All-America Selections and other awards for its exceptional year-round ornamental value — a compact (2–3 feet) mounding shrub that changes color through the seasons from spring's golden-yellow new growth through summer's bright green-and-yellow variegation to fall's spectacular orange, red, and burgundy tones. Small, tubular, white to pale pink fragrant flowers appear continuously from spring through fall, adding a floral dimension to the primarily foliage-based ornamental value. Abelia is one of the most butterfly-attractive landscape shrubs available — the small, tubular, nectar-rich flowers are visited by virtually all butterfly species present in zone 9 from spring through fall, making Kaleidoscope an effective pollinator garden plant that is also ornamental enough for formal landscape use. The compact habit, multi-season interest, and tolerance of partial shade make Kaleidoscope one of the most versatile small shrubs for Gulf South landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Kaleidoscope develops its most vivid yellow-to-orange foliage color in full sun — in partial shade the leaf color is more yellow-green and less intense.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Kaleidoscope is the most celebrated and widely planted variegated abelia cultivar — named for its remarkable seasonal foliage color changes that shift through a wide range of colors through the growing season. The new spring growth emerges brilliant golden-yellow to chartreuse; through summer the leaves display yellow margins on green centers; in fall the foliage transitions to vivid orange, red, and burgundy-red — an essentially continuous foliage display that provides more sustained ornamental interest than almost any other compact landscape shrub. The small, white to pale-pink tubular flowers bloom prolifically from spring through frost, adding light fragrance and excellent butterfly and hummingbird value throughout the season. The arching, well-branched habit stays compact at 2.5–3.5 feet tall and wide with minimal pruning. Kaleidoscope won the award of the American Nursery & Landscape Association and has become one of the most popular landscape shrubs introduced in the early twenty-first century. Like all abelias, it is extremely tough — tolerating drought, clay soil, heat, humidity, and partial shade with minimal care. Essentially pest-free; deer-resistant. Prune lightly after spring bloom to shape; remove any all-green reverted shoots immediately to prevent them from overtaking the variegated growth.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil; this hybrid mayapple establishes and spreads more slowly than the native species, so be patient and avoid frequent disturbance.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil and be patient, since this hybrid mayapple establishes and spreads slowly compared to the native species. It is grown chiefly for its spectacular umbrella-shaped leaves, which emerge deep chocolate-mahogany with irregular jade-green mottling before shifting to a more solid bronze-green as the season progresses. Small nodding flowers appear beneath the foliage canopy in spring, but the plant is prized almost entirely for its foliage display in a shaded border or container. Mulch to keep roots cool and protect emerging shoots from late frost.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to sandy, well-drained to seasonally wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Kalm's St. John's wort is extremely adaptable to soil moisture extremes, native to the rocky and sandy shorelines of the Great Lakes.
directions: Plant in average to sandy soil, tolerant of both seasonally wet and fairly dry conditions, in full sun to partial shade; Kalm's St. John's wort is a compact, rounded native shrub from Great Lakes shorelines and rocky lakeshores, valued for bright, sunny-yellow flowers with a prominent burst of long stamens that bloom over a long stretch of summer, set against fine-textured, blue-green foliage. Older stems develop attractive exfoliating, peeling bark that adds interest through winter after the leaves drop. It is remarkably adaptable to difficult sites — tolerating both periodic flooding and dry, sandy soil, as well as wind and some salt exposure — which makes it a useful, low-maintenance choice for rain gardens, pond and shoreline edges, and other spots with unpredictable moisture. Deadheading is not required for continued bloom; a light shearing in early spring keeps the mounded shape tidy and encourages fresh flowering wood. Pollinators, particularly bees, visit the flowers heavily.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into sharply drained, humus-poor, acidic rocky or gravelly soil in a sheltered rock garden or trough.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into sharply drained, humus-poor, acidic rocky or gravelly soil in a sheltered rock garden or trough, echoing the serpentine outcrops of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains where this Oregon endemic is found nowhere else on Earth. In spring it bears small, bright rose-pink, rhododendron-like flowers over a dense mound of tiny evergreen leaves, making it a prized miniature for alpine and rock gardens. It demands cool nights, high humidity, and drainage that never stays soggy, so raised beds or scree plantings suit it far better than ordinary garden soil.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost after 3 months of cold stratification at 40°F; transplant to a shaded, moist, humus-rich location in spring. Division of established clumps in spring is the most reliable propagation method.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, deep, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Kamchatka bugbane is one of the most valuable late-season shade perennials, producing tall, elegant bottlebrush spikes of fragrant, white to pale pink flowers in September and October — a time when very few shade plants are in bloom. The attractive compound foliage emerges in spring and provides good texture through summer. Selections with dark purple-bronze foliage (such as 'Brunette', 'Hillside Black Beauty', and 'James Compton') are especially striking — the dark foliage glows in dappled shade and contrasts dramatically with nearby light-colored hostas and ferns. Performs best in cooler climates; in the warmth of zone 8, provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture. Formerly classified as Cimicifuga simplex.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting 2-3 inches deep with growing tip up; Kamchatka Trillium is an East Asian species (Japan, Korea, China, Russian Far East) bearing pure white, three-petaled flowers above a whorl of broad green leaves. Never dig from the wild.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2 to 3 inches deep with the growing tip pointed upward. Kamchatka Trillium is widely distributed across the cool moist forests of Japan, Korea, northeastern China, and the Russian Far East, geographically and taxonomically distinct from the familiar North American trillium species, bearing a broad, pure-white, three-petaled flower above a whorl of three deep-green leaves in early to mid spring, closely resembling and closely related to the beloved Trillium grandiflorum of eastern North America. Never dig plants from the wild, since trilliums take five to seven years to bloom from seed and wild populations are vulnerable to overcollection; purchase only nursery-propagated stock. It naturalizes slowly under deciduous trees alongside ferns and other spring woodland wildflowers.

plant_note: Plant small cuttings or divisions at any point in the growing season into very well-drained, dry, average to lean, neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Kamschatka stonecrop is one of the most widely used low sedum groundcovers in temperate gardens.
directions: Plant cuttings or divisions in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Kamschatka stonecrop forms a dense, slowly spreading mound of toothed, spoon-shaped, glossy green leaves that flush attractive orange-red tones in fall and cold weather. Flat clusters of bright golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers cover the mat in early to midsummer, drawing bees and other pollinators, and the variegated cultivar 'Variegatum,' with creamy white leaf margins tinged pink, is nearly as widely planted as the plain green species. It tolerates more shade and slightly more moisture than many other low sedums, making it a versatile choice for rock gardens, border edges, and green roof plantings across a wide range of climates. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if the center becomes bare or woody.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown plants in spring; kangaroo paw requires very well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil. High humidity and wet soil are the main threats — raise beds or plant on slopes in humid climates.
directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy, low-nutrient soil in full sun; kangaroo paw is a grass-like Australian native perennial producing the most unusual tubular flower clusters in horticulture — densely woolly, claw-shaped flower tubes in red, orange, yellow, pink, or bicolored combinations that are irresistible to hummingbirds and the floral emblem of Western Australia. The tall (2–5 foot) flower stems rise above the strap-shaped basal leaves in spring and summer. The major challenge in humid climates is ink disease (Alternaria), a fungal disease that turns leaves black — Anigozanthos flavidus is the most disease-resistant and robust species, making it the best choice for Gulf Coast gardens. Remove spent flower stems by cutting to the base after blooming.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Kanjiro blooms October–December in zone 9 — fall planting gets it established before its bloom season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Kanjiro is one of the most popular sasanqua camellia cultivars in Gulf Coast landscapes, producing abundant, medium-sized (2–2.5-inch), semi-double flowers in a distinctive deep rose-pink to carmine-rose color from October through December in zone 9 — a color that is richer and more vivid than the typical light-pink sasanquas. The flowers are produced in overwhelming quantity on vigorous, dense, upright-to-spreading plants that reach 5–8 feet in zone 9, covering the entire plant in color for 6–8 weeks. Kanjiro is also known by the synonym 'Hiryu' in older nursery trade literature. The semi-evergreen to evergreen foliage is dark, glossy, and fine-textured, making the plant attractive even out of bloom as a hedge, screen, or foundation plant. Like all sasanqua camellias, Kanjiro is more sun-tolerant than japonicas and produces the heaviest bloom in a position receiving 4–6 hours of sun. It is also somewhat drought-tolerant once established compared to camellia japonicas. The combination of cold hardiness, heat tolerance, and prodigious bloom production makes Kanjiro one of the most dependable fall-flowering shrubs for zone 9.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring.
directions: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with the pink eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, since peonies planted too deep may fail to flower. Choose a full-sun site with rich, well-drained soil and avoid crowding by nearby shrubs or trees. Kansas produces sturdy stems topped with intensely saturated, rounded double blooms in a clear cherry-red that holds its color well and resists fading in the sun. It is a vigorous, long-lived heirloom cultivar that has remained popular for cut-flower use since its introduction in the 1940s.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, moist to average soil in full sun; kapok is a major tropical tree requiring frost-free conditions and grows naturally in tropical forests of Central and South America, West Africa, and Southeast Asia.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, moist to average soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–12; kapok is one of the most recognized tropical trees in the world — the sacred World Tree (Ceiba) of Maya cosmology, the largest tree in Central American rainforests, and the source of kapok fiber (used historically to stuff life preservers, sleeping bags, and pillows before synthetic fills). The enormous, buttressed trunk with its distinctive large, pointed spines on the bark is unmistakable. The leafless tree produces masses of cream-to-white flowers for bat and moth pollination when the dry-season canopy is open. The seed pods split to release a mass of fine, silky kapok fibers that carry the seeds on the wind. The tree is the sacred national tree of Guatemala. In South Florida, a few mature specimens exist as landscape curiosities; it is better known as an indoor botanical garden and tropical greenhouse specimen.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Kardinal is a bright red mophead cultivar bred primarily for the cut-flower trade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Kardinal bears vivid, bright red mophead blooms, a color that resists shifting toward purple or blue even in acidic soil more strongly than many other red or pink hydrangea cultivars, making it a favorite for florists needing a dependable, true red. Its sturdy stems and long vase life suit it especially well for cutting. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent wilting.

common_name: Karl Foerster Feather Reed Grass (Upright Feather Reed Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Karl Foerster is unusual among ornamental grasses in tolerating partial shade as well as heavy clay soils — both qualities expand its planting options in typical residential landscapes.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Karl Foerster Feather Reed Grass was named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2001 and is the single most important ornamental grass in American landscape design — a sterile, non-invasive hybrid producing stiffly upright, narrow clumps of arching green foliage that in late spring through summer send up tall (4–5 feet), feathery, reddish-purple flower plumes that gradually dry to warm buff-gold and persist beautifully through winter. The four-season interest of Karl Foerster is exceptional: spring green vertical foliage, summer red-purple flower plumes, fall buff-gold dried plumes, and winter structural sculptural form — all without any invasive seeding or aggressive spreading. The narrow, upright, 2–3 foot wide clumps fit neatly into smaller garden spaces where spreading grasses would be impractical. Karl Foerster tolerates clay soil, periodic wetness, drought once established, and partial shade better than most ornamental grasses — qualities that make it remarkably adaptable across a wide range of residential landscape conditions. The sterile nature (no viable seed set) makes it entirely safe to plant near natural areas without invasive risk. Cut to 4–6 inches in late February before new growth emerges; it is otherwise essentially maintenance-free.

common_name: Karl Rosenfield Peony (Deep Red Double Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and set a peony ring in place early in spring before growth fills in. Introduced in 1908 and still one of the best-selling red peonies grown, Karl Rosenfield produces enormous, fully double, deep crimson-red flowers with a light, fresh fragrance on strong, well-branched stems that generally need less staking than other doubles of similar size. It is a vigorous, disease-resistant, long-blooming selection well suited to cutting, holding its color well as flowers age. Like other Paeonia lactiflora cultivars it needs sustained winter chill to flower well and is best in zones 3–8; cut foliage to the ground each fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Karley Rose Fountain Grass (Vivid Rose-Pink Ornamental Grass)
plant_note: Divide clumps or plant container-grown starts in spring in full sun and well-drained, average to lean soil; Karley Rose is a sterile hybrid selection, so it must be propagated by division rather than seed and does not seed around the garden.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, allowing room for the vigorous, mounding clump to fill in over its first two seasons. Karley Rose is the most widely planted selection of oriental fountain grass, prized for larger, more numerous, and more intensely rose-pink flower spikes than the species, held well above the fine-textured gray-green foliage from early summer into fall and glowing when backlit by low sun. It is more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many fountain grasses, performs reliably in the Gulf South, and, as a sterile hybrid, spreads only by clump expansion rather than self-seeding, making it a tidier choice than seed-grown fountain grasses for formal or mixed borders. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide every three to four years if the center begins to die out.

common_name: Karma Choc Dahlia (Chocolate-Burgundy Waterlily Cut-Flower Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep after soil has warmed following the last frost; stake at planting since stems can be lax under heavy bloom load.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep after soil has warmed following the last frost. This Karma-series cut-flower dahlia produces waterlily-form double blooms 4–6 inches across in a velvety chocolate-brown shading to deep burgundy at the petal edges, an effect that intensifies in cool fall weather. Foliage and stems are notably dark, nearly black, echoing the flower tone. Bred specifically for the commercial cut-flower trade, Karma Choc holds up exceptionally well in the vase and blooms prolifically from midsummer through frost; stake plants since stems can be lax under heavy bloom load.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Karwinski's giant sage grows into a very large, shrubby specimen in a single season and needs room to reach full size.
directions: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Karwinski's giant sage grows into a very large, shrubby specimen in a single season and needs room to reach full size. Large, velvety, gray-green leaves cover a fast-growing, shrubby Mexican sage that can reach ten feet or more in a single warm season, producing tall spikes of small, rose-pink to magenta flowers with fuzzy, felted calyxes in late fall, a display that arrives just as many other salvias are finishing for the year. Its dramatic, fast growth and late-season flowering make it a bold architectural addition to the back of a large border or a tropical-style planting, though it dies to the ground in all but the mildest winters and regrows from the root each spring in marginal zones. Provide plenty of space, water regularly through the growing season, and cut the frost-killed top growth back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Kate Bletilla (Variegated Cream-Margined Hardy Ground Orchid)
plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Kate bears cream-margined variegated foliage that adds ornamental value even before the plant flowers.
directions: Plant pseudobulbs or divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, mulching to protect the shallow pseudobulbs over winter in the colder parts of its hardiness range. Kate produces attractive, pleated, lance-shaped leaves edged in crisp cream-white variegation, giving the plant garden interest well before its orchid-like magenta-pink flowers open in late spring on slender stems held above the foliage. Unlike most terrestrial orchids, which are notoriously fussy, this species is remarkably easy and reliable in an ordinary garden border with consistent moisture, spreading gradually by offset pseudobulbs into a fuller clump over the years. Established plantings need little care beyond a yearly topdressing of compost and division every several years if clumps become overcrowded.

common_name: Katharina Zeimet Rose (White Baby Rambler Polyantha)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Katharina Zeimet, a 1901 polyantha nicknamed the White Baby Rambler, blooms nearly continuously on a compact, low-maintenance plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Katharina Zeimet, introduced in 1901 and nicknamed the White Baby Rambler, is a compact polyantha rose bearing large clusters of small, pure white, lightly fragrant flowers almost continuously from spring through frost. Its low, dense, well-behaved habit makes it a reliable choice for borders, edging, and mass plantings, needing far less spraying and maintenance than many modern roses to look good all season. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, and expect vigorous rebloom within a few weeks after each flush is spent.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; reticulata iris needs a dry summer dormancy and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil, performing best in a rock garden or raised bed. A hybrid between two dwarf iris species, this uniquely marked cultivar produces pale, luminous, ice-blue and pale yellow flowers netted with fine gray-blue veining, an intricate, almost translucent pattern quite unlike the solid deep blue of most other reticulata iris, opening low to the ground in very early spring. One of the most popular and widely photographed small bulb cultivars for its unusual, subtle color pattern, it naturalizes readily in favorable rock garden conditions once its exacting drainage requirements are met. Allow foliage to die back naturally before removing it, and avoid any summer moisture, which quickly rots the small bulbs during their required dry dormancy.

common_name: Katherine Phlox (Lavender-Blue with White Eye Garden Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space at least 18 inches apart for good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Katherine bears rounded flower heads in soft lavender-blue, each petal marked with a small white eye, a cool, gentle color that stands apart from the hot pinks and reds typical of most garden phlox, carrying the classic sweet fragrance of the species through a long midsummer-to-early-fall bloom season. It benefits from full sun, steady moisture, and generous spacing to reduce powdery mildew. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in any moist to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Katie is a compact, largely sterile dwarf selection of Mexican petunia bred to spread far less aggressively than the straight species, making it the recommended choice for residential borders and edging where the full-sized species can become a spreading nuisance.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 10-14 inches apart for a solid groundcover effect. Katie is a dwarf cultivar of Mexican petunia, staying under a foot tall compared to the species' 2-4 foot height, and is prized as the responsible choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want the plant's nonstop purple bloom and toughness without its tendency to spread aggressively by runners and self-sown seed — the straight species is considered invasive in natural areas across Florida and other Gulf states. Each funnel-shaped purple flower lasts only a single day, but the compact, well-branched clumps produce so many buds that bloom appears continuous from spring through frost. It is remarkably heat, drought, and salt tolerant once established, tolerating conditions that stress most other low-growing perennials, and works well as a dense edging plant, in mass plantings, or in containers. Shear back by about a third in mid-season if plants become leggy to refresh the display.

common_name: Katsura Pieris (Wine-Red New Growth Evergreen Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Katsura bears striking wine-red new growth that matures to green, along with red-tinted flower buds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and winter winds; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity. Katsura bears vivid wine-red new growth in spring that gradually matures to dark green, extending its colorful season well beyond the typical spring flush of most Pieris cultivars, and carries red-tinted flower buds through winter that open into cascading clusters of white to pale pink, urn-shaped blooms in late winter to early spring. Its long-lasting foliage color gives it multi-season interest beyond the flower display alone. Water during dry spells and prune lightly after flowering to shape.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in spring or fall; katsura requires consistent soil moisture especially during the first 2–3 years, and is prone to leaf scorch in hot, dry conditions. Afternoon shade is beneficial in inland climates with hot summers. In fall, the dropped leaves emit the famous caramel-cotton candy fragrance.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; katsura tree is one of the most beautiful ornamental trees for four-season interest, producing small, heart-shaped, scalloped-edged leaves that move through a sequence of striking colors — emerging in spring with bronze-red or purplish new growth, maturing to clean blue-green through summer, then turning in autumn to brilliant shades of yellow, apricot, and pink. As the leaves fall they emit an extraordinary fragrance universally described as caramel, cotton candy, or freshly baked sugar — one of the most enchanting scents in the autumn garden. The tree also develops attractive, finely furrowed, shaggy russet-brown bark on older specimens that is ornamental through winter. Native to mountain forests of Japan and China, it grows as a graceful, pyramidal tree that softens with age, often with multiple ascending trunks. A magnificent specimen for a moist, partly shaded position where its four-season sensory qualities can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Katy Road Pink Rose (Found Texas Polyantha)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Katy Road Pink is a Texas 'found rose,' rescued and named for the road it was discovered growing on, closely related to Caldwell Pink but slightly larger-flowered and equally tough.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Katy Road Pink is one of the classic Texas 'found roses' rescued by rose rustlers from an old homesite along the road that gives it its name, and like most found roses it is grown own-root, making it far more resilient to freeze dieback than grafted roses since any new growth from the base is still the same good rose. It produces clusters of small, semi-double, clear pink flowers in nearly continuous flushes from spring through fall, on a compact, dense, twiggy shrub that needs almost no spraying to stay healthy through the Gulf South's humid summers. Give it an occasional light shaping and a spring feeding; otherwise it thrives on neglect, making it an outstanding low-maintenance landscape or hedge rose.

common_name: Kauai Rose Wishbone Flower (Compact Early-Blooming Bicolor Torenia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kauai Rose is a compact, early-blooming, heat-tolerant wishbone flower bred for hand-painted bicolor rose-and-yellow blooms.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil consistently moist through the heat of summer. Kauai Rose is part of a compact, early-flowering wishbone flower series bred for uniform, hand-painted bicolor blooms combining rich rose-pink outer petals with a bright yellow throat, held on a tidy, mounding plant that begins flowering earlier in the season than older torenia strains. It thrives in the shaded conditions where many other flowering annuals struggle, blooming continuously from late spring through frost with excellent heat and humidity tolerance, making it a reliable Gulf South shade bedding and container annual. No deadheading is required to keep it flowering. Water regularly during dry spells, since consistent moisture keeps the display at its best.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Kay Parris performs well in partial shade but blooms most prolifically with 6+ hours of direct sun.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Kay Parris is a named Southern magnolia cultivar selected for its superior cold hardiness, narrow columnar form, and early and prolific bloom — a combination of attributes that makes it one of the finest magnolias for zone 6–10 residential landscapes. The naturally narrow, upright habit (20–30 feet tall with a relatively tight 10–15 foot spread) fits medium-sized residential landscapes better than the broadly spreading species without requiring the extremely compact size of Little Gem. Kay Parris begins blooming at young age, producing large (6–8 inch), intensely fragrant white flowers from May through September in zone 9. The cultivar was selected and named by nurseryman David Parris for his wife Kay. A notable characteristic is the exceptionally cold-hardy performance for a Southern magnolia — Kay Parris has been successfully grown into zone 6 with protection, significantly colder than most Southern magnolia selections. The leaves show the characteristic glossy dark-green upper surface and reddish-bronze to cinnamon undersurface. The narrow form suits planting near buildings, driveways, and in limited spaces where the standard Southern magnolia would eventually overwhelm the landscape.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Kazanlik is the classic damask rose grown commercially in Bulgaria's Rose Valley for rose oil (attar of roses) production.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Kazanlik is the historic damask rose grown at commercial scale in Bulgaria's famed Rose Valley for centuries to distill attar of roses, the concentrated rose oil at the heart of the perfume industry, bearing loosely double, soft pink blooms with an intensely rich, classic rose fragrance considered among the finest of any rose. Like most damask roses it blooms in a single strong flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably cold-hardy and disease-resistant, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; keeled garlic naturalizes freely from self-sown seed and bulbils produced in the flower heads — it can spread aggressively in favorable well-drained, open garden soils. Subsp. pulchellum (purple-flowered) is more commonly grown ornamentally than the pink-flowered type species. The flowers are attractive to bees and butterflies. Mild garlic scent when foliage is bruised.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; keeled garlic is a European mountain allium — native to the rocky, subalpine meadows and open woodlands of central and southern Europe from the Alps to the Balkans — that is grown ornamentally for its airy, late-summer flower display: loose, open umbels of nodding to spreading, small, pink to reddish-pink to purple (in subsp. pulchellum) bells on slender stems, the individual florets having a pendulous grace that differs from the tight, spherical pompom-type alliums. The flower heads often contain a mix of open flowers and small bulbils — a propagation strategy that makes keeled garlic a prolific self-spreader in open, well-drained garden soils. The bloom period (July–August in most of Europe) provides ornamental value in the midsummer to late-summer garden at a time when many other bulbs have finished. Subsp. pulchellum, with richer purple-pink flowers on taller, more elegant stems, is the form most widely grown ornamentally and is sometimes sold as a separate entity. Outstanding for naturalizing in gravel gardens, dry rock garden slopes, and sunny border fronts where its self-seeding habit creates naturalistic colonies over time.

common_name: Kees Nelis Tulip (Fire-Red Triumph Tulip Edged Golden Yellow)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Kees Nelis is a Triumph-class tulip with fire-red petals edged in golden yellow, blooming midseason.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Kees Nelis, a Triumph-class tulip, bears vivid fire-red petals crisply edged in golden yellow, a bold bicolor combination blooming in midseason on sturdy, medium-height stems typical of the versatile Triumph group, which bridges early singles and late Darwin hybrids in bloom timing. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or sow directly once soil warms; Kees' Orange is a Dutch-bred African marigold selection valued for its large, fully double, deeply ruffled blooms that hold up unusually well as a cut flower.
directions: Sow directly after frost danger passes or start indoors for a head start, barely covering the seed; Kees' Orange is a large-flowered African marigold selection producing fully double, ruffled, deep-orange pompon blooms on sturdy, well-branched plants that stay more compact than older tall African types like Crackerjack. Plant in full sun where its pungent foliage helps deter nematodes and many garden pests, making it a classic companion plant near tomatoes and vegetables as well as a strong performer in a cut-flower border — the sturdy stems and long vase life make it a favorite for market bouquets. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the plant flowering steadily through the heat of summer into fall.

common_name: Kelos Fire Red Celosia (Heat-Tolerant Plumed Celosia)
scientific_name: Celosia argentea var. plumosa 'Kelos Fire Red'
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Kelos Fire Red is a compact, uniform plumed celosia in the Kelos landscape series, bred for weather resistance and season-long color in bedding lines.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Kelos Fire Red is a compact, uniform, plumed (feathery) celosia bred as a weather-resistant landscape bedding plant, producing dense, upright, velvety deep-red flame-shaped plumes held well above tidy, even foliage from early summer through frost. It was bred specifically to tolerate the heat, humidity, and heavy summer rain that cause older plumed celosia strains to flop, discolor, or rot, making it a dependable performer for Gulf South summer beds and containers where many other bedding annuals struggle. Deadhead spent plumes to extend bloom, though the Kelos series is bred to keep flowering vigorously with minimal maintenance. Plants tolerate heat and some drought once established but bloom best with consistent moisture and a light monthly feeding.

common_name: Kelvin Floodlight Dahlia (Giant Golden-Yellow Dinnerplate Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Kelvin Floodlight is a classic giant dinnerplate dahlia producing enormous, clear golden-yellow blooms on tall, sturdy plants, one of the most widely grown large-flowered exhibition and garden dahlias. Stake plants early since the very heavy blooms require support.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately, since Kelvin Floodlight produces some of the largest blooms of any commonly grown dahlia. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. A longtime favorite in exhibition and garden circles, Kelvin Floodlight bears massive, clear golden-yellow, informal decorative blooms that can reach 10-12 inches across on strong, tall stems, giving it a genuinely dramatic presence in the summer and fall border. Its bright, pure yellow color holds up well through the season compared to some of the more subtly toned modern dahlia varieties, providing reliable, bold color from midsummer to frost with regular deadheading. Because the flowers are so large and heavy, disbudding side buds to focus energy into fewer, larger blooms is common practice for exhibition-quality flowers, though leaving buds intact still produces an impressive garden display. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

common_name: Kelway's Glorious Peony (Large Fragrant White Double Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Kelway's Glorious was introduced by the famed English Kelway's nursery in 1909.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Kelway's Glorious carries huge, rounded, pure white double flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance long considered among the finest of any peony, opening from blush-tinted buds to flowers that can reach 8 inches or more across on a vigorous, floriferous plant. It has remained a benchmark white peony among collectors and breeders for well over a century since its introduction by England's famed Kelway's nursery. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Direct sow or press small starter plants into crevices in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial shade; Kenilworth ivy readily self-sows once established, tucking its own seed pods into nearby cracks and crevices, so a single planting often spreads on its own without further help.
directions: Plant or sow into average to poor, well-drained soil in partial shade, tucking seed or small starts directly into the crevices of a shaded stone wall, retaining wall, or old masonry steps where it will look most at home; Kenilworth ivy is a delicate, trailing perennial with small, ivy-shaped leaves and tiny snapdragon-like lavender flowers with a yellow throat, blooming from spring through fall. After each flower fades, the seed stalk curves and grows away from the light, pushing the ripening seed pod deep into a dark crevice to germinate there — an adaptation that lets the plant colonize vertical stone and brickwork on its own over time. It is a classic self-seeding plant for softening the look of old shaded walls, steps, and rockeries, and tolerates poor, dry, alkaline soil that would stress most other groundcovers. It can naturalize enthusiastically in the right conditions, so it is best given a spot, like a stone wall, where its spread is welcome rather than a small formal bed.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial shade; kentia palm is the most tolerant of all palms of indoor low-light conditions and is the premier interior landscape palm. Outdoors it prefers shade or dappled light and moist, fertile, well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial to full shade; kentia palm is the world's most popular indoor palm and one of the most important ornamental plants in the global interior plant industry — exported from its tiny native range (Lord Howe Island, Australia) in the form of seeds and seedlings for over 150 years to supply interior landscape plantings worldwide. The graceful, arching, dark green pinnate fronds and the extremely high tolerance of low light, low humidity, and neglect make it the standard palm for hotel lobbies, office buildings, and living rooms. Outdoors in zones 9–11, kentia palm is an attractive garden palm for shaded or semi-shaded positions under larger trees, unusually shade-tolerant for a palm. The seed germination is notoriously slow and erratic (months to a year). One of the few palms genuinely adapted to deep shade — a valuable characteristic that distinguishes it from almost all other palms.

plant_note: Sow seed in early fall (45–65°F soil temperature) or early spring in well-prepared, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Kentucky bluegrass establishes slowly from seed (2–4 weeks to germinate, 6–8 weeks to usable turf) but forms a dense, self-repairing sod via underground rhizomes once established. It goes dormant and turns tan during drought or summer heat; resume growth in fall.
directions: Sow in fall or early spring in well-prepared, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade; Kentucky bluegrass is the premier cool-season lawn grass of the northern United States — the standard against which other turf grasses are measured for fine texture, dense sod, deep-green color, and ability to repair itself through underground rhizomes (stolons). It produces a rich, blue-green, fine-textured carpet that performs best in cool (55–75°F) temperatures of spring and fall, going summer-dormant in heat and drought only to green up vigorously in autumn. The key advantage over other cool-season grasses is its rhizomatous spread — unlike bunch-forming tall fescue or ryegrass, Kentucky bluegrass fills in bare spots and repairs foot-traffic damage through vegetative spread. Establishing a Kentucky bluegrass lawn is slower from seed than from sod, but the resulting turf is superior in long-term density and durability. It is commonly blended with perennial ryegrass (for fast establishment) and fine fescues (for shade tolerance) in premium lawn seed mixes.

plant_note: Scarify seeds by nicking the hard seed coat or soaking in hot water (not boiling) for 24 hours before planting. Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to slightly acidic, deep soil in full sun. Caution: seeds and pods are toxic if ingested raw; roasting destroys the toxic alkaloids.
directions: Kentucky Coffeetree is one of the most architecturally dramatic of the eastern native trees, native to the bottomlands, river terraces, and moist upland woods of the central and mid-south United States from New York and Nebraska south to Tennessee and Oklahoma, immediately recognizable in winter by its massive, stout, few-branched silhouette, deeply ridged gray bark, and enormous, persistent, dark brown seed pods up to 10 inches long that hang through winter — one of the most bold and graphic of all bare winter tree forms. The enormous, doubly-pinnate leaves (up to 3 feet long and 2 feet wide) unfurl very late in spring and drop early in fall, giving it one of the shortest leafy seasons of any native tree; in late spring it produces hanging clusters of fragrant white flowers attractive to long-tongued native bees. The hard seeds were roasted and used as a coffee substitute by early settlers and Native American tribes (raw seeds contain toxic alkaloids destroyed by roasting); the pods were fed to pigs and cattle historically. Extremely drought-tolerant, pollution-tolerant, and adaptable to urban conditions once established; an outstanding underused native street and shade tree.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall into consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Kentucky lady's slipper is the most heat- and humidity-tolerant native Cypripedium and the best-suited species for Gulf South and mid-South woodland gardens.
directions: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall into consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade, mimicking the rich floodplain and streamside hardwood forests of Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and the mid-South where it grows wild. It bears the largest flower of any native lady's slipper, with twisted, greenish-bronze lateral petals framing a huge, pale ivory-cream pouch veined in soft rose, opening in late spring and lasting for several weeks. Unlike the more cold-adapted northern Cypripedium species, Kentucky lady's slipper genuinely tolerates hot, humid Gulf Coast summers, making it the realistic choice for a shaded southern woodland garden rather than the classic pink lady's slipper of northern bogs. Never dig from the wild — populations are scattered and slow to recover — and expect several years of patient care with deep, consistently moist mulch before a nursery-grown division reaches full flowering size.

plant_note: Best planted in early spring in moist, well-drained woodland soil. Prefers sheltered spots near streams or in moist ravines that mimic its native rocky woodland habitat.
directions: Select a site in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil that mimics its native rocky streambank habitat. Plant container-grown specimens in early spring, backfilling with a mix of native soil and compost. Water deeply each week during the first two growing seasons to encourage a deep root system. White flower clusters emerge in late spring and give way to blue-black berries that are a valuable food source for migrating and resident birds throughout autumn.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants (named cultivars are preferred over seedlings for reliable flowering) in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Provide a very sturdy support structure — arbor, pergola, or strong trellis — capable of bearing the substantial weight of a mature plant.
directions: Kentucky Wisteria is the hardiest and most well-behaved of the native wisterias, native to the bottomland forests, streambanks, and moist woodland edges of the south-central United States from Illinois and Missouri south to Louisiana and Texas, producing in late spring (and often again in late summer) dense, fragrant, lavender-to-purple flower racemes 6–12 inches long that are visually spectacular on an arbor or pergola — and doing so while behaving far less aggressively than the invasive Japanese and Chinese wisterias that have escaped cultivation and naturalized throughout the southeastern United States. Named cultivars such as 'Blue Moon', 'Aunt Dee', and 'Thunderstruck' are reliable repeat-bloomers and are the preferred choice over seedlings, which may take years to bloom and produce inferior flowers. Unlike Asian wisterias, Kentucky Wisteria twines in a clockwise direction and is significantly less vigorous and easier to manage, though it still requires a strong support and annual pruning. Grow in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which promotes excessive foliage at the expense of flowers.

common_name: Kermesina Blue Flag Iris (Wine-Red Native Iris Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant divisions of the rhizome in heavy soil at the pond margin or in a submerged container so the crown sits at or just below the waterline, in full sun to light shade.
directions: Set rhizome divisions into heavy garden soil at the pond edge or in a submerged aquatic container so the crown rests at or just below the waterline, choosing a spot with full sun to light shade. This selection of the native blue flag iris produces richly saturated wine-red to magenta-purple flowers with yellow-and-white signal markings in late spring, held above upright, sword-shaped foliage. Like the wild species, it tolerates both shallow standing water and consistently moist soil, spreading gradually by rhizome without becoming aggressive. It offers a deeper, moodier color option than the typical blue-violet species for pond margins, rain gardens, and native plant bog plantings.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness; seeds need darkness to germinate.
directions: Sow the fine seed in darkness indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, since light inhibits germination. Also called painted tongue, this variety bears sprays of velvety, deep-blue, trumpet-shaped flowers from summer until frost.
