It stays under 18 inches and is suitable for small gardens, containers, woodland borders, and shaded corners where larger ferns would overwhelm the space. Native to rocky woodland slopes of Japan, Korea, and China, it is more tolerant of dry shade than most ferns once established. Excellent for the front of a shaded border alongside hostas, hellebores, and woodland wildflowers.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean spice viburnum blooms on old wood, so avoid pruning until after flowers fade in late spring.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean spice viburnum is arguably the most sweetly fragrant of all flowering shrubs — the dense, rounded heads of small pink buds opening to white flowers in early spring produce an extraordinary spicy-sweet perfume that fills the garden on warm spring days and can be detected from 50 feet away. The fragrance is strongest on still mornings and in the evening warmth. The rounded shrub is neat and symmetrical, reaching 4–5 feet tall and wide over many years, with dull dark-green leaves that turn wine-red to burgundy in fall where summers are not too hot. It performs best in zones 4–7 where winter cold is reliable — in zone 8 and warmer, it often fails to bloom well due to insufficient winter chilling hours and may decline over time. Site it where the fragrance can be fully appreciated: near the entrance, beside a path, or outside a frequently used window. Prune lightly if needed immediately after flowering to maintain shape.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean stewartia resents root disturbance — do not move after planting. Site in a protected location away from hot afternoon sun and drying winds. Mulch to maintain even soil moisture.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean stewartia is a four-season specimen tree widely regarded as one of the most beautiful of all small ornamental trees. In summer, it produces large, white, camellia-like flowers with showy orange stamens over several weeks. As summer transitions to fall, the foliage turns brilliant shades of orange, red, and purple. In winter and spring, the intricate, flaking bark — peeling in irregular patches to reveal a mosaic of gray, orange, tan, and cinnamon — provides some of the most dramatic winter interest of any tree. The tree is pyramidal in youth and gradually broadens with age. More heat-tolerant than Japanese stewartia and slightly more adaptable to zone 8 conditions. One of the finest specimen trees for the transitional South, performing best in partial afternoon shade in zones 7–8.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Korean waxbells is closely related to the more commonly grown Kirengeshoma palmata but has a more upright habit and larger, more outward-facing flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Korean waxbells is a refined woodland perennial with large, maple-like leaves on sturdy dark stems, topped in late summer and early fall with clusters of thick-textured, pale-yellow, shuttlecock-shaped flowers that hang slightly outward rather than nodding straight down, a subtle distinction from its better-known relative Kirengeshoma palmata that gives it a somewhat bolder floral presence. It blooms late in the season, when few other shade perennials are still flowering, extending color in the woodland garden into fall. It combines beautifully with ferns, hostas, and other moisture-loving shade perennials in a humus-rich bed that never dries out completely. Established clumps need little care beyond a spring topdressing of compost and consistent moisture through summer; cut old stems back in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant trained onto a moss pole or bark slab in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Korthals' shingle vine presses its juvenile leaves flat against a climbing support and needs that vertical surface to grow well.
directions: Grow as a houseplant trained onto a moss pole or bark slab in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Korthals' shingle vine presses its juvenile leaves flat against a climbing support and needs that vertical surface to grow well. In its juvenile climbing stage, small, glossy, overlapping leaves press tightly flat against tree bark or a moss pole in a dense, shingled pattern, a distinctive growth habit shared with a handful of other aroid vines and prized by collectors for the tidy, textured wall of foliage it creates. As the vine matures and reaches better light, its leaves grow progressively larger and eventually become perforated, similar in appearance to a small monstera, once it is well established and climbing vigorously. Provide a broad, moist support such as a sphagnum-covered pole for the aerial roots to grip, mist regularly to keep humidity high, and be patient, since the shift from small shingling leaves to larger mature foliage can take considerable time.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings under mist in early summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; Cornus kousa is significantly more resistant to dogwood anthracnose and borers than the native Cornus florida, making it the preferred choice for landscapes where these pests are a serious concern.
directions: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kousa dogwood is a Japanese, Korean, and Chinese small deciduous tree that blooms approximately three to four weeks later than the native flowering dogwood (Cornus florida) — producing its characteristic four-pointed, star-shaped, white or pink bracts in June rather than April — and is considered by many gardeners to be even more ornamental over the full year. The pointed, white (occasionally pink) bracts surround the small true flowers in the center and remain attractive for 4–6 weeks. In late summer and fall, large, bumpy, pink-red, strawberry-like composite fruit clusters ripen and are edible (sweet, slightly grainy, and pleasant-tasting, used to make jam in Japan). The fall foliage is outstanding — purplish-red to scarlet. On mature specimens the bark becomes attractively mottled and exfoliating. It is significantly more resistant to dogwood anthracnose disease and dogwood borer than C. florida — one of the primary reasons for preferring it in areas where these pests are problematic. 'Milky Way' (very heavy flower production), 'Satomi' (deep-rose-pink bracts), and 'Wolf Eyes' (white-variegated leaves) are outstanding cultivars.

common_name: Kramer's Beauty Camellia (Deep Red Peony-Form Camellia japonica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Kramer's Beauty is a sport of the fragrant Kramer's Supreme camellia, sharing its deep red color and rich scent on a peony-form flower.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Kramer's Beauty bears large, deep red, peony-form flowers and carries the same notable fragrance as its parent, Kramer's Supreme, an unusual trait since most camellias have little to no scent. The vigorous, upright evergreen shrub blooms in mid-season, providing dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its fragrant winter flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kramer's Supreme is unusually tolerant of cold — one of the most cold-hardy red camellia cultivars available, surviving temperatures to 10–15°F.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kramer's Supreme is one of the most significant Camellia japonica cultivars because it is reliably fragrant — a quality extremely rare in camellias, which are otherwise almost completely scentless. The large (4–5 inch), peony-form to informal double, vivid turkey-red flowers have a light but distinct, pleasant fragrance that is surprising in a camellia, making this cultivar uniquely valuable for gardens where fragrance is a priority. The flower color is an especially vivid, pure turkey-red without the blue-purple tones of Mathotiana — a clean, electric red that is among the most brilliant flower colors available for the winter garden. Kramer's Supreme blooms in midseason (November–February in zone 9), providing brilliant red winter color when few other shrubs are in bloom. Its exceptional cold hardiness (to zone 6, surviving temperatures to 10–15°F) makes it the most reliably winter-hardy red camellia cultivar, growing further north than most other japonica types. The upright to spreading habit grows 6–10 feet tall with regular pruning. In zone 9, Kramer's Supreme is an outstanding long-lived landscape shrub that requires only light pruning after bloom and supplemental iron (from acidic fertilizer) to prevent chlorosis in alkaline Gulf Coast soils.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Krimson Queen hoya colors most vividly in bright light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Krimson Queen hoya colors most vividly in bright light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound. Thick, waxy, oval leaves are edged in broad creamy-white margins that blush distinctly pink in bright light, especially on new growth, growing on vigorous, twining vines that eventually produce rounded clusters of small, star-shaped, fragrant pink flowers with a deep red center from the same reusable flowering spurs year after year. One of the most popular variegated hoya cultivars for its reliable, colorful foliage even when not in bloom, it climbs or trails readily and rewards a bright window with steady growth and repeat flowering. Provide a trellis or hanging basket for the twining stems, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flowering spurs, which continue to rebloom for years.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; single-flowered peonies like this one carry their blooms on notably sturdy stems and rarely need staking. Introduced in 1928, Krinkled White bears large, single, pure white flowers with crepe-paper-textured, ruffled petals surrounding a prominent boss of bright golden stamens, giving it a simpler, more naturalistic look than the double cultivars. Bees and other pollinators favor single peonies like this one for the open, accessible center, and the flowers are excellent, long-lasting cut blooms despite their delicate appearance. It blooms in midseason and is one of the most award-winning white single peonies in cultivation, valued for its garden-worthy habit as much as its flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kris Plant is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kris Plant is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Deeply cut, arrow-shaped leaves with pronounced wavy, serrated edges are glossy dark green with bold silvery-white veins and a metallic sheen, the jagged leaf margin giving the plant its common name after the wavy-bladed Southeast Asian kris dagger. Native to the Philippines and considered vulnerable in the wild due to habitat loss, it is a striking specimen for a shaded, humid patio or bright bathroom, its deeply lobed leaf shape distinguishing it at a glance from the broader, more solid-edged leaves of other commonly grown alocasias. Provide high humidity, protect from direct hot sun which scorches the leaves, and expect the plant to go dormant and lose its leaves if temperatures drop much below 55°F, resprouting from the rhizome once warmth returns.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Krossa Regal develops a distinctive upright vase-shaped form rather than the mounded habit of most hostas, creating an architectural accent in the shade garden.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Krossa Regal is among the most structurally distinct hostas — rather than forming the typical low mound, it produces large, strongly upright, arching, glaucous blue-gray leaves that create a dramatic vase-shaped form 28–36 inches tall and up to 5 feet wide at maturity. This architectural habit makes it an outstanding focal point in shaded borders, particularly when contrasted with the mounding form of surrounding plants. The tall flower scapes — often reaching 4–5 feet — produce pale lavender flowers that are among the most ornamental of any hosta. The thick, waxy, blue-gray leaf surface is notably resistant to slug damage. It is slow to establish but very long-lived, forming impressive, multi-crowned clumps over many years. Provide consistent moisture and mulch heavily; the upright leaves funnel rainwater to the crown, helping maintain soil moisture during dry spells.

common_name: Kudos Coral Agastache (Compact Coral-Pink Hummingbird Mint)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Kudos Coral is part of a compact, heavy-flowering agastache series bred for garden performance and improved winter survival compared to older hummingbird mint selections.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage is the single most important factor for overwintering success, since agastache crowns are prone to rot in wet, heavy soils. Kudos Coral forms a dense, compact mound topped with tightly packed spikes of coral-pink flowers over aromatic, anise-scented foliage from early summer well into fall. The long, continuous bloom season and rich nectar make it a strong draw for bumble bees, honey bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies, and the compact habit keeps it tidy and self-supporting without staking. Leaving the seed heads standing through winter provides additional interest and food for finches.

common_name: Kudos Mandarin Agastache (Compact Orange Hummingbird Mint)
plant_note: Transplant out after the danger of frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Kudos Mandarin is a compact, heavy-blooming hummingbird mint bred by Terra Nova Nurseries for a tidy, floriferous habit.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential, since this hummingbird mint is far more prone to winter rot in heavy, wet soil than to any problem from summer drought. Kudos Mandarin forms a compact, densely branched mound of aromatic foliage covered from early summer to frost in tightly packed spikes of warm orange flowers, blooming from the base of the plant to the tip rather than thinning out partway up the spike as many older agastache cultivars do, and it draws hummingbirds and bees in steady numbers all season. Its tidy, well-branched habit needs no staking and holds up well through summer storms. Cut back old flowering stems in late winter just before new growth resumes, and avoid winter mulch piled against the crown, which encourages rot.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; kuma bamboo spreads by underground rhizomes and can colonize large areas over time — use as a vigorous groundcover or install a rhizome barrier to define boundaries.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to consistently moist soil in shade to partial shade; kuma bamboo is a low-growing Japanese dwarf bamboo celebrated for its dramatic winter foliage effect — the leaf margins die back in cold weather to create a striking natural cream or parchment-colored border around each dark green blade, giving the plant an appearance of variegation through winter and early spring. This leaf withering is a natural adaptation, not a sign of damage, and the distinctive marginal color disappears when fresh green growth emerges in summer. Growing only 2–4 feet tall, it forms a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover ideal for shaded areas under trees, Japanese-style gardens, and naturalistic woodland settings in zones 6–9. Like other Sasa species, it spreads moderately by rhizomes and should be managed to prevent it from overrunning smaller companion plants.

common_name: Kumasaka Camellia (Cold-Hardy Rose-Pink Japanese Heirloom Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kumasaka is an old Japanese Camellia japonica cultivar noted for exceptional cold hardiness among japonica cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Kumasaka is a historic Japanese Camellia japonica cultivar producing rose-pink, rose-form double flowers with neatly overlapping petals, valued not only for its classic, elegant bloom form but for cold hardiness above average for the species, which has helped it remain in cultivation across a broader hardiness range than many other japonica cultivars. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in midseason and provides dense, glossy year-round structure. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

subcategory: Australian native drought-resistant ornamental shade tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained to dry, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline to neutral soil in zone 8–11; Kurrajong is a beautiful, long-lived, drought-hardy Australian native tree from the dry slopes, woodlands, and grasslands of New South Wales and Victoria — bearing attractive, cream-white, bell-shaped flowers with red and purple interior spotting in summer, variable, lobed or unlobed lustrous leaves, and boat-shaped woody seed pods with edible seeds — an outstanding shade tree for hot, dry garden conditions.
directions: Plant Brachychiton populneus in full sun in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, deep soil (it develops a strong taproot); it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and adapts to alkaline, heavy clay soils that challenge most trees; avoid overwatering, especially in youth. Kurrajong is a superlative drought-tolerant ornamental tree for hot, dry climates — native to the slopes, foothills, and grasslands of inland southeastern Australia where it is drought and heat adapted. The leaves are remarkably variable on the same tree: some deeply multi-lobed, others simple and oval, giving the tree a naturally textured, organic appearance. The cream to white, cup-shaped flowers with red and purple interior spotting are produced in summer in clusters and are attractive up close. The woody seed pods (follicles) split to reveal yellow, edible seeds surrounded by irritating hairs — the seeds are roasted to remove the hairs and then eaten or ground into flour; Aboriginal Australians roasted the seeds as a significant food and ground the inner bark fiber for fiber and string. The fat-storing capacity of the young roots was also exploited as a water source in dry conditions. A valuable shade tree for Texas, the Gulf Coast, and dry-summer climates where it withstands drought, alkaline soils, and heat that defeat most ornamental trees. Moderately frost-hardy to about 18–20°F.

plant_note: Plant divisions (fans) in spring or fall in full sun to partial shade in almost any well-drained soil; Kwanso is the classic double-flowered sport of the orange ditch daylily and, like the species, spreads by stolons and is completely sterile, so it survives and spreads only by hand division and pass-along sharing.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in almost any well-drained soil; Kwanso is a centuries-old double-flowered sport of the orange ditch daylily, producing ruffled, tawny-orange blooms with extra petals crowded into the center of each flower instead of the species' simple six-petaled form. Like its parent, each flower lasts only a single day but the clump produces a long, heavy succession of bloom over three to four weeks in early summer, and the plant is triploid and essentially sterile, spreading only vegetatively by stolons and thick, fleshy roots. It shares the species' legendary toughness, shrugging off clay, drought, heat, and root competition from nearby trees, and has been passed along between Southern gardeners for generations as an easy, reliable heirloom. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigorous bloom and to share starts with other gardeners, exactly as it has spread for centuries.

common_name: Kwanzan Flowering Cherry (Double Pink Ornamental Cherry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Kwanzan is the most widely planted flowering cherry cultivar, blooming a week or two later than Yoshino cherry with an even showier, fully double flower.
directions: Kwanzan is the classic double-flowered ornamental cherry, its dense clusters of vivid rosy-pink, fully double, pompom-like blooms covering the bare branches in mid-spring before the bronze-tinted new leaves emerge, producing one of the showiest flowering tree displays available in a temperate garden. Unlike Yoshino cherry, Kwanzan sets essentially no fruit, avoiding fruit litter, and its vase-shaped, upright-spreading habit and reddish-bronze fall color add further seasonal interest beyond the spring bloom. Give it moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to minimize disease entry through large wounds, and expect a relatively short lifespan of 15-20 years typical of ornamental cherries, which are prone to canker and borer problems as they age.

common_name: Kyoto Dwarf Mondo Grass (Miniature Super-Dwarf Mondo Grass)
plant_note: Plant small divisions or plugs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kyoto Dwarf grows extremely slowly, so set plugs closer together than standard mondo grass if a solid carpet is wanted within a few seasons.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping the planting consistently watered while the tiny tufts knit together into a mat. Kyoto Dwarf is the smallest form of mondo grass in general cultivation, forming dense tufts of thread-fine, dark green, grass-like foliage that rarely exceeds 2 inches tall, far shorter than standard mondo grass, and it spreads by short rhizomes at a notably slow pace. Its diminutive scale makes it a favorite for filling the joints between stepping stones and pavers, edging small shade beds, and miniature or Japanese-style gardens where a finer, lower texture than standard mondo or liriope is wanted. It is evergreen, deer resistant, and tolerant of light foot traffic once established, but division and fresh planting are the only practical way to fill an area quickly, since growth from seed is impractically slow for most gardeners.

common_name: Kyushu Hydrangea (Upright Glossy-Leaved White Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Kyushu bears glossy foliage and an upright habit distinct from many looser panicle hydrangea cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Kyushu bears creamy white, conical flower panicles with a light fragrance on an upright, vigorous shrub with notably glossy, dark green foliage, a tidier and more polished look than many looser-habited panicle hydrangea cultivars. Its strong upright growth also makes it adaptable for training as a small standard tree form. Prune in late winter to shape and control size, cutting back last year's growth by about a third to encourage strong new flowering stems.

plant_note: Plant nursery shrubs in fall or early spring in a sheltered, partly shaded spot.
directions: This evergreen camellia shrub is best planted from a nursery specimen in fall or early spring in a location with morning sun and afternoon shade, sheltered from harsh wind. It thrives in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, so mulch the shallow roots and avoid planting too deeply. From winter into spring it bears playful blooms of white or soft pink streaked with red, with no two flowers alike. Water regularly during dry spells and prune lightly just after flowering to shape the plant.

common_name: La Bourboule Dianthus (Compact Alpine Pink with Toothed Petals)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; La Bourboule is a compact, mat-forming alpine pink with small single, bright rose-pink, toothed-petal flowers.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. La Bourboule forms a dense, tight, mat-forming cushion of fine blue-green foliage rarely more than a few inches tall, topped in spring with abundant small, single, bright rose-pink flowers with delicately toothed petal edges, an alpine-scale garden pink well suited to rock gardens, troughs, and tight crevices between paving stones. Its low, spreading habit makes it one of the most useful dianthus selections for a small-scale rock garden setting. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown container specimens in fall into consistently moist, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade, replicating the sphagnum bogs and boreal peatlands where this evergreen shrub naturally grows.
directions: Plant nursery-grown container specimens in fall into consistently moist, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade, replicating the sphagnum bogs and boreal peatlands of the Great Lakes region and points north where this evergreen ericaceous shrub naturally grows. Clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are visited by bees and flies, while the dense, leathery, rust-fuzzed foliage provides year-round cover for birds along bog and wetland edges. Leaves are aromatic and were historically brewed as tea, though they contain compounds that are toxic to livestock if browsed in quantity, so this is a plant for wildlife habitat and ornamental bog gardens rather than for foraging. Best suited to a dedicated acidic bog garden alongside pitcher plants, sundews, and cranberry rather than average garden soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Labrador violet is an outstanding self-seeding groundcover for shaded areas, particularly valued for its purple-flushed foliage that adds color contrast to green shade plantings.
directions: Plant in spring or fall in moist, humus-enriched soil in partial to full shade; Labrador violet self-seeds freely once established and naturalizes into a charming, informal ground cover under trees and in shaded woodland gardens. Viola labradorica is a native North American violet of cool woodland, alpine, and subarctic habitats, distinguished from other violets by its distinctively purple-flushed to dark violet foliage — particularly striking in light shade where the leaves often take on a nearly burgundy coloration that contrasts beautifully with the tiny, lavender-purple flowers produced from early spring through summer. It is much smaller than most violet species, forming low mats only 3–6 inches tall that spread by self-seeding and gradually colonize an area; the heart-shaped leaves with their characteristic purple flush make it instantly recognizable among other shade groundcovers. An excellent, low-maintenance companion to hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Labuffarosea rain lily naturalizes readily in Gulf South gardens and flowers in flushes after rainfall through the warm season.
directions: Plant bulbs in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Labuffarosea rain lily naturalizes readily in Gulf South gardens and flowers in flushes after rainfall through the warm season. A historic Texas hybrid between Zephyranthes bifida and Z. grandiflora, it produces grassy foliage and funnel-shaped, soft rose-pink flowers that emerge reliably within days of a good rain from late spring through fall, giving the classic rain lily bloom trigger its common name. Long grown as a heirloom pass-along plant across the Gulf South, it multiplies steadily by bulb offsets into dense, long-lived clumps that need dividing only when flowering begins to decline from overcrowding. Plant it along a border edge or in a lawn-adjacent bed where its surprise flushes of bloom after summer thunderstorms can be enjoyed, and leave clumps undisturbed for years for the best display.

plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Labyrinth is a large formal decorative dahlia producing warm blush-to-orange blooms that shift in tone across the flower, a popular cut-flower variety alongside Café au Lait among floral designers. Stake plants early since the heavy blooms on tall stems require support.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage branching and more blooms per plant. Labyrinth is a large formal decorative dahlia bearing full, densely petaled blooms that open a soft peachy-blush at the center and deepen toward warm orange-apricot tones at the outer petals, a complex, layered coloring that has made it a favorite alongside Café au Lait among wedding and cut-flower growers seeking warm, muted tones. Blooms run 6-8 inches across on strong stems well suited to cutting, and the plant produces continuously from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading and harvesting. In zone 9, peak summer heat can dull flower color and reduce bloom size somewhat, with the best color and largest blooms typically appearing in the cooler weather of early summer and fall. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

common_name: Lace Aloe (Guinea Fowl Aloe, Aristaloe aristata)
plant_note: Divide and replant offset rosettes in spring into gritty, well-drained soil, setting the base at the same depth it grew previously.
directions: Grow in containers or rock gardens with sharply drained soil and light afternoon shade in hot climates, watering only when the soil has dried out completely. It tolerates brief light frosts better than many aloes, making it useful in border zones between hardy and tender succulent plantings. The stemless rosette of dark green, white-spotted leaves edged in soft translucent teeth resembles a small starfish and slowly offsets into a dense clump. Coral-orange tubular flowers appear on slender stalks above the foliage in spring.

common_name: Lace Hedgehog Cactus (Lace Cactus, Comb Hedgehog Cactus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or plant rooted offsets/transplants in spring into sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than soil fertility.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; this low-growing, clump-forming cactus native to the limestone hills and prairies of Texas, Oklahoma, and northern Mexico is covered in densely interlacing, comb-like (pectinate) white to pinkish spines that lie flat against the stem in an intricate lattice pattern, giving rise to the common name. In mid-to-late spring, mature clumps produce a flush of large, satiny, magenta-pink flowers with a pale throat that can nearly obscure the plant, followed by small, spiny, edible red fruit. Among the most cold-hardy of the hedgehog cacti, it tolerates winter lows well below zero Fahrenheit provided the soil stays dry, and rot from wet, poorly drained soil is the single greatest threat to the species in cultivation. It is an excellent choice for rock gardens, gravel beds, and crevice plantings across the southern Great Plains and Texas Hill Country.

plant_note: Propagate by rooting the plantlets that form on trailing stolons, or by division of an established mat; pot into shallow, wide containers or hanging baskets. Best started in spring or summer. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.
directions: Unlike its bolder, colorful-leaved cousin Episcia cupreata, this species is grown for its abundant small white flowers with deeply fringed, lace-like edges, set against small, plain green, quilted leaves on wiry trailing stolons. Grow in bright, indirect to shaded light — an east window or a spot a few feet from a south window — since direct sun stresses the thin foliage. Pot in a light, peaty, well-drained mix and keep evenly moist without letting the pot sit in water; consistently high humidity encourages the heaviest, most continuous bloom. Excellent in a hanging basket or as a groundcover in a large terrarium, where the trailing stems root into the mix as they spread and can be divided freely to share or restart plants.

plant_note: Plant small container-grown trees in fall or early spring in well-drained, alkaline, rocky or limestone soil in full sun; Lacey oak, a Texas Superstar tree, is slow-growing and best planted young, since it establishes more reliably as a smaller container tree than as a large balled-and-burlapped specimen.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline, rocky or limestone-derived soil in full sun; Lacey oak is a Texas Superstar-designated Hill Country native, valued for smoky blue-green summer foliage that emerges with an attractive soft pink flush in spring, along with excellent resistance to oak wilt, the vascular disease that has devastated live oaks and red oaks across parts of Texas. It grows slowly into a graceful, moderately sized shade tree well suited to the alkaline, rocky, drought-prone soils of the Texas Hill Country and similar limestone-based Gulf South sites where many other shade trees struggle. Its slow, controlled growth rate also means a naturally strong branch structure that needs relatively little corrective pruning compared to fast-growing trees. Once established, it is highly drought tolerant and needs no supplemental irrigation in most climates within its range. Give it plenty of room and full sun to develop its best form.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring into dry, lean, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; lacy tansyaster is a tough Great Plains and Southwest native that flowers best with minimal water and no supplemental fertility.
directions: Direct sow into dry, lean, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; lacy tansyaster is a short-lived native perennial of dry prairies, rocky slopes, and roadsides from the Great Plains west into the desert Southwest, producing finely divided, spiny-toothed foliage and abundant bright yellow, daisy-like flowers over a long summer-into-fall bloom season. It is exceptionally drought- and heat-tolerant once established, thriving in the same lean, sun-baked, rocky conditions that stress most garden perennials, and rich, moist soil or regular fertilizer tends to shorten its life and reduce flowering. A dependable, low-maintenance filler for a xeriscape, gravel garden, or dry native wildflower border, it self-seeds modestly in favorable open, sunny sites to maintain a sustained population.

common_name: Lady Banks Rose (Thornless Climbing Heirloom Rose)
plant_note: Plant container roses in spring against a strong, large support such as an arbor, pergola, or fence, since Lady Banks eventually becomes an enormous, vigorous climber; it is thornless and blooms only once in spring but very heavily.
directions: Plant against a substantial support in well-drained soil in full sun. A Southern heirloom favorite introduced from China in the early 1800s, Lady Banks Rose is a nearly thornless, extremely vigorous climber that can eventually cover an entire arbor, porch, or old tree with a spectacular single spring flush of small, rosette-shaped flowers, typically pale yellow or white depending on the form grown, often accompanied by a light violet fragrance. Unlike repeat-blooming modern roses, it flowers only once a year but with such abundance that a mature plant can be smothered in thousands of blooms for several weeks. It is remarkably drought-tolerant and pest-free once established, needs only occasional pruning right after bloom to control its size, and is a classic sight on old homes throughout the Gulf South.

common_name: Lady Clare Camellia (Large Semi-Double Rose-Pink Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Lady Clare, also known as Akashigata in Japan, is a classic large semi-double camellia with deep rose-pink flowers and prominent golden stamens, a long-favored Southern garden cultivar.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Lady Clare, known in its native Japan as Akashigata, is a classic large semi-double camellia bearing loosely arranged, deep rose-pink petals surrounding a prominent, showy cluster of golden-yellow stamens, a looser and more informal look than fully double camellia forms. Its vigorous, spreading, somewhat weeping growth habit and large flower size have made it a long-standing favorite for Southern gardens and historic camellia collections, often trained as a specimen or espalier to show off its graceful branching. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it flowers in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9, when little else is in bloom. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

common_name: Lady Emma Hamilton Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Lady Emma Hamilton's dark reddish-purple new foliage is part of its ornamental appeal and contrasts strikingly with the vivid flower color.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2005, Lady Emma Hamilton produces vivid orange-red buds opening to peachy-orange, cupped blooms that darken toward the petal edges, carrying a strong, fruity, tea-like fragrance, on a compact, well-branched shrub whose new growth emerges an unusual deep reddish-purple before maturing to green. The combination of saturated warm flower color and dark young foliage gives it strong two-tone appeal, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Lady Hillingdon Rose (Apricot-Yellow Tea Rose with Plum-Colored New Growth)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Lady Hillingdon, introduced in 1910, bears apricot-yellow tea rose blooms with distinctive plum-colored young stems and foliage, also known through a popular climbing sport.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3 to 3.5 feet apart. Lady Hillingdon, introduced in England in 1910, bears elegant, loosely double, apricot-yellow blooms with a rich tea fragrance, distinguished from other tea roses by its striking plum-purple young stems and new foliage that provide ornamental interest even between flushes. Like other tea roses it flowers almost continuously from spring to frost and shows good resistance to blackspot in the humid Gulf South compared with modern hybrid teas; a vigorous climbing sport of the same cultivar is also widely grown where more height is wanted. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter.

common_name: Lady Jane Species Tulip (Slender Pink-and-White Clusiana Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; as a species tulip, Lady Jane is more likely than hybrid tulips to naturalize and return for several years in warm-winter gardens.
directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; species tulips generally tolerate drier, leaner conditions than large hybrid tulips. Lady Jane produces slender, elegant, candy-striped flowers with rose-pink exteriors that open in full sun to reveal a pure white interior, closing again each evening in a graceful daily rhythm typical of species tulips. Its smaller stature and naturalizing tendency make it a good choice for rock gardens, gravel beds, or the front of a border, and it is considerably more likely to return and multiply for several years in mild-winter Southern gardens than the large-flowered hybrid types. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom to support next year's flowering.

common_name: Lady Margaret Passionflower (Red Hybrid Passion Vine)
plant_note: Plant out after the last frost in a warm, sheltered spot with a trellis or wire support, in rich, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist.
directions: Give this fast-growing hybrid a wire trellis, obelisk, or fence in a warm, sheltered spot, and keep the soil evenly moist but well drained. It bears an abundance of small, richly colored deep red-and-pink flowers with a dark maroon-purple center almost continuously from late spring until frost, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds to the garden. In frost-free climates it stays semi-evergreen and can be left to cover a large structure, while in cooler areas it is best grown in a container and brought indoors or treated as a fast annual climber. Cut back hard in late winter where it is hardy to keep new growth vigorous and floriferous.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; lady palm is one of the most shade-tolerant palms available — thriving in conditions that would stress most palms, including deep shade, indoor light levels, and enclosed patios. In zone 9 it is an outstanding landscape palm for shaded positions where other palms fail. Slow-growing but very long-lived; old clumps become multi-stemmed specimens of considerable grace. Widely used as an interior plant in subtropical and tropical regions.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; lady palm is one of the most shade-tolerant and most elegantly refined of all the palms — a multi-stemmed, clumping, fan-leafed palm of Chinese origin (native to southern China, probably Guangdong province) that has been cultivated in Japan for centuries as an esteemed garden and indoor specimen, with numerous named cultivars developed over generations of Japanese horticulture. The palm grows as a dense clump of multiple, slender, bamboo-like stems 1–1.5 inches in diameter, each covered in the distinctive dark-brown, woven-fiber leaf-base sheathing, the whole clump increasing in number of stems over the years to form a graceful, multi-stemmed mass of considerable elegance. The fan-shaped leaves are deeply divided into 5–8 broad, blunt-tipped, ridged segments of a rich, deep glossy green, arranged in a spreading, circular pattern at the tips of the slender stems. The overall effect of a mature clump — multiple slender fiber-covered stems of different heights, each topped with a circular fan of broad, deep-green leaf segments — is one of the most graceful and refined of any palm. The exceptional shade tolerance — growing well in conditions equivalent to bright indirect indoor light — makes it uniquely valuable as a landscape palm for shaded positions where most palms fail: under tree canopy, on north-facing walls, in covered outdoor rooms and patios, and in spaces where strong shade prevents the use of most ornamental plants. Slow-growing but very long-lived; established clumps in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens persist for decades.

common_name: Lady Rothschild's Orchid (Rothschild's Bulbophyllum, Red Fan Bulbophyllum)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork or in a slatted basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to partial direct morning light; Bulbophyllum rothschildianum is one of the most spectacular of the large Bulbophyllum species, producing pendant, fan-shaped inflorescences 10–14 inches wide bearing 8–12 large flowers arranged in a semicircle — the flowers red-and-white striped with long, thread-like sepal appendages and a small, motile lip. Prefers intermediate to warm temperatures (days 70–85°F, nights 60–70°F). Keep consistently moist. The flowers have an unpleasant odor for a few days but are extraordinarily ornamental. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow mounted on cork or in a slatted basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun — Lady Rothschild's Orchid is one of the most spectacular and sought-after of the large-flowered Bulbophyllum species and rewards careful culture with extraordinary inflorescences that rank among the most unusual flower forms in the orchid family. Bulbophyllum rothschildianum is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to India (specifically the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya) and Myanmar, one of the largest-flowered species in the enormous genus Bulbophyllum (which contains approximately 2,000 species, making it one of the largest plant genera in the world). The plant produces oval pseudobulbs spaced along a creeping rhizome, each carrying a single, large, leathery, dark-green leaf. From the rhizome, pendant flower spikes emerge bearing a remarkable inflorescence: a broad, fan-shaped or semicircular arrangement of 8–12 large flowers (2–3 inches each) arranged in a precise, symmetrical arc like a peacock's tail display. Each flower has large, broadly oblong dorsal and lateral sepals in cream-white to pale yellow with vivid red to maroon striping and veining, and extraordinarily long, thread-like extensions (up to 6 inches) from the sepal tips that wave in air movement. The small lip is dark, shiny, and highly motile — moving in the slightest air current to deceive fly pollinators. The flowers produce a smell for a few days that attracts these pollinators but dissipates quickly. One of the crown jewels of Bulbophyllum culture. Named in honor of Lady de Rothschild. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant in fall; perennializes well in warm dry climates.
directions: Plant lady tulip bulbs in fall about five inches deep in sharply drained soil and full sun. Unlike hybrid tulips, this dainty species perennializes reliably and naturalizes in warm, dry climates. The slender flowers are white or yellow with a bold red or pink exterior stripe and open flat in sun. Keep the site dry during summer dormancy to encourage the bulbs to return and multiply for years.

common_name: Lady Vansittart Camellia (Variegated White-and-Pink Striped Camellia japonica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Lady Vansittart is a long-cultivated antique Camellia japonica notable for the striking, unpredictable white-and-pink striping of its blooms.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Lady Vansittart is a historic Camellia japonica cultivar dating to the 1800s, prized for its semi-double flowers striped and marbled in white and rose-pink in an irregular, ever-varying pattern from bloom to bloom, occasionally producing solid pink or solid white flowers on the same plant, a trait long fascinating to camellia collectors. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in mid-season and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its striking winter and early spring flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Lady in Pink Fern (Rose-Pink-Stemmed Lady Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Lady in Pink carries rose-pink stems and midribs, a softer color companion to the red-stemmed Lady in Red.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and keep the soil from drying out, since lady fern wilts quickly in dry conditions and does not recover well from prolonged drought stress. Lady in Pink bears finely divided, lacy, light green fronds rising from distinctive rose-pink stems (stipes) and midribs (rachises), a softer, warmer color companion to the more common red-stemmed Lady in Red selection, and the pink coloring is most vivid on new spring growth. Its fine texture and colorful stems make it a good contrast plant among broader-leaved hostas and heucheras in a shaded border or woodland garden. Cut back tattered fronds in late winter before new growth emerges in spring, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Lady in Red Fern (Red-Stemmed Lady Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Lady in Red is more tolerant of summer heat and drier conditions than Japanese painted fern, making it somewhat more reliable in zone 9 — though consistent moisture remains important.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Lady in Red is an exceptional and distinctive lady fern selection with bright cherry-red to deep wine-red stems (stipes) that contrast dramatically with the lacy, light-green fronds — one of the most striking color effects in shade-garden ferns. The vivid red-to-burgundy stem color persists from spring emergence through fall, providing a seasonal color effect unmatched by most other ferns. The fronds are finely divided and lacy, with the characteristic lady fern form — lighter and more delicate in texture than southern shield fern or wood fern, creating a soft, airy quality in the shade garden. Lady in Red grows larger and more vigorously than Japanese painted fern (18–30 inches vs. 12–18 inches) and is somewhat more heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant, making it more reliable in zone 9. Like most lady ferns, it is deciduous in zone 9 — dying back in late fall and re-emerging in spring — but the spring growth is vigorous. Outstanding for moist shade situations such as stream banks, bog gardens, and the deep shade of large trees. Pair with hostas, toad lilies, and Solomon's seal for layered shade-garden compositions.

common_name: Lady in Red Salvia (Red Texas Sage, Scarlet Salvia coccinea)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 6 weeks early; in zone 9, Lady in Red often self-seeds so prolifically that it naturalizes as a perennial colony — once established, allow the self-seeded seedlings to fill in around the original planting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Lady in Red is a compact, All-America Selections winning selection of Salvia coccinea — the native Texas sage or scarlet salvia — producing vivid, true scarlet-red tubular flowers on compact, well-branched plants from spring through frost in zone 9. Unlike the sprawling, leggy habit of unselected Salvia coccinea, Lady in Red stays compact and bushy at 18–24 inches with neat, square-stemmed, slightly aromatic foliage. The brilliant red tubular flowers are intensely attractive to hummingbirds, which hover around each bloom spike, and the plant is nearly always in active use by feeding hummingbirds during the long Gulf South summer. In zone 9, Lady in Red is treated as a short-lived perennial or vigorous annual that typically self-seeds so freely it naturalizes into a colony that perpetuates indefinitely without replanting. The naturalized seedlings are genetic variations that may range slightly from the named cultivar, but generally maintain the compact habit and red flower color of the parent. The salvia's ability to grow in partial shade as well as full sun makes it more versatile than most red-flowering summer annuals, fitting under light tree canopy and in dappled-light conditions. Outstanding for butterfly and hummingbird gardens.

common_name: Lady of Shalott Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Lady of Shalott is known for exceptional disease resistance and vigor even in hot, humid climates, and can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2009, Lady of Shalott bears warm apricot-orange, tea-and-spice-scented blooms that open from red-orange buds into loosely cupped rosettes, held on strong, arching, thorny canes that resist bending in rain far better than many old-style roses. It is one of the most disease-resistant and heat-tolerant English roses available, holding up well to Gulf South humidity and blooming almost continuously from late spring through frost, and its vigorous growth allows it to be trained as a short climber against a fence or trellis if given support.

common_name: Lady of the Night (Night Jasmine, Brunfelsia americana)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil; Lady of the Night thrives in the dappled shade of large trees and performs poorly in full afternoon sun in zone 9. In zone 9a, it requires frost protection or container culture that can be brought indoors; in zone 9b-10, it grows as a reliable evergreen shrub. The fragrance is most intense after dark — plant near outdoor seating areas for evening enjoyment. All parts are toxic.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Lady of the Night is one of the finest shade-tolerant fragrant shrubs for zone 9-11 Gulf Coast gardens, where its powerful nocturnal fragrance fills outdoor spaces on warm spring and summer evenings. Brunfelsia americana is an evergreen shrub from the Caribbean (Jamaica, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Lesser Antilles) in the Solanaceae family closely related to Yesterday Today Tomorrow (B. pauciflora and B. australis). Its single-day flowers begin as pure white tubes and age through cream to pale yellow — the reverse color change from B. pauciflora's purple-to-white progression. The flower fragrance is released most powerfully after dark and is one of the most intensely sweet and complex fragrances in the plant world — often described as combining jasmine, vanilla, and gardenias — with a reach that can fill a large garden or patio on warm, still evenings. In zone 9, Lady of the Night blooms from spring through fall with peak flowering in late spring and early summer. The combination of shade tolerance and extraordinary nocturnal fragrance makes it one of the most valuable plants for shaded evening garden spaces, planted near patios, decks, and seating areas. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic — contain brunfelsamidine and other alkaloids causing neurological symptoms if ingested.

common_name: Lady of the Night Orchid (Brassavola nodosa, Starwhite Orchid)
plant_note: Mount on cork bark, a tree fern slab, or grow in a slatted orchid basket with bark media; Brassavola nodosa grows in full sun to bright indirect light and cannot tolerate frost. In zone 9b-10, it can be grown outdoors year-round on trees or cork mounts in sheltered spots — it tolerates brief temperatures to 35°F when dry. The plant performs very well in zone 9 on shaded covered porches, blooming multiple times per year. Never let the pseudobulbs dry completely for extended periods. Allow to dry briefly between waterings. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial shade — Brassavola nodosa tolerates brighter light than many orchids but performs well in the bright indirect light of a shaded porch or east-facing window. Brassavola nodosa is a compact, easily grown, free-blooming epiphytic orchid native to coastal and tropical areas from Mexico and the Caribbean through Central America to Colombia and Venezuela, one of the most cold-tolerant and adaptable of the commonly grown tropical orchids. The plant produces clusters of narrow, terete (cylindrical), slightly fleshy leaves and blooms in fall through winter with clusters of 3–7 flowers — the waxy, star-shaped flowers are greenish-white to pure white with a large, heart-shaped white lip fringed with tiny teeth, each flower 3–4 inches across. The flowers are inconspicuously fragrant by day but at night release an intensely sweet, vanilla-lilac perfume to attract pollinating sphinx moths — the nocturnal fragrance, sweet, penetrating, and far-carrying on warm evenings, earned the plant the name 'Lady of the Night' (not to be confused with Brunfelsia americana, another nocturnal fragrant plant with the same common name). Brassavola nodosa is used extensively in hybridization with Cattleya and related genera to produce the 'B. nodosa hybrids' with the characteristic nocturnal fragrance. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in early spring; lady’s mantle can also be direct sown on the soil surface in early spring as the seed needs light and moisture to germinate. It self-sows freely once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; lady’s mantle is treasured for its large, rounded, softly pleated and densely hairy leaves that bead morning dew and rain into perfect silver droplets — one of the most beloved effects in the garden. The frothy sprays of tiny chartreuse-yellow flowers bloom over many weeks in early summer, creating an airy effect that blends beautifully with everything. Shear spent flower stems and old foliage back hard in midsummer to produce a flush of fresh new growth. In warm climates (zone 7 and up) lady’s mantle may go dormant in summer heat — it strongly prefers cool, moist conditions and performs best in the Pacific Northwest and Upper South in partial shade.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 4-8 weeks before last frost, or sow directly in fall; ladybell forms a long taproot and resents transplanting once established, so set out young plants while still small or sow in place.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to partial sun; ladybell is an East Asian relative of the bellflowers, producing slender, wiry stems clothed in whorled leaves and topped from mid to late summer with airy, nodding sprays of small, pale blue-violet, bell-shaped flowers that bring gentle color to the woodland edge when many spring shade bloomers have finished. The young leaves and shoots are used as a cooked vegetable in Korean and Japanese cuisine, and the thick taproot has a history of use in East Asian herbal medicine, though most Western gardeners grow it purely as an ornamental. Because it develops a deep taproot early on, it establishes best when sown or transplanted young rather than moved as a mature plant, and once settled it is long-lived and easy-care, tolerating light shade and average garden soil without fuss. Deadhead spent flower stems to tidy the plant; it self-seeds modestly where conditions suit it.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Ladybird Scarlet's dwarf habit suits edging and containers where taller sulfur cosmos would overwhelm the space.
directions: Ladybird Scarlet is a dwarf, extra-compact selection of sulfur cosmos bred to bring the same heat- and drought-tolerant, brilliantly colored flowers of standard Cosmos sulphureus onto a low, tidy plant well under knee-height. Its vivid scarlet-orange single blooms open early and continue prolifically through summer heat that slows many other bedding annuals, and the short, well-branched habit needs no pinching or staking. It is well suited to the front of a border, edging, or containers, and its nectar-rich flowers draw butterflies and other pollinators throughout the season.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to bright partial shade; ladyfinger cactus clusters and offsets freely, making division the easiest way to propagate and multiply plants.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to bright partial shade; ladyfinger cactus produces slender, finger-like stems densely covered in fine, golden-yellow to bronze spines arranged in a neat spiral pattern, clustering and offsetting readily into a dense mound of dozens of stems within a few years. Small, star-shaped, pale yellow to cream flowers ring the tips of mature stems in spring, followed by small pink to red fruit. It is one of the easiest and most forgiving cacti for beginners, tolerating light shade and occasional neglect far better than most barrel or columnar species, though it still requires sharp drainage and minimal winter watering to avoid rot. Detach and pot up individual offsets any time during the growing season to control clump size or start new plants.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or plant rooted offsets in spring into sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; ladyfinger cactus is native to the brushlands of South Texas and northern Mexico and forms sprawling mats of slender, finger-like stems.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; ladyfinger cactus is a low, sprawling native of the South Texas brushlands and adjacent Mexico, its slender, finger-thick stems rooting where they touch the ground to form a loose, spreading mat rather than an upright clump. In spring it produces a spectacular flush of large, satiny, magenta-pink flowers with a darker throat, often nearly covering the plant for several days at a time, among the showiest blooms of any native hedgehog cactus. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than more northern Echinocereus species and performs best in the milder winters of zones 8 to 10, where it makes an excellent groundcover for a rock garden, gravel bed, or the sunny, well-drained edge of a xeriscape planting. Good drainage is essential, since standing winter moisture quickly rots the shallow-rooted stems.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence to support the climbing canes; Lamarque is a vigorous 1830 Noisette climber well adapted to Gulf Coast heat and humidity.
directions: Plant at the base of a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence in well-drained soil in full sun, tying in the vigorous climbing canes as they grow. Lamarque, introduced in 1830, is a classic climbing Noisette rose bearing large, creamy-white, lemon-scented blooms in generous clusters, repeating through the growing season on a vigorous plant that can climb 15 to 20 feet or more where conditions favor it. Like other Noisettes it was bred for the heat and humidity of the American South and remains one of the best-performing large climbers for that climate, tolerating the disease pressure that limits many modern climbing roses. Train canes horizontally along a support to encourage the most flowering laterals, and prune lightly after the main flush to maintain shape and promote continued rebloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; lamb's ear requires perfect drainage and actually performs better in dry, poor soil — it rots quickly in wet, humid conditions or heavy clay. In zone 9a, site in a raised bed or slope with excellent air circulation to avoid summer rot.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun; lamb's ear is prized above all for its extraordinary tactile foliage — thick, felt-like silver leaves 4–6 inches long covered in dense white wool that is impossibly soft to the touch, giving the plant its evocative common name. The silver-gray foliage is among the most effective of all for brightening dark borders, creating contrast with purple or yellow flowers, and providing texture in the dry garden. Tall woolly stems rise in summer carrying whorls of small lavender flowers attractive to bumblebees; the non-flowering cultivar 'Silver Carpet' is a denser, neater groundcover. Lamb's ear requires excellent drainage and good air circulation — in humid zone 9a summers the center of clumps may rot; divide and replant in fall after the heat breaks, selecting drier, elevated sites. Deer resistant.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in poor to average, well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in partial to full sun; lamb's ears struggles in wet, humid conditions — ensure excellent drainage, especially in the humid South, and do not mulch around the crowns.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in poor to average, well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in partial to full sun; lamb's ears struggles in wet, humid conditions — ensure excellent drainage, especially in the humid South, and do not mulch around the crowns. Stachys byzantina is grown almost entirely for its spectacular dense-woolly, silver-white, softly tactile leaves that form a spreading, mat-forming groundcover and make an elegant foil for colorful perennials; in late spring to summer it sends up fuzzy, silver-lavender flower spikes that some gardeners remove to keep the foliage display clean. Divide every 2–3 years in early spring to remove dead centers and maintain a tidy mat. Excellent at the front of borders, edging paths, and as dry-garden groundcover.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors since light aids germination; transplant after frost.
directions: Surface-sow the seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, since light aids germination. This monarda is covered with tiered whorls of lavender-pink flower clusters that attract butterflies, hummingbirds, and bees. The edible petals can replace oregano in savory dishes, be steeped into tea, or float in punch. Grow in full sun to part shade with good air circulation to limit mildew, and deadhead to extend flowering.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Lanai verbena is bred for improved powdery mildew resistance compared to older verbena strains.
directions: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Lanai verbena is bred for improved powdery mildew resistance compared to older verbena strains. Dense clusters of small, brightly colored flowers in a wide range of colors from white and pink to red, purple, and bicolor patterns cover trailing, mat-forming stems nearly continuously through the growing season, bred for improved resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem that plagued older bedding verbena varieties in humid climates. Its trailing, spreading habit and improved disease resistance make it a reliable choice for a hanging basket, container spiller, or groundcover in a sunny, well-drained bed. Water when the top inch of soil dries, avoid overhead watering which promotes fungal disease, and deadhead if seed set becomes heavy to encourage continued bloom.

common_name: Lanai Twister Pink Verbena (Bicolor Pink-and-White Trailing Verbena)
plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Lanai Twister Pink is part of the popular Lanai trailing verbena series, producing dense clusters of bicolor flowers with a bright pink outer edge surrounding a white center, giving each flower cluster a distinctive pinwheel, two-toned effect unlike the solid-color verbena cultivars more commonly grown. Its low, spreading, trailing habit fits hanging baskets, window boxes, and the tops of raised beds and retaining walls where it can cascade over the edge, blooming nearly continuously from spring through frost. Shear the plant back by about a third periodically through the season to keep growth dense and encourage continued bloom, and expect it to perform as a warm-season annual outside its hardy zones.

common_name: Lanarth White Hydrangea (Classic Pure White Lacecap Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Lanarth White is a classic pure white lacecap hydrangea, an RHS Award of Garden Merit winner.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Lanarth White bears crisp, pure white lacecap blooms, a flat outer ring of showy sterile florets surrounding a central disk of small fertile flowers, unaffected by soil pH the way blue and pink cultivars are since white pigments don't shift with aluminum availability. Its clean, classic lacecap form and reliable performance have earned it a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent wilting.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; lance leaf coreopsis is one of the most floriferous and reliable native wildflowers for Gulf Coast and southern gardens and naturalized meadow plantings — it thrives on neglect in lean, well-drained soil.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall or early spring by pressing lightly into well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom season. Coreopsis lanceolata (lance-leaf coreopsis or sand coreopsis) is one of the most abundantly flowering native wildflowers of the Gulf Coastal Plain and eastern North America — a long-lived perennial producing masses of bright, 2-to-3-inch, golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers with serrated ray petals on tall, branching stems above narrow, lance-shaped, mostly basal leaves from May through July (and often reblooming in fall). It is one of four coreopsis species designated as the State Wildflower of Florida and one of the most widely used native perennials in southeastern wildflower meadow restorations, roadside plantings, and naturalistic gardens. Unlike many coreopsis species, C. lanceolata is exceptionally drought-tolerant, self-seeds reliably (but not aggressively), and maintains a neat, upright habit in garden settings. The flower heads are extremely attractive to native bees and small native butterflies. It is one of the most recommended low-maintenance native perennials for full-sun, lean-soil garden situations throughout the Gulf South.

common_name: Lance-Leaf Begonia (Amphioxus Begonia, Spotted Sarawak Begonia)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, porous potting mix with excellent drainage; Begonia amphioxus is a trailing to semi-erect cane begonia best displayed in a hanging basket or allowed to cascade over a pot edge. Maintain consistent moisture but allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings. This species appreciates moderate humidity (50%+) and good air circulation. Propagate from stem cuttings. A terrarium plant in temperate climates; zone 11-12 outdoor shade garden in tropical conditions. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix — Lance-Leaf Begonia performs best in the bright, diffuse light of a shaded indoor position or sheltered tropical shade garden and produces its most vivid leaf spotting in good indirect light. Begonia amphioxus is a small, trailing to semi-erect begonia native to Sarawak, Malaysia (Borneo) in the Begoniaceae family, one of the most visually distinctive of the hundreds of wild Begonia species collected by tropical plant enthusiasts for its remarkable combination of leaf shape and surface pattern. The leaves are the defining feature: narrow, lance-shaped to narrowly ovate (2–4 inches long but only 0.5–1 inch wide — extremely elongated relative to the width), with a strongly tapering, spear-like tip that gives the species its name 'amphioxus' (Greek for 'pointed at both ends'). On this narrow, bright green surface, scattered crimson-red to scarlet spots and blotches of varying sizes are distributed irregularly — the effect is of a thin bright-green ribbon patterned with vivid red paint droplets. The undersides are deep red. The plant also produces small pink flowers in clusters from the leaf axils throughout the growing season. A collector's begonia valued for its completely distinctive and unusual leaf shape — the extreme narrowness distinguishing it from nearly all other cultivated begonia species. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; lance-leaved loosestrife grows naturally in moist woodland openings, stream banks, and meadow edges across eastern North America. It spreads by rhizomes and self-sows to form loose colonies.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in moist woodland borders, stream banks, and rain gardens; lance-leaved loosestrife is a slender, upright native perennial with narrow, lance-shaped leaves and cheerful, star-shaped yellow flowers in midsummer. It is one of the more adaptable native loosestrifes, tolerating somewhat drier conditions than the wetland species while still preferring consistent moisture. The flowers provide nectar for small native bees, including Macropis bees that are specialists on Lysimachia pollen and oil. The plant spreads steadily by rhizomes and seeds to form naturalistic colonies in appropriate moist, shaded areas, combining naturally with native ferns, sedges, and woodland wildflowers. A native alternative to the highly invasive purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria) for moist areas, though unrelated botanically.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface in spring after last frost — seeds need light to germinate; in zone 9, sow in early spring (February–March) or in late summer for fall flowers. The plant behaves as an annual in most of the South but sometimes overwinters in zones 8–10.
directions: Scatter seeds on bare, dry, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost — this wildflower requires excellent drainage and poor, even sandy soil; in rich, moist soil it becomes floppy and short-lived. Lanceleaf blanket flower is native to sandy plains and open disturbed ground from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas, with narrow lance-shaped leaves (unlike the wider leaves of the hybrid garden gaillardia) and bright yellow to orange-tipped ray flowers with purple-red centers that bloom continuously from summer through frost. A superb plant for hot, dry sandy gardens and roadsides in the Southeast where it attracts skippers, bumblebees, and goldfinches (which eat the seed heads). Minimal care once established — simply leave the seed heads in place for self-sowing.

common_name: Lanceleaf Coreopsis (Native Perennial Yellow Tickseed Wildflower)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in fall or early spring; Lanceleaf Coreopsis is a native perennial that self-seeds prolifically once established — a single planting will naturalize and expand over years without replanting. In zone 9, sow fall (September–November) or late winter (January–February) for bloom in spring (April–June) of the same or following season. Coreopsis planted from fall will frequently bloom the following spring; from spring seed, blooms appear by late summer. The species is extremely drought-tolerant once established — one of the most reliably undemanding native perennials for the well-drained, sunny portions of zone 8–9 gardens.
directions: Scatter seeds on prepared, weed-free soil and press in without covering; coreopsis seeds need some light for germination. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom and prevent self-seeding where not desired. Lanceleaf Coreopsis (Coreopsis lanceolata) is a native perennial wildflower of the eastern and central United States — distributed naturally in open meadows, prairies, roadsides, and disturbed areas from the Atlantic Coast to the Great Plains, south to the Gulf Coast. The bright golden-yellow flowers (1.5–2 inches across) have the characteristic daisy-like form with slightly toothed or lobed ray petals and a central button — instantly recognizable as the defining coreopsis look that has made the genus a staple of native plant and pollinator gardens across North America. As a native plant, Lanceleaf Coreopsis evolved with and provides premium pollinator habitat: the flowers are highly attractive to native bees (bumblebees, mining bees, sweat bees), skippers, and butterflies, providing nectar and pollen from spring through midsummer. The seeds are consumed by native sparrows and small finches, making this a multi-function wildlife plant. Unlike many prairie natives, Lanceleaf Coreopsis blooms heavily in its first year from fall planting, making it more immediately rewarding than species that require two or more seasons to establish before flowering. Its minimal water needs and tolerance of poor, dry soil make it ideal for rain gardens, unirrigated native plantings, and naturalized areas.

plant_note: Set divisions or plugs in spring into consistently damp to seasonally wet soil, letting trailing stems root along the ground.
