More sun-tolerant than many shade sedges, it also performs well in dappled or morning-sun sites. It spreads gradually by both self-seeding and short rhizomes to fill in as a dense, low-maintenance groundcover that needs no fertilizer or irrigation once established, and it tolerates the periodic dry spells common in Gulf South summers better than cool-season lawn grasses growing in shade.

plant_note: Broadcast seed onto lightly raked, moist soil in spring or fall; tolerates both a fall sowing for spring bloom and a spring sowing for summer color.
directions: Broadcast seed onto lightly raked, moist soil in spring or fall, since this Florida native tolerates both a fall sowing for spring bloom and a spring sowing for summer color. As the official state wildflower it is planted along Florida highways and low pinelands for its long parade of small yellow, brown-centered daisies that feed native bees and support skipper and sulphur butterfly larvae. It thrives in the humid, sandy soils common across the northern Gulf Coast and readily reseeds each year if some spent flower heads are left standing. Keep soil evenly moist during germination but avoid waterlogging once seedlings are established.

plant_note: Plant pup offsets in spring in full sun in extremely well-drained, alkaline, rocky desert soil; lechuguilla is the indicator species of the Chihuahuan Desert — wherever it grows, you are in the Chihuahuan Desert. It is a key component of Chihuahuan Desert garden design and Big Bend National Park landscapes.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, alkaline, rocky, thin desert soil with no supplemental water once established; lechuguilla (Agave lechuguilla) is the defining indicator plant of the Chihuahuan Desert, forming dense colonies on rocky limestone slopes from west Texas through New Mexico and into Mexico. The stiff, narrow, sharply-tipped leaves earned the common name 'shin-dagger' for the painful punctures they inflict on hikers. Indigenous peoples of the Chihuahuan Desert used lechuguilla extensively — the fibers from the leaves were woven into rope, sandals, and baskets; the leaf sap was used medicinally; and the heart was cooked and eaten. The flowering stalk, which can reach 10–15 feet, is spectacular but marks the plant's death. An authentic Chihuahuan Desert specimen plant for Texas and New Mexico landscapes.

common_name: Leda Rose (Painted Damask, Creamy White Edged Crimson)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Leda, known as the Painted Damask, bears creamy white petals edged in crimson, most vivid on the buds.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Leda, popularly called the Painted Damask, bears creamy white double blooms delicately edged in crimson-red, the contrasting rim most vivid and vibrant on the tightly furled buds and softening slightly as the flower fully opens, a distinctive hand-painted look unique among damask roses. Like most damask roses it blooms in a single strong flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Legend of the Fall Fothergilla (Long-Holding Multi-Color Fall Foliage Hybrid)
scientific_name: Fothergilla x intermedia 'ALICE' (Legend of the Fall)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Legend of the Fall is an upright Proven Winners fothergilla hybrid bred for strong white bottlebrush blooms and an especially long-lasting red-orange-yellow fall color display.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat. Legend of the Fall is an upright fothergilla hybrid bred for a heavy show of fragrant, honey-scented, bottlebrush-like white flower spikes in spring before the leaves emerge, followed by blue-green summer foliage that turns a spectacular, long-holding blend of red, orange, and yellow in fall — the display persists notably longer than in many older fothergilla selections. Its upright, four to five foot habit suits a shrub border, woodland edge, or foundation planting. Requires minimal pruning; simply remove dead or crossing wood after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Legion of Honor Marigold (Classic Heirloom Single Gold with Maroon Blotch)
plant_note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or sow directly once soil warms; Legion of Honor, a classic heirloom known since 1903 as Little Brownie, bears single gold flowers marked with maroon blotches at the base.
directions: Start seeds indoors for a head start or sow directly after frost danger passes, barely covering them. Legion of Honor, a classic heirloom French marigold long known also as Little Brownie and grown since 1903, bears simple, single, golden-yellow flowers with a distinctive dark maroon blotch marking the base of each petal, an old-fashioned, less showy bloom form than modern double French marigolds but valued for its heirloom pedigree. Plant in full sun where the strong scent helps deter garden pests. Deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming all summer.

plant_note: Sow directly in fall into shaded, well-drained soil; seeds benefit from cool, moist conditions during stratification before spring germination.
directions: Leibnizia is a low-growing rosette perennial native to central Mexico, Guatemala, and the mountains of northwestern Chihuahua, prized among botanically curious gardeners for its remarkable dual flower strategy: showy open (chasmogamous) white-and-purple daisy flowers appear in spring, while a second flush of closed, self-pollinating (cleistogamous) flowers is produced later in the season without ever opening. This unusual adaptation allows the plant to set seed reliably even without pollinators, making it a resilient choice for dry shade conditions under trees or on north-facing slopes. Sow seeds in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with partial shade; established plants form tidy, attractive basal rosettes that spread slowly over time. It pairs well with other dry-shade natives such as woodland sedges and low ferns, requiring only occasional watering during extended dry periods once roots are established.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lemoine deutzia is a classic, cold-hardy hybrid valued for its profuse, pure white late-spring flower display.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lemoine deutzia is a classic, cold-hardy hybrid valued for its profuse, pure white late-spring flower display. This historic French hybrid, bred by the renowned Lemoine nursery in the late nineteenth century, smothers its arching branches in dense clusters of small, pure white, star-shaped flowers in late spring, one of the most floriferous of the classic deutzia hybrids and a mainstay of cottage-garden and heritage shrub borders for over a century. Reliable and easy-care, it tolerates a range of soils and climates, providing a reliable flush of white bloom each spring with minimal maintenance beyond occasional renewal pruning. Prune immediately after flowering to shape and remove some of the oldest canes at the base periodically to keep the shrub renewed and full from the ground up.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost, or direct sow when warm.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow when soil is warm, covering lightly. These bushy, compact signet marigolds form dense mounds of lacy, scented foliage topped with profuse single lemon and tangerine blooms. The petite flowers are edible and can be infused into oil or vinegar for salad dressings. Grow in full sun with average soil, deadhead to keep blooms coming, and use them as tidy edging or rock-garden accents.

plant_note: Anchor stem cuttings 1 inch into aquarium substrate in small clusters; the thick, succulent stems are brittle and root best when handled gently and not buried too deeply.
directions: Native to wetlands and slow streams across the southeastern and south-central United States, this thick-stemmed, round-leaved plant is grown fully submersed as a background or mid-ground species in freshwater planted aquaria, not planted in outdoor garden soil. It grows under medium aquarium lighting and does not require CO2 supplementation, though growth is sturdier and more compact with it. The crushed foliage carries a distinctive lemon scent, a useful identifying trait at the aquarium store. Propagate by cutting healthy stem tips and replanting them directly into the substrate; older lower stems tend to defoliate over time and should be trimmed away.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural stratification and spring germination in the South and Gulf Coast, where it blooms in spring and early summer; Monarda citriodora is a Texas and Great Plains native annual with strongly lemon-scented foliage and whorled spikes of pink to lavender flowers that are among the finest nectar sources for native bees.
directions: Scatter seed on the soil surface in fall in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 12 inches in spring. Monarda citriodora (lemon beebalm, lemon mint) is a widespread native annual or short-lived perennial of the central grasslands from Texas to Kansas and east to the Gulf Coast, growing on dry prairies, roadsides, and disturbed sites in calcareous, well-drained soils; it is the most aromatic of the native beebalms, with strongly lemon-scented foliage that can be used as a culinary and tea herb. The whorled flower spikes produce rings of pink to lavender flowers with distinctive purple-spotted bracts at intervals along the stem in late spring and early summer — among the most important early nectar sources for native bees including bumblebees and Monarda specialist bees. Naturalizes readily from self-seeding in dry, sunny sites; a superb plant for wildflower meadows and native bee gardens throughout the South.

common_name: Lemon Coral Sedum (Bright Chartreuse Spreading Groundcover Sedum)
plant_note: Set out transplants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; drought-tolerant once established and well suited to containers, rock gardens, and groundcover use.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, since this succulent groundcover is intolerant of soggy conditions. Lemon Coral is a spreading sedum bred for its vivid, bright chartreuse-yellow, needle-like foliage that forms a dense, glowing mat or spills attractively over container edges, adding brilliant color contrast to mixed plantings even without flowering. Small star-shaped yellow flowers appear in summer, though the foliage color is the plant's main ornamental draw throughout the growing season. Highly drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on neglect and needs only occasional watering during extended dry spells, making it an easy, low-maintenance choice for rock gardens, green roofs, container spillers, and sunny groundcover areas where soil stays on the drier side.

plant_note: Divide spreading clumps in spring or fall; lemon daylily spreads readily by underground rhizomes to form extensive colonies and may become too vigorous for small spaces. In rich, moist soils it spreads more aggressively. Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun to part shade. This ancient species has been cultivated in European gardens since the 1500s.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; lemon daylily is one of the oldest ornamental plants in European garden history — a Chinese native introduced to European gardens in the late 1500s that appears in botanical illustrations from the 1600s and has grown in cottage gardens and farmsteads continuously ever since. The flowers are clear, clean, bright-yellow and strongly sweet-fragrant, carried on arching stems above fine-textured, narrow foliage in May and June — among the earliest daylilies to bloom. The fragrance is a classic, fresh, sweet lily-like scent that carries well in still evening air. Unlike most hybrid daylilies (which are crosses from several species including this one), lemon daylily is a true species that spreads modestly by rhizomes to form naturalized drifts and can be found half-wild in old rural gardens across temperate regions. The earliest-blooming daylily species in temperate gardens, filling the gap before the early hybrids begin their season. Buds and young flowers are edible as a vegetable in Chinese cooking.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost, or direct sow when warm.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow when soil warms, covering about 1/4 inch. 'Lemon Drop' bears cheerful sunny-yellow flowers on compact plants perfect for the front of the bed, patio pots, and window boxes. It takes little space in the vegetable garden and may help reduce soil nematodes. Grow in full sun with average soil, and deadhead regularly to encourage continuous bloom through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9 plant February–April for spring and September–October for fall. Like all signet marigolds, Lemon Gem blooms continuously without deadheading and tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers better than most other annual flowers.
directions: Broadcast seed on the soil surface or barely cover in well-drained soil; Lemon Gem is the yellow-flowered counterpart to Tangerine Gem in the signet marigold group (Tagetes tenuifolia), producing a mound of fine, lemon-scented, ferny foliage covered continuously with bright yellow single flowers from late spring through fall. The flowers and young leaves are edible with a sharp, citrusy, slightly spicy flavor that works well as a garnish or in salads. The strongly aromatic foliage repels whiteflies, aphids, and nematodes, making signet marigolds the most pest-deterrent marigold type for interplanting with vegetables. The compact, mounded habit is ideal for edging beds, container planting, and window boxes. Self-seeds modestly, often returning year after year in zone 8–9 gardens.

common_name: Lemon Lime Nandina (Bright Chartreuse Compact Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color is brightest with several hours of direct sun, while some afternoon shade helps prevent scorch in peak Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Lemon Lime is a dwarf, mounding nandina selected for foliage that emerges bright chartreuse-lime rather than the red tones typical of most nandina cultivars, holding that fresh lime-green color through summer without the burgundy winter shift seen in other dwarf types. Its compact, dense habit and unusual color make it a useful accent for brightening a shaded bed or breaking up the heavier greens and burgundies of a typical foundation planting. Like other modern dwarf nandina selections it is sterile and produces no berries, avoiding the self-seeding that has made standard nandina invasive in parts of the Southeast, and it needs little pruning beyond removing occasional damaged canes.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost; succession sow for continuous bloom.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the last frost, and sow again every 2 to 4 weeks until three months before first fall frost for continuous bloom. Majestic multi-branched plants produce many soft lemon-yellow flowers ideal for cutting all summer. Easy to grow in almost any well-drained soil, these sunflowers are drought-tolerant once established. Give them full sun, and leave late seed heads for birds to enjoy in autumn.

common_name: Lemon Queen Swamp Sunflower (Pale-Yellow Compact Native Fall Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Lemon Queen blooms in fall (September–November) and develops its full height by mid-summer — place toward the back of borders where the tall stems are supported by adjacent plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Lemon Queen is a compact cultivar of swamp sunflower (Helianthus angustifolius) producing pale-yellow, lemon-colored flowers rather than the golden-yellow of the species — a softer, cooler yellow that creates a different aesthetic quality in the fall garden. The pale lemon-yellow flowers with dark brown centers bloom in September–November when few other perennials are at peak display, filling the fall garden with a naturalistic cloud of soft-yellow daisy-form flowers that are outstanding for cut flowers and highly attractive to migrating monarch butterflies, native bees, and seed-eating birds. 'Lemon Queen' is somewhat more compact than the straight species (4–6 feet rather than 6–10 feet for vigorous species plants) and less likely to require staking — a practical advantage for typical residential borders where the species' tall, floppy stems can be problematic. The pale yellow flower color allows combination with blue-purple asters, violet-flowered plants (ironweed, ageratum), and warm orange-red tones (ornamental grasses, late salvias) in fall combinations without the color intensity of the golden-yellow species. Division every 3–4 years in spring prevents center die-out in mature clumps. An outstanding choice for rain gardens, moist spots, and naturalistic borders where fall native color and pollinator support are priorities.

common_name: Lennei Magnolia (Full-Petaled Deep Purple-Pink Saucer Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Lennei blooms somewhat later than Alexandrina, giving it a bit more protection from late-season frost damage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Lennei is a classic saucer magnolia cultivar valued for its unusually full, heavy-petaled flowers in a deep rose-purple on the outside with a paler, almost white interior, giving each bloom a rounded, goblet-like fullness distinct from the more open form of many other saucer magnolia cultivars. It flowers on bare branches in early to mid spring, somewhat later than Alexandrina, and grows into a broad, spreading, multi-stemmed small tree that needs little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood. Established trees are long-lived, low-maintenance landscape specimens, though a late hard freeze can still brown open flowers in an unusually cold spring.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in early fall or late winter; lenten rose establishes most reliably from container-grown plants rather than bare-root divisions and resents frequent transplanting once established — site carefully.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; lenten rose (Helleborus × hybridus) is one of the most valuable and irreplaceable shade garden perennials in temperate gardens — an evergreen clump of bold, leathery, dark-green, deeply palmate leaves that produces nodding, cup-shaped flowers in an extraordinary color range (pure white, cream, pale yellow, soft pink, rose, deep magenta, plum, near-black, and every bicolor and picotee combination) from late winter through early spring, often blooming through snow. Unlike most spring flowers it opens during the coldest months of late winter, providing garden color at the bleakest time of year. The flowers face downward, so tilt them gently upward to appreciate the intricate inner markings — spotted, veined, and blotched patterns of stunning complexity are characteristic of the named hybrid selections. Plants are long-lived (decades), deer-resistant, slug-resistant, and self-seed freely to form expanding colonies. 'Wedding Party Series', 'Winter Jewels Series', and 'Frostkiss Series' offer named selections in predictable colors. Do not cut old foliage until new growth emerges in late winter. An absolute cornerstone plant for the shade garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; hellebores resent disturbance once established — plant in a permanent location and do not divide unless essential. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial to full shade; lenten rose (Helleborus x hybridus) is one of the finest and most prized of all shade garden perennials — a nearly evergreen perennial that flowers in late winter (February–March in zone 8–9) with nodding, cup-shaped flowers 2–4 inches across in an extraordinary range of colors: white, cream, pale yellow, pink, rose, burgundy, deep plum, near-black, and spotted or picotee bicolors. No other garden plant offers such refined beauty in the dead of winter shade. The leathery, deeply divided leaves persist year-round, creating outstanding year-round texture. In zone 9a, site in deep shade with excellent drainage to avoid summer root rot. It thrives in the Southeast under deciduous trees and is remarkable for blooming when almost nothing else does in deep shade. Deer resistant. All parts toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant dormant bulbs in autumn 4-6 inches deep in cool, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but sharply drained acidic soil in dappled woodland shade.
directions: Grow this Sino-Himalayan bulb in a cool, sheltered woodland border where summers stay mild and soil never dries out or becomes waterlogged; a raised bed of leaf mold and grit over clay works well. In early-to-midsummer, wiry stems carry nodding, outward-facing bowls of white to soft pink, each petal blotched with maroon-purple spots reminiscent of a small martagon lily. Plants are slow from seed, often taking four to six years to flower, so most gardeners start with dormant bulbs and top-dress annually with leaf mold rather than manure. Mulch for winter protection in zone 6 gardens and shield from late spring frosts, which can damage emerging shoots.

plant_note: Plant rhizomatous bulbs in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; leopard lily spreads by rhizomatous bulbs to form large colonies over time. It prefers stream-bank conditions with consistent moisture and partial shade but is more adaptable than many native lilies.
directions: Plant rhizomatous bulbs in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; leopard lily is the most widely cultivated and vigorous of the western native lilies, native to stream banks, seeps, and moist openings in the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges of California and southern Oregon. The reflexed orange flowers with red-spotted centers on tall, wiry stems are produced in midsummer. More adaptable than many native lilies — it spreads by interconnected rhizomatous bulbs to form substantial clumps and is considerably more heat- and drought-tolerant than it appears, provided consistent soil moisture is maintained at root depth. Naturalizes well in gardens with moist but well-drained conditions. The subspecies and cultivar 'Giganteum' grows to 8 feet with over 30 flowers per stem. An important parent of the classic 'Bellingham Hybrid' garden lilies.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; leopard plant is one of the finest shade perennials for the Gulf Coast, tolerating both deep shade and the summer heat and humidity that defeat many shade perennials in zone 8–9.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to deep shade — leopard plant is one of the most valuable and underused shade perennials for the Gulf Coast, producing extraordinarily bold, round, glossy, deep-green, leathery leaves up to 18 inches across that retain a tropical freshness through the hottest Gulf Coast summers. The common cultivar 'Aureomaculatum' (spotted leopard plant) has large yellow spots scattered across the dark green leaves, giving a striking, almost artificial-looking pattern. Yellow daisy flowers appear in fall to winter on tall stalks, providing late-season color when most shade perennials are shutting down. Completely evergreen in zone 8–10; the leathery leaves resist frost damage better than most shade perennials and the plant is reliably root-hardy through zone 7 winters. Clumps increase slowly and need division only every 5–7 years. An outstanding long-term, zero-maintenance shade perennial for Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; leopard Solomon's seal spreads by creeping rhizomes to form an evergreen groundcover and, unlike deciduous Polygonatum, keeps its foliage through winter in zones 7 and warmer.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; leopard Solomon's seal spreads by creeping rhizomes to form an evergreen groundcover and, unlike deciduous Polygonatum, keeps its foliage through winter in zones 7 and warmer. Disporopsis fuscopicta is a low, arching Chinese relative of Solomon's seal grown for its glossy, dark green, lance-shaped leaves speckled and mottled with maroon-purple blotches, with small, dangling, greenish-cream bells appearing beneath the foliage in spring followed by dark berries. It is a choice, slow-spreading evergreen groundcover for shaded borders and woodland gardens in the warmer half of the country, holding its patterned foliage year-round where winters are mild. Water regularly during dry spells, mulch to retain soil moisture, and divide congested clumps in early spring to spread the planting or share with other gardeners.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or container plants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; leopard's bane is one of the earliest-blooming spring perennials and goes dormant by midsummer — mark its location.
directions: Plant divisions in early fall or set out container plants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; leopard's bane is among the first perennials to bloom in spring, producing bright yellow daisy-like flowers in March or April above heart-shaped, hairy basal leaves — a welcome sight when virtually nothing else is in color. The plants go completely summer-dormant by July; mark their locations so they are not disturbed during the dormancy period. Combine with hostas and ferns that will fill in the gaps left by dormant leopard's bane by summer. Divide congested clumps every 2–3 years in late summer just before the new fall rosettes emerge. Excellent for cutting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Leslie Ann is a Louisiana Super Plants selection and 1961 Ralph Peer Camellia Award winner, a long-proven fall-blooming sasanqua for the Gulf South landscape.
directions: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun; Leslie Ann is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated sasanqua camellia with a long track record, having won the Ralph Peer Camellia Award back in 1961 and remaining a proven, reliable landscape performer in the decades since. It produces large, semi-double flowers combining pink, blush, and white in each bloom, opening from October through December when few other shrubs are in flower, and provides glossy evergreen structure through the rest of the year. Like other sasanquas it is more sun-tolerant and generally faster-growing than Camellia japonica, but still benefits from some afternoon shade and consistently moist, well-drained, acidic soil. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.

plant_note: Transplant tubers in early spring into a site that mimics semi-shaded European woodland with neutral to slightly calcareous soil. Handle tubers gently to avoid bruising, and plant at the same depth as the original growing position. Consistent soil moisture through the first growing season is essential for establishment.
directions: Plant in partially shaded spots beneath deciduous trees where dappled sunlight reaches the forest floor, in neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil. This orchid produces its sweetly vanilla-scented flower spikes in early summer and relies on night-flying moths for pollination, so undisturbed sites near hedgerows or woodland edges are ideal. Avoid over-mulching around the base, as this can smother the rosette of basal leaves that appear in spring. Established plants are long-lived and best left undisturbed; clumps should only be divided when visibly overcrowded.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers or bulbils in fall, 1-2 inches deep, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade under deciduous trees; lesser celandine emerges and blooms in earliest spring before tree canopies leaf out, then dies back completely to underground tubers by early summer. It spreads readily by tubers and is regarded as an invasive weed in much of the northeastern and mid-Atlantic United States, so plant only well-behaved, sterile ornamental cultivars and never near streams, floodplains, or natural areas.
directions: Plant tubers in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to dappled sun beneath deciduous trees; lesser celandine is a low, mat-forming spring ephemeral native to Europe and western Asia that carpets the shaded woodland floor with glossy, heart-shaped leaves and glistening, bright yellow, buttercup-like flowers in the first mild weeks of spring, then vanishes completely underground by early summer as the tree canopy closes overhead. The species itself spreads with great vigor from both underground tubers and small bulbils that form in the leaf axils, and it has escaped cultivation to become a serious invasive weed of moist floodplain forests across much of the northeastern and mid-Atlantic United States, where it can carpet the forest floor and crowd out spring-blooming native wildflowers before most of them emerge. Gardeners who want its bright, glossy foliage should instead choose named ornamental selections such as the dark bronze-purple-leaved 'Brazen Hussy' or the fully double-flowered 'Flore Pleno', both of which set little or no viable seed and spread far more slowly than the wild type; even so, these should be planted in contained beds away from wild woodlands and watercourses. Once dormant in summer, mark planting locations, since the foliage disappears entirely until the following late winter.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall directly onto moist, cool, humus-rich soil in a shaded or partly shaded position, as this alpine European species requires a period of cold stratification to germinate reliably — fall outdoor sowing provides this naturally. Press seeds lightly into the surface and keep the seedbed consistently moist; seeds will germinate the following spring as temperatures moderate. Cold stratification is essential: germination rates drop significantly for seeds sown without a winter chill period.
directions: Direct-sow in fall onto moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, allowing the winter cold to provide the stratification this alpine species needs before germinating in spring. Seeds are small, so scatter them thinly over a prepared seedbed and press gently to ensure good soil contact without burying them deeply. This compact masterwort produces deeply divided, palmate leaves and delicate pincushion flower heads in early to midsummer — smaller in scale than A. major, making it well-suited to rock garden pockets and intimate shade plantings. Keep the soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, and divide established clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain flowering vigor.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings or divisions 12–18 inches apart in spring or fall; stems root wherever they contact soil, filling in gaps quickly once plants establish.
directions: Plant in almost any soil in partial to deep shade; lesser periwinkle is one of the toughest shade groundcovers, tolerating dry shade under mature trees once established. The trailing stems root at nodes to form a weed-suppressing mat studded with periwinkle-blue pinwheel flowers in spring, with scattered repeat bloom into fall. Variegated forms such as 'Illumination' and 'Ralph Shugert' brighten dark spaces. Shear plants back by half in early spring to maintain density and remove dead or straggling stems. Note that Vinca minor can spread into natural areas — consider native alternatives (Pachysandra procumbens, Asarum canadense) in gardens bordering woodlands.

common_name: Let's Dance Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Bigleaf Hydrangea Series)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance is a compact, reblooming bigleaf hydrangea series that flowers on both old and new wood, giving reliable summer bloom even after a late frost damages the previous year's buds.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Let's Dance is a breeding series of compact, reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas that stay under 3 feet tall, considerably smaller than older mophead cultivars, while still flowering on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year. This reblooming trait means a late spring frost that kills the old flower buds does not prevent a good summer bloom, unlike older hydrangea cultivars that flower only once per year on old wood. Individual cultivars within the series vary in flower form (mophead or lacecap) and color. Flower color shifts with soil pH the way most macrophylla hydrangeas do, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since hydrangea's large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

common_name: Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue is a Proven Winners reblooming bigleaf hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, giving a longer bloom season than older mophead varieties that bloom only on the prior year's growth.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in the Gulf South. Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue is part of the Proven Winners Let's Dance series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas, bred to flower reliably on new growth as well as on old wood, so a late freeze that damages the previous year's stems doesn't wipe out the whole season's bloom the way it can on older mophead cultivars. Its compact, rounded habit fits smaller foundation plantings and containers better than full-sized mopheads, and the large, rounded flower clusters shift from blue to pink depending on soil pH, staying truest blue in acidic soil amended with aluminum sulfate if needed. Deadhead spent blooms and prune lightly to shape in late winter, avoiding heavy pruning that would remove the current season's developing flower buds.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; benefits from cool soil to germinate.
directions: Lewis blue flax is a graceful native perennial that opens clear sky-blue flowers each morning atop slender, wiry stems. Sow seeds directly in spring or fall on well-drained soil, pressing them in lightly and keeping the surface moist until they sprout. Once established it is remarkably drought tolerant and thrives in full sun across a wide range of conditions. Allow spent flowers to set seed and it will self-sow to form drifts over time.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Lewis's mock orange is the state flower of Idaho and one of the most cold-hardy and fragrant native mock oranges.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Lewis's mock orange is drought-tolerant once established and adapts to a wide range of soils including rocky slopes and thin, dry soils. Philadelphus lewisii is a native western North American shrub (state flower of Idaho) producing clusters of large, 4-petaled, pure-white flowers with a pronounced, sweet, citrus-orange fragrance in late spring and early summer — one of the most powerfully perfumed of all flowering shrubs. Unlike the commonly cultivated European species (P. coronarius), this native is more drougt-tolerant, cold-hardy, and has excellent wildlife value; it provides important cover and nesting habitat for birds, and the fragrant flowers attract butterflies and native bees. The multi-stemmed, arching habit is attractive even out of bloom.

plant_note: Plant container trees in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Leyland cypress is highly prone to Seiridium and Botryosphaeria canker disease in the hot, humid, poorly drained conditions common in the Gulf South, so good drainage, wide spacing for airflow, and avoiding overhead irrigation are essential for long-term success.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving trees generous spacing for airflow, since crowding and poor drainage are the leading causes of the canker diseases that shorten this tree's life in humid climates. Leyland cypress is a fast-growing hybrid conifer long popular across the South for quickly establishing a dense, narrow, evergreen privacy screen, capable of adding 3 feet or more of growth per year in its early years to reach a mature height of 40–60 feet with soft, feathery, blue-green foliage. Its rapid growth rate made it the default screening tree for decades, but it is increasingly susceptible to fatal canker diseases in the Gulf South's heat, humidity, and heavy clay soils, particularly when planted too closely together or in poorly drained sites, so many extension services now recommend Green Giant arborvitae or other alternatives for new plantings in this region. Where Leyland cypress is already established or planted with excellent drainage and spacing, minimal pruning is needed beyond an occasional light shearing to maintain shape.

common_name: Li'l Bang Daybreak Coreopsis (Dwarf Disease-Resistant Bicolor Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Daybreak is a dwarf sibling of the Big Bang coreopsis series bred by Darrell Probst, noted for strong disease resistance and a compact habit well suited to small beds and containers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Daybreak is a compact coreopsis from the Li'l Bang series, a dwarf line bred from the disease-resistant Big Bang parentage, producing bright orange-red and yellow bicolor flowers over a dense, tidy mound. Its small size and disease resistance make it a strong choice for the front of a border, edging, or a sunny container where a taller coreopsis would be out of scale. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall and tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established. Shear the plant back lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

common_name: Li'l Bang Starstruck Coreopsis (Dwarf Rosy-Pink Disease-Resistant Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Starstruck is a dwarf, rosy-pink-flowered member of the disease-resistant Li'l Bang coreopsis series, a compact size well suited to small Gulf Coast beds and containers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Starstruck is a compact coreopsis from the Li'l Bang series, standing out for its unusual rosy-pink flower color among a genus more often known for yellow and orange tones, held over a dense, tidy mound of fine foliage. It shares the series' strong disease resistance and blooms heavily from early summer into fall, tolerating heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established. Its small stature makes it a good fit for the front of a border, edging, or a sunny container. Shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 in deep in spring as soon as the soil can be worked; they establish quickly and bloom the first season.
directions: Plant corms 3–4 in deep with the flat side down in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; rich or wet soil leads to floppy growth. Liatris is unique in opening its flowers from the top of the spike downward, prolonging the bloom period for 3–4 weeks in midsummer. The purple to rose-pink spikes are outstanding cut flowers and highly attractive to butterflies and bees; stems last 10–14 days in a vase. Clumps multiply steadily; divide every 3–4 years in spring to prevent overcrowding and maintain strong bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Liberty is a large, show-stopping hosta that requires 3–4 years to develop full size and leaf character — the wide gold margin becomes more prominent and the overall plant more impressive with each passing season.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Liberty is a large hosta with a striking bicolor pattern — blue-green, deeply corrugated, puckered centers surrounded by an exceptionally wide, 3–4 inch irregular margin that transitions from creamy white in spring through gold and yellow in summer. It was named the American Hosta Growers Association Hosta of the Year in 2012. The very wide margin distinguishes it from Frances Williams (its likely parent) and creates a bolder, more dramatic variegation. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in midsummer. Like all large hostas with H. sieboldiana background, Liberty performs best when given generous space, consistent moisture, and deep organic mulch. The wide margin may show some margin burn in zone 8–9 during prolonged summer heat, making deep shade and consistent moisture essential in warm climates. A spectacular long-lived perennial for mature shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil or attach to rough bark in partial to full shade; licorice fern is an epiphytic Pacific Coast fern that grows naturally on mossy boulders, tree trunks, and cliff faces — it requires excellent drainage but consistent moisture during its winter growing season and goes dormant in summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — most charming when allowed to grow on the surface of mossy boulders, log stumps, or the rough bark of large-trunked trees; licorice fern is a graceful, small, creeping fern of the cool, moist Pacific Coast woodlands, named for the sweet licorice-like flavor of its slender rhizomes, which were chewed fresh by Pacific Northwest indigenous peoples to sweeten foods and treat respiratory ailments. The fronds are bright, glossy green, simply pinnate, and arch gracefully; the plant is unusual in that it grows actively through the cool, wet winter months and goes completely dormant in summer when conditions become warm and dry. In gardens it performs best in mild coastal climates (Pacific Coast, mild Atlantic coast) with cool, moist winters and moderate summers. Established plants drape beautifully over mossy surfaces and create a lush, ancient, fern-grotto effect in shaded rock gardens.

common_name: Lightning Jewel Orchid (Golden Jewel Orchid, Macodes petola)
plant_note: Grow as a terrarium specimen or high-humidity windowsill plant in zone 9; Macodes petola requires consistently high humidity (70–80%) and will deteriorate rapidly in dry indoor air without supplemental humidity from a terrarium, cloche, or humidity tray. It prefers slightly cooler temperatures (65–75°F) than many tropical houseplants and performs poorly in very warm rooms. Use a fine-textured, moisture-retaining but well-draining mix (sphagnum moss or orchid mix with added coco fiber). Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in low to moderate shade — Lightning Jewel Orchid thrives in the dim conditions of its native deep-forest habitat and is one of the few ornamental plants that benefits from genuinely low light (a north window or the floor level of a bright room). Macodes petola is a small terrestrial orchid from the tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Philippines, Java, Borneo, Sumatra) in the subfamily Goodyerinae — the 'jewel orchid' group grown for foliage rather than flowers. The common name 'Lightning Jewel Orchid' comes from the extraordinary pattern on the leaves: dark emerald-green to near-black, velvety, oval leaves decorated with an iridescent network of veins in vivid gold to golden-green that branch and rebranch in a pattern precisely resembling lightning bolts or an elaborate golden circuit board. The metallic sheen of the veins is real — it results from the cellular structure of the leaf reflecting light at specific angles, creating an electrifying golden glow in even dim conditions. The effect in low light is genuinely startling — the golden veins seem to glow from within. Macodes petola is the most dramatic of the jewel orchids in terms of vein contrast and iridescence and is considered a crown jewel of terrarium and vivarium culture. Produces small, inconsequential reddish-brown flowers. Non-toxic.

common_name: Lightning Strike Toad Lily (Variegated Gold-and-Green Foliage Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to mostly shade with even moisture; Lightning Strike is a Japanese selection valued for boldly striped gold-and-green variegated foliage in addition to its typical toad lily flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to mostly shade with consistent moisture; Lightning Strike is a striking variegated toad lily, its arching stems and leaves streaked in gold and green like bolts of lightning, providing strong foliage interest for months before the mauve-purple, heavily spotted flowers open on two-foot arching stems in late summer to fall. Because the variegation develops best with a bit more light than deep shade allows, give it a spot with morning sun or dappled light rather than the darkest part of the garden. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch with leaf litter, and divide congested clumps in spring as needed to maintain the plant's vigor and variegation quality.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; lignum vitae is frost-tender, extremely slow-growing, and native to South Florida hammocks and the Keys.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; lignum vitae is frost-tender, extremely slow-growing, and native to South Florida hammocks and the Keys. Small, leathery, evergreen leaflets cover a dense, rounded canopy that bursts into a profusion of vivid blue-purple flowers, often several times a year, followed by bright yellow-orange seed capsules that split to reveal striking red-coated seeds, making it one of the most ornamentally distinctive native trees of South Florida. Its extremely dense, heavy wood — historically the source of the actual lignum vitae timber prized for its self-lubricating properties in ship propeller shaft bearings — reflects an exceptionally slow growth rate that has made wild populations vulnerable to historical overharvesting, so cultivated specimens from nursery-propagated stock help support the species. Extremely drought- and salt-tolerant once established, it thrives on poor, rocky, alkaline soil with essentially no supplemental care, making it a valuable, low-maintenance native specimen tree for a South Florida landscape.

common_name: Ligtu Hybrid Alstroemeria (Classic Mixed-Color Chilean Strain)
plant_note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Ligtu hybrids are a classic mixed-color strain derived from Chilean species, blooming in a broad range of pastel and warm tones.
directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, handling the brittle roots carefully. Ligtu hybrids are a long-cultivated Chilean-derived seed strain producing orchid-like flowers across a wide range of colors including cream, pink, orange, salmon, and red, often with contrasting streaking on the upper petals, blooming heavily in late spring to early summer before going dormant in the heat. Because it is a mixed seed strain rather than a single named clone, individual plants vary somewhat in color, giving naturalized drifts extra variety. Pulling rather than cutting spent flower stems from the base stimulates continued rebloom during the flowering season. In colder zones mulch heavily for winter protection or lift the roots for storage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Himalayan geranium spreads gently by rhizome to form a loose, weaving groundcover rather than staying in a tight clump.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and provide afternoon shade and even moisture where summers are hot. Native to the Himalayas and Central Asia, Geranium himalayense forms a loose, spreading mound of deeply lobed, softly hairy leaves and bears large, saucer-shaped, violet-blue flowers with darker veining and a small white eye through late spring and early summer. It weaves attractively among neighboring perennials without becoming aggressive, and its rich blue flower color is among the truest blues found in hardy geraniums, making it a valuable companion for pink- and yellow-flowered border plants. Cut the plant back hard after its main flush to tidy the foliage and often coax a lighter rebloom later in the season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to keep growth vigorous.

common_name: Lilac Wonder Colchicum (Early Rosy-Lilac Autumn Crocus)
plant_note: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer to early fall, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Lilac Wonder is one of the earliest colchicum cultivars to bloom, often flowering in late summer before most others.
directions: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Lilac Wonder produces goblet-shaped, rosy-lilac flowers with a white basal blush, blooming leafless directly from bare ground earlier in the season than many colchicum cultivars, often as early as late summer, and reliably multiplying into generous clumps over the years. The following spring brings large, glossy, strap-shaped leaves with no flowers, which must be left to die back naturally by early summer to recharge the corm for the next autumn's bloom. Its compact size compared to some larger colchicum hybrids makes it a good choice for smaller naturalized plantings or rock gardens. All parts are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from areas where pets or livestock might graze.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Lilafee epimedium tolerates dry shade once established but establishes fastest with regular watering through its first season.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Lilafee epimedium tolerates dry shade once established but establishes fastest with regular watering through its first season. New leaves emerge deep bronze-purple in early spring before greening for summer, and in the same flush the plant sends up wiry stems bearing showy, large, deep violet-purple, four-spurred flowers that hover like tiny orchids over the unfurling foliage — among the largest and darkest flowers of any commonly grown epimedium. Cut back old winter foliage to bare crowns in late winter just before new growth starts, since last year's leaves otherwise obscure the flower display. A superb choice for underplanting deciduous shrubs or lining a shaded path, it is deer- and rabbit-resistant and spreads slowly into a dense, weed-suppressing patch over several years.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm soil, covering seeds about 1/4 inch, or start indoors a few weeks early. 'Lilliput' produces a never-ending show of vibrant, small double pompon flowers on long stems all summer. Cutting the blooms for bouquets encourages the plants to produce even more, delighting butterflies and bees. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to limit mildew, and deadhead or harvest often to keep it flowering.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Magnolia liliiflora is the parent species that was crossed with M. denudata in China to produce the famous saucer magnolia (M. x soulangeana), and is itself a beautiful spring-flowering small shrub or tree with deep purple-red to rose-purple flowers.
directions: Plant in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; avoid sites with late spring frosts as the flowers can be damaged in zone 5–6. Magnolia liliiflora is the wild lily magnolia of central and western China, a small, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree (8–12 feet) that produces distinctive, tulip-shaped flowers with deep purple-red to rose-magenta exteriors and white to pale lilac interiors from late March to May (late spring); it is the parent species crossed with M. denudata by Chinese and French horticulturalists to produce the beloved saucer magnolia (M. x soulangeana). The flowers are later-emerging than many magnolias and more reliably miss late freezes in zones 5–6. Grown as an elegant specimen or mixed border plant; 'Nigra' is the most widely grown cultivar, with deeper purple flowers than the species. The species has been cultivated in Chinese gardens for over 1,400 years.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; pot-bound clumps bloom most freely — divide only when clumps are truly congested.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade after the last frost; lily of the Nile is one of the most effective summer-blooming perennials for the Gulf South, producing large globular heads of tubular blue or white flowers on tall naked scapes rising above strap-like evergreen foliage from early to midsummer. Water regularly during the growing season but reduce watering in fall and winter to trigger the rest period that promotes heavy flowering. Clumps perform best when somewhat pot-bound and should be divided only every 5–7 years. In zones 7–8, protect crowns with a heavy mulch over winter or grow in containers to move indoors.

plant_note: Plant pips (rhizome divisions) in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; lily of the valley spreads aggressively by rhizomes in suitable conditions and is best confined or planted where it can naturalize freely.
directions: Plant pips (root divisions) shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; lily of the valley is one of the most beloved and recognizable shade groundcovers in the world, producing two broad, ribbed leaves per stem and delicate sprays of tiny, perfectly bell-shaped, intensely and sweetly fragrant white flowers in late spring that are legendary in perfumery and bridal traditions. The plant spreads by underground rhizomes to form dense colonies that suppress weeds effectively. It goes dormant in summer; allow adequate space and companion plant to cover the bare ground. Thrives in cool, moist northern climates but performs poorly in the hot, humid deep South. All parts are extremely toxic — never confuse with wild garlic. 'Rosea' has pale pink flowers; 'Flore Pleno' has double flowers.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; lily-leaved twayblade grows in rich deciduous woods and shaded slopes across the eastern and midwestern US and depends on soil mycorrhizae, so wild-dug plants rarely survive transplant.
directions: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Lily-leaved twayblade produces two broad, shiny, ribbed basal leaves that could easily be mistaken for a small hosta, but in late spring it sends up a loose spike of unusual dusky purple-brown flowers with a wide, translucent lip, giving it a subtle, almost otherworldly charm among more familiar woodland wildflowers. It grows scattered through rich deciduous forest, floodplain woods, and shaded slopes across much of the eastern and midwestern United States, typically appearing as isolated individuals or small colonies rather than dense stands. Like most native terrestrial orchids it relies on a long-term relationship with soil fungi, so wild-collected plants almost never survive transplant; source only from specialist native orchid nurseries and avoid disturbing the soil around an established planting once it is settled.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall; plants establish quickly and begin spreading within the first growing season.
directions: Plant in almost any well-drained soil, from deep shade under dense evergreens to full sun, though the darkest green foliage color develops in partial shade. This evergreen, clump-forming groundcover produces spikes of violet flowers in late summer followed by black berries that persist through winter; it is one of the most reliable plants for covering problem areas under trees where lawn grasses fail. Shear or mow plants to 3–4 inches in late winter before new growth begins to remove tattered winter foliage. Divide congested clumps every 4–5 years to maintain vigor; divisions establish quickly and can be replanted immediately.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; limber pine is highly drought tolerant once established and adapted to thin, rocky, nutrient-poor subalpine soils. Very long-lived — excellent for dry, high-elevation or exposed site plantings.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; limber pine is a classic five-needle (white pine group) pine of the Rocky Mountains and Great Basin, named for its extraordinarily flexible young branches and branchlets that can be tied in knots without breaking — a key adaptation to the heavy snow loads of its high-elevation, exposed, windswept native habitats on rocky ridges and subalpine parklands from Montana south to Arizona and New Mexico. Often grows alongside bristlecone pine and whitebark pine at the highest elevations, reaching 2,000–5,000 years of age in some ancient specimens. The large, wingless seeds (lacking the wind-dispersal wing of most pines) are dispersed almost exclusively by Clark's nutcracker, which caches thousands of seeds annually. Like whitebark pine, it is threatened by white pine blister rust (Cronartium ribicola). An excellent cold-hardy, drought-tolerant ornamental pine for high plains, foothills, and rocky mountain sites.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, surface sowing since the fine seed needs light to germinate; Lime Green produces unusual chartreuse-green, star-shaped flowers that pair well with almost any other flower color and are fragrant in the evening.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost danger passes. Lime Green is a favorite flowering tobacco cultivar among garden designers and cut-flower growers for its unusual, muted chartreuse-green, star-shaped flowers, a soft color that blends easily into nearly any planting scheme rather than competing for attention. The tubular flowers open in clusters atop sticky, aromatic foliage and release a noticeable sweet fragrance in the evening, attracting moths and other night-flying pollinators. It blooms over a long summer season with routine deadheading and self-seeds modestly in a favorable site, and tolerates the heat and humidity of a Gulf South summer better than many old-fashioned flowering annuals.

common_name: Lime Marmalade Heuchera (Chartreuse Ruffled Coral Bells)
plant_note: Set divisions or potted plants in spring in rich, well-drained soil, spacing about a foot apart and watering consistently while roots establish.
directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil and avoid heavy clay or standing water, which quickly rots the shallow crown of most coral bells. Bright, indirect light or a few hours of morning sun keeps the ruffled leaves glowing chartreuse without bleaching them out in hot afternoon exposure. Its large, deeply lobed, lime-green leaves stay vivid through the growing season and take on warmer amber tones in cool fall weather, with airy sprays of tiny cream flowers in early summer. The vivid color makes it a strong focal point in a shaded container or border where it lights up darker corners of the garden.

common_name: Lime Rickey Heuchera (Lime Rickey Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Lime Rickey shows good heat tolerance and performs better than many green-leafed heucheras in the South as long as drainage is excellent and afternoon shade is provided.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Lime Rickey is a distinctive chartreuse-to-lime-green heuchera producing brilliant, highly ruffled, almost neon-yellow-green leaves that are especially vibrant in spring before summer heat causes some fading. In the garden it functions as a luminous accent that brightens dark corners of the shade border, combining beautifully with deep purple or burgundy companions such as Obsidian heuchera, dark astilbes, and black-leafed Colocasia. Small white flowers appear on fine-textured scapes in early summer. Unlike dark-leafed heucheras, which hold color best in partial shade, Lime Rickey intensifies its chartreuse coloring with a little direct morning sun and can tolerate more light than most. Good drainage is the most critical cultural requirement for heucheras in warm, humid climates — root rot from standing water or poorly drained soil is the primary cause of decline in zone 8–9.

common_name: Lime Sizzler Firebush (Variegated Chartreuse Hummingbird Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lime Sizzler is a Louisiana Super Plants selection, a variegated chartreuse-and-lime firebush cultivar that keeps the species' hummingbird-attracting orange-red flowers while adding colorful foliage.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lime Sizzler is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated firebush selection with striking variegated foliage — leaves in bright chartreuse-lime with contrasting red-toned veining — that turns this reliable hummingbird shrub into a colorful foliage accent even between flushes of bloom. It keeps the tubular, red-orange flowers of the species, produced continuously from late spring through frost, which are a magnet for hummingbirds and butterflies throughout the long Gulf South growing season. In zone 9, it behaves as a root-hardy perennial in a well-protected, sheltered spot, dying back after a hard freeze and resprouting from the roots in spring, or it can be grown as a fast-filling warm-season annual shrub farther from the coast where winters are more severe. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, and prune out any winter-damaged wood in spring once new growth resumes.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rhizomes after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Lime Zinger is a compact xanthosoma reaching 2–3 feet (smaller than most elephant ears), making it well-suited for containers and small garden spaces. In zone 9 it grows vigorously in summer heat and humidity, reaching full size by midsummer. Unlike Colocasia, Xanthosoma does not need as much moisture and tolerates slightly drier conditions. In zone 9 the rhizomes can often overwinter in the ground with heavy mulching but are safest dug and stored indoors in frost-free conditions.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil; Lime Zinger is a compact Xanthosoma cultivar with exceptionally vivid, clear chartreuse to lime-yellow-green leaves that glow with an almost electric intensity in shaded garden settings. While most elephant ears are dark green or dramatically colored with dark burgundy or black, Lime Zinger's brilliant chartreuse-yellow foliage brings an entirely different quality of light and energy to shade gardens — the luminous yellow-green leaves reflect and amplify ambient light in ways that dark-foliaged plants cannot, visually brightening shaded areas that typically appear gloomy and low-energy. The compact 2–3 foot height distinguishes Lime Zinger from the 4–6 foot stature of larger elephant ear varieties, making it practical for smaller spaces, container cultivation, and foreground positions in shade garden designs. In zone 9's humid subtropical climate, Lime Zinger thrives from late spring through fall, rapidly producing new leaves that emerge chartreuse and mature to lime green with each unfurling adding drama to the seasonal garden progression.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential to prevent crown rot.
directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; wet or heavy ground causes rot far more readily than this sedum is bothered by drought. Lime Zinger produces bright chartreuse-green succulent foliage edged in a fine, contrasting cherry-red margin, a color combination that intensifies with more sun exposure, topped by clusters of pink summer flowers that draw bees and butterflies. Its compact, mounding habit and season-long foliage color make it a strong choice for rock gardens, border edges, and mixed succulent containers where a low-maintenance, drought-tolerant color accent is wanted. Shear back lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and tidy, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years to renew vigor.

common_name: Lime-Bark Crape Myrtle (Uncommon Smooth Pale-Bark Species)
plant_note: Plant container trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Lagerstroemia limii is an uncommon crape myrtle species grown chiefly for its smooth, pale, flaking bark.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Lagerstroemia limii is an uncommon species crape myrtle valued primarily for its smooth, pale bark that flakes away in thin patches to reveal lighter tones beneath, a subtler bark effect than the boldly mottled trunks of subcostata or fauriei types, paired with modest clusters of small white summer flowers. Its rarity in cultivation makes it more a collector's specimen than a mainstream landscape plant, best suited to gardeners specifically seeking species-level crape myrtle diversity beyond the common indica and fauriei hybrids. Site it where the trunk can be appreciated, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches to preserve the multi-trunked form that shows off the bark.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Limelight tolerates full sun in zone 9 better than French hydrangea but benefits from afternoon shade — morning sun with afternoon shade maintains the attractive chartreuse color longer before it fades to white.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Limelight is the most celebrated panicle hydrangea cultivar — a Dutch introduction that has become one of the most popular landscape shrubs in America in the early twenty-first century, distinguished from the classic PeeGee hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata) by its unique flower color: the large, cone-shaped flower panicles (10–12 inches long) open in a distinctive pale chartreuse-green rather than white, gradually changing to creamy white as they mature, then transitioning to dusty pink and finally parchment-buff as they age through summer into fall — providing nearly five months of evolving ornamental interest from a single set of flowers. The opening chartreuse color is particularly distinctive and unusual in the landscape — fresh, cool-looking, and completely unlike any other flowering shrub color. Limelight blooms on new wood and can be pruned hard in late winter to control size and encourage vigorous new shoots with maximum flower production. In zone 9, Limelight performs well in morning sun and afternoon shade; full day sun may cause wilting during peak summer heat. The large flower heads dry beautifully on the plant for fall and winter ornamental interest.

common_name: Limelight Prime Hydrangea (Compact Improved Lime-Green Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Limelight Prime is a more compact, sturdier-stemmed improvement on the original Limelight, needing less staking to hold its heavy flower panicles upright.
directions: Limelight Prime carries the same fresh lime-green flower panicles that made the original Limelight one of the most popular panicle hydrangeas ever introduced, but on a somewhat more compact plant with stronger, more upright stems that better resist flopping under the weight of the large flower heads. The panicles age to soft pink and then tan through fall, extending the season of color well beyond the initial green flush, and because it blooms on new wood it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply during dry spells for the fullest, most weather-resistant flower panicles.

plant_note: Plant offsets in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, alkaline, gravelly or limestone-based soil in full sun.
directions: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; native to limestone scree in the French and Italian Alps, this species performs best where soil pH runs neutral to alkaline rather than acidic. Sempervivum calcareum forms neat, symmetrical blue-gray rosettes with distinctive dark maroon to blackish leaf tips that intensify in strong sun and cold weather, a color pattern that has made it a parent of many hybrid sempervivum cultivars grown today. It spreads slowly and modestly compared to more vigorous sempervivum hybrids, staying tidy in small crevice gardens, alpine troughs, and tufa plantings without swamping neighboring plants. Each rosette flowers once on a stout stalk after several years and then dies, leaving offsets behind to continue the clump.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in moist, fertile, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; limestone meadow sedge tolerates a wider range of light and moisture conditions than many sedges, from wet meadows to average garden soil.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil, tolerant of neutral to alkaline conditions, in partial shade to full sun; limestone meadow sedge is an easy-care native with attractive blue-green foliage, naturally found in wet meadows, moist woodland edges, and floodplains across much of the eastern and central US. It is more adaptable than many sedges, handling everything from consistently moist meadow soil to average garden conditions and tolerating both more sun and more shade than fussier species, which has made it a popular, forgiving choice at native plant nurseries for rain gardens, meadow plantings, and naturalistic borders. It spreads gradually to form a soft, low-textured groundcover and combines well with other native perennials in a mixed planting. Established clumps need little maintenance beyond routine moisture during dry spells.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost in rocky, calcareous, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; cold-moist stratify seeds for 3–4 weeks before sowing to improve germination. Best sited in rock garden settings or along limestone-based slopes and canyon edges where drainage is excellent and competition from taller plants is limited.
directions: Plant in rocky, calcareous, lean, very well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Limestone Milkvine is a native twining perennial vine of canyon edges, open rocky woodlands, and limestone outcrops in Texas and adjacent Oklahoma. It produces somewhat rough, heart-shaped leaves and small, dark maroon to brownish-purple, 5-petaled star-shaped flowers with a slight odor that attracts small flies as pollinators, followed by spindle-shaped seed pods that split to release wind-dispersed, plume-tailed seeds. Once established it is notably drought-tolerant and thrives without supplemental water in rocky, calcareous soils where most vines fail. It is an ecologically appropriate native vine for Texas Hill Country gardens seeking regionally adapted, low-water climbing plants.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to moderately moist, neutral to slightly alkaline, rocky or gravelly woodland soil in partial to full shade; limestone oak fern is one of the few ferns that prefers alkaline conditions and grows naturally in shaded limestone cliff crevices and rocky calcareous woods.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, neutral to slightly alkaline, rocky or gravelly, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; limestone oak fern is one of the few ferns with a preference for calcareous (limestone-rich) substrates, making it valuable for alkaline woodland gardens where most ferns struggle. Gymnocarpium robertianum is a delicate, graceful fern of shaded limestone cliffs, rocky calcareous woods, and talus slopes in northern North America and Europe, producing small (6–15 inch), broadly triangular, three-pinnate fronds with a slightly glandular texture and pleasant scent, arising from slender, creeping rhizomes that spread slowly to form loose colonies. It is closely related to G. dryopteris (common oak fern) but differs in its glandular fronds, preference for calcareous rock, and slightly larger stature. An unusual and choice fern for the rock garden or shaded limestone garden wall; combine with Cystopteris bulbifera and Polypodium virginianum on limestone outcrops.

subcategory: Gulf Coast native woodland pollinator perennial
plant_note: Set divisions or transplants into humus-rich, partly shaded soil in spring; this woodland native spreads gently by rhizome once established under Gulf Coast tree canopy.
directions: Plant in a woodland-edge or partly shaded bed with rich, moisture-retentive soil, spacing plants a foot or so apart so the clumps can knit together as a groundcover. Native to bottomland woods and shaded ravines across the Gulf South, this smooth-leaved wild petunia bears pale lavender trumpet flowers from late spring through fall that attract bees and serve as a larval host for buckeye and other butterflies. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form an attractive, low-maintenance patch under high shade where turf struggles. Established plantings tolerate both the wet spells and brief dry stretches typical of Gulf Coast summers.

common_name: Linde Armstrong Cleome (Compact Spineless Dwarf Spider Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Linde Armstrong is a compact, spineless cleome selection much shorter than the tall, thorny heirloom spider flower, making it far easier to handle and better suited to smaller beds and containers.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Linde Armstrong is a dwarf, spineless cleome selection that solves two common complaints about traditional tall spider flower: its sharp thorny stems and its ungainly, leggy height. This compact form stays under a foot and a half tall, producing the same fragrant, spidery, rose-pink flower clusters over a long summer season, without spines, making it much more pleasant to work around in a mixed border or container. It self-seeds modestly, tolerates heat and drought well once established, and draws hummingbirds and butterflies just as effectively as its taller heirloom relatives.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in early spring in moist, well-drained loam in partial shade to full sun; plant two or more unrelated seedlings or cultivars nearby, since a single plant fruits poorly on its own.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained loam in partial shade to full sun; linden viburnum tolerates a wide range of soils and takes on some drought tolerance once its roots are established. The broad, felted, toothed leaves resemble those of a linden tree, giving the shrub its common name, and turn shades of russet and wine-red in autumn. Domed clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are followed, on cross-pollinated plants, by a heavy fall crop of glossy red berries that persist into winter and draw overwintering songbirds.
