Its dense, rounded form and reliable fruit set make it a good understory screening shrub for a woodland edge or shaded property line.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; Lindheimer ironweed is native to dry, rocky limestone hillsides of central Texas and the Edwards Plateau and thrives in hot, drought-prone conditions where many other perennials fail.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, rocky to sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; once established, Lindheimer ironweed is drought-tolerant and virtually maintenance-free. Vernonia lindheimeri (Lindheimer ironweed or woolly ironweed) is a native Texas ironweed distinguished from common ironweed (V. fasciculata) by its dramatically white-woolly leaf undersides and stems — covered in dense, white, cobwebby hairs that give the plant a distinctly silver-woolly appearance, especially striking against the deep violet-purple of the late-summer flower heads. Named for Ferdinand Jacob Lindheimer, the 'Father of Texas Botany,' this species is native to the dry limestone hillsides and cedar glades of the Edwards Plateau and central Texas, where it thrives in the rocky, alkaline, well-drained conditions that defeat most perennials. Like all ironweeds, it produces brilliant violet-purple, thistle-like flower heads in late summer (August–September) that are extraordinarily attractive to monarch butterflies, swallowtails, gulf fritillaries, and native bees. The white woolly stems and leaf undersides create a beautiful silver-and-purple effect unique among Texas natives and make Lindheimer ironweed a particularly ornamental species compared to other ironweeds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Lindheimer muhly is native to limestone outcrops and dry slopes in central Texas and is outstanding for hot, dry, alkaline, infertile conditions characteristic of central Texas caliche and limestone soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Lindheimer muhly is highly drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the calcareous, rocky soils of the Texas Hill Country. Muhlenbergia lindheimeri (Lindheimer muhly or big muhly) is a large-growing, clump-forming native grass endemic to central Texas limestone country, producing stately, upright clumps of blue-gray, fine-textured foliage that erupt in spectacular fall bloom — from September through November, the 4-to-6-foot clumps are topped with 12-to-18-inch, airy, silvery-blue to silver-gray flower plumes that catch and hold the light in autumn sun with extraordinary effect. Unlike the related and more widely known pink muhly (M. capillaris), Lindheimer muhly's plumes are silver-blue to whitish rather than pink-purple, creating a cooler, more elegant color effect. It is distinctly larger and more imposing than M. capillaris and is better suited to large landscape-scale plantings and mass drifts. In Texas Hill Country gardens and Gulf Coast landscapes, Lindheimer muhly is a landscape signature plant — combined with Texas sage (Leucophyllum), autumn sage (Salvia greggii), and native asters for a definitive Texas xeriscape composition.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost in well-drained, dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Lindheimer's ironweed grows naturally on dry limestone slopes, cedar glades, and rocky calcareous soils of central Texas. It is significantly more drought-tolerant than eastern ironweeds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry to moderately dry, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Lindheimer's ironweed is a Texas endemic named for Ferdinand Jacob Lindheimer, the 'father of Texas botany,' and one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant ironweeds in North America. While the more common New York and tall ironweeds require moist, fertile soils, this species is adapted to the thin, rocky limestone soils and extreme drought of the Edwards Plateau and Gulf Coastal Plains of central and south Texas. The brilliant magenta-purple flower heads — intensely saturated even by ironweed standards — are produced from midsummer into fall on stems silvery with fine white hairs. An outstanding zone 9a perennial for dry limestone garden conditions where other ironweeds struggle. Irresistible to migrating monarch butterflies, pipevine swallowtails, and numerous native bees. Texas-specific alternative to the eastern ironweed in hot, dry gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Lindheimer's muhly is native to limestone-based soils of the Edwards Plateau and south-central Texas and is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Lindheimer's muhly is one of the most striking large ornamental grasses native to Texas, forming graceful, arching clumps of narrow blue-green leaves 3–4 feet tall that turn golden-tan in fall, topped with silky silver-gray flower plumes 4–5 feet high from fall through winter. Named for Ferdinand Lindheimer, the pioneering Texas botanist, it is remarkably tough and adaptable — thriving in heat, drought, alkaline soils, and even rocky caliche where most ornamental grasses fail. The large, dramatic clumps provide outstanding winter structure and movement. It is somewhat tolerant of clay soils if drainage is adequate. Cut to 6 inches in late winter before new growth begins; established clumps need division only every 4–5 years when they become hollow in the center.

common_name: Lindley's Butterfly Bush (Weeping Purple Buddleja Species)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Lindley's butterfly bush is a spreading, suckering species that dies back to the ground in colder parts of its range and regrows from the roots each spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, giving it room to spread since this species suckers and colonizes an area over time rather than staying in a tidy clump. Lindley's butterfly bush produces distinctive one-sided, arching racemes of small tubular reddish-purple flowers from summer into fall, a looser and more graceful bloom form than the dense conical spikes of the common Buddleja davidii, and it attracts butterflies and hummingbirds just as readily. In the northern part of its hardiness range it behaves as a woody-based perennial, dying back to the ground each winter and resprouting vigorously in spring, so cut old stems to the ground in late winter to keep growth tidy. It tolerates poor soil and drought once established and needs little care beyond an annual hard pruning and removal of unwanted suckers at the edge of the planting.

common_name: Linen Zinnia (Improved Pastel Cream-Blush Cut-Flower Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Linen bears improved pastel cream-to-blush colored blooms, a modern cut-flower breeding introduction.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches. Linen bears large, fully double blooms in soft cream and blush tones, an understated, neutral color that pairs well with almost any bouquet or garden color scheme and has made it a favorite among cut-flower growers seeking a versatile neutral. Plants bloom heavily from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading or harvesting to encourage continuous production. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds or transplant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; lion's tail is fast-growing from seed and may flower in its first season. It is a large, woody-based sub-shrub reaching 4–6 feet in mild climates; in zones 8 and colder it dies back in winter but regrows strongly from the base. Outstanding for hummingbirds and butterflies. The leaves and flowers have traditional medicinal uses in South Africa, where 'dagga' is used colloquially (not to be confused with Cannabis).
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; lion's tail is one of the most visually striking tall sub-shrubs for warm climate gardens — a South African native producing from late summer through autumn and into winter (September through February in mild climates) long, upright, square-stemmed shoots bearing at regular intervals dense, globular whorls of velvety-textured, tubular, two-lipped, brilliant deep-orange to orange-scarlet flowers — the stacked orange rings of flowers arranged up the stem creating the 'lion's tail' silhouette that gives the plant its common name. Each individual flower is a vivid, velvet-textured, deep orange tube about 2 inches long projecting upward from the whorl, and a large plant in full bloom with multiple stems bearing stacked rings of vivid orange is one of the most spectacular displays in the subtropical garden. The color is a specific, saturated, warm orange-to-vermillion that attracts hummingbirds powerfully — migrating hummingbirds on the Gulf Coast flyway visit lion's tail repeatedly. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, requiring little supplemental water in zone 9 after the first season. Fast-growing from seed, potentially blooming in the first year. The traditional South African medicinal plant known as 'wilde dagga' (wild hemp) — no relation to cannabis.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall in a partially shaded woodland bed; cold stratification over winter significantly improves spring germination rates, and seeds should be pressed onto the soil surface with only a light dusting of leaf litter as cover.
directions: Lion's-foot is a tall, upright native perennial of the chicory family, with deeply lobed and variable leaves and drooping clusters of tiny, nodding, creamy white to pale lavender composite flowers that open in late summer and fall — one of the few native woodland wildflowers to bloom during this season under shade. Native to dry to moist open woods, forest edges, and thickets throughout eastern North America, it exudes a white milky sap when stems are cut or broken, a characteristic trait of the Cichorieae tribe. Grow in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade, where the nodding, whisker-like flower clusters add delicate late-season interest to the shade garden. Plants self-sow moderately in undisturbed leaf-litter and establish slowly, so patience through the first two seasons is rewarded with a long-lived, trouble-free shade perennial.

common_name: Lipstick Plant (Lipstick Vine, Red Bugle Vine)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket or trailing container plant in bright indirect to moderate shade; Lipstick Plant is a classic epiphytic trailer that performs beautifully cascading from hanging baskets on shaded porches and patios in zone 9. It cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F — bring containers indoors when temperatures drop. A 4–6 week cool, dry period (50–65°F) in fall can trigger the spring bloom flush. Propagate from stem cuttings in spring. Avoid overwatering — the succulent, epiphytic stems are prone to rot.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in fast-draining, well-aerated growing medium (an orchid bark mix or coarse potting soil with added perlite); Lipstick Plant is naturally epiphytic and requires excellent drainage to prevent root and stem rot. Aeschynanthus pulcher is a trailing, semi-succulent epiphytic vine from Malaysia and Java in the Gesneriaceae family — the same family as African Violets and Gloxinias. The common name comes from the flowers: vivid scarlet to red tubular blooms 2–3 inches long that emerge from dark maroon or dark brown tubular calyxes — the effect is precisely that of a red lipstick emerging from its case. The flowers are produced at the tips of the trailing stems (and sometimes along the stems) in winter-spring flush and sporadically throughout the year, and are an outstanding hummingbird attractant when the plant is grown outdoors in season. The stems are clothed in fleshy, glossy, dark-green, oval leaves that overlap along the stems. The cascading habit and attractive foliage make it excellent for hanging baskets and wall planters even when not in flower. Numerous hybrids and cultivars offer flowers in orange, yellow, pink, and bicolors in addition to the classic red.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 14–16 weeks before last frost date; lisianthus requires a very long lead time and is challenging from seed.
directions: Surface-sow tiny, pelleted seeds on sterile, fine-textured mix; do not cover as seeds need light and maintain steady 70–75°F. Seedlings grow extremely slowly for the first 8–10 weeks, so patience is essential — do not overwater at this stage as damping off is common. Transplant carefully after last frost into rich, well-drained, alkaline-leaning soil in full sun. The ruffled, rose-like blooms in white, purple, pink, and bicolor make lisianthus one of the finest cut flowers; harvest stems when 2–3 buds per stem have opened.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky, acidic soil in full sun; lithodora is intolerant of alkaline soils and poorly drained conditions. Root or stem cuttings taken in early summer are the most reliable propagation method.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; lithodora is one of the most intensely blue-flowered plants in horticulture, with flowers of a saturated, true azure-blue that stops visitors in their tracks when the plant is in full bloom in spring and early summer. It forms a low, spreading, woody-based mat of small, dark green, evergreen leaves covered in tiny blue trumpets. Formerly classified as Lithospermum diffusum. The cultivar 'Grace Ward' has particularly large, deep blue flowers; 'Heavenly Blue' is the most commonly cultivated. Strictly requires acidic, free-draining soil — it collapses rapidly in alkaline or heavy soil. Excellent in rock gardens, along walls, and cascading over raised bed edges. Best in areas with cool, humid summers (Pacific Northwest, coastal areas) and struggles in hot, humid inland climates.

common_name: Little Adder Agastache (Dwarf Compact Purple-Blue Hyssop)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Little Adder is a compact sport of the popular Black Adder agastache, retaining the dark purple-blue flower spikes on a smaller, more garden-scale plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, spacing plants closely enough to form a dense, low drift of color. Little Adder carries dense, narrow spikes of deep purple-blue flowers over aromatic, anise-scented foliage from midsummer into fall, and its compact scale suits smaller borders and containers where the larger Black Adder would be out of proportion. The tightly packed flower spikes are rich in nectar and draw bees and butterflies consistently through the bloom season, while the fine-textured foliage remains attractive even between flushes of bloom. As with other agastache, sharp drainage is critical for reliable overwintering.

common_name: Little Beeswings Dahlia (Small Orange-Bronze Ball Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Little Beeswings is a small ball dahlia with orange-bronze blooms flushed gold.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage bushier growth and more blooms. Little Beeswings bears small, tightly formed ball flowers in warm orange-bronze flushed with gold, a rich autumnal color combination on a compact, floriferous plant well suited to cutting gardens and mixed borders. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming through the season, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in spring in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; little bluestem thrives in poor, rocky, clay, or sandy soils and performs poorly if over-fertilized. Container transplants establish quickly in spring or fall.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in spring or plant container transplants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; little bluestem is the quintessential native prairie grass of the American continent and one of the finest ornamental grasses for dry, infertile sites. Blue-green to blue-silver in summer, it transforms to brilliant shades of russet, copper, and burgundy in fall, holding that color through winter while the fluffy white seed tufts shimmer in low sunlight. Outstanding for dry meadow plantings, naturalized prairie restorations, rain garden edges, and as a matrix grass for native perennial combinations. Leave standing through winter as the seed tufts are critically important to juncos, sparrows, and other seed-eating birds; cut back to 4–6 inches in early spring.

common_name: Little Bunny Fountain Grass (Miniature Fountain Grass)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Little Bunny is the smallest and most compact fountain grass commonly available — excellent for container gardens, small borders, and edging where even the compact Hameln would be too large.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Little Bunny is the most compact Pennisetum alopecuroides selection available — a true miniature fountain grass reaching only 12–18 inches in both height and spread, compared to the 24–36 inch Hameln and 36–48 inch standard species. Despite its tiny size, Little Bunny produces the characteristic fountain grass form in perfect miniature: the fine-bladed, arching, clumping foliage topped by small, fluffy, white to cream-colored bottle-brush plumes that sway gracefully with the slightest breeze. The diminutive scale makes it perfect for the front edge of borders, rock gardens, container plantings, and formal edging uses where even the most compact standard fountain grass selections would be oversized. In zone 9, Little Bunny blooms in late summer (August–September) and the plumes persist attractively through winter. Like all Pennisetum alopecuroides selections, Little Bunny is a warm-season grass that emerges late in spring, grows actively through summer, flowers in late summer, and is cut back to 4–6 inches in late winter (February in zone 9) before new growth begins. Very drought-tolerant once established; essentially maintenance-free except for annual cutback. Low-seeding — less invasive spreading than some fountain grass types.

common_name: Little Business Daylily (Miniature Wine-Red Floriferous Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Little Business is a compact, extremely floriferous miniature daylily with wine-red flowers, excellent for edging and containers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Little Business bears small, rounded, wine-red flowers with a bright green throat on a compact plant that produces an unusually high number of branches and buds per scape, giving it one of the longest and most prolific bloom displays of any widely grown miniature daylily. Its small stature and heavy flowering make it a favorite for edging paths, containers, and the front of a mixed border where larger daylily cultivars would overwhelm the space. Divide every three to four years when bloom declines, and deadhead spent scapes to keep the planting tidy.

common_name: Little Carlow Aster (Vigorous Hybrid Lavender-Blue Autumn Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Little Carlow is a vigorous hybrid aster bearing masses of small lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisies in autumn, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Little Carlow, a vigorous hybrid believed to derive from Aster cordifolius parentage, produces an exceptionally heavy late-season display of small, lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisies held in airy, branching sprays above heart-shaped lower leaves, earning it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It tolerates light shade better than most asters and shows good resistance to powdery mildew. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring, and stake or grow among sturdy neighbors if grown in rich soil, since strong growth can flop under the weight of bloom.

common_name: Little Cuties Adorable Heuchera (Miniature Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Little Cuties Adorable is a Proven Winners miniature heuchera bred especially for small containers, fairy gardens, and tight edging spaces.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Little Cuties Adorable is a miniature coral bells cultivar from the Proven Winners Little Cuties series, bred to stay notably smaller than standard heucheras, with ruffled leaves in soft rose-pink to amber tones on a diminutive mound just a few inches tall. Its tiny scale makes it ideal for small containers, fairy gardens, rock garden pockets, and tight edging spots where a full-sized heuchera would quickly overwhelm the space. Small flower spikes rise just above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the compact, colorful leaf display. Provide consistent moisture and sharp drainage, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Little Cuties Peppermint Heuchera (Miniature Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Little Cuties Peppermint is a Proven Winners miniature heuchera bred especially for small containers, fairy gardens, and tight edging spaces.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Little Cuties Peppermint is a miniature coral bells cultivar from the Proven Winners Little Cuties series, bred to stay notably smaller than standard heucheras, with crinkled, minty-green leaves overlaid with silvery highlights and fine dark veining on a diminutive mound just a few inches tall. Its tiny scale makes it ideal for small containers, fairy gardens, rock garden pockets, and tight edging spots where a full-sized heuchera would quickly overwhelm the space. Small flower spikes rise just above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the compact, colorful leaf display. Provide consistent moisture and sharp drainage, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Little Devil Ninebark (Dwarf Dark-Purple Foliage Ninebark)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in any well-drained to moist, acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; the dark foliage color holds best in full sun.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; ninebark is an exceptionally tough native shrub tolerating clay, poor soil, and drought once established. Little Devil is a true dwarf ninebark selection, staying under 4 feet tall and wide — roughly a third the size of the straight species and more compact than even 'Diabolo' or 'Summer Wine' — while still producing the same deep purple-black foliage and clusters of small white to pale-pink spring flowers that draw native pollinators. Its small scale makes it a good fit for foundation plantings and smaller mixed borders where full-size dark-leaf ninebark cultivars would be too large. Exfoliating bark on older stems adds winter texture; prune out the oldest stems at the base every 2–3 years to keep growth vigorous.

common_name: Little Gem Candytuft (Compact Dwarf Evergreen Candytuft)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Little Gem is a compact, dwarf candytuft selection well suited to rock gardens and small-space edging where larger candytuft cultivars would spread too wide.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential, since candytuft declines quickly in heavy, wet soil. Little Gem is a dwarf, compact perennial candytuft selection that stays smaller and neater than most cultivars, forming a tight, low mound of glossy evergreen foliage well suited to rock gardens, trough plantings, and tight edging where a spreading, larger candytuft would take up too much space. It produces the same clean white spring flowers typical of the species over its compact mound, and tolerates poor, rocky soil and drought well once established. Shear back lightly after flowering to keep the mound tidy and encourage the best bloom the following spring.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Gem is one of the few magnolia cultivars that can be maintained as a large shrub or espalier-trained against a wall for a completely different landscape effect.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Gem is the single most important and most widely planted named cultivar of the Southern magnolia — a compact, narrow-form selection introduced by Warren Steed of Steed's Nursery in Candor, North Carolina, that has transformed the usability of this iconic Southern tree for residential landscapes. The standard Southern magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora) can reach 60–80 feet and 30–40 feet wide, making it a poor choice for typical modern residential lots. Little Gem reaches 15–25 feet tall with a dense, narrow spread of 7–10 feet — fitting foundation plantings, narrow screening situations, and typical residential lots that the species magnolia would overwhelm. Most remarkably, Little Gem begins blooming at 2–3 years of age — compared to 10–15 years for seed-grown species trees — producing medium-sized (3–4 inch), intensely fragrant white flowers from May through fall in zone 9 with periodic bloom throughout the growing season. The leaves have the characteristic deep green upper surface and rich cinnamon-brown woolly undersurface (indumentum) of the species. Little Gem also makes an outstanding espalier subject, pruned flat against a fence or wall to create a formal evergreen screen. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil; Southern magnolias dislike wet feet.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Little Goldstar is an All-America Selections winner selected for compact form (16–20 inches vs 24–30 for 'Goldsturm') and extended bloom season. The mounding, non-flopping habit holds its form through bloom without staking — a consistent problem with standard-sized Rudbeckia cultivars in humid, fertile conditions. Deadhead or cut back spent flower stems to stimulate additional flowering; the main bloom is August–October in zone 9. Divide every 3–4 years when clumps become crowded and flower production declines.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Little Goldstar Rudbeckia adapts to a wide range of soils, is drought tolerant once established, and blooms most freely in full sun; Little Goldstar is an All-America Selections award-winning compact cultivar of Orange Coneflower (Rudbeckia fulgida), producing a dense, mounding form covered with the classic single, golden-yellow daisy flowers with prominent dark brown central cones that define the black-eyed susan. The compact selection (16–20 inches) is specifically bred to address the most common problem with standard Rudbeckia — the tendency to flop and decline in the heat and humidity of Southern gardens — by reducing height, increasing stem stiffness, and selecting for heat tolerance. Black-eyed susans are the quintessential late-summer and fall native perennial for the American garden, providing the most vivid and extensive golden-yellow display available from any native plant in the August–October timeframe when garden color is often difficult to maintain. As a native plant across the Eastern US, Rudbeckia fulgida supports native bees, seed-eating birds (goldfinches prize the seed heads), and beneficial insects throughout the blooming and seeding period that extends from summer through winter.

common_name: Little Grapette Daylily (Popular Miniature Grape-Purple Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; its compact habit makes it ideal for edging and small-space borders.
directions: Bred by Pauline Henry and registered in 1985, Little Grapette produces abundant small, grape-purple blooms with a green throat on compact, grassy foliage clumps, making it one of the most widely grown miniature daylilies ever introduced. Plant it in average, well-drained garden soil and it will form dense, floriferous clumps that need division only every several years. Its diminutive size, heavy bud count, and reliable performance across a wide climate range have made it a mainstay for rock gardens, mixed borders, and container plantings alike.

common_name: Little Hard Fern / Alpine Water Fern
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade; space closely for quick coverage of difficult ground under trees.
directions: Plant in deep to partial shade in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, making it an excellent choice for the difficult dry shade under conifers if additional moisture and organic matter are worked in at planting. Set small clump divisions just shallowly enough that the rhizomes sit near the soil surface, spacing them 12 to 18 inches apart; the creeping rhizomes will knit together over time to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat. Keep the soil consistently moist during the first growing season to establish the colony. Avoid alkaline soils and overhead irrigation with hard water, which can cause the fronds to yellow.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Little Henry is a dwarf compact selection (18–24 inches) of Virginia Sweetspire — far smaller than the straight species (3–5 feet) and better suited for low foundation plantings, border edges, and small garden spaces. It suckers slowly to form a colony; remove unwanted suckers to maintain a compact clump. In zone 9 the outstanding fall color (burgundy to orange-red to crimson, lasting weeks into November) is the most dramatic ornamental feature. Tolerates wet soils and periodically flooded conditions better than most ornamental shrubs.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Little Henry Virginia Sweetspire performs well in the partial shade typical of the Gulf South understory, with good color and flowering in conditions too shaded for many ornamental shrubs; Little Henry (sold under the trade name 'Little Henry', patent name 'Sprich') is a compact selection of Virginia Sweetspire (Itea virginica), a native deciduous shrub of the Gulf South coastal plain that provides three distinct seasons of ornamental interest — fragrant white bottlebrush flower spikes in June–July, healthy green summer foliage, and an extraordinary fall color display of burgundy, orange-red, and crimson that persists for weeks longer than most shrubs in zone 9's mild autumns. The fragrant white flower spikes (4–6 inches long) appear in June when relatively few other ornamental shrubs bloom, attracting pollinators during a midsummer gap in the landscape flowering sequence. As a native Gulf Coast species, Virginia Sweetspire is perfectly adapted to the heat, humidity, and periodic flooding of Gulf South landscapes — tolerating wet soils along pond edges, creek banks, and low-lying areas where introduced landscape shrubs often fail. The compact scale of Little Henry makes the ornamental quality of the species accessible for residential landscapes where the spreading colonizing habit of the straight species would be inappropriate.

common_name: Little Henry Virginia Sweetspire (Compact Fragrant White Native Shrub for Partial Shade)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained to moderately wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Little Henry spreads slowly by root suckers to form an expanding colony — a desirable quality for naturalizing in shrub borders, but plant where the slow spread can be accommodated.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Little Henry is a compact selection of Virginia Sweetspire (Itea virginica) — one of the most valuable and reliable native shrubs for eastern North American shade and partial-shade gardens, providing three distinct seasons of ornamental interest in a small, manageable size suitable for mixed borders and foundation plantings. In late spring to early summer (May–June in zone 9), Little Henry produces long, arching, fragrant white flower racemes (3–4 inches) that droop gracefully from the branches, providing light sweetly-scented bloom when many shrubs have finished flowering. The summer foliage is clean, medium-green, and disease-free. Then in autumn, Little Henry delivers one of the most reliable and vivid fall color displays of any native shrub adapted to Gulf South conditions — the leaves turn scarlet, burgundy, purple-red, and orange, often holding the fall color longer than most other shrubs and providing persistent autumn interest through October and into November in zone 9. The compact habit (2–3 feet versus 4–5 feet for the standard species) makes Little Henry more versatile in typical garden settings. Virginia Sweetspire is native to moist woods and stream banks throughout the eastern US, including Gulf Coast regions, providing excellent ecological value — it is a larval host for several moths and provides wildlife habitat through the winter.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Little Honey's golden foliage colors best with some morning sun but scorches in hot, direct afternoon sun, especially in the Gulf South — site with afternoon shade protection.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; keep evenly watered, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry, hot conditions. Little Honey is a compact, dwarf, golden-leaved sport of the classic native oakleaf hydrangea, Hydrangea quercifolia, selected for foliage that emerges bright chartreuse-gold in spring and holds strong golden color through summer before turning shades of orange-red in fall — a dramatic color echo of the oakleaf's already excellent native fall display. Creamy white, cone-shaped flower panicles appear in early summer, aging to soft pink, though the golden foliage is the primary draw of this compact cultivar, which stays considerably smaller than the species and fits well into smaller shaded gardens where a full-sized oakleaf hydrangea would be too large. An outstanding foliage-color accent for a partly shaded border, zone 5–9.

common_name: Little Joe Joe Pye Weed (Compact Native Butterfly Perennial)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Joe is a compact Joe Pye weed selection that brings the same pollinator value as full-sized Joe Pye species into a much smaller footprint suited to typical garden borders.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Little Joe brings the excellent late-summer butterfly appeal of Joe Pye weed into a compact plant roughly half the size of the towering wild species, producing dense, rounded clusters of dusty rose-purple flowers that draw swallowtails, monarchs, and bees in large numbers without needing the several feet of space required by taller Joe Pye selections. Its smaller stature fits a typical perennial border or rain garden far more easily than full-sized Joe Pye weed, while still providing an excellent native nectar source late in the season. It tolerates average garden moisture better than some Joe Pye species, though consistently moist soil produces the strongest growth and best bloom.

common_name: Little Joe Viburnum (Dwarf Native Walter's Viburnum)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Joe is a compact, low-growing selection of native Walter's viburnum, useful as a dense low hedge or foundation shrub in a fraction of the space the straight species eventually needs.
directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart for a low hedge. Little Joe is a dwarf cultivar of Walter's viburnum, a Southeastern native shrub, selected for a naturally low, dense, mounding habit that tops out around 2-3 feet, dramatically smaller than the straight species, which can reach 10-20 feet as an untrimmed large shrub or small tree. Small, glossy, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves (in the Gulf South, foliage often persists through mild winters) provide fine texture, and clusters of small white flowers appear in spring, followed by small red fruit that ripens to black and draws songbirds. Its compact size and native heritage make it a low-maintenance, wildlife-friendly choice for foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where the full-sized species would quickly outgrow the space. It tolerates a range of soil moisture from average garden conditions to occasionally wet sites, reflecting its native habitat in low woods and along streams, and needs little pruning to maintain its naturally tidy, compact form.

common_name: Little John Bottlebrush (Dwarf Compact Red-Flowered Bottlebrush)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained soil in full sun; Little John is a dwarf, compact bottlebrush cultivar reaching only 2-3 feet, well suited to smaller gardens and containers.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; bottlebrush tolerates heat, humidity, and short dry spells once established, though it does not tolerate wet feet. Little John stays notably compact and dense for a bottlebrush, reaching only about two to three feet tall and wide, yet produces the same brilliant red, bristly bottlebrush-shaped flower spikes as full-sized cultivars, blooming heavily in spring with lighter repeat flushes through the warm season and drawing hummingbirds reliably. Its dwarf, tidy habit fits foundation plantings, containers, and small garden beds where larger bottlebrush shrubs would be out of scale. Prune lightly after the main spring bloom to shape, and protect from hard freezes in the coolest parts of its range.

common_name: Little King River Birch (Fox Valley Dwarf Compact Selection)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or shrubs in fall or early spring before new growth starts; Little King, sold under the trade name Fox Valley, is a true dwarf river birch reaching only 10-12 feet, fitting spaces too small for standard river birch.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically flooded soil. Little King, marketed under the trade name Fox Valley, is a genuine dwarf selection of river birch that stays a compact, dense, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree only 10 to 12 feet tall, retaining the same attractive exfoliating cream-to-tan bark and fine-textured foliage as full-sized river birch cultivars but scaled for foundation plantings, small yards, or as a large shrub border specimen. It tolerates the heat, humidity, and periodic flooding of Gulf South conditions well. Fall color is a modest yellow, and it needs minimal pruning to maintain its naturally rounded, dense form.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Little Kitten maiden grass is one of the most compact miscanthus cultivars, well suited to small gardens and containers where full-sized miscanthus would be too large.
directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Little Kitten maiden grass is one of the most compact miscanthus cultivars, well suited to small gardens and containers where full-sized miscanthus would be too large. Fine, narrow, arching green foliage forms a dense, dwarf mound rarely more than two feet tall, topped in fall by small, coppery-pink plumes typical of miscanthus but scaled down to match the plant's diminutive size. Its small stature makes it one of the few maiden grass cultivars genuinely appropriate for a small border, foundation planting, or large container, offering the classic miscanthus texture and fall plume display without overwhelming a limited space. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Best established in spring from nursery-grown divisions into dry, open sites with sandy or gravelly, low-fertility soil. Avoid clay and consistently moist soils, which promote root rot.
directions: Choose a sunny spot with dry, infertile, well-draining sandy or rocky soil — conditions that would starve most garden plants but suit this diminutive orchid perfectly. Loosen the planting area to about six inches deep, mix in a small amount of coarse sand if drainage is questionable, and set the tuberous roots at their original depth. Water lightly after planting and then rely almost entirely on rainfall once the plant has settled in; overwatering is the most common cause of failure. Because of its tiny stature, plant little ladies' tresses in small drifts of three or more and mark the site, as the foliage disappears after flowering and the plant is easy to accidentally disturb.

common_name: Little Lamb Hydrangea (Fine-Textured Panicle Hydrangea with Small Dainty Blooms)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Lamb blooms on new wood, so it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing that season's flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; afternoon shade helps sustain flower quality through the hottest part of summer in zone 9. Little Lamb is a panicle hydrangea selected for smaller, more refined flower panicles made up of many tiny individual florets, giving the plant an airier, more delicate texture than the large, heavy blooms of cultivars like Limelight, and earning its name from the fluffy, lamb's-wool appearance of the massed small white flowers. Blooms open pure white in mid- to late summer and age to soft pink as temperatures cool in fall, held on sturdy stems that resist the flopping some large-flowered panicle hydrangeas suffer after rain. As with all Hydrangea paniculata, it blooms reliably on new wood, so hard pruning in late winter to shape the plant and encourage vigorous new growth does not sacrifice the coming season's bloom.

common_name: Little Lime Hydrangea (Compact Lime-Green Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Lime stays 3–5 feet — significantly smaller than the full-size Limelight hydrangea (6–8 feet) — making it practical for typical residential borders.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Lime is the compact version of the celebrated Limelight hydrangea — a dwarf selection (3–5 feet) that produces the same distinctive chartreuse-to-cream flower panicles in a proportionate size for smaller residential garden spaces where the full-size Limelight (6–8 feet) would dominate. The flower color progression is identical to Limelight: opening chartreuse-green in midsummer, maturing to creamy white, and transitioning through pink to dusty rose and finally buff-parchment as the flowers age through summer into fall — providing a 4–5 month evolving color display from a single set of flower heads. Like all Hydrangea paniculata cultivars, Little Lime blooms on new wood and is pruned hard in late winter (to 12–18 inches) to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum flower production. This makes it essentially foolproof — unlike French hydrangeas that lose flowers if pruned at the wrong time, Little Lime reliably flowers on whatever new wood it produces after any pruning regime. In zone 9, morning sun with afternoon shade is preferred — sufficient sun for good flower production with heat protection during the intense Gulf South afternoon. The compact size makes Little Lime suitable for foundation plantings, smaller landscape spaces, and containers.

common_name: Little Lime Punch Hydrangea (Compact Pink-Red Aging Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Lime Punch keeps the compact size of Little Lime but was selected for a deeper, faster color shift as the panicles age through the season.
directions: Little Lime Punch is a compact panicle hydrangea that opens the same fresh lime-green flower panicles as its parent Little Lime, but ages through a more pronounced rosy-pink-to-red flush by late summer and fall, giving a bolder two-tone color progression on a plant scaled for a smaller border or foundation planting. Sturdy stems hold the flower heads upright without staking, and because it blooms on new wood it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply during dry spells for the fullest panicles and the most vivid late-season color change.

common_name: Little Midge Palm Sedge (Compact Bamboo-Like Shade Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; Little Midge is a compact selection of palm sedge reaching only 8-10 inches, with the same whorled, bamboo-like foliage as the species.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; palm sedge tolerates wet soils better than most ornamental grasses, making it useful near a rain garden or pond edge. Little Midge bears the same distinctive whorled, palm-frond-like foliage arrangement as the species, but stays notably compact at eight to ten inches, well suited to smaller shaded borders or as an edging plant where full-sized palm sedge would be too large. Its bright green, fine-textured foliage brightens a shaded planting through the growing season. Divide congested clumps in spring, and keep soil from drying out during summer heat.

common_name: Little Nipple Cactus (Corky-Seed Cactus, Nipple Beehive Cactus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, gritty cactus mix, or set out nursery-grown plants in spring into rocky, alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun.
directions: Start seed indoors in a sterile, gritty cactus mix under warm conditions, or set out nursery-grown plants in spring into rocky, alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun; native to south and central Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico, this low, often solitary globose cactus grows nearly flush with the ground and is easy to overlook until its ring of small white to pink flowers opens around the crown in spring. Showy club-shaped red-pink fruits follow later in the year and persist for months, adding color long after bloom has finished. The plant's small size and slow growth make it well suited to rock gardens, trough plantings, and gravel beds where it can be viewed up close, and it needs no supplemental water once established in appropriately gritty soil. Avoid rich or moisture-retentive soils, which quickly lead to rot in this drought-adapted species.

common_name: Little Ollie Dwarf Olive (Fruitless Compact Landscape Olive)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Little Ollie sets little to no fruit, avoiding the mess and staining that full-sized fruiting olives can cause near patios and walkways.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Little Ollie is a compact, naturally dwarf, non-fruiting selection of common olive, prized for the same fine-textured, silvery-gray evergreen foliage as full-sized olive trees but on a dense, easily maintained shrub that fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and containers far better than a full-scale olive tree. Because it produces little or no fruit, it avoids the dropped-olive mess and staining that can be a drawback of ornamental fruiting olives planted near hardscape. It is extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soils, and needs only occasional shearing to maintain a tidy, rounded form, making it a low-maintenance evergreen backbone plant for xeriscape and Mediterranean-style landscapes.

common_name: Little Poncho Kousa Dogwood (Dwarf Heavy-Flowering Kousa Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Poncho is a dwarf kousa dogwood reaching only 8 to 10 feet, well suited to small gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Little Poncho stays notably compact for a kousa dogwood, reaching only about eight to ten feet at maturity, yet blooms as heavily as full-sized cultivars, covering itself with creamy-white, four-bracted flowers in early summer despite its small stature. Its diminutive size makes it one of the few kousa dogwoods practical for a small urban lot or foundation planting. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Little Princess blooms most prolifically in full sun — at least 6 hours of direct sun is required for the best flower display.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Little Princess is a classic compact Japanese spiraea — a neat, mounding dwarf shrub staying 18–30 inches tall with a wider spread, producing masses of small, rose-pink flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) in late spring to early summer against mid-green foliage. Where Magic Carpet spiraea is grown primarily for foliage color, Little Princess is grown primarily for its prolific pink summer flower display — the small, densely packed flower heads cover the plant in a vivid pink display for 4–6 weeks and attract bees and butterflies intensively during bloom. The compact, mounding habit and fine-textured blue-green to medium-green summer foliage that transitions to orange-red in fall provide seasonal interest beyond the spring bloom. Shear lightly immediately after flowering to promote a second, lighter summer flush and maintain the naturally compact mounding form — cutting back by one-third after spring bloom encourages fresh new growth and often produces additional flowering in late summer. Little Princess is among the most cold-hardy Japanese spiraea cultivars, and its compact size and adaptability to clay and average soils make it one of the most practical and reliable deciduous flowering shrubs for zone 4–8 landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after the main bloom flush to tidy the mound and encourage a modest rebloom. Little Princess is a compact, mounded spirea grown primarily for its abundant clusters of rose-pink flowers that blanket the blue-green foliage in early summer, rather than for foliage color as with the gold-leaved spirea cultivars. Its dense, tidy, low habit suits it to low hedges, foundation plantings, and mixed borders where a reliable flush of pink summer bloom is wanted on a plant that stays in bounds without heavy pruning. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor soil and urban heat with minimal maintenance.

common_name: Little Quick Fire Hydrangea (Compact Early-Blooming Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Quick Fire is roughly two-thirds the size of the original Quick Fire, fitting foundation plantings and smaller borders where the full-size selection would quickly outgrow the space.
directions: Little Quick Fire is a compact sport of Quick Fire hydrangea, keeping the same early bloom timing and unusually fast color change but on a dense, rounded shrub well under half the mature size of most panicle hydrangeas. White flower panicles open several weeks ahead of standard panicle hydrangeas in early summer, then shift to pink and finally deep wine-red within weeks, giving a long season of color change on sturdy stems that hold the flower heads upright without staking. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it tolerates a hard late-winter pruning to control size or renew an aging plant without sacrificing the coming season's bloom, and it takes more sun than mophead hydrangeas without wilting.

common_name: Little Quickfire Hydrangea (Compact Early-Blooming Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Quickfire is a compact sport of Quickfire panicle hydrangea, bred for a smaller mature size while keeping the same early-season white-to-pink bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangeas tolerate considerably more sun than bigleaf types. Little Quickfire is a compact sport of the popular Quickfire panicle hydrangea, offering the same trait of blooming several weeks earlier than most other panicle hydrangeas, with conical flower clusters opening white and aging to a rich pink-to-burgundy as the season progresses, but on a smaller-scale plant that fits foundation plantings and smaller beds where full-sized Quickfire would be too large. Unlike bigleaf hydrangeas, flower color is not affected by soil pH, and flower buds form on new wood, so it can be pruned back hard in late winter without sacrificing that year's bloom. Water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads in late winter to tidy the plant before new growth begins.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Richard is a compact, heavy-blooming white-flowered abelia selection.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Little Richard forms a rounded, compact shrub bearing abundant clusters of fragrant white flowers from late spring into fall, blooming more heavily and over a longer season than many other compact abelia selections. Its manageable size and long bloom period make it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a foundation planting or low hedge that draws pollinators for months. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs only light pruning to maintain shape.

common_name: Little Rocket Ligularia (Compact Spiked Leopard Plant)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently wet to moist soil, spacing clumps a couple feet apart to allow for their spreading habit.
directions: Plant in heavy, fertile soil that stays consistently wet, such as along a pond edge or low spot, since ligularias wilt dramatically in dry conditions even in shade. Morning sun with shade from the hot afternoon reduces wilting and leaf scorch during summer heat. A more compact form of the well-known 'The Rocket' ligularia, this cultivar produces the same near-black stems and bold, triangular toothed leaves but stays shorter and better behaved in smaller gardens, with narrow spikes of yellow flowers rising above the foliage in mid to late summer. It brings dramatic vertical form and bold texture to a shaded bog garden or streamside planting.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Little Ruby is grown for its foliage, not its flowers — the tiny white flowers are insignificant. In zone 10+ it persists as a perennial; in zone 9 it grows as a long-season annual that may overwinter in sheltered locations. The compact, mounding habit (12–18 inches) makes it ideal for borders, containers, and low-edging applications where the deep purple-red foliage provides consistent color contrast throughout the season. Pinching tip growth promotes dense, compact branching. In partial shade the foliage develops a deep burgundy-purple; in full sun it may become more red-toned.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Little Ruby is a compact cultivar of Alternanthera dentata (Brazilian joyweed) selected for its intensely deep purple-red foliage and compact, tidy mounding habit — an improvement over older, taller alternanthera varieties that required frequent cutting back to maintain appearance. The deep, saturated burgundy-red to purple-red leaf color provides a rich, jewel-toned contrast to chartreuse, lime-green, and silver foliage companion plants in container combinations and formal bedding designs. Alternanthera is grown entirely as a foliage plant for its color effect — the small, white, inconsequential flowers do not add to the ornamental value and the plant is typically sheared off when flowering begins to redirect energy into producing vibrant new foliage. In zone 9's hot, humid summer conditions, alternanthera thrives — heat intensifies rather than fades the foliage color, making it one of the few plants that actually looks better during zone 9's harshest summer months. Little Ruby's partial shade tolerance allows use in garden positions that receive less than 6 hours of direct sun.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall for spring germination after cold stratification; seeds require 3–4 months of cold stratification. Little silverbell grows in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade — a classic understory tree of the southeastern mixed forest.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; little silverbell is the smallest of the native silverbells (Halesia), forming a shrubby small tree to 25 feet with the genus's characteristic white, bell-shaped flowers in spring before leaf-out. The flowers hang in clusters along the bare winter stems and create a charming early spring display. The fruits develop the distinctive winged structure typical of the genus. This species is native to the Gulf Coastal Plain and Piedmont from South Carolina to Texas and is better adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South (zone 9a) than the more commonly planted Carolina silverbell (H. tetraptera). An excellent native understory tree for partial shade in moist, acidic, woodland garden settings.

common_name: Little Spire Russian Sage (Compact Russian Sage)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; Russian sage requires excellent drainage — it will not survive in heavy clay or wet soil, and is particularly susceptible to crown rot in zone 9's summer humidity if planted in poorly drained sites.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Little Spire is a compact Russian sage cultivar that stays 18–30 inches — roughly half the height of standard Russian sage — making it manageable in typical residential borders where the full-size species (3–5 feet) would require staking and frequent division to remain attractive. The characteristic soft, lavender-blue, hazy flower spikes and silver-white, finely cut aromatic foliage are present in the compact form, creating the same misty, blue-silver cloud effect but in a more contained, neater habit. Russian sage is named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 1995 and remains one of the finest blue-silver perennials for full-sun, dry situations. The hazy lavender-blue flower spikes provide weeks of color from midsummer through fall, and the silver-white stems remain attractive through winter as a structural element in the garden. Strongly deer-resistant; exceptionally drought-tolerant once established; attracts bees and butterflies. The key challenge in zone 9 is the combination of summer heat and humidity — Russian sage succeeds with absolutely excellent drainage, lean soil, and good air circulation. In heavy clay or wet sites, it is short-lived or fails to establish. In well-drained, raised bed conditions or gravelly soils, it is reliably perennial in zone 9.

plant_note: Surface-sow the tiny seed in spring on well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in a meadow, glade, or rock-garden setting.
directions: Surface-sow the tiny seed in spring on well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in a meadow, glade, or rock-garden setting, since this compact, non-spreading Oenothera stays tidy compared to its more aggressive relatives. Unlike many evening primroses, its inch-wide lemon-yellow flowers open in daytime as well as evening, drawing both day-flying bees and dusk-active moths, including specialist bees that visit only Oenothera pollen. It forms a low basal rosette with slender flowering stems and works well massed at the front of a dry native border. Deadheading is unnecessary, as seed capsules provide a modest food source for small birds through fall.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; prefers cool weather.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep in cool, moist soil in early spring. Unlike vining sweet peas, 'Little Sweetheart' is a dwarf bush type with profuse, lightly scented small flowers in a rainbow of colors. Its compact habit suits hanging baskets, patio containers, window boxes, and the front of a border. Keep roots cool and evenly moist, and cut blooms often to prolong flowering before summer heat.

common_name: Little Woody Redbud (True Dwarf Vase-Shaped Redbud)
plant_note: Plant nursery stock in spring or early fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Little Woody is a true dwarf redbud selection, staying only 10-12 feet tall at maturity, well suited to small Gulf Coast landscapes where a standard-sized redbud would quickly outgrow the space.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Little Woody is a genuine dwarf redbud, selected in 2000 by North Carolina plantsman Paul Woody, reaching only 10-12 feet at maturity with a tidy, vase-shaped form rather than the larger spreading canopy of the straight species. In early spring, the bare branches are covered in the classic rosy-pink, pea-like redbud flowers before the heart-shaped leaves emerge, providing the same spectacular native spring display as a standard redbud but scaled for a small yard, courtyard, or foundation planting. Water deeply during the first two years to establish the root system, then supplement only during dry spells once established. Prune lightly just after flowering if any shaping is needed.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; deadhead spent seed heads before they mature and avoid siting near natural areas, since Miscanthus sinensis is classified as invasive in parts of the eastern and midwestern United States.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, cutting the prior year's foliage back hard in late winter before new blades emerge. A compact, dwarf sport of zebra grass, it forms a tidy rounded clump of arching blades horizontally banded in cream and green, with coppery plumes rising just above the foliage in late summer. Because this species is documented as invasive in parts of the eastern and midwestern United States, gardeners in those regions should remove flower heads before seed set, avoid planting near wild areas, and check local invasive-species guidance before adding it to the landscape.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or fall and replant immediately; hexastylis grows slowly to form dense mats and is best divided from established nursery plants. It requires consistent moisture, humus-rich acidic soil, and can colonize dry shade under oaks once established.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained to moist soil in full to part shade; Hexastylis arifolia (littlebrownjug, heartleaf) is a native evergreen groundcover of the southeastern United States closely related to wild ginger (Asarum) — the two genera were formerly combined. The thick, leathery, arrow-shaped to heart-shaped leaves are deep glossy green, often with silvery-gray marbled patterns, and remain attractive year-round even in the coldest winters within its range. The flowers are inconspicuous ground-level jugs (hence 'littlebrownjug') hidden beneath the foliage, relying on fungus gnats for pollination. It is superb for covering ground in dry to moist shade under deciduous oaks, pines, and other native trees where its slow-but-steady spread creates a dense, weed-suppressing mat. An important food plant for the pipevine swallowtail butterfly.

plant_note: Plant small container-grown trees (1–2 gallon) in winter or early spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; live oak establishes best when young. Large container or balled-and-burlapped trees are slow to re-establish. Plant acorns immediately upon collecting in fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; live oak is the defining tree of the Gulf Coast landscape, forming magnificent broad, sweeping canopies of twisted horizontal branches draped with Spanish moss, with a single mature tree providing habitat for hundreds of species of insects, birds, and wildlife. The leaves are semi-evergreen in zone 8 (dropping briefly in late winter as new leaves emerge) and evergreen in zone 9–10. It tolerates salt spray, sandy soils, and periodic drought once established and grows steadily — 1–2 feet per year when young. The small acorns are critically important fall and winter food for blue jays, wild turkeys, squirrels, and deer. Plant far from structures and utility lines — mature trees reach 40–60 feet tall with 60–100 foot spread. A heritage landscape tree meant for centuries.

plant_note: Transplant small clumps with intact rhizomes in early fall in moist, well-drained, alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees; liverleaf is slow-growing and very long-lived, preferring undisturbed conditions once established.
directions: Transplant small clumps in early fall in moist, well-drained, alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; liverleaf (hepatica) is one of the earliest native wildflowers to bloom in eastern North American woodlands — its lavender-blue to white, delicate, many-stamened flowers push directly through the leaf litter in late winter to early spring, often before any other woodland wildflower. The three-lobed, leathery leaves persist through winter, often turning deep purplish-bronze in cold weather, and are replaced by fresh green leaves after bloom. Very slow-growing but extremely long-lived, persisting undisturbed for decades in suitable woodland conditions. Requires alkaline to neutral soil (unlike most woodland natives that prefer acid), making it suitable for limestone-rich areas. Nearly impossible to buy and best obtained from native plant seed exchanges.

plant_note: Pot small nursery plants or separate mature clumps in spring into a very lean, mineral, extremely fast-draining mix with minimal organic matter; living stones need almost no water while establishing and are far more likely to be killed by overwatering than underwatering.
directions: Grow in a shallow pot of very lean, gritty, mineral succulent mix in bright, direct sun, following a strict seasonal watering rhythm rather than a fixed schedule. Lithops (living stones, pebble plants) are southern African mesembs that mimic the pebbles and stones of their native habitat as camouflage from grazing animals, each plant consisting of a single pair of fused, fleshy leaves with a translucent 'window' at the top that admits light to the photosynthetic tissue below while the plant sits nearly buried in the substrate. Each year a new leaf pair emerges from the center and slowly absorbs the old pair, which shrivels and splits away, a process that requires almost no supplemental water; water sparingly in fall as the growing season begins, taper off through winter, and withhold water almost entirely while the old leaves are being reabsorbed in spring, resuming light watering only once new leaves are fully formed. Bright, direct sun year-round is essential to keep the body compact and prevent the plant from stretching; daisy-like white or yellow flowers, larger than the plant body itself, open from the cleft between the leaves in autumn.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in shallow water (1–4 inches) or saturated soil at pond or stream margins in partial shade once soil warms; requires consistent moisture and will not survive drought.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in shallow water or saturated, slightly acidic soil at pond or stream margins in partial shade; lizard's tail is a distinctive native aquatic perennial of southeastern swamps, stream banks, and freshwater wetlands, producing arching spikes of tiny white fragrant flowers that droop at the tip like a lizard's tail in midsummer, above large glossy heart-shaped leaves. It grows naturally in standing water and at stream margins from Quebec to Florida, and is an excellent choice for pond margins, boggy borders, and rain gardens where its attractive foliage and unusual flowers provide interest through the season. The plant spreads by rhizome to form naturalistic colonies. The fragrant flowers attract many small native bees and beetles. Excellent combined with pickerel rush and blue flag iris for a native wetland plant community.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost in spring into dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; plants establish quickly in heat and self-sow in open ground.
directions: Lizard-tail Gaura, now reclassified into Oenothera, is a native annual or biennial of dry, open, sandy or rocky ground across Texas and adjacent south-central states, producing long, wand-like spikes of small, 4-petaled white to pale pink flowers that open in the evening and fade to pink or red by the following morning. More compact and freely self-seeding than the widely cultivated Oenothera lindheimeri, it is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant and thrives with complete neglect in hot, dry conditions. Direct sow after last frost in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; plants resent clay or wet soils and will decline quickly if overwatered or crowded. In suitable open, disturbed, or sandy sites, plants self-sow freely and maintain a persistent colony.

plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark or in a shallow basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to filtered direct light; Bulbophyllum lobbii is one of the easier large Bulbophyllum species for intermediate indoor conditions. The single large flower per spike emerges from the base of the pseudobulb and holds itself somewhat upright — the lateral sepals, which are the longest parts of the flower, rock gently in air movement, a motion that mimics an insect to attract pollinators. Maintain moderate humidity and water regularly. Blooms spring–summer. Protect from temperatures below 50°F. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow mounted on cork or in a shallow basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to filtered direct light — Lobb's Bulbophyllum grows most vigorously when its roots can spread freely across a flat surface (mount) or in the shallow, free-draining conditions of a flat basket. Bulbophyllum lobbii is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, Borneo, Sumatra, Java, and the Philippines in the Orchidaceae family, one of the finest and most readily available large-flowered Bulbophyllum species for tropical orchid collections. Bulbophyllum is the largest genus of orchids (over 2,000 species), and B. lobbii is considered one of the most ornamentally satisfying for its balance of large flower size, pleasing fragrance, and relative ease of cultivation. The plant produces round, ribbed pseudobulbs each with a single, broad, thick, leathery leaf. From the base of the pseudobulb, a single (occasionally 2) flower stem emerges carrying one large (3–4 inch) flower: creamy yellow to pale lemon-yellow with variable dark spotting in pink, purple, or reddish-brown on the petals, and long, tapering lateral sepals that project outward and downward. These lateral sepals are hinged at the base and rock freely back and forth in any air movement — a movement that mimics an insect in flight and is thought to attract pollinators. The flowers emit a pleasant, slightly musky sweet fragrance. Named for Thomas Lobb, the famous 19th-century plant collector. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Nestle small divisions or spore-raised plants into shallow soil pockets on shaded sandstone or acidic rock outcrops; best in a dedicated rock or crevice garden with sharp drainage.
directions: Nestle small divisions or spore-raised plants into shallow soil pockets on shaded sandstone or acidic rock outcrops, replicating the crevice habitat this eastern native occupies as a naturally stabilized fertile hybrid between ebony spleenwort and walking fern. Its small, evergreen fronds range from simple lobed blades near the base to more deeply cut tips, giving each plant a variable, almost sculptural form. Best reserved for dedicated rock or crevice gardens with sharp drainage rather than typical garden borders, where it rarely thrives.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; palmate violet grows in dry to moist, open deciduous woodland and forest edge habitats across the eastern US.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; palmate violet is distinguished by its deeply palmately lobed, finger-like leaf divisions — distinctly different from the typical heart or arrow-shaped leaves of most native violets. The leaf shape is variable, with the spring leaves often deeply lobed and the later summer leaves less so. The violet-purple flowers in early spring are typical of the native blue violets. Growing in dry to moderately moist woodland conditions, it is more tolerant of dry shade than the moisture-requiring woodland violets. Like all native violets, it provides larval food for multiple fritillary butterfly species including the great spangled fritillary, Diana fritillary, and regal fritillary. An ecologically important woodland plant for butterfly gardeners.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; loblolly bay requires strongly acidic, consistently moist to wet soil — it will not grow in neutral, alkaline, or dry conditions and must have peaty, humus-rich, well-aerated acid soil.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich, peaty, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun — loblolly bay is a spectacular native evergreen tree of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic coastal plain bay swamps and wet pine flatwoods, producing 2.5–3 inch, pure white, camellia-like flowers with prominent gold stamens that appear from June through October in the hottest part of the summer when few other flowering trees bloom. The dark, glossy, evergreen leaves are handsome year-round; the bark is attractively furrowed and gray. It grows naturally in the acidic, peaty, frequently saturated soils of bay swamps, seeps, and wet flatwood depressions — conditions exactly matching an acidic, moist bog garden or the wet margins of a natural pond. It is closely related to the camellia family and equally demanding in its soil pH requirements; failure is almost always caused by insufficiently acidic soil. An outstanding native flowering tree for wet, acidic, shaded garden sites in zone 7–9.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root seedlings in fall or early spring in average to moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; loblolly pine grows quickly on a wide range of soils and is the dominant commercial timber pine of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain.
directions: Plant container-grown or bare-root seedlings in fall or early spring in average to moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; loblolly pine grows quickly on a wide range of soils and is the dominant commercial timber pine of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain. Long, dark green needles in bundles of three clothe a fast-growing, straight-trunked tree that can add two or more feet of height per year on a good site, eventually reaching well over 100 feet with a broad, rounded crown at maturity, making it one of the most economically important timber and pulpwood trees in the American South. It reseeds itself readily on disturbed and cutover ground and is a familiar, defining tree of the region's forests, providing habitat and seed for a wide range of birds and mammals including favored nesting habitat for red-cockaded woodpeckers in older stands. Give it plenty of room to reach full size, since it is not a small-yard tree, and avoid planting where ice storms or hurricane-force wind could bring down large limbs near structures.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after temperatures are reliably above 65°F in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; heliconia requires consistently warm temperatures to thrive — avoid planting while soil remains cool. Divide clumps in spring every 2–3 years to maintain vigor.
