directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; heliconia is one of the most exotic and spectacular tropical plants available for zone 9–12 gardens, producing large, bold banana-like foliage and dramatic flower bracts in brilliant shades of red, orange, and yellow that attract hummingbirds prolifically. H. psittacorum (parrot heliconia) is one of the smaller and most adaptable species, with slender upright stems 3–5 feet tall and colorful upright flower bracts in red-orange with green and yellow tipping — produced nearly year-round in frost-free gardens. The flowers are outstanding in tropical cut flower arrangements. Heliconias require consistent heat, moisture, and humidity to thrive; they are not drought tolerant and decline quickly when chilled below 50°F. In zone 9a they may suffer frost damage to foliage but regrow from rhizomes in spring if the soil does not freeze. Apply a thick layer of mulch to protect roots during cold snaps.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, average to lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; lodgepole pine is highly adaptable, tolerating boggy, acidic soils (coastal form) through well-drained mountain soils. The inland form (var. latifolia) is used for large landscape and windbreak plantings; the coastal form (var. contorta) is more compact.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, average to lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; lodgepole pine is one of the most ecologically important and ecologically fascinating conifers in western North America — growing from bog edges at sea level on the Pacific Coast (shore pine, var. contorta) through the montane forests of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada (var. murrayana) to the vast subalpine lodgepole forests of the Rocky Mountains (var. latifolia). Named for its traditional use by Native peoples as the straight, slender poles for constructing tipis and lodges. The Rocky Mountain lodgepole is famous for its serotinous cones — cones sealed with resin that remain on the tree for years, opening only in the intense heat of a forest fire, releasing a massive seed rain to regenerate burned areas. This fire-adaptation allows lodgepole to be the dominant post-fire forest species across millions of acres of the Rockies. Severely impacted by mountain pine beetle (Dendroctonus ponderosae) outbreaks, which have killed over 70,000 square miles of lodgepole forest in western Canada and the US since 2000.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings under mist in early summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; Loebner magnolia blooms 1–2 weeks later than Magnolia stellata, making it slightly less susceptible to late-frost flower damage — an important practical advantage in zone 4–5 gardens.
directions: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Loebner magnolia is a hybrid between Magnolia kobus (Kobus magnolia) and M. stellata (star magnolia), combining the tree-like stature and vigor of the kobus parent with the larger, more numerous flower petals and earlier flowering of the stellata parent to produce a superior garden tree. In April the bare branches become covered with large, many-petaled, white to pale-pink, starry, fragrant flowers before the leaves emerge, creating a spectacular spring display. The cultivar 'Merrill' — vigorous, reliably flowering at a young age, and very cold-hardy — is the most widely planted and commercially available selection, and is considered one of the finest magnolias for zones 4–8. 'Leonard Messel' produces pale-pink to rose-purple flowers with typically 12 petals and is outstanding in a soft-pink color scheme. Both are superior to M. stellata in size, vigor, and visual impact. Tolerates partial shade and clay soil better than most magnolias. An excellent choice as a single specimen or small grove in lawns, borders, and naturalistic gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil; log fern resents drought and requires reliably moist conditions throughout the growing season.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade in zones 5–9; log fern is a naturally occurring hybrid between the Goldie's fern (Dryopteris goldiana) and the swamp wood fern (Dryopteris ludoviciana), combining the large size of Goldie's fern with the semi-evergreen habit of the swamp fern. The broad, lustrous dark green fronds are among the most striking of any eastern US fern, and the plant is especially valuable in the Southeast because it thrives in the heat and humidity of zones 7–9 where many northern ferns languish. It is commonly found growing on the moist, decaying logs and hummocks of southeastern bottomland forests, giving rise to its common name. Mulch heavily in zones 5–6 to protect the crowns in winter.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Lola echeveria holds its best pastel color and tightest rosette form in bright light and rots quickly in wet soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Lola echeveria holds its best pastel color and tightest rosette form in bright light and rots quickly in wet soil. A popular hybrid between Echeveria lilacina and E. 'Perle von Nurnberg,' it forms a tight, perfectly symmetrical rosette of smooth, powdery, pale lavender-pink leaves with a soft, almost pastel glow that intensifies in bright light and cooler temperatures. Its compact size and refined coloring make it a favorite for succulent arrangements, wedding favors, and mixed containers, and it offsets readily to form small clusters over time. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves to protect their delicate powdery coating, and provide bright light to prevent the rosette from stretching and losing its tight form.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; London Pride forms a dense, spreading evergreen rosette mat and tolerates deep shade and root competition from established trees better than most flowering groundcovers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tolerates deep, dry shade under mature trees better than most flowering shade groundcovers once established. Saxifraga × urbium (London Pride) is a classic cottage-garden hybrid saxifrage forming neat, evergreen rosettes of small, spoon-shaped, leathery leaves that knit together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat. In late spring, airy, wiry stems rise well above the foliage carrying loose sprays of small, star-shaped, pale pink flowers speckled with deeper pink and red spots — a delicate, long-lasting display that contrasts nicely with the low, tidy foliage below. Long a staple of English shade gardens, it has largely fallen out of fashion in American gardening despite being one of the toughest, most reliable evergreen groundcovers for difficult dry shade, tolerating root competition, poor soil, and neglect better than most alternatives. An excellent, underused choice for edging a shaded path or filling in beneath established shrubs and trees, zone 6–8.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade in spring; long beech fern requires cool, moist, acidic conditions and is most successful in zones 2–6 in cool, shaded ravines, stream banks, and moist forest understories.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade near streams or in cool, moist ravines; long beech fern (northern beech fern) is a delicate native fern of cool, moist, acidic northern forests, recognizable by the characteristic shape of its fronds — triangular in overall outline with the lowest pair of pinnae (leaflets) angled sharply downward and forward, giving each frond a distinctive winged appearance as if the bottom pair of segments were stretched down toward the ground. The fronds are soft-textured, softly hairy, and bright green with a fresh, cool quality. Plants spread slowly by underground rhizomes to form loose colonies on moist, shaded stream banks and in ravines. Requires consistently moist, cool, acidic conditions similar to its forest habitat and is not suited to drier or warmer gardens south of zone 6. Excellent for naturalizing in cool, moist, shaded stream-side gardens alongside ostrich ferns, interrupted ferns, and blue cohosh.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full to partial shade; long sedge grows naturally in wet woods, seeps, and bog margins and is valued as much for its unusual inflated seed heads as for its foliage.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; long sedge is a native wetland woodland sedge grown as much for its distinctive seed heads as for its arching, medium-green foliage — in summer it produces unusually large, inflated, spiky seed capsules clustered along the flowering stems, giving it a coarser, more textural presence than most fine-leaved sedges and making it a conversation piece in a shaded rain garden or bog planting. It grows naturally in wet woods, seeps, and bog margins and needs reliably moist to wet, acidic soil to perform well, tolerating standing water for extended periods. A good choice for the consistently damp, shaded low spot in a rain garden where turf and most perennials struggle. Established clumps need little care beyond adequate moisture.

common_name: Long-Lobed Alocasia (Malaysian Monster, Longiloba Elephant Ear, Tiger Taro)
plant_note: Plant rhizome or division in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a warm, humid location; Alocasia longiloba is a striking medium-to-large elephant ear from Malaysia and Borneo with dark, blue-green, slightly metallic leaf blades marked with pale blue-gray to silver veins and very long basal lobes that extend downward, giving each leaf an elongated, blade-like silhouette quite different from the broader-lobed appearance of most elephant ears. Grows best in high humidity, warm temperatures (above 60°F), and consistent moisture. May die back in zone 9b freezes but resprouts from rhizomes in spring. CAUTION: calcium oxalate in all parts; toxic to cats, dogs, and humans if consumed raw.
directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Long-Lobed Alocasia grows best in the warm, humid, partially shaded conditions of a protected tropical garden or shaded patio and produces its most dramatic foliage in consistent warmth and moisture. Alocasia longiloba is a rhizomatous, medium-to-large perennial aroid in the Araceae family native to Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo, and Sumatra — one of the many ornamentally valuable Alocasia species from the tropical forests of Southeast Asia. The plant produces large, elongated, leaf blades on sturdy petioles: each leaf is narrowly sagittate (arrowhead-shaped) with characteristically long, drooping basal lobes that extend significantly downward, creating a leaf silhouette that is more blade-like and elongated than the broader shield-shape of Alocasia macrorrhizos or A. odora. The upper leaf surface is dark blue-green with a slightly metallic or satiny sheen, and the prominent midrib and primary veins are pale blue-gray to silvery-white — creating a strong, graphic contrast of dark ground and light veins. The underside of the leaf is pale gray-green to lavender. The overall appearance is of a dramatically architectural, dark-and-silver tropical foliage plant of considerable beauty. Multiple horticultural forms and cultivars exist under the name longiloba with varying degrees of vein prominence and leaf color intensity. In zone 9, plants die to the ground in hard freezes but regrow vigorously from rhizomes in spring. CAUTION: all Alocasia parts are toxic if consumed raw — calcium oxalate crystals cause severe irritation.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow natural cold-moist stratification over winter; seeds germinate in spring when temperatures warm. Can also be cold-stratified in the refrigerator for 4–6 weeks and sown in early spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky or gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade or dappled sunlight, mimicking its native Texas canyon and limestone hillside habitat. The pale yellow, sweetly fragrant flowers bear extraordinarily long spurs — 3 to 4 inches — that are adapted for hawk moth pollination and are also visited by hummingbirds hovering at the long tube. Like other columbines, it self-sows freely once established and is short-lived (3–5 years) but perpetuates itself readily in place. Cut back spent flower stalks to prevent excessive self-seeding and to tidy the mounding foliage.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; long-flowered alumroot has slender, tubular flowers held on taller, more graceful stems than many heuchera species, giving it an airier presence in a woodland border.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; long-flowered alumroot has slender, tubular flowers held on taller, more graceful stems than many heuchera species, giving it an airier presence in a woodland border. Heuchera longiflora is an Appalachian native forming a low mound of softly hairy, rounded, lobed leaves and sending up wiry, branching stems of narrow, elongated, greenish-cream, tubular flowers in summer that hang somewhat bell-like rather than the more open, starry flowers of many other heuchera species. It is valued in native plant gardens for supporting hummingbirds and native bees over a long summer bloom period, and its shade tolerance and mounding habit make it a good textural companion for ferns and Solomon's seal. It is easy to grow under standard heuchera conditions and self-sows modestly in favorable sites.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early fall or immediately after flowering in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade; long-leaved lungwort is notably more heat- and drought-tolerant than other Pulmonaria species, which is significant for gardeners in zones 6-8 where summer heat limits most lungworts. The cultivar Bertram Anderson has exceptionally heavy silver spotting on very long, narrow leaves and is the most widely grown selection.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; long-leaved lungwort is the most distinct species in the genus, immediately recognizable by its extraordinarily long, very narrow, lance-shaped leaves that can reach 20-24 inches in length — far longer than the broader, more rounded leaves of other Pulmonaria species. These elongated leaves are heavily marked with irregular silver-white spots and splashes that cover much of the leaf surface, particularly in the cultivar Bertram Anderson which has some of the most heavily spotted leaves of any shade perennial. The late-winter and early-spring flowers are deep violet-blue to blue-violet, produced in drooping cymes on 8-12 inch stems. Compared to other lungworts, P. longifolia shows better heat and drought tolerance during summer, making it a better performer in warmer parts of the range. The distinctive long, spotted leaves provide an elegant, sophisticated texture in the shade garden throughout the growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; long-spurred violet is an Appalachian mountain species that performs best in cool, moist, shaded conditions with good drainage and slightly acidic soil.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — long-spurred violet is one of the most distinctive and elegant of all native violets, immediately recognizable by its unusually long nectar spur — 0.5 to 0.75 inches long, compared to the very short spurs of most violets — and its pale lavender flowers with darker veining and a darker eye. The long nectar spur specifically coevolved with certain long-tongued bees and butterflies that can access the nectar. It grows naturally in cool, moist, rich Appalachian woodland from Pennsylvania south to the Carolinas, preferring the well-drained, acidic, forest soils of mountain slopes and ravine banks. Less adaptable to hot, humid lowland conditions than most native violets. A beautiful specialty violet for cool-climate woodland gardens and native plant collections in zones 4–8, and a host plant for native fritillary butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very dry, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun for natural winter cold stratification and spring germination; in mild desert climates (zones 8–10) seeds can also be sown in early winter. Do not amend or fertilize — Longbeak Streptanthella thrives in the same impoverished desert soils where most plants fail. Scatter seed thinly across bare or sparsely vegetated ground and press lightly into contact with soil surface.
directions: Direct sow in fall in lean, very dry, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun for spring germination and bloom; Longbeak Streptanthella is a slender native annual in the mustard family (Brassicaceae) found on dry, sandy or gravelly desert flats and open creosote scrub from California to Texas. It produces very narrow, clasping stem leaves and elongated racemes of small, pale yellow to white, 4-petaled mustard flowers in spring that are followed by the distinctive, very long and narrow, strongly curved seed pods that give the plant its common name. It is one of many early-blooming native annual mustards that can carpet desert flats in favorable wet years, providing important early nectar for native bees and small butterflies emerging in spring. It is entirely self-sufficient once established in appropriate lean desert soils and requires no irrigation, fertilization, or maintenance.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into dry, well-drained, low-fertility soil in a sunny to partially shaded location. Seeds are minute; surface-sow and press lightly to ensure soil contact without covering. Cold winter exposure promotes spring germination.
directions: Longleaf Bluet is an excellent choice for dry rock gardens, gravelly slopes, and naturalized prairie or meadow plantings where its tolerance for poor, well-drained soils gives it a competitive advantage. Sow seeds in fall directly onto a raked, weed-suppressed seedbed, pressing them into the surface without cover, as light aids germination after winter cold stratification. Avoid amending soil with compost or fertilizer, as rich conditions favor weedy competitors and cause Longleaf Bluet to decline. Plants form tight clumps that bloom profusely in late spring and are long-lived when sited in a dry, open exposure with minimal soil disturbance.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; longleaf lobelia grows naturally in wet, sunny to partially shaded habitats of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain — wet flatwoods, seepage slopes, and marsh margins.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; longleaf lobelia is a native wetland lobelia of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, growing in wet flatwoods, seepage slopes, and the moist to wet margins of ponds and streams. The plant is distinguished by its unusually long, narrow leaves (longleaf) and produces typical two-lipped, bright blue-purple lobelia flowers on tall spikes in late summer and fall — a critical nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds during fall migration. Like cardinal flower (L. cardinalis), it belongs to the hummingbird-pollinated blue-purple lobelia guild of wetland habitats. An excellent native for moist to wet, partially shaded garden areas in zone 9a where its combination of height, bold flower spikes, and hummingbird attraction make it a standout plant.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in wet to moist, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; longleaf milkweed is a specialist of wet pine savannas and flatwoods, requiring wet, acidic, nutrient-poor, sandy soil that mimics its natural firebreak-maintained longleaf pine habitat. Avoid rich or amended soils.
directions: Plant in moist to seasonally wet, sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor soil in full sun; longleaf milkweed is a native of the wet pine savannas, flatwoods, and pocosins of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, growing in the unique combination of wet, acidic sand and frequent fire disturbance that characterizes longleaf pine ecosystems — one of the most biodiverse and most threatened habitats in North America. It has distinctively long, narrow, grass-like leaves (giving the species its common name) that are quite unlike the broader leaves of most milkweeds, making it texturally interesting in the garden. The pink-tinged white flowers attract monarchs and specialist milkweed bees. Because it requires wet, acidic, lean sand, it performs best in zone 9 coastal gardens with naturally sandy, poorly drained soils and is an exceptional plant for wet, acidic areas in the garden that challenge most other species.

common_name: Longleaf Pine (Gulf South Restoration Native Conifer, America's Most Ecologically Important Pine)
plant_note: Plant nursery container trees in fall or early spring; Longleaf Pine (Pinus palustris) is the signature tree of the Gulf South coastal plain — historically covering an estimated 90 million acres of the southeastern United States in a vast longleaf pine savanna ecosystem that stretched from Virginia to Texas. Today, less than 3% of the original longleaf range remains, making Longleaf Pine one of the most important trees for conservation planting and ecosystem restoration in the eastern United States. In zone 9, Longleaf Pine grows naturally on well-drained sandy and loamy soils from the coastal plain to upland ridges. Young trees (up to age 7–15) spend years in the 'grass stage,' appearing as a dense tuft of very long (10–15 inch) dark green needles with essentially no height gain — the tree is developing an enormous root system before growing upward. After exiting the grass stage, Longleaf grows rapidly, reaching 40–50 feet in 20–30 years.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in full sun with well-drained sandy or loamy soil. Do not fertilize or amend heavily — Longleaf is adapted to nutrient-poor soils. Longleaf Pine is not merely a native tree — it is the keystone species of an entire ecosystem that shaped the Gulf South landscape for thousands of years and still supports hundreds of associated plant and animal species, many of which cannot persist without the open, fire-maintained Longleaf Pine savanna. The original Longleaf Pine ecosystem extended from the Virginia piedmont to eastern Texas in a belt following the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains, and the extraordinary longevity of individual trees (documented specimens over 500 years old), combined with fire resistance provided by thick bark and the grass-stage growth pattern, made Longleaf ecosystems among the most stable and fire-dependent in North America. The ecosystem's collapse — driven by intensive logging for the world's largest timber market in the 19th–20th centuries, naval stores production (turpentine and tar extraction), and fire suppression — is one of the greatest ecological losses in American history. The 97% reduction in Longleaf Pine acreage has driven numerous associated species (the Red-cockaded Woodpecker, Bachman's Sparrow, gopher tortoise, and hundreds of plant species) to threatened or endangered status. For Gulf South homeowners and landowners, planting Longleaf Pine on appropriate sites (well-drained, sandy or sandy-loam soils with full sun) is the most ecologically significant native tree planting choice available — each established tree connects to and supports the broader restoration of one of North America's most imperiled ecosystems.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification over winter; cold exposure improves germination rates significantly.
directions: Longleaf Wild Buckwheat is a native perennial of dry, rocky or sandy open ground throughout the southeastern and south-central US — one of the few Eriogonum species native east of Texas. It produces mounded clumps of long, narrow, woolly-white basal leaves and slender upright flowering stems bearing clusters of small white to pale cream flowers in summer, followed by seed heads heavily consumed by native sparrows and finches. Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Established plants are notably drought-tolerant and long-lived once rooted into well-drained ground.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring (cold stratify for 4–6 weeks) in moist to average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; longsepal penstemon is one of the more shade-tolerant eastern penstemons and grows naturally along woodland edges, disturbed roadsides, and open glades. It is longer-lived than some penstemons but benefits from periodic division or reseeding to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; longsepal penstemon is a native eastern North American penstemon of woodland edges and disturbed areas from Ohio south to Georgia and west to Missouri — one of the more shade-tolerant penstemons in the eastern native plant palette, making it useful for semi-shaded positions where most western garden penstemons would decline. The flowers are rose-pink to lavender-pink with pale-pinkish-white interior tube and two pale guide lines on the interior of the corolla, typical of the eastern penstemon group. Larger and more robust in stem and leaf than many prairie penstemons. Blooming in May through June, it is visited by bumblebees and ruby-throated hummingbirds. Naturally adapted to the woodland-edge conditions typical of much of the eastern United States garden landscape — the open, moderately moist, slightly acidic conditions of old fields, woodland clearings, and roadsides. A valuable native plant for gardens wanting native penstemons that succeed in something other than full sun, dry, western conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in late spring in moist to wet soil in full sun; Longspike Tridens is a tall (3-4 foot) wet-prairie native bunchgrass with dense, spike-like brownish-purple flower clusters, a seed source for birds and mammals and larval host for butterflies.
directions: Direct sow in consistently moist to wet, average soil in full sun, at a pond margin, rain garden, or wet meadow site. Longspike Tridens forms an upright, clumping native bunchgrass reaching 3 to 4 feet, topped in late summer by dense, narrow, spike-like flower and seed clusters in a rich brownish-purple that stand out among the more typically airy or open panicles of other native grasses. As a genuine wet-prairie specialist, it fills a wet-soil niche that most ornamental grasses cannot tolerate, and its abundant seed provides food for birds and small mammals through fall and winter while also serving as a larval host plant for several native butterfly and skipper species. It requires little care beyond adequate moisture once established. Cut back old growth in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every few years if increase is wanted.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring (before new growth begins) or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade; longspur barrenwort is exceptional among shade groundcovers in its ability to spread and bloom under the root competition and drought of large deciduous trees — established plants require remarkably little supplemental water once the root system is well established.
directions: Divide clumps in early spring or fall, or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade; longspur barrenwort is a Japanese and Korean woodland perennial that is one of the most versatile, tough, and ultimately rewarding shade groundcovers for temperate gardens — it produces a weed-suppressing carpet of heart-shaped, compound leaves that emerge in spring with striking copper-bronze to rose-red new-growth coloring before maturing to medium-green, and in mid-spring bears airy sprays of delicate, spidery flowers with four prominent long spurs in white, pink, purple, or bicolor combinations depending on the variety. The species is among the most drought-tolerant of all shade-garden perennials once established, thriving in the dry, competitive root zone of mature deciduous trees where most other groundcovers would languish. Many species and cultivars are semi-evergreen, with the previous season's foliage persisting through winter in a rust-bronze color that is ornamental in its own right. 'Album' (white), 'Rose Queen' (pink), and 'Violet Queen' (violet-purple) are among the best-known cultivars; the Japanese nursery industry has produced hundreds of species hybrids.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; longstalk hosta is native to rocky streamside slopes in Japan and tolerates more sun and better drainage than many hosta species if given consistent moisture.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; longstalk hosta is native to rocky streamside slopes in Japan and tolerates more sun and better drainage than many hosta species if given consistent moisture. Hosta longipes is a wild species valued by collectors for its glossy, wavy-margined, heart-shaped leaves and tall flowering scapes bearing pale purple, funnel-shaped flowers with darker purple veining in late summer and fall, later in the season than most hosta cultivars bloom. Its rock-dwelling native habitat gives it better tolerance of sharp drainage and dappled sun than typical hybrid hostas, making it a good choice for a shaded rock garden or slope planting alongside ferns and epimedium. It has also been an important parent species in hosta hybridizing programs, contributing glossy foliage and late bloom to many modern cultivars.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; longstalked holly is unusual among hollies in having non-spiny, smooth-margined leaves resembling those of a camellia. Plant both male and female plants for berry production.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; longstalked holly is a Japanese evergreen holly quite unlike the typical image of holly — the leaves are entire, smooth-margined, and spineless, with a glossy, dark green appearance resembling camellia leaves. The small, bright red berries are borne on unusually long, slender stalks (reflecting the name 'pedunculosa' — long-stalked) that hold the berries away from the foliage in a distinctive dangling display quite unlike any other holly. One of the hardiest broad-leaved evergreen hollies, tolerating temperatures to –20°F in zone 5 with protection. Excellent bird food: the bright berries attract thrushes, waxwings, and mockingbirds in fall and winter. A refined and underused evergreen screening shrub or small tree that adds elegant, season-long interest. Requires both male and female plants for berry set.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Longwood Blue bluebeard is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Longwood Blue bluebeard is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring. Aromatic, silvery-green foliage sets off dense clusters of vivid, true-blue, fringed flowers that wreathe the upper stems from late summer into fall, a bloom period that provides valuable late-season nectar for bees and butterflies when many other shrubs have finished flowering. Introduced by Longwood Gardens and prized for its especially rich, saturated blue flower color compared to older caryopteris cultivars, it is a compact, easy-care choice for the front or middle of a sunny border, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established. Cut the whole plant back to a few inches from the ground in late winter, since it flowers on new wood and benefits from hard annual pruning to stay compact and floriferous.

common_name: Longwood Purple American Wisteria (Non-Invasive Native Wisteria Selection)
plant_note: Plant container vines in spring near a very strong support; unlike seed-grown American wisteria, named cultivars like Longwood Purple bloom reliably from a young age.
directions: Plant near a very strong trellis, pergola, or fence in full sun to partial shade; unlike the invasive Asian wisterias, this native selection is well-behaved and will not escape into natural areas. Longwood Purple, selected at Longwood Gardens, is a vigorous, heavy-blooming American wisteria cultivar with dense, fragrant, blue-purple flower clusters in late spring and good repeat bloom through summer, a reliability that seed-grown American wisteria does not consistently offer. It flowers at a younger age than seed-grown plants and responds well to pruning, staying more manageable than the aggressive Chinese and Japanese wisteria species widely sold. Prune twice yearly — once after the main spring bloom and again in late winter — to maintain size and encourage flowering spurs.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Looking Glass needs consistent moisture and appreciates a spot sheltered from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, which can scorch its thin silver leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; keep evenly watered through summer heat and divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early spring or fall. Looking Glass is a striking Brunnera macrophylla cultivar bred for nearly solid, luminous silver foliage, with only the finest tracery of green veins remaining visible — among the most reflective, brightest foliage of any shade perennial, capable of lighting up a dim woodland bed from a distance. In early spring, sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the emerging leaves before the silver coloration fully develops. The heart-shaped leaves hold their color and quality through the growing season better than many older silver-leaf brunnera cultivars, provided the plant is kept out of hot, direct sun and never allowed to dry out. An outstanding textural and color contrast plant for shaded borders and woodland gardens in zone 3–8.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination.
directions: Sow seeds directly into dry, sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in fall, pressing seed into the surface without covering, as light aids germination. Cold stratification over winter triggers reliable spring germination and establishment. Once seedlings emerge in spring, thin to 12-18 inches apart and avoid supplemental water once plants are established. Excellent for longleaf pine understory restorations and sandy native wildflower gardens in zones 6-9, where its loose, airy panicles of white to pale pink, lavender-marked flowers bloom in April and May.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; loose-flowered woodland sedge grows naturally in rich mesic forests and forested slopes throughout eastern North America. It is one of the most shade-tolerant native sedges.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; loose-flowered woodland sedge is one of the finest native groundcover sedges for deep shade conditions in eastern North American woodland gardens, producing graceful, arching, medium-width leaves of fresh green that provide attractive texture throughout the growing season. The nodding flower spikes in spring are loosely arranged — giving the species its name — and have a delicate, casual elegance. It grows naturally in rich mesic forests, forested slopes, and streamside woodlands on fertile, well-drained to moist soils. Substantially more shade-tolerant than lawn alternatives and an excellent low-maintenance substitute for turf beneath mature trees where grass struggles. Maintains attractive appearance with minimal water or care once established. Pair with native ferns, wild ginger (Asarum), and trilliums for a natural-looking native groundcover.

common_name: Lord Baltimore Hardy Hibiscus (Classic Dinner-Plate Crimson-Red Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Lord Baltimore is a classic 1955 hybrid hardy hibiscus, still one of the most widely grown red-flowered selections, producing enormous ruffled crimson blooms on a large, sturdy plant.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer since this wetland-edge native hibiscus wilts quickly in dry conditions. Lord Baltimore is a landmark 1955 hybrid, bred from a mix of native swamp and rose mallow hibiscus species, and remains a garden standard decades later for its huge, ruffled, crimson-red flowers that can reach up to 10 inches across, blooming from midsummer into fall on a robust, well-branched plant. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location and be patient rather than assuming it has died. It is generally pest-free and undemanding given consistently moist, fertile soil, rewarding minimal care with a spectacular tropical-looking summer display from a fully cold-hardy perennial.

common_name: Lord Derby Caladium (Classic Pink Strap-Leaf Translucent Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Lord Derby is a strap-leaf type with higher sun tolerance than most fancy-leaf pink caladiums — it performs well in morning-sun positions that would damage large fancy-leaf types.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Lord Derby is one of the oldest continuously grown caladium cultivars — a classic strap-leaf (lance-shaped leaf) type producing elongated, narrowly heart-shaped leaves with an unusual translucent, rose-pink to deep-pink coloration that allows light to pass through the thin leaf blade, creating a jewel-like, luminous quality that is distinctly different from the opaque coloration of most other caladiums. The translucent quality of Lord Derby's leaves — similar in concept to stained glass — is most striking when backlit by morning sun or viewed against a bright sky, creating an almost glowing rose-pink effect quite unlike any other commonly grown shade plant. The strap-leaf form produces a finer-textured, more graceful display than large fancy-leaf types, and the higher sun tolerance of strap-leaf caladiums generally allows Lord Derby to be planted in positions receiving 3–4 hours of direct morning sun without the bleaching and leaf collapse that damages large white or pink fancy-leaf types. Lord Derby has been maintained in commercial production for well over a century — a testament to the unique visual quality of the translucent rose-pink coloring that has no equivalent in other modern caladium varieties. In zone 9, Lord Derby produces reliably through the warm season with tubers overwintering in-ground. Excellent in mass edging applications along shaded walks and beds.

plant_note: Soak seeds and sow in cool early-spring soil at the base of a trellis.
directions: Lord Nelson is a richly fragrant heirloom sweet pea with deep, nearly navy-blue blooms on vigorous climbing vines. Soak seeds overnight and sow in cool early-spring soil at the foot of a trellis or fence, since sweet peas thrive in chilly starts and fade in heat. Keep the roots cool and evenly moist and pick flowers frequently to keep new buds forming. Provide sturdy vertical support for the five- to six-foot vines.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; lords and ladies grows in the cool, moist months (autumn through spring) and is dormant in summer. The glossy, dark-green, arrow-shaped leaves (often spotted with dark purple-brown blotches, though unspotted forms exist) emerge in autumn and are present through winter and spring — providing attractive winter-green foliage in the shade garden. All parts are highly toxic — especially the attractive orange-red berries. Keep away from children.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; lords and ladies is the classic British and European woodland arum — one of the most familiar and architecturally interesting plants of the deciduous forest floor, producing in early spring a distinctive, pale green to whitish-cream spathe (the outer hood) surrounding a dark maroon-purple, club-like spadix (the 'lords') — the whole structure exuding a brief period of heat and a faint odor to attract small insects for pollination. The broad, glossy, dark-green, arrow-shaped leaves (frequently spotted with dark purple-brown blotches) emerge in autumn and persist as an attractive winter-green groundcover through the cold months, disappearing in summer dormancy. In late summer the flowering stem, now leafless, bears a dense cluster of brilliant, traffic-light-orange berries in a tight cylinder on the persistent spadix — one of the most startling and visually striking berry displays of any woodland plant, the vivid orange-red contrasting brilliantly against the dark woodland floor. Self-seeds freely in moist, shaded garden soil to build naturalizing colonies. All parts are highly toxic if ingested — especially the attractive berries, which resemble no edible fruit. A classic plant for a woodland garden, shaded wall planting, or naturalistic woodland-edge garden in zones 5–9.

common_name: Louis Philippe Rose (Classic Deep South Heirloom China Rose)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Louis Philippe is an old Deep South China rose that blooms nearly continuously in the long growing season of the Gulf Coast and needs very little winter protection in zone 8-9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Introduced from China in the 1830s and long naturalized around old homesites and cemeteries across the Deep South, Louis Philippe is a classic 'found rose,' still turning up growing untended for a century or more with little care, testament to its exceptional heat tolerance, disease resistance, and toughness. It produces rich crimson-red, cupped, moderately fragrant blooms almost continuously through the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season, a trait that made China roses like this one especially valuable to Southern gardeners long before modern repeat-blooming roses existed. It thrives on neglect, needs only an occasional shaping prune, and is highly resistant to the black spot and powdery mildew that trouble many modern hybrid roses in humid climates.

common_name: Louise Arny Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Historic Orchid-Pink Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louise Arny, introduced in 1956, bears ruffled orchid-pink flowers on a historic Louisiana iris cultivar.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Louise Arny, introduced in 1956, bears softly ruffled orchid-pink flowers, a historic cultivar from the influential Arny breeding line that has remained popular among Louisiana iris collectors for its refined color and form. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: Louise Odier Rose (Fragrant Warm-Pink Bourbon Rose)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Louise Odier, a Bourbon rose from 1851, performs well in the heat and humidity of Southern gardens with good repeat bloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Louise Odier, introduced in 1851, is a classic Bourbon rose bearing warm rose-pink, cupped, densely petaled flowers with an exceptionally strong, rich fragrance, produced in generous flushes through the growing season on an upright, well-branched shrub. Bourbon roses like this one bridge the gap between antique once-blooming roses and modern repeat-flowering hybrids, and Louise Odier remains one of the most fragrant and reliable of the class for warm-climate gardens. Feed and water a bit more generously than tougher China or Tea roses, since Bourbons appreciate slightly richer soil, and prune lightly after each bloom flush to encourage continued rebloom.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; cold-stratify seed 6-8 weeks if starting from seed, since fresh seed germinates unevenly. Never dig from wild colonies — buy nursery-propagated stock only.
directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana phlox is a spring-blooming woodland perennial endemic to the longleaf pine and hardwood forests of Louisiana and adjacent states, forming loose, fuzzy-leaved mounds topped in April with fragrant clusters of pink to lavender-pink flowers. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form an attractive, non-aggressive woodland groundcover rather than the mat-forming habit of creeping phlox species. Give it the same conditions as other spring woodland wildflowers: consistent moisture in spring while blooming, a bit more tolerance for dry shade once established under trees, and a leaf-litter mulch that mimics its native forest floor habitat. Powdery mildew can appear on foliage in late summer humidity; good air circulation and morning sun help minimize it. An excellent, under-planted native choice for Gulf South shade gardens looking for spring color under pines and hardwoods.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana sedge grows naturally at the shaded margins of Gulf Coast swamps, bottomland woods, and pond edges and needs reliable moisture to perform well.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana sedge is a Gulf Coast native of shaded bottomland woods, swamp margins, and pond edges, forming arching clumps of medium-textured green foliage well suited to the wet-shade conditions that stump many other groundcovers. It is a good choice for the shaded, poorly drained corner of a yard, the margin of a rain garden basin under tree canopy, or the damp ground beside a pond or stream where standing water is common after rain. Established clumps spread slowly and need little care beyond adequate moisture; they tolerate occasional flooding without harm. Like other native sedges, it provides structure and habitat value with none of the maintenance demands of a mowed lawn, and it combines well with ferns and other wet-shade natives in a naturalistic planting.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana trillium is a Mississippi Delta and Gulf Coastal Plain sessile species that thrives in the same rich, seasonally flooded hardwood terraces as spring ephemerals like trout lily and bloodroot.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana trillium is a Mississippi Delta and Gulf Coastal Plain sessile species that thrives in the same rich, seasonally flooded hardwood terraces as spring ephemerals like trout lily and bloodroot. Closely related to the more widespread Trillium cuneatum, it produces broad silver-mottled leaves in a whorl of three beneath a stalkless, upright flower whose narrow maroon-to-bronze petals appear in late winter to early spring, well before the deciduous canopy leafs out. It is one of the few trilliums reliably suited to warm, humid Gulf South gardens rather than cooler Appalachian conditions, making it a good match for shaded beds under live oak or hackberry from Louisiana into coastal Texas and Mississippi. Top-dress with leaf mold each fall and avoid summer irrigation once the foliage yellows and goes dormant, since the dormant rhizome prefers to dry out somewhat during the hot months.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; nigella dislikes transplanting.
directions: Direct sow in early spring where plants are to grow, since nigella resents transplanting. 'Delft Blue' bears distinctive dual-colored blooms of violet-blue over snowy white with burgundy stamens amid feathery foliage. Drought-tolerant and easy to grow, it is perfect for borders and attracts pollinators, while the ornamental seed pods are prized for arrangements. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, and let some pods mature so plants self-sow for next year.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; do not start too early indoors as plants grow quickly and become rootbound.
directions: Sow seed on the soil surface and press lightly — seed needs light to germinate. Direct sowing is preferred as plants grow fast and resent transplanting. Thin seedlings to 18–24 in to allow the dramatic, rope-like crimson tassels to develop fully. The hanging panicles can be cut and hung upside down to dry when they reach full length.

common_name: Love-Lies-Bleeding Amaranth (Classic Long Trailing Red Tassel Amaranth)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Love-Lies-Bleeding produces long, drooping, rope-like tassels of tiny deep red flowers that can trail two feet or more, a dramatic, old-fashioned cottage garden and cut-flower favorite.
directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed; overly rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of the dramatic flower tassels. Love-Lies-Bleeding is a long-cultivated ornamental amaranth grown for its striking, long, rope-like, drooping tassels of deep crimson-red tiny flowers that can cascade two feet or more from the top of the plant, an eye-catching, old-fashioned cottage garden focal point and a favorite for both fresh and dried arrangements. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and self-seeds readily in a favorable spot, sometimes becoming a welcome volunteer in following years. Harvest the flower tassels for drying just as they reach full color, hanging them upside down in a cool, dry, dark spot.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; press seeds into the soil surface or barely cover with 1/8 inch of fine soil. Succession-sow every 2 weeks through spring for continuous bloom.
directions: Direct sow in early spring 4 weeks before last frost by pressing seeds lightly into the soil surface in full sun; nigella does not transplant well because of its taproot, so sow in place and thin seedlings to 6–9 inches apart after they emerge. The delicate blue, white, or pink flowers are surrounded by a wispy cage of thread-like green bracts that give the plant its fanciful name, and the inflated, papery seed pods that follow are equally ornamental and dry beautifully for flower arrangements. Succession-plant every 2–3 weeks through spring for continuous bloom; plants decline and set seed in summer heat. Nigella self-sows reliably and will naturalize in cool-season beds once established.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost; in zone 9 sow March–May for summer and fall display. Love-in-a-Puff self-seeds prolifically in zone 9–10 and will return each year from dropped seeds without replanting. It is a native vine in the Gulf South and will naturalize in moist, sunny garden edges.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; nick the seed coat or soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination. Love-in-a-Puff (Cardiospermum halicacabum) is a delightful lightweight twining annual vine native throughout the tropics and subtropics including the Gulf Coast, where it scrambles through shrubs and fence wire producing a continuous display of tiny white flowers and its signature inflated, papery, three-winged seed pods that look exactly like miniature balloons or Japanese paper lanterns — the pods are responsible for the plant's whimsical common name. Inside each round green pod are three round, black seeds, each with a perfect white heart-shaped marking where they were attached to the pod wall — the 'heart seed' of the scientific name Cardiospermum. The vine is lightweight and delicate, climbing trellises, fences, and other plants to 8–10 feet by twining tendrils, never heavy or smothering. In zone 9–10, it naturalizes freely from dropped seeds. The leaves and seeds are used medicinally in Ayurvedic medicine for joint inflammation; research has identified anti-inflammatory compounds in the plant. An excellent, low-care vine for adding airy texture and charming seed pods to Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Divide and transplant in early spring before fronds fully unfurl; water thoroughly after planting.
directions: Choose a shaded location with rich, moist soil such as a woodland garden floor or the base of a slope where moisture collects naturally. Plant divisions in spring at the same depth they were previously growing, and water generously through the first growing season. Do not be alarmed if fronds yellow and die back during dry summer spells; this species is summer-deciduous in drier conditions and will reliably re-emerge in fall with cooler temperatures and increased moisture. Supplement with compost or leaf litter each year to maintain the fertile, woodland-soil conditions this fern prefers.

common_name: Loyalist Hosta (White-Centered Dark Green-Margined Reverse Patriot Sport)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil. Loyalist is a reverse-variegated sport of the popular Patriot, with a white center and dark green margin.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partly to fully shaded site, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Loyalist arose as a reverse-variegated sport of the popular Patriot hosta, flipping the pattern so a bright white center is surrounded by a dark green margin, a striking inversion of its well-known parent's coloring. It produces lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer, though the bold, high-contrast foliage is the primary ornamental feature. Mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system from summer heat, and divide congested clumps every several years in spring.

common_name: Lu Shan Snow Camellia (Cold- and Heat-Tolerant White Species Selection)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Lu Shan Snow is a selection of tea-oil camellia noted for unusually broad climate tolerance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Lu Shan Snow is a selection of Camellia oleifera, the tea-oil camellia, bearing simple, fragrant, single white flowers with prominent gold stamens on a large, vigorous shrub or small tree, and it stands out among camellias for tolerating both harsher winter cold and hotter, drier summer conditions than most cultivars, a useful trait for gardeners at the edges of typical camellia range. It flowers in fall, and its tough constitution makes it a good rootstock or breeding parent as well as a garden plant in its own right. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Lucifer is a Crocosmia masoniorum hybrid and one of the most widely grown named crocosmia cultivars, valued for its exceptionally vivid, large, blazing-red flowers and strong garden vigor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Lucifer is arguably the most famous named crocosmia cultivar, a Crocosmia masoniorum hybrid bred by British plantsman Alan Bloom and prized for its extraordinarily vivid, saturated red flowers held in arching, one-sided sprays above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer. It is among the hardiest and most vigorous crocosmia cultivars available, tolerating colder winters than many other crocosmia and multiplying readily by corm offsets into substantial clumps within a few years. The intensely red, tubular flowers are a magnet for hummingbirds and make excellent, long-lasting cut flowers. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection; in zone 8–9 it is reliably hardy in the ground year-round. Give it full sun to light afternoon shade and consistently moist, well-drained soil for the best flower display.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Lucky series lantana is bred for a compact, uniform, mounding habit well suited to containers and small-space plantings.
directions: Plant transplants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Lucky series lantana is bred for a compact, uniform, mounding habit well suited to containers and small-space plantings. Clusters of small, brightly colored flowers in shades of yellow, pink, red-orange, and bicolor tones cover a dense, compact mound smaller and more uniform than older lantana selections, blooming continuously from late spring through frost and drawing butterflies and hummingbirds throughout the season. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives through the hottest, most humid part of summer with minimal care, tolerating poor soil and neglect far better than most bedding plants. It behaves as a root-hardy perennial in zones 8-11, dying back to the ground in a hard freeze and resprouting from the base the following spring, or is grown as a heat-loving annual further north.

common_name: Luna Blush Hibiscus (Compact Blush-Rimmed Red-Eyed Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost or set out container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Luna Blush is part of the compact Luna series, bred for garden and container use, staying well under half the height of older hardy hibiscus varieties.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer to keep this wetland-edge native from wilting in hot weather. Luna Blush bears white flowers with a soft blush-pink rim and a bold dark red center, on the same compact, well-branched, 24-30 inch frame that defines the Luna series, resisting the flopping common in taller hardy hibiscus. It flowers continuously from mid to late summer into fall, providing bold, tropical-looking color from an entirely cold-hardy perennial that dies back to the crown each winter and returns reliably each spring even after a hard freeze. Cut the dead stalks back to a few inches above ground in late winter, and note that new growth emerges late in spring, so avoid mistaking a dormant crown for a dead plant.

common_name: Luna Pink Swirl Hibiscus (Compact Picotee-Patterned Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost or set out container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Luna Pink Swirl is part of the compact Luna series, bred for garden and container use, staying well under half the height of older hardy hibiscus varieties.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer to keep this wetland-edge native from wilting in hot weather. Luna Pink Swirl bears distinctive picotee-patterned flowers, a swirled blend of pink shades radiating from a dark red center, on the same compact, well-branched, 24-30 inch frame that defines the Luna series, resisting the flopping common in taller hardy hibiscus. It flowers continuously from mid to late summer into fall, providing bold, tropical-looking color from an entirely cold-hardy perennial that dies back to the crown each winter and returns reliably each spring. Cut the dead stalks back to a few inches above ground in late winter, and note that new growth emerges late in spring, so avoid mistaking a dormant crown for a dead plant.

common_name: Luna Red Hibiscus (Compact Deep-Red Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost or set out container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Luna Red is part of the compact Luna series bred for garden and container use, staying well under half the height of older hardy hibiscus varieties.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer to keep this wetland-edge native from wilting in hot weather. Luna Red is a compact, well-branched hardy hibiscus cultivar bred for garden and large-container use, producing an abundance of enormous, deep red, 6–8 inch flowers over a sturdy 24–30 inch frame that resists the flopping common in taller hardy hibiscus. It flowers continuously from mid to late summer into fall, providing bold, tropical-looking color from an entirely cold-hardy perennial that dies back to the crown each winter and returns reliably each spring even after a hard freeze. Cut the dead stalks back to a few inches above ground in late winter, and note that new growth emerges late in spring, so avoid mistaking a dormant crown for a dead plant.

common_name: Luna White Hibiscus (Compact Red-Eyed White Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost or set out container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Luna White is part of the compact Luna series, bred for garden and container use, staying well under half the height of older hardy hibiscus varieties.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer to keep this wetland-edge native from wilting in hot weather. Luna White bears crisp white, 6-8 inch flowers with a bold, contrasting red central eye, on the same compact, well-branched, 24-30 inch frame that defines the Luna series, resisting the flopping common in taller hardy hibiscus. It flowers continuously from mid to late summer into fall, providing bold, tropical-looking color from an entirely cold-hardy perennial that dies back to the crown each winter and returns reliably each spring even after a hard freeze. Cut the dead stalks back to a few inches above ground in late winter, and note that new growth emerges late in spring, so avoid mistaking a dormant crown for a dead plant.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in a shaded, moist site; division is the most reliable propagation method.
directions: Plant in deep shade to partial shade in humus-rich, consistently moist soil; lungwort is one of the best shade perennials, offering both attractive silver-spotted foliage and early spring flowers. Pink buds open to blue or violet tubular flowers in early spring, often when little else is in bloom, providing nectar for early pollinators. In hot, dry summers the leaves may develop powdery mildew — shear back affected foliage after flowering and new, fresh leaves will emerge. Divide clumps every 3–4 years immediately after flowering to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; lungwort is among the first shade perennials to bloom in late winter and requires consistently moist soil throughout the growing season.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, spacing 12–18 inches apart; the silver-spotted leaves emerge before most shade perennials awaken and the funnel-shaped flowers that shift from pink buds to blue as they open make lungwort a standout in early spring. Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged — plants wilt dramatically in drought but recover quickly after watering. Shear the foliage to the ground in midsummer if it looks tired or shows powdery mildew; fresh leaves will emerge within weeks and carry the plant through autumn in good condition. Divide every 3–4 years in early fall when clumps begin to die out in the center.

plant_note: Direct sow outdoors in early spring or fall; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination.
directions: Scarify seeds with sandpaper or soak overnight in water to soften the hard seed coat before sowing 1/4 in deep in cool, slightly acidic, well-drained soil. Lupines fix atmospheric nitrogen via root nodules and thrive in lean soils without heavy fertilization — too much nitrogen promotes foliage over flowers. They prefer cool summers; in hot climates, they often perform as cool-season annuals, blooming in late spring and fading by midsummer. Deadhead promptly after the first flowering spike fades to encourage a second flush and prevent excessive self-seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil in sun to partial shade; lurid sedge is among the most adaptable native wetland sedges — it tolerates both seasonal flooding and brief drying, making it excellent for rain gardens and wet-site landscaping.
directions: Plant in moist to seasonally wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; lurid sedge is a widely distributed native sedge of streambanks, ditches, wet meadows, and pond margins throughout eastern North America. The distinctive, densely packed, cylindrical to oval female flower heads — pale green when young, becoming dark and almost blackish at maturity — give it a bold, architectural appearance in the rain garden or bioswale. The species name refers to the dark, somewhat somber coloring of the mature fruiting heads. Lurid sedge is highly adaptable: it tolerates temporary inundation, moderate drought once established, clay or sandy soils, and pH ranging from 5.5 to 7.5 — an unusual combination that makes it one of the most versatile natives for challenging wet sites. Excellent for stream bank stabilization and rain garden margins where it spreads by short rhizomes to form erosion-controlling colonies.

plant_note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; lurida moraea follows the Cape winter-rainfall growth cycle — emerging in autumn, blooming in spring (September–November in South Africa), going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer. The flowers, which smell unpleasant to deter most insects but attract certain flies for pollination, are nonetheless visually striking. This is a rare species in cultivation — of botanical and collector interest.
directions: Plant corms in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; lurida moraea is a botanically unusual Cape iris — unusual primarily in two respects: the flower colors are in the warm brown-yellow-orange-cream range with contrasting dark spots and dark-patterned nectar guides (a lurid, dark-spotted quality that gives the species name 'lurida', meaning 'pale, sallow, discolored, lurid'), and the flowers emit a smell that, rather than attracting bees or butterflies, specifically attracts certain blowflies and carrion flies through a somewhat unpleasant odor — a pollination strategy of sapromyiophily (fly-pollination through deception). The flowers, however, are visually interesting and somewhat exotic-looking, with their warm, spotted, dark-centered color pattern. For the collector of unusual Cape irids, it occupies a different niche from the brilliant pure-blue geissorhizas or the vivid red-and-white gladioli — providing a curious, botanically interesting, darkly-patterned flower type that represents the diversity of pollination strategies evolved by Cape plants. A plant for botanical curiosity and collection rather than mass ornamental display.

common_name: Luscious Bananarama Lantana (Compact Non-Fading Yellow Trailing Lantana)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained soil in full sun; Bananarama holds a steady bright yellow color rather than shifting through orange and red like standard Lantana camara, and its lower, more spreading habit suits hanging baskets and container edges as well as beds.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Luscious Bananarama is part of Proven Winners' Luscious lantana series, bred for a lower, more mounding and trailing habit than upright landscape lantana, with clear, consistent golden-yellow flower clusters held over the foliage from spring through frost without deadheading. Its compact size and spreading habit make it equally at home cascading from hanging baskets and containers or filling beds and borders, and like other modern lantana selections it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving through the hottest stretch of a Gulf South summer. The flowers are strong pollinator magnets, drawing butterflies and bees throughout the long bloom season. In zone 9 it typically dies back to the roots in a hard freeze but resprouts vigorously from a well-established root system.

common_name: Luscious Lantana (Sterile Non-Seeding Landscape Lantana Series)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Luscious was bred to be sterile or nearly so, producing very few seeds and reducing the self-seeding and bird-spread naturalization that has made some older lantana cultivars invasive in mild climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, and water sparingly once established, since lantana is highly drought-tolerant and prone to root and crown rot in consistently wet soil. Luscious is a vegetatively propagated lantana series bred for a low, spreading, well-branched habit and a bright range of citrus and berry-toned flower colors, produced in continuous flushes from spring through frost that draw butterflies and hummingbirds heavily. Its low seed set is a meaningful improvement over older, heavily self-seeding lantana cultivars that have become weedy or invasive in warm, frost-free climates, making Luscious a more responsible choice for gardeners in the Deep South and similar regions. In milder winters the roots often survive to resprout in spring; where hard freezes occur it is grown as a warm-season annual.

plant_note: Divide and replant clumps in early spring while dormant, keeping the fleshy roots shallow and well spread in humus-rich soil.
directions: Plant in loose, well-drained soil generously amended with compost, sited where the finely cut foliage will get morning sun and afternoon shade. Unlike old-fashioned bleeding hearts, this hybrid keeps its handsome blue-green, fern-like leaves looking fresh through summer instead of going dormant, and it deadheads and rebounds quickly with light watering during dry stretches. Slender arching stems carry cherry-red, heart-shaped flowers from spring well into fall in cooler climates, giving far longer bloom than the species types. It combines beautifully with hostas, ferns, and heucheras as a long-season anchor for the shade border.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; named selections are grown from cuttings rather than seed.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Lydia broom forms a low, cascading mound of fine blue-green stems that is smothered in brilliant golden-yellow pea-shaped flowers for several weeks in late spring. It is exceptionally well suited to spilling over rock walls, covering dry slopes, or edging a gravel bed, and unlike some brooms it stays naturally tidy and compact without aggressive reseeding. Good drainage is essential — it declines quickly in heavy clay or soil that stays wet — but once sited correctly it needs almost no irrigation or fertilizer.

common_name: Lynn's Legacy Cenizo (Texas Superstar Reliable-Blooming Texas Sage)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in extremely well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Lynn's Legacy is a Texas Superstar cenizo selection named for plantsman Lynn Lowrey, chosen for blooming more reliably and over a longer season than typical cenizo, regardless of humidity swings.
directions: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline soil; Lynn's Legacy is a Texas Superstar-designated cenizo, discovered by plantsman Lynn Lowrey near Monterrey, Mexico, and selected because it blooms more consistently and for a longer stretch of the growing season than typical Leucophyllum cenizo, which famously flushes into bloom mainly around rain events. It shares the classic silvery, felted foliage that reflects heat and reduces water loss, along with clusters of lavender-purple tubular flowers, but with a more upright, slightly more refined growth habit than the common species. Never overwater, fertilize heavily, or amend the planting hole with organic matter, since excess moisture and rich soil are the most common causes of decline in cenizo. Outstanding for xeric, native, and wildlife gardens across zones 8-11.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Lynwood Gold requires full sun for maximum flower production — plants in partial shade produce fewer flowers but good foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Lynwood Gold is the most widely planted forsythia cultivar and perhaps the most familiar early-spring flowering shrub in American horticulture — a vigorous, upright-arching shrub that literally covers itself with vivid golden-yellow flowers in late February through March (in zone 8) before any leaves emerge, creating an explosive, golden-yellow color display that signals the end of winter. The flowers are produced on second-year wood along the entire length of the arching stems before any foliage appears — when in full bloom, a mature Lynwood Gold shrub is a mass of pure golden yellow visible from a considerable distance. This spectacle is the quintessential early spring garden moment in zone 5–8. Note: forsythia's flower bud hardiness is its limiting characteristic for zone 9 use — the flower buds require a period of cold dormancy and are damaged by extended warm winters in zone 9, where reliable flowering cannot be counted on every year. In zone 9, forsythia may flower well in cool-winter years and produce sparse bloom in mild winters. For zone 9 plantings, consider Karl Sax and Meadowlark cultivars with enhanced flower bud cold-hardiness, or accept the variable bloom performance of standard cultivars.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; lyre-leaf sage is one of the few native sages tolerant of part shade and self-sows freely in lawns, woodland edges, and open disturbed areas across the Southeast.
directions: Sow direct in fall in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; lyre-leaf sage self-sows prolifically once established and can naturalize in lawns, under deciduous trees, and along woodland edges — it is one of the most shade-tolerant native sages in North America, which is remarkable given that most Salvia species require full sun. Salvia lyrata is a native biennial to short-lived perennial of the eastern United States producing a basal rosette of deeply lobed, lyre-shaped (lyrate) leaves that are often flushed with attractive purple-maroon coloring in winter and early spring; in its flowering year it sends up slender, upright stems bearing whorls of tubular, pale blue to blue-violet flowers from April through June that are visited by native bumblebees, small bees, and ruby-throated hummingbirds. The winter rosette is evergreen in mild climates and provides early-season ground cover; plants self-sow abundantly enough to persist as a self-perpetuating colony. It is particularly effective naturalized under deciduous oaks and in partly shaded lawn areas where few other native wildflowers will bloom.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the soil has warmed and frost has passed; lift and store tubers over winter in cold zones.
directions: Maarn is a classic orange ball dahlia that produces an abundance of round, uniform blooms perfect for cutting. The plants are large and well-balanced, often standing without staking, and they generate plenty of tubers for dividing. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost has passed. Cut flowers frequently and deadhead spent blooms to keep the plant producing all season. In zones colder than 8, dig and store the tubers in a cool, dry place over winter.

common_name: Mac 'n' Cheese Coneflower (Double Cheddar-Orange Domed Center)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Mac 'n' Cheese bears a double form with a cheddar-orange domed center and a short fringe of yellow-orange petals.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.
