Mac 'n' Cheese bears an unusual double form with a raised, cheddar-orange domed center rimmed by a short fringe of yellow-orange petals, a playful, food-inspired color combination and shape distinct from the flat-petaled species form. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Macho Mocha Mangave (Giant Speckled Agave-Manfreda Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant rooted offsets or nursery divisions in spring into very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this hybrid is clonally propagated only, since it does not come true from seed.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, giving it generous room since 'Macho Mocha' is among the largest and most vigorous mangave cultivars, forming a broad rosette of thick, wavy-margined, olive-green leaves heavily speckled with maroon-burgundy spots that intensify in bright light and cool weather. As a hybrid between Agave and Manfreda parentage it inherits the softer, more pliable leaves and hummingbird-pollinated flower spikes of manfreda along with the bold rosette form of agave, and importantly it is polycarpic, meaning the rosette survives flowering rather than dying like a true century plant. It grows considerably faster than pure agave species, reaching full size in just a few seasons, and has become a popular large-scale accent for Gulf South and Texas xeriscape beds and containers. Sharp drainage and good air movement are essential, since rot from wet soil is the primary risk to an otherwise low-maintenance plant.

plant_note: Divide and transplant in early spring before fronds fully unfurl, into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; upland brittle fern grows naturally on rocky wooded slopes and talus rather than the damp bottomland preferred by the closely related lowland bladder fern.
directions: Divide and transplant in early spring before fronds fully unfurl, siting the fern in well-drained, humus-rich soil tucked among rocks or on a sloped woodland bank in partial to full shade. Upland brittle fern forms a delicate, finely cut, light-green clump that closely resembles the lowland bladder fern but favors drier, rockier upland woods and talus slopes rather than damp valley bottoms, and its fronds are especially brittle and easily snapped at the stem base, a trait shared across the genus. It is summer-deciduous in drought, dying back when conditions turn hot and dry and re-emerging with cooler, moister fall weather, so do not mistake dormancy for plant loss. A good choice for a shaded rock garden or the dry edge of a woodland border where richer, constantly moist soil is not available.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mackenzie sedge tolerates salt spray and coastal wind and appreciates cooler summer conditions.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mackenzie sedge tolerates salt spray and coastal wind and appreciates cooler summer conditions. Broad, strap-like, glossy dark-green leaves form a bold, tussocky clump from which triangular flower stems rise in summer, bearing chunky, pale-brown seed heads that add coarse textural contrast to finer-leaved companions. Native to coastal cliffs and tussock grasslands of New Zealand, it is prized in maritime and Pacific Northwest gardens for its salt and wind tolerance, making it a strong choice for coastal borders, large containers, and rain gardens. It performs best where summers stay relatively cool and moist, and may struggle with prolonged heat and humidity in hot inland climates.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade; macrantha toad lily differs from most toad lilies in bearing nodding, tubular bell-shaped yellow flowers rather than the flat-open, starry flowers typical of the genus — it is an elegant collector's plant best suited to sheltered, humus-rich woodland gardens.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart; macrantha toad lily is a Japanese woodland species that stands apart from most other toad lilies by producing nodding, tubular, bell-shaped flowers rather than the open, starry, orchid-like blooms of the more familiar T. hirta and T. formosana. The pendant, 1-inch yellow flowers are spotted with reddish-brown inside and hang from arching stems in late summer and fall, giving the plant the look of an elegant woodland bell. Tricyrtis macrantha requires consistently moist, humus-rich soil in deep or partial shade and performs best in sheltered, cool woodland gardens; it is less tolerant of drought and heat than the common toad lily and is considered an advanced collector's plant rather than a garden workhorse. Protect from slugs, which can damage the foliage, and provide a light mulch to retain moisture and protect the crowns in colder zones.

plant_note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on an extremely sturdy pergola or arbor built to carry the mature vine's substantial weight.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on an extremely sturdy support structure, since mature vines become massive and heavy over time. Macrobotrys is grown above all for its astonishing flower racemes, violet-blue and fragrant, that can trail two to three feet long, among the longest of any wisteria, creating a dramatic curtain effect when trained over a tall pergola where the full length of each raceme can hang free. Like other Japanese wisteria it twines clockwise and is a vigorous, potentially aggressive grower that needs firm annual pruning, both in summer to control rampant new growth and in late winter to shape and encourage flower bud formation. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity, and be prepared for a genuinely large, long-term structural commitment in the landscape.

plant_note: Plant as a container specimen in zone 9 — Madagascar Dragon Tree is damaged by temperatures below 35°F and cannot be safely planted outdoors in zone 9a year-round. Bring containers indoors or to a frost-free space when temperatures drop below 40°F. In zone 10-11, plant outdoors in partial shade with well-drained soil. Excellent for patios and atriums as a year-round container plant that goes outdoors in warm weather.
directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained soil or potting mix; Madagascar Dragon Tree adapts to low-light conditions better than most tropical plants, making it one of the premier houseplants and patio container specimens. Dracaena marginata (Madagascar Dragon Tree) is native to Madagascar and Mauritius and has become one of the most popular large houseplants and outdoor landscape specimens in subtropical and tropical regions worldwide. The narrow, red-edged, strap-like leaves radiate in rosettes from the tips of slender, branching stems that develop a distinctive bottle-palm-like silhouette as they age. Multiple color forms are available: the standard 'Marginata' (red-edged green leaves), 'Tricolor' (green, cream, and red stripes), 'Colorama' (dark red-purple throughout), and 'Tarzan' (wide, arching leaves). Dracaena marginata is exceptionally forgiving of neglect — it tolerates low light, infrequent watering, dry indoor air, and occasional drought better than almost any other large tropical plant. Plants that get regular outdoor exposure to bright indirect light and occasional fertilization in the growing season grow substantially faster and maintain better color than those kept exclusively indoors. In zone 10-11 it can be planted outdoors as a landscape specimen reaching 15–20 feet with multiple branching trunks. NASA Clean Air Study data suggest it removes formaldehyde, benzene, and trichloroethylene from indoor air.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer in moist perlite or plant container specimens on a trellis in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to partial shade; stephanotis requires consistent warmth and resents root disturbance.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens on a trellis in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to partial shade; stephanotis is a twining vine from Madagascar prized for its waxy, pure-white, intensely fragrant tubular flowers in clusters from spring through summer — the flowers have one of the most exquisite perfumes in the plant kingdom and are traditionally used in bridal bouquets and leis. Keep the root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged. The vine requires a period of cool, dry rest in winter (55–60°F) to set flower buds for the following season. Plants resent being moved once established; keep in the same pot or location for best performance. Grow outdoors year-round only in frost-free zones.

plant_note: Plant in full sun in sandy, extremely well-drained soil; Pachypodium geayi is frost-sensitive and cannot tolerate temperatures below about 40F, so grow as a large container specimen moved indoors for winter outside of zone 10-12. The plant drops its leaves in winter dormancy; resume watering when new growth appears in spring.
directions: Plant in full sun in sandy, gravelly, or any extremely well-draining soil medium, since this Madagascar succulent tree rots quickly in heavy or moisture-retentive soil. Pachypodium geayi is very similar to and frequently confused with the more common Pachypodium lamerei in the nursery trade, but can be distinguished by its narrower, longer, more silvery-gray leaves with fine hairs along the margins, giving the crown a softer, more silvered appearance than lamerei's broader, glossier green leaves. Like its relative, it grows as a tall, spine-covered succulent column that is not a true palm despite the common name, eventually branching with age and producing fragrant, pinwheel-shaped white flowers at the stem tips on mature specimens grown in strong light. The milky sap is toxic and irritating to skin and eyes, so wear gloves when pruning or repotting, and site the sharp, spine-covered trunk away from foot traffic.

common_name: Madagascar Palm (Spiny Club, Club-Foot, Lamerei Pachypodium)
plant_note: Plant in full sun with sandy, extremely well-drained soil; Madagascar Palm is frost-sensitive and cannot tolerate temperatures below 40°F. In zone 9, grow as a large container specimen moved inside in winter. The plant goes fully dormant in winter — it is normal for all leaves to drop; resume watering in spring when new leaves appear. Water moderately in the growing season (spring–fall); water very sparingly in winter dormancy. The trunk and stems contain a milky toxic sap — wear gloves when working near the plant. The 3 long, sharp spines at each leaf scar are painful.
directions: Plant in full sun in sandy, gravelly, or any extremely well-draining soil medium — Madagascar Palm rots rapidly in heavy or moisture-retaining soils and must never sit in standing water. Pachypodium lamerei is a tall, columnar succulent tree native to the arid regions of southern Madagascar in the family Apocynaceae (the same family as Plumeria, Oleander, and Hoya), one of the most striking and distinctive succulents regularly available in the horticultural trade. Despite the common name 'Madagascar Palm,' it is not a palm at all — it belongs to no monocot group but is instead a tropical succulent adapted to the dry, spiny deserts of Madagascar. The plant grows as a tall, single column (branching occasionally with age) of silvery-gray to greenish, ridged stem covered along its entire length with clusters of three sharp, gray-white spines 1–2 inches long at each leaf scar — the spines and the architectural, column-like form create an immediate visual impression of a cactus from the American deserts but represent an entirely convergent adaptation on another continent. From the top of the column, a rosette of long, narrow, dark-green leaves appears in the growing season. On mature specimens, the column tip produces fragrant, white, pinwheel-shaped flowers (resembling Plumeria) — rare and prized in cultivation. The milky sap is toxic. A dramatic, architectural container specimen or landscape accent for hot, dry, zone 10-11 gardens.

common_name: Madame Alfred Carriere Rose (White-Blush Vigorous Climbing Noisette Rose)
plant_note: Plant own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy trellis or fence; Madame Alfred Carriere is a vigorous, cold-hardier climbing Noisette that tolerates some shade.
directions: Plant own-root stock in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy trellis, wall, or fence. Madame Alfred Carriere bears large, fragrant, white blooms tinted with soft blush-pink, opening in flushes almost continuously through the warm season on an exceptionally vigorous, cold-hardier climbing Noisette that reaches greater heights than many others in its class and tolerates a north-facing or partly shaded wall better than most roses. Its combination of toughness, shade tolerance, and repeat bloom has made it one of the most widely planted antique climbers. Prune lightly after each bloom flush and train canes horizontally along the support to maximize flowering side shoots.

common_name: Madame Butterfly Snapdragon (Double Azalea-Flowered Cut-Flower Mix)
plant_note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. An All-America Selections winner grown for fully double, azalea-shaped blooms.
directions: Surface-sow the fine seed indoors under bright light 12-16 weeks before transplanting, since it needs light to germinate and should be left uncovered. Madame Butterfly is an All-America Selections-winning snapdragon series notable for fully double, azalea-shaped blooms that give the flower spikes a ruffled, almost rose-like appearance quite different from the single spurred flowers of classic snapdragons. The 24-30 inch plants are widely adapted and bloom in a broad color range including red, pink, orange, yellow, purple, and white, making dense, showy spikes prized for cutting. Like other snapdragons it thrives in cool weather and fades once summer heat sets in, so plan for a spring or fall harvest window.

common_name: Madame Chereau Bearded Iris (Historic 1844 Plicata Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Madame Chereau is an 1844 French heirloom bearded iris and one of the earliest plicata (picotee-edged) cultivars still grown.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Bred in France in 1844, Madame Chereau is among the oldest plicata-pattern bearded irises still in cultivation, its white petals finely stippled and edged in soft blue-violet along every margin, a delicate pattern that was strikingly novel for its era. Nearly two centuries in gardens have proven it a tough, dependable heirloom, multiplying steadily into long-lived clumps that ask for little beyond full sun and sharp drainage. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep flowering strong.

common_name: Madame Emile Mouilliere Hydrangea (Antique White Mophead with Colored Eye)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this French cultivar dates to 1909 and remains one of the finest white mopheads.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Introduced in France in 1909, Madame Emile Mouillere bears large, rounded, pure white mophead blooms with a delicate pink or blue eye at the center of each floret depending on soil pH, a refined color combination that has kept it in cultivation for well over a century. Unlike the fully pH-responsive blue-or-pink cultivars, its white petals stay white regardless of soil chemistry, while only the small central eye shifts color, giving a subtler, more restrained effect than a fully colored mophead. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in the Gulf South to prevent wilting in peak summer heat.

common_name: Madame Galen Trumpet Vine (Less-Aggressive Orange-Red Trumpet Creeper)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun on a strong, permanent support such as a large arbor or sturdy fence; Madame Galen is a hybrid trumpet vine that spreads less aggressively by root suckers than the straight native trumpet creeper, though it still grows vigorously.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun against a strong, permanent structure, since this vigorous woody vine becomes heavy over time and can damage weak supports or siding it is allowed to climb directly. A hybrid between American trumpet creeper and Chinese trumpet vine, Madame Galen produces abundant clusters of large, salmon-orange to apricot-red trumpet-shaped flowers through summer that are a favorite of hummingbirds. It is somewhat less prone to aggressive root suckering than the wild American species, though it still needs a firm hand with pruning to keep it in bounds and off of nearby structures. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease, and a hard pruning in late winter keeps the vine full and encourages the current season's flowering growth.

common_name: Madame Hardy Rose (Pure White Green-Eyed Damask Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; introduced in France in 1832, Madame Hardy is considered one of the finest white Damask roses ever raised.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Hardy tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough 19th-century Damask. Introduced in France in 1832, it bears exquisitely formed, pure white double blooms that open flat with a distinctive small green button eye at the center, a refined and much-admired detail that has made it a benchmark white old garden rose for nearly two centuries, carrying a fresh, lemony Damask fragrance. Like other Damasks it blooms just once, in a spectacular fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Madame Isaac Pereire Rose (Fragrant Bourbon Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall in full sun in rich, well-drained soil against a fence or low wall if grown as a climber; Madame Isaac Pereire is a vigorous Bourbon that performs well through the humid Gulf South growing season, though it benefits from good air circulation to limit blackspot.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, compost-enriched soil, and prune back by about a third after the main spring flush to encourage a strong repeat bloom later in the season. Bred by Garçon in France and introduced in 1881, Madame Isaac Pereire is a Bourbon rose renowned as one of the most fragrant roses ever raised, bearing very large, deeply cupped, ruffled blooms in a rich magenta-pink that release an intense, raspberry-like old-rose perfume detectable from a distance. Its vigorous, somewhat lax growth habit allows it to be kept as a large rounded shrub or trained as a short climber on a wall or pillar for extra height and better air movement through the dense foliage. Deadhead through summer to encourage the sporadic rebloom that follows its heavy spring display.

common_name: Madame Joseph Schwartz Rose (Ivory-Blush Sport of Duchesse de Brabant)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Joseph Schwartz, introduced in 1871, is a white-blush sport of the classic Tea rose Duchesse de Brabant and shares its toughness and rebloom in Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Madame Joseph Schwartz, introduced in 1871, is an ivory-white Tea rose blushed with soft pink that arose as a sport of the classic Duchesse de Brabant, sharing its parent's cupped, informal flower form, rich fragrance, and outstanding heat tolerance. Long grown as a 'found rose' in old Texas and Deep South gardens, it blooms in flushes almost continuously through the growing season and requires little care beyond a sunny, well-drained site and occasional light pruning after each flush. Its excellent disease resistance and easygoing nature have kept it a favorite in heirloom rose collections for generations.

common_name: Madame Julia Correvon Clematis (Wine-Red Nodding Viticella Clematis)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Madame Julia Correvon is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Madame Julia Correvon bears an abundance of nodding, wine-red flowers with slightly twisted petals over a long summer season, on a vigorous vine well suited to scrambling through a large shrub or covering a fence quickly. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so it can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter, a far simpler pruning routine than the large-flowered old-wood types. Its rich color and easy care have made it one of the most popular viticella cultivars.

common_name: Madame Pierre Oger Rose (Pale Pink-and-Cream Cupped Bourbon Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Pierre Oger is a repeat-blooming Bourbon rose whose delicate cupped blooms deepen in color with more sun.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Madame Pierre Oger bears delicate, cupped, double blooms in pale cream-pink that deepen to a richer rose-pink with stronger sun exposure, opening on a graceful, upright Bourbon shrub with the strong, sweet fragrance typical of the class. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a genuine advantage of Bourbon roses over many once-blooming old garden rose classes. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

plant_note: Sow in darkness indoors; seeds need darkness to germinate.
directions: Sow seed in darkness indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, since light inhibits germination. Above slim, silvery foliage, tiny star-shaped blooms form 2 to 3 inch pincushion-like flowerheads with a light scent that draws pollinators. This Australian wildflower is a soft, fragrant beauty that makes a lovely, airy cut flower. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, provide support in windy sites, and harvest stems for delicate bouquets.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Magellan stays notably compact and sturdy compared to most large-flowered zinnias, making it a good choice for beds and containers where taller cut-flower zinnias would flop.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Magellan is an All-America Selections winner bred for large, fully double, dahlia-like flowers on unusually compact, sturdy plants, giving the visual impact of a tall cut-flower zinnia on a dwarf, well-branched habit that rarely needs staking. It blooms in a wide range of colors from cream and yellow through orange, salmon, pink, and deep red, flowering heavily from midsummer to frost with regular deadheading. Its compact size and strong garden performance make it well suited to bedding, borders, and containers, and good air circulation between plants helps reduce the powdery mildew that affects zinnias in humid climates.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–2 weeks before the last frost date, surface-sowing onto moist seed-starting mix at cool room temperature (50–65°F), as this subantarctic species prefers cool germination conditions. Transplant outside after frost danger has passed into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from drying winds. This bold architectural plant performs best in cool, moist climates with reliably damp soil throughout the growing season.
directions: Start seeds at cool temperatures (50–65°F) by pressing them onto the surface of damp seed-starting mix without covering, then keep trays consistently moist until germination occurs in 10–21 days. Grow on in a cool, bright location and transplant outdoors in spring once frost risk has passed, into deep, consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial shade. This imposing South American perennial produces enormous paddle-shaped leaves topped by tall stems bearing clusters of large white daisy flowers in summer, followed by ornamental gray-woolly seed heads. Mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and prevent drought stress, which causes premature leaf collapse.

common_name: Maggie Rose (Found Texas China-Bourbon Antique Rose)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Maggie is a found rose rediscovered growing at old Texas homesites, believed to be a China-Bourbon hybrid, valued for rich magenta-pink, cupped, fragrant blooms on a tough, low-care shrub.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Maggie needs little beyond an occasional deep watering once established. Like many of the antique roses preserved through the Texas rose rustling movement, Maggie is a found rose, rediscovered growing untended at an old homestead and propagated from cuttings rather than traced to a known breeder or introduction date, and it is generally considered a China-Bourbon hybrid based on its growth habit and bloom. It produces richly fragrant, cupped, deep magenta-pink flowers in generous flushes from spring through fall on a vigorous, well-branched shrub that shrugs off Southern heat, humidity, and poor soil with the same toughness that let it survive decades of neglect at its original homesite. Its resilience and near-constant bloom make it an excellent low-input choice for a Gulf Coast heirloom border, and it asks for little beyond an occasional shaping prune after the heaviest spring flush.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors since light aids germination; snapdragons like cool weather.
directions: Surface-sow the fine seed indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, since light aids germination. This dwarf snapdragon blend offers a lovely mix of colors that charms in flower beds, borders, containers, and hanging baskets. Snapdragons prefer cool weather, so transplant hardened seedlings out around the last frost. Grow in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil, pinch young plants to encourage branching, and deadhead to prolong bloom.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Magic Carpet's best leaf color — vivid red-orange new growth — develops in full sun; in partial shade the foliage is more yellow-green and less vivid.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Magic Carpet is one of the most spectacular compact spiraea cultivars for foliage color — a dwarf selection staying 12–24 inches tall that produces a dramatic seasonal foliage display beginning with vivid red-orange to scarlet new growth in spring, maturing to yellow-gold through summer, and transitioning to orange-red fall color. The three-season foliage interest — red spring, gold summer, orange fall — combined with pink summer flowers creates year-round ornamental value rarely matched by such a compact shrub. The flower heads are pink, produced in early summer above the colorful foliage, but the foliage is the primary ornamental feature. Magic Carpet's extremely compact size makes it outstanding for edging, mass planting as a colorful ground cover, container gardens, and foreground positions in shrub borders where larger spiraea would overwhelm. Like all Japanese spiraea cultivars, it is extremely tough and adaptable — tolerating drought, clay soil, urban conditions, and the heat of zone 9 with minimal care. Shear lightly after flowering and again in late summer to encourage fresh, colorful new growth. In zone 9, Magic Carpet tends to be slightly more compact than in cooler zones and performs best in full sun with good drainage. Deer-resistant once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted stolons in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Tricolor' is less cold-hardy and less vigorous than the plain green species, so it is best grown as a container or hanging-basket plant outside its reliably hardy zones.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted stolons in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Tricolor' is less cold-hardy and less vigorous than the plain green species, so it is best grown as a container or hanging-basket plant outside its reliably hardy zones. This colorful sport of strawberry begonia forms rounded, scalloped leaves edged in cream and flushed rose-pink, sending out thin red runners tipped with small plantlets in the same strawberry-like fashion as the species, with airy sprays of small white flowers in late spring. Its bright variegation makes it a favorite for shaded hanging baskets, terrariums, and container groundcover where its trailing runners can cascade over an edge. It is slower and less aggressive than the green species, so it rarely becomes a groundcover pest, and benefits from bright indirect light to maintain strong variegation.

common_name: Magic Flowers (Hot Water Plant, Cupid's Bower, Achimenes, Orchid Pansy)
plant_note: Start scaly rhizomes (caterpillar-like propagules) indoors in shallow trays of moist peat-perlite mix in late winter; the common name 'hot water plant' comes from the old practice of watering with warm water to stimulate sprouting. Plant in hanging baskets or shade garden beds in partial to full shade once temperatures are consistently above 60°F. Achimenes goes dormant in fall — allow plants to dry and store the tiny rhizomes at 50–60°F through winter. In zone 9, rhizomes left in ground with heavy mulch may survive mild winters. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in well-draining, humus-rich, slightly acidic potting mix — Magic Flowers performs best in the bright, indirect or filtered light of a sheltered shade garden or covered porch and will scorch in direct summer sun. Achimenes hybrida encompasses the large group of garden hybrid achimenes (family Gesneriaceae) developed from crosses among approximately 25 wild species native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and other parts of Central America — a genus valued as one of the finest shade-garden summer-blooming plants available. The plants grow from tiny, caterpillar-shaped scaly rhizomes (the 'scales' are actually modified leaves with overlapping bracts) that sprout readily when planted in warm conditions. The resulting plants produce trailing to semi-upright stems of soft, dark-green, hairy, opposite leaves covered in a continuous flush of flowers from early summer through fall — each individual flower a flat-faced, broadly funnel-shaped bloom 1–2 inches across in the full color range: white, pink, rose, magenta, purple, lavender, red, and bicolors. The prolific, non-stop flowering habit in the shade — a position where many other summer flowers fail — is the defining advantage of Achimenes hybrida. Excellent in hanging baskets and window boxes in a shaded location, where the trailing stems create a summer-long cascade of color. Non-toxic.

common_name: Magic Fountains Delphinium (Compact Mixed-Color Seed Strain)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall for cool climates; Magic Fountains is a compact seed strain of tall border delphinium bred to need less staking than older varieties.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Magic Fountains is a compact seed strain of classic tall border delphinium, producing dense spikes of large, double flowers in a full range of colors including blues, purples, pinks, and white, on plants shorter and sturdier than older delphinium strains, needing less staking to stay upright. In warm climates it is typically grown as a cool-season annual or short-lived biennial since it declines in summer heat, while in cooler zones it persists as a reliable short-lived perennial. All parts are toxic if ingested. Cut back hard after the first bloom flush to encourage a possible second round of flowering.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just at the soil surface in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; magic lily performs best when allowed to dry out after the spring foliage dies — do not water heavily in June–July as the bulbs are dormant.
directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or near the soil surface in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun — magic lily earns its name by following a seemingly magical seasonal cycle: broad, strap-like leaves emerge in early spring, grow through April, then disappear entirely by June, leaving no trace for two months. Then, in July or August, apparently bare ground suddenly produces clusters of tall, leafless stalks topped with large (3–4 inch), fragrant, pink to lavender-pink lily-like flowers in a spectacular summer surprise that inspired the common names 'surprise lily' and 'resurrection lily.' The flowers last 1–2 weeks. Interplant with hostas, daylilies, or groundcovers to hide the disappearing spring foliage. Clumps increase slowly and bloom more prolifically when undisturbed — divide only every 7–10 years when overcrowded. One of the most reliably carefree bulbs for the southern garden.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors since light aids germination; prefers cool, moist conditions.
directions: Surface-sow the tiny seed indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, since light aids germination. This mix dazzles with blooms in yellow, orange, pink, and red on plants ideal for borders, containers, and wildflower gardens. Monkey flower thrives in cool, moist conditions and blooms continuously from spring into summer. Grow in sun to part shade, keep the soil consistently moist, and deadhead to keep the colorful show going.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light with very high humidity (70–80%); Anthurium magnificum is strictly a tropical collector's plant in zone 9 and requires consistently warm temperatures (65–85°F) and the humid conditions of its native Colombian cloud forest habitat. Use a chunky, well-aerated epiphytic mix and water thoroughly when the top layer dries. The leaves are very large and prone to mechanical damage — handle carefully. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Anthurium magnificum produces its most spectacular foliage in conditions of consistent bright filtered light, ideally from a bright north or east window, and will decline in dim corners. Anthurium magnificum is a large, terrestrial to lithophytic anthurium native to the cloud forests of Colombia, closely related to Anthurium crystallinum and belonging to the same 'velvet anthurium' group. The species name 'magnificum' is apt: the mature plant produces truly magnificent large leaves — broadly heart-shaped, up to 24–30 inches across, with a thickly leathery, velvety texture, very dark emerald-green surface, and a bold network of raised, pale ivory to cream veins that create an intricate pattern across the dark leaf face. The leaves are quadrangular-cordate (squarish heart shape) with distinctly angled basal lobes, a feature that distinguishes it from the more rounded lobes of A. crystallinum. The combination of large size, cardboard-thick leaf texture, dramatic vein pattern, and rich coloration makes A. magnificum one of the most impressive velvet anthuriums available. The species' considerable variation in the wild has led to complex classification and collector debate over 'true magnificum.' All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Magnoliiflora, an 1888 Japanese heirloom, bears smaller, semi-double blush-pink flowers resembling a small magnolia bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Magnoliiflora is an antique Camellia japonica cultivar dating to around 1888, named for its smaller, semi-double, soft blush-pink flowers whose loosely arranged petals and prominent stamens give them a delicate resemblance to a small magnolia bloom, a distinctive form among the many fuller, more formal camellia types. It flowers later in the season than many other japonica cultivars, extending camellia bloom into late winter and early spring. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub provides dense, glossy year-round structure. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Magnus Coneflower (Classic Flat Deep Rose-Purple Perennial Plant of the Year)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Magnus was named the 1998 Perennial Plant of the Year for its large, flat, deep rose-purple flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Magnus, named the 1998 Perennial Plant of the Year, bears large, single, deep rose-purple flowers with petals held unusually flat rather than drooping downward, a classic, widely imitated form that helped popularize coneflower as a mainstream garden perennial. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall, attracting bees, butterflies, and goldfinches that feed on the dried seed heads through winter. Deadhead to prolong bloom or leave seed heads standing for winter bird interest, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Mahogany Fern (Maidenhair Tree Fern, Hump Fern, Truncate Didymochlaena)
plant_note: Plant in deep to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil; Didymochlaena truncatula is one of the most elegant and distinctive shade ferns for zone 10-12 outdoor use or a shaded indoor container. The new fronds emerge in rich copper-pink to bronze-mahogany color before maturing to glossy dark green — the color sequence from which the common name 'Mahogany Fern' derives. Sensitive to temperatures below 45°F; bring indoors or protect in zone 9. Water consistently — allow the medium to approach dryness between waterings but never fully dry. Slow to establish but long-lived once settled. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in deep to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil — Mahogany Fern grows most beautifully in the cool, moist, deeply shaded conditions of a sheltered porch, conservatory, or jungle garden in zone 10-12 and is one of the most elegant of all shade ferns when well-established. Didymochlaena truncatula is a large, upright-growing terrestrial fern in the Didymochlaenaceae family (sometimes placed in Dryopteridaceae) with a broadly pan-tropical distribution — native to moist forests in tropical Africa, Madagascar, Asia, Australia, the Pacific Islands, the Caribbean, and tropical Americas. The plant produces a broad, erect rosette of large, bipinnate fronds 24–48 inches long, each frond having a distinctive architectural quality: the individual pinnules (small leaflets) are oblong with truncated (squared-off) bases and tips, giving the frond a clean, precise, almost geometric appearance unlike the delicate filigree of most ferns. The young fronds emerging from the crown are the plant's most spectacular feature — they emerge in rich mahogany-bronze to coppery-pink, a color that glows in shaded light before gradually maturing to glossy, dark forest-green. The contrast between the soft, metallic young fronds and the dark mature fronds creates a year-round multi-tonal display. The trunk gradually develops a short, upright base over many years, giving old specimens a tree-fern-like quality. An elegant, distinctive shade fern of botanical interest. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Mahogany plains coreopsis self-sows readily and naturalizes into drifts in favorable meadow or wildflower plantings.
directions: Direct sow in early spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Mahogany plains coreopsis self-sows readily and naturalizes into drifts in favorable meadow or wildflower plantings. This selection of the widespread native plains coreopsis produces small, solid, deep mahogany-red flowers with no yellow banding, a richer, more uniform color than the classic red-and-yellow bicolor form of the wild species, blooming prolifically on airy, finely branched stems from summer through fall. Extremely easy from seed and adaptable to a wide range of soils and climates, it is a staple of native wildflower meadow mixes across North America, providing abundant nectar and pollen for a wide range of small native bees and other pollinators. It self-sows readily once established, requiring no fertilizer or supplemental water, and is best massed in a meadow or informal border where its airy, branching form can be appreciated in drifts.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring when soil has warmed; miscanthus establishes best in warm soil and can be slow in cold springs.
directions: Plant divisions in full sun in any well-drained to moderately moist soil; maiden grass forms large, dramatic clumps with arching, green or variegated foliage and showy, feathery silver plumes in late summer and fall. Cut back hard in late winter or early spring before new growth emerges — use pruners or a chainsaw on large clumps; tie the clump with twine before cutting to simplify cleanup. Divide every 3–5 years in spring when the center of the clump dies out. Some cultivars are sterile; check before planting, as seeding types can naturalize aggressively in some regions.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained soil; maiden pinks germinate readily in cool conditions. Thin to 6 inches and expect first-year flowering. They can also be planted from divisions or plugs in spring or fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; maiden pinks is a low, mat-forming European native dianthus that covers itself with small, richly colored flowers in shades of rose, crimson, white, and bicolored combinations. The flowers have toothed or fringed petal margins and many have a darker central ring ('eye'), giving them a jewel-like quality. In flower from late spring through summer, maiden pinks self-sows to naturalize readily in gravel paths, between paving stones, and on dry sunny slopes. It is excellent for rock gardens, cottage garden edging, and low green roofs. The blue-green, needle-like foliage forms an attractive evergreen mat through winter.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or plugs in spring in shallow water (0–12 inches), wet marsh margins, or permanently saturated soil in full sun; maidencane spreads aggressively by rhizomes in aquatic conditions — site where it has room to spread or contain with barriers in smaller water features.
directions: Maidencane is the dominant emergent aquatic grass of the Gulf Coastal Plain's freshwater marshes, lake margins, and slow-moving waterways — forming vast, grass-like stands in shallow water from Texas to Florida that serve as one of the most important waterfowl habitat grasses in the southeastern United States. Dabbling ducks including mallards, teal, mottled ducks, and wood ducks consume the seeds profusely during fall migration; the emergent stands also provide critical nesting cover for king rails, common gallinules, and purple gallinules. In constructed wetlands, stormwater retention ponds, and rain garden overflow areas, maidencane stabilizes wet banks and shallow margins with its extensive rhizome system while providing year-round wildlife value. It spreads rapidly in aquatic conditions by rhizomes and self-seeding and can form dense monocultures in productive conditions — appropriate for naturalized pond and wetland margins but requires management in small water gardens to prevent it from overwhelming other plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; maidenhair fern grows slowly but is long-lived in appropriate conditions with consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; northern maidenhair fern is one of the most graceful ferns in cultivation, with distinctive, horseshoe-shaped fronds of fan-shaped, bright-green leaflets carried on delicate, wiry, shining black stems that tremble in the slightest breeze. New growth in spring emerges as coppery-pink croziers (fiddleheads) before expanding to full size. It requires consistently moist soil and fails in dry, compacted, or alkaline conditions. Excellent in combination with trilliums, Solomon's seal, and other woodland perennials. Divide in early spring by lifting and cutting the rhizome mass — do not allow divisions to dry out before replanting. The tropical maidenhairs (A. raddianum and relatives) require completely different culture.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants or small divisions tucked into crevices of a rock garden or dry stone wall in partial to full shade, in neutral to slightly alkaline, freely draining, rocky or gritty soil. Maidenhair Spleenwort is a rock crevice specialist and thrives in the tight drainage and consistent humidity of dry stone walls and rocky outcrops.
directions: Maidenhair Spleenwort is one of the world's most widely distributed and delightful small ferns, native to rock crevices, cliff faces, and mortared stone walls throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere from North America to Europe, Asia, and beyond, where its neat rosettes of tiny, dark-stemmed, pinnate fronds tuck into the smallest gaps between stones with remarkable grace. The evergreen, arching fronds — typically 4–8 inches long with rounded, alternating pinnae on wiry, dark, lustrous stems — are persistent through winter and provide delicate year-round texture in rock gardens, dry stone walls, and shaded rocky outcrops. Unlike most ferns that prefer moist, humus-rich soil, Maidenhair Spleenwort is adapted to excellent drainage and even slightly alkaline conditions derived from limestone or mortar — making it ideal for growing in rock garden crevices and the joints of dry stone walls, where its fine texture contrasts beautifully with the rugged stone. Plant in tight crevices with minimal amended soil and virtually no supplemental watering once established.

plant_note: Divide established clumps immediately after flowering or in early fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Majeste is a French-bred lungwort selection, introduced in the 1980s, prized for foliage that is almost solid silver rather than spotted.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Majeste is often cited as one of the finest silver-leaved lungworts, its broad leaves covered almost entirely in shimmering silver with only a thin green margin remaining, giving it a more uniformly bright appearance than the spotted patterning typical of most lungwort cultivars. Clusters of small, funnel-shaped flowers open pink and age to soft blue in early spring, appearing just as the striking foliage begins to unfurl. The dense clump makes an excellent, long-lasting groundcover once established, and the light-reflecting foliage is especially effective for brightening dark shade through summer. Keep soil consistently moist, since lungworts wilt and decline in dry shade, and divide after flowering if clumps become congested.

common_name: Majestic Beauty Indian Hawthorn (Tree-Form Large Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Majestic Beauty grows considerably larger than standard Indian hawthorn and can be trained as a small multi-trunked tree or large screening shrub.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Majestic Beauty is a hybrid Indian hawthorn selected for its unusually large mature size, growing into a substantial large shrub or small tree rather than the compact rounded mound typical of most Indian hawthorn cultivars, which makes it useful for screening, specimen planting, or a small flowering tree in coastal landscapes. In spring it produces abundant clusters of fragrant, light pink flowers followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds, all on glossy, leathery, disease-resistant foliage. It shares the species' outstanding tolerance for salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soils, making it a strong performer in exposed coastal Gulf sites, though good air circulation helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions.

common_name: Majestic Giant Pansy (Classic Large-Flowered Pansy Series)
plant_note: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, covering lightly and keeping the seed tray cool and dark for germination, then transplant out as soon as the soil can be worked; Majestic Giant also performs well as a fall-planted pansy in mild-winter zones.
directions: Transplant into full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil, and deadhead regularly to keep the long bloom season going strong. Majestic Giant is a long-standing standard pansy series bred for exceptionally large, 3-4 inch blooms in a wide range of colors and bold blotched patterns, on compact, well-branched plants that hold up well in cool weather and light frost. It performs as a cool-season annual, flowering heavily in spring and again in fall in most climates, and in the Gulf South it is commonly planted in fall for color that carries through a mild winter into early spring. Water at the base rather than overhead to reduce leaf spotting, and shear back lightly if plants stretch or thin out during a warm spell to encourage fresh, compact regrowth.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants in late spring once soil has warmed, choosing a site with rich, constantly moist soil since this Madagascar river-margin species is far thirstier than most landscape palms.
directions: Set out container-grown Majesty Palms in late spring once soil has warmed, choosing a site with rich, constantly moist soil since this Madagascar river-margin species is far thirstier than most landscape palms. Give it high shade or filtered sun in its early years and full sun once established, and mulch heavily to buffer root temperature swings at the northern edge of its range. Its dense, upright crown of soft feathery fronds reads as an instant tropical focal point beside pools, ponds, and courtyard entries. In zone 9, site it in a warm microclimate and be prepared to protect it during hard freezes.

common_name: Major Wheeler Coral Honeysuckle (Best Native Hummingbird Honeysuckle Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Major Wheeler blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates more shade than most flowering vines — half-day sun produces good bloom in Gulf South conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Major Wheeler is widely considered the finest cultivar of native coral honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) — a vigorous, non-invasive, native vine producing intense scarlet-red tubular flowers in large clusters throughout the spring and early summer with rebloom through fall. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica), Coral honeysuckle is well-behaved, manageable, and ecologically beneficial — a twining vine that climbs to 6–12 feet without smothering everything in its path, and one of the premier hummingbird plants in eastern North American gardens. 'Major Wheeler' was selected for exceptionally heavy and prolonged bloom compared to the straight species — the flower clusters are larger, more numerous, and the rebloom period more consistent, making it the overwhelming choice among coral honeysuckle cultivars for maximum ornamental and hummingbird value. The vivid red tubular flowers have no fragrance (unlike Japanese honeysuckle) but attract ruby-throated hummingbirds with exceptional consistency from spring through fall. The semi-evergreen, blue-green, oval leaves are attractive even when not in bloom. In zone 9, Major Wheeler performs best with afternoon shade protection during the hottest summers. Red berries persist into fall, providing late-season food for thrushes, mockingbirds, and other frugivorous birds.

plant_note: Plant container vines in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a trellis, fence, or arbor support — Major Wheeler is a twining vine that requires vertical support and will reach 10–15 feet at maturity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with vertical support; Major Wheeler is widely considered the finest cultivar of trumpet honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) — the native American hummingbird vine — selected for its exceptionally prolific and long flower production. While the species is already outstanding for hummingbirds, Major Wheeler produces dramatically more flowers per season and repeats bloom flushes more reliably than unselected species plants. The 1.5–2 inch, tubular scarlet-to-coral-red flowers are produced in dense terminal clusters from spring through fall in zone 9, creating an almost unmatched hummingbird feeding resource — Ruby-throated hummingbirds visit repeatedly, and the vine at peak bloom will attract multiple hummingbirds simultaneously. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica), trumpet honeysuckle is a well-behaved native that does not self-seed aggressively or spread invasively. The semi-evergreen foliage is attractive, with the characteristic perfoliate leaves (the vine stem appears to grow through the center of the leaf pairs) near the flowers. Major Wheeler is drought-tolerant once established and adaptable to a wide range of soils and light conditions from full sun to partial shade. The profusion of red flowers followed by small red berries provides exceptional wildlife value throughout the year.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; Maki is commonly clipped as a hedge or espalier.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Maki is a shorter, denser, more shrubby form of yew podocarpus than the columnar tree form, with narrower, shorter needle-like leaves densely packed on upright stems, widely used throughout the Gulf South as a clipped hedge, foundation shrub, or trained espalier. Like the species, it tolerates significant shade, clay soil, salt spray, and drought far better than most needled evergreens, and it accepts frequent shearing well, holding a crisp, formal shape when clipped regularly or growing more loosely and naturally if left alone. Its small, fleshy, red-purple fruit receptacles are attractive to birds; it is essentially pest-free in Gulf Coast landscapes.

subcategory: East African and Malagasy ornamental cycad
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–12; Malagasy Cycad is a large, palm-like cycad native to Madagascar, the Comoros Islands, East African coastal forests (Mozambique, Tanzania, Kenya), and the Mascarene Islands — producing an arching crown of long, glossy, bright-green fronds on a stout trunk, and growing to impressive size over many decades in warm, frost-free gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Cycas thouarsii is drought tolerant once established and does not tolerate waterlogged soils — excellent drainage is essential; water deeply but infrequently and apply balanced slow-release fertilizer once or twice per year. Cycas thouarsii (Malagasy Cycad, East African Cycad, or Madagascar Cycad) is a large, striking cycad native to the coastal and lowland forests of Madagascar, the Comoros, and the East African coastline (Mozambique, Tanzania, coastal Kenya), making it the only Cycas species native to Africa or its offshore islands. The plant is a slow-growing, long-lived, architectural specimen cycad developing a stout, palm-like trunk topped by a crown of long (up to 6 feet), graceful, arching, pinnately compound fronds with glossy, bright-green, narrowly lanceolate leaflets. Like all cycads, it is extremely slow-growing but exceptionally long-lived — specimens hundreds of years old are known. Cycas thouarsii is somewhat more cold-tolerant than other large Cycas species and performs well in zones 9–12, making it among the most useful large cycads for Gulf Coast, Florida, and warm subtropical gardens. A distinctive and dramatic specimen plant for large tropical-style landscape settings. All parts of the plant contain cycasin and other neurotoxins — not edible and should be kept away from children and pets.

plant_note: Root stem tip cuttings under high humidity or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, orchid-bark-amended soil in bright indirect light or partial shade after frost; medinilla requires high humidity (above 60%), consistent warmth, and an orchid-like open, free-draining substrate — standard potting soil compacted around its roots causes root rot and decline.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich, acidic, bark-amended soil in bright indirect light or partial shade; Malaysian orchid (rose grape, showy medinilla) is a Philippine tropical epiphyte of the family Melastomataceae — one of the most spectacular flowering plants in the world — that produces enormous, pendant, bougainvillea-like flower panicles composed of clusters of small, deep-rose-pink to magenta flowers hanging from pale-pink to rose-red, waxy bracts, dangling in dramatic, chandelier-like cascades from the tips of the stiff, upright, square stems with large, sessile, dark-green, prominently veined leaves. The entire flower structure is breathtakingly ornamental and can reach 12–18 inches in length on established specimens. As an epiphyte, medinilla naturally grows on tree branches in the Philippine rainforest and is adapted to excellent drainage, high humidity, and warm, bright-shade conditions — it requires an open, orchid-like substrate and consistent humidity rather than consistently moist soil. In zone 10–12 it can be grown outdoors in bright shade; elsewhere it is a challenging but rewarding conservatory or greenhouse specimen.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; male fern is one of the most adaptable of all ferns, tolerating dry shade, poor soils, and challenging urban conditions that defeat most other species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; male fern is one of the most widely grown and adaptable ferns in the world, forming large, vase-shaped, semi-evergreen clumps with lance-shaped, dark-green fronds that are both elegant and extremely tough. It tolerates dry shade, poor soils, periods of neglect, and more urban pollution than virtually any other fern. New fronds emerge as tightly coiled croziers (fiddleheads) in spring. Semi-evergreen in mild winters; cut old fronds to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges to improve appearance. Excellent for difficult, challenging shaded spots. Named varieties include 'Barnesii' (narrow, upright) and 'Linearis Polydactyla' (narrow, crested frond tips). Divide clumps every 5–7 years in spring.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown transplants in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich, poorly drained to seasonally wet soil in partial shade to full sun. Maleberry thrives in the wet, acidic conditions of pocosins, bog margins, and wet flatwoods where most other ornamental shrubs will not succeed.
directions: Maleberry is a native deciduous shrub of wet, acidic soils across the eastern United States, found in pocosins, bog margins, wet flatwoods, and seasonally flooded stream banks from Maine south to Florida and west to Texas. The clusters of small, urn-shaped white flowers in late spring attract native bees and bumblebees, while the attractive fall foliage ranges from yellow to orange-red in appropriate sunlight. A member of the blueberry family (Ericaceae), Maleberry shares the extreme soil requirements of its relatives — strongly acidic, humus-rich, poorly drained to saturated conditions that would stress most landscape shrubs. Well-suited for wet, acidic garden settings including bog gardens, rain garden overflow zones, and moist native plant hedges in acid soil conditions, Maleberry is rarely cultivated but deserves wider use for challenging wet, acidic sites. Plant rooted cuttings in strongly acidic, moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun with room to reach its mature 6-7 foot height; tolerates a range of soils but performs best with consistent moisture during establishment.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun with room to reach its mature 6-7 foot height. Bred by German nurseryman Ernst Pagels to flower reliably even in cooler, shorter-season climates, Malepartus produces broad green foliage with a fine white midrib and sends up large, silky plumes in late summer well ahead of most other Miscanthus sinensis selections. The plumes open a warm pinkish-copper, deepen to rust-red through fall, and finally fade to shimmering silvery-white, persisting well into winter above a strong, upright-arching clump. Foliage turns shades of orange, red, and bronze in autumn, adding a second season of color before the plant is cut back hard in late winter.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in fall into well-drained, rocky to loamy soil in partial sun; mallow ninebark is native to dry montane forest understories of the Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in fall into well-drained, rocky to loamy soil in partial sun, matching the dry, open coniferous forest understory this species naturally inhabits across the Northern Rockies and Pacific Northwest. Mallow ninebark forms a dense, rounded mound of maple-like lobed leaves with clusters of small white to pinkish flowers in early summer that draw native bees and other pollinating insects. Its inflated seed capsules are eaten by songbirds through fall, while the foliage and twigs are browsed by deer and elk, making it an important component of wildlife habitat in dry western forests. Peeling, multi-layered bark gives the shrub interest through the winter months and shelter for overwintering insects.

plant_note: Direct sow after the danger of hard frost has passed, since the taprooted seedlings resent transplanting; thin to final spacing once seedlings have a couple of true leaves.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, since the deep taproot makes this Mediterranean annual a poor candidate for transplanting from cell packs. Malope produces large, satiny, mallow-like flowers in shades of magenta, pink, or white, each backed by three enlarged leafy bracts that continue to enlarge and remain attractive as the seed pod matures, giving the plant a long season of interest beyond the bloom itself. Sturdy, upright, and free-flowering over a long summer season, it makes an easy, old-fashioned cottage garden and cutting-garden annual that needs little more than deadheading to keep producing new flowers. Once established it tolerates heat and some drought well, and it self-sows modestly where the soil is left undisturbed.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or direct sow in fall for spring germination; Maltese cross self-sows freely and can become a weed in favorable conditions — deadhead before seeds mature to limit spread. It is short-lived (2–4 years) but self-sows to maintain colonies. Plants in poor soil stay compact; rich soil produces tall, floppy plants that may need staking.
directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Maltese cross is a classic cottage-garden perennial from Russia and Siberia producing one of the most intensely saturated and vivid scarlet reds available in early-summer perennials — upright, bristly-hairy stems topped with flat-topped, dense clusters of small flowers, each petal notched into a distinctive cross shape that gives each floret a Maltese cross outline, and in the aggregate creating round, vivid-scarlet flower heads of high visual impact. The scarlet is hot, clear, and uncompromising — a true scarlet without orange or pink dilution. This saturated color, in combination with the flat-topped, dense cluster form, creates one of the most eye-catching early-summer effects in the mixed border. It is a traditional cottage garden plant with centuries of cultivation. It combines dramatically with blue delphiniums or white Shasta daisies in the classic red-white-blue color schemes of traditional English cottage gardens. Self-sows freely to maintain colonies; the white form 'Alba' is also available. Tends to be short-lived but perpetuates itself by seed.

common_name: Malvern Hills Rose (David Austin English Rambling Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun to partial shade with sturdy support, since Malvern Hills is an extremely vigorous rambler best trained over a large arch, pergola, or fence where its long canes have room to spread.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, training the long, flexible canes over sturdy support such as an arch, pergola, or large fence, since Malvern Hills is one of the more vigorous, rambling David Austin introductions rather than a compact border shrub. Small, soft yellow, rosette-shaped flowers open in dense clusters in a single heavy flush in late spring, carrying a light, fresh fragrance, and the shrub's shade tolerance and vigor make it useful for covering a difficult structure or fence line that would defeat a less rambunctious climber. Prune immediately after the spring bloom to shape and remove old wood, since it flowers primarily on growth made the previous year.

common_name: Maman Cochet Rose (Large-Flowered Antique Tea Rose)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Maman Cochet, introduced in 1893, is one of the most widely grown Tea roses across the old Deep South, valued for large, high-centered blooms and strong heat tolerance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Maman Cochet, introduced in 1893, produces large, full, high-centered flowers in soft pink shaded with cream on the reverse of the petals, opening from long, elegant buds that made it a favorite cut flower and exhibition rose in its era. It remains one of the most widely planted and beloved Tea roses in old Southern gardens for its combination of exceptional bloom size, repeat flowering through the growing season, and the toughness and heat tolerance characteristic of Tea roses. Prune lightly after each flush to encourage continued rebloom, and expect strong resistance to black spot and powdery mildew even in humid Gulf Coast summers.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; likes cool weather.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep in cool, moist soil in early spring. Mammoth sweet peas boast extra-large, sweetly scented flowers on long stems that are perfect for cutting. Bred from an Early Multiflora Gigantea Spencer type, this blend offers extra drought and heat resistance for a longer season. Provide a tall trellis, keep roots cool and evenly moist, and cut flowers frequently to prolong the bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or corms after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Mammoth grows rapidly in zone 9's warm, humid summer conditions — plants can reach full height and enormous leaf size by midsummer from a spring planting. Provide consistent moisture, especially during peak summer growth; Colocasia thrives in wet to consistently moist conditions and can even grow in shallow water. In zone 9 the corms often survive winter in the ground with heavy mulching; in colder areas of zone 9 dig and store corms above 50°F. The enormous leaves can reach 4 feet across — a single plant in optimal conditions creates a truly dramatic, tropical focal point.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Mammoth Colocasia thrives in consistently moist conditions, bog edges, and even shallow water where drainage is poor; Mammoth is a large-growing selection of common taro (Colocasia esculenta) selected and named for its exceptional leaf size — producing the largest leaves of any widely available Colocasia cultivar, with individual leaves reaching 3–4 feet long and nearly as wide under optimal conditions. The enormous, heart-shaped, velvety, medium-to-dark green leaves on sturdy, upright petioles create an overwhelming tropical presence in the garden that is unmatched by almost any other hardy temperate-climate plant — a single well-grown Mammoth plant is a landscape focal point that demands attention and creates an immediate tropical atmosphere in whatever garden space it occupies. The enormous leaf surface is simultaneously visually dramatic and ecologically functional: Mammoth creates deep shade beneath its canopy (useful for understory shade plants), captures rainfall and funnels it to the soil (an adaptation to tropical forest conditions), and provides cover for garden wildlife. In zone 9 Mammoth thrives in the humid heat that is its native climate — producing increasingly large leaves through summer as the plant approaches its full potential.

plant_note: Soak and sow in cool spring soil beside a trellis.
directions: This mammoth sweet pea mix delivers large, fragrant blooms in soft rose, pink, lavender, and white on vigorous vines. Soak seeds overnight and sow in cool early-spring soil against a trellis, since these cottage-garden climbers love a chilly start. Keep roots cool and moisture steady, and harvest often to encourage a long succession of scented flowers. The five- to six-foot vines need sturdy support to climb.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; likes cool weather.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep in cool, moist soil in early spring. This Mammoth selection produces striking, extra-large blooms in deep velvety purple-blue atop long stems ideal for cutting gardens. Bred from Early Multiflora Gigantea, it offers Spencer-type beauty with added drought and heat resistance. Provide a tall trellis, keep roots cool and evenly watered, and cut flowers often to extend flowering.

common_name: Mammoth Russian Sunflower (Classic Giant Single-Stem Sunflower)
plant_note: Sow after the last frost when soil is warm; Mammoth Russian is a classic giant heirloom sunflower producing a single towering stalk topped by an enormous seed head, grown as much for edible, harvestable seed as for ornamental impact.
directions: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed. Mammoth Russian is one of the oldest and most iconic giant sunflower heirlooms, reliably reaching ten to twelve feet or more on a single sturdy stalk topped by a massive, heavy flower head that matures into a dense disc of large, striped seeds prized for roasting, snacking, and bird feed. Because of its impressive height and heavy seed head, it benefits from a somewhat sheltered site out of strong wind, and very tall specimens may need staking. Once the back of the flower head turns yellow-brown and petals drop, the seed head can be cut and hung to dry before threshing out the seeds for harvest or leaving it up for birds.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; needs warm soil and full sun.
directions: This giant heirloom sunflower grows on a single stem to ten or twelve feet and crowns it with a massive golden head up to a foot across. Sow seeds an inch deep directly in warm soil after frost, spacing generously so the huge plants have room. Give full sun and steady water, and stake tall stems in exposed sites to keep them from toppling. The abundant seeds are excellent for roasting or feeding birds once heads mature.

common_name: Mammy Croton (Dark Twisted-Leaf Red-and-Gold Croton Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mammy's strongly twisted and contorted leaf form is a defining ornamental characteristic — the spiral, corkscrew-shaped leaves distinguish it from all other commonly grown croton cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mammy Croton is one of the most distinctive and recognizable croton cultivars — immediately identifiable by its strongly twisted, spiraling, contorted leaves that curl and spiral along their length rather than lying flat, creating an unusual three-dimensional texture unlike any other commonly available ornamental foliage plant. The leaf color is darker and more intensely red-dominated than Petra: deep, burgundy-red to red-and-gold coloring on a dark green base, with the red tones more predominant and the yellow more restricted to the midrib and splashes near the veins. The overall effect is a darker, moodier palette than the brighter, more orange-dominated Petra — making Mammy especially effective in tropical designs with other dark-leaved companions like black elephant ear, purple ti plant, and dark caladiums. In zone 9, Mammy is typically used as a warm-season container plant or annual-style tropical that is moved indoors before frost; in zone 10b-12 it grows as a permanent perennial shrub. The twisted leaf form is most pronounced in high light conditions — leaves in deep shade tend to become more flattened and less dramatically spiral. The unusual form makes Mammy Croton a striking conversation-piece plant in tropical container arrangements.

plant_note: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5) soil or potting mix in full sun to partial shade; mandevilla requires warm temperatures above 50°F at all times — cold damage occurs below 45°F. In zone 9–10 it may be grown in the ground in a protected location; elsewhere treat as a container plant brought indoors in winter.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; mandevilla is one of the most popular tropical vines for patio containers in the United States, producing large, trumpet-shaped flowers 3–4 inches across in brilliant pink, red, or white from spring through frost. The climbing stems have glossy, dark green leaves that are attractive even out of bloom. Modern compact ('Sundaville' and 'Sun Parasol') series stay under 3 feet and are outstanding in large pots and hanging baskets. The larger vining types need a trellis or support and can reach 8–10 feet. Feed every 2 weeks with a bloom-booster fertilizer for maximum flower production. In zone 9–10 mandevilla may be left outdoors year-round in a sheltered location; in zone 8a bring inside at first frost and keep barely moist through winter. Very sap is milky white and mildly toxic — wear gloves when pruning.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mango bears a warm, soft orange-peach spathe with a deeper throat.
directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where hot afternoon sun will not scorch the foliage. Mango bears a soft, warm orange-peach spathe deepening toward a richer orange throat, a gentler tone than the more fiery reds and oranges of some calla lily hybrids, on narrow, glossy green foliage that rises through summer before the plant goes dormant in fall. Its warm, blendable color pairs well with both hot-colored and pastel summer plantings. In zones 8-10 it can be left dry in the ground through a mild winter, while in colder climates the rhizomes should be lifted and stored dry like dahlia tubers. Reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall to encourage the plant into its natural dormant period.

common_name: Mango Popsicle Red Hot Poker (Compact Orange Dwarf Kniphofia)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Mango Popsicle is a compact, dwarf red hot poker bred for smaller borders and container growing.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; good drainage is essential year-round, since standing moisture around the crown quickly causes rot. Mango Popsicle bears compact, torch-like flower spikes in warm mango-orange, blooming on a much shorter, more compact plant than traditional tall red hot poker cultivars, which suits it well to smaller borders, rock gardens, and large containers where a full-size Kniphofia would be out of scale. Its shorter grassy foliage and reduced overall size also make winter protection easier in colder parts of its range. The tubular flowers attract hummingbirds through the summer bloom season. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering begins to decline.

common_name: Mango Tango Agastache (Vivid Orange-Red Hummingbird Mint)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential for winter survival, since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.
directions: Mango Tango carries dense, tightly packed flower spikes in a vivid orange-red over aromatic, gray-green, anise-scented foliage, one of the warmest, most saturated colors available among hardy hummingbird mints.
