The loose, twining stems 6–15 feet long bear small, dark green, slightly succulent leaves and are covered in vibrant orange blooms that attract butterflies. The orange color is exceptionally vivid and warm, excellent for combining with blue salvias or purple queen for autumn and winter color. In zone 8a it is killed to the ground in hard freezes but established root systems resprout reliably each spring to bloom again by mid-summer.

plant_note: Direct-sow or allow to self-sow in almost any well-drained soil including wall crevices, paving gaps, and gravel; Mexican fleabane is a prolific self-seeder that naturalizes readily and is best established by simply allowing seeds to find their own level in the garden. It is short-lived as an individual plant (2–3 years) but self-sows perpetually, filling gaps and softening edges throughout the garden.
directions: Sow in almost any well-drained soil, including crevices in walls and paving, in full sun; Mexican fleabane is one of the most charming and generous self-seeding plants for temperate gardens, producing a near-continuous display of small daisy flowers from late spring through autumn — the flowers open white, then age through blush-pink to deep rose over the course of several days, so a flowering plant simultaneously carries white, pink, and rose flowers creating a multicolor cottage-garden effect. The plants themselves are small and airy, with tiny, narrow leaves, creating fine-textured mounds that tuck into gaps in walls, cascade over stone edges, spill from urns, and fill paving cracks — places where larger plants cannot grow. The combination of extremely long bloom, color change, minimal size, and willingness to grow in dry, lean conditions in full sun makes this one of the most useful 'spontaneous' plants in the garden. Originally from Mexico and Central America, it has naturalized widely in the Mediterranean, parts of Australia, and coastal California and Pacific Northwest in the US.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, lean, rocky to gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in zone 7–11; Mexican Grass Tree is a striking, long-lived architectural accent plant native to the highlands of Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas, Mexico — forming a huge, rounded, porcupine-like mass of extremely long, narrow, unarmed leaves (to 6 feet) radiating from a central stem that eventually develops into a tree trunk, used as a dramatic focal point in hot, dry Southwestern desert and xeriscape gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, rocky to gravelly, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Dasylirion longissimum requires excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water once established — it is highly drought and heat tolerant but will rot in poorly drained, wet, or clay soils. Dasylirion longissimum (Mexican Grass Tree or Toton Palm) is a dramatic, slow-growing architectural succulent in the Asparagaceae family native to the semi-arid highland mountains of Nuevo Leon, Coahuila, and Tamaulipas in northeastern Mexico, where it grows on rocky limestone slopes and ridges in full sun. Unlike the spoon-leaf Dasylirion species (D. wheeleri, D. texanum) whose leaves have serrated or spiny edges, D. longissimum is distinguished by its extremely long (to 6 feet), narrow, strap-like, essentially unarmed and smooth-edged leaves that radiate from the growing center in an enormous, perfect sphere — giving the plant an appearance of a giant teal-green sea urchin or porcupine. Over many years and decades, the plant develops a raised, cylindrical trunk beneath the leaf mass, eventually reaching 10–20 feet in old age. The flower stalk when it finally appears is a spectacular 10–15 foot spike covered with thousands of tiny cream flowers. Excellent for Southwestern desert gardens, xeriscape plantings, and architectural accent positions in hot, dry, alkaline-soil landscapes in zones 7–11.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican heather establishes quickly and begins blooming almost immediately after transplanting. In zones 9–10 it often self-sows freely and may behave as a short-lived perennial; it is used as an annual in zones 8 and colder.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican heather is a fine-textured, dense-growing tropical perennial that produces a continuous profusion of tiny lavender, pink, or white flowers on compact mounds of tiny, shiny, narrow leaves — resembling true heather (Calluna) in growth habit and foliage texture but adapted to tropical heat rather than cool climates. It blooms almost without pause from planting through frost and is one of the best butterfly and skipper nectar plants available for Gulf Coast gardens. In zone 9 it is typically a short-lived perennial that often reseeds to maintain a permanent presence. It is outstanding as a low edging plant, in mass plantings, along pathways, or at the front of mixed borders where its fine texture contrasts beautifully with coarser tropical foliage. Requires almost no deadheading or maintenance; simply trim lightly in early spring to refresh the habit.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Mexican Hens holds its ruffled leaf form and frosty color best in bright light with cooler nights.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Mexican Hens holds its ruffled leaf form and frosty color best in bright light with cooler nights. Thin, wavy, deeply ruffled leaves coated in a fine, frosty, powdery bloom form an elegant, undulating rosette in shades of soft pink, lavender, and gray, one of the most delicately textured and colorful echeveria species commonly grown, with color intensifying in cooler weather and bright light. Native to rocky slopes in Mexico, it offsets to form small clusters over time and is a favorite for succulent arrangements and collector displays for its uniquely ruffled, almost paper-thin leaf texture. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves to protect the delicate powdery coating, and provide bright light for the best ruffling and color.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in partial shade to full sun with well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mexican Honeysuckle grows rapidly in zone 9 and begins blooming in its first season. In zone 9a, plants freeze back in hard winters but resprout reliably from the root crown in spring. In zone 9b-10, it grows as a reliable semi-evergreen perennial shrub blooming nearly year-round. Prune by one-third after each bloom flush to maintain compact form and stimulate reblooming. Roots readily from stem cuttings. An excellent hummingbird plant.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Mexican Honeysuckle blooms most prolifically in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9 and actually benefits from afternoon shade during the peak of summer heat. Justicia spicigera is a large, soft-stemmed, fast-growing shrub from Mexico and Central America in the Acanthaceae family, closely related to the more commonly grown Jacobinia (Justicia carnea) and Shrimp Plant (Justicia brandegeana). The species' common name 'Mexican Honeysuckle' refers not to any botanical relationship with true Lonicera honeysuckles but to the nectar-rich tubular flowers, which are intensely attractive to hummingbirds and butterflies — the long, tubular, orange to orange-red flowers emerging from softly fuzzy, velvety calyxes are among the most reliable hummingbird attractants in the zone 9 garden. The flowers are produced in terminal spikes and bloom over an exceptionally long season, essentially year-round in zone 9b-10 with brief pauses between flush cycles. The large, soft, gray-green, velvety leaves give the plant an attractive textural quality even out of bloom. In Mexican folk medicine, Justicia spicigera leaves (Mohintli) have traditional uses as a blue dye plant and herbal remedy. Among the most underused but most hummingbird-effective shrubs for Gulf Coast partial-shade garden beds.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after last frost into well-drained, poor to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; in zones 9–10 plants can be direct sown in fall for spring bloom.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant to well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Mexican hyssop is among the best hummingbird and pollinator plants for hot, dry, alkaline conditions across the Southwest and Gulf South, producing dense spikes of tubular rose-pink to cherry-red flowers from midsummer through fall that hummingbirds, hawk moths, and butterflies work heavily. The crushed foliage has a pleasant licorice-mint fragrance. Unlike North American Agastache species, Mexican hyssop is adapted to alkaline, rocky, dry conditions and performs poorly in acidic, heavy soils. Short-lived as a perennial in warm climates but self-sows readily to maintain a colony without replanting. Drought-tolerant once established.

common_name: Mexican Lilac (Quick Stick, Mother of Cocoa)
plant_note: Plant container stock or large hardwood cuttings (which root directly in the soil) in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; gliricidia is one of the world's most important multipurpose tropical trees — outstanding for living fences, shade for cocoa, and nitrogen fixation in tropical agroforestry systems.
directions: Plant container stock or large (2–4 foot) hardwood cuttings directly in the ground in spring; gliricidia establishes from large cuttings planted directly in the soil — a useful trait for creating instant living fence posts. Gliricidia sepium (Mexican lilac, quick stick, or mother of cocoa) is one of the most widely planted multipurpose tropical trees in the world — a Central American legume tree grown throughout the humid tropics for nitrogen fixation, living fences, shade for cacao and coffee plantations ('mother of cocoa' in Costa Rica), green manure, and fodder. The tree has an extraordinary capacity to root from large, dormant hardwood cuttings planted directly in the ground — a common practice for creating instant living fence posts that then leaf out and grow into full trees. In spring (usually January–March when dormant), the bare branches are covered with stunning clusters of bright pink-lavender pea-like flowers resembling redbud (Cercis) — one of the showiest tropical trees in bloom. The leaves and branches are nitrogen-rich and used as green mulch in organic farming; however, the leaves are toxic to mammals (including horses and dogs) if consumed in large quantities. CAUTION: Seeds, bark, and leaves are toxic to mammals — do not plant where livestock have access.

plant_note: Divide offsets in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; Mexican lily is damaged below about 15-20 degrees F and is best suited to zones 7-10. The spectacular flower scape, reaching 6 feet or more, appears once after the plant reaches maturity and then the main rosette dies, leaving offsets to continue the colony.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Mexican lily is a dramatic, architecturally imposing relative of the agave from the mountains of central Mexico, forming a bold rosette of broad, soft, blue-green, sword-shaped, yucca-like leaves that are spineless and non-lethal to touch — unlike true agaves. When mature, the plant produces one of the most spectacular flowering events in the succulent world: a massive, arching, coral-red to orange-red flower scape that bends dramatically under its own weight and grows to 5-7 feet, bearing drooping clusters of pendant, tubular, red-and-green flowers along its entire length. The coral-red scape itself is ornamental for weeks before and after the flowers open. The combination of dramatic arching scape, vivid coral-red color, and pendant green-tipped flowers is unlike anything else in hardy horticulture. After flowering, the main rosette dies but produces offsets at its base. An outstanding architectural specimen for warm, sheltered, well-drained gardens in zones 7-10, particularly effective with other bold-textured plants.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; in zone 7 site against a south- or west-facing wall for winter frost protection, as hard freezes can damage the foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; Mexican orange blossom is one of the most popular fragrant evergreen shrubs for warm-climate gardens, producing clusters of pure white, star-shaped flowers with a powerful, sweet orange-blossom fragrance in spring and frequently reblooming again in fall. The glossy, trifoliate leaves are aromatic when crushed, releasing a sharp citrus-like scent. It is borderline hardy in zone 7 and may suffer leaf damage in hard freezes, but typically recovers vigorously from the root system — planting against a warm south-facing wall significantly improves winter survival. The compact cultivar 'Sundance' (golden-yellow foliage) and the more cold-tolerant 'Aztec Pearl' (narrower leaflets, very fragrant pink-tinged flowers) are excellent named selections.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in any moist to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican petunia is extremely adaptable and spreading — contain with deep edging if planting near lawn or naturalistic areas, as it spreads aggressively by underground runners and self-sown seed in warm climates. Use the compact, non-invasive cultivar 'Purple Showers' or 'Katie' in contained plantings.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican petunia is one of the most widely used and lowest-maintenance flowering perennials in Gulf Coast landscapes, producing a continuous display of funnel-shaped flowers in purple, pink, or white from spring through frost on upright stems with narrow, dark-green leaves. Each individual flower lasts only one day, but the plant produces new flowers in such abundance that the display is uninterrupted throughout the season. It is remarkably drought, heat, and salt tolerant once established and thrives in the conditions that challenge most other perennials. However, it spreads aggressively by underground runners and abundant self-seeding — R. simplex is considered invasive in natural areas in Florida and other Gulf states. Compact, sterile cultivars such as 'Purple Showers' and 'Katie' (dwarf, 8–12 inches) are strongly recommended for residential use as they do not spread by seed. Deadhead or shear to refresh and stimulate new bloom flushes.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost in dry, sandy, well-drained soil; seed requires warmth to germinate reliably.
directions: A freely self-seeding annual prickly poppy native to tropical Mexico and the Caribbean, now widely naturalized in disturbed, dry, open ground throughout the southern US and tropical regions worldwide; produces deeply lobed, spine-tipped, silvery-veined, blue-green leaves and golden-yellow, 4-6-petaled flowers 1.5-2 inches across from spring through fall. The yellow sap and seeds are toxic — do not ingest. Direct sow in spring in dry, sandy, well-drained, lean soil; self-sows prolifically and can become weedy in favorable conditions. Grown in folk medicine traditions across tropical America for its analgesic properties.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican redbud requires scarification to break seed dormancy — nick or abrade the hard seed coat and soak 24 hours before planting. It grows naturally on rocky, limestone canyon walls and slopes of west Texas and Mexico.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican redbud is a shrubby to small-tree redbud native to the rocky limestone mountains and canyon walls of west Texas (Big Bend country) and adjacent Mexico, distinguished from eastern redbud (C. canadensis) by its smaller stature, smaller and more rounded leaves with unusually wavy, scalloped margins, and greater tolerance of dry, alkaline, rocky soils. The bright magenta-pink spring flowers appear on bare branches before the leaves, like other redbuds. Heat, drought, and alkaline soil tolerance superior to eastern redbud makes it better suited to the dry limestone terrain of central and west Texas. A fine specimen shrub-tree for the xeric, alkaline, rocky garden in zone 9a where standard redbud struggles on thin, calcareous soils.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; in zone 8 it may die back to roots in hard freezes but re-sprouts in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Mexican sage is a large, bold, shrubby species with broad, deeply veined, highly aromatic leaves and long wands of blue-purple flowers from late summer through fall that attract hummingbirds and bumblebees. It is native to mountain forests and canyon edges in central Mexico at moderate elevation and tolerates partial shade better than most sages, making it useful in the lightly shaded areas of a Gulf Coast or zone 8–9 garden. The foliage has a strong, pleasant herbal fragrance when brushed and is deer resistant. It grows rapidly to a large sub-shrub in one season and may be damaged or killed by hard freezes but typically re-sprouts from the root crown in zone 8. Shear back by half in mid-spring to encourage compact, heavily blooming growth.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade, giving this large Mexican highland sage plenty of room to reach full size before blooming in fall.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade with room to grow into a large, upright shrub; Mexican scarlet sage produces some of the largest, most dramatic flowers of any commonly grown salvia, with brilliant orange-red tubular blooms emerging from near-black calyces on tall spikes that appear from late summer into fall. It is a late-season showstopper and one of the most reliable hummingbird magnets available for a fall garden, drawing migrating hummingbirds heavily as they pass through in September and October. Because it flowers so late in the year, an early hard freeze in the northern part of its range can cut the display short, so site it in a warm, sheltered spot at the cold edge of its hardiness. Pinch young plants once or twice in early summer to encourage bushier growth and more flowering stems, and cut back to the base after a killing frost, mulching well over winter.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Mexican snowball requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of wet soil, especially in the center of the rosette — the most common cause of death is crown rot from standing water.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil or succulent potting mix in bright sun to part shade; allow soil to dry completely between waterings. Echeveria elegans (Mexican snowball) is one of the classic and most widely grown echeverias — a Mexican succulent producing perfect, symmetrical, pale-blue-grey to ice-blue rosettes of dense, fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves 4–6 inches across, with a powdery glaucous coating that gives the rosette a cool, icy-blue appearance and inspired the common name 'Mexican snowball.' In spring and summer, it produces arching, coral-pink flower stems with nodding, yellow-tipped, pink flowers that are attractive to hummingbirds. The plant offsets freely (producing 'chicks' around the central 'hen'), allowing easy propagation by division; leaf and stem cuttings also root readily. Echeveria elegans is the foundation of much of the interest in succulent container gardening and succulent wreaths, and is one of the best echeverias for humid climates (it tolerates more moisture than many succulents if drainage is excellent). In zone 9, it grows outdoors in well-drained rockeries, raised beds, and container gardens; bring indoors during hard freezes.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting (after soil warms to 70°F+) in well-drained, average to poor, neutral soil in full sun; tithonia is extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms better in lean, dry soil.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting (after soil warms to 70°F+) in well-drained, average to poor, neutral soil in full sun; tithonia is extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms better in lean, dry soil. Tithonia rotundifolia is the premier late-summer annual for attracting monarch butterflies, swallowtails, and native bumblebees — in high summer and early fall, a patch of blooming Mexican sunflowers will be covered with butterflies from dawn to dusk. The plant produces vivid, velvety, 3-inch, orange-scarlet flowers with a golden-yellow center on tall, branching, slightly hairy stems from midsummer through frost; hollow stems must be seared before using as cut flowers to prevent wilting. It is an outstanding back-of-border annual for hot, sunny gardens in zones 9–11 and is perennial in frost-free areas.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade sheltered from wind; give it room to spread its broad arching crown as the trunk slowly builds height over years.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade, protected from drying wind that shreds the soft fronds. Water generously and regularly, since it does not tolerate drought the way tougher landscape ferns do. Over years it develops a shaggy, fiber-covered trunk topped by a graceful crown of finely textured, soft-green arching fronds, making it one of the more elegant tree ferns for a shaded tropical courtyard or large container specimen in cooler climates.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; established clumps are drought-tolerant but look best with regular water through the first two seasons.
directions: This subtropical clumping bamboo produces extremely fine-textured, blue-green foliage on thin culms that arch gracefully outward in a fountain-like habit, giving it a soft, willowy look unlike any timber bamboo. It is a true clumper with tight rhizomes, so it never becomes invasive and is a popular specimen or screening plant around pools and patios in Florida, coastal California, and the Gulf South. It tolerates poor, rocky soil once established but grows fastest and fullest with occasional deep watering and a light annual feeding. Foliage can be damaged by hard freezes, but established clumps generally resprout from the base after cold snaps in zone 8b-9 gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in winter or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexican white oak, a Texas Superstar tree, grows considerably faster than most oaks and tolerates heat, wind, and drought better than many shade tree alternatives.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexican white oak, also called Monterrey oak, is a Texas Superstar-designated shade tree native to both a small area of south Texas and much of northeastern Mexico, prized for a faster growth rate than most oaks along with attractive peach-to-bronze new spring growth that matures to glossy green. It is semi-evergreen to evergreen in mild winters, dropping and replacing its leaves quickly in late winter rather than standing bare for long, and tolerates heat, wind, and drought impressively well once established, making it a strong, adaptable shade tree choice for difficult urban and suburban Texas and Gulf South sites. Its faster growth compared to slower native oaks makes it useful where a newly planted landscape needs shade sooner rather than decades later. Give it plenty of room to reach its substantial mature size, and provide regular water during the first couple of years to establish a deep root system before easing off to only occasional supplemental irrigation.

common_name: Mexican Yellow Water Lily (Yellow Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 2–4 inches deep in heavy aquatic planting mix in containers submerged 6–18 inches below the water surface; Mexican yellow water lily spreads vigorously by stolons and can naturalize in shallow ponds and slow-moving water throughout zones 8–11.
directions: Plant tubers in heavy aquatic soil (NOT potting mix — which floats) in containers submerged 6–18 inches below the water surface in full sun; Mexican yellow water lily is a native aquatic perennial of ponds, marshes, and slow-moving waters of the Gulf Coast region from Texas to Florida and into Mexico, producing the classic water lily form — floating, round pads and fragrant, multi-petaled flowers — but in a soft, clear yellow color that distinguishes it from most cultivated water lilies. It is notably more heat-tolerant and better adapted to warm, humid climates than the European water lily (N. alba) or most cultivated tropical water lily hybrids. The cheerful yellow flowers open in the morning and close by afternoon. This species spreads readily by horizontal rhizomes (stolons) to colonize pond edges in warm climates — beneficial in a natural pond setting, manageable in a contained water garden. An excellent choice for water gardens in zone 9a.

common_name: Mexican Zinnia (Little Classic Zinnia, Haage Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mexican zinnia is more drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and disease-resistant than common garden zinnia (Z. elegans) and is outstanding for hot, humid Gulf Coast summers where powdery mildew can devastate Z. elegans plantings.
directions: Direct sow seeds in warm soil in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; thin to 8–12 inches. Zinnia haageana (Mexican zinnia) is a compact, fine-leaved, heat-tolerant Mexican native zinnia species that produces cheerful bicolor and tricolor daisy flowers in orange, red, yellow, and mahogany combinations from summer through frost. Unlike the common large-flowered garden zinnia (Z. elegans), Z. haageana is dramatically more drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and resistant to powdery mildew — the disease that devastates Z. elegans in hot, humid climates. In zone 9, Mexican zinnias perform with vigor through the summer while common garden zinnias may defoliate from mildew. The 'Aztec' series is the most widely grown, with single or semi-double flowers in warm orange-red, yellow-orange, and burnt-orange combinations that are extremely attractive to butterflies, especially Gulf Fritillaries and Sulphurs. The compact habit and narrow, lance-shaped leaves create a finer texture than Z. elegans. Z. haageana is also used as a parent in interspecific zinnia hybrids ('Profusion,' 'Zahara') bred specifically for heat, humidity, and disease resistance.

common_name: Miami Crape Myrtle (Dark Pink Cinnamon-Bark Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Miami is a U.S. National Arboretum indica x fauriei hybrid released in 1979, growing into a tall, mildew-resistant tree with striking exfoliating bark.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Miami is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei hybrid releases, combining the flower power of common crape myrtle with the disease resistance and exceptional bark of Lagerstroemia fauriei. It produces abundant dark-pink flower clusters from summer into early fall on a tall, upright tree, and as it matures the outer bark exfoliates to reveal smooth, rich cinnamon-brown inner bark that becomes a major ornamental feature through fall and winter after the leaves drop. Its strong resistance to powdery mildew, the primary disease problem of straight Lagerstroemia indica cultivars, makes it a reliable choice for humid Gulf South summers. Its eventual height puts it among the larger crape myrtle selections, better suited to a specimen planting or street tree role than a small foundation bed. Never top or hard-prune the main framework; prune selectively in late winter only to remove crossing or crowded growth.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall into moist, disturbed woodland soil; seeds require cold stratification to break dormancy and will germinate naturally in late winter or early spring for bloom in April and May. Seeds can also be stratified in the refrigerator for 4-6 weeks and sown in earliest spring.
directions: Phacelia purshii is a delicate spring annual native to moist woodland edges and disturbed forest floors across eastern North America, producing loose clusters of finely-fringed lavender-blue and white flowers from April through June. Scatter seeds in fall across bare or lightly raked soil in partial shade; the seeds need a cold, moist period to break dormancy and will germinate on their own schedule in late winter. Plants grow quickly in cool weather, bloom prolifically, then set abundant seed before summer heat arrives, often naturalizing into self-sustaining colonies. It combines beautifully with other spring ephemerals such as Virginia bluebells and wild ginger.

common_name: Miami Supreme Gardenia (Heat-Tolerant Large Double White Gardenia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Miami Supreme was bred specifically for reliable flowering under the intense heat and humidity of the Deep South and Florida.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Miami Supreme bears large, fully double, intensely fragrant white flowers on a vigorous, upright shrub bred specifically to hold up to the extreme heat and humidity of the Deep South and Florida, where some gardenia cultivars struggle to set or hold buds. Its bold flower size and dependable performance under tough summer conditions have made it a favorite for Gulf Coast gardens. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer through the growing season, keep soil consistently moist, and prune right after the main spring-into-summer bloom to shape.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in sharply well-drained, gritty or sandy soil in partial shade or sun in fall, 6–10 weeks before first frost; Michael's fritillary is native to alpine and subalpine meadows in northeastern Turkey and must have excellent drainage year-round, particularly dry conditions during summer dormancy — planting in raised beds or incorporating coarse grit into heavy soils is strongly recommended.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in sharply well-drained, gritty soil in partial shade or full sun in autumn for April–May bloom; Michael's fritillary is one of the most visually striking of all small fritillaries — a compact, 4–8-inch species from the mountains of northeastern Turkey producing clusters of pendant, bell-shaped flowers whose coloring is among the most dramatic of the genus: the upper two-thirds of each bell is a deep, rich purple-maroon to mahogany-purple, shading abruptly to a bright, clear canary-yellow band at the flared petal tips, creating an intensely eye-catching bicolor effect quite unlike anything else in the spring garden. Multiple bells are carried per stem, intensifying the display. Like all Middle Eastern alpine fritillaries, it insists on perfect drainage and a dry summer dormancy; it is intolerant of prolonged wet conditions at any season and will fail in heavy, moisture-retentive soils. Best grown in a gravel garden, raised bed, alpine trough, or bulb frame. When conditions suit, it multiplies freely by bulb offsets. A rare but readily available gem for the enthusiast collector.

plant_note: Sow on bare limestone-derived soil in fall; seeds require cold stratification over winter to germinate in late winter or early spring. Do not add organic matter or compost — this species demands thin, nutrient-poor, calcareous substrate.
directions: Michaux's Gladecress is a tiny, jewel-like native winter annual of limestone cedar glades in Tennessee, Kentucky, and adjacent states, one of the earliest wildflowers to bloom in the entire eastern flora, opening its single white 4-petaled flowers with yellow centers on thread-like stems as early as February through April. It completes its entire life cycle on the exposed, thin-soiled faces of limestone outcrops that experience brief seasonal saturation followed by intense summer drought — conditions nearly impossible to recreate in conventional gardens. Grow in thin, rocky, calcareous, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, deliberately avoiding soil amendments or fertilizer that would favor competing vegetation. It is an ecological specialist of rare, imperiled cedar glade habitat and is best suited for limestone glade restoration projects rather than traditional garden settings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, rocky or gravelly soil in partial shade; Michaux's saxifrage is an Appalachian high-elevation endemic growing on moist, rocky, north-facing cliffs and rock outcrops above 2000 feet elevation in the southern Blue Ridge Mountains.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, rocky or gravelly, shaded to partially shaded conditions; Michaux's saxifrage is a rare, high-elevation Appalachian endemic named for the French botanist André Michaux who explored the southern Appalachians in the late 18th century. The plant grows on moist, shaded rock outcrops, north-facing cliffs, and rocky streamsides at higher elevations in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Small white flowers appear in summer. The deeply toothed, spatula-shaped leaves with distinctive reddish-brown dried leaf bases are ornamentally attractive in rock garden and alpine trough settings. Only suitable for cool-summer gardens in zones 4–7; does not tolerate heat. A challenging but rewarding plant for the rock garden specialist — available from native plant specialists and botanical garden plant sales.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall at 3–4 inches depth in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Michigan lily is one of the tallest native lilies and prefers consistently moist, fertile soil along stream banks, moist meadows, and moist prairie edges. Thrives with dappled afternoon shade.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun along stream banks, moist meadows, and moist prairie edges; Michigan lily is a tall native lily of the Midwest and Great Plains, naturally growing in moist prairies, stream banks, and open woodland margins. Like Turk's cap lily (L. superbum), it produces nodding, orange-red, spotted flowers with strongly reflexed petals, but Michigan lily is more common in the central and western part of the range where Turk's cap is absent. The tall stems can reach 7 feet, bearing up to a dozen or more flowers per stem in mid-summer. The drooping flowers are adapted for pollination by large, strong bumblebees and the great spangled fritillary butterfly. A superb native for moist meadow gardens, rain gardens, and naturalistic plantings in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Michigan lily is a superb native Turk's cap-type lily for moist meadows, prairie margins, and stream banks in zones 3–8.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Michigan lily performs best in consistently moist, fertile soil and is especially beautiful planted at the margins of ponds and along stream banks where consistent moisture is available. Lilium michiganese is a native lily of the upper Midwest and Great Plains tallgrass prairies, moist meadows, and stream margins; it closely resembles the Turk's cap lily (L. superbum) but has smaller, more numerous flowers and a more compact habit. It produces whorled leaves on stout stems reaching 3–6 feet tall and bears 3–10 (occasionally more) nodding, strongly reflexed, orange to orange-red flowers with dark-maroon spots in mid-summer — a spectacular sight when established in large naturalized clumps. Outstanding for moist native plant gardens and prairie restoration plantings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Middendorff weigela is the only yellow-flowered weigela species, distinct from the pink, red, and white tones of common hybrid weigela.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Middendorff weigela is the only yellow-flowered weigela species, distinct from the pink, red, and white tones of common hybrid weigela. Funnel-shaped flowers open a soft primrose-yellow marked with fine orange spotting in the throat, an unusual color among weigelas, which are overwhelmingly bred in shades of pink, red, and white, blooming on a compact, low-growing shrub native to cold woodland edges in northeastern Asia and Japan. Its distinctive yellow flower color and smaller stature compared to common hybrid weigela cultivars make it a worthwhile specialty addition to a shrub border or collector's garden seeking something beyond the usual pink and red weigela palette. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood like other weigela species.

common_name: Midnight Bayou Heuchera (Midnight Bayou Coral Bells)
plant_note: Install divisions in partial shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil, where the deeply lobed, glossy foliage can be appreciated up close along a path or container edge.
directions: Install divisions in partial shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil, where the deeply lobed, glossy foliage can be appreciated up close along a path or container edge. Midnight Bayou is a vigorous, spreading hybrid with lustrous purple-black leaves overlaid with a silvery sheen and prominent red-purple veining, a striking contrast plant among lighter-colored hostas and ferns. Wiry, pinkish-white flower stems rise above the foliage in early summer, though the plant's main appeal is its season-long dark, glossy leaf color. It tolerates heavier soils and more sun than many heuchera cultivars, provided moisture is consistent.

common_name: Midnight Marvel Hibiscus (Near-Black Foliage Red-Flowered Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Midnight Marvel pairs near-black purple foliage with huge, vivid true-red flowers, one of the most dramatic color combinations in the Summerific hardy hibiscus series.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Midnight Marvel pairs deep, near-black purple foliage — among the darkest available in hardy hibiscus — with enormous, 8-inch, vivid true-red flowers that create striking contrast against the dark leaves, making it one of the most visually dramatic cultivars in the compact, well-branched Summerific breeding series. It blooms in a steady succession of huge flowers from midsummer into fall, each lasting only a day but replaced continuously by new buds, giving the plant a long, reliable season of color. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring — often not until late May in many climates — so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown. It is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil, though Japanese beetles can be a significant pest on the foliage and flowers where present.

common_name: Midnight Rose Heuchera (Midnight Rose Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Midnight Rose is a sport of Obsidian and shares its parent's need for well-drained soil and partial shade to maintain the characteristic black leaf color with pink spotting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Midnight Rose is a sport of Obsidian heuchera distinguished by its extraordinary foliage — deep black-purple leaves randomly spotted with vivid pink and cream flecks that make the plant appear bejeweled. The spotting is variable and unpredictable from leaf to leaf, ranging from a few small dots to large, splashed pink areas; no two leaves are identical. This speckled pattern creates an arresting, jewel-like effect in the shade garden, especially when the glossy black background reflects light from nearby sources. The pink flecking tends to be more prominent in spring and fall when temperatures are cooler and less distinct in the heat of summer. Small cream to pink flowers appear on wiry scapes in early summer. Like Obsidian, it requires perfect drainage in humid climates and benefits from division every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. An outstanding cultivar for creating focal points in dark, shadowed spots of the garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; foliage color and bloom are both best with at least six hours of direct sun, and Midnight Wine's very low, spreading habit suits it to edging and small-space plantings.
directions: Midnight Wine was the original dwarf dark-leaved weigela that later inspired the even smaller Fine Wine, staying under 18 inches tall and wide with dense, deep burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season. Clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers appear in a heavy late-spring flush that draws hummingbirds, and the low, spreading, mounded habit works well as a border edge, small-space accent, or mixed container planting where taller weigela cultivars would be out of scale. It is drought-tolerant and largely trouble-free once established, needing only a light shaping right after the main spring bloom and an occasional renewal cut to the oldest wood to keep growth vigorous.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part shade.
directions: Mighty Chocolate Cherry is a tall astilbe with dramatic cherry-red plumes rising above green-burgundy chocolate-toned foliage. It brings bold vertical color to shaded, moist borders and woodland gardens. Plant in partial shade in rich soil that stays evenly moist, since astilbe suffers if it dries out. Water regularly and mulch to conserve moisture and keep roots cool. Cut back spent foliage in late fall and divide clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Surface sow; needs light and dislikes transplanting.
directions: Direct sow mignonette on the soil surface, as it needs light to germinate and resents root disturbance. The unremarkable greenish flower spikes release an intensely sweet raspberry-like fragrance beloved in Victorian gardens. Grow in full sun to light shade in cool weather and fertile, alkaline soil. Position it near paths and seating where its perfume can be enjoyed, and make successive sowings for a long season.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; resents transplanting.
directions: Sow directly where plants are to grow, as California poppies have a taproot and dislike transplanting. Scatter seed on prepared soil in early spring or fall and press in lightly. This selection bears saucer-shaped, bright orange-red flowers that open in sun and close at night or on cloudy days. Heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it needs little care and often self-sows for years of color.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring where plants will grow; do not transplant.
directions: This California poppy strain glows with deep red-orange, saucer-shaped blooms that open in sun and close at night. Sow seeds directly in early spring where they are to grow, pressing them onto the surface since the taproot resents transplanting. Full sun and lean, well-drained soil suit it best, and it needs little water once established. It self-sows reliably to return and naturalize in gardens and meadows.

common_name: Mikawa Yatsubusa Japanese Maple (Dwarf Dense Layered Bonsai-Type Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, or grow in a container; Mikawa Yatsubusa is a dwarf, densely layered maple popular for bonsai and small-garden use.
directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, or grow in a container where its dwarf, densely branched habit is easy to display up close. Mikawa Yatsubusa forms a slow-growing, tightly congested mound of overlapping, layered green foliage with unusually short internodes, giving it a dense, textural look prized both as a landscape dwarf specimen and as classic bonsai stock. Its very slow growth rate and compact ultimate size make it one of the most practical Japanese maples for small gardens or container culture. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape.

common_name: Milk and Honey Astilbe (Cream-White Plumed Astilbe)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in shade to dappled shade; Milk and Honey bears soft cream-white plumes and needs steady moisture through the growing season to avoid leaf scorch.
directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade to dappled shade; Milk and Honey produces feathery, plume-shaped flower spikes in a soft cream-white with faint honey-gold undertones, a gentler, more muted color than the vivid pinks and reds common in many astilbe cultivars, standing above deep green, finely divided foliage in early to mid summer. The pale plumes glow softly in a shaded border and pair particularly well with dark-leaved companions such as bronze heucheras or purple-leaved coral bells. Astilbe does not tolerate drought and will brown and decline quickly without steady moisture, so mulch well and water regularly through the growing season, especially in a hot, humid Gulf South summer. Leave the dried plumes standing through fall and winter for ornamental interest, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Milk and Wine Crinum (Striped White-and-Pink Fragrant Gulf South Crinum Lily)
plant_note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Milk and Wine Crinum prefers planting with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface — planting too deep reduces flowering; divide congested clumps every 5–7 years to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant large bulbs in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Milk and Wine Crinum is one of the most beloved and long-lived heirloom bulbs of Gulf South gardens — a heritage Crinum hybrid producing large clusters of fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers with white petals boldly striped with wine-red to rosy-pink along the midrib of each petal, creating the distinctive 'milk and wine' appearance that gives the variety its evocative name. The large, heavily fragrant flowers (6–8 per umbel, 4–5 inch diameter) are produced in flushes from late spring through fall, typically blooming most heavily after rainfall events similar to the related Zephyranthes rain lilies. The sweet fragrance — particularly intense in the evening — is one of the most distinctive qualities of Crinum lilies generally, and the large flower clusters create an arresting display at the back of the border or as a specimen planting. Milk and Wine Crinum is extremely long-lived and persistent — established clumps in old Gulf South gardens often persist for many decades, growing into very large clumps with dozens of flowering stalks annually without any attention. The massive bulbs (sometimes reaching the size of a football in old, undivided clumps) have few pests and diseases. The handsome, strap-shaped evergreen foliage (3–4 feet long) provides year-round architectural interest. Tolerates periodic flooding, drought, salt spray, and heavy clay soils — one of the most adaptable ornamental bulbs for challenging Gulf South conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Milkshake bears fully double, rounded, pure white pompom blooms with no visible cone or ray petals.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Milkshake produces unusual, fully double, creamy white pompom blooms in which the petals have multiplied into a rounded mass with no distinct cone visible, a striking novelty form quite different from the simple daisy shape of straight-species coneflower. It blooms over a long summer season and tolerates heat and drought well once established, though the fully double flowers are generally less valuable to pollinators than single-flowered coneflowers. Deadhead for continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratify seed or fall sow for best germination.
directions: Cold-moist stratify the seed for several weeks or sow in fall to break dormancy for this heirloom perennial. Direct sow where plants will grow, as the deep taproot resists transplanting. From summer onward it produces clusters of fiery red-orange flowers, a preferred nectar source for monarchs and other pollinators, followed by ornamental seed pods. Drought tolerant once established, it is best left undisturbed to form a long-lived clump.

plant_note: Surface-sow; seed needs light to germinate. One of the tallest garden campanulas and may benefit from staking or the support of nearby plants.
directions: Surface-sow seed in early spring or fall, pressing it lightly onto well-drained, fertile soil without covering, or plant divisions from an established clump. Milky bellflower is one of the tallest garden campanulas, sending up sturdy, well-branched stems topped with airy, open clusters of pale lavender-blue, pink, or white bells from midsummer into fall, native to the mountains of the Caucasus and northern Turkey. It performs best in rich, evenly moist soil with full sun in cooler climates or afternoon shade where summers are hot, and larger cultivars often benefit from staking or the support of nearby plants to stay upright. Cut spent stems back hard after the first flush of bloom to encourage a second round of flowering into fall.

common_name: Milky Way Cast Iron Plant (White-Speckled Deep-Shade Aspidistra)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade. Milky Way is a striking selection of the legendary cast iron plant, its broad, strap-shaped, leathery evergreen leaves densely dusted with small white speckles across the entire leaf surface, a starry, luminous pattern distinct from the bolder longitudinal stripes of other variegated aspidistra cultivars. Like the species, it tolerates the deepest, driest shade of nearly any ornamental perennial, thriving in the difficult dark, root-filled ground under mature live oaks and other dense-canopy trees where few other plants survive. It is essentially maintenance-free once established, extremely drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and slow-growing enough that division is rarely needed except to propagate new plantings.

common_name: Milky Way Kousa Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming White Kousa Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade; kousa dogwood is more sun-tolerant and disease-resistant than the native flowering dogwood.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Milky Way is an exceptionally floriferous kousa dogwood cultivar, its June flower display of creamy-white, pointed bracts so dense the branches appear covered in a blanket of white — a later bloom time than native flowering dogwood, extending the dogwood flowering season into early summer — followed in fall by raspberry-like red fruit that is edible and attracts wildlife, and by strong burgundy-red fall foliage color. As an Asian species, it is generally more resistant than native Cornus florida to the anthracnose and dogwood borer problems that trouble flowering dogwood in humid climates. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Milky Way Morning Glory (White with Purple-Red Star Streaks)
plant_note: Nick or soak seeds overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow after last frost; morning glories resent transplanting.
directions: Nick the seed coat with a file or soak overnight, then direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a trellis or fence. Milky Way opens predominantly white flowers streaked and flushed with fine purple-red rays radiating from the throat, giving each bloom a soft, starry appearance quite different from solid-colored morning glory cultivars. It climbs vigorously by twining stems and, like other Ipomoea purpurea types, opens fresh each dawn and closes by early afternoon. Deadhead spent flowers before seed set to prevent unwanted volunteers the following year, since morning glories self-sow readily in warm climates.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Milky Way carries an especially dense scattering of silver spots across the leaf surface, giving a starry, night-sky effect.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture and good drainage together keep the fleshy roots healthy while preventing leaf scorch in drier sites. Milky Way bears a dense, uniform scattering of small silver spots across its green leaves, evoking a starry night sky, with clusters of pink buds opening to blue flowers in early spring that provide welcome color before most other shade perennials emerge. The richly spotted foliage remains attractive through the growing season, making it a strong textural and color companion to hostas, ferns, and other woodland shade plants. Cut back foliage after flowering if powdery mildew develops in humid summer weather, encouraging fresh new growth, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in fall or early spring.

common_name: Millenium Ornamental Onion (2018 Perennial Plant of the Year)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring (or fall in mild climates) in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Millenium is a sterile hybrid that forms tight, glossy clumps and needs division only when clumps become crowded after several years.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Millenium ornamental onion tolerates heat, humidity, and short dry spells better than most ornamental alliums, which is part of why it was named the Perennial Plant Association's 2018 Perennial Plant of the Year. It forms a tidy, deer- and rabbit-resistant mound of glossy, strap-like foliage topped from midsummer into early fall by two-inch, rose-purple globe flowers that draw heavy traffic from bees, butterflies, and other pollinators for weeks on end. Unlike many ornamental onions, this hybrid is sterile and does not set seed, so it stays in a neat, non-spreading clump rather than self-sowing through the garden. It holds up well in the humid Gulf South as long as drainage is good, and pairs nicely with coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, and ornamental grasses in a late-summer pollinator border.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Millie Mac azalea is a selection of the Gulf Coast native orange azalea with distinctive white-edged flowers.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Millie Mac azalea is a selection of the Gulf Coast native orange azalea with distinctive white-edged flowers. A striking selection of the native Florida flame azalea, it produces fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers in warm gold and orange tones distinctly edged in crisp white, a bicolor pattern not found in the straight species, opening in mid-spring on bare branches before or just as new leaves emerge and filling the garden with sweet fragrance. Like other native deciduous azaleas, it thrives in the dappled shade and acidic, humus-rich soil of a woodland edge, providing important early-season nectar for native bees and swallowtail butterflies migrating through the Gulf South. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid heavy pruning since it flowers on the previous year's wood, and site in a location with good air movement to reduce fungal disease pressure.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; million bells is vegetatively propagated (sterile hybrids do not come true from seed) and sold exclusively as rooted cuttings or potted plants.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; million bells (superbells) are trailing, mounding hybrids derived from South American Calibrachoa species that produce thousands of tiny, one-inch, petunia-like flowers throughout the growing season in virtually every color — from pure white through yellow, pink, coral, red, purple, magenta, and bicolor combinations. They are among the top-selling container annuals in the US for their continuous bloom, compact trailing habit, and resistance to flopping and deadheading requirements (they are self-cleaning). Require consistently moist, well-fertilized growing media — plants in containers quickly exhaust the available nutrients and benefit from weekly liquid fertilizer at half-strength during active growth. Excellent in hanging baskets, window boxes, and as trailers over container edges.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 sow March–May. Million Gold is a compact, very early-flowering melampodium selection that begins blooming in just 50–70 days from seed — among the earliest-blooming selections in this genus. The plant is extremely self-sufficient once established — no deadheading, no pinching, no staking, and minimal water requirements after root establishment. In zone 9 melampodium performs best in the heat of summer (May–October), with declining performance as fall temperatures cool. The bright golden-yellow flowers complement blue, purple, and white companions effectively; excellent with angelonia, vinca, and ornamental sweet potato. Plants can be started from direct sow seed — unusually easy for a warm-season annual.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Million Gold Melampodium thrives in hot, dry conditions and performs most reliably in full sun with minimal water once established; Million Gold Melampodium is a compact selection of Medallion Flower (Melampodium divaricatum), a warm-season annual from Mexico producing a neat, mounding, self-branching plant covered with small (1–1.5 inch), bright golden-yellow, single daisy flowers with deep yellow centers that bloom continuously from late spring through fall frost without any deadheading or flower removal. Melampodium is one of the most genuinely self-sufficient summer annuals available for zone 9 — requiring no deadheading (spent flowers drop cleanly from the plant), minimal water once established, no pinching or shaping, and performing actively through the peak zone 9 summer heat without the bloom reduction or disease issues that affect less heat-adapted annuals. The consistent, clean golden-yellow of the flowers — produced in sufficient quantity to give the plant a solid golden appearance — combined with the dwarf, non-flopping habit and absolute minimal-care requirements makes Million Gold one of the most practical choices for no-maintenance summer color in full-sun beds, borders, and containers throughout zone 9's long summer season.

common_name: Million Hearts Plant (Heart Leaf Dischidia, Rosary Dischidia)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket, mounted epiphyte, or container plant in bright indirect to moderate shade; Million Hearts Plant cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. Mount on cork bark or tree fern slabs like an orchid for the most natural display, securing young stems with fishing line until roots establish. In a container, use a chunky mix of orchid bark and perlite with excellent drainage. Water thoroughly then allow to dry almost completely between waterings — overwatering causes rapid stem rot in this epiphyte. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade with exceptional drainage — Million Hearts Plant is a true epiphyte that rots quickly in heavy, moisture-retaining growing media. Dischidia ruscifolia is a small-leafed trailing epiphytic vine from the Philippines and Southeast Asia in the family Apocynaceae (the same family as Hoya and Stephanotis), producing thin, wiry, trailing stems clothed in pairs of tiny, heart-shaped, slightly fleshy, pale to medium-green leaves approximately half an inch across. The massed effect of hundreds of small green hearts cascading from a hanging basket gives the plant its popular common name — 'Million Hearts' — a name that perfectly captures the charming, delicate abundance of the foliage. As a true epiphyte from the humid forests of Southeast Asia, Dischidia grows naturally attached to rough tree bark in conditions of excellent air circulation, bright filtered light, and periodic drought — the small, slightly succulent leaves store water against dry periods between tropical rainstorms. Tiny, white, urn-shaped flowers appear sporadically along the stems. Multiple cultivars exist, including 'String of Nickels' (rounder, slightly larger leaves) and the slightly more compact 'Imbricata.' Non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; mimosa is fast-growing and extremely adaptable to poor, dry, or compacted soils but has weak, brittle wood and a short 10-20 year lifespan. CAUTION: mimosa self-seeds prolifically and is listed as invasive in Gulf South and southeastern states — remove seed pods where possible and avoid planting near natural areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; established mimosas tolerate drought, heat, salt spray, and poor soils far better than most flowering trees. Mimosa is a fast-growing, umbrella-shaped, deciduous tree valued for its finely divided, fern-like bipinnate foliage and its abundant clusters of fragrant, silky, pink pompom flowers produced from late spring through late summer, which are irresistible to hummingbirds and butterflies. The wood is weak and prone to storm damage, the roots can be aggressive near pavement, and the species is highly susceptible to Fusarium mimosa wilt, which can kill mature trees within a season or two. CAUTION: mimosa is classified as invasive throughout much of the southeastern United States, including the Gulf South, where it escapes cultivation readily along roadsides and disturbed woodland edges from its abundant, long-lived seed; gardeners in this region should weigh its ornamental value against its weedy tendencies and consider deadheading spent flowers before pods form.

plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat; direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Minarette is a dwarf strain needing less staking than full-size Russell lupines.
directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing with sandpaper before sowing, then direct sow into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Minarette is a compact, dwarf strain derived from the classic Russell garden lupine, producing the same dense, colorful spikes in a full mix of blues, purples, pinks, reds, yellows, and bicolors, but on a much shorter, sturdier plant that needs little to no staking, unlike the taller full-size Russell strains. Its smaller scale suits container growing, small borders, and front-of-border plantings where taller lupines would be out of proportion. Like other Russell-type lupines it thrives in the cool, moist summers of northern gardens but declines quickly in heat and humidity, making it best suited to zones 7 and cooler. Deadhead spent spikes promptly to encourage a possible second flush of bloom.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Mine-no-Yuki has a wide, spreading, almost groundcover-like habit that sets it apart from the more upright sasanqua cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Mine-no-Yuki, whose name translates roughly to 'snow on the peak,' is a classic sasanqua camellia grown for its wide, spreading, low-mounding habit and its abundant, large, white, semi-double to double flowers produced in a heavy fall flush, offering both a groundcover-scale alternative to upright sasanquas and reliable late-season color when little else is blooming. Its sprawling form makes it useful for espalier, bank plantings, or training against a wall as well as an informal low hedge. Setsugekka and other sasanquas tolerate more sun than japonicas, and Mine-no-Yuki follows that pattern, blooming well in partial shade to full sun. Prune only lightly to shape after flowering, since flower buds set later in the growing season.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Minerva is one of the most popular and widely available amaryllis cultivars, bearing bold red flowers with a crisp white star pattern at the center.
directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Minerva bears large, vivid red flowers with a distinctive crisp white star radiating from the center of each bloom, making it one of the most recognizable and widely sold amaryllis cultivars, striking both in the garden and as a classic holiday container bulb. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, naturalizing and multiplying into an increasingly full clump over the years. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering rather than cutting it early, since the leaves recharge the bulb, and for container forcing plant with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix for traditional winter bloom indoors.

common_name: Minerva Rose of Sharon (Lavender-Pink Red-Eyed Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Minerva is one of the original US National Arboretum rose of sharon introductions and remains one of the most widely available cultivars.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Minerva bears large, single to semi-double, lavender-pink flowers with a bold reddish-purple eye at the center, opening over a long season from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Like its sibling introductions Aphrodite and Diana, it is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection that sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older, seed-grown rose of sharon while remaining tough and heat-tolerant. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and maximize flowering wood.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite under intermittent mist, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade after frost; ming aralia is sensitive to cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, which cause leaf drop — protect from cold air movement and avoid sites exposed to winter winds in zone 10, where the plant is marginally hardy.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; ming aralia (parsley aralia, wild coffee tree) is an Indo-Pacific tropical evergreen shrub in the ginseng family (Araliaceae) that produces some of the most intricately textured and refined tropical foliage available for shaded garden positions — the leaves are compound and deeply divided, with each leaflet further divided into multiple, small, toothed, crinkled, irregular segments that create a dense, feathery, parsley-like to fern-like appearance at close range and an impression of extraordinary, finely subdivided textural richness from a distance. The thin branches grow in a graceful, architectural, often slightly irregular pattern that resembles a natural bonsai. Ming aralia is frequently grown as an indoor specimen and shaped into bonsai form. Outdoors in zone 10–12 it grows into a substantial shrub or small tree to 15 feet with similarly intricate foliage at a much larger scale. The combination of shade tolerance, fine texture, and elegant form makes it one of the most useful and refined tropical foliage shrubs for shaded positions in the tropical garden.

common_name: Mini Monstera (Piccolo Monstera, Ginny Philodendron, Rhaphidophora)
plant_note: Grow on a moss pole or bark support in bright indirect light in well-draining, chunky aroid mix; Raphidophora tetrasperma climbs vigorously and produces progressively larger, more deeply split leaves as it ascends a support — provide a tall moss pole for best results. Despite widespread common names referencing Monstera and Philodendron, it belongs to neither genus. Allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Maintain moderate humidity (50%+). Propagate from stem cuttings. All parts mildly toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in well-draining, aerated potting mix on a climbing support — Mini Monstera produces its most attractive, deeply split leaves as it climbs and becomes less impressive when allowed to trail without a support. Raphidophora tetrasperma is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to southern Thailand and Malaysia in the Araceae family — not a Monstera, not a Philodendron, despite being widely marketed under both names. The plant produces deeply split, pinnatifid (partially divided rather than fully perforated), glossy, dark-green leaves on slender, fast-growing climbing stems. In young plants, the leaves are small and undivided; as the plant climbs, they become progressively larger (up to 12 inches) and more deeply cut into opposite pairs of oval lobes separated by incisions extending almost to the midrib — a leaf pattern strikingly similar to a miniature Monstera deliciosa. The combination of this attractive, deeply-split leaf pattern, fast growth rate, compact size relative to true Monstera, and ease of cultivation in indoor and tropical garden conditions has made Raphidophora tetrasperma one of the most popular aroids in the contemporary houseplant boom. It grows significantly faster than true Monstera and is substantially more compact, making it better suited to average indoor and small tropical garden spaces. Mildly toxic.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container vine; Rhaphidophora tetrasperma is strictly tropical and cannot tolerate temperatures below 55°F. Provide a moss pole, bamboo stake, or trellis for the aerial roots to attach to — the plant grows much faster and develops larger, more fenestrated leaves when it can climb. Propagate from stem cuttings with one node — root in water or moist sphagnum moss within 2–3 weeks. Despite being commonly sold as 'Mini Monstera,' it is a completely different genus from Monstera.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade; Mini Monstera grows fastest in bright indirect light (3–6 feet from a sunny window) and develops larger leaves with more pronounced fenestrations when given good light and a climbing support. Rhaphidophora tetrasperma is a fast-growing, climbing tropical vine from southern Thailand and Malaysia that has become one of the most popular houseplants in the recent era of tropical plant collecting, despite being entirely unrelated to the true Monstera genus. It is sold in virtually every garden center and box store under the trade name 'Mini Monstera' because the deeply lobed, fenestrated, bright-green leaves bear a strong resemblance in miniature to Monstera deliciosa — the iconic 'Swiss Cheese Plant' — though R. tetrasperma leaves are smaller (4–8 inches) and thinner. The plant climbs by aerial roots, producing new leaves quickly and making it one of the fastest-growing popular tropical foliage plants. Each new leaf is larger than the last when the plant is given adequate light, warmth, and a climbing structure. Like Monstera, the leaf splits (fenestrations) are thought to be an adaptation for surviving high winds in the rainforest understory by reducing wind resistance on large leaves. Mildly toxic if chewed; the calcium oxalate crystals cause mouth irritation.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; Mini Pearl performs best with 6+ hours of direct sun but tolerates a few hours of afternoon shade in Gulf South summers without loss of bloom.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Mini Pearl, registered by Pauline Henry in 1982, is one of the most widely planted miniature daylilies for its small, clear light-pink, 2.75-inch flowers with a soft green throat held on grassy, narrow-leaved clumps well under 20 inches tall. It is exceptionally floriferous, producing a heavy count of buds per scape and reblooming steadily through summer where heat and moisture allow, which makes it a dependable low-edging or mass-planting daylily rather than a single-specimen accent. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in early spring or immediately after bloom to keep flower counts high.

common_name: Mini Penny Hydrangea (Dwarf Reblooming Blue Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Mini Penny is a dwarf sport of the reliable reblooming cultivar Penny Mac, staying compact enough for small gardens and large containers while retaining its parent's dependable rebloom.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Mini Penny is a dwarf sport of the widely grown, reliably reblooming Penny Mac hydrangea, retaining its parent's strong performance — flowering on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year — while staying considerably more compact, typically under 2 feet tall, making it well suited to small gardens, foundation plantings, and large containers where a full-sized hydrangea would be too large. Because it reblooms on new wood, a late spring frost that damages old buds does not prevent a strong summer bloom. Flower color shifts with soil pH the way most macrophylla hydrangeas do, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

common_name: Mini Stella Daylily (Dwarf Reblooming Golden Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Mini Stella is a dwarfer, smaller-flowered relative of Stella de Oro, well suited to edging and container growing.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Mini Stella takes the reblooming, compact model of the landmark daylily Stella de Oro and scales it down further, with a smaller overall plant size and daintier golden-yellow flowers that suit small-space edging, rock gardens, and containers better than the somewhat larger Stella de Oro. Like its relative, it blooms continuously from late spring through frost rather than in a single flush, and tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and average soil with equal ease. Deadhead spent scapes to keep the planting tidy and encourage continued rebloom; clumps are long-lived and rarely need dividing except to control size or propagate new plants.

plant_note: Plant small tubers in spring after soil warms in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in deep shade to part shade; miniature caladium is the smallest-leaved caladium species with delicate, naturally small foliage and is an excellent choice for container gardens, terrariums, shaded rock gardens, and fine-textured shade border edging.
directions: Plant small tubers 1 inch deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in deep shade; keep consistently moist and protect from any cold. Caladium humboldtii (miniature caladium) is a distinct Venezuelan caladium species producing naturally compact, small-leaved plants reaching only 6–12 inches tall with small (2–4 inch), elegantly proportioned, arrow-shaped leaves in classic white-with-green-veining coloration that is more restrained and subtle than the bold fancy-leaf cultivars. While less commonly grown than Caladium bicolor cultivars, C. humboldtii is valuable for smaller spaces — terrariums, small container arrangements, fine-textured shade borders, and rock garden pockets — where the scale of fancy-leaf caladiums would be overwhelming. It is also more shade-demanding than C. bicolor and thrives in deeper shade conditions. The species has contributed to miniaturized caladium cultivars bred for compact size. In zones below 10, lift tubers before the first frost and store indoors at 55–60°F; they may be replanted the following spring.
