directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Moon Bay is a compact, naturally mounding nandina selection staying 18–30 inches tall — smaller and more tightly formed than Gulf Stream or Harbour Dwarf, making it the most compact of the commonly available dwarf nandina cultivars. The graceful, fine-textured, finely divided foliage is a beautiful glossy-green through summer, turning vivid orange-red to scarlet-red in fall and winter when cold temperatures arrive. Moon Bay's compact, mounding form and outstanding fall/winter color combination make it an exceptionally practical and ornamental foundation shrub for zone 9 gardens where its reliability, low maintenance, and multi-season interest make it one of the most useful small evergreen shrubs in the landscape palette. Like all nandinas, Moon Bay is remarkably adaptable — tolerating clay, drought once established, heat, humidity, and partial shade without significant loss of performance or appearance. The foliage compound texture, graceful habit, and outstanding winter red color make it visually effective in all four seasons. Note: Nandina domestica berries are toxic to birds and the plant has invasive potential in some Gulf South natural areas — plant in contained garden settings away from natural areas.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the green species form tolerates more direct sun, while the brightly colored grafted forms sold as 'moon cactus' need protection from intense direct sun.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; the green species form tolerates more direct sun, while the brightly colored grafted forms sold as 'moon cactus' need protection from intense direct sun. In its natural green form this small, rounded, ribbed cactus from Paraguay and Brazil bears attractive pale pink to white flowers, but it is far better known in cultivation for its chlorophyll-free color mutants — brilliant red, orange, yellow, or pink globes — which lack the green pigment needed to photosynthesize and are grafted as small caps atop a green Hylocereus or Selenicereus cactus rootstock to survive. These colorful grafted 'moon cactus' combinations are common, inexpensive houseplants but are ultimately temporary, since the graft union eventually fails after a few years even with good care, at which point the colorful top can sometimes be re-grafted onto fresh rootstock. Water sparingly, avoid direct hot sun which can scorch the color mutant tops, and expect the brightly colored forms to need eventual regrafting rather than indefinite growth on their own roots.

common_name: Moon Vine (Large-Flowered White Night-Blooming Tropical Vine for Evening Gardens)
plant_note: Nick or soak seeds overnight before planting to speed germination; direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Moon Vine is best planted where it can climb a trellis, fence, or arbor and be viewed in the evening when the flowers open — the flowers close by mid-morning each day.
directions: Nick or soak seeds overnight, then direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Moon Vine (Ipomoea alba) is the classic evening and night garden vine — a tropical twining vine that produces extraordinarily large (4–6 inch), pure white, funnel-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and evening, perfuming the garden with a sweet, rich, jasmine-like fragrance that intensifies as darkness falls. The flowers are among the largest of any commonly grown annual vine and the pure white color reflects low light beautifully, appearing to glow under moonlight, porch lights, or landscape lighting — creating the ethereal moonlit effect that gives the plant its common name. Moon Vine is a rapid, enthusiastic climber, gaining 15–20 feet in a single growing season in warm Gulf South conditions — it covers fences, arbors, pergolas, and mailboxes with dense, large-leaved foliage and a continuous supply of evening flowers from mid-summer until frost. The flowers each last only one evening, but numerous buds open in succession for months of nightly bloom. In Gulf South zone 9, Moon Vine is grown as a warm-season annual from spring through fall. In zone 10–12, it grows as a perennial twining vine. The rapid growth and profuse bloom make it one of the most rewarding evening-garden plants for summer arbors and screens. Often combined with common morning glory (I. purpurea) to create a 24-hour floral display from the same genus.

common_name: Moonbeam Coreopsis (Classic Pale Yellow Long-Blooming Perennial Thread-Leaf Coreopsis)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Moonbeam requires excellent drainage and lean soil — plants in heavy clay or overly fertile soil tend to be short-lived and flop open; raised beds and amended soil provide the drainage needed for long-term success in Gulf South clay soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Moonbeam is one of the most beloved and awarded garden perennials of the late 20th century — a Coreopsis verticillata cultivar that received the Perennial Plant of the Year award in 1992 and remains a gold standard for long-blooming, low-maintenance perennial gardens. The distinctive feature of 'Moonbeam' compared to other coreopsis is its unique pale primrose-yellow to cream-yellow flower color — softer and more subtle than the vivid golden-yellow of most coreopsis cultivars — combined with the fine-textured, thread-like foliage of C. verticillata that creates an airy, delicate visual mass very different from the coarser leaves of C. grandiflora and C. lanceolata. The extremely long bloom season — from early summer through frost with deadheading — and the soft yellow color that harmonizes with virtually every other garden color make Moonbeam one of the most versatile perennials for border combinations. It blooms most prolifically with lean soil and moderate drought stress — overly rich, moist conditions produce lush foliage and reduced bloom. In zone 9, Moonbeam performs best with afternoon shade protection during peak summer and requires well-drained soil to persist as a perennial rather than a short-lived annual-style planting.

plant_note: Start indoors 2–4 weeks before last frost after nicking or soaking seed; transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Nick or soak seeds in warm water for 12 hours before sowing 1/2 in deep. Moonflower is a vigorous, fast-growing vine that needs a strong trellis or fence. Unlike morning glories, its large, fragrant white blossoms open in the evening and remain open through the night and into the following morning. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers to encourage blooming.

common_name: Moonflower Vine (Night-Blooming White-Flowered Annual Ipomoea Vine)
plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination. In zone 9, plant March–April; moonflower is a tropical perennial in frost-free areas but grown as a fast annual. Provide sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence — vines reach 10–15 feet in one season. Moonflower's fragrant white flowers open in the evening and close by midmorning, making it the ideal choice for planting near outdoor seating areas or porches used in the evening. Excellent paired with Heavenly Blue morning glory (which opens in the morning when moonflower closes).
directions: Nick seed coat or soak overnight; direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a sturdy trellis or arbor. Moonflower Vine is the large-flowered night-blooming cousin of morning glory — a tropical Ipomoea species producing enormous (4–6 inch diameter) white, saucer-shaped flowers with a sweet, tropical fragrance that unfurl rapidly at dusk and remain open through the night until midmorning, when they close as morning glories open. The dramatic daily opening — moonflowers can be watched as the buds spirally unfurl in minutes at dusk — is one of the most theatrical performances in the plant world. The very large flowers are pure white, satiny, with a star-shaped pattern visible in the petals, and the heavy, sweet, tropical fragrance carries well on still evening air, perfuming the garden and attracting sphinx moths (hummingbird moths) that are primary pollinators. Moonflower is a fast-growing, robust vine (10–15 feet per season) that covers a standard garden arbor or pergola quickly. The combination of its dramatic evening show and fragrance makes moonflower ideal for planting near outdoor dining or seating areas — evening patio dinners become special when the moonflowers open at dusk around the pergola. In zone 9–10, moonflower is a short-lived perennial that may persist between mild winters.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Moonlight's chartreuse-to-cream coloration makes it one of the brightest caladiums for deep shade illumination.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Moonlight is a large-leaved, predominantly chartreuse to cream-white caladium with an unusual warm, yellow-green to near-white leaf color that creates one of the brightest and most luminous foliage effects of any fancy caladium cultivar. The warm, slightly yellow-tinged white-to-cream color differs from the pure, cool white of 'Candidum' — Moonlight has a warmer, softer quality that creates a glowing, moonlit effect particularly striking in the dim light of deep-shade garden areas at dusk and in low-light conditions. In brighter partial shade, the color is a vivid chartreuse-green that gradually lightens toward cream-white at the center of each leaf as temperatures rise through summer. The large leaf size and predominantly light-colored foliage maximize the light-reflective effect in shade positions — Moonlight is an outstanding choice for illuminating dark corners and brightening shaded foundation areas. The chartreuse-cream color contrasts beautifully with dark-foliaged companions like Black Magic elephant ear, 'Obsidian' heuchera, or dark ajuga groundcovers, creating a vivid light-dark foliage combination. Consistent moisture, humus-rich soil, and protection from direct afternoon sun produce the largest leaves and best color in Gulf South conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike compact bedding nasturtiums, Moonlight is a true climbing type and needs a trellis, fence, or nearby shrub to scramble up.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor, since Moonlight is a vigorous climbing nasturtium capable of scrambling 6 to 8 feet by twining leaf stems rather than tendrils. Its soft, pale primrose-yellow flowers glow in evening light, giving the variety its name, and provide a gentler color note than the hot oranges and reds of most nasturtiums. As with other nasturtiums, keep soil on the lean side, since overly rich soil produces abundant foliage but fewer flowers, and both leaves and blooms are edible with the characteristic peppery, watercress-like bite. Plants bloom from early summer until frost and make an easy, fast-growing vertical accent for a vegetable garden trellis or fence line.

common_name: Moonlight Scindapsus (Treub's Scindapsus, Dark Form Scindapsus, Satin Pothos Relative)
plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in well-drained, moist, chunky aroid mix with a moss pole, bark board, or rough surface to climb; Scindapsus treubii has two widely grown forms — 'Moonlight' (silver-green leaves with strong silver-white overlay) and 'Dark Form' (very deep, almost black-green leaves with subtle steel-blue iridescence). Both forms are highly sought collector aroids. The plant is closely related to Scindapsus pictus (Satin Pothos) but produces narrower, more elongated, distinctly different leaves. Keep warm (above 60°F) and provide consistent humidity. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, well-aerated aroid mix with a rough support to climb — Moonlight Scindapsus produces its most ornamental foliage in bright indirect to low light conditions and is an outstanding climbing shade vine for shaded indoor and outdoor tropical positions. Scindapsus treubii is a climbing, hemiepiphytic perennial aroid in the Araceae family native to Borneo, Java, and Southeast Asia — a member of the genus Scindapsus, which is closely related to but distinct from both Epipremnum (pothos) and Monstera, in the tribe Monstereae. The plant produces elongated, narrowly ovate leaves (4–6 inches long, distinctly narrow compared to S. pictus) on climbing stems that ascend with adhesive aerial roots. Two distinct leaf color forms have become highly popular in the collector aroid market: the 'Moonlight' form, which produces silver-green to pale sage-green leaves with a strong silver overlay that gives each leaf a luminous, silver-washed quality — and the 'Dark Form,' which produces leaves of a very deep, saturated dark forest-green to near-black, with a subtle, gunmetal blue-green iridescence in certain light. Both forms are striking and distinctly different from any common houseplant. The plant climbs readily when given a rough moss pole or bark board and develops larger, more lustrous leaves as it ascends. Moderately fast-growing in warm conditions. One of the most sought-after collector aroids of the past decade. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

common_name: Moonlit Masquerade Daylily (Lavender-Purple with Cream Appliqué Band Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Moonlit Masquerade won the American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal in 2008 for its lavender-purple petals edged in a wide cream-white band.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Moonlit Masquerade bears lavender-purple petals bordered by a wide, distinct cream-white edge often described as an appliqué band, a striking two-tone pattern that earned it the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2008, the organization's highest honor for a daylily cultivar. Its large, ruffled blooms open over a long summer season on well-branched scapes carrying a high bud count for extended flowering. Divide every three to four years when bloom declines, and deadhead spent scapes to keep the planting tidy.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their full mature width to develop. Moonrock is a compact panicle hydrangea bred for exceptionally sturdy, thick stems that hold its dense, rounded flower panicles fully upright without staking, even after heavy rain — a common problem with older, larger panicle hydrangea cultivars. Flowers open creamy white in mid to late summer and age to a soft green before finishing pink-blushed in fall, giving a long season of changing color on a plant sized for smaller foundation plantings and mixed borders. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be pruned back hard in late winter without losing that year's bloom; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.

plant_note: Divide established rhizome clumps in early spring before new growth emerges and replant at the same depth in moist, humus-rich soil; keep consistently moist through the first growing season.
directions: Moonseed is a deciduous, twining native vine of moist woodland edges, stream banks, and thicket margins throughout eastern North America, valued for its bold, broadly shield-shaped leaves and striking blue-black berries in fall. The crescent-shaped seed inside each berry inspired the common name and distinguishes it from the true wild grapes it resembles — the berries are highly toxic and must never be eaten. It spreads readily by underground rhizomes to form dense, colonizing patches, making it ideal for naturalizing moist, shaded slopes and stabilizing stream banks. Grow in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; it tolerates periodic flooding and deep shade better than most native vines.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Moonshine produces leaves almost entirely covered in bright, luminous silver with only a thin green edge, one of the most heavily silvered lungwort cultivars available, glowing in dim shade in a way few other foliage plants can match. Clusters of small, funnel-shaped flowers open pink and mature to blue in early spring, appearing before many companion shade perennials leaf out and providing an early nectar source for emerging bumblebees. Its bright, near-white foliage effect makes it a strong accent for lighting up dark corners; divide congested clumps in early fall every few years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Moonshine snake plant holds its pale silvery color best out of direct hot sun, which can bleach or scorch the broad leaves.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Moonshine snake plant holds its pale silvery color best out of direct hot sun, which can bleach or scorch the broad leaves. Broad, solid, pale silvery-green leaves with a subtle darker green margin form an upright fan distinct from the horizontally banded, dark green leaves of the classic snake plant, giving this cultivar a cool, almost metallic glow that stands out in a low-light interior. Like other snake plants it stores water in thick, succulent leaves and tolerates long stretches of neglect and low light, making it one of the most forgiving houseplants for offices, hallways, and other spots that receive little natural light. Water only when the soil is fully dry, and divide congested clumps to propagate or refresh an overcrowded pot.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; Moonshine requires excellent drainage — it will not survive in heavy clay or wet soil, particularly during summer humidity in zone 9.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; Moonshine is the standard hybrid yellow yarrow cultivar — a cross between Achillea clypeolata and A. taygetea — producing large, flat-topped clusters of rich sulfur-yellow flowers from late spring through midsummer above finely cut, aromatic, silver-gray to gray-green, feathery foliage. The cool, muted sulfur-yellow flower color is softer and more refined than the golden-yellow of species yarrow, making Moonshine a superb mixer in the perennial border — it harmonizes with blue flowers (salvias, catmints), orange and coral tones, and white without the dominating brightness of brighter yellows. The silver-gray foliage is attractive even when the plant is not in flower. Moonshine was named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 1990, recognizing its outstanding landscape performance. Like all yarrows, it is extraordinarily drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant — performing best in lean, dry soils where many perennials struggle. The key limitation in zone 9 is summer humidity: yarrow is susceptible to crown rot and foliar diseases in hot, humid, wet conditions. In zone 9, excellent drainage and lean soil are essential; amended sandy or gravelly soils work better than clay. The dried flower heads are excellent for arrangements. Divide every 2–3 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Lay individual leaves or short stem cuttings on the surface of dry, very well-drained succulent mix in spring; moonstones roots and produces new plantlets readily from detached leaves, which is the standard home propagation method.
directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, and water only after the soil has dried out completely. Pachyphytum oviferum (moonstones) produces plump, egg-shaped leaves in soft pastel shades of lavender, blue-grey, and pale pink, coated in a powdery white farina that gives the plant its frosted, gumdrop-like look; avoid touching the leaves, since fingerprints permanently remove the protective bloom. The trailing, sprawling stems eventually flop over the edge of a container as they lengthen, so it works well in a shallow pot or hanging arrangement, and old stems can be cut back and re-rooted to renew a tidy rosette shape. Intense, direct afternoon sun in hot climates can scorch the leaves, so bright morning sun with some midday protection gives the best color without burning. In winter, arching stems of coral-red, bell-shaped flowers rise above the foliage on well-grown plants.

common_name: Moor Place Dahlia (Compact Deep Wine-Red Pompon Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Moor Place is a compact pompon dahlia bearing deep wine-red globe flowers.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage bushier growth and more blooms. Moor Place is a true pompon dahlia, its small, densely quilled florets curling inward to form an almost perfectly spherical deep wine-red globe, one of the richest, darkest colors available in the pompon class. The dainty, uniform blooms are produced in great abundance on wiry stems, making them a favorite for posies, buttonholes, and mixed bouquets. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the top third of the bulb above the soil surface in moist to consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; Moore's crinum is notable among crinums for its strong shade-tolerance — it grows naturally in the moist, shaded, coastal forests of the Eastern Cape. The long, distinctive neck on the bulb (to 12 inches or more in old plants) is a diagnostic feature. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant bulbs (upper third exposed) in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; Moore's crinum is the most shade-tolerant of the commonly grown crinum species and one of the few large, summer-flowering bulbs that genuinely thrives in the deep, dry shade under large trees — making it exceptional value in the shade garden where bold summer flowers with tropical presence are difficult to achieve. The flowers are large, lily-like, pale to medium pink, funnel-shaped funnels opening to 4–5 inches across, borne in umbels of 5–10 on stout scapes, fragrant in the evening. Unlike many crinums that require full sun and hot conditions, Moore's crinum originates in the moist, shaded, humid coastal forest margins of the Eastern Cape where it grows with clivias and other shade-lovers. In the shade garden it provides a refreshingly bold, tropical-scale bulb plant for positions under tree canopy, combining naturally with hostas, clivias, and other shade perennials. The long, distinctive, elongated bulb neck — a diagnostic feature of the species, sometimes reaching 12 inches long in old specimens — should be left exposed above the soil when planting. One of the parent species of Crinum x powellii (with C. bulbispermum).

common_name: Moorhexe Purple Moor Grass (Strictly Upright Dark Purple-Black Flower Stems)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Moorhexe forms a compact, strictly upright clump with dark purple-black flower stems.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; purple moor grass performs best with consistent moisture and struggles in hot, dry conditions. Moorhexe, German for 'moor witch,' forms a tight, strictly upright clump of fine green foliage topped by narrow, dark purple-black flower stems held rigidly vertical, a striking architectural contrast to the more relaxed, arching forms of other Molinia selections. Its compact, upright habit and dark flower color make it a strong vertical accent in a small border or container. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Mops mugo pine is extremely slow-growing and needs excellent drainage, tolerating drought and poor soil once established.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Mops mugo pine is extremely slow-growing and needs excellent drainage, tolerating drought and poor soil once established. Dense, dark green needles are held on tightly congested, irregularly rounded branches that grow just an inch or two per year, forming a naturally globe-shaped, tousled mound reminiscent of a mop head, one of the most popular true-dwarf mugo pine selections for foundation plantings and rock gardens. Its slow growth rate means it holds its neat, rounded form for decades with essentially no pruning required, making it an exceptionally low-maintenance evergreen accent for a small garden or entryway planting. Water during establishment and prolonged drought, and avoid heavy, poorly drained soils that can lead to root rot.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; or nick and soak seed overnight then start indoors 2–4 weeks early.
directions: Nick the hard seed coat with a file or soak in warm water for 8–12 hours before sowing 1/2 in deep to speed germination. Morning glories need a fence, trellis, or other support and are best sown directly at the base of their support. Avoid over-fertilizing, which promotes leaves at the expense of flowers. Blooms open in the morning and close by afternoon on each individual day.

plant_note: Nick seed coat with sandpaper or soak overnight before sowing directly in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil after last frost; do not start indoors as tap root is damaged by transplanting.
directions: Nick seed coat with sandpaper or soak overnight before sowing directly in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil after last frost; do not start indoors as tap root is damaged by transplanting. Ipomoea tricolor is the parent of the famous 'Heavenly Blue' morning glory, a fast-growing annual twining vine with heart-shaped leaves and large (3–4 inch), funnel-shaped flowers that open a vivid sky-blue or blue-violet each morning and fade to pink-purple by afternoon — one of the most startling and beautiful morning colors in the annual garden. Provide a trellis, fence, or other support to 8–12 feet; it will naturally scramble up any available structure. The seeds contain lysergic acid amides and are mildly toxic if eaten in quantity. Morning glories bloom most prolifically in lean, dry soil with minimal fertilization; rich soil produces excessive foliage.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Morning Light performs best in full sun — adequate moisture is important during summer in zone 9, where extended drought combined with reflected heat can stress plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Morning Light is widely considered one of the most elegant ornamental grasses available — a refined, fine-textured miscanthus producing very narrow (one-eighth-inch wide) blades edged with a thin white margin that gives the entire plant a silvery-white luminous quality, almost as if the plant is lit from within. The effect is subtle but beautiful: from a distance, the plant appears silver-white; close up, each blade shows a green center stripe and cream-white margins. The narrow, refined foliage and compact, vase-shaped habit reach 4–6 feet, substantially smaller than the larger maiden grass selections. In late summer and fall, feathery, copper-pink plumes emerge above the foliage and last well into winter. Morning Light is notable among miscanthus for being sterile or low-seed-producing in most conditions, which reduces the invasive spread concern that affects some miscanthus selections in the Southeast. In zone 9, flowering typically occurs in September–October; the plant grows as an evergreen or semi-evergreen, requiring cutting back in late winter. An outstanding specimen or mass-planting grass for full-sun locations where its distinctive silver-white effect can be appreciated.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–October in zone 9) for winter and spring bloom, or in earliest spring; Moroccan toadflax is a cool-season annual that must bloom before summer heat arrives — it performs best sown in fall in mild-winter climates and in very early spring in colder regions.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall or very early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; press in lightly and keep moist — seeds need light to germinate. Linaria maroccana (Moroccan toadflax) is a slender, delicate, cool-season annual producing miniature snapdragon-like flowers just 1/2 to 3/4 inch long with a small spur on dense, upright spikes in an exceptional range of colors — violet, pink, red, orange, yellow, white, and bicolor — all with a yellow or orange eye that gives the flowers a jewel-like quality at close range. The extremely fine, thread-like foliage is nearly invisible under the mass of flowers. 'Fairy Bouquet' is the classic mixed-color strain; 'Northern Lights' has larger flowers; 'Fantasy' is dwarf (8–9 inches). Moroccan toadflax self-seeds freely in suitable gardens and can naturalize in rock gardens and gravel paths. In zone 9, fall-sown plants bloom from December through March — providing cool-season color when few annuals are in bloom. It is outstanding combined with poppies, larkspur, and bachelor buttons in cool-season cutting gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; golden featherflower is one of the most difficult of all Western Australian natives to cultivate outside its native habitat — it requires perfect drainage, lean soil, and the precise conditions of the sandy coastal plains of the Perth area. Grafted plants on Darwinia or Calytrix rootstocks have improved success. It is the floral emblem of Western Australia's capital region. Not for beginners; a challenge-and-reward plant for dedicated native plant enthusiasts.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; golden featherflower is one of the most spectacular of all the Australian native shrubs in bloom — a Western Australian coastal heath specialist from the sandy coastal plains around Perth (where it is so abundant in spring that it colors whole hillsides brilliant yellow-gold, and is the informal floral symbol of the Perth region) that produces in late winter and spring an astonishing, total-coverage, smothering mass of tiny (0.5 inch), yellow to orange-yellow, feathery-edged flowers covering every stem and twig of the plant in a dense, almost furry, golden-yellow coating. The 'feather' texture of the flowers — each individual flower with finely fringed, feathery-textured petals — gives the genus its common name (Verticordia, meaning 'turning hearts', is sometimes called the featherflower genus), and the density of the yellow flowers on a mature plant in full bloom creates an effect like a shrub dipped in gold or covered in bright-yellow powder. It is considered one of the most spectacular and beautiful spring-flowering shrubs of Australia's west coast. The difficulty of cultivation outside its native sandy coastal habitat is well known — it is considered one of the 'holy grail' plants of Australian horticulture, requiring very specific conditions.

plant_note: Float rooted divisions directly on the surface of a warm, still, full-sun pond well after last frost; mosaic plant needs consistently warm water above 65°F and is grown as a warm-season annual outside frost-free zones.
directions: Float rooted divisions directly on the surface of a warm, still, full-sun pond well after last frost; mosaic plant needs consistently warm water above 65°F and is grown as a warm-season annual outside frost-free zones. Diamond-shaped, glossy, bronze-green leaves arranged in tight, overlapping, geometric rosettes float flat on the water's surface in a striking mosaic or tile-like pattern unlike any other pond plant, punctuated by small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers that open just above the leaf rosettes on sunny days. Native to slow-moving tropical waters of South America, it spreads by runners across a still pond surface and is a favorite accent for a formal or tropical-style water garden, though it needs warm, calm water and full sun to thrive and perform well. Where winters bring freezing water temperatures, bring a few rosettes indoors to a warm, sunlit aquarium or bowl to overwinter and restart the following season.

common_name: Mosaica Copper Plant (Multi-Color Tropical Foliage Shrub for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mosaica develops the most vivid multi-color leaf patterning in full sun — partial shade produces larger leaves but significantly reduces the intensity and complexity of the copper, red, orange, and yellow mosaic color pattern.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mosaica is a cultivar of Acalypha wilkesiana (copper leaf, copperleaf, Jacob's coat) — a tropical shrub from the Pacific Islands grown primarily as a foliage plant for the extraordinary multi-color patterning of its large, broad leaves. The 'Mosaica' cultivar produces leaves with a complex, patchwork mosaic of copper, red-orange, bronze, gold-yellow, and reddish-purple tones — different colors appearing as irregular patches, blotches, and streaks across each leaf surface, creating a richly complex pattern that is genuinely different from plant to plant. The result in full sun is one of the most vivid and complex foliage colors available in a commonly grown landscape plant: a tropical tapestry of warm colors that creates intense visual interest in mixed subtropical plantings. Acalypha wilkesiana grows rapidly in Gulf South summer heat, reaching 4–6 feet in a single growing season when planted in warm soil with adequate nutrition. The inconspicuous catkin-type flowers are secondary to the foliage display. In zone 10–12, copper leaf is an evergreen perennial shrub. In zone 9, it grows as a warm-season annual — planted after the last frost and growing rapidly through summer and fall until frost kills it. The rapid growth and striking color make it one of the most effective single-season tropical foliage plants for Gulf South summer borders and container combinations.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; daylilies tolerate a wide range of soil conditions and need little care once established.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; daylilies tolerate a wide range of soil conditions and need little care once established. Vivid orange-red petals with a darker red eyezone and a bright greenish-yellow throat combine for a bold, fiery color display that lives up to the cultivar's name, opening on well-branched scapes that carry numerous buds for an extended bloom season on an established, well-grown clump. As with all daylilies, each individual flower lasts only a single day, but a healthy plant produces a steady daily succession of new blooms over several weeks, and this cultivar's strong, saturated color makes it a standout accent among softer pastel daylily companions. Deadhead spent blooms and remove finished flower scapes at the base, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to keep the planting vigorous.

plant_note: Scatter a handful of the tiny floating fern directly onto the pond surface after the water has warmed; no planting medium is needed since it floats freely and multiplies on its own.
directions: This tiny free-floating fern forms a dense carpet of overlapping scale-like fronds that shade out algae and turn reddish in strong sun or cool weather. Simply toss a starter mat onto the water; it doubles rapidly through vegetative fragmentation and needs no rooting medium. Skim off excess growth regularly to prevent it from completely covering the surface and cutting off oxygen exchange, and treat it as an annual in cold climates since it is killed by hard freezes, though warm-region growers should check local rules as it can be weedy in mild-winter ponds and waterways.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings after flowering or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; moss phlox requires excellent drainage and rots in wet soil. Shear or cut back by one-third after flowering to maintain compact mounded form and prevent the center from dying out — this keeps plants attractive and full for many years.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; moss phlox is one of the most spectacular spring-blooming groundcovers in temperate gardens, native to rocky outcrops, sandy barrens, and thin-soiled slopes of eastern North America and covering itself so completely with flowers in April and May that the foliage is entirely hidden — creating a solid carpet of color, typically in shades of pink, white, lavender, or red-purple depending on cultivar. The plant itself is a dense, needle-leaved, semi-evergreen mat barely 4–6 inches tall that cascades beautifully over walls, slopes, and rock garden edges and provides attractive dark-green foliage texture through the rest of the season. After the spectacular spring bloom, trim it back by one-third to maintain dense, compact growth and prevent the center from opening up. Extremely drought-tolerant and cold-hardy once established, and among the few groundcovers that holds its own on steep, dry slopes where nothing else will establish. The cultivar range is enormous — 'Emerald Blue,' 'Candy Stripe,' 'Fort Hill,' 'Scarlet Flame,' and many others offer colors from pure white through pink to deep rose and lavender-blue.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface after last frost (seeds need light — do not cover) or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; portulaca demands dry, poor, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and will rot in heavy, moist, fertile conditions — this is the annual for the hot, dry, rocky spots where nothing else will grow.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface after last frost (seeds need light — do not cover) or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; portulaca demands dry, poor, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and will rot in heavy, moist, fertile conditions — this is the annual for the hot, dry, rocky spots where nothing else will grow. Portulaca grandiflora is a prostrate, succulent annual adapted to hot, dry, sandy conditions that makes a spectacular low groundcover with bright green, needle-like leaves and a profusion of large (1–2 inch), tissue-paper-textured, cup-shaped flowers in vivid shades of red, magenta, orange, yellow, and white; flowers are single-day bloomers that open in full sun and close at night or in cloudy weather. It is virtually indestructible in the heat, requires essentially no water once established, is perfect for hot pavement cracks, dry slopes, and rock gardens, and provides important nectar for specialist Portulaca-visiting native bees. Modern double-flowered varieties stay open longer through the day.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Moss Verbena is a sprawling, low-growing perennial (annual in zones 6–7, short-lived perennial in zones 8–10) with finely dissected, moss-like foliage and continuous lavender-purple flowers from spring through frost — it is one of the most drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and weed-suppressing ground cover plants for sunny dry areas in the Gulf South.
directions: Sow directly or use transplants in full sun; Moss Verbena requires excellent drainage — it thrives in sandy, rocky, or poor soils and dies in heavy clay that stays wet; once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and self-sows freely in warm climates; shear lightly after peak bloom to encourage fresh new growth. Moss Verbena (Verbena tenuisecta) is a sprawling, mat-forming wildflower native to South America but thoroughly naturalized throughout the Gulf South states and Texas, where it has spread along roadsides, rocky disturbed areas, and dry meadows to become one of the most common and beloved wildflowers in the region. The finely dissected, pinnately cut leaves have a delicate, moss-like or fern-like appearance that is distinctly different from the large, lobed leaves of garden verbena; this distinctive leaf texture gives the plant its 'Moss Verbena' name. The small lavender to purple flowers (occasionally white in some populations) are produced in dense clusters at the stem tips from spring through fall, virtually non-stop in warm climates — one of the longest bloom periods of any flowering plant. Moss Verbena is exceptional as a low-maintenance ground cover for dry, sunny areas in zones 8–11 where it spreads by stolons and self-sowing to cover bare ground, suppresses weeds by smothering, and provides continuous bloom with virtually no care. Heavily used by native bees and butterflies as a nectar source. Zone 9a gardens (Chester's area) experience Moss Verbena as a perennial that may die back partially in cold winters but regrows from the base or self-sows prolifically.

common_name: Moth Orchid (Moon Orchid, Amabilis Phalaenopsis, White Moth Orchid)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in zone 9; Phalaenopsis amabilis cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Grow in slatted orchid pots or clear plastic pots in coarse orchid bark media with excellent drainage. Water thoroughly once or twice per week, allowing the media to dry partially between waterings. A brief 2–4 week period of cooler nights (55–65°F) in fall stimulates flower spike initiation. Never remove a green flower spike — reblooming occurs from side branches. Repot every 1–2 years when the bark has decomposed. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Moth Orchid prefers the bright indirect light of an east or shaded south window (direct sun burns the thick leaves) and will rarely rebloom in genuinely dim conditions. Phalaenopsis amabilis is a large, monopodial epiphytic orchid native to the tropical islands of Southeast Asia and northwestern Australia (Java, Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi, the Moluccas, and Queensland), discovered in 1750 by Georg Eberhard Rumphius and named 'amabilis' (lovely) for its extraordinary flowers. The species is the primary ancestor of virtually the entire modern commercial Phalaenopsis hybrid industry — the enormous, flat, moth-shaped flowers with rounded sepals and petals, pure white with yellow and red markings at the lip, and the elegant arching stems bearing 10–20 or more flowers simultaneously, established the floral template that modern breeders have reproduced and amplified across thousands of hybrid cultivars. The commercial Phalaenopsis orchids sold at every supermarket, garden center, and box store worldwide are overwhelmingly hybrids in which P. amabilis is a primary parent — the single most economically significant orchid species in global horticulture. The flowers last 2–4 months on the plant and are among the longest-lasting of any floral display. Genuinely non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Plant divisions, or detach and root the small plantlets that form on mature fronds, in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mother fern propagates unusually easily from its own frond-borne baby plants.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mother fern produces finely divided, arching, lacy fronds notable for the small plantlets, or bulbils, that form directly on the upper surface of mature fronds and can be detached, once they have a few tiny roots and leaves, and pressed onto moist potting mix to grow into new independent ferns. This viviparous habit makes it one of the easiest ferns to propagate and share, needing no spore culture or division of the crown. In frost-free gardens it forms a full, fountain-like clump that works well in shaded borders, under trees, or in large containers, and it also thrives as a houseplant in bright, indirect light and consistent humidity where winters are too cold for it outdoors. Keep soil evenly moist and humidity high, since dry air causes browning frond tips, and remove old, tattered fronds at the base to keep the clump looking fresh.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; dislikes transplanting.
directions: Surface sow the fine seed directly in early spring or fall, as poppies need light to germinate and resent root disturbance. This blend glows in soft shades of pink, white, and purple with crepe-paper petals and contrasting dark centers. Low-maintenance and drought-tolerant, it is stunning massed along borders and self-sows to return each year. Thin seedlings to give plants room.

plant_note: Press or lightly bury the small plantlets that drop from mature leaf margins onto moist, well-drained succulent mix in spring or summer; each plantlet already has tiny roots forming and establishes within days, so propagation is essentially automatic once a plant is producing them.
directions: Grow in bright light, including some direct sun, in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only when the soil has dried out. Kalanchoe daigremontiana (mother of thousands, alligator plant) forms an upright rosette of long, grey-green, purple-blotched leaves edged with rows of miniature plantlets that root wherever they touch soil, a reproductive strategy that gives the plant its common name and makes it one of the most effortlessly propagated houseplants in cultivation. Because of that same trait it self-sows aggressively and is classified as invasive in frost-free parts of the Gulf Coast, Florida, Hawaii, and other subtropical regions, so it is best confined to a container on a windowsill or patio rather than planted in the ground in warm climates, and spent flower stalks or dropped plantlets should be cleaned up promptly. All parts contain cardiac glycosides (bufadienolides) that are toxic if ingested by pets or livestock, so site it out of reach of curious animals and children.

common_name: Mother-in-law Tongue (Dracaena Snake Plant, Bowstring Hemp)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to full shade; Dracaena trifasciata (the current accepted name for snake plant) grows outdoors year-round only in frost-free zones 10–12 but is widely grown as a houseplant in all zones.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in any light condition; Dracaena trifasciata survives in deep shade but grows more slowly and maintains better leaf color with moderate indirect light. Dracaena trifasciata is the current taxonomically accepted name for the plant long known as Sansevieria trifasciata (which see for the full cultural description); the transfer from Sansevieria to Dracaena was proposed in 2017 based on molecular phylogenetic studies showing that the two genera are not distinct. Garden centers and nurseries continue to sell plants labeled under both names, and both are correct in common usage. The plant is a West African native producing stiffly upright, sword-shaped, succulent-textured leaves with horizontal dark-and-light green banding and often yellow or cream leaf margins. In zones 10–12, it grows outdoors in subtropical and tropical landscapes as a clump-forming ground layer plant; in cooler zones it is one of the most popular and low-maintenance houseplants worldwide. The fiber from the leaves (historical source of the common name 'bowstring hemp') was once used to make rope and bowstrings in West Africa.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Mother-of-Hundreds cactus clusters vigorously into a large mound and needs a spacious pot to accommodate its spread.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Mother-of-Hundreds cactus clusters vigorously into a large mound and needs a spacious pot to accommodate its spread. Flattened, densely clustering stems armed with stout white to brownish spines multiply rapidly from a single plant into a wide, dense mound of dozens of individual heads, living up to its common name within just a few years of vigorous offsetting, topped each spring by a ring of small, bright pink-purple flowers. Native to central Mexico, it is one of the fastest-clustering and most reliably free-flowering mammillaria species, making an impressive large specimen for a sunny patio or greenhouse given enough years and pot space to spread. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright direct light, and repot into a wider container as the clustering mound grows to accommodate its spread.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; mottled epimedium spreads more freely than many species via slender running rhizomes, making it a good choice where a faster-filling groundcover is wanted.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; mottled epimedium spreads more freely than many species via slender running rhizomes, making it a good choice where a faster-filling groundcover is wanted. Epimedium leptorrhizum is a Chinese species with slender, wide-running rhizomes that let it spread more readily into a groundcover mat than clump-forming epimediums, bearing arrow-shaped, sometimes bronze-mottled leaflets and unusually large, showy, pale pink to lilac flowers with long spurs in mid-spring. Its larger, more colorful flowers and faster spread make it a striking choice for covering a good-sized area of dry shade under trees, where it forms an attractive, weed-suppressing carpet within a few seasons. Cut back old foliage in late winter to fully display the spring flowers, and give it typical epimedium conditions of humus-rich soil with reliable moisture during active growth.

plant_note: Plant clump divisions in early spring in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in deep to partial shade; Mottled Wild Ginger is slow-growing and long-lived. Maintain consistent moisture until established, then reduce watering as the plant is drought-tolerant in deep shade once its root system is developed.
directions: Mottled Wild Ginger is a beautiful native evergreen ground cover of the southern Appalachians and upper coastal plain, producing low mounds of heart-shaped, leathery leaves decorated with silver and pale green mottling against dark green — one of the most ornamentally spectacular native shade plants of the southeastern United States. Unlike the more northern Asarum canadense, which is deciduous, Mottled Wild Ginger retains its attractively patterned foliage through winter and forms a weed-suppressing carpet in dry to moist shade where few other plants grow reliably year-round. The curious, urn-shaped brownish-purple flowers are produced near the soil surface in late spring, hidden beneath the foliage where they are pollinated primarily by ground beetles and ants attracted to their earthy fragrance. Plant divisions in spring in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in deep to partial shade; plants spread very slowly but are virtually permanent once established, gradually forming dense colonies that suppress weeds under deciduous trees.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Moudry fountain grass self-sows more readily than named seedless cultivars, so deadhead spent seed heads to control spread if that is a concern.
directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Moudry fountain grass self-sows more readily than named seedless cultivars, so deadhead spent seed heads to control spread if that is a concern. Arching, medium-green foliage forms a tidy fountain-shaped clump topped in late summer by dense, bottlebrush-like flower spikes that emerge almost black before aging to dark purple-brown, a striking color rarely seen in ornamental grass seed heads and one of the darkest of any commonly grown fountain grass. Its compact size and bold, near-black plumes make it a strong textural and color accent at the front or middle of a border, contrasting well against lighter-colored companions. Cut the whole clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes each spring.

common_name: Moulin Rouge Sunflower (Deep Red Pollen-Free Cut Flower Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; for succession harvests, sow every 2–3 weeks through summer. Moulin Rouge is a pollen-free variety, making it exceptional for cut flower arrangements — no pollen drop on tablecloths or clothing. For cut flower production, harvest when the outer ring of petals has fully unfurled but the center disk is still compact and not yet shedding pollen. In zone 9, it can be sown in fall for winter blooms.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches apart for best stem quality and branching. Moulin Rouge is a premium cut flower sunflower developed and popularized by Johnny's Selected Seeds that produces fully double or semi-double flowers in an exceptionally deep, saturated burgundy-red to mahogany-maroon color — the deepest red available among annual sunflowers and a dramatic departure from the yellow, gold, and orange tones that dominate the sunflower palette. The name references the famous Parisian cabaret's signature deep red aesthetic. The deep color is most intense at cool temperatures and when harvested just as the petals fully open; heat and full sun through summer can lighten the red to more orange-red tones, while spring and fall production in cooler conditions maintains the darkest burgundy shades. Moulin Rouge is pollen-free — an important trait for cut flower arrangements, as pollen-producing sunflowers drop yellow pollen onto table linens, furniture, and clothing during vase life. The branching habit produces multiple flowers per plant over an extended summer season when succession-planted. An outstanding specialty cut flower that provides a uniquely dark, dramatic color for flower arrangements and one of the most requested sunflower varieties by florists who want alternatives to the standard yellow.

common_name: Mound Lily Yucca (Spanish Dagger, Glorious Yucca, Soft-Tipped Yucca)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; Yucca gloriosa is native to the southeastern coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and west through the Gulf Coast, where it grows in dunes, sandy maritime forests, and coastal scrub — one of the most architectural ornamental yuccas for large-scale landscaping in zone 6–10 gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in excellent drainage; Mound Lily Yucca is larger than most garden yuccas and eventually forms a multi-stemmed shrub 5–10 feet tall; remove spent flower spikes after bloom; the species is slower-suckering than many yuccas and generally stays as a single or few-stemmed specimen for many years. Mound Lily Yucca is a large, architecturally bold native yucca of the southeastern United States coastal plain — one of the signature plants of the Atlantic and Gulf Coast dune systems, where it stabilizes sandy soils and provides year-round structural interest with its dramatic rosettes of broad, blue-green leaves. Unlike most garden yuccas, Yucca gloriosa grows to significant size over time, eventually developing a thick woody trunk or multi-stemmed shrub to 5–8 feet (sometimes 10 feet), with large rosettes of stiff, 2–3 foot leaves at the branch tips — creating a palm-like or tree-like silhouette unlike the low ground-hugging form of Yucca filamentosa. The common name 'Spanish Dagger' refers to the stiff, somewhat flexible leaf tip: while sharp, it is softer and less needle-like than the truly dangerous Y. aloifolia (Spanish Bayonet), making Mound Lily Yucca a somewhat safer choice for garden settings near walkways and play areas — though still requiring care. The dramatic 4–6 foot flower spike bearing hundreds of creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers appears in late summer to fall, creating one of the most spectacular flowering events of the late-season garden; the flowers are both edible and attractive to moths that pollinate them at night. Widely used in coastal landscape design for its salt tolerance and sandy-soil adaptation.

common_name: Mount Airy Fothergilla (Premier Large Honey-Scented Fall-Color Fothergilla)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mount Airy is the premier large fothergilla selection, prized for reliable brilliant orange-red-yellow fall color and honey-scented white bottlebrush flowers, tolerating shadier sites than most flowering shrubs.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mount Airy tolerates shadier conditions than most spring-flowering shrubs while still delivering reliable bloom and fall color. Widely regarded as the finest fothergilla cultivar available, Mount Airy was discovered as a superior seedling at the Mount Airy Arboretum in Cincinnati and combines fragrant, honey-scented white bottlebrush flowers in mid-spring, before the leaves emerge, with an exceptionally consistent and vivid fall display blending brilliant orange, red, and yellow on the same plant, often on the same leaf, a color show that rivals or exceeds many more commonly planted shrubs. Its dense, rounded, well-behaved habit needs little pruning to look tidy. An outstanding, low-maintenance choice for the shaded or partly shaded shrub border, requiring no spraying and tolerating both heat and cold well within its range.

common_name: Mount Everest Allium (Giant White Ornamental Onion)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Mount Everest produces one of the largest pure white flower globes among ornamental onions, often 6-8 inches across.
directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep and 10-14 inches apart in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun; standing water around the bulbs in winter causes rot. Mount Everest sends up a tall, sturdy, leafless stem in late spring topped by a dense, perfectly round globe of small starry white flowers that can reach 6 to 8 inches across, one of the largest and showiest white ornamental onions available, holding its form as a dramatic vertical accent in the border for several weeks. Like other large alliums, its strappy basal foliage yellows and dies back before or during bloom, so plant it behind or among later-emerging perennials that will mask the fading leaves. Deer- and rabbit-resistant and drought-tolerant once established, it multiplies slowly by offsets and is best left undisturbed for years, with the dried seed heads adding continued architectural interest into fall if left standing.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mount Hood daffodil is a classic, widely adapted large-trumpet variety that naturalizes well in most temperate gardens.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mount Hood daffodil is a classic, widely adapted large-trumpet variety that naturalizes well in most temperate gardens. Large, classically shaped flowers open pale creamy-yellow, with the long trumpet fading to pure white as the bloom matures, giving each flower a soft, two-toned transition over its bloom period that is a hallmark of this long-popular heirloom trumpet daffodil. A dependable, vigorous grower since its introduction, it multiplies steadily into large drifts when left undisturbed, making it a favorite for mass plantings, naturalized lawns, and cutting gardens alike. Let the foliage die back naturally after flowering before removing it, and divide crowded clumps every four to five years once dormant in late summer.

common_name: Mount Tacoma Tulip (Pure White Peony-Form Double Late Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Mount Tacoma is a Double Late (peony-flowered) class tulip with pure white, fully double blooms, flowering late in the season.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from strong wind, since the large double flower heads can be heavy. Mount Tacoma bears large, densely ruffled, pure white double blooms with the full, rounded form of a garden peony rather than a typical single tulip flower, opening late in the season and providing a clean, elegant counterpart to the blush-pink Angelique within the same Double Late class. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mountain allium is a compact, early-blooming ornamental allium ideal for rock gardens and border fronts. It blooms in late spring (May–June), earlier than the large hybrid alliums, with open, lax umbels of bright, deep-rose-pink star-shaped flowers. It increases by offsets and seeds to form small clumps. Mild garlic scent when foliage is crushed.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mountain allium is a compact, low-growing allium from the mountain meadows of Central Asia — Turkey, the Caucasus, and Central Asia — that offers one of the most intense, saturated pink-rose flower colors in the ornamental allium range on a plant small enough for the rock garden, border front, or naturalizing in thin, stony turf. The flowers are borne in late spring in rather open, lax, flat-headed umbels of 6–20 individual, six-petaled, starry flowers in a clear, deep magenta-rose to carmine-pink, the petals with a slightly darker central midrib, creating small open umbels of vivid, concentrated pink color on 8–12 inch stems above two narrow, channeled, grass-like leaves. Unlike the large hybrid alliums, the flower head is open and non-spherical, giving it a more informal, naturalistic appearance suited to wild-flower style or rock garden plantings. It blooms before the tall hybrid alliums, filling the late spring bulb gap between the main daffodil-tulip season and the early summer perennial season. Outstanding in combination with Allium hollandicum and later alliums for an extended ornamental allium succession.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; mountain aloe is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere grown as a large container specimen.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; mountain aloe is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere grown as a large container specimen. Massive, thick, blue-gray leaves armed with reddish-brown thorns along the margins and scattered across both leaf surfaces form an enormous, single-trunked rosette that ranks among the largest and most architecturally imposing of all cultivated aloe species, topped in winter by branching flower spikes bearing dense clusters of orange to red tubular flowers. Native to rocky hillsides and savanna across southern Africa, it is a slow-growing but ultimately massive specimen well suited to a large-scale xeriscape or succulent garden where its bold, spiny form can be a focal point. Water only occasionally once established, provide full sun and excellent drainage, and give it ample room to eventually develop its substantial mature size.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring or plant divisions in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mountain alyssum is drought-tolerant and thrives in hot, dry rock gardens and on sunny, exposed banks.
directions: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mountain alyssum is intolerant of shade and wet soil — it is a plant of hot, dry, rocky habitats and thrives on neglect and poor soil. Alyssum montanum is a low, mat-forming European perennial alyssum (not to be confused with the annual sweet alyssum, Lobularia maritima) with gray-green, densely hairy leaves and bright-yellow, honey-scented, 4-petaled flowers in dense, rounded clusters in early to mid-spring; the honey fragrance is less pronounced than sweet alyssum but still pleasant. It forms attractive, low mats on dry, rocky banks, in rock gardens, between paving stones, and on dry walls; it is drought-tolerant, long-lived, and essentially maintenance-free in appropriate conditions. More compact and lower-growing than gold dust alyssum (A. saxatile/Aurinia saxatilis).

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into gritty, well-drained soil; seeds require cold stratification over winter to germinate in spring. Thin seedlings to final spacing once established.
directions: Direct sow seed in fall into sharply drained, gritty or rocky soil that mimics its alpine home. Cold stratification through winter breaks dormancy naturally, and seedlings emerge in spring once temperatures moderate. This compact perennial prefers cool summers and excellent drainage; it performs best in rock gardens, troughs, or the front of a cool-climate border. Allow the attractive feathery seed heads to develop after the golden flowers fade for continued ornamental interest.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; mountain bellwort is smaller and more compact than the larger-flowered Uvularia grandiflora, making it a good choice for tucking into tight spots in a woodland rock garden.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; mountain bellwort is smaller and more compact than the larger-flowered Uvularia grandiflora, making it a good choice for tucking into tight spots in a woodland rock garden. Uvularia puberula is a compact southeastern native bellwort found on rocky, acidic slopes and forest edges, forming a low clump of glossy, perfoliate leaves with small, twisted, pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers dangling from the stem tips in mid-spring, followed by three-angled seed capsules. Its diminutive scale and tolerance of drier, rockier soil than other bellworts make it well suited to a shaded rock garden or the front of a woodland border alongside foamflower and dwarf sedges. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is best left undisturbed once established, since plants take time to recover from transplanting.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Mountain Camellia is somewhat easier to establish than Silky Camellia (Stewartia malacodendron) and more cold-hardy; avoid waterlogged or alkaline soils.
directions: Mountain Camellia is a striking native understory shrub or small tree, native to rich, moist, wooded slopes, ravine walls, and stream terraces in the southern Appalachians from Virginia and Kentucky south to Georgia and Alabama, blooming in July and August with large, white, five-petaled flowers bearing a prominent cluster of orange-tipped stamens. Larger than Silky Camellia (Stewartia malacodendron) and more cold-hardy (to zone 5), Mountain Camellia blooms later in summer when few other native shrubs are flowering, extending ornamental interest deep into the season. The smooth, exfoliating gray bark provides attractive winter interest, and the foliage turns shades of orange and red in fall. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade — it is somewhat more tolerant of garden conditions than Silky Camellia and establishes more readily from nursery transplants, though it is still slow-growing and long-lived.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or direct-sow in fall; mountain cornflower spreads by underground rhizomes and self-sows freely — it can be invasive in some regions and should be deadheaded before seeds ripen to limit spread. After the main late-spring flush, shear plants back hard to encourage a fresh crop of foliage and often a second flush of bloom in late summer.
directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade; mountain cornflower is the perennial version of the annual bachelor's button — a stout, spreading perennial from European mountain meadows producing large (2–3 inch), spidery, brilliant violet-blue to deep blue-violet cornflower heads with deeper violet centers and contrasting purplish-maroon outer florets, displayed on upright stems above soft, gray-green, woolly foliage from late spring through early summer with a possible second flush in late summer if cut back hard after the first flowering. The cobalt-blue and violet tones are among the truest and most saturated blues available in early-summer perennials, and the large, spidery flower heads have a more romantic, wildflower quality than the more refined blue of delphiniums. White ('Alba'), pink ('Carnea'), and bicolor cultivars exist but the species violet-blue is generally considered the most ornamental. Spreads vigorously and is potentially aggressive in fertile soils; more restrained in lean, dry conditions. Self-sows freely and can naturalize rapidly — an asset in a wildflower garden, a management concern in a formal border.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; mountain death camas requires good winter cold and is best suited to northern regions and mountain elevations.
directions: Anticlea elegans (formerly Zigadenus elegans, white camas) is a graceful bulbous perennial native to moist mountain meadows, subalpine slopes, and streambanks across western and central North America from Alaska to New Mexico, producing a basal cluster of narrow, grass-like leaves and an erect stem in summer bearing a loose raceme of saucer-shaped, creamy white to greenish-white flowers with distinctive greenish glands at the petal bases. Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; the plant requires good winter cold and is best suited to northern regions and mountain elevations. All parts of the plant are highly toxic — it is closely related to and easily confused with edible camas (Camassia), so never harvest from mixed populations without expert identification. An elegant addition to a native wildflower garden in cool climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; mountain devil requires excellent drainage and no phosphorus fertilizer (like all Proteaceae). It is a slow-growing shrub with unusual, distinctively shaped seed pods — woody follicles with prominent curved, curved horns at the opening — that have given it the common name 'mountain devil' for the devil-like horned silhouette of the pods. The scarlet, tubular flowers bloom intermittently throughout the year in mild climates.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; mountain devil is an Eastern Australian Proteaceae shrub of the Sydney sandstone heathlands that has become well-known for a botanical curiosity: the woody seed pods, when mature and dried, have a distinctive shape with two prominent, curved, tusk-like horns projecting from the opening of each follicle — the overall silhouette of the pod resembling a tiny devil or horned face, giving the plant its memorable and accurate common name. These distinctive horned seed pods have made mountain devil a popular dried-floral material in Australia; the pods are collected, sometimes dyed, and used in wreaths and arrangements. In the garden it is also a rewarding ornamental plant producing throughout the year (most heavily in late winter and spring) terminal clusters of 7 tubular, scarlet-red flowers with prominent, recurving, scarlet petals — vivid, hummingbird-attracting flowers of considerable color impact. Like all Proteaceae it requires excellent drainage and no phosphorus fertilizer. The combination of attractive red flowers and the remarkable, collectible, horned seed pods makes it a plant of multiple ornamental seasons.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into gritty, acidic, rocky or sandy soil in a cool, partially shaded rock garden setting; cold stratification over winter is highly beneficial, and seeds should not be buried — surface sow and firm gently into the growing medium.
directions: Mountain Dwarf Dandelion is a rare endemic native perennial restricted to high mountain rocky summits, cliff faces, and seepage slopes in the southern Appalachians of North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee — far more cold-adapted and persistently perennial than the other species in this small genus. Plants produce slender, leafless scapes topped with solitary, bright golden-yellow dandelion-like flower heads that open in summer above neat basal rosettes of narrow leaves. Grow in cool, well-drained to moist, rocky or sandy, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun — conditions that mimic its native mountain seep and rocky outcrop habitats. This species is an exceptional choice for alpine troughs, crevice gardens, and rock garden settings in the upper South but is not suited to hot, humid lowland gardens where summer heat and poor drainage will be fatal.

common_name: Mountain Fire Japanese Pieris (Red New-Growth Andromeda)
plant_note: Plant container stock in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in part shade alongside azaleas and rhododendrons, which share the same cultural needs.
directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in part shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind. Mountain Fire is grown chiefly for its brilliant fire-engine-red new growth in spring, considered among the most vivid of any Pieris cultivar, which matures to bronze and then glossy dark green as the season progresses. Cascading chains of small white urn-shaped flowers open in late winter to early spring before the new flush, giving two distinct ornamental moments. It is slow-growing and low-maintenance once established, needing little pruning beyond removing spent flower clusters.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; mountain fleece is exceptionally adaptable and performs in a wide range of conditions from full sun to quite deep partial shade.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to moderately dry, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; mountain fleece (red bistort) is a Himalayan perennial that has become one of the most celebrated and widely grown border perennials in European gardens for its extraordinary five-month flowering period — from late June through November it produces an uninterrupted succession of small, upright, bottle-brush-like flower spikes of rich, deep crimson-red, rosy-red, or white on compact, well-foliaged plants, outperforming most border perennials in duration of bloom by a considerable margin. The plant forms a well-behaved, non-spreading clump of large, heart-shaped leaves that provide an attractive foliage mass independent of the flowers. It tolerates partial shade well, maintaining its blooming performance in dappled light where many full-sun perennials would fail to flower. 'Firetail' (deep crimson-red), 'Golden Arrow' (gold-variegated leaves), 'Album' (white), and 'Inverleith' (compact, dark red) are widely grown cultivars. The flower spikes are attractive to bumblebees throughout the season.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall after scarifying and cold-stratifying seeds; plant in well-drained soil in full sun and allow natural winter conditions to complete stratification.
directions: Mountain Golden Banner is a showy, robust native perennial in the pea family, producing stout leafy stems with trifoliate lupine-like leaves and dense upright racemes of bright golden-yellow pea flowers in May and June — one of the most striking yellow wildflowers of the Rocky Mountain landscape. It is native to mountain meadows, open slopes, and forest clearings from Montana to New Mexico, spreading by rhizomes to form large, persistent colonies over time. Direct sow in fall after scarifying and cold-stratifying seeds, in well-drained soil in full sun; seeds may take one to two seasons to germinate and plants typically reach first bloom in their second year. This species is intolerant of summer heat and humidity and is not suited to gardens south or east of USDA zone 7, making it ideal for Rocky Mountain and intermountain western gardens.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, deep, humus-rich, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade; mountain hemlock grows naturally at subalpine elevations (5,000–11,000 feet) along the Pacific Crest from Alaska to California, requiring cold winters and cool, moist summers. Does not tolerate heat, drought, or alkaline soils.
