directions: Root stem cuttings or plant specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full shade; nerve plant (mosaic plant, painted net leaf) is a Peruvian tropical creeping groundcover of the family Acanthaceae, producing small, oval, intensely patterned leaves in which a dense, intricate network of bright-white, pink, or red veins forms a complete lacework overlay on the dark-green leaf surface, creating a mosaic-like pattern that gives the plant its alternative common name. The leaf patterning is extraordinarily precise and complex — the entire leaf surface is filled edge-to-edge with this fine vein network, with no undecorated green area visible. As a creeping, mat-forming groundcover it spreads horizontally across the soil surface to create a dense, living carpet of patterned leaves in terrarium and deep-shade garden conditions. Fittonia is among the most humidity-demanding of all tropical foliage plants — it wilts dramatically at the first sign of dry air, then recovers equally dramatically when humidity is restored. This complete intolerance of dry conditions makes it ideal for terrariums and glass cases but challenging in open interior environments. Pink-veined ('Argyroneura'), red-veined ('Rubra'), and white-veined forms are the primary selections.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown container trees in fall in rocky, dry, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; net-leaf hackberry is a tree of canyon walls, rocky arroyos, and desert wash margins in the arid Southwest — it requires excellent drainage and tolerates alkaline soils better than sugar hackberry.
directions: Net-leaf hackberry is the western species of hackberry, found on rocky canyon walls, limestone bluffs, and desert arroyo margins from the Texas Hill Country west to California and south into Mexico, where it often clings to near-vertical cliff faces and survives in conditions of extreme drought and heat. Its distinctive deeply veined, rough, sandpaper-textured leaves (the 'reticulata' means net-veined) and tolerance of alkaline limestone soils make it the hackberry for dry, rocky, alkaline landscapes of the southwest where eastern hackberry (Celtis occidentalis) is poorly adapted. Like all hackberries, it is a primary host plant for hackberry emperor and American snout butterflies, and its small, dark red to black berries are eaten by 30+ bird species including robins, mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and migrating thrushes. In south and central Texas and the southwestern states, it is an important native tree for dry, rocky, alkaline soil landscape situations and for restoring native woodland structure in arroyo and canyon habitats.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or cold-stratify seeds for 60 days and sow indoors in late winter. This vine dies back to the ground in winter and re-emerges from the root in spring. Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; netleaf leather flower is a slender native vine of the southeastern Coastal Plain that scrambles through shrubs and over fences with modest vigor. The unique, urn-shaped flowers have thick, leathery tepals in shades of dull purple with pale-veined markings — resembling tiny pitchers that hang from the vine stems in summer. Unlike the more showy garden clematis, this species is subtle and discovered on close inspection. The feathery seed heads that follow are silvery and attractive. The netted or reticulated (net-like) veins of the leaves give the species its name. This is one of the native leather flower clematis of the Gulf Coastal Plain (related to C. crispa and C. viorna) and a rare but valuable plant for a low-water, naturalistic southern garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in wet to consistently moist, peaty, acidic soil in partial to full shade; netted chain fern is well adapted to boggy woodland margins and shaded swale edges where soils remain saturated for extended periods.
directions: Woodwardia areolata is a small, deciduous native fern of eastern North American bogs, swamps, and shaded wet woodland margins, producing simply pinnate (not bipinnate) sterile fronds with broad, lobed, ladder-like pinnae and a distinctive netted venation pattern that gives the plant its common name; its fertile fronds are narrower with elongated sori arranged in chain-like rows along the midrib of each pinna. It spreads steadily by slender rhizomes to form a low, dense groundcover in wet, acidic, shaded sites and is an excellent native choice for rain garden margins, shaded bog edges, and the wet fringes of pond plantings in zones 3–9. Unlike many ferns, it tolerates standing water and waterlogged soils well, making it one of the few ferns suited to intermittently flooded conditions. Combine with blue flag iris, pitcher plants, and native sedges in naturalized wet woodland or bog plantings.

plant_note: Surface sow seeds in early spring or fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade; nettle-leaf bellflower self-sows freely and can naturalize in woodland garden conditions. It has a history as a medicinal herb: the botanical name trachelium refers to the Greek word for throat (trachea) as it was used in folk medicine to treat sore throats.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part to full shade; nettle-leaf bellflower is a shade-tolerant European native of hedgerows, woodland edges, and scrub, producing coarsely toothed, roughly textured leaves reminiscent of stinging nettle (hence the common name, though unrelated and harmless) and in July–August, upright stems bearing clusters of large (1–1.5 inch), broadly cup-shaped, violet-blue to blue-purple flowers — somewhat more openly bell-shaped than C. latifolia and carried in more branching clusters. Like C. latifolia, it is genuinely shade-tolerant and thrives in the moist, lightly shaded conditions where most bellflowers decline. It was used historically in herbal medicine for throat ailments (trachelium derives from the Greek for throat). A traditional English hedgerow plant, it naturalizes readily in the semi-shaded woodland garden. The double-flowered cultivar 'Bernice' (fully double, lilac-blue flowers) is the most decorative available form. Self-sows reliably in moist, shaded situations and can be used to create naturalized colonies under deciduous shrubs and trees.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; nettle-leaf sage is one of the most shade-tolerant native Salvia species in eastern North America and is best suited to woodland edge and dappled-shade settings.
directions: Sow direct in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; seeds benefit from natural cold stratification over winter and germinate in spring — nettle-leaf sage adapts to the kind of moderately moist, shaded woodland floor where most sun-loving sages fail. Salvia urticifolia is a uncommon and underused native perennial sage of the southeastern Appalachians and adjacent piedmont, native to moist, shaded slopes, woodland edges, and stream margins; it is distinguished by its large, nettle-like, coarsely toothed, aromatic leaves (urticifolia = nettle-leaved) that give it a lush, bold texture in shaded garden settings. It produces upright stems bearing whorls of tubular, blue to blue-purple flowers from May through July that are attractive to native bumblebees and hummingbirds — a notable distinction in a genus where most species require full sun. Nettle-leaf sage is an excellent choice for shaded native plant gardens, woodland edges, and naturalistic plantings in the mid-Atlantic and upper South; it self-sows modestly and is not aggressively spreading.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil (do not cover — seeds need light) in early spring or early fall; nettle-leaved mullein is a genuine long-lived perennial, unlike the common biennial mullein, returning reliably year after year. It self-sows moderately to maintain a colony. The cultivar Album has white flowers with the same mauve-purple stamens and is equally ornamental.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; nettle-leaved mullein is the most reliably perennial and garden-worthy of the mulleins, distinct from both the common biennial mullein (Verbascum thapsus) and the silvery Turkish mullein (V. bombyciferum) in being a genuine long-lived perennial that returns each year. The flower spikes reach 3-5 feet and are densely packed with yellow flowers, but the most distinctive and ornamental feature is the prominent, woolly, mauve-purple filaments of the stamens visible in the center of each flower — a striking purple-and-yellow bicolor combination visible across the garden. The cultivar Album produces white flowers with the same contrasting purple-mauve stamens — an unusual and beautiful combination. Native to central and southern Europe, it thrives in the lean, well-drained, alkaline soils of traditional cottage-style dry borders, rock gardens, and gravel plantings. Combines beautifully with Mediterranean herbs, silver-leafed plants, and ornamental grasses.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; ctenanthe tolerates the deepest shade of the prayer plant family and maintains its leaf coloring in quite low light conditions where stromanthe and calathea would fade.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; never-never plant is a Brazilian tropical perennial of the prayer plant family (Marantaceae) that produces long, lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive, precisely patterned, feathered silvery-gray variegation on a rich dark-green background — the alternating dark and light bands create a herringbone or fish-bone pattern that has a formal, almost graphic quality unlike the more organic markings of calathea. The undersides of the leaves are deep burgundy-red to maroon. It is among the most shade-tolerant of the Marantaceae family, maintaining acceptable growth and variegation in quite dim interior spaces where other prayer plant relatives would decline. Like calathea and maranta, the leaves exhibit nyctinasty (night leaf movement), folding upward in the evening. More tolerant of irregular watering than calathea. 'Tricolor' (cream, white, and green irregular blotching) is the most widely grown cultivar selection.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; never-never plant is an excellent tropical shade perennial for zone 9b–11 gardens or as a container plant brought indoors in winter in cooler zones — grown primarily for its stunning silver and dark green striped foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; never-never plant is intolerant of drought, direct sun, and cold temperatures below 50°F. Ctenanthe setosa is a Brazilian rainforest native in the prayer plant family (Marantaceae) prized for its spectacular foliage: long, oval leaves with dramatic silver-grey stripes on a dark olive-green background and deep burgundy-purple undersides that flash when the leaves move in a breeze. Like other Marantaceae, the leaves fold upward at night in a sleep movement (nyctinasty) that gives the family its common name 'prayer plant.' Grow in deep, consistent shade with high humidity and regular moisture but excellent drainage; use as a bold tropical accent in shaded island beds in zone 10–11 or as a high-impact container plant for patios in cooler zones. Propagate by dividing clumps in spring.

plant_note: Tuck small rosette divisions into moss-covered rock crevices or lean gravelly soil in spring; avoid disturbing roots more than necessary.
directions: Nevius' stonecrop is a diminutive, mat-forming succulent native to river-bluff rock outcrops of the southern Appalachians in Tennessee, Alabama, and Georgia, where it roots directly into thin pockets of moss and lichen on gneiss and phyllite ledges. Small rosettes of blue-green, spoon-shaped leaves spread slowly by short stolons, forming loose colonies that hug exposed rock. In late spring, wiry flowering stems lift clusters of small white star-shaped flowers just above the foliage, drawing small native bees and other early-season pollinators. In the garden, give it a sharply drained rock garden, dry-stacked wall, or gravel crevice with light shade and lean soil that mimics its cliffside origins; it resents heavy or consistently moist ground.

common_name: New Dawn Rose (Ever-Blooming Doctor Van Fleet)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring against a sturdy support structure; New Dawn requires strong architectural support — a substantial fence, arbor, or pergola capable of supporting a mature plant that can weigh several hundred pounds.
directions: Plant against a sturdy support in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; New Dawn holds the distinction of being the first plant ever patented in the United States (Plant Patent No. 1, 1931) and remains one of the most beloved climbing roses in cultivation, producing masses of medium-pink, lightly fragrant, semi-double flowers on long, arching canes that can reach 15–20 feet. New Dawn is a sport of 'Dr. Van Fleet' that gained its fame partly by blooming repeatedly rather than once in spring — an unusual quality in vigor climbing roses of its era. The silvery-pink flowers fade gradually to nearly white and are produced in large clusters in spring with reliable repeat bloom in fall. The vigorous, arching canes with glossy, disease-resistant foliage require substantial annual tying and training to maintain the climbing habit; left unsupported it forms a large sprawling shrub. New Dawn tolerates partial shade better than most climbing roses, making it valuable for training on north-facing or partially shaded walls and fences.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; cold stratification for 4–6 weeks improves germination.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds for 4–6 weeks in a damp paper towel in the refrigerator before sowing indoors to improve germination rates. Pinch plants back by one-third in late spring to encourage bushier growth and delay bloom until fall, when their purple flowers are invaluable for pollinators. Tall varieties may need staking or can be grown through a peony cage. Divide clumps every 2–3 years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent the center from dying out.

common_name: New Gold Lantana (Compact Golden-Yellow Gulf Coast Lantana)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; New Gold is sterile (does not produce fruit) — a significant advantage over fertile lantana cultivars that produce berries consumed by birds and potentially spread invasively in Gulf Coast natural areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; New Gold is the premier golden-yellow lantana cultivar — a Texas A&M University release selected for its uniform, pure golden-yellow flower color (no color changes as in the standard Lantana camara, which shifts from yellow to orange to red as individual flowers age within the cluster), its sterility (no viable seeds — a major ecological advantage in the Gulf South where fertile lantana spreads into natural areas via bird-dispersed berries), and its compact, mounding habit. New Gold blooms continuously from the last frost through hard frost in zone 9 — essentially a 10-month blooming season with no significant dormant period and no deadheading required. The uninterrupted, consistent golden-yellow flower display and the plant's extraordinary heat, drought, and humidity tolerance make New Gold one of the finest low-maintenance flowering perennials for the Gulf South landscape. The golden-yellow flowers are outstanding pollinator magnets — drawing gulf fritillary and monarch butterflies in remarkable numbers, along with many bee species, throughout the long bloom season. New Gold is evergreen and woody perennial in zones 9–11, dying back to the roots in hard freezes but recovering vigorously. Established plants tolerate drought and heat that would kill most flowering perennials. An indispensable plant for zone 9 full-sun borders.

common_name: New Gold Lantana (Sterile Golden-Yellow Pollinator Lantana for Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; New Gold is sterile and will not produce the potentially invasive berries of the straight species — an important environmental advantage for Gulf South Gulf Coast plantings near natural areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; New Gold is a sterile hybrid lantana producing a continuous flush of bright golden-yellow to deep-gold flowers from spring through frost — one of the most floriferous and pollinator-attractive annuals and perennials for Gulf South full-sun gardens. The sterile nature of 'New Gold' is its most important horticultural virtue: unlike Lantana camara (common lantana), which is invasive in coastal areas of Florida and Texas where its berries are consumed and dispersed by birds, 'New Gold' produces no viable seed and no berries, eliminating the invasive spread concern that limits use of the species in sensitive native habitats. The golden-yellow flower color provides a particularly effective nectar resource for monarch and queen butterflies, swallowtails, skippers, and numerous native bee species — the warm-yellow flowers are among the most reliably butterfly-visited of any commonly grown annual in the Gulf South. In zone 8, New Gold is a perennial returning from the root each spring after winter dieback; in zone 10-11, it may persist as an evergreen subshrub. The trailing to mounding habit makes it outstanding for sunny borders, retaining wall edges, and large container plantings where the branches cascade naturally. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; excess water and nitrogen reduce flowering.

common_name: New Guinea Impatiens (Busy Lizzie, Star Impatiens)
plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in partial to full shade; in zone 9, New Guinea Impatiens performs best March through November when planted in morning sun or dappled shade with afternoon protection from the intense summer sun. Unlike common Impatiens (I. walleriana), it tolerates more direct morning sun and is less susceptible to Impatiens downy mildew. Pinch stem tips at planting to encourage bushy growth and prolific flowering. In zone 9b, it sometimes persists into winter in sheltered spots.
directions: Plant in morning sun to partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained, organically rich soil; New Guinea Impatiens requires more light than common impatiens and will become leggy and bloom poorly in deep shade, but performs best with protection from the harsh afternoon sun of zone 9 summers. Impatiens hawkeri is a species native to Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands that served as the primary genetic source for the large-flowered New Guinea Impatiens hybrids that have become among the most popular shade-tolerant annual flowers in American horticulture since their introduction in the 1970s. The flowers are significantly larger (2–3 inches) and the foliage more diverse than common I. walleriana — leaves may be dark green, bronze, variegated cream-and-green, or deeply colored — and many modern hybrids carry contrasting leaf and flower colors simultaneously. New Guinea Impatiens are critically important for gardeners as a replacement for the traditional common impatiens (I. walleriana) following the widespread outbreak of Impatiens Downy Mildew (Plasmopara obducens) beginning around 2010, which devastated I. walleriana plantings across the US. New Guinea Impatiens are resistant to the mildew and have largely taken the place of common impatiens in commercial and home landscapes. Flowers come in every color except true blue: white, red, orange, pink, salmon, coral, lavender, and bicolors.

common_name: New Harmony Elm (Disease-Tolerant Upright American Elm)
plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; New Harmony, released alongside Valley Forge by the USDA National Arboretum, combines strong Dutch elm disease tolerance with a more upright, compact habit than some other resistant selections.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. New Harmony was released by the USDA National Arboretum as a companion selection to Valley Forge, chosen from the same disease-screening program for combining strong Dutch elm disease tolerance with a somewhat more upright, uniform growth habit that some growers prefer for street and boulevard plantings. Like other resistant American elm cultivars it restores the tall, graceful, arching form long associated with the species, and it has performed reliably in urban conditions including compacted soil, heat, and air pollution. Water deeply during the establishment years, prune early to encourage a strong central leader and well-spaced scaffold branches, and allow ample overhead and root space for the tree's eventual large size.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; new Jersey tea has an extremely deep taproot and is very difficult to transplant once established — site it carefully the first time.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; New Jersey tea is a remarkable native shrub with one of the most interesting histories in American botany — the dried leaves were widely used as a tea substitute during the Revolutionary War when British tea was boycotted. The fluffy clusters of tiny white flowers in early summer are among the most important nectar sources in the native prairie and woodland edge, attracting dozens of bee species, skippers, and hairstreak butterflies. The roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility over time. This shrub is exceptionally drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established, thriving on rocky, infertile, dry soils where few shrubs succeed. The spring bee value alone makes it an outstanding native garden plant. It resents being moved after establishment, so site it correctly from the start.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets (pups) in spring into very well-drained, gritty, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; New Mexico century plant is one of the most cold-hardy agave species, tolerating temperatures near 0°F once established in sharply drained soil.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, rocky soil in full sun; New Mexico century plant forms a compact, symmetrical rosette of thick, gray-green to blue-green leaves edged with small, closely spaced teeth and a sharp terminal spine, native to limestone hills and grasslands of the Chihuahuan Desert borderlands. It is remarkably cold-hardy for a true agave, tolerating hard freezes that would kill most other agave species, provided the soil drains sharply and the crown stays dry through winter. Like all agaves, it is monocarpic, spending a decade or more building the rosette before sending up a single tall, branched flower stalk once in its lifetime, after which the main rosette dies while offsets typically continue the clump. Water only sparingly to establish young plants, since overwatering in heavy or poorly drained soil is the most common cause of failure with this otherwise tough, long-lived species.

plant_note: Set out container plants or nursery divisions in spring after the ground is workable. Cold stratification of seeds for 4-6 weeks improves germination rates.
directions: New Mexico Checker-mallow is a native perennial of moist mountain meadows, stream banks, and valley grasslands throughout the southwestern US and Great Basin, thriving across New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, and Arizona. It produces slender, upright spikes of bright rose-pink to lavender-pink mallow flowers from June through August, adding long-lasting color to summer gardens. Plant in well-drained, moderately moist soil in full sun; once established it tolerates periods of dryness better than most other Sidalcea species. Grow from container plants or nursery-propagated divisions for best results, as transplants establish more reliably than direct-seeded plants in garden settings.

common_name: New Mexico Privet (Desert Olive, Elbow Bush)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, caliche, or sandy soil in full sun to part shade; New Mexico privet is native to dry, rocky limestone hillsides and arroyos of the Chihuahuan Desert, Trans-Pecos Texas, and adjacent New Mexico and Oklahoma — it is extremely drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; once established, no supplemental irrigation is needed. Forestiera pubescens (New Mexico privet or desert olive) is a native Texas and New Mexico shrub — a member of the olive family (Oleaceae) producing olive-like, small (1/4-inch), blue-black drupes in fall that are eagerly consumed by migrating and resident birds, including mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings. The shrub is a multi-stemmed, densely branching, semi-evergreen plant with small, light-green, opposite leaves and tiny, inconspicuous, yellowish flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge. As a landscape plant, Forestiera pubescens is valued for extreme drought and limestone tolerance, dense wildlife-supporting structure, and use as a native hedge or screen plant that requires no supplemental water once established. It is an outstanding alternative to non-native privets (Ligustrum species) in dry southwestern and southern landscapes, providing equivalent screening value with native habitat benefits. The small, clustered fruits produced in fall are an important berry food source for fall migrants moving through the southwestern plains.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; New Year lily is a Cape winter-rainfall species that blooms in winter (January in South Africa, its summer; December–February in zone 9 cultivation), producing vivid scarlet-red flowers with white teardrop markings on the lower petals. It is native to wet mountain seeps and waterfall margins (hence 'Waterfall Gladiolus') in the Western Cape. This species is one of the parent plants of the modern garden gladiolus hybrid complex.
directions: Plant corms in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; New Year lily has a historical distinction that makes it botanically significant beyond its beauty: it is one of the primary wild species from which the entire complex of modern hybrid garden gladioli was developed, contributing especially the brilliant scarlet-red color and the broad, well-formed floret shape that characterize the best hybrid gladioli. In its own right it is a beautiful species — producing in winter (unusually early, hence 'New Year lily') tall spikes of vivid, clear, true-scarlet to cardinal-red, hooded, gladiolus-type flowers with two distinctive, teardrop-shaped, white blotches on the lower three petals, the white markings providing a crisp, contrasting accent to the vivid scarlet. It grows naturally on wet mountain cliffs and waterfall margins in the Cederberg and Hottentots Holland Mountains of the Western Cape — habitats of constant water seepage and mist — and therefore tolerates and prefers the moist conditions of its native waterfall-spray habitat better than most gladioli. The winter bloom timing, in December through February, creates the unusual situation of brilliant-red gladiolus flowers in the zone 9 midwinter garden.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; or divide established clumps in early spring. Division every 2-3 years keeps plants vigorous and prevents the center die-out typical of older clumps.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile to average, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade; New York aster is among the most profusely blooming of the native fall asters, producing dense masses of violet-blue to purple or white daisy flowers from late August through October and serving as one of the most important late-season nectar sources for migrating monarchs, painted ladies, and bumble bee queens preparing for winter. Divide clumps every two to three years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent the hollow center that develops in older undivided plants. Many cultivars offer compact habits, deeper colors, and extended bloom periods. Susceptible to powdery mildew in hot, humid climates; choose resistant varieties and provide good air circulation.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; New York fern spreads readily by rhizomes and will naturalize to form a weed-suppressing groundcover in moist, shaded woodland settings.
directions: Thelypteris noveboracensis is a light-green, deciduous native fern of eastern North American moist woodlands, instantly recognizable by its distinctive frond shape — the pinnae taper gradually toward both the tip and the base of the frond, creating a narrowed appearance at both ends that has inspired the saying that it "burns at both ends." It spreads steadily by slender, branching rhizomes to form a delicate, airy groundcover that is excellent for naturalizing large shaded areas under deciduous trees, and its light, fresh green color brightens deeply shaded spots in spring and early summer before the fronds fade to yellow and go dormant by fall. New York fern prefers moderately moist, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic woodland soils and does not tolerate waterlogging or drought, though it is more adaptable than many woodland ferns once established. Pair with wild ginger, mayapple, and Solomon's seal for a classic eastern woodland groundcover planting.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; New York ironweed tolerates consistently wet soils and is excellent in rain gardens, moist meadows, and along streams.
directions: Sow direct in spring or start indoors with 4–6 weeks of cold stratification; New York ironweed prefers moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade and is one of the best native perennials for consistently wet, sunny sites. Vernonia noveboracensis is a magnificent, tall (4–7 feet), upright native perennial of eastern North American moist meadows, stream margins, and wet prairies; it produces narrow, lance-shaped, toothed leaves on stout stems and bears large, flat-topped clusters of brilliant, deep royal-purple, fluffy, disc flowers (no ray petals) in late summer through fall — one of the most intensely saturated purples in the native plant palette and a standout in late-season gardens. The flowers are exceptional late-season nectar sources for monarchs, swallowtails, and native bees; the persistent, reddish-brown seed heads provide winter interest. Name does not restrict its range — it occurs throughout much of the eastern and central US.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring into lean, well-drained soil; keep out of paths and play areas since the spiny burrs cling to socks, fur, and bare feet.
directions: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring into lean, well-drained soil; the ferny bronze-copper foliage spreads quickly into a tight mat that hugs rocky slopes and fills gaps between pavers. It is an effective erosion binder for sunny banks, but the reddish spiny burrs that follow the summer flowers cling readily to socks, fur, and bare feet, so it is best kept out of paths and play areas. Trim back hard in early spring if the mat becomes patchy to encourage fresh, dense regrowth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally within sight or scent of the coast; strictly a warm coastal plant, suffering damage below the high 20s F.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally within sight or scent of the coast; New Zealand Christmas tree is prized above all for its extreme tolerance of salt spray, wind, and sandy soil, thriving on exposed bluffs and beachfronts where few other flowering woody plants survive. Established plants are strikingly drought tolerant, drawing on deep roots once they are past their first year or two in the ground. Brilliant crimson, bottlebrush-like flower clusters cover the leathery, silver-backed leaves in a spectacular late-spring to early-summer display, and the plant can be maintained as a dense large shrub or screen with pruning, or allowed to develop into a picturesque small tree over many years. It is strictly a warm coastal plant, suffering damage below the high 20s F.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun to part shade; New Zealand flax is extremely adaptable, tolerating coastal salt spray, clay soils, seasonally wet conditions, and moderate drought. Named cultivars with bronze, red, purple, pink-striped, or variegated foliage are widely available and maintain their color best in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; New Zealand flax is one of the most architecturally powerful foliage plants for temperate and warm climates, producing bold, erect, sword-like leaves 3–10 feet long in green or in the many named cultivars, spectacular foliage in bronze, dark purple-red, pink-striped, variegated cream-and-green, or orange-flushed combinations. In summer, mature clumps send up dramatically tall flower spikes (up to 15 feet) bearing tubular red-orange flowers rich in nectar that attract hummingbirds and honeybirds in its native range. The Maori people of New Zealand used the leaf fibers extensively for weaving baskets, mats, and garments — one of their most important fiber plants. In warm-climate landscapes (zones 8–11) it provides bold, year-round architectural structure as a specimen, in mixed borders, or in mass plantings, tolerating coastal exposure, salt spray, wind, and drought once established. Smaller species P. cookianum is more shade-tolerant and suitable for partly shaded positions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; New Zealand iris prefers cool, moist coastal conditions and may struggle in hot, dry summer climates without supplemental irrigation.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; New Zealand iris forms upright, fan-shaped clumps of narrow, rigid, dark-green, iris-like foliage that is evergreen in mild climates and produces clusters of pure white, three-petaled flowers in late spring followed by bright orange seed capsules that persist through fall — providing three distinct seasons of ornamental interest. The neat, architectural foliage clumps are excellent for edging paths, front-of-border placement, and contemporary garden designs. Excellent drought resistance once established but benefits from supplemental water during extended hot, dry spells. In zone 8 the foliage may be damaged by hard freezes; cut back in early spring and new growth re-emerges rapidly.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist but well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; New Zealand iris is evergreen and provides structural foliage through the year. It tolerates both dry and seasonally moist conditions once established. The orange-tinted winter foliage (in some forms intensifying to bright orange in cold weather) is a distinctive seasonal feature. Named 'mikoikoi' in Maori.
directions: Plant in moist but well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; New Zealand iris is a structural, evergreen, iris-family perennial from New Zealand that provides year-round interest through two distinct phases: the foliage and the flowers. The sword-shaped, narrow, bright-green to orange-tinted leaves are held in the classic iris-family flat fan arrangement, and in cool weather (particularly winter) the leaves often intensify to bright orange, golden-orange, or bronze-orange in some forms, creating a warm, glowing winter-foliage effect that is particularly striking in a bare-winter border. In spring through early summer the plant produces branching, airy panicles of small, white, three-outer-petaled flowers — each individual flower small, pure white, and open-faced, collectively creating a light, airy, fine-textured spray of white above the structural foliage. The combination of the structural, strap-like fans of orange-tinged leaves with the sprays of white flowers above them is architecturally satisfying throughout the year. The Maori name 'mikoikoi' acknowledges the plant's deep cultural history in New Zealand. Outstanding in zone 9 Gulf Coast borders as a year-round structural foliage plant with spring flowers.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; New Zealand rock lily is particularly suitable for dry shade under trees where it succeeds where many competitors fail. It tolerates brief frosts to approximately 20°F but performs best in zones 8b–10 in frost-free or near-frost-free conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; New Zealand rock lily is a handsome, clump-forming perennial native to New Zealand's coastal and lowland forests that produces arching rosettes of broad, strap-like, glaucous, gray-green to blue-green leaves in a loosely spreading clump, then in spring sends up branching, airy sprays of small, nodding, pure-white, star-shaped flowers with distinctive reflexed petals that hover above the foliage on slender stems — an effect of elegant, understated refinement. The 'renga' in its Maori name refers to its use as a food source (the fleshy roots were an important carbohydrate in traditional Maori diet). In gardens, it is valued as a shade-tolerant, drought-tolerant groundcover for mild climates — one of the few plants producing genuinely ornamental flowers in dry shade under large trees. The selection 'Te Puna' has especially good, compact foliage. Outstanding as a container specimen and as mass planting in shaded coastal gardens.

common_name: Nick Shaylor Peony (Bomb-Form Blush Pink Fading to Cream)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nick Shaylor is a classic bomb-form double peony in blush pink fading to creamy white.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Nick Shaylor bears large, tightly domed bomb-form flowers that open a soft blush pink and gradually fade to creamy white as they mature, giving a single planting a gentle gradient of color over its bloom period, opening from broad outer guard petals surrounding the rounded petaloid center typical of the bomb form. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Nicky Phlox (Deep Magenta-Purple Mildew-Resistant Garden Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space at least 18 inches apart for good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Nicky bears large, rounded flower heads in deep magenta-purple, a bold, saturated color that holds up well through the heat of summer, blooming over a long stretch from midsummer into early fall with the classic sweet fragrance of tall garden phlox. It shows better than average resistance to powdery mildew compared to older pink and purple cultivars, though full sun and generous spacing still help keep foliage clean. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings.

common_name: Nicolas Japanese Forest Grass (Green-to-Orange Fall Color Hakonechloa)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring as new growth begins in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; growth is slow the first two seasons.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and cut the whole clump back to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Nicolas is a solid-green Japanese forest grass selection prized for its dramatic seasonal transformation, holding rich green, cascading foliage through summer before turning striking shades of orange and copper-red in fall, a more pronounced color shift than many hakonechloa cultivars offer. Its bold fall display extends the season of interest for this slow, graceful, arching grass well past the typical late-summer peak of most shade perennials. Divide congested clumps in early spring every 4–5 years as growth increases.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; self-sows readily where happy.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost. This species nicotiana has a wiry, airy, well-branched habit distinct from stockier bedding cultivars, carrying masses of small, nodding, bell-shaped chartreuse-green flowers whose mouths reveal a striking ring of sky-blue pollen-bearing anthers. It is a favorite of garden designers for softening bold color combinations and mixing into cut arrangements, where its unusual lime tone reads almost as a foliage accent. It self-sows readily where happy and draws pollinators steadily through the season.

plant_note: Start indoors, surface-sowing the fine seed since it needs light to germinate; transplant after frost danger passes into a spot with room for the tall, airy, branching habit to develop fully.
directions: Start seed indoors, pressing it lightly into the surface of the mix without covering, and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade once frost danger has passed. This tall, gracefully branching flowering tobacco produces hundreds of small, star-shaped blooms that open white or pale pink and darken through rose to deep magenta as they age, giving each plant a cloud of multiple colors at once — the trait behind both its common name and species epithet. Unlike the more compact bedding nicotianas, it blooms freely in daylight rather than mainly at dusk, making it a favorite for cutting gardens and airy, see-through plantings toward the back of a border. It self-sows readily in mild climates and, though grown as an annual, can persist as a short-lived perennial in zone 9 and warmer.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface sow as light aids germination.
directions: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, pressing the fine seed onto the surface since light aids germination. This spicy-scented snapdragon bears dark red blooms that deepen to near-black in fall, with foliage that darkens too. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and set out after hardening off. A bumblebee favorite that makes long-lasting, striking cut flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Night Before Christmas has wide white centers that intensify in light shade — deep shade may cause the white to become somewhat translucent and less vivid.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Night Before Christmas is a medium hosta producing striking foliage with the color pattern reversed from most variegated hostas — a broad, bright white center surrounded by a dark green margin rather than the more common green center with lighter margin. The wide white center areas create exceptional brightness in dark shaded locations, almost appearing luminous in deep shade, making this one of the most effective hostas for illuminating dark corners of the garden. The white portion may show some sun scorch if exposed to afternoon sun, so full shade or dappled light is best. Near-white flowers appear on tall scapes in midsummer. Night Before Christmas is a steady-growing medium cultivar that reaches mature size in 3–4 years and forms a well-mannered clump without the rapid spreading tendencies of some smaller hostas. The bold, unusual reversed variegation makes it a prized addition to the serious hosta collection.

common_name: Night Embers Daylily (Dark Red Velvet Daylily)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or fall; set crowns just 1 in below soil level in full sun to light afternoon shade.
directions: Plant fans with the crown about 1 in deep, spreading roots outward over a small mound of soil in the hole, and water thoroughly after planting. Night Embers bears deep, velvety wine-red flowers with a darker red eye zone and a faint gold edge picking up the light, a rich, smoldering color that gives the cultivar its name, blooming heavily over a long midseason display. Its dark, saturated color reads best against a lighter background — pale gravel, light-colored mulch, or silver-foliaged companions — where the depth of the red is not lost in shadow. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines, and remove spent scapes after all buds open to keep the planting tidy.

common_name: Night Heron Fairy Bells (Black-Stemmed Canton Fairybells)
plant_note: Plant divisions of the clumping rhizome in spring into rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, shaded bed, mulching to protect the crown through winter at the cooler end of its range.
directions: Plant divisions of the clumping rhizome in spring into rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, shaded bed, mulching to protect the crown through winter at the cooler end of its range. Tall, cane-like stems emerge near-black and arch upward, clothed in glossy, dark green, lance-shaped leaves, with small creamy bell-shaped flowers dangling from the leaf axils in spring and dark berries following in fall. The striking near-black stems give this selection a bold, almost bamboo-like presence that stands out among hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than the wild species, so gardeners at the cold end of its range should give it a protected spot and a heavy winter mulch.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in cool weather or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; night phlox opens its flowers only at dusk and in overcast conditions, releasing its extraordinary fragrance — the flowers close tightly during daylight hours. Plant near pathways, seating areas, or bedroom windows to experience the nocturnal fragrance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; night phlox is a remarkable South African native that has evolved a unique relationship with night-flying moth pollinators — the flowers close completely during the day and in bright sunlight (appearing as tight, white-edged, crimson-backed buds), then open at dusk to release one of the most extraordinarily powerful and sweet fragrances of any garden plant. The fragrance has been compared to honey, vanilla, almonds, and chocolate, and a single plant in full bloom can perfume an entire garden on a still evening. The opened flowers reveal five petals, white on the inner (upper) face, deep crimson to maroon on the outer (lower) face, creating a white flower with crimson reverse. A South African Cape native, it performs best in cool seasons and mild climates, blooming through spring and into summer before declining in heat. Plant directly beside a path, a garden bench, or beneath a bedroom window to enjoy the extraordinary nocturnal fragrance — during the day the plant with its closed flowers is unremarkable, but after dusk it transforms the garden into something extraordinary.

common_name: Night Sky Petunia (Deep Purple Starry White-Speckled Petunia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Night Sky's speckled pattern varies from flower to flower and shifts with temperature, showing fewer white flecks in hot weather and a more heavily speckled look in cooler conditions.
directions: Night Sky became an overnight sensation for its deep violet-purple flowers randomly speckled and streaked with white, giving each bloom a starry-night appearance unlike any solid-colored petunia, with no two flowers marked exactly alike. The pattern is temperature-sensitive, appearing with fewer white speckles during hot weather and more pronounced flecking as temperatures cool in spring and fall, adding an extra layer of seasonal variation to an already novel bloom. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and deadhead or shear back by half in midsummer if the mounded, spreading habit becomes leggy, which encourages fresh growth and a renewed flush of the distinctive speckled flowers.

common_name: Night-Blooming Cereus (Queen of the Night, Dutchman's Pipe Cactus)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic cactus or orchid bark mix in bright indirect shade; despite being a cactus, this epiphytic species grows naturally in tropical forest canopies and prefers shade and higher humidity than desert cacti. Allow the cut end to callus 1–2 days before planting.
directions: Root cuttings in well-drained cactus or orchid bark mix in bright indirect shade; night-blooming cereus is one of nature's most theatrical performances — the enormous, pure white, intensely fragrant flowers 10–12 inches across bloom only after dark, open for a single night, and wilt before dawn. The flowers, which appear irregularly in summer and fall, often cause garden 'watching parties' when buds are spotted, as the opening in real-time over a few hours is mesmerizing. Unlike most cacti, this epiphytic cactus from tropical forests grows best in partial shade and moist, well-drained organic soil rather than full sun and dry conditions. The flat, leaf-like stems are unremarkable until they flower. In zone 9a it is an outstanding container plant kept on a shaded porch, brought indoors before frost. The fruit is edible and sweet.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix at 70–80°F in spring and plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9–12 plant container-grown specimens directly into the landscape.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in spring after frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained, moist soil in zone 9–12; night-blooming jasmine is the most powerfully fragrant shrub for warm-climate gardens, releasing an almost overwhelming sweet tropical scent from small, tubular, white-to-yellowish-green flowers that open only after dark and fill the evening air for considerable distances. Flowers appear in clusters multiple times per year in frost-free climates, making it an exceptional plant for near patios, porches, and bedroom windows where the nocturnal fragrance can be enjoyed. Though not a true jasmine (it is in the nightshade family), its fragrance is incomparable; note that the plant is toxic if ingested. Prune lightly after each flowering flush to maintain a tidy, compact shrub form.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; night-scented gladiolus grows in winter and spring (following the Cape winter-rainfall cycle), producing its pale, cream-ivory flowers in late winter and spring with a powerful evening fragrance. Unlike most garden gladioli, this species grows from autumn through spring and goes summer dormant. Native to wet marshes and seeps of the Cape coastal zone; it tolerates seasonally moist to waterlogged conditions better than other gladioli.
directions: Plant corms in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; night-scented gladiolus is one of the most fragrant of all gladiolus species — producing in late winter and spring slender, elegant flower spikes bearing 6–10 pale cream-ivory, creamy-yellow, or very pale greenish-white flowers of delicate, almost translucent quality that in the daytime appear quietly beautiful but subdued, and in the evening fill the surrounding air with an extraordinarily sweet, powerfully rich, vanilla-jasmine-like fragrance that far surpasses any hybrid gladiolus in scent intensity. This powerful evening fragrance — evolved to attract night-flying hawk moths — is the species' defining feature and the reason for both the common name (night-scented) and the species epithet 'tristis' (sad, mournful — referring perhaps to the pale, ghostly flowers that show their best quality only after dark when they become intensely fragrant). Native to the moist coastal seeps and wetland margins of the Western Cape, it is unusual among gladioli in tolerating and even preferring seasonally wet conditions, making it valuable for moist borders and rain garden sites in zones 8–11. A plant to site near a window or garden seating area where the evening fragrance can be fully appreciated.

plant_note: Plant the large, flattened, turnip-like tuber with its top just below the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; night-scented pelargonium follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — growing and flowering in winter and spring, going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer dormancy. This species holds the botanical distinction of being the first pelargonium introduced to European horticulture — brought to Leiden Botanic Garden in 1601.
directions: Plant tuber near the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; night-scented pelargonium holds a unique place in botanical history as the first pelargonium species to reach European gardens — introduced to Leiden Botanic Garden in 1601 from the Cape of Good Hope, marking the beginning of the enormously influential European fascination with South African Pelargonium species that eventually produced the entire zonal and regal geranium garden industry. The plant itself is modest but charming: a stout, flattened, turnip-shaped tuber produces in winter and spring a rosette of finely-divided, almost fern-like, deeply-pinnate, dark green leaves of considerable delicacy, and small clusters of typical pelargonium flowers in dull yellow-brown to purplish-brown — not showy in daylight, which gave rise to the species epithet 'triste' (sad, dull) and the common name 'Sad Geranium'. But in the evening, the flowers emit a powerfully sweet, vanilla-like fragrance that explains why this modest-looking plant attracted such attention from seventeenth-century botanists. It is a nocturnal moth-pollinated species, scentless by day, intensely fragrant after dark. A plant of profound historical and botanical significance and unusual sensory quality.

common_name: Nigra Lily Magnolia (Deep Purple-Red Tulip Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Nigra bears deep purple-red, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact shrub that sporadically reblooms into summer and fall.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Nigra bears narrow, upright, tulip-shaped flowers in the deepest purple-red of any commonly grown lily magnolia cultivar, opening in mid-spring as the leaves begin to emerge and continuing sporadically through summer into fall, an unusual and valuable trait among flowering magnolias. Its compact, shrubby habit tops out smaller than the tree-form magnolias, making it a good fit for foundation plantings or a mixed shrub border. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune lightly after the main spring flush to shape.

common_name: Nikko Blue Hydrangea (Classic Blue Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5 for blue flowers), well-drained soil in partial shade; Nikko Blue flowers blue in acidic soil (pH below 5.5) and pink in alkaline soil (pH above 6.5) — add aluminum sulfate to lower pH and intensify the blue color in Gulf South alkaline soils.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nikko Blue is the most widely grown blue mophead hydrangea cultivar and a classic of the American garden — producing large (8–10 inch), rounded, fully double, sky-blue to cornflower-blue flower heads in early summer from June through August. The iconic blue mophead hydrangea flower is inseparable from the image of the classic American coastal and southern garden, and Nikko Blue has been the most popular blue mophead for decades. The characteristic pH-dependent color change is part of Nikko Blue's management: acidic soil (pH 5.0–5.5) produces the richest true blue; alkaline soil (pH above 6.5) produces pink. In Gulf South alkaline soils, amending with aluminum sulfate (2 lbs per 100 sq ft) and acidifying fertilizers in spring maintains the blue color. Nikko Blue blooms on old wood — meaning the flower buds form in late summer for the following year's bloom. This means the primary rule is: do NOT prune in fall, winter, or spring before bloom; prune only by removing spent flowers immediately after bloom to shape. In zone 9, Nikko Blue is evergreen to semi-evergreen and performs best in morning sun with afternoon protection from the intense Gulf South summer heat.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Nikko deutzia stays low and spreading rather than upright like most deutzia, making it useful as a flowering groundcover or low border shrub.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Nikko deutzia stays low and spreading rather than upright like most deutzia, making it useful as a flowering groundcover or low border shrub. This dwarf, mounding selection of slender deutzia forms a low, wide mat of fine-textured, dark green foliage that turns burgundy-red in fall, smothered in a profusion of small, star-shaped white flowers in mid to late spring. Its low, spreading habit sets it apart from taller deutzia cultivars, making it well suited to a foundation planting, low informal hedge, or the front of a shrub border where a flowering groundcover effect is wanted. It tolerates part shade better than many flowering shrubs while still blooming well, and needs only light pruning after flowering to maintain a tidy shape.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; nimblewill is naturally adapted to shaded conditions and grows in woodland gardens, dry slopes, and disturbed shaded lawns throughout eastern North America.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; nimblewill is a native creeping muhly grass that is one of the more shade-tolerant warm-season grasses of eastern North America, growing at the edges of woodland gardens, on shaded slopes, and in disturbed areas with some shade. The fine-textured, soft green stems root at the nodes and spread to form a low, soft, mat-like ground cover that turns an attractive warm tan-beige in winter. While sometimes treated as a lawn weed, nimblewill is a native grass providing soft ground cover in the dry shade under trees — one of the few warm-season grasses capable of functioning as a lawn alternative in shade. It is the host plant for the Cobweb Skipper butterfly. In winter, the bleached, straw-colored mat persists and actually has decorative winter interest.

plant_note: Sow seed directly where it is to grow in fall, since the long, carrot-like taproot resents transplanting once established; seed needs roughly 60-90 days of natural winter chilling to break dormancy.
directions: Sow seed directly where it is to grow in fall, since the long, carrot-like taproot resents transplanting once established; the seed needs roughly 60-90 days of natural cold-moist winter chilling to break dormancy and sprout the following spring. This is a classic dry-slope wildflower of the interior Pacific Northwest, thriving in gravelly or rocky soils with excellent drainage and almost no summer water. Its finely divided foliage emerges very early in spring and serves as a key larval host for the Anise Swallowtail and, in rockier habitats, the Indra Swallowtail.

plant_note: Plant with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and shade or mulch the root zone while training the vine up a trellis or through a shrub into full sun; light pruning group, so remove only dead or weak stems in late winter.
directions: Bred in Poland by Władysław Noll, Niobe is one of the deepest, most saturated red large-flowered clematis cultivars widely grown, with velvety ruby-red 5 to 6 inch blooms set off by contrasting gold-yellow stamens that darken toward maroon as they age. It flowers heavily on old wood in late spring and early summer, then produces a lighter rebloom on new growth later in the season, so pruning should be light — just tidying and removing weak growth in late winter rather than a hard cutback. Like most clematis, it performs best with its roots kept cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun, a classic pairing achieved by underplanting with low groundcover or mulch.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nippon spirea blooms on old wood — prune immediately after flowering (never in fall or late winter) to avoid removing flower buds for the following year. Deadheading extends the flowering display and maintains a tidy appearance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nippon spirea is a Japanese native and one of the finest white-flowering deciduous shrubs for the temperate garden — a rounded, arching shrub producing small, dark blue-green, oval leaves and in late spring through early summer, an exceptional display in which flat clusters of small, pure-white, button-like flowers cover every branch and arching stem so completely that the shrub appears to be draped in white lace, creating the characteristic mounded, snowdrift effect that earns the cultivar 'Snowmound' its name. The small, dark leaves provide an effective foil for the white flowers, and the contrast of the dark foliage and white bloom gives the plant a particularly fresh, clean appearance. Blue-green foliage color is distinctive throughout summer after bloom. Compact enough for foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders, it performs best with consistent moisture and full sun. Other cultivars include 'Halward's Silver' (lower and more compact) and 'June Bride' (particularly dense flower clusters). Widely used in residential landscaping across the northern United States.

common_name: Nirvana Annual Vinca (Disease-Resistant Compact Vinca Series)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; this series shows good resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight, a serious fungal disease of annual vinca in hot, humid conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; overly wet or poorly drained soil quickly leads to root and stem rot. Nirvana is a compact, uniform annual vinca series bred with strong resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight, a fungal disease that devastates less resistant vinca plantings during hot, humid, rainy summers typical of the Gulf South. It produces abundant, flat-faced flowers in a range of colors over a dense, well-branched mound that tolerates heat, drought, and reflected heat from pavement better than almost any other bedding annual, blooming continuously from late spring through frost with essentially no deadheading required. It is an excellent low-maintenance choice for hot, sunny beds, medians, and containers where many other annuals struggle.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; variegation is best appreciated with some indirect light rather than the deepest shade.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Nishiki is a variegated selection of rohdea (sacred lily, omoto), a Japanese collector's plant with a centuries-long cultivation history, bearing glossy, dark-green, strap-shaped leaves marked with irregular cream-to-yellow striping that gives the clump a jeweled, patterned appearance distinct from the solid-green species. Like the plain species, it tolerates extreme shade and dry, root-filled soil under mature trees that defeats most other evergreen perennials, and inconspicuous spring flowers are followed by bright red berries in fall. Extremely long-lived, drought-tolerant once established, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free; berries are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Niveum epimedium is more compact and slower to spread than most barrenworts, so give it a protected spot where it will not be crowded out.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Niveum epimedium is more compact and slower to spread than most barrenworts, so give it a protected spot where it will not be crowded out. This dainty hybrid barrenwort produces small, heart-shaped leaflets tinged bronze-red on emergence in spring, maturing to soft green, with airy sprays of small, pure white, spurred flowers held just above the foliage on wiry stems. Shear the previous year's tattered leaves to the ground in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge, since old foliage otherwise hides the bloom display. It is an excellent small-scale edger or front-of-border groundcover for dry shade under trees, tolerating root competition and summer drought once established better than most shade perennials.

common_name: Noble Dendrobium (Nobile Orchid, Cane Orchid, Spring Orchid)
plant_note: Grow in a slatted orchid pot or basket with coarse bark media in bright indirect to partial direct light; Dendrobium nobile is one of the more cold-tolerant orchids, surviving temperatures to 40°F if kept dry — its Himalayan origin predisposes it to cool winters. In zone 9, grow on a shaded porch or bright indoor windowsill. CRITICAL for blooming: withhold water almost completely (barely misting monthly) for 6–8 weeks in fall when nights cool to 50–55°F — this cool-dry rest is essential for flower bud development. After rest period, resume normal watering to trigger bud development. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct morning sun — Noble Dendrobium blooms most prolifically in good light with an unobstructed east or shaded south exposure; it will survive but rarely bloom in dim conditions. Dendrobium nobile is a sympodial, cane-forming epiphytic orchid native to the Himalayan foothills of India (Assam, Sikkim, Meghalaya), Nepal, Bhutan, southern China, Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam, growing at elevations of 2,000–5,000 feet in a climate with cool, dry winters and warm, wet summers. The plant produces upright, cane-like pseudobulbs (stems) 12–24 inches tall clothed in leaves that are sometimes deciduous in winter. In late winter and spring, after the essential cool-dry rest period, flower buds emerge from the nodes along the previous year's canes and open to clusters of 3–5 flowers per node, covering the entire length of each cane — in a well-bloomed specimen, dozens of clusters may open simultaneously. The flowers are large (2–3 inches), waxy, fragrant, in shades of white to lavender-purple with a dark purple center in the lip — a classically beautiful orchid flower. Dendrobium nobile is the parent species of the large Dendrobium nobile hybrid orchids widely sold as gift plants in spring, which share the clustered-blooming habit. More cold-tolerant than most popular orchids. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in full sun; noble fir grows naturally at high elevations (2,000–5,500 feet) in the Cascades and Siskiyous, requiring cool, moist, well-drained conditions. Does not tolerate hot, dry, or poorly drained sites.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in full sun; noble fir is the Christmas tree of the Pacific Northwest — the most widely grown Christmas tree in the Pacific Northwest states, valued for its beautiful, stiff branches, perfect conical form, blue-gray needles, and exceptional needle retention after cutting. In the wild it is one of the largest and most impressive native firs, reaching 200+ feet in old-growth Cascade forests. The enormous cylindrical cones — up to 10 inches long — are covered with prominent, downward-pointing bract tips that give them a distinctly bristly appearance and make them the showiest cones of any North American fir. Nobel fir foliage boughs are the primary decorative greenery used throughout the Pacific Northwest holiday season, cut and sold in vast quantities from plantation-grown trees. Widely planted as a specimen ornamental in gardens in zones 4–7.

common_name: Noble Pearl Camellia (Large Coral-Pink Peony-Form Reticulata Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Noble Pearl is a vigorous, upright reticulata camellia with large coral-pink peony-form blooms.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind. Noble Pearl bears large, full peony-form blooms in warm coral-pink on a vigorous, upright shrub with the bold, leathery foliage typical of Camellia reticulata, flowering in mid-to-late winter into spring. Its strong, upright growth habit makes it easier to train as a specimen or espalier than some of the more sprawling reticulata cultivars. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

plant_note: Divide established clumps after flowering or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade; nodding clivia has a more pendulous flower than C. miniata and produces longer, narrower leaves. Like all clivias, it requires a dry winter rest period to trigger reliable spring flowering — reduce watering significantly from late autumn through winter. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; nodding clivia is the first described species in the Clivia genus and is the most pendulous-flowered — producing in spring a drooping umbel of 20–40 tubular-funnel flowers that hang downward more decisively than C. miniata, in shades of orange-red to salmon with yellow-green tips on the outer petal margins, creating a pendant, chandelier-like cluster of nodding tubes. The leaf blades are narrower and longer than C. miniata, with a slightly wavy or recurved texture. It grows naturally in the dense, humid, coastal forests of the Eastern Cape near the sea, an environment very different from the drier, higher-altitude KwaZulu-Natal forests of C. miniata. In cultivation it provides the same outstanding shade tolerance — thriving in the deep, dry shade under large trees — with the somewhat less spectacular but more refined pendant flower form. Like C. miniata, it is evergreen, long-lived, and requires the dry winter rest period to flower. A plant for clivia collectors and those who appreciate the more nuanced, quiet elegance of the drooping flower form over the bold upward-facing clusters of C. miniata.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers or transplants in fall in moist to moderately wet, acidic to neutral, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; nodding ladies' tresses is the most adaptable of all native terrestrial orchids and can succeed in a wider range of conditions than most, including moist meadows and roadsides.
directions: Nodding ladies' tresses is the most common and widely distributed of all North American native orchids — a fall-blooming terrestrial orchid found in moist meadows, roadsides, and open woodland edges across virtually the entire eastern United States, producing delicate spiral-whorled spikes of small, pure white, vanilla-scented flowers that are a surprise and delight when discovered blooming in September and October when orchids are the last thing most people expect to find flowering. Its late-season bloom coincides with the final nectar demand of native bumblebee queens preparing for winter, and the white, fragrant flowers are heavily visited by yellow-and-black native bumblebees that are attracted from considerable distance by the fragrance. Unlike most native terrestrial orchids, nodding ladies' tresses is found in a wide variety of habitats including disturbed sites, roadsides, golf courses, and moist lawns, making it potentially the most accessible native orchid for cultivation — it has established itself from naturally windblown seed in appropriate garden conditions without deliberate planting. A beautiful orchid available from specialist native nurseries that can succeed in average moist garden conditions when other native orchids would fail.

plant_note: Divide rhizome clumps in fall or plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Nodding Mandarin is less common in cultivation than Yellow Mandarin but adapts well to the same moist woodland garden conditions.
directions: Nodding Mandarin is a beautiful native woodland perennial distinguished from its close relative Yellow Mandarin (Disporum lanuginosum) by its larger, pure white, purple-spotted, bell-shaped flowers that dangle conspicuously from arching branch tips in April and May — an unusual and eye-catching display in the spring shade garden. Native to moist, rich, deciduous cove forests and north-facing slopes of the Appalachians from Ohio and Pennsylvania south to Georgia and Alabama, it grows in similar conditions to Solomon's seal and False Solomon's seal, with which it often associates. The red-orange berries that follow in summer attract birds and add late-season interest; the plant slowly spreads by rhizome to form loose, graceful colonies over time. Divide clumps in fall, or plant nursery transplants in spring in deeply amended, consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full shade.

plant_note: Plant fresh rhizomes in late summer or early fall at 2–3 in depth in moist, humus-rich woodland soil; from seed, expect 4–7 years to first bloom as seeds require double dormancy — a warm period followed by cold before germination, then another year before the seedling emerges. Plant divisions are far more practical.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, deep, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in full to partial shade; nodding trillium is distinguished by its white flower that hangs below the leaves on a recurved peduncle, making it easy to overlook in the wild but charming on close inspection. The flower faces downward and is pollinated by bumblebees that must hover or enter from beneath. Plant rhizomes pointed-end up at a depth of 2–3 inches in fall, and mulch with shredded leaves to mimic the natural leaf litter of its woodland floor habitat. Never harvest plants from the wild — all trilliums are extremely slow-growing from seed and wild populations decline quickly when disturbed. Shade and cool, moist conditions are essential throughout the growing season.

common_name: Noel Sutton Sweet Pea (Mid-Blue Fragrant Spencer Sweet Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Noel Sutton is a widely grown mid-blue Spencer-type sweet pea prized as a benchmark for its color class.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Noel Sutton bears large, ruffled, richly fragrant Spencer-type flowers in a true, clear mid-blue considered one of the finest blue sweet peas ever raised, long used as the benchmark against which other blue cultivars are judged by exhibitors and breeders. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows the vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

plant_note: Start tubers indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, or transplant seedlings after hardening off, into rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nonstop Mocca begonia is a compact series bred for reliable, continuous summer bloom in shaded containers and beds.
directions: Start tubers indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, or transplant seedlings after hardening off, into rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nonstop Mocca begonia is a compact series bred for reliable, continuous summer bloom in shaded containers and beds. Large, fully double, rose-like flowers in warm apricot-orange tones are held above deep bronze-black foliage, a striking dark-leaf selection within the popular Nonstop tuberous begonia series bred for compact size and near-continuous bloom from early summer through fall frost.
