The fragrant white flowers are the renowned source of prized tupelo honey, a light-colored, mild-flavored honey with unique fructose chemistry that resists crystallization and commands premium prices at market. Plant in permanently wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this species is intolerant of drought or alkaline conditions and grows best where roots reach permanent water.

plant_note: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep alluvial or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; Oglethorpe oak grows naturally in moist, rich bottomland woods and ravine slopes of a very small native range in Georgia and South Carolina. It is extremely rare in the wild.
directions: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy or alluvial soil in partial shade to full sun; Oglethorpe oak is one of the rarest native oaks in North America, known from only a handful of scattered populations in bottomland and ravine forests of northern Georgia and adjacent South Carolina — the total wild population numbers only a few thousand trees. Taxonomically unusual within oaks, it produces very small, rounded acorns on distinctively long stalks, and the leaves are large, dark green, and deeply lobulate with rounded tips. The species was not scientifically described until 1940, found in a ravine near Oglethorpe County, Georgia. Despite its extreme rarity in the wild, it grows vigorously in cultivation and has proven adaptable to a wider range of conditions than its limited natural distribution suggests. A conservation-worthy ornamental that horticultural planting can help save from extinction. Fast-growing and handsome, with good fall color and excellent form.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–April. Ogon Sweet Flag prefers consistently moist soil and tolerates wet conditions — it grows naturally along stream banks and pond margins. Unlike most ornamental grasses, it thrives in shade and performs poorly in full sun in the South, where heat and sun bleach the golden foliage. Divide every 3–4 years when clumps become crowded. Ogon is excellent in container water gardens, naturalistic pond margins, and as a finely textured edging plant for shaded areas with consistent moisture. The fan-shaped growth pattern is a distinguishing ornamental feature — each clump fans upward from the crown in a flat plane.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Ogon Japanese Sweet Flag thrives in moist, shaded conditions and can grow in shallow water or consistently saturated soil; Ogon is the golden variegated cultivar of Japanese Sweet Flag (Acorus gramineus), producing narrow, strap-like, bright golden-yellow to chartreuse-gold leaves in dense, fan-shaped clumps that grow in a flat plane from the crown — a distinctive, architectural growth form that is unlike any other commonly grown ornamental grass or grass-like plant. The vivid golden-yellow leaf color is exceptionally valuable in the shade garden: the luminous, clean gold provides a strong color accent that brightens dark corners, creates contrast against dark-foliaged companions, and reflects light in a way that makes shaded areas appear more open and bright. Unlike most golden or variegated plants that need sun to maintain their color, Ogon's gold intensity actually improves in shade — the yellow pigmentation is more stable and vivid without the bleaching effect of direct sun. The fine, grass-like texture and modest scale (10–14 inches) make it useful as a textural ground cover, border edging, and pond margin plant in partially shaded locations with adequate moisture.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ogon spiraea holds its bright gold foliage color best in full sun and greens up somewhat in shade.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ogon spiraea holds its bright gold foliage color best in full sun and greens up somewhat in shade. Fine, narrow, willow-like leaves emerge bright golden-yellow in spring and hold good color through summer before turning shades of orange and copper in fall, providing season-long foliage interest on a graceful, arching shrub that is also covered in small white flowers along bare branches in very early spring, ahead of the emerging gold foliage. Its combination of early spring bloom and vivid, long-lasting golden foliage makes it a valuable multi-season color accent for a mixed shrub border, standing out clearly against green-leaved companions from spring through fall. Prune lightly after flowering to shape, and provide full sun for the brightest, most sustained gold foliage color through the growing season.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in fall while soils are still warm to allow root establishment before winter; if transplanting seed, sow fresh nuts immediately after collection in fall as they lose viability rapidly when dried.
directions: Plant in moist, deep, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ohio buckeye is the state tree of Ohio and a striking native specimen tree with large, palmately compound leaves that emerge very early in spring and put on a vivid orange-red fall color display — often the first tree to color and drop leaves in autumn. Upright panicles of yellow-green flowers appear in April and May, attracting early-emerging pollinators, and ripen into the distinctive spiny husks that split to reveal the rich brown nuts that give the tree its name. All parts of the plant — bark, leaves, and especially the nuts — are toxic to humans, livestock, and dogs and should not be planted where children or grazing animals have access. Provide consistent moisture, especially during establishment, as it is poorly adapted to drought and will drop leaves early under heat stress.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for winter cold-moist stratification, or plant divisions/container stock in spring; Ohio goldenrod is a calciphile that grows best in consistently moist, mineral-rich fen and wet prairie soils.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, calcareous soil in full sun. Ohio goldenrod is a regional specialty of Great Lakes-area prairie fens, calcareous wet meadows, and interdunal wetlands, where it grows alongside other fen specialists such as Riddell's goldenrod and grass-of-Parnassus. It is distinguished by smooth, glossy, mostly basal leaves and flat-topped, corymb-like clusters of bright yellow flowers held above the foliage on unbranched stems from late summer into fall. Like other late-blooming goldenrods it is an important nectar and pollen source for native bees and migrating monarch butterflies at a time when few other wildflowers remain in bloom, and its heavy, insect-transported pollen does not cause hay fever (that is the wind-borne pollen of ragweed, which blooms at the same time). Because it depends on steady soil moisture and calcium-rich conditions in the wild, it performs best in rain gardens, pond edges, and naturally wet low spots rather than average well-drained garden soil, and it is a good conservation-value choice for restoring regional fen and wet prairie plant communities.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Ohio spiderwort spreads by self-sowing and forms expanding clumps — divide every 2–3 years in spring to control spread and rejuvenate vigor.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Ohio spiderwort is adaptable and drought-tolerant once established, performing well in dry to average soils and tolerating clay — rich, fertile soils encourage excessive flopping. Tradescantia ohiensis is a native prairie and woodland-edge perennial of the central and eastern United States producing upright, glaucous, blue-green stems bearing long, strap-like leaves and terminal clusters of bright blue-violet, three-petaled flowers from April through June; each individual flower lasts only a single morning, opening at dawn and wilting by noon, but the plant produces a long succession of blooms over several weeks. It is a significant early-season pollen source for native bumblebees, mason bees, and specialist Tradescantia-foraging sweat bees; the flowers are visited almost exclusively in the morning hours when they are open. Ohio spiderwort goes summer-dormant in hot, dry weather, cutting back naturally in July — this is normal; plant it among later-emerging perennials to fill the gap, and it will re-emerge and often rebloom in the cool of early fall.

common_name: Okame Cast Iron Plant (Broad White-Striped Aspidistra)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade. Okame is a classic Japanese cast iron plant selection with broad, bold, creamy-white longitudinal stripes running the length of each leathery, strap-shaped leaf, a strong, high-contrast variegation pattern that brightens the darkest corners of a shade garden. Like the species, it tolerates extraordinary neglect — drought, poor light, root competition from trees, and long stretches without care — making it a cornerstone of low-maintenance Gulf South shade gardening under live oaks and other dense-canopy trees. It is slow-growing, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free once established; division is rarely needed except to propagate new plants.

common_name: Okame Flowering Cherry (Early Bright-Pink Heat-Tolerant Cherry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Okame is among the most heat- and humidity-tolerant flowering cherries, making it a more reliable choice than many ornamental cherry cultivars for the Gulf South.
directions: Okame is a hybrid flowering cherry bred from Taiwan cherry and Fuji cherry, prized for opening its single, vivid carmine-pink flowers earlier in spring than most other ornamental cherries and for tolerating heat and humidity noticeably better than Yoshino or Kwanzan, a real advantage in the Gulf South where many flowering cherries struggle and decline. Its smaller, more upright-vase-shaped habit fits a modest yard, and reddish-orange fall foliage color extends the season of interest beyond the early spring bloom. Give it moist, well-drained soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to limit disease entry through large wounds, and expect a shorter lifespan than longer-lived shade trees, typical of the flowering cherry group.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Oklahoma redbud is particularly well-adapted to alkaline limestone soils of the Edwards Plateau and to the heavy clay soils of the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Oklahoma redbud is a Texas-native botanical variety of eastern redbud that is substantially more heat- and drought-tolerant than the standard eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis), making it the superior choice for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where summer heat and drought stress often cause the standard species to decline. The cultivar 'Oklahoma' was selected for exceptional dark rose-magenta to rosy-purple flower color — deeper and more saturated than the typical light pink-lavender of species redbud — and for glossy, leathery, rich dark-green leaves that are waxy-looking and more heat-resistant than the soft, matte leaves of the standard species. The flower display appears on bare branches in February–March in zone 9 and is spectacular — the vivid magenta-rose flowers cover the branches in dense clusters before the leaves emerge. The glossy-leaved foliage provides excellent summer interest and greater resistance to summer leaf drop than standard eastern redbud. Oklahoma redbud is smaller and more compact than the eastern species, reaching 12–20 feet tall and wide, making it appropriate for smaller residential landscapes. Superior drought tolerance, heat resistance, and adaptability to alkaline and clay soils make Oklahoma redbud one of the finest ornamental trees for zone 9.

plant_note: Direct sow in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; Oklahoma is a compact scabiosa-flowered zinnia series with smaller, double blooms produced in great abundance.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil. The Oklahoma series produces smaller, fully double, scabiosa-form blooms — with a raised, cushion-like center of tightly packed petals — across a full range of colors, in far greater numbers per plant than large-flowered zinnia types, making it a favorite for cutting gardens where volume of stems matters as much as individual flower size. Thin plants for good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew in humid conditions, and deadhead regularly to keep the prolific bloom going from planting through frost.

common_name: Old Blush Rose (Parson's Pink China, One of the Oldest Cultivated Roses)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Old Blush is one of the original four China roses introduced to Europe in the 1750s-1790s and is credited with bringing repeat bloom into modern rose breeding.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Old Blush is one of the four founding China roses brought to Europe in the late 1700s and is historically significant as one of the first roses to introduce genuine repeat bloom to Western rose breeding, which until then relied on once-blooming European roses. It produces semi-double, silvery-pink flowers that deepen in color with age and heat, blooming in flushes nearly continuously through the growing season, and remains a tough, easygoing garden rose with excellent heat tolerance and good resistance to black spot. Grown for over two centuries across the Gulf South, it needs little more than an occasional shaping prune and is a good choice for gardeners who want an authentic heirloom with real historical rose-breeding significance.

common_name: Old Coral Louisiana Iris (Historic Coral-Toned Breeding Parent Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Old Coral, bred in 1949 by Louisiana iris pioneer Caroline Dormon, bears coral-toned flowers and was an important early breeding parent for the class.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Old Coral, bred in 1949 by influential Louisiana naturalist and iris pioneer Caroline Dormon, bears warm coral-toned flowers and holds historic importance as an early breeding parent whose genetics influenced many later Louisiana iris introductions. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: Old Faithful Itoh Peony (Deep Red Intersectional Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Old Faithful bears large, semi-double to double flowers in a deep, rich red, one of the darkest colors available among Itoh hybrids, held on strong, woody-based stems that support the heavy blooms without staking or flopping. Its glossy, deeply cut foliage stays clean and disease-resistant through summer well after bloom finishes, giving good structure to the border for the rest of the growing season. Like other intersectional hybrids it combines tree peony flower form and color range with the cold-hardy, die-back-to-the-ground habit of herbaceous peonies, tolerating more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight Paeonia lactiflora cultivars. Divide only when absolutely necessary, since Itoh peonies resent disturbance and can take a couple of seasons to rebloom fully after moving.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; Old Lady Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; Old Lady Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil. A rounded, clustering cactus densely covered in long, fine, white hairs that give it a soft, shaggy, almost fur-covered appearance among sharp little spines, it produces a ring of small, bright pink to magenta flowers around the crown in spring, a cheerful contrast to its snowy-white body. Native to central Mexico, it is a popular, easy-care species for a sunny windowsill or outdoor xeriscape container, clustering readily with age into an attractive mounded colony of multiple heads. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright direct light for the fullest hair coverage, and protect from frost and prolonged cold, damp conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; Old Man Banksia is a slow-growing large shrub to small tree requiring many years to reach mature size and first flower. Like all Proteaceae, it requires excellent drainage and absolutely no phosphorus fertilizer. It is fire-adapted — the large, persistent woody cones (follicles) open to release seeds after fire. In the garden it grows more slowly without fire; the seed cones can be individually heated to release seeds. Famous in Australia as the model for 'Big Bad Banksia Men' in May Gibbs's classic Gumnut Babies stories.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; Old Man Banksia is Australia's most culturally iconic banksia — famous both as a botanical landmark and as the model for the 'Big Bad Banksia Men' in May Gibbs's classic 1918 Australian children's book series 'Gumnut Babies', where the gnarled, leathery, toothy-faced spent flower cones with their hairy, follicle-covered surface became the memorable villains of Australian childhood imagination. As a living plant it is one of the most ancient-looking trees in the Australian flora — a large, rugged, slow-growing shrub to small tree with deeply fissured, rough gray bark, thick, leathery, saw-toothed (serrata) leaves with pale undersides, and in summer through autumn, large, cylindrical, cream-yellow to pale-gold flower spikes 6–8 inches long composed of thousands of individual small, densely packed flowers — the whole structure eventually developing into the large, woody, hairy-textured, persistent seed cone that inspired the 'Banksia Man' appearance. The flower spikes are excellent nectar sources for honeyeating birds, bees, and in cultivation, hummingbirds. A very long-lived tree where conditions are suitable, eventually forming gnarled, large specimens of great character.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Pacific Northwest native sedum tolerates cooler, moister conditions than many drought-adapted sedum species.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Pacific Northwest native sedum tolerates cooler, moister conditions than many drought-adapted sedum species. Small, rounded, opposite-paired, jelly-bean-like leaves in bright green often blush red at the tips in bright light, forming a low, spreading mat on rocky outcrops and cliffs from the Cascades to coastal bluffs of the Pacific Northwest, topped with small star-shaped yellow flowers in summer. Adapted to a cooler, wetter climate than many popular garden sedums bred from Mediterranean or Mexican species, it is a good native groundcover choice for a Pacific Northwest rock garden or dry border where more heat-loving sedums may struggle with the cooler summers. Water occasionally, particularly during establishment, and divide congested mats to propagate or control spread.

common_name: Old Mexico Zinnia (AAS-Winning Mahogany-Red Double Tipped Gold)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Old Mexico, a 1962 All-America Selections winner and RHS Award of Garden Merit holder, bears mahogany-red double and semi-double flowers tipped gold on a compact 12-18 inch mound.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 8-12 inches. Old Mexico, a 1962 All-America Selections winner holding a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, bears rich mahogany-red, double and semi-double flowers with each petal tipped in gold, a warm, richly textured bicolor pattern on a compact, well-branched mound. Its dense, prolific flowering and manageable size have kept it a garden favorite for over sixty years. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into dry, lean soil; plants spend the first year as a basal rosette and flower in their second year.
directions: Old Plainsman is a tall, strikingly elegant native biennial or short-lived perennial found on dry, open prairies, mesquite grasslands, and roadsides primarily in Texas and adjacent south-central states. In its first year it produces an aromatic, white-woolly basal rosette of deeply dissected, fern-like foliage; in its second year it erects much-branched stems to 5 feet tall, topped with flat, dense clusters of small creamy-white to yellowish composite flowers from May through July that are highly attractive to native bees and small butterflies. Grow in dry, calcareous or sandy, well-drained, lean soil in full sun — it will not tolerate heavy, wet, or highly fertile soils. Allow plants to self-sow to maintain a continuing colony; the airy, open texture and tall stature make it an outstanding component of Texas Hill Country and western prairie native gardens.

common_name: Old Spice Sweet Pea (Antique Highly Fragrant Mixed Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for a late winter to spring bloom; provide a trellis for the twining tendrils to climb.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the vines to climb. Old Spice is a mixed strain of antique, small-flowered sweet peas assembled from pre-1900 grandiflora-type cultivars and selected specifically to preserve the intense, old-fashioned sweet pea fragrance that later, larger-flowered modern hybrids gradually lost in breeding for bigger blooms. The mix produces flowers across the full classic sweet pea color range — pinks, purples, reds, whites, and bicolors — on vigorous climbing vines that bloom over a long cool-season window. Pick frequently for bouquets, since cutting flowers before they set seed is the single most effective way to extend a sweet pea vine's overall bloom period, and enjoy the fragrance indoors, which is often strongest in the cool of morning.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; almost always propagated by cuttings since seed germination is slow and unreliable.
directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — site it away from areas where livestock, pets, or small children graze on foliage, and never burn the trimmings, since the smoke carries toxic compounds. Root cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; oleander shrugs off heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil, which is why it lines highway medians and beachfront properties across the Gulf Coast and Southern California. Clusters of single or double flowers in white, pink, red, salmon, or yellow appear almost continuously from late spring through fall on new wood, so prune lightly right after a bloom flush rather than in late winter. Cold snaps below the high teens can kill it to the ground in zone 8, but established plants typically resprout vigorously from the root crown.

common_name: Olive Bailey Langdon Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Wide Gold Margin)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; the gold margin on Olive Bailey Langdon develops best with some morning sun.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, with some gentle morning sun helping to develop the fullest gold margin color. Olive Bailey Langdon bears large, heavily corrugated, blue-green leaves edged in a broad, bright gold-yellow margin, a bold two-tone combination that holds up well through the season and stands out strongly against plain green shade companions, with pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer. Its substantial size and strong variegation make it a good specimen plant in a mixed shade border. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on the tender new growth in spring, and divide congested clumps only after several years, since hostas generally resent frequent disturbance.

common_name: Olivia Rose Austin (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring or fall in soil enriched with compost; Olivia Rose Austin was named for the breeder's granddaughter and combines strong disease resistance with an exceptionally long repeat-flowering season.
directions: Set plants in full sun with at least six hours of direct light and rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply and regularly during the first year to establish a strong root system. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to keep flushes of bloom coming. Olivia Rose Austin was bred by David Austin and named for his granddaughter, and it has become one of the most widely planted English roses for combining soft, cupped, blush-pink double blooms with a fruity fragrance and notably strong disease resistance compared to many older English rose cultivars, holding clean foliage through humid summers better than most. Its compact, bushy, well-branched habit makes it useful for smaller borders and mixed plantings where a full-sized shrub rose would be too large, and it repeats reliably from late spring through frost with regular deadheading.

common_name: Olympic Fire Mountain Laurel (Red-Budded Mountain Laurel)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun, which stresses mountain laurel in hot climates.
directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Olympic Fire is a mountain laurel selection prized for exceptionally deep, wine-red buds that open to lighter pink flowers, giving a stronger two-tone contrast than the species' typical pink-and-white banding. It shares the species' gnarled, sculptural habit and evergreen foliage, making it a strong specimen or woodland-border shrub. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in fall for spring germination, or in early spring; Olympic mullein is a biennial that forms a large, felted rosette in year one and sends up a spectacular candelabra-branched flower stem in year two. It self-sows abundantly in dry, sunny, gravelly conditions to maintain a permanent colony. Distinct from the silver mullein (V. bombyciferum) in its more dramatically branched candelabra form and slightly less intensely silver foliage.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Olympic mullein is the most dramatically architectural of the large biennials, native to rocky, dry, mountainous regions of Greece and the Balkans. In its first year it forms a large, flat, broadly spreading rosette of large, soft, gray-white woolly leaves. In its second year it sends up a stout, multi-branched, candelabra-like flower stem reaching 6-8 feet, with numerous spreading side branches each densely packed with bright-yellow flowers that open progressively from the bottom upward over many weeks. The overall effect — a massive, symmetrical candelabra of yellow flowers on a central architectural column — is unlike anything else in the biennial or perennial garden and creates a focal point of extraordinary structural impact. Unlike common mullein (Verbascum thapsus), the Olympic mullein produces a genuinely branched, multi-stemmed candelabra rather than a single spike. It self-sows freely in dry, gravelly conditions to create a self-perpetuating colony.

plant_note: Move small clumps with generous surrounding native soil into cool, moist, acidic humus in deep conifer shade, taking care not to break up the fine root system that ties this plant to its fungal partners.
directions: Move small clumps with generous surrounding native soil into cool, moist, acidic humus in deep conifer shade, taking care not to break up the fine root system that ties this plant to its fungal partners. Each slender stem bears a single loose rosette of small rounded leaves and lifts one nodding, waxy-white, sweetly fragrant flower with a prominent green style in early to midsummer. It is among the most difficult native wildflowers to establish outside its natural forest floor, so gardeners are best served by protecting existing colonies rather than attempting to relocate them into cultivated beds. Where it does persist, its solitary, jewel-like blossom makes it one of the most charming finds on a shaded woodland walk.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural cold stratification or plant container-grown specimens in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; one-seed juniper is among the most drought-tolerant and cold-hardy junipers of the Southwest, growing naturally on dry mesas and rocky slopes from 3,500–7,000 feet elevation.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; one-seed juniper is the most abundant and widespread tree of the Colorado Plateau and central New Mexico highlands, forming the characteristic juniper-piñon woodland that covers millions of acres of the Southwest at mid-elevations. The name comes from the berry-like cones, each containing only one seed (rather than the 2–3 of most junipers). A characteristically multi-trunked, dense, irregularly shaped tree with scaly, gray-green foliage and shredding reddish-brown bark. Often grows as a twisted, gnarled form in exposed, rocky, windswept sites. Extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived — ancient trees 300–500 years old are common. The 'berries' are important food for many birds including bluebirds and robins. The wood is used for fence posts and fuel; the shredded bark was used by Indigenous peoples for basket-making and insulation. An excellent low-maintenance xeriscape tree for hot, dry, rocky sites in the Southwest.

common_name: Only the Lonely Nicotiana (Giant Fragrant Woodland Tobacco)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; site where its evening perfume reaches a patio, porch, or open window.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost. This dramatic architectural annual forms a basal rosette of huge paddle-shaped leaves before sending up tall, sturdy spikes topped with clusters of long, pendant, trumpet-shaped white flowers. The blooms release an intense jasmine-like fragrance that carries widely at night, making it one of the most powerfully scented garden annuals available from seed. Its height and bold foliage make it an effective specimen or back-of-border plant, and it self-sows in milder climates once established.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Onondaga is a Sargent viburnum selection with maroon-tinted new foliage and pink-tinted lacecap flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Onondaga emerges with striking maroon-purple new growth that matures to green with a maroon overlay, and bears flat lacecap flower clusters of white fertile florets rimmed by showy pink-tinted sterile florets, followed by red fruit that ripens to black. Its dramatic, multi-season foliage color sets it apart from most green-leaved viburnum species, making it a strong focal shrub in a mixed border. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Onyx Odyssey Hellebore (Winter Jewels Series Near-Black Lenten Rose)
plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Onyx Odyssey is part of the Winter Jewels breeding series and produces some of the darkest, near-black flowers available in hellebores, blooming in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist while the plant establishes. Onyx Odyssey is part of the acclaimed Winter Jewels hellebore breeding series and stands out for flowers in an unusually deep, glossy near-black purple, one of the darkest colors available among Lenten roses, held above leathery, evergreen, deeply divided foliage. Like other Lenten roses it blooms very early, often through late-season snow or hard frost, providing color in the shade garden when almost nothing else is flowering. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to showcase the flowers, and note that all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where pets or children graze.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; tolerates light frost.
directions: Direct sow in early spring, covering seed as darkness aids germination; calendula prefers cool weather and tolerates light frost. This compact variety bears single and double blooms in orange, cream, and yellow tipped with fiery orange. Deadhead often to keep the profusion of blooms going, and pair with blue or purple annuals in containers. The petals are edible and attractive in salads.

plant_note: Set divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall or early spring, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool through summer.
directions: Set divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall or early spring, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool through summer. Opal is prized for its unusually soft, pale ice-blue flowers, a subtler and cooler tone than the typical pink-to-blue pulmonaria palette, held above lightly spotted, softly hairy green leaves in earliest spring. It provides one of the season's first nectar sources for emerging bumblebees and pairs elegantly with hellebores and early daffodils. Shear off tattered summer foliage to encourage a fresh, cleaner-looking flush of leaves for the rest of the season.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; resents transplanting.
directions: Sow seed directly where plants will grow in early spring or fall, since the taproot dislikes transplanting. This heirloom, the state flower of California, produces golden-orange flowers that open in sun and close at night. Drought tolerant and low-maintenance, it attracts pollinators and self-sows freely for naturalized hillsides of color. Grow in full sun and lean, well-drained soil.

common_name: Orange Clock Vine (Brilliant Pure-Orange Continuous-Blooming Tropical Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants or transplants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Orange Clock Vine is a vigorous, fast-growing vine — provide a trellis, fence, or support structure at planting; the vine covers a 6–8 foot fence section in a single warm season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Orange Clock Vine (Thunbergia gregorii) is an African climbing vine producing one of the most brilliantly pure-orange flower displays available in a commonly grown ornamental vine — the 1.5-inch, five-petaled, open-faced flowers are a vivid, saturated orange-to-apricot-orange with no dark center (the 'clock' of the common name refers to the open flower face), blooming in continuous succession from summer through frost. The pure, clean orange color without dark center markings or contrasting color zones creates a uniformly vivid orange effect that is quite different from Black-eyed Susan Vine (T. alata), which has a dark eye, or clock vines with throats of different colors. The fast-growing, twining stems cover trellises, fences, and arbors quickly — an established plant can produce a solid curtain of orange flowers across a 6–8 foot fence section. In zone 9, Orange Clock Vine grows as a warm-season perennial vine that may be killed by hard freezes but returns from the roots in protected positions with mulching; in zone 10-12, it grows as an evergreen perennial vine that blooms most of the year. The pure orange color makes it outstanding in tropical designs combining orange, yellow, and red — particularly effective with yellow allamanda, red mandevilla, and golden angel's trumpet for a warm tropical palette.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring; seed requires cold stratification but the cultivar 'Goldsturm' comes true from seed with stratification.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Rudbeckia fulgida is the perennial species behind the famous 'Goldsturm' cultivar that revolutionized native plant gardening in the 1980s. Unlike the biennial R. hirta (common black-eyed Susan), this species returns reliably from the crown each year and spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form impressive colonies. The bright orange-yellow flowers with dark brown centers bloom from July through September and attract finches to the persistent seed heads all winter. Divide every 4 years in spring to maintain vigor; plants in rich, moist soil may need staking but grow more compact in lean conditions.

common_name: Orange Daylily (Tawny Daylily, Tiger Daylily, Ditch Lily)
plant_note: Plant divisions (fans) in spring or fall in full sun to partial shade; Orange Daylily adapts to a wide range of soils but blooms most profusely in full sun. It spreads vigorously by stolons and fleshy roots and can become invasive in ideal conditions — mow or divide regularly to control spread. In zone 9, it blooms May–June; in hot summers the foliage goes semi-dormant. Division every 3–5 years maintains vigor. The species form is triploid and produces no viable seed; it spreads only vegetatively.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in almost any well-drained soil; Orange Daylily is among the most adaptable and indestructible of all garden perennials, tolerating clay, sand, drought, and competition from tree roots while spreading steadily by stolons. Hemerocallis fulva is native to Asia and has been cultivated in gardens for over two thousand years, spreading throughout Europe and North America so thoroughly that it is now naturalized along roadsides, railroad embankments, and woodland edges across most of the continent. The large, bright orange, lily-like flowers — each bloom lasting just one day (hence 'day lily') but produced in succession over 3–4 weeks — bloom in May–June in zone 9. The plant has naturalized so widely in North America because it is triploid and cannot produce viable seed; all spread is vegetative, but each original planting can slowly colonize a large area. Despite its commonness, the orange daylily remains a beautiful garden plant — the species form provides a reliable, bold orange bloom in late spring when few other perennials are at peak. The tender young shoots and flower buds are edible and used as a vegetable in Chinese cuisine (golden needles or 'gum jum'). Young daylily buds are also used in moo shu pork and hot-and-sour soup.

common_name: Orange Form Aechmea (Blanchetiana Bromeliad, Amber Star Bromeliad)
plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) or container-grown stock in spring once nights stay above 50°F; Aechmea blanchetiana is hardy outdoors year-round only in zone 9b-11 and needs container culture with winter protection farther north. Foliage color is most intense in bright light and fades to plain green in deep shade.
directions: Plant in fast-draining soil or a coarse bark-and-perlite mix in bright, filtered light to partial sun — full sun brings out the most intense foliage color, while deeper shade keeps leaves plain green and softer in texture. Aechmea blanchetiana is a large, clumping, terrestrial bromeliad native to the coastal restinga scrub of eastern Brazil, forming bold rosettes of broad, stiff, strap-shaped leaves that flush brilliant orange to red-orange in strong light, an effect widely used as a dramatic color accent in South Florida and Gulf Coast landscapes. In late winter to spring, a mature rosette sends up a tall, branched flower spike with small yellow flowers held above showy orange-red bracts, after which the rosette slowly declines while offsets ('pups') fill in around it to keep the clump going indefinitely. Keep the central cup filled with water where practical, water sparingly at the roots, and protect plants from temperatures below the upper 20s°F, since foliage is damaged by frost and the plant is killed outright by a hard freeze.

common_name: Orange Globe Amaranth (Strawberry Fields Gomphrena, Haage's Globe Amaranth)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm, or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for earlier bloom; Gomphrena haageana is a distinct species from the commonly grown G. globosa (globe amaranth), producing vivid orange-red to scarlet clover-like button heads on taller, more branching plants — the parent species of the popular 'Strawberry Fields' variety (though 'Strawberry Fields' is actually a hybrid between G. haageana and G. globosa).
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep after last frost in full sun; orange globe amaranth is extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, thriving in the summer heat that wilts most other annuals; excellent for cut flowers, dried flowers, and pollinator gardens; the button-like heads dry beautifully on the stem and retain their orange-red color for months. Orange globe amaranth is a warm-season annual native to Mexico and the southwestern United States, closely related to the commonly grown purple or pink globe amaranth (Gomphrena globosa) but producing flowers in vivid orange-red to scarlet rather than the lavender-purple typical of G. globosa. The most important commercial variety derived from this species is 'Strawberry Fields' — actually a hybrid between G. haageana and G. globosa that combines the intense orange-red color of haageana with some characteristics of globosa — which became popular after its introduction in the 1990s. However, open-pollinated G. haageana selections produce flowers in a range of warm tones from bright orange to deep brick-red that are distinct from the Strawberry Fields hybrid and equally attractive. Like all globe amaranths, the 'flowers' are actually colorful papery bracts (modified leaves) surrounding a tiny true flower — the papery texture is what gives globe amaranths their everlasting quality. Orange globe amaranth thrives under conditions that challenge most summer annuals: heat above 90°F, droughty soil, and humidity that causes other flowers to rot — making it particularly valuable in the hot, humid summer climates of zone 9a and the Gulf South.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or plant container-grown stock in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; orange hummingbird mint is native to dry, rocky desert grasslands and demands perfect drainage and low soil fertility to thrive.
directions: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or plant container-grown stock in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; orange hummingbird mint is native to dry, rocky desert grasslands and demands perfect drainage and low soil fertility to thrive. Agastache aurantiaca is a compact, drought-tolerant Southwestern native with aromatic, mint-scented foliage and dense spikes of brilliant orange to orange-red to bicolor (orange and yellow) tubular flowers from midsummer through late fall that are outstanding for ruby-throated and black-chinned hummingbirds; it is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant agastaches and is an essential plant for xeriscape and hummingbird gardens in zones 6–10. The cultivar 'Apricot Sunrise' (with apricot-orange flowers) and 'Tango' (deep orange) are the most widely grown selections; plants are often short-lived but self-seed freely in well-drained soil.

common_name: Orange Jessamine (Mock Orange, Chalcas, China Box)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after last frost; in zone 9 plant February–April for the longest establishment period before summer heat. Orange Jessamine tolerates light freezes (28–32°F) but will be damaged by temperatures below 28°F — in zone 9a plant in a sheltered south-facing location or near a heat-retaining wall for best winter survival. It blooms multiple times per year in zone 9-10 when temperatures are warm.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Orange Jessamine is one of the most intensely fragrant shrubs available for zone 9 Gulf Coast and Florida gardens, producing multiple flushes of tiny, pure-white, star-shaped flowers throughout the warm months — the fragrance has been described as a combination of orange blossom and jasmine and is one of the strongest and most intoxicating scents in the subtropical plant world. Murraya paniculata is closely related to citrus (family Rutaceae) and is native from South Asia through southern China and into Malaysia; it has been naturalized in South Florida where it occasionally escapes into natural areas. The glossy, dark-green, aromatic foliage is attractive year-round; after the white flowers fade, small oval berries ripen from green to orange-red, adding additional ornamental interest. In zone 9, Orange Jessamine is an excellent fragrant hedge, privacy screen, or specimen shrub reaching 8–15 feet; it can also be maintained as a small tree with lower branch removal. It tolerates light shade well and performs admirably as a foundation shrub under building overhangs or in bright indirect light. Prune immediately after flowering to control size; the plant flowers on new wood. NOTE: Murraya paniculata is a host plant for citrus greening disease (Huanglongbing) and its import is restricted in some states — check local regulations before purchasing.

common_name: Orange King Bougainvillea (Warm Copper-Orange Bougainvillea Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Orange King blooms most prolifically under slight water stress — allow the soil to dry somewhat between waterings and limit nitrogen fertilizer to promote flowering over vegetative growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Orange King is a bougainvillea cultivar producing bracts in warm copper-orange to apricot-orange tones — a distinctly different color character from the hot pinks and magentas of Barbara Karst or the scarlet-red of San Diego Red, offering instead a warmer, earthier color tone that reads more tropical and less vivid in the landscape. The orange-copper bracts combine particularly well with terracotta container materials, yellow walls, and companion plants in warm orange, yellow, and bronze tones. Orange King blooms in the same seasonal pattern as other bougainvillea cultivars in zone 9 — most heavily in spring and fall as temperatures moderate, with reduced bloom during peak summer heat and winter cold. The bract color in Orange King tends to fade to salmon-pink and peachy tones as the bracts age on the plant, creating a natural color progression from rich copper-orange at peak freshness to faded salmon-apricot as the bloom matures — a pleasing multi-tone effect during extended bloom periods. The growth rate and vigor are typical of bougainvillea: rapid once established in zone 9 conditions, capable of covering substantial wall or fence areas. The copper-orange color has become popular in Spanish Colonial, Mediterranean, and Southwestern landscape styles where the warm tones harmonize with stucco walls and warm architectural palettes.

common_name: Orange Marmalade Celosia (Vivid Compact Wheat-Type Celosia)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost risk passes; celosia thrives in heat and grows fastest during the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Orange Marmalade is a wheat-type celosia bred for a compact, well-branched habit and abundant slender, plumed flower spikes in a vivid, warm orange, a bright, uniform color that reads well both in the garden and in cut arrangements. Unlike the large single crested heads of cockscomb-type celosia, the wheat-type spikes are smaller and more numerous, giving a fuller, airier look to plantings and bouquets alike, and the plant blooms continuously through the heat of summer with minimal deadheading needed. Harvest stems for fresh or dried arrangements once spikes are fully colored, since the sturdy, long-lasting flowers hold their shape and color exceptionally well when air-dried.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Crossandra is a tropical perennial that grows as a tender perennial or treated as an annual in zone 9 — established plants may survive mild winters in sheltered, well-mulched locations but should be considered annual in exposed sites. Crossandra tolerates and actually prefers partial shade to deep shade in zone 9's summer, where full sun exposure combined with summer heat can stress the plant and reduce flower quality. The salmon-orange fan-shaped flower clusters are produced continuously from late spring through fall without deadheading. Excellent performance in humid, hot conditions makes Crossandra one of the most reliable partial-shade flowering plants for Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun (morning sun, afternoon shade preferred) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil — Crossandra thrives in warm, humid, partially shaded conditions that mimic its native South Asian forest understory habitat; Orange Marmalade is an improved cultivar of Crossandra (Crossandra infundibuliformis), a compact tropical perennial producing fan-shaped clusters of overlapping, distinctively asymmetrical salmon-orange to coral flowers on short spikes above glossy, dark green, undulating leaves. The flower shape is unusual and attractive — the individual flowers have five rounded petals arranged in a slightly asymmetrical fan, a characteristic flower structure of the Crossandra genus that creates a layered, tiered appearance on the flower spikes. Crossandra's most valuable landscape quality is its continuous production of attractive blooms through the heat, humidity, and partial shade of zone 9 summers — conditions that limit or stop flowering in many ornamental annuals and tender perennials. While impatiens are the default shade annual for many Gulf South gardeners, Crossandra handles the heat-humidity combination of summer significantly better than most Impatiens walleriana varieties, making it the more reliable summer shade bloomer when temperatures remain in the 90s for weeks at a time.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; protect from afternoon sun in zone 8–9 to keep the gold leaf center from bleaching or scorching.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Orange Marmalade produces broadly heart-shaped leaves with a bright gold to chartreuse center that deepens toward orange-gold tones as the season progresses, set off by a narrow, irregular dark green margin. It forms a tidy, mounded clump of medium size, making it useful as a specimen or grouped along a shaded bed edge where its warm coloring stands out against the more common blue and green hosta tones. Pale lavender flowers rise on scapes above the foliage in mid to late summer. Divide congested clumps in early spring as new growth emerges, and mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool through hot Gulf South summers.

plant_note: Sow seed in fall onto the surface of moist, acidic, low-nutrient sandy or peaty soil so winter cold can break dormancy, mimicking the bogs, seepage slopes, and wet pine savannas where it grows wild.
directions: Sow seed in fall onto the surface of moist, acidic, low-nutrient sandy or peaty soil so winter cold can break dormancy, mimicking the bogs, seepage slopes, and wet pine savannas where it grows wild. The flame-orange, densely packed flower spikes are unmistakable and bloom over a long season from late spring through fall, drawing bumblebees, small native bees, and butterflies looking for nectar in low-fertility wetland habitats. It performs poorly in rich or fertilized garden soil and is best suited to a dedicated bog garden, rain garden, or restored savanna planting kept consistently damp. Established plants may act as short-lived perennials, reseeding themselves modestly if conditions stay favorably wet and open.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Orange River lily is one of the most cold-hardy crinums — surviving to zone 7b with winter mulching. It is native to the banks of the Orange River in South Africa and tolerates both periodic flooding and significant drought. One of the parent species of the hybrid Crinum x powellii. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant bulbs (neck exposed) in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Orange River lily is the South African crinum that gives its extraordinary cold-hardiness to the widely grown hybrid Crinum x powellii (which has C. bulbispermum as one parent) — surviving to zone 7b, significantly colder than most tropical crinum species, and tolerating the brief hard frosts of zone 7 winters with root protection. The flowers are white to pale pink with a deep-rose central stripe on each outer petal surface — borne in summer (July–September) in umbels of 6–15 large, funnel-shaped, lily-like blooms on stout, hollow scapes up to 3 feet tall, sweetly fragrant in the evening. The broad, bright-green, strap-shaped leaves form an impressive, fountain-like rosette. It grows naturally along the Orange River in the Northern Cape, where it tolerates periods of seasonal flood and extreme drought, giving it exceptional adaptability in cultivation. Outstanding for zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens where large, fragrant, summer-blooming bulbs with tropical presence are needed — and the superior cold-hardiness compared to other crinums makes it a reliable garden perennial rather than a tender-treated container plant.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants after last frost; orange sedge is a New Zealand native that tolerates mild frosts but is damaged below about 10°F. It grows well in a range of soils from well-drained to moderately moist and tolerates light shade, developing its best color in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist soil in part shade to full sun; orange sedge is a New Zealand native producing fine, arching, evergreen foliage that emerges olive-green then develops warm orange-tan to bronze-orange tones that intensify in cooler temperatures and full sun — providing year-round color interest that complements orange, bronze, and copper-toned companion plants. The fine, thread-like foliage has a delicate, airy quality that contrasts well with bolder-leaved plants. It makes an excellent container plant, where its warm tones complement dark-leafed heucheras, black mondo grass, and orange-toned tulips and perennials. Unlike the more tender New Zealand sedges, C. testacea handles brief dips to single-digit temperatures when established. The orange-bronze coloration intensifies through fall and winter, making it most striking during the cooler months.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring every 2-3 years or plant container-grown plants in moist to moderately dry, fertile, neutral soil in full sun; orange sneezeweed blooms June-July, considerably earlier than the common sneezeweed (H. autumnale), which blooms August-September, making it valuable for filling the midsummer bloom gap in the perennial border. All parts of the plant can cause dermatitis in sensitive individuals.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, fertile, neutral soil in full sun; orange sneezeweed is a western North American native of the Rocky Mountains and Sierra Nevada that blooms in June and July — significantly earlier than the common eastern sneezeweed (Helenium autumnale) that flowers in August and September. The large, golden-orange to orange-yellow daisy flowers have drooping, three-lobed ray petals surrounding a prominent, dark-orange to brown-orange central cone, creating a warm, bright, sunflower-like effect. It grows taller and more robust than many heleniums and is an excellent cut flower. Native to mountain meadows, streambanks, and moist subalpine slopes from Oregon to New Mexico, it is fully cold-hardy to zone 3 and adapts well to the humid east as long as soils are well-drained and not excessively wet in winter. Like all heleniums, the flowers are extremely attractive to bees, butterflies, and specialist native bees throughout the bloom period. Divide every 2-3 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, neutral soil in full sun; orange star grows on a Mediterranean cycle — cool-season growth, spring bloom, summer dormancy — and naturalizes in zone 9–11. In zone 7–8, lift bulbs after foliage yellows and store dry through summer. It is also widely grown as a cut flower and an indoor pot plant.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, neutral soil in full sun; orange star is a South African Ornithogalum producing clusters of brilliant orange to yellow-orange, star-shaped flowers — entirely atypical for the genus, which is almost exclusively white-flowered — that are long-lasting both in the garden and as cut flowers. The dense, dome-shaped clusters of orange stars are vivid and eye-catching in late winter to spring. As a South African Cape bulb, it grows through the cool season, blooms in late winter to spring, and goes dormant in summer — requiring dry conditions during its summer dormancy to prevent bulb rot. In zone 9–11 it naturalizes as a perennial in well-drained, sunny beds. It is one of the most widely sold cut flower bulbs globally. Despite its common name 'Orange Star,' the flower color varies from bright orange to yellow-orange to orange-red depending on the clone, with the most vivid orange forms being the most ornamental. Long-lasting in a vase — up to 3 weeks — making it an outstanding cut flower.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the orange-flowered form of fragrant tea olive is a Gulf South favorite for its intensely apricot-scented fall bloom.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it near a window, porch, or path where its powerful fragrance can be enjoyed. Orange Tea Olive bears small, warm orange flowers, more strongly colored than the creamy-white blooms of the common fragrant tea olive, releasing an intense, sweet, apricot-like scent that carries a considerable distance on the air, most heavily in fall with lighter, scattered flushes through the rest of the year in mild climates. Its dense, glossy, evergreen foliage makes it useful as a large screening shrub, informal hedge, or small specimen tree over time, tolerating shearing well if a more formal shape is wanted. It is slower-growing and generally less cold-hardy than the plain white-flowered species, so it performs best in the milder parts of the Gulf South, and established plants need only routine watering during dry spells and an occasional shaping after the heaviest bloom flush.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface sow as light aids germination.
directions: Start indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, pressing seed onto the surface as light aids germination. This variety wows with peachy-orange blossoms brushed with pink above lush green foliage on long stems. Pinch young plants for bushier growth and cut freely for long-lasting bouquets. The blooms are edible and make a whimsical garnish for salads and desserts.

common_name: Orangeola Japanese Maple (Cascading Orange-Red Lace-Leaf Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil, protecting it from drying wind and hot afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in part shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and the harshest afternoon sun. Orangeola produces one of the most colorful seasonal displays among lace-leaf Japanese maples, with finely dissected leaves emerging brilliant orange-red in spring, deepening to bronze-red through summer, and finishing in a fiery orange-scarlet fall display, on a cascading, semi-weeping form that grows somewhat more upright than fully pendulous cultivars like Tamukeyama. Its strong, layered branching and vivid seasonal color changes make it a standout specimen near a patio or entry where it can be viewed up close through the year. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Oranges and Lemons blanket flower is short-lived like most gaillardia and benefits from being allowed to self-sow to maintain the planting.
directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Oranges and Lemons blanket flower is short-lived like most gaillardia and benefits from being allowed to self-sow to maintain the planting. Warm, glowing flowers open bright golden-yellow at the tips fading through orange to a soft apricot center, a smooth color gradient rather than the sharp banded bicolor pattern of the wild species, giving each bloom a warm, sunset-like glow that blooms continuously from early summer through frost. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on poor, lean, well-drained soil and struggles in rich, moist, or heavily fertilized ground, making it a strong choice for a xeriscape border or gravel garden. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, and expect the plant to be relatively short-lived (two to three years), relying on self-sown seedlings to maintain the planting over time.

plant_note: Root a mature, callused stem cutting in a fast-draining, chunky orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; keep slightly root-bound in a fairly small pot, since these jungle-cactus hybrids often flower more reliably when their roots are somewhat crowded.
directions: Grow in a fast-draining, humus-rich orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light, with only gentle early-morning direct sun tolerated in mild climates. These sprawling, flat- or triangular-stemmed hybrids descend from generations of breeding among wild epiphytic jungle cacti, chiefly Epiphyllum, Disocactus, and Selenicereus species from Central and South American rainforest canopies, and are grown almost entirely for their spectacular flowers, which can reach 6-10 inches across in nearly every color but true blue. Each bloom typically lasts only a day or two in late spring or summer, so many growers track bud development closely to catch the show. Feed lightly with a diluted bloom-boosting fertilizer during the growing season, water thoroughly and then allow the mix to dry somewhat before watering again, and protect from frost, since this tender hybrid is grown outdoors year-round only in zone 10-11 and elsewhere as a container or greenhouse plant.

common_name: Orchid Frost Lamium (Silver-Leaved Lavender-Pink Dead Nettle)
plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Orchid Frost bears nearly solid silver leaves with a narrow green margin and clear lavender-pink flowers, and is notably more vigorous and mildew-resistant than older Lamium cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun, which scorches the pale foliage. Orchid Frost bears striking, nearly solid silver leaves edged with a narrow band of green, among the brightest foliage of any Lamium cultivar, topped by clear lavender-pink flowers from late spring into summer, and shows improved vigor and resistance to the powdery mildew that troubles older, less-refined Lamium selections. It spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, quickly knitting together a dense, weed-suppressing, low groundcover beneath trees and shrubs, brightening dark corners of the shade garden with its luminous foliage even when not in bloom. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to encourage fresh growth and tidy the mat, and divide congested patches in spring if increase or containment is needed.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; orchid primrose is short-lived but produces a uniquely shaped bicolor flower spike unlike any other primrose.
directions: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring, keeping the soil evenly damp through the growing season. Primula vialii is unmistakable among primroses for its dense, conical flower spike that opens from the bottom up, starting bright red-violet in bud and opening to lavender-blue flowers, creating a striking two-toned, poker-like bloom reminiscent of an orchid or a small red-hot-poker plant. Though often short-lived, it self-sows readily in congenial conditions to maintain a presence in the garden, making it a novel accent for a moist, partly shaded border or streamside planting where its unusual flower form stands out.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; orchid trees grow rapidly — up to 3–5 feet per year — and begin flowering within 3–5 years from seed.
directions: Start seeds in moist potting mix after soaking 24 hours, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; orchid tree is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the subtropical world, producing large, pink-to-magenta 5-petaled flowers that truly resemble orchid blossoms from late winter to spring before or as the distinctive two-lobed (camel's foot-shaped) leaves emerge. Trees grow rapidly and begin flowering in 3–5 years, reaching 20–30 feet at maturity. They are relatively cold-hardy compared to other tropical trees, tolerating brief freezes to 22°F once established. Young trees require frost protection in zone 9 until the trunk reaches 4–5 inches in diameter. Prune after bloom to shape and remove any frost-damaged wood.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown vines after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; orchid vine is damaged below 30°F. In zone 9 it may die back in cold winters but resprouts vigorously from established roots. It grows rapidly in warm conditions and needs a strong trellis, fence, or support structure.
directions: Root cuttings in warm conditions and train on a trellis or fence in full sun to part shade; orchid vine (butterfly vine) is a South American twining vine producing clusters of intricate, butter-yellow flowers with fringed, wavy petals that closely resemble small orchid flowers or the wings of a butterfly, giving the plant both its common names. The flowers are followed by samara-style winged fruits that are ornamental in their own right. Stigmaphyllon ciliatum grows rapidly to 10–25 feet and provides attractive coverage for fences, trellises, pergolas, and arbors with its somewhat heart-shaped, textured leaves and near-constant bloom from summer through fall. The unusual flower form makes it immediately recognizable and a conversation piece in the garden. Related S. littorale (Amazon vine) is more salt-tolerant and suitable for coastal Gulf Coast conditions. An excellent and underused tropical vine for zone 9–11 gardens.

plant_note: Plant in fall in moist bottomland soils along Pacific Northwest streams, seasonal wetlands, or low-lying yards that stay damp through the wet season; monitor for emerald ash borer.
directions: Plant in fall in moist bottomland soils along Pacific Northwest streams, seasonal wetlands, or low-lying yards that stay damp through the wet season, since this is the only ash native west of the Rocky Mountains. Its broad, rounded canopy and compound leaves provide strong seasonal shade, turning yellow before dropping in autumn. It tolerates seasonal flooding and heavy clay soils better than most shade trees, making it valuable for riparian buffer and stormwater plantings. As with other native ashes, monitor for emerald ash borer as the pest continues to spread westward.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring after last frost; cold stratification of seed for 4-6 weeks improves germination if starting from seed.
directions: Oregon Checker-mallow is a robust native perennial of moist meadows, wet prairies, and stream margins from Washington to northern California, producing tall, upright spikes of bright pink to rose-pink, 5-petaled mallow flowers 1 to 1.5 inches across from June through August. It is one of the showiest and most widely cultivated western Sidalcea species, performing best in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade. Plant container-grown transplants in spring, spacing generously to allow mature clumps to develop over several seasons; established plants are long-lived and drought-tolerant once roots reach moist subsoil. It is an excellent choice for Pacific Northwest native gardens, rain gardens, and perennial borders, where it serves as a larval host for West Coast lady butterflies and draws specialist native bees to its nectar-rich blooms all summer.

plant_note: Tuck divisions into shallow pockets of gritty, well-drained soil among rocks or in a crevice garden in spring.
directions: Tuck divisions into shallow pockets of gritty, well-drained soil among rocks or in a crevice garden in spring, echoing the cliffs and talus slopes this widespread western native inhabits from the Rockies to the Pacific Coast, with disjunct populations near the Great Lakes. The small, deciduous, twice-pinnate fronds die back cleanly in late summer heat and return reliably each spring, making it a tidy, low-water choice for rock gardens and dry shaded walls. It is best grown where winter and spring moisture are followed by a drier summer rest.

common_name: Oregon Grape Holly (Tall Oregon Grape, Mountain Grape)
plant_note: Plant container stock or bare-root plants in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade; Oregon grape holly is native to Pacific Northwest forests and is most successful east of the Rockies in part shade with protection from winter winds and afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade; avoid exposed sites with afternoon sun or harsh winter winds, which cause foliage burn; protect with burlap in zone 5. Mahonia aquifolium is a Pacific Northwest native evergreen shrub with bold, leathery, pinnate leaves composed of 5–9 spiny, holly-like leaflets that are lustrous dark-green in summer and turn attractive bronze-purple to red-purple in fall and winter, especially in sun — a highly ornamental combination with the spring flowers and summer berries. Dense clusters of brilliant-yellow flowers cover the branch tips in March–April before most other spring-flowering shrubs, providing exceptional early-season pollinator value; the flowers are followed by clusters of blue-black, grape-like berries coated in blue-white bloom (powder) that ripen in August and are relished by many birds. The berries are edible (tart, high in vitamin C) and can be used for jelly or syrup; the roots and inner bark yield a yellow dye historically used by Indigenous peoples. The genus Mahonia is now often merged with Berberis by modern taxonomists.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Oregon stonecrop tolerates cooler, moister Pacific Northwest conditions better than many drought-adapted sedum species.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Oregon stonecrop tolerates cooler, moister Pacific Northwest conditions better than many drought-adapted sedum species. Glossy, spoon-shaped, bright green leaves often flush bronze-red in bright light or dry conditions, forming a low, spreading mat on rocky outcrops, forest edges, and coastal bluffs from California to British Columbia, topped with bright yellow, star-shaped flower clusters in early summer. One of the more shade-tolerant native western sedums, it grows in both open rock gardens and the light shade of a coastal forest edge, making it a versatile native groundcover for a Pacific Northwest rock garden or dry woodland border. Water occasionally, particularly during establishment, and divide congested mats to propagate or control spread.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall or spring in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Oregon sunshine is drought-tolerant once established and is best adapted to the lean, rocky, or sandy soils of its Pacific Coast native habitat. In rich, moist garden soil it becomes floppy and short-lived. An outstanding front-of-border perennial for dry, sunny western gardens.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Oregon sunshine is a widespread Pacific Coast native perennial of rocky outcrops, dry slopes, and lean, sandy soils from British Columbia to northern California, producing a low mound of densely woolly-white, deeply lobed, silver-gray leaves and from late spring through summer, a generous display of bright, clear golden-yellow daisy flowers (1–1.5 inches across) with yellow central discs that appear to float above the silver foliage. The combination of the felty, woolly, white-silver foliage and the clear yellow flowers creates a striking, drought-tolerant, rock-garden effect in full sun. The name reflects both the woolly (lanatum = woolly) leaf surface and the Oregon origin of the species. It is highly variable across its range, with many recognized subspecies and geographical forms varying from compact 6-inch cushions to taller, looser plants 18 inches high. Outstanding for western rock gardens, dry slope stabilization, and the front of the sunny, drought-tolerant border where its silver foliage provides good contrast. Attracts native bees and is one of the primary native bee foraging plants in its range.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth immediately upon collection in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; Oregon white oak acorns do not require cold stratification and germinate readily. They lose viability quickly and should not be stored dry for long.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, dry to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Oregon white oak (Garry oak) is the only native oak of the Pacific Northwest north of California, forming open oak savannas and woodlands from British Columbia to California. It is a slow-growing, long-lived, massive tree that can live over 500 years, developing deeply furrowed gray bark and massive, gnarled limbs with age. The oak savannas it creates support extraordinary biodiversity — over 200 species of bees use Oregon white oak, and it supports more invertebrate biodiversity per tree than any other northwest native plant. This ecosystem is now highly threatened, with less than 5% of original oak savanna remaining. The acorns are sweet and palatable, historically processed by indigenous peoples into acorn meal and flour. A landmark native tree for large-scale restoration planting in the Pacific Northwest.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions or rooted plantlets in spring in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from cold, drying winds; mulch the crown heavily in autumn where winters approach the cold edge of its range.
directions: Oriental chain fern is a bold, arching evergreen fern whose broad, glossy, pinnate to bipinnate fronds emerge coppery orange in spring before maturing to deep green, eventually reaching four feet tall and wide or more where winters stay mild. Small plantlets form along the mature fronds and root readily where they touch soil, so gardeners can propagate new plants simply by pegging a frond tip down or removing rooted offsets in autumn. Best sited in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil, it takes the heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer in stride but appreciates a dry winter mulch at the cooler edge of its range. Its coarse, tropical texture makes a strong architectural counterpoint to fine-textured Dryopteris and Athyrium plantings in a warm-climate shade border.
