plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; oriental cherry is the species from which most Japanese ornamental cherry cultivars are derived, including 'Kwanzan', 'Shirofugen', and 'Ukon'. Grafted cultivars are most commonly available.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; oriental cherry (Japanese flowering cherry) is the parent species of dozens of the most famous ornamental cherry cultivars in the world, including the double-flowered 'Kwanzan' (dark pink), 'Shirofugen' (white fading to pink), and 'Ukon' (pale yellow-green). In Japan, cherry blossom viewing (hanami) centered on this species and its cultivars is a centuries-old cultural tradition celebrating the brief but spectacular spring bloom. Most widely planted ornamental cherries in American gardens are cultivars derived from P. serrulata. The double-flowered cultivars produce no fruit (the extra petals replace stamens), limiting wildlife value, but the spectacle of spring bloom — covering the bare branches in clouds of pink or white — makes them among the most celebrated ornamental trees worldwide. Short-lived compared to some other ornamentals (25–30 years).

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or direct-sow seeds after soil warms in full sun, well-drained, average to lean soil; oriental fountain grass is more cold-hardy than the popular Pennisetum setaceum (tender fountain grass) and survives to zone 6 with good drainage. Cut back to 4–6 inches in late winter before new growth begins.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; oriental fountain grass is a compact, well-behaved, hardy perennial ornamental grass producing graceful, arching mounds of fine-textured, gray-green foliage topped by exceptionally soft, fluffy flower spikes in shades of soft pink, rose, and cream from June through September — the inflorescences catching the light with a glowing, backlit quality in the evening garden. It is significantly more cold-hardy than the widely grown but tender Pennisetum setaceum (annual fountain grass in zones 6–7) while offering similar mounding, fountain-like habit and soft-colored flower heads. The selection 'Karley Rose' is widely available and offers particularly strong rose-pink coloring on the spikes. It thrives in heat, drought, and poor soil once established and requires only annual cutting back in late winter. An outstanding perennial grass for dry, sunny mixed borders where summer color, fine texture, and movement in the breeze are all desired.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall or early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; fall planting is preferred in zones 4–7.
directions: Plant bulbs 6–8 in deep (3 times the bulb diameter) in well-drained, organically rich, slightly acidic soil; apply mulch to keep roots cool. Oriental lilies prefer to have their heads in the sun and their feet in the shade — interplant with low perennials to shade the root zone. The large, intensely fragrant blooms appear in mid- to late summer; deadhead after flowering but allow foliage to remain until it yellows naturally. Avoid overhead watering to reduce the risk of botrytis; stake tall cultivars against wind damage.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring; light aids germination.
directions: Surface sow in early spring, pressing the fine seed onto the soil since light aids germination. This variety forms a low, spreading carpet of fragrant deep purple blooms that flower all season and spill nicely over container edges. Withstanding heat and drought, it is an ideal rock garden and edging plant that draws pollinators. Shear lightly midseason if flowering slows.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; seeds need cool soil and germinate best when sown directly outdoors.
directions: Surface-sow seeds in early spring on well-prepared, well-drained soil; seeds need cool temperatures and light, so press firmly without covering. Oriental poppies bloom for a brief but spectacular 2–3 weeks in late spring to early summer with crepe-paper petals in orange, red, pink, or white up to 6 in across. Plants go dormant after bloom leaving a bare spot — interplant with late-emerging annuals like baby's breath or dahlias to fill the gap. Divide clumps in late summer while dormant; established plants dislike being moved during the growing season.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to average, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; oriental spruce grows naturally in mountain forests of the Caucasus and northeastern Turkey, making it tolerant of cold winters and moderate summer heat — more heat-tolerant than most spruces.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to average, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; oriental spruce is considered by many horticulturists to be the most beautiful of all the spruces — the extremely short needles (only 1/4 to 1/3 inch, the shortest of all spruces) are tightly pressed along the branchlets, creating an unusually dense, lustrous, deep-green, almost 'lacquered' appearance quite different from other, coarser-needled spruces. The small, narrowly cylindrical, violet-purple cones ripen to reddish-brown and are very ornamental. The spring growth of new bright lime-green needles contrasting with the dark older foliage is striking. More heat-tolerant than Norway spruce or Colorado blue spruce, adapting reasonably well to the warmer parts of its zone range. The cultivar 'Skylands' with permanently golden-yellow foliage is one of the most sought-after ornamental conifers in the nursery trade. An outstanding specimen tree for larger landscape settings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Orion bears unusually large flowers for a hardy geranium and blooms over a long season with occasional shearing.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in hot climates. Orion produces exceptionally large, vivid violet-blue flowers with a small white center, bigger than most hardy geranium cultivars, held above a vigorous, mounding clump of deeply cut foliage that blooms heavily from late spring into summer. Its strong color and generous flower size make it a standout in the perennial border, and shearing the plant back by half after the first flush of bloom fades encourages a tidy regrowth of foliage and a good second round of flowers later in the season. It tolerates heat and some drought once established, though consistent moisture supports the longest bloom period, and dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring keeps the plant vigorous.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall where winters are mild.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring as they need light and cool temperatures to germinate; do not cover seeds. Orlaya produces flat-topped umbel flowers with large, irregular outer florets that create a delicate lace effect in pure white, ideal as a cut flower filler. It prefers lean, well-drained soil — overly rich conditions produce lush foliage at the expense of flowers. Plants self-sow readily where happy, returning reliably if the ground is not disturbed; collect seed or allow them to fall for the following year.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall, 4–8 weeks before the ground freezes, for late-spring to early-summer bloom.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall at a depth of 3 times their diameter in sharply drained soil; the large-flowered types like 'Globemaster' can be planted 12 in deep for stability. Foliage often begins to yellow while the flowers are still in bloom — interplanting with perennials helps mask the dying leaves. Deer and rodents avoid alliums, making them a good choice for wildlife-prone gardens. Spherical seedheads are ornamentally interesting and can be dried for arrangements.

plant_note: Plant purchased transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; ornamental bacopa (Sutera) is a cool-to-mild-season annual or tender perennial that blooms most heavily in spring and fall in zone 9 and struggles in summer heat — it is best used as a cool-season annual or in shaded locations in warm climates.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; in zone 9, plant in fall or early spring for best bloom before summer heat; cut back lightly after the spring bloom flush to encourage new growth. Sutera cordata (ornamental bacopa or snowflake) is a South African tender perennial grown as a cool-season annual in most climates, producing masses of tiny, 4-petaled, white (or pink or lavender) flowers on a trailing, mounding plant with small, rounded, bronze-green, hairy leaves — the overall effect is a frothy cascade of tiny flowers that are exceptional in hanging baskets, window boxes, and as container spillers. NOTE: Despite being commonly marketed as 'Bacopa,' Sutera cordata is entirely unrelated to the medicinal herb Bacopa monnieri (water hyssop), which is an aquatic plant in the family Plantaginaceae — the shared common name is a marketing confusion. Sutera cordata performs best in cool to mild weather (55–75°F), blooming prolifically in spring and fall in zone 9 and going largely dormant in summer heat. It combines beautifully with petunias, calibrachoa, and lobularia in cool-season combination containers.

plant_note: Divide offset pups from the base of established clumps or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; ornamental banana requires rich, moist, organic soil and grows most rapidly with monthly fertilization during the growing season — poor soil and drought produce stunted, unattractive plants.
directions: Divide offset pups or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; ornamental banana is an Indian and Southeast Asian tropical banana grown for its ornamental qualities rather than its edible fruit — the small fruit clusters are not edible — and is notable for producing one of the most beautiful inflorescences of any banana, with dramatically ornate, upright flower spikes bearing brilliant, deep-rose-pink to purple-pink, waxy bracts that contrast with the small, pale-yellow to white flowers and create a vivid and decorative floral display that is distinctly more ornamental than the simple, greenish-yellow flower bracts of fruiting bananas. The plant's relatively modest stature (5–10 feet), its tolerance of partial shade, and its cold-hardiness to around 28–30°F in zone 9 (the underground rhizomes surviving and reshooting after the tops are killed by frost) make it a practical ornamental banana for Gulf Coast zone 9–12 gardens where the plant can be used as a permanent specimen. The broad, paddle-shaped, typically unspotted green leaves provide bold tropical texture. Spreads by producing basal offsets (pups).

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost at 70–75°F; transplant after frost danger passes into full sun and fertile, well-drained soil — warm soil is essential for strong establishment. Grown as an annual for its striking deep burgundy-purple foliage and the large, cylindrical flower/grain heads that arch gracefully under their own weight in late summer. An excellent anchor plant in tropical-style or mixed annual borders, and the dried seed heads are useful in arrangements. Highly attractive to birds in fall — leave some plants intact for wildlife value.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or divide established plants; grow in sharply drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun. Named cultivars including Herrenhausen, Hopley's Purple, and Rosenkuppel are consistently more floriferous than seedlings and must be propagated by cuttings or division to maintain flower character. Dead-head or cut back after the first bloom flush to encourage re-blooming through fall.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; ornamental oregano is an outstanding long-season pollinator plant from rocky hillsides of Turkey and Cyprus, producing masses of tiny tubular purple-pink flowers on wiry, branching stems from June through October — a bloom period of four to five months that makes it one of the longest-flowering hardy perennials available. The numerous small flowers are irresistible to bees, butterflies, and hoverflies throughout the long season. The foliage is aromatic like culinary oregano but the plant is grown primarily as an ornamental rather than for cooking, since the essential oil content is lower than culinary Greek or Italian oregano. The cultivar Herrenhausen is the most widely available and produces dense, upright clusters of deep rose-purple flowers on burgundy-flushed stems; Hopley's Purple is taller with more open, airy clusters. The dried seed heads and wiry stems remain attractive through winter and make excellent filler in dried arrangements. Excellent for the front of a dry border, Mediterranean-style plantings, and rock gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or slips in spring after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; ornamental sweet potato vines are among the most vigorous and colorful summer trailing annuals for beds, borders, and containers in zone 9 and perform outstandingly through Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in warm soil after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; ornamental sweet potato grows extremely vigorously and may need periodic trimming to keep in bounds. Ipomoea batatas 'Tricolor' (ornamental sweet potato vine) is one of the most widely grown summer ornamental foliage annuals — a vigorous, trailing or mounding, tender perennial vine grown for its spectacular, large (3–5 inch), deeply lobed or heart-shaped leaves in bold foliage colors ranging from chartreuse to lime green ('Margarita'), deep burgundy-purple to nearly black ('Blackie'), and multicolored ('Tricolor' with pink, white, and green variegation). The plants trail vigorously up to 3–8 feet during the summer season and are used as groundcovers, in hanging baskets, and as 'spillers' in container combinations. Unlike edible sweet potatoes, the ornamental varieties have been selected for foliage rather than tuber quality, though the small tubers produced are edible. Ornamental sweet potato vine performs outstandingly in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers and is one of the few colorful trailing plants that maintains vigor through August heat. Note: the leaves and small tubers are mildly toxic to cats and dogs.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; ornate star cactus needs excellent drainage and grows slowly, taking years to reach flowering size.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; ornate star cactus needs excellent drainage and grows slowly, taking years to reach flowering size. A tall, ribbed, columnar cactus is patterned with scattered flecks of white, star-like wool against dark green skin, arranged along pronounced vertical ribs edged with stiff yellow-brown spines, eventually producing large, pale yellow flowers at the crown once the plant matures after many years. Native to central Mexico, it is prized by collectors for its striking geometric ribbing and starry white speckling, growing slowly into an impressive columnar specimen over a decade or more of patient cultivation. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide as much direct sun as possible for tight, well-defined ribs, and protect from frost and excess winter moisture.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; Orphanides' tulip requires hot, dry summer dormancy to persist — suited to Mediterranean-climate gardens and dry, well-drained rock garden or raised bed conditions in hotter, drier zones. The Whittallii and Hageri forms (sometimes treated as varieties or separate species) have warm bronze, apricot, and orange-bronze color forms. It naturalizes well in lean, dry, sunny conditions.
directions: Plant bulbs in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Orphanides' tulip is a wild tulip species from the rocky, sun-exposed, dry hillsides and stony garigue of Greece and Turkey that occupies a distinctive niche among wild tulips: the flowers are warm-toned in bronze, apricot, terracotta, orange-bronze to brick-red with a pale or contrasting outer petal surface — colors that are rarely seen in tulips and difficult to describe precisely, varying through the population from burnt-orange to warm bronze to dark coppery-red, often with a contrasting buff, cream, or olive-yellow on the outer surface of the petals, creating a bicolor effect when open that shifts through several harmonious warm tones from bud to full bloom. The related Hageri form has darker, more saturated brick-red to terracotta flowers; the Whittallii form has vivid orange and is among the most orange-flowered of all tulips. All forms are excellent naturalizers in lean, very well-drained, hot, sunny positions where summer is dry — rock gardens, gravel gardens, raised beds with lean substrate — gradually building colonies of the distinctive warm-toned flowers that bridge the spring-to-early-summer gap in the tulip season.

common_name: Osage Crape Myrtle (Semi-Dwarf Light Pink Cinnamon-Bark Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Osage, one of the earliest U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series releases (1975), is a semi-dwarf crape myrtle noted for smooth cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Osage was one of the earliest U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series crape myrtles, released in 1975, and remains valued for its light, clear pink flowers and especially smooth, glossy cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark, which many gardeners consider among the most attractive of any crape myrtle cultivar for winter interest. Its semi-dwarf, well-branched habit fits smaller landscapes better than some of the larger Indian-series introductions while still showing good resistance to powdery mildew. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Osaka Red Ornamental Kale (Rose-Purple Flowering Cabbage)
plant_note: Start seed indoors in mid-to-late summer for fall and winter color and transplant out as temperatures cool; the deep rose-purple center intensifies with each hard frost rather than being damaged by it.
directions: Start seed indoors in mid-to-late summer and transplant into full sun with steady moisture, since ornamental kale needs a long cool season to size up before its color peaks. Osaka Red forms a broad, smooth-edged rosette of blue-green outer leaves surrounding a large, richly colored rose-to-purple-red center that deepens further with each cold snap, giving fall and winter beds and containers a bold splash of color when most other bedding plants have finished. Its round, cabbage-like form and relatively large size make it a strong focal point in mixed fall containers or mass plantings, distinct from the more deeply fringed, feathery kale types. The leaves are technically edible but are grown almost entirely for ornamental display rather than the table; plants hold their color and form through hard freezes and typically decline only when sustained heat returns in late spring.

common_name: Osakazuki Japanese Maple (Green Summer Foliage with Brilliant Scarlet Fall Color)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Osakazuki is grown chiefly for its exceptionally brilliant scarlet fall color, considered among the best of any Japanese maple.
directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Osakazuki bears plain green summer foliage on a larger, upright tree, unremarkable through most of the growing season, but transforms each fall into one of the most brilliant, saturated scarlet-red displays of any commonly grown Japanese maple, a dramatic payoff that has made it a longtime favorite among collectors specifically for autumn color. Its larger mature size suits it to a specimen role in a spacious garden where its fall show can be viewed from a distance. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

plant_note: Plant bulb divisions in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; osceola plume requires consistently moist, acidic, low-nutrient conditions similar to those of Gulf Coast pine flatwoods and pitcher plant bogs.
directions: Plant bulb divisions in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; osceola plume (formerly Zigadenus densus) is a native bulbous perennial of Gulf Coast and South Atlantic pine flatwoods, wet savannas, and pitcher plant bogs from Florida to North Carolina, producing narrow, grass-like basal leaves and slender flowering stems 2–4 feet tall bearing a dense, showy, plume-like raceme of small white flowers in May and June — one of the most floriferous and ornamental members of the bunchflower family. It is an excellent companion plant in acidic bog gardens alongside pitcher plants (Sarracenia), sundews (Drosera), rose pogonia orchids, and grass-pink orchids. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested; do not confuse with edible bulbs. The species has a limited native range in the coastal plain and is becoming commercially available through specialty native plant nurseries as interest in Gulf Coast bog gardens grows.

common_name: Osiris Fantaisie Ligularia (Compact Bicolor Purple-Backed Foliage)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from afternoon sun; Osiris Fantaisie is a compact Quebec-bred ligularia cultivar, more manageable in a smaller bed than full-sized types like Desdemona, but like all ligularias it needs a cool, sheltered, consistently damp site to perform well in zone 9 heat.
directions: Plant in constantly moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from afternoon sun and heat; Osiris Fantaisie is a compact ligularia cultivar bred at Les Jardins Osiris in Quebec, bearing leathery, heart-shaped leaves in deep olive-green flushed burgundy on top with contrasting purple undersides and purple stems, topped in summer by racemes of bright yellow daisy flowers. Its more compact size, to about three feet, makes it easier to fit into a smaller shade bed than larger ligularia cultivars. Like all ligularias it wilts visibly during midday heat and recovers overnight, normal behavior for the genus that signals a need for cooler, damper conditions rather than disease; give it the coolest, most sheltered, consistently moist spot available and mulch heavily to protect the roots through a Gulf South summer. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Oso Easy Italian Ice Rose (Pink-and-Cream Bicolor Landscape Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Oso Easy Italian Ice is part of a landscape rose series bred for disease resistance and low-maintenance repeat bloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Oso Easy Italian Ice bears unusual bicolor blooms opening pink and cream and shifting in tone as they age, so a single plant can show several shades at once, a distinctive novelty color pattern among landscape shrub roses. Bred for strong disease resistance and continuous bloom without deadheading, it fits low-maintenance foundation plantings and mixed borders where spraying and fussing over roses isn't practical. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well and need only an annual light pruning in late winter to stay compact and floriferous.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ostbo Red is one of the deepest red-budded mountain laurel cultivars and needs the same acidic, well-drained conditions as other mountain laurels.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ostbo Red is one of the deepest red-budded mountain laurel cultivars and needs the same acidic, well-drained conditions as other mountain laurels. Deep, rich red buds open to reveal cupped, saucer-shaped flowers with a paler pink interior, opening in intricate, crimped, origami-like folds typical of mountain laurel, one of the earliest and darkest-red cultivars bred by pioneering Pacific Northwest hybridizer Endre Ostbo in the mid-twentieth century. Native to the eastern United States, mountain laurel is an important broadleaf evergreen understory shrub, and this early red-flowered selection helped spark the modern wave of mountain laurel breeding for improved bud and flower color that followed in subsequent decades. Provide the same acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and dappled shade the species requires, mulch to keep roots cool, and avoid heavy pruning, since mountain laurel resents hard cutting back.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early to mid-spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; ostrich fern thrives in riparian and floodplain conditions and spreads vigorously by stolons, so allow ample space for a colony to develop.
directions: Matteuccia struthiopteris is a large, dramatic, deciduous native fern of eastern and northern North America, producing tall, vase-shaped clusters of bright-green sterile fronds that resemble the plumes of an ostrich and reach 3–5 feet tall; shorter, dark-brown fertile fronds emerge in the center of the vase in late summer and persist through winter, releasing spores in early spring. It spreads assertively by underground stolons and will form a bold, large-scale colony in moist, cool, shaded sites, making it ideal for naturalizing along stream banks, pond edges, and shaded rain gardens in zones 3–7, though it struggles in the heat and humidity of the Deep South. The tightly coiled spring fiddleheads are a celebrated edible delicacy — harvest only a few per plant when they are still tightly coiled and no more than a few inches tall, and cook thoroughly before eating as raw fiddleheads contain a heat-labile toxin. Pair with native wildflowers such as Virginia bluebells, Jack-in-the-pulpit, and trout lily for a classic northeastern floodplain garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ostrich Plume is a late-blooming thunbergii hybrid whose drooping plumes open well after most arendsii-type astilbes have finished.
directions: Set crowns in rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade, spacing plants far enough apart to show off their arching habit. Ostrich Plume carries loose, weeping sprays of soft rose-pink flowers on gracefully bowed stems above dark green, deeply cut foliage, a distinctly drooping silhouette that sets thunbergii-type astilbes apart from the stiffer upright plumes of most arendsii hybrids. Its later bloom time extends the astilbe season into midsummer, but the same trait that gives it a looser, more sun-tolerant habit also means it needs steady, uninterrupted moisture to avoid crispy leaf margins during hot spells. In the Gulf South, give it afternoon shade, mulch heavily, and expect it to appreciate irrigation during dry summer stretches more than most other perennials in the bed.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Otaksa is among the oldest named hydrangea cultivars, introduced to the West from Japan in the 19th century.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Otaksa is one of the earliest named hydrangea cultivars introduced to Western gardens from Japan in the 19th century by the plant collector Philipp von Siebold, who reportedly named it after a Japanese companion. Its large, rounded mophead blooms shift between rose-pink and blue depending on soil pH, in the same manner as later cultivars, and its historic significance lies in being one of the founding introductions behind the whole class of garden mophead hydrangeas grown today. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and site it with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent wilting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; like all ligularia, Othello wilts dramatically in afternoon sun or dry soil, so site it in a reliably damp, sheltered spot.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; site it in reliably damp ground, since plants scorch and wilt badly in anything less regardless of shade level. Othello is a classic Ligularia dentata cultivar, its large, rounded leaves tinted purple-bronze on top with a deep mahogany-purple underside, topped in mid to late summer by tall clusters of vivid orange-yellow, daisy-like flowers that contrast strongly with the dark foliage. It has been a garden standard for its combination of bold dark leaves and bright late-summer bloom, making a dramatic accent at a pond edge, rain garden, or the moist, shaded portion of a mixed border. Slugs can be a persistent problem on the tender young growth in consistently damp settings; handpick or use organic slug controls as needed.

common_name: Otto Luyken Cherry Laurel (Dwarf English Laurel)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Otto Luyken' stays low and dense without shearing, making it a standard low hedge and foundation shrub in shaded sites.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, and water regularly the first year to establish a dense root system before drier summers. 'Otto Luyken' is a compact, low-mounding selection of cherry laurel with narrower, glossier leaves than the species and abundant upright spikes of small white flowers in mid-spring, followed by small black fruits that birds favor. Its naturally tidy, spreading habit and shade tolerance make it one of the most reliable low hedges and mass foundation plantings for shaded entryways and woodland-edge borders, requiring only occasional shaping rather than regular shearing to stay dense.

common_name: Otto's Thrill Dahlia (Giant Soft-Pink Dinnerplate Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep after soil has warmed; sturdy staking is essential from planting time since flower heads are heavy.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep after soil has warmed, staking sturdily from planting time since flower heads are heavy. A classic dinnerplate-type dahlia bearing enormous, fully double blooms 8–10 inches across, occasionally larger, in soft pink shading darker toward the center, with broad, symmetrically arranged petals that give the flower a lush, rounded form. It has earned numerous American Dahlia Society awards and a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for consistent bloom quality. Plants benefit from disbudding side buds to maximize bloom size.

plant_note: Direct sow spring or fall; biennial that blooms in year two.
directions: Direct sow in spring or fall against a wall or fence that can support the towering spikes; as a biennial it typically blooms the second year. Barely cover the seed and keep moist until germination. This old cottage-garden hollyhock reaches several feet tall with a long bloom period, and the flowers are edible though bland. Stake in windy sites and allow some plants to self-sow for continuous stands.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ovens wattle is one of the most cold-hardy ornamental acacias — surviving to zone 7b when established in a sheltered, well-drained position. The highly distinctive, angular, triangular phyllodes (the leaf-like stems) arranged in a compressed zigzag along arching stems give it an unusual structural appearance unlike other acacias. It blooms in spring, producing masses of fragrant, golden-yellow pompom flowers along the arching stems.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ovens wattle is a compact to medium Australian wattle from the high-altitude mountain forests of the Victorian Alps and Snowy Mountains — the most cold-hardy ornamental acacia commonly available, surviving temperatures to about 5°F (-15°C) in sheltered, well-drained positions. The foliage is distinctive and easily recognized: the phyllodes (leaf-like stems) are very small, almost triangular to rhomboidal, with a sharp point, and arranged in a compressed, angled zigzag along the arching, pendulous stems — creating a unique angular, scale-like texture quite different from the fine-pinnate leaves of A. baileyana or the large oval phyllodes of A. podalyriifolia. The angular phyllodes give the whole plant an unusual structural character. In late winter and spring, the arching stems are densely packed with small, spherical, golden-yellow, fragrant pompom flowers — in some springs the stems become almost entirely golden with flower clusters. The weeping, arching habit with angular foliage and golden flower cascades makes it an excellent specimen plant for cold-climate gardeners who cannot grow the more tender Australian wattles.

plant_note: Plant young container-grown trees in fall in wet to seasonally flooded, poorly drained, clay or loamy soil — overcup oak is a bottomland species adapted to extended winter flooding and is one of the best native oaks for wet, compacted, or periodically inundated sites.
directions: Overcup oak is the definitive native tree for chronically wet, flood-prone sites across the Gulf Coastal Plain and Mississippi Alluvial Valley — its name refers to the unusual acorn, where the cup nearly completely encloses the nut, a characteristic unique among North American oaks. Trees are exceptionally flood-tolerant, naturally occurring in swamp forests, seasonally flooded bottomlands, and poorly drained clay flats where other oaks cannot survive periodic inundation, making it the native oak of choice for rain garden margins, detention basins, and low-lying wet areas. Mature trees develop deeply furrowed, blocky gray bark and a broad, spreading crown that provides excellent wildlife value: dozens of species of woodland birds and mammals rely on the mid-sized, nutritious acorns for fall and winter food. Overcup oak grows slowly but lives for centuries — use it as a lasting structural tree in native woodlands, riparian plantings, and large-scale landscape restorations.

common_name: Overdam Feather Reed Grass (Variegated Upright Reed Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Overdam is a variegated sport of Karl Foerster feather reed grass, staying slightly shorter and less vigorous than its parent, with cream-edged leaf blades that provide season-long color contrast.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Overdam arose as a variegated sport of the popular Karl Foerster feather reed grass, sharing the same stiffly upright, non-invasive clumping habit but with narrow leaf blades edged in creamy white that brighten through the season, sometimes taking on a pink flush in cool fall weather. Feathery, upright flower plumes appear in early summer, aging to a warm buff tan that stands well through winter for structural interest. It tolerates heavier clay soils and somewhat more shade than most ornamental grasses, and like its parent is sterile, posing no invasive seeding risk. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

plant_note: Break off and callus a rooted offset or stem cutting for a day or two, then set shallowly in a very gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in bright light with some protection from harsh midday sun; established clumps can also be divided at the same time of year.
directions: Plant in a very gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in bright light, with light shade from the most intense midday sun in hot climates. This low, clustering South African succulent forms mats of soft, toothed, four- to five-angled stems and produces unusual star-shaped flowers banded in maroon and cream-yellow, each with a raised, ring-like center that resembles a lifesaver candy, giving the plant both of its common names. The blooms release a faint carrion scent to attract fly pollinators rather than bees. Water sparingly, letting the mix dry completely between waterings, since the shallow root system rots quickly in wet, poorly drained soil; grow as a container or houseplant outside of zone 9b-11, bringing it indoors well before frost.

common_name: Ox Eye Sunflower (False Sunflower, Smooth Oxeye)
plant_note: Direct sow in spring (or fall for best germination) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; false sunflower self-seeds freely and establishes permanent colonies in suitable sites — a reliable long-blooming perennial wildflower that is one of the most important midsummer native pollinator plants.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; thin to 18–24 inches. Heliopsis helianthoides (false sunflower or ox eye) is a native prairie and woodland-edge perennial producing masses of 2-to-3-inch, bright-yellow daisy flowers with yellow or yellow-brown cone centers from late June through September — a blooming duration of 8–10 weeks that makes it one of the most valuable summer-blooming natives for pollinators, including bumble bees, native sweat bees, and monarch butterflies. Unlike true sunflowers (Helianthus), false sunflower is reliably perennial, returning year after year and gradually expanding from a central clump while self-seeding moderately. The cultivar 'Loraine Sunshine' (white-marbled leaves with green veins) is grown as much for foliage as flowers; 'Summer Nights' has deep-orange flowers; 'Prairie Sunset' has coppery-orange blooms on bronze-tinged foliage. It tolerates clay soil, drought, and brief flooding better than many comparable native perennials.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in early spring or fall in full sun in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil; ox-eye daisy thrives in poor, dry soil and self-seeds prolifically — it is listed as invasive or noxious in several western US states, so check local regulations before planting.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in early spring or fall in full sun in lean, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; ox-eye daisy is the classic white-and-yellow European meadow daisy that has naturalized across most of North America, producing a reliable and long-lasting display of 2-inch flowers on tall branching stems from late spring through midsummer. It thrives in poor, rocky, or disturbed soil and performs poorly in rich, moist, heavily fertilized conditions where it becomes floppy and disease-prone. Deadhead to prevent the prolific self-seeding that makes it weedy in some settings — it is listed as invasive in several western states. Divide overcrowded clumps every 2–3 years in early fall to maintain vigor; ox-eye daisy is an excellent cut flower and a valuable pollen source for generalist bees.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in late summer or early fall; once planted, oxblood lily resents disturbance and should be left alone permanently to naturalize. Do not dig or divide unless absolutely necessary.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the oxblood lily is one of the most beloved and iconic heirloom bulbs of the Gulf South, an old-fashioned schoolhouse garden staple that has been passed along in this region for over 150 years since its introduction from Argentina. The brilliant deep-red trumpet flowers (2–3 per stem) appear suddenly in late August through September, before the leaves, seemingly overnight after the first significant fall rain — hence the alternate name 'hurricane lily.' The strap-like leaves follow in fall and winter, dying back by summer. The bulbs are nearly indestructible in zone 7–9, naturalizing freely and increasing year after year, with established stands producing hundreds of stems in late summer. They thrive in dry, lean conditions and actually perform worse with too much water or fertilizer. A piece of living southern garden history.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall (cold stratification over winter triggers spring germination) or cold-stratify for 4–6 weeks before indoor sowing in late winter; oxlip grows best in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade. It naturalizes in woodland and meadow settings and was historically associated with specific ancient woodland indicator communities in England. All parts are toxic if ingested in quantity.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part to full shade; the oxlip is one of the three native British primroses and occupies an interesting ecological and horticultural position between the two more familiar species — it is rare in the wild (restricted in Britain to a few hundred ancient woodland sites in East Anglia), yet it has the pendant, one-sided cluster of pale-yellow flowers on a single stem characteristic of the cowslip combined with the broader, primrose-like leaves and woodland habitat of the primrose. Where cowslip and primrose both grow, the oxlip hybrid (Primula x variabilis, better known as the polyanthus) arises naturally. The true oxlip has pale, almost-cream-yellow pendant flowers in one-sided clusters on stems 6–12 inches tall, appearing in April and May. In cultivation it requires the woodland conditions of its native habitat — moist, shaded, slightly alkaline soil — and is somewhat less easily pleased than cowslip or primrose. A collector's plant for the serious woodland garden, valuable for the historical significance of its conservation ecology and the delicate beauty of its pale spring flowers.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in midsummer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; Magnolia sieboldii is one of the most shade-tolerant magnolia species and blooms more reliably in partial-shade positions than virtually any other magnolia — siting in partial shade also slows spring growth and reduces the risk of early flowers being caught by late frosts.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Oyama magnolia is an East Asian deciduous magnolia that flowers in late spring to early summer (May–June) — well after frost risk has passed — producing pendant, nodding, cup-shaped, pure-white, intensely lemon-and-vanilla-fragrant flowers with a prominent central boss of deep crimson-red stamens that contrast dramatically with the white petals and give each flower a jewel-like center. The flowers nod downward on their stems and are best viewed from below or on a gentle slope, where their pendant display and scarlet centers are most visible. It is one of the very few magnolias that performs in genuine partial shade, blooms reliably in dappled light, and does not require full sun for good flowering — making it uniquely valuable for shaded woodland gardens where other magnolias would fail to bloom properly. The large, bold, bright-green leaves are themselves attractive. A refined, fragrant, and very different-looking magnolia suited to the naturalistic shade garden rather than the formal sunny border.

plant_note: Divide rosette offsets or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade after the last frost; oyster plant tolerates poor soil, drought, and salt spray, making it one of the most useful and indestructible shade groundcovers for Gulf Coast landscapes.
directions: Divide rosette offsets or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial to full shade; oyster plant (Moses in the cradle, boat lily) is a Central American native that forms dense, suckering rosettes of stiff, lance-shaped leaves that are glossy dark green on the upper surface and rich purple-violet on the lower surface — a two-tone combination that makes it one of the most distinctive tropical groundcovers available. Small white flowers are cradled within paired, boat-shaped bracts in the leaf axils (giving the common name Moses in the cradle). The plant is extremely tough — tolerant of drought, poor soil, salt spray, and deep shade — and spreads by offsets to form dense, weed-suppressing groundcover colonies in difficult spots under trees and on shaded embankments. An essential low-maintenance groundcover for Gulf Coast zone 8–11 landscapes. Tender to hard frost but rebounds from root in zone 8; root-hardy to approximately 25°F.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring or plant divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Ozark bluestar tolerates consistently wet soil and is outstanding for moist prairie and streamside plantings in the Midwest.
directions: Sow direct in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Ozark bluestar tolerates consistently wet, poorly drained soils better than the commonly grown Arkansas bluestar (A. hubrichtii) and is the best bluestar for consistently moist to wet sites. Amsonia illustris is a native bluestar of Ozark glades, stream banks, and moist prairies in Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Arkansas, with broader, more lustrous (illustris = shining) leaves than other amsonias and the same starry, light-blue flowers on upright stems in mid-spring; it has excellent golden-yellow fall color. Like other bluestars, it is long-lived, clump-forming, deer-resistant, drought-tolerant once established, and one of the most carefree of all native perennials; this species' greater tolerance of wet soil makes it an outstanding choice for rain gardens and pond margins.

plant_note: Sow seeds in late fall or early spring in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Ozark sundrops develops a deep taproot that makes transplanting difficult after the first season — direct seeding or planting very small container plants while young is preferable. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the dry, alkaline soils of limestone-based gardens.
directions: Sow seeds or plant small container plants in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Ozark sundrops produces the largest flowers of any Oenothera — enormous, four-petaled, silky-bright-yellow flowers reaching 4-5 inches across that open in the evening and often remain open through the morning of the following day, giving them more garden visibility than most evening primroses. The large, bowl-shaped flowers glow with an almost luminous yellow in the low-angle evening light. The plant itself is low-growing and spreading, typically only 6-12 inches tall, with narrow, lance-shaped leaves that form a mat-like groundcover decorated with these spectacular flowers from May through July. After flowering, the plant produces distinctive large, winged seed pods (macrocarpa = large fruit) that are ornamental when mature. Native to the dry, limestone and chalk prairies of the Ozarks and central Great Plains, it is exceptionally drought-tolerant and long-lived in well-drained, alkaline soils with minimal supplemental watering once established.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; PJM rhododendron is exceptionally cold-hardy and tolerates more sun than most large-leaved rhododendrons.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; PJM rhododendron is exceptionally cold-hardy and tolerates more sun than most large-leaved rhododendrons. Small, aromatic, dark green leaves turn an attractive plum-purple in cold weather, providing year-round color, and the shrub is smothered in a profusion of small, vivid lavender-pink flowers in very early spring, often the first rhododendron to bloom in a northern garden. Named for breeder Peter J. Mezitt and bred specifically for extreme cold hardiness, it tolerates far colder winters than most large-leaved rhododendron hybrids and adapts to more sun exposure, making it one of the most widely planted and reliable rhododendrons across the colder regions of North America. Mulch to keep roots cool, avoid planting in heavy or poorly drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; tolerates light frost.
directions: Direct sow in early spring, covering seed since darkness aids germination; calendula thrives in cool weather and tolerates light frost. This classic cottage-garden blend bears gold and orange flowers from spring to fall on drought- and heat-tolerant plants. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and save the edible petals for teas, salads, and salves. Grow in full sun for the fullest flowering.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost in cool soil.
directions: Sow Pacific Beauty calendula a quarter inch deep near your last frost date, favoring the cool weather this heirloom loves. It produces a cheerful daisy-like mix of gold, orange, and cream blooms on plants up to two feet tall. The petals are both edible and valued in herbal skin-care preparations. Deadhead regularly for a long season, and let a few blooms set seed to self-sow.

common_name: Pacific Blue Ice Hens and Chicks (Silvery-Blue Sempervivum)
plant_note: Plant offsets in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun.
directions: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun; strong sun deepens the cool, frosty color this cultivar is grown for. Pacific Blue Ice is a Pacific hybridizer selection prized for its tight, symmetrical rosettes of powdery, silvery blue-gray leaves with a faint violet blush at the tips, a cooler, icier tone than the greens, reds, and purples typical of most hens and chicks. It offsets freely to form a slowly spreading mat, making it a good color-contrast companion to the warmer-toned sempervivum cultivars in a mixed trough or crevice planting. As with all sempervivums, sharp drainage is essential — the plant tolerates drought and poor soil far better than it tolerates wet feet.

plant_note: Start indoors early; chilling seed improves germination.
directions: Start seed indoors early, chilling it briefly to improve germination for this award-winning heirloom perennial. Set plants in rich, well-drained soil and grow in groups of three or more for impact. Tall, elegant spires pack large blossoms in pink, violet, and many shades of blue; stake the stems against wind. Cut back after the first flush to encourage a second bloom, and provide steady moisture.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Pacific ninebark is an excellent riparian shrub for stream banks, rain gardens, and moist native plant gardens on the West Coast.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade along stream banks, pond margins, or in rain gardens; Pacific ninebark is a native riparian shrub of the Pacific Northwest excellent for stabilizing stream banks and moist slopes. Physocarpus capitatus is a large, vigorous, deciduous native shrub of western North American stream banks and moist slopes producing lobed, maple-like leaves, rounded clusters of small, creamy-white flowers in late spring, and ornamental, papery, red-bronze seed capsules in fall and winter; the exfoliating bark (which gives ninebark its name) peels in thin, multi-layered strips to reveal mahogany-colored inner bark, providing attractive winter texture. It is an important wildlife shrub, providing nesting cover, shelter, and browse for deer and elk; the flowers support native bees and butterflies. More vigorous and adapted to wet conditions than the eastern ninebark (P. opulifolius).

plant_note: Transplant balled or container shrubs in fall into acidic, well-drained forest soil rich in organic matter, keeping the crown at grade and mulching with conifer needles or shredded bark.
directions: Transplant balled or container shrubs in fall into acidic, well-drained forest soil rich in organic matter, keeping the crown at grade and mulching with conifer needles or shredded bark. This is the dominant evergreen shrub layer beneath Douglas fir and redwood forests from British Columbia to California, so it thrives in dense to dappled shade and resents hot, exposed sites with reflected heat. Large trusses of pink to rosy-purple bell-shaped flowers appear in late spring above leathery, dark green leaves, giving structure and winter interest to a shaded native garden long after bloom. It is the state flower of Washington and pairs naturally with sword fern, salal, and huckleberry in a Pacific Northwest woodland planting.

common_name: Pacino Sunflower (Compact Dwarf Branching Pot Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost; Pacino stays compact enough to grow in large containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Sow in full sun in average garden soil or a large container with drainage; Pacino stays a compact 14-20 inches tall, far shorter than typical branching sunflowers, while still producing multiple golden-yellow blooms per plant. Its dwarf, bushy habit makes it one of the few sunflower cultivars genuinely suited to patio pots and small-space gardens without staking. Flowers open earlier than most sunflower types, often within about seven to eight weeks of sowing, giving a quick, reliable display for container plantings or edging a bed. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the compact plants tidy and encourage additional side blooms through summer.

plant_note: Propagate from offsets or leaf cuttings in very well-drained cactus mix; paddle plant develops the most intense red-orange leaf color when exposed to bright full sun and cool temperatures (below 50°F). In warm, shaded conditions the leaves remain mostly green. It is monocarpic — the rosette dies after flowering — but leaves numerous offsets before doing so.
directions: Grow in very well-drained, lean cactus mix in full sun; paddle plant is a dramatic South African succulent grown primarily for its extraordinary foliage — large, flat, rounded, paddle-shaped leaves arranged in a stacked, overlapping rosette pattern like a fan of stacked poker chips or a head of red-tinted cabbage, each leaf reaching 4–6 inches across. In full sun and cool temperatures, the leaves develop vivid, coral-red to orange-red margins and suffused coloring, with the intensity of red color directly proportional to sun and cold stress. In winter sun, the entire rosette can become a burning red-orange — one of the most dramatic color effects achievable with any succulent. The plant is monocarpic, producing a tall flower spike of tubular yellow flowers after several years of growth and then dying, but it generates offsets that continue the colony. Long confused with the similar K. thyrsiflora, which has yellow flowers and powdery-white leaf coatings — K. luciae has red-edged leaves and is the true 'paddle plant.' Excellent in containers, rock gardens, and succulent borders in zone 9–11.

plant_note: Divide basal suckers or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring after frost; pagoda flower spreads by underground stolons and requires ample space — allow 6 feet on each side for a mature, freely suckering clump.
directions: Divide suckers or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; pagoda flower (scarlet clerodendrum, tower of gold) is a Southeast Asian tropical shrub that produces one of the most impressive flower structures of any tropical plant — enormous, upright, tiered panicles reaching 18–24 inches in height, composed of hundreds of small, intensely orange-scarlet, tubular flowers arranged in dense whorls that give the flower head the appearance of a brilliantly colored pagoda structure. The large, dark-green, boldly lobed leaves are themselves dramatic, and the entire plant creates a powerful tropical statement in summer and fall borders. It spreads steadily by underground suckers to form colonies, which can be controlled by mowing the perimeter. Hummingbirds and butterflies are strongly attracted to the flower heads. Semi-shade tolerant — performs well in dappled light under high canopy trees. In zone 9 top growth is sometimes killed by frost but resprouts vigorously from the root. 'Starburst' is a popular selection.

common_name: Pagoda Trout Lily (Yellow Hybrid Trout Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous shade; Pagoda is a vigorous hybrid trout lily that naturalizes more readily than the wild species and tolerates a slightly wider range of conditions, though it still prefers cool woodland soil and benefits from a mulch of leaf litter.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil, then leave undisturbed to naturalize and multiply into drifts over several years. Pagoda is a robust hybrid trout lily (a cross involving Erythronium tuolumnense and E. californicum) producing mottled, glossy green leaves and nodding, bright sulfur-yellow, reflexed flowers with a brownish base held on wiry stems in early to mid spring, typically two to three blooms per bulb rather than the single flower of most wild species. It is one of the easiest and most vigorous trout lilies for the garden, spreading by offsets to form substantial colonies faster than native species, and pairs beautifully with hellebores, epimedium, and early ferns in a shaded border. Foliage yellows and goes dormant by early summer, so interplant with later-emerging perennials to cover the gap.

plant_note: Plant rhizomatous bulbs just below the soil surface in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; paintbrush lily requires consistent moisture during growth (spring through fall) but prefers reduced watering when dormant in winter. The flowers often appear before the leaves in spring. All parts are highly toxic if ingested. Plants resent disturbance — choose a permanent location.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; paintbrush lily is one of the most dramatically beautiful shade-garden bulbs in the world — a South African native of forest margins and shaded kloofs (ravines) producing in spring (often before the leaves emerge) a spectacular, dense, globe-like umbel of 50–100 individual, bright scarlet-red to orange-red flowers on a stout stem, each flower having a slender, tubular perianth with projecting stamens, the aggregate effect being a large, spherical, brilliant-red paintbrush head of exuberant, vivid color. The flower heads are 6–8 inches across — a substantial, tropical-looking display on a moderate-sized plant. After the flowers fade, large, broad, matte-green leaves with prominent veins emerge to provide attractive foliage through summer. Orange-red berries follow the flowers. In zones 9–11, it is an outstanding shade-garden perennial for the tropical or subtropical garden, combining with other shade-tolerant South African species. A few specimens in a shaded border create an unmistakably tropical, bold statement in the spring garden.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds immediately after collecting in fall, 1-2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil; painted buckeye seeds lose viability quickly and should not be allowed to dry out before planting. Plant in a location with at least some shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; painted buckeye is a native small tree or large shrub of the southeastern US Piedmont and Coastal Plain, naturally growing in the understory of moist woodland slopes and stream banks. It is the most heat-tolerant native buckeye, making it an excellent choice for southern gardens where the more common red buckeye (A. pavia) and Ohio buckeye (A. glabra) can struggle in summer heat. The pale cream to yellow flower clusters in spring attract ruby-throated hummingbirds and large bees. Like all buckeyes, the large, shiny seeds are toxic to humans and livestock, but are an important food source for squirrels which chew through the outer covering to reach the seed. The foliage often develops excellent yellow fall color.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in cool soil.
directions: This tricolor painted daisy opens bold three-inch blooms with concentric rings of white, pink, red, or yellow around a dark bullseye center. Sow seeds directly in early spring in cool soil, covering lightly and thinning seedlings once they establish. Grow in full sun with average moisture, and stake if plants grow lanky in rich soil. Deadhead to extend the display and cut stems for cheerful, long-lasting bouquets.

plant_note: Sow in place in early spring for summer color.
directions: Direct sow annual painted daisy in early spring where plants are to bloom. The colorful banded daisies with contrasting central rings make superb long-lasting cut flowers. Grow in full sun and average, well-drained soil, staking taller plants in windy sites. Deadhead frequently to prolong flowering, and the plants often self-sow lightly in favorable conditions.

common_name: Painted Drop Tongue (Crinkle-Leaf Chinese Evergreen, Silver Queen Aglaonema)
plant_note: Grow in shade to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or a well-draining container mix; Aglaonema crispum is one of the parent species behind the thousands of hybrid 'Chinese Evergreen' cultivars sold in the houseplant trade. It is one of the most shade-tolerant of all ornamental plants, thriving in deep interior shade where virtually no other ornamental plant will survive. In zone 10-12, it can be grown as a permanent outdoor shade groundcover or low accent plant; in zone 9, it is a container plant that should be protected from temperatures below 50°F. CAUTION: all Aglaonema contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic to pets and irritating if the sap contacts skin.
directions: Grow in shade to deep shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil — Painted Drop Tongue is one of the most shade-tolerant ornamental plants available and will grow in the dim light of a north-facing room or the deep shade under dense tree canopy where nearly all other plants fail. Aglaonema crispum is a clumping, stemmed, tropical perennial in the Araceae family native to the Philippines and Southeast Asia — one of the approximately 25 species of Aglaonema, the group broadly marketed under the common name 'Chinese Evergreen,' and an important parent species in the development of the many hundreds of cultivated hybrids. The species form produces erect stems with large (12-inch), broadly ovate to elliptic leaves in dark, lustrous green with irregular blotches and streaks of silver-gray to pale green — a naturally variegated pattern that makes the leaves ornamental in the low-light conditions where the plant thrives. The crisped or wavy leaf margin (reflected in the species name crispum and some common names) adds texture. In bright indirect to low light, Aglaonema crispum produces consistent ornamental foliage year-round with minimal inputs. Occasional small aroid spathes (white spathe, white to green spadix) appear in mature plants but are not the ornamental feature. Grown as one of the most reliable and adaptable shade ornamentals available for indoor, patio, and outdoor shade garden use in zone 10-12. CAUTION: sap contains calcium oxalate; toxic to pets.

common_name: Painted Fingernail Plant (Fingernail Bromeliad, Spectabilis Neoregelia)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or in a shaded, frost-free container garden; Painted Fingernail Plant tolerates only brief dips near 40°F and needs protection below that. Pot in a coarse, well-draining bark-based bromeliad mix, since the roots mainly serve to anchor the plant rather than take up water. Keep the central cup filled and offset the parent rosette's pups into their own pots once they have a few roots of their own.
directions: Provide bright, indirect light — stronger light intensifies the red leaf tips that give this species its common name, while low light produces an all-green rosette. Neoregelia spectabilis is a medium-sized epiphytic bromeliad native to the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, forming a broad, open rosette of stiff, olive-green to bronze strap-shaped leaves that are each tipped in vivid red, resembling a hand of freshly painted fingernails; the leaf undersides carry fine silvery-gray cross-banding. Like other Neoregelias, its true flowers are small and largely hidden within the central water-filled cup, so the plant is grown chiefly for its foliage color and form rather than its bloom. It tolerates a wider range of light than many bromeliads and adapts well to bright windowsills, making it a popular beginner species among Neoregelia collectors.

plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Painted Lady gladiolus is a winter-growing, summer-dormant Cape species that produces its soft pink, dark-marked flowers in late spring, following the same reverse growth cycle as other winter-rainfall South African bulbs.
directions: Plant corms in fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and allow the foliage to die back naturally in early summer without supplemental water; Painted Lady gladiolus follows the winter-growing, summer-dormant cycle typical of Cape winter-rainfall bulbs, so it needs to stay dry and undisturbed through the hot months. Gladiolus carneus bears loose, one-sided spikes of three to twelve softly funnel-shaped, pale pink to cream flowers marked with deep carmine feathering on the lower petals, blooming for up to a month in late spring. It is native to sandstone and clay slopes of the Western Cape and performs best in zones 8-10 where winters stay mild and wet while summers turn dry, making it a good companion for other Cape bulbs like Sparaxis and Babiana in a Mediterranean-style bulb border. Where summer irrigation cannot be avoided, grow it in containers that can be kept dry and dormant through summer.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Painted Lady bears soft salmon-pink single flowers on a vigorous tropical hibiscus shrub.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Painted Lady bears large, single flowers in a soft, warm salmon-pink, a gentler and more subdued tone than the bold reds and oranges typical of many tropical hibiscus, making it a good choice for a pastel-themed tropical planting or as a softer accent among brighter companions. It flowers steadily from spring through frost in warm climates, with each individual bloom lasting only a single day before a fresh flush of buds takes its place. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Painted Lady philodendron holds its bright lime and yellow coloring best with strong, consistent indirect light.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Painted Lady philodendron holds its bright lime and yellow coloring best with strong, consistent indirect light. Glossy, heart-shaped leaves emerge a bright chartreuse-yellow speckled and streaked with darker green flecks, a lively, sunny leaf coloring that brightens a shaded corner far more than the deep greens typical of most climbing philodendrons, with the mottled pattern varying somewhat from leaf to leaf. A vigorous climber, it develops larger, more vividly patterned leaves when trained up a moss pole rather than left to trail, and its bright color makes an eye-catching contrast against darker-leaved houseplant companions. Provide bright indirect light to maintain the vivid yellow-green coloring, keep humidity moderate to high, and water when the top inch of potting mix has dried.

common_name: Painted Lady Sweet Pea (1730s Historic Bicolor Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for a late winter to spring bloom; provide a trellis for the twining tendrils to climb.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, training the twining tendrils onto a trellis or netting. Painted Lady is among the oldest named sweet pea cultivars still in cultivation, documented in England since the 1730s, prized for its charming bicolor blooms — soft rose-pink standards paired with white or pale blush wings — and a strong, classic sweet pea fragrance closer to the wild species than many modern, less-scented hybrids. The relatively small, dainty flowers are less showy than modern grandiflora sweet peas but bloom prolifically over a long cool-season window and make outstanding, richly perfumed cut flowers for small bouquets. In mild Gulf Coast winters, sow in fall so vines establish through the cool months for a strong late-winter to early-spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 4-6 weeks before) in well-drained, average to poor, neutral soil in full sun; painted sage is a drought-tolerant, heat-loving annual that blooms best in lean soil with minimal fertilizer, and deadheading extends the display.
directions: Salvia viridis (syn. S. horminum) is an annual Mediterranean sage grown primarily for its striking, colored bracts — terminal clusters of papery, veined, pink, purple, or white leaf-like structures surrounding tiny, insignificant flowers — that provide vivid color for 2-3 months in summer and are outstanding both in the garden and as dried flowers (the colored bracts hold their color well when dried and are superior to many everlastings). The plant has a mild sage-like fragrance and has some historical use as a beer flavoring. The cultivar series 'Oxford Blue', 'Pink Sunday', and 'White Swan' are the most widely grown ornamental selections.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant 2–3 weeks before last frost as plants tolerate light frost.
directions: Sow seeds in the dark (cover lightly and keep the tray in darkness) at 60–70°F; darkness improves germination for salpiglossis. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the petunia-like flowers with intricate veining in yellow, red, purple, maroon, and bicolor thrive in cool weather. Provide light support with twiggy stakes since plants can flop in wind; pinch tips once for bushier plants. Plants decline in summer heat — treat them as a spring and fall flower in warm climates or plant where afternoon shade moderates temperatures.

plant_note: Plant divisions immediately upon receiving in early spring in very acidic, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this plant is difficult to establish and should be purchased only from reputable nursery-propagated sources as it is protected in many states.
directions: Plant in moist, very acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; painted trillium is widely regarded as the most beautiful of the eastern trilliums, producing white flowers with a vivid magenta-pink V-shaped painted mark at the base of each petal in late spring that gives the plant its common name. It grows in coniferous and mixed forest understories with strongly acidic soil, particularly in association with hemlock and pine. It is more demanding of soil acidity than the common great white trillium (T. grandiflorum) and more difficult to establish in the garden. Purchase only nursery-propagated divisions from reputable sources, as wild populations are declining due to collection pressure and deer browsing. Very slow from seed — divisions from established colonies are the only practical propagation method.

common_name: Palace Purple Coral Bells (AAS Deep Bronze-Purple Foliage Shade Perennial)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Palace Purple develops its best deep bronze-purple foliage color in partial shade with some morning sun — full deep shade dulls the color toward brownish-green, while intense afternoon sun in zone 9 can scorch the leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Palace Purple is the original All-America Selections Heuchera winner that launched the contemporary interest in foliage-first coral bells breeding — producing distinctive broad, maple-like leaves in deep bronze-purple to burgundy-red with metallic overtones that hold their color through the growing season in appropriate conditions, brightening shaded garden beds with warm, rich color unavailable from most other shade perennials. The foliage is the primary ornamental feature: the deeply lobed, mahogany-bronze leaves are striking in partial-shade borders where they contrast with green or chartreuse companions. Tall, airy scapes of small cream-white to pale pink flowers appear above the foliage in late spring, providing delicate vertical interest and nectar for small pollinators. Palace Purple is grown primarily from seed and shows some variability in foliage color intensity — the best seedlings display deep, uniform bronze-purple while weaker selections tend toward greenish-bronze. In Gulf South conditions, Heuchera is somewhat heat-sensitive — zone 9 is at the warm edge of reliable performance, and siting in morning-sun-afternoon-shade positions with consistent moisture is essential. Well-drained soil that avoids waterlogging is critical: crown rot in poorly drained or waterlogged soil is the primary cause of heuchera failure. Division every 2–3 years when the crown becomes woody and elevated from the soil surface rejuvenates the plant and maintains vigor.

common_name: Palace Purple Heuchera (Palace Purple Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions or transplants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Palace Purple is the classic dark-leafed heuchera that spawned an entire generation of dark-foliage coral bells, and remains one of the best performers in heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Palace Purple heuchera was the groundbreaking plant-of-the-year when it received the Perennial Plant of the Year award in 1991 — the first dark-leafed heuchera to receive widespread commercial distribution, it opened the door for the enormous wave of purple-, bronze-, and dark-foliage heucheras that followed. The large, lobed leaves emerge deep burgundy-purple in spring and hold their color best in partial shade with some direct light; in dense shade they fade toward bronze-green. Small creamy-white flowers on wiry stems appear in early summer above the foliage and attract pollinators. Palace Purple is one of the more heat-tolerant heucheras available, performing well in zone 8–9 with afternoon shade, consistent moisture, and good drainage. Divide every 3–4 years in fall or early spring when the crown heaves out of the ground; replant the vigorous offsets and discard the woody center.

plant_note: Start seeds after cold-moist stratification for 4–8 weeks, or direct sow in fall for natural stratification, in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun.
directions: Start seeds after cold-moist stratification for 4–8 weeks, or direct sow in fall for natural stratification, in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun. Echinacea pallida is a midwestern prairie native easily distinguished from other coneflowers by its unusually long (up to 4 inches), very narrow, drooping, pale-pink to pale-mauve ray petals that give the flower a distinctive "swept back" or "mop-headed" appearance unlike any other coneflower; it is native to dry to mesic prairies from Michigan and Tennessee west to Nebraska and is an important source of late-spring to early-summer nectar for bumblebees and specialist coneflower bees. The root is used medicinally like other echinaceas; it is somewhat more floriferous and heat-tolerant than E. angustifolia and easier to establish in garden conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; pale corydalis germinates in cool soil and self-sows freely in rocky, lean, acidic, well-drained soil. It is a biennial to short-lived perennial that grows naturally in disturbed rocky soils, talus slopes, and open rocky woods across northeastern North America.
