directions: Direct sow in fall in rocky, well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; pale corydalis is a delicate, finely cut-leaved, blue-green biennial of rocky, disturbed soils in northeastern North America, producing small, tubular, pink-tipped flowers with yellow ends from spring through summer. The flowers have the distinctive spurring and shape of the Corydalis/Fumitory family, with petals fused into two pairs, the outer pair spurred. The feathery blue-green foliage is attractive throughout the growing season. Self-sows freely in appropriate rocky, lean conditions to persist indefinitely. An excellent plant for dry, rocky garden walls, scree beds, and disturbed rocky soil in partial shade. The flowers attract long-tongued bees and hummingbirds. Often establishes spontaneously in rocky garden edges and wall crevices in the Northeast.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean woodland or disturbed soil in partial shade to shade; pale corydalis is a weedy annual that germinates in fall or early spring and grows in disturbed woodland edges, open woodlands, and roadsides across the eastern US. Self-sows prolifically.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean woodland, edge, or disturbed soil in partial shade; pale corydalis is a widespread eastern US native annual or biennial, smaller and more adaptable than yellow fumewort, growing in a wider range of disturbed, edge, and open woodland habitats from the Midwest south and east to the Atlantic Coastal Plain. The pale cream to yellow, small, spurred flowers are typical of the Corydalis genus. It is more tolerant of dry conditions and disturbed soils than yellow fumewort, commonly appearing as a winter annual in disturbed sites, roadsides, and the edges of open woods across its range. The lacy, fernlike foliage is consistently attractive. An easy, self-sowing, low-maintenance annual for naturalizing in lightly shaded gardens, woodland edges, and naturalistic settings where the delicate ferny texture provides spring interest before disappearing in early summer.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring into lean, well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; pale evening primrose spreads by rhizomes in loose, sandy ground and naturalizes readily once established.
directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; pale evening primrose is a low, spreading native of dry plains and sandy desert grassland, with narrow gray-green leaves and large, satiny white flowers that open in late afternoon and evening, fading to pale pink as they age the following day. The fragrant, moth-pollinated blooms make it a valuable addition to an evening or moon garden, where the pale flowers glow in low light and draw sphinx moths and other night-flying pollinators. It spreads by shallow, creeping rhizomes to form a loose colony in loose, sandy soil, tolerating extreme heat, drought, and poor fertility better than nearly any bedding annual. Avoid rich soil and heavy irrigation, which encourage floppy, less floriferous growth in this drought-adapted plains native.

plant_note: Sow stratified seed on the soil surface in fall since it needs light and winter chilling to germinate; be patient, plants typically take two to three years to reach flowering size.
directions: Sow stratified seed on the soil surface in fall since it needs light and winter chilling to germinate, and be patient — plants typically take two to three years to reach flowering size. Clusters of creamy-yellow, bottle-shaped flowers open in late summer at the stem tips of this upland prairie and woodland-edge species, and they are almost exclusively pollinated by large bumblebees strong enough to force the petals apart. Plant it in a mesic to dry-mesic prairie planting or oak savanna restoration where it will not be shaded out or overtopped by aggressive neighbors. Once established the deep-rooted crown is long-lived and rewards minimal disturbance.

plant_note: Best fall-sown or cold-moist stratified for 60 days, since seed benefits from winter chilling; established plants are long-lived and need little further attention.
directions: Sow stratified seed or set out plugs in prairie or meadow plantings with well-drained to average soil; the smooth, glaucous, silver-backed leaves make a bold textural statement even before the flat-topped clusters of small ivory flowers open in mid to late summer. It is a favorite nectar source for a wide range of small bees, wasps, and beetles, and its architectural height and pale foliage pair well with grasses and taller composites in a naturalistic border. Once established the deep taproot makes the plant very drought tolerant and it rarely needs staking despite its height. Leave seed heads standing through winter for visual interest and to let it self-sow modestly.

plant_note: Self-sows freely and typically requires no direct sowing once established in a moist, shaded location; plants emerge from the previous year's seed bank in late spring. In new locations, direct sow in moist soil in shade after last frost and keep evenly moist until germination.
directions: Allow to naturalize in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; pale jewelweed is a native annual of moist, shaded forest floors, streambanks, and seepy woodland edges across eastern North America. Closely related to the orange-flowered spotted jewelweed (I. capensis), this species produces clear, pale yellow flowers with a more open, cup-like shape and faint reddish-brown spotting. The explosive seed pods are famously touch-sensitive — ripe pods rupture with a forceful spring mechanism when touched, flinging seeds several feet — a feature particularly delightful for children. The succulent, translucent stems produce a watery sap long used to soothe poison ivy rash and insect stings. An excellent self-sowing shade annual that naturalizes rapidly in moist woodland gardens, forming showy drifts of yellow from midsummer through fall. Hummingbirds and bumblebees pollinate the flowers.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; Clematis versicolor is a native vine of glades, cedar barrens, and rocky limestone woods in the Ozarks and surrounding region, producing urn-shaped, pale lavender to greenish flowers in midsummer followed by showy, feathery seed heads.
directions: Plant at the base of a fence, trellis, or shrub where the roots can be shaded; shade the root zone with a stone or low groundcover while allowing the vine to climb into sunlight. Clematis versicolor (pale leatherflower) is a rare and seldom-cultivated native vine of the Ozarks and Interior Highlands of Missouri, Arkansas, and adjacent states, found on rocky, limestone-derived glades and open cedar-hardwood barrens in thin, alkaline soil; its urn-shaped or pendent, pale lavender to greenish-purple flowers (about 1 inch long) appear in midsummer after most other clematis have finished blooming, followed by large, globe-shaped, feathery seed heads that are attractive in fall. One of the leatherflower clematis group (Viorna section), sharing the nodding, urn-shaped flower form with C. crispa and C. pitcheri. Exceptionally drought-tolerant once established; grows naturally in dry, thin soils over rocky limestone and does not want summer irrigation. An outstanding rare native vine for dry, partially shaded garden settings.

plant_note: Surface sow in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; pale lobelia is an annual or biennial that self-seeds readily in suitable conditions, maintaining itself in the garden from year to year without replanting.
directions: Lobelia appendiculata is a delicate, small-flowered annual to biennial native lobelia of moist disturbed sites, roadsides, sandy flats, and open pine flatwoods in the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Texas; it produces wispy, branching stems with very narrow leaves and small pale-blue to white, two-lipped flowers with a distinctive appendage (hence appendiculata) on the calyx lobes, blooming from spring through summer. It is one of the smaller and more delicate native lobelias, useful as a naturalistic, self-seeding filler in moist native garden settings in the Deep South and Gulf Coast. Surface sow in fall without covering seeds; the plant self-seeds readily once established and will naturalize in appropriate moist, open conditions.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic (pH 3.5-5.5), nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum bog medium in full sun; keep standing in a tray of pure rain water or distilled water 1-2 inches deep year-round — never fertilize and never use tap water.
directions: Pale pitcher plant is the characteristic Sarracenia of the longleaf pine savannas and bogs of the western Gulf Coastal Plain, native from the Florida Panhandle through Louisiana, Texas, and southern Arkansas, distinguished by pale yellow-green to cream pitchers with fine reddish veining and a broad, wavy-edged, hood-like lid that helps keep rain out of the trap. Like its relatives, it lures insects with nectar-like secretions along the pitcher rim, and prey slide down the slick, downward-hair-lined interior into digestive fluid at the base. Nodding, cream to pale yellow flowers with a faint sweet fragrance appear on separate leafless stalks in early spring, ahead of or alongside the season's first pitchers. As the most naturally Gulf Coast-adapted pitcher plant species, it tolerates the region's hot, humid summers particularly well and is an excellent choice for a home bog garden in zone 7b-9, needing only pure water, full sun, and nutrient-poor, consistently wet acidic soil — never fertilize or plant in ordinary garden soil, both of which quickly kill Sarracenia.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, dry, rocky soil in full sun; pale poppy mallow is native to the dry, calcareous prairies and cedar glades of the south-central and central US, distinguished from other winecups by its lighter pink to nearly white flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; pale poppy mallow is a lower-growing, softer-colored winecup species with flowers in shades of pale pink to almost white — a softer, more delicate palette than the intense magenta-wine of most Callirhoe. The plant is native to dry, calcareous prairies, cedar glades, and rocky outcrops of the central US. Its lower stature (8–18 inches) makes it useful as a front-of-border wildflower or rock garden perennial. Like other Callirhoe, it develops a deep, fleshy taproot that makes it drought tolerant once established but difficult to transplant when mature. The pale flowers are produced from spring through summer, providing a long season of soft color. A charming and unusual alternative to the more commonly grown deep-colored winecups.

plant_note: Fall sowing or cold stratification improves germination of this native seed.
directions: Pale purple coneflower is a native prairie perennial with elegant, drooping lavender-pink petals around a tall spiky cone. Sow seed outdoors in fall or cold-stratify before spring sowing to break dormancy. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, where the deep taproot makes it very drought tolerant once established. It draws bees and butterflies in bloom and finches to the seed heads, which can be left standing for winter interest.

plant_note: Sow direct at or just after last frost in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; pale touch-me-not often grows alongside orange jewelweed (I. capensis) in moist wooded areas.
directions: Sow direct at last frost in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; pale touch-me-not self-seeds prolifically in favorable conditions and once established naturalizes reliably without further intervention. Impatiens pallida is the yellow-flowered counterpart of the orange jewelweed (I. capensis) and is found in similar moist, shaded habitats across eastern North America; it produces succulent, translucent stems and pale-yellow, lightly spotted, spurred flowers from mid-summer to frost that are less intensely colored than the orange species but equally attractive to hummingbirds and long-tongued bumblebees. Like its relative, the seed pods explode when ripe, dispersing seeds vigorously. The two species frequently grow side by side and make a complementary pair in naturalized, moist woodland gardens; pale touch-me-not tends to prefer slightly less acidic, slightly less wet conditions than orange jewelweed. Stems can be used in the same folk remedies as I. capensis.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pale yellow-eyed grass is larger and bolder than the blue-flowered North American sisyrinchiums — it forms iris-like fans of gray-green, sword-shaped leaves and produces in late spring–early summer multiple upright flower spikes of small, pale creamy-yellow, six-petaled flowers with purple veining. It self-sows freely and can form substantial naturalized clumps. Short-lived perennial that maintains itself by seeding.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pale yellow-eyed grass is a significantly larger and more architectural plant than the familiar blue-flowered North American sisyrinchiums — it forms bold, iris-like fans of flat, sword-shaped, gray-green leaves (distinctly iris-like in form and arrangement, unlike the grass-like leaves of smaller sisyrinchiums) and in late spring through early summer produces multiple, upright, stiffly erect flower spikes of small, cup-shaped, pale cream to soft primrose-yellow flowers with delicate purple veining, packed along the upper portions of the stem in the manner of a slender poker lily. The effect is refined and distinctive — pale, cream-yellow flowers on architectural gray-green sword-leaf fans — both restrained and elegant in the border. A short-lived perennial that replenishes itself freely from self-sown seed in open, well-drained, disturbed soil — functioning practically as a self-maintaining garden plant in zones 5–8. The cultivar 'Aunt May' (variegated cream-striped leaves) is widely available and more commonly grown than the type. Native to Argentina and Chile; naturalized in parts of western Europe.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination or direct sow in early spring; paleleaf sunflower prefers moderately dry to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun, growing naturally at woodland edges, dry upland forest margins, and disturbed clearings across the eastern US.
directions: Plant in moderately dry to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; paleleaf woodland sunflower is one of the most shade-tolerant native sunflowers, growing naturally at the margins of woodlands, dry upland forest edges, and open clearings where it receives dappled to partial shade. The pale green undersides of the leaves distinguish it from similar species. Bright yellow daisy flowers in late summer provide excellent late-season pollinator value — the seeds are important food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. As a woodland-edge sunflower, it is particularly valuable for the partial-shade garden where most sunflowers would not bloom reliably. Spreads by rhizomes to form modest colonies without being overly aggressive. A natural companion for native asters and goldenrods in late-season partial-shade borders.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring into well-drained, dry, alkaline, rocky or clay-loam soil in full sun to light shade; paleleaf yucca is a stemless, slow-growing Texas prairie and woodland-edge endemic best propagated by division.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown rosettes in well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun to light shade; paleleaf yucca forms a stemless, symmetrical rosette of broad, pale blue-green leaves distinctly softer and paler than most yuccas, with smooth or minimally fibrous leaf margins. A tall flower spike of creamy white, bell-shaped blooms rises 3 to 5 feet above the foliage in late spring, pollinated by the same specialized yucca moths as other Yucca species, and is a striking accent even when the plant is not in bloom. Native to the North Central Texas Blackland Prairie and Cross Timbers, it tolerates heavy clay and limestone soils better than many desert yuccas, as long as drainage is adequate and standing water is avoided. Extremely low maintenance once established, it needs no fertilizer or supplemental water beyond an occasional deep soak in extended drought.

plant_note: Surface sow seeds (do not cover — need light to germinate) in moist, slightly acidic soil in spring; palespike lobelia grows naturally in a wide variety of open to semi-shaded habitats including dry roadsides, open woods, meadows, and prairies across most of eastern North America. It is shorter-lived than great blue lobelia (L. siphilitica) but self-sows readily to maintain colonies.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to average soil in full sun to part shade; palespike lobelia is one of the most widely distributed and ecologically adaptable native lobelias in eastern North America — native to dry roadsides and disturbed soils, open prairies, open woodlands, and rocky glades from Quebec to Florida and west to North Dakota. It produces erect, unbranched spikes bearing a dense, elongating raceme of small, pale-blue to nearly-white, two-lipped lobelia flowers from June through September — the flowers significantly smaller and paler than the showier great blue lobelia (L. siphilitica) or cardinal flower (L. cardinalis), but produced freely and over a very long season on a more adaptable and drought-tolerant plant. This adaptability to dry and disturbed conditions makes it useful in difficult sites where the more demanding, moisture-loving native lobelias would fail. It is visited by native bees and an important native plant for open-habitat gardens. Self-sows to maintain colonies in appropriate conditions. More drought-tolerant and sun-tolerant than great blue lobelia, and better suited to natural, low-maintenance naturalistic garden settings.

common_name: Palibin Dwarf Korean Lilac (Compact Long-Lived Fragrant Dwarf Lilac)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Palibin's naturally dwarf, dense habit needs no shearing to keep a tidy rounded form, making it useful for foundation plantings and low hedges.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and prune only lightly right after bloom to remove spent flower heads, since Palibin naturally keeps a dense, rounded, proportionate form without regular shearing. This dwarf Korean lilac is smothered each spring in masses of small, intensely fragrant pale lavender-pink flower panicles that are proportionate to its compact size, unlike many lilacs where large blooms overwhelm a small shrub. Its naturally tidy habit, fine-textured blue-green foliage, and good resistance to powdery mildew have made it one of the most widely planted dwarf lilacs for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and low informal hedges. Like other lilacs it needs real winter chill to flower reliably and performs best at the cooler end of its hardiness range, but established plants are tough, long-lived, and essentially maintenance-free.

plant_note: Plant divisions after all danger of frost has passed in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; palm grass is root-hardy in zones 9b and warmer and will resprout from the base after mild frost, but tops are killed by temperatures below 28°F.
directions: Plant in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in zones 9–11, or grow as a container specimen brought indoors in colder climates; palm grass is a dramatic tropical ornamental grass from Southeast Asia and the Pacific, producing enormous pleated and corrugated leaves 2–4 feet long that closely resemble miniature palm fronds, creating a bold exotic statement in shaded tropical and subtropical gardens. It thrives in the conditions that challenge most ornamentals — deep shade, humid heat, and competition from tree roots — making it invaluable for tropical understory plantings. Caution: palm grass has naturalized and become invasive in parts of Florida, Hawaii, and other frost-free regions; check local regulations before planting in zones 10–11. In the tropics, the young shoots are used as a vegetable similar to bamboo shoots.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring after all cold weather has passed, positioning the crown at or just above soil level in a shaded bed enriched with compost.
directions: Plant divisions in rich, well-draining soil in a fully or deeply shaded location, spacing clumps 24-36 inches apart to allow the pleated, palm-like leaves to spread without crowding. Water regularly to keep the soil evenly moist, but avoid standing water around the crown. Apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer in spring and again in midsummer to support vigorous foliage. Divide established clumps every 3-4 years in spring to rejuvenate growth and propagate new plants.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, shaded sites; palm sedge can also be started from seed indoors with cold moist stratification but divisions establish far more reliably.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; palm sedge is one of the most dramatic native sedges, producing whorls of long, arching, bright green leaves arranged around the stem nodes in a pattern strikingly reminiscent of a miniature palm tree — hence the common name. It is one of the finest large sedges for moist shade gardens, growing vigorously under tall trees where few grasses survive. The golden fall color and persistent dried winter form add year-round interest. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies and is excellent massed under deciduous trees or along the shaded margins of rain gardens and ponds.

plant_note: Direct sow once the soil has warmed after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks earlier for an earlier display.
directions: Sow directly in well-drained soil once nights stay warm, since this Mediterranean native thrives in heat and resents soggy conditions. Space plants generously to let their rounded, bushy habit fill out, and pinch young growth to encourage more branching and flowers. Bright green, aromatic, feathery foliage is covered from midsummer into fall with cheerful yellow daisy blooms that open from lime-green buds, giving borders and gravel gardens a long season of drought-tolerant color and making it a useful filler for late-summer cutting gardens.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich, freely draining potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; palm-leaf begonia tolerates lower humidity than most large begonias and is more drought-tolerant between waterings than the soft-stemmed types.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; palm-leaf begonia is a Brazilian cane begonia of exceptional architectural distinction — it grows with a tall, upright, woody-stemmed, clump-forming habit reaching 4–8 feet, and each leaf is dramatically and uniquely palmate (palm-shaped), divided into 7–16 long, narrow, deep-green, finger-like leaflets radiating from the leaf stalk like the fingers of an open hand or the fronds of a small palm, creating an unexpectedly tropical, palm-like silhouette that bears almost no resemblance to the typical begonia leaf form. The deeply cut, palmate leaves are themselves ornamentally distinctive and create a refined, unusual tropical foliage effect quite unlike any other begonia species. Periodically the plant produces large, pendulous clusters of small, white, fragrant flowers. The woody, bamboo-like stems develop a corky texture with age. An outstanding architectural begonia for shaded tropical patios, conservatories, and zone 10–12 gardens where its distinctive form can be displayed as a specimen.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost with a month of cold-moist stratification, into very well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Palmer's penstemon self-seeds readily once established and often behaves as a reseeding short-lived perennial.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, sandy or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Palmer's penstemon is one of the tallest and most fragrant of the native penstemons, sending up stout flower spikes 3 to 5 feet high packed with large, pale pink to lilac, snapdragon-like blooms with a distinctive sweet fragrance that carries well through the garden. Broad, gray-green, clasping leaves surround the base and lower stem, giving the plant a somewhat succulent appearance even before flowering begins in late spring. It readily self-sows in loose, disturbed, well-drained soil, often persisting in a planting for many years as a rotating population of new seedlings even though individual plants may be relatively short-lived. Cut spent flower stalks back after bloom if reseeding is not wanted, and avoid rich soil or regular summer irrigation, which shortens its lifespan.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into well-drained, calcareous to neutral rocky or sandy soil.
directions: Palmleaf Scurfpea is a low-growing native perennial of dry, rocky, calcareous prairies and hillsides in Texas and Oklahoma, notable for its palmately compound leaves with five to seven spreading, finger-like leaflets that give the species its name. In spring it produces dense, short spikes of blue to purple pea flowers above silvery-hairy, mat-forming clumps. Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into very well-drained, calcareous to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun. It is an excellent choice for limestone rock gardens and dry prairie restoration plantings, and is highly drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established.

common_name: Pam Puryear Turk's Cap (Pink-Flowered Native Turk's Cap)
plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery plants in spring once frost danger has passed; this soft-pink heirloom Turk's cap selection roots easily and establishes quickly in Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Plant in a bed with morning sun and afternoon shade, or in dappled light beneath trees, and water regularly the first season until the woody base is established. Discovered and popularized by Texas plantswoman Pam Puryear, this selection of the native Turk's cap bears the same twisted pink-red hibiscus-like blooms as the species but in a softer pink shade, opening continuously from late spring through fall. Hummingbirds visit the flowers constantly and songbirds eat the small apple-flavored fruits that follow, making it a dependable wildlife shrub for shady Gulf Coast gardens. It dies back in hard winters but resprouts reliably from the roots each spring.

common_name: Pam's Choice Foxglove (White with Deep Maroon Throat Spots)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors or sow directly in late summer for fall transplanting; in zone 9 foxglove is grown as a winter annual or biennial. Pam's Choice bears white flowers heavily spotted with deep maroon in the throat.
directions: Plant in partial shade — filtered light under tall trees suits it well — in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil. Pam's Choice bears tall spikes of pure white, tubular flowers with dramatic, deep maroon spotting concentrated inside the throat, a striking high-contrast color combination that has made it one of the most popular named foxglove cultivars for cottage-garden and cut-flower use. As a true biennial, plants form a low rosette of foliage in year one and send up the tall flowering spike in year two, though fall-sown plants in mild-winter zones can bloom the following spring; it self-seeds readily where happy. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where children or pets might sample the foliage or flowers.

common_name: Pampas Grass (South American Giant Ornamental Plume Grass)
plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges, or plant container-grown plants in spring after last frost; pampas grass is slow to establish in its first year and then grows rapidly — mature clumps reach full ornamental size (6–10 feet) by year 2–3. Plant in a permanent location with full sun and excellent drainage; the sharp leaf blades require leather gloves when dividing or handling. In zone 9, pampas grass is evergreen to semi-evergreen and rarely needs division for 5–10 years.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; once established, pampas grass is extremely drought-tolerant and requires virtually no supplemental irrigation except during establishment. Pampas grass (Cortaderia selloana) is one of the most dramatic and instantly recognizable ornamental grasses in cultivation — a native of the pampas (grasslands) of Argentina, Brazil, and Chile that forms enormous clumps of arching, sharp-edged, blue-green leaves 4–6 feet tall topped by tall stalks bearing spectacular, feathery, silky white to cream (female) or more narrow silver (male) plumes that emerge in late summer and persist through fall and winter, providing exceptional dried-flower display for 4–6 months. Female plants produce the larger, showier plumes preferred in ornamental use; most commercial plants are female. The plumes, which can reach 12 feet in total height, are outstanding as fresh-cut or dried arrangements and are long-lasting on the plant through winter. Pampas grass is so visually dominant that a single specimen becomes a landscape focal point — the feathery white plumes blowing in late-summer breezes have become iconic in coastal and tropical garden landscapes. In Gulf Coast zone 8–9 conditions, pampas grass is evergreen to semi-evergreen, forming an expanding clump that may need division every 5–7 years as the center dies out. Plants are best divided with a sharp spade or mattock; the razor-sharp leaf margins make leather gloves and long sleeves essential for any hands-on work. Note: pampas grass has become invasive in coastal California and New Zealand and should not be planted in fire-prone areas or where it may escape into natural areas.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm, or start indoors.
directions: Direct sow after frost into warm soil, or start indoors a few weeks earlier, pressing the fine seed onto the surface for light. This blend produces large, feathery plumes ranging from golden-yellow to scarlet on long, straight stems that attract pollinators. The multi-branching plants have handsome foliage and love heat. Harvest for fresh bouquets or hang to dry for lasting arrangements.

plant_note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; panakenake spreads by creeping stems that root as they go, knitting into a solid mat within a season or two under reliable moisture.
directions: Plant divisions or starter plugs in consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; panakenake is a New Zealand native creeping groundcover forming a very low, dense carpet of small, rounded, glossy leaves, studded in summer with tiny white star-shaped flowers followed by an unusual show of small, rounded, deep magenta-purple berries that persist for weeks — a distinctive feature that sets it apart from similar low flowering groundcovers, which typically lack showy fruit. It roots as it spreads and tolerates light foot traffic once established, making it useful between shaded stepping stones or as a lawn substitute in a damp, shaded nook. Keep the soil from drying out, since it thins quickly in drought, and provide reliable shade in hot climates to keep the foliage from scorching. Divide congested patches in spring to fill bare spots or start new plantings.

common_name: Panama Pacific Water Lily (Historic Viviparous Violet-Purple Tropical Day-Bloomer)
plant_note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after water has warmed well past last frost; Panama Pacific, introduced in 1914, is a viviparous tropical day-bloomer producing small plantlets directly on the leaf surface, and shows somewhat better cold tolerance than most tropical water lilies.
directions: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 12 to 18 inches deep in a full-sun pond, waiting until the water has warmed well above 70°F. Panama Pacific, introduced in 1914 and still grown over a century later, bears rich violet-purple, star-shaped day-blooming flowers, and is notable among tropical water lilies for being viviparous, sprouting small new plantlets directly on the leaf surface that can be detached and grown into new plants, an easy and reliable propagation method. It also shows somewhat better cold tolerance than many other tropical cultivars, extending its useful range a bit further into cooler zones before winter dormancy sets in. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly through the growing season, remove spent flowers and yellowing pads, and detach and pot up plantlets as they form.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Panama rose requires acidic soil and reacts to alkalinity with iron deficiency chlorosis — supplement with chelated iron or soil acidifiers if yellowing between the veins occurs.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Panama rose is a Cuban and Central American tropical evergreen shrub in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that produces rounded clusters of small, tubular, brilliant coral-orange to red-orange, five-lobed, fragrant flowers with a yellow eye, borne in profusion at the shoot tips from late spring through fall and intermittently at other seasons — the vivid coral-orange color and sweet fragrance combine to create an attractive and useful shade-tolerant flowering shrub for zone 9–11 gardens. The glossy, dark-green, oval, wrinkled leaves create an attractive foliage backdrop for the bright flowers. Panama rose is shade-tolerant for a tropical flowering shrub and performs acceptably in partial-shade conditions where most comparable orange-flowered shrubs would fail to bloom. It requires acidic soil and is sensitive to alkalinity. In zone 9 it is often damaged or killed by hard freezes but may regrow from established roots. An underused but excellent shade-tolerant flowering shrub for the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; panda plant rarely flowers or sets viable seed in home cultivation, so it is propagated almost exclusively from cuttings and offsets rather than seed.
directions: Grow in bright light with some direct morning sun in very well-drained, gritty cactus mix, watering only after the soil has dried completely. Kalanchoe tomentosa (panda plant) is a Madagascar native prized for its thick, silvery-grey, felted leaves edged in chocolate-brown scalloped markings that resemble a panda's ears, with a dense coat of fine hairs covering the whole plant. Water at the soil line rather than overhead, since the fuzzy leaves trap moisture against the surface and are prone to rot or unsightly spotting if wetted; the same fuzz makes leaf-cutting propagation less reliable than stem cuttings, which root readily in a few weeks. Left to its own devices it forms an upright, sparsely branched shrublet on a windowsill or in a container, and leggy stems can be pinched or cut back hard to encourage bushier new growth from the base.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; dislikes transplanting.
directions: Surface sow the tiny seed in early spring or fall, as poppies need light to germinate and resent transplanting. Tall, slender stems are topped with two- to three-inch silky double and semi-double blooms that shift from deep burgundy to soft pinkish-red, each striped with silver. Pollinators love them, and no two flowers look alike. Thin seedlings and let some self-sow for next season.

common_name: Pandora's Box Daylily (Award-Winning Miniature Eyed Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Pandora's Box is a miniature-flowered daylily bred by Talbott and released in 1980, long a favorite for its sharply contrasting eye zone.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Pandora's Box is an award-winning miniature daylily with cream-colored petals set off by a sharply defined, deep cranberry-purple eye zone around the throat, a striking contrast that has kept it a long-standing garden favorite since its 1980 introduction. The small (under 3 inch), abundant flowers open over a compact, well-branched scape, giving a long, floriferous bloom season typical of the best miniature daylilies. Like other daylilies it tolerates heat, humidity, and average to poor soil with ease once established, needing only routine deadheading of spent scapes to keep the planting tidy. Clumps are long-lived and multiply steadily; divide every four to six years when flowering begins to decline from overcrowding.

common_name: Pandora's Box Hosta (Miniature White-Centered Narrow Green-Margined Hosta)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pandora's Box Hosta is a miniature cultivar with white-centered leaves and narrow green margins, well suited to containers and small garden spaces.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Pandora's Box is a diminutive miniature hosta bearing small leaves with bright white centers edged in a narrow green margin, a high-contrast variegation pattern packed into a tiny mature footprint. Its small size fits containers, rock gardens, and the front edge of a shaded border where larger hosta cultivars would be out of scale. Divide clumps every four to five years in spring if increased numbers are wanted, since the compact habit means division is rarely necessary for plant health.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangea is the most sun and heat tolerant of the garden hydrangeas — it blooms on new wood, so pruning in late winter encourages the largest flower panicles.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — panicle hydrangea is the most heat, sun, and cold tolerant of all hydrangeas, thriving from zone 3 to zone 9 in conditions that would stress or kill bigleaf hydrangeas. It blooms on new wood (unlike bigleaf hydrangeas that bloom on old wood), making it immune to late-frost damage to buds — simply prune hard in late winter and it will bloom reliably every year. The enormous, cone-shaped flower panicles (12–18 inches long) open white or cream in July–August and age to pink and then burgundy-parchment in fall, remaining attractive through winter. Modern cultivars like 'Limelight' (with chartreuse-green flowers), 'Little Lime' (dwarf), 'Quick Fire' (earliest to bloom), and 'Pinky Winky' (deep pink) greatly expand the ornamental range of the species. Flower color cannot be changed by soil pH, unlike bigleaf hydrangeas.

plant_note: Start indoors early in darkness; cool-season bedding plant.
directions: Start seed indoors in darkness eight to ten weeks before setting out, since pansies germinate best without light and prefer cool conditions. This gold-standard performer brightens cool-season gardens with rosy-red blooms and yellow centers on a compact, well-branched habit that resists winter weather. Grow in full sun to part shade in borders, containers, or mass plantings. The flowers are edible and hold up to frost.

plant_note: Start indoors 12–14 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or start in late summer for fall transplanting. Plants tolerate hard frost once established.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 in deep in a moist starting mix; cover the tray with dark plastic as darkness aids germination. Transplant outdoors several weeks before the last frost, as cool weather brings out the richest colors and most abundant bloom. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to prevent seed set, which stops flowering. Plants decline as summer heat arrives; remove and replace with heat-tolerant annuals.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–14 weeks before fall transplant date (August–September in zone 9) in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Viola tricolor is the wild European species parent of modern hybrid pansies and is smaller-flowered, more self-seeding, and more cold-hardy than hybrid types — outstanding for naturalistic winter-garden settings.
directions: Start seeds indoors or sow in place in fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Viola tricolor self-seeds prolifically and naturalizes readily in suitable gardens. Viola tricolor (heartsease or wild pansy) is the original wild European violet from which all modern garden pansies and violas have been derived — a small, free-flowering, self-seeding annual or short-lived perennial producing an abundance of charming, 3/4-to-1.5-inch, three-colored (typically violet-purple, yellow, and white) face-patterned flowers from fall through spring in mild climates. Unlike modern hybrid pansies (Viola × wittrockiana), the species heartsease is smaller-flowered, more prolific, more self-seeding, and more graceful — it naturalizes into a delightful ground-covering mass in cool-season beds, cottage gardens, and informal settings. The plant has a centuries-long history in European folk medicine and culinary use: the edible flowers have been used as garnishes, crystallized for confectionery decoration, and used to make flower teas and infusions (heartsease tea is a traditional folk remedy). In zone 9, sow in September–October for fall-through-spring bloom; the plants self-seed and return annually with minimal intervention. All Viola flowers are edible and mild-flavored.

plant_note: Plant in sharply drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; keep on the dry side, watering only during active summer flushes, since soggy soil in cool weather is its main vulnerability.
directions: Plant this southwestern Chinese cycad in sharply drained soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, taking advantage of its unusual ability among sagos to shrug off brief hard freezes into the teens once mature. Its stiff, gray-green pinnate crown on a low, often branching trunk gives a rugged, sculptural presence to rock gardens and dry Mediterranean-style beds. Keep it on the dry side, watering only during active summer flushes, since soggy soil in cool weather is its main vulnerability. It is an excellent substitute for King Sago in colder zone 8 gardens where Cycas revoluta struggles.

plant_note: Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in early spring, ideally clustered in groups of three or more where the papery, exfoliating bark can be admired year-round.
directions: Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in early spring, ideally clustered in groups of three or more where the strikingly white, papery, exfoliating bark can be admired year-round against evergreens or dark backdrops. This fast-growing, relatively short-lived pioneer tree tolerates cold climates exceptionally well but struggles in prolonged heat and drought, so it performs best in northern gardens rather than the warmer end of its range. Its golden fall color and open canopy make it a favorite specimen for naturalized woodland edges, and the bark historically provided material for canoes and baskets. Keep roots consistently moist and mulched, since paper birch is prone to bronze birch borer when stressed by heat or drought.

plant_note: Do NOT plant in Florida where this species is a listed invasive; in other zone 9–11 regions, sow fine seeds on the surface of moist soil without covering, as they require light to germinate. Nursery-grown transplants establish more reliably than seed.
directions: Outside of Florida, plant Paperbark in full sun in moist to wet soils where its tolerance of flooding, salt spray, and periodic drought makes it an exceptional landscape tree for difficult sites. The distinctive spongy, white papery bark peels in thick layers year-round and is one of the most visually striking bark textures available in subtropical horticulture. Creamy white bottlebrush-like flower spikes appear multiple times per year and attract nectar-feeding birds and insects. This species is federally listed as invasive in Florida and must not be planted there; gardeners in other Gulf Coast and Pacific Coast subtropical regions should confirm local regulations before planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in spring or fall; paperbark maple is slow-growing but tolerant of a wide range of soil conditions. It grows well in part shade, which can actually highlight the cinnamon-colored exfoliating bark better than full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; paperbark maple is widely considered to have the finest bark of any temperate deciduous tree — the rich cinnamon-orange to mahogany-red outer bark peels in papery, tissue-thin curling sheets year-round, revealing layers beneath in a constantly changing mosaic that glows in winter sunlight. The trifoliate leaves turn blazing red-orange in fall, making it a multi-season treasure. It grows slowly to 20–30 feet over 30–40 years, making it appropriate for smaller residential landscapes. Originally from central China, it has been widely planted in the United States since the early 1900s and is reliable in zones 4–8. The combination of exceptional bark, good fall color, and small stature makes it arguably the single best ornamental tree for the four-season garden where space is limited.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; paperbush sets its silvery, silky flower buds in fall and holds them ornamentally through winter before opening in late winter, so avoid pruning after midsummer or next year's display will be lost.
directions: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; paperbush sets its silvery, silky flower buds in fall and holds them ornamentally through winter before opening in late winter, so avoid pruning after midsummer or next year's display will be lost. Edgeworthia chrysantha is a striking Asian shrub with a distinctive tiered, architectural branching structure and large, soft, blue-green leaves, producing rounded clusters of intensely fragrant, tubular, golden-yellow flowers that open from silvery, fur-covered buds in late winter to earliest spring before the leaves emerge. Its combination of bold winter structure, ornamental buds held through the cold months, and richly fragrant late-winter bloom makes it a premier specimen shrub for a shaded winter garden, best sited near a path or entrance where its fragrance can be appreciated. The bark has traditionally been used to make high-quality paper in Japan and China, giving the plant its common name, and it prefers a sheltered site out of harsh winter wind at the colder edge of its hardiness range.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost into lean, gravelly, sharply drained soil, barely covering the fine seed since it germinates best with light exposure.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost into lean, gravelly, sharply drained soil, barely covering the fine seed since it germinates best with light exposure. Established plants form silvery-gray mounds that bloom almost continuously from spring through fall with clusters of small, papery yellow daisies that dry in place rather than dropping. It is an important nectar source for small native bees and butterflies across the Chihuahuan and Sonoran desert grasslands and needs shearing back hard after flowering flushes to stay compact. Avoid rich soil or regular irrigation, which causes floppy, short-lived growth.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade in October–November; unlike most daffodils, paperwhites require no cold chilling period and bloom naturally in the warmth of the Gulf South winter, typically December–February. In zone 9–10 they naturalize and multiply freely.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall; paperwhites are the most reliable and easy-to-grow winter-blooming bulb for the Gulf South, where they naturalize freely and bloom reliably every December–February without any cold treatment. The clusters of small, pure white, extremely fragrant flowers are a joy in the winter garden and make excellent cut flowers — the strong musky-sweet scent is distinctive and potent (dilute in mixed arrangements for those sensitive to strong fragrances). Unlike yellow daffodils, paperwhites persist and multiply in the warm, mild winters of zone 8–11. Plant new bulbs in fall for the first year; established naturalized clumps increase every year and require only to be divided when crowded. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after blooming to feed the bulbs for next year.

common_name: Papillilamina Anthurium (Black Velvet Anthurium, Dark Velvet Anthurium, Panama Velvet Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow in deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky aroid mix with high humidity; Anthurium papillilaminum is an exceptionally velvety anthurium from Panama producing large, oval, heart-shaped leaves in very deep, almost black-green with a pronounced velvety texture from dense papillae covering the upper leaf surface. The velvet quality is among the most pronounced of all cultivated anthuriums and the dark color intensity is exceptional. Requires warm (above 60°F), humid (60%+) conditions and deep shade. A prestigious collector's aroid. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in deep shade in moist, well-drained, chunky aroid mix with high humidity and consistently warm temperatures — Papillilamina Anthurium is one of the most intensely velvety and deeply colored of all the ornamental velvet anthuriums, producing leaves of extraordinary depth of color and texture in the proper conditions. Anthurium papillilaminum is a climbing, hemiepiphytic anthurium in the Araceae family native to Panama, belonging to the section Cardiolonchium — the velvet-leaved anthurium group that includes A. crystallinum, A. clarinervium, A. warocqueanum, and A. regale. The plant produces large, broadly cordate (heart-shaped) leaves 12–20 inches long with a surface that is quite remarkable for the intensity of its velvet quality: the entire upper leaf surface is densely covered in papillae (small, rounded surface protrusions) that scatter light diffusely, creating a matte, velvet-fabric appearance that rivals the famous velvety texture of A. warocqueanum. The color of the leaf is a very deep, saturated, near-black forest-green — darker and more intense than most other velvet anthuriums, giving the leaf an almost black appearance in low light. The leaf undersides are pale to medium green. Primary veins are silver-white and moderately prominent, though less dramatically contrasting than in species like A. regale or A. magnificum. The combination of near-black color and pronounced velvet texture makes A. papillilaminum one of the most dramatically dark-foliaged ornamental aroids available. A prestigious collector's plant for serious aroid enthusiasts. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Paprika requires excellent drainage and will not tolerate heavy, wet clay, particularly through summer humidity.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; heavy clay or consistently wet soil quickly kills yarrow, especially in humid summers. Paprika produces flat-topped flower clusters that open a vivid brick-red and gradually fade through shades of salmon-orange and soft gold as they age, often showing several colors on the same plant at once, held above finely cut, aromatic, fern-like gray-green foliage. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and spreads slowly by rhizomes to form an expanding patch, making it a good choice for a xeric border or meadow-style planting. Deadhead spent flower clusters to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring or fall.

plant_note: Divide clumps or plant container stock in spring in full sun in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil or shallow water (2–12 inches deep) in zone 9–12; Papyrus is a large, dramatic, aquatic sedge native to the Nile Basin and sub-Saharan Africa — the plant from which the ancient Egyptians produced the world's first writing surface (papyrus paper) — producing tall, triangular stems topped by spectacular, spherical, radiating umbels of fine, thread-like bracts resembling giant green fireworks.
directions: Plant in full sun in consistently wet, fertile soil or shallow water (2–12 inches deep) in pots set in ponds, bog gardens, or rain gardens; Cyperus papyrus is a water-loving plant that must never dry out — grow at the edge of ponds, in aquatic containers in water features, or in persistently moist bog areas with at least 6 hours of full sun. Cyperus papyrus (Papyrus or Egyptian Papyrus) is a tall, dramatic, rhizomatous, aquatic sedge native to the margins of the Nile River, Lake Chad, and the shallow freshwater marshes, lakeshores, and riverbanks of tropical Africa from Egypt south through East Africa to Madagascar. It is one of the most historically significant plant species in human civilization: the stems of Cyperus papyrus provided the material from which ancient Egyptians manufactured papyrus paper — the world's first practical writing and documentation surface, produced from thin, crisscrossed strips of the pith — enabling the record-keeping and administrative systems that underlie ancient Egyptian, Greek, and early Roman civilization. The triangular, 3-sided stems (typical of the sedge family, hence the field-guide maxim 'sedges have edges') are hollow, spongy, and grow to 5–12 feet tall, topped by dramatic spherical umbels of 100+ fine, radiating, thread-like stems with tiny brown flower clusters — the visual effect is of enormous green fireworks or celestial spheres. Ornamentally outstanding as a bold water-garden or pond accent in zone 9–12; can become invasive in year-round warm climates where it naturalized beyond the garden.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty potting mix; parachute plant stores water in its succulent stems and tubers and prefers to dry out between waterings.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty potting mix; parachute plant stores water in its succulent stems and tubers and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thin, wiry, trailing succulent stems bear pairs of small heart-shaped leaves and unusual, pale green flowers shaped like a tiny umbrella or parachute, complete with a fringe of fine hairs around the rim that trap small fly pollinators temporarily inside the flower before releasing them dusted in pollen. Native to South Africa, it grows from a small underground tuber that stores water and energy through dry periods, and its slender trailing stems make it a good candidate for a small hanging basket where its odd, whimsical flowers can be seen up close. Water only when the potting mix is fully dry, provide bright indirect light, and avoid overpotting this slow-growing tuberous vine.

plant_note: Start indoors; cold stratification aids germination.
directions: Start seed indoors, giving it a cold-moist stratification period to improve germination for this first-year-flowering dwarf echinacea. Set plants in full sun and well-drained soil where the vibrant blooms will draw pollinators. Nearly care-free once established and drought tolerant, it makes a fine fresh or dried cut flower. Leave the seed cones standing for winter interest and to feed birds.

common_name: Parakeet Heliconia (Lobster Claw Heliconia, Tan Heliconia, Expanded Heliconia)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring when soil temperature reaches 65°F+ in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Heliconia latispatha is one of the most adaptable and widely grown heliconias for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, tolerating moderate drought once established better than many species. In zone 9, the rhizomes survive mild winters underground with heavy mulch protection; in zone 9b-10, it grows as a reliable perennial clump. Divide and spread clumps every 3–4 years. Excellent as a tropical cut flower with 2–3 week vase life.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Parakeet Heliconia grows well in partial shade and can tolerate more direct sun than many heliconias, making it more versatile in zone 9 garden conditions. Heliconia latispatha is a clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to an extremely wide range from Mexico through Central America and into Ecuador, Colombia, and Peru in the Heliconiaceae family — one of the most geographically widespread of the heliconias, which explains its adaptability to diverse growing conditions. The plant produces the characteristic banana-like paddle-shaped leaves on tall upright pseudostems and, in the warm months, erect inflorescences with boat-shaped bracts in yellow-orange to orange-red with vivid green tips (in the most common form), arranged alternately along the stem in a 'lobster claw' pattern. Multiple color forms exist, ranging from purely yellow to orange to red, with various tip and margin colorations. The flowers within the bracts are small and white, pollinated by hummingbirds attracted to the brightly colored bracts. Heliconia latispatha is considered one of the best heliconias for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens because of its relative cold tolerance, adaptability to partial shade, and consistent blooming performance through the warm months. The inflorescences are long-lasting cut flowers.

common_name: Pardon Me Daylily (Red Miniature Reblooming Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pardon Me is a compact reblooming red daylily excellent for containers, edging, and mass plantings in zone 3–10.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pardon Me is the premier compact red reblooming daylily — producing velvety, deep cranberry-red flowers with a small yellow-green throat on compact 18–22 inch stems from early summer through fall with reliable repeat bloom throughout the season. It won the Stout Silver Medal in 1994 and remains one of the most consistent compact red daylilies available. The deep red color holds through summer heat without significant fading, an important quality in red-pigmented daylilies that can bleach in direct sun. Pardon Me is a fragrant cultivar with a pleasant fruity-floral scent detectable especially in morning and evening. In zone 9 it begins blooming in April and continues through November in good conditions. Divide every 3–4 years when bloom declines.

common_name: Pardon My Cerise Bee Balm (Compact Cherry-Pink Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pardon My Cerise is a compact bee balm bred with better-than-average powdery mildew resistance, a real advantage for a Gulf South summer where mildew often defoliates older Monarda varieties.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Pardon My Cerise is a compact bee balm bearing dark cherry-pink, shaggy tubular flowers on an eighteen-inch plant, considerably shorter than heirloom bee balm types and bred with better-than-average resistance to the powdery mildew that commonly defoliates taller Monarda varieties in humid summer weather. Its bright flowers draw hummingbirds and butterflies through the summer, and the compact size fits more easily into a mixed perennial border than older, sprawling bee balm cultivars. Provide good air circulation with adequate spacing to further reduce mildew pressure. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Pardon My Purple Bee Balm (Extremely Compact Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pardon My Purple is an extremely compact bee balm bred with good resistance to the powdery mildew that plagues taller, older Monarda cultivars in humid Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Pardon My Purple is a compact bee balm cultivar, standing barely a foot tall, bred with notably better powdery mildew resistance than many older, taller Monarda varieties that often defoliate badly by midsummer in humid conditions. It produces the classic shaggy, tubular purple flowers beloved by hummingbirds and bees, on a tidy mound scaled for a smaller border or container rather than the back of a bed. Good air circulation, achieved through adequate spacing, further reduces mildew pressure. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in loose, well-drained soil, setting the crown level with the surrounding soil to avoid rot.
directions: Site in humus-rich soil with good drainage and water regularly the first season while the fibrous root system spreads, then taper off once established. Part shade suits this cultivar best, since deep near-black coloring can fade in intense sun but the plant still needs enough light to stay compact and full. Ruffled, glossy leaves emerge nearly black with a subtle red undertone, holding color through the season better than many dark heucheras, and thin stems lift small white flowers above the foliage in early summer. Its dramatic, dark foliage makes a striking contrast plant next to silver brunnera or golden sedges in a shaded bed.

plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Park Princess is an unusually vigorous, compact cactus dahlia that can be grown from seed as well as tubers and often blooms its first season.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up, or start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost for first-year bloom. Park Princess produces cheerful cyclamen-pink cactus-type blooms with narrow, quilled petals on compact, well-branched plants that need less staking than taller cactus dahlias. Its shorter stature and seed-grown vigor have made it a long-time favorite for borders and cutting beds alike, blooming freely from midsummer to frost with regular deadheading. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or simply treat as an annual and start fresh from seed each year.

common_name: Parlor Palm (Neanthe Palm, Good Luck Palm, Bella Palm)
plant_note: Grow in containers in zone 9 — Parlor Palm cannot tolerate frost and must be kept above 50°F year-round. In zone 10-11, plant outdoors in deep, consistently shaded spots with moist, well-drained soil. As a container plant, repot every 2–3 years when roots fill the pot; a slightly root-bound plant is fine. Low humidity is the main indoor problem — mist regularly or use a humidity tray. Do not overwater — allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings.
directions: Grow in low to bright indirect light; Parlor Palm is one of the most shade-tolerant palms available, thriving in the reduced light levels of interior rooms, offices, and north-facing windows where most palms would quickly decline. Chamaedorea elegans is a small, graceful, clustering palm native to the cloud forests and rainforest understory of southern Mexico (Veracruz, Oaxaca, San Luis Potosí) and Guatemala at elevations up to 5,000 feet — its adaptation to the deeply shaded forest floor makes it uniquely suited to indoor conditions. Since the 19th century, when cut fronds became popular as floral arrangements and the plants were grown in Victorian parlors (hence the name), Chamaedorea elegans has become one of the most widely sold and cultivated houseplants in the world. The palm forms a slow-growing, multi-stemmed clump of slender, bamboo-like stems carrying dark-green, pinnately-compound fronds 2–3 feet long. It produces small, yellow, bead-like flowers (occasionally borne even on young plants) followed by small black fruits if pollinated. Parlor Palm is on the NASA Clean Air Study list for removing benzene, formaldehyde, and trichloroethylene from indoor air. Non-toxic to pets and children — one of the few large palms confirmed safe for households with cats and dogs.

plant_note: Anchor stem cuttings in moist aquatic substrate or simply drop bunches into still, warm water in full sun in zone 6–11 once frosts have passed; Parrot Feather is a vigorous, feathery South American aquatic plant with emergent, bright-green, whorled, finely divided leaves that extend above the water surface — widely used in water gardens, fish ponds, and aquariums for its ornamental value and oxygenating properties, but invasive outside its native range.
directions: Anchor Myriophyllum aquaticum stem bunches in aquatic substrate at the pond margin or in water 3–12 inches deep in full sun; plants spread vigorously by stem fragments — contain in aquatic pots to prevent spread, and never dispose of cuttings in natural waterways. Parrot Feather is native to the Amazon River basin and adjacent South America and has become naturalized as an invasive aquatic plant throughout much of North America, Europe, Australia, and beyond — spreading through watercourses via stem fragments and posing serious ecological risk. Despite its invasive status, it remains widely sold and planted for its exceptional ornamental value: the bright-blue-green, pine-like emergent shoots are genuinely beautiful and create an attractive, feathery texture at the water's edge. In garden ponds, grow only in contained aquatic pots and never plant near natural waterways, drainage ditches, or irrigation systems. Note: regulated or banned in many US states — check local regulations before purchasing or planting. In zone 6–8, tops die back to the water after hard frost but re-emerge in spring; in zone 9–11, it grows year-round.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic medium in partial to full shade in zone 10–12, or grow as an annual indoors or on a shaded patio in cooler zones; Parrot Impatiens (African Impatiens, Congo Impatiens) is a large, spectacular, shade-loving tender perennial from the rainforests of tropical Central Africa — bearing elongated, dramatic flowers with brilliant red pouched spurs tipped with bright yellow, strongly resembling tiny, hovering parrots — continuously blooming in warm conditions.
directions: Root Impatiens niamniamensis tip cuttings in moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in a warm, shaded location; keep evenly moist — never waterlogged — and protect from any frost; pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushy growth; fertilize monthly with a balanced liquid fertilizer during active growth. Parrot Impatiens is one of the most extraordinary of all shade-loving plants — the unusual, elongated, hooded flowers with their brilliant scarlet-and-yellow coloring genuinely resemble small parrots or tiny shoes, creating a remarkable conversation piece in the shaded garden or container. Native to the dense rainforests of Uganda, DRC, and adjacent Central Africa, where it grows in deep, humid shade in rich, moist forest floor soil, it is perfectly adapted to the dappled shade of tropical and subtropical gardens. The species is a reliable hummingbird plant in its adopted range; in Florida and South Texas, it attracts ruby-throated and rufous hummingbirds. Unlike many Impatiens, it has robust, somewhat succulent stems and grows into a substantial plant 2–3 feet tall; it does not wilt as readily in partial sun as the more tender I. walleriana but still performs best in partial to full shade with consistent moisture. In zone 10–12, it grows as a perennial shrub; in cooler areas, an excellent container plant for shaded patios and sunrooms.

plant_note: Plant outdoors only after all danger of frost has passed and temperatures remain consistently warm. In frost-free climates (zones 10–11), can be planted year-round in a sheltered, shaded spot.
directions: Propagate from stem cuttings taken in spring or summer, rooting them in moist perlite or a well-draining potting mix in a warm, humid environment. Plant in deep to partial shade with rich, consistently moist but well-draining soil amended with compost. Water regularly to keep the root zone evenly moist, and mist foliage occasionally to raise humidity in dry conditions. Bring indoors before the first frost; it makes an excellent houseplant in a bright, indirect-light position.

plant_note: Plant tuberous roots in spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; parrot lily has naturalized widely across the Gulf South and can spread aggressively by underground stolons once established.
directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, handling the brittle roots carefully. Parrot lily bears striking, dark red flowers streaked and tipped in deep maroon-green, distinctive markings that give the plant its common name, blooming on wiry stems from spring into summer. Unlike many Peruvian lily hybrids, this species has naturalized extensively across the Gulf South, spreading by underground stolons to form substantial colonies in shaded gardens, old homesites, and woodland edges, so give it room or plan to periodically thin it where a contained planting is wanted. It goes dormant in the heat of summer and resprouts with cooler fall weather in many gardens, and established colonies are extremely drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once settled in.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum in full sun; parrot pitcher plant tolerates periodic flooding and brief submersion better than other Sarracenia species — an advantage in seasonally wet Gulf Coast bogs.
directions: Parrot pitcher plant is the most unusual and architecturally distinctive of all North American pitcher plants — its fat, lobster-trap pitchers lie horizontally or at low angles rather than upright, with a hooded, beaked lid resembling a parrot's head (the name 'psittacina' means parrot-like) and a complex network of transparent windows that allow light in but confuse trapped insects attempting to escape. Unlike upright pitcher plants that fill with rainwater, parrot pitcher plant traps insects in a dry chamber and floods seasonally in its native Gulf Coast bogs; it is actually adapted to tolerate periodic submersion in floodwater, which passively provides additional drowned prey. This distinctive form and short stature make it a valuable companion plant to tall pitchers in bog garden designs, providing a low, ground-level layer of carnivorous plants that adds visual variety. Native to the Gulf Coastal Plain from Georgia to Louisiana, it thrives in the wet pine savannas of the Gulf Coast where it should be cultivated in appropriate bog conditions to support habitat awareness and conservation of this threatened ecosystem.

plant_note: Plant in fall in a sheltered spot; blooms are heavy.
directions: Plant parrot tulip bulbs in autumn six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and a spot sheltered from wind. The flamboyant fringed and twisted petals are streaked and feathered in bold colors, making dramatic cut flowers. Because the large blooms can flop, choose a protected location and stake if necessary. Let foliage die back naturally, and in mild-winter areas chill bulbs before planting.

plant_note: Plant offsets in very well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, rocky to sandy, extremely dry soil in full sun; Parry's agave is one of the most cold-hardy agaves, surviving temperatures below 0°F when established in sharply-drained soil — wet conditions in cold weather kill it even when temperatures would otherwise be survivable.
directions: Plant offsets in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, extremely dry soil in full sun — Parry's agave is one of the hardiest and most ornamentally refined of all agaves, forming tight, symmetrical, compact rosettes of short, broad, blue-gray to silver-gray leaves with dark terminal spines and toothed margins — an architectural perfection that makes it one of the finest structural plants for dry gardens. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert and Mexican highlands, it is among the most cold-tolerant agaves, hardy to zone 5–6 with adequate drainage. The tall, impressive flower spike of orange-yellow flowers is produced once after 15–25 years of growth; the plant dies after flowering but produces offsets that continue the colony. The piña (heart) was roasted and eaten by indigenous peoples of the Southwest — the source of the common name 'mescal agave.' An outstanding specimen plant for dry, sunny rock gardens, slope stabilization, and xeriscaping in zone 5–11.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost into dry, sandy, lean, well-drained desert soil in full sun.
directions: Parry's Marina is a delicate native annual legume of dry, sandy desert washes and open plains in the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts of California, Arizona, and adjacent Mexico. It produces slender, branching stems with tiny, pinnate, gland-dotted leaves and small but brilliant blue-violet to purple pea flowers with yellow centers from spring through summer; native desert bees are particularly attracted to the blooms. Direct sow into dry, sandy, lean, very well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; no soil amendment or irrigation is needed once seedlings are established. Parry's Marina self-sows in suitable desert garden settings and makes a charming, rarely cultivated native addition to California and Arizona desert wildflower mixes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, sandy or gravelly well-drained soil; seeds germinate with winter rains and bloom March through May.
directions: Parry's Phacelia is a southern California native annual bearing some of the most intensely colored flowers of any native plant — vivid, deep violet-purple, bell-shaped blooms clustered in coiling, fiddlehead-style cymes atop upright, glandular-hairy stems. It is native to dry, rocky, and sandy soils in coastal scrub and chaparral of Los Angeles, San Diego, and Baja California, blooming from March through May. Direct sow in fall on bare, dry, sandy, or gravelly well-drained soil in full sun; no soil amendment is needed and rich soil reduces flowering. Handle plants with gloves as the hairy stems can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive individuals, and expect native bees — including specialist phacelia bees — to visit heavily.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; parsley hawthorn tolerates more shade than most hawthorns and grows naturally as an understory tree in bottomland forests.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; parsley hawthorn is the most delicate and ornamental of the southeastern hawthorns, distinguished by its exquisitely cut, deeply lobed leaves that truly resemble flat-leaf parsley — giving it an unusually fine, lacy texture among native trees. White flower clusters in spring are followed by small red berries in fall that provide wildlife food. It grows naturally as an understory tree in moist bottomland forests and shaded river banks throughout the Southeast and tolerates shade better than most hawthorn species. The gray-brown bark flakes to reveal attractive smooth orange-tan underbark. An underused native tree that deserves much wider garden use for its ornamental leaf texture and wildlife value.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in poor, sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; scarify seeds with sandpaper or soak 24 hours before sowing to improve germination. Partridge pea self-sows abundantly to perpetuate itself.
directions: Direct sow scarified or soaked seeds after last frost in poor, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; partridge pea is a native Eastern North American annual legume that fixes nitrogen, produces cheerful yellow flowers from midsummer through fall, and provides essential food and cover for quail, pheasants, and songbirds that eat the seeds and nest in the dense foliage. It thrives on neglect in dry, infertile soils where most ornamentals struggle, naturalizing by prolific self-seeding to fill roadsides, meadows, and wildlife gardens. Do not enrich the planting soil — excess nitrogen reduces flowering. It is a larval host plant for several native sulfur butterfly species. Plant in sweeps of at least 10–20 plants for best ecological impact.

plant_note: Transplant rooted stem cuttings or small clumps in moist, very acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade in spring; partridgeberry demands acid soil (pH 4.5–5.5) and is best established in prepared, pine-bark-enriched beds under large oaks, pines, or rhododendrons.
directions: Transplant rooted cuttings or small clumps in moist, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full shade in spring; partridgeberry is a native evergreen groundcover of eastern North American forest floors that forms a tight, creeping mat of small, paired, round, glossy dark-green leaves marked with pale veins, producing pairs of tiny, fused, fragrant white tubular flowers in summer followed by a single, paired-scar, brilliant-red berry that persists through winter and is prized food for grouse, turkeys, foxes, and songbirds. The berries are edible to humans and mildly pleasant-tasting, though rarely produced in quantity. It is an exquisite but demanding terrarium and woodland garden plant requiring deep shade, consistently moist acid soil, and excellent drainage. One of the finest fine-textured native groundcovers for the darkest spots.
