common_name: Party Punch Caladium (Dwarf Hot Pink Sun-Tolerant Strap-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Party Punch is a dwarf strap-leaf caladium bred for sun tolerance in containers, with hot pink centers and red veining.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to nearly full sun with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. Party Punch bears vivid hot pink centers with contrasting red veining on narrow strap-shaped leaves, on a dwarf, compact plant bred specifically for reliable sun performance in containers and mixed plantings. Its small stature and bright, saturated color make it a strong choice for pots, window boxes, and the front of a shaded or partly sunny border. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall; sap and foliage can irritate skin — handle with gloves and avoid contact with eyes.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in a sunny, gravelly, or rocky, very well-drained site; pasque flower germinates best from fresh seed with natural cold stratification and is slow to establish but extremely long-lived once settled. Silky, nodding purple, lavender, or white flowers emerge in early spring from the fuzzy, hairy foliage and are followed by fluffy, ornamental seedheads similar to clematis. Perfectly drained, lean, alkaline or neutral soil is essential — clay or continuously wet conditions are fatal. Resents transplanting; sow in situ or plant container-grown specimens when small.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to dry, poor to average, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; path rush is one of the most adaptable and commonly overlooked native rushes, growing naturally along compacted paths, in disturbed areas, woodland edges, and open understory throughout eastern North America.
directions: Plant in moist to average, poor to average, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; path rush is one of the most ubiquitous and overlooked native rushes, a slender, wiry plant of paths, roadsides, woodland edges, and compacted soils throughout eastern North America. It is named for its habit of growing along beaten paths and in disturbed areas where compacted, nutrient-poor soil discourages competition. The very fine, wiry, dark green culms are cylindrical and leafless in the true rush manner, producing small, compact clusters of flowers and seeds near mid-culm. While not showy, path rush is an excellent native filler for difficult, shaded, or compacted areas where other plants struggle. It self-sows freely in appropriate conditions and provides fine-textured contrast to broader-leaved shade plants. The seed heads are eaten by sparrows and other small birds. A reliable, low-maintenance component of ecological plantings in disturbed, shaded areas.

plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Patriot's wide white margins light up shaded areas effectively and the plant is vigorous and easy to establish. Divide every 4–5 years when clumps become very large.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Patriot is one of the most popular hostas ever introduced and winner of the American Hosta Society's Hosta of the Year award in 1997 — a vigorous medium-sized hosta producing mounds of dark green leaves with remarkably wide, crisp white margins that illuminate shade gardens with a luminous quality. The bold contrast between the deep forest-green center and the wide (1–1.5 inch) chalk-white margin makes Patriot one of the most visually striking hostas available, creating the brightest light effect in deep shade of any hosta. It is a sport of 'Francee' but with a substantially wider white margin; the two are often grown together. Lavender flowers appear in midsummer. Patriot is vigorous, adaptable, and tolerates a range of soil and moisture conditions better than many showier hostas.

common_name: Patty's Plum Poppy (Dusky Plum-Mauve Oriental Poppy)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Oriental poppies go dormant and disappear entirely in summer, so mark the spot to avoid disturbing the dormant crown.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Oriental poppies resent wet, heavy soil and summer humidity, so good drainage is essential. Patty's Plum bears large, single flowers in an unusual, subtle dusky plum-mauve rather than the fiery orange-red typical of most Oriental poppies, a sophisticated, muted color that pairs beautifully with silver-leaved companions and other pastel perennials in a late-spring border. Like other Oriental poppies it flowers in late spring, then dies back to dormancy through summer heat before re-emerging with fresh foliage in fall, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown during the summer gap. It performs best in climates with cooler summers and struggles in the humid, hot conditions of the Deep South.

common_name: Paul's Glory Hosta (Classic Gold-Centered Blue-Margined Hosta)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Paul's Glory develops its brightest gold center with some morning sun and is notably more sun-tolerant than many gold hostas without losing color, though the blue margin holds its cast best in shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with a few hours of morning sun for the brightest gold color at the center of the leaves. Introduced in the 1980s and named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 1999, Paul's Glory bears large, thick, cupped leaves that open chartreuse and mature to a rich, glowing gold center edged in an irregular blue-green margin, one of the most widely grown and influential variegated hosta cultivars ever released. Near-white flowers appear on tall scapes above the foliage in summer. Its heavy leaf substance provides good resistance to slug damage, and its combination of striking color, vigor, and reliability has made it a parent to numerous later hosta introductions. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring as new growth emerges.

common_name: Paul's Himalayan Musk Rose (Extremely Vigorous Blush-Pink Rambler)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun with an exceptionally sturdy, large support, such as a mature tree, since this rambler can grow 30 feet or more.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing an extremely sturdy, large support such as a mature tree, since Paul's Himalayan Musk is among the most rampant ramblers grown, capable of climbing 30 feet or more into a tree canopy. Once each early summer it produces a spectacular single flush of small, soft blush-pink, musk-scented double flowers borne in huge cascading clusters that can smother an entire tree in bloom. Because of its enormous ultimate size and single bloom season, it is best suited to a large property where it can be left to scramble freely rather than a small, formal garden. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood, ideally right after the summer bloom.

common_name: Paula Fay Peony (Early-Blooming Bright Coral-Pink Semi-Double)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Paula Fay is an early-blooming semi-double peony with bright coral-pink flowers on a vigorous landscape plant.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Paula Fay bears bright, clear coral-pink, semi-double flowers with a ring of golden stamens visible at the open center, blooming notably early in the peony season, which extends the flowering window when paired with later-blooming cultivars. The vigorous, floriferous plant is a strong landscape performer valued as much for its garden presence as for cut flowers. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Plant in full sun in consistently moist to wet soil, since it naturally occurs in Everglades sloughs and marsh margins and tolerates poor drainage better than almost any other landscape palm.
directions: Plant this multi-trunked Florida and Caribbean native fan palm in full sun in consistently moist to wet soil, since it naturally occurs in Everglades sloughs and marsh margins and tolerates poor drainage better than almost any other landscape palm. Its slender clustered trunks topped with bright green, fan-shaped fronds create a dense screening mass ideal for pond edges, rain gardens, and wet low spots where other palms fail. It is more cold-tolerant than its tropical origin suggests, recovering readily from foliage damage in hard freezes. Thin occasional suckers if a more open, multi-stem silhouette is preferred over a dense thicket.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in deep to moderate shade; peace lily requires warmth (above 60°F) and protection from direct sun and drying drafts. It is toxic to cats and dogs — the calcium oxalate crystals cause mouth irritation if ingested.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep shade; peace lily is one of the most adaptable, forgiving, and widely grown of all tropical shade plants — equally at home as an outdoor ground cover in zone 10–12 deep shade and as a low-light houseplant in virtually any indoor setting. It produces broad, glossy, dark green leaves and distinctive white spathes (modified leaves) surrounding a cream-colored spadix from spring through summer, and often reblooms in fall. It is one of very few flowering plants that tolerates genuine deep shade with limited light, making it indispensable for covered patios, north-facing rooms, and the deepest shade under trees. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry; the plant will droop dramatically when too dry but recovers quickly after watering. A NASA Clean Air Study plant found to remove formaldehyde, benzene, and trichloroethylene from indoor air.

common_name: Peace Rose (Gloria Dei, Mme. A. Meilland)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Peace is vigorous and more disease-resistant than many hybrid tea roses, but benefits from preventative fungicide application and consistent feeding in humid climates.
directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Peace rose holds a unique place in horticultural history — introduced during World War II and officially named at the San Francisco United Nations conference in 1945, it is considered by many the most famous rose of the 20th century. The large, high-centered flowers are distinguished by their remarkable color combination: soft yellow petals edged with carmine-pink that intensifies with age, creating an unusually warm, layered flower. It is more vigorous and disease-resistant than most hybrid teas of its era, with large, glossy, dark-green foliage. Peace is still widely grown and performs reliably in zone 4–9 with standard hybrid tea care. The story of its distribution during World War II — with cuttings smuggled out of France before the Nazi occupation — and its formal naming at the historic UN conference make it one of the most culturally significant plants ever grown. Prune hard in late winter; feed with rose fertilizer monthly through the growing season.

plant_note: Set divisions or potted plants in spring after the soil has warmed, in rich, moisture-retentive soil, and water deeply until established.
directions: Grow in fertile, consistently damp soil enriched with compost, and keep a layer of mulch over the roots to buffer summer heat and moisture swings. Filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade brings out the best flower color without scorching the fine foliage. This older Arends hybrid produces soft salmon-pink plumes over mounds of dark green, deeply cut leaves in early summer, blooming a bit ahead of many other astilbe cultivars. Its gentle color and reliable performance make it a good companion for hostas and ferns along a shaded stream bank or border edge.

plant_note: Transplant container-grown plants in spring into well-drained soil, spacing closely for a continuous low border or mass planting.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly the first season and reducing frequency once the compact root system is established. Prune back by roughly a third in late winter to keep the mounded habit dense and encourage abundant new flowering shoots. Double, peach-to-coral blooms that fade to soft pink open in large clusters over low, spreading mounds of small glossy foliage, part of the Drift series developed by crossing groundcover and miniature roses. Its diminutive size and long bloom season from late spring to frost make it well suited to container plantings, rock gardens, and small-space borders.

common_name: Peach Flambe Heuchera (Peach Flambe Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, siting the plant where it gets some morning sun to intensify its warm coloring without scorching the foliage.
directions: Plant divisions in partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, siting the plant where it gets some morning sun to intensify its warm coloring without scorching the foliage. Peach Flambe produces ruffled, rounded leaves that emerge glowing peach-orange and shift through amber and copper tones as the season progresses, brightest in cool spring and fall weather. Small bell-shaped flowers appear on wiry stems in early summer, but the plant is grown mainly as a season-long foliage accent along a shaded path or border edge. Like most modern heuchera hybrids it benefits from division every three to four years to prevent the woody crown from heaving out of the soil.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; dislikes root disturbance.
directions: Direct sow the large seed about half an inch deep after frost, as nasturtiums dislike transplanting; soaking overnight speeds sprouting. This compact variety bears creamy peach blooms with red centers above rounded leaves. Both flowers and leaves have a peppery, watercress-like flavor that livens up salads. Grow in lean soil and full sun, since rich soil promotes leaves over flowers.

common_name: Peach Seduction Yarrow (Soft Peach-Pink Fading Yarrow)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or transplant divisions in spring, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Peach Seduction is part of the Seduction series bred for compact habit and a long color-fade sequence.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; excellent drainage matters more than soil fertility, since wet, rich soil produces weak growth and invites crown rot. Peach Seduction opens a warm, soft peach-pink and gradually fades to a pale cream as each flower cluster ages, giving a gentle multicolor effect across the compact plant, held above aromatic, finely cut gray-green foliage from late spring through summer. Its more compact habit than older, taller yarrow cultivars fits smaller borders and mixed containers without staking. Deadhead spent flower clusters to prolong bloom, and expect exceptional drought and heat tolerance once established; divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigorous, floriferous growth.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or plant container-grown stock in spring, into well-drained, average garden soil; peach-leaved bellflower prefers cooler summers and benefits from afternoon shade and reliable moisture in the heat of a Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade in warm climates, or full sun where summers are milder, and keep the shallow, fibrous roots from drying out. Campanula persicifolia is a classic European cottage-garden perennial named for its narrow, willow-like leaves that resemble peach foliage, sending up slender, wiry stems in late spring to early summer topped with a loose spire of large, upward-facing, cup-shaped blue or white flowers that are outstanding as cut flowers. The airy, see-through growth habit makes it a good middle-of-border plant that does not block the view of what is planted behind it. Deadhead spent flower spikes to encourage a possible rebloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in fall or early spring to keep plants vigorous; in hot, humid climates the plant appreciates a bit of afternoon shade and does best treated as a slightly short-lived perennial refreshed periodically from new divisions.

common_name: Peacock Begonia (Iridescent Begonia, Blue Sheen Begonia)
plant_note: Grow as a terrarium specimen or high-humidity houseplant in zone 9; Begonia pavonina requires consistently high humidity (60–80%) and cool to moderate temperatures (60–75°F) and will deteriorate in dry air or high heat. Its natural habitat on the shaded forest floor of highland Malaysian rainforest means it prefers conditions different from most tropical begonias — cooler, more humid, and with less direct light. Excellent for enclosed terrariums and paludariums. Propagate from leaf cuttings.
directions: Grow in low to moderate shade — Peacock Begonia is one of the very few decorative plants that performs optimally in very low light, where its iridescent leaf shimmer is most dramatic and where, in nature, this adaptation would maximize photosynthesis. Begonia pavonina is a small rhizomatous begonia from the highland cloud forests of the Cameron Highlands region in Peninsular Malaysia, discovered growing in conditions of exceptionally deep shade on the forest floor — so deep that most plants could not photosynthesize effectively. The plant's extraordinary adaptation to this extreme shade environment is structural iridescence: the leaves are dark green in normal reflected light but in dim, directional light reveal a brilliant metallic blue-green to peacock-blue shimmer, produced by chloroplasts arranged in regular stacks that function as thin-film optical interference filters, reflecting blue wavelengths while transmitting red wavelengths deeper into the leaf for photosynthesis — an elegant evolutionary engineering solution to low-light photosynthesis that was the subject of significant scientific interest when described. The iridescence is most visible in angled, dim light and disappears in bright light or from certain viewing angles. Small pink flowers appear seasonally. The combination of the unusual blue iridescence, deep forest requirements, and scientific interest make Peacock Begonia one of the most remarkable shade plants available for terrarium culture.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 1–2 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; peacock ginger requires warm temperatures to sprout — be patient, as the rhizomes may take 4–6 weeks to emerge after planting. Allow the foliage to die back completely in fall before lifting and storing rhizomes if in zone below 9.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; peacock ginger is a Southeast Asian tropical ginger grown for its exceptionally ornamental foliage — the low-growing, ground-hugging leaves lie flat on the soil surface, each leaf broadly oval and elaborately patterned with a striking, iridescent, silver-green, feathered variegation over a deeper green background, creating a pattern resembling the eye-spot on a peacock feather. The leaves emerge directly from the soil with no visible stem and spread flat in an overlapping rosette that effectively covers the shaded ground beneath with a dense, elaborately patterned carpet. In summer, small, lilac-purple to pale-pink flowers emerge directly from the center of the leaf rosette, opening one or two at a time for a brief morning display, each flower beautiful on close inspection. Like other kaempferia species, the plants are summer-active and go completely dormant in winter. Excellent as a fine-textured, ornamentally patterned groundcover in partial to full shade, where the iridescent leaf marking is most vivid. Multiplies readily by rhizome division.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions after the last frost threat in moist, well-drained, organically rich, slightly acidic soil in full shade to partial shade; peacock ginger goes completely dormant in winter and re-emerges reliably in spring in zones 8–11 with minimal care.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions after last frost in moist, well-drained, organically rich, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; peacock ginger is a Southeast Asian cousin of culinary ginger grown purely for its extraordinarily beautiful foliage — broad, flat leaves that lie close to the ground and are decorated with intricate patterns of dark-green, silver-gray, bronze, and chocolate in overlapping concentric zones, resembling the eye-pattern on a peacock feather. Small, lavender-pink flowers appear among the leaves in summer. The plant goes completely dormant in winter, disappearing below ground level. Ideal as a weed-suppressing, low groundcover in shade gardens and under tall trees in Gulf Coast and subtropical landscapes. Spreads slowly by rhizomes to form attractive colonies. Related species K. rotunda and K. elegans offer similar ornamental value.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 1 inch deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; peacock ginger thrives in bright indirect light or filtered shade and actually struggles in full sun in hot climates. It goes completely dormant in winter — mark its location to avoid disturbing rhizomes.
directions: Plant rhizomes in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; peacock ginger is one of the most beautiful and unusual tropical perennials for shaded Gulf Coast gardens, producing large, flat, spreading leaves marked with an intricate silver-green pattern (resembling peacock feathers) that lie almost flat on the ground and create a fascinating low carpet in the shade garden. Small but lovely white and pale purple flowers emerge directly from the leaf surface in late spring and summer, nestled among the ornamental foliage. The aromatic rhizomes are used medicinally in Southeast Asian traditional medicine and as a culinary spice (known as 'kencur' in Indonesian cuisine). The plant is completely dormant from late fall through early spring — all top growth dies back, but the rhizomes persist in the ground and emerge vigorously when warm weather returns. An outstanding understory plant for the shaded tropical garden in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in sharply drained, sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in fall; peacock moraea grows through the cool season (October–April) and requires complete dryness during summer dormancy. In zones 9–10 with perfect drainage, corms can remain in the ground year-round. In other climates, lift corms after foliage dies and store dry until fall.
directions: Plant corms in fall in sharply drained, lean, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; peacock moraea is one of the most spectacular members of the iris family — a South African endemic whose three outer petals each bear an iridescent, peacock-eye marking of brilliant blue-purple or violet in the center, surrounded by a contrasting ring of yellow or orange against a white or purple petal background. This extraordinary pattern closely mimics the eyespot of a peacock feather, making each flower an art object of botanical precision. The plant is a winter-grower of the Western Cape fynbos and blooms in spring (February–April), producing flowers that last only a single day each but appear in succession from multiple buds. It requires the characteristic fynbos growing cycle of wet winters and bone-dry summers, making perfect drainage and summer dryness absolute requirements. Fascinating for the specialist bulb grower and extraordinary as a cut flower or container specimen in a cold frame where the summer dry period can be managed.

plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for late-summer bloom; peacock orchid is tender (damaged below 28 degrees F) and in most zones is treated as an annual or the corms are lifted after frost and stored frost-free over winter. In zones 9-10 the corms can be left in the ground year-round in well-drained soil. The distinctive fragrance — sweet, vanilla-like, noticeable from several feet away — is most pronounced in the evening.
directions: Plant corms after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; peacock orchid is the most distinctive and fragrant member of the gladiolus genus — in fact it was long classified in a separate genus (Acidanthera bicolor var. murielae) because its flowers are so unlike typical garden gladiolus. The pure white, star-shaped flowers, each with a prominent, deep maroon-purple blotch at the center of each petal, are carried on tall, slender stems in August and September, nodding from the top of the stem in a loose, graceful arrangement quite unlike the stiffly formal, upright spikes of garden gladiolus. Most importantly, peacock orchid is fragrant — sweetly, distinctly scented, the fragrance carrying on the air in the evening — an unusual quality in the gladiolus family. The combined effect of the white-and-purple flowers, graceful drooping habit, and sweet fragrance has made it a favorite for cutting gardens and mixed borders. Native to the high-altitude Ethiopian Highlands of East Africa. Plant in quantity for the best effect.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; peacock orchid (now classified as Gladiolus callianthus in current taxonomy) blooms in late summer and early autumn (August–October), producing white flowers with a dark maroon-purple blotch at the throat. The fragrance is powerfully sweet, particularly in the evening. In zones 7 and colder, lift corms after frost and store dry over winter; in zones 8–10 it may overwinter in the ground.
directions: Plant corms in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; peacock orchid is a beloved and exceptional corm — grown primarily for its combination of large, elegant white flowers and exceptional fragrance. In late summer and early autumn, the tall, narrow, sword-leaved stems carry on slender, arching stems a sequence of large (3-inch), pure-white, star-shaped flowers, each with a dramatic, well-defined, dark maroon-purple to blackish-purple blotch at the base of each petal that creates a bold, contrasting star pattern at the throat of each white flower. The flower form alone would be sufficient to recommend it — graceful, large, pure-white, star-shaped — but the fragrance transforms it into something exceptional: an intensely sweet, rich, spicy scent that intensifies in the evening and can fill a garden area with a perfume comparable to tuberose or Lilium regale in power and quality. Native to the Ethiopian highlands and East Africa, it blooms in late summer and early autumn (August–October) when most other fragrant bulbs have finished. Technically now classified as Gladiolus callianthus in current molecular taxonomy but still widely sold and grown under the Acidanthera name. Outstanding near seating areas and open windows where the evening fragrance can be appreciated.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; in zone 9, plant corms in February–March for summer bloom; in zone 9 the corms may overwinter in the ground if protected with 3–4 inches of mulch or in a warm, sheltered location.
directions: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; Peacock Orchid (also known as Acidanthera or Abyssinian gladiolus) is one of the most fragrant summer bulbs available for the warm-season garden — producing tall, slender stems (3–4 feet) bearing 6–8 staggered, pure-white, star-shaped flowers with a prominent, deep maroon-purple blotch at the center of each flower, creating a dramatic color contrast. The intense, sweet, orchid-like fragrance that distinguishes Peacock Orchid from all other gladiolus relatives is its most celebrated quality: a single stem in a vase perfumes an entire room, and a planting of 20–30 corms fills the garden with fragrance on warm evenings. The flowers open successively along the spike over 2–3 weeks, extending the display season. The combination of the white flower with dark center, tall elegant stem, and exceptional fragrance makes Peacock Orchid outstanding for cutting gardens. The corms are somewhat tender and must be lifted and stored in zone 6 and colder; in zone 9, they often overwinter successfully in well-drained soil with mulch protection and naturalize to form expanding clumps over several years. Plant in succession every 2–3 weeks from March through May for continuous summer bloom. The fragrant flowers open in the afternoon and evening, making Peacock Orchid particularly effective near patios and outdoor seating areas.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; peacock plant is one of the most humidity-demanding of the Marantaceae — crispy leaf edges and fading leaf patterns are the primary symptoms of insufficient humidity.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; peacock plant (cathedral windows, cathedral plant) is a Brazilian tropical perennial of the prayer plant family (Marantaceae) considered by many to have the finest and most elaborate leaf patterning of any ornamental tropical plant — the oval leaves are covered with an intricate pattern of dark-green ovals and irregular markings on a silver-green background that exactly replicates the eye-spot pattern of a peacock's tail feather, with deeper-green undersurface markings visible through the semitranslucent leaf when backlit. The effect is almost stained-glass-like when the leaves are held up to light. Requires genuinely high ambient humidity (above 60%) for the leaves to maintain crisp edges and clear, sharp variegation — in dry conditions, the leaf edges turn brown and the pattern loses clarity. An outstanding houseplant for humid environments and a spectacular specimen for outdoor tropical shade gardens in zones 10–12. Sensitive to fluoride and chlorine in tap water; use distilled or rain water.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted stem sections in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in deep shade with high humidity; it scrambles and climbs over neighboring plants and structures, so give it room or a support to sprawl on.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted stem sections in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in deep shade, and maintain high humidity, since the delicate foliage browns quickly in dry air. Its sprawling, climbing stems root as they spread, so it works well scrambling over logs, pot edges, or other groundcovers rather than staying in a tidy mound. What makes it unlike any other spikemoss in cultivation is its structural blue-green iridescence, a true optical effect from thin layers within the leaf surface rather than pigment, which glows almost metallic in low light. It is a favorite for shaded terrariums and humid tropical shade gardens where that shimmering color can be appreciated up close.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; peanut cactus is one of the easiest flowering cacti, tolerating some neglect and irregular watering.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; peanut cactus is one of the easiest flowering cacti, tolerating some neglect and irregular watering. Slender, finger-like, pale green stems covered in soft white spines sprawl and branch loosely, forming a low, spreading clump that resembles a pile of small peanuts, and it rewards even minimal care with a generous flush of large, brilliant orange-red, funnel-shaped flowers in late spring that dwarf the small stems bearing them. Native to Argentina, it is easy to grow and propagate, readily forming offsets that root wherever a stem segment touches soil, making it a favorite beginner cactus for a bright windowsill or hanging basket. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide plenty of direct sun for the best flowering, and separate rooted offsets to propagate.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; pearl bush establishes readily but benefits from consistent moisture during its first season to develop a strong root system before summer heat.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial sun; pearl bush thrives in most average garden soils and tolerates clay provided drainage is adequate, but performs best with moderate supplemental irrigation during dry spells in its first two years. Exochorda racemosa is a multi-stemmed, arching Chinese ornamental shrub celebrated for its spectacular spring bloom: in April and May the entire plant becomes blanketed in pure white, five-petaled flowers borne in long racemes, rivaling any flowering shrub in the garden. Prune immediately after flowering if needed to maintain shape, as flower buds are set on the previous season's wood; removing up to one-third of the oldest stems to the ground each year keeps the plant vigorous and open.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; pearl bush blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering. The cultivar 'The Bride' is compact, heavily flowering, and significantly better than the straight species, and is the most widely available selection.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; pearl bush is an underappreciated Asian flowering shrub producing, in mid-spring, an extraordinary display of pure-white flowers in rounded clusters that cover the plant so densely the individual flowers resemble a cascade of lustrous white pearls — a display that rivals the visual impact of the best spring flowering shrubs. The flowers are 5-petaled, circular, and exquisitely symmetrical, giving the plant its common name. Unlike many early-spring shrubs, pearl bush has a refined and elegant quality rather than blowsy exuberance. The cultivar 'The Bride' is a compact, densely flowering form that spreads wider than tall (3–4 feet tall, 4–6 feet wide) and has become the preferred selection for small modern gardens. It is long-lived and low-maintenance, requiring only light pruning immediately after flowering and an appropriate site that does not become waterlogged. An excellent alternative to spireas and deutzias for the spring border.

plant_note: Press the dust-fine seed onto the soil surface without covering, since light aids germination, and start indoors about six weeks before the last frost or direct-sow outdoors once frost danger has passed.
directions: Press the dust-fine seed onto the soil surface without covering, since light aids germination, and start indoors about six weeks before the last frost or direct-sow outdoors once frost danger has passed. This tough, silvery-leaved native spreads slowly by rhizome in lean, well-drained soil and shrugs off drought once established, making it a good fit for meadow and gravel gardens. It is a primary caterpillar host for the American Lady butterfly, which wraps silk-and-leaf shelters around the felted foliage, and the dried, papery flower clusters give the plant its "everlasting" reputation for cut-flower use.

common_name: Pearly Gates Morning Glory (Pure White Large-Flowered Morning Glory)
plant_note: Nick or soak seeds overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow after last frost; morning glories resent transplanting.
directions: Nick the seed coat with a file or soak overnight, then direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a trellis or fence. Pearly Gates is the pure white counterpart to the classic Heavenly Blue morning glory, sharing the same large flower size and vigorous, fast-growing habit but opening flawless white blooms that glow at dusk and dawn, making it an excellent choice for a moon garden or evening seating area. Like other Ipomoea tricolor types it opens fresh each dawn and closes by early afternoon, blooming most heavily as days shorten in late summer. Deadhead spent flowers before seed set to prevent unwanted volunteers the following year, since morning glories self-sow readily in warm climates.

common_name: Pecos Crape Myrtle (Compact Pink Mildew-Resistant Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pecos is a compact U.S. National Arboretum indica x fauriei hybrid bred for smaller landscapes and foundation plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pecos is one of the more compact selections from the U.S. National Arboretum's mildew-resistant Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei breeding program, staying small enough for foundation plantings, smaller landscapes, and large containers where full-size crape myrtles would quickly outgrow the space. It produces abundant clear-pink flower clusters through summer on a dense, well-branched dwarf-to-medium shrub, along with the strong powdery mildew resistance characteristic of the fauriei-hybrid crape myrtles. Its small mature size means it needs little to no size-control pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter — never top or hard-prune crape myrtles, since this ruins the naturally graceful branching form. A dependable, low-maintenance choice for a smaller garden that still wants the long summer bloom crape myrtles are known for.

common_name: Pee Wee Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dwarf Oakleaf Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pee Wee is the most compact oakleaf hydrangea cultivar widely available and provides all the species' ornamental attributes in a much smaller package appropriate for foundation plantings and small gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pee Wee is a compact dwarf selection of the native oakleaf hydrangea that stays only 2.5–4 feet tall and wide — dramatically smaller than the standard species that can reach 6–8 feet or more — making it appropriate for foundation plantings, smaller shade gardens, and situations where the full-size species would be overwhelming. Despite the smaller size, Pee Wee provides all the ornamental attributes that make oakleaf hydrangea outstanding: conical white flower clusters in late spring that age through pink to papery tan; deeply lobed, large, textured foliage that turns rich burgundy-red in fall in zone 9; and attractive exfoliating cinnamon-brown bark that provides winter interest. The flowers are proportionally smaller than the species but still conspicuous and attractive. Pee Wee is one of the few native shade shrubs that truly provides four-season interest in the Gulf Coast garden. Like all oakleaf hydrangeas, it blooms on old wood — never prune in fall or winter, trim only immediately after the main bloom period if shaping is needed. Pee Wee is outstanding for shaded rain gardens and areas with seasonal moisture variation.

common_name: Peggy Clarke Japanese Apricot (Double Deep-Pink Flowering Mume)
subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree
plant_note: Plant grafted specimens in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Peggy Clarke blooms in mid-to-late winter, often while the tree is still bare and while few other plants are in flower, so a sheltered site helps protect the blooms from harsh winter wind.
directions: Peggy Clarke is a Japanese apricot selection grown almost entirely for its ornamental winter flowers rather than for fruit, bearing fully double, deep rose-pink blooms with a light, sweet fragrance on bare branches in the coldest part of winter, often January into February, when almost nothing else in the garden is flowering. Like the species it forms a graceful, small-to-medium, vase-shaped tree, and while it does set the small, sour, apricot-like fruit typical of Prunus mume, ornamental cultivars like Peggy Clarke are grown chiefly for the flower display rather than for a culinary crop. Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and prune to an open vase shape right after flowering to maintain form and encourage strong bloom the following winter.

common_name: Peggy Mac Louisiana Iris (Foundational Historic Lavender-Pink Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Peggy Mac, introduced in 1943, is a foundational lavender-pink Louisiana iris cultivar influential in many modern breeding lines.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Peggy Mac, introduced in 1943, bears soft lavender-pink flowers and holds historic significance as one of the foundational Louisiana iris cultivars whose genetics run through many later, more refined pink and lavender hybrids, making it of particular interest to collectors tracing the class's breeding history. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Set out dormant or potted plants in spring after hard frost.
directions: Plant this vigorous climber from a potted or bare-root plant in spring, setting it in full sun with rich, well-drained soil at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence. It offers a cascading display of soft pink blooms and is renowned for thriving in tough conditions with minimal care, even shrugging off common rose troubles. Train the long canes horizontally to maximize flowering and water deeply while establishing. A fast grower that rewards patience with abundant bloom.

common_name: Peggy Martin Rose (The Katrina Rose, Thornless Found Climber)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a fence, arbor, or trellis for the vigorous climbing canes; Peggy Martin is a thornless found rose famous for surviving weeks of brackish floodwater in a New Orleans garden after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
directions: Plant at the base of a sturdy fence, arbor, or trellis in well-drained soil in full sun, and let the long, nearly thornless canes ramble and climb. Peggy Martin became famous across the Gulf South as the 'Katrina Rose' after a specimen in a Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana garden survived two weeks submerged in brackish Hurricane Katrina floodwater and leafed out again the following spring, after which cuttings were propagated and distributed to raise funds for hurricane-ravaged gardens and parks. It produces large sprays of small, deep pink, mildly fragrant blooms in a spectacular once-a-year spring flush, on a vigorous, once-blooming climber that is exceptionally tough, disease-resistant, and tolerant of poor or even storm-damaged soil. Give it strong support to climb, and prune only lightly right after the spring bloom to control size, since it flowers on old wood.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container starts in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; set crowns just at soil level and mulch with leaf litter to keep roots cool and evenly moist.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from drying wind and afternoon sun. Keep the soil evenly moist through summer, since the broad leaves wilt quickly in dry spells, and top-dress yearly with compost or leaf mold to mimic its native forest floor. This uncommon Japanese woodlander forms slowly spreading clumps of rounded, peltate, softly hairy leaves on wiry stems, topped in early summer by loose sprays of small pale yellow flowers. It pairs beautifully with hostas, ferns, and other choice shade perennials as a textural accent in a moist woodland or shade border.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 10–12; the Pemba Island Palm is a rare, clustering, feather-leaved palm endemic to Pemba Island off the coast of Tanzania — producing graceful arching fronds on slender stems from a suckering base, and one of the lesser-known gems in the Dypsis genus transplanted to tropical gardens.
directions: Plant Dypsis pembana in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a site with bright indirect light or partial sun; protect from frost, extended drought, and waterlogged conditions; young palms prefer more shade and gradually accept more sun as they mature. The Pemba Island Palm is an attractive clustering feather palm from Pemba Island in the Zanzibar Archipelago of Tanzania — an island known for its extraordinary biodiversity and high levels of endemism. The palm forms multi-stemmed clumps of slender, graceful stems bearing arching pinnate fronds that create a lush, tropical effect in the garden; the suckering habit makes it an excellent screen plant in frost-free gardens. Like many island-endemic palms, Dypsis pembana is threatened in its native habitat due to land conversion and is rarely seen in cultivation outside of specialist palm collections; sourcing nursery-propagated material supports conservation. In zone 10–12, plant in a sheltered position with regular moisture during the establishment period; once settled, it requires only moderate supplemental irrigation.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to consistently wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; pendulous sedge thrives in wet, shaded conditions beside ponds, streams, and in rain gardens where few ornamental grasses perform.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to consistently wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; pendulous sedge (weeping sedge) is a large, bold, evergreen European sedge that forms impressive arching clumps of broad, strap-like, bright-green leaves, with long, pendulous flower spikes that arch gracefully outward and downward in late spring and summer — the elongated, cylindrical brown catkin-like flower spikes dangling from arching stems are one of the most distinctive and structurally elegant features in the shade garden. It thrives in wet, shaded conditions beside ponds and streams where few ornamental grasses can grow. The dense, lush foliage creates dramatic textural contrast with broadleaf shade plants like hostas and astilbes. Can self-sow prolifically in ideal moist conditions; remove seed heads before they mature if unwanted seedlings are a concern. One of the most architecturally impressive sedges for large-scale shade and water garden compositions.

common_name: Penelope Hybrid Musk Rose (Fragrant Creamy Apricot-Pink Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Penelope is a classic, richly fragrant hybrid musk shrub rose that tolerates a bit of shade.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hybrid musk roses tolerate more shade than most rose classes, blooming reasonably well with just a half-day of direct sun. Penelope bears large clusters of semi-double, creamy apricot-pink blooms fading to soft white, with a strong, musky-sweet fragrance carried well beyond the plant itself, followed in fall by coral-pink hips if left undeadheaded late in the season. The lax, arching shrub repeats bloom reliably through the growing season and can be trained as a short climber against a wall. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through summer to encourage continued flowering.

plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Penhill Watermelon is a ball-type dahlia producing perfectly round, densely petaled blooms in a vivid rose-watermelon pink, valued by cut-flower growers for its neat form and excellent vase life.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants for support as they grow. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage branching and increase the number of blooms. Penhill Watermelon is a ball dahlia, a form characterized by perfectly spherical, densely and evenly packed blooms roughly 3-4 inches across, in a bright, saturated rose-pink reminiscent of watermelon flesh that holds its color well through the season. The tidy, uniform bloom shape and mid-sized flower make it especially popular with cut-flower growers and floral designers, since ball dahlias hold their form and color exceptionally well in the vase, often lasting a week or more after cutting. Plants are relatively compact compared to giant dinnerplate types, making them useful in mixed borders as well as dedicated cutting gardens. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the plant producing from midsummer through frost. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring or early fall; space 6–12 inches apart and expect plants to fill in within 2–3 seasons. Pennsylvania sedge establishes slowly but once settled requires virtually no maintenance.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry soil in partial to full shade; Pennsylvania sedge is one of the best native lawn substitutes for shaded areas under oak trees and other large deciduous trees where grass fails. It forms a fine-textured, low, arching carpet of narrow dark-green blades that stays semi-evergreen through mild winters and requires no mowing when grown as a groundcover. It spreads steadily by rhizomes without becoming invasive and tolerates the dry, root-competitive shade under mature trees that challenges most groundcovers. Unlike lawn grasses, it requires no fertilizer, pesticides, or irrigation once established, and its dense mat effectively suppresses weeds.

common_name: Penny Mac Hydrangea (Reliable Reblooming Blue Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Penny Mac blooms on both old and new wood, so it reliably reflowers through summer even after a late frost damages the previous year's buds.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Penny Mac was an early and long-proven rebloomer among mophead hydrangeas, flowering on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year, which means a late spring frost that kills the old flower buds does not prevent a good summer bloom as it would on older mophead cultivars. Flower color shifts with soil pH the way most macrophylla hydrangeas do, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments if a particular color is desired. Keep soil consistently moist, since hydrangea's large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; seeds benefit from 4 weeks of cold stratification.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds for 4 weeks in damp medium in the refrigerator before sowing indoors for best germination; transplant after the last frost into well-drained to dry soil. Penstemon thrives in poor, gravelly soil and is one of the most important native nectar plants for hummingbirds and native bees. The tubular white to pale pink flowers appear in late spring to early summer; deadhead to a basal rosette of leaves after bloom. Excellent drainage is critical — wet winter conditions are the leading cause of plant loss.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting, or purchase bedding plants; in zone 9, plant in spring through early fall in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pentas is one of the most reliable butterfly and hummingbird plants for hot, humid Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; deadhead spent clusters to encourage continuous bloom. Pentas lanceolata (star flower or pentas) is a tropical East African shrub grown as a warm-season annual or perennial in zones 9–12, producing dense, 3-to-4-inch, domed clusters of small, star-shaped, 5-petaled flowers in red, pink, lavender, white, and bicolor combinations on bushy, upright plants that bloom continuously from spring through frost and beyond in frost-free climates. It is among the best and most reliable butterfly plants for Gulf Coast gardens — the flat-topped flower clusters are perfectly designed for butterfly feeding, attracting Gulf Fritillaries, Sulphurs, Swallowtails, Monarchs, and many other species in numbers not equaled by most other plants. Pentas also attracts hummingbirds to red and pink cultivars. In zone 9, it thrives through the hot, humid summer when many other plants struggle, blooming non-stop in summer heat; the plant often survives mild winters in zone 9b as a perennial, producing larger plants and more blooms in subsequent seasons. The 'Graffiti' and 'Lucky Star' series are among the most compact and floriferous.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Penwiper Plant tolerates somewhat lower light than many succulents but colors and flowers best with bright light.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Penwiper Plant tolerates somewhat lower light than many succulents but colors and flowers best with bright light. Broad, rounded, pale gray-green leaves are boldly marked with large, irregular, purplish-brown blotches, a striking mottled pattern that gives the plant its whimsical common name from a supposed resemblance to a stained cloth used for wiping pens. Native to Ethiopia and East Africa, it produces clusters of white, waxy, fragrant flowers on tall stems in winter, a welcome bloom period when few other succulents are flowering. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright indirect to full light for the boldest leaf markings, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes; eyes no deeper than 1–2 in below soil surface.
directions: Plant roots with the pink eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface — planting too deeply is the most common reason peonies fail to bloom. Peonies require 6 weeks of temperatures below 40°F to set flower buds, so they need cold winters and are not suited to zones 9+. Expect minimal bloom the first 1–2 years as the plant establishes; mature plants can live 50+ years with little care. Cut foliage to the ground in fall to remove potential disease inoculum.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; dislikes transplanting.
directions: Surface sow the fine seed directly in early spring or fall, as these poppies need light to germinate and resent root disturbance. Fully double, three- to five-inch ruffled flowers in many colors rise above soft, blue-green foliage that pollinators adore. Thin seedlings to give each plant room, and leave the decorative seed pods for dried arrangements. Fairly low-maintenance and self-sowing.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Peppermint Ice is part of the Winter Jewels breeding series, with white to pale pink flowers veined and edged in rose-red, blooming in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist while the plant establishes. Peppermint Ice is part of the acclaimed Winter Jewels hellebore breeding series, producing crisp white to pale pink flowers with fine rose-red veining and a picotee edge that gives each bloom a fresh, striped candy-cane appearance, held above leathery, evergreen, deeply divided foliage. Like other Lenten roses it blooms very early, often through late-season snow or hard frost, providing reliable color in the shade garden when little else is flowering. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to best showcase the flowers, and site it away from areas where pets or children graze, since all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Peppermint Mountain Laurel (Bold Pink-and-White Candy-Striped Bands)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Peppermint bears bold, candy-striped pink-and-white flower bands, a bright, distinctive pattern among mountain laurel cultivars.
directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Peppermint bears bold, crisply defined candy-cane-striped bands of pink against white on each flower, a brighter, higher-contrast pattern than the softer pink-white banding typical of the species, opening on the classic gnarled, sculptural evergreen shrub. Its vivid, striking pattern makes it a strong specimen or woodland-border accent. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; loves heat.
directions: This zinnia produces cheerful 2 to 4 inch blooms striped and speckled in bright colors, with no two flowers exactly alike. Heat-loving and easy to grow, it brightens beds, borders, and containers until fall frost and makes an excellent cut flower. Sow directly in warm soil or start indoors, and deadhead spent blooms to keep flowering. Give it full sun and good airflow to limit powdery mildew.

common_name: Peppermint Twist Phlox (White with Magenta Candy-Stripe Garden Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Peppermint Twist bears distinctive candy-striped petals unlike most solid-colored garden phlox.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Peppermint Twist bears white petals striped down the center with a bright magenta-pink candy stripe, a novelty pattern that stands out sharply from the solid-colored blooms typical of most garden phlox, carrying the classic sweet fragrance of the species. It benefits from full sun, steady moisture, and generous spacing to reduce powdery mildew, and stripe patterning can vary somewhat from flower to flower. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings, which revert to solid colors.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in moist to well-drained soil in any light condition; peppervine is one of the most shade-tolerant native vines and grows naturally in the forest understory and along shaded streambanks.
directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun along fences, trellises, and at woodland edges; peppervine is a native southeastern vine distinguished from grapes and other ampelopsis by its twice-compound leaves — the leaflets are themselves divided, giving the foliage a lacy, highly decorative texture quite unlike any other native vine. The small berries pass through shades of green, lavender, white, and finally dark purple-black as they ripen in fall — a stunning polychrome effect on the same cluster that makes this plant highly ornamental. The berries are important food for mockingbirds, bluebirds, and other fruit-eating birds in fall and winter. The plant tolerates partial shade better than most fruiting vines and is an excellent choice for naturalized areas in the woodland garden or at the edge of a forest.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Percy Wiseman is a compact yakushimanum-type hybrid well suited to smaller gardens than many larger rhododendron cultivars.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Percy Wiseman is a compact yakushimanum-type hybrid well suited to smaller gardens than many larger rhododendron cultivars. Flowers open a soft peachy-cream fading to pale primrose-yellow with a hint of pink at the edges, a subtle, changeable color combination typical of the finest yakushimanum-heritage hybrids, on a compact, dense, mounding shrub with attractive, felted new growth. Its manageable mature size, exceptional flower quality, and the sturdy constitution inherited from its Rhododendron yakushimanum parentage have made it a multi-award-winning cultivar and a favorite for smaller gardens where full-sized rhododendrons would be too large. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid hot afternoon sun in warmer zones, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Percy's Pride Red Hot Poker (Unusual Pale Yellow-Green Kniphofia)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Percy's Pride bears unusual pale yellow-green flowers, a departure from the typical hot reds and oranges of the genus.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; good drainage is critical year-round, since standing moisture around the crown quickly causes rot. Percy's Pride bears tall, torch-like flower spikes in an unusual pale, cool yellow-green shade, a striking departure from the hot reds, oranges, and golds typical of red hot poker cultivars, giving it a softer, more sophisticated presence in the border. Its long, arching, grassy foliage and tall flower stems make a strong architectural statement from summer into fall, and the tubular flowers draw hummingbirds despite the unusually cool color. In colder parts of its range, tie the foliage together over the crown and mulch deeply before the first hard freeze to protect the growing point, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering declines.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in warm, moist sand or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun after last frost; peregrina grows rapidly in warm climates and produces flowers almost continuously in frost-free zones.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun in the warmest microclimates of zone 10–12; peregrina is a Cuban native with strikingly red star-shaped flowers borne in clusters nearly year-round, making it one of the most continuously blooming ornamentals in tropical and subtropical landscapes. Plants attract butterflies and hummingbirds avidly. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — the seeds in particular are very poisonous and should not be accessible to children or pets. Drought-tolerant once established. In zone 9 container culture, bring indoors to a bright location before frost.

plant_note: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun in early spring or fall; perennial blanket flower requires excellent drainage and actually blooms more abundantly in lean soils than in rich, moist ones. It is the parent species of the hybrid Gaillardia x grandiflora and is hardier and longer-lived in harsh conditions than the hybrids. Direct seeding is preferable as the taproot resents disturbance.
directions: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; perennial blanket flower is the native wildflower parent of the hybrid blanket flowers sold in garden centers, native to the open, dry grasslands, prairies, and meadows of the Rocky Mountains and Great Plains from British Columbia to Colorado and Nebraska. The flowers are large, vivid daisy-like composites with bright-yellow ray petals banded at the base with orange-red, surrounding a prominent, rounded, dark-orange to reddish central disk — a flame-like, sunset color combination that is unmistakably blanket flower. As the true perennial species (unlike annual G. pulchella), it reliably returns each year from deep taproots and, given excellent drainage and lean soil, can persist for many years. It is more cold-hardy and drought-tolerant than the hybrid G. x grandiflora and succeeds in difficult, dry positions where the hybrids fail. Blooms continuously from June through frost in favorable conditions, providing months of vivid color for butterflies, bees, and other pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; nick and soak seed to aid germination.
directions: Nick and soak the hard seed, then direct sow in early spring at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor for this everlasting perennial sweet pea. The long, lush trailing vines ramble beautifully over shrubs or serve as a groundcover and return each year. It withstands summer heat well, is fairly drought tolerant, and attracts pollinators, though unlike annual sweet peas the flowers are not fragrant. Note that the seeds are not edible.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; perennial honesty blooms most freely in the dappled light of open deciduous woodland where it receives good spring light before the canopy leafs out, then is protected from summer desiccation by the shade.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; perennial honesty is a European shade woodland perennial — the long-lived, truly perennial species of the honesty family — that differs from the common biennial honesty (Lunaria annua) in being a genuine perennial that returns for many years without replanting, in producing intensely sweet, lilac-scented flowers (rather than the unscented flowers of the biennial), and in having oval rather than round seed pods. In late spring the plant produces tall stems bearing dense clusters of small, four-petaled, lilac-purple to white, powerfully honey-and-violet-fragrant flowers above large, heart-shaped, toothed leaves. After flowering, the flattened, elliptical, papery, silvery seed pods develop and dry to a translucent, pearly-white, decorative finish that is highly ornamental for dried arrangements. It grows naturally in the dappled light of deciduous woodland edges and is genuinely shade-tolerant — one of few flowering perennials that produces good flower and seed pod displays in partial to full shade. Spreads gradually by self-seeding.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained soil; established plants are drought-tolerant.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil — perennial salvia is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established and will rot in soggy conditions. Shear plants back by one-third to one-half after the first flush of deep violet-blue spikes fades to trigger a strong second (and sometimes third) bloom. The aromatic foliage deters deer and rabbits, making it a reliable choice for wildlife-challenged gardens. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to keep them vigorous.

plant_note: Sow seeds or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; perennial sea lavender develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established — site carefully. It tolerates salt spray, coastal conditions, and alkaline soils better than most perennials. Do not over-water; wet winter conditions cause root rot.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; perennial sea lavender is the long-lived perennial statice — a superior plant to the familiar annual Limonium sinuatum of florist bouquets, producing massive, airy clouds of tiny, papery, lavender-blue to violet flowers in billowing sprays from July through September. Each individual flower consists of two parts: an outer papery calyx in a rich purple and an inner true flower in cream, both of which retain their color when dried — making the plant outstanding for everlasting dried arrangements. The flower sprays rise 2–3 feet above a rosette of large, leathery, basal leaves, the whole creating an airy, haze-like display in the late-summer border. It is exceptionally tolerant of coastal salt spray, dry conditions, and alkaline soils — thriving in the coastal gardens of the Northeast and mid-Atlantic where it can self-sow into rock crevices and wall tops. Excellent as a long-lasting cut flower (fresh or dried) and as a companion plant for late-season color with ornamental grasses and salvias.

plant_note: Nick or soak seeds for 24 hours before sowing to improve germination; direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or sow in fall for spring germination. Perennial sweet pea grows from a deep, fleshy rootstock and is difficult to transplant — direct seeding or container-starts in deep pots are recommended.
directions: Nick seeds and sow in early spring at the base of a trellis, fence, or shrub; perennial sweet pea is a vigorous, deep-rooted climbing perennial that produces small clusters of magenta-pink, rose, or white flowers from June through August — different in color and somewhat smaller than the annual sweet pea but with the same climbing, clasping, and twining habit. It climbs by tendrils to 6–10 feet and tolerates poor, dry soils and heat far better than the annual sweet pea, making it an easy-care perennial vine for difficult spots. Unlike the annual, it has no fragrance, a tradeoff for its tough perennial character. It self-sows readily and can naturalize on disturbed soil and roadsides. The 'White Pearl' and 'Red Pearl' selections provide specific flower color control. All parts of the plant are mildly toxic if consumed in large quantities.

common_name: Perfect Storm Hibiscus (Dark Foliage Pink-Flowered Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Perfect Storm combines deep purple-black foliage with large pale pink flowers featuring a bold red eye, a compact, heavily branched Summerific series cultivar bred for exceptional flower count.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Perfect Storm combines dark, near-black-purple foliage with large, 6-8 inch, soft pink flowers marked by a bold, deep red eye at the center, a striking two-tone effect set against the dark leaves. It is among the most compact and heavily branched cultivars in the Summerific series, bred to produce an unusually high number of blooms per plant while staying tidy enough for smaller garden spaces and large containers. Flowering runs from midsummer into fall, with new buds opening continuously as older flowers fade after a single day. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown. It is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil, though Japanese beetles can damage foliage and flowers where present.

common_name: Perfecto Mundo Hot Pink Azalea (Reblooming Sun-Tolerant Compact Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Perfecto Mundo was bred for particularly strong sun tolerance and reliable rebloom, making it a good option for a bed that gets more direct light than azaleas traditionally prefer.
directions: Perfecto Mundo Hot Pink is a compact, reblooming azalea bred as a Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction with an emphasis on strong sun tolerance and dense, well-branched growth, producing vivid hot-pink flowers in flushes from spring through fall rather than the single spring bloom of traditional azaleas. Its compact size and tidy, mounded habit suit foundation plantings and mixed containers, and it needs minimal pruning to hold shape through the season. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, giving it more direct sun than older azalea types tolerate, and water deeply during dry spells to sustain the extended bloom cycle; light pruning right after the heaviest spring flush avoids removing developing buds for later color.

common_name: Perfecto Mundo White Azalea (Reblooming Sun-Tolerant Compact White Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Perfecto Mundo was bred for particularly strong sun tolerance and reliable rebloom, making it a good option for a bed that gets more direct light than azaleas traditionally prefer.
directions: Perfecto Mundo White is a compact, reblooming azalea bred as a Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction, producing clean white flowers in repeated flushes from spring through fall on a dense, well-branched, sun-tolerant shrub. Its neutral flower color and tidy, mounded habit make it a versatile mixer in foundation plantings and containers alongside other colors, needing minimal pruning to hold shape through the season. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, giving it more direct sun than older azalea types tolerate, and water deeply during dry spells to sustain the extended bloom cycle; light pruning right after the heaviest spring flush avoids removing developing buds for later color.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; perfoliate bellwort is distinguished from the similar large-flowered bellwort (U. grandiflora) by its smaller, paler yellow flowers and by the granular-papillose (roughened) texture on the inner surface of its petals.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting rhizomes about 2 inches deep; perfoliate bellwort is a native spring wildflower of eastern North American deciduous forests that closely resembles the large-flowered bellwort (U. grandiflora) but is distinguished by its smaller, paler, lemon-yellow flowers and by a distinctive granular-roughened texture on the inner surface of its petals visible on close examination. Like U. grandiflora, the stem of U. perfoliata appears to pass directly through the leaves (perfoliate), giving both species their characteristic appearance; however, perfoliate bellwort tends to be somewhat less vigorous and slightly more shade tolerant than its larger relative. It goes dormant by midsummer and should be planted with late-emerging companions such as hostas or ferns to fill the gap. Spreads slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies and is an excellent naturalizer in shaded native plant gardens from New England to Florida.

common_name: Perforated Rhaphidophora (Window Rhaphidophora, Foraminous Rhaphidophora, Hole-Leaf Rhaphidophora)
plant_note: Grow on a moss pole, rough bark board, or tree trunk in partial to deep shade with high humidity; Rhaphidophora foraminifera produces leaves with natural circular to elongated holes (fenestrations) perforating the blade — similar in concept to the holes in Monstera deliciosa but produced through a different morphological mechanism. The holes develop as the leaf matures, often beginning as slits at the leaf margin that become closed holes as the leaf expands. Very fast-growing once established. Requires warm, humid conditions and a rough climbing surface. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow on a rough bark surface or moss pole in partial to deep shade in moist, humid conditions — Perforated Rhaphidophora climbs rapidly when given a rough surface and produces its distinctively perforated, window-like leaves most dramatically when allowed to ascend and provided consistently warm, humid conditions. Rhaphidophora foraminifera is a climbing, hemiepiphytic aroid in the Araceae family native to Southeast Asia (Borneo, Sabah, Malaysia), a member of the genus Rhaphidophora in the tribe Monstereae — the same tribe as Monstera, Epipremnum, and Scindapsus. The plant is grown for the unusual quality of its mature adult leaves: broadly oval to oblong, dark glossy green, with a scattered array of circular to irregular holes (fenestrations or foramina — from which the species name foraminifera, 'bearing holes,' derives) perforating the leaf blade. The holes begin forming in medium-sized, maturing leaves and range from small (0.5 inch) to larger irregular perforations scattered across the leaf surface. The fenestration pattern in R. foraminifera differs from Monstera deliciosa both in hole size and distribution, and in the mechanism of formation, but the visual effect — a glossy, dark-green leaf with natural window-like holes — gives the plant an appearance that immediately suggests an unusual tropical relative of the Swiss Cheese Plant. The plant climbs rapidly with adhesive aerial roots and can cover large surfaces of rough bark or moss poles with attractive, window-paned foliage. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; nick and soak seed to aid germination.
directions: Nick and soak the seed, then direct sow in early spring at the foot of a trellis, as sweet peas relish cool weather and need support to climb. This rainbow blend of large, ruffled flowers in purple, red, rose, scarlet, white, blue, cream, and bicolors carries an exquisite old-fashioned fragrance. More heat resistant than many strains, it still fades in high summer, so sow early. Cut often to keep the fragrant blooms coming.
