plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Perle d'Azur is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Perle d'Azur, introduced from France in 1885, bears an extraordinary abundance of sky-blue, four-petaled flowers over a long summer season, covering the vine so thoroughly that established plants can look like a solid sheet of blue. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so it can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter, a far simpler pruning routine than the large-flowered old-wood types. Its vigor and free-flowering habit make it an excellent choice for scrambling through a large shrub or covering a fence quickly.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Perle d'Or is an 1884 French polyantha, often compared to the similar Cecile Brunner, valued for clusters of small, apricot-pink, old-fashioned blooms on a tough, easygoing shrub.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Perle d'Or needs little beyond an occasional deep watering once it's established. Introduced in France in 1884, Perle d'Or is a classic polyantha rose closely related to the better-known Cecile Brunner, producing abundant clusters of small, high-centered, apricot-to-golden-pink blooms with a spicy-sweet fragrance held above neat, small foliage on a tough, twiggy shrub. It blooms in nearly continuous flushes from spring through frost, tolerates poor soil and Southern heat and humidity with minimal disease trouble, and its small flower size and clustered habit make it an excellent choice for cutting or for a low, informal hedge. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape the shrub and encourage vigorous new growth loaded with flower buds.

common_name: Perle des Jardins Rose (Fragrant Creamy-Yellow Antique Tea Rose)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Perle des Jardins, a French Tea rose introduced in 1874, was historically valued as a florist's rose for its fragrant, pale creamy-yellow blooms.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Perle des Jardins, introduced in France in 1874, bears full, richly fragrant, pale creamy-yellow flowers that were prized historically as a cut flower and greenhouse florist rose before becoming a mainstay of heirloom garden collections. Like other Tea roses it repeats reliably through the growing season and tolerates heat and humidity with far less disease pressure than many modern hybrid teas, needing only a sunny, well-drained spot and occasional light pruning after each bloom flush. Its soft yellow color and strong fragrance make it a distinctive addition to an antique rose collection or mixed border.

common_name: Perle von Nurnberg Echeveria (Iridescent Purple-Pink Rosette Succulent)
plant_note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Perle von Nurnberg requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water, especially in the center of the rosette, which quickly leads to rot.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Perle von Nurnberg is a classic hybrid echeveria prized for its large, iridescent rosettes of dusty mauve-purple leaves with a pearlescent pink-lavender sheen that shifts subtly with the light, one of the most striking color combinations among ornamental echeveria hybrids. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings, and it makes an excellent container or rock garden specimen in the warm, dry conditions it prefers. In zone 9a it can be grown outdoors in a well-drained container or bed but should be moved under cover or indoors during hard freezes, since it has little cold tolerance.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or plant container-grown plants in moist to dry, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; this hybrid is one of the most drought-tolerant epimediums once established. Cut old foliage back to the ground in late winter (February) before the new flowers and leaves emerge to display the early spring show.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; Perralchicum barrenwort is one of the most vigorous, robust, and drought-tolerant epimediums — a hybrid between E. perralderianum (Algerian barrenwort) and E. pinnatum subsp. colchicum, producing broadly heart-shaped, dark-green, leathery leaves that are semi-evergreen to evergreen and form a dense, reliable groundcover under trees where few other plants will grow. In early spring, before the foliage, slender wiry stems carry loose clusters of small, bright-yellow, four-petaled flowers with short spurs — like a miniature rain of golden stars above the crown. The primary cultivar 'Frohnleiten' is widely available and particularly vigorous. It spreads steadily by rhizomes and is among the most effective ground covers for dry shade under large trees — tolerating the challenging conditions of root competition, deep shade, and summer drought that defeat even other epimediums. Once established, it requires essentially no maintenance beyond cutting back old foliage annually.

common_name: Perry's Baby Red Water Lily (Dwarf Hardy Deep Red Container Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 6-12 inches deep in a full-sun pond or tub after last frost; Perry's Baby Red, a 1989 introduction, is a true dwarf hardy water lily bearing deep red cup-shaped flowers, ideal for small ponds and container water gardens.
directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers only 6 to 12 inches deep in a full-sun pond or even a half-barrel tub garden, since Perry's Baby Red is a genuine dwarf, staying small enough that it does not need the large ponds most hardy water lilies require. Introduced in 1989 by hybridizer D. Stetson Perry, it bears compact, cup-shaped flowers in a deep, rich red held just above small, neat pads, making it one of the best hardy water lily choices for a container water garden, small preformed pond, or any spot too small for a standard cultivar. It overwinters in the pond in most temperate climates as a true hardy type. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly through the growing season, remove spent flowers and yellowing pads, and divide congested rhizomes every few years.

common_name: Perry's Blue Siberian Iris (Historic Soft Blue Self, One of the Oldest Named Cultivars)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Perry's Blue, registered in 1912, is one of the oldest named Siberian iris cultivars still commonly grown.
directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Perry's Blue, registered in 1912 by English horticulturist Amos Perry, is one of the oldest named Siberian iris cultivars still widely grown today, bearing soft, clear blue self-colored flowers over narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. Its long garden history and reliable performance have kept it in cultivation for over a century. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Perry's Fire Opal Water Lily (Hardy Orange-Red Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant the tuberous rootstock horizontally in a wide aquatic container of heavy clay loam topped with pea gravel, then submerge so the crown sits 6 to 18 inches below the water surface in a sunny, still section of the pond.
directions: Set the rootstock in a wide planting basket of heavy garden soil capped with gravel to keep it in place, then lower the pot so the growing crown rests six to eighteen inches beneath the surface in full sun. This hardy Perry D. Slocum hybrid was bred for its unusually warm coloring among hardy lilies, opening a fiery orange that deepens toward red-orange as each flower ages. Star-shaped blooms sit just above rounded green pads from late spring through fall, with a moderate spread that suits small to mid-sized garden ponds and large tubs. Regular removal of spent flowers and yellowing pads keeps the plant blooming steadily through the season.

common_name: Perry's Giant Sunburst Lotus (Large Lemon-Yellow Slocum Hybrid Lotus)
plant_note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after water has warmed past last frost; Perry's Giant Sunburst, bred by Perry D. Slocum, bears large lemon-yellow flowers 8-12 inches across.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 12 to 18 inches deep in a full-sun pond, waiting until the water has warmed past danger of frost. Perry's Giant Sunburst, bred by the renowned lotus and water lily hybridizer Perry D. Slocum, bears enormous, richly fragrant lemon-yellow flowers 8 to 12 inches across held well above the water on tall, sturdy stems, one of the largest-flowered yellow lotus cultivars available, followed by the distinctive flat seed pods prized for dried arrangements. Once the huge, round, umbrella-like leaves and blooms emerge in early summer, the plant grows vigorously and needs a fairly large, deep container or open pond bottom to reach its full size. Lotus goes dormant and dies back completely each winter, re-emerging from the tuber the following late spring; divide overcrowded tubers every few years in spring.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep and 6–8 inches apart in well-drained soil in fall; Persian allium bulbs naturalize well in sunny, dry spots and increase year over year.
directions: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in well-drained to dry soil in full sun in fall; Persian allium is one of the most popular large-flowered ornamental alliums, producing perfectly spherical 4–5 inch flower balls of hundreds of tiny star-shaped purple flowers on tall stiff stems in late spring. The cultivar 'Purple Sensation' is among the deepest purple-flowering bulbs available. Foliage appears in early spring and often dies back by bloom time, so plant alliums among hostas, daylilies, or other perennials that will fill in around the fading leaves. Alliums are strongly deer-resistant. After blooming, the spherical seed heads dry to silvery brown and remain ornamental through summer and fall.

plant_note: Soak claws (tubers) in water for 3–4 hours before planting; plant claw-side down, 2 inches deep, 6 inches apart. In zones 8–11, plant in October–November for winter and spring bloom. In zones 4–7, plant in early spring as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: Plant soaked claw-shaped tubers in well-drained, cool soil in full sun; Persian buttercup is the cream of the cool-season cut flower garden, producing fully double flowers 2–4 inches across with dozens of silky petals arranged in concentric layers in every color of the rainbow — cream, yellow, gold, orange, red, pink, magenta, purple, and white, many with picotee edges. They are extraordinarily beautiful as cut flowers, lasting 7–10 days in a vase. In zone 8‑9, the October-to-spring season is ideal — plant in fall, enjoy blooms from January through April. Plants go dormant in summer heat and can be left in the ground in well-drained sites or dug and stored dry. Modern Cloni and Elegance series produce the most enormous, peony-like flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; this narrow-leaved Mexican zinnia handles hot, dry conditions with ease. It bears bicolored single and double flowers in gold, burgundy, cream, red, and orange that bloom until first frost. Compact and reliable, it suits beds, borders, and containers and needs little water once established. Deadhead to extend the display and draw pollinators.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring after flowering; Persian epimedium spreads steadily by underground rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat in dry to moist shade. Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Persian epimedium from the Caucasus and northern Iran is one of the most vigorous and reliable epimediums for shade ground cover, producing cheerful bright yellow flowers in spring and dense, semi-evergreen foliage that smothers weeds effectively. The species is particularly valuable for dry shade under trees where it colonizes aggressively enough to form a solid cover but is not invasively weedy in garden beds. The subspecies subsp. colchicum is especially commonly grown, with larger, brighter yellow flowers and more robust spreading. Epimediums as a genus are among the most underused dry-shade perennials, thriving where other plants struggle. Shear or mow the old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to show the flowers clearly.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep and 8-10 inches apart in sharply well-drained, alkaline to neutral, gritty or sandy soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun position in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; Persian fritillary is native to rocky, well-drained slopes in Turkey, Iran, and the Middle East and absolutely requires excellent drainage — it will rot in wet or heavy clay soils. In areas with wet winters, plant in raised beds or incorporate grit generously to improve drainage. It may take 2-3 seasons to settle in before flowering freely.
directions: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in sharply well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in fall for April bloom; Persian fritillary is one of the most dramatically beautiful and architecturally impressive of all spring bulbs, producing stout, upright stems 24-36 inches tall clothed in whorls of glaucous blue-grey leaves and terminating in a long, densely flowered raceme of 20-30 or more pendant, narrowly bell-shaped flowers in an extraordinarily rich, deep plum-purple to near-black — a color unmatched in depth and intensity by any other commonly grown spring bulb. The cultivar 'Adiyaman' is particularly dark and free-flowering. Native to rocky limestone slopes, scrub, and dry meadows across Turkey, Iran, and the Levant, it demands the sharp drainage, alkaline soil, and summer baking of its native habitat to perform well, and it is less forgiving of wet, heavy soils than most spring bulbs. In well-suited conditions in a warm, sheltered border with free-draining soil it is a stunning, long-lived perennial that draws attention from every visitor to the spring garden.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow onto moist seed-starting mix and keep at 60 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit until germination, then transplant out after frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last expected frost, pressing them onto the surface of a moist, well-draining seed-starting mix at 60 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit; do not cover deeply as light aids germination. Transplant seedlings into a sunny site with sharply drained, lean soil after all frost risk has passed, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart to allow airflow around the aromatic foliage. Once established, Persian Germander is highly drought-tolerant and thrives on neglect — avoid rich soil and heavy watering, which promote floppy growth at the expense of the dense, upright flower spikes. Cut plants back by about one-third after the first flush of bloom to encourage a second wave of the deep purplish-red flowers that are so attractive to bees and butterflies.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in spring or fall; Persian ironwood adapts to a wide range of soil types including clay and dry soils once established and is notably more heat- and drought-tolerant than its forest origins might suggest. Its multi-stemmed, vase-shaped habit develops best when lower branches are allowed to sweep to the ground.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Persian ironwood is one of the finest four-season ornamental trees available, native to the Alborz Mountains and Caspian lowlands of northern Iran where it grows as a dominant forest species. In late winter and very early spring (January–March), before any leaves appear, the branches are lit with clusters of tiny, brilliant-red staminate flowers — among the earliest flowers of any woody plant. The leaves that follow are large, wavy-edged, and glossy, producing some of the most spectacular autumn color of any tree in deep shades of scarlet, orange, yellow, and burgundy all simultaneously present on one tree. Through winter, the mottled, exfoliating bark in tones of gray, green, and brown creates a patchwork pattern similar to the London plane tree, giving outstanding year-round bark interest. The wood is among the hardest of all deciduous trees, hence its common name. Increasingly recognized as an outstanding landscape tree that offers something of interest in every season.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring or fall in any well-drained soil in shade; Persian ivy establishes quickly and is less prone to the leaf spot and spider mite problems that affect English ivy in hot, humid summers of the South.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full to partial shade — Persian ivy is more tolerant of deep shade than English ivy and produces dramatically larger leaves, up to 8–10 inches across, with a bold, tropical quality that makes it stand apart as a groundcover or climbing vine in shaded areas. The dark, leathery, heart-shaped leaves have a glossy surface and a pleasant resinous fragrance when handled. Unlike the widely planted English ivy (H. helix), Persian ivy is far less invasive and rarely escapes into natural areas in North America. The cultivar 'Sulphur Heart' features leaves with bold yellow centers and dark green edges, making it one of the most striking shade groundcovers available; 'Dentata Variegata' has cream-margined leaves. Berries are toxic — do not plant where children or pets may ingest them. Excellent on north-facing slopes and under dense tree canopies.

plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter Gulf Coast gardens for spring bloom; nigella resents transplanting and is best direct sown where it is to flower.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun, since the fine taproot resents disturbance and rarely transplants successfully. Persian Jewels is a classic mixed-color strain of love-in-a-mist, blending sky blue, white, pink, rose, and violet-purple flowers, each one nestled in a delicate, thread-fine haze of feathery foliage that gives the plant its common name. After the flowers fade they are followed by inflated, papery, striped seed pods that are just as ornamental as the blooms and prized for dried arrangements. Nigella grows and blooms fastest in the cool part of the season, going to seed once summer heat sets in, and self-seeds readily where happy, often popping up as volunteers the following year without any replanting.

plant_note: Divide and transplant bare-root fans in spring or late summer, spreading roots out in a shallow planting hole with the crown just below the soil surface.
directions: Set bare-root fans in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, spreading roots evenly and covering the crown with about an inch of soil before watering in thoroughly. Give plants a full growing season to establish before expecting peak bloom. Persian Market is a tetraploid daylily bred by Stamile with ruffled, lavender-purple petals surrounding a bold chartreuse-green throat, giving the flower strong color contrast and substance. Its large, well-formed blooms and vigorous branching scapes have made it a widely grown modern classic among purple-toned daylilies.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall at a depth of 3–4 times the bulb diameter (typically 4–6 in) in well-drained soil; bulbs establish roots through winter and send up foliage in early spring with blooms in late spring.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Persian onion produces softball-sized spherical flowerheads in rich violet-purple on straight stems 24–36 inches tall in late spring — a striking vertical accent among lower perennials. The dried seedheads maintain their globe form and are attractive into summer, making them excellent for cutting and drying. Persian onion is an important parent species of the popular garden variety 'Purple Sensation,' which shares its intense color and large globe form. Plant in drifts among roses, peonies, or late-flowering alliums to create a succession of color. The foliage dies back after bloom, so plant among perennials that will mask the yellowing leaves. Reliable and long-lived in zones 4–8 with good drainage; bulbs often naturalize and gradually multiply.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after temperatures are consistently above 65°F in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Persian shield performs best in bright, filtered shade and may develop leaf scorch in direct afternoon sun in hot climates. It roots readily from stem cuttings and can be overwintered indoors in colder zones.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Persian shield is one of the most flamboyantly beautiful foliage plants available for shaded tropical gardens, with large, lance-shaped leaves of iridescent silver-purple that shimmer with metallic, jewel-like blue-purple-silver tones that change with the viewing angle and lighting conditions — an almost impossibly vivid foliage display unlike anything else in the garden. In zone 8–11 it thrives outdoors in the warm, humid conditions of the Gulf Coast, particularly in sheltered, brightly shaded spots where the metallic leaves glow dramatically. Pinch growing tips frequently to encourage dense, bushy growth — unpinched plants become tall and leggy. It is outstanding as a container plant that can be moved indoors as a houseplant in winter (where it performs beautifully in indirect light) in colder zones. Propagates effortlessly from 4-inch stem cuttings rooted in moist potting mix.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil where they can naturalize undisturbed for years.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 2-4 inches apart in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, positioning them where they will not be disturbed since they resent transplanting once established. Pale silvery-blue, star-shaped flowers with a darker central stripe on each petal open in very early spring, often emerging alongside the last snowdrops and before most other squills. The short flower stalks and low grassy foliage make it a good choice for rock gardens, bulb lawns, or the front edge of a border where early color is welcome. Left undisturbed, it slowly forms dense, long-lived colonies.

subcategory: compact tender bedding and container annual
plant_note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost since it is slow to reach blooming size, and transplant outdoors only once nights are reliably warm.
directions: Press the tiny seed onto the surface of a moist, well-draining seed mix and keep warm and humid under cover, as it germinates slowly and needs light to sprout. Grow on in bright, indirect light and pinch seedlings once to build a rounded mound before setting plants out in a sheltered spot with dappled shade in hot regions. Compact plants form neat domes of glossy foliage covered in small, fragrant, saucer-shaped violet-blue or white flowers with contrasting yellow anthers, making it a long-blooming choice for shaded borders, window boxes, and indoor pots.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in deep shade; persistent trillium is a federally threatened species restricted to a handful of gorge forests along the Tallulah and Chattooga Rivers in northeast Georgia and northwest South Carolina, and wild collection is illegal.
directions: Plant only nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in deep shade beneath rhododendron or mountain laurel, mimicking the steep gorge-forest understory where this species survives in the wild. Persistent trillium is a federally threatened pedicellate species known only from a small cluster of populations in the deep river gorges of the Tallulah and Chattooga watersheds in northeast Georgia and adjacent South Carolina, named for its narrow pink-to-white petals, which stay fresh and open far longer than those of most trilliums before fading. Because natural populations are so restricted and legally protected, it should be grown only from nursery-propagated stock as a specialty addition to a cool, deeply shaded woodland garden, never collected from the wild. It is slow to establish and slower still to reach flowering size, so patience and consistently cool, moist conditions are essential to success.

common_name: Peru Monstera (Karstenianum Monstera, Monstera sp. Peru)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Peru Monstera cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Unlike many Monsteras that trail well, Peru Monstera is relatively compact and climbs tightly — a small moss pole or trellis is ideal. The leaves remain similar in size whether trailing or climbing, unlike the dramatic juvenile-to-adult size transformation of M. deliciosa. Propagate from stem cuttings with one node. Use a well-draining aroid potting mix. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Peru Monstera maintains attractive foliage in moderate indoor light and is more adaptable to typical room conditions than many of the collector Monsteras. Monstera sp. 'Peru' (sometimes called Monstera karstenianum, though this name has uncertain formal botanical status) is a compact climbing aroid from Peru and neighboring South American countries in the Araceae family, sold widely under the name 'Monstera Peru' in the houseplant trade. The leaves are its defining feature: small to medium-sized (typically 4–8 inches), dark green to nearly blue-green, rigidly leathery, and covered with a distinctive topographic texture — the leaf surface is not smooth but deeply embossed with a pattern of raised veins and sunken areas creating a strongly three-dimensional, almost crinkled or hammered-metal appearance. The leaves are glossy and intensely colored, and the rigid, structural texture of each leaf is the quality that makes the plant immediately recognizable among the many Monsteras now popular in cultivation. Unlike M. deliciosa and M. adansonii, Peru Monstera does not develop fenestrations (holes) even in maturity — the ornamental value is entirely in the texture and color of the solid leaf surface. It is generally adaptable to indoor conditions and grows at a moderate pace. All parts are toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; adapted to hot, dry climates, this species-type zinnia asks little water once established. Its simple, open, single flowers make ideal landing pads for pollinators and self-sow to return year after year. Give full sun and good airflow to limit mildew, and cut or deadhead to keep the airy plants blooming. A charming, drought-tolerant choice for naturalized plantings.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Hymenocallis x festalis bulbs can remain in the ground year-round in zone 9 if given winter protection with heavy mulch; in colder zones dig and store bulbs above 40°F during winter. The white, fragrant flowers appear in late spring and early summer (May–July in zone 9) on tall scapes — each scape bears 3–5 flowers. The fragrance is sweetly powerful in the evening. Plants in zone 9 produce increasing numbers of flowering scapes each year as the bulbs multiply — well-established clumps can produce 20–30 flower scapes in a single season. The bulb is toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil — Peruvian Daffodil performs particularly well in partial shade in zone 9 where afternoon shade reduces the stress of peak summer heat during the blooming period; Peruvian Daffodil (Hymenocallis x festalis) is a spider lily hybrid of South American origin producing among the most elegant and exotic-looking white flowers of any summer bulb — each pure white flower has a large, central, funnel-shaped cup (corona) surrounded by six long, narrow, reflexed white petals that extend outward like spider legs, creating a dramatic, intricate structure entirely different from any conventional lily or daffodil form. The powerful sweet fragrance, strongest in the evening, is one of the most intensely pleasant of any summer-blooming flower — filling a garden area with a rich, sweet, tropical scent that attracts sphinx moths (hawkmoths) as pollinators. The combination of exotic flower structure, intense fragrance, white color (which reflects beautifully in the dusk and evening garden), and adaptability to partial shade makes Hymenocallis one of the most distinctive and memorable summer bulbs available for zone 9 gardens.

plant_note: Plant tuberous roots in spring; superb cut flower.
directions: Plant Peruvian lily tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil, handling the brittle roots carefully. The orchid-like flowers in warm oranges, pinks, and reds are among the longest-lasting of all cut flowers. Grow in full sun to light shade with consistent moisture, and pull rather than cut spent stems to stimulate rebloom. In colder zones mulch heavily for winter or lift the roots for storage.

common_name: Peter Pan Agapanthus (Dwarf Blue Agapanthus, Dwarf Lily of the Nile)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Peter Pan is drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms more prolifically when slightly root-bound — avoid dividing too frequently and allow plants to form mature, congested clumps before dividing.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Peter Pan is the most widely planted dwarf agapanthus cultivar — a compact, clump-forming evergreen perennial reaching only 12–18 inches tall in the foliage mass, with flower scapes rising to 24–30 inches above the clump in summer and bearing clusters of clear blue-lavender, trumpet-shaped flowers that are highly attractive to hummingbirds and bees. The compact size makes Peter Pan suitable for situations where the larger agapanthus species would be overwhelming — edging, containers, mass ground cover plantings under trees, and low borders. In zone 9, Peter Pan blooms reliably in June–August and the strap-like, dark-green, evergreen foliage provides attractive year-round ground cover. The key cultural insight is that agapanthus blooms most prolifically when the roots are somewhat constrained — plants that are allowed to fill their container or planting space without division for several years produce the heaviest flowering. Peter Pan is drought-tolerant once established, tolerates reflected heat from paving and walls, and requires minimal maintenance beyond occasional division every 5–7 years when the clump becomes overcrowded. Division is best done in late winter in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season; Peter Pears was named for the English tenor and remains a favorite warm-toned exhibition and cutting gladiolus.
directions: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes as the ruffled blooms open. Peter Pears carries warm apricot-orange florets accented by a deeper red-orange throat blotch, a rich, glowing color that has kept it popular for both garden display and exhibition since its introduction. The tall, densely flowered spikes open from the bottom up over one to two weeks, giving a long window for cutting. Cut spikes once the lowest florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm, and lift and store corms after foliage yellows in colder zones.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface sow as light aids germination.
directions: Start seed indoors eight to ten weeks before the last frost, pressing the tiny seed onto the surface since light is essential for germination. This compact blend blooms prolifically all summer in red, rose, scarlet, salmon, violet, and white, attracting butterflies and pollinators. Set out after frost in full sun in window boxes, borders, and containers. Deadhead and feed regularly to sustain the heavy flowering.

common_name: Petra Croton (Classic Multi-Color Bold-Foliage Tropical Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; maximum color intensity in Petra requires high light — move to more shade only to protect from extreme summer heat, not as a routine growing position.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Petra is the most widely planted croton (Codiaeum variegatum) cultivar in the United States — the standard by which other crotons are measured, producing large, boldly lobed, leathery leaves with spectacular multi-color variegation in green, yellow, orange, and bright red that develops most intensely in high light. A single leaf may display all four colors simultaneously, with yellow at the midrib transitioning through orange to red at the leaf margins and green background — creating the kind of botanical fireworks impossible to achieve with any other commonly available ornamental. 'Petra' is named for its large, broadly lobed leaf form with relatively uniform multicolor patterning, distinguishing it from more narrowly-leaved or sparsely variegated croton selections. In zone 9, Petra is widely used as a warm-season container plant for patios and entryways, providing dramatic tropical foliage from April through October before being moved indoors to overwinter in a bright window or warm greenhouse. In zone 10-12, Petra grows as an evergreen perennial shrub to 4–6 feet with permanent outdoor planting. The spectacular foliage combines effectively with solid-color tropicals — red ginger, golden canna, purple confederate rose — where the multi-color leaves tie together the surrounding single-color plants.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow tiny seed on the surface of moist starting mix — do not cover, as petunias need light to germinate. Pinch transplants by one-third when planting to encourage branching. Deadhead or shear back leggy plants by half in midsummer to renew vigor and flush of bloom. Feed every two weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer for best performance.

common_name: Peve Minaret Bald Cypress (Dwarf Narrow-Conical Bald Cypress)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Peve Minaret is a true dwarf selection of bald cypress that fits small landscapes and container culture where the towering native species would be far too large.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, though it also tolerates average well-drained garden soil once established. Peve Minaret is a dwarf, densely conical selection of the native bald cypress, growing to a fraction of the height of the species while retaining the same soft, ferny, deciduous foliage that turns rusty orange-brown in fall, making it a rare option for gardeners who want the character of a bald cypress in a small yard, foundation planting, or large container. Like the species it handles both flooded and ordinary soil with equal ease and needs little care once established beyond occasional watering during drought. Its compact, narrow form eliminates the need for the corrective pruning larger bald cypress selections often require near structures or power lines.

common_name: Pewter Lace Fern (Silvery Hybrid Painted Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Pewter Lace bears finely cut, lacy fronds in a cool, metallic pewter-silver overlaid with darker gray-green tones and deep burgundy-red stems, a more finely dissected, delicate frond texture than the broader-cut leaves of many Japanese painted fern hybrids. Its refined, silvery texture provides a soft, luminous accent in a shaded border, contrasting well with the bolder leaves of hostas and heucheras nearby. Cut back old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Pewter Veil is one of the older, widely proven painted fern selections and adapts readily to average shade-garden conditions.
directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Pewter Veil is one of the older, widely proven painted fern selections and adapts readily to average shade-garden conditions. Broad, silvery-gray fronds are overlaid with a soft metallic sheen and centered with deep maroon-purple midribs, giving the whole clump a cool, luminous glow that brightens even the darkest corners of a shade garden. One of the earliest painted fern cultivars to reach wide distribution, it received early recognition for garden performance and remains a benchmark against which newer selections are compared, combining reliably with hostas, astilbe, and heuchera. Deciduous and easy, it dies back in fall and simply needs old fronds cut away and soil kept from drying out through the growing season.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangeas tolerate considerably more sun than bigleaf types.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangeas tolerate far more direct sun than bigleaf types and are not affected by soil pH the way blue-and-pink mophead hydrangeas are. Phantom produces some of the largest flower panicles of any hydrangea cultivar, often 12–15 inches long, opening creamy white and aging to a soft pinkish blush, on a large, sturdy shrub whose thick stems hold the huge flower heads upright without flopping even after rain. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing that year's flowers, making size management straightforward for such a large-flowered cultivar. Water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Pharaoh's Mask Elephant Ear (Green Leaf with Bold Black Hand-Painted Veins)
plant_note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Pharaoh's Mask bears green leaves with bold, raised black midribs and veins that look hand-painted, a striking pattern among elephant ear cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9. Pharaoh's Mask bears large green leaves crossed with bold, raised, near-black midribs and veins that stand out sharply against the lighter leaf surface, giving the foliage a dramatic, almost hand-painted appearance unlike the more uniformly colored leaves of most colocasia cultivars. The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every two to three years to control spread. Provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions, as elephant ear grows naturally along streamsides and in boggy areas.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 6–8 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; pheasant's eye narcissus is the most shade-tolerant daffodil species and naturalizes beautifully under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant bulbs 6–8 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees — the bulbs receive full sun in spring before leaves emerge, and the summer shade helps keep them cool and dry during dormancy. Narcissus poeticus is the wild narcissus of southern European mountain meadows, the most fragrant of all daffodil species, with pure-white petals and a tiny, flat, yellow cup edged in red (the "pheasant's eye") — a simple, elegant flower of extraordinary fragrance used in the production of genuine Diorissimo and other fine perfumes. Unlike most daffodils, it flowers very late (often after tulips) in mid- to late spring, extending the daffodil season considerably; it is among the most shade-tolerant of daffodils and naturalizes superbly under deciduous trees. The selected form 'Actaea' is the classic large-cupped cultivar widely available.

common_name: Pheasant's Tail Grass (New Zealand Wind Grass)
plant_note: Set out nursery divisions or transplants in spring after frost danger passes, spacing plants to allow the arching foliage room to display its fountain shape.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in well-drained soil, choosing a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hotter climates to keep the foliage color from bleaching. It tolerates light, infrequent irrigation once established but performs best with even moisture and does not like winter wet combined with heavy clay. The narrow, arching leaves emerge olive-green and shift to copper, bronze, and orange tones through the seasons, and airy purplish flower panicles rise above the mound in summer, giving it a soft, self-seeding presence in mixed borders and gravel gardens. In cold climates it is usually grown as an annual or protected in a container over winter.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or spring-sow after moist chilling, in moist, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Philadelphia fleabane self-seeds readily and naturalizes quickly into damp meadows, ditches, and woodland edges.
directions: Plant in moist, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Philadelphia fleabane is one of the most widespread native fleabanes in eastern North America, found naturally in damp meadows, ditches, roadsides, and open woodland edges, where it produces an abundance of small, daisy-like flowers with dozens of very fine, thread-like pink-to-white rays around a bright yellow center. It blooms early, from mid-spring into summer, providing an important nectar source for small native bees, syrphid flies, and other early-season pollinators before many summer wildflowers begin blooming. Plants form loose rosettes that send up multiple flowering stems and self-seed readily, naturalizing into cheerful colonies in a damp meadow or the informal edge of a rain garden without becoming aggressively weedy in a maintained bed. It is short-lived as an individual plant (often biennial or short-lived perennial) but persists reliably in a planting through continuous self-seeding. Cut back after the main bloom flush to tidy the planting and encourage a possible rebloom later in the season.

plant_note: Divide clumps or plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in deep shade in zone 10–12; Philippine Evergreen is a robust, clumping aroid native to the Philippines and Sulawesi — the wild parent species of the wide array of ornamental Aglaonema cultivars grown as houseplants worldwide — bearing attractive, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves with silver-gray variegation in a slow-growing, durable, extraordinarily shade-tolerant clump.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in deep shade to bright indirect light; Aglaonema commutatum is among the most shade-tolerant and low-light-tolerant plants in cultivation — thriving in conditions with as little as 25–50 foot-candles of light; avoid direct sun, cold drafts, and overwatering. Aglaonema commutatum (Philippine Evergreen or Chinese Evergreen) is a slow-growing, clumping, rhizomatous aroid native to the humid tropical forests of the Philippines and Sulawesi, and the wild ancestor of dozens of cultivated Aglaonema varieties grown as among the most popular and durable foliage houseplants and low-light landscape plants in the world. The wild species produces lance-shaped, dark-green leaves with attractive silver-gray markings and variegation patterns in variable degrees, typically forming clumps 1–3 feet tall with arching stems. Aglaonema commutatum and its cultivated hybrids are celebrated as among the most tolerant of all ornamental plants to low light, neglect, dry indoor air, and irregular watering — making them a first-choice recommendation for deep-shade landscape positions, dim interior corners, offices, shopping centers, and any low-light situation where most plants fail. The wild species has been intensively hybridized to create hundreds of ornamental cultivars ranging from silver-variegated to red-pink, orange, and multi-colored forms. Outdoors in zone 10–12, it performs as an excellent, very low-maintenance, deep-shade groundcover or accent plant. All Aglaonema parts contain calcium oxalate crystals — mildly toxic if ingested.

common_name: Philippine Ground Orchid (Large Purple Ground Orchid, Tall Spathoglottis)
plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or container-grown clumps in spring in partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, orchid bark-enriched soil; Spathoglottis plicata is the most garden-adaptable of the ground orchids, tolerating a much wider range of soil and light conditions than epiphytic orchids. In zone 9-10, established clumps may survive mild winters with mulch protection — in zone 9a, treat as a perennial with some dieback risk in freeze years. Blooms repeatedly through the warm months. Divide clumps every 3–4 years. An excellent beginner-friendly orchid for outdoor subtropical gardens. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Plant in partial shade to bright indirect light in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil — Philippine Ground Orchid performs best in the filtered light and moist, organically rich conditions of a shaded garden bed and will produce fewer flowers and show leaf stress in intense full sun. Spathoglottis plicata is a clump-forming terrestrial orchid native to a vast natural range from the Philippines, Malaysia, and Indonesia through the Pacific Islands to northern Australia and New Caledonia in the Orchidaceae family — one of the easiest-to-grow orchid species for outdoor gardens in zone 9-12 because, unlike most commonly grown orchids, it is truly terrestrial: it grows in ordinary garden soil rather than requiring bark mounts or special epiphyte media. The plant produces oval to egg-shaped pseudobulbs that store water, topped with 2–4 narrow, pleated (the 'plicata' — folded), bright green leaves 12–24 inches long. From the pseudobulbs emerge tall flower scapes (18–36 inches) bearing 6–20 flowers in succession — each flower a typical orchid shape (3 sepals, 2 petals, 1 lip) in shades of deep rose-pink to magenta-purple with a yellow throat and slightly marked lip. The plant blooms repeatedly through spring, summer, and fall in zone 9-10, with individual scapes blooming for several weeks before a new scape emerges. An outstanding and underused orchid for zone 9-11 shade and partial-shade garden beds. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container transplants after nighttime temperatures are consistently above 55°F; Philippine violet blooms on new growth and should be pruned back by one-third in early spring to encourage a flush of new flowering stems.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun — Philippine violet is a prolific-blooming tropical shrub from South Asia that thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast, producing masses of attractive tubular, five-lobed flowers in shades of lavender-blue, violet, or white from fall through spring. It blooms most heavily during the cooler months when many other tropical plants have shut down, making it a valuable addition to the fall and winter garden palette. The soft, somewhat hairy foliage is attractive year-round in zone 10–11. It performs beautifully in partial shade and tolerates considerable drought once established — an outstanding plant for dry-shade situations along building foundations and under trees in zone 9–10. In zone 9 top growth may freeze back in hard winters but the plant regrows vigorously; cut back to 6 inches in late winter each year to encourage vigorous new blooming growth.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain consistently above 60°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and bring indoors before temperatures approach 50°F. Micans is a velvety-leaved cultivar of Heartleaf Philodendron — the same species as the standard green Heartleaf Philodendron but with an iridescent, bronze-green, velvety texture on the leaf surface that catches and reflects light in an unusual way. Stem cuttings root easily in water or moist propagating mix, making propagation simple. In zone 9 the warm, humid summer promotes lush, rapid growth on shaded patios, pergolas, and covered outdoor living spaces.
directions: Plant in bright indirect light to shade — never in direct sun, which bleaches and scorches the velvety leaf surface — in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil; Micans is a velvety-leaved cultivar of Heartleaf Philodendron (Philodendron hederaceum) producing heart-shaped leaves in bronze-green with a distinctive iridescent, velvet-textured surface that catches light differently at different angles — shifting from deep bronze-green in direct viewing to a warmer, almost copper-gold sheen when light strikes the leaf surface obliquely across the fine surface trichomes that create the velvety texture. The leaf color and texture of Micans distinguishes it clearly from the standard smooth, glossy-green Heartleaf Philodendron, creating a more sophisticated, jewel-like foliage quality that has made it one of the most sought-after trailing philodendrons among contemporary plant collectors. New growth emerges in a warmer pinkish-bronze before deepening to the mature bronze-green, creating an additional decorative effect as the plant actively grows. The trailing, vining habit — identical to the parent species — makes Philodendron Micans excellent for hanging baskets, trailing container edges, and shaded climbing situations where the long, velvety stems cascade attractively over the container lip.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors 4-6 weeks earlier.
directions: Direct sow after frost or start indoors four to six weeks earlier for this tall African marigold. It produces large, bright yellow, fully double blooms on sturdy stems that make excellent cut flowers. Give it full sun and space to reach its mature height, staking if needed in exposed sites. Deadhead to keep the big, cheerful flowers coming from summer until frost.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; physic nut is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. All parts of the plant, especially the seeds, are toxic if ingested, so site away from children and pets.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; physic nut is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. All parts of the plant, especially the seeds, are toxic if ingested, so site away from children and pets. Thick, succulent stems and broad, lobed leaves cover a fast-growing, drought-tolerant shrub long used as a living fence across the tropics for its ease of propagation from simple stem cuttings, more recently studied worldwide as a source of biodiesel from the high oil content of its toxic seeds. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on poor, marginal soils with minimal care, but every part of the plant, particularly the oil-rich seeds, contains toxic compounds that cause severe illness if ingested by people or animals. Grow it as a hedge or specimen shrub in a location away from curious children, pets, or livestock, and handle pruned material with gloves, since the sap can irritate skin.

common_name: Pica Bella Purple Coneflower (Mt. Cuba Top-Performing Compact Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pica Bella was rated a top performer in the Mt. Cuba Center's Echinacea trial for its compact, floriferous habit and strong pollinator appeal.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pica Bella is a purple coneflower selection that earned a top score in the Mt. Cuba Center's rigorous multi-year Echinacea trial, valued for a compact, well-proportioned habit that produces an exceptionally heavy flush of classic purple-pink blooms with a prominent orange-bronze cone. Its strong, reliable flower production makes it a magnet for bees and butterflies through a long summer bloom season. Like other coneflowers it is drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond deadheading to prolong bloom. Leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering starts to decline.

common_name: Picasso Calla Lily (White with Deep Purple Throat)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Picasso bears white spathes with a dramatic deep purple throat that bleeds partway up the petal edges.
directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where hot afternoon sun will not scorch the foliage in warm climates. Picasso bears elegant, funnel-shaped spathes in creamy white with a striking, deep purple-violet throat that bleeds a thin margin of color up the petal edges, a bold two-tone effect that has made it one of the most popular colored calla lily hybrids. Narrow, glossy green leaves rise from the rhizome through summer, and the plant goes dormant in fall. In zones 8-10 it can be left dry in the ground through a mild winter, while in colder climates the rhizomes should be lifted and stored dry like dahlia tubers. Reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall to encourage the plant into its natural dormant period.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in containers of heavy clay soil and submerge in 4–12 inches of water after water temperatures reach 60°F; or plant directly in shallow pond margins.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in shallow water (4–12 inches deep) in clay-loam soil in full sun; pickerel rush is one of the most essential native aquatic plants for pond margins, rain gardens, and wetland restoration, providing blue-violet flower spikes from June through October that are heavily used by bumblebees and long-tongued native bees. The glossy, arrow-shaped leaves provide cover for frogs, herons hunt at the plant's base, and waterfowl eat the seeds. Remove spent flower stalks to encourage rebloom. Divide crowded colonies every 3–4 years in spring, keeping each division attached to a healthy rhizome section.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring at the margins of a pond, stream, or water garden with the crown at or just below the waterline; pickerelweed grows best in 2–6 inches of standing water but will establish in saturated mud at water's edge. Space divisions 18–24 inches apart in containers of heavy aquatic soil submerged just below the water surface, or plant directly into the soft sediment of a natural pond margin.
directions: Plant at the shallow margins of a pond, rain garden, or water feature in 2–6 inches of standing water or saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; pickerelweed is a native emergent aquatic perennial found naturally in marshes, sluggish streams, lake margins, and ditches across eastern North America and is one of the most ornamental and wildlife-valuable native aquatic plants available. Pontederia cordata produces bold, heart-shaped, glossy dark-green leaves and upright spikes of violet-blue, two-lipped flowers from June through October — one of the longest-blooming of any native aquatic — that are excellent nectar sources for bumble bees, honey bees, skippers, and swallowtails. The small, hard fruits that follow are eaten by ducks and other waterfowl; the plant also provides critical cover and nesting substrate for frogs, fish, and aquatic insects. Spreads by rhizomes to form attractive colonies at pond edges and can be easily divided every few years to share or control spread.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Pickwick crocus naturalizes well in a lawn or border and multiplies steadily by cormlets over the years.
directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Pickwick crocus naturalizes well in a lawn or border and multiplies steadily by cormlets over the years. Large, goblet-shaped flowers are boldly striped in silvery-lilac and deep purple with a bright orange center, one of the largest-flowered and most strikingly patterned of the classic large-flowering Dutch crocus cultivars, opening wide in full sun each early spring day and closing again at dusk or on cloudy days. Long popular for naturalizing in lawns, where its foliage dies back and disappears before the grass needs its first mowing, it multiplies steadily over the years by producing small cormlets around the parent corm. Allow foliage to die back naturally before mowing over a naturalized planting, and divide congested clumps in summer dormancy if flowering begins to decline.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Picturata scorches badly in direct sun and needs deeper shade than most variegated shrubs.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, avoiding direct sun, which scorches and bleaches the distinctive foliage. Picturata is an eye-catching aucuba cultivar with an unusual variegation pattern reversed from the more common gold-dust type: each glossy, leathery leaf has a bold splash of gold-yellow in the center surrounded by a dark green margin, rather than gold speckles scattered over green. Like other aucubas, it is one of the few broadleaf evergreen shrubs that thrives in deep, dry shade under trees where little else stays attractive, making it valuable for difficult shaded foundation plantings and understory beds. Female plants produce bright red berries in winter if a male aucuba is nearby for pollination; little pruning is needed beyond removing damaged or leggy stems in spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil; avoid planting too deep — the crown should be at or just above soil level.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in dappled shade to light sun; the Piedmont azalea is among the most beautiful and fragrant of the native deciduous azaleas, naturally found in woodland edges and along streams from Virginia to Florida and Texas. The pale pink to white flowers with long, exserted stamens appear in early spring before or with the new foliage, giving the plant a delicate, open appearance very different from the dense evergreen hybrid azaleas. Unlike most garden azaleas it tolerates zone 9 Gulf Coast summers well. Prune only after flowering, removing no more than one-third of the plant at once; never shear. Amend soil heavily with compost and pine bark before planting.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Piedmont rhododendron is smaller in leaf and stature than catawba or rosebay rhododendron and tolerates more heat, making it a better choice for lowland southeastern gardens.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Piedmont rhododendron is smaller in leaf and stature than catawba or rosebay rhododendron and tolerates more heat, making it a better choice for lowland southeastern gardens. Rhododendron minus is a compact, evergreen southeastern native with small, leathery, dark green leaves and clusters of pink to rose-purple, funnel-shaped flowers in late spring to early summer, occurring naturally on dry rocky slopes and bluffs from the Carolinas into the Gulf South. Its smaller stature and greater heat and drought tolerance compared with the large-leaved mountain rhododendrons make it one of the more practical evergreen rhododendrons for lowland southeastern gardens, including well-drained Gulf Coast sites with some afternoon shade. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and avoid heavy, poorly drained clay, which this species tolerates poorly despite otherwise being one of the tougher rhododendron species for the Deep South.

common_name: Pig's Ear Plant (Round-Leaf Navelwort, Cotyledon orbiculata)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings after callusing for several days, then plant into gritty, well-drained soil in a full-sun bed or container once frost danger has passed.
directions: Grow in full sun in fast-draining soil, watering deeply but infrequently and allowing the soil to dry between waterings to keep the fleshy stems from rotting. It forms a small, woody-based shrub over time, tolerating coastal wind and salt spray as well as drought. Thick, chalky gray-green paddle-shaped leaves often develop a reddish, crinkled margin in strong sun, giving the plant its pig's-ear common name. Clusters of dangling, tubular orange to red flowers rise on tall stalks above the foliage in summer, attracting hummingbirds and other pollinators.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained, moist soil in zone 9–12; Pigeon Berry (Golden Dewdrop, Skyflower) is a fast-growing, ornamental tropical shrub from the Caribbean and tropical Americas — producing cascading sprays of small, lavender-blue to white tubular flowers beloved by butterflies and hummingbirds, followed by clusters of striking golden-yellow, berry-like drupes — widely planted in Gulf Coast gardens but caution: all parts of the plant, especially the berries, are toxic to humans, dogs, and cats.
directions: Plant Duranta erecta in fertile, well-drained, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun to partial shade; prune regularly to control size and shape — it can become a large, arching shrub or small tree without pruning; in zone 9, it dies back to the ground after hard frost but re-emerges in spring. CAUTION: Berries and leaves are toxic — do not plant where young children or pets have unsupervised access; the golden-yellow berries are attractive but cause severe gastroenteritis if ingested. Pigeon Berry is one of the most popular ornamental shrubs in Gulf Coast, tropical, and subtropical gardens for good reason — the cascading clusters of lavender-blue, tubular flowers with a fringed appearance (the 'sky flower') are produced in extraordinary abundance from spring through fall, creating a lavender haze that is irresistible to butterflies (particularly swallowtails, sulphurs, and monarchs) and hummingbirds. Following the flowers, clusters of bright golden-yellow berries persist through winter, providing excellent bird food for mockingbirds, robins, and thrushes — but the berries should not be eaten by people or pets. Several cultivars are available: 'Aurea' with golden-yellow foliage, 'Alba' with white flowers and yellow berries, and 'Golden Edge' with gold-margined leaves. In zone 10–12 it can become a large, sprawling shrub or small tree 15–18 feet tall without regular pruning.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds after last frost or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade in spring; pigeonberry self-seeds prolifically in suitable shaded areas of Gulf Coast gardens and functions essentially as a self-maintaining native groundcover once established.
directions: Direct-sow or plant container specimens in well-drained to moist, average soil in partial shade after frost; pigeonberry (rouge plant, baby peppers, coralito) is a native perennial sub-shrub of the Gulf South, Caribbean, and Central America that is one of the most wildlife-friendly and adaptable shade-tolerant native plants for zone 7–11 — simultaneously producing clusters of tiny, star-shaped, white to pale-pink flowers and brilliant translucent red-orange berries on the same plant throughout most of the growing season, providing months of ornamental interest and a constant food source for mockingbirds, Carolina wrens, white-eyed vireos, and numerous other fruit-eating birds. The plant is low-growing, semi-woody at the base, and self-seeds freely in shaded garden beds, under trees, and at woodland edges to create ever-expanding naturalized colonies. An excellent native alternative to non-native shade groundcovers, it fills the ecological role of producing berries in shaded conditions where most fruiting plants will not bloom. Berries are considered mildly toxic to humans but are consumed in quantity by birds.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plantlets in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; piggyback plant readily propagates itself from the small plantlets that form at the base of mature leaves — simply pin a leaf to moist soil to root a new plant.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; keep consistently moist, since the shallow-rooted foliage wilts quickly in dry conditions. Tolmiea menziesii (piggyback plant, or youth-on-age) is a native Pacific Northwest woodland groundcover named for its unusual and endearing method of vegetative reproduction: new baby plantlets sprout directly at the base of each mature, hairy, maple-like leaf, riding piggyback on the parent leaf until the weight bends the stem to the ground, where the plantlet roots and becomes an independent plant. Small, unusual, chocolate-brown and green tubular flowers appear on slender stalks in spring, though the fresh green, textured foliage and self-propagating habit are the plant's main appeal. It forms a dense, low, weed-suppressing mat in consistently moist, shaded woodland conditions, and its easy self-propagation makes it simple to share and spread through a shade garden. Also grown widely as a houseplant, it performs equally well outdoors in the reliably moist, cool shade it needs, zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant in full sun with consistently moist, well-drained soil, well suited to containers and the front of small borders; appreciates supplemental watering during dry spells.
directions: Plant in full sun with consistently moist, well-drained soil, well suited to containers and the front of small borders. Introduced by Brent Horvath of Intrinsic Perennial Gardens from a seedling of the popular cultivar Hameln, Piglet is even smaller than its already-compact parent, forming a tight mound of soft, fine-textured green foliage. In late summer it produces silvery to pinkish-white, bottlebrush-shaped flower spikes that stand just above the foliage and persist into fall. Its diminutive size, typically under 2 feet tall and wide, makes it one of the smallest garden fountain grass selections available, useful where even Little Bunny or Hameln would be too large.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Piilu is a compact, Estonian-bred clematis well suited to containers and small trellises, blooming on old wood with a second flush on new growth.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade, on a compact trellis, obelisk, or large container support. Piilu bears semi-double flowers in soft pink with a deeper pink central bar down each petal, opening earlier in the season on the previous year's growth and reblooming with simpler single flowers on new growth later in summer. Its shorter, more restrained vine habit than many large-flowered clematis makes it well suited to container growing, small trellises, or the front of a mixed border where a full-sized clematis would be too vigorous. Prune lightly in late winter, removing only dead or weak stems, to preserve the early double flush while still allowing continued bloom through the season.

common_name: Pike's Pink Dianthus (Double Orchid-Pink Opening from Creamy Buds)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Pike's Pink bears double orchid-pink flowers opening from creamy-yellow buds on a low, wide blue-green mound.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Pike's Pink bears double, fragrant, orchid-pink flowers that emerge from distinctive creamy-yellow buds, opening over a low, wide-spreading mound of fine blue-green foliage that makes an excellent edging or rock garden plant. Its dense, cushion-like habit and reliable spring bloom have kept it a long-standing favorite for sunny, well-drained borders. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pillans's watsonia is evergreen (unlike many other watsonia species) and blooms in autumn (February–April in South Africa; August–October in the Northern Hemisphere) rather than spring. This autumn bloom timing, combined with the evergreen habit, makes it distinctive among the watsonias. It is a robust species that spreads by corm offsets and self-seeds in favorable conditions.
directions: Plant corms in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pillans's watsonia stands apart from the commonly grown, spring-blooming pink watsonia (W. borbonica) by two characteristics: it blooms in autumn (August–October in the Northern Hemisphere) rather than spring, and the flowers are a warm orange to orange-red to salmon-orange rather than the pink to magenta of the spring-blooming species — the warm-toned tubular gladiolus-like flowers on the tall, upright, spike-like stems standing out distinctly in the autumn border when the warm orange-red of watsonia is available at the same time as autumn perennials in yellow and bronze. The plant is also evergreen, maintaining its broad, iris-like, sword-shaped fans of deep-green leaves through winter. The autumn bloom timing fills a gap in the South African iris-family plant calendar in the garden — providing the characteristic watsonia spike-form in the autumn season when no other watsonia species is in bloom. Combined with autumn-blooming agapanthus, late kniphofias, and autumn grasses, it provides a warm, orange-accented, late-season contribution to the South African plant garden.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost date and transplant after last frost into well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, average-fertility soil in full sun; pincushion flower blooms most freely in lean conditions and resents acid or wet soil.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant into well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, average-to-lean soil in full sun; pincushion flower produces a long succession of lavender-blue, lilac, or white domed flower heads on wiry stems from early summer through frost that are excellent for cutting and highly attractive to butterflies and native bees. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to prolong the season. Plants are relatively short-lived in hot, humid climates and in acidic soils; top-dress with garden lime in acidic beds. In zones 8–9, treat as a cool-season annual and sow in fall for winter-to-spring bloom. The similar annual species S. atropurpurea blooms in a single season from seed.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed into a sunny, alkaline-friendly site.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost, sowing 1/4 in deep in a light germination mix; transplant outdoors after frost into well-drained, slightly alkaline or neutral soil. The domed, pincushion flowers in rich maroon, lavender, white, pink, and burgundy are magnets for butterflies and superb for cutting. Deadhead consistently to prevent self-seeding and extend the long bloom period from early summer through frost. Avoid rich, wet soils — scabiosa thrives in moderately lean conditions and is drought-tolerant once established.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or well-drained soil in full sun; pincushion hakea requires excellent drainage and lean soil — it is native to dry, sandy soils of southwestern Australia. Do not fertilize with phosphorus. It blooms in autumn through winter (April–July in Australia; October–January in the Northern Hemisphere), providing winter color. The flowers are outstanding for nectar-feeding birds (honeyeaters in Australia; hummingbirds in cultivation).
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; pincushion hakea is one of the most spectacular Australian shrubs — a large, erect shrub or small tree from southwestern Australia producing in autumn and winter remarkable, spherical, sea-urchin-like flower heads 2–3 inches across: dense, globular clusters of cream-yellow to pale-cream tubular flowers from which project numerous long, curved, crimson to bright-red styles — the combined effect of the cream flower and scarlet projecting styles creating the distinctive 'pincushion' or 'sea urchin' appearance from which the common names are drawn. The contrast of the cream-colored flowers and brilliant red styles is vivid and immediately eye-catching. The leaves are long, narrow, lance-shaped, blue-green to gray-green, providing a fine-textured, somewhat willow-like foliage year-round. Blooming in autumn and winter when few other dramatic flowers are available, it provides an exceptional, long-lasting (the flowers persist on the shrub for weeks) winter display and, in cultivation, proves to be a reliable hummingbird attractor. Like all Proteaceae, it requires excellent drainage, lean soil, and absolutely no phosphorus-based fertilizer.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; pincushion protea requires excellent drainage and absolutely no phosphorus fertilizer — phosphorus is lethal to all Proteaceae. Use only Proteaceae-specific or phosphorus-free fertilizers. It blooms in late winter through spring, producing large, spherical, brilliant-orange flower heads composed of densely packed, projecting styles (the 'pins' of the pincushion). Outstanding cut flower with long vase life. Does not tolerate frost below about 28°F/-2°C.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; pincushion protea is one of the most spectacular and widely grown of all South African fynbos plants in cultivation — producing in late winter through spring extraordinary, spherical to dome-shaped flower heads of brilliant orange to orange-red to golden-orange composed of densely packed, long, tubular perianths each tipped with a projecting style that creates the exact, unmistakable texture of a pincushion densely stuck with orange-headed pins, 4–5 inches across per head. The flowers are bold, vivid, warm orange — a color that dominates and energizes any planting composition — and have exceptional vase life as cut flowers (10–14 days), making the pincushion protea one of the important South African cut flower exports worldwide. In the garden it forms a substantial, mounding, evergreen shrub with attractive, leathery, blue-gray-green, heart-shaped leaves (giving the species name cordifolium) providing year-round structure. Like all Proteaceae it requires excellent drainage, lean soil, and absolutely no phosphorus fertilizer. The parent species of many important Leucospermum hybrids. A signature plant for California and zone 9 Gulf Coast Mediterranean-style gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in moist to moderately wet, sandy, acidic, poorly drained or seasonally wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Pine Barren Goldenrod is one of the few goldenrods that tolerates and prefers seasonally wet flatwoods and pine barren conditions. Established plants spread steadily by rhizomes.
directions: Pine Barren Goldenrod is a native perennial of the moist to seasonally wet sandy pine barrens, flatwoods, and boggy savannas of the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Louisiana, distinguished among goldenrods by its hollow, pithy stem (fistulosa means 'hollow' or 'pipe-like') and its tolerance for the wet, acidic, nutrient-poor soils of flatwood depressions and moist pine barrens. The bright yellow flower spikes in fall are an outstanding nectar source for monarch butterflies, native bees, and numerous other pollinators migrating or overwintering along the southeastern coastal plain. Spreading reliably by rhizomes to form colonies in appropriate conditions, Pine Barren Goldenrod is an excellent choice for wet meadow, rain garden, and moist flatwood restoration plantings. Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants naturalize readily in wet, open, seasonally flooded settings.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in wet to moist, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; pine barrens coreopsis grows in wet pine savannas, pitcher plant bogs, and seasonal wetlands of the Gulf Coastal Plain and is one of the few coreopsis adapted to waterlogged, nutrient-poor conditions.
