directions: Plant in wet to moist, strongly acidic, nutrient-poor, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; pine barrens coreopsis is a specialist of wet pine savannas, boggy pine flatwoods, and pitcher plant bogs of the Gulf Coastal Plain — one of the biologically richest and most threatened habitats in North America. Unlike the drought-tolerant cultivated coreopsis of garden centers, this species grows in consistently wet, nutrient-poor, acidic conditions typical of longleaf pine bog communities. The delicate, almost leafless stems bear a single, large, bright pink to lavender-rose flower — a striking departure from the yellow of most coreopsis — making it one of the most ornamentally distinctive species in the genus. The pink flowers are produced in spring and early summer, attracting native bees. This is a relatively rare plant outside of its bog habitats, and growing it from specialty nursery sources supports conservation awareness of longleaf pine ecosystem species.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, low-nutrient soil in full sun; pine lily grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods and savannas of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain. It requires fire-maintained, open, acidic, wet conditions and is imperiled by fire suppression and habitat loss.
directions: Plant in moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, low-nutrient soil in full sun in wet pine flatwoods or bog garden conditions; pine lily is among the most spectacularly beautiful native flowers of the Gulf Coastal Plain, producing single, large, upward-facing flowers with orange-red petals spotted with purple and with a distinctive long, tapered tube base — unlike the nodding, reflexed form of most other native lilies. The upright, face-up flower orientation makes it a standout for pollinators and human observers alike. Unfortunately pine lily is increasingly imperiled throughout its range due to fire suppression (it requires periodic fire to maintain open pine flatwood habitat), drainage, and development. It is the larval host for the rare tiger moth species and an important nectar source for swallowtail butterflies. A critical species for pine flatwood restoration in zone 9.

common_name: Pine Pink (Purple Bletia, Rose Pogonia, Cuban Ground Orchid)
plant_note: Plant corms or pot-grown divisions in spring in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Bletia purpurea grows naturally in Florida's pine flatwoods and sandy, open habitats and needs good drainage rather than the consistently moist conditions favored by many orchids. In zone 9, established plants typically overwinter successfully with the corms protected by mulch. The plant goes partially dormant in winter. The vivid magenta-pink flowers are produced primarily in spring. Propagate by dividing corm clusters. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, sandy, lean soil — Pine Pink grows naturally in Florida's nutrient-poor, sandy pine flatwoods and scrub habitats and performs better in lean, well-drained soil than in rich, fertile garden beds. Bletia purpurea is a corm-producing terrestrial orchid native to Florida (central and southern), the Florida Keys, the Caribbean (Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica, Puerto Rico, the Lesser Antilles), Mexico, and Central America in the Orchidaceae family. The plant grows from clusters of corms (fleshy, rounded, underground storage organs) that produce 2–4 narrow, pleated, grass-like leaves and, in spring, one or more erect flower spikes 18–36 inches tall bearing 5–15 flowers in vivid, clear magenta-pink to bright rose-purple — one of the most vivid and cheerful flower colors available from a Florida-native terrestrial orchid. The bright pink flowers have a similar intensity and quality to a hardy Cattleya alliance hybrid, and the naturalness of their occurrence in Florida's sandy pinelands makes them particularly meaningful as a native plant. Pine Pink has demonstrated the ability to naturalize and spread in sandy, disturbed ground in Florida lawns and gardens — one of the few Florida native orchids that can be sustainably cultivated and propagated from legally sourced stock. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring after soil warms; lift where not hardy.
directions: Plant pineapple lily bulbs in spring about five inches deep in rich, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed. Each stout stem produces a dense spike of starry flowers topped by a tuft of leafy bracts resembling a pineapple. Grow in full sun with regular summer moisture, and it also performs beautifully in large containers. In cold climates lift the bulbs before frost or grow them in pots moved indoors for winter.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pineapple Queen coleus holds its bright chartreuse-gold color well in both sun and shade.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pineapple Queen coleus holds its bright chartreuse-gold color well in both sun and shade. Bright, glowing chartreuse-yellow leaves with a fine reddish edge cover a vigorous, well-branched plant that lights up a shaded bed or container with sunny color even in dim corners where flowering plants struggle to bloom. Its bright, luminous color and adaptability to both sun and shade make it a versatile filler for mixed containers or a colorful accent massed in a shady border, pairing well with darker-leaved coleus and other foliage companions for contrast. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushy, compact growth, and remove flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy focused on foliage production.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, coarse or sandy-loam soil in zone 9–11; Lepidozamia peroffskyana (Pineapple Zamia) is a magnificent, large cycad native to subtropical and tropical Queensland rainforest margins in Australia — producing very long, glossy, arching, pinnate fronds in a large, impressive crown and enormous female cones resembling pineapples that are among the largest of any cycad.
directions: Plant Lepidozamia peroffskyana in well-drained, coarse soil (sandy loam with added grit or perlite) in partial shade to full sun; avoid overwatering and ensure excellent drainage as cycads are highly susceptible to root rot in waterlogged soil; apply a slow-release cycad fertilizer with minor elements in spring. Caution: all parts of Lepidozamia peroffskyana are toxic — seeds contain cycasin and cause severe neurological damage if ingested — keep away from children and livestock. Pineapple Zamia is one of the most impressive cycads in cultivation — native to subtropical and warm-temperate rainforest margins in coastal Queensland — and produces a stately, fountain-like crown of very long, glossy-green, arching pinnate fronds that can reach 8–10 feet in length. The name 'Pineapple Zamia' refers to the massive female reproductive cones, which can weigh 20–35 kg (44–77 lbs) and closely resemble giant pineapples. Like all cycads, it is a living fossil — cycads have changed little since the Mesozoic Era when they formed a significant part of dinosaur-era forests. Growth is slow: adding one new flush of fronds per year; a mature, cone-bearing specimen in a garden represents decades of patient cultivation. The striking glossy fronds and bold architectural form make it a supreme specimen plant for subtropical gardens throughout zone 9–11.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring after temperatures warm consistently in sandy, well-drained, infertile, acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Pineland Heliotrope thrives in the dry pinelands and open sandy habitats of Florida and the Caribbean and self-seeds prolifically in hospitable conditions.
directions: Pineland Heliotrope is a native low-growing wildflower of the dry pinelands, pine flatwoods, and open sandy habitats of Florida and the Caribbean, producing a profusion of tiny yellow to creamy-white flowers on small, spreading, leafy mats throughout the warm season. A member of the borage family, the small flowers display the characteristic scorpioid cyme (coiled flower arrangement) of the heliotrope group and provide nectar for small native bees, Ceraunus Blue butterflies, and other small pollinators of the Florida pineland community. The narrow, resin-dotted, gland-bearing leaves give the plant a pleasant, somewhat spicy fragrance when brushed. Direct sow seeds in spring in sandy, well-drained, infertile, acidic soil in full sun; Pineland Heliotrope self-seeds freely in appropriate sandy conditions and is a useful groundcover for open, xeric Florida gardens where its continuous bloom and compact form fill bare sandy spaces with pollinators.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; pineland milkweed is adapted to fire-maintained sandy pinelands and needs sharp drainage.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; pineland milkweed is adapted to fire-maintained sandy pinelands and needs sharp drainage. Softly hairy, oval, gray-green leaves and rounded clusters of small, dull greenish-white to pale yellow flowers give this milkweed a subtler, more muted appearance than the bright orange or pink of showier relatives, but it serves the same essential role as a monarch butterfly larval host plant across the sandy pine woodlands of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain. Native to fire-adapted longleaf pine sandhills and open sandy woods, it tolerates the dry, nutrient-poor, well-drained soils typical of that ecosystem and benefits from occasional disturbance or periodic burning in a restoration context, though a home garden planting simply needs sharp drainage and full to partial sun. It requires no supplemental water or fertilizer once established in appropriately lean, sandy soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plugs in spring into sandy, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; pineland twinflower spreads gently by rhizomes to form a low, informal groundcover in pine flatwoods and open sandy sites.
directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; pineland twinflower is a low, spreading Gulf Coast and Florida native groundcover with small, oblong leaves and delicate, pale lavender-blue, funnel-shaped flowers produced in loose pairs nearly continuously through the warm months. It is the primary larval host plant for the common buckeye butterfly in much of its range, so expect and welcome some caterpillar feeding as part of supporting a full butterfly life cycle rather than a purely ornamental planting. Spreading gently by rhizomes, it knits together into a soft, low groundcover under open pines and in sunny to lightly shaded sandy beds, tolerating both drought and the periodic light fire regimes of its native flatwoods habitat. Cut back by about half in late winter to refresh the planting before the new season's growth and bloom begin.

subcategory: southwestern native evergreen perennial pollinator plant
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, gravelly soil in full sun; pineleaf milkweed forms a shrubby, evergreen clump of fine, pine-needle-like foliage and blooms nearly continuously in warm climates.
directions: Plant in sharply-draining, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun after the last frost; pineleaf milkweed is native to the Sonoran Desert borderlands of Arizona, Texas, and Mexico and forms a rounded, woody-based, shrubby perennial with fine, needle-like leaves that give it an almost conifer-like texture unlike any other milkweed. Small clusters of white flowers appear repeatedly through the warm months, drawing native bees and butterflies, and the plant serves as a larval host for monarch and queen caterpillars in low-desert gardens. Its low water needs and evergreen, well-behaved habit make it a popular structural choice in southwestern xeriscape and pollinator plantings.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost with a 3–4 week cold-moist stratification for best germination, or set out nursery divisions in spring, into very well-drained, dry, gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; pineleaf penstemon is a compact, woody-based, evergreen subshrub from the mountains of the American Southwest and northern Mexico, with narrow, needle-like leaves that persist year-round and give the plant its pine-like texture even when not in bloom. Slender, tubular, brilliant orange-red to scarlet flowers cover the mounding plants from late spring through summer and are outstanding hummingbird forage, reblooming readily if lightly sheared after the first flush. It is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant of all penstemons, thriving in rock gardens, dry borders, and gravel mulch plantings where excess moisture and rich soil would quickly rot it. Shear back lightly in early spring to remove winter-damaged growth and keep the mound dense and compact.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; pineywoods dropseed is a native grass of the longleaf pine flatwoods and sandhills ecosystem, adapted to the driest, most infertile sandy soils of the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pineywoods dropseed is a fine-textured, wire-like native bunchgrass of the longleaf pine ecosystem, with very narrow, curling leaves and graceful, open, airy seed heads that appear misty when backlit in fall. It grows in the driest, most infertile, white-sand sites of the Gulf Coastal Plain pine flatwoods — a very specialized habitat. The plant is fire-adapted and is one of the most drought and heat tolerant native grasses of zone 9a. In the garden, it provides a delicate, fine-textured contrast to bold-leaved shade plants and coarser wildflowers in naturalistic pine flatwoods plantings. The seeds are tiny but produced in quantity and consumed by small ground-foraging birds.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Pink Allusion syngonium colors most vividly with bright indirect light and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Pink Allusion syngonium colors most vividly with bright indirect light and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11. Arrow-shaped juvenile leaves emerge a warm coral-pink and mature to a soft rosy-salmon with green margins, a color progression that gives each stem a two-toned, blushing effect distinct from the plain green or white-variegated arrowhead plants more commonly sold. Young plants hold an upright, bushy form and can later be encouraged to climb a moss pole, where mature leaves develop the deeper lobes and arrow shapes typical of adult syngonium foliage. Pinch growing tips to keep the plant compact and bushy, and note that, like other syngoniums, its sap can irritate skin and is toxic if chewed by pets.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Pink Autumn Sage is among the most cold-hardy of the Salvia greggii selections, with robust performance across zones 7–9. Prune plants back to 6–8 inches in late winter to remove winter-killed stems and stimulate dense, floriferous new growth. In zone 9 blooms most heavily spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) with reduced but continuous bloom through summer. The soft pink flowers attract hummingbirds and butterflies through both bloom peaks.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — Pink Autumn Sage thrives in dry, rocky, calcareous conditions and is one of the most drought-tolerant flowering perennials for zones 7–9; Pink is the soft pink-flowered form of Autumn Sage (Salvia greggii), producing the same compact evergreen shrub habit and nearly continuous bloom from spring through fall as the red-flowered form but in a softer, more pastel warm pink that complements a broader range of garden color palettes. The pale to medium pink flowers (slightly larger than the red form on some selections) provide a refined alternative to the vivid scarlet that is the standard Salvia greggii color — useful for gardeners who prefer harmonious soft-toned plantings over vivid red accent plants. Like all S. greggii selections, Pink Autumn Sage is a highly effective hummingbird and butterfly plant — the tubular flower structure and nectar production attract Ruby-throated Hummingbirds and a variety of butterflies throughout the growing season. The combination of drought tolerance, extended bloom, wildlife value, and reliable performance in the dry, calcareous soils of zone 7–9 makes this one of the most practical flowering perennials for water-wise gardens in the region.

plant_note: Divide and plant pups in spring after all frost danger has passed, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Pink Banana is one of the smaller ornamental bananas, reaching only 4–6 feet, and is well-suited to containers or small garden spaces where larger bananas would be overwhelming.
directions: Pink Banana is one of the most ornamental of the small bananas, native to the forests of Assam, India, and grown worldwide for the striking combination of its vivid pink, velvety flower bracts and small, bright pink, hairy fruits that split open when ripe to reveal sweet white flesh studded with seeds — an unusual display that makes the plant a conversation piece in any garden. Growing only 4–6 feet tall, it is well-suited to container culture, small garden spaces, and use as an accent among larger tropical foliage plants, and it blooms and fruits within its first year from a good-sized pup. In zones 8–9 the pseudostem may die to the ground in freezing weather, but the rhizome re-sprouts reliably in spring; in zones 9b–11 it is effectively evergreen. Divide pups from the parent clump in spring, plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun, and water and fertilize generously throughout the growing season.

common_name: Pink Beauty Caladium (Classic Rose-Pink Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; plant an inch or two deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Pink Beauty is a long-established fancy-leaf caladium cultivar producing large, heart-shaped leaves in soft rose-pink centers with darker green veining and margins, a gentler, more pastel color combination than the bright reds of many other classic caladium cultivars. It provides months of reliable, low-maintenance color in shaded beds, borders, and containers without needing flowers, pairing especially well with ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Pink Beauty Doublefile Viburnum (Lacecap White Aging to Pink)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Beauty is a doublefile viburnum selection whose white lacecap flowers age to pink.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Pink Beauty bears flat, lacecap flower clusters held in two rows along horizontally tiered branches, the classic doublefile viburnum form, opening white and gradually aging to soft pink as the blooms mature, so a single plant can show both colors at once during peak bloom. Its strong horizontal branching habit gives it striking architectural structure even out of bloom, and red fruit follows in summer. Prune lightly right after flowering to maintain the tiered branch structure, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; pink calla lily tolerates drier soil between waterings than white calla lily and is well suited to a large container.
directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; pink calla lily tolerates drier soil between waterings than white calla lily and is well suited to a large container. Narrow, dark green leaves speckled with translucent white spots set off elegant, funnel-shaped spathes in shades of soft pink to deep rose-red, smaller and more delicate than the familiar white calla lily but no less striking massed in a border or container. Native to summer-wet, winter-dry grasslands of South Africa, it goes dormant and can be left dry in the ground through a mild winter in zones 8-10, or lifted and stored like a dahlia tuber in colder climates. Plant in light shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, and reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall to encourage the plant into its natural dormant period.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Pink Champagne bears large, mottled foliage speckled with maroon spots over green, particularly striking as new growth emerges in spring, paired with dainty sprays of pink-and-white spurred flowers held above the leaves. Its patterned foliage provides ornamental interest well beyond the relatively brief spring bloom period, making it a strong textural and color accent for a shaded border or woodland planting. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh and show off the spring display.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Pink Champion anthurium wants consistent warmth and humidity and blooms best with steady bright indirect light.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Pink Champion anthurium wants consistent warmth and humidity and blooms best with steady bright indirect light. Glossy, heart-shaped, deep green leaves set off long-lasting, waxy, bright pink spathes surrounding a pale, contrasting spadix, produced nearly year-round under good indoor conditions and prized as long-stemmed cut flowers as well as a flowering houseplant. Like other flamingo-flower anthuriums it is an epiphyte in habitat and performs best in a loose, chunky, orchid-bark-based mix that drains quickly rather than a dense potting soil that holds excess moisture around the roots. Feed lightly during the growing season to sustain repeat bloom, keep humidity above 50 percent where possible, and remove spent spathes at the base to tidy the plant.

common_name: Pink Chimes Japanese Snowbell (Pale Pink-Flowered Snowbell Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pink Chimes bears pale pink-flushed flowers on a broad, rounded small tree, and does not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally as an understory tree beneath high-canopy shade; Japanese snowbell is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Pink Chimes bears pendant, bell-shaped flowers softly flushed with pale pink rather than the pure white of the species, hanging in rows beneath the horizontal branching in late spring to early summer for the same elegant, layered floral display Japanese snowbell is known for. Its subtle pink coloring adds a gentler tone to the classic snowbell look, particularly appealing planted where the pendant blooms can be viewed from below. Mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches, since the tree's natural layered form needs little shaping.

plant_note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Pink China taro thrives at a pond edge or in a large moisture-retentive container as much as in a border.
directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Pink China taro thrives at a pond edge or in a large moisture-retentive container as much as in a border. Large, matte, blue-green, heart-shaped leaves are carried on tall, distinctly pink-blushed petioles and stems, giving this taro selection a softer, more subtly colorful presence than the near-black or solid-green elephant ears more commonly grown. It brings bold, tropical foliage texture to a shaded bog garden, pond margin, or large container, tolerating standing water at the root zone as well as consistently moist ordinary garden soil. In zones colder than 8, lift and store tubers indoors over winter like dahlias, or grow the plant as a dramatic single-season annual.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Cloud beautybush flowers most heavily in full sun and tolerates poor soil and drought once established.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Cloud beautybush flowers most heavily in full sun and tolerates poor soil and drought once established. In late spring the entire arching, fountain-shaped shrub disappears beneath a dense, week-long cloud of small, bell-shaped, soft pink flowers with a yellow throat, a bloom so heavy it can obscure the foliage entirely, followed by bristly, bronze-pink seed capsules that add subtle texture into fall. Selected for its especially profuse, richly colored bloom compared to the species, it is an easy, tough, low-maintenance shrub once established, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil with minimal care, and its peeling, tan-brown bark provides winter interest after the leaves drop. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, removing some of the oldest stems at ground level each year to keep the shrub renewed and full from the base.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; pink coreopsis is unusual among coreopsis species in tolerating and even preferring more moisture than typical yellow coreopsis. It naturally occurs in wet sandy soils, lake margins, and moist open barrens along the Atlantic coastal plain. Unlike drought-tolerant species coreopsis, it declines in hot, dry conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pink coreopsis is a genuinely unusual and valuable native plant from the sandy coastal plain of the northeastern United States — unusual within the coreopsis genus for two distinctly non-typical features: its flowers are pink to nearly white with a yellow center rather than the bright yellow universal to almost all other coreopsis species, and it grows naturally in moist to wet, sandy soils rather than the lean, dry conditions most coreopsis prefer. The small, fine-textured flowers (3/4 to 1 inch across) are produced in mass on a spreading, somewhat floppy, fine-textured plant with very narrow, thread-like leaves from June through September. The clear, soft pink color — a genuine pink rather than a pink-tinged yellow — is what makes this species uniquely valuable in the native plant palette. The cultivar 'American Dream' is more compact and has deeper rose-pink flowers. Combines beautifully with grasses and other fine-textured wetland-edge plants in moist native gardens. An imperiled native plant due to coastal plain habitat loss.

common_name: Pink Delight Butterfly Bush (Clear Pink Buddleja)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; deadhead spent flower spikes regularly to extend bloom and limit self-seeding.
directions: Pink Delight is a classic, long-grown butterfly bush cultivar carrying long, dense, conical spikes of clear rose-pink flowers on a large, vigorous, arching shrub, one of the most reliable and widely available pink-flowered buddleja selections. The clean pink tone pairs easily with both cool and warm companion colors in a mixed border, and like other butterfly bush cultivars it draws swallowtails, monarchs, and hummingbirds heavily throughout its long summer-into-fall bloom season. In zone 9 it dies back hard over winter and should be cut to about 12 inches from the ground in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth for the coming season.

common_name: Pink Diamond Hydrangea (White Panicles Aging to Pink)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Diamond is an RHS Award of Garden Merit panicle hydrangea whose white flowers age to deep pink.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Pink Diamond opens large, conical white flower panicles that gradually deepen to a rich pink as they age through late summer into fall, so a single plant shows both colors at once, a color-change trait shared by several panicle hydrangea cultivars and recognized with a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. It grows into a large, vigorous shrub or small tree form over time. Prune in late winter to shape and control size, cutting back last year's growth by about a third to encourage strong new flowering stems.

plant_note: Plant container roses in early spring or fall in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pink Double Knock Out shares the disease resistance and repeat bloom of the rest of the Knock Out family but carries fully double, ruffled flowers rather than the single five-petaled blooms of the original.
directions: Pink Double Knock Out combines the legendary disease resistance and near-continuous rebloom of the Knock Out rose family with a fuller, more traditionally rose-shaped flower, carrying densely petaled, medium-pink, ruffled double blooms instead of the simple five-petaled flowers of the original red Knock Out. Like its relatives it is essentially self-cleaning, dropping spent petals cleanly without deadheading, and shows outstanding natural resistance to black spot and powdery mildew in the humid Gulf South. It blooms in flushes from spring through frost and needs only a hard prune to 12-18 inches in late winter to renew vigorous flowering growth for the coming season; avoid planting in less than a full six hours of direct sun, which reduces bloom significantly.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring just below soil level with the crown at the surface, in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, and top-dress with compost each spring to keep the glossy foliage lush. Pink Dragonfly is a compact Terra Nova Nurseries bergenia bred for deep rose-pink flower clusters held on dark red stems in early spring, paired with rounded, leathery leaves that flush deep purple-red through winter cold. Its smaller stature compared to species bergenias suits it to shaded rock gardens, woodland edges, and mixed containers where a bold-textured, low-maintenance evergreen accent is wanted. It is deer- and rabbit-resistant and spreads slowly by rhizome to form a dense weed-smothering patch; divide congested clumps every 4–5 years in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained to dry, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; pink evening primrose spreads aggressively by rhizomes and self-sowing and is best suited to naturalized areas, roadsides, or wildflower meadows where spreading is acceptable — it can be difficult to control once established in enriched soils.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, well-drained to dry, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; pink evening primrose is exceptionally easy to establish from seed and requires no soil amendment — rich, fertile, or regularly irrigated soils encourage rank, weedy growth and even more aggressive spreading than usual. Oenothera speciosa is a low, spreading native perennial of the Gulf Coast, southern prairies, and open disturbed ground from Kansas south through Texas and into Mexico, widely naturalized across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic; it spreads vigorously by shallow rhizomes and prolific self-seeding to form broad, low-growing colonies that in late spring (April–June) are covered in large, delicate, cup-shaped flowers of soft pink to nearly white with darker pink veining and a central yellow eye — misnamed 'evening primrose,' its flowers actually open in the morning and close in afternoon heat. It is visited by native bees, particularly specialist Oenothera-foraging sweat bees and long-tongued bees that collect its sticky, thread-connected pollen; it also supports the white-lined sphinx moth as a larval host. Plant in dry, lean settings and be prepared for it to spread — it is best treated as a naturalized groundcover rather than a border plant, and is spectacular when allowed to colonize dry roadsides, rocky slopes, and meadow edges.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade; pink fawn lily grows naturally in moist, shaded stream banks, redwood forest floors, and moist mixed evergreen forest of the California and Oregon Coast Ranges. Requires moisture during the growing season but tolerates summer drought when dormant.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade; pink fawn lily is arguably the showiest of the native Pacific Coast fawn lilies, producing intensely mottled brown-and-green leaves and large, strongly reflexed, deep rose-pink flowers with a yellow center on stems 8–16 inches tall. Native to moist coastal forest and stream-bank habitats from northern California to British Columbia, it naturalizes readily in woodland gardens and increases readily from offsets to form clumps and colonies. The pink color distinguishes it from the cream-white Oregon fawn lily (E. oregonum). The cultivar 'Johnsonii' and the pink-flowered hybrid 'Pagoda' (E. revolutum x E. tuolumnense) are widely available in commerce and are excellent, robust garden plants that increase readily. Goes fully summer-dormant; plant where it won't be disturbed in summer.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, organically rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, siting it in morning sun with afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Cornus florida f. rubra is the classic pink-flowering form of the native flowering dogwood, its showy pink to rose-pink bracts opening in early spring before the leaves fully emerge, followed by clusters of glossy red fall fruit that draw songbirds and bright red-purple fall foliage. Seedlings grown from this form show a range of pink intensity, so gardeners wanting a guaranteed, consistent shade of pink should choose a named, vegetatively propagated cultivar rather than seed-grown stock. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, since dogwoods are shallow-rooted and stressed by drought; prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Pink Frost Hellebore (Gold Collection Marbled-Leaf Hybrid Hellebore)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in fall or early spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pink Frost is a compact Gold Collection hybrid prized for silver-marbled, spiny-edged foliage and clusters of dusty-pink to plum-flushed white flowers that open in late winter and deepen in color with age.
directions: Set divisions or container plants into humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial shade, since this Helleborus niger x lividus hybrid resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought. Pink Frost stands out among hellebores for its silvery, marbled evergreen leaves veined in green, which remain attractive through the growing season and pair well with the nodding, rose-flushed white flowers produced on branching stems above the foliage in late winter. Being a patented Gold Collection selection, it is propagated by division or tissue culture rather than seed, and clumps benefit from occasional dividing every three to four years to maintain vigor. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to showcase the flowers.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Giant is a pink-flowered selection of glory-of-the-snow with larger flowers than the typical blue species.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; glory-of-the-snow naturalizes readily under deciduous trees and in lawns. Pink Giant bears larger star-shaped flowers than the typical blue species, opening a soft, dusty pink with a paler center, among the earliest bulbs to bloom in very early spring, often flowering right alongside the last snow in colder climates. Its unusual color offers a departure from the blues and whites of most glory-of-the-snow plantings, working well combined with early crocus and snowdrops for a mixed drift of very early spring color. Allow the grass-like foliage to die back naturally after flowering before mowing over naturalized plantings, and it will self-seed and multiply by offset bulbs to form larger colonies over time.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in cool weather 4–6 weeks before last frost or in fall in mild climates; pink hawk's beard is a cool-season annual that performs best before summer heat sets in. It self-sows freely and can maintain naturalized colonies in mild climates by fall and spring self-sowing. It does not transplant well — always direct sow.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in full sun in any well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil; pink hawk's beard is a charming Italian native annual producing basal rosettes of dandelion-like toothed leaves and from spring through early summer, slender stems bearing several cheerful, clear pink to rose-pink flowers closely resembling small, elegant, pink dandelion flowers — each one individually attractive, with strap-like ray florets in clear rose-pink radiating from a central disc, all held on slender, branching stems above the foliage. In the aggregate, mass plantings create a low carpet of bright pink that is effective at close range and has the unaffected, wildflower charm of a meadow plant rather than a cultivated ornamental. It is one of the few pink-flowered members of the dandelion tribe and is grown as a cool-season annual for spring color. Self-sows freely in favorable conditions to maintain colonies. Easy to grow and useful for cottage garden edges, naturalizing in light grass, and filling gaps in spring borders before summer annuals are planted.

common_name: Pink Haze Siberian Iris (Soft Pink Midseason Iris)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Pink Haze bears soft pink flowers, one of the earliest widely available pink-toned Siberian iris cultivars.
directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Pink Haze bears soft, gentle pink flowers, one of the earlier introductions to bring true pink tones to the largely blue-and-purple Siberian iris palette, blooming in midseason over narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Icicle camellia is valued for cold-hardy, reliable winter bloom in cold-tolerant camellia breeding lines.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Icicle camellia is valued for cold-hardy, reliable winter bloom in cold-tolerant camellia breeding lines. Semi-double to peony-form flowers open a soft, cool pink with a lighter, almost frosted edge to the petals, blooming reliably through the coldest part of winter on a vigorous, upright shrub bred from cold-hardy camellia lines developed to extend the range of camellia cultivation into colder climates than the classic Gulf South and coastal camellia belt. Its combination of improved cold tolerance and dependable winter flower production has made it a popular choice for gardeners at the northern edge of camellia hardiness wanting to grow this classic Southern shrub outside its traditional warm-climate range. Mulch well to protect roots through winter, provide the dappled shade and acidic soil all camellias require, and avoid planting in a site exposed to harsh winter wind.

common_name: Pink Impression Tulip (Deep Rose-Pink Darwin Hybrid Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Pink Impression is a Darwin hybrid tulip with huge, globe-shaped, deep rose-pink flowers on sturdy stems.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Pink Impression, a Darwin hybrid tulip bred for extra-large flowers on strong, tall stems, produces huge, globe-shaped blooms in deep, saturated rose-pink that have made it one of the most widely planted pink tulips for mass displays and cut flowers. Darwin hybrids like Pink Impression also tend to perennialize somewhat better than many other tulip types in climates with adequate winter chill, though in mild-winter zone 8-9 gardens they are still usually most reliable treated as a fresh fall planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a trellis, fence, or arbor in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9, Pink Jasmine blooms most heavily in January–March when the cooler temperatures trigger bud set — the fragrance in a good bloom year can be detected from across a garden. Avoid heavy pruning in fall as flower buds form in fall for winter bloom. Prune immediately after flowering. In zone 9a, occasional hard freezes may kill some top growth but established vines resprout from the crown. Established vines can be invasive in mild climates — manage by removing seed pods.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Pink Jasmine blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates morning sun with afternoon shade in zone 9's summer climate, which can actually extend the blooming season. Jasminum polyanthum is a twining, evergreen vine native to the mountains of Yunnan province in southern China and Burma (Myanmar) at 5,000–9,000 foot elevations — a naturally cool-adapted plant that translates beautifully to zone 8–9 winter garden conditions. In late winter (January–March in zone 9), the vine produces clouds of intensely fragrant, star-shaped flowers that open white from deep rose-pink buds — the pink buds contrasting with the pure white open flowers creates a beautiful two-tone effect. The fragrance is intensely sweet and reminiscent of jasmine absolute — one of the most powerfully scented of all cultivated jasmines, detectable from remarkable distances on warm winter afternoons. A well-established vine covering a fence or arbor in full late-winter bloom is one of the most memorable garden sights of the zone 9 winter garden, drawing visitors to investigate the fragrance source. Pink Jasmine is also widely grown as a houseplant and patio container plant, where the fragrance of winter-blooming potted specimens fills indoor spaces. Listed as invasive in some Pacific island and mild coastal California locales where the climate allows year-round seeding.

plant_note: Plant container roses in early spring or fall in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pink Knock Out shares all the low-maintenance attributes of the original red Knock Out — self-cleaning, disease-resistant, repeat-blooming — but in soft pink tones that complement mixed border plantings.
directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pink Knock Out is a member of the breakthrough Knock Out rose family, sharing the original cultivar's extraordinary disease resistance, self-cleaning habit, and continuous bloom production but with medium-pink semi-double flowers that are lighter and softer than the cherry-red original. The pastel pink color blends naturally with both warm and cool companion plants, making it more versatile for mixed plantings than the strong red. It blooms from late spring through frost in flushes every 5–6 weeks, requires no deadheading, and shows outstanding resistance to black spot — the most common and damaging rose disease in humid climates. Prune hard (to 12–18 inches) in late winter; light selective pruning during the season is optional but not required. In zone 9, apply 2–3 inches of mulch over the root zone to prevent moisture loss and reduce root zone temperature stress in the peak summer heat.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; pink kopsia is one of Singapore's most recognizable ornamental shrubs — a member of the Apocynaceae family (related to frangipani and Vinca) producing clusters of pretty, pinwheel-shaped, five-petaled, soft-pink flowers nearly year-round; CAUTION: All parts of the plant contain alkaloids — toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; prune lightly after flowering flushes to maintain compact shape; CAUTION: All parts are toxic — do not ingest. Kopsia fruticosa (pink kopsia or Singapore rose) is a compact, tropical evergreen shrub in the Apocynaceae (dogbane) family — the same family as frangipani (Plumeria), vinca (Catharanthus), and allamanda — native to the forests and forest edges of Southeast Asia, particularly the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, and Indonesia. The shrub is an extremely popular and widely planted ornamental in Singapore, Malaysia, and tropical Southeast Asia, where it is one of the most recognizable roadside and garden shrubs. The flowers are similar in shape to periwinkle or frangipani flowers: five-petaled, pinwheel-shaped, 1–1.5 inch across, soft pink to rose-pink with a slightly darker center, produced in small clusters at the branch tips nearly continuously throughout the year in a warm, tropical climate. The effect is of a neat, clean, cheerful, softly-colored shrub covered in pastel-pink flowers year-round. The glossy, elliptic, dark-green leaves provide an attractive backdrop. Like most Apocynaceae, kopsia contains alkaloids (kopsingine and related compounds) that make all plant parts toxic if ingested; do not eat any part of the plant. A must-have for tropical gardens seeking reliable, long-blooming, moderate-sized ornamental shrubs.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens — never transplant from the wild (it is illegal in most states and plants almost never survive wild transplanting); plant in fall in acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), moist, humus-rich, sandy or rocky soil with full mycorrhizal fungal support in partial to full shade.
directions: Pink lady's slipper is perhaps the most iconic wildflower of eastern North American forests — its single inflated, pouched, rose-pink to magenta flower with a central cleft is instantly recognizable and has captured the imagination of generations of woodland hikers. It grows in acidic, humus-rich, sandy or rocky soil under pines, oaks, and hemlocks throughout eastern North America, requiring a very specific soil-dwelling fungus (Rhizoctonia species) to germinate from seed and to survive through its multi-year seedling stage. This fungal dependence, combined with slow growth (plants take 10–15 years to reach blooming size from seed) and sensitivity to transplanting, makes it one of the most challenging native wildflowers to establish; wild plants are strictly protected in most states. Purchase only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens from specialist native orchid nurseries and establish them in an area that has never been disturbed — once established in a suitable location, individual plants may persist and bloom for 50 or more years. Never collect from the wild.

plant_note: Plant pips (rhizome divisions) shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; the crown should rest just at or barely below soil level. Pink lily of the valley spreads by rhizomes like the white species and can be invasive in ideal conditions — plant where it can naturalize freely or contain with buried edging.
directions: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; pink lily of the valley is the rare pink-flowered cultivar of the beloved woodland groundcover, producing the same pairs of broad, ribbed, deep-green leaves and the same arching sprays of tiny, perfectly formed, intensely fragrant pendant bells as the familiar white species — but in a delicate, warm soft pink that gives a distinctly different and romantic character to the planting. The flowers are sweetly and powerfully fragrant, as in the white form, and bloom in late spring (April–May). It spreads by underground rhizomes to form dense colonies, going summer-dormant as conditions warm. It thrives in cool, moist northern climates and woodland gardens where conditions mimic its native European forest habitat. All parts are highly toxic if ingested. Pips of the pink form may be slightly slower to establish than the white species but are fully as hardy and ultimately just as vigorous. An exceptional and coveted form for the shade garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained gritty soil in a cool site with some afternoon shade.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained gritty soil in a cool site with some afternoon shade, mimicking the snowmelt-fed subalpine and alpine meadows of the Cascades, Sierra Nevada, and northern Rockies. Its heather-like needle foliage and nodding, bell-shaped pink flowers in early summer make it a favorite for high-elevation rock gardens and are visited by native bumblebees. It needs consistent moisture through the growing season and cool nights, so it is best suited to mountain or maritime climate gardens rather than hot lowland sites.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring; avoid fall planting in zones 6–7 as plants need a full season to establish before winter.
directions: Plant in full sun and well-drained, lean to average soil; muhly grass is tolerant of sandy soil, heat, humidity, and drought once established and is an outstanding choice for hot, dry southern landscapes. The main attraction is the spectacular cloud of airy, rose-pink flower plumes in September–October that transform the planting into something otherworldly when backlit by low autumn sun. Cut back to 4–6 in in late winter before new growth begins; avoid heavy organic mulching which can cause crown rot in humid climates. Divide every 4–5 years in spring to rejuvenate large clumps.

common_name: Pink Pearl Hyacinth (Deep Pink Dense-Spike Hyacinth)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.
directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Pink Pearl bears one of the deepest, most saturated pink spikes among garden hyacinths, its tightly packed, waxy florets opening a rich rose-pink that holds its color well and carries the same powerful, sweet fragrance typical of the species. Its bold color makes it a strong accent in mixed spring bulb plantings or forced indoors in a bulb vase, where the fragrance fills a room. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled hyacinth bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since the bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for good flowering in subsequent years without repeat chilling.

common_name: Pink Perfection Camellia (Shell Pink Camellia japonica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal in zone 9 — deep shade reduces bloom production while direct afternoon sun causes leaf scorch and flower bud drop.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Perfection is a classic, long-cultivated Camellia japonica cultivar — one of the most widely grown and beloved camellias in American Southern horticulture — producing perfectly formed, small to medium, fully double, shell-pink to pale-blush-pink flowers with tightly spiraling petals arranged in a formal decorative pattern of exceptional precision and beauty. The shell-pink color is softer and more refined than the deeper rose-pink of many camellias, with a cool, porcelain quality that has made Pink Perfection a perennial favorite for cut-flower use and formal garden settings. Bloom season in zone 9 runs from mid-season through late season (January through March), making Pink Perfection one of the later-blooming reliable japonica cultivars — an attribute that makes it more likely to miss the worst freeze events in zone 9. The growth habit is upright and moderately vigorous to 5–10 feet tall with dense, glossy dark-green evergreen foliage. Pink Perfection is considered one of the most reliable japonica camellia cultivars for zone 9 performance, with consistent flower production and good disease resistance. Fertilize with azalea-camellia specific acidic fertilizer in spring and fall; maintain 3–4 inches of pine bark mulch over the shallow root zone year-round.

common_name: Pink Pewter Lamium (Pewter-Silver Soft Pink Dead Nettle)
plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Pink Pewter bears pewter-silver foliage with a thin green edge and soft, pale pink flowers, forming a tidy, non-aggressive mat.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun, which scorches the pale foliage. Pink Pewter bears soft, silvery pewter-toned leaves with a thin green margin, a gentler, more muted metallic look than the brighter silver 'Orchid Frost', paired with delicate, soft pink flowers from late spring into summer. Its habit is tidy and relatively restrained compared to more aggressive Lamium selections, making it well suited to smaller shaded beds or mixed woodland plantings without overwhelming neighbors. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a dense, weed-suppressing low groundcover beneath trees and shrubs. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to encourage fresh growth, and divide congested patches in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Pink Pickerelweed (Pink-Flowered Native Marginal Pond Plant)
plant_note: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2-6 inches deep at the pond margin in full sun after last frost; Pink Pons is a pink-flowered sport of the usually blue-flowered native pickerelweed.
directions: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 2 to 6 inches deep at the shallow margin of a pond in full sun. Pink Pons is a naturally occurring pink-flowered sport of native pickerelweed, an easy-to-grow, tough marginal aquatic normally seen with blue-violet flower spikes, offering an unusual soft pink color option on the same reliable, glossy heart-shaped foliage and upright habit. It blooms over a long season from late spring into fall, drawing bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds to its flower spikes, and provides habitat and cover for pond wildlife. As a true native wetland plant, it tolerates a wide range of water depths and spreads gradually by rhizomes to form an increasing colony at the pond edge. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade after frost; pink porterweed blooms most continuously with regular light pruning of spent flower spikes and regular fertilization — tip-pruning every 6–8 weeks encourages dense, bushy growth and maximizes the number of new flower spike tips produced.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in partial shade; pink porterweed (changeable porterweed, coral porterweed) is a large Central American tropical shrubby herb in the verbena family (Verbenaceae) that produces some of the most continuously attractive, hummingbird-visited, long-season flower display of any soft-wooded tropical perennial — it grows with a large, upright, somewhat sprawling, freely branching habit and produces at the tips of every shoot long, dense, spike-like, candle-like racemes in which the individual small, tubular, rich coral-pink to salmon-pink to deep-rose flowers open progressively from bottom to top of each spike, with each new flower opening daily for weeks. The vivid coral-pink color, continuous production of new spikes, and intense hummingbird and butterfly attraction make it one of the premier wildlife-garden plants for the Gulf South. Unlike the common blue porterweed (S. jamaicensis), which is a spreading groundcover, pink porterweed grows as a large, upright shrub. Killed by frost in zone 9 but regrows readily from established roots or from new transplants in spring.

common_name: Pink Powderpuff (Spectacular Tropical Small Tree with Giant Pink Pompom Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Powderpuff is frost-sensitive and should be planted in the most frost-protected garden location in zone 9 — against south-facing walls, under building eaves, or in large containers that can be moved indoors during the brief winter freeze events that periodically affect zone 9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Powderpuff (Calliandra haematocephala) is one of the most visually spectacular flowering trees available for Gulf South zone 9b–12 gardens — a tropical South American legume tree producing large (3–4 inch diameter), perfect spherical pompoms composed entirely of long, bright pink to deep rose-red stamens, creating a flower display that looks like enormous powder puffs or fireworks suspended from the branches. The flower structure is unique: what appear to be the 'petals' are actually hundreds of long, silk-fine stamens arranged in a perfect sphere, each stamen tipped with a tiny bead of pollen — the combined effect of many stamens creating the full, lush, velvet-textured pompom that makes this plant immediately recognizable and unlike any other commonly grown flowering tree. The dramatic flowers appear in late winter through spring and often again in fall, hanging from branch tips in clusters that can cover the tree completely during peak bloom. In zone 9a, Pink Powderpuff is frost-sensitive and requires protection during hard freezes — many zone 9a gardeners grow it in large containers for easy winter protection, where it blooms abundantly. In zone 9b–12, it is a reliable, fast-growing evergreen tree. Hummingbirds visit the flowers for nectar; the long, silky stamens make it one of the most hummingbird-attractive trees in the tropical garden palette.

common_name: Pink Powderpuff (Surinam Powderpuff, Pink Mimosa Bush)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after last frost in full sun to partial shade; Pink Powderpuff grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and benefits from placement against a south or west wall in zone 9a for added frost protection. In zone 9a, freeze damage is common but the plant usually resprouts from the base in spring; in zone 9b, it blooms nearly year-round. Prune to shape immediately after the heaviest bloom flush; avoid heavy pruning in fall. Excellent as a large container specimen on a warm patio.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Pink Powderpuff thrives in the heat, humidity, and seasonal drought of zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, performing even better in zone 9b–11 where frost is rare. Calliandra surinamensis is a multi-stemmed tropical shrub or small tree native to Surinam and Brazil, producing the distinctive Calliandra flower type: spherical to semi-spherical clusters of numerous elongated stamens that collectively form a powder-puff appearance — in this species a beautiful bicolor combination of rose-pink at the outer stamen tips fading to white at the center. The individual flowers are small but borne simultaneously in numerous rounded clusters along the branches, and the overall effect of a plant in full bloom is a profusion of softly glowing pink puffballs distributed throughout the canopy. Flowers appear throughout the warm season in zone 9 and nearly year-round in zone 10-11. The feathery, twice-pinnate foliage is ornamentally attractive even out of bloom, giving the plant a delicate, lacy texture that contrasts beautifully with bold-leaved tropical neighbors. Highly attractive to hummingbirds, which probe the stamen clusters for nectar. Distinguishable from the Red Powderpuff (C. haematocephala) by its pink-and-white rather than solid red flowers and more compact habit.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Pink Princess philodendron needs strong indirect light to develop and hold its pink variegation and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Pink Princess philodendron needs strong indirect light to develop and hold its pink variegation and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11. This highly sought-after cultivar produces near-black, glossy leaves irregularly splashed and marbled with bright bubblegum-pink patches, a chimeric variegation pattern that varies from leaf to leaf and can revert to solid dark green on stems that receive too little light. Left unstaked it sprawls and vines, but is often grown on a moss pole to encourage larger, more dramatically variegated leaves as the plant matures. Prune out any all-green reverted growth promptly to keep the plant's energy directed toward pink-variegated stems, and rotate the pot regularly for even light exposure.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the surface of sandy, well-drained, infertile soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed to 70°F; do not cover seeds, as they require light to germinate. Pink Purslane self-seeds prolifically in sandy soil and may establish itself as a recurring volunteer in the garden.
directions: Pink Purslane is a native annual wildflower of the southeastern United States and tropical Americas, sprawling across sandy roadsides, coastal dunes, dry flatwoods openings, and disturbed sunny areas with tiny, vivid magenta-pink flowers that open in the morning sunshine and close by midday. A close relative of the Moss Rose (Portulaca grandiflora) sold in garden centers, Pink Purslane is smaller and more delicate but shares the same remarkable heat and drought tolerance that makes portulacas ideal for hot, dry, infertile spots where other flowering annuals fail. The fleshy, succulent leaves are edible — with a slightly sour, mucilaginous texture similar to common purslane — and were eaten by various indigenous peoples of the Americas. Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in full sun after soil warms to 70°F; Pink Purslane self-seeds prolifically in sandy, infertile, well-drained soil and may establish as a recurring garden volunteer.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained woodland or conifer forest soil in partial to full shade; pink pyrola establishes slowly but is extremely cold-hardy and long-lived once settled in the right conditions — it requires specific soil acidity and mycorrhizal associations to thrive.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained conifer woodland or mixed forest soil in partial to full shade; pink pyrola requires specific mycorrhizal associations and will not establish in standard garden beds without undisturbed woodland soil. Pyrola asarifolia is a circumpolar wintergreen of boreal and montane forests throughout northern North America, Asia, and Europe, producing a rosette of glossy, leathery, dark-green, round to kidney-shaped evergreen leaves and a nodding raceme of pink to deep rose-pink flowers in late spring and early summer on an upright stem 6–12 inches tall — among the most beautiful of all the native pyrolas. It grows naturally under conifers, in moist mossy bogs, and along shaded stream banks where the soil is consistently moist and strongly acidic. In garden settings, plant in undisturbed, leaf-mulched acidic woodland soil near established conifers or rhododendrons; transplant small container-grown plants rather than attempting seed propagation. Once established, pink pyrola is virtually maintenance-free.

plant_note: Place outdoors in shade after temperatures remain above 55°F; in zone 9 use outdoors April–October and bring indoors in winter. Pink Quill Tillandsia is an epiphytic bromeliad — it can be grown mounted on driftwood, in a shallow container with fast-draining orchid bark mix, or attached to a tree branch in zone 10–11. Absorbs water and nutrients through the leaf scales (trichomes); mist or soak the plant 2–3 times weekly in warm weather, ensuring it dries fully between mistings. The spectacular pink inflorescence — a flat, paddle-shaped, bright rose-pink quill — is the primary ornamental feature, lasting 2–3 months before the blue-violet flowers emerge from its edges and then fade. After flowering, the plant produces offsets (pups) from the base that can be separated when they reach half the parent size.
directions: Plant in bright indirect light to deep shade — never in direct sun, which bleaches and damages the foliage — mounted on driftwood or in a container with very fast-draining orchid bark; water by misting or soaking the entire plant; Tillandsia cyanea (Pink Quill Plant) is an epiphytic bromeliad from Ecuador that produces one of the most visually dramatic floral structures available in any commonly grown houseplant or shade-tolerant ornamental — a striking, large, flat, paddle-shaped, bright hot-pink to rose inflorescence (the 'quill') up to 6 inches tall from which 1-inch violet-blue flowers sequentially emerge along both edges over a period of weeks. The color combination of the hot-pink bracts and violet flowers is exceptional and entirely natural — creating a bicolor display that would seem improbably vivid if it were not a real, wild-type species rather than a hybridized selection. As an epiphyte, Pink Quill Tillandsia requires no soil — it grows naturally attached to tree branches, absorbing water and nutrients through the specialized leaf trichomes (scales) that cover the gray-green leaves. For zone 9 gardeners with covered porches, pergolas, and outdoor living spaces that receive no direct sun, Pink Quill Tillandsia offers one of the most spectacular and conversation-provoking shade ornamental plants available, with minimal care requirements beyond regular misting.

common_name: Pink Rain Lily (Caribbean Rosy-Pink Summer Rain-Triggered Zephyranthes)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Rain Lily responds to the rain and humidity of Gulf South summer storms with explosive simultaneous blooming — the flowers appear 3–5 days after heavy rain events, with all blooms opening within a short window before closing and fading.
directions: Plant bulbs in spring 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Rain Lily (Zephyranthes rosea) is a Caribbean bulb from Cuba and other West Indian islands, producing small (1.5–2 inch), clear rose-pink to warm deep-pink funnel-shaped flowers that appear in coordinated, simultaneous flushes days after summer rain — a uniquely responsive blooming trigger that makes rain lily displays brief, intense, and tied directly to Gulf South summer storm events. The pink color of Z. rosea is warmer and deeper than the blush-tinged white of the native Atamasco lily, providing a more vivid summer color accent; the genus name Zephyranthes means 'flower of the west wind', reflecting the traditional association of these bulbs with rains coming from storm systems. In Gulf South zone 9, Pink Rain Lily is one of the most reliable and easily naturalized of all small summer bulbs — it multiplies freely by offsets to form dense clumps that bloom repeatedly through summer and fall, naturalizing in lawn edges, rock gardens, and perennial border fronts. The narrow, rush-like leaves appear with or before the flowers and remain through summer. Excellent naturalized in drifts under partially shaded garden beds where summer rainfall triggers reliable repeat bloom. Bulb clumps can be divided every 3–4 years when overcrowding reduces bloom, though undisturbed clumps often bloom more reliably.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in spring after last frost, or in fall in zone 8–10 where they are hardy; the bulbs naturalize quickly and bloom most reliably after summer rain events.
directions: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; pink rain lily is the most commonly grown zephyr lily in the South, producing soft rose-pink funnel-shaped flowers that emerge just days after summer and fall rainfall — an event that earns them the name 'rain lily.' The bulbs go dormant through winter and dry summers, then spring to life reliably after soaking rains from June through October. In zone 9–10 they may also bloom sporadically through winter with sufficient moisture. Plant in drifts of 20 or more for the most impactful display along path edges, in rock gardens, or at the front of borders. The bulbs naturalize readily and multiply over years into showy colonies. In zones colder than 7, lift and store bulbs dry through winter.

common_name: Pink Rock Orchid (Kingianum Orchid, Australian Rock Orchid)
plant_note: Divide congested clumps in spring after flowering and pot in a fast-draining bark-and-perlite mix in a shallow container; Dendrobium kingianum is a lithophytic species from rocky outcrops in eastern Australia and is among the most cold-tolerant orchids grown, surviving brief drops to near freezing when kept dry, so it can summer outdoors in a bright spot in most temperate climates.
directions: Grow in bright light with some direct morning sun — more light than a typical Phalaenopsis needs — and let the compact, clustering canes dry between waterings. Dendrobium kingianum forms tight clumps of short, tapering, cane-like pseudobulbs and is one of the easiest and most reliably floriferous orchids for beginners, producing clusters of small, fragrant, white-to-deep-pink flowers at the cane tips in late winter and spring. A distinct, cool, dry rest from late fall into winter, with night temperatures allowed to drop into the 40s°F, is essential for heavy flowering and also toughens the plant against occasional cold snaps. Because it tolerates more cold and neglect than most orchids, it is widely sold as a beginner-friendly "rock orchid" and adapts well to being grown outdoors on a porch or patio for much of the year in mild climates.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; dislikes transplanting.
directions: Direct sow in spring where plants will grow, as rose mallow dislikes transplanting, and expect blooms in about sixty-five days. The lush plants stand two to four feet tall and cover themselves in pink, hibiscus-like flowers that magnetize pollinators. Give full sun and average soil, thinning seedlings for good air movement. It reseeds readily, so leave a few flowers to set seed for next year.

common_name: Pink Ruffles Azalea (Ruffled Pink Southern Indica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Ruffles is a Southern Indica azalea grown for its heavily ruffled, wavy-edged pink petals, distinct from the flatter blooms of most other Southern Indica cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. Pink Ruffles is a Southern Indica azalea distinguished from most other cultivars in the group by its heavily ruffled, wavy-margined petals, giving the bright pink spring flowers extra texture and dimension against the large, evergreen shrub's dense foliage. Like other Southern Indica cultivars it produces its heaviest bloom in a single spectacular spring flush and provides substantial year-round structure the rest of the year. Water deeply during establishment and dry spells, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.

common_name: Pink Sensation Water Lily (Vigorous Deep Pink Hardy Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun; Pink Sensation is a vigorous grower and benefits from a larger container than more compact water lily cultivars.
directions: Pink Sensation is a vigorous, free-flowering hardy water lily prized for its rich, deep pink, star-shaped flowers held well above the water surface, a stronger, more saturated pink than many older hardy cultivars, opening reliably even in the heat of a Gulf South summer. Its robust growth quickly fills a pond or large container with attractive round green pads, providing shade cover for fish as well as flowers, and it tends to bloom more heavily and over a longer season than more compact cultivars. Divide rhizomes every two to three years when they crowd their container, and feed during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets pushed into the soil for the best bloom.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Pink Silver hoya colors most vividly in bright indirect light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Pink Silver hoya colors most vividly in bright indirect light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound. Narrow, dusky green leaves are heavily speckled with silvery flecks and flush pink to burgundy along the margins in bright light, growing on vigorous, twining vines that produce rounded clusters of small, dark maroon-pink, fuzzy-centered flowers with a musky, spicy fragrance most noticeable at night. A popular, fast-growing selection of one of the most variable hoya species, it tolerates a wider range of indoor conditions than many finer hoyas and rewards a sunny window with abundant, repeat blooms from the same flowering spurs. Provide a trellis or moss pole for climbing, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flower spurs, which rebloom for years.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Pink Skyrocket forms a tidy, slowly spreading clump well suited to shaded borders, rock gardens, and container plantings.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Pink Skyrocket is a distinctive foamflower cultivar with very narrow, deeply and sharply cut, almost spidery leaflets — among the most finely dissected foliage in the genus — giving the clump a delicate, lacy texture quite different from the broader, maple-like leaves of most Tiarella. In spring, slim spikes crowded with small, star-shaped, pink-flushed flowers rise just above the foliage, deepening the pink tones already present in the new leaves. The refined, textural foliage remains an asset through the whole season, long after bloom has finished, making this a strong choice for a woodland shade garden or as a textural accent among broader-leaved shade perennials like hostas and heucheras. Zone 4–9.

plant_note: Sprinkle seeds on the surface of moist, acidic, nutrient-poor medium (live sphagnum moss or 50/50 peat and perlite) without covering; keep standing in a tray of pure rain water or distilled water in full sun — pink sundew self-seeds prolifically in appropriate bog conditions.
directions: Pink sundew is the most common and widespread native sundew of the Gulf Coastal Plain, found abundantly in open, wet, acidic pine flatwoods, bogs, and roadside ditches from Virginia to Texas and Florida — its tiny rosettes of reddish, glistening, gland-tipped leaves studded with sticky droplets of mucilage trap and digest tiny insects (especially gnats, midges, and small flies) to supplement nutrients in its nutrient-poor habitat. Despite its miniature size (rosettes rarely exceed 2 inches across), pink sundew produces an outsized display of delicate, pink flowers on long stems in late spring, and in appropriate bog conditions it self-seeds prolifically to form dense mats of glittering, glandular rosettes that capture insects throughout the warm season. One of the easier carnivorous plants to grow from seed or to establish in a native bog garden alongside pitcher plants and grass pink orchids; seeds require no stratification and germinate readily on the surface of moist sphagnum or peat.
