Grow in standing water (the tray method) using rain water or distilled water only — tap water hardness kills all carnivorous plants over time.

common_name: Pink Symphony Caladium (All-Pink Large Fancy-Leaved Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Pink Symphony requires consistent moisture — irregular watering causes leaf tip burn that reduces the ornamental quality of the display.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Pink Symphony is a large-leaved, primarily pink-toned fancy caladium producing heart-shaped leaves with varying shades of rose-pink to medium pink as the dominant leaf color, with pink-veined or green-veined patterning depending on individual leaf development. The soft, warm pink coloration creates an elegant, romantic atmosphere in shade garden plantings — distinctly different from the cool white-and-green of 'Candidum' or the vivid red-and-green of 'Florida Cardinal'. Pink caladiums like Pink Symphony are among the most frequently requested by gardeners seeking warm-season color in shaded foundation beds and areas under trees where traditional flowers fail. In zone 9, Pink Symphony performs reliably through the entire warm season (May–October) and the tubers increase in size each year, producing larger and more numerous leaves as the planting matures over successive seasons. The soft pink foliage combines beautifully with white-flowered shade companions (impatiens, begonias, white vinca), silver-leaved plants, and the blue-green tones of hostas for a classic, romantic shade garden color scheme. Maintain consistent moisture throughout the growing season and mulch heavily to maintain soil temperature and moisture.

subcategory: late-summer South African pink iris corm
plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; pink tritonia blooms in late summer (July–September) on upright stems with flowers arranged alternately in two rows (disticha = two-rowed) along the upper stem. Unlike the Cape winter-rainfall tritonias, this species is summer-growing, tolerating summer moisture well. It can naturalize in mild-winter, well-drained garden conditions and spreads by corm offsets.
directions: Plant corms in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; pink tritonia is a late-summer blooming South African iris-family plant from the summer-rainfall areas of the Drakensberg — producing in July through September upright, slender stems bearing alternating rows of medium-sized, open-faced, clear to deep pink flowers with slightly darker veining, each flower funnel-shaped with reflexing petals, arranged in two precise rows along the upper stem (the botanical meaning of 'disticha'). The flowers are produced successively along the stem over a 4–6 week period, providing extended late-summer color in an individually distinct and refined flower form. The clear pink color, clean and uncomplex, is particularly valuable in the late-summer border when pink is difficult to source in iris-family plants. It is a summer-rainfall species tolerating summer moisture well, making it more practical for the Gulf Coast and humid-summer gardens of zones 7–10 than the more demanding Cape winter-rainfall iris species. It spreads gradually by corm offsets to form larger clumps, and naturalizes modestly in favorable well-drained, sunny garden conditions over time.

common_name: Pink Truffles Baptisia (Decadence Series Dusty Pink False Indigo)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Pink Truffles is a compact Decadence-series hybrid with unusual dusty mauve-pink flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Pink Truffles bears dense spikes of unusual, dusty mauve-pink, pea-like flowers, a soft, muted color rarely seen in the genus, on a compact, upright plant that is part of the Decadence series bred for more manageable garden size than the sprawling wild Baptisia species while keeping the genus's legendary toughness and longevity. Following bloom, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest, and the plant serves as a larval host for several native butterfly species. It is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free once established. Avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants; simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun in spring; pink trumpet tree (formerly Tabebuia rosea) flowers most reliably when it experiences a distinct dry season in winter — the moisture stress and cool temperatures of a dry winter followed by the onset of rain and warmth in spring triggers the spectacular leafless flowering display.
directions: Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; pink trumpet tree (formerly Tabebuia rosea, now Handroanthus roseus) is a large tropical deciduous tree native to Central America and northern South America that produces one of the most breathtaking spring flowering displays in the tropical world — in spring (late dry season), before or as the leaves emerge, the entire leafless tree becomes covered in large, funnel-shaped, lavender-pink to pale-purple-pink, trumpet-form flowers borne in dense, rounded clusters at every branch tip, transforming the canopy into a billowing cloud of soft-pink that is visible from great distances. The flowering display lasts 2–4 weeks, with the fallen pink petals carpeting the ground beneath the tree in a second display. The broad, palmate, compound, five-leaflet leaves are attractively tropical during the growing season. Pink trumpet tree is widely planted as a street and park tree throughout Central America, the Caribbean, and South Florida, where it is one of the most dramatic ornamental trees available for tropical zone 10–12 landscapes.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in warm, moist potting mix or plant container specimens near a strong trellis, fence, or arbor in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; pink trumpet vine blooms most heavily in fall and early winter in Gulf South climates.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens on a sturdy trellis, pergola, or fence in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; pink trumpet vine is a South African twining vine that produces large clusters of soft pink, trumpet-shaped flowers with red-striped throats from fall through early winter, filling a bloom gap when most vines have stopped flowering. The pinnate, deep-green glossy leaves are attractive throughout the growing season. The vine grows moderately (10–20 feet), is much less aggressive than Campsis radicans, and is suitable for structures that cannot support heavy, vigorous vines. Drought-tolerant once established. In zone 9 cut back frost-damaged stems in late winter; plants re-sprout reliably from the base.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring; pink turtlehead is one of the best late-blooming shade perennials for wet conditions — it performs at its best beside streams, ponds, and in rain gardens where the soil remains consistently moist.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in consistently moist to wet, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade; pink turtlehead is a southeastern Appalachian native shade and moisture perennial of the family Plantaginaceae that produces upright spikes of inflated, two-lipped, deep-rose-pink flowers in late summer and early fall (August–October) — the unique, puffy, snapdragon-like flowers have a distinctly turtle-headed shape (the two lips nearly closed) that gives the plant its charming common name, and are visited preferentially by bumblebees large enough to force apart the lips and access the nectar. It blooms at the same time as asters and late sedums, extending the partial-shade flowering season into autumn. The plant thrives in the wet, partially shaded conditions of streambanks, pond edges, and moist woodland gardens where it spreads gradually by rhizomes to form attractive colonies. 'Hot Lips' (particularly vivid rose-pink with a white throat) and 'Tiny Tortuga' (more compact, 18-inch form) are excellent cultivars. An important nectar plant for migrating monarch butterflies and late-season native bees.

common_name: Pink Velour Crape Myrtle (Dark Purple-Leaved Pink-Flowered Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pink Velour holds dark burgundy-purple foliage color best with full sun exposure, fading toward green in shadier sites.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun for the deepest, most saturated foliage color. Pink Velour pairs dramatic, near-black burgundy-purple foliage that emerges nearly black in spring and matures to a deep wine-purple with rich rose-pink flower clusters through summer, a striking contrast that makes it a strong specimen or accent even before bloom. Its medium size fits smaller landscapes and foundation plantings better than the largest white crape myrtle cultivars, and it shares the good powdery mildew resistance of modern breeding programs. Prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or twiggy growth and maintain an open form; avoid heavy topping, which destroys the natural vase shape and reduces next season's bloom.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; pink velvet banana is a compact ornamental species from Assam and northeastern India, growing to 4–6 feet and producing distinctive, vivid pink, velvet-textured, self-peeling fruits about 3 inches long. The fruits are ornamental and technically edible but filled with hard seeds and are not grown for culinary use. More cold-hardy than most ornamental bananas — surviving to zone 8 with some protection. Outstanding as a seasonal or permanent tropical ornamental in zone 8–11 gardens.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; pink velvet banana is a compact, ornamental banana from the hill forests and moist slopes of northeastern India (Assam) and Bangladesh that provides two distinct ornamental seasons in the garden: a summer season of lush, tropical, paddle-shaped banana foliage in a compact (4–6 foot) plant suitable for small gardens and containers, and a late-summer to autumn fruiting season producing clusters of the remarkable, distinctive, vivid pink, velvet-textured fruits that give the species its common names. The fruits are small — about 3 inches long — and covered in a dense, soft, velvety pink to hot-pink skin of bright, saturated pink-magenta color that is completely unlike the yellow-green of edible bananas. They are technically edible but filled with numerous very hard, black seeds and are gathered primarily for their ornamental value — the clusters of vivid pink velvet fruits against the tropical green foliage are a striking visual combination. The name 'self-peeling' banana refers to the fruit's tendency to split and peel back naturally when ripe, revealing the cream-white interior. More cold-hardy than many ornamental bananas, this species tolerates zone 8 winters with mulch protection over the rhizome and regrows reliably in spring. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a permanent, clumping perennial that provides compact tropical foliage and the unique pink-velvet ornamental fruit display annually.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in dry to well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; pink wild bean is a native annual vine of sandy, coastal, and inland dry habitats, fixing nitrogen and providing important wildlife food.
directions: Direct sow in dry, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; pink wild bean is a native twining annual legume of dry, sandy coastal plain habitats from Long Island to Florida and Texas, producing small, rose-pink to pinkish-lavender flowers typical of wild beans followed by narrow seed pods. The seeds are eaten by bobwhite quail and other ground-foraging birds, making it a valuable wildlife plant for naturalistic meadow and coastal garden settings. As a native nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves soil fertility while providing summer flowering interest. The plant twines readily through other vegetation or on a small trellis. In zone 9a, it grows rapidly as a summer annual from seed and self-sows to perpetuate itself in appropriate dry, sandy soils.

plant_note: Plant small bulbils in spring in average to well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; pink wood sorrel spreads readily by bulbils and self-sown seed, naturalizing rapidly in disturbed areas, lawn edges, and garden beds throughout the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in zones 8–11; pink wood sorrel is a South American species widely naturalized throughout the Gulf South and subtropical regions, where it is familiar as a low, spreading perennial of lawns, garden edges, and disturbed ground. The characteristic trifoliate clover-like leaves fold up at night and reopen each morning in a consistent daily rhythm. The bright rose-pink flowers with darker veining are produced profusely from fall through spring in zone 9 — the opposite of most temperate plants — making it a valuable cool-season color plant that performs when annuals have been killed by frost. The small underground bulbils spread the plant readily, so it can become persistent in garden beds; it is best managed as a groundcover in areas where its spreading habit is acceptable. The leaves are edible with a pleasant, mild lemon-sorrel flavor from oxalic acid.

plant_note: Plant bulb divisions or container transplants in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; pink woodsorrel is a reliable, low-care groundcover that spreads slowly by bulb offsets to fill shaded areas — it can also be grown as a container or hanging basket plant.
directions: Plant bulb divisions in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade — pink woodsorrel is a compact, ever-blooming bulbous perennial producing bright pink, five-petaled flowers nearly year-round in mild climates above neat, dark green, three-leaflet clover-like foliage that is ever-present and attractive. Unlike the common weedy Oxalis species that invade lawns, this species is a tidy, manageable ornamental that spreads slowly by bulb offsets without becoming a nuisance. It is especially effective as a low groundcover or container plant for partially shaded areas, and blooms reliably in conditions of moderate to bright indirect light. The 'Alba' form offers pure white flowers; 'Rosea' produces deeper rose-pink. An underused and highly rewarding perennial for consistently blooming color in the partial-shade border or container garden in zone 7–10.

plant_note: Surface-sow and press in; seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Press the tiny seed onto the soil surface without covering it, since light aids germination. This reddish-pink heirloom yarrow forms feathery, aromatic foliage topped with flat clusters of bloom above soft leaves. Once established it is exceptionally drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, and divide clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Pink Young's Barrenwort (Roseum, Nodding Pink Bishop's Hat)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Roseum bears nodding, purplish-pink flowers, a distinct color from the white-flowered 'Niveum' form of the same hybrid already common in gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Roseum is a classic, long-cultivated cultivar of Young's Barrenwort bearing dainty, nodding, purplish-pink flowers with paler spurs in mid-spring, held just above neat, compact mounds of heart-shaped leaflets that emerge bronze-tinted before turning green, a soft pastel color option alongside the white-flowered 'Niveum' form of the same hybrid. Its compact, dense habit makes it well suited to the front of a shaded border or as a small-scale groundcover beneath shrubs and trees. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to fully display the blooms, and divide congested clumps in early spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Pink Zazzle Gomphrena (Large Ball-Form Bright Pink Globe Amaranth)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting, or direct sow after last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Pink Zazzle bears unusually large, bright pink, ball-shaped flower heads.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Pink Zazzle bears notably large, rounded, vivid bright pink flower heads, bigger than standard globe amaranth blooms, on a compact, well-branched plant that flowers continuously from summer through frost with no deadheading required, since spent heads dry naturally on the plant. It is among the most reliable Gulf South summer annuals for sustained bloom through brutal heat and humidity that collapses many other bedding plants, and it draws butterflies readily. Excellent as a fresh or dried cut flower, with the dried flower heads holding color for months.

common_name: Pink and White Shower Tree / Java Cassia
plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper or nick with a file before sowing to improve germination rates; sow in spring when temperatures are consistently warm. Container-grown nursery stock establishes more predictably than direct seeding and blooms sooner.
directions: Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and ample room for the tree's characteristically wide, horizontal branching structure; avoid sites with standing water or heavy clay. Java Cassia blooms most heavily when dry-season stress triggers flowering, so reduce irrigation in late winter before the expected spring bloom flush. The bicolor pink-and-white flowers open in waves across the canopy and are highly attractive to bees and butterflies. Stake young trees for the first one to two seasons to develop a strong central leader before the spreading canopy takes over.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Brewer's clarkia does not transplant well and should always be sown in place. In mild-winter climates, fall sowing for spring bloom is ideal. It performs best in cool weather and declines in summer heat. Self-sows freely in appropriate lean, open soils.
directions: Direct sow seeds in cool weather in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Brewer's clarkia (pinkfairy) is a California native annual notable for being one of the very few annual wildflowers with a pronounced, sweet floral fragrance — the delicate, lavender-pink to rose-pink, four-petaled flowers, each only about 1 inch across with deeply fan-shaped petals notched at the tip, carry a light, rose-like fragrance that makes them pleasant both in the garden and as a cut flower, unusual among California native annuals. Named for the American botanist William Brewer, it grows naturally in the open, chaparral and oak woodland understory of the Sierra Nevada foothills and Coast Ranges of California. The flowers are produced in loose racemes on branching stems from spring through early summer. Outstanding as a companion to other California native annuals — California poppies, gilia, clarkia species — in native plant meadow mixes and cottage gardens. The fragrance, rare in the genus, makes it particularly valuable near garden seating areas and along paths where the flowers can be appreciated up close.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in late winter on sterile, mineral-rich cactus mix, then harden off and transplant into the garden once nights stay above freezing.
directions: Start seed indoors in late winter on sterile, mineral-rich cactus mix, then harden off and transplant into the garden once nights stay above freezing. Native to higher-elevation grasslands and woodlands of the Southwest, this species tolerates more cold than many hedgehog cacti and rewards growers with large, brilliant pink-purple blooms each spring. It slowly clusters into small mounds, making it well suited to xeric rock gardens at higher elevations. Excellent drainage is essential, since this species is more susceptible to rot than to cold injury.

common_name: Pinkie Indian Hawthorn (Classic Compact Pink Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Pinkie is one of the oldest and most widely planted Indian hawthorn cultivars, a garden standard for decades, bearing soft pink flower clusters in spring above dense, glossy, leathery evergreen foliage, followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds. Its low, mounding, compact habit fits foundation plantings and low hedges, and it shares the species' reliable tolerance for salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils, a long-proven performer in coastal Gulf landscapes. Good air circulation between plants helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions.

common_name: Pinkie Magnolia (Little Girl Series Fuchsia-to-Pale-Pink Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Pinkie is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred for later, frost-dodging bloom on a compact, upright plant.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Pinkie is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later bloom timing, producing tulip-shaped flowers colored deep fuchsia-pink at the base fading to pale pink at the tips, with a white interior, on a compact, multi-stemmed plant. Its later flowering window gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, consistently acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to light shade. Pinkshell Azalea requires reliable moisture and good air circulation and does not tolerate dry, alkaline, or compacted soils; it is most reliable in cool, high-humidity environments in Zones 4–7.
directions: Pinkshell Azalea is a beautiful and rare native deciduous azalea endemic to a small area of the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, where it grows on boggy hillsides, stream banks, and acidic seeps at elevations above 3,000 feet — one of the most restricted native azaleas in the eastern United States, known from fewer than 20 natural populations. The delicate, five-petaled, light to deep pink flowers borne in early spring before leaf emergence have a distinctive butterfly shape lacking the long floral tube typical of most azaleas, making the blooms uniquely recognizable among native azalea enthusiasts and adding exceptional elegance to the spring garden. Among the hardiest of all native azaleas, surviving USDA Zone 4 winters with ease, Pinkshell Azalea is a superb choice for northern gardens seeking a spectacular, native spring-flowering shrub for moist, partially shaded spots. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation; it requires reliable moisture and high humidity to perform well, especially in warmer zones.

common_name: Pinky Winky Hydrangea (Two-Tone Pink-and-White Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Pinky Winky performs best with full morning sun and afternoon shade in zone 9 — sufficient sun for maximum flower production with shade protection during peak summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Pinky Winky is a distinctive panicle hydrangea cultivar distinguished by its unusual two-tone flower display — the large, conical (12–16 inch) flower panicles open pure white in midsummer and then progressively change color from the bottom of the panicle upward, with the lower, older florets turning from white to deep pink to rose-red while the upper, younger florets remain white. This creates a striking bicolor effect of white-on-pink within a single flower head that provides weeks of ornamental interest as the color change progresses. The vigorous, upright-arching habit grows more vigorously than Limelight — Pinky Winky can reach 6–8 feet tall with strong, upright stems. Like all Hydrangea paniculata cultivars, Pinky Winky blooms on new wood and can be pruned hard in late winter to stimulate maximum new growth and flower production. It is among the hardiest of all hydrangeas (to zone 3) and tolerates clay soils, full sun (with adequate moisture), and some drought better than French hydrangeas. In zone 9, the pink color develops most intensely in cooler fall temperatures and may be less vivid in very hot summers.

common_name: Pinky Winky Prime Hydrangea (Compact Improved Bicolor Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Pinky Winky Prime is a more compact, sturdier-stemmed improvement on the original Pinky Winky, needing less staking to hold its heavy bicolor flower panicles upright.
directions: Pinky Winky Prime carries the same distinctive two-tone flower panicles as the original Pinky Winky, with the lower portion of each panicle turning deep pink while the upper tip stays white, giving each flower head a bicolor effect as the bloom season progresses, on a more compact plant with stronger, more upright stems than the original cultivar. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers, and its improved stem strength holds the heavy panicles upright through summer storms better than many older panicle hydrangea cultivars. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply during dry spells for the fullest, most colorful panicles.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sections in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade; pinnate bittercress is a spring ephemeral — it emerges early, flowers, and begins going dormant by early summer. Mark the planting site to avoid disturbance. It spreads by brittle, easily-broken rhizome segments that are scattered around the planting site by digging — each fragment regenerates into a new plant.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; pinnate bittercress is a handsome spring-ephemeral from the beech forests of southern Europe, larger and more boldly architectural than the common weedy bittercresses — producing fresh, bright-green, pinnately-divided leaves with seven (or more) leaflets arranged along the stalk in the neatly ordered pattern characteristic of the genus, and in April through May producing substantial clusters of relatively large, four-petaled flowers in clear white to pale lilac-pink above the attractive foliage. The whole plant is a spring ephemeral — beginning to go dormant by early summer as the tree canopy closes above — but the spring show is attractive and the spreading rhizomes form an effective, gradually expanding colony in moist, shaded conditions. The brittle, white, tooth-like rhizomes break apart easily when disturbed, each fragment capable of regenerating a new plant — making it very easy to propagate by simply working the soil around established plants. Combines naturally with bluebells, wood anemones, and wild garlic in the spring woodland garden.

common_name: Pinstripe Calathea (Pin Stripe Plant, Calathea ornata)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in zone 9; Calathea ornata cannot tolerate temperatures below 60°F or dry air. It requires consistent moisture, high humidity (above 50%), and bright indirect light to maintain its best appearance. Use filtered, distilled, or rainwater — fluoride and chlorine in tap water cause leaf tip browning. Propagate by dividing the rhizome clump at repotting time in spring. Leaves fold upward at night (nyctinasty) and return to horizontal position in daylight.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Calathea ornata performs best 3–6 feet from a bright window and will not tolerate direct sun which scorches the dramatic leaf markings. Calathea ornata is a tropical prayer plant from Colombia and Venezuela in the family Marantaceae, prized for its extraordinary leaf markings: the large, elongated, dark emerald-green leaves are decorated with precise, parallel, feather-like stripes of pale pink to cream in the juvenile phase (turning white as leaves mature) that radiate from the midrib, creating a pattern resembling elaborate hand-painted porcelain. The underside of each leaf is deep burgundy-purple. At night, the leaves fold upward (nyctinasty) — a behavior common to all Calatheas and Marantas that gives them the collective name 'prayer plants.' Calathea ornata's beautiful patterned foliage has made it one of the most sought-after decorative houseplants of the current era, though it has a well-deserved reputation for sensitivity: it is easily stressed by low humidity, fluoride in tap water, cold drafts, and overwatering, developing brown leaf tips and edges. The key to success is consistently warm temperatures, high humidity, and filtered water. Despite the challenges, a healthy, well-grown specimen is extraordinarily beautiful.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in fall or spring in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; like other aeoniums, pinwheel aeonium is a winter-growing, summer-dormant Canary Islands succulent, so cuttings establish best during the cool season rather than in summer heat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun to part shade, watering moderately from fall through spring and withholding water in summer when growth pauses. Aeonium haworthii (pinwheel aeonium) is smaller and more freely branching than the larger tree aeonium, forming a rounded, multi-stemmed shrublet topped with neat 4-to-5-inch rosettes of blue-green, spoon-shaped leaves edged in a fine red-pink line that gives the compact rosette its 'pinwheel' look. It shares the unusual reverse growing season of its genus, actively growing through cool, moist winters and going semi-dormant with reduced leaf turgor in hot, dry summers, when watering should be cut back sharply. This species is the parent of several popular variegated and colored cultivars, including 'Kiwi' and 'Tricolor', and readily branches from cut stems, making it easy to shape or propagate from tip cuttings. It suits rock gardens, mixed succulent containers, and coastal Mediterranean-style plantings in zone 9-11.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; nick and soak seed to aid germination.
directions: Nick and soak the hard seed, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis or fence for these quick-growing heirloom vines. Heart-shaped leaves and pinwheel-patterned blossoms open to greet the morning, with a fresh set of flowers each day. Give full sun and support to climb, and avoid overly rich soil, which favors leaves over blooms. Note that morning glory seeds are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, very well-drained soil in partial shade; pinxter azalea requires excellent drainage and strongly acidic conditions — it will not survive in alkaline or clay soils. Mulch heavily with pine bark to maintain acidic soil pH and moisture.
directions: Plant in moist, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, very well-drained soil in partial to dappled shade — pinxter azalea is a graceful, open-branching deciduous native azalea of the eastern piedmont and coastal plain, producing masses of pale to deep pink tubular flowers with long, exserted stamens in April–May before or just as the leaves unfurl, filling shaded woodland gardens with a lovely, sweet-spicy fragrance. Unlike evergreen azaleas, pinxter's open, airy form is beautiful even out of bloom, with yellow-green to orange fall foliage. It grows naturally in acidic, sandy, well-drained soils at the edges of pine and oak woodlands and along stream banks in the Southeast. Slower-growing and longer-lived than most garden azaleas, with exceptional cold and heat tolerance for zone 5–9. An outstanding native alternative to introduced evergreen azaleas that thrives in the challenging, sandy, acidic soils of Gulf Coast pine woodlands without the pest and disease issues of Asian azalea species.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines near a sturdy trellis, pergola, or tree trunk in partial to full shade; the vine grows quickly once established but may be slow to emerge in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; pipevine is a vigorous native climbing vine with enormous heart-shaped leaves that creates a dense, lush shade canopy and unusual curved pipe-shaped brown flowers in late spring that lure and temporarily trap small flies as pollinators. It is the essential host plant for the stunning pipevine swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs exclusively on Aristolochia species — the caterpillars absorb aristolochic acids from the plant, making both larva and adult butterfly toxic to predators. Plant several vines together to provide enough leaf mass for the caterpillars. Train on a sturdy arbor, pergola, or fence; the vine can grow 20–30 feet and covers itself with tropical-looking foliage by midsummer. Cut back hard in late winter to control size.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy or rocky, infertile soil in full sun; pitch pine is adapted to the poorest, most fire-prone habitats of the eastern US — the Pine Barrens, rocky ridges, and sandy outwash plains where other trees cannot persist.
directions: Plant in dry, strongly acidic, sandy or rocky, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pitch pine is one of the most fire-adapted trees in eastern North America, able to re-sprout from dormant buds in the bark after fire damage — a trait unique among northeastern pines. The New Jersey Pine Barrens, one of the most ecologically important and unusual ecosystems in the eastern US, is dominated by pitch pine, which requires periodic fire to maintain the open, scrubby canopy and prevent succession to other forest types. The tree produces pitch (resin) in extraordinary quantities — historically harvested for naval stores, tar, and turpentine. An extremely tough, gnarled, characterful tree for the driest, most infertile, fire-maintained habitats in the Northeast and Appalachians. Not suitable for zone 9 — limited to zones 4–7.

plant_note: Plant with crown at soil level in well-drained, limestone-based or neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; Pitcher's clematis is a prairie-edge species naturally found on limestone bluffs, rocky slopes, and thicket edges in the south-central US.
directions: Pitcher's clematis is a native vine of the south-central United States — Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and adjacent states — producing nodding, pitcher- or urn-shaped flowers of purplish-blue to violet-blue with thick, recurved petal tips from May through August on a twining vine that scrambles through shrubs and fences with a restrained, manageable habit. Its distinctive flowers are adapted to specialist bee pollinators and are particularly visited by native metallic green sweat bees that navigate the closed floral tube; the feathery, silvery seedheads that follow persist into winter as the seed plumes expand and catch the light. As a species adapted to drier, alkaline limestone soils, Pitcher's clematis is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant of all native clematis, performing well in zones 7–9 where summer heat and occasional drought challenge other species in the genus. Cut stems back to 12–18 inches in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and prolific flowering the following season.

plant_note: Sow seed directly into loose, well-drained sand in fall so it experiences natural winter cold-moist stratification; plant only nursery-grown seed-sourced stock, since this dune specialist is federally threatened.
directions: Sow seed directly into loose, well-drained sand in fall so it experiences natural winter cold-moist stratification, mimicking its native habitat on open, active Great Lakes sand dunes. This silvery, deeply lobed thistle spends several years as a low rosette before sending up a single flowering stalk of pale pink to cream blooms that are an important nectar source for native bees and migrating monarch butterflies, after which the plant sets seed and dies. It is a federally threatened dune specialist, so plant only nursery-grown seed-sourced stock and give it full sun and undisturbed, sandy, low-nutrient soil with excellent drainage. Established plantings help stabilize dune habitat while supporting pollinators that few other dune plants can sustain.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring onto a lightly disturbed, open soil surface in full sun; press seed into contact with the soil without deep burial and keep the seedbed evenly moist until germination occurs in two to three weeks.
directions: Scatter seed onto a lightly raked seedbed in full sun in early spring, pressing it firmly into the soil and watering until seedlings emerge and begin to establish their root systems over the first month. Pitchfork paspalum is a native warm-season grass of the southeastern coastal plain and eastern prairies, recognized by its distinctive forked seed heads — two to several spreading racemes that give the species its name — which emerge in mid to late summer and persist attractively into fall. It thrives in open, well-drained prairies, pine savannas, and dry roadsides, tolerating drought and lean soils once the deep root system is established, and providing important seed and cover for grassland birds. Allow plants to self-sow into adjacent open ground to gradually build a naturalized stand; division of established clumps in spring is also effective for expanding plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; nick and soak seed to aid germination.
directions: Nick and soak the seed, then direct sow in spring where plants will grow, as lupines resent transplanting. This compact variety stays just twelve to eighteen inches tall with loose eight-inch spikes in pink, blue, purple, and white, some bicolored. Plant in groups for a splash of color in smaller gardens or containers. Provide full sun and well-drained soil, and deadhead spent spikes to prolong bloom.

plant_note: Surface-sow; needs light to germinate. Self-seeds readily.
directions: Scatter seed on prepared soil and barely press it in, as light triggers germination. This easy native annual, also called calliopsis or golden tickseed, opens bright yellow petals marked with burgundy centers from early summer to fall. It thrives in poor, dry soil and full sun, quickly filling meadows and borders with color. Allow some flowers to set seed and it will reliably return the following season.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral riparian soil in full sun; plains cottonwood is the dominant riparian tree of the Great Plains, forming gallery forests along rivers and streams in the otherwise treeless prairie landscape. It grows extremely fast and requires consistently moist soil.
directions: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral riparian soil in full sun; plains cottonwood is the subspecies of eastern cottonwood (Populus deltoides) adapted to the semi-arid Great Plains, forming the iconic riparian forest galleries along the Platte, Republican, Arkansas, and other prairie rivers of the central US. In the treeless expanses of the Great Plains, cottonwood groves along rivers are biological oases — the only substantial tree cover across thousands of square miles of grassland. They support nesting red-tailed hawks, great horned owls, heron colonies, orioles, and dozens of other bird species that simply cannot exist without tree canopy in the open prairie. The brilliant yellow fall foliage is a spectacular landmark in an otherwise somber fall landscape. The female trees produce cottony seed release in early summer that can be messy — male plants are preferred in urban settings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; plains larkspur is native to dry, open prairies and disturbed ground of the Great Plains and south-central US. Seeds require cold stratification to germinate well.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; plains larkspur is a native perennial of dry prairies and plains grasslands from Manitoba south to Texas and east to Illinois, producing pale white to pale blue flower spikes (more white or cream than the vivid blues of mountain larkspurs) on upright stems in late spring. The foliage and seeds are toxic to cattle and horses — a significant issue for rangeland management in the Great Plains — and all parts should be treated as toxic to humans as well. In the garden, the delicate, lacy foliage and tall flower spikes provide vertical interest in dry, native prairie plantings and meadow gardens. Self-sows in open, disturbed, dry conditions to naturalize over time. Important for pollinators including bumblebees, native bees, and hummingbirds during its spring bloom period.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring into rocky or sandy, well-drained upland soil; can also be fall-seeded to allow cold stratification over winter for stronger spring germination.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in spring on exposed, well-drained soil after the last frost, or fall-sow to let winter cold naturally stratify the seed for improved spring germination. Thin seedlings to 18–24 inches and avoid amending soil with compost, as plains muhly is native to lean, alkaline uplands and tends to flop in overly rich conditions. Plants form tidy, wiry clumps that produce airy seed panicles from late summer into fall, providing both visual interest and forage for native sparrows and finches. Cut clumps back to 4–6 inches in late winter before new growth resumes to keep the planting looking fresh.

plant_note: Scarify the hard seed coat lightly and sow in fall or early spring into well-drained, dry, sandy or clay-loam soil in full sun; plains poppy mallow forms a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established, so sow it where it is to grow.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained, dry soil in full sun; plains poppy mallow is a sprawling Great Plains and south-central native with deeply lobed leaves and cup-shaped, rich wine-red to magenta flowers held above the foliage on wiry stems from spring through early summer. A thick taproot makes established plants extremely drought tolerant and essentially impossible to move successfully, so choose a permanent, well-drained location before sowing rather than planning to transplant later. The trailing stems weave attractively through low grasses and other prairie perennials without smothering them, making it an excellent component of a naturalistic prairie or meadow planting rather than a tidy formal border. It needs no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established and self-sows modestly in open, undisturbed soil.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of dry, lean, sandy or gravelly soil after last frost; press seed into soil but do not cover deeply, as light aids germination.
directions: A bold, spiny-stemmed native annual or biennial poppy with deeply lobed, blue-gray, spine-tipped leaves and enormous, tissue-paper-white flowers 3-4 inches across with golden-yellow stamens; native to dry, open prairies, roadsides, and disturbed ground of the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain foothills. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested and the milky yellow sap causes skin irritation — handle with thick gloves. Direct sow in spring in dry, lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; self-sows prolifically and naturalizes in open, disturbed, dry ground. An excellent, drought-tolerant native annual for large-scale prairie plantings.

plant_note: Let a harvested pad callus for a week in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end an inch into very well-drained, gritty, sandy soil in full sun in late spring; plains pricklypear roots readily from single pad cuttings.
directions: Plant a callused pad in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; plains pricklypear is one of the most cold-hardy of all opuntias, native from the southern Great Plains north into areas with prolonged sub-zero winters, where it survives by shrinking and wrinkling its pads until spring growth resumes. Flattened, blue-green pads bear tufts of small barbed bristles (glochids) as well as scattered longer spines, and are topped in late spring with large, silky, lemon-yellow flowers that sometimes show a reddish center, followed by reddish-purple, edible fruit (tunas) in late summer. It spreads slowly by rooting pads to form a low, sprawling colony useful for dry slopes, rock gardens, and unirrigated xeriscape beds where turf and border perennials struggle with drought and poor soil. Handle pads and fruit with heavy gloves and tongs, since the fine glochids embed painlessly in skin and are difficult to remove.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, deep soil in full sun; plains wild indigo has a very deep taproot and resents disturbance once established — sow where it will remain permanently. Scratch seed lightly and cold-stratify before spring sowing.
directions: Sow scarified seed in fall in well-drained, average to poor, deep soil in full sun — plains wild indigo is a low, spreading prairie legume of the Great Plains and midwestern prairies producing dense racemes of cream to pale yellow pea flowers in early spring, among the earliest native prairie plants to bloom. Unlike the tall blue false indigo (B. australis), plants remain compact and spread broadly rather than upright — the procumbent, mounded form covered with 4-inch cream flower spikes is striking in the spring landscape. A nitrogen-fixing prairie legume with an extremely deep taproot that survives drought and fire. Extremely long-lived once established (decades) but slow to establish from seed. Excellent for prairie garden restoration and native plant meadow plantings in zones 4–9. The inflated black seed pods are interesting ornamentally and rattle when dry. A host plant for specialist bees and several moth species.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; plains yellow primrose requires excellent drainage and is native to the dry, calcareous soils of the Great Plains and western prairies. It is very drought-tolerant once established but will rot in heavy, wet soils. A good choice for rock gardens, gravel gardens, and dry prairie restorations in the central states.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; plains yellow primrose is a low-growing, spreading native perennial of the calcareous prairies, rocky glades, and dry bluffs of the central Great Plains — from the Dakotas south to Texas and west to the Rocky Mountains — producing narrow, slightly toothed leaves on spreading stems and a profuse display of clear, bright yellow, four-petaled flowers about 1–1.5 inches across from late spring through summer. The flowers have a soft, crepe-paper texture characteristic of the evening primrose family and open in the morning rather than in the evening, despite the family association. An exceptionally drought-tolerant plant of dry, calcareous soil, it is well-adapted to the same difficult conditions as the central Texas Hill Country where limestone-based, thin, droughty soil is the norm. It spreads moderately by both seed and spreading stems to form a low groundcover in dry, open positions. Excellent for the xeric prairie garden, rock garden, and any lean, calcareous soil situation where a low, spreading, yellow-flowered native perennial is needed. Visited by native bees and other pollinators throughout its extended bloom season.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, dry, gravelly or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; plains zinnia is native to shortgrass prairie and high plains grassland and needs sharp drainage far more than it needs fertility.
directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; plains zinnia is a low, spreading perennial relative of the common bedding zinnia, native from the high plains south through the Chihuahuan Desert. Narrow gray-green leaves and small, bright golden-yellow flowers with a darker center cover the low mounding to creeping mats from late spring through fall, drawing butterflies and native bees even in extreme summer heat and drought. It spreads slowly by underground rhizomes to form a dense, tough, walkable groundcover in xeriscape beds, dry slopes, and rock gardens, and is essentially untroubled by pests, disease, or deer once established. Avoid rich soil, extra irrigation, and winter-wet sites, all of which shorten its life and encourage rot in this drought-adapted, deep-rooted species.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Planer Tree tolerates and prefers seasonally flooded conditions. Seeds should be sown fresh in moist, saturated soil as soon as they ripen in spring, as viability diminishes quickly.
directions: Planer Tree — also called Water Elm — is a small and uncommon native tree of permanently wet swamps, river floodplains, and cypress-tupelo bottomlands of the coastal plain from South Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, where it often grows in the understory beneath bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp cottonwood. The small, rough-textured leaves and warty, inconspicuous drupes superficially resemble those of the closely related elms, but the single nutlet with a distinctly rough, tuberculate surface is the diagnostic feature that separates Planera from Ulmus. Seeds should be collected and planted fresh in moist to wet, acidic soil under light shade, as viability drops quickly; container-grown nursery transplants are the most reliable method for establishing this species in cultivation. Planer Tree is rarely grown in ornamental settings but makes a distinctive small specimen for rain gardens, pond margins, and naturalized floodplain plantings where saturated soils and periodic flooding prevent most woody plants from thriving.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; plantain-leaf sedge grows naturally in moist, rocky, north-facing woodland slopes in rich, deep soil and requires similar conditions in the garden.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; plantain-leaf sedge is the most architecturally distinctive of all the native shade sedges, immediately recognizable by its unusually broad, pleated, dark green leaves (1–2 inches wide) with prominent parallel veins resembling plantain (Plantago) leaves — a completely different aesthetic from typical narrow-leaved sedges. The leaves remain evergreen or semi-evergreen through winter, providing year-round ground-level interest in the woodland garden. Burgundy-red stems bear small, elegant fruiting spikes in early spring before most other plants emerge. It grows naturally on moist, north-facing, rocky woodland slopes in the Appalachians and eastern US. Slower to spread than some native sedges but forms a beautiful, refined groundcover in appropriate conditions. An outstanding accent plant for the front of a shaded border or as a specimen among ferns and hostas.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in dry to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; plantain-leaf pussytoes tolerates poor, rocky soil and is ideal for naturalizing on dry slopes or beneath high-canopied trees where little else will grow.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in dry, poor to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; plantain-leaf pussytoes is exceptionally tolerant of drought, rocky substrates, and the dense dry shade beneath high-branched deciduous trees. Antennaria plantaginifolia forms dense mats of silvery-gray, woolly foliage that spreads steadily by stolons to create a weed-suppressing groundcover, bearing clusters of tiny white button-like flower heads in early spring that attract native bees before most other plants are in bloom. This dioecious native of eastern North American open woodlands and rocky hillsides thrives where moisture and fertility are too low for conventional groundcovers, making it invaluable for difficult dry-shade situations.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, rocky to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; plateau live oak is significantly more cold and drought tolerant than the coastal live oak (Q. virginiana) and is the live oak of choice for inland Texas gardens away from the mild Gulf Coast climate.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, rocky to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — plateau live oak is the iconic evergreen oak of the Texas Hill Country, Edwards Plateau, and Balcones Escarpment, where it forms the defining, spreading, ancient trees of the landscape. Nearly identical to the coastal live oak (Q. virginiana) in appearance, it is distinguished by its superior cold tolerance (surviving zone 6 winter cold without damage) and extreme drought tolerance, adapted to the thin, rocky, alkaline limestone soils of the Hill Country where moisture is scarce. Trees develop the same magnificent, broadly spreading, rounded crown with leathery, dark evergreen leaves and massive, gnarled trunks as coastal live oak but in harsher conditions. Small acorns in the red oak group ripen in two years. This is the live oak for central and west Texas gardens — offering the same magnificent landscape presence as its coastal relative but with dramatically greater cold hardiness and drought performance.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Plena bears an unusual double set of white bracts giving each bloom a fuller, rose-like appearance.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; understory planting beneath high, open tree canopy mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. Plena bears an unusual double layer of white bracts, up to eight per bloom rather than the typical four, giving each flower a fuller, rose-like appearance that sets it apart from standard flowering dogwoods, along with good resistance to anthracnose. Its distinctive double-bracted form has made it a favorite among collectors seeking something beyond the common dogwood look. Water during dry spells, especially the first two years, and avoid deep planting or heavy mulch piled against the trunk.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Pleniflora' suckers more vigorously than single-flowered kerria and is best given room to form a naturalized colony or planted where suckers can be mowed or pulled to control spread.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Pleniflora' suckers more vigorously than single-flowered kerria and is best given room to form a naturalized colony or planted where suckers can be mowed or pulled to control spread. This double-flowered kerria selection produces the same bright green, arching, bamboo-like canes as the species but with fully double, pompom-shaped, golden-yellow flowers in mid-spring that resemble small ranunculus blooms and last longer than the single form. It tolerates considerably more shade than most flowering shrubs while still blooming reliably, making it a good choice for a woodland edge, foundation planting, or naturalized shrub border, and its green stems provide subtle winter interest after leaf drop. Prune out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering each year to keep the colony vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Plum Crazy Hardy Hibiscus (Dark Plum Foliage White-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Plum Crazy's dark foliage color is most intense with full sun exposure and consistent moisture through the growing season.
directions: Plum Crazy pairs deep plum-purple, near-black foliage with enormous white, dinner-plate-sized flowers marked by a bold dark red-purple eye at the center, a striking contrast between dark leaves and pale bloom that stands out from the greener-leaved hardy hibiscus cultivars. Like other Hibiscus moscheutos selections it is naturally a wetland-edge plant and performs best in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun, flowering from midsummer into fall on a robust, well-branched perennial. It dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown, and expect it to be generally trouble-free once established given adequate water.

common_name: Plum Gorgeous Loropetalum (Compact Deep Plum-Purple Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Plum Gorgeous is a compact, mounding loropetalum selection grown for deep plum-purple foliage that holds its color well through the growing season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with at least a few hours of direct sun each day to bring out the deepest foliage color, since plants grown in heavy shade fade toward green. Plum Gorgeous is a compact, mounding loropetalum selected for rich, deep plum-purple foliage that holds its color through summer heat better than many older loropetalum cultivars, paired with bright pink fringe flowers that appear in a heavy spring flush and continue sporadically into summer and fall. Its manageable, rounded size fits foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders without the frequent shearing larger loropetalums need to stay in bounds, and the dark foliage makes an effective color contrast against golden or chartreuse companion plants. Loropetalums as a group are among the most heat- and humidity-tolerant flowering shrubs for the Gulf South and are largely trouble-free once established in well-drained soil; avoid waterlogged sites, which invite root rot.

common_name: Plum Passion Nandina (Deep Plum-Red New Growth Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; new-growth color is most intense with several hours of direct sun, while afternoon shade helps prevent scorch in peak Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Plum Passion is a compact nandina selected for new foliage that emerges a deep plum-red to burgundy, maturing to green through the growing season before shifting back to purple-red tones in fall and winter cold, giving a longer window of rich color than many dwarf nandina cultivars that show red only in cool weather. Its dense, mounding habit fits foundation plantings and mixed borders without the tall, leggy cane growth of standard nandina, and like other modern dwarf selections it produces few or no berries, reducing the self-seeding that has made straight-species nandina invasive in parts of the Southeast. It needs little care beyond occasionally removing damaged canes to keep its naturally tidy shape.

common_name: Plum Pudding Heuchera (Silver-Veined Purple Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Plum Pudding is a long-popular cultivar valued for deep purple, ruffled foliage overlaid with prominent silvery venation that shows best with a few hours of morning sun.
directions: Set divisions into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving a few hours of gentle morning sun where possible to intensify the leaf color without scorching. Plum Pudding forms a tight mound of ruffled, rounded leaves in a rich aubergine-purple with a network of raised silver veins and wine-red undersides, holding its color well into autumn. It sends up thin, wiry flower stalks with small greenish-white bells in early summer, which many gardeners shear off to keep the focus on foliage. This older, well-tested cultivar is reliably vigorous and clumping rather than spreading, and benefits from division every few years once the central crown begins to heave out of the soil.

common_name: Plum Tart Gladiolus (Rich Deep Plum-Purple to Magenta)
plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season. Plum Tart bears rich, deep plum-purple to magenta blooms.
directions: Plum Tart bears rich, deep plum-purple to magenta blooms, a saturated jewel-toned color that stands out among the more common pastel and primary gladiolus shades, well suited to autumn-themed or dramatic cutting-garden color schemes. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; grass-leaved iris is one of the very few irises that performs well in partial shade and is native to shaded woodland margins in southern Europe.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; grass-leaved iris is one of the very few irises that performs well in partial shade and is native to shaded woodland margins in southern Europe. Iris graminea is a delightful, small-flowered iris of European woodland edges and shaded grasslands, forming compact clumps of narrow, grass-like leaves among which the small, purple-and-white, typical iris-form flowers are half-hidden in late spring — but the flowers make themselves unmistakably known by their extraordinary fruity fragrance, described universally as exactly like ripe Victoria plums or plum tarts, one of the most surprisingly sweet and specific scents of any iris. The plant is compact, slow-spreading, and absolutely trouble-free in partial shade; use it at the front of a shaded border or beneath deciduous shrubs where its fragrance can be appreciated when passing. It will not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to average soil in full sun to part shade; plume poppy spreads vigorously by rhizomes and can be invasive in ideal conditions — plant only where spreading is welcome or where it can be contained by a barrier. The milky, orange-yellow sap can irritate sensitive skin. In rich, moist soil it may exceed 10 feet in height.
directions: Plant in moist to average, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; plume poppy is a majestic, large-scale perennial from China and Japan that creates an extraordinary tropical effect in the temperate garden. The enormous, deeply scalloped, fig-leaf-shaped leaves — each up to 12 inches across — are carried alternately along tall, glaucous, blue-gray stems and have striking bluish-gray surfaces with contrasting creamy-white undersides that flash pale when the wind moves through them. In mid to late summer, the plant produces enormous, branching plumes of hundreds of tiny, petal-less, buff-cream to pink flowers on stems reaching 6-10 feet, creating an airy, feathery mass that floats above the bold foliage below. It spreads freely by rhizomes and can colonize a large area quickly, but this vigor makes it invaluable for large-scale screening and rapid ground coverage in difficult areas. A single plant creates a dramatic focal point of scale and presence rarely achieved by any other hardy perennial. The orange-yellow sap is irritating to skin; handle with gloves.

common_name: Plumed Celosia (Feathery Plume Cockscomb Summer Annual)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is consistently above 65°F; celosia resents root disturbance and direct sowing usually outperforms transplants. In zone 9, plant April–June for summer and fall bloom. Celosia thrives in heat and humidity — it is one of the summer annuals that blooms more vigorously (not less) in the Gulf South's hot, humid conditions, unlike many other annuals that slow down in summer.
directions: Sow seeds 0.125 inch deep after last frost; thin to 8–14 inches. Plumed celosia is a variety group of Celosia argentea producing feathery, upright, flame-like flower plumes rather than the flat, brain-shaped crests of the cockscomb (var. cristata) type. The plumes are dense, velvety, and upright, ranging from 4–8 inches tall, in brilliant colors: deep scarlet, crimson, orange, salmon, yellow, cream, and hot pink — hot colors that intensify in summer heat. Celosia is one of the most heat-tolerant summer annuals available, thriving in conditions that cause most other plants to retreat — the combination of intense heat, humidity, and high soil temperatures that characterize Gulf South summers promotes vigorous blooming rather than reducing it. The long-lasting cut flowers are prized in both fresh and dried arrangements: the plumes hold their color and shape well when dried, making them valuable for dried flower crafts and fall arrangements. Young leaves and flowers are edible and used as cooked greens in West African and Southeast Asian cooking, where celosia is grown as a vegetable crop. Garden series include Kimono, Fresh Look, and Intenz, each offering improved uniformity and specific color ranges.

plant_note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1–2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; do not water until new growth appears — plumeria cuttings rot easily if kept wet before rooting. Established plants are dormant and leafless in winter and require complete dryness during dormancy.
directions: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun — plumeria is a tropical American tree sacred in Buddhist and Hindu cultures, widely planted around temples throughout Asia and used in Hawaiian leis, and one of the most intensely fragrant of all flowering plants. The waxy, 4-inch flowers in white, yellow, pink, red, or multicolor combinations have a powerful sweet tropical scent that is strongest at night. Plumeria is deciduous (leafless in winter), drought tolerant, and thrives in heat — full sun and excellent drainage are its only requirements. In zone 9a it is widely grown in containers: bring indoors dry and leafless when temperatures drop below 40°F, store in a frost-free location, and return outdoors in spring. Hundreds of named cultivars are prized by collectors; the Singapore White (P. obtusa) is an evergreen species suited to zone 10+.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; keep crown at or above soil level. Do not allow to dry out during establishment.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in partial to full shade; plumleaf azalea holds a unique distinction among native deciduous azaleas — it blooms in July and August, later than every other native azalea species, and is therefore in bloom when every other azalea in the garden has long finished. The large, brilliant orange-red (rarely yellow) flowers appear on the shrub in midsummer, providing color and hummingbird nectar in a season when the woodland garden often lacks bloom. This is one of the rarest native azaleas in the wild, found only in southwestern Georgia and eastern Alabama, but it is a superb and underused garden plant. It tolerates the heat and partial shade of zone 8–9 summers better than most native azaleas. Mulch heavily with pine bark to maintain soil moisture and acidity.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, ideally sheltered from drying winds; a named clonal fern selection, propagated by division rather than spores to remain true to type.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, ideally sheltered from drying winds. This is among the most finely dissected soft shield fern cultivars available, with fronds so densely and repeatedly divided that they take on a soft, feathery, almost moss-like texture unlike any other hardy fern. Evergreen in all but the harshest winters, it holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit and is prized by fern collectors for its exceptionally refined texture in a shaded rockery or woodland setting. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter just before the new crosiers unfurl.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Plush Plant flowers reliably with bright light and needs excellent drainage to avoid rot.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Plush Plant flowers reliably with bright light and needs excellent drainage to avoid rot. Thick, softly fuzzy, velvety green leaves edged in red give this shrubby Mexican succulent an appealingly plush, tactile texture unlike the smoother, glossier leaves of most other echeveria species, topped by clusters of vivid orange-red, bell-shaped flowers that resemble tiny firecrackers, giving the plant its alternate common name. Its upright, branching, shrub-like habit sets it apart from the flatter rosette form typical of most echeverias, making it a good textural and structural accent in a succulent container arrangement. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact growth and reliable flowering, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; the fine hairs covering the leaves make leaf-propagation less reliable than in smooth-leaved echeverias, so stem cuttings are the preferred home method.
directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering only after the soil has dried out completely. Echeveria pulvinata (plush plant) is a Mexican succulent covered from stem to leaf tip in a soft coat of fine white hairs that gives the whole rosette a velvety, chenille-like texture unlike smooth-leaved echeverias. The leaf tips and margins flush a vivid red in bright, cool conditions, deepening into the 'Ruby Blush' color that gives the popular selection its name, while shaded plants stay mostly green. Water carefully at the soil line rather than from overhead, since the hairy leaf surface holds moisture and can scorch or spot if droplets sit in direct sun. It branches on short stems as it matures, tending toward a low shrublet rather than a single tight rosette, and produces clusters of orange-red, bell-shaped flowers in winter that are a valuable nectar source for hummingbirds where grown outdoors.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall in mild-winter climates for earlier bloom; succession sow every few weeks to keep flowers coming through the aphid season.
directions: Scatter seed directly over prepared soil in a sunny spot, tucking it along vegetable bed borders and pathways where its low, spreading habit will not shade neighboring crops. The white-and-yellow, egg-yolk-centered flowers bloom prolifically for weeks and are one of the most reliable draws for hoverflies, whose aphid-eating larvae make this a favorite in organic vegetable gardens. It thrives in cool weather and tends to fade or stop flowering once summer heat arrives, so many gardeners treat it as an early-spring and fall companion planting rather than a summer-long bloomer. Deadheading lightly extends bloom, but it also self-seeds readily and will often return on its own the following year.

common_name: Pocomoke Crape Myrtle (True Dwarf Groundcover-Type Rose-Pink Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Pocomoke's true dwarf size makes it useful as a low border or mass planting rather than a tree, and it needs little to no annual pruning.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pocomoke is one of the true dwarf National Arboretum crape myrtle selections, staying under three feet tall and wide, useful as a low border, mass planting, or large-scale groundcover rather than the shade-tree role most crape myrtles fill. It produces rich rose-pink flower clusters over a long summer season and, like other National Arboretum hybrids, shows good resistance to powdery mildew. Its very small mature size means it needs almost no pruning beyond removing dead wood, in sharp contrast to the standard practice of cutting back larger crape myrtles.

plant_note: Set container-grown divisions in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; poet's laurel is exceptionally slow to establish and is almost always propagated by division of mature clumps rather than seed.
directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, mulching well since roots resent drying out; poet's laurel is an Asparagaceae relative of butcher's broom grown not for flowers but for its arching stems of glossy, dark green, leaf-like cladodes that are a mainstay of the florist trade for their remarkable vase life. Tiny greenish flowers in spring are followed, on pollinated plants, by orange-red berries that persist through winter and add interest to the deep-shade planting. Growth is very slow, with clumps taking several years to reach mature size, so treat new plantings as a long-term investment and avoid disturbing established clumps once they are settled in. It tolerates dry shade and heavy shade better than nearly any other broadleaf evergreen, making it valuable under mature trees where little else will grow.

common_name: Poinsettia (Mexican Christmas Star, Easter Flower, Noche Buena Garden Shrub)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil; in zone 9a and the Gulf South, poinsettia is a perennial GARDEN SHRUB growing 6–12 feet tall that blooms every winter in response to the shortening days of November–December — it is NOT just a houseplant; established plants naturalize and self-sow freely in zone 9–10 and bloom reliably each winter without indoor protection.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun or morning sun with afternoon shade; prune heavily after blooming (January–February in zone 9) — cut plants back by one-third to one-half to prevent legginess and encourage compact growth and more prolific flowering the following winter; avoid any artificial light at night in October–November which will delay or prevent flowering since poinsettia requires uninterrupted long nights (14+ hours of darkness) to initiate flower (bract) color. Poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima) is primarily known as a holiday houseplant in most of the United States, but in zone 9–11 (tropical and subtropical Gulf Coast, California, Hawaii, Florida) it is a perennial garden SHRUB that grows 6–12 feet tall, often becoming a significant landscape element that blooms dependably every winter. In the wild, poinsettia is native to Mexico — particularly the Pacific coastal region of Taxco, Guerrero — where it grows as a semi-deciduous shrub or small tree 10–15 feet tall in the dry tropical forest and blooms in response to the shortening days of November–December, turning entire hillsides red with its bracts (the colorful parts are modified leaves, not petals — the true flowers are the small yellow structures at the center). The plant takes its common English name from Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first U.S. Ambassador to Mexico, who introduced it to the United States in 1825. In zone 9a, poinsettia grown outdoors blooms reliably from November through January with minimal care, and established plants develop woody trunks and can become large impressive shrubs. The characteristic that determines bloom timing is photoperiodism — poinsettia requires uninterrupted dark periods of 14 hours or more to initiate bract coloration, which occurs naturally as nights lengthen in autumn. Streetlights or interior lights shining on the plant at night will disrupt this cycle and delay or prevent coloring.

common_name: Pointleaf Tick Trefoil / Large-flowered Tick Trefoil
