The flowers are 'ephemeral' in the literal sense — each individual bloom opens at dawn and is closed and wilted by midday, having lasted only a single morning — but the plant produces a succession of blooms over several weeks, and a naturalized colony in bloom can produce dozens of the pure-blue morning flowers at once. The name 'celestial' perfectly captures the sky-blue color. Native to the rocky limestone prairie, sandy post oak savanna, and open woodlands of the central US, it is an outstanding native plant for prairie garden and naturalistic meadow plantings in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall, 2–3 inches deep, into well-drained, average, prairie-type soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie celestial goes fully dormant in summer heat, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the resting corm.
directions: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie celestial is a small, exquisite native bulb of tallgrass and mixed-grass prairies, sending up a few grass-like, pleated leaves in late winter followed by delicate, sky-blue to violet-blue, three-petaled flowers in mid-spring. Individual flowers open only for a single morning and close by early afternoon, especially on sunny days, so the best display is seen on a walk through the planting before midday during the brief two- to three-week bloom window. After flowering and setting seed, the foliage yellows and the plant disappears entirely underground for the rest of the year, re-emerging reliably the following late winter. Because the corm is completely dormant and invisible for most of the year, mark plantings carefully and avoid deep cultivation nearby, and interplant with summer-active prairie grasses or perennials that fill the space once the foliage has died back.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost, or direct sow in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sidalcea tolerates light shade but blooms most prolifically in full sun.
directions: Start transplants indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost, or direct sow in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sidalcea tolerates light shade but blooms most prolifically in full sun. Prairie checker mallow is a graceful western native perennial in the mallow family with deeply lobed, palmate leaves and slender, upright racemes of rosy-pink to lavender-pink, five-petaled flowers resembling small hollyhocks from late spring through midsummer; it is the primary larval host plant for the West Coast Lady butterfly (Vanessa annabella) and an important nectar source for native bumblebees and mining bees. Cut back after the first flush of bloom to encourage rebloom; plants are drought-tolerant once established and are exceptional in California-style meadow gardens and dry borders.

plant_note: Direct sow on dry to average, well-drained soil in fall or early spring; prairie coneflower prefers poor, lean soils — excessive fertility leads to floppy stems and reduced flowering; self-seeds freely to form naturalizing colonies in dry prairies and meadows.
directions: Prairie coneflower (Mexican hat) is one of the most distinctive and drought-tolerant of all native prairie wildflowers — the flowers have a tall, thimble-shaped, elongated central cone surrounded by reflexed, drooping golden to red-brown ray petals that create the unmistakable 'Mexican sombrero' silhouette that inspired its popular name. Native to prairies, roadsides, and dry grasslands from Canada to Mexico, it is among the toughest of all native wildflowers in the heat and drought of the southern plains, remaining reliably perennial in zones 3–10 with essentially no supplemental water once established in lean, well-drained soil. The aromatic foliage has a distinctive camphor-like smell when crushed and is rarely browsed by deer; the long, wiry stems sway gracefully in wind, earning it a place in naturalistic meadow plantings throughout the Great Plains and Gulf Coast. Grows well mixed with black-eyed Susans, blue wild indigo, and native grasses in drought-tolerant native meadows and highway wildflower plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie cordgrass is a dominant native of tallgrass prairie wetlands and edges and is one of the best tall grasses for consistently wet, even seasonally flooded conditions in the landscape.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie cordgrass spreads rhizomatously and can form large colonies in suitable wet conditions — allow ample space or use rhizome barriers to contain it. Spartina pectinata is a tall, imposing native grass of the tallgrass prairie region and eastern coastal plain, growing 4–7 feet tall with sharply-edged, arching leaves and distinctive comb-like (pectinate) flower spikes in late summer that are striking in silhouette against the sky; the leaves turn rich golden-yellow in fall and bleach to an attractive tan in winter. An extremely valuable grass for erosion control on wet slopes, rain gardens, bioswales, pond margins, and stream banks where its vigorous rhizome system stabilizes soil; it tolerates seasonal flooding better than almost any other native upland grass. The variegated cultivar 'Aureomarginata' has yellow-striped leaves.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie coreopsis spreads by rhizomes and can form expanding colonies in appropriate conditions — an asset in prairie restorations and naturalized areas, but may need containment in formal borders. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established in sandy or rocky soil.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie coreopsis is a native perennial of the central North American prairie, one of the most drought-tolerant and cold-hardy of all the coreopsis species, spreading by rhizomes to form expanding colonies of stiff, upright stems with distinctive, deeply three-lobed or palmate (finger-like) leaves — quite different from the simple, undivided leaves of most coreopsis. In early summer (June–July) it produces a cheerful display of bright golden-yellow daisy flowers with yellow centers, each about 1.5 inches across, carried on slender stems above the dense foliage. It thrives in the exact difficult conditions of its native habitat — poor, dry, rocky, sandy prairie soils in full sun — and in rich, moist garden soils becomes rank and floppy. An excellent choice for prairie restorations, meadow gardens, and road banks where lean soil conditions naturally limit competition from aggressive non-native plants. The rhizomatous spread makes it effective for erosion control and slope stabilization. Less commonly grown than threadleaf coreopsis (C. verticillata) but distinctively different in leaf form and equally tough.

plant_note: Plant young trees in spring into well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun; prairie crabapple is adapted to the fencerows, savannas, and old fields of the tallgrass prairie region and tolerates drought once rooted.
directions: Plant young trees in spring in well-drained, average to dry soil and full sun, giving the thorny, wide-spreading crown room in an open fencerow, savanna, or pasture edge planting. Prairie crabapple is more drought tolerant than many crabapples once established, reflecting its origin on the tallgrass prairie and midwestern plains. Its very fragrant, rose-pink blossoms open in late spring and are heavily worked by native bees, while the small, waxy, greenish-yellow fruit persists into winter and is eaten by foxes, raccoons, deer, and fruit-eating birds after repeated freezing and thawing softens it. Dense, thorny branching also offers secure nesting sites for grassland and edge-dwelling birds.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow winter cold stratification; seeds require exposure to cold and moisture to break dormancy and will germinate in spring without any additional treatment.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall to take advantage of natural cold stratification, and expect germination the following spring after a period of consistent cold. Prairie dock is one of the most visually dramatic native prairie plants, producing enormous rough-textured basal leaves up to 18 inches long that resemble the ears of an elephant — these bold leaves persist all season and provide striking foliage interest even when the plant is not in bloom. In midsummer, nearly leafless flowering stems shoot up to 5–8 feet tall and are topped with loose clusters of small yellow daisy flowers that attract a wide range of native pollinators through late summer. Like all Silphium, prairie dock is extremely slow to mature from seed but extraordinarily long-lived, forming a deep resinous taproot that anchors it through drought and fire.

plant_note: Surface sow seeds without covering — prairie dropseed requires light for germination; press seeds firmly onto moist soil and keep evenly moist until established; plugs are often preferred as the species is slow to establish from seed.
directions: Prairie dropseed is considered one of the finest native ornamental grasses for the garden, forming an elegant, fine-textured mound of arching dark-green foliage that cascades like a fountain and turns brilliant amber-orange in fall. In late summer airy panicles of tiny flowers rise above the foliage bearing a remarkable fragrance often described as buttered popcorn, cilantro, or warm spice — making it one of the few ornamental grasses with a notable garden scent. It is slow to establish from seed, typically requiring 3 years to reach a full clump size, but once settled it is extremely long-lived and very drought tolerant, thriving in lean, well-drained soils of average to low fertility without supplemental irrigation. Plants self-sow modestly; shear lightly in early spring to remove old foliage and allow the fresh new growth to emerge cleanly.

common_name: Prairie Dusk Penstemon (Cold-Hardy Rose-Purple Hybrid Beardtongue)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Prairie Dusk is a Nebraska-bred hybrid penstemon noted for excellent cold hardiness and reliable perennial return, though in the Gulf South it especially needs sharp drainage to avoid winter and summer root rot in humid, poorly drained soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, choosing a raised or sloped site if garden soil tends to stay wet; Prairie Dusk is a hybrid penstemon developed in Nebraska from a cross of Penstemon barbatus and Penstemon strictus, bearing tall spikes of tubular, rose-purple flowers in early summer that are a strong draw for hummingbirds and bumblebees. It is notably cold-hardy and, given the sharp drainage penstemon generally demands, an easygoing, long-lived perennial in climates with well-drained soil. In humid Gulf Coast gardens, good drainage matters more than fertility for success — amend heavy clay with grit or plant on a raised berm to keep the crown from sitting in wet soil, which is the most common cause of penstemon failure in the region. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the plant and encourage a possible light rebloom.

common_name: Prairie Fire Carex (Orange-Red New Zealand Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color intensifies with more sun exposure.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color deepens and intensifies with more direct sun exposure. Prairie Fire is a New Zealand sedge cultivar with fine, arching foliage that shifts through warm tones of orange, copper, and red depending on season and light, a fiery color unlike the greens and blues typical of most ornamental sedges. Its low, fountain-like mound provides season-long color and texture in a rock garden, border edge, or mixed container without needing bloom to carry visual interest. Comb out dead blades by hand each spring rather than shearing, since cutting the evergreen foliage back hard can leave the clump looking ragged for weeks; divide congested clumps in spring every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Prairie Fire develops its best red summer foliage color in full sun — in partial shade the foliage remains more green through summer before turning red in fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Prairie Fire is one of the most distinctive switchgrass cultivars — a compact selection that develops an early and sustained red-to-burgundy foliage color through the summer growing season, rather than the typical green-turning-to-red-in-fall pattern of most switchgrass cultivars. In full sun from July onward, Prairie Fire's foliage transitions progressively from green to red-tipped to fully wine-red — providing a strong red color contribution throughout the second half of the growing season when most other ornamental grasses are still green. The compact habit (3–4 feet tall, compared to 5–6 feet for species switchgrass) makes it proportionate for typical residential garden beds and mixed perennial borders. Like all Panicum virgatum cultivars, Prairie Fire is a North American prairie native that is exceptionally adaptable: tolerating clay, drought, wet conditions, and the full range of Gulf South weather extremes. The early red coloration makes it excellent for mixed perennial borders where the early fall-like color creates a dramatic seasonal transition effect while summer still has weeks to run. Plant in masses for maximum visual impact — the red-burgundy foliage color is most effective when multiple plants create a sweeping color echo across a broad planting area.

plant_note: Surface-sow in fall and leave uncovered, since seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Surface-sow in fall across the eastern two-thirds of Texas, Louisiana, and the broader Gulf South, where it germinates as a winter rosette and sends up wiry stems topped with small white to pale-pink, yellow-centered daisies from late spring into summer. It is one of the earliest and most dependable native nectar sources for small bees, syrphid flies, and butterflies in disturbed fields, roadsides, and open meadows. Left unmowed, it self-sows freely without becoming weedy in most garden settings, and its fine, airy texture makes a good filler among coarser prairie perennials. It tolerates average to slightly moist soils and light, sandy loam typical of Gulf Coast lowlands.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moist to moderately dry, loamy to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie gentian grows naturally in wet prairies, roadsides, and disturbed areas in the Gulf Coast region and self-sows readily in open, sunny, slightly alkaline conditions.
directions: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moderately moist to dry soil in full sun — prairie gentian is the wild ancestor of the popular florist lisianthus, a Gulf Coast native annual of wet prairies and roadsides from Texas to Florida that produces elegant, upward-facing, funnel-shaped flowers in clear blue-purple with a velvety texture and a prominent yellow and white center — one of the most beautiful wildflower blooms on the Gulf Coast prairies. The florist lisianthus (E. grandiflorum) is a cultivated form of this species bred for larger, showier, often double flowers in expanded color ranges. The native species is shorter, tougher, and self-sows freely in Gulf Coast gardens, returning annually in open, sunny, slightly alkaline areas. The silvery-blue to blue-gray, glaucous, clasping leaves are attractive even out of bloom. A lovely wildflower for naturalistic prairie plantings, roadsides, and open, sunny garden borders in the Gulf Coast region.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; prairie golden-pea forms a deep taproot and spreads slowly by rhizome once established, so allow it room to naturalize.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; prairie golden-pea forms a deep taproot and spreads slowly by rhizome once established, so allow it room to naturalize. One of the earliest prairie wildflowers to bloom, it sends up short spikes of bright yellow, pea-shaped flowers in early spring — historically noted by settlers and Indigenous peoples as one of the first signs of the growing season on the northern plains, appearing around the time bison calves ('buffalo') were born. Silvery-green, three-parted leaves persist after bloom, and the plant spreads gradually by rhizome to form loose colonies in native prairie and rangeland restorations. It is extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, needing no irrigation or fertilizer, and its nitrogen-fixing roots benefit surrounding prairie soil.

subcategory: South American–naturalized Gulf Coast iris relative
plant_note: Plant small corms 2 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie iris has naturalized extensively on the Texas Gulf Coast, roadsides, and open areas, blooming in spring and early summer. It is originally from South America (Argentina, Uruguay) but has naturalized so thoroughly in coastal Texas that it is now treated ecologically as part of the local flora. Each blue flower lasts only a single day. The corms multiply quickly to form colonies.
directions: Plant corms in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie iris is a South American iris-family corm that has naturalized so extensively on the Texas Gulf Coast — roadsides, vacant lots, suburban lawns, open fields — that it has become a characteristic and beloved part of the Gulf Coast spring flora, blooming from March through May in flushes of sky-blue, six-petaled, open-faced flowers with yellow throats, each flower lasting a single day but the colony producing successive blooms over weeks. The flowers are slightly smaller than those of Nemastylus geminiflora but similarly pure blue-violet with yellow center markings, and the plant is significantly more adaptable and self-seeding than the native prairie irises, spreading freely in disturbed and maintained areas of coastal Texas. For Gulf Coast gardeners in zone 9a, calydorea has already naturalized in their region — it is familiar as a spring roadside wildflower — and including it in native prairie and naturalistic garden plantings supports the locally established population of this spring blue. A prolific, low-maintenance, self-sustaining small bulb that, once established, provides years of spring color without any attention.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, setting the rhizome shallowly at or just below the surface; prairie iris grows naturally in open wet savannas and pine flatwoods rather than the deep marsh favored by other Louisiana iris species, so it tolerates a somewhat less saturated garden spot.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, setting the rhizome shallowly with its top at or just below the surface. Prairie iris is the most recently recognized of the Louisiana iris species, native to open, fire-maintained wet savannas and pine flatwoods across the Gulf Coastal Plain from Louisiana to the Florida panhandle, distinguished from its wetland relatives by its smaller, more compact stature and preference for seasonally moist rather than permanently flooded ground. Its blue-violet flowers, carried on branched stalks above narrow sword-shaped leaves, open in mid-spring and draw bumblebees and swallowtails. Because it comes from open, sunny habitat, it tolerates more direct sun than copper or giant blue iris and suits a wet meadow planting or the damp, sunny margin of a rain garden as well as a shadier pond edge.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie lily is native to the limestone prairie soils and rocky hillsides of central and south Texas, where it blooms reliably after summer rain events — the characteristic 'rain lily' flush of flowers appearing 5–7 days after heavy summer rainfall. It is one of the largest-flowered Zephyranthes species, with white to very pale pink, upright, funnel-shaped flowers 3–4 inches across. Heat- and drought-tolerant once established; naturalizes freely in Gulf Coast landscapes.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie lily is the largest-flowered native rain lily of Texas and the central Gulf Coast, producing in summer — typically 5–7 days after heavy rainfall events — large, upright, pure-white to very pale blush-pink, funnel-shaped flowers up to 4 inches across on stems 10–16 inches tall, each flower facing upward and outward with six broad, satiny white tepals of clean elegance. The rain-triggered flowering mechanism is one of the most distinctive behaviors of the Zephyranthes and Cooperia genera: the plants remain dormant through dry periods and flower synchronously with dramatic precision following significant rainfall, creating spectacular mass-blooming events across the central Texas prairies and limestone hills. In garden plantings, a deep summer watering can trigger the same response. The grassy, bright-green leaves emerge before or with the flowers and persist through the growing season. Native from Texas to northern Mexico, it is extraordinarily heat-tolerant and drought-adapted, requiring virtually no supplemental irrigation once established in the Gulf Coast climate where summer rains naturally trigger its bloom cycle. An outstanding, low-maintenance native bulb for zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Overseed into an established stand of native bunchgrass in fall, since seedlings must attach to grass roots as a partial parasite to grow vigorously.
directions: Overseed into an established stand of native bunchgrass in fall, since seedlings must attach to grass roots as a partial parasite to grow vigorously; sowing bare paintbrush seed alone in fertile garden soil will disappoint. Native to calcareous prairies from the Edwards Plateau north into the Cross Timbers, it is longer-lived than the familiar annual Texas Indian paintbrush and blooms in shades from yellow to orange, red, or purple depending on variety. Its tubular flowers are an important early hummingbird and long-tongued bee resource in Hill Country and adjacent Gulf Coast prairie plantings. Keep it in lean, well-drained calcareous soil and resist fertilizing, which favors the host grass over the paintbrush.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or cold-moist stratify 60-90 days before a spring sowing; it resents transplanting once its taproot is established.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained prairie soil, dry-mesic meadow plantings, or gravelly slopes where competition is low, since it establishes a deep taproot early and does not transplant well. In its second year it sends up flat yellow umbels in mid-spring, among the earliest umbellifer blooms available to emerging native bees and small pollinators. As a true prairie relict it tolerates drought and poor soil once established but is intolerant of heavy, wet clay. Let seed heads mature and shatter naturally to maintain a self-sustaining population, since it is a short-lived perennial that relies on some recruitment from seed.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after cold stratification for 30 days, or sow in fall for natural stratification; plants may rebloom in fall in cool climates.
directions: Direct sow cold-stratified seed in early spring in lean, well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; prairie phlox is more drought tolerant and heat tolerant than the commonly planted P. divaricata and grows in dry prairie soils and open woodland edges across the eastern US. The fragrant pink to lavender flower clusters bloom in late spring and attract swallowtail butterflies and native bee species. The downy (pilosa) stems give the plant a soft texture throughout the season. Shear back by one-half after bloom to prevent disease and encourage fresh growth; plants in rich soil or shade are more susceptible to powdery mildew. Excellent combined with native grasses in a dry meadow or prairie planting.

plant_note: Surface-sow the fine seed in fall or early spring on well-drained prairie or savanna soil, pressing it in without covering since light aids germination.
directions: Surface-sow the fine seed in fall or early spring on well-drained prairie or savanna soil, pressing it in without covering since light aids germination. This basal-rosette species sends up branched clusters of small daisy-like yellow flowers in late spring, well ahead of most tallgrass prairie bloomers, making it an important early-season nectar and pollen source for small bees and emerging butterflies. It self-sows modestly and naturalizes well in dry, sandy or gravelly prairie restorations without becoming aggressive. Leave the winter rosettes undisturbed, as they are evergreen and provide early cover in the off-season.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring 2–3 inches deep in full sun in well-drained, rocky to sandy-loam soil in zone 7–10; Prairie Rain Lily is a Texas and northeastern Mexico native bulbous perennial — appearing in masses across limestone grasslands, cedar-oak savannas, and roadside prairies after summer rains — with large, pure-white, powerfully fragrant flowers that open at dusk and stay open through the night, making it an outstanding native plant for moon gardens and evening landscapes.
directions: Plant Cooperia pedunculata bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy-loam soil in full sun; provide a dry period through spring, then allow summer rains (or supplemental soaking) to trigger blooming; avoid overwatering during dormancy as bulbs rot easily in wet winter soils. Prairie Rain Lily is a beloved Texas wildflower that carpets limestone roadsides, ranch grasslands, and cedar-oak savannas with brilliant white after summer rains — sometimes appearing by the thousands seemingly overnight. The genus Cooperia is now often merged into Zephyranthes by modern taxonomists, but the species is distinct in its nocturnal blooming behavior: flowers open fully at dusk, are powerfully sweet-fragrant, pure white, and 2–3 inches wide — perfectly adapted to pollination by sphinx moths and hawk moths that fly at night. A superb choice for naturalistic meadow plantings, moon gardens, and dry-summer landscapes throughout the Texas Hill Country and Gulf Coast. Bulbs naturalize in thin, rocky soil far better than in rich garden beds — excess fertility delays flowering. Divide crowded clumps in late summer after foliage yellows; bulbs can be moved dry during dormancy.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie rose is the only native climbing rose in the Midwest and East and is remarkably adaptable to difficult sites.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie rose is the only native climbing rose of the Midwest and Great Plains, producing clusters of beautiful deep pink, single, 2-inch flowers in early to midsummer on long arching canes that trail or climb through shrubs and fences. The flowers attract native bees including leafcutter bees and mason bees; the red hips persist into winter providing food for mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. Unlike most garden roses, prairie rose requires no spraying, no deadheading, and no special care — once established it is remarkably drought-tolerant and adaptable. It blooms only once in summer (it is not repeat-blooming) but the display is spectacular. The 3-leaflet leaves give it a distinctive character among roses. An excellent native rose for naturalistic gardens, fence lines, and erosion control on slopes.

common_name: Prairie Rose Gentian (Texas Star, Meadow Pink)
plant_note: Direct sow seed on the soil surface in fall in full sun in moist, open, disturbed ground; seedlings overwinter as small rosettes and bloom the following late spring into summer, typical of many Gulf Coast prairie annuals.
directions: Direct sow seed on bare, disturbed soil in fall since seeds need light and cold-season moisture to germinate; plants overwinter as low rosettes and shoot up the following spring in full sun and evenly moist, open ground. Prairie rose gentian is a slender, branching annual wildflower of Gulf Coast prairies, roadsides, and open meadows from Texas through Louisiana, bearing bright pink, five-petaled, star-shaped flowers with a greenish-yellow eye that open through late spring and summer. Bees and small butterflies visit the flowers readily, and plants reseed freely once established, making them a low-maintenance addition to a wildflower meadow or naturalized prairie planting. Because it thrives in the same lean, seasonally moist soils common across the Gulf Coast, it pairs well with other native prairie annuals without needing supplemental fertility.

plant_note: Plant in average garden loam to wet or clay ground in full sun; needs minimal irrigation once established.
directions: Plant in average garden loam to wet or clay ground in full sun; tolerates a wide range of soils and needs minimal irrigation once established. Prairie Sky is prized among switchgrass cultivars for its strongly powder-blue foliage, a color it holds from spring through summer before shifting to soft yellow and then tan in late fall. Its columnar, strictly upright habit resembles the popular cultivar Heavy Metal but grows taller and bluer, sending up airy, dark rusty-red flower panicles above the foliage from late summer into fall that persist as a shimmering seed cloud through winter. Use it in mass plantings, screens, or naturalistic borders where its blue color and vertical form provide strong contrast to green-leaved perennials.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification; or start indoors in late winter with 8–10 weeks of cold moist stratification.
directions: Sow seeds in fall and allow winter cold to naturally stratify them, or cold-stratify indoors for 8–10 weeks before spring sowing; plant in lean, well-drained to dry soil in full sun. The nodding, burgundy-pink flowers in mid-spring are followed by the spectacular feathery, smoke-like seed plumes that give the plant its name and provide ornamental interest for weeks. Prairie smoke is a rugged, drought-tolerant native wildflower that thrives in rocky or sandy soils where more demanding plants struggle. It spreads slowly into a weed-suppressing groundcover in open, sunny areas.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions into dry, rocky or caliche-rich soil in spring; this low prairie native spreads slowly by rhizome once established.
directions: Native to the prairies of Texas and Oklahoma, this low mounding perennial produces small lavender-blue tubular flowers over an extended bloom from spring through fall. It thrives in poor, rocky, or caliche soils where competition is low and rainfall is unreliable, needing almost no supplemental water once established. Its spreading habit makes it a useful groundcover for a hot, dry native bed, and its flowers draw a steady stream of small native bees and butterflies. Trim lightly after a flush of bloom to keep the mound tidy and encourage repeat flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie spiderwort self-sows readily and naturalizes in prairies and open areas. The three violet-blue petals have a distinctive triangle formation typical of all Tradescantia species.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist to well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun to partial shade — prairie spiderwort is a Great Plains native Tradescantia closely related to the more widely grown Ohio spiderwort (T. ohiensis), producing the same distinctive three-petaled violet-blue to pink-purple flowers whose delicate petals last only a single morning before shriveling, but with new buds opening daily over many weeks in spring and early summer. Like all spiderworts, the clear blue-violet flowers are striking when massed, creating a wave of cool color in the spring garden. Prairie spiderwort is generally more compact and drought-tolerant than Ohio spiderwort, reflecting its origin on drier Great Plains prairies. Foliage goes dormant and yellows in midsummer heat — plant with later-emerging perennials to fill in. An excellent native for dry, sunny to partly shaded prairie gardens and informal settings in zones 3–9.

common_name: Prairie Splendor Coneflower (AAS-Winning Compact Seed-Grown Rose-Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Prairie Splendor, an All-America Selections winner, is a compact, seed-grown rose-pink coneflower strain with uniform habit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Prairie Splendor, an All-America Selections winner, bears clear rose-pink single flowers on a compact, uniform, seed-grown plant bred to flower reliably the first year from seed, making it especially economical for filling large beds with consistent coneflower color. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall, attracting bees, butterflies, and goldfinches. Deadhead to prolong bloom or leave seed heads standing for winter bird interest.

common_name: Prairie Sun Rudbeckia (Large Golden Green-Eyed Black-Eyed Susan)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Prairie Sun is an All-America Selections gold medal winner — one of the most vigorous and long-blooming large-flowered Rudbeckia hirta cultivars available.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Prairie Sun is one of the finest large-flowered Rudbeckia hirta cultivars — producing very large (4–5 inch diameter), pure golden-yellow flowers with a distinctive apple-green central disc rather than the dark-brown or black center of most black-eyed Susan cultivars. The unusual lime-green center creates a fundamentally different flower appearance — Prairie Sun is technically a 'green-eyed Susan' rather than black-eyed — with the green disc creating a fresh, unconventional combination that is immediately distinctive in the garden. The very large flower size (4–5 inches compared to the 2–3 inches of standard types) and the green center make Prairie Sun outstanding in cut flower arrangements and mass plantings where the large, bold flowers create maximum visual impact. The pollenless flowers (a practical advantage for cut flower use) and exceptional heat and drought tolerance make Prairie Sun outstanding for Gulf South summer gardens. An All-America Selections gold medal winner recognized for its exceptional landscape performance. Plants bloom prolifically from summer through fall without deadheading — though removing spent flowers extends the season. In zone 9, Prairie Sun is typically grown as a summer annual, though it may self-seed and persist in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes.
directions: Sow seed directly after the last frost, one-half inch deep in warm, well-drained soil. This branching native annual produces many small yellow flowers with reddish-brown centers on graceful stems. It is highly drought-tolerant and thrives on the lean soils of open meadows and restoration plantings. Bees feed on the blooms while finches and other birds harvest the ripe seed in fall.

plant_note: Direct-sow this low, gray-green summer annual after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into lean, dry, disturbed, or rocky soil.
directions: Direct-sow this low, gray-green summer annual after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into lean, dry, disturbed, or rocky soil where it naturally colonizes glades, pastures, and prairie edges. It asks for essentially no care, tolerating poor soil and drought, and will self-sow modestly from year to year once introduced. Its chief garden value is as one of only a handful of documented hosts for the Goatweed Leafwing butterfly, whose caterpillars feed on the small, felted leaves, and its seed is also eaten by quail and dove.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall immediately after ripening; trillium seeds require 18+ months of warm+cold stratification before germination — plants take 5–7 years from seed to first flower. Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade. Rhizome division in late summer is faster.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; prairie trillium is a distinctive sessile trillium (flowers without stems, sitting directly on the leaves) native to the moist, rich bottomland forests, floodplain woodlands, and upland mesic forests of the central US Midwest — from Michigan and Ohio west to Iowa and south to Arkansas. The dark maroon-purple petals and strongly mottled leaves with brownish-green markings (resembling a snake skin) distinguish it from other trilliums. It grows naturally in rich alluvial forest soils and tolerates slightly more open conditions than some woodland trilliums. Like all trilliums, it takes many years from seed to flowering and is legally protected in several states — purchase only nursery-propagated plants from ethical native plant nurseries. Forms slow-spreading colonies over decades.

plant_note: Plant corms immediately after division in late summer or early fall, 3-4 inches deep, in well-drained, calcareous prairie or glade soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike its woodland relatives, prairie trout lily is native to open tallgrass prairie and limestone glades from Texas to Kansas and Missouri and tolerates more sun and drier summer soil.
directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep immediately after division in late summer or early fall in well-drained, calcareous prairie or rocky glade soil in partial shade to full sun. Prairie trout lily is a Great Plains counterpart to the woodland Erythronium species, native to tallgrass prairie remnants and limestone glades from central Texas north through Kansas and Missouri, where its plain green, unmottled to faintly mottled leaves and pale lavender-white, star-shaped flowers appear in very early spring and are held more upright than the nodding blooms of its forest cousins. Because it grows naturally in open, sun-exposed prairie rather than deep shade, it tolerates a drier, better-drained garden spot than most trout lilies, making it a good fit for a native prairie or rock-garden planting rather than a woodland border. Like other trout lilies it goes fully dormant by late spring, so mark the spot and interplant with warm-season prairie grasses or forbs that fill in as it disappears.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, neutral to alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; prairie verbena requires excellent drainage and tolerates no standing water. Self-sows readily to naturalize across open, dry areas.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into very well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — prairie verbena is a sprawling, finely cut-leaved native groundcover of the southern Great Plains and Gulf Coast prairies, producing clusters of bright rose-pink to lavender-pink flowers nearly year-round in warm climates from fall through spring and sporadically through summer. It is one of the most important native nectar plants for low-growing prairie butterflies including the Phaon crescent, bordered patch, and sulfur species. The silvery-green, finely dissected foliage forms an attractive, trailing mat that roots where stems contact soil, spreading to cover rocky slopes, dry banks, and open gravel. It thrives in the alkaline, caliche-heavy, or sandy soils of the southern Gulf Coast that defeat many garden plants. Essentially no supplemental irrigation is needed in adapted soils; good drainage is critical — the plant will not survive in wet or clay soils.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry soil in full sun; prairie verbena spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a dense, low mat and is among the most common native verbenas of Texas roadsides and prairies.
directions: Direct sow into lean, well-drained, dry soil in full sun; prairie verbena forms a low, spreading mat of finely divided, ferny leaves topped almost continuously from spring through fall with rounded clusters of small lavender-purple flowers that draw butterflies in large numbers. It is one of the most common and durable native groundcover wildflowers of the southern Great Plains, coloring roadsides, prairies, and disturbed ground with a long-lasting purple haze through the growing season. Trailing stems root as they spread, quickly filling in bare, sunny ground and tolerating foot traffic and mowing far better than most flowering perennials, which makes it a good choice between stepping stones or as an informal lawn substitute in hot, dry sites. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and needs no supplemental fertilizer, blooming most heavily in lean, unimproved soil.

plant_note: Sow seed outdoors in fall so a natural 60-day cold-moist winter chill breaks dormancy, into well-drained prairie soil in full to part sun.
directions: Sow seed outdoors in fall so a natural 60-day cold-moist winter chill breaks dormancy, into well-drained prairie soil in full to part sun; this deeply lobed, fine-textured violet is markedly more drought-tolerant than woodland violet species. It stays low and compact, making it well suited to short-grass prairie plantings and border edges rather than shaded gardens. Prairie violet is a critical larval host for the increasingly rare Regal Fritillary butterfly, whose restoration in the Midwest depends heavily on reestablishing violet-rich prairie remnants.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring before leafout; cuttings root readily if kept moist and placed in sand or moist potting mix. Direct seed is possible but seeds lose viability within days of ripening and must be sown immediately.
directions: Plant in well-drained to slightly moist, sandy or loamy soil in full sun to light shade; prairie willow is one of the few willows adapted to dry upland sites rather than wetlands, making it valuable for stabilizing dry slopes and prairie edges. The fuzzy silver catkins emerge in earliest spring before the leaves — earlier than most other willows — providing critical pollen and nectar for queen bumblebees and early-emerging native bees. Prairie willow is an important larval host plant for the viceroy butterfly and several species of giant silk moths. The plant forms colonies through root suckering and tolerates fire.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Prayer peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky, succulent-type potting mix; Prayer peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thick, folded, translucent-green leaves are shaped like tiny curved trumpets or canoes, held upright along fleshy stems in a form so distinctive it is instantly recognizable among succulent-leaved peperomias, with a pale window-like stripe running down each folded leaf that lets light filter into the plant's interior. Native to dry rocky slopes in Peru, this fully succulent species tolerates missed waterings far better than soggy soil and is prone to rot if kept constantly moist, making a gritty, fast-draining mix and cautious watering essential. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact, well-formed growth, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, peat-based, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in bright indirect shade; maranta requires consistent moisture, high humidity, and warmth above 60°F. Avoid hard water — use rainwater or allow tap water to sit 24 hours before using to allow chlorine to off-gas.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, peat-based soil in bright indirect shade; the prayer plant is named for its remarkable circadian leaf movement — the broad, oval leaves with their intricate dark green and silver herringbone pattern are flat during the day but fold upward in the evening in a prayer-like posture, then return to horizontal at dawn. This nyctinasty (night-time leaf folding) is especially dramatic in the variety 'Erythroneura,' which has brilliant red veins against velvety dark green with light green feathering — one of the most beautiful leaf patterns of any plant. As an outdoor shade plant in zone 10–12, maranta spreads as a low groundcover under trees and in shaded planting beds. Indoors it thrives in any room with bright indirect light. Keep soil consistently moist and mist frequently or place on a pebble tray with water to maintain humidity.

common_name: Praying Hands Hosta (Narrow Upright Twisted-Leaf Novelty Hosta)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Praying Hands is a distinctive novelty hosta with narrow, upright, twisted leaves that stay folded together along the midrib, resembling hands held in prayer, a striking departure from typical flat hosta foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade. Praying Hands is one of the most distinctive novelty hostas available, its narrow, dark green, gold-margined leaves staying folded together along the center vein rather than opening flat, so each leaf remains upright and twisted in a shape that closely resembles two hands pressed together in prayer. This unusual leaf form gives the plant a strong vertical, sculptural presence quite unlike the typical broad, spreading hosta mound, making it a conversation-piece accent in a shade border or container planting. Lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Its narrow, upright habit takes up relatively little horizontal space compared to standard hostas, making it useful for tight spots where a bolder, spreading hosta would not fit. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

common_name: President Canna (Classic Heirloom Solid Scarlet-Red Canna)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in warm, fertile, moist soil in full sun; President is a classic, widely planted heirloom canna with plain green leaves and large, bold scarlet-red flowers, historically one of the most common garden cannas.
directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in warm, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun. President is a long-cultivated heirloom canna bearing broad, solid green leaves and large, brilliant scarlet-red flowers on sturdy, compact stalks, representing the classic, unfussy garden canna look that anchored countless Southern flower beds for generations before the modern trend toward colorful striped and bronze-leaved cultivars. Its reliable, heavy bloom and tough constitution have kept it in continuous cultivation despite flashier newer introductions. Like other cannas it thrives with generous water and rich soil. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage; in zone 8-10 gardens it can typically be left in the ground with a heavy mulch layer for winter protection.

common_name: President Clay Azalea (Classic Salmon-Orange Southern Indica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; President Clay is a classic Southern Indica azalea long grown in historic Gulf South gardens for its warm salmon-orange bloom color.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, allowing plenty of room for the shrub's mature spread. President Clay is a historic Southern Indica azalea cultivar bearing warm salmon-orange flowers in a heavy spring flush, one of the classic color selections that have anchored Deep South azalea gardens and public azalea trails for generations. The large, vigorous evergreen shrub provides dense year-round structure and a spectacular seasonal display, making it a strong choice for large borders, screens, and historic garden restorations. Water deeply while establishing and during dry periods, and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's flower buds form soon after bloom ends.

common_name: President Hedley Louisiana Iris (Historic Reddish-Purple Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. President Hedley is a historically significant Louisiana iris cultivar from the early era of Louisiana iris breeding, producing rich reddish-purple flowers that helped establish the modern range of colors available in cultivated Louisiana iris hybrids. Like other Louisiana iris selections it performs best in reliably moist to wet soil and is an excellent choice for pond margins, ditch banks, and rain gardens where standing water is common after rain. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to keep the planting vigorous.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; President is an old, vigorous tropical hibiscus cultivar grown for its large, reliable red single flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. President bears large, single, classic red flowers with a prominent central staminal column, on a vigorous, fast-growing shrub that has remained a garden favorite for generations thanks to its dependable, near-continuous bloom through the warm season. Its bold, traditional red is a good anchor color for a mixed tropical hibiscus planting, especially alongside the more novel bicolor and pastel cultivars that have become common in recent decades. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season.

common_name: Pretoria Canna (Yellow-Green Striped Foliage Orange Canna)
plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Pretoria is a classic large-leaved canna cultivar with bold yellow-and-green striped foliage and vivid orange flowers, one of the longest-cultivated striped-leaf canna varieties.
directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun. Pretoria is a classic, long-cultivated canna prized for large, bold, paddle-shaped leaves striped lengthwise in bright yellow and green, topped with vivid orange summer flowers, similar in overall effect to the more recently introduced Bengal Tiger but with a somewhat larger, more substantial leaf. Its bold tropical foliage makes it a striking specimen or focal point even when not in bloom, useful for anchoring a tropical-themed border or providing a backdrop for smaller plants. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

common_name: Pretty Much Picasso Petunia (Chartreuse-Edged Purple Petunia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pretty Much Picasso's vigorous, spreading habit fills containers and hanging baskets quickly and needs little deadheading to keep flowering.
directions: Pretty Much Picasso carries hot magenta-purple flowers irregularly bordered in bright chartreuse-green, a bold, artistic hand-painted look that made it one of the most talked-about petunia introductions of its release year and remains a standout in mixed containers. The vigorous, trailing, self-cleaning habit spreads readily over pot edges and needs no deadheading to keep producing new flowers through the season. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, fertilize regularly to sustain its rapid growth, and give it a midsummer trim if the trailing stems become overly long or sparse in the heat, which prompts fresh, bushier regrowth and renewed bloom.

common_name: Pretty Shooting Star / Western Shooting Star
plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall onto the surface of a moist, prepared bed; cold stratification over winter is required to break dormancy, and seedlings will emerge in early spring.
directions: Scatter fresh seed in fall onto the surface of a moist, well-prepared bed in partial shade, pressing seed lightly into the soil without covering, as light and cold together aid germination. Winter temperatures provide the stratification needed to break dormancy, and rosettes will emerge the following spring. Keep the planting area consistently moist through the brief spring growing window, then allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally as the plant enters its characteristic summer dormancy. Once colonies are established, Pretty Shooting Star will self-sow into surrounding areas, gradually spreading into a naturalized drift.

common_name: Preziosa Mountain Hydrangea (Mophead Aging Pink to Deep Rose)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Preziosa is a compact mountain hydrangea whose mophead blooms age from pink to a deep rose-red.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Preziosa is a compact mountain hydrangea, a smaller, more shade- and heat-tolerant relative of bigleaf hydrangea from the mountains of Korea and Japan, bearing rounded mophead flower clusters that open pink and deepen through the season to a rich rose-red, a color progression more dramatic than most macrophylla cultivars show. Its modest size makes it more practical than bigleaf hydrangea in smaller gardens, and it flowers reliably even in warm-climate gardens where H. macrophylla can struggle. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 8–11; Prickly Cycad is one of the most widely cultivated and shade-tolerant of the Encephalartos cycads, native to the coastal forests and forest margins of eastern South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape) — producing large, dark-green, glossy fronds with spiny leaflets in a lush, tropical-looking crown, and growing well in considerably more shade than most cycads.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; Encephalartos villosus prefers more moisture and shade than most Encephalartos species — mulch the root zone and water moderately to maintain the moist, humus-rich forest-floor conditions of its native coastal forest habitat. Encephalartos villosus (Prickly Cycad or Villous Cycad) is one of the most horticulturally popular and widely cultivated Encephalartos species, native to the dense, subtropical coastal forests and forest margins of eastern South Africa from the Eastern Cape north through KwaZulu-Natal. Unlike many Encephalartos species adapted to open, dry, sunny habitats, E. villosus naturally inhabits shaded forest understory positions — making it one of the most shade-tolerant of all Encephalartos species and an excellent choice for partially shaded garden positions where many cycads would struggle. The fronds are large (up to 2 meters long), arching, dark-green, glossy, and set with numerous spiny leaflets that give the plant a bold, tropical texture. The common name 'Prickly Cycad' refers to these spiny leaflets. Plants can grow as acaulescent (nearly stemless) individuals for many years before developing a trunk. Encephalartos villosus is CITES Appendix II listed; only purchase nursery-propagated plants from reputable suppliers and never remove plants from the wild. All cycad parts are toxic.

plant_note: Plant cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; prickly phlox is a native California chaparral shrub adapted to hot, dry, rocky slopes and sandy coastal scrub, tolerating drought and heat once established. Avoid excess water or clay soil.
directions: Plant cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; prickly phlox is a native California shrub of chaparral, coastal sage scrub, and dry rocky slopes in the California Ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills, producing densely needle-like, prickly foliage (much sharper and more aggressive than any true phlox) and profuse, bright rose-pink, five-petaled flowers that closely resemble garden phlox in spring. The combination of phlox-like flowers and needle-prickle foliage is unmistakable. Despite belonging to the same family (Polemoniaceae) as true phlox, it is in a different genus. A spectacular, California-native flowering shrub for dry, hot, well-drained gardens in zones 8–10, producing one of the showiest spring flower displays of any California native shrub. Excellent for slope stabilization, xeriscape, and fire-resistant California native gardens. Hummingbirds and native bees visit the flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; pricklyleaf dogweed thrives on poor, dry, caliche soils and needs no fertilizer or supplemental watering once established.
directions: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; pricklyleaf dogweed thrives on poor, dry, caliche soils and needs no fertilizer or supplemental watering once established. Finely divided, aromatic, thread-like foliage forms a low, dense mound studded with small, bright yellow, daisy-like flowers over an unusually long season from spring through fall, drawing small native bees and butterflies to even the driest, rockiest corner of a garden. Native to limestone outcrops, caliche flats, and dry plains across Texas and the southwestern United States, it is a tough, long-lived, low-maintenance filler for rock gardens, gravel gardens, and xeriscape borders. Established plants need no irrigation beyond natural rainfall and resent rich, moist, or heavily mulched soil.

common_name: Pride of Augusta Carolina Jessamine (Double-Flowered Evergreen Vine)
plant_note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a trellis, arbor, or fence; Pride of Augusta blooms most heavily in full sun but tolerates partial shade with somewhat reduced flowering.
directions: Plant against a sturdy trellis, arbor, mailbox post, or fence in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and train young vines onto their support until the twining stems take hold on their own. Pride of Augusta is a heritage double-flowered selection of Carolina jessamine, the southeastern native evergreen vine, bearing fully double, ruffled, deep golden-yellow flowers with a sweet fragrance that smother the vine in late winter to early spring, a showier and longer-lasting display than the single flowers of the standard species. Its glossy, twining evergreen foliage provides year-round cover for a fence or arbor even when not in bloom, and once established the vine is highly drought-tolerant and easy-care, asking for little beyond an annual light pruning after flowering to control size and shape. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where livestock or small children might be tempted to chew the foliage or flowers.

common_name: Pride of Barbados (Red Bird of Paradise)
plant_note: Direct sow scarified or nicked seed 1 inch deep after the last frost, or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier; pride of barbados germinates rapidly after scarification in warm soil. The plant dies back to the ground after hard freezes in zone 8 but regrows vigorously from established roots and can bloom within the first season from seed.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — sandy, rocky, and even alkaline soils are acceptable; pride of barbados is one of the most spectacular flowering tropical shrubs for hot, dry, difficult sites, producing large showy clusters of exotic-looking flowers in brilliant shades of red-orange with long protruding red stamens (resembling a bird of paradise arrangement) over finely pinnate, lacy green foliage from summer through frost. It is exceptionally heat, drought, and poor-soil tolerant and blooms most prolifically in the hottest part of the summer when many other plants flag. The entire shrub is typically killed to the ground by hard freezes in zone 8 but regrows robustly each spring, often re-blooming within 60 days. In zone 9–12 it is woody and persistent, reaching shrub-tree size. Seeds germinate quickly after the hard seed coat is nicked or soaked. All parts are toxic if ingested. An outstanding butterfly and hummingbird plant for xeric, full-sun gardens.

common_name: Pride of Burma (Orchid Tree of Burma, Queen of Flowering Trees)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in partial shade with consistently moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Pride of Burma is strictly a zone 10-11 tree and requires warm, humid, protected conditions to thrive. It performs best in partial shade and protection from strong winds, which damage its unusually large, pendant new leaves. The new foliage emerges in a remarkable coppery-red to orange-pink pendulous cascade before stiffening and turning green. This species is considered among the most demanding of tropical ornamental trees to cultivate well outside its native habitat.
directions: Plant in partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Pride of Burma is one of the most demanding of all ornamental trees and requires the warm, humid, protected conditions of its native Myanmar habitat — consistently high humidity, warm temperatures year-round, shelter from drying winds, and fertile moist soil. Amherstia nobilis is an evergreen tree from the tropical forests of Myanmar (Burma), monotypic in its genus (the only species of Amherstia), and considered by many botanists and horticulturists to be the single most beautiful flowering tree in the world — a claim contested only by a handful of other extraordinary trees. The tree produces its flowers in pendant racemes hanging from the branch tips: each raceme carries 15–30 individual flowers of extraordinary complexity — vivid scarlet-red sepals, yellow-tipped petals, scarlet wings, arranged in a structure resembling an ornate tropical orchid flower in brilliant red and yellow. Each flower is 3–4 inches long; a single raceme in full development is among the most spectacular botanical displays in existence. The new leaves that emerge before the flowers are equally remarkable: they hang in long, copper-red to orange-pink, perfectly limp pendant tassels up to 3 feet long before gradually stiffening and turning green as they mature. Named in honor of Lady Amherst, wife of the Governor-General of India, who first preserved specimens for Western science in 1826.

common_name: Pride of Houston Yaupon Holly (Upright Berry-Producing Native Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pride of Houston is an upright, female selection of native yaupon holly that sets heavy crops of red berries and can be grown as a large shrub or limbed into a small multi-trunked tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Pride of Houston is an upright, densely branched selection of native yaupon holly that, unlike the compact dwarf yaupon forms, is a female clone that produces abundant bright red berries prized for winter interest and wildlife value, holding well into the colder months. It grows into a substantial large shrub or can be pruned up into a small evergreen tree for use as a screen or specimen, and like all yaupon selections it is extremely tolerant of heat, drought, wind, salt spray, and poor soil, making it one of the toughest Gulf Coast landscape plants available. It needs only occasional shaping and no supplemental water once established.

common_name: Pride of Mobile Azalea (Deep Watermelon-Pink Southern Indica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pride of Mobile is a classic Southern Indica azalea named for the historic Mobile, Alabama azalea trail gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with room for the shrub to reach full size. Pride of Mobile is a historic Southern Indica azalea associated with the famed azalea trail gardens of Mobile, Alabama, prized for its deep, saturated watermelon-pink flowers produced in a spectacular spring flush on a large, vigorous evergreen shrub. Like other Southern Indica cultivars it has proven itself over generations of Gulf Coast gardens for reliability, size, and sheer bloom impact, making it a striking specimen or hedge plant in large landscapes. Water deeply during establishment and dry periods, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next spring set soon after bloom ends.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pride of Rochester grows considerably taller and more upright than dwarf deutzia cultivars and needs room to reach its full arching, vase-shaped mature size.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pride of Rochester grows considerably taller and more upright than dwarf deutzia cultivars and needs room to reach its full arching, vase-shaped mature size. This heirloom nineteenth-century deutzia cultivar produces an abundance of double, pale pink-tinged white flowers packed densely along arching branches in late spring, one of the showiest bloom displays among old-fashioned flowering shrubs, followed by peeling, cinnamon-colored bark that adds winter interest. Its large size and old-fashioned charm make it a good choice for the back of a shrub border, an informal flowering hedge, or a specimen where its fountain-like form and heavy spring bloom can be fully appreciated. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes to the ground right after flowering each year to keep the shrub vigorous and well-shaped over time.

common_name: Pride of Summerville Azalea (Deep Rose-Pink Charleston-Area Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pride of Summerville is a Southern Indica azalea associated with the historic azalea gardens around Summerville and Charleston, South Carolina.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, allowing plenty of room for the mature shrub's spread. Pride of Summerville is a historic Southern Indica azalea long associated with the famed heirloom azalea gardens around Summerville and Charleston, South Carolina, prized for its deep, rich rose-pink flowers produced in an overwhelming spring flush on a large, vigorous evergreen shrub. Like other Southern Indica cultivars it provides substantial year-round structure and a spectacular seasonal display, making it a strong choice for large borders, screens, and historic garden restorations. Water deeply during establishment and dry periods, and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's flower buds form soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Primal Scream Daylily (Award-Winning Vivid Orange-Red Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Primal Scream is an award-winning daylily cultivar known for large, intensely saturated orange-red flowers with a darker eye zone, blooming heavily over a long midsummer season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Primal Scream is a widely acclaimed daylily cultivar bearing large, ruffled, intensely saturated orange-red flowers accented by a darker red eye zone and a bright yellow-green throat, a bold color combination that reads vividly even from a distance. It received the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal, the organization's highest honor, in recognition of its outstanding garden performance, vigorous growth, and heavy, reliable bloom production over a long midsummer season. The strong, well-branched scapes hold plenty of buds for an extended flowering display, and the plant multiplies steadily into a robust, floriferous clump. Like other daylilies it is easy to grow in average soil with routine watering, tolerating heat and a range of soil conditions well. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Primo Black Pearl Heuchera (Large Near-Black Glossy Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Primo Black Pearl is part of a heuchera breeding line selected for unusually large, substantial leaves and vigorous garden performance.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; good drainage combined with steady moisture keeps the crown from rotting while preventing the plant from drying out in summer heat. Primo Black Pearl produces unusually large, glossy, deeply lobed leaves in a rich near-black purple, part of a Primo breeding line selected for bigger, more substantial foliage and sturdier garden performance than many older, smaller-leaved heuchera cultivars. Its bold scale makes a strong dark accent in mixed shade plantings, especially paired with chartreuse or silver companions for contrast. Small pale flower spikes appear above the foliage in late spring but are secondary to the season-long leaf color and texture. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent the crown from becoming woody and less productive.

plant_note: Surface sow seed on moistened starting mix without covering — primrose seed needs light to germinate and germinates best below 65°F; start 10–12 weeks before last frost or in late summer for fall planting.
directions: Grow in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; primrose blooms in late winter or early spring and struggles in climates with hot, dry summers, where it benefits from deeper shade and consistent moisture. Surface sow seed at 55–60°F and provide strong light to prevent damping off; seedlings are tiny and slow-growing in early stages. In mild climates plants are nearly evergreen; in colder zones they die back and re-emerge in early spring. Divide established clumps every 2–3 years immediately after flowering to maintain vigor and prevent die-out in the center.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; primrose jasmine is semi-evergreen in mild climates and cascades attractively over a wall or bank.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; primrose jasmine is semi-evergreen in mild climates and cascades attractively over a wall or bank. Bright, semi-double, pale yellow flowers resembling small primroses open along arching green stems in late winter and early spring, larger and showier than the flowers of winter jasmine though sharing that relative's lack of fragrance and cascading, wall-draping growth habit. Its glossy, semi-evergreen foliage and long, arching canes make it a good choice for softening a retaining wall, bank, or trellis in mild-winter climates, providing an early, cheerful splash of yellow color when little else is blooming. Prune immediately after flowering to control size and shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and it tolerates hard pruning to rejuvenate an overgrown planting.

common_name: Primrose Lady Marigold (AAS-Winning Fully Double Primrose-Yellow)
plant_note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or sow directly once soil warms; Primrose Lady, an AAS winner, bears fully double, 3-inch primrose-yellow blooms on 20-inch plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors for a head start or sow directly after frost danger passes, barely covering them. Primrose Lady, an All-America Selections winner, bears large, fully double, soft primrose-yellow blooms up to three inches across on sturdy, uniform 20-inch plants, a gentler, paler yellow than the deep golds and oranges typical of many African marigolds. Plant in full sun where the strong scent helps deter garden pests, making it a classic vegetable-garden companion. Deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming all summer and pinch young plants to encourage branching.

plant_note: Plant container-grown cycads in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Prince Sago tolerates more cold and grows notably faster than the common sago palm, but still needs protection from hard freezes when young.
directions: Plant container-grown cycads in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Prince Sago tolerates more cold and grows notably faster than the common sago palm, but still needs protection from hard freezes when young. Closely related to and often confused with the ubiquitous sago palm (Cycas revoluta), this Taiwanese cycad grows considerably faster and develops a taller, more slender trunk with a fuller, more graceful crown of glossy, dark green, feathery fronds, making it an increasingly popular alternative where a bigger, quicker-growing cycad specimen is wanted. Like all cycads it is an ancient, primitive plant lineage predating flowering plants, tolerant of poor soil and drought once established, and slow enough overall that a young specimen still represents a significant long-term investment despite its faster relative growth rate. Water sparingly once established, protect young plants from hard freezes with covering during cold snaps, and avoid overwatering, which is the most common cause of root and stem rot in cycads.

common_name: Prince Tut Papyrus (Medium Dwarf Egyptian Papyrus)
plant_note: Grow in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy garden soil so the crown and lower stems sit an inch or two underwater at the pond's edge, or in consistently saturated soil; Prince Tut is a medium-sized dwarf papyrus, taller than Baby Tut but more compact than King Tut, well suited to a mid-sized container water garden.
directions: Set potted divisions into a submerged aquatic container of heavy garden soil so the crown and lower stems sit an inch or two underwater along the pond's edge, or grow it in a large container of constantly saturated soil kept in a saucer of water. Prince Tut is a mid-sized dwarf selection of Egyptian papyrus, taller and fuller than the very compact Baby Tut but noticeably more manageable than full-sized King Tut, forming a dense clump of slender, leafless stems topped with fine, mop-like tufts of thread-like bracts that sway in the breeze. It brings strong vertical, textural interest to a water garden or bog planting and works equally well in a large mixed container as a dramatic thriller element, provided its roots stay constantly wet. Outside its hardy range it is grown as a warm-season annual or brought indoors and kept in a water-filled saucer over winter as a houseplant.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Prince of Orange philodendron is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no support or moss pole.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Prince of Orange philodendron is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no support or moss pole. New leaves emerge a vivid orange-red and pass through peach and yellow-green tones as they mature to deep glossy green, so a single healthy plant displays several leaf colors at once in an eye-catching, ever-changing progression. Its neat, upright, non-vining rosette habit keeps it compact and tidy on a shelf, desk, or tabletop without the sprawl of climbing philodendrons, making it a popular low-maintenance choice for smaller spaces. Provide bright indirect light for the most vivid new-leaf color, and allow the top inch of potting mix to dry between waterings.

common_name: Princess Alexandra of Kent Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Princess Alexandra of Kent's fragrance intensifies as each bloom ages, so established, well-fed plants tend to be the most fragrant.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2007, Princess Alexandra of Kent produces rich, pure pink, cupped rosette flowers with a fresh tea fragrance that grows stronger as each bloom matures, on a vigorous, healthy, well-branched shrub with glossy, disease-resistant foliage. It is regarded as one of David Austin's more robust, easy-care introductions, tolerating heat and humidity well, and it repeat-blooms generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.
