common_name: Princess Flower (Glory Bush, Purple Glory Tree, Brazilian Spider Flower)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), organic-matter-rich soil; Tibouchina strongly prefers well-drained soil and suffers from root rot in waterlogged conditions. In zone 9–10, plants are perennial shrubs that grow to 8–15 feet; they are frost-sensitive and benefit from a protected south- or east-facing microclimate in the cooler end of zone 9. Hard frosts kill the above-ground portion; plants often regenerate from the root crown in zone 9a.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic, organically rich soil; water consistently but ensure excellent drainage, as Tibouchina is intolerant of wet feet. Princess flower (Tibouchina urvilleana) is one of the most magnificent flowering shrubs for Gulf South and tropical gardens — a native of southern Brazil that produces enormous (3–4 inch), five-petaled, royal-purple flowers of a saturated, jewel-toned violet-purple color rarely found in any other woody plant. The flowers are borne singly or in small clusters at the branch tips continuously from summer through fall, with the heaviest bloom often in late summer and early fall; the large, soft, velvety leaves with their strongly ribbed texture add tactile and visual interest even when not in flower. Plants grow 4–15 feet depending on frost exposure and cultural conditions — in frost-free climates Tibouchina becomes a large shrub or small tree; in zone 9 where hard freezes occur, plants die back to the crown in cold winters and return as smaller shrubs each spring. The rich purple flower color pairs exceptionally well with golden or orange flowering plants, bougainvillea, and tropical foliage plants; Tibouchina is frequently used as a focal-point specimen shrub in Gulf Coast landscapes and performs well in large containers (12+ gallon) where it can be moved to frost protection in winter. Slightly acid soil (pH 5.5–6.5) with added organic matter is important for sustained health and heavy flowering — alkaline soil causes interveinal chlorosis.

common_name: Princess Margaret Rose Gladiolus (Fiery Mixed Red-Orange-Yellow)
plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season. Princess Margaret Rose bears a fiery mix of red, orange, and yellow in closely set ruffled florets.
directions: Princess Margaret Rose bears a fiery, warm blend of red, orange, and yellow tones within closely packed, ruffled florets, one of the most vividly multicolored gladiolus cultivars available, standing out strongly in a mixed cutting garden. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; princess tree grows extremely fast (up to 15 feet per year) and is invasive in the eastern US — listed as invasive in many states. Plant only in contained situations or where it can be managed; do not plant near natural areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, with caution regarding invasive potential; princess tree is a Chinese ornamental tree that has become invasive across the eastern and southern United States, spreading prodigiously by wind-dispersed seeds into disturbed habitats, roadsides, riverbanks, and forest margins. The spring flower display is extraordinary — large, erect panicles of lavender-purple, foxglove-shaped flowers bloom in April before the very large, velvety, heart-shaped leaves emerge, creating a spectacular early spring display. The wood is prized in Japan as the finest, lightest, most resonant wood for musical instruments and traditional craft; female dolls and furniture are traditionally made from paulownia wood. Despite its beauty, plant responsibly — avoid locations near natural areas and never plant where it could escape cultivation into native habitats.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Princeton was selected long before Dutch elm disease became widespread, purely for form and vigor, and only later proved to carry unusually strong disease tolerance, making it one of the most widely planted elm replacements today.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing generous room for the tree's wide, arching, classic vase-shaped canopy to develop. Princeton is a selection of American elm originally chosen in the 1920s for its fast growth, dense glossy foliage, and handsome symmetrical form, only to later prove one of the most Dutch-elm-disease-tolerant American elm selections available, which has made it the standard replacement elm for streets, parks, and campuses across much of the country. It restores the soaring, cathedral-like street-tree silhouette that made American elm so beloved before the disease devastated the species, while resisting infection far better than seedling-grown trees. Water deeply during establishment, provide good air circulation and avoid wounding the bark, since even resistant cultivars can occasionally succumb under heavy disease pressure, and prune to maintain a strong central structure while the young tree is developing its canopy.

common_name: Princeton Sentry Ginkgo (Narrow Columnar Seedless Male Ginkgo)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Princeton Sentry is a grafted male clone selected specifically for a narrow, upright form and reliable seedlessness, making it a popular street and formal landscape tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; ginkgo tolerates urban conditions, air pollution, and compacted soil better than almost any other large landscape tree, making it a favorite for street and parking-lot plantings. Princeton Sentry is a male ginkgo selection prized for a distinctly narrow, upright, columnar form that fits streets and tight urban spaces where a full-spreading ginkgo would be impractical, while still developing the species' brilliant, uniform golden-yellow fall color that drops in a dramatic, near-simultaneous leaf fall. As a male clone it never produces the malodorous, messy fruit of female ginkgo trees, avoiding the notorious smell and slip hazard those seeds cause on walkways. Slow-growing and exceptionally long-lived, ginkgo is essentially pest- and disease-free once established, needing only a deep, infrequent watering during extended drought and no routine maintenance beyond structural pruning while young to establish a strong central leader.

common_name: Prinses Irene Tulip (Orange with Purple Flame Triumph Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Prinses Irene is a mid-season Triumph tulip valued for its unusual smoky orange-and-purple coloring.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Prinses Irene bears warm orange petals brushed with a purple-violet flame running up each petal from the base, an unusual smoky color combination that pairs beautifully with dark tulips, wallflowers, and other early-to-mid spring companions. Its sturdy, medium-height stems and compact habit make it a reliable performer in both garden beds and containers, blooming in mid-spring. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season.
directions: Priscilla is a ruffled gladiolus with creamy white petals edged in soft pink and a yellow throat, a fragrant heirloom-style bicolor that has remained popular for cutting since its introduction. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall, since Priscilla is not reliably winter hardy outside zone 8 and warmer.

common_name: Prism Sunshine Petunia (Clear Yellow Grandiflora Petunia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Prism Sunshine is an AAS-winning grandiflora petunia noted for unusually clear, weather-resistant yellow color.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Prism Sunshine bears large, clear, buttery-yellow grandiflora blooms that hold their color and form better in rain and heat than most earlier yellow petunias, a trait that earned it All-America Selections recognition when introduced. Its bright, cheerful color works well in mixed plantings with purples and blues, providing strong contrast without the harshness of orange or red. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, and shear back by half in midsummer if plants become leggy, which encourages fresh, bushy regrowth.

common_name: ProCut Bicolor Sunflower (Single-Stem Red-and-Gold Cut Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is above 60°F, succession sowing every 1-2 weeks for staggered harvests since the whole planting blooms together.
directions: Plant on close 6-9 inch spacing in full sun; like other members of the ProCut series, Bicolor puts its energy into a single strong stem and one flower rather than branching. Its petals open deep red at the base and shade to gold at the tips, giving each bloom a two-toned, painterly look that stands out among the mostly solid-color sunflowers used in bouquets. The pollen-free flowers won't shed onto tablecloths or clothing, and uniform stem height and bloom timing make the crop easy to plan for market bunches. Harvest when petals have just begun to unfurl but the center disk is still tight, and cut in the cool morning for the best vase life.

common_name: ProCut Orange Sunflower (Single-Stem Golden-Orange Cut Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is above 60°F, and repeat sowings every 1-2 weeks through midsummer for a continuous cut-flower supply.
directions: Sow seeds 0.5 inch deep on tight 6-9 inch spacing in full sun so plants channel all their growth into a single unbranched stem topped with one flower. ProCut Orange is the vivid golden-orange member of the industry-standard ProCut single-stem series, distinguished by a warmer, deeper hue than the yellow and lemon shades in the line, on a plant that flowers uniformly and all at once about 55-65 days after sowing. Because the flowers are pollen-free, they hold up well in mixed bouquets without dropping pollen on fabric or other blooms. Stake or support plantings in exposed sites, and harvest as petals just begin to unfurl for the longest vase life.

common_name: ProCut Red Sunflower (Single-Stem Deep Red Cut Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is above 60°F; for a continuous cut-flower harvest, sow a new short row every 1-2 weeks through midsummer, since ProCut Red flowers all at once rather than over an extended period.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in full sun and space plants closely, 6-9 inches apart, since ProCut Red is bred as a true single-stem variety that puts all its energy into one flower on one straight, unbranched stem rather than producing side shoots. Part of the industry-standard ProCut cut-flower series, ProCut Red bears deep mahogany-red petals around a dark center on strong, uniform stems, and its pollen-free flowers won't drop pollen and stain fabric or tablecloths, a key trait for cut-flower use. Because plants bloom together rather than over a stretched-out season, succession sowing every one to two weeks through midsummer is the way to keep a steady supply of stems coming for arrangements. Harvest when petals have just begun to unfurl but the central disk is still tight for the longest vase life, and provide support or a single stake in windy sites to keep the tall, top-heavy stems from bending.

common_name: ProCut Sunflower (Industry-Standard Single-Stem Cut Flower Series)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; for succession harvests, sow every 1-2 weeks through summer. ProCut is the industry-standard commercial cut-flower sunflower series, bred as single-stem, pollen-free, uniform-height plants specifically for high-volume, high-quality cut-flower production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; grow on a tight spacing of 6-9 inches, since ProCut is bred as a true single-stem variety that puts all its energy into one large flower on one straight stem rather than branching. ProCut is the benchmark commercial cut-flower sunflower series used by professional flower farms worldwide, prized for exceptional uniformity in height, bloom timing, and flower size, along with pollen-free flowers that make it ideal for arrangements and bouquets without dropping pollen on fabric or furniture. The series is available in multiple colors including gold, lemon, bicolor, and red tones, all sharing the same single-stem habit and reliable, predictable performance that makes succession planting for continuous harvest straightforward. Because each plant produces only one flower, close spacing maximizes stems per square foot, and because there is no branching, ProCut plantings are typically harvested all at once about 55-65 days after sowing rather than picked over an extended period. Harvest when the petals have just begun to unfurl but the center disk is still tight, for the longest vase life.

common_name: Professor Anton Kippenberg Aster (Compact Semi-Double Lavender-Blue New York Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Professor Anton Kippenberg is a compact New York Aster with semi-double lavender-blue flowers, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike many drought-tolerant native asters, New York Aster cultivars perform best with consistent moisture. Professor Anton Kippenberg is a compact, long-cultivated selection bearing masses of semi-double, lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisies in early to mid fall, its dwarf habit and reliable form having earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit over many decades of garden use. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and reduce the powdery mildew that can affect crowded New York Aster plantings, and pinch stems back by a third in early summer for a bushier, more floriferous plant.

common_name: Professor Barnard Crimson Flag Lily (Deep Carmine-Red Hesperantha)
plant_note: Divide and plant rhizomes in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Professor Barnard is a richly colored crimson flag lily cultivar, bearing deep carmine-red, star-shaped flowers on wiry stems well into autumn, later in the season than many perennials are still blooming. It forms grassy, evergreen-in-mild-climates clumps that spread steadily where soil stays reliably moist, making it well suited to pond margins, stream banks, or rain garden edges. Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering. Its intense red coloring is deeper and more saturated than the pinks common in the species, making it a striking late-season accent among ornamental grasses or ferns.

common_name: Professor Ike Louisiana Iris (Historic Red Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Professor Ike is one of the historic named Louisiana iris cultivars still grown for its rich red flowers, which helped define red as one of the classic color classes within this group of Gulf South native iris. It is a vigorous, easy-to-grow heirloom well suited to naturalizing along a pond edge or in a consistently damp border. Keep the soil evenly moist through spring bloom and the rest of the growing season, feed lightly in early spring, and divide crowded clumps every four to five years in late summer to keep the clump vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Professor Sargent Camellia (Prof. Sargent Japanese Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Professor Sargent is a cold-hardy japonica camellia that blooms January–March in zone 9 — one of few flowering shrubs providing color in midwinter.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Professor Charles S. Sargent is one of the most reliably cold-hardy and long-lived Japanese camellia cultivars — a classic selection named after the founder of Harvard's Arnold Arboretum, with dark crimson-red, full peony-form flowers produced from January through March in zone 9, providing brilliant color in the depths of winter when little else is in bloom. The full peony-form flowers are large (3–4 inches), with irregular layers of ruffled, petals that give each bloom a luxuriously full, dense appearance. The plant is a strong grower reaching 8–12 feet tall with a dense, pyramidal to oval habit and outstanding glossy, dark-green foliage. Professor Sargent is considered one of the most reliably cold-hardy japonicas — surviving to zone 7 reliably and even zone 6b with protection — which made it the standard japonica for northern camellia growers for much of the 20th century. In zone 9 it thrives and produces heavy bloom loads. Japonicas bloom on old wood — never prune in winter or spring, only prune lightly immediately after bloom if needed. The midwinter bloom is vulnerable to hard freezes below 20°F that can brown open flowers.

common_name: Professor Tsai Camellia (Wavy-Petaled Rose-Pink Reticulata Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Professor Tsai bears semi-double to loose peony-form blooms with distinctively wavy petals.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind. Professor Tsai bears rose-pink, semi-double to loose peony-form blooms with irregular, wavy petal edges that give the flower a slightly ruffled, informal look on an upright shrub with the bold, leathery foliage typical of Camellia reticulata. It flowers in mid-to-late winter into spring, growing more openly and slowly than japonica camellias. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Profusion Beautyberry flowers on new wood; cut plants back hard to 12–18 inches in late winter to promote maximum new growth and fruit production. Without this annual rejuvenation pruning, plants become open and leggy. The spectacular violet-purple berry clusters — tightly packed in rings along the stems — appear September–November when most other shrubs have finished fruiting. The berries persist after leaf drop, showing most dramatically against bare winter stems. Berries attract bluebirds, robins, and cedar waxwings.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Profusion Beautyberry is adaptable to a range of light conditions and performs well in the partial shade typical of zone 9 landscapes under the filtered canopy of high-branched trees; Profusion is a cultivar of Chinese Beautyberry (Callicarpa bodinieri), producing one of the most spectacular and unusual fall fruiting displays of any landscape shrub — clusters of intensely violet-purple to magenta berries packed tightly in whorls along the length of the arching stems in September through November. The color of the berries is genuinely unusual — a saturated, electric, jewel-like violet-purple that has no equivalent among common native berrying shrubs, creating a fall display that stops observers who are unfamiliar with the plant. Profusion was selected for particularly heavy berry production compared to the straight species, bearing abundant clusters on vigorous, arching stems that achieve maximum visual impact in full fruit. The fall berry display works well in combination with the native American Beautyberry (Callicarpa americana), whose berries are a slightly different, more pink-magenta shade — the two species together providing a visual study in the range of violet-purple available within the Callicarpa genus. As a wildlife plant, beautyberry berries are consumed by at least 40 bird species across the US, making it a high-value habitat shrub for landscape designs focused on bird support.

common_name: Profusion Double Deep Salmon Zinnia (AAS-Winning Fully Double Heat-Tolerant Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost into full sun; this fully double Profusion selection blooms nonstop from early summer through frost with the series' signature resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep after the last frost in full sun, or set out transplants; the compact, mounded plants need no staking and bloom continuously without deadheading. Profusion Double Deep Salmon is an AAS Winner in the interspecific Profusion series, bred to add fully double, ruffled, rose-like blooms in a warm deep salmon-orange to the line's signature disease resistance and weather toughness, a texture previously available only in the series' single- and semi-double-flowered members. It shares the same exceptional heat, humidity, and drought tolerance and strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot that make the Profusion series far more reliable than older tall zinnia varieties through a hot, humid Gulf South summer. Its dense, self-cleaning habit and nonstop bloom suit it well to beds, borders, and containers with minimal upkeep beyond occasional light feeding.

common_name: Profusion Orange Zinnia (AAS-Winning Disease-Resistant Heat-Proof Single Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is consistently warm (70°F+) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Profusion Orange was bred specifically to resist the powdery mildew that typically devastates standard large-flower zinnias (Z. elegans) in Gulf South summer humidity — plant it where standard zinnias have failed.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Profusion Orange is an All-America Selections winner — part of the Profusion zinnia series developed as a breakthrough in zinnia breeding for humid, heat-stressed climates where standard large-flowered zinnias (Zinnia elegans) historically succumb to powdery mildew and plant decline by midsummer. The Profusion series (Zinnia marylandica, a hybrid between Z. elegans and Z. angustifolia) combines the powdery mildew resistance and heat tolerance of the narrow-leafed zinnia (Z. angustifolia) with the flower size and color range of Z. elegans, producing smaller but abundant, clean single flowers on a compact, bushy plant that maintains healthy foliage through Gulf South summer conditions that devastate regular zinnias. Profusion Orange produces warm orange single flowers (2–2.5 inch) with golden-yellow centers, creating a compact mass of color from planting through frost without the white powdery mildew coating that eventually ruins Z. elegans plantings in humid conditions. The self-cleaning habit (dropping spent flowers without deadheading) and continuous bloom production from a relatively small, mounding plant make it practical for garden edges, container planting, and cutting. Monarch butterflies and swallowtails visit the flowers extensively. For maximum Gulf South reliability, the Profusion series is one of the most consistently recommended zinnia alternatives to the otherwise problematic large-flowered types.

common_name: Profusion Red Yellow Bicolor Zinnia (AAS-Winning Two-Tone Disease-Resistant Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost into full sun; this bicolor Profusion selection blooms nonstop from early summer through frost with strong resistance to the powdery mildew and leaf spot that trouble older zinnia varieties in humid weather.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep after the last frost in full sun, or set out transplants; the compact, mounded plants need no staking and bloom continuously without deadheading. Profusion Red Yellow Bicolor is an AAS National Award Winner in the popular interspecific Profusion series, opening single, daisy-like flowers with a red outer edge shading into a bright yellow center that shifts and deepens in color as each bloom ages, giving a single plant a naturally multicolored look. Like the rest of the Profusion series, it combines exceptional heat, humidity, and drought tolerance with strong resistance to powdery mildew and leaf spot, making it far more reliable than older tall zinnia varieties through a hot, humid Gulf South summer. Its dense, weather-resistant habit and nonstop bloom suit it well to beds, borders, and containers with minimal maintenance beyond an occasional light feeding.

common_name: Profusion Red Zinnia (AAS-Winning Disease-Resistant Heat-Proof Single Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is consistently warm (70F+) in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Profusion Red was bred for the same powdery-mildew resistance and heat tolerance as the rest of the Profusion series, which was bred to hold up in Gulf South summer humidity where standard large-flower zinnias typically fail.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Profusion Red is an AAS-winning member of the Profusion zinnia series (Zinnia marylandica, a hybrid between Z. elegans and Z. angustifolia), bred for the same powdery mildew resistance and heat tolerance as its Profusion Orange and Profusion White stablemates, producing abundant clean, single, deep-red flowers on a compact, bushy, mounding plant that keeps healthy foliage through a full Gulf South summer that would defoliate a standard large-flowered zinnia. It is self-cleaning, dropping spent flowers without deadheading, and blooms continuously from planting through frost. Its compact scale and continuous color make it a dependable choice for garden edges, mass plantings, and containers, and the flowers draw butterflies heavily throughout the season.

plant_note: Direct sow in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–June for summer bloom or August–September for fall bloom. Profusion White, like all Profusion series zinnias, is a fully interspecific hybrid zinnia (Z. elegans x Z. angustifolia) that produces single to semi-double flowers with superior disease resistance over standard Z. elegans varieties — the interspecific parentage provides natural resistance to powdery mildew that is a serious problem for Z. elegans in humid Gulf South summers. The medium-sized (2–3 inch), pure white flowers bloom continuously without deadheading. Profusion White won an All-America Selections award — the AAS Flower Award — specifically for its combination of heat tolerance, disease resistance, and continuous flowering in summer trial gardens across the US.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Profusion White zinnia thrives in hot, sunny conditions and blooms most prolifically with minimal water stress; Profusion White is an All-America Selections award-winning interspecific zinnia hybrid producing a spreading, mounding plant covered with clean white, single to semi-double flowers (2–3 inches) from early summer through frost. The interspecific hybrid origin (Zinnia elegans x Z. angustifolia) gives Profusion White significantly superior powdery mildew resistance compared to standard large-flowered Z. elegans varieties — a critical practical advantage in zone 9's summer humidity where mildew routinely disfigures and eventually kills non-resistant zinnia varieties. The pure white flowers provide an exceptionally versatile garden color — combining harmoniously with virtually every other color, useful as a neutral presence that separates vivid hues without disappearing into the background, and reflecting light effectively in evening gardens when white flowers glow at dusk. The continuous flowering without deadheading and the compact, spreading habit (rather than the tall, upright habit of large-flowered types) make Profusion White an excellent mass-planting zinnia for zone 9 borders, containers, and butterfly gardens where the prolific white flowers attract skippers, sulphurs, and painted ladies throughout the summer.

common_name: Profusion Zinnia (AAS-Winning Interspecific Disease-Resistant Compact Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4–6 weeks earlier; Profusion zinnias are more compact than standard Z. elegans types and well-suited to containers and border edging. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer bloom and again August for fall. Profusion's exceptional disease resistance makes it the best zinnia for humid Gulf South summers where powdery mildew devastates standard zinnia types. The plants self-clean (no deadheading needed) and bloom continuously from planting until frost.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 10–14 inch spacing. No deadheading required — old blooms fall cleanly and new buds replace them continuously. Profusion is a series of interspecific hybrid zinnias (Zinnia elegans × Zinnia angustifolia) developed by PanAmerican Seed and introduced in 1999, when the original Profusion Orange and Profusion Cherry received the first AAS Award ever given to a zinnia — an unprecedented recognition that launched the interspecific zinnia category. The Profusion hybrid combines the larger flower size of Z. elegans with the heat tolerance, powdery mildew resistance, and continuous-blooming, self-cleaning nature of Z. angustifolia, solving the primary problems that limit zinnia use in warm, humid climates: powdery mildew (which can defoliate standard zinnias by midsummer in the Gulf South) and the need for constant deadheading to maintain bloom. Profusion plants are compact (10–16 inches tall), dome-shaped, and covered with 2–2.5 inch single and semi-double flowers that fall cleanly when spent without intervention. The extreme heat tolerance and low maintenance make Profusion the zinnia of choice for Gulf South landscapes where most annual flowers struggle in the summer heat.

plant_note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Prolific is a heavy-flowering Chinese wisteria selection valued for consistent, abundant bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a very sturdy support structure built to carry the mature vine's considerable weight. Prolific was selected from Chinese wisteria specifically for its reliably heavy flowering, opening dense, fragrant, violet-blue racemes all at once before the leaves fully emerge, in the classic Chinese wisteria style, for a bolder, more uniform floral display than seedling-grown plants often produce. Like other Chinese wisteria it twines counterclockwise, in contrast to the clockwise twining of Japanese wisteria, and is a vigorous, potentially aggressive grower that needs firm annual pruning both in summer and late winter to control growth and encourage flowering. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity and plan for a genuinely large, long-term structural commitment.

subcategory: Gulf Coast native spring iris-family corm
plant_note: Plant small corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; propeller flower is native to the coastal prairies and open grasslands of Texas and Louisiana, blooming through late spring and summer with flowers that each open for only a single afternoon.
directions: Plant corms in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; propeller flower is a striking Gulf Coast native iris relative of Texas and Louisiana prairies, producing wiry stems topped with unusual, pinwheel-shaped flowers whose three narrow, twisted outer petals are deep maroon-purple mottled with cream and yellow at the base, giving the bloom a distinctive spinning-propeller look unlike any other native wildflower. Each flower opens for a single afternoon, but a healthy corm produces a long succession of blooms from late spring into summer, longer than most of its spring-only iris-family relatives. Adapted to the region's hot, humid summers and mild winters, it is an excellent, low-maintenance choice for a Gulf Coast prairie or native wildflower planting in lean, well-drained soil, needing little supplemental water once established.

common_name: Prosperity Hybrid Musk Rose (Fragrant White Cluster-Flowered Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Prosperity is a fragrant, white-flowered hybrid musk shrub rose that tolerates a bit of shade.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hybrid musk roses tolerate more shade than most rose classes, blooming reasonably well with just a half-day of direct sun. Prosperity bears large, dense clusters of double, creamy white blooms tinged with pale pink in bud, with a strong, musky-sweet fragrance, opening against glossy dark foliage on a dense, rounded shrub. It repeats bloom well through the growing season and its pale color makes it a versatile choice for a white or moon garden. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through summer to encourage continued flowering.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or plant container-grown plants in deep, moist, humus-rich, fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade; Przewalski's ligularia requires consistently moist soil and wilts dramatically in hot afternoon sun even when well-watered — site in dappled shade with good air circulation. The popular hybrid The Rocket (L. stenocephala x L. przewalskii) has similar cultural requirements but more heat tolerance.
directions: Plant in deep, moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in part shade; Przewalski's ligularia is one of the most architecturally spectacular shade moisture perennials, producing a dramatic combination of ornamental features rarely found together in one plant. The large, deeply and finely divided, almost feathery, palmate leaves — more intricately cut than those of other ligularias — are carried on long stems that form bold, tropical-looking clumps of striking textural interest. From these clumps in July and August arise tall, slender, black-stemmed flower spires — the distinctly dark purple-black stems are ornamental in themselves — bearing dense, narrow columns of small, bright-yellow, daisy-like flowers that create luminous, candelabra-effect spires against the shade. The black stems against yellow flowers is a stunning color combination. Native to northern China, it grows naturally along stream banks, wet meadow margins, and in moist mountain scrub. The hybrid The Rocket, crossed with L. stenocephala, is more heat-tolerant and widely grown in warmer regions.

plant_note: Direct sow into lean soil after last frost; avoid rich or heavily fertilized beds, which push foliage growth at the expense of flowers.
directions: Psyche is a long-grown heirloom cosmos strain distinguished by semi-double and crested, ruffled-petal flowers in a mix of white, pink, and crimson, a fluffier texture than the flat single blooms of standard Cosmos bipinnatus. Plants keep the same tall, airy, finely cut foliage typical of the species and are just as easy from direct seed, thriving in poor, lean soil where richer conditions would produce excess foliage and fewer flowers. The ruffled flower form makes Psyche a favorite for cutting gardens and informal cottage borders where a bit of texture is wanted alongside classic single-flowered cosmos.

plant_note: Install in full sun during warm months, giving it generous overhead and lateral clearance since it eventually forms one of the thickest trunks and largest crowns in the genus.
directions: Install this massive Caribbean sabal in full sun during warm months, giving it generous overhead and lateral clearance since it eventually forms one of the thickest trunks and largest crowns in the genus. It adapts to a wide range of soils, from sandy coastal ground to heavier inland loam, and tolerates both drought and brief flooding once rooted in. Reserve it for large-scale landscapes, parks, or long avenues where its massive fan-leafed canopy can be appreciated at full size. Young plants are slow to trunk, so plant it as an investment piece rather than for quick impact.

common_name: Pugster Amethyst Butterfly Bush (Dwarf True-Purple Compact Buddleja)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth on this dwarf, thick-stemmed selection.
directions: Pugster Amethyst is part of the dwarf Pugster butterfly bush series, bred for unusually thick, sturdy stems and large flower spikes on a plant that stays under two feet tall, a striking contrast to the tall, willowy growth of standard Buddleja davidii. It produces true purple-amethyst flowers continuously from early summer through frost, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds just as reliably as full-size cultivars despite its diminutive stature, and its low, dense habit fits containers, small borders, and mass plantings where larger butterfly bush would overwhelm the space. Like other modern Buddleja hybrids it is sterile and does not self-seed, and it needs only an annual hard cutback in late winter to stay compact and free-flowering.

common_name: Pugster Blue Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Sterile Reblooming Buddleja)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pugster Blue is a compact, sterile, non-invasive butterfly bush that stays under 2 feet tall, fitting into small garden beds and large containers where standard butterfly bush is too large.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pugster Blue is part of the Pugster series of dwarf butterfly bushes, bred to stay compact — under 2 feet tall and wide — while producing full-sized, densely packed, true-blue flower spikes on unusually thick, sturdy stems that hold up well without flopping. Unlike older Buddleja davidii cultivars, the Pugster series is bred to be sterile or very low-seeding, largely eliminating the self-seeding invasiveness concern associated with standard butterfly bush in parts of the country, so it can be planted more responsibly near natural areas. It blooms from early summer through frost with only light deadheading needed to keep flowers coming, and like all butterfly bush it is a strong draw for butterflies, particularly swallowtails and monarchs, as well as hummingbirds. In zone 9, plants die back partially in winter and resprout vigorously from the base in spring; cut back hard in late winter to encourage a full flush of new flowering growth. Its small stature makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, mixed perennial borders, or large containers where a full-sized butterfly bush would overwhelm the space.

common_name: Pugster Periwinkle Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Reblooming Blue-Purple Buddleja)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Pugster Periwinkle is part of a dwarf, sterile butterfly bush series bred for compact size and continuous rebloom without deadheading.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since butterfly bush is far more likely to be lost to wet winter soil than to cold or drought. Pugster Periwinkle bears dense spikes of blue-purple flowers with a small orange eye on a naturally dwarf, sturdy, well-branched plant, part of the compact, non-invasive Pugster series bred for a tidy habit and continuous bloom from late spring through frost without the need for deadheading. Its low, rounded shape fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and large containers where the towering size of old-fashioned butterfly bush would overwhelm the space, and its sterile flowers do not set the abundant seed that has made some older Buddleja davidii cultivars invasive in parts of the country. Cut the whole plant back hard in late winter each year, since it flowers on new growth and responds with denser, more floriferous regrowth.

common_name: Pugster Pink Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Pink Buddleja)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth on this dwarf, thick-stemmed selection.
directions: Pugster Pink shares the same thick-stemmed, dwarf habit as the rest of the Pugster butterfly bush series, staying under two feet tall while still carrying large, dense flower spikes in a clear rose-pink, blooming continuously from early summer through frost. The compact, sturdy form fits small borders, containers, and foundation plantings where standard butterfly bush cultivars grow far too large, and it draws butterflies and hummingbirds with the same intensity as full-size cultivars. It is sterile and does not self-seed like older Buddleja davidii selections, and needs only an annual hard cutback in late winter, to about 6-12 inches, to stay dense and floriferous.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Pumila' spreads by stolon into a dense, low groundcover rather than staying in a tight clump like most astilbe cultivars, and blooms later in the season than taller Chinese astilbe selections.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Pumila' spreads by stolon into a dense, low groundcover rather than staying in a tight clump like most astilbe cultivars, and blooms later in the season than taller Chinese astilbe selections. This dwarf Chinese astilbe selection forms a low, spreading mat of finely cut, dark green foliage topped in late summer by upright, fuzzy, lilac-pink plumes that appear after most other astilbes have finished blooming, extending the shade border's flowering season. Its low, groundcover habit makes it useful for edging shaded paths, filling in beneath taller shrubs, or massing as a flowering lawn substitute in consistently moist shade where turfgrass will not grow. Astilbe chinensis selections tolerate more sun and drier soil than other astilbe species, but 'Pumila' still performs best with regular moisture and appreciates a yearly topdressing of compost.

common_name: Pumila Dwarf Pampas Grass (Compact Ornamental Plume Grass)
plant_note: Plant container divisions after last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pumila is a compact cultivar of pampas grass, reaching roughly a third the size of the straight species, making it more manageable for a smaller residential garden.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pumila is a compact selection of pampas grass, reaching only about 4–6 feet in bloom compared to the 8–10-plus feet of the straight species, which makes it far more practical for a standard residential landscape while retaining the same dramatic, silvery-white plumes held well above the arching, fine-textured foliage from late summer into fall. It is a tough, drought-tolerant grass once established, tolerating heat, wind, and poor soil with ease, and works well as a specimen, screen, or accent at a scale that overwhelms most gardens when the full-sized species is used instead. The narrow leaf blades have sharp, saw-toothed edges, so wear gloves and long sleeves when cutting the clump back hard in late winter before new growth begins. Because pampas grass can self-seed and naturalize in some regions, deadhead spent plumes before seed drop if planting near natural areas, and confirm local guidance, since it is considered invasive in parts of the Gulf South and West Coast.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in wet to seasonally flooded, poorly drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pumpkin ash is adapted to swamps and bottomlands and tolerates standing water far better than upland ash species.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in wet to seasonally flooded, poorly drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pumpkin ash is adapted to swamps and bottomlands and tolerates standing water far better than upland ash species. Named for the swollen, pumpkin-shaped base that often develops on trees growing in permanently flooded ground, this large wetland tree bears compound leaves and winged seeds typical of ash, providing food for wildlife and dense shade over the bottomland hardwood forests and cypress-tupelo swamps of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain. It is among the most flood-tolerant of all ash species, capable of growing in standing water for extended periods, making it valuable for restoring wet bottomland sites where few other large shade trees will survive. Like other native ash species it is vulnerable to the invasive emerald ash borer, so plant it as part of a diverse wetland tree planting rather than a monoculture.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; seeds cold-stratify naturally and germinate with winter rains for spring bloom.
directions: Punchbowl Clarkia is a charming southern California and Baja California native annual with slender, branching stems bearing small, 4-petaled, rose-pink to lavender-pink flowers with darker veins along dry, rocky, partially shaded chaparral and canyon slopes. It is one of the few Clarkia species that tolerates and even prefers partial shade, making it particularly valuable under native oaks and along shaded garden borders. Direct sow in fall on dry, lean, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, pressing seeds lightly into the surface without covering — like all Clarkia, it does not transplant well and must be direct sown. Once established it self-sows in suitable conditions and is an excellent shade-tolerant native annual for California dry gardens and open chaparral garden settings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Punktchen bears green blades flecked with small yellow spots rather than the horizontal banding typical of zebra grass cultivars, on a compact plant.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; maiden grass tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden conditions well once established. Punktchen, German for 'little dot,' bears green blades flecked with small, scattered yellow spots along their length rather than the bold horizontal cross-banding typical of zebra grass cultivars, giving a more subtle, speckled variegation on a more compact plant than many Miscanthus selections. Its smaller mature size fits a mid-border planting where full-sized maiden grass cultivars would be too large. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Purity Candytuft (Classic Evergreen White-Flowered Perennial Candytuft)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Purity is a classic evergreen perennial candytuft producing a dense mat of glossy dark green foliage smothered in pure white flowers in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential, since candytuft quickly declines in heavy, wet soil. Purity is a classic, widely grown perennial candytuft producing a dense, low, spreading mat of glossy, dark evergreen foliage that provides year-round structure at the front of a border or in a rock garden, completely smothered each spring in masses of small, pure white flowers. It is drought-tolerant once established and tolerates poor, rocky soil well, making it a reliable, low-maintenance edging plant. Shear the mat back lightly after flowering to keep growth dense and compact and to encourage the best bloom the following spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring after last frost in full sun with well-drained soil; Purple Allamanda is a vigorous grower that can be trained as a large sprawling shrub or tied to a trellis as a vine. In zone 9a, frost damage is likely in winter — grow in a large container or plant in a protected microclimate. In zone 9b-10, it grows as a perennial shrub-vine and blooms from late spring through fall. The milky sap is toxic and a skin and eye irritant.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Purple Allamanda requires full sun for best flowering and will produce fewer blooms in shaded conditions. Allamanda blanchetii (sometimes listed as A. violacea) is a large, vigorous, scrambling shrub or lax vine from Brazil, closely related to the common Golden Allamanda (A. cathartica) but producing rich rose-purple to magenta, trumpet-shaped flowers 3–4 inches in diameter rather than the familiar yellow. The flowers are stunning — the color a deep, saturated rose-magenta that is unusual among tropical vines — and are borne in successive flushes from late spring through frost in zone 9. Like its golden relative, Purple Allamanda has a sprawling, lax habit that can be trained on a fence or trellis by tying stems, or allowed to cascade down a bank or over a wall. The stems exude a milky white sap when cut, similar to the toxic latex of its relatives in the Apocynaceae family — this sap is a skin irritant and toxic if ingested, with all plant parts considered poisonous. In zone 9, Purple Allamanda is used as a warm-season annual or half-hardy perennial; in zone 10-11 it grows as a large, floriferous evergreen shrub that blooms nearly year-round.

common_name: Purple Beauty Creeping Phlox (Rich Violet-Purple Moss Phlox)
plant_note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; moss phlox performs best in sharply drained, lean soil, since rich, moist soil promotes lush foliage at the expense of flowering.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky, lean soil in full sun. Purple Beauty is a richly colored moss phlox selection producing an especially vivid, deep violet-purple spring flower display over a dense, low, evergreen, needle-textured mat, one of the more saturated colors available among moss phlox cultivars. Like other moss phlox it thrives in sharply drained, lean, sunny sites and struggles in rich, wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a rock garden, sunny slope, or cascading over a retaining wall. Shear the mat back lightly after flowering to maintain dense growth and encourage the strongest bloom the following year.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; this Asian beautyberry is more compact than the native American beautyberry (C. americana) and produces incredibly vivid violet-purple berries that are among the most electric colors of any fall fruiting shrub.
directions: Plant in spring or early fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; purple beautyberry performs best in partial afternoon shade in zone 7–8 which prevents leaf scorch while maintaining prolific berry production. Callicarpa dichotoma is the Asian counterpart to the native American beautyberry, producing a more compact shrub (3–5 feet) with arching branches and, in fall, spectacular clusters of vivid violet-purple berries so intense in color they seem almost artificial — these berries are among the most electric and eye-catching of any fruiting shrub in the temperate garden and are invaluable for fall color. The small, lavender flowers in summer are attractive to pollinators. Plant in groups of 3 or more for best berry set; prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and heavy fruiting. The berries are mildly toxic to humans.

plant_note: Start indoors 10 weeks early; slow to establish.
directions: Start purple bell vine indoors ten weeks before the last frost, surface sowing the fine seed and providing warmth. This delicate climber produces dangling flowers with rosy-pink parasol-shaped calyces and dark tubular petals. Grow on a light trellis or in hanging baskets in full sun to partial shade with rich, moist soil. It is grown as a tender annual in most climates and blooms until frost.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or fall; purple bergenia's distinctive red-purple winter coloration is most vivid when the plant receives some cold and some winter sunlight — deep full shade and consistently mild winters suppress the purple coloration.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; purple bergenia is a Himalayan shade evergreen perennial distinguished from other bergenia species by its exceptional and consistent winter foliage coloring — from autumn through winter, the large, rounded, leathery, shiny leaves turn a deep, vivid, wine-red to purple-red that intensifies with cold weather and sunlight exposure, creating one of the finest winter foliage color effects available from any shade-tolerant evergreen groundcover plant. In spring the foliage gradually returns to dark green as temperatures warm. The flowers, produced in March–April on upright, red-stalked stems, are deep rosy-pink to magenta and particularly vivid against the purplish-red foliage of late winter. Purple bergenia is one of the primary species in the background of many Bergenia hybrid cultivars bred specifically for enhanced winter foliage coloring, including 'Bressingham Ruby' and 'Sunningdale'. It is among the most ornamental species of the genus for four-season interest, combining spring flowers, summer foliage groundcover, and rich winter purple coloring into a single, low-maintenance, long-lived evergreen.

plant_note: Float a handful of stems in a sunny pond, water garden, or tub without soil; purple bladderwort has no roots and drifts or loosely anchors among other aquatic vegetation — use rain or pond water rather than chlorinated tap water.
directions: Place a clump of stems in a sunny, still or slow-moving acidic pond, water garden, or tub without adding soil; purple bladderwort floats free or drifts loosely among other aquatic plants and needs no planting medium at all. Its finely branched, whorled underwater stems carry small bladder traps, though unlike most bladderworts it is thought to rely on them more for anchorage and some prey capture than as its primary feeding strategy, since it also photosynthesizes readily in the nutrient-poor, tannin-stained waters it favors. From summer through early fall it produces small but vivid purple, orchid-like flowers held just above the water surface on slender stalks, among the most ornamental of the native bladderworts. It spreads readily in warm, acidic, still water across much of the eastern and southeastern US and is easily thinned by hand if it becomes too vigorous in a small water garden.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in fall into well-drained, rocky or gravelly soil in a partially shaded woodland edge or open glade. Seeds are very fine; mix with sand for even distribution and press lightly onto the soil surface without covering.
directions: Purple Bluet is well suited to lean, rocky soils at woodland edges and cedar glades where competition from aggressive grasses is naturally limited. Direct sow seeds in fall by scattering them onto a prepared, weed-free surface and pressing them gently into contact with the soil without burying them. Plants develop slowly in the first year, establishing a root system before putting on significant top growth, so mark planting areas carefully to avoid accidental disturbance. Once established, Purple Bluet self-seeds reliably and gradually spreads to form attractive clumps that bloom from mid-spring into early summer.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Purple Candles is a chinensis-type astilbe noted for handling sun and dry spells better than most arendsii-hybrid selections.
directions: Grow in humus-rich soil with reliable moisture in partial shade, though established clumps tolerate brief dry spells better than most astilbes once rooted in. Purple Candles sends up tall, narrow, densely packed spikes of dark purplish-red flowers held well above a mound of coarse, deeply incised, bronze-green foliage, with color that gradually softens to lighter purple as each plume ages over its long bloom period. As a chinensis-type selection it spreads more readily by rhizome than arendsii hybrids, gradually forming a broader clump rather than staying in a tight crown. Its improved sun and drought tolerance make it one of the more forgiving astilbes for a Gulf Coast shade border, though it still colors and blooms best with consistent moisture through the heat of summer.

plant_note: Plant in very well-drained, rocky, calcareous, alkaline to neutral crevices in partial shade to full sun; purple cliffbrake grows on dry limestone outcrops, rock faces, and cliff ledges and is exceptionally drought-tolerant for a fern. Do not plant in moist, shaded conditions.
directions: Plant in dry, rocky, calcareous, alkaline to neutral, well-drained crevices and ledges in partial shade to full sun; purple cliffbrake is one of the most drought-tolerant ferns in North America — an unusual xeric specialist that grows on dry limestone cliffs, ledges, and rocky outcrops where moisture is minimal and other ferns cannot survive. The wiry, dark purple-black stems (the trait giving the plant its name) emerge from rocky crevices with arching, blue-green, leathery fronds that curl in drought and rehydrate when rain returns. This extraordinary drought tolerance makes it the ideal fern for rock garden settings, dry stone walls, and limestone outcrops where moisture-loving ferns would decline. Entirely undemanding in dry, alkaline, rocky conditions; it declines in rich, moist, acidic soils where it is outcompeted by more vigorous plants. An outstanding rock garden fern with architectural, all-season interest.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall for natural cold-moist stratification and spring germination, or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost after 8 weeks of cold stratification in the refrigerator; established transplants planted in spring or fall bloom reliably in their second year and beyond.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for natural cold stratification, or start from transplants; purple coneflower is one of the most ecologically valuable and widely grown native perennials of the eastern and central US prairie, producing large rosy-purple daisy-like flowers with prominent orange-brown spiny central cones from midsummer through early fall that attract an extraordinary diversity of pollinators. The roots and leaves have a centuries-long history as the most widely used plant in North American traditional medicine, and Echinacea extracts remain among the best-selling herbal supplements for immune support. Allow seed heads to mature and stand through winter — they are a primary food source for American goldfinches and many other songbirds. Grows best in lean soil; excessive fertility produces floppy stems and poor flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms, or cold stratify seed for 4 weeks to improve germination.
directions: This native heirloom is a long-lived perennial that blooms for a month or more from midsummer, with pinkish-purple petals surrounding a large dark cone. Sow seed in spring after the last frost, or cold stratify beforehand to break dormancy. Space plants a foot or more apart in well-drained soil and full sun to part shade. Once established it is drought tolerant and self-sows. Leave spent cones standing to feed goldfinches through fall and winter.

plant_note: Scatter seeds on bare, dry, disturbed ground in fall and press lightly into the soil surface; do not cover, as seeds need light to germinate.
directions: Purple Cudweed is a silvery-woolly native annual or biennial that forms a low basal rosette of soft, spatulate leaves coated in white wool before sending up dense leafy spikes of small rose-purple to brownish composite flower heads from spring through early summer. It is an important larval host plant for the American Painted Lady butterfly and attracts small native bees seeking pollen. Grow it in dry, sandy, lean, or disturbed open ground in full sun; rich or moist soils suppress growth and reduce self-seeding. Direct sow on bare soil in fall, pressing seeds lightly against the surface without burying them, and allow plants to complete their cycle and self-sow for a self-sustaining colony.

common_name: Purple Diamond Loropetalum (Compact Deep-Purple Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Diamond holds its rich purple foliage color best in full sun, and its naturally compact, dense habit needs little pruning to stay tidy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water regularly the first season to establish before easing into a lower-maintenance routine. Purple Diamond is part of the First Editions breeding program and stands out among Loropetalum chinense cultivars for its unusually dense, rounded, naturally compact habit and consistently deep, dark purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season rather than fading to green, punctuated by frilly magenta-pink flowers in spring with scattered rebloom into fall. Its tidy, slow-to-medium growth rate makes it lower-maintenance than larger loropetalum cultivars, suiting foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders without frequent shearing. Prune lightly right after the spring flower flush if shaping is needed, since later pruning removes next year's flower buds.

common_name: Purple Dome Aster (Compact Deep Purple New England Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Purple Dome is a compact New England aster selection that stays low and mounded without the floppy growth and staking that taller New England asters usually require.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Purple Dome is a compact selection of native New England aster, forming a tidy, dense, dome-shaped mound covered in deep violet-purple daisy flowers with golden centers in fall, without the tall, sprawling growth habit that often requires staking in the wild species. This shorter stature makes it far more practical for a mixed perennial border, and like other New England asters it is an exceptional late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies and other migrating pollinators. It performs best with consistent moisture through summer and can be divided every few years in spring to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: Purple Dragon Lamium (Silver-Leaf Deep Violet Dead Nettle)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Purple Dragon has almost entirely silver foliage narrowly edged in green, topped with deep violet-purple flowers, one of the showiest color combinations among lamium cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Purple Dragon produces nearly solid silvery-white foliage with just a thin green margin, among the most striking silver-leaved lamium cultivars, topped in spring with clusters of deep violet-purple flowers that stand out sharply against the pale foliage. It spreads by surface runners to form a dense groundcover mat fairly quickly, making it useful for brightening a dark, shaded bed under trees or shrubs, and it tolerates fairly dry shade once established better than many groundcovers. Shear back after flowering if the mat becomes tired-looking in summer heat to encourage fresh new growth for fall.

common_name: Purple Emperor Sedum (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Stonecrop with Pink Fall Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like other upright sedums, Purple Emperor is drought-tolerant once established and rots readily in wet, heavy soil.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; rich, moist soil produces floppy, weak growth in upright sedums, so avoid heavy feeding or fertile ground. Purple Emperor is an upright border sedum selected for deep purple-black foliage and stems that hold their dark color through the growing season, topped in late summer and fall by broad, flat clusters of dusky pink flowers that draw butterflies and bees in large numbers just as many other perennials are fading. Its sturdy, self-supporting stems generally resist the flopping that troubles older tall sedum cultivars, and the dark foliage provides strong color contrast against silver, gray, or chartreuse companion plants all season, not just at bloom time. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on neglect in a sunny border and needs only occasional division every few years to keep the clump vigorous; spent flower heads can be left standing through winter for structural interest and bird food.

plant_note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed; nasturtiums resent transplanting.
directions: This trailing variety carries deeply veined petals in shades of purple fading to lavender and dusty rose, making it ideal for hanging baskets or as a flowering ground cover. Sow the large seeds directly where they are to grow once the soil has warmed, planting about half an inch deep. Avoid rich soil and heavy feeding, which produces leaves at the expense of blooms. It is fairly drought tolerant once established. Both the peppery blossoms and leaves are edible and add a colorful kick to salads.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in consistently moist to wet soil, preferably at a streambank, pond margin, or rain garden; Physostegia purpurea spreads by rhizomes and will naturalize into a colony in reliably wet conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to saturated soil at a streambank, pond edge, or rain garden where roots can stay consistently wet; this species is distinct from the more common Physostegia virginiana and thrives in wetter, shadier conditions than its relative. The vivid purple-pink tubular flowers appear in fall and are held on upright spikes; each individual flower can be repositioned laterally on the stem and will stay put, a quirk that earns the plant its common name 'obedient plant.' Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent the colony from overcrowding neighboring plants.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in warm, moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; pseuderanthemum colors most intensely in bright indirect light — deep shade causes the purple coloring to fade toward green.
directions: Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade; purple false eranthemum (Jacob's coat, eldorado) is a Pacific Islands tropical shrub grown for its spectacular, large, glossy, dark-purple to maroon leaves dramatically overlaid with scattered spots, streaks, and blotches of pink, rose, gold, and white — one of the most richly colored foliage plants available for tropical and subtropical gardens. The unusual combination of dark background coloration with bright-colored irregular markings creates a bold, jewel-like quality unlike any other landscape shrub. Small, pale-lavender to white, tubular flowers appear in terminal spikes throughout the year in frost-free climates but are secondary to the remarkable foliage. Excellent combined with chartreuse-leaved plants (golden pothos, lime coleus) for high-contrast tropical compositions. Grown as a houseplant in cool climates; in zone 10–12 it forms an outdoor foliage shrub of 2–4 feet. 'Tricolor' and 'Rubrum' are cultivar selections emphasizing different color combinations.

plant_note: Direct sow among established native grasses at or just after last frost; seeds require contact with host grass roots for successful establishment.
directions: Purple False Foxglove is a native annual hemi-parasite of eastern North American prairies, pine savannas, and wet meadows, drawing supplemental nutrition through root connections to neighboring grasses while also performing its own photosynthesis. To grow it successfully, direct sow seeds among established native warm-season grasses such as little bluestem or broomsedge in full sun — without host grass roots present, germination and survival rates drop sharply. The plant produces a profusion of showy, rosy-purple, trumpet-shaped flowers with spotted throats from August through October, providing a critical late-season nectar source for native bees and supporting the caterpillars of the buckeye butterfly. Sow seeds on the soil surface at or just after last frost and keep the planting moist until germination; once established, plants are largely self-sufficient.

common_name: Purple Flora Gladiolus (Large Velvety Violet-Purple Ruffled)
plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season. Purple Flora bears large, velvety violet-purple ruffled flowers opening from dark indigo buds.
directions: Purple Flora bears large, velvety violet-purple, ruffled flowers that open from dark indigo buds, a rich, saturated color that provides strong contrast in a mixed cutting bed of brighter reds, pinks, and yellows. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants after last frost; this cultivar does not come true from seed and is propagated by division.
directions: Plant after last frost in full sun and very well-drained soil; purple fountain grass is grown as an annual north of zone 9 for its arching burgundy-red foliage and showy, rose-tinged plumes from midsummer through frost. It thrives in heat and drought once established but requires consistent moisture the first few weeks after transplanting. In frost-free climates it is a perennial that can become invasive — avoid planting near natural areas and remove flower heads before seeds ripen. Bring container-grown specimens indoors before frost to overwinter as a houseplant in colder zones.

common_name: Purple Globe Amaranth (Heat-Proof Deep Purple Clover-Like Annual for Hot Summers)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Purple Globe Amaranth is among the best summer annuals for sustained performance in brutal Gulf South summer heat and humidity — it actually performs better in August than June in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Purple Globe Amaranth (Gomphrena globosa) produces compact, globe-shaped, clover-like flower heads in rich magenta-purple — papery, button-like structures (1/2–3/4 inch) that maintain their color indefinitely when dried, making globe amaranth one of the premier cut-and-dried flower annuals for summer gardens. The papery bracts retain their vivid purple color when dry because they are composed of pigmented, non-photosynthetic modified leaves rather than the true petals (which would bleach on drying) — the same quality that makes strawflowers, statice, and immortelle persist when dried. In the summer garden, globe amaranth is outstanding for one key quality: it genuinely thrives in the brutal Gulf South summer heat that collapses most other annuals in July and August. The vivid purple clover-like heads continue to produce without pause through extreme heat and humidity, providing consistent garden color when most other summer annuals have declined. Butterflies visit the flowers consistently through the bloom season. The dried flower heads retain their color for months and are outstanding in dry arrangements. Low fertility and good drainage extend bloom; excess nitrogen promotes leafy growth over flowers.

common_name: Purple Glory Tree (Brazilian Spider Flower, Princess Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Purple Glory Tree grows rapidly and should be planted in a location with room to develop a multi-branched canopy 15–25 feet wide. In zone 9a, it freezes back hard in cold winters but resprouts vigorously from the trunk or base in spring; in zone 9b-10, it is semi-evergreen to evergreen. The most spectacular bloom occurs in fall (September–November) and a second flush in spring; do not prune in late summer to preserve flower buds.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, organically rich soil; Purple Glory Tree grows most vigorously in full sun but tolerates afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Tibouchina granulosa is a large, fast-growing tree from the Atlantic rainforest of Brazil, producing one of the most spectacular purple floral displays of any tree in the subtropical world. In late summer through fall, the entire canopy becomes covered with large (2–3 inch) royal purple to intense violet flowers borne in broad, flat-topped clusters at every stem tip — the effect is breathtaking, with a well-established specimen appearing as though it has been draped in a cascade of purple velvet. Each flower has prominent purple anthers on curved filaments that give the genus the common name 'Spider Flower.' The large, velvet-textured, dark-green, prominently ribbed leaves are attractive year-round. Tibouchina granulosa (the tree form) is distinguished from the shrubby Princess Flower (T. urvilleana, 6–10 feet) by its potential tree height of 25–40 feet in zone 10-11 and its tendency to develop a single dominant trunk. In zone 9, hard pruning after frost damage stimulates vigorous regrowth and heavy flowering on new wood. An outstanding specimen tree for subtropical Gulf Coast landscapes.

common_name: Purple Gown Camellia (Full Peony-Form Rose-Purple Reticulata Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Purple Gown is a slow-growing, historic Chinese reticulata camellia cultivar with very full peony-form blooms.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind. Purple Gown, one of the historic Chinese reticulata cultivars, bears very full, rose-purple peony-form blooms up to 6 inches across, densely packed with irregular petals in a rich, saturated color unusual among camellias. It grows more slowly than most reticulata cultivars, forming a compact, dense shrub over time rather than the open, rangy habit typical of the species. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May or September–October. Purple Heart is a tender perennial in zone 7–9 that may die back to the ground in hard freezes but resprouts reliably from the roots in spring. The trailing, spreading stems root wherever nodes contact moist soil, rapidly covering ground in sunny to partially shaded areas. Stem cuttings root extremely easily — simply cut a stem and place it in moist soil or water, where roots develop within 1–2 weeks. The vivid purple color intensifies in full sun and fades somewhat in shade; in very deep shade the foliage may appear more green-purple than the vivid, saturated purple of full-sun plants.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Purple Heart is drought tolerant once established and blooms most freely with the most vivid purple foliage in full sun, while tolerating partial shade; Purple Heart (Tradescantia pallida, formerly Setcreasea pallida) is one of the most striking purple-foliaged plants available for zone 9 gardens, producing a intense, saturated, clear purple color on both the trailing stems and the large (4–5 inch), lance-shaped leaves that is unique among commonly grown ground covers and border plants. Small, three-petaled, bright pink-magenta flowers appear at the stem tips in summer, providing a complementary floral dimension to the primary foliage display. The trailing, ground-covering habit (stems rooting where they contact soil) makes Purple Heart one of the most effective and low-maintenance purple ground covers available — spreading steadily without becoming invasive in most garden contexts, rooting easily from stem pieces, and recovering quickly from damage or drought when conditions improve. In zone 9 Purple Heart is at its best — thriving in the summer heat that stresses many ornamentals and maintaining its vivid color through the entire growing season from spring through fall. The vivid purple provides exceptional contrast with chartreuse, silver-gray, and gold-foliaged companion plants.
