plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Raspberry Splash flowers very early in spring, often among the first shade perennials to bloom, and its heavily silver-spotted leaves provide season-long foliage interest afterward.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Raspberry Splash produces clusters of small, funnel-shaped raspberry-pink flowers in very early spring, among the first blooms in the shade garden each year, held above heavily silver-spotted, softly bristled leaves that continue to provide strong foliage texture and contrast for the rest of the growing season. Like other lungworts it combines beautifully with hostas, ferns, and hellebores in a woodland border, and it tolerates fairly dry shade once established better than many shade perennials, though consistent moisture during establishment gives the best results. Divide congested clumps in early fall every few years to maintain vigor and refresh the planting.

common_name: Raspberry Wine Bee Balm (Deep Pink-Red Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Raspberry Wine spreads by underground stolons and benefits from division every two to three years to keep the colony within bounds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew. Raspberry Wine produces large, shaggy clusters of deep magenta-pink flowers in midsummer above aromatic, mint-scented foliage, drawing hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies in large numbers over a long bloom period. It shows notably better resistance to powdery mildew than many older bee balm cultivars, a disease that commonly disfigures monarda foliage by midsummer in humid climates, though good spacing and airflow still help keep plants looking their best. Divide every two to three years in spring to control its spreading habit and maintain vigorous, healthy growth.

common_name: Raspberry Wine Beebalm (Wine-Red Mildew-Resistant Bee Balm)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Raspberry Wine is a tall, vigorous bee balm cultivar with deep wine-red flowers and notably better mildew resistance than many older red and pink Monarda didyma selections.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Raspberry Wine is a vigorous bee balm cultivar bearing large, shaggy flower heads in a deep, rich wine-red color, held on tall, sturdy stems above aromatic, mint-scented foliage. It shows notably better resistance to powdery mildew than many older red and pink Monarda didyma cultivars, an important trait in the humid Gulf South where mildew commonly disfigures bee balm foliage by midsummer, though good air circulation and consistent moisture still help keep it looking its best through the season. Hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies visit the tubular flowers heavily from early to midsummer. Like other bee balms, it spreads by underground stolons to form an expanding clump; divide every two to three years in early spring to control spread, renew vigor, and reduce crowding that can encourage mildew. Deadhead spent flowers to tidy the plant, or leave some seed heads standing for winter interest and finch forage.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; rat tail cactus is an epiphytic forest cactus and prefers more humidity and less intense sun than desert cacti.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; rat tail cactus is an epiphytic forest cactus and prefers more humidity and less intense sun than desert cacti. Long, thin, trailing, spine-covered stems cascade densely from a hanging basket, growing several feet long over time, and in spring the plant produces a profusion of brilliant magenta-pink, tubular flowers all along the trailing stems, a spectacular flush of color from an otherwise unassuming, snake-like plant. Native to Mexican and Central American forests, where it grows draped over tree branches rather than rooted in desert soil, it appreciates more regular watering and higher humidity than typical desert cacti, though it still stores water in its fleshy stems and should not sit in soggy mix. Hang where its long trailing stems can cascade freely, water when the mix approaches dryness, and avoid disturbing the plant while flower buds are forming, since they can drop if the pot is moved or turned.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade with tall trees or structures to climb; Rattan (Calamus rotang) is a clustering, spiny, climbing palm native to the tropical forests of India and Sri Lanka — the original source of 'rattan' furniture cane — producing extraordinarily long, flexible, spiny stems that climb forest canopy trees using backward-pointing hook-tipped whips.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with tall trees or very strong support structures for climbing — Calamus rotang is a vigorous, long-stemmed climber that can reach enormous heights in mature forest and requires substantial support to reach fruiting size; handle with thick gloves as the entire plant is armed with sharp, recurved spines and hooks. Calamus rotang (Rattan, Common Rattan, or Indian Rattan Palm) is a clustering, spiny, climbing palm in the Arecaceae family native to the tropical coastal forests, moist forests, and forest edges of southern India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu) and Sri Lanka, and widely naturalized throughout Southeast Asia — the progenitor of the global rattan furniture and basketry industry. Calamus rotang and its relatives (Calamus species are the largest genus in the palm family, with 300+ species) produce extraordinarily long, slender, solid, flexible, spiny stems by climbing to the forest canopy using backward-pointing, hook-covered whips (cirri) that grab onto adjacent vegetation. The harvested and processed stems — stripped of spines, bundled, and steamed — are the 'rattan cane' used worldwide for wicker furniture, baskets, mats, walking sticks, and traditional crafts. Global rattan is a multi-billion-dollar industry, primarily from Indonesian and Malaysian forests. Calamus rotang is one of the few rattan species adapted to cooler, drier conditions outside equatorial rainforest and can be grown as an ornamental curiosity in zone 10–12 gardens with ample space and support.

plant_note: Scarify seeds lightly with sandpaper or soak overnight in warm water before direct-sowing at the surface of well-drained sandy or loamy soil after the last frost; no thinning needed as plants remain compact.
directions: Direct-sow after the last frost in well-drained, infertile to moderately fertile soil in full sun; rattlebox thrives in dry sandy fields, roadsides, and open woodland edges where it fixes nitrogen through root nodules and improves soil structure with minimal inputs. Bright yellow pea-like flowers appear from midsummer onward, followed by inflated pods that turn black and papery at maturity, causing the loose seeds inside to rattle audibly in the wind — giving the plant its common name. It is an important larval host plant for the ceraunus blue butterfly and several native moth species. Allow plants to set seed and self-sow freely for a self-renewing colony; the entire plant is toxic if ingested by livestock or humans.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in moist, rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade in spring; rattlesnake fern is mycorrhizal-dependent and very slow-growing from spores, so start only from nursery-grown crowns and expect a long establishment period.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in moist, rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade in spring; rattlesnake fern is mycorrhizal-dependent and very slow-growing from spores, so start only from nursery-grown crowns and expect a long establishment period. Each plant sends up a single broad, finely divided, lacy sterile blade in early spring, from the base of which a separate upright fertile stalk emerges bearing a branched cluster of bead-like spore cases that resembles a rattlesnake's rattle once it browns in summer. It is one of the earliest ferns to unfurl in rich deciduous woods each spring and disappears by mid- to late summer once spores are shed, so mark its location or interplant with later-emerging shade perennials to avoid bare patches. Undisturbed leaf litter and consistent moisture through spring are essential to its survival.

common_name: Rattlesnake Ginger (Yellow Rattle Calathea, Rattlesnake Plant, Yellow Wax Calathea)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in late spring in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Calathea crotalifera prefers partial shade but tolerates full shade — it grows naturally as an understory plant in humid tropical forests. In zone 9, treat as a container plant moved indoors in winter as the plant cannot tolerate frost. The distinctive yellow, waxy, overlapping-bract inflorescences are excellent cut flowers (2–3 week vase life). Propagate by rhizome division. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Rattlesnake Ginger produces its best foliage and inflorescence display in the bright, filtered light of a shaded tropical garden position or sheltered patio. Calathea crotalifera is a clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to Mexico, Central America, and northern South America in the Marantaceae family, grown for its remarkable, novelty inflorescences as much as for its large, paddle-shaped foliage. The inflorescences are 8–14 inches long, erect to arching, and composed of tightly overlapping, waxy, bright yellow to golden-yellow bracts stacked in a precise, shingle-like pattern along the central axis — the bract arrangement, when viewed from the side, closely resembles the segmented rattle of a rattlesnake, explaining the common name 'Rattlesnake Plant.' From between the bracts, small white to pale yellow flowers emerge in succession. The yellow, waxy inflorescences are long-lasting (several weeks on the plant and 2–3 weeks as cut flowers) and have commercial value in the tropical cut flower industry. The large, green, paddle-shaped leaves provide an attractive, lush background to the colorful inflorescences. Multiple inflorescences can be produced simultaneously by established clumps through the warm months. An attractive zone 10-11 shade garden plant and excellent tropical cut flower.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification; transplants poorly due to deep taproot.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in a sunny prairie or meadow garden in lean, well-drained soil; rattlesnake master develops a deep taproot and resents being moved after establishment. The dramatic, yucca-like basal rosette of spiny blue-green leaves is topped by tall branched stems bearing small, spiny, globe-shaped white flower heads in midsummer that are highly attractive to native bees. It is extremely drought-tolerant and actually performs better in poor, sandy or rocky soil than in rich garden beds. The sculptural seedheads provide winter interest and are prized for dried arrangements.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 9; Rattlesnake Plant requires consistent warmth (65–85°F), moderate indirect light, and high humidity (50%+) for best appearance. Water with filtered or rainwater to avoid fluoride damage to leaf tips. The narrow, upright leaves make it one of the more efficient space users in the Calathea group. Propagate by rhizome division in spring when repotting. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in moist, well-drained, well-aerated potting mix; Rattlesnake Plant is one of the most adaptable Calatheas for indoor conditions, tolerating somewhat lower humidity and slightly less consistent care than many of its relatives while maintaining attractive foliage. Calathea lancifolia (sometimes reclassified as Goeppertia insignis) is a prayer plant from the tropical rainforests of Brazil, producing distinctively narrow, elongated lance-shaped leaves up to 18 inches long decorated with a precise, alternating pattern of dark oval spots along the midrib that graduates to wavy, irregular dark green edges — a marking pattern that strikingly resembles the scale pattern of certain rattlesnakes, particularly the timber rattlesnake, hence the common name. The undersides of the leaves are deep purple-red, creating a dramatic visual effect when the leaves move through their daily opening and closing cycle (nyctinasty). Among the popular Calatheas, Rattlesnake Plant is often recommended as the best choice for beginners due to its relatively higher tolerance for imperfect conditions — it is more forgiving of occasional dry periods, lower humidity, and temperature fluctuation than species like C. ornata or C. makoyana, while still producing the characteristic dramatic patterned foliage that makes the group so appealing.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Raven ZZ plant tolerates the same low light and infrequent watering as the standard green ZZ plant and is equally forgiving of neglect.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Raven ZZ plant tolerates the same low light and infrequent watering as the standard green ZZ plant and is equally forgiving of neglect. New leaflets emerge bright lime-green and darken over several weeks to a deep, glossy near-black, giving mature plants a dramatic, almost otherworldly color unlike any other common houseplant, while retaining the same thick, water-storing rhizomes and waxy, pinnate leaves as the species. It tolerates low light, infrequent watering, and general neglect better than almost any other foliage houseplant, making it a favorite for offices and low-light interiors, but grows fastest and darkest with bright indirect light. Allow the potting mix to dry out well between waterings, since the plant's rhizomes rot quickly in constantly wet soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun in spring; ravenna grass thrives in hot, dry, poor conditions and actually performs better in infertile soil — rich, fertile soil produces excessive, floppy growth.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; ravenna grass (Plume grass, Hardy pampas grass, Erianthus) is the cold-hardy alternative to pampas grass for northern zone 6–9 gardens — an enormous, dramatic, clump-forming grass that rises to 8–14 feet with wide, arching, blue-gray-green leaves developing attractive silvery and purplish tones in autumn, and produces enormous, feathery, silvery-white, pampas-like flower plumes in late summer that arch dramatically from the top of the plant and dry to a warm, creamy-tan for winter. The scale is truly impressive — a single established clump rivals the visual impact of a small tree and provides a genuine architectural focal point in the large-scale landscape. Hardy to zone 6 (unlike true pampas grass, Cortaderia selloana, which is limited to zone 7 or 8 in most regions), making it the choice for gardeners in zones 6–8 who want the pampas grass effect. Thrives in hot, dry, poor conditions. Can self-seed in some regions — monitor and remove unwanted seedlings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Ray Hartman ceanothus needs excellent drainage above all else and is intolerant of summer irrigation once established, which promotes root rot.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Ray Hartman ceanothus needs excellent drainage above all else and is intolerant of summer irrigation once established, which promotes root rot. A vigorous, large-growing hybrid between two California native ceanothus species, it produces masses of medium-blue flower clusters over glossy, deep green foliage in early spring, growing quickly into a substantial evergreen shrub or small multi-trunked tree that can be trained with a single leader for a more tree-like form. One of the most reliable and widely planted ceanothus hybrids in California native gardens, it tolerates poor soil and heat with essentially no supplemental water once established, and its abundant spring bloom is a major early-season draw for native bees. Water only during the first year or two of establishment, then withhold summer irrigation entirely, and prune lightly after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Raydon's Favorite Aster (Drought-Tolerant Native Aromatic Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Raydon's Favorite is one of the most widely planted aromatic aster cultivars, prized for exceptional drought tolerance and a dense, floriferous fall display.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Raydon's Favorite is a beloved selection of native aromatic aster, forming a dense, rounded mound of fragrant gray-green foliage that becomes smothered in masses of small, violet-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers in fall, providing an important late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and other pollinators when few other perennials are still blooming. It is exceptionally tolerant of heat, drought, and poor soil once established, thriving with minimal supplemental water even through Gulf South summers, and resists the powdery mildew that troubles many other asters in humid climates. Cut the plant back by about half in late spring to keep growth compact and promote the fullest fall bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification over winter for improved spring germination.
directions: A highly unusual native sunflower of the southeastern coastal plain entirely lacking ray flowers, bearing only chocolate-brown disk heads on stiff, upright stems in summer and fall. Native to wet flatwoods, longleaf pine savannas, and bog margins from North Carolina to Florida and Mississippi, it thrives in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil in full sun. Despite lacking petals, the dark disk heads attract specialist native bees and provide seed for songbirds through fall and winter. An unusual and conversation-worthy specimen for native savanna gardens and rain gardens in zones 7-9, it pairs well with other wet-flatwoods natives such as Liatris and native sedges.

common_name: Razzleberri Loropetalum (Dwarf Burgundy-Foliage Hot-Pink Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Razzleberri is a dwarf, mounding loropetalum selection with burgundy foliage and hot-pink flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, where the deepest foliage color develops. Razzleberri forms a dense, mounding shrub with rich burgundy-purple foliage held year-round and covered each spring in vivid hot-pink, fringe-petaled flowers, with foliage color holding better through summer heat than some older loropetalum selections. Its dwarf, mounded habit suits it to foundation plantings, low borders, and mass plantings without the need for constant pruning. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

common_name: Razzmatazz Coneflower (Pioneering Fully Double Hot-Pink Pompom Echinacea)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Razzmatazz was one of the first true fully double coneflowers introduced, bearing a dense hot-pink pompom with no visible cone.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Razzmatazz holds historical importance as one of the first true, stable, fully double coneflower cultivars ever introduced, bearing a dense, hot-pink pompom bloom with the central cone entirely replaced by a mass of small petaloids, a breakthrough form that opened the door to the many double coneflower cultivars bred since. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Recurvifolium is a wavy-leaved sport of Japanese privet long grown as a tough Southern hedge and screen shrub.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; established plants tolerate considerable heat, drought, and poor soil once rooted in. Recurvifolium is a distinctive selection of Japanese privet named for its glossy, deep-green leaves that curl and twist along their edges, giving the whole shrub a wavy, textured look that sets it apart from the flat-leaved species at a glance. Left unpruned it grows into a dense large shrub or small multi-trunked tree useful as a tall screen, but it also takes shearing well for a formal clipped hedge. Clusters of small white flowers appear in late spring with a fragrance some gardeners find heavy in close quarters, followed by blue-black berries that draw birds; site it away from bedrooms or patios if the bloom scent is a concern.

plant_note: Propagate from tissue culture or sow seeds (slow) or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; red Abyssinian banana does not produce offsets like Musa species and must be propagated by seed, division of the main trunk base, or tissue culture — it is a non-clumping, clonal specimen plant.
directions: Propagate from tissue culture or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; red Abyssinian banana is the most dramatically colored of all ornamental banana plants — a non-clumping, monocarpic (flowers once then dies) Ethiopian banana species in the cultivar 'Maurelii' that produces enormous, paddle-shaped leaves (up to 8 feet long) in a spectacular combination of deep maroon-red midrib, burgundy-red leaf margins and undersides, and dark-green to olive-green central leaf surface, creating a massive, bold, jewel-toned tropical foliage effect that is unlike any other large-leaved tropical plant. The purple-red coloration is most vivid on young leaves emerging from the center and fades somewhat as each leaf matures, but the overall plant maintains its rich, dark, dramatic coloring throughout. Unlike fruiting bananas (Musa), Ensete ventricosum is a non-clumping banana species that grows from a single, non-suckering pseudostem to 10–15 feet in zone 10–12, producing leaves throughout its vegetative phase before the terminal inflorescence and dying after setting seed. In zone 9, it is often grown as a summer annual, started fresh from tissue culture plants each spring for its spectacular single-season tropical display.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Red Alternanthera is used extensively in zone 9 as a colorful, low-growing bedding and border-edging plant — often planted in mass to create geometric patterns (carpet bedding) in formal garden designs. Shear plants lightly every 4–6 weeks to maintain compact, dense form and prevent legginess; unpruned plants become open and produce fewer of the intensely colored leaves. The color is most vivid in full sun; partial shade produces larger, slightly less vivid leaves. In zone 9 it performs as a warm-season annual (tender below about 35°F), though established plants may resprout from stems in mild winters.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil — Red Alternanthera produces the most vivid leaf color in full sun but tolerates partial shade and is often used in partially shaded border situations; Red Alternanthera (Alternanthera ficoidea 'Red') is a low-growing, densely leafed foliage annual producing small, narrow leaves in vivid shades of red, burgundy, and bronze-red — creating a solid color mass of warm, intensely pigmented foliage that is used in traditional carpet bedding, border edging, and colorful pattern planting. Unlike the more rounded, dark-red-leaved Alternanthera dentata varieties, A. ficoidea has smaller, narrower leaves and a lower, denser growth habit, making it particularly useful for tight geometric patterns and fine-textured edging where a compact, fine-textured plant is needed. The richly colored leaves provide the same seasonal color function as flowering annuals but with purely foliage-based appeal — valuable in designs where consistent, uniform color without the maintenance of deadheading or the variability of flower timing is preferred. Red Alternanthera thrives in zone 9's summer heat and humidity, which would stress many cool-season foliage plants, growing most vigorously and producing its most intensely colored leaves in the hottest months of the year.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or summer; unlike most Brugmansia, B. sanguinea is adapted to cool Andean conditions and actually prefers temperatures of 50–70°F for best bloom. In hot Gulf Coast summers it may decline — site in afternoon shade, keep well-watered, and expect the best display in spring and fall. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Root cuttings and grow in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in part shade; red angel's trumpet is the most distinctive Brugmansia species — unlike the white, pink, and yellow angels' trumpets (B. x candida and relatives) that prefer warm conditions, B. sanguinea is native to the cool, cloud forest elevations of the Andes (5,000–11,000 feet) in Peru, Chile, Colombia, and Ecuador, producing exceptionally large, pendant, bicolored tubular flowers that are red-orange at the flared tip fading to yellow at the base, with a prominent green calyx. The flowers are in continuous production on established plants and are pollinated by hummingbirds in their native habitat — making them strongly attractive to hummingbirds in cultivation. The cool-preference nature makes it better suited to coastal California and mild Pacific Northwest climates than to tropical Gulf Coast summers, where afternoon shade, ample water, and well-drained fertile soil are essential. All plant parts are highly toxic; contain scopolamine, atropine, and related tropane alkaloids.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Red Autumn Sage is a hardy, long-lived perennial shrub in zone 9 — established plants can persist for 10+ years with minimal care. Prune to 6–8 inches in late winter to remove dead wood and stimulate fresh, densely flowering new growth; without annual pruning plants become leggy and produce fewer flowers. In zone 9 blooms most heavily in spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) — flowering is reduced during the heat of July–August but rarely stops entirely. The small, tubular, vivid red flowers are one of the premier hummingbird nectar sources among all landscape plants.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — Red Autumn Sage is a Texas limestone native demanding excellent drainage and thriving in the lean, dry conditions that produce the most abundant flowering; Red Autumn Sage (Salvia greggii) is a small evergreen shrub native to the Chihuahuan Desert region of Texas and Mexico that has become one of the most valuable and widely planted ornamental sages for zones 7–9 — providing reliable, continuous flowering from spring through fall in the heat, drought, and alkaline soil conditions where most ornamental plants require intensive support. The vivid scarlet to cherry-red tubular flowers are produced in dense spikes on arching stems in successive flushes through the growing season, with the richest flowering in the cool-weather periods of spring and fall in zone 9. Salvia greggii is one of the most reliably effective hummingbird plants in the Gulf South — the tubular red flowers are specifically adapted to hummingbird pollination and attract Ruby-throated Hummingbirds and other hummingbird species wherever they occur in the plant's range. The combination of drought tolerance, heat tolerance, alkaline soil adaptation, compact evergreen habit, continuous bloom, and hummingbird value makes Red Autumn Sage effectively irreplaceable as a low-maintenance, wildlife-supporting perennial for the warmer, drier parts of zones 7–9.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; red baneberry is easily grown in any cool, moist, shaded site and spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding to form handsome clumps over time.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; red baneberry is easily grown in any cool, moist, shaded site and spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding to form handsome clumps over time. Actaea rubra is a native North American woodland perennial in the buttercup family with large, compound, twice-ternate leaves that give it a delicate, airy texture; in mid-spring it produces fluffy, white bottle-brush-like flower clusters on leafy stems, followed in summer by brilliant, glossy, red (occasionally white in form neglecta) berries in compact clusters on red pedicels that are among the most ornamental of any native woodland fruit but are highly toxic — all parts of the plant are poisonous. It is an excellent companion for black cohosh, white baneberry, ferns, and hostas in shaded woodland gardens; the red berries are eagerly eaten by birds and provide important late-summer wildlife food.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; red barrenwort establishes readily and spreads steadily to form dense colonies, and is one of the most cold-hardy epimedium hybrids available.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this popular hybrid between E. grandiflorum and E. alpinum produces small crimson-red and white bicolored flowers in spring just as striking red-tinted new foliage unfurls. The seasonal foliar interest extends into autumn when leaves again take on red and bronze tints before going fully dormant in colder zones. Cut back old leaves in late winter before new growth emerges to give the delicate spring flowers full prominence. Red barrenwort is one of the most cold-hardy epimedium hybrids, making it a reliable choice for gardens in zones 4–8 where other species may struggle.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Red Beauty colors most intensely with a little morning sun and consistently moist soil.
directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Red Beauty colors most intensely with a little morning sun and consistently moist soil. Fronds emerge with an unusually heavy wash of wine-red and burgundy across silvery-gray pinnae, carrying more red pigment and less green than most Japanese painted fern selections, an effect that intensifies as fronds mature through the season. Deciduous and easy-going, it dies back cleanly in fall and returns reliably each spring, combining beautifully with green-leaved hostas, heucheras, and other ferns where its unusual color can stand out. Keep soil evenly moist through summer and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Red Bells Enkianthus (Deep Red-Veined Bell-Flowered Selection)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Red Bells bears bell-shaped flowers with deeper red veining than the straight species, followed by brilliant fall color.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, in the same conditions favored by rhododendrons and azaleas. Red Bells bears dangling clusters of small, cream-based, bell-shaped flowers etched with noticeably deeper red-pink veining than the species form, held along horizontally tiered branches in late spring, followed in fall by a spectacular display of red, orange, and yellow foliage color that ranks among the finest of any woodland shrub. Its tiered, layered branching habit provides distinctive year-round structure even without flowers or fall color. It combines beautifully with rhododendrons, azaleas, and other acid-loving woodland shrubs sharing the same partial-shade, moisture-retentive growing conditions. Prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Philodendron squamiferum cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Provide a moss pole or rough climbing support for best leaf development — the leaf lobes become more deeply divided on climbing specimens. Use a well-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil. Maintain moderate humidity (50%+) for best appearance. Propagate readily from single-node stem cuttings. All parts are toxic if chewed.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Red Bristle Philodendron produces its largest, most dramatically lobed leaves with adequate bright indirect light and a climbing support to grow upward. Philodendron squamiferum is a climbing philodendron from French Guiana, Suriname, and northern Brazil, one of the most immediately distinctive and recognizable collector philodendrons because of its unique combination of leaf shape and petiole texture: the leaves are large (10–18 inches), deeply and irregularly lobed into five distinct lobes (like an oak leaf or a flattened hand), rich dark green, with a thick, leathery texture — but the plant's most distinctive feature is the petioles (leaf stalks), which are covered in dense, soft, bristle-like red hairs or scales. These bright rust-red to coral-red bristled petioles are unique among commonly grown aroids and give the plant the common names 'Red Bristle Philodendron' and 'Hairy Philodendron.' The contrast between the dark green lobed leaves and the vivid red furry stems creates an ornamental effect quite different from the smooth-stemmed philodendrons that dominate the market. The species is generally adaptable and grows well in indoor conditions with moderate care. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fresh seeds planted immediately after collecting in fall also establish reliably. All parts of the plant are toxic — the seeds especially so.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; red buckeye is one of the finest native shrubs for the shaded garden, producing upright panicles of brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers in April and May precisely timed to the return of ruby-throated hummingbirds from migration. The flowers are visited almost exclusively by hummingbirds and are among the most important early-season hummingbird plants available. It grows naturally as a forest understory shrub throughout the Southeast and performs exceptionally well in zone 8–9 Gulf Coast gardens in partial shade. The glossy, palmate compound leaves are attractive all season but the plant goes fully dormant in summer heat — mark its location and interplant with later-season companions. The large, mahogany-colored seeds are toxic to humans and livestock.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; red button ginger blooms most freely in partial shade and is one of the most shade-tolerant of the tropical gingers — it actually produces more flowers in dappled light than in full sun, where the foliage tends to bleach and the plant may experience heat stress.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; red button ginger is a Central American tropical spiral ginger that produces one of the most continuously ornamental flower displays of any shade-tolerant ginger — the inflorescence is a compact, cone-shaped structure of tightly overlapping, bright-red, waxy, button-like bracts from which small, orange-yellow, tubular flowers emerge one or two at a time throughout the warm season. The cone structure persists and remains ornamental even between flowering periods, providing months of red-cone interest. The plant has a distinctive habit characteristic of all Costus gingers — the leaves are arranged in a precise, slightly ascending spiral around each stem rather than the flat-spreading arrangement of other gingers, creating an elegant, corkscrew-like effect that is architecturally attractive. The stems die back after flowering, with new stems emerging from the base the following season. Red button ginger performs at its best in partial shade with consistent moisture, and is an excellent understory plant for the shaded tropical garden. Excellent near water features and in moist, shaded borders in zone 9–12.

common_name: Red Button Ginger / Scarlet Spiral Ginger
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once all danger of cold has passed, setting them 2-3 inches deep in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in a shaded or partially shaded location.
directions: Plant divisions in rich, well-draining soil in a shaded to partially shaded location, spacing clumps 24-36 inches apart to allow the glossy, spirally arranged leaves to develop their full architectural presence. Water regularly throughout the growing season to keep the soil evenly moist, and feed monthly with a balanced liquid fertilizer from spring through late summer to support the production of the dramatic scarlet cone-like inflorescences. Remove spent flowering canes at the base after blooms fade to encourage fresh new growth and repeated flushes of color. In zone 9 where light frost may occur, cut tops back and mulch the root zone deeply in fall to protect the rhizomes through winter.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once temperatures are reliably warm, setting them 2-3 inches deep in humus-rich soil in a partially shaded position.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, organically rich soil in partial shade, setting rhizomes 2-3 inches deep and spacing clumps 3-5 feet apart to accommodate their spiraling, upright canes. Water consistently during the growing season, and apply a high-potassium fertilizer monthly from spring through late summer to fuel the production of the vivid red terminal bracts. Cut older canes to the ground after they finish flowering to encourage fresh growth from the base. In zone 9 where light frost may occur, mulch the root zone heavily in fall to protect the rhizomes through winter.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; red campion is dioecious (separate male and female plants) — sow generous quantities so that both sexes are represented. It self-sows prolifically and can naturalize readily in hedgerows, woodland edges, and semi-shaded garden areas. Plants live 2–4 years but self-sow continuously.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to woodland edge; red campion is a widespread European wildflower of woodland edges, hedgerows, and shaded banks — among the most common and cheerful May-flowering wildflowers of the British countryside, producing branched stems of deeply rose-pink, five-petaled, notched flowers from May through September in a cheerful, informal, prolific display that weaves among other wildflowers and garden plants with naturalizing ease. It is dioecious — male and female flowers occur on separate plants, the males slightly smaller and more numerous — and freely hybridizes with the white campion (Silene latifolia) where both occur, producing the intermediate hybrid Silene x hampeana with pale-pink flowers. A classic companion to bluebells and cow parsley in the British spring and early-summer hedgerow. In the garden it naturalizes beautifully in semi-shaded borders, woodland-edge gardens, and cottage-garden plantings, self-sowing to maintain colonies without invasive behavior. Double-flowered forms ('Flore Pleno') with pompom-like blooms are available and particularly ornamental.

common_name: Red Charm Peony (Deep Crimson-Red Bomb-Form Exhibition Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Charm is a benchmark bomb-form exhibition peony in deep crimson-red.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Red Charm bears large, tightly domed bomb-form flowers in deep, velvety crimson-red, the rounded petaloid center rising from a ring of broader outer guard petals, a classic exhibition form that has made it a benchmark red peony among collectors and breeders since its introduction. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for earlier bloom.
directions: Each medium bloom showcases deep, sultry red petals around a vivid yellow center on compact, deer-resistant plants only six to ten inches tall. Sow directly after the last frost or start indoors a few weeks early for a quicker show. These marigolds thrive in full sun and average, well-drained soil. Deadhead regularly to keep them flowering until frost. Their compact size makes them ideal for edging beds, borders, and containers while drawing in pollinators.

plant_note: Surface-sow on prepared soil in early spring or fall; needs light and does not transplant well.
directions: Scatter the fine seed on the soil surface in early spring or fall, as it needs light and resents transplanting. This iconic Flanders poppy opens tissue-paper scarlet petals with dark centers in late spring and early summer. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil where its deep taproot makes it drought-tolerant. Let flowers form seed pods and it will self-sow generously for years to come.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Red Crown Cactus flowers most reliably when given a cool, dry winter rest followed by increased water and light in spring.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Red Crown Cactus flowers most reliably when given a cool, dry winter rest followed by increased water and light in spring. Small, flattened, globular stems covered in short, fine spines cluster readily at the base into a low mat, and in spring the plant produces a ring of brilliant orange-red, funnel-shaped flowers encircling the crown, disproportionately large and vivid for such a small cactus body. Native to high-elevation grasslands in Bolivia and Argentina, it is one of the most reliable and free-flowering of the small globular cacti, often blooming as a very young plant and continuing for years with minimal care. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide a distinct cooler, drier winter rest to trigger the next season's bloom, and separate offsets to propagate a colony.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; red dome blanketflower is a compact Southwest native adapted to desert grassland and dry mesas, more finely textured than the common bedding blanketflower.
directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; red dome blanketflower is a compact Southwestern desert grassland native with finely cut, grayish-green leaves and cheerful yellow, red-based flowers surrounding a domed reddish-brown center, blooming over a long season from late spring through fall in response to warm-season rainfall. It is more finely textured and lower-growing than the widely sold hybrid bedding blanketflowers, with a wiry, deep-rooted habit suited to harsh, dry, exposed sites where richer garden perennials fail. Deadheading extends the bloom season, though the plant reseeds readily on its own in lean, undisturbed soil, often naturalizing into a self-sustaining colony over a few years. It tolerates intense heat, reflected sun, and extended drought once established, needing no supplemental irrigation beyond occasional deep watering in the harshest dry spells.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Dragon Japanese maple holds its deep red color better in more sun than many other laceleaf cultivars, but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Dragon Japanese maple holds its deep red color better in more sun than many other laceleaf cultivars, but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Finely dissected, lacy, deep burgundy-red leaves cover a compact, mounding, weeping laceleaf form that holds its rich color from spring through summer better than many older red-leaved cultivars, which often fade toward green by midsummer, before finishing with a bright crimson fall display. Its dense, cascading, umbrella-like habit makes it a striking specimen for a container, rock garden, or the front of a shaded border, providing structure and color even without flowers. Provide afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, keep soil consistently moist but well drained, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through summer heat.

common_name: Red Drift Rose (Low-Growing Red Groundcover Rose)
plant_note: Plant container roses in late winter through spring in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in full sun; Red Drift requires at least 6 hours of direct sun daily for best flowering; in zone 9 the long warm season allows nearly year-round bloom with only a brief winter rest.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Red Drift is the red-flowered member of the Drift series of groundcover roses — a series developed by Meilland International that combines the disease resistance and landscape adaptability of groundcover roses with the repeat-blooming, dense coverage of modern landscape roses. Red Drift stays very low (12–18 inches tall, 24–36 inches wide), creating a carpet of semi-double, rich red flowers from spring through hard frost. The Drift series was specifically bred to be self-cleaning — spent flowers drop cleanly without deadheading, maintaining a tidy appearance without maintenance pruning. This self-cleaning quality combined with outstanding disease resistance (exceptional black spot and powdery mildew resistance compared to standard tea roses), heat tolerance, and continuous bloom makes Drift roses among the most low-maintenance roses available. Red Drift's low habit makes it outstanding for edging borders, planting on slopes for erosion control, ground covering under taller plants, and mass plantings where its red carpet effect and long bloom season are maximized. In zone 9, Red Drift blooms from February through December with only brief pauses; the disease resistance is maintained even in zone 9's humid summers when black spot devastates unresistant roses. A truly modern, low-maintenance landscape rose.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Red Emerald philodendron is a vigorous climber that develops larger leaves when given vertical support.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Red Emerald philodendron is a vigorous climber that develops larger leaves when given vertical support. Glossy, elongated heart-shaped leaves in rich emerald green are set off by wine-red new growth, petioles, and stems, a classic color combination that made this one of the most widely grown climbing philodendrons since its introduction decades ago. As a true climbing aroid it develops larger, more mature foliage and stronger red coloring when trained up a moss pole or trellis rather than left to trail, and it grows quickly under good indoor light with minimal care. Wipe dust from the glossy leaves periodically, provide bright indirect light for the best stem color, and prune to control length and encourage branching.

common_name: Red Emperor Tulip (Fosteriana Type Very Early Giant Red Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Red Emperor is a Fosteriana-type tulip prized for blooming very early in the tulip season with unusually large flowers on relatively short, sturdy stems.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Red Emperor, also known as Madame Lefeber, is a Fosteriana-type tulip celebrated for opening enormous, brilliant scarlet-red flowers very early in spring, well ahead of most other tulip types, giving an early burst of bold color while many other bulbs are just emerging. Its wide, bowl-shaped blooms open fully in sun to reveal a black-based interior that adds drama to the display, and the sturdy, relatively short stems hold up well to wind and rain. As with other tulips, mild-winter Southern gardens generally get the best results treating it as a fresh fall bulb planting rather than relying on it to perennialize reliably.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; typically propagated by semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; red escallonia produces glossy, aromatic, dark green leaves and clusters of small, tubular, crimson-red flowers over a long summer bloom season that draws hummingbirds and bees. It is a mainstay hedge and screening shrub of coastal California and Pacific Northwest gardens because of its outstanding tolerance for salt spray, wind, and fog, though it prefers more consistent moisture than a true desert xeriscape plant. Shear or hand-prune after the main flush of bloom to keep an informal hedge dense, and site it where air circulates freely to minimize leaf spot in humid coastal conditions.

common_name: Red Flash Ageratum (Unusual Brick-Red Floss Flower)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; performs in full sun to light afternoon shade.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost. Red Flash breaks from the usual blue-and-white ageratum palette with fuzzy flower clusters in a deep brick-red to rusty terracotta shade, set off by dark bronze-tinged green foliage. Its mounding, well-branched habit suits mixed containers and warm-toned borders where typical powder-blue ageratum would clash. It blooms steadily from early summer to frost and is more self-cleaning than older ageratum strains.

common_name: Red Flash Caladium (Red-Centered Green-Margined Fancy Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Red Flash is one of the most sun-tolerant caladium cultivars, performing acceptably in 3–4 hours of morning sun.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to partial sun; Red Flash is one of the most striking and popular fancy-leaved caladium cultivars — producing large, heart-shaped leaves with vivid red centers, green margins, and distinctive pink to white spots scattered across the red central area, creating a complex, colorful pattern unique among caladium cultivars. The red center, spotted texture, and dark-green margins combine into a leaf with more visual complexity and depth than solid-colored cultivars. Red Flash is notable among caladiums for its higher sun tolerance — it performs acceptably in morning sun positions (3–4 hours direct sun) that would bleach or damage most white-leaved caladiums. This sun tolerance makes Red Flash more versatile for partially shaded locations that receive some direct morning light. The large, boldly patterned leaves create outstanding tropical texture in mixed shade plantings, container gardens, and as mass ground covers under trees. In zone 9, Red Flash produces foliage from late April or May through October before cold temperatures trigger dormancy. The tubers increase in size each year, producing progressively larger and more numerous leaves as the clumps mature. Red Flash is also well-suited to container production, where the combination of good sun tolerance and striking foliage makes it an outstanding patio and deck plant.

common_name: Red Fountain Grass (Burgundy-Purple Tropical Ornamental Grass)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; 'Rubrum' is a sterile cultivar — it does not set viable seed, unlike the invasive straight species Pennisetum setaceum, making it safe to plant without concern for naturalization.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; Red Fountain Grass ('Rubrum') is one of the most visually dramatic warm-season ornamental grasses for Gulf South gardens — producing mounding, arching clumps of narrow, burgundy-purple to dark wine-red leaves topped by reddish-bronze to copper-colored bottle-brush flower plumes in summer and fall that create an elegant, soft-textured, colorful mass that stands out brilliantly against green or silver companions. The foliage color — maintained throughout the growing season from spring through fall rather than only at bloom time — provides a sustained burgundy accent that few other ornamental grasses offer. The 'Rubrum' cultivar is sterile and does not set viable seed, making it non-invasive despite the parent species (Pennisetum setaceum) being a serious invasive in some warm climates (Hawaii, California) — the sterility of 'Rubrum' is an important ecological distinction. In zone 9, Red Fountain Grass is reliably perennial, dying back in cold winters but returning from the roots in spring; in zone 9b and 10, it may remain semi-evergreen through mild winters. Drought-tolerant once established and excellent in full-sun, reflected-heat positions that challenge many ornamental grasses. Outstanding in containers, as a specimen accent, in mixed borders, and in combination with silver companions (dusty miller, Powis Castle artemisia) where the burgundy-red and silver combination is striking.

plant_note: Divide clumps by separating rhizomes with a sharp spade in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; red ginger blooms best in bright light but tolerates the partial shade under high-canopy trees in zone 10–12 landscapes.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; red ginger (Ostrich plume ginger, pink cone ginger) is one of the most visually dramatic tropical ornamentals available, producing tall, cane-like stems bearing long, glossy, banana-like leaves and topped by spectacular upright or arching flower spikes with densely packed, overlapping bracts in vivid scarlet-red, pink, or white — the bracts (not petals) are the showy feature, lasting for months as both living spikes and cut flower material. The plant is the dominant decorative ginger seen in Hawaiian lei-making and floral arrangements worldwide. Small bulbils often develop in the flower head after bloom and can be removed and replanted. In zone 10–12 it is essentially everblooming. Excellent combined with bird of paradise, heliconias, and tropical foliage plants for a lush, tropical garden effect.

common_name: Red Head Fountain Grass (Oversized Dark Red-Brown Bottlebrush Plumes)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Head is a larger-growing fountain grass selection with oversized, dark reddish-brown bottlebrush flower spikes.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; fountain grass is heat- and drought-tolerant once established. Red Head grows notably larger than the common Hameln fountain grass, producing oversized, dark reddish-brown bottlebrush flower spikes above arching green foliage from late summer into fall, a bolder and darker flower display than most other Pennisetum alopecuroides selections. Its larger scale and dramatic plumes make it a strong specimen or focal point in a sunny mixed border. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Red Heart Rose of Sharon (Classic White with Red Center Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Heart is an older, long-cultivated rose of sharon and, unlike the sterile National Arboretum triploid introductions, can self-seed, so remove spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Red Heart is a classic, long-cultivated rose of sharon bearing large, single, pure white flowers with a bold crimson-red center, a simple but striking color combination that has kept it in continuous cultivation for generations. Blooming heavily from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub, it is tough, heat-tolerant, and easy to grow in average garden soil, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and encourage the current season's flowering wood.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Red Hills azalea is native to the Gulf Coastal Plain of Alabama and Georgia and is well adapted to the heat and humidity of a Deep South garden.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Red Hills azalea is native to the Gulf Coastal Plain of Alabama and Georgia and is well adapted to the heat and humidity of a Deep South garden. Rhododendron colemanii is a large, vigorous deciduous azalea only formally described in 2008 from the Red Hills region of Alabama and Georgia, producing intensely fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers in shades of cream, pale pink, orange, and yellow in late spring to early summer, with considerable variation in color among individual plants. As a genuine Gulf South native azalea, it is exceptionally well suited to zone 8–9 gardens where many other native azaleas struggle with heat and humidity, making it an excellent choice for a naturalized woodland border in the Deep South. It tolerates more heat than mountain-native azaleas but still needs consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil and the dappled light of a high pine or hardwood canopy to perform well.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed in spring.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep and maintain even moisture at 65–75°F until germination. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — good drainage is critical, especially in winter, as plants rot in waterlogged conditions. The torch-like flower spikes transition from red or orange in bud to yellow as the florets open, creating a two-toned effect that attracts hummingbirds throughout summer and fall. In zones 5–6 tie the leaves together and mulch deeply around the crown before the first hard freeze to protect the growing point.

subcategory: dark-barked ornamental gum with pink to red flowers
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; red ironbark is one of the more cold-hardy ornamental eucalyptus — surviving to zone 7b in sheltered, well-drained positions. It is a long-lived tree with deeply furrowed, dark-red to almost black, persistent ironbark that provides year-round structural interest. The flower color is variable — white, cream, pink, and deep crimson forms occur, with 'Rosea' being the most ornamental dark-pink selection. Excellent for birds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; red ironbark is the most structurally dramatic ornamental eucalyptus for cold climates (surviving to zone 7b) — a long-lived, stately tree developing over decades a deeply furrowed, persistent, very dark red-brown to almost black-red ironbark (the iron-like, very hard, deeply grooved bark that never sheds as in the smooth gums) that creates a powerful, dark, architectural trunk structure of great character in mature specimens. The contrast of the very dark, almost black ironbark with the blue-gray-green, lance-shaped leaves and, in winter and spring, clusters of white to cream to pink to vivid crimson-rose flowers (depending on form) is a multi-season, multi-textural ornamental composition of considerable sophistication. The dark bark catching winter light against pink flowers in the background blue-gray of the canopy is one of the most striking winter tree compositions available in zones 7–11. The cultivar 'Rosea' produces the most vivid, deep-pink to rose-red flowers. Outstanding as a long-term specimen tree where its slow development into a structurally impressive large tree is a generational investment in a garden.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in shade to part shade; Red ivy is a low, spreading tropical Southeast Asian groundcover grown for its distinctive leaves — metallic dark green-gray with a purple reverse and a wrinkled, waffle-textured surface — it is one of the finest shade groundcovers for tropical gardens and performs well in containers and hanging baskets.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; keep consistently moist for best foliage color. Hemigraphis alternata (red ivy or waffle plant) is a low-growing, creeping tropical perennial from Java and other parts of Southeast Asia in the acanthus family (Acanthaceae), grown primarily as an ornamental for the distinctive foliage: the leaves are oval to heart-shaped, with a deeply wrinkled, puckered, waffle-like texture on the upper surface (hence 'waffle plant') and are metallic dark greenish-gray with silver highlights on top, contrasting with a vivid, wine-red to magenta-purple underside. The undersurface color gives the plant its other common name, 'red ivy,' especially as it spreads along the ground and the underside is visible. Stems root readily at the nodes, allowing the plant to spread as a groundcover in warm, humid conditions. Small, white, tubular flowers are produced but are inconspicuous — the foliage is the feature. As a shade container or hanging basket plant, red ivy is outstanding: the trailing stems with metallic-textured leaves create an elegant, unusual display. In zone 10–12, it functions as a year-round shade groundcover. It is also popular as a tropical aquarium plant and terrarium subject. One of the most distinctive-looking low groundcovers for warm, humid shade.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; red justicia tolerates more shade and slightly more regular water than chuparosa, its desert-wash relative in the same family.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; red justicia is a compact, rounded Arizona and Sonoran shrub with small, bright green leaves and clusters of vivid red-orange, tubular flowers produced heavily in spring and again in fall, with lighter, sporadic bloom through summer in favorable conditions. It is a reliable, easy-care hummingbird plant for desert gardens, tolerating both reflected heat in full sun and the dappled light of a partially shaded courtyard or wash-side planting. Established plants are quite drought tolerant, though occasional deep watering during the hottest, driest stretches keeps the foliage fuller and encourages more consistent flowering. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to maintain a dense, rounded form, and expect frost damage to the top growth in a hard freeze, with recovery from the base typical the following spring.

common_name: Red King Humbert Canna (Classic Bronze-Leaf Heirloom Canna)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes after danger of frost has passed, 3-4 inches deep in rich, heavily amended soil; this early-1900s heirloom pairs bold bronze-maroon foliage with large orange-red flowers.
directions: Give this heirloom canna full sun and steady moisture, including standing water at pond margins where it thrives. Introduced in the early 1900s, it remains one of the most widely grown bronze-leaved cannas for its combination of dark maroon-red foliage and vivid orange-scarlet blooms that appear from summer through fall. Deadhead spent flower stalks to prolong bloom, and in zone 8 either mulch heavily to overwinter rhizomes in place or lift and store them after the first killing frost. Divide congested clumps every two to three years to keep flowering strong.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in its native range (California and Oregon); seeds benefit from cool temperatures and natural cold-moist stratification to break dormancy and germinate in late winter or early spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky or sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; red larkspur is a California and southern Oregon native of shaded canyon slopes and mixed evergreen forest edges, distinguished from all other delphiniums by its unusual orange-red to scarlet flowers — a color virtually unheard of in the genus. The tubular, upward-facing flowers are exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds. It is a short-lived perennial or annual in cultivation and goes summer-dormant in dry California summers, so allow the foliage to die back naturally without summer irrigation. Like all delphiniums, all parts are toxic.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Red Latan Palm is a striking, slow-growing, large fan palm endemic to the island of Réunion in the Mascarene Islands — critically endangered in the wild — bearing enormous, circular, blue-green fan fronds with distinctive red midribs, petioles, and leaf sheaths in juvenile plants that give it an extraordinary color display unique among fan palms.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy, lean to average, alkaline-tolerant soil; Latania lontaroides is adapted to well-drained coastal soils and tolerates salt spray, drought, and exposed coastal conditions — avoid waterlogged clay soils. Latania lontaroides (Red Latan Palm or Latanier Rouge) is a large, majestic, slow-growing fan palm critically endangered in its native habitat — it is endemic to the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean Mascarene Islands, where remaining wild populations are severely threatened by habitat loss and invasive species. The palm is celebrated for one of the most spectacular color displays in the palm family: juvenile and young plants (up to 10–15 years old) bear enormous, circular fan fronds with vivid blood-red to crimson midribs, petioles, and sheaths that contrast dramatically against the blue-green frond blades — the color gradually fading to reddish-brown and then gray as plants mature. Even mature plants retain reddish-tinged frond bases and produce an imposing crown of large, slightly glaucous, waxy fan fronds on a stout, prominently ring-marked trunk. Latania lontaroides is dioecious; both male and female plants display the color. Widely cultivated in botanical gardens and by palm collectors worldwide for its extraordinary juvenile coloration. Well adapted to coastal limestone soils, salt spray, and drought conditions in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck of the bulb at or just above soil surface; in zone 9 plant January–March for spring bloom or September for fall bloom. In zone 9 amaryllis bulbs can remain in the ground year-round as permanent perennials, blooming in spring (March–April) and sometimes again in fall. Established outdoor clumps in zone 9 bloom prolifically with minimal care. When grown in containers (as holiday houseplants), plant with 1/3 of the bulb above the potting mix; a single large bulb will typically produce 2 scapes each bearing 4 large flowers. Allow the foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering to rebuild the bulb for next season.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Red Lion Amaryllis performs best with some shade protection in zone 9's summer heat, which can stress the bulb during summer dormancy; Red Lion is the defining red amaryllis cultivar — a large-flowered, velvety, deep red to scarlet selection that has become the standard commercial red amaryllis in the US market, producing the classic amaryllis flower form: massive, trumpet-shaped blooms 6–8 inches across borne in groups of 4 on thick, hollow scapes that emerge directly from the bulb. The bold, trumpet-form flowers in vivid red with a subtle lighter central stripe represent the most widely recognized and purchased amaryllis color — available in virtually every garden center and holiday gift catalog and producing a dramatic indoor or outdoor floral display that few other bulb flowers can match in sheer size and color impact. In zone 9, outdoors, Red Lion amaryllis is a permanent garden perennial rather than a temporary holiday novelty — the large bulbs naturalize in the ground, multiplying steadily over years and producing spring flower displays of increasing size as clumps develop. The combination of easy culture, spectacular flowers, and permanent naturalization in zone 9 makes amaryllis one of the most rewarding large-flowered bulbs available for Gulf South gardens.

plant_note: Insert stem cuttings 1 inch into fine aquarium gravel or planted-tank substrate in small groups; space groups several inches apart to allow the reddish foliage to fill in as a mid-ground or background mass.
directions: A native wetland stem plant of the southeastern and south-central United States, cultivated submersed in freshwater aquaria as one of the most reliable red-toned planted-tank species. Leaf color shifts from olive-green to coppery red as light intensity increases, so grow under medium to high aquarium lighting for the best coloration; CO2 injection and a nitrogen-limited, iron-rich fertilizing routine intensify the red tones further. It roots readily from stem cuttings pushed into nutrient-rich substrate and tolerates a wide range of water hardness and temperature. Trim and replant stem tops regularly to keep growth bushy rather than leggy.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring before flowering or immediately after blooms fade, splitting the crown into sections with both roots and foliage. Replant promptly in prepared, moisture-retentive soil in shade and water thoroughly. Cut back any tattered foliage after dividing to reduce transplant stress.
directions: Grow red lungwort in full to partial shade in soil enriched with compost or leaf mold, where it will spread steadily into an attractive groundcover. Divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding, replanting at the same depth and watering well. The unspotted, velvety evergreen leaves are an ornamental feature year-round; cut back any damaged foliage in late winter before new growth emerges. Good air circulation and consistent moisture help prevent the powdery mildew that can affect lungworts in warm, dry conditions.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown propagules or container stock in spring in coastal, estuarine, or tidal wetland substrate in full sun; Red Mangrove is viviparous — the seed germinates on the parent tree, producing a cigar-shaped propagule that drops and anchors in the mud. Planting in protected tidal areas with shallow water and fine sediment gives the best establishment results. Never plant Red Mangrove outside of its natural range.
directions: Red Mangrove is one of the most ecologically important coastal trees in the subtropical and tropical Americas, forming the seaward fringe of mangrove forests along sheltered tidal coasts, estuaries, and coastal lagoons of Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean, where its arching prop roots create a complex three-dimensional habitat supporting hundreds of species of fish, invertebrates, birds, and reptiles. The species is viviparous — the seeds germinate on the parent tree itself, producing cigar-shaped propagules up to 12 inches long that drop into the water and drift with currents before anchoring in tidal mudflats and developing new trees. Red Mangrove forests provide irreplaceable ecological services including coastal erosion control, storm surge buffering, carbon sequestration, and water quality filtration; removing them is illegal in Florida and most coastal states. Plant nursery-grown material only in appropriate tidal coastal zones in full sun in Zones 9–11; Red Mangrove is cold-sensitive and should not be planted north of its natural range.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately wet soil in full sun; red maple establishes readily and grows quickly. Avoid alkaline or compacted soils, which cause chlorosis and stunted growth.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun for best fall color; red maple is one of the most widely distributed and commonly planted native trees in eastern North America, naturally ranging from Newfoundland to Florida and adaptable to an enormous range of soil moisture conditions from wet bottomlands to dry upland ridges. True to its name, red maple puts on a red display in virtually every season: tiny red flowers cluster on bare branches in late winter (often the earliest tree to bloom), red samaras (winged seeds) ripen in spring, the leaf stalks are red through summer, and fall foliage blazes in brilliant shades of orange-red to crimson. The samaras are consumed by squirrels, grosbeaks, and finches; red maple is also a significant larval host plant for the Cecropia moth and numerous other native insects. With a growth rate of 1.5–2.5 feet per year and wide site adaptability, it is one of the most practical large native shade trees for gardens of all sizes.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for earlier bloom.
directions: This color-shifting marigold is deep burgundy in cool weather, then develops splashes of yellow as temperatures warm and reverts to solid burgundy when it cools again. Sow directly after the last frost or start indoors for earlier blooms. Full sun and well-drained soil produce the sturdiest, most colorful plants. Deadhead often to prolong flowering through the season. It makes a striking garden hedge and attracts pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; red milkweed grows naturally in freshwater and brackish marshes, wet pine flatwoods, and tidal ditches of the Coastal Plain. Tolerates seasonal flooding but not prolonged submersion.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun at pond margins, rain gardens, and tidal wetland edges; red milkweed is one of the most brilliantly colored of all native milkweeds, producing vivid, bicolored flowers with red-orange reflexed petals and orange hoods — the most intensely colored flower heads in the Asclepias genus. It grows naturally in freshwater and brackish marshes and wet pine flatwoods of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, making it ideally suited to rain gardens and wet bioswales in zone 9a. The striking flowers attract monarchs, swallowtails, and a wide range of other pollinators, and the plant is an important monarch host plant in Gulf Coast wetlands. The tall, narrow habit with narrow, willow-like leaves gives it a graceful, architectural form in the moist garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or small starts in spring into very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Red Mountain ice plant is a cold-hardy South African hardy ice plant selection valued for its intense red-orange flower color.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Red Mountain ice plant forms a dense, low mat of small succulent leaves smothered in late spring to early summer with vivid red-orange, satiny flowers that hold their color intensity better in heat than many other hardy ice plant selections. It is part of a group of cold-hardy Delosperma species and hybrids that have expanded ice plant use well beyond the frost-free regions where tender South African species are normally limited, tolerating winters that would kill Lampranthus or Aptenia outright. Sharp drainage remains essential, since winter wet rather than cold is the main threat to this otherwise tough and drought-tolerant groundcover. Use it in rock gardens, gravel mulch beds, and dry slopes where its mat-forming habit and long bloom season provide reliable color with minimal maintenance once established.

common_name: Red October Big Bluestem (Native Prairie Grass with Wine-Red Fall Color)
