directions: Site in humus-rich soil that stays reliably moist and add a couple inches of mulch to prevent the shallow root system from drying between waterings. Part shade with protection from hot afternoon sun keeps the bright pink plumes from fading quickly. One of the earliest-blooming Arendsii astilbes, it sends up dense, bubblegum-pink flower spikes over glossy dark green foliage in early summer, extending the astilbe bloom season when paired with later cultivars. It reads well massed along a shaded path or combined with hostas and heucheras for season-long texture.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in lean, well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic soil in full sun; rhizomatous little bluestem differs from common little bluestem (S. scoparium) by having shallow rhizomes that allow it to spread into a loose, spreading mat rather than a tight bunch — making it more effective as a groundcover grass.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, dry to moderately moist, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rhizomatous little bluestem is a Gulf Coastal Plain endemic closely related to the widely cultivated little bluestem (S. scoparium) but with the important additional trait of short rhizomes that allow the plant to spread into a loose colony — a significant advantage for erosion control on sandy slopes and for naturalizing large dry areas with a weed-suppressing native grass groundcover. The blue-green summer foliage, silvery-white fall seed heads, and brilliant copper-bronze winter color mirror the ornamental qualities of common little bluestem, while the spreading habit provides better coverage of large areas. Native to dry pine flatwoods, sandhills, and sandy openings in the Gulf states from Florida to Texas. An outstanding native grass for large-scale sandy slope plantings and mass groundcover applications in the warm-season Gulf South garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, setting the root ball slightly high with a thick mulch of pine bark or leaf litter over the shallow roots.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, setting the root ball slightly high with a thick mulch of pine bark or leaf litter over the shallow roots. Choose a site in dappled woodland shade or a boggy edge where soil stays cool and evenly damp, since this species naturally grows in bog margins, wet thickets, and open coniferous woods across the northeastern United States and eastern Canada. In May, before its leaves fully expand, the low twiggy shrub covers itself in clusters of rosy-purple flowers with an unusual two-lipped shape. It is one of the hardiest and most cold-tolerant native azaleas and works well in a naturalized woodland or rain garden planting where taller shade trees keep the summer sun off its foliage.

plant_note: Plant container-grown palms in spring in a wind-sheltered full-sun location with fertile, well-drained soil; in zone 9 choose a warm microclimate near a south-facing wall to protect from brief freezes.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with consistent moisture; the ribbon fan palm is prized for its enormous fan leaves whose outer leaflets droop into graceful, ribbon-like weeping tips that set it apart from other fan palms. Mature specimens can reach 50 feet with individual leaves spanning 10 feet, making this an architectural statement palm for large landscapes and parks. It is among the more cold-tolerant of the Livistona genus and can handle brief dips into the upper 20s°F when established in a sheltered microclimate. Fertilize three times per year with a slow-release palm fertilizer high in magnesium and manganese to maintain the deep green frond color.

common_name: Ribbon Orchid (Long-Petaled Bulbophyllum, Whip Orchid, Long-Sepal Bulbophyllum)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to partial direct morning light with high humidity; Bulbophyllum longissimum is grown for the extraordinary length of its lateral sepals — flowers on well-grown specimens produce thread-like sepal extensions 8–12 inches (sometimes to 20 cm) long that hang from the flower in whip-like filaments. The flowers are pale yellow to cream with pink to purple spotting and the long sepal threads, which wave gently in air movement. The inflorescence itself is only 3–4 inches in main flower size, but the hanging filaments create a dramatically different visual impact. Intermediate to warm temperatures. The flowers have a mild unpleasant odor for the first few days. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow mounted on cork bark or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to partial direct light with good humidity and air movement — Ribbon Orchid is one of the most extraordinary of the long-sepal Bulbophyllum species and is grown entirely for the remarkable visual effect of its hanging, whip-like lateral sepal filaments. Bulbophyllum longissimum is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Thailand, Malaysia, and the Malay Peninsula — one of a distinctive group of Bulbophyllum species (section Cirrhopetalum or Cirrhopetalum alliance) in which the lateral sepals of the flowers are extended into long, thread-like filaments that can reach extraordinary lengths. In B. longissimum, the lateral sepal extensions are particularly dramatic: in well-grown specimens, these filaments reach 8–12 inches (to 20+ cm), hanging from the flower in graceful, whip-like threads that wave in the slightest air movement. The flower itself is 3–4 inches in the main sepal-and-petal body — pale yellow to cream with irregular pink to purple spotting — and the thread filaments emerge from the tips of the lateral sepals. The single-flower (or occasionally 2-flower) inflorescences emerge on short stems from the base of the pseudobulbs. The visual effect of several flowers in bloom simultaneously — each with its pair of long, waving white threads hanging from the flower body — is unique and unforgettable among orchids. The flowers produce a mild, unpleasant odor for the first 1–3 days of blooming to attract fly pollinators, then the odor dissipates. An extraordinary orchid for collectors interested in unusual flower forms. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on well-drained to moist, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil; rice button aster self-sows prolifically once established and tolerates a wide range of soil moisture from moist meadows to moderately dry areas. It spreads by rhizomes to form colonies in appropriate conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; rice button aster is one of the most floriferous and adaptable of the native fall asters, producing clouds of tiny white to pale lavender flowers with yellow centers (the disk turns reddish with age) from late August through November on much-branched, bushy stems. The individual flowers are noticeably small — about the size of a grain of rice — but they are produced in such enormous numbers that a single plant in full bloom appears to be covered in a white mist. This is one of the most important late-season nectar plants in the Southeast, attracting dozens of bee species, butterflies, and other pollinators when few other wildflowers remain in bloom. The abundant seeds feed songbirds into winter. Native across the entire eastern US from the Gulf Coast to New England, it is reliably adapted to zone 9a gardens.

plant_note: Root small clusters of stem segments after a brief callusing period in a loose, well-drained orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light to light shade; this epiphyte grows on trees and rocks in humid South American forests and tolerates lower light better than most cacti.
directions: Grow in a loose, well-drained orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light to light shade, keeping it lightly moist and misting occasionally to mimic its humid native habitat. Native to the rainforest canopies of Brazil and Argentina, this spineless jungle cactus branches profusely into dense, airy clusters of tiny cylindrical, rice-grain-like segments, giving mature plants a soft, coral-like texture that spills attractively over a hanging basket rim. Small cream-white flowers appear along the stems in spring, followed by translucent pinkish-white berries. It is more shade-tolerant and humidity-loving than most cacti and should never be allowed to dry out completely for long periods, though standing water and heavy, poorly drained soil will still cause stem rot.

plant_note: Sow or press seed into consistently wet to saturated soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; rice cutgrass thrives at pond margins, ditches, and other permanently moist to shallowly flooded sites.
directions: Plant in consistently wet to saturated soil, or shallow standing water at the immediate pond edge, in full sun to partial shade; rice cutgrass is a rhizomatous native perennial grass of marshes, wet ditches, and stream banks throughout most of North America, spreading steadily by underground rhizomes to stabilize saturated soil and shorelines. Fine, harshly barbed leaf margins give the plant its common name and deter grazing wildlife and careless handling alike, while airy, drooping seed heads appear in late summer and provide food for waterfowl and songbirds. It is a valuable choice for rain garden basins, bioswales, and pond-margin plantings where its spreading habit helps filter runoff and control erosion in consistently wet ground. Because it spreads aggressively in ideal wet conditions, confine it with a barrier or ample open space rather than placing it in a small, mixed wetland planting.

plant_note: Divide suckers in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost danger has passed; rice paper plant spreads by underground stolons and requires ample space — allow 6–8 feet on all sides. Cut to ground after frost in zone 8; it rebounds vigorously from the root.
directions: Divide underground stolons or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; rice paper plant (Chinese rice paper plant) is a bold, dramatic Asian shrub that produces some of the largest leaves of any hardy to zone 8 plant — enormous, deeply lobed, palmate leaves that can reach 3 feet or more across on stems that rise to 6–15 feet, creating an instantly tropical, jungle-like effect with no equivalent in temperate gardening. The felted undersides of the leaves provide a contrasting silver-gray texture. The traditional Chinese paper used for making rice paper paintings is made from the pith of the stems. It spreads steadily by underground stolons to form expanding colonies, which can be managed by mowing around the perimeter; this spreading habit also makes it excellent for covering large areas. In zone 8, top growth is killed by frost but the plant rebounds from underground stolons vigorously each spring, often reaching 8–10 feet by summer. 'Steroidal Giant' is a selection with even larger leaves.

common_name: Richard Wallace Canna (Classic Heirloom Clear-Yellow Canna)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every two to three years.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun. Introduced in 1902 and still in commerce, this Crozy-group heirloom canna is prized for producing the clearest, truest yellow of any widely grown canna, with lightly ruffled petals and fine orange-red speckling in the throat. Foliage is a fresh apple-green, providing a bright, uncluttered backdrop that lets the flowers stand out. It flowers continuously from midsummer into early autumn atop sturdy stalks; divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Richmondensis Begonia (Bronze-Leaf Heirloom Angel Wing Begonia)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this old hybrid roots readily from stem cuttings and is rarely grown from seed.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, pinching young plants to encourage the branching, cane-like habit typical of angel wing begonias. A hybrid dating to the early 20th century still valued today, Richmondensis bears glossy, bronze-green, angel-wing-shaped leaves with a reddish underside and hanging clusters of soft pink flowers produced through summer and fall. Its tough, easy-care constitution and heirloom pedigree have kept it in circulation among begonia collectors and Southern gardeners for generations, tolerating both container culture and shaded garden beds. Take stem cuttings in late summer to overwinter indoors where winters bring hard freezes.

common_name: Ricki Magnolia (Little Girl Series Large-Flowered Deep Pink Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Ricki is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias, noted for its unusually large flowers, bred for later, frost-dodging bloom.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Ricki is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later bloom timing, producing unusually large, deep purple-pink, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact, multi-stemmed plant. Its later flowering window gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts, and its larger bloom size stands out among its Little Girl siblings. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for winter cold-moist stratification, or plant divisions/container stock in spring; Riddell's goldenrod prefers consistently moist to seasonally wet calcareous soils and is a signature species of prairie fens and wet meadows.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, calcium-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade. Riddell's goldenrod is a distinctive wetland species of Midwestern prairie fens, wet-mesic prairies, and calcareous sedge meadows, easily recognized by its narrow, folded, boat-shaped leaves that curve upward along the stem below flat-topped clusters of golden-yellow flowers in late summer and early fall. It is an excellent late-season nectar source for native bees, migrating monarch butterflies, and other pollinators, blooming alongside asters and other fall composites. Because it depends on consistently saturated to seasonally wet, mineral-rich soils in the wild, it is best suited to rain gardens, pond margins, and low, poorly drained spots in the landscape rather than average dry garden beds. It spreads gradually to form a modest colony but is far less aggressive than the well-known Canada goldenrod, making it a good choice for smaller wetland-style native plantings.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Ring of Fire philodendron is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no moss pole or trellis.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Ring of Fire philodendron is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no moss pole or trellis. Deeply serrated, oak-leaf-shaped foliage emerges heavily speckled and streaked in shades of cream, yellow, orange, and pink over a green base, with each leaf displaying a unique, unpredictable mix of colors and patterns that shift as it matures, giving the plant an almost painterly, ever-changing appearance. Its compact, non-vining rosette habit and deeply cut leaf margins set it apart texturally from smoother, rounder-leaved philodendrons, and the unpredictable color patterning makes each individual plant unique. Provide bright indirect light to maintain the vivid multicolor variegation, water when the top inch of potting mix dries, and rotate the pot occasionally for even growth.

common_name: Ring of Fire Sunflower (Bicolor Red-and-Gold Branching Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; Ring of Fire is a branching, pollen-free bicolor sunflower with rings of deep burgundy-red at the petal base fading to golden-yellow tips, a striking bicolor pattern popular for cut-flower arrangements.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches for good branching. Ring of Fire produces striking bicolor blooms with a deep burgundy-red ring at the base of each petal fading outward to bright golden-yellow tips, creating a fiery, sunset-like halo effect that stands out clearly from single-toned sunflower varieties. As a branching type, each plant produces multiple flowers over an extended harvest window rather than a single bloom, making it productive for both garden display and cut-flower use, and the flowers are pollen-free, keeping arrangements and clothing free of the yellow pollen standard sunflowers shed. Deadhead or harvest spent blooms to encourage continued branching and flowering through the season. Grow in full sun with support in windy sites, since the branching habit and multiple large flowers can make plants somewhat top-heavy.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in partial shade; ring-cupped oak grows naturally in the understory of moist mountain forests of Japan, China, and the Himalayas, making it more shade-tolerant than most oaks. Tolerates hot summers in the southeastern US.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in partial shade; ring-cupped oak is a beautiful East Asian evergreen oak widely distributed from Japan through China, Korea, and the Himalayas — an important component of warm-temperate and subtropical Asian forests. The attractive, evergreen, lanceolate to oblong leaves have characteristic waxy, blue-gray (glaucous) undersides that give the species its name. The acorn cups have distinctive concentric ring-shaped ridges (hence 'ring-cupped'). More shade-tolerant than most oaks — an unusual characteristic that makes it appropriate for partially shaded sites where most oaks would struggle. In Japanese gardens it is used as a refined evergreen specimen tree. Adaptable to the warm, humid southeastern US climate in zones 7–9. The glossy, dark-green, evergreen foliage provides year-round interest. An underused Asian evergreen oak for southern US gardens where holm oak might also be grown.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early spring; Arisaema ringens is more tolerant of mild winter temperatures than many Asian arisaema species and is one of the better choices for zone 7–9 woodland gardens, where other species may not reliably overwinter.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; ringed cobra lily is a Japanese and Chinese woodland Arisaema species with one of the most dramatic and architecturally distinctive flower structures of the genus — the broad, rounded, glossy spathe (hooded 'pulpit') is boldly striped with deep purple-brown, greenish, and white bands running vertically, and the hood is dramatically arched forward and downward with a prominent, beak-like tip, giving the entire flower the striking appearance of a rearing cobra with a patterned hood — the basis for the species' common name. Two large, three-parted leaves, each with three broad leaflets, emerge from a single tuber. Like all Arisaema species, the plants are deciduous and go completely dormant by midsummer. Ringed cobra lily is among the most cold-tolerant of the Asian arisaemas and performs better in zone 7–9 gardens than many other species. It requires cool, moist, acidic, humus-rich woodland soil and resents summer heat and drought. Over time a single tuber produces offsets to form small colonies. A distinctive collector's plant for the serious woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring into very well-drained, dry, alkaline, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; Rio Bravo sage blooms most heavily right after summer rain events, functioning as a natural 'barometer bush.'
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, alkaline soil in full sun; Rio Bravo sage is a South Texas native shrub in the cenizo group, with small, silvery-gray, felted leaves and abundant lavender-purple, trumpet-shaped flowers that burst into bloom within a day or two of rain or a sharp rise in humidity, a trait that has earned cenizo shrubs the folk name 'barometer bush' across South Texas. It stays somewhat more compact than the widely planted Texas sage (Leucophyllum frutescens) and tends to flower even more heavily and reliably after rain events. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, it thrives in poor, rocky, or caliche soil that would stress most ornamental shrubs, needing only excellent drainage and full sun. Prune minimally and only to shape, since heavy shearing removes the natural silvery, rounded form and reduces the flush of bloom that follows each rain.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, hanging basket, or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Rio philodendron is an easy, fast-growing variegated selection tolerant of average indoor conditions.
directions: Grow as a houseplant, hanging basket, or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Rio philodendron is an easy, fast-growing variegated selection tolerant of average indoor conditions. A variegated form of heartleaf philodendron, it produces narrow, distinctively wave-edged and lobed leaves streaked in shades of yellow, cream, and light green over darker green, giving the trailing vine a more sculptural, textured look than the plain heartleaf or the broader-striped 'Brasil' cultivar. It roots easily from stem cuttings, grows quickly under average indoor light, and trails attractively from a hanging basket or shelf, making it a forgiving, low-maintenance choice for gardeners newer to variegated aroids. Pinch trailing stems to encourage bushier growth and provide bright indirect light to keep the variegation crisp.

plant_note: Set tubers out after the last spring frost when the soil is warm.
directions: Rip City bears dramatic dark red-black blooms on long, easy-to-cut stems from early in the season. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil after frost danger passes, and stake the plants early since the tall stems benefit from support. This variety is a strong tuber producer, so plants can be divided at season's end. Deadhead spent flowers to keep new blooms coming through fall. Lift tubers before hard frost in cold-winter regions.

common_name: Rip Van Winkle Daffodil (Shaggy Double Miniature Heirloom Daffodil)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; Rip van Winkle is a shaggy, fully double heirloom miniature daffodil dating to the 19th century.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Rip van Winkle bears small, shaggy, fully double golden-yellow flowers with narrow, twisted petals that give the bloom an unruly, tousled appearance quite unlike the neat, formal shape of most daffodils, a distinctive 19th-century heirloom that has remained in cultivation for its charm and novelty. Its miniature size suits rock gardens and containers. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun to partial shade; river birch transplants readily and establishes quickly. Multi-stem clump forms are widely available and provide year-round ornamental interest.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically flooded soil in full sun to light partial shade; river birch is the most adaptable and heat-tolerant native birch in North America, naturally occurring along streambanks and floodplains from New Hampshire to Florida and west to Kansas. Unlike the European white birch, river birch is highly resistant to the bronze birch borer and bronze birch clearwing, making it a far more reliable long-term landscape tree throughout most of the eastern US. The ornamental exfoliating bark — cinnamon to salmon-pink to creamy-white — peels in papery curls to reveal new inner bark throughout the year, providing outstanding four-season interest. River birch grows quickly (1.5–2 feet per year) and tolerates both wet, poorly drained soils and moderate drought once established, an unusually wide site adaptability. The small winged seeds are relished by chickadees, redpolls, and pine siskins in late winter.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, average soil in partial to full shade; River Mist sea oats holds its variegation best out of hot afternoon sun and tolerates the same range of soils as the green species.
directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, average soil in partial to full shade; River Mist sea oats holds its variegation best out of hot afternoon sun and tolerates the same range of soils as the green species. Broad, bamboo-like leaves are crisply edged and streaked in creamy white, brightening shaded ground with a soft, luminous variegation before the plant sends up the same arching sprays of flat, oat-like seed heads in late summer that dangle and shimmer with the slightest breeze, aging from green to golden bronze. Like the straight native species, it self-sows in moist soil and can naturalize into drifts under trees, though seedlings of variegated cultivars often revert to plain green, so remove any all-green volunteers to maintain the display. Cut old foliage back in late winter before new shoots emerge in spring.

common_name: River Oats (Native Shade-Tolerant Ornamental Grass with Nodding Flat Seed Heads)
plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; River Oats self-sows prolifically in favorable conditions — allow it to naturalize in shade garden areas but prevent seeding into naturalized areas where it can spread aggressively beyond the garden.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; River Oats (Chasmanthium latifolium) is one of the most valuable and beautiful native ornamental grasses for Gulf South gardens — uniquely, it is one of the very few ornamental grasses that performs well in partial to full shade, filling the difficult niche of shade-tolerant ornamental grass that few other species can occupy. The slender, arching, bamboo-like stems carry flat, compressed, oat-like seed heads in an elegantly nodding arrangement — the flat seed heads rattle and shimmer in the slightest breeze, creating continuous gentle movement that adds life and animation to static shade plantings. The seed heads emerge green in summer and gradually ripen to warm tan-gold through fall, persisting on the plant into winter and providing months of ornamental interest. In fall, the leaves also develop warm copper-bronze tones before the plant goes dormant. River Oats is native to moist woodlands, stream banks, and shaded slopes throughout the eastern US, including Gulf Coast states, making it an ecologically appropriate native grass for Gulf South shade garden designs. It spreads by self-seeding and can naturalize enthusiastically in favorable moist conditions — this exuberant self-seeding can be welcome in large naturalistic areas but may require editing in smaller formal gardens. Deer tend to avoid it. An outstanding grass for woodland garden understory, shade border edges, and moist streamside gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; river wattle has produced numerous excellent ornamental cultivars with fine weeping habits and attractive foliage, including 'Lime Magic' (chartreuse-lime green), 'Burgundy Cascade' (purple-bronze), and 'Cousin Itt' (very compact, ground-hugging mound of fine foliage). More moisture-tolerant than most acacias. The dense, weeping, fine-foliage habit is primarily valued over the flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; river wattle is valued primarily for its graceful, weeping, architectural foliage character rather than its flowers — producing dense, cascading fountains of very narrow, slightly curved, bright-green to dark-green phyllodes (leaf-like stems) of fine, soft texture that hang in long, sweeping, pendulous masses from arching branches, creating a weeping, willow-like cascade of fine-textured, green or colored foliage. The cultivar 'Cousin Itt' has become an extremely popular ground-hugging garden curiosity: an extremely compact, low, spreading mound (only 12–18 inches tall) of the same cascading, fine-textured foliage that creates a dense, completely circular, ball-like ground mound resembling the cartoon character 'Cousin Itt' from The Addams Family. Other cultivars include 'Lime Magic' (bright chartreuse-lime-yellow foliage) and 'Burgundy Cascade' (burgundy-purple-tinted foliage). The spring flowers are small, yellow, fragrant pompoms in clusters — pleasant but not the primary ornamental quality. More moisture-tolerant than most acacias, native to the stream banks and river margins of southeastern Australia.

common_name: Riviera Sky Blue Lobelia (Compact Non-Trailing Edging Lobelia)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; shear plants back lightly after summer heat slows bloom to encourage a fall flush.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost. Riviera is a compact, mounding lobelia series (not trailing) bred for earlier bloom and better heat tolerance than older lobelia strains, though it still performs best where summers stay relatively cool. Riviera Sky Blue smothers itself in small, clear sky-blue flowers with a tiny white eye, forming a dense low carpet ideal for edging, rock gardens, and front-of-border plantings. Bloom often slows in peak summer heat; shearing plants back lightly encourages a strong flush of rebloom as temperatures moderate.

common_name: Roald Dahl Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Roald Dahl is bred for strong disease resistance and reliably repeats through the season with routine feeding and deadheading.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2016 and named for the celebrated children's author, Roald Dahl bears warm peachy-pink, cupped rosette flowers with a light, fresh tea fragrance, on a healthy, compact, disease-resistant shrub bred to hold clean foliage through humid summers with minimal spraying. It flowers freely and repeats reliably from late spring through frost, making it a dependable, easy-care choice for gardeners wanting classic English-rose form without a demanding maintenance routine.

common_name: Robert Poore Garden Phlox (Heat-Tolerant Mildew-Resistant Magenta Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, spacing generously for airflow; Robert Poore was selected in Texas specifically for resistance to powdery mildew in hot, humid summers.
directions: Plant in moist, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, with generous spacing for air circulation; Robert Poore is a heirloom Texas selection of garden phlox found growing in a San Antonio-area yard and prized for combining tall, vigorous, magenta-purple flower trusses with outstanding resistance to powdery mildew, the disease that disfigures most garden phlox by midsummer in the humid South. It has repeatedly ranked among the top performers for mildew resistance and heat tolerance in regional perennial trials, making it one of the most reliable tall garden phlox for Gulf Coast gardens. Plants form sturdy, upright clumps three to four feet tall that bloom from midsummer into early fall and draw butterflies and hummingbirds heavily. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, and remove faded flower heads before they set seed to prevent seedlings that revert to muddy magenta and gradually overwhelm the named cultivar.

common_name: Robin Holly (Bronze-Red New Growth Screening Holly)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped hollies in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Robin is a female cultivar and needs a male holly pollinator nearby for the heaviest berry production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Robin is a pyramidal hybrid holly notable for the striking bronze-red flush of its new spring growth, which matures to glossy dark green and contrasts attractively with the bright red berries produced later in the season when a compatible male holly is planted nearby for pollination. Its dense, upright form and moderate size make it a versatile choice for screening, hedging, and specimen use in the landscape, requiring only occasional shaping to maintain a neat outline. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established, and consistent watering during the first couple of seasons speeds root establishment.

plant_note: Plant after frost when soil reaches about 60 F.
directions: Robin Hood produces large salmon-orange blooms whose saturation shifts through the growing season, making each flower slightly different. Because the big blooms are heavy, stake or corral this variety early so stems stay upright. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in loose, fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Feed with a low-nitrogen fertilizer to favor flowers over foliage. Cut blooms freely to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Robin's plantain spreads gently by stolons and self-seeding to form a low, weed-suppressing patch along woodland edges and shaded lawns.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; tolerates light foot traffic and mowing after bloom, making it a good native alternative to lawn in lightly shaded areas. Erigeron pulchellus (Robin's plantain) is a low, spreading native perennial of open woods, meadows, and woodland edges across eastern North America, forming rosettes of soft, hairy, spoon-shaped leaves that stay low and semi-evergreen through much of the year. In mid-spring, slender stems rise above the foliage carrying cheerful, daisy-like flowers with thin, numerous lavender-to-pink-tinged white rays around a bright yellow center — an important early nectar source for native bees and small butterflies, appearing alongside the earliest spring wildflowers. It spreads gently by both stolons and self-seeding into an attractive, low-maintenance patch without becoming aggressive, and it tolerates part shade as well as more open, sunny sites. A cheerful, easy native for the front of a woodland-edge border or naturalized meadow planting in zone 3–8.

common_name: Robinetta Gladiolus (Red Streaked with White, Compact Habit)
plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Robinetta bears red flowers streaked with white, up to seven per stem, on a compact 18-24 inch habit shorter than most gladiolus.
directions: Robinetta bears vivid red flowers streaked with white, carrying up to seven florets per stem on a notably compact 18 to 24 inch plant, much shorter than the typical 3 to 4 foot gladiolus, making it more self-supporting and better suited to a mixed border without staking. Plant corms in well-drained soil, cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, and leave at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; plants usually bloom the second year.
directions: This perennial painted daisy, also called Persian daisy, produces bright long-stemmed blooms that make excellent cut flowers and pair beautifully with columbine and delphinium. Sow seed in spring in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil. Plants typically flower in their second season and attract pollinators. Divide clumps every few years to keep them vigorous. Some people may experience contact dermatitis, so handle the foliage with care.

common_name: Robinsoniana Wood Anemone (Lavender-Blue Historic Wood Anemone Selection)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Robinsoniana, one of the oldest and most popular colored selections, bears lavender-blue flowers, distinct from the white species form.
directions: Plant thin, brittle rhizomes 2 inches deep, horizontally, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees. Robinsoniana, one of the oldest and most widely grown colored selections of wood anemone, bears soft lavender-blue flowers with a silvery reverse, a gentle departure from the pure white of the wild species, opening in early to mid spring and closing at night and in overcast weather. Like other wood anemones, it spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes to form an increasingly dense carpet over the years in a favorable woodland setting, then goes fully dormant by early summer, disappearing until the following spring. It combines beautifully with early daffodils, trilliums, and other spring woodland ephemerals. Once established, it requires essentially no care and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent site.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in bright partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–11; Ceratozamia robusta is a large, impressive cycad endemic to the tropical rainforests of Veracruz and Oaxaca, Mexico — producing a stout trunk with long, arching, pinnate fronds bearing many pairs of broad, glossy, dark-green leaflets — one of the most ornamental of the Ceratozamia genus, and threatened in the wild by habitat loss and illegal collection.
directions: Plant Ceratozamia robusta in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-enriched soil in bright partial shade; protect from frost below 28°F, direct summer sun (which bleaches the glossy fronds), and waterlogged conditions; fertilize with a slow-release cycad fertilizer containing trace elements twice yearly in spring and summer. Caution: all parts of Ceratozamia robusta are toxic — seeds, leaves, and roots contain cycasin — keep away from children and livestock. Robust Horncone is one of the largest and most impressive species in the genus Ceratozamia — a Mexican cycad group distinguished from other New World cycads by the paired 'horns' on the tops of male and female cone scales. The species is native to humid tropical and montane forests of Veracruz and Oaxaca at elevations from near sea level to about 1,500 meters, where it grows as a forest understory plant in deep, humus-rich soil. Long, arching pinnate fronds (each 4–6 feet in length) bearing numerous pairs of broad, glossy dark-green leaflets create a dramatic, palm-like effect in the shade garden. Growth is very slow; a cone-bearing adult specimen represents many decades of cultivation and is a highly prized collector's plant. Ceratozamia robusta is listed on CITES Appendix I (the most restrictive protection level) due to severe wild population declines from habitat clearing and poaching; purchase only from reputable nurseries with documentation of nursery origin.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Rochfordianum holly fern tolerates heat, humidity, salt spray, and dry shade better than most ferns, making it a Gulf Coast landscape standard.
directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Rochfordianum holly fern tolerates heat, humidity, salt spray, and dry shade better than most ferns, making it a Gulf Coast landscape standard. Glossy, leathery, deep-green pinnae are more deeply and irregularly toothed than the straight species, giving each frond a fringed, ruffled outline that reads as more refined and textured in mass plantings. Extremely tough and adaptable, it holds up to coastal wind and salt spray, dry shade under eaves, and heavy summer humidity that would rot more delicate ferns, and it stays evergreen through mild Gulf South winters. Remove damaged fronds after any hard freeze and let new growth flush from the crown; established clumps rarely need division.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rock daffodil is a miniature species of Iberian limestone rocks requiring excellent drainage and summer drought.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; rock daffodil requires excellent drainage and summer drought during its dormant period — it performs best in raised beds, rock gardens, or on sharply drained slopes. Narcissus rupicola is a charming miniature wild daffodil of the Iberian Peninsula growing on limestone rocks and dry, sunny slopes; it produces slender, rush-like, blue-green leaves and small (1 inch across), bright-yellow flowers with a flat, slightly six-lobed, darker-yellow cup in mid-spring, often earlier than most daffodils. It is one of the most delicate and refined of all miniature daffodils, best appreciated up close in a rock garden, raised alpine bed, or container where its small scale can be properly seen. Excellent combined with other small bulbs such as Iris reticulata and Crocus species.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained upland soils or limestone-based ground; shows somewhat better Dutch elm disease resistance than American elm.
directions: Plant in spring in well-drained upland soils or limestone-based ground where this slow-growing elm forms a narrow, pyramidal crown distinct from the vase shape of American elm. Distinctive corky wings often develop along its branches, giving winter interest that sets it apart from other native elms. Rock elm shows somewhat better resistance to Dutch elm disease than American elm, making it a worthwhile alternative for restoration plantings and long-lived shade in northern landscapes. Its exceptionally dense, heavy wood was historically valued for tool handles and shipbuilding, reflecting the tree's slow, sturdy growth habit.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, dry, rocky, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rock muhly grows on dry, rocky canyon walls, limestone outcrops, and talus slopes of the Chihuahuan Desert and surrounding mountains. Extremely drought and heat tolerant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry, rocky, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rock muhly is a small, delicate native grass of rocky canyon walls and limestone outcrops in the Chihuahuan Desert of Texas, New Mexico, and Mexico, adapted to the extreme drainage and heat of vertical rock faces where few other plants survive. The very fine, hair-like foliage forms small, wispy tufts that root into rock crevices, and the airy, purple-tinted seed heads in fall create a delicate haze of color against the rock. Extremely drought-tolerant once its roots reach the moisture retained in rock crevices. A specialist plant for dry, rocky, calcareous scree and rock garden settings in the arid Southwest. More drought-tolerant than any other commonly available muhly grass. Excellent for planting in crevices of dry limestone walls and rocky garden outcrops in zone 9.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; rock penstemon is adapted to limestone cliffs and ledges and rots quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil.
directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; rock penstemon is adapted to limestone cliffs and ledges and rots quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil. Small, glossy, evergreen leaves clothe woody-based stems that form a low, shrubby mound, studded from summer into fall with tubular, bright red-orange flowers that are outstanding hummingbird forage during a season when many other penstemons have finished blooming. Native to limestone canyon walls and rocky slopes of the Trans-Pecos and Edwards Plateau regions of Texas into northern Mexico, it is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant penstemons available, thriving in the reflected heat of a rock garden or dry stone wall. Established plants need no supplemental water beyond natural rainfall and benefit from a light trim after the main flowering flush to keep the mound tidy.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; rock pink requires excellent drainage and will rot in heavy, wet soils. It is native to limestone glades, rock outcrops, and dry prairies of the south-central United States. The flowers open in the afternoon and close by evening — a feature of its polemonium-like adaptation to heat-of-the-day bee pollinators.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rock pink is a native succulent perennial of the limestone glades and rocky prairies of the south-central United States — from the Missouri Ozarks south through Kansas and Oklahoma to Texas — producing succulent, cylindrical, bright-green leaves in dense tufts and in summer (June–August) an abundance of bright, clear, rose-pink to magenta-pink, five-petaled flowers (1 inch across) on slender stems that open in the afternoon and close by evening, creating a daily recurrence of cheerful color in hot, dry, full-sun positions. The succulent foliage is attractive even out of flower, providing bright green contrast to the rocky surroundings. It is genuinely adapted to the extreme conditions of limestone glade habitats — thin, rocky, limey soil, baking summer heat, drought, and full sun — conditions that defeat most ornamentals. A rewarding native plant for rock gardens, glade restorations, and any lean, sunny position with well-drained to dry, calcareous soil in zones 4–9. Self-sows modestly to maintain colonies in open, lean-soil conditions.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of frost passes in very well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; rock purslane is perennial in zones 9–11 and extremely drought-tolerant once established. In colder zones grow as a tender annual from seed. The succulent, gray-green foliage provides attractive texture even when not in bloom.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; rock purslane is a Chilean native succulent perennial producing rosettes of thick, fleshy, glaucous gray-green succulent leaves and from spring through fall, slender, wiry stems bearing flowers of an astonishingly vivid, pure, hot fuchsia-magenta color — one of the most intense and eye-catching flower colors achievable in the drought-tolerant garden. Each individual bloom is a simple, five-petaled cup of brilliant, saturated magenta-cerise on a delicate stem, and the contrast of these vivid flowers against the cool, gray-green succulent foliage is exceptional. It is more drought-tolerant than most flowering plants with such saturated color, native to the dry, rocky coastal hills of Chile where it forms sprawling mats over exposed rocky ground. In zones 9–11 it grows as a substantial, semi-woody, spreading perennial that blooms for much of the year. In colder zones treat as a tender annual from early-started seed. Outstanding in containers, rock gardens, and dry stone wall plantings where both the fleshy foliage and vivid flowers provide interest, and where drought tolerance is essential.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant after all danger of frost passes in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; rock purslane is perennial in frost-free zones (9–11) and treated as a tender annual in colder climates. Formerly classified as Calandrinia grandiflora. Like other succulent-leaved purslane relatives, it requires excellent drainage and thrives on neglect.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; rock purslane is a Chilean coastal hill native producing large rosettes of thick, fleshy, gray-green succulent leaves of impressive scale (up to 6–8 inches long) and from spring through summer, tall, branching stems bearing multiple clusters of vivid, intense, hot-magenta-fuchsia flowers (1.5–2 inches across) in clear, pure, un-muddied color — one of the most visually arresting single colors available from any succulent or drought-tolerant plant. The contrast of the cool, gray-green, fleshy foliage with the hot, electric fuchsia-magenta flowers is striking and tropical in quality. In zones 9–11 it grows as a long-lived, semi-woody perennial up to 4 feet tall that blooms for much of the year in mild seasons. In colder zones it is grown as a tender annual from early-started seed. Formerly classified as Calandrinia grandiflora, it was reclassified into Cistanthe based on molecular evidence. Outstanding in containers, on dry rock slopes, and in the front of drought-tolerant borders in subtropical and Mediterranean-climate gardens.

common_name: Rock Rose (Texas Pavonia, Rose Mallow Pavonia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; pavonia is native to the Edwards Plateau and south Texas and is adapted to alkaline limestone soils — it actually grows better in lean, rocky conditions than in rich garden soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas pavonia is one of the most outstanding native shrubs for the Gulf Coast garden — a compact, woody perennial shrub that produces a profusion of small (1.5 inch) single rose-pink flowers with yellow stamens continuously from spring through frost, with peak bloom in summer. Each individual flower lasts only a day, but the plant produces new flowers constantly for 6+ months, creating a long-lasting display. It tolerates alkaline soil, drought, and heat and actually blooms better under mild stress than in rich, moist conditions. Deer resistant and attractive to hummingbirds and butterflies. In zone 7–8, top growth may be killed by hard freezes but roots resprout vigorously in spring. Light pruning in late winter promotes compact, bushy growth.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost when soil has warmed.
directions: Rock Run Ashley is a smaller smoky-salmon dahlia that blends beautifully in mixed bouquets and is a favorite with florists. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the soil warms, spacing plants about 12-18 inches apart. Pinch young plants to promote branching and more cut stems. Keep soil evenly moist during bloom but let it dry slightly between waterings to prevent tuber rot. Harvest flowers in the cool of the morning for the longest vase life.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rock soapwort is one of the most spectacular and vigorous rock garden and dry wall plants, spilling in cascades of bright-pink flowers.
directions: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; rock soapwort is an extremely vigorous spreader when well established — site it where it can spill freely over walls or banks without smothering smaller plants. Saponaria ocymoides is a trailing, mat-forming European alpine perennial in the pink family that completely covers itself with a stunning carpet of bright, deep-pink to rose-pink, 5-petaled flowers in late spring and early summer — one of the most floriferous of all rock garden plants, and one of the best for cascading over walls where it hangs in sheets of pink. The leaves contain saponin and produce a slight soapy lather when rubbed with water (giving the genus its name). After the first flowering, shear plants back hard to encourage a second flush and to keep the plant compact. One of the easiest and most rewarding alpine plants for sunny, dry sites.

common_name: Rock and Roll Alstroemeria (Variegated Cream-and-Green with Pink Flowers)
plant_note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Rock and Roll bears cream-and-green variegated foliage that provides ornamental value even before the plant flowers.
directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, handling the brittle roots carefully. Rock and Roll bears attractive cream-and-green variegated foliage that provides ornamental interest even when the plant is not in bloom, topped by clear pink, orchid-like flowers with darker pink and yellow streaking through the growing season. Its variegated leaves make it a good textural companion in a mixed container or border even before flowering begins. Pulling rather than cutting spent flower stems from the base stimulates continued rebloom. In colder zones mulch heavily for winter protection or lift the roots for storage, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring if flowering declines.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Hosta rupifraga is unusual among hostas in tolerating more sun and drier conditions than most species, reflecting its origin on rocky, cliff-face habitats in Japan.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Hosta rupifraga is a small-to-medium Japanese species hosta named for its native habitat — growing on rocky cliff faces and rock outcrops (rupifraga = rock-splitting) in central Japan, a distinctly different habitat from the moist, shaded woodland floors where most hostas grow. The small, ovate leaves with characteristic wavy margins and pale midribs are attractive. Because it evolved on exposed, rocky cliff habitats, it is more tolerant of drier conditions, higher light, and poorer soils than typical hostas — making it a more versatile species for gardens where moisture and shade are variable. The lavender flowers are attractive in late summer. One of the less-known Japanese species hostas, it is increasingly of interest to hosta collectors and breeders as a source of drought-tolerance genes for new hybrid varieties. Forms compact, attractive clumps that can be divided every few years.

common_name: Rockapulco Red Impatiens (Fully Double Rose-Bud Impatiens)
plant_note: Plant purchased transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full shade. Rockapulco is a Proven Winners series bred for fully double, rose-bud-like flowers and improved heat and humidity tolerance compared to older double impatiens strains.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Rockapulco Red is a Proven Winners impatiens bred for fully double, ruffled, rose-like red blooms that resemble small roses more than a typical five-petaled impatiens flower, held over a compact, mounding plant that continues flowering non-stop from spring through frost in deep shade where few other bedding annuals bloom well at all. Like other Impatiens walleriana selections it remains susceptible to impatiens downy mildew, the fungal disease that has caused serious losses in impatiens plantings across North America since 2011; provide good air circulation, avoid overhead watering, and consider New Guinea impatiens or SunPatiens in areas with a known history of the disease. Deadheading is not required since spent blooms drop cleanly on their own, and consistent moisture keeps the display at its best through summer heat.

subcategory: fragrant cool-season candytuft for cutting and edging
plant_note: Direct sow a few weeks before the last frost in cool soil, since this hardy annual germinates and grows best in cooler temperatures.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in well-drained soil as soon as it can be worked, then thin seedlings to their final spacing since crowded plants produce fewer flower spikes. Succession sow every few weeks in spring for a continuous supply of blooms before summer heat shortens the display. Unlike the flat-topped clusters of common candytuft, this species bears dense, upright, hyacinth-like spikes of small, fragrant white or lilac flowers that are excellent for cutting and draw bees and other pollinators to the border or cutting garden.

common_name: Rocket City Daylily (Tall Tetraploid Orange Daylily)
plant_note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Rocket City is a vigorous, heavy-blooming tetraploid that clumps up quickly and tolerates Gulf South heat and humidity without complaint.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and water deeply through the first season while the fans establish. Bred by Orville Fay and introduced in the early 1970s, Rocket City bears large, brilliant tangerine-orange, ruffled flowers with a green throat on tall, well-branched scapes that hold well above the foliage, and its tetraploid vigor gives it thick-textured petals and a heavier bud count than older diploid orange daylilies. Individual flowers have an extended bloom habit, staying open later into the evening than a typical single-day bloom, which stretches out the display during its main flowering flush in early summer. Deadhead spent scapes to keep the clump tidy and divide congested plantings every three to four years to maintain strong, floriferous growth.

common_name: Rocket Larkspur (Tall Annual Larkspur, Cool-Season Delphinium Relative)
plant_note: Direct sow in place (larkspur does not transplant well and the taproot is sensitive to disturbance); sow in fall in zone 9 — seed needs cool temperatures (45–55°F) for germination and seeds left on cold soil through winter will germinate when conditions are right. In zone 9, sow October–December for bloom February–April. Larkspur blooms heavily in the cool of late winter and spring and dies when summer heat arrives; it self-seeds reliably and returns each fall. All parts of larkspur are toxic if ingested.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall on or near the soil surface; do not transplant. Rocket Larkspur (Consolida ajacis, previously Delphinium ajacis) is a tall annual relative of the perennial delphinium — producing the same elegant, towering spikes of densely packed, spurred flowers in shades of blue, purple, lavender, pink, white, and bicolors on upright, 3–5 foot stems, but completing its entire life cycle in one cool season rather than requiring years of perennial establishment. For Gulf South gardeners in zone 8–10, annual larkspur fills the role that perennial delphinium cannot — delphinium is not reliably perennial in the South due to heat and humidity, but annual larkspur thrives in the mild Gulf South winter, blooming prolifically from February through April before summer arrives. The tall, graceful flower spikes are among the most beautiful and romantic elements of the cool-season garden, resembling miniature cottage-garden spires that evoke English country garden aesthetics. Larkspur self-seeds with great reliability — once established in a suitable location, it may naturalize and return each fall from self-sown seed without further planting, creating a self-sustaining annual display over years. All parts are toxic if eaten.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; rocket ligularia wilts dramatically in full sun and afternoon heat, signaling water stress even when soil is moist — afternoon shade is essential in zones 6–8.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; rocket ligularia (the rocket) is one of the most dramatic and architecturally impressive shade garden perennials available — the cultivar 'The Rocket' produces enormous, rounded-to-triangular, deeply veined, dark-green leaves on tall, dark-mahogany stems, and in midsummer erupts into flowering with tall, bold, upright spires of small, sharp-yellow, daisy-like flowers packed densely along 3–4-foot stems that tower dramatically above the foliage mound. The combination of bold, tropical-scale foliage and tall, vivid-yellow flower spires creates an unforgettable effect in the moist shade garden. Ligularia is notorious for wilting dramatically in warm afternoon sun even when soil is moist (a physiological response to transpiration demand exceeding root uptake), making afternoon shade essential; plants look perfectly healthy in the morning and collapsed by afternoon. This is a normal behavior and plants recover when temperatures drop in the evening. Excellent beside ponds, streams, and rain garden margins. 'The Rocket' (Japan), 'Britt-Marie Crawford' (very dark, near-black foliage), and 'Little Rocket' (compact) are key cultivars.

common_name: Rocket Snapdragon (Tall Cut-Flower Annual Snapdragon Mix)
plant_note: Start indoors 12–16 weeks before expected transplanting; snapdragon seed is tiny and needs light (surface sow without covering). Chill-treated seeds or germinate at 60–65°F. In zone 9, start seeds in September–October and transplant November–December for bloom January–April — the Gulf South's mild winter is ideal for snapdragons, which bloom in the cool but collapse in summer heat. Rocket is the tall cut-flower type (24–36 inch stems), appropriate for cutting gardens and back of borders.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, sterile starting mix under bright lights; do not cover — needs light. Transplant after hardening off. Rocket Snapdragon is the tall cut-flower class of Antirrhinum majus — producing long (18–24 inch), sturdy flower stems with densely-packed, spurred flowers in a wide range of colors including red, pink, orange, yellow, white, lavender, and bicolors, ideal for cutting. Snapdragons are quintessential cool-season annuals, performing beautifully in the Gulf South fall through spring garden (September–April in zone 9) and collapsing when summer heat arrives. For zone 9 gardeners, snapdragons are a fall-planted flower that fills the gap between summer annuals and creates a spectacular late-winter and spring cutting garden from November through April — producing abundant long-stemmed flowers during the cool months that rival any season's production. The Rocket series is the premier tall cut-flower snapdragon from PanAmerican Seed, designed specifically for market garden cut-flower production with the longest, straightest stems and best holding quality of any snapdragon class. The individual snap flowers on each spike open from the bottom up, with each flower having the characteristic dragon-snapping mechanism that children (and many adults) find irresistible.

common_name: Rockin' Salvia (Vigorous Heat-Tolerant Hummingbird Sage Series)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rockin' salvia grows larger and more vigorously than the species type, so give it room to spread into a substantial clump over the season.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and give this vigorous selection plenty of room to grow into a large, well-branched clump by late summer. Rockin' is a bred selection of Salvia guaranitica (anise sage) valued for larger flowers, more vigorous growth, and better heat tolerance than the species or older cultivars like Black and Blue, producing spikes of large, deep blue to purple tubular flowers continuously from summer through frost that are outstanding for hummingbirds. Its exceptional vigor and heat tolerance make it a standout performer through the peak of Gulf South summer, when many perennials slow their bloom, and the substantial size makes it a strong anchor plant for the back of a mixed border. Where winters are mild the rhizomatous roots often survive to resprout in spring; further north it can be treated as an annual or mulched heavily for winter protection.

common_name: Rockspray Cotoneaster (Low Spreading Fishbone-Branched Groundcover with Red Berries)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Rockspray tolerates poor, rocky, or dry soil and is often used to stabilize slopes and banks where its low, spreading branches root lightly as they spread.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants tolerate drought, poor rocky soil, and wind, making this a reliable choice for slopes, banks, and low-maintenance beds where little else thrives. Rockspray cotoneaster is named for its distinctive herringbone or 'fishbone' branching pattern, with stiff horizontal branches that hug the ground and layer over each other as the plant spreads, studded with small glossy dark green leaves that turn red-orange in fall. Small white to pink flowers appear in late spring and are followed by abundant bright red berries that persist into winter, providing food for birds and strong seasonal color over bare or rocky ground. It needs minimal pruning beyond removing dead wood, and its low, wide-spreading habit make it a classic choice for cascading over walls and covering banks where mowing is impractical.

plant_note: Plant tubers outdoors once the danger of frost has passed.
directions: Rockstar is a dark anemone-type dahlia with distinctive foliage that blooms continuously through the season and holds well in the vase. Plant the tuber 4-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil after frost, positioning the eye upward. Provide full sun and support tall stems as needed. Deadhead regularly and cut blooms often to keep the plant productive. In cold climates dig and store tubers before the first hard freeze.

plant_note: Direct sow seed after last frost in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Rocky Mountain bee plant self-sows prolifically and naturalizes in open, sunny, dry areas — no supplemental water is needed once plants are established.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — Rocky Mountain bee plant is a native annual of the Great Plains, Rocky Mountain foothills, and desert Southwest, producing clusters of showy, spidery, pink to white flowers on tall, branching, slightly pungent-scented stems from summer through fall. It is one of the most important native bee plants of the central US: bumblebees, mason bees, and honey bees are intensely attracted to the nectar-rich flowers, working the plants all day in good weather. The plant was an important food source for indigenous peoples of the Plains and Pueblos, who boiled the leaves as a green vegetable and rendered the plant to make a black dye used in pottery painting. It self-sows prolifically to naturalize in dry, open, sandy or rocky soils across a wide climate range. The musky scent (a defense against some insect herbivores) is more noticeable up close than at a distance.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; cold stratification improves germination.
directions: The state flower of Colorado, this heirloom columbine bears long-lasting pale violet and white blossoms above delicate blue-green, fern-like foliage. Sow seed in early spring or fall and expose it to a cold period, as chilling greatly improves germination. It is at home in part shade and moist, well-drained soil. Plants bloom in their second year and self-sow readily. Leave a few seed heads to naturalize the patch over time.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; seed benefits from cold stratification.
directions: This long-lived heirloom penstemon sends up exquisite blue-violet flower spikes that bloom for about a month in early summer and attract pollinators. Sow seed in fall or early spring and give it a cold, moist period to break dormancy. Provide full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, as it is drought tolerant once established. Evergreen basal rosettes carry the plant through winter. Leave the satiny brown seedpods for interest and self-sowing.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral or slightly acidic, dry to average, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; Rocky Mountain juniper tolerates a wide range of soil types and is very drought tolerant once established. Use container-grown plants for best success — bare-root establishment can be difficult.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral or slightly acidic, dry to average, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; Rocky Mountain juniper (also called Colorado red cedar) is the western counterpart of eastern red cedar — the dominant juniper of the Rocky Mountains and Great Plains, growing from British Columbia south through the Rockies and east across the northern Great Plains to North Dakota and Kansas. Valuable wildlife tree — the blue-glaucous berry-like cones are an important food source for cedar waxwings, Townsend's solitaires, and many other birds. Widely used for windbreaks and shelterbelts on the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain foothills. The cultivar 'Skyrocket' (also sold as J. virginiana 'Skyrocket') is one of the most narrowly columnar ornamental conifers available — forming a tight, fastigiate column only 2–3 feet wide and 15–20 feet tall, ideal for narrow spaces. Blue-foliaged cultivars like 'Wichita Blue' and 'Moonglow' are popular landscape specimens. Extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; or cold-stratify seeds in the refrigerator for 90-120 days and sow in early spring. Transplant seedlings when small, as the roots develop quickly.
directions: Plant in moist, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Rocky Mountain maple is a multi-stemmed native small tree or large shrub found from Alaska to New Mexico in canyon bottoms, streamside areas, and the cool slopes of the Rocky Mountains and Cascades. It is one of the most important browse plants for mule deer, elk, and moose in the West. The distinctive three-lobed leaves are bright green in summer, turning yellow, orange, and red in fall — a spectacular display in mountain settings. More drought-tolerant than most maples once established. The samaras are consumed by small birds and squirrels. Excellent for naturalizing in shaded, moist spots in western gardens and mountain landscapes where conditions suit its northern and montane origins.

plant_note: Start transplants after 4–6 weeks cold stratification (or direct sow in fall), in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rocky mountain penstemon is one of the most adaptable western penstemons for eastern gardens if given excellent drainage.
directions: Start transplants after 4–6 weeks cold stratification (or direct sow in fall), in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rocky mountain penstemon is one of the most adaptable western penstemons for eastern gardens if given excellent drainage. Penstemon strictus is a robust, upright western penstemon native to the Rocky Mountain foothills and sagebrush steppe from Wyoming to New Mexico, producing glaucous (blue-green), leathery leaves and 1–3 foot racemes of vivid blue-purple to violet-purple tubular flowers in June and July that are outstanding for native bumblebees and bumblebee-mimic hoverflies, and provide nectar for hummingbirds; it is one of the most reliable and vigorous of the blue penstemons in garden culture, adapting to a wider range of soils than most western species. Excellent in sunny, dry-slope rock gardens and xeric borders.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a moist, sheltered spot; rodgersia requires consistently moist to wet soil and is often at its best beside ponds, streams, or in boggy woodland areas. Emerging leaves in spring are vulnerable to late frosts — site in a sheltered location or protect with fleece.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, fertile, slightly acidic soil; rodgersia is a bold, architectural shade perennial with enormous horse-chestnut-like compound leaves up to 24 inches across that emerge bronze-tinged in spring and deepen to dark green through summer. The fluffy astilbe-like flower plumes in creamy white to pink rise dramatically above the foliage in midsummer. It is one of the most dramatic foliage plants available for wet, shaded locations — particularly impressive at the edge of a pond or naturalistic woodland garden where its scale commands attention. The roots are massive and rhizomatous; once established, plants resent disturbance. In southern gardens (zone 7–8) it benefits from consistently moist soil and afternoon shade to prevent leaf scorch in summer heat.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into thin, rocky, limestone-derived soil in partial shade to full sun; Roemer's phlox is a Texas Hill Country endemic annual that germinates with fall rains, overwinters as a small rosette, and blooms the following spring.
directions: Direct sow in fall onto thin, rocky, limestone-influenced soil in dappled shade to full sun beneath oaks and junipers, mimicking the woodland-edge slopes and canyons where this Texas Hill Country endemic grows wild. Seedlings overwinter as small rosettes and bolt in early spring into loose sprays of five-petaled, lavender to pink flowers, each marked with a distinctive yellow-gold eye that gives the plant its common name, blooming alongside bluebonnets in Hill Country wildflower displays. Plants complete their life cycle and set seed by early summer as temperatures rise, then die back and reseed themselves in soil that is not disturbed or heavily mulched. Once established in a compatible thin, rocky, well-drained site, it self-sows reliably year after year and needs no irrigation beyond natural rainfall.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in late summer to early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; roof iris is among the most shade-tolerant of all iris species.
directions: Plant rhizomes with the tops just at or slightly below the soil surface in late summer in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; roof iris (named because Japanese gardeners traditionally planted it on thatched roof ridges) is the most shade-tolerant iris species, producing lilac-blue or white flowers with distinctive dark-veined crests in late spring on stems to 15 inches, followed by flat fans of fresh green foliage that remain attractive all season. Unlike bearded iris, it performs beautifully under trees and in dappled light, making it invaluable for shaded borders and woodland edges. Divide congested rhizomes every 4–5 years in late summer to early fall after bloom. The white form 'Album' is equally vigorous.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Rooguchi has a scrambling rather than strongly climbing habit and benefits from being tied loosely to a support or allowed to weave through companion shrubs.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs or scrambles into full sun to light shade. Rooguchi is a distinctive Japanese viticella-type hybrid bearing nodding, bell-shaped, thick-petaled flowers in deep purple-blue with a paler, twisted, recurved petal tip, a form entirely different from the flat, open flowers of most large-flowered clematis, blooming continuously from early summer into fall. Its lax, semi-climbing habit works well trained on a low trellis or obelisk, woven through a shrub, or left to sprawl at the front of a border, and unlike many clematis it flowers on new growth, so it can be cut back hard in late winter. Its long, prolific bloom season and unusual flower form have made it a favorite among clematis collectors and gardeners looking for something different from the typical large-flowered hybrids.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist to average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Rooper's red-hot poker blooms in autumn (September–November) rather than summer like most kniphofias, making it valuable for extending the season of dramatic red-hot poker flower spikes. It is somewhat more moist-tolerant than many species.
directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Rooper's red-hot poker provides a unique seasonal value among kniphofias — it blooms in autumn (September through November) rather than in summer like the majority of red-hot pokers, extending the season of dramatic, torch-like flower spikes deep into the fall border season when most summer perennials have finished. The flower spikes are globular to egg-shaped (more oval than the elongated cylinders of most kniphofias) and in the characteristic two-toned red-and-yellow combination — orange-red to scarlet upper florets fading to golden-yellow at the base — creating distinctive bicolored rounded torches on tall stems above the typical, strap-leaved rosettes.
