The fall blooming time coincides with the southward migration of hummingbirds along the Atlantic and Gulf coastal flyways, making these flower spikes valuable late-season hummingbird nectar sources. Outstanding at the back of the fall border, combined with ornamental grasses, late asters, and goldenrods in a late-season color composition. More moisture-tolerant than many kniphofias from drier South African habitats.

common_name: Root Beer Heuchera (Ruffled Cinnamon-Bronze Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Root Beer bears large, heavily ruffled leaves in a warm cinnamon-bronze color with a glossy, almost caramel-toned sheen, a distinctive warm tone that stands apart from the more common purple, silver, and gold heuchera palettes. Its bold texture and rich brown-bronze color make it a versatile companion for both warm- and cool-toned shade plantings, pairing especially well with orange- or rust-toned flowers. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosa Mundi is a centuries-old Gallica sport dating to at least the 16th century, blooming once in a single heavy spring flush.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosa Mundi tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough historic Gallica. Recorded since at least the 1500s, this striking sport of the Apothecary's Rose bears semi-double blooms irregularly striped and splashed in shades of pink, crimson, and white, no two flowers looking quite alike, on dense, compact, relatively thorny canes. Like other Gallicas it blooms just once, in a spectacular, fragrant flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2 inches deep once soil has warmed well above 65°F, since cold soil causes rot and stalled growth; keep soil consistently moist through summer.
directions: Plant tubers 2 inches deep once soil has warmed well above 65°F, since cold soil causes rot and stalled growth. This lance/strap-leaf caladium produces narrow, elongated pink-centered leaves with ruffled margins and a defined green edge, forming a dense, low mound well suited to edging and mixed containers. Its compact habit and smaller leaf size distinguish it from the broad fancy-leaf types, and it tolerates more sun than most shade-bred caladiums without significant fading. Keep the soil consistently moist and lightly fertilized for continuous new leaf production through summer.

plant_note: Propagate by hardwood cuttings taken in late winter or by digging and transplanting rooted suckers in early spring before new growth begins.
directions: Take hardwood cuttings 6 to 8 inches long from dormant stems in late winter and root them in a sandy propagation medium with bottom heat. Alternatively, dig rooted suckers from established clumps in early spring and transplant directly to the desired location. Plant in full sun in well-drained, even poor or sandy soil, as rich conditions encourage excessive suckering at the expense of flowering. Install a root barrier if planting near walkways or structures, as this shrub spreads vigorously by underground stolons.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; rose cactus (Pereskia bleo) is a primitive, leafy, climbing cactus from Colombia and Panama — the most un-cactus-like cactus, producing true, broad, succulent-edged leaves and large, rose-like orange flowers, with the leaves used as a vegetable in Malaysia and the Philippines where the plant has naturalized.
directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; provide support for climbing stems. Pereskia bleo (rose cactus or wax rose) is a Colombian and Panamanian climbing cactus that challenges every expectation of what a cactus looks like: it produces true, broad, elliptical, dark-green leaves (2–4 inches long) on stout, armed (spiny) stems — not the water-storing leafless paddles of familiar cacti. Pereskia species are the most evolutionarily 'primitive' of all cacti, representing the ancestral form from which leafless cacti evolved by gradually reducing their leaves while enlarging their stems as water storage organs. Rose cactus produces attractive, 2-inch, bright-orange to salmon-orange, multi-petaled flowers resembling wild roses or thin-petaled hibiscus, followed by fleshy, pear-shaped, orange-yellow fruits. In Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines — where the plant has naturalized — the leaves are eaten as a vegetable: the thick, slightly succulent, mildly flavored leaves are blanched, stir-fried, or added to soups. In traditional medicine across Southeast Asia, the leaves are used topically for skin conditions and as an anti-inflammatory preparation. A fascinating specimen plant for tropical collectors and those interested in the botanical history of cacti.

plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or container-grown divisions in spring in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Calanthe rosea is a deciduous species — its leaves die back in fall and the pseudobulbs rest through winter. Withhold water almost completely during dormancy (October–January) and resume as new growth starts in spring. Protect pseudobulbs from frost — zone 10 minimum for outdoor planting, zone 9 in containers. The delicate rose-pink flowers emerge in late fall to winter on leafless pseudobulbs. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil during the active growing season — Rose Calanthe needs consistent moisture and shade to develop strong pseudobulbs, but requires a near-dry winter dormancy period to trigger the delicate flower display on the leafless pseudobulbs. Calanthe rosea is a deciduous terrestrial orchid native to the Philippines and adjacent Southeast Asia in the Orchidaceae family, closely related to the widely grown tropical deciduous calanthes and producing one of the most refined and delicate flower displays available from a terrestrial orchid. The plant grows large, egg-shaped pseudobulbs with broad, pleated, fresh-green leaves in the growing season (spring through fall); as temperatures cool in fall, the leaves yellow and drop, leaving the bare pseudobulbs. On these leafless pseudobulbs, arching flower spikes emerge in late fall to winter, bearing 10–20 small (1-inch) flowers in delicate shades of rose-pink to clear pink with a slightly frilled lip — the pure, soft color and graceful arching of the spike over the bare pseudobulbs creates a distinctly elegant display. The flowers are lightly fragrant. Calanthe rosea is grown in tropical orchid collections for both its ornamental flower quality and its interesting deciduous habit — the emergence of flower spikes from bare pseudobulbs with no leaves is a striking seasonal event. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring around last frost date; plants may bloom the first fall from an early sowing or establish and bloom their second year.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in well-drained soil; germination is fast and reliable. Plant in full sun in poor to average, very well-drained soil — rose campion thrives under dry, sunny conditions that would stress many perennials. The intensely magenta-crimson flowers glow against the woolly, silver-white felted stems and leaves, which are ornamental throughout the growing season. Individual plants are short-lived (2–3 years) but self-sow abundantly so colonies persist indefinitely; thin or transplant self-sown seedlings to prevent overcrowding.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in poor to average, well-drained soil in full sun; rose campion prefers lean conditions and self-sows prolifically, filling in gaps in dry, sunny borders year after year.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; rose campion is a short-lived perennial or biennial that self-sows abundantly to maintain itself in the garden, producing dense rosettes of silver-white, woolly leaves the first year and branching stems bearing vivid magenta-crimson flowers for 4–6 weeks in early to midsummer the second year. The silver foliage provides excellent contrast with blue- and purple-flowered neighbors throughout the season even when plants are not in bloom. Do not over-fertilize or plant in rich soil — lean, dry conditions produce the best silver coloring and most compact growth. Leave some spent flowerheads to set seed for next year's colony.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Rose Creek is one of the most cold-hardy abelia selections and also one of the most compact — excellent for small foundation plantings and tight spaces.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rose Creek is a compact, cold-hardy abelia cultivar selected for its tight, mounding growth habit (2–3 feet tall and wide), exceptional cold hardiness (reliably hardy to zone 5 with protection, zone 6 without), and profuse white flower production from spring through frost. The white, tubular flowers are produced on arching stems in clusters and have the characteristic sweet, light fragrance of abelia flowers that attracts butterflies and hummingbirds. The small, dark-green foliage turns attractive bronze-reddish in fall and winter, providing seasonal color change interest. Rose Creek is somewhat more upright and compact than standard Abelia × grandiflora and its smaller stature makes it appropriate for tight foundation positions and smaller garden spaces where standard abelia would become too large. Like all abelias, Rose Creek is remarkably adaptable — tolerating clay soils, drought, heat, humidity, and partial shade that challenge many flowering shrubs. Minimal pruning is needed — remove any winter-damaged stems in late winter and lightly shape immediately after spring bloom if size control is needed. Plant 3–5 for foundation borders or in masses for sweeping effect.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens after the last frost in spring into moist, fertile, well-drained soil. In zone 7, mulch the root zone heavily in late autumn to protect the roots from hard freezes.
directions: Plant in partial sun with rich, evenly moist soil; in hotter climates, afternoon shade helps prevent wilting and keeps the large leaves looking their best through summer. The enormous domed clusters of fragrant rose-pink flowers appear from July through September and are highly attractive to butterflies. Be aware that this shrub spreads aggressively by root suckers, especially in zone 9 and warmer — install a root barrier or remove suckers promptly to prevent unwanted spread. In zones 7 and 8 the top growth is often killed by frost but roots reliably resprout in spring; cut dead stems to the ground and apply a thick mulch layer over the root zone each winter.

common_name: Rose Glow Barberry (Mottled Pink-and-Purple Foliage Dwarf Barberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; check state and local regulations before planting, as Japanese barberry is classified as invasive or restricted in a number of states due to its tendency to naturalize in woodlands.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since the mottled pink-purple color develops most intensely with good light exposure. Rose Glow is a compact, thorny barberry cultivar valued for new growth that emerges deep purple heavily mottled and splashed with rose-pink and white, giving each shrub a distinctive marbled, variegated look that matures to a more uniform reddish-purple as leaves age through the season. Its dense, twiggy, thorned branching makes it useful as a barrier planting or accent, and small yellow spring flowers are followed by red berries that persist into winter. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and low-maintenance, needing only an occasional shaping prune, but because Japanese barberry seeds into wild areas and displaces native understory plants in much of the eastern and midwestern US, gardeners should confirm it is not restricted or invasive in their area before planting.

plant_note: Plant small corms 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun; rhodohypoxis requires moist conditions during the growing season (spring through fall) but must be kept completely dry in winter when dormant, as wet-cold conditions cause rotting. In wetter climates, grow in containers that can be kept dry in winter or lift corms for frost-free dry storage.
directions: Plant small corms in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun; rose grass is a jewel-like South African alpine perennial from the Drakensberg mountains producing diminutive tufts of narrow, hairy, grass-like leaves (hence 'rose grass') only 2–4 inches tall, completely smothered in bright, cheerful, six-petaled flowers throughout summer from May to September. The flowers — individually only half an inch across but produced in remarkable abundance relative to the plant's tiny size — are in rich shades of deep rose-pink, pale pink, or white depending on the cultivar. The resulting effect is a dense carpet of concentrated, happy color disproportionate to the miniature plant size, making it exceptional for rock gardens, alpine troughs, container gardens, and front-of-border edging. It requires the unusual combination of moist summer growing conditions and completely dry winter dormancy — easy to provide in a pot, more challenging in open ground in wet climates.

plant_note: Scarify hard seed coat before sowing to speed germination.
directions: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before sowing to encourage even germination in warm soil. This native hibiscus produces large, pink, tropical-looking blooms and thrives in moist to wet ground. Give it full sun and steady water, making it ideal for pond edges, rain gardens, and low, damp spots. The plant dies back in winter and returns from the root, drawing bees and hummingbirds each summer.

common_name: Rose Marvel Salvia (Rose-Pink Compact Meadow Sage)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Rose Marvel offers a rose-pink flower color that is uncommon among meadow sage cultivars, most of which run to blue, violet, or purple tones.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, and avoid heavy, wet clay where the crown can rot over winter. Rose Marvel forms a compact clump of upright spikes packed with small rose-pink flowers from late spring into summer, offering a warm-toned alternative to the blue and violet shades typical of the species, and it pairs well with silver-foliaged companions like artemisia or lamb's ear. Cutting back the first flush of spent flower stalks encourages a repeat bloom later in the season. Bees work the flower spikes steadily through the bloom period, and the compact habit suits the front to middle of a sunny perennial border.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratify seed for 30 days; often blooms the second year.
directions: Cold-stratify the seed for about a month, then sow into moist soil in spring. Also called swamp milkweed, this native perennial bears clusters of fragrant dusty-rose flowers atop narrow-leaved stems. Unlike common milkweed it tolerates wet ground, making it perfect for rain gardens and pond margins in full sun. It is an essential Monarch host and nectar source, so avoid pesticides and let caterpillars feed on the foliage.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Rose Pincushion Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Rose Pincushion Cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil. Densely packed, hooked golden-brown spines cover a cylindrical, slowly clustering stem topped each spring with a striking ring of vivid rose-pink to magenta flowers that circle the crown just below the growing point, one of the more reliably free-flowering mammillaria species for a sunny windowsill collection. Native to central Mexico, it slowly forms small clusters of stems over years of growth, eventually developing into an attractive mounded specimen without the aggressive, rapid offsetting of faster-clustering mammillaria species. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright direct light for the best spine color and most reliable flowering, and protect from frost.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into a prepared seedbed of lean, well-drained soil; seeds need a period of winter cold to break dormancy and will germinate naturally the following spring.
directions: Rose Pink is a native annual or biennial of eastern North American meadows, clearings, and open woodland edges, instantly recognized by its four-angled (winged) stems and intensely fragrant, vivid pink, five-petaled flowers that appear July through August. Scatter seeds in fall on the surface of lean, well-drained soil in partial to full sun; plants resent rich or heavily amended beds and will become floppy and bloom-shy in fertile garden soil. In its second year as a biennial, the plant produces a profuse flush of bloom, drawing bumblebees and long-tongued native bees before setting abundant seed and dying. Allow seed to fall in place each year to establish a self-perpetuating colony, as Rose Pink relies on natural reseeding rather than vegetative spread.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in spring in saturated to wet, acidic (pH 3.5–5.5), nutrient-poor, peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; rose pogonia is a true bog obligate that will not survive in typical garden soil — it requires constantly wet, open, acidic bog conditions with no fertilizer.
directions: Rose pogonia is a delicate and charming bog orchid native to open, acidic wetlands — bogs, bog meadows, seeps, and sphagnum-filled depressions — across eastern North America from Newfoundland to Florida and west to Texas, where it blooms in June and July with a single rose-pink flower bearing a conspicuous fringed and bearded lip that smells faintly of raspberries. Like grass pink orchid, it practices deceptive pollination, offering no reward to pollinators — native bumblebees visit the flower expecting nectar but find none, and only return occasionally due to the lack of reward, which is sufficient for cross-pollination between widely spaced plants in bog meadows. Rose pogonia is one of the more tractable native bog orchids for cultivation because it spreads vegetatively by horizontal rhizomes in appropriate bog conditions, gradually forming small colonies in sphagnum moss or wet, peaty soil without the extreme mycorrhizal fungal dependence of many other native orchids. An essential component of a native bog garden in zones 3–9 alongside pitcher plants, sundews, and butterworts in nutrient-poor, constantly wet, acidic conditions.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Rose Quartz is part of the Winter Jewels breeding series, with pale double pink flowers blooming in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist while the plant establishes. Rose Quartz is part of the acclaimed Winter Jewels hellebore breeding series, producing rounded, outward-facing, fully double flowers in a pale, translucent pink reminiscent of the mineral it is named for, densely packed with extra petaloids for a full, rose-like appearance, held above leathery, evergreen, deeply divided foliage. Like other Lenten roses it blooms very early, often pushing through late-season snow or hard frost, providing reliable color in the shade garden when little else is flowering. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to showcase the flowers at their best, and site it away from areas where pets or children graze, since all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Rose Queen is a classic older cultivar bearing rose-pink flower spikes, an unusual color among meadow sage cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Rose Queen bears dense spikes of rose-pink flowers on a sturdy, upright plant, a warmer, softer color than the blue and violet tones that dominate most Salvia nemorosa cultivars, pairing well with silver foliage and other pastel perennials. Shear spent flower spikes back by half after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom later in the season. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond occasional deadheading and dividing congested clumps every few years.

common_name: Rose Queen Spider Flower (Classic Rose-Pink Self-Seeding Annual for Summer Borders)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost (or in early fall in zone 9 for winter-spring bloom) in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Rose Queen self-sows prolifically — once established, it will return as volunteers each year without replanting in most Gulf South gardens, though seedlings are variable in color.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Rose Queen is a rose-pink selection of Cleome hassleriana (spider flower) — one of the most heat-tolerant, drought-resistant, self-sufficient large annuals for Gulf South summer gardens, producing large, airy flower heads of rose-pink to warm-pink flowers with long, protruding stamens that give each floret its characteristic spider-like appearance. Cleome is uniquely suited to Gulf South summer heat: it grows vigorously through July and August when other summer annuals stall or decline, reaching 4–5 feet and producing continuous bloom from the elongating flower head at the top of each stem. The slightly sticky, aromatic stems and foliage are characteristic of the species and can be sticky to the touch — a minor trait that does not detract from the plant's considerable garden value. The large flower heads, combined with the tall habit and self-sowing tendency, create a semi-naturalized effect in borders that successive generations of gardeners have found to be exactly what hot, difficult summer borders need — a tall, self-sustaining plant that provides color and structure without requiring constant attention. Rose Queen produces predominantly rose-pink flowers but may show some color variation in self-sown seedlings, which can include white ('Alba') and lavender-purple forms within the same planting. An outstanding plant for butterflies and sphinx moths, which are particularly effective at accessing the long-stamened flowers. In Gulf South zone 9, Cleome can be fall-sown for spring bloom.

common_name: Rose Supreme Gladiolus (Peachy-Salmon Ruffled Tall Gladiolus)
plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season. Rose Supreme bears peachy-salmon flowers with ruffled edges on tall 3-4 foot spikes.
directions: Rose Supreme bears soft, peachy-salmon flowers with gently ruffled petal edges on tall, sturdy 3 to 4 foot spikes, a warm, sunset-toned color valued by cut-flower growers for its versatility in mixed bouquets. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

plant_note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade; this plant requires reliable moisture and will stress in drought. Blooms 2–3 weeks earlier than the white species (Chelone glabra).
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; rose turtlehead produces deep rose-pink inflated flowers from midsummer into fall, blooming 2–3 weeks earlier than the similar white turtlehead and offering richer color. It grows naturally along stream banks, wet meadow margins, and boggy woodland edges from Maryland south into the Southeast. Bumblebees that are heavy enough to force open the closed flower mouth are its primary pollinators. Plant in groups of three or more for best visual impact. Divide clumps every 4 years in spring to maintain vigor; cut to the ground after hard frost. Excellent in rain gardens and wet borders where the reliable summer moisture it needs is naturally available.

plant_note: Sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or cold-stratify seeds for 4–6 weeks before direct sowing in early spring. Surface sow and lightly press into soil; seeds need light to germinate.
directions: Surface sow in fall or after a 4–6 week cold stratification in spring, pressing seeds lightly into the soil surface as they require light for germination. Rose Vervain is a low-spreading native perennial that produces abundant clusters of rose-pink to purple flowers from spring through fall, making it one of the longest-blooming native groundcovers available for hot, dry sites. It spreads by trailing stems that root at nodes and self-seeds to gradually colonize sunny, dry borders, rock gardens, and slopes. Deadheading spent flower clusters encourages continued bloom and reduces self-seeding if naturalization is not desired.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost; zinnias grow quickly in warm soil.
directions: Abundant four- to five-inch rosy pink blooms range from dusty rose to warm pink, evoking an old-fashioned cottage garden when planted in drifts. Sow seed directly into warm soil after the last frost. Cut and deadhead frequently to keep the plants producing into fall. Full sun and good spacing for airflow help avoid powdery mildew. Pollinators, including butterflies, love the long-lasting flowers.

common_name: Rose de Mai Dianthus (Earliest-Blooming Intensely Clove-Scented Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Rose de Mai is the earliest-blooming garden pink, often flowering in March, with clear-pink, double, intensely clove-scented flowers.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Rose de Mai is prized as the earliest-blooming garden pink cultivar, often opening its clear-pink, double, intensely clove-scented flowers as early as March, well ahead of most other dianthus selections, extending the fragrant-pink season at the start of spring. Its compact, evergreen, blue-green foliage mound provides tidy structure at the front of a border year-round. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

common_name: Rose de Rescht (Persian Compact Fuchsia-Magenta Portland Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rose de Rescht is a Persian-origin Portland rose popularized in the West by rose historian Nancy Lindsay, prized for its compact size and intense fragrance.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Rose de Rescht, of Persian origin and popularized in Western gardens by rose historian Nancy Lindsay, bears densely double, vivid fuchsia-magenta flowers with an intense, rich fragrance on a notably compact bush, one of the smaller-growing Portland roses and well suited to a mixed border or smaller garden where larger old garden roses would overwhelm the space. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a hallmark advantage of the Portland class over many once-blooming old garden rose types. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Rose du Roi (Historic Bright Red Portland, Hybrid Perpetual Ancestor)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rose du Roi, introduced in 1815, is historically important as an ancestor of the later Hybrid Perpetual rose class.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Rose du Roi, introduced in France in 1815, bears bright, fragrant red double flowers and holds significant historical importance as a key ancestor in the development of the later Hybrid Perpetual rose class, which dominated nineteenth-century rose breeding and eventually gave rise to the modern hybrid tea. It repeats bloom well through the growing season, a hallmark advantage of the Portland class over many once-blooming old garden rose types. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Rose of Venezuela (Scarlet Bouquet Tree, Brownea grandiceps)
plant_note: Plant in partial shade with consistently moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Brownea grandiceps is an understory tree from humid tropical forests and grows best with protection from intense afternoon sun and drying winds. It is frost-sensitive and best suited to zone 10-11 outdoors. The new leaves emerge as remarkable bronze-pink, limp pendant tassels that gradually stiffen and turn green — protect these emerging leaf tassels from mechanical damage. Site where the spectacular flower heads can be viewed from below or from eye level.
directions: Plant in partial shade to dappled light in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Brownea grandiceps is a natural tropical forest understory tree that grows in the bright, filtered light beneath the forest canopy and performs best in garden conditions that replicate this environment. Brownea grandiceps is a medium-sized evergreen tree from Venezuela and adjacent Colombia in the family Leguminosae (Fabaceae), considered one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the tropical world — alongside Amherstia nobilis and Delonix regia — for the extraordinary quality and appearance of its flowers. The inflorescences are large, dense, spherical or dome-shaped heads of 50–100 individual tubular flowers, each 2–3 inches long, in vivid scarlet to orange-red with pale yellow stamens — the combined head is 8–14 inches across and resembles a massive, burning, scarlet cushion or bouquet emerging directly from the branch tips. The flowers are produced in successive flushes, primarily in spring and fall, and at peak bloom an established tree may carry dozens of the massive heads simultaneously. The emerging new leaves are equally spectacular: they appear as long, limp, silky, coppery-pink tassels hanging vertically from the branch tips before gradually stiffening and turning green — a phenomenon called 'juvenile leaf wilting' that occurs in many rainforest trees as a strategy to make young leaves unattractive to herbivores. Among the most prized ornamental trees in zone 10-11 tropical collections.

common_name: Rose of Venezuela (Scarlet Flame Bean, Mountain Rose)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; Rose of Venezuela is a South American leguminous tree considered one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the tropics — it produces large, tightly-packed, dome-shaped clusters of brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers directly on the branches and trunk, and displays new leaves as hanging, pale-pink 'ribbons' or 'tassels' before they harden to green.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; provide irrigation during dry periods. Brownea coccinea (Rose of Venezuela or scarlet flame bean) is a tropical South American tree widely regarded as one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the tropics — a standard in tropical botanical gardens worldwide precisely because of two extraordinary visual displays. The first: large, dome-shaped, tightly packed heads (capitula) of brilliant scarlet-red, tubular flowers — 6–10 inches across — that emerge directly from the branches and trunk (cauliflory), creating a dense, ball-like cluster of brilliant red against the green foliage. The second: the remarkable display of new leaf growth — young leaves emerge in hanging 'pendant' clusters, beginning as soft, limp, pale-pink to cream-colored 'ribbons' of young leaflets that hang limply below the branch tips before gradually stiffening, darkening to green, and taking their mature position. This juvenile 'drooping' display of new leaves is one of the most unusual and memorable sights in tropical horticulture. Brownea is in the legume family (Fabaceae) and is related to the flamboyant tree. In zone 10–12, it makes an outstanding specimen tree for tropical gardens, botanical collections, and large spaces where a genuinely rare and spectacular ornamental is desired.

common_name: Rose-Painted Calathea (Medallion Plant, Dottie Calathea, Rose-Painted Prayer Plant)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light — no direct sun, which bleaches and scorches the patterned leaves. Use well-draining peat-based or peat-free porous mix; keep consistently moist but never waterlogged. Calatheas are sensitive to fluoride in tap water — use rainwater, distilled water, or water that has stood overnight. Maintain high humidity (60%+ preferred). Propagate by dividing rhizomes in spring. The cultivar 'Medallion' (dark green with pink midrib and silver-green margins) and 'Dottie' (nearly black leaves with pink margins) are widely available. All parts non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light to dim interior light — Rose-Painted Calathea is one of the most shade-tolerant of the ornamental calatheas and tolerates low-light conditions that would defeat most other foliage plants. Calathea roseopicta is a rhizomatous, clump-forming tropical perennial native to northwestern Brazil and adjacent Colombia in the family Marantaceae, one of the most widely grown and ornamentally important of the approximately 200 Calathea species for indoor and tropical shade garden use. The leaves are large (6–12 inches long), broadly oval, carried upright on graceful petioles, and decorated with some of the most elaborate natural patterns of any houseplant: the upper surface is dark green with a feathered lighter green center stripe, bordered by a band of bright rosy pink or silvery white, then a dark green margin — a concentric color pattern that earned the plant the name 'Rose-Painted Calathea.' The undersides are uniformly deep purple-maroon. Like other Marantaceae members, C. roseopicta exhibits nyctinasty — the leaves fold upward at night to reveal the purple undersides, then open again at daybreak, driven by a circadian rhythm. Multiple named cultivars with varying color expressions are widely available: 'Medallion' (classic pink-banded), 'Dottie' (near-black leaves with bright pink margins), 'Rosey' (silvery-green with pink), and 'Medallion Fusion.' Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; rosea ice plant forms a fine-textured, low, dense mat that roots as it spreads across bare ground.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; rosea ice plant forms a fine-textured, densely branched mat of tiny, glistening, cylindrical leaves covered so thickly in pale pink to lilac-pink flowers each spring that the foliage nearly disappears beneath the bloom for several weeks. Its finer texture and lower profile compared to trailing ice plant make it especially useful for softening the edges of paths, rock walls, and gravel beds where a delicate groundcover is wanted. Extremely drought tolerant once established, it thrives on minimal water in full sun and mineral, fast-draining soil, and it spreads and roots along the ground to knit bare areas together within a season or two. Being frost-tender, protect or take cutting insurance in colder parts of its zone range, and shear lightly after bloom to maintain a tight, tidy mat.

plant_note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Rosea is a soft pink-flowered form of Japanese wisteria, an unusual color among wisterias.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a very sturdy support structure built to carry the mature vine's considerable weight. Rosea bears long, fragrant racemes in an unusual pale, dusty pink, a soft, romantic departure from the violet-blue or white that dominates most wisteria, making it a distinctive choice for a pastel garden scheme. Like other Japanese wisteria it twines clockwise and grows vigorously, needing firm summer pruning to control rampant new growth and a shaping late-winter prune to encourage flowering rather than pure vegetative sprawl. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity and plan for a genuinely large, long-term structure to support it.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped plants in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Rosea is a classic pink-toned star magnolia selection, its buds flushed with pink fading to near-white as they open.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Rosea opens from pink-flushed buds into star-shaped flowers that fade to a soft near-white as they mature, giving the bloom a two-toned effect across the flowering period in late winter to early spring before the leaves emerge. It is one of the older and more widely available pink-toned star magnolia cultivars, with the same fine-textured, multi-tepaled flower form and light fragrance typical of the species. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Rosea is a historic 1906 cultivar with salmon-pink flower spikes, distinct from the white-flowered 'Sixteen Candles' and the deeper pink 'Ruby Spice' already common in cultivation.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; summersweet tolerates shade well and is commonly used as understory planting beneath larger trees, though it flowers most heavily with a few hours of morning sun. Rosea, introduced in 1906 and one of the oldest named summersweet cultivars still in cultivation, bears dense, upright spikes of fragrant, soft salmon-pink flowers in midsummer, buds opening a deeper rose-pink that fades gently as they age, a distinct, historic color option from the pure white 'Sixteen Candles' and 'September Beauty' and the deeper 'Ruby Spice' selected decades later. Its intensely sweet, spicy fragrance perfumes the garden for weeks and draws heavy pollinator traffic from bees and butterflies. It tolerates wet soil better than most shrubs, making it useful along ponds or low spots, and suckers gently over time to form a colony. Prune immediately after flowering if size control is needed.

plant_note: Plant young container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; rosebay rhododendron tolerates deeper shade than almost any other flowering broadleaf evergreen — it naturally grows in the dark understory beneath hemlock and hardwood canopy.
directions: Rosebay rhododendron (great laurel) is the largest native rhododendron in North America — capable of reaching 20–35 feet in the moist, cool, deep shade of Appalachian stream gorges and hemlock forests — and produces massive trusses of white to pale pink, spotted flowers in June and July, a month later than most other rhododendrons, making it the last and largest-flowered of all native flowering shrubs in the eastern forest. Its enormous, glossy, dark green leaves (up to 10 inches long) curl tightly during cold weather as a frost protection mechanism, a distinctive winter character; the dense, multi-stemmed growth creates impenetrable evergreen thickets in shaded stream valleys that are critical winter shelter for ruffed grouse, white-tailed deer, and black bears. It is the most shade-tolerant of all native rhododendrons — thriving in the darkest understory beneath eastern hemlock, where little else with ornamental value grows — and represents one of the few truly shade-tolerant, large-scale evergreen flowering shrubs for the eastern native garden. Grows slowly but long-lived; once established it requires minimal care in appropriate conditions.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in sharply drained, lean, phosphorus-poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rosemary grevillea requires excellent drainage above all else — wet, heavy clay soils or overwatering are the primary causes of failure. Use low-phosphorus fertilizer only. It is moderately frost-tolerant once established, surviving to 15–20°F in zone 8.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rosemary grevillea is an Australian shrub named for its narrow, rosemary-like needle leaves (prickly to the touch) on arching, graceful stems that form a loose, airy, medium-sized shrub 3–6 feet tall. From late autumn through spring it produces clusters of spidery, deep-pink to crimson-red flowers in the distinctive grevillea style — curved, nectar-rich, toothbrush-shaped clusters that are irresistible to hummingbirds and honey-producing bees, providing critical winter nectar during the period when almost no other nectar source flowers in California and the Southwest. One of the most consistently winter-flowering garden shrubs in zones 8b–10. Drought-tolerant once established (requires no summer water in Mediterranean climates), long-lived, and largely pest- and disease-free in appropriate conditions. An essential plant for California native wildlife gardens and for year-round hummingbird habitat.

common_name: Roseraie de l'Hay Rose (Fragrant Wine-Red Rugosa Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; Roseraie de l'Hay is a vigorous, intensely fragrant wine-red rugosa rose named for the famed French rose garden.
directions: Plant in average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; rugosa roses excel in poor, dry, or coastal soils that would stress most other roses. Roseraie de l'Hay bears large, loosely double, rich wine-red to magenta blooms with an intense, spicy-sweet fragrance considered among the strongest of any rugosa, opening on a large, vigorous shrub that can be used as an informal flowering hedge. It sets few hips compared to other rugosas since its heavily petaled blooms are less fertile, so it is grown primarily for its exceptional flower color and fragrance. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since rugosas bloom on both old and new growth and resent hard pruning.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to high open shade under deciduous trees. Roseshell Azalea tolerates somewhat drier and rockier conditions than most native azaleas and is the hardiest species, performing well in Zones 3–7.
directions: Roseshell Azalea is a fragrant native deciduous azalea of the northeastern United States and Appalachian Mountains, producing profuse clusters of deep rose-pink to light pink flowers with a strong, sweet clove-like fragrance that perfumes entire gardens in late spring — a quality unique among native azaleas that makes it an outstanding choice wherever fragrance is a garden priority. The most cold-hardy of all native azaleas, surviving USDA Zone 3 reliably, Roseshell Azalea grows in rocky, dry-to-moist, open woods, cliff edges, and forest margins from Quebec south to the Virginia mountains, tolerating somewhat drier and stonier conditions than most other native azalea species. The compact, naturally rounded growth habit, spectacular fragrant flowers, and brilliant orange-red to crimson fall foliage make this a superb multi-season native shrub for northern and mountain landscapes. Plant in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to high, shifting shade under deciduous trees.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Roseum Elegans is one of the most cold-hardy and widely adaptable rhododendron cultivars, tolerating heat, cold, and poor soil better than many fussier hybrids.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Roseum Elegans is one of the most cold-hardy and widely adaptable rhododendron cultivars, tolerating heat, cold, and poor soil better than many fussier hybrids. Large, dense trusses of lavender-pink flowers with a faint orange-brown blotch cover this old, extremely reliable catawba rhododendron hybrid each late spring, backed by large, leathery, deep green evergreen leaves that provide year-round structure to a shaded border. Introduced in the nineteenth century and still one of the most widely planted rhododendron cultivars in North America, it owes its enduring popularity to exceptional cold hardiness, heat tolerance, and general toughness compared to more temperamental modern hybrids, thriving in a wider range of climates and soils. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid planting too deep or in poorly drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

plant_note: Set out nursery plants in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil.
directions: This hardy evergreen shrub produces clusters of soft pink, trumpet-shaped blooms in spring above lush foliage. Plant it in spring or fall in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and site it in dappled shade or morning sun. Keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist with a mulch of pine bark or leaves. Avoid deep planting, as the crown must stay near the surface. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape the plant.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; surface sow as seed needs light to germinate.
directions: This sweetly scented alyssum forms low mats covered in tiny rose-pink flowers in mini-rosettes, perfect for rock gardens, walls, paths, and container edges. Sow seed directly in early spring, pressing it onto the surface since it needs light to germinate. Full sun to light shade and well-drained soil keep it blooming. Shear lightly if it fades in summer heat to spur a fresh flush. The mildly grassy, mustardy flowers are edible and draw in pollinators.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; rosilla is a California and Oregon native sneezeweed adapted to moist, seasonally flooded grasslands and stream margins.
directions: Sow direct in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rosilla is a wetland-affiliated native that thrives in consistently moist conditions near streams, ponds, and in rain gardens — it is poorly adapted to dry soils. Helenium puberulum is a California and Oregon native sneezeweed of moist grasslands, stream margins, and valley bottoms; it produces winged stems with decurrent leaf bases (a distinguishing feature of helenium) and yellow, daisy-like flowers with reflexed ray petals around a prominent, rounded yellow to greenish disk in summer through fall. Like all heleniums, it is an excellent late-season pollinator plant, providing nectar for a broad range of native bees, butterflies, and wasps; the yellow flowers are intensely attractive to bumblebees. It naturalizes readily in moist, sunny California-native gardens and is effective in mass plantings at pond margins and in wet meadow restorations.

common_name: Rosina Sweet Violet (Long-Blooming Pink Fragrant Violet)
plant_note: Plant divisions of Rosina in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs, where it spreads slowly by short stolons into a fragrant, well-mannered groundcover.
directions: Plant divisions of Rosina in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs, where it spreads slowly by short stolons into a fragrant, well-mannered groundcover. Unlike the deep-purple species type, Rosina bears soft pink, sweetly perfumed flowers over an unusually long season from late winter into spring, with a light repeat in fall in mild climates. Both the flowers and young leaves are edible, the blossoms often crystallized in sugar, tossed into salads, or steeped into a fragrant syrup, with a mild, faintly sweet flavor and the same honeyed violet scent. Its shade tolerance, extended bloom, and edible flowers make Rosina a useful choice for a woodland edge or shaded cottage bed where color and food value are both wanted.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained to average, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to loam soil in full sun; rosinweed is a deep-rooted prairie plant that takes 2–3 years to bloom but becomes virtually indestructible once established — site it where it can remain permanently.
directions: Sow seed in fall in well-drained to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun — rosinweed is the most compact and garden-adaptable of the native Silphium genus, producing bright yellow, 2–3 inch daisy-like flowers from late summer through early fall on branching stems 3–5 feet tall. Like all silphiums, rosinweed is a deep-rooted prairie species with extraordinary drought and heat tolerance once established — the deep taproot (sometimes 12 feet deep in mature specimens) accesses moisture unavailable to shallow-rooted plants. The rough, sandpaper-textured opposite leaves are distinctive. The flat, disc-shaped seeds are highly attractive to goldfinches, which perch on the sturdy stems to extract them. It is being researched as a potential perennial grain crop because the seeds have a high oil content. More compact and less rank than compass plant or prairie dock, making it more suitable for smaller prairie garden settings. Extremely long-lived — prairie specimens are known to be over 100 years old.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; Rosso peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings, like other ripple peperomias.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; Rosso peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings, like other ripple peperomias. Deeply quilted, ruffled, dark green leaves with a metallic sheen are strikingly backed in solid burgundy-red, an eye-catching two-tone effect visible whenever a leaf turns or catches the light, set off by slender, upright, mouse-tail-like flower spikes above the compact rosette. Its naturally tidy, symmetrical growth habit needs little pruning or shaping, and the plant's small scale suits a windowsill, desk, or terrarium as well as a mixed dish garden. Water only when the top inch of potting mix has dried, and propagate easily from leaf cuttings rooted in moist soil.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall in mild climates; clarkia dislikes transplanting.
directions: Graceful branching stems carry a profusion of delicate pink, white, and salmon blooms from spring into summer, swaying in the breeze. Sow seed directly where it is to grow, as clarkia resents root disturbance. It prefers cool weather, so sow in early spring or in fall where winters are mild. Give it full sun to part shade and lean, well-drained soil. Pollinators love the flowers, which also last well when cut.

plant_note: Plant in early spring in deep, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil. Softwood cuttings taken in summer root under mist propagation; seeds should be sown fresh in autumn in a cold frame as they lose viability quickly.
directions: Plant in partial sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with protection from harsh wind; Dipelta floribunda develops into a large arching shrub of 10–15 ft and needs generous space to display its full elegance. In late spring, fragrant pale pink flowers with distinctive orange-yellow throats cover the gracefully drooping branches in a display reminiscent of a giant Weigela. After the flowers fade, the papery, wing-like seed bracts persist through summer and add ornamental interest that extends the plant's season of appeal. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape, removing only the oldest and weakest stems; heavy pruning is unnecessary and detracts from the natural arching habit.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosy ice plant needs sharp drainage and full sun for its best flowering display.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosy ice plant needs sharp drainage and full sun for its best flowering display. Slender, cylindrical, gray-green leaves cover a mounding, semi-woody South African succulent that produces a dazzling flush of glistening, deep rose-pink, daisy-like flowers each spring, densely covering the plant in color for several weeks and giving the whole planting a shimmering, iridescent quality typical of the ice plant group. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in coastal and Mediterranean-climate gardens, tolerating salt spray, poor soil, and neglect while providing a reliable, showy spring flower display for a sunny bank, rock garden, or xeriscape border. Water only occasionally, shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound tidy and encourage denser growth, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.

common_name: Rosy Lights Azalea (Cold-Hardy Fragrant Deciduous Rose-Pink Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Rosy Lights, part of the University of Minnesota Northern Lights series bred for exceptional cold hardiness, bears fragrant rose-pink flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Rosy Lights, part of the University of Minnesota's Northern Lights azalea series bred specifically for extreme cold hardiness, bears clusters of fragrant, rose-pink, funnel-shaped flowers on bare branches in mid-spring before the deciduous foliage fully expands, followed by good yellow-orange fall color. Unlike the evergreen azaleas more common in Southern landscapes, this deciduous type drops its leaves each winter but rewards gardeners at the colder edge of azalea range with reliable, fragrant bloom. Water deeply during dry spells and prune lightly right after flowering, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.

plant_note: Direct-sow into deep, dry sandy soil after the last frost, choosing an open, disturbed, or lean site.
directions: Direct-sow into deep, dry sandy soil after the last frost, choosing an open, disturbed, or lean site since this Texas native resents rich, moisture-retentive beds. Found naturally in sandy soils along the middle Texas Gulf Coast, the post oak belt, and the Rolling and High Plains, it produces thimble-shaped lavender-pink flowers with a distinctive dark red style from June through November. It is a strong late-season nectar source for bees, butterflies, and moths, and several butterfly and moth larvae use it as a host plant. Its extended bloom window makes it a valuable filler for a Gulf Coast dry-meadow planting once summer heat has stalled other wildflowers.

common_name: Rosy Rain Lily (Cuban Pink Miniature Fall Rain Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Zephyranthes rosea naturalizes freely in Gulf South gardens, multiplying rapidly by offsets and self-seeding — plant in masses of 25+ bulbs for best display and allow to spread into expanding naturalized colonies.
directions: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Zephyranthes rosea (Rosy Rain Lily or Cuban Rain Lily) is a small but charming fall-blooming bulb native to Cuba and Guatemala that has naturalized widely through the Gulf South as a garden escape — producing small (1.5–2 inch diameter), funnel-shaped, rose-pink to warm-pink flowers on 6–8 inch stems in flushes triggered by rainfall events from late summer through fall. The delightful blooming response to rainfall — a period of dry weather followed by a good rain triggers near-simultaneous flowering across an established colony within 2–3 days — creates the characteristic rain lily display that is one of the most charming garden phenomena of the Gulf South fall season. Zephyranthes rosea is the smallest and most miniature of the commonly grown rain lily species, with flowers somewhat smaller than Z. grandiflora but produced in great profusion on well-established colonies. The warm rose-pink color is more saturated and vivid than the pale shell-pink of Z. grandiflora — a clear, definite pink that reads well at a distance in naturalized mass plantings. Established colonies multiply rapidly by bulb offsets and prolific self-seeding, eventually forming dense patches that provide reliable annual display with no maintenance. Outstanding for naturalizing along lawn edges, in rock gardens, under deciduous trees, and along garden paths where the self-seeding habit can fill in naturally.

common_name: Rosy Returns Daylily (Pink Reblooming Miniature Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Rosy Returns reblooms most vigorously when kept consistently moist between bloom cycles.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Rosy Returns is a compact prolific-reblooming daylily producing rose-pink flowers with a yellow-green throat and darker rose eye zone from early summer through fall in multiple reliable flushes. It was bred as a Stella d'Oro companion that extends the rebloom series into pink tones while maintaining the same outstanding rebloom habit. The soft rose-pink coloring is attractive and distinctive among reblooming daylilies, which tend to be dominated by yellow and orange. Rosy Returns combines beautifully with white, purple, or blue perennial companions in the long-season border. In zone 9 it begins blooming in March or April and typically continues through November, often with semi-evergreen foliage through mild Gulf Coast winters. Divide every 3–4 years.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in early spring, spacing at 8–12 inches for coverage within 2 years; tolerates very dry shade once established.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; rosy sedge is one of the finest native groundcovers for dry shade under mature deciduous trees, where it forms dense tufts of arching, fine-textured, glossy green foliage. It is not a spreader in the invasive sense — each clump slowly expands but does not colonize aggressively — making it well-suited to a refined shade garden. The plant tolerates drought better than Pennsylvania sedge (C. pensylvanica) and handles the dense root competition of established trees. Self-sows lightly once established to fill gaps over time.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to deep shade; rosy twisted stalk is a slow-growing woodland perennial of cool northern and mountain forests that requires consistent moisture and cool summer temperatures.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; established plants spread slowly by rhizomes and form loose colonies over many years without becoming invasive. Streptopus roseus is a graceful, Solomon's-seal-like woodland perennial of boreal and montane forests across northern and eastern North America, producing arching stems 12 to 24 inches tall with broad, sessile, parallel-veined leaves; uniquely, its tiny rose-pink, bell-shaped flowers hang singly beneath each leaf from a distinctly kinked or twisted flower stalk — the characteristic that gives the plant its common name. Small red berries follow the flowers in late summer and are eagerly eaten by forest birds, though they are considered mildly toxic to humans. This is a plant for patient gardeners: seed exhibits double dormancy requiring two cold periods before germination, making division the practical propagation method for most gardeners.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in cool, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; rosy twisted-stalk is native to cool, moist mountain and northern forests and performs best in a sheltered, cool microclimate rather than a hot southern exposure.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in cool, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; rosy twisted-stalk is native to cool, moist mountain and northern forests and performs best in a sheltered, cool microclimate rather than a hot southern exposure. Streptopus lanceolatus produces a distinctive zigzagging stem with clasping, parallel-veined leaves and small, rose-pink to purplish, bell-shaped flowers dangling on thread-like, kinked stalks from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by translucent red berries in late summer. The twisted flower stalks (the source of both the genus name and common name) and zigzag stem give it a wiry, delicate texture that contrasts nicely with broader-leaved shade perennials like hosta and ginger. It needs consistently cool, moist conditions and struggles in hot, humid summers or dry shade, making it best suited to northern and higher-elevation gardens or shaded, moisture-retentive microclimates further south.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or late summer in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; rosy-leaf sage is damaged below 28 degrees F and killed at 25 degrees F. In zones 8-11 it overwinters as a perennial and grows as a substantial shrubby plant; in colder zones it can be grown as a large annual or lifted and overwintered frost-free. It blooms very late — September through November — when most other flowering plants have finished.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; rosy-leaf sage is a tall, shrubby Mexican salvia producing some of the most unusually beautiful flowers in the genus — the large, prominently inflated pink-carmine calyx tubes (the involucre that gives it its name) persist and enlarge to become ornamental bracts that frame the rosy-pink to carmine flower tubes, giving each flower cluster a double-layered, large-scale, almost peony-like appearance quite unlike the typical small-flowered salvia. The flowers appear in terminal clusters in September through November — later than almost any other salvia — making it an invaluable late-season nectar source for migrating hummingbirds. In zones 8-11 it grows as a substantial perennial shrub 4-6 feet tall; in zones 6-7 it can be grown as a late-season annual in a large container. The cultivar Bethellii has particularly large flower clusters and is the most widely grown form.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost in dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; self-sows moderately in open disturbed ground.
directions: Rothrock's Knapweed is a native annual or biennial of mountain meadows, roadsides, and open disturbed ground in Arizona, New Mexico, and adjacent Mexico — one of the few Centaurea species native to the southwestern United States. It produces showy, rose-purple, thistle-like composite flower heads on branching stems from summer through fall, attracting native bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Unlike many knapweeds in the genus, this native species is non-invasive and ecologically appropriate for southwestern US gardens. Direct sow in spring after last frost in dry, well-drained, lean soil in full sun; plants self-sow moderately and establish naturally in open, rocky, or disturbed ground.

plant_note: Plant in full sun and average to lean, well-drained soil; established plants are drought- and salt-tolerant and need little maintenance beyond an early spring cutback.
directions: Plant in full sun in average to lean, well-drained soil, since established plants are drought- and salt-tolerant and need little maintenance beyond an early spring cutback. Introduced by German breeder Karl Foerster in the late 1960s, Rotstrahlbusch is one of the older switchgrass selections grown for reliably early and intense red coloring, with leaf tips flushing red by midsummer well before the burgundy fall color typical of most switchgrass cultivars. It is shorter and finer-textured than the wild species, forming a dense upright clump topped by airy, reddish-tinged seed heads in late summer that fade to beige through winter. The strong, non-flopping habit and compact size make it useful in smaller borders where taller switchgrass cultivars would overwhelm the planting.

common_name: Rotunda Holly (Dwarf Chinese Holly, Mounding Chinese Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter through spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rotunda is a sterile male clone and does not produce berries — it is grown purely for its compact mounding form and dark-green foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rotunda is one of the most widely planted compact foundation shrubs in the Gulf South — a male Chinese holly selection with a dense, rounded, mounding form that stays compact (2–4 feet tall, slightly wider) without the frequent pruning that many other Chinese holly cultivars require to maintain shape. Rotunda does not produce berries (it is a sterile male clone) and is grown purely for its clean, dark-green, heavily spined foliage and reliable, slow-growing mounded form. The extremely sharp, multiple-spined leaves make Rotunda an outstanding security planting under windows and along boundaries — the spines deter entry more effectively than most other barrier plants. Despite the spiny leaves, Rotunda is one of the most versatile, trouble-free foundation shrubs in the Gulf South: it tolerates heavy clay, drought, heat, partial shade, and the year-round humidity without significant pest or disease pressure. In typical residential foundation plantings, Rotunda maintains a clean, tight mound for years with minimal to no pruning — a significant advantage over faster-growing hollies that require aggressive trimming 2–3 times per season. Deer-resistant; essentially maintenance-free in well-drained soil.

common_name: Rotundiloba Fruitless Sweetgum (Seedless Round-Lobed Sweetgum with No Gumballs)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; Rotundiloba produces no seed balls, avoiding the spiny gumball litter of standard sweetgum on lawns and walkways.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; Rotundiloba is a naturally occurring seedless selection of American sweetgum, prized for producing the species' spectacular multicolored fall foliage display of yellow, orange, red, and burgundy-purple without the spiny seed balls that make standard sweetgum a nuisance on lawns, patios, and walkways. Its distinctive rounded, scalloped leaf lobes (rather than the pointed star shape of typical sweetgum) also make it easy to identify at a glance even before fall color develops. Like the species it grows into a large, handsome shade tree with a somewhat narrower, more upright habit than seed-grown sweetgum, transplanting readily when young and establishing quickly in the landscape. Because it sets no seed, it also does not provide the winter seed-ball forage that goldfinches and other birds rely on from wild sweetgum, a worthwhile tradeoff to weigh where wildlife value is a priority.

plant_note: Set the crown two to three inches deep at planting time to protect against clematis wilt, and mulch the root zone while letting the top growth reach for sun.
directions: This French-bred cultivar is valued for its velvety, deep ruby-red blooms with contrasting cream-yellow anthers, produced in flushes from early to late summer. As a pruning group three vine, cut all stems back to a strong bud pair roughly twelve inches above the soil in late winter each year to keep growth vigorous and floriferous. It performs best with its roots shaded and cool and its foliage and flowers reaching into full sun on a trellis, fence, or through a shrub. Regular moisture and an annual topdressing of compost help sustain its rich color through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; sunflowers grow best sown where they will bloom.
directions: This stunning true-red sunflower blooms on multi-branching plants, offering a dramatic accent in beds, borders, and bouquets. Sow seed directly into warm soil after frost, spacing plants closer together for longer stems and smaller flowers ideal for cutting. Full sun and steady moisture produce the best display. Cut stems just before the flowers fully open for the longest vase life. Successive sowings extend the bloom season into fall.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; rough agave is a Chihuahuan Desert native with distinctly rough-textured, gray-green leaves and moderate cold tolerance for the genus.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, rocky soil in full sun; rough agave forms a broad, symmetrical rosette of thick, gray-green leaves with a distinctly rough, sandpaper-like surface texture and reddish-brown marginal teeth, native to rocky hillsides and desert scrub of the Chihuahuan Desert. Its imposing rosette makes a strong architectural focal point in a xeriscape bed for years before the plant reaches flowering maturity, when it sends up a tall, branched flower stalk lined with yellow blooms in its single flowering event before the rosette dies. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than agaves like Agave neomexicana or Agave havardiana, so gardeners at the cooler edge of its range should site it in a protected, reflective location such as against a south-facing wall. Water only to establish, since mature specimens are extremely drought tolerant and prone to rot in heavy, slow-draining, or frequently irrigated soil.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; rough blazing star requires cold stratification for reliable germination and grows from a corm — established corms can also be planted in spring 2–3 inches deep; avoid rich or clay-heavy soils that cause crown rot.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy, loamy, or rocky soil in full sun; rough blazing star is among the most drought-tolerant Liatris species, native to the dry prairies, open woodlands, and rocky glades of the central United States from North Dakota south to Texas and east to Ohio, where it thrives in the kind of lean, dry, well-drained soils where L. spicata fails. Liatris aspera grows from a rounded corm and produces a slender, rough-textured (aspera = rough) stem bearing alternate, linear to lance-shaped leaves and, from August through October, a spike of rounded, button-like, rosy-lavender to pink-purple flower heads with slightly fringed bracts — unlike the more densely spiked L. spicata and L. pycnostachya, the heads are spaced somewhat apart along the spike, giving it a looser, more open appearance; like all Liatris, flowers open from the top of the spike downward. It is an exceptional pollinator plant for migrating monarch butterflies in late summer and fall, and is also heavily visited by native bumblebees, sweat bees, skipper butterflies, and cloudless sulphur; the dried seed heads are eaten by goldfinches and American tree sparrows. Rough blazing star is an excellent choice for dry, lean, native meadow plantings, prairie restorations, and rock gardens where it out-competes weeds once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade; rough maidenhair fern is more drought tolerant than most adiantums and better adapted to humid subtropical conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; rough maidenhair fern is broadly adapted and heat-tolerant, native to tropical Africa, Asia, and Australia, and far better suited to humid subtropical conditions of zone 8-11 than the delicate northern maidenhair fern. New fronds emerge in shades of coppery-pink or bronze before maturing to bright fresh green. The distinctive palmate frond arrangement with leaflets resembling a spread hand is elegant and recognizable. More tolerant of occasional dryness than other maidenhair ferns, making it more forgiving in garden conditions where desiccation is a common maidenhair killer.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification over winter; seeds require a cold, moist period to break dormancy reliably in spring.
directions: A native perennial prickly poppy of dry, rocky slopes, canyon walls, and disturbed open ground in the Rocky Mountains and Great Plains; more persistently perennial than annual Argemone species; produces white, tissue-paper-textured flowers 2-3 inches across on densely spiny, branching stems with blue-gray, deeply lobed, spine-tipped leaves. The yellowish sap is toxic. Direct sow in fall in rocky, very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun; established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived. Excellent for rocky slopes and xeriscape gardens in zones 4-9.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; rough rosinweed grows in dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, open prairie and savanna soils. Develops a deep taproot over years; best sown directly where it is to grow permanently.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rough rosinweed is a drought-tolerant native Silphium of open prairies, dry savannas, and open woodlands across the southeastern US, producing multiple-branched stems with numerous yellow daisy flowers in summer. The stiffly rough, sandpaper-textured leaves give the plant a tactile distinctiveness. Like all rosinweeds, it produces a resinous, aromatic sap and develops a deep taproot that makes established plants very drought tolerant and also nearly impossible to transplant. Direct sow is strongly preferred over transplanting for this species. The seeds are highly attractive to goldfinches and other finches in late summer and fall. A mid-to-tall native prairie plant providing excellent structural interest and wildlife food in naturalistic gardens.

subcategory: South American tropical spiral ginger ornamental
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Rough Spiral Flag is a tall, tropical spiral ginger from the lowland rainforests of Central and South America — bearing rough-textured, spirally arranged leaves on tall canes and distinctive, elongated red-orange bracts with yellow flowers — one of the taller and more architectural of the cultivated Costus species.
directions: Plant Costus scaber divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; provide consistent moisture throughout the warm season and protect from temperatures below 40°F; cut old canes to the ground after they finish blooming and new shoots will emerge from the base; divide clumps every 2–3 years. Rough Spiral Flag is named for the distinctively rough, slightly sandpapery texture of its large, spirally arranged leaves — a texture that sets it apart visually from the smoother-leaved Costus species. The elongated red-orange to brick-red bracts with yellow flowers create a more narrow, torch-like shape than the rounder cones of Costus spicatus. Native to tropical lowland forests and forest margins in Central and South America, it prefers warm, humid conditions in partial shade — making it better adapted to deeply tropical zone 10–12 gardens than the more cold-hardy C. spicatus. Young leaf shoots and tender stem tips of several Costus species, including C. scaber, have been used as edible vegetables by Indigenous peoples throughout their range in tropical America, cooked as pot herbs or eaten raw as salad greens. The plant provides a bold, architectural tropical statement in the garden throughout the warm months and is particularly effective when massed under the canopy of large shade trees.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; rough velvetseed is frost-tender and native to coastal hammocks and pinelands of South Florida.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; rough velvetseed is frost-tender and native to coastal hammocks and pinelands of South Florida. Rough, sandpaper-textured leaves cover a large shrub or small tree bearing small, fragrant, white to cream flowers followed by red berries that turn black as they ripen, providing food for a range of native birds and wildlife across its hammock and coastal scrub habitat. Well adapted to the poor, well-drained, often rocky limestone soils typical of South Florida's native plant communities, it tolerates both dry, sunny sites and the partial shade of a hammock understory, making it a versatile choice for naturalistic native landscaping. It needs little supplemental water or fertilizer once established and provides good wildlife habitat value with minimal maintenance.
