directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Russell's sage is a Turkish native and one of the most structurally interesting and drought-tolerant perennials for the sunny border — forming bold, spreading mounds of large, heart-shaped, rough-textured, wrinkled, gray-green leaves and in June through July producing upright stems carrying whorled tiers of soft, butter-yellow, hooded, sage-like flowers arranged in distinct rings at regular intervals up the stem, creating an architectural, tiered candelabra form. After the flowers fade, the calyx whorls remain on the dried stems through autumn and winter as attractive, rigid, tiered seed structures in warm brown, providing months of winter architectural interest and seeds for finches. The dried winter stems are so decorative that Chelsea Flower Show designers have used them as a winterbourne architectural element in naturalistic plantings. Outstanding for the gravel garden, prairie-style border, and drought-tolerant plantings combined with ornamental grasses and other drought-adapted plants. Visited heavily by bumblebees.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into moist, well-drained soil in a partially sunny woodland glade or forest edge. Surface sow or barely cover seeds, as they need light and cold stratification over winter to germinate reliably in spring.
directions: Russell's Wild Bergamot is a rare and regionally distinctive bee balm native to Ozark glades, open woodlands, and rocky forest edges, where it thrives in well-drained soils with dappled to partial sun. Sow seeds in fall by pressing them lightly onto a prepared soil surface in the planting site, as they benefit from natural cold stratification over winter and will germinate the following spring. Space plants 18 to 24 inches apart to ensure good air circulation, which helps maintain the superior mildew resistance this species displays compared to other Monarda. Once established, plants spread slowly by rhizomes to form clumps and can be divided every few years in spring to rejuvenate the planting and propagate new starts.

plant_note: Plant in spring after last frost in lean, well-drained soil; established plants are extremely drought-tolerant.
directions: Plant in poor to average, sharply drained soil in full sun — Russian sage declines quickly in fertile or moist soil and is highly susceptible to root rot in clay. Cut plants back hard in early spring (to about 6 in) just as new basal growth emerges; do not cut back in fall as the woody framework helps protect the crown. The airy silver stems and lavender-blue flowers create a haze of color from midsummer through fall and are beloved by pollinators. Deer avoid this plant due to its strongly aromatic foliage.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; surface sow as seed needs light.
directions: This Asian wildflower has an unusual spiky habit and rosy color that adds welcome contrast to the landscape and long-lasting cut and dried flowers. Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, pressing it onto the surface for light. Transplant into full sun and well-drained soil after frost. It tolerates heat and dry conditions once established. Harvest stems when most of the tiny flowers have opened for the best dried bouquets.

common_name: Rustica Rubra Magnolia (Later-Blooming Rose-Red Saucer Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Rustica Rubra's later bloom time than Alexandrina and Lennei helps it dodge late frosts that damage earlier saucer magnolia cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Rustica Rubra produces deep rose-red, cup-shaped flowers with a paler interior, blooming somewhat later in spring than Alexandrina and Lennei, which gives it a real practical advantage in regions prone to late hard freezes that can blacken the open flowers of earlier saucer magnolia cultivars. The tree grows into a broad, spreading, multi-stemmed small tree or large shrub, requiring little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, and its rich color makes it a striking spring focal point once established. Give it a sheltered site with consistent moisture for the healthiest growth and most reliable annual bloom.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist soil in fall for spring germination, or sow in early spring — seeds require light to germinate and must not be covered with soil. Unlike common foxglove which is biennial, Digitalis ferruginea is typically a short-lived perennial persisting 3–5 years in ideal conditions. It self-sows freely to maintain a permanent colony in the garden.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; rusty foxglove is a tall, refined species from southeastern Europe and Turkey producing exceptionally architectural flower spikes — much more densely packed and finely detailed than common foxglove. The flowers are small (3/4 to 1 inch), closely arranged along the spike, and colored in warm, tawny russet-brown to rusty-orange-cream with intricate darker veining and netting visible inside the tube, giving the whole spike a burnished, antiqued quality from which it takes its name. Unlike common foxglove (Digitalis purpurea), which typically dies after flowering, D. ferruginea is a genuine short-lived perennial persisting 3–5 years in favorable conditions while self-sowing freely to maintain a colony. The upright spikes can reach 4–7 feet in excellent conditions and are extraordinarily architectural in the border. Combines beautifully with ornamental grasses, purple-leafed shrubs, and golden-foliaged plants where the warm rusty flower color finds its best complement.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in dry to moist, well-drained, sandy, highly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Rusty Staggerbush is adapted to the dry, scrubby flatwoods and ridge habitats of the Florida peninsula and coastal plain, and requires excellent drainage to thrive.
directions: Rusty Staggerbush is a coarse-textured evergreen shrub or small tree, native to the dry, sandy, scrubby flatwoods, pine ridges, and xeric hammocks of the Florida peninsula and coastal plain from South Carolina to Alabama, distinguished by its large, leathery leaves with rust-colored (ferruginous) scales on the undersides that give the species its common name. In spring it produces clusters of white to pale pink, urn-shaped flowers typical of the heath family (Ericaceae), which are important nectar sources for native bees; the plant may grow 8–20 feet tall in ideal conditions, forming small trees in open scrub habitats. All parts are toxic if ingested by livestock — the 'staggerbush' name refers to the neurological symptoms caused in cattle that graze the foliage. Grow in dry to moist, well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; it is drought-tolerant once established and an important component of Florida scrub restoration plantings.

plant_note: Plant small divisions in early spring into crevices or well-drained rocky soil; avoid wet or clay-heavy sites.
directions: Grow in a partly shaded rock garden or on a retaining wall with excellent drainage and a gritty, low-nutrient substrate; avoid rich soils which can cause overly lush growth prone to collapse. Tuck small divisions into crevices filled with a mix of grit and coarse humus, mimicking the alpine outcrops where this fern thrives naturally. Water sparingly once established, as this species is notably drought-tolerant once its roots have anchored into the rock substrate. The distinctive rust-colored hairs on the frond undersides intensify in sunnier exposures, making a partly open site preferable to deep shade.

common_name: Ryan's Pink Chrysanthemum (Hardy Soft Pink Garden Mum)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Ryan's Pink is a hardy garden mum grown for genuine perennial garden performance rather than one-season florist pot display.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build a compact, heavily budded plant. Ryan's Pink bears soft, clear pink semi-double daisy flowers in mid fall on a sturdy, well-branched plant selected for its ability to survive winters in the ground and return reliably the following year. Its gentle color works well massed in a fall border alongside asters, ornamental grasses, and goldenrod. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and free-flowering.

common_name: S. Arnott Snowdrop (Large Fragrant Vigorous Hybrid Snowdrop)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; S. Arnott bears large, strongly honey-scented flowers on a vigorous hybrid snowdrop widely regarded as one of the best garden snowdrops for reliable increase and flower size.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees where they receive good light before the canopy leafs out. S. Arnott, holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, is widely regarded by snowdrop growers as one of the finest and most garden-worthy hybrid snowdrops available, bearing unusually large, rounded, pure-white flowers with a strong, sweet honey fragrance, held on tall, sturdy stems well above the foliage, and increasing vigorously and reliably into substantial drifts faster than many named cultivars. It flowers in late winter to very early spring, among the first bulbs of the year. Divide and transplant clumps while still in leaf ('in the green'), immediately after flowering while the foliage is still active, for the most reliable transplant success. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Sabre-Leaf gasteria is one of the largest gasteria species and needs a substantial container as it matures.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Sabre-Leaf gasteria is one of the largest gasteria species and needs a substantial container as it matures. Long, curved, sword-like leaves streaked with irregular light and dark green mottling radiate outward in a large, distichous rosette, one of the biggest gasteria species commonly grown, eventually producing tall, arching flower stalks bearing clusters of the characteristic pink-and-green, stomach-shaped flowers that give the genus its name. Native to coastal cliffs in South Africa's Eastern Cape, its considerably larger mature size compared to the many miniature gasteria species makes it a bold specimen for a large container or shaded succulent bed rather than a small windowsill collection. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright indirect light, and give it ample room to reach its substantial mature size.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sacajawea combines creamy-white flowers with cream-margined variegated foliage, giving two seasons of ornamental interest.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; camassia tolerates seasonally wet spring soil better than most bulbs but prefers drier conditions during summer dormancy. Sacajawea pairs creamy-white, star-shaped flowers on tall spring spikes with strappy foliage edged in a crisp white-cream variegation, giving the plant ornamental value both in and out of bloom, unlike the plain green foliage of most camassia selections. Native in form to wet meadows of the Pacific Northwest, it naturalizes well in a moist border or meadow setting and pairs nicely with blue-flowered camassia cultivars or late tulips for contrast. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering to recharge the bulb for next year, and established clumps need minimal care beyond occasional division after many years if flowering declines.

plant_note: Plant in spring in sharply drained, rocky or gravelly alkaline soil in full sun. Avoid clay or organically rich soils; this rose is adapted to hot, dry limestone slopes of the American Southwest.
directions: Establish in a hot, sunny spot with extremely well-drained, gritty or rocky soil; Sacramento Rose is native to desert mountain slopes and is uniquely adapted to alkaline, low-nutrient conditions that would stress most cultivated roses. Its unusual gooseberry-like divided leaves and bristly stems make it visually distinctive even when not in bloom. Water sparingly after the first season — established plants are highly drought-tolerant and resent overwatering. Propagate by taking semi-hardwood cuttings in early summer and rooting them in very gritty, low-fertility compost; seeds benefit from a warm stratification period followed by cold stratification before germination.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost once soil has warmed to at least 70°F; nick or lightly scarify seeds before sowing to improve germination rates.
directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC — leaves, flowers, seeds, and roots contain potent tropane alkaloids (scopolamine, hyoscyamine, atropine) that can cause severe anticholinergic poisoning or death; do not plant where children or pets have unsupervised access and wash hands thoroughly after handling. Datura wrightii is a fast-growing native of the American Southwest and Mexico that produces enormous, sweetly fragrant, white to pale-purple funnel-shaped flowers up to 8 inches across that open at dusk and attract sphinx moths in a spectacular display of night-garden drama. Direct sow lightly scarified seeds into well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun after the soil has warmed; this plant thrives on neglect, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established. In zones 8–11 it returns reliably from a deep taproot each spring; in zones 7–8 treat it as a warm-season annual, allowing plants to self-seed for natural reestablishment.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; rohdea tolerates the deepest, driest shade of any ornamental perennial for zone 7–10 and is specifically useful in the most difficult dark corners of the landscape.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; rohdea (sacred lily, Nippon lily, omoto) is a Japanese native that has been cultivated and revered in Japan for centuries as a symbol of good fortune and longevity, with thousands of cultivars developed by Japanese enthusiasts — some producing extravagantly variegated, ruffled, crested, or otherwise unusual foliage prized as collector's items. For garden use, the plain species produces handsome, glossy, dark-green, strap-shaped leaves in dense, upright clumps and tolerates extreme shade conditions — including the dark, dry shade under mature trees — that defeat most other evergreen perennials. Inconspicuous spike-like flowers in late spring are followed by brilliant red berries in autumn. Extremely long-lived, drought-tolerant once established, and essentially maintenance-free. An excellent deer-resistant shade plant for zone 7–10 gardens. Berries are toxic.

plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Safrano is an 1839 tea rose long grown in Southern gardens for its saffron-apricot buds, strong tea fragrance, and excellent tolerance of Gulf Coast heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-3.5 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1839, Safrano is one of the oldest tea roses still in general cultivation and was long prized for its long, elegant, saffron-orange buds that open to loosely double, apricot-to-buff blooms with a rich, classic tea fragrance — the scent for which the entire tea rose class is named. Like other tea roses it flowers almost continuously from spring to frost, with the buds often considered more beautiful than the fully open bloom, and it shows good resistance to blackspot in the humid Gulf South compared with modern hybrid teas. The lightly arching, twiggy shrub works well in mixed borders or as an informal low hedge. Minimal pruning is needed — remove dead or crossing wood in late winter and avoid hard cutting back, which reduces the flush of bloom.

plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sagae was named Hosta of the Year in 2000 for its large, upright, vase-shaped clump of blue-green leaves broadly margined in creamy white to gold, one of the most architecturally striking hosta cultivars available.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the best margin color. Sagae was named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 2000, prized for its distinctive upright, vase-shaped growth habit — unusual among hostas, most of which form low, spreading mounds — with large, glossy, blue-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white that often deepens to soft gold as the season progresses. Tall scapes of pale lavender flowers rise well above the foliage in summer. Its architectural, upright form and large mature size make it an excellent specimen or focal point at the back of a shade border, distinct in silhouette from the many mound-forming hosta cultivars. The margin coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic contrast. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; perfect drainage is the primary cultural requirement — sago palms decline rapidly in heavy clay or waterlogged soils. All parts of the plant are extremely toxic to humans and pets — manganese deficiency (yellow fronds) is common in alkaline soils and is treated with chelated manganese.
directions: Plant in very well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; despite the common name, the sago palm is not a true palm but a cycad — one of the oldest surviving plant lineages on Earth, essentially unchanged since the Mesozoic Era. The dramatic, crown of stiff, glossy, dark-green fronds radiating from a thick, rough-textured trunk (which grows extremely slowly — gaining only 1–2 inches per year) makes it one of the most architecturally striking landscape plants available for zones 8–12. An established specimen with multiple trunks is an invaluable focal point in any tropical or subtropical garden. The plant produces bright orange-red seeds in large cone-like structures; every part of the plant — seeds, leaves, and trunk — is extremely toxic to humans and pets. In coastal Gulf Coast gardens it is one of the most reliable landscape plants available, tolerating salt, drought, heat, and wind with ease. Apply palm-formulated fertilizer with added manganese in spring to prevent the common yellowing from micronutrient deficiency.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in very well-drained, alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; saguaro is extremely slow-growing (one inch in the first year from seed) and grows best in the desert Southwest where it is protected by law in Arizona — it is illegal to harvest or damage saguaro on public land or to transplant wild specimens without a permit. Purchase only from reputable nurseries that propagate them legally.
directions: Plant legally sourced transplants in very well-drained, alkaline, desert-type soil in full sun; saguaro is the iconic columnar cactus of the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and northwestern Mexico — recognized worldwide as the symbol of the American Southwest, appearing on the Arizona state seal and in countless Western films. The great columnar stems, which can reach 40–50 feet in extreme old age (100–200 years), develop 'arms' only after 75–100 years of growth. The fluted, ribbed trunks store enormous quantities of water during monsoon rains, allowing the plant to survive extreme drought. In May and June, large, white, night-blooming flowers open at the stem tips — the Arizona state wildflower — attracting white-winged doves, bats, and native bees. The red, fig-like fruits are sweet, edible, and culturally significant to the Tohono O'odham people, who harvest the fruit with long poles to make syrup, wine, and jelly. LEGAL NOTE: saguaro are protected by Arizona law — obtain only from licensed nurseries.

common_name: Salet Moss Rose (Repeat-Blooming Pink Moss Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Salet is a repeat-blooming moss rose, an advantage over most once-blooming moss cultivars.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Salet bears fragrant, clear pink double blooms surrounded by soft, resinous, moss-textured sepals that release a distinctive balsam scent when touched, a hallmark of moss roses, and unlike most of its class it reliably repeats bloom through the season rather than flowering just once. Its balance of the classic mossy old-rose look with genuine repeat flowering has made it one of the most practical moss roses for a modern mixed border. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after each bloom flush.

common_name: Salmon Rose Zinnia (Giant Coral-Pink Cut-Flower Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Salmon Rose is a giant-flowered coral-pink selection from the Benary's Giant zinnia series, producing large, fully double blooms in a warm salmon-rose tone popular for soft, romantic floral arrangements.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches. Salmon Rose is a giant-flowered zinnia from the Benary's Giant series, producing large, fully double, dahlia-like blooms 4-5 inches across in a warm, soft coral-pink shade that reads as gentle and romantic rather than bold, making it a favorite for wedding and garden-style floral arrangements. As part of one of the premier cut-flower zinnia series, it shares the group's large flower size, long, sturdy stems, and excellent vase life of five to ten days. Plants are tall and vigorous, blooming heavily from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading or harvesting to encourage continuous production. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates, and stake in windy sites since the large blooms can be top-heavy on the tall stems.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost when the soil has warmed.
directions: Salmon Runner is a well-balanced salmon-colored dahlia that produces abundant cut flowers without needing staking. Plant the tuber 4-6 inches deep in loose, fertile soil after the last frost, eye facing up. This sturdy variety stands on its own but still benefits from pinching to increase stem count. Water deeply and consistently once growth is established, and cut blooms often to prolong flowering. Lift and store tubers over winter in regions colder than zone 8.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Salome daffodil naturalizes well and its trumpet color changes distinctly as the flower matures.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Salome daffodil naturalizes well and its trumpet color changes distinctly as the flower matures. Broad, overlapping white petals surround a trumpet that opens soft yellow and gradually fades through apricot to a soft peachy pink as the flower ages, a striking color transformation that means a single planting shows several different trumpet shades at once across flowers of different ages. This large-cupped daffodil is a long-standing garden favorite for its unusual, evolving pink coloring, naturalizing well into larger clumps over the years in a border or lightly shaded woodland planting. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer once dormant.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Salsa is a compact sneezeweed selection with deep, saturated red flowers on a shorter, more self-supporting plant.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sneezeweed thrives in moist soils and is poorly suited to dry conditions. Salsa bears deep, saturated red flowers with reflexed petals fanning back from a prominent rounded disk, on a notably compact, sturdy plant that needs no staking, unlike many taller Helenium selections. Its shorter stature and intense color make it well suited to the middle of a border or a large container, blooming from summer into fall and drawing native bumblebees and specialist Helenium-foraging bees. Divide established clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in spring into saline or alkali soils, spacing plugs 12–18 inches apart; plants spread vigorously by rhizome once roots are established and require no soil amendment.
directions: Set divisions into saline, alkali, or seasonally flooded soil in full sun during spring, pressing roots firmly into the planting site and watering in well to eliminate air pockets. Salt grass is one of the few natives that thrives in coastal salt marshes and alkali flats where soil salinity would kill most other plants, making it an excellent choice for erosion control along tidal edges and dune margins. Plants spread steadily by rhizome to form a dense, low mat that suppresses weeds and stabilizes disturbed soils without any supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established. Allow the planting to spread naturally, and mow or cut back only if needed to control boundaries.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to wet, neutral to slightly saline, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; salt meadow cordgrass is one of the most salt-tolerant ornamental grasses and can tolerate periodic inundation with brackish water — essential for coastal restoration and salt marsh edge plantings.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, neutral to slightly saline soil in full sun to partial shade; salt meadow cordgrass (marsh hay cordgrass) is a native grass of coastal salt marshes, barrier island meadows, and estuarine edges from eastern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico that forms graceful, fine-textured, wispy, arching mounds of narrow, wiry, medium-green to golden-green leaves that wave and rustle attractively in coastal breezes, turning golden-tan in autumn. It is one of the most salt-tolerant native grasses and is essential for coastal restoration work, stabilizing salt marsh edges, protecting coastal shorelines from erosion, and naturalizing the transitional zone between dry upland and tidal marsh. The plant is extremely valuable in the ecology of coastal systems — it is a primary nesting habitat for Nelson's sparrows, saltmarsh sparrows, and other coastal specialty birds, and its dense root systems trap sediment and build marsh soil. For ornamental use, it creates a fine-textured, naturalistic groundcover in wet coastal gardens where few grasses perform.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in irregularly flooded high marsh zones, salt flats, or moist brackish soils; salt meadow cordgrass occupies the high marsh zone flooded only by storm tides, above the daily inundation zone of smooth cordgrass.
directions: Salt meadow cordgrass (formerly Spartina patens) is the characteristic grass of the high salt marsh zone — the broad expanses of short, dense, cowlick-patterned grass visible from coastal roads and causeways along both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Its lower height, finer texture, and characteristic 'cowlick' growth pattern (where wind and tidal currents lay the grass in whirling mats) easily distinguish it from the taller smooth cordgrass of the lower marsh. Historically harvested as 'salt hay' for bedding and fodder from colonial times through the early 20th century, salt meadow cordgrass was the backbone of colonial coastal agriculture; today it is a primary plant for high marsh restoration, living shoreline construction, and tidal wetland mitigation projects throughout the eastern United States. Dense stands provide critical nesting habitat for salt marsh sparrows, seaside sparrows, and willets, and the seeds are consumed by migrating birds; the grass also functions as important muskrat, vole, and meadow mouse habitat in coastal marshes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into damp, saline-to-brackish, sandy or silty soil along marsh edges, ditches, and low coastal meadows, or set out spring divisions where a period of standing or seasonally wet soil can be provided.
directions: Direct sow in fall into damp, saline-to-brackish, sandy or silty soil along marsh edges, ditches, and low coastal meadows, or set out spring divisions where a period of standing or seasonally wet soil can be provided. This low, spreading aster tolerates salt spray and periodic tidal flooding that would kill most garden perennials, making it a workhorse for restoring pollinator habitat in Gulf Coast marsh fringes and brackish swales. Its late-season lavender ray flowers open from September into November, a critical nectar bridge for migrating monarchs and native bees just before frost. Cut back dead growth in late winter to encourage vigorous rebloom the following fall.

plant_note: Plant bare-root plugs or divisions in spring in wet, brackish to saline, sandy or muddy soil at the tidal marsh edge or in wet, salt-tolerant garden settings; saltmarsh cordgrass must have consistent moisture and tolerates flooding and salt spray that would kill most plants.
directions: Plant in consistently wet, brackish to saline, sandy or muddy soil in full sun at tidal marsh edges, coastal restoration sites, or wet, salt-influenced garden areas; saltmarsh cordgrass is the foundational native grass of Atlantic and Gulf Coast salt marshes, forming the vast meadows of gently waving green that define the coastal landscape from Maine to Texas. It tolerates full tidal flooding, saline soils, and constant wave action that no other ornamental grass can withstand, making it irreplaceable for coastal restoration and stabilization. The coarse, upright stems reach 2–6 feet and produce seed heads in late summer that feed coastal sparrows, rails, and other marsh birds. Rhizomatous roots spread to stabilize shorelines, prevent erosion, and trap sediments. Essential for living shoreline projects, coastal restoration, and saline wet-garden situations in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens near the bay or marsh. Not appropriate for ordinary garden use but outstanding in naturalized coastal settings where its ecological function and native character make it irreplaceable.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade; Saltmarsh Fleabane self-seeds prolifically in zone 9-10 moist conditions and will naturalize in wet garden edges, rain gardens, and coastal plantings. It grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions. In zone 9, it may behave as a short-lived perennial in mild winters, returning from the crown for 2-3 years before dying out.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, average to poor soil; Saltmarsh Fleabane thrives in conditions that challenge most ornamentals — waterlogged clay soils, salt-spray exposure, and the intense summer heat of Gulf Coast wetland margins. Pluchea odorata is a native North American wildflower found in salt marshes, mangrove edges, coastal prairies, disturbed moist areas, and roadsides throughout the Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida and up the Atlantic coast to the Carolinas. The plants produce strongly aromatic, camphor-scented foliage (the source of common names 'Camphorweed' and 'Sweetscent') and flat-topped clusters of small rose-pink to violet-pink flowers from July through October that attract skippers, hairstreak butterflies, and small native bees. The plant is valuable in coastal and wetland restoration plantings, rain gardens, and moist meadow plantings where its tolerance of salt, flooding, and poor soils outperforms most cultivated plants. In the wild, it provides critical late-summer and fall nectar for migrating butterflies along the Gulf Coast. The aromatic leaves have traditional use in folk medicine for fever, arthritis, and respiratory complaints in Gulf Coast and Caribbean traditions.

plant_note: Transplant divisions or nursery starts into consistently moist to wet soil after the last frost; this brackish-marsh native spreads by rhizome and needs damp ground to establish.
directions: Set plants in full sun along the margins of ponds, ditches, or rain gardens where soil stays consistently moist to occasionally brackish, giving the twining stems something low to scramble over. Native to Gulf Coast marshes and estuary edges from Texas to Florida, it produces arrowhead-shaped leaves and funnel-form pink-lavender flowers through the warm months that attract bees and sphinx moths. It is an excellent choice for stabilizing damp, low-lying ground where few other flowering vines will thrive. Once rooted it tolerates both standing water after storms and short dry spells between rains.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into moist to wet, brackish or sandy soil in full sun; this fast-growing shrub establishes quickly along ditches, pond edges, and low spots that flood with brackish water after storms.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs into moist, brackish, or occasionally flooded soil in full sun; saltwater false willow is a fast-growing, upright native shrub of Gulf and South Atlantic coastal marshes with narrow, slightly succulent leaves that tolerate salt spray and fluctuating soil salinity better than most woody plants. It is dioecious, with male and female flowers on separate plants, and produces small tufted seed heads in fall that support pollinating insects late in the season. Because it thrives in the low, wet, salt-influenced spots where many landscape shrubs fail, it is a practical screening or erosion-control choice along the back edge of a Gulf Coast property near a ditch, pond, or brackish waterway. It tolerates hard pruning if a denser, shorter form is wanted.

plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Samantha's cream-and-green variegated foliage colors up best in strong sun and tends to revert to plain green in shade, so give it the sunniest spot available.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun after the last frost, and let the trailing stems spill over a wall, container edge, or raised bed where the foliage can be appreciated up close. Samantha is a low, spreading lantana cultivar grown as much for its striking cream-and-yellow variegated foliage as for its clusters of golden-yellow flowers, which deepen slightly toward orange at the center as they age. The variegation gives it season-long visual interest even between flushes of bloom, making it a popular choice for hanging baskets, mixed containers, and sunny groundcover plantings where its trailing habit can spread and cascade freely. Like other lantana, it is highly drought- and heat-tolerant once established and attracts butterflies heavily through the growing season; where winters bring hard freezes it is best treated as an annual or overwintered indoors.

common_name: Samaritan Kousa Dogwood (White-Margined Variegated Kousa Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Samaritan bears white-margined variegated foliage and a showy display of white bracts, and benefits from some afternoon shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure that can scorch the variegated leaves. Samaritan bears leaves boldly margined in creamy white around a green center, paired with a heavy early-summer display of showy white bracts, giving the tree strong ornamental appeal both in and out of bloom. Its variegated foliage brightens shaded plantings and provides contrast against darker-leaved companion shrubs. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into dry, well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade.
directions: Sampson's Snakeroot is a native perennial legume of dry, open woods, prairie margins, and rocky or sandy open ground throughout the southeastern and south-central United States. It produces gland-dotted, trifoliate leaves with distinctive purple-black glands visible when held to light, and slender, spike-like racemes of blue-violet pea flowers from May through July that are highly attractive to native bees. Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun to light shade. Drought-tolerant once established, it is an ecologically valuable native legume for dry native gardens, open woodland edges, and dry prairie restoration plantings.

common_name: Samurai Orchid (Fuukiran, Wind Orchid, Japanese Fan Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on bark, in a small slotted pot with moss, or in the traditional Japanese method of loose sphagnum moss in a ceramic pot; Neofinetia falcata is one of the most cold-hardy of all epiphytic orchids and will survive winter temperatures to 20°F when properly established, making it suited for zone 7-12 outdoor culture in all but the coldest climates. In zone 9, it can be grown outdoors year-round on shaded porches or attached to tree bark. The flowers are small (0.75 inch), pure white, and intensely fragrant with a spicy-sweet vanilla-jasmine scent that is strongest at night. Treasured in Japan for centuries as a formal horticultural art. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial morning sun, mounted on bark, in loose sphagnum moss, or in the traditional Japanese manner in a small ceramic pot with loose moss — Samurai Orchid is remarkably cold-tolerant for a tropical epiphyte and adapts to year-round outdoor culture in zone 8-12 with appropriate moisture and light. Neofinetia falcata is a miniature, monopodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Japan (Ryukyu Islands, Kyushu, Shikoku), Korea, and China — one of the most historically significant and culturally revered orchids in East Asian horticulture. The plant has been cultivated in Japan as a formal horticultural art for over 300 years, with samurai-class collectors developing hundreds of named cultivars (especially variegated-leaved forms called Fuukiran) and specialized cultivation practices that persist to the present day. The plant is small and compact — the fan-shaped rosette of stiff, curved, two-ranked, gray-green leaves rarely exceeds 6 inches in height or spread. In summer, short racemes of 3–7 small (0.75-inch) pure white, long-spurred flowers emerge from the leaf axils. The flowers are the plant's outstanding quality: the long, curving nectary spur (up to 2 inches) and pure white coloration are beautiful, but the fragrance is extraordinary — an intensely sweet, spicy, vanilla-and-jasmine scent produced in the evening hours and capable of perfuming a room or patio. The cold-hardiness (surviving frost to 20°F in established form), small size, fragrance, and cultural history make Neofinetia falcata one of the most appealing miniature orchids for zone 8-12 outdoor culture. Non-toxic.

common_name: San Diego Red Bougainvillea (Vivid Scarlet-Red Large Vigorous Tropical Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average soil in full sun; San Diego Red is among the most cold-hardy bougainvillea cultivars — it survives brief temperature drops to 25–28°F with some dieback but typically returns from the base.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; San Diego Red (also sold as 'Scarlett O'Hara' or 'Rosenka') is a large, vigorous bougainvillea cultivar known for its vivid scarlet-red to brilliant red bract color — one of the most intensely red bougainvilleas available, producing masses of brilliant red bracts that create a bold, high-impact tropical display when the vine is in full bloom. The bract color is described as more purely red (rather than the magenta-red of Barbara Karst) — a cleaner, more saturated crimson-to-scarlet tone that creates a different visual temperature in the landscape. San Diego Red is also noted as one of the more cold-hardy bougainvillea cultivars for zone 9 — surviving brief periods below freezing better than many other varieties, with some gardeners in zone 9a successfully maintaining it as a returning perennial with winter protection. Like all bougainvilleas, San Diego Red blooms most prolifically under slightly stressful conditions: periodic dry-down between waterings, lean soil without excessive nitrogen, and full sun exposure produce the heaviest flower display. The large, vigorous vine can reach 20+ feet on a wall or pergola structure in favorable conditions. Outstanding trained against a south or west-facing wall where reflected heat enhances bloom production and the structure protects the vine from cold north winds in zone 9 winters.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix in warmth and humidity, or plant container specimens in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to bright indirect light after last frost; sanchezia colors most intensely in bright indirect light.
directions: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix in a warm, humid environment, or plant container specimens in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to partial shade; sanchezia is a Peruvian rainforest shrub grown for its dramatically large, glossy leaves with bold yellow or white veins that glow against the deep green leaf surface — a stunning foliage plant that makes a strong tropical statement in shaded landscapes. Spikes of red-and-yellow tubular flowers appear intermittently. Plants prefer consistently moist, warm conditions and do not tolerate cold, dry winds or temperatures below 50°F. In zone 9 grow in large containers and bring indoors before frost to a warm, bright location. Fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer during active growth.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into sandy, well-drained soil; seeds benefit from natural winter cold stratification and will germinate in early spring when soil temperatures rise above 60°F.
directions: Sand Blue-eyed Grass is a delicate, grass-like native perennial of the southeastern coastal plain, producing small but jewel-like violet-blue flowers with a bright yellow center from spring through early summer atop flat, iris-family stems that blend naturally into sandy meadows and open pinelands. Despite its common name, it is not a true grass but a member of the iris family (Iridaceae), and its fine, strap-like foliage forms low, slowly spreading clumps that are nearly invisible when not in bloom. It thrives in dry to moist, lean, sandy or gravelly soils in full to partial sun and strongly resents heavy clay, poor drainage, or high-fertility garden beds where competing vegetation quickly overtops it. Sow seeds in fall by scattering them on the surface of sandy soil, allowing winter cold to break dormancy naturally; established clumps can also be gently divided in fall to expand a planting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in spring into moist to seasonally wet, sandy soil in full sun; established clumps expand slowly outward and rarely need division once sited in a low, damp spot.
directions: Plant divisions or nursery clumps into moist, sandy soil in full sun, in a wetland margin, pond edge, or seasonally damp low spot; sand cordgrass forms tight, fountain-like clumps of fine arching blades that tolerate both standing brackish water and drier upland sand once roots are established, unlike its rhizomatous cordgrass relatives that spread aggressively along tidal shorelines. It stays evergreen through mild Gulf Coast winters and provides cover for marsh birds and small wildlife while its dense root mass helps stabilize pond banks and low drainage areas against erosion. Use it as a substitute for non-native ornamental grasses in a rain garden, retention pond edge, or naturalized wet meadow planting where its clumping habit will not overrun neighboring plants.

common_name: Sand Dropseed (Extremely Drought-Tolerant Sandy-Soil Native Bunchgrass)
plant_note: Direct sow in late spring in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; Sand Dropseed is a widespread, extremely drought-tolerant native bunchgrass of sandy soils, complementing the more ornamental prairie dropseed with even greater toughness in poor, dry sites.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; Sand Dropseed is among the most drought-tolerant native grasses available, thriving in loose, sandy, nutrient-poor soils where few other grasses persist. It forms an open, wiry-leaved clump topped by an airy, diffuse seed panicle in late summer that often breaks free and tumbles in the wind, dispersing seed widely, a distinct habit from the tighter, more formal seed heads of prairie dropseed already common in cultivation. Its extensive root system stabilizes loose, sandy, or eroding soil effectively, and the abundant small seeds are an important food source for songbirds and small mammals. It requires essentially no supplemental water or fertilizer once established, making it ideal for xeriscape plantings, dune stabilization, and low-water native landscaping. Cut back old growth in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in any well-drained, alkaline, dry to average soil in full sun; sand hackberry is a thorny, drought-resistant shrub of south Texas and the Rio Grande Valley — it grows rapidly and tolerates poor, alkaline, caliche soils with no irrigation.
directions: Sand hackberry (granjeno in south Texas) is a thorny native evergreen shrub of the lower Rio Grande Valley and south Texas brush country, producing small, yellowish-orange to red fruits abundantly year-round that are among the most important food sources for resident and migratory birds in the region — it is one of the top-ranked native plants for bird feeding in the Rio Grande Valley by wildlife managers and birders. The dense, thorny thickets provide impenetrable nesting and escape cover for green jays, Altamira orioles, and dozens of other brushland birds; the plant is a cornerstone of the native south Texas chaparral community. Hackberry emperor butterflies use this species as a larval host, and white-tipped doves, plain chachalacas, and chestnut-fronted macaws consume the fruits. In south Texas wildlife habitat gardens and Rio Grande Valley native plantings, granjeno is one of the highest-priority native shrubs for creating dense, self-sustaining wildlife habitat that provides food, cover, and nesting resources year-round without supplemental irrigation.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown container trees in fall in dry, sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sand live oak is adapted to deep, excessively drained coastal sands and does not tolerate poorly drained, heavy clay, or alkaline soils.
directions: Sand live oak is a native evergreen tree of coastal sand dunes, scrub habitats, and sandy pinelands of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, closely related to live oak (Quercus virginiana) but distinctly adapted to excessively drained, nutrient-poor, acidic sands of ancient coastal terraces. It is distinguished from live oak by its smaller, more narrow leaves with rolled-under (revolute) margins, lower growth habit, and adaptation to dry sand rather than the moist, fertile soils favored by live oak. In coastal dune restoration and sandy barrier island plantings, sand live oak serves as one of the primary stabilizing species for ancient coastal plain sands, where it eventually develops into sprawling, wind-sculpted specimens of great character; it is more salt spray tolerant than live oak. Like all oaks, it supports an enormous diversity of native moths, butterflies, and beetles as larval hosts; its small acorns feed migrating wood ducks, and the dense evergreen canopy provides nesting habitat for many songbirds. A valuable evergreen tree for coastal sandy sites in zone 7–10 where typical live oak would not thrive.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring on sandy, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; sand lovegrass requires sharp drainage and lean soils — it declines rapidly in heavy clay or moist, fertile garden conditions and is best suited to sandy prairies and xeric landscape situations.
directions: Sand lovegrass is a taller, more robust native lovegrass of deep sandy soils and sandy prairies across the south-central United States, producing large, open, feathery panicles of light pinkish-green to tan spikelets in late summer that wave gracefully in any breeze — its airy, fountain-like form makes it one of the most elegant of all native prairie grasses for dry, sandy garden situations. Found naturally in sand prairies, sandy bottomlands, and open sandy oak woodlands of the Central Plains and Gulf Coast region, it is adapted to deep, well-drained, infertile sandy soils that challenge most ornamental grasses; it is significantly more tolerant of sand and drought than blue grama or buffalo grass while producing a more visually dramatic plant. The seed panicles provide food for native sparrows and finches through fall and winter, and the dried tufts remain attractive through the cold season. Excellent companion for prairie grasses like indiangrass, big bluestem, and prairie dropseed in sandy-soil native meadow plantings from Texas to the Midwest.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into loose, deep, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; sand palafox is adapted to shifting coastal and inland dunes and performs poorly in heavy clay or richly amended soil.
directions: Direct sow after last frost into loose, deep, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; sand palafox is adapted to shifting coastal and inland dunes and performs poorly in heavy clay or richly amended soil. Tall, slender stems carry narrow, fuzzy gray-green leaves and are topped from late summer into fall with airy clusters of pink to lavender, fringed, thistle-like composite flowers that are a strong late-season draw for bees and butterflies. Native to deep sand dunes, sandhills, and disturbed sandy ground across the western Gulf coastal plain and adjacent Texas sand sheet, it is an excellent choice for stabilizing loose, dry, sandy sites where few other showy wildflowers will grow. It self-sows readily in sandy soil once established and needs no irrigation or fertilizer beyond its first few weeks of establishment.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in very well-drained, sandy to rocky soil; sand phlox requires excellent drainage and will rot in heavy, wet soils. It also performs well in slightly alkaline soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; sand phlox is a low-growing native prairie groundcover that covers itself with fragrant lavender to white flowers with distinctively notched or cleft petals in early spring. It forms a dense mat of needle-like evergreen foliage and blooms so profusely that the foliage is completely hidden by flowers. Unlike the creeping phlox (P. subulata) of garden centers, sand phlox is native to the midwestern prairies and is adapted to slightly drier conditions. Shear or mow lightly immediately after blooming to encourage compact, dense new growth. An outstanding plant for rock gardens, dry slopes, and edging in well-drained sites.

plant_note: Transplant container-grown seedlings in spring in very well-drained, dry, pure white sand in full sun; sand pine is adapted to the most nutrient-poor, droughty, xeric white sand soils in Florida and adjacent states where no other pine survives. Do not amend planting soil.
directions: Plant in dry, infertile, pure white to light-colored, acidic sand in full sun; sand pine is a Florida endemic of the ancient marine sand ridges and white sand scrub habitats of the Florida peninsula and coastal panhandle — one of the most ecologically specialized trees in North America. It is the primary tree of Florida scrub, growing in soil so nutrient-poor and drought-prone that it excludes virtually all other tree species. Two populations exist: a serotinous scrub variety (var. clausa) with cones that remain closed until opened by fire — releasing a mass of seeds after fire removes competing vegetation — and an open-cone variety (var. immuricata) along the Gulf Coast. The scrub habitat it creates is among the most biodiverse ecosystems in Florida, harboring endemic species including the Florida scrub jay, Florida mouse, and dozens of rare plant species. An extremely site-specific tree that should only be planted in authentic white-sand scrub conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring onto bare, sandy, or gravelly soil in full sun; press seed lightly into the surface and keep the site moist until seedlings emerge, then reduce watering as plants develop their deep root system.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a loose, infertile sandy or gravelly seedbed in full sun in early spring, pressing it lightly into the soil surface and watering until seedlings establish over the first few weeks. Sand reed grass is a deep-rooted native of the central Great Plains and interior dune systems, where its extensive rhizome network anchors shifting sand and withstands the full force of plains wind and drought with ease. Plants produce graceful, feathery seed plumes in late summer that persist through winter, providing outstanding visual interest and valuable wildlife cover in prairie restorations, dry meadows, and stabilized dune plantings. Avoid fertilizing or irrigating once established, as lean, dry conditions produce the strongest roots and the most attractive, wind-resilient growth.

plant_note: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet, saturated to seasonally flooded soil in full sun to partial shade at pond margins, bog gardens, or low-water areas; sand spikerush spreads by rhizome to form a dense mat and tolerates periodic drying once established.
directions: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet, saturated to seasonally flooded soil in full sun to partial shade at pond margins, bog gardens, or low-water areas; sand spikerush spreads by rhizome to form a dense mat and tolerates periodic drying once established. Slender, leafless, rush-like green stems rise in dense tufts from spreading rhizomes, each tipped with a small brown spikelet, forming a fine-textured, grass-like turf across mud flats, pond shallows, and seasonally wet low spots. It is a valuable erosion-control and habitat plant for the shallow-water margins of a constructed pond or wetland, spreading readily to stabilize saturated soil while providing food and cover for waterfowl and shorebirds. Once established it tolerates both standing water and the seasonal drawdown typical of retention ponds and rain gardens.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; sand-myrtle demands sharp drainage and is native to coastal-plain sandhills and rock outcrops, so amend heavy soils generously with coarse sand or grit before planting.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; sand-myrtle demands sharp drainage and is native to coastal-plain sandhills and rock outcrops, so amend heavy soils generously with coarse sand or grit before planting. Leiophyllum buxifolium is a compact, mounding, evergreen heath-family shrub with tiny, glossy, boxwood-like leaves that bronze attractively in winter, smothered in a profusion of small white to pink star-shaped flowers in mid-spring. Its fine texture and low, tidy habit make it a good substitute for boxwood in acidic-soil gardens, and it works well massed as a foundation planting, in a rock garden, or along a sunny woodland edge. Give it consistently sharp drainage and lean soil, since it is intolerant of wet feet or rich, heavily amended garden beds, and avoid fertilizing beyond a light acidic feeding in spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; sandankwa viburnum is the workhorse hedge viburnum of the Gulf Coast and central Florida, thriving where northern viburnums struggle in summer heat and humidity. Avoid planting in poorly-drained sites; it tolerates light drought once established but will not stand waterlogged roots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; sandankwa viburnum is the most widely used broadleaf evergreen hedge and screening shrub in Gulf Coast and central Florida landscapes — an easy-growing, tough, relatively drought-tolerant Japanese species that forms a dense, 5–8 foot mound of glossy, dark green, oval leaves and produces clusters of small, fragrant white to pale pink flowers in winter and early spring when few other shrubs bloom. The flowers are followed by red fruits that mature to black, attracting birds. It tolerates partial shade well and performs reliably in the heat and humidity that limits many northern shrubs in zone 8b–10 gardens. Widely used for foundation planting, privacy hedges, and screening in Florida and along the Gulf Coast; easy to shear to a formal shape or allow to grow naturally as an informal screen.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or stakes directly into moist, sandy, or silty streambank soil in very early spring; stems 12–24 in long can be pushed directly into moist soil where they root almost instantly, making sandbar willow the easiest willow to propagate for streambank restoration.
directions: Plant in wet to moist, sandy or silty soil in full sun along stream banks, pond margins, and flood-prone areas; sandbar willow colonizes bare mineral soils and gravel bars faster than almost any other native woody plant, making it invaluable for erosion control and streambank stabilization following disturbance. The long, narrow silver-green leaves give the plant an elegant, fine-textured appearance that contrasts nicely with coarser riparian vegetation. Mature plants form dense thickets through aggressive root sprouting, providing nesting cover for warblers, wrens, and yellowthroats. The species is ecologically keystone in southwestern riparian corridors where it provides critical streambank structure and willow-dependent pollinator forage.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, sandy, infertile, acidic soil in full sun; sandhill milkweed is native to the dry, sandy pine flatwoods and sandhills of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, where it grows in the challenging, xeric conditions typical of the longleaf pine ecosystem.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, infertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; sandhill milkweed is a prostrate to spreading Gulf Coastal Plain milkweed adapted to the extreme xeric conditions of longleaf pine sandhills — the type of habitat that receives very little soil moisture even during rainy seasons due to the high permeability of deep, white sand. The plant lies almost flat along the ground, with large, round, grayish-green leaves that help reduce water loss, and produces clusters of pale pink to lavender flowers in summer. It is a primary monarch butterfly host plant in the longleaf pine flatwoods ecosystem and an important nectar source for numerous native bees. One of the most drought-tolerant milkweeds available, making it an outstanding pollinator plant for dry, sunny, sandy landscapes in zone 9a.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; sandhill oak is endemic to the ancient scrub habitats of central Florida and is a legally protected Florida state plant. Never collect from the wild — obtain only nursery-grown plants.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; sandhill oak is a Florida scrub endemic — one of the most specialized and geographically restricted oaks in North America, found only in the ancient inland scrub habitats of central Florida's Lake Wales Ridge and surrounding areas. These scrub habitats on ancient sand dunes are among the most threatened ecosystems in the US, harboring numerous endemic species including the Florida scrub-jay, which depends on low scrub oaks like Q. inopina for acorn food and low, open habitat structure. The plant forms a spreading shrub to small tree with glossy, nearly evergreen leaves and is adapted to the driest, most nutrient-poor sandy soils of the ancient scrub ecosystem. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants from Florida-certified native nurseries; wild collection is illegal.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated bulbs or scales in fall, 4-6 inches deep, in consistently moist to wet, acidic, sandy-peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; sandhills bog lily is native to fire-maintained seepage bogs and streamhead pocosins of the North Carolina and Virginia Sandhills and needs steady moisture year-round.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated bulbs or scales 4-6 inches deep in fall in consistently moist to wet, acidic, sandy-peaty soil in full sun to partial shade. Sandhills bog lily is a rare, narrowly distributed native lily discovered growing in the fire-maintained longleaf pine seepage bogs and streamhead pocosins of the North Carolina and Virginia Sandhills, where recurring fire keeps competing shrubs low and lets its tall, wiry stems and nodding, orange-red, strongly recurved Turk's-cap-type flowers stand out in mid to late summer. Unlike most garden lilies it wants year-round wet feet rather than the well-drained soil most Lilium demand, making it best suited to the sunny, boggy margin of a rain garden or pond edge alongside pitcher plants and sundews rather than a conventional lily border. Because natural populations are small and highly restricted, plant only nursery-propagated bulbs, and mulch lightly with pine straw to hold moisture and suppress weeds around the shallow root system.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1 inch depth in well-drained, rocky, calcareous, dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sandpaper oak grows on dry, rocky, limestone slopes and desert grasslands of west Texas and New Mexico where it forms dense, scrubby thickets adapted to poor, alkaline, dry conditions.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, rocky, calcareous, dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sandpaper oak is a small, shrubby to tree-like, semi-evergreen oak of dry, rocky, limestone slopes in west Texas and New Mexico, named for the distinctively rough, sandpaper-textured upper surface of the small, leathery, holly-like leaves with spiny teeth. It forms dense, thorny, impenetrable thickets in its natural habitat that serve as important cover for scaled quail, roadrunners, and various lizards in the Chihuahuan Desert. The small acorns provide food for wildlife in an arid region where food sources are sparse. A tough, dry-land shrub-oak for rocky, alkaline, exposed garden conditions in west Texas and the Southwest where most ornamental plants struggle. Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established. Can form a functional barrier hedge in harsh, exposed xeric conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; sandpaper verbena spreads aggressively by rhizomes in Gulf Coast conditions — it is most appropriate in large open areas or as a slope cover where spreading is desired.
directions: Plant or direct sow in well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — sandpaper verbena is a tough, spreading perennial from South America that has naturalized widely across the Gulf Coast and Deep South, producing brilliant purple to magenta flat-topped flower clusters almost continuously from spring through hard frost. The rough, sandpapery-textured, deeply veined leaves and stems give it a distinctive texture; the plant spreads rapidly by underground rhizomes to cover large areas in hot, dry conditions where lawn and other groundcovers fail. It is an outstanding butterfly plant with exceptional drought tolerance and makes a bold, colorful slope cover, median planting, or informal groundcover in sunny, dry areas. In zone 7–8 it may die back in winter but resprouts reliably from established roots. The intense purple flower color is unusually vivid in the landscape and combines beautifully with yellow or orange companions. Too aggressive for small formal beds but invaluable for large-scale planting.

common_name: Sandpaper Vervain (Rough Wetland and Tidal-Marsh Native Verbena)
plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet soil in full sun; Sandpaper Vervain is a wetland and tidal-marsh native with distinctly rough-textured leaves that extend down onto the stem, adapted to consistently damp conditions.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun, at a pond margin, rain garden, or low spot that stays reliably damp, since Sandpaper Vervain is native to wetland edges and even tidal freshwater marshes. Its leaves are notably rough and sandpaper-textured to the touch, tapering down and extending onto the stem in a way that distinguishes it from the drier-adapted native verbena species more commonly planted, bearing slender spikes of small pale lavender to white flowers from summer into fall that draw bees and butterflies. As a genuine wetland specialist, it fills a habitat niche that upland verbena species cannot, making it valuable for a rain garden, pond edge, or naturalized wet meadow planting. It self-sows readily in suitable damp conditions; thin seedlings as needed to control spread.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, consistently wet to seasonally flooded soil in full sun to partial shade; sandweed grows naturally in Gulf South pine flatwoods ponds, bog margins, and ditches and tolerates standing water for extended periods.
directions: Plant in acidic soil that stays consistently wet to seasonally flooded, in full sun to partial shade; sandweed is a native wetland shrub of Gulf South pine flatwoods ponds, bog margins, and roadside ditches, with narrow, needle-like leaves and bright golden-yellow flowers with a prominent tuft of stamens blooming through summer. Older stems develop attractive reddish, peeling, exfoliating bark that adds winter interest after the leaves drop, giving the plant its 'peelbark' common name. It tolerates standing water for extended periods better than almost any other flowering shrub, making it a genuinely useful choice for the wettest part of a rain garden, pond margin, or low spot that floods after storms and stays soggy for weeks. Pollinators, especially bees, visit the flowers heavily through the long summer bloom season. Once sited in appropriately wet, acidic ground it needs very little care.

plant_note: Nick or lightly scarify hard seed coats and sow in fall into loose, well-drained, sandy, low-fertility soil in full sun; sandyland bluebonnet was the original 1901 Texas state flower selection, later broadened to include several related Lupinus species.
directions: Scarify seed lightly and direct sow in fall into loose, sandy, well-drained, lean soil in full sun, since seedlings overwinter as small rosettes and bloom the following spring. Sandyland bluebonnet is shorter and more compact than the better-known Texas bluebonnet (Lupinus texensis), with slightly narrower, more silvery leaflets and a preference for deep, sandy soils over the heavier clays that texensis tolerates. Dense spikes of blue flowers with a white to pale yellow banner spot open in early spring, coinciding with roadside bluebonnet displays throughout its native sandy-soil range in South and East Texas. Do not fertilize or amend the planting site, since this nitrogen-fixing legume performs best in the same lean, low-fertility sand it evolved in, and rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of bloom. Allow seed pods to fully dry and split on the plant before removing spent growth, since the developing pods reseed the planting for future years.

common_name: Sangria Caladium (Compact Wine-Red Sun-Tolerant Strap-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Sangria is a compact, sun-tolerant strap-leaf caladium with wine-red leaves and darker veining.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to nearly full sun with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. Sangria bears deep wine-red leaves with darker veining on a compact, sun-tolerant plant, providing rich, saturated color in containers and mixed beds that get more light than fancy-leaf caladiums can handle. Its small stature suits pots, window boxes, and the front of a border. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Sangria Ornamental Pepper (Deep Purple-to-Red Fruit Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Sangria is a compact ornamental pepper bred for fruit color display and does well in containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Sangria is compact enough for containers and makes a colorful seasonal accent for patios and borders. Its small, upright, tapered fruits ripen from deep purple-black through wine-red, giving the plant a rich, saturated color palette named for the sangria drink, held densely above dark green foliage on a tidy, mounded plant. Grown primarily for ornamental fruit display through summer and fall rather than culinary use, though the fruit is technically edible and carries significant heat; its compact size and heavy, colorful fruit set suit mixed containers, border edges, and fall seasonal plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun; sanguine coneflower is native to the sandy, acidic soils of the coastal plain and pineland habitats of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun; sanguine coneflower is native to the sandy, acidic soils of the coastal plain and pineland habitats of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma. Echinacea sanguinea is the coneflower of the southeastern coastal plain pineland habitats, producing narrow, strongly reflexed, rose-red to blood-red ray petals and a tall, conical, brownish-orange central disk; its tolerance of sandy, acidic soils and the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast region makes it the best-adapted true-species echinacea for zone 7–9 southern gardens. It is rare in cultivation but increasingly available from native plant nurseries in the South, and is important for ecological gardens in its native range where it supports specialist native bees.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; sanguine coneflower is native to the dry, open pine savannas and sandy, open woodlands of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; sanguine coneflower is a rare Echinacea species endemic to the piney woods of eastern Texas, Louisiana, and neighboring states, producing attractive coneflowers with pale lavender to rose-pink ray petals and the characteristic spiny orange-brown central cone. Named sanguinea (blood-red) for the reddish coloration of the cone at certain stages, it is closely related to and sometimes confused with E. purpurea. The species is adapted to the sandy, slightly acidic soils and mild winters of the East Texas piney woods ecosystem, making it better adapted than many coneflowers to the conditions of zone 9a. An important pollinator plant attracting numerous native bees and monarch butterflies. The seeds are consumed by goldfinches and other finches in fall.

common_name: Santa Barbara Mexican Bush Sage (Compact Mexican Sage)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Santa Barbara is a compact selection that grows about half the size of the standard Salvia leucantha and is suitable for smaller garden spaces where the full-size species would overwhelm.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Santa Barbara is a compact selection of Mexican bush sage (Salvia leucantha) — a smaller, more garden-friendly alternative to the full-size species that can reach 4–6 feet. Santa Barbara stays 2–3 feet tall and wide, making it practical for smaller beds and borders where the full-size species would quickly become overwhelming. Like the species, Santa Barbara produces spectacular, long (6–12 inch) velvety-purple and white flower spikes from late summer through fall — the velvety-purple calyxes enclose small white flowers in a distinctive bicolor spike that is exceptional for late-season pollinator value and cut-flower use. The long, arching, purple flower spikes of Mexican sage provide the single most dramatic fall display of any commonly grown Gulf Coast perennial — no other plant matches the intensity and quantity of the purple-and-white flower production in September through November. Santa Barbara's compact habit blooms slightly earlier than the full-size species, making it more practical in zone 9 where the species sometimes misses the first frost deadline. Cut back to 12 inches after blooming; the plant regrows vigorously from the woody base. Drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free in well-drained soil.

common_name: Santa Barbara Mexican Sage (Compact Velvety Purple Fall-Blooming Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Santa Barbara requires the same fall bloom trigger as the species — shorter day length in late summer and fall initiates flowering regardless of other conditions; plants in areas with significant artificial night lighting may not bloom as freely.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Santa Barbara is a compact selection of Mexican bush sage (Salvia leucantha) — more suitable for typical garden spaces than the standard species, which can reach 4–5 feet. At 2–3 feet, Santa Barbara produces the same spectacular display of velvety, deep purple to purple-and-white bicolor flower spikes as the species in a more manageable size. Mexican bush sage flowers in response to shortening day length (photoperiod-triggered), blooming from August through December — one of the most valuable late-season ornamentals for Gulf South gardens that provide important late-summer nectar for migrating monarch butterflies. The flower spikes are composed of velvety, fuzzy purple calyces (even in the bicolor 'white flowers' version, the calyces are purple) with white or purple corolla flowers — the texture is unique among commonly grown sages. In zone 9, Santa Barbara grows as a semi-evergreen perennial, returning from the base after hard freezes; it is at its drought-tolerant best once established in lean soil. Excellent as a late-season companion for fall-blooming Salvia coccinea, Gulf muhly grass, and swamp sunflower. Hummingbirds and gulf fritillary butterflies visit the flowers extensively during the fall bloom period.

plant_note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Santa Claus dahlia produces large blooms and benefits from staking to support the heavy flower heads.
directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Santa Claus dahlia produces large blooms and benefits from staking to support the heavy flower heads. Large, semi-cactus flowers are boldly striped and splashed with vivid red over a white base in an irregular, festive pattern that gives this cultivar its holiday-themed name, with no two flowers patterned quite identically, making each bloom a small surprise. Its bold, novelty bicolor pattern makes it a conversation-starting accent in a cutting garden or mixed border, standing out clearly against solid-colored dahlia companions. Stake individual stems to support the substantial flower heads, deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost.

common_name: Santa Cruz Sunset Begonia (Cascading Orange-Red Bolivian Begonia)
plant_note: Set out transplants or tubers after the last frost into partial shade to morning sun in rich, well-drained soil; Santa Cruz Sunset is grown as a cascading hanging-basket or container plant and does not need pinching to flower heavily.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to gentle morning sun, and keep the shallow root system evenly moist without letting the crown sit in standing water. Santa Cruz Sunset belongs to a series of Begonia boliviensis hybrids bred for a trailing, cascading habit that spills gracefully over the edge of a hanging basket or raised container, bearing narrow, pointed leaves and a nonstop flush of pendant, elongated, single flowers in fiery orange-red from late spring through frost. Unlike fibrous or tuberous bedding begonias grown for mounded garden beds, this Bolivian species is best displayed at eye level or overhead where its cascading stems and bright color can be seen from below. It holds up to heat and light rain far better than old-fashioned tuberous begonias, but still prefers a spot sheltered from the most intense midday sun and from strong wind, which can shred the relatively thin, brittle stems.
