directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — sensitive briar is a fascinating native trailing groundcover of the Gulf Coast and southern prairies, with two remarkable properties: the delicate, fern-like, bipinnate leaves fold closed immediately when touched (thigmonastic movement — the same sensitivity as the tropical 'sensitive plant'), providing an entertaining and educational garden element, and the stems are lined with small, recurved prickles similar to rose thorns. The spherical, bright pink pompom flowers in late spring and summer are delightful and attract native bees. It spreads flat along the ground to cover dry, rocky, or sandy open areas. As a legume, it fixes nitrogen from the air, improving soil fertility for neighboring plants. An outstanding native for dry, sunny slopes, caliche hillsides, and disturbed areas where its drought tolerance and sprawling habit control erosion while providing summer bloom and ecological interest.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; sensitive fern naturalizes aggressively in wet areas by underground rhizomes and can become invasive in bog gardens.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun near ponds, streams, and in rain garden edges; sensitive fern produces large, broadly triangular, bright-green fronds that are coarser and less typical-looking than most ferns and die back at the first frost (hence the name 'sensitive'). Separate fertile fronds bear persistent clusters of small, bead-like brown spore cases that remain standing through winter, providing attractive winter silhouette and food structure for birds. The plant spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes in consistently moist conditions and is best used in large-scale naturalistic plantings where its spread can be accommodated. The hardiest fern for wet, disturbed sites across North America.

plant_note: Start indoors; nick or soak the hard seed coat and keep warm. Transplant after frost.
directions: This novelty rapidly folds its fern-like leaves when touched, exposing spines as a defense, delighting children and adults alike. Nick or soak the hard seed and start it indoors in warmth, then grow on as a houseplant or transplant outdoors after frost. Give it bright light, full sun to part shade, and consistently moist, well-drained soil. It is frost tender and typically grown as an annual or potted plant outside the tropics. Handle sparingly to enjoy repeated leaf-folding without stressing the plant.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; 'September Beauty' tolerates wet soils and extends the summersweet bloom season about a month later than most other cultivars.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and mulch well, since summersweet suffers in dry conditions but thrives with damp roots. 'September Beauty' is valued for blooming roughly a month later than most other Clethra alnifolia selections, sending up dense, upright, 6-inch white flower spikes in late summer into September that fill the garden with a strong, sweet fragrance right as many other shrubs finish flowering. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit heavily during this late nectar flush, making it a valuable late-season pollinator resource. As an understory shrub it tolerates significant shade as long as soil moisture is maintained, and it may sucker gently over time to form a broader colony in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast plantings.

common_name: September Charm Japanese Anemone (Clear Pink Fall Anemone)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; plant in spring for establishment before the summer heat; newly transplanted Japanese anemones may be slow to establish but become vigorous spreaders once settled.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; September Charm is one of the finest pink-flowered Japanese anemone cultivars — producing clear, medium-pink, single flowers with a slightly deeper pink exterior and prominent yellow stamens on stems somewhat shorter and more compact than Honorine Jobert. The clear, unmuddied pink color (neither the pale blush of some cultivars nor the strong cerise of others) is one of September Charm's most consistently praised qualities: the pink is bright, cheerful, and long-lasting over the 6–8 week fall bloom season. The individual flowers are slightly smaller than Honorine Jobert (2–2.5 inches) but are produced in similar abundance on well-branched stems. September Charm typically begins blooming in late August in zone 7–8 — one to two weeks earlier than many other Japanese anemone cultivars — then continues through October. The earlier bloom start extends the display season significantly. Like all Japanese anemones, September Charm spreads by underground stolons and benefits from spring division every 4–6 years. The dark-green, deeply lobed foliage is attractive from spring through hard frost. Pair September Charm with Honorine Jobert for a contrasting white-and-pink combination in the fall shade garden — the two cultivars bloom simultaneously and create a complementary display.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, limestone-based upland soil in full sun to partial shade; September elm tolerates the same range of soils as other native elms and needs little care once established.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, limestone-based upland soil in full sun to partial shade; September elm tolerates the same range of soils as other native elms and needs little care once established. Unlike every other native elm, which flowers in late winter or very early spring before leafing out, this uncommon species flowers and sets its winged seeds in September and October, giving the tree its distinctive common name and making it easy to identify in fall when its papery samaras are conspicuous against the still-green foliage. Native to scattered limestone bluffs and upland woods across the mid-South and lower Midwest, it is considered rare and local throughout its range, making cultivated plantings valuable for conserving the species' genetic diversity outside isolated wild populations. Like other American elms it is susceptible to Dutch elm disease, though reportedly to a somewhat lesser degree than American elm, and provides the same wildlife and shade value as more common elm species where it can be sourced from a specialty native nursery.

common_name: Sequestered Sunshine Itoh Peony (Pale Yellow Intersectional Peony)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Sequestered Sunshine produces large, semi-double flowers in a soft, pale butter-yellow, a gentler tone than the bright lemon-yellow of Bartzella, giving it a quieter presence in the border that pairs easily with pastel companions. Its strong, woody-based stems hold the large flowers upright without staking, and the deeply cut, disease-resistant foliage stays attractive well after bloom finishes, providing good structure through summer and into fall. Like other Itoh hybrids it tolerates more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight herbaceous peonies, performing into zone 9 with afternoon shade, and dies back to the ground each winter like an herbaceous peony rather than persisting as a woody shrub.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or divide established clumps in spring; Serbian bellflower spreads vigorously by surface runners and can become invasive in small rock gardens or between paving stones. It self-sows modestly. Shear back hard after the main June–July flush to encourage a repeat bloom in late summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; Serbian bellflower is one of the most prolific and cheerful bellflowers — a low, trailing, vigorously spreading perennial from the Dalmatian limestone mountains producing a relentless flood of small, star-shaped, lavender-blue to lilac flowers from June through August (with a possible rebloom in fall if cut back), carried on trailing stems 6–8 inches tall that spread outward over rocks, walls, and pavement in a cheerful scrambling cascade. The flowers, though individually simple and small, are produced in such extraordinary abundance that a mature clump is a solid color mass for weeks. Outstanding for trailing over walls, filling cracks between stone, scrambling down banks, and naturalizing in difficult dry positions in part shade. It spreads more vigorously than most bellflowers and can colonize large areas over time. The cultivar 'Stella' has a somewhat more compact habit than the species.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline, average, loamy or clay soil in full sun to partial shade; Serbian spruce is one of the most adaptable and ornamentally outstanding spruces — tolerating both acidic and alkaline soils, air pollution, and a wide range of growing conditions.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline, average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Serbian spruce is one of the most beautiful and narrowly columnar spruces in cultivation — a naturally slender, spire-shaped tree with gracefully pendulous branchlets, dark green needles with conspicuous silvery-white stomatal bands on the undersides, and very small, dense cones. The narrowly pendulous, weeping-branched form creates an elegant vertical exclamation mark in the landscape. Native to a tiny relict population in a limestone canyon of the Drina River valley in western Serbia — one of the rarest conifers in the wild, with fewer than 60,000 wild trees. Ironically, it has proven one of the most adaptable spruces in cultivation, tolerating a wider range of soils (including alkaline) and air pollution than most spruces. One of the best spruces for urban conditions and for narrow garden spaces where a vertical, densely columnar form is desired. More adaptable than Norway spruce in warm summers.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Angelonia is one of the most genuinely heat-tolerant flowering annuals for zone 9 — actively thriving in the peak summer heat (June–September) that causes many annuals to stop blooming, become diseased, or die. The Serena series is one of the most widely grown and commercially successful compact angelonia series — bred for uniform habit, early flowering, and deep purple color intensity. Plants bloom continuously from planting through frost without deadheading. The foliage has a pleasant grape-like fragrance when brushed. Angelonia is increasingly used as a substitute for snapdragon in heat-tolerant summer situations — it provides a similar spike-form flower in conditions that kill snapdragons.
directions: Plant in full sun — angelonia requires full sun for maximum flowering and compact growth; partial shade causes leggy, reduced bloom — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist soil; Serena Purple Angelonia is a compact cultivar of Angelonia (Angelonia angustifolia), a tropical perennial from Mexico grown as a warm-season annual, producing upright spikes of small, two-lipped, orchid-like deep purple flowers continuously throughout the summer growing season in zone 9 without deadheading or special care. The unusual flower form — small, orchid-like flowers with two prominent lobes arranged alternately along the spike — is entirely different from most annual flowers, providing a distinctive floral texture that works well in mixed container and border compositions. Angelonia angustifolia is one of the best-adapted flowering annuals for the zone 9 climate: actively growing and blooming through the hottest, most humid part of zone 9 summer (July–September) when temperatures regularly exceed 95°F and humidity remains high — conditions that stress and reduce flowering in most other summer annuals. The combination of unmatched heat tolerance, continuous non-stop bloom without deadheading, attractive spike-form flowers, and pleasant fragrance makes Serena Purple one of the most practically valuable purple-flowering annuals for zone 9 summer beds and containers.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Serena angelonia is a compact, seed-grown series that flowers reliably through Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Serena angelonia is a compact, seed-grown series that flowers reliably through Gulf South summer heat. Spikes of small, orchid-like flowers in shades of purple, pink, white, and lavender rise above narrow, glossy foliage on a compact, well-branched plant that blooms continuously through the hottest, most humid part of summer without deadheading, making it one of the most heat- and humidity-tolerant bedding annuals available for a Gulf South garden. Its compact, uniform, seed-grown habit and outstanding summer heat performance have made it a mainstay of commercial and home landscaping across the warm-summer South, holding color and form when many other bedding annuals falter in extreme heat. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and expect vigorous, low-maintenance bloom through the entire summer without deadheading.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Serenita Angelonia is sold primarily as transplants rather than direct seeded — seed germination is reliable indoors but the long growing season before bloom makes direct seeding impractical. In zone 9 angelonia performs magnificently in summer heat, blooming prolifically from spring through fall frost without the heat-related decline seen in snapdragons and other cool-season spike flowers. Deadheading is not necessary — plants are self-cleaning and bloom continuously without intervention.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — angelonia is remarkably drought-tolerant once established and performs well in the lean, dry summer conditions of zone 9; Serenita Pink is a heat-loving annual from the Serenita series of compact angelonia (summer snapdragon), producing upright spikes of soft pink, two-lipped flowers that closely resemble miniature snapdragon blooms while performing in summer heat conditions that cause true snapdragons to fail completely. Angelonia is one of the very best summer annuals for zone 9 and the Gulf South precisely because it thrives rather than merely survives in high heat and humidity — blooming continuously from late spring through frost in the conditions that challenge most other annual flowers. The soft pink flowers with their delicate, slightly grape-scented fragrance (angelonia has a subtle sweet scent that intensifies in warm weather) add a refined, airy texture to summer garden beds through their vertical spike form and light color. The Serenita series was selected for compact habit, early flowering, and excellent branching — producing well-branched, tidy plants that do not require pinching or deadheading to maintain a full, floriferous appearance through the entire season.

plant_note: Plant transplants in fall (September–October in zone 9) for fall and winter bloom, or plant in late winter (January–February) for spring bloom. Osteospermum (African daisy) closes its flowers at night and on cloudy days — the flowers are diurnal. The Serenity series was developed for improved heat tolerance compared to older osteospermum series, allowing some flowering even in mild zone 9 summers. Plants may be cut back by one-third in June to encourage more compact growth and fall rebloom. The deep purple-violet flowers with distinctive blue-black centers produce a rich, jewel-toned color that provides excellent contrast with yellow, orange, and white companions in the cool-season garden.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist soil — Osteospermum requires full sun for maximum flowering; the flowers close in shade and on overcast days; Serenity Purple Osteospermum is a compact, heat-tolerant cultivar of African Daisy (Osteospermum ecklonis) producing vivid purple-violet to deep mauve-purple, single daisy flowers with distinctive blue-black central discs that create a striking two-tone color effect between the saturated petals and the nearly black center. The Serenity series represents one of the most heat-tolerant and widely grown osteospermum breeding lines — bred to extend the practical bloom season of this South African native from the strictly cool-only performance of older series into warm-season conditions where mild summers allow continued flowering. Osteospermum provides the richest saturated cool-tone daisy colors available from cool-season annual plants — the purple, pink, and white color range of osteospermum varieties providing the most vivid and large-scale cool-color cool-season flower display available in zone 9's fall-through-spring annual garden. The combination of large flower size (2–3 inches), vivid color, compact mounding form, and the unusual blue-black center disc that creates a subtle bicolor contrast makes Serenity Purple one of the most visually distinctive cool-season annual offerings available for zone 9 fall and winter containers and garden beds.

common_name: Serissa (Tree of a Thousand Stars, Snow Rose)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in bright light with some direct morning sun; established Serissa tolerates brief light frost outdoors in zone 8b-9, but is grown mainly as a houseplant or patio plant brought under cover before hard freezes.
directions: Grow in bright light with some direct morning sun, in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil kept evenly moist. Serissa is a small-leaved evergreen shrub from Southeast Asia grown for its tiny, glossy, dark-green foliage and its remarkably long, nearly year-round flush of small, star-shaped white flowers (double or single depending on cultivar) that gives the plant its common name; several popular variegated cultivars offer cream-white leaf margins for added interest. Like Fukien tea, it is a classic indoor and patio bonsai subject valued for naturally fine branching and a woody, gnarled trunk that develops quickly, but it shares a reputation for dropping leaves in response to sudden changes in light, temperature, or watering, so keep conditions as consistent as possible. Prune and wire young growth in spring and summer to train bonsai shape, feed lightly during active growth, and repot every one to two years into fresh, fast-draining mix.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; serrated jack-in-the-pulpit is variable in size and color across its native range, so choose nursery stock selected for reliable garden performance.
directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; serrated jack-in-the-pulpit is variable in size and color across its native range, so choose nursery stock selected for reliable garden performance. Arisaema serratum is a widespread Japanese woodland aroid with divided, sharply toothed leaflets and a striking hooded flower (spathe) that ranges from green with white stripes to deep purple-black depending on the form, appearing in mid-spring before the compound leaves fully unfurl, followed by a spike of bright red-orange berries in fall. Its variability in size and coloration make different named forms collectible for a shaded woodland garden, where it associates well with hosta, ferns, and other Arisaema species for a layered, textural planting. As with other Arisaema, the plant contains calcium oxalate crystals that irritate skin and mouth if handled or chewed, so keep the attractive berries away from curious pets or children.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring or fall in moist to average, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; sessile bellwort is the most shade-tolerant and cold-hardy of the bellworts and is distinguished from U. perfoliata and U. grandiflora by its sessile (not perfoliate) leaves — the stem does NOT pass through the leaves.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring or fall in moist to average, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; sessile bellwort is the smallest and most cold-hardy of the eastern North American bellworts, reaching only 6–12 inches tall and bearing narrow, pale cream-yellow, pendant flowers on slender stems in April and May. Critically, Uvularia sessilifolia is distinguished from the perfoliate bellworts (U. grandiflora and U. perfoliata) by its sessile leaves — the stem clasps but does NOT pierce through the leaf blade, so the leaves appear to wrap around the stem at the base rather than to be skewered by it. It is more tolerant of dry shade and deeper shade than its relatives and is the best bellwort for difficult, low-light situations; it spreads slowly by rhizomes to form loose, refined colonies. Also known as wild oats for the grass-like appearance of its narrow leaves and pendant seed capsules; goes dormant by midsummer like all bellworts.

plant_note: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, deep soil in full sun; sessile oak grows naturally on acidic, well-drained soils in hilly or upland areas — it prefers better-drained conditions than English oak (Q. robur) and is more common in the highland areas of Britain and western Europe.
directions: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, deep soil in full sun; sessile oak is the co-dominant great oak of Europe alongside English oak (Q. robur), but distinguished by its stalkless (sessile) acorns held directly on the twigs (whereas English oak acorns hang on long stalks). The two species hybridize freely wherever their ranges overlap, producing intermediate forms. Sessile oak tends to grow on better-drained, more acidic, hillside soils while English oak occupies clay vales and wetlands. The 'ancient oakwoods' of Wales, Ireland, Scotland, and the western Highlands are typically sessile oak — including the famous Wistman's Wood on Dartmoor and the ancient semi-natural oakwoods of the Lake District. The wood is highly valued for fine furniture, flooring, and wine and whiskey barrel staves. An exceptionally long-lived tree reaching over 1,000 years. Provides the full suite of habitat value as English oak for British and Irish wildlife.

plant_note: Divide clumps in fall and plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Sessile-leaf Bellwort tolerates somewhat drier conditions than Uvularia grandiflora and adapts well to a wider range of shade garden soils.
directions: Sessile-leaf Bellwort is a delicate native woodland wildflower, native to moist to mesic deciduous forests and forest edges from New Brunswick and Manitoba south to Georgia and Oklahoma, spreading slowly by rhizome to form loose, airy colonies in the shade garden. Smaller and more delicate than Large-flowered Bellwort (Uvularia grandiflora), it produces pale cream-yellow, narrowly bell-shaped pendant flowers in April and May on slender, branching stems; the leaves are sessile (non-clasping) rather than perfoliate, distinguishing this species from its cousin. An easy-going, adaptable native wildflower that tolerates slightly drier soil than U. grandiflora, Sessile-leaf Bellwort is a good choice for gardeners working with thinner, drier woodland soils where other spring wildflowers struggle. Divide clumps in fall, plant in humus-rich soil, mulch with leaf litter, and allow colonies to naturalize.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall (September–October) or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; fall planting in zone 9 allows establishment before the plant blooms and coincides with its peak growing period.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Setsugekka is widely regarded as one of the finest and most beloved sasanqua camellia cultivars, producing large (3–4-inch), snow-white, semi-double flowers with a prominent central boss of golden stamens from October through December in zone 9 — a time when few other shrubs are blooming. The flowers are lightly fragrant with a clean, sweet scent that perfumes the garden on warm fall days. The upright, arching habit reaches 8–12 feet tall with an elegant, slightly weeping branch structure that is attractive even out of bloom. Setsugekka is notably sun-tolerant compared to japonicas — it performs in full sun as well as partial shade, and more sun generally means more abundant bloom production. In zone 9, the fall and winter bloom season aligns perfectly with the region's most pleasant outdoor weather, making Setsugekka an outstanding choice for high-visibility landscape positions, espalier on walls or fences, screening, and informal hedges. The graceful branch structure also makes it an outstanding candidate for training as a small ornamental tree by gradually removing lower branches over several years.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; seven-son flower adapts well to a range of soils and exposures. Its exfoliating bark is particularly ornamental on multi-stemmed specimens where older trunk sections peel in attractive vertical strips of gray, brown, and cream.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; seven-son flower is one of the most underrated multi-season ornamental shrubs or small trees, native to central China and offering a remarkable sequence of interest from late summer through winter. Fragrant, small white flowers appear in clusters in late August and September — later than virtually any other woody shrub — followed by an unusual second display: the sepals surrounding the spent flowers enlarge and turn bright rose-red in October, extending the colorful season by several weeks and often mistaken for the flowers themselves. The exfoliating bark on mature stems peels in long, curling strips of gray, brown, and cream, creating striking winter interest similar to crape myrtle or birch. The bold, dark-green, distinctly veined leaves are tropical-looking for a hardy shrub. Adaptable to zones 5–9 and to a range of soil conditions, it combines late-season bloom, extended fall color, and ornamental bark in a single low-maintenance plant.

plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost date.
directions: Severn Sunrise offers a softer palette than most crocosmias, with pale apricot-pink flowers that open from coral-orange buds and fade toward cream at the base of each petal. Bred by plantsman Eric Smith, it holds its unusual coloring best with some afternoon shade in hot climates, though full sun elsewhere yields the sturdiest stems. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season and divide crowded clumps in spring every three to four years. The gentle pastel tones make it easy to combine with blues and purples in a mixed perennial border, unlike the typical hot reds and oranges of the genus.

common_name: Sexy Pink Heliconia (Chartacea Heliconia, Strawberry Cream Heliconia, Peach Heliconia)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in late spring in partial shade to full sun with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, fertile soil; Heliconia chartacea is a large, frost-sensitive species suited to zone 10-11 outdoor planting. This species grows to impressive dimensions — 6–15 feet tall — and its pendant inflorescences are among the most prized in the heliconia family for cut flower use, with vase lives of 3–4 weeks. The cultivar 'Sexy Pink' (pale pink and cream bracts) and 'Burle Marx' (deeper pink) are widely available. Provide ample space and consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, fertile, well-draining soil — Sexy Pink Heliconia grows most impressively with regular moisture and some shade protection from the most intense afternoon sun in zone 10 conditions. Heliconia chartacea is a large, clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Brazil in the Heliconiaceae family, producing what many heliconia enthusiasts consider the most beautiful and sophisticated inflorescences in the entire genus — inflorescences so striking that the most popular cultivar was given the flamboyant trade name 'Sexy Pink.' The inflorescences are large (18–36 inches long), pendant (hanging downward on arching peduncles), and composed of broadly boat-shaped, overlapping bracts in the most delicate coloration of any heliconia: soft, creamy pale pink to rosy pink, with a velvety or slightly glossy texture and a subtle color gradation from base to tip — the 'Sexy Pink' cultivar is perhaps the palest, most pastel, most refined of the pendant heliconias. The 'Burle Marx' cultivar (named for the famous Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx) has deeper, richer pink to rose-pink bracts. The large, banana-like foliage provides an impressive tropical backdrop. In the cut flower industry, H. chartacea inflorescences command premium prices for their elegance and exceptional vase life (3–4 weeks). One of the finest pendant heliconias for zone 10-11 tropical gardens.

common_name: Señorita Blanca Cleome (Sterile Spineless White-Flowered Cleome)
plant_note: Set out transplants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; sterile and non-seeding, so it blooms continuously all season without setting the messy seed pods of older cleome varieties, and will not self-seed or spread as a volunteer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Señorita Blanca is a sterile companion to the popular Señorita Rosalita cleome, bred to be entirely spineless and non-seeding, eliminating both the thorny stems and the prolific self-seeding that made older heirloom cleome varieties a nuisance in some gardens, while still producing abundant clusters of airy white flowers with long, delicate stamens from spring through frost. Because the plant never sets seed, all its energy goes into continuous flower production rather than seed development, resulting in exceptionally long, uninterrupted bloom without any deadheading required. The tall, bushy habit works well as a filler in mixed borders or as a temporary informal hedge, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and drought well once established.

plant_note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Shade Fanfare was bred by hosta pioneer Paul Aden and released in 1986, and colors best with a bit more morning sun than most hostas need.
directions: Plant in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade, giving it a bit more morning sun than most hostas need to bring out its best color contrast. Shade Fanfare, a 1986 introduction from noted hosta breeder Paul Aden and a sport of the older cultivar Flamboyant, has heart-shaped, softly corrugated chartreuse-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white, with pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer. It forms a neat, well-proportioned mound and has proven itself over decades as a reliable, widely available variegated hosta for the front or middle of a shaded border. Provide consistent moisture, especially during the heat of summer, and protect emerging spring growth from slugs, which favor the tender new foliage.

plant_note: Direct sow in very early spring or fall; seed germinates best in cool soil and darkness.
directions: Tall spikes of light and dark blue blossoms make a compelling backdrop for beds and bouquets and reseed readily. Sow seed directly in very early spring or in fall, as it needs cool soil and darkness to germinate and dislikes transplanting. Larkspur blooms in the cool weather of late spring and early summer. Provide full sun and well-drained soil, and stake in exposed sites. All parts are toxic if eaten, so site it away from grazing animals.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; surface sow as seed needs light to germinate.
directions: This spectacular perennial sends up multiple graceful spikes of white, pink, deep rose, violet, and purple flowers that attract butterflies. Sow seed in spring or fall, pressing it onto the soil surface since it needs light to germinate. It is fast growing and fairly drought tolerant, excelling in dry landscape gardens or mass plantings. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil. Cut spent spikes to encourage rebloom and use the flowers in arrangements.

common_name: Shadow Witch Orchid (Racemose Ponthieva, Wild Orchid, Moccasin Flower)
plant_note: Plant in fall in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil; Ponthieva racemosa grows naturally in moist, shaded, calcareous woodland soils throughout the southeastern US and is one of the few native orchids that can be successfully grown in woodland garden conditions. The basal leaf rosette overwinters in zone 8-10; the plant blooms in fall and winter. Best established from small plants or divisions from reputable nurseries propagating this native species legally — never collect from the wild. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil — Shadow Witch Orchid grows naturally in the deep, moist, humus-rich soils of shaded floodplain forests, seepage slopes, and limestone woodland margins throughout the southeastern US and requires cool, moist shade conditions for successful establishment. Ponthieva racemosa is a deciduous terrestrial orchid with a wide natural range from Virginia and Florida south through the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, and into South America in the Orchidaceae family. The plant produces a flat, ground-level rosette of 3–5 broadly elliptic to oval, dark-green, slightly fleshy basal leaves that overwinter and persist until spring in the southern part of the range. In fall and early winter, an erect, somewhat glandular-hairy flower spike 10–20 inches tall emerges bearing 10–25 small (0.5-inch) flowers in white to greenish-white with the two upper petals distinctively patterned with green veins and spots — the petals held in an unusual, somewhat spreading, wing-like position that gave rise to the poetic common name 'Shadow Witch.' The flowers are self-fertilizing in many populations, ensuring seed set without pollinators. One of the more shade-tolerant and cold-hardy of the southeastern native orchids, making it suitable for woodland garden cultivation in zone 8-10 with appropriate moist, shaded conditions. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; shaggy shield fern is more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many Asian ferns and adapts well to typical garden soil.
directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; shaggy shield fern is more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many Asian ferns and adapts well to typical garden soil. New fronds unfurl a striking near-black at the emerging crosiers and stipe scales before maturing to narrow, upright, glossy dark green fronds with a strongly vertical, almost architectural habit, giving the clump a bold, semi-evergreen presence through much of winter in milder zones. Native to woodlands of China, Japan, and Korea, it is a strong textural contrast plant for a shaded border, pairing well with broader-leaved hostas and rounder ferns. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter before the new flush of dark, unfurling crosiers appears.

common_name: Shaina Japanese Maple (Dwarf Dense Red Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; its dwarf size makes Shaina well suited to large containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun. Shaina is a dwarf, densely branched sport of the classic 'Bloodgood' Japanese maple, growing as a compact, rounded shrub-like small tree with the same deep maroon-red foliage color but reaching only a fraction of Bloodgood's mature size, making it a good fit for small gardens, foundation plantings, and large containers where a full-size Japanese maple would eventually outgrow the space. Its tight branching and small, deeply lobed leaves give it a fine, dense texture that holds up well through the growing season before a bright scarlet fall display. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter.

plant_note: Start seed indoors with a cold stratification period of 60-90 days before transplanting in spring; plant into very gritty, sharply drained soil.
directions: Shale Barren Wild Buckwheat is a rare endemic restricted to the ancient shale barrens of West Virginia and Virginia — one of only a handful of Eriogonum species native to eastern North America. It forms a compact, rosette-shaped perennial with woolly, spoon-shaped leaves and open clusters of yellow to cream-yellow flowers in summer, thriving on extreme, thin, hot, and dry rocky shale soils where little else survives. Grow in very well-drained, gritty, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and avoid any organic-rich or moisture-retentive amendments that encourage rot. This species is an exceptional choice for specialized rock and alpine garden collections in zones 4-7.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes horizontally 2–3 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; in zones 8–9 mulch rhizomes heavily in fall to protect from frost. Shampoo ginger is one of the most shade-tolerant of the Zingiber species, producing dramatic cone-like inflorescences that turn brilliant red as they mature and exude a slippery, soapy fluid used traditionally as a hair conditioner in tropical Asia.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally 2–3 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; in zone 8–9 mulch rhizomes heavily in fall to protect from frost. Zingiber zerumbet is a tall, dramatic tropical ginger grown both for its bold ornamental foliage and its unusual cone-like inflorescences — initially green and cream-banded, turning brilliant red as they mature — that produce a slippery, soapy fluid traditionally used as a hair conditioner and shampoo in tropical Asia; the plant is widely used in SE Asian cooking and traditional medicine. It grows naturally in moist, shaded tropical forests and is one of the most shade-tolerant of the Zingiber species; in zone 9–10 gardens it makes a spectacular background plant for shaded tropical borders, producing dramatic red cone heads even in quite deep shade. The rhizomes have a pungent, camphor-like scent and some medicinal uses in Ayurveda.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Shamrock inkberry is a compact selection that holds a denser form than the species without the legginess older inkberry cultivars develop.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Shamrock inkberry is a compact selection that holds a denser form than the species without the legginess older inkberry cultivars develop. Small, glossy, spineless evergreen leaves cover a dense, rounded native shrub that serves as a broadleaf evergreen alternative to boxwood, tolerating wetter soil and more shade than boxwood while providing similar year-round structure for a foundation planting or low hedge. Native to wetlands and pinelands of the eastern and southeastern United States, it is more compact and less prone to the bare, leggy lower growth that plagues many older inkberry cultivars, and only female plants produce the small black berries valued by birds, requiring a male pollinator nearby for fruit set. Shear lightly if a more formal shape is wanted, and provide consistently moist, acidic soil, since inkberry tolerates wetter conditions than most broadleaf evergreens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in moist, well-drained soil in spring or fall; Shantung maple is notably tolerant of drought, alkaline soils, heat, and urban conditions — making it far more adaptable to the South and Southwest than its more common relatives. The 'Norwegian Sunset' and 'Pacific Sunset' cultivars are common hybrid selections (A. truncatum x A. platanoides).
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral or even alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; Shantung maple is a medium-sized Chinese maple of outstanding toughness and ornamental value — the young spring leaves emerge in shades of rich purple-burgundy before maturing to glossy, deep green, and the fall color is consistently a rich orange-red, comparable to red maple in intensity. It grows 20–30 feet with an upright-oval to rounded crown and is among the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant maples available, thriving in the hot, dry, alkaline conditions of the Great Plains and Southwest where most other maples fail. Unlike Norway maple, it is non-invasive and better-behaved in the landscape. 'Norwegian Sunset' and 'Pacific Sunset' (A. truncatum x platanoides hybrids) have been widely planted in street tree programs across the western and central United States for their exceptional adaptability.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in moist to moderately dry, sandy to loamy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Sharp Blazingstar tolerates somewhat moister soils than many blazingstars and thrives in the coastal prairie and savanna conditions of Texas and Louisiana where periodic seasonal flooding alternates with drought.
directions: Sharp Blazingstar is a native perennial of the Gulf Coast prairies, savannas, and open meadows of Texas and Louisiana, producing dense spikes of pinkish-purple flower heads from late summer through fall that provide important nectar for migrating monarchs and native bees during the critical fall migration period along the Gulf Coast. Unlike many blazingstars that prefer dry, xeric conditions, Sharp Blazingstar tolerates moist prairie soils and the seasonal flooding that characterizes the Gulf Coast prairie ecosystem, making it suitable for a broader range of garden conditions than its dry-country relatives. The tight, upright spike of densely packed flower heads is similar in appearance to Prairie Blazingstar but more compact in stature. Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in moist to moderately dry, sandy to loamy, acidic soil in full sun; corms develop slowly but become very drought-tolerant once established in appropriate open conditions.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed immediately after harvest in late spring or early summer directly into the garden or into outdoor containers; seed requires a warm period followed by cold stratification and will not germinate until the following spring. Alternatively, plant nursery-grown divisions in fall in neutral to slightly alkaline, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil that is neutral to slightly alkaline (pH 6.5–7.5) in full to partial shade, ideally under deciduous trees where early spring sunlight reaches the forest floor before leaf-out; sharp-lobed hepatica is among the earliest wildflowers of the eastern North American woodland, pushing up delicate white, pink, or lavender flowers on fuzzy stems in February and March before any leaves are visible, often while snow still lingers. It is distinguished from the closely related round-lobed hepatica (H. americana) by its three-pointed, sharply tipped leaf lobes and its preference for neutral to calcareous rather than acidic soils, making it the better choice for limestone-derived soils in the Midwest and mid-Atlantic. The mottled, three-lobed evergreen leaves persist through winter and are attractive throughout the season. Plant in drifts of 10 or more for best effect; it spreads slowly by self-sowing in ideal conditions and is long-lived once established. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants.

plant_note: Plant fibrous root divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly to moderately calcareous, humus-rich, stony woodland soil in deep shade. Sharp-Lobed Hepatica prefers richer, more base-rich soils than Round-Lobed Hepatica. Do not plant deeply — the crown should be at or just below the soil surface.
directions: Sharp-Lobed Hepatica is one of the first native wildflowers to bloom in the eastern woodlands, producing delicate white, pink, blue, or lavender flowers on slender, hairy stems in late winter to early spring — often while frost still covers the ground — before the deciduous forest canopy has begun to leaf out. The three-lobed, leathery leaves remain green through the winter as an evergreen basal rosette, often acquiring beautiful reddish-purple tones in the cold months; distinguished from Round-Lobed Hepatica by the pointed (acute) tips of its three leaf lobes, it prefers slightly richer, more alkaline woodland soils with good calcium content. A long-lived, slow-growing wildflower of exceptional garden character, Sharp-Lobed Hepatica is best established from fall-planted divisions of existing clumps rather than from seed, which requires 2–3 years of stratification cycles before germination. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly calcareous, humus-rich soil with some grit or stone in deep shade under deciduous trees.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; Sharry Baby orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; Sharry Baby orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11. One of the most widely grown Oncidium-alliance hybrids, it produces tall, branching sprays of dozens of small, deep maroon-red to chocolate-brown flowers edged in white, famous for an intense fragrance that many growers describe as smelling exactly like chocolate or vanilla, strongest on warm, sunny mornings. Vigorous and free-flowering compared to many orchid hybrids, it blooms readily under bright windowsill or greenhouse conditions and is a favorite for its combination of showy, long-lasting flower sprays and genuinely pleasant scent. Water when the bark mix approaches dryness, feed lightly with a balanced orchid fertilizer during active growth, and repot every one to two years once the bark breaks down.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist potting mix and keep at 60–70°F for germination; transplant after the last frost into well-drained soil. Shasta daisies often bloom lightly the first year from seed and fully the second year — named cultivars from division or plugs bloom more reliably in year 1. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage repeat blooming from midsummer into fall. Divide clumps every 2–3 years in spring, discarding the woody center and replanting vigorous outer sections.

common_name: Shasta Doublefile Viburnum (Compact Horizontal-Branching Flowering Viburnum)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Shasta is a compact doublefile viburnum selection with an especially heavy show of horizontally tiered white flower clusters in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; doublefile viburnum blooms on the previous year's wood and should be pruned, if needed, only right after flowering. Shasta is a compact, wide-spreading selection of doublefile viburnum, producing an exceptionally heavy display of pure white, flat-topped lacecap flower clusters held in tiers along strongly horizontal branches in spring, followed by red berries that ripen to black and attract birds, and burgundy-red fall foliage color. Its strikingly tiered, horizontal branching habit gives the shrub a distinctive architectural presence even out of bloom, and it spreads noticeably wider than it grows tall, so allow ample lateral space when siting it.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; give Shasta ample width to display its horizontal branching habit without crowding.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing plenty of lateral room for the wide, tiered, horizontal branching this cultivar is known for. Bred by the U.S. National Arboretum, Shasta is among the most spectacular doublefile viburnum cultivars, its strongly horizontal, tiered branches lined in spring with rows of flat, lacecap-like flower clusters so dense the branches appear snow-covered, followed by red berries that ripen to black and draw songbirds in late summer. Its wider-than-tall habit makes it a strong specimen for open lawn areas or the edge of a woodland garden where its architectural branching pattern can be fully appreciated from a distance. Prune only lightly and selectively right after bloom, since heavy shearing destroys the natural tiered structure that is the plant's chief ornamental asset.

common_name: Shawnee Brave Bald Cypress (Narrow Columnar Bald Cypress)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Shawnee Brave is a narrow, columnar selection of bald cypress that fits street and boulevard plantings where the broader native species would need more room.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, though established trees also tolerate average well-drained garden soil once roots are developed. Shawnee Brave is a narrow, densely pyramidal selection of the native Southern bald cypress, holding a much more upright, columnar shape than the broadly spreading wild species, which makes it far better suited to street plantings, narrow side yards, and formal allees where space is limited. Like the species, it tolerates both flooded and ordinary garden soil with equal ease, developing the picturesque flared trunk base and soft, ferny, deciduous foliage that turns rusty orange-brown in fall before dropping. It is highly wind- and storm-resistant once established and essentially free of serious pests or diseases, making it an excellent long-lived specimen or street tree throughout the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, consistently moist, well-drained to boggy soil in partial shade; sheep laurel grows naturally in acidic bogs, barrens, and open woodland margins across eastern North America and needs the same acidic, humus-rich conditions as its relative mountain laurel.
directions: Plant in acidic, consistently moist, well-drained to boggy soil in partial shade; sheep laurel is a low, compact native evergreen shrub of eastern bogs, barrens, and cutover woodland, closely related to mountain laurel but shorter and distinguished by its flowering habit — clusters of small, deep rose-pink, cup-shaped flowers appear along the stem below the current year's new leafy growth rather than at the branch tips, giving mature plants a distinctive layered look with new green growth rising above a band of bloom in early summer. It is a useful native shrub for the acidic, moist end of a woodland or bog garden and provides nectar for native bees and other pollinators. As the common names 'sheep laurel' and 'lambkill' warn, all parts of the plant contain grayanotoxins that are toxic if ingested by livestock and by people — keep it out of pastures and away from grazing animals, and do not consume any part of the plant. Prune lightly after flowering only if needed to shape; it resents heavy cutting.

plant_note: Sow seeds or divide established clumps in early spring in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sheep's fescue is intolerant of heavy, wet, clay soils and humid summer heat — it performs best in cool, dry climates and partial shade in hot summer regions. Cut or comb out dead foliage in early spring. Note: F. glauca (blue fescue) is a closely related and often confused species with more consistently blue-gray foliage.
directions: Sow in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sheep's fescue is a fine-textured, drought-tolerant cool-season bunchgrass native to poor, dry, thin soils of European mountains and moorlands, widely used as an ornamental edging grass, meadow component, and low-maintenance lawn grass in cool, dry climates. The narrow, wiry, blue-green to gray-blue leaves form tight, rounded tufts that remain attractive through most of the year — evergreen in mild winters, dormant in summer heat. The related Festuca glauca (blue fescue), with more intensely blue-gray coloring in selected cultivars like 'Elijah Blue,' is the standard ornamental garden selection. Sheep's fescue itself is used more in low-maintenance lawn seed mixes for poor, dry sites including sandy banks and dry slopes where conventional lawn grasses fail. Among the most drought-tolerant of all cool-season turf species, requiring little supplemental water once established in appropriate conditions.

common_name: Sheffield Pink Chrysanthemum (Hillside Sheffield Pink Mum)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February-March or September-October. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to keep growth compact, since unpinched plants stretch tall and lean under the weight of the fall flower flush.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Sheffield Pink is a Chrysanthemum x rubellum selection closely related to (and often confused with) 'Clara Curtis', but it grows taller and more lax, and its single daisy flowers open a soft apricot-buff in bud before fading to a warm salmon-pink as they mature, giving each cluster a two-toned effect. Like other rubellum hybrids it is a genuinely long-lived garden perennial rather than a disposable florist pot mum, spreading gradually into loose colonies and blooming heavily from mid-October into November in zone 9, after most other perennial color has finished. Stake or grow through peony rings in richer soil, where the taller, willowy stems benefit from support to keep the late-season flower display from flopping.

subcategory: large tropical ornamental ginger with pendulous flower clusters
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to consistently moist soil in partial shade after last frost; shell ginger is one of the most spectacular ornamental gingers for subtropical gardens, producing long, drooping racemes of waxy, porcelain-white buds that open to reveal pink-and-yellow-marked flowers in spring and summer. In zone 8 the top growth may die back in hard freezes but the rhizomes survive and resprout vigorously; in zones 9–11 it remains semi-evergreen. Plant divisions 2–3 feet apart. The variegated cultivar 'Variegata' (yellow-striped leaves) is widely grown as an ornamental.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade after last frost; shell ginger is native to East Asia and produces one of the most beautiful inflorescences in the ginger family — long, pendulous, branched racemes of porcelain-white, waxy, egg-shaped buds that dangle like strings of shells before opening to reveal flowers with white petals and a broad, yellow-and-red-marked labellum. The broadly lance-shaped, glossy, deep-green leaves are large and handsome, providing a lush tropical effect throughout the growing season, and the leaves and rhizomes are used in Southeast Asian cooking to wrap foods and flavor dishes. In zones 8–9 the aerial stems may be killed by hard freezes but rhizomes typically survive the winter underground and resprout with vigor in spring; in zones 10–11 it is essentially evergreen. Clumps spread steadily over time and should be divided every 3–5 years to maintain vigor. The popular variegated form 'Variegata' has striking yellow-and-green-striped foliage and is slightly less vigorous but equally ornamental.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring after soil warms in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Shenandoah switchgrass develops its best fall red color in full sun — in shade or with excessive fertility, fall color is less vivid and the compact habit becomes loose.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Shenandoah is the most popular compact switchgrass cultivar — a German selection of Panicum virgatum that stays a neat 24–36 inches tall with an upright, fine-textured habit and produces one of the most spectacular fall color transformations available in any ornamental grass. Beginning in August and intensifying through October, the fine-bladed green foliage transitions through wine-red to deep scarlet-red, creating a glowing color display against the delicate clouds of airy pink-red seed heads. Switchgrass is a native North American prairie grass naturally adapted to a wide range of conditions from wet bottomlands to dry upland prairies across the Gulf Coast region, and Shenandoah maintains this native adaptability while providing improved compactness and superior fall color compared to unselected species. It is highly drought-tolerant once established, needs no supplemental fertilization in most soils, and is resistant to deer browsing. The airy seed heads are wildlife food for sparrows, towhees, and juncos in winter. Cut back to 4–6 inches in late winter (February in zone 9) before new growth begins. Shenandoah performs best in lean to average soils; rich, heavily amended soils cause floppy stems and reduced fall color intensity.

common_name: Sherwood Purple Creeping Phlox (Deep Violet Woodland Groundcover Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Sherwood Purple spreads by surface stolons to knit together as a low, semi-evergreen mat.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Sherwood Purple is a long-popular selection of creeping phlox valued for its saturated violet-purple flowers, a noticeably deeper and more vivid color than the species' typical lavender-blue, held just above a low, spreading mat of semi-evergreen foliage in mid-spring. Like the species, it spreads by surface stolons that root as they travel, gradually knitting together into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover well suited to shaded slopes, woodland garden edges, and beneath deciduous trees. It performs best where summers stay relatively cool and humid soils are consistently moist, and like most Phlox stolonifera selections it struggles in the hottest, most humid zone 9 summers unless given a consistently cool, moist, deeply shaded microclimate with reliable irrigation. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tidy and encourage dense regrowth; divide every few years if the center of the patch thins out.

common_name: Sherwood Red Azalea (Compact Bright Red Kurume-Type Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Sherwood Red is a compact, semi-dwarf Kurume-type azalea bred for a dense habit and bright red spring bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Sherwood Red is a compact, semi-dwarf Kurume-type azalea prized for its bright, clear red flowers produced in a dense spring flush on a tidy, well-branched shrub that fits easily into foundation plantings, borders, and mass plantings without regular pruning. Its smaller mature size compared to Southern Indica cultivars makes it a practical choice where space is limited but a vivid red spring display is still wanted. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sherwoodii is a fine-textured, dense, compact abelia selection that rarely sets flowers, grown mainly for its neat foliage form.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Sherwoodii forms an unusually dense, fine-textured mound of small, glossy leaves, arching gracefully like other glossy abelia cultivars but staying more compact and tidy, and flowering only sparsely compared to typical abelia, making it valued primarily as a refined foliage shrub rather than for bloom. Its neat, rounded habit suits low hedges, foundation plantings, and mixed borders where a fine texture is wanted without the arching sprawl of larger abelia selections. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs only light pruning to maintain shape.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; shield-leaf begonia wants consistent humidity and moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; shield-leaf begonia wants consistent humidity and moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11. Rounded, olive-green leaves are attached to their stalks from the center of the leaf rather than the edge, a peltate arrangement that gives the foliage a distinctive umbrella-like symmetry, with small white to pale pink flowers rising above the foliage on slender stems. Native to Central American cloud forests, it forms a tidy, low, rhizomatous clump well suited to a terrarium or humid shaded windowsill, its neat, symmetrical leaf shape providing a calm textural contrast to the more heavily patterned rex-type begonias. Keep humidity high, water when the soil surface begins to dry, and avoid direct sun, which quickly scorches the leaves.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in well-drained, moderately fertile, acidic to neutral, loamy to clay-loam soil in full sun to light shade. Shingle Oak is more adaptable to clay and moderately compacted urban soils than many oaks and makes an excellent large shade tree for challenging sites.
directions: Shingle Oak is a distinctive and underappreciated native oak of the eastern United States from New England south to Georgia and west to Kansas, immediately recognizable among oaks by its entire, unlobed leaves resembling those of a water beech — a surprising feature for an oak — making it an excellent conversation piece in any landscape. The dried leaves persist on the branches well into winter in a quality called marcescence, providing landscape texture and winter interest, while the abundant small acorns are a reliable annual mast crop for wood ducks, turkeys, white-tailed deer, and numerous songbirds. An adaptable and durable large shade tree for urban and suburban landscapes, Shingle Oak tolerates heavier clay soils and greater pH variability than many oaks, and develops a graceful, broadly pyramidal to rounded crown at maturity with modest fall color ranging from yellow to russet brown. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade.

common_name: Shingle Plant (Silver Shingle Plant, Cryptantha Shingle Vine, Shingle Vine)
plant_note: Grow against rough bark, a moss pole, or a flat board in partial to deep shade with high humidity; Rhaphidophora cryptantha is one of the ultimate 'shingle plants' — it grows pressed completely flat against a surface, with its leaves arranged in overlapping, shingle-like rows, the entire leaf surface adhering to the substrate. In juvenile form (the only form usually cultivated), the leaves are small (1–3 inches), silvery-gray-green, and completely flat against the surface — the plant looks more like a lichen or bark overlay than a conventional plant. Very slow-growing. Requires warm (above 60°F), humid conditions. CAUTION: contains calcium oxalate; toxic to pets.
directions: Grow pressed against a rough bark surface or tree trunk in partial to deep shade with consistent warmth and humidity — Shingle Plant is one of the most unusual growing habits of any cultivated aroid and must be given a vertical, rough-barked surface to adhere to in order to develop its characteristic shingled growth form. Rhaphidophora cryptantha is a creeping, climbing, sympodial aroid in the Araceae family native to the rainforests of Papua New Guinea, a member of the large genus Rhaphidophora that includes several other popular climbing aroids. The plant exhibits one of the most extreme forms of the 'shingle plant' growth habit found in the Araceae: in juvenile form (which is the form commonly encountered in cultivation), the plant grows pressed entirely flat against a vertical surface, with each leaf arranged in an overlapping, shingled sequence along the climbing stem — the leaf blade, petiole, and stem all flattened against the surface as if laminated onto the bark. The leaves themselves are oval to oblong, 1–3 inches, in a silvery to gray-green color with subtle darker veining. The overall effect is of an intricate, overlapping mosaic of small metallic shields pressed against the substrate — genuinely unlike any other commonly grown plant in appearance. In mature, arboreal form (rarely achieved in cultivation), the leaves expand greatly in size and become more typical aroid leaf shape. The shingle plant growth habit is an evolutionary adaptation to the sheltered, low-light conditions of tropical rainforest tree trunks and buttresses. An extraordinary collector's plant for warm, humid, shaded environments. CAUTION: toxic to pets if ingested.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions or rooted stem-tip cuttings in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade in spring; shining clubmoss depends on soil mycorrhizal fungi and almost never survives transplanting from wild-collected material, so source only nursery-grown stock.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions or rooted stem-tip cuttings in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade in spring; shining clubmoss depends on soil mycorrhizal fungi and almost never survives transplanting from wild-collected material, so source only nursery-grown stock. This evergreen fern ally forms low, glossy, dark-green tufts of forking stems clothed in narrow, shining, needle-like leaflets, spreading slowly by both creeping stems and leaf-tip gemmae that fall and root nearby. It is a signature groundcover of cool, moist, undisturbed eastern hardwood and hemlock forests and reads as a miniature, evergreen conifer at the forest floor, pairing well with partridgeberry and wood ferns. Keep soil constantly moist and never let it dry out or sit in standing water; it resents heat, drought, and disturbed or compacted ground.

plant_note: Divide established clumps every 3-4 years in early spring or plant container-grown plants in moderately fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun; shining coneflower is a tall, vigorous plant (5-7 feet) that may need staking in exposed positions or can be planted where surrounding tall plants provide support. The cultivar Herbstsonne (Autumn Sun) is the most widely grown selection and the standard bearer for late-summer yellow daisy perennials.
directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun; shining coneflower is one of the tallest and most impressive of all coneflowers, reaching 5-7 feet in excellent conditions, with large, single daisy flowers from August through September that have prominent, distinctive green cone centers rather than the dark-brown central cones of the familiar black-eyed Susan. The large, golden-yellow ray petals are proportionally longer and more gracefully reflexed than most rudbeckias, giving the flowers an especially elegant, slightly drooping appearance. The cultivar Herbstsonne (German for Autumn Sun) is justly celebrated as one of the great late-summer perennials, producing masses of these large, yellow-and-green daisies on tall, self-supporting stems above broad, strong foliage that is healthy and disease-resistant throughout the growing season. Native to the southeastern US, it grows well in heat and humidity — better than many coneflowers in the southern states — while also being fully cold-hardy to zone 4. An outstanding back-of-border plant that provides scale and late-season color at a time when the garden needs it most.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained to poorly drained soil in full sun to full shade; shining fetterbush naturally occurs in wet flatwoods, bay swamps, and moist pocosins and is exceptionally tolerant of wet, poorly drained, acidic soils.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to full shade; shining fetterbush performs remarkably well in wet, poorly drained conditions that challenge most ornamental shrubs, making it valuable for rain gardens, pond margins, and wet woodland settings. Lyonia lucida is an evergreen native shrub of the southeastern coastal plain with exceptionally handsome, glossy, dark-green, alternate leaves with a prominent revolute (rolled-under) margin that gives the plant a polished, refined appearance unusual in native shrubs; small, pink to white, urn-shaped flowers are produced in axillary clusters along the previous season's stems in March–April before many other shrubs flower, providing important early-season nectar for native bumblebees and other early-flying pollinators. The glossy foliage (the source of the epithet 'lucida,' meaning shining) is effective year-round and provides excellent winter interest. Shining fetterbush is native to wet flatwoods, bay swamps, and pocosins from Virginia to Florida and Louisiana and is an outstanding native choice for wet, acidic-soil sites in zones 7–10 where drainage is poor.

common_name: Shining Spider Lily (Coastal Plain Spider Lily)
subcategory: coastal Southeast US native spider lily
plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist to seasonally wet, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; shining spider lily is native to the flatwoods, wet prairies, and pond margins of the coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Mississippi. It tolerates periodic flooding and requires consistently moist to wet soil during the growing season. The flowers are strongly fragrant in the evening.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist to wet, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; shining spider lily is a native coastal Southeast US Hymenocallis — growing naturally in the wet flatwoods, longleaf pine savannas, and seasonally flooded prairies and pond margins from Virginia to Florida and west along the Gulf Coast — that produces in summer the classic spider lily flower: a pure-white, fragrant, reflexed-petaled star with the distinctive central funnel-cup (the staminal cup or corona) and six long, narrow, spreading, white, ribbon-like outer perianth segments radiating outward from the cup. The flowers, 3–4 per scape, are sweetly fragrant in the evening, carried on sturdy stems above broad, strap-shaped, bright-green leaves. The species epithet 'rotata' (wheel-shaped) refers to the wide, flat, open rotation of the spreading perianth segments. An excellent native alternative to the more commonly grown tropical Hymenocallis species for moist or wet garden sites in the coastal Southeast, including rain gardens, pond margins, and consistently moist borders. The native ecological context — flatwoods, savannas, wet prairies — gives it outstanding adaptation to the natural seasonal wet-dry cycles of the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; grown from semi-hardwood cuttings since seed propagation is not commercially practiced.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; shiny xylosma is grown chiefly for its glossy, bronze-red new growth maturing to lustrous bright green foliage rather than for its small, inconspicuous, fragrant greenish-yellow flowers, which are followed by black berries on female plants. It responds exceptionally well to shearing and is widely used as a formal or informal hedge, screen, espalier, or small patio tree in California, Texas, and Gulf Coast landscapes. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and urban conditions with ease, and the arching, somewhat thorny branches make it a useful barrier planting as well as an ornamental one.

common_name: Shirley Pope Siberian Iris (Vibrant Velvety Red-Purple with White Signal)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Shirley Pope bears vibrant velvety red-purple flowers with a contrasting white signal.
directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Shirley Pope bears vibrant, velvety red-purple flowers with a bright white signal at the throat that provides sharp contrast against the deep petal color, opening over narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

plant_note: Surface sow on cool soil; do not cover the fine seed.
directions: Scatter the tiny Shirley poppy seed on the surface of cool, moist soil in very early spring, or sow in fall in mild regions. Do not cover the seed, which needs light and cold to germinate well. The delicate crepe-paper flowers in pink, red, and white are classic cottage and meadow plants. Poppies resent transplanting, so always direct sow, and let some pods ripen for self-seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (October–November in zone 9) for winter establishment and spring bloom; poppies do not transplant well and must be direct-sown. Cool soil (50–65°F) is required for germination — do not bury seed; press lightly into the soil surface or rake in shallowly. In zone 9 fall sowing produces the best plants and bloom; spring sowing in warming soil produces poor results. Shirley Poppy was developed by Reverend Wilks in Shirley, England in the 1880s by selecting from wild Corn Poppy — the Shirley strains producing single and semi-double flowers with translucent, tissue-thin petals in pink, red, rose, salmon, and white, typically with a white center ring. Plants self-seed readily in zone 9 to naturalize in sandy, well-drained soils. All parts of Papaver rhoeas are mildly toxic.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — Shirley Poppies demand full sun and poor to moderately fertile, lean soil; in rich, fertilized soil they produce excessive foliage with reduced flowering; Shirley Poppy Mix is a classic selection of Corn Poppy (Papaver rhoeas), producing the tissue-thin, crinkled-petal, bowl-shaped flowers in an extended color range of pink, rose, salmon, red, and white — often with picotee edges, darker veining, or a distinctive white base ring — that have made Shirley poppies one of the most beloved and evocative of all annual wildflowers for the cottage and cutting garden. The distinctive visual quality of Shirley poppy flowers — the tissue-paper-thin petals catching and transmitting light, creating a slightly translucent, glowing quality particularly effective in morning and evening light — is entirely different from the opaque, solid color of most other annual flowers, producing an effect of delicacy and refinement at odds with the plant's actually tough, drought-tolerant character. Corn Poppy (Papaver rhoeas) is native to the Mediterranean and Middle East and has been associated with remembrance, sleep, and beauty in European and Mediterranean culture for thousands of years — the simple, vivid flowers carrying cultural weight disproportionate to the plant's modest agricultural weed origins. In zone 9 fall-sown Shirley poppies bloom in February–April in a naturalistic wildflower display that self-renews through seed-drop each year once established.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Scatter the tiny seed on the soil surface in early spring or fall, pressing lightly but not covering since it needs light to sprout. This 1880s heirloom bears delicate two-to-three-inch blossoms on slender, nodding stems that dance in the breeze. Poppies resent transplanting, so always direct sow where they are to grow and thin gently. As a carefree annual it readily self-sows, making it ideal for naturalized areas and meadow plantings. Water sparingly once established, as these plants tolerate lean, dry conditions.

common_name: Shirley Temple Peony (Fragrant Double Fading Soft Pink to Near-White)
