plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Shirley Temple is a fragrant double peony opening soft pink and fading to near-white.
directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Shirley Temple bears large, fully double flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening a soft pale pink and fading to nearly white as the bloom matures, giving a single planting a gentle gradient of color over its bloom period. Its fragrance and classic double form have made it a long-standing favorite for cutting and for scenting a spring garden. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

plant_note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Wisteria brachybotrys is a less commonly grown Japanese species valued for large individual flowers on shorter racemes.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support structure. Shiro-kapitan belongs to the less commonly grown silky wisteria species, distinguished by soft, velvety foliage and shorter but denser racemes of unusually large, pure white, intensely fragrant flowers compared to the longer, more open racemes of Japanese wisteria. Its more compact raceme length and refined flower size make it a good choice for gardeners who want the wisteria experience on a slightly smaller scale than the sprawling Macrobotrys-type cultivars. Like other wisteria it needs firm annual pruning, both in summer to control vigorous new growth and in late winter to shape and encourage flowering, and several years to reach flowering maturity on a genuinely sturdy long-term support.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Shirobana is unusual among spirea in producing white, pink, and deep rose-red flower clusters simultaneously on the same plant.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun; spirea flowers most heavily and holds the tightest habit in full sun, tolerating partial shade with looser growth and fewer blooms. Shirobana is a distinctive Japanese spirea that produces flat clusters of white, soft pink, and deep rose-red flowers all at once on the same shrub, an unusual multicolor effect rather than the single, uniform flower color typical of most spirea cultivars, blooming heavily in late spring with scattered rebloom through summer. Its fine-textured blue-green foliage provides an attractive backdrop to the mixed-color flower clusters and takes on russet tones in fall. Shear off spent flower clusters after the first flush to tidy the plant and encourage continued summer bloom, and cut the whole shrub back by a third in late winter every few years to renew vigorous growth.

common_name: Shirofuji Mountain Hydrangea (Double White Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Shirofuji bears unusually double white lacecap florets.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Shirofuji bears lacecap flower heads in which the outer sterile florets are fully double, layered like tiny white pompoms ringing the smaller central fertile flowers, an elegant, refined texture among mountain hydrangea cultivars. This compact, shade- and heat-tolerant type performs reliably in warm-climate gardens where straight bigleaf hydrangea can struggle. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Shishi-Gashira is a compact, dwarf sasanqua camellia widely used as a low foundation shrub or informal hedge.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Shishi-Gashira is one of the most widely planted dwarf sasanqua camellias, valued for its compact, dense, mounding habit that stays low without regular pruning, making it a popular foundation shrub, low hedge, or mass planting in Gulf South landscapes. It produces abundant, deep rose-pink, semi-double flowers in a heavy fall flush, offering reliable color when few other shrubs are blooming, and like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica cultivars, blooming well in partial shade to full sun. Its naturally tidy, slow-growing form means it rarely needs shearing to maintain shape, and pruning, if wanted, should be done lightly right after flowering.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Shishigashira is a naturally low, dense grower that blooms later in the sasanqua season than many cultivars, extending camellia color into winter.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Shishigashira is a compact, mounding sasanqua camellia noted for its unusually low, dense, wider-than-tall habit compared to the more upright growth of most sasanquas, making it useful as a large-scale groundcover, low hedge, or foundation planting. It produces semi-double, rose-pink flowers with ruffled petals in late fall into winter, later in the season than earlier-blooming sasanqua cultivars, extending camellia interest further into the cold months. Like other camellias it needs consistently moist, acidic soil and benefits from a layer of mulch to protect shallow roots and conserve moisture through the year.

common_name: Shoal Creek Chaste Tree (Classic Large-Spike Gulf South Vitex Selection)
plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Shoal Creek, introduced in 1983 by Goodness Grows Nursery in Georgia, is the classic vitex selection for the Gulf South, valued for larger violet-blue flower spikes and faster, more vigorous growth than the straight species.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Shoal Creek is the standard Gulf South chaste tree selection, chosen for noticeably longer, more densely flowered lavender-blue spikes and faster, more vigorous growth than seed-grown plants of the species. It blooms profusely on new growth from summer through fall, tolerating the heat, drought, and poor soil that defeat many other flowering shrubs, and the fragrant, gray-green palmately compound foliage adds a pleasant sage-like scent to the garden. Cutting back hard in late winter to 12-18 inches above ground produces vigorous new growth and the best flower display. It is a favorite of bees and butterflies through its long bloom season.

common_name: Shock Wave Purple Tie Dye Petunia
plant_note: Start indoors early and surface sow; seed needs light. Transplant after frost.
directions: This petite petunia bears one-and-a-half to two-inch variegated purple flowers with tie-dye patterns that shift with temperature and light, so no two blooms match. Start the tiny seed indoors eight to ten weeks before the last frost, pressing it onto the surface for light. Transplant after frost into full sun and well-drained soil. Its compact, mounded, spreading habit makes it ideal for hanging baskets and containers. Feed regularly and pinch to keep it full and blooming all season.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; sunflowers grow best sown where they will bloom.
directions: Yellow-tipped, bronze-red petals and contrasting purple-tinged stems make this well-branched sunflower a striking cut flower. Sow seed directly into warm soil after frost, spacing closer for longer stems suited to bouquets. The blooms are pollenless, so they will not shed on tabletops. Give the plants full sun and steady moisture. The edible petals add a bittersweet pop of color to salads.

plant_note: Wedge a small division into the fibrous boot bases of a cabbage palm trunk, a mounted piece of bark, or a hanging basket of coarse, well-drained epiphytic mix in humid, deep shade; shoestring fern grows naturally as an epiphyte and resents standing in wet soil.
directions: Mount divisions on the fibrous trunk boots of a cabbage palm, a piece of rough bark, or a basket of coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix in deep, humid shade; shoestring fern is a distinctive Florida and Gulf Coast native epiphyte with long, narrow, grass-like fronds that hang and drape rather than growing upright, giving the plant its descriptive common name. It grows naturally tucked into the boots left by old palm frond bases on live cabbage palms, drawing moisture from humid air, rainfall, and decomposing organic debris rather than soil. Provide consistent humidity and dappled to deep shade, misting during dry spells if grown away from its preferred palm-trunk habitat, and avoid any planting medium that stays soggy, which quickly rots the fine roots. It is an excellent choice for mounting on palm trunks, in hanging baskets, or in a humid greenhouse or lanai setting throughout its frost-free range.

common_name: Shoo Fly Plant (Apple of Peru, Lantern-Pod Nicandra)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; self-seeds readily, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted the following year.
directions: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Shoo Fly Plant is a tall, bushy South American annual bearing pale lavender-blue, bell-shaped flowers with a white-and-purple throat through summer, followed by papery, inflated, lantern-like seed pods that resemble those of Chinese lantern (Physalis) and are popular in dried arrangements. Its old common name comes from a folk belief that the plant's foliage repels houseflies when hung or grown near a doorway, though this has not been scientifically confirmed. It self-seeds readily and can naturalize in a bed once established, so deadhead spent flowers before pods mature if volunteer seedlings are unwanted; all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, as with many nightshade-family relatives.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade after frost; shooting star performs best in bright indirect light or light-dappled shade — deep shade diminishes its leaf patterning, while intense direct sun bleaches and scorches the variegated leaves.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; shooting star is a Pacific Island tropical shrub of the family Acanthaceae grown primarily for its striking foliage — the oval to lance-shaped leaves are broadly variegated in an irregular blotch pattern of deep purple, green, cream, and ivory-white, creating a bold, multicolored effect that is ornamental year-round and serves a similar role to coleus in the shaded tropical garden. Periodically through the year, the plant produces loose clusters of small, tubular, white flowers with purple-spotted throats, adding to the display. The cultivated forms include purple-leaved and cream-variegated variants, all under the variable species classification. It requires genuine tropical warmth (zone 10–12) and resents cold temperatures — even brief chilling below 50°F can cause leaf discoloration and drop. Most effective in the warm, bright-shade microclimate of an established tropical garden, where its bold variegated foliage provides a strong mid-border accent. Excellent for shaded container plantings and outdoor tropical rooms in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in the garden for natural cold stratification; seeds require at least 60 days of cold moist conditions before they will germinate in spring. Division of established crowns is the faster propagation method.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; the plant is a spring ephemeral that blooms in early spring with distinctive nodding clusters of swept-back petals in white to pink with a yellow ring at the center. After flowering and setting seed in late spring, the foliage yellows and the plant goes fully dormant by midsummer — mark the location well and interplant with later-emerging shade perennials. Plants grown from seed typically require 2–3 years to produce their first bloom. Naturalize in groups of a dozen or more for the most impactful display in a woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; shooting star is a spring ephemeral that dies back completely by early summer — mark planting location to avoid disturbing the dormant roots during summer dormancy.
directions: Plant in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade — shooting star is one of the most spectacular native spring wildflowers, producing umbels of 3–20 nodding flowers whose swept-back petals (white to lavender to deep magenta) and prominent yellow anther cone pointing downward create an unmistakable shooting-star silhouette. The flowers are buzz-pollinated exclusively by bumblebees, which grip the anther cone and vibrate at a specific frequency to release the pollen. A spring ephemeral of open woodland, prairies, and moist slopes, shooting star goes completely dormant by early summer and must be marked to avoid disturbing the underground corms. It grows slowly and persists for decades in appropriate conditions. Requires good drainage despite needing moisture in spring — summer-wet conditions cause rot. Outstanding for naturalizing in moist, open woodland gardens with hostas, ferns, and other spring wildflowers.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Shooting Star hoya has a more upright, shrubby habit than most trailing hoya species and benefits from light staking when young.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Shooting Star hoya has a more upright, shrubby habit than most trailing hoya species and benefits from light staking when young. Glossy, lance-shaped leaves clothe a semi-upright, shrubby plant that produces dramatic, dense clusters of dozens of small, narrow, swept-back yellow-to-white flowers with reflexed petals, resembling a burst of tiny shooting stars and giving the plant its common name. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it blooms more readily and at a younger age than many hoya species, and its shrubbier, less vining habit makes it a good choice for a floor or tabletop specimen rather than a hanging basket. Provide bright indirect light for reliable flowering, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flowering spurs, which rebloom for years.

common_name: Shooting Star Viburnum (Upward-Facing White Doublefile Viburnum)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Shooting Star blooms on the previous year's wood, so prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed.
directions: Shooting Star is a doublefile viburnum selected for lacecap flower clusters whose outer sterile florets twist and curl upward and outward as they mature, giving each cluster a starburst appearance rather than the flat, symmetrical disc of most doublefile types. It carries the same strongly tiered, horizontal branching habit as other doublefile selections, producing a heavy spring bloom followed by red berries that ripen to black and are readily taken by birds, with burgundy fall color to close the season. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade and allow generous width, since the layered branches spread further than the plant grows tall.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in sandy, well-drained, even infertile soil in full sun; shore juniper tolerates salt spray, seaside conditions, and poor, dry soils, making it excellent for difficult coastal and sandy exposures.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, well-drained to poor soil in full sun; shore juniper is native to the sandy coastal cliffs and beaches of Japan and is exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, wind, drought, and nutrient-poor soils, making it a premier choice for coastal gardens, seaside slopes, and hot, sandy bank stabilization. The needles are notably sharper and more prickly than most prostrate junipers, so plant away from paths. The blue-green foliage often takes on attractive steel-blue tones in winter. The cultivar 'Blue Pacific' is particularly low-growing and dense with blue-green color; 'Emerald Sea' has bright green needles. Unlike many groundcovers, shore juniper is largely free of serious pests and diseases in hot, dry conditions where others struggle.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in average to moist, well-drained, woodland or open-edge soil in partial shade; Short's aster establishes readily and tolerates the dappled light of open woodland edges and north-facing slopes better than most asters, making it especially valuable for bridging the sun-to-shade transition zones in naturalistic garden designs.
directions: Plant divisions in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, where it performs best at open woodland edges, lightly shaded slopes, and north-facing exposures that receive morning sun and afternoon shade; Short's aster is a tall, graceful species native to the limestone woodlands and open forest edges of the central and eastern United States, producing branching stems 2–4 feet tall that bear abundant violet to blue daisy flowers with yellow centers from August through October, an important nectar source at a season when many woodland plants have finished blooming. Named for Dr. Charles Wilkins Short, a prominent 19th-century Kentucky botanist and physician, this species fills the niche of a shade-tolerant late-blooming aster that the more commonly grown garden asters cannot fill; it is an excellent choice for the understory garden in combination with golden rod, native ferns, and fall-blooming natives. Divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor; the plant self-seeds modestly and seedlings can be moved in spring.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; short-leaved aloe is compact, cold-tender, and clusters readily into a tidy mat over time.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; short-leaved aloe is compact, cold-tender, and clusters readily into a tidy mat over time. Thick, triangular, pale blue-gray leaves edged with small white teeth form a tight, dense rosette that offsets freely at the base, quickly forming a low, clumping mat, with spikes of coral-orange, tubular flowers rising well above the foliage in spring, attracting hummingbirds where grown outdoors. Native to South Africa's Western Cape, it is one of the smaller, more compact aloe species commonly grown, making it well suited to a succulent dish garden, rock garden pocket, or mixed container where larger aloes would be out of scale. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide full sun for the best blue coloring, and separate offsets to propagate or control spread.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; short-horned epimedium is deciduous and notably cold-hardy, going fully dormant in winter before reliable spring regrowth even in colder gardens.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; short-horned epimedium is deciduous and notably cold-hardy, going fully dormant in winter before reliable spring regrowth even in colder gardens. Epimedium brevicornu is a Chinese species with soft, deciduous, spiny-edged leaflets and delicate sprays of white to pale pink flowers with short, stubby spurs (the source of its common and scientific names) in mid-spring, held on wiry stems above the emerging foliage. Its strong cold hardiness and easy garden adaptability make it one of the more reliable choices for gardeners in colder climates who want to grow epimedium species beyond the typically grown hybrids. It has also long been used in traditional Chinese medicine as a source of yin yang huo, and in the garden it spreads steadily by rhizome to form an attractive, low-maintenance deciduous groundcover.

plant_note: Surface sow in spring in moist to seasonally wet, moderately acidic soil in partial sun; shortleaf lobelia is characteristic of the longleaf pine ecosystem and performs best in open, fire-maintained settings with low competition from aggressive grasses or invasive shrubs.
directions: Lobelia brevifolia is a coastal plain endemic of the southeastern United States, characteristic of longleaf pine upland bogs, pitcher plant savannas, and seepage slopes where it is distinguished from similar lobelias by its notably short, reduced leaves — the feature that gives it its name; it produces blue flowers on erect stems in late summer and fall. This species is a high-fidelity indicator of intact longleaf pine ecosystem habitats and is rarely encountered outside of conservation-quality remnant sites, making it a meaningful ecological garden plant for those working to restore or reconstruct the rapidly disappearing longleaf pine savanna plant community. Sow surface seeds in spring in moderately acidic, moist to seasonally wet soil with good light penetration; avoid heavy mulching or crowding with taller competing vegetation.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in fall in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun. Shortleaf Pine adapts to a wide range of well-drained, acidic soils from dry sand to moist clay loam, and is one of the most widely distributed southern pines — tolerating both droughty uplands and moderately moist conditions.
directions: Shortleaf Pine is one of the most widely distributed southern pines, native to 22 states from New York and New Jersey south to Florida and west to Texas and Oklahoma, growing in dry to moderately moist, acidic, well-drained to somewhat poorly drained soils across a remarkable variety of upland and foothill conditions — a broader soil and climate tolerance than almost any other southern pine. Its most distinctive adaptive trait is the ability to regenerate from dormant basal buds (called 'root sprouts') after top-killing fire or mechanical damage — a trait shared with longleaf pine but uncommon among other pines — that allows it to recover from disturbance without relying solely on seeding. Shortleaf Pine has been a major timber species in the South for over 200 years and is commercially important for lumber and pulpwood; in restoration contexts it is a key species for re-establishing mixed pine-hardwood forests on former agricultural and cutover lands in the Ozarks and upper Gulf Coastal Plain. Grow in full sun in any well-drained, acidic soil; it is more drought-tolerant than most other southern pines and one of the hardiest (to zone 5) of the typically warm-climate southern pines.

common_name: Shortwood Phlox (Clear Pink High-Performance Garden Phlox)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Shortwood is a top-performing pink garden phlox in university trial gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation between plants. Shortwood bears large, clear pink flower heads on tall, vigorous stems, and has repeatedly ranked among the top-performing tall garden phlox cultivars in university trial gardens for its combination of strong color, mildew resistance, and reliable vigor. It carries the classic sweet fragrance of the species through a long midsummer-to-early-fall bloom season. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend bloom and prevent unwanted seedlings, which typically revert toward magenta.

common_name: Shot Silk Camellia (Satiny Bright Pink Reticulata Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Shot Silk is a vigorous, willowy reticulata camellia noted for a satiny sheen on its petals.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind. Shot Silk bears large, semi-double, bright pink blooms with a distinctive satiny, almost iridescent sheen that shifts in appearance depending on the light, a quality that gives the cultivar its name. The vigorous, willowy shrub grows taller and more upright than many other reticulata cultivars, blooming in mid-to-late winter into spring. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Show Off requires full sun for the heaviest flower coverage, and its more compact size than older forsythia cultivars needs less pruning to control.
directions: Show Off is a compact forsythia bred to flower along the entire length of every branch, from the base to the tip, rather than mainly at the branch tips as in older cultivars, producing an unusually dense, solid mass of golden-yellow flowers in late winter before the leaves emerge. Its smaller mature size, roughly half that of standard border forsythia, fits foundation plantings and smaller gardens without the annual hard pruning that larger forsythia cultivars need to stay in bounds. Like all forsythia, flower bud hardiness is the limiting factor outside its ideal cold-winter range — flower buds need a period of cold dormancy and can be damaged by extended warm spells in mild winters, so bloom performance in zone 9 varies from year to year depending on winter chill.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall for natural cold-moist stratification and spring germination, or stratify seed for 4–6 weeks at 40°F and sow in early spring; showy aster is native to coastal plain pine barrens and sandy, acidic, dry soils where it is most vigorous — avoid rich, moist garden soils that promote floppy growth.
directions: Sow seed in fall directly into well-drained, dry to average, acidic, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; showy aster is a coastal plain native endemic to the pine barrens, sandy oak woodlands, and dry acidic uplands from New England to the Carolinas, where it produces vivid violet-purple ray flowers with yellow centers from August through October in conditions that would challenge most other flowering perennials. It is one of the most intensely colored native asters, the petals a rich violet-purple that stands out strongly against the sandy, sparse-vegetation landscapes it colonizes in the wild. Because it is adapted to lean, dry, infertile soils, planting in rich or moist garden conditions produces tall, floppy plants with diminished flowering — restrict soil richness and irrigation to keep plants compact and free-flowering. Divide or transplant with care, as the taproot resents disturbance once established.

plant_note: Plant corms 4-6 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil, ideally before flowers emerge leafless from bare ground.
directions: Set corms 4-6 inches deep and about 6-9 inches apart in a sunny to lightly shaded bed with rich, well-drained soil, planting in late summer so goblet-shaped flowers appear on bare stems weeks later. Broad strap-like leaves emerge the following spring, photosynthesize, then die back well before the naked blooms return in autumn. The large rosy-lilac flowers are showier than common autumn crocus and work well naturalized under deciduous shrubs or in a rock garden. All parts are toxic if ingested, so site away from grazing animals and small children.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or fall and replant immediately in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Geranium x magnificum is a sterile hybrid and cannot be grown from seed — propagate only by division. After the main June flowering, cut back hard to encourage a fresh rosette of foliage (with occasional scattered rebloom in summer and autumn).
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; showy cranesbill is arguably the finest and most reliable of the large-flowered hardy geraniums — a robust sterile hybrid (G. ibericum x G. platypetalum) producing dense mounds of large, deeply lobed, richly textured leaves and in June, a spectacular and prolonged flush of large (1.5–2 inch) flowers in vivid violet-blue with finely veined darker purple veining that gives the flowers a luminous, saturated intensity unusual among blue-flowered perennials. The flowers are produced in such density that they nearly cover the foliage at peak bloom. It is notably heat-tolerant among the large-flowered hardy geraniums. Because it is a sterile hybrid it does not self-sow. After the June display, cutting the entire plant back hard to 4–6 inches stimulates a fresh crop of deeply lobed, ornamental leaves for summer and autumn — the foliage alone is attractive through the season. The autumn foliage turns red and orange. An indispensable component of the mixed perennial border, particularly in sun-to-shade transition zones.

plant_note: Surface-sow; needs light to germinate. Spreads vigorously by runners.
directions: Surface-sow the seed and press it in lightly, as light encourages germination. Commonly called pink ladies, this spreading native perennial opens delicate pink, cup-shaped flowers over a long season. It thrives on neglect in full sun and dry, poor soil, spreading readily by runners to cover slopes and difficult sites. Give it room to roam or contain it, and expect a carefree groundcover loved by bees and butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; showy fleabane is native to montane meadows and aspen groves of the Rocky Mountains and adapts well to average garden conditions at lower elevations.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; showy fleabane forms a tidy clump of narrow leaves topped in early to midsummer by abundant lavender-blue, daisy-like flowers with dozens of narrow petals surrounding a bright yellow center, giving the blooms a fine, almost fringed texture reminiscent of a small aster. It is native to montane meadows and aspen groves of the Rocky Mountains, where it blooms heavily for several weeks and attracts a wide range of native bees and butterflies. Unlike many fleabanes, it holds its color and form well without flopping, making it useful as a front-of-border perennial or in naturalistic pollinator plantings at lower elevations outside its mountain habitat. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in spring; showy goldenrod is one of the most garden-worthy of all native goldenrods — less aggressively spreading than common goldenrod and producing more upright, elegant flower plumes.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; showy goldenrod is one of the most ornamentally refined of all native goldenrods — producing stiffly erect, clump-forming stems (rather than the invasive rhizomatous spread of S. canadensis) topped in late summer and fall by large, dense, pyramidal plumes of vivid golden-yellow flowers that provide the most intense and lasting goldenrod bloom display available and are exceptionally attractive to monarch butterflies, native bees, and late-migrating birds seeking seed. Its more controlled growth habit and superior flower presentation make it a far more garden-worthy selection than common goldenrod for the formal border and prairie garden. It does not cause hay fever — the pollen is too heavy to be wind-dispersed and is spread only by insects. Thrives in average to lean soil and tolerates drought well once established; rich, fertile, moist soil encourages excessive vegetative growth at the expense of flowering.

common_name: Showy Jasmine (Florida Jasmine, Yellow Jasmine Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in partial shade to full sun; Showy Jasmine is more cold-hardy than most jasmines and adapts well to zone 9 conditions, including heavy clay soils and summer humidity. It blooms most heavily in spring (March–May in zone 9) with lighter bloom repeats through fall. Prune after the main spring bloom to shape; avoid hard pruning in fall which removes flower buds. It is more shrubby and less sprawling than some jasmines, forming a mounded 3–5 foot specimen.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil; Showy Jasmine is adaptable to a range of soil types and is more tolerant of clay soils than many ornamental shrubs. Jasminum floridum is a semi-evergreen to evergreen shrubby jasmine native to China (cultivated in Chinese gardens for centuries and naturalized in parts of the southern US, hence its occasional listing as 'Florida Jasmine'). Unlike the vining habit of most popular jasmines (J. officinale, J. polyanthum), Showy Jasmine grows as a compact, mounding, multi-stemmed shrub with arching branches and small, dark-green, glossy, trifoliate or 5-leaflet compound leaves. The bright yellow, 5-petaled, tubular flowers bloom in spring and sporadically through the warm season, providing cheerful color without the fragrance of white-flowering jasmines — the flowers are pleasantly scented but not as intensely aromatic as J. polyanthum or J. officinale. Showy Jasmine is one of the better-adapted jasmines for zone 9 Gulf South conditions — tolerating summer heat, humidity, and clay soils better than the more tender tropical species while providing reliable cold hardiness through zone 7 winters. It makes an excellent landscape shrub for partially shaded foundation plantings, mixed shrub borders, and parking lot islands.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall in moist to wet, neutral to slightly alkaline, calcium-rich, humus-rich soil in partial shade; showy lady's slipper prefers cooler, wetter conditions and neutral to basic pH (pH 5.5–7.5) unlike most native orchids that need acidic soil.
directions: Showy lady's slipper is the largest and most spectacularly beautiful of all North American native orchids — the official state wildflower of Minnesota — with large, pure white upper petals surrounding a dramatically inflated, rosy-pink to magenta pouch that is rivaled in size only by tropical orchids. Unlike most eastern orchids that need acidic soil, showy lady's slipper prefers neutral to slightly alkaline, calcium-rich soils in cool, moist, shaded swamp forests, tamarack bogs, and calcareous seeps — a habitat preference that makes it more restrictive than yellow lady's slipper but potentially suitable for gardens with moist, organic, neutral soil in zones 2–7. Individual plants are remarkably long-lived and slow-growing, capable of persisting in the same location for 50–100 years when undisturbed, slowly expanding into multi-stemmed clumps of increasing grandeur. As with all native terrestrial orchids, purchase only tissue-cultured nursery propagated specimens — wild collection of any Cypripedium is illegal in most states and ecologically devastating. Note: handling the foliage can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall sowing into very well-drained, rocky or gravelly, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun in cool climates.
directions: Showy Locoweed is a remarkably beautiful native locoweed of dry, rocky alpine and subalpine slopes in the northern Rockies and northern Great Plains, producing unusually dense, silky-woolly silver foliage that makes the plant appear frosted even in midsummer. The brilliant blue-violet to rose-purple flower spikes appearing in early summer are among the most intensely colored wildflowers of the northern plains and mountains. CAUTION: like other locoweeds, it is toxic to livestock and should be sited away from grazing animals. Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into very well-drained, rocky or gravelly, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; it performs best in cool, dry climates and is an outstanding rock garden and alpine garden native for zones 2 through 7.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall, or cold stratify seed 4-6 weeks before spring sowing.
directions: This robust heirloom perennial hosts monarch butterflies and draws many pollinators with clusters of star-shaped blooms above green to silvery foliage. Sow seed in fall or cold stratify it for several weeks before spring sowing to break dormancy. It grows best in full sun and well-drained soil and is drought tolerant once established. Its deep roots dislike transplanting, so sow it in place. Leave seed pods to spread the patch and support monarch populations.

plant_note: Sow shallowly and cover; seed germinates best in darkness.
directions: Sow seed lightly covered, since this annual phlox germinates best in darkness. It produces a colorful blend of five-petaled, lightly fragrant blooms on low, spreading plants. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil, sowing in early spring or fall in mild climates for the best bloom. Deadhead to prolong flowering and enjoy the bright carpets it forms in beds, borders, and containers.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring into cool, moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this boreal native prefers cooler climates and struggles in hot, humid summers.
directions: Plant young trees in spring in cool, moist, well-drained, acidic soil and full sun to light shade, sited where summers stay relatively cool since this northern species declines in hot, humid regions. Showy mountain ash is native to boreal forests, rocky shorelines, and cold uplands across the northern United States and Canada, forming a small, rounded tree with flat clusters of white spring flowers that attract bees and other pollinators. The large, bright orange-red berry clusters ripen in early fall and persist into winter, becoming a magnet for migrating and overwintering cedar waxwings, pine grosbeaks, and other winter finches once softened by frost. Its open branching structure also provides good perching and nesting sites for songbirds.

common_name: Showy Pansy Orchid (Brazilian Miltonia, Spectabilis Orchid)
plant_note: Divide clumps of 3+ pseudobulbs in spring just as new growth emerges and pot in a fine bark-and-sphagnum mix in a shallow, well-drained container; Miltonia spectabilis is a warm-growing Brazilian lowland species and, unlike its cooler-growing relative Miltoniopsis, tolerates typical indoor room warmth without complaint.
directions: Provide bright, filtered light — an east or lightly shaded south window — with high humidity and good air movement around the flattened, oval pseudobulbs. Miltonia spectabilis is an epiphytic orchid from the Atlantic coastal forests of Brazil, producing broad, flat, pansy-shaped flowers 2–3 inches across in late summer and fall: white to rose-pink sepals and petals surround a large, flaring lip that is white with a bold purple-red blotch radiating from its base. Keep the bark mix evenly moist through the growing season and reduce watering only slightly after flowering, since this species has no pronounced dry dormancy and resents prolonged drying at the roots. It is one of the classic "pansy orchids" of the trade and considerably easier in average home warmth than the similarly named but cooler-growing Miltoniopsis hybrids.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; showy penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, tolerating summer dry periods without supplemental water.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; showy penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, tolerating summer dry periods without supplemental water. Thick, blue-green leaves clasp tall, sturdy flower stalks topped with dense clusters of large, funnel-shaped, violet-blue to lavender-pink flowers in spring, one of the tallest and showiest of the Southern California native penstemons and a favorite of bees and hummingbirds. Native to dry chaparral and coastal sage scrub slopes of Southern California and Baja California, it is a long-lived, drought-tolerant perennial well suited to a xeriscape or native plant border, providing bold vertical structure and color when massed. Cut back spent flower stalks after bloom to tidy the plant, and avoid overwatering or rich soil, which shortens its lifespan.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees. Showy Skullcap performs best in the cool, dappled shade of eastern deciduous forest understories — it is one of the few native wildflowers that produces exceptional bloom in moderate to deep shade.
directions: Showy Skullcap is an outstanding native woodland wildflower of the central Appalachians and adjacent regions, producing some of the most vivid blue-violet flowers of any shade-garden native from May through early June — a relative rarity among plants that genuinely thrive in moderate to deep deciduous forest shade. The clear blue, two-lipped tubular flowers are produced in terminal and axillary clusters on 12–24 inch stems and are a significant nectar source for bumblebees and other long-tongued native bees that visit the forest understory in spring. Native to moist, fertile, slightly acidic, humus-rich soils of deciduous woodlands in the central Appalachian region, Showy Skullcap is an ideal native perennial for the shaded garden border, woodland path edge, or native plant shade garden where deep blue flowers in late spring fill a critical color gap. Direct sow seeds in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; established plants are long-lived and slowly colonize appropriate shaded spots.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; showy stonecrop is extraordinarily drought-tolerant once established and is best planted in poor to average, dry soil — rich, moist soils cause floppy, weak growth.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and very well-drained, lean, average to poor soil; showy stonecrop thrives on neglect and drought — it rots in heavy, wet, or overly fertile soil, and rich soil produces tall, floppy stems that fall open in the center. Hylotelephium spectabile (formerly Sedum spectabile) is a succulent perennial forming neat, upright clumps of thick, fleshy, blue-green leaves on sturdy stems, producing large, flat-topped, broccoli-like flower heads that open rose-pink in August, deepen to dusty rose and brick-russet through September and October, and persist as attractive buff-brown seedheads through winter — making it one of the most important late-season perennials for pollinators, with bees, butterflies, and hoverflies crowding the flowers well into fall. The iconic cultivar 'Autumn Joy' (syn. 'Herbstfreude') is the most widely grown sedum in the world and is essentially identical to the species. Plants are best divided every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor; simply pull clumps apart and replant divisions.

plant_note: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water 12 hours before direct sowing in average to poor, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; showy tick trefoil fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules and improves poor, degraded soils.
directions: Scarify seeds and soak in warm water 12 hours before direct sowing in average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; showy tick trefoil is a tall, robust native prairie legume that produces large, branching panicles of small, rosy-pink, pea-like flowers from July through August — one of the most generously blooming of all native prairie wildflowers in its season and exceptional for attracting a wide diversity of native bees, bumble bees, and butterflies. As a legume, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules and actively improves impoverished prairie and meadow soils. Seed capsules break into individual hooked segments that cling to fabric and animal fur for dispersal — the classic 'tick trefoil' seed. The large, compound, three-part leaves are attractive through the growing season. Excellent for native plant meadow restorations, prairie gardens, and wildlife habitat plantings where its late summer bloom fills a critical pollinator-support gap.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; shredded umbrella plant is a slow-establishing but very long-lived perennial — patience through the first two seasons is rewarded with permanent, essentially maintenance-free shade garden coverage thereafter.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; shredded umbrella plant is one of the most unusual and conversation-inspiring perennials in the shade garden — each spring the new leaves emerge in a remarkable juvenile form, looking like a closed, tattered umbrella with deeply divided, drooping, shaggy segments still folded together; as the leaves expand and unfurl, they reveal mature, deeply palmate, aconitum-like leaves with elegant, fingerlike divisions held flat in an umbrella shape. The effect of the emerging juvenile growth is bizarre and fascinating. Mature plants bear small, inconspicuous, white daisy flowers in late summer. The plant is native to shaded rocky hillsides and open woodlands in Korea, China, and Japan and is completely winter-hardy while tolerating heat better than many shade perennials. An excellent foliage specimen for collectors, shade garden enthusiasts, and gardeners who appreciate unusual plant texture and form over flashy flowers. Slow to establish from division; patience is required.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; shrimp plant grows rapidly and roots easily from stem cuttings — pinch tips frequently during the first few months to encourage branching and a fuller habit before allowing it to bloom.
directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; shrimp plant is one of the most charming and long-blooming perennials for shaded Gulf Coast gardens, named for the distinctive overlapping reddish-brown bracts (modified leaves) that form arching, drooping spikes 3–4 inches long, closely resembling a cooked shrimp — from the tip of each bract emerges a delicate white two-lipped flower. Bloom is essentially continuous from spring through frost and often persists in warm winters. It performs equally well in light shade or partial sun, making it versatile for difficult spots under the canopy of large trees. Hummingbirds visit the flowers readily. A yellow-bracted form ('Fruit Cocktail' or 'Yellow Queen') provides the same long bloom season in a lighter color. Pinch the plant back after bloom flushes to keep it compact and stimulate fresh growth. Propagate from stem cuttings, which root readily in moist soil.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; shrubby cinquefoil is tolerant of clay, alkaline soils, and cold once established. Prune out oldest stems to the base every few years to maintain vigorous flowering. It blooms on new wood and benefits from light shearing after the main flush.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; shrubby cinquefoil is among the toughest, most cold-hardy, and longest-blooming deciduous shrubs in cultivation — a circumboreal native of arctic and alpine regions of the Northern Hemisphere that produces a dense mound of fine-textured, small, pinnate leaves and, from late spring through autumn, a near-continuous succession of cheerful five-petaled flowers resembling small wild roses in yellow, white, cream, pink, or orange depending on the cultivar. The bloom season is exceptionally long — often six months in favorable conditions — making it one of the most reliably flowering shrubs per season of any woody plant in cold climates. It tolerates cold to zone 2, clay soil, alkaline soil, drought once established, and salt spray. Dozens of named cultivars are available including 'Goldfinger' (deep yellow), 'Primrose Beauty' (pale yellow), 'Abbotswood' (pure white), 'Pink Beauty' (soft pink), and 'Red Ace' (orange-red, which fades to yellow in heat). Outstanding for low-maintenance shrub borders, highway medians, and mass plantings in cold climates.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; shrubby germander tolerates pruning well and can be sheared into a formal low hedge or shaped as a specimen. It is damaged below about 15 degrees F and is best suited to zones 8-11. The cultivar Azureum has more intensely blue-lavender flowers than the typical species.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; shrubby germander is a standout evergreen Mediterranean shrub valued for its exceptional silver-white foliage that glows brilliantly in the sun. The entire plant — stems, leaves, and undersides — is covered in dense, white, woolly hairs that give it an almost luminous silver-white appearance in the garden, making it one of the most silver-foliaged of all hardy shrubs. From spring through summer it produces a long succession of two-lipped, pale-blue to lavender flowers with a prominent lower lip, carried singly in the leaf axils along the branches. Native to the western Mediterranean in Spain, Portugal, and North Africa, it thrives in lean, alkaline, well-drained soils and intense sun and is extremely drought-tolerant once established. It is widely used in Mediterranean-style, California, and Gulf Coast gardens as a specimen shrub, low screening hedge, or silver foliage accent. Responds well to shearing and can be kept as a formal hedge of 3-4 feet.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; shrubby penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, thriving in a rock garden or dry border.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; shrubby penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, thriving in a rock garden or dry border. Small, evergreen, toothed leaves cover a low, woody-based, mounding subshrub that produces an abundant flush of large, vivid lavender-blue to violet flowers in late spring, native to rocky slopes, ridges, and open pine forests across the inland Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies. Its semi-woody, shrubby structure gives it more year-round garden presence than many herbaceous penstemons, holding a tidy mounded shape through winter, and its drought tolerance and rock-garden scale make it well suited to a xeriscape border or scree planting. Cut back lightly after flowering to maintain a compact form, and avoid rich soil or excess summer water, both of which shorten this dryland native's lifespan.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; shrubby St. John's wort is adaptable to moist or dry soils and tolerates periodic light flooding better than golden St. John's wort.
directions: Shrubby St. John's wort is one of the most adaptable and cold-hardy native flowering shrubs of eastern North America — a rounded, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub that produces bright, butter-yellow five-petaled flowers with showy stamens prolifically in July and August, when the garden's early-summer bloom has faded and few other native shrubs are at peak flower. It grows naturally in a wider range of moisture conditions than most native shrubby Hypericums, tolerating both dry rocky slopes and moist, seasonally wet bottomland edges, making it one of the more versatile native shrubs for mixed landscape situations. Native bees — particularly specialist pollen collectors in the family Melittidae and Apidae — are the primary pollinators, attracted by the abundant pollen (this genus provides no nectar); the persistent, star-shaped seed capsules are ornamental through winter and consumed by some birds. An excellent choice for naturalistic shrub borders, rain garden edges, and native landscape plantings in the cold northern half of its range where golden St. John's wort is less reliably hardy.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall or container trees in early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Shumard oak establishes faster than most oaks and tolerates brief flooding, making it an excellent street and yard tree in the South.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall or container trees in early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Shumard oak is the premier large native oak of the Gulf Coast and Deep South, growing faster than most oaks (2–3 feet per year when young) while developing into a large, long-lived specimen tree with spectacular deep red-to-scarlet fall color — one of the best oaks for fall color in zone 7–9 where many trees fail to color reliably. It tolerates brief flooding and clay soils better than many oaks, making it an excellent choice for urban and suburban landscapes in the South. The deeply lobed leaves with pointed tips are similar to pin oak but without the drooping lower branches. The acorns provide important fall food for turkeys, deer, and numerous bird species. An outstanding Gulf Coast street tree, shade tree, and wildlife tree.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Shuttleworth's wild ginger is more slowly spreading than Asarum canadense and has exceptionally attractive, silver-mottled, evergreen foliage.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Shuttleworth's wild ginger is slower-spreading than the common eastern wild ginger (A. canadense) but is evergreen and much more ornamental in foliage, making it superior for groundcover use in shaded gardens. Asarum shuttleworthii is a southern Appalachian native evergreen wild ginger with large, heart-shaped, leathery, dark-green leaves beautifully mottled and marbled with silvery patterns; the intricate mottling intensifies with the age of the plant and varies considerably between individual plants, making each one somewhat unique. Like all Asarum, it bears curious, jug-shaped, brownish-purple flowers concealed at the base of the leaves near the soil in spring; the leaves smell faintly of ginger when crushed and were used historically as a seasoning though the plant contains toxic compounds and is not recommended for internal use.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 2–3 inches deep in spring after soil warms to 65°F or above in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; Siam tulip produces stunning upright flower spikes with pink bracts in summer and thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Plant rhizomes 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun after soil warms; rhizomes go dormant in winter. Curcuma alismatifolia (Siam tulip) is a Thai and Southeast Asian tropical ginger producing one of the most beautiful and unusual flower structures in the tropics — an upright, tulip-shaped cluster of colorful, papery bracts (modified leaves) in pink, lavender, white, or bicolor (pink and white) with small, insignificant flowers hidden within, atop a bare stalk 18–24 inches tall. The flowers resemble a stylized tulip from a distance but are actually inflorescences with showy bracts rather than true petals. Plants emerge from dormant rhizomes in late spring, bloom in summer, and go dormant again after fall — a clean growth cycle suited to Gulf Coast gardens. As a cut flower, Siam tulip is extremely long-lasting (2–3 weeks in a vase). It is one of Thailand's most important commercial cut flower crops and is widely grown in tropical floriculture worldwide. In zone 8–11, the rhizomes can be left in the ground year-round; in colder zones, lift and store at 55°F. Excellent in container plantings.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is reliably warm; in frost-free zones 9-12 seed can be sown at any time during the warm season.
directions: Vigorous tropical perennial herb or shrub in the aster family with opposite, triangular leaves and dense clusters of white to pale lavender fluffy composite flowers from fall through winter, popular with monarch butterflies and small native bees. Native to tropical America and widely naturalized in open disturbed habitats throughout the tropics and subtropical US, it grows extremely fast in warm, humid climates and is considered invasive in parts of Africa and Asia. In frost-free zones 9-12 it makes an effective naturalistic backdrop or wildlife garden plant but requires containment in smaller gardens. Plant in full sun in average to moderately moist soil and cut back hard after flowering to maintain a manageable shrubby form.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or fall; Siberian bergenia is one of the most cold-tolerant evergreen shade groundcover plants available and is fully hardy to zone 2 (-50°F) — invaluable for cold-climate shade gardens where most broadleaf evergreens are not reliably hardy.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siberian bergenia is an Asian shade evergreen perennial renowned primarily for its exceptional cold-hardiness (to zone 2, or approximately -50°F) and its ability to maintain its large, rounded, leathery, glossy, dark-green leaves through the harshest winters with minimal damage — the massive, cabbage-like, evergreen leaves provide bold textural interest throughout the year, and the foliage develops rich bronze, red, and burgundy tones in cold weather, particularly when planted in a position receiving some winter sun. In late winter and early spring (February–April depending on zone), bright-pink to magenta, bell-shaped flowers on thick, reddish stalks emerge directly from the crown, often appearing before the snow has fully melted. Siberian bergenia is one of the two or three most cold-tolerant evergreen shade groundcovers available for temperate gardens and is an essential plant for shaded positions in zone 2–4 gardens where most competing shade groundcovers are not reliably hardy. Spreads steadily by thick, creeping rhizomes to form dense weed-excluding colonies.

plant_note: Plant container divisions or transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; brunnera is a cool-season performer that looks best in spring and early summer, typically going summer-dormant in hot, humid climates.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Siberian bugloss is a spring gem of the shade garden — forming low mounds of large, deep-green, heart-shaped leaves covered from early to mid-spring in tiny, vivid sky-blue flowers that exactly resemble forget-me-not blossoms. The flowers appear before the leaves reach full size, creating an airy blue haze above the emerging foliage. After flowering, the large, textured leaves expand to 8–10 inches wide and provide attractive coverage through early summer. In climates with hot, humid summers, brunnera may go partly summer-dormant, which is normal — the leaves decline but the plant revives in fall. Named cultivars add silver variegation: 'Jack Frost' has entire silver leaves with only green veining, 'Looking Glass' is nearly all-silver, and 'Sea Heart' has silver patterns with dark margins. All cultivars need consistent moisture and protection from afternoon sun to maintain their silver markings. Self-seeds freely in cool, moist shade garden conditions.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; Siberian bugloss is larger in leaf and more vigorous than the better-known B. macrophylla, but lacks the popular silver-leaved cultivars of that species. It forms dense groundcover colonies in moist, shaded conditions and is more drought-tolerant once established than its appearance suggests. The tiny, bright-blue forget-me-not flowers appear in spring before the large leaves are fully expanded.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; Siberian bugloss is the larger and more vigorous Brunnera species — surpassing the more commonly grown B. macrophylla in leaf size (the heart-shaped, rough-textured, bright-green leaves can reach 12 inches across), vigor, and spreading capacity. In early spring, before the large leaves are fully expanded, it produces a cloud of tiny, brilliant sky-blue, five-petaled flowers identical in form to forget-me-nots (the borage-family relationship is clear) — held in loose, branching sprays above the emerging foliage. After flowering, the large, coarse-textured, heart-shaped leaves expand to form a bold, weed-smothering groundcover through the remainder of the growing season, at a scale that is more dramatic and architectural than B. macrophylla. Native to the forests and shaded river banks of Siberia and adjacent regions, it is among the hardiest of all shade perennials, surviving to zone 3, and thrives in the cool, moist, shaded conditions that suit it in zones 3–7. An excellent large-scale shade groundcover for woodland gardens where bold, weed-suppressing foliage through summer and brilliant spring blue flowers are both desired.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall where plants are to grow permanently — fresh seed germinates readily in cool conditions; Siberian corydalis has a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established. It self-sows freely around the parent plant when happy. After the spring flowering and seed set, the plant goes summer dormant and disappears completely until the following spring.
directions: Sow seeds in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Siberian corydalis is the largest and most architectural of the commonly grown corydalis species — a bold-leaved spring ephemeral native to Siberia and central Asia producing finely divided, glaucous, blue-gray-green foliage of remarkable quality and elegance, and in early to mid-spring, dense, upright clusters of substantial yellow flowers with dark-brown to purple inner petal markings at the tip of each floret. The flowers are significantly larger than those of C. lutea or C. ochroleuca, the clusters more imposing, and the whole effect more dramatically architectural. After setting seed, the plant disappears completely into summer dormancy — the site should be marked to avoid inadvertent disturbance. It combines beautifully with late-emerging perennials (hostas, ferns, daylilies) that will fill in as it goes dormant. Often uncommon in nurseries despite being easy from fresh seed. Self-sows modestly to maintain a colony once established.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow onto moist seed-starting mix and do not cover, as seeds need light to germinate.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last expected frost by pressing them onto the surface of moist seed-starting mix under grow lights, maintaining soil temperatures around 65 degrees Fahrenheit. Transplant seedlings outdoors after frost danger has passed into deep, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun. Plants grow slowly in their first year but develop into bold architectural clumps by the second season, sending up whorled-leaf stems topped with pink to lilac candelabra flower spikes in midsummer. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and share this underused pollinator plant with other gardeners.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers or divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siberian fumewort is a spring ephemeral that goes fully dormant by early summer, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant tubers later in the season.
directions: Plant dormant tubers or divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siberian fumewort is a spring ephemeral that goes fully dormant by early summer, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant tubers later in the season. Corydalis ambigua is a diminutive East Asian woodland ephemeral producing finely divided, ferny blue-green foliage and short spikes of vivid sky-blue to purple-blue, spurred flowers in earliest spring, often blooming alongside snowdrops and crocus before the tree canopy leafs out. It naturalizes gently from self-sown seed and offsets in a woodland rock garden or beneath deciduous shrubs, disappearing completely by summer to leave room for later-emerging perennials. Plant it in generous drifts for the best display, since individual plants are small, and avoid summer irrigation over the dormant tubers, which prefer to stay drier once foliage has died back.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring (just as growth begins) or fall, setting just below the soil surface in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Siberian iris tolerates wet soils and partial shade far better than bearded iris and requires much less maintenance.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring (just as growth begins) or fall, setting just below the soil surface in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Siberian iris tolerates wet soils and partial shade far better than bearded iris and requires much less maintenance. Iris sibirica is widely considered the most refined and garden-worthy of all the iris species, producing slender, grass-like, attractive foliage throughout the season and elegant, five-inch flowers with gracefully drooping falls in shades of violet-blue, purple, white, pink, and yellow in late May to June; unlike bearded iris, it rarely needs dividing (every 5-7 years only), is disease-resistant, and is virtually deer-proof. It thrives at pond margins, in rain gardens, and in consistently moist borders; the attractive, upright seedpod clusters provide winter interest and self-seeding; it is an outstanding cut flower with slender, upright foliage that remains attractive all season.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall; seeds germinate best at cool temperatures (55–65°F) and benefit from a brief cold-moist stratification period of 1–2 weeks before sowing.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; unlike the tall border delphiniums (D. elatum hybrids), Siberian larkspur forms a compact, mounded plant 12–18 inches tall that rarely needs staking and is far more heat-tolerant. The brilliant gentian-blue to violet flowers cover the plant in late spring and early summer and will often rebloom if cut back hard after the first flush. In warm climates (zone 7+) it is frequently grown as a cool-season annual or biennial, as it declines in summer heat; in cooler zones it is a reliable short-lived perennial. All parts are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Siberian pea tree is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, alkaline conditions where most shrubs fail. It is one of the most cold-tolerant of all nitrogen-fixing leguminous shrubs and is a standard permaculture and shelterbelt species for the northern Great Plains and prairie provinces.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Siberian pea tree is one of the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant nitrogen-fixing shrubs available, native to Siberia and northern China and reliably hardy to zone 2 — surviving temperatures of -50°F — making it invaluable for the most extreme northern climates where few other leguminous shrubs survive. The yellow pea flowers in spring are attractive and nectar-rich, providing early-season bee forage. The seed pods (up to 2 inches long) contain small seeds that are technically edible — they were eaten by indigenous Siberian peoples as a protein source in famine conditions — and are eaten by birds and small mammals. In permaculture design, Siberian pea tree serves as a cold-hardy nitrogen-fixing component for food forests, shelter belts, and northern homesteads. It is widely used for windbreaks and shelterbelt plantings on the northern Great Plains of North America and the prairie provinces of Canada. The weeping form 'Pendula' is sometimes grown as an ornamental grafted specimen.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 3 inches deep and 3 inches apart in fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Siberian squill naturalizes by self-seeding and offsets to form large, sweeping colonies under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant small bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun under deciduous trees; Siberian squill is one of the most intense true-blue flowers in the spring garden, producing small nodding bells of vivid cobalt-blue in earliest spring, often emerging through late snow. It is one of the best naturalizing bulbs for shaded areas, spreading slowly by both seed and offsets to carpet woodland floors with color by late March. After bloom the foliage yellows and disappears by late spring, leaving no trace. Plant in drifts of 100 or more under deciduous trees or in lawn areas for the most striking seasonal display. They are not harmed by mowing once the foliage has yellowed.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 6-8 inches apart in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Sicilian honey garlic is extremely easy to grow in any well-drained soil and is highly adaptable to sun or partial shade. It self-seeds with some freedom and the persistent, papery seed heads are an attractive ornamental feature in their own right — deadhead after flowering if you wish to limit self-seeding.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for late spring to early summer bloom; Sicilian honey garlic is among the most unusual and elegant of all the ornamental allium relatives — a tall, statuesque bulb producing long, strap-like basal leaves with a keel that smell of garlic when bruised, then in late May or early June sending up stiff, slender stems to 2-3 feet topped with large, loose, umbel-like clusters of 10-30 pendant, bell-shaped flowers in a subtle, sophisticated palette of cream, pale green, pink, and rich maroon-red, the colors shifting and blending from bud to flower to seed in a remarkable way. After the flowers fade, the seed heads turn abruptly upright on their pedicels, becoming stiffly erect papery capsules that persist on the stem and are highly valued for dried arrangements. It is an outstanding cut flower both in bud and in seed. The plant self-seeds modestly and slowly builds into a naturalized colony in suitable conditions; it is adaptable to poor, dry soils and thrives with minimal care.

plant_note: Direct sow onto dry, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in fall; seeds benefit from exposure to winter moisture and temperature cycling and should be pressed lightly onto the soil surface without covering in a site with full sun and no competing vegetation.
directions: Sickle-leaved Coreopsis is a native perennial of dry, open, sandy pine savannas and flatwoods along the southeastern coastal plain, immediately recognizable by its narrow, linear to distinctly sickle-shaped leaf segments that set it apart from all other coreopsis species. Bright yellow, daisy-like flowers with a maroon-tinged central disk zone open in summer above the fine-textured foliage, attracting native bees and small butterflies throughout the season. Native to fire-maintained longleaf pine ecosystems of the Carolinas and Florida, this species thrives in poor, sandy, acidic, extremely well-drained soil in full sun and becomes more floriferous and compact under the lean conditions it evolved with — avoid rich soil or supplemental fertilizer, which produce floppy, weak growth. An excellent choice for longleaf pine savanna restorations, dry native meadows, and open native gardens in zones 7 through 9.

plant_note: Sow direct after last frost in warm, well-drained to dry, lean soil in full sun; sicklepod is a warm-season annual that germinates quickly in hot soil and is well adapted to disturbed, dry, open ground across the southeastern United States.
directions: Sow direct after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 70°F in well-drained to dry, lean soil in full sun; sicklepod germinates rapidly in hot conditions and is not suited to heavy clay or consistently wet soils — it thrives in the kind of dry, open, disturbed ground where many other plants struggle. Senna obtusifolia is a native warm-season annual of the southeastern United States and Gulf Coast, producing pinnately compound leaves with broadly obovate leaflets and paired, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers from June through September; its common name refers to the distinctive curved, sickle-shaped seed pods that follow the flowers and are a key identification feature. The roasted seeds have a long history of use as a coffee substitute — known as 'java bean' or 'foetid cassia coffee' — and the young leaves are used as a food vegetable in parts of West Africa, where the plant has naturalized extensively; it is also an important host plant for cloudless sulphur and other native sulfur butterflies. Sicklepod self-sows prolifically in warm climates and can naturalize in open sandy or disturbed ground; it is well suited to naturalistic plantings, butterfly gardens, and dry roadsides in the Deep South.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; do not fertilize as this is a plant of lean, poor soils.
directions: Direct sow in early spring in lean, well-drained, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; side oats grama is the official Texas state grass and one of the finest warm-season native grasses for ornamental use, with slender upright stems bearing distinctive oat-like seed heads all arrayed on one side of the stem in a graceful line. It establishes quickly from seed, tolerates drought and heat extremely well once established, and provides excellent winter structure with its bronze-tan seed heads. Mow or cut back once in late winter before new growth begins. Excellent for low-maintenance meadow plantings, slopes, and bird-supporting landscape borders. The seed is harvested by sparrows, finches, and native buntings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained conifer or boreal woodland soil in partial to full shade; sidebells wintergreen is a creeping, slowly stoloniferous ground cover that requires acidic woodland conditions and mycorrhizal associations to thrive.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained conifer woodland soil in partial to full shade; sidebells wintergreen is a creeping, slowly spreading subshrub that requires mycorrhizal soil associations and should be planted in undisturbed woodland soil near established conifers or other acid-loving plants. Orthilia secunda (formerly Pyrola secunda) is the most distinctive of the wintergreens, instantly recognizable by its one-sided flowering habit — the nodding, greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers are all borne on one side of the arching, 4–8 inch stem — hence the common names sidebells and one-sided pyrola. It is a circumboreal species of cold, moist, conifer and mixed woodland floors throughout northern North America, Europe, and Asia, forming low, creeping mats of small, ovate, toothed, evergreen leaves. It is rarely available commercially but will naturalize in suitable acidic woodland gardens with patience, spreading slowly by stolons. A charming and unusual ground cover for the serious native plant gardener in cold climates.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly after last frost in prepared, weed-free soil at a light 1/4-inch depth; sideoats grama establishes well from seed and is often included in dry prairie and meadow seed mixes.
directions: The state grass of Texas, sideoats grama is a compact, highly drought-tolerant native grass reaching 18–30 inches, distinctive for its arching flower stems bearing small oat-like seed clusters that all hang neatly from one side — a characteristic unique among North American grasses. It excels in hot, dry, rocky, or sandy soils with excellent drainage and full sun, making it among the best choices for difficult xeric sites across the Great Plains, Southwest, and upper South. Foliage is blue-green through summer, turning orange-tan in fall, with the attractive hanging spikelets persisting into winter for subtle seasonal interest. Cut back in late winter to tidy the planting; it is also highly valued for erosion control and restoration seedings on dry slopes and disturbed ground.
