plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring as new growth emerges, or plant container-grown stock in spring or early fall in rich, evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; Siebold's hosta is one of the largest and most imposing hosta species and grows slowly to a massive clump but rarely needs division.
directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; Siebold's hosta performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, or light, dappled shade from deciduous trees. Hosta sieboldiana is the most imposing of all hosta species in size and foliage impact — producing enormous, deeply corrugated, puckered, blue-gray to blue-green leaves that can reach 12–15 inches long and 10–13 inches wide on mature plants, with a velvety, glaucous surface that gives the leaves a distinctive waxy sheen and outstanding slug resistance. The near-white, pale-lavender flowers bloom in June–July on stems just above the leaf mound and are relatively inconspicuous compared to the spectacular foliage. This is a slow-growing but very long-lived hosta that takes several years to achieve its full, majestic clump size — but once established it is essentially maintenance-free and can remain undisturbed for decades. H. sieboldiana is the parent of many of the most famous large-leaved hosta cultivars including 'Frances Williams,' 'Elegans,' and 'Great Expectations.'

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; Siebold's hosta is one of the larger-leafed hostas — allow generous spacing as clumps can eventually reach 4 feet across.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade — Siebold's hosta is one of the most majestic and widely grown of all hosta species, producing enormous, boldly corrugated, glaucous blue-green to blue-gray leaves up to 18 inches long that give the shade garden a dramatic, tropical-foliage effect. The sluggish pale lavender flowers on low, barely-visible scapes in early summer are secondary to the spectacular foliage. Famous cultivars derived from this species include 'Elegans' (intensely blue, deeply corrugated), 'Frances Williams' (blue with gold-green margins), and 'Big Daddy' (deeply puckered, intensely blue). The waxy, powder-coated leaf surface repels water and resists slug damage somewhat better than thin-leaved hostas. While this species is at its finest in cool-climate zone 4–7 gardens, it grows adequately in zone 8 in deep shade with consistent moisture and limited afternoon sun exposure.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta sieboldii is one of the smaller-growing true hosta species — a parent of many modern landscape hosta cultivars. Spreads by offsets to form clumps.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta sieboldii is a smaller-leaved, lance-leafed Japanese hosta species with characteristic narrowly-edged creamy-white margins on its dark green, wavy-margined leaves — one of the most distinctive and charming of the species hostas, parent of many white-margined cultivars in the modern hosta trade. The lavender flower scapes rise above the foliage in midsummer, topped with funnel-shaped, lightly fragrant flowers. More heat-tolerant than some hostas, making it a good choice for southern gardens in zones 7–9. The white-edged foliage remains attractive even in light shade conditions. A good parent species for understanding the range of hosta diversity — more grass-like and delicate than the massive blue-leaved Siebold hostas. Multiplies readily into clumps that can be divided every 3–4 years for propagation.

plant_note: Plant container or balled shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Siebold's viburnum tolerates the light shade of a woodland margin better than many large flowering shrubs and grows into a substantial small tree over time.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Siebold's viburnum is a large, handsome, tree-like viburnum from Japan with bold, deep-green, leathery leaves and, in late spring, dense, rounded clusters of creamy-white flowers with a distinctive, somewhat pungent fragrance that carries on the air. The real show follows in late summer as the fruit clusters ripen through a striking sequence from green to pink to bright red and finally glossy black, all held on showy, persistent, contrasting red stalks (pedicels) that remain colorful even after the birds strip the berries. Give it room to grow, since with age it develops into a substantial small tree well suited to the back of a shrub border, a woodland margin, or as a specimen with high, filtered shade from taller trees overhead. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood; the naturally handsome, layered branching habit needs little shaping. A tough, long-lived, four-season shrub for a partly shaded spot with room to spare.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siebold's wood fern is slow to establish and slow to spread, so allow it a couple of seasons to settle in before expecting a full, mature clump.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siebold's wood fern is slow to establish and slow to spread, so allow it a couple of seasons to settle in before expecting a full, mature clump. Dryopteris sieboldii is an unusual East Asian fern that looks nothing like a typical feathery fern — its stiff, leathery, evergreen fronds are divided into just a few broad, undivided, strap-like leaflets radiating from the frond tip, giving the whole plant a bold, almost palm-like texture. This coarse, architectural form makes it a striking textural contrast to lacy ferns like maidenhair or Japanese painted fern in a shaded border or fern collection, and its thick, leathery fronds are notably more drought- and heat-tolerant than most woodland ferns once established. It spreads slowly to form a tidy clump and needs little maintenance beyond removing any winter-damaged fronds in early spring.

common_name: Sierra Linda Autumn Sage (Compact Coral-Red Salvia greggii)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; performs best with lean soil and minimal supplemental irrigation once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Sierra Linda is a compact, bushy Salvia greggii selection bred for a denser, more uniform mounding habit than the straight species, producing vivid coral-red, two-lipped flowers in continuous flushes from spring through hard frost. Its smaller, tidier scale suits foundation plantings, border edges, and mass plantings where a very drought-tolerant, long-blooming Texas native is wanted without the looser, more open growth of older Salvia greggii selections. It draws hummingbirds and native bees throughout its long bloom season; cut back hard to 6–8 inches in late winter to promote fresh, dense growth and abundant spring flowering, and shear lightly after each bloom flush to keep production continuous.

common_name: Sikes Dwarf Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact Oakleaf Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Sikes Dwarf is the most compact of the commonly available oakleaf hydrangea cultivars — staying 3–4 feet tall, half the size of the standard species.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sikes Dwarf is a compact oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia) selected for its smaller, more manageable size — reaching 3–4 feet tall and wide — compared to the standard oakleaf hydrangea species that can grow 6–8 feet. Like the species, Sikes Dwarf has all the outstanding multi-season qualities that make oakleaf hydrangea the finest native flowering shrub for the Gulf South: conical white flower panicles from June through August that dry to tan-parchment and persist ornamentally through winter; large, distinctive oak-shaped leaves with outstanding reddish-purple to burgundy fall color; attractive cinnamon-orange peeling bark for winter interest; and excellent adaptation to the heat, humidity, clay soils, and partial to full shade of Gulf South gardens. Oakleaf hydrangea is native to the southeastern United States, making it perfectly adapted to zone 9 conditions without the special care that exotic hydrangea species may require. In deep shade (3 hours or less of sun), it flowers less but still provides outstanding foliage, bark, and fall color. The compact size makes Sikes Dwarf suitable for foundation plantings, shade borders, and garden positions where the full-size species would be too large.

plant_note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a stream or pond margin in partial shade in spring; Sikkim cowslip is closely related to Primula florindae and shares its need for permanently damp soil.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently wet, humus-rich soil at a stream, pond, or bog margin in partial shade in spring. Primula sikkimensis is native to alpine meadows and stream banks of the eastern Himalayas, producing an upright stem topped with a nodding cluster of fragrant, pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers coated with a fine white mealy powder in early summer, blooming somewhat earlier than its close relative the giant Himalayan cowslip. Its fragrant, softly colored flowers and preference for reliably damp ground make it a good companion for candelabra primroses and moisture-loving ferns in a shaded bog garden or the damp margin of a woodland pond.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cut back to a few inches before new growth emerges in spring.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. One of the oldest and most influential Miscanthus sinensis cultivars in the trade, Silberfeder forms a large upright-arching clump of narrow green leaves topped in late summer by tall, airy plumes that open sparkling pinkish-silver and mature to shining silvery-white by fall. It is among the tallest garden-scale maiden grasses, often reaching 7 to 8 feet in flower, making it best suited to large borders, screens, or specimen use rather than small beds. The foliage turns a soft wheat tone in autumn and the seed heads remain attractive and structurally sound through much of winter.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in extremely well-drained, infertile, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Silk Bay will quickly decline in heavy, wet, or overly fertile soils. It is highly susceptible to laurel wilt disease spread by the redbay ambrosia beetle — plant in isolated or protected settings.
directions: Silk Bay is a Florida endemic member of the laurel family, native to the ancient, fire-maintained scrub habitats of the central and southern Florida peninsula, where it grows in pure white sand alongside Scrub Hickory, Florida Rosemary, and scrub oaks in conditions of extreme infertility and drainage. The leaves are smaller and silkier than those of the closely related Red Bay and Swamp Bay, with a distinctive silky pubescence on the undersides; small, dark blue-black drupes produced in summer and fall provide important food for Florida Scrub-Jays, fish crows, and migratory songbirds. Like all native bays in the genus Persea, Silk Bay is highly susceptible to laurel wilt disease, an exotic fungal pathogen spread by the redbay ambrosia beetle that has devastated native bay populations across the Southeast. Plant in extremely well-drained, infertile, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; this species demands perfect drainage and will quickly decline in heavy, wet, irrigated, or highly amended soils.

common_name: Silk Floss Tree (Palo Borracho, Pink Floss Silk Tree, Ceiba speciosa)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Ceiba speciosa grows rapidly in zone 9-10 and is surprisingly cold-tolerant for a tropical-looking tree — established specimens survive temperatures to 25°F with damage to young growth. The trunk is typically covered with large, sharp conical spines, especially on young trees (the spines may diminish on older trunks). In zone 9-10, the tree typically drops its leaves in fall just before the spectacular pink bloom flush. The large seed pods release abundant white silky floss in late winter.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Silk Floss Tree is drought-tolerant once established and resents waterlogged conditions. Ceiba speciosa (formerly Chorisia speciosa) is a large, fast-growing ornamental tree native to the Gran Chaco and Atlantic Forest regions of South America (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay) in the family Malvaceae (the mallow family, which also includes Hibiscus and cotton). The tree is immediately identifiable at any age by its green to gray-green trunk studded with large, conical, bottle-shaped spines that cover the bark from ground to canopy — the spines function as water-storage adaptations during the dry season of its native habitat and create a sculptural, primeval appearance. In fall (October–November in zone 9), after the leaves have dropped, the bare, spiny branches produce an extraordinary display of large (4–6 inch), 5-petaled flowers in shades of bright pink to rose-magenta with a white and yellow-streaked center — a bloom so striking on leafless branches that the tree resembles a pink-flowering cloud when viewed from a distance. The large, oval seed pods that follow split open in late winter to release abundant silky white floss that carries the seeds on the wind. Established trees are impressively cold-tolerant — a remarkable quality in a tree with so tropical an appearance.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; silk tassel bush is native to the fog-belt coastal chaparral of central and northern California and performs best in cool, moist coastal climates with dry summers. It establishes poorly from transplants in summer heat and drought. The cultivar 'James Roof' produces the longest catkins — up to 14 inches.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; silk tassel bush is a California native evergreen shrub or small tree producing some of the most dramatic winter catkins of any temperate plant — long, silky, pale gray-green to silver catkins that hang in cascading clusters from the branch tips of male plants from December through February, swaying in the winter wind and creating an arresting spectacle during the garden's emptiest period. On the male cultivar 'James Roof' (the most widely grown), these catkins can reach 14 inches long and are present in such abundance that the entire shrub seems draped with silver-gray fringe. Female plants produce grape-like clusters of purple berries if a male pollinator is nearby. The foliage is leathery, wavy-edged, and deep glossy green with woolly gray undersides, giving the shrub excellent texture year-round. Drought-tolerant once established and native to coastal California chaparral and mixed evergreen forest, it thrives in mild climates but resents excessive summer irrigation. An outstanding specimen for dry gardens, woodland edges, and shrub borders where winter interest is most needed.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun; silky aster is adapted to poor, gravelly, or sandy prairie soil and performs best without extra fertility or moisture, which encourage floppy growth.
directions: Plant in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun; highly drought-tolerant once established and prone to flopping or declining in overly rich or moist soil. Silky aster is a compact native prairie perennial named for the fine, silvery, silky hairs that densely cover its narrow gray-green leaves, giving the whole plant a soft, shimmering appearance that stands out from other fall-blooming asters. In late summer and fall, the wiry stems are covered in a profusion of small, vivid violet-purple, gold-centered flowers that make an excellent late-season nectar source for native bees and migrating monarch butterflies. Its diminutive size and drought tolerance make it a good choice for the front of a dry, sunny prairie planting, rock garden, or gravel bed where richer soil would cause taller, floppier asters to sprawl. Zone 3–8.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. Silky Camellia is slow to establish and resents transplanting; choose the permanent location carefully and amend the soil deeply before planting.
directions: Silky Camellia is widely regarded as one of the most beautiful native shrubs in North America, native to moist, acidic forest understories from Virginia and Tennessee south to Florida and west to Arkansas and Texas, where it blooms in May through July with large, pure white, five-petaled flowers featuring a central boss of deep bluish-purple filaments with yellow anthers — a combination found nowhere else in the native flora and reminiscent of a Japanese camellia. The flowers open sequentially over several weeks and are followed by attractive woody capsules; the fall foliage turns shades of orange and scarlet. Despite its beauty, Silky Camellia is notoriously slow-growing and slow to establish, taking many years to reach blooming size and resenting transplanting once established — but gardeners who invest the time and proper siting conditions are rewarded with a genuinely spectacular flowering shrub. Provide moist, deeply amended, acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; mulch heavily and water regularly during the first several years.

common_name: Silky Oak (Australian Silver Oak, Fern-Leaf Grevillea)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; silky oak is a spectacular Australian native tree with deeply-cut, fern-like, silver-green foliage and brilliant orange-yellow brush flowers — it grows rapidly to 60–80 feet and is widely used as a street tree in zone 8–11 throughout Florida, California, South Africa, and India.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; silky oak is drought-tolerant and fast-growing — site with ample space. Grevillea robusta (silky oak or Australian silver oak) is a large, fast-growing Australian native tree from the subtropical rainforests of Queensland and New South Wales — one of the most widely planted and recognizable Australian trees in subtropical and warm-temperate regions worldwide. The tree produces extraordinarily beautiful, deeply pinnate to bi-pinnate, fern-like leaves with a silver-silky underside (the 'silky' in the name) that create a delicate, lacy, architectural texture rare in a tree of this size. In spring, the tree is covered with striking, elongated clusters of golden-orange to rusty-orange 'brush' flowers (each a typical Proteaceae flower with a long, curling style) that attract bees, butterflies, and in Australia, honeyeaters. In the US, silky oak is used as a street tree and large specimen in zone 8–11 Florida and California, where it grows rapidly to 50–80 feet. In India, silky oak is one of the most commonly planted shade trees on tea plantations, providing canopy shade for tea bushes (and its wood is the traditional material for Indian furniture in colonial-era designs). It tolerates lean, acidic soils and drought once established — very low maintenance once past establishment. CAUTION: Contact dermatitis reported in some individuals from handling leaves or wood.

plant_note: Scarify or cold-stratify seeds before fall direct sowing into sandy, dry soil in full sun.
directions: Silky Prairie Clover is a showstopping Great Plains native covered in silky white hairs that give the whole plant a silvery-gray sheen, topped in summer with dense cylindrical spikes of vivid rose-pink to magenta flowers with prominent orange anthers. Sow seeds directly in fall into loose, sandy, very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; seeds benefit from scarification or a brief cold-moist stratification period before planting. Once established, the deep root system makes this plant highly drought-tolerant and long-lived. It is an outstanding specialist bee plant rarely available commercially but invaluable in authentic Great Plains prairie restorations.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors or direct sow in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; silky-spike melic thrives on poor, dry soils and develops floppy, weak growth if the soil is too rich or moist.
directions: Start transplants indoors or direct sow in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; silky-spike melic thrives on poor, dry soils and develops floppy, weak growth if the soil is too rich or moist. Narrow, blue-green foliage forms a tidy clump topped in early summer by dense, cylindrical, silvery-white flower spikes covered in silky hairs that catch the light and sway with the slightest breeze, aging to a soft buff tan that persists into fall. Native to dry, rocky, calcareous slopes across central and southern Europe, it is a well-mannered, non-spreading clumper ideal for a gravel garden, rock garden, or dry border where taller grasses would overwhelm smaller companions. Cut the previous season's foliage back hard in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Siloam Double Classic Daylily (Ruffled Double Pink Miniature Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Siloam Double Classic is part of the celebrated Siloam series of small-flowered daylilies bred by Pauline Henry, producing fully double, ruffled pink blooms on a compact plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Siloam Double Classic is part of the renowned Siloam series of miniature and small-flowered daylilies bred by Pauline Henry of Siloam Springs, Arkansas, whose decades of breeding work produced some of the most refined small-flowered daylily cultivars available. Siloam Double Classic bears fully double, ruffled, rose-pink flowers with a deeper pink eye zone, on a compact plant well suited to smaller gardens, edging, and mass plantings where full-sized daylilies would be too large. Like other daylilies it is easy to grow in average soil with routine watering and tolerates heat well. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Siloam June Bug Daylily (Chartreuse-Green Siloam Series Daylily)
plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or fall; set crowns just 1 in below soil level in full sun to light afternoon shade.
directions: Plant fans with the crown about 1 in deep, spreading roots outward over a small mound of soil in the hole, and water thoroughly to settle the soil. Part of the celebrated Siloam breeding line developed by Pauline Henry, Siloam June Bug bears unusual chartreuse-green flowers with a deeper green throat, a color rarely seen in daylilies and one that reads almost lime-yellow in bright light, on a compact, dwarf-scale plant. Its small stature and unusual color make it a distinctive accent in a mixed border or collector's daylily bed, standing apart from the more common pink, red, and gold Siloam introductions. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to alkaline, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; silver beardgrass grows naturally on dry, rocky prairies, limestone outcrops, and dry hillsides across the south-central US. Drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, slightly acidic to neutral or alkaline, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; silver beardgrass is a native grass of dry prairies, limestone outcrops, and rocky hillsides across the south-central United States, particularly abundant on dry, calcareous soils of the Edwards Plateau and Texas Hill Country. The plant produces an unusually showy display for a grass — the seed heads are covered in long, bright white hairs that create a shimmering silver effect across the entire upper portion of the plant in summer, making it appear as if the grass is in bloom with silver flowers. The effect is particularly dramatic when mass planted or when backlit by afternoon sun. Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established; thrives in the limestone-derived, thin, rocky soils typical of Texas rangelands. An outstanding ornamental native grass for dry, sunny gardens and prairies in zones 5–10.

common_name: Silver Bells Browallia (White-Flowered Bush Violet for Shade)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Silver Bells bears pure white flowers, a bright counterpart to the blue-toned Browallia cultivars more commonly grown.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, watering regularly to keep soil consistently moist. Silver Bells bears an abundance of star-shaped, pure white flowers on a compact, mounding plant, a bright, clean color option among browallia cultivars that are more typically bred in shades of blue and violet, brightening dark corners of the shade garden or a shaded container planting. It blooms continuously from planting through frost without deadheading, tolerating heat and humidity well, and is one of the true shade-loving flowering annuals, performing better in shade than in full sun where the foliage can scorch. Treat as a warm-season annual outside its tender perennial zone range, and pinch stems occasionally to encourage a fuller, bushier habit.

plant_note: Divide established clumps immediately after flowering or in early fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Silver Bouquet is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction bred by Janet Egger, noted for good mildew resistance and heat tolerance that suits it to Southern shade gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Silver Bouquet bears slender, narrow, almost entirely silver leaves that give it a more delicate, refined texture than broader-leaved lungwort cultivars, while still lighting up a dark shade bed effectively. Coral-pink, funnel-shaped flowers appear in early spring, opening before the foliage reaches full size and providing early-season color alongside daffodils and hellebores. It has been noted for good resistance to powdery mildew and better heat tolerance than many older lungwort selections, an advantage in a humid Gulf South summer. Keep soil consistently moist, since dry shade quickly causes lungworts to wilt and decline, and divide congested clumps after flowering.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Silver Bract pachyphytum holds its powdery silver coating best when kept dry and undisturbed.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Silver Bract pachyphytum holds its powdery silver coating best when kept dry and undisturbed. Thick, plump, oval leaves coated in a heavy, chalky, silvery-white powder are stacked densely at the tips of thick, upright-then-trailing stems, one of the more substantial pachyphytum species with larger leaves than the related and often-confused moonstones cultivars, producing red-and-white bell-shaped flowers on tall stalks in season. Native to rocky slopes in Mexico, it is easy to grow and propagate, though the delicate powdery coating rubs off easily with handling and should be protected to preserve the plant's silvery appearance. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid touching or wetting the leaves to protect the powdery bloom, and propagate from stem or leaf cuttings.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown plants in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; silver bush requires excellent drainage — poorly drained or wet soil causes root rot and death. It is one of the most drought-tolerant garden shrubs and requires little to no water once established in appropriate conditions.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; silver bush is a compact Mediterranean shrub of the bindweed family prized for its outstanding foliage — small, narrow, lance-shaped leaves so densely covered with fine, silky, silver hairs that the entire plant appears to be fashioned from spun silver, creating a brilliant, luminous effect in the hot, sunny garden. From spring through summer it produces successive flushes of typical bindweed-shaped flowers, each a pure white funnel with a faint pink exterior, emerging from distinctly pinkish buds and opening into clean white — the contrast of the metallic silver foliage and snow-white flowers being extraordinary. A Mediterranean cliff and limestone plant from rocky coastal scrub, it requires the same lean, dry, well-drained, sunny conditions as lavender and rosemary and performs best with no summer irrigation in appropriate climates. Outstanding in combination with other silver-leafed and drought-tolerant Mediterranean plants in water-wise gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky coastal soil in full sun; silver buttonwood grows naturally in coastal strand, mangrove fringes, and rocky coastal hammock of south Florida and the Caribbean, highly tolerant of salt spray, wind, and drought.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky coastal soil in full sun; silver buttonwood is a variety of buttonwood (Conocarpus erectus) distinguished by its striking silvery-gray foliage — the leaves are covered with fine, silky, silver-gray hairs (sericeus = silky) that give the entire plant a luminous, metallic quality unlike any other coastal plant. An outstanding ornamental for coastal landscapes in zone 10–11, it provides year-round silver foliage color with outstanding resistance to salt spray, drought, wind, and shallow rocky soils. Extremely tolerant of coastal exposure and one of the most salt-tolerant broadleaf trees for South Florida coastal plantings. Widely used as a coastal hedge, specimen shrub, or small tree in South Florida landscaping. The small, rounded flower clusters and button-like fruiting heads give the buttonwoods their common name. A native of coastal hammocks and mangrove transitions.

plant_note: Install nursery plugs or divisions in spring on eight to twelve inch centers into fast-draining soil, watering regularly the first several months until the mat knits together.
directions: Install nursery plugs or divisions in spring on eight to twelve inch centers into fast-draining soil, watering regularly the first several months until the felted gray-green foliage knits together into a tight, walkable mat. It is one of the best true no-mow lawn substitutes for mild, dry climates and fills beautifully between stepping stones, where its tiny yellow daisies appear along the leaf margins in summer. Once established it tolerates foot traffic and extended drought, but it is not reliably cold hardy below the mid-teens Fahrenheit, so it is mainly suited to zones 8-11.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Silver Chimes is a multi-flowered tazetta/triandrus hybrid daffodil that performs well and reblooms reliably in the mild winters typical of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Silver Chimes bears clusters of three to six dainty, nodding, sweetly fragrant flowers per stem, white petals with a soft pale yellow cup, combining traits from its tazetta and triandrus parentage into a graceful, late-blooming daffodil well suited to mild-winter climates where it perennializes more reliably than many large trumpet daffodils bred for colder regions. Its multi-flowered habit and light, airy form make it a lovely addition to naturalized plantings as well as cut flower arrangements. Allow the foliage to die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

common_name: Silver Cloud Philodendron (Quilted Silver Leaf Philodendron, Mamei Philodendron)
plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or a chunky aroid mix; Philodendron mamei is a creeping, terrestrial-to-climbing philodendron that produces its most dramatic foliage in warm, humid, shaded conditions. The large leaves (12–24 inches) have a distinctly quilted, puckered surface texture between the lateral veins, with irregular silver-gray blotches on a dark green background — the 'Silver Cloud' pattern for which it is named. Grows best when allowed to creep and self-head along the ground or climb low onto a rough surface. Protect from temperatures below 55°F. CAUTION: all Philodendron parts contain calcium oxalate; toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil — Silver Cloud Philodendron produces its most dramatic, large-leaved, heavily silvered foliage in the warm, moist shade conditions of a protected tropical garden or sheltered indoor space in zone 10-12. Philodendron mamei is a crawling, self-heading to low-climbing, terrestrial philodendron in the Araceae family native to Ecuador and Peru, belonging to the diverse subgenus Meconostigma within Philodendron (the same group as Philodendron bipinnatifidum and P. selloum). Unlike the more familiar climbing philodendrons, P. mamei is primarily a creeping, ground-hugging plant that spreads by elongating stems close to the ground surface rather than aggressively climbing. The leaves are the plant's primary ornamental feature: large, broadly heart-shaped to ovate, 12–24 inches long, in dark, lustrous, forest-green with irregular silver-gray blotches scattered across the surface in a cloud-like, unpredictable pattern — the 'silver cloud' effect that gives the plant its popular name. The leaf surface between the lateral veins has a pronounced quilted, puckered texture, creating a tactile three-dimensionality unusual in philodendrons. The cataphylls (leaf sheaths) are a distinctive light green. Philodendron mamei grows moderately fast in warm conditions and remains manageable in size, making it appropriate for collectors' shade gardens, covered terraces, and shaded container plantings in zone 10-12. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.

plant_note: Divide corms or separate offsets in spring, or plant container-grown specimens in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade after frost; silver cloud taro is more shade-tolerant than most colocasias and performs better in deep shade with consistent moisture than in full sun, where the silvery leaf markings may bleach.
directions: Divide corms or plant container specimens in moist to wet, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade; silver cloud taro is a smaller, more refined, and more shade-tolerant Colocasia species from Southeast Asia — unlike the bold, large-scale giant taros (C. esculenta, C. gigantea), this species produces compact, 18–30-inch plants with relatively smaller but more ornately marked leaves, each heart-shaped, dark-green leaf decorated with a distinctive, broad, silvery-gray to silver-white zone in the center of the leaf surface that fades to dark-green at the margins — creating a soft, clouded, misty silvery-green effect that justifies its cultivar name 'Silver Cloud'. The silvery leaf marking is unique among colocasias and creates a quieter, more refined tropical foliage effect than the large, plain green forms. It grows best in consistently moist to wet soil in partial to full shade, where the silvery marking is most pronounced. More cold-tolerant than most colocasias (to approximately 20°F in zone 8 with protection). Excellent in shaded water gardens, bog gardens, and as a refined shade groundcover under large trees in zone 8–12.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; silver dollar gum is fast-growing and may require pruning to maintain as a shrub rather than a large tree. In zone 9 it can reach 25–40 feet but is most commonly grown and coppiced as a large shrub for foliage production. The round, silver-blue juvenile leaves (the 'silver dollars') are the primary ornamental feature and are highly valued as cut foliage; adult leaves are narrower and less ornamental.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; silver dollar gum is one of the most widely grown and commercially important ornamental eucalyptus species in warm-climate horticulture — prized almost exclusively for the extraordinary beauty of its juvenile foliage. The juvenile leaves of E. cinerea are perfectly circular to nearly circular, stalkless (clasping the stem), and a beautiful, soft, silver-blue to gray-blue color, arranged in opposite pairs that create a precise, architectural pattern of round blue-silver coins along the young stems — the 'silver dollars' of the common name. These round, blue-silver juvenile leaves are the standard cut-foliage 'gum leaf' used worldwide in floral arrangements, wedding floristry, and decorative foliage, exported in massive quantities from Australian and California eucalyptus plantations. The foliage is aromatic — the eucalyptus oil in the leaves releasing the characteristic refreshing, camphor-eucalyptus scent when crushed. To maintain juvenile foliage (which is the entire ornamental point), the tree can be coppiced (cut to the ground) every few years, stimulating the continuous production of young, round-leaved growth. As a zone 9 garden tree it provides outstanding silver foliage and drought tolerance; as a coppiced cut-foliage plant it provides continuous stem material for floristry.

plant_note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; silver dollar jade is slow-growing and eventually forms a small, gnarled, tree-like trunk, so container culture with occasional repotting into a slightly larger pot suits it well.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the soil dry between waterings. Crassula arborescens (silver dollar jade, silver jade plant) is a South African relative of the common jade plant, distinguished by larger, nearly circular, powdery blue-grey leaves edged in red that intensifies with bright light and cooler temperatures. It grows more slowly and stays more compact for longer than Crassula ovata, but over years develops a similar thick, woody, tree-like trunk and can be trained as a striking succulent bonsai in a shallow container. Propagate from stem or leaf cuttings allowed to callus for a day or two before rooting in dry succulent mix; established plants tolerate brief dry spells well but are quick to rot if left in soggy soil, especially in winter. Small pale-pink, star-shaped flower clusters may appear in late winter on mature specimens grown in strong light.

common_name: Silver Edge Siberian Iris (Picotee-Edged Blue-Violet Iris)
plant_note: Plant divisions in late summer or early fall in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil; Silver Edge is a 1992 Siberian iris cultivar valued for its fine picotee edging, an unusual trait in this species.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in full sun to light shade, unlike bearded iris this species tolerates and even prefers soil that stays consistently damp. Introduced in 1992, Silver Edge is a Siberian iris prized for its fine white picotee edging around each violet-blue fall, a delicate contrast trait that is unusual in this typically solid-colored species. The narrow, grass-like foliage forms neat clumps that need no staking and hold up well through summer and fall as a textural border element long after bloom finishes in late spring. Unlike bearded iris it has no bare rhizome to rot in wet soil, making it a good choice for rain gardens or the moist edge of a pond; divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer.

common_name: Silver Falls Fern (Cascading Silvery Painted Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Silver Falls produces heavily silvered fronds with a soft, arching, slightly weeping habit that cascades gracefully over its own crown, deep burgundy-red stems providing strong color contrast against the pale silver-gray frond color. Its arching, flowing form suits it well to the edge of a raised bed, container, or rock garden where the cascading fronds can drape over an edge, in addition to standard use in a shaded border alongside hostas and heucheras. Cut back old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Silver Heart Brunnera (Silver Heart Siberian Bugloss)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system evenly cool and moist.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system evenly cool and moist. Silver Heart carries broad, heart-shaped leaves that are almost entirely silvered, interrupted only by fine dark-green veining, giving it one of the brightest all-silver effects among brunnera cultivars, topped in early spring by sprays of small sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers. It forms a tidy, non-invasive clump that lights up a dim woodland corner from spring through frost. Established plantings rarely need division and tolerate deep shade better than most variegated shade perennials.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; silver king artemisia spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes and should be sited where its spreading habit can be contained or accommodated.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; silver king artemisia is a native North American prairie and plains plant grown for its exceptionally bright, woolly-silver, aromatic foliage that is among the most useful and effective silver foliage plants in the temperate garden — the upright, wand-like stems and broadly lance-shaped silver-white leaves create a luminous, light-gathering effect in borders that is especially effective in the evening. The plant is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in hot, dry, alkaline conditions. It spreads by underground rhizomes to form large colonies; divide every 2–3 years in spring to maintain vigor and control spread. Excellent as a foil for richly colored flowers and for cutting and drying. 'Silver Queen' (broader leaves, more compact) and 'Valerie Finnis' (bright silver, outstanding form) are fine named selections.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in shade; silver lace fern is excellent in sheltered, frost-free positions in zones 9-12, or in containers brought indoors in winter in colder zones.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade to bright indirect light; silver lace fern is one of the most ornamental small ferns available, with intricate fronds where each leaflet is dramatically marked with a broad central stripe of silvery white against dark green margins. The cultivar Victoriae has an especially bold silver central band. Grows to 10-18 inches and makes an excellent groundcover for deeply shaded spots or a container specimen. In zone 9, grow in a sheltered, frost-protected position or in a container moved indoors below 32°F. Native to tropical and subtropical Asia and the Pacific.

common_name: Silver Lace Vine (Russian Vine, Mile-a-Minute Vine)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; silver lace vine is extremely vigorous — plant ONLY where you intend to allow its aggressive growth, as it can quickly overwhelm structures and neighboring plants. It is listed as invasive in some areas.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; silver lace vine (Russian vine, or 'mile-a-minute' vine for its extraordinary growth rate — up to 15 feet per year) is one of the fastest-growing hardy vines available, capable of covering an entire structure, fence, or wall in a single growing season with dense, twining stems. In late summer and early autumn it produces masses of tiny white to pinkish-white flowers in enormous, frothy plumes covering the entire vine — creating one of the most spectacular displays of any vine in bloom, resembling a cloud of white foam or lace. Native to central Asia (Tajikistan and Afghanistan). Despite its aggressive growth, the vine dies completely to the ground in cold winters, making management easier in zones 4–6 than in milder climates where it may remain semi-evergreen. Valuable for quickly covering unsightly fences, walls, and structures where nothing else would grow fast enough. Do not plant near delicate or small plants it might overwhelm. Potentially invasive — check local status.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade after frost; silver lady fern is sensitive to both drought and standing water — maintain even moisture and excellent drainage simultaneously with organic mulch.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; silver lady fern (dwarf tree fern) is a Pacific Island native that is one of the most architecturally impressive of the smaller tropical ferns — it develops a short, stout, fibrous trunk topped by an elegant crown of spreading, once-pinnate, ladder-like fronds with smooth, glossy, dark-green pinnae that give the plant a clean, refined, almost tropical prehistoric quality. As the plant matures it resembles a miniature tree fern, with the arching crown of fronds rising from an increasingly taller fibrous stem, eventually reaching 3–4 feet in height with an elegant, sculptural silhouette distinctly different from the bushier, non-trunked appearance of most ferns. An excellent specimen fern for shaded tropical gardens, container plantings, and indoor bright-shade locations. More tolerant of dry indoor air than many tropical ferns. In zone 9, protect from frost — the crown is the most vulnerable part. 'Silver Lady' is the standard cultivar widely grown.

common_name: Silver Leaf Philodendron (Brandt's Philodendron, Olive Leaf Philodendron)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Philodendron brandtianum cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. It grows well in a hanging basket as a trailing vine or can be trained up a moss pole to produce progressively larger leaves. Provide a well-draining potting mix with added orchid bark and perlite. Water thoroughly and allow the top inch to dry between waterings. Propagate readily from single-node stem cuttings in water or moist mix. All parts are toxic if chewed.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Silver Leaf Philodendron is adaptable to lower light levels than many collector philodendrons but produces its best growth and most vibrant silver leaf coloration with consistent bright indirect light. Philodendron brandtianum is a climbing philodendron from Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, and Peru, valued for its distinctive and unusually colored foliage: the heart-shaped to oval leaves emerge in shades of rich olive-bronze and mature to a striking combination of grayish-green base color overlaid with irregular patches and blotches of silver and pale gray, creating an iridescent, metallic quality in the leaf that is unusual among philodendrons. The contrast between the olive-toned base and the silvery markings is most visible in raking or indirect light and varies somewhat depending on growing conditions. The leaves are smaller than many philodendrons (typically 4–8 inches), giving the plant a neater, more compact form well-suited to hanging baskets and medium-sized containers. New leaves emerge on vivid red-pink petioles that fade to green as the leaf matures, adding further ornamental interest. Philodendron brandtianum is generally regarded as more adaptable and easier to grow than most collector aroids, tolerating imperfect humidity and temperature fluctuation with less damage to its appearance than the demanding velvet types. All parts toxic due to calcium oxalate.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to neutral or slightly acidic, fertile to average, deep loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; silver linden is the most drought- and heat-tolerant of the lindens, native to southeastern Europe where summers are hot and dry. More suitable for urban conditions than other lindens.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to neutral or slightly acidic, fertile to average, deep loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; silver linden is distinguished from other lindens by the distinctive silver-white felt of dense, soft hairs on the undersides of the dark green leaves — when a breeze stirs the canopy, the alternating flash of dark green upper surfaces and brilliant silver-white undersides creates a shimmering, sparkling effect quite unlike any other tree. The heavily fragrant, creamy-white flowers in summer are powerfully honeyed and sweet — the flowers are harvested for linden flower tea (tilleul) across European countries, used as a relaxing, mildly sedative herbal remedy. The most heat- and drought-tolerant of the European lindens — surviving hot, dry summers in southeastern Europe better than other linden species. More adaptable to urban conditions (heat, air pollution, drought) than American basswood or littleleaf linden. An excellent street and shade tree where its large scale is appropriate. The silver leaf underside display when windblown is one of the finest effects of any ornamental tree.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, deep soil in full sun to partial shade; Silver Maple is most appropriately planted near permanent water features, in rain gardens, or in low-lying, wet areas where its moisture requirement is naturally met. Avoid planting near sewer lines or foundations — the roots are aggressive in seeking moisture.
directions: Silver Maple is the fastest-growing of the native maples, native to the streambanks, bottomlands, and moist lowlands of eastern North America from New Brunswick to Florida and west to the Dakotas, producing a new flush of growth each season that can exceed 3 feet per year in rich, moist alluvial soil. It is among the first native trees to bloom in late winter (February–March), producing clusters of tiny red flowers on bare branches that are one of the most important early pollen and nectar sources of the year for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. The leaves are deeply lobed with silvery-white undersides that shimmer and flash in the breeze, creating a beautiful display in summer wind storms; fall color is modest — pale yellow to orange. The wood is softer and weaker than other maples and Silver Maple is prone to branch breakage in ice storms, making maintenance planning important; it is most appropriate for wet, low-lying sites near water where its moisture tolerance, fast growth, and wildlife value are assets. Keep away from foundations and sewer lines.

common_name: Silver Monstera (Siltepecana Monstera, El Salvador Monstera)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Monstera siltepecana cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Provide a moss pole, coco coir totem, or other rough climbing surface — the plant produces dramatically larger, more fenestrated leaves when allowed to climb upward, a phenomenon called 'juvenile vs. adult form' dimorphism that is extreme in this species. In the trailing or hanging basket form, the leaves remain in the small, silver-marked juvenile stage. Propagate from stem cuttings with at least one node and aerial root.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Silver Monstera is more tolerant of lower light than Monstera deliciosa but produces its best growth and most dramatic leaf size with consistent bright indirect light. Monstera siltepecana is a small-to-medium Monstera species native to southern Mexico (Chiapas, hence 'siltepecana' from the Siltepec region) south through Central America to El Salvador, producing one of the most striking examples of heterophylly (dramatic leaf-form difference between juvenile and adult stages) in the Araceae family. In the juvenile or trailing phase, the plant produces small (3–5 inch), elongated leaves with a distinctive silver or gray-blue metallic sheen overlaid on the dark green surface — silvery markings between the lateral veins that create an unmistakable iridescent effect, giving the species its common name 'Silver Monstera.' When provided a vertical climbing support and allowed to mature, the same plant produces dramatically larger adult leaves (12–24 inches) that develop fenestrations (holes) and lose the juvenile silver coloration entirely — a transformation so complete that juvenile and adult forms were historically treated as separate species. The juvenile silver form is what is sold commercially and is the reason for the plant's popularity. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate.

common_name: Silver Moon Agapanthus (Cream-Edged Variegated Foliage Agapanthus)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Silver Moon is grown as much for its cream-variegated foliage as for its blue flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade helping to prevent leaf scorch on the variegated foliage in the hottest climates. Silver Moon carries strap-shaped leaves edged in creamy white year-round, providing ornamental interest well beyond its summer show of blue flower umbels, making it a good textural accent even out of bloom. Its variegation is most vivid in bright but not scorching light. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; silver mound artemisia absolutely requires excellent drainage and deteriorates rapidly in wet, heavy, or humus-rich soil.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; silver mound artemisia forms an impeccably neat, mound-shaped clump of finely divided, intensely silver-white, silky foliage that serves as the quintessential contrast and edging plant in the mixed perennial border, glowing with particular brightness when planted beside purple or blue flowers. It requires excellent drainage — wet, heavy, or humus-rich soil causes the mound to collapse and rot in summer. Cut back any collapsed or brown sections in late summer after heat stress; the plant resprouts vigorously from the base. Divide every 2–3 years in early spring to maintain the tight, dense mound form. An extremely useful design plant for creating visual coherence and brightness in mixed plantings.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in fall for spring germination, or in early spring; seeds require light to germinate and must not be covered. Silver mullein forms a large, flat basal rosette in year one and sends up a towering flower spike in year two. It self-sows freely in appropriate conditions to maintain a colony. The cultivar Arctic Summer is an improved selection with large, bright-yellow flowers on pure-white woolly stems.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in lean, well-drained, neutral to alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; silver mullein is one of the most visually striking biennials available, distinguished by its extraordinary silver-white woolly texture that covers every surface — leaves, stems, flower buds, and bracts — in a dense layer of fine, silky, white hairs that make the entire plant appear frosted or dipped in silver. In the first year it forms a large, flat, dramatically architectural basal rosette of broadly oval, felted-white leaves that can reach 2 feet across. In the second year, a stout, silvery, candelabra-branched flower spike rises 4-7 feet bearing densely packed, bright-yellow flowers with purple-pink stamens against the silver stems — a striking color contrast. Native to rocky, dry, alkaline slopes of northwestern Turkey, it thrives in very well-drained, lean soils where excess moisture does not cause crown rot. A magnificent structural plant for the dry border, gravel garden, or as a seasonal focal point surrounded by lower-growing perennials.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in zone 10–12; Silver Palm is an elegant, slow-growing Caribbean native fan palm from the Florida Keys, Bahamas, Cuba, and Hispaniola — adapted to alkaline, rocky, coastal limestone soils where few other palms thrive — bearing beautiful, circular, silver-backed fan fronds that shimmer in coastal breezes and small, round, dark-purple, edible berries.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, alkaline to neutral, lean soil — Silver Palm is highly adapted to coastal limestone conditions; avoid clay, overwatering, or organically enriched soil that promotes lush growth at the expense of cold and drought tolerance. Coccothrinax argentata (Silver Palm or Florida Silver Palm) is an elegant, slow-growing, single-trunked fan palm native to the rocky coastal pinelands, hammocks, and scrublands of the Florida Keys, the Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, and other Caribbean islands, where it inhabits the harshest, most exposed coastal limestone environments. The palm is named for the distinctive silvery-white underside of the fan fronds — circular, deeply divided, dark-green above and shimmering silver-white beneath — which catch the light beautifully in coastal breezes, creating a distinctive two-tone shimmer. The small (1/2 inch), round, dark-purple to black berries that follow the small, creamy, fragrant flowers are edible and eaten by birds, and reportedly used in Caribbean folk medicine. Coccothrinax argentata is native to the calcareous, thin, nutrient-poor soils of the Caribbean limestone environment and is extremely well adapted to South Florida's alkaline soils — growing vigorously where many palms suffer from iron deficiency and limestone toxicity. An outstanding accent palm for South Florida and Caribbean gardens, especially in dry, exposed, coastal positions with alkaline soil.

common_name: Silver Plectranthus (Silver Spurflower, Silver Spur Flower)
plant_note: Plant cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in partial shade to full sun; Silver Plectranthus roots quickly from tip cuttings placed in water or moist soil and is one of the easiest tropical plants to propagate. In zone 9, grow as a warm-season annual or container plant that is brought indoors during frost. It grows rapidly and may need pinching to maintain a compact, bushy habit — pinch or cut tip growth every 4–6 weeks during the growing season. Excellent for filling large containers with dramatic silver foliage.
directions: Grow in partial shade to full sun — Silver Plectranthus produces its finest, most silvery foliage color in partial shade, where the iridescent silver hairs on the large, textured leaves catch available light; in full afternoon sun in zone 9 the leaves can become bleached and less attractively colored. Plectranthus argentatus is a large, fast-growing, soft-stemmed tropical shrub from Queensland, Australia, grown for its large (4–6 inch), rounded, deeply veined, heavily silver-pubescent leaves that give the plant an extraordinary metallic silver-gray appearance — one of the most intensely silver-foliaged plants available for the shade garden. The silver effect comes from a dense covering of fine white hairs on all leaf surfaces and stems. In zone 9, it grows as a dramatic warm-season annual that can reach 3–4 feet and fill a large space with its bold silver presence from May through November. In late fall, established plants produce tall spikes of small, white to pale blue flowers that attract bees and butterflies. The combination of large silver leaves, easy culture, and rapid growth makes Silver Plectranthus an outstanding foliage accent for shade gardens, mixed tropical containers, and contrasting with dark or brightly colored neighbors.

plant_note: Direct sow or divide established clumps in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; silver plumegrass grows naturally in moist, open areas, stream banks, and forest margins across the southeastern US.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; silver plumegrass is a native tall grass of the southeastern Coastal Plain producing spectacular, large, feathery, silvery-white plume seed heads in fall that shimmer in the breeze — one of the most ornamentally dramatic of all native grasses. The plumes are produced on tall, robust culms reaching 5–10 feet, creating a bold, upright architectural statement in the late-summer and fall landscape. The silky-silver plumes are as showy as those of ornamental miscanthus but on a native plant that supports native wildlife — the seeds provide food for numerous sparrows and finches, and the dense clumps provide nesting habitat. A superb bold specimen grass for moist roadsides, stream banks, naturalistic borders, and the back of large native plantings in zones 5–9. The plumes persist through winter, providing long-lasting seasonal interest.

common_name: Silver Ponyfoot (Silver Falls Dichondra, Silver Nickel Vine)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist mix or plant container transplants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; silver ponyfoot requires excellent drainage and actually thrives in poor, rocky, dry soils where other groundcovers fail. It is sensitive to overwatering and cold below 25°F.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun; silver ponyfoot (Dichondra argentea) is a stunning silvery native groundcover and container trailing plant, native to dry rocky slopes of south Texas, New Mexico, and Mexico. The small, round, kidney-shaped leaves are densely covered in fine silver hairs that give the plant its brilliant silver color — one of the most intensely silver of any plant, creating a shimmering pool of metallic light in the garden. It is spectacular trailing from containers and hanging baskets, where the silver cascading stems create a waterfall effect. As a groundcover it stays low (2–4 inches) and spreads to cover rocky, dry areas. It thrives in heat and drought, requiring little to no irrigation once established. Excellent for edging, rock gardens, and container combos where its silver tone contrasts beautifully with deep purple or lime-green companions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or bedding transplants in spring after frost danger has passed in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; silver falls dichondra is one of the most effective and dramatic trailing annuals for hanging baskets and container 'spillers,' producing cascading curtains of silver foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; silver falls dichondra is drought-tolerant and more vigorous in warm, dry conditions than in humid, wet ones. Dichondra argentea (silver ponysfoot or Silver Falls dichondra) is a Texas and Mexican native trailing plant producing cascading stems of small (3/4-inch), perfectly round, silver-white, densely hairy leaves that create a spectacular waterfall of shimmering, reflective foliage when allowed to trail from hanging baskets, window boxes, or retaining walls — the 'Silver Falls' selection is grown primarily for this effect. The silver color comes from dense white hairs covering the round, kidney-shaped to circular leaves. Unlike many trailing annuals, Silver Falls is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant, often performing better in dry conditions than in humid, rainy weather (which can cause stem rot). It is one of the most effective annual 'spillers' in container gardening for creating dramatic, flowing, silver curtain effects. The plant's native habitat is the dry rocky slopes and cliffs of the Chihuahuan Desert and Trans-Pecos Texas. In zone 9, it may survive mild winters as a semi-perennial; it dies back in cold but resprouts if roots are protected.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix in bright indirect light to deep shade; silver pothos is one of the most forgiving and adaptable tropical shade vines for indoor and outdoor tropical garden use, tolerating lower light conditions than most variegated tropical plants.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix in bright indirect light to shade; allow the top inch to dry slightly between waterings. Scindapsus pictus (silver pothos or satin pothos) is a Southeast Asian tropical vine prized for its extraordinary leaf texture — heart-shaped, matte-surfaced leaves 4–6 inches long overlaid with an irregular, splashed pattern of silver spots and variegation that has a unique, almost luminous 'satin' quality unlike the shiny surface of true pothos (Epipremnum aureum). The silver spotting pattern varies from light splashing (in 'Argyraeus') to heavy, nearly complete silver covering (in 'Exotica' or 'Silver Splash'). In the wild, the plant climbs large trees in Southeast Asian rainforests, producing larger, more deeply patterned leaves as it ascends toward the canopy. In cultivation, it trails or climbs moderately and adapts well to hanging baskets, climbing poles, and shaded wall coverage in tropical gardens. CAUTION: Like most aroids, silver pothos is toxic to cats and dogs if ingested. It tolerates lower light levels than many tropical vines, making it particularly valuable for deeply shaded interior spaces.

subcategory: weeping ornamental gum with pink-red flowers
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; silver princess is native to the rocky granite outcrops of southwestern Western Australia — it requires excellent drainage and lean, low-phosphorus soil. It blooms in late winter and spring (July–November in Australia). The cultivar 'Silver Princess' (subsp. magna) has larger, deeper-pink to bright-red flowers and is the most ornamental form. The silvery-white powdery bark (the 'caesia' of the species name, meaning blue-gray) is an additional ornamental feature.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; silver princess is regarded by many Australian plant enthusiasts as the single most ornamental of all the mallees (multi-stemmed, shrubby eucalyptus) — combining several outstanding ornamental qualities in one plant. The form is broadly weeping to pendulous, with graceful, arching branches sweeping to the ground. The bark is silvery-white and powdery (caesia = blue-gray), giving the stems a ghostly, glaucous-white texture. The buds are spectacular: large, urn-shaped, covered in white, waxy powder with long, conical, pointed caps — some of the most beautiful eucalyptus buds of any species. The flowers, when the caps fall, are deep pink to crimson-red to vivid rose-pink with contrasting golden-yellow stamens — large (3-inch), showy, spider-like clusters of brightly colored stamens against the silver-white branch structure. The combination of the weeping form, powdery-silver bark, spectacular urn-shaped buds, and vivid pink-red flowers makes it a multi-season ornamental of exceptional beauty. Native to a small area of granite outcrops in southwestern Western Australia; in cultivation it requires good drainage and thrives in zone 9 warm, dry conditions.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a deep shade location after temperatures remain above 60°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and bring indoors when temperatures approach 50°F. Chinese evergreen is among the most sensitive common tropical foliage plants to cold — chilling injury occurs at temperatures below 50°F and frost kills plants immediately. Zone 9 summers (May–October) provide ideal conditions for outdoor display on shaded patios and in covered garden areas. Keep out of direct sun at all times — even brief exposure to direct midday sun in zone 9 causes immediate, irreversible leaf bleaching and burn. Leaf sap is a skin irritant in some individuals.
directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light — never in direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil; Silver Queen is one of the classic Chinese Evergreen cultivars, producing lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive silver-green variegation pattern — a silver-gray to cream central area on each leaf with darker green margins and irregular darker green markings that create a subtle, sophisticated foliage pattern. Chinese Evergreen (Aglaonema) is one of the most adaptable and tolerant foliage plants for low-light conditions — genuinely thriving in the deep shade conditions where most other ornamental plants cannot survive or maintain acceptable appearance. Silver Queen's tolerance of genuinely low light levels, combined with the refined, silver-variegated foliage and relatively compact scale, makes it one of the most practically useful plants for the specific challenge of decorating and greening shaded spaces — covered porches, pergolas with overhead cover, north-facing entries, and any situation where light levels are insufficient for most ornamental plants but where lush, attractive foliage is desired. As an outdoor container plant in zone 9's humid summers, Chinese Evergreen thrives in the warm, humid conditions on shaded patios that replicate its native Southeast Asian forest understory habitat.

common_name: Silver Saw Palmetto (Silvery-Blue Coastal Saw Palmetto)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Silver Saw Palmetto is a prized silvery-blue-leaved coastal-dune form of the native saw palmetto, distinct from the more common green form.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; saw palmetto tolerates poor, dry, or salty coastal soils exceptionally well once established. Silver Saw Palmetto is a striking silvery-blue-leaved form of the native saw palmetto, most commonly found naturally along coastal dunes, offering the same slow-growing, spreading, low-trunked or trunkless habit of the species with the added ornamental impact of icy-blue fan fronds that contrast beautifully with green landscape plantings. Like the species it is extremely tough, drought- and salt-tolerant, and long-lived, making it an excellent low-maintenance native accent for xeriscape and coastal Gulf South gardens. It is very slow-growing, so patience is needed for a young plant to reach a substantial size, and it requires almost no supplemental care once established beyond removal of old fronds.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Silver Sceptre produces narrow, arching blades edged in crisp silvery-white, keeping its brightest variegation where afternoon sun is filtered.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Silver Sceptre is a variegated selection of Japanese sedge, forming a tidy, fountain-like clump of fine, arching, dark-green leaves each edged in a crisp band of silvery white, brightening shaded borders and woodland edges without the maintenance a flowering perennial demands. It holds its evergreen foliage through mild winters and keeps its variegation strongest when protected from harsh midday sun, which can scorch or fade the white margins. Established clumps need only the occasional combing-out of tattered old leaves in early spring, and division every three to four years keeps plantings vigorous and prevents the center of the clump from thinning out.

common_name: Silver Scrolls Heuchera (Silver-Purple Veined Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Silver Scrolls is a longtime favorite heuchera cultivar with large, glossy, silvery-gray leaves traced by bold, dark purple veining that stands out sharply against the pale metallic background, an early and influential introduction in the wave of silver-leaved heucheras that followed. In early summer it sends up tall, wiry stems of small white flowers above the foliage that draw hummingbirds and pollinators. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

plant_note: Root short stem cuttings directly in moist terrarium substrate, where they take within a week or two under warm, humid conditions; Silver Sprinkles Pilea is one of the fastest-rooting, fastest-filling terrarium groundcovers available and can overrun slower neighbors if not trimmed back.
directions: Grow in medium to bright indirect light in a light, well-draining, moisture-retentive mix — this trailing pilea (widely sold under the trade name 'Aquamarine' and often labeled Pilea glauca or Pilea glaucophylla, though its exact botanical origin remains debated among growers) produces tiny, rounded, blue-gray-green leaves with a fine silvery sheen on thin, wiry, cascading reddish stems, giving a delicate, fern-like texture reminiscent of baby tears but more drought-tolerant. It spreads quickly by rooting along trailing stems and makes an excellent low terrarium groundcover, hanging basket subject, or spiller at the edge of a mixed planter. Allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings when grown in an open pot, but keep the substrate consistently moist in a closed terrarium. Trim stems back hard whenever growth becomes sparse or leggy — it fills back in within weeks from any remaining node. Small white flowers appear sporadically but are inconspicuous; the plant is grown strictly for foliage texture.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Silver Sword philodendron climbs readily and develops larger, more elongated leaves with vertical support.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Silver Sword philodendron climbs readily and develops larger, more elongated leaves with vertical support. Narrow, elongated, arrowhead-shaped leaves have a matte, silvery-blue-green cast and a soft, almost velvety sheen, a cool, muted coloring that stands out among the mostly solid green or variegated philodendrons more commonly grown. A selection of Philodendron hastatum, it climbs steadily up a moss pole, producing progressively larger, more elongated silvery leaves as the vine matures, and its understated, elegant color makes it a popular choice for a minimalist or monochromatic plant display. Provide bright indirect light to maintain the silvery sheen, keep humidity moderate to high, and let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Silver Thatch Palm is highly drought- and salt-tolerant and is excellent for the thin, rocky, alkaline soils of the Florida Keys where other palms struggle.
directions: Silver Thatch Palm is a graceful, slender native palm, native to the rocky, alkaline limestone soils of the Florida Keys, extreme southern Miami-Dade County, and the Caribbean, where it grows in coastal hammocks and pine rocklands as one of the most salt- and drought-tolerant palms in the Florida native flora. Its most distinctive feature is the brilliant silver-white coloration of the undersides of the fan-shaped fronds, which flash dramatically in the breeze and give the tree a shimmering, two-toned effect unlike any other native Florida palm. Slow-growing but long-lived, Silver Thatch Palm produces small white flowers in summer followed by round, dark purple berries consumed by birds; historically the leaves were used for thatching (hence the common name). An outstanding specimen palm for the thin, rocky, alkaline marl and limestone soils of South Florida gardens where faster-growing palms would quickly exhaust the substrate — plant in full sun to partial shade, provide excellent drainage, and supply minimal supplemental water once established.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Silver Torch Cactus is one of the more cold-tolerant columnar cacti, handling brief light frost once mature, but still needs sharp drainage.
