plant_note: Direct sow in spring in consistently moist, acidic soil in partial to full shade; slender woodoats is native to wet pine savannas, bog margins, and swamp edges across the southeastern coastal plain and, unlike its larger relative inland sea oats, wants steadier moisture and tolerates less drying between rains.
directions: Direct sow in consistently moist, acidic soil in partial to full shade; slender woodoats is a smaller, more delicate southeastern relative of the better-known inland sea oats, native to wet pine savannas, bog edges, and swamp-margin woods from Virginia to Texas. It forms a low, fine-textured clump of narrow blades topped in summer by slender, nodding spikelets, lighter and airier than the broader, more pendulous seed clusters of Chasmanthium latifolium, and it persists into winter as a soft tan accent. Because it comes from consistently damp, acidic ground, it performs best at a pond margin, rain garden, or the wet, shaded edge of a bog planting rather than an average shade border, and it does not tolerate the same periodic drying that inland sea oats shrugs off. Self-sows modestly in favorable conditions; thin volunteer seedlings where a tidier clump is wanted.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before sowing and direct sow in fall into dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the deep taproot establishes during the first growing season and the plant blooms fully in subsequent years.
directions: Slimflower Scurfpea is a deep-rooted native perennial legume of dry, open prairies, sandy plains, and disturbed ground throughout the Great Plains and south-central US, producing wiry, much-branched stems with delicate pinnate leaves covered in tiny resinous glands and loose clusters of blue-violet, pea-like flowers from May through July. Scarify seeds mechanically or with sandpaper before sowing to improve germination rates, then direct sow in fall into dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun — avoid fertile or amended soil, which favors weedy competition over this tough prairie native. The extensive taproot makes established plants extremely drought-tolerant and difficult to transplant; plants may go dormant in midsummer drought but return vigorously each spring and serve as an important nitrogen-fixer and nectar source for native prairie bees.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun to partial shade. Slippery Elm is moderately susceptible to Dutch Elm Disease but less so than American Elm; it is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions including clay, limestone soils, and occasionally flooded areas.
directions: Slippery Elm is a large, somewhat coarser native elm than American Elm, native to rich, moist forest slopes, bottomlands, and upland woods throughout eastern North America from Quebec to Florida and west to the Dakotas, named for the distinctive slippery, mucilaginous quality of its inner bark, which has been used medicinally for centuries as a demulcent (soothing agent) for sore throats, coughs, and gastrointestinal inflammation — the FDA has recognized the inner bark as a safe and effective over-the-counter demulcent. The rough, sandpaper-textured leaves are distinctive and diagnostic for the species; the reddish, hairy leaf buds in late winter are among the first signs of life in the spring forest. While moderately susceptible to Dutch Elm Disease, Slippery Elm is adaptable to a wider range of soil conditions than American Elm, tolerating clay, limestone, and occasionally wet soils. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; the coarse texture and broad shade make it a valuable native alternative to cultivated elms.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; small anise tree is more shade-tolerant and faster-growing than Florida anise (I. floridanum) and is especially effective as a tall, screening shrub in deep shade situations.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; small anise tree is more shade-tolerant and faster-growing than Florida anise (I. floridanum) and is especially effective as a tall, screening shrub in deep shade situations. Illicium parviflorum is a large, fast-growing, evergreen native shrub or small tree endemic to central Florida and historically occurring only in Volusia and Seminole counties, though now widely cultivated throughout the Gulf South for its outstanding performance as a screening plant in difficult shaded and wet conditions; it produces bright, lime-green to medium-green, aromatic, elliptic leaves and tiny, inconspicuous, pale yellowish flowers in spring. A workhorse screening shrub and hedge plant for zones 7–10 that can reach 8–15 feet tall quickly; it naturalizes along shaded stream banks, pond margins, and moist ravines.

plant_note: Sprinkle seed on the surface of moist, acidic, nutrient-poor medium (milled sphagnum or 50/50 peat and sand) without covering; keep standing in a tray of pure rain water or distilled water in full sun to partial shade — small butterwort is the tiniest of the Gulf Coast Pinguicula species and grows naturally in open, wet pine savanna.
directions: Small butterwort is the smallest of the native Gulf Coast Pinguicula, forming a flat rosette barely an inch or two across of pale yellow-green, sticky-glandular leaves that trap and digest tiny insects such as gnats and fungus flies, growing naturally in the open, wet, acidic pine savannas and seepage bogs of the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains. Delicate pale lavender to white flowers, each on a thin, wiry stalk well above the foliage, appear from spring into summer and self-seed readily in suitably wet, nutrient-poor conditions. Sow seed on the surface of milled sphagnum or a lean peat-sand mix and keep the pot standing in pure rain water or distilled water year-round in full sun to light shade, since tap water minerals and ordinary fertile soil will kill it within a season. It is easiest to grow alongside sundews and smaller Sarracenia species in a shallow, sunny bog garden or a bog-in-a-pot on a porch.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; small crowea is one of the most reliably flowering Australian native shrubs — blooming from late summer through winter with extraordinary prolificacy. The clear, rose-pink, five-petaled star flowers are produced almost continuously for 4–6 months on a healthy plant. Tip pruning after spring promotes dense, bushy growth. More tolerant of shading than many Australian natives.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; small crowea is one of the most valuable and reliably long-blooming Australian native shrubs for the garden — producing from late summer through autumn and winter an almost continuous succession of five-petaled, clear rose-pink to deep pink, open-faced, star-shaped flowers on a compact, bushy, densely-leaved mound of narrow, aromatic, dark-green foliage. The bloom period of 4–6 months (August through February in warm climates) makes it one of the longest-blooming of all Australian native shrubs. The flowers are in the clear, clean, warm-pink to deep-rose range — not the orange-red of many Australian natives — providing a color that is unusual in winter-flowering Australian plants. The aromatic, narrow, pointed leaves (the plant is in the Rutaceae family, related to citrus and boronia) release a characteristic pleasant scent when brushed. The compact, neat, naturally rounded habit requires little pruning to maintain. Excellent in part shade — one of the few Australian shrubs that tolerates meaningful shade and continues to flower well. A consistently reliable and rewarding garden shrub for zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, acidic, peaty soil in partial to full shade; small green wood orchid grows in boggy woods, seepage swamps, and streamhead pocosins across a wide range from Canada to the Gulf Coast, tolerating more shade than most native bog orchids.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, acidic, peaty soil in partial to full shade, never from wild-collected stock. Small green wood orchid is a diminutive, easily overlooked native bog orchid with an unusually wide range from eastern Canada south to the Gulf Coast, distinguished by its small spikes of pale greenish-white flowers with a distinctive club-shaped spur, blooming in mid to late summer in the boggy, shaded woods, seepage swamps, and streamhead pocosins it calls home. Unlike the sun-loving fringed orchids of open savannas, it tolerates and even prefers the dappled shade of a wooded bog margin, making it a useful native orchid for a shaded corner of a bog garden that gets too little sun for showier species. It depends on soil mycorrhizal fungi like other native orchids, so keep the planting undisturbed and consistently wet with rain water or distilled water rather than mineral-rich tap water.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; CAUTION — white wandering jew is invasive in Florida, the Gulf South, parts of California, and many tropical and warm-temperate regions where it forms dense mats that exclude native understory plants — verify local regulations before planting.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile soil in shade to part shade; CAUTION — invasive in Florida and warm-temperate regions; never plant near natural areas. Tradescantia fluminensis (small leaf spiderwort or white wandering jew) is a South American succulent trailing perennial closely related to the more commonly grown 'wandering Jew' (T. zebrina) and tradescantia group. This species is smaller-leaved with glossy, oval, bright-green leaves on trailing stems, producing tiny white flowers. It is widely used as a shade groundcover indoors and in warm gardens for its easy growth, shade tolerance, and rapid spreading habit. However, T. fluminensis is classified as an invasive weed in Florida, South Africa, New Zealand, Hawaii, and other warm regions where it escapes cultivation and forms dense, impenetrable mats in woodland understories, smothering native understory vegetation. In New Zealand, it is considered one of the most damaging environmental weeds in coastal forest understories. Where legal and appropriate (i.e., in fully contained indoor or urban settings far from natural areas), it is an effective low-maintenance shade groundcover. Note: causes skin irritation in some individuals. Grow with caution and responsibility.

plant_note: Direct sow on or just after the last frost date; seeds germinate readily in warm sandy soil and plants grow quickly to bloom.
directions: Small Palafox is a slender, branching native annual of the aster family, found naturally in dry, sandy grasslands, prairies, and open roadsides across Texas and adjacent south-central states. It produces clusters of small, rose-pink to pale lavender composite flowers with a deeper rose disc from midsummer through fall, providing reliable late-season color in hot, dry gardens. Sow seeds directly in spring after the last frost into dry, sandy, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; plants thrive on neglect and perform best without supplemental fertilizer or irrigation. Small Palafox self-sows freely in open, disturbed sandy ground, making it a reliable naturalizer and low-maintenance filler for Texas native wildflower plantings and sandy prairie restorations.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall onto thin, rocky or sandy, calcareous to slightly acidic, very well-drained soil; winter cold provides natural stratification.
directions: Direct sow in fall onto thin, rocky or sandy, calcareous to slightly acidic, very well-drained soil in full sun, pressing seed lightly onto the surface and allowing winter cold to stratify it naturally before spring germination. This diminutive native perennial is one of the smallest-statured Scutellaria species in eastern North America, at home in cedar glades, thin-soiled limestone outcrops, and calcareous prairies from the eastern seaboard through the central states. Tiny, tubular, blue to violet-blue, 2-lipped flowers appear on thread-like stems with small, rounded, often toothed leaves from May through July. Plants spread slowly by shallow rhizomes to form loose, low colonies and are excellent in rock garden crevices, glade restorations, and dry, infertile native plant settings where taller competitors are kept in check.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; small Solomon's seal spreads steadily by rhizomes to form colonies and is best planted in generous drifts of at least 5–7 rhizomes.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; small Solomon's seal spreads steadily by rhizomes to form colonies and provides four seasons of interest — emerging foliage in spring, hanging white flowers in late spring, blue-black berries in summer, and golden-yellow fall color. Polygonatum biflorum is the smaller native eastern North American species of Solomon's seal (compared to the great Solomon's seal, P. commutatum), producing arching stems 18–36 inches long with alternate, oval, parallel-veined leaves and paired, pendant, tubular, white to cream flowers dangling from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by glaucous blue-black berries beloved by wildlife. The common name comes from the circular, seal-like scars left on the rhizome where old stems have attached; the rhizome was used medicinally and the young shoots are edible. Outstanding for naturalizing in shaded woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall into consistently moist, neutral to alkaline, calcium-rich soil in partial shade; never dig from the wild, and expect slow establishment but a long-lived clump once sited correctly.
directions: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens in fall into consistently moist, neutral to alkaline, calcium-rich soil in partial shade, replicating the calcareous fens and prairie wet meadows of the Great Lakes and upper Midwest where this, the smallest native lady's slipper, naturally occurs. Its compact white pouches with twisted, maroon-striped lateral petals bloom in late spring and are pollinated by small bees that enter seeking non-existent nectar and exit dusted with pollen. Populations have declined sharply with fen and prairie wetland loss, so it is state-listed as rare or threatened across much of its range; never dig from the wild, and expect a slow-establishing but long-lived clump once sited correctly. A rewarding specialty plant for a constructed calcareous seep or fen garden rather than average acidic woodland soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; small woodland sunflower spreads by rhizome and, unlike most sunflowers, blooms reliably in the dappled light beneath high tree canopy.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; small woodland sunflower spreads by rhizome and, unlike most sunflowers, blooms reliably in the dappled light beneath high tree canopy. Helianthus microcephalus is an eastern native perennial sunflower adapted to woodland edges and open forest understory, producing slender, branching stems and a profusion of small, delicate, pale yellow flower heads in late summer and fall that are an important late-season nectar source for bees and butterflies as sunnier flowers fade. Its shade tolerance and airy, small-flowered habit make it a good choice for naturalizing along a wooded property line or the high, filtered shade of mature trees where full-sun sunflower species will not thrive. It spreads by rhizome to form a colony over time and can be divided in spring to control its spread or share with other gardeners.

common_name: Small World Dahlia (Pure White Pompon Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Small World is a pure white pompon dahlia forming tight, perfectly round 1-2 inch globes.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage bushier growth and more blooms. Small World is a true pompon dahlia, its small, densely quilled florets curling inward to form an almost perfectly spherical pure white globe barely 1 to 2 inches across, a clean, crisp counterpoint to the huge dinnerplate types grown for size. The dainty, uniform blooms are produced in great abundance on wiry stems, making them a favorite for posies, buttonholes, and mixed bouquets. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Small's penstemon tolerates partial shade better than most penstemons and is one of the few species that naturalize reliably in the humid Southeast. It self-sows freely and forms naturalized colonies in appropriate conditions.
directions: Sow seeds or plant divisions in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; Small's penstemon is an Appalachian native producing spikes of large, tubular flowers in a distinctive combination of rosy-purple and white — the wide throat of each flower is striped with purple guidelines on a white background, giving a bicolored effect. It blooms in late spring (May–June), a slightly earlier time than many penstemons. Unlike western penstemons that often fail in humid southeastern gardens, Small's penstemon is native to the humid forest edges and rocky slopes of the southern Appalachians from Virginia to Georgia and is naturally adapted to the summer humidity and rainfall of the Southeast. It is one of the most garden-worthy penstemons for humid zone 7–9 gardens where western species typically struggle or die after one season. An important early nectar source for hummingbirds and native bumblebees.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Small's ragwort forms an evergreen basal rosette groundcover that spreads gradually and works well massed along a woodland edge or dry shaded bank.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Small's ragwort forms an evergreen basal rosette groundcover that spreads gradually and works well massed along a woodland edge or dry shaded bank. Packera anonyma is a southeastern native forming a low mat of semi-evergreen, toothed basal leaves that sends up wiry stems topped with clusters of small, bright yellow, daisy-like flowers in late spring, providing early-season nectar for a range of small native bees and other pollinators. It tolerates dry, poor soil and light shade better than many groundcover perennials, making it useful for naturalizing along woodland margins, dry banks, and other tough sites where richer soil groundcovers struggle. It spreads readily by seed and short rhizomes to form a colony over a few seasons and needs essentially no supplemental care once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; small-flowered alumroot is a Pacific Northwest native that tolerates deeper shade than most heucheras, making it useful as a shade groundcover under conifers where few perennials survive.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; small-flowered alumroot is a Pacific Northwest native that tolerates deeper shade than most heucheras, making it useful as a shade groundcover under conifers where few perennials survive. Heuchera micrantha is the Pacific Northwest native alumroot most closely associated with the famous 'Palace Purple' cultivar and the cascade of bronze- and purple-leafed garden heucheras that followed; the species itself has large, lobed, light-to-medium-green leaves with silver mottling and produces tall, open, airy panicles of tiny white flowers in late spring. It is native to moist, forested cliffs and shaded stream banks from British Columbia to northern California and is an important parent species in Heuchera hybridization programs; in the garden it is a tough, reliable shade perennial for the Pacific Northwest and is more tolerant of dry shade than most species once established.

common_name: Small-Flowered Campylocentrum (Leafless Florida Orchid, Ghost Orchid Relative)
plant_note: Mount on rough-barked wood or cork with exposed aerial roots in bright indirect to partial direct light; Campylocentrum micranthum is a leafless epiphytic orchid — like the related Ghost Orchid (Dendrophylax lindenii), it produces no leaves and obtains all photosynthesis through flat, green, chlorophyll-containing roots. The roots must receive light (bright indirect to partial direct) to support the plant. A very slow-growing, specialist orchid for patient collectors with appropriate high-humidity conditions. Wild plants are protected. Zone 10-12 outdoors. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow mounted on rough bark or cork in partial indirect to dappled direct light with high humidity — Small-Flowered Campylocentrum is a leafless, photosynthetic-root orchid that requires light on the roots and consistently warm, humid conditions to thrive. Campylocentrum micranthum is a minute, leafless, epiphytic orchid native to southern Florida (Collier and Miami-Dade counties), Puerto Rico, the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, and South America in the Orchidaceae family, representing one of the fascinating group of 'ghost orchids' — orchids that have eliminated their leaves entirely and adopted a photosynthetic root system. The plant is visible only as a mass of flat, strap-like, green to gray-green roots spreading across the bark surface of its host tree. From these roots in summer and fall, tiny (2–3 mm) cream-white to yellowish flowers emerge on short racemes — the flowers microscopic by orchid standards, requiring a hand lens for appreciation, but formally complete with sepals, petals, lip, and column. Campylocentrum is a genus of approximately 60 species distributed from the Caribbean through tropical America, related to the more famous Dendrophylax genus that includes Florida's Ghost Orchid (D. lindenii). In south Florida, C. micranthum grows naturally on live oaks, pond apples, and other hardwood trees in hammock forests. A specialist's orchid of genuine ecological interest, particularly for collectors drawn to Florida's remarkable native orchid flora. Non-toxic.

common_name: Small-Flowered Cuphea (Candy Corn Cuphea, Micropetal Cuphea)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil after last frost; Cuphea micropetala is one of the more cold-tolerant Cuphea species, surviving temperatures to 25–28°F in established plants and often regrowning from the root crown after light freezes in zone 9. The orange-and-yellow tubular flowers are exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds and are produced almost continuously from spring through frost. The common name 'Candy Corn Cuphea' reflects the bicolored orange-yellow flower resembling candy corn. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Small-Flowered Cuphea blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates partial shade and is more drought-tolerant than many tropical-looking ornamental shrubs once established. Cuphea micropetala is a compact, semi-woody, perennial shrub native to Mexico and Guatemala in the Lythraceae family, one of the most cold-hardy and ornamentally valuable of the approximately 260 Cuphea species for zone 8-11 gardens. The plant produces a dense, upright to somewhat mounding form with narrow, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves and an exceptionally free-flowering habit — producing dozens to hundreds of tubular flowers at the leaf axils simultaneously through the warm months from spring through fall. Each flower is a small (0.5-inch), tubular, slightly curved structure in orange to orange-red with a yellow-green tip — a bicolored orange-and-yellow pattern that strongly resembles a piece of candy corn, explaining the marketing name 'Candy Corn Plant' sometimes applied to this species. The nectar-rich, tubular, hummingbird-adapted flowers attract Ruby-throated, Rufous, and other hummingbird species reliably, with hummingbirds visiting and revisiting a flowering Cuphea micropetala plant dozens of times daily during migration. Greater cold hardiness (to zone 8) than most ornamental Cuphea species makes this a particularly valuable selection for zone 9 gardens. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root 4–6 inch stem cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat mix, then pot into a hanging basket once rooted. Best rooted in spring or early summer so trailing stems fill out before shorter winter days. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.
directions: A finer-textured, more densely trailing relative of the larger Columnea gloriosa, this epiphyte carries tiny rounded leaves along thin, wiry stems that can cascade 2–3 feet from a hanging basket. Pot in a loose, fast-draining epiphytic mix and grow in bright, indirect light — direct sun scorches the small leaves, while too little light suppresses the tubular red-orange flowers that appear along the stems in winter and early spring. Keep humidity moderate to high and let the mix dry slightly between waterings, since the fine roots are prone to rot in constantly wet mix. A cooler winter rest period with reduced watering encourages the heaviest bloom the following season.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic, rocky or sandy soil in partial to full shade; small-flowered alumroot is a limestone cliff and cave-entrance specialist native to the Appalachians, preferring the cool, consistently moist, very well-drained conditions of shaded rock overhangs and cliff faces.
directions: Plant in moist, very well-drained, humus-rich, rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; small-flowered alumroot is an Appalachian native of limestone cliffs, cave entrances, and shaded rocky outcrops, naturally growing in the perpetually cool, moist, well-drained environment of rock overhangs where moisture seeps through rather than pooling. The rounded, maple-like, dark green leaves form low, neat rosettes and are attractive year-round as a semi-evergreen groundcover in appropriate rocky, shaded garden settings. The tiny, white flowers on airy, branching panicles in late summer are less showy than garden heuchera cultivars but provide nectar for small native bees. An excellent choice for shaded rock gardens, crevices in stone walls, and the base of large boulders in woodland gardens in zones 4–8.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; small-headed blazing star grows naturally in dry, rocky, calcareous soils of the Cumberland Plateau and surrounding Appalachian region, in open glades and rock outcrops in full sun.
directions: Plant in dry, rocky, calcareous or slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; small-headed blazing star is a distinctly more slender, more narrowly adapted liatris than the widely cultivated Liatris spicata, native to the open rocky glades and dry, calcareous slopes of the Cumberland Plateau of Tennessee and surrounding areas. The small flower heads give it a more airy, delicate appearance than the more robust blazing stars, and it blooms in late summer with the typical rose-purple liatris color. Like all Liatris species, the flowers open from the top of the spike downward, and it serves as an important late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies and native bees during their fall migration period. An excellent, drought-tolerant species for dry, rocky, calcareous garden soils.

plant_note: Surface-sow on moist soil at or just after last frost; do not cover seeds, as light aids germination.
directions: Slender, freely branching native annual or short-lived perennial smothered in masses of small white to pale lavender daisy-like flowers with yellow centers from late summer through October. Native to moist, open, disturbed habitats, ditches, and pond margins throughout the southeastern US, it is much more delicate in appearance than the larger Boltonia asteroides. Surface-sow on moist soil in full sun after last frost; plants naturalize readily by self-seeding in consistently moist sites. An excellent fine-textured filler for the back of rain garden borders and native wetland restorations where consistent moisture is available.

plant_note: Lightly scarify seeds with sandpaper or soak overnight in warm water before sowing to improve germination, though seeds will often sprout without treatment.
directions: Sow seeds in spring directly into their permanent location or into deep containers to accommodate early taproot development. Plant in full sun in dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil — this shrub thrives in poor, alkaline, or sandy conditions where most plants struggle. Once established it requires virtually no supplemental irrigation and tolerates wind, drought, and severe cold with ease. Use in mass plantings for erosion control, shelterbelts, or wildlife hedgerows across challenging exposed sites.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into sandy, rocky, or gravelly well-drained soil in full sun; Nuttall's milkvetch is adapted to naturally disturbed, nutrient-poor ground and requires excellent drainage — it will rot in heavy, wet, or clay soils.
directions: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into sandy, rocky, or gravelly well-drained soil in full sun; nick the hard seed coat lightly before sowing to improve germination and inoculate with a legume rhizobium inoculant to encourage nitrogen fixation from the outset. Astragalus nuttallianus is a native annual of the south-central United States — primarily Texas, Oklahoma, and New Mexico — producing small purple pea-like flowers in spring on low, spreading stems that thrive in the same disturbed, calcareous, sandy soils where it naturally occurs along roadsides, cedar glades, and open rangeland. This inconspicuous but ecologically significant species is a documented larval host for the Reakirt's Blue butterfly, a specialist of leguminous plants found across the arid Southwest, making it a valuable addition to native wildflower mixes in its natural range.

plant_note: Set divisions of the shallow, creeping rhizome into consistently moist, humus-rich soil beneath a closed woodland canopy in early spring, spacing plants to allow the arching stems room to spread.
directions: Set divisions of the shallow, creeping rhizome into consistently moist, humus-rich soil beneath a closed woodland canopy in early spring, spacing plants to allow the arching stems room to spread. Paired lance-shaped leaves line each gently curving stem, and in mid-spring pairs of ivory, bell-shaped flowers dangle beneath the foliage before giving way to orange-red berries in late summer. Native to moist coastal forests from British Columbia to central California, it thrives in the same deep shade and leafy soil favored by ferns, wild ginger, and trillium. It spreads gradually into a loose colony but is never aggressive, making it a good textural companion in a naturalistic shade border.

plant_note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; smooth agave is less cold-hardy and less heavily armed than many agave species, tolerating light frost but not hard freezes.
directions: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; smooth agave is less cold-hardy and less heavily armed than many agave species, tolerating light frost but not hard freezes. Broad, smooth-edged, glossy yellow-green leaves lack the sharp marginal teeth of many agave species, making it a more approachable choice for a planting near a walkway or patio where passersby might brush against it, tapering to a single sharp terminal spine at each leaf tip. Popular variegated selections with creamy yellow leaf margins are especially widely grown in mild-winter landscapes, forming an attractive symmetrical rosette that offsets readily to form a cluster over time. Like other agaves it is monocarpic, flowering once on a tall spike after many years and then dying, but the numerous offsets produced beforehand ensure the planting continues.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; smooth aster tolerates a wide range of soils, from lean prairie ground to average garden soil, and is one of the more adaptable native asters for general garden use.
directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and generally sturdy and self-supporting without staking. Symphyotrichum laeve (smooth aster, or smooth blue aster) is a native tallgrass prairie perennial distinguished by its smooth, waxy, blue-green foliage — a notable contrast to the coarser, hairier leaves of many other native asters — and its clouds of lavender-blue, yellow-centered flowers that open from late summer into fall. It is considered one of the most valuable late-season native asters for pollinators, providing critical nectar for native bees, honeybees, and migrating monarch butterflies as they refuel for their journey south, and it also serves as a larval host plant for pearl crescent butterflies. Its sturdy, upright habit and long fall bloom period make it an excellent choice for the middle of a sunny native perennial border or prairie-style planting, zone 3–8.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratify seed for 30 days; often blooms the second year.
directions: Give seed a month of cold-moist stratification, then sow in spring. This dependable native perennial bears clouds of small lavender-blue, daisy-like flowers in late summer and fall. Plant in full sun and average, well-drained soil where its smooth blue-green foliage resists disease. It provides critical late-season nectar for bees and migrating butterflies as other flowers fade.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Bougainvillea glabra blooms most heavily under mild drought stress (slightly dry) and full sun — avoid rich, wet soil or excessive fertilization, which promotes vegetative growth at the expense of the showy bracts.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide a sturdy trellis, wall, or fence for climbing support. Bougainvillea glabra (smooth bougainvillea) is the species most commonly sold as 'bougainvillea' in the nursery trade — a vigorous, thorny, sprawling vine or shrub from Brazil producing masses of small, white, tubular true flowers surrounded by the magnificently colored bracts (modified leaves) in magenta, purple, red, orange, yellow, white, or bicolor combinations that are the ornamental feature of the plant. B. glabra differs from the common hybrid Bougainvillea spectabilis in having smooth (glabrous, as the name implies) stems and leaves vs. hairy stems and is generally considered more free-blooming and compact. Bougainvillea blooms most heavily after mild water stress in full sun; withhold water before anticipated bloom periods to trigger flowering. In zone 9, it may die back in hard freezes but resprouts vigorously from roots when established; in zones 10–12, it is a dramatic year-round bloomer. Stems are armed with sharp thorns; handle with heavy gloves.

plant_note: Direct sow cold-stratified seed in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to gravelly, thin soil in full sun to partial shade; smooth coneflower is a Federally Threatened species adapted to disturbed, thin-soil openings in cedar-hardwood woodland — it requires good drainage and open mineral soil.
directions: Sow cold-stratified seed in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to gravelly soil in full sun to partial shade — smooth coneflower is a Federally Threatened native coneflower of the Appalachian piedmont and Blue Ridge foothills, declining primarily due to habitat loss and canopy closure over its characteristic thin-soil, semi-open woodland and roadside habitats. It is distinguished from the more common purple coneflower (E. purpurea) by its smooth (not rough) stems and leaves and its adaptation to disturbed, thin, rocky soils — often in partially shaded situations unlike most other Echinacea. The pale to deep rose-purple ray flowers and prominent central cone are characteristic of the genus and equally attractive to pollinators and beneficial for gardens. Growing this species supports its conservation by maintaining cultivated populations and seed banks. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants from reputable native plant nurseries.

plant_note: Plant plugs or bare-root divisions in spring in regularly flooded tidal flats, muddy marsh edges, or constructed tidal wetlands; smooth cordgrass must be planted in the intertidal zone where it is flooded by saltwater twice daily — it will not persist in fresh water or fully upland sites.
directions: Smooth cordgrass (formerly Spartina alterniflora) is the dominant grass of tidal salt marshes along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of North America — arguably the single most ecologically important native grass on the eastern seaboard, as it forms the structural foundation of the salt marsh ecosystem. Dense monocultures of smooth cordgrass trap sediment, reduce shoreline erosion, export enormous amounts of organic material (detritus) that feeds estuarine food webs, provide nesting habitat for clapper rails, marsh wrens, and seaside sparrows, and serve as the primary nursery habitat for shrimp, blue crab, flounder, and dozens of commercially important fish species. In coastal restoration projects, smooth cordgrass is the primary plant used to revegetate denuded tidal mudflats, eroding shorelines, and disturbed salt marsh: it establishes from plugs or bare-root divisions within a single growing season and spreads by rhizomes to form self-sustaining colonies. Use for tidal marsh restoration, living shoreline projects, and coastal erosion control where intertidal conditions are present.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into sandy or average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; seeds overwinter and germinate the following spring.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall onto the surface of sandy or average, well-drained soil in a partially shaded to fully sunny spot, allowing winter cold to promote germination the following spring. This distinctive southeastern native forms a bold basal rosette of large, rough, spatula-shaped leaves from which wiry, branching stems rise 12-24 inches and bear small, fuzzy, lilac-pink composite flower heads in late summer and fall, providing nectar for native bees and small butterflies at a time when many other plants have finished blooming. It differs from the closely related Elephantopus tomentosus in having noticeably smoother leaves and stems. Plants adapt well to open woodland gardens, partial-shade borders, and disturbed natural areas with average to moderate soil moisture, and they naturalize steadily from self-sown seed without becoming invasive.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil at woodland edges, streambanks, or shaded rain gardens; Stachys tenuifolia spreads by stolons and establishes readily in reliably moist, partially shaded sites.
directions: Stachys tenuifolia is a shade-tolerant native mint-family perennial that forms spreading colonies via stolons in moist woodland edges and floodplain margins where other plants struggle. Small pink-lavender flowers are held on upright spikes in mid-summer and provide nectar for native bees and small pollinators. Plant in reliably moist to wet, organically rich soil and avoid dry or compacted sites; it pairs well with other native wetland-edge plants such as Lobelia cardinalis and Physostegia species. Divide colonies every few years in early spring to keep the planting tidy and share divisions with other moist garden areas.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; this hydrangea blooms on new wood — cut it back to 12 inches in late winter for the largest, most vigorous flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; smooth hydrangea is the native parent of the enormously popular cultivars 'Annabelle' and 'Incrediball', which have transformed shade gardens with their enormous round white flower heads up to 12 inches across. Unlike oakleaf hydrangea, smooth hydrangea blooms on new wood — cut all stems to 12–18 inches in late winter for the strongest, most floriferous performance. It grows naturally along stream banks, woodland edges, and cliff faces across the eastern US and tolerates more shade and competition than most shrubs. If flower heads become too heavy for stems, cut back less severely the following year. Pollinators of many species use the tiny fertile flowers at the center of the flower heads.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; smooth penstemon adapts to moist woodland edges as well as dry upland sites in the Southeast, making it more versatile than most penstemons for Gulf Coast garden conditions.
directions: Smooth penstemon is the most widely distributed native penstemon in the southeastern United States, found in open woodland edges, roadside banks, and moist to dry uplands from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas — it is one of the more adaptable penstemons for Gulf Coast gardens, tolerating the heat and humidity of the Deep South better than many western species that struggle in the muggy Southeast. The whorled, tubular lavender-to-white flowers appear in April through June and are eagerly worked by large native bumblebees, hummingbirds, and long-tongued native bees; the plant's smooth, glossy leaves (the 'laevigatus' means smooth) and upright flower spikes provide attractive structure in native garden borders. It adapts to both moist woodland edges with partial shade and dry, sunny upland slopes — a versatility unusual among penstemons that makes it a reliable choice for varied garden conditions in the Southeast. Self-seeds modestly and forms small colonies over time; divide crowded clumps in fall every 3–4 years.

plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; smooth phlox is adapted to moist, streamside woodland edges and is more tolerant of partial shade and consistent soil moisture than meadow phlox (P. maculata) or the dry-adapted P. carolina.
directions: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; smooth phlox is adapted to moist, streamside woodland edges and is more tolerant of partial shade and consistent soil moisture than meadow phlox (P. maculata) or the dry-adapted P. carolina. Phlox glaberrima is a smooth-stemmed native phlox of moist to wet lowland prairies, stream edges, and open forest glades throughout the southeastern and central United States, producing dense, rounded clusters of rich pink to magenta-pink flowers in late spring to early summer on unbranched to lightly branched upright stems; it is disease-resistant (less prone to powdery mildew than P. paniculata), moist-soil tolerant, and heat-hardy in zones 7–9. An outstanding native alternative to garden phlox for moist, sunny to partially shaded borders and rain gardens, supporting hummingbirds, swallowtails, and hummingbird hawk-moths.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, shaded, rocky or sandy soil; cold winter temperatures provide the stratification needed to break seed dormancy. Plants form a basal rosette in the first year and bloom in their second spring.
directions: Smooth Rock Cress is a native biennial or short-lived perennial of moist, shaded rocky woodland slopes, bluff bases, and cliff ledges throughout eastern North America, quietly filling in some of the season's earliest wildflower gaps. In its first year it forms a flat, silvery-green basal rosette of smooth, clasping leaves; in its second spring it sends up a slender, upright stem bearing small, white to pale lavender, 4-petaled mustard flowers that attract early-season bees and native insects. The smooth, glossy stem leaves clasp the stalk with distinctive ear-like auricles that make identification easy. Direct sow in fall in moist, slightly acidic, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil under partial shade; it naturalizes steadily in woodland borders by self-sowing, gradually colonizing rocky slopes and ledges with little intervention.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into dry, sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor, very well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Smooth Scurfpea is a rare, conservation-priority native perennial legume of dry, open longleaf pine flatwoods and sandy pinelands in the Mississippi-Alabama coastal plain region. It is unusual among legumes in producing simple or unifoliolate leaves rather than compound leaves, a trait encoded in its species name simplex, and bears short, spike-like racemes of blue to purple pea flowers in summer. Grow in dry, sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor, very well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding clay or amended soils that this lean-soil specialist cannot tolerate. Scarify seeds before fall direct sow; source plants or seeds only from reputable native nurseries given its conservation status, and use it in longleaf pine restoration or dry sandhill plantings in zones 6 through 9.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade; like all winterberries, this species is dioecious — plant at least one male for every 5–6 female plants for good fruit set. Smooth winterberry is slightly more compact than common winterberry (I. verticillata).
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; smooth winterberry is a native deciduous holly of the Atlantic Coastal Plain, closely related to but slightly smaller and more southern-adapted than common winterberry (I. verticillata). The glossy leaves and more tapered, smooth-margined leaflets distinguish it from the more northern species. In fall, the bright orange-red to scarlet berries are produced in exceptional abundance — smaller than I. verticillata berries but often in denser clusters — and persist into winter. The plant grows naturally in bog edges, wet flatwoods, and pond margins from Maine south to Georgia, making it well-suited to zone 9a moist conditions where it is more reliable than its northern relative. The berries are critically important winter food for bluebirds, robins, and cedar waxwings. Like all hollies, the berries are toxic to humans.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; snail vine grows rapidly in warm conditions and may re-sprout from the root in zone 9 after light frosts. Train on a trellis or fence.
directions: Direct sow after frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; snail vine is a vigorous tropical vine from South America producing some of the most uniquely shaped flowers in the legume family — the petals are twisted into a tight spiral or snail-shell shape, creating a flower that looks as if it has been wound up like a corkscrew. The flowers are lavender-purple to pink and emit a rich, honey-vanilla fragrance that intensifies in the afternoon and evening. A rapid grower once established, covering a trellis or fence with lush, tropical foliage and weeks of unusual, fragrant flowers from midsummer through fall. Thomas Jefferson famously grew snail vine at Monticello, where he valued it as an ornamental and edible bean — the pods and seeds are edible. In zone 9a, it may perennialize in warm microclimates.

plant_note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Snake air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering.
directions: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Snake air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering. A bulbous base tapers into long, slender, snaking leaves marked with irregular purplish-maroon speckles and blotches over green, an unusual mottled pattern combined with the plant's writhing, serpentine form that gives it its common name, topped with a spike of purple flowers emerging from pink bracts at maturity. Native to humid forests from Mexico through Central America, it prefers slightly more shade and humidity than desert-adapted tillandsia species, thriving mounted in a shaded, humid spot such as a covered porch or bathroom window. Soak or mist thoroughly two to three times weekly, ensure good air circulation to dry the base fully afterward, and avoid direct hot sun, which can scorch the mottled leaves.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average soil; Snake Bean Tree is a West and Central African legume tree producing extraordinary, long, twisted, snake-like seed pods hanging in pendulous clusters from the branches — pods reach 1.5 to 3 feet long — and bears white and yellow pea-family flowers in striking axillary clusters.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor soil; Swartzia madagascariensis is drought tolerant once established and adapted to seasonal dry conditions — water regularly in the first two years for establishment, then reduce to deep, infrequent watering or rely on seasonal rainfall in tropical climates. Swartzia madagascariensis (Snake Bean Tree or Worm Tree) is a large, semi-deciduous to evergreen legume tree native to the woodland savannas, miombo forests, and bushveld of tropical and sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal east through Ethiopia and south through East Africa to Zimbabwe and Mozambique, where it is recognized as one of the most distinctive fruiting trees of the African savanna by its extraordinarily long, pendulous, corded, snake-like or worm-like seed pods — each 18 to 36 inches long, twisted and constricted between seeds, hanging in spectacular cascades from the branches. The creamy-white and yellow flowers carried in dense clusters attract pollinators before the pods develop. The hard, heavy, dark-reddish-brown heartwood is highly valued as a traditional timber for construction, tool handles, musical instruments, and carving across the tree's range. The bark and roots are widely used in traditional African medicine for pain relief, wound healing, and anti-parasitic applications. An exceptional specimen tree for large tropical gardens, wildlife areas, and agroforestry systems.

plant_note: Root leaf sections or offset divisions in well-drained cactus or succulent mix at 70–80°F in bright indirect to low light; in zone 9–12 it may be planted outdoors year-round in very well-drained soil in deep to partial shade.
directions: Root leaf cuttings or offset divisions in well-drained cactus mix in bright indirect light to very low light; the snake plant (formerly Sansevieria trifasciata, reclassified to Dracaena in 2017) is one of the most forgiving indoor plants available, surviving weeks of neglect, poor light, and inconsistent watering that defeat most other houseplants. Water sparingly — no more than once every 2–3 weeks in winter and once a week in summer — allowing the soil to dry completely between waterings; root rot from overwatering is by far the most common cause of decline. In zone 9–12 it can be grown as an outdoor landscape plant in full shade to partial shade in very well-drained soil, where it forms bold architectural clumps of stiff, upright, green-and-yellow banded foliage to 4 feet tall. Note that the leaves are mildly toxic to cats and dogs if ingested.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained to dry, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to full sun; snake plant is one of the most drought- and neglect-tolerant houseplants and outdoor shade plants and will survive in almost any indoor or outdoor light condition except cold temperatures below 50°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in any light condition from deep shade to full sun; water infrequently — allow soil to dry completely between waterings. Sansevieria trifasciata (snake plant or mother-in-law's tongue — now sometimes classified as Dracaena trifasciata, a separate entry) is among the most indestructible of all cultivated plants — a West African succulent producing stiff, upright, sword-shaped leaves 18–48 inches tall with distinctive horizontal gray-green and dark-green banding (which gives it the 'snake plant' name from the pattern resembling snakeskin), often bordered with yellow margins in the popular 'Laurentii' cultivar. It tolerates neglect, drought, deep shade, bright sun, low humidity, and infrequent watering with virtually no complaints — making it the number-one recommended plant for beginning gardeners and those who cannot provide consistent care. Mature, pot-bound plants occasionally produce clusters of fragrant, white, vanilla-scented flowers on long stalks. Note: Sansevieria trifasciata is taxonomically equivalent to Dracaena trifasciata; some authorities retain the Sansevieria name, others use Dracaena — plants sold in nurseries may be labeled under either name.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moisture-retentive soil in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; snake's head fritillary performs best in partial shade in moist, leafy soil similar to a damp meadow or woodland edge — avoid hot, dry, or strongly alkaline sites. Plant in large numbers for the best naturalistic effect; this species self-seeds freely and will increase into generous colonies under favorable conditions.
directions: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade in fall for late March-April bloom; snake's head fritillary is one of the most extraordinary and visually arresting spring bulbs in cultivation — a slender, nodding species producing solitary or occasionally paired pendant bells of an intricate, precisely patterned chequered design in rich dusky pink-purple or pure white, each square of the tessellation separated by a deeper or lighter shade in an effect that perfectly mimics the markings of a guinea fowl or the scales of a snake, which gives the plant its common name. Native to damp, traditionally managed flood meadows across Europe, it is tragically endangered in its wild British habitats due to agricultural change, yet it is among the easiest and most rewarding of all spring bulbs in cultivation, naturalizing freely in damp grass, woodland edges, and partial shade where few other bulbs thrive as well. The combination of the hauntingly beautiful flowers, tolerance of shade and moist conditions, cold hardiness to zone 3, and free self-seeding habit makes it one of the finest spring bulbs for naturalistic and woodland plantings.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost as plants tolerate light frost.
directions: Press seed onto the surface of moist starting mix and do not cover — seed needs light to germinate. Pinch seedlings once to promote multiple spikes. Transplant to the garden a few weeks before the last frost, as snapdragons thrive in cool conditions and can tolerate a light freeze. After the primary spike blooms, cut it off to encourage a second flush from side branches.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container divisions in spring in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; sneezeweed tolerates seasonally wet conditions and is one of the few tall late-season native perennials that will perform in consistently moist to occasionally flooded sites.
directions: Plant container divisions or direct-sow seeds in spring in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately wet soil; sneezeweed is a stately native perennial of moist eastern prairies and meadows that blooms in late summer through fall — when most other perennials have finished — with large, daisy-like flowers in rich shades of red, copper, bronze, yellow, and bicolors depending on cultivar. The common name comes not from the flowers causing sneezing, but from the historical use of dried leaves as a snuff; the flowers themselves are an important late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies and bumblebees. Pinch stems in early summer to reduce height and encourage branching, or the plants can grow quite tall and may need staking. Divide every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor; popular cultivars include 'Moerheim Beauty' (red-bronze) and 'Sahin's Early Flowerer'.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost has passed and soil is warm.
directions: Snoho Doris is a tall, productive dahlia bearing salmon-coral blooms with uniquely patterned petals on very long, easy-to-harvest stems. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil after the last frost, and provide light support for the tall plants. Pinch the central shoot early to encourage more branching and stems. Cut flowers frequently to encourage continued blooming into fall. A great choice for beginning dahlia growers thanks to its reliable production.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last spring frost when soil warms.
directions: Snoho Jojo is a productive, short-statured dahlia with smoky mauve blooms carried on long stems that are excellent for cutting. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger passes. The compact plant produces cut-worthy stems from the start of the season. Deadhead and cut regularly to keep blooms coming through fall. In cold climates, lift the tubers before the first hard freeze and store them in a cool, dry place.

plant_note: Sow in fall for natural cold stratification, into lean, sandy or gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun on open, dry ground.
directions: A shrubby buckwheat of arid sagebrush steppe and sandy scabland from the Columbia Basin through the Great Basin, forming a rounded clump of narrow white-woolly leaves topped from late summer into fall by dense, snowy-white flower clusters that stand out sharply against surrounding dormant grasses. Because it blooms later than most other native buckwheats, it provides an outsized late-season nectar resource for native bees, wasps, and migrating butterflies preparing for winter. Grow in lean, sandy or gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun with no summer irrigation once established; it is highly drought tolerant and poorly suited to amended or clay garden soil. A valuable addition to dryland pollinator gardens and restoration plantings where fall-blooming natives are scarce.

common_name: Snow Bunting Crocus (White with Lilac Feathering)
plant_note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Snow Bunting is an early-blooming species crocus, flowering ahead of the larger Dutch hybrids and naturalizing readily in lawns and rock gardens.
directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; good drainage prevents corm rot during summer dormancy. Snow Bunting produces small, fragrant, creamy-white flowers delicately feathered with soft lilac-purple on the outer petals and a bright orange-yellow throat, opening among the earliest crocus of the year, often before the last snow has fully melted in colder climates. Its small scale and early bloom make it well suited to naturalizing in a lawn, rock garden, or the front of a border where it can be enjoyed up close before larger spring bulbs take over the show. Allow the grass-like foliage to die back naturally after bloom before mowing over a naturalized planting, and it will multiply steadily by cormlets to form larger drifts over the years.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; snow bush develops the most vibrant white, pink, and red coloring in full sun but tolerates and performs acceptably in partial shade.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; snow bush (snowbush, calico plant) is a Pacific Islands tropical shrub that produces some of the most elaborately variegated foliage available in tropical landscaping — the small, oval leaves are mottled, splashed, spotted, and streaked with white, pink, red, and green in patterns that vary from leaf to leaf and intensify in color through the growing season, creating a continuously shifting kaleidoscope of color. Young growth is especially vibrant, flushing pink and red before developing its characteristic multi-colored pattern. The cascading, arching branch habit creates a graceful, cottage-garden character despite the dramatic coloring. Excellent as a colorful accent in tropical mixed borders, as a container specimen, and as a vibrant informal hedge in zones 10–12. Full sun intensifies the coloring; partial shade softens it. Frost-sensitive — protect or bring indoors when temperatures approach 35°F. The cultivar 'Roseo-Picta' is the standard ornamental selection with the fullest color range.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall; naturalizes and resists squirrels.
directions: Plant snow crocus corms in fall about three inches deep in well-drained soil and full to partial sun. This early species crocus naturalizes rapidly in lawns and borders and is more squirrel-resistant than large Dutch crocus. The slender lavender flowers are among the first blooms of late winter, providing vital early forage for bees. Leave the foliage undisturbed until it withers to allow the corms to multiply.

plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil so they can flower at the earliest thaw.
directions: Plant small corms 3-4 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in fall in a well-drained, sunny site, since standing winter moisture is the main cause of rot. This species blooms even earlier than common Dutch crocus, often pushing through late snow to open cup-shaped flowers in shades of gold, cream, and blue-purple, frequently with contrasting feathered markings. Its grassy foliage is inconspicuous and disappears quickly after bloom, making it ideal for tucking into lawns, rock gardens, and the front of borders. The early nectar is an important first food source for emerging bees.

common_name: Snow Crystals Alyssum (AAS-Winning Large-Flowered White Alyssum)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in early spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade; Snow Crystals is an AAS-winning alyssum with larger individual flowers and a more vigorous, mounding habit than older, finer-textured alyssum varieties.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade. Snow Crystals is an All-America Selections-winning alyssum bred for larger individual florets and a more vigorous, denser mounding habit than older, fine-textured alyssum varieties, while retaining the same sweet honey fragrance and nonstop bloom. It forms a low, spreading carpet of small white flowers, excellent for edging, rock gardens, and filling gaps between pavers, and performs best in cool spring and fall weather, often slowing or fading in the peak heat of a Gulf South summer. Shearing the plant back by about half if it becomes leggy or stops flowering in summer heat encourages a fresh flush of bloom as temperatures cool.

common_name: Snow Flurry Aster (Prostrate Groundcover White Heath Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Snow Flurry is a prostrate, groundcover-form selection of native heath aster.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun. Snow Flurry hugs the ground in a dense, spreading mat only a few inches tall, smothered each fall in tiny white daisy flowers, an unusual groundcover form of the native heath aster useful for rock gardens, slopes, or the front edge of a sunny border where a low-growing fall bloomer is wanted. It tolerates poor, lean soil and drought well once established, in keeping with its origin as a tough native wildflower. Cut back in late winter to tidy the mat before new growth emerges in spring.

common_name: Snow Flurry Camellia (Cold-Hardy White Ackerman Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Snow Flurry is another of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy Winter-series camellia hybrids, grown for its abundant white anemone-form flowers and improved cold tolerance.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, with some protection from harsh winter wind in the coldest parts of its range. Snow Flurry is one of the most floriferous of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy Winter-series camellia hybrids, smothering its spreading, dense evergreen branches in small, white, anemone-form flowers with ruffled centers over a long fall-into-winter bloom season. Its Camellia oleifera parentage gives it notably better cold hardiness than standard Camellia japonica, letting gardeners at the colder edge of camellia range enjoy a heavy floral display that would otherwise be unreliable. The naturally spreading, slightly weeping habit also makes it useful for a low, wide evergreen groundcover-like planting rather than the more upright shape typical of most camellias. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune lightly only to shape.

common_name: Snow Fountains Weeping Cherry (Cascading White-Flowered Dwarf Cherry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped, grafted trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Snow Fountains is grafted onto an upright trunk, so the cascading branches need occasional guiding or staking while young to establish an attractive weeping form.
directions: Snow Fountains is a compact, strongly weeping flowering cherry, its slender branches cascading nearly to the ground and smothered in small, single, pure white flowers in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge, giving a fountain-like effect that suits it well as a specimen near a patio or entry where its form can be appreciated up close. It stays considerably smaller than most flowering cherries, making it a good fit for a modest-sized yard, and its glossy green summer foliage turns orange-red in fall for additional seasonal interest. Give it moist, well-drained soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to shape and remove crossing branches, and expect the shorter lifespan typical of ornamental cherries, which are prone to canker and borer problems as they age.

common_name: Snow Hill Salvia (White-Flowered Compact Meadow Sage)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Snow Hill is a compact white-flowered meadow sage, an uncommon color among Salvia nemorosa cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Snow Hill bears dense spikes of clean white flowers on a compact, tidy plant, a rare white-flowered selection among the typically blue and violet Salvia nemorosa cultivars, useful for cooling down a hot-colored border or pairing crisply with silver foliage. Shear spent flower spikes back by half after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom later in the season. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond occasional deadheading and dividing congested clumps every few years.

common_name: Snow Lady Shasta Daisy (Compact Dwarf White Shasta Daisy)
plant_note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Snow Lady is an AAS-winning dwarf shasta daisy that blooms the first year from an early seed start and stays much more compact than the tall classic shasta daisy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Snow Lady is a compact, All-America Selections-winning shasta daisy cultivar producing classic, crisp white, yellow-centered daisy flowers on a dwarf plant well under a foot tall, much shorter than the standard shasta daisy, making it a good fit for the front of a border, edging, or containers where taller cultivars would be out of scale. It flowers reliably the first year from an early seed start and continues blooming over a long summer season with regular deadheading. It is easy to grow in average garden soil and, like other shasta daisies, benefits from division every two to three years to maintain vigor as clumps become congested.

common_name: Snow N Summer Asiatic Jasmine (Variegated White-Splashed Groundcover)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Snow N Summer colors up brightest with a few hours of direct sun but tolerates the same dry shade conditions as plain green asiatic jasmine.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and mulch and water regularly until the low, twining stems knit together into a solid mat. Snow N Summer is a variegated sport of Asiatic jasmine bearing small, glossy leaves heavily splashed in white and cream over green, with new growth often flushed pink in cool weather, giving the groundcover noticeably brighter, more varied color than the plain species. It shares the same dense, weed-suppressing, low-maintenance habit prized in Asiatic jasmine, making it useful for lightening dry shade under trees, slopes, and other spots where mowing is impractical, though its variegated leaves are somewhat less vigorous and slower to fill in than solid green Asiatic jasmine. Shear back hard in early spring every couple of years to remove old woody growth and encourage dense, colorful new foliage, and watch for any all-green reverted shoots, cutting them out to keep the planting true to type.

common_name: Snow Nymph Tropical Sage (White Salvia coccinea)
plant_note: Transplant after the last frost into warm soil; this pure-white tropical sage selection performs best through the long humid Gulf Coast growing season.
directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in average, well-drained garden soil, giving each plant about a foot of room to branch into a loose mound. This all-white selection of the Gulf Coast native tropical sage lights up evening gardens and pairs well with red or purple companions, while still drawing hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies all summer long. It handles heat and humidity with ease, needs little supplemental water once rooted, and will often reseed itself in beds along the coast. Deadheading spent spikes encourages continuous rebloom from late spring through the first fall frost.

common_name: Snow Panda Loropetalum (Green-Foliage White-Flowered Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Snow Panda is a green-foliage, white-flowered loropetalum selection with a compact mounding habit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Snow Panda pairs clean green evergreen foliage with abundant white, fringe-petaled flowers in spring and scattered rebloom later in the season, a softer, more traditional look than the burgundy-leaved, pink-flowered loropetalum cultivars that dominate the trade. Its compact, mounding habit works well as a low hedge, foundation planting, or mixed-border companion to burgundy loropetalum for contrast. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; eomecon spreads vigorously by stolons and should be sited where it can colonize freely or be contained by hard edging.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and allow stolons to spread freely; eomecon is most effective when given space to form a weed-suppressing groundcover colony beneath large shrubs or trees. Eomecon chionantha is a distinctive Chinese woodland perennial producing large, scalloped, glaucous blue-green leaves on long petioles and bearing delicate white four-petaled flowers resembling small single poppies from late spring through early summer. When stems or roots are cut, the plant exudes a striking orange-red latex sap; it spreads readily by underground stolons and can colonize significant areas, making it both a vigorous groundcover and a plant that requires thoughtful siting.

plant_note: Plant transplants at or shortly after last frost; in zone 9 plant February–April and again September–November. Snow Princess is a vegetatively propagated variety (sold as transplants only, not seed) selected for superior heat tolerance vs. standard seed-grown alyssum — it continues blooming in summer heat that causes other alyssum to stop flowering. In zone 9 use as a spring and fall annual; it may slow in the hottest summer weeks but typically rebounds when temperatures moderate. The spreading, mounding habit (6–10 inches tall, 18–24 inches wide) makes it excellent for container spillers and front-border edging.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — sweet alyssum thrives in the cooler conditions of partial shade in warm climates and benefits from afternoon protection; Snow Princess is a vegetatively propagated sweet alyssum cultivar developed for exceptional heat tolerance and extended bloom compared to standard seed-grown alyssum varieties. The cascading mounds of tiny, pure white, honey-scented flowers create one of the most intensely fragrant annual flower effects available — a cloud of sweet, delicate honey fragrance that can fill an entire garden space from a relatively small planting. Sweet alyssum's fragrance is particularly concentrated in the cooler parts of the day (morning and evening), intensifying when dew is present or during spring and fall in zone 9. Snow Princess blooms continuously from planting and is self-cleaning — tiny spent flowers drop without deadheading to maintain the pristine white appearance. The spreading habit makes Snow Princess outstanding for container edges, hanging basket trailing, and as a fragrant ground cover between stepping stones where foot traffic releases the characteristic honey scent.

common_name: Snow Queen Oakleaf Hydrangea (Upright Classic Oakleaf Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, allowing room for its full 5–7 foot spread at maturity. A Georgia-bred, Award of Garden Merit-winning selection introduced in the 1960s, Snow Queen is one of the most widely planted oakleaf hydrangea cultivars, valued for its unusually erect, well-branched flower panicles that stand upright rather than nodding, and its heavier-than-average flower production compared to the wild species. Flowers open white in early summer, age to a rich pink-bronze by late summer, and can be left standing through fall and winter for continued interest, while the bold, deeply lobed foliage turns brilliant shades of red, orange, and burgundy in fall before the shrub's cinnamon, exfoliating bark takes over as the winter feature. Blooms form on old wood, so prune, if needed, only in the weeks right after flowering.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in a gritty, humus-rich, well-drained woodland or rock-garden soil in partial to full shade, setting the small rhizome about 1-2 inches deep; snow trillium is one of the very earliest spring ephemerals and needs sharp drainage rather than the constantly wet soil favored by larger trilliums.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, only 1-2 inches deep, in a spot that stays cool and does not become waterlogged over winter. Trillium nivale is the smallest and among the earliest-blooming of the North American trilliums, often pushing its tiny white flowers up through late snow cover weeks before most other woodland wildflowers appear. Its diminutive scale suits a shaded rock garden, trough, or the front edge of a woodland path where such an early bloomer would otherwise be overlooked. Purchase only nursery-propagated stock, since wild populations are uncommon and slow to recover from collection.

common_name: Snow White Indian Hawthorn (Compact White-Flowered Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Snow White is a compact Indian hawthorn cultivar producing abundant clusters of pure white flowers in spring, followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds, all on a dense, rounded mound of glossy, leathery, disease-resistant foliage. Its low, tidy habit fits foundation plantings, low borders, and coastal landscape beds, and it shares the species' outstanding tolerance for salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils, making it a dependable performer in exposed Gulf Coast sites. Good air circulation between plants helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost; euphorbia dislikes root disturbance.
directions: Crisp white-edged bracts look hand-painted and give a luminous, frosted glow even in summer heat, brightening beds and contrasting with deeper greens. Sow seed directly around the last frost, since this euphorbia resents transplanting. It thrives in full sun to part shade and average, well-drained soil and tolerates heat and drought. Wear gloves, as the milky sap can irritate skin and eyes. The variegated foliage makes a fine cut accent when the stem ends are seared.

plant_note: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery divisions in spring once soil is workable, spacing plants a foot or more apart.
