directions: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery divisions in spring once soil is workable, spacing plants a foot or more apart since the woolly silver foliage spreads quickly by trailing stems. Use it as a sun-baked lawn substitute on slopes or as edging along walkways, where its white star flowers create a frothy carpet in late spring. Shear the mat back by half right after bloom to keep it tight and prevent the center from opening up and going woody. It struggles in hot, humid summers, so gardeners south of zone 7 should treat it as short-lived and give it maximum drainage.

common_name: Snowball Agapanthus (Dwarf White Lily of the Nile)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Snowball is a compact white-flowered agapanthus selection well suited to containers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Snowball bears dense, rounded, pure white flower heads on compact scapes above narrow, dark-green strap leaves, offering a crisp, clean alternative to the blue and violet tones typical of most agapanthus. Its dwarf habit fits neatly into containers, border edges, or smaller garden spaces where larger agapanthus cultivars would be too imposing. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

plant_note: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with excellent air circulation; Snowball air plant is adapted to arid conditions and needs much lighter, less frequent misting than most tillandsias to avoid rot.
directions: Mount on bark or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with excellent air circulation; Snowball air plant is adapted to arid conditions and needs much lighter, less frequent misting than most tillandsias to avoid rot. Slender, curling leaves are so densely coated in thick, woolly, silvery-white trichomes that the entire plant appears to be covered in a soft blanket of snow, one of the fuzziest and most visually striking of all commonly grown air plants and a favorite for terrarium and driftwood displays. Native to high-elevation, fog-fed cliffs and dry Andean slopes in Ecuador and Peru, it absorbs most of its moisture from humid air and fog rather than rainfall, making it more prone to rot from overwatering than nearly any other air plant in cultivation. Mist lightly only once or twice a week rather than soaking, ensure the plant dries completely and quickly afterward, and provide bright light and strong air movement to replicate its native high-altitude habitat.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions or transplants in fall in average to dry, well-drained to moist, alkaline or acidic soil in partial shade; snowberry is one of the most shade-tolerant of all native fruiting shrubs and thrives under forest canopy where other fruiting shrubs fail.
directions: Snowberry is a low-growing, thicket-forming native shrub of North American forests and woodland edges, producing the remarkable clusters of pure white, waxy berries (technically drupes) in fall that gave the plant its name — the berries are striking against the bare winter stems, remaining on the plant through November and December as one of the last fruits visible in the winter woodland. The berries are technically mildly toxic to humans (containing saponins) but are consumed by birds including ruffed grouse, pheasants, and robins, as well as by black bears and other mammals; they were used medicinally by several indigenous tribes. Snowberry spreads freely by stolons to form dense, erosion-controlling thickets — excellent for stabilizing slopes and difficult, shaded problem areas where other shrubs struggle to establish. The small, pink tubular flowers in summer are a critical nectar source for hummingbirds and are also visited by native bees; the twinberry hummingbird (Calypte anna) in the west is particularly associated with Symphoricarpos species as a nectar plant.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, fast-draining, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; snowbrush ceanothus is a fire-adapted native of dry western forests and resents rich, wet, or heavily amended soil.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, fast-draining, rocky soil in full sun, choosing a dry slope or open site similar to the burned or disturbed forest ground this species naturally colonizes across the mountain West. Snowbrush ceanothus fixes atmospheric nitrogen at its roots, allowing it to thrive in poor soils where it also improves fertility for neighboring plants. Its dense, fragrant clusters of small white flowers in early summer are among the most heavily visited native shrub blooms for bees, butterflies, and other pollinators, while deer and elk browse the evergreen foliage and small mammals and birds eat the seed. The thick, glossy leaves and low, spreading form also provide valuable cover for ground-nesting birds.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs in fall, 3 in deep; alternatively plant 'in the green' (just after bloom) for better establishment.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 in deep in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees or in a shaded border; snowdrops are one of the first bulbs to bloom, often in January or February. They establish most successfully when transplanted 'in the green' — lifted and divided just after blooming while foliage is still active. Clumps multiply steadily and benefit from division every 3–4 years right after flowering to prevent overcrowding. Allow foliage to die back naturally; avoid mowing naturalised areas until leaves have fully yellowed.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in early spring or set out container plants; snowdrop anemone spreads by stolons and will form expanding colonies over time. Fall division is also possible.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; snowdrop anemone is a delightful spring-blooming European native producing pure white 2-inch flowers with prominent yellow stamens above deeply cut, soft green leaves. It blooms for 4–6 weeks in mid-spring and often produces a second flush of bloom in fall, making it exceptional value among shade perennials. After blooming, fluffy white seedheads resembling small puffballs follow the flowers. The plant spreads steadily by underground stolons to form a colony but is not aggressively invasive — simply pull unwanted shoots to contain the spread. It performs best in climates with cool springs and is an outstanding companion for spring bulbs under deciduous trees.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Snowflake produces unusually large individual flowers and broader foliage compared to older candytuft cultivars, giving a bolder spring display.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential, since candytuft declines quickly in heavy, wet soil. Snowflake is a robust perennial candytuft selection with larger individual flowers and broader, more substantial evergreen foliage than many older cultivars, creating an especially bold, dense carpet of white bloom in spring. It provides good year-round structure as a low evergreen groundcover for the front of a border or rock garden, and tolerates poor, rocky soil and drought well once established. Shear back lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, compact habit and encourage strong bloom the following year.

common_name: Snowflake Creeping Phlox (Pure White Moss Phlox)
plant_note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; moss phlox performs best in sharply drained, lean soil, since rich, moist soil promotes lush foliage at the expense of flowering.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky, lean soil in full sun. Snowflake is a pure white-flowered selection of moss phlox, forming a dense, low, needle-textured evergreen mat that becomes completely smothered in small white flowers for several weeks in early spring, one of the classic rock garden and slope groundcovers for that season. It thrives in the same sharply drained, lean, sunny conditions that suit other moss phlox cultivars, struggling in rich, wet soil, and works beautifully cascading over a rock wall or covering a sunny bank. Shear the mat back lightly after flowering to keep the foliage dense and encourage strong bloom the following spring.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Snowflake blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after bloom if needed, never in fall or winter.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Snowflake oakleaf hydrangea is a superior selection of the native oakleaf hydrangea, distinguished by its remarkable double flowers — each individual floret in the large panicle cluster bears extra petals and sepals that give the entire flower head a dense, fully doubled appearance unlike the single-flowered species. The enormous, conical flower clusters can reach 12 inches long and are an extraordinary display in late spring and early summer in zone 9 (May–June). The flowers open pure white, age to soft rose-pink over several weeks, then become a papery tan-cream that persists through fall as attractive dried flower heads. Snowflake was selected and patented by plantsman Jeff Beasley of Piccadilly Farm in Georgia. The large, deeply lobed, oak-like leaves develop outstanding burgundy-red to reddish-purple fall color in September–October in zone 9 — exceptional for a shade shrub. The attractive exfoliating cinnamon-brown bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Snowflake grows somewhat larger than the single-flowered species but retains the same outstanding adaptability to humid southeastern conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Snowline sedge is a slow, compact clumper well suited to small-scale plantings and container culture.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Snowline sedge is a slow, compact clumper well suited to small-scale plantings and container culture. This dwarf Japanese sedge forms tight, dome-shaped tufts of narrow, dark green leaves crisply edged in white, staying well under a foot tall and spreading only gradually into a neat mound. Its diminutive scale makes it ideal for the front edge of a shaded rock garden, tucked between stepping stones, or as a container and fairy-garden accent where larger sedges would overwhelm the space. It needs little maintenance beyond an occasional comb-out of old leaves and rarely requires dividing.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early.
directions: Delicate ivory pincushion blooms with frilled petals appear continuously from early summer to fall on sturdy two-foot stems ideal for cutting. Sow seed directly around the last frost or start indoors a few weeks early. Provide full sun and well-drained soil and deadhead often to keep the honey-scented flowers coming. Bees and butterflies are drawn to the blooms. The strong stems make it a reliable cut-flower workhorse.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Snowstorm is a vigorous, heat-tolerant bacopa series bred to hold up better through summer heat than older bacopa varieties, which often decline once temperatures climb.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping soil consistently moist since bacopa wilts quickly if allowed to dry out. Snowstorm produces a dense, trailing mound of small, dark green leaves smothered in tiny, pure white, five-petaled flowers nearly all season, making it one of the most popular spiller plants for containers and hanging baskets, especially paired with more upright annuals. It was bred for improved heat tolerance compared to older bacopa selections, which historically struggled and stopped flowering once summer temperatures climbed, though consistent moisture and a partly shaded site in the hottest part of the day still help it perform its best through a Gulf South summer. Regular fertilizing supports its continuous bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; snowy woodrush is one of the most ornamental woodrushes for bright, clumping foliage and showy white flower clusters in early summer.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; snowy woodrush tolerates dry shade better than many shade plants once established, though it looks best with consistent moisture. Luzula nivea is a clumping, evergreen woodrush native to central and southern European mountain forests, producing bright green, grass-like leaves edged with fine white hairs that give it a frosted, silvery appearance, and showy, loose clusters of brilliant white flowers in early summer that are among the showiest of any rush or sedge and are excellent as cut flowers. The fine-textured evergreen foliage provides year-round interest in shaded borders, and the plant is useful as an underplanting for shade trees, along stream banks, and as a textural contrast to broad-leaved shade perennials like hostas and astilbe.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; So Sweet is a mid-size hosta with narrow, pointed, deep-green leaves edged in a creamy-white margin, forming a neat, symmetrical mound that works well as an accent or in mass plantings under trees. In midsummer it sends up tall scapes of pale lavender flowers with an unusually strong, sweet fragrance detectable from several feet away, a trait shared by relatively few hosta cultivars and one that adds a second season of interest beyond the foliage. Divide congested clumps in early spring or fall every 4–5 years to maintain vigor, and watch for slugs, which can disfigure the leaves in consistently damp conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; soap aloe is one of the more cold-tolerant and adaptable aloe species, spreading readily by offsets into a dense colony.
directions: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; soap aloe is one of the more cold-tolerant and adaptable aloe species, spreading readily by offsets into a dense colony. Broad, spotted, blue-green leaves marked with irregular white blotches form a dense rosette that offsets freely into a spreading colony, topped by branching spikes of coral-orange to red flowers over an unusually long season, and the leaf sap has traditionally been used across southern Africa as a soap substitute, giving the species its common name. One of the toughest and most adaptable aloe species in cultivation, it tolerates more cold, drought, and neglect than many other aloes, spreading steadily by offsets to form an increasingly showy colony over time. Water only occasionally once established, and divide congested clumps to propagate or control spread as needed.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; soaptree yucca, the New Mexico state flower, is native to Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert grasslands and eventually forms a slender trunk with age.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; soaptree yucca is the state flower of New Mexico, an iconic desert grassland plant with narrow, flexible, blue-green leaves edged in white, curling fibers that top a slender trunk which develops slowly over many decades, eventually reaching tree height in old specimens. A tall, arching flower stalk rises well above the foliage in late spring, densely packed with creamy white, bell-shaped flowers pollinated exclusively by the yucca moth in an obligate partnership found throughout the genus. The roots and trunk contain natural saponins historically used by Native American and Mexican communities as a soap and shampoo substitute, the source of its common name. It is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant, requiring virtually no supplemental water once established, and makes a striking, slow-growing architectural specimen for xeriscape and desert-style landscapes.

common_name: Soapweed Yucca (Small Soapweed, Great Plains Yucca)
plant_note: Set root divisions or nursery transplants in spring into a sunny, well-drained bed and avoid disturbing the deep taproot once established.
directions: Plant in full sun on dry, sandy or rocky ground and skip supplemental irrigation once roots are established, since this prairie native thrives on neglect. It is one of the most cold- and drought-tolerant yuccas, surviving harsh Great Plains winters and prolonged summer drought without protection. Narrow, rigid, blue-green leaves with curling white fibers along the margins form low clumping rosettes that stay evergreen year-round. In early summer a stout central stalk rises with a cluster of large, waxy, greenish-white bell-shaped flowers favored by native pollinators.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; soapwort gentian is demanding in its moisture requirements and is best planted at the margin of moist woodland areas or along stream banks.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; soapwort gentian is a late-blooming native perennial producing striking, intensely deep-blue, bottle-shaped flowers in October and November — among the latest blooming native wildflowers and a vital nectar source for bumblebees in the fall garden. The flowers remain tightly closed at the top — the bumblebee must force its way inside to access the nectar, making soapwort gentian one of the most specialized pollinator plants for late-season bees. The upright stems carry pairs of opposite leaves, topped by clusters of 1–3 brilliant blue blooms. Consistent moisture is non-negotiable — this plant grows naturally at forest edges, moist meadows, and streambanks in the eastern US and will quickly decline if allowed to dry out. The extraordinary blue flower color in October distinguishes it from any other native plant in the fall shade garden.

common_name: Sodom Apple (Rubber Bush, Dead Sea Apple)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy dryland soil in full sun; Sodom apple is a drought-resistant tropical shrub native to Africa and the Middle East — producing distinctive, large, hollow, inflated seed pods resembling smooth apples that contain silky, white, cottony fiber around the seeds; ALL parts are toxic — the milky latex causes severe skin and eye irritation; excellent for xeriscape and dryland ornamental plantings in zone 9–12.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy dryland soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant; CAUTION: All parts are highly toxic; the milky latex causes severe skin and eye irritation — wear gloves and eye protection when handling. Calotropis procera (Sodom apple, rubber bush, or Dead Sea apple) is a drought-resistant tropical shrub native to the dryland regions of sub-Saharan Africa, the Sahel, North Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia — naturalized across warm, arid, disturbed habitats worldwide. The plant is related to and resembles crown flower (C. gigantea) but is typically smaller and better adapted to drier, harsher conditions. The most distinctive feature of C. procera is its unusual fruit: large (2–3 inch), perfectly round, hollow, inflated pods that look like smooth, apple-green, apple-shaped balloons — hence 'Sodom apple' (the reference to Sodom in the Dead Sea region where it is found). When ripe and dry, the pods burst open to release small seeds attached to long, silky, white, cottony fibers similar to milkweed floss; this floss has been used as stuffing material and in traditional rope-making. Small (1-inch), waxy, lavender and white, star-shaped flowers are produced abundantly. The milky white latex is extremely toxic and caustic — used historically as an arrow poison in Africa. Despite its toxicity, the fiber and bark have traditional uses across Africa and Asia.

plant_note: Plant offsets in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; soft agave is the most shade-tolerant of the commonly grown agaves — it actually performs better in partial shade in hot climates, where full sun can bleach the leaves.
directions: Plant offsets in well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — soft agave is unique among agaves in having spineless, flexible, blue-gray to pale green leaves without a terminal spine, making it the only agave safe to plant near foot traffic, children's play areas, and along walkways. The large, architectural rosettes of softly recurving, powdery blue-gray leaves are among the most beautiful foliage effects in the succulent garden. Unlike most agaves, it tolerates partial shade and actually performs better in dappled light in hot climates where full sun bleaches the gray leaf color to yellow-green. The spectacular arching flower spike (10–15 feet, resembling a giant foxtail) is produced once at maturity, then the parent rosette dies leaving offsets. Cold hardiness is limited to about 26–28°F; excellent for zone 9–11 landscapes and large containers in cooler zones.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; soft agrimony is distinguished from other agrimonies by its softly hairy stems and leaves and is native to rich, moist deciduous forests throughout eastern North America.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade for spring germination after natural cold stratification. Soft agrimony is distinguished from the related beaked agrimony (A. rostellata) by its taller stature, softly hairy stems and foliage, and larger leaflets — the downy texture gives the whole plant a gentle, velvety appearance. Like other agrimonies, it produces slender, vertical spikes of small, bright yellow, 5-petaled flowers from mid-summer into fall that provide modest late-season color in shaded native plantings, followed by hooked seed capsules that disperse by attaching to animal fur. Soft agrimony grows in rich, moist, slightly acidic to neutral deciduous forest soils throughout eastern North America and is a good, low-maintenance filler plant for the shaded native garden, especially effective when naturalized in large masses under tall forest canopy.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Soft Caress is significantly more shade-tolerant than most other mahonia species and thrives in the deep shade under tree canopies where few other shrubs perform.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Soft Caress is a revolutionary mahonia introduction from China — the first mahonia to produce completely thornless, soft, fine-textured leaves that can be touched without the painful spines that characterize traditional mahonias like Mahonia bealei and M. aquifolium. The soft, narrow, willow-like leaflets are arranged in the typical pinnate mahonia pattern but are smooth-edged and as soft to the touch as fine grass — making Soft Caress the first mahonia that can be used in foot-traffic adjacent plantings, children's play areas, and along pathways without hazard. The graceful, arching form (3–5 feet tall, similar spread) with cascading, fine-textured leaflets creates an exceptionally refined and unusual texture in the shade garden — unlike any other widely available shade shrub. In fall and early winter (October–December), Soft Caress produces racemes of bright-yellow flowers along the stem tips, followed by small, blue-black, powdery-coated fruits that are attractive to birds. The plant thrives in deep shade where few other shrubs grow well — performing under dense tree canopies that exclude even azaleas and camellias. Cold-hardy to the low-single-digits Fahrenheit, it is reliably perennial throughout zone 7–9. A landmark introduction for shade gardeners.

plant_note: Direct-sow into sandy, well-drained soil in spring, siting in longleaf pine sandhills, turkey-oak ridges, or similar disturbed conditions.
directions: Direct-sow into sandy, well-drained soil in spring, siting it in the longleaf pine sandhills, turkey-oak ridges, or disturbed roadside conditions it favors from east Texas and Louisiana across the Gulf Coastal Plain to Florida. The soft, hairy-leaved rosette sends up branching stems bearing yellow daisy flowers with a chocolate-tinted, papery green calyx that persists after bloom, giving the plant its common name. Its nectar and pollen support a range of native bees and butterflies through a long summer bloom season. It is closely related to Texas greeneyes but is better adapted to the sandy, humid conditions of the coastal plain rather than the drier Hill Country and West Texas range of its cousin.

Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; soft shield fern is more drought-tolerant than many ferns once established and adapts well to dry shade, making it one of the most garden-worthy of all European ferns. Polystichum setiferum is a beautiful, semi-evergreen to evergreen European fern producing arching, broadly lanceolate fronds with finely textured, soft, lacy pinnae that give it an exceptionally delicate appearance; it has a sprawling, vase-shaped habit with fronds lying nearly flat to the ground in many of the popular cultivars such as 'Herrenhausen' and 'Proliferum', which produce bulbils along the midrib of older fronds and can be used to propagate new plants. It is one of the most ornamental and widely used ferns for shaded woodland gardens in zones 5–9 and pairs beautifully with hellebores, cyclamen, and shade-flowering bulbs.

common_name: Soft Touch Holly (Spineless Dwarf Mounding Japanese Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Soft Touch has soft, spineless foliage unlike most hollies and a naturally low, rounded mounding habit that needs minimal pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Soft Touch is a Japanese holly selection valued for its genuinely soft, spineless foliage, pleasant to brush against or work around unlike the prickly leaves of Chinese hollies, combined with a naturally dense, low, rounded mounding habit that stays tidy with little to no pruning. Its fine-textured, boxwood-like appearance makes it a popular low-maintenance substitute for boxwood in foundation plantings and low borders, especially in humid climates where boxwood can struggle with disease. It prefers consistently moist, well-drained, acidic soil and tolerates a range of light conditions from partial shade to nearly full sun, needing only an occasional light shearing if a more formal outline is wanted.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container plants in spring in any well-drained soil in full to partial sun; among the most adaptable and Gulf Coast-appropriate yuccas, with soft, flexible leaf tips that do not injure passersby and a refined appearance suitable for close-quarters landscape use.
directions: Plant offsets or container-grown plants in spring in any well-drained to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and require virtually no maintenance once established. Yucca recurvifolia is among the most garden-friendly of all yuccas because its long, blue-green leaves recurve or droop gracefully at the tips rather than ending in a sharp point, making it safe to plant along walkways and in high-traffic areas; it produces tall (3–5 ft) spikes of large, creamy white, bell-shaped flowers in early summer that are pollinated by yucca moths and are dramatic and beautiful. The plant spreads slowly by offsets to form attractive colonies and is extremely tolerant of heat, drought, salt spray, and poor sandy soils — a nearly indestructible landscape plant for Gulf Coast and zone 8–11 gardens.

plant_note: Sow onto bare, sandy soil in fall so seedlings can establish a basal rosette over winter before flowering the following summer.
directions: Sow onto bare, sandy soil in fall so seedlings can establish a basal rosette over winter before sending up soft, gray-green hairy stems topped with classic yellow, dark-centered coneflowers the following summer. Native to the Florida Panhandle, southern Georgia, and Alabama sandhills and pine flatwoods, it is well suited to the dry, well-drained sandy soils found across the Gulf Coastal Plain. Its blooms attract a wide range of native bees, butterflies, and beneficial wasps, and the seed heads feed goldfinches into fall and winter. Give it full sun and lean soil, since rich, moist conditions promote floppy growth and shorten its life.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plug transplants in spring in wet to consistently moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; softrush is adapted to shallow water, pond margins, rain gardens, and wet ditches and tolerates standing water for extended periods.
directions: Plant divisions in wet to consistently moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil at pond margins, in rain gardens, and in wet ditches in full sun to partial shade — softrush is a graceful, clump-forming native rush of wet areas throughout the Americas, producing upright, round, deep-green, leafless stems that form arching, fountain-like clumps at the water's edge. The inconspicuous brownish flower clusters appear to emerge from the side of the stems (actually from a bract that appears continuous with the stem), adding subtle texture in summer. Softrush is a critical habitat plant for many wetland birds that weave it into nest construction, including marsh wrens and red-winged blackbirds; the seeds are consumed by waterfowl. An outstanding structural plant for rain gardens, bioswales, and natural pond margins that also serves as excellent water quality filtration for stormwater. The curly-leaved cultivar 'Spiralis' (Corkscrew Rush) is popular as an ornamental in containers and wet garden beds.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or plugs in spring directly into shallow water (up to 12 inches deep) or saturated soil at a pond or wetland margin in full sun; softstem bulrush spreads readily by rhizomes to form a dense stand and is often used in constructed wetlands for its strong water-filtering ability.
directions: Plant in shallow standing water or permanently saturated soil in full sun; spreads by rhizomes into a dense colony and tolerates both fresh and brackish water. Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani (softstem bulrush) is a tall, native wetland perennial forming striking, leafless, blue-green, rounded stems that rise straight up from the water like a stand of green pencils, topped in summer with small drooping clusters of brown flower spikelets. It is one of the most widely used native plants for pond margins, rain gardens, and constructed wetlands, valued for its dense root system's exceptional ability to filter and stabilize sediment and take up excess nutrients from runoff, as well as for the cover and nesting habitat it provides for waterfowl, red-winged blackbirds, and other wetland wildlife. The tall, architectural, vertical stems also provide strong textural contrast against broader-leaved pond plants like pickerelweed and arrowhead. An excellent, functional native choice for the wet margins of a pond, rain garden, or bioswale, zone 4–10.

common_name: Soiree Kawaii Red Shades Vinca (Micro-Bloom Disease-Resistant Vinca)
plant_note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, or plant purchased transplants; set out only when nights are consistently above 55F. Soiree Kawaii is bred with improved resistance to Phytophthora, the soilborne rot that is the most common cause of vinca bedding failures in hot, wet conditions.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun only after nights are reliably warm, since cold, wet soil stalls and yellows young vinca plants. Soiree Kawaii Red Shades is a compact annual vinca bred for a profusion of small, closely spaced deep-red flowers in a tidy mounding habit, along with meaningfully improved resistance to Phytophthora root and stem rot, the fungal disease most responsible for sudden vinca collapse in the humid, rain-prone conditions of a Gulf South summer. Like other vinca it is naturally heat- and drought-tolerant and self-cleaning, needing no deadheading to keep flowering non-stop through the hottest part of the season, and it generally outperforms impatiens and other shade annuals in a full-sun bed once truly warm weather sets in. Avoid overwatering and improve soil drainage before planting, since even disease-resistant vinca still performs poorly in soggy soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade; Solar Eclipse is a Heucherella prized for deeply lobed, near-black leaves rimmed in bright chartreuse-green, spreading gradually by short stolons to form a groundcover patch.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial shade, since Heucherella hybrids generally need more consistent moisture than pure Heuchera selections. Solar Eclipse produces deeply cut, star-shaped leaves that emerge dark purple-black in the center fading to a bright green rim, a dramatic combination that intensifies in cooler weather. Unlike clumping heucheras, this Heuchera x Tiarella hybrid spreads slowly by short stolons, eventually knitting together into a dense groundcover patch useful for edging shaded beds. Loose sprays of small white flowers appear in late spring; shear spent stalks after bloom and divide the spreading mat every few years to control its size or propagate new plants.

common_name: Solar Flare Baptisia (Yellow-to-Orange-Red Aging False Indigo)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; part of the compact Decadence breeding series, choose its planting site carefully since baptisia resents transplanting once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since the deep taproot resents transplanting once established. Solar Flare produces flower spikes that open golden yellow and shift dramatically to burnt orange and red-orange as they age, so a single spike often shows several colors at once, a striking effect distinct from the solid-color flowers of most baptisia cultivars. Its more compact, Decadence-series habit fits modern garden borders better than the tall, wide-spreading straight species while retaining baptisia's legendary toughness and longevity, and the flowers are followed by ornamental dark seed pods that persist into fall. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and essentially pest-free, needing no division and improving for many years.

plant_note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Solfatare is one of the oldest named crocosmia cultivars still in commerce, dating to the 1880s, valued as much for its bronze-tinted foliage as for its soft apricot-yellow flowers, which are held on gracefully arching sprays in mid to late summer above the smoky-bronze, sword-like leaves. The combination of warm foliage color and soft flower tone gives it a more subdued, sophisticated look than the vivid reds and oranges of most crocosmia cultivars, pairing well with other bronze- or burgundy-foliaged perennials. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 10–12; Solitaire Palm is an elegant, slender, solitary-trunked palm native to the tropical and subtropical rainforests of Queensland, Australia — producing a compact, formal crown of arching, gracefully pinnate fronds above a clean, prominently ring-marked trunk, and bearing small, bright-red ornamental fruits in drooping clusters beneath the crown shaft.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ptychosperma elegans grows well in partial shade when young — excellent for planting under light tree canopy — and can be moved to more sun as it establishes; water regularly and fertilize monthly with palm-specific fertilizer. Ptychosperma elegans (Solitaire Palm or Seaforthia Palm) is a slender, elegant, single-trunked feather palm native to the tropical and subtropical rainforests and forest margins of coastal Queensland, Australia — from Cairns south through the Wet Tropics to Brisbane — where it typically grows in moist, well-drained positions in lowland and lower-montane rainforest. The palm is distinguished by its exceptional formal elegance: a smooth, prominently ring-marked, pencil-slender trunk supporting a compact, tidy crown of arching, pinnate, bright-green fronds with a characteristic 'jagged' appearance to the leaflet tips (fish-tailed, or praemorse, leaflet ends) that give the fronds a slightly irregular but attractive quality. Masses of small, brilliant-red fruits in drooping infructescences appear periodically and add ornamental interest. Ptychosperma elegans is tolerant of partial shade, making it an excellent choice for shaded or filtered-light positions in zone 10–12 gardens, and it also adapts to full sun in humid coastal conditions. Widely planted in Hawaii, South Florida, Caribbean gardens, and tropical Asia as a refined, formal landscape accent.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown at soil level in fertile, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun with roots kept cool by mulch or low companion plants.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with the roots shaded and cool, and stake loosely or let plants sprawl through neighboring perennials since this species has no tendrils to climb with. Unlike its vining relatives, Clematis integrifolia is a true herbaceous perennial that forms an upright to sprawling clump of un-lobed leaves topped from early to midsummer with nodding, bell-shaped, deep blue-violet flowers with distinctively twisted, recurved petal tips. It combines beautifully at the front to middle of a mixed border, weaving through roses and other perennials for support, and makes an excellent, long-lasting cut flower both in bloom and as fluffy silvery seed heads afterward. Cut the entire plant back to a few inches in late winter, since it blooms on new growth each year.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; solitary pussytoes is well suited to dry woodland understory conditions in the southeastern US where summer heat and shade combine to eliminate many groundcover options.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil beneath deciduous or mixed woodland in partial to full shade; solitary pussytoes is one of the best low-growing native groundcovers for the difficult dry shade of southeastern hardwood forest understories. Antennaria solitaria is distinguished from other pussytoes by producing only a single flower head per stem rather than the clustered heads typical of the genus, a characteristic reflected in both its common and scientific names. It spreads reliably by stolons to form a fine-textured, silvery-green mat that suppresses weeds and provides early-season forage for native bees in woodlands, slopes, and shaded areas throughout the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 1–2 inches deep in fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist, deeply humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; plants take 2–3 years from division to reach full flowering size — space generously as they spread slowly by creeping rhizomes.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Solomon's plume is one of the most graceful native plants of the eastern woodland understory, producing arching stems with pairs of broad, smooth, strongly veined leaves, topped in mid-spring with fluffy, creamy-white plumes of tiny fragrant flowers — superficially similar to Solomon's seal but blooming above the leaves rather than below. The flowers are followed in fall by clusters of berries ripening from white with reddish speckles to full red, providing excellent songbird food. Young shoots are edible in spring as a cooked potherb with a mild asparagus-like flavor, and the rhizomes were used medicinally by many eastern woodland tribes. Spreads slowly by creeping rhizome to form attractive, low-maintenance colonies under deciduous trees — an indispensable native for the shaded naturalistic garden.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring before growth begins or in early fall; Solomon's Seal establishes slowly from division (2–3 years to full size) and tolerates transplanting poorly if moved in summer. In zone 9, plant divisions October–February for spring emergence. Solomon's Seal spreads slowly by rhizome to form a steadily expanding colony — space at 12–18 inches and allow 3–5 years for a full-coverage planting. Young shoots emerging in spring are edible and were used by Native Americans.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with a pH of 5.5–7.0; mulch annually with leaf mold or compost. Solomon's Seal (Polygonatum biflorum) is a graceful native woodland wildflower and groundcover found throughout eastern and central North America, from the coastal forests of New England to the eastern Texas Piney Woods — a true shade plant that thrives in the dappled light and moist, humus-rich conditions of deciduous forest understory. The arching, elegant stems (18–36 inches) with alternating pairs of oval, parallel-veined leaves and the signature dangling pairs of small, cream-white bell flowers along the stem undersides are one of the most distinctive and beautiful sights of the spring woodland. The name 'Solomon's Seal' references the circular rhizome scars left when old stems die back, which resemble official wax seals. Solomon's Seal is a remarkable shade garden plant: it emerges reliably each spring, arches gracefully throughout the growing season, produces the bell flowers and later blue-black berries attractive to birds, and then dies back cleanly in fall. Slowly expanding clumps fill the deep shade under oaks and other hardwoods where almost nothing else will grow. Young spring shoots are edible and have a history of use by Native American peoples as a cooked green similar to asparagus.

common_name: Sombrero Adobe Orange Coneflower (Compact Heat-Tolerant Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Sombrero Adobe Orange is a Proven Winners/Darwin Perennials coneflower bred for compact size, heavy branching, and strong heat and drought tolerance, well suited to a hot Gulf South summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Sombrero Adobe Orange is part of the popular Sombrero coneflower series, bred for a compact, sturdy, heavily branched habit that produces far more flowers per plant than older coneflower varieties. The vivid, warm orange, sun-facing blooms hold their color well through summer heat, and the plant's heat and drought tolerance make it a strong performer once established in a Gulf South pollinator or perennial border. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering starts to decline.

common_name: Sombrero Echinacea Series (Compact Branching Coneflower Series)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Sombrero is a coneflower breeding series bred for compact size, improved branching, heavy bloom, and a wide range of flower colors.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. The Sombrero series is a modern coneflower breeding line selected for compact, well-branched plants that produce an unusually heavy volume of flowers over a long summer-to-fall bloom season, available in a wide range of colors from classic purple-pink through red, orange, and yellow shades not found in the wild species. Its improved branching habit means more flowers per plant without staking, and like other coneflowers it is highly drought-tolerant once established and attracts butterflies, bees, and seed-eating birds. Deadhead to prolong bloom, or leave a final flush of seed heads standing for winter interest and bird forage. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Sombrero Salsa Red Coneflower (Compact Hardy Orange-Red Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Salsa Red is a Sombrero-series coneflower bred for improved winter hardiness and branching over earlier coneflower hybrids, giving reliable perennial return in a Gulf South border.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Salsa Red bears single, orange-red flowers on a compact, well-branched plant bred as part of the Sombrero series for improved hardiness and vigor over some earlier coneflower hybrids that struggled to reliably return as perennials. The strong branching habit produces a heavier flush of bloom than older single-stem coneflower types, and the plant tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead to prolong bloom through summer, or leave seed heads standing into fall and winter for goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering starts to decline.

common_name: Sombreuil Rose (Antique White Climbing Tea Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall at the base of a support; Sombreuil is an 1850 climbing tea rose prized for flat, quartered, creamy-white blooms and strong performance in the heat and humidity of Gulf South gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor, allowing 4-6 feet for its climbing spread. Introduced in France in 1850, Sombreuil is a climbing tea rose bearing large, flat, densely quartered, creamy-white blooms tinged with the faintest blush of pink, carrying a light tea fragrance and considered one of the finest white antique climbers for its old-fashioned flower form. It blooms repeatedly from spring through fall, most heavily in spring, and performs reliably in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South with good resistance to blackspot compared to many climbing roses. Train the long canes horizontally along a fence or arbor rather than straight up a post, since horizontally trained canes produce far more flowering side-shoots than vertical ones. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to remove spent wood, saving any structural pruning for full winter dormancy.

common_name: Something Old Something New Morning Glory
plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm; nick or soak the hard seed coat first.
directions: This blend pairs nostalgic favorites like sky-blue Heavenly Blue with newer starred varieties for a mix of climbing morning glory flowers. Nick or soak the hard seed, then sow directly into warm soil after frost near a fence or trellis for the twining vines to climb. Give the plants full sun and average soil; overly rich soil favors foliage over flowers. Water regularly to keep the vines vigorous through summer. Note the seeds are toxic if eaten, so keep them away from children and pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this tetraploid cultivar produces heavily ruffled, substantial blooms that benefit from full sun to develop their best color and form.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Something Wonderful is a tetraploid daylily prized for large, heavily ruffled lavender-pink flowers with a contrasting green throat, the ruffled edge giving the bloom exceptional substance and a lightly gold-dusted sheen in bright light. It is a vigorous, floriferous grower that produces well-branched scapes carrying many buds per stem, extending the effective bloom season well beyond a single flush. Remove spent scapes after flowering finishes to keep the clump tidy and redirect energy into the crown for the following year. Divide every three to four years in spring as clumps become congested, replanting divisions promptly to minimize root stress.

common_name: Sonata Cosmos (Compact Dwarf Bedding Cosmos Series)
plant_note: Direct sow after frost in average soil; overly rich soil reduces blooms. Sonata is a compact, dwarf cosmos series bred for bedding displays and containers, staying shorter and sturdier than tall heirloom cosmos types.
directions: Direct sow in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, since overly fertile soil produces excess foliage at the expense of flowers. Sonata is a dwarf cosmos series bred to stay compact and sturdy, avoiding the tall, floppy growth of many heirloom cosmos varieties, which makes it much better suited to bedding displays, borders, and containers where a shorter, self-supporting plant is needed. It produces the same large, daisy-like flowers in white, pink, and crimson over a long summer season, drawing bees and butterflies, and its shorter stature means it rarely needs staking even in open, windy sites. Deadheading spent blooms extends the flowering season into fall.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Song of India is a slow-growing, easy-care dracaena that tolerates lower indoor light better than many variegated foliage plants.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Song of India is a slow-growing, easy-care dracaena that tolerates lower indoor light better than many variegated foliage plants. Narrow, gracefully arching leaves are edged in bright creamy-yellow with a soft green center, densely whorled around slender canes that branch and thicken with age into a full, multi-stemmed small tree, the yellow margins often flushing pink on new growth in bright light. One of the more forgiving variegated dracaenas, it tolerates the lower light and drier air of a typical home or office better than many showier foliage plants, making it a popular, long-lived floor or tabletop specimen depending on its stage of growth. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, avoid overwatering which causes root rot, and wipe dust from the leaves periodically.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; deadhead spent flower clusters through summer to encourage continued rebloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and deadhead spent flower clusters through the summer to keep the rebloom cycle going. Unlike traditional weigela cultivars that flower only in a single spring flush on old wood, the Sonic Bloom series flowers on both old and new wood, producing a heavy spring display of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers followed by continued waves of bloom through summer into fall — dramatically extending the season of interest for a shrub usually valued for only a few spring weeks. Its hummingbird-attracting flowers and repeat bloom make it a strong choice where a longer season of color is wanted from a single shrub. Little pruning is required beyond removing dead or crossing branches, since rebloom on new wood makes timing far less critical than with old-wood-only weigela cultivars.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; Sonoma sage spreads by rooting stems to form a low, wide-spreading groundcover mat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; Sonoma sage is a low, mat-forming California native groundcover with soft, gray-green, aromatic leaves and short spikes of pale lavender-blue flowers held just above the foliage in late spring, drawing bees and occasional hummingbirds. Trailing stems root as they spread, gradually covering considerable ground and making it a valuable low-water groundcover alternative to turf on dry slopes, under oaks, and in chaparral-style landscaping. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established, going dormant or semi-dormant with reduced leaf size during the hottest, driest part of summer and flushing fresh growth with fall and winter rains, in keeping with its Mediterranean-climate origins. Avoid summer irrigation on established plantings, which encourages root rot and fungal problems in this drought-adapted native.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost, or start indoors 6-8 weeks early for a head start on bloom.
directions: Sonora carries an unusually wide mahogany-red band circling each ray petal's base, tipped in bright gold, giving the large 5-6 inch blooms a bold two-color banded look distinct from the mostly solid-gold black-eyed Susans typically grown from seed. Its branching, compact habit produces heavy bud counts on relatively short stems, making it well suited to containers and the front of sunny borders as well as cut-flower rows. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this warm-season plant germinates and flowers quickly from seed, usually blooming within ten weeks of sowing. Deadhead to prolong the show through summer heat, when many other bedding annuals begin to fade.

common_name: Sooty Dianthus (Dark Chocolate Foliage with Near-Black Crimson Flowers)
plant_note: Direct sow or plant transplants in fall for spring bloom in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Sooty is a Victorian-era Sweet William cultivar grown as much for its near-black foliage as its flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Sooty is a striking Victorian heirloom Sweet William grown as much for its dark, chocolate-maroon foliage as for its clusters of small, near-black crimson flowers, a dramatically dark color combination unusual among garden dianthus and useful for adding contrast next to silver or chartreuse companions. Sweet William is technically a short-lived biennial or short-lived perennial, often grown as a biennial sown one year to bloom the next, and it self-sows readily where happy. Deadhead spent flower clusters to extend bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding if a tidier planting is desired.

common_name: Sops in Wine Dianthus (Maroon-and-White Fringed Heirloom Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Sops in Wine is an old English cottage pink historically used to flavor wine and ale.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Sops in Wine is an old English heirloom cottage pink bearing deep maroon-red petals with a white base, each finely fringed along the edge, and carries the traditional clove fragrance the species is named for; historically the flowers were steeped in wine and ale to add flavor and color, giving the cultivar its name. It forms a low, tidy mat of gray-green foliage that stays attractive between bloom flushes. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and encourage a possible second flush.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; Soraya is an All-America Selections winning branching sunflower producing abundant, bright golden-orange blooms on strong, well-branched plants, valued for both garden display and cut-flower use.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches for good branching. Soraya was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its outstanding combination of bright, rich golden-orange flowers, strong branching habit, and excellent garden performance, producing an abundance of medium-large blooms over a long season rather than a single giant flower. The sturdy, well-branched plants hold up well in the garden and produce enough stems for repeated cutting without depleting the display, making Soraya equally useful as a garden specimen and as a reliable cut-flower producer for home bouquets. Deadhead or harvest spent blooms regularly to encourage continued branching and flowering from midsummer through the first frost. Grow in full sun, and stake or provide wind protection in exposed sites, since well-branched plants loaded with multiple large flowers can become top-heavy in storms.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting, or plant transplants in fall; in zone 9 plant transplants September–November for fall and winter bloom, or January–February for spring bloom. Sorbet XP Orange is an All-America Selections winner selected for earlier blooming (15–20 days faster than standard Sorbet series) and the rare, vivid true orange color in viola — distinct from the yellow-orange or peach-orange of most orange viola selections. In zone 9 violas (Viola cornuta) perform far better than pansies (Viola x wittrockiana) in winter and early spring heat — the smaller, more numerous flowers of viola are more heat-tolerant and continue blooming as temperatures rise in March–April, lasting 3–4 weeks longer into spring than pansies. The XP suffix designates early-blooming performance.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade — in zone 9 afternoon shade extends the cool-season bloom period before summer heat causes decline — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil with good drainage; Sorbet XP Orange Viola is an All-America Selections award-winning compact viola producing very early, prolific, vivid true-orange flowers in the small, rounded, five-petaled form characteristic of Viola cornuta — a more heat-tolerant, smaller-flowered viola species that outperforms pansies (V. x wittrockiana) in the zone 9 climate where winter temperatures are too mild for pansy to set flower buds reliably and spring warmth arrives before pansies peak. The vivid orange color of Sorbet XP Orange is genuinely rare in violas — most 'orange' viola selections trend toward yellow-orange or salmon rather than the clear, saturated mid-orange that this selection provides — making it a distinctive and visually striking addition to winter and spring cool-season plantings. The extremely high flower count, compact spreading habit, and extended bloom season relative to pansies make Sorbet XP Orange one of the most practically useful and reliable cool-season annual selections for zone 9 winter containers, window boxes, and border plantings, providing color from November through April in the mild, pleasant part of zone 9's garden year.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the upper half of the large, multi-layered bulb exposed above the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Boophone disticha is extremely slow-growing — bulbs may take 10–20 years to reach flowering size. The bulb is highly toxic — one of the most toxic South African plants — containing alkaloids used by San Bushmen to poison arrows. The fan of stiff, wavy-edged leaves is arranged in a distinctive flat plane (disticha = two-ranked).
directions: Plant large bulbs (upper half exposed) in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Boophone disticha is one of the most remarkable botanical curiosities of the South African flora — a plant of multiple botanical distinctions that make it a prize for collectors and botanically curious gardeners. The flat fan of stiff, wavy-margined, strap-shaped leaves arranged in a strict, two-ranked, fan-like plane (the disticha arrangement that gives the species name) is immediately distinctive and architecturally impressive. In spring, a dense, spherical to hemispherical umbel of 50–100 individual, bright-pink to deep-rose, tubular flowers appears on a stout scape from the large, grapefruit-to-soccer-ball-sized, multi-layered bulb — a vivid, spherical pompon of pink. After flowering, the entire, now-papery-dry seed head detaches from the scape and tumbles across the landscape like a tumbleweed, dispersing seeds by wind as it rolls — an extraordinary and unique seed-dispersal strategy for a bulb plant. The common name 'Sore-Eye Flower' refers to the traditional belief that its pollen causes irritation; the bulb is highly toxic and was used by indigenous peoples to poison arrowheads. The extraordinary combination of unique leaf arrangement, spectacular flower ball, tumbleweed seed dispersal, and legendary toxicity makes this one of the most interesting bulbs in the world. A patience plant — 10+ years to first flower from seed.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring after last frost in well-drained to dry soil in full sun; sorrelvine dies back to the ground after hard freezes in zone 8-9 but re-emerges vigorously from thickened roots in spring. It grows naturally on rocky limestone slopes and caliche in central and south Texas.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, rocky, alkaline or neutral soil in full sun in zones 7–11; sorrelvine is a native Texas vine of the same family as grapes, naturally scrambling over limestone slopes, rocky draws, and caliche outcrops across central and south Texas. The trifoliate leaves superficially resemble poison ivy — enough to cause alarm — but sorrelvine has tendrils (poison ivy doesn't) and causes no skin irritation. The small black berries are eaten by birds but toxic to humans. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, with thickened roots that store water. In zone 9a it makes a vigorous summer vine that provides quick cover on a fence or trellis during the hottest part of the year. Dies back after hard frost but re-sprouts reliably from the base in spring.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and keep the root zone consistently moist.
directions: Souliea vaginata is a little-grown Ranunculaceae relative of Actaea and Cimicifuga, native to cool montane forests of western China, forming a low clump of glossy, compound, dark-green leaflets. In spring it sends up short spikes of unusual purple-brown, cup-shaped flowers held just above the foliage, followed later by inflated, papery seed pods that add a second season of interest. It prefers the same cool, humus-rich, evenly moist woodland conditions favored by hepaticas and epimediums, and resents hot, dry summer exposure. A curiosity for specialist shade gardeners building a collection of unusual Asian woodland genera.

common_name: Soulmate Swamp Milkweed (Compact Rose-Pink Native Milkweed Selection)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring into consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun; Soulmate is a compact selection of swamp milkweed bred to stay shorter and more floriferous than the wild species without losing its wetland toughness.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Soulmate is a compact selection of the native swamp milkweed, bred to stay a shorter, tidier 18 to 24 inches while still producing the dense, rose-pink, vanilla-scented flower clusters that make the species a monarch and pollinator magnet. Its shorter, sturdier habit fits more easily into a mixed perennial border or rain garden than the taller wild species, which can reach four feet or more, while still tolerating the wet soils and occasional standing water it needs to thrive. As a larval host for monarch butterflies and a heavy nectar source for many other butterflies and native bees, it is a strong choice for a pollinator garden with a moist low spot or pond margin. Cut back spent flower stalks after seed pods form to prevent excess self-seeding, or leave pods to split and release silky-tufted seed for wildlife interest.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring; sourwood resents transplanting once established and requires strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) — alkaline soil causes rapid, permanent decline. Avoid disturbing the root zone once planted.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; sourwood is a native American forest tree considered by many horticulturalists to be the finest small to medium-sized ornamental tree native to the eastern United States, offering four seasons of distinction: long, drooping panicles of small, white, lily-of-the-valley-like flowers in July and August (a rare native tree that flowers in midsummer when few other trees bloom); spectacular fall foliage in fiery scarlet-red to deep crimson — among the earliest and most vivid trees to color in autumn; persistent, creamy-white seed capsules that decorate the bare branches through winter; and elegant, slightly drooping branch tips that give the tree a graceful, somewhat weeping quality year-round. Sourwood honey (made by bees collecting nectar from the flowers) is considered among the finest American honeys. Strictly requires strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) and declines rapidly if planted in alkaline or compacted soils. Resents root disturbance after planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with a pH of 4.5–6.0 in partial shade to full sun; sourwood is naturally an understory tree in the Appalachians and is remarkably shade tolerant when young, making it an excellent choice beneath high-canopy oaks and hickories. It resents root disturbance and transplants best while young from containers; avoid alkaline soils and compacted clay. Top-dress annually with pine bark or leaf mulch to maintain soil acidity and moisture.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil; sourwood is among the most multi-season native trees of eastern North America, earning its place in the landscape with four distinct seasons of interest — it is a member of the heath family (Ericaceae) and one of the few trees in that family to achieve canopy stature. In July, when most trees offer nothing but foliage, sourwood erupts in long, arching, drooping panicles of small white urn-shaped flowers reminiscent of lily-of-the-valley — these are the primary source of the prized sourwood honey produced by Appalachian beekeepers, considered by many to be the finest American varietal honey. Fall color is nothing short of spectacular: leaves turn vivid scarlet to deep crimson while the persistent creamy seed capsules hang in graceful clusters, often coinciding with yellow foliage of neighboring trees for a striking contrast. The glossy, lance-shaped leaves have a pleasantly sour taste (hence the common name) and the tree's naturally layered branching habit provides excellent winter structure; it is exceptionally long-lived, low-maintenance, and virtually pest-free when sited in appropriately acidic soils.

plant_note: Divide established clumps after flowering in late spring (when the foliage begins to die back) or plant container-grown plants in fall; South African bulbinella grows in winter and flowers in late winter through spring (blooming when the South African Cape experiences its cool, moist season), then goes summer dormant. It requires moist conditions during the growing season and dryness during summer dormancy.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; South African bulbinella is a bold, cool-season-active perennial from the Cape mountains of South Africa, producing tufts of bright-green, strap-shaped or broader, succulent-tinged leaves that emerge in autumn, grow through winter, and in late winter through spring send up upright, dense, bottlebrush-like spikes of vivid, golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers — each spike 12–18 inches long, packed with hundreds of individual yellow blooms creating a dense cylindrical shape similar to a yellow bottlebrush or a very fat, yellow cat's tail. The bloom coincides with the Cape fynbos wet season and represents a flash of intense yellow color in the late-winter to spring garden at a time when few other bold yellow flowers are available. After flowering and seed-set in early summer, the plant goes completely summer dormant, disappearing until autumn rains trigger new growth. Outstanding for Mediterranean-climate gardens and zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where the seasonal rhythm of cool-wet/hot-dry matches the plant's natural South African Cape requirements.

common_name: South Pacific Scarlet Canna (AAS-Winning Seed-Grown Canna)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or seed-grown transplants once soil has warmed; South Pacific Scarlet was an All-America Selections winner bred to flower reliably from seed in a single season, producing vivid scarlet-red blooms on compact, uniform plants with attractive green foliage.
directions: Plant rhizomes or seed-grown transplants a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun. South Pacific Scarlet was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its ability to flower reliably and uniformly from seed within a single growing season, an important breakthrough for a genus traditionally propagated by rhizome division, which made cannas slower and more expensive to bring to market as bedding plants. It produces vivid, true-scarlet flowers on compact, well-branched plants with clean green foliage, blooming continuously from early summer through frost. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump over time. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; South Seas is an award-winning tetraploid daylily prized among collectors for its rich melon-coral color and heavy substance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. South Seas is a tetraploid daylily bred by well-known hybridizer Curt Hanson, admired for its large, rich melon-to-coral-red flowers with a contrasting green throat and heavy, substantial petals that hold their color well through the heat of summer. Its award-winning bloom quality has made it a favorite among daylily collectors seeking strong, saturated warm colors distinct from the more common yellows and pastels. Like other daylilies it is easy to grow in average soil with routine watering, and mature clumps can be divided every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and increase the planting.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to filtered sun in spring; adder's-tongue fern is mycorrhizal-dependent, easy to overlook, and slow to increase, so mark plantings clearly and avoid disturbing the soil around them.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to filtered sun in spring; adder's-tongue fern is mycorrhizal-dependent, easy to overlook, and slow to increase, so mark plantings clearly and avoid disturbing the soil around them. Each plant produces just a single smooth, undivided, oval sterile blade with a separate slender fertile spike rising from its base, tipped with a row of embedded spore cases that suggest a snake's tongue — a form unlike any typical fern. It grows in damp meadows, fens, and open moist woodland edges, going dormant underground for much of the year and reappearing only briefly each growing season, so patience and consistent soil moisture matter more than active care. Because populations are small and easily lost to mowing or soil compaction, it is best grown in a protected, undisturbed corner of a shade or bog garden.

plant_note: Ideal for rain gardens, swales, and wet edges of ponds or streams. Plant in early spring in moist to wet soil; tolerates periodic flooding and heavy clay soils better than most viburnums.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in a location that receives partial shade, such as the edge of a woodland, streambank, or rain garden basin. Unlike most shrubs, this viburnum tolerates and even benefits from periodic inundation and clay soils. Water generously through the establishment period and maintain steady soil moisture thereafter — it will not perform well in dry conditions. White flower clusters open in spring and attract numerous native pollinators, while the dark blue fall berries are eagerly consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and other frugivorous birds.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or cold-stratify seeds at 40°F for 4–6 weeks, then sow indoors 8 weeks before last frost. Southern beardtongue tolerates poor, sandy, acidic soil better than most penstemons.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky, lean, acidic soil in full sun; southern beardtongue is a slender, wiry native of the southeastern Coastal Plain from Virginia to Florida, well adapted to the acidic sandhills, pine flatwoods, and open dry woods where most penstemons would fail. The tubular flowers in late spring through early summer are pink-lavender with two-lipped openings, arranged on spikes that attract ruby-throated hummingbirds and bumblebees. Unlike many penstemons, this species tolerates the humid heat of zones 7–9 and the highly acidic, low-fertility sandy soils characteristic of the southeastern Coastal Plain. Short-lived as a perennial (typically 3–5 years) but self-seeds reliably to maintain a colony. An underutilized native wildflower for naturalistic plantings in the Southeast.

common_name: Southern Belle Hibiscus (Classic Mixed-Color Seed-Strain Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants or start seed indoors in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Southern Belle is a classic seed-strain giving mixed white, pink, and red 10-inch blooms on a tall, four-to-six-foot plant.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Southern Belle is a classic, long-cultivated seed strain producing enormous, 10-inch dinner-plate flowers in a mix of white, pink, and red on the same planting, giving a colorful, varied display on tall, robust, four-to-six-foot plants. Its seed-grown, mixed-color nature makes it economical for filling a large area with bold summer color. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location, and watch for Japanese beetle damage where present.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in sandy, well-drained, acidic, infertile soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring. Southern Blazingstar thrives in the longleaf pine savanna and coastal flatwood conditions of the southeastern coastal plain.
directions: Southern Blazingstar is a small, slender native perennial of the sandy, open longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods, and coastal plain prairies of the Gulf and South Atlantic states from Georgia to Louisiana, producing dense wand-like spikes of small pink-purple flower heads in early fall that attract monarch butterflies, skippers, and native bees during the critical fall migration period. Less showy than the larger Liatris species but ecologically significant in its native longleaf pine ecosystem, Southern Blazingstar is a component of the diverse herbaceous layer that characterizes intact coastal plain savannas. Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in sandy, infertile, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; established corms are drought-tolerant and long-lived, forming tight clumps that slowly expand over time in appropriate open, sunny conditions.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil at the water's edge or in shallow water up to 4 inches deep; fall planting allows roots to establish before spring bloom.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil at the margin of a pond, stream, or rain garden in partial shade to full sun; southern blue flag is the native wetland iris of the coastal South and Southeast, growing naturally in swamps, freshwater marshes, wet meadows, and pond margins from Virginia to Florida. The violet-blue flowers veined with white and yellow in late spring are extraordinarily beautiful and important for early bumblebees and native bee species large enough to pollinate the structured flowers. The bold, sword-like leaves provide vertical structure in water gardens. Plant where the rhizome can stay moist — unlike bearded irises, this species must not dry out. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested. A superb companion to pickerel rush, arrowhead, and swamp lily in water garden designs.

plant_note: Set container-grown plants into humus-rich, well-drained soil in spring or fall, spacing to allow for suckering spread.
directions: Plant in average to humus-rich soil with reliable moisture, siting in partial shade to filtered woodland light where afternoon sun is softened; it tolerates deeper shade than most flowering shrubs but blooms more heavily with some morning sun. This southeastern US native suckers gently to form a low colony, producing clusters of tubular pale-yellow flowers from early to late summer that age to orange-red, giving a long, two-toned bloom display. New growth cultivars selected from this species show burgundy-black or bronze foliage that colors best with a bit more light exposure.
