In zones 9–10 with excellent drainage it can be grown in the open garden with a reliable summer dry period. Naturalizes freely in California coastal climates similar to its native habitat.
directions: Plant corms in fall in sharply drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; spider iris is among the most bizarre and visually fascinating members of the iris family — a South African fynbos endemic producing flowers of extraordinary complexity, with six wavy, crinkled, spider-leg-like tepals in cream, brown, purple-black, and maroon arranged in intricate combinations and textures, the wavy margins and darkly mottled patterns creating a flower that resembles a small, ornate mosaic. The flowers are short-lived (each lasting a single day or two) but appear successively over several weeks in winter and spring and carry a distinctive, musky-vanilla fragrance that is strong and reminiscent of chocolate to some observers. It grows through the cool season of its native winter-rainfall Western Cape habitat and must be kept completely dry in summer. Related to the moraeas, it belongs to the same iridaceae tribe and requires identical cultivation. A collector's plant of unique character, grown for its botanical bizarreness as much as its fragrance.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist to wet, well-drained to moderately drained fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; hymenocallis thrives near water features, pond margins, and in moist low-lying areas of zone 7–11 gardens.
directions: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun near water features, pond edges, or in moist low spots; the spider lily produces one of the most structurally distinctive flowers in the summer garden — a white central cup is surrounded by six long, narrow, arching white petals that give each flower an elegant spider-like form, and the intensely sweet perfume is released especially in the evening hours. The broad, strap-like, semi-evergreen foliage remains attractive throughout the year in zone 9–11. Established clumps multiply by offsets and require minimal care; divide every 4–5 years in late fall after the foliage dies back when clumps become crowded. In zone 7–8, lift bulbs after the first frost and store in a cool, dry location through winter.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or fall; set crowns just 1 in below soil level in full sun to light afternoon shade.
directions: Plant fans with the crown about 1 in deep, spreading roots outward over a small mound of soil in the hole, and water thoroughly to settle the soil. Spider Miracle belongs to the spider class of daylilies, defined by petals at least four times longer than they are wide, producing dramatically narrow, twisting, lavender-purple petals with a lime-green throat that give each flower a starburst, spidery form very different from the rounder, more overlapping petals of classic daylily types. Its tall scapes and unusual flower form make it a strong textural contrast planted among rounder-flowered daylily cultivars. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; spider orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; spider orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11. Extraordinarily long, narrow, wavy-margined, pale green to yellow-green petals and sepals radiate outward from each flower in a dramatic, spidery silhouette that gives the species its common name, dotted with warty green markings near the flower's center that are believed to mimic spiders and attract wasp pollinators seeking prey. Native to Central American cloud forests, it thrives with the same intermediate warmth and bright, filtered light as many other epiphytic orchids, and its unusual, architectural flower form makes it a striking specimen even among a broader orchid collection. Water when the bark mix approaches dryness, feed lightly with a balanced orchid fertilizer during active growth, and provide bright indirect light for the most reliable flowering.

common_name: Spider Orchid (Arching Brassia, Colombian Spider Orchid, Arcuigera Brassia)
plant_note: Grow in a medium-to-large pot with medium bark or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to partial direct light; Brassia arcuigera is one of the largest-flowered Brassia species, with individual spidery flowers reaching 6–10 inches tip to tip of the longest extended sepals. The flowers are vivid yellow-green to yellow with brown to cinnamon spotting and blotching on the sepals and petals, with a light, pleasant fragrance. Blooms primarily in spring. The spidery flowers mimic female spider wasps, and male wasps attempt to mate with the lip, effecting pollination. Intermediate temperatures preferred. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light in medium bark — Spider Orchid grows most vigorously in intermediate temperatures with bright, filtered light and produces its extraordinary long-sepaled flowers most freely when given generous pot size and adequate root room. Brassia arcuigera is a robust, sympodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru — one of the larger-flowered Brassia species (a genus sometimes called 'spider orchids' for the elongated, spreading, insect-leg-like sepals of their flowers). The plant produces flattened, compressed pseudobulbs 4–5 inches tall with 2–3 broad, somewhat fleshy, strap-like leaves. In spring, long (to 24 inches), arching flower spikes emerge bearing 6–10 large flowers, each one remarkable for the extraordinary length of the sepals: the lower lateral sepals extend downward and outward in a strongly arching pattern (giving the species name arcuigera, 'bearing an arch') to total flower widths of 6–10 inches tip-to-tip. The flower color is vivid yellow-green to bright yellow with irregular brown to cinnamon spotting concentrated toward the sepal bases, and the broad lip is white with brown spots. The spidery appearance of the flower is an adaptation to its pollination system — male spider wasps (Pepsis species) mistake the lip for a large female wasp and attempt to mate with it, picking up pollinaria in the process. A spectacular orchid of extraordinary flower form. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root plantlets (spiderettes) by pinning them to moist soil or placing in water; in zone 9b–11, spider plant can be grown as an outdoor groundcover in deep shade where its stolons will root and spread to cover ground. In zone 8–9a, treat as a container plant or protect from frost.
directions: Root spiderette plantlets in water or moist soil and plant in any moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade — spider plant is one of the world's most popular houseplants and a valuable outdoor shade groundcover in tropical and subtropical gardens, producing fountains of long, arching, strap-like leaves (solid green or with bold cream-white centers or margins) and long, arching stolons tipped with miniature plantlets that root wherever they contact moist soil. In zone 9b–11 it grows as a naturalized groundcover in deep shade under trees, producing a lush carpet that requires almost no care. It tolerates deep shade, inconsistent watering, and low soil fertility better than almost any other shade groundcover. The variegated form (cream-and-green striped) is especially bright in dark shade. NASA studies identified spider plant as one of the most effective air-purifying houseplants, removing formaldehyde and other volatile organic compounds from indoor air.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Spider Web is a variegated Fatsia japonica cultivar with fine white speckling scattered across each large, glossy, deeply lobed leaf, giving the foliage a frosted, cobweb-like appearance.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, protected from direct hot afternoon sun, which scorches the fine variegation faster than it would plain green foliage. Spider Web is a striking variegated sport of the popular architectural shade shrub Fatsia japonica, with each large, glossy, hand-shaped leaf speckled in fine white flecks that give the whole plant a frosted, almost cobweb-dusted look distinct from the bolder white-edged variegation of other Fatsia cultivars. It brings dramatic tropical-looking texture to a deep shade bed where few other shrubs perform, and its bold foliage pairs well with ferns, hostas, and other fine-textured shade perennials as a contrasting anchor plant. Established plants tolerate the humid Gulf Coast summer well but appreciate protection from hard freezes in the colder parts of their range; a hard frost may damage foliage even where the roots survive and resprout in spring. Prune only to remove damaged or overly leggy stems, since Fatsia branches slowly and responds well to renewal pruning if it becomes overgrown.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Spider's Web' is less vigorous and more cold-sensitive than plain green fatsia, so give it a sheltered site or grow it in a container that can be moved for winter protection.
directions: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Spider's Web' is less vigorous and more cold-sensitive than plain green fatsia, so give it a sheltered site or grow it in a container that can be moved for winter protection. This striking fatsia selection carries the same bold, glossy, deeply lobed, tropical-textured leaves as the species but heavily speckled and mottled with white, giving each leaf a frosted, web-like appearance that brightens a deeply shaded corner. Rounded clusters of small white flowers appear in fall on mature plants, followed by black berries, though the plant is grown almost entirely for its dramatic variegated foliage rather than its modest bloom. Because variegated growth is less vigorous than solid green fatsia, prune out any reverted all-green shoots promptly to keep the plant's variegation strong, and protect from hard freezes and drying winter wind at the colder edge of its range.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring around last frost date; cold stratification for 4 weeks improves germination of seed.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds for 4 weeks before sowing; established divisions establish more reliably than seed-grown plants and can be done in spring or fall. Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, average to rich soil; plants tolerate wet conditions and make excellent rain garden plants. The three-petaled flowers in purple, blue, pink, or white open only for a single morning but are produced in rapid succession over many weeks. Shear the entire plant to 8 in after the main bloom flush to stimulate fresh foliage and a second round of flowers in fall.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; spike winter hazel is among the most widely available Corylopsis species in US nurseries and is known for unusually long, many-flowered racemes. Site in a sheltered location to protect from late winter frosts.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade, sheltered from late winter frosts; spike winter hazel is a Japanese species distinguished from other Corylopsis by the unusually long, cylindrical racemes containing up to 20 lemon-yellow flowers each — the longest pendulous flower clusters of commonly grown winter hazels. The flowers are slightly larger than those of C. pauciflora and carry a soft, sweet, cowslip-like fragrance that is particularly pleasant in the mild days of late winter and early spring. The purple-tipped stamens create a colorful contrast with the pale yellow petals. Leaves emerge with an attractive reddish-purple flush that matures to blue-green, turning golden yellow in fall. Hardy to zone 5, this is one of the more reliable winter hazels for cold-climate gardens. Combines beautifully with early-blooming witch hazels (Hamamelis) for an extended winter flowering display.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–12; Spiked Costus is a Caribbean and tropical American native spiral ginger — naturalized in Florida and widely found in Gulf Coast gardens — producing tall, spiraling, leafy canes topped by brilliant scarlet-red, pine-cone-like flower spikes from which small, bright-yellow flowers emerge successively from spring through fall, and thriving in the partial shade of large trees.
directions: Plant Costus spicatus rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; mulch well to retain moisture and protect the rhizome in zone 9 where frost kills the tops but the roots re-emerge in spring; divide clumps every 2–3 years to maintain vigor and increase; harvest the mature scarlet bracts for use as attractive cut foliage. Spiked Costus is native to the West Indies and adjacent mainland tropical Americas and has become naturalized in moist, disturbed areas of South and Central Florida, where it thrives in partial shade under oaks and palms in the Gulf Coast climate. The spirally arranged leaves on the tall, cane-like stems and the handsome scarlet-red, waxy, bract-covered cone at the tip — from which small, yellow, tubular flowers emerge one at a time — create a bold, tropical effect in the shade garden from late spring through fall. The bracts and stems are decorative in arrangements, lasting well. A highly reliable and tough plant for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens — dying back to the ground after frost in zone 9 and re-emerging vigorously each spring from the spreading rhizome. Hummingbirds visit the flowers regularly. The stems have been used in traditional medicine in the Caribbean. Naturalizes readily in suitable moist, shaded conditions and can spread to form large colonies.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; spiked ginger lily is among the more cold-hardy Hedychium species, tolerating brief freezes once its rhizomes are established and mulched.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; spiked ginger lily is among the more cold-hardy Hedychium species, tolerating brief freezes once its rhizomes are established and mulched. Broad, banana-like leaves rise from stout canes topped in late summer by dense, upright spikes of fragrant, pale yellow to cream flowers with a prominent orange-red throat marking, followed by showy orange seed capsules that split to reveal bright red seeds persisting into fall. Native to Himalayan forests from Afghanistan to southwestern China, its aromatic rhizome has long been used in traditional medicine and incense in its native range, and the plant itself brings both fragrance and bold tropical texture to a shaded or partly sunny border. Mulch heavily over winter at the colder end of its range and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall or divide clumps in spring; spiked wood oats is more shade and drought tolerant than the related inland sea oats (Chasmanthium latifolium) and performs well in dry to moderately moist conditions in full to partial shade.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — spiked wood oats is a fine-textured native grass of the southeastern and south-central US, closely related to inland sea oats (C. latifolium) but notably more drought and shade tolerant and somewhat smaller and narrower in leaf. It grows naturally in dry, rocky, or sandy woodland soils under hardwood forest canopies and along dry bluffs and ridges, where its minimal water requirements make it a standout among shade grasses. The attractive seed heads emerge in summer, erect rather than pendulous, and turn a warm tan by fall, providing winter interest and wildlife food. An excellent grass for filling dry shade under oaks and other trees where irrigation is unavailable, or for naturalizing in shaded woodland garden settings. Self-sows moderately; cut back to the ground in late winter to encourage fresh growth.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; blooms on old wood, so prune, if needed, immediately after flowering.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and remove the oldest flowered stems right after bloom to keep the compact shrub from becoming crowded at its base. Spilled Wine is a dwarf weigela roughly half the size of the species, producing dense, arching mounds of deep burgundy-purple foliage topped with a heavy flush of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds reliably. Its small stature and consistently dark foliage make it a strong color-contrast shrub for the front of a mixed border or foundation planting where a full-size weigela would be too large. It is tough and adaptable, tolerating a range of soils once established, with minimal pruning needed given its naturally compact, well-behaved habit.

plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Spilt Milk is grown for its unusual white speckled and streaked leaf pattern rather than a solid-color margin.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously. Spilt Milk carries an unusual, irregular pattern of white speckles and streaks scattered across its green leaves, as though milk had literally been splashed and dried across the foliage, a distinctive break from the more common solid-margin or two-tone variegation patterns found in most hosta cultivars. The speckling is most pronounced on new growth in cooler spring conditions and may soften somewhat as summer heat sets in. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer, though the unusual leaf pattern is the main ornamental draw. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on tender new growth, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; spindle palm is frost-sensitive and requires frost-free conditions. Native to Rodrigues Island (Mauritius), where it is critically endangered in the wild with fewer than a few dozen specimens remaining.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–11; spindle palm is closely related to bottle palm (both in the genus Hyophorbe), and while both have distinctively shaped trunks, spindle palm's trunk swells in the MIDDLE rather than at the base, creating a spindle or fusiform shape — widest in the center of the trunk and tapering toward both the base and the crownshaft. The taller, more slender crown of arching pinnate fronds and the graceful spindle-shaped trunk distinguish it clearly from the squat bottle palm. Like bottle palm, it is critically endangered in the wild (native to Rodrigues Island, Mauritius), but very widely cultivated as an ornamental throughout the tropical world. Slightly taller and more slender than bottle palm, with a more graceful overall form. Both Hyophorbe species are outstanding ornamentals for small garden spaces in frost-free climates where their compact size and architectural trunks are advantages.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Spine Tingler bears glossy, evergreen leaves edged in fine, prickly spines, a distinctly bold, holly-like texture unlike the smooth-margined foliage of most epimedium cultivars, topped in spring by sprays of pale yellow flowers with a delicate, spurred form. Its spiny-edged, deer-resistant foliage provides year-round textural interest in a shaded border or woodland garden even outside the spring bloom season. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh and show off the spring display.

common_name: Spineless Yucca (Soft Leaf Yucca, Giant Yucca)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in any well-drained soil; Spineless Yucca grows quickly in warm conditions and requires excellent drainage — it will rot in clay that stays wet after rain. Plant 6–10 feet from buildings and walkways to allow for mature spread. In zone 9a, plants may defoliate in hard freezes but resprout from the trunk if the growing tips are not frozen.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Spineless Yucca is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives on neglect in appropriate conditions. Yucca elephantipes (also sold as Yucca gigantea) is a native of Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico that has become one of the most widely planted tropical accent plants in Gulf Coast zone 9–11 landscapes and a standard large houseplant and container specimen throughout the world. Unlike most yuccas whose stiff leaf tips can pierce skin (earning the family name 'needles and thread'), the Spineless Yucca's long, dark-green, strap-like leaves have soft, flexible tips that cause no injury — making it safe around children and pets and usable in high-traffic landscape situations where spiny yuccas would be hazardous. The plant develops multiple trunks over time, each eventually producing dramatic 3–4 foot spikes of creamy-white, pendant, bell-shaped flowers. It makes an excellent large container specimen for patios, entryways, and atriums where the bold form contrasts with fine-textured plants. When planted directly in the ground in zone 9b–11, it can grow to 30 feet with multiple branching trunks and a truly impressive specimen presence. Very popular in formal tropical and Mediterranean-style Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Divide crowns in early spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; spinulose wood fern tolerates a range of moisture conditions from consistently moist to moderately dry under tree canopy once established. It is one of the most widely distributed ferns in the temperate Northern Hemisphere and adaptable to a wide range of shaded garden conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; spinulose wood fern is one of the most common and widely distributed woodland ferns in the temperate Northern Hemisphere, found across North America, Europe, and Asia in moist, deciduous and coniferous forests. The medium-sized, triangular, lacy fronds are elegantly divided two or three times, with small, sharply toothed (spinulose) segments that give the fronds a fine, delicate texture distinguishing them from the coarser Dryopteris filix-mas. The plant forms vase-shaped clumps of light-green to medium-green fronds that are semi-evergreen in mild winters. It is one of the most adaptable, tolerant, and widely planted ferns for woodland gardens, succeeding in a wide range of shade and moisture conditions. It hybridizes freely with other Dryopteris species, including producing the common hybrid D. x complexa with D. affinis. An excellent, dependable fern for naturalizing in woodland settings and for combining with hostas, hellebores, and woodland wildflowers.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; spiny acanthus is more drought-tolerant and more deeply cut in its foliage than soft acanthus (A. mollis) — it is also more heat-tolerant and better adapted to dry summer conditions. Wear gloves when handling as the leaf tips bear sharp spines.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun to part shade; spiny acanthus is the superior species for hot-summer and dry-summer gardens — the deeply lobed, spiny-tipped, dark-green leaves are more dramatic in outline than soft acanthus (A. mollis), and the plant is more cold-hardy, more drought-tolerant, and more adaptable to a wide range of conditions. The leaves inspired the capital designs of Corinthian columns in classical Greek and Roman architecture, one of the most ancient uses of any plant in decorative art. In summer, spectacular vertical spikes 3–5 feet tall arise carrying hooded, two-toned flowers: purple-maroon bracts surrounding white flowers with prominent spiny bracts between each flower. These spikes are among the most architecturally impressive flower structures of any perennial and the flowers are visited by bumblebees that are strong enough to push into the hooded blooms. Once established, acanthus spreads by thick underground roots and can be difficult to eradicate — site it where it can expand freely.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; spiny black olive grows naturally in tropical coastal hammocks and the edges of mangrove in south Florida and the Caribbean, tolerating salt spray, thin alkaline soils, and drought.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, coastal soil in full sun; spiny black olive is a native tree of tropical coastal hammocks and scrub of south Florida and the Caribbean, not related to the olive (Olea) but named for the dark, fleshy, olive-like fruits. The tree has an attractive, fine-textured, weeping canopy with long, drooping branchlets bearing small, leathery, elongated leaves and (on young growth) short, stiff spines that have given it one common name. The small fruits are eaten by tropical birds. Well adapted to coastal conditions including salt spray, rocky limestone soil, and drought — all characteristic of the Keys habitat. Widely used as an ornamental and windbreak tree in South Florida coastal landscapes. A smaller relative of the commonly planted (and non-native) black olive (Bucida buceras), which is the dominant street tree of Miami.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun. Suited to California and mild coastal climates; protect from hard freezes. Once established, this shrub thrives on neglect and minimal water.
directions: Choose a sunny site with fast-draining, lean soil — rich or moist soils encourage weak growth and root rot in this chaparral native. Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in late summer, or transplant nursery-grown starts in spring. Water only to establish during the first season, then reduce to occasional deep irrigation in summer. The spiny branches form an effective barrier hedge while the bright red berries draw birds throughout fall and winter.

plant_note: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, gravelly to rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; spiny star cactus needs sharp drainage and is best grown in a raised bed or rock garden in wetter climates.
directions: Plant container-grown cactus in spring in lean, gravelly to rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; spiny star cactus needs sharp drainage and is best grown in a raised bed or rock garden in wetter climates. Small, cylindrical, densely spined stems slowly cluster into small groups, producing vivid magenta-pink, star-shaped flowers in spring that open wide in full sun and rank among the more striking blooms of the smaller Chihuahuan Desert cacti. Native to limestone hills and desert scrub of west Texas and northern Mexico, it thrives on poor, rocky, alkaline soil and full desert sun, making it a good choice for a small-scale rock garden or trough planting alongside other miniature desert cacti and succulents. Water only occasionally once established, provide sharp drainage above all else, and protect from prolonged winter wet, which is more damaging than cold.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in a lean, sterile cactus mix, or plant offsets in spring into rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely cold hardy compared to most cacti.
directions: Start seed indoors in a lean, sterile cactus mix, or plant offsets in spring into rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; this small, densely spined, clustering cactus ranges from the southern Canadian prairies through the Great Plains into the Texas Panhandle and Trans-Pecos, making it one of the most cold-hardy cacti native to North America. Globe-shaped stems bear a starburst pattern of radiating spines and slowly form tight clumps of a dozen or more heads, topped in late spring by bright pink to magenta flowers followed by small green fruit that ripens the following year. Because it thrives on neglect and rots quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil, plant it in a raised bed or scree garden of coarse gravel and mineral soil and water only during active summer growth. Its extreme cold tolerance makes it a good choice for xeric rock gardens well outside the range of most other ornamental cacti.

plant_note: Plant nursery starts in spring on a raised, gritty scree slope that drains rapidly and never sits in standing water.
directions: Site on a steep, well-drained slope or raised bed of gritty, mineral-rich soil that mimics its native mountain habitat, and avoid summer overhead watering that can rot the tightly packed leaves. This alpine aloe tolerates cold and occasional snow better than most aloes but demands excellent drainage year-round. Mature rosettes form a striking five-pointed spiral of thick, blue-green leaves that can spiral clockwise or counterclockwise. Established plants send up dense spikes of red-orange tubular flowers in late spring, though it may take several years to bloom from a young offset.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rhizomes in spring after soil warms in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Spiral Ginger is one of the most cold-tolerant Costus species — surviving to zone 9 (and marginally zone 8) with root protection during freezes.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Spiral Ginger is a tropical shade perennial in the Costus genus — producing erect, cane-like stems with the characteristic spiral arrangement of broad, tropical-looking leaves that give the entire Costus group their common name. The leaves are arranged in a beautiful, precise spiral up each cane that is architecturally distinctive and visually arresting. In late summer and fall, large (3–4 inch), white, tissue-paper-thin flowers emerge from reddish-brown cone-like terminal bracts, providing a dramatic contrast against the deep-green foliage. Spiral Ginger creates outstanding tropical shade garden effects in zone 9–11, where its combination of bold, spiraling foliage and dramatic late-season flowers provides multi-season ornamental interest. In zone 9, the tops are killed by hard freezes but the underground rhizomes typically survive to zone 9a when mulched, re-sprouting vigorously in spring. The bold tropical foliage texture combines beautifully with other shade tropical plants — caladiums, gingers, and philodendrons — to create a lush, jungle-like understory effect under high-canopy trees. Division of established clumps every 3–4 years maintains vigor and provides divisions for expanding the planting.

subcategory: deep blue spectacular South African Cape corm
plant_note: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; splendid wine cups follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — autumn emergence, winter-spring bloom, complete summer dormancy. Keep bone dry in summer. The species name 'splendidissima' (most splendid) is justified: the flowers are among the most intense, saturated, pure deep blue of any plant in the world. Best in containers in areas with wet summers to control summer moisture.
directions: Plant corms in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; splendid wine cups — the botanical superlative in the species epithet 'splendidissima' (most splendid) is fully earned — is one of the most intense, saturated, deep-blue flowering plants in existence, producing in late winter and spring wide-open, cup-shaped flowers of extraordinary, gemlike, deep ultramarine-blue to dark royal-blue that is so saturated and vivid it appears almost luminescent in sunlight, with a small, contrasting white or very pale center zone at the base of each petal that intensifies the optical power of the surrounding dark blue. Unlike the bicolor G. radians (blue with red center blotches), G. splendidissima achieves its beauty through the purity and depth of a single, extraordinary, supremely saturated blue — arguably the deepest, most intense, most unmistakably magnificent pure blue of any spring-flowering plant regularly available to gardeners. Native to a restricted area of the coastal Western Cape fynbos where it grows in sandy, peaty, seasonally moist soils on the coastal flats. A collector's prize — not widely available but obtainable from specialist Cape bulb suppliers — of singular botanical distinction for the quality of its flower color alone.

common_name: Split-Leaf Monstera (Pinnatipartita, Peru Monstera, Broad-Leaf Monstera)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Monstera pinnatipartita cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Provide a moss pole or climbing support to achieve the dramatically pinnate adult leaf form — the transformation from juvenile simple leaves to deeply split adult leaves is one of the most striking in the genus. In zone 10-11 outdoors, it can climb tree trunks in deep shade. Propagate from stem cuttings with at least one node. Use a well-draining aroid potting mix. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Monstera pinnatipartita transitions from its juvenile to its extraordinary adult leaf form most rapidly with adequate bright indirect light and a climbing support. Monstera pinnatipartita is a climbing aroid from Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia in the Araceae family, producing one of the most dramatically transformative leaf progressions in the genus Monstera — the group named for their 'monstrous' leaves. In the juvenile trailing or hanging phase, the plant produces relatively small (4–6 inch), simple, elongated, glossy dark-green leaves that give no indication of what is to come. As the plant climbs a vertical surface and matures, the leaves transform dramatically: they enlarge significantly and become deeply pinnately lobed — divided almost to the midrib into numerous (8–12 pairs or more) distinct lobes — creating a leaf structure that is deeply slashed rather than fenestrated (holed), with the individual lobes remaining attached to the central rib like a feather. The adult leaves, reaching 24 inches or more, are among the most striking in the genus. Monstera pinnatipartita is frequently confused in commerce with Monstera siltepecana (which is similar in juvenile form), Rhaphidophora decursiva (similar in adult form), and even Epipremnum pinnatum — accurate identification is helpful for appropriate care and expectation setting. All parts are toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral, dry soil in full sun; splitbeard bluestem is a low-nutrient-requiring grass that performs best in poor, sandy, acidic pine flatwoods soils — excessive fertilization leads to rank growth and reduced ornamental quality.
directions: Splitbeard bluestem is one of the most ornamentally appealing native grasses of the Gulf Coastal Plain and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine country — in fall, the paired flower spikes develop silky, glistening white or silvery seed heads with a distinctive forked, Y-shaped arrangement that gives the species both its common names (splitbeard for the paired stalks, chalky for the whitened seed heads). The plants have a somewhat tufted, wiry character and typically stay shorter than big bluestem or bushy bluestem, making them appropriate for small to medium native garden settings; their chalky-white winter seedheads contrast beautifully with the coppery-bronze stems and leaves. Naturally found in open, dry, longleaf pine savannas, sandhills, and coastal plain flatwoods, splitbeard bluestem is adapted to the fire-maintained, nutrient-poor sandy soils of the Gulf South — combine with native wildflowers like blazing stars, black-eyed Susans, and goldenrods for an authentic pine flatwoods meadow garden.

plant_note: Sow in fall into sandy, well-drained soil to allow natural cold stratification before spring germination.
directions: Spoonleaf Barbara's Buttons is a compact southeastern native wildflower adapted to the sandy, nutrient-poor soils of longleaf pine uplands, where it produces distinctive spoon-shaped basal leaves and delicate white to pale pink pincushion blooms in spring. Direct sow seeds in fall into well-drained, acidic sandy soil with good sun exposure, spacing plants at least 9 inches apart to accommodate their slow-spreading habit. This drought-tolerant perennial is well-suited to rock gardens, native plant borders, and open pine understory plantings where many other flowers struggle. It thrives with minimal fertilization, as overly rich soils can reduce flowering and encourage lush but bloom-sparse foliage.

plant_note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; spoonleaf sundew tolerates a wider range of climates than round-leaved sundew, from cold bogs to warm coastal plain seeps.
directions: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; spoonleaf sundew tolerates a wider range of climates than round-leaved sundew, from cold bogs to warm coastal plain seeps. Narrow, spoon-shaped leaves tipped with sticky, glistening, red tentacles are often held semi-upright rather than lying flat, trapping small insects across the wet, sunny bogs, seeps, and pond margins where it grows natively across a wide range spanning from cold northern peatlands to warm Gulf coastal plain wetlands. Its broader climate tolerance compared to the more cold-dependent round-leaved sundew makes it a good choice for a bog garden across a wider range of USDA zones, including warmer Southern climates where round-leaved sundew struggles without a hard winter. Keep the growing medium constantly wet with pure water, provide bright light for the best coloring and dew production, and allow a period of reduced growth over winter even in milder climates.

plant_note: Surface-sow; light aids germination. Short-lived but self-sows.
directions: Surface-sow the seed and press it in, as light helps it germinate. Also called dotted horsemint, this native produces tiered whorls of yellow flowers spotted with purple, set off by showy pink bracts. It thrives in full sun and sandy, dry soil, and its aromatic foliage deters deer. A biennial to short-lived perennial, it self-sows freely and is a magnet for bees, wasps, and other beneficial pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; spotted beebalm requires excellent drainage and is intolerant of heavy or consistently moist soils — it thrives in the kind of dry, sandy, or rocky ground where most other wildflowers struggle, cold-stratifying naturally over winter for spring germination.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or rocky soil in full sun; spotted beebalm is strictly a plant of dry, open ground and will not tolerate heavy clay or consistently moist soils — it is one of the finest native wildflowers for hot, dry, infertile conditions where richly blooming plants are difficult to establish. Monarda punctata, also called horsemint, is one of the most botanically unusual native wildflowers in eastern and central North America: its flowers are small, spotted yellow-white with purple-brown dots and held in multiple tiered whorls along the stem, each whorl subtended by showy, leaf-like bracts in soft pink, lavender, or white that persist long after the flowers fade, giving the plant a dramatic, sculptural appearance from July through September that is wholly unlike any other native wildflower. It is one of the very best native plants for small native bees, including many specialist solitary bees that visit Monarda; it is also heavily worked by bumblebees, sweat bees, long-tongued bees, and various wasps, and the aromatic foliage contains high concentrations of thymol, the same antiseptic compound found in garden thyme. Spotted beebalm is a short-lived perennial or biennial that self-sows prolifically in appropriate dry, sandy soils — allow seed heads to ripen and fall in place to maintain a self-sustaining colony, and avoid amending or irrigating the soil, which dramatically shortens the lifespan of individual plants.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring or divide established clumps in spring or fall; spotted bellflower spreads by underground rhizomes and can be aggressive — choose a site where some spread is welcome or confine with a root barrier. It is notably heat-tolerant among bellflowers and performs well in the warmer parts of its zone range.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; spotted bellflower is a Japanese and Korean native that produces some of the largest, most unusual flowers in the bellflower genus — long (2 inches), drooping, tubular bells in cream to soft pink, each distinctly spotted and freckled inside with red-purple dots, hung in nodding clusters on plants only 12–18 inches tall. The interior spotting, only visible by looking up into the pendant flower, is exquisite and gives the flowers a quality more reminiscent of foxglove or digitalis than of typical bellflowers. It blooms in early summer and spreads vigorously by underground rhizomes to form colonies in semi-shaded woodland conditions. Several cultivars and hybrids are available including 'Cherry Bells' (deep rose-pink) and 'Bowl of Cherries.' The rhizomatous spread, while vigorous, makes it an effective groundcover under shrubs and trees. Somewhat more heat-tolerant than most temperate bellflowers, succeeding in the warmer zones of its range.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep in moist, moderately fertile soil in spring; spotted calla lily requires dry summer dormancy (unlike Z. aethiopica which is summer-active) — stop watering when leaves yellow after flowering and keep dry through summer. It is the parent species of many hybrid calla lilies with spotted, translucent-spotted leaves. Suitable for zones 8–11 outdoors; lift and store dry in colder zones.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in part shade; spotted calla lily is the primary parent species of the hybrid calla lily group with the characteristic white-spotted, translucent-spotted foliage — the dark-green, arrow-shaped leaves are decorated with numerous white, translucent dots and spots of varying size, creating an attractively patterned foliage effect even before the flowers appear. The flowers are typical calla-form — a creamy-white to pale-yellow or greenish-white spathe surrounding a yellow spadix — smaller and more elegant than the large Z. aethiopica. Unlike Z. aethiopica, it follows a summer-dormant, winter-active pattern (reflecting its summer-dry South African native habitat) and must have dry conditions during summer dormancy to prevent rhizome rot. In zones 8–11 it can remain in the ground with withheld summer water. It is the parent of most hybrid calla lily cultivars with spotted foliage, now available in a wide range of spathe colors from white through yellow, orange, pink, and dark burgundy-purple. Outstanding in containers where the summer dormancy can be easily managed by simply withholding water.

plant_note: Transfer small divisions of the coral-like rhizome in early spring, taking care to keep a portion of the surrounding native soil attached to preserve active fungal partners. Plant in undisturbed forest duff beneath mature deciduous or coniferous trees where leaf litter accumulates naturally. Do not attempt to grow in sterile or amended potting mix; success depends entirely on intact mycorrhizal networks already present in the native soil.
directions: Establish divisions beneath a closed woodland canopy in rich, humus-laden soil where minimal light reaches the forest floor, as this plant produces no chlorophyll and gains all nutrition through its fungal symbiont. Because it never photosynthesizes, it is entirely invisible above ground for most of the year, emerging only as a leafless reddish-brown stem bearing small spotted flowers in late spring or summer. Mark planting locations carefully to avoid accidental disturbance during the dormant season. Supplemental watering is rarely needed where natural leaf litter maintains consistent soil moisture, but avoid flooding or allowing the soil to dry out completely.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the upper half exposed above the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; spotted crossyne flowers in late summer and autumn (February–April in South Africa) before the leaves emerge (hysteranthous). Keep dry in summer. The species name 'guttata' means spotted — the individual flowers are white to pale pink and often marked with darker spots or streaks. A rare collector's bulb native to the fynbos of the Northern Cape.
directions: Plant bulbs (upper half exposed) in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; spotted crossyne is a rare, collectible South African bulb in the Amaryllidaceae family — related to Brunsvigia and Boophone — from the arid, rocky, fynbos and Namaqualand landscapes of the Northern Cape. Like Brunsvigia and Boophone it flowers in late summer and autumn on a leafless scape that emerges before the leaves (hysteranthous), producing a rounded, somewhat hemispherical umbel of 20–40 individual, tubular-funnel, white to pale pink flowers that are frequently spotted or streaked with darker markings — the 'guttata' (spotted) character. The whole flower head has a somewhat informal, airy quality compared to the more spectacular Brunsvigia josephinae or the bizarre Boophone disticha, but it provides the authentic autumn bloom timing and the spotted flower pattern that make it of botanical interest for the collector of South African autumn-blooming amaryllids. After the autumn flowers, the strap-shaped, grey-green leaves emerge and persist through winter and spring. A specialist plant for the dedicated Cape bulb collector; not widely available in commerce.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant divisions in spring; spotted dead nettle establishes quickly and begins spreading within the first season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; spotted dead nettle is one of the most reliable shade groundcovers available, prized for its silver-marked leaves that light up dim spaces under trees. The small hooded flowers in pink, white, or purple appear in spring and continue sporadically through summer. Shear plants back by one-third in midsummer if they become straggly to promote fresh new growth. Named cultivars with highly silvered or patterned foliage — 'White Nancy', 'Beacon Silver', 'Hermann's Pride' — are superior to the straight species. Tolerates dry shade once established but performs best in consistently moist conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; space 12–18 inches apart for quick coverage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, avoiding heavy clay that stays waterlogged in winter; spotted deadnettle forms a quick-spreading mat of silver-marked foliage that suppresses weeds effectively under trees and shrubs. The small pink, white, or purple flowers appear in late spring and continue sporadically through summer. Cut plants back hard in midsummer if they become leggy or stressed by heat to encourage a flush of fresh foliage. The silver-splashed leaves of popular cultivars like 'White Nancy' and 'Beacon Silver' brighten dark corners more effectively than most groundcovers. Divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratify seed for 30 days; surface-sow as light aids germination.
directions: Cold-stratify the seed for a month and surface-sow, since light improves germination. This tall native perennial produces large, domed clusters of fragrant rose-pink flowers from August into September. Grow it in full sun to part shade and consistently moist to wet soil, ideal for rain gardens and pond edges. Its towering stems are a butterfly favorite and add bold structure to the back of the border.

common_name: Spotted Leopard Plant (Yellow-Spotted Bold-Leaf Shade Perennial for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; the yellow spotting of Aureomaculatum is caused by viral variegation and is therefore heritable but not transmissible to other plants — propagate only by division to maintain the spotted pattern.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Aureomaculatum is the spotted form of Farfugium japonicum — the same bold-textured, large-leaved shade perennial as the green species but with distinctive irregular yellow spots and blotches distributed randomly across the dark green leaf surface, resembling paint splattered across the leaves and creating a strikingly unusual variegation pattern not found in other commonly grown shade perennials. The yellow spots of Aureomaculatum are the result of a viral variegation — genetically stable but caused by a specific viral interaction in the plant tissue — which means the spotting pattern is propagated faithfully by division but cannot be transmitted to adjacent plants. Each leaf produces a uniquely arranged set of yellow spots, and the number and size of spots varies from leaf to leaf, creating an irregular, artistically random variegation that is more visually interesting than uniformly-patterned variegation. The spotted pattern brightens deep shade positions significantly — the yellow spots appear luminous in low-light conditions, functioning like scattered points of light in the dark garden. Otherwise, the cultural requirements and fall yellow flowers of Aureomaculatum are identical to the green-leaved species. In Gulf South shade gardens, the spotted form provides a higher ornamental value than the straight species and is worth seeking out from specialty nurseries and plant societies. Both forms are equally cold-hardy and reliable in zone 7–10.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic to slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade. A coastal plain specialist, Spotted Trillium thrives in the warm, moist forests of Georgia, Alabama, and the Florida panhandle.
directions: Spotted Trillium is a sessile trillium of the southeastern coastal plain, native to moist, rich hardwood forests from South Carolina south to Florida and west to Alabama, where it often grows with sweetbay magnolia, titi, and evergreen shrubs in lowland forest understories. Its heavily marbled, silver-spotted leaves and nearly black maroon sessile flowers make it one of the more dramatic members of the genus, and the flowers carry a faint spicy scent that attracts fly pollinators. Rhizome divisions establish best when planted in fall in deeply amended, consistently moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.0) in full shade; the plants go completely dormant by early summer and should never be disturbed while dormant. Source only from reputable nurseries growing their own stock — this species is never legitimately available from wild collection.

plant_note: Carefully transplant small rooted sections with attached soil and intact root structure in early spring; spotted wintergreen requires very specific conditions — dry, infertile, sandy or rocky, strongly acidic soil in deep shade with established ectomycorrhizal fungi. Only plant nursery-propagated stock; never collect from the wild.
directions: Plant in dry, lean, sandy or rocky, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade; spotted wintergreen is one of the most beautiful native evergreen groundcovers of the eastern forest understory — a low, spreading plant with glossy, dark green leaves dramatically patterned with white or pale silver along the veins, creating a vivid variegated effect. Small, waxy, fragrant white flowers are produced in summer on upright stalks. The plant requires the presence of specific ectomycorrhizal fungi and strongly dislikes root disturbance, fertilization, or soil amendments — making it notoriously difficult to establish in cultivated settings. The best approach is to acquire nursery-propagated plugs (never wild-collected), plant in dry, acidic, sandy soil near the base of oaks or pines that support appropriate mycorrhizal networks, and then largely leave it undisturbed. Once established, it spreads slowly to form colonies that are permanent features of the native shade garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Spotty Dotty is a hybrid mayapple selection prized for enormous, deeply lobed leaves boldly splashed with chocolate-maroon spots, providing dramatic textural impact in the shade garden well beyond its brief spring bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sited where its bold foliage has room to spread. Spotty Dotty is a hybrid Podophyllum selection, likely involving the Chinese species P. delavayi, bred for enormous, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves heavily marbled and spotted with chocolate-maroon blotches over rich green, a striking effect that makes it one of the boldest textural statements available for a shaded border. In spring, dark maroon-red, nodding, cup-shaped flowers appear beneath the emerging foliage, followed later by red fruit, though the flowers are often hidden by the leaves and the foliage display is the plant's main draw. Unlike the common native mayapple (Podophyllum peltatum), which spreads by rhizome and goes dormant by midsummer, Spotty Dotty forms a slowly expanding clump and holds its dramatic foliage well into fall in consistently moist soil. Mulch with leaf litter or compost each fall to mimic its native woodland habitat, and avoid letting the soil dry out during the growing season, since drought causes the large leaves to scorch.

plant_note: Divide established mats or plant small rooted sections in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade; spreading club moss requires constantly moist soil and high humidity — it desiccates rapidly in dry conditions. Excellent for terrariums, woodland floors with consistent moisture, and the margins of streams and ponds in zones 7–10.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade; spreading club moss is a South African moss-relative (actually a vascular plant, unrelated to true mosses) that creates a dense, emerald-green to bright-golden-green flat mat of exceptionally fine-textured, scale-like leaves that spreads steadily over moist shaded surfaces — creating a seamless carpet of living green over forest floors, terrarium floors, and other consistently moist, shaded situations. The golden-green cultivar 'Aurea' (gold club moss) is especially popular in terrariums and miniature gardens for its warm, luminous color in deep shade. It spreads by prostrate stems that root at intervals, eventually covering large areas where the consistently moist conditions it requires are maintained. Not drought-tolerant at all — the foliage wilts and browns rapidly if allowed to dry out. An ideal companion to ferns, mosses, and woodland wildflowers in moist, shaded sites with reliable moisture. Also widely used in vivaria and terrariums as a naturalistic ground layer.

plant_note: Divide established rhizome clumps in early spring, or cold-stratify and direct-sow seed shallowly once the soil has warmed.
directions: Site in well-drained soil in partial sun to light shade at a woodland edge or dry meadow margin, where its wiry, branching red-tinged stems and pairs of oval leaves form a low, spreading colony. Clusters of small, fragrant, pink-striped bell flowers nod from the branch tips in early summer and are intensely attractive to bumblebees, small butterflies, and moths, which are drawn to the sweet nectar despite the flower's slick, trap-like structure. The milky sap it shares with its dogbane relatives makes the foliage unpalatable to deer and rabbits, a useful trait in a naturalized pollinator planting. Give it space to spread underground and avoid rich, heavily amended soil, which encourages floppy growth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; spreading phlox is a high-elevation cushion plant that needs sharp drainage and struggles with heat, humidity, and rich soil.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; spreading phlox is a high-elevation cushion plant that needs sharp drainage and struggles with heat, humidity, and rich soil. Tiny, needle-like evergreen leaves form a dense, low cushion or mat that all but disappears beneath a smothering flush of small, fragrant, pale pink to lavender-blue flowers in late spring, native to dry, rocky, high-elevation slopes and open pine forests from the Cascades and Sierra Nevada into the Rocky Mountains. Its tight, mat-forming habit and tolerance of thin, gravelly, alpine soil make it an excellent choice for a rock garden, scree bed, or trough planting in a cool-summer climate, blanketing bare rocky ground with color for several weeks each spring. Water sparingly, ensure sharp drainage, and avoid rich or heavily amended soil, which causes this lean-soil alpine specialist to decline.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spreading sedge colonizes slowly by long stolons to form a low groundcover that is easy to control if needed.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spreading sedge is a low-growing native sedge of eastern woodland floors, distinguished by its unusually wide leaves (up to 3/4 inch wide, broad for a sedge) that are a beautiful glaucous blue-green color with a matte, almost frosted surface. The prostrate to arching leaves spread loosely to form a lax groundcover very different in character from the more upright native sedges — relaxed, natural-looking, and graceful. It spreads slowly by long stolons to form a loose, open mat. The cultivar 'Hobb' (sold as 'Blue Bunny') offers especially pronounced blue-green foliage and is widely available in the native plant trade. An outstanding groundcover for the shaded woodland garden in zone 4–8, especially effective paired with native spring wildflowers, ferns, and bleeding heart.

common_name: Spreading Sunset Lantana (Trailing Multicolor Sunset-Toned Groundcover Lantana)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Spreading Sunset bears multicolor orange-red-yellow flower clusters on a low, trailing, groundcover-type lantana.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, and avoid overwatering, since lantana is highly drought-tolerant once established and prone to root problems in soggy soil. Spreading Sunset bears vivid multicolor flower clusters blending orange, red, and yellow tones that shift as they age, on a low, vigorously trailing plant well suited to groundcover use, spilling over walls, or filling large containers and hanging baskets. It blooms nonstop from spring through frost and draws butterflies heavily throughout the season. In the coldest parts of its hardiness range it dies to the ground in winter and returns from the roots in spring; further north it is grown as a summer annual.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in shade to dappled light; tolerates heavier moisture than many wood ferns and spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form a weed-suppressing colony.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full shade to dappled woodland light; the spreading wood fern produces broad, arching, triangular-ovate fronds on dark stalks, forming graceful mounds that soften woodland garden paths and shaded borders with fresh spring-green color that deepens to rich forest green through summer. Semi-deciduous to deciduous, it spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a natural-looking weed-suppressing colony. Tolerates heavier moisture than many wood ferns and establishes readily in the humus-rich leaf-mold soils typical of mature deciduous woodland.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Sprenger's tulip is the latest of all tulip species to bloom (June in northern gardens) and is among the very best naturalizers — spreading freely by seed in garden conditions when allowed to set seed without cutting. A single planting builds into large colonies over 5–10 years. Bulbs are small and difficult to source; seed or specialist tulip nurseries are the main supply route.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade; Sprenger's tulip has two unique distinctions that set it apart from all other tulip species: it is the latest to bloom (flowering in late May through June after all other tulips have finished, bridging the gap between spring bulbs and summer perennials), and it is arguably the best naturalizer in the tulip genus — self-seeding freely in garden conditions to build large, spreading colonies of plants that increase reliably year after year without lifting, dividing, or replanting. The flowers are a vivid, warm, scarlet-red to deep orange-red (with occasional yellow-flushed outer petal surfaces), starry, six-petaled, pointed-oval in bud and opening to a broad, open, star-like display of satiny red in bright sun. For a species that blooms so late and self-seeds so freely, it is perplexingly rare in general cultivation — partly because the small bulbs are difficult to produce commercially and mostly available through specialist sources and from seed. A colony established from seed or a first planting of small bulbs gradually becomes a self-sustaining treasure in the garden, the late-season red tulip display filling a slot in the spring bulb calendar that nothing else occupies. Naturalized colonies have been established in old gardens and appear completely at home in the borderline-shade of deciduous tree canopy.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–May or September–October. Sprengeri Fern grows from tuberous roots that allow it to survive periods of drought and some winter cold. In zone 9 it behaves as a semi-evergreen perennial, surviving mild winters with minimal damage and resprouting vigorously after hard freezes kill the above-ground stems. The trailing, cascading stems make it excellent in hanging baskets, window boxes, and container plantings where the growth can hang freely. Small, fragrant white flowers appear on established plants followed by red berries — attractive but mildly toxic if ingested. Can become invasive where birds drop seeds in warm, frost-free areas.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sprengeri Fern adapts to a wide light range but produces the most lush, dense growth in consistent partial shade with regular moisture; Sprengeri Fern is the most widely grown ornamental asparagus cultivar — a trailing, cascading, arching plant with airy, needle-like cladodes (the green, needle-like modified stems that function as leaves) clothing long, flexible stems that naturally arch and cascade 2–4 feet from their point of origin. Despite the common name, Sprengeri is not a true fern but an asparagus relative (Asparagus densiflorus) native to South Africa, sharing only the fine, feathery texture that gives it a fern-like appearance. The light, airy, bright green texture of cascading Sprengeri stems is one of the most versatile elements in both container design and cut flower arranging — the stems add a loose, naturalistic, fine-textured complement to virtually any floral combination, and the sprays remain fresh for an extended period after cutting. As a container plant for shaded patios and porches in zone 9, Sprengeri's cascading habit and fine texture provide an essential design element that trails gracefully from the edges of containers while tolerating the heat and partial shade conditions of covered outdoor spaces.

plant_note: Plant small corms in early fall in deep, moist, well-drained, rich woodland soil in full shade under deciduous trees; spring beauty naturalizes by self-sowing and corm offsets into large, sweeping colonies over many years.
directions: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in early fall in moist, rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade under deciduous hardwoods; spring beauty is one of the quintessential Eastern North American spring ephemerals, forming extensive carpets that produce thousands of small pink-striped white flowers in earliest spring before the tree canopy leafs out, then disappearing completely by late spring. The dime-sized corms are edible, with a starchy-sweet flavor resembling water chestnuts, and were an important food source for Eastern Native peoples. Plants naturalize slowly by both self-seeding and corm offsets to create breathtaking sweeps of spring color in undisturbed woodland gardens. Purchase nursery-propagated corms only.

common_name: Spring Beauty Siberian Squill (Large-Flowered Deep Blue Scilla)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Spring Beauty is the most widely sold Siberian squill selection, with larger flowers and a more vigorous habit than the wild species.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Siberian squill naturalizes vigorously under deciduous trees and in lawns, tolerating deep shade once trees leaf out for the summer. Spring Beauty bears larger, more richly colored, deep cobalt-blue, nodding, bell-shaped flowers than the wild species, opening in very early spring and often carpeting large areas once established, since it self-seeds and multiplies by offset bulbs readily. It is one of the most reliable and low-maintenance early spring bulbs for naturalizing, tolerating a wide range of soil and light conditions and largely ignored by deer and rodents. Allow the narrow, strappy foliage to die back naturally after flowering before mowing over naturalized lawn plantings.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Spring Bouquet is a compact selection of laurustinus (Viburnum tinus) valued for dense evergreen foliage, winter-into-spring flower clusters, and a naturally tidy rounded form that requires little pruning.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge. Spring Bouquet is a compact cultivar of laurustinus, prized for its dense, dark green, glossy evergreen foliage and abundant clusters of small, fragrant, pinkish-white flowers that open from reddish-pink buds in late winter and early spring, one of the earliest flower displays in the evergreen shrub border. Flowers are followed by small blue-black berries that add fall and winter interest and attract birds. Its naturally rounded, well-proportioned habit holds a tidy shape with far less pruning than many broadleaf evergreens, making it useful for foundation plantings, informal hedges, and mixed borders. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established, though good drainage improves long-term performance, and it shows good resistance to the pests and diseases that trouble some other Southern landscape evergreens. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering to avoid removing the next year's flower buds.

plant_note: Set divisions or plugs a foot or so apart in spring into well-drained soil; tolerates light foot traffic once it has knit together.
directions: Set divisions or plugs a foot or so apart in spring into well-drained soil; the semi-evergreen foliage spreads by short runners to form a low mat that can substitute for turf on sunny slopes or fill spaces between stepping stones. Bright yellow, strawberry-like flowers cover the mat for several weeks in mid-spring, and the planting tolerates light foot traffic once it has knit together. It is drought tolerant once rooted in and needs little care beyond an occasional trim to keep edges tidy.

plant_note: Plant small corms just below the soil surface (1 inch deep) in humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil under deciduous trees; spring cyclamen grows and flowers in winter and spring while deciduous trees are leafless, then goes dormant in summer when tree shade intensifies. Dry summer dormancy is essential — do not water during this period.
directions: Plant corms just below the surface in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade under deciduous trees; spring cyclamen is the third species of hardy garden cyclamen (after the autumn-blooming C. hederifolium and the winter-blooming C. coum) — a Mediterranean native of olive groves and deciduous woodlands in southern Europe that flowers in spring (March–April) with elegantly reflexed, rose-pink to carmine, fragrant flowers above beautifully silver-marbled, ivy-shaped leaves. Like its relatives, it grows actively in winter and spring when deciduous tree canopies are open, then retreats into summer dormancy under the dense shade of summer foliage. The flowers have a subtle, sweet fragrance uncommon in this genus. Hardier than the florist cyclamen (C. persicum) but somewhat less cold-tolerant than C. hederifolium, thriving in sheltered woodland gardens in zones 7–9. Together, C. hederifolium, C. coum, and C. repandum extend hardy cyclamen interest from August through April — nearly year-round in mild gardens.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall before ground freezes; spring fumewort is a spring ephemeral — it emerges and blooms early, sets seed, and then dies down completely by early summer, leaving bare soil, so mark its position and interplant with later-emerging perennials to fill the gap.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall; spring fumewort (fumitory, bird-in-a-bush) is a European woodland spring ephemeral bulb in the fumitory family — one of the earliest woodland bulbs to flower, emerging and blooming in early spring (March–April) simultaneously with snowdrops, early crocuses, and Scilla sibirica, before the deciduous tree canopy leafs out and shades the ground. The compact plants produce racemes of small, tube-spurred, two-lipped flowers in shades of deep rose-pink, magenta, red, lilac, or white with darker purple tips, above finely divided, gray-green, fernlike leaves. Like other spring ephemerals, it completes its entire growth cycle — emergence, flowering, seed-set, and dormancy — before deciduous trees fully shade the ground. It naturalizes readily under deciduous trees, spreads by self-seeding and by the division of the solid round tubers. The named cultivar 'George Baker' (deep, vivid salmon-red) is considered the finest individual form. Plant in large drifts of 25 or more bulbs for best effect under deciduous shade.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Spring Green is an eye-catching celosia standing about 40 inches tall with fresh lime-green plumes that thrive through late summer heat. Start seed indoors 6 to 4 weeks before the last frost, barely covering it and keeping soil warm around 75 degrees F for best germination. Transplant into full sun after frost danger passes, spacing plants for good airflow. The long, sturdy stems make excellent fresh or dried cut flowers and attract pollinators. Deadhead or harvest regularly to keep the display coming through the growing season.

common_name: Spring Green Tulip (Ivory-White Viridiflora Tulip with Green Flame)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Spring Green is a Viridiflora-class tulip with ivory-white petals marked by a central green feathered flame, blooming late in the season.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Spring Green, one of the most popular Viridiflora-class tulips, bears creamy ivory-white petals streaked down the center with a feathered flame of green, the distinctive partial-green coloring that defines the Viridiflora group, blooming late in the tulip season with a soft, subtle look that pairs beautifully with nearly any garden color scheme. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in early spring into consistently moist, open ground with full sun to light shade. Incorporating organic matter improves establishment in heavier soils, but avoid excessive fertility.
directions: Site spring ladies' tresses in a moist meadow, rain garden, or roadside planting with full sun to partial shade and consistently moist, humus-enriched soil that does not dry out in summer. Prepare the planting area by removing competing sod and loosening the soil to allow the fleshy roots to establish without obstruction. Plant divisions at their original depth, firm the soil around the roots, and water thoroughly; continue to keep the soil evenly moist through the first growing season. This orchid blooms in spring rather than fall, making it an excellent companion to other early-season natives, and it will slowly colonize suitable areas once the mycorrhizal community is established.

plant_note: Start indoors in cool conditions; transplant in early spring or fall.
directions: Midnight Glow features rich velvet-purple petals with glowing yellow centers that fade into deep purple edges, producing large 3-inch blooms on uniform, well-branched plants. Start seed indoors in cool conditions and dark until germination, then grow on in bright, cool light before transplanting. Pansies thrive in cool, short-day weather, making them ideal for early spring and fall displays. Set plants in full sun to part shade in rich, moist soil and deadhead to prolong bloom. The edible flowers make a colorful garnish for salads and desserts.

plant_note: Divide and replant established clumps in early spring before new growth emerges, setting pseudobulbs just at the soil surface in a fast-draining orchid mix in a shaded location.
directions: Grow in a fast-draining mix of bark, perlite, and leaf mold in a deeply shaded location that receives bright indirect light, spacing clumps 9-15 inches apart to allow the narrow grassy foliage to form tidy mounds. Water moderately during the growing season, allowing the mix to approach dryness between waterings, and reduce water significantly in late autumn to encourage the formation of spring flower spikes. Apply a dilute balanced orchid fertilizer every two to three weeks from spring through summer, switching to a low-nitrogen formula in fall to harden growth. Divide clumps every three to five years in early spring, ensuring each division retains at least three to five pseudobulbs to guarantee flowering within one to two seasons.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spring snowflake is one of the earliest bulbs to bloom, often flowering before the last frosts, and naturalizes steadily to form increasingly beautiful drifts over time.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spring snowflake blooms in very early spring — often alongside snowdrops and well before most bulbs — producing one to three white, drooping, bell-shaped flowers per stem with distinctive green (sometimes yellow) spots at the tip of each petal, creating a dainty, charming display. Unlike the taller summer snowflake (L. aestivum), L. vernum is dwarf and delicate, blooming for 2–3 weeks in late winter to early spring. It naturalizes steadily by bulb offsets in suitable moist, shaded conditions and is one of the finest companion bulbs for snowdrops, winter aconites, and early crocus under deciduous trees. All parts are mildly toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Texas spider lily is native to wet meadows, creek margins, and roadside ditches in south Texas, Louisiana, and the Gulf Coastal Plain and thrives in seasonally moist to wet conditions where many other bulbs fail.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Texas spider lily tolerates and even prefers seasonally flooded or consistently wet conditions.
