directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Stellar Pink dogwood is a Rutgers-bred hybrid with strong resistance to dogwood anthracnose and borers, which trouble many flowering dogwoods. A hybrid between the native flowering dogwood and the Asian kousa dogwood developed at Rutgers University, it combines the classic large, showy, soft pink bracts of flowering dogwood with the improved disease and pest resistance of its kousa parent, addressing the anthracnose and borer problems that have devastated many straight Cornus florida plantings in recent decades. Blooming in mid-spring between the earlier flowering dogwood and later kousa dogwood bloom windows, it provides reliable pink flower color on a tough, adaptable small tree well suited to a woodland edge or specimen planting. Water during establishment and dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool, and avoid the anthracnose and borer problems common to straight dogwood species by choosing this resistant hybrid for new plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into dry, sandy, infertile soil in full sun; avoid amended or fertile soils.
directions: A distinctive, low-growing native ironweed that appears nearly stemless, with large, broadly elliptic, rough-textured basal leaves lying flat to the ground and short upright flowering stems bearing clusters of deep purple composite flowers in summer. Native to dry, sandy, open pine flatwoods and barrens of the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida, it is much shorter and more drought-tolerant than other Vernonia species. Grow in dry, sandy, infertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; rich or amended soils cause rank growth and reduce flowering. An excellent choice for sandy native gardens and longleaf pine flatwood restorations in zones 6-9.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral coastal soil in full sun; stemodia grows naturally in coastal strand, saltmarsh margins, and disturbed coastal sandy habitats of the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. It tolerates salt, drought, and nutrient-poor sandy soils.
directions: Direct sow in sandy, salty, slightly alkaline to neutral, coastal soil in full sun; stemodia is a small, sprawling annual of coastal sandy habitats from the Gulf Coast to the Caribbean, producing tiny, attractive, two-lipped violet to lavender flowers on small, aromatic, glandular-hairy plants. The plant has some culinary and ethnobotanical interest in the Caribbean as a flavoring herb (used in some Jamaican cooking) and traditional medicine. More importantly it is an ecological component of coastal sand plant communities and a useful groundcover for sandy, salty, nutrient-poor coastal soil where few other flowering plants will grow. The aromatic, glandular foliage has a pleasant scent when brushed. A small, obscure but ecologically interesting native of Gulf Coast beach and dune back-areas, useful for detailed ecological plantings of coastal strand communities.

plant_note: Plant in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade to a bit more sun than most hellebores tolerate; H. x sternii, a cross of H. argutifolius and H. lividus, is grown chiefly for its stiff, silver-marbled, purple-tinged evergreen foliage as much as for its pale green flowers flushed pink.
directions: Grow in gritty, well-drained soil with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH in partial shade; this hybrid tolerates more sun and dry spells than most hellebores, a trait inherited from its Mediterranean parent species. Helleborus x sternii forms a tidy, shrubby clump of leathery, spine-toothed leaves heavily veined and marbled in silver over blue-green, often flushed with purple-red along the margins and stems, giving strong foliage interest even without bloom. In late winter, branched clusters of cupped, pale jade-green flowers often tinged rose-pink appear above the foliage, echoing the purplish stem color. Because named selections do not come true from seed, propagate by division of the crown or by basal cuttings taken in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to take advantage of winter rains, or set out nursery starts in fall or early spring, into well-drained, lean, dry to average soil in full sun to partial shade along the coast.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun near the coast or partial shade inland; sticky monkeyflower is a resilient California chaparral and coastal scrub subshrub with narrow, sticky, resinous, dark green leaves and an extended bloom season of open-faced, snapdragon-like flowers ranging from cream and pale yellow through peachy orange to deep red-orange depending on the population. Flowers appear nearly year-round in mild coastal gardens, tapering off only during the hottest, driest part of summer, and are a favored nectar source for hummingbirds and native bees. It is drought-deciduous in harsh conditions, dropping leaves during severe heat or drought and flushing new growth with the return of cooler, wetter weather, so do not mistake dieback for plant failure. Lightly prune leggy stems after the main flowering flush to keep growth dense, and avoid regular summer irrigation once plants are established.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, dry, sandy or rocky, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; stiff aster is adapted to poor, thin soils over rock or sand and struggles in rich, moist garden beds.
directions: Plant in lean, dry, sandy or gravelly, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; thrives in poor, thin soil that would stress most perennials and declines in fertile, moist garden conditions. Ionactis linariifolius (stiff aster, also called sandpaper aster for its rough-textured leaves) is a compact, wiry native perennial of dry rocky outcrops, sandy barrens, and open pine woods across eastern North America, forming a low, bushy mound of narrow, needle-like, evergreen leaves quite different in texture from the broader leaves of most asters. In late summer and fall, the stiff stems are topped with numerous small, violet-purple, yellow-centered flowers that provide valuable late nectar for native bees and butterflies. Its tolerance of poor, dry, rocky soil and compact size make it an excellent, low-maintenance choice for a rock garden, dry sunny bank, or gravel planting where richer-soil perennials would fail, zone 3–8.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; stiff dogwood grows naturally in wet, moist bottomland woodlands, swamp edges, and stream banks of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; stiff dogwood is a native multi-stemmed shrub of wetland margins and moist bottomland forests throughout the southeastern Coastal Plain, distinguished from gray dogwood (C. racemosa) by its more southern range and adaptation to moist to wet conditions. The flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers in spring attract many native bees and flies. The small, blue-black berries on red stems in fall are critically important food for numerous bird species including warblers, thrushes, and vireos during fall migration — one of the most productive native bird-food shrubs for the Gulf South. Spreads by root sprouts to form multi-stemmed thickets in wet conditions. An essential native shrub for wet, shaded garden margins and naturalistic wetland plantings in zone 9a.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in partial shade to full sun; stiff gentian grows naturally in moist, open woodlands, woodland edges, and roadsides of the eastern US and Appalachian Mountains, blooming in late summer and fall after two years of growth as a biennial.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in partial shade to full sun; stiff gentian (agueweed) is a native biennial of the eastern US, producing stiffly upright, branched stems with clusters of small, pale violet to blue-violet, tubular flowers at the stem tips in late summer through fall. Less showy than the fringed or bottle gentians, stiff gentian compensates with its prolific branching and production of many smaller flowers. The common name 'agueweed' comes from a traditional use — the bitter roots were used medicinally for fevers (ague) by eastern Native Americans and early settlers. The bitter principle (gentiopicrin) shared by all gentians has been used in digestive bitters. Biennial, reliably self-seeding in moist, partially shaded woodland garden edges and disturbed areas to maintain persistent colonies. A useful, relatively easy native for woodland garden edges and naturalistic settings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to light shade; stiff goldenrod is drought tolerant and thrives in poor, well-drained soils — it will not thrive in wet or highly fertile conditions where it becomes floppy.
directions: Direct sow in fall or transplant in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — stiff goldenrod is one of the most ornamentally attractive native goldenrods, producing broad, flat-topped clusters of bright golden-yellow flower heads in August–October that contrast beautifully with the coarse, grayish-green, almost sandpapery-textured leaves. Unlike many goldenrods with arching, plume-like inflorescences, stiff goldenrod holds its flowers in rigid, organized, flat-topped corymbs with an unusually bold, architectural quality. It is one of the most valuable late-season pollinator plants on the continent: dozens of specialist bee species including eastern bumble bees, mining bees, and sweat bees depend on goldenrod pollen in late summer as a critical pre-winter protein source, and the flowers host hundreds of beneficial insect species. The stiff, upright habit (rarely needing staking despite the name) makes it more manageable than spreading goldenrod species in garden settings. Blooms reliably with virtually no care in adapted soils.

common_name: Stiff Sunflower (Classic Tallgrass Prairie Rhizomatous Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Stiff Sunflower is a classic tallgrass-prairie species bearing fewer, larger flower heads than most native sunflowers, spreading by rhizomes and tolerant of drought.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; established plants tolerate considerable drought once their rhizomatous root system is settled. Stiff Sunflower is a defining species of the tallgrass prairie, bearing fewer but noticeably larger flower heads than most other native perennial sunflowers, on sturdy, upright, rough-textured stems that hold up well without staking. It spreads gradually by rhizomes to form an increasing colony, blooming from late summer into fall and providing valuable nectar and pollen for native bees and butterflies during a season when many spring bloomers have finished, followed by seed heads that feed goldfinches and other birds through fall and winter. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant and low-maintenance, well suited to a native prairie planting or meadow garden. Divide congested colonies every few years in spring to control spread.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors or divide existing plants in spring; plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun; stiff-leaf aster is adapted to dry, infertile conditions and will become weedy and floppy in rich, moist soil.
directions: Start transplants indoors or divide existing plants in spring; plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun; stiff-leaf aster is adapted to dry, infertile conditions and will become weedy and floppy in rich, moist soil. Ionactis linariifolius is a compact, fine-textured native aster of rocky outcrops, sandy barrens, and dry acidic woodlands, with stiff, needle-like, linear leaves (hence linariifolius) and a profusion of small, 3/4-inch, bright violet-blue to lavender flowers with yellow centers in September and October; it is one of the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant of the native asters, thriving in lean sandy soils and rocky barrens where most asters cannot establish. An excellent choice for dry, naturalistic rock gardens and sandy pine barrens-style gardens; it is a specialist larval host for the scalloped sallow moth and provides nectar for specialist aster bees.

plant_note: Plant in spring in partial shade to full shade in deep, fertile, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil with high humidity in zone 11–12; Stilt Palm (Seychelles Stilt Palm) is a single-trunk palm endemic to the steep, humid forests of the granitic Seychelles islands — one of the botanical jewels of the Seychelles — unique among palms for its conspicuous mass of aerial stilt roots supporting the lower trunk above the forest floor, producing simple (undivided), large pinnate-ribbed leaves and a dramatically exotic appearance in the shaded tropical garden.
directions: Plant Stilt Palm in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to deep shade with year-round high humidity; maintain consistently moist soil; never expose to frost or dry air; protect from direct sun, which scorches the leaves. Verschaffeltia splendida is among the world's most botanically distinctive palms — endemic to the granitic Seychelles islands and found naturally in the steep, humid, shaded ravines and forest slopes of Mahé and Praslin. Its most striking feature is the prominent mass of aerial stilt roots that emerge from the lower trunk and arch outward to anchor the palm in the steep, leaf-litter-covered forest slopes — an adaptation to the unstable, steep hillside habitats it occupies, allowing the palm to maintain stability while the main trunk rises straight and slender above. The leaves are entire (undivided) when young, becoming irregularly split with age in a distinctive pattern not seen in most palms. Reaching 20–40 feet at maturity, with a smooth, slender gray trunk rising dramatically above the radiating stilt root mass, the Stilt Palm is one of the most sought-after and visually extraordinary palms for specialist tropical collectors and botanical garden palm collections. It requires consistent high humidity, shade, and moist soil year-round — a demanding palm for zone 12 conditions only, but extraordinarily rewarding.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Stingray alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Stingray alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. This distinctive hybrid produces long, narrow, undulating leaf blades that taper to a slender, whip-like drip tip, giving each leaf a striking silhouette reminiscent of a stingray's body and tail unlike the broad, arrow-shaped leaves of most other alocasias. Its unusual leaf form makes it a conversation-piece specimen for a shaded patio container or the protected understory of a tropical-themed border, where high humidity and consistent moisture keep the foliage looking its best. Protect from direct hot sun, which scorches the leaves, and from cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit, which causes the plant to go dormant or suffer dieback.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; stinking hellebore is the most shade-tolerant and most distinctly colored of the commonly grown hellebores, producing in midwinter through early spring nodding, bell-shaped, pale chartreuse-green flowers with a maroon rim at the petal margin. Unlike most hellebores, it is fully evergreen with handsome, deeply divided, dark-green palmate leaves that persist year-round. Self-seeds freely in suitable conditions. The unpleasant foliage odor when crushed gives it the common name.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; stinking hellebore is the most architecturally distinctive and most unusually colored of all the hellebores — a robust, fully evergreen shade perennial native to woodland edges, rocky limestone slopes, and scrub across western and central Europe from Britain and France through the Mediterranean region. The deeply divided, palmate, dark-green, leathery leaves are arranged in a dramatic, spreading, star-like pattern on erect stems that persist through the full year — giving the plant a bold, almost tropical-looking architectural foliage presence in the shade garden throughout all twelve months. In midwinter through early spring (January through April in zone 9), the erect stems produce terminal clusters of numerous small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers of an unusual, distinctive pale chartreuse-green color, each flower tipped with a thin, dark maroon-purple rim at the petal margin that creates a distinctive two-toned, green-and-maroon effect quite unlike the warm pinks, purples, and creams of H. orientalis hybrids. The plant self-seeds freely under suitable conditions — in sheltered gardens with consistent moisture and part shade it can naturalize into spreading colonies. The foliage emits an unpleasant odor when bruised, hence the common names 'stinking' hellebore and 'bear's foot' (for the palmate leaf shape). One of the best winter-flowering shade perennials for zone 5–9 gardens with a preference for alkaline soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, average to poor soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; stinking iris tolerates dry shade under mature trees better than almost any other flowering perennial and is remarkably adaptable to poor, dry conditions.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial to full shade; stinking iris (Gladwin iris, gladdon) is one of the most versatile and underappreciated evergreen perennials for dry, deep shade — its leathery, dark-green, sword-shaped leaves provide attractive year-round foliage structure in conditions where little else thrives, including deep dry shade under dense trees. The small, lilac to pale-mauve flowers in June are modest rather than spectacular, but the true ornamental event comes in fall and winter, when the fat seed pods split open to reveal brilliant rows of hard, glistening, orange-scarlet seeds that persist for months, providing one of the finest berry-like winter displays available in the shade garden. The common name refers to the mildly unpleasant smell of crushed leaves. 'Variegata' (cream-striped leaves) is an ornamental cultivar for brighter effect. Extremely drought-tolerant once established. An essential plant for solving dry, deep-shade problem spots.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; stinking passionflower is a self-sowing annual to short-lived perennial that naturalizes readily in zone 9. The sticky, hairy leaves trap insects — a possible protocarnivorous adaptation.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; stinking passionflower is a weedy, delicate annual vine producing small white to pale lavender passion flowers enclosed in intricate, hair-fringed bracts that resemble lace or mist around the flower — giving it the poetic alternative name 'love-in-a-mist'. The red to orange ripe berries enclosed in the lacy bracts are edible and consumed by birds and children. The plant is a larval host for the gulf fritillary butterfly, adding to its conservation value. The leaves have a slightly unpleasant odor when crushed (hence 'foetida') and the glandular hairs on the bracts are sticky and may trap small insects. Self-sows prolifically in zone 9 to naturalize as a charming summer vine, flowering continuously through the season until frost.

plant_note: In zone 8–10, start seeds indoors in September–October and transplant to the garden in October–November for winter–spring blooms; stock requires cool growing conditions (40–65°F nights) to flower well and will not bloom in summer heat. Pinch seedlings to encourage branching.
directions: Start seeds in fall and transplant to cool-season beds in full sun; stock is one of the most intensely fragrant of all garden flowers — the densely clustered, four-petaled flowers in white, pink, red, lavender, or yellow on upright spikes have a clove-like scent that carries 20 feet on still evening air. In zone 8–10 it is grown as a cool-season annual planted in fall and blooming through the mild winter months, filling the winter garden with color and fragrance when little else is in bloom. The double-flowered forms are more fragrant than singles. Stock performs best at temperatures of 40–65°F and declines as summer heat arrives. Plant with pansies, snapdragons, and dianthus for a classic cool-season fragrant border. An outstanding and long-lasting cut flower.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost after cold-stratifying for 4–6 weeks; transplant after last frost.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds in moist medium at 35–40°F for 4–6 weeks before sowing indoors; germination is slow but improved by stratification. Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; Stokes' aster is native to the American Southeast and tolerates heat and humidity well but dislikes wet winter conditions. The large, cornflower-like blooms in blue, lavender, or white appear from early summer to fall and are excellent for cutting. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor; plants spread slowly and are well-behaved in the border.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; stonecrop tolerates poor, rocky, and dry soils extremely well and rots quickly in rich, wet, heavy conditions.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; tall stonecrop (formerly Sedum spectabile, now Hylotelephium spectabile) is a classic late-season border perennial producing bold, flat-topped flower heads of tiny, star-shaped pink to mauve flowers from late summer through fall that attract monarch butterflies, bumblebees, and native bees in extraordinary numbers. The succulent, fleshy, grey-green leaves are attractive from spring through fall, and the dried seed heads remain ornamental through winter and provide food for birds. Excellent drought tolerance once established; the main enemy is wet, poorly drained, or rich soil where it rots. Popular cultivars include 'Autumn Joy', 'Matrona', and 'Neon'.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Stoplight develops the most vivid red center coloration with some morning light — in deep shade the red becomes less saturated while the chartreuse margin becomes more dominant.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Stoplight is one of the most striking Heucherella cultivars — a hybrid between Heuchera and Tiarella (foam flower) that combines the bold foliage color of the former with the finely lobed leaf shape of the latter. The distinctive leaves display a brilliant red-cherry to crimson central blotch surrounded by a wide chartreuse-yellow to lime-green margin — the red-and-green color combination that gives the variety its 'Stoplight' name. The bold foliage contrast makes Stoplight one of the most visually arresting ground-covering shade plants available, and a group planting creates a striking color combination effect in dark garden corners. In late spring, airy, branching wands of small, white, foam-flower-like blossoms rise above the foliage on delicate stems, adding a light, delicate contrast to the bold leaves. Heucherella cultivars are more heat-tolerant and adaptable than many Heuchera cultivars, performing well through zone 9's summer heat when given adequate moisture and shade from afternoon sun. The slowly spreading clumps fill in over 2–3 seasons and require virtually no maintenance beyond dividing when crowded (every 3–4 years). Excellent in shaded borders, woodland gardens, and as a ground cover under ornamental trees.

common_name: Storm Cloud Agapanthus (Deep Blue-Purple Lily of the Nile)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Storm Cloud's dark flower color is most intense in full sun — in partial shade the blue-purple color remains attractive but may not achieve the deepest navy tones.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Storm Cloud agapanthus is a mid-sized cultivar distinguished by unusually dark, deep blue-purple to near-navy flowers — among the darkest flower color available in any common agapanthus selection — produced on upright scapes in midsummer above clumps of narrow, dark-green strap leaves. The intense flower color provides maximum contrast with lighter companion plants — white-flowering perennials, silver-foliage plants, and pale yellow companions create dramatic color combinations with the deep blue-purple Storm Cloud. At 2.5–3 feet tall in flower, it fits mixed perennial borders more easily than the large Ellamae-type selections. Storm Cloud is evergreen in zone 9, providing attractive groundcover foliage year-round, and it is reliably winter-hardy to zone 7 with occasional protection. Like all agapanthus, Storm Cloud is drought-tolerant once established, thrives with minimal fertilization in moderately fertile soils, and actually tends to produce fewer flowers in overly rich soil or with excessive nitrogen fertilization. Outstanding for mass plantings where the deep blue-purple color creates a bold seasonal statement.

plant_note: Biennial; sow in spring or summer for bloom the following year.
directions: Canterbury bells, also called bellflower, is an elegant, tall biennial that makes a dramatic backdrop for shorter annuals and perennials. Surface sow the fine seed, which needs light to germinate, and grow seedlings on before transplanting into rich, moist, well-drained soil. As a biennial, plants form a leafy rosette the first year and send up their cup-and-saucer bloom spikes the second season into early summer. Site in full sun to part shade and stake tall stems in windy spots. The nectar-rich flowers attract bees and other pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moist to moderately dry, rocky, slightly acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in partial shade to full sun. Stout Goldenrod is native to rocky Appalachian woodland edges and tolerates partial shade better than most goldenrods.
directions: Stout Goldenrod is a native perennial of rocky Appalachian woodlands, cliff edges, shale barrens, and dry to moderately moist forest margins from New England south to the mountains of Tennessee and North Carolina, valued as one of the more shade-tolerant goldenrods and distinctive for its stout, robust stems and narrow, leafy inflorescence of bright yellow flowers in August and September. Unlike many goldenrods that require full sun and open meadows, Stout Goldenrod grows happily at shaded rock outcrops, rocky woodland edges, and forest margins with only partial sun, making it a useful native plant for challenging semi-shaded, rocky garden sites. The dense clusters of small yellow flowers attract native bees and late-season butterflies as one of the last significant nectar sources before fall in Appalachian woodland habitats. Direct sow seeds in fall in moist to moderately dry, rocky, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are long-lived and require little maintenance.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; strap-leaf anthurium is best displayed hanging so its long pendulous leaves can drape freely.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; strap-leaf anthurium is best displayed hanging so its long pendulous leaves can drape freely. Extraordinarily long, narrow, ribbon-like leaves dangle several feet down from a short central stem, an unusual pendulous growth form completely unlike the broad heart-shaped leaves of florist anthuriums, with slender, string-like fruit spikes that dangle even further once the plant flowers and sets seed. Native to Ecuadorian and Colombian cloud forests, where it grows as an epiphyte high in the tree canopy, it is best mounted or grown in a hanging basket where its dramatic trailing foliage can be fully appreciated rather than confined to an upright pot. Water when the mix approaches dryness, maintain high humidity, and provide bright, filtered light for the longest, healthiest leaves.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted stolons in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; spreads by long, thread-like stolons that root at the tip to form new plantlets.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted stolons in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; strawberry begonia spreads by long, thread-like stolons that root at the tip to form new plantlets, similar to strawberry runners — divide and replant rooted offsets in spring or fall. Saxifraga stolonifera is an East Asian native groundcover saxifrage that is not related to begonias at all, but earned its common name from the rounded, silver-veined, hairy leaves that resemble certain begonia foliage and the strawberry-like runners that spread to form low mats; in late spring and early summer it produces open panicles of asymmetric, white flowers with two petals much longer than the other three — a delicate, airy, somewhat unusual flower structure. It is an excellent, low, shade groundcover for zones 6–9, performing especially well in the Mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest; in the Gulf South (zone 8–9), provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture and it will thrive as an evergreen to semi-evergreen mat.

common_name: Strawberry Blonde Sunflower (Soft Rose-Pink Branching Cut Flower Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; Strawberry Blonde is a branching, pollen-free sunflower with soft rose-pink to strawberry-red petals fading to a lighter blush at the tips, a departure from the typical yellow-gold sunflower palette popular for romantic cut-flower arrangements.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches for good branching. Strawberry Blonde produces soft rose-pink to strawberry-red petals that fade to a paler blush near the tips, a warm, muted bicolor effect quite different from the bold golds and reds of most sunflower varieties, making it a favorite for romantic, soft-toned floral arrangements and mixed cutting gardens. As a branching type, each plant produces multiple medium-sized blooms over an extended harvest window rather than a single flower, and the blooms are pollen-free, keeping arrangements and clothing free of the yellow pollen standard sunflowers shed heavily once open. Deadhead or harvest spent blooms regularly to encourage continued branching and flowering through the season, from midsummer into fall. Grow in full sun and provide support in windy, exposed sites, since branching plants with multiple flowers can become top-heavy.

common_name: Strawberry Candy Daylily (Pink Reblooming Daylily with Rose Eye)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Strawberry Candy is a popular, widely grown reblooming daylily with rose-pink flowers marked by a deeper raspberry-rose eye zone, valued for its vigor, heavy rebloom, and ease of growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Strawberry Candy is one of the most widely planted modern daylily cultivars, bearing bright rose-pink flowers with a distinct, deeper raspberry-rose eye zone and a matching ruffled edge, a cheerful, candy-like color combination that has made it a garden center staple. It reblooms readily over a long season from early to late summer, producing far more flowers per plant than older, single-bloom-cycle daylily varieties, and it is exceptionally easy to grow, tolerating a wide range of soil types and requiring little care beyond routine watering. The compact, well-branched scapes and reliable performance make it a favorite for mass plantings, borders, and low-maintenance landscaping. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Strawberry Fields Gomphrena (Haage Globe Amaranth, Wild Globe Amaranth)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; soak seeds for 12–24 hours before sowing; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gomphrena haageana is slightly more heat-tolerant and larger-growing than common globe amaranth (G. globosa) and produces superior long-stemmed cut flowers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting (soaking seeds first improves germination); plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Gomphrena haageana (Haage globe amaranth) produces clover-like, papery, rounded flower heads 1–1.5 inches across in vivid orange-red to scarlet (the 'Strawberry Fields' cultivar) or golden-orange, on taller, more upright stems than common globe amaranth (G. globosa). The papery flower heads maintain their color perfectly when dried — making them among the best everlasting flowers for dried arrangements, where the orange-red 'Strawberry Fields' color is one of the most sought-after and unique in the dried flower palette. Heat and drought tolerance is exceptional — plants bloom prolifically through Gulf Coast summers without mildew or decline. The flowers are also outstanding for fresh cutting and as a long-season garden annual. Butterflies visit the rounded flower heads frequently. 'Strawberry Fields' (vivid red-orange) is the most widely grown cultivar; 'QIS Orange' is selected for commercial cut-flower production.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or transplant divisions in spring, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Strawberry Seduction opens vivid cherry-red and fades gracefully through pink to cream as flowers age.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; like other yarrows, it will not tolerate heavy clay or consistently wet soil, especially through humid summers. Strawberry Seduction opens a vivid, saturated cherry-red and gradually fades through rose-pink to soft cream as each flat-topped flower cluster ages, so a single plant displays several colors simultaneously atop finely cut, aromatic, gray-green ferny foliage. It blooms from late spring through summer, and deadheading spent flower stems encourages continued flowering and a tidier appearance. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it performs best in lean, sharply drained soil where richer perennials would struggle, and dividing congested clumps every two to three years in spring keeps the plant vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Strawberry Sundae Hydrangea (Compact Pink-Red Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their mature width to fill in. Strawberry Sundae produces conical flower panicles that open creamy white and quickly flush strawberry-pink from the base upward, creating a two-toned, sundae-like effect as the color moves up each flower cluster through summer, eventually deepening to a richer rose-red in fall. Its mid-size, well-branched habit fits mixed borders and foundation plantings without the bulk of larger panicle hydrangea cultivars. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be pruned back hard in late winter without losing that year's flowers; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Sow seed on the surface of moist starting mix and press lightly — light aids germination, so barely cover seed. Strawflowers tolerate drought and poor soils remarkably well. For drying, harvest stems when the central button of each head is still closed, before the outer bracts fully open; they will continue to open as they dry. Deadhead garden plants regularly to maintain continuous bloom.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring by carefully separating rhizomes, or transplant container-grown plants into consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in part shade; stream orchid grows naturally along seeps, stream banks, and wet canyon floors and requires consistent soil moisture without standing water. It is the most easily cultivated terrestrial orchid native to North America.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in part shade; stream orchid is the most garden-amenable of North America's native terrestrial orchids, found naturally along spring-fed seeps, stream banks, and wet canyon floors throughout western North America from British Columbia to Texas. It produces upright stems with broad, pleated, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately along their length, and in late spring to early summer bears intricate, nodding flowers loosely arranged along the upper stem — each bloom unmistakably orchid-shaped with a cupped, lip petal striped and marked in green, pink, and purple-maroon, like a small, graceful wild orchid spike. Unlike many terrestrial orchids that refuse garden cultivation, E. gigantea establishes well from divisions in consistently moist, partly shaded sites near streams, ponds, or rain gardens. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form modest colonies over time and is an outstanding plant for a naturally moist shade garden where reliably wet soils support it.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, well-drained soil. Soak seeds in near-boiling water for 24 hours before sowing to scarify the hard seed coat and significantly improve germination.
directions: Streambank Wild Hollyhock is a bold, shrubby native perennial found along rocky stream banks, moist meadows, and avalanche tracks in the Rocky Mountains from British Columbia south to New Mexico. It grows into impressive, large-leaved plants with deeply lobed, maplelike foliage topped by tall spikes of rose-pink to lavender flowers 2-3 inches across from June through August. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; it thrives in garden sites that mimic its native riparian habitat and benefits from consistent moisture through the growing season. Soak seeds in near-boiling water for 24 hours before sowing to break dormancy, and expect plants to reach full flowering size in their second or third year.

common_name: Strict Tillandsia (Rosy Air Plant, Brazilian Air Plant, Stricta)
plant_note: Mount on cork bark, wood, or wire in bright indirect to gentle direct light; Tillandsia stricta is one of the more cold-tolerant air plants, surviving temperatures to 28–30°F briefly when dry. In zone 9, plants can be grown outdoors year-round in sheltered positions with good air circulation. Water by dunking in water for 20–30 minutes or misting thoroughly every 2–3 days; allow to dry completely within 4 hours. Produces abundant pups after blooming, quickly forming dense, attractive clumps. Excellent for mounting in groups on boards or logs. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct morning sun — Tillandsia stricta adapts to a range of light conditions better than most Tillandsias and is one of the recommended starter air plants for outdoor use in zone 8-9. Tillandsia stricta is a compact, clump-forming epiphytic bromeliad native to Venezuela, Trinidad, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana, Brazil, and Argentina — a very wide natural range spanning multiple climate zones that explains its reputation as one of the most adaptable and cold-tolerant of the commonly grown Tillandsias. The plant forms a small (4–6 inch) rosette of narrow, somewhat stiff, silvery-green leaves arranged in a spherical to fan-shaped pattern. At bloom time, the rosette produces an upright flower head with bright pink to red bracts from which small, deep blue-violet tubular flowers emerge — a brilliant pink-and-purple color combination that makes the blooming plant particularly striking. After blooming, T. stricta is among the most prolific producers of offsets — a well-established clump can develop 5–10 pups from a single parent, forming a large, multi-rosette cluster in a relatively short time. In zone 8-9, mounted clumps of T. stricta grown outdoors year-round on tree branches, drift wood, or bark panels have become a popular low-maintenance ornamental feature in sheltered garden areas.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Strictus is more upright and stiffer than most miscanthus cultivars and does not require staking — a significant advantage in exposed positions where wind would topple arching types.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Strictus, also known as Porcupine Grass, is the most distinctive upright miscanthus cultivar — sharing the yellow banding characteristic of Zebrinus (zebra grass) but with an importantly different growth habit: while Zebrinus has a loose, arching, spreading form that can sprawl untidily, Strictus grows rigidly upright with a narrow, stiff, columnar form that stays tightly together and doesn't flop. The horizontal yellow bands that stripe each leaf perpendicular to its length create the unusual porcupine-stripe appearance that gives this cultivar both its common name and its striking visual effect — the banding is only visible at relatively close range but creates an unusual texture effect that is distinctive and unusual. The upright, narrow form (6–8 feet tall, 4 feet wide) makes Strictus outstanding for screening, privacy hedges, and vertical accent use where the wide-spreading form of other miscanthus types would be inappropriate. In fall, copper-bronze flower plumes rise above the foliage before drying to a persistent, ornamental winter structure. Like all Miscanthus sinensis cultivars, cut to 6 inches in late winter before new growth begins. Note invasive potential in some eastern states.

common_name: String Theory Amsonia (Dwarf Fine-Textured Threadleaf Blue Star)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun. String Theory is a dwarf selection of threadleaf blue star, staying under 18 inches — roughly half the height of the species — while keeping the same finely textured, needle-like foliage and pale blue, star-shaped spring flowers, then putting on the same spectacular golden-yellow fall foliage display the species is prized for. Its smaller scale fits border edges and smaller gardens where full-size Amsonia hubrichtii, which can reach 3 feet, would eventually crowd the space. It is deer-resistant, drought-tolerant once established, and essentially pest-free, needing no staking or routine division.

plant_note: Lay or lightly bury stem cuttings on top of a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in spring or summer in bright indirect light to partial sun; roots form readily along the stem nodes within a few weeks.
directions: Grow in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, watering only once the soil has dried completely. This South African trailer is a close relative of string of pearls but carries small, curved, banana-shaped succulent leaves along thin, fast-growing stems that can trail 2-3 feet from a hanging basket or shelf edge. In late winter to spring it can produce small, white, cinnamon-scented daisy-like flowers. It grows noticeably faster and is somewhat more forgiving of brighter light than string of pearls, but shares the same intolerance for wet feet, so err on the side of underwatering. All parts are considered toxic if ingested by pets or people.

common_name: String of Buttons (Necklace Vine, Crassula perforata)
plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings after the cut end has callused for a few days, then insert into gritty succulent mix and keep barely moist until roots take hold.
directions: Grow in hanging baskets or shallow pots with fast-draining succulent mix, providing bright but filtered light to avoid scorching the pale foliage. Let the soil dry out fully between waterings and reduce water further in winter. Triangular gray-green leaves are stacked in opposite pairs along trailing stems, threading through each other in a way that gives the plant its common name. In warm weather mature plants send up small clusters of star-shaped white or pale pink flowers at the stem tips.

common_name: String of Dolphins (Dolphin Plant, Dolphin Necklace)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun after allowing the cut ends to callus for a day; this hybrid roots slower than string of pearls, so keep the mix barely moist, not wet, until new growth appears.
directions: Grow in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, watering only when the mix has dried completely. This whimsical intergeneric hybrid, a cross between string of pearls and the candle plant (Curio articulatus), bears crescent-shaped, faintly ribbed leaves that curve like a pod of leaping dolphins along trailing stems, making it a favorite conversation piece for hanging baskets and shelves. It shares the low-water, fast-draining needs of both parents and rots quickly if left in soggy mix, so let it dry out fully between waterings, especially in winter. As with its string-of-pearls parent, it is considered toxic if ingested by pets.

common_name: String of Hearts (Rosary Vine, Chain of Hearts)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright indirect light to partial sun; String of Hearts is typically grown as a hanging basket or trailing container plant rather than in the ground, since it has very little cold tolerance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial sun, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings. String of Hearts produces long, thin, trailing stems draped with small, heart-shaped, marbled gray-green and silver leaves, occasionally accented with a pink or purple blush, making it a favorite hanging basket and shelf plant that cascades gracefully over a container edge. It is a true succulent and rots quickly in overly wet, poorly drained soil, so err on the side of underwatering, particularly in winter when growth slows. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container that can be moved indoors or under cover during freezes, since it has very little cold tolerance, unlike more cold-hardy garden succulents.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket, or mount on a slab, in bright, indirect light in a loose, fast-draining, orchid-bark-based epiphytic mix; string of nickels is a true epiphyte and rots quickly in dense, moisture-retentive potting soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket, or mount on a slab, in bright, indirect light in a loose, fast-draining, orchid-bark-based epiphytic mix; string of nickels is a true epiphyte and rots quickly in dense, moisture-retentive potting soil. Small, round, coin-like succulent leaves are strung closely along thin, wiry, trailing stems, forming a dense curtain of tiny green discs that cascades attractively from a hanging basket or mounted slab, punctuated occasionally by small, inconspicuous pale flowers. Native to Southeast Asian and Pacific rainforest canopies, where it grows attached to tree bark rather than rooted in soil, it stores water in its fleshy leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings rather than sit in consistently moist mix. Provide bright, filtered light and excellent air circulation, and mist occasionally to boost humidity without saturating the roots.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty, slightly alkaline to neutral succulent potting mix in bright indirect light to part sun; string of pearls requires perfectly draining substrate and infrequent watering — the spherical leaves store water and will rot quickly if kept wet.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light; water only when soil is completely dry. Senecio rowleyanus (string of pearls) is one of the most distinctive and sought-after trailing succulents in cultivation — a South African native producing trailing stems up to 2–3 feet long densely clothed in perfectly round, pea-sized, green, bead-like succulent leaves with a distinctive translucent stripe on each sphere. The spherical leaf shape is a remarkable adaptation for water storage and light transmission: the round form minimizes the surface-area-to-volume ratio (reducing water loss) while the translucent stripe allows light to penetrate to the interior of the leaf for photosynthesis. The resulting trailing curtains of pearl-like leaves cascading from hanging baskets or trailing over pot edges are one of the most charming and photogenic effects in indoor or outdoor succulent gardening. In late winter, plants may produce small, white, cinnamon-scented flowers. CAUTION: Toxic to cats and dogs if ingested. String of pearls requires careful watering — the most common error is overwatering; allow soil to dry completely between waterings.

common_name: String of Raindrops (String of Watermelons, String of Gooseberries)
plant_note: Lay stem cuttings on the surface of a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in spring or summer in bright indirect light to partial sun and mist lightly until roots establish along the buried nodes.
directions: Grow in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, allowing the mix to dry fully before watering again. Trailing stems carry plump, teardrop-shaped leaves with fine translucent striping reminiscent of tiny watermelons, a South African relative of string of pearls that is somewhat larger-leaved, faster growing, and slightly more tolerant of brighter light. Clusters of small white, faintly fragrant flowers can appear in winter on mature plants. As with its relatives, overwatering and poorly drained soil are the most common causes of failure, so keep it on the dry side, especially in winter when growth slows.

common_name: String of Stars Hoya (Wax Vine, Linearis Hoya, Thread-Leaf Hoya)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket in bright indirect to moderate shade; Hoya linearis is more cold-tolerant than most Hoyas, surviving brief temperatures to 40°F if the root zone is dry — its native Himalayan habitat means it experiences cool dry winters. In zone 9 it may survive outdoors in a protected spot, but container culture is safer. Use a very well-draining, airy mix. The narrow, soft leaves are more susceptible to root rot from overwatering than the succulent-leaved Hoyas. Propagate from stem cuttings in moist mix. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Hoya linearis is somewhat more shade-tolerant than the succulent-leaved Hoyas but requires good light to bloom. Hoya linearis is a cascading epiphytic vine from the Himalayas of Nepal, Bhutan, northeastern India, and southwestern China, growing naturally on mossy tree branches and rock faces at cool elevations of 5,000–8,000 feet — one of the few Hoyas to originate from a genuinely cool mountain environment. The plant looks startlingly different from the typical Hoya: instead of thick, waxy, succulent leaves, Hoya linearis produces long, narrow, slightly hairy, soft-textured, thread-like leaves less than an inch long that are densely arranged along trailing stems, creating a cascading, fern-like or rosemary-like texture entirely unlike other popular Hoyas. Long stems hang in soft curtains from hanging baskets, creating an elegant waterfall of narrow foliage. In summer, the plant produces tight umbels of small, pure white, star-shaped flowers with a sweet, slightly waxy fragrance. The combination of unusual fine-textured foliage and delicate white flowers makes Hoya linearis one of the most distinctive trailing houseplants available, prized by Hoya collectors and general houseplant enthusiasts alike. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Root short stem or single-node cuttings in a fast-draining, chunky mix (standard potting soil amended with extra perlite or fine bark); String of Turtles is slow to root and slow-growing overall compared with most terrarium plants, so patience is needed. Keep only lightly moist — this species is unusually prone to rot for a peperomia.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a very fast-draining, chunky mix, and let the soil dry substantially between light waterings — String of Turtles is a diminutive, semi-succulent, trailing Brazilian peperomia that has become one of the most sought-after small houseplants for its tiny, thick, rounded leaves patterned with dark green and silvery-gray marbling in a shape strongly resembling a miniature turtle shell, strung along thin wiry reddish stems. Despite its succulent-like water storage, the fine root system is easily damaged by overwatering, and the species is notably more rot-prone than its chunky leaves might suggest — it is generally considered a plant for growers already comfortable with succulent watering habits rather than a beginner terrarium plant. It thrives in bright light (some morning direct sun toughens growth) and appreciates a shallow, wide pot or terrarium placement with excellent drainage over a moisture-retentive but not soggy substrate. Slow-growing compared with most peperomias, it rewards patience by eventually cascading in dense strands of shell-like leaves ideal for terrarium edges, small hanging pots, or shelf displays.

plant_note: Plant stem fragments or divisions at any point in the growing season into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; stringy stonecrop spreads unusually fast for a sedum via long, thin, wiry runners that root at every leaf node.
directions: Plant stem fragments in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; stringy stonecrop is a fast, low, trailing sedum with whorls of narrow, bright yellow-green, succulent leaves along thin, wiry stems that root readily wherever they touch soil, spreading noticeably quicker than most other low-growing sedums. Clusters of small, star-shaped yellow flowers appear in early summer above the foliage, though the plant is grown chiefly for its rapid, dense groundcover habit rather than for floral display. It handles more shade and slightly more moisture than typical rock-garden sedums, making it useful for covering bare ground quickly under high, open shade or in a semi-shaded rock wall where faster establishment is wanted. Because it spreads so readily, confine it with a mowed edge, walkway, or container rather than placing it directly among smaller, choice rock garden plants it could overrun.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded terrarium plant in zone 9; Begonia listada cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It prefers high humidity (50–70%) and well-draining, slightly acidic potting mix. Allow the top half-inch of soil to dry between waterings. Excellent for terrariums, enclosed plant cases, and high-humidity indoor displays where its striking foliage can be appreciated at close range. Propagate from leaf cuttings or stem tip cuttings.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Striped Begonia prefers the bright indirect light of a north or east window and will bleach in direct sun, though it can flower in lower light levels than many begonias. Begonia listada is a small, upright to slightly trailing begonia native to southern Brazil, one of the most distinctively marked of the many begonia species in cultivation. The leaves are the primary ornamental feature: dark emerald-green, slightly puckered and hairy, with a distinctive pale green to yellow-green stripe that runs precisely along the entire length of the central midrib, creating a two-toned leaf that appears to have been painted with a lime-green brush stroke down the center. The undersides of the leaves are dark red-purple. The combination of the dark green leaf with the bright central stripe and the hairy, textured surface creates a compact plant with strong graphic appeal. Begonia listada produces small but attractive white flowers with a reddish calyx that adds to the ornamental display. The plant's compact size and high-humidity requirements make it well-suited to terrarium culture, where the consistent moisture, gentle air circulation, and close viewing distance allow the detailed foliage markings to be appreciated. A parent species in some hybrid begonia programs, contributing the central-stripe leaf pattern.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall into well-drained woodland soil; cold winter temperatures fulfill stratification requirements for spring germination.
directions: Sow seed in early fall into a woodland garden bed with well-drained, slightly acidic soil, pressing seed to the surface and covering with only a dusting of soil or leaf litter. Cold stratification through winter is essential for breaking dormancy, and seedlings should emerge by mid-spring. This rare southeastern gentian is sensitive to waterlogged roots, so ensure drainage is adequate even in moist woodland conditions. Plants typically require two or more growing seasons before producing their striking fall-blooming, purple-striped flowers.

common_name: Striped Lily of the Valley (Variegated Convallaria)
plant_note: Plant dormant pips or divisions in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade in fall, or in early spring where fall planting is impractical.
directions: Plant pips a few inches deep with the growing tip just below the soil surface in rich, cool, evenly moist soil, then leave undisturbed for several years as the rhizomes spread into a naturalized patch. Stripes are strongest on emerging spring foliage and tend to fade somewhat by midsummer, especially in warmer climates, so this form is best appreciated as an early-season accent. Each cream-and-green striped leaf pair frames the same intensely fragrant, nodding white bell flowers of the species in mid-spring. It brings extra visual interest to a shaded spring border even before the flowers open, and like the species it spreads readily to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under trees.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in late winter or early spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, cool, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; striped maple is a cool-climate understory tree that requires protection from afternoon sun and heat in zone 6+ and will not thrive in zone 7 and warmer.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, cool soil in partial to full shade — striped maple is one of North America's most beautiful native understory trees, instantly recognizable by the striking vertical white-and-green striping on the young bark (giving it the alternate name 'snakebark maple' or 'moosewood'). The large, three-lobed leaves turn butter yellow in fall. It is a true understory specialist that grows naturally in the shade beneath taller hardwoods in cool, moist, acidic mountain forests — it is shade-tolerant enough to regenerate in nearly complete shade. Moose browse the bark in winter (giving the common name). Not suited to zone 7 and warmer, where the heat and humidity are too much for this cool-climate species. An outstanding ornamental tree for the shaded garden in zone 3–6, particularly in New England, the upper Midwest, and the Appalachian highlands. The ornamental bark is visible year-round and is spectacular.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3 inches apart in well-drained, average to humus-rich soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; striped squill is an extremely cold-hardy and adaptable early spring bulb that performs especially well in partial shade under deciduous trees, where it receives full early spring sun before the canopy closes. It naturalizes steadily and is an excellent choice for planting in lawns or woodland edges.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich to average soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for very early spring bloom; striped squill (Puschkinia, Lebanese squill) is one of the earliest and most adaptable of all spring bulbs — a small, graceful, extremely cold-hardy bulb producing loose, upright racemes of pale icy-blue to silvery-white flowers, each petal delicately striped down its center with a deeper blue-grey line that gives the flowers their distinctive, precise, etched appearance. It blooms very early, typically alongside Scilla siberica and early Chionodoxa in March and April, forming a luminous, cool-toned carpet of pale blue-white flowers. Native to rocky slopes and open woodland from the Caucasus to Lebanon, it is perfectly adapted to life under deciduous trees and shrubs, thriving in the bright spring light that reaches the ground before trees leaf out. It naturalizes steadily and combines beautifully with snowdrops, early crocus, and Scilla in naturalized plantings. Excellent for planting in the lawn, at woodland edges, or beneath specimen trees.

common_name: Striped Torch Bromeliad (Florida Guzmania, West Indian Tufted Airplant)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, mounted epiphyte, or shaded container specimen; Striped Torch has no frost tolerance outside its native south Florida hammocks and swamps, where it grows as a protected epiphyte. It can be mounted on a piece of wood or bark like a Tillandsia, or potted in a very open, fast-draining orchid-bark mix. This species is state-listed as endangered in Florida due to habitat loss and over-collection, so only source nursery-propagated plants and never remove it from the wild.
directions: Provide bright, filtered light similar to dappled canopy shade — this species naturally grows as an epiphyte on tree limbs in humid hammocks, so it favors more airflow and slightly less constant moisture in its cup than tank-forming Guzmanias. Guzmania monostachia is native to south Florida (including Everglades and Big Cypress hammocks), the Caribbean, and Central and South America, forming a soft, arching rosette of light green, strap-shaped leaves. Its inflorescence is distinctive among Guzmanias: a slender, upright spike of white to cream bracts striped and tipped with green and, later, red, topped with small white flowers, rather than the flat colorful star of bracts typical of Guzmania lingulata. Mist occasionally and keep a small amount of water in the central cup, flushing it periodically to prevent stagnation.

plant_note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; Striptease is a relatively fast-growing hosta that forms good-sized clumps within 3–4 years and is one of the most eye-catching of the tricolor hostas.
directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; Striptease retains good variegation in moderate to full shade, making it more versatile than many hostas that need some sun to hold their color. Hosta 'Striptease' is one of the most visually striking of all hosta cultivars — named for its unique tricolor variegation pattern in which dark-green leaf margins surround a bright gold-yellow center separated by a narrow, precise bright-white stripe that runs the full perimeter of the central gold section; this crisp, three-colored, sharply-defined pattern is unlike most hosta variegation and gives 'Striptease' a bold graphic quality rare in shade-garden plants. The medium-sized leaves are 7–8 inches long with an upright, slightly wavy habit. Near-white lavender flowers appear in late summer. 'Striptease' was introduced by Tony Avent and received the American Hosta Society's Alex J. Summers Distinguished Merit Hosta award. It is a vigorous, relatively fast-growing cultivar that forms impressive clumps within 3–4 seasons.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; stromanthe requires consistently high humidity — in dry conditions, leaf edges brown and the striking variegation fades. Misting or a humid microclimate is beneficial.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; stromanthe (Triostar, 'Tricolor') is a Brazilian tropical perennial of the prayer plant family (Marantaceae) that produces some of the most dramatically colored foliage of any shade tropical plant — the long, lance-shaped, leathery leaves are boldly painted in irregular splashes, streaks, and blotches of cream-white, pale green, and deep forest green on the upper surface, while the undersides are uniformly, intensely wine-red to magenta, creating a bicolor leaf display that is visible from both above and below. Like its relatives calathea and maranta, the leaves fold upward in the evening (a response called nyctinasty, hence 'prayer plant' family), revealing the red undersides in a daily display. Requires consistently moist soil and high humidity — the primary challenge of growing stromanthe successfully in hot, dry climates. Excellent in shaded tropical borders, outdoor living spaces, and bright-shade patio containers in zones 10–12. The cultivar 'Triostar' is the standard variegated selection widely grown.

common_name: Strutter's Ball Daylily (Deep Purple Daylily with Green Throat)
plant_note: Divide and transplant bare-root fans in spring or late summer, spreading roots out in a shallow planting hole with the crown just below the soil surface.
directions: Set bare-root fans in spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, fanning the roots downward and covering the crown with about an inch of soil. Water deeply after planting and keep beds weeded until clumps are established. Introduced in the early 1980s, Strutter's Ball produces velvety, deep purple-black blooms with a sharp, luminous green throat that provides striking contrast against the dark petals. Its rich color and vigorous clump-forming habit have kept it one of the most recognizable dark-toned daylilies in cultivation.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in warm, fertile, moist soil in full sun; Stuttgart is grown primarily as a dramatic foliage accent, with large leaves heavily marbled and streaked in white over gray-green, needing a bit more shade protection than green-leaved cannas to avoid leaf scorch.
directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in warm, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, since the heavily variegated white-and-gray leaves can scorch in the most intense sun and heat. Stuttgart is grown chiefly as a bold foliage accent, with large leaves dramatically marbled and streaked in white over a soft gray-green base, giving it a ghostly, eye-catching presence that stands apart from typical solid-green or brightly striped canna foliage; its small orange flowers are secondary to the striking leaves. Like other cannas it thrives with generous water and rich soil, tolerating even boggy ground at a pond edge. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage; in zone 8-10 gardens it can typically be left in the ground with a heavy mulch layer for winter protection.

common_name: Subcostata Crape Myrtle (Cold-Hardy Species with Exfoliating Bark)
plant_note: Plant container trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Lagerstroemia subcostata is a cold-hardy crape myrtle species grown primarily for its outstanding exfoliating bark.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Lagerstroemia subcostata is grown chiefly for its outstanding ornamental bark, which peels away in patches to reveal a smooth, mottled tapestry of cinnamon, gray, and cream tones, providing four-season interest that outshines its relatively modest clusters of small white summer flowers. It is notably more cold-hardy than most ornamental crape myrtle hybrids and has been used as breeding stock to pass improved bark quality and cold tolerance into modern cultivars. Site it where the trunk can be seen and appreciated year-round, such as near a patio or entry, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches, since heavy pruning sacrifices the multi-trunked form that best displays the bark.

common_name: Substantial Evidence Daylily (Heavily Ruffled Cream-Gold Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; the heavy ruffling and substance of this cultivar develop best with consistent moisture and a full day of light.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Substantial Evidence produces large, extremely thick-substanced, heavily ruffled cream-to-gold flowers with a lightly gold-edged ruffle, bred to hold their crisp form through the heat of the day when thinner-petaled daylilies wilt or go limp by afternoon. Vigorous branched scapes carry numerous buds, extending bloom over several weeks rather than a single flush. Remove spent scapes after flowering to keep the clump tidy and channel energy back into the crown. Divide every three to four years in spring as the clump becomes congested, watering divisions well until re-established.

plant_note: Plant container trees in spring or fresh seed in fall in any well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, clay to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; sugar hackberry is exceptionally adaptable to difficult soil conditions including alkaline soils, clay, and brief flooding.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade — sugar hackberry is the primary Celtis species of the Gulf Coast and Deep South, better adapted to the heat, humidity, and occasional flooding of zone 7–9 than the common hackberry (C. occidentalis). The distinctive warty, corky-gray bark is unmistakable and one of the most interesting bark textures of any native tree. Small orange to purple-black berries in fall are among the most important food sources for migrating songbirds — more than 50 species consume the berries, including yellow-rumped warblers and hermit thrushes. The tree is the exclusive larval host for the hackberry emperor butterfly and American snout butterfly, two distinctive native butterflies wholly dependent on Celtis species. It tolerates urban conditions, compacted soils, drought, and alkaline pH remarkably well. A keystone wildlife tree for the Gulf Coast landscape.

plant_note: Transplant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil away from road salt and compacted urban sites, since sugar maple is sensitive to both.
directions: Transplant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil away from road salt and compacted urban sites, since sugar maple is sensitive to both. This long-lived tree develops a dense, rounded crown prized for the brilliant orange and scarlet fall color that defines much of the eastern hardwood forest, and mature stands are the traditional source of maple syrup sap. It provides excellent shade for large residential and park settings but needs consistent moisture during establishment and should be kept out of confined urban tree pits. Give it room to grow undisturbed for decades, as it is intolerant of heavy pruning and soil disturbance near its roots.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Sugar Shack is a compact selection reaching only 4–5 feet, far smaller than the 8–12 foot species; it fits into residential landscapes where the full-sized species would be too large. Buttonbush is a wetland native that grows along stream banks, pond edges, and in low-lying areas with poor drainage — it is one of the very few ornamental shrubs suitable for consistently wet or periodically flooded sites. Blooms on new wood; prune in late winter to control size and stimulate maximum flowering.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sugar Shack Buttonbush thrives in the poorly drained, wet soils that defeat most landscape shrubs and is actually native to swamp and wetland margins; Sugar Shack is a compact cultivar of native Buttonbush (Cephalanthus occidentalis), introduced by Bailey Nurseries as a landscape-appropriate size selection of one of the most ecologically valuable native shrubs in North America. The extraordinary round, spherical, 1–1.5 inch white flower heads that appear in July–August are genuinely unusual — the flower ball is densely packed with tiny, long-tubed white florets with projecting styles that give the whole ball a pin-cushion or sputnik-like radiating texture unlike any other common landscape plant. This unusual flower structure is extremely attractive to butterflies (especially swallowtails and skippers), bumblebees, and other nectar-seeking pollinators — making Buttonbush one of the highest-value native pollinator plants available. The subsequent seed heads remain through winter as small, persistent brown balls that provide food for ducks, songbirds, and small mammals. As a native species adapted to Gulf Coast wetlands, Sugar Shack Buttonbush fills the specific niche of a flowering shrub for wet, low-lying sites that are often the most challenging spots in residential landscapes.

common_name: Sugar Tip Rose of Sharon (Variegated Sterile Pink Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; variegation is brightest with several hours of direct sun.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Sugar Tip stands apart from other rose of sharon cultivars for its striking blue-green foliage crisply edged in creamy white, providing ornamental interest even before the double, soft pink flowers open from midsummer into fall. As a sterile selection, it sets little to no seed, avoiding the self-sowing weediness of older rose of sharon while adding season-long variegated foliage color that few other rose of sharon cultivars offer. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established, making it a low-maintenance, multi-season shrub for a sunny border.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sugar and Spice forms a slowly spreading, non-invasive clump and benefits from consistent moisture, especially in warmer parts of its range.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, mulching with leaf litter to keep roots cool and evenly moist. Sugar and Spice is a foamflower cultivar with deeply cut, maple-like green leaves marked by a bold, dark burgundy-purple central blaze that intensifies in cooler weather, topped by fluffy spikes of pale pink to white star-shaped flowers in spring that give the plant its common name. It forms a dense, slowly spreading, non-aggressive clump ideal for the front of a shaded border, a woodland path edge, or massed as a groundcover beneath deciduous trees, and pairs well with heuchera, hosta, and ferns for season-long foliage contrast. Foliage often takes on additional reddish tones through fall and can remain semi-evergreen in milder climates.

subcategory: South African Cape fynbos signature shrub
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; sugarbush protea requires excellent drainage — wet, heavy soils are fatal. Do not fertilize with phosphorus (phosphorus kills Proteaceae). Use only Proteaceae-specific or low-phosphorus fertilizers. It blooms in winter and spring, is adapted to fire, and produces large quantities of sweet nectar. Outstanding for birds (sunbirds in South Africa; hummingbirds in cultivation). The dried flower heads are widely used in the floral trade.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; sugarbush is the most widely distributed and historically significant protea species — the signature Cape fynbos plant of the mountains and coastal hills of the Western Cape from which the Cape Floral Kingdom takes much of its iconic visual identity. The flower heads are typical protea form — a rounded 'artichoke' of overlapping bracts enclosing the central mass of flowers — in white to cream-white to pale pink, sometimes streaked or flushed with deeper pink or rose, each individual flower head 4–5 inches across. They bloom in winter and spring (May–October in South Africa) and produce so much sweet nectar that the common name 'sugarbush' refers to the honey-like sweetness that children and sugarbirds alike consume directly from the flower — the traditional source of 'proteabosse stroop', a traditional Cape syrup. The nectar production and flower structure are extraordinary among ornamental plants; in cultivation, hummingbirds visit the flowers repeatedly. The large, dried flower heads, with their sculptural, papery bracts, are a major cut-flower and dried-flower export from South Africa. A magnificent signature plant for zone 9 Mediterranean-climate gardens — requiring the specific drainage, lean soil, and low-phosphorus conditions of its fynbos habitat.
