plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, rich, well-drained to moist soil in full to partial sun; sugarcane plumegrass tolerates a wider range of moisture conditions than bent-awn plumegrass and can be planted in moist woodland edges, stream banks, and moist meadow margins.
directions: Sugarcane plumegrass is the tallest native grass of the eastern United States, reaching 6–10 feet in height and producing enormous, feathery, white-to-copper-tinted plumes in fall that rival pampas grass in spectacle while being fully native and ecologically appropriate across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plains. As a close relative of sugarcane in the genus Saccharum, it shares similar bold, architectural characteristics — long, broad, pointed leaves with white midribs, reed-like stems with prominent nodes, and a strongly upright, vase-shaped form that provides a dramatic focal point in any large native planting. The silky plumes attract and shelter migrating birds in fall and provide nesting material for marsh and meadow birds; the tall, dense clumps create excellent wildlife screening habitat. Best suited to moist, rich woodland edges, stream banks, and rain garden borders where its imposing size can be fully appreciated — the fall plumes are stunning backlit by afternoon or evening sun in October and November.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in average to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately well-drained soil in full sun in early spring; stratify seeds cold for 30 days in the refrigerator before sowing to improve germination rates. Sullivan's milkweed does not transplant well once established due to a deep taproot — plant it where it can remain permanently.
directions: Direct sow stratified seeds in average to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sullivan's milkweed (smooth milkweed) is a superior native milkweed alternative to common milkweed (A. syriaca) for garden settings — it produces the same essential monarch butterfly breeding habitat but in a more refined, clump-forming growth habit without the aggressive rhizomatous spread that makes common milkweed difficult to manage in ornamental borders. The smooth, hairless, blue-green leaves and stems are handsomely architectural, and large, fragrant, rosy-pink flower clusters appear in June and July — slightly more ornamental than the common milkweed. The inflated, warted seed pods split in fall to release silky-plumed seeds. Considered an excellent monarch host plant for formal and semiformal garden settings where common milkweed's spread would be problematic. Less common in the nursery trade than some milkweeds but increasingly available from native plant specialists.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; Sulphur bears dark green leaves margined in sulfur-yellow that matures to creamy white.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; sun causes unattractive yellowing and leaf scorch, so this is one of the best broadleaf evergreens for the darkest corners of the garden. Sulphur bears dark green leaves edged with a band of sulfur-yellow that softens to creamy white as the foliage matures, giving a more subtly variegated look than the boldly speckled Aucuba cultivars. As a female selection it needs a male Aucuba such as 'Mr. Goldstrike' nearby to set the bright red berries that persist through winter. It tolerates salt spray, pollution, and heavy shade under large trees better than nearly any other broadleaf evergreen.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 3–4 weeks before) in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil in full sun; sulphur cosmos is even more heat- and drought-tolerant than C. bipinnatus and blooms most freely in lean conditions — do not fertilize.
directions: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 3–4 weeks before) in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil in full sun; sulphur cosmos is even more heat- and drought-tolerant than C. bipinnatus and blooms most freely in lean conditions — do not fertilize. Cosmos sulphureus is the warm-colored cosmos native to tropical Mexico and Central America, producing semi-double to double flowers in vivid yellow, gold, orange, and red on compact, branching plants; it is much more heat-tolerant than the familiar pink-and-white C. bipinnatus and provides brilliant color through the hottest summer periods when other cosmos decline. The flowers are excellent for small native bees, hoverflies, and monarch butterflies; sulphur cosmos is particularly heat-adapted and is the better cosmos choice for zone 8–11 southern gardens. It self-seeds prolifically in warm climates.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Epimedium establishes slowly in the first season but spreads steadily thereafter, forming dense, weed-suppressing colonies under trees where other ground covers struggle. Once established, it is remarkably drought tolerant for a shade plant — making it one of the few ground covers that thrives in the dry, shaded conditions under mature trees where soil moisture is depleted by tree roots. Cut back the old foliage to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges to reveal the delicate spring flowers. In zone 9 the foliage is semi-evergreen to nearly evergreen in mild winters.
directions: Plant in shade to dappled shade in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sulphur Epimedium is exceptional among shade ground covers for its tolerance of dry shade under tree canopies where most ground covers struggle to survive; Sulphureum is one of the most widely planted and reliable Epimedium cultivars, a hybrid ground cover producing heart-shaped, compound leaves on wiry stems with a subtle bronze-red tint on new spring growth and persistent semi-evergreen foliage that provides year-round texture. In early spring, before or with the emerging foliage, delicate sprays of small, spurred, clear sulfur-yellow flowers appear on arching stems — creating a brief but charming floral display that is easily the most delicate and refined spring flowering of any commonly available shade ground cover. Epimedium's genuine value lies in its ability to colonize and thrive under the specific conditions created by large, established shade trees — dry, rooty, shaded soil with heavy competition for moisture and nutrients — conditions where hostas, ferns, and most other shade perennials eventually decline. As a permanent ground cover in these challenging dry-shade situations, Sulphur Epimedium is effectively irreplaceable, providing low-maintenance, visually attractive coverage in the most difficult zone 9 planting conditions.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring; sulphur epimedium prefers well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade. A hybrid between E. pinnatum and E. diphyllum, it combines vigor with attractive semi-evergreen foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; sulphur epimedium is a naturally occurring or garden hybrid producing pale sulphur-yellow (creamy-yellow) flowers in spring — a softer, more refined color than the bright yellow of E. pinnatum. The semi-evergreen foliage provides attractive ground cover through most of the year in mild climates. Like the best garden epimediums, it spreads steadily by underground rhizomes to form a weed-suppressing colony without becoming invasively aggressive. An excellent choice for naturalizing under mature deciduous trees where the canopy creates challenging dry shade conditions — one of the few perennials that not only survives but thrives in these conditions. Shear back the old foliage in late winter to reveal and enjoy the spring flowers.

common_name: Sulphur Queen Spider Lily (Yellow-Flowered Hymenocallis Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sulphur Queen is a yellow-flowered spider lily cultivar, a less common color than the more typical white-flowered hymenocallis types.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Sulphur Queen produces the same delicate, spidery, fragrant flowers typical of hymenocallis, but in an unusual soft yellow rather than the classic white of most spider lily cultivars, giving a fresh color option for the summer bulb border. The strappy, dark green foliage stays attractive through the growing season, and the fragrant blooms open over several weeks in summer, drawing evening pollinators like moths. It multiplies slowly by offset bulbs to form an expanding clump over time and is generally low-maintenance once established, needing only routine watering during dry spells and winter mulch protection in the cooler parts of its range.

plant_note: Sow in fall so seed overwinters and cold-stratifies naturally, into lean, gritty, very well-drained, dry soil in full sun; sulphur-flower buckwheat is a widespread Rocky Mountain and Intermountain West native of dry, rocky slopes and open pine forest.
directions: Plant in gritty, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; sulphur-flower buckwheat forms a low mat of rounded, gray-green leaves topped from early to midsummer by flat clusters of bright sulfur-yellow flowers on wiry stems, aging to rust-orange and copper tones that remain attractive well into fall and winter. It is an important larval host and nectar source for numerous native butterflies, including several blue butterfly species, and its persisting dried seed heads feed overwintering birds. Extremely drought and cold tolerant once established, it thrives in the same rocky, mineral, low-fertility soils that most garden perennials reject, making it a natural fit for rock gardens, dry slopes, and high-elevation xeriscape plantings. Avoid rich soil, fertilizer, and supplemental summer water, all of which shorten its life and cause floppy, less colorful growth.

common_name: Sultan's Ruby Siberian Iris (Deep Magenta with Gold Signal)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Sultan's Ruby bears deep magenta standards and velvety magenta falls with a round gold signal.
directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Sultan's Ruby bears deep magenta standards and velvety magenta falls set off by a round gold signal at the throat, among the richest, most saturated colors available in a Siberian iris, opening over narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division, and when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Sum and Substance is more sun-tolerant than most hostas and can take morning sun in zone 9 without scorching, but afternoon shade is essential in the South. Established plants are drought-tolerant.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Sum and Substance is the most widely grown large golden-yellow hosta in American gardens and winner of the American Hosta Society's Hosta of the Year award in 2004 — an enormous specimen hosta producing clumps 4–6 feet wide with individual leaves 18–24 inches long in bright chartreuse-gold that deepens to golden-yellow in full sun. The scale is spectacular: a mature clump becomes a ground-covering mass of large, ribbed, luminous leaves that make it a landscape statement plant rather than merely an accent. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in midsummer. 'Sum and Substance' is more slug-resistant than many hostas because of its thick, leathery leaf texture — a practical advantage in moist garden settings where slug damage is a persistent problem with thinner-leaved varieties. In zone 9 it is a reliable perennial that goes fully dormant in winter and returns strongly each spring.

common_name: Summer Beauty Ornamental Onion (Long-Blooming Pink-Purple Allium)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring (or fall in mild climates) in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Summer Beauty tolerates more shade and heavier soil than many ornamental onions. It forms a tidy, glossy, deer- and rabbit-resistant clump of strap-like foliage topped from midsummer into early fall by rounded, rosy-purple globe flowers that draw heavy bee and butterfly traffic for weeks — one of the longest bloom periods of any ornamental allium. It performs reliably in the humid Gulf South as long as drainage is adequate, and its glossy foliage resists the rust that can disfigure some ornamental onions in humid climates. Divide congested clumps only when they become crowded after several years; it pairs well with coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, and ornamental grasses in a late-summer pollinator border.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Summer Chocolate holds its rich foliage color best with a half-day or more of direct sun and shows some improved resistance to Fusarium wilt over the green species, though it is not immune. CAUTION: like the species, it can self-seed — remove spent seed pods if volunteer seedlings near natural areas are a concern.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Summer Chocolate is a purple-leaved sport of mimosa selected for its deep bronze-chocolate, finely divided, fern-like foliage, which holds its dark color through the heat of summer far better than most other purple-leaved trees and provides a striking, season-long contrast to the pale pink, silky pompom flowers produced from early summer into fall. It is somewhat smaller and more restrained in habit than the straight green species, typically reaching 15-20 feet, and its weak, brittle wood still benefits from a sheltered planting site away from strong winds. Because it is grafted or vegetatively propagated onto known rootstock, Summer Chocolate is more predictable in size and color than seed-grown mimosas, but gardeners in the Gulf South should still watch for and remove volunteer seedlings, as the cultivar remains capable of setting viable seed.

common_name: Summer Drummer Allium (Very Tall Late-Summer-Blooming Ornamental Onion)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Summer Drummer is an unusually tall allium reaching up to 6 feet, blooming later in summer than most ornamental onions.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Summer Drummer stands out among ornamental onions for its exceptional height, reaching up to six feet on strong, sturdy stems topped by loose, creamy-white starburst flower heads with a purple-tinted base, blooming later in the season, from midsummer into late summer, than the spring-blooming alliums most gardeners are familiar with. Its towering height and late bloom timing make it a dramatic back-of-border accent that extends the ornamental allium season well past the typical spring display. The dried seed heads persist and add winter interest if left standing. Allium foliage often yellows and dies back before or during bloom, so plant lower companion perennials in front to hide the fading leaves.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep after danger of frost has passed once soil has warmed in spring.
directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep and 8-12 inches apart after the last spring frost in fertile, well-drained soil, choosing a sheltered spot since the tall flower spikes can catch wind. Strap-shaped bluish-green leaves rise first, followed in late summer by arching racemes of pendulous, fragrant white bell flowers reminiscent of giant hyacinths or summer-blooming galtonia relatives. It combines well toward the back of a mixed border or among ornamental grasses, and the cut flower spikes hold up well in arrangements. In climates colder than about zone 7, lift and store the bulbs indoors over winter as you would gladiolus or dahlias.

common_name: Summer Jewel Lavender Salvia (Compact Early-Blooming Hummingbird Sage)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 sow March-May or September for a fall planting. Summer Jewel Lavender blooms several weeks earlier from seed than standard-sized Salvia coccinea and stays compact at 18-24 inches.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; Summer Jewel Lavender is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most freely in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9. It rounds out the All-America Selections-winning Summer Jewel series alongside Red and Pink, offering the same compact, early-blooming, heat-tolerant habit of tropical sage in a soft, cool lavender-blue that reads differently in the border than its warm-toned siblings, borne on whorled spikes atop upright, well-branched plants from late spring to frost. Like the rest of the series it is bred from a Gulf Coast and Caribbean native wildflower that normally reaches 3-4 feet, condensed here into a garden-scaled size that still draws hummingbirds and butterflies reliably. It self-seeds readily in zone 9, and established plants need little beyond an occasional deep watering during extended dry spells.

common_name: Summer Jewel Pink Salvia (Compact Early-Blooming Hummingbird Sage)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 sow March–May or September for a fall planting. Summer Jewel Pink blooms 3–4 weeks earlier from seed than standard-sized Salvia coccinea and stays compact at 18–24 inches.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; Summer Jewel Pink is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most freely in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9. This All-America Selections award-winning companion to Summer Jewel Red carries the same compact, early-blooming, heat-tolerant habit of tropical sage but in clear soft pink, borne on whorled spikes atop upright, well-branched plants from late spring to frost. Like its red counterpart, it is bred from a Gulf Coast and Caribbean native wildflower that normally reaches 3–4 feet, condensed here into a more garden-scaled size without sacrificing the free flowering or hummingbird appeal of the species. It self-seeds readily in zone 9, letting one season's plants volunteer reliable color the following year, and needs little more than an occasional deep watering during extended dry spells once established.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 sow March–May or September for a fall planting. Summer Jewel Red is an All-America Selections award-winning selection of Texas Sage (Salvia coccinea), a native annual of the Gulf Coast and Southeast US that naturalizes prolifically in warm gardens. In zone 9 it self-seeds abundantly — allowing one generation of plants to set seed ensures volunteers in subsequent years. The compact form (18–24 inches) blooms 3–4 weeks earlier from seed than standard-sized Salvia coccinea. The vivid red tubular flowers are among the most reliable hummingbird plants available for zone 9 summer gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Summer Jewel Red Salvia is drought tolerant once established and blooms most freely in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9; Summer Jewel Red is an All-America Selections award-winning compact cultivar of Tropical Sage (Salvia coccinea), a native annual wildflower of the Gulf Coast, Caribbean, and Central America that produces bright red, tubular flowers organized in whorled spikes on upright, hairy stems. The compact selection (18–24 inches) was specifically bred from a species that normally reaches 3–4 feet, creating a more garden-appropriate size while maintaining the free-flowering, heat-tolerant, hummingbird-attractive character of the wild species. Salvia coccinea is one of the most effective hummingbird plants available for zone 9 — the vivid red, narrow tubular flowers are precisely adapted for hummingbird pollination and attract Ruby-throated and other hummingbirds with unusual reliability wherever the plant is grown in their range. As a native species, Tropical Sage supports native bees and hummingbirds while naturalizing through self-seeding to create stable, self-renewing populations in zone 9 gardens once established. The combination of hummingbird value, heat tolerance, shade adaptability, self-seeding naturalization, and low maintenance needs makes it one of the most practical ornamental annuals for Gulf South summer gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger in warm soil and full sun.
directions: Summer Lovin bears a mix of creamy lemon-tipped petals with burgundy or strawberry-pink centers, often several color variations on a single plant. Direct sow the large seed after the last frost in warm, well-drained soil and full sun, planting about an inch deep. The tall, branching stems are pollenless and stiff, perfect for clean cut-flower bouquets. Thin seedlings to give plants room and stake if needed in exposed sites. Harvest often to encourage more blooms across the summer.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Summer Nights bears vivid, saturated magenta-pink petals held outward to slightly downward around a prominent dark orange-brown cone, on a compact, sturdy, well-branched plant that produces far more flowers per stem than older coneflower selections. Its intense color and heavy bloom make it a strong pollinator draw through summer, and its heat and drought tolerance suit it well to a Gulf South perennial border once established. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering starts to decline.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Summer Nights develops its darkest stem and foliage color in full sun with consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Summer Nights is a German-bred selection of the native false sunflower, chosen for its near-black, purple-flushed stems and dark green foliage with purple undertones that provide dramatic contrast to its abundant golden-orange, daisy-form flowers produced from midsummer through early fall. The long, sturdy stems make it a favorite for cut flower use, and the extended bloom period makes it one of the most reliable, long-flowering native-species perennials for the summer border. Like the wild species, it is highly attractive to a wide range of native bees, butterflies, and other pollinating insects, and its seed heads provide food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds if left standing into fall and winter. It is tolerant of heat and average garden conditions once established, benefits from division every three to four years to maintain vigor, and generally does not require staking despite its height, thanks to its sturdy, dark stems.

common_name: Summer Pastels Yarrow (Mixed Soft-Color Seed Strain)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow after frost danger has passed, into very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Summer Pastels is a classic All-America Selections-winning mixed-color seed strain.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since yarrow rots readily in heavy, wet soil. Summer Pastels is a classic All-America Selections-winning seed strain producing a soft mix of cream, apricot, salmon, pink, and lavender flowers across a planting, a gentler palette than the bright golds and reds of many named yarrow cultivars, held on sturdy stems above aromatic, finely cut gray-green foliage from early summer through fall. Deadheading spent flower clusters extends the bloom season and keeps the planting tidy. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it performs best in lean, sharply drained soil, and because it is seed-grown, individual plants within a planting will vary somewhat in exact color, adding to its informal, cottage-garden charm.

common_name: Summer Skies Delphinium (Light Sky-Blue Pacific Giant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall for cool climates; Summer Skies is a classic Pacific Giant delphinium strain bearing pale sky-blue flowers with a white bee.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, staking tall flower spikes to protect them from wind and summer storms. Summer Skies bears towering spikes of large, semi-double flowers in a soft, pale sky-blue, each centered with a contrasting white 'bee,' a gentler, more pastel counterpart to the deep violet-blue of King Arthur within the classic Pacific Giant delphinium series. Its light color works well woven through a cottage-style border or cutting garden alongside pinks and whites. In warm climates it is typically grown as a cool-season annual or short-lived biennial since it declines quickly in summer heat and humidity. All parts are toxic if ingested. Cut spent flower spikes back hard after the first bloom flush to encourage a possible secondary, shorter round of flowering later in the season.

common_name: Summer Sky Coneflower (Pink-and-Orange Bicolor Big Sky Coneflower)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Summer Sky is part of the Big Sky series of hybrid coneflowers, bearing bicolor pink-and-orange blooms.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Summer Sky bears petals that shift from soft pink at the base to warm orange at the tips around a coppery-orange cone, a sunset-toned bicolor effect distinctive among the Big Sky series of hybrid coneflowers bred to expand the traditional purple-pink coneflower palette. It blooms over a long summer season and tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead for continued bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; despite its common name, summer snowflake blooms in spring (March-April), not summer — the name refers to the season of its native European habitat rather than its bloom time. It is outstanding planted beside ponds, streams, or in low-lying areas that stay moist, and naturalizes well in partial shade under deciduous trees where soil moisture is adequate.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade or sun in fall for March-April bloom; summer snowflake is a taller and later-blooming relative of the spring snowflake (L. vernum), producing erect, hollow stems 12-18 inches tall that each carry a cluster of 2-5 pendant, white, bell-shaped flowers with a distinctive bright green dot at the tip of each rounded petal — giving the flowers a delicate, precise, spotted appearance that distinguishes them from all other white spring bulbs. Despite its misleading common name, it blooms in spring, typically in March and April alongside mid-season daffodils. It is a moisture-loving bulb by nature, native to wet meadows, riverbanks, and alluvial woodlands across Europe, and it thrives in conditions too damp for most bulbs — beside water features, in low-lying areas, or in partial shade where soil remains evenly moist. It naturalizes readily by offsets into large, robust clumps that increase year after year without division, and the selected cultivar 'Gravetye Giant' is a larger, more vigorous form with especially bold flowers.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Summer Snowflake is more upright and narrower than most doublefile viburnums, making it a better fit for a foundation planting or narrow side-yard bed.
directions: Summer Snowflake is a doublefile viburnum valued for producing a strong flush of flat, white lacecap flower clusters in mid-spring and then continuing to open scattered new clusters sporadically through summer into early fall, a much longer bloom window than the single spring flush typical of most doublefile selections. Its growth habit is narrower and more upright than the wide-spreading species, fitting more easily into foundation plantings and smaller garden spaces, while still producing the tiered horizontal branching, red-to-black fall berries, and burgundy fall foliage typical of the group. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, and prune, if needed, only right after the main spring flush to avoid removing the buds that produce the later summer rebloom.

common_name: Summer Torch Bromeliad (Foolproof Plant, Pyramidal Billbergia)
plant_note: Plant outdoors in partial shade to filtered sun in zone 9b-11; Summer Torch tolerates brief drops into the upper 20s°F once established and is regularly grown as a permanent, low-maintenance groundcover under tree canopies across Florida and the Gulf Coast. In zone 9, mulch heavily over winter or grow in a container that can be moved under cover during hard freezes. Divide crowded clumps by separating rooted offsets any time during active growth.
directions: Grow in filtered sun to partial shade — Summer Torch is among the more sun-tolerant tank bromeliads and can handle a few hours of direct morning sun outdoors, though hot afternoon sun will scorch the leaves. Billbergia pyramidalis is a clump-forming bromeliad native to Brazil and the Caribbean, earning the nickname 'foolproof plant' for its tolerance of neglect, drought, and a wide range of soils and light. Its loose, vase-shaped rosettes of glossy green leaves send up a short, dense, pyramid-shaped flower head in summer, packed with brilliant scarlet-red bracts and blue-tipped petals that make it one of the showiest and easiest bromeliads to bloom reliably outdoors. Keep the central cup topped with water, but the plant also tolerates the cup drying out briefly, unlike more sensitive tank bromeliads. Established colonies spread readily by offsets and naturalize into dense drifts.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. Summer Wave Blue is a trailing variety that cascades beautifully in hanging baskets, window boxes, and over the edges of raised beds. It blooms continuously without deadheading in shade conditions where most annual flowers fail. In zone 9 it performs through summer heat better than most shade annuals when given consistent moisture and afternoon shade protection from the most intense heat.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Summer Wave Blue Torenia (wishbone flower) is a trailing, shade-tolerant annual producing a continuous display of snapdragon-like flowers with deep violet-blue upper petals and a pale lavender lower lip with a bright yellow throat — one of the most vivid blue-flowered shade annuals available. The Summer Wave series from Suntory Flowers was specifically selected for superior heat tolerance and continuous flowering without deadheading in shaded conditions where standard impatiens may struggle in humid summer heat. The trailing habit (spreading 24–36 inches on 6-inch-tall stems) makes it exceptional for hanging baskets, window boxes, and shade containers where the cascading stems display the colorful flowers at eye level. Torenia thrives in the moist, warm, shaded conditions that characterize summer weather in the Gulf South — zone 9 gardens with humid summers provide near-ideal growing conditions. The wishbone-shaped stamens inside each flower give the plant its common name.

common_name: Summer Wave Torenia (Heat-Tolerant Shade Wishbone Flower Annual)
plant_note: Plant container transplants after the last frost in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Summer Wave Torenia is one of the most heat-tolerant shade annuals for Gulf South gardens — maintaining good bloom through the humid summer months when impatiens and other shade annuals fail.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Summer Wave Torenia (Torenia fournieri) is a spreading, trailing shade annual producing small (1-inch) two-lipped, tubular flowers in blue-purple with white and yellow markings — the wishbone-shaped stamen arrangement that gives the family its common name visible within each flower. The 'Summer Wave' series was developed by Proven Winners specifically for the trailing, spreading habit that fills containers and ground-level shade plantings with cascading growth rather than the upright habit of older torenia varieties. In Gulf South gardens, torenia occupies an important ecological niche: a heat-tolerant shade annual for summer months when impatiens (the other primary summer shade annual) increasingly fails due to impatiens downy mildew disease that has devastated impatiens performance across the southeastern US. The shade tolerance and heat performance of Summer Wave Torenia make it one of the most reliable summer annuals for partial-shade positions in zone 9 where few flowering plants provide consistent bloom through July–September. The spreading, self-branching habit fills 18–24 inch containers without pinching, and plants in ground-level beds spread quickly to provide solid coverage. Colors in the Summer Wave series range from blue to lavender to large white to berry colors — all with the characteristic wishbone flower form.

common_name: Summer Wine Ninebark (Compact Wine-Red Foliage Ninebark)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Summer Wine is a more compact ninebark cultivar than Diabolo, with deep wine-red foliage, fitting smaller borders and foundation plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Summer Wine brings the same striking dark foliage color popularized by Diabolo into a considerably more compact plant, better suited to foundation plantings, smaller borders, and mass plantings where a full-sized ninebark would grow too large. The deep wine-red leaves hold their color well through the season, especially in full sun, and clusters of small white flowers in late spring add contrast before fading to reveal reddish seed capsules later in summer. It requires minimal care beyond occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems each year to maintain a full, vigorous shrub.

common_name: Summerific Hardy Hibiscus (Compact Large-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus Series)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Summerific series hibiscus were bred for a more compact, well-branched habit than older hardy hibiscus, which tend to grow tall and leggy, while still producing dinner-plate-sized flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. The Summerific breeding series was developed to bring the enormous, dinner-plate-sized flowers of hardy hibiscus into a shorter, sturdier, more floriferous plant than older cultivars, which often grow tall, sparse, and prone to flopping. Depending on the specific cultivar in the series, flower colors range from pure white and soft pink to deep red and near-black-leaved forms, all blooming from midsummer into fall. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown, and it is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in late spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; summersweet tolerates seasonally wet, boggy conditions and thrives along stream banks and pond margins.
directions: Root softwood cuttings in late spring or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; summersweet (sweet pepperbush) is one of the finest native shrubs for shaded, moist gardens, producing upright spikes of small, pure-white to pale-pink, intensely and deliciously fragrant flowers in mid- to late summer — filling a bloom gap when few shade-tolerant shrubs flower. The clean, lustrous, dark-green foliage turns bright golden-yellow to orange in fall. It suckers to form multi-stemmed colonies in suitable conditions. Excellent for stream banks, rain gardens, woodland edges, and shaded borders with consistently moist soil. 'Hummingbird' (compact, 2–3 feet), 'Ruby Spice' (deep pink flowers), and 'Sixteen Candles' are superb cultivars. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit the fragrant flowers heavily.

common_name: Sun Mandevilla (Tropical Vine with Large Showy Summer Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; provide a trellis, obelisk, or other support for the twining stems — mandevilla climbs by twining and requires vertical support to display its full ornamental potential.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sun Mandevilla (Mandevilla x hybrida, marketed under trade names including 'Sun Parasol') is a tropical climbing vine producing large (3–5 inch diameter), trumpet-shaped flowers in shades of brilliant red, deep pink, rose, pale pink, or white throughout the warm season. The large, glossy, dark-green leaves and continuous production of oversized, flamboyant flowers make mandevilla one of the most dramatically ornamental vines for Gulf South container gardens, trellis plantings, and patio displays. In zone 9, mandevilla grows vigorously through the warm season (April–November), producing continuous flowers without deadheading. The twining stems require a trellis, post, or support structure to climb — without support, mandevilla sprawls as a mounding container plant, which is also ornamentally effective. Zone 9b and 10 gardeners can treat mandevilla as a perennial vine that returns from the roots after mild winters; in zone 9a, the plants may be killed by severe freezes but return from persistent roots with mulch protection, or be overwintered as container plants in a frost-free garage or greenhouse. Red-flowered cultivars are attractive to hummingbirds. Container-grown mandevilla requires more frequent watering and fertilization than in-ground plants — use a balanced liquid fertilizer every 2 weeks through the growing season for best bloom production.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Sun Parasol Crimson is a selection from the Sun Parasol brand mandevilla series bred for outdoor performance in warm climates. The plant twines naturally and needs a trellis, fence, pergola, or other structure to climb. In zone 9 it grows vigorously from spring through fall, blooming continuously without deadheading from first planting through first frost. In the warmest zone 9 locations the plant may survive mild winters as a semi-woody perennial; in most of zone 9 treat as an annual or move container-grown plants indoors before frost. The milky sap is irritating to some people — wear gloves when pruning.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sun Parasol Crimson Mandevilla blooms most abundantly in full sun with consistent moisture; Mandevilla (Mandevilla x amabilis) is a tropical twining vine producing large, funnel-shaped flowers with five broadly overlapping petals in a classic five-lobed arrangement — the Sun Parasol Crimson selection bearing vivid crimson to deep rose-red flowers 3–4 inches across that create a striking, uninterrupted bloom display from late spring through frost. Mandevilla's combination of tropical flower size (far larger than most annual vines), glossy deep green foliage, continuous bloom without deadheading, and ability to quickly cover a trellis, pergola, or fence with an impressive tropical display makes it one of the most impactful ornamental vines for zone 9 summer gardens. The large, funnel-shaped flowers are hummingbird-attractive — the trumpet form, bright crimson color, and sweet nectar production make mandevilla a reliable hummingbird plant wherever hummingbirds occur. In zone 9's warm, humid climate, mandevilla performs as one of the finest summer flowering vines available — thriving in the heat that defeats many vine species and providing the tropical character that suits the Gulf South climate.

plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, since Sun Power tolerates more light than many hostas but still needs protection from harsh midday sun. Water deeply during dry spells to prevent leaf scorch on the thin gold foliage. This upright, vase-shaped cultivar bears large, ruffled, chartreuse-to-gold leaves that brighten as the season progresses, topped by pale lavender flowers in summer. Bred by Paul Aden, it is valued for its bold vertical form and vivid color in partly shaded borders.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; sun-changing begonia colors most dramatically with bright indirect light and consistent humidity.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; sun-changing begonia colors most dramatically with bright indirect light and consistent humidity. This unusual Brazilian species is named for its remarkable ability to shift leaf color through the day, its rounded, lightly ruffled leaves turning from soft chartreuse-green to a striking golden yellow-green in bright light before settling back to green in lower light, an adaptive color response rather than fixed variegation. Its ever-changing foliage color makes it a conversation piece among collectors, and it is best displayed where its subtle daily transformation can actually be observed, such as a bright kitchen or sunroom window. Keep humidity moderate to high, water when the soil surface begins to dry, and protect from harsh direct sun, which can scorch rather than simply color the leaves.

common_name: SunPatiens Compact Orange Impatiens (Sun-Tolerant Season-Long Bedding Impatiens)
plant_note: Set out transplants after the last frost into full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; unlike traditional impatiens, SunPatiens tolerates full sun and heat without wilting and is also resistant to downy mildew, the disease that has devastated standard impatiens plantings.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, and feed regularly through the season to sustain the vigorous growth and nonstop bloom this series is bred for. SunPatiens Compact Orange is a vegetatively propagated, downy-mildew-resistant impatiens hybrid bred to tolerate full sun and heat that would scorch or collapse traditional Impatiens walleriana, holding a dense, well-branched, self-cleaning mound covered in bright orange flowers from spring through frost. The Compact series stays more tidy and controlled than the larger Vigorous SunPatiens line, making it well suited to smaller beds, borders, and container plantings where a large spreading mound would be too much. Consistent moisture is important during establishment and through the hottest stretch of summer, though established plantings tolerate brief dry spells better than traditional impatiens.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. SunPatiens are a Sakata Seed trademark and are sold as vegetatively propagated transplants only — not as seed. The Compact series plants are smaller (18–24 inches) than the Vigorous series (24–36 inches), making Compact Pink better suited to containers and formal beds. SunPatiens bloom continuously without deadheading and are self-cleaning. In zone 9 they perform well from spring through fall in both sun and partial shade, withstanding summer heat and humidity significantly better than traditional bedding impatiens.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil — SunPatiens tolerate more sun than traditional impatiens and are suitable for both shaded and full-sun locations; SunPatiens Compact Pink is part of the SunPatiens line from Sakata Seed — an interspecific impatiens hybrid (Impatiens x hybrida) developed to solve the critical problem of impatiens downy mildew (Plasmopara obducens) that devastated traditional bedding impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) populations beginning around 2011–2012. The interspecific hybrid parentage gives SunPatiens resistance to this downy mildew disease that rendered conventional impatiens unreliable for shade garden use in warm, humid climates. SunPatiens Compact Pink produces large (1.5–2 inch), bright candy-pink flowers continuously from planting until frost, with glossy, slightly succulent foliage that is more heat-tolerant than standard impatiens. The unique sun-and-shade tolerance allows SunPatiens to be used across a wider range of light conditions than any traditional impatiens variety — from deep shade to full sun — making it one of the most versatile summer annuals for varied garden situations.

common_name: SunPatiens Vigorous Lavender New Guinea Impatiens (Large Vase-Habit Downy-Mildew-Resistant Impatiens)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; SunPatiens Vigorous Lavender is the large-form, vase-habit tier of the SunPatiens line, reaching 30-36 inches, with strong resistance to downy mildew.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, watering regularly to keep soil consistently moist. SunPatiens Vigorous Lavender is the largest-growing tier of the SunPatiens breeding line, forming a substantial, upright, vase-shaped plant 30 to 36 inches tall covered in soft lavender-pink flowers from spring through frost, a dramatically bigger scale than the compact, mounding SunPatiens forms bred for smaller beds and containers. Like the rest of the SunPatiens line, it carries strong resistance to the downy mildew that devastated old-fashioned impatiens walleriana plantings, and tolerates considerably more sun than traditional shade impatiens while still performing well in partial shade. Its size makes it useful as a substantial seasonal hedge, back-of-border filler, or large container centerpiece. No deadheading is needed to keep it blooming continuously.

common_name: SunRich Lemon Sunflower (Pollen-Free Single-Stem Pale Yellow Cut Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; succession sow every 1-2 weeks through summer since the crop matures all at once.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep on 6-9 inch spacing in full sun. SunRich Lemon grows as a single unbranched stem bred for uniform height and bloom timing, producing pale, soft lemon-yellow petals around a dark center disk that offer a gentler, more pastel look than the deep golds typical of most cut-flower sunflowers. Because the flowers are pollen-free, they're a clean choice for mixed arrangements and won't stain fabric or drop pollen on tablecloths. Plan on harvesting the entire planting within a narrow window, roughly 55-65 days after sowing, and cut when petals have just started to open for maximum vase life.

common_name: SunRich Orange Sunflower (Pollen-Free Single-Stem Orange Cut Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; succession sow every 1-2 weeks through summer since the crop matures all at once.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep on 6-9 inch spacing in full sun; SunRich Orange grows as a single unbranched stem bred for uniform height and bloom timing, the traits that make the SunRich line a favorite of commercial growers. The rich, deep-orange petals surround a dark center disk and hold their color well in the field and in the vase, offering a bolder alternative to the paler golds and lemons elsewhere in the series. Because the flowers are pollen-free, they're a clean choice for mixed arrangements and won't stain fabric. Plan on harvesting the entire planting within a narrow window, roughly 55-65 days after sowing, and cut when petals have just started to open for maximum vase life.

common_name: SunRich Sunflower (Pollen-Free Single-Stem Cut Flower Series)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; for succession harvests, sow every 1-2 weeks through summer. SunRich is a major commercial single-stem, pollen-free cut-flower sunflower series bred for uniform bloom timing and strong stems, widely used alongside ProCut in professional cut-flower production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; grow on a tight spacing of 6-9 inches to encourage the single, unbranched flowering stem this series is bred to produce. SunRich is one of the leading commercial cut-flower sunflower series, offering pollen-free flowers in gold, lemon-yellow, orange, and other colors on strong, straight, single stems bred specifically for uniformity, making it a favorite of market growers who need predictable, evenly timed harvests. Because plants do not branch, close spacing maximizes stem count per bed, and the whole planting typically matures and is harvested together roughly 55-65 days after sowing. The pollen-free trait keeps arrangements and clothing clean of the yellow pollen that standard sunflowers shed heavily once open. Harvest when petals have just begun to unfurl but the center disk remains tight for the best vase life, and succession sow every one to two weeks through the growing season for a continuous cut-flower supply.

plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; unlike single-stem seed sunflowers, Sunbelievable is a vegetatively propagated, sterile hybrid that branches continuously and never needs deadheading or staking for a single giant bloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, and expect a mounded, heavily branching plant rather than the tall single stalk of a traditional sunflower. Sunbelievable is a sterile hybrid sunflower series bred for nonstop bloom, covering itself in hundreds of small, 2-inch, brown-eyed golden flowers continuously from late spring until frost without ever needing deadheading, since sterile flowers do not go to seed and stop blooming the way fertile sunflowers do. Its dense, self-branching, weather-resistant habit holds up well in wind and rain without staking, making it a reliable choice for containers, borders, and mass plantings where a traditional sunflower's single giant bloom and floppy stem would be impractical. Because it is a sterile hybrid, it is propagated only from cuttings and sold as a rooted plant rather than from seed.

plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Suncredible produces a large number of full-sized flowers on a well-branched, taller plant, blooming continuously without the deadheading a traditional single-stem sunflower requires.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, and expect a taller, more upright, heavily branching habit than compact landscape sunflower series. Suncredible is a vegetatively propagated sunflower bred for continuous rebloom, producing full-sized, classic golden sunflower blooms with dark centers in huge numbers from a single well-branched plant over a long summer-to-frost season, without the need to deadhead or replant as is required with traditional single-bloom seed sunflowers. Its taller stature and heavier bloom load make it a strong choice for the middle or back of a sunny border, a cutting garden, or a large container where its abundant flowers can be enjoyed both in the garden and as cut flowers. Stake in windy sites if needed, and feed regularly through the season to sustain its extended, heavy bloom production.

common_name: Sundae Fraise Hydrangea (Compact Strawberry-Pink Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Sundae Fraise is a compact panicle hydrangea, smaller than Vanilla Strawberry, that fits foundation plantings and smaller gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Sundae Fraise produces upright, conical flower panicles that open creamy white in midsummer and gradually flush from the base upward through pink to a rich strawberry-red as the season progresses, giving a bicolor effect similar to the larger Vanilla Strawberry but on a more compact, three-dimensional, well-branched shrub better suited to smaller yards and foundation plantings. Its strong stems hold the panicles upright without flopping even as they mature and gain weight. Like other H. paniculata cultivars it blooms on new wood, so prune hard in late winter to a low framework to encourage vigorous new growth and the largest flower panicles the following summer.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm. In zone 9 plant March–May. Sunday Orange celosia is heat-loving and actually blooms better and more vividly as temperatures increase — it is one of the few annuals that performs better in summer heat rather than declining. The large, feathery plumes are excellent for fresh cutting and dry extremely well on the plant, making them outstanding for dried flower arrangements.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Sunday Orange is a plume-type (feather) celosia producing dramatic, soft, feathery plumes in vivid pure orange — one of the most saturated and vividly colored of any annual flower, with an almost unreal intensity of color that makes it instantly eye-catching in summer garden displays and mixed cut flower arrangements. The plume-type celosia (as opposed to the crested cockscomb type) has soft, delicate, branching flower heads that resemble bright-colored feathers or flames, which explains the common name 'plumed cockscomb' or 'feather celosia'. Sunday Orange was developed for uniformity, large plume size, and early bloom — beginning to flower 60–75 days from transplant and continuing continuously until frost without requiring deadheading. Celosia is genuinely heat-loving: plants grow slowly in cool weather and then rapidly accelerate in hot summer conditions, blooming most freely in zone 9's intense summer heat. The flowers dry in place on the plant and can be cut for dried arrangements at any stage of development.

plant_note: Fall sow or cold-stratify seed; taproot resents transplanting.
directions: Sundial lupine, also called wild lupine, is a heirloom perennial native to the eastern U.S. and a vital host plant for the Karner blue butterfly. Scarify or cold-stratify the hard seed and direct sow in fall or early spring, since the deep taproot dislikes transplanting. Grow in full sun in lean, sandy, well-drained soil where it naturalizes in wildflower gardens and meadows. Its blue flower spikes appear in late spring to early summer and draw many pollinators. Avoid rich soil and excess water, which this drought-tolerant native does not need.

common_name: Sundial Mango Portulaca (AAS-Winning Warm Mango-Orange Moss Rose for Summer Heat)
plant_note: Surface-sow seeds after the last frost in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; do not cover seeds — portulaca seeds require light for germination; Sundial Mango blooms reliably even in cloudy conditions unlike older portulaca varieties that closed their flowers on overcast days.
directions: Surface-sow seeds on well-drained, lean to sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sundial Mango is an All-America Selections award-winning portulaca (moss rose) — part of the Sundial series selected for an important improvement over older portulaca varieties: the ability to remain open and in bloom on overcast days. Traditional portulaca varieties close their flowers in shade, cloudy weather, and in the afternoon, significantly limiting their ornamental value to only the sunniest morning hours. The Sundial series maintains flower opening throughout the day in typical light conditions, including partial overcast. The Mango color — warm, sunny, deep apricot-orange to mango-orange — is one of the richest and most distinctive in the Sundial color range, producing a warm, vibrant display in the rock garden, gravel mulch, and dry border positions where portulaca excels. Portulaca is one of the most truly drought-tolerant and heat-resistant summer annuals for full-sun Gulf South positions — thriving in lean, sandy, or gravelly soil where other annuals would fail, and continuing to bloom through the driest and hottest periods of Gulf South summer. The succulent stems and leaves store water to bridge dry periods without wilting. The low, spreading mounding habit (6–8 inches tall, 12–18 inches wide) makes portulaca ideal for rock walls, gravel gardens, and the fronts of full-sun borders.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–May. The Sundial series is one of the most widely grown portulaca series in North America, selected for flowers that remain open longer than older portulaca — traditional portulaca closes in shade and on cloudy days, while Sundial remains open in lower light conditions. Do not cover seed — portulaca requires light for germination. Direct sow on the soil surface and press in lightly. Thin seedlings to 8–10 inches. In zone 9 portulaca is one of the most dependably heat and drought-tolerant annuals available — thriving in the harshest summer conditions while continuing to flower prolifically. Excellent for rock gardens, sandy banks, and other hot, dry situations where few other annuals can perform.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Portulaca demands full sun and excellent drainage; it thrives in the dry, hot conditions that defeat most other annuals and declines rapidly in shade or wet soil; Sundial Orange Portulaca is a compact, semi-double to double portulaca producing vivid orange flowers in the Sundial series, one of the most improved portulaca strains available — with flowers that remain open in lower light conditions than older portulaca varieties that close completely on cloudy days and in shade. The succulent stems and leaves of Portulaca grandiflora (from its South American native range) store water and enable the plant to withstand drought conditions at which most annual flowers wilt and decline — making portulaca uniquely valuable for hot, dry, full-sun situations including sandy banks, rock gardens, paving cracks, and dry border edges where conventional annuals would require frequent irrigation to survive. The brilliant orange of Sundial Orange provides one of the most saturated and vivid warm-color tones available from a low-growing annual — particularly effective as an edging or mass planting against stone or gravel surfaces where the orange flowers glow against neutral backgrounds. In zone 9's peak summer heat portulaca improves in performance while most other annuals decline, making it the go-to choice for reliably colorful, extremely low-maintenance summer color in the most challenging hot, dry sunny situations.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–June. Sundial series portulaca flowers stay open later into the afternoon than older varieties (which close in overcast or afternoon conditions), making them more useful as a continuous-color bedding plant throughout the day. In zone 9 portulaca thrives in the hottest, driest summer conditions — a perfect full-sun annual for hot, dry slopes, rock gardens, and containers where irrigation is minimal. Sow seeds thinly on the surface of the soil (do not cover — seeds require light to germinate) and mist gently until seedlings establish.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty, neutral to slightly acidic soil — portulaca demands excellent drainage and actually blooms best in poor, dry soil, languishing in rich or wet conditions; Sundial Pink is a large-flowered (1.5-inch) semi-double portulaca (moss rose) with bright cerise-pink blooms from the Sundial series, which was specifically developed to solve portulaca's traditional failing: the original moss roses closed their flowers in afternoon heat, overcast conditions, and late in the day, leaving the plant bloomless for much of the day. The Sundial series flowers stay open significantly longer than older varieties — an important improvement for a plant intended to provide continuous color in hot, sunny garden locations throughout the day. The succulent, needle-like leaves store water in their tissues, giving portulaca remarkable drought tolerance that allows it to survive periods of complete neglect and to thrive in the kind of hot, dry, reflected-heat locations (paved beds, rocky slopes, container walls) that would kill almost any other flowering annual. In zone 9's brutal summer heat, portulaca is among the very few flowering plants that genuinely improves in performance as temperatures rise.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring around or just before the last frost date in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; sundrops self-seeds readily once established and spreads by rhizomes to form attractive colonies — site it where it has room to naturalize.
directions: Direct sow in early spring in lean, well-drained, average to poor, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; sundrops is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in poor, dry soils — rich, moist conditions produce weak, floppy growth and reduce flowering. Oenothera fruticosa is a native eastern North American perennial evening primrose relative that, unlike most of its nocturnal relatives, opens its bright, butter-yellow, 4-petaled, 1–2-inch flowers in full daylight throughout the day — making it a true daytime ornamental rather than a night-bloomer; the clear yellow flowers appear abundantly from May through July atop reddish, upright stems with lance-shaped, glossy, dark-green leaves that often develop attractive red and bronze tints in fall and spring. It is an excellent native wildflower for sunny, dry, low-maintenance borders and meadow plantings, spreads gradually by rhizomes and self-seeding to form colonies, and is highly attractive to bees and other native pollinators. The red-budded subspecies glauca (sometimes sold as ssp. glauca or 'Fyrverkeri'/'Fireworks') has particularly ornamental red flower buds that contrast vividly with the yellow open flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification through winter; seeds will germinate in spring as soils warm.
directions: Sunflower-leaved Coreopsis is a robust southeastern native perennial distinguished by its broad, undivided leaves that closely resemble small sunflower leaves — quite unlike the finely cut foliage of most other Coreopsis. Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; it tolerates a wider range of conditions than many of its relatives and is more forgiving of heavier soils. Classic bright yellow daisy flowers with maroon-tinged central discs appear on upright stems from June through August, reliably attracting bees and butterflies. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes to form attractive, long-lived clumps that require little maintenance in prairie gardens or open sunny borders.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; good for containers due to compact habit.
directions: Sow seed one inch deep after the last frost once soil warms. This dwarf heirloom grows just two to three feet tall, producing dozens of fluffy, double golden-yellow pom-pom blooms. Its compact, branching habit suits containers, borders, and small gardens, and the sturdy stems make fine cut flowers. Give it full sun and moderate water, and deadhead to keep new blooms coming through the season.

common_name: Sunkiss Coreopsis (AAS-Winning Bicolor Red-Ringed Yellow Coreopsis)
plant_note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sunkiss is an AAS-winning bicolor coreopsis blooming heavily the first year from an early start.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Sunkiss is an All-America Selections-winning coreopsis producing bright golden-yellow flowers marked with a bold burgundy-red ring around the center, a striking bicolor pattern that stands out against the plain gold of most coreopsis cultivars. It blooms heavily from its first year onward and continues over a long summer season with regular deadheading, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil with ease once established. Like other coreopsis, it performs best in lean soil with sharp drainage, since overly rich or wet conditions promote excess foliage and shorten the plant's life; dividing congested clumps every few years helps maintain vigor.

common_name: Sunny Border Blue Veronica (Perennial Plant of the Year Deep Blue Speedwell)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Sunny Border Blue was named Perennial Plant of the Year for its long bloom season, glossy dark green foliage, and dependable performance across a wide range of conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Sunny Border Blue was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 1993 and remains one of the most reliable, widely grown veronica cultivars, producing dense spikes of rich violet-blue flowers over glossy, deep green, crinkled foliage from early summer well into fall with deadheading. Its exceptional garden performance and long bloom season across a wide range of soil and climate conditions have made it a benchmark perennial for sunny borders, and it draws bees and butterflies reliably throughout its bloom period. Divide the clump every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor as the center becomes congested.

common_name: Sunny Charms Abelia (Low Mounding Chartreuse-Gold Abelia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sunny Charms stays low and mounded, fitting foundation plantings and border fronts where taller abelia cultivars would need frequent pruning to control size.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; full sun produces the brightest chartreuse-gold foliage color and the heaviest flowering. Sunny Charms forms a naturally low, dense, rounded mound of bright yellow-green foliage that holds its color through the growing season, topped from late spring through fall with small, fragrant, white-to-pale-pink flowers that draw butterflies and hummingbirds. Its compact scale suits low borders, mass plantings, and foundation beds where larger abelia cultivars would need constant cutting back, and it needs little pruning beyond an occasional light shaping after the heaviest bloom flush. It tolerates heat and humidity well once established and is generally trouble-free, making it a low-maintenance option for year-round foliage color in the Gulf South landscape.

common_name: Sunny Delight Japanese Forest Grass (Sun-Tolerant Chartreuse-Gold Hakonechloa)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Sunny Delight tolerates more sun than most Hakonechloa cultivars while keeping its bright chartreuse-gold color.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Sunny Delight tolerates more direct sun than most Japanese forest grass cultivars without scorching, though afternoon shade still gives the best color and texture in the hottest climates. It bears cascading, arching blades of bright chartreuse-gold edged in a fine green line, forming a graceful, flowing mound prized for its soft texture and movement in a breeze. Its improved sun tolerance makes it more versatile than 'Aureola' for borders that get more than dappled light. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if needed.

common_name: Sunny Knock Out Rose (Yellow Knock Out)
subcategory: landscape shrub rose, Knock Out series
plant_note: Transplant container-grown plants in spring after the last hard freeze, into well-drained soil with room for the shrub's mature rounded form.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, watering deeply during the first season and then only during dry spells once established. Light shearing in late winter keeps the rounded shrub form tidy and encourages fresh bloom flushes through the season. Single, bright yellow flowers that fade to creamy white open continuously from spring to frost on this low-maintenance landscape shrub, part of the widely planted Knock Out series bred for disease resistance and repeat bloom without deadheading. Its compact size and self-cleaning flowers make it popular for mass plantings and foundation beds.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants after frost danger passes, into well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sunray flowers reliably from seed the first year on a compact, well-branched plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sunray earned the All-America Selections bedding plant award in 1990 for producing fully double, golden-yellow, pompon-like flowers on wiry stems from an otherwise typical single-flowered species, giving it a fluffier, more ruffled look than most tickseed cultivars. Bushy and free-branching, it flowers heavily from early summer into fall and holds up well as a cut flower thanks to its sturdy stems. Like other Coreopsis grandiflora selections it is relatively short-lived in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast, so allow some flowers to set seed for volunteer replacements or plan to start fresh seed every two to three years. Sharp drainage and lean soil keep plants compact; rich, moist conditions cause floppy, sparse-flowering growth.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; soak or nick seed to speed germination.
directions: Sunrise Blend offers a colorful assortment of trumpet blooms that flutter against vigorous heart-shaped foliage from midsummer to the first fall frost. Soak or nick the hard seed coat, then direct sow after the last frost near a trellis, fence, or arbor for the climbing vines to scale. The flowers open in early morning and may stay open on cloudy or cool days. Grow in full sun in average soil, avoiding overly rich ground that favors leaves over flowers. Note that the seeds are poisonous if eaten, so keep them away from children and pets.

common_name: Sunrise Coneflower (Soft Yellow Big Sky Series Coneflower)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunrise is part of the Big Sky series of hybrid coneflowers bred for expanded color range.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Sunrise bears large, soft lemon-yellow blooms with slightly drooping petals around a coppery-orange cone, part of the Big Sky series of hybrid coneflowers bred to expand the color palette beyond the traditional purple-pink of straight Echinacea purpurea. It blooms over a long summer season and, like other coneflowers, tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead for continued bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches.

plant_note: Set out young plants or rooted softwood cuttings in spring in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; performs poorly where summer heat and humidity are extreme, so it suits Mountain West, high-plains, and Pacific Northwest xeriscapes better than the humid Gulf Coast.
directions: Set out young plants or rooted softwood cuttings in spring in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; sunrose forms a low, spreading, semi-evergreen mat of small gray-green leaves that disappears under a flush of single or double, saucer-shaped flowers in yellow, orange, pink, red, or white for several weeks in late spring and early summer. It is a classic choice for rock gardens, dry stone walls, and gravel edging in cooler, drier climates, but performs poorly where summer heat and humidity are extreme, so it suits Mountain West, high-plains, and Pacific Northwest xeriscapes better than the humid Gulf Coast. Shear lightly after the main bloom to encourage a tidier habit and occasional rebloom, and avoid rich soil or excess water, both of which shorten its lifespan.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in early spring, or plant divisions, into lean, very well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; sunset foxglove is a true perennial species, unlike the biennial common foxglove.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since this Mediterranean species is far more likely to be lost to wet winter soil than to drought. Sunset foxglove, native to dry hillsides of Spain and North Africa, bears unusual, small, tubular flowers in warm coppery-orange to russet-brown shades with darker reticulated veining inside the throat, a departure from the pinks, purples, and whites typical of common foxglove. As a true short-lived perennial rather than a biennial, it can persist and rebloom for a few years in the lean, dry, well-drained conditions of a rock garden or gravel bed. All parts are toxic if ingested. Cut back spent flower spikes to tidy the plant, and avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which shortens its lifespan considerably.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to a very well-drained site in full sun; sunset hyssop requires excellent drainage and thrives in lean, rocky, alkaline soils — rich, moist soils promote disease and weak growth. Established plants are very drought-tolerant and heat-loving.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sunset hyssop is a native agastache of the dry mountains of New Mexico and Arizona, producing aromatic, narrow, gray-green leaves with an intensely pleasant combined licorice-mint-root-beer fragrance and long, narrow spikes of small tubular flowers in a spectacular orange-pink to salmon-coral color that shades toward orange at the base of the tube and pink at the tip — precisely the color of a sunset sky. The blooms appear from midsummer through fall and are intensely attractive to hummingbirds throughout the season. Unlike the more common anise hyssop, sunset hyssop is more heat-tolerant, much more drought-tolerant, and thrives in the hot, arid, alkaline soils of the Southwest and Gulf Coast. It is short-lived (2–4 years) but self-sows readily. Deer resistant.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; loves heat and dry soil.
directions: Sunshine Blend gazania is a heat- and drought-loving groundcover in warm colors from yellow to mauve, with lush low foliage and blooms held high on their stems. Start seed indoors 6 to 4 weeks before the last frost, covering lightly since darkness aids germination, then transplant after frost danger passes. Grow in full sun in sandy, well-drained soil where the daisy-like petals unfurl in sunshine and close under clouds. Water sparingly once established, as this tough plant tolerates drought and poor soil. Deadhead to keep the color coming through summer.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun for best golden color; Sunshine Ligustrum is a sterile, non-fruiting sport selected specifically to avoid the invasive seeding of common Chinese privet.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, where the foliage colors most brightly; in shadier sites the leaves stay more chartreuse-green than gold. Sunshine Ligustrum was selected as a sterile, non-flowering, non-fruiting sport of common Chinese privet specifically to provide the same tough, brightly colored foliage without the invasive seeding that has made the wild species a serious problem in Southern woodlands. Because it never flowers or sets berries, it channels its energy into dense, compact growth and vivid golden-yellow foliage color that holds through the heat of summer, making it a popular low hedge, mass planting, or color accent shrub. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease and needs only occasional shearing to maintain a tidy shape.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in any well-drained, sunny soil; sunshine mimosa spreads vigorously by stolons to form a dense mat — excellent for replacing lawn areas in full sun, but control spread in small gardens by periodic edging.
directions: Sunshine mimosa is the premier native groundcover lawn substitute for the Gulf Coast region — a low-growing, stoloniferous perennial that forms dense, fine-textured mats covered with pink, feathery pompom flowers from spring through fall, handling foot traffic better than most native groundcovers. As a member of the legume family, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, improving soil fertility as it spreads, and it tolerates the heat, drought, and poor sandy soils of Gulf Coast gardens that defeat other groundcovers. The sensitive leaves fold slightly when brushed or walked on — a charming touch-me-not response that delights children — and the spectacular pink pompom flowers are a prolific nectar source for native bees and butterflies throughout the growing season.
