directions: Start seed indoors requiring cold-moist stratification or plant nursery divisions in wet to consistently moist, humus-rich, neutral soil in partial shade in spring; swamp saxifrage is a wetland-edge native that wants boggy ground, not average garden soil. A basal rosette of broad, coarsely toothed leaves sends up a tall, sticky-hairy flower stalk in mid-spring bearing loose, branched clusters of small, star-shaped, greenish-white to purple-tinged flowers that are an early-season draw for small bees and flies. It occurs naturally in wet meadows, marsh edges, and seepage areas and is an easy, low-maintenance choice for the damp, partly shaded margins of a rain garden or pond where turf grass struggles. It is monocarpic in some populations, flowering once from a mature rosette and then dying back, but self-sows readily to persist in a consistently moist planting.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in wet to moist, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp spider lily thrives in pond margins, wet ditches, and boggy, shaded spots where few other bulbs will grow. It is winter-hardy to zone 7 and resprouts reliably from established bulbs.
directions: Plant bulbs in wet to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun — the swamp spider lily is a spectacular Gulf Coast native wildflower found naturally in wet prairies, swampy ditches, stream banks, and the margins of cypress swamps from Texas to Georgia. In spring it produces clusters of 3–6 intensely fragrant, spider-like white flowers on leafless scapes 18–24 inches tall — the long, narrow, reflexed petals surrounding a prominent cup-like corona are architecturally striking and fill the garden with a rich, sweet perfume. The broad, strap-like leaves emerge in spring and die back by late summer. It naturalizes freely in wet conditions, forming spectacular colonies in roadside ditches and pond margins throughout the Gulf Coast region. Unlike many spider lilies, it thrives in partial shade and wet soils where most other bulbs fail. Excellent at the edge of rain gardens, retention ponds, and boggy low spots.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; plants can also be started from divisions in spring for faster bloom.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; swamp sunflower is arguably the most spectacular of the native sunflowers for fall bloom, producing hundreds of bright yellow flowers on tall multibranching stems from October through frost — often when almost nothing else is blooming. It grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods, swamp margins, and roadside ditches across the coastal South and is perfectly suited to Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens where the late season heat and moisture support its growth. The plant spreads aggressively by rhizome and self-seeding; give it space or divide annually in spring. Monarch butterflies and native bees mob the flowers. Pinch tips twice in early summer for a shorter, more compact plant.

plant_note: Sow in fall into consistently moist soil so seed stratifies over winter; keep beds evenly damp through spring germination.
directions: Plant in consistently wet to moist soil in a low spot, rain garden, or pond margin with full to partial sun; unlike its spinier upland relatives, swamp thistle has a nearly spineless stem that is comfortable to handle. It grows as a rosette the first year and flowers the second or third year on tall stalks topped with clusters of pink-purple blooms that are a favorite nectar stop for swallowtails, bumblebees, and the American goldfinch, which later feeds on the down-tufted seed. Because it needs sustained moisture, it is best suited to wet meadows and streambank plantings rather than average garden beds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil; swamp titi tolerates periodic flooding and grows naturally in bog margins, cypress swamps, and pitcher plant bogs of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain. Propagate from softwood cuttings in summer.
directions: Plant in wet to moist, acidic, peaty or humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; swamp titi is a native Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain shrub of remarkable ornamental and ecological value that is still underused in landscape horticulture. The long, drooping racemes of small white honey-scented flowers in late spring and summer are among the most important nectar sources for honey production in the Florida Panhandle, where 'titi honey' is a regional specialty. The semi-evergreen to evergreen, leathery leaves turn vivid red and orange in fall before dropping. It tolerates flooding, poor acid soil, and full sun in swampy conditions — exactly the site conditions where most ornamental shrubs fail. In zone 9a, it makes an excellent native screen in wet or poorly drained areas.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in wet to moist, acidic, slightly sandy or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade. Swamp Tupelo is adapted to seasonally or permanently flooded conditions and develops distinctive swollen (buttressed) trunk bases in very wet soils; it is most appropriate for rain gardens, wet bottomlands, and natural pond margins.
directions: Swamp Tupelo is a dominant native tree of the permanent swamps, bay forests, and river floodplains of the southeastern coastal plain from Delaware to Florida and west to Texas, often growing alongside bald cypress and water tupelo in pure stands in the deepest, most permanently flooded low-lying land in the South. It is distinguished from the more upland Black Gum (Nyssa sylvatica) by its narrower leaves, preference for wetter conditions, and more southern distribution; in very wet sites it develops the distinctive swollen, buttressed trunk base characteristic of swamp-adapted trees. In fall Swamp Tupelo produces one of the finest foliage displays of any native tree — brilliant crimson, scarlet, and orange — providing spectacular autumn color even in the deep South where fall foliage is often muted. Small blue-black drupes in fall are consumed by a wide variety of birds and mammals. Plant in consistently wet to seasonally flooded, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates standing water better than almost any other native upland tree.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall or container trees in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; swamp white oak tolerates extended flooding and clay soils better than most oaks and is an excellent choice for wet, low-lying areas.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; swamp white oak is the premier large native oak for wet, clay-heavy, or periodically flooded sites — conditions where most other oaks decline. The exfoliating, peeling bark on the upper branches is a distinctive and attractive identification feature, revealing lighter bark beneath. The acorns are large, borne in pairs on long stalks (2–4 inches), and are among the most important fall-winter food for wood ducks (which nest in cavities of old trees), turkeys, deer, and dozens of other species. Fall color is yellow to bronze. The tree develops into a large, rounded specimen 50–60 feet tall with a broad, open crown. Its tolerance of wet, clay, compacted, and temporarily flooded conditions makes it an outstanding choice for low areas of the landscape, stream buffers, and rain gardens where it can manage stormwater.

common_name: Swan Lake Dahlia (Pure White Waterlily-Form Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Swan Lake is a pure white waterlily-form dahlia with broad, gently overlapping petals.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants in exposed sites to support the broad, flat blooms in wind. Swan Lake bears shallow, cupped, waterlily-form flowers in pure white, the broad, gently overlapping petals creating a flatter, less densely layered bloom than decorative or ball dahlia types, resembling an actual water lily floating in a pond. Its clean white color pairs well with almost any garden color scheme and makes an elegant cut flower. Deadhead spent blooms regularly, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks early; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start Swan River daisy indoors about six weeks before the last frost for earliest bloom. The dainty, fragrant daisies in blue, mauve, and white cover mounding plants ideal for edging, containers, and hanging baskets. Provide full sun and well-drained soil, avoiding overly rich conditions that soften growth. Shear lightly after the first flush and feed lightly to keep the plant blooming through summer.

subcategory: papery everlasting for drying and cutting
plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost, or as soon as the ground can be worked, since this fine-rooted annual dislikes transplanting.
directions: Scatter seed thinly over well-drained soil and press in lightly, then thin seedlings once they have true leaves because crowded plants stretch and flop. Provide lean, gritty soil and steady sun, as overly rich conditions produce weak stems and fewer blooms. Wiry stems carry papery, daisy-form flowers in pink, rose, and white with a bright central disc that keep their color and shape when air dried, making this a classic everlasting for dried arrangements as well as a cheerful cut flower fresh from the garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to average, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to shade; Swan's sedge grows naturally in moist to dry woodland understory and meadow edges throughout eastern North America. Division of established clumps in spring is the most reliable propagation method.
directions: Plant in moist to average, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade; Swan's sedge is a common and adaptable woodland sedge of eastern North America, forming neat, arching clumps of medium-width, bright green leaves that remain attractive through the growing season. Unlike some native sedges adapted to wet or strictly dry conditions, Swan's sedge thrives across a broad range of soil moisture from average to moderately moist woodland soil, making it one of the more garden-adaptable woodland natives. The nodding flower spikes in late spring are unremarkable but the foliage is clean and attractive as a mid-height groundcover or clump accent in the shade garden. Naturalizes readily in shaded areas and combines well with ferns, native gingers, and woodland wildflowers in the layered shade garden.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; alyssum tolerates light frost and prefers cool weather.
directions: Scatter seed on the soil surface and press gently — light aids germination; just barely cover if needed to prevent the seed from blowing away. Sweet alyssum may slow or stop blooming in peak summer heat; shear plants back by half and they will rebound strongly when temperatures cool in early fall. The honey-scented flowers attract beneficial insects throughout the season.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; sweet autumn clematis establishes quickly and blooms the first year from transplant — keep cool in summer by mulching around the base and providing afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline soil with the crown at or just below the soil surface; sweet autumn clematis explodes into bloom in late summer and fall with masses of small, starry white flowers that cover the vine in a frothy blanket of fragrance reminiscent of vanilla. The plant can grow 15–20 feet in a season once established and needs a strong trellis, arbor, or fence to climb. Prune back hard in late winter (cut to 12–18 inches from the ground) to control size and encourage vigorous new growth, since it blooms on current-season growth. Important note: sweet autumn clematis self-seeds prolifically and is considered invasive in portions of the eastern US; deadhead before seeds mature or remove seedlings promptly to prevent spread into wild areas. Excellent on chain-link fences, pergolas, and as a late-season screen.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; sweet azalea is naturally a streamside and moist woodland plant and requires consistent soil moisture. It blooms 6–8 weeks after most other deciduous azaleas, filling the early-summer gap in the native azalea sequence from May through July.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil in part shade; sweet azalea is one of the latest-blooming native deciduous azaleas of eastern North America, native to streambanks, moist woodlands, and cool mountain ravines from Pennsylvania to Alabama, producing its flowers in late June through July — 6–8 weeks after most other azaleas have finished — creating invaluable sequence of color in the native woodland garden. The flowers are exceptional among azaleas for their fragrance: strongly and sweetly scented, with a light, honeysuckle-like fragrance that perfumes the surrounding air, reminiscent of heliotrope or vanilla. The blooms are white to pale blush-pink with prominent, very long red stamens that extend well beyond the petals, giving the open flowers a delicate, spider-like appearance against the green foliage. The foliage is glossy and smooth (giving rise to 'smooth azalea'), turning attractive red and orange in fall. Among native azaleas, it is one of the most adaptable in the garden and one of the most underplanted, despite combining fragrance, late bloom season, and attractive form in a single shade-tolerant shrub.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; avoid bare-root transplanting as magnolias resent root disturbance. Site carefully as the roots are shallow and wide-spreading.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acid soil in full sun to partial shade; this native magnolia naturally inhabits swampy lowlands and stream banks from Massachusetts to Florida and is one of the best large shrubs or small trees for wet areas in the southern garden. The creamy-white, lemon-scented flowers appear over a long season from late spring through summer, and the semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves (depending on winter severity) have a striking silver underside. In the Gulf South it can reach 30 feet as a multi-stemmed, nearly evergreen tree; in colder zones it is smaller and more deciduous. The red fruit clusters provide fall and winter food for songbirds and small mammals.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; never collect from wild populations. Sweet Betsy is a sessile trillium — its maroon flowers sit directly on the three large, attractively mottled leaves without a stalk.
directions: Sweet Betsy trillium is one of the finest sessile trilliums in the Southeast, native to rich, moist deciduous forests from Virginia and Kentucky south to Georgia and Mississippi, where it carpets shaded forest floors with its dramatically silver-mottled leaves topped by stalkless dark maroon to reddish-purple flowers in March and April. The cuneate (wedge-shaped) base of the leaves distinguishes this species from the very similar Trillium sessile, and the flowers emit a faint, sweet fragrance in warm weather that attracts fly pollinators. Like all trilliums, Sweet Betsy requires 5–7 years to bloom from seed — always purchase plants from ethical nurseries propagating their own stock, and never collect from wild populations, which are protected in many states. Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) in partial to full shade; mulch lightly with leaf litter, keep consistently moist, and allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally each summer.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, cool, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Sweet Birch is an Appalachian mountain tree that performs best in cool, moist, north-facing situations in zones 3–6; in zone 7 it may struggle in hot summer conditions and requires a sheltered, cool, moist site.
directions: Sweet Birch is an elegant native birch of the Appalachian Mountains and northeastern North America, native to cool, moist, well-drained forest slopes and ravines from Maine and Ontario south through the Appalachians to Georgia and Alabama, distinguished from other birches by its dark, cherry-like bark (not peeling white or papery) and the intensely sweet, wintergreen fragrance released when the bark, twigs, or leaves are crushed — the essential oil methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) was historically distilled from the bark and twigs for flavoring and as a precursor to salicylic acid. Rich, golden-yellow fall color, pendant pollen catkins in early spring, and an attractive, slightly furrowed dark bark provide four-season ornamental interest in the woodland garden. Sweet Birch is host to dozens of native Lepidoptera species (caterpillars) and provides high-quality nesting habitat for cavity-nesting birds in mature specimens. Grow in cool, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; it is most appropriate for the cooler portions of its range and struggles in the heat of zones 7–8.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in average to moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; sweet black-eyed Susan benefits from natural cold stratification over winter for reliable spring germination and blooms in its second year from seed, producing its best floral display from year 3 onward once established.
directions: Sow direct in fall in average to moderately moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring — sweet black-eyed Susan is more tolerant of clay and consistently moist soils than most Rudbeckia species, and performs best with reliable moisture during its establishment period. Rudbeckia subtomentosa is a tall, clump-forming native prairie perennial of the central United States producing softly hairy (subtomentosa = somewhat woolly) stems and large, three-lobed leaves with a distinctive pleasant anise or sweet fragrance when crushed — a unique trait among native coneflowers that gives this species its common name; from August through October it bears large numbers of bright yellow daisy-like flowers with long, reflexed ray petals surrounding a prominent dark brown to nearly black, dome-shaped central disk. It is an outstanding late-season pollinator plant for native bees, bumble bees, and migrating monarch butterflies; the persistent seed heads feed goldfinches and other seed-eating birds through fall and winter. Sweet black-eyed Susan is longer-lived and more robust than Rudbeckia hirta, forming steadily expanding clumps that can be divided every 3–4 years in spring; it is an excellent choice for the back of a native meadow planting, wet prairie restoration, or a tall native border where its height and late bloom season add value.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring or fall; sweet box spreads slowly by suckers to form a dense colony over many years.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; sweet box is a refined, slow-growing, suckering Asian shrub with small, polished, lance-shaped leaves and inconspicuous tiny white flowers in late winter to early spring that produce one of the most intensely sweet vanilla-honey fragrances in the plant world — remarkable for their power from such small, unshowy blooms. Small, glossy black berries follow in late summer. The plant is entirely shade-adapted and makes an excellent low-maintenance, deer-resistant groundcover or fragrant foundation planting under trees where little else succeeds. 'Purple Stem' (Sarcococca hookeriana var. humilis) stays more compact at 18 inches. No significant pruning required.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in partial to full shade; Sweet Box establishes readily and is low-maintenance once settled. It tolerates both dry shade and moderately moist conditions. In zone 9, it performs as an evergreen shrub blooming December–February; the tiny white flowers are barely visible but produce an intense, sweet vanilla-honey fragrance detectable from 10–15 feet away on mild winter days. Hardy to about 0°F when established.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist to dry, well-drained soil; Sweet Box is exceptionally tolerant of dry shade and root competition, making it one of the best low-growing shade shrubs for planting beneath established trees. Sarcococca confusa is a low, spreading, slowly suckering evergreen shrub in the boxwood family (Buxaceae) native to China, notable for producing its tiny but extraordinarily fragrant flowers in the dead of winter — December through February in zone 7–9 — when little else in the garden is blooming. The individual white flowers are barely noticeable: small tufts of stamens without petals, hidden among the glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves. But the fragrance they produce is intensely sweet and reminiscent of vanilla and honey, and on mild winter days it carries remarkably far from a planting, making Sweet Box one of the most valuable fragrant plants for the shade garden. After flowering, small black or red berry-like fruits provide additional ornamental interest and are eaten by birds. The plant spreads gradually by underground suckers to form a dense, ground-covering colony 2–3 feet high and 4–6 feet across over many years. Essentially pest- and disease-free, drought-tolerant in shade, and long-lived, it is among the finest low-maintenance shade shrubs available.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown stock in early spring into well-drained, preferably alkaline or chalky soil. If raising from seed, cold-stratify for 90–180 days before sowing under cover.
directions: Choose a sunny spot with lean, well-drained soil; Sweet Briar thrives on chalky or limestone ground and the apple scent of its foliage is most pronounced in warm sun after a light rain. Propagate by hardwood cuttings taken in late autumn and rooted in gritty compost over winter. Avoid rich soils or heavy feeding, which promote excessive vegetative growth at the expense of flowers and hips. Thin old woody stems every few years to keep the plant open and productive, and wear heavy gloves — the hooked thorns are notably sharp.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Bronze Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Bronze-Purple Ornamental Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the Sweet Caroline series was bred with a more compact, less rampant habit than older ornamental sweet potato vines, making it easier to keep in bounds in mixed containers.
directions: Sweet Caroline Bronze produces deeply lobed, ivy-like leaves in a warm bronze-purple, a softer, more finely cut alternative to the broad near-black leaves of the older cultivar Blackie, on a plant bred to be more compact and manageable in containers than earlier ornamental sweet potato vine selections. Its trailing stems cascade over pot edges and retaining walls, and the finely lobed foliage texture pairs well with both bold tropical companions and fine-textured annuals in a mixed planting. Give it well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; like other ornamental sweet potato vines it is extremely heat-tolerant and grows fastest in the peak of Gulf South summer, needing only occasional trimming to keep it in scale.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Light Green Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Chartreuse Ornamental Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the compact Sweet Caroline habit fits smaller container combinations better than the more vigorous, rambling growth of older chartreuse ornamental sweet potato vine cultivars like Margarita.
directions: Sweet Caroline Light Green carries bright chartreuse-green, deeply lobed foliage on a more compact, restrained vine than older lime-colored sweet potato vine cultivars, making it easier to keep proportionate in a mixed container rather than letting one plant take over the whole pot. The luminous foliage color brightens shaded corners and pairs naturally with cool blue and purple flowering companions or bold dark-leaved foliage plants for contrast. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates a bit more shade than most chartreuse foliage plants while still holding good color, and needs only occasional trimming to control its trailing spread through the heat of summer.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in average to slightly moist, well-drained soil in full to partial sun; sweet coneflower adapts to a wide range of soil types and moisture levels and self-seeds moderately, forming clumps that should be divided every 3–4 years.
directions: Sweet coneflower is one of the most fragrant of all native coneflowers — the flowers emit a noticeable sweet, anise-like scent, particularly on warm afternoons — and is native to moist to dry prairies, savannas, and open woodlands of the central United States from Texas to Illinois. Its 2-foot-wide clumps of deeply textured, softly hairy leaves (the 'subtomentosa' refers to the downy leaf texture) support multiple branched stems bearing dozens of cheerful gold-petaled flowers with dark brown central cones from July through September. A popular parent of many prairie garden cultivars, sweet coneflower is valued by horticulturists for its outstanding heat tolerance, mildew resistance (unlike many Rudbeckia species in humid southern climates), and adaptability from clay to sand soils. The seed heads remain ornamental through winter and feed goldfinches, chickadees, and sparrows; pair with prairie grasses and ironweeds for a dramatic native meadow planting.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; sweet crabapple prefers open sites at woodland edges and old fields.
directions: Plant young trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil and full sun to light shade, choosing an open site at a field or woodland edge where the rounded crown has room to spread. Sweet crabapple, native to the eastern and midwestern United States, produces intensely fragrant pale pink blossoms in mid-spring that draw large numbers of native bees and other pollinators before most other trees have leafed out. The small, hard, greenish-yellow fruit ripens in fall and often clings into winter, becoming an important food source for foxes, deer, and overwintering birds such as robins and cedar waxwings once it softens after frost. Its dense branching also offers good nesting cover for songbirds.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in evenly moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike most catmints, Nepeta subsessilis selections such as Sweet Dreams tolerate consistently moist soil and light shade without declining.
directions: Plant in evenly moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; this species tolerates more moisture and shade than the more drought-adapted Nepeta racemosa and Nepeta x faassenii cultivars. Sweet Dreams forms an upright, non-sprawling clump of broad, dark green foliage topped with dense clusters of rose-pink flowers from mid to late summer, giving it a tidier habit and a flower color distinct from the blue and lavender tones typical of most catmints. It combines well at the edge of a woodland border or in a perennial bed with part-day sun, and its late-season flowers are a valuable nectar source for bees and butterflies when many earlier-blooming perennials have finished.

common_name: Sweet Drift Rose (Clear Pink Double Groundcover Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Drift is part of the low-growing, spreading Drift groundcover rose series bred for continuous bloom and disease resistance.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun. Sweet Drift bears clear, soft pink, fully double flowers in dense clusters on a low, spreading, groundcover-type shrub, part of the Drift series bred by crossing miniature roses with groundcover roses to combine compact size with vigorous, disease-resistant, everblooming performance. Its low, mounding habit suits it to edging a border, cascading over a low wall, or massing as a flowering groundcover, and it blooms continuously from spring to frost with minimal deadheading required. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well and need little more than an annual light pruning in late winter to stay tidy.

common_name: Sweet Emily Kate Camellia (Ruffled Deep Pink Compact Sasanqua)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Sweet Emily Kate's compact, columnar-to-rounded habit fits a narrower planting space than many spreading sasanqua cultivars.
directions: Sweet Emily Kate carries ruffled, deep rose-pink, semi-double to double flowers with a distinctive curled petal texture, held on a compact, upright, well-branched sasanqua shrub that blooms heavily through the fall. Its narrower growth habit than many older sasanqua cultivars makes it a good fit for a tighter foundation planting or narrow side-yard bed, and its rich, ruffled flower color provides strong seasonal interest during a season when few other shrubs are flowering. Like other camellias it needs consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and a layer of mulch to protect its shallow roots; prune, if needed, only lightly right after flowering to avoid removing next season's buds.

plant_note: Surface sow directly at or just after last frost into a disturbed, bare soil patch, as seeds require light to germinate and should not be covered.
directions: Sweet Everlasting is a native annual or biennial of dry, open fields and forest margins throughout eastern North America, beloved for its silvery-white, woolly everlasting flower clusters that emit an intensely sweet vanilla-like fragrance both fresh and dried. Direct sow onto the surface of well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, pressing seeds lightly into the soil without covering them, as light is required for germination. Plants are drought-tolerant once established and thrive in poor soils where competition is low, making them excellent for dry wildflower meadows, roadside plantings, and naturalized areas. Cut stems just before the flower clusters fully open and hang upside-down to dry; the fragrance persists for many months in dried arrangements.

plant_note: All Acorus calamus in North America is triploid and sterile and does not set viable seed — propagate exclusively by rhizome division in early spring. Plant at or just below the waterline in boggy soil or shallow water up to 4 inches deep.
directions: Sweet Flag is a grass-like aromatic perennial grown for its bright green, sword-shaped leaves that emit a distinctive sweet, spicy fragrance when bruised or crushed. It thrives at pond margins, in rain gardens, and in boggy soils where it tolerates partial shade admirably. Because all North American populations of Acorus calamus are triploid and sterile, the plant reproduces solely by rhizome — divide clumps every 3-4 years in early spring to maintain vigor and spread. Plant rhizomes horizontally just below the soil surface at the water's edge or in shallow standing water.

plant_note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed into warm, well-drained soil in full sun; seeds germinate quickly in warm conditions.
directions: Direct sow seeds after the last frost date into full sun and well-drained, even poor soil, as this Mexican native thrives in lean conditions similar to its native desert habitat. Flowers open each afternoon and release an extraordinary sweet fragrance that intensifies into the evening, drawing hawk moths and hummingbirds. In zones 9 and above the tuberous roots are perennial; in cooler climates dig and store the tubers frost-free over winter, much like dahlias, to replant the following spring. Allow 12 to 16 weeks from sowing to first bloom, and plant near a patio or path where the evening fragrance can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Sweet Iris (Orris Root Iris, Dalmatian Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to fall, setting the rhizome shallow with its top exposed to the sun in well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Iris is an old dooryard-garden heirloom passed along by division for centuries and is the historic source of orris root, the dried, violet-scented rhizome once widely used in perfumery.
directions: Plant rhizomes shallow, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Iris is an old Mediterranean bearded iris long grown in Southern dooryard gardens and passed hand to hand as a heirloom pass-along plant. It bears fragrant, soft lavender-blue flowers with a sweet, grape-like scent in mid-spring above handsome silvery gray-green foliage that stays attractive through summer even after bloom finishes. Historically, its dried, aged rhizome was the primary commercial source of orris root, prized in perfumery and sachets for a violet-like fragrance that develops only after long curing, though modern gardeners grow it mainly for its flowers and foliage. Like other bearded irises, it resents wet feet and rich, heavy soil — give it excellent drainage and avoid mulch piled against the rhizome to prevent rot.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; sweet Joe-Pye weed is one of the tallest and most spectacular late-summer native perennials, reaching 4–7 feet tall.
directions: Sow direct in spring or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; sweet Joe-Pye weed tolerates more shade than most large native perennials and performs well in the transition zone between sunny meadows and shaded woodland. Eutrochium purpureum (formerly Eupatorium purpureum) is a majestic native perennial of the eastern and central US, producing stout, wine-stained purple stems bearing whorls of large, coarsely toothed, vanilla-scented (when crushed) leaves and large, domed clusters of tiny, mauve-pink to rosy-purple flowers from late summer through early fall that are among the finest late-season pollinator plants available — a single mature plant can support hundreds of individual butterflies over a season, including monarchs, tiger swallowtails, and fritillaries. Its massive size (4–7 feet) makes it most appropriate at the back of borders, along pond margins, and in naturalized meadow plantings; the seed heads provide winter interest and bird food.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Sweet Kate goes semi-dormant in the heat of mid-summer, dying back to the ground — cut back the tired foliage in July and it will resprout fresh golden foliage in fall. The bright yellow-gold foliage color is most vivid in spring and fall when temperatures are moderate; some green may develop in summer heat. Divide every 2–3 years when clumps become crowded. Partial shade maintains the golden leaf color better than full sun and prevents the leaf scorching that can occur on the thin, golden foliage in extreme summer heat.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sweet Kate performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, which maintains the golden foliage color and prevents summer leaf scorch; Sweet Kate is a spiderwort cultivar valued primarily for its extraordinary bright golden-yellow foliage rather than its flowers, creating an unusual color combination when the vivid blue-violet, three-petaled spiderwort flowers open against the luminous gold-yellow leaf background. The foliage color — a genuine, clear, clean golden-yellow rather than the chartreuse-green or lime-yellow of many 'gold' plants — provides exceptional contrast potential with dark-foliaged companions (black-eyed Susan, dark-leaved coral bells) and with blue-flowered plants. The flowers themselves, like all Tradescantia, are produced in succession — each individual flower lasts only a single morning before collapsing, but new buds continue opening from the same cluster over weeks, maintaining the blue-and-gold display from late spring through early summer. Sweet Kate's combination of unusual leaf color and blue flower-against-gold-foliage display makes it one of the most visually distinctive herbaceous perennials for spring and fall interest in partial shade.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or hardwood cuttings in fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; sweet mock orange blooms on the previous year's wood — prune immediately after flowering by removing the oldest, flowered stems to encourage new growth from the base.
directions: Root cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; sweet mock orange is a European deciduous shrub that produces one of the most intensely and purely sweet fragrances of any flowering shrub available to temperate gardeners — the large, pure-white, four-petaled flowers, borne in dense clusters along the arching branches in late May to June, fill the garden air with a sweet orange-blossom and honey fragrance that is produced in such quantity that a single established shrub can perfume an entire garden. The flowers have a simple, classic, white-on-white beauty that complements the fragrance perfectly. Individual flowers are relatively brief (2–3 weeks), but the overall display is impressive and the fragrance lingers. 'Aureus' has golden-yellow spring foliage that fades to chartreuse-green in summer; 'Variegatus' has white-margined leaves. It tolerates partial shade and clay soil better than most fragrant shrubs. Prune immediately after flowering to maintain shape and encourage vigorous flowering growth for the following year. One of the most valuable and time-tested fragrant flowering shrubs in the temperate garden tradition.

plant_note: Plant container stock in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Sweet Olive is a signature shrub of Gulf Coast and Deep South gardens in zones 8–10, prized above nearly all other plants for its intensely sweet, apricot-like fragrance.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Sweet Olive performs best with at least 4 hours of sun but tolerates and even thrives in the dappled shade of open woodland gardens, where its fragrance is often more concentrated. Osmanthus fragrans is perhaps the most intensely fragrant shrub or small tree in temperate horticulture — its tiny, creamy-white to pale-apricot flowers, only a few millimeters across and produced in small axillary clusters, carry an extraordinarily powerful and sweet fragrance described variously as apricot, peach, jasmine, and vanilla that can perfume an entire garden on still evenings, carrying 50–100 feet from the plant. The fragrance blooms emerge in fall (September–November), often again in spring, and sporadically year-round in warm climates — the fall flush, just as the garden is losing other interest, makes it especially prized. In zones 8–10 it grows as an evergreen shrub or small multi-stem tree 6–20 feet tall; in zone 7 it may be semi-evergreen and die back to the roots in severe winters. The form 'Aurantiacus' has orange flowers with even more intense fragrance than the typical white-flowered form. Essential for zone 9 gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow outdoors 4–8 weeks before last frost; seeds prefer cool soil (55–65°F) and young plants tolerate frost.
directions: Nick or soak seeds overnight before sowing 1 in deep in cool, enriched soil at the base of a trellis. Sweet peas perform best during cool weather and decline as summer heat arrives — sow as early as possible. Cut flowers frequently, as even a few fading blooms left on the plant will trigger seed set and halt blooming. Provide sturdy support from the start, as vines climb to 4–6 ft.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum in full sun; sweet pitcher plant has several geographically distinct subspecies adapted to different habitats from the Carolinas to Alabama — select subspecies appropriate to your region.
directions: Sweet pitcher plant earns its name from the intensely sweet, rose-like fragrance of its spring flowers — deep crimson-red blooms that open in April and May on tall, leafless stalks well above the pitchers, producing a fragrance that can be detected several feet away and is considered the most sweetly scented of any Sarracenia flower. The compact, narrow pitchers of this species grow 8–24 inches tall depending on the subspecies and have a distinctive red-veined, green-and-purple coloration that varies widely among the multiple recognized subspecies (Sarracenia rubra ssp. rubra, ssp. jonesii, ssp. gulfensis, ssp. wherryi, and others) distributed across different parts of the coastal plain from North Carolina to Alabama. Subspecies gulfensis (Gulf Coast sweet pitcher plant) is native to the Florida panhandle and Alabama, where it grows in seepage bogs adjacent to other Gulf Coast carnivorous plants; it is one of the most threatened Sarracenia subspecies due to habitat loss. As with all native pitcher plants, purchase only nursery-propagated specimens from ethical native plant dealers and grow in pure water, acidic medium, and full sun.

plant_note: Sow in fall or early summer for bloom the following spring; sweet rocket self-sows prolifically and functions as a perennial in most gardens once established; considered invasive in some northern states — check local regulations.
directions: Sow seed on the soil surface in fall or early summer for spring bloom the following year, in moist but well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; sweet rocket is a European biennial or short-lived perennial producing tall spikes of white, lilac, and purple four-petaled flowers from spring to early summer with an extraordinarily sweet, strong evening fragrance similar to violets and stock that intensifies at dusk — a classic cottage garden and moon garden plant. It self-sows freely once established, functionally making it a perennial. Sometimes confused with garden phlox; sweet rocket has four petals (true phlox has five). Classified as invasive in some northern states; use with awareness of local regulations.

plant_note: Sow in spring or summer; often blooms the second year as a biennial.
directions: Sweet Rose Magic delights with flowers that open white, shift to soft pink, and mature into rich rose, creating a tricolor display on a single stem. Start seed indoors and barely cover it, or sow outdoors in late spring, transplanting into rich, well-drained soil. As a biennial it typically forms foliage the first year and blooms the second, though it may flower the first season from an early start. Grow in full sun to part shade and deadhead for repeat bloom. The clustered flowers are lightly clove-scented and excellent for cutting.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks early for cut flowers.
directions: Start sweet scabious indoors about six weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once soil warms. The domed pincushion flowers in deep maroon, pink, and white are long-lasting cut flowers and pollinator magnets. Grow in full sun and fertile, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil, staking tall stems if needed. Harvest or deadhead frequently to keep the plants producing new blooms all summer.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; does not transplant well due to taproot.
directions: Sow seeds directly in a sunny, well-drained location in early spring; thin to 9–12 in apart as seedlings emerge. The fragrant, fringed, powder-puff flowers in shades of pink, purple, yellow, and white are excellent for cutting, with a pleasant, musky sweet scent. Plants prefer cool weather and will begin to decline as summer heat intensifies — make a second sowing in late summer for fall bloom in warm climates. Successive sowings every 3–4 weeks in spring extend the flowering season through early summer.

common_name: Sweet Tea Heucherella (Amber-Copper Ruffled Foliage Heucherella)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sweet Tea holds its warm amber-copper foliage color well through the season and tolerates more heat than many heucherella cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, with mulch to keep roots cool and moist. Sweet Tea is a popular heucherella cultivar prized for its large, deeply ruffled, maple-shaped leaves in a warm amber-to-copper color that deepens further in cooler weather, providing months of foliage interest well beyond its modest sprays of small white flowers in late spring. As a heucherella, it combines the bold, colorful foliage typical of heuchera with a more vigorous, ground-covering habit inherited from its foamflower parentage, spreading gradually to fill in a shaded bed. It pairs well with blue-green hostas, ferns, and dark-leafed heuchera, and benefits from being divided every few years in spring or fall as the clump matures.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; sweet viburnum grows 2–3 feet per year when established and can be maintained as a dense formal hedge by trimming 2–3 times per year, or allowed to develop into an informal screen or small tree reaching 15–20 feet. It is damaged at temperatures below 15°F.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; sweet viburnum is one of the most widely planted evergreen screening shrubs of the Gulf Coast, Deep South, and Florida — valued for its large, glossy, dark-green leaves, rapid growth rate, and the intensely fragrant white flower panicles produced in late March through May that fill the surrounding garden with a sweet, orange-blossom-like fragrance. After flowering, clusters of small fruits ripen from red to black and attract birds. The plant adapts equally well to full sun and part shade and grows rapidly to form a dense privacy screen or hedge 10–20 feet tall. It tolerates brief dips to 15°F but is most reliable from zone 8b southward. Shearing 2–3 times per year maintains it as a tight formal hedge; left unpruned it develops into a handsome large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with layered, spreading branches. The cultivar 'Emerald Lustre' offers especially large, deeply glossed leaves. One of the fastest and most reliable evergreen privacy solutions for Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes.

plant_note: Plant divisions or stolons in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; sweet violet spreads by stolons and self-sown seed to naturalize under deciduous trees. Cold-stratify seed 4–6 weeks if starting from seed.
directions: Plant divisions in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich soil in fall or early spring; sweet violet is one of the oldest cultivated flowers in the Western world, prized for its intoxicating honey-sweet fragrance and fully edible blooms that appear in late winter to early spring in shades of deep violet, lavender, rose, or white. Both flowers and young leaves are edible — the flowers are crystallized with sugar as classic confections, used fresh in salads, infused into vinegars and syrups, or candied for cake decoration. The plant spreads by stolons and self-sown seed to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under trees and shrubs. Deadhead spent blooms to reduce excessive self-seeding where spread is unwanted. The cultivar 'Königin Charlotte' is considered the most fragrant; 'Rosina' produces soft pink blooms and is slightly less vigorous. An outstanding edible ornamental for shaded paths and beds under deciduous trees in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in deep, moist, rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in a cove-forest woodland setting; sweet wakerobin grows in the same rich southern Appalachian coves as the closely related Trillium vaseyi and Trillium erectum.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in deep, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Sweet wakerobin is a southern Appalachian pedicellate trillium, native to rich cove forests of North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia, easily confused in the field with its relatives Trillium vaseyi and Trillium erectum but distinguished by its pure white, outward-facing petals held above the leaves and a light, sweet fragrance rather than the fetid odor typical of many large trilliums. It blooms in April and May, later than most sessile trilliums, and slowly forms an expanding clump where the deep, consistently moist cove-forest conditions it needs are maintained. Give it the richest, most humus-laden soil available and a thick annual leaf-litter mulch, and expect several years before divisions reach full flowering size, since trillium rhizomes resent disturbance and recover slowly from transplant.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, cool, well-drained soil in deep shade; sweet white violet is one of the most shade-tolerant native violets and grows in cool, moist, acidic forest conditions in the Northeast and Appalachians.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained soil in deep shade under deciduous trees; sweet white violet is one of the smallest and most shade-tolerant native violets of the eastern woodland, producing tiny, delicate white flowers with purple veining in early spring — often the first violet to bloom in cold-climate woodlands. The small, heart-shaped leaves form attractive, glossy ground cover mats in moist, acidic shade. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes and produces aboveground stolons in summer to colonize nearby areas. An excellent species for the deep shade of northern woodland gardens where its requirement for cool, moist, acidic conditions is easily met. Like all native violets, it serves as a host plant for multiple fritillary butterfly species. In zone 7 and below only — does not tolerate the heat and humidity of the Gulf South.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant can go out 2–4 weeks before last frost as plants are frost-tolerant.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in well-drained germination mix; germination is fast and reliable at 65–70°F. Plant in full sun in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; sweet William is technically a biennial that flowers in its second year, but modern annual varieties bloom the first year from an early indoor start. The domed, fragrant flower clusters in vivid shades of red, pink, white, and bicolor appear in late spring and early summer. Deadhead spent clusters promptly to extend the blooming period; plants self-sow readily to maintain a colony from year to year.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring bloom; or sow in fall in mild climates (zones 7–9) for a winter-spring annual that blooms prolifically before summer heat arrives; a charming cottage garden annual that self-seeds reliably.
directions: Direct sow in early spring while nights are still cool, or in fall for zone 7–9 winter-spring bloom; barely cover seeds with soil and keep moist until germination. Sweet William catchfly (also called None-So-Pretty and Sweet William silene) is a delightful European annual producing slender, somewhat sticky stems with clusters of small, magenta-pink, five-petaled flowers with notched petals in tight, rounded clusters that bloom prolifically from spring through early summer; it strongly resembles sweet William but is a much more compact plant. The sticky glands on the stem trap small insects — hence 'catchfly' — but this causes no harm to the plant. An excellent self-seeding cottage garden annual that naturalizes nicely in gravel paths, rock gardens, and between pavers; butterflies and small native bees visit the flowers reliably. Direct sow in drifts for best effect.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted stem sections in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in spring; sweet woodruff naturalizes rapidly in cool, moist, shaded conditions and can become invasive in ideal habitat.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted stem pieces in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; sweet woodruff is a delicate-looking European native that forms a low, weed-suppressing carpet of bright, fresh-green whorled leaves topped with a froth of tiny, pure-white, four-petaled flowers in late spring that are classically used to flavor May wine (Maibowl). The fresh plant has a faint, pleasant hay-like scent; dried foliage intensifies to a strong, sweet, vanilla-like fragrance of coumarin used in perfumery and pot-pourri. It naturalizes beautifully as a groundcover under deciduous trees and in woodland gardens, spreading steadily by creeping stems without becoming overwhelming in average garden conditions, though it can run in moist, loose soils. Semi-evergreen in mild winters; dies to the ground in cold climates.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; sweetbay magnolia is more tolerant of wet, boggy soils than most magnolias and thrives in the heavy, seasonally wet soils common in southeastern gardens.
directions: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; sweetbay magnolia is more tolerant of wet, boggy soils than most magnolias and thrives in the heavy, seasonally wet soils common in southeastern gardens. Magnolia virginiana is the finest native magnolia for year-round SE gardens — semi-evergreen in zones 7–10 with smooth, blue-gray bark; large, glossy, dark-green leaves with silver undersides that flutter beautifully in the breeze; and creamy-white, lemon-scented flowers 2–3 inches across that open throughout summer, providing a long season of fragrance and pollinator value. The red, berry-like seeds in fall are consumed by birds, and the tree supports specialist Promethea silk moth and tiger swallowtail caterpillars; it grows naturally in swampy, streamside habitats from Massachusetts to Texas.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to part shade; sweetbox is one of the most elegant and fragrant small shrubs for shaded gardens, thriving under high-canopy trees where few shrubs succeed.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to part shade; avoid dry soil or full sun, which bleaches and scorches the leaves. Sarcococca hookeriana (Himalayan sweetbox) is one of the finest shade shrubs for temperate and mild-winter gardens — a compact, slowly spreading, Himalayan evergreen shrub producing small, glossy, narrow, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves on gracefully arching stems, and tiny, thread-like, white flowers of almost no visual impact but extraordinary fragrance in January–March, filling the winter air with an intense, vanilla-like perfume that is among the most powerful and pleasing of any garden plant in bloom. The flowers are followed by small, glossy, black drupes (berries) attractive to birds. Plants spread slowly by rhizomes to form tidy, weed-suppressing colonies. The variety humilis (dwarf form, to 24 inches) is lower and more spreading; var. digyna is slightly taller with narrower leaves. Sweetbox is superbly adapted to the dry shade and root competition under large trees — one of the most underused shrubs for difficult shaded spots. In zone 9, protect from afternoon sun and provide reliable summer moisture.

plant_note: Divide established root suckers in early spring or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy to gravelly, infertile soil in full sun to partial shade; sweetfern resents fertile soil and will not thrive in amended or enriched garden soil — this is a plant specifically for lean, acidic, infertile conditions.
directions: Divide root suckers in early spring or plant container specimens in well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy, infertile soil in full sun to partial shade; sweetfern is one of the most distinctive and characterful of all North American native shrubs — though it looks like a miniature fern with deeply lobed, linear, fern-like leaves, it is actually a nitrogen-fixing, aromatic shrub related to bayberry (Morella), not a fern at all. The leaves have a remarkable, intensely spicy-sweet, resinous fragrance when bruised or crushed — one of the most evocative natural scents of the northeastern American outdoors, instantly recognizable to anyone who has walked through sunny pine barrens, rocky slopes, and sandy blueberry barrens in summer. It thrives in extremely infertile, dry, sandy, acidic soils where virtually nothing else will grow, and is essential for naturalizing and stabilizing infertile, acidic slopes and disturbed areas. The nitrogen-fixing root system slowly enriches the surrounding soil, making it useful as a nurse plant for subsequent native plantings. Essentially impossible to transplant bare-root; always use container stock.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; sweetgum transplants readily when young and establishes quickly, growing 2–3 feet per year in good conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; sweetgum is one of the most visually spectacular native trees for fall color in the South, producing star-shaped leaves that turn a stunning mosaic of yellow, orange, red, and burgundy-purple — often all colors simultaneously on a single tree — rivaling the best maples in fall display. It is a major component of bottomland and upland forests throughout the eastern United States and grows rapidly into a large, pyramidal to oval tree. The distinctive spiny spherical seed balls (gumballs) that persist through winter provide important food for goldfinches, pine siskins, and purple finches but can be a nuisance underfoot on lawns; fruitless cultivars such as 'Rotundiloba' are available for situations where the seed balls are problematic. The sweetgum is one of the most ecologically important trees for wildlife in the Southeast.

common_name: Sweetheart Hoya (Heart Leaf Hoya, Lucky-Heart Plant, Valentine Hoya)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light with excellent drainage; Hoya kerrii cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 50°F. The single-leaf cuttings sold as 'Sweetheart Hoyas' around Valentine's Day will root and survive for years but cannot develop into full climbing plants — they lack the axillary node that produces new growth. A complete vine cutting (with at least one node) will develop into a full flowering vine. Grow in a chunky, well-draining potting mix. Water thoroughly and allow the soil to dry almost completely between waterings. The thick succulent leaves store water against long dry periods. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Sweetheart Hoya is more shade-tolerant than most succulents but produces its best growth and flowers (on mature vines) in bright indirect light; it will not flower in low light. Hoya kerrii is a succulent-leaved epiphytic vine native to the hill and montane forests of Southeast Asia (Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia, southern China), belonging to the family Apocynaceae alongside other Hoyas and Dischidias. The common name 'Sweetheart Hoya' and the plant's enormous commercial popularity around Valentine's Day both derive from the uniquely heart-shaped leaves: thick, fleshy, dark-green, perfectly symmetrical cordate (heart-shaped) leaves that give the plant an immediately charming, gift-ready appearance. The single rooted leaf cuttings sold in tiny pots — ubiquitous in florist shops and garden centers every February — are cute but limited: because a single leaf has no axillary bud (node), it can root and survive indefinitely but can never produce new growth or develop into a full plant. Only stem cuttings with a node can develop into the full trailing vine, which in time produces small, white, star-shaped flowers in umbels with a faint sweet fragrance. The complete vine form, with its thick, overlapping heart leaves and occasional fragrant flowers, is the superior ornamental plant. Non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; sweetleaf is a true understory species of southeastern woodlands and performs best sited beneath a high pine or hardwood canopy rather than in open sun.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath established trees; adaptable to a range of soil textures as long as it is not waterlogged. Symplocos tinctoria (sweetleaf, or horse sugar) is a semi-evergreen to evergreen native shrub or small tree of southeastern woodlands, named for its distinctly sweet-tasting leaves — historically browsed eagerly by livestock (hence 'horse sugar') and once used by farmers as emergency fodder. In late winter to earliest spring, before or as new leaves emerge, the bare branches are lined with small, fragrant, pale yellow flower clusters that provide an important early nectar source for native bees at a time when little else is blooming. The foliage is a larval host plant for several moth species, including the striking io moth, adding real ecological value to a woodland garden planting. An underused, ecologically valuable native for the shaded understory of a southeastern woodland garden, zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or rooted softwood cuttings in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; sweetshrub thrives in the dappled shade at the edges of deciduous woodland.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; sweetshrub is an excellent native shrub for the woodland garden, producing unusual maroon-to-burgundy, many-petaled, strap-petaled flowers in late spring with a sweet, fruity, strawberry-spice fragrance that has been treasured for centuries — historically the dried flowers were placed in sachets and closets for perfuming linens. Fragrance intensity varies considerably among individuals, so select plants when in bloom or seek named fragrant cultivars like 'Athens' (buttery-yellow flowers) and 'Michael Lindsey'. The large, dark-green leaves turn butter-yellow in fall. Adaptable and low-maintenance once established; it suckers moderately to form a naturalistic clump.

common_name: Swing Low Distylium (Prostrate Groundcover Evergreen Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Swing Low's very low, ground-hugging habit makes it useful as a durable evergreen groundcover in spots too shaded for most flowering groundcovers.
directions: Swing Low is one of the lowest-growing distylium selections available, spreading wide while staying under 18 inches tall, which makes it a tough, evergreen alternative to traditional shade groundcovers like liriope or mondo grass in beds too shaded for turf. Its small, glossy, leathery leaves resist deer browsing and stay attractive year-round, with new growth tinged bronze-red before maturing to green, and inconspicuous small red flowers appear in late winter without significant ornamental impact. Like other distylium selections it is remarkably adaptable, tolerating wet or dry soil, heat, humidity, and both full sun and deep shade with minimal disease or pest pressure, and needs only an occasional trim to keep its spreading habit in bounds.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Swingtime is a classic trailing double-flowered fuchsia grown for hanging baskets.
directions: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun and intense summer heat, which fuchsias tolerate poorly. Swingtime is a classic trailing fuchsia bearing an abundance of large, fully double flowers with vivid red tubes and sepals surrounding a puffy white corolla, dangling like little ballet skirts along cascading stems, a favorite for hanging baskets and porch containers for generations. It flowers most heavily in cool, humid conditions and slows or stalls in peak summer heat, so afternoon shade and consistent moisture are essential in warm-summer climates. Pinch growing tips when young to encourage a fuller, more floriferous basket, and feed regularly through the growing season to sustain its continuous bloom.

common_name: Swiss Cheese Vine (Monkey Mask Plant, Adanson's Monstera)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Swiss Cheese Vine cannot tolerate frost and must be protected from temperatures below 50°F. It thrives in indirect light and is one of the best choices for filling hanging baskets, climbing moss poles, or trailing from shelves in shaded indoor and outdoor spaces. Propagate easily from stem cuttings — a node with one leaf and an aerial root inserted in moist potting mix roots readily in 2–3 weeks. Feed monthly with balanced fertilizer during the growing season.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade; Swiss Cheese Vine performs best with bright indirect light (2–4 feet from a sunny window) and will tolerate lower light than the larger Monstera deliciosa, though growth slows significantly in very dim conditions. Monstera adansonii is a tropical vine from Central and South America in the Araceae family closely related to but smaller-leaved than the iconic Monstera deliciosa. Its heart-shaped to oval, dark-green leaves are perforated by numerous oval holes (fenestrations) of varying sizes — the perforations develop naturally as the leaves expand and are thought to allow wind and rain to pass through without damaging the leaf in the turbulent rainforest understory. The fenestrated leaves, smaller than M. deliciosa (3–8 inches versus 12–18 inches), are nevertheless extremely ornamental and have made Swiss Cheese Vine one of the most popular and widely sold trailing houseplants in the current era of 'indoor jungle' interior design. The plant grows quickly in good conditions and can cascade several feet from a hanging basket or climb enthusiastically up a moss pole. In zone 10-11, it can be planted outdoors in deeply shaded, humid spots and will eventually climb trees to considerable height. All parts are mildly toxic if chewed.

plant_note: Start indoors in cool, dark conditions; transplant in early spring or fall.
directions: This Swiss heirloom is the parent of most modern pansies, producing low, bushy plants covered in showy, large, velvety flowers. Start seed indoors in cool conditions and darkness, then grow seedlings on in bright light before transplanting in early spring or fall. Pansies thrive in cool weather and make a fine companion to spring bulbs. Grow in full sun to part shade in rich, moist soil and deadhead to extend bloom. The edible petals garnish soft cheeses and baked goods.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Strawflowers live up to their name, with stiff, papery bracts that look like colored straw and never wilt, making them the classic everlasting cut flower. Surface sow the seed indoors since light aids germination, then transplant after frost into full sun and well-drained soil. Swiss Giants produce extra-large double blooms in bright shades on long, sturdy stems. Cut flowers just before they fully open and hang them upside down to dry for lasting arrangements. Deadhead spent blooms to keep plants flowering, and enjoy the pollinators they attract.

plant_note: Sow indoors and cover; seed germinates best in darkness and cool conditions.
directions: Start seed indoors covered and in darkness, keeping the soil cool for best germination. This heirloom mix produces large, velvety, edible blossoms in blue, purple, yellow, orange, and burgundy. Pansies love cool weather, so transplant in early spring or fall and grow in full sun to part shade with steady moisture. Deadhead often and they will bloom prolifically until summer heat or hard freezes arrive.

plant_note: Plant divisions of the rhizomatous colony in spring in moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; switchcane spreads by vigorous underground rhizomes to form dense thickets in appropriate moist conditions, mimicking its natural streambank and pocosin habitat.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun along streambanks, pond margins, and in wet bottomlands; switchcane is the smaller of two native North American bamboos (the other being giant cane, A. gigantea), naturally forming dense canebrake thickets in wet, poorly drained soils of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain. While historically common, natural canebrake habitats have been reduced by over 95% since European settlement, making switchcane increasingly rare in the wild. It provides important habitat for several rare and declining species, including the Swainson's warbler, which nests almost exclusively in canebrake thickets. Leaves are consumed by white-tailed deer and the cane structure provides winter cover for numerous birds. The Arogos skipper butterfly uses native cane as its larval host plant. Spreads aggressively by rhizomes — excellent for ecological restoration of wet areas, less suitable for small formal gardens.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in spring in full sun in any well-drained to moderately wet soil; switchgrass is highly adaptable and grows in a broader range of soil conditions than most prairie grasses — from dry upland sand to seasonally flooded clay.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in spring or plant container transplants in any well-drained to moderately wet, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; switchgrass is one of the most important and ecologically valuable native grasses of the North American prairie, valued for its extraordinary adaptability — it grows from Canada to Florida, from dry upland sand to seasonally flooded clay, and tolerates salt, drought, and flooding with equal resilience. The midsummer cloud of airy, panicle flowers dances above the upright, blue-green foliage, turning to golden seed heads by fall that feed dozens of native bird species. Selected cultivars offer outstanding landscape value: 'Shenandoah' turns deep red in summer, 'Prairie Sky' has intense blue foliage, and 'Northwind' is strongly upright. Cut back to 6 inches in late winter before new growth begins.

plant_note: Float a rosette in a sunny pond or water garden without soil; swollen bladderwort forms its own free-floating raft of spongy, inflated spokes and needs no anchoring — use rain or pond water rather than chlorinated tap water, and site it only in a contained water feature within its native Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain range.
directions: Float a rosette in a sunny, still, acidic pond or water garden without adding soil; swollen bladderwort is unmistakable among native bladderworts for the spoked, inflated float it produces where its finely divided, bladder-covered stems meet the water surface, buoying up a central cluster of showy, bright-yellow, snapdragon-like flowers held several inches above the water in summer. It is native to quiet, acidic, tannin-stained ponds and ditches across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, where its submerged stems trap tiny aquatic invertebrates in bladder traps while the plant drifts freely with the wind. In a home water garden it adds an architectural floating element unlike any typical aquatic plant, though it spreads readily in favorable warm, nutrient-poor water and should be thinned periodically and kept within a contained feature rather than released into open waterways outside its native range.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline, rocky limestone or loamy soil in partial shade to filtered sun. Sycamore-leaf Snowbell is a Texas endemic adapted to the alkaline limestone soils of the Edwards Plateau and adjacent Hill Country.
directions: Sycamore-leaf Snowbell is a beautiful native understory shrub or small tree, endemic to the limestone canyons, creek banks, and rocky woodland slopes of the Texas Edwards Plateau and Hill Country, where it grows in the shaded understory of live oak and Texas cedar elm woodlands in thin, alkaline, limestone-derived soils. In April and May it produces clusters of fragrant, white, pendant bell-shaped flowers similar to those of other snowbells (Styrax species), with the blooms arranged more openly than the closely related American Snowbell (Styrax americanus). The large, maple-like (plataniform) leaves are a distinctive characteristic that sets it apart from other native snowbells. An excellent shrub for Texas Hill Country native landscapes and limestone-soil gardens in zones 7–9, it is drought-tolerant once established in well-drained alkaline soil and requires no fertilizer or supplemental irrigation after the first two seasons. Source from specialty native Texas plant nurseries.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sydney golden wattle is extremely fast-growing — potentially reaching 20 feet in 3–5 years — and is used as a quick-growing screen or windbreak plant. It blooms in winter and spring (July–October in Australia; January–April in zone 9). More coastal and moisture-tolerant than many wattles. Listed as invasive in parts of the Mediterranean region, Portugal, and South Africa — use with awareness in mild climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sydney golden wattle is one of Australia's most fast-growing, most fragrant, and most adaptable coastal wattles — native to the sandy coastal heaths, dune systems, and dry sclerophyll forests along the entire Australian east coast from Queensland to Victoria. Unlike the finely-divided, feathery bipinnate leaves of A. baileyana or A. dealbata, Sydney golden wattle is a phyllode-bearing species with long, narrow, lance-shaped, bright-green phyllodes that create a dense, willow-like screen of dark-green foliage year-round. In winter and spring, the branches are covered in dense, cylindrical spikes of small, bright-golden-yellow flowers (rather than spherical pompoms) with a powerful, sweet, characteristic wattle fragrance. The cylindrical spike form (rather than pompom) is immediately distinguishing. Its fast growth — reaching 15–20 feet in only a few years — makes it valuable as a quick-growing, fragrant, flowering screen or windbreak in coastal zone 9 gardens. More tolerant of coastal conditions, sandy soils, and occasional moisture than the inland species. The outstanding fragrance and very fast growth make it a practical choice for rapid effect in new gardens.

common_name: Symphony Chrysanthemum (Exhibition Spider Mum, Feathery Russet-Orange-Bronze)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Symphony is an exhibition spider mum with long, feathery russet-orange-bronze petals.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; spider mums generally need more sun and staking support than compact garden mum types. Symphony, a favorite exhibition spider mum, bears long, feathery, curling petals in warm russet-orange-to-bronze tones, prized on the show bench for the elegant, flowing form of its petals, which distinguish spider mums from the tighter, more compact button and decorative garden mum types. Stake plants to support the tall stems and heavy flower heads, and disbud side buds if larger, showier terminal blooms are the goal.

plant_note: Direct sow stratified seeds in spring in very well-drained, rocky, acidic, lean soil in full sun; table mountain pine is strictly adapted to dry, rocky, high-elevation habitats and performs poorly in rich, moist, or lowland conditions. Plant on exposed, sunny slopes or rocky outcrops in the Appalachian region.
directions: Plant in dry, rocky, very well-drained, acidic, lean soil in full sun on exposed ridges and slopes; table mountain pine is an Appalachian endemic restricted to dry, exposed, rocky ridge tops from Pennsylvania to Georgia, typically growing on south- or west-facing outcrops at elevations of 2000–4000 feet. The most distinctive feature is the armored cones — among the most ferociously spiny of any North American pine, with stout, curved, sharp spines on each scale. These serotinous cones remain closed on the tree for decades and require the intense heat of a wildfire to open and release seeds, an adaptation to the fire-maintained pine barrens community of dry Appalachian ridges. The tree has a gnarled, picturesque growth habit from constant exposure to wind and drought on rocky summits. Of limited garden use outside its native range but outstanding for naturalistic plantings on rocky, thin, dry, acidic slopes in Appalachian zones 4–7.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or plant container-grown plants in deep, moist, humus-rich, fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; astilboides requires consistently moist to wet soil and should never be allowed to dry out. It is slow to establish but becomes impressively bold once settled. Protection from wind is important as the enormous leaves can be damaged by strong gusts.
