directions: Plant in deep, moist to wet, humus-rich, fertile soil in part to full shade; tabletop astilboides is grown for what may be the most dramatically impressive foliage of any hardy perennial — individual circular, peltate (the stem attaches to the center of the leaf, like an umbrella handle) leaves that reach 2-3 feet across in mature specimens, creating enormous, flat, table-like platforms of bold textural interest in the shade garden. The leaf surface is light green, somewhat hairy, with prominent lobes and veining visible across the whole expanse. In early summer, the plant produces tall stems bearing large, branching panicles of small, cream-white flowers above the foliage, adding floral interest to the already spectacular leaf display. Native to moist valleys and stream margins in northeastern China and Korea, it requires consistently moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in a shaded position — drying out causes the enormous leaves to scorch rapidly. An irreplaceable plant for creating a bold tropical effect in cool, moist shade gardens alongside hostas, ligularias, and rodgersias.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; Tahiti is a long-standing double daffodil cultivar mixing yellow petals with orange-red segments.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Tahiti bears fully double blooms mixing rich yellow petals with segments of vivid orange-red, giving each flower a ruffled, layered look quite different from the simple trumpet-and-perianth form of most daffodils. It has remained in commerce for decades thanks to its warm, cheerful color combination and reliable performance in the garden. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over the years.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring, even before the last frost date, into well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Tahoka daisy self-seeds freely and is often easiest to establish by fall sowing where winters are mild.
directions: Direct sow into lean, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun as soon as soil can be worked, since seedlings tolerate light frost; Tahoka daisy is a fast, drought-tough Great Plains and Southwest native annual with finely cut, ferny, aromatic foliage. Large lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers open in profusion from late spring through fall, closing at night and on cloudy days, and are a strong draw for native bees and butterflies. Plants sprawl and self-seed generously in loose, dry soil, so it naturalizes readily in wildflower meadows and gravel gardens once introduced, often returning from seed for years with no replanting. It needs no supplemental fertilizer and little to no irrigation once seedlings are established, making it a reliable, low-maintenance filler for hot, dry, sunny sites.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Taiwan cherry blooms in January–February in mild climates and is the best ornamental cherry for mild-winter, zone 8–10 gardens where standard Japanese cherries bloom poorly due to insufficient winter chill.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Taiwan cherry blooms in January through February in zone 8–10, producing small, bell-shaped (campanulata = bell-shaped) flowers in a vivid, deep cerise-pink to crimson-red — among the most intensely colored of all cherry blossoms. Unlike most Japanese ornamental cherries that require cold winters for satisfactory bloom, Taiwan cherry thrives in mild winters and requires minimal winter chill. It is the ornamental cherry of choice for gardeners in the Gulf South, Pacific Southwest, and other mild-winter areas where cold-requirement Japanese cherries languish. A hummingbird magnet — the intensely colored, nectar-rich flowers attract Anna's and rufous hummingbirds throughout their bloom period. The small, dark red fruits are edible though small and tart. Blooms in late winter before most other flowering trees.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, fertile loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Taiwan cypress grows naturally in mountain cloud forests of Taiwan at 3,000–9,000 feet elevation, requiring cool, humid conditions with excellent drainage. Rare in cultivation outside of botanical gardens and conifer specialist collections.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, fertile loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Taiwan cypress is one of the most massive and ancient conifers in Asia — the ancient forests of Taiwan contain trees that are the oldest and largest living organisms in East Asia, with some trees estimated at 2,000–3,000 years old and measuring over 60 feet in trunk circumference. The ancient tree 'Alishan Giant' and other Taiwan cypress giants in the Alishan Forest Recreation Area are Taiwan's most celebrated natural treasures. The reddish, furrowed bark and spreading, cathedral crown of these ancient specimens are extraordinary. In cultivation outside Taiwan it is rarely grown and poorly known compared to its relatives Chamaecyparis lawsoniana and C. obtusa. The wood has historically been an important construction timber in Taiwan and Japan. Grown primarily in botanical gardens and specialist collections in mild, humid climates — zones 7–9 with adequate rainfall.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Taiwan toad lily spreads more assertively by stolons than hairy toad lily (T. hirta) and can form substantial colonies in favorable conditions.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart; Taiwan toad lily is the most commonly grown toad lily in American gardens and is distinguished from the similar hairy toad lily (T. hirta) by its terminal flower clusters (borne at the branch tips, not in the leaf axils), its upright rather than strictly arching stems, and its slightly wider hardiness range extending to zone 9. Tricyrtis formosana produces white to pale lilac flowers heavily spotted with purple and with a yellow-centered throat from August through October, on 18–30 inch stems that may branch near the top; the blooms genuinely resemble miniature orchids and appear when virtually no other shade perennials are in flower. It spreads more freely than T. hirta by underground stolons, gradually forming substantial colonies; divide in early spring every few years to manage spread and rejuvenate clumps. Excellent paired with hostas, Japanese forest grass, and late-season ferns in the shade border.

common_name: Takil Windmill Palm (Rare Cold-Hardy Himalayan Windmill Palm)
subcategory: cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Takil is a rare, distinct windmill palm species native to high elevations in the Kumaon Himalayas, sought by palm collectors for cold hardiness that can exceed even the more common Trachycarpus fortunei.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade. Takil is a rare windmill palm species native to high-elevation forests in the Kumaon region of the Himalayas, distinct from the far more commonly planted Trachycarpus fortunei, and prized among palm enthusiasts pushing the limits of cold-hardy palm cultivation for its exceptional tolerance of cold, sometimes cited as comparable to or better than standard windmill palm. It develops a similar fiber-covered trunk and fan-shaped fronds but can be slower growing and harder to source than the common windmill palm. Water regularly while establishing, then reduce to occasional deep watering during dry spells, and remove old, dead fronds as they brown to keep the trunk tidy.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or plant transplants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. The Talent series is one of the most popular silver-leaved gazania strains — the silvery-white, pubescent foliage providing an additional ornamental dimension beyond the vivid orange flowers. Gazania flowers open fully only in sun and close on cloudy days and at night. The plants are highly drought-tolerant once established and perform best in lean, well-drained, sandy soils — excessive moisture or fertility causes root rot and reduced flowering. Gazania is borderline perennial in zone 9 — the plants may survive mild winters as semi-woody perennials but are most reliably grown as warm-season annuals. The orange flowers provide strong warm-color contrast with blue and purple companion plants.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Gazania requires full sun (flowers close in shade) and excellent drainage; it thrives in hot, dry, coastal conditions where many other annuals decline; Talent Orange Gazania is a silver-leaved selection of Treasure Flower (Gazania rigens), a South African perennial grown as a warm-season annual — producing vivid orange, large (3-inch), single daisy flowers with darker orange or brown striping at the base of the ray petals that creates a striped, star-patterned floral display above a low, spreading rosette of distinctive silver-gray, deeply divided leaves. The silver-white foliage of the Talent series is one of the most striking and unusual features of this selection — the densely pubescent leaf surface covering the leaves in fine silver hairs that give the entire plant a silvery, reflective quality, adding a year-round foliage interest that makes the plant attractive even when not in bloom. Gazania's South African coastal origin (fynbos and coastal scrub) gives it exceptional adaptability to hot, dry, sandy, salt-air conditions that are common in Gulf Coast home gardens — making it one of the most practical ornamental annuals for beach-adjacent and coastal zone 9 gardens where other annuals struggle with salt, sand, and periodic drought. The combination of vivid orange flowers, attractive silver foliage, extreme drought and heat tolerance, and compact mounding habit makes Talent Orange one of the most useful full-sun, low-water annuals for zone 9.

subcategory: Sri Lankan giant monocarpic fan palm
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral deep soil in zone 10–12; Talipot Palm is the largest of all fan palms — native to southern India and Sri Lanka — and produces the largest branched inflorescence of any plant on Earth, bearing 6–8 million individual flowers at once on a terminal spike 20–25 feet tall and 30–40 feet wide, after which the entire palm dies; a remarkable, once-in-a-lifetime natural spectacle requiring 40–80 years to mature.
directions: Plant Talipot Palm in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; it grows relatively quickly once established into an impressive palm that may be the largest fan palm a gardener ever grows; water regularly during establishment and periodically in dry periods; avoid poorly drained sites. Talipot Palm is one of the most extraordinary plants in existence — a palm that spends 40–80 years growing slowly to maturity, accumulating enormous reserves in its massive trunk, then produces the largest inflorescence of any plant on Earth: a single terminal flower spike 20–25 feet tall and 30–40 feet wide, bearing an estimated 6–8 million individual cream-white flowers — then dies. The entire plant's reproductive output is concentrated into this one monumental effort. Native to the moist lowland forests of Sri Lanka and adjacent Kerala, India, the palm was historically of immense cultural importance: the huge leaves (up to 25 feet across) were used for umbrellas (the species name umbraculifera means 'umbrella-bearing'), as writing surfaces (palm leaf manuscripts on which much of South Asian religious literature was recorded), for thatching, and as food service vessels. Growing one in a zone 10–12 garden is an investment in a multi-generational botanical specimen — most planted individuals will never be seen to flower by the person who plants them, but the journey is rewarding in its own right.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall (cold stratification improves germination) in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tall bellflower is a biennial that blooms in its second year — establish a planting from seed in two successive years to ensure continuous bloom thereafter.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — tall bellflower is a striking native biennial of eastern forest understories that can reach 3–6 feet tall when in bloom, producing a long terminal raceme and lateral branches covered with flat, five-lobed blue-violet flowers that open wide (unlike the nodding, bell-shaped flowers of most bellflowers) throughout summer. It is one of the most shade-tolerant native wildflowers capable of producing impressive flowering stems in quite deep shade. The long, curved styles and protruding stamens give the flowers a distinctive star-burst appearance. The plant is a true biennial — forming a rosette in year one, blooming and setting seed in year two, then dying. Self-sows reliably in appropriate conditions to maintain a naturalized colony. An outstanding native plant for creating a vertical accent in the shaded native garden in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; seed needs darkness to germinate.
directions: Bachelor's button, also known as cornflower, is a drought-tolerant, low-maintenance annual with flowers great for cutting or drying and edible petals for garnishing salads. Direct sow in early spring, covering the seed since it needs darkness to germinate, and thin seedlings once up. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil. This tall blend self-sows readily, naturalizing for another crop of flowers the following year. Deadhead or harvest often to prolong the bloom period and support pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or cold-stratify seeds 90 days and sow indoors in late winter. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil at the edge of a stream or in a moist woodland.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade at stream banks, moist woodland edges, and wet mountain meadows; tall bluebells is the western counterpart of Virginia bluebells (M. virginica), native to streamside habitats from the Rocky Mountains through the Great Basin. The hanging clusters of blue tubular flowers in late spring are typical of the genus — opening from pink buds and maturing to clear sky-blue — and are heavily visited by bumblebees and hummingbirds. The plant goes fully dormant by midsummer after setting seed, so mark its location to avoid digging through the dormant rootstock. Combines beautifully with marsh marigolds, skunk cabbage, and riparian sedges in moist, shaded stream-bank planting. Best in cool-summer climates.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; tall coreopsis self-sows freely and naturalizes in meadow plantings, prairie gardens, and along woodland edges.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun where the plant's height can be accommodated; tall coreopsis is the largest coreopsis species native to North America, reaching 4–8 feet and producing hundreds of cheerful, small yellow daisy-like flowers from midsummer through early fall. Unlike short-lived tickseed cultivars, the straight species is a robust, long-lived prairie perennial that establishes deeply and persists for decades without division. The anise-scented foliage is deer-resistant. Excellent for the back of meadow borders, along fences, and in rain garden margins where it adds bold vertical interest while feeding native bees and butterflies throughout the blooming season. Leave seed heads standing through winter for songbirds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; flat-topped aster spreads by rhizomes to form large colonies in suitable moist conditions and can be aggressive in small gardens — use it in large native plantings and rain gardens where spread is welcome.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; flat-topped aster spreads by rhizomes to form large colonies in suitable moist conditions and can be aggressive in small gardens — use it in large native plantings and rain gardens where spread is welcome. Doellingeria umbellata is a robust, tall native perennial of moist meadows, wet prairies, streambanks, and open shrubby swamps throughout eastern North America, producing many-branched stems with large, flat-topped to umbellate clusters of numerous small, white to pale lavender-white flowers with yellow centers from August through October. The flat-topped flower clusters are exceptional landing pads for pollinating insects — the flowers attract an extraordinary diversity of native bees, wasps, flies, and butterflies, providing an important late-season nectar resource as most other wildflowers decline. It spreads vigorously by rhizomes and is best used in large-scale naturalistic plantings rather than formal borders.

plant_note: Surface sow in spring as seed needs light to germinate; division of established clumps in early spring is more reliable and faster.
directions: Scatter seed on the surface of average, well-drained soil in full sun; tall goldenrod is the single most important plant for migrating monarch butterflies and late-season native bees, providing nectar during the critical fall migration period. Despite its reputation for causing hay fever (the actual culprit is ragweed, which blooms simultaneously), goldenrod pollen is heavy and insect-pollinated, not airborne. The plant spreads aggressively by rhizome in fertile soil; divide every 2–3 years to maintain vigor, using divisions to fill new areas. Excellent companion for ironweed (Vernonia), asters, and Joe-Pye weed in a late-season native garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for winter cold-moist stratification, or cold-stratify seed 60 days before spring sowing; tall green milkweed is slower to establish than common milkweed but is more compact and well-behaved once mature.
directions: Plant in dry to mesic, well-drained soil, including sandy and rocky ground, in full sun. Tall green milkweed is a lesser-known prairie species that once ranged widely through remnant tallgrass and sand prairies of the Midwest and Northeast but has become locally uncommon as native grasslands were converted to agriculture, making garden plantings valuable for regional monarch and pollinator conservation. It bears dense, rounded clusters of greenish-white flowers with a faint fragrance in early to midsummer, held tightly against narrow, willowy leaves on an upright, non-spreading stem, giving it a tidier and less rangy habit than common milkweed. As with all milkweeds it serves as a larval host plant for monarch butterflies and is visited by a wide range of native bees and other pollinators for nectar. It tolerates lean, dry soils and heat well once its taproot is established, and unlike Asclepias syriaca it does not spread aggressively by rhizome, making it a good choice for smaller native plant beds.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or sow indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in spring after frost risk passes — tall ironweed self-seeds freely in moist meadows and stream margins.
directions: Tall ironweed earns its name — plants commonly reach 8 to 10 feet in moist bottomland meadows and woodland edges, bearing brilliant magenta-purple, flat-topped flower clusters in late summer and early fall that stand above neighboring prairie plants and attract a spectacular diversity of butterflies and native bees. As one of the tallest native perennials in the eastern United States, it provides a dramatic vertical accent in native gardens, meadows, and rain garden margins where few other plants achieve its scale while remaining fully native. The intense royal purple flowers are among the most vivid of any North American wildflower — the color is caused by anthocyanin pigments and does not fade even in full southern sun. Cut plants back by half in late June to reduce height and encourage branching if growing in a formal border; allow spent flower heads to stand through winter to feed goldfinches and sparrows.

plant_note: Sow seed outdoors in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally; established plants resent transplanting once their taproot forms.
directions: Sow seed outdoors in fall so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally, or refrigerate moist seed before spring sowing; established plants resent transplanting once their taproot forms. This upright, late-summer-blooming larkspur sends up narrow spikes of deep blue-violet flowers that are a favorite of long-tongued bumblebees and are visited by hummingbirds as well. It is native to open woodlands, rocky slopes, and prairie-woodland transitions of the Appalachians and lower Midwest, and appreciates a lean, well-drained soil rather than rich garden loam. Because it is regionally uncommon in the wild, garden-grown stock helps take pressure off native populations while still supplying valuable late-season forage.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors; snapdragons tolerate cool weather when hardened off.
directions: This tall blend of snapdragons adds classic charm to gardens and cut-flower arrangements, and its blooms are a bee magnet as bumblebees climb right into the mouths. Surface sow the tiny seed indoors since light aids germination, and grow seedlings on before transplanting into rich, well-drained soil. Snapdragons prefer cool weather, so set out hardened plants a bit before the last frost and provide late-afternoon shade in hot regions. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and stake the tall spikes if needed. The edible flowers make a pretty garnish, and deadheading prolongs the display.

plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; tall meadow rue is native to wet meadows, stream banks, and wet woods and demands consistent moisture to thrive — it is ideal for rain gardens, wet meadow borders, and streamside plantings.
directions: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; tall meadow rue is native to wet meadows, stream banks, and wet woods and demands consistent moisture to thrive — it is ideal for rain gardens, wet meadow borders, and streamside plantings. Thalictrum polygamum is the tallest native North American meadow rue, a dramatic architectural plant reaching 5–7 feet in good conditions with large, compound, blue-green leaves and enormous, cloud-like panicles of tiny, creamy-white, fragrant flowers with prominent white stamens in midsummer; it is one of the finest plants for providing vertical scale in large native rain gardens and streamside plantings and provides exceptional late-spring and summer nectar for native bees and beneficial wasps.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for cold stratification and spring germination; or cold stratify seeds for 30–60 days and sow indoors in late winter. Tall meadow rue grows naturally in moist, shaded floodplain forests and wetland edges across eastern North America.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; tall meadow rue is the largest of the native eastern meadow rues, producing elegant, airy columns of blue-green, compound leaves with rounded lobes that resemble maidenhair fern in texture — providing exceptional, fine-textured foliage contrast in the shade garden through the entire growing season. In midsummer, fluffy, creamy-white, tassel-like flowers are produced in large, airy panicles on tall stems, creating a misty, cloud-like effect at the garden's top. Dioecious — male plants produce showier, fluffy staminate flowers while female plants produce seedier fruiting clusters. Excellent at the shaded woodland edge and in moist, shaded rain gardens where its tall, airy presence fills the mid-to-upper strata with graceful, fine-textured foliage. The feathery flowers attract numerous small bees and beneficial insects.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving the very tall flower scapes a sheltered spot at the back of a border; Tall Night-Blooming Daylily opens its flowers in late afternoon and evening rather than in the morning like most daylilies.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, siting toward the back of a bed where its exceptionally tall scapes won't shade shorter neighbors. Native to China, Hemerocallis altissima is one of the tallest species in the genus, sending up slender flower stalks well over 5 feet topped with clusters of pale yellow, sweetly fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and stay open through the night, closing again by the following midday, an unusual habit among daylilies that mostly bloom for a single day. This late-summer bloom time and strongly evening-fragrant character make it a valuable addition to a moon garden or evening seating area where its perfume can be enjoyed after dusk. Established clumps are long-lived and rarely need division more than once every five years or so.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into moist to seasonally wet, acidic, low-fertility soil in full sun to partial shade; tall nutrush grows naturally in wet meadows, pine savannas, and prairie swales across the eastern and southeastern US.
directions: Direct sow or plant divisions into moist to seasonally wet, acidic, low-fertility soil in full sun to partial shade. Tall nutrush is a slender, upright wetland sedge easily identified by its small but strikingly hard, shiny, pearly-white to gray seeds, which persist decoratively into fall and are readily eaten by songbirds and small mammals. It grows naturally in wet meadows, prairie swales, and open pine savannas across the eastern and southeastern United States, adding fine, grass-like texture and subtle late-season interest to a native wet meadow or rain garden planting. It tolerates a range of moisture from consistently damp to briefly saturated soil and needs little care beyond occasional division of congested clumps to keep the planting vigorous.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tall stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tall stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance. Among the largest-growing of the stewartias, this Japanese species develops smooth, richly colored cinnamon-red exfoliating bark considered by many collectors to be the finest of any stewartia, alongside small white summer flowers and reliable orange-red fall color, all on a taller, more substantial tree form than most of its garden-scale relatives. Its combination of eventual larger size and exceptional bark color makes it a valuable specimen tree for a spacious woodland garden where its slow but steady growth into a true small-to-medium shade tree can be accommodated over the years. Provide consistent moisture, dappled shade, and acidic, humus-rich soil, and avoid disturbing the root zone once established, since stewartias establish and transplant slowly.

common_name: Tall Tails Oriental Fountain Grass (Elongated Soft White-Pink Plumes)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Tall Tails is a taller, more vigorous oriental fountain grass with elongated, soft white-pink flower spikes rising well above the foliage.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; fountain grass is heat- and drought-tolerant once established. Tall Tails grows taller and more vigorously than the species, sending up elongated, soft white-pink flower spikes well above the fine-textured foliage mound from late spring through summer, a longer bloom season than most Pennisetum alopecuroides cultivars provide. Its taller flower display and extended bloom window make it a strong mid-border choice for continuous seasonal interest. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained to average, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moist soil in partial shade; tall thimbleweed self-sows readily and naturalizes in appropriate dry to moist woodland conditions without being invasive.
directions: Sow seed in fall in well-drained to average, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moist soil in partial shade — tall thimbleweed is an upright, woodland-edge native anemone whose white, 1–1.5 inch flowers are followed by the plant's most distinctive feature: elongated, thimble-shaped seed heads that are covered in cottony white fibers (resembling a thimble wrapped in white fluff) and persist well into winter, providing long-lasting ornamental value. The flowers attract solitary native bees and small beetles. It grows naturally in dry to moist open woodland, woodland edges, and clearings throughout the eastern and central US, tolerating the dry shade beneath dense tree canopies better than most native wildflowers. The persistent cottony seed heads are useful in dried arrangements. More drought-tolerant than most anemone species. An excellent and underused native for dry, shaded woodland garden settings.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost after cold-stratifying for 1–2 weeks; often blooms from seed the first year.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds in moist towels for 1–2 weeks at 35–40°F, then sow indoors at 65–75°F; germination remains erratic over 14–28 days. Plant in full sun in poor to average, well-drained soil; this South American native is drought-tolerant and naturalizes readily once established. The wiry, branching stems carry clusters of small purple flowers from midsummer through frost at an unusual height that allows it to weave transparently through other plants. Grown as an annual north of zone 7, it self-sows prolifically even in cold climates and seedlings replace killed parent plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; tall white lettuce grows naturally in moist, shaded deciduous forests and forest margins throughout eastern North America. It tolerates deep shade better than most tall composite-family plants.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; tall white lettuce is one of the tallest composite-family plants adapted to true forest shade, growing naturally in the understory of moist deciduous forests where it can reach 9 feet. The large, deeply lobed, variable leaves resemble those of garden lettuce — the plant is indeed related to Lactuca — and produce a milky sap when broken. The small, creamy-white, nodding flower heads in late summer and fall are subtly beautiful and attract specialist native bees. The fluffy seed heads provide food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds in fall. The plant's ability to grow in deep forest shade makes it one of the few tall, imposing plants appropriate for heavily shaded woodland gardens where most large plants fail. Self-sows readily in appropriate conditions.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before direct sowing in fall into rocky, calcareous, well-drained soil.
directions: Talus Scurfpea is a native perennial of rocky limestone talus slopes, calcareous dry prairies, and dry hills from Kansas south through Texas. It produces palmately compound leaves covered in resin dots and dense, upright spikes of blue-violet pea flowers in late spring and early summer. Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into very lean, rocky, or gravelly, well-drained calcareous soil in full sun. Once established, it is highly drought-tolerant and develops a deep, starchy tuberous root; avoid disturbing or transplanting.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tama Beauty's flower pattern can vary somewhat from bloom to bloom, part of the charm of many peppermint-striped camellia cultivars.
directions: Tama Beauty is a camellia japonica prized for its semi-double flowers streaked and flecked in rose-pink over a white background, a lively peppermint-candy pattern that stands out from the solid-colored blooms of most camellia cultivars, with prominent golden stamens at the center. It flowers in mid-to-late winter into early spring on a compact, well-branched, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub, providing weeks of color during the coldest part of the year when little else in the garden is blooming. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mulch to keep roots cool, and prune only lightly to shape right after flowering, since flower buds for the following season set over the summer.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Tama-no-Ura was discovered growing wild on the Gotō Islands of Nagasaki, Japan, in 1947 and is prized for its clean white-edged red flowers, a distinctive natural pattern that seldom reverts.
directions: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind and hot midday sun; Tama-no-Ura is a celebrated Japanese camellia cultivar discovered growing wild on the Gotō Islands off Nagasaki in 1947, bearing single, rich red flowers cleanly edged in white — a naturally occurring bicolor pattern that, unlike many mottled or streaked camellias, holds true and rarely reverts to solid color. The glossy, deep-green evergreen foliage provides year-round structure, and the plant blooms in winter into early spring, when few other shrubs are in flower. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it needs consistently moist but well-drained, acidic soil and benefits from a site with some shelter from strong afternoon sun, which can bleach and brown open flowers. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly after flowering only to shape, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.

common_name: Tamukeyama Japanese Maple (Weeping Red Lace-Leaf Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil, protecting it from drying wind and hot afternoon sun; one of the most heat- and sun-tolerant weeping lace-leaf cultivars, though it still benefits from afternoon shade in Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in part shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and the harshest afternoon sun. One of the oldest and most reliable weeping lace-leaf Japanese maple cultivars in cultivation, Tamukeyama forms a low, dome-shaped, cascading mound of finely dissected, deep burgundy-red leaves that hold their color through summer heat better than most other red lace-leaf cultivars, a trait that has made it a Gulf South and Deep South favorite. Its wider-than-tall, mounding habit makes it a strong specimen for the edge of a pond, atop a slope, or spilling over a low wall. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, especially through the first few years, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches, preserving the natural cascading form.

common_name: Tangerine Beauty Crossvine (Native Apricot-Orange Tubular Flower Spring Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Tangerine Beauty is one of the most cold-hardy and adaptable native flowering vines for Gulf South gardens, performing equally well in full sun and partial shade — one of few vines with significant shade tolerance.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Tangerine Beauty is a selected cultivar of crossvine (Bignonia capreolata), a native southeastern vine notable for its warm apricot-orange to copper-orange flower color — a softer, warmer tone than the typical red-and-yellow of the straight species. The 2-inch, tubular, trumpet-shaped flowers are produced in dense clusters along the vine in March–May, creating a spectacular spring display of orange-toned blooms that attract hummingbirds with exceptional consistency — the tubular flower form and warm color combination is highly attractive to ruby-throated hummingbirds during their spring migration through the Gulf South. Crossvine clings to surfaces with adhesive tendrils and disk-like holdfasts similar to Boston ivy — it can climb masonry, wood, and bark without a separate trellis. The semi-evergreen, compound leaves (two leaflets flanking a tendril) turn deep burgundy-red in winter cold, providing attractive winter foliage color before the spring bloom. Unlike many vines, Tangerine Beauty tolerates considerable shade — growing well on north-facing fences and under tree canopy where most flowering vines fail. The native origin makes it valuable for wildlife gardens: hummingbirds in spring, and specialist native bee species that visit the flowers. The vine is manageable in typical garden settings, growing to 10–20 feet rather than the 50+ feet of some other vines.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9 plant February–April for spring and September for fall. Tangerine Gem marigolds are more heat-tolerant than French or African marigold types and bloom continuously throughout the Gulf Coast growing season with minimal deadheading.
directions: Sow directly on the soil surface or lightly covered in any well-drained soil; Tangerine Gem is a signet marigold (Tagetes tenuifolia) with a mounded, airy habit covered in small, single, deep orange flowers with a fine, ferny foliage that is intensely lemon-scented — deer and rabbits strongly avoid it. Unlike the larger French and African marigolds, signet types tolerate partial shade, bloom without deadheading, and have edible, pleasantly spicy-citrusy flowers suitable for use as a garnish in salads, desserts, and herbal teas. The intense lemon-scent of the crushed foliage deters whiteflies and aphids when planted near vegetables. Plants are drought-tolerant once established and reseed moderately in warm-winter zones.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring onto a lightly raked, open seedbed in partial shade; press seed into the soil surface without deep covering and keep the area evenly moist until germination occurs in two to three weeks.
directions: Scatter seed in early spring onto a lightly disturbed, open soil surface in partial shade, pressing seeds into contact with the soil and watering gently to maintain moisture through germination. Tapered rosette panicgrass is a native of eastern North America's woodland edges and sandy clearings that forms a distinctive flat basal rosette of soft, hairy leaves in fall and winter, then sends up flowering culms 12–24 inches tall in late spring. It thrives in the dappled light of open woodlands and forest margins where few other grasses establish, making it a valuable groundcover and wildlife forage grass in naturalistic plantings. Allow the plant to self-sow freely, as seedlings are easy to identify by their characteristic winter rosette and help naturalize shaded areas over time.

common_name: Tapien Verbena (Fine-Textured Mildew-Resistant Spreading Groundcover Verbena)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9 Tapien performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons, since it can decline in the most humid, wet stretch of high summer.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, since good drainage and air movement are essential to keep this fine-textured verbena free of the powdery mildew that troubles older verbena selections in humid weather. Tapien is a vegetatively propagated groundcover verbena series bred in Japan for finely cut, almost fern-like foliage and a low, dense, fast-spreading habit that quickly carpets ground or spills over container edges in shades of blue, pink, violet, and white. Its improved mildew resistance compared to older verbena makes it noticeably more reliable through humid weather, though like most verbena it still prefers excellent drainage and dislikes soggy soil. Shear plants back by about a third if they become leggy in midsummer to refresh dense flowering, and expect the strongest performance during spring and fall in zone 9's mild-winter climate.

common_name: Tara Ginger Lily (Hardy Scarlet Ginger Lily)
plant_note: Set out divisions in spring after soil has warmed in fertile, well-watered beds; Tara is among the most cold-hardy ginger lily selections and one of the more reliable for the cooler edge of zone 8.
directions: Plant in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade and keep the soil consistently moist through summer for tall stands of orange-red flower spikes from late summer into fall. Tara was selected for its exceptional winter hardiness among Hedychium coccineum forms, making it a good choice for gardeners near the zone 8a/8b line. Mulch heavily after the first freeze knocks back the foliage, and divide dense clumps every few years to renew bloom and share plants.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Tara prairie dropseed is slow to establish in its first year or two before its extensive root system takes hold, so keep young plantings weeded and watered.
directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Tara prairie dropseed is slow to establish in its first year or two before its extensive root system takes hold, so keep young plantings weeded and watered. Bred at Iowa State University for a more uniform, compact habit than the wild species, this selection forms a neat, fine-textured fountain of glossy, hair-thin green leaves that turns bright orange to copper in fall, with airy seed panicles in late summer that release a distinctive fragrance often compared to popcorn or coriander. It holds its shape through winter and needs no staking or division, making it one of the lowest-maintenance native grasses for a formal border edge, mass planting, or prairie-style garden. Cut the whole clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes each spring.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil where clumps can be left undisturbed to naturalize.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in fall in a sunny site with sharp drainage, since unlike hybrid tulips this species performs best when left in the ground for years rather than lifted annually. Each bulb sends up several low, sprawling stems that each open into a cheerful star-shaped flower with bright yellow centers and white-tipped petals, several blooms opening together from a single clump. Its compact, spreading habit suits rock gardens, gravel beds, and the front of a sunny border far better than a formal tulip bed. Given good drainage, it reliably returns and slowly multiplies, unlike many modern tulip hybrids that decline after the first season.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Tardiva blooms several weeks later than most panicle hydrangeas, extending color into early fall, and benefits from afternoon shade in the hottest Gulf South gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants generously to accommodate its large mature size. Tardiva is a classic, tall-growing panicle hydrangea cultivar, dating to the early 20th century, valued for flowering three to four weeks later than most Hydrangea paniculata selections, opening airy, loosely branched white flower panicles composed mostly of small fertile florets with scattered showy sterile florets in late summer that age to a soft pinkish-bronze through fall. Its later bloom time and more open, elegant panicle shape distinguish it from denser modern cultivars like Limelight, making it valued by gardeners who want hydrangea color extending into September and October. Like all panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood regardless of pruning timing, so it can be cut back hard in late winter to control size and encourage strong new flowering stems; the large habit also makes it useful as a big-shrub anchor at the back of a mixed border or as a small specimen tree when limbed up.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; tarflower is adapted to the fire-prone pine flatwoods and scrub of the Gulf South and tolerates poor, dry, sandy soil once established.
directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; tarflower is a native evergreen shrub of Gulf South pine flatwoods and sandy scrub, blooming in late summer with clusters of fragrant, white-to-pink, sticky flowers whose petals are edged with tiny glandular hairs that exude a resinous, tar-like substance — hence the common name, and a genuine curiosity, since bees visiting the flowers often end up with a bit of sticky residue on their bodies. It is a fire-adapted plant of longleaf pine ecosystems, resprouting vigorously after burns in the wild, and is highly drought tolerant in the deep, fast-draining sand it evolved in. Grown occasionally by native-plant nurseries for wildlife gardens and low-water landscaping within its native range, it asks for little beyond sharp drainage and lean, acidic soil; rich garden soil or poor drainage are more likely to cause problems than neglect. Its long late-summer bloom period is valuable for native pollinators when many other shrubs have finished flowering.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich to average soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Tasman flax lily establishes quickly and spreads steadily by underground runners — plant 18–24 inches apart and divide every 3–4 years when the center of large clumps begins to die out.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich to average soil in partial shade to full sun; Tasman flax lily is an Australian evergreen perennial groundcover that combines ornamental foliage, flowers, and berries across a long season — it grows in spreading, grass-like clumps of narrow, strap-shaped, dark-green, stiff, arching leaves and in late spring produces loose, delicate, branching panicles of small, sky-blue to soft-lilac, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers on tall, wiry stems. The flowers are followed by the plant's most ornamental feature: clusters of intensely vivid, shining, deep-blue to purple-blue berries that persist on the plant for weeks and are striking against the dark foliage. The berries are the primary ornamental feature that distinguishes Dianella from similar grass-like perennials. The plant is notably shade-tolerant and drought-tolerant once established and spreads steadily by underground stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover. An excellent, easy-care, low-maintenance shade groundcover for zone 8–11 with four-season interest.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Tasmanian tree fern is more cold-hardy than most tree ferns and can survive brief light frosts once established, but the growing crown should be mulched heavily ahead of any hard freeze.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Tasmanian tree fern is more cold-hardy than most tree ferns and can survive brief light frosts once established, but the growing crown should be mulched heavily ahead of any hard freeze. Dicksonia antarctica is a slow-growing but exceptionally cold-tolerant Australian tree fern with a thick, shaggy, fibrous trunk and a broad crown of dark green, leathery, arching fronds, forming a striking specimen for a sheltered shaded courtyard or woodland garden. It grows more slowly than Cyathea species, typically only an inch or two of trunk per year, but tolerates cooler, more temperate conditions and light frost better than most of its tropical relatives, making it the tree fern of choice for gardeners at the cooler edge of tree-fern-growing range. Keep the growing crown watered from above regularly, especially in dry weather, since the trunk has no true root system and absorbs much of its moisture through the fibrous trunk itself.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in shade or bright indirect light; avoid waterlogged soils — good drainage paired with consistent moisture suits it best.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in shade or bright indirect light; tassel fern earns its name from the distinctive golden-bronze, tassel-like croziers that unfurl in early spring before expanding into glossy, lustrous, deep evergreen fronds — one of the most refined and elegant shade ferns for temperate gardens, with outstanding year-round presence. Avoid waterlogged soils; good drainage paired with consistent moisture is ideal. Slugs can damage emerging croziers severely in spring — early protection is worthwhile.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; thrives in heat.
directions: Direct sow tassel flower after the last frost in warm, well-drained soil. The small brush-like scarlet and orange flowers rise on wiry stems above tidy rosettes, adding fine texture to arrangements. It thrives in heat and full sun and blooms freely all summer with little care. Deadhead to prolong flowering and allow occasional self-sowing for future plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; brickellia is highly drought-tolerant once established and thrives in lean soils where most plants struggle.
directions: Direct sow in spring in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; brickellia is highly drought-tolerant once established and thrives in lean soils where most plants struggle. Brickellia grandiflora is a perennial subshrub native to open rocky slopes, canyon walls, and dry meadows throughout the western United States, producing aromatic, triangular, coarsely toothed leaves with pale undersides and numerous nodding, tassel-like heads of creamy-white flowers from July through October that are exceptional late-season nectar sources for migrating monarch butterflies and specialized native bees in the aster family. The plant is one of the most important native late-season nectar plants in western gardens and serves as an important floral resource when most other composites have finished blooming.

plant_note: Plant small cuttings or divisions at any point in the growing season into very well-drained, dry, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; six-sided stonecrop is often confused with biting stonecrop but lacks its sharp, burning taste.
directions: Plant cuttings or divisions in very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; tasteless stonecrop forms a dense, low mat of tiny, cylindrical, bright green leaves arranged in neat, tightly spiraled rows around each stem, giving the foliage a distinctly geometric, six-sided appearance up close. Clusters of small, star-shaped yellow flowers cover the mat in early summer, similar to the closely related biting stonecrop but without the sharp, burning taste that gives that species its common name and mild toxicity warning. It spreads readily by rooting stem fragments to form a tough, walkable groundcover useful for green roofs, gravel gardens, and rock wall crevices where little else survives. Established mats need essentially no care beyond an occasional shearing if growth becomes woody or thin in the center, and they tolerate drought, poor soil, and heat with ease.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring into average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Tatarian aster is an unusually tall, sturdy East Asian aster that rarely needs staking despite its height.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Tatarian aster is a robust, back-of-border East Asian perennial that towers over most other garden asters, sending up sturdy, largely self-supporting stems topped with broad, flat-topped clusters of lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers in mid to late fall, among the latest of any hardy aster to bloom. Large, coarse basal leaves form a substantial rosette before the flowering stems rise, giving the plant a strong presence even before bloom. Its late timing makes it valuable for extending pollinator forage right up to the first hard frosts, when few other nectar sources remain. Despite its height, it is notably wind- and rain-resistant compared to many tall perennials, though staking or growing among other sturdy neighbors is still helpful in very exposed sites; divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

subcategory: deciduous shrub grown for winter stem color
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in spring or fall.
directions: Site in evenly moist to boggy soil in partial shade, where this cold-hardy Asian dogwood tolerates far less light than most flowering shrubs and often colors its bark most vividly with some shade protection from harsh winter sun-scald. Small, flat clusters of creamy white flowers open in late spring followed by white to pale blue berries, but the main ornamental feature is the coral-red to blackish-purple young stems that light up the winter garden once leaves drop. Many variegated cultivars are grown for shaded borders and pond edges, pairing white- or gold-edged summer foliage with dramatic bare-stem winter color. Cut one-third of the oldest stems to the ground each early spring to keep a steady supply of brightly colored young wood.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; tatting fern is less vigorous than plain lady fern and is best sited where its unusual fronds can be viewed up close rather than massed at a distance.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; tatting fern is less vigorous than plain lady fern and is best sited where its unusual fronds can be viewed up close rather than massed at a distance. This curious heirloom Victorian-era cultivar of lady fern produces narrow fronds reduced to small, round, bead-like pinnae strung along the frond like lace tatting, an oddity that has been passed down by division among fern collectors since the nineteenth century rather than reproduced reliably from spores. Its small, dainty scale and unique texture make it a conversation-piece specimen for a shaded rock garden, trough, or the front of a fern collection, though it lacks the vigor and fullness of standard lady fern cultivars. Divide clumps carefully in spring to propagate, since the cultivar does not come true from spores and must be maintained vegetatively.

plant_note: Direct sow into saturated, acidic, peaty or muck soil in fall, allowing winter moisture and cold to break seed dormancy naturally.
directions: Direct sow into saturated, acidic, peaty or muck soil in fall, allowing winter moisture and cold to break seed dormancy naturally. Unlike the earlier-blooming, hummock-forming tussock cottongrass, this species spreads by rhizomes to form loose colonies and produces its tawny-brown cottony seed heads in late summer into fall, extending the bloom season in a bog or wet-meadow planting. The fluffy seed heads provide nesting fiber for birds and songbirds forage the seeds, while the dense root mass helps filter and stabilize saturated soils along pond and bog margins throughout the Appalachian and Great Lakes wetland range. Pair it with sundews, pitcher plants, or sedges for an authentic acidic bog planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Tawnyberry Holly is dioecious — both male and female plants are needed for berry production. It is best suited to frost-free Zone 10–11 landscapes in south Florida.
directions: Tawnyberry Holly is a native evergreen holly tree of the Florida Keys, Miami-Dade rockland hammocks, and Caribbean islands, producing small clusters of tawny-orange to reddish-black berries that are eagerly consumed by white-crowned pigeons, mockingbirds, and other fruit-eating birds in the subtropical forests of southernmost Florida. Growing as a slender understory tree to small specimen tree in the hammock community, Tawnyberry Holly has glossy, dark green evergreen leaves and small, inconspicuous white flowers in spring. An important component of the rare Florida Keys and Miami-Dade pine rockland hammock community — one of the most imperiled plant communities in the United States — this species deserves wider cultivation as an ornamental holly in frost-free south Florida landscapes. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in Zone 10–11; both male and female plants are needed for berry production.

common_name: Taylor Juniper (Narrow Columnar Eastern Red Cedar)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Taylor is an extremely narrow, columnar selection of native eastern red cedar discovered in Missouri, useful as a slim vertical accent or narrow screen where a standard red cedar's broader form would not fit.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 4-6 feet apart for a narrow screen or hedge. Taylor is a naturally occurring selection of the native eastern red cedar discovered growing in a Missouri cemetery, prized for an exceptionally narrow, columnar form — often only 3-4 feet wide at maturity despite reaching 15-25 feet tall — that gives it the vertical, formal look of an Italian cypress while retaining the cold hardiness, heat tolerance, and adaptability of native red cedar. The dense, blue-green, scale-like evergreen foliage provides year-round structure, privacy screening, and wildlife cover in a fraction of the horizontal space a standard-form red cedar or arborvitae would require, making it a popular choice for narrow side yards and tight property-line screens. Like other eastern red cedars, it tolerates poor, dry, rocky, or alkaline soils, drought, and heat once established, and needs essentially no supplemental irrigation after the first year or two. Little to no pruning is required to maintain its naturally narrow form; avoid planting in poorly drained sites, since red cedar is prone to root problems in consistently wet soil.

plant_note: Plant in fall; includes paperwhites for forcing.
directions: Plant tazetta daffodil bulbs in fall six inches deep in well-drained soil, or force paperwhite types indoors in pebbles and water. These clustered, intensely fragrant narcissi are well suited to mild-winter gardens and bloom early. Give them full sun and let the foliage die back naturally outdoors. Forced bulbs are generally discarded after flowering, while garden bulbs naturalize in suitable zones.

common_name: Tea Cup Elephant Ear (Compact Cupped-Leaf Colocasia)
plant_note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Tea Cup is a smaller-statured sport of Coffee Cups with shiny green cupped leaves forming a distinct bowl shape, well suited to containers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9. Tea Cup, a smaller-statured sport of the popular Coffee Cups elephant ear, bears glossy green leaves with strongly upturned margins forming a pronounced cup shape that collects rainwater, on a plant scaled down enough to suit large containers where full-sized Coffee Cups would be too big. The cupped leaves shimmer and hold water in dappled light, creating a living water feature and wildlife attraction on a more manageable scale. The plant spreads readily by stolons; divide every two to three years to control spread, and provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Tea Oil Camellia is notably more cold-hardy than most ornamental camellias and its late-fall bloom often escapes damage from early frosts.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Grown for centuries in China for the edible oil pressed from its seeds, Tea Oil Camellia produces fragrant white flowers in late fall into winter and is notably more cold-hardy than the familiar ornamental camellias, tolerating temperatures well below what damages Camellia japonica or sasanqua. The glossy evergreen foliage and modest size make it a useful dual-purpose shrub for a partly shaded border, valued both as an ornamental flowering evergreen and, where enough plants are grown, for pressing the oil-rich seeds. It tolerates a range of light conditions from woodland shade to fairly sunny sites and needs the same acidic soil and good drainage as other camellias.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in early spring in well-drained, mildly acidic soil sited in partial shade to protect the airy, upright form from wind damage; a second unrelated seedling nearby improves the fall berry display.
directions: Plant in well-drained, mildly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, giving the shrub room to develop its open, arching, vase-shaped habit rather than crowding it against other plantings. Tea viburnum is grown chiefly for its heavy fall display of long-lasting, translucent orange-red berries that dangle from the branches on drooping stalks well into winter, set off by narrow, willowy leaves that turn bronze-red before dropping. The common name comes from the historical use of dried young leaves as a tea substitute in parts of China, though it is grown ornamentally today. Because it flowers on old wood, prune only right after the spring bloom to avoid removing the berries that follow; light shade during the hottest afternoon hours helps keep foliage from scorching in warmer parts of its range.

common_name: Teasing Georgia Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since Teasing Georgia is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber against a wall, fence, or pillar.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1998, Teasing Georgia bears deep yellow buds opening to cupped, rich yellow blooms that soften with age, carrying a strong tea fragrance, on long, arching canes that reach 8 feet or more when trained as a climber, or can be kept pruned as a large freestanding shrub. Its vigor and rich, saturated yellow color have made it one of David Austin's most popular climbing selections, and it repeat-blooms well from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Techno Heat White Lobelia (Heat-Tolerant Trailing Lobelia)
plant_note: Start the very fine seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, pressing it onto the surface since it needs light to germinate. Techno Heat is bred to keep flowering through summer heat rather than shutting down the way standard trailing lobelia typically does once temperatures climb.
directions: Start the very fine seed indoors, pressing it onto the surface of moist mix without covering since it needs light to germinate; transplant after frost danger has passed into moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Techno Heat White is a trailing lobelia bred specifically to resist the summer heat dieback that causes most Lobelia erinus varieties to stop blooming and go into decline once temperatures climb into the 80s and 90s, extending its display of small, pure-white flowers over cascading, fine-textured foliage well into the hot part of the growing season. It works well in hanging baskets, window boxes, and container edges. Keep soil consistently moist, since lobelia has a shallow root system that dries out quickly in containers, and provide afternoon shade in the hottest climates to further extend bloom. A light midseason shearing encourages a fresh flush of flowers if the plant thins out.

common_name: Techny Arborvitae (Broad Pyramidal Winter-Hardy Green Arborvitae)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, spacing for a hedge if a screen is wanted; Techny holds its deep green color through winter better than many arborvitae cultivars, which tend to bronze in cold weather.
directions: Techny is a broad, dense, pyramidal arborvitae grown for its reliable deep green color that holds through winter cold far better than many other Thuja occidentalis selections, which often bronze or yellow in freezing weather. Its wider, fuller pyramidal shape makes it a substantial specimen or privacy screen, slower-growing and more compact than towering cultivars like Green Giant, and it needs only light shearing, if any, to maintain a tidy form. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; arborvitae generally performs best in cooler climates and struggles with the intense heat and humidity of the Deep South, so it is best suited to the northern edge of its range.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall (September–November in zone 9) for winter and spring bloom; ranunculus corms must be pre-soaked 3–4 hours in cool water before planting to rehydrate the dry corms. Plant with the claw-like corm facing downward, 2 inches deep. The Tecolote series is one of the premier commercial ranunculus series in the world — bred by C. Aris in the Carpinteria, California area, which is one of the world's major ranunculus production centers. In zone 9 ranunculus blooms February–April, producing one of the most spectacular, high-value floral displays of any cool-season bulb. The corms cannot tolerate summer heat — dig and store in a cool, dry location after foliage yellows, or treat as annuals (replace each fall). In zone 9 with good drainage and appropriate timing, ranunculus is one of the most rewarding and spectacular cut flowers that can be grown at home.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist soil — ranunculus requires excellent drainage, especially in winter; wet soil causes corm rot; Tecolote Red Ranunculus is a named color selection in the Tecolote Series — one of the finest commercial ranunculus strains available, producing the large, fully double, multi-petaled flowers that represent the highest development of the flower form in Ranunculus asiaticus. The flowers are composed of densely packed, tissue-thin petals in concentric rings that create a structure resembling a perfectly formed, layered rose or peony at 3–4 inches in diameter — the Tecolote Red selection providing vivid scarlet-red flowers with the extraordinary petal density and precision of form that makes Tecolote ranunculus the premium choice for high-end cut flower production and upscale spring garden display. Persian Buttercup (Ranunculus asiaticus) produces some of the most spectacularly beautiful cut flowers available from any garden plant — the large, fully double, multi-layered flowers in vivid, clear colors lasting 1–2 weeks in a vase and providing a level of floral sophistication normally associated with peonies, garden roses, or lisianthus. In zone 9, planted in fall for February–April bloom, ranunculus provides a spectacular spring floral display during the critical late-winter window when few other garden plants produce flowers of comparable quality.

plant_note: Plant well-callused stem segments (joints) in spring into very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; handle only with long tongs or a folded towel, as the barbed, easily detaching spines readily embed in skin and clothing.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun, well away from foot traffic and pets; teddy bear cholla is a Sonoran and Mojave Desert native (Arizona, southeastern California, northwestern Mexico) forming a densely spined, silvery, teddy-bear-soft-looking trunk and branches that are anything but soft to the touch. Individual stem segments detach at the slightest touch and cling by barbed spines to passing animals or clothing, a dispersal strategy that gives the plant its 'jumping cholla' nickname, so it is best sited as a specimen or barrier planting away from paths. Established plants are extremely drought tolerant, thriving on rainfall alone in low-desert gardens, and bear small, pale greenish-yellow flowers in spring followed by spineless, tuberculate fruits. It is markedly more cold-sensitive than prickly pear and performs best in the warmest zones of the Southwest and coastal Gulf xeriscape, generally suffering damage below about 15-20 degrees Fahrenheit.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil and full sun.
directions: Teddy Bear produces fluffy, bright-yellow puffball blooms 3 to 5 inches across on a compact, multi-branching plant 24 to 36 inches tall. Direct sow the seed about an inch deep after the last frost in warm soil and full sun. Thin seedlings to give each plant room to branch and form its many pompom flowers. It works beautifully as a short hedge and makes a fabulous, long-lasting cut flower. Water steadily while young and enjoy the double blooms all summer.

common_name: Teddy Bear Magnolia (Compact Fuzzy-Backed Southern Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Teddy Bear is a compact, dense southern magnolia selection well suited to smaller residential lots where a full-sized Magnolia grandiflora would eventually overwhelm the space.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Teddy Bear is a compact, densely pyramidal southern magnolia selection notable for its thick, glossy dark green leaves with dense, fuzzy cinnamon-brown undersides, a texture that gives the plant its name and provides striking contrast when wind or hand movement flips the leaves to show their reverse side. Its narrower, more upright form and smaller mature size than the massive straight species make it a practical evergreen specimen or screen for typical residential lots, while it still produces the large, fragrant, creamy white summer flowers magnolias are prized for. It requires little pruning to maintain its naturally tidy pyramidal shape and tolerates the same range of soil conditions as other southern magnolia selections.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in shallow standing water or saturated, acidic, sandy to peaty soil in full sun; ten-angle pipewort grows naturally in the shallow, nutrient-poor pools and ditches of Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine savannas alongside pitcher plants and grass pink orchids.
directions: Plant divisions in shallow standing water or saturated, acidic, sandy to peaty soil in full sun; ten-angle pipewort produces a low tuft of grass-like leaves and, in summer, tall, wiry, ribbed flower stalks tipped with small, tight, button-like white flower heads that stand well above the foliage like a field of pins stuck upright in the bog, giving rise to the common name hatpins. It grows naturally in the shallow, nutrient-poor pools, ditches, and savanna wetlands of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, often standing in an inch or two of water alongside pitcher plants, grass pink orchids, and sundews, and makes an unusual vertical accent in a home bog garden pool. Keep the crown in consistently saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic, low-fertility soil and full sun, and avoid any fertilizer, which quickly favors weeds over this slow, specialized wetland native.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in rocky, very well-drained, lean, calcareous or sandy soil in full sun; not suited to heavy clay or moist soils.
directions: Ten-petal Blazingstar is a spectacular Great Plains and Rocky Mountain foothills native, bearing the largest flowers of any Mentzelia native to the United States — creamy-white, 10-petaled blooms up to 4 inches across that open at dusk and fill the evening air with a strong, sweet fragrance, drawing hawk moths and other night pollinators from considerable distances. It grows on dry, rocky, calcareous or sandy bluffs and open slopes from Nebraska to Texas and New Mexico, forming an upright, branching perennial clump clothed in rough, barbed leaves that cling to passersby. The combination of enormous blooms and intensely sweet evening scent makes it an extraordinary centerpiece for night and moonlight garden designs. Direct sow in fall in lean, rocky, fast-draining, calcareous or sandy soil in full sun; established plants are extremely drought-hardy and resent supplemental irrigation or organically rich soils.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich soil over limestone or other calcareous rock, tucked into shaded ledges.
directions: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich soil over limestone or other calcareous rock, tucked into shaded ledges or the base of rock walls where this eastern and midwestern native naturally colonizes crevices and talus. The lacy, twice-pinnate deciduous fronds arise from a fertile, stabilized hybrid lineage between fragile fern and bulblet bladder fern, and it often self-sows modestly along suitable rock outcrops. It pairs well with walking fern and other calciphile species in a shaded limestone rock garden.

plant_note: Direct sow cold-stratified seed in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, thin, rocky, cedar glade soil in full sun; Tennessee coneflower is adapted to the extreme conditions of limestone cedar glades and requires excellent drainage — it will rot in clay or wet soils.
directions: Sow cold-stratified seed in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, thin rocky soil in full sun — Tennessee coneflower is a Federally Threatened native species known from only a handful of cedar glade sites in Davidson and Rutherford counties of central Tennessee, where it grows in the extremely shallow, rocky, alkaline soil over limestone bedrock that characterizes these rare ecosystems. It is distinguished from other coneflowers by its upward-reflexed (rather than drooping) ray petals, giving the flower a more open, daisy-like appearance. The species was removed from the federal endangered species list in 2011 after recovery efforts increased its wild populations — a conservation success story. It performs well in gardens as a drought-tolerant, heat-hardy perennial for well-drained, sunny, alkaline to neutral soils in zones 4–9. Growing this species in cultivation helps maintain genetic diversity and reduces collection pressure on wild populations. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky soil in full sun; Tennessee coneflower is federally threatened in the wild but adapts well to cultivation in zones 5–8.
directions: Sow direct in fall for cold stratification and spring germination in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or gritty soil in full sun; Tennessee coneflower is adapted to thin, calcareous, rocky cedar glades in Middle Tennessee and requires excellent drainage and lean soil — avoid rich, heavy soils. Echinacea tennessensis is a federally threatened coneflower endemic to a tiny area of cedar glades in Middle Tennessee; it is distinguished from other echinaceas by its reflexed ray petals that curve strongly downward along the central cone and its preference for alkaline, rocky soils. Despite its limited natural range, it is adaptable in cultivation throughout zones 5–8 in well-drained, lean soils; it is a beautiful, narrow-endemic wildflower of conservation significance and an important ornamental for butterfly gardens. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants.

plant_note: Plant dormant tuberous roots two to three inches deep in fall so they can root through the cool season; seed germinates erratically and needs 60-90 days cold-moist stratification.
directions: Plant dormant tuberous roots two to three inches deep in fall so they can root through the cool season and emerge as one of the very first Texas wildflowers to bloom, often as early as late January in South Texas. The greenish-white to purplish-blue flowers open on wiry stems above finely divided foliage, then the whole plant vanishes underground by early summer to escape the heat, so it pairs well with later-emerging perennials in a mixed bed. It prefers well-drained sandy or calcareous clay soils typical of Texas prairies and needs minimal supplemental water even in a dry Gulf Coast winter. Its early pollen is an important resource for the season's first native bees.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; like all yarrows, Terra Cotta requires excellent drainage and lean soil — organic-rich, moist soil promotes soft growth, disease, and short plant life.
