directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Terra Cotta is an outstanding Achillea millefolium cultivar from the Galaxy series — a hybrid selection producing flat-topped flower clusters in a distinctive, warm terra-cotta to salmon-orange color that is unique among common yarrow cultivars. Most commonly grown yarrows come in yellow or white; Terra Cotta's warm orange-salmon tones extend the yarrow color palette into the sunset range, making it excellent for warm-toned color schemes with bronze ornamental grasses, yellow-gold companions, and dark-leafed perennials. The flower color changes as it ages — opening with deep terra-cotta orange and fading to soft salmon-buff as the flowers mature, creating an interesting multi-tonal effect on a single flower head. The finely cut, feathery, aromatic, medium-green foliage is attractive when not in flower. Terra Cotta blooms from early summer through fall with deadheading, and the dried flower heads hold their warm tones well for dry arrangements. Like Moonshine, it is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant but requires excellent drainage to persist in the humid Gulf South — it is often treated as an annual in heavy clay or wet zone 9 conditions. Divide every 2–3 years to maintain vigor and prevent the center from dying out.

plant_note: Plant tubers outdoors after the last frost when the soil is warm.
directions: Terracotta produces romantic terracotta-bronze blooms with wavy petals on long stems, making it an outstanding cut flower and a strong tuber producer. Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil once frost has passed, laying them horizontally with the eye up. Provide full sun and stake tall plants to keep the long cutting stems upright. Cut flowers frequently and deadhead to encourage continuous bloom into fall. Dig and store the tubers before hard frost in cold climates.

common_name: Tess of the d'Urbervilles Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Tess of the d'Urbervilles blooms in generous flushes and benefits from regular deadheading to sustain repeat flowering through the season.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1998 and named for the Thomas Hardy novel, Tess of the d'Urbervilles bears dark crimson-red, rosette-shaped blooms with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous, well-branched shrub with glossy foliage. Its rich, velvety red color and classic old-rose form and scent have made it a favorite among David Austin's darker-flowered introductions, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; Tete-a-Tete is a popular miniature daffodil often forced for winter and early spring container color, and in zone 9 it may be best treated as an annual display bulb rather than a reliable long-term perennial.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. Tete-a-Tete is one of the most widely grown miniature daffodils, valued for its small stature, early bloom, and habit of producing two or more small, bright golden-yellow flowers per stem, giving a cheerful, multiplied display from each bulb. Its compact size makes it especially popular for containers, rock gardens, and small-space plantings, and it is often sold as a potted, forced bulb for indoor winter color as well as an outdoor garden plant. Like other daffodils it is completely resistant to deer and rodents, and foliage should be allowed to yellow and die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors; seed needs light to germinate. Transplant when hardened off.
directions: Start seed indoors on the soil surface under light, since it needs light to germinate. This mix produces tall, upright spikes of ruffled, nectar-rich blooms in vivid colors. Snapdragons prefer cool weather, so transplant in early spring for strong stems and abundant flowers. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and cut spikes regularly for long-lasting bouquets and repeat bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Texanum ligustrum tolerates heat, humidity, and heavy pruning well, a mainstay hedge shrub across the Gulf South.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Texanum ligustrum tolerates heat, humidity, and heavy pruning well, a mainstay hedge shrub across the Gulf South. Broad, glossy, dark green, wax-textured leaves cover a dense, fast-growing shrub topped in early summer by conspicuous clusters of small white flowers with a strong, sweet scent some find pleasant and others find overpowering, followed by small dark berries that birds readily consume and disperse. A more compact, rounder-leaved selection than the straight species, it has long been one of the most widely planted hedge and screening shrubs across the warm, humid South, tolerating heavy shearing, heat, and drought once established, though it can self-sow aggressively and is considered invasive in some regions. Shear regularly to control size and maintain a formal hedge, and monitor for self-sown seedlings in naturalistic areas, since birds spread the berries widely.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained sandy soil in partial shade beneath high pine or hardwood canopy, mimicking the streamside pine-forest understory where this azalea naturally grows.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained sandy soil in partial shade, keeping roots consistently moist but never waterlogged. Texas azalea is a deciduous native shrub of the West Gulf Coastal Plain, found wild in sandy pine woods and along shaded stream banks of East Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma, where it forms a mounding, spreading thicket of slender branches. In mid-to-late spring, after or alongside the emerging leaves, clusters of narrow, glandular, white to pale pink tubular flowers open with a distinctive lemony-spice fragrance that carries well beyond the plant. Because it flowers later than many spring azaleas, it extends the native azalea bloom season in a partly shaded woodland border, and it is a useful nectar source for late-season pollinators including sphinx moths.

common_name: Texas Baby Blue Eyes (Large-Flowered Baby Blue Eyes)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September-November) into humus-rich, well-drained soil; the plant overwinters as a low rosette and will not bloom well if sown in spring, much like Texas bluebonnets.
directions: Direct sow seed in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun, covering seed lightly since exposure to light aids germination; like Texas bluebonnets, this native annual establishes as a low rosette over winter and needs the cold season to flower well the following spring. Give it filtered light beneath oaks or along woodland edges and keep soil evenly moist through germination and bloom, then allow it to dry out with summer heat. In March and April the sprawling plants are covered in inch-wide sky-blue flowers with white throats, considerably larger and showier than the related California Baby Blue Eyes, making a soft companion groundcover to bluebonnets and other spring ephemerals. Once established, self-sown seedlings return reliably in the same beds each fall.

common_name: Texas Barrel Cactus (Turk's Head Cactus, Glory of Texas)
plant_note: Start seed indoors in warm, sterile mineral cactus mix, or transplant nursery stock in spring into sharply drained, gravelly or caliche soil in full sun.
directions: Start seed indoors in warm, sterile mineral cactus mix, or transplant nursery stock in spring into sharply drained, gravelly or caliche soil in full sun; native to the Rio Grande Plains of South Texas and adjacent Mexico, this ribbed, cylindrical barrel cactus is armed with stout, strongly hooked central spines for which it is named. Bright yellow flowers with a reddish throat open at the crown in summer, followed by fleshy yellow fruit, and older solitary stems can eventually reach two feet or more in height over many years. It is somewhat less cold hardy than the more northern Ferocactus wislizeni, so in the coolest parts of its recommended zones a covered or south-facing site helps protect it from prolonged hard freezes. Water only sparingly during the growing season and keep it essentially dry over winter, as this species is highly susceptible to rot in wet or poorly draining soil.

plant_note: Direct sow seed or plant divisions in fall in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas betony is native to dry limestone slopes and rocky arroyos and requires excellent drainage — it declines quickly in heavy, wet clay soils. The plant self-sows to naturalize in appropriate, well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas betony is a native wildflower of the limestone hills of Texas and the arid Southwest, producing tubular, brilliant scarlet flowers in whorls along the square stems of a spreading mint-family plant from late winter through frost — one of the longest-blooming native perennials in the Southern garden. The vivid red flowers are irresistible to hummingbirds and provide one of the best native hummingbird plants for xeric, alkaline-soil gardens. It is extremely drought and heat tolerant, thriving in the conditions that defeat most flowering perennials in the hot, dry Southwest. The felted, gray-green leaves provide attractive texture even between bloom cycles. Self-sows freely in appropriate, well-drained conditions to naturalize. Outstanding in native plant gardens, xeric landscapes, and rock gardens in zone 7–11.

plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper or nick with a knife before sowing — this is essential as the hard seed coat dramatically reduces germination without scarification. Direct sow in fall (September–November in zones 7–10) into well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil; Texas Bluebonnets must overwinter as rosettes to bloom the following spring and will not flower if spring-sown. Do not sow in spring.
directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing with coarse sandpaper or nicking the hard coat with a knife, then direct sow in fall (September through November) into thin, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun — Texas Bluebonnets must overwinter as basal rosettes to set flower buds and will not bloom if sown in spring. The Texas state flower produces stunning sky-blue and white upright flower spikes in March–April, spreading along roadsides and meadows in one of the most iconic wildflower displays in North America. Like all lupines, plants fix nitrogen through root nodules and resent transplanting due to a deep taproot; sow seeds in their permanent location and thin to 6–12 inches after seedlings are established. Plants self-seed reliably where conditions suit them, building in density each year.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seeds for 4–6 weeks before sowing indoors; plant out after last frost in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil. The plant dies to the ground in winter and re-emerges from the root in spring. Can also be started from softwood cuttings taken in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas clematis is the only North American clematis species with urn-shaped, non-opening flowers in shades of scarlet to coral-pink — a dramatic departure from the typical flat, open clematis bloom. In its native Texas limestone hill country habitat, it scrambles through shrubs and along rocky slopes. The plant is one of the most drought-tolerant clematis species once established and thrives in the alkaline soils and intense heat of zone 8–9 where many clematis struggle. Its native-species hybrid offspring, including the popular 'Princess Diana' (coral-pink) and 'Duchess of Albany' (pink), are more widely available than the straight species but share its ornamental urn shape. Prune back hard in late winter as the vine blooms on new growth.

common_name: Texas Columbine (Native Longspurred Yellow Wildflower Columbine)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Aquilegia longissima requires cold stratification for reliable germination — fall sowing outdoors provides natural stratification; seeds benefit from surface sowing as light aids germination.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade with afternoon protection from the hottest sun; Texas Columbine (Aquilegia longissima) is a native wildflower of the Edwards Plateau and the Chihuahuan Desert transitional zone, producing pale golden-yellow to cream-yellow flowers with extraordinarily long, elegant spurs reaching 4–6 inches — the longest flower spurs of any North American native columbine, creating a distinctly different and more delicate floral form than the compact-spurred garden columbine hybrids. The very long, thread-like spurs are specifically adapted to pollination by hawk moths (Sphingidae) whose long proboscises can reach the nectar at the spur tip — a co-evolutionary relationship that has driven the extreme spur length unique to this species. Aquilegia longissima is more heat-tolerant than most columbine species, performing reliably in zone 9 where other columbines are short-lived or summer dormant — making it one of the few columbines that works in Gulf South gardens as a reliable perennial rather than a brief cool-season performer. The airy, finely textured blue-green foliage is attractive from fall through spring, and the elegant flowers in April–June attract hummingbirds and hawk moths. Outstanding naturalized under deciduous trees and along shaded woodland garden edges where it self-sows modestly to maintain its population.

plant_note: Set out transplants in spring after soil has warmed, or direct sow in fall into prepared beds; this coastal-prairie native tolerates seasonally wet clay and needs no coddling once established.
directions: Plant in full sun in beds with average to seasonally moist soil, spacing plants about a foot apart so the slender branching stems can fill in as a airy clump. Once roots are established this Texas and Louisiana coastal-prairie native shrugs off summer heat, humidity, and short dry spells with little care. Each stem carries small drooping yellow rays around a dark cone from summer into fall, drawing bees, skipper butterflies, and other pollinators. Its narrow habit and long bloom window make it a good filler among grasses in a Gulf Coast wildflower meadow or rain garden edge.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in spring or fall in rocky, well-drained soil; Texas copper lily naturalizes readily in limestone soils and gravelly banks throughout central and south Texas and the Gulf Coast. In zone 7–10 it is fully perennial with no winter protection needed. Clumps bloom most spectacularly in late summer–fall after periods of heat and dry stress followed by rain.
directions: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained to rocky soil in full sun; Texas copper lily is a small but charming native bulb found growing in thin limestone soils from Texas into Mexico, bearing funnel-shaped copper-orange flowers on slender stems in August–October. Like other habranthus, the blooms emerge reliably after summer rains following a dry period — the heat-rain cycle acts as a trigger for the spectacular flush of flowers. Each stem carries a single, upward-facing bloom unlike the outward-facing flowers of rain lilies (Zephyranthes), distinguishing the genus. The fine, grass-like foliage is unobtrusive during the growing season and the bulbs multiply steadily over years into impressive drifts. Excellent for naturalizing in dry, rocky, Texas-style landscapes — plant in masses for the most effect.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas dandelion is a common winter-annual roadside wildflower across the southern Great Plains and Gulf South, self-seeding readily once introduced.
directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas dandelion produces a low rosette of narrow, deeply lobed leaves and, despite the misleading common name, pale lavender-pink rather than yellow, dandelion-like flowers on slender stalks in spring, followed by fluffy seed heads relished by goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. It is a common, easygoing winter annual of roadsides, pastures, and open fields across the southern Great Plains and Gulf South, thriving in ordinary, unimproved soil with little care beyond a sunny to lightly shaded spot. Once introduced it self-seeds readily, naturalizing in a native wildflower meadow or informal lawn alternative, and its early, extended spring bloom period provides useful nectar for small native bees ahead of the main spring wildflower flush.

common_name: Texas Dawn Water Lily (Vigorous Louisiana-Bred Hardy Yellow Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun; Texas Dawn, bred by Louisiana hybridizer Kenneth Landon, is an exceptionally vigorous hardy yellow water lily well suited to the Gulf South.
directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun. Texas Dawn, bred by Louisiana water lily hybridizer Kenneth Landon, is a vigorous hardy water lily producing large, bright yellow, star-shaped flowers held above the water on strong stems, with a growth habit exceptionally well suited to the heat and long growing season of Gulf South ponds. Its regional breeding gives it particularly strong performance in warm Southern water gardens compared with some hardy water lily cultivars developed for cooler climates. Divide rhizomes every two to three years when they crowd their container, and feed during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets pushed into the soil for the best bloom.

plant_note: Transplant in spring into moist, calcareous, well-drained soil; site in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist through the first summer.
directions: Texas Dutchman's Pipe is a twining native perennial vine of moist, calcareous woodland edges and bottomland thickets in Texas and adjacent Oklahoma, recognized by its large, prominently net-veined, heart-shaped leaves and brownish-purple, pipe-shaped flowers that bloom from spring into early summer. It is a critical larval host plant for the Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor) in central and south Texas, and a single well-established plant can support multiple generations of caterpillars through a growing season. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline, limestone-based soil in partial shade to full sun; the plant spreads by underground rhizomes and will form a colonizing patch over time. It is an essential component of butterfly garden plantings for the Texas Hill Country, cross-timbers region, and adjacent areas with alkaline soils.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in alkaline, well-drained, clay or sandy loam soil in full sun; Texas ebony is slow-growing and long-lived — plant young trees for establishment, as older specimens transplant poorly due to deep taproots.
directions: Texas ebony is one of the finest ornamental trees native to south Texas and northeastern Mexico, producing a dense, rounded crown of small, dark green compound leaves on thorny branches — the tree's extremely hard, black-brown heartwood (comparable in density to commercial ebony) is prized for wood turning and tool handles, and the species' name reflects this extraordinary wood quality. Clusters of fragrant, creamy-white to pale yellow flowers appear in summer and fall and are heavily visited by native bees and honeybees, producing a distinctive honey; the large, woody seed pods split open in fall to reveal shiny black seeds that are edible when roasted and were an important food source for indigenous peoples of the Rio Grande Valley. In south Texas (zone 9–10) it is among the most recommended native trees for year-round evergreen screening, wildlife habitat, and creating dense shade in landscapes — slow-growing but extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived once established. It also provides one of the most important nesting trees for the endangered ferruginous pygmy owl in the lower Rio Grande Valley.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas false dragonhead spreads by rhizomes and self-seeds to form colonies in appropriate conditions — provide ample moisture for best performance.
directions: Texas false dragonhead is a rare native perennial of Texas endemic to rocky, moist, calcareous prairies and streamside meadows in the Edwards Plateau and surrounding regions — producing flower spikes similar to the more widely known obedient plant (Physostegia virginiana) but with deeper, brighter pink-purple flowers and a more compact, heat-adapted growth habit suited to south-central Texas conditions. Like other Physostegia species, the individual tubular flowers are hinged and will stay in position when pushed — the 'obedient' character that gives the related species its common name — making them a quirky, interactive feature of native garden tours. Pollinators, especially bumblebees and hummingbirds, visit the tubular, orchid-like flowers throughout summer; in gardens it provides a reliable mid-season pollinator spike when many spring bloomers have finished. It spreads by rhizomes similarly to its relatives and can form assertive colonies in moist, rich soil — site where spreading is welcome or divide regularly to control.

common_name: Texas Gold Columbine (Big Bend Golden Columbine)
plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall to allow natural cold-moist stratification and spring germination, or cold-stratify seed for 3-4 weeks at 40F and sow in early spring; Texas Gold is a Texas Superstar selection of a rare Big Bend native columbine with especially large golden flowers and strong heat tolerance.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Texas Gold is a Texas Superstar-designated selection of a rare native columbine found only in a few canyons of Big Bend National Park, producing exceptionally large, long-spurred, bright golden-yellow flowers on sturdy stems from spring into summer. Selected specifically for outstanding heat and drought tolerance compared to typical garden columbines, it holds up notably well through a Texas or Gulf South summer with far less decline than European columbine hybrids. The long nectar spurs make it an excellent hummingbird and sphinx moth plant. Like other columbines it is relatively short-lived as an individual plant but self-sows readily where happy, naturalizing into a persistent colony over a few seasons if seed heads are allowed to mature and drop.

plant_note: Direct sow in late spring in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; Texas Grama is a small, tough native bunchgrass of Texas and Oklahoma with distinctive one-sided spike clusters, a larval host for several skipper and satyr butterflies.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; Texas Grama tolerates poor, shallow, alkaline soils that defeat most turf grasses and ornamental perennials. This small, tough native bunchgrass of Texas and Oklahoma forms a low, fine-textured clump bearing distinctive comb-like, one-sided seed spikes on wiry stems in summer, adding subtle textural interest to a native prairie or xeriscape planting. It serves as a larval host plant for several native skipper and satyr butterfly species, adding wildlife value beyond its drought-tolerant, low-water landscaping role. It requires essentially no supplemental water or fertilizer once established and is well suited to rock gardens, dry meadow plantings, and low-water native landscaping. Cut back old growth in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Direct sow into lean, rocky or limestone-derived soil; this drought-tough Hill Country native resents rich, wet ground and needs excellent drainage to persist.
directions: A close cousin of soft greeneyes, Texas greeneyes carries cheerful yellow ray flowers around a papery green-and-maroon disk from early summer well into fall. It favors the drier, rockier limestone prairies and open woods of central and west Texas, where its deep taproot lets it shrug off drought once established. Give it a hot, sunny spot with sharp drainage and avoid overwatering, which shortens its lifespan. The long bloom season makes it a steady nectar source for native bees through the hottest months.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in disturbed areas, roadsides, or moist-to-moderate soil; Texas Groundsel is an annual or biennial native wildflower blooming from February through April in Texas and the Gulf South with masses of small, bright yellow daisy-like flowers — one of the earliest spring wildflowers in Central and South Texas and an important early-season nectar source for native bees.
directions: Scatter seeds in fall over prepared, moderately moist soil; Texas Groundsel self-sows prolifically once established and will naturalize in disturbed areas, roadsides, and meadows; best in moist to average soils (unlike most Texas native wildflowers which prefer dry conditions). Texas Groundsel (Packera ampullaceus, formerly classified as Senecio ampullaceus) is one of the earliest-blooming native spring wildflowers in Central and South Texas, producing masses of small, bright golden-yellow, daisy-like composite flowers on leafy stems from February through April before most other spring wildflowers have begun to bloom. The species belongs to the groundsel/ragwort group (genus Packera, family Asteraceae), and like its relatives it has slightly succulent, lobed basal leaves and erect branching stems bearing numerous flower heads; the bright yellow coloration and prolific production of small flowers make stands of Texas Groundsel visually striking in early spring when the landscape is still brown. As one of the earliest wildflowers to bloom, Texas Groundsel provides a critical early nectar and pollen source for native bees emerging in late winter and early spring before other flowers are available — particularly important for native queen bumblebees that must feed immediately after emerging from winter dormancy. The species grows in moist to moderately moist soils, particularly around stream edges, woodland openings, and disturbed roadsides where it can form large colonies. It is a short-lived annual or biennial that reproduces entirely from seed.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant transplants in spring in dry, well-drained, rocky or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Texas Indian mallow is a low, drought-tough native subshrub of Texas and the southern Great Plains, thriving in the same lean, sun-baked conditions favored by scarlet globemallow and other xeric wildflowers.
directions: Direct sow or plant transplants in dry, well-drained, rocky or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun. Texas Indian mallow is a low, softly gray-velvety native subshrub of Texas, Oklahoma, and adjacent states, producing small, apricot to soft yellow-orange, cup-shaped flowers over a long season from spring through fall on wiry, sprawling stems clothed in fuzzy, heart-shaped leaves. It grows naturally on caliche flats, limestone slopes, and dry prairie roadsides, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil that would stress most garden perennials once established, and needs no supplemental water beyond an establishment period. Its soft gray foliage and long bloom season make it a useful, low-maintenance filler for a sunny xeriscape or native wildflower border, and its flowers are visited by a range of small native bees. Cut back lightly in late winter to encourage fresh, compact new growth for the coming season.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas ironweed is more compact and better behaved in a garden border than the larger, coarser ironweed species.
directions: Start transplants or plant divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas ironweed is more compact and better behaved in a garden border than the larger, coarser ironweed species. Slender, upright stems carry narrow leaves and flat-topped clusters of small, intensely purple, fringed flowers from late summer into fall, drawing swallowtails, skippers, and other butterflies in large numbers during a season when many other nectar plants have finished blooming. Native to open prairies, woodland edges, and roadsides across Texas, Oklahoma, and Louisiana, its smaller stature compared to relatives like New York and giant ironweed makes it a better fit for mixed perennial borders and smaller pollinator gardens. It is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond cutting stems back in late winter.

plant_note: Plant container stock after last frost in well-drained, dry soil; Texas lantana is drought-tolerant once established and requires very little care. It may die back to the roots in zone 8 hard freezes but re-sprouts vigorously in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, even rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Texas lantana is a native alternative to the non-native common lantana sold at garden centers, with the same heat tolerance and butterfly-magnet qualities but a more compact, less rampant habit that doesn't pose the invasive risk of L. camara in tropical areas. The small, multi-colored flowers progress from yellow through orange to red as they age on the same cluster, creating a striking tricolor effect that attracts swallowtails, skippers, and monarchs all summer long. The plant is toxic to livestock and pets if ingested. In zone 8, it dies back to the root crown after hard freezes and regrows as a true perennial; in zones 9-11 it stays semi-evergreen. An excellent plant for hot, dry slopes, driveways, and sunny borders where heat and drought defeat most other plants.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to light shade; Texas larkspur is a cool-season annual or biennial that requires cold stratification — fall sowing in Gulf Coast gardens provides natural stratification and leads to bloom in April–May before summer heat arrives.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — Texas larkspur is the native delphinium of southern prairies, limestone cedar glades, and rocky roadsides from Texas to the Carolinas, producing tall, slender spikes of deeply blue, white, or blue-and-white bicolored flowers in April–May before summer heat arrives, with the delicate, finely cut, ferny foliage typical of the delphinium family. The flowers are intensely attractive to ruby-throated hummingbirds and long-tongued native bees. Unlike the Pacific Giant and other hybrid garden delphiniums that struggle in heat and humidity, Texas larkspur is fully adapted to the alkaline limestone soils, hot springs, and dry summers of the southern prairies. It self-sows readily to maintain naturalized colonies in open, well-drained, sunny conditions and is excellent for wildflower meadow plantings in the southern Gulf Coast and Texas Hill Country. All parts are toxic if consumed.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Texas Lilac is a Texas Superstar-promoted chaste tree selection heavily marketed for extreme heat and drought toughness across Texas and the Gulf South.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Texas Lilac is a widely promoted vitex selection valued for its dense, fragrant, lavender-blue flower spikes and reliably strong performance under the extreme heat, drought, and poor soil conditions typical of Texas and Gulf South summers, where it has become a landscape staple as a tough, low-maintenance flowering large shrub or small tree. It blooms heavily on new growth from late spring through fall, with the fragrant, gray-green palmately compound foliage adding a light sage-like scent to the garden. Cut back hard in late winter to about 12-18 inches above ground each year to encourage vigorous new growth and the best flower display, and to keep the plant at a manageable size. Bees and butterflies visit the long-lasting flower spikes heavily.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in rocky to gravelly, alkaline, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Texas milkweed grows naturally in canyon seeps and rocky washes and tolerates more shade than most milkweed species.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in rocky to gravelly, alkaline, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Texas milkweed grows naturally in canyon seeps and rocky washes and tolerates more shade than most milkweed species. Slender stems carry narrow leaves and loose clusters of pure white, sweetly fragrant flowers from spring through fall, serving as both nectar source and larval host for monarch and queen butterflies in the limestone canyons of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos where it is native. Its tolerance of partial shade makes it a valuable milkweed choice for the dappled light of a canyon garden, rocky woodland edge, or the north side of a xeriscape planting where most sun-loving milkweeds struggle. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond cutting spent stems back in late winter.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in alkaline, rocky, well-drained soil; extremely slow-growing but extremely long-lived. Scarify seeds before sowing to aid germination.
directions: Plant in alkaline to neutral, rocky or caliche, sharply drained soil in full sun; this aristocratic native evergreen shrub of the Texas Hill Country and desert Southwest is prized for its intensely fragrant violet-purple flower clusters that smell like Concord grape candy and appear in early spring. It is extremely slow-growing (6–12 inches per year), drought tolerant once established, and virtually pest and disease free. The distinctive woody seed pods contain bright red seeds that are highly toxic if eaten. Give it an excellent drainage and poor alkaline soil — rich, moist conditions cause root rot. An excellent foundation or specimen plant for Gulf Coast and zone 8–9 gardens where winter temperatures stay above 10°F.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, rocky, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas muhly grows naturally on dry, rocky, limestone slopes and canyon walls of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos of Texas. It is adapted to very dry, calcareous, vertical or steep rocky substrates.
directions: Plant in dry, rocky, well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas muhly is a small, tufted native grass of the limestone hills and rocky canyon walls of central and west Texas, adapted to the thin, calcareous, excessively well-drained soils of the Edwards Plateau. The delicate, airy seed heads in late summer and fall create a fine-textured, golden haze above the compact green clumps. Unlike the larger, showier muhlys (M. capillaris, M. sericea), Texas muhly is a fine-textured, more compact plant appropriate for smaller-scale rocky, dry garden settings and rock garden pockets in calcareous soil. Excellent for crevices in limestone walls and dry rock garden beds in zone 9a. Plants grown in rich, moist soil tend to flop; the lean, dry conditions of its native limestone habitat produce the best compact form.

common_name: Texas Olive (Mexican Olive, Anacahuita, Wild Olive)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Texas olive is native to extreme south Texas and northeastern Mexico and prefers alkaline, calcareous soils. It is tolerant of clay and caliche but requires excellent drainage and is damaged at 22–25°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas olive is one of the most spectacular native flowering trees of the Rio Grande Plains and an outstanding ornamental for zone 8–11 gardens. The large, tropical-looking leathery leaves and stunning pure white, 2-inch funnel-shaped flowers with a yellow throat are produced year-round in warm weather, attracting bees, butterflies, and birds. The olive-like fruits ripen to white and are eaten by mockingbirds and other wildlife. The tree is semi-evergreen, holding its large velvety leaves in mild winters and dropping them only in cold or drought. It is highly drought tolerant once established and grows naturally on rocky limestone slopes, chaparral, and thorny brush country of the Rio Grande Plains. In zone 8a it may be killed to the ground in severe winters but resprouting from roots is common.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (October–November in zones 7–9) on established lawn or native grass areas where grass hosts are present; Texas Paintbrush is hemiparasitic, attaching root haustoria to the roots of nearby grass plants for water and nutrients — it cannot grow without host grasses and should not be planted in bare soil; scatter seed directly into existing grass or native wildflower turf.
directions: Scatter seeds directly onto existing lawn or native grass in fall without tilling; do not cover seeds (light aids germination); Texas Paintbrush is obligate-hemiparasitic and must attach to grass roots to survive — sowing into bare soil always fails; keep grass host mowed to 3–4 inches. Texas Paintbrush (Castilleja indivisa) is one of the most iconic wildflowers of Texas and the Gulf Coast, appearing in brilliant red-orange masses across meadows, roadsides, and prairies from Austin and San Antonio south to the Gulf every spring from March through May. The flaming red-orange 'flowers' are actually highly modified bracts (modified leaves) surrounding the small, tubular true flowers; the brilliant coloration serves as a long-distance signal to the ruby-throated hummingbirds and long-tongued bees that pollinate the species. Texas Paintbrush is a hemiparasite — unlike full parasites, it can photosynthesize but augments its nutrition by attaching root haustoria to the roots of nearby grasses and extracting water, minerals, and some photosynthate from the host plant. This obligate relationship with grass hosts makes it impossible to grow in containers or in bare soil; it must be established directly into existing grass or wildflower turf. Texas Paintbrush is an annual in most of its range, completing its lifecycle and setting seed by summer; the seeds persist in the soil and germinate in fall with winter rains, producing a rosette of gray-green foliage through winter before the brilliant spring bloom. One of the 'Big Three' Texas wildflowers alongside bluebonnets and drummond phlox.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Texas palafox grows naturally on deep sand deposits and sandy roadsides across central and south Texas and self-seeds readily in similar loose, dry soil.
directions: Direct sow into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Texas palafox is a tall, wiry native annual of deep-sand habitats across central and south Texas, producing loose, airy clusters of fragrant, pale to deep pink flowers with long, prominent, needle-like stamens from summer through fall that give the plant its common name and draw a steady stream of bees and butterflies. It is highly adapted to loose, infertile sand and gravel where richer garden soil actually works against it, so avoid heavy amendment or fertilizer and let it grow lean and tall as it does in the wild. Once introduced to a suitably sandy, sunny site it self-seeds readily, returning reliably each year, and its airy, see-through form works well massed at the back of a native wildflower meadow or scattered through a xeric gravel garden.

common_name: Texas Palmetto (Mexican Palmetto, Rio Grande Palmetto)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, fertile to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Texas palmetto transplants with difficulty (large specimens require professional installation) — plant small, young specimens and let them grow in place.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun; once established, Texas palmetto is drought-tolerant and requires little supplemental water. Sabal mexicana (Texas palmetto or Mexican palmetto) is the native palm of the lower Rio Grande Valley and the southernmost tip of Texas — the most cold-hardy of the larger Sabal species and the only palm native to continental Texas. It produces a massive, solitary trunk up to 50 feet tall topped with a globular crown of large, fan-shaped (palmate), blue-green fronds 4–6 feet across on 8-to-10-foot petioles; the base of old petioles persist on the trunk as a distinctive boot-like attachment giving the trunk a characteristic rough texture. The palm is closely related to the Cabbage Palm (Sabal palmetto) of the Florida/Carolina coast, but is larger and adapted to the limestone, alkaline soils of southern Texas and northern Mexico. It is the dominant palm of the Texas Gulf Coast and Rio Grande Valley and is important as an ornamental landscape tree, wildlife food source (fruits are eaten by numerous bird species including Hooded Orioles), and cultural symbol of the Rio Grande Valley. More cold-hardy than most large palms, surviving brief drops to 15°F when established.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; Texas pink skullcap is a Mexican drylands native that rots in heavy, poorly drained, or overwatered soil.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; Texas pink skullcap is a Mexican drylands native that rots in heavy, poorly drained, or overwatered soil. Fine, needle-like evergreen foliage forms a dense, tidy mound smothered from spring through fall in small, tubular, cherry-pink to magenta flowers that are a magnet for bees and hummingbirds throughout the long Gulf South growing season. Native to limestone slopes in northeastern Mexico, it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving in the reflected heat of a rock garden, dry border, or xeriscape bed where it needs no deadheading to stay in near-continuous bloom. Shear lightly in late winter to remove any cold-damaged growth and keep the mound compact.

plant_note: Sow seed indoors on well-drained mineral mix in late winter, then move seedlings outside after the last frost into a bed with sharp drainage and reflected heat.
directions: Sow seed indoors on well-drained mineral mix in late winter, then move seedlings outside after the last frost into a bed with sharp drainage and reflected heat. This cylindrical, banded-spine cactus from the Chihuahuan Desert produces enormous, fragrant flowers in shades of yellow, peach, or magenta that open for several days in succession each spring. It is typically solitary or forms only a few stems, making it a striking specimen plant for a xeriscape bed or trough. Give it a gravel mulch and minimal summer water to mimic its native rocky slopes.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in well-drained, rocky to loamy, alkaline to slightly acidic, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas redbud is significantly more drought, heat, and alkaline-soil tolerant than the standard eastern redbud — it is the variety to choose for Gulf Coast and South Texas gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — Texas redbud is the heat-and-drought-hardy western variety of our native eastern redbud, offering the same spectacular early spring bloom — dense clusters of magenta-pink pea-flowers covering every branch before the leaves emerge — with significantly improved performance in the rocky limestone soils, alkaline caliche, and intense summer heat of the western Gulf Coast and Edwards Plateau. The foliage is rounded, glossy, and notably thicker and more heat-tolerant than the standard species, holding up through brutal Texas summers without scorching. Selected cultivars like 'Oklahoma' (with very dark, glossy foliage and wine-red flowers) and 'Texas White' (clear white flowers) offer outstanding ornamental refinements over the species. An outstanding small patio or understory tree for dry, alkaline, sunny to lightly shaded garden sites in zone 6–9, requiring minimal water once established.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky or gritty soil in full sun; Texas rock yucca is endemic to the limestone outcrops of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau and thrives in the thin, rocky, alkaline soil conditions of that region. It is smaller and more compact than most yuccas, making it better suited to residential gardens than the large tree yuccas.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky soil in full sun; Texas rock yucca is an endemic Texas Hill Country species producing the most distinctively twisted and curving leaves of any common yucca — flat, dark-green, strap-like leaves with yellow-green margins that twist and curl as they lengthen, creating a characteristic spiral effect on the rosette. Unlike most yuccas, which produce straight, upright leaves, the twisted leaves of Y. rupicola give it an immediately recognizable and distinctive appearance. It stays compact — reaching only 18–30 inches in spread without the stiff trunk of larger yuccas — making it more manageable in residential garden settings. Excellent for Texas Hill Country-style native gardens, rock gardens, limestone soil gardens, and dry xeriscapes in zone 7–11. Summer flower spikes of white, bell-shaped, fragrant yucca flowers are visited by yucca moths. The plant slowly produces offsets over many years to form modest clumps.

common_name: Texas Sabal Palm (Rio Grande Palmetto, Mexican Palmetto)
plant_note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Texas sabal palm is extremely drought tolerant once established and native to the Rio Grande Delta, where it grows in sandy, saline, and seasonally flooded soils. It is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant native palms in the US.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; the Texas sabal palm is the only native palm of the Rio Grande Delta — a majestic, fan-leafed palm native to the last remaining wild groves at the southern tip of Texas, now found in only a few protected areas such as the Sabal Palm Sanctuary near Brownsville. It is closely related to the familiar Sabal palmetto of Florida and is one of the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant of all native palms. The massive, deeply curved fan leaves on 5-6 foot stalks create a dramatic tropical silhouette; established trees develop a broad, imposing crown. Black fruits ripen in fall and are relished by birds. A premier palm for zone 8–11 Gulf Coast gardens — exceptionally wind, salt, and drought tolerant once established and requiring little maintenance. Grow from locally sourced nursery stock; wild populations are endangered.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas sacahuista is native to dry, rocky limestone plains and hillsides of central and west Texas and the Trans-Pecos and demands sharp drainage and lean soil — it will not tolerate wet, clay, or rich soil conditions.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; once established, Texas sacahuista requires no supplemental irrigation. Nolina texana (Texas sacahuista or Texas beargrass) is a native Texas perennial producing a dense, stemless rosette of very narrow (1/4-inch wide), fibrous, tough, grass-like leaves up to 3 feet long — creating a fountain-like mound of fine-textured, dark-green foliage that persists year-round. In late spring, mature plants send up a tall (3–5 foot), branching flower stalk bearing large panicles of tiny, white to cream flowers. Native Americans and early settlers used the tough, durable leaf fibers extensively for weaving baskets, mats, and sandals — sacahuista (the Mexican Spanish name) has roots in indigenous craft traditions of the Southwest. As a landscape plant, Texas sacahuista is valued for its extreme drought and heat tolerance, fine leaf texture, and year-round evergreen structure in hot, dry, alkaline gardens — an excellent companion to agaves, sotol, and native grasses in xeriscaping. It is also outstanding for erosion control on dry, rocky slopes. The flower stalks can be cut and used in dried arrangements.

plant_note: Direct-sow after last frost or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas sage is native to the alkaline limestone soils of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos and performs best in lean, well-drained, dry conditions. Rich or moist soil produces lush but floppy growth with fewer flowers. It will behave as a short-lived perennial in zone 8–10 and is reliably perennial in zone 9–10.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas sage (not to be confused with Leucophyllum frutescens, also called 'Texas sage') is a small, slender-stemmed perennial salvia native to the limestone hills and rocky grasslands of central and west Texas, producing airy spikes of clear, bright-blue flowers through spring and again in fall after rains — an extremely drought-tolerant native that blooms in the same heat and dry conditions that defeat most garden plants. The plant is open and wiry in habit, with small, oval, slightly aromatic leaves, and relies on its profusion of vivid blue flowers rather than bold foliage for ornamental effect. Native bee-adapted with the classic two-lipped, tubular salvia flower, it attracts native bees, mason bees, and hummingbirds. Excellent for low-water Texas Hill Country-style gardens, rock gardens, dry slopes, and xeriscape designs in zones 7–10 where its need for excellent drainage and alkaline soil can be met.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in well-drained to average, moist soil in shade or partial shade; Texas sedge is adapted to the dry, shaded conditions under live oaks and cedar elms of Texas and is among the most drought-tolerant sedges available for zone 7–9 shade gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil in partial to full shade; Texas sedge is one of the most valuable native groundcovers for the difficult dry-shade conditions found under live oaks, cedar elms, and other dense-canopy trees in Texas and the Gulf Coast. The very fine, soft, bright green blades stay only 4–8 inches tall and spread slowly to form a delicate turf that can be mowed occasionally or left unmowed as a naturalistic groundcover. It is notably more drought tolerant than most carex species, surviving the dry summers under mature trees where more moisture-demanding groundcovers wilt and die. Excellent as a lawn alternative in shade where traditional turfgrasses thin out and fail. Seeds are tiny and eaten by many ground-foraging birds. Evergreen in zone 8–10.

plant_note: Direct sow into disturbed, well-drained soil after the last frost; this rangeland annual germinates readily on bare ground and needs no coddling.
directions: Named for its habit of keeping its lemon-yellow ray flowers closed until around midday, this branching Texas and Oklahoma native colonizes disturbed prairie, roadsides, and stream banks with minimal care. It tolerates poor, dry sand or clay and largely shrugs off summer heat once seedlings are established. Leave some plants unpulled at season's end so seed can scatter and refresh the patch the following year. It is a reliable, low-input filler for a wildflower meadow mix rather than a formal border plant.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in well-drained to xeric, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; sotol requires excellent drainage and grows best in rocky, limestone-based soils. It is extremely slow-growing and patience is required — established plants can live for many decades.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; Texas sotol is a dramatic native xeriscape plant of the Chihuahuan Desert and Edwards Plateau, forming a globe of many hundreds of narrow, finely toothed, spoon-based leaves with serrated margins and a distinctive dried-flower-arrangement appearance year-round. Established plants occasionally send up towering flower stalks 10–15 feet tall bearing dense clusters of small white flowers in summer, then produce fruit and seeds over the following months before dying back — the vegetative rosette survives and eventually produces another stalk. The base of the leaves was a critical food staple for the Chihuahuan people who roasted and ate the heart (similar to agave); the leaves are used to make sotol fiber and baskets. Slow-growing but extremely long-lived and virtually maintenance-free once established.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into average, well-drained prairie soil in full sun; Texas thistle forms a rosette the first year and flowers the following late spring — a native, non-invasive biennial thistle that is one of the most reliable spring nectar sources on the southern Great Plains and Gulf prairies.
directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained prairie soil in full sun; Texas thistle grows wild across the prairies, savannas, and roadsides of Texas, Oklahoma, and adjacent states, forming a spiny basal rosette its first year and sending up a branched flower stalk topped with rose-pink to lavender blooms the following late spring and early summer. It is a magnet for native bees, swallowtail and monarch butterflies, and hummingbirds during a season when many other prairie wildflowers have yet to bloom, and its seed heads are relished by goldfinches once they ripen. As a true native prairie species it is well-behaved in a garden setting and does not spread aggressively like the introduced pasture thistles most gardeners are taught to fear. Plant it toward the back of a sunny native prairie or pollinator bed, away from paths given its spiny leaves, and allow a modest amount of self-seeding to maintain the colony from year to year.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Texas trillium is native to damp baygalls and seepage-slope pine-hardwood forest of the western Gulf Coastal Plain and needs steadier moisture than most upland trilliums.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Texas trillium is native to damp baygalls and seepage-slope pine-hardwood forest of the western Gulf Coastal Plain and needs steadier moisture than most upland trilliums. Unlike its mottled-leaved cousins, it carries plain green leaves and a pedicellate, nodding-to-erect white flower that ages to pink, blooming in early spring in the wet, acidic soils of southeast Texas and adjacent Louisiana. Rare and highly localized in the wild, it is best grown from nursery-propagated stock in a shaded bog garden or the damp margin of a rain garden alongside pitcher plants, sundews, or Virginia sweetspire. Keep the soil reliably moist through the growing season and mulch with pine straw to hold moisture and mimic its native acidic litter layer.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Texas verbena overwinters as a basal rosette in zone 7–9 and blooms prolifically in spring before summer heat arrives, then self-sows to maintain a persistent colony.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in full sun — Texas verbena is a delicate-looking but tough native annual of the Gulf Coast prairies and open roadsides of Texas, Louisiana, and adjacent states, producing slender, erect stems topped with small but brilliantly colored lavender-pink to pink-purple flower spikes from late winter through spring. Despite its fine, airy texture, it is remarkably heat and drought tolerant and is one of the most important early-season nectar plants for gulf fritillary and phaon crescent butterflies emerging from winter dormancy. It self-sows prolifically in open, disturbed soils to maintain self-sustaining colonies in roadsides, meadows, and sunny, dry garden borders. Excellent for adding fine texture and early spring color to wildflower meadow plantings alongside bluebonnets, Indian paintbrush, and Indian blanket. Essentially no maintenance once established from seed.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; like other Texas-variety redbuds, Texas White tolerates heat, drought, and alkaline soils notably better than standard eastern redbud.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Texas White is a white-flowered selection of the Texas botanical variety of eastern redbud, combining the glossy, leathery, heat-tolerant foliage and superior drought resistance of Texas redbud with pure white spring flowers instead of the typical magenta-pink. The crisp white bloom against bare branches in late winter to early spring provides a striking contrast to pink- and purple-flowered redbuds nearby, and the same waxy, dark green summer leaves resist the leaf scorch and drop that afflicts standard eastern redbud in Gulf Coast heat. Like other Texas redbud selections it is well adapted to alkaline, clay, and rocky soils and needs little supplemental water once established, making it a reliable, low-maintenance small flowering tree for the Gulf South.

common_name: Texas Yellow Star (Texas Star Daisy, Lindheimera)
plant_note: In zone 9, direct sow in fall (October–November) for late winter and spring bloom; in zone 7–8 sow in early spring. Lindheimera texana is endemic to limestone hills of central Texas and needs excellent drainage — avoid clay soils or supplement with coarse sand and gravel. Self-sows readily in zone 9 gardens and returns year after year with no replanting once established.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface or barely covered with fine grit in very well-drained, lean, alkaline-tolerant soil in full sun; Texas Yellow Star does not require rich soil — in fact, excessive fertility produces weak, floppy stems with few flowers. Lindheimera texana is a delightful annual wildflower endemic to the limestone Hill Country of central Texas and is one of the few monotypic genera in the Asteraceae — the only species in its genus, named for Ferdinand Jacob Lindheimer, the pioneering 19th-century Texas botanist. The cheerful, bright-yellow, five-rayed daisy flowers cover the compact plants from March through June in Texas, and self-seeding plants bloom into summer wherever drainage is excellent. Flowers have a slightly unusual structure: the ray florets are not ligulate but have distinctly notched petals that give them a whimsical, multi-pointed star appearance. An excellent companion in wildflower meadows alongside bluebonnets, wine cups, and Indian paintbrush in zone 8–9 limestone garden settings. Once self-seeding populations establish in a well-drained spot, they return reliably each year without replanting. Deer resistant.

common_name: Thai Beauty Caladium (Pink and White Variegated Fancy Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Thai Beauty is a larger, more vigorous caladium than most fancy-leaved cultivars — provide ample space and consistent moisture for maximum leaf development.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Thai Beauty is one of the most strikingly patterned and vigorous fancy-leaved caladiums available — producing large to extra-large heart-shaped leaves with a complex pattern of pink and white variegation on a green base, with irregular pink and white sectors, streaks, and markings creating a kaleidoscopic pattern that varies from leaf to leaf. The intricate, non-repeating pattern of each leaf — with pink, white, and green sectors arranged differently on each successive leaf — gives the plant an unusual, almost watercolor-painted appearance that is visually complex and continuously interesting as new leaves unfurl with slightly different patterning. Thai Beauty grows vigorously and produces large leaves, creating an impressive tropical foliage mass in summer shade gardens. The soft pink and white tones create a cooler, more pastel effect than the bold red-and-white contrast of 'White Queen' or the pure color masses of 'Florida Cardinal' — making Thai Beauty an excellent choice for mixed caladium plantings where different color combinations are desired. As with all fancy-leaved caladiums, provide consistent moisture throughout the growing season, mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and moderate root temperature, and allow the foliage to yellow naturally in fall before removing the withered stems.

plant_note: Place outdoors in a shade to bright indirect light location after temperatures remain above 60°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October. Thai Constellation is a tissue-culture selection that produces consistent, stable cream-and-green variegation on every leaf — unlike naturally occurring variegated Monstera (var. albo-variegata) which can revert to solid green. Protect from any direct sun, which causes permanent bleaching of the white variegated areas. Provide a moss pole or other climbing support; Monstera naturally climbs by aerial roots in its native forest understory. As the plant matures, leaf fenestrations (the characteristic holes and splits) develop and become progressively larger and more elaborate on successive leaves.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light — never in direct sun, which irreversibly bleaches and kills the pale variegated areas of the leaf — in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil; Thai Constellation is a variegated cultivar of Swiss Cheese Plant (Monstera deliciosa) that was developed through tissue culture in Thailand and produces spectacular cream-and-green marbled variegation on the large, deeply fenestrated (perforated and split) leaves — creating one of the most visually dramatic and internationally collectible foliage plants in the contemporary indoor and outdoor tropical plant market. The variegation pattern is unique on each leaf: irregular cream-white to yellow-white splashes, sectors, and marbling on the dark green background create a different constellation of pale color on every leaf — never exactly the same twice — which explains the cultivar name. The characteristic Monstera leaf fenestrations (windows and splits in the large leaves) combined with the cream-and-green variegation creates a leaf form and color pattern that has become one of the most recognized symbols of contemporary tropical plant culture and indoor garden design. As an outdoor shade container plant for zone 9's warm season, Thai Constellation provides an extraordinary level of foliage sophistication on covered patios and shaded garden areas.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring once temperatures are consistently warm; treat cut ends with rooting hormone and maintain high humidity until roots establish.
directions: Take semi-hardwood cuttings in spring, treat with rooting hormone, and root in a warm, humid environment with bottom heat around 75 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit until a strong root system develops before transplanting. Choose a site with full sun, good drainage, and ample space, as this large tree can reach 20 to 30 feet tall and wide at maturity in frost-free climates. Water regularly during the first two years to establish deep roots, then reduce irrigation as the tree becomes more self-sufficient during dry periods. In zone 9, plant in a sheltered microclimate and mulch heavily at the base to protect roots if a rare frost threatens, as even brief freezes can cause significant dieback.

plant_note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun; Thailand Giant is among the largest-leaved colocasia available and needs abundant water, fertility, and space to reach full size.
directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun; Thailand Giant is among the largest-leaved colocasia available and needs abundant water, fertility, and space to reach full size. Enormous, matte blue-green, heart-shaped leaves can reach four feet or more in length on tall, thick stems, making this one of the largest and most dramatic elephant ears grown, capable of creating an instant jungle effect at the back of a border or beside a pond in a single warm season. Unlike ordinary colocasia grown mainly for foliage, mature plants also occasionally produce large, fragrant, upright white flower spikes reminiscent of a giant peace lily bloom, an unusual bonus for a plant typically valued for leaf size alone. Feed heavily and water generously through the growing season to support its massive leaf production, and in zones colder than 8, lift and store the tuber indoors over winter or grow it as a dramatic single-season annual.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Thalia daffodil is one of the more heat-tolerant, reliably perennializing daffodils for warmer climates where many modern hybrids fail to return.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Thalia daffodil is one of the more heat-tolerant, reliably perennializing daffodils for warmer climates where many modern hybrids fail to return. Introduced in 1916 and still widely grown over a century later, this elegant heirloom triandrus-type daffodil produces two to three nodding, pure white, reflexed flowers per stem with a light, sweet fragrance, giving it a graceful, orchid-like poise distinct from the single, forward-facing trumpet of most daffodils. Its old, proven garden performance and good heat tolerance for a daffodil make it one of the more dependable choices for naturalizing in warmer zones where modern large-trumpet hybrids often fail to rebloom reliably. Let foliage yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer once dormant.

common_name: Thanksgiving Cactus (Crab Cactus, False Christmas Cactus)
plant_note: Root two- or three-segment stem cuttings after callusing for a day or two in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright indirect light; in autumn, give the plant roughly six weeks of long uninterrupted nights and cool temperatures near 50-55 degrees F to initiate flower buds.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping it evenly moist during active growth and allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings. This Brazilian rainforest epiphyte carries flattened, jointed stem segments with pointed, claw-like serrated edges, the feature that distinguishes it from the smoother-scalloped true Christmas cactus, Schlumbergera x buckleyi; most cactus plants sold in stores in November and December under the name Christmas cactus are actually this earlier-blooming species. Vivid pink, red, orange, purple, or white flowers dangle from the segment tips once the plant has had a cool, short-day autumn rest. Keep it away from cold drafts, heating vents, and sudden temperature swings, which can cause buds and even whole segments to drop.

common_name: The Alnwick Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; The Alnwick Rose's compact, rounded habit fits a smaller border position than many other David Austin cultivars.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001 and named for Alnwick Garden in Northumberland, The Alnwick Rose bears rich rose-pink, cupped rosette flowers with a strong, sweet old-rose fragrance, on a compact, rounded, well-branched shrub that fits smaller borders more easily than larger English rose cultivars. It repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost, and its dependable habit and strong fragrance have made it a long-standing favorite in David Austin's catalog.

common_name: The Blues Little Bluestem (Fine-Textured Powder-Blue Native Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; like other little bluestem selections, The Blues performs poorly in rich, overfed soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; little bluestem thrives in poor, rocky, clay, or sandy soil and performs poorly if overfed. The Blues produces exceptionally fine-textured, powder-blue foliage through summer, among the most intensely blue of the little bluestem cultivars, turning warm copper-orange in fall with fluffy silvery seed heads that catch low autumn and winter light beautifully. Its upright, airy habit and strong color make it a striking textural contrast against darker-foliaged perennials and shrubs in a naturalistic border or meadow planting. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and provides valuable seed and cover for birds; cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; seed germinates in darkness.
directions: The Bride stands out among bachelor's buttons for its unusual snowy-white, frilly blooms and captivating honey fragrance. Direct sow in early spring, covering the seed since darkness aids germination, and thin the seedlings once established. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil where this drought-tolerant annual needs little care. Frequent cutting or deadheading keeps the plants producing their pollinator-friendly flowers, which draw bees and butterflies. Leave a few flowers to set seed and it will often self-sow.

plant_note: Plant the potted or bare-root shrub in spring after frost danger passes.
directions: The Champion Sunblush is an easy-care flowering rose shrub with brilliant, sun-kissed petals suited to both beginner and experienced gardeners. Set the plant in full sun in rich, well-drained soil, digging a hole wide enough for the roots and watering in well. Provide consistent moisture at the base to keep foliage dry, and mulch to conserve water and moderate soil temperature. Prune in late winter to shape the shrub and remove dead or crossing canes, and feed in spring as growth begins. Hardy in zones 5 to 9, it rewards steady care with repeat blooms through the season.

common_name: The Chatelaine Lupine (Pink and White Bicolor Russell Strain)
plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat; direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil.
directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing with sandpaper before sowing, then direct sow into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. The Chatelaine is a long-cultivated named selection from the classic Russell strain of garden lupine, bearing soft bicolor flowers combining rose-pink standards with white wings on tall, dense spikes above handsome palmately compound foliage, a gentler color combination than the more common blues and purples of the genus. Its cottage-garden charm has kept it in cultivation as an heirloom selection for many decades. Like other Russell-type lupines it thrives in the cool, moist summers of northern gardens but declines quickly in heat and humidity, making it best suited to zones 7 and cooler. Deadhead spent spikes promptly to encourage a possible second flush of bloom, and avoid disturbing the deep taproot once established.

common_name: The Fairy Polyantha Rose (Low, Spreading Pink Ground Cover Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; The Fairy is a low, spreading polyantha rose useful as a flowering ground cover or low border.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the low, spreading habit works well as a flowering ground cover, low informal hedge, or the front of a mixed border. The Fairy produces dense clusters of small, double, soft pink rosette blooms almost continuously from late spring through fall, on a compact, glossy-leaved shrub that is exceptionally disease-resistant and easy to grow without spraying. Its long bloom season and low maintenance have made it one of the most widely planted polyantha roses in modern gardens. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom, and prune lightly in late winter to maintain shape.

plant_note: Plant container roses in late winter through spring in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in full sun; The Fairy is one of the most adaptable and disease-resistant roses available and tolerates a wider range of soils and partial shade than most landscape roses.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; The Fairy is a classic polyantha rose introduced in 1932 by Ann Bentall that has remained continuously popular for nearly a century — a testament to its exceptional combination of qualities: outstanding disease resistance, long blooming season from late spring through hard frost, profuse clusters of small (1-inch), cupped, double, soft-pink flowers in dense panicles, and a compact, spreading mounding habit requiring minimal pruning. Where modern tea rose hybrids are high-maintenance plants demanding regular spraying for black spot and disease control, The Fairy is genuinely low-maintenance — rarely requiring fungicide treatment even in humid Gulf South climates — and blooms dependably season after season without the intensive care that classic hybrid teas demand. The small, button-like pink flowers are produced in large, dense clusters on arching stems, creating an effect reminiscent of a compact, pink-flowering hydrangea at peak bloom. The Fairy is widely used as a landscape rose, groundcover rose, and in container plantings where its naturally arching, cascading habit is particularly attractive. The mild, apple-and-rose fragrance is pleasant but light. In zone 9, The Fairy is essentially evergreen to semi-evergreen and blooms from March through December — one of the longest bloom seasons of any commonly grown rose.

common_name: The Generous Gardener Rose (David Austin Climbing English Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring or fall in soil enriched with compost near a support structure; The Generous Gardener can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber, with fragrant, soft pink blooms and better shade tolerance than most roses.
directions: Set plants in full sun to light partial shade with rich, well-drained soil, and provide a trellis, fence, or pergola if training it as a climber, since it flowers well trained flat against a support or left as a large, arching, informal shrub. Prune to shape in late winter, removing only crossing or damaged canes if grown as a climber, and deadhead through the season to encourage repeat bloom. The Generous Gardener is a David Austin rose valued for its large, cupped, soft blush-pink double flowers with a strong, classic old-rose fragrance carrying notes of musk and myrrh, produced in generous flushes from late spring into fall. It tolerates a bit more shade than most roses, making it a useful choice for a partly shaded fence or wall where a typical rose would bloom poorly, and its long, flexible canes make it easy to train horizontally to maximize flowering along a support.

common_name: The Giant Colchicum (Large Pale Lilac-Pink Autumn Crocus)
plant_note: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer to early fall, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; corms often begin flowering within days of planting, even before they are in the ground.
directions: Plant corms as soon as available in late summer, 4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. The Giant is one of the largest and most vigorous colchicum hybrids, sending up goblet-shaped, pale lilac-pink flowers with a white throat directly from the ground in early fall, appearing before any foliage emerges, which is followed the next spring by large, glossy, strap-like leaves that die back by early summer and must be left to yellow naturally to recharge the corm. Its unusual bloom sequence — flowers with no leaves in fall, leaves with no flowers in spring — surprises gardeners unfamiliar with the genus, so mark planting locations to avoid accidental disturbance. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas grazed by pets or livestock, and its large spring foliage needs room among companion plants that will not be smothered.

common_name: The Governor Lupine (Deep Blue and White Bicolor Russell Strain)
plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat; direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil.
directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing with sandpaper before sowing, then direct sow into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. The Governor is a long-cultivated named selection from the classic Russell strain of garden lupine, bearing striking bicolor flowers combining deep royal blue standards with crisp white wings on tall, dense spikes above handsome palmately compound foliage. Its bold color contrast has kept it a favorite heirloom lupine selection for generations of cottage gardeners.
