Like other Russell-type lupines it thrives in the cool, moist summers of northern gardens but declines quickly in heat and humidity, making it best suited to zones 7 and cooler. Deadhead spent spikes promptly to encourage a possible second flush of bloom, and avoid disturbing the deep taproot once established, since this plant resents transplanting.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown rhizome divisions in consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; The King ostrich fern spreads by rhizome as vigorously as the species and needs room to naturalize.
directions: Plant nursery-grown rhizome divisions in consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; The King ostrich fern spreads by rhizome as vigorously as the species and needs room to naturalize. Selected in the United Kingdom for larger, more robust, upright fronds than typical ostrich fern, this selection forms a bold, vase-shaped shuttlecock of bright green, finely divided fronds that can tower over most other hardy ferns by midsummer, with separate dark, feather-like fertile fronds persisting through winter. It colonizes moist ground along stream banks, pond edges, and low spots by spreading rhizomes, making it best suited to naturalized plantings or spacious shade borders rather than small, contained beds. Where fiddleheads are foraged in early spring, harvest only a portion of each clump's emerging crosiers to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: The Pilgrim Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since The Pilgrim is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber against a wall, fence, or pillar.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1991, The Pilgrim carries soft, clear yellow, deeply cupped rosette flowers with a strong myrrh fragrance, on long, arching canes that reach 8 feet or more when trained as a climber, or can be kept pruned as a large freestanding shrub. It was one of the earlier David Austin introductions to combine a strong yellow color with reliable repeat bloom and good disease resistance, and it continues to flower generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

plant_note: Plant with the crown a couple of inches below soil level, shading the root zone while the vine climbs a trellis, arbor, or fence into full sun; light pruning group — trim lightly in late winter rather than cutting hard to the ground.
directions: Introduced in England in 1876, The President remains one of the most reliable and widely planted large-flowered clematis more than a century later, prized for its rich purple-blue, star-shaped 5 to 6 inch flowers with contrasting reddish-purple stamens and silvery reverse petals that catch the light as they twist in the breeze. It reblooms twice in a season — a strong flush in late spring to early summer followed by a lighter repeat in late summer — and its long garden pedigree has earned it lasting popularity. As with other clematis, keep the roots cool and shaded (mulch or low companion planting works well) while the vine itself grows into full sun.

plant_note: Plant nursery stock in spring after the ground thaws; can also plant in early fall.
directions: The Rising Sun redbud is a small deciduous tree prized for new growth that emerges in fiery apricot, orange, and gold before aging to lime and green. Site it in rich, well-drained soil where it receives morning sun and some afternoon shade in hot climates. Rosy-pink pea-like flowers cover the bare branches in early spring before the leaves unfurl. Water deeply during the first two years to establish the root system, then supplement only in dry spells. Prune lightly after flowering to shape the canopy.

common_name: The Rocket Ligularia (Black-Stemmed Award-Winning Bog Perennial)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in constantly moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from afternoon sun; The Rocket is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit winner, though like all ligularias it struggles in zone 9 heat and needs a cool, sheltered, consistently damp site.
directions: Plant in constantly moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from afternoon sun and heat; The Rocket is a dramatic, architectural ligularia bearing bold, toothed, triangular leaves topped in mid to late summer by tall, striking spikes of small yellow flowers held on near-black stems that rise well above the foliage. It is one of the classic pond-edge and bog-garden perennials in cooler climates, holding a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for garden performance. Like all ligularias it wilts dramatically during midday heat, recovering overnight, which is normal behavior for the genus rather than disease; it performs best in climates with mild summers and struggles in zone 9 heat, so give it the coolest, most consistently damp spot available and mulch heavily to keep roots cool. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or summer; biennial that blooms the second year.
directions: The Watchman appears nearly black from a distance but reveals a rich purplish-burgundy cast up close on towering flower spikes. Direct sow the seed in spring or summer, barely covering it, since this biennial usually forms a rosette the first year and blooms the second. Grow in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and stake the tall spikes in windy locations. The dramatic towers make an excellent backdrop for pink, red, yellow, or white flowers and attract bees and butterflies. Let some flowers set seed and it will readily self-sow for future years.

plant_note: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; thick-stemmed pelargonium grows from a stout, woody, succulent trunk base that stores water and gives the plant a caudex-like appearance similar to a small succulent tree. It follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — growing and flowering in winter and spring, going summer dormant. Keep dry in summer. The swollen, elephant-leg-like trunk base is the primary ornamental feature of mature plants.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; thick-stemmed pelargonium is one of the more unusual succulent pelargoniums from the arid, rocky environments of Namaqualand and the Northern Cape — developing over years a swollen, fleshy, woody, bulbous trunk base of increasing size and eccentricity, from which emerge the annual stems bearing finely divided, somewhat hairy, green leaves and small clusters of white to cream-white pelargonium flowers with typical geranium-family two-upper/three-lower petal arrangement. The swollen, water-storing trunk base — sometimes described as 'elephant-foot' or 'caudex-like' — is the primary ornamental distinction, giving mature plants the appearance of tiny, gnarled, succulent trees. In the arid, rocky Namaqualand environment it is an adaptation to water storage through the long, summer drought periods. For collectors of succulent plants and unusual geranium-family species, the novelty of a pelargonium developing into a swollen-trunked, bonsai-like succulent miniature tree over many years makes it a rewarding long-term specimen. The genus Pelargonium includes many such succulent-stem species from the arid Cape, of which P. carnosum is one of the more robust and accessible.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; thimble cactus offsets prolifically and is one of the easiest, fastest-clustering small cacti to grow.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; thimble cactus offsets prolifically and is one of the easiest, fastest-clustering small cacti to grow. Small, cylindrical, pale green stems covered in fine white spines detach easily and root readily wherever they fall, causing the plant to spread and cluster with unusual speed compared to most mammillaria species, quickly filling a dish garden or small pot with dozens of small offsets. Small, pale yellow-white flowers ring the crown of mature stems in spring, though the plant is grown chiefly for its easy, fast-multiplying habit rather than a dramatic bloom display. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact growth, and simply replant any detached offset segments to propagate more plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, average to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; thimbleweed is more drought-tolerant than Canada anemone and prefers better-drained, drier soils in open woodland or prairie edge settings.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, average to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; thimbleweed is more drought-tolerant than Canada anemone and prefers better-drained, drier soils in open woodland or prairie edge settings. Anemone virginiana is a compact, clump-forming native with deeply dissected leaves, and produces greenish-white, sometimes pink-tinged flowers from June through August, followed by its most distinctive and ornamental feature: cylindrical, spool-shaped seed heads covered in cottony white seeds that persist well into winter and provide excellent winter interest; the fluffy seed heads catch the winter light and are outstanding when used in dried arrangements. It naturalizes modestly from self-seed without becoming invasive and is well-suited to dry shade gardens, woodland margins, and native butterfly garden plantings.

plant_note: Sow stratified seed shallowly in fall or set out divisions in early spring along woodland edges, thickets, or partly shaded meadow margins.
directions: Sow stratified seed shallowly in fall or set out divisions in early spring along woodland edges, thickets, or partly shaded meadow margins where this rhizomatous sunflower can spread into loose colonies. It tolerates more shade than most sunflowers and produces smaller, more numerous 2-inch yellow blooms from late summer into fall. The flowers draw a wide range of bees, hoverflies, and butterflies, while goldfinches and other seed-eating birds work the ripening heads through autumn. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep vigor up and prevent overcrowding of neighboring plants.

common_name: Thomas Edison Dahlia (Classic Large Deep Purple Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Thomas Edison is a classic large decorative dahlia producing huge, fully double, deep royal purple blooms on a tall, sturdy plant that benefits from staking.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally, four to six inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Thomas Edison is a long-cherished large decorative dahlia cultivar, producing huge, fully double flowers in a rich, deep royal purple that hold their color well and make outstanding, long-lasting cut flowers. The tall, vigorous plants benefit from staking to support the heavy flower heads, and pinching the growing tip when young encourages a bushier plant with more flowering stems. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with good drainage and heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler zones ensures the most reliable survival from year to year.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; Thompson's yucca is more compact and smaller than Y. rostrata but is sometimes confused with it. It is native to the limestone mountain ranges of the Big Bend region of Texas and northern Mexico and is adapted to the same extreme drought and alkaline limestone soils.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky soil in full sun; Thompson's yucca is a blue-gray-leafed native of the Trans-Pecos limestone mountains of west Texas — one of the most ornamental small to medium tree yuccas, developing a slowly lengthening trunk over many years and producing a symmetrical, rounded head of narrow, blue-gray, finely toothed leaves. Its blue-gray foliage is similar to Yucca rostrata but the plant stays somewhat more compact and typically doesn't develop as tall a trunk. The narrow, glaucous leaves create a fine-textured, spherical crown that is outstanding as a landscape specimen and combines well with native grasses, agaves, and other desert-adapted plants. In spring, impressive, branched flower spikes 4–6 feet tall bear numerous large, white, bell-shaped flowers. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert and adjacent ranges in Texas and Mexico, it is excellent for dry, alkaline, rocky landscape situations in zones 6–10.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Thornbird bears an intricate tan-and-lavender veined pattern typical of the finest modern bearded iris breeding.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Thornbird bears warm tan-gold standards over falls delicately veined and washed with lavender-violet, an intricate, softly blended pattern characteristic of modern exhibition-quality bearded iris breeding, opening on tall, well-branched stems. Its subtle, complex coloring rewards close viewing and pairs beautifully with both warm and cool-toned companion plantings. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep the rhizomes in full sun with sharp drainage to avoid rot.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; thorny elaeagnus is extremely tough and adapts to a wide range of difficult conditions including drought, salt spray, and heavy soils.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; thorny elaeagnus is a large, vigorous, thorny, evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub from Asia with distinctive silvery-brown scales on the lower leaf surfaces that give the foliage an attractive metallic sheen. Small, intensely fragrant, white to cream-colored flowers appear in October–November — one of the few strongly scented fall-flowering shrubs — followed by reddish berries (edible but tart) in spring. It is extremely tough — among the most stress-tolerant shrubs for dry, salty, alkaline, or compacted soils and full shade — and fixes nitrogen through root nodules. Excellent for barrier hedges, windbreaks, and difficult dry or salt-spray sites in the Gulf South. 'Fruitlandii' (larger, more silver leaves) and 'Maculata' (golden-splashed variegation) are popular selections.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring, or sow seed in fall after scarifying the seed coat for natural cold stratification over winter; thread-leaf bluestar resents frequent disturbance once established and is best sited permanently in lean, very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun — avoid heavy clay or consistently moist soils, which cause root rot and poor performance.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, sandy or rocky, dry to average soil in full sun; thread-leaf bluestar is closely related to Hubricht's bluestar (A. hubrichtii) and shares its extraordinary fine-textured, thread-like foliage and brilliant golden-yellow fall color, but has a broader natural range across the sandy pinelands, rocky outcrops, and dry prairies of the southeastern United States from North Carolina to Texas, making it better adapted to heat and more drought-tolerant than its Ozark relative. In spring, before the foliage matures, it produces terminal clusters of small, pale powder-blue, star-shaped flowers that are excellent nectar sources for native bees and early butterflies; throughout the growing season the mounded, almost needle-like foliage provides an exceptional fine-textured contrast to broader-leaved perennials in the sunny border or native meadow planting. Thread-leaf bluestar is distinguished from A. hubrichtii by the ciliate (fringed with fine hairs) margins of its leaves — hence the epithet ciliata — and by its somewhat broader ecological amplitude in dry, sandy, infertile soils where it is extremely long-lived and essentially self-sufficient once established. It is deer-resistant, pest- and disease-free, and tolerates both the heat and humidity of the South and the cold of Zone 5, making it one of the most adaptable and underused native perennials for challenging dry, sunny conditions across the eastern and central United States.

plant_note: Sprinkle seeds on moist sphagnum moss or peat/perlite mix in full sun; thread-leaf sundew produces tall, erect, thread-like leaves to 12 inches that are covered in mucilaginous glands — one of the most spectacular of all sundews, capable of trapping large insects including damselflies.
directions: Thread-leaf sundew is one of the most spectacular of all North American carnivorous plants — producing upright, thread-like leaves up to a foot tall that are covered along their entire length with long, glistening, red-tipped tentacles dripping with sticky mucilage, making the plant look like something from a science fiction film. Native to coastal plain bogs of New Jersey and the Carolinas, it is one of the largest and most dramatic of all North American sundews, capable of trapping insects as large as damselflies and small bees on its long, adhesive leaves. Pink flowers appear on tall stalks in summer; the plant goes dormant in winter in zones 5–7, forming a tight, dry bud (hibernaculum) at the soil surface that is cold-hardy to well below freezing, making it one of the more cold-tolerant carnivorous plants for outdoor bog gardens. It produces gemmae (vegetative propagules) in fall that can be planted to create new individuals — an easy propagation method that makes it more accessible than many other carnivorous plants. Grow in the standard wet, acidic, nutrient-poor bog conditions with pure water only.

plant_note: Surface sow seed in early spring or start transplants; threadleaf coreopsis is more reliably propagated by division than seed — divisions establish quickly in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Grow in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade — threadleaf coreopsis is the most finely textured and perhaps the most garden-adaptable of all native coreopsis species, producing a season-long display of bright golden-yellow daisy flowers above delicate, needle-like whorled foliage from early summer through fall frost. Unlike most coreopsis, the thread-like leaves create an exceptionally fine-textured mound that contrasts beautifully with bold-leafed perennials. It spreads steadily by rhizome to form wide, weed-suppressing clumps and thrives in poor, dry soils where richer garden perennials struggle. Named cultivars 'Moonbeam' (pale yellow), 'Zagreb' (bright gold, compact), and 'Golden Gain' are widely available and extremely garden-worthy. Deadheading is optional — the plant reblooms regardless, but removing spent flowers extends peak flowering. One of the longest-blooming native perennials available.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; three-flower melic grass is an under-planted southeastern woodland native, a good alternative to the more commonly grown Chasmanthium (inland sea oats) for a shaded grass with less self-seeding vigor.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; three-flower melic grass is a graceful, under-planted native woodland bunchgrass, producing soft mounds of fine green foliage topped in late spring by open, airy flower panicles with distinctive drooping, oat-like spikelets that catch light beautifully in dappled shade. It offers a similar naturalistic, woodland-grass look to the more widely planted inland sea oats (Chasmanthium latifolium) but with a noticeably more restrained, clump-forming habit and far less aggressive self-seeding, making it a better-behaved choice for a smaller or more formal shade garden bed where self-sown seedlings would be unwelcome. It goes dormant and dies back by mid-summer in its native range, so plan companion plantings to carry interest through the second half of the growing season. Established clumps need little care beyond routine moisture and a spring cleanup of old foliage.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall or divide established mats in early spring; three-leaf bittercress spreads by creeping rhizomes and over time forms an effective, low groundcover in moist, shaded situations. It is semi-evergreen to fully evergreen in mild winters, maintaining its attractive dark-green, trifoliate leaves year-round. Best planted in drifts for maximum groundcover effect under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; three-leaf bittercress is a quietly attractive European woodland groundcover producing neat, dark-green, three-parted (trifoliate) leaves that have the quality of large, dark, clover-like foliage and are semi-evergreen through mild winters — forming a low carpet of attractive rounded leaflets that suppresses weeds and covers ground effectively under trees. In spring it produces a cloud of small, four-petaled, pure-white cruciform flowers on 4–6 inch stems that hover just above the foliage in a brief but cheerful display before the tree canopy closes above. The simple white flowers and clean, dark, rounded foliage make it quietly pleasing throughout the season. Spreads steadily by creeping rhizomes to form expanding patches — useful in competition with tree roots, where it can make progress without heavy soil disturbance. An underused woodland floor plant for temperate shade gardens, valuable for its evergreen quality and ability to spread slowly in competition with the root systems of large trees.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring into lean, sandy, or rocky soil where richer garden loam would encourage floppy growth.
directions: Plant divisions in spring into lean, sandy, or rocky soil where richer garden loam would encourage floppy growth; this North American native forms a low, glossy trifoliate mat that turns bronze-red in fall and holds slopes against erosion in even the poorest ground. Small white flowers appear over summer above the foliage, and once established it needs little supplemental water. It is exceptionally cold hardy, native to alpine barrens and rocky outcrops from Greenland south through the Appalachians, making it a strong choice for lean, sunny sites where turfgrass fails.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in shallow standing water or saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; three-way sedge is the only living species in its genus and grows naturally along pond and lake margins across nearly all of North America.
directions: Plant divisions in shallow standing water (up to a few inches deep) or saturated soil in full sun to partial shade. Three-way sedge is an unmistakable native wetland plant, its jointed, hollow, upright stems and neat three-ranked leaves giving it a distinctly bamboo-like appearance unlike any other native sedge, an effect enhanced by small brownish flower spikelets that dangle along the upper stem in summer. It grows along the shallow margins of ponds, lakes, and slow streams across nearly the entire United States and southern Canada, spreading by rhizome to form an attractive colony that provides cover for waterfowl and other wetland wildlife. In a home pond or rain garden it makes a striking vertical accent at the water's edge, tolerating both standing water and saturated soil, and it can be divided in spring to control spread or to start new plantings elsewhere.

plant_note: Set plugs or rhizome divisions into saturated soil at the brackish or freshwater marsh edge in spring; keep soil consistently wet through establishment.
directions: This triangular-stemmed rush colonizes the mid-marsh zone of Gulf Coast estuaries and freshwater shorelines, where its dense rhizome mats resist erosion and filter runoff before it reaches open water. Historically its tough, pliable stems were split and woven for chair seats and baskets, giving the plant its common name. Plant into consistently wet to seasonally flooded soil in full sun; it tolerates brackish water up to moderate salinity and periodic tidal inundation better than most freshwater sedges. Use it in living-shoreline plantings alongside smooth cordgrass and black needlerush to build a graded marsh transition.

common_name: Thryallis (Galphimia, Rain of Gold, Golden Thryallis)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Galphimia glauca is one of the most heat-tolerant flowering shrubs for zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes, blooming continuously from spring through fall and tolerating brief frosts to about 25–28°F when established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Galphimia glauca (commonly called Thryallis, Rain of Gold, or Golden Thryallis) is a Mexican and Central American shrub that is one of the most reliably blooming and low-maintenance flowering shrubs for Gulf Coast and South Texas zone 8–10 landscapes — producing a nearly continuous shower of small, five-petaled, bright golden-yellow flowers on terminal spikes from spring through fall (and sometimes year-round in zone 10+). The effect of hundreds of small golden flowers covering the fine-textured, blue-green foliage is spectacular and sustained, unlike many flowering shrubs that bloom only briefly. Thryallis tolerates heat, humidity, and drought exceptionally well once established, requires minimal fertilization, and is rarely bothered by pests or diseases — the combination of beauty, durability, and low maintenance makes it one of the finest choices for reliable color in challenging Southern landscapes. The shrub grows into a well-behaved, rounded mound (4–8 feet tall and wide over time) without aggressive spreading. Excellent as a specimen, mass planting, or informal hedge. Freezes to the ground in hard winters in zone 8 but resprouts from roots with vigor; essentially evergreen in zone 9b–12.

common_name: Thryallis (Shower of Gold, Rain of Gold)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; thryallis is a fast-growing, drought-tolerant Mexican native shrub producing masses of small, brilliant-yellow flowers on gracefully arching branches nearly year-round in warm climates — one of the most reliable and cheerful flowering shrubs for zone 9–12 Gulf Coast and tropical gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after flowering to maintain compact shape. Galphimia gracilis (thryallis, shower of gold, or rain of gold) is a graceful, fast-growing, shrubby Mexican native in the Malpighiaceae family — one of the most reliably cheerful and floriferous flowering shrubs for zone 8–11 Gulf Coast and tropical gardens. The plant produces long, arching branches tipped with clusters of small (1/2-inch), five-petaled, brilliant golden-yellow flowers produced abundantly almost year-round in warm, frost-free climates — hence the evocative common names 'shower of gold' and 'rain of gold.' In zone 9–11, thryallis blooms nearly continuously from spring through fall, pausing only during the coldest months. The fine-textured foliage, graceful, fountain-like habit, and prolific golden flower production make it outstanding for mixed borders, foundation plantings, and as a flowering accent in drought-tolerant landscapes. It is also highly attractive to butterflies. Thryallis is more cold-hardy than many Mexican tropical shrubs, surviving brief dips to about 25°F once established in zone 8b; it dies back in cold winters but regrows from the root. A tremendously reliable and low-maintenance choice for hot, sunny, dry gardens throughout the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall; space 5-6 ft apart for a solid privacy screen.
directions: Thuja Green Giant is a fast-growing evergreen conifer widely used as a living privacy hedge, adding several feet of dense, rich green foliage each year. Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil, spacing plants 5 to 6 feet apart for a continuous screen. Water regularly the first season to establish deep roots; once mature it tolerates heat, humidity, and brief drought. Its naturally pyramidal habit rarely needs pruning, though it takes shearing well if a formal shape is desired. It resists deer browsing and most pests.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sunny, well-drained spot.
directions: Thuja Virginian is a compact arborvitae hybrid that offers the dense evergreen screening of Green Giant in a more manageable size for smaller yards. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water consistently through the first growing season to establish. Its tight, upright pyramidal form makes an excellent privacy hedge or specimen without heavy pruning. Mature plants tolerate heat and humidity and stand up to deer better than many evergreens. Mulch the root zone to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil and full sun.
directions: Thumbelina is a charming dwarf zinnia and 1963 All-America Selections winner, producing abundant cheerful blooms in a wide range of colors on compact plants. Direct sow after the last frost in warm soil and full sun, thinning seedlings for good airflow. Its small stature suits containers, edging, and the front of borders. Deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming through summer and into fall. Water at the base to reduce foliar disease, and enjoy the pollinators the flowers attract.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted softwood cuttings in early spring or fall into average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Thunberg spirea roots readily from cuttings and establishes quickly.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; Thunberg spirea is among the earliest-blooming of all spireas, opening masses of tiny, five-petaled white flowers along slender, arching branches in very early spring, often before or alongside forsythia, giving rise to its baby's-breath-like common name. Fine-textured, narrow blue-green leaves follow the bloom and often color soft yellow-orange in fall before dropping. The fountain-like, twiggy habit is best left unsheared and only lightly thinned right after flowering, removing a portion of the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep the shrub airy and floriferous rather than dense and shaded out. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and is a reliable, low-fuss flowering shrub for foundation plantings, informal hedges, and mixed borders.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or divide established crowns in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Thunberg's bush clover dies back to woody crowns each winter and may appear dead long into spring before new growth emerges — do not prune until new growth confirms the crown is alive. It grows very rapidly each spring. The cultivar Gibraltar is the most widely grown, with particularly deep rose-purple flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Thunberg's bush clover is one of the most spectacular late-season perennials available, producing dense, cascading wands of small, rosy-pink to rose-purple pea flowers in August and September — when almost nothing else in the garden is blooming with this abundance — on long, gracefully arching branches that create a weeping, fountain-like form of exceptional elegance. Each individual stem carries hundreds of small flowers in a dense, continuous spike, and a single established plant produces dozens of such stems that cascade toward the ground under their own weight, creating a foamy, waterfall effect of pink bloom that can span 5-7 feet. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves soil over time. Native to China and Japan, it dies back to the woody crown each winter and emerges late in spring, growing rapidly to blooming size by midsummer. Extraordinary for filling the late summer gap in the perennial border with a dramatic, long-lasting display highly attractive to bees and butterflies.

common_name: Thunberg's Daylily (Late-Blooming Fragrant Yellow Species Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Thunberg's daylily blooms notably later than most species and hybrid daylilies, extending the bloom season into midsummer, and its flowers open in late afternoon and stay open into evening.
directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Native to Japan and Korea, Hemerocallis thunbergii is a tall wild species bearing lightly fragrant, lemon-yellow flowers held well above the foliage on slender scapes, blooming later in the season than most daylilies and, unusually, opening in late afternoon and remaining open into the evening rather than closing by dusk like typical daytime-blooming daylilies. Its late bloom time makes it a useful parent for extending daylily flowering into midsummer and a valuable collector's plant in its own right. The clump forms a tidy, upright mass of grassy foliage and is slow to spread, rarely needing division more than once every several years to remain vigorous and floriferous.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Thunberg's jack-in-the-pulpit has unusually long, thread-like extensions trailing from its hooded spathe, a distinctive feature best appreciated planted where it can be viewed up close.
directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Thunberg's jack-in-the-pulpit has unusually long, thread-like extensions trailing from its hooded spathe, a distinctive feature best appreciated planted where it can be viewed up close. Arisaema thunbergii is a Japanese woodland aroid with glossy, divided, umbrella-like leaves and a dark purple-black to green hooded flower (spathe) in spring, drawn out into a remarkably long, whip-like tail that can trail six inches or more beyond the hood — one of the most dramatic flower forms among cultivated Arisaema. It is a choice specialty plant for a shaded woodland or collector's garden, best massed with other Arisaema species and woodland ephemerals for a layered spring display, followed by a spike of bright red berries in fall. Like other Arisaema, all plant parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are irritating if chewed, so site away from areas where pets or children might sample the showy berries.

common_name: Thunder Cloud Texas Sage (Deep-Purple Compact Cenizo Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–8.0), lean soil in full sun; Thunder Cloud absolutely requires excellent drainage — it will not tolerate standing water or heavy wet clay, and root rot in poorly drained soil is the primary cause of failure in humid Gulf South gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Thunder Cloud is one of the most compact and richly colored Texas sage (cenizo) cultivars — producing the species' characteristic silvery-gray, small, soft-textured foliage on a more restrained 3–4 foot plant, with deep purple-violet flowers that are more saturated and darker than the typical medium-purple of the species and many other cultivars. The compact habit makes Thunder Cloud proportionate for typical residential borders and containers where the sprawling, larger selections would overgrow the planting space. Like all cenizo, Thunder Cloud blooms in remarkable, synchronized flushes triggered by periods of high humidity or moisture after dry weather — the sudden appearance of masses of purple flowers across an entire planting following a rain or fog event is one of the most dramatic of Gulf South garden phenomena. The silvery foliage is attractive year-round — the pale gray-silver leaf color provides an effective contrast to green or dark foliage companions. Leucophyllum requires excellent drainage — in the humid Gulf South east of San Antonio/Houston, site in raised beds, berms, or rocky slopes where water moves away from roots quickly. Once established in appropriate drainage conditions, Thunder Cloud requires virtually no supplemental watering or fertilization. An outstanding choice for xeriscaping, reflected-heat positions, and caliche/alkaline soils where other ornamental shrubs struggle.

plant_note: Set out divisions or transplants in spring into full sun and well-drained soil, allowing room for the tall clump and its billowing flower panicles.
directions: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in full sun on average to sandy soil; established clumps tolerate both drought and occasional wet spells, making this a forgiving choice for open beds and meadow-style plantings. Cut the prior season's stems back in late winter before new growth emerges. Sturdy blue-green blades stay upright through summer storms and are topped in late summer by an unusually dense, dark, cloud-like haze of tiny flowers that gives the cultivar its name, followed by tan seed heads that persist for winter interest and birds.

plant_note: Plant after the last frost in spring in a hot, sunny location.
directions: Thunderstruck Coral Boom is a fast-growing crape myrtle that produces large panicles of vivid coral-pink blooms from early summer into fall. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; more sun means more flowers and better mildew resistance. Its multi-season interest includes attractive exfoliating bark in winter and colorful fall foliage. Prune in late winter to remove crossing branches and shape the canopy, avoiding heavy topping. Water regularly while establishing, after which it becomes notably heat- and drought-tolerant.

plant_note: Plant after the last frost in a warm, sunny spot.
directions: Thunderstruck Rumblin' Red is a crape myrtle celebrated for its fiery red summer blooms and strong year-round interest. Site it in full sun in well-drained soil, where abundant light maximizes flowering and helps prevent powdery mildew. The dark-tinged foliage and smooth exfoliating bark add appeal beyond the long bloom season. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain a tree-like structure rather than topping it hard. Once established it is quite tolerant of heat and dry conditions, needing supplemental water only in extended droughts.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; thyme-leaf fuchsia is a Mexican cloud-forest species that appreciates cooler summer conditions and consistent moisture.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; thyme-leaf fuchsia is a Mexican cloud-forest species that appreciates cooler summer conditions and consistent moisture. Fine, small, thyme-like leaves clothe delicate, arching branches studded nearly year-round with small, slender, pale pink to rose-red flowers, giving the shrub an airy, refined texture distinct from the larger-leaved, gaudier hybrid fuchsias. Native to oak and pine-oak woodlands of Mexico and Central America, it is more heat-tolerant than many species fuchsias while still preferring the dappled shade and humidity of a woodland setting, making it a good choice for a shaded border in warmer climates where typical fuchsias struggle. Pinch growing tips periodically to encourage a bushy habit and continued bloom, and protect from hard freezes in marginal zones.

plant_note: Root tip cuttings or 'log' sections in moist potting mix or water at 70–80°F; in zone 10–12 plant outdoors in partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained fertile soil. Grow as a container plant in colder climates, bringing indoors before frost.
directions: Root tip cuttings or stem sections ('logs') in moist potting mix or water at 70–80°F, then plant outdoors in partial shade in moist, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile, well-drained soil in zone 10–12; the ti plant has been a sacred and culturally significant plant in Pacific Island and Hawaiian cultures for millennia, prized for its deep burgundy, pink, green, or tricolor strap leaves and grown outdoors year-round in tropical gardens. Bright filtered shade deepens the leaf coloration — full sun bleaches the colors and deep shade reduces vibrancy and causes leggy growth. Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged and fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer during the growing season. Outside zone 10–12, grow as a houseplant or deck container in the highest indirect light available and bring indoors before the first frost.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a warm, sheltered location with high humidity. Prefers rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. In zone 9, site against a south-facing wall or in a container that can be moved indoors during cold snaps.
directions: Propagate from softwood or semi-hardwood cuttings in summer, keeping them warm and humid until well rooted before potting on. Transplant to the garden only in frost-free zones 10-11, or grow in a large container in zone 9 and overwinter indoors above 55°F. Maintain consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and fertilize monthly with a balanced tropical-plant fertilizer throughout the growing season. The pinwheel-shaped white flowers bloom repeatedly in warm weather and are at their most fragrant in the evening, making this tree a standout near patios and entryways.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tibetan cherry is grown primarily for its extraordinary bark — not its flowers. Site it where the trunk is visible in winter and where you will brush against it to feel the satiny surface.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tibetan cherry from western China is grown almost exclusively for its extraordinary, burnished, mahogany-red to copper-brown bark that peels in horizontal strips to reveal gleaming, polished, metallic-looking new bark beneath — arguably the most ornamental bark of any tree in temperate gardening. The effect is amplified in winter sun when the bark catches raking light and glows like burnished copper. The flowers are white and relatively small, appearing with or just before the narrow, willow-like leaves in spring. The dark red fruits are small but attractive to birds. Position where winter sun will illuminate the trunk, and keep it clear of competing vegetation at the base. The bark develops its best coloring as the tree matures — young trees are less impressive. A specimen tree for its stem and bark character.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs into humus-rich, well-drained soil in spring, allowing room for arching, suckering growth.
directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, where this Chinese relative of spirea produces long, gracefully arching canes lined with toothed, birch-like leaves. In late spring and early summer, drooping racemes of small tubular pink flowers with reddish calyces dangle along the branches, drawing bees and giving a soft, cottage-garden effect beneath high canopy trees. It spreads slowly by suckers to form an informal thicket, making it useful for naturalizing along a shaded woodland edge or shrub border. Thin out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering to maintain an open, fountain-like habit.

plant_note: Plant divisions or offsets in spring in fertile, humus-rich, evenly moist, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this evergreen woodland groundcover resents heat and drought and needs consistent moisture and cool root conditions to thrive.
directions: Plant divisions or offsets in spring in fertile, humus-rich, evenly moist, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this evergreen woodland groundcover resents heat and drought and needs consistent moisture and cool root conditions to thrive. Ypsilandra thibetica forms tight rosettes of glossy, strap-shaped evergreen leaves from which upright spikes of small, intensely fragrant white flowers with prominent purple-black anthers emerge in late winter to early spring, well before most other woodland perennials break dormancy. A relative of Helonias and native to moist forests of the eastern Himalaya and southwestern China, it slowly forms a dense, weed-suppressing colony at the front of a shaded border or along a woodland path, and its evergreen foliage and deer, rabbit, and slug resistance make it a useful year-round groundcover where hardy. Provide a steady mulch of leaf litter to buffer soil temperature and moisture, and avoid sites that bake in summer sun or dry out between waterings.

common_name: Tickled Pink Veronica (Compact Long-Blooming Pink Spike Speedwell)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; deadheading spent spikes promptly encourages a strong repeat bloom later in the season.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid heavy, poorly drained ground where veronica is prone to crown rot over winter. Tickled Pink is a compact spike speedwell bred for a long season of clear pink flower spikes held upright over neat, dark green foliage, blooming from late spring into summer and again in fall if deadheaded promptly after the first flush. Its tidy, well-branched habit needs no staking and suits the front to middle of a sunny perennial border, where it draws bees and butterflies over an extended bloom period. Established plants are drought-tolerant once rooted and benefit from division every three to four years to maintain vigor and flowering, since older clumps can become woody and bloom less freely at the center.

plant_note: Sow in fall or early spring; a reliable wildflower for meadows.
directions: Scatter tidy tips seed on cool, moist soil in fall or early spring and rake in lightly. This California native produces cheerful yellow daisies tipped in white that attract native bees and butterflies. It thrives on lean soil with minimal water once established, making it ideal for wildflower meadows and drought-tolerant plantings. Allow some flowers to set seed for reliable self-sowing in future seasons.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tiffany is a mid-to-late season camellia blooming January through March in zone 9, providing winter interest when many other landscape plants are dormant.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tiffany is a magnificent large-flowered Camellia japonica cultivar producing extremely large (4.5–5 inch), semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a distinctive warm orchid-pink to light lavender-pink color with slightly wavy, cupped petals surrounding a prominent cluster of bright-yellow stamens. The large, open, somewhat informal flower form and the distinctive orchid-pink color (neither the deep red of Mathotiana nor the pure pink of Debutante, but a warm intermediate with lavender tones) make Tiffany instantly recognizable and uniquely beautiful among red and pink camellia cultivars. Tiffany was selected from a seedling in California and has become one of the most popular and widely grown large-flowered japonica cultivars in American gardens. The blooms are produced mid to late season (January through March in zone 9) on an upright, vigorous shrub that can reach 6–12 feet with excellent annual growth rate. As with all Camellia japonica cultivars in zone 9, plant in dappled shade or morning sun with afternoon shade; consistent moisture and acidic soil are essential for healthy growth and maximum bloom production. Supplement iron with chelated iron fertilizer if leaves show yellowing between veins (chlorosis) — a common sign of iron deficiency in alkaline Gulf South soils.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container plants in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; tiger aloe naturally grows in rock crevices and the partial shade of cliff faces in its native South Africa and is one of the few aloes that actively prefers some shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade — unlike most aloes that demand full sun, tiger aloe is unique in preferring partial shade or bright indirect light, making it one of the most valuable and unusual succulents for shaded dry garden conditions. The compact, triangular, dark green leaves arranged in three ranks are beautifully marked with irregular white horizontal bands and spots — a striking, ornamental pattern that gives rise to the common names tiger and partridge breast. The salmon-pink to coral-red tubular flowers on tall stalks appear in winter and spring, providing color when the garden needs it most. Compact enough for windowsills, containers, and small garden pockets; it produces offsets slowly to form small clusters. Native to the scrubby karoo shrubland and rocky hillside outcrops of South Africa. Outstanding as a houseplant in bright indirect light or as an outdoor container plant in shade in Gulf Coast zone 9–11.

common_name: Tiger Eyes Sumac (Golden Cutleaf Staghorn Sumac)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun in spring or fall; because Tiger Eyes is grafted onto straight-species rootstock, remove any green-leaved suckers that arise below the graft union, since they will overtake the golden scion if left to grow.
directions: Tiger Eyes is a compact sport of staghorn sumac selected for deeply cut, lacy, fern-like foliage that emerges chartreuse-yellow in spring, holds bright gold through summer on contrasting pink-red leaf stalks, then finishes with fiery orange-scarlet fall color, giving three seasons of striking foliage color on a shrub roughly half the size of the wild species. It still spreads by root suckers to form a colony over time, though far less aggressively than the species, and its fuzzy, cone-shaped red berry clusters persist into winter and feed birds. Give it some afternoon shade in hot climates, since the pale gold leaves scorch more readily than green foliage in intense summer sun; this cultivar is best suited to cooler regions and can struggle with the combination of extreme heat and humidity found deep in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; each exotic three-petaled flower lasts only one day but new buds open in succession over weeks. The vivid blooms come in yellow, orange, red, pink, and white, typically with a heavily spotted or blotched center cup. Plant in groups of a dozen or more for a showy display from midsummer into fall. In zones colder than 8, dig bulbs after first frost, dry thoroughly, and store in paper bags in a cool, frost-free location.

plant_note: Divide offset clumps or root stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; tiger jaws clumps steadily with age, so mature plants are easy to split into several new pots.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering only after the soil has dried out and cutting back further in winter. Faucaria tigrina (tiger jaws) is a South African mesemb related to Lithops, forming pairs of thick, triangular, blue-green leaves edged with soft, white, tooth-like projections that interlock across the opposing leaf pairs like an open jaw, giving the plant its common name; the 'teeth' are soft and harmless rather than sharp spines. Individual rosette pairs are short-lived but the plant continuously produces new pairs from the center, gradually building into a low, spreading clump of interlocking 'jaws' over a few years. Large, daisy-like, bright yellow flowers open in the afternoon sun in autumn, closing again by evening, and are a reliable bloomer even on young plants given enough direct light. Keep the winter rest period dry, since like most South African mesembs it is far more prone to rot from overwatering in cool weather than from drought.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep and 12 inches apart in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light partial shade in early spring; tiger lily multiplies rapidly from the characteristic black bulbils that form along the leaf axils in summer and can be planted immediately for new plants.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep and 12 inches apart in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light partial shade in early spring; tiger lily multiplies rapidly from the characteristic black bulbils that form along the leaf axils in summer and can be planted immediately for new plants. Lilium lancifolium is the showiest, most vigorous, and most carefree of all garden lilies, producing 4-6 foot stems in midsummer with up to 20 pendant, strongly reflexed flowers of vivid orange with black spots and recurved petals that are among the most dramatic mid-summer ornamentals in any garden; individual plants bloom for 2-3 weeks and clumps increase rapidly. This lily can carry Lily Symptomless Virus without showing symptoms and can transmit it to other lily species via aphids — plant it away from other Lilium species, especially the more susceptible Asiatic and Oriental hybrids.

common_name: Tiger Stanhopea (Downy Stanhopea, Inverted Orchid, Upside-Down Orchid)
plant_note: MUST grow in an open slat basket or mesh basket — NEVER in a solid pot; Stanhopea's flower spikes grow downward and penetrate through the basket bottom to bloom below the plant. A solid pot prevents flowering entirely. Use coarse bark medium. Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun. Water regularly in active growth; reduce slightly in winter. The flowers last only 3–5 days but the fragrance is extraordinary. Bloom season is summer. Protect from temperatures below 50°F. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in a slatted or open-mesh hanging basket in bright indirect to filtered direct light — Tiger Stanhopea MUST be grown in an open-bottom container because its flower spikes emerge from the base of the pseudobulbs and grow downward through the basket medium to bloom below the plant — a pot with a solid bottom prevents flowering. Stanhopea tigrina is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to Mexico (Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas, Puebla) in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most fascinating orchids in cultivation for several reasons: its extraordinary downward-blooming habit, its large and complex flowers, and its remarkable fragrance. The plant produces oval pseudobulbs with broad, heavily-veined leaves, and in summer, one to four flower spikes per pseudobulb emerge from the base, push through the bark medium, and emerge hanging downward below the basket — where they open simultaneously into 3–8 of the most bizarre and dramatic flowers in the orchid family. Each flower is large (4–5 inches), waxy, and complex in shape: the sepals and petals are pale yellow heavily spotted and blotched with maroon-purple spots (the 'tigrina' — tiger-spotted), with a sculptural, two-part, boat and hook-shaped lip. The fragrance is powerful, complex, and sweet-spicy (vanilla, cinnamon, and eucalyptus are described), used by male Eulaema bees to attract females. Flowers last 3–5 days. Non-toxic.

common_name: Tiki Torch Caladium (Flame-Patterned Red-Orange Sun-Tolerant Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Tiki Torch is a sun-tolerant strap-leaf caladium with flame-like red-orange coloring radiating up the leaf.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to nearly full sun with consistent moisture; strap-leaf caladiums tolerate more direct sun than fancy-leaf types. Tiki Torch bears vivid red-orange coloring that radiates up each narrow, strap-shaped leaf in a flame-like pattern, a fiery, warm-toned caladium well suited to sunnier spots than most fancy-leaf selections tolerate. Its bold color and sun tolerance make it a strong choice for containers and mixed beds that get more than dappled light. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.

common_name: Tiki Torch Coneflower (Single Vivid Orange Fragrant Big Sky Series Echinacea)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Tiki Torch, part of the Big Sky hybrid series, bears vivid orange, spicy-fragrant flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Tiki Torch, part of the Big Sky hybrid coneflower series, bears large, single, vivid orange flowers with a distinctive spicy fragrance not found in most coneflower cultivars, on tall, sturdy stems held well above the foliage. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall, attracting bees, butterflies, and goldfinches that feed on the dried seed heads through winter. Deadhead to prolong bloom or leave seed heads standing for winter bird interest, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade.
directions: Tilt-A-Swirl is a bigleaf hydrangea whose mophead blooms shift through pink, red, and green as the season progresses, with flower color influenced by soil pH. Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil where it gets morning sun and shade during the hottest part of the day. Keep the soil consistently moist, especially in summer, as this species wilts quickly when dry. It blooms on old and new wood, so avoid heavy pruning; simply remove spent flowers and dead stems in late winter. Amend soil with aluminum sulfate for bluer tones or lime for pinker ones.

common_name: Timeless Beauty Southern Magnolia (Compact Heavy-Blooming Selection)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Timeless Beauty is a compact southern magnolia selection noted for especially heavy, reliable flowering at a younger age than the species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Timeless Beauty bears the classic large, creamy-white, lemon-scented southern magnolia blooms in heavy abundance from a younger age than many seedling-grown trees, on a more compact, densely branched form than the largest species specimens, making it a strong choice where a full-sized magnolia's eventual scale is a concern but heavy flowering is still wanted. Water deeply during establishment, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune only to remove dead or damaged wood, since magnolias need little routine pruning.

common_name: Timeless Treasure Heuchera (Silver-Overlay Rose-Veined Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Timeless Treasure bears large, ruffled leaves in silvery-rose overlaid on a purple base, with contrasting darker veining that traces each leaf in a lace-like pattern, giving the foliage a rich, layered, almost painted look that holds up well through the growing season. Its bold leaf size and dramatic coloring make it a strong accent plant in shaded containers and border fronts. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Tineke rubber tree holds its cream-and-green variegation best with consistent bright indirect light and needs protection from direct hot sun.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Tineke rubber tree holds its cream-and-green variegation best with consistent bright indirect light and needs protection from direct hot sun. Large, glossy, leathery leaves are marbled in shades of dark green, gray-green, and creamy white with pink-tinged new growth, giving this variegated rubber tree cultivar a soft, marbled color pattern quite different from the solid dark green of the standard species. Grown as a tall, architectural floor plant indoors, it develops into a substantial small tree over years, with new leaves unfurling from a distinctive protective red sheath that drops away as each leaf expands. Wipe dust from the large leaves periodically to keep pores clear, water when the top inch of potting mix dries, and rotate the pot occasionally for even, symmetrical growth.

common_name: Tinkerbell Agapanthus (Dwarf Variegated Pale Blue Lily of the Nile)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Tinkerbell is a dwarf, variegated agapanthus well suited to container growing and small border spaces.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, in a container or garden bed. Tinkerbell forms a compact, dwarf clump of narrow, strappy leaves edged in a crisp cream-white variegation, giving the plant ornamental value even before bloom, topped in summer by rounded clusters of pale, soft blue, trumpet-shaped flowers on short scapes held just above the foliage. Its small scale and attractive variegated foliage make it especially well suited to containers, small borders, and edging where larger agapanthus cultivars would be out of proportion. In regions colder than its hardiness range, grow it in a container and bring it into a cool, frost-free space for winter, or apply heavy mulch over the crown if planted in the ground near the edge of its hardiness zone. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering declines.

common_name: Tiny Rubies Dianthus (Miniature Double Rose-Pink Cheddar Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; Tiny Rubies is a miniature cheddar pink forming a very dense, low mat.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Tiny Rubies forms an exceptionally dense, low mat of fine, silvery-blue foliage smothered each spring in tiny, fully double, rose-pink flowers, its miniature scale making it well suited to rock gardens, gravel paths, and the edges of stone walls where larger dianthus would look out of proportion. Like other cheddar pinks it thrives in lean, sharply drained, rocky-to-sandy soil and shows good heat tolerance compared to alpine dianthus species. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring; seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Tiny Tim is a compact, honey-scented sweet alyssum that stays covered in tiny flowers all season with no need to shear back. Surface sow the seed in early spring since light aids germination, pressing it into the soil without covering. Grow in full sun to part shade in average, well-drained soil where it forms a fragrant, spreading groundcover. It withstands heat and drought while drawing beneficial insects and pollinators. Use it to edge beds, tuck between pavers, or spill from containers and hanging baskets.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil; ideal for containers or small beds.
directions: Tiny Tower is a very slow-growing dwarf Alberta spruce that keeps a naturally dense, narrow pyramidal shape without shearing, making it perfect for small gardens, entryways, and containers. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and provide good air circulation to discourage spider mites, its main pest. Water regularly the first two seasons and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. In hot climates give it some afternoon shade to prevent needle scorch. Its compact evergreen form also serves as a living holiday tree.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Tiny Wine's compact size fits foundation plantings and small borders where larger ninebark cultivars like Diabolo would quickly outgrow the space.
directions: Tiny Wine is a compact ninebark selection carrying the same deep wine-red to purple maple-like foliage as larger dark-leaved cultivars but on a rounded shrub roughly half the size, staying well under 5 feet tall and wide. Clusters of small white-to-pink spring flowers draw pollinators and are followed by reddish seed capsules, while the exfoliating bark provides winter interest once the leaves drop. Like other ninebarks it tolerates a very wide range of soil conditions, including clay and periodic flooding, and full sun brings out the darkest, richest foliage color; renewal-prune by removing some of the oldest stems at the base every few years to keep the plant full and vigorous.

plant_note: Soak seed overnight and sow deep; resents transplanting so direct sow.
directions: Soak the large seed overnight and sow about half an inch deep directly in the garden after frost. This dwarf, non-trailing variety produces a cheerful mix of yellow, red, and orange blooms held above the foliage. Both the peppery leaves and flowers are edible, making it a favorite for salads and companion planting. Grow in full sun and lean soil, since rich ground yields lots of leaves but fewer flowers.

common_name: Tipu Tree (Pride of Bolivia, Rosewood of Bolivia, Tipu)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Tipu Tree grows rapidly in zone 9-10 and can add 3–5 feet of height per year in good conditions. It is semi-evergreen to briefly deciduous in zone 9, dropping leaves in late winter before the spring leaf flush and peak bloom. The flower display occurs just after (or just before) the new leaf flush — the entire tree covered in yellow-orange flowers is a spectacular annual display. The distinctive single-winged seed pods (samaras) are ornamental. Root system is invasive — plant away from paving and structures.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Tipu Tree grows most vigorously in full sun and well-drained soil, becoming drought-tolerant once established. Tipuana tipu is a fast-growing, large, semi-evergreen to deciduous ornamental tree native to Bolivia, Argentina, and Brazil in the legume family (Fabaceae), monotypic in its genus. The tree has become one of the most widely planted street and shade trees in Mediterranean-climate cities worldwide (particularly in California, Spain, Argentina, South Africa, and Australia) and in zone 9-11 Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes. In late spring to early summer, the tree produces its annual bloom: an explosion of small, pea-like flowers in rich apricot-yellow to golden-orange covering the entire canopy — the display can be so dense that the foliage is temporarily obscured by the flowers, and the falling petals create a golden carpet beneath the tree. The flowers are followed by distinctive single-winged samara seed pods that spin as they fall. The broad, spreading canopy (often exceeding the tree's height in spread) provides exceptional shade on large lawns and public spaces. The compound leaves — each composed of 13–21 paired leaflets — are a fine-textured, light green that dances in the breeze. A magnificent specimen tree for large residential and public zone 9-11 landscapes.

common_name: Titan Annual Vinca (Large-Flowered Vigorous Vinca Series)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; this series shows good resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight, a serious fungal disease of annual vinca in hot, humid conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; overly wet or poorly drained soil quickly leads to root and stem rot. Titan is a vigorous annual vinca series bred for unusually large, bold flowers relative to plant size, along with the same excellent heat and drought tolerance and good disease resistance typical of modern vinca breeding. It produces a dense, mounding plant covered in wide, flat-faced blooms across a range of colors from late spring through frost, thriving in the hottest, sunniest, most exposed parts of a Gulf South garden where many other bedding annuals fail. It requires minimal maintenance beyond routine watering during establishment and is an excellent low-water, low-input choice for mass plantings, medians, and containers.

common_name: Titan's Glory Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Deep Violet-Blue Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and sharply drained soil; Titan's Glory won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal for its huge, richly colored blooms and vigorous growth.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil in full sun; soggy conditions invite rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Titan's Glory earned the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal for its exceptionally large, deep violet-blue flowers with excellent form and substance, held on tall, sturdy, well-branched stems that carry an unusually high bud count for a long bloom season. Its vigorous growth and heavy increase have made it a widely grown garden and exhibition standard for decades. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans; good drainage is essential to prevent rhizome rot.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring as growth begins; they establish quickly and bloom in their first season from divisions.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained shade; toad lily is an elegant late-season bloomer that produces exotic-looking, orchid-like flowers in white, purple, or lilac with dark spots from late summer through fall. The arching stems with clasping leaves create a graceful, architectural presence throughout the season. Consistent moisture is essential — plants decline in dry soil; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and temperature. Divide every 3–4 years in early spring to manage the slowly spreading clumps.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, compacted or disturbed, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; toad rush is a cosmopolitan annual of seasonally moist, disturbed, and compacted ground — path edges, tire ruts, pond margins, and mudflats. It establishes and sets seed rapidly before conditions dry out.
directions: Scatter seed on moist, compacted, disturbed soil at the margins of ponds, seasonal wetlands, and wet disturbed areas; toad rush is a tiny, nearly grass-like annual rush that grows naturally in the muddy margins of ponds, seasonal pools, tire tracks, path edges, and any temporarily moist, disturbed ground across virtually all of North America and most of the world. The very small stature and wiry stems bear tiny flowers along most of their length. While not ornamental, toad rush is an important ecological pioneer plant that quickly colonizes bare, moist, disturbed soil before other species establish, providing early ground cover and preventing erosion. The tiny seeds are eaten by various shorebirds and wading birds that forage in its typical shallow-water and mudflat habitat. It self-sows automatically in any appropriate seasonal mud habitat without management.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; never collect toadshade from wild populations — purchase only nursery-propagated plants. The stalkless (sessile) flower sits directly atop the three mottled leaves.
directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions in fall in humus-rich, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — toadshade trillium is one of the most distinctive of the eastern native trilliums, recognizable immediately by its sessile (stalkless) dark maroon flower that sits directly upon the three large, dramatically mottled leaves without an intermediate stalk. The heavily mottled, silver-and-green leaves are among the most beautiful of any native spring wildflower, providing ornamental interest even before the flowers open. A wide natural range stretches from New York west to Kansas and south to Georgia, growing in rich, moist hardwood forests and along stream banks. Like all trilliums, toadshade takes 7 years to bloom from seed — always purchase nursery-propagated plants and never collect from wild populations. The flowers attract small flies and beetles as pollinators; the seeds are dispersed by ants. An outstanding native wildflower for the shaded woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Toffee Chip is a slower-spreading, more compact ajuga than older cultivars, better behaved in small borders.
directions: Plant in average, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; good drainage is important, since ajuga crowns can rot in constantly waterlogged soil despite the plant's general preference for moisture. Toffee Chip forms a low, dense mat of small, rounded leaves in a distinctive bronze-caramel color edged with a creamy border, a warmer, more muted palette than the deep purple or burgundy tones of older ajuga cultivars, with short spikes of blue flowers rising just above the foliage in spring. It spreads more slowly and stays more compact than many older, more aggressive ajuga cultivars, making it a better-behaved choice for small borders, rock gardens, and edging where a running groundcover could become a nuisance. It tolerates foot traffic lightly and needs little care beyond dividing and replanting congested patches every few years.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Toffee Twist produces fine, curling, warm bronze-copper foliage that forms a graceful cascading mound, an unusual foliage color for a shade-tolerant sedge.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Toffee Twist is a distinctive New Zealand sedge grown for its fine, thread-like, warm bronze-copper foliage that curls and cascades into a loose, tousled, fountain-like mound, an unusual warm color that contrasts beautifully with green- and blue-leaved shade perennials like hostas and ferns. It tolerates a range of light from fairly sunny to shaded sites and adapts to both moist and moderately dry soil once established, needing only an occasional combing-out of old, dead foliage to keep the mound looking fresh. Its arching, tactile texture makes it a favorite for containers and border edges where its curling leaves can be appreciated up close.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring as shoots emerge; tokudama hosta is slow-growing but extremely long-lived once established. Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Takes 3–5 years to reach mature size — plan to leave it undisturbed long-term.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tokudama hosta is one of the most prized species hostas in cultivation, valued for its exceptionally deeply cupped, puckered, glaucous-blue to blue-gray leaves that are among the most intensely textured of all hostas. The deep cupping and puckering of the heavy, corrugated leaf surface gives an almost sculptural quality that makes each plant a focal point in the shade garden. It is a slow-growing hosta species that takes several years to reach full size, but its garden longevity and unique foliage quality make it worth the wait. Several important hosta cultivars derive from this species, including the famous 'Halcyon' (via hybridization). Pale lavender flowers in mid-summer. Slug damage is less severe on the heavily puckered, waxy leaves than on smooth-leaved hostas.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant after frost into part shade.
directions: Tom Thumb Blend is a compact, shade-loving balsam standing 12 to 16 inches tall with bushy plants that come alive with violet, white, and rose double flowers. Start seed indoors and barely cover it, keeping soil warm, then transplant after frost into part shade and rich, moist soil. Bumblebees and hummingbirds are drawn to the array of blooms tucked along the stems. Keep the soil consistently moist, as balsam wilts quickly when dry. Its tidy size makes a charming centerpiece for shady beds and containers.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Tom Thumb crassula is a compact selection well suited to a small pot or dish garden.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Tom Thumb crassula is a compact selection well suited to a small pot or dish garden. Tightly stacked, triangular, blue-green leaves alternate up trailing stems in a distinctive braided, chain-like pattern, blushing red-edged in bright light, on a more compact and slower-growing selection than the straight species that suits a smaller container or succulent dish garden. Its tidy, manageable size and interesting stacked-leaf texture make it a popular choice for succulent arrangements and windowsill collections where a naturally compact plant is preferred over more sprawling species. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for the best red edging, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.
