Each flower is distinctly tricolored: the cream-white to pale yellow sepals and petals are densely spotted and blotched with maroon-brown to chestnut-brown markings, and the large, three-lobed lip is a vivid rose-purple to magenta — a striking, complex color pattern that makes the flower immediately recognizable. The flowers emit a pleasant, spicy-sweet fragrance, strongest in morning. The species is one parent of the large-flowered hybrid Vanda 'Rothschildiana' (V. coerulea × V. tricolor) and many other ornamental hybrids. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in spring or fall; trident maple is remarkably adaptable to urban conditions — compacted soils, air pollution, drought, heat, and alkaline soils — making it one of the most stress-tolerant small to medium deciduous trees available.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; trident maple is a small to medium-sized Chinese maple that has become one of the most valued urban and street trees in temperate regions for its exceptional toughness, adaptability, and multi-season ornamental character. The distinctive three-lobed leaves resemble a trident in silhouette, turn brilliant orange-red to burgundy in fall, and the exfoliating orange-tan bark on mature specimens is decorative in winter. Trident maple is one of the most popular species for bonsai cultivation, where its small leaves, fine branching, and easily trained habit produce classical specimens. As a landscape tree it is tolerant of heat, drought, alkaline soil, and urban pollution far beyond most maples — making it the preferred maple for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where standard sugar maple and red maple often struggle in the heat.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; trillium-leaf foamflower is native to moist Pacific Northwest conifer forests and, like other foamflowers, spreads gradually to form an attractive shaded groundcover.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; trillium-leaf foamflower is native to moist Pacific Northwest conifer forests and, like other foamflowers, spreads gradually to form an attractive shaded groundcover. Tiarella trifoliata differs from the familiar eastern Tiarella cordifolia in its distinctly three-parted, trillium-like leaflets rather than a single lobed leaf, with slender, airy spikes of small white to pale pink starry flowers rising above the foliage in late spring and early summer. It forms loose colonies in consistently moist, humus-rich forest soil, making it a good textural companion for ferns, vanilla leaf, and other Pacific Northwest woodland natives in a shaded garden. Keep soil evenly moist and mulched with leaf litter, and divide congested clumps in fall to propagate or maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant outdoors after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May and bring containers indoors before temperatures drop below 35°F in fall. In zone 10–11 Schefflera arboricola can remain outdoors year-round as a landscape shrub reaching 8–15 feet. In zone 9 it is best managed as a container specimen or porch plant — moved outdoors for the warm season and overwintered indoors. Prune leggy stems in spring to maintain bushy compact form; Schefflera responds well to pruning. Remove any all-green reversion shoots on variegated plants immediately to prevent them from overtaking the cream-variegated growth.
directions: Plant in bright indirect light to partial shade outdoors — Trinette Schefflera thrives in shade conditions where direct sun is absent or minimal, making it one of the most useful large foliage plants for covered patios, deep porches, and shaded landscape settings; Trinette is a variegated cultivar of Dwarf Umbrella Plant (Schefflera arboricola), producing the characteristic glossy, palmate, compound leaves of schefflera in a green-and-cream to yellow-green variegated form that provides significantly more ornamental interest than the plain green species. Each palmately compound leaf is composed of 7–9 leaflets radiating from a central point in the classic umbrella arrangement that gives the plant its common name, with the Trinette cultivar's cream-yellow variegation adding a bright, light-catching quality to the foliage that works especially well in shaded settings. As a patio or porch container plant in zone 9, Trinette Schefflera fills the role of a large, architectural foliage plant for shaded outdoor living spaces — providing a tropical, lush texture that transforms a covered porch or shaded patio into an outdoor room with lush, jungle-like plant material. The size and bold foliage make it a genuine statement plant for large containers on shaded patios, and it overwinters successfully as an indoor houseplant in bright indirect light.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry-to-average sandy or rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; triplet lily is dormant and completely dry in summer — do not water during summer dormancy or the corms will rot.
directions: Plant corms in fall in very well-drained, dry-to-average, sandy or rocky soil in full sun to partial shade — triplet lily is a spectacular western native bulb of California and Oregon grasslands and open woodlands, producing umbels of 15–30 funnel-shaped blue-violet to purple flowers (2 inches long) on 18–24 inch stems in late spring to early summer. The flowers are among the bluest of all native American wildflowers and provide important nectar for native bumblebees and long-tongued bees. The plant is entirely summer-dormant — it emerges in early spring, blooms, and then disappears as summer approaches, requiring dry summer conditions for healthy corm development (do not irrigate in summer). Excellent for naturalizing in dry, warm-summer climates in well-drained rocky or sandy soils — it multiplies steadily by corm offsets in appropriate conditions. An outstanding native bulb for Mediterranean-climate and dry western gardens.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 6-8 inches deep before ground freezes.
directions: Plant Triumph tulip bulbs in fall about six to eight inches deep and four to six inches apart in well-drained soil. This mid-season class offers sturdy stems and classic egg-shaped blooms in a vast color range, excellent for beds and cutting. Provide full sun and allow the foliage to yellow naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb. In warm climates pre-chill bulbs for ten to fourteen weeks before planting, or treat them as annuals.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings under mist or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; mussaenda flowers most prolifically in the warmest, most humid months and benefits from regular fertilization throughout the growing season to maintain vigor and continuous flower production.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; tropical dogwood (Ashanti blood, red flag bush) is a West African tropical shrub in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that creates one of the most spectacular and unusual flowering effects available in the tropical garden — the small, true yellow flowers are relatively inconspicuous, but each is surrounded by one or more greatly enlarged, modified, leaf-like, blood-red to rose-red calyx lobes (sepals) that function as the visual attractor, and in full flowering these large, papery, brilliantly colored bracts cover the entire plant in a mass of vivid red-orange or pink that resembles a bougainvillea in intensity. The Philippine white mussaenda (Mussaenda philippica) is a white-bracted form of similar effect. The bracts are produced most abundantly through the warm season. All parts of the plant are reportedly toxic if ingested. In zone 10–12 it grows as a large, evergreen, freely-branching shrub; in zone 9 it may be grown as a container specimen moved indoors in winter. An extraordinary tropical specimen for zone 10–12 gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock after last frost danger in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–12; Tropical Hydrangea is a fast-growing East African shrub or small tree that produces spectacular, large, drooping globular clusters of pink to deep rose flowers in winter and spring — resembling oversized hydrangea flower heads on a tropical tree — and is one of the most ornamental flowering trees for Gulf Coast and tropical gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Dombeya wallichii is fast growing and responds well to pruning after flowering to maintain a compact form — cut back one-third of the plant after each bloom cycle to encourage bushiness and the next flush of blooms. Dombeya wallichii (Tropical Hydrangea or Pinkball Tree) is a large, fast-growing evergreen to semi-deciduous shrub or small tree native to Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, and the East African highlands, where it grows at elevations of 3,000–7,000 feet in forest edges, clearings, and disturbed habitats. The large, pendulous, globular clusters of pink to deep rose, 5-petaled flowers closely resemble oversized hydrangea flower heads and appear dramatically in winter and early spring, often nearly obscuring the large, velvety, heart-shaped leaves. The dried, spent flower clusters remain attractively on the plant for weeks after petal fall, persisting as papery, straw-colored globes. Dombeya is a consistent performer in zones 9–12, flowering reliably in winter when few other large flowering shrubs are in bloom — making it exceptionally valuable for winter interest in Gulf Coast, Florida, and Southern California gardens. Mulch well, maintain consistent moisture, and fertilize monthly during the growing season for best flowering. Plants freeze to the ground in zone 9a frost events but typically regrow rapidly from the root crown.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost or direct sow after frost; in zones 9–11 cut plants back to 6 inches in late fall and early winter to interrupt the year-round bloom cycle and deter Monarch butterflies from overwintering rather than migrating.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost or sow directly after frost danger passes in well-drained, average soil in full sun; tropical milkweed produces orange-and-yellow bicolor flowers continuously from late spring through frost and is the most reliably available milkweed for Monarch butterfly gardeners in warm climates, serving as both a nectar source and larval host plant. In frost-free zones (9–11), cut plants back to 6 inches in November–January to remove OE parasite spores that accumulate on the foliage and to prevent Monarchs from staying put year-round rather than migrating — a critical management step that affects monarch population health. Plants regrow rapidly after cutting. Native milkweed species (A. incarnata, A. tuberosa) are preferable where they grow reliably.

plant_note: Direct sow outdoors after last frost or start indoors 6–8 weeks early; tropical sage self-sows prolifically in Gulf South gardens and often naturalized colonies require no replanting after the first year.
directions: Direct sow or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; tropical sage is a native of the southeastern US, Caribbean, and Mexico that produces a continuous display of loose spikes of two-lipped, brilliant scarlet flowers from late spring through frost — it is one of the finest hummingbird and butterfly plants available for southern gardens and thrives in partial shade where most salvias fail. Plants often self-sow freely to naturalize in Gulf South landscapes, maintaining a persistent colony that renews itself annually. 'Lady in Red' (compact, pure red) won an All-America Selections award; 'Coral Nymph' (bicolor coral and white) and 'Snow Nymph' (white) are popular alternatives. Deer-resistant.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; tropical snowball establishes quickly in warm weather and may bloom within 2 years from cutting-grown plants. It dies back after hard frost but re-sprouts from the roots in zone 9.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in zones 9-12; tropical snowball is one of the most spectacular flowering small trees for warm-climate gardens, producing enormous, round clusters of soft pink to deep pink flowers in late winter and spring when little else is in bloom. The large, heart-shaped leaves are bold and tropical. The pendant flower clusters hang like ornaments from the branches and are extraordinarily fragrant — filling the surrounding air with a sweet, honeyed perfume. Native to Madagascar, the tree is now widely planted in tropical and subtropical gardens worldwide. In zone 9, it may be damaged by hard freezes but typically re-sprouts vigorously from the base in spring, behaving as a large perennial shrub. It is a magnet for butterflies and bees. Prune after flowering to maintain a tidy shape.

common_name: Tropical Turk's Cap (Sleeping Hibiscus, Cardinal's Hat)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to heavy partial shade; tropical Turk's cap is more frost-tender than the native Malvaviscus arboreus — in zone 9a it needs frost protection or may die back to the roots; in zone 9b–12 it is a true perennial shrub. Like M. arboreus, it is a hummingbird magnet.
directions: Root stem cuttings in moist sand or plant divisions in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tropical Turk's cap is a Mexican species closely related to the native Turk's cap (Malvaviscus arboreus) but distinctly different — producing pendulous, elongated, deep red, twisted flowers 2–3 inches long that hang downward on long stalks rather than the upright flower of M. arboreus, giving it a more dramatic, drooping floral display. Like its relative, the flowers never fully open — they remain twisted into a tube, accessible only to hummingbirds whose long bills can reach the nectar at the base. Tropical Turk's cap is a large, fast-growing shrub reaching 6–10 feet with large, tropical-looking leaves and year-round bloom in frost-free areas, making it one of the most reliably productive hummingbird plants for zone 9b–12 gardens. It tolerates significant shade and grows vigorously under tree canopies where other flowering shrubs struggle. More frost-tender than the native species, requiring protection or regrowth from roots in zone 9a.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tropicana is an AARS 1963 winner bred by Mathias Tantau and one of the best-selling roses of the 20th century, though like many older hybrid teas it benefits from a preventative fungicide program in humid climates.
directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tropicana, also sold as Super Star, is a landmark hybrid tea rose bred in Germany and released to enormous acclaim in the early 1960s, celebrated for its almost fluorescent coral-orange color — a shade so vivid it was said to have been a genuine breeding breakthrough at the time — carried on large, high-centered blooms with a strong, fruity fragrance. It became one of the best-selling roses of the 20th century and remains a benchmark for vivid orange rose color. As with most classic hybrid teas, expect to manage black spot and powdery mildew with a regular preventative spray program in humid climates. Prune hard in late winter, feed monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to sustain the repeat-flowering cycle.

common_name: Tropicanna Canna (Phasion Canna, Striped-Foliage Tropical Canna)
plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil when soil temperatures are above 60°F; each division should have at least one eye (growing point). In zone 9, established clumps overwinter in ground and regrow vigorously each spring — established plants put up new shoots from March onward. In zone 7–8, lift rhizomes after frost kills the foliage, allow to dry, and store frost-free over winter.
directions: Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun; feed with a balanced fertilizer monthly during the growing season for maximum foliage color and flowering. Tropicanna (also sold under the European trademark name 'Phasion') is the most widely grown ornamental canna in the world and arguably the most visually spectacular — selected specifically for its extraordinary foliage, which is striped in vivid bronze, green, gold, pink, and red bands running the length of each paddle-shaped leaf, creating a tropical stained-glass effect unlike any other common garden plant. The foliage alone is bold enough to justify growing Tropicanna as a pure foliage plant, but the plants also produce vibrant bright orange flowers on tall stalks above the foliage from summer through fall, adding another layer of tropical color. Each individual plant grows to 4–6 feet tall with an equally bold spread; in mass plantings or as specimen plants in large containers, Tropicanna creates instant tropical impact that takes most ornamentals years to achieve. The foliage color is most intense in full sun — shaded plants develop a solid green that loses most of the characteristic striping. In zone 9, Tropicanna overwinters reliably in the ground and expands by rhizome division each year, requiring periodic thinning to prevent overcrowding. Provide consistent moisture — cannas are heavy feeders and drinkers — but excellent drainage is equally critical, as standing water causes rhizome rot.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Tropicanna Gold produces the brightest, most vivid golden-yellow-striped foliage in the Tropicanna series — each leaf is green with prominent golden-yellow to cream-yellow stripes running the length of the leaf. The vivid orange flowers provide a complementary warm-toned floral display above the striped foliage. In zone 9 canna rhizomes can remain in the ground year-round as permanent perennials, forming spreading clumps that increase in size each season. Divide clumps every 2–3 years when they become crowded. Water stress and nutrient deficiency reduce foliage color intensity — maintain consistent moisture and fertilization for the best striped effect.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil — Tropicanna Gold Canna produces the most vivid foliage color in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9 where afternoon shade reduces the heat stress on the large foliage; Tropicanna Gold is a golden-striped foliage canna producing extraordinarily vivid green-and-gold variegated leaves — broad, paddle-shaped, tropical leaves with prominent longitudinal golden-yellow to cream-yellow stripes that create a boldly patterned tropical foliage effect unlike any other commonly grown garden plant. The combination of the large scale of canna foliage (leaves 12–18 inches wide on plants 4–5 feet tall) with the vivid yellow-striped pattern creates one of the most dramatic tropical foliage statements available in the summer landscape — immediately visible from a distance and creating a strong focal point in any garden composition. Above the spectacular striped foliage, Tropicanna Gold produces bright orange flowers in the classic canna form, which extend the ornamental display from late spring through frost in zone 9 and provide hummingbird nectar. In zone 9 canna is one of the most permanent and reliable tropical perennials available — surviving winter in the ground, re-emerging and producing increasingly large clumps each year, and creating a progressively more impressive foliage display as the planting matures.

plant_note: Plant fresh corms immediately in early fall — do not allow them to dry out — in deep, humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in full shade under deciduous hardwoods; plant 3–4 inches deep and 3–4 inches apart.
directions: Plant fresh corms in early fall in deep, humus-rich, moist, acidic soil in full shade under deciduous hardwoods, never allowing them to dry out between digging and replanting; trout lily is a native spring ephemeral of the Eastern U.S. forest floor whose mottled brown-and-green leaves (which resemble a brook trout's speckled flank) and nodding yellow flowers emerge in earliest spring before the tree canopy leafs out and go completely dormant by early summer. Single corms produce only a leaf for the first 3–7 years before producing two leaves and the first bloom — patience is essential. Enrich soil deeply with leaf mold before planting. Purchase only nursery-propagated corms; wild-dug plants almost never establish.

common_name: Truffula Pink Gomphrena (Tall Wand-Form Globe Amaranth)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Truffula Pink thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf South summers, holding up better than many annuals during the peak of the season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, and expect minimal maintenance beyond routine watering, since gomphrena is highly heat- and drought-tolerant once established. Truffula Pink is a tall, vigorous gomphrena selection producing an abundance of rounded, papery, bright pink flower globes held well above the foliage on long, airy stems, creating a wand-like effect that stands out in a border or cutting garden and gives the plant its whimsical name. The flowers hold their color exceptionally well both in the garden and after cutting, making Truffula Pink a favorite for fresh and dried arrangements, and its nonstop bloom from summer through frost provides reliable color when many other annuals falter in Gulf South heat. It is also highly attractive to butterflies and other pollinators throughout its long bloom season. Deadheading is not required for continued bloom, though removing spent stems keeps the planting tidy.

common_name: Trumpet Creeper (Trumpet Vine, Cow Itch Vine)
plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained to dry, poor to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; trumpet creeper is an exceptionally vigorous native vine that can overwhelm weaker support structures and spread aggressively — give it a sturdy masonry wall, fence, or large arbor and do not plant near small trees or delicate plants.
directions: Plant in poor to moderately fertile, well-drained to dry soil in full sun on a very sturdy support; never plant on wooden fences or near small trees as the vigorous vine can destroy them within a few years. Campsis radicans (trumpet creeper) is a native deciduous woody vine of exceptional ornamental value and hummingbird attraction — its large, trumpeted, 3-inch orange-red to scarlet flowers bloom prolifically in clusters of 4–12 from July through September on the current season's growth, creating an irresistible magnet for ruby-throated hummingbirds which are the primary pollinators. The vine climbs by clinging rootlets that attach firmly to masonry, bark, and wood and can scale heights of 20–40 feet or more. It is one of the most vigorous plants in American horticulture — spreading by root suckers and self-seeding freely — and should be sited with awareness of its potential to overtake its space: do not plant on wooden structures, near small trees, or where spread cannot be controlled. The cultivar 'Flamenco' has yellow-orange flowers; 'Crimson Trumpet' has deeper red flowers; 'Indian Summer' is more compact. Despite its vigor, trumpet creeper is extraordinarily valuable for wildlife and native garden plantings on large, sturdy supports.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall or early spring; never let dry out.
directions: Plant trumpet lily bulbs in fall or early spring about eight inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil. The tall stems carry many large, powerfully fragrant trumpet-shaped flowers in midsummer and often need staking. Give them full sun with cool, shaded roots and never allow the bulbs to dry out completely. Leave stems standing until they yellow so the bulbs can store energy for the following year.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; trumpet tree is a frost-tender, fast-growing pioneer species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; trumpet tree is a frost-tender, fast-growing pioneer species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Large, distinctive, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves radiate from hollow, jointed stems on this extremely fast-growing Neotropical pioneer tree, which colonizes disturbed clearings and forest gaps throughout Central and South America, its hollow stems famously providing a home for symbiotic Azteca ants that protect the tree from herbivores in exchange for shelter and food. Growing many feet per year when young, it is one of the fastest-growing woody trees in the American tropics but is relatively short-lived and structurally weak, better suited to quickly establishing shade or a distinctive architectural specimen in a tropical garden than a long-term landscape anchor. Water regularly while young, provide full sun for the fastest growth, and expect a relatively short lifespan compared to slower, longer-lived tropical trees.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring against a very sturdy support — trumpet vine becomes extremely heavy with age and requires a substantial structure such as a fence post, large arbor, or mature tree. Full sun is essential for the best flowering.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants against a very sturdy structure in full sun in any well-drained soil; trumpet vine is a vigorous native climber of the eastern US that attaches by aerial rootlets and can ultimately reach 20–40 feet, producing masses of large, brilliant orange-red trumpet flowers from midsummer through fall that are the single most effective hummingbird plant for zone 4–9 gardens during the critical midsummer period. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially indestructible, but its vigor must be respected — it spreads by suckers that emerge from the roots, can become invasive in some settings, and the aerial rootlets can damage masonry and wood siding. Prune aggressively in late winter to control size; it blooms on new growth so hard pruning never reduces flowering. The cultivar 'Flava' has clear yellow flowers; 'Crimson Trumpet' is a deep red.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts in spring into a coarse, low-nutrient mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark; keep the medium moist year-round with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide warm, humid conditions — never use tap water or ordinary garden soil.
directions: Truncate pitcher plant is native to lowland forests of Mindanao in the Philippines and is named for its distinctive broad, truncated leaf blades, which set off some of the largest pitchers in the entire genus — mature lower pitchers can be a foot or more tall with a massively thickened, ribbed peristome. As a lowland species it wants warm, humid, greenhouse-like conditions year-round and considerable room to spread, but tissue-culture propagation has made it much more widely available to home growers than it once was. Pot it in a coarse, low-nutrient mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark, and water exclusively with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater, since tap water minerals build up in the medium and damage the roots. Keep humidity high and light bright but filtered, and never fertilize the soil directly.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, sandy or clay soil; best suited to California's summer-dry Mediterranean climate.
directions: Truncated Rosin Weed is a glandular-sticky, resinous native annual tarweed of dry, open foothill grasslands and chaparral margins in northern and central California, notable for its white to cream-white, 3-lobed ray flowers surrounding yellow disk florets — one of the few white-rayed tarweeds in California's flora. The strong, characteristic resinous scent of crushed foliage is typical of the tarweed tribe, and the sticky stems can trap small insects. Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, well-drained sandy or clay soil in full sun; plants germinate with winter rains and bloom from June through September with no supplemental irrigation. This species is best adapted to California's summer-dry Mediterranean climate and is well suited to dry garden naturalization and native grassland restoration plantings.

common_name: Trusty Rusty Coleus (Award-Winning Rust-and-Magenta Gold-Edged Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Trusty Rusty is an RHS Award of Garden Merit winner with large rust-and-magenta leaves edged golden-yellow, tolerant of both sun and part shade.
directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Trusty Rusty, a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit winner, bears large leaves in warm rust and magenta tones edged with a bright golden-yellow margin, a rich, warm color combination that has made it a standout in trial gardens. Its adaptability to a range of light conditions and strong garden performance suit it to mixed borders, containers, and mass plantings alike. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds (after cold stratification for 4–6 weeks) in early spring in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tube white penstemon is short-lived (2–4 years) but self-sows to maintain colonies in lean, dry, open soils. It is native to glades, rocky prairies, and limestone-based habitats throughout the central and southeastern United States.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tube white penstemon is a native prairie penstemon of the central and southeastern United States, unusual among penstemons in its pure-white flowers — most penstemons in this region are purple, lavender, or pink, making the clean, tubular-white flowers of this species distinctively different. The flowers are slightly longer and more narrowly tubular than many penstemon flowers (hence 'tubaeflorus,' meaning 'tube-flowered'), arranged in loose whorls on upright stems from late spring through early summer. A prairie and glade native adapted to the hot, dry, limestone-based soils common through the ozarks, glades, and limestone-prairie regions of the central states, it is more heat-tolerant than many penstemons and suited to zone 9 gardens in Texas. The white flowers attract native bumblebees, solitary bees, and various hummingbirds. It is relatively short-lived as an individual plant but self-sows in lean, open soil to maintain colonies. Combines naturally with prairie companions — grasses, black-eyed Susans, coreopsis, and native asters — in naturalistic prairie garden compositions.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after soil warms to 60°F; tuberose requires a long, warm growing season to bloom — plant early and do not allow soil to remain cold and wet, which causes rot. In zone 9–11 tubers can remain in the ground year-round with light mulch.
directions: Plant tubers 2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; tuberose is one of the most intensely fragrant flowers in the world — the pure white, waxy flowers on tall spikes in late summer have a heavy, sweet, complex scent that intensifies at night and has been prized for centuries in perfumery and garlands. It is the principal flower in traditional South Asian garlands and is widely used in the Indian perfume industry (the absolute is one of the most expensive floral extracts). The single-flowered variety blooms slightly earlier than the double; 'The Pearl' is the most widely grown double-flowered cultivar. In zone 9–11 the clumping tubers naturalize to form large colonies that bloom reliably each summer; in colder zones dig and store tubers dry through winter. An outstanding cut flower with exceptional vase life of 10–14 days.

plant_note: Start tubers hollow-side up in barely moist potting mix 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost date, in a warm bright location at 70–75°F; transplant outdoors after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Start tubers indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost by placing them hollow-side up, barely covered, in moist peat-based mix at 70 to 75°F; keep the medium just slightly moist until shoots appear to prevent rot. Grow on in bright indirect light and transplant outside into partial shade after all frost danger has passed, spacing plants 10 to 14 inches apart in rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil. Tuberous begonias perform best where summer nights are cool; in hot, humid climates provide afternoon shade and good air circulation to reduce disease pressure. Before the first fall frost, cut stems back and lift the tubers, cure them in a dry location for a week, then store in barely damp peat moss at 45 to 50°F over winter.

plant_note: Start tubers hollow-side up in shallow trays of moist peat-free starting mix 6–8 weeks before last frost; move outdoors only after all frost danger has passed and nights remain above 50°F.
directions: Place tubers concave-side up, barely covered with moist growing medium, at 65–70°F until sprouts appear, then move to bright indirect light and keep evenly moist. Tuberous begonias produce spectacular 3–6 inch double flowers in every color but blue and thrive in the cool, shaded spots where few flowering annuals succeed. Remove the small single flowers (male) flanking the large showy central bloom to direct energy to the main display. As nights cool in fall, reduce watering; after the first frost blackens the foliage, dig tubers, cure for two weeks in a warm dry spot, and store in barely moist peat at 45–50°F for replanting the following spring.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; tuberous Jerusalem sage is one of the most cold-hardy phlomis species (to zone 3) due to its tuberous roots that protect it through severe winters. As with P. russelliana, leave the dried whorled stems standing through winter for ornamental interest and wildlife value.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; tuberous Jerusalem sage is one of the most frost-hardy phlomis species — surviving reliably to zone 3 due to its fleshy tuberous roots — and differs from the more common P. russelliana in producing rosy-mauve to lilac-pink whorled flowers (rather than yellow) on taller, more upright stems reaching 4–5 feet. The flower color in shades of warm mauve-pink is unusual in the phlomis genus, which is more commonly represented by yellow species. Like all phlomis, the flowers are arranged in distinct, evenly-spaced whorls along the upright stem, creating the characteristic, architecturally tiered, candelabra effect at bloom time in June and July. The dried stems and calyx whorls persist through winter as attractive structures. More upright and taller than P. russelliana. Native to central and eastern Europe and central Asia in dry, rocky, steppic grassland. Outstanding for prairie-style plantings, gravel gardens, and large-scale naturalistic designs where drought tolerance and winter stem interest are both valued.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in deep shade to partial shade in zone 8–11; Tuberous Sword Fern is a robust, vigorous fern native to tropical Asia and East Africa, widely naturalized in warm climates worldwide, distinguished from the common Boston Fern by small, round, white storage tubers on its stolons — highly drought tolerant for a fern because of these tubers — and one of the best large, shade-tolerant groundcovers for hot, humid southern landscapes.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Nephrolepis cordifolia is considerably more drought tolerant than Boston Fern due to its water-storing root tubers — once established it tolerates periods of dry soil that would wilt typical ferns. Nephrolepis cordifolia (Tuberous Sword Fern or Ladder Fern) is a robust, clumping, stoloniferous fern native to tropical and subtropical Asia, East Africa, and the Pacific Islands, now widely naturalized in Florida, the Caribbean, Central America, Hawaii, and New Zealand — where it has become invasive in some regions due to its vigorous growth and prolific stolon production. The plant is distinguished from the very similar common Boston Fern (N. exaltata) by small, round, white, marble-sized tubers borne on the stolons — starchy, edible in some regions as bush food — which function as water-storage organs allowing the plant to survive drought periods that would desiccate typical ferns. The pinnate fronds are erect to arching, bright green, 1–2.5 feet long, on multiple crowns that spread and colonize by stolons. Tuberous Sword Fern is an excellent, tough, large-scale shade groundcover for hot, humid, subtropical gardens in zones 8–11, performing well under trees, on shaded slopes, and in difficult dry-shade situations where most ferns fail. Monitor for spreading in warm climates where it can become invasive.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Tuff Stuff is a Proven Winners mountain hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, giving it a much longer rebloom window and better resistance to losing a season's flowers to a late spring freeze than bigleaf hydrangeas that bloom on old wood only.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some protection from hot afternoon sun; Tuff Stuff is a compact reblooming mountain hydrangea (Hydrangea serrata) bred by Proven Winners to flower on both old and new growth, so even if a hard late freeze damages the previous year's buds, the plant still produces a strong flush of lacecap blooms on new wood later in the season — a real advantage over bigleaf hydrangeas that bloom only on old wood and can lose an entire year's flowering to a bad spring frost. Flower color shifts with soil pH, from blue in acidic soil to more pink or purple tones in neutral to alkaline soil, the same way it does in bigleaf hydrangea. Mountain hydrangea is generally more cold-hardy and sun-tolerant than bigleaf hydrangea, and its compact size fits well into smaller foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders. Water regularly during dry spells, since hydrangeas wilt quickly in dry soil, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat.

common_name: Tufted Evening Primrose / White Evening Primrose
plant_note: Direct sow in well-drained to dry, rocky or sandy, poor to average soil in full sun; tufted evening primrose demands sharp drainage and will rot in heavy clay or consistently moist soil.
directions: Oenothera caespitosa is a low-growing western native perennial that forms stemless rosettes of large, silvery-gray, wavy-margined leaves at ground level and produces a succession of enormous (3-4 inch diameter), pure white, four-petaled flowers with bright yellow centers from late spring through midsummer; the flowers open at dusk, last one night, and turn pink as they age the next morning, making this one of the finest plants for a moonlight garden or evening patio. The intensely sweet fragrance is extraordinary at night and attracts sphinx moths (hawkmoths) that are the primary pollinators; it is also a larval host plant for several sphinx moth species. Exceptional for dry rock gardens, wall crevices, and xeriscape plantings in zones 3-7.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; tufted hair grass is one of the few ornamental grasses that performs well in partial shade and is especially effective in moist, partially shaded garden settings where most grasses fail.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; tufted hair grass is one of the most graceful and versatile of cool-season ornamental grasses, forming dense, dark-green, fine-textured tufts of narrow, arching leaves that produce extraordinary airy clouds of delicate, silvery-tan, open-panicle flower heads on slender, arching stems in early summer — when backlit by morning or evening sun, the massed flower heads create a luminous, misty, gossamer effect that is among the most beautiful of all grass effects in the garden. It is distinctively shade-tolerant compared to most ornamental grasses and thrives in moist, cool, partially shaded sites. The flower heads dry in place and provide multi-season interest through winter. 'Goldtau' (gold-tinted), 'Schottland' (tall, graceful), and 'Bronzeschleier' (bronze veil) are superb cultivars. Excellent with hostas and astilbes in moist shade gardens.

common_name: Tukana Verbena (Vigorous Large-Flowered Spreading Landscape Verbena)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Tukana's vigorous, fast-spreading habit covers ground quickly, making it useful for large beds, slopes, and mass plantings as well as containers.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants generously to allow room for this vigorous series to spread quickly. Tukana is a vegetatively propagated verbena series bred for larger flower clusters and stronger vigor than finer-textured groundcover verbena types, spreading rapidly to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat covered in color from spring through fall in shades of red, pink, purple, and white. Its rapid coverage makes it a practical choice for filling large sunny beds, slopes, and mass landscape plantings where quick, showy results matter, while good air circulation and well-drained soil keep it free of the powdery mildew that troubles older verbena in humid conditions. An occasional shearing back after a heavy flush of bloom keeps growth dense and encourages continued flowering through the season.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall when soil temperatures drop below 55°F, about 4–8 weeks before hard frost.
directions: Plant bulbs pointed end up at a depth of 3 times their height, typically 6–8 in deep, in well-drained soil — standing water will cause rot. In warmer zones (7–8), pre-chill bulbs for 6–8 weeks in the refrigerator before planting to simulate the cold period they need. Most hybrid tulips perform best in year 1; replanting fresh bulbs annually is common practice in mild climates. Allow leaves to die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb.

plant_note: Plant in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil with room to grow large.
directions: The tulip poplar is a fast-growing native shade tree that reaches towering heights, with distinctive four-lobed leaves and cup-shaped, greenish-yellow tulip-like flowers in late spring. Give it a large, open site in full sun with deep, moist, well-drained soil, as its extensive root system needs room. Water regularly for the first few years to establish; mature trees are fairly self-sufficient. Its rapid growth makes it excellent for quick shade, though the soft wood benefits from a sheltered location. Foliage turns clear golden-yellow in autumn.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tumbleweed allium requires a dry summer dormancy period and is not suited to sites with summer irrigation or heavy, wet soils.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tumbleweed allium produces the largest and most dramatically structured flower head of all ornamental alliums — a massive spherical umbel up to 18–20 inches in diameter composed of dozens of star-shaped flowers on ray-like stalks of dramatically varying lengths, creating a loose, three-dimensional, snowflake-like burst that literally resembles a fireworks explosion. The flower is one of the most remarkable structural elements in the late-spring garden. After bloom, the dried seed head detaches from the stem and tumbles across the ground like a tumbleweed (hence the name), distributing seeds. The dried heads are superb in floral arrangements and last for months. Unusual and conversation-stopping in the garden.

common_name: Tuolumne Fawn Lily (Vigorous Bright-Yellow Plain-Leaf Trout Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Tuolumne Fawn Lily bears vigorous bright-yellow flowers over plain, glossy, unmottled leaves, distinct from the mottled-leaf trout lily species more commonly grown.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it. Native to the Sierra Nevada foothills of California, Tuolumne Fawn Lily is distinguished from most other Erythronium species by its plain, glossy green, unmottled leaves rather than the brown-marbled foliage typical of the genus, and it is also one of the most vigorous and easily grown species, readily multiplying by offsets to form an increasing clump of bright, clear yellow, backswept flowers in early spring. It naturalizes well in a cool, humus-rich woodland setting beneath deciduous trees and is often used as a parent in Erythronium hybrid breeding for its vigor. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to full shade; Turk's cap is one of the most shade-tolerant of all flowering shrubs and is outstanding for shaded garden spots where flowering shrubs rarely bloom — it produces its characteristic twisted red flowers prolifically in sun or shade.
directions: Plant in moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun to full shade; Turk's cap tolerates a wide range of soil conditions and is virtually maintenance-free once established. Malvaviscus arboreus (Turk's cap or wax mallow) is one of the most beloved and useful native shrubs of south Texas and the Gulf Coast — a large, sprawling, multi-stemmed shrub native from Florida through Texas and deep into Mexico and Central America, producing a continuous show of small, unique, hibiscus-like flowers whose petals never fully open but instead remain spirally twisted around the central column, creating a distinctive, turban-shaped, bright-scarlet-red 'Turk's cap' flower from late summer through fall. It is among the very best plants for attracting hummingbirds and butterflies to the Gulf Coast garden. What distinguishes Turk's cap ecologically is its outstanding shade tolerance — it blooms prolifically under large live oaks, in deep woodland margins, and in full shade where almost no other flowering shrub succeeds. It is also drought-tolerant, deer-resistant in many areas, and nearly carefree. The small, red berries are edible (mildly sweet, jelly-like) and can be used to make preserves; they are also consumed by wildlife.

common_name: Turk's Cap (Turk's Cap Mallow, Wax Mallow)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Turk's Cap is outstanding in partial to full shade where it is one of the most shade-tolerant flowering native shrubs for the Gulf Coast and Southeast, blooming reliably in conditions that defeat most flowering shrubs.
directions: Plant in spring in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to deep shade; Turk's Cap is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant native shrubs of the Gulf Coast and is also one of the most shade-tolerant flowering plants in the region. Malvaviscus arboreus var. drummondii (Turk's Cap) is a native perennial shrub of the Gulf Coast and Texas lowlands from Louisiana to Mexico, producing distinctive, red, partially-opened hibiscus-like flowers with petals that never fully unfurl (remaining curled around the prominent staminal column in the distinctive 'turban' or 'fez' shape that gives it the common name). The tubular, nectar-rich flowers are among the most important hummingbird food sources in Gulf Coast and Texas gardens from summer through late fall; native bees and butterflies also visit. Edible small red fruits follow the flowers and are eaten by mockingbirds and other wildlife. Dies to the ground in freezes north of zone 9 but re-sprouts from the root crown reliably. Outstanding for shaded gardens, natural areas, and wildlife plantings in zones 7–11.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after last frost in any well-drained soil; this is one of the few true shade-tolerant flowering shrubs that performs in deep shade while also thriving in full sun. Dies to the ground in hard frost zones but re-sprouts vigorously.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to deep shade; Turk's cap is one of the South's most versatile and valuable flowering shrubs, producing bright red nodding flowers with tightly spiraled petals that never fully open (resembling a Turkish fez) from summer through frost — and in zone 9–10, flowering nearly year round. It is outstanding in dry shade under large trees where little else will bloom, and is equally at home in full blazing sun. Ruby-throated and rufous hummingbirds are its primary pollinators and mob the flowers from summer through migration. In zone 8 it dies back to the roots in hard freezes but re-sprouts reliably in spring and reaches full size by July. Do not overwater; it tolerates considerable drought once established.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Turk's Cap Cactus needs consistent warmth year-round and excellent drainage, and does not tolerate any frost.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Turk's Cap Cactus needs consistent warmth year-round and excellent drainage, and does not tolerate any frost. A ribbed, barrel-shaped green body armed with stout amber spines grows for years before eventually producing a distinctive woolly, bristled, cap-like structure called a cephalium at its crown, from which small pink flowers and bright red-pink fruit emerge in succession for the rest of the plant's life, resembling a fez or turban perched atop the cactus. Native to the Caribbean islands, it requires many years of growth before the cephalium forms, after which the main body stops growing wider and channels its energy into flowering and fruiting from the cap. Water sparingly and only in warm weather, provide full sun, and keep it consistently warm, since it is more cold-sensitive than most desert cacti and can be damaged by even brief chilly, damp conditions.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in early spring at 4–6 inch depth, in groups of 3–5 for best effect; handles more shade than most lilies and prefers consistently moist soil.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to light sun; Turk's cap lily is the tallest native eastern lily, and in optimal conditions can reach 8 feet with dozens of richly spotted orange reflexed (turkscap-shaped) flowers per stem in July–August. Unlike cultivated Asiatic or Oriental lilies, it grows naturally in wet meadows and forest edges and requires consistently moist soil throughout the growing season. It tolerates more shade than most lilies and is valuable in the lightly shaded, moist native garden border. Ruby-throated hummingbirds are primary pollinators. The foliage and bulbs may be toxic to cats; keep away from where cats roam.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun where broad foliage can be displayed.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 8-10 inches apart in fall in full sun and well-drained soil, giving each bulb room since it produces unusually broad, wavy-edged, gray-green strap leaves that lie close to the ground. In late spring a stout stalk rises just above the foliage to open a dense, softball-sized umbel of dusty pink to lilac starry florets that dries attractively and holds its shape for weeks. Its low, wide habit makes it a striking edger or front-of-border accent quite different from the tall, leafless-stemmed look of most ornamental onions. The foliage begins to fade around bloom time, so pair it with later-emerging perennials to hide the dying leaves.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; Turkestan tulip is one of the earliest species tulips to bloom and naturalizes readily by both offsets and self-sown seed in favorable rock-garden conditions.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; Turkestan tulip is one of the earliest species tulips to bloom and naturalizes readily by both offsets and self-sown seed in favorable rock-garden conditions. Each bulb sends up multiple slender stems bearing several small, star-shaped flowers per stem, creamy white with a golden-yellow base, opening among the very first bulbs of the season, often before crocuses have finished. Native to rocky slopes of Central Asia, it is exceptionally cold-hardy and low-maintenance, multiplying steadily in a rock garden, gravel bed, or naturalized lawn planting where sharp drainage keeps the small bulbs from rotting through summer dormancy. Allow foliage to die back naturally before removing it and avoid summer watering in its dormant season.

plant_note: Plant young, nursery-grown container plants in fall in dry, white, sandy or sandy loam, acidic soil in full sun; turkey oak is adapted to the driest, most nutrient-deficient sandy soils of the coastal plain and requires sharp drainage — it does not tolerate clay or moist soils.
directions: Turkey oak is a native small to medium tree endemic to the scrub and sandhill habitats of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from Virginia to Louisiana — one of the most adapted trees in North America to the white, nutrient-deficient, excessively drained sands of the ancient coastal plain terraces where it forms nearly pure stands alongside longleaf pine and sand live oak. Its deeply 3–5 lobed leaves are large, glossy, and architectural — among the most decorative of all oak foliage — and turn vivid shades of red, orange, and burgundy in fall, providing exceptional autumn color even in warm climates where most oaks turn only dull brown. Turkey oak is the critical host tree for the Florida scrub-jay, one of the most endangered birds in North America, which depends on turkey oak acorns as its primary food; the tree is also habitat for dozens of rare invertebrates endemic to scrub habitats. In sandy coastal plain gardens with excessively drained, acidic, nutrient-poor soil — exactly the conditions that challenge most ornamental trees — turkey oak thrives with no supplemental care once established.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in moist to moderately dry, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Turkey tangle fogfruit is a native North American groundcover that spreads rapidly by stolons and is outstanding for wildlife habitat — it is a critical larval host plant for three species of buckeye and cloudywing butterfly caterpillars.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist to dry, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; fogfruit spreads by stolons and self-seeds to form a dense mat. Phyla nodiflora (turkey tangle fogfruit or frogfruit) is a low-growing, mat-forming native perennial groundcover of the southeastern United States, Gulf Coastal Plain, and tropical Americas — one of the most important native groundcovers for butterfly habitat in the Gulf South. The plant produces trailing, rooting stems and tiny, oval leaves, with small (1/4-inch), pink-to-lilac-white flower clusters on short stalks throughout the warm season. What makes fogfruit ecologically significant is its role as a larval host plant: it is the primary or sole caterpillar host plant for Common Buckeye (Junonia coenia), White Peacock (Anartia jatrophae), and Phaon Crescent (Phyciodes phaon) butterflies in the Gulf South — caterpillars of these abundant butterflies feed almost exclusively on fogfruit leaves. As a no-mow lawn substitute or habitat groundcover, fogfruit is outstanding for hot, sunny, moist-to-dry situations. It is also occasionally used as a lawn grass substitute in India and South Asia (karpooravalli) for its drought tolerance.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring just as new growth begins, or in early fall; plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade sheltered from harsh winter wind, which can damage the evergreen leaves.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Turkish epimedium is native to woodlands of the Balkans and Turkey and is among the tallest and most vigorous of the commonly grown epimedium species, forming a substantial evergreen clump of heart-shaped leaflets that emerge coppery-bronze before maturing to glossy dark green. In mid-spring, wiry stems carry open sprays of small, pale creamy-yellow flowers held well above the foliage, showier in quantity than in individual flower size. Once established, it tolerates dry shade under trees better than many perennials and needs little supplemental water beyond normal rainfall. Comb out or shear tattered old foliage in late winter before new leaves and flower stems emerge to keep the display clean.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moderately moist, neutral to alkaline soil; Turkish sage is a vigorous spreader by rhizomes and will fill in a large area over several years. Unlike shrubby Jerusalem sage, this is a herbaceous perennial that dies back to the ground in winter. It tolerates partial shade and poorer soils better than most Phlomis.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; Turkish sage is a herbaceous perennial from Turkey and Syria with one of the most dramatic architectural presences of any medium-sized perennial. The large, broadly heart-shaped, soft, sage-textured leaves form a ground-covering rosette that spreads steadily by rhizomes to fill a substantial area, effectively suppressing weeds with bold foliage. In early summer, stout, upright flower stalks rise 3-4 feet above the foliage bearing the distinctive whorled, tiered clusters of soft-yellow flowers arranged in evenly spaced rings around the stem — an unusual and eye-catching form. After flowering, the persistent, orbicular, pale-buff seed whorls remain erect and attractive through winter, providing exceptional structure and interest in the dormant garden. Unlike the shrubby Jerusalem sage (P. fruticosa), P. russeliana is fully herbaceous and cold-hardy to zone 4, making it adaptable across a much wider range of climates. More shade-tolerant than most Phlomis species.

plant_note: Set out plugs on roughly ten-inch centers in spring; recovers quickly from occasional foot traffic once established, needs virtually no mowing.
directions: Set out plugs on roughly ten-inch centers in spring; this extremely low, tight evergreen mat of glossy round leaves was specifically developed and promoted as a mowable, steppable lawn substitute for hot, dry regions. Deep blue flowers blanket the foliage for several weeks in late spring, and the planting recovers quickly from occasional foot traffic once established. It is remarkably drought and heat tolerant compared with most turf alternatives and needs virtually no mowing, just an annual light trim if it starts to mound.

common_name: Turnera (White Buttercup, Sulphur Alder, Politician's Bush)
plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; Turnera subulata thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers and blooms continuously from spring through frost in zone 9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; once established, turnera is drought-tolerant and thrives with minimal care. Turnera subulata (white buttercup or turnera) is a warm-climate shrubby perennial from South America producing masses of cheerful, 5-petaled, white flowers each about 1 inch across, with a distinctive yellow eye at the center — each flower opens for only a single day (a brief daily flowering phenomenon characteristic of the genus), but the continuous succession of new buds from spring through frost maintains constant bloom. The yellow-centered white flowers bloom prolifically on compact, rounded bushes with toothed, dark-green, slightly aromatic leaves. Turnera is outstanding for Gulf Coast gardens where it grows as a near-evergreen perennial shrub in zone 9–10, providing reliable bloom through summer heat and humidity when many other plants struggle; in colder zones, it is used as a summer annual. It naturalizes in warm climates and can become mildly weedy in tropical gardens. Highly tolerant of drought, poor soil, and coastal salt spray once established.

subcategory: uniquely colored South African Cape bulb
plant_note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface in fall in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; like all lachenalias it follows the Cape winter-rainfall growth cycle — emerging in autumn, blooming in late winter and spring, then going completely summer dormant. Keep dry in summer. This species is notable for its unique turquoise-green flower color, one of the only true blue-green (teal) flower colors in the plant kingdom.
directions: Plant bulbs near the soil surface in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; turquoise lachenalia is one of the most botanically remarkable flowering bulbs in the world for a single, astonishing reason — its flowers are turquoise-green to blue-green, a color so unusual in the plant kingdom that it qualifies as genuinely unique among commonly cultivated bulbs. True blue-green (teal) flowers are exceedingly rare in nature; this color is achieved through a combination of unusual pigment concentrations in the pendant, tubular bells that gives the entire flower head a distinct turquoise to blue-green hue that appears almost artificial or painted when seen for the first time. The effect is unlike any other flower color in the bulb garden. The flowers appear in dense, upright racemes of 10–20 pendant tubular bells on stems 6–10 inches tall in late winter and early spring above two strap-shaped, somewhat spotted, succulent-tinged leaves. Like all Cape Lachenalia, it requires the strict winter-growth, summer-dormancy schedule of the Mediterranean-climate Cape fynbos. A collector's plant of extraordinary botanical interest for its completely unprecedented flower color.

plant_note: Plant outdoors in partial shade to filtered sun in zone 9b-11; Turtle Bromeliad is one of the tougher, more cold-tolerant tank bromeliads in general landscape use, handling brief dips into the upper 20s°F once established. In zone 9, site it in a protected spot or mulch heavily over winter. Divide crowded clumps by separating rooted offsets from the base of the parent rosette.
directions: Grow in filtered sun to partial shade — Quesnelia testudo tolerates more direct light than many tank bromeliads, which suits it to open shade-tree plantings rather than only deep shade. Native to the Rio de Janeiro region of Brazil, it has been in cultivation since the 1800s and forms a stiff, arching rosette of grayish-green, spine-edged strap leaves. Its common name comes from the compact, domed flower head of coral-pink bracts and blue-violet flowers, which some growers liken to the shape of a turtle's shell rising from the foliage. Keep the central cup topped with water and grow in a coarse, fast-draining bromeliad or orchid mix; established clumps are tough, forgiving, and long-lived in the landscape.

common_name: Turtle Vine (Creeping Inch Plant, Miniature Inch Plant)
plant_note: Plant stem cuttings in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained potting mix or garden soil in part shade to full shade; turtle vine is a tiny-leaved, trailing shade plant from Central and South America that is outstanding for hanging baskets, terrariums, vivarium substrate, and shaded groundcover in warm, humid climates.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral potting mix or garden soil in shade; keep consistently moist. Callisia repens (turtle vine or creeping inch plant) is a tiny-leaved, mat-forming, trailing succulent from Central and South America in the Commelinaceae family — related to tradescantias and wandering Jews — producing dense, low, creeping mats of round, succulent, overlapping, bright-green leaves just 1/2-inch across on trailing stems, with the leaves overlapping on the stems like shingles or scales (the 'turtle vine' name suggests the scale-like leaf pattern). The plant is one of the most popular terrarium and vivarium plants due to its miniature scale, shade tolerance, and ease of care; it is also used as a hanging basket subject and in fairy garden designs. A purple-leaved cultivar ('Pink Lady') with pink-purple leaves is widely grown and striking. Turtle vine roots extremely easily — virtually any stem fragment with a node will root in moist soil. It is also commonly used as a supplemental diet food for many species of reptiles and tortoises, who eat the leaves. Virtually indestructible in humid shade conditions.

common_name: Tuscany Superb Rose (Dark Velvety Maroon-Purple Gallica)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Tuscany Superb is an improved 19th-century form of the historic Gallica rose Tuscany.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Tuscany Superb tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough 19th-century Gallica. An improved, larger-flowered form of the historic rose Tuscany, it bears dense, semi-double blooms in the darkest velvety maroon-purple of any Gallica, with prominent golden stamens providing striking contrast against the near-black petals, and a strong, classic old-rose fragrance. Like other Gallicas it blooms just once, in a spectacular flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

plant_note: Plant after the last frost in a sunny, well-drained spot.
directions: Tuscarora is a vigorous crape myrtle that bears long-lasting panicles of hot coral-pink flowers from midsummer into fall. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil to maximize bloom and reduce the chance of powdery mildew. Its smooth, mottled cinnamon bark and orange-red fall color extend the interest well past the flowering season. Prune only lightly in late winter to preserve its graceful vase-shaped structure rather than cutting it back hard. Established plants tolerate heat and drought, needing extra water mainly during long dry stretches.

plant_note: Surface-sow; seed needs light to germinate. Often blooms the second year.
directions: Press seed onto the soil surface without covering, since light is needed for germination. Also called Carpathian bellflower, this compact perennial forms neat mounds covered in violet-blue, upward-facing bells. Grow it in full sun to part shade and cool, well-drained soil, ideal for rock gardens, edgings, and containers. Shear after the first bloom flush to tidy the plant and encourage a second round of flowers.

plant_note: Sow seed onto the surface of consistently saturated, acidic peat or sphagnum in fall so winter cold provides natural stratification, or transplant divided tussocks directly into a bog garden or constructed wetland.
directions: Sow seed onto the surface of consistently saturated, acidic peat or sphagnum in fall so winter cold provides natural stratification, or transplant divided tussocks directly into a bog garden or constructed wetland. Over years each plant builds a raised hummock of tightly packed leaf bases topped with fluffy white cottony seed heads in late spring, which provide nesting material for birds and cover for small wetland fauna. It is a keystone structural species of northern peatlands and bogs found across the Great Lakes region, and its tussocks help stabilize saturated, nutrient-poor soils where few other plants thrive. Best suited to a dedicated bog or rain-garden feature with permanently wet, acidic conditions rather than a typical border.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; tussock sedge grows naturally in swamps, wet meadows, and the shallow margins of ponds and streams, where it forms the characteristic elevated pedestals (tussocks) that are an important ecological feature of northeastern wetlands.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; tussock sedge is the most ecologically important and structurally distinctive native sedge of northeastern North American wetlands — forming the characteristic large, elevated 'tussocks' (raised, columnar mounds of tightly packed dead and living stems) that are one of the most recognizable features of northeastern sedge meadows, swamps, and wet prairies. The tussocks serve as elevated nesting and resting platforms for many wetland birds and small mammals, and as elevated refuges from standing water. Blue-wing teal, sedge wrens, and least bitterns nest among tussock sedge clumps. Old established tussocks can reach 3–4 feet in height and diameter after decades of growth. An essential species for ecological wetland plantings, bioswales, rain gardens with wet zones, and naturalistic wet-meadow restorations.

common_name: Tutti Frutti Agastache (Vivid Raspberry-Pink Anise Hyssop)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Tutti Frutti requires excellent drainage, since it is prone to rot in heavy, wet clay or standing water, particularly through humid Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; raised beds or amended soil help ensure the sharp drainage this plant needs. Tutti Frutti produces tall, dense spikes of vivid raspberry-pink flowers over aromatic, licorice-scented foliage from summer into fall, drawing hummingbirds and bees in large numbers over its long bloom season. Like other hyssop hybrids it is somewhat shorter-lived in humid, high-rainfall climates than in drier regions, and excellent drainage is the single most important factor in getting it to persist for more than a season or two. Deadheading spent spikes encourages continued flowering, and the aromatic foliage is generally left alone by deer and rabbits.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade after frost; tweedia is one of the very few true pure sky-blue flowers available as an annual, making it exceptionally valuable as a cut flower and container accent.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; tweedia (blue milkweed) is a Brazilian native sub-shrub grown as an annual that produces one of the rarest colors in the flower world — a pure, clear, true sky-blue that does not shade toward purple or lavender. The small, star-shaped flowers open turquoise-blue from pink buds, gradually deepen to rich sky-blue at maturity, and then age through lilac to pink as they fade, providing three distinct flower colors simultaneously on the same plant. The soft, hairy, heart-shaped leaves and lax, scrambling stems give the plant a relaxed, cottage-garden character. Excellent as a cut flower — the unusual blue color is in extreme demand for floral arrangements and wedding work. Plants bloom most freely in full sun but tolerate partial shade. In zones 9–11 it overwinters as a perennial sub-shrub.

plant_note: Start indoors well before last frost; slow to germinate.
directions: Tweedia, or blue milkweed, offers rare true-blue, aquamarine star-shaped flowers with lavender buds and older blooms adding extra flair. Start the slow-germinating seed indoors 8 to 6 weeks before the last frost in warm soil, and transplant out after frost danger passes. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil where the sweetly scented flowers draw pollinators. Unlike common milkweeds it stays compact, making it well suited to containers and cut-flower use. Handle the stems with care, as the milky sap can irritate skin.

common_name: Twilight Magic Crapemyrtle (Plum-Foliage Disease-Resistant Purple-Leaf Alternative)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Twilight Magic is a First Editions crapemyrtle bred for deep plum foliage with high resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew, marketed as a heat-tolerant, disease-resistant alternative to purple-leaf plum trees that often defoliate in Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Twilight Magic bears deep plum-purple foliage that holds its color through the heat of a Gulf South summer, providing dramatic contrast against clusters of fuchsia-pink blooms from summer into fall. It was bred with high resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew, holding its dark foliage cleanly through humid conditions that cause many purple-leaved landscape shrubs and small trees to decline or defoliate. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood, preserving the plant's natural form rather than heavily topping it.

plant_note: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and heavy clay with minimal care.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and cut back in late winter before new growth begins. Twilight Zone stands out among little bluestem selections for its iridescent, silvery-mauve foliage that develops through midsummer and deepens toward rich purple tones as autumn arrives. New growth in spring emerges a cool blue-green before taking on its signature pastel coloring, giving the upright, columnar clump a shifting, almost metallic appearance across the season. Fluffy silver-white seed heads follow the narrow blue-toned foliage in fall, adding textural contrast and catching low autumn light. Native to North American prairies, it thrives in lean soil and tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and heavy clay with minimal care.

common_name: Twilite Prairieblues Baptisia (Bicolor Violet-and-Yellow False Indigo Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall into deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Twilite Prairieblues is a hybrid between Baptisia australis and Baptisia sphaerocarpa bred at the Chicago Botanic Garden, combining traits of both native parents.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; like its native Baptisia parents, Twilite Prairieblues develops a substantial taproot and strongly resents transplanting once established, so choose a permanent site from the start. This hybrid of blue wild indigo and yellow wild indigo produces striking bicolor flower spikes that open deep violet-purple and age to smoky charcoal-lilac with yellow-tinged keels, combining the vigor and bicolor interest of both native species into a single robust, shrub-like clump. It flowers over a long spring season and is heavily visited by bumblebees and other native bees, while the blue-green foliage and blackening seed pods provide structure through summer and fall. Established plants are extremely drought- and heat-tolerant and need no staking, fertilizing, or division, making them essentially maintenance-free once their deep root system is in place.

common_name: Twin Sisters Daffodil (Butter and Eggs Tazetta)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Twin Sisters is an ancient sterile tazetta hybrid spread entirely by bulb division and has been passed hand to hand between Gulf South gardeners for well over a century, naturalizing at old homesites, cemeteries, and roadsides.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Twin Sisters gets its common name from its habit of producing exactly two fragrant flowers per stem, each with pure white perianth segments surrounding a small, pale yellow cup, blooming earlier than most trumpet daffodils in mid to late winter. It is an ancient sterile hybrid that sets no seed, so like Grand Primo and Grand Monarque it has survived and spread across the Deep South for generations purely as a pass-along bulb, still turning up blooming reliably each year at abandoned homesites long after everything else planted there is gone. Give it a low-chill spot in full sun, let the foliage die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply for years.

common_name: Twin-Flowered Agave (Rabo de León, Gemini Agave)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; Agave geminiflora is one of the most distinctive and ornamental agaves for zone 9a and tropical gardens, producing a symmetrical globe of hundreds of extremely narrow, thread-like leaves edged with long, loosely curling white fibers — creating a dramatic spherical specimen plant that is unusual among succulents for its fine, grass-like texture despite being a stiff-leaved agave.
