directions: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; Agave geminiflora is a compact, slow-growing agave that suits containers and small spaces better than most species; it rarely if ever offsets (monocarpic in its entire life), blooming once after 10–15 years and producing the characteristic paired (gemini) flower arrangement, then dying without leaving pups; propagate from seed. Twin-Flowered Agave is one of the most visually distinctive of the ornamental agaves — distinguished immediately by its extremely unusual leaf form: rather than the broad, blade-like leaves of most agaves, Agave geminiflora produces hundreds of very narrow, almost grass-like leaves (only 1/4–1/3 inch wide but 12–24 inches long) each edged with long, loosely curling white fibers that give the compact spherical rosette a softly frilled or filigree appearance unique in the genus. The overall effect is a perfect globe of fine, dark green, fiber-edged leaves that catches light beautifully and looks dramatic from all angles. The species name 'geminiflora' refers to the characteristic arrangement of flowers on the bloom spike — the yellow flowers are borne in pairs (gemini = twin) on each branch of the 10–15 foot tall flower stalk that appears after 10–15 years. Native to the state of Nayarit on the Pacific coast of Mexico, it is somewhat tender (zone 8b–11) and may suffer frost damage in hard freezes below 20°F. In zone 9a, provide excellent drainage and a sheltered south-facing microclimate for maximum cold protection. An exceptional specimen plant for containers, courtyards, and focal points in xeric gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; twin-leaf epimedium is one of the smallest and daintiest species, best used at the front of a bed or in a trough where its delicate scale can be appreciated.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; twin-leaf epimedium is one of the smallest and daintiest species, best used at the front of a bed or in a trough where its delicate scale can be appreciated. Epimedium diphyllum is a diminutive Japanese species named for its distinctive leaves, which are divided into just two heart-shaped leaflets rather than the many leaflets typical of most epimedium, forming a low, tidy tuft topped with small, pure white, four-petaled flowers in spring. Its miniature scale and simple, elegant leaf structure make it a choice specialty plant for a shaded rock garden or the edge of a woodland path among other small treasures like dwarf hosta and Iris gracilipes. It spreads slowly and is easy to grow given consistent moisture and humus-rich soil, requiring little maintenance once established.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted softwood cuttings in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; twinberry honeysuckle naturally colonizes streambanks and moist woodland edges and establishes best where it gets consistent soil moisture while young.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where twinberry honeysuckle naturalizes readily along stream edges and under an open woodland canopy across its wide native range from Alaska south through the Pacific Northwest and Rockies. In spring the shrub bears small, paired, tubular yellow flowers tinged with red, followed in summer by shiny black berries held in pairs against a showy pair of deep red bracts — an unmistakable, almost theatrical fruit display that gives the plant its common name. The berries are bitter and unpalatable to people but are readily eaten by robins, waxwings, and other songbirds, and the shrub's dense, arching form provides valuable cover for nesting birds. It tolerates wet soil better than most shrubs sold for shade, making it a strong choice for the damp, low-light corners of a woodland or rain garden where few other flowering shrubs thrive.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions in spring in cool, moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; twinflower demands consistently cool root temperatures and high humidity, and succeeds best in northern gardens and Pacific Northwest conditions — it will not tolerate summer heat or drought.
directions: Plant in cool, moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; twinflower is a delicate trailing boreal woodland plant that spreads by slender rooting stems to form a fine-textured mat of small rounded leaves. In summer, pairs of tiny pink pendant bell-shaped flowers arise on forked stems above the foliage — sweetly fragrant, exquisite in detail, and perfectly matched to their Y-shaped stalks. Named for Carl Linnaeus himself, who considered it his favorite plant, L. borealis is a rewarding challenge best suited to cool northern and Pacific Northwest gardens. It will not tolerate summer heat, drought, or compacted or alkaline soils; mulch heavily with pine needles or leaf mold to maintain the cool, moist root zone it requires.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in fine, fast-draining orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Twinkle oncidium's small, mounted-friendly size and modest water needs make it well suited to a windowsill collection.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in fine, fast-draining orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Twinkle oncidium's small, mounted-friendly size and modest water needs make it well suited to a windowsill collection. This popular miniature hybrid produces sprays of numerous small, star-shaped white, pink, or yellow flowers with an intense, sweet vanilla-like fragrance that belies the plant's diminutive size, blooming reliably even on a young, small specimen unlike many larger orchid hybrids that take years to reach flowering maturity. Its compact size makes it one of the easiest oncidium-type orchids for a limited windowsill or grow-light collection, tolerating slightly less light than larger cattleya-alliance orchids while still flowering dependably multiple times a year. Water when the mix approaches dryness, feed lightly with a diluted orchid fertilizer during active growth, and repot every one to two years once the fine bark mix breaks down.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or sow fresh seed in fall; Twinleaf is a charming and underused native woodland plant of the barberry family named in honor of Thomas Jefferson by its discoverer William Bartram, producing distinctive deeply two-lobed leaves that resemble a folded butterfly wing and ephemeral white flowers in early spring.
directions: Plant in spring in deeply humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; Twinleaf is slow to establish but long-lived and gradually expands into a colony through root divisions. Jeffersonia diphylla (Twinleaf) is a native eastern North American woodland plant of the barberry family named by the American botanist Benjamin Smith Barton in honor of Thomas Jefferson in 1792 for Jefferson's wide-ranging botanical and scientific curiosity; the common name 'twinleaf' refers to the distinctive paired, deeply bilobed leaves that appear to consist of two separate mirror-image halves folded together along a central crease — unlike any other North American wildflower leaf. In early spring (March–April) the plant produces solitary, eight-petaled, pure white flowers on bare stems before the leaves fully expand; the flowers last only a day or two. After flowering the leaves expand to their full size and remain attractive through summer. An unusual and botanically interesting native wildflower for moist woodland gardens; relatively rare in cultivation.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun a few weeks before last frost; twinspur performs best in cool weather and may go semi-dormant in peak summer heat, rebounding in fall.
directions: Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in cool spring or fall weather; twinspur is a South African relative of snapdragons that produces delicate, open-faced, two-lipped flowers of soft to vivid pink, salmon, coral, or white with characteristic twin spurs projecting backward from the base of each flower — a charming, cottage-garden character of the individual flowers. Plants produce a loose, mounding, spreading habit with abundant bloom in cool spring and fall weather and are self-cleaning (no deadheading required). Like bacopa and lobelia, they may go semi-dormant in peak summer heat and should be trimmed back slightly and watered through the worst heat to encourage fall rebloom. Excellent in hanging baskets, window boxes, and container edges. 'Coral Belle', 'Elegance Series', and 'Whisper Series' are widely grown. Perennial in zones 7–9 where winters remain above 25°F.

common_name: Twist of Lime Abelia (Lime-and-Cream Variegated Abelia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; variegation is brightest with several hours of direct sun, and new growth flushes pink before settling into its lime-and-cream pattern.
directions: Twist of Lime is an abelia selection grown chiefly for its foliage, small leaves margined in creamy yellow around a lime-green center, with new growth emerging flushed pink before settling into the mature variegated pattern, giving the shrub a bright, multicolored look through most of the growing season. It still produces the small, fragrant, white-to-pale-pink tubular flowers typical of abelia from late spring into fall on gracefully arching stems, and like other abelia cultivars it is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay soil, heat, humidity, and drought with minimal care once established. Prune lightly after the main flush of spring bloom if shaping is wanted, and watch for occasional reversion shoots of plain green foliage, which should be cut out to keep the variegation strong.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; flowers blue in acidic soil (pH below 5.5) and pink in alkaline soil (pH above 6.5), like other macrophylla cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and remove spent flower heads through the season to encourage continued rebloom. Part of the Endless Summer collection, Twist-n-Shout is a reblooming lacecap hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, producing flat clusters of pink or blue fertile florets ringed by showy sterile ray flowers from early summer through fall, with the deep red-tinged stems adding fall and winter interest after leaf drop. Because it blooms on new growth as well as old, an errant late-frost or a hard pruning does not eliminate the whole season's flowers the way it does on old-wood-only cultivars, making it more forgiving for gardeners uncertain about pruning timing. Keep soil consistently moist — hydrangeas wilt readily in summer heat — and mulch to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; twisted trillium grows on rich wooded slopes and ravine bottoms of Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee and is easy to identify by its distinctively twisted, horizontally spreading petals.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Twisted trillium is a sessile species of the mid-South, native to rich wooded slopes and ravines in Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee, named for its narrow maroon-purple petals, which spiral and twist as they spread out nearly horizontally above the mottled leaves rather than standing upright like most sessile trilliums. It blooms in early spring, with a faintly fetid scent typical of fly-pollinated trilliums, and its low, outstretched flower makes an eye-catching accent along a shaded woodland path where visitors can look down into the twisted petals. Give it the same rich, well-drained, humus-heavy soil favored by Trillium cuneatum, and avoid moving established clumps, since trillium rhizomes take years to recover fully from transplant.

common_name: Twister Agapanthus (White Petals Edged in Blue Bicolor)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Twister is a distinctive bicolor agapanthus with blue-edged white petals.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Twister bears rounded umbels of white flowers each finely edged in blue, an unusual bicolor pattern that gives the flower heads a frosted, two-toned look at a distance, distinct from both solid white and solid blue agapanthus. It flowers in summer above clumps of narrow, dark green strap foliage and combines well with either pure blue or pure white companions in a mixed border. Like other agapanthus it is drought-tolerant once established and blooms best when slightly pot-bound, so avoid dividing established clumps too frequently.

plant_note: Sow seed direct in early spring after scarifying or soaking overnight; alternatively, sow in fall and allow the seed to cold-stratify naturally over winter — this Mediterranean perennial establishes most reliably from seed sown in situ, as its spreading rhizomes resent disturbance once established.
directions: Sow scarified or overnight-soaked seed 1 inch deep into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, with a trellis, wire, or shrub for support; two-flowered everlasting pea is considered the most ornamental of the perennial peas, bearing pairs of exceptionally large, richly colored deep-pink to magenta flowers on each stem from early to midsummer — the blooms are substantially larger than those of the common everlasting pea (Lathyrus latifolius) and make a striking display on arches, obelisks, or through open shrubs. It spreads steadily by rhizomes and will naturalize freely in well-drained soils, forming sizeable clumps in time; site it where it can expand without crowding small neighbors. Like most perennial peas it is drought-tolerant once established and fixes its own nitrogen, performing best in lean rather than heavily enriched soils.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in well-drained, moderately fertile, humus-rich soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; two-leaf squill is one of the very earliest spring bulbs to emerge and bloom, often flowering in February in mild climates or March further north, before most other bulbs have broken dormancy. It naturalizes freely and thrives under deciduous trees and shrubs, forming expanding colonies that bloom more prolifically each year.
directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade in fall for very early spring bloom; two-leaf squill is one of the earliest and most charming of the squill family, producing loose, arching racemes of intense, vivid blue star-shaped flowers — a singularly saturated, pure blue rarely matched among early spring bulbs — on short stems above just two (occasionally three) glossy, strap-like basal leaves, from which its species name derives. It blooms in February to March, often emerging through the last frosts of late winter alongside snowdrops and winter aconite, and thrives particularly well in the partial shade beneath deciduous trees and shrubs, where it colonizes the leaf-littered ground with a spreading carpet of brilliant blue. It naturalizes freely by both offsets and self-seeding, increasing steadily to form sizeable drifts over the years with no attention required. A choice companion for snowdrops, Eranthis, and early crocus in woodland-edge or naturalistic plantings.

plant_note: Sow fresh seeds in fall immediately when ripe (seeds require cold stratification over winter to germinate in spring), or divide established clumps carefully in early spring; two-leaved mitrewort grows in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil under deciduous trees and should not be allowed to dry out in summer. It self-sows modestly where conditions are suitable.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade under deciduous trees; two-leaved mitrewort is a delicate eastern North American woodland wildflower producing a basal rosette of maple-leaf-shaped, three-lobed, slightly hairy leaves with two smaller, opposite stem leaves at mid-stem, and in April and May, slender, airy racemes 8–14 inches tall bearing a succession of exquisitely tiny flowers that reward close examination — each bloom a miniature snowflake of fringed, thread-like, feathery white petals arranged in a star with intricate, almost lacy dissection. The flowers are so small and intricate that a hand lens reveals their true beauty. A quiet, refined native wildflower without showy impact, it is valued in the naturalistic shade garden as a companion to spring ephemerals, wild ginger, and ferns, naturalizing in moist woodland soil to form small colonies over time. The common name 'bishop's cap' refers to the small, mitre-shaped seed capsule that follows the tiny flowers. Native to moist deciduous forest from Quebec to Georgia and west to Minnesota.

common_name: Two-Lobed Aerangis (Bilobed Aerangis, West African Star Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark or wood with exposed aerial roots in bright indirect to filtered direct light; Aerangis biloba is a miniature, monopodial epiphyte that thrives when the roots are fully exposed to air, drying between waterings. Mist or dunk the roots daily in summer; water weekly in winter. Provide good air circulation — still, humid air promotes fungal issues. The pendant racemes of fragrant, white, nocturnally-fragrant flowers bloom in fall and winter. Protect from temperatures below 55°F. Excellent as a terrarium or windowsill orchid. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow mounted on cork or wood with freely exposed aerial roots in bright indirect to filtered direct light — Aerangis biloba is a miniature monopodial epiphyte that performs best when mounted without any medium, allowing its silver roots to dry between mistings in the manner of its natural tree-branch habitat. Aerangis biloba is a small, monopodial epiphytic orchid from West Africa (Cameroon, Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Sierra Leone) in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most rewarding of the approximately 50 Aerangis species for beginning and experienced orchid collectors. The plant is compact: a single upright stem with overlapping ranks of 4–8 oblong, dark-green, strap-shaped leaves 4–6 inches long with two rounded lobes at the tip (the 'biloba' — two-lobed). The aerial roots are silvery-white, thick, flat, and numerous. In fall and winter, the plant produces pendant racemes 8–16 inches long carrying 8–18 flowers in two ranks along the stem — each flower a small (1-inch), pure white, star-shaped bloom of the Angraecoid type (6 pointed petals in a flat arrangement with a long spur). The flowers open pure white and are intensely, sweetly fragrant at night. The pendant display of pristine white flowers on an arching stem, combined with the night fragrance, makes Aerangis biloba one of the most delightful of the African miniature orchids for indoor or protected porch culture. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant bulbs after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; two-tone pineapple lily is half-hardy and benefits from a thick winter mulch in zones 7-8 or lifting where winters are more severe.
directions: Plant bulbs after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; two-tone pineapple lily is half-hardy and benefits from a thick winter mulch in zones 7-8 or lifting where winters are more severe. Broad, wavy-edged, strap-shaped leaves with purple-spotted undersides form a bold rosette from which a thick flower spike rises in summer, densely packed with star-shaped, pale green flowers edged in maroon-purple and topped with a tuft of leafy bracts that mimics a pineapple crown, giving the whole plant its distinctive common name. Native to South Africa, it is a long-blooming, low-maintenance summer bulb that provides months of unusual textural and color interest in a border or large container, attracting bees to its abundant small flowers. Water regularly through summer growth, reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall, and mulch heavily over winter or lift and store bulbs in colder zones.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; two-toned grape hyacinth produces only a single broad, strap-shaped leaf per bulb (unlike the multiple narrow leaves of M. armeniacum) and flowers in mid-spring, later than many grape hyacinths. It naturalizes freely in suitable conditions. The bicolor effect of dark-violet lower florets and sky-blue sterile upper florets on the same spike is unique among muscari.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade; two-toned grape hyacinth stands apart from other muscari species through a striking, built-in bicolor effect on each individual spike: the lower portion of the densely packed raceme carries the typical, deep, dark-blue-violet to navy-blue, urn-shaped, fertile florets of the grape hyacinth type, while the upper portion of the same spike carries distinctly lighter, sky-blue to pale-blue, sterile florets that are more elongated and open — creating a natural two-toned spike that grades from dark violet at the base to pale sky-blue at the tip. This gradation of two distinct blues on a single small flower spike is botanically unique among commonly grown muscari and creates a more complex, interesting flower display than the single-toned spikes of M. armeniacum. A single broad leaf (vs the several narrow leaves of other species) gives the foliage a distinctive, lush quality. The bulbs increase steadily and naturalize in part shade under deciduous trees and shrubs, where the bicolor spring spikes create a particularly attractive display in the dappled light. An outstanding, underused grape hyacinth for the woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; two-winged silverbell is native to rich, moist woodland slopes and streambanks of the southeastern Coastal Plain and performs best where afternoon shade moderates summer heat. It is more heat-tolerant than Halesia carolina and is the preferred silverbell for zones 8–9 gardens. Seed requires a double dormancy — warm stratification for 3 months followed by cold stratification for 3 months — and may take two seasons to germinate; container transplants are strongly recommended.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; two-winged silverbell is a graceful southeastern native small tree that puts on one of the most charming spring flower displays of any native woody plant — in March and April, before or just as the leaves emerge, the pendulous branches are draped in clusters of pure-white, four-petaled, nodding bell-shaped flowers that dangle like delicate ornaments along every stem, providing exceptional early nectar for pollinators. Halesia diptera is distinguished from the more commonly grown Carolina silverbell (H. carolina) by its two-winged fruits rather than four-winged, and by its superior heat tolerance, making it the silverbell of choice for gardens in the Deep South and Gulf Coast regions where H. carolina struggles. The fruits that follow are decorative in their own right, persisting on the branches well into fall, and the clean oval foliage turns yellow in autumn before dropping. An outstanding specimen tree for woodland garden edges, naturalistic streamside plantings, and residential lawns in zones 5–9 where a refined, low-maintenance flowering tree of genuine native provenance is desired.

common_name: Two-flowered Dwarf Dandelion, Orange Dwarf Dandelion
plant_note: Sow in fall in well-drained to moderately moist, average to slightly acidic soil in partial shade; cold stratification through the winter naturally breaks seed dormancy and promotes strong germination in early spring — fall direct sowing in place is the most reliable establishment method.
directions: Krigia biflora is a cheerful, underused native perennial of woodland margins, forest clearings, and disturbed open areas across eastern North America from Kansas to New England and south into the Appalachians, producing bright orange-yellow, dandelion-like flower heads on branching, leafy stems from late spring into summer — an unusually long bloom season for a member of the chicory family. Unlike the common dandelion, it tolerates meaningful shade and thrives at the transition zone between open lawn and shaded woodland edge, making it an excellent native substitute in naturalistic or no-mow plantings where other sun-loving wildflowers struggle. The milky-sapped stems branch repeatedly after the first blooms, extending the flowering display, and the plant gradually spreads by seed to form attractive loose colonies; direct sow in fall and allow seeds to overwinter naturally for best results.

plant_note: Plant tubers eye-up, 4-6 inches deep, in full sun after the soil has warmed following the last frost.
directions: Twyning's After Eight is a compact bishop-type dahlia with near-black, finely cut foliage that sets off pure white single flowers with a small yellow eye. Its low, bushy habit and small flower size make it well suited to container growing and the front of a border, where the foliage color reads as a design feature even before it flowers. Pinch the growing tip early to build a bushier plant, and deadhead regularly to keep new buds forming through summer. Gardeners often grow it specifically for the dark-leaf, white-flower combination, which is unusual among compact bedding dahlias.

common_name: Türkenlouis Poppy (Deeply Fringed Red Oriental Poppy)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Oriental poppies go dormant and disappear entirely in summer, so mark the spot to avoid disturbing the dormant crown.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Oriental poppies resent wet, heavy soil and summer humidity, so good drainage is essential. Türkenlouis stands out among Oriental poppies for its unusual, deeply cut and fringed red petals with a dark central blotch, giving each bloom a shaggy, almost carnation-like texture quite different from the smooth-petaled forms typical of the species. Like other Oriental poppies it flowers in late spring, then dies back to dormancy through summer heat before re-emerging with fresh foliage in fall, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown. It performs best in climates with cooler summers and struggles in the humid, hot conditions of the Deep South.

common_name: Ukigumo Japanese Maple (Floating Clouds Heavily Variegated Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Ukigumo, meaning 'floating clouds,' bears heavily variegated white, pink, and green mottled leaves.
directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure that can scorch the delicate variegated leaves. Ukigumo, Japanese for 'floating clouds,' bears leaves heavily mottled and speckled in white, pink, and green in an irregular, ever-shifting pattern that makes each leaf slightly different, one of the most dramatically variegated Japanese maple cultivars available, on a slow-growing, upright small tree. Its striking, ethereal foliage pattern makes a strong focal specimen in a shaded or partly sunny border where its color can be appreciated up close. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape.

plant_note: Plant transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Ultra Violet autumn sage is drought-tolerant once established and blooms over an unusually long season from spring through fall.
directions: Plant transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Ultra Violet autumn sage is drought-tolerant once established and blooms over an unusually long season from spring through fall. Fine, aromatic foliage covers a compact, well-branched shrub topped with a near-continuous flush of rich violet-purple flowers from spring through the first hard frost, one of the deepest, truest purple tones among the many autumn sage color selections bred from this exceptionally floriferous Texas and Mexico native. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in the reflected heat of a xeriscape border or gravel garden, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies throughout its long bloom season with minimal care. Shear lightly after each flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and cut back hard in late winter to remove old woody growth and rejuvenate the plant.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant to sharply drained, lean soil in full sun after danger of frost passes; calandrinia is short-lived but self-sows in mild climates. In zones 7–9 it may overwinter in a sheltered position with excellent drainage. The flowers close in overcast conditions and open only in full sun.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; umbellate calandrinia is a compact Chilean native producing low mounds of narrow, slightly fleshy, slightly hairy leaves and in summer a succession of intense, brilliant crimson-magenta, five-petaled flowers (3/4 to 1 inch across) in loose, umbellate clusters on short stems — the flowers opening only in full sun and closing in shade or overcast conditions, creating a display that varies dramatically between bright sun and cloud cover. The saturation and purity of the crimson-magenta color is exceptional — a true, vivid, unmuddied crimson-red rather than pink or orange-red. It thrives in the lean, dry, rocky, and well-drained conditions of alpine and coastal rocky habitats in Chile. Outstanding in rock gardens, gravel gardens, and any lean, sun-baked position where its compact size and vivid color can be appreciated at close range. Self-sows in mild climates to maintain naturalized colonies in appropriate lean, open positions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 5–9; Umbrella Bamboo is the ideal bamboo for most temperate gardens — a non-invasive, extremely cold-hardy clumping bamboo native to the mountains of Hunan Province, China, forming elegant, arching, fountain-like clumps of slender culms and fine-textured leaves — completely non-invasive and perfect for small to medium gardens needing screening or specimen interest without rhizome spreading.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Fargesia murielae performs best in cool, moist conditions with some shade protection from hot afternoon sun — in hot climates (zone 7b–9) choose a north-facing or east-facing position to prevent leaf scorching in summer heat. Fargesia murielae (Umbrella Bamboo or Muriel Bamboo) is one of the most popular and widely grown bamboos for temperate gardens across Europe and North America, prized precisely for its qualities opposite to the notorious running bamboos: it is a tight, non-invasive clumper with pachymorph rhizomes that never run or spread aggressively. Native to the high mountains of Hunan and Sichuan Provinces, China, at elevations of 6,000–10,000 feet, it is extremely cold hardy to zone 5 (-10°F) — surviving conditions that kill most bamboos. The graceful, arching culms (1–2 inch diameter, 6–15 feet tall) are covered with fine-textured, lance-shaped leaves that cascade in elegant, weeping fountain-form clumps — outstanding as a specimen plant, privacy screen, or container plant. Fargesia murielae is the primary food bamboo of the wild giant panda in Hunan Province — nearly all wild Fargesia murielae populations in China flowered and died simultaneously in the 1980s in a masting event, causing a severe panda food shortage. Important note: all Fargesia species are monocarpic — they flower once after 80–100+ years and die; plants from the post-1980s regeneration are not yet at flowering age.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Fargesia bamboos are clump-forming (not running/invasive) and can be planted without containment barriers, unlike Phyllostachys and other runner bamboos.
directions: Divide established clumps or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; umbrella bamboo (Chinese fountain bamboo) is one of the most ornamental and garden-appropriate of all bamboos for temperate gardens — a graceful, arching, clump-forming (non-invasive) bamboo that produces dense clusters of slender, elegant culms (canes) that arch gracefully outward and downward like a fountain of cascading foliage, bearing short, narrow, lance-shaped leaves that create a rustling, whispering sound in the breeze. Unlike the running bamboos (Phyllostachys, Pseudosasa) that spread invasively by underground rhizomes, Fargesia bamboos form compact, tightly restrained clumps that expand slowly and require no containment barriers. Tolerates shade better than most bamboos. Excellent as a screen, specimen, or large container plant. Unlike some Fargesias, this species flowers infrequently. 'Simba' and 'Jumbo' are popular cultivar selections.

plant_note: Transplant divisions with a section of the stout rhizome in early fall, or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic, cool, shaded soil near a stream or seepage area in early fall; umbrella leaf requires constantly moist, cool conditions and is best planted beside permanent water features or in north-facing slopes.
directions: Transplant divisions in early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full shade near streams or seepage areas; umbrella leaf is a rare and spectacular native perennial of high Appalachian mountain stream edges, grown for a sequence of three distinct ornamental features across the season — in spring, each stem bears two enormous, deeply lobed leaves that spread horizontally like open umbrellas up to 20 inches across (one of the most dramatic basal leaf effects in hardy perennials), followed by flat-topped clusters of white flowers in early summer, followed in turn by the most prized feature: clusters of vivid, intensely blue berries on bright red stalks in late summer — a color combination of scarlet stems and brilliant blue-purple fruits that is uniquely eye-catching in the shade garden and is the plant's greatest ornamental asset. Requires constantly moist, cool, shaded conditions similar to its streamside mountain habitat. Fairly difficult to establish but long-lived and spectacular when content.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; umbrella magnolia grows naturally as an understory tree in moist ravines and shaded slopes and tolerates deep shade better than most flowering trees.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; umbrella magnolia is a distinctive native understory tree of the Appalachians and Southeast named for the pattern of its enormous leaves — 12–24 inches long — arranged in a dramatic whorl around the branch tips like the spokes of an umbrella, creating a striking bold-textured tropical effect in the shaded garden. The large creamy-white flowers (6–10 inches) in late spring have an unusual, slightly unpleasant fragrance but are still attractive from a distance. Red cone-like fruit clusters in late summer and fall are ornamental and eaten by songbirds. It grows naturally as a subcanopy tree in moist, acidic ravines and tolerates shade better than most Magnolia species, making it one of the few flowering trees that performs well in partial to light shade. The extraordinarily large leaves and exotic texture make it an excellent specimen in shaded woodland gardens.

plant_note: Root stem tip cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container specimens in well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost; schefflera grows rapidly in warm climates — up to 2–3 feet per year — and becomes a large specimen tree in frost-free zones.
directions: Root stem tip cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to full sun; umbrella plant grows rapidly to become a large, multi-stemmed tree in zones 10–12 with bold, palmate, compound leaves of 7–16 leaflets arranged like the ribs of an umbrella, creating a striking tropical silhouette. Mature trees produce dramatic, upright clusters of small red flowers that attract birds. Outdoors it can reach 40 feet tall; as a container plant or indoor specimen in filtered light it stays manageable at 4–8 feet. Plant has become invasive in Florida and Hawaii — consider the smaller, non-invasive Schefflera arboricola (dwarf schefflera) as an alternative in those states. Container plants tolerate low light exceptionally well.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beside ponds, streams, and in rain gardens in spring; umbrella plant thrives in shallow water (up to 6 inches deep) and wet boggy soil and requires consistently moist conditions throughout the growing season.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beside water; umbrella plant (Indian rhubarb) is a native Californian and Oregon perennial of streambanks and wet canyon floors with two distinct ornamental seasons: in early spring, before any leaves emerge, clusters of small, flat-topped, pale-pink flowers appear on 3-foot, bare, hairy reddish stems — a surprising and charming early display; then throughout summer and fall, enormous, round, peltate (stalked from the center) leaves up to 2 feet across rise on tall, thick, hairy petioles to 3–4 feet, creating a bold, parasol-like effect that is one of the most architecturally dramatic of any streamside or bog perennial. The leaves turn to rich coppery-orange in autumn before dying back. An excellent specimen plant for large-scale naturalistic plantings beside ponds and streams where its scale and requirement for constantly wet soil can be accommodated. Similar in scale to Petasites (butterbur) but native to western North America and much better-behaved (non-spreading).

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in consistently wet to standing-water conditions in full sun to part shade; umbrella plant grows in boggy soil, shallow water up to 6 inches deep, or ordinary moist container mixes. It can be overwintered indoors as a houseplant in cold climates and is one of the most popular container and pond plants.
directions: Grow in consistently wet soil, boggy margins, or shallow standing water in full sun to part shade; umbrella plant is a Madagascar native sedge in the papyrus family producing tall, straight, triangular stems topped with graceful, radiating whorls of narrow, grass-like bracts that spread like the ribs of an umbrella — an architectural silhouette immediately distinctive in any water garden or container planting. It grows best in shallow water (2–6 inches) or in saturated boggy soil at pond margins, and is equally successful as a houseplant in a water-filled saucer. The upright, bamboo-like stalks create bold vertical interest in water features, and the plant is prolific enough to supply cut foliage for arrangements. In zones 9–11 it is perennial outdoors; in colder climates it is widely grown as a pool ornamental moved indoors for winter or maintained as a houseplant year-round. Propagation is uniquely simple — cut off a head of bracts and float it upside-down in water, where it will root from the bracts.

common_name: Umbrella Tree (Octopus Tree, Queensland Umbrella Tree)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; umbrella tree is adaptable to a wide range of conditions but prefers bright indirect light for best indoor performance — outdoors in zone 9b-12 it is a fast-growing shade tree. CAUTION: Listed as invasive in Florida — check local regulations.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; CAUTION — invasive in Florida and Hawaii; do not plant near natural areas. Schefflera actinophylla (umbrella tree or octopus tree) is an Australian tropical tree that has become one of the most popular houseplants in the world while simultaneously becoming a serious invasive species in Florida and Hawaii. As a landscape tree in zone 10–12, it grows to an impressive 25–40 feet with a distinctive canopy of large, palmate (hand-shaped) compound leaves with 5–16 leaflets radiating like the ribs of an umbrella — each leaflet 4–10 inches long and glossy. The common name 'octopus tree' comes from the bizarre flowering structure: dark-red, finger-like flower spikes emerging from the branch tips like tentacles — striking in flower and producing small, dark-red berries consumed by birds (which has spread the plant into natural areas). As an indoor plant, the large-leafed forms create a bold tropical statement; 'Amate' is a popular, more compact cultivar. CAUTION: Listed as an invasive Category I exotic pest plant in Florida — do not plant near wild areas or waterways.

plant_note: Plant in groups of three or more in full sun for the strongest color display; thrives in heavy alkaline clay as well as sandy or rocky soils.
directions: Plant in groups of three or more in full sun for the strongest color display; thrives in heavy alkaline clay as well as sandy or rocky soils and tolerates both drought and periodic waterlogging. Selected in 2003 by horticulturists Lauren Springer and Scott Ogden from a vigorous wild population in north-central Texas, Undaunted is a 2014 Plant Select winner valued for extending true pink muhly grass color into colder zones than the straight species can reliably handle. Its fine, mid-green, sometimes curling foliage forms a rounded mound that erupts in early fall into a haze of bright reddish-pink seed heads, fading to warm tawny brown through winter. It is markedly more cold-hardy and adaptable than the straight species, with strong deer resistance and virtually pest-free performance once established.

common_name: Under the Sea Coleus (Uniquely Lobed Fringed-Leaf Coleus Series)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Under the Sea selections tolerate more sun than traditional shade coleus but still benefit from afternoon shade protection in the hottest Gulf South locations.
directions: Plant in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and keep soil consistently moist to support the lush, textural foliage this series is grown for. Under the Sea is a distinctive coleus series bred for unusual, deeply lobed, ruffled, or fringed leaf shapes that resemble coral, anemones, or seaweed, giving each named selection within the series a strikingly different silhouette and texture from typical broad-leaved coleus, in a range of colors from deep burgundy to chartreuse and coral-pink. The novel foliage forms make the series a favorite for adding textural contrast and conversation-piece interest to shaded containers, fairy gardens, and mixed beds alongside broader-leaved companions like hosta and heuchera. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy in leaf production, and pinch growing tips periodically for a fuller, bushier habit through the season.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Underwood's Trillium is a warm-climate sessile species suited to the moist hardwood and mixed pine-hardwood forests of the Florida panhandle, Georgia, and Alabama.
directions: Underwood's Trillium is a southeastern sessile trillium native to the moist, mixed hardwood forests of the Florida panhandle, Georgia, and Alabama, where it blooms in February through April with dark maroon to nearly black sessile flowers nestled among three strongly mottled, glossy leaves. It occupies an ecological niche similar to other coastal plain sessile trilliums but tolerates somewhat warmer and more humid conditions than its montane relatives, making it an appropriate choice for gardeners in zones 7–9 seeking native spring woodland plants. Obtain only nursery-propagated plants, as wild collection is destructive and in many areas illegal; plant rhizome divisions in fall in well-amended, moist, acidic soil in the shade of evergreen or deciduous trees. Like all trilliums, it blooms for only a few weeks before going dormant, so interplant with later-emerging shade perennials to fill the gap.

common_name: Unicorn Monstera (True Swiss Cheese Plant, Obliqua Monstera, Ghost Monstera)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-draining, chunky, highly aerated aroid mix; true Monstera obliqua is one of the rarest Monsteras and most plants sold under this name in the trade are actually Monstera adansonii. Genuine M. obliqua has leaves where the fenestrations (holes) exceed the remaining leaf tissue in area — the leaf appears to be more hole than leaf. Requires high humidity (70%+), warm temperatures (65–85°F), and a climbing support. Very slow-growing. Propagate from stem cuttings. All parts toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in chunky, well-aerated aroid potting mix with a climbing support — true Monstera obliqua is an extremely slow-growing, delicate climbing aroid that requires consistent warmth, high humidity, and careful watering to thrive. Monstera obliqua is a rare, hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to Panama, Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, and Brazil in the Araceae family, one of the most coveted and least commonly available plants in the tropical collector world. The reason for its rarity and fascination is its extraordinary leaf fenestration pattern: true M. obliqua produces thin, delicate leaves in which the holes (fenestrations) are so large and numerous that they actually occupy more area than the remaining green leaf tissue — the leaf is literally more hole than leaf, a lace-like structure of the most extreme fenestration of any Monstera species. This quality makes the true plant fragile, photosensitive, and extremely challenging to cultivate compared to the robust Monstera adansonii that is frequently sold as 'M. obliqua' in the plant trade. Collectors who obtain true M. obliqua consider it one of the pinnacles of the aroid hobby. Important note: the vast majority of plants labeled 'Monstera obliqua' in commercial horticulture are actually Monstera adansonii, which is more robust and has much less fenestration. All parts of true M. obliqua are toxic.

common_name: Unique Hydrangea (Vigorous Very Large White Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Unique is a vigorous panicle hydrangea bearing some of the largest flower panicles in the species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Unique produces very large, dense, cone-shaped white flower panicles on a vigorous, large-growing shrub, among the biggest blooms and biggest overall plants in the panicle hydrangea group, making it a substantial specimen or informal screen where its eventual size can be accommodated. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new growth regardless of soil pH, so flower color never shifts. Prune in late winter to shape and control size, cutting back last year's growth by about a third to encourage strong new flowering stems.

common_name: UpTick Coreopsis (Large-Flowered Long-Blooming Compact Tickseed Series)
plant_note: Set out container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; UpTick blooms the first year and continues nonstop through summer into fall without deadheading.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid heavy, poorly drained ground where coreopsis crowns are prone to rot over winter. UpTick is a vegetatively propagated coreopsis series bred for unusually large flowers, up to three inches across, on compact, well-branched plants that bloom continuously from late spring through frost without deadheading, a marked improvement over the smaller flowers and shorter bloom window of older seed-grown tickseed cultivars. Its dense, mounded habit and strong repeat bloom make it a reliable performer at the front of a sunny border, and established plants are notably heat- and drought-tolerant, thriving in the same lean, well-drained conditions native Coreopsis grandiflora prefers in the wild. Deadheading is not required to keep it flowering, though shearing lightly midseason can refresh a tired-looking plant.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Upland Boneset is a shade-tolerant woodland species with sessile, non-clasping leaves, distinct from wetland-loving common boneset.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, in dry to average woodland conditions rather than the consistently wet soil that common boneset prefers. Upland Boneset is a genuinely dry-adapted, shade-tolerant thoroughwort of upland woods and woodland edges, distinguished from wetland-associated Eupatorium relatives by its narrow, tapering, sessile leaves that do not clasp or fuse around the stem, topped by flat clusters of white flowers in late summer to early fall that provide valuable nectar for bees and butterflies as many other blooms fade. Its tolerance for drier, shadier conditions makes it a useful native option for a dry woodland garden where the classic wetland boneset would struggle. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Upland White Goldenrod (Prairie Goldenrod, White Aster-Goldenrod)
plant_note: Fall-sow onto well-drained, lean soil or cold-moist stratify 30-60 days before spring sowing; it establishes best in gravelly or rocky prairie-type ground rather than rich garden beds.
directions: Grow in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil such as limestone glades or gravelly prairie plantings, since this unusual goldenrod bears flat-topped clusters of white, aster-like ray flowers rather than the typical yellow plumes of its relatives, a trait that once led botanists to classify it as an aster. It blooms in late summer and fall, complementing true asters and providing a valuable pale counterpoint to yellow prairie goldenrods while still attracting the same broad range of native bees, wasps, and butterflies. Unlike many goldenrods it stays compact and well-behaved, spreading slowly rather than aggressively colonizing by rhizome. It performs best where soil stays on the dry, mineral side and struggles in rich, moisture-retentive garden loam.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; upright hosta forms an unusually vertical, vase-shaped clump rather than the low mound typical of most hostas, making it useful as a textural accent among lower groundcovers.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; upright hosta forms an unusually vertical, vase-shaped clump rather than the low mound typical of most hostas, making it useful as a textural accent among lower groundcovers. Hosta rectifolia is a wild species from Japan and the Russian Far East with narrow, elongated, dark green leaves held in a distinctly upright, funnel-shaped rosette, sending up tall spikes of pale purple flowers in late summer that stand well above the foliage. Its narrow, vase-like habit reads differently from mounding hosta cultivars and adds vertical structure to a shaded border, while its exceptional cold hardiness makes it a reliable choice even in far northern gardens. It is easy to grow under standard hosta conditions and divides readily in spring to increase the planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; unlike its relative wild ginger, Saruma has upright stems rather than a low creeping habit and self-seeds modestly in a favorable woodland setting.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade. Saruma henryi is a monotypic Chinese woodland genus closely related to wild ginger, but unlike its low, creeping cousin it grows upright stems clothed in heart-shaped, softly hairy leaves, forming a small clump rather than a mat. In late spring it produces small, nodding, pale yellow flowers shaped much like those of wild ginger, followed by modest self-seeding in a hospitable shade garden. It combines well with hostas, ferns, and hellebores in a woodland border, tolerates a range of shade conditions once established, and needs little care beyond a yearly topdressing of leaf compost.

plant_note: Direct sow in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–May for summer bloom or August–September for fall bloom. Uproar Rose is a tall variety (24–30 inches) that may benefit from staking in exposed locations. For the longest bloom season, deadhead spent flowers regularly — though Uproar Rose blooms profusely with or without deadheading. Thin to 12 inches apart for best air circulation; zinnias are susceptible to powdery mildew when crowded, especially in humid conditions. The large, rose-pink flowers are outstanding cut flowers lasting 7–10 days in a vase.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — zinnias thrive in hot, sunny, moderately fertile conditions; Uproar Rose is an All-America Selections award-winning zinnia producing particularly large (4–5 inch), fully double, deep rose-pink flowers on tall, sturdy stems that are among the most impressive cut flowers available from direct-sown seed in the summer garden. The rich, saturated rose-pink color — more vibrant and deeper than pale pink varieties — maintains its intensity through summer heat, making Uproar Rose one of the most reliable large-flowered pink zinnias for the hot conditions of zone 9 summers. Zinnias in general are the quintessential summer annual for the Gulf South — they thrive in the heat that defeats many summer flowers, blooming continuously and heavily from planting through frost with minimal care. The large flowers are exceptional butterfly magnets, attracting swallowtails, fritillaries, monarchs, and sulphurs throughout the summer season, making zinnia plantings important pollinator habitat during the hottest months when many other nectar plants are stressed. Uproar Rose's combination of cut flower quality, striking color, heat tolerance, and pollinator value makes it one of the most multi-purpose zinnias available.

common_name: Uproar Scarlet Zinnia (Huge Uniform Scarlet-Red Disease-Tolerant Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Uproar Scarlet bears huge, uniform scarlet-red flower heads on sturdy, disease-tolerant plants, a modern cut-flower breeding introduction.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches. Uproar Scarlet bears exceptionally large, uniform, brilliant scarlet-red blooms on tall, sturdy, disease-tolerant plants bred specifically for reliable cut-flower production, standing out for its consistency of flower size and vivid, saturated color across the entire planting. Plants bloom heavily from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading or harvesting to encourage continuous production. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

common_name: Ursula Red Fern (Deep Burgundy Japanese Painted Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the deepest red coloring develops with bright, indirect light.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, providing bright indirect light for the most intense foliage color. Ursula Red is a Japanese painted fern selection bred for exceptionally deep, saturated burgundy-red coloring throughout the fronds, considerably darker and richer than the silver-and-maroon coloring of the classic Japanese painted fern, making it a dramatic accent in shaded borders and container plantings. The compact, well-behaved clump stays tidy without spreading aggressively, and the deep red color contrasts strikingly against green-leaved shade companions like hosta, heuchera, and other ferns. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring, and keep soil consistently moist, since painted fern selections are less drought-tolerant than many tougher native ferns.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in partial shade in spring; dicliptera is drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms better in poor, dry soil than in rich, fertile conditions — avoid heavy fertilization which produces rank foliage at the expense of flowers.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade; Uruguayan firecracker plant (hummingbird plant) is a South American perennial of the family Acanthaceae that stands out from other hummingbird plants by its distinctive silvery-gray, softly hairy foliage — the felt-like, silver-green leaves create a refined, cool-toned foliage effect that combines beautifully with the bright, tubular, orange-red flowers borne in clusters at the stem tips from late spring through fall. The silver foliage and orange-red flowers together create a sophisticated color combination that is warm, vivid, and unusual. It is notably drought- and heat-tolerant, shade-tolerant, and hardy to approximately 15°F in zone 8 (freezing back and regrowing reliably from the root). The clusters of bright-orange tubular flowers are irresistible to hummingbirds and produce nectar continuously through the warm season. It spreads moderately by underground stolons to form manageable colonies that make it effective as a groundcover on slopes and dry, shaded areas. An outstanding plant for hot, dry, partially shaded conditions in zone 8–11 where many flowering perennials fail.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container-grown starts in spring in a raised bed or slope of coarse, mineral gravel with no organic mulch against the crown.
directions: Plant in full sun on a rocky slope or berm with fast-draining, gravelly soil, keeping the crown high and dry to survive freezing winters. This is among the cold-hardiest agaves, tolerating temperatures well below freezing as long as its roots stay dry. The compact, symmetrical rosette of narrow, blue-gray leaves is armed with small marginal teeth and a sharp terminal spine, forming clumps over time through basal offsets. Like other agaves it is monocarpic, sending up a tall flower spike once after many years before that individual rosette dies.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural cold stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to arid, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Utah juniper is supremely adapted to the cold desert climate and thin soils of the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau at 3,000–8,000 feet elevation.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to arid, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Utah juniper is the defining tree of the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau desert — the dominant woody plant of the vast juniper-sagebrush and piñon-juniper woodlands that characterize the landscape of Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, and adjacent states at mid-elevations. More adapted to the cold desert continental climate (extreme heat, extreme cold, minimal rainfall) than almost any other tree species. Often grows in nearly pure stands on rocky mesas, canyon slopes, and valley floors. The species name 'osteosperma' means 'bony-seeded' — the hard seed within the fleshy berry-like cone. Important forage and browse plant for deer, pronghorn, and other wildlife. The berries are a critical food source for many birds. An excellent xeriscape tree for high desert gardens (zone 4–8) where water conservation is paramount — virtually no irrigation needed after establishment.

common_name: Valentine Day Camellia (Clear Pink Formal Double Reticulata Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this reticulata-japonica hybrid, bred by Howard Asper, is prized for exceptionally long-lasting formal double blooms.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind. Valentine Day bears clear, formal double to peony-form pink blooms, bred by Howard Asper from reticulata and japonica parentage, and is especially valued among exhibition growers for flowers that hold their perfect form for weeks on the plant, longer than most camellias. It grows into an upright shrub and flowers in winter into early spring. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

common_name: Valentine Sunflower (Pale Lemon-Yellow Branching Pollen-Free Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; space plants well to let the branching habit develop for a longer bloom season.
directions: Plant in full sun with 12-18 inches between plants so the multi-branching habit has room to fill out. Valentine produces pale, creamy lemon-yellow petals around a chocolate-brown center, a soft pastel look that fits cottage-garden and wedding-style arrangements better than the saturated golds and oranges of most sunflowers. Its branching habit means each plant yields a steady succession of medium-sized blooms over many weeks rather than a single large flush, and the pollen-free flowers keep vases and tablecloths clean. Regular cutting or deadheading of spent flowers keeps the plant producing new buds until frost.

common_name: Valerie Finnis Grape Hyacinth (Pale Ice-Blue Muscari)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Valerie Finnis is a pale, ice-blue sport of the common grape hyacinth, a softer color than the typical deep cobalt-blue species.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; grape hyacinth naturalizes readily and needs little care once established. Valerie Finnis bears dense spikes of small, tightly packed, urn-shaped florets in a soft, silvery ice-blue, a gentler and more unusual color than the deep cobalt-blue of the common species, blooming in mid-spring alongside daffodils and tulips. Its pale color makes it a versatile companion for pastel spring combinations where the standard deep-blue grape hyacinth might read as too strong. Foliage emerges in fall and persists through winter before the flower spikes appear in spring, then dies back by early summer; leave it undisturbed to die back naturally, and clumps will multiply steadily by offset bulbs to form larger drifts over the years.

common_name: Valley Forge Elm (Highly Disease-Tolerant American Elm)
plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Valley Forge, released by the USDA National Arboretum, ranks among the very highest of all American elm cultivars for Dutch elm disease tolerance, though it grows with a somewhat looser, faster habit than Princeton and benefits from early structural pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the tree room for its broad, classic vase-shaped canopy. Valley Forge was released by the USDA National Arboretum after extensive screening trials and stands out for having some of the strongest documented Dutch elm disease tolerance of any American elm cultivar, making it a leading choice for restoring the American elm to streets and parks where the species was once devastated by the disease. It grows quickly, often faster than other resistant cultivars, though its structure can be somewhat more open and irregular, so early formative pruning helps develop a strong central framework as the tree matures. Water deeply while establishing, avoid trunk and root wounds that can allow disease entry, and expect a large, long-lived shade tree well suited to the wide, open sites where American elm has always excelled.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, valley or foothill soil in full sun; valley oak requires deep soil to accommodate its extensive taproot. It grows naturally in deep valley soils and does not tolerate shallow, rocky, or waterlogged conditions. Never summer-irrigate established trees.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; valley oak is the largest of California's native oaks, reaching 40–100 feet tall with massive, sprawling crowns up to 80 feet wide — widely regarded as one of the most majestic and iconic trees of California. It grows naturally in deep valley soils and oak savanna throughout California's Central Valley and coast ranges. Valley oaks can live over 600 years and develop massive, deeply furrowed, gray trunks and wide-spreading canopies of graceful, deeply-lobed leaves. The large acorns were the primary food staple of numerous California indigenous cultures. CRITICAL: never irrigate established valley oaks in summer — summer water near the root zone encourages Phytophthora root rot (sudden oak death) and kills otherwise healthy trees. Plant away from irrigated lawns and landscapes. A landmark tree requiring ample space but magnificent at maturity.

plant_note: Plant tubers after all danger of frost when soil has warmed.
directions: Valley Porcupine is a spiky, pink-and-white cactus-type dahlia that is both an excellent cut flower and a reliable tuber producer, making it a great choice for beginners. Plant tubers horizontally about 4 to 6 inches deep after the soil warms in spring, with the eye facing up. Site in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and stake tall plants to support the heavy blooms. Pinch the growing tip when plants are about a foot tall to encourage bushier growth and more flowers. In cold zones, lift and store the tubers indoors over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost when soil is warm.
directions: Valley Rust Bucket is a smaller red-orange dahlia whose warm autumn tones blend beautifully with bronze and copper companions in the cutting garden. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Stake the plants and pinch the central shoot early to promote branching and a fuller flush of blooms. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep the plant producing through the season. Lift the tubers before hard freezes in colder regions and store them in a cool, dry place for replanting.

common_name: Valley Valentine Pieris (Deep Rose-Red Flowered Evergreen Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Valley Valentine bears unusually deep rose-red flower clusters, among the darkest-colored of any Pieris cultivar.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and winter winds; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity. Valley Valentine bears cascading clusters of deep rose-red, urn-shaped flowers in late winter to early spring, among the darkest and most saturated flower color of any widely grown Pieris cultivar, opening against glossy, dark evergreen foliage with the reddish-bronze new growth typical of the species. Its intensely colored blooms provide a striking early-season accent when little else in the shade garden is flowering. Water during dry spells and prune lightly after flowering to shape, since Pieris needs little routine pruning.

common_name: Van Houtte Sage (Van Houtte's Scarlet Sage, Red Velvet Sage)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings in spring after last frost in partial shade to full sun; Van Houtte Sage grows vigorously in zone 9 and can reach 4–6 feet in a single season. It roots readily from tip cuttings in water or moist soil. In zone 9a, plants may be damaged by hard frost but resprout from the root crown in spring; in zone 9b-10, it overwinters reliably as a semi-evergreen perennial. Prune by half after each bloom flush to stimulate repeat blooming and maintain compact habit.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Van Houtte Sage grows fastest in full sun but tolerates and even appreciates afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat, where it continues blooming through July–August when other sages shut down. Salvia van-houttei is a large, vigorous, soft-stemmed tropical sage from Brazil that produces some of the most theatrical and unusual flowers in the genus. The whorled flower spikes are covered with large, deeply-veined, velvety, dark burgundy-red to wine-colored calyxes that persist long after the scarlet corolla flowers inside them have fallen — the persistent, showy calyxes give the entire spike a dramatic deep-red to black-purple appearance and extend the ornamental interest of each bloom spike for weeks. The flowers themselves are tubular, bright scarlet, and intensely attractive to hummingbirds and large butterflies including swallowtails. The large, soft, dark-green, pebbly-textured leaves are aromatic and give the plant a bold, tropical presence even out of bloom. Van Houtte Sage is one of the most underused and undervalued of the tropical sages available for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens — combining long bloom season, hummingbird attraction, heat tolerance, and an exotic tropical appearance that rivals showier but less adaptable ornamentals.

common_name: Vanessa Bell Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Vanessa Bell blooms heavily and benefits from regular deadheading to keep the semi-double flowers coming through the season.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2016 and named for the Bloomsbury Group painter, Vanessa Bell carries semi-double, soft butter-yellow flowers that fade toward cream as they age, with a fresh, tea-and-lemon fragrance, on a healthy, free-flowering, medium-sized shrub. Its semi-double form exposes more stamens than fully double English roses, giving a slightly looser, more relaxed look that also makes it useful to pollinators, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanhoutte spiraea blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering to avoid removing the following year's flower buds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanhoutte Spiraea, commonly called Bridal Wreath, is one of the most beloved flowering shrubs in American horticulture — a large, wide-arching shrub that in April and May (zone 7–8) produces such a profusion of small, pure-white flower clusters along the entire length of each cascading branch that the branches appear covered with a white veil, creating the bridal wreath effect that gives the plant its common name. The arching, fountain-like form with flowers distributed along every branch tip is one of the most graceful and spectacular spring flowering shrub effects available in the northern and mid-South garden. Vanhoutte spiraea is a hybrid of Spiraea cantoniensis and S. trilobata that has been cultivated since the 1860s — more than 150 years of continuous popularity testify to its landscape merit. Unlike summer-blooming Japanese spiraea (S. japonica) cultivars that bloom on new wood, Vanhoutte blooms on old wood and must be pruned immediately after flowering — never in fall or winter, which would remove the following year's flower buds. In zone 9's heat, Vanhoutte performs best in zone 8 and colder; in the hottest parts of zone 9a, the summer heat can stress the plant.

common_name: Vanilla Cream Baptisia (Decadence Series Creamy Yellow-White False Indigo)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Vanilla Cream is a compact Decadence-series hybrid with soft creamy yellow-white flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Vanilla Cream bears dense spikes of soft, creamy yellow-white, pea-like flowers, a gentler tone than the bright yellow of many false indigo cultivars, on a compact, upright plant that is part of the Decadence series bred for more manageable garden size than the sprawling wild Baptisia species while keeping the genus's legendary toughness and longevity. Following bloom, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest, and the plant serves as a larval host for several native butterfly species. It is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free once established. Avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants; simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil and full sun.
directions: Vanilla Ice brings a creamy, light-yellow color to the garden on multi-branched plants about 5 feet tall bearing sweet 3-to-5-inch flowers. Direct sow the seed about an inch deep after the last frost in warm soil and full sun. Thin seedlings so the branching plants have room to develop their many blooms. Practically care-free, these sunflowers provide months of color and lovely cut flowers, and are striking in a moonlit garden. Water steadily while young and enjoy the pollinators and birds they attract.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; vanilla leaf is native to moist conifer forests of the Pacific Northwest and spreads by rhizome into a dense colony once its cultural needs for cool, consistent moisture are met.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; vanilla leaf is native to moist conifer forests of the Pacific Northwest and spreads by rhizome into a dense colony once its cultural needs for cool, consistent moisture are met. Achlys triphylla forms a uniform, deciduous groundcover of distinctive three-lobed, fan-shaped leaves atop wiry stems, with slender spikes of tiny white flowers lacking petals rising above the foliage in late spring; the dried leaves release a sweet, vanilla-like fragrance, giving the plant its common name and traditional use as a natural air freshener and insect repellent by Pacific Northwest indigenous peoples. It makes an elegant, uniform textural carpet under conifers and other acid-loving shade plants such as rhododendron and huckleberry, though it needs consistently cool, moist soil and does not tolerate hot, dry summers or heavy clay. Once established in the right conditions it requires little care beyond an annual leaf-litter mulch to replicate its native forest floor.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in full sun in well-drained soil; Vanilla is one of the palest African marigold cultivars, bred for a soft ivory-white flower color rare in the species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Vanilla bears large, fully double, creamy ivory-white blooms, one of the closest approaches to a true white flower yet achieved in African marigold breeding, most African marigold cultivars running toward gold, orange, and yellow. Its soft, pale color makes it a versatile companion in mixed plantings and a striking contrast against darker-flowered marigolds or bronze foliage. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming through summer heat, and it blooms reliably from planting until frost with minimal care.

common_name: Vanilla Spice Summersweet (Large-Flowered Fragrant White Clethra)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Vanilla Spice tolerates wet, periodically flooded soils and works well in a rain garden or pond-edge planting in dappled shade, the same conditions as other Clethra alnifolia selections.
directions: Vanilla Spice was bred for unusually large flower spikes, nearly twice the size of the species, packed with small white, intensely sweet-scented flowers that open in mid-to-late summer and draw heavy pollinator traffic from bumblebees, honeybees, and butterflies during a period when many other shrubs have finished blooming. Like other summersweet selections it forms a dense, suckering, upright shrub with glossy dark-green foliage that turns clear yellow in fall, and its fragrance carries well through a partly shaded garden on a warm evening. Keep soil consistently moist in partial to full shade, since summersweet does not tolerate prolonged drought, and expect the shrub to slowly spread by suckers to form a colony over time, useful for naturalizing a moist, shaded area.
