plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanilla Strawberry blooms on new wood — prune hard in late winter to stimulate vigorous new growth for maximum flower production.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanilla Strawberry is one of the most spectacular and distinctive panicle hydrangea cultivars — producing enormous, upright, conical flower panicles (up to 12–16 inches long) that undergo a dramatic color transformation through the growing season: opening pure creamy-white in early summer, then progressively blushing from the base of each panicle upward from pink to vivid strawberry-red as summer advances, creating a bicolor white-and-strawberry effect that is unlike any other hydrangea. At peak color in late summer and early fall, the large panicles display a gradient from strawberry-red at the base through pink to creamy-white at the tip — an extraordinary color combination that has made Vanilla Strawberry one of the fastest-selling new shrubs since its introduction. The shrub grows 6–8 feet tall and 4–6 feet wide with a strong, upright habit and sturdy stems that support the heavy flower panicles without flopping — an advantage over some other large-flowered H. paniculata types. Like all H. paniculata, it blooms on new wood and is pruned hard in late winter. In zone 9, morning sun with afternoon shade produces optimal results — the intense strawberry-red color develops best with some direct sun but the flowers hold color better if protected from the intense afternoon Gulf South sun.

common_name: Vanille Fraise Hydrangea (Bicolor White-to-Strawberry-Red Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanille Fraise is a French-bred panicle hydrangea whose panicles shift from white to strawberry-red as they age.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Vanille Fraise opens creamy white flower panicles at the base that shift dramatically to a deep strawberry-red toward the tip as the season progresses, so a single panicle displays a striking gradient of color, a French-bred introduction that has become one of the most popular bicolor panicle hydrangea cultivars. Its sturdy stems hold the heavy panicles upright well through wind and rain. Prune in late winter to shape and control size, cutting back last year's growth by about a third to encourage strong new flowering stems.

common_name: Vanity Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Clear Pink Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced in the early 1970s and a Dykes Medal winner, Vanity bears tall, softly ruffled, clear rose-pink flowers of exceptional form and substance on strong branched stems, and its clean, unfading pink long made it a benchmark for pink bearded iris breeding. It remains a vigorous, floriferous grower decades after introduction, valued for reliable rebloom of full stalks year after year rather than novelty coloring. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizome and replanting healthy outer fans; good drainage is essential to prevent rot.

common_name: Vardar Valley Boxwood (Low Broad Flat-Topped Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Vardar Valley is a low, broad boxwood selected from seed collected in Macedonia for exceptional heat and cold tolerance.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with some direct sun. Vardar Valley grows into a distinctive low, broad, flat-topped mound with dark blue-green foliage, wider than it is tall, making it a good choice for a low, informal hedge or foundation planting where a rounded ball shape isn't wanted. Selected from wild seed collected in the Balkans, it shows notably good tolerance of both summer heat and winter cold compared to many other boxwood cultivars. It grows slowly and holds its shape well with only light annual shearing.

common_name: Variable Maxillaria (Yellow and Red Maxillaria, Tufted Maxillaria, Variabilis Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on bark or in a small basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to partial direct light; Maxillaria variabilis is one of the most tolerant and adaptable of the Maxillaria species, growing in a wide range of temperature and light conditions — cool, intermediate, and warm — and producing single, small (0.75-inch) flowers in variable colors (yellow, orange-red, red, or brown) singly from between the pseudobulbs and leaf bases on short stems. The plant forms increasingly large clumps over time, eventually producing dozens of flowers simultaneously over many months. A good beginner orchid for zone 9-11 outdoor culture. Tolerates brief temperatures to 35°F. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light mounted on bark or in a small basket — Variable Maxillaria is one of the most adaptable and undemanding of the smaller Maxillaria species, tolerating cool to warm temperatures, a range of light conditions, and irregular watering better than many more exacting orchids. Maxillaria variabilis is a sympodial, clustering, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, and Colombia — widely distributed in the cloud forests and humid montane forests of Central America and northern South America. The plant produces compact, somewhat flattened pseudobulbs 1–2 inches tall arranged tightly on a clustering rhizome, each topped with a single, narrow, grass-like leaf 4–8 inches long. The species name variabilis refers to the remarkable variation in flower color across the natural range: from clear, bright yellow in some populations to orange-red, brick-red, deep red, or brown-red in others, with all intermediate shades represented. The flowers are small (0.75 inch), produced singly on short stems from the bases of the pseudobulbs, and are faintly fragrant. The real value of the plant lies in its clumping habit: over several years, a plant develops into a large, multi-headed clump producing dozens of flowers simultaneously over the extended blooming season (spring and early summer primarily, with scattered bloom at other times). Very adaptable and rewarding in zone 9-11. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to dry, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; variable panicgrass is a woodland species native to the understory of open deciduous and mixed forests, one of the few native grasses truly adapted to shaded conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; variable panicgrass is one of the most important native Dichanthelium species of woodland and forest-edge habitats across eastern North America. The Dichanthelium grasses are a unique genus of native panicgrasses that form rosettes of broad basal leaves in fall and winter, bloom in spring, then produce a second wave of smaller flowers through summer — an unusual bimodal blooming pattern shared across the genus. This species occupies the woodland understory with particular success, tolerating a degree of shade that excludes most native grasses. The fine, loosely branched seed panicles are a critical, high-quality food source for woodland-edge sparrows, juncos, and other granivorous birds. Excellent in the shaded section of a rain garden, at woodland edges, and as a low-growing grass layer beneath canopy trees in native plant gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on moist, acidic, sandy soil; cold stratification over winter improves germination rates.
directions: Native perennial sunflower of wet pine flatwoods and longleaf pine savannas of the southeastern coastal plain, producing bright yellow daisy-like flowers 2-3 inches across in late summer and fall on tall, upright stems. The narrow, rough basal leaves differ markedly in shape from the smaller stem leaves, giving the plant its common name. Grows best in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil in full sun but tolerates seasonal standing water; plant in mass for the most striking late-season display. Seeds attract finches and sparrows, making it an underused native sunflower for wet, full-sun pollinator and bird gardens in the Gulf Coast region.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; varicolored angel's trumpet is notable for flowers that change color as they age — typically opening white and gradually turning peach, apricot, or orange. CAUTION: All parts extremely toxic.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; varicolored angel's trumpet is an Ecuadorian species named for its distinctive flower color change — the enormous pendant trumpets open white and gradually transition through cream, peach, and apricot to a final orange tone as they age, so a single plant displays multiple flower colors simultaneously, creating an exceptional multicolor effect rare in tropical ornamentals. The flowers, up to 14 inches long among the largest in the genus, have a pleasant, sweet fragrance. Like all Brugmansia, all parts are dangerously toxic and the plant must be sited away from children and animals. The enormous, tropical-looking foliage and dramatic pendant flowers create the most architectural and dramatic tropical statement in the warm-climate garden. Heavy fertilization and consistent moisture are essential for maximum performance; drought or nutrient stress cause immediate flower drop.

plant_note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Variegata is an older classic Brunnera selection with irregular cream-white leaf margins.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the variegated foliage. Variegata bears heart-shaped green leaves irregularly edged in creamy white, one of the older and longest-cultivated Brunnera variegated selections, topped in early spring by sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers before the foliage fully expands. Its bright, irregular leaf margins add textural contrast to a shaded planting alongside hostas and ferns. Keep soil consistently moist, especially during summer heat, and divide congested clumps in early spring or fall.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese iris wants more moisture than bearded iris and benefits from standing in shallow water briefly during its spring growing season.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese iris wants more moisture than bearded iris and benefits from standing in shallow water briefly during its spring growing season. Crisply white-striped, sword-shaped leaves provide months of bright variegated texture before the classic large, flat, deep reddish-purple Japanese iris flowers open in early summer, a striking foliage-and-flower combination that extends the ornamental season well beyond the relatively brief bloom period typical of the species. Native to wet meadows and marsh edges across East Asia, it wants acidic, consistently moist to wet soil unlike the drier, alkaline conditions bearded iris prefers, making it a good companion for the wet margin of a pond or rain garden. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season, avoid lime or alkaline amendments, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring or right after flowering.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this classic, long-cultivated variegated sedge clumps steadily without running.
directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this classic, long-cultivated variegated sedge clumps steadily without running. Narrow, arching, evergreen leaves are striped white along the margins in a crisper, more strongly contrasting pattern than many newer sedge cultivars, forming a dense, fountain-like tuft that holds its shape through the seasons. One of the oldest variegated Japanese sedge selections still widely grown, it is a dependable, low-maintenance edger for shaded borders and pathways and a reliable filler for mixed containers in shade. Groom out old foliage by combing with gloved fingers in late winter and divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years.

plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Variegata bears classic cream-yellow striped leaf margins, one of the older and most widely available variegated liriope selections.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; liriope tolerates the full range of Gulf South conditions from clay to sandy soils and from moist to periodically drought-stressed. Variegata bears strap-shaped, dark green leaves edged in creamy yellow stripes, one of the classic, long-established variegated liriope selections that brightens border edges and mass plantings, topped in late summer by spikes of small lavender-purple flowers followed by black berries that persist into winter. As one of the most versatile groundcover plants for Gulf South landscapes, it works equally well as a border edge, foundation planting, or mass groundcover under trees. Divide established clumps every three to five years when they become overcrowded and flowering declines.

common_name: Variegata Purple Moor Grass (Compact Cream-and-Green Striped Mound)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Variegata forms a compact, cream-and-green striped mound and tolerates more shade than the taller purple moor grass selections.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; this compact cultivar tolerates more shade than the taller purple moor grass selections. Variegata forms a neat, low mound of narrow blades crisply striped cream and green, topped by delicate, airy purple-tinted flower spikes in summer, all on a scale far more modest than the tall, see-through Skyracer and Transparent selections. Its compact, bright-foliaged form fits the front of a border or a container planting. Cut back to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps in spring.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Variegata holds its cream-edged foliage as a bright accent through the growing season, well after the spring flowers fade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. A long-established classic among variegated shrubs, Variegata weigela produces soft green leaves broadly edged in creamy white that brighten a mixed border all season, paired with clusters of soft pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds. The variegated foliage provides ongoing visual interest well beyond the relatively brief flowering period typical of weigela cultivars. It performs best with a light shaping prune right after flowering, since blooms form on the previous year's wood, and is otherwise a tough, easy shrub tolerant of average soil and normal garden care.

common_name: Variegata di Bologna Rose (Striped Red-White-Purple Bourbon Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Variegata di Bologna bears dramatically striped red-purple-and-white blooms, mostly on a single strong spring flush.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy support, since the vigorous canes can be trained as a short climber. Variegata di Bologna bears large, fully double blooms boldly striped in raspberry-red and purple over a white ground, an eye-catching, painterly pattern among Bourbon roses, with a strong, sweet fragrance. Unlike some repeat-blooming Bourbons it flowers mainly in a single dramatic spring flush with only light rebloom later, so plant it where its once-yearly show provides maximum impact. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood.

common_name: Variegated Cast Iron Plant (Cream-Striped Deep-Shade Aspidistra Groundcover)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; the variegated form is somewhat slower-growing than the all-green species and slightly less tolerant of extreme neglect — provide consistent moisture and avoid direct sun which burns the cream variegation.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Variegated Cast Iron Plant is a stunning selection of the legendary Aspidistra elatior — the most shade-tolerant of all commonly grown ornamental plants — producing the same broad, strap-shaped, leathery evergreen leaves as the green species but with distinctive cream-white to ivory longitudinal stripes that create a luminous, light-reflecting effect in the deepest, darkest shade positions where few other plants survive. The cream stripes typically run the length of the leaf blade in widths varying from thin lines to broad bands, producing a gently variegated pattern that brightens dark garden areas while maintaining the bold, tropical foliage character that makes cast iron plant a cornerstone of Gulf South shade gardening. Aspidistra elatior earned its common name through extraordinary tolerance of neglect, drought, poor light, dry soil, and root competition from trees — but the variegated form is slightly more demanding than the green species and produces its best appearance with consistent moisture and protection from sun. In zone 9, Variegated Cast Iron Plant grows as a reliable perennial groundcover under live oaks, magnolias, and other dense-canopy trees where the combination of root competition, deep shade, and summer drought would eliminate most alternatives. The cream stripes are most vivid in the variegated form grown in good but indirect light — deep shade in poor soil dulls the variegation over time.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near a sturdy trellis or arbor; variegated chocolate vine is a vigorous twining climber and needs a strong support, plus occasional pruning to control spread.
directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near a sturdy trellis or arbor; variegated chocolate vine is a vigorous twining climber and needs a strong support, plus occasional pruning to control spread. Palmate, five-lobed leaves are irregularly splashed and marbled in creamy white, a bright variegated counterpart to the plain green species, twining vigorously up any nearby support and producing small, chocolate-scented, maroon-purple flowers in spring, occasionally followed by unusual sausage-shaped purple fruit with sweet, edible pulp in favorable conditions. Its vigorous, twining growth can become aggressive and self-seed in mild climates, so site it where its spread can be managed and monitor for volunteer seedlings, particularly since escaped chocolate vine has become invasive in parts of the eastern United States. Prune hard in late winter to control size and shape, and provide a sturdy arbor, fence, or trellis strong enough to support its vigorous twining growth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a trellis or fence for the twining stems; variegated confederate jasmine holds its cream-margined variegation best in bright light.
directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a trellis or fence for the twining stems; variegated confederate jasmine holds its cream-margined variegation best in bright light. Glossy, dark green leaves are irregularly edged in creamy white, often blushed pink on new growth in cooler weather, providing year-round variegated color even outside the plant's intensely fragrant late-spring flowering period, when small, pinwheel-shaped white flowers cover the twining vine with classic jasmine scent. Slightly less vigorous and cold-hardy than the plain green species, it still makes a fine trellis, fence, or mailbox-post vine in warm-climate gardens or a colorful container specimen further north, brought indoors or into a greenhouse for winter outside its hardiness range. Provide a support for the twining stems, water regularly during establishment, and prune after flowering to control size and shape.

common_name: Variegated Creeping Broadleaf Sedge (Cream-Striped Deciduous Woodland Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this creamy white-striped form of the broad, grass-unlike Japanese and Korean woodland sedge is a slow-spreading deciduous groundcover.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Unlike most sedges, this species bears broad, lance-shaped, distinctly grass-unlike leaves, and the Variegata form brightens the woodland floor with crisp creamy-white longitudinal stripes running the length of each leaf, spreading slowly by rhizomes to form a low, deciduous groundcover that dies back in winter and re-emerges fresh each spring. It combines well with hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials, providing a fine-textured, brightly variegated foil for bolder foliage nearby. Water during dry spells, since it prefers consistent moisture over drought, and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

plant_note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions in fall, or container-grown plants in spring, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade; this is a distinct species from the more common Polygonatum odoratum 'Variegatum' sold under a nearly identical name, with broader leaves and a stouter, more upright arch.
directions: Plant dormant rhizome divisions in fall, or container-grown plants in spring, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade; this is a distinct species from the more common Polygonatum odoratum 'Variegatum' sold under a nearly identical name, with broader leaves and a stouter, more upright arch. Gracefully arching stems carry broad, creamy-white-edged leaves in two ranks, with clusters of two to five small, tubular, greenish-white bells dangling from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by blue-black berries. Native to European woodlands, this variegated form of the classic Solomon's seal brings strong vertical structure and season-long brightness to a shaded border, combining well with hostas, ferns, and hellebores. Top-dress annually with compost or leaf mold and keep soil from drying out in summer; established clumps need dividing only every five to seven years.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average to poor soil in full to deep shade; Variegated Goutweed bears crisp white-margined leaves that brighten deep, dry shade where little else thrives, and young spring shoots have historically been eaten as a pot-herb. Site with care, since it spreads aggressively by rhizomes and is best confined to contained or difficult sites.
directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in full to deep shade, and choose the planting site with care, since Variegated Goutweed spreads vigorously and persistently by rhizomes and can be difficult to remove once established; it is best used in a contained bed, a hard-to-plant difficult site such as under a deck or between buildings, or bordered by pavement or a buried barrier. Its crisply white-margined, green-centered leaves brighten deep, dry shade far better than most groundcovers tolerate, forming a dense, weed-suppressing carpet that spreads where turf and most perennials fail to grow. Small white flower umbels appear in early summer but are usually removed before seed sets, since the variegated form can occasionally revert to the more aggressive plain-green species. Historically, young spring shoots were gathered and cooked as a pot-herb similar to spinach, though the plant is grown today almost exclusively as an ornamental groundcover.

common_name: Variegated Greater Periwinkle (Vinca major with Cream-White Leaf Margins)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Variegata bears larger leaves edged in cream-white than plain Vinca major, and spreads vigorously, so site it where it can be contained.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, average soil, siting it where its vigorous spread can be contained by a bed edge, path, or other barrier, since Vinca major can naturalize aggressively in mild climates. Variegata bears larger, glossy leaves boldly edged in cream-white around a green center, brightening a shaded bank or slope more than the solid-green species, along with the same lavender-blue, pinwheel-shaped spring flowers typical of greater periwinkle. Its trailing stems root readily wherever they touch soil, making it effective for erosion control on shaded slopes, though its vigor means it needs monitoring near naturalized woodland areas. Cut back hard in late winter if growth becomes leggy or overgrown.

plant_note: Set rooted divisions or nursery plugs into moist, acidic, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade in spring or early fall.
directions: Space plugs or divisions evenly in loose, acidic soil amended with leaf mold, and water regularly until the creeping stems knit together into a solid mat, which is slower to fill in than the plain green form. Once established, shear back any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the planting uniformly variegated. Leaves are edged and mottled in creamy white around a soft green center, giving a brighter, more finely textured look than standard pachysandra, with the same small white spring flower spikes. It is a dependable, low, spreading evergreen for dry shade under trees where turf and most flowering perennials struggle.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in wet, fertile soil in shallow standing water up to 4 inches deep or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; variegated Japanese water iris needs constant moisture and struggles if allowed to dry out.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in wet, fertile soil in shallow standing water up to 4 inches deep or consistently saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; variegated Japanese water iris needs constant moisture and struggles if allowed to dry out. Sword-shaped leaves are crisply striped in white and green through spring and early summer, gradually fading to solid green by midsummer, providing months of bright variegated texture at a pond margin or rain garden before the deep blue-purple flowers with a yellow signal patch open above the foliage in early summer. Native to marshes and pond edges across East Asia, it tolerates standing water better than most bearded irises, making it a good structural, upright accent for the shallow-water zone of a water garden alongside pickerelweed and arrowhead. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or immediately after flowering to maintain vigor and variegation.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegata pittosporum is highly salt-tolerant and is an excellent choice for coastal landscapes within a mile of the Gulf or Atlantic coast.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegated pittosporum is one of the most reliable and widely planted foundation and landscape shrubs for zone 8–11 coastal and Gulf Coast gardens — a compact, rounded, evergreen shrub producing distinctive, leathery, spatula-shaped leaves in dark green irregularly edged and streaked with creamy white to gray-green variegation. The variegated foliage provides year-round visual interest and brightness in both full sun and partial shade conditions. In spring, the shrub produces small, creamy-white, intensely orange-blossom fragrant flowers — the fragrance is remarkably strong for such small flowers and perfumes the surrounding garden. Variegated pittosporum is among the most salt-tolerant and wind-tolerant of common landscape shrubs, making it exceptional for coastal exposures where most shrubs struggle with salt spray and marine wind. The compact, naturally mounding habit stays 3–5 feet tall and wide with minimal pruning, though it can be pruned to control size immediately after spring bloom. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; tolerates clay soil, alkaline conditions, and reflected heat from paving. Avoid wet, poorly drained sites where Phytophthora root rot can be a problem. Essentially pest-free in zone 9. The standard green species Pittosporum tobira grows larger and is also widely planted in Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; variegated screw pine develops sharp, tooth-edged leaves, so site it away from high-traffic areas and handle with care.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; variegated screw pine develops sharp, tooth-edged leaves, so site it away from high-traffic areas and handle with care. Long, arching, sword-shaped leaves striped in white and green spiral around a central growing point in a distinctive corkscrew pattern that gives the whole plant genus its common name, with fine, sharp spines along the leaf margins and midrib. As the plant matures it develops thick, stilt-like prop roots at the base that help anchor and support the increasingly top-heavy rosette, an unusual and architectural feature that adds to its appeal as a bold specimen plant for a bright room or shaded tropical patio. Wipe dust from the leaves carefully with gloves due to the sharp edges, water when the top inch of potting mix dries, and provide bright indirect light to maintain crisp variegation.

common_name: Variegated Shell Ginger (Cream-and-Green Striped Tropical Ginger Specimen)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Variegated Shell Ginger prefers afternoon shade protection — full-day direct sun can cause the cream variegation to bleach to white and the leaf margins to burn in Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Variegated Shell Ginger is one of the most spectacular foliage plants for Gulf South tropical garden designs — a large, bold ornamental with broad, strap-shaped leaves (12–18 inches long) brilliantly streaked with alternating bands of deep green and creamy-white to ivory-yellow variegation that creates one of the most visually striking striped foliage effects of any commonly available ornamental plant. The creamy-white striping covers 30–50% of each leaf surface in irregular, painterly bands that vary in width and distribution, creating a luminous effect in partial shade where the cream bands glow against the dark-green background. In spring or early summer, mature established clumps produce pendant clusters of shell-shaped white flowers with yellow and red markings — beautiful but secondary to the spectacular foliage display. The variegated form is significantly more ornamental than the solid-green Alpinia zerumbet (shell ginger) but slightly slower-growing and more heat-sensitive — the cream portions of the variegated leaves are more vulnerable to sun scorch than the all-green type. In zone 9, Variegated Shell Ginger is a perennial that may be top-killed by hard freezes but returns from the rhizome in spring — heavy mulching protects the roots through zone 9a winters. The bold, tropical scale and spectacular variegation make this an outstanding specimen plant for partially shaded entryways, courtyard gardens, and tropical-theme garden designs.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full sun; variegated shell ginger is more shade-tolerant than common shell ginger and the variegated foliage is brightest in morning sun with afternoon shade — full shade produces less crisp variegation but plants still thrive.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; provide morning sun for best foliage color. Alpinia vittata (variegated shell ginger) is a Pacific Island native ginger producing one of the most striking foliage displays of any tropical plant — upright, 3-to-5-foot stems with long (18-inch), lance-shaped leaves dramatically striped with alternating bands of green and creamy yellow, creating a bold, bright, bamboo-like architectural effect. Unlike common shell ginger (A. zerumbet) which is grown for both foliage and flowers, variegated shell ginger is primarily a foliage plant — the striped leaves are the main ornamental feature, providing year-round tropical color in shade and part-shade situations. The shell ginger flowers (nodding racemes of white and pink flowers resembling porcelain shells) are less freely produced than in the straight species. In zone 8–12, the plant persists as a perennial; the above-ground parts may die back in a hard freeze but the rhizomes survive in the ground with mulch protection. An outstanding tropical foliage specimen for part-shade situations in Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Place outdoors in shade to partial shade after temperatures remain above 55°F; in zone 9 use outdoors April–October and bring indoors when temperatures approach 45°F. Laurentii is a variegated cultivar with the distinctive bright yellow margin stripe — this variegation is propagated by division only (leaf cuttings revert to plain green). Dracaena trifasciata 'Laurentii' (formerly Sansevieria trifasciata 'Laurentii') is one of the most studied plants for indoor air quality — NASA's Clean Air Study identified it as effective at removing formaldehyde, benzene, and other VOCs from interior air. The upright, strap-leaved form takes up minimal floor space relative to its visual impact, making it effective in confined container situations.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light — tolerates extremely low light conditions where most plants cannot survive, while also adapting to bright indirect light — in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil or potting mix; Variegated Snake Plant (Dracaena trifasciata 'Laurentii') is the classic variegated form of Mother-in-Law's Tongue, producing the familiar upright, stiff, strap-shaped leaves with the distinctive pattern of dark green cross-banding on a lighter green ground — and in the 'Laurentii' form, an additional bright golden-yellow stripe running the full length of both leaf margins. The combination of the detailed cross-banded central pattern and the bold, clean yellow margin stripe creates a more visually striking and decorative effect than the plain green species, making 'Laurentii' the most commonly sold and planted snake plant variant worldwide. Dracaena trifasciata tolerates neglect — infrequent watering, low light, temperature fluctuations, and irregular fertilization — at levels that would kill most other decorative foliage plants, making it genuinely practical for situations (covered porches, low-light indoor corners, weekend homes) where consistent care cannot be guaranteed. The extremely low water requirement (tolerating complete drought for weeks) combined with the low-light tolerance and the clean, architectural upright form makes the Variegated Snake Plant one of the most practically useful shade and low-light ornamentals available.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring just as new growth emerges, or plant in early fall, placing rhizomes horizontally 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; variegated Solomon's seal establishes slowly but becomes a long-lived, low-maintenance shade perennial. Mark the planting area as it emerges late in spring.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; variegated Solomon's seal is the most widely grown and most ornamentally striking form of Polygonatum odoratum (angular Solomon's seal), bearing the same elegantly arching unbranched stems as the species but with each oval leaf edged in a broad, creamy-white to pale-cream margin that provides striking variegated foliage from emergence in spring through autumn dormancy. In late spring, small pairs of white, sweetly fragrant, tubular pendant bells dangle beneath the leaf axils along the full length of the arching stem, followed by blue-black berries. The arching stems with their precisely alternating variegated leaves create one of the most refined and architecturally graceful effects available for the shaded garden, combining beautifully with hostas, ferns, hellebores, and dark-leaved plants where the creamy leaf margins glow in low light. It spreads slowly by rhizomes into gradually expanding colonies. All parts are toxic if ingested. An indispensable classic of the shade garden.

plant_note: Place outdoors in shade to partial shade after temperatures remain above 50°F; in zone 9 use outdoors April–October and bring indoors before freezing temperatures. Vittatum produces the classic center-white, green-margined stripe pattern — the reverse pattern from 'Variegatum' (which has green centers and white margins). Spider plants produce long, arching runners bearing miniature plantlets (spiderettes) that can be snipped and rooted in water or moist soil. In zone 9 outdoors in summer, spider plants grow vigorously in the humid heat, producing abundant runners and plantlets. The thick, fleshy roots store water, making spider plants more drought tolerant than their lush appearance suggests.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light — spider plants tolerate extremely low light conditions and are among the most adaptable shade container plants available — in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral potting mix with consistent moisture; Variegated Spider Plant (Chlorophytum comosum 'Vittatum') is one of the most widely grown and genuinely shade-tolerant foliage plants in cultivation — producing gracefully arching rosettes of long, narrow leaves with a central white stripe and green margins, and sending out long, arching stolons that produce miniature plantlets (spiderettes) at their tips that dangle in the air like a cascade of tiny spiders. The vittatum pattern — white center stripe, green margins — creates a bright, luminous effect in shaded settings where the white stripe catches and reflects available light, making spider plants one of the most effective brightening plants for deeply shaded corners and covered patios where other plants would fade to monotone green. The cascading runners and plantlets extend 2–3 feet below the container in a hanging basket, creating a dramatic, lush, cascading display with almost no care beyond periodic watering. The combination of extreme adaptability to low light and neglect, air-purifying capability, prolific production of easily shared plantlets, and the bright variegated foliage makes spider plant one of the most practical and rewarding shade foliage plants for zone 9 porches, patios, and interiors.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after last frost in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; variegated Swedish ivy roots readily from cuttings and spreads quickly in warm, humid conditions.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after last frost in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; variegated Swedish ivy roots readily from cuttings and spreads quickly in warm, humid conditions. Rounded, scalloped, aromatic leaves are edged in a broad, creamy-white margin over soft green centers, trailing along succulent stems that root wherever they touch soil, quickly filling a hanging basket or groundcover area with variegated texture and a light, minty fragrance when brushed. One of the easiest and most reliable trailing houseplants and shade groundcovers, it tolerates the low light and dry air of typical indoor conditions as well as the humid shade of an outdoor porch or patio in warm climates. Pinch growing tips to encourage bushier growth, water when the top inch of soil dries, and propagate easily from stem cuttings rooted in water or moist soil.

common_name: Variegated Water Clover (Mottled Bicolor Four-Leaf Floating Fern Ally)
plant_note: Plant rooted stock in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in shallow submerged containers in a full-sun to partial-shade pond after all frost danger has passed; Variegated Water Clover bears distinctive mottled bicolor four-part leaves floating on the water's surface.
directions: Plant rooted stock in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in shallow submerged containers just a few inches deep, in full sun to partial shade. Variegated Water Clover produces distinctive four-part leaves that closely resemble a four-leaf clover, floating flat on the water's surface, each leaflet attractively mottled in bands of green and yellow-green, a more striking, patterned foliage effect than the plain green Marsilea species more commonly grown. This unusual fern relative spreads by creeping rhizomes to form a low, textural mat over shallow water or damp mud, useful at a pond margin, in a bog garden, or in a shallow water feature. It is frost-tender and best suited to warm, frost-free ponds year-round; in cooler zones grow as a summer annual or overwinter indoors. Thin spreading colonies periodically to keep them in bounds.

plant_note: Divide clumps and replant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade during spring or fall.
directions: Plant divisions in loose, well-drained soil and water regularly the first year until the clumping rhizomes spread and fill in. Once settled it needs little care beyond an occasional trim of old or winter-damaged foliage. The arching, grass-like leaves are broader than common mondo grass and are edged in creamy white, brightening dim corners even before the arching spikes of small white summer flowers appear, which are followed by blue-violet berries. It makes a durable, low-maintenance edging or mass planting for shaded walkways where its variegated foliage provides year-round contrast against darker-leaved neighbors.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Variegatus requires full sun to keep its crisp white-and-green striped blades from reverting toward plain green in shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Variegatus is one of the oldest and most classic maiden grass cultivars, producing arching, gracefully drooping blades boldly striped lengthwise in crisp white and green, creating a luminous, almost silvery effect in the garden that brightens even from a distance. In late summer it sends up tall, feathery, coppery-pink flower plumes that age to fluffy tan seed heads persisting through winter for structural interest. The large, fountain-like clump makes an excellent specimen or screen, though it needs a good amount of room to display its full arching habit; cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Variegatus is one of the oldest and most classic variegated false holly cultivars, its spiny, holly-like leaves crisply edged in creamy white around a dark green center, providing bright, reliable, year-round contrast in a shaded border without depending on bloom for interest. Tiny, sweetly fragrant white flowers appear tucked among the leaves in fall, easy to miss visually but noticeable by scent alone. Its dense, evergreen, deer-resistant foliage makes it a durable choice for shaded foundation plantings, informal hedges, and screens; little pruning is needed beyond light shaping after fall bloom.

plant_note: Direct sow in early autumn or divide established clumps in spring; autumn sowing allows roots to establish before winter.
directions: Direct sow in early autumn onto a lightly prepared seedbed under deciduous trees or in dappled shade, pressing seed into the soil surface without covering deeply, as light aids germination. Unlike most ornamental fescues that demand full sun, this species genuinely performs well in moderate to full shade, maintaining attractive dark-green, thread-fine foliage throughout the season. Plant or thin to 12 to 18 inches apart to allow each clump to develop its full, loose arching character. Divide clumps every three years in early spring to prevent center die-out and to maintain the fresh, dense texture that makes this fescue a standout groundcover in shaded situations.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall or late winter in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial sun; native to Gulf South woodlands and resents heavy, poorly drained clay.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection, mulching well to keep roots cool. Varnadoe is a selected form of Piedmont azalea (Rhododendron canescens), a widespread Gulf South and Southeastern native, chosen for an especially heavy flush of fragrant, pale pink flowers with prominent, showy stamens on a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed shrub in early spring before the leaves fully emerge. Like other native deciduous azaleas, it is far better adapted to the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Deep South gardens than most Asian evergreen azalea hybrids, and its intense honeysuckle-like fragrance carries well beyond the plant itself. Site it at a woodland edge or under high pine or hardwood canopy, similar to the conditions where it grows wild along stream banks and bluffs.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in deep, moist, rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in a woodland garden setting. Vasey's Trillium is a large pedicellate species that blooms somewhat later than sessile trilliums — April to May in the Southern Appalachians.
directions: Vasey's Trillium is one of the largest and most striking of the native eastern trilliums, native to rich, moist cove forests and sheltered ravines of the southern Appalachians from Virginia and North Carolina south to Georgia and Alabama, where it blooms from April through May with dramatic, deep wine-red petals that recurve strongly back toward the stem, hanging below the leaves and emitting a strong, sweet fragrance to attract fly pollinators. It grows markedly larger than most sessile trilliums, with broad three-parted leaves and stems reaching 24 inches, and its flowers hang on a distinct pedicel below the leaf whorl — a characteristic setting it apart from sessile species. Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in the deepest, most richly amended soil you can provide — cove forest conditions with high organic matter, consistent moisture, and full shade — and mulch heavily with leaf litter. Vasey's Trillium takes 5–7 years to reach blooming age from seed, making nursery divisions the only practical route for most gardeners.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor; introduced in Germany in 1909, Veilchenblau is a once-blooming rambler grown for its unusual violet-purple color.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor, and note that it tolerates more shade than most roses, blooming reasonably well in partial shade. Introduced in Germany in 1909, Veilchenblau bears a single spring flush of small, semi-double flowers that open magenta-violet streaked with white and fade through smoky lavender-gray as they age, a genuinely unusual color range among roses that has earned it the nickname "blue rose" despite never being a true blue. Its thornless canes and light, sweet fragrance add to its appeal for training over an arbor or fence where visitors brush past. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins. Replant divisions immediately at the same depth in consistently moist, humus-rich soil. Shelter from afternoon sun to prevent leaf wilting.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in moist to wet, organically rich soil with dappled or partial shade, particularly protection from harsh afternoon sun. Ligularia veitchiana is one of the most dramatically scaled perennials for the moist shade garden, with leaves that can exceed 18 inches across and flower spikes rising 4 to 6 feet in midsummer. Keep soil consistently moist throughout the growing season, as plants will wilt dramatically during dry spells even in shade. This bold specimen works well planted in large groups near water features or as a backdrop plant in sheltered woodland borders.

plant_note: Grow as a shaded, cool, humid houseplant or greenhouse specimen in a fine, well-drained orchid mix; Veitch's masdevallia is a cool-growing Andean cloud-forest species that struggles in hot, dry conditions and is best suited to an air-conditioned room or shaded, humid greenhouse.
directions: Grow as a shaded, cool, humid houseplant or greenhouse specimen in a fine, well-drained orchid mix; Veitch's masdevallia is a cool-growing Andean cloud-forest species that struggles in hot, dry conditions and is best suited to an air-conditioned room or shaded, humid greenhouse. Brilliant, glowing orange-red, triangular flowers with a fine, iridescent, shimmering texture rise on slender stems above a low tuft of leathery leaves, a color and shine so vivid that it was noted by nineteenth-century orchid hunters as one of the most striking flowers in the Peruvian Andes. Native to high-elevation cloud forests, it requires consistently cool temperatures, high humidity, and constant air movement, making it a challenging but rewarding species for growers able to replicate cloud-forest conditions rather than a plant for an average warm home. Keep the mix constantly moist but never soggy, and avoid any temperature above the mid-80s Fahrenheit, which stresses and can kill the plant.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; Boston ivy clings tightly to masonry surfaces and is difficult to remove once established, so site carefully.
directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; Boston ivy clings tightly to masonry surfaces and is difficult to remove once established, so site carefully. One of the original introduced forms of the classic ivy-league-covering vine, it produces smaller, more deeply three-lobed leaves emerging purplish-bronze in spring before maturing to glossy green and turning a spectacular scarlet-crimson in fall, clinging tightly to brick and stone with adhesive tendril discs to blanket entire building facades. Extremely vigorous and self-clinging, it needs no additional support once established but can grow large enough to obscure windows and gutters if not pruned, and removing an established planting from masonry can leave persistent tendril residue. Prune annually to keep growth away from windows, doors, and roof edges, and consider the vine's vigorous, decades-long coverage potential before planting against a valued building surface.

common_name: Veitchii Gardenia (Classic Florist Gardenia with Everblooming Double White Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Veitchii was historically the standard florist gardenia for cut flowers and corsages and produces more compact, more regularly shaped flowers than the larger, showier 'Fortuniana' — both fragrant but with different use profiles.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Veitchii is the classic florist and corsage gardenia cultivar — the variety that shaped the public image of gardenia for most of the 20th century as the preferred white flower for corsages, wedding bouquets, and cut flower arrangements, valued for its perfectly formed, fully double, pure-white flowers and the intense, sweet, iconic gardenia fragrance that makes it one of the most recognizable flower scents in the world. The flowers of Veitchii are somewhat smaller than those of the larger-flowered 'Fortuniana' and 'Mystery' cultivars but are more precisely and symmetrically formed — tight spirals of white petals forming a perfect double flower that is simultaneously elegant and lush. The key practical advantage of Veitchii over earlier cultivars is repeat or continuous bloom (sometimes described as 'everblooming') — unlike once-blooming gardenias that flower only in spring, Veitchii produces flowers from late spring through summer and into fall, a trait that made it invaluable commercially. The intense gardenia fragrance is full and true across all blooming periods. The plant grows as a compact to medium evergreen shrub (3–5 feet) with the characteristically glossy, deep-green foliage of gardenia. In zone 9, Veitchii is somewhat cold-sensitive — mulching the roots and planting against a south-facing wall provides winter protection in zone 8–9a. Strongly acidic soil and iron availability are the most common cultural challenges.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Veitchii is an older lacecap hydrangea whose white sterile florets age to soft pink or blue.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Veitchii bears lacecap blooms that open crisp white and gradually age to soft pink or blue depending on soil pH, giving the flower head a two-toned effect as older and newer florets sit side by side, unlike white cultivars whose color never shifts. It has been in cultivation since the 19th century and remains valued for its refined lacecap form. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent wilting.

common_name: Velvet Arrowhead (Wendland's Syngonium, Silver Goosefoot Plant, Dark Velvet Syngonium)
plant_note: Grow in full shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil or on a moss pole for climbing; Syngonium wendlandii is the darkest and most velvety of the commonly cultivated Syngonium species, producing deeply colored, dark forest-green leaves with a striking white central stripe and a velvety texture from tiny, light-scattering surface hairs. It is an outstanding indoor or sheltered outdoor shade plant for zone 10-12 or a protected outdoor position in zone 9b. Keep from temperatures below 50°F. The leaves are beautiful when backlit. CAUTION: all Syngonium parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested by pets or children — toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in full to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil — Velvet Arrowhead is one of the most shade-adapted and visually distinctive of the Syngonium species and thrives in the low-light conditions of a shaded porch, bright interior room, or understory garden in zone 10-12. Syngonium wendlandii is a climbing, rhizomatous tropical vine in the Araceae family native to Costa Rica and Central America, one of the most sought-after species in the genus for the extraordinary visual quality of its leaves. The leaves are a deep, saturated dark forest-green on their upper surfaces, with a broad, brilliant white to silver-white midrib and primary veins creating a dramatic two-tone pattern of dark and light. The surface of the leaf has a distinctly velvety texture from tiny surface papillae that scatter light in a way reminiscent of velvet fabric — making the leaves appear almost three-dimensional, like cut velvet or dark plush. Juvenile plants produce smaller, arrowhead-shaped leaves on compact, low-growing stems. As the plant matures and begins to climb a support, the leaves take on a larger, more broadly lobed form up to 10–12 inches across, with the white markings becoming even more pronounced. Syngonium wendlandii is one of the classic collector aroids now widely appreciated both as a houseplant and as a shaded outdoor container or landscape plant in frost-free climates. The deep shade tolerance, compact juvenile form, and extraordinary leaf pattern make it ideal for shade gardens and sheltered patios. CAUTION: toxic to pets if ingested — keep away from cats and dogs.

plant_note: Transplant in spring into desert washes, irrigated yards, or streambank sites across the Southwest, where this drought-adapted ash tolerates alkaline soils and intense heat.
directions: Transplant in spring into desert washes, irrigated yards, or streambank sites across the Southwest, where this drought-adapted ash tolerates alkaline soils and intense summer heat far better than eastern ash species. Its velvety young twigs and leaflets give the tree a soft gray-green texture, and its dense canopy makes it a popular fast-growing shade tree in arid urban landscapes. It benefits from periodic deep irrigation during establishment even though mature trees can survive on minimal supplemental water in wash habitats. Watch for emerald ash borer as its range continues to expand into the Southwest.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; velvet begonia is more sun- and drought-tolerant than most begonias and rots quickly in constantly wet soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; velvet begonia is more sun- and drought-tolerant than most begonias and rots quickly in constantly wet soil. Thick, rounded, succulent leaves are densely covered in soft, silvery-white, felted hairs that give the whole plant a plush, frosted appearance and a texture unlike almost any other begonia, with clusters of white, waxy, fragrant flowers appearing over a long season. Native to coastal sand dunes and rocky outcrops in Brazil and Uruguay, it is unusually tolerant of full sun, salt spray, and drought for a begonia, reflecting its exposed native habitat, and it thrives with more light and less water than the shade-loving rex and cane-type begonias more commonly grown. Water only when the soil has dried and provide bright light for the fullest, most compact growth and best flowering.

common_name: Velvet Cardboard Anthurium (Clarinervium, White Veined Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light; Anthurium clarinervium requires consistent warmth (65–85°F), high humidity (60–80%), and excellent drainage. Use a chunky, well-aerated epiphytic mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil — never dense potting compost. Water thoroughly when the top layer of the mix dries; the plant is more drought-tolerant than humidity-tolerant, and chronic overwatering causes rapid root rot. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Anthurium clarinervium needs adequate light for healthy leaf production but will bleach and burn in direct sun. Anthurium clarinervium is a terrestrial to epiphytic anthurium endemic to the limestone cliff faces (karst) of Chiapas, Mexico, where it grows in the crevices and rock faces of cloud forest — an unusual natural habitat that explains its particular cultivation requirements: excellent drainage, high humidity, and bright filtered light in a calcareous substrate. The leaves are the defining ornamental feature: large, broad, heart-shaped, and thickly textured with a distinctive velvety or cardboard-like feel (giving the species the common name 'Cardboard Anthurium'), rich dark emerald-green to blue-green, covered with a network of precisely delineated, bright white to silvery-white raised veins in a complex branching pattern. Young leaves emerge in shades of rose to bronze before deepening to the mature dark green. The combination of bold leaf shape, velvety texture, and dramatic white venation has made Anthurium clarinervium one of the most sought-after velvet anthuriums among tropical plant collectors worldwide. The spathe flowers are small and inconsequential. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

common_name: Velvet Cloak Smokebush (Deep Purple Compact Smoke Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained to dry, average to lean soil in full sun; Velvet Cloak is valued for holding a deeper, more consistent purple foliage color through summer heat than older purple smokebush cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, average to lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; like other smokebush cultivars it tolerates rocky, sandy, and drought-prone sites better than richer, consistently moist soil. Velvet Cloak produces deep, rich wine-purple foliage that resists fading to green or bronze through summer heat better than many older purple-leaved smokebush selections, holding strong color from spring leaf-out into fall, when it turns brilliant scarlet-orange before dropping. Its billowing, airy, pink-purple summer flower panicles create the characteristic smoky haze that gives the plant its common name, standing out well against the dark foliage. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, needing only occasional thinning in late winter to maintain an open, well-branched form and remove any dead or crossing wood.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Velvet Leaf kalanchoe tolerates somewhat lower light than many succulents but colors best in bright conditions.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Velvet Leaf kalanchoe tolerates somewhat lower light than many succulents but colors best in bright conditions. Rounded, scalloped, gray-green leaves are covered in a soft, dense, velvety fuzz with faint bronze mottling along the margins, giving this Madagascar succulent a plush, tactile texture and subtle patterning quite different from the smoother, glossier leaves of most kalanchoe relatives. Its soft, fuzzy texture and manageable size make it a favorite for touch-friendly succulent displays where children or visitors can safely handle the plant without spines or sharp edges. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for the best coloring, and propagate easily from stem or leaf cuttings.

common_name: Velvet Mocha Coleus (Rich Mocha-Maroon Sun Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Velvet Mocha, part of the ColorBlaze series, bears rich, solid mocha-maroon foliage bred for heat tolerance and minimal flowering, so the color show lasts all season.
directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Velvet Mocha, part of the ColorBlaze series bred specifically for full-sun garden performance, bears rich, velvety mocha-maroon foliage with almost no pattern or variegation, giving it a deep, uniform color that reads almost solid from a distance and pairs well as a dark foil for brighter companion plants. Like other ColorBlaze selections it flowers very late in the season, so the foliage display continues largely uninterrupted through summer without frequent pinching. Water regularly during establishment and pinch growing tips occasionally to maintain a full, bushy habit.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; branching habit produces many blooms.
directions: Sow seed one inch deep directly in the garden after the last frost once soil warms. This heirloom bears velvety, multi-toned blooms in mahogany, bronze, and burnt orange on branching five- to seven-foot stems. Its many pollen-rich flowers make excellent cut material and feed bees throughout summer and fall. Give it full sun and moderate water, staking tall plants in exposed sites to prevent lodging.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts in spring into a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite; keep the medium moist year-round with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide bright, above-average humidity — never use tap water or ordinary garden soil.
directions: Ventrata pitcher plant is a naturally occurring hybrid between N. ventricosa and N. alata that combines the cool tolerance of one parent with the heat tolerance of the other, making it exceptionally adaptable and by far the most widely sold Nepenthes in general nurseries and garden centers. Its vigorous growth, fast pitchering, and tolerance of average indoor humidity make it the standard recommendation for a first-time carnivorous plant grower. Grow it in a well-draining medium of sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite, watering only with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater, since tap water minerals accumulate in the mix and damage the roots over time. Provide bright, indirect light and above-average humidity, and never fertilize the soil.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts in spring into a loose mix of sphagnum moss and perlite or fine orchid bark; keep the medium moist year-round with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide bright, humid conditions — never use tap water or ordinary garden soil.
directions: Ventricosa pitcher plant grows wild only on a handful of volcanic peaks on Luzon in the Philippines, where cool cloud-forest nights shape a plant that tolerates lower temperatures than most other Nepenthes, making it one of the best highland species for a bright windowsill or unheated sunroom. Its pitchers are easy to recognize by their narrow, strongly in-curved mouth and thick, waxy walls that are usually pale green flushed with red to deep maroon. Grow it in a loose, low-nutrient mix of sphagnum moss and perlite or fine orchid bark, watering exclusively with distilled or rainwater, as mineral buildup from tap water quickly damages the fine root system. Provide bright, filtered light and consistently high humidity, and never add fertilizer to the potting medium.

common_name: Venus Chrysanthemum (Hardy Korean-Type Single Pink Mum)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Venus is a Korean-type hardy chrysanthemum valued for its simple single daisy form and reliable garden hardiness.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build bushy, well-branched growth loaded with buds. Venus produces clear, soft pink single daisy flowers with a yellow center, a simple and graceful form descended from the tough Korean hybrid mums bred for garden hardiness rather than the double, ball-shaped blooms of florist pot mums. It flowers reliably in fall and, as a genuinely perennial garden plant, spreads gradually into a substantial clump over the years rather than needing yearly replacement. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

plant_note: Plant container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0) soil in partial shade; Venus is more heat-tolerant and disease-resistant than Cornus florida and performs better in zone 9 than the native species.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Venus is the US National Arboretum's most celebrated hybrid dogwood introduction — a first-generation hybrid between the native American flowering dogwood (Cornus florida) and the Chinese kousa dogwood (C. kousa) that produces flower bracts of extraordinary size: individual bracts (modified leaves surrounding the true flowers) reach 3–4 inches long, making the overall flower display twice the visual impact of either parent species. The enormous, pure-white, overlapping bracts create a spectacular late-April to May floral display (blooming slightly later than C. florida, extending the dogwood season) on a vigorous, upright tree. Venus inherits the best qualities of both parents: the early spring bloom timing and dense flowering of C. florida, combined with the superior heat tolerance, drought resistance, and disease resistance of C. kousa — specifically resistance to dogwood anthracnose that has devastated native C. florida populations. In zone 9, Venus performs reliably where native dogwood often struggles — the C. kousa genetics provide significantly better adaptation to Gulf South heat, humidity, and the summer conditions that stress C. florida. The large fruits that follow bloom are more showy than those of either parent. A landmark introduction for southern gardeners who love dogwoods.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, nutrient-poor, acidic medium (50/50 peat moss and perlite or long-fiber sphagnum moss) in full sun; water only with rain water or distilled water — tap water minerals and all fertilizers will kill plants. Venus flytrap requires a winter dormancy period (50°F for 3–4 months).
directions: Venus flytrap is the world's most famous carnivorous plant — a native of the Green Swamp region of North and South Carolina, where it grows in wet, nutrient-poor, acidic pine savannas maintained by periodic fire, trapping and digesting insects and spiders with its hinged, toothed, snap-trap leaves to supplement the minimal nutrients available in its impoverished native habitat. Each trap closes in milliseconds when two trigger hairs inside the trap are touched in quick succession — a failsafe mechanism that prevents wasted closure on raindrops or wind-blown debris; the trap then seals tightly and secretes digestive enzymes over 7–10 days to dissolve the prey. Despite its exotic appearance, Venus flytrap is hardy to zone 7 and requires a cold winter dormancy of 3–4 months (50°F) to remain healthy long-term; in zones 7–9 it can be grown outdoors year-round in appropriate bog conditions. Grow in a mix of 50% peat moss and 50% perlite or sand (no potting soil, no fertilizer), keep the medium wet using rain water or distilled water only, and provide maximum sun — the most common causes of failure are tap water, fertilizer, and insufficient sun.

common_name: Venusta Queen of the Prairie (Deep Pink Meadowsweet Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, rich soil; this cultivar wants more water than most perennials and thrives at pond edges, in rain gardens, or low wet meadow spots.
directions: Give this selection steady moisture and rich soil; it struggles and scorches in dry conditions but forms an impressive stand of coarse, astilbe-like foliage topped by feathery deep-pink plumes in early to midsummer where sited well. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and control spread. It is an excellent architectural plant for the back of a moist border or a rain garden, and its plumes are noticeably deeper pink than the species. Bees and butterflies visit the frothy flower heads, and the seed heads provide additional late-season texture.

common_name: Vera Cruz Rose Plumeria (Fragrant Deep Pink Plumeria)
plant_note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Vera Cruz Rose is a widely grown plumeria cultivar with rich, deep pink flowers and a strong, sweet, classic tropical fragrance.
directions: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Vera Cruz Rose is a widely grown, long-established plumeria cultivar producing rich, saturated deep pink flowers with a lighter blush toward the yellow-white center, carrying a strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance that intensifies in the evening. It is one of the more reliably vigorous and free-flowering pink plumeria cultivars, making it a popular choice for both garden specimens and lei-flower production in Hawaii. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to prevent stem rot. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Vera Jameson's low, sprawling stems make it better suited to a border edge or wall than the upright sedums it's often paired with.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Vera Jameson is a low, spreading sedum with smoky purple-gray succulent foliage on lax stems that sprawl outward rather than standing upright, topped in late summer by dusky rose-pink flower clusters that draw butterflies and bees. Its trailing habit makes it useful for softening the front of a border, tumbling over a low wall, or filling a container, where the dark foliage contrasts nicely against green-leaved neighbors. Like other sedums it thrives on neglect, needing no fertilizer and very little water once established, and can be divided every few years in spring if the clump gets thin in the center.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Verbanica is a late-blooming saucer magnolia with rosy-pink cupped flowers and coppery fall foliage color.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Verbanica bears cup-shaped, rosy-pink flowers with a paler interior, opening later in spring than most saucer magnolia cultivars, which lets its blooms largely escape the late hard freezes that damage earlier-flowering selections. The foliage turns an attractive coppery-bronze in fall, adding a second season of interest beyond the spring bloom. The tree grows into a broad, multi-stemmed small tree with minimal pruning needs beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Vermillionaire is a sterile hybrid propagated by cuttings, sold as a rooted plant, and blooms nonstop through summer heat without setting seed.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, and feed regularly through the growing season to fuel its continuous bloom. Vermillionaire is a sterile hybrid cuphea bred as a non-invasive, seedless alternative to the older, self-seeding cigar plant, producing an even heavier, nonstop display of small, tubular, bright orange flowers on a well-branched, mounding plant that draws hummingbirds from the moment it opens its first flowers until frost. Because it never sets seed, it does not spread or naturalize the way older cigar-flower cuphea can, making it a better-behaved choice for borders, mixed containers, and pollinator gardens. It is winter hardy only in the warmest zones and is typically grown as a summer annual elsewhere, propagated from cuttings taken before frost to overwinter indoors.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade to full sun; vernal witch hazel tolerates moist soil and periodic flooding along streams better than most other witch hazels.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade — vernal witch hazel is the earliest-blooming native Hamamelis species, opening its strap-petaled flowers in January through March while the plant is still dormant, even in the coldest conditions of zone 4–5. The flowers come in shades from pale yellow to orange to deep brick-red (dark orange-red in the commonly grown form) and have a sweet, spicy fragrance. Unlike the common witch hazel (H. virginiana), which blooms in fall, H. vernalis blooms in late winter and is the best native species for early-season pollinator value — providing nectar for early queen bumblebees and native mining bees on warm winter days. It is native to the gravel bars and rocky streambanks of the Ozarks and tolerates moist to wet conditions. The fall foliage is brilliant orange-yellow.

common_name: Vernal Witch Hazel, Ozark Witch Hazel
plant_note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; vernal witch hazel is native to the Ozark plateau and grows naturally along stream gravels — it is more tolerant of dry, calcareous soils than H. virginiana and slightly more drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; vernal witch hazel is native to the Ozark plateau and grows naturally along stream gravels — it is more tolerant of dry, calcareous soils than H. virginiana and slightly more drought-tolerant once established.
