Hamamelis vernalis is among the first woody plants to bloom in late winter, producing intensely fragrant, small, yellow to reddish-orange, ribbon-petaled flowers on bare stems from January through March, filling the dormant winter garden with a spicy-sweet scent on any mild winter day; the flowers close when temperatures drop below freezing and reopen when temperatures rise, allowing them to survive late-winter freezes. The fall foliage is outstanding in shades of gold and orange; it is a major improvement over Asian witch hazels for naturalizing in eastern North American native gardens because it supports specialist witch hazel bees and other native insects.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil; excellent drought tolerance once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; speedwell is notably drought-tolerant and performs poorly in soggy or heavy clay conditions. The upright spikes of blue, pink, or white flowers bloom from late spring into summer and are excellent for cutting. Deadhead by removing spent spikes back to a lateral bud or leaf to extend the flowering period and prevent excessive self-seeding. Divide every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor and an attractive mounding habit.

plant_note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Verrone's Obsidian pairs deep, near-black bronze foliage with small, single, deep red flowers, grown as much for its dramatic dark leaves as for its blooms.
directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, where the darkest foliage color develops with the most direct light. Verrone's Obsidian belongs to the group of dark-foliage dahlias grown as much for their near-black, deeply bronzed leaves as for their flowers, and its small, single, deep red blooms with a contrasting yellow center provide a bright accent against the almost black foliage rather than dominating the plant. The bold, dark leaf color makes it a striking accent or backdrop plant in a mixed border, especially paired with silver or chartreuse foliage companions for contrast. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the compact plant blooming through summer, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store the tubers indoors after the first hard frost blackens the top growth.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring before new growth begins or in fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade; versicolor barrenwort tolerates dry shade under large conifers and shallow-rooted trees better than almost any other ornamental groundcover — it is one of the first plants to try in those notoriously difficult positions.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade; versicolor barrenwort (Epimedium × versicolor) is a hybrid between E. grandiflorum and E. pinnatum subsp. colchicum that is widely regarded as the most vigorous, adaptable, and drought-tolerant of the garden epimediums — the cultivar 'Sulphureum' is particularly popular, with semi-evergreen, heart-shaped, compound leaves that emerge with a rich copper-red mottling in spring before maturing to medium green, and bright-yellow, four-spurred flowers produced in loose, airy sprays in mid-spring. The plant spreads more vigorously than the straight species epimediums by rhizomes, forming an increasingly dense, weed-suppressing groundcover mat that is exceptional in dry shade under conifers, maples, beeches, and other notoriously difficult root-competitive trees. In mild winters the foliage is semi-evergreen, providing year-round cover. Once established it is extraordinarily drought-tolerant and requires essentially no supplemental irrigation. 'Sulphureum' remains the standard against which other yellow-flowered epimediums are measured.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this mayapple relative is grown chiefly for its large, glossy, deeply lobed umbrella-like foliage that emerges bronze before turning deep green.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving each clump ample room for its large leaves to spread. Podophyllum versipelle is a Chinese woodland species prized for its bold, glossy, deeply cut leaves held on tall petioles like a cluster of umbrellas, with small maroon flowers hidden beneath the foliage in spring followed by orange-red fruit in fall. Its dramatic, oversized leaf form makes it an excellent architectural foliage plant for the back of a shaded border or a shaded courtyard bed where its scale can be appreciated against finer-textured companions like ferns or epimediums.

common_name: Vertigo Fountain Grass (Dramatic Dark Purple-Black Ornamental Grass)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions after the last frost into full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Vertigo grows as a fast, dramatic annual accent outside its tropical hardiness range and is usually replanted each year or overwintered indoors as a houseplant.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and feed regularly through the season to fuel this grass's exceptionally fast, dramatic growth. Vertigo is a dwarf selection of Napier grass bred for strikingly dark, near-black-purple blades on a tall, upright, fountain-like clump, providing bold vertical color contrast in beds and large containers unmatched by most other purple ornamental grasses. It grows remarkably quickly through a single warm season, often reaching full size within a few months of planting, and the color deepens with more sun exposure and warmth. Outside the warmest zones it is grown as a dramatic annual accent or container specimen and either replaced each spring or, where a bright indoor spot is available, cut back and overwintered as a houseplant to save the clump for the following year.

common_name: Vestal Wood Anemone (Fully Double Pure-White Pompon-Centered Anemone)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Vestal bears a fully double, pure white flower with a pompon-like tufted center, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit.
directions: Plant thin, brittle rhizomes 2 inches deep, horizontally, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees. Vestal, holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, bears a fully double flower with an outer ring of pure white petals surrounding a dense, tufted, button-like pompon center of smaller white segments, one of the most elegant and sought-after wood anemone forms, opening in early to mid spring and closing at night and in overcast weather. It spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes to form a gradually increasing carpet in a favorable woodland setting, then goes fully summer-dormant, disappearing until the following spring. It combines beautifully with early daffodils, trilliums, and other spring woodland ephemerals. Once established it requires essentially no care and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent site.

common_name: Vestitum Calanthe (Swan Calanthe, Christmas Calanthe, White-Cloaked Calanthe)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-draining terrestrial mix (bark, perlite, coco coir); Calanthe vestita is a deciduous orchid that loses its large, pleated leaves in fall as the pseudobulbs ripen — this is normal and expected. Reduce watering as leaves yellow in fall, then keep dry through the winter blooming period. The arching flower spikes bearing 10–25 large, white to pale rose flowers emerge from the leafless pseudobulbs in late fall and winter, making this an outstanding Christmas-season bloomer. Resume watering as new growth starts in spring. Tolerates brief temperatures to 35–40°F when dry. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-draining terrestrial orchid mix — Vestitum Calanthe grows most successfully when its seasonal deciduous cycle is respected: active growth and heavy watering in spring and summer, a gradual dry-down in fall, a dry winter rest during bloom, then resumption of watering with new spring growth. Calanthe vestita is a deciduous, terrestrial to semi-terrestrial, sympodial orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Myanmar (Burma), Thailand, Laos, and Malaysia — a member of the large, diverse genus Calanthe which includes both evergreen and deciduous species. Among the deciduous Calanthe species, C. vestita stands out for its large, elegant flowers and its bloom timing: the arching flower spikes, 18–24 inches long and bearing 10–25 flowers, emerge from the leafless pseudobulbs in November through January — making it one of the finest winter-blooming orchids. Each flower is large (1.5–2 inches), long-lasting, and elegant: the broad, spreading sepals and petals are pure white to very pale pink, framing a large, four-lobed or three-lobed lip that is white with a distinctive orange, yellow, or rose-red callus or marking at the center — the 'cloak' (vestita, meaning cloaked) of the species name. The flowers are unscented but of a clean, formal beauty appropriate to their winter blooming season. Calanthe vestita contributed important parentage to many classic Calanthe hybrids developed in Victorian times, when deciduous Calanthe orchids were among the most popular orchids in cultivation. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late autumn or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; vetchleaf sophora is adapted to dry, rocky, alkaline hillsides in China and tolerates drought, poor soils, and extreme heat better than most flowering shrubs. Avoid rich, moist soils which produce lush but uncharacteristically vigorous growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; vetchleaf sophora is a spreading, elegant Chinese shrub in the pea family producing silvery-gray, pinnately divided foliage that has a delicate, fern-like texture throughout the season — and producing in May and June loose clusters of small, pale-blue to lilac-white pea flowers flushed with purple that are attractive to bees and butterflies. The combination of silvery, soft-textured foliage and subtle blue-white flowers gives the shrub a refined, mediterranean quality, somewhat resembling a drought-tolerant version of false indigo (Baptisia). It develops a somewhat stiff, twiggy branching structure that can be shaped to enhance the garden form, and the dried seed pods are ornamental in winter. Very drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in lean, rocky, alkaline soils similar to those of the Chinese highland slopes where it grows naturally — an excellent plant for dry, alkaline sites where most flowering shrubs perform poorly.

plant_note: Plant divisions or slips 18–24 inches apart in rows along the contour of a slope in full sun; vetiver is sterile and does not self-sow, making it non-invasive in spite of its vigorous growth. Established plants tolerate drought, flooding, and extreme heat.
directions: Plant slips or divisions along contour lines on slopes in full sun in any well-drained soil; vetiver is the world standard for low-cost erosion control on steep slopes — a tropical grass from South Asia with an extraordinary root system that penetrates 6–10 feet straight down (not laterally) and holds soil with remarkable efficiency against both water and wind erosion. The World Bank promotes vetiver hedgerow systems in developing countries as the most effective and affordable slope stabilization technology available. The aromatic roots are distilled to produce vetiver essential oil, a base note used in hundreds of fine perfumes. Unlike most grasses used for erosion control, vetiver is sterile and non-invasive — it produces no viable seed and spreads only by division. In zone 8–11 it is an outstanding low-maintenance erosion control plant for steep slopes, stream banks, and road cuts.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before first fall frost for spring bloom; in zone 9 sow October–November for February–April flowering. Victoria Blue forget-me-not is typically grown as a winter annual in zone 9 — seeds sown in fall germinate through cool weather, overwinter as small rosettes, and produce flowers in late winter through spring before setting seed and dying as temperatures rise. The self-seeding characteristic means a planting once established will typically reseed itself year after year in favorable locations. In zone 9 partial shade extends the blooming season by keeping the soil cooler and delaying bolting.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — forget-me-nots prefer cool, moist conditions and partial shade in warm climates; Victoria Blue is a compact, early-flowering forget-me-not cultivar producing an exceptional azure-blue that is one of the most intensely saturated blues available among spring-blooming cool-season plants. The tiny (0.25-inch), five-petaled flowers in the classic azure-blue with a white or yellow eye completely cover the low, mounding plant in a carpet of pure blue in late winter and spring — creating a luminous blue ground-level effect that is unmatched by any other cool-season annual. The 'Victoria' in the name refers to the compact, mounding habit selected by breeders for more formal garden use — unlike the sprawling, loose habit of wild forget-me-not, Victoria Blue forms tidy compact mounds ideal for edging, underplanting spring bulbs, and filling in between larger plants in spring garden combinations. The traditional spring combination of azure forget-me-nots with orange or yellow tulips creates one of the most visually striking color contrasts in the spring garden. In zone 9 forget-me-nots bloom in late winter (February–March), providing garden interest in the color-limited cool season.

plant_note: Sow in spring or summer; biennial that blooms the following spring.
directions: Victoria Blue is a darling, compact forget-me-not with petite, star-shaped blue flowers perfect for the front of a shade garden or alongside spring bulbs. Direct sow the seed in spring or summer, covering it lightly since darkness aids germination. As a biennial or short-lived perennial it often blooms the spring after sowing and then self-sows to return. Grow in part shade in moist, rich soil where it heralds spring with its cheerful color. Keep the soil evenly moist and let plants naturalize for a lasting display.

common_name: Victoria Blue Salvia (Classic Dark-Blue Compact Mealy Sage for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting or plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Victoria Blue is one of the most reliable cut flowers for Gulf South summer arrangements — the flower spikes hold their color well for 7–10 days in water.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Victoria Blue is the classic, standard-setting Salvia farinacea (mealy blue sage) cultivar — one of the most widely planted blue-flowering perennials for Gulf South gardens, producing dense spikes of deep violet-blue flowers with the white-powdery (mealy) stems that give the species its common name. The flower color of Victoria Blue is one of the most purely blue and deeply saturated available in a commonly grown summer perennial — the cobalt-blue to violet-blue spikes are more intensely colored than most Salvia farinacea varieties, providing a vivid blue accent in summer borders where true blue is difficult to achieve. Victoria Blue is seed-grown and therefore more variable than named vegetatively-propagated cultivars — but the best plants from a seed-grown flat are outstanding. In Gulf South zone 9, Victoria Blue grows as a short-lived perennial that often persists 2–4 years with occasional winter dieback and spring regrowth; it also performs as a long-lived annual from winter-grown transplants set out in spring. The long bloom season (spring through frost), excellent heat and drought tolerance, and outstanding cut-flower quality make Victoria Blue one of the most versatile blue annuals/perennials for Gulf South summer gardens. An excellent companion for Rudbeckia, Lantana, and Gulf muhly grass in summer and fall borders.

common_name: Victoria Falls Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Light Blue Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced in 1977 and a Dykes Medal winner, Victoria Falls bears tall, elegant, clear light-blue flowers on strong, well-branched stems, with a form and substance that set a benchmark for blue bearded iris breeding for years afterward. Its clean, luminous color and vigorous, floriferous habit have kept it in wide cultivation long after many of its contemporaries faded from commerce. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizome and replanting healthy outer fans; good drainage is essential to prevent rot.

plant_note: Sow in spring or summer; biennial that blooms the following spring.
directions: Victoria Pink is a compact forget-me-not with petite, star-shaped pink flowers that attract pollinators and pair beautifully with spring bulbs. Direct sow the seed in spring or summer, covering it lightly since darkness helps germination. As a biennial or short-lived perennial it typically blooms the spring after sowing and self-sows to return year after year. Grow in part shade in moist, rich soil, keeping it evenly watered. Let plants naturalize at the front of shady beds for a soft, spreading carpet of color.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Victoria is a cold-hardy southern magnolia selection with rounded, glossy leaves, originating from a hardy Canadian-grown specimen.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Victoria bears the classic large, creamy-white, lemon-scented southern magnolia blooms on a tree noted for exceptional cold hardiness beyond typical species range, with rounded, glossy dark-green leaves and good resistance to winter leaf burn. Its improved cold tolerance extends southern magnolia's usable range further north than most cultivars, while it performs equally well in the milder Gulf South. Water deeply during establishment, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune only to remove dead or damaged wood.

common_name: Victoria Water Lily (Royal Water Platter, Queen Victoria Water Lily)
plant_note: Start from seed indoors in warm water (80–90°F) in late winter and transplant to an outdoor pond or large water feature after last frost when water temperature reaches 75°F+; Victoria amazonica grows extremely rapidly once established in warm water. It requires a large water feature (minimum 20×20 feet, 3–4 feet deep) to reach its full glory. In zone 9, grow as a warm-season annual — plants cannot survive cold water below 60°F. Botanical gardens and public water gardens throughout the Gulf South grow Victoria species annually as statement plants.
directions: Plant in full sun in large, warm, fertile ponds or water features — Victoria amazonica requires the warmest, sunniest conditions and a large volume of nutrient-rich water for its enormous, rapid growth. Victoria amazonica is the world's largest water lily, producing the most spectacular leaves of any aquatic plant: circular, flat, floating pads up to 10 feet across (in exceptional specimens) with upturned margins 4–8 inches high that give them the appearance of enormous green trays or pizza-pan platters on the water surface. The underside of each pad is covered with sharp spines (to deter fish feeding) and a matrix of rigid, air-filled ribs of extraordinary structural efficiency — the geometry of these ribs, allowing the leaf to support a weight of 100+ pounds distributed evenly across its surface, inspired Victorian engineer Joseph Paxton's design for the Crystal Palace in London (1851). The flowers are large (12–18 inches), open white at night and release an intense pineapple-vanilla fragrance to attract scarab beetles as pollinators, then close at dawn, trap the beetles, release pollen, and reopen the following night — now brilliant pink to rose-red. In zone 9, Victoria amazonica is grown as an annual summer spectacle in public water gardens and large private ponds.

common_name: Victoriae Lady Fern (Victorian Crested Lattice-Frond Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Victoriae is a striking Victorian-era lady fern cultivar prized by fern collectors for a genuinely unusual frond structure, in which the leaflets cross and overlap in a distinctive lattice or crisscross pattern rather than lying flat in the typical fern arrangement, creating a lacy, almost woven texture unlike any ordinary fern. This heirloom cultivar has been maintained in cultivation since Victorian times specifically for its ornamental oddity, and it makes a genuine conversation piece and focal point in a shaded fern collection or woodland garden bed. Culture is otherwise identical to standard lady fern: consistent moisture, rich organic soil, and full to partial shade, with clumps dying back each winter and re-emerging reliably each spring.

common_name: Victorian Lady Abutilon (Ruffled Pink Flowering Maple)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Victorian Lady bears large, ruffled, bell-shaped flowers in soft pink with darker pink veining, hanging gracefully from a tall, upright, well-branched shrub with maple-shaped leaves, blooming nearly year-round in mild climates. Its old-fashioned, cottage-garden charm and long bloom season make it a favorite for mixed borders and large containers where its upright habit fits better than trailing abutilon types, and hummingbirds visit the pendant flowers regularly. In zone 8, expect frost dieback most winters, with plants often resprouting from the base if roots are mulched and protected; where hard freezes are common, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

common_name: Victory Hosta (Large Green Hosta with Creamy-White Margin)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Victory is a large, vigorous hosta needing ample room to display its full, imposing mature form.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving the plant ample room to reach its large mature size over several seasons. Victory bears substantial, deeply veined, deep green leaves edged in a wide, creamy-white to yellow margin, forming an imposing, symmetrical mound that makes a strong specimen or focal point in a shaded border, with pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in mid to late summer. Its large scale and clean variegation hold up well through the growing season without excessive fading. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on tender spring growth, and divide only when the clump becomes overly congested after many years, since large hostas resent frequent disturbance.

common_name: Viette's Little Suzy Black-Eyed Susan (Compact Deer-Resistant Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Viette's Little Suzy was bred by noted Virginia perennial grower André Viette for a notably compact, sturdy habit compared to the popular Goldsturm black-eyed susan.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Viette's Little Suzy is a compact black-eyed susan cultivar, notably shorter and tidier than the widely grown Goldsturm, bred by longtime Virginia perennial nurseryman André Viette for a sturdy, floriferous plant that fits into smaller borders and front-of-bed plantings. It produces the familiar golden-yellow, dark-centered daisy flowers over a long summer bloom season, drawing bees and butterflies while resisting deer and drought once established. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the display tidy and encourage continued bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter for goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Villa Taranto Japanese Maple (Narrow Strap-Leaf Compact Dome Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Villa Taranto is a linearilobum-type maple with narrow, strap-like reddish-green lobes on a compact, dome-shaped bush.
directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Villa Taranto, a linearilobum-type Japanese maple, bears unusually narrow, strap-like leaf lobes in reddish-green that give the foliage a fine, feathery, almost willow-like texture distinct from the broader lobed leaves of typical maple cultivars, on a compact, dome-shaped shrub. Its fine texture and manageable size make it a good specimen for a small garden or container where a delicate, airy foliage effect is wanted. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape.

plant_note: Plant with the crown two to three inches below soil level to help the vine recover from stem dieback, keeping roots shaded and cool while the top grows into sun.
directions: Introduced in France in 1899, this heirloom clematis bears bright carmine-red blooms with a paler central bar, fading slightly as they age through summer. As a pruning group three cultivar, cut all stems back hard to a strong pair of buds about a foot from the ground in late winter, which keeps the vine compact and floriferous. Provide a trellis, obelisk, or shrub to climb, and keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist. It flowers on new growth from midsummer into fall, making it a reliable companion for climbing roses that bloom earlier in the season.

common_name: Ville de Nantes Camellia (Red-and-White Marbled French Heirloom Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ville de Nantes, introduced in France in 1910, bears distinctive red flowers marbled and streaked with white on loosely notched petals.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Ville de Nantes, introduced in France in 1910, is a distinctive antique Camellia japonica cultivar bearing loose, peony-form red flowers irregularly marbled and streaked with white, the notched, informal petal edges giving each bloom a slightly ragged, old-fashioned character unlike the smoother forms of many other camellias. It blooms in mid to late season on an upright, vigorous evergreen shrub that provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its unusual flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Vinca (Rosy Periwinkle, Annual Vinca, Madagascar Periwinkle)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting (slow-growing from seed); or purchase bedding plants; in zone 9, plant after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; annual vinca is among the most heat-tolerant summer annuals and thrives through Gulf Coast summers where many other annuals struggle.
directions: Plant bedding plants in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; avoid overwatering or heavy mulch against stems, which promotes Phytophthora stem and root rot. Catharanthus roseus (annual vinca or Madagascar periwinkle) is one of the top summer annuals for hot, humid Gulf Coast and Deep South gardens — an exceptionally heat-tolerant, long-blooming Madagascar native producing 1.5-to-2-inch, 5-petaled, pinwheel-shaped flowers in red, pink, rose, magenta, white, lavender, and bicolor (with contrasting eye) in profusion from spring through frost, with shiny, dark-green, camellia-like leaves. Unlike impatiens (which struggles or dies in humid summers due to downy mildew), annual vinca thrives through the hottest, most humid months. It is also valuable medically — Catharanthus roseus is the source of the alkaloids vincristine and vinblastine, critical chemotherapy drugs used worldwide for leukemia and lymphoma treatment. The 'Titan,' 'Cora,' and 'Pacifica' series are modern, improved cultivars with exceptional heat tolerance and disease resistance to aerial Phytophthora.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in shade; softwood cuttings taken in early summer can be rooted under mist. Seeds require 3-4 months of cold stratification before germinating.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; vine maple is the most shade-tolerant native tree on the Pacific Coast, growing as a multi-stemmed understory tree or large shrub in the dense Douglas-fir and western red cedar forests of the Pacific Northwest from British Columbia to northern California. The circular, 7-9-lobed leaves turn brilliant orange, scarlet, and gold in autumn, making it one of the premier fall-color plants of the region. In deep shade, the stems often lean, twist, and arch to seek light, creating a sculptural form used in Japanese-inspired gardens. The small red flowers appear in spring and the winged samaras ripen in summer. It adapts better to garden conditions than most native Pacific Northwest trees and is excellent for shaded Pacific Coast gardens.

common_name: Vintage Jade Distylium (Compact Spreading Evergreen Shade Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Vintage Jade is a compact, wide-spreading distylium selection that stays under 4 feet tall while spreading considerably wider, useful as a durable evergreen groundcover-like shrub in deep shade where few broadleaf evergreens perform well.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Vintage Jade is a low, wide-spreading distylium selection that matures to roughly 3-4 feet tall but spreads 5-8 feet across, making it one of the most useful large-scale evergreen groundcover shrubs for difficult shady sites where azaleas, boxwood, and other traditional shade shrubs often struggle. Like other distyliums, it produces small, glossy, leathery, dark green leaves and inconspicuous, petal-less red-stamened flowers in late winter that add subtle color before most shrubs break dormancy. Its defining feature is extraordinary adaptability — it tolerates full sun, deep shade, wet or dry soil, and both acid and moderately alkaline pH with no serious pest or disease problems and virtually no pruning required to look tidy, and deer generally leave it alone. Because it spreads wider than tall, space plants according to their eventual width rather than the young nursery size, and use it in mass plantings, foundation beds, or as a substitute where foundation shrubs have failed in a heavily shaded spot.

plant_note: In zone 9 start seeds indoors August–September and transplant October–November for winter and early spring bloom. Stock requires vernalization (6–8 weeks of temperatures below 50°F at night) to initiate flowering in most varieties — zone 9 winters typically provide enough cool nights for flowering from December through March. The Vintage series was selected for lower vernalization requirements, making it better adapted to mild-winter climates than older stock varieties. Grow as a winter annual in zone 9; plants rarely survive into summer heat.
directions: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — stock performs poorly in acidic soil and benefits from lime in naturally acidic garden soils; Vintage White stock (Matthiola incana) is one of the most intensely fragrant cut flowers available to home gardeners — the vertical spikes of pure white, densely petaled, ruffled flowers produce a rich, warm, vanilla-and-clove fragrance that is among the strongest and most complex of any garden flower. The fragrance of stock is categorically different from most flowers: warm, spicy, and complex rather than floral-sweet, filling an entire room from a single cut stem. Stock flowers are primarily valued as cut flowers for winter and early spring arrangements where the long, sturdy stems (18–24 inches) and exceptional fragrance make them among the most sought-after seasonal flowers for bouquets and arrangements. The Vintage series was developed for earliness and adaptation to warmer winter climates, making it practical for zone 9 winter gardens where adequate cold for vernalization is reliable but extreme cold is uncommon. Vintage White provides a classic, sophisticated white cut flower from December through March in zone 9 — a season when relatively few flowers are available.

common_name: Vintage Wine Coneflower (Double Deep Wine-Purple Pompom)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Vintage Wine bears deep wine-purple double pompom blooms on a well-branched, sturdy plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Vintage Wine bears fully double, deep wine-purple pompom flowers on a well-branched, sturdy plant that produces heavy bud counts through the summer, a rich, saturated color deeper than most other double coneflower cultivars. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant several weeks before last frost as plants tolerate mild freezes.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 in deep in a cool, moist starting mix; darkness during germination is beneficial. Violas are more petite and heat-tolerant than pansies, often self-sowing prolifically in the garden. Deadhead to extend flowering, or allow seed to set for naturalized self-seeding the following year. They shine in early spring containers and border edges.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in fall for natural cold-moist stratification, or sow in spring after 30–60 days of cold stratification; plant in well-drained, dry to mesic soil in partial shade at the edge of open woodlands.
directions: Sow scarified seeds in fall or stratified seeds in early spring in dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil in partial shade at the edges of open deciduous woods, woodland clearings, or dry savannas; violet bush clover is a slender, graceful native legume of the eastern United States, producing a profusion of small, bright violet pea-shaped flowers in loose panicles in mid to late summer — a season when few other native perennials are in bloom, making it a valuable late-season nectar source for native bees, skippers, and sulphur butterflies. Unlike the weedy Asian lespedezas that have invaded roadsides across the East, this species is well-behaved and does not spread aggressively. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it enriches the soil and performs best in the lean, dry, slightly acidic soils that characterize the open woodlands and dry savannas of its native range; rich, moist soils cause floppy, rank growth. The trifoliate leaves are small and attractive; stems are reddish and arching. An excellent understory addition to dry native plant gardens and oak savanna restorations.

common_name: Violet Iochroma (Violet Tubes, Blue Bells Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs after last frost; in zone 9a, plant in a sheltered south-facing or south-wall-adjacent location and mulch heavily at the base to protect roots from frost. Iochroma cyaneum may freeze to the ground in zone 9a winters but often resprouts vigorously from the root crown in spring if the soil did not freeze deeply. In zone 9b-10, it blooms nearly year-round.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; in zone 9's intense summer sun, afternoon shade improves performance and prevents leaf burn. Iochroma cyaneum is a soft-wooded shrub in the Solanaceae family (related to Brunfelsia and nightshade) native to the Andes of Ecuador and Colombia, where it grows in moist montane cloud forests at 6,000–10,000 feet elevation. In zone 9 Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes, it is grown for its spectacular pendant clusters of deep violet-blue, 1.5-inch tubular flowers that dangle from the branch tips in profuse flushes throughout the warm season. The deep, pure violet-blue color is among the most saturated blues available in a large tropical shrub — not lavender, not purple, but true rich violet-blue. The flowers are intensely attractive to hummingbirds, which hover at the pendant clusters throughout the blooming season. The plant grows quickly, reaching 6–10 feet by the end of its first full season. Prune back hard after each major bloom flush to encourage repeat flowering and a more compact, bushy habit. All parts of the plant are mildly toxic if ingested. An outstanding hummingbird and ornamental shrub for zone 9b–11.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; violet moth orchid needs consistent warmth (65-85°F) and cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; violet moth orchid needs consistent warmth (65-85°F) and cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Thick, waxy, star-shaped flowers in rich violet-purple with a contrasting white or green center carry an intense, sweet fragrance most noticeable in the warmth of midday, opening just one or two at a time from a short stem rather than the long arching sprays typical of the hybrid moth orchids commonly sold in stores. Native to the hot, humid lowland rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, it requires warmer year-round temperatures than most commercial phalaenopsis hybrids, thriving best in a warm greenhouse or bright bathroom where heat and humidity stay consistently high. Water when the bark mix approaches dryness, maintain high humidity and warmth above 65°F even at night, and provide bright but filtered light for the best flowering and fragrance.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost in full sun.
directions: Violet Queen is a clary-type annual salvia grown for its showy, long-lasting violet bracts rather than its tiny true flowers, with aromatic foliage and blooms. Direct sow around the last frost in full sun and average, well-drained soil, barely covering the seed. It blooms non-stop through summer; simply remove spent spikes to encourage continual color. Drought-tolerant once established, it mixes well with bright annuals in beds and borders. The colorful bracts also dry nicely and draw hummingbirds, butterflies, and other pollinators.

common_name: Violet Queen Spider Flower (Deep Violet-Purple Heirloom Cleome)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Violet Queen is the deep purple member of the classic Queen series of spider flower and self-sows readily once established.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Violet Queen is the richest, deepest-colored member of the classic Queen series of spider flower, its large, airy flower heads opening a saturated violet-purple with the same long, protruding stamens that give every cleome bloom its spidery look. Like its Rose Queen and Cherry Queen relatives it shrugs off the worst of Gulf South summer heat, growing vigorously through July and August when many other annuals stall, and blooming continuously from the top of each elongating stem until frost. The slightly sticky, aromatic foliage is typical of the species, and established plantings self-sow freely, drawing hummingbirds, butterflies, and sphinx moths all summer.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; violet silverleaf needs excellent drainage and full sun to bloom well and rots in heavy, wet, or overwatered soil.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; violet silverleaf needs excellent drainage and full sun to bloom well and rots in heavy, wet, or overwatered soil. Small, densely felted, brilliant silvery-white leaves cover a compact, rounded shrub that erupts into a profuse flush of rich violet-purple flowers following summer rains, a dramatic and reliable bloom response shared by other Texas silverleaf species and prized for the way it signals rainfall across the Chihuahuan Desert landscape it calls home. Native to limestone hills of the Trans-Pecos region and northern Mexico, it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, needing no supplemental irrigation beyond natural rainfall, and its striking silver foliage provides season-long textural interest between bloom flushes. Prune lightly to shape if needed, avoiding heavy shearing which reduces the natural rounded form and flowering, and plant in the leanest, best-drained spot available.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; violet wild petunia is a well-behaved native alternative to the aggressively self-seeding Mexican petunia (Ruellia simplex) sold widely in nurseries.
directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; violet wild petunia is a true Texas and Gulf South native wildflower with narrow, hairy leaves and funnel-shaped, violet-purple flowers that open in the morning and typically drop by afternoon, refreshing with new blooms daily over a long spring-through-fall season. It serves as a larval host for the common buckeye butterfly and is visited regularly by native bees, offering solid wildlife value without the aggressive rhizomatous spread of the widely sold, non-native Mexican petunia often confused with it. Plants form a modest, well-mannered clump rather than running aggressively, making them safe to place in mixed beds without fear of them taking over neighboring plants. Cut back hard after the first hard freeze in colder parts of its range, mulching the crown, since it dies back to the roots and resprouts in spring.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs (corms) 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; violet woodsorrel naturally grows in open prairies, rocky glades, and open woodland edges and prefers well-drained to slightly dry conditions.
directions: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun — violet woodsorrel is a charming native bulb of the eastern US prairies and open woodlands, producing clusters of small, five-petaled, rose-purple to violet flowers in spring above neat clover-like leaves with three heart-shaped leaflets that fold at night and in cloudy weather. It is one of the earliest-blooming spring bulbs in the native prairie garden, appearing alongside spring beauty and pasque flower. The corms multiply slowly each year to form small colonies that naturalize in open, well-drained, sunny to partially-shaded conditions. The leaves have a pleasant, mild lemony flavor (from oxalic acid, same as other woodsorrels and sheep sorrel) and can be eaten sparingly in small quantities as a tart, lemony salad accent. It goes dormant in summer heat and reemerges in fall with a brief second bloom before going dormant for winter.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in fall for spring germination, or sow in early spring; viper's bugloss is a biennial that germinates and forms a basal rosette in year one, then flowers in year two. It self-sows prolifically in dry, sunny, well-drained conditions to maintain a permanent colony. It thrives in sandy, gravelly, chalky, or lean soils and actually blooms more abundantly in poor, dry soils than in rich ones.
directions: Sow seeds in lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral, sandy or chalky soil in full sun; viper's bugloss is one of the supreme bee and butterfly plants of European wildflower meadows — a bristly, rough-textured biennial covered from late spring through midsummer with brilliant, vivid blue (occasionally pink or white) flowers that are produced in extraordinary profusion from the curving, scorpioid flower clusters characteristic of the borage family. In a good year a single plant produces hundreds of flowers over a period of months, each flower visited repeatedly by bumblebees, honeybees, and solitary bees. The name comes from the snake-like shape of the nutlets (seeds) which resemble a snake's head. Native to dry, sunny, chalky grasslands and disturbed ground throughout Europe, it thrives in the lean, alkaline, well-drained soils of roadsides, banks, and gravel gardens where it self-sows freely to maintain a permanent colony. Note: while naturalized across much of North America, it is classed as a noxious weed in some western states due to toxicity to livestock from pyrrolizidine alkaloids.

plant_note: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade near a fence, trellis, or shrubby thicket; virgin's bower scrambles through shrubs and climbs by leaf petioles — site where it can naturalize freely as it self-seeds prolifically.
directions: Virgin's bower is the most widespread and cold-hardy of all native North American clematis, scrambling through shrubs and small trees along streams, roadsides, and woodland edges from Nova Scotia to Florida — in late summer it smothers its support in masses of small, four-petaled white flowers that are intensely fragrant and attract a spectacular diversity of native bees, wasps, beetles, and butterflies seeking late-summer nectar. After bloom, the flowers are replaced by feathery, silvery seed plumes that persist through fall and winter, creating a spectacular 'old man's beard' effect in the landscape — a three-season ornamental vine of understated elegance. While not as showy as large-flowered hybrid clematis, its fine-textured floral masses and subsequent silky seedheads provide months of changing interest with zero maintenance; it is drought-tolerant once established and pest-free. Self-seeds freely to form spreading colonies — allow it to naturalize in native shrub borders or along a fence where it can sprawl without becoming an obstacle.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; virginal mock orange is a classic, widely grown hybrid group prized for heavily double, intensely fragrant flowers.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; virginal mock orange is a classic, widely grown hybrid group prized for heavily double, intensely fragrant flowers. Large, semi-double to fully double, pure white flowers cover the upright, somewhat leggy branches in late spring, carrying an intense, sweet orange-blossom fragrance that made this old hybrid group a mainstay of cottage and heritage gardens since the early twentieth century. Less refined in habit than some newer compact mock orange cultivars, it is grown chiefly for the strength of its fragrance and flower fullness, best sited toward the back of a border or near a window or path where the scent can be appreciated during its bloom period. Prune immediately after flowering, removing some of the oldest canes each year at the base to keep the naturally leggy shrub renewed and full at the bottom.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall immediately after harvest in moist, rich, neutral to slightly alkaline woodland or floodplain soil in partial to full shade; seeds require cold stratification over winter and germinate in early spring — do not allow seeds to dry out before sowing as viability drops rapidly.
directions: Direct sow fresh seed in fall immediately after harvest in moist, rich, neutral to slightly alkaline floodplain or woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds require cold stratification over winter and germinate in early spring — do not allow seeds to dry out before sowing as viability drops rapidly. Virginia bluebells is the finest eastern North American spring ephemeral wildflower; it emerges with smooth, blue-green, glaucous foliage in early spring and produces arching clusters of trumpet-shaped flowers that open pink from the bud and mature to a luminous, sky-blue color in April and May, creating a breathtaking drift of color beneath flowering redbuds and dogwoods. The plant goes completely dormant by early summer, leaving no trace; mark its location and plant late-emerging hostas, ferns, or annuals to fill the gap. It naturalizes prolifically along stream banks and moist woodland floors and is a premier pollinator resource for native bumblebees.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Virginia bunchflower requires consistently moist conditions and does best in wet meadows or along stream margins.
directions: Melanthium virginicum is a stately native perennial of eastern North American wet meadows, bogs, and stream margins, producing tall stems 3–5 feet in height from a clump of long, strap-like leaves, topped in summer (June–July) with a large, showy, pyramidal panicle of creamy white to pale greenish-white flowers that age to deep purple-green, creating a striking color transition over several weeks of bloom. It grows naturally in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soils in partial shade to full sun and is an excellent choice for rain garden margins, pond banks, and moist native meadow plantings in the mid-Atlantic and Southeast. The large flower panicles provide nectar for native bees and insects; leaves have a pleated, corn-like texture. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested; handle rhizomes with gloves.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), wet to moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Virginia chain fern tolerates deeper standing water than most ferns and can colonize the margins of swamps, bogs, and wet ditches.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), wet to moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Virginia chain fern is a robust, twice-pinnate native fern of Atlantic coastal plain bogs, swamps, and wet pine flatwoods — larger and more dramatic than the similar netted chain fern, with bipinnate fronds reaching 2–5 feet in saturated acidic soil. The sori are arranged in the chain-like pattern that names the genus, running in long lines parallel to the midrib. It tolerates standing water around the root zone and is one of the best native ferns for establishing in swampy, waterlogged, acidic conditions where few other plants thrive. Spreads steadily by rhizome to form bold colonies in appropriate wet, acid conditions. An important structural plant in wetland restoration and naturalistic bog gardens in the Southeast and coastal plain from New England to Florida.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Virginia chain fern thrives in bogs, wet woodland depressions, and the permanently moist margins of streams and ponds.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Virginia chain fern is a native North American fern of bogs, swamps, and wet woodland floors, producing distinctive fronds with alternating sterile and fertile pinnae that create a chain-like pattern — the source of its common name. The fertile fronds are somewhat narrower and browner than the sterile ones and remain erect through winter, providing structure and winter interest. Spreads by rhizomes to form dense, weed-suppressing colonies in appropriate wet, shaded conditions. Excellent for naturalizing wet, shaded areas of the garden where few other plants thrive. Tolerates standing water seasonally. The larger related species W. fimbriata (giant chain fern) is native to the Pacific Coast.

plant_note: Plant container vines in spring near a structure, tree, or fence; the vine clings by adhesive suction-cup pads that do not penetrate surfaces or damage mortar. Do not confuse with poison ivy (three leaflets); virginia creeper has five.
directions: Plant in virtually any soil — wet or dry, rich or poor, sandy or clay — in full sun to deep shade; Virginia creeper is one of the most versatile native vines, blanketing fences, walls, trees, and arbors in deep shade where few other plants grow, and producing a stunning curtain of brilliant crimson-scarlet-burgundy fall color that is among the most vivid of any plant in the North American flora. The small dark blue-black berries that follow in fall are an essential food for migrating thrushes, waxwings, bluebirds, and woodpeckers. It clings by adhesive pads (not invasive roots), making it appropriate on stone and brick. The sap and berries are toxic to humans and can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive individuals; the similar five-leaflet compound leaf distinguishes it from three-leaflet poison ivy. Prune aggressively in late winter to control size.

plant_note: Scatter seed in fall or as soon as ground is workable in early spring onto bare, thin, or sandy soil; do not cover, as seeds require light for germination and will find their own crevices in open, undisturbed ground.
directions: Virginia Dwarf Dandelion is a diminutive native annual of the daisy family, producing miniature golden-yellow flower heads barely half an inch across on thread-like stems from early spring through early summer in thin, dry, sandy, or gravelly, undisturbed soil across eastern North America. One of the earliest native spring wildflowers to bloom, it fills an important ecological role as a nectar source for small native bees — particularly Lasioglossum and Andrena species — when almost nothing else is in flower. Grow in thin turf, bare sandy patches, lichen-covered rock outcrops, or powerline rights-of-way where it naturalizes freely without any competition from vigorous grasses or perennials. Best established by scattering seed in fall onto prepared bare ground and leaving it alone; this tiny annual thrives precisely where gardeners struggle to grow anything else.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring after last frost in dry, sandy, gravelly, or rocky, well-drained, infertile soil in full sun to light shade. Virginia False Aloe is extremely drought-tolerant once established; do not amend with compost, fertilize, or irrigate routinely, as overly rich or moist soil causes crown rot and rapid decline.
directions: Virginia False Aloe is a native succulent wildflower of the southeastern United States, producing a compact basal rosette of fleshy, strap-like, often maroon-spotted leaves from sandy or rocky, well-drained soils in prairies, cedar glades, open woodlands, and roadsides from Virginia south to Florida and west to Nebraska. Unlike the dangerous spiny agaves to which it is closely related, False Aloe has soft, non-rigid leaf tips, making it entirely safe to handle; after several years of vegetative growth, it sends up a single spectacular flower spike reaching 4–6 feet tall, bearing fragrant, tubular, greenish-brown to purple flowers that open at night and attract sphinx moths as their primary pollinators. Once the flower stalk sets seed, the rosette dies but is replaced by offsets from the base, allowing clumps to expand gradually over many years without becoming invasive. Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly, infertile, rocky soil in full sun; False Aloe is highly drought-tolerant and long-lived in appropriate conditions but quickly rots in wet, poorly drained, or heavily amended soils.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in ordinary, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; jumpseed tolerates dry shade under mature trees better than most woodland perennials once established and self-sows modestly where happy.
directions: Plant in ordinary, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, including the dry shade under established trees where it tolerates competition better than most woodland perennials once its roots are established. Virginia jumpseed is a tough eastern North American native prized less for its wiry spikes of small greenish-white flowers than for its explosive seed dispersal — ripe seeds are launched several feet when the wand-like flower stalks are brushed, a trait that gives the plant its common name and makes it a fun teaching plant for children's gardens. The variegated cultivar sold as 'Painter's Palette', with a dark V-shaped chevron and creamy speckling splashed across each leaf, is grown chiefly as a striking dry-shade foliage plant and reseeds true enough to keep a colorful patch going for years. Cut plants back hard in late winter to clear the previous year's dried stems before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Scarify seeds lightly and direct sow in early spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Virginia Mallow self-sows from year to year; established plants develop a persistent woody crown and re-sprout each spring.
directions: Virginia Mallow is a tall, bold native perennial, native to the rich, moist soils of bottomlands, riverbanks, woodland edges, and disturbed clearings from Virginia and Pennsylvania south to Georgia and west to Indiana, growing to 8–10 feet tall in fertile, moist soil and producing a continuous succession of small, five-petaled, white flowers from July through September that attract an exceptional diversity of native bees, including many specialist bees that are important pollinators. The large, palmately lobed leaves and towering height give Virginia Mallow a dramatic architectural quality in the native garden, providing bold structure in the back of borders and in naturalized meadow plantings. The abundant seeds are consumed by goldfinches, sparrows, and other seed-eating birds in fall and winter; the plant's stems provide nesting material and stem-nesting sites for solitary native bees. Grow in fertile, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; it is surprisingly adaptable and self-sows reliably once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or direct sow in spring in moist to wet, very acidic, sandy or peaty, low-nutrient soil in full sun to partial shade; Virginia meadow beauty is adapted to the wet, acidic, nutrient-poor conditions of bogs, pitcher plant bogs, and moist pine savannas — it does not tolerate enriched garden soil or alkaline conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or peaty, low-nutrient soil in full sun to partial shade; Virginia meadow beauty is a native perennial of wet, acidic bogs, pitcher plant bogs, moist pine savannas, and seepage-wet flatwoods. The four-petaled, bright rose-pink flowers with distinctive, curved, bright yellow anthers are produced from mid-summer through fall. The distinctive jug-shaped seed capsule that follows the flowers is attractive and ornamental, persisting into winter. Meadow beauties are poll-collected by specialist buzz pollinators — bumblebees and certain specialist bees that vibrate the anthers at a specific frequency to release pollen, making them important for native bee diversity. Requires very acidic, lean, moist soil; will not thrive in neutral or fertilized garden conditions. Perfect for bog gardens, pitcher plant gardens, and the wet, acidic margins of natural ponds.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, humus-rich soil in fall to allow cold stratification over winter. Do not cover seeds, as they require light to germinate. Best established by transplanting small divisions from existing colonies rather than starting from seed.
directions: Virginia Pennywort thrives in the deep shade of moist deciduous forests and requires a rich, organic soil with consistent moisture year-round. Scatter seeds directly on the forest floor in fall, pressing lightly into the leaf litter without burying them, as they need cold winter temperatures to break dormancy. This partially parasitic plant depends on mycorrhizal fungi associated with tree roots, so siting it near established oaks, beeches, or maples significantly improves establishment success. Avoid disturbing the soil around established plants, as the shallow root network is easily damaged.

plant_note: Direct sow stratified seeds in spring in well-drained, sandy, acidic, poor soil in full sun; Virginia pine colonizes dry, infertile, disturbed sites naturally and establishes readily from seed. It is one of the most important pines for wildlife plantings on poor soils in the mid-Atlantic and upper South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, poor, acidic soil in full sun; Virginia pine is a pioneer species of the mid-Atlantic and upper South, naturally colonizing dry, infertile, disturbed, and eroded sites where richer soils and better drainage favor other trees. It is a relatively small, irregularly shaped pine with short, twisted needles in pairs and persistent small cones that remain on the tree for years, providing seeds and cover for wildlife through winter. The tree's value for wildlife planting on poor soils is exceptional — it is a primary host for numerous moth and butterfly caterpillars, and the cone seeds are eaten by finches, chickadees, and other birds. Used extensively in reclamation planting on strip-mined land and abandoned agricultural soils in Appalachia and the Piedmont. Though not a timber tree, it serves as an important nurse tree that prepares infertile sites for succession to mixed hardwood forest.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container divisions in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Virginia rose is extremely cold hardy and tolerates a wide range of soils, including poor, sandy, and dry conditions once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — Virginia rose is one of the most ecologically valuable of all native roses, producing simple, five-petaled, clear pink flowers in late spring with a pleasant light fragrance, followed by the best hips of any eastern wild rose: large, bright red, glossy fruits that persist on the canes through winter and provide critical food for catbirds, mockingbirds, robins, and cedar waxwings. The foliage turns brilliant shades of red, orange, and burgundy in autumn — outstanding fall color for a shrub. It spreads by suckers to form dense, wildlife-valuable thickets in naturalistic settings, along fencerows, and at the edges of woodland, and tolerates salt spray, poor sandy soils, and moderate drought. Disease resistance is excellent compared to hybrid roses: no spraying required. Prune out oldest canes after flowering to keep the plant productive; remove suckers to control spread in small spaces.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Virginia snakeroot is a small woodland understory herb that needs the same rich, leafy shade conditions as trilliums and other spring ephemerals.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Virginia snakeroot is a small woodland understory herb that needs the same rich, leafy shade conditions as trilliums and other spring ephemerals. Slender, zigzagging stems carry heart-shaped leaves close to the forest floor, with small, curved, pipe-shaped brownish-purple flowers produced low at the base of the plant, largely hidden beneath the leaf litter and pollinated by small flies. As a member of the pipevine family, it serves as a larval host plant for pipevine swallowtail butterflies, though it is a smaller, less vigorous host than the woody pipevine (Aristolochia macrophylla) more commonly planted for that purpose. Historically valued in traditional medicine for its aromatic rhizome, it is grown today mainly as a woodland native curiosity and butterfly host plant, spreading slowly by rhizome in rich, undisturbed shade.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall; plants establish quickly and begin blooming the following spring. Direct seeding is possible but takes longer — divisions are the preferred propagation method.
directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Virginia spiderwort is a native wildflower of open woods and roadsides producing three-petaled flowers in shades of blue-violet to purple, pink, or white that open in the morning and close by early afternoon. The strap-like, grass-like foliage is bold and attractive in the spring garden. After flowering, plants go semi-dormant in midsummer heat and may look tatty — cut back hard to 4–6 inches to encourage a flush of fresh foliage. Plants self-seed prolifically and spread by clump division; thin as needed. The closed flowers and young shoot tips are edible in salads, and the plant has a long history of use by eastern woodland peoples.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated stock in early spring along a streambank or seasonally scoured floodplain edge in consistently moist, gravelly to sandy soil, since wild populations depend on periodic flood disturbance to persist.
directions: Virginia spiraea is a federally threatened, rhizomatous shrub restricted to a scatter of high-gradient river and stream banks in the central Appalachians, where its dense root mats stabilize scoured cobble bars against flood erosion. In cultivation it forms a low, arching, suckering thicket topped in early to midsummer by flat-topped clusters of small white to pale pink flowers that draw a wide range of native bees and butterflies. Because the species is adapted to periodic flooding and mechanical scouring, it tolerates seasonally saturated soil and occasional inundation far better than most garden spireas, but it should never be collected from the wild given its rarity. Site it along a pond margin, rain garden, or streambank restoration planting with reliable moisture and light shade for part of the day.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall or transplant tiny corms 2–3 inches deep in autumn; plants require winter cold to break dormancy and will bloom the following spring. Once established, they self-seed to naturalize freely.
directions: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees; Virginia spring beauty is a spring ephemeral wildflower that carpets the woodland floor with pink-striped white flowers in early spring before tree canopies close. The narrow, fleshy leaves and small corms are edible — the corms taste like a mild potato and were gathered by Indigenous peoples of eastern North America. Plants go fully dormant by late spring, leaving bare soil where they grew; interplant with ferns, hostas, or other summer-active groundcovers to fill the gap. Self-seeds freely once naturalized — scatter seed right after it ripens in late spring to establish new colonies.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, very slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade — virginia stewartia is notoriously difficult to establish and absolutely requires excellent drainage, consistently moist (not wet) soil, and protection from afternoon heat in zones 8–9; mulch heavily to maintain cool, moist root conditions.
directions: Stewartia malacodendron is the most beautiful and rarest of the native stewartias, a slow-growing, multi-stemmed shrub to small tree of open forest understories in the coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and Texas, producing extraordinarily showy, wide-open, camellia-like white flowers 3–4 inches across with distinctive, dramatic, purple-blue stamens and dark-purple anthers in June and July — the most spectacular flowers of any stewartia. It also has handsome, flaking, mottled gray-and-cinnamon bark and brilliant red autumn foliage. A coveted collector's plant for shaded native woodland gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds where they are to grow 4–6 weeks before last frost in cool weather (or in fall in mild climates); Virginia stock matures so quickly — as little as 4–5 weeks from sowing to first flower — that successive sowings every 3–4 weeks from early spring through early summer and again in early fall extend the season. It does not transplant well and should always be direct-sown where it is to grow.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in full sun in any moderately fertile, well-drained soil; Virginia stock (despite its common name, a Mediterranean native unrelated to American Virginia) is one of the fastest-flowering annuals in existence — germinating in less than a week and producing flowers within 4–5 weeks of sowing, making it ideal for impatient gardeners, children's gardens, and gaps in the border that need instant color. The flowers are small (half an inch), simple four-petaled cruciform blooms in the traditional cross shape of the Brassicaceae family, in cheerful shades of lilac, pink, red, white, and yellow — all usually sold as a mixed color packet. The plants grow quickly, flower prolifically, set seed, and die within their first season, but self-sow freely to maintain colonies. The flowers have a light, sweet, clove-like fragrance. Excellent for filling gaps rapidly in mixed beds, cottage-garden style plantings, and children's gardens where the fast germination-to-flower timeline provides immediate satisfaction. Sow in broad sweeps for the best effect; individual small plants can look weedy but mass sowings create cheerful carpets of color.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in spring; Virginia sweetspire is notably adaptable and tolerates poorly drained, wet soils where most shrubs fail. It spreads slowly by root suckers to form loose colonies and can be divided in early spring.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full shade; Virginia sweetspire is an outstanding native shrub for difficult moist or shaded sites, producing long (2–6 inch) arching spikes of fragrant white flowers in early summer and then delivering some of the richest fall foliage of any native shrub — leaves turn crimson, scarlet, orange, and burgundy-purple and often hold into early winter long after most deciduous shrubs have dropped their leaves. The multi-stem arching habit is graceful year-round. Unlike many shade shrubs, it tolerates both periodically wet conditions and drought once established, making it excellent for rain gardens, woodland edges, and stream banks. 'Henry's Garnet' is the most widely grown cultivar, with outstanding wine-red to deep scarlet fall color and somewhat larger flower spikes than the species.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring before new growth; fresh seed can be sown in fall for spring germination. Virginia waterleaf spreads by rhizomes and self-sows to form colonies in favorable conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; Virginia waterleaf is a native perennial named for the distinctive pale, water-stained markings on its young leaves that look as though water has splashed on them — these marks fade as the leaves mature. It produces small clusters of white to pale lavender bell-shaped flowers beloved by native bees in spring, then large attractive foliage through summer. The young leaves and shoots are edible and were gathered as spring greens by Eastern Woodland peoples. It spreads reliably by rhizomes to create dense, weed-suppressing colonies under tall hardwood canopies — one of the most effective native groundcovers for deep shade in the eastern US.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall (preferred) or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Virginia wildrye is one of the rare native grasses that genuinely thrives in partial shade, making it invaluable for woodland edges and shaded naturalized areas.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Virginia wildrye is one of the most ecologically important and ornamentally useful native grasses for shaded sites in eastern North America — a cool-season bunchgrass forming attractive upright to arching clumps of medium-green leaves, topped in late spring and summer by distinctive awn-tipped seed heads that arch gracefully and provide significant wildlife food value for native sparrows, towhees, and other seed-eating birds. Unlike most ornamental grasses that require full sun, Virginia wildrye genuinely thrives in partial shade under deciduous trees, making it an excellent groundcover-level grass for naturalized woodland edges. It also tolerates wet conditions, river floodplains, and clay soils — a broad adaptability that makes it an outstanding restoration and native plant garden grass. Spreads by self-seeding in appropriate conditions. An outstanding wildlife-supporting grass for zone 9 woodland gardens.

common_name: Viridis Japanese Maple (Classic Green Mounding Lace-Leaf Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Viridis is a classic mounding green lace-leaf maple with fine-textured foliage and gold-orange fall color.
directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Viridis forms a graceful, low, mounding dome of finely dissected, lacy green foliage, the classic green counterpart to the many red-leaved lace-leaf cultivars, turning brilliant gold and orange in fall for a dramatic seasonal transformation. Its wider-than-tall, cascading habit makes it a strong specimen for the edge of a pond, atop a slope, or spilling over a low wall. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, especially through the first few years, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches, preserving the natural mounding form.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring for late spring color.
directions: Direct sow viscaria thinly in early spring where plants are to bloom. The dainty rose, blue, and white five-petaled flowers cover slender stems and suit cottage gardens and cutting beds. It appreciates full sun and well-drained soil and blooms quickly from seed. Thin seedlings for good air movement and deadhead to prolong the flowering period.

common_name: Viscountess Byng Crimson Flag Lily (Late-Blooming Pale Pink Hesperantha)
plant_note: Divide and plant rhizomes in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Viscountess Byng is one of the latest-flowering crimson flag lily cultivars, holding off until well into autumn to open its pale, soft-pink, star-shaped blooms, often continuing until the first hard frost cuts them down. Its late timing makes it valuable for extending color in the perennial border after most other bloomers have finished. Grow it in consistently moist soil near pond edges or in rain gardens, and divide clumps every three years in spring to keep flowering strong. The delicate pink flowers pair well with ornamental grasses and asters that share its autumn bloom window.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a shaded, moist location.
directions: Vision In Pink is a shade-loving perennial astilbe that sends up soft pink, feathery flower plumes above mounds of deep green, finely cut foliage in summer. Plant in partial to full shade in humus-rich, consistently moist soil; it will not tolerate dry conditions. Divide clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and increase your planting. Cut back spent plumes or leave them for winter interest, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. It is an excellent choice for woodland gardens, shaded borders, and near water features.

common_name: Vision in Red Astilbe (Dark Red-Plumed Bronze-Leaved Astilbe)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial shade; Vision in Red is part of the Dutch Vision series of astilbe chinensis hybrids, bred for compact size and unusually good drought tolerance compared to most astilbe, though it still performs best with reliable moisture in a Gulf South summer.
directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Vision in Red bears dense, dark purplish-red plumes over bronze-tinted green foliage on a compact plant, one of the more richly colored selections in the popular Vision series of astilbe chinensis hybrids. Like other Vision-series astilbe, it is somewhat more tolerant of dry spells than older astilbe cultivars, though it still performs best and blooms most heavily with consistent moisture through summer. Leave the dried plumes standing through fall and winter for ornamental interest, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Visions is a compact Astilbe chinensis selection that tolerates somewhat drier soil and more sun than most astilbe cultivars, though consistent moisture still gives the best results.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Visions is a compact Astilbe chinensis cultivar producing dense, bottlebrush-like plumes of rich raspberry-pink flowers in mid-to-late summer above glossy, dark green, finely cut foliage, blooming somewhat later in the season than many Arendsii-type astilbe cultivars. Its Chinese astilbe parentage gives it better tolerance of drier soil and more sun exposure than most astilbes, though it still performs best with consistent moisture and appreciates deep shade and heavy mulch through the hottest part of a zone 9 summer. The dried flower plumes remain attractive well after bloom, and clumps can be divided every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Visions in Red Astilbe (Deep Red Compact Astilbe)
