plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; more tolerant of drier soil and sun than most astilbe cultivars, though consistent moisture gives the best results.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Visions in Red produces dense, bottlebrush-like plumes in a deep, saturated wine-red, a richer and darker color than the raspberry-pink of the original Visions astilbe, above glossy, dark bronze-green, finely cut foliage that adds color contrast even before bloom. Like other Astilbe chinensis selections, it tolerates somewhat drier soil and more sun than Arendsii-type astilbes, though it still performs best with consistent moisture and appreciates deep shade and heavy mulch through the hottest part of a zone 9 summer. The dried flower plumes remain attractive well after bloom; divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant in spring with the crown set a couple of inches below the soil surface and the base shaded, giving the vine a fence, trellis, or shrub to climb into full sun; blooms entirely on new wood, so it can be cut back hard each late winter.
directions: Plant nursery starts in spring with the crown set a couple of inches below the soil surface and the roots shaded and cool, giving the vine a fence, trellis, or shrub to scramble into in full sun. Viticella clematis is one of the toughest and most disease-resistant of the large clematis groups, producing an abundance of smaller, nodding, four- to six-petaled flowers in shades of purple, magenta, and blue from midsummer into fall on the current season's growth. Because it blooms entirely on new wood, it can be cut back hard to 12–18 inches each late winter, a simple pruning routine that also makes it easy to grow through and rejuvenate an early-blooming shrub or rose. Its resistance to clematis wilt and reliable late-season color have made it a parent species behind many popular modern hybrids, including the 'Ernest Markham' and 'Polish Spirit' cultivars already bred from it.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Vivid Obedient Plant spreads by underground rhizomes — divide every 2–3 years to prevent aggressive spreading in smaller gardens. The common name 'Obedient Plant' comes from the unusual behavior of the individual flowers: each bloom can be pushed to one side on the flower spike and will stay in its new position ('obediently'), making it interesting for demonstration and a unique cut flower. In zone 9 the late-summer bloom (August–October) aligns with hummingbird migration, making the tubular pink flowers an important nectar source for migrating Ruby-throated Hummingbirds.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Vivid Obedient Plant performs well in partial shade and tolerates the moist, partially shaded conditions along stream banks and pond margins where it naturally grows; Vivid is a compact cultivar of Obedient Plant (Physostegia virginiana), a native eastern North American perennial producing upright, four-angled stems topped with dense, terminal spikes of tubular rose-pink to magenta flowers in late summer and fall. The 'Vivid' selection was chosen for its particularly rich, vivid rose-pink color and compact habit (24–30 inches rather than the 3–5 foot height of the unimproved species), making it much more manageable in garden settings where the species' tendency to flop and spread aggressively is less welcome. The late-season bloom timing of Obedient Plant (August–October in zone 9) is one of its most valuable landscape qualities — providing strong pink color in the native perennial garden at exactly the moment when most spring and summer native perennials have finished blooming and fall asters haven't yet reached peak. As a native species, Physostegia supports native bumblebees, long-tongued bees, and hummingbirds with its abundant nectar.

common_name: Volcano Purple with White Eye Garden Phlox (Highly Mildew-Tolerant Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing generously for airflow; the Volcano series was bred from an Eastern European heirloom line noted for exceptional powdery mildew tolerance, a significant advantage for tall garden phlox in the humid Gulf South.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants generously for good air circulation; this Volcano-series garden phlox produces richly fragrant purple flowers with a crisp white eye, held in dense trusses that can carry over a hundred blooms per stem at peak. The Volcano series was bred from a mildew-tolerant Eastern European heirloom line specifically to overcome the powdery mildew problems that plague many older tall phlox cultivars in hot, humid climates, making it a strong choice for a Gulf South perennial border. Deadhead the central flower cluster once it fades to encourage side-shoot rebloom, and avoid overhead watering to further support disease resistance. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–4 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early spring; the tuber will flower without being planted at all — a bare voodoo lily tuber placed in a pot without soil or water will flower using energy stored in the tuber, then must be planted to develop foliage and replenish energy for the following year.
directions: Plant corms in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; voodoo lily (monarch of the East, red calla) is a South Asian aroid that performs one of the most remarkable botanical tricks available to the home gardener — the large, smooth, gray-mottled, flattened tuber, when stored through winter and brought out in spring, will spontaneously produce a single, dramatic, brownish-maroon, speckled, mottled spathe surrounding a dark-purple-brown, club-like spadix, without any soil or water, powered entirely by energy reserves within the tuber. The flower produces an intensely foul, rotting-meat odor for about 24 hours to attract fly pollinators — a single spectacular performance rather than an extended display. After flowering, plant the tuber in shaded, moist soil, where it produces a single, large, deeply divided, elegantly patterned, dark-green leaf on a mottled stem that provides months of bold tropical foliage. The leaf dies down in fall and the tuber is stored dry through winter. A reliable shade garden conversation piece for zone 6–10, hardy to approximately 0°F when mulched.

common_name: Voodoo Lily (Monarch of the East, Dead Horse Arum, Sacred Lily of India)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring 2–4 inches deep in partial shade in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Typhonium venosum (formerly Sauromatum venosum) is remarkable for its ability to bloom without any soil at all — a dormant tuber placed on a plate at room temperature will produce its spathe and spadix unaided, drawing entirely on stored energy. The inflorescence produces a powerful, unpleasant odor for 1–2 days to attract fly pollinators. After this brief bloom, plant the tuber in soil where it will produce its ornamental, spotted, mottled foliage for the summer. In zone 9+, tubers overwinter in the ground and are very cold tolerant. Non-toxic external contact; ingestion causes irritation.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Voodoo Lily thrives in the same moist, shaded conditions as Amorphophallus and Arisaema and is one of the most cold-hardy of the large ornamental aroid genera, surviving winters well into zone 6 when the tuber is adequately mulched. Typhonium venosum (formerly Sauromatum venosum, often still sold as Sauromatum guttatum) is a tuberous, deciduous, perennial aroid native from East Africa through India, Southeast Asia, and China in the Araceae family — widely grown since Victorian times as a botanical curiosity for its ability to bloom from a bare, soil-less tuber. In spring, a single, exotic inflorescence emerges from the dormant tuber: a large, mottled, maroon-and-green spathe 12–18 inches tall surrounds an erect, dark purplish-maroon spadix with a long, whip-like terminal appendage (up to 12 inches). For 1–2 days, the inflorescence produces a powerful, fetid odor mimicking rotting flesh to attract the blowflies and carrion beetles that pollinate it — after which the odor dissipates entirely. Following this bloom, the tuber should be planted in soil, where it produces the handsome summer foliage: a single, large, dramatically divided, deeply lobed, mottled leaf on a spotted petiole that is quite ornamental in a shaded setting. A strange and fascinating botanical specimen with genuine garden presence in tropical and subtropical shade gardens. The tubers multiply steadily over time. Irritating if ingested; keep from pets and children.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Voodoo is among the darkest-colored of the creeping stonecrops, holding deep burgundy-red foliage color all season rather than just in cool weather.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; standing winter moisture, not cold, is what kills this drought-proof succulent groundcover. Voodoo forms a dense, low mat of tiny, fleshy, deep burgundy-red leaves that hold their rich color through the growing season and intensify further in cool fall weather, topped in summer by flat clusters of small, star-shaped pink flowers that draw bees and small butterflies. Its low, spreading habit fills rock garden pockets, green roof plantings, and hot, dry slopes where little else thrives, tolerating poor, gravelly soil and reflected heat from pavement without complaint. It needs essentially no maintenance beyond an occasional trim to keep it within bounds and division every several years if a mat becomes bare in the center.

plant_note: Plant tubers 1–2 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade after frost; voodoo taro emerges rapidly once soil temperatures warm above 65°F — if tubers are planted when the soil is still cool, they will rot rather than sprout. The inflorescence, which emerges before or simultaneously with the leaves, has a pungent, unpleasant odor that is brief and fades once pollination is complete.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; voodoo taro (red stem taro) is a tropical aroid native to South and Southeast Asia with an unusual combination of ornamental foliage and jack-in-the-pulpit-style flowers — the deeply three-lobed, triangular, arrow-shaped, rich dark-green leaves are held on erect, slender, attractively mottled, dark-green and purple petioles and are prominently veined, creating a bold, tropical texture in the shade garden. Before or alongside the foliage, the plant produces a distinctive inflorescence: a narrow, dark-maroon to green spathe surrounding a long, filiform, deep-purple, tail-like appendage at the tip of the spadix, with a brief but pungent, carrion-like scent that attracts fly pollinators (the characteristic pollination strategy of many Araceae). After pollination, clusters of bright-red berries form on the lower portion of the spadix and remain ornamental for several weeks. The plant goes dormant in winter and reemerges in spring when soils warm. An unusual and interesting shade-garden aroid for collectors and those who appreciate the quirky botanical spectacle of carrion-scented, fly-pollinated tropical plants in zone 9–12.

common_name: Vulcan Hibiscus (Large Ruffled Deep Red Tropical Hibiscus)
plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Vulcan bears exceptionally large, deeply ruffled deep red flowers on a vigorous tropical hibiscus shrub.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Vulcan bears exceptionally large, deeply ruffled single flowers in an intense, saturated deep red, among the boldest and most substantial blooms of any commonly grown tropical hibiscus cultivar, opening a striking focal point in the garden even though, as with all hibiscus, each flower lasts only a single day. A well-grown plant produces a steady succession of new buds for continuous color from spring through frost in warm climates. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season.

common_name: Vyvyan Pennell Clematis (Double Violet-Blue Early-Season Clematis)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Vyvyan Pennell produces double flowers on old wood in late spring and single flowers on new growth later in the season.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Vyvyan Pennell is unusual for producing two distinct flower forms in a single season: fully double, violet-blue rosette-like blooms from old wood in late spring, followed by simpler single flowers in a similar color on new growth later in summer. This dual bloom pattern means pruning strategy matters more than with most clematis, so limit spring pruning to dead or weak stems in order to preserve the spectacular early double display. Its extended, two-phase bloom season has made it a favorite among clematis collectors.

common_name: Wabash Bearded Iris (Historic Dykes Medal Amoena Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Wabash won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1940 and remains a garden-worthy heirloom bicolor.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Introduced in 1936 and awarded the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1940, Wabash is a classic amoena-type bearded iris pairing crisp white standards with deep violet-purple falls, a striking two-tone combination that made it one of the most influential parents in mid-20th-century iris breeding. The sturdy stems hold their large ruffled blooms well above the fan of foliage in mid-spring, and established clumps multiply steadily, benefiting from division every three to four years to keep bloom quality high. Good drainage is essential, since soggy soil quickly leads to rhizome rot.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings well after last frost into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wagner's sage is a large, understory Central American salvia more cold-sensitive than most other tender sages and needs a sheltered site at the cold edge of its zone range.
directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wagner's sage is a large, coarse-textured Central American salvia with broad, bold leaves and dramatic winter to early-spring flower spikes wrapped in showy, rose-pink to mauve bracts that persist attractively even as the small white and pink flowers inside them fade. Its understory origin in humid mountain forests makes it more tolerant of shade and humidity than many other tender salvias, and it performs best with protection from hot, direct afternoon sun and from drying wind. Because it is among the more cold-sensitive of the commonly grown tender sages, plant it in a sheltered microclimate in zone 9, and expect significant dieback or loss in a hard freeze without heavy mulching over the crown. Where winter cold is a concern, growing a potted specimen that can be moved under cover is a safer option than relying on in-ground survival.

common_name: Wagnerianus Windmill Palm (Compact Stiff-Leaved Windmill Palm)
subcategory: cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Wagnerianus is a smaller, stiffer-leaved variety of windmill palm with notably better wind tolerance than the species, since its shorter, tougher fronds resist tearing and shredding in storms.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade. Wagnerianus is a compact variety of windmill palm bearing smaller, stiffer, more rigid fan fronds than the species form, a trait that makes it noticeably more resistant to wind damage and shredding in storms, a real advantage along the Gulf Coast where tropical storm winds are a regular hazard for broad-leaved palms. It shares the species' excellent cold hardiness, tolerating temperatures into the single digits Fahrenheit once established, and its smaller, tidier crown fits narrower planting spaces than the standard windmill palm. Water regularly while establishing, then reduce to occasional deep watering during dry spells, and remove old, dead fronds as they brown to keep the trunk tidy.

common_name: Waikiki Elephant Ear (Green Leaf with Dark Maroon Center Blotch)
plant_note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; Waikiki, part of the Royal Hawaiian series, bears green leaves with a dramatic dark maroon-burgundy center blotch, tolerating partial shade to shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9. Waikiki, part of the Royal Hawaiian elephant ear series, bears bright green leaves marked with a dramatic dark maroon-burgundy blotch radiating from the center, a bold two-tone pattern that makes a strong focal point in a shaded bog garden or large container. The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every two to three years to control spread. Provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions, as elephant ear grows naturally along streamsides and in boggy areas.

common_name: Waithman Beauty Dianthus (Ruby-Red Marked with Pink-White Lacing)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Waithman Beauty bears ruby-red to dark magenta-maroon flowers marked with pale pink-white lacing, sweetly clove-scented.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Waithman Beauty bears deep ruby-red to dark magenta-maroon flowers finely marked with pale pink-white lacing, a rich, dramatic laced pattern on a strongly clove-scented old-style garden pink, opening over compact, evergreen blue-green foliage. Its dark, jewel-toned color makes a bold accent at the front of a sunny border. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Wakaebisu is a classic Satsuki azalea especially popular as a bonsai subject in Japan.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Wakaebisu bears salmon-pink flowers on a low, spreading Satsuki azalea prized in Japan as one of the classic cultivars for bonsai training, valued for its tolerance of the repeated root and branch pruning that bonsai technique requires as much as for its late-spring bloom. Grown as a garden shrub rather than trained as bonsai, it forms a dense, low mound similar to other Satsuki types, blooming weeks after Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas have finished. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil; this hybrid is sterile and increased only by division.
directions: 'Waldenbuch' is a looser, more arching alternative to the ubiquitous 'Karl Foerster' feather reed grass, forming a tight clump of deep green foliage beneath softly nodding flower stems. The plumes emerge silvery green in midsummer and mature to a golden tan, standing well into winter before they shatter, while the foliage turns light yellow in fall. Choose this cultivar where a slightly more relaxed, less rigid silhouette is wanted than the stiffly vertical 'Karl Foerster'. It tolerates heavy clay and part shade better than many ornamental grasses, and needs only a hard cutback in late winter.

plant_note: Hang bare-root in a slatted teak or wire basket with little to no medium so the thick aerial roots dry quickly after watering; Vanda sanderiana is a lowland Philippine species that needs very bright light, warm year-round temperatures, and high humidity, and it is now rare in the wild, so only nursery-propagated stock should be acquired.
directions: Provide very bright light and strong air movement around the exposed roots, watering or misting the root mass thoroughly once or twice daily in warm weather and allowing it to dry within a few hours to prevent rot. Known as Waling-Waling and closely associated with Davao in the southern Philippines, Vanda sanderiana bears some of the largest, flattest flowers in the genus — 4 to 6 inches across, with the upper half of the flower rose-pink and the lower half warm tawny-brown overlaid with fine reddish tessellation. Established, well-grown plants can flower more than once a year given consistently warm temperatures and high humidity. This species has been extensively used in hybridizing large-flowered, brightly patterned Vanda and Ascocenda hybrids and remains one of the most historically important species in Vanda breeding.

common_name: Walker's Cattleya (Miniature Cattleya, Compact Walkeriana Orchid)
plant_note: Mount small divisions on a cork or tree-fern slab, or pot loosely in coarse bark in a small clay pot, so roots dry quickly between waterings; Cattleya walkeriana is a compact, rock- and tree-dwelling Brazilian species that stays under 8 inches tall, making it one of the few full-sized-flowered Cattleyas suited to a bright windowsill rather than a greenhouse bench.
directions: Grow in bright, filtered light similar to other Cattleyas — a lightly shaded south or unobstructed east window — and allow the small pseudobulbs to dry noticeably between waterings. Cattleya walkeriana, native to rocky outcrops and tree branches in Minas Gerais and Goiás, Brazil, is unusual among Cattleyas for its miniature stature paired with large, intensely fragrant, 3–4-inch lavender-pink to white flowers that open from the base of a new growth before or as the single leaf fully expands. Give a brief, cooler, drier rest in late winter after growths mature to encourage the following season's flower buds, then resume regular watering as new roots appear in spring. Its compact size and outsized, fragrant blooms have made it one of the most sought-after species for breeding smaller, windowsill-friendly Cattleya hybrids.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Walker's Low requires excellent drainage and lean soil — in rich, moist soil the stems become floppy and the plant loses its characteristic compact mounding form.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Walker's Low is the most celebrated catmint cultivar — named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2007 and consistently one of the top-rated perennials in American horticulture for its outstanding combination of compact mounding habit, long bloom season, aromatic silver-gray foliage, and abundant lavender-blue flower production. Despite the name 'Low,' Walker's Low is actually a relatively large catmint reaching 18–24 inches tall with a 24–36 inch spread — the name refers to the garden in Northern Ireland where it was discovered. The characteristic mounding habit, covered from late May through July in zone 9 with dense spikes of lavender-blue flowers, creates one of the most effective mass-planting perennials available for full-sun, dry borders. After the main bloom flush, cut the entire plant back by half — this stimulates vigorous fresh growth and typically produces a substantial second bloom in late summer. The aromatic, silver-gray, textured foliage is attractive when not in flower. Walker's Low is extremely drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free in well-drained soil. In zone 9, it performs best in zones 4–8 — in the hottest parts of zone 9, summer heat and humidity can stress the plant, but with excellent drainage and lean soil it often persists successfully.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Walker's Low is sterile and mildly aromatic, discouraging deer and rabbits while drawing bees in large numbers, and shearing it back hard after the first flush produces a strong rebloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Named Perennial Plant of the Year in 2007, Walker's Low forms a broad, billowing mound of soft gray-green, aromatic foliage topped with airy spikes of lavender-blue flowers over an exceptionally long bloom season from late spring into fall. Despite its name it grows considerably taller and wider than the name suggests, and shearing the whole plant back by about a third after the first big flush of bloom keeps it tidy and triggers vigorous reflowering. It is highly drought-tolerant once established, rarely troubled by deer or rabbits thanks to its pungent foliage, and one of the most reliable long-season bee and pollinator plants for a sunny border edge.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Walker's Low is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established — it performs best in lean soils and declines rapidly in heavy, wet clay without amendment and drainage improvement.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Walker's Low is the Perennial Plant Association's 2007 Plant of the Year and one of the most reliable, versatile, and long-blooming perennials available for the full-sun border — producing a continuous display of small, tubular, lavender-blue flowers in dense whorls along arching stems from May through September (with shearing after the first main flush to stimulate repeat bloom). The aromatic gray-green foliage emits a pleasant minty-catmint fragrance when brushed or disturbed — similar to the scent of catnip, though Walker's Low is far less potent to cats than true catnip (Nepeta cataria). The mounding, gently arching form with a soft, hazy, lavender cloud effect is one of the most effective and widely used planting combinations in contemporary perennial garden design: Walker's Low paired with ornamental grasses, roses, and Russian sage creates a classic soft-textured, long-season color composition. Walker's Low is highly attractive to pollinators — bees of many species, hummingbirds, and butterflies visit constantly during the long bloom season. Shear to 6 inches after the main late-spring flush to stimulate dense new growth and a strong repeat bloom in late summer. In zone 9, plant in well-drained soil — Walker's Low will not tolerate standing water or consistently wet soil in the Gulf South summer heat.

plant_note: Plant divisions or transplants in moist, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous (limestone-based), humus-rich, very well-drained soil in deep shade; walking fern is highly specific in its substrate requirements — it grows naturally on shaded, moist, mossy limestone and calcareous rocks and will not thrive in acidic or poorly-drained soils.
directions: Plant in moist, calcareous, humus-rich, very well-drained soil on shaded limestone surfaces, moss-covered rocks, or alkaline woodland beds in deep shade — walking fern is a unique and fascinating native fern of the eastern US, producing long, narrow, tapering fronds with heart-shaped bases that extend to 12–18 inches and root at their tips wherever they contact moist substrate, slowly 'walking' outward to colonize a shaded limestone outcrop or mossy rock wall. The entire plant is distinctive and easily recognized: its uncut, lance-shaped fronds bear no resemblance to typical fernlike foliage. It is strictly associated with shaded, moist, mossy limestone and calcareous rock faces in the eastern deciduous forest, growing in deep shade of overhanging cliffs, ravine walls, and shaded limestone boulders. It is an outstanding plant for the specialized shaded rock garden with limestone substrate, adding a uniquely charming and ecologically interesting element to native wildflower rock gardens.

plant_note: Divide clumps or detach and pot the plantlets that form at the flower-stalk tips, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; walking iris is one of the finest and most reliable shade-tolerant flowering perennials for zone 9–12 and blooms intermittently throughout the warm season in quite deep shade conditions.
directions: Divide clumps or pot up rooted plantlets from stem tips in moist, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; walking iris (Apostle Plant) is a Brazilian tropical evergreen perennial of the iris family (Iridaceae) that is one of the most valuable and widely used shade-tolerant flowering plants for Gulf Coast and tropical gardens — producing beautiful, iris-like, white flowers with purple and brown markings on upright, flat, sword-like stems that resemble those of a large iris, blooming intermittently through the warm season in partial to full shade conditions. The common name 'walking iris' refers to the plant's ingenious self-propagating method: after flowering, the flower stalk bends under the weight of a new plantlet (a miniature plant complete with leaves and roots) that forms at the stalk tip and, when the stalk touches the ground, the plantlet roots in and starts a new plant — 'walking' the colony progressively outward from the parent. This gives it the ability to spread and colonize shade garden areas without any gardener intervention. An excellent, easy-to-grow, and self-spreading shade groundcover for zone 9–12 tropical shade gardens. Blooms most freely with about 13 leaves present — hence 'Apostle Plant'.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; walking iris tolerates a range of light conditions but performs best and blooms most freely in bright filtered shade. In zone 9 it may be damaged by hard freezes but regrows vigorously from established rhizomes.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; walking iris (Neomarica gracilis) takes its name from its fascinating method of reproduction: after the short-lived fragrant iris-like flowers (white with blue and brown markings) appear at the tip of a fan-shaped leaf stalk, plantlets form at the same tip and the stalk bends under their weight until the plantlets touch the ground and root — 'walking' the plant outward from the mother clump. The tropical-looking, fan-shaped clumps of stiff, flat, strap-like leaves grow in dense stands that are ornamental year-round. The flowers appear several times through the warm season, each lasting only a day but produced in succession over weeks. Also called the 'apostle plant' because the original observation was that each stalk must produce 12 leaves (one for each apostle) before flowering — an observation that is approximately correct for mature stalks. An outstanding low-maintenance shade plant for zone 9–12 that naturalized easily in humid, subtropical gardens.

plant_note: Sow on the soil surface in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun to part shade; wall bellflower is a natural crevice plant and thrives in gaps between paving stones, in dry stone walls, and in rock garden crevices where perfect drainage around the crown prevents winter rotting. Less spreading than C. poscharskyana.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; wall bellflower is a compact, neat, semi-evergreen perennial from rocky cliff faces of Dalmatia, Croatia, producing masses of rich, deep blue-purple, bell-shaped flowers in June and July above a carpet of small, dark-green, heart-shaped, slightly toothed leaves. More compact and more neatly behaved than its relative C. poscharskyana, it is particularly outstanding for planting in the crevices of dry stone walls and between paving stones, where its natural cliff-dwelling habit is replicated and perfect drainage around the crown prevents the crown rot that afflicts it in heavy soils. The dark, saturated blue-purple of the flowers is notably rich compared to the lighter lavender of C. poscharskyana. Semi-evergreen to evergreen in mild winters. One of the standard reliable perennials for rock gardens, wall crevices, and alpine troughs, performing best in thin, lean soils where better-fed companions would outcompete it.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in shade to part shade; Wallich's wood fern is slow to establish but extremely long-lived once settled. The emerging croziers (fiddleheads) are strikingly covered with jet-black or dark-brown scales, creating a dramatic spring display before the fronds unfurl.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full to part shade; Wallich's wood fern is one of the most architecturally spectacular hardy ferns available, producing an upright, vase-shaped shuttlecock of long, elegant, yellow-green to deep-green fronds with prominent dark midribs and distinctive black to dark-brown scales on the rachis (midrib) that remain visible and ornamental throughout the growing season. The emerging croziers in spring are covered with striking jet-black scales, creating a dramatic architectural display weeks before the fronds unfurl. Each frond can reach 3–4 feet in length, forming bold clumps of impressive visual impact in the shade garden. Unlike many decorative ferns, it is also surprisingly tolerant of dry conditions once established, making it useful under trees where other ferns struggle. Native to mountain woodlands from the Himalayas to Japan and Africa.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Reifler's Dwarf is a compact selection (4–6 feet) compared to the species which can reach 15–18 feet, making it manageable for landscape use. Walter viburnum grows naturally in wet to moist, often flooded, acidic soils along stream banks and wetland margins throughout the coastal plain — it is one of the most flood-tolerant ornamental shrubs available. Cross-pollination with another Walter viburnum or selection is needed for berry production; plant two or more specimens for fruit.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, acidic to slightly acidic soil — Walter viburnum naturally grows in the wet, acidic soils of coastal plain wetlands and is highly tolerant of flooding and poor drainage; Reifler's Dwarf is a compact cultivar of Walter Viburnum (Viburnum obovatum), a native Florida and Gulf Coast evergreen viburnum that provides exceptional ecological value as a wildlife food source while offering ornamental merit in difficult, wet, or shaded landscape conditions. The small, rounded, dark green leaves and compact habit create a dense, fine-textured evergreen shrub suitable for hedging, screening, and naturalistic plantings in the challenging moist-to-wet soil conditions where many landscape plants struggle. In late winter and early spring (February–March), Walter viburnum produces flat clusters of small white flowers that attract early-season pollinators before most other landscape shrubs begin blooming. The small, red-to-black fruits that mature in summer are eaten by dozens of bird species — making Walter viburnum a high-value wildlife plant for zone 9 landscapes designed to support native birds. The native provenance means Walter viburnum is adapted to the exact soil, climate, and pest pressures of the Gulf South without the cultural challenges of introduced alternatives.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in moist to wet, well-drained to poorly drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Walter viburnum is one of the most versatile and tough native Florida and Gulf Coast shrubs, thriving in both wet and dry soils and performing well from full sun to part shade.
directions: Plant in moist to wet or well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Walter viburnum tolerates flooding, drought, clay, and sand — one of the most site-adaptable native shrubs for Florida and the Gulf Coast. Viburnum obovatum is a native Florida and Gulf Coast viburnum with small, leathery, dark-green, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves that give the plant a fine texture uncommon among viburnums; flat-topped, 2-to-3-inch clusters of small white flowers appear in February–March and are followed by red berries that ripen to black, providing outstanding value for songbirds including thrushes, mockingbirds, and waxwings through winter. The shrub ranges from 3–12 feet tall depending on conditions — compact in dry, sunny sites and larger in moist, shaded conditions — and responds well to pruning into a dense hedge or wildlife planting. The cultivar 'Mrs. Schiller's Delight' is a compact, 3–4 foot selection with proportionally small leaves, ideal for residential gardens. Walter viburnum is native to wet flatwoods, swamp margins, and stream banks from Virginia to Florida and is an outstanding choice for rain gardens, wet spots, and bird gardens in zones 7–10.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in average, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Walter's aster is a Southeastern coastal plain native that blooms notably late in the season, well after many other native asters have finished.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Walter's aster is a Southeastern coastal plain native perennial found naturally in open pine woods, savannas, and woodland edges from the Carolinas to the Gulf Coast, producing wiry, well-branched stems studded with small, pale lavender-to-white ray flowers and yellow centers. Its standout feature is bloom timing — flowering runs from late summer into late fall, often continuing later into the season than many other native asters, making it a valuable late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and the last generations of native bees active before winter. Plants are airy and gracefully branched rather than dense, working well threaded through a mixed native border or naturalized under high pine canopy where its light shade tolerance suits it well. It tolerates the sandy, well-drained soils typical of the coastal plain and needs only routine moisture, without the wet, boggy conditions some other native asters prefer. Cut back by about a third in early summer to encourage bushier growth and more abundant fall bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Walter's dogwood is an underused Chinese species valued for its strong trunk character, reliable flowering, and excellent drought tolerance once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Walter's dogwood is a large shrub or small tree from central and northern China distinguished among dogwoods by its striking deeply furrowed, interlacing bark — among the most dramatically textured trunks of any dogwood — and by notable drought tolerance once established. The flat-topped clusters of small, creamy-white flowers in early summer are followed by blue-black berries consumed by birds. Like other Cornelian-cherry relatives, the fall color is an attractive red-purple. Significantly more drought and heat tolerant than flowering dogwood (C. florida) and less susceptible to dogwood anthracnose, making it a more durable choice for Southern gardens in zones 7–9 where C. florida often struggles. An underused specimen tree that deserves wider planting for its ornamental bark and adaptability.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Walter's viburnum tolerates both wet, low sites and drier upland soils once established, and takes shearing well when grown as a formal hedge.
directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; adaptable to both periodically wet and average garden soils, and tolerates shearing into a formal hedge as well as being left to grow into a graceful large natural shrub or small tree. Viburnum obovatum (Walter's viburnum) is a native evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub of wetland margins, stream banks, and hammocks across the Gulf South and Florida, distinguished from other native viburnums by its small, glossy, finely textured leaves that give it a refined, boxwood-like appearance even without pruning. In late winter to early spring, the branches are covered in small, fragrant, white flower clusters that draw abundant pollinators, followed by small red fruits that ripen to black and are readily eaten by songbirds. Its fine texture, evergreen habit, and tolerance of both hedge shearing and natural form make it one of the most versatile native shrubs for a Gulf South screen, hedge, or woodland-edge planting, zone 7–9.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; Walter's violet spreads by stolons to form a creeping ground cover mat in shaded woodland settings — one of the most shade-tolerant native violets.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Walter's violet is a low-growing, creeping native violet of the southeastern Coastal Plain woodland understory, spreading by above-ground stolons to form a dense, attractive mat of small, rounded, mottled-silver leaves. The leaves often have attractive silver or grayish variegation that makes the plant ornamentally distinguished even when not in flower. The small, lavender-blue to pale violet flowers in spring are charming on close inspection. As a creeping, rhizomatous violet, it is one of the most effective native alternatives to invasive ground covers for shaded, moist woodland floors in zone 9a. The larvae of numerous fritillary butterfly species use native violets as their host plant — including the variegated fritillary, gulf fritillary, and great spangled fritillary.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Walther Funcke holds an intense brick orange-red color longer than many warm-colored yarrow cultivars before fading.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential, as this drought-loving perennial declines quickly in heavy, wet soil. Walther Funcke bears intensely colored, brick orange-red flower clusters that hold their saturated color longer into the season than many similarly toned yarrow cultivars before gradually softening toward copper and gold, set above finely cut, gray-green aromatic foliage from early summer into fall. Its rich, warm color pairs especially well with blue salvias, catmints, and ornamental grasses in a sunny mixed border. Deadhead spent flower heads to encourage continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous, since older yarrow clumps can become woody and open in the center.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in wet to moist, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; wand goldenrod is a wetland-affiliated species of the Gulf Coastal Plain that prefers seasonally saturated sites — it thrives in moist pine flatwoods, wet savannas, and pond margins.
directions: Wand goldenrod is a native goldenrod of the Gulf Coastal Plain's seasonally wet habitats — wet pine flatwoods, boggy depressions, and moist savannas from New Jersey to Texas — producing upright, unbranched or sparsely branched stems with small basal leaves and terminal wand-like flower spikes of golden yellow that are distinctive among goldenrods for their narrow, column-like form rather than the typical arching plume. Because it grows naturally in wet, acidic, sandy soils — habitats shared with pitcher plants, sundews, and rare orchids in Gulf Coast longleaf pine country — it is an appropriate companion plant for native bog gardens, seepage slopes, and the moist margins of rain gardens in the Deep South. The late-summer to fall bloom coincides with peak monarch migration and provides a critical nectar source for southbound monarchs; native bees are also heavily attracted to the dense, accessible flower clusters. In Gulf Coast flatwoods restorations, wand goldenrod is a keystone species of the low pine savanna ground layer.

plant_note: Root 3–4 inch stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix; cuttings root in 1–2 weeks and can be transplanted to beds or containers. In zone 9–11, establish in spring for summer groundcover coverage. Keep soil moist and provide light shade to partial shade for best foliage color.
directions: Root cuttings in water and transplant to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Tradescantia zebrina (wandering jew) is one of the fastest-spreading and most colorful of all tropical groundcovers for shaded areas, producing a mat of trailing stems with striking elliptical leaves in deep green and silver stripes with brilliant purple undersides — the tricolor effect is particularly vivid in good light. Small pink-purple three-petaled flowers are produced nearly year-round. In zone 9–11 it spreads freely as a low groundcover under trees and in shaded planting beds, rooting wherever stems touch moist soil; it can be aggressive and should be kept away from natural areas. For containers, the trailing stems are beautiful in hanging baskets on covered porches. The contact sap may cause contact dermatitis in some people; handle with caution. Easy to propagate from cuttings and nearly impossible to kill.

common_name: Ward's Ruby Azalea (Compact Dark Red Kurume Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ward's Ruby is a slow-growing, compact Kurume azalea valued for its very dark red flowers and good cold hardiness to zone 8.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Ward's Ruby is a slow-growing, compact Kurume azalea bearing very dark, saturated red flowers in a dense spring flush, its small mature size making it especially useful for foundation plantings, rock gardens, and smaller borders where larger Southern Indica cultivars would not fit. Its good cold hardiness and manageable size have kept it a reliable, long-favored selection among compact red azaleas. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Warley barrenwort is a vigorous hybrid grown for its coppery-orange spring flowers set against semi-evergreen, spiny-edged foliage.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, then cut back old foliage in late winter before new flower spikes emerge. Epimedium x warleyense is a robust hybrid named for the historic Warley Place garden in England, valued for its unusual coppery-orange, yellow-centered flowers that appear in loose sprays above bronze-tinted new foliage in spring. It is more vigorous and sun-tolerant than many epimedium species, spreading steadily by rhizome to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under trees and shrubs. Its warm flower color pairs well with the more common yellow and white epimediums for extended seasonal contrast in a shaded border.

common_name: Warren's Red Possumhaw Holly (Heavy-Fruiting Female Deciduous Holly for Winter Bird Food)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Warren's Red is a heavy-fruiting female selection of native deciduous holly, its persistent red berries a critical winter food source for cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds. Plant a male pollinator within range for fruit set.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a male possumhaw within range for pollination, since hollies are dioecious and only fertilized female plants produce berries. Warren's Red is one of the most widely planted and heaviest-fruiting selections of native possumhaw, or deciduous holly, dropping its leaves each fall to reveal branches absolutely laden with small, bright red berries that persist through much of winter, a dramatic and highly ornamental display in the bare-branch season when few other plants offer color. Those berries are a critical late-winter food source for cedar waxwings, American robins, mockingbirds, and other fruit-eating birds, often stripped in a single flock visit once fully softened by cold. It tolerates a wide range of soils, including seasonally wet sites, and needs little maintenance once established. Prune to shape immediately after the fruit display fades, if needed.

common_name: Warszawska Nike Clematis (Velvety Reddish-Purple with Silver Reverse)
plant_note: Plant with the crown a couple of inches below soil level, shading the root zone while the vine climbs a trellis, arbor, or fence into full sun; Warszawska Nike, a Polish-bred Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit cultivar, bears velvety reddish-purple flowers with silvery undersides.
directions: Bred in Poland and holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, Warszawska Nike bears large, velvety, deep reddish-purple flowers with silvery-mauve undersides and bright yellow stamens, opening from early summer through fall on a vigorous, free-flowering vine. Its rich, saturated color and long bloom season have made it one of the most widely planted purple large-flowered clematis cultivars worldwide. As with other clematis, keep the roots cool and shaded (mulch or low companion planting works well) while the vine itself grows into full sun, and prune according to its bloom group for the best flowering.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Warszewicz's philodendron is a self-heading (non-climbing) species that needs no moss pole or trellis.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Warszewicz's philodendron is a self-heading (non-climbing) species that needs no moss pole or trellis. Deeply pinnately lobed leaves resemble an oak leaf blown up to dramatic scale, with narrow, finger-like divisions radiating from a strong central rib, giving this Central American species a bold, sculptural silhouette distinct from the smoother, heart-shaped leaves of many common philodendrons. Its non-vining, upright rosette habit stays compact and self-supporting even as leaves grow quite large, making it a striking floor or tabletop specimen without the need for a climbing support. Provide bright indirect light for the best leaf division and size, wipe dust from the deeply cut leaves periodically, and water when the top inch of potting mix has dried.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Wasabi is a vigorous, sun-tolerant coleus cultivar with bright chartreuse-green, deeply ruffled and jagged-edged leaves, providing bold color contrast in both sun and shade plantings.
directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Wasabi is a widely grown, vigorous coleus cultivar bred for improved sun tolerance, distinguished by large, brilliantly chartreuse-green leaves with deeply cut, ruffled, almost oak-leaf-like edges. Its intensely bright, almost glowing chartreuse color makes it an outstanding accent against darker-foliaged companions in both container plantings and garden beds, and the bold, ruffled leaf texture adds visual interest beyond color alone. Like other modern sun coleus, Wasabi handles considerably more direct sun than older shade-only coleus varieties, though the color is often most vivid with some afternoon shade in the hottest climates. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear, since coleus flowers are insignificant and pinching redirects the plant's energy into larger, more colorful foliage and a fuller, more branched habit. In zone 9's long warm season, Wasabi can grow into a large, impressive specimen by late summer.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in average, adaptable soil in full sun; Washington hawthorn tolerates a wide range of soils including alkaline, clay, and occasionally wet conditions — one of the most urban-tough of all native hawthorns.
directions: Washington hawthorn is the most widely planted of all native North American hawthorns in cultivation — an exceptionally ornamental small tree with multiple seasons of interest: dense clusters of white flowers in May, glossy, deeply lobed leaves turning orange-red in fall, and abundant clusters of small bright red fruits that persist into winter. It is one of the highest-value wildlife trees available for the eastern garden: at least 20 species of birds consume the fruits, including cedar waxwings, robins, and bluebirds; the dense, thorny structure (1–3 inch curved thorns) provides nesting habitat for catbirds, thrashers, and kingbirds; and over 150 species of Lepidoptera use native Crataegus as larval host plants. Washington hawthorn adapts to urban conditions including soil compaction, air pollution, and alkaline pH better than most native landscape trees, making it suitable for street planting, parking lots, and urban parks where native trees are rarely successful. A top choice for combining year-round ornamental interest with maximum wildlife value in limited space.

common_name: Watch Chain Crassula (Rattail Crassula, Zipper Plant)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; watch chain crassula stores water in its tightly packed leaves and rots quickly if left in soggy soil.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; watch chain crassula stores water in its tightly packed leaves and rots quickly if left in soggy soil. Tiny, scale-like, bright to yellow-green leaves are stacked in four tight, overlapping columns along thin, upright-then-trailing stems, giving each stem the look of a braided cord, zipper, or chain of tiny watch links, an unusual, almost architectural texture unlike typical rounded succulent leaves. Native to dry regions of southern Africa, it is easy and fast-growing, tolerating bright light, drought, and general neglect, and it branches and spreads readily to fill a container or rock garden pocket with its distinctive braided stems. Water only when the soil is fully dry, propagate easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus before potting, and provide bright light to keep growth compact rather than stretched.

common_name: Watchet Azalea (Large Pale Pink Dark-Blotched Robin Hill Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Watchet is a Robin Hill azalea with unusually large, dark-blotched pale pink flowers on a spreading habit.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Watchet bears unusually large, pale pink flowers marked with a bold, dark blotch, opening on a low, wide-spreading Robin Hill azalea bred for large flower size on a compact, cold-hardy plant. Its spreading habit suits it to underplanting taller shrubs or massing as a flowering groundcover in dappled shade. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring at the shallow margins of a wildlife pond or bog, setting the rhizome horizontally just below the water surface or in permanently saturated soil.
directions: Position rhizome divisions horizontally at the boggy margins of a pond or slow-moving stream, with the rhizome just at or barely below the waterline and roots anchored in mud. Small white spathes reminiscent of miniature calla lilies appear in late spring and early summer, followed by tightly clustered bright red berries that are highly attractive to wildlife. This circumpolar native spreads gradually by rhizome, slowly colonizing suitable wet margins without becoming invasive in cold-climate gardens. It thrives in the coldest zones where many aquatic ornamentals cannot survive, making it invaluable for northern and mountain water gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow winter cold stratification to break dormancy naturally. Seeds will germinate the following spring. Moist, rich soil in partial shade gives best results.
directions: Sow seeds directly in fall into a prepared bed of moist, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded location. Cold winter temperatures naturally stratify the seeds so they sprout reliably in spring without pre-treatment. Water avens thrives at the edges of woodland ponds, along shaded stream banks, or in rain gardens where soil moisture stays consistently high. The nodding, dusky rose flowers appear in late spring and the decorative feathery seed heads extend the ornamental interest well into summer.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring or plant container specimens in wet to moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil or submerged in a water feature; water canna tolerates standing water up to 6 inches deep and can be grown in containers submerged in garden ponds — it is one of the few cannas that actually thrives in permanently flooded conditions and can be treated as an aquatic plant in shallow ponds and water features.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in wet to moist, humus-rich, fertile soil or in shallow water in full sun to partial shade; water canna (Louisiana canna) is a wetland and aquatic canna native to South America and the Caribbean, growing naturally at the edges of streams and ponds and in shallow standing water — it differs from garden hybrid cannas in its distinctively narrow, lance-shaped, blue-green to gray-green, powdery-glaucous foliage (the species name 'glauca' refers to this gray-blue waxy leaf bloom) and its slender, elegant, pale-to-deep yellow, narrow-petaled flowers that are considerably more graceful and refined than the large-flowered hybrid cannas. Unlike garden hybrid cannas, water canna tolerates permanently boggy, saturated, or even inundated soils and can be grown in containers standing in several inches of water in garden ponds and water features. It is also more shade-tolerant than hybrid cannas, performing creditably in partial shade. It is one parent of the heat-tolerant Louisiana hybrid aquatic cannas, which inherit its moisture-tolerance. Hardy to approximately 10°F in zone 7 with roots protected by water or mulch.

plant_note: Plant rooted runners in shallow aquatic pots of loam so the clover-like leaflets can either float on the surface or stand just above shallow water.
directions: This low-growing aquatic fern produces distinctive four-leaflet fronds resembling a four-leaf clover and spreads by creeping rhizomes across mud or shallow water at the pond margin. Plant divisions in submerged or bog-margin containers of heavy soil, and trim back runners regularly since it forms a dense mat that can overtake open water in mild climates. It is a useful low, textural contrast plant next to taller marginals like pickerelweed or Louisiana iris, and dies back to a hardy rhizome that survives freezing in the pond mud.

plant_note: Sow seed in fall directly into consistently wet to seasonally flooded, acidic, sandy soil along pond edges, ditches, and pine savanna wetlands, since it germinates poorly without a season of natural cold-moist stratification.
directions: Sow seed in fall directly into consistently wet to seasonally flooded, acidic, sandy soil along pond edges, ditches, and pine savanna wetlands, since it germinates poorly without a season of natural cold-moist stratification. Slender, nearly leafless hollow stems rise from a cluster of thin basal leaflets and open into flat white umbels of tiny flowers in late summer, resembling a delicate wild carrot relative built for standing water. As a member of the carrot family it is an important larval host plant for black swallowtail butterflies in wetland habitats, and its late flowers also draw small native bees, wasps, and flies. Keep the root zone wet through the growing season; it is not suited to average garden beds that dry out between waterings.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors after cold-moist stratification of 4-6 weeks; transplant into permanently moist or wet soil in spring once seedlings are well established.
directions: Water Eryngo is a tall, robust native perennial of coastal plain marshes, wet pine savannas, and stream borders, producing rounded, thimble-like blue-gray flower heads on strongly upright, branching stems in late summer. It develops a deep taproot that makes established plants difficult to transplant, so choose the permanent planting site carefully and provide consistently wet, full-sun conditions from the start. Seeds benefit from a cold-moist stratification period before sowing, and young transplants should be kept well watered during their first season. This species also serves as a larval host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly, adding significant wildlife value to rain gardens and native wetland plantings.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown aquatic plants in consistently wet, mucky, or submerged (up to 4 inches deep) soil in part shade to full sun; water forget-me-not is a true aquatic perennial that thrives at pond edges, in bog gardens, and in shallow water — quite different from the common woodland forget-me-not (M. sylvatica) which is a dry-garden annual. It spreads to form attractive floating mats in shallow water.
directions: Plant in consistently wet, boggy, or shallow-water conditions in part shade to full sun; water forget-me-not is the aquatic, perennial member of the forget-me-not genus — a genuine wetland native that grows naturally at pond and stream margins, in bogs, and with stems and bases submerged in shallow water, where it forms attractive spreading mats of trailing, bright-green stems with the same pure, sky-blue, yellow-eyed flowers familiar from the common garden forget-me-not, but from May into July and on a plant that returns every year rather than dying after seeding. The brilliant, clear blue of the small flowers is one of the most saturated, pure blues in the plant kingdom, providing a vivid focal point at the pond's edge throughout late spring and early summer. In shallow water features, the trailing stems and leaves float attractively on the surface while flowers arise above the water. An essential plant for naturalistic water gardens, rain gardens, and bog gardens where it softens the edges with a haze of blue flowers.

plant_note: Plant the knobby tuber in a submerged aquatic basket of heavy loam set 12 to 24 inches below the water surface so the strap-like leaves float freely on top; thrives in cool water and full sun to light shade.
directions: Set the tuber horizontally in a wide aquatic planting basket filled with heavy garden soil, then lower the container to a depth of one to two feet so the oblong leaves reach the surface and float. It performs best in cool water and can be grown in ponds that ice over lightly in winter, provided the tuber stays below the freeze line. Forked spikes of fragrant, vanilla-scented white flowers with black anthers appear mainly during cooler months, often blooming in fall and again in spring when most water lilies are dormant. The floating foliage also offers shade and cover for fish, making it a useful companion plant in mixed water gardens.

plant_note: Place rooted plantlets or offshoots on still or slow-moving water after all frost danger passes; in zone 9–11 water hyacinth is perennial year-round and should be managed to prevent spread to natural waterways. Provide full sun for best flowering.
directions: Float on still or slow-moving water in full sun; water hyacinth is an extraordinary aquatic plant producing glossy, inflated-petiole rosettes that float freely on the water surface, anchoring delicate feathery roots downward into the water column where they filter nutrients from the water. The lavender-blue flowers — each cluster on an erect spike — are among the most beautiful of any aquatic plant, with the upper petal marked by a purple spot and yellow dot. In zone 9–11 water hyacinth is a perennial that blooms repeatedly through the warm months. IMPORTANT: Water hyacinth is federally listed as one of the world's worst aquatic invasive weeds; it must never be released into natural waterways where it can form impenetrable mats that block sunlight, deplete oxygen, and destroy aquatic ecosystems. Use only in contained ponds and water features, and remove all plant material to the compost bin rather than to any water body. Its ornamental value and water-filtering ability make it outstanding for contained pond and water garden use where it can be responsibly managed.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; wrightia is one of the classic bonsai subjects of Southeast Asia and its naturally fine-twiggy branching pattern, small leaves, and appealing flower production make it ideal for bonsai training — it tolerates aggressive pruning and responds with dense, profuse new growth.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; water jasmine (sacred Buddhist tree, wild water plum) is a Southeast Asian tropical evergreen shrub widely cultivated throughout the tropical world — particularly in Thailand, Cambodia, and Malaysia — both for its ornamental beauty and its deep spiritual significance, as it is traditionally planted at temples and sacred sites, and its dangling clusters of small, pure-white, five-petaled, star-shaped flowers with long filamentous corona lobes are used as Buddhist temple offerings. The flowers are produced continuously and profusely throughout the warm season on the drooping, fine-twiggy branches, with a sweet, delicate fragrance, creating a graceful, weeping, white-flowered effect. The plant belongs to the Apocynaceae (oleander family) and exudes a milky sap when cut; all parts are toxic if ingested. In addition to its garden use as a specimen and informal flowering hedge, wrightia is one of the preeminent tropical bonsai subjects, widely grown in competitive Southeast Asian bonsai culture. Excellent in containers and as a specimen in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Place rooted offshoots on still water after all frost danger passes; water lettuce spreads rapidly by stolons to produce new rosettes that cover the water surface, shading algae and providing habitat for fish. In zone 9 it is a perennial that requires management to prevent overgrowth of the pond surface.
directions: Float on still or slow-moving water in partial to full shade; water lettuce forms floating rosettes of velvety, ribbed, blue-green leaves that closely resemble a head of lettuce — up to 10 inches across — with dense feathery roots trailing below the surface. It thrives in partial to full shade in warm water and is one of the few aquatic plants that genuinely prefers shade, making it outstanding for shaded ponds and water features. The roots provide important habitat for fish and aquatic invertebrates, while the dense leaf canopy controls algae by shading the water surface. It spreads rapidly by horizontal stolons, producing daughter plants prolifically. IMPORTANT: Like water hyacinth, water lettuce is a serious aquatic invasive in warm states; it must never be released into natural waterways, ditches, or drainage systems. Florida prohibits its sale. Use only in contained, sealed water features and compost removed plants. Outstanding for contained water gardens in warm climates where it performs beautifully as a living water filter.

plant_note: Scarify seeds and plant nursery transplants in spring in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep alluvial or clay-loam soil in full sun. Water Locust tolerates prolonged flooding and is an excellent native tree for the most difficult, permanently wet bottomland sites where other large trees fail.
directions: Water Locust is the swamp-adapted cousin of Honey Locust (Gleditsia triacanthos), native to the permanently flooded bottomlands, river swamps, and slough edges of the southeastern and south-central United States from South Carolina and Florida west to Illinois and Texas, where it tolerates standing water for extended periods that most other large trees cannot survive. Like Honey Locust it bears formidable branched thorns on the trunk and branches, but the seed pods are shorter and usually contain only one or two seeds rather than the many seeds in Honey Locust's long pods. The flat seed pods that fall into floodwater are buoyant and dispersed by currents, making Water Locust an effective natural colonizer of new bottomland habitats after flooding. A valuable riparian restoration tree for wet, bottomland habitats in zones 5–9, providing large tree structure in permanently flooded sites where bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp cottonwood grow as associates. Plant in full sun in wet, rich, slightly acidic alluvial soil.

plant_note: Plant small container trees in winter or spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to wet soil; water oak is fast growing for an oak (2–3 feet per year when young) and establishes readily from planting.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun; water oak is one of the most common and fast-growing native oaks of the coastal South, easily identified by its distinctively variable leaf shape — three-lobed duck-foot leaves, paddle-shaped leaves, and narrow elliptic leaves can all appear on the same tree. It grows naturally in bottomland forests, wet stream banks, and moist upland soils from New Jersey to Texas and is among the fastest-growing oaks in the South (2–3 feet annually). The very small, nearly round acorns produced in enormous quantities beginning at 10–15 years are critically important for wood ducks, mallards, wild turkeys, squirrels, and deer. Water oak is smaller than live oak (40–70 feet) and better suited to residential landscapes where space is limited. It typically lives 60–80 years.

plant_note: Plant in very shallow water (0-6 inches deep) or saturated mud at pond margins in spring; or sow seeds on the surface of wet mud in spring. Plants grow quickly in warm weather and begin flowering the first year.
directions: Plant in shallow water (1-6 inches) or saturated mud at the margins of ponds, streams, and bog gardens in full sun; water plantain produces attractive oval to heart-shaped leaves on long stalks and whorled branching stems of tiny pale pink to white flowers in summer that attract numerous small insects. The plant grows in both standing water and wet soil at the pond's edge, making it versatile for water garden margins. Native to North America, Europe, and Asia, it colonizes disturbed, muddy waterways naturally. The seeds are consumed by waterfowl. In traditional medicine, the rhizome was used by Asian and Native American peoples as a diuretic and to treat kidney and urinary conditions. Allow the plant to go to seed to establish new colonies; remove excess plants if spreading beyond desired boundaries.

plant_note: Plant divisions in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy loam set 2-8 inches below the water surface once water temperatures are consistently warm.
directions: Water poppy produces glossy, rounded floating leaves and cheerful three-petaled yellow flowers that open in succession just above the water through summer, giving a long season of bloom in a small water-lily-like package. Grow it in a submerged pot of heavy garden soil topped with gravel, positioned in full sun in shallow to moderately deep water, and divide the spreading rhizome every year or two to keep it in bounds. It is frost-tender and will not survive a freeze, so gardeners north of USDA zone 9 should overwinter a potted division indoors in a bright spot or heated greenhouse and treat it as a seasonal pond annual otherwise.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring, anchoring in the muddy bottom of a pond or slow stream at a depth of 1–5 feet. Water Shield spreads by rhizome to form floating mats; provide adequate space in larger ponds where it can naturalize without overpowering other plantings.
directions: Water Shield is a distinctive native floating-leaf aquatic plant found in slow ponds, lakes, bogs, and sluggish streams throughout North America, Asia, and Australia, immediately identifiable by the thick, gelatinous mucilage that coats the undersides of the small, peltate (shield-shaped), olive-green floating leaves and the stems — a characteristic not found in any other native aquatic plant. Small, dark maroon to purplish flowers appear just above the water surface in summer, and the leaves and young stems, with their gelatinous coating, have been used as food in Japan (where it is called junsai) and by Native American tribes. Water Shield is a valuable aquatic plant for wildlife ponds, providing food and cover for frogs, turtles, waterfowl, and invertebrates; the floating leaf mats shade the water and suppress algae. Plant rhizomes in soft mud at the pond bottom at 1–5 feet depth; the plant spreads slowly but steadily in favorable conditions.

common_name: Water Snowflake (White Fringed-Petal Floating Pond Plant)
plant_note: Plant rooted stock in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after all frost danger has passed; Water Snowflake bears small, white, fringed-petal flowers above floating heart-shaped pads, distinct from the yellow-flowered Nymphoides already common in cultivation.
directions: Plant rooted stock in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 4 to 12 inches deep in a full-sun pond. Water Snowflake produces small, rounded, heart-shaped floating pads resembling miniature water lily leaves, with delicate white flowers whose petal edges are finely fringed and frilled, giving each bloom a lacy, snowflake-like texture, opening in succession through the warm months just above the water's surface. It spreads by runners to cover open water, providing shade that helps suppress algae while remaining light and airy in appearance compared to bolder-leaved pond plants. It is frost-tender and best suited to warm, frost-free ponds; in cooler zones it can be grown as a summer annual or overwintered indoors. Thin and divide regularly, since it spreads readily in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Float a small starter clump on the pond surface once nights stay reliably above 50°F; it needs no soil or anchoring and will multiply on its own in warm water.
directions: Water spangles is a free-floating fern with paired oval fronds covered in water-repellent hairs that trap air and keep the plant buoyant, plus a submerged root-like frond that absorbs nutrients. It provides quick surface shade for fish ponds and helps suppress algae, but reproduces so quickly by fragmentation that it is best grown in a contained water feature and skimmed out regularly rather than an open pond. It is frost-tender and collapses at the first hard freeze, so treat it as a seasonal annual outside USDA zone 9 and dispose of excess plants in the trash rather than a waterway, since it is a regulated invasive species in parts of the southern US.

common_name: Water Spider Orchid (Creeping Bog Orchid, Floating Orchid, Repen's Habenaria)
plant_note: Grow in shallow water (0–3 inch depth) or constantly saturated soil at pond edges, in rain gardens, or in containers of aquatic soil kept submerged; Habenaria repens is unique among orchids in that it genuinely thrives in aquatic and flooded conditions where most orchids would drown. The plant spreads by producing floating runners (stolons) that carry new plantlets — in a pond, these runners float across the surface and root wherever they contact soil. In zone 9, established colonies survive winters. Place where the delicate white flowers can be viewed at close range. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in shallow water, saturated soil, or pond margins in partial shade to full sun — Water Spider Orchid is unique among cultivated orchids in tolerating and preferring genuinely wet to aquatic conditions, making it an excellent choice for rain gardens, pond edges, and water features. Habenaria repens is a small, semi-aquatic terrestrial orchid native to the southeastern United States (Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Texas, North Carolina), the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, and South America in the Orchidaceae family. It is one of the few orchids in the world genuinely adapted to aquatic and flooded environments — it grows naturally in shallow water, flooded ditches, pond margins, and wet prairies where standing water is normal, and spreads by producing floating stolons (horizontal runners) that carry small plantlets that root when they contact saturated soil or float to new locations. The plant produces upright stems of bright, fresh, green, succulent leaves. In summer and fall, the stems terminate in racemes of small (0.5-inch), intricate, bright white flowers with deeply fringed, spider-like petals — the fringed white petals arranged in a precise, delicate pattern that earned the common name 'Water Spider Orchid.' A fascinating and highly unusual orchid for water garden features in zone 8-12. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Float or lightly root plants in the pond, fully or partially submerged, in partial shade to full sun after all frost danger has passed; Water Sprite is an unusual floating or submerged fern, entirely distinct in form and habit from any terrestrial garden fern.
