directions: Float plants freely on the pond surface or lightly anchor rooted stock in a submerged planting basket, in partial shade to full sun, in warm, calm water. Water Sprite is an unusual true fern that grows either floating on the water's surface or fully submerged, with finely divided, lacy, bright green fronds that provide fine-textured contrast to broader-leaved pond plants, entirely different in form and habit from any terrestrial fern grown in the garden. It reproduces readily by tiny plantlets that form along the frond margins, dropping off to grow into new plants and quickly multiplying to cover open water, which also makes it valuable as shelter and spawning habitat for pond fish and as a nutrient-absorbing plant that helps keep water clear. It is frost-tender and treated as a warm-season plant outside the mildest zones, either replaced annually or overwintered indoors in an aquarium or heated container.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring in wet to flooded, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; water tupelo is one of the very few large trees that tolerates prolonged seasonal flooding of 6–12 feet and thrives in swamp, bottomland, and floodplain conditions inaccessible to most trees.
directions: Plant in wet to seasonally flooded, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to loamy bottomland soil in full sun to partial shade — water tupelo is one of the dominant trees of the Deep South's most iconic wetland ecosystems: the cypress-tupelo swamp. It develops a dramatically buttressed, swollen trunk base that allows gas exchange during prolonged flooding, standing in water for months at a time in the bottomlands of the Gulf Coast and Mississippi River corridor. The large, elliptic leaves turn brilliant orange, scarlet, and crimson in fall, making it one of the finest fall-color trees for wet sites. Clusters of small, oblong, dark blue to black fruit in late summer and fall are among the most sought by migrating birds. Water tupelo honey — gathered by bees from the small spring flowers — is renowned as a premium monofloral honey with an exceptionally delicate, fruity sweetness and crystallization-resistant properties. An outstanding large tree for naturalizing in wet, swampy, or bottomland areas.

common_name: Waterfall Japanese Maple (Vigorous Green Weeping Lace-Leaf Maple)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; give this vigorous, wide-spreading cultivar plenty of horizontal room to cascade.
directions: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun, allowing plenty of lateral room for its cascading spread. Waterfall is a vigorous green weeping lace-leaf Japanese maple, its finely dissected, bright green leaves cascading over long, arching branches in a form that lives up to its name, turning brilliant gold to orange-yellow in a long-lasting fall display that is among the showiest of any green-leaf cultivar. Its wide, mounding, cascading habit makes it an outstanding specimen for the top of a slope, the edge of a pond, or any spot with room to let the branches drape naturally. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches.

plant_note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer before they sprout, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs.
directions: Colchicum 'Waterlily' is a sterile double-flowered hybrid cultivar (a cross of C. autumnale and C. speciosum) prized for its large, many-petaled, rosy-lilac blooms that resemble a waterlily floating on bare soil, opening leafless in early autumn well before the coarse, strap-like foliage emerges the following spring. The heavy double flowers are more prone to flopping in rain than single colchicums, so siting under the light, dappled shade of deciduous trees or shrubs helps keep blooms cleaner and more upright than a fully exposed bed. Because the broad spring foliage persists for months and looks untidy as it yellows, interplant with later-emerging shade perennials such as hostas or ferns that will mask the dying leaves. All plant parts are toxic if ingested and should be planted away from grazing animals or edible garden beds.

common_name: Waterlily Star Magnolia (Pale Pink Many-Petaled Star Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped plants in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Waterlily is a star magnolia cultivar with an unusually high petal count opening from silvery-pink buds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Waterlily opens from soft silvery-pink buds into fragrant, nearly ice-white flowers with up to 25 narrow, strap-like tepals, a fuller flower form reminiscent of a waterlily bloom that has made it one of the most sought-after star magnolia selections. Like other star magnolias it flowers on bare branches in late winter to early spring before any foliage appears, creating a striking floral display, though the early bloom timing can leave flowers vulnerable to browning from a late hard freeze. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil where clumps can be left undisturbed to naturalize; typically the earliest tulip species to flower each spring.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall in a sunny site with sharp drainage, leaving clumps undisturbed to naturalize rather than lifting them annually like hybrid tulips. Waterlily tulip is typically the earliest tulip to bloom each spring, opening its slender, pointed buds into wide, flat flowers on sunny days — the flattened, multi-petaled look that gives the species its common name — usually in bicolor combinations of red, cream, and yellow, and closing again at night or in overcast weather. Native to the mountains of Central Asia, it is shorter and generally longer-lived in the garden than large hybrid tulips, spreading gradually into a low carpet of bloom well suited to rock gardens and the front of a sunny border. Give it excellent drainage, since like all tulips it is prone to bulb rot in soggy soil, especially through its summer dormancy.

common_name: Watermeal (World's Smallest Flowering Plant, Native Floating Novelty)
plant_note: Scatter a starter colony directly onto calm pond water in full sun to partial shade after last frost; Watermeal is a native, rootless, free-floating relative of duckweed and is considered the world's smallest flowering plant, valued as a novelty and as fish and waterfowl forage.
directions: Scatter a small starter colony directly onto calm, still pond water in full sun to partial shade, where it will multiply rapidly on its own. Watermeal consists of tiny, rootless, oval green grains barely visible to the naked eye, individually among the smallest flowering plants known to science, floating in dense colonies that can carpet the water's surface in favorable, nutrient-rich conditions. Though easy to dismiss as a nuisance, it is a valuable natural food source for fish, ducks, and other waterfowl, and, like duckweed, absorbs excess nutrients from the water that would otherwise feed algae blooms. It multiplies extremely quickly in warm, nutrient-rich water and can cover a pond's surface faster than duckweed, so thin regularly with a net or skimmer if full coverage isn't wanted, since a thick surface mat can block light and oxygen exchange for submerged plants and fish below.

common_name: Watermelon Begonia Vine (Trailing Watermelon Begonia, Pellionia)
plant_note: Root 3-4 inch stem tip cuttings directly in moist terrarium substrate or a light, well-draining potting mix; Watermelon Begonia Vine roots readily at the leaf nodes where trailing stems touch soil, making it one of the easiest terrarium plants to propagate and fill in. Keep humidity high and temperatures above 55°F.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium light and high humidity — Pellionia repens is a low, creeping, succulent-stemmed groundcover from Southeast Asia in the nettle family (Urticaceae), long a staple of closed terrariums and vivariums for its speed of coverage and its fleshy, olive-green leaves with a dusty purplish-pink cast along the margins, evoking watermelon rind (hence the common name, unrelated to true begonias). The trailing stems root at every node they touch, so a single cutting will carpet a terrarium floor or spill over a pot rim within a few months. Keep the substrate evenly moist but not waterlogged; the semi-succulent stems tolerate brief dryness but stall in growth if humidity drops much below 50%. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep growth dense rather than leggy, and trim hard if it outgrows its space — it rebounds quickly from cut-back. Best used as a terrarium groundcover, hanging basket trailer, or humid-bathroom houseplant; it fades and drops leaves in dry indoor air outside an enclosure.

plant_note: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in partial shade to full sun; more sun intensifies pink and burgundy tones while shade favors more green.
directions: Plant container starts in spring after the last frost in partial shade to full sun. This classic vegetatively propagated coleus carries frilly, ruffled leaves with bright magenta-pink centers, veins of deeper burgundy bleeding outward, and a netted lime-green margin, an effect reminiscent of watermelon flesh and rind. More sun intensifies the pink and burgundy tones while shade favors more green, giving gardeners some control over the color balance. Its compact, bushy, mounded habit with smaller leaves makes it well suited to container plantings and border edging.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant; Watermelon Peperomia is strictly a zone 10-12 outdoor plant and cannot survive frost. In zone 9, grow in containers that can be moved indoors when temperatures drop below 50°F. Plant in a small pot — Peperomia prefers to be slightly root-bound and is prone to root rot if overwatered in too large a container. Propagate by leaf cuttings: detach a leaf with stem, insert the cut end in moist perlite, and new plants emerge from the stem within 4–6 weeks.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Watermelon Peperomia cannot tolerate direct sun (leaves bleach and scorch) and thrives in the lower light levels of north-facing windows, office interiors, and deeply shaded patios. Peperomia argyreia is a compact, rosette-forming tropical from South America (Brazil, Bolivia, Venezuela) prized for its extraordinarily decorative foliage: the thick, succulent, shield-shaped, dark olive-green leaves are marked with precisely parallel silver-gray stripes running from the center stem to the leaf edge in a pattern that mimics exactly the markings on a watermelon rind — an exceptional example of natural mimicry that makes the plant immediately recognizable and beloved. Each leaf is also subtly satin-textured, adding another dimension to the ornamental effect. The plant stays small and compact (under 12 inches) indefinitely, making it ideal for small pots, terrariums, dish gardens, and desktop displays. Watering is the key cultural challenge: Watermelon Peperomia has succulent stems and leaves that store considerable water, and overwatering causes rapid root rot — allow the top inch or two of soil to dry completely between waterings. Like all Peperomias, it is non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Transplant in spring into dry, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in a location with afternoon shade; avoid overwatering, as this desert species is highly susceptible to root rot in heavy or poorly drained soils.
directions: Watson's Dutchman's Pipe is a slender, drought-adapted native perennial vine of desert washes, rocky canyon slopes, and scrubby edges in southern Arizona, New Mexico, and adjacent Mexico. It produces narrow, elongated leaves and distinctive, S-curved, brownish-purple pipe-shaped flowers that serve as an exclusive larval host for the Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor) — female butterflies seek it out specifically to lay eggs, and the caterpillars sequester the plant's defensive alkaloids for their own protection. Grow in dry, well-drained, rocky or sandy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade; established plants are highly drought tolerant and should be watered only sparingly. This unassuming vine is among the most ecologically important plantings a Southwestern gardener can make for supporting native pollinators.

plant_note: Plant corms after last frost in spring for summer bloom; in mild-winter climates (zones 9–10) plant in fall.
directions: Plant corms 3–4 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil; watsonia closely resembles gladiolus and thrives in similar conditions. The tall, sword-like foliage produces elegant spikes of tubular flowers in shades of pink, red, coral, white, and bicolor throughout summer. In frost-free climates corms multiply into large colonies and can become invasive — divide every few years to manage spread. In colder zones lift corms after frost kills the foliage, cure, and store in a cool, dry, frost-free location.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in fall (September–November in zone 8–9) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; watsonia corms planted in fall establish roots before winter and bloom the following spring. In zone 9 Gulf South they naturalize readily and can be left in the ground year-round in well-drained sites.
directions: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; watsonia is a South African cormous perennial of the iris family that produces tall, elegant, narrowly branching spikes of funnel-shaped, soft-pink to bright-pink or lavender-pink flowers in spring, carried on sturdy, 3–5-foot stems above a fan-like base of narrow, sword-shaped, bright-green leaves resembling those of a large gladiolus. The individual flowers are attractive and open sequentially up the spike over several weeks. Watsonia has naturalized extensively in parts of coastal Australia and in suitable Gulf South areas and can form large, self-perpetuating colonies in well-drained soil — the corms persist and multiply year to year without lifting, making it more reliably perennial than gladiolus in zone 8–10. After flowering the foliage dies back in summer, and the plants rest through the heat before resuming growth in fall. An excellent and easily naturalized spring-blooming ornamental and cut flower for Gulf Coast mild-winter gardens.

common_name: Wave Purple Petunia (Classic Original Spreading Groundcover Petunia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Purple Wave was the original spreading, groundcover-type petunia that launched the entire Wave series.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving it ample room to spread. Purple Wave was the groundbreaking original introduction that launched the entire Wave petunia series, spreading rapidly into a low, dense, weed-suppressing mat covered in vivid purple flowers from spring through frost, unlike the more upright, mounding habit of traditional petunias. Its vigorous, low-growing spread makes it especially effective as a flowering groundcover, spilling over walls, or filling large landscape beds and containers. It is largely self-cleaning and needs little deadheading, though a mid-season trim can rejuvenate the planting if it becomes overly leggy in the heat of summer.

common_name: Wave of Love Anthurium (Plowman's Anthurium, Ruffle Anthurium, Bird's Nest Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow in shade to partial shade in well-drained, moist, humus-rich, aerated aroid mix; Anthurium plowmanii is a bird's-nest type anthurium that produces an upright rosette of large, strongly ruffled and undulate leaves 24–36 inches long with dramatically wavy, crinkled margins — the 'wave' in the popular name 'Wave of Love.' Unlike the climbing velvet anthuriums, it is a terrestrial, self-heading plant that spreads by producing offsets from the base. It grows best in warm, humid, deeply shaded conditions. Water moderately, allowing the mix to partially dry between waterings. CAUTION: calcium oxalate in all parts; toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky mix — Wave of Love Anthurium grows most beautifully in the warm, humid, deeply shaded conditions of a sheltered tropical garden or protected patio in zone 10-12, where its unusually textured, undulate leaves create a dramatic, bold-textured presence. Anthurium plowmanii is a large, terrestrial, bird's-nest type anthurium in the Araceae family native to Bolivia, Peru, and Brazil, belonging to the section Pachyneurium — the group of anthuriums that form upright, self-heading rosettes rather than climbing vines. The plant produces an erect, open rosette of large (24–36 inch) leaves that are narrowly elliptic to strap-like, with the most distinctive feature being their strongly undulate, ruffled, crinkled margins — the leaf edges are so dramatically wavy and ruffled that they form a complex, three-dimensional edge pattern unlike any other commonly grown anthurium. The leaf surface is dark to medium green, smooth, and glossy, with the contrasting undulate margin creating a rippled effect. The plant produces inflorescences with a narrow spathe and erect, pencil-like spadix, followed by small berry clusters. Over time, the central rosette produces side offsets that can be separated for propagation. A bold, architectural shade plant of genuine presence for zone 10-12 sheltered outdoor spaces. CAUTION: toxic to pets if ingested.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in consistently moist, rich soil in part to full shade after the last frost.
directions: Grow this cultivar in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded bed or large container, watering deeply whenever the soil surface starts to dry since the broad leaves wilt quickly in dry conditions. It rewards a sheltered spot near a downspout or pond edge where humidity stays high through summer. The rounded, glossy leaves have a pronounced undulating, wavy margin that catches light differently than the flatter-leaved forms of the species, and clusters of small daisy-like yellow flowers appear on tall stalks in fall. Its bold, rippled foliage adds strong textural contrast among ferns and hostas in a shaded border.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, dry to average, sandy, rocky, or peaty, lean soil in partial shade; wavy hairgrass grows naturally in dry, acidic, rocky or sandy woods, moors, and heathlands of the northern hemisphere. More tolerant of dry shade than tufted hairgrass.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, dry to average, sandy, rocky, or peaty, lean soil in partial shade; wavy hairgrass is a fine-textured, tufted perennial grass of acidic, rocky, open woodland and moorland habitats across the Northern Hemisphere — common in pine barrens, heathlands, and rocky mountain forests of North America and Europe. The extremely fine, thread-like leaves form dense, dark green tufts, and the summer flower panicles are delicate and airy with a distinctive wavy (flexuosa) arrangement of branches. Attractive bronze-purple tints appear in the foliage in autumn. More drought and shade tolerant than tufted hairgrass (D. cespitosa), making it valuable for dry, shaded, acidic sites under conifers and in sandy woodland gardens where few ornamental grasses grow. Valuable for underplanting under pines and rhododendrons. Self-sows modestly in appropriate lean, acidic conditions.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; wavy-leaved hosta is one of the classic variegated hostas, with creamy-white centers and twisted, undulating leaves that make it a visual standout even in deep shade.
directions: Plant dormant crowns 1–2 inches deep in spring in moist, organically rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; keep consistently moist but never waterlogged. Hosta undulata is one of the original classic variegated hostas, producing medium-sized, undulating (wavy) leaves with creamy-white to pure white centers and irregular green margins that brighten shaded borders considerably; it naturalizes reliably in deep shade where many other variegated hostas fade or revert to solid green. The distinctive twisted, rippled leaf texture gives it a dynamic quality that catches light even in dim conditions. Lavender flowers on 18–24 inch scapes in mid-summer are fragrant; divide every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor. Slug control is essential — apply iron phosphate bait or diatomaceous earth around emerging growth in early spring.

plant_note: Sow seeds in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, clay or rocky soil in full sun in early spring or fall; wavyleaf coneflower grows in soils with a higher clay content than many echinaceas. It has narrower, more drooping (reflexed) ray petals than E. purpurea and blooms June-July, slightly earlier than E. purpurea. Cold stratification of seeds for 30-60 days improves germination rates.
directions: Sow seeds in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; wavyleaf coneflower is a distinct native species of the Ozark region of Missouri, Arkansas, Illinois, and Tennessee, readily distinguished from the common purple coneflower (E. purpurea) by its narrow, wavy-margined (undulate) leaves, more strongly reflexed (drooping) rose-pink to pale-pink ray petals, and earlier bloom time (June-July versus August for E. purpurea). The flowers are also notably fragrant, with a sweet, mild honey-like scent that contributes to its attractiveness to bumblebees, native bees, and butterflies. In the wild, it grows in rocky, often clay-based, glades and woodland openings in the Ozarks — adapted to heavier soils than some other echinaceas. As with all echinaceas, the persistent, spiny seed heads are highly attractive to goldfinches and other seed-eating birds in fall and winter. A genuinely distinct species worth growing alongside other echinaceas for its earlier bloom time, drooping ray style, and fragrance.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before last frost (seeds are nearly microscopic — surface-sow on moistened germinating mix and press lightly, do not cover) or plant container-grown transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before last frost (surface-sow only — seeds require light for germination) or plant transplants after frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade; wax begonia is the most widely grown shade-tolerant annual, producing an uninterrupted cascade of small, neat, single or double flowers in red, pink, salmon, coral, orange, or white on compact, self-cleaning mounds of glossy, waxy, green or bronze-tinted foliage from transplant to killing frost. Unlike tuberous begonias, wax begonias tolerate significant summer heat and humidity and are far easier to grow — they require almost no attention beyond deadhead-free, continuous bloom. Bronze-leaved selections ('Cocktail Series') handle full sun better than green-leaved forms. Excellent for massed bedding, container work, window boxes, and edging shaded walks and borders. In zones 10–12 they persist as tender perennials; in cooler climates they are lifted and overwintered indoors or discarded after frost. One of the most reliable and widely available bedding plants available.

plant_note: Surface sow dust-fine seed on moist starting mix without covering 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Surface sow seed on moistened fine-textured starting mix at 70°F and cover the tray with plastic to retain humidity — seeds need light and consistent moisture to germinate. Seedlings emerge in 2–3 weeks and are among the slowest-growing bedding plants; prick out when cotyledons are fully open and grow on under bright lights. Wax begonias flower continuously from transplant until hard frost without deadheading, making them among the most reliable shade-tolerant bedding annuals. Green-leaved types tolerate deeper shade; bronze-leaved types handle more sun and heat. In zones 10–11 they naturalize as tender perennials; elsewhere take cuttings in fall to overwinter on a sunny windowsill.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting (seeds are extremely fine — sow on surface without covering); or purchase transplants; plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; wax begonias are among the most reliable flowering shade annuals for Gulf Coast summers and perform well through heat and humidity.
directions: Plant bedding transplants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in part shade; avoid overwatering, which promotes stem rot. Begonia cucullata (wax begonia or fibrous begonia) is the ubiquitous, versatile bedding begonia sold by the billions as a summer-shade annual — an evergreen South American perennial grown as an annual in temperate gardens. The plants form compact, bushy mounds of glossy, waxy-looking, rounded to shield-shaped leaves in bright green or rich bronzy-chocolate, covered continuously with small, 1-to-1.5-inch, four-petaled flowers in white, pink, rose, red, and salmon from late spring through frost. Wax begonias are remarkable for their shade tolerance combined with genuine heat tolerance — they thrive in conditions that defeat most summer-shade annuals, performing reliably in the high heat and humidity of the Gulf South. The 'Cocktail' and 'Big' series offer bronze-leaved types with outstanding heat tolerance; the 'Super Olympia' series has performed especially well in deep South trials. In zone 9, plants may overwinter if not hit by hard frost. Wax begonia also tolerates more sun than most begonias — the bronze-leaved forms are most sun-tolerant.

common_name: Wax Mallow (Turk's Cap, Mexican Turk's Cap)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, average fertility, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wax mallow is a fast-growing native shrub of the Gulf Coastal Plain that blooms prolifically from summer through frost, tolerating drought and heat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average fertility, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wax mallow (the Texas Turk's cap) is closely related to Malvaviscus arboreus but distinguished by flatter, less deeply lobed leaves. Like its relative, it produces characteristic semi-tubular, never fully-opening, bright red flowers throughout the long Gulf Coast growing season — from summer well into winter in mild years. The nectar-rich flowers are a critically important hummingbird nectar plant in the Gulf South, visited constantly by ruby-throated and rufous hummingbirds throughout their migration. The small red fruits are edible fresh and can be used for jelly. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established; dies to the ground after hard freezes but regrows vigorously from the root in spring. An essential native plant for the hummingbird garden in zone 9a.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings (with at least two nodes) in moist perlite or sphagnum moss, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average soil in partial shade; wax plant requires a period of cool, dry dormancy in winter (reduced water, no fertilizer, temperatures to 50°F) to initiate the following season's flower buds — plants kept warm and wet year-round often refuse to bloom.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, lean soil in partial shade; wax plant (porcelain flower) is an East Asian tropical vining succulent of the milkweed family (Apocynaceae) that produces clusters of utterly distinctive, perfectly formed, waxy flowers — each cluster a spherical umbel of 20–40 small, star-shaped, pale-pink or white flowers, each flower centered with a smaller red-pink, five-pointed, star-shaped corona that gives the cluster an intricate, jewel-like appearance, and the entire flower cluster glistening with sweet, clear nectar droplets. The flowers are intensely fragrant, especially in the evening. The thick, succulent, oval, glossy, dark-green leaves on the twining stems provide attractive year-round foliage coverage. Flowering requires patience — established plants may take several years to bloom — and a cool, dry winter rest period (the opposite of most tropical plants) to initiate the process. Once blooming age is reached, it flowers reliably from the same spur-like peduncles that should never be removed. 'Krimson Queen' (white-cream leaf margins), 'Tricolor', and the double-flowered 'Compacta' are popular cultivars. A long-lived, low-maintenance succulent vine once established.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Wayet's hoya trails naturally and looks best allowed to cascade rather than staked upright.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Wayet's hoya trails naturally and looks best allowed to cascade rather than staked upright. Narrow, pointed, deep green leaves often flush purple-red along the margins in bright light, growing densely along slender, gracefully trailing stems that produce small clusters of dark maroon-red, star-shaped flowers with a sweet fragrance most noticeable in the evening. Native to the Philippines, it is a compact, easy-care hoya well suited to a hanging basket or shelf where its cascading stems can drape freely, and, like other hoyas, it blooms repeatedly from the same short flowering spurs, which should never be removed. Allow the potting mix to dry between waterings and provide bright indirect light for the best leaf color and most reliable flowering.

plant_note: Plant container or balled shrubs in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil, including chalky or alkaline ground, in full sun to partial shade; wayfaring tree is exceptionally tough and adaptable, tolerating drought, wind, and difficult soil once established.
directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil, including dry, chalky, or alkaline ground, in full sun to partial shade; wayfaring tree is a large, rugged, deciduous viburnum long used for hedging and windbreaks across Europe, with felted, gray-green, textured leaves and flat clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring that develop into berries passing through red on their way to a final glossy black, so a single cluster often shows both colors together in late summer — a striking two-tone effect that also feeds birds. Fall color runs from yellow to deep red-purple. It is one of the toughest large viburnums available, shrugging off poor soil, wind, drought, and neglect once established, and works well as an informal hedge, screen, or woodland-margin shrub where a tidier plant would struggle. Prune right after flowering if shaping is needed; otherwise it needs very little routine care. The felted leaves and stems are a useful identification feature that distinguishes it from smoother-leaved viburnums.

plant_note: Plant pups or container-grown stock in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil in full sun; give it plenty of room since it grows faster and larger than most ornamental agaves.
directions: Set pups or nursery plants slightly proud of grade in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; Weber's Agave is one of the largest and fastest-growing commonly cultivated agaves, forming a huge symmetrical rosette of smooth, gray-green to blue-green leaves that lack the marginal teeth found on most agave species, making it a safer choice near walkways and pool decks. It was historically grown in San Luis Potosí, Mexico for pulque and mezcal production and is sometimes confused with Agave americana, which it resembles but outgrows. Like other true agaves it is monocarpic, sending up a tall branched flower stalk after roughly 8-15 years and then dying back while leaving a ring of offsets. Its rapid growth and imposing scale make it a strong choice for large-scale xeriscape beds, medians, and desert-style landscaping where a fast architectural statement is wanted.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Wedding Ring's variegated margin is brightest with some direct sun, but plants benefit from afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 summer heat.
directions: Wedding Ring is a variegated boxwood selection whose small, glossy leaves are edged in creamy yellow around a green center, giving hedging or specimen plantings a lighter, brighter look than the solid dark green of standard boxwood cultivars. It holds a naturally rounded, dense habit and takes shearing well for those who want a crisper formal shape, though it can also be left to its own tidy form for a more relaxed planting. Give it moist, well-drained soil, protection from harsh afternoon sun in the Deep South, and watch for boxwood leafminer and boxwood blight, the two most significant pest and disease pressures on boxwood in Southern gardens.

common_name: Wedelia (Beach Creeper, Bay Biscayne Creeper, Orange Wedelia)
plant_note: Plant stem cuttings (rooted or unrooted) in full sun in any well-drained soil; Sphagneticola trilobata (formerly Wedelia trilobata) is one of the most vigorous and fast-spreading groundcovers available for zone 9-12, rooting at stem nodes and spreading to cover large areas within a single season. Excellent for slopes, coastal areas, and difficult-to-maintain areas where dense, weed-suppressing coverage is desired. The cheerful orange-yellow daisy flowers are produced almost continuously through the warm months. In zone 9, established plants cut back in hard freezes but regrow from the root crown vigorously in spring. Classified as invasive in some jurisdictions — check local regulations before planting, and do not plant near natural areas or waterways.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil — Wedelia establishes and spreads rapidly in full sun and is one of the most drought-tolerant, low-maintenance groundcovers for warm-climate landscapes once the initial establishment period is complete. Sphagneticola trilobata (formerly Wedelia trilobata, Wedelia paludosa) is a vigorous, mat-forming, spreading perennial in the Asteraceae family native to the Caribbean, Mexico, and Central and South America, now widely naturalized and planted throughout the tropical and subtropical world as an ornamental groundcover. The plant produces prostrate to semi-erect, fleshy stems that root at each node where they contact moist soil, enabling rapid, dense coverage of large areas. The leaves are dark green, coarsely toothed, and slightly succulent. Through the warm months (and year-round in zone 10-12), the plant produces quantities of small (1-inch), bright orange-yellow daisy-like flowers with notched ray petals surrounding a prominent raised central disk — a cheerful, consistent bloom that continues for months. The densely rooting stems form a weed-suppressing mat 6–18 inches deep. Wedelia is exceptionally useful for covering slopes, banks, and erosion-prone areas in zone 9-12 where a tough, low-maintenance groundcover with attractive flowers is desired. It is also widely planted in coastal areas for its salt and wind tolerance. Listed as invasive in many tropical countries — plant responsibly, keep contained, and avoid areas near natural lands. Non-toxic.

common_name: Wee Bit Grumpy Hydrangea (Dwarf Reblooming Deep Blue-Purple Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wee Bit Grumpy blooms on both old and new wood, so it reliably reflowers through summer even after a late frost damages the previous season's buds.
directions: Wee Bit Grumpy is a dwarf, reblooming mophead hydrangea staying compact enough for a large container or small foundation bed, producing rounded flower heads that read as intense deep blue in acidic soil or purple-pink in more neutral to alkaline soil, following the same pH-driven color shift typical of macrophylla hydrangeas. Because it flowers on both old and new wood, a late spring freeze that damages the previous season's buds does not prevent a strong summer rebloom. Keep soil consistently moist in partial shade, since the leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning sacrifices the earliest old-wood flowers.

common_name: Weeping Blue Atlas Cedar (Sculptural Silvery-Blue Cascading Cedar)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; stake and train the leader upright for several years if height is wanted, since unstaked plants sprawl as a low, wide mound.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, staking and training the central leader upright for the first several years if a taller, cascading form is desired, since left untrained this cultivar sprawls as a wide, undulating mound. Weeping Blue Atlas Cedar is a dramatic, sculptural conifer with long, weeping branches clothed in striking silvery-blue needles, prized as a specimen tree that can be trained into strikingly different forms — tall and serpentine, mounded and groundcover-like, or trained flat against a wall — depending on staking and pruning in its early years. Its bold color and highly individual, sculptural character make it one of the most dramatic focal-point conifers available, though its ultimate size and shape are unpredictable and shaped largely by the grower's training choices. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant and require little routine care beyond removing dead wood.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to average soil in full sun in spring or fall; weeping bottlebrush is extremely drought-tolerant once established and performs well in poor, dry, sandy soils — it is actually less vigorous and may develop root rot in rich, wet, or poorly drained soil.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun; weeping bottlebrush is an Australian evergreen tree that is one of the most spectacular flowering trees for the Gulf Coast and Deep South — in spring (primary bloom), and intermittently throughout the year, the long, arching, weeping branches become covered from tip to base with the plant's signature cylindrical, bright-crimson-red, bottlebrush-like flower spikes, each composed of hundreds of long, projecting red stamens with yellow tips that form the dense, brush-like structure for which the plant is named. The weeping habit and the brilliant red flower display against the fine-textured, narrow, willow-like, evergreen leaves make it one of the most visually impressive medium-sized flowering trees available for zone 8–11. It flowers most heavily in spring but continues to produce scattered bloom through summer and fall. Attracts hummingbirds and orioles with exceptional reliability. Drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established. Hardy to approximately 15°F in zone 8.

plant_note: Plant in late spring when soil and air are warm; Weeping Fig is sensitive to cold (leaf drop below 40°F) and should not be planted outdoors until all danger of cold nights has passed. In zone 9a, plant in the most protected microclimate available — south or east facing walls, urban heat pockets, or under structural overhangs. In zone 9b and warmer, it can be planted as a landscape specimen with minimal frost protection.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; in zone 9, afternoon shade protection extends the plant's cold hardiness and prevents leaf scorch during heat waves. Ficus benjamina is the world's most widely cultivated indoor tree and one of the most popular tropical landscape trees in zone 9b–11 Gulf Coast, Florida, and California landscapes, where mature specimens with their gracefully arching, weeping branches laden with small, glossy, pointed leaves create an elegant, tropical canopy. In warm climates, trees grow to 50–60 feet with an equally broad spreading crown. The smooth gray trunk often develops aerial roots in humid conditions. The plant produces small, inedible figs in zone 10-11 but rarely fruits in zone 9. Ficus benjamina is notorious indoors for dropping leaves when conditions change — any shift in light, temperature, humidity, or watering schedule triggers a stress response. For outdoor landscape use in zone 9b, choose a permanent location as transplanting established trees causes significant leaf drop. The aggressive root system can damage sidewalks, foundations, and underground utilities within 20-30 feet; avoid planting near hardscape or infrastructure. A spectacular specimen when given room and a frost-free site.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; final height and form depend heavily on whether the tree was trained upright on a stake when young or left to sprawl along the ground.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the leader upright when young if a taller, cascading specimen is wanted, since left unstaked this cultivar sprawls along the ground as a wide, low mound instead. Weeping Norway spruce produces long, pendulous branches draped in dark-green needles that cascade dramatically once the tree gains some height, making a dramatic, sculptural specimen whether trained tall and narrow or allowed to spread as a groundcover-like mound over a slope or wall. No two plants develop exactly alike, since the ultimate form depends on training and the individual habit of the grafted specimen, giving each tree a unique, almost bonsai-like character. Little routine pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood and guiding the leading shoot if a taller form is desired.

plant_note: Plant in spring in moist ground, away from pipes and foundations.
directions: The Weeping Willow is a graceful, fast-growing shade tree with long, sweeping branches that trail nearly to the ground and sway in the slightest breeze. Plant in full sun in moist to wet soil, ideally near a pond or stream where its thirsty roots have ample water. Keep it well away from septic lines, drains, and foundations, as the aggressive roots seek out moisture. Water deeply and regularly, especially in dry spells and during establishment. Prune in late winter to remove crossing or damaged branches and to raise the canopy as it matures.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist to dry, acidic to slightly alkaline, well-drained to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Pendula is a female selection and will produce berries without a separate male plant if other male yaupon hollies are in the vicinity — or plant alongside a male yaupon cultivar to maximize berry production.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, acidic to slightly alkaline, well-drained to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Weeping Yaupon is a dramatic, architecturally distinctive native holly cultivar with strongly pendulous, cascading branches that create an elegant weeping form quite unlike any other native landscape tree. The long, drooping branches cascade downward from the upright central leader, creating a columnar-weeping silhouette in winter and a dense, cascading curtain of small, glossy, dark-green evergreen leaves during the growing season. In winter when the female plant bears translucent red berries against the dark green foliage along the drooping branches, the display is spectacular. Weeping yaupon is a female Ilex vomitoria selection and requires a nearby male yaupon holly (the species or a male cultivar) within about 100 feet for reliable berry production. Like the species, Weeping Yaupon has extraordinary adaptability — thriving in the full spectrum of Gulf Coast conditions from seasonally flooded clay soils to dry sandy uplands, salt spray, alkaline soils, and both full sun and partial shade. It grows 12–18 feet tall with a cascading, somewhat narrow spread of 6–10 feet. The weeping form makes it outstanding as a specimen, accent, or garden focal point where its distinctive silhouette can be appreciated.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: The Weeping Yoshino is a flowering cherry with gracefully cascading branches that in spring become a fountain of delicate, blush-white blossoms before the leaves emerge. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and provide good air circulation to limit fungal issues. Water regularly during establishment and mulch the root zone, keeping mulch away from the trunk. Prune only lightly right after flowering to maintain the weeping shape, as cherries are prone to disease through large cuts. It makes a spectacular focal point in a lawn or beside a patio.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or hardwood cuttings in winter, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; weigela blooms on old wood — prune immediately after flowering by removing the oldest, flowered stems to prevent the shrub from becoming overgrown and bare at the base.
directions: Root cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; weigela is a Chinese deciduous flowering shrub that has been a cornerstone of the North American spring garden since the Victorian era — producing masses of trumpet-shaped, 1-inch flowers densely covering the arching branches in late May to June in shades ranging from deep crimson-red and rose-pink to pale pink and white, depending on cultivar, at the same time as azaleas and late lilacs, creating one of the richest spring flowering displays available in zone 4–8. Modern cultivars have dramatically expanded the ornamental value beyond the original species, adding dark-purple, burgundy, or gold foliage to the flowering display: 'Wine and Roses' (deep-purple foliage, bright-pink flowers), 'Midnight Wine' (compact, dwarf, burgundy leaves, rose-pink flowers), and 'Sonic Bloom' series (repeat-flowering from spring through frost) are standout introductions. It attracts hummingbirds reliably. Tolerates partial shade acceptably. One of the easiest and most adaptable flowering shrubs for the temperate garden.

common_name: Welch's Pink Beautyberry (Soft Pink-Berried American Beautyberry)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; Welch's Pink is a selected form of native American beautyberry bearing soft pink rather than magenta-purple berry clusters.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil. Welch's Pink is a selected color form of the native American beautyberry, bearing the same tight, globe-shaped berry clusters ringing the arching stems in late summer and fall, but in a soft rosy pink rather than the species' typical vivid magenta-purple, offering a gentler color option for gardeners who want the beautyberry effect with a different palette. Like the species it provides valuable late-season food for mockingbirds, robins, and other wildlife once the berries ripen, and the small, pale pink summer flowers attract pollinators. Prune hard in late winter, cutting back to within 6-12 inches of the ground, to encourage vigorous new growth and the heaviest berry production, since berries form on new wood and unpruned plants can become leggy and sparse over time.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds on the soil surface (do not cover — seeds require light for germination) in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in fall for spring germination, or in very early spring; Welsh poppy self-seeds so freely in suitable shaded, moist conditions that a single planting typically results in permanent, self-sustaining colonies — subsequent hand-sowing is rarely necessary.
directions: Surface-sow seeds on moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in fall or early spring; Welsh poppy is a European woodland and rocky-ledge annual or short-lived perennial — unique among poppies as the only species that genuinely thrives in shade — producing a continuous succession of cheerful, bright-orange or yellow, four-petaled, simple poppy flowers from late spring through summer above rosettes of divided, bright-green, fernlike leaves. It is also unique among its family in tolerating and actually preferring cool, shaded, moist woodland conditions, making it an invaluable source of cheerful color in the shade garden at a season when few other shade plants offer comparable brightness. It self-seeds prolifically in suitable conditions to form permanent, self-renewing colonies under trees and in shaded rocky crevices. The double-flowered form, with fully petaled orange or yellow flowers, is particularly ornamental. Unlike the Himalayan blue meconopsis, Welsh poppy is genuinely easy to grow and is essentially maintenance-free in a suitable site. Considered invasive in some Pacific Northwest gardens where conditions perfectly suit it.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Wendlinger's anthurium is best displayed hanging so its long pendulous leaves can drape freely.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Wendlinger's anthurium is best displayed hanging so its long pendulous leaves can drape freely. Long, glossy, strap-shaped leaves with a distinctly quilted, corrugated surface texture hang gracefully downward, similar in overall form to the related strap-leaf anthurium but with broader, more heavily textured foliage and a more pronounced pleated pattern along each leaf. Native to Costa Rican and Panamanian cloud forests, it grows epiphytically in the wild and is best replicated in cultivation with a hanging basket or mounted display that allows its pendulous leaves to hang free rather than a standard upright pot. Water when the mix approaches dryness, maintain high humidity, and provide bright, filtered light for the best leaf texture and length.

plant_note: Set out nursery starts after frost danger has passed in well-drained, amended beds or large containers; this Australian-bred hybrid blooms nearly nonstop through the hot, humid Gulf Coast season.
directions: This vigorous chance seedling produces magenta-pink flowers with wine-colored calyces on sprawling, arching stems from spring through frost. Give it full sun and good drainage; it tolerates heat and humidity better than many salvias and is a strong hummingbird and butterfly plant for Gulf Coast borders. Cut back hard in late winter to renew growth, and take softwood cuttings in fall as insurance since plants can be short-lived in wet winter soils. In colder zone 8 pockets treat as a root-hardy perennial and mulch the crown heavily.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, fertile to average soil in full sun; West Indian mahogany is one of the few native mahogany trees in North America, naturally occurring in tropical hardwood hammocks of extreme south Florida and the Keys.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun in zone 10–12; West Indian mahogany is one of the most prized timber trees in the world — the original 'true mahogany' of the Caribbean cabinet-making tradition, producing close-grained, durable, reddish-brown wood used in fine furniture, musical instruments, and boat building since the 16th century. It is the state tree of the Dominican Republic. In south Florida and the Keys, it grows naturally in tropical hardwood hammock and is the only native mahogany in North America. Widely planted as a street and shade tree in Miami, it develops into a stately, large, semi-deciduous tree with a dense, spreading canopy. The large, hanging seed capsules split into five valves to release winged seeds. Critically endangered in its natural range due to centuries of timber harvesting; planting supports conservation of this culturally important species.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants in fall or early spring into loose, well-drained, acidic soil amended with leaf mold or conifer duff, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer.
directions: Set out container-grown plants in fall or early spring into loose, well-drained, acidic soil amended with leaf mold or conifer duff, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer. It grows naturally along streambanks and in open, partly shaded woods from California into southern Oregon, so give it filtered light beneath high canopy and steady moisture in its first few seasons while it establishes deep roots. Fragrant white to pale pink flowers with a yellow blotch open in early summer on a rangy, multi-stemmed shrub, and the scent carries well through a shaded border or informal woodland edge. Established plants tolerate summer drought better than most azaleas once their roots reach cooler subsoil.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; western bleeding heart spreads by rhizomes and self-sows to form attractive groundcover colonies in cool, moist, shaded sites.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, spacing 12–18 inches apart; western bleeding heart is a Pacific Coast native that differs from the Eastern Dicentra spectabilis (which goes dormant in summer) by remaining in active growth and bloom through most of the season in cool, moist climates, producing delicate, dissected blue-green ferny foliage and dangling chains of rose-pink heart-shaped flowers from spring into summer. In hot climates it may go summer-dormant but reliably re-emerges in fall. It spreads pleasantly by rhizomes and self-sowing to colonize shaded areas, and is an excellent groundcover under conifers and deciduous trees on the West Coast and in cool-summer regions. Divide in early spring to increase plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall for natural cold-moist stratification; alternatively, cold-stratify seed for 3–4 weeks at 38–40°F and sow in spring. Western columbine self-sows prolifically in cool, moist Pacific Northwest gardens and will naturalize readily if allowed to set seed.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mimicking the woodland edge and streamside habitats it occupies naturally along the Pacific Coast from Alaska to Baja California and east through the Rocky Mountains; Aquilegia formosa is distinguished by its vivid red-and-yellow bicolor flowers with short, straight, red spurs — a color combination specifically evolved to attract hummingbirds — and it is one of the most important native hummingbird plants of the Pacific Northwest and mountain West, with hummingbirds and bumblebees being its primary pollinators. It is a natural parent of many popular red-and-yellow hybrid columbines and imparts heat tolerance and reliable performance to its cultivated offspring. Like most columbines, it is a short-lived perennial of 3–5 years that perpetuates itself freely by self-seeding; allow seed to disperse naturally to maintain the planting. Columbine leaf miners may create pale tunnels in the foliage but rarely harm plant health.

subcategory: prairie and glade native pollinator annual
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring onto bare, well-drained soil, since seed needs light to germinate and should not be buried deeply; it also self-sows readily once established in a bed.
directions: Scatter seed onto lightly raked, well-drained soil in a sunny rock garden, glade planting, or short-grass prairie mix and press in without covering, since germination is light-dependent. The small white-to-pale-lavender, yellow-centered daisies resemble a miniature aster and bloom heavily from mid-spring into early summer, attracting small native bees and syrphid flies. It behaves as a short-lived annual or biennial in most gardens, persisting through reseeding rather than by rootstock, so avoid mulching too heavily over the seedbed. It is well suited to lean, rocky, or sandy soils where more aggressive perennials would crowd it out.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; western hemlock grows naturally in the moist Pacific coastal and Cascade forests where high humidity and consistent soil moisture are available year-round. Does not tolerate drought or heat.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; western hemlock is the state tree of Washington and one of the dominant trees of the moist Pacific Northwest forests from northern California to Alaska — often growing alongside Sitka spruce, Douglas-fir, and Pacific red cedar in the classic coastal rainforest community. The nodding leading shoot and graceful, pendulous branch tips distinguish it from all other conifers. The small, oval cones (less than an inch long) are among the smallest of any large conifer. Western hemlock is remarkable for its shade tolerance — young seedlings establish readily in the deep shade of old-growth forest and slowly grow up to eventually overtop their nurse trees. The inner bark was used by Pacific Northwest indigenous peoples as an emergency food source. The hemlock bark is high in tannin and was an important tanning material in the Pacific Northwest leather industry.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in average to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; western ironweed spreads by rhizomes once established, so give it room or plant it where a colonizing habit is welcome, such as a large native meadow planting.
directions: Plant in average to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; western ironweed is adaptable to poor, dry, or occasionally clay soils and needs no irrigation once established. Vernonia baldwinii is a coarse, upright prairie perennial native from Texas and Louisiana north through the central Plains to Nebraska and Iowa, producing broad, flat-topped clusters of vivid red-violet, thistle-like flower heads from midsummer through fall that are heavily worked by monarchs, swallowtails, skippers, and native bees during a season when many other prairie flowers have finished blooming. It spreads by rhizomes to form expanding colonies over time, so it is best suited to naturalized meadow plantings, roadsides, or large borders rather than small, tidy beds. The tough, deep-rooted plants tolerate heat, drought, and occasional mowing better than most late-season pollinator perennials, and the dried seed heads provide texture and food for birds into winter.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown container specimens in fall into consistently moist, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade; belongs in a dedicated acidic bog garden rather than ordinary soil.
directions: Plant nursery-grown container specimens in fall into consistently moist, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade, replicating the mountain bogs, fens, and streambanks from British Columbia and the Cascades south to California and east to the Rockies where this evergreen shrub grows wild. Rounded clusters of small white flowers open in early summer above aromatic, leathery, woolly-backed leaves, drawing bees and other pollinators, while the dense foliage offers year-round shelter in wetland habitats. Closely related to the eastern Labrador tea but distinct to western wetlands, it belongs in a dedicated acidic bog garden rather than ordinary garden soil, since both drying out and alkaline conditions are quickly fatal.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after cold stratification in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; western larch is one of the fastest-growing conifers of the Pacific Northwest, requiring full sun and well-drained, mineral soils. Does not tolerate shade, drought, or poorly drained conditions.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; western larch is the largest and most commercially important of the North American larches, reaching 100–180 feet in the forests of the inland Pacific Northwest. A deciduous conifer — like all larches it drops its needles in fall after they turn a brilliant, luminous golden-yellow, one of the most spectacular fall displays in the western mountains. The needles grow in characteristic larch clusters of 14–30 needles from woody spur shoots on older wood, with single needles on the leading growth. Western larch wood is the strongest and most rot-resistant of the western conifers, used for structural lumber, railroad ties, and telephone poles. The thick, fire-resistant bark protects old trees from low-intensity forest fires. A magnificent landscape tree where space allows, providing the rare combination of exceptional scale, distinctive form, and spectacular fall color.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade in spring; western maidenhair naturally roots into rocky streambank seeps and appreciates a gritty, well-aerated planting mix.
directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade in spring; western maidenhair naturally roots into rocky streambank seeps and appreciates a gritty, well-aerated planting mix. Wiry, glossy blackish-purple stems fan out into delicate, finely divided, blue-green fronds in a distinctive upright, hand-shaped arrangement, giving the plant a more architectural, vase-like habit than the similar eastern maidenhair fern. Native to moist, rocky slopes, cliff seeps, and streambanks from Alaska south through the Pacific coast ranges and disjunct populations in the East, it is a choice specimen for a shaded rock garden, waterfall edge, or container where its fine texture and dark stems can be appreciated up close. Keep soil evenly moist and sheltered from drying wind, and mulch lightly with leaf litter over winter in colder zones.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into consistently moist, acidic, gritty soil in a cool site with light shade.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into consistently moist, acidic, gritty soil in a cool site with light shade, matching the rocky alpine and subalpine slopes of the Pacific Northwest and Sierra Nevada where it grows in mats fed by melting snowbanks. Its tiny, scale-like leaves densely clothe wiry stems, and in early summer it is studded with small white, bell-shaped flowers nodding on thread-like stalks, a classic sight of high mountain heather meadows. It is exacting about cool roots and steady moisture, making it best suited to a shaded scree bed, trough, or high-elevation native rock garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; western mountain ash prefers cooler mountain climates and struggles with heat and drought in lowland gardens.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; western mountain ash prefers cooler mountain climates and struggles with heat and drought in lowland gardens. Flat clusters of small white flowers open in early summer above compound, fern-like leaves on this small native tree of high-elevation forests and mountain slopes across western North America, followed by bright orange-red berry clusters that persist into fall and winter, providing important food for grouse, waxwings, and other mountain wildlife. Its compact size and showy fruit display make it a good choice for a native mountain or high-elevation garden, but it is not well adapted to hot, humid, or low-elevation conditions far from its cool mountain forest habitat. Water during establishment and dry spells, and site in a location with cool summer temperatures and good air circulation for the best long-term performance.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or small trees in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; western redbud is much more drought-tolerant and sun-demanding than eastern redbud and thrives in the dry summers of California, Nevada, and Arizona where the eastern species would fail. Established plants are highly drought-tolerant and require minimal supplemental irrigation in their native climate range.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; western redbud is the California and Great Basin counterpart of the eastern redbud, native to rocky hillsides, chaparral, and dry canyon walls throughout California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah. It is a distinctly different plant from eastern redbud in several ways: typically growing as a large, multi-stemmed shrub rather than a single-trunked tree (reaching 10-15 feet rather than 20-30 feet), with round rather than heart-shaped leaves, and substantially higher drought tolerance adapted to the dry-summer Mediterranean climate of the American West. In early spring, the leafless stems are covered in brilliant, vibrant magenta-pink pea flowers identical in form to eastern redbud, creating a breathtaking display. The round, deep-green summer leaves have attractive fall color. An outstanding California native for xeriscaping, wildlife gardens, and drought-tolerant landscapes, and increasingly valued as a garden plant in the Gulf Coast and Southeast where its heat tolerance is an advantage.

plant_note: Plant rooted suckers or container stock in spring into average to dry, well-drained soil in full to partial sun; this tough plains shrub tolerates heavy clay, drought, and cold with ease.
directions: Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in spring in average to dry soil and full to partial sun, spacing plants to allow the colony to spread naturally by underground rhizomes into a dense thicket. Western snowberry needs little care once established and tolerates heavy clay, drought, and harsh prairie winters better than most ornamental shrubs. Small pink-tinged bell flowers in early summer draw bumblebees and other native pollinators, and the waxy white berries that follow persist into winter, feeding sharp-tailed grouse, pheasants, and small mammals when other food is scarce. The dense, thicket-forming habit also provides valuable nesting and escape cover for grassland songbirds.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after removing the fleshy seed coat and scarifying; soak 24 hours before planting in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun. Western soapberry grows naturally on dry, rocky, calcareous slopes and plains across the south-central US.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous to sandy soil in full sun; western soapberry is a native tree of the south-central US, growing on dry, rocky, calcareous plains and hills from Kansas and Missouri south to Mexico. The fleshy, translucent, golden-amber berries contain saponins — natural soap compounds — and are high enough in saponin concentration that the crushed berries lather in water and have been used historically as soap for washing clothes and hair by indigenous peoples. The fruits are technically toxic if eaten in quantity due to the saponins. The pale yellow-green fall foliage, persistent golden berries through winter, and handsome pinnate leaves provide multi-season ornamental interest. Excellent urban tree tolerating drought, heat, alkaline soils, and neglect — one of the toughest native trees for harsh, dry, calcareous landscape conditions in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant small corms in fall 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; western spring beauty is a true spring ephemeral that grows from a small, deep corm and disappears completely by early summer. It grows naturally in mountain meadows and open forests as snow melts.
directions: Plant corms in fall 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade; western spring beauty is the Rocky Mountain and Pacific Northwest counterpart of the familiar eastern spring beauty (Claytonia virginica), producing lanceolate rather than grasslike leaves and charming clusters of white to pale pink flowers with darker pink veins in early spring as snow melts. A small, delicate spring ephemeral growing from a deep, starchy corm (called bitterroot or Indian potato) that was an important food for mountain Native Americans and early explorers. Bears ate the newly emerged flowering plants after emerging from winter dens. Naturalizes in appropriate conditions, spreading by corms and self-sowing. Goes completely dormant by early summer. Perfect for planting under deciduous trees or shrubs where it will receive ample spring light but summer shade will not be a problem, as the plant is long gone.

plant_note: Fall-sow or cold-moist stratify 30-60 days before spring sowing; established plants spread slowly by rhizome and are best left undisturbed once sited.
directions: Plant in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun, where its distinctive basal rosette of leaves and nearly leafless flowering stalks distinguish it from the taller, leafier sunflowers most gardeners already grow. Bright yellow, 2 to 3 inch composite flowers open from late summer into fall on wiry stems, providing a valuable late-season nectar and pollen source for bees and butterflies as many earlier bloomers fade. It is notably drought tolerant and thrives in poor, sandy, or rocky soils where richer ground would cause it to flop or be outcompeted. Divide clumps every few years if they become congested, and avoid overly fertile or irrigated beds, which promote lanky growth.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; western sword fern is exceptionally drought tolerant for a fern once established and can grow in drier conditions than most shade ferns. Best suited to mild coastal gardens and the Pacific Coast; tolerates moderate heat in zone 9 with adequate moisture.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; western sword fern is the dominant groundcover fern of the Pacific Coast forest — so abundant under the conifer canopy from Alaska to California that it defines the character of the Pacific Northwest woodland aesthetic. It produces large, upright vase-shaped crowns of long, lance-shaped, once-pinnate, deep-green fronds with distinctive little ear-like pinnae at the base of each pinnule. The fronds are evergreen and persistent, providing year-round cover and beauty. Unlike many ferns, western sword fern is remarkably drought tolerant once established, making it suitable for drier shaded conditions under conifers where moisture-loving ferns fail. The leathery fronds are long-lasting as cut foliage in arrangements. A superb structural fern for the cool, moist shade garden; it works at large scale as a groundcover under conifers, at woodland edges, and in large drift plantings where its bold, persistent fronds create a dependable year-round backdrop.

plant_note: Scatter seed on bare or lightly raked soil in fall; seeds require cold winter temperatures to break dormancy and will germinate naturally in early spring. No covering is needed — simply press seed into contact with the soil surface.
directions: Western Tansy Mustard is a native annual of dry, open, sandy or rocky ground across the western US and Great Plains, producing finely pinnate, fern-like leaves with a pleasant aroma and dense racemes of small, pale yellow, 4-petaled mustard flowers from March through June. The cylindrical seed pods that follow are eagerly eaten by mourning doves, quail, and native sparrows, making it a high-value plant for bird-friendly gardens and prairie restorations. Direct sow in fall into lean, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; it thrives in poor soils where competition from other plants is minimal. It self-sows prolifically in open, disturbed ground and will naturalize a site with little intervention once established.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; western trillium is the Pacific Northwest counterpart to white trillium — purchase nursery-propagated divisions only, never wild-dug plants.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; western trillium requires the same conditions as eastern white trillium (T. grandiflorum) — cool, moist, shaded conditions and years of patience before it establishes and flowers reliably. Trillium ovatum is the dominant trillium species of Pacific Northwest old-growth forests, producing the classic trillium form of three broad leaves and a single, three-petaled, white flower in early spring that ages to pink and finally purple-red over its two-to-three-week bloom period; it differs from eastern T. grandiflorum primarily in its narrower, more pointed petals. Like all trilliums, it requires 5–7 years from seed to first bloom; divisions from nurseries are the only ethical source — wild collection is destructive and depletes natural populations. Outstanding for shaded native plant gardens in the Pacific Northwest and similar climates.

plant_note: Plant in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Well-suited to the dry summers of the Pacific Northwest and northern California; irrigation should be minimal once established to avoid root rot.
directions: Choose a site that receives morning sun and afternoon shade, with fast-draining, rocky or sandy soil that stays dry in summer. This is the only Viburnum native to Oregon and California, and it is adapted to summer drought — avoid planting in lawn areas or anywhere that receives regular irrigation. Plant in spring, water to settle the roots, and then allow natural rainfall to take over after the first season. Clusters of white flowers in late spring attract native pollinators, and the dark berries that follow are eaten by western scrub-jays, towhees, and other Pacific coast birds.

common_name: Western White Fawn Lily (Oregon Fawn Lily)
plant_note: Plant corms in fall (2–3 inches deep) in well-drained to dry, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or loamy woodland soil in partial shade to shade; western white fawn lily grows naturally in open, rocky oak and Douglas fir woodlands and grassy balds of the Pacific Northwest. Goes completely summer-dormant after setting seed.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained to dry, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or loamy woodland soil in partial shade; western white fawn lily is a native spring ephemeral of the Pacific Northwest, producing pairs of beautiful, mottled, brown-and-green basal leaves and nodding, creamy-white to white flowers with reflexed petals that reveal bright yellow anthers within — an elegant, understated woodland lily of great beauty. After the seeds ripen in late spring, the plant retreats completely underground until the following spring — perfect under deciduous trees where summer shade would harm other plants. Native to open Garry oak woodlands, rocky slopes, and the margins of Douglas fir forests from Vancouver Island south through Oregon. The mottled leaves (reminiscent of a fawn's spotted coat, giving the genus its common name) are almost as ornamental as the flowers. Multiply slowly from offsets; best established from corms in fall.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist to average, fertile to average, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; western white pine grows naturally in moist mountain forests of the Pacific Northwest and requires adequate moisture. Susceptible to white pine blister rust — use only certified rust-resistant stock when available.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist to average, fertile to average, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; western white pine (Idaho white pine) is the state tree of Idaho — a magnificent five-needle pine that once dominated vast stretches of the northern Rocky Mountains and Cascades, forming some of the most majestic forest stands in North America. The trees are tall, narrowly pyramidal when young but developing a broad, somewhat irregular crown at maturity, with long (5–8 inch), bluish-green needles in bundles of five and distinctive, elongated, curved cones 5–12 inches long. The wood was once the most important commercial timber in Idaho and the Pacific Northwest — light, straight-grained, and ideal for fine millwork, matchsticks, and patterns. White pine blister rust (Cronartium ribicola), an introduced fungal disease, decimated western white pine populations throughout the 20th century. Breeding programs have produced rust-resistant varieties now used in restoration plantings. A beautiful, fast-growing ornamental for large landscape sites in cool, moist mountain climates.

common_name: Wesuwe Salvia (Early Long-Blooming Deep Violet-Blue Meadow Sage)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Wesuwe is an early-blooming, long-flowering Salvia nemorosa cultivar with deep violet-blue spikes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Wesuwe bears dense spikes of deep violet-blue flowers, opening earlier in spring than many meadow sage cultivars and continuing over an unusually long season, especially with prompt deadheading.
