Its sturdy, upright habit and rich color make it a reliable anchor for the front or middle of a sunny border. Shear spent flower spikes back by half after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Weyer's Butterfly Bush (Orange-Gold Globe-Flowered Buddleja Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; this hybrid butterfly bush blooms on new wood, so an annual hard cutback in late winter keeps it compact and encourages the heaviest flowering.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, and cut the entire shrub back hard, to within a foot or so of the ground, in late winter each year, since flowers form on new growth and a severe annual pruning keeps the shrub compact and floriferous rather than large and leggy. Buddleja x weyeriana is a cross between the familiar purple butterfly bush (B. davidii) and the yellow-flowered B. globosa, combining the long, arching bloom season of the former with rounded, ball-shaped flower clusters closer to the latter, opening in shades of warm orange, gold, and apricot from midsummer through fall. Like other butterfly bushes it is a magnet for butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds, and its distinctive globe-shaped flower clusters and unusual color range set it apart from the more common purple- and pink-flowered Buddleja davidii cultivars. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, and deadheading spent flower clusters through the season helps prolong the bloom display.

common_name: Whale Tongue Agave (Blue Whale Agave, Cadena de Plata)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in extremely well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Agave ovatifolia is one of the best-adapted agaves for zone 9a Texas and Gulf Coast landscapes — it handles the combination of intense summer heat, periodic drought, occasional freezes to 5°F, and alkaline clay soils better than most ornamental agaves, and its relatively large, symmetrical blue-gray rosette is one of the most architecturally impressive plants for xeric gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry soil, slightly elevated if in clay to prevent rot at crown; Whale Tongue Agave establishes quickly compared to many agaves and begins showing its distinctive character within 2–3 years; it rarely offsets (unlike many agaves) and is usually a solitary rosette; blooms once after 15–20 years then dies. Whale Tongue Agave is a spectacular ornamental agave native to the Sierra Madre Oriental mountains of northeastern Mexico (particularly Nuevo León state), where it grows on rocky limestone hillsides at elevations of 3,000–6,000 feet — an origin that gives it both excellent heat tolerance (hot summers) and remarkable cold hardiness (mountain winters to about 5–10°F). The common name 'Whale Tongue' describes the broad, paddle-like shape of each leaf: unlike the narrow, dagger-like leaves of most agaves, Whale Tongue's leaves are distinctively wide, somewhat spoon-shaped, and have a pronounced broadening toward the middle before tapering to a stout terminal spine — each leaf literally resembles a large, blue-gray whale tongue. The color is one of the most beautifully glaucous (blue-gray waxy powdery) of any agave, making the symmetrical 3–5 foot wide rosette a striking architectural centerpiece in any xeric planting. This species is particularly valued in Texas and the Gulf South because it tolerates the humid heat of summer better than many desert agaves, handles alkaline clay soils with good drainage better than most succulents, and provides bold structure with minimal care. Named for its entire leaf shape (Latin ovatifolius = oval-leafed). One of the top recommended agaves by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension.

common_name: Whale's Tongue Agave (Broad-Leaved Silvery Blue Agave)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil in full sun; Whale's Tongue Agave is notably more cold-hardy than many other agave species and forms a large, symmetrical rosette of broad, thick, powdery blue-gray leaves.
directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; agave requires perfect drainage and quickly rots in heavy clay or wet sites. Whale's Tongue Agave forms one of the boldest and most architectural rosettes among cold-hardy agave species, with wide, cupped, powdery blue-gray leaves that curve upward like a whale's tongue, giving strong sculptural presence in a xeric or Mediterranean-style garden. It is notably more cold-tolerant than many ornamental agave species, making it a good choice at the cooler edge of typical agave range, and it needs essentially no supplemental water once established beyond occasional deep soaking in extended drought. Like most agaves it is monocarpic, flowering once on a tall stalk after many years and then dying, though it may produce offsets (pups) before or after flowering that can be separated and replanted.

common_name: Wheat Celosia (Flamingo Feather, Plumosa Spike Celosia)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 2–4 weeks before last frost (celosia dislikes transplanting — use peat pots to minimize root disturbance) or direct sow after soil warms to 70°F; wheat celosia thrives in hot, humid conditions and is outstanding for zone 9 summer and early fall gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors 2–4 weeks before transplanting in peat pots, or direct sow after soil warms; plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil. Celosia spicata (wheat celosia) is distinct from the more familiar plumed celosia (C. argentea var. plumosa) and cockscomb (C. argentea var. cristata) in producing elegant, tapering, wheat-head-like flower spikes 3–4 inches long on upright, branching stems — the spikes are deep rose-pink to magenta-pink aging to silvery-white, creating a two-toned, naturalistic effect that looks right in both cottage-garden and cutting-garden contexts. The 'Flamingo Feather' series is the most widely grown cultivar group, producing uniform, graceful spikes excellent for cutting and drying. Unlike plumed celosias, wheat celosia has a lighter, more elegant texture that mixes naturally with other flowers rather than dominating the composition. It is drought-tolerant once established, thrives in summer heat, and provides long-lasting cut flowers that hold their color when dried. Zone 9: sow in March for summer bloom, again in August for fall color.

common_name: Wheat Celosia Flamingo Feather (Slender Spike Cockscomb for Drying)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Flamingo Feather celosia is a spicata type that grows in an elegant, more open, branching habit than cockscomb (cristata) or plume (plumosa) types, producing many narrow, wheat-like spikes per plant. In zone 9, plant April–June. The graceful, narrow spikes are valued for both fresh cutting and dried flower arrangements where the pale pink to rose-pink color and wheat-head form add texture without bulk.
directions: Direct sow 0.125 inch deep after last frost; thin to 8–14 inches. Flamingo Feather is a variety of Celosia argentea var. spicata — the wheat celosia type, distinctly different from the compact cockscomb (var. cristata) and the feathery plume types (var. plumosa). Spicata-type celosias produce many slender, elongated, cylindrical to slightly tapered flower spikes resembling wheat or barley heads, each spike 4–8 inches long, on branching plants that develop an open, airy architecture quite different from the dense, compact forms of other celosia types. Flamingo Feather's color is characteristic: the flower spikes emerge with a rosy-pink to salmon-pink coloration that fades gracefully to pale pink to cream as the spikes age — a color progression that adds visual interest to bouquets and arrangements over time. The wheat-like spikes hold their form beautifully when dried (hang upside down in a dry, dark location) and maintain good color, making Flamingo Feather one of the most valuable annual flowers for dried wreath and arrangement work. Fresh in vases, the elegant, slender spikes provide a soft, feathery texture contrast to the rounder forms of zinnias, sunflowers, and celosias of other types.

common_name: Wheee! Hosta (Intensely Wavy Twisted Green Margin)
plant_note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil. Wheee! is distinguished by intensely wavy, twisted green leaf margins unlike almost any other hosta.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partly to fully shaded site, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Wheee! bears solid green leaves with dramatically wavy, twisted, undulating margins, a lively, almost animated texture that sets it apart from the flatter-leaved hosta cultivars, living up to its playful exclamation-point name. It produces lavender flowers on scapes in summer, though the distinctive leaf texture is the main attraction. Mulch to conserve moisture and protect the shallow root system from summer heat, and divide congested clumps every several years in spring.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wheeler's Dwarf tolerates salt spray and coastal conditions well, making it a common choice near the Gulf.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wheeler's Dwarf tolerates coastal salt spray, wind, and poor soil better than many broadleaf evergreens, making it a reliable low hedge or foundation plant in Gulf Coast landscapes. This dwarf pittosporum forms a dense, mounding shrub of small, glossy, leathery, deep-green leaves rarely reaching more than 2 feet tall, with clusters of small, cream-white flowers in spring that carry a strong orange-blossom fragrance detectable from several feet away, the trait that gives the species its common name of mock orange. Its naturally low, tidy habit needs little shearing to maintain shape, and it holds up well to both heat and the Gulf Coast's high humidity. Prune, if needed, right after the spring bloom to preserve next year's flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Wherry's foamflower is a clumping, non-spreading species ideal where a well-behaved groundcover is needed without invasive spread.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Wherry's foamflower is a clumping species (unlike the stoloniferous T. cordifolia) and is better behaved in the garden without aggressive spreading, making it suitable for smaller shaded spaces. Tiarella wherryi is a native foamflower of the central and southern Appalachians producing deeply lobed, often bronze-veined, maple-like leaves in low mounds and slender spikes of small, delicate, white to pinkish flowers with prominent, thread-like stamens that give the flower spike its foamy appearance in mid-spring; the foliage often develops attractive burgundy or chocolate central veining or mottling that deepens in cool weather. It is an outstanding native groundcover for shaded rock gardens, woodland paths, and under-planted shrub borders; parent of many of the compact, non-running tiarella cultivars now popular in the trade.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 4–5 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; whipcord jack-in-the-pulpit is one of the tallest and most vigorous Arisaema species and benefits from a sheltered site out of strong wind.
directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 4–5 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; whipcord jack-in-the-pulpit is one of the tallest and most vigorous Arisaema species and benefits from a sheltered site out of strong wind. Arisaema tortuosum is a dramatic Himalayan species with a tall, mottled false stem supporting a whorl of large, divided leaflets and an upright green hooded flower topped by a long, twisted, whip-like appendage that curls distinctively above the foliage, blooming in early summer. Its imposing height and unusual, contorted flower spike make it one of the most architectural Arisaema species for a shaded border or woodland garden, standing well above the low mounding perennials typically grown nearby. It multiplies steadily by offsets from the tuber and self-sows modestly in favorable conditions, and, like other Arisaema, contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals that make all parts unpleasant to handle or ingest.

common_name: Whirligig Zinnia (Picotee Bicolor Cut-Flower Zinnia Mix)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; thin to spacing for good air circulation. Whirligig is grown for its picotee bicolor petal pattern, which gives blooms a pinwheel-like look.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost once the soil has warmed, thinning seedlings so plants have good air circulation. Whirligig is a zinnia mix known for its picotee patterning, where each semi-double to double bloom carries a contrasting band or tip color around the petal edge, giving the flowers a pinwheel-like look that sets it apart from solid-colored zinnia types. The bushy, roughly 20-inch plants produce abundant 3-4 inch flowers over a long summer season and respond well to regular cutting or deadheading. Like other zinnias it draws butterflies reliably and performs best in hot, sunny conditions with soil that isn't kept constantly wet.

common_name: Whirling Butterflies Gaura (Airy Long-Blooming White Wandflower)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Whirling Butterflies produces airy sprays of small white flowers on thin, wiry stems that dance in the slightest breeze, giving the plant its common name.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, since gaura resents wet, poorly drained soil, especially in winter. Whirling Butterflies produces masses of small, white, four-petaled flowers tinged with pink on tall, airy, wiry stems that seem to hover and flutter above the foliage like a cloud of small butterflies, blooming continuously from late spring through frost with minimal deadheading needed. Its deep taproot makes it exceptionally drought-tolerant once established but also means it resents being moved or divided, so choose its planting site carefully. It combines beautifully with bolder-textured perennials and ornamental grasses, adding lightness and movement to a sunny border.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; protect from afternoon sun in zone 8–9 to keep the white margin from scorching.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Whirlwind bears twisted, wavy-margined leaves with a green center and a crisp white edge, the distinctive twist giving the clump an animated, swirling texture unlike the flatter-leaved hostas around it. It is a moderately vigorous grower that increases into a well-formed mound over a few seasons. Pale lavender flowers rise on scapes in mid to late summer above the foliage. Divide congested clumps in early spring as new growth emerges, and site it where its unusual twisted form can be viewed up close along a path or bed edge.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile potting mix in full sun; Whirlwind is a vegetatively propagated selection bred for improved vigor and heat tolerance over older scaevola cultivars, performing especially well through Gulf South summer humidity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile potting mix in full sun after the last frost, and water consistently, since scaevola performs best without letting the root zone dry out completely between waterings. Whirlwind is a heat-tolerant, vigorously trailing fan flower selection producing an abundance of distinctive, one-sided, fan-shaped flowers in blue, purple, or white continuously from spring through frost, spilling attractively over the edges of hanging baskets, window boxes, and raised containers. Bred for stronger heat and humidity tolerance than older scaevola cultivars, it holds up notably well through the peak of Gulf South summer, when many trailing annuals decline, and requires no deadheading to keep blooming. Its long, trailing stems benefit from an occasional light trim if growth becomes overly leggy, encouraging fuller, more floriferous regrowth.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost date when soil has warmed to 55°F; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall-through-spring bloom. Whirlybird is compact and well-suited to containers, hanging baskets, and small garden spaces. Soak large seeds overnight before planting for faster germination. In zone 9 nasturtiums thrive in the cool season and decline with summer heat — let them reseed for fall germination.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, poor-to-moderate soil — nasturtiums bloom most profusely in lean soil; Whirlybird is an All-America Selections Award winner distinguished from standard trailing nasturtiums by its compact mound habit and spurless flowers that face upward (toward the viewer) above the foliage rather than hiding below the leaves like older varieties. The upward-facing semi-double flowers in a mix of cherry, tangerine, gold, mahogany, and cream shades make Whirlybird the most impressive nasturtium for cut flower use and garden display — the flowers are fully visible from above rather than requiring you to lift the leaves to appreciate them. The spurless character (no nectar spur) also means the flowers are technically easier to use as edible garnishes where the spur's somewhat bitter flavor is eliminated. Like all nasturtiums, the flowers, leaves, and seeds are edible — the peppery, watercress-like flavor of the leaves and the bright, slightly sweet-peppery flowers are popular in salads, compound butters, and as garnishes.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white angel's trumpet is the most widely cultivated Brugmansia species with the strongest fragrance. CAUTION: All parts are extremely toxic. Do not plant where children or pets have unsupervised access.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white angel's trumpet is the most fragrant and widely grown Brugmansia species, producing pendant, white, trumpet-shaped flowers up to 12 inches long with an intensely sweet, heady tropical fragrance most pronounced in the evening — one of the most powerfully scented flowers of any tropical plant. The fragrance on a warm summer evening can perfume an entire garden. Multiple flushes of bloom occur throughout the warm season. Like all Brugmansia, all parts are dangerously toxic — do not grow where children or curious pets have access. In zones 9–10, it grows as a large semi-evergreen shrub; in zone 8 it dies to the ground in winter and re-sprouts from the base. Heavy feeding with balanced fertilizer and consistent moisture produce the largest and most prolific flowers. Widely available in both white and cream-to-pale-yellow double-flowered forms.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white ash establishes readily and grows at a moderate to fast rate. Consider planting only where emerald ash borer biocontrol programs (parasitoid wasps) are active in your region.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white ash is a magnificent native canopy tree of eastern North American forests, producing large, compound leaves that turn exceptional shades of yellow, orange, and deep burgundy-purple in fall — among the finest fall color of any native tree. IMPORTANT: White ash is critically threatened across its entire range by the emerald ash borer (EAB), an invasive beetle from Asia that has killed hundreds of millions of ash trees since its detection in Michigan in 2002; all native Fraxinus species in North America are vulnerable. Planting is still worthwhile in areas where USDA-approved biocontrol programs using parasitoid wasps (Tetrastichus planipennisi and others) are actively established, as these programs are showing meaningful suppression in treated areas. Consult your state forestry agency or Cooperative Extension service for current EAB biocontrol status in your region before planting. The historically important wood — used for baseball bats, tool handles, and furniture — and the tree's exceptional ecological value as a host for hundreds of native insects make white ash worth preserving wherever possible.

common_name: White Autumn Sage (Pure White Everblooming Salvia greggii Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; 'Alba' has the same excellent drought and heat tolerance as other Salvia greggii cultivars — it performs best with lean soil and minimal supplemental irrigation once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; 'Alba' is the pure-white flowered cultivar of Salvia greggii (autumn sage), a Texas native subshrub that produces small, two-lipped, pure-white flowers in continuous flushes from spring through hard frost. The clean white color is distinctive in the Salvia greggii palette (which otherwise runs through red, pink, coral, salmon, and bicolor combinations) — providing a true white that is uncommon among drought-tolerant Texas native salvias and outstanding for brightening shaded edges of full-sun borders, for white-and-blue combinations with blue salvias (Blue Queen, Indigo Spires), and for white garden themes. 'Alba' has the same exceptional drought tolerance, heat performance, and wildlife value as the red-flowered Salvia greggii species — the white flowers attract hummingbirds, large carpenter bees, and numerous native bee species throughout the long bloom season. The semi-evergreen to deciduous shrub reaches 2–3 feet with a similar spread and benefits from a hard cutback to 6–8 inches in late winter to promote fresh, dense growth and abundant spring flowering. In zone 9, 'Alba' reliably overwinters and produces its best flowering in the spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) shoulder seasons; summer bloom continues in the heat but may be somewhat reduced. Light shearing after each main flush encourages continuous production.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for cold stratification and spring germination; or divide established clumps in early spring. White avens self-sows reliably in moist, shaded woodland gardens and naturalizes readily once established.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; white avens is a common but underappreciated native woodland perennial of rich forest floors and moist woodland edges across eastern North America. The small, five-petaled white flowers on branching stems in early summer are modest in size but individually elegant, producing burr-like seed heads with long, hooked styles that cling to passing animals for dispersal. The basal foliage consists of pinnately compound leaves with a large, rounded terminal leaflet — fresh green and attractive throughout the growing season. White avens self-sows freely in moist woodland soils to fill gaps in the native groundcover layer, functioning as both an ornamental and a highly effective colonizer of bare shaded ground. An excellent low-growing, self-sustaining native for difficult shaded spots where other plants struggle to establish from seed.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants or rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; white baneberry is very slow from seed (requiring two winters to break double dormancy) — purchase nursery stock only.
directions: Plant nursery-grown transplants or rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; white baneberry is very slow from seed (requiring two winters to break double dormancy) — purchase nursery stock only. Actaea pachypoda is a bold native perennial of eastern North American deciduous forests, producing large, compound, deeply toothed leaves and cylindrical clusters of white flowers with distinctive stamens in spring, followed by the plant's most dramatic feature: clusters of pure white berries, each with a prominent black dot, on thick red pedicels that remain on the plant into October, creating an eerie, memorable display. All parts of the plant — especially the berries — are highly toxic; the berries can cause cardiac arrest if eaten and must be kept away from children. An outstanding specimen for shaded native plant gardens, it is one of the most distinctive-looking native perennials in late summer.

common_name: White Bat Flower (Large White Bat Flower, Tacca Lily, White Devil's Tongue)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with high humidity; Tacca integrifolia requires the same deeply shaded, warm, humid conditions as its relative the Black Bat Flower (T. chantrieri), but produces flowers in white to pale purple rather than black, making it arguably even more ethereal in appearance. The bat-like bracts (4–6 inches wide) spread out like wings above the central flowers and the long, thread-like floral filaments can reach 20–28 inches. Needs consistently warm temperatures above 60°F and high humidity (60%+). Difficult but rewarding. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with consistently warm temperatures and high humidity — White Bat Flower is one of the most unusual and spectacular of all shade-loving tropical perennials, producing otherworldly flowers unlike those of any other commonly grown plant. Tacca integrifolia is a rhizomatous, evergreen perennial in the Taccaceae family (now often placed in Dioscoreaceae) native to the tropical forests of Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Borneo, India), a close relative of the Black Bat Flower (T. chantrieri) but producing flowers in white to pale lavender-purple rather than dark maroon-black. Both Tacca species are grown for the same extraordinary quality: the inflorescence, which consists of two large, wing-like bracts (modified leaves) 4–6 inches across spreading horizontally above the central cluster of small flowers like a bat's wings in flight, with long, thread-like appendages (filiform bracts) hanging 20–28 inches below — creating the impression of a ghostly bat hovering among the leaves. The overall color of T. integrifolia is white to pale green-white with occasional pale lavender or purple tints, giving it a more ethereal, moonlit quality compared to the dramatic darkness of T. chantrieri. Both the large bracts and the hanging filaments are characteristic of the genus. Tacca integrifolia grows from a shallow rhizome that spreads slowly in moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade. It produces large, glossy, undivided, broadly elliptic leaves 18–24 inches long that create an attractive foliage display year-round. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Surface-sow seed onto saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic peat or sand in fall, leaving seed uncovered since it needs light plus winter cold to germinate the following season.
directions: Surface-sow seed onto saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic peat or sand in fall, leaving seed uncovered since it needs light plus winter cold to germinate the following season. This small, wiry, tufted sedge produces distinctive bristly white beaked spikelets in summer that stand out against the dark peat of bogs and poor fens, and its abundant seed is foraged by waterfowl and sparrows through fall and winter. It is a characteristic, low-competition component of acidic bog and fen plant communities across the Great Lakes and Appalachian highlands, helping fill in bare peat and stabilize saturated substrates alongside sundews and pitcher plants. Best used in a constructed bog garden or wetland restoration planting rather than conventional garden soil.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, calcium-rich to neutral soil in deep shade; white bear sedge is a limestone-loving sedge of rich, moist, beech-maple-basswood forests of the eastern US Midwest. It germinates best after cold stratification.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, calcium-rich to neutral soil in deep to partial shade; white bear sedge is a distinctive native sedge of rich mesic forests over limestone, particularly common in the mixed mesophytic and beech-maple forest communities of the eastern US interior. The broad, flat leaves are unusually wide for a sedge — among the broadest of the native Carex — and have a soft, somewhat glaucous appearance. In the garden, white bear sedge excels as a ground layer plant under deciduous trees in rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil, where its lush, wide-leaved appearance provides a different texture from the finer-leaved wood sedge cultivars. It tolerates deep shade well and is semi-evergreen in mild winters. A good companion for mayapple, trillium, and other spring ephemerals in the shade garden.

common_name: White Beauty Fawn Lily (Large Recurved White Trout Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; White Beauty is a superior selection with larger, recurved white flowers with maroon-ringed centers and heavily mottled leaves.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it. White Beauty is a superior named selection of the California fawn lily, bearing larger, gracefully recurved white flowers marked with a distinctive maroon-brown ring at the throat, held above handsomely mottled, brown-and-green marbled leaves, one of the showiest and most sought-after selections in the genus. It naturalizes gradually in a cool, humus-rich woodland setting beneath deciduous trees, going summer-dormant after flowering. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs. Once established, it requires minimal care and slowly increases into an attractive spring-blooming colony.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Lactea' is propagated by cuttings to preserve its white-fruited trait, since seedlings often revert toward the species' typical magenta berry color.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil; 'Lactea' is a naturally occurring white-fruited selection of American beautyberry, identical to the wild species in habit, foliage, and pale lilac summer flowers but bearing clusters of translucent, ivory-white berries instead of the typical magenta-purple, for a strikingly different look against the same arching, deciduous stems. The pale berries persist into fall and are just as valuable to mockingbirds and other fruit-eating birds as the species type, though some gardeners note the paler fruit can be slightly less visible to foraging wildlife against green foliage. Because seed-grown plants frequently revert to the common purple-berried form, propagate only from rooted cuttings taken from a confirmed white-fruited plant to preserve the trait. Prune hard in late winter, as with the species, since flowers and berries form on the current season's new growth.

common_name: White Beautyberry (White-Berried Form of Native American Beautyberry Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; White Beautyberry produces the most prolific berry clusters in partial shade with morning sun — deep shade reduces berry production significantly, while full sun requires consistent moisture to prevent drought stress.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; White Beautyberry is the white-fruited selection of Callicarpa americana — the native American beautyberry that is one of the most striking native fruiting shrubs of the Gulf South, now in the unusual and elegant white-berry form that provides a distinct ornamental alternative to the standard vivid-purple berry clusters. The white (ivory to pale cream-white) berry clusters of 'Alba' are arranged in the same dense, tightly-packed rings around the stems at each leaf axil as the purple species — the distinctive whorled ring pattern that makes beautyberry unmistakable — but the white color creates a different visual effect: quieter and more sophisticated in combination with dark green foliage, and particularly effective in evening garden settings or combined with dark purple or burgundy companions where the contrast is strong. The berry clusters are produced abundantly in August through November, persisting on the bare stems into winter after the leaves fall, providing food for at least 40 species of songbirds and game birds. The leaves of American beautyberry contain callicarpenal, a compound with documented mosquito-repellent activity that has long been used in folk tradition. Beautyberry grows as a loose, arching shrub that benefits from hard pruning in late winter — cutting back by one-third to one-half stimulates vigorous new growth that produces the most prolific berry clusters in the same year. Self-sows in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Divide basal suckers in spring or plant large container-grown specimens in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white bird of paradise grows slowly to tree proportions and requires ample space — allow at least 10 feet on all sides for a mature specimen.
directions: Divide basal suckers or plant large container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; white bird of paradise is the giant tree-form relative of the familiar orange bird of paradise (S. reginae), developing massive, paddle-shaped, blue-green leaves up to 6 feet long on tall, bamboo-like trunks — producing a dramatic, tropical architectural effect in the landscape. The flowers are spectacular when they appear: large, boat-shaped spathe bracts of deep purple-blue cradle blue-and-white flower petals. The plant is extensively used as a dramatic indoor specimen (the most popular tropical foliage plant in US interior landscaping) and as an outdoor landscape focal point in zones 10–12. Tolerates partial shade and indoor low light better than most tropical trees, though outdoor plants in full sun are most vigorous. Outstanding as a large-scale specimen in courtyards, entrances, and pool gardens in zone 10–12 landscapes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination, or plant container-grown divisions in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun in spring; white blue-eyed grass is a prairie and glade species that tolerates drier, leaner soil than the more common blue-flowered Sisyrinchium species.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant container divisions in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; white blue-eyed grass grows in tallgrass prairies, limestone glades, and open woodland edges across the central and eastern US, producing the same grass-like, iris-family foliage as its blue-flowered relatives but with delicate white to pale lavender, yellow-centered flowers opening in mid-spring. It tolerates drier, leaner soil than the more common blue-eyed grass species, making it a good fit for a sunny prairie planting or rock garden rather than a consistently moist border. It self-seeds modestly in favorable open, sunny conditions, gradually forming small drifts, and combines well with other spring prairie natives like prairie phlox and golden alexanders.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; white boneset grows naturally in dry to moist, sandy, acidic, open pine woods, flatwoods, and sandhills of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain. It is better adapted to dry, sandy conditions than common boneset.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, sandy, lean, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; white boneset is a Coastal Plain native eupatorium of dry sandy pinewoods and sandhills, particularly common across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain from Virginia to Texas. Unlike the moisture-loving common boneset (E. perfoliatum), white boneset thrives in dry, sandy, acid soils of longleaf pine flatwoods — making it an outstanding native pollinator plant for dry, infertile, sandy soils where few other flowering perennials excel. The flat-topped clusters of pure white flowers in late summer attract an extraordinary diversity of small native bees, wasps, flies, beetles, and butterflies including both skippers and swallowtails. Plant in dry, sandy naturalistic garden settings in zone 9a where it requires almost no supplemental water once established.

common_name: White Burma Orchid (Snow-White Thunia, Phaius Thunia)
plant_note: Plant divisions or detached leafy stem sections in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained orchid bark and soil mix; Thunia alba is a deciduous orchid — its tall, reed-like canes grow actively in spring and summer, flower at the tips in early summer, then shed their leaves in fall as the canes die back, leaving dormant cane bases. Keep nearly dry through winter. Requires cool to moderate winter temperatures (45–60°F) for best performance. The terminal clusters of large white flowers in June–July are spectacular. Propagate from stem cuttings or by removing offsets. Zone 9 in containers; outdoors zone 10+. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil or orchid bark mix during the active growing season — White Burma Orchid grows vigorously in warm, humid conditions from spring through early fall and requires consistent moisture to develop its tall, leafy canes. Thunia alba is a deciduous terrestrial to semi-epiphytic orchid native to Myanmar (Burma), Yunnan Province of China, northeastern India, and Nepal in the Orchidaceae family, producing one of the most spectacular terminal flower displays of any terrestrial orchid relative to its size. The plant grows tall, upright, reed-like canes (2–4 feet) clothed in alternate, elliptical, gray-green leaves throughout the growing season. In early summer (June–July), the growing tip of the cane produces a large, pendant, multi-flowered inflorescence of 5–12 large (2–3 inch) flowers: pure white petals and sepals with a yellow-orange to orange, fringed lip decorated with purple veins — the combination of the pure white outer parts and the brightly colored, frilled, intricate lip creating a flower of considerable beauty. After blooming, the canes continue to grow slightly, then begin shedding leaves from the base upward as the plant enters dormancy. The leafless canes can be detached and rooted as cuttings — a convenient propagation method. A showy and relatively easy deciduous orchid for zone 9-11 with cool winters. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; white butterfly ginger is one of the most powerfully fragrant flowering plants cultivated in warm climates — the pure white, butterfly-shaped flowers releasing an intense, sweet, exotic fragrance that carries a considerable distance in evening air. It is the national flower of Cuba (known as Mariposa) and has naturalized throughout the tropical world. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a reliable perennial, dying back in winter and resprouting vigorously in spring. Thrives in moist, boggy conditions; can grow at pond margins.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; white butterfly ginger is regarded by garden enthusiasts in warm climates as one of the most intensely fragrant of all flowering plants — a native of the Himalayan foothills of India and Nepal (naturalized throughout tropical Asia, the Caribbean, and subtropical America) that produces in summer and autumn large, terminal spikes of pure-white, butterfly-shaped flowers with an extraordinarily powerful, sweet, exotic, slightly jasmine-like fragrance of unusual complexity and intensity that fills the garden air, particularly in the warm evenings when the fragrance intensifies and carries for considerable distances. The individual flowers are the distinctive hedychium form: a long, narrow, trumpet tube opening to three spreading, pure-white upper petals (the 'butterfly' shape) with a central, broad, pure-white labellum and two narrow, lateral staminodes creating the characteristic butterfly appearance. They are produced in succession on terminal spikes held above the long, lance-shaped, bright-green, ginger-family foliage for weeks in summer and fall. In zone 9 the rhizomes survive winter underground and resprout with considerable vigor each spring, producing clumps of erect, 5–7-foot stems by midsummer. Cuba named it the national flower under the name 'Mariposa' (butterfly). The national flower of Cuba and one of the quintessential plants of tropical and subtropical garden traditions worldwide.

common_name: White Calanthe (White Nun Orchid, Triple-Winged Calanthe, Evergreen Calanthe)
plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or container-grown divisions in spring in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Calanthe triplicata is one of the most cold-tolerant Calanthe species, surviving brief temperatures to 28–30°F with mulch protection in zone 9a. It is evergreen (unlike the deciduous Japanese ebine calanthes), requiring moisture year-round. The tall spikes of white flowers with orange-red centers are produced in spring. Excellent for naturalistic shade gardens under large trees. Divide every 3–4 years. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — White Calanthe thrives in the deep, moist, organic-rich conditions of a shaded garden bed under large trees and will decline in dry or sunny positions. Calanthe triplicata is a clump-forming terrestrial orchid with an exceptionally wide natural range — one of the most geographically widespread of all orchid species, native from Japan, China, and India through all of Southeast Asia to Australia, New Zealand, and many Pacific Islands in the Orchidaceae family. The plant produces robust, oval pseudobulbs and 3–4 broad, pleated, rich-green leaves (12–20 inches) per pseudobulb. In spring, one or more erect flower spikes 18–36 inches tall emerge from the base, each bearing 10–25 flowers in a showy raceme. The flowers are white to pure white, approximately 1.5 inches across, with the central lip distinctly yellow-orange to orange at the center and three-lobed — the 'triplicata' (triple) refers to this three-lobed lip structure. The two-toned white and orange center creates a clean, elegant flower display. As one of the most cold-tolerant of the Calanthe species (rated to zone 9), and as an evergreen species requiring no winter rest period, C. triplicata is among the most adaptable and reliable of the terrestrial orchids for zone 9-12 shade garden planting. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for spring germination, or sow in early spring; white campion self-seeds freely to naturalize and often behaves as a short-lived perennial or biennial in garden conditions.
directions: Sow direct in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; white campion self-seeds freely and often naturalizes in gardens, roadsides, and meadows without intervention once established. Silene latifolia (syn. Melandrium album) is a common European short-lived perennial or biennial weedy wildflower naturalized throughout North America; it produces softly hairy, sticky stems bearing oval leaves and sweetly fragrant, pure-white, 5-petaled flowers with deeply notched petals that open in the evening and at night, making it particularly attractive to moth pollinators. The nocturnal fragrance is delightful in the summer garden; white campion is an important pollinator plant and naturalizes beautifully in wildflower meadows and cottage-garden borders. Male and female flowers are on separate plants (dioecious); both are needed for seed production.

common_name: White Cedar (Pink Trumpet Tree, Variable-Leaf Tabebuia, Caribbean Lapacho)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Handroanthus heterophyllus is one of the more cold-tolerant Handroanthus species, surviving temperatures to 24–28°F with some damage. In zone 9, established trees produce reliable spring bloom and may recover well from cold damage. Like other trumpet trees, it blooms best on bare branches after a dry period. Semi-deciduous — the leaves drop before spring bloom in cool or dry conditions. The common name 'White Cedar' reflects historical Caribbean timber use; the wood is extremely hard and durable.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil — White Cedar is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in the sandy, alkaline soils of coastal Gulf and Florida landscapes. Handroanthus heterophyllus (formerly Tabebuia heterophylla) is a medium-sized, semi-deciduous flowering tree native to the Caribbean islands (Puerto Rico, Hispaniola, Cuba, Jamaica, and the Lesser Antilles) in the family Bignoniaceae, the national tree of Puerto Rico. The species name 'heterophyllus' (variable leaf) refers to the variation in leaf form on individual trees — sometimes simple, sometimes 3-leaflet, sometimes 5-leaflet compound. In spring, the tree produces clusters of large (3–4 inch), trumpet-shaped flowers in soft lavender-pink to light rose-pink, blooming on bare or nearly bare branches before the new leaf flush — the delicate pink coloration is softer and more pastel than the vibrant magenta-pink of H. impetiginosus, creating a distinctly elegant bloom display. The tree is widely used in Caribbean and tropical American landscapes as a medium-sized flowering shade tree, and has proven successful in zone 9 Gulf South conditions where its relative cold tolerance, drought adaptability, and spring flower display make it one of the better choices among the many beautiful but sometimes tender Handroanthus trumpet trees.

common_name: White Chiffon Rose of Sharon (Sterile Double-Flowered White Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; as a sterile triploid, White Chiffon sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance of older rose of sharon.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood, since bloom occurs on new growth. White Chiffon bears large, semi-double, pure white flowers with a soft, ruffled cluster of extra petals at the center that gives each bloom a fuller, more anemone-like look than the typical single rose of sharon flower, blooming from midsummer into fall. As a sterile selection, it produces almost no seed, sidestepping the self-sowing weediness that has given older rose of sharon a mixed reputation, while still delivering months of clean white color from a tough, low-maintenance shrub. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring when soil temperature reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant April–June. In zone 9 caladiums are perennial — leave tubers in the ground year-round in frost-free areas, but lift and store in mild zones where frost occurs. White Christmas is particularly striking in dappled shade under trees, where the bright white leaves illuminate dark areas. Reduce water and allow tubers to go dormant when foliage declines in fall; store at 60°F minimum if digging.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, acidic soil — caladiums require warmth above all else and tolerate deep shade better than most foliage plants; White Christmas is one of the most classic and enduring caladium cultivars, producing large, arrow-shaped leaves with dramatic nearly all-white blades set off by bright green veins and a narrow green margin — the effect of a mass planting under tree shade is startlingly bright and luminous, as the white leaves reflect available light and appear to glow in shade conditions where most plants would appear dull. Caladium is among the most effective plants for brightening dark, shaded areas of the landscape, and White Christmas is specifically sought for high-contrast shade planting because its white leaves provide the maximum illuminating contrast. The tropical foliage effect — large, bold, dramatic leaf patterns — also works extremely well in containers on shaded patios and porches. In zone 9 White Christmas performs as a reliable perennial, returning each summer from established tubers with increasing size and vigor each year.

common_name: White Cloud Muhly Grass (White-Flowered Gulf Coast Muhly Grass Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Cloud produces its best display in late September through November in the Gulf South — plant in spring for full development by fall bloom time.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Cloud is the pure-white-flowered cultivar of Gulf Coast muhly grass (Muhlenbergia capillaris) — producing the same spectacular fall display of airy, cloud-like flower and seed head masses as the standard pink-to-reddish-pink species, but in a pure, soft white rather than the warm pink-magenta of the species. The white flower clouds have a cool, ethereal quality — a mist of white above the fine-textured green foliage — that creates an entirely different aesthetic from the warm, romantic pink of standard muhly: White Cloud works beautifully in white-and-silver garden themes, with blue-violet companions (blue salvias, ageratum, fall asters), or in naturalistic plantings where a softer, more naturalistic tone is desired. The fall bloom season (September–November) is identical to the species — a time when few other native grasses or perennials are at peak display, making White Cloud outstanding for fall garden interest. Like the species, White Cloud is exceptionally drought-tolerant, adapted to full sun, and thrives in poor, lean soils where fertility is minimal and drainage is good. Shear close to the ground in late winter before new growth begins. White Cloud is native in origin, supports a wide range of native seed-eating birds through winter, and requires absolutely minimal maintenance once established.

common_name: White Cloud Texas Sage (White-Flowered Cenizo Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–8.0), lean soil in full sun; White Cloud absolutely requires excellent drainage — it will not tolerate standing water or heavy wet clay soil; plant in raised beds or berms in the humid eastern Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; White Cloud is the white-flowered cultivar of Texas sage (cenizo, Leucophyllum frutescens) — producing the same outstanding silver-gray, small, soft, woolly foliage and the remarkable humidity-triggered synchronized blooming behavior as the purple-flowered species, but with pure white flowers that create an entirely different aesthetic. The white-flowered display is particularly striking against the silver-gray foliage — an all-silver-and-white combination that has a cool, refined quality in contrast to the warm purple-on-gray of standard cenizo cultivars. White Cloud's bloom response to humidity or rainfall (a sudden mass flowering of white across the entire shrub following a rise in relative humidity or rain event) is one of the most dramatic natural phenomena in southwestern ornamental horticulture. The white flowers pair beautifully with blue-purple companion plants (blue salvias, Russian sage) for a traditional blue-and-white planting combination, and with ornamental grasses whose warm golden tones provide contrast. Like all Leucophyllum, White Cloud requires excellent drainage and lean soil — excessive water and fertility produce soft growth and reduce the tight, silver-gray character of the natural plant. In zone 9 west of the high-humidity coastal zone (San Antonio area, central Texas), White Cloud is exceptionally hardy and reliable; in the humid Gulf Coast proper, good drainage is essential.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; white colicroot grows naturally in acidic, seasonally wet savannas, flatwoods, and bogs and requires specific acidic, low-nutrient soil conditions — do not add lime or fertilizer.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or peaty, low-nutrient soil in partial shade to full sun; white colicroot is a native perennial of the eastern and southeastern US coastal plain and Piedmont, growing naturally in open, wet, acidic savannas, pine flatwoods, bogs, and roadside ditches, where it produces a flat basal rosette of smooth, pale-green, lance-shaped leaves and a tall, wand-like spike of small, mealy-white, tubular flowers with a distinctive bumpy, granular texture — the species name farinosa means 'floury' and refers to the rough, mealy surface of the flower tube. In bloom from May to August, the white wand-like spikes are one of the more distinctive and unusual native wildflower forms and are excellent for naturalistic planting with pitcher plants, sundews, and other bog-community species. The plant has a long history of use in traditional Appalachian and Native American medicine for digestive ailments. Never add lime, compost, or fertilizer to the planting site.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; white correa is the most salt-tolerant and coastal-hardy of the commonly grown correas — native to the exposed coastal cliffs and headlands of southeastern Australia where it experiences constant salt spray and wind. It blooms in autumn through winter, providing white star-shaped flowers when few other correas are in bloom. The dense, rounded habit with attractive silver-green foliage provides year-round interest.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; white correa differs from the pendant-tubular C. reflexa in producing starry, white, open, four-petaled flowers — the petals reflexing fully to create an open, flat, white star rather than a hanging tube. The flowers are produced in autumn through winter from terminal clusters on the tips of arching branches covered in attractive, oval, gray-green leaves with a slightly woolly or tomentose texture underneath. The overall effect of a plant in flower — masses of small, clean, white, four-petaled stars scattered across the dense mound of gray-green foliage — is simple and elegant. Native to the exposed, salt-sprayed coastal cliffs and headlands of southeastern Australia from New South Wales to South Australia and Tasmania, it is the most salt-tolerant and wind-resistant of all the commonly grown correas — thriving in positions that defeat most ornamental shrubs. An excellent, reliable plant for coastal gardens in zone 9 where salt spray, wind, and lean, sandy soil combine to limit the range of ornamental shrub choices. Provides winter flowers, attractive foliage, and year-round bird habitat.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–May. Plant with the neck of the bulb at or just below soil surface — do not bury too deep. Crinum x powellii 'Album' is among the most cold-hardy of all crinum lilies, tolerating temperatures to about 5°F when the bulbs are well-mulched — hardy in zones 7–10 as a permanent landscape bulb. In zone 9 it is essentially evergreen, with the large, strap-like foliage persisting through mild winters. Established clumps multiply freely; dig and divide offsets every 4–5 years when blooming declines. The large bulbs resent disturbance once established — site carefully and allow permanent placement.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Crinum x powellii 'Album' adapts to a wide range of soil and light conditions and is one of the most versatile large bulbs for zone 9; White Crinum is one of the most reliably large and spectacular summer-blooming bulbs for Southern gardens, producing huge, fragrant, pure white funnel-shaped flowers (4–5 inches across) on tall, sturdy scapes that emerge above the broad, strap-like foliage in July and August — the peak of summer when most spring bulbs are long finished and fall-blooming plants have not yet begun. Crinum x powellii 'Album' is a hybrid between two South African species that has proven exceptionally cold-hardy for a crinum, extending the growing range well north of most other crinum lilies. The pure white, lily-like flowers (each scape bears 6–12 blooms in succession) are powerfully fragrant in the evening — a feature that makes White Crinum particularly effective near patios, walkways, and outdoor living areas where the fragrance can be appreciated. As a permanent, low-maintenance, long-lived landscape bulb for zone 9 that returns reliably year after year and gradually multiplies into impressive clumps, White Crinum fills the large-scale, summer-blooming bulb niche with a kind of reliable permanence that annual summer bulbs cannot match.

common_name: White Diamonds Hydrangea (Sturdy Upright White Panicle Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the plant room to reach its full mature size as a large specimen shrub or small tree form. White Diamonds bears large, conical, pure white flower panicles on strong, rigid stems that stay upright through summer storms without staking, aging to a soft pink blush by fall. Its vigorous, well-branched, tree-like habit can be trained as a small single- or multi-stem specimen tree as well as grown as a large shrub, giving it more design flexibility than more compact panicle hydrangea cultivars. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing bloom; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.

common_name: White Dome Hydrangea (Lacecap Flat-Headed Smooth Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; White Dome is a lacecap-form smooth hydrangea, an airier alternative to the rounded mophead form of Annabelle.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. White Dome bears large, flat, lacecap-form flower heads with showy sterile white florets ringing a center of smaller fertile flowers, a more open, naturalistic look and much better resistance to flopping in rain than the heavy round mophead form of Annabelle-type smooth hydrangeas. It blooms reliably on new growth each year regardless of winter cold, so bloom performance isn't at risk from bud damage. Cut stems back hard, to 12-18 inches, in late winter to encourage a fresh flush of sturdy flowering stems.

common_name: White Doves Camellia (Compact Small-Flowered White Sasanqua)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; White Doves is a compact, spreading sasanqua camellia bearing small, anemone-form white flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. White Doves is a compact, spreading sasanqua camellia producing an abundance of small, pure white, anemone-form flowers with a fluffy center of golden stamens in a heavy fall flush, offering delicate, dove-like blooms when little else is in flower. Its manageable, spreading habit fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders without the size of many larger camellia cultivars. Like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica, blooming well in partial shade to full sun. Prune only lightly to shape after flowering, since flower buds set later in the growing season.

common_name: White Duranta (White-Flowered Golden Dewdrop Shrub with Golden Berries)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; the golden-yellow berries of Duranta are toxic if eaten by humans and pets — plant away from areas where berry consumption is likely.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; White Duranta ('Alba') is the white-flowered form of golden dewdrop (Duranta erecta) — a widely grown tropical shrub native to the Americas that produces arching, cascading branches of small, white flowers (rather than the blue-purple of the species) followed by the showy strings of golden-yellow berries that give the plant its common name 'golden dewdrop'. The white flower and golden berry combination creates an elegant, clean color scheme distinct from the blue-and-gold of standard Duranta. Duranta is one of the most important butterfly and hummingbird plants for Gulf South gardens — the flowers attract monarch butterflies, queen butterflies, sulphur butterflies, and a wide range of native bees throughout the long bloom season (summer through fall), making it an outstanding pollinator plant in full-sun borders and along fence lines. The golden-yellow berry clusters persist through fall and are consumed by mockingbirds, catbirds, and other frugivorous birds. In zone 9, Duranta grows as a perennial shrub in protected locations, often killed to the ground by hard freezes but returning vigorously from the roots in spring. The fast-growing, arching habit means established plants can reach 6–8 feet in a single warm season. The berries are toxic if eaten — a caution for households with small children or pets that might be attracted to the colorful fruits.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; white edge sedge is a graceful native woodland sedge that tolerates both drier upland shade and consistently moist woodland soil.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; white edge sedge is a graceful eastern woodland native with slender, arching foliage and delicate, drooping flower spikes in late spring that give the plant a soft, airy texture distinct from the stiffer, more upright habit of many other sedges. Growing naturally in deciduous forest understory across a range of moisture conditions, from drier upland woods to moist bottomland, it adapts well to typical shade garden soil without demanding consistently wet ground. It combines nicely with ferns, wildflowers, and other native shade perennials, adding fine textural contrast to bolder-leaved companions. Established plants need little maintenance beyond routine watering during extended dry spells; leave old foliage in place over winter and tidy up in early spring before new growth emerges.

subcategory: Egyptian sacred night-blooming aquatic water lily
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring in full sun in aquatic pots with heavy clay loam under 6–18 inches of warm water in zone 9–12; the White Egyptian Lotus is a tropical night-blooming water lily native to the Nile Delta, East Africa, and Southeast Asia — one of the most ancient sacred aquatic plants in human history — bearing large, fragrant, white flowers with prominent yellow stamens that open at dusk and close by midmorning.
directions: Plant Nymphaea lotus tubers in heavy, unamended clay loam in large aquatic pots submerged under 6–18 inches of warm water in full sun; top-dress monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets and maintain water temperatures above 65°F for active growth; lift tubers and overwinter indoors in a bucket of water in zone 9 and colder. The White Egyptian Lotus is a night-blooming tropical water lily sacred in ancient Egyptian religion and art — depicted extensively on temple walls, papyrus scrolls, and tomb paintings, where it symbolized creation, rebirth, and the sun. Unlike the Blue Lotus (Nymphaea caerulea) which opens at sunrise, Nymphaea lotus opens at dusk and closes the following morning; flowers are strongly fragrant, white to pale pink at the tips, 6–10 inches across, and held well above the water on strong stalks. The toothed, slightly wavy leaf margins distinguish Nymphaea lotus from other white water lilies. Native to the Nile Delta and East Africa, the species has also become naturalized throughout Southeast Asia where it grows wild in rice paddies and irrigation canals. In zone 9, overwinter as for other tropical water lilies; in zone 10–12, it may persist year-round in garden ponds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 10–12; White Elephant Palm is an extremely rare, slow-growing, understory fan palm endemic to just two forest areas in peninsular Thailand (Khao Nor Chuchi in Krabi Province) — critically endangered in the wild — producing a crown of large, circular fan fronds with brilliant white undersides that flash silvery-white when the fronds move in the wind.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly to strongly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Kerriodoxa elegans requires consistently moist, humid, shaded conditions — protect from direct sun, cold below 45°F, and dry winds; the white frond undersides are the primary ornamental feature and must be positioned where they can be viewed from beneath. Kerriodoxa elegans (White Elephant Palm or Elegant Kerriodoxa) is an exceptionally rare, slow-growing, monotypic fan palm endemic to an extremely restricted habitat: the lowland rainforests of Khao Nor Chuchi and one or two adjacent forest areas in Krabi Province, peninsular Thailand, making it one of the rarest palms in the world by natural distribution — classified as Critically Endangered by IUCN. The name 'White Elephant Palm' references both the rarity (white elephants being considered sacred and extremely rare in Thai culture) and the striking ornamental feature: large, circular fan fronds (2–3 feet across) with deep-green upper surfaces and brilliant, chalky-white to silver-white lower surfaces — when the fronds move in a breeze, the alternating flash of green and white is spectacular. The palm is short to medium-trunked, reaching 10–15 feet in cultivation over many years, with a compact, elegant habit. Primarily of interest to specialized tropical palm collectors and botanical gardens. Always purchase nursery-propagated specimens — never wild-collected.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; white enkianthus stays more compact than redvein enkianthus and works well as a foundation shrub or low hedge in an acidic-soil shade garden.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; white enkianthus stays more compact than redvein enkianthus and works well as a foundation shrub or low hedge in an acidic-soil shade garden. Enkianthus perulatus is a compact Japanese shrub with fine-textured foliage and clusters of small, pure white, urn-shaped flowers dangling beneath the branches in mid-spring, followed by outstanding fall color that ranges from bright red to orange-scarlet, among the most reliable fall foliage displays of any acidic-soil shrub. Its smaller size compared with redvein enkianthus makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, low hedges, or the middle layer of an azalea and rhododendron border in partial shade. It needs the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil as its relatives and requires little pruning beyond removing any dead or crossing branches.

subcategory: Pacific Northwest native shade spring bulb
plant_note: Plant corms in fall 3–4 inches deep in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in zone 4–8; White Fawn Lily (Oregon Fawn Lily) is a graceful, spring-blooming native bulb of Pacific Northwest open woodland and forest edges from Vancouver Island and western Oregon to northern California — producing beautiful, reflexed, pure-white flowers with creamy-yellow centers above pairs of handsomely mottled, bronzy-green and silver-grey leaves.
directions: Plant Erythronium oregonum corms in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; keep consistently moist in spring and allow to dry out somewhat in summer during dormancy; plant in colonies of 10–25 for the best naturalistic effect; mark planting areas as the plants disappear completely by midsummer. White Fawn Lily is one of the most elegant of all Pacific Northwest native wildflowers — blooming early in spring before the tree canopy leafs out in the dappled shade of western red cedar, Douglas-fir, and bigleaf maple forests. The reflexed, nodding flowers with their upswept petals (resembling the style of a Turk's Cap lily) are pure white with bright yellow anthers and a cream-yellow center; below the flower, a pair of broad, succulent leaves with beautiful maroon-and-silver mottling emerges from the ground. Naturally forms spreading colonies from corm offsets and self-sowing; in suitable woodland garden conditions it will slowly naturalize and spread to carpet large areas. The mottled leaves are among the most attractive foliage patterns in spring bulbs. An outstanding companion for Trillium, native ferns, Dicentra, and spring wildflowers in Pacific Northwest woodland gardens; tolerates more summer moisture than many Erythronium species.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; white fir is the most drought-tolerant of the native North American firs, adapting to drier, more continental conditions than other firs. More tolerant of heat and drought stress than Engelmann spruce or balsam fir.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; white fir is among the most elegant and garden-worthy of the native North American firs — notable for its long, curved, distinctively blue-gray to blue-green needles that are arranged in a beautifully symmetrical pattern on each branch. The blue-gray form (sometimes called 'concolor fir' in the nursery trade) has striking, ice-blue foliage that rivals Colorado blue spruce in color intensity but with a much more graceful habit. White fir is significantly more drought tolerant than most firs, native to the drier mountain forests of the Sierra Nevada, Rocky Mountains, and Great Basin from Colorado to southern California. The Christmas tree industry uses white fir as an alternative to Fraser and balsam firs in western states, and it is one of the premier ornamental firs for large landscape settings in the West. Relatively more tolerant of dry summers than other firs.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after temperatures are reliably above 50°F in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; white firespike is even more shade tolerant than red firespike and performs beautifully as an understory plant under large shade trees in humid Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; white firespike is a lesser-known but equally attractive relative of the scarlet-flowered firespike (Odontonema tubaeforme), producing tall, graceful spikes of pure white tubular flowers on dark, glossy-leaved plants in late summer and fall. It is an outstanding shade-garden perennial for zone 9–12, providing important late-season white flower color in deep shade conditions where most other white-flowering plants require more light. The white flowers are particularly effective at brightening dark corners of the garden and glow beautifully in evening light. Like red firespike, it grows most vigorously and productively in the bright shade of large trees or pergolas; it is somewhat more cold-sensitive than the red species and benefits from mulching in zone 9. Propagate from stem cuttings taken in summer. White firespike is less commonly available than red firespike but increasingly offered by specialty nurseries in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, acidic, peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; never collect plants from the wild — source only from reputable native plant nurseries with documented propagation.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, acidic, peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade, never from wild-collected stock. White fringed orchid is one of the showiest native bog orchids of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, producing a dense spike of pure white flowers in mid to late summer, each bloom trimmed with a delicately fringed lip that gives the species its name, rising above narrow grass-like leaves in open, sunny sphagnum bogs and wet pine savannas. It grows alongside pitcher plants and sundews in the wild and makes a spectacular companion for them in a home bog garden, though like most native orchids it depends on specific soil mycorrhizal fungi and resents root disturbance, so leave established plantings undisturbed once sited. Keep the growing medium constantly wet using rain water or distilled water, since mineral-laden tap water and ordinary fertile soil are both fatal to bog orchids over time.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped specimens in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; white fringetree establishes slowly but is long-lived and exceptionally adaptable once rooted in. It is dioecious — female plants produce ornamental blue-black fruits attractive to wildlife if a male is nearby, though both sexes flower showily. Seed requires warm stratification followed by cold stratification and may take 18 months to germinate; nursery-grown transplants are strongly preferred.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; white fringetree is one of the most spectacular native flowering trees of the eastern United States, erupting in late April and May in airy, drooping panicles of pure-white, strap-like petals that give the effect of shimmering white fringe covering the entire canopy — often before or just as the leaves emerge, which amplifies the floral display dramatically. Chionanthus virginicus is dioecious: female plants produce loose clusters of olive-sized, blue-black, grape-like fruits in late summer that are highly attractive to birds, particularly thrushes, mockingbirds, and waxwings; male plants typically produce slightly showier and more fragrant flower clusters. Exceptionally adaptable to a wide range of soil types including clay, loam, and sandy soils, and tolerant of urban conditions, air pollution, and occasional flooding once established — making it an outstanding choice for residential landscapes, streetscapes, and naturalistic borders throughout zones 3–9. Grows slowly at 6–10 inches per year; patience yields a magnificent specimen that can live for decades with virtually no maintenance.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall where plants are to grow, or allow existing plants to self-sow freely; white fumewort self-sows into cracks and crevices in walls, steps, and paving where it often thrives better than in cultivated soil. It tolerates dry shade under trees. Unlike blue-flowered C. flexuosa, this species blooms continuously from spring through fall without a summer rest.
directions: Sow seeds in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; white fumewort is one of the finest and most long-blooming shade perennials available — a European native producing delicate, finely divided, blue-green foliage resembling bleeding heart or maidenhair fern, topped continuously from April through November with clusters of small, tubular flowers in creamy-white with a yellow tip. Unlike many shade perennials with limited bloom seasons, this species is genuinely in flower for most of the growing season in mild climates, filling the shade garden with a constant veil of soft white. It is a natural wall and pavement plant, spontaneously colonizing cracks in stone, brick, and mortar where it often self-sustains indefinitely, and is particularly charming growing from walls and between paving stones where organic soil would be unsuitable. Related to the blue C. flexuosa and yellow C. lutea, it occupies the same garden role as the yellow species but in white — longer-blooming and more shade-tolerant than many competitors.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant in spring into well-drained soil.
directions: White gaura brings airy elegance with long, delicate stems and butterfly-like white blooms that dance in the breeze above the foliage. Start seed indoors 8 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun and lean, well-drained soil. Its deep taproot makes it drought-tolerant once established, so avoid soggy ground and heavy feeding. Cut back spent flowering stems to encourage a fresh flush of bloom through summer and fall. Hardy in zones 5 to 9, it adds graceful height and motion to beds and borders.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–4 inches deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun after soil warms above 60°F; white ginger lily thrives in dappled light under tall trees and along stream banks in zone 7–11.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 2–4 inches deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered light in spring after soil warms above 60°F; white ginger lily is outstanding for Gulf Coast and zone 7–11 gardens where its intensely fragrant butterfly-white flowers perfume the garden in late summer and fall with one of the sweetest scents in the plant world. The tall, reed-like stems with broad tropical-looking leaves create bold textural interest from late spring through frost, making it an excellent specimen and a striking backdrop in mixed borders.
