Unlike the more familiar purple-leaved Oxalis triangularis ('purple shamrock'), O. regnellii has bright, clean green foliage that is cooler and more restrained in its effect, yet equally attractive. It grows from small, segmented, rhizome-like tubers that multiply into colonies over time; in zone 9, it is perennial outdoors in protected shaded spots, going dormant in extreme cold or heat and resprouting from tubers. It is also outstanding as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant, blooming through much of the year indoors. The foliage closes at night and reopens in morning light — a 'sleep movement' (nyctinasty) characteristic of the Oxalis genus.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or autumn; plant at the same depth and water in well.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in any reasonably moist, well-drained soil, where it will form tidy, slowly spreading clumps of hairy, grass-like foliage. This woodrush tolerates a wider range of conditions than many of its relatives, including brief dry spells and more heat, making it a practical groundcover under deciduous trees. Divide established clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor and to propagate new plants; divisions establish readily when kept moist for the first few weeks. The loose white flower panicles that appear in early summer add a delicate, airy texture to the shade garden before fading to tan seed heads.

plant_note: Surface-sow and press in; seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Press the fine seed onto the soil surface without burying it, as light aids germination. This native heirloom yarrow bears flat clusters of white flowers above soft, feathery, aromatic foliage. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in full sun and lean, well-drained soil. Deadhead to prolong bloom and divide clumps every few years; the flowers are valued in medicinal and dye gardens and dry well for arrangements.

plant_note: Plant container-grown camellias in fall (September–November in zone 9); fall planting allows root establishment before the winter-spring bloom season. Camellias strongly prefer acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5); test and amend soil if needed before planting. Do not plant too deeply — the crown should be at or slightly above soil level. In zone 9 camellias bloom October through March, with peak flowering December–February — providing the only large, colorful blooms in the landscape during the coldest months. Avoid planting in locations with afternoon western sun, which can cause petal browning on open flowers in warm spells.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered light — camellias prefer the bright, indirect light of open shade under tall pines or high-branched trees, avoiding deep shade or full afternoon sun; White by the Gate is a registered Camellia japonica cultivar producing elegant white flowers in the formal double or peony form that represents one of the most refined and sophisticated floral displays available from any landscape shrub in zone 9's winter garden. The pure white flowers — whether formal double, semi-double, or peony form — provide a clean, luminous, refined contrast to the dark, glossy, evergreen foliage of the camellia shrub, creating a winter display of formal elegance that has made white camellias a staple of Southern estate and garden district plantings for generations. Camellia japonica is one of the defining landscape plants of the American Gulf South — thriving in the same partial shade, acidic, well-drained conditions that characterize the longleaf pine and mixed hardwood forests native to the region. The combination of large (3–6 inch) formal flowers in January–March when nothing else of comparable size or quality blooms in the landscape, glossy evergreen foliage year-round, and the exceptional longevity of well-sited camellias (specimens over 100 years old are documented in the Gulf South) makes camellia japonica cultivars essentially irreplaceable in zone 7–9 winter garden design.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum bog medium in full sun; keep standing in pure rain water or distilled water — white pitcher plant is a Gulf Coast native that performs reliably in zones 7–9 outdoor bog gardens.
directions: White-top pitcher plant may be the most visually stunning of all native North American pitcher plants — its tall, erect pitchers are dramatically bi-colored with deep green lower tubes transitioning to brilliant, white, red-veined upper sections that function as translucent windows to attract and confuse trapped insects attempting to escape. It is endemic to the Gulf Coastal Plain of Alabama, Florida panhandle, Georgia, Mississippi, and Louisiana, where it grows in open, frequently burned, wet longleaf pine savannas — one of the most threatened habitats in North America, having lost over 97% of its original extent. White pitcher plant grows second pitchers in fall (alongside the primary summer pitchers) that are among the most ornamental of any carnivorous plant in the autumn garden, and the spectacular crimson flowers in spring are pollinated by queen bumblebees. A critical conservation indicator species, white pitcher plant should only be purchased from reputable nurseries propagating from cultivated stock; wild populations are legally protected and ecologically irreplaceable. Grow in an outdoor bog garden in full sun for the most impressive pitcher development.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall on the surface of moist, acidic soil; the distinctive white phyllary bracts are visible even before flowers open and help confirm identification in the garden.
directions: White-bracted Thoroughwort is a native perennial of wet, acidic meadows, bogs, and coastal plain pinelands with a range extending from Massachusetts south to Florida, making it one of the more cold-hardy wet-soil Eupatoriums available to northern gardeners. The flat-topped clusters of white composite flowers that appear in late summer and fall are distinguished by strikingly bright white phyllary bracts that give the plant an unusually crisp, clean appearance compared to other species in the genus. Grow in moist to wet, sandy or peaty, acidic soil in full sun and pair with other wet meadow natives for a naturalistic rain garden or low-area planting that provides exceptional late-season support for native bees and butterflies.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, well-drained soil with the crown set just below the soil surface; keep the root zone shaded and cool with a thick layer of mulch, and provide a trellis or fence for the twining stems to climb.
directions: White-leaf Leather Flower is a twining native perennial vine of moist woodland edges, stream banks, and thickets in the southeastern United States, instantly recognizable by the striking glaucous — blue-gray and waxy-white — undersurfaces of its leaves that flash silver whenever a breeze stirs the foliage. In spring it bears nodding, urn-shaped flowers with recurved purplish-pink to rose petals, followed by showy, feathery silvery seed heads in fall that extend the ornamental season well into winter. Grow in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, keeping the root zone cool and consistently moist; it climbs by twining leaf petioles and benefits from a sturdy support. The glaucous foliage sets it apart from all other native clematis and makes it a distinctive choice for moist fencerows and woodland garden edges in zones 5-9.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in dry to average, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; white-tinged sedge is more drought-tolerant in dry shade than most native sedges and establishes readily from divisions.
directions: Plant divisions in spring or fall in dry to average, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; white-tinged sedge is more drought-tolerant in dry shade than most native sedges and establishes readily from divisions. Fine, wiry, arching blue-green leaves form small, tidy tufts that spread gradually into a loose, informal groundcover under oaks and pines, with inconspicuous flower spikes in spring that give way to small, pale, silvery-tinged seed heads. It is among the more drought-tough native sedges once established, tolerating the dry, root-filled soil of established woodland far better than moisture-loving sedge species, and needs no mowing, fertilizing, or irrigation in a naturalized planting. Use it as a fine-textured lawn substitute or filler between larger shade perennials in dry woodland gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring, or set out divisions, into consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy soil such as roadside ditches, wet pine savannas, and pond margins.
directions: Direct sow in early spring, or set out divisions, into consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy soil such as roadside ditches, wet pine savannas, and pond margins. This low rosette-forming fleabane sends up airy stems topped with abundant small white-rayed, yellow-centered flowers in spring and early summer, providing an early nectar source for small native bees and syrphid flies before many summer wildflowers begin blooming. It spreads modestly by short rhizomes and self-seeding to form loose drifts in wet meadow plantings. Keep soil damp through establishment; it does not tolerate prolonged drought once mature growth has begun.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, sandy, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white-topped sedge grows naturally in the wet pine flatwoods, bogs, and seepage slopes of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain. Excellent in rain gardens and wet-site landscapes in zone 9.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, sandy or peaty, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; white-topped sedge is one of the most ornamentally distinctive native sedges of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, producing a starburst of narrow white bracts (leaf-like structures) surrounding the inconspicuous true flowers — creating a bold, star-shaped white ornamental display that is visually striking from a distance. The white bracts are produced prolifically on rush-like, fine-textured dark green foliage from late spring through summer. It grows naturally in wet, sandy, acidic flatwoods and boggy seepage slopes of the coastal plain from Maryland to Texas. In rain gardens, pond margins, and boggy areas in zone 9, it is a superb native ornamental that blooms when few other wetland plants have such visual impact. The plant spreads by rhizomes to form attractive colonies in appropriate wet conditions. A non-showy but excellent addition to native-themed wet gardens.

plant_note: Plant seeds (stratified) or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky, lean to average soil in full sun; whitebark pine is a keystone subalpine species growing at treeline and requiring cold winters, cool summers, and excellent drainage. Threatened by blister rust, mountain pine beetle, and climate change. Plant only rust-resistant stock from reputable sources.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring (use only rust-resistant certified stock) in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky, lean to average soil in full sun; whitebark pine is a keystone subalpine species of the highest Rocky Mountain treeline zones — one of the most ecologically critical trees in the western mountain ecosystem, providing essential high-calorie seeds for grizzly bears (up to 50% of pre-denning grizzly diet in some years), black bears, Clark's nutcrackers, and many other wildlife species. The tree has no seed wing — its seeds cannot be wind-dispersed; instead Clark's nutcracker (Nucifraga columbiana) is the primary and essentially only effective seed disperser, harvesting thousands of seeds per bird per year and caching them in groups that, when uncollected, establish new trees. Severely threatened — white pine blister rust, mountain pine beetle, and climate change have killed the majority of whitebark pines in many areas. Listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act in 2022. Ancient trees at treeline grow as wind-sculpted krummholz mats no taller than the winter snow. One of the most ecologically important trees in the western US.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification over winter for spring germination; Pycnanthemum albescens prefers well-drained to dry, average to poor soil in full to partial sun and is notably drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Pycnanthemum albescens is a coastal plain endemic of the southeastern US with striking silvery-white leaf bracts that surround and contrast dramatically with the small purple flowers in mid- to late summer, creating a two-toned effect visible from a distance. It is among the most valuable native plants for pollinators, drawing extraordinary numbers of native bees, wasps, beneficial flies, and butterflies to its long-blooming flower clusters. Direct sow seeds in fall on the soil surface without covering, as they need light and cold stratification; seedlings transplant poorly so sow in place. Once established, the plant is drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, well-drained soils with little or no supplemental irrigation.

common_name: Whiteleaf Sunflower (Southern Appalachian Endemic Woodland-Gap Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Whiteleaf Sunflower is a rare Southern Appalachian endemic with waxy, white-undersided leaves, adapted to woodland gaps rather than open prairie.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, in a woodland-edge or clearing setting rather than open prairie. Whiteleaf Sunflower is a rare endemic of the Southern Appalachian Mountains, considered vulnerable across its limited range, distinguished by leaves with a striking waxy, white-glaucous underside that contrasts sharply with the deep green upper surface, an ecologically distinct woodland-gap species among perennial sunflowers, most of which are open-prairie or meadow specialists. It bears typical bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads in late summer, drawing bees and butterflies, followed by seed heads valuable to goldfinches and other birds. Its shade tolerance makes it a useful native option for a woodland clearing or partly shaded native garden where open-prairie sunflower species would struggle. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring if increase is wanted.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; whitetop sedge grows naturally in wet pine savannas, bog margins, and seepage wetlands of the Coastal Plain from North Carolina to Texas. It requires consistently moist to wet, acidic, low-nutrient soil.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, nutrient-poor soil in full sun to partial shade; whitetop sedge is one of the most ornamentally striking native wetland sedges of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, creating a spectacular display in late spring and summer when the broad, white-tipped bracts (modified leaves) surrounding the flower heads turn brilliant white — creating the illusion that the plant is covered in large, pure white flowers. The white coloration comes from the dramatically broadened, leaf-like bracts that subtend the small true flowers, a feature unique to the genus Rhynchospora. In naturalistic wet gardens, rain gardens, pond margins, and bog plantings in zones 7–10, whitetop sedge provides exceptional ornamental interest that no other native plant can match. The white display lasts for weeks and brightens moist, shaded areas dramatically. Requires consistently wet, acidic, low-nutrient soil similar to a pine flatwood.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Whitewater combines a graceful weeping habit with heart-shaped leaves boldly marked in white and cream, giving it striking multi-season interest beyond the typical redbud's spring flower display.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting where its cascading branches have room to arch downward without crowding. Whitewater is a weeping redbud cultivar whose branches cascade gracefully from a central leader, giving it a fountain-like silhouette distinct from the typical vase-shaped redbud form. In early spring, the bare, pendulous branches are covered in the classic rosy-pink pea-like flowers typical of the species, followed by heart-shaped leaves heavily variegated in white and cream over green, a striking combination that provides ornamental interest all summer rather than just during the brief spring bloom. Because variegated foliage photosynthesizes less efficiently than solid green leaves, growth is somewhat slower than standard redbud cultivars, and the tree stays more compact, making it a good choice for smaller landscapes or as a specimen near a patio where its cascading, patterned foliage can be appreciated up close. Provide afternoon shade in zone 8-9 to prevent leaf scorch on the variegated foliage, and plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are highly susceptible to rot in wet sites.

common_name: Whitney Snake Plant (Dwarf Silver-Green Mottled Sansevieria)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Whitney is a dwarf, rosette-forming snake plant well suited to small containers, dish gardens, and windowsill growing.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix. Whitney forms a low, dense rosette of broad leaves mottled in silvery gray-green, a dwarf, compact form that stays well under a foot tall and wide, making it well suited to a small pot, dish garden, or windowsill planting where a full-size upright snake plant would be too large. Like other snake plants it is extremely tolerant of low light, infrequent watering, and general neglect, making it one of the easiest houseplants for beginners or low-light spaces. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent; it also does well in a shaded outdoor container through the warm season.

plant_note: Broadcast seed in fall directly among an established stand of native grasses or Artemisia, since seedlings must attach to a host plant's roots within their first year to survive.
directions: Wholeleaf Indian paintbrush is a clump-forming perennial of dry rocky slopes, piñon-juniper woodland, and short-grass prairie from the southern Rocky Mountains through Arizona and New Mexico, distinguished from other regional paintbrushes by its undivided, entire leaf margins and brilliant orange-red bracts that appear from spring into midsummer. Like all Castilleja, it is a hemiparasite that taps into the root systems of nearby grasses, sagebrush, or buckwheat for water and minerals, so seed is best broadcast into an already-planted native bed rather than grown alone in isolated pots. Established plants are a major early-season hummingbird and butterfly nectar source in high-desert gardens and are largely deer- and rabbit-resistant. Because of its parasitic root dependency, transplanting mature plants is rarely successful; direct seeding onto a compatible host planting gives the most reliable results.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Whopper grows notably larger and more vigorously than standard wax begonias, living up to its name.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in well-drained, fertile soil. Whopper is a landscape begonia bred for exceptional vigor, growing into a large, substantial mound of glossy foliage topped with abundant clusters of red or rose-pink flowers, filling a bed or large container far faster than standard wax begonias. Its bold scale and heavy flowering make it an efficient choice for mass plantings where quick, dense coverage is the goal. It tolerates more sun than many shade begonias if soil moisture is kept consistent, but still performs best with some protection from the harshest afternoon heat.

common_name: Whorled Class Walter's Viburnum (Compact Florida Native Hedge Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; space plants for a hedge or let them stand as a rounded specimen, since 'Whorled Class' holds a dense, uniform shape with little pruning.
directions: Grow in average garden soil with regular watering through the first year, after which this tough Florida native tolerates both dry spells and occasionally soggy ground. 'Whorled Class' takes its name from the distinctive whorled arrangement of three leaves per node along its stems, giving the dense, rounded shrub an unusually fine, textured look among viburnums. Lightly fragrant white flowers with buttery-yellow throats cover the plant from late winter into early spring, followed by red fruit that ripens to black and draws songbirds through the season. It handles heat, humidity, and light shade from overhead trees with ease, making it a reliable evergreen hedge or foundation shrub for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; plants spread steadily by rhizome and can naturalize in appropriate moist woodland settings. Do not confuse with purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria), an invasive wetland plant — this is a completely different, well-behaved native species.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; whorled loosestrife is a charming native woodland wildflower of eastern North America, recognizable by its distinctive architecture — the lance-shaped leaves are arranged in precise whorls of 4 around the stem, and small five-petaled yellow flowers with a red center arise from the axil of each leaf in the whorl, creating a very regular, geometric flowering pattern in early summer. It is in no way related to the invasive purple loosestrife (Lythrum) — this is a well-behaved native Lysimachia that spreads slowly by rhizome in appropriate moist, acidic woodland conditions. It provides early-summer pollen and floral oils for specialist native bees in the family Macropis. A lovely, understated wildflower for the naturalized woodland garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to average, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; whorled milkweed spreads slowly by rhizomes to form small colonies and benefits from natural cold stratification over winter for reliable spring germination — do not amend soil or it will become lax and weedy.
directions: Sow direct in fall in dry to average, very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; whorled milkweed tolerates poor, sandy, rocky, or gravelly soils with ease and is well-adapted to the dry, open prairies, roadsides, and pastures of the central and eastern United States where it is native across a remarkably wide range from the Great Plains east to the Atlantic Coast. Asclepias verticillata is among the most distinctive of native milkweeds: its very fine, thread-like (linear) leaves are arranged in dense whorls of 3–6 around slender, upright stems, giving the plant a delicate, almost grass-like texture that is unlike any other milkweed species; in midsummer (July–August) it produces small clusters of tiny, greenish-white flowers with white corona hoods, modest in individual size but produced in great abundance and richly fragrant. It is an important host plant for monarch butterfly larvae and is also used by queen butterflies; because it emerges relatively late in spring, it should be marked to avoid accidental disturbance. Whorled milkweed spreads slowly by rhizomes to form modest colonies and self-sows in appropriate conditions; it is one of the most drought-tolerant milkweeds in North America and is an excellent choice for lean, dry native meadow plantings where the larger, showier milkweeds fail.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; whorled rosinweed prefers well-drained to dry, moderately fertile to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Slow to establish from seed but long-lived and deep-rooted once mature.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; whorled rosinweed is a distinctive Silphium species recognized by its leaves arranged in neat whorls of 3–4 around the stem — an unusual arrangement among the rosinweeds, most of which have opposite or alternate leaves. The bright yellow daisy flowers in mid to late summer attract native bees and provide seed food for goldfinches. Like all Silphiums, it develops a deep taproot over years and becomes extremely drought tolerant once fully established, but is slow to transplant and performs best when seeded in place. The genus name Silphium references the mysterious ancient plant traded from North Africa in classical times, though the American rosinweeds are unrelated to it. An underused native perennial for dry, prairie-style gardens and naturalistic meadow plantings.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline woodland soil in partial to full shade; whorled Solomon's seal has an upright, unbranched habit rather than the arching form of most Polygonatum and reads as a strong vertical accent among lower shade groundcovers.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline woodland soil in partial to full shade; whorled Solomon's seal has an upright, unbranched habit rather than the arching form of most Polygonatum and reads as a strong vertical accent among lower shade groundcovers. Polygonatum verticillatum is a Eurasian woodland species with narrow leaves arranged in tiers of whorls up a stiffly upright stem, producing small, pendant, greenish-white to pale pink tubular flowers in the leaf axils in late spring followed by red berries in fall. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form an open colony and is well suited to woodland gardens, shaded rock gardens, and the base of deciduous shrubs where its distinctive whorled, tiered foliage sets it apart from other Solomon's seals. Give it consistent moisture during the growing season and a leaf-litter mulch to mimic its native forest floor habitat.

common_name: Wichita Blue Juniper (Upright Silver-Blue Screening Conifer)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun; Wichita Blue is very drought tolerant once established and resents heavy, wet, poorly drained soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun; Wichita Blue is a Rocky Mountain juniper cultivar prized for its dense, broadly pyramidal form and intense, silvery powder-blue foliage that holds its color well through winter, when many blue conifers dull to green or purple-brown. It grows at a moderate, predictable rate into a strong architectural accent or informal screen, and its upright habit and cold hardiness make it a popular choice from the Great Plains through the upper South. Established plants are highly drought tolerant and need little maintenance beyond occasional light shearing to maintain shape, and they should be sited with good air circulation to reduce the fungal blight issues that can affect junipers in humid climates.

common_name: Wichita Crape Myrtle (Large Lavender-Flowered Tree-Form Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Wichita is a large, tree-form U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series crape myrtle grown for bright lavender flower panicles and cinnamon-mahogany exfoliating bark.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving this large tree-form cultivar plenty of room to mature. Wichita is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, producing bright lavender flower panicles through summer on a large, upright tree, with richly colored cinnamon-to-mahogany exfoliating bark that provides striking winter interest once the leaves drop. Its size and vigor make it well suited as a specimen shade tree or street tree in larger landscapes rather than a foundation shrub. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Wide Brim's broad cream to white margin is brightest and most attractive in partial shade with some morning light — deep shade may reduce the vividness of the contrast.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Wide Brim is a striking medium-sized hosta producing broadly oval to heart-shaped leaves with a deep olive-green center surrounded by a wide, irregular cream to creamy-white margin — one of the boldest and most clearly defined white-margined hostas with a broad, contrasting edge that creates a dramatic two-tone foliage effect. The wide creamy-white margin (often 1–2 inches wide on mature leaves) against the deep green center provides a luminous brightness in shadowy garden settings. Wide Brim is a medium-large hosta reaching 18–24 inches tall and 30–42 inches wide at maturity with an arching, mounding habit and good sun tolerance for a cream-to-white variegated hosta — most cream-margined hostas are more susceptible to leaf scorch in brighter conditions, but Wide Brim handles partial shade locations with some morning sun relatively well. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in mid-summer. The white-margined foliage brightens dark shade conditions and provides maximum contrast with deep green or dark-leafed companion plants. Like all hostas, slug management is important — regular monitoring and iron phosphate bait applications prevent the unsightly slug damage that can disfigure an otherwise beautiful hosta specimen.

plant_note: Sow seed on the soil surface in fall (seed needs light and a period of cool, moist conditions to germinate), into very well-drained, thin, lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; widow's cross self-seeds readily once established and naturalizes best in a spot mimicking its native rock-outcrop habitat.
directions: Sow or set out in very well-drained, thin, lean, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant and intolerant of rich soil, competition, or standing moisture. Sedum pulchellum (widow's cross) is a diminutive native succulent of glades, granite and limestone rock outcrops, and thin prairie soils across the central and southeastern United States, forming low, spreading mats of narrow, cylindrical, bright green leaves that often blush red in dry, sunny conditions. In late spring to early summer, the plant sends up distinctive flower clusters arranged in a four-branched, cross-like pattern (the source of the common name), each branch lined with small, star-shaped, pink to rose-purple flowers that draw in small native bees and other pollinators. As a true annual or biennial, it completes its life cycle in a single season or two and relies on self-seeding to persist, readily colonizing bare rocky or gravelly ground where little else will grow. An excellent, easy, true-to-habitat choice for a rock garden, green roof, or gravel bed in zone 5–9.

plant_note: Direct-sow or transplant in moist to average, well-drained to slightly moist soil in part shade to full shade; widow's tears naturalizes readily and self-sows to maintain a colony. In zone 9–11 it grows as a perennial from fleshy roots; in zone 7–8 it may die back but resprouts in spring. It tolerates dry shade under trees, a rare quality among flowering plants.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; widow's tears (whitemouth dayflower) is a native perennial of the Gulf Coast, Southeast, and tropical America — one of the most genuinely shade-tolerant flowering perennials for the South. The small but intricate flowers are distinctive: three-petaled, with two large, vivid bright-blue upper petals and one tiny, reduced white lower petal, creating a charming, asymmetric, sky-blue and white pattern that inspired the common name 'dayflower' (each flower lasts only one day). The plant blooms continuously from spring through fall, producing a constant succession of new flowers, and self-sows to maintain naturalized colonies in the shade garden. It tolerates dry shade under large trees — a critical landscape niche where few flowering plants will grow. The foliage is attractive and grass-like, with lance-shaped, pleated leaves. In zone 9–11 it grows from fleshy roots and persists as a perennial. An excellent, low-maintenance flowering groundcover for the shaded edges of Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in average to dry, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; wild bergamot cold-stratifies naturally over winter for reliable spring germination and spreads by rhizomes and self-seeding to form loose colonies — avoid rich, consistently moist soils that encourage lax, floppy stems and powdery mildew.
directions: Sow direct in fall in average to dry, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; wild bergamot cold-stratifies naturally over winter and germinates readily in spring without any additional treatment — it is one of the easiest native prairie wildflowers to establish from direct-sown seed. Monarda fistulosa is one of the most widespread and adaptable native wildflowers in North America, ranging from the eastern seaboard to the Rocky Mountains across prairies, open woodlands, roadsides, and meadow edges; from July through September it produces shaggy, two-lipped lavender-pink to pale purple flower heads above aromatic, gray-green foliage that smells strongly of oregano and thyme when crushed — the common name wild bergamot refers to a superficial scent resemblance to bergamot orange, the flavoring in Earl Grey tea. It is an exceptional pollinator plant and is especially important for native mining bees (Andrena spp.) and long-tongued bees; it is also a primary nectar plant for ruby-throated hummingbirds, swallowtail butterflies, and a wide range of native bee species. Wild bergamot spreads slowly by rhizomes to form gradually expanding clumps and self-seeds freely in lean, open conditions; divide clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor, and site in lean, dry soil to minimize powdery mildew — the species is far more mildew-resistant than the cultivated bee balm Monarda didyma when grown in appropriate dry, well-ventilated conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; unlike the common bleeding heart (L. spectabilis), this native eastern species blooms from spring through hard frost if kept consistently moist.
directions: Plant root divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; this eastern North American native handles the summer heat far better than the Asian garden bleeding heart and does not go summer-dormant as long as it receives regular moisture. Wild bleeding heart produces delicate, finely cut, blue-green ferny foliage and pendant clusters of small rose-pink to magenta heart-shaped flowers that continue blooming from late spring through fall frost under ideal moist, shaded conditions — one of the longest-blooming native perennials for deep shade. Cut back faded stems to encourage continued flowering and apply a mulch of shredded leaves to keep the root zone cool and moist through summer. An excellent companion for hostas, ferns, and astilbe under deciduous trees.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall after scarifying seed coat with sandpaper and allowing natural winter cold stratification; wild blue indigo is extremely slow from seed — expect 3–5 years before first bloom — but becomes a massive, long-lived, drought-tolerant prairie cornerstone once established.
directions: Sow direct in fall after scarifying the hard seed coat with sandpaper or nicking it with a knife, then pressing seeds into the surface of lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring — transplanting is not recommended as wild blue indigo develops a very deep, extensive taproot that resents disturbance. Baptisia australis is one of the most spectacular and long-lived native perennials of the eastern tallgrass prairie and open woodland edges, producing stout, blue-green, glaucous stems bearing trifoliate leaves and dense, upright racemes of deep indigo-blue, pea-like flowers from April through June that are highly attractive to native bumblebees and large carpenter bees. After flowering, the inflated, charcoal-black seed pods are persistent and ornamentally valuable through fall and winter, rattling audibly in the wind; the entire plant turns charcoal-black at frost and can be left standing for winter interest and wildlife cover. Wild blue indigo is an exceptional prairie restoration plant and a nitrogen-fixer; once established after its slow juvenile period, it is essentially indestructible and may live for decades, forming clumps 4 feet wide and wide — do not move or divide established plants.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in early fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; wild blue phlox naturalizes well under deciduous trees as a spring-blooming groundcover.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees or shrubs, spacing 9–12 inches apart; wild blue phlox spreads gently by rooting stems to form a soft groundcover that produces fragrant lavender-blue to pale violet flowers for 3–4 weeks in mid-spring, bridging the gap between spring ephemerals and summer perennials. Unlike the mildew-prone garden phlox, the semi-evergreen foliage stays clean through summer and into fall. Trim stems by half after bloom to encourage denser growth and a possible repeat flush; the plant remains attractive even when not in flower. Self-sows lightly without becoming weedy and naturalizes readily in cool, moist, shaded sites.

plant_note: Scatter seeds on moist prepared soil in fall or early spring, pressing lightly onto the surface; wild violet self-seeds prolifically and is best established by allowing naturally germinated seedlings to develop in place in moist, shaded locations.
directions: Scatter seeds directly on prepared moist soil in fall or early spring, pressing lightly onto the surface without burying; wild blue violet germinates best after a period of cool, moist stratification over winter. Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained soil under trees or along woodland edges where it will naturalize freely by self-seeding and underground rhizome spread. Both the heart-shaped leaves and small purple-blue spring flowers are edible and have a long culinary history as salad greens, garnishes, and tea; harvest young spring leaves sparingly for the best mild flavor. This native groundcover is a critical early nectar source for pollinators and a required host plant for several native fritillary butterfly species in eastern North America.

plant_note: Anchor rooted divisions into muddy or sandy substrate 12 to 36 inches below the water surface of a pond or water garden in full sun to partial shade; wild celery is a true submerged aquatic and will not grow outside standing water.
directions: Anchor rooted plants into soft mud or sandy substrate well below the water surface in a pond or water garden in full sun to partial shade; wild celery is a submerged native aquatic with long, ribbon-like, translucent green leaves that sway gently in current and provide excellent cover and oxygenation for fish and pond life. It spreads by runners across the pond bottom to form dense underwater meadows and is one of the single most important native food plants for migrating waterfowl, particularly canvasback ducks, which rely heavily on its starchy tubers and seeds. Female flowers are carried to the surface on long, coiling stalks for pollination and then draw back underwater to mature, a distinctive reproductive strategy among aquatic plants. It requires clear water with reasonable light penetration to thrive, so avoid excessive nutrient loading or turbidity that would shade out the submerged foliage, and thin congested colonies periodically to keep the planting healthy and open.

common_name: Wild Coco (Wild Coco Orchid, Alta Eulophia, Haitian Orchid)
plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or divisions in spring in partial shade to full sun in moderately moist, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; Eulophia alta is one of the most adaptable terrestrial orchids for zone 9-11 outdoor cultivation — it naturally grows in disturbed sites, lawns, roadsides, and open woodlands and tolerates a wider range of soil and light conditions than most orchids. In zone 9, established plants survive mild winters; mulch in hard freeze years. Self-seeds and can naturalize as a 'lawn orchid' in warm, moist conditions. Divide clumps every 3–5 years. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moderately moist, well-drained, loamy or sandy soil — Wild Coco is one of the most adaptable terrestrial orchids available, tolerating full sun to partial shade and a range of soil moisture levels, making it far easier to establish in zone 9-11 gardens than most orchids. Eulophia alta is a large, robust terrestrial orchid native to Florida (central and southern portions), the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, South America, and tropical Africa in the Orchidaceae family — one of the most widely distributed of all terrestrial orchids, inhabiting an enormous range from Florida lawns to African grasslands. The plant produces large, clustered, corn-like pseudobulbs with 3–5 long, broad, pleated, bright-green leaves forming an impressive clump. In spring and summer, tall erect flower spikes (2–4 feet) emerge bearing 8–25 flowers in shades of brownish-purple on the outside with a pale pink to whitish, three-lobed lip — not the most brightly colored orchid, but perfectly attractive and interesting. The species has a remarkable ability to establish itself spontaneously in lawns and open ground in warm Florida and Gulf Coast areas, earning the informal title of 'lawn orchid.' For gardeners who want to add Florida-native orchids to outdoor garden beds without the demanding cultural requirements of most epiphytic orchids, E. alta is the most accessible starting point. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Wild Coffee is one of the finest native shade shrubs for south Florida landscapes and is an important larval host plant for several native butterfly species.
directions: Wild Coffee is one of the most valuable native shade shrubs for south Florida and tropical hammock gardens, native to the dense, shaded understories of tropical hardwood hammocks, coastal hammocks, and pinelands from Brevard and Hillsborough counties south through the Florida Keys and into the Caribbean. Its large, glossy, strongly quilted or pleated dark green leaves with prominent veins are among the most attractive foliage textures in the Florida native palette, providing a lush, tropical appearance in deep shade where few other shrubs thrive. Small white flowers appear year-round, followed by clusters of bright red berries in fall and winter that are a vital food source for migrating warblers, robins, and thrushes. Despite the common name, it is not a true coffee (Coffea), though the plants share family membership; the berries are not edible by humans. An outstanding shade shrub for zone 9b–11 landscapes that fills the difficult deep-shade role with year-round beauty and wildlife value.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil; wild columbine requires 4–8 weeks of cold-moist stratification and germinates readily the following spring. It self-seeds freely once established.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, or start indoors with 4–6 weeks of cold stratification; wild columbine is one of the most important early hummingbird nectar flowers of eastern North America, producing nodding, lantern-shaped flowers with distinctive red-and-yellow spurred petals from mid-spring through early summer at exactly the time ruby-throated hummingbirds return from their winter migration. It self-seeds freely in suitable conditions to naturalize under deciduous trees, along rock outcrops, and in woodland garden edges. Short-lived (3–5 years) but perpetuated by abundant self-seeding that maintains a persistent colony. The lacy, blue-green, compound foliage is attractive from late winter through fall before dying back.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, cold-moist stratifying for 60 days first, or transplant divisions in spring or fall, into average to dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees.
directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tolerant of dry shade once established, a valuable trait for planting beneath established trees. Cynoglossum virginianum (wild comfrey, or wild hound's tongue) is a native woodland perennial of the eastern United States, forming a basal rosette of large, coarse, hairy, tongue-shaped leaves — the source of its common name — from which a branching flower stalk rises in mid-spring, carrying loose clusters of small, pale blue to lavender, forget-me-not-like flowers. It is an unassuming but reliable early to mid-spring bloomer for the dry shade beneath hardwoods, a notoriously difficult site for many perennials, and its coarse foliage provides useful textural contrast to finer-leaved woodland companions like ferns and sedges. After flowering, the plant produces bur-like seed clusters that cling to fur and clothing for dispersal, in the manner typical of the borage family. A tough, easy native for a naturalistic dry shade garden, zone 4–8.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wild cucumber is a vigorous annual vine that grows naturally along stream banks, woodland edges, and roadsides, climbing rapidly by tendrils over shrubs and small trees. Self-sows freely in moist conditions.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in moist, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wild cucumber is a vigorous native annual vine of moist woodland edges, streambanks, and disturbed riparian areas across most of North America, climbing rapidly by branching tendrils over shrubs, fences, and small trees to produce a dense, large-leaved screen in a single season. The large, maple-like leaves create excellent temporary screening. Small, white, star-shaped male flowers in large, fluffy panicles are mildly fragrant and attractive to many small native bees. The distinctive, spiny, oval, cucumber-like fruits (about the size of a golf ball) are ornamental and give the plant both its common names — the inflated, papery fruits are balsam-apple shaped and resemble tiny cucumbers covered in soft spines. The fruits split at maturity to release 4 large, flat seeds. An excellent, fast-growing native annual for covering trellises, fences, or unsightly structures in partially shaded, moist locations.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist, well-drained soil with a trellis or support in zone 9–12; Wild Cucumber Vine is a slender, fast-climbing African cucurbit vine — native to tropical Africa and naturalized widely in warm regions — producing small, white flowers and clusters of very small, oval, green fruits that ripen to brilliant scarlet-red, creating an ornamental effect similar to tiny hanging lanterns, and providing excellent wildlife value as the fruits are relished by birds.
directions: Direct sow Zehneria scabra seeds in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a trellis, fence, or shrub for the slender tendrils to climb; water moderately and fertilize lightly during active growth; harvest decorative red fruits for displays or leave for birds. Wild Cucumber Vine is a vigorous, scrambling, African cucurbit vine in the Zehneria genus — a group of small, wild cucumbers native to Africa, Asia, and Australia that are less known than their cultivated relatives but often equally ornamental. The plant climbs by tendrils to 5–8 feet, producing small but numerous cream-white flowers followed by masses of tiny, glossy, oval fruits about the size of a grape that ripen from green through yellow to brilliant glossy scarlet-red, creating a cheerful, berry-like display. The fruits are not edible for humans (bitter) but are eaten enthusiastically by birds, making this an excellent plant for wildlife gardens. The rough-textured leaves (scabra means 'rough') are typical of the cucurbit family. In zone 9–12, it grows as a perennial vine from a persistent rootstock; in zone 8, it can be grown as a warm-season annual. Useful for quickly covering fences, trellises, and outbuildings in warm climates with minimal care, while providing ornamental value and wildlife support.

plant_note: Plant container stock after last frost danger in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in warm climates (zone 9–11); Wild Gardenia is a South African native woodland tree bearing intensely fragrant, pure-white 8-petaled flowers followed by hard, white, ribbed, woody fruits used traditionally as medicine and a source of yellow dye.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Gardenia thunbergia tolerates more sun than the common Gardenia jasminoides and is considerably more drought-tolerant once established — water deeply but infrequently, allowing the top few inches of soil to dry between irrigations. Gardenia thunbergia (Wild Gardenia or Woodland Gardenia) is a medium to large shrub or small tree native to the coastal forests and bushveld of South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and Tanzania, differing from the familiar florist gardenia in producing strikingly symmetrical, 8-petaled, white waxy flowers — intensely fragrant in the evening — on a naturally sculptural, dark-barked tree that can reach 20–30 feet. The large, hard, ribbed woody fruits are distinctive — oval, white-grey, prominently ridged, and woody-shelled — and have historically been used as snuff containers, children's toys, and a source of yellow to gold fabric dye across southern Africa. Unlike Gardenia jasminoides, which suffers in alkaline soils, G. thunbergia is somewhat more tolerant of soil variation. It is prized in warm-climate gardens for its refined branching habit, glossy foliage, and exceptional evening fragrance, and makes an outstanding specimen tree or large fragrant hedge in zones 9–11.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost risk has passed. Choose a site with well-drained, slightly acidic soil and protection from cold winds. Mulch the root zone to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature.
directions: Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in late spring or summer, dipping the cut end in rooting hormone before inserting into a well-draining mix of perlite and peat. Transplant rooted cuttings outdoors in spring once nighttime temperatures reliably stay above 50°F. Gardenia thunbergia is more heat- and drought-tolerant than common gardenia, but consistent moisture during the first growing season promotes rapid establishment. Fertilize with an acid-formulated fertilizer in spring and midsummer to encourage lush foliage and the best display of its large, intensely fragrant white blooms.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early fall or early spring, ensuring each division has several eyes and a portion of the rhizome; wild geranium can also be grown from seed sown in fall to cold-stratify naturally over winter, though seedlings take 2 years to reach flowering size — fall division is the most reliable propagation method for garden use.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; wild geranium is one of the finest native spring wildflowers of the eastern deciduous forest, producing deeply lobed, palmately divided leaves and clusters of five-petaled, rose-pink to magenta flowers from April through June — it blooms during the critical window before the tree canopy fully leafs out, making it an ideal companion for spring ephemerals and shade-garden perennials. Native across a broad range from Manitoba to Georgia and west to Kansas, it is among the most adaptable of eastern woodland wildflowers, tolerating a wide range of soil pH, moderate summer drought once established, and everything from dappled shade under deciduous trees to fairly deep shade — the foliage often takes on attractive reddish-autumn tones before dying back. The deeply lobed leaves provide attractive foliage from spring through frost and the plant slowly spreads by rhizome to form modest, well-behaved colonies; it is an excellent substitute for non-native Geranium species in shaded native gardens and is an important early-season pollen source for native bees, particularly specialist mining bees. Plant in groups of three or more for the best floral display and allow it to naturalize in a woodland garden setting where it will gradually form a loose, low-maintenance groundcover under deciduous shrubs and trees.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in well-drained to moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; wild hyacinth is the eastern counterpart to the more widely grown C. quamash and is better adapted to the heavier clay soils and summer humidity common across the eastern US. It naturalizes freely and is excellent for planting in large drifts in meadow gardens, native plant borders, or along pond edges.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained to moderately moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for April-May bloom; wild hyacinth is a graceful native spring bulb widespread across the eastern United States, producing tall, slender spikes of loosely arranged, star-shaped flowers ranging from pale lavender to near-white, the individual blossoms arranged in a loose raceme that opens progressively upward for a long bloom period in mid-spring. It is the eastern ecological counterpart to the western Camassia quamash and shares its history of importance as a food source — Native American peoples across its range harvested, cooked, and dried the nutritious bulbs as a significant caloric staple. In the garden it is one of the most valuable native spring bulbs for naturalizing in meadow plantings, rain gardens, and low areas where the soil stays moderately moist in spring, tolerating both partial shade and heavier clay soils better than most spring bulbs. It combines beautifully with native ferns, Virginia bluebells, and late tulips.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky, alkaline to neutral, coastal soil in full sun. Wild Lime is highly drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established but is cold-sensitive and best suited to frost-free or nearly frost-free landscapes in Zone 9b–11.
directions: Wild Lime is a native evergreen shrub or small tree of coastal hammocks, rocky pinelands, and scrub edges of southern Florida and coastal Texas, recognizable by its small, dark green leaflets attached to a winged rachis — a distinctive feature of the citrus family — that release a sharp lime fragrance when crushed. A critical host plant for the giant swallowtail butterfly, the largest native butterfly in North America, Wild Lime provides the caterpillar's only food source in many south Florida hammock habitats, and its dense, spiny growth makes it an excellent barrier plant or habitat hedge in tropical and subtropical landscapes. The small, gland-dotted aromatic fruits and leaves are used in Caribbean folk medicine and regional cooking, and the plant's salt tolerance and drought-hardiness make it particularly valuable in coastal south Florida settings. Plant in well-drained, sandy to rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established plants require virtually no irrigation or maintenance in appropriate Zone 9b–11 landscapes.

plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper or nick the seed coat, then direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination. Wild Lupine develops a long, deep taproot that makes transplanting nearly impossible — choose the permanent site carefully and sow in place. Requires acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), sandy, infertile, well-drained soil; rich or clay soils will cause decline.
directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing lightly with sandpaper or nicking the hard seed coat with a knife, then direct sow in fall into permanently selected, dry, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), sandy or gravelly, infertile soil in full sun — Wild Lupine will fail in rich, clay, or wet conditions. This native perennial produces handsome palmate foliage and blue-violet flower spikes in May–June and is the sole larval host plant of the federally endangered Karner Blue butterfly, making it a conservation priority for eastern dry oak savanna and pine barren restorations. Do not attempt to transplant established plants; the deep taproot is extremely sensitive to disturbance, and plants will almost always die if moved. Once established, Wild Lupine is essentially self-sufficient, fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, and will self-seed modestly to form a small colony in suitable conditions.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; one of the few native evergreen shrubs that performs in partial to full shade in the Southeast.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; wild olive is the native North American member of the same genus as the prized Asian fragrant sweet olive (O. fragrans), and though its white flowers in late spring are smaller and less flamboyant, they carry a delicate, sweet fragrance and are borne abundantly on large shrubs or small trees in woodland settings. It grows naturally in moist, shaded coastal plain forests and ravine forests of the Southeast, making it well-suited to garden use under tall trees where it provides refined, glossy-leaved evergreen structure year-round. The small, dark blue berry-like drupes ripen in fall and provide wildlife food. Slow growing but extremely long-lived; excellent as a foundation shrub or informal hedge in shade.

plant_note: Start from seed (surface sow, seeds need light) 10–12 weeks before last frost or purchase transplants; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after last frost; deadhead regularly to extend bloom and pinch back leggy stems to maintain a bushy habit.
directions: Start from seed (surface sow, seeds need light) 10–12 weeks before last frost or purchase transplants; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after last frost; deadhead regularly to extend bloom and pinch back leggy stems to maintain a bushy habit. Petunia integrifolia is one of the primary wild parent species of all modern hybrid petunias, a semi-trailing South American native with small (1–1.5 inch), violet-purple to rose-magenta funnel-shaped flowers on sticky, hairy stems; it is both more heat-tolerant and more attractive to bumblebees than most hybrid petunias (which have been bred with flowers too large for native bees to access efficiently). In zone 9–10 gardens it can be grown as a short-lived perennial and self-seeds modestly in suitable conditions; the species is being rediscovered as a more ecologically valuable alternative to hybrid petunia mixes for pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, sandy to rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; wild petunia self-sows prolifically in appropriate conditions and can naturalize in dry, open areas — a welcome attribute in a native meadow but worth noting in a more formal setting.
directions: Sow seed in fall in well-drained, dry to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — wild petunia (Ruellia humilis) is a native prairie perennial that produces a continuous succession of lavender to pale violet, 1.5-inch funnel-shaped flowers remarkably similar in appearance to garden petunias through summer and into fall, making it a genuinely ornamental native for dry, sunny or partly shaded settings. Individual flowers last only a day, but new ones open continuously over many weeks on the low, hairy, sessile-leaved plants. It grows naturally in dry, open prairies, rocky glades, and open woodland edges. Unlike tropical Ruellia (Mexican petunia, R. simplex), native wild petunia is not invasive — it self-sows modestly and is well-behaved in most gardens. Excellent for rock gardens, dry slopes, and native plant gardens. An important nectar source for bumblebees and long-tongued native bees.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; this plant grows naturally in dry, sandy upland soils and pine woods — do not plant in heavy clay or rich, moist soils.
directions: Direct sow in dry, sandy, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; wild petunia is a delicate native wildflower of the dry sandy pine flatwoods and upland forests of the Southeast, producing lavender-blue tubular flowers resembling petunias (though not related) throughout the growing season from spring through fall. It grows naturally in infertile, dry conditions where it avoids competition from more aggressive plants. The trumpet-shaped flowers are visited by hummingbirds, sphinx moths, and small native bees. Plant in rock gardens, in sandy soils under pines, or at dry woodland margins; it will not tolerate wet or clay soils. It self-sows reliably and naturalizes into small colonies in ideal conditions. In zone 9–10 it may behave as an evergreen short-lived perennial.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in dry, rocky, very well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; wild pink grows naturally in extremely well-drained, rocky or sandy woodland soils and will not survive in poorly drained sites.
directions: Plant in dry, rocky, very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wild pink is a charming, mat-forming native perennial of the eastern Piedmont and Appalachians, producing clusters of vivid pink, 5-petaled flowers atop low, sticky-stemmed rosettes in mid-spring. The bright cerise-to-magenta flower color is outstanding in the late-spring garden and attracts butterflies. The common name 'sticky catchfly' refers to the sticky stems that trap small insects, though the plant is not carnivorous. Wild pink grows naturally on rocky ledges, sandy barrens, and dry oak-pine woodland edges where the soil drains rapidly and conditions alternate between exposed sun and light shade from scattered trees. It is extremely sensitive to poor drainage — in heavy clay or consistently wet soil it will quickly rot. An outstanding plant for rock gardens, dry shade under pines, and naturalized woodland edges in the Southeast. Self-seeds sparingly in appropriate conditions.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; wild plantain is a large, vigorous grower that spreads by rhizomes to form impressive clumps — allow adequate space (6–10 feet) for its full lateral spread.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; wild plantain is a large Caribbean heliconia that produces some of the most dramatic and brightly colored of all heliconia inflorescences — the erect, upright-held flower spikes consist of stacked, boat-shaped, waxy bracts in vivid combinations of red and yellow, or red, orange, and yellow, alternately arranged in zigzag fashion up the vertical stem, with small, white, tubular flowers visible within the bracts' waxy cavities. The inflorescences are produced year-round in the tropics on mature clumps and are exceptionally long-lasting as cut flowers (3–4 weeks). The large, paddle-shaped, banana-like leaves on the vegetative pseudostems provide bold tropical foliage throughout the year. Wild plantain is larger and more vigorous than most Heliconia psittacorum types and requires more space. It grows best in warm, humid, partially shaded conditions with consistently moist, fertile, organic soil. An important nectar plant for hermit hummingbirds in its native Caribbean range. Excellent as a large-scale tropical landscape specimen or in naturalistic tropical garden settings.

plant_note: Start transplants from stratified seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; wild quinine develops a deep taproot after the first year and becomes highly drought-tolerant.
directions: Start transplants from stratified seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; wild quinine develops a deep taproot after the first year and becomes highly drought-tolerant. Parthenium integrifolium is a tough, adaptable native perennial producing bold clusters of flat-topped, button-like white flower heads from late spring through summer on sturdy, upright, 2–4 foot stems with large, textured, rough-hairy leaves; it was used medicinally by Native Americans as a quinine substitute (hence the common name) for fever treatment. The flat flower clusters are outstanding for butterflies, small native bees, and wasps; the plant is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once deep-rooted and thrives in clay or loamy soils in full sun with no supplemental irrigation, making it an outstanding low-maintenance prairie garden plant.

plant_note: Set out container plants after frost in well-drained soil; established plants are more cold-tolerant.
directions: Root cuttings in a moist, well-drained medium in warm conditions and transplant to the garden in spring once nighttime temperatures remain above 40 degrees F. Unlike the invasive Lantana camara, this native species is well-behaved and blooms with small white to pale lavender flower clusters nearly year-round in frost-free regions. The pungently fragrant foliage deters browsing by deer, and the blooms are a premier nectar source for swallowtails, skippers, and other butterflies. Water sparingly once established and prune lightly in late winter to shape the plant and encourage fresh flowering stems.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall after scarifying the hard seed coat with sandpaper; wild senna seeds have impermeable seed coats that require scarification for reliable germination — fall sowing after scarification allows cold-stratification over winter and strong germination in spring.
directions: Sow direct in fall after scarifying the hard seed coat with sandpaper or soaking in hot water for 24 hours; wild senna has a physical seed dormancy due to an impermeable seed coat that must be broken before water can enter and germination can proceed — without scarification, germination rates are very poor. Senna marilandica is a bold, tall native perennial of eastern North American prairies, meadows, and open woodland edges producing pinnately compound, fine-textured leaves on robust stems and clusters of bright yellow, five-petaled flowers from July through August that are exceptional for pollinators — it is a host plant for several native sulfur butterflies and cloudless sulphur, and the flowers are heavily visited by bumblebees harvesting pollen. It is a nitrogen-fixing legume, improving soil fertility over time; established plants develop a deep taproot and become very drought-tolerant despite their large size, though they perform best with moderate moisture during establishment. Wild senna spreads moderately by self-sowing and by short rhizomes; the persistent, straight, flattened seed pods provide wildlife food and winter garden interest — it is an ideal structural plant for the back of a native border or meadow planting.

plant_note: Plant small divisions or cuttings in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic, very well-drained, rocky or gravelly soil in partial to full shade; wild stonecrop establishes easily from stem cuttings pressed into moist soil and spreads to form dense mats in appropriate conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic, well-drained, rocky or gravelly soil in partial shade; wild stonecrop is the only native Sedum of eastern North America adapted to shade — a low, mat-forming succulent producing whorls of three small, fleshy, bright-green rounded leaves on trailing stems that root where they contact moist soil. In spring, upright flowering stems rise 3–6 inches to produce clusters of small, star-shaped white flowers attractive to early pollinators. It is an outstanding native groundcover for shaded rocky slopes, woodland paths, and difficult spots where soil is dry, well-drained, and in partial shade — conditions where most shade plants struggle. Unlike other stonecrops, which demand full sun, wild stonecrop genuinely thrives in shade and performs poorly in direct sun. It spreads at a moderate rate to form solid mats that suppress weeds and stabilize slopes. Deer usually ignore it. An underused but excellent native for naturalized woodland groundcover plantings.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, calcareous or sandy soil in full sun; wild tamarind grows naturally in the subtropical hammocks and rocky pinelands of south Florida and the Florida Keys, thriving in the thin, rocky, alkaline soils over oolitic limestone typical of south Florida.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, thin, rocky, calcareous soil in full sun; wild tamarind is a striking native tree of subtropical south Florida, the Florida Keys, and the Caribbean, producing an exceptionally graceful, lacy, filtered-shade canopy of bipinnately compound leaves that resemble tamarind foliage. The tree forms a high, open canopy that provides filtered light — one of the best native trees for creating dappled shade in south Florida landscapes without completely blocking light. Small, fragrant, white pompom flowers in spring attract numerous pollinators. A nitrogen-fixing legume (like true tamarind) that improves soil fertility. The flat, papery seed pods persist through the dry season. Butterfly gardeners prize it as a host plant for large orange sulphur butterfly larvae. The finest native shade tree for zone 10 rocky, calcareous, limestone soil conditions where other trees struggle.

common_name: Wild Thing Salvia (Vigorous Hot-Pink Hybrid Sage)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Wild Thing grows larger and more vigorously than most Salvia greggii selections, so give it extra room to spread.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and give this vigorous hybrid room to grow into a substantial, well-branched mound over its first two seasons. Wild Thing is a Texas A&M introduction resulting from a cross between Salvia greggii and S. microphylla, combining the best traits of both parents into a larger, more heat-tolerant plant that produces an especially heavy, near-continuous display of vivid hot-pink, two-lipped flowers from spring through frost. Its larger stature and exceptional bloom production make it a standout hummingbird and butterfly plant for a sunny border or mixed shrub planting, and like its parent species it is highly drought-tolerant once established, thriving on lean soil with minimal supplemental water. Cut back hard in late winter to renew growth and keep the plant from becoming woody and sparse at the base.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in fall; unlike most hybrid tulips, Tulipa sylvestris reliably perennializes and spreads vegetatively by stolons — it does not need lifting and replanting annually. It tolerates partial shade and naturalizes well under deciduous trees and in grass. Allow foliage to die back naturally after blooming to build bulb reserves.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; wild tulip is a species tulip that dramatically differs from the large hybrid garden tulips in its ability to reliably naturalize and return year after year — spreading vegetatively by underground stolons to form expanding colonies that flower more profusely over time rather than declining as do most hybrid tulips. The flowers are smaller and more delicate than hybrid tulips, elegantly star-shaped when fully open, in clear, warm, soft yellow with a faint greenish flush on the outer petals — and they have a pleasant, sweet fragrance absent from most tulips. Native across a vast range from the Mediterranean to central Asia, it has naturalized in historical European orchards and vineyards where it was planted during the Renaissance. Outstanding for naturalizing in grass under deciduous trees, in orchard lawns, and in rock gardens where its modest size and naturalizing habit suit semi-wild plantings. One of the few tulips that succeeds in zone 9 because it does not require deep cold to perform.

common_name: Will Fleming Yaupon Holly (Narrow Columnar Native Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Will Fleming is a naturally narrow, upright male selection of native yaupon holly that never needs shearing to maintain its columnar shape.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Will Fleming is a naturally narrow, strictly upright, columnar selection of the Gulf Coast native yaupon holly, discovered and named for a Texas landscape architect, and valued for providing the vertical accent of a formal columnar evergreen without any shearing or shaping required to maintain the shape. As a male selection it does not produce the red berries typical of yaupon holly, but its extreme drought tolerance, adaptability to both wet and dry soils, and complete indifference to heat and poor soil make it one of the toughest, most maintenance-free narrow accent shrubs available for Gulf Coast gardens. It works well as a narrow screen, foundation accent, or repeated vertical element along a walk or drive.

common_name: Will Goodwin Clematis (Large Pale Lavender-Blue Clematis)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Will Goodwin is an early large-flowered cultivar that blooms on both old and new wood, so needs only light pruning.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis, arbor, or fence. Will Goodwin bears large, pale lavender-blue flowers with a soft, luminous quality and gently ruffled petal edges, opening earlier in the season than many large-flowered clematis and often reblooming lightly later in summer. Its clear, gentle color pairs well with roses and other early-summer perennials trained on the same support. Because it blooms on both old wood from the previous season and new growth, it needs only light, selective pruning in late winter to remove dead or weak stems rather than the hard annual cutback required by later-blooming, new-wood cultivars.

common_name: Will Scarlet Hybrid Musk Rose (Vivid Scarlet-Red Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Will Scarlet is a vivid scarlet-red sport of the pink hybrid musk Skyrocket, tolerating a bit of shade.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hybrid musk roses tolerate more shade than most rose classes, blooming reasonably well with just a half-day of direct sun. Will Scarlet, a vivid scarlet-red sport of the hybrid musk Skyrocket, bears large clusters of semi-double blooms with a light, musky fragrance and golden stamens, opening on a tall, vigorous shrub that can be trained as a short climber against a wall or fence. It repeats bloom well through the growing season and often sets attractive orange hips in fall if lightly deadheaded. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood.

common_name: Will's Wonderful Chrysanthemum (Hardy Bronze-Red Garden Mum)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Will's Wonderful is a reliably cold-hardy garden mum bred for garden persistence rather than florist pot display.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build a compact, heavily budded plant instead of tall, sparse growth. Will's Wonderful bears semi-double, bronze-red daisy flowers with a warm, glowing tone in mid fall, on a plant selected specifically for the ability to survive cold winters in the open garden rather than be discarded after a single season like most florist pot mums. Its dependable hardiness has made it a longtime favorite among gardeners building a true perennial fall border rather than replanting mums every year. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: William Baffin Rose (Cold-Hardy Explorer Series Climber)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall against a trellis, fence, or arbor in full sun; bred for extreme cold hardiness in Canada's Explorer series, William Baffin also performs reliably in warm Gulf South gardens thanks to its outstanding disease resistance and vigor.
directions: Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil against a sturdy support, and expect vigorous growth that needs little more than occasional shaping once established.
