Bred by Agriculture Canada's Ogilvie/Svejda rose breeding program and introduced in 1983 as part of the cold-hardy Explorer series, William Baffin bears large clusters of semi-double, deep pink blooms with a light fragrance in a heavy spring flush and steady rebloom through summer and fall. Although developed for Canadian winters down to roughly zone 3, its outstanding vigor and near-immunity to blackspot and powdery mildew make it just as valuable in hot, humid Gulf South gardens, where many modern climbers struggle with disease pressure. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing canes in late winter, since the plant blooms reliably on both old and new wood.

common_name: William Lobb Moss Rose (Purple-Magenta Fading to Lavender-Grey)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; William Lobb is a tall, vigorous moss rose whose flower color shifts dramatically as blooms age.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the tall, arching canes benefit from support or a spot where they can lean into a fence or shrub. William Lobb opens deep purple-magenta double blooms that fade through smoky mauve to a striking lavender-grey as they age, so a single bush shows several colors at once, all carried on brownish, heavily mossed sepals with the characteristic balsam fragrance of the class. Like most moss roses it blooms just once, in a fragrant flush in late spring. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: William Shakespeare 2000 Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; William Shakespeare 2000 replaced David Austin's earlier William Shakespeare introduction with a more disease-resistant plant carrying the same deep crimson color.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2000 as an improved replacement for his earlier William Shakespeare rose, this cultivar carries deep velvety crimson-purple, fully double blooms with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous shrub bred for markedly better disease resistance than the original 1987 introduction, which was notoriously prone to black spot. It repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading, and its dark, saturated color makes a dramatic accent among lighter companion plantings.

common_name: William Sim Dianthus (Foundation Scarlet Florist Carnation)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; William Sim is the historic foundation parent behind the modern florist Sim carnation line grown commercially worldwide.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. William Sim bears single, vivid scarlet-red flowers on tall, sturdy stems, and while less commonly grown as a garden plant today, it holds a special place in horticultural history as the foundation parent behind the entire modern line of Sim-type florist carnations grown commercially around the world for the cut-flower trade. In the garden it performs like other carnations, benefiting from sharp drainage and full sun, and rewarding with the classic sweet clove fragrance of the species. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bloom and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Willo's Violet Dahlia (Rich Violet-Purple Dwarf Pompon Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Willo's Violet is a pompon dahlia with rich violet-purple, perfectly globular blooms on a dwarf plant.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage bushier growth and more blooms. Willo's Violet is a true pompon dahlia on a notably dwarf plant, its small, densely quilled florets curling inward to form an almost perfectly spherical rich violet-purple globe, the compact habit fitting containers and small border spaces better than taller dahlia types. The dainty, uniform blooms are produced in great abundance, making them a favorite for posies and mixed bouquets. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, and lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

plant_note: Plant small container trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; willow oak transplants more easily than most oaks and is one of the best native trees for urban street and lawn use in the Southeast.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; willow oak is one of the most graceful and distinctive of the native oaks, bearing narrow, willow-like leaves that give the tree an unusually fine-textured, airy appearance very different from other oaks. It grows naturally in moist bottomland forests and upland slopes throughout the Southeast and is one of the most widely planted native oaks as a street and lawn tree, valued for its tolerance of urban soils, relatively fast growth (1–2 feet per year), and adaptability. The small acorns produced abundantly from age 15 onward are a critical food source for wood ducks, mallards, wild turkeys, and many songbirds. The fine foliage turns attractive golden-yellow in fall before dropping cleanly, and the tree's upright-oval form matures into a large, handsome landscape specimen.

common_name: Willow Wand Camellia (Weeping Narrow-Habit Deep Pink Reticulata Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Willow Wand is a distinctively narrow, weeping-branched reticulata camellia unlike the typically broad, open habit of the species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protected from harsh winter wind. Willow Wand is unusual among reticulata camellias for its narrow, willowy, weeping branch structure, giving the shrub a graceful, arching silhouette quite different from the typically broad, open habit of the species, and bears semi-double, deep pink blooms in mid-to-late winter into spring. Its narrow footprint makes it useful where a tall but space-conscious camellia is needed. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's growth.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; willow-leaf ox-eye thrives in poor, dry, alkaline, limestone-derived soils that are typical of its native Alpine meadow habitat. In rich soils it becomes floppy and short-lived. Deadhead regularly for a long bloom season; divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; willow-leaf ox-eye is a useful and underused European native perennial from Alpine and subalpine meadows of central and southern Europe, producing slender, willow-like leaves on upright stems and a prolonged succession of yellow, asterlike daisy flowers (1.5–2 inches across) with slightly twisted ray petals and darker yellow disc centers from June through September — one of the longest natural bloom seasons of any daisy-type perennial in undemanding conditions. The slightly twisted ray petals give the flowers an informal, loosely spidery quality distinguishing them from the more precisely regular rays of Leucanthemum or Helenium. It thrives in the poor, dry, alkaline soils of limestone gardens where more demanding perennials decline, making it a good choice for difficult, free-draining situations. Excellent for prairie-style plantings, gravel gardens, and naturalistic wildflower areas on calcareous soils. Long-lived in lean conditions, shorter-lived in rich soils. Attractive to bees and butterflies throughout its long season.

plant_note: Start transplants or plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; willowleaf aster naturally grows at the wetter, sunnier edge of prairies and marshes and tolerates periodic flooding better than most asters.
directions: Start transplants or plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; willowleaf aster naturally grows at the wetter, sunnier edge of prairies and marshes and tolerates periodic flooding better than most asters. Narrow, willow-like leaves clothe tall, upright stems that spread gradually by rhizome into loose colonies, topped in fall by masses of small, lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers that are an important late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and native bees. Native to wet prairies, marsh edges, and low meadows across the central and eastern United States, it is a strong choice for the moist portion of a pollinator garden or the sunnier fringe of a rain garden where it can spread without crowding out smaller neighbors. Cut stems back in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every three to four years.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun; willowleaf sunflower cold-stratifies naturally over winter and germinates reliably in spring; like Maximilian sunflower it benefits from lean, drier soils that keep stems upright and plants better proportioned — rich, moist soils encourage excessive vegetative growth and floppy stems.
directions: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun; willowleaf sunflower is one of the most architecturally distinctive native perennial sunflowers in North America, immediately recognizable by its exceptionally long, narrow, willow-like leaves (4–8 inches long, less than half an inch wide) that clothe the stem in dense, drooping, grass-like foliage from base to tip, creating a feathery, almost bamboo-like texture that is unlike any other sunflower species. From September through October the stems are topped with clusters of bright yellow, 2–3 inch daisy flowers with yellow-brown disk centers, providing the same important late-season food resources as Maximilian sunflower for pollinators and seed-eating birds at a critical time when most wildflowers have finished. Native to the rocky, dry prairies, limestone glades, and rocky hillsides of the south-central United States from Nebraska to Texas and Louisiana, it is naturally adapted to thin, alkaline, rocky soils and extreme drought — it performs best in lean, dry conditions that emphasize its graceful texture rather than producing excessive, floppy vegetative growth. Willowleaf sunflower spreads by rhizomes into handsome colonies and is an excellent structural plant for the back of a sunny native border, tall prairie planting, or naturalistic meadow where its fine-textured foliage provides visual interest from spring through frost.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a sunny, well-drained spot or a container that can move indoors in cold zones.
directions: Wilma Goldcrest is a lemon cypress with glowing golden-green foliage that releases a fresh citrus scent when brushed, and a narrow, upright form perfect for tight spaces. Grow it in full sun to keep the foliage brightest, in fast-draining soil that never stays waterlogged. In containers it stays around 3 to 5 feet, while in the ground in mild climates it can reach 10 feet. In zones colder than 7, grow it in a pot and bring it indoors near a bright window over winter. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and avoid soggy roots.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in midsummer under mist or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; Wilson's magnolia is best appreciated when planted at the top of a slope, retaining wall, or above a path so that the pendulous, nodding flowers can be admired at face level or viewed from below.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Wilson's magnolia is a Chinese deciduous magnolia introduced from Sichuan province by plant hunter E.H. Wilson in 1908 that produces, in May and June, the most exquisitely formed pendant flowers of any magnolia species — pure-white, circular, saucer-shaped, deeply cupped flowers about 3–4 inches across, with nine large, rounded, pure-white petals surrounding a magnificent, bold, central boss of deep crimson-red to rose-red stamens, hanging nodding on slender stalks from the tips of the branches so that they look directly downward, like ornamental lanterns. The brilliant contrast of the white petals against the vivid crimson stamen cone makes each flower a miniature work of art. Like M. sieboldii, it performs well in partial shade — making it particularly valuable for the woodland garden — and the late flowering season (May–June) means frost damage to the flowers is rare. A connoisseur's magnolia for zone 6–9 gardens seeking unusual shade-tolerant flowering trees. Closely related to and similar to M. sieboldii, distinguished by its slightly larger flowers and different leaf shape.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in California; seed requires cool, moist conditions to germinate and blooms in spring before summer heat arrives.
directions: A delicate California native annual related to the California poppy, producing slender, upright stems with finely cut leaves and vivid brick-red to salmon-orange, 4-petaled flowers with a deep maroon basal blotch in spring; native to grassy chaparral burns, open hillsides, and disturbed ground of California's Coast Ranges and foothills. Often appears in abundance after wildfire, earning it the name 'fire follower.' Direct sow in fall in dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; does not transplant well. An outstanding, rarely cultivated annual for California native gardens and fire-follower wildflower mixes.

subcategory: most cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; windmill palm is the most cold-hardy fan palm widely available, surviving to about 5–10°F (-15 to -12°C) when established. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a reliable, permanently hardy landscape palm reaching 20–30 feet over decades. In part shade it grows more slowly but maintains its characteristic single, slender, fiber-covered trunk with spreading fan leaves. Produces fragrant yellow flower clusters in spring, followed by blue-black fruits on female plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; windmill palm is the most cold-hardy fan palm in general cultivation — a native of the mountain forests of central China and Japan at elevations up to 7,500 feet, where it endures significant cold, frost, and even snow on its characteristic fan-shaped leaves. The hardiness extends to approximately 5–10°F (-15 to -12°C) when the palm is established and planted in a sheltered, well-drained position, making it a genuine, permanent landscape palm for gardens as cold as zone 7b — including much of the mid-Atlantic coast, the Pacific Northwest, the British Isles, and large areas of the American Southeast where other palms cannot survive. The distinctive characteristic of the species is the single, slender trunk covered in dense, dark-brown, burlap-like fibrous matting — the remains of old leaf bases — giving it an instantly recognizable, rough-textured, shaggy appearance quite unlike the smooth, gray trunks of many tropical palms. The circular, fan-shaped, blue-green leaf blades, divided into numerous stiff, radiating segments, are held on long petioles at the top of the trunk. In spring, the palm produces arching clusters of small, fragrant, yellow flowers from among the leaf bases; female plants (the species is dioecious) subsequently produce small, blue-black, waxy fruits. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a completely reliable, permanently established landscape palm that grows steadily over decades. One of the defining plants of warm-climate gardening in zones 7–11.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Window haworthia spreads by underground rhizomes to form a slowly expanding mat.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Window haworthia spreads by underground rhizomes to form a slowly expanding mat. Fleshy, triangular leaves with translucent, window-like tips arranged in a spiraling rosette allow light to filter down into the leaf tissue, an adaptation shared with several small haworthias native to rocky crevices in southern Africa where much of the plant hides below the soil surface for protection from intense sun. Unlike clustering haworthias that offset from a central rosette, this species spreads by underground rhizomes, sending up new rosettes at a distance from the parent to form a slowly expanding colony over time. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light, and divide the spreading rhizome mat to propagate or share.

plant_note: Set pseudobulbs half-buried in a gritty, well-drained orchid mix in early spring just as new growth begins, positioning them in a shaded to partially shaded location that stays cool and frost-free through winter.
directions: Half-bury pseudobulbs in a gritty mix of fine bark, perlite, and leaf mold in a shaded position, placing them 4-6 inches apart in a shallow pan or raised bed where their shallow roots can spread freely. Water sparingly when new growth first emerges in spring, gradually increasing moisture as the single pleated leaf and showy pink to lilac flowers develop, then reducing water steadily as foliage yellows in autumn. Keep pseudobulbs cool and nearly dry but frost-free during their winter dormancy, as prolonged freezing will kill them even in zone 7 without protective mulch or cold-frame shelter. Each autumn, lift and separate the daughter pseudobulbs that form alongside the original, discarding the spent parent bulb and replanting the offsets to steadily increase your colony.

common_name: Windy City Ornamental Onion (Large-Flowered Long-Blooming Hybrid Allium)
plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring, or bulbs in fall, in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Windy City is a sterile hybrid bred as a companion to Millenium with larger flower heads on taller stems.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Windy City is a sterile hybrid ornamental onion bred from the same breeding program as the popular Millenium allium, but selected for notably larger rosy-purple globe flowers held on taller, sturdier stems above strap-like, deer- and rabbit-resistant foliage. It blooms from midsummer into early fall, drawing heavy bee and butterfly traffic for weeks, and because it is sterile it does not set seed or self-sow, staying in a tidy, non-spreading clump. Its heat and humidity tolerance make it more reliable in the Gulf South than many ornamental onions, provided drainage is good, and it combines well with coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, and ornamental grasses in a late-summer pollinator planting. Division is needed only occasionally, when clumps become crowded after several years.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Wine Cup crassula has an unusual funnel-shaped leaf and needs excellent drainage to avoid water pooling in the cupped foliage.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Wine Cup crassula has an unusual funnel-shaped leaf and needs excellent drainage to avoid water pooling in the cupped foliage. A single, oddly fused, funnel- or wine-cup-shaped leaf tops a short stem on this diminutive South African succulent, an extraordinary and instantly recognizable growth form unlike any other commonly grown crassula, with small white flowers rising from the center of the cup at maturity. Slow-growing and best displayed as a specimen where its unusual form can be appreciated up close, it is a favorite curiosity among succulent collectors for its bizarre, singular leaf shape. Water sparingly and carefully to avoid water pooling and rotting in the natural cup shape, provide bright indirect light, and propagate from leaf cuttings.

subcategory: spectacularly bicolored South African Cape corm
plant_note: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean to slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; wine cups follows the Cape winter-rainfall growth cycle — emerging in autumn with rains, blooming in late winter and spring (August–October in South Africa, February–April in the Northern Hemisphere), then going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer dormancy. One of the most spectacularly colored small Cape corms. Best in containers in areas with wet summers.
directions: Plant corms in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; wine cups is one of the most dramatically, improbably beautiful small Cape corms — a botanical rarity that produces flowers of such striking, sharply contrasting bicolor perfection that the first sight of a blooming plant reliably produces disbelief. Each flower is a shallow, open, wide-faced cup (the 'wine cup') of pure, deep, vivid blue-violet to royal blue — and at the center of each petal, precisely positioned, a bold, dark wine-red to maroon-red blotch that creates a starburst pattern of wine-red at the center of the blue cup, the two colors absolutely saturated and sharply demarcated in a bicolor combination of electric blue and blood-red that appears painted by an artist rather than produced by a plant. The common name 'Sentry-in-a-Box' refers to the traditional observation that the red markings look like a small figure standing in a blue sentry box. Native to a small area of the Western Cape around Darling in the sandy coastal fynbos, it is one of the Cape's many microendemic botanical wonders — a plant of restricted range but astonishing floral beauty. Outstanding in pots and alpine house conditions where summer dryness is easily controlled; a collector's gem of the highest order.

plant_note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Wine Eyed Jill is a collarette-type dahlia valued for its open, single-flowered, pollinator-friendly form.
directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Wine Eyed Jill is a collarette-type dahlia valued for its open, single-flowered, pollinator-friendly form. A single ring of bright yellow outer petals surrounds a distinctive inner collar of shorter, deep wine-red petaloids around a dark central disc, a two-tiered, open flower form characteristic of collarette dahlias that exposes the central disc to visiting pollinators far more than fully double dahlia forms. Its open, accessible flower structure makes it one of the better dahlia types for attracting bees and other pollinators, in addition to providing a distinctive, layered look for cut-flower arrangements. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, stake tall stems in windy sites, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost.

common_name: Wine and Roses Gladiolus (Pink Fringed with Wine-Red Throat)
plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season. Wine and Roses bears pink, slightly fringed flowers with a wine-red throat edged in white.
directions: Wine and Roses bears soft pink, slightly fringed flowers with a wine-red throat outlined in white, a layered, romantic color combination that has made it a favorite for wedding and event floral work. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall.

common_name: Wine and Roses Weigela (Dark Purple-Leaf Pink-Flowered Weigela)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Wine and Roses holds its dark purple foliage color best with at least six hours of direct sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Wine and Roses was a breakthrough weigela introduction for combining rich, dark burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season with abundant clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped spring flowers that stand out sharply against the dark leaves. Hummingbirds are drawn strongly to the tubular flowers, and the plant provides months of foliage-color interest even after the main spring bloom flush ends. It is generally trouble-free, tolerating heat and average garden soil well, and needs only a light shaping prune right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood and heavy pruning at the wrong time removes the next season's flower buds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring in well-drained to moderately moist, loamy or clay soil in full sun to light shade. Winged Elm seeds ripen in early spring before leafout and must be sown fresh immediately upon collection, as viability is lost within days; transplanting from nursery stock is the practical choice for most gardeners.
directions: Winged Elm is a medium-sized native tree of dry to mesic upland woods, rocky slopes, fence rows, and disturbed roadsides across the southeastern and south-central United States from Virginia to Florida and west to Kansas, readily identified by the distinctive corky, wing-like ridges that develop along younger branches — a feature unique among eastern elms. The seeds ripen in early spring before the leaves emerge and must be sown fresh in moist, well-drained soil immediately upon collection, as germination viability drops to near zero within days of ripening; nursery transplants are the practical method for establishing this species. Winged Elm is among the toughest and most adaptable of the native elms, tolerating drought, compacted clay, alkaline soils, and periodic flooding, and shows some tolerance to Dutch elm disease, making it a useful native tree for difficult urban sites and naturalized roadsides. The vase-shaped canopy, small rough-textured leaves, and light-yellow fall color provide multi-season ornamental interest with minimal maintenance.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; in mild climates (zones 8–10) sow in fall for winter-spring bloom; winged everlasting is an Australian native grown worldwide as an everlasting cut flower — the papery white flower heads with yellow centers dry beautifully on the plant and retain their papery texture for 1–2 years in dried arrangements.
directions: Surface sow or barely cover seed; winged everlasting tolerates poor, dry, sandy soils and needs excellent drainage; harvest stems for drying when the yellow central disc is still tight and the papery white bracts are just opening; hang upside-down in small bundles in a dry, airy location to dry; the papery quality is retained for years in dry conditions. Winged everlasting (Ammobium alatum) is an Australian native wildflower grown around the world as a premier dried-flower crop and garden annual, valued for its distinctive papery flower heads that retain their appearance almost indefinitely after drying. The plant grows from a basal rosette of leaves with woolly-white undersides, sending up erect, distinctively winged stems (the 'alatum' = 'winged' in Latin refers to the prominent flanges running down the length of each stem) topped by clusters of small, round, papery-bracted flower heads about 3/4 inch across — white papery outer bracts surrounding a compact yellow central disc. The white papery bracts have the characteristic texture of everlasting flowers: they are neither petals nor sepals in the conventional sense but specialized, scale-like bracts that are naturally dry and paper-textured even on the living plant. When cut and dried, the flowers maintain their white color and papery texture with minimal shrinkage and no loss of the characteristic form, making Ammobium one of the longest-lasting and most reliably drying of all the everlasting flower genera. The flowers are freely produced over a long season (6–8 weeks or more), and plants often self-sow reliably in well-drained garden situations. Used extensively in dried flower arrangements, wreaths, and craft projects.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratify seed for 30 days, then surface-sow in moist to wet soil in full to partial sun once temperatures warm.
directions: Sow into consistently moist to wet soil along pond edges, ditches, or low meadow spots, pressing seed onto the surface without covering since it needs light to germinate. This slender native wildflower is an entirely different, well-behaved species from the invasive Eurasian purple loosestrife it is sometimes confused with, staying in a modest clump rather than spreading into wetlands. From midsummer into fall it produces slim spikes of small magenta-pink flowers along winged stems that draw in bumblebees, small native bees, and skipper butterflies. It pairs well with other wetland natives such as blue flag iris and swamp milkweed in a rain garden setting.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts in spring into a loose, well-draining mix of long-fiber sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite; keep the medium moist year-round with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide high humidity — never use tap water or ordinary garden soil.
directions: Winged pitcher plant is native to a broad range of Philippine islands, where it grows as a scrambling vine at low to mid elevations and produces the narrow, ribbed 'wings' running down the front of its pitchers that give the species its common name. It is one of the more forgiving Nepenthes for home growers, tolerating the moderate day-to-night temperature swings of a typical house or sunroom rather than demanding the cool nights of high-elevation species. Pot it in a well-draining mix of long-fiber sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite, and water only with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or collected rainwater, since the dissolved minerals and salts in tap water accumulate in the sensitive roots and kill the plant over time. Keep humidity high with regular misting or a pebble tray, provide bright filtered light, and never fertilize the soil — feed sparingly, if at all, by dropping a small dead insect directly into a mature pitcher instead.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow after soil warms to 70°F in full sun; wingpod purslane requires no watering once established in sandy or gravelly soil. Unlike moss rose (P. grandiflora), the flowers of P. umbraticola (used to breed most modern Portulaca hybrids) do not close in cloudy weather — an important horticultural advantage. Most nursery 'Portulaca' sold as 'Sundial', 'Yubi', or 'Pazzazz' series are derived from or are this species.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; wingpod purslane is a heat-loving succulent annual native to the southern United States and tropical America that is the primary parent species behind most modern portulaca hybrids sold under names like 'Sundial', 'Yubi', and 'Pazzazz.' It produces succulent, cylindrical to flat, glossy, bright-green leaves on sprawling, succulent stems and from early summer through frost, vivid, tissue-paper-textured flowers (1–2 inches across) in the full range of hot portulaca colors — crimson, scarlet, magenta, orange, yellow, white, and bicolors — that, importantly, stay open longer in cloudy conditions than the related moss rose (P. grandiflora), making them a better choice for regions with overcast summer weather. Absolutely the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant of all colorful summer annuals, thriving in pure sand or gravel with no supplemental irrigation in the hottest summer conditions. Outstanding for the tops of dry stone walls, sandy road edges, the front edge of gravel driveways, and any impossible, hot, dry location where virtually nothing else will flower. An essential plant for Gulf Coast and zone 9 summer gardens where heat and drought defeat most annuals.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist, fertile soil in partial shade; plants establish readily and spread by rhizome and self-seeding, naturalizing aggressively once happy. Do not plant in small gardens without containment.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wingstem is a bold, tall native wildflower of moist woodland edges and stream banks with distinctive narrow wings running down the length of the stem (giving it the common name), topped with loose clusters of raggedy yellow flowers in August through October that are outstanding late-season nectar sources for bees, wasps, and butterflies. The plant is one of the most shade-tolerant of the tall native yellow-flowered composites, blooming reliably in significant shade where few similar plants perform. It spreads aggressively by rhizome and should be given a naturalized area of its own or managed by division. The persistent seed heads are eaten by goldfinches and other seed-eating birds through fall and winter.

plant_note: Plant the potted or bare-root climber in spring after hard frosts.
directions: Winner's Circle is a vigorous climbing rose with bright, cherry-red double blooms and a strong, upright habit that flowers spring through fall. Plant the potted or bare-root rose in spring in full sun and rich, well-drained soil near a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence to support the canes. Tie in the long canes as they grow and train them horizontally to encourage more blooms. Water at the base to keep foliage dry, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune in late winter to shape and remove old wood. Hardy in zones 4 to 10, it rewards care with repeat flushes of color.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Winnifred Gilman sage needs sharp drainage and is more compact and better suited to smaller gardens than the species.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Winnifred Gilman sage needs sharp drainage and is more compact and better suited to smaller gardens than the species. Intensely aromatic, wrinkled gray-green leaves cover a rounded, well-branched shrub topped with dense whorls of vivid violet-blue flowers held on distinctive purple-black flower stalks, a strong color contrast that makes this one of the most popular selections of Cleveland sage grown in California native gardens. Its compact size compared to the straight species, combined with exceptional fragrance and a long bloom season that draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds, makes it a standout choice for a sunny xeriscape border or native pollinator garden. It needs no supplemental water once established and resents rich soil, heavy mulch, or summer irrigation, all of which shorten its naturally long lifespan.

common_name: Winston Churchill Sweet Pea (Crimson-Scarlet Spencer Sweet Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Winston Churchill is a classic crimson Spencer-type sweet pea long popular with exhibitors.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Winston Churchill bears large, ruffled, fragrant Spencer-type flowers in a deep, vivid crimson-scarlet, a bold, saturated color that has kept it a favorite among sweet pea exhibitors and cutting gardeners since its introduction. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows the vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

plant_note: Plant tubers (actually small, knobbly rhizomes) 2-3 inches deep as soon as they are available in late summer or very early fall — ideally in August or September while the tubers are still plump and fresh, as they dry out and fail quickly if stored; soak dry tubers in water for 24 hours before planting to rehydrate them. Winter aconite establishes most reliably when planted immediately after purchase into moist, humus-rich, alkaline-leaning soil beneath deciduous trees.
directions: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep as early as possible in fall in moist, humus-rich, preferably alkaline soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees for late January to March bloom; winter aconite is the earliest of all spring bulbs — it blooms while snow is still on the ground, often beginning in January or February, producing solitary bright golden-yellow, buttercup-like flowers cupped in a distinctive ruff of bright green, finely cut leaves that makes the flower look as though it is wearing a small green collar. It is the perfect companion for snowdrops (Galanthus) — the golden flowers of winter aconite and white flowers of snowdrops bloom simultaneously, creating one of the most celebrated sights of the late-winter garden. Unlike most bulbs, winter aconite is actually a small tuber (rhizome) that performs best in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that stays cool and slightly moist even in summer, and it thrives under the light shade and root competition of deciduous trees — conditions it encounters in its native woodland habitat across southern Europe. It self-seeds freely once established to form large colonies, but initial establishment can be slow, particularly from dried tubers; fresh tubers or green transplants succeed best.

plant_note: Plant this Mediterranean evergreen clematis in autumn with its roots shaded and cool; prune lightly right after flowering.
directions: Plant this Mediterranean evergreen clematis in autumn with its roots shaded and cool while its ferny, sometimes bronze-tinted foliage climbs into brighter light above, the classic cool-roots-sunny-head rule relaxed here since the vine tolerates partial shade throughout. Nodding, bell-shaped cream to pale yellow flowers, often freckled maroon inside, open through winter into early spring when little else in the garden is blooming. It is a useful choice for softening a shaded wall or fence with off-season interest and a light almond scent in some selections. Prune lightly right after flowering to tidy growth without sacrificing next winter's buds.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial to full shade or full sun in spring; winter creeper is extremely adaptable and tolerates a wide range of soil types, sun levels, and difficult conditions including drought and air pollution.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in shade to full sun; winter creeper is one of the most versatile and widely planted evergreen groundcovers in North American landscaping — a trailing to climbing shrub with glossy, dark-green, oval leaves that naturally roots where stems contact soil, making it an effective weed-suppressing groundcover on slopes and under trees, or a wall-covering vine when given support. Numerous cultivars offer varying leaf size, growth habit, and variegation: 'Coloratus' (leaves turn purple-red in winter, excellent groundcover), 'Emerald Gaiety' (white-margined, compact), 'Emerald 'n Gold' (yellow-margined, colorful), and 'Vegetus' (large-leaved, vigorous). Very tolerant of shade, drought, poor soil, air pollution, and pruning. Important caution: in parts of the eastern US and Midwest it can escape cultivation to become invasive in woodland settings; check local invasive species listings before planting in naturalized areas.

plant_note: Plant corms 1–2 inches deep in fall (with the flat side down) in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; winter cyclamen goes dormant in summer and should be planted where it will not receive summer irrigation.
directions: Plant corms flat-side down, 1–2 inches deep, in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; winter cyclamen (Eastern Mediterranean cyclamen) is a delightful small hardy cyclamen that blooms in late winter to early spring — often from December through February — producing tiny, swept-back, bright carmine, pink, or white flowers and beautifully marbled, kidney-shaped silver-patterned leaves that emerge in fall and persist through winter, disappearing entirely in summer dormancy. The plant naturalizes slowly by self-seeding to form expanding colonies under deciduous trees and in sheltered rock gardens. Less demanding than the tender florist's cyclamen; this species is reliably hardy and garden-worthy. Best planted in masses of 25 or more for a significant winter flowering effect.

plant_note: Plant in early fall or spring in sharply drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; daphne is notoriously difficult to transplant — choose the permanent location carefully as plants do not move well.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade and choose the site carefully — winter daphne resents transplanting and should be considered permanent once established. The intensely sweet fragrance of its pink-purple flower clusters from late winter to early spring is one of the most powerful and pleasant in the garden and can perfume the air for 20 feet or more. Excellent drainage is the single most critical cultural requirement; root rot in wet soil kills plants quickly and without warning, a phenomenon so common that gardeners joke that daphne 'dies for no reason.' Keep well-watered during dry spells in summer. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — handle with care and wash hands after pruning.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Winter Gem requires protection from hot afternoon sun in zone 9 — partial shade is preferred and helps prevent the bronzing and bleaching that can affect boxwood foliage in intense summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun with afternoon shade protection; Winter Gem is the most widely planted Korean boxwood cultivar — a tight, globe-forming selection that maintains exceptional dense, rounded form with small, dark-green, lustrous leaves that hold their color better than many boxwood cultivars through winter and summer. The deep, rich green color with a slightly glossy sheen is particularly attractive as a formal edging or clipped topiary subject. Unlike many Buxus sempervirens cultivars, Winter Gem shows markedly superior resistance to boxwood blight (Calonectria pseudonaviculata), which has devastated English boxwood plantings across much of the Eastern United States — this disease resistance is a major reason Korean boxwood cultivars have increased in popularity. Winter Gem tolerates zone 9 summer heat better than English boxwood selections, provided afternoon shade protects from the most intense sun. Boxwoods require well-drained soil — they are extremely susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet, poorly drained sites. No serious pests affect boxwood in Gulf Coast gardens except the boxwood leafminer, which causes blistering of the leaves; treat with systemic insecticide if infestation is severe. Shear or hand-prune to maintain desired formal shape in late winter or after spring flush.

common_name: Winter Gold Winterberry (Rare Gold-Apricot-Berried Native Winterberry)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Winter Gold bears unusual gold-to-apricot berries, distinct from the red-fruited winterberry cultivars more commonly grown. Plant a compatible male pollinator within range for fruit set.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a compatible male winterberry within range for pollination, since hollies are dioecious and only fertilized female plants produce berries. Winter Gold is a rare and distinctive winterberry selection bearing berries in a warm gold-to-apricot tone rather than the classic bright red of most cultivars, a striking, unusual color option that stands out in the winter landscape and in cut branches used for holiday arrangements. The berries persist on the bare branches well into winter after leaf drop, providing the same valuable food source for robins, cedar waxwings, and other birds as red-fruited winterberry selections. It tolerates wet soil better than most shrubs, making it useful in a rain garden or low spot, and requires little routine care once established. Prune to shape in late winter before new growth begins, if needed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter honeysuckle blooms on bare branches in late winter, filling the garden with fragrance well before spring.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter honeysuckle blooms on bare branches in late winter, filling the garden with fragrance well before spring. Small, creamy white, unassuming flowers open along the bare branches in late winter to very early spring, easy to overlook visually but releasing an intense, sweet, lemon-and-jasmine-like fragrance that carries a remarkable distance on a still winter day, making this shrub prized for scent rather than showy bloom. A large, rounded, semi-evergreen to deciduous shrub, it is best sited near a door, window, or path where its understated but powerful winter fragrance can be enjoyed up close during the coldest, least colorful part of the year. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, and note that it has naturalized and become weedy in some regions, so monitor for unwanted seedlings and consider a well-behaved native alternative where invasive spread is a local concern.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; this species iris blooms extremely early, sometimes emerging through snow, and needs a dry summer dormancy to persist.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; this species iris blooms extremely early, sometimes emerging through snow, and needs a dry summer dormancy to persist. Large, richly patterned deep blue to violet flowers with white, gold-flecked markings on the falls open remarkably early, often the very first bulb to flower in late winter, well ahead of crocus and even before its own grassy foliage has fully developed. Native to the mountains of Turkey, it is the wild species behind many of the popular reticulata iris hybrids more commonly sold, and grows and multiplies well in a rock garden or raised bed with the same sharp drainage its hybrid offspring require. Allow foliage to mature and yellow naturally after bloom before removing it, and avoid summer watering, which is fatal to the bulbs during their dry dormant season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter jasmine tolerates poor soil and looks best cascading over a wall or bank where its arching stems can drape freely.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter jasmine tolerates poor soil and looks best cascading over a wall or bank where its arching stems can drape freely. Bright yellow, star-shaped flowers open along bare, arching green stems from late winter into early spring, well ahead of most other flowering shrubs, providing a welcome flush of cheerful color during the last cold weeks of winter dormancy despite lacking the fragrance of its jasmine relatives. Its long, sprawling, cascading stems root wherever they touch soil, making it a useful, tough groundcover for a bank or the top of a retaining wall where its arching branches can spill downward and its winter bloom can be appreciated from below. Prune immediately after flowering to shape and control spread, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and it tolerates hard renewal pruning if the planting becomes overgrown.

common_name: Winter Moonbeam Hellebore (Silver-Veined Early-Blooming Hybrid Hellebore)
plant_note: Transplant container-grown plants in fall or early spring into humus-rich, neutral-to-alkaline soil, disturbing the roots as little as possible.
directions: Plant in well-drained but moisture-retentive soil enriched with compost, ideally beneath deciduous shrubs or trees that provide summer shade and winter light. Established clumps need little care beyond an annual topdressing of compost and removal of old, tattered leaves in late winter to showcase the emerging flowers. This hybrid between Helleborus niger and H. sternii forms leathery, silver-veined evergreen foliage and produces abundant clusters of pink-blushed white flowers from midwinter into early spring, well ahead of most other hellebores. Its combination of ornamental foliage and extra-early bloom makes it a standout for a winter shade garden.

common_name: Winter Red Winterberry Holly (Heavy-Fruiting Compact Female Winterberry)
plant_note: Plant female shrubs alongside a compatible male pollinator such as Jim Dandy in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; Winter Red is among the most widely planted and heaviest-fruiting winterberry cultivars available.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, and site a compatible male pollinator such as Jim Dandy within pollinating range, since winterberry is dioecious and female plants need a male nearby to set fruit. Winter Red bears an exceptionally heavy, dense crop of bright red berries that coat the bare branches after leaf drop and persist well into winter, considered one of the most reliably prolific and widely available winterberry cultivars on the market. Its dependable, showy fruit display makes it a favorite for winter interest, holiday decorating, and feeding overwintering songbirds. Prune only lightly and only after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Winter's Beauty Camellia (Cold-Hardy Pink Semi-Double Ackerman Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Beauty is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series of cold-hardy camellias.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Winter's Beauty belongs to the Ackerman-bred Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids, bearing semi-double pink blooms with a dense, ruffled center on a vigorous, dense shrub, blooming over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in flower. Its compact growth suits foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders alike. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

common_name: Winter's Charm Camellia (Cold-Hardy Lavender-Pink Peony-Form Ackerman Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Charm is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series of cold-hardy camellias bred for fall-into-winter bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Winter's Charm belongs to the Ackerman-bred Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids, bearing full, peony-form lavender-pink blooms on an upright, vigorous shrub, one of the more richly colored members of the series. It flowers over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in bloom. plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Hope is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series of cold-hardy camellias.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Winter's Hope belongs to the Ackerman-bred Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids, opening from buds tinged pink into semi-double to peony-form blooms that fade toward white as they mature, giving a soft, two-toned effect over the bloom period. It flowers over a long season from fall into early winter on a vigorous, upright shrub. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Interlude is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series of cold-hardy camellias bred for fall-into-winter bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Winter's Interlude belongs to the Ackerman-bred Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids, producing anemone-form shell-pink blooms on a spreading, wider-than-tall shrub that works well as a low, informal hedge or mass planting. It flowers over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in bloom. plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Joy is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series of cold-hardy camellias bred for fall-into-winter bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Winter's Joy belongs to the Ackerman-bred Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids, bearing neat, formal double pink blooms on a dense, compact shrub that fits foundation plantings and smaller gardens well. It flowers over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in bloom. plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Rose is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series of cold-hardy camellias bred for fall-into-winter bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Winter's Rose belongs to the Ackerman-bred Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids, notable for its small, formal double, soft pink blooms and unusually dense, compact growth habit compared to other Winter series cultivars, making it well suited to foundation plantings or containers. It flowers over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are blooming. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Snowman is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series, among the most cold-hardy white-flowered members.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Winter's Snowman belongs to the Ackerman-bred Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids, bearing crisp white anemone-form blooms on a vigorous, upright shrub, among the hardiest and most reliably cold-tolerant members of the series. It flowers over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in bloom. common_name: Winter's Star Camellia (Cold-Hardy Orchid-Pink Ackerman Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Star is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series of cold-hardy camellias, bred for reliable fall-into-winter bloom and better cold tolerance than standard camellias.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold snaps. Winter's Star belongs to the Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids developed at the U.S. National Arboretum, crossing Camellia oleifera into the hardier fall-blooming Camellia hiemalis lineage to combine dependable fall-into-winter flowering with markedly better cold tolerance than most camellias. It produces single, orchid-pink flowers with prominent golden stamens on a vigorous, spreading evergreen shrub, blooming over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in flower. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Winter's Waterlily is part of Dr. William Ackerman's Winter series, bred for formal double white blooms resembling a waterlily.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold. Winter's Waterlily belongs to the Ackerman-bred Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids, its formal double white blooms opening in tidy, symmetrical layers reminiscent of a waterlily, on a dense, compact shrub well suited to foundation plantings. It flowers over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in bloom. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

plant_note: Plant at least one male and three female shrubs for berry production; one male can pollinate up to five females. Match the male cultivar's bloom time to the female's — choose male cultivar recommendations from the nursery that match your female selection.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; winterberry is a spectacular native deciduous holly that produces brilliant red (or yellow or orange in some cultivars) berries that encrust every branch after leaf drop in fall, providing dazzling winter interest from October through February when birds finally strip them. It grows naturally in swamps, stream banks, and wet woodland margins and performs best with consistent moisture. This species is dioecious — you must plant both male and female plants, matching cultivars that bloom at the same time, to get berries. Named female cultivars like 'Winter Red', 'Sparkleberry', and 'Red Sprite' (compact) are widely available; match them with the appropriate male. Mulch to maintain soil moisture and acidity.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring just below soil level with the crown at the surface, in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fall planting also succeeds in mild climates.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, and pull off tattered older leaves by tugging them sharply downward to snap them free from the rhizome. Winterglow is a compact, Terra Nova Nurseries selection prized for its glossy, rounded evergreen leaves, which turn a rich burgundy-red through the cold months, and its clusters of white flowers that age to soft pink, opening on sturdy red stems in early spring. Its dense, tidy habit makes it a better fit for small shade gardens and container plantings than larger species bergenias, while still providing the same tough, deer-resistant groundcover value. Divide crowded clumps every 4–5 years in spring by cutting through the woody, surface-creeping rhizomes.

common_name: Wintergold Hellebore (Gold Collection Golden-Flowered Hybrid Hellebore)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wintergold is a vigorous Gold Collection cross of Helleborus niger and H. argutifolius that combines spiny, leathery foliage with unusually soft golden-yellow flowers blushed pink as they age.
directions: Site in fertile, humus-rich soil with good drainage in partial shade, mulching lightly to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature over winter. Wintergold inherits the coarse, spiny-toothed, dark evergreen foliage of Corsican hellebore parentage along with the earlier, more floriferous blooming habit of Christmas rose, producing abundant outward-facing flowers that open a soft primrose-yellow and age to dusky pink as the season progresses. This nigercors hybrid is notably vigorous and more heat-tolerant than pure Helleborus niger selections, making it a useful choice where straight Christmas rose struggles. As a patented clone it is increased by division rather than seed; established clumps can be lifted and split in early fall once flowering slows.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Wintergreen boxwood holds its green winter color better than many boxwood cultivars, which often bronze in cold weather.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Wintergreen boxwood holds its green winter color better than many boxwood cultivars, which often bronze in cold weather. Small, glossy, bright green leaves cover a dense, rounded, exceptionally cold-hardy boxwood selection bred for reliable survival in harsh northern winters where many traditional boxwood cultivars suffer dieback, while retaining fresh green foliage color through the coldest months rather than the bronzing common in less hardy types. Its combination of superior cold hardiness and good winter color has made it a popular substitute for English boxwood in colder climates, used for low hedges, edging, and formal shapes much like its more tender relatives. Shear in late spring or early summer to maintain a formal shape, water during establishment and dry spells, and provide good air circulation to reduce the fungal disease pressure that affects many boxwood plantings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; wintersweet is slow to establish and slow to reach flowering size from seed, so container stock is the standard way to plant it.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a warm wall or in a sheltered spot near a path where its fragrance can be appreciated up close; wintersweet is an old Chinese garden shrub grown for one thing above all — intensely sweet, spicy fragrance from small, waxy, translucent pale-yellow flowers with maroon-purple centers that open on bare gray branches in the dead of winter, often during a warm spell between freezes, well before the glossy leaves emerge. A single stem cut and brought indoors will scent an entire room. The shrub itself is an unremarkable, rangy, multi-stemmed grower with plain foliage the rest of the year, so site it where winter interest matters and something else can carry the summer show, such as near an entry or a frequently used winter path. It tolerates partial shade but flowers most heavily with several hours of sun. Prune immediately after flowering, since next winter's buds form on the current year's growth; older plants can be renovated by cutting the oldest stems to the ground.

plant_note: Establish from nursery plugs in spring in full sun in dry, sandy, infertile, well-drained soil; wiregrass is the dominant native groundcover grass of longleaf pine flatwoods and savannas across the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Establish from container-grown plugs in spring in full sun in lean, sandy, well-drained soil, since wiregrass struggles in rich or poorly drained ground. This fine-textured, wiry bunchgrass forms tight blue-green clumps and sends up slender flowering stalks in fall that catch afternoon light beautifully, echoing the look of the longleaf pine savannas it dominates across the Gulf Coastal Plain. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and historically depended on periodic fire to flower and reseed, so gardeners typically cut clumps back hard in late winter to mimic that cycle. Use it in sandy, low-fertility beds, native plant meadows, or pine-savanna-style landscaping where showier, moisture-loving grasses would fail.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Surface-sow tiny seeds on moist mix without covering; they need light to germinate at 70–75°F. Torenia is one of the best flowering annuals for shaded and part-shaded spots in hot, humid climates where impatiens are lost to downy mildew. The bicolored, snapdragon-like flowers in purple, pink, white, or yellow bloom profusely without deadheading throughout summer. Keep soil consistently moist, as plants wilt quickly when dry but recover readily; fertilize monthly with a balanced liquid feed.

common_name: Wisley Blue Spring Starflower (Deep Blue Ipheion Selection)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Wisley Blue is a superior selection of spring starflower with larger, deeper blue flowers than the species.
directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; spring starflower tolerates surprisingly dry summer conditions once established and multiplies readily by offset bulbs. Wisley Blue bears larger, more richly colored, deep lavender-blue, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers than the plain species, held on slender stems above narrow, grass-like foliage that smells faintly of onion when crushed, betraying its relationship to the allium family. It blooms freely over several weeks in early to mid-spring, performing equally well in open sunny borders and in the light shade of deciduous trees. The bulbs multiply steadily, slowly forming dense clumps well suited to edging, rock gardens, or naturalizing in rough grass, and need essentially no maintenance once established beyond allowing the foliage to die back naturally after bloom.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in early spring or late fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; the plant transplants well from container stock but is slow to establish from seed. The species blooms October–December; vernal witch hazel (H. vernalis) blooms in late winter.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; American witch hazel is the latest-blooming native shrub, producing clusters of fragrant, spidery yellow flowers on bare branches from October through December — often while the leaves are still falling around the flowers. It is a stunning sight in the November woodland garden when nothing else is in bloom. Growing naturally as a multi-stemmed understory tree in moist woodland slopes and ravines across eastern North America, it tolerates full shade but blooms more heavily with some dappled light. The bark and leaves are the botanical source of witch hazel astringent. Allow it to grow naturally as a large multi-stemmed specimen; it resents heavy pruning. The seed pods pop open explosively to disperse seeds.

common_name: Wizard Golden Coleus (Seed-Grown Chartreuse Foliage Coleus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; pinch out small flower spikes as they form to keep energy in foliage production.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost. The Wizard series was an early AAS-winning breakthrough in raising coleus reliably and uniformly from seed rather than cuttings, and it remains one of the most widely grown seed coleus lines. Wizard Golden bears bright chartreuse-gold leaves with a small maroon center blotch, brightening shaded beds and mixed containers all season on compact, well-branched plants. Pinching out the small blue flower spikes as they form keeps the plant's energy in foliage production and prevents legginess.

common_name: Wizard Mix Coleus (Seed-Grown Multicolor Coleus Blend)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, surface-sowing since coleus seed needs light to germinate; transplant out after all frost danger has passed and nights stay reliably above 50°F.
directions: Surface-sow seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, since light aids germination, and transplant into partial shade to filtered sun once nights are reliably warm. Wizard Mix was one of the original All-America Selections-winning coleus lines bred to come true and uniform from seed rather than requiring cuttings, and the mix packet produces a full range of the series' signature colors on compact, well-branched plants, from deep maroon and rose to salmon, chartreuse, and bicolor combinations edged in green or cream. Pinch out the small blue flower spikes as they form to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage rather than seed production, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage bushy, well-filled plants. Wizard Mix tolerates more sun than older coleus strains but still colors up best and holds its leaves longest with some afternoon shade in hot Gulf South summers.

common_name: Wizard Mosaic Coleus (Green Foliage Speckled with Red Mottling)
plant_note: Start seed indoors or plant after all frost danger has passed; Wizard Mosaic is a compact, seed-grown coleus with bright green leaves speckled and splotched with red in a mottled mosaic pattern.
directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Wizard Mosaic bears bright green leaves irregularly speckled and blotched with red in a distinctive mottled pattern that gives each leaf a unique, mosaic-like appearance, distinguishing it from solid-colored coleus cultivars. Its compact, uniform, heat-tolerant habit and tolerance of both sun and shade make it a versatile choice for edging, mass bedding, and containers. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.

common_name: Wizard Scarlet Coleus (Compact Bright Red Seed-Grown Coleus)
plant_note: Start seed indoors or plant after all frost danger has passed; Wizard Scarlet is a compact, seed-grown Wizard series coleus with bright red, slightly ruffled leaves edged in green, tolerant of both sun and shade.
directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Wizard Scarlet bears bright, slightly ruffled red leaves edged in a contrasting green margin on a compact, uniform, seed-grown plant bred for reliable garden performance from a young age. Its small stature and adaptability to a wide range of light conditions make it a versatile choice for edging, mass bedding, and containers where a compact, colorful foliage plant is wanted. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Wizard Sunset coleus grows quickly and fills in beds and containers with brilliant warm-toned foliage. Pinch flower spikes as soon as they appear to maintain the foliage color and compact shape — flowering signals the end of the plant's productive foliage season. In zone 9 the long warm season allows extended growth; the plants can be maintained as large specimens through the year in frost-free areas.
directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Wizard Sunset is part of the Wizard coleus series — a compact, seed-grown coleus series known for uniform habit and a wide range of color selections. The Sunset color in the Wizard series features leaves in a warm blend of sunset orange, gold, red-orange, and bronze arranged in irregular patterns, capturing the warm glow of an evening sky. The compact, 12–18 inch height and dense branching habit of the Wizard series makes it one of the most practical seed-grown coleus for formal bedding patterns, edging, and container planting where a consistent, predictable size is required. Unlike the large-leaved vegetatively propagated coleus varieties, seed-grown Wizard types are uniform in size, color, and habit — each plant from the same packet is nearly identical, making them reliable for mass planting effects. In partial shade the warm sunset colors are often most vivid; deep shade tends to deepen the red tones while reducing the gold and orange.

plant_note: Direct-sow in fall for biennial flowering in spring of the second year, or sow in very early spring; woad is a biennial or short-lived perennial in the mustard family. INVASIVE WARNING: Woad is a listed noxious weed in multiple western US states (Idaho, Colorado, Utah, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, and others) and should not be planted in those states. Check local regulations before planting.
directions: Sow in well-drained, average soil in full sun — INVASIVE in western US states: check local regulations; woad is the ancient European source of blue dye that predates the introduction of tropical indigo (Indigofera tinctoria) — the same compound, indigotin, is present in both plants, but in smaller concentrations in woad. The blue woad dye produced from fermented, composted leaves was the primary blue textile dye of Europe for thousands of years, from prehistoric times through the Middle Ages, and was used to produce the blue in medieval stained glass pigments, illuminated manuscripts, and textiles. The Picts of Scotland famously used woad to paint their bodies blue. The plant itself is an upright biennial producing rosettes of blue-green basal leaves in the first year and tall branching flower stalks bearing masses of small, bright-yellow flowers in the second year, followed by distinctive, hanging, black, paddle-shaped seed pods that are ornamental. It was supplanted by imported indigo in the 16th–17th centuries. Now grown primarily as a historical, educational, and natural dye plant.

common_name: Wolf Eyes Kousa Dogwood (Variegated Dwarf Kousa Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; variegated foliage scorches in intense afternoon sun and benefits from some shade protection.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure that can scorch the variegated leaves. Wolf Eyes is a dwarf, slow-growing kousa dogwood grown as much for its striking foliage as its flowers, with leaves crisply edged in creamy white around a gray-green center, turning shades of pink and burgundy-red in fall, along with a modest early-summer flush of white bracts against the variegated backdrop. Its smaller mature size and dense, compact habit make it a strong specimen for smaller gardens or as a focal accent near a patio where the foliage can be appreciated up close. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Wollerton Old Hall Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since Wollerton Old Hall is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber against a wall, fence, or pillar.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes as a climber; prune lightly to shape after the main flush rather than hard-pruning, which sacrifices height. Introduced by David Austin in 2011, Wollerton Old Hall produces soft apricot-cream, cupped rosette flowers carrying one of the strongest myrrh fragrances of any English rose, on long, arching, thornier-than-average canes that can reach 10 feet or more when trained upright, or be kept as a large freestanding shrub with pruning. Its vigor, fragrance, and repeat bloom from late spring through frost have made it a favorite for both border and climbing use in warm-climate gardens.

common_name: Woman's Tongue (Siris Tree, East Indian Walnut)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Woman's Tongue is a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing, tropical legume shade tree famous for its persistent, flat, papery seed pods that rattle noisily in the wind (hence the evocative common name) — CAUTION: classified as a Category I invasive exotic in Florida where it naturalizes aggressively in disturbed areas and natural habitats.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established. CAUTION: invasive in Florida — do not plant near natural areas. Albizia lebbeck (woman's tongue or siris tree) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous-to-semi-evergreen tropical legume tree native to South Asia and tropical Africa, now widely naturalized throughout the tropics as both a valued shade tree and an invasive species. The plant is named 'woman's tongue' for its persistent, flat, tan, papery, 6–10 inch long seed pods that hold their seeds loosely and rattle loudly in the slightest breeze — the metaphorical association being obvious.
