As a landscape tree, Woman's Tongue is excellent: it grows rapidly (3–5 feet per year), provides dense, spreading shade, fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root bacteria, produces attractive cream-white, fragrant, powder-puff flower clusters in late spring, and is extraordinarily drought-tolerant on poor soils. The bark has traditionally yielded saponins used as a soap substitute in India. The wood is highly valued as a timber for furniture and construction in South Asia. IMPORTANT CAUTION: In Florida, coastal Gulf South states, and Hawaii, Albizia lebbeck is classified as an invasive exotic pest plant — it naturalizes in disturbed areas, roadsides, and natural areas aggressively. Do not plant in proximity to natural lands in Florida or coastal Gulf states.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; plant in generous drifts of at least 25–50 rhizomes for best effect.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; wood anemone spreads steadily by rhizomes to form extensive, low carpets under deciduous trees and looks best when planted in generous drifts of at least 25–50 rhizomes. Anemone nemorosa is a diminutive, spring-ephemeral European woodland perennial producing a low carpet of deeply cut, dark-green, three-lobed leaves above which rise slender, 6–12-inch stems each bearing a single, star-shaped, white (sometimes pink or pale blue in cultivars) flower with 6–8 petal-like sepals and a ring of golden stamens in early to mid-spring; the plant goes completely dormant by early summer. It naturalizes beautifully under deciduous trees and in combination with spring bulbs such as snowdrops, glory of the snow, and miniature daffodils; cultivars include the lavender-blue 'Robinsoniana' and the pure white, semi-double 'Vestal'. All parts are mildly toxic.

plant_note: Divide the slender creeping rhizomes in fall and plant shallowly in loose, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees where the colony can receive bright early-spring light; seed germination is slow and erratic, so division is the practical propagation method.
directions: Divide the slender creeping rhizomes in fall and plant shallowly in loose, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees where the colony can receive bright early-spring light. Native to eastern North American woodlands, this dainty spring ephemeral bears five-parted leaflets and solitary white, often pink-blushed flowers that open in mid to late spring, then the whole plant goes dormant and disappears by midsummer as the canopy closes overhead. It differs from the similar European wood anemone in leaflet number and is a well-behaved, slow-spreading groundcover rather than an aggressive colonizer. Best combined with other spring ephemerals like trout lily or spring beauty that share the same fleeting bloom window.

plant_note: Plant divisions near suitable host plant roots in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; wood betony is hemiparasitic primarily on grasses and some forbs — it performs best in native plant communities with a diversity of host species.
directions: Plant divisions or carefully transplant container-grown plants in spring near the roots of grasses and native forbs in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade or light dappled sun; wood betony is hemiparasitic and performs best embedded in a diverse native plant community with ample grass and forb roots to tap. Pedicularis canadensis is a native eastern North American hemiparasitic perennial of woodland edges, prairies, and open rocky slopes; it produces attractive, deeply pinnately lobed, fernlike leaves in a basal rosette and stout spikes of clustered, tubular flowers with distinctive, hooded upper lips in colors ranging from yellow through red in mid-spring, one of the most beautiful and architecturally interesting of the spring wildflowers. It is among the most important early-season nectar plants for queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation. Like paintbrush, it benefits from diverse host-plant associations and is most successful in native meadow and woodland garden settings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled sun in spring; wood cranesbill is native to the cool woodlands and meadows of Europe and western Asia and tolerates more sun than most woodland geraniums where summers stay mild.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled sun in spring, working in compost to improve moisture retention in lean soils. Wood cranesbill forms a tidy mound of deeply lobed, softly hairy leaves topped in late spring to early summer by abundant violet-blue to purple-pink flowers with a small white eye. It tolerates more sun than most woodland geraniums in cooler climates but appreciates afternoon shade and consistent moisture where summers turn hot and humid. Shear the entire clump back by half after the main flush of bloom to tidy the foliage and often coax a lighter rebloom later in the season.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall at 3–4 inches depth in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; wood lily is one of the few native lilies that holds its flowers upright (facing the sky) rather than drooping. It requires good drainage and benefits from light shade in warmer zones.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; wood lily is one of the most striking native wildflowers of eastern and central North America, producing upward-facing, brilliantly orange to orange-red, spotted flowers on relatively short stems — unlike the drooping, turk's-cap form of most other native lilies. The upright orientation makes wood lily a natural hummingbird flower, and ruby-throated hummingbirds are among its most important pollinators. The plant is increasingly rare in the wild due to deer browsing, loss of fire-maintained habitat, and illegal collection. In the garden, wood lily requires excellent drainage and is short-lived in rich, moist conditions. Plant in sandy soil on a slope or raised bed with consistent but moderate moisture and light afternoon shade in warmer zones.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; wood melic grass grows naturally in shaded woodland on alkaline or neutral soils and is specifically suited to shade conditions — it does not perform well in full sun.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; wood melic grass is a European woodland grass that is one of the few true ornamental grasses suited to deep shade — it forms loose, delicate tufts of soft, flat, rich-green leaves and produces loose, arching panicles of nodding, dark-purple to bronze, single-spikeleted flowers from late spring through early summer that glisten with a silky, metallic quality when backlit. The overall effect of wood melic in flower is ethereal and refined — far more subtle and naturalistic than most ornamental grasses. Excellent for naturalizing as a groundcover in shaded woodland gardens under deciduous trees and in formal shade borders where a soft, grassy textural element is needed without the full-sun requirements of most grasses. The cultivar 'Variegata' (cream-striped leaves) is slightly more ornamental. Self-sows moderately in suitable shaded, humus-rich conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist woodland soil for natural cold stratification and spring germination; this native shade perennial naturalizes readily from self-seeding and is among the brightest and longest-blooming yellow wildflowers for shaded sites.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; cold stratification occurs naturally over winter and seeds germinate in early spring. Wood poppy is a native eastern North American woodland perennial in the poppy family with deeply lobed, blue-green, poppy-like leaves and large (1.5–2 inch), brilliant golden-yellow flowers with four petals that bloom from early spring through summer in shaded conditions, making it one of the brightest and most prolific yellow-flowering shade plants for the eastern US — a standout with spring bloomers like wild ginger, bleeding heart, and ferns. It self-seeds freely without becoming invasive, gradually naturalizing into a cheerful drift under deciduous trees. All parts of the plant exude orange sap when broken; do not ingest.

common_name: Wood Rose (Yellow Morning Glory, Hawaiian Wood Rose)
plant_note: Direct sow or plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; wood rose is a vigorous tropical vine grown for its extraordinary, large, pale-yellow morning glory flowers and, uniquely, for the spectacular dried seed pods — the opened, star-shaped, woody calyces resemble carved wooden roses and are prized in dried floral arrangements.
directions: Direct sow scarified seeds in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; wood rose is drought-tolerant and vigorous once established — provide a very strong support. Merremia tuberosa (wood rose or Hawaiian wood rose) is a large, fast-growing tropical vine in the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae) native to Mexico and Central America, now naturalized and widely grown throughout the tropics. It produces large (3-inch), beautiful, pale golden-yellow, funnel-shaped morning glory flowers throughout the warm season. But the real treasure of wood rose is its extraordinary seed pod: as the flower fades and the fruit ripens, the calyx (the five-lobed green backing of the flower) expands and stiffens into a large, starfish-shaped, papery-woody structure 2–3 inches across, remaining on the vine to dry naturally. When fully dry, these calyces are deep chestnut-brown, rigid, and resemble intricately carved wooden roses — hence the name. The dried pods are highly prized in the craft and dried flower market, used in wreaths, arrangements, and floral crafts. Seed the pods during summer, collect in fall, and air-dry for use. In Hawaii, where the vine has naturalized widely, it is considered invasive in some native plant habitats. NOTE: Seeds may contain mildly psychoactive ergot alkaloids (similar to morning glory seeds) — do not ingest.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or root basal cuttings in early summer; Salvia x sylvestris is a sterile hybrid and must be propagated vegetatively. After the first main bloom flush, cut the entire plant back by half to two-thirds to promote a reliable second flush of bloom in late summer. It is drought-tolerant once established and performs best in lean, well-drained soils.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; woodland sage hybrid is the parent species of many of the finest cultivated garden salvias — a complex hybrid (S. nemorosa x S. pratensis) producing dense, bushy, upright plants clothed in aromatic gray-green leaves and, from late spring through summer (with reblooming after cutting back), dense upright spikes of rich violet-blue, blue-violet, or pink tubular flowers with contrasting bracts that maintain their color and decorative quality even after the flower petals drop. The named cultivars derived from this hybrid group are among the most widely planted perennials in temperate horticulture: 'May Night' ('Mainacht', deep violet-blue with dark bracts, Gold Medal Award winner), 'Blue Hill' ('Blauhugel', clear sky-blue), 'Rose Queen' (rose-pink), and 'Caradonna' (violet flowers on distinctive dark, near-black stems). Drought-tolerant, long-blooming with proper deadheading, and reliable across a wide zone range from 4 to 9 — qualities that make this hybrid group among the most useful and versatile of all garden perennials for the sunny, low-maintenance border.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this variety does not come true from seed, so division of rooted rhizome sections is the standard way to propagate it. Once settled it spreads on its own and rarely needs replanting.
directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, including the dry, root-filled ground beneath mature trees where few other evergreens thrive; wood spurge forms low rosettes of leathery, dark-green leaves on creeping underground rhizomes, and in mid-spring each rosette sends up a stem topped with a dome of long-lasting, acid-yellow-green bracts that light up shaded corners for six weeks or more before fading to green for summer. It spreads steadily by rhizomes to knit together a dense, weed-smothering evergreen carpet, and tolerates dry shade, root competition, and neglect better than almost any other flowering groundcover, making it a workhorse under hedges, shrub borders, and shade trees. Wear gloves when dividing or cutting it back, since the milky latex sap is a skin and eye irritant common to all euphorbias; site it away from paths where bare skin might brush against broken stems. Deer and rabbits leave it alone. Shear off flowering stems after bloom to keep growth tidy and prevent excessive self-seeding of the straight species where it may be nearby.

common_name: Wood's Dwarf Nandina (Very Compact Fiery Winter-Color Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wood's Dwarf is one of the smallest nandina selections available, with intense fiery winter foliage color.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, where the most intense winter color develops. Wood's Dwarf is among the most compact nandina selections in the trade, forming a dense, tidy mound that turns a vivid fiery red-orange in cold weather, providing dramatic seasonal color in a footprint small enough for tight foundation plantings or containers. Like other dwarf nandina cultivars it never flowers or sets the invasive berries of the straight species. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs little routine care.

plant_note: Plant rooted suckers, cuttings, or container stock in spring into average, well-drained soil in full to partial sun; Wood's rose is widespread across western and central North America and tolerates cold, drought, and poor soil.
directions: Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in spring in average, well-drained soil and full to partial sun, allowing room for the thicket-forming shrub to spread by underground rhizomes into a dense, thorny colony. Wood's rose ranges from the Great Plains to the Pacific Coast and from Canada into Mexico, tolerating cold winters, drought, and poor soils better than most cultivated roses. Its fragrant pink single flowers in early summer feed native bees, and the bright red hips that follow persist through winter, providing critical food for grouse, pheasants, and songbirds along with browse for deer. The dense, prickly thickets also create some of the safest nesting cover available to grassland and shrubland birds.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into loose, humus-rich woodland soil, spacing them close together to encourage the rhizomes to knit into a groundcover more quickly.
directions: Plant into rich, well-drained woodland soil with a good layer of leaf litter or compost worked in, and water regularly the first season while the spreading rhizomes establish. Full to dappled shade under deciduous trees matches its native habitat, and once settled it tolerates the dry shade common under mature trees better than many sedges. Slender, arching blue-green leaves emerge early in spring and spread gradually by rhizomes to form a loose, natural-looking carpet, with inconspicuous flowers in April. It makes an easy, low-maintenance native alternative to turf or pachysandra beneath trees and along woodland paths.

common_name: Wood's White Knight Water Lily (Huge Fragrant Night-Blooming Tropical White)
plant_note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond after water has warmed well past last frost; Wood's White Knight bears huge, fragrant, night-blooming white flowers 10-12 inches across with 28-30 petals.
directions: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers 12 to 18 inches deep in a full-sun pond, waiting until the water has warmed well above 70°F. Wood's White Knight is one of the largest-flowered night-blooming tropical water lilies in cultivation, producing enormous, richly fragrant white blooms 10 to 12 inches across with 28 to 30 slender petals, opening in the evening and remaining open into the following morning, making it a spectacular choice for a pond viewed at dusk or enjoyed with evening entertaining. It is a vigorous grower requiring a fairly large pond to accommodate its substantial pads and flowers. In zones below its perennial range it is typically grown as a warm-season annual or overwintered indoors as a dormant tuber. Feed with aquatic plant tablets monthly through the growing season and remove spent flowers and yellowing pads.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil with the roots shaded and the stems in sun; woodbine tolerates partial shade better than Japanese honeysuckle and is preferred for informal hedgerows and native garden settings across Europe.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the root zone cool and shaded while allowing stems to climb toward light; woodbine is the native European honeysuckle celebrated in Shakespeare's writings and the source of the intensely sweet evening fragrance associated with English cottage gardens. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica), this species is non-invasive and suitable for planting in naturalistic gardens. The tubular flowers, creamy-white flushed with pink and purple, are exceptionally fragrant in the evening and attract hawk moths; the red berries feed warblers, thrushes, and other birds in late summer. Popular cultivars include 'Serotina' (late Dutch, deep purple outside), 'Graham Thomas' (creamy white aging to yellow), and 'Belgica' (early Dutch honeysuckle). Prune lightly after flowering to shape.

common_name: Woodbridge Rose of Sharon (Classic Rosy-Pink Red-Eyed Althea)
plant_note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Woodbridge is one of the most popular and widely available older rose of sharon cultivars, and unlike the sterile National Arboretum triploid introductions it can self-seed, so remove spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Woodbridge is one of the most popular and long-cultivated rose of sharon selections, bearing large, single, rich rosy-pink flowers with a deep red eye at the center, blooming prolifically from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its rich, saturated color and reliable heavy bloom have kept it a garden favorite for decades, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden soil with ease, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions or container stock in fall with the crown just below the soil surface, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade.
directions: Paeonia obovata is a true forest-dwelling peony from Japan, Korea, and China, unlike most garden peonies which demand full sun. It produces soft blue-green, rounded leaflets and single, cupped white to soft pink flowers with prominent golden stamens in mid to late spring, followed by striking seed pods that split open to reveal glossy blue-black fertile seeds beside bright red infertile ones. It thrives in the dappled light beneath deciduous trees where full-sun peonies would fail, and its foliage often takes on attractive purple-red fall tones. Give it rich, well-drained woodland soil and avoid disturbing the crown once established, as peonies resent transplanting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery transplants in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; woodland phlox naturalizes by self-sown seed and stolons. If starting from seed, cold-stratify 60–90 days before sowing; germination is slow and erratic.
directions: Plant divisions in partial shade in moist, humus-rich soil in fall or early spring; woodland phlox is one of the most beautiful native spring wildflowers of eastern North America, producing masses of fragrant flat-faced flowers in shades of pale blue, lavender, violet, and white in mid-spring — blooming at the same time as Virginia bluebells and trilliums to create spectacular native wildflower combinations. The semi-evergreen foliage forms spreading mats that suppress weeds throughout the growing season, and unlike tall garden phlox (P. paniculata), woodland phlox is rarely troubled by powdery mildew when given good air circulation in a shaded site. Selected cultivars include 'Clouds of Perfume' (fragrant blue-violet), 'London Grove Blue' (deep blue), and 'Fuller's White' (pure white). An excellent pollinator plant attracting hummingbirds, swallowtail butterflies, and long-tongued native bees. Spreads slowly by rooting stolons to fill woodland edges and shaded borders naturally.

plant_note: Plant bulb offsets in spring, 4–6 inches deep, into humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; woodland spider lily is native to bottomland woods and shaded stream terraces and needs shade rather than full sun to perform well.
directions: Plant bulbs in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; woodland spider lily is a true forest-floor native, found wild in bottomland hardwood forests and along shaded stream terraces across the southeastern and south-central United States. Strap-like leaves emerge in spring, followed in late summer by clusters of fragrant, spidery white flowers with narrow, curving petals surrounding a central cup, held on tall, leafless stalks above the foliage. It multiplies slowly by offsets into a modest colony over the years and is one of relatively few bulbs that genuinely thrive in deep or dappled shade rather than merely tolerating it, making it valuable for woodland gardens, shaded borders, and naturalistic plantings under deciduous trees. Leave the foliage in place after bloom to recharge the bulb for next year, and divide congested clumps only when flowering noticeably declines, since it resents frequent disturbance.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in dry to average, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; woodland sunflower spreads by rhizome to form large colonies and is best used where aggressive naturalization is welcome — it is exceptionally effective at naturalizing along dry woodland edges and under oak canopies.
directions: Sow seed in fall or divide in spring in dry to average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade — woodland sunflower is one of the very few perennial sunflowers genuinely adapted to partial shade, producing 2–3 inch yellow daisy flowers in mid-to-late summer on upright stems 3–6 feet tall in conditions where most sunflowers refuse to bloom. It grows naturally in dry, open woodlands, woodland edges, and clearings throughout the eastern US and is especially common along the edges of oak woodland, thriving in the dry shade beneath the oak canopy that challenges most sun-loving perennials. It spreads vigorously by rhizome — use this to advantage in naturalizing dry, shaded areas with low-maintenance native cover and late-season pollinator value. The seeds are eaten by goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. An outstanding native for filling the challenging dry, part-shade niche.

plant_note: Surface sow (seeds need light) indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost on moist seed-starting mix; do not cover seeds. Transplant to partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil after last frost.
directions: Surface sow (seeds need light) indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost on moist seed-starting mix; do not cover seeds. Transplant to partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil after last frost. Nicotiana sylvestris is a spectacular ornamental tobacco from northwestern Argentina, producing enormous (up to 24 inches wide), rough-hairy, basal rosettes of bold, dark-green leaves and tall, candelabra-like clusters of long, pendant, tubular white flowers in early summer that are intensely, sweetly fragrant — particularly at dusk and night, when the fragrance carries 50 feet or more. The flowers are adapted to sphinx moth pollination and their nocturnal fragrance attracts hawkmoths in the evening; they also attract hummingbirds. All parts are toxic; do not ingest. A spectacular annual for the back of shaded or partially shaded borders, where its bold texture and evening fragrance create a dramatic effect.

common_name: Woods Blue Aster (Compact Mildew-Resistant Blue-Violet New York Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Woods Blue is a compact, mildew-resistant New York aster selection well suited to smaller borders.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Woods Blue forms a compact, dense mound smothered in small, blue-violet, daisy-form flowers each fall, considerably more resistant to the powdery mildew that often disfigures larger New York aster cultivars by late summer. Its tidy, low habit suits it to the front of a border or a mass planting where a compact fall-blooming perennial is wanted. Pinch or shear back by one-third in early summer to keep growth bushy and delay bloom slightly, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

common_name: Woods Pink Aster (Compact Mildew-Resistant Clear Pink New York Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Woods Pink is a compact, mildew-resistant New York aster selection well suited to smaller borders.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Woods Pink forms a compact, dense mound smothered in small, clear pink, daisy-form flowers each fall, considerably more resistant to the powdery mildew that often disfigures larger New York aster cultivars by late summer. Its tidy, low habit and soft color suit it to the front of a border or a mass planting where a compact fall-blooming perennial is wanted. Pinch or shear back by one-third in early summer to keep growth bushy and delay bloom slightly, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; in zone 9, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator (not freezer) for 6-8 weeks before planting in December-January, since hyacinths need cold they may not otherwise get in mild winters.
directions: Plant pre-chilled bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full sun. Woodstock is prized for its unusually deep, dramatic magenta-purple color, among the darkest of any commonly grown hyacinth, opening dense spikes that read almost burgundy in low light and add a rich, moody accent to a spring bulb display. Its intense color makes a striking companion to pale yellow or white hyacinths and early tulips. In warm-winter Gulf South gardens, treat pre-chilled hyacinth bulbs as an annual display planted in December or January for February-March bloom, since the bulbs rarely rebuild the cold exposure needed for good flowering in subsequent years without repeat chilling.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants in fall or early spring into deep, loose sand; avoid heavy or poorly drained soils, which quickly rot the roots.
directions: Native to the scrub and stabilized secondary dunes of the Florida Panhandle and Gulf Coast, this rounded evergreen shrub produces silvery, resinous foliage and a showy flush of small yellow flower heads in mid to late fall. It is extremely drought and salt tolerant once rooted, thriving in deep, sterile beach or scrub sand where few other flowering shrubs survive. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and resist the urge to fertilize or irrigate beyond the first season. It works well massed on dune crests or in xeric coastal gardens where its fall bloom complements late-season grasses like muhly and bluestem.

plant_note: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade at pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens; woolgrass tolerates both standing water and periods of drier soil once established.
directions: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade at pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens; woolgrass tolerates both standing water and periods of drier soil once established. Tall, coarse, grass-like clumps send up arching stems topped in late summer by loose, drooping clusters of reddish-brown flower spikelets that mature into soft, woolly, tan-brown seed heads persisting through fall and winter, giving the plant its common name and strong textural presence in a wetland planting. Native to marshes, wet meadows, and pond margins across most of North America, it is an excellent, fast-establishing choice for stabilizing the wet edges of a rain garden or retention pond while providing cover and seed for waterfowl and songbirds. Cut old growth back in late winter before new shoots emerge.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; woolly butterfly bush is far more compact and drought tolerant than the common Buddleja davidii sold widely in nurseries.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; woolly butterfly bush is a compact, rounded Chihuahuan Desert shrub with small, felted, silvery-gray leaves densely covered in soft wool-like hairs, and small, tight, ball-shaped clusters of bright orange flowers in spring and again after summer rains. Unlike the fast-growing, sometimes weedy Buddleja davidii common in nurseries, this species stays naturally compact and slow-growing, making it far better suited to small xeriscape gardens and rock plantings without becoming leggy or invasive. Its dense silvery foliage and modest size pair well with agaves, yuccas, and other true desert plants in a mixed xeriscape border, and it is visited by butterflies and bees during its bloom periods. It requires excellent drainage and minimal water once established, needing only light shaping after flowering to maintain its naturally tidy, rounded form.

common_name: Woolly Congea (Shower Orchid Vine, Lilac Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; woolly congea is a spectacularly beautiful tropical vine from Thailand and Southeast Asia — the ornamental display consists of large clusters of pale-lavender to white, woolly, three-lobed bracts (petal-like modified leaves) that cover the vine in winter and early spring in a display sometimes compared to seeing falling lavender snow; actual flowers are tiny, hidden within the dramatic bracts.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; woolly congea is a vigorous vine requiring strong support and can become very large — provide a sturdy pergola or large fence. Congea tomentosa (woolly congea, shower orchid vine, or lilac vine) is one of the most spectacular and unusual tropical flowering vines available for zone 10–12 gardens — a native of Thailand, Myanmar, and Southeast Asian dry tropical forests where it scrambles over trees in the deciduous forest canopy. The ornamental display of congea is completely different from most flowering vines: the actual flowers are tiny and inconspicuous, but each small cluster is surrounded by three large, petal-like, woolly bracts (modified leaves) that are the true ornamental display. These bracts, 1–2 inches long, are produced in enormous quantities in dense, cascading clusters that cover the vine during the cool, dry season (winter to early spring in zone 10–12) — pale lavender-lilac when fresh, fading to silvery-white as they age. The overall effect of a flowering congea is one of cascading pale-lavender to white woolly clusters hanging in billowing masses from the vine — sometimes compared to a waterfall of lavender or a shower of lilac snow. The vine can reach enormous size (30–50 feet) on a large pergola or tree. After flowering, the silvery dried bracts persist attractively for weeks. A breathtaking and rare ornamental vine for large tropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant container vines or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; woolly Dutchman's pipe is the southeastern-native species of Aristolochia, hardier and better adapted to Gulf Coast conditions than A. macrophylla.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun with a sturdy support structure; woolly Dutchman's pipe is the southeastern US native species of Aristolochia, distinguished from A. macrophylla by its dense woolly coating of soft hairs on the leaves and stems — a beautiful textural detail. Like all native Aristolochia species, it is the exclusive larval host plant for the pipevine swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor), one of the most spectacular black-and-iridescent-blue native butterflies in eastern North America. A single established vine supports dozens of caterpillars each season. The unusual curved, yellowish-green to brown pipe-shaped flowers are insect-trapping devices that temporarily trap small flies for pollination. Twining stems reach 10–20 feet and provide rapid screening in partial shade. Highly recommended for butterfly gardens in zones 5–9, particularly in the Southeast where this species is native.

plant_note: Tuck divisions into rock crevices or very well-drained, gritty, alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; woolly lip fern is one of the most drought-tolerant true ferns, native to dry limestone bluffs and rock outcrops.
directions: Tuck plants into rock crevices, dry stone walls, or gritty, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; woolly lip fern breaks the usual rule that ferns need constant moisture and shade, growing naturally on exposed limestone bluffs, cliffs, and rocky slopes across the central and southern United States. Small, finely divided fronds are covered on the undersides with dense, woolly, grayish-white hairs that reduce water loss and give the foliage a soft, felted texture and appearance. Like resurrection fern, it curls and appears shriveled and dead during extended drought, then re-expands and greens up again within a day or two of rain, an adaptation to its harsh, sun-exposed native habitat. Avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, and regular irrigation, all of which cause crown rot in this uniquely drought-adapted fern, and use it in rock gardens or dry stone features where conventional ferns would fail.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall into dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, matching the open pine flatwood conditions this southeastern native prefers. Rake seeds shallowly into the soil surface and allow winter rains to settle them in place. Avoid clay-heavy or moisture-retentive soils, which cause root rot; established plants are highly drought-tolerant and require little to no supplemental irrigation.
directions: Sow seeds in fall directly onto a prepared, lean, sandy or gravelly seedbed in full sun — this species from the dry southeastern coastal plain requires excellent drainage and will not persist in heavy soils. Lightly rake seeds into the top quarter-inch of soil and water once to settle; subsequent rains will carry the seeds through winter stratification. The distinctive silvery-woolly basal rosettes appear in early spring and the bright yellow flowers open in mid-spring, often before most summer wildflowers have emerged. Once established after the first season, plants are reliably drought-tolerant and will self-sow modestly into bare soil nearby.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, well-drained soil; avoid low, wet spots since it is prone to rot in poorly drained or consistently soggy soil.
directions: Plant divisions in spring into gritty, well-drained soil; the soft gray-woolly foliage spreads into a dense low mat that works well tucked between flagstones or cascading over the edge of a raised bed. Small blue or pink-veined flowers smother the foliage in mid-spring, and the mat tolerates being lightly walked on once it has filled in. It handles heat and drought well but is prone to rot in poorly drained or consistently soggy soil, so avoid low, wet spots.

plant_note: Plant transplants in fall in moist, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; woolly sunbonnets is adapted to the longleaf pine savanna and flatwood conditions of the southeastern coastal plain and performs best with periodic disturbance or open canopy that mimics its native fire-maintained habitat.
directions: Plant transplants in fall in moist, well-drained sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun, choosing a site that approximates the open longleaf pine flatwood conditions of its native range in the southeastern coastal plain. Chaptalia tomentosa produces a flat basal rosette of leaves that are deep green on top and strikingly white-woolly on the undersides, giving the plant year-round textural interest even out of bloom. The unusual daisy-like flowers appear from winter through spring, nodding in bud like a sunbonnet before opening to reveal white to pale lavender rays, making this native wildflower a valuable cool-season bloomer in mild southeastern gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade; woolly sweetspire is a Coastal Plain relative of the common summersweet (C. alnifolia) with notably woolly-hairy leaves and stems.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; woolly sweetspire is a native ericaceous shrub of wet, acidic Coastal Plain habitats — pocosins, bay edges, moist pine flatwoods, and the margins of Carolina bays — from Virginia to Georgia. The dense, white, fragrant flower racemes in midsummer are intensely perfumed and highly attractive to native bees, particularly bumblebees, which find the tubular flowers accessible. The woolly-textured leaves and stems (more densely hairy than C. alnifolia) give the plant a distinctive soft appearance. Fall foliage turns orange to red. As with all sweetspires, it thrives in moist, acidic woodland gardens and wetland edges — excellent for rain gardens and moist shade borders in zones 5–9. Spreads slowly by stolons to form colonies.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; woolly-stemmed sage is frost-tender and is damaged below 30 degrees F. In zones 9-11 it grows as a large, shrubby perennial; in colder zones it can be grown in large containers and overwintered frost-free. It is a large plant — allow 3-4 feet of space. Fertilize monthly to support its vigorous growth and abundant flowering.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; woolly-stemmed sage is a dramatically bold Brazilian salvia producing some of the most visually striking flower spikes in the genus. The entire plant is covered in a dense layer of russet-orange to tawny-brown woolly hairs — on the stems, leaf undersides, and calyx — that create a warm, velvety texture throughout. The flower spikes, which appear from late summer through frost, carry deep orange-red to crimson-scarlet tubular flowers from rusty-orange woolly calyces in dense, compact whorls, creating a warm, glowing effect unlike the typically blue or purple tones of most salvias. The large leaves are roughly textured and prominently veined, with hairy surfaces on both sides. At 4-6 feet tall and as wide, it is a commanding plant in the late-season border or tropical-style garden. It is powerfully attractive to hummingbirds throughout the bloom period. In zones 9-11 it grows into a large perennial shrub; elsewhere it is a dramatic container specimen.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural winter chilling, or cold-stratify seed 30 days before spring sowing; woollypod milkweed is adapted to California's dry-summer climate and resents summer irrigation once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil, including clay and decomposed granite, in full sun. Woollypod milkweed is a California foothill and chaparral native named for the dense, felt-like white wool that covers its distinctive large seed pods, which split open in fall to release silky-tufted seed. Its broad, gray-green, softly fuzzy leaves and rounded clusters of pale pink-to-purplish flowers make it one of the more ornamentally striking western milkweeds, and it is an important larval host for monarch butterflies across its range in the coastal and interior foothills of California and the Sierra Nevada. It is deeply drought tolerant once its taproot is established, going summer-dormant or semi-dormant in the driest sites, and performs best with no supplemental irrigation beyond the establishment period. Note that woollypod milkweed's foliage is considered relatively higher in cardenolide toxicity than some other milkweed species and should be sited away from grazing livestock.

common_name: Wormvine Vanilla (Leafless Vanilla, Barefoot Vanilla, Florida Vanilla)
plant_note: Grow on rough-barked trees or cork with exposed aerial roots in partial shade; Vanilla barbellata is a leafless, photosynthetic-root Vanilla species — unlike V. planifolia, it produces no leaves, obtaining all photosynthesis through its flat, green, chlorophyll-containing aerial roots. These roots must be exposed to light (partial shade to filtered light) for the plant to thrive. Wild plants are protected in Florida (endangered) — only cultivate from legally propagated nursery stock. Hand pollinate the short-lived flowers for occasional pod set. Zone 10-12 outdoors. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow on rough-barked trees or cork mounts in filtered, indirect light — Wormvine Vanilla is a leafless climbing orchid that obtains all its photosynthesis through chlorophyll-containing aerial roots that must receive adequate light, making it unlike most orchids in its light requirements for the roots rather than the leaves. Vanilla barbellata is a leafless, climbing, epiphytic orchid native to the Florida Keys, the Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, and Jamaica in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most distinctive of the Vanilla species and a genuinely fascinating botanical curiosity. The plant produces no leaves at any life stage — instead, the flat, strap-like, dark-green aerial roots serve dual function as both anchoring/water-absorbing organs and as photosynthetic structures, containing chloroplasts and performing all the plant's carbon fixation. The stems are thin, wiry, and flexible, climbing by these flatly-adhering roots up tree trunks and branches. The flowers (produced on short racemes from leaf axils) are pale green to white with a white lip, short-lived (single day), and produce occasional small vanilla pods with some fragrance but of much less commercial value than V. planifolia. As a native Florida Keys and Caribbean species, V. barbellata is protected under Florida law and by CITES. In cultivation, it provides a fascinating example of leafless photosynthesis. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3 inches apart in early to mid-fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; Woronow's snowdrop establishes best when planted 'in the green' immediately after flowering in late winter, but dry bulbs planted promptly in fall will succeed in suitable shade conditions.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in early to mid-fall in moist, humus-rich, woodland soil in partial to full shade; Woronow's snowdrop is one of the most shade-tolerant snowdrops available and excels under deciduous trees and shrubs where it naturalizes freely. Galanthus woronowii is a Caucasian species snowdrop immediately distinguished from the common snowdrop (G. nivalis) by its exceptionally bright, glossy, apple-green, strap-shaped leaves that remain vivid and fresh-looking even in the coldest weather — giving rise to the common name 'Green Snowdrop'; the white, nodding, single flowers with green-marked inner petals appear from January through March, pushing through snow and frozen ground. It naturalizes readily by offsets and self-seeding under deciduous trees and performs particularly well in shaded gardens where it receives winter and spring sunlight through bare branches and summer shade; this dappled-shade tolerance makes it one of the most reliable snowdrops for woodland gardens. Like all snowdrops, it goes dormant by early summer and benefits from undisturbed, leaf-mold-enriched soil.

plant_note: Plant tubers in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 7–9; provide complete summer drought; Wreath Nasturtium is a spectacular, large-scale trailing Chilean nasturtium from the Atacama-Andes transition zone — producing masses of brilliant golden-yellow flowers on long, far-spreading stems with distinctive, pale blue-green, glaucous, many-lobed leaves — one of the most striking of all tuberous nasturtiums in cool-winter gardens.
directions: Plant Tropaeolum polyphyllum tubers in fall in extremely well-drained, lean, sandy to gritty soil in full sun; provide absolutely no summer water — summer drought is essential; the plant grows over winter and spring in the cool, moist season, dies back completely in early summer, and re-emerges the following fall. Wreath Nasturtium is one of the largest and most spectacular of the Chilean tuberous nasturtiums — producing wide-spreading, mat-forming or trailing stems that can travel 3–6 feet in a single season, bearing distinctive blue-grey-green, multi-lobed, glaucous leaves that emerge with a smoky bloom and masses of bright golden-yellow flowers along the entire length of the stems. The effect in full bloom is extraordinary: a wide sweep of yellow flowers over a blue-grey foliage carpet, created from a single tuber that develops into a substantial, carrot-like storage root. Native to the Atacama Desert transition zone in Chile and Argentina, where winter rains trigger growth and summer drought forces dormancy, its cultivation requires strict adherence to this rainfall pattern — no summer water whatsoever. Grow in raised beds, scree, or containers moved under cover in summer. The tuber grows very large over successive years (sometimes reaching over a foot long); the large, gnarled tubers are occasionally used as an edible root vegetable in its native Chile, with a pleasant, slightly peppery flavor.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; Wright's skullcap is a Texas Hill Country limestone native that needs sharp drainage and struggles in humid, poorly drained conditions.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; Wright's skullcap is a Texas Hill Country limestone native that needs sharp drainage and struggles in humid, poorly drained conditions. Small, gray-green leaves form a low, dense mound studded with two-lipped, violet-blue flowers held on short spikes from spring through summer, providing season-long nectar for native bees on some of the thinnest, rockiest soils in a xeriscape planting. Endemic to limestone outcrops and rocky slopes of central Texas, it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and thrives in crevice or rock gardens where richer soil would cause it to rot. Shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage repeat flowering and keep the mound tidy.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall or early spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; wrinkleleaf goldenrod tolerates consistently wet soil and is one of the best goldenrods for rain gardens, pond margins, and moist meadows.
directions: Direct sow in fall or provide 4–6 weeks of cold stratification before spring sowing; wrinkleleaf goldenrod thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade and is one of the best native goldenrods for persistently wet, difficult sites. Solidago rugosa is a robust, upright to arching eastern North American goldenrod with wrinkled, rugose (rough and deeply veined) leaves and arching, one-sided racemes of bright yellow flowers in late summer through fall; it tolerates consistently wet soil better than most goldenrods, making it valuable for rain gardens, pond margins, and moist meadow restorations. The cultivar 'Fireworks' is a spectacular garden selection with strongly arching, fountain-like flowering branches creating a dramatic display; it spreads vigorously by rhizomes in moist, fertile soils. Outstanding late-season pollinator plant for monarchs, bees, and wasps.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Wushan epimedium is an evergreen species from Chongqing and Sichuan provinces of China, named for the Wushan Gorge area of the Three Gorges. It is one of the most dramatic large-leaved epimediums and exceptionally ornamental.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Wushan epimedium is one of the most dramatic and large-growing epimediums in cultivation, producing very large, evergreen, narrowly ovate leaflets with a fine, spiny-toothed margin and a bold, dark green appearance that persists through winter. The flower display in spring is spectacular — large racemes of pale yellow to soft yellow flowers with slightly reflexed outer petals and long, curved, slightly orange-tipped spurs, born on tall, airy stems well above the foliage. One of the largest-growing and most vigorous epimediums, it can form substantial clumps in good woodland soil. The evergreen foliage makes it an excellent year-round groundcover that suppresses weeds effectively even in dry shade under trees. The cultivar 'Caramel' is particularly sought after for its rich caramel-bronze new growth.

plant_note: Sow in fall so seed cold-stratifies naturally over winter, into lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun on dry slopes or sagebrush-steppe openings.
directions: A widespread Intermountain West and Pacific Northwest native of dry, rocky slopes, sagebrush steppe, and open pine woodland, forming a mounded clump of woolly gray-green leaves topped by broad, flat-topped umbels of cream to pale yellow flowers in early to midsummer that often blush rusty pink with age. It is an important nectar plant for native bees and a larval host for several blue butterflies, and its dried flower heads feed songbirds into winter. Grow in lean, sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; avoid fertile garden soil and supplemental summer water, both of which shorten its lifespan and cause weak, floppy growth. Well suited to rock gardens, dry slopes, and high-elevation xeriscape borders.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost once soil has warmed.
directions: Wyns New Pastel is a tall, vigorous dahlia bearing big pink-and-yellow blended blooms all season on a well-branched, hedge-like plant. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed. Because of its height, provide sturdy staking early and pinch the central shoot to encourage branching. Cut flowers freely and deadhead to keep new buds forming through summer and fall. In cold climates, dig and store the tubers over winter, replanting them the following spring.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Wyoming is a classic large canna cultivar with dark bronze-purple foliage and bright orange flowers, a long-standing favorite for tropical-style borders.
directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun. Wyoming is a classic, long-cultivated canna bearing large, deep bronze-purple leaves that provide dramatic dark color and bold tropical texture through the growing season, topped with bright, true-orange flowers that stand out sharply against the dark foliage. Its substantial size and strong color contrast make it a favorite anchor plant for tropical-themed borders and mixed plantings alongside cannas of contrasting leaf color. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

plant_note: Divide basal offsets or plant container-grown specimens after frost into rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Xanadu forms a tidy, non-vining, self-heading clump considerably more compact than its parent, selloum.
directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Xanadu is a compact, self-heading philodendron hybrid selected for its neat, rounded mound of deeply lobed, glossy dark green leaves that never develop the sprawling scale or trunk of full-sized selloum, making it far better suited to foundation plantings, mixed shade borders, and mass plantings in smaller garden spaces. It holds a tidy, symmetrical form with minimal care, needing only the occasional removal of an old lower leaf to stay attractive year-round in frost-free climates. Container culture works well anywhere, with plants moved indoors to a bright spot before the first frost in climates colder than its hardiness range. Established outdoor plantings tolerate brief light frost with foliage damage but generally recover from the crown, much like other tender aroids grown in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain above 45°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. In zone 9a Xanadu Philodendron is borderline hardy — the rhizome may survive light frost when mulched, but temperatures below 28°F will kill the above-ground foliage. Manage as a container plant on a shaded porch or patio and bring indoors when frost threatens, or plant in the ground in the most frost-protected garden microclimate. In zones 10–11 it grows as a fully hardy landscape shrub reaching 4 feet by 5 feet. The deeply lobed leaves create a refined tropical effect in shaded outdoor living spaces, and the plant handles zone 9's summer heat and humidity well if maintained with consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in partial to deep shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil — Xanadu Philodendron thrives in the shade conditions of tropical forest understories, performing best where direct sun is excluded; Xanadu (Thaumatophyllum xanadu, formerly Philodendron xanadu) is a compact, self-heading philodendron producing a dramatically architectural mound of deeply pinnately lobed, dark glossy green leaves that create a refined, sophisticated tropical texture at a manageable scale — growing to a tidy 2–4 foot mound rather than the sprawling, climbing habit of many philodendron species. Each large leaf (up to 18 inches long on established plants) is divided into deeply cut lobes along the length that create a feathery, textured appearance fundamentally different from the entire or shallowly lobed leaves of most shade tropicals. Xanadu's architectural foliage — the precise, repeating cut-leaf pattern, the glossy dark surface, the mounding form — creates a modern, clean aesthetic that works well in contemporary landscape design as well as in tropical garden styles. As an outdoor shade plant for zone 9 patios and covered garden areas, Xanadu provides a tropical character with more refined foliage texture than elephant ears or cannas, creating a sophisticated shade garden texture suitable for formal as well as casual landscape settings.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Xanthos is a pale yellow-flowered cosmos, an unusual color achieved through breeding since Cosmos bipinnatus does not naturally produce true yellow.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; cosmos actually blooms better in poor soil, which keeps plants from growing overly tall and floppy. Xanthos bears semi-double, pale primrose-yellow blooms on airy, ferny foliage, an unusual color breakthrough for Cosmos bipinnatus, a species that naturally flowers only in pinks, whites, and magentas, with true yellow historically found only in the unrelated Cosmos sulphureus. Its soft color blends easily with both warm and cool-toned companions in a cutting garden. Deadhead regularly to prolong bloom, and it flowers from early summer until frost with little care.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; prefers to be direct sown as transplants disturb its taproot.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in full sun with lean, well-drained soil; xeranthemum is one of the easiest everlastings to grow and tolerates poor, dry conditions well. The papery, daisy-like flowers in shades of lavender, pink, purple, and white are naturally self-preserving and air-dry on the stem. Harvest stems for drying when flowers are about two-thirds open; hang upside down in a warm, airy location for 2–3 weeks. Successive sowings 2–3 weeks apart can extend the harvest season into early fall.

common_name: Xerographica Air Plant (King of Air Plants, Silver Ball Tillandsia)
plant_note: Display on open cork board, in a bowl, or mounted in bright direct to indirect light; Tillandsia xerographica is native to dry tropical forests (the specific epithet means 'dry writing') and is significantly more drought-tolerant than most tillandsias. Water by misting heavily once per week in summer or dunking briefly for 5–10 minutes monthly — overwatering is the primary killer. Allow to dry within 4 hours. In zone 9, it can be grown outdoors year-round in exposed, bright spots and tolerates temperatures to 32°F when dry. One of the slowest-growing tillandsias — a large silver ball represents many years of growth.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to direct morning sun — Tillandsia xerographica is more sun-tolerant than most tillandsias and actually requires brighter light than T. ionantha and other small species to look its best; it will become loose and etiolated in inadequate light. Tillandsia xerographica is a large, slow-growing, epiphytic bromeliad native to the semi-arid tropical dry forests of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and southern Mexico, listed as a protected species in CITES Appendix II due to over-collection from the wild. It has been called the 'King of Air Plants' — a title that reflects both its commanding size (a mature specimen forms a rounded silver ball 12–30 inches across) and its dramatic appearance. The long (12–24 inch), silvery-white to pale gray, curling, strap-like leaves spiral outward and curl back at their tips in a loose, sculptural, spherical arrangement that is among the most architecturally elegant of all bromeliads. The silver color comes from the dense coating of trichomes that cover every leaf surface, maximizing atmospheric moisture absorption from the dry habitats where the plant grows. In spring or summer, a tall flower spike rises from the center producing an inflorescence of pink, green, and purple bracts surrounding small violet tubular flowers. Tillandsia xerographica is extraordinarily long-lived and slow-growing — a prized, prestigious specimen plant for distinctive decorating.

common_name: Yaezaki Farfugium (Jitsuko's Star, Double-Flowered Leopard Plant)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade; Yaezaki (trade name Jitsuko's Star) is a double-flowered leopard plant selection, distinct from the more common single-flowered farfugium cultivars already grown for their bold, glossy foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to full shade; Yaezaki is grown as much for its glossy, rounded, leathery evergreen leaves as for its flowers, giving the shade garden a bold, almost tropical texture that contrasts well with finer-textured ferns and hostas. In fall it produces double, fully ruffled yellow daisy-like flowers on tall stems above the foliage, a showier display than the simple single flowers of most farfugium cultivars. Give it protection from direct afternoon sun and hard freezes, since the large leaves scorch in strong sun and can be damaged by hard frost, though the crown typically survives and resprouts in zone 8 with adequate mulch. Slugs and snails are drawn to the tender new growth, so watch for damage in damp conditions.

plant_note: Plant in full sun in reasonably drained soil; drought-tolerant once established and fits easily into small residential gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in reasonably drained soil; this drought-tolerant selection asks for little beyond a sunny spot once established. Named for Japan's Yaku Island, this selection is the most diminutive commonly grown form of Miscanthus sinensis, forming a tidy, fine-textured clump of narrow, gracefully arching green blades well under half the size of the species. Buff-colored plumes with a light reddish tinge appear in late summer, rising just above the foliage before fading to silver and persisting into winter. Its compact size makes it far more versatile than full-size maiden grasses, fitting easily into mixed perennial borders, foundation plantings, and smaller residential gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs shallowly in spring or fall into acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch lightly to keep the fibrous surface roots cool and moist.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs shallowly in spring or fall into acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch lightly to keep the fibrous surface roots cool and moist. Native to the mountain summit of Yakushima Island in Japan, it grows naturally in a harsh, exposed habitat but has become a parent of countless compact hybrids because of its dense, mounded form and heavy woolly indumentum on the undersides of its leaves. Rounded trusses of pale pink flowers fading to white open in late spring against foliage that looks silvery and felted from below, giving the shrub interest even when not in bloom. Its naturally dwarf, tidy habit makes it useful in smaller shaded foundation plantings where larger rhododendron species would quickly outgrow the space.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface in early spring (seeds need light to germinate) or plant divisions in spring or fall in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; yarrow thrives in poor, dry soil and actually performs better without fertilizer — rich soil causes floppy, weak growth.
directions: Direct sow or divide in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; yarrow is one of the most drought-tolerant and adaptable native perennials of North America, producing flat-topped clusters of tiny flowers in white (wild type) or warm shades of yellow, gold, salmon, pink, and red in named cultivars from summer through fall. The ferny, deeply divided aromatic foliage is attractive throughout the season. Yarrow is exceptional for dry, sunny, difficult sites — it tolerates poor soil, heat, drought, and deer grazing and is one of the best perennials for planting on slopes and in gravel gardens. The flat flower heads are important landing platforms for beneficial insects including parasitic wasps, lacewings, and hover flies. Cut stems back by half after the first flush to encourage reblooming; divide every 3 years as plants spread outward. Outstanding long-lasting cut and dried flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into open, sandy soil near the root zones of oaks or native shrubs that will serve as hosts for this hemi-parasitic annual.
directions: Yaupon Blacksenna is a native annual hemi-parasite of the southeastern United States, growing in open, sandy longleaf pine habitats and roadsides where it parasitizes the roots of oaks and native shrubs to supplement its photosynthesis — direct sow seeds near the root zones of established native oaks or shrubs, as plants depend on host root contact and will not persist in open, host-free soil. Its finely dissected, ferny, Senna-like foliage gives plants an airy, lacy texture quite unlike most other native annuals, and small bright yellow flowers appear throughout summer and fall. It performs best in poor, well-drained, sandy soils in full sun and declines quickly in heavy clay or high-fertility garden beds. Yaupon Blacksenna is an excellent botanical specimen for longleaf pine garden restorations and is an important nectar plant for specialist native bees.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown stock in spring or fall in virtually any soil type in full sun to full shade; yaupon holly is one of the most adaptable native shrubs in North America, tolerating drought, flooding, poor soils, salt spray, and heavy shade. It is dioecious — plant at least one male for every 3–6 females to ensure berry production on female plants.
directions: Plant in full sun to full shade in virtually any well-drained to periodically wet soil — yaupon holly is among the most stress-tolerant of all native North American shrubs, thriving in sand, clay, limestone caliche, brackish coastal soils, and dry urban sites once established. Ilex vomitoria is the only native North American plant known to contain significant quantities of caffeine, and its dried leaves were used by Indigenous peoples of the Southeast to brew a stimulating ceremonial tea called 'Black Drink' — today it is being explored commercially as a sustainable source of caffeine for teas and beverages. Female plants produce masses of small, translucent-red (rarely yellow) berries that persist through winter and provide critical food for cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, bluebirds, and many other bird species. Outstanding cultivars range from large screening shrubs to weeping forms, dwarf groundcovers, and topiary specimens, giving landscape designers exceptional versatility with a genuinely native, wildlife-supporting plant.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Yeddo hawthorn is slower-growing and more compact than Indian hawthorn (R. indica) with larger, thicker, darker leaves and larger white flowers — a more refined species for formal use.
directions: Plant in spring or early fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Yeddo hawthorn is drought-tolerant once established and extremely tolerant of salt spray and coastal conditions, making it an outstanding choice for beachfront and coastal zone 8–10 landscapes. Yeddo hawthorn (R. umbellata) is the Japanese species of Raphiolepis, larger and slower-growing than the commonly sold Indian hawthorn (R. indica), with distinctly thick, leathery, very dark green rounded leaves and showy clusters of large, pure white fragrant flowers in spring followed by dark blue-black berries attractive to birds; the overall appearance is more refined and dramatic than other Raphiolepis. Excellent as a specimen plant, in foundation plantings, or as a formal hedge in coastal and Gulf Coast landscapes where salt tolerance is essential.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; yellow African iris is remarkably drought-tolerant once established and requires no supplemental irrigation in zone 8–9 after the first growing season.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; yellow African iris (biscuit plant) is a South African native that produces clumps of stiff, sword-shaped, evergreen leaves and repeatedly blooms with pale-yellow, iris-like flowers distinctly spotted with dark-brown to maroon spots near the flower center, giving each flower the appearance of a painted Japanese screen panel. Unlike bearded irises, the individual flower stalks do not need to be cut after blooming but instead produce additional flowers from the same stem over the course of a season — do not cut the flowering stems until they have completely finished producing buds. Dietes bicolor is slightly more compact and drought-tolerant than the related D. iridioides (white African iris) and performs especially well in the dry, hot conditions of zone 8–11 Gulf Coast and southwestern gardens. Excellent as a low-maintenance evergreen clump in dry, sunny or partially shaded borders, medians, and slopes. Self-seeds modestly. Completely maintenance-free once established.

subcategory: small-flowered everlasting for edging and drying
plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date once soil has warmed slightly, or start indoors a few weeks earlier where the growing season is short.
directions: Sow shallowly in well-drained soil after frost danger passes and keep evenly moist until seedlings establish, then let the planting dry down slightly between waterings once mature. Compact, finely branched plants form tidy mounds of ferny foliage topped with dense, flat clusters of tiny golden-yellow everlasting flowers that resemble a sunny take on ageratum. The long-lasting blooms hold their color well after cutting and drying, making this an easy, low-maintenance edging plant and a useful filler for dried bouquets.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade after frost; yellow alder self-seeds prolifically in Gulf Coast gardens and will naturalize as a persistent, freely self-maintaining annual or short-lived perennial once established.
directions: Direct-sow or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; yellow alder (West Indian holly, mariposa, butter daisy, ramgoat dashalong) is a Caribbean native tropical shrub that has naturalized throughout south Florida, the Gulf Coast, and tropical landscapes worldwide, producing bright, clear-yellow, five-petaled flowers with dark-yellow centers on a continuous, self-seeding basis from late spring through frost. Individual flowers are open only in the morning hours, closing by noon, but the plant produces such a continuous succession of buds that the overall display appears constant throughout the warm season. It grows rapidly from seed, blooms within weeks of germination, and self-seeds with such vigor in suitable warm climates that it functions essentially as a permanently self-maintaining annual or short-lived perennial groundcover once introduced to a sunny area. Deer-resistant, drought-tolerant, and heat-adapted. Useful as a low-maintenance color plant for hot, dry areas and disturbed ground in zone 9–12 gardens.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 3-5 inches apart in sharply well-drained, dry to average, preferably lean soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Yellow Allium is native to dry, rocky Mediterranean and Central European hillsides and thrives in the hot, dry conditions of a rock garden, gravel planting, or the front of a dry sunny border. It self-seeds readily in suitable well-drained conditions and will naturalize freely to form expanding colonies over several years.
directions: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in sharply well-drained, dry, lean to average soil in full sun in fall for summer bloom; Yellow Allium is one of the very few ornamental alliums to offer yellow flowers, producing loose, airy, umbel-like heads of small, pendant, golden-yellow, bell-shaped flowers on slender 6-12-inch stems with attractive thread-like, blue-green foliage in midsummer, after the main flush of spring alliums has passed. The flowers are held on unequal pedicels that give the open umbel a spraying, graceful appearance quite different from the tight, geometric globes of the larger ornamental alliums, and they are attractive to bees and other small pollinators. It is best suited to rock gardens, sunny gravel plantings, dry stone walls, or the front of a hot, dry border where its small stature and love of lean, sharply drained soil can be accommodated; rich or moist soils encourage weak, lush growth and reduced flowering. It self-seeds freely in well-drained conditions and over time can naturalize into loose, informal drifts.

plant_note: Plant in moist, acidic, organically rich, well-drained to moist soil in full to partial shade; yellow anise tree performs best in the filtered shade of tall pines or oaks and adapts to wet to seasonally dry conditions across the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Yellow anise tree is a rare Florida native evergreen shrub endemic to the Ocala National Forest and surrounding central Florida scrub and flatwoods, closely related to Florida anise (Illicium floridanum) but producing small, inconspicuous yellow flowers rather than red ones — its primary appeal is its dense, lustrous evergreen foliage and exceptional shade tolerance that make it one of the finest screening shrubs for difficult deep-shade sites in Gulf Coast landscapes. All parts of the plant contain toxic compounds similar to true star anise (Illicium verum) and emit a strong, pleasant anise-like fragrance when crushed, making deer browsing rare — an excellent choice where deer pressure limits other evergreen shrubs. Plants grow moderately quickly into dense, mounding 5–10 foot specimens that provide excellent year-round privacy screening in shaded settings where hollies and other broadleaf evergreens might struggle; they tolerate periodic flooding and are well-suited to moist, organic soils. As a critically rare Florida endemic, yellow anise tree deserves wider use in horticulture throughout zones 7–10 wherever a tough, fragrant, shade-tolerant evergreen screening shrub is needed.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial to full shade in spring; yellow archangel spreads aggressively by long, arching, rooting stolons — site carefully away from natural areas where it can escape and become invasive. Excellent within contained bed borders.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to moderately dry, average soil in partial to full shade; yellow archangel (golden dead-nettle) is a vigorous, fast-spreading shade groundcover with one of the most attractive and persistent foliage displays in the low-maintenance shade garden — the soft, nettle-shaped leaves are heavily marked with silver variegation in patterns that retain their brilliance through winter, creating bright, light-reflecting patches of color in the darkest corners of the shaded garden throughout the year. In late spring the plant produces whorled clusters of bright yellow, hooded, snapdragon-like flowers on upright stems above the groundcover mat. It spreads with considerable vigor by long, arching stems that root wherever they touch the ground, making it an effective, weed-suppressing groundcover but potentially problematic in gardens bordering woodland areas where it has been documented as invasive in some regions of the Pacific Northwest and northeastern United States. Most commonly grown as the variegated cultivar 'Variegatum' (silver-marked) or the compact 'Hermann's Pride' (heavily silver-marked, less aggressive). Excellent for large, shaded areas under dense trees where maintaining other groundcovers would be difficult.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; yellow archangel spreads aggressively by stolons and should only be planted where its spread can be managed — it is invasive in some Pacific Northwest regions.
directions: Plant stem cuttings or divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade where spreading groundcover is desired; yellow archangel produces silvery-marked, semi-evergreen leaves year-round and bright yellow, hooded mint-family flowers in mid-spring that light up dark shade corners. It spreads vigorously by long, arching stolons that root where they touch the ground, forming a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under established trees and shrubs within 1–2 seasons. Note: Lamiastrum galeobdolon 'Variegatum' and related cultivars are considered invasive in the Pacific Northwest and should not be planted where they can escape into natural areas — check local regulations before planting. Plant only in contained or managed sites in those regions.

common_name: Yellow Bauhinia (Bell Bauhinia, St. Thomas Tree)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; yellow bauhinia is a deciduous to semi-evergreen shrub or small tree from tropical Africa and India — producing large (3–4 inch), distinctive bell-shaped, pale-yellow flowers with a dark maroon to near-black stain on one petal; different from the more commonly grown orchid trees (B. variegata and B. purpurea) in its smaller stature and unique yellow-and-dark-red flower color combination.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape. Bauhinia tomentosa (yellow bauhinia, bell bauhinia, or St. Thomas tree) is a deciduous to semi-evergreen shrub or small tree from the tropical dry forests and savannas of East Africa, India, and Sri Lanka — a member of the enormous Bauhinia genus (orchid trees) but markedly different in appearance from the more commonly cultivated purple orchid tree (B. variegata) and red orchid tree (B. blakeana). The flowers of B. tomentosa are distinctive and elegant: large (3–4 inch), bell-shaped with five petals that do not spread as broadly as other orchid tree flowers, colored a soft pale-yellow to cream-yellow with one petal bearing a dramatic deep-maroon to near-black central stain — a striking bicolor combination unlike any other Bauhinia.
