The leaves are the characteristic twin-lobed 'butterfly' shape shared by all Bauhinia species (resembling two joined leaves — the genus name honors botanist Gaspard and Johann Bauhin, twin brothers, for this two-lobed leaf). In zone 8–11, yellow bauhinia is a more compact and cold-hardy Bauhinia option than many tropical relatives, making it useful in zone 8b gardens that cannot support larger tropical Bauhinia species. The bark has traditional medicinal uses in Indian Ayurveda.

subcategory: Bolivian yellow tuberous begonia parent species
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil or container mix in zone 8–10; Yellow Begonia (Pearce's Begonia) is a compact, tuberous begonia species native to the Bolivian Andes — one of the primary parent species of the entire modern tuberous hybrid begonia group — bearing abundant bright-yellow, flat-faced single flowers above distinctive dark-green leaves with silver spotting, and far more heat-tolerant than modern large-flowered tuberous hybrid begonias.
directions: Plant Begonia pearcei tubers in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; water consistently but ensure excellent drainage; fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer; allow foliage to die back in fall and store tubers dry and cool in winter in zone 8–9; repot each spring. Yellow Begonia holds a special place in horticultural history as one of the five wild Bolivian and Peruvian Andean begonias that, when hybridized in Belgium in the 1860s–1870s, produced the entire line of large-flowered tuberous hybrid begonias that became one of the most popular bedding plants in history. Begonia pearcei contributed the yellow flower color — absent from other Andean begonia species — making possible the spectacular range of yellow, orange, and bicolored modern tuberous begonias. The species itself is a charming garden plant: compact, with attractive dark-green leaves marked with silver spots, and producing masses of bright, clear-yellow single flowers in partial shade throughout summer. Unlike the large-flowered modern hybrids which struggle in heat, the species form is more tolerant of warm temperatures. In the garden, it excels in containers, shaded window boxes, and as a groundcover in partially shaded borders. Tubers increase steadily by division over years.

plant_note: Direct sow seed or plant container-grown plants in spring after frost danger passes in any well-drained soil in full sun; esperanza grows rapidly from seed and can bloom the first year. It dies back to the ground after hard freezes in zone 8 but regrows strongly from established roots in spring — do not cut back until new growth confirms the roots have survived.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained to dry soil — sandy, rocky, alkaline, and poor soils are all acceptable; esperanza or yellow bells is a native flowering shrub and small tree of Texas, the Southwest, and Mexico that produces brilliant golden-yellow trumpet-shaped flowers in large clusters almost continuously from late spring through frost. It is among the most heat tolerant and drought resistant flowering plants available for zone 8–11 landscapes, thriving in conditions that challenge almost everything else. The showy flowers attract hummingbirds and butterflies prolifically throughout the summer. The cultivar 'Gold Star' is the most widely planted, selected for compact habit and extra-large flower clusters. Esperanza grows vigorously and may need annual cutting back in mild winters; in zone 9 it is woody and persistent year-round while in zone 8 it typically dies to the ground in winter and regrows from roots. It blooms on new wood, so frost damage sets back the plant temporarily, not permanently.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich, cool soil in partial shade to full sun. Yellow Birch does not tolerate heat, drought, alkaline soils, or heavy clay and is best suited to cool northern or mountain climates in Zone 3–7.
directions: Yellow Birch is a graceful, long-lived native tree of moist, cool Appalachian and northeastern forests from eastern Canada south to the mountains of Georgia and Tennessee, distinguished by its golden-yellow to bronze, papery bark that peels in thin, curly horizontal strips and provides remarkable year-round ornamental interest. The young twigs and inner bark carry a distinctive sweet wintergreen fragrance from the natural methyl salicylate they contain, and the sap can be tapped in late winter for a birch syrup similar to maple syrup; the bark was historically distilled to produce oil of wintergreen. An important component of northern hardwood forest ecosystems, Yellow Birch provides critical nesting habitat for warblers, vireos, and thrushes while moose, deer, and snowshoe hares browse the twigs and bark through winter. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich, cool soil in partial shade to full sun; Yellow Birch demands consistently cool, moist conditions and is not suitable for hot, dry, or alkaline climates.

common_name: Yellow Bird of Paradise (Desert Bird of Paradise)
plant_note: Scarify seeds or soak overnight before sowing; plant container-grown shrubs in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Yellow bird of paradise reseeds prolifically and can naturalize aggressively in desert climates — verify local invasive status before planting in the Southwest. It dies back in hard freezes but resprouts from established roots in zone 8.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; yellow bird of paradise is a native of Argentina that has naturalized extensively in the American Southwest and Mexico, prized for its brilliant, eye-catching flowers — large, canary-yellow petals surrounding long, dramatic, brilliant-red stamens that extend 2–3 inches beyond the petals in striking contrast. The flowers appear in loose, upright clusters at the branch tips from summer through fall — a spectacularly colorful display during the dry season when many desert plants are dormant. The compound, ferny, blue-green foliage is attractive on its own. It is among the most drought-tolerant ornamental shrubs available, requiring virtually no water once established in desert climates, but can be grown throughout zones 8–11 with well-drained soil. Caution: it reseeds prolifically and has naturalized invasively in parts of the Sonoran Desert and adjacent areas; check local invasive status before planting in Arizona and southern New Mexico.

plant_note: Plant fresh (unsoaked) nuts in fall in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, well-drained soil in partial shade; unlike most trees, yellow buckeye performs best in partial shade, especially afternoon shade in zone 7–8. The fresh nuts lose viability rapidly — plant within weeks of collection.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade — yellow buckeye is unusual among trees in that it actually performs better in partial shade than full sun, making it one of the best large native trees for the shaded garden. Native to rich mountain forests of the southern Appalachians, it produces beautiful upright clusters of yellow flowers in spring that attract hummingbirds and long-tongued native bees, and large smooth seed pods containing 1–3 mahogany-brown nuts with pale patches — striking ornamental fall fruit. The palmate compound leaves of 5 leaflets are among the first to emerge in spring and first to drop in fall (often by August in drought). It tolerates understory conditions and is frequently found growing as a subcanopy tree beneath tulip poplar and basswood. The nuts are toxic to humans but consumed by squirrels. Often considered the most beautiful of the North American buckeyes.

subcategory: fragrant cream-yellow tropical ginger, shade perennial
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; yellow butterfly ginger is nearly identical to white butterfly ginger (H. coronarium) in garden habits and cold hardiness but produces cream-yellow to pale-yellow flowers with a yellow labellum rather than pure white. In zone 9 it is a reliable, returning perennial from underground rhizomes. It has naturalized in Hawaii, Florida, and other subtropical areas. Slightly more vigorous and faster-spreading than H. coronarium. Provides several weeks of fragrant summer bloom.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; yellow butterfly ginger is the cream-yellow counterpart of the iconic white butterfly ginger (Hedychium coronarium) — a closely related species from the Himalayan foothills of India and Nepal producing in summer and early autumn terminal spikes of sweetly fragrant, butterfly-shaped flowers in pale cream-yellow to soft butter-yellow with a contrasting deeper-yellow labellum (central lip), the whole flower having the characteristic hedychium butterfly silhouette of narrow upper petals and a broad, spreading lower lip. Like H. coronarium, it is powerfully fragrant, the sweet, warm, somewhat vanilla-like scent carrying through the garden on summer evenings. The growth habit, cultural requirements, and winter hardiness are nearly identical to H. coronarium — erect rhizomatous clumps reaching 5–7 feet with large, lance-shaped, fresh-green ginger-family leaves, dying back to the ground in cold winters and resprouting vigorously in spring. It has naturalized in Hawaii, the Florida panhandle, and other subtropical Atlantic and Gulf Coast areas. The cream-yellow flower color provides a warm, soft alternative to the pure white of H. coronarium in gardens where a slightly warmer color palette is desired. Outstanding as a fragrant, tropical-character shade and part-shade perennial for zone 7–11 moist gardens.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in spring in wet, acidic to neutral, nutrient-poor, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; yellow butterwort is a Gulf Coast native that tolerates the humid summers of zones 7–9 better than most temperate butterworts.
directions: Yellow butterwort is a native carnivorous plant of the Gulf Coastal Plain's wet pine flatwoods and seepage slopes, producing flat rosettes of bright yellow-green, greasy-textured leaves covered in sticky glands that capture small insects and fungus gnats — the oily, buttery texture of the leaves inspired the 'butterwort' common name. In late winter and spring, beautiful, pale yellow, five-petaled flowers on long, delicate stalks emerge from the center of each rosette, appearing before many other wildflowers in the Gulf Coast bog community. Unlike the complex snap-trap mechanism of Venus flytrap or the drowning pitchers of Sarracenia, butterworts use a simple passive flypaper strategy — insects land on the sticky leaves and are unable to escape; digestive glands then secrete enzymes to break down the prey. Yellow butterwort is relatively easy to grow among carnivorous plants, adapting to a range of wet, acidic to neutral conditions and tolerating the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast winters when other carnivorous plants may struggle. Propagate readily from leaf cuttings laid on moist sphagnum moss in bright light.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in spring; Pentland's calla follows a dry summer dormancy (like Z. albomaculata and Z. rehmannii, not the summer-active Z. aethiopica) — withhold water as foliage yellows after spring flowering and keep dry through the summer. Distinguished from Z. elliottiana by its unspotted foliage and typically larger, deeper-yellow spathe.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in part shade; Pentland's calla is a rare but beautiful South African calla lily species from the Drakensberg mountains that produces large, deep-golden-yellow spathes — among the most richly saturated yellows of any Zantedeschia — above plain, unspotted, dark-green, arrow-shaped foliage. The species is less commonly grown than the spotted-leaved Z. elliottiana or Z. albomaculata but has a simpler, cleaner elegance: the combination of the unspotted, deep-green leaves with the vivid pure-gold spathe is uncomplicated and very beautiful. Like the other summer-dormant species (as opposed to Z. aethiopica which is summer-active and evergreen in mild climates), it goes completely dormant in summer, requiring dryness, and re-emerges in autumn or spring depending on climate. The natural habitat is rocky stream banks and moist grasslands of KwaZulu-Natal at mid-altitude, where it experiences cool, moist winters and warm, dry summers. A collector's species that is rarely seen in trade outside specialist bulb suppliers.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring after frost; yellow calla lily requires dry summer dormancy (reduce or stop watering after the leaves die back) to initiate the following season's flower buds — gardeners who keep the soil moist through summer typically get good foliage but poor flower production the following season.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; yellow calla lily is a South African summer-dormant bulb that produces large, elegant, golden-yellow calla spathe flowers similar in form to the familiar white calla (Zantedeschia aethiopica) but in a warm, deep-yellow to butter-yellow color that is distinctly different in character — the yellow spathe surrounding the upright, golden-yellow spadix is held on a stout stem above large, semi-upright, heart-shaped, dark-green leaves that are ornamentally decorated with translucent white spots and blotches (a characteristic feature of this species). The spotted foliage is itself ornamental throughout the growing season. Unlike the common white calla, yellow calla lily requires a dry summer dormancy for good subsequent blooming — reducing water after leaf dieback allows the tuber to ripen and develop its flower buds. Hardy to approximately 15°F in zone 8 with good drainage. The yellow and orange-flowered spotted-leaf Zantedeschia species (Z. elliottiana, Z. pentlandii, Z. rehmannii) are the parents of the modern garden calla hybrid cultivars in yellow, orange, red, pink, and purple.

plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; unlike most terrestrial orchids, Bletilla species are genuinely easy to grow in an ordinary garden bed without special mycorrhizal requirements, spreading gradually by pseudobulb offsets into a larger clump.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; mulch in colder parts of its range to protect the shallow pseudobulbs over winter. Bletilla ochracea (yellow Chinese ground orchid) is a rare, genuinely garden-friendly terrestrial orchid from China, closely related to the more commonly available purple-flowered Bletilla striata but distinguished by its soft, buttery yellow blooms — an unusual flower color among hardy garden orchids. In late spring, slender stems rise from pleated, lance-shaped leaves carrying several elegant, orchid-shaped flowers that persist for weeks, followed by attractive seed pods if left unpicked. Unlike most native terrestrial orchids, which require a very specific symbiotic soil fungus and are essentially impossible to establish from purchased stock, Bletilla species grow readily in ordinary humus-rich garden soil and slowly multiply into an increasingly showy clump, making them one of the few hardy orchids genuinely suitable for typical home garden conditions. An excellent, unusual specimen for a partly shaded border, zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–November or February–April. Yellow Clivia requires a dry winter rest period of 6–8 weeks with reduced watering to trigger spring flowering — this is often the most critical management factor. In zone 9 the mild, drier winters naturally provide the needed rest period. Divide congested clumps every 4–5 years in early spring after flowering; divisions bloom within 1–2 years.
directions: Plant in deep to partial shade in well-drained, organically rich soil; Yellow Clivia is a rare and highly prized yellow-flowered form of Clivia miniata, producing umbels of 12–20 nodding, funnel-shaped, pale to deep golden-yellow flowers on sturdy stems in late winter to spring — a striking departure from the familiar orange of standard clivia and extremely valuable in shade gardens where yellow-flowered plants are scarce. The strap-like, dark green, leathery leaves form architectural clumps that are ornamental year-round and provide deep-shade ground cover where few other plants will grow. Yellow clivia forms were once extraordinarily rare and expensive (individual plants sold for thousands of dollars in South African and Japanese specialty markets) but have become more widely available through tissue culture and selected open-pollinated seed. In zone 9 and 10 clivia thrives under established tree canopies, on north-facing exposures, and in the deep shade of eaves and overhangs — precisely the difficult situations where gardeners have few flowering options. Avoid replanting once established; clivia blooms most freely when root-bound.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; unlike many Arisaema species, this one tolerates drier soil and more sun once its foliage has expanded, making it useful in a woodland edge planting.
directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in a partly shaded woodland-edge bed; give it drier conditions in summer dormancy than most cobra lilies require. Arisaema flavum has an extraordinarily wide native range across the Himalayas, the Middle East, and East Africa, and stands out among jack-in-the-pulpits for its small, bright egg-yolk-yellow spathe rather than the typical green or purple-striped hood. Its compact size and unusual sunny color make it a distinctive accent for a partly shaded rock garden or the front of a woodland bed, where it multiplies gradually by offsets over time.

plant_note: Sow seeds in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun in early spring or fall; yellow echinacea grows well in lean, dry soils similar to other echinaceas. Cold stratification of seeds for 30-60 days improves germination rates significantly. It is a critical parent species used in breeding yellow and orange hybrid coneflowers and is the only yellow-petaled species in the genus.
directions: Sow seeds in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; yellow echinacea is the botanical paradox of the coneflower genus — named paradoxa because it has bright, clear, lemon-yellow to butter-yellow ray petals that droop downward from the central cone, unlike every other Echinacea species which has pink, purple, or white petals. It is the only naturally occurring yellow-flowered species in the genus, native to dry, rocky, limestone glades and cedar barrens of the Ozarks in southern Missouri, northern Arkansas, and eastern Oklahoma. The unusual drooping yellow petals surrounding a prominent dark-orange to brown central cone create a flower quite different in character from the familiar purple coneflower, with a more elegant, crane-like appearance. As a parent species, it is of enormous horticultural importance — virtually all the yellow, gold, and orange hybrid coneflowers now widely sold (Sunrise, Harvest Moon, Art's Pride) have E. paradoxa as a major parent. Attracts butterflies, native bees, and goldfinches that harvest the seeds in fall.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in late summer or early fall directly in cool, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; plants self-sow abundantly and often establish in wall crevices and shaded rock garden pockets.
directions: Sow fresh seed directly in fall or set out container plants in spring in partial to full shade in well-drained, average to humus-rich soil; yellow corydalis produces lacy blue-green ferny foliage and a near-continuous display of golden-yellow spurred flowers from spring through frost, blooming even when most shade plants are between cycles. It self-sows prolifically and naturalizes quickly in cool, shaded spots including wall crevices, gaps in flagstone, and the dry shade under evergreens. Plants go summer-dormant in hot climates but regrow in fall where winters are mild. Deadhead spent flowering stems to limit unwanted spread if needed.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into shaded borders, wall crevices, or rock gardens; yellow corydalis self-seeds freely once established and cold stratification from winter temperatures triggers reliable spring germination.
directions: Direct sow in fall in partial to full shade, allowing natural cold stratification over winter to break dormancy; yellow corydalis thrives in the thin, gritty soil of wall crevices, rocky outcrops, and shaded borders where it naturalizes freely by self-seeding. Pseudofumaria lutea produces ferny, blue-green foliage and an exceptionally long succession of small, spurred yellow tubular flowers from spring through fall, making it one of the longest-blooming shade perennials available. Once established it requires little care and will colonize appropriate niches throughout the garden, though it is shallow-rooted and never aggressively weedy.

plant_note: Plant bulbils or divide rhizomes in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade in zone 9–12; Yellow Dancing Ladies Ginger is a delicate, shade-loving ginger-family perennial native to Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, and Southeast Asian forests, producing graceful, drooping inflorescences of small bright-yellow flowers with reflexed yellow petals and yellow stamens dancing on arching stems in summer — an outstanding shade-garden ornamental.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade with consistent moisture; Globba schomburgkii is shade-adapted and suffers in direct sunlight — the best location is filtered light beneath trees or in deep shade of structures, with consistently moist soil and high humidity. Globba schomburgkii (Yellow Dancing Ladies Ginger) is one of dozens of graceful, shade-tolerant Globba species native to the humid forests of Southeast Asia (Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia), where these delicate perennials are adapted to deep forest-floor understory light conditions. The inflorescences are distinctively graceful — arching, pendulous racemes of small, bright-yellow to golden-yellow, two-lipped flowers on dangling, pedicellate stalks that dance in the lightest air movement, explaining the poetic common name 'Dancing Ladies.' Many Globba species also produce curious bulbils (small, rounded, violet-purple or green buds) in the inflorescence that can be collected and grown into new plants. The foliage is also attractive — neat, alternately arranged, lanceolate leaves on upright, reedy stems. Plants die back to dormant rhizomes in winter, re-emerging reliably in spring. Among the most effective and unusual shade-garden ornamentals for zone 9–12 warm climates. Plant en masse under trees or shade structures for the most impactful display.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring before shoots emerge, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yellow fairy bells establishes steadily and expands into an increasingly attractive clump — the rhizome is somewhat sensitive to drying out, so divisions should be replanted promptly and kept moist during establishment.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yellow fairy bells is a Korean woodland perennial in the lily family (Liliaceae / Colchicaceae) that shares the same arching, leafy-stemmed, graceful habit as the related Solomon's seal (Polygonatum) and false Solomon's seal (Maianthemum) — each stem is an elegant, arching or erect, 24–36-inch wand clothed in broadly oval, parallel-veined, bright-green, sessile leaves from whose tips in spring hang clusters of pendant, narrowly cylindrical to tubular, rich golden-yellow, bell-shaped flowers with slightly flared mouths, creating a warm, jewel-like, yellow pendant-bell display at the shoot tips that brightens the spring shade garden. The yellow color is more vivid and saturated than most shade perennials, which tend to flowers in white, lavender, or pink, making D. flavens a valuable source of true yellow in the shade garden. Black berries follow the flowers. The rhizomes spread slowly to form a gradually expanding clump. An increasingly popular and valued shade perennial for the woodland and shade garden in zone 5–8.

plant_note: Plant divisions of the clumping rootstock in fall or early spring into rich, evenly moist soil in a lightly shaded bed, and top-dress with leaf mold to mimic its native forest floor.
directions: Plant divisions of the clumping rootstock in fall or early spring into rich, evenly moist soil in a lightly shaded bed, and top-dress with leaf mold to mimic its native forest floor. Slender, bamboo-like stems arch outward and carry glossy, pleated leaves, with clusters of soft yellow, pendant, tubular flowers dangling from the stem tips in mid-spring. Native to woodlands in China, Korea, and Japan, it forms a tidy, slowly expanding clump rather than running underground, so it stays well behaved among hostas, hellebores, and other shade perennials. Cut back the fading foliage in autumn to keep the planting tidy through winter.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; yellow fire lily is a rare yellow-flowered Cyrtanthus species from the Drakensberg grasslands that blooms in summer, triggered by fire or drought stress in nature. Unlike the scarlet-red C. elatus (Scarborough Lily), this species produces clusters of small, bright-yellow, tubular flowers in summer umbels. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; yellow fire lily fills an unusual niche in the Cyrtanthus genus — yellow-flowered fire lilies are distinctly uncommon compared to the dominant red, orange, and pink species. C. breviflorus produces in summer compact umbels of 3–8 small, bright yellow, nodding, tubular flowers on stems 12–18 inches tall above narrow, strap-shaped, deciduous leaves that die back in winter. The short, wide flower tubes (giving the species epithet 'breviflorus', short-flowered) are bright, clear yellow — a warm, clean, sunflower-yellow tone that stands out distinctly from the red and orange fire lilies. It comes from the summer-rainfall grasslands of the Drakensberg and Natal midlands in South Africa, where it flowers in summer following fires that burn the dry winter grass — a characteristic fire-adapted ecology shared by many Cyrtanthus species (which collectively are called 'fire lilies' for this flower-triggering behavior). In the garden it flowers reliably in summer even without fire stimulus when provided with a dry period in late winter and spring followed by watering as temperatures rise. An unusual yellow flowering option for the zone 9 summer bulb garden.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions at the water's edge or in wet, mucky soil in partial shade to full sun; yellow flag iris spreads rapidly by both rhizome and prolific seed set in wet conditions — it is listed as invasive in many US states and should not be planted near natural waterways, wetlands, or drainage areas. Deadhead promptly to prevent seed spread.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions at pond margins, in wet ditches, or in containers submerged in water gardens in full sun to partial shade — yellow flag iris is one of the most spectacularly showy wetland plants in the world, producing large, bright golden-yellow iris flowers in late spring on tall, sword-leaved clumps 3–5 feet high, thriving in standing water, stream banks, and boggy soils where few other ornamentals succeed. It is a superb water garden marginal and naturalizes rapidly in any wet, disturbed area. However, it is introduced from Europe and is listed as an invasive plant in much of the eastern and western US, crowding out native wetland vegetation — do not plant it near natural wetlands, ponds, streams, or drainage systems, and remove seed heads immediately after blooming. For water gardens, contain the rhizomes in submerged pots to prevent spread. The native blue flag iris (I. virginica) or southern blue flag (I. virginica var. shrevei) are strongly preferred alternatives in most areas.

plant_note: Scarify or nick seeds before sowing to improve germination, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun in spring; yellow flame tree is fast-growing, drought-tolerant once established, and highly adaptable to different soil types including coastal sands — it is one of the most successful street trees in tropical cities throughout Southeast Asia and the Caribbean.
directions: Scarify seeds before direct-sowing or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun; yellow flame tree (copper pod, copperpod) is a large tropical tree native to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia and widely planted throughout the tropical world as a street, shade, and ornamental tree of exceptional quality — it produces dense, spreading canopy of finely divided, bipinnate, feathery, dark-green leaves that create a graceful, filtered shade, and from summer through fall, produces large, upright, terminal and lateral panicles of vivid yellow, five-petaled, fragrant flowers that bloom in flushes and can blanket the canopy in golden yellow. After the flowers, the tree produces masses of distinctive, flat, winged pods that mature through russet-brown to bright copper-red, persisting ornamentally on the tree for months and giving it the common name 'copper pod'. The tree's fine foliage, yellow flowers, copper seedpod clusters, and attractive form make it ornamental across multiple seasons. It is fast-growing, drought-tolerant once established, and widely used as a street tree in tropical cities across Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and South Florida.

plant_note: Direct-sow onto dry, disturbed or gravelly prairie soil a few weeks before the last frost; keep on lean soil with reduced competition rather than in a rich, crowded bed.
directions: Direct-sow onto dry, disturbed or gravelly prairie soil a few weeks before the last frost, since this short-lived annual or biennial establishes quickly and often self-sows to persist in a planting once introduced. Small, bright yellow five-petaled flowers open for only a few morning hours through summer, closing by early afternoon, and are visited by small native bees and syrphid flies during their brief daily window. It is a pioneer species well suited to filling bare or recently disturbed patches in a prairie restoration while slower perennials establish around it. Because it is not competitive in dense vegetation, keep it on lean soil with reduced competition rather than in a rich, crowded bed.

plant_note: Divide rooted crowns and plant in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy garden loam, then set the pot 6-18 inches below the water surface so the small heart-shaped leaves can float and spread.
directions: Pot divisions in loam-filled aquatic containers topped with gravel and submerge them so the mottled, lily-pad-like leaves reach the surface and produce clusters of small fringed yellow flowers through summer. It spreads by both rhizomes and floating stem fragments, so keep it confined to a container in ponds and remove excess growth each season to prevent it from choking open water; it is listed as invasive in parts of North America outside its native Eurasian range. Overwinter the rootstock below the ice line in the pond, since dormant crowns tolerate hard freezes as long as they do not dry out.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; yellow foxglove is a true perennial unlike the common biennial foxglove and returns reliably each year without needing to self-sow to perpetuate.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; yellow foxglove is a true perennial (unlike the common biennial D. purpurea) native to European woodlands, producing tall spikes of tubular, pale creamy-yellow flowers with light brown veining and spotting inside in early to midsummer — a refined and elegant foxglove in a soft color that pairs beautifully with blue salvias, geraniums, and hostas in a shade border. The plant is reliably long-lived and returns for many years without needing to reseed itself. All parts are toxic, as with all foxgloves. Self-sows in suitable conditions. Excellent in combination with the biennial common foxglove (D. purpurea) for a continuous succession of foxglove interest. Tolerates more shade than most other foxgloves.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist soil without covering — seeds require light to germinate — in early spring or fall; yellow foxglove is considerably more long-lived than common foxglove, persisting as a true perennial for many years in suitable conditions. Divide established clumps in early spring to propagate named selections and rejuvenate older plants.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; yellow foxglove is the most genuinely long-lived foxglove species, behaving as a true perennial for 5–10 or more years rather than the typical 2-year biennial cycle of common foxglove — a crucial distinction for the perennial border. It produces dense spikes 2–3 feet tall of small, pale-yellow to cream tubular flowers with faint darker veining inside the tube in early summer, and often reblooms on lateral shoots if cut back after the main flowering flush. The foliage is glossy, dark-green, and forms a neat, semi-evergreen clump in mild climates that is attractive throughout the year. More shade-tolerant than most foxgloves, it succeeds in dappled woodland shade under deciduous trees where the common foxglove often fails to bloom well. A refined, dependable, long-lived plant for the shaded border that deserves far wider use than its quieter color gives it.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, nutrient-poor soil in full sun to partial shade; yellow fringed orchid requires the acidic, wet soils of bogs, seepage slopes, and moist pine flatwoods — plant in partnership with appropriate mycorrhizal fungi.
directions: Yellow fringed orchid is among the most spectacularly beautiful of all North American native wildflowers — a magnificent spike of dozens of bright golden-orange to deep orange flowers, each with a dramatically fringed lower lip that creates a feathery, lace-like appearance unique among wildflowers, blooming in July and August in open bogs, moist savannas, and wet pine flatwoods throughout the Gulf Coastal Plain and eastern United States. The long, slender nectar spur extending from each flower can only be reached by long-tongued swallowtail butterflies (especially tiger and spicebush swallowtails), which are the primary pollinators — the match between floral anatomy and pollinator tongue length is so precise that no other insect can effectively pollinate the flowers. Found throughout the Gulf Coast longleaf pine flatwoods and seepage bogs from Texas to Florida, where it blooms in late summer heat alongside pitcher plants, sundews, and other carnivorous plants of this unique, fire-maintained ecosystem. An unforgettable sight when in full bloom and worth every effort to establish in a properly maintained bog garden.

subcategory: Western US native dry spring bulb
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun to partial shade in very well-drained, dry, sandy or gritty soil in zone 3–8; Yellow Fritillary (Yellow Bells, Pudding Onion) is a charming, small, early-spring-blooming native bulb of the western United States — found from British Columbia to California east to the Rockies in sagebrush steppe, bunchgrass prairies, and open pine forest — bearing one to three nodding, bright golden-yellow bell flowers on each short stem, among the first native wildflowers to bloom in late winter and early spring.
directions: Plant Fritillaria pudica bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in very well-drained, dry, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; they require dry summer dormancy and are intolerant of summer moisture — grow in raised beds, scree, or containers to control drainage; provide minimal water during winter and spring, then dry out completely by early summer. Yellow Fritillary is a small but disproportionately delightful native bulb — its bright golden-yellow, nodding bells appearing remarkably early in late winter and early spring when little else is in bloom in its native Western sagebrush and bunchgrass habitat. The bulbs are surrounded by numerous rice-grain bulblets that produce offsets and spread into small colonies over several years. Indigenous peoples throughout its range used the small bulbs as a food source — eaten raw, roasted in the coals, or boiled and mixed with other foods. The main challenge in cultivation outside the West is providing the perfectly dry summer dormancy the bulbs require; in humid summer climates, growing in pots that can be stored dry under a bench from July through October is the most reliable approach. Plant among early spring companions like Phlox subulata, spring-blooming Allium, or in a naturalistic Western xeriscape.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in shade to partial shade; yellow fumewort self-sows freely in moist woodland understories, appearing as tiny ferny seedlings in early spring and completing its cycle by late spring before summer heat. A true spring ephemeral annual.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, rich woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; yellow fumewort is a small, delicate woodland annual of rich, moist floodplain forests and mesic slope forests of the eastern US, producing finely dissected, ferny, pale blue-green foliage and tiny clusters of small, pale yellow, spurred flowers in early spring. Despite the modest size and inconspicuous flowers, yellow fumewort makes a charming and understated element in woodland gardens, filling in the bare ground under deciduous trees in early spring when little else is growing. Self-sows reliably in appropriate moist, shaded woodland soil to naturalize and expand each year. The plant is gone entirely by early summer, leaving no trace — true spring ephemeral behavior. Often found growing alongside Dutchman's breeches, spring beauty, trout lily, and other spring ephemerals in rich eastern floodplain forest. A specialist plant for authentic native woodland garden compositions.

plant_note: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; yellow giant hyssop tolerates partial shade better than most agastaches and grows vigorously along woodland edges and in open, naturalized meadows.
directions: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; yellow giant hyssop tolerates partial shade and adapts to a wider range of moisture conditions than purple giant hyssop, naturalizing along woodland borders and stream margins. Agastache nepetoides is the tallest of the eastern North American native giant hyssops, reaching 4–6 feet tall with large, heart-shaped, minty-scented leaves and dense, elongated spikes of tiny, pale-yellow to white flowers with protruding yellow-green bracts in mid- to late summer that attract enormous numbers of native bees, bumblebees, and butterflies. Despite the somewhat inconspicuous individual flowers, the plant's tall, vertical form and prolific blooming make it a standout in naturalized meadow and woodland-edge plantings; the seed heads persist through winter and provide food for seed-eating birds. It self-seeds moderately in favorable locations.

common_name: Yellow Ginger Lily (Golden Butterfly Ginger, Yellow Garland Lily, Flavum Ginger)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Hedychium flavum is a vigorous, rhizomatous ginger lily that produces fragrant, clear yellow to pale-yellow flowers in dense, terminal spikes in summer and fall. More cold-hardy than many tropical gingers, it is root-hardy to zone 7 and recovers reliably from frost in zone 8-9 when mulched. The fragrance is sweet, intense, and jasmine-like, strongest in the evening. Excellent in moist, partially shaded positions near seating areas where the fragrance can be appreciated. Divide clumps every 2–3 years for best bloom. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Yellow Ginger Lily thrives in the warm, moist conditions of Gulf Coast summers and produces its fragrant yellow flower spikes most prolifically when given consistent moisture through the growing season. Hedychium flavum is a tall, rhizomatous, evergreen to deciduous perennial ginger in the Zingiberaceae family native to the Himalayas (Nepal, India, Bhutan, southern China) — one of the most cold-hardy and fragrant of the ornamental ginger lilies, known since Victorian times as a prized garden plant for the tropical-appearing foliage and the intensely perfumed, clear yellow flowers. The plant produces robust, cane-like stems 3–6 feet tall clothed in broad, glossy, bright-green, lance-shaped leaves 12–18 inches long — the overall effect lush and tropical. In summer and fall, the stem tips are crowned by dense, cylindrical, 6–10 inch flower spikes bearing 15–30 flowers. Each flower is a classic Hedychium bloom: a narrow yellow tube flares into a larger, reflexed, bright-yellow, three-petaled corolla with a single prominent stamen and style in the same clear yellow. The fragrance is the plant's outstanding quality — intensely sweet, rich, and jasmine-like, filling the surrounding air in the evening hours when it is strongest. This fragrance quality, combined with the cold hardiness (to zone 7 with mulching), makes H. flavum one of the most useful and rewarding of the ginger lilies for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens. Non-toxic.

common_name: Yellow Ground Orchid (Pubescent Spathoglottis, Hairy Ground Orchid)
plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or divisions in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Spathoglottis pubescens is slightly less cold-tolerant than S. plicata but grows in similar conditions. The distinctive yellow to golden-yellow flowers distinguish it from the pink-purple S. plicata. Plant alongside S. plicata for a colorful mixed ground orchid bed. Divide every 3–4 years. The common name 'pubescens' refers to fine hairs on the flowers and plant surfaces. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Yellow Ground Orchid performs best in the filtered light of a shaded garden bed with regular moisture and organic-rich soil, conditions that approximate its native forest-margin habitat. Spathoglottis pubescens is a clump-forming terrestrial orchid native to southern China, India, the Himalayas, Thailand, Vietnam, and adjacent Southeast Asia in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most attractive Spathoglottis species for its distinctive flower color: unlike the rose-pink to magenta flowers of the more commonly grown S. plicata, S. pubescens produces flowers in clear, bright golden-yellow to canary-yellow with a darker orange-yellow lip — a warm, cheerful color that stands out particularly well against the green foliage of a shaded garden bed. The plant has a similar growth habit to S. plicata — oval pseudobulbs, pleated green leaves, and tall (18–30 inch) flower scapes bearing 5–15 flowers in succession — but the yellow coloration and the fine, soft hairs on the flowers and plant surfaces (the 'pubescens' — hairy) distinguish it from its pink relative. Planted together, yellow S. pubescens and pink S. plicata create an attractive bicolor ground orchid display that provides weeks of sequential bloom through the warm months. One of the finest terrestrial orchids for zone 9-12 shade gardens. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in fall or early spring in average to moist, well-drained soil near a trellis, fence, or shrub to climb; yellow honeysuckle tolerates partial shade and can be trained as a scrambling groundcover or trained vertically for hummingbird gardens.
directions: Yellow honeysuckle is a native semi-evergreen vine of the Ozarks and Appalachian foothills, one of the most ornamentally beautiful of all American honeysuckles — its showy clusters of vivid golden-yellow to orange-yellow trumpet flowers in spring are magnets for ruby-throated hummingbirds during their northward migration and are also visited by long-tongued bumblebees and sphinx moths. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica) that has escaped across the South, yellow honeysuckle is a well-behaved native that twines moderately and stays in bounds without smothering trees or shrubs; it is semi-evergreen in mild winters in the South. Small red berries ripen in summer and are eaten by mockingbirds and other fruit-eating birds. Train on a picket fence, stone wall, arbor, or through a native shrub border — it blooms most profusely in partial shade to full sun and combines beautifully with coral honeysuckle for extended bloom.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds where plants are to grow permanently in spring or fall; yellow horned poppy has a deep taproot and resents transplanting. It is biennial to short-lived perennial — forming a rosette the first year and flowering from the second year onward. It self-sows freely in appropriate conditions. All parts are toxic if ingested. The conspicuously long (6–12 inch) seed pods are the source of the 'horned' common name.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; yellow horned poppy is a coastal biennial or short-lived perennial native to the shingle beaches, sea cliffs, and dry wasteland of the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts of Europe — one of the most dramatically attractive plants of shingle habitats, producing a large rosette of deeply lobed, wavy-edged, intensely glaucous, blue-gray, rough-textured, almost metallic-appearing leaves in the first year, and from June through September of the second year, a succession of large (2–3 inch), crinkled-petaled, vivid butter-yellow poppy flowers followed by the plant's most extraordinary feature — slender, horn-like seed pods up to 12 inches long that curve and arc dramatically, giving the plant an immediately recognizable, sculptural quality when seeding. The combination of the intensely silver-blue foliage and the bright yellow flowers on a large, architecturally dramatic plant is one of the finest available in dry, coastal or gravel gardens. Self-sows modestly to maintain colonies in appropriate lean, well-drained conditions.

common_name: Yellow Ipe (Brazilian Trumpet Tree, Yellow Lapacho, Guayacan Amarillo)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Handroanthus serratifolius is moderately cold-hardy, surviving temperatures to 26–28°F in established specimens, making it viable in protected zone 9b-10 locations. The tree blooms most spectacularly on bare branches in spring after a dry period — withhold irrigation through February to trigger maximum bloom. The serrated leaflets (the 'serratifolius' — serrated leaves) distinguish this species from related Handroanthus species. Drought-tolerant once established. One of the national symbols of Brazil.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Yellow Ipe is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in the sandy, well-drained soils common throughout Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes. Handroanthus serratifolius is a large, deciduous to semi-deciduous tree native to Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, and Brazil in the Bignoniaceae family, one of several South American species collectively called 'Ipê Amarelo' (Yellow Ipe) — celebrated as among the most spectacular flowering trees in the world. In late winter to spring, the tree drops its leaves and then, on the leafless branches, produces one of the most dramatic flower displays in all of the tree kingdom: the entire canopy simultaneously explodes in masses of large, 3-inch, brilliant golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers covering every branch without a single leaf to distract from the flower display — the tree appears from a distance as a cloud of pure, intense yellow gold. After the bloom, the new leaves emerge as the flowers fall, carpeting the ground with a golden layer of spent petals. The wood of Ipê (called 'ironwood' in lumber trade) is one of the hardest, most durable timbers in the world — rated Class A for marine and ground-contact use and used for heavy decking, bridges, and structural applications across South America and in exported form worldwide. In the ornamental world, the bloom display alone justifies the tree's cultivation in zone 9-12 landscapes.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated, tissue-cultured specimens from specialist orchid nurseries in fall; yellow lady's slipper is the most adaptable of the native Cypripedium species and can succeed in more garden conditions than pink lady's slipper — plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade.
directions: Yellow lady's slipper is the most widely distributed and arguably the most garden-adaptable of all native North American orchids — growing in moist, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soils across an enormous range from Canada to the Gulf Coast states, and tolerating a wider range of pH and soil conditions than the highly acid-demanding pink lady's slipper. The golden-yellow, pouch-shaped flowers with maroon-striped lateral petals and a rich, sweet-spicy fragrance emerge in May from stems bearing 1–3 blooms; bumblebee queens are the primary pollinators, entering the pouch to discover there is no nectar and escaping through a back exit that brushes them with pollen — a deceptive but effective pollination mechanism. Like all Cypripedium, it forms a long-lived clump that slowly expands by rhizomes; established plants purchased from nurseries and planted in appropriate woodland conditions can persist for decades, eventually forming spectacular multi-stemmed flowering colonies. The most rewarding and accessible native terrestrial orchid for the shaded woodland garden when purchased as tissue-cultured nursery stock.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist to moderately wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; yellow loosestrife spreads aggressively by rhizomes in moist, fertile conditions and is best used where spreading can be contained or accommodated.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to moderately wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; yellow loosestrife is a robust European garden perennial producing whorled, lance-shaped leaves and cheerful, bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers held in loose spikes from early to midsummer — an excellent, long-lasting yellow for the partially shaded border, particularly in moist conditions where many perennials struggle. The plant spreads freely by rhizomes in fertile, moist soil and can colonize large areas in garden borders; edge annually to control spread or plant in a contained bed. Excellent for stream banks, pond margins, and rain garden edges. 'Alexander' (creamy-gold variegated leaves) and 'Golden Alexander' are popular selections that are slightly less vigorous than the straight species. Not to be confused with the invasive purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria), which is a different genus.

plant_note: Divide rhizome clumps in fall or plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Yellow Mandarin slowly spreads by rhizome to form colonies in the moist woodland garden.
directions: Yellow Mandarin is an elegant native woodland perennial, native to rich, moist, deciduous forests of eastern North America from Ontario south to Georgia and Alabama, with arching stems bearing alternating, broadly oval, clasping leaves and pendant, creamy-yellow, bell-shaped flowers dangling from branch tips in April and May — an effect reminiscent of Solomon's seal but with larger, more distinctly yellow-green flowers. The small, red to orange berries that follow in late summer are attractive and eaten by some birds, adding late-season interest to the shaded garden. Yellow Mandarin spreads slowly by rhizome to form loose, graceful colonies and is one of the most architecturally pleasing of the native spring woodland wildflowers, providing strong vertical structure in layers under taller shade trees. Divide clumps in fall, or plant nursery transplants in spring in well-amended, consistently moist, humus-rich soil.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; yellow mandarin forms slow-spreading clumps and is best massed with other native ephemerals and ferns rather than used as a single specimen.
directions: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; yellow mandarin forms slow-spreading clumps and is best massed with other native ephemerals and ferns rather than used as a single specimen. Prosartes lanuginosa (formerly classified as Disporum lanuginosum) is an eastern North American woodland native with downy, arching stems bearing alternate, pointed leaves and small, pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers dangling beneath the foliage in mid-spring, followed by orange-red berries in summer that ripen to a rich red. It is a quiet, textural companion for trillium, wild ginger, and Solomon's seal in a shaded native garden, valued more for its graceful arching form and berries than for showy bloom. Give it consistent moisture and a leaf-mold-rich soil similar to its native rich cove and slope forest habitat, and avoid soils that dry out or become waterlogged.

subcategory: California native dry summer grassland bulb
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun in very well-drained, dry, lean, clay-loam to sandy soil in zone 7–10; withhold water completely from late spring through fall; Yellow Mariposa Lily is a spectacular California native bulb of the Central Valley foothills and inner Coast Ranges — bearing large, bright-golden-yellow, three-petaled, cup-shaped flowers with brown-red markings at the petal bases — one of the easiest Calochortus for drier California gardens and naturalistic plantings.
directions: Plant Calochortus luteus bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in lean, dry, clay-loam or sandy soil in full sun; provide winter and spring moisture (natural rainfall is usually sufficient in California), then allow to go completely dry from June onward — no summer water is essential for long-term success. Yellow Mariposa Lily is one of the most cheerful and showy of all California spring wildflowers — forming grassland and foothill scrub meadows of pure brilliant yellow across the Central Valley foothills when conditions are right. The large, satiny-petaled, chalice-shaped flowers are a bright, clear yellow with a small reddish-brown blotch inside at the base of each petal above the nectar gland. Unlike the more variable Calochortus venustus, the yellow color is consistent and reliable, making it an excellent choice for naturalistic meadow plantings and spring wildflower gardens in California and other dry-summer climates. Calochortus luteus grows naturally in heavy clay-loam soils of California's inner Coast Ranges and foothills — a habitat that floods in winter and bakes concrete-hard in summer — and adapts surprisingly well to similar heavy soils in the garden. An excellent companion to poppies, lupines, and blue dicks in California native wildflower meadows.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or plant container-grown plants in moist to wet, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; yellow meadow rue is adapted to moist conditions including wet meadows and stream margins. The subspecies glaucum (Spanish Meadow Rue) has particularly glaucous, blue-green foliage and is slightly more drought-tolerant than the species.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately wet, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; yellow meadow rue is a tall, elegant European perennial distinguished by its outstanding glaucous (blue-green) foliage — the divided, finely cut, columbine-like leaves are a particularly intense, powdery, blue-green color that provides striking cool contrast in the summer garden independent of the flowers. In early to midsummer, the plant produces fluffy, branching clusters of numerous small, lemon-yellow, petal-less flowers at the top of tall, upright stems — the fluffy effect comes from the prominent, crowded yellow stamens that form the visible flower structure, as the true petals have been reduced to small sepals. Native to moist meadows and streambanks throughout Europe, it is adapted to consistently moist conditions and succeeds beside water features, in bog gardens, and in moist, partly shaded borders. The subspecies glaucum from Spain and Portugal has particularly intensely glaucous foliage and is more drought-tolerant than the typical species. Excellent as a tall filler in the moist or partly shaded border.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out transplants in consistently moist to wet soil in early spring; yellow monkeyflower is a streamside and seep native that needs steady moisture and struggles in average garden soil that dries out between waterings.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil along pond margins, rain gardens, or stream edges in partial shade to full sun, since this species is naturally found growing with its roots at or near the water table. Yellow monkeyflower is a widespread North American wildflower named for the whimsical, grinning face suggested by the dark red spotting inside its bright yellow, snapdragon-like flowers, which bloom over a long season from spring into summer and draw bumblebees and other native pollinators reliably. Plants often behave as short-lived perennials or reseeding annuals, sprawling and rooting at the nodes where stems touch wet soil, which makes them useful as a low, moisture-loving edge planting for water features. Keep the soil from drying out, since this is the single most common cause of failure; in a genuinely wet, boggy spot it needs very little other care.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, gritty, well-drained soil in a cool, partly shaded site.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, gritty, well-drained soil in a cool, partly shaded site, recreating the high alpine and subalpine slopes of the Cascades and northern Rockies where it often grows beside its pink-flowered relative. Clusters of small, urn-shaped, greenish-yellow to cream flowers open in early summer above dense needle-like foliage, and where the two species overlap they hybridize into an intermediate-colored form. Give it steady moisture and cool summers; it declines quickly in hot, dry, or poorly drained garden conditions.

common_name: Yellow Oleander (Lucky Nut, Be-Still Tree, Cascabela thevetia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Yellow Oleander grows rapidly in zone 9-10 and begins blooming in the first year. In zone 9a, it may be damaged by hard frost but resproots from the root crown in spring. In zone 9b-10, it grows as a reliable evergreen shrub blooming nearly year-round. Prune after each bloom flush to shape and stimulate reblooming. The milky sap is a severe skin and eye irritant. EXTREME CAUTION: All parts contain highly toxic cardiac glycosides — seeds especially dangerous and have caused accidental poisoning fatalities worldwide.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil; Yellow Oleander is drought-tolerant once established and will rot in heavy, consistently wet soils. Cascabela thevetia (formerly Thevetia peruviana) is a large, evergreen shrub or small tree from Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean in the Apocynaceae family — distantly related to Oleander (Nerium) and sharing its extreme toxicity. The plant produces long, narrow, deep green, glossy, lance-shaped leaves that densely clothe the arching stems, and bears funnel-shaped, slightly fragrant flowers 2–3 inches across in brilliant yellow — occasionally orange-yellow or peach in some forms. Flowering occurs year-round in zone 10-11 and from spring through fall in zone 9, with peak bloom in warm months. In tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, Yellow Oleander is one of the most commonly planted ornamental shrubs for hot, dry, full-sun landscapes — its combination of attractive foliage, continuous flowers, and extreme drought and heat tolerance makes it exceptionally useful. EXTREME CAUTION: All parts of Yellow Oleander contain highly toxic cardiac glycosides (thevetin A and B, neriifolin) that affect the heart — the large black seeds are particularly concentrated and have caused accidental poisonings and intentional toxicity events worldwide; do not plant where children, pets, or livestock have access.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; yellow passionflower is the most shade-tolerant of the native Passiflora species and naturalizes readily in shaded woodland edges and fence lines in zone 6–9.
directions: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; yellow passionflower is the most shade-tolerant native Passiflora species and is far less aggressive than maypop (P. incarnata), making it more suitable for smaller gardens and shaded areas. The flowers are smaller than other passionflowers but share the same intricate, layered structure — creamy yellow-green petals and a distinctive corona of filaments — and are visited by long-tongued native bees for nectar. Like all native Passiflora, yellow passionflower is a host plant for the larvae of gulf fritillary, variegated fritillary, and zebra longwing butterflies. The small dark purple fruits are eaten by birds. It grows naturally along shaded woodland edges, thickets, and roadsides throughout the southeastern US and is one of the best native vines for adding butterfly-host value to a shaded fence or trellis.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to part shade; yellow patrinia self-sows moderately once established, maintaining a colony without becoming invasive. Established plants develop a deep taproot and should not be moved; site carefully from the start.
directions: Sow seeds in moist, well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; yellow patrinia is a Japanese and Korean perennial that has become a valued late-season component in naturalistic perennial designs, producing airy, branching sprays of small, bright-yellow flowers from July through September — an unusually long bloom period — carried on slender, branching stems above deeply cut, dark-green basal foliage. The finely divided flower clusters create a golden haze effect when massed and combine beautifully with blue salvias, purple asters, ornamental grasses, and late-season rudbeckias. As autumn proceeds, the yellow flowers gradually age to a warm bronze-orange and are joined by ornamental seed heads, extending the season further. Yellow patrinia is a significant and long-lasting cut flower, popular in Japanese ikebana arrangements and increasingly in Western floral design. The plant self-sows reliably without becoming weedy and is attractive to wasps, small bees, and butterflies. It is long-lived once established and thrives in a remarkably wide range of conditions.

plant_note: Plant fleshy tuber clusters in spring 6 inches deep in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 7–10; Yellow Peruvian Lily (Chilean Lily, Orange Alstroemeria) is a vigorous, spreading, tuberous perennial from the Andean foothills and grasslands of Chile and Argentina — bearing abundant, trumpet-shaped, warm-golden-yellow to orange flowers with contrasting dark inner streaks from early summer through fall — the wild parent species from which most modern hybrid Alstroemeria cut flowers derive their warm color range.
directions: Plant Alstroemeria aurea tubers 6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during active growth; deadhead spent flowers to extend blooming; divide clumps every 3–4 years as needed; the plant spreads vigorously by rhizomatous tubers and can become quite extensive. Yellow Peruvian Lily is one of the most widely grown wild Alstroemeria species and the parent (or grandparent) of the majority of modern hybrid cut-flower Alstroemerias in the trade. The species itself is extremely vigorous and free-flowering — producing abundant, 2-inch, trumpet-shaped flowers in warm golden-yellow to rich orange with distinctive brown to maroon inner petal streaks from early June through September. Unlike many Alstroemeria, A. aurea is quite cold-hardy (to zone 7) and spreads enthusiastically in garden conditions, forming large colonies that bloom reliably year after year. The resupinate (upside-down) leaves characteristic of all Alstroemeria are evident in this species. An excellent cut flower with exceptional vase life — stems can last 2–3 weeks in water. Spreads widely enough in fertile soil to become quite assertive — give it room or contain the rhizomatous tubers with buried barriers. In zone 8–10 Gulf Coast gardens, the warm colors and extended bloom period make it particularly valuable for summer borders.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic (pH 3.5–5.5), nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum bog medium in full sun; keep standing in a tray of pure rain water or distilled water 1–2 inches deep year-round — never fertilize and never use tap water.
directions: Yellow pitcher plant is one of the tallest and most spectacular native carnivorous plants of North America — producing elegant, yellow-green, trumpet-shaped pitchers up to 4 feet tall with distinctive reddish veining, topped by an arching, umbrella-like lid and a flaring collar that guides insects into the prey-filled, rain-protected trap. Insects are attracted by colorful nectar-like secretions around the pitcher mouth, slide down the waxy inner surface, and drown in the accumulated fluid at the base where bacteria and enzymes digest them; a single pitcher can trap dozens of insects per week. Large, drooping yellow flowers appear on separate stalks in April before the pitchers emerge fully, and have an unusual musty, cat-like scent that attracts early spring pollinators including queen bumblebees, solitary bees, and flies. Native to the wetland pine savannas of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from Virginia to Florida, this plant is an outstanding garden specimen for acidic bog gardens in zones 6–9 — it requires no special care beyond pure water, wet conditions, and full sun, and will thrive for decades as a dramatic living sculpture in a properly maintained bog.

common_name: Yellow Polystachya (Concrete Polystachya, Pan-Tropical Epiphytic Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on rough bark or in a small slatted basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light; Polystachya concreta is an adaptable, relatively tolerant epiphyte. In zone 9-10, it can be grown outdoors on shaded trees and porches through the warm months and protected indoors in winter. The small, yellow-green flowers with a slightly resupinate lip arrangement (lip on top) are characteristic of the Polystachya genus. Blooms spring–summer. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light mounted on bark or in a small slatted basket — Yellow Polystachya adapts well to both mounted and potted culture in good indirect light with adequate air circulation. Polystachya concreta is a small, sympodial, epiphytic orchid with one of the widest natural ranges of any orchid species in the world — it occurs naturally across all of tropical Africa, tropical Asia, Australia, the Pacific Islands, the Caribbean, Florida, Mexico, Central America, and tropical South America — a genuinely pantropical distribution that makes it one of the most geographically widespread orchid species known. In Florida, it grows naturally in Highlands, Miami-Dade, Monroe, and Collier Counties as a native epiphyte. The plant produces small, narrow, flattened pseudobulbs with 2–3 narrow, dark-green, somewhat fleshy leaves. In spring and summer, short, erect to arching flower spikes bear 5–20 small (0.5-inch) flowers in yellow-green to yellowish-cream, each with a slightly darker green spotted center and a white to cream three-lobed lip. A distinctive feature of Polystachya flowers is that they are non-resupinate — the lip is held uppermost rather than below as in most orchids, an unusual orientation. While not as showy as many tropical orchids, P. concreta's remarkable adaptability, wide tolerance of conditions, and status as a Florida-native epiphyte make it a meaningful and historically interesting addition to orchid collections. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in full sun to partial shade in still or slow-moving water 1–4 feet deep in zone 3–10; the Yellow Pond Lily (Brandy Bottle) is a vigorous, cold-hardy, native aquatic perennial found across Europe, North America, and western Asia — forming spreading colonies of large, heart-shaped, floating leaves and cheerful bright-yellow, globe-shaped flowers above the water surface from late spring through summer.
directions: Plant Nuphar lutea rhizome sections horizontally in heavy clay loam in large aquatic containers or directly in the pond bottom in 1–4 feet of still or slow-moving water; top-dress with aquatic fertilizer tablets in spring; thin colonies in fall by dividing and removing excess rhizome sections as needed. The Yellow Pond Lily is one of the most cold-tolerant and widely adaptable of all aquatic perennials — native across a broad swathe of the Northern Hemisphere from North America and Europe to western Asia — and perfectly suited to ponds and naturalistic water gardens where winters are too severe for tropical water lilies. The bright yellow, globe-shaped flowers (the old name 'Brandy Bottle' refers to their faint alcoholic scent) are held just above the water surface and attract native bees and beetles as pollinators. Large, waxy, heart-shaped leaves float on the surface, providing excellent shade that reduces algae growth and offers fish cover beneath. Unlike tropical water lilies, Yellow Pond Lily goes dormant in winter and re-emerges from thick rhizomes in spring; rhizomes can form substantial colonies over time and may need periodic thinning in smaller ponds. The seeds and rhizomes are edible and were historically used by Native Americans.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring, anchoring the thick horizontal rhizome in heavy clay or loamy pond-bottom soil at a depth of 1–4 feet of standing water. Yellow Pond Lily thrives in slow-moving streams, ponds, bayous, and blackwater swamps and should not be planted in fast-moving water.
directions: Yellow Pond Lily is a vigorous native floating-leaf aquatic plant, native to the slow ponds, sluggish streams, bayous, and blackwater swamps of eastern North America from New Brunswick to Florida and across the Gulf states to Texas, bearing large, heart-shaped floating leaves up to a foot across and distinctive globular yellow flowers on stout stems from spring through fall — the flowers are pollinated by beetles and tiny bees attracted to the scent and heat generated by the floral chamber. The thick, horizontal rhizomes anchor in muddy pond bottoms and can spread aggressively, making Yellow Pond Lily best suited to large natural ponds and water gardens where it can spread freely; its roots, seeds, and leaf bases are important food for wood ducks, beaver, and muskrats. Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil at the pond bottom at a depth of 1–4 feet; once established, plants require no care and will spread naturally to cover the water surface, providing excellent shade that suppresses filamentous algae.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; yellow prairie flax is a short-lived, wiry-stemmed Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau native that self-seeds readily.
directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; yellow prairie flax is a slender, wiry-stemmed native wildflower of Texas limestone hills and prairies, with fine, needle-like leaves and small, bright golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers that open fresh each morning and shatter by afternoon, replaced by a new flush of blooms the following day over a long spring and early summer season. Individual plants are short-lived, typically persisting only a couple of seasons, but self-sow readily in lean, undisturbed, rocky soil to maintain a naturalized population over time. Its fine, airy texture works well threaded through a rock garden or dry prairie planting among bunchgrasses and other low, drought-tolerant wildflowers rather than as a stand-alone specimen. Avoid rich soil, mulch, and regular irrigation, which shorten its already brief lifespan and reduce self-sowing.

common_name: Yellow Rain Lily (Bright Yellow Fall Zephyranthes Bulb)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Yellow Rain Lily naturalizes freely in zone 8–10 gardens, self-seeding and producing offsets to form expanding colonies that require minimal maintenance — plant and allow to spread.
directions: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Zephyranthes citrina (Yellow Rain Lily) is one of the finest low-growing, naturalizing bulbs for Gulf South gardens — producing small (2–3 inch), bright golden-yellow, funnel-shaped flowers on 6–8 inch stems in flushes that follow rainfall events from summer through fall. The characteristic blooming response to rainfall gives rain lilies their common name: a period of dry weather followed by rain triggers an almost simultaneous flowering display across an established colony — hundreds of flowers opening within days of a rain event, creating a carpet-effect display that is one of the most charming garden phenomena. Yellow Rain Lily is distinguished from the more common pink and white species by its pure, vivid golden-yellow color — a bright, clean yellow with no orange or orange tones. The small flowers are jewel-like individually and spectacular en masse. Zephyranthes citrina is among the most heat-adapted and drought-tolerant of the rain lilies — naturally adapted to Mexican and Central American seasonally dry habitats and outstanding in the heat and periodic drought of the Gulf South. Established bulbs multiply rapidly by offsets and self-seeding to form large, low-maintenance colonies that naturalize freely in turf edges, rock gardens, and border edges. Plant in masses of 25–50 or more for best display effect — individual bulbs disappear among other plantings.

plant_note: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; roscoea emerges late in spring, so mark the planting spot to avoid disturbing what looks like bare soil. Excellent winter drainage is essential to prevent root rot.
directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Roscoea cautleyoides is a compact, cold-hardy member of the ginger family from the high-elevation forests and meadows of southwestern China, prized for its orchid-like flowers in a wider color range than most roscoea, including soft yellow, cream, white, and pale purple selections depending on the seed strain or named form. Like other hardy roscoea, it emerges quite late in spring and quickly produces a neat rosette of narrow, upright leaves topped by two-lipped, hooded blooms held just above the foliage in early to midsummer, giving an unexpectedly tropical, orchid-like accent to a temperate shade or woodland border. Sharp winter drainage is critical, since the fleshy storage roots are prone to rot in cold, waterlogged soil; raised beds or a gritty soil amendment help in heavier gardens. Combine with hostas, hellebores, and ferns for a layered woodland planting.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall in dry to moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; yellow star grass blooms prolifically in spring and early summer and is one of the native wildflowers that tolerates the light shade and root competition under pine trees — a very useful quality for southern landscapes.
directions: Plant small corms 1–2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; yellow star grass tolerates both dry and moderately moist conditions and is easily established in open woodland, pine barrens, and prairie settings. Hypoxis hirsuta is a tiny, charming native wildflower found throughout eastern North America from the Great Plains to the Atlantic coast, producing grass-like, hairy leaves 4–8 inches long and star-shaped, six-petaled, brilliant yellow flowers 1/2–3/4 inch across held on slender stems above the foliage from April through June; despite its small stature, a colony in full bloom is eye-catching. It grows from a corm and tolerates a wide range of conditions from dry pine woods to moist meadows, making it an adaptable choice for naturalizing in rough grass, woodland edges, and pollinator gardens. Native bees visit the flowers readily for pollen.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; yellow thistle forms a spiny basal rosette the first year and flowers on a tall stalk the second spring — a native, non-invasive biennial thistle valuable to pollinators, not to be confused with introduced noxious thistles.
