Popular cultivars include 'Meyer' (coarse, very cold-hardy), 'Emerald' (fine-textured, shade-tolerant, Gulf South standard), 'Palisades' (excellent drought and shade tolerance), and 'Zeon' (ultra-fine, premium home lawns).

plant_note: Start indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant out once frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant after the weather warms, or direct sow in warm regions. Also called Monarch of the Veldt, this heat- and drought-tolerant South African annual produces 3 to 4 inch daisy-like flowers above silver-tinged foliage from midsummer to fall. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil, and avoid overwatering as it prefers drier conditions. The blooms attract bees, birds, and butterflies. Flowers close at night and on cloudy days.

common_name: Zuni Crape Myrtle (Compact Lavender-Pink Semi-Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Zuni's smaller mature size makes it a good fit for tight residential spaces where larger crape myrtles would eventually crowd the site.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Zuni is one of the smaller National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles, producing lavender-pink flower clusters from summer into early fall on a compact, semi-dwarf tree well suited to smaller residential landscapes and foundation plantings. Like other National Arboretum hybrids it shows good resistance to powdery mildew, a common disease problem on older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars, and develops attractive exfoliating bark with age. Fall foliage turns shades of orange-red. Remove root suckers as they appear and prune only to remove crossing or dead branches rather than heavily topping the plant.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Zwartkop aeonium develops its darkest near-black color in bright, cool-season light and greens somewhat in shade or heat.
directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Zwartkop aeonium develops its darkest near-black color in bright, cool-season light and greens somewhat in shade or heat. Large, glossy rosettes of deep, near-black purple leaves top branching, woody stems on one of the most dramatic and widely recognized dark-foliaged succulents grown, creating striking silhouettes against lighter-colored companions in a mixed succulent bed or container arrangement. Unlike many succulents, aeoniums actively grow through the cooler months and can go semi-dormant or stressed in extreme summer heat, so afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps the plant look its best through summer. Water occasionally through the cooler growing season, reduce watering during the summer semi-dormant period, and propagate easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus before rooting.

plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in well-draining bark-based medium (not mounted); Zygopetalum mackayi grows naturally at moderate elevations (2,000–5,000 feet) in the Atlantic Forest of Brazil and appreciates cooler nights (50–60°F) that are essential for triggering bloom — without cool nights in fall and winter, the plant may not flower. Water regularly during active growth; reduce in winter. Blooms fall–winter, emitting a powerful, sweet, hyacinth-like fragrance. One of the more cold-tolerant sympodial epiphytic orchids. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in well-draining bark medium — Zygopetalum mackayi needs good light to bloom and will not flower in dim conditions, but is damaged by direct summer sun on the foliage. Zygopetalum mackayi is a sympodial, epiphytic to semi-terrestrial orchid native to the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil (Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo) at elevations of 2,000–5,000 feet in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most distinctive and ornamentally striking orchids in terms of flower coloration. The flowers of Zygopetalum are immediately recognizable: large (3–4 inches), with three sepals and two petals in the same rich coloration — a combination of green with broad bands and blotches of chocolate-brown to deep maroon — and a dramatically contrasting broad, spreading lip in pure white to pale lilac heavily marked with bold veins of deep purple to dark violet, creating a complex pattern of purple lines and dots on a white or pale background. The color combination of maroon-spotted green petals against a purple-veined white lip is unique among commonly grown orchids and immediately eye-catching. The flowers are strongly, sweetly fragrant — a powerful, hyacinth-like scent that fills a room. Multiple flowers per spike (5–12), with tall erect spikes in fall and winter. A prized and underused orchid for zone 9-11 collectors who can provide cool nights in fall to trigger bloom. Non-toxic.

scientific_name: Vitis riparia x Vitis rupestris '3309 Couderc'
plant_note: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; 3309 Couderc is grown as a phylloxera-resistant understock, not for its own fruit.
directions: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; 3309 Couderc is grown as a phylloxera-resistant understock, not for its own fruit. A classic French-American hybrid rootstock bred in the nineteenth century from two native North American grape species specifically to resist the root-feeding phylloxera aphid that devastated European wine grape vineyards, it remains one of the most widely planted grape rootstocks worldwide for its reliable phylloxera and some nematode resistance, moderate vigor, and good performance in well-drained, moderately fertile soils. Its long track record and predictable, moderate vigor have made it a benchmark rootstock against which many newer selections are compared, though it is less well suited to very dry or high-lime soils than some other rootstock options. Graft a desired named wine or table grape variety onto young rootstock, and provide well-drained soil, since it performs poorly in wet or poorly aerated ground.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; A4 macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued commercially for high oil content and cracking quality.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; A4 macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued commercially for high oil content and cracking quality. One of the classic Hawaiian-selected macadamia cultivars developed for commercial orchards, it produces medium-sized nuts with a high proportion of premium-grade, whole-kernel cracking quality and rich, high oil content prized by processors, making it a benchmark variety in Hawaiian macadamia production for decades. Like other macadamias it needs consistent warmth, protection from frost, and several years of growth before reaching significant bearing age, along with a compatible cross-pollinator variety for the best nut set. Water regularly during nut development, allow nuts to mature and fall naturally before harvest, and provide the same warm, humid, frost-free conditions the species requires throughout the year.

common_name: AU Buck IV Chestnut (Auburn University Annual-Bearing Chinese Chestnut)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU Buck IV is an open-pollinated selection out of AU-Cropper, bred for the heat and humidity of Alabama and the wider Gulf South, and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Buck IV is part of a numbered series (AU Buck I through V) of Chinese chestnut selections patented by Auburn University from open-pollinated seedlings of the AU-Cropper cultivar, chosen for blight resistance, precocious bearing, and dependable annual cropping rather than the alternate-bearing pattern common in seedling chestnut trees. It sets a medium to heavy crop of large nuts most years once established, and like other Auburn chestnut releases it is bred specifically to perform under the heat, humidity, and soilborne disease pressure of the Deep South. Space trees widely for a broad mature canopy and good air circulation, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar nearby, since chestnuts are not reliably self-fruitful. Harvest nuts from the ground in September-October as the spiny burrs split open, and refrigerate cured nuts to sweeten the starches before eating.

common_name: AU Gobbler II Chinese Chestnut (Early Extended-Drop Auburn University Chestnut)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU Gobbler II was selected by Auburn University for early, extended nut drop beginning in early September and continuing four to five weeks, a companion to the earlier AU Gobbler I.
directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Gobbler II, developed through Auburn University's chestnut breeding program specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the Deep South, was selected for its early and unusually extended nut drop, beginning around the first week of September and continuing over four to five weeks, spreading the harvest window and the wildlife forage value well beyond that of single-flush cultivars, and complements the related earlier-released AU Gobbler I. Its smaller nuts (roughly 5.7 grams) are typical of trees bred with wildlife food-plot use in mind, though it is equally suited to home orchard planting for its reliable annual bearing and blight resistance. Space trees widely for their broad mature canopy and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range.

common_name: AU-Cherry Plum (Auburn Disease-Resistant Southern Japanese Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; AU-Cherry sets a good crop on its own but benefits from a second Japanese plum cultivar nearby, and is well suited to home orchards across the Southeast.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second plum cultivar nearby to boost fruit set even though AU-Cherry is largely self-fruitful. Released from Auburn University's fruit breeding program, AU-Cherry was selected specifically for the disease pressures of the humid Southeast, showing strong resistance to bacterial leaf spot and plum leaf scald that limit many older plum cultivars in the region. The small, dark red, cherry-like fruit ripens about two weeks after Methley with a sweet, juicy flavor good for fresh eating. Trees are noted for staying vigorous and productive for many years, making AU-Cherry a dependable long-term choice for Southern home orchards.

common_name: AU-Cropper Chestnut (Auburn University Precocious Chinese Chestnut)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Cropper was selected by Auburn University specifically for the heat and humidity of the Deep South and bears young, but still needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set.
directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Cropper is a Chinese chestnut selection released through Auburn University's chestnut breeding program, developed specifically for reliable, precocious production under the heat, humidity, and disease pressure typical of Alabama and the broader Gulf South. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that eliminated American chestnut from Eastern forests, and begins bearing meaningful crops within a few years of planting rather than the decade or more required by seedling trees. Nuts drop free of the spiny burr at maturity in September–October for easy hand or ground collection. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy and to maintain the air circulation that helps limit fungal disease pressure in humid Southern summers, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range, since chestnuts are not reliably self-fruitful.

common_name: AU-Homeside Plum (Disease-Resistant Auburn University Gulf South Plum)
plant_note: Plant a grafted or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; AU-Homeside is an Auburn University plum release bred with strong resistance to bacterial spot, canker, and leaf scald, the diseases that most trouble plums under Gulf South humidity, ripening mid-summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, and plant a second, compatible plum cultivar nearby for pollination and reliable fruit set. AU-Homeside, part of Auburn University's plum breeding program alongside AU-Rosa, AU-Amber, AU-Producer, and AU-Cherry, was developed specifically for strong resistance to bacterial spot, bacterial canker, and leaf scald, the trio of fungal and bacterial diseases that most limit plum production under the humid, disease-favoring conditions of the Deep South. It bears a solid mid-summer crop of flavorful fruit on a tree that requires substantially less fungicide input than susceptible standard plum cultivars to stay productive and healthy. As with the rest of the AU series, it is well matched to Gulf South heat, humidity, and disease pressure, making it a lower-maintenance choice for home orchards in the region. Prune to an open center for good air circulation, which further reduces disease pressure.

common_name: AU-Homestead Chestnut (Auburn University Southeastern Chinese Chestnut)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Homestead was released by Auburn University alongside AU-Cropper as part of the same Southeastern-adapted chestnut breeding effort, and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for full cross-pollination.
directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Homestead is a Chinese chestnut cultivar developed through Auburn University's chestnut improvement program as a companion release to AU-Cropper, selected for good nut quality and disease tolerance under the heat, humidity, and soil conditions typical of Alabama and the wider Gulf South. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it inherits strong resistance to chestnut blight, the introduced fungal disease that historically devastated American chestnut, and begins cropping within a few years of planting on a grafted tree. Space trees widely to accommodate the broad, spreading mature canopy typical of Chinese chestnut, and interplant with a second, unrelated named cultivar within pollination range, since chestnuts require cross-pollination for a full nut set. Harvest nuts from the ground in September–October as burrs split and drop, and store cured nuts refrigerated for the sweetest flavor, since chestnut starches convert to sugar during cold storage.

common_name: AU-Leader Chestnut (Auburn University Precocious Chinese Chestnut)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Leader was released by Auburn University alongside AU-Cropper and AU-Homestead from the same Deep South-adapted breeding population, and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut cultivar nearby for full cross-pollination.
directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU-Leader is a Chinese chestnut selection from Auburn University's chestnut improvement program, drawn from the same precocious, blight-resistant seedling population that also produced AU-Cropper and AU-Homestead, and was chosen for a strongly upright, single-leader growth habit that makes it easier to train and maintain than the sprawling form typical of many chestnut selections. Like its sibling releases it inherits good resistance to chestnut blight and begins bearing at a young age on a grafted tree. Nuts run large for a Chinese chestnut, averaging roughly a dozen grams each, and mature and drop free of the split burr in early-to-mid September, ahead of many other Southern-adapted cultivars. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy, and interplant with a second unrelated chestnut cultivar within pollination range for a full nut set.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kola nut is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kola nut is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. This West African rainforest tree bears large, star-shaped pods containing caffeine-rich seeds that are chewed fresh across much of West Africa as a stimulant and used ceremonially to welcome guests, and were historically the original flavoring source for early cola soft drinks before synthetic flavorings largely replaced them. Trees take many years to reach bearing age and need consistently warm, humid, partly shaded conditions similar to their native rainforest understory habitat, limiting cultivation outside the tropics to botanical collections and large frost-free properties. Water regularly, especially while young, and provide the dappled shade of taller companion trees where possible to mimic natural forest conditions.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; abiu is a South American tropical tree suited to zones 10–12 that performs best in consistently warm, humid conditions with ample rainfall or irrigation. Grafted trees from superior selections begin fruiting in 3–4 years and produce smooth, bright yellow fruits with translucent, very sweet, jelly-like flesh.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 10–12; abiu (Pouteria caimito) is a tropical Sapotaceae tree native to the Amazon basin that produces smooth, glossy, bright lemon-yellow fruits with a custardy, translucent white flesh of exceptional sweetness — often described as tasting of caramel, vanilla, or crème brûlée — that clings to a small number of large seeds. The fruit is eaten fresh by scooping out the flesh, taking care to avoid the slightly sticky latex in the skin, which can irritate the lips if left in contact. Abiu is widely grown in Brazil and Queensland, Australia, where its productivity and flavor have made it one of the most popular exotic Sapotaceae fruits among tropical fruit enthusiasts. Trees respond well to regular fertilization with a balanced tropical fruit fertilizer and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development; mulch heavily to conserve soil moisture and maintain root health.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; acai palm is a frost-tender floodplain species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse with high humidity.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; acai palm is a frost-tender floodplain species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse with high humidity. Native to the seasonally flooded várzea forests of the Amazon River basin, this multi-stemmed, clustering palm produces heavy clusters of small, dark purple, antioxidant-rich berries that are pulped fresh into the acai bowls and juices that have become a global health-food phenomenon, though the fruit itself is highly perishable and must be processed within a day of harvest. It thrives in wet, swampy, even periodically flooded soil unlike most palms, reflecting its floodplain origin, and forms multiple clustering trunks over time rather than a single stem. Water generously and consistently, since it does not tolerate drought, and expect several years of growth before the first fruit clusters are produced.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or grafted stock in spring after all frost danger; in zone 9 site against a south-facing wall for extra warmth.
directions: Acerola produces cherry-like fruits with one of the highest natural concentrations of vitamin C of any food plant — up to 65 times that of an orange. The shrubby tree is self-fertile and can bear multiple times per year in truly frost-free climates; it is very sensitive to cold below 30°F and root systems are damaged below 28°F. Plant in well-drained, slightly acid to neutral soil and fertilize lightly with a balanced fertilizer three times per year. Fruit ripens very quickly from green to red and is extremely perishable — harvest when fully red and process (freeze, juice) within 24–48 hours for maximum vitamin C retention.

common_name: Acerola Cherry (Barbados Cherry, Highest Vitamin C Natural Tropical Fruit)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery plants in spring after last frost in full sun; acerola is a frost-sensitive tropical shrub that is damaged below 28°F and killed by temperatures below 25°F. In zone 9, plant against a south-facing wall for frost protection, in containers that can be moved indoors, or in frost-protected microclimates. Acerola produces 3 or more fruit crops per year in frost-free conditions — the plant blooms and fruits almost continuously in warm, humid conditions. The fruits should be harvested at full red ripeness and consumed or processed immediately — acerola loses Vitamin C rapidly after harvest (50% within 24 hours at room temperature). Stem cuttings root readily.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; protect from frost. Prune lightly after harvest to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting wood. Acerola Cherry (Malpighia emarginata, Barbados Cherry, West Indian Cherry) is a tropical American shrub producing small, bright red, cherry-shaped fruits with the highest Vitamin C content of any commonly cultivated fruit — measured at 1,600–4,700 mg per 100 grams of fresh fruit, compared to 50–90 mg per 100 grams in oranges. This extraordinary Vitamin C concentration — 30–100 times that of citrus — makes acerola one of the most nutritionally significant fruits available to home gardeners in zone 9–11, where the plant is well-adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South. The fruits are small (0.5–1 inch), three-lobed, brilliantly red at ripeness, with soft, juicy, somewhat tart flesh — the tartness masks the sweetness but reflects the very high ascorbic acid content. Acerola fruit has extremely limited commercial availability in North America because the ripe fruits are too soft and perishable for commercial shipping; the best quality fruit is available only to gardeners who can harvest and consume them immediately. Acerola is used for fresh eating, juicing, smoothies, and is commercially important in South America (especially Brazil) for vitamin supplement production from the concentrated juice.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; achachairu is more cold-tolerant than mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana) and reportedly survives brief dips to 28–30°F when established. Young trees are more sensitive to cold than mature ones — protect for the first several years. It is commercially grown in Bolivia at elevations up to 3,000 feet.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; achachairu is a Bolivian fruit tree in the same genus as mangosteen (Garcinia) and widely considered the superior subtropical Garcinia for warm temperate gardens — significantly more cold-tolerant than true mangosteen (which requires tropical conditions) while producing excellent fruit. The oval, orange-yellow fruits are 2–3 inches long with a thick, hard rind and sections of white, juicy, translucent flesh with a flavor profile that directly recalls mangosteen: sweet, tropical, slightly acidic, and complex, with an aromatic quality unique in temperate fruits. The tree is dense, dark-green, and attractive as an ornamental, with glossy leaves and a naturally compact, rounded form. Commercially grown in Bolivia, the fruit is popular fresh and in juices, ice creams, and desserts. It grows much faster than mangosteen and begins fruiting in 7–10 years from seed. Australia has embraced it as a commercial orchard crop, and it is increasingly available in subtropical zones 9–11 in the United States.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; ackee requires warm tropical conditions in zones 10–12 to fruit reliably; in zone 9, it may survive in protected locations but rarely fruits without summer heat accumulation.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; avoid planting in frost-prone sites. Blighia sapida (ackee) is a West African tree that became the national fruit of Jamaica, where the arils (fleshy seed coverings) of the opened, ripe fruit are the key ingredient in Jamaica's national dish, ackee and saltfish. The three large, black seeds of each red ackee pod are surrounded by creamy-yellow, buttery, scrambled-egg-textured arils that taste mildly savory and are typically sautéed with salt cod, onions, and peppers. IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: Unripe ackee (pods not fully opened naturally) contains hypoglycin A, a toxin that can cause Jamaican Vomiting Sickness — consume only the fully ripe arils after the pod has opened completely on the tree and seeds have developed fully. The ripe arils are nutritious, high in protein, fat, and niacin. The tree is an attractive, medium-sized evergreen with pinnate leaves and small white flowers. Fresh ackee is available in Jamaican and Caribbean communities in South Florida; canned ackee (already safely processed) is widely available.

plant_note: Plant the dormant or potted grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Adams produces an abundant spring flush of deep rose-red buds opening to rose-pink flowers, followed by small, glossy, cherry-red fruit about half an inch across that persists into winter and draws robins, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. It is a reliably disease-resistant crabapple, showing good resistance to apple scab and cedar-apple rust that plague many older, less-improved cultivars, and its rounded, well-branched form makes it a dependable small flowering shade tree for a home landscape. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Adams Elderberry (Classic High-Yield Large-Cluster American Elderberry Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Adams is one of the best pollinators for Bob Gordon and Nova elderberry cultivars — planting two or more different cultivars consistently produces 30–50% heavier fruit crops than single-variety plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Adams is one of the oldest and most widely established named elderberry cultivars — selected from wild American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) populations and long used as the benchmark for comparison in elderberry cultivar trials. It produces large, flat-topped flower clusters (cymes) in June–July — among the largest of named elderberry cultivars — followed by heavy, pendant clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late August–September. Adams is valued not only for its direct productivity but as an exceptionally effective cross-pollinator for other cultivars: planting Adams near Bob Gordon, Nova, or other cultivars consistently boosts overall production across the planting. The heavy, well-formed berry clusters of Adams are well-suited to all standard elderberry processing: elderberry syrup (a popular immune support product), elderberry wine, elderberry jelly, and elderflower preparations from the spring flowers. The large flower clusters are among the most attractive of any elderberry cultivar for elderflower cordials, fritters, and other culinary uses. As with all American elderberry, Adams spreads vigorously by root suckers and can naturalize in favorable moist conditions — manage the suckering to maintain a defined shrub rather than a spreading thicket. In zone 9, elderberry performs best in the slightly cooler, moister areas — near water features or in low spots where soil moisture is consistent.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Adams Pearmain is a reliable, easy-to-grow classic English russet apple well suited to a home orchard.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Adams Pearmain is a reliable, easy-to-grow classic English russet apple well suited to a home orchard. An old English variety first recorded in the early nineteenth century, it bears medium, elongated, pearmain-shaped apples with a dull red flush over a russeted yellow ground and dense, crisp, nutty-sweet flesh, ripening in mid-fall as a reliable, well-flavored traditional dessert apple. Its consistent, moderate cropping and good disease tolerance compared to some other classic English varieties have made it a dependable choice for a home orchard wanting an easy-to-grow heirloom russet-type apple. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for a few weeks to a couple of months for the best rich, nutty dessert flavor.

common_name: Advance Loquat (Early-Ripening Gulf Coast Orange-Fleshed Loquat)
plant_note: Plant grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Advance is one of the earliest-ripening loquat varieties available, with fruit typically mature 2–3 weeks ahead of standard varieties like Premier or Champagne — a significant advantage in the Gulf South where early spring frosts sometimes damage late-blooming varieties or where extended harvest overlapping with other fruit crops creates scheduling conflicts.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil; Advance loquat ripens earlier than most other varieties, often beginning in January–February in zone 9a, making it the first fresh tree fruit of the year in Gulf Coast gardens; fruits are medium, orange-fleshed, and sweet with moderate acidity; harvest sequentially as individual fruits ripen since this variety does not ripen all at once. Advance is an early-ripening loquat cultivar prized in Gulf Coast and Florida gardens for its ability to bring the first fresh homegrown tree fruit of the year to the table — typically ripening in January or February in zone 9a, 2–3 weeks ahead of the standard loquat season. This early ripening characteristic is agriculturally significant in two ways: it extends the effective loquat season (allowing home growers to plant multiple varieties for a longer fresh-fruit window from January through April), and it potentially reduces frost-damage risk to the developing fruit since early-ripening varieties complete their fruit development before the most severe January-February cold events. The fruits of Advance are medium-sized, rounded, with orange to golden-orange skin and firm, sweet orange flesh that is well-flavored without being as intensely aromatic as some other varieties. The tree is moderately vigorous and productive, and its earlier bloom time (September–October) compared to later-season varieties means some cross-pollination timing considerations when planting alongside other loquat varieties. Advance is a standard recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for Gulf Coast home gardeners who want reliable loquat production.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Ae Ae is grown chiefly for its dramatic white-and-green variegated foliage and fruit and needs protection from cold and strong wind, which can shred the tender leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade after the last frost, in a spot sheltered from strong wind; Ae Ae is a historic Hawaiian banana cultivar prized above all for its striking variegation, with broad white-and-green striped leaves and fruit that also shows white-and-green striping before ripening to a more solid yellow. It is grown as much as an ornamental tropical foliage specimen as for its sweet, edible fruit, and the variegated leaves are notably more prone to wind tatter and sunscald than solid-green banana cultivars, so a protected courtyard or the shelter of taller plantings improves its appearance. Because variegated plants generally grow more slowly than their all-green counterparts, give Ae Ae rich soil, consistent moisture, and regular feeding to keep it vigorous. Cold tolerance is limited like most ornamental Musa cultivars, so plan on container culture or serious winter protection in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; African breadfruit is a large, majestic West African tree — the largest member of the breadfruit/jackfruit family (Moraceae) — producing enormous globose fruits (12–36 inches across, up to 65 lbs) unlike common breadfruit: the edible part is the large starchy seeds rather than the flesh, and they are a major dietary staple in Nigeria, Cameroon, and Central Africa.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; a very large tree requiring considerable space — suitable primarily for large tropical properties in zone 11–12. Treculia africana (African breadfruit or ize) is one of the most ecologically and nutritionally important food trees of West and Central Africa — a massive, buttressed tropical tree native to the humid forests of Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, DRC, and Central Africa, producing the largest fruits of any species in the breadfruit/jackfruit family (Moraceae). The enormous globose fruits (12–36 inches across, weighing 10–65 lbs) erupt directly from the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) and are technically similar to jackfruit or breadfruit in structure, but used very differently: unlike common breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis, where the flesh is eaten) and jackfruit (where the flesh is the food), in African breadfruit, the edible product is the starchy, protein-rich seeds embedded in the fibrous flesh. The seeds are extracted, boiled or roasted, ground into flour, fermented (to make ugba or ukpaka — a traditional condiment in southeastern Nigeria), made into porridge, or pressed for oil. The fermented seed product (ukpaka) is a major flavor ingredient in Igbo cuisine, used similarly to cheese or miso as an aged, complex-flavored condiment. African breadfruit seeds are exceptionally protein-rich (21%) compared to other starchy staples. The tree is too large and slow-growing for most home gardens but represents one of the most important indigenous food forest trees of sub-Saharan Africa.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical climates (zone 11–12) in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil; African Bush Mango (Ozigo) is a large rainforest tree of Central and West Africa in the same genus as Safou (D. edulis) — bearing elongated, oblong, oil-rich, dark-blue to black fruits boiled and eaten as a sauce or condiment in Central African Gabonese and Cameroonian forest communities.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Dacryodes buettneri requires consistently high rainfall and humidity typical of tropical rainforest conditions — water abundantly during dry spells, mulch heavily, and maintain high organic matter content. Dacryodes buettneri (African Bush Mango, Ozigo, or Arbre à Beurre in French) is a large, emergent to canopy rainforest tree native to Gabon, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, and the Congo Basin forests, a member of the same Burseraceae genus as the widely grown African olive (Dacryodes edulis / Safou). Like safou, D. buettneri produces oblong, oil-rich fruits with thin, waxy skin ripening from green to dark-blue or black-purple, cooked (boiled or roasted) rather than eaten raw — the soft, creamy, rich, butter-like pulp develops a flavor somewhat reminiscent of avocado or a rich olive when heated. The fruits are an important food and oil source for forest-dwelling communities in Gabon and Cameroon, and the extracted fat is used for cooking and traditional personal care. Dacryodes buettneri is a tall-growing, high-humidity, tropical rainforest species best suited to humid equatorial climates in zones 11–12; it does not tolerate drought, salt, or cold and needs rich, moist, forest-type soils to perform well.

subcategory: African dryland cucurbit ornamental fruiting vine
plant_note: Direct sow or plant tuber divisions in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in zone 9–12; African Cucumber is a drought-adapted cucurbit vine from sub-Saharan Africa — producing charming, small, green-and-white striped, oval fruits that ripen to bright orange and red, and growing from a large, water-storing tuberous rootstock that allows it to survive months-long dry seasons — ornamental and wildlife-valuable in dry gardens and xeriscape plantings.
directions: Plant Kedrostis africana seeds or tuber sections in very well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; water sparingly during establishment and infrequently once growing — the large tuberous roots store water for extended dry periods; allow to dry down significantly in winter (the plant may appear dead); new growth emerges from the tuber in spring. African Cucumber is one of the most drought-adapted vines in the Cucurbit family — a member of the extraordinary African flora adapted to seasonal drought — growing from a large, knobby, water-storing tuber (caudex) that can persist underground through months-long dry seasons without any rainfall. Slender, twining vines emerge from the tuber in the wet season and bear small, deeply lobed leaves and clusters of tiny, exquisite, green-and-cream-striped oval fruits that look like perfect miniature watermelons as they develop, then ripen through yellow-orange to bright scarlet-red, splitting to reveal black seeds. In African folklore and traditional medicine, the tuberous roots and fruits of related Kedrostis species have various documented uses; the fruits are eaten by birds and mammals in the wild. The ornamental miniature fruits make it a conversation piece in the dry garden; it is well suited to succulent gardens, xeriscapes, and dry South Africa-inspired plantings in zone 9–12 Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, deep, sandy to loamy, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in zone 9–12; African Fan Palm is the African counterpart of the Asian Toddy Palm (Borassus flabellifer) — a massive, stately, long-lived fan palm native to the savanna, woodland, and floodplain regions of sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal to Kenya and south to Zimbabwe, producing very large, heavy, orange-brown fruits whose jelly-like germination tissue, fleshy mesocarp, and young shoots are all consumed as food.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, sandy to loamy, alkaline-tolerant soil; Borassus aethiopum is drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry periods of African savanna — water regularly only in the first few years of establishment; growth is very slow initially as the palm develops its extensive root system before vertical growth. Borassus aethiopum (African Fan Palm or African Palmyra) is one of the largest and most ecologically important palms of sub-Saharan Africa — a massive, solitary-trunked fan palm native to the savanna, woodland, and seasonal floodplain ecosystems of tropical and subtropical Africa from Senegal east through Nigeria, Sudan, Kenya, Tanzania, and south to Zimbabwe and Mozambique. The closely related Asian Toddy Palm (Borassus flabellifer) is a separate species adapted to South and Southeast Asian monsoon climates. The African Fan Palm reaches impressive dimensions — trunks to 80+ feet topped by a large, rounded crown of enormous, pleated, circular fan fronds up to 10 feet across. The large (4–6 inch), smooth, orange-brown fruits are economically important: the jelly-like germinating seed tissue is eaten by children and livestock; the fleshy mesocarp is eaten raw or cooked; palm sap tapped from the crown is fermented into 'African palm wine.' The hard, extremely dense, durable black palm heartwood is used for construction, tool handles, and musical instruments across its range. A dramatic, long-lived specimen palm for large tropical landscapes in zone 9–12 with patience — first 5–10 years of growth are slow as the root system establishes.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, sandy-loam soil in full sun; African locust bean (dawadawa or nere) is one of the most important food trees of West Africa — the seeds are fermented into dawadawa, one of sub-Saharan Africa's most important and most pungent flavor condiments (similar in culinary function to fish sauce, miso, or soy sauce), while the sweet, yellow, powdery pulp around the seed pods is eaten fresh and used as a sweetener.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep, sandy-loam to clay-loam soil in full sun; African locust bean is drought-tolerant once established and fixes nitrogen. Parkia biglobosa (African locust bean, dawadawa, or nere) is a massive, wide-canopied leguminous tree from the West African savanna and Sudan zone — one of the most economically and nutritionally important trees across a broad band of West Africa from Senegal to Ethiopia. The tree produces striking, spherical, red to orange pompom flower heads on pendulous stalks — spectacularly ornamental. The fruits are long pods containing seeds embedded in a dry, yellow, powdery, sweet pulp. The sweet pulp (high in sugar, vitamin C, and tannins) is eaten fresh or dissolved in water as a sweet drink. The seeds are the critical product: fermented over several days into dawadawa (called iru in Yoruba, ogiri-nono in Igbo, sumbala in Mande-speaking regions) — an intensely aromatic, deeply umami-flavored condiment with a pungent smell similar to very strong blue cheese or natto. Dawadawa is the essential flavoring in West African soups, stews, and sauces in the same way that fish sauce is essential in Southeast Asia — providing deep umami richness. The tree also fixes atmospheric nitrogen (Rhizobium symbiosis), improving soil fertility. A supremely important multi-use tree for tropical food forests in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant in the warm, wet tropics; strictly frost-free.
directions: The African mango, or bush mango, is a large tropical tree grown for its mango-like fruit and especially its oil-rich seed kernel, called dika nut. It demands a hot, humid, frost-free climate with abundant moisture and deep, fertile soil. Plant in full sun with plenty of room, as mature trees become tall and broad. Trees are slow to bear from seed, so grafted stock fruits sooner; harvest the fallen fruit and dry the prized kernels.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; African mangosteen is more cold-hardy than the tropical mangosteen (G. mangostana) and tolerates light frost once established.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; African mangosteen tolerates brief light frosts to about 28°F when established, making it considerably more cold-hardy than tropical mangosteen and viable in zone 9 sheltered locations. Garcinia livingstonei is an African native shrub or small tree grown for its small (1–2 inch), orange-yellow to orange-red, edible fruits with juicy, sweet-tart, apricot-like flesh and 1–3 large seeds; the flavor is pleasant and described as a combination of apricot and mango, and the fruits are eaten fresh, made into juices, and used to make a fermented beverage in southern Africa. Unlike tropical mangosteen (G. mangostana), which is notoriously difficult to cultivate outside the humid tropics, African mangosteen is adaptable, drought-tolerant when established, and significantly more cold-hardy — an excellent choice for Gulf Coast subtropical gardens in zones 9–11.

plant_note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; atemoya generally needs hand pollination for reliable fruit set in US gardens, since its natural beetle pollinators are absent.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. African Pride is a popular commercial and home garden atemoya cultivar known for a more compact tree size and heavy, reliable fruit production compared to some other cultivars, making it a practical choice where space is somewhat limited. The rich, sweet, custard-like flesh is classic atemoya quality, and hand pollination in the morning hours, transferring pollen from male-stage to female-stage flowers, significantly improves fruit set and size. Harvest when the fruit softens slightly and the skin lightens in color, then let it finish ripening at room temperature for the best eating quality.

common_name: African Walnut (Gaboon Nut, Walnut of the Congo)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in part shade; African walnut is a large West African rainforest tree producing olive-to-cherry-sized fruits with a hard shell enclosing a single, walnut-flavored edible kernel — one of the most important wild nut foods of the rainforest zone of Cameroon, Gabon, Nigeria, and the Congo Basin — eaten fresh, roasted, or boiled by forest-dwelling communities.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in part shade; African walnut is a slow-growing canopy tree for large properties in zone 11–12 humid tropics. Coula edulis (African walnut or Gaboon nut) is a large, slow-growing canopy tree of the humid tropical rainforests of West and Central Africa — native to Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Congo, and the DRC — and one of the most important wild nut-producing trees of the Central African forest zone. The tree produces small (1–1.5 inch), olive-to-cherry-sized, oval to round fruits with a thin, olive-like outer flesh and an extremely hard, woody shell inside (in the Olacaceae family, related to the African walnut group). The single kernel within the hard shell has a distinctly walnut-like flavor — nutty, oily, and rich — and is eaten fresh (raw), roasted in hot ashes, or boiled by forest communities across its range. The nuts are gathered from wild trees and are sold in markets in Cameroon, Gabon, and DRC as an important forest food product and source of income for forest-dependent communities. The high fat content (40–50%) makes the kernels calorie-dense and nutritionally valuable. Coula edulis is listed as a species of conservation concern in parts of its range due to overharvesting of wild nuts and habitat loss. A remarkable and entirely unknown tree outside West Central Africa.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; African wild mango (ogbono) is a large West African forest tree producing mango-like fruits with sweet, edible pulp — but valued primarily for the large, hard-shelled seeds (ogbono or dika nuts), which are dried and ground into ogbono powder, the critical thickening and flavoring agent in Nigeria's beloved ogbono soup and other West African forest-zone soups.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; African wild mango grows as a large forest tree requiring considerable space in zone 10–12. Irvingia gabonensis (African wild mango, ogbono, or dika nut) is a large, canopy forest tree native to the humid tropical forests of West and Central Africa — particularly Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, Ivory Coast, and the Congo Basin — and one of the most economically important non-timber forest trees of the West African rainforest zone. The tree produces round to oval, 2–3 inch fruits that superficially resemble small mangoes externally (hence 'African wild mango') but are unrelated: the fruit flesh (mesocarp) is sweet, yellowish, edible, and pleasant, but it is the large, hard-shelled seeds inside that represent the primary economic and culinary product. The seeds (ogbono nuts or dika nuts) are dried, smoked, or processed into ground ogbono powder — the essential thickening and flavoring agent in Nigerian ogbono soup (also called draw soup for its slimy, mucilaginous texture) and related soups across the forest zone of West Africa. Ground ogbono has a distinctive, complex, slightly bitter, earthy-nutty flavor and contains mucilaginous compounds (similar to okra) that create the characteristic 'draw' texture of the soup. The seeds also yield dika oil (Gaboon chocolate), used in confectionery. The tree gained international attention as a weight-loss supplement ingredient (IGOB131 extract) in the 2000s, with preliminary studies suggesting effects on blood lipids.

common_name: Akane Apple (Tokyo Rose, Early Scab-Resistant Tart-Sweet Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Akane blooms and ripens early in the season and needs a pollinator such as Jonathan or Golden Delicious that flowers at the same time.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible early-blooming pollinator. Bred in Japan from a cross of Jonathan and Worcester Pearmain and released in 1970, Akane produces small-to-medium, bright red apples with crisp, juicy, tart-sweet flesh reminiscent of Jonathan but with better resistance to apple scab. It ripens in late summer, ahead of most main-season apples, making it a good choice for gardeners who want an early harvest without spraying heavily for disease. Fruit is best used fresh or in sauce shortly after picking, as it does not store as long as later-season varieties.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Al-Sirin-Nar is a Turkish pomegranate cultivar prized for large fruit with deep-red, soft-seeded arils and rich, sweet-tart flavor. Self-fertile; no cross-pollination needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Al-Sirin-Nar, a Turkish cultivar whose name translates roughly to 'sweet pomegranate,' bears large fruit filled with deep-red, notably soft-seeded arils and a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that has made it one of the more sought-after fresh-eating pomegranate cultivars among collectors. Trees are vigorous and productive, ripening fruit in the fall for fresh eating, juicing, or preserving. Trees are drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood.

plant_note: Plant grafted or air-layered trees in spring once soil has warmed; in zone 9b–10 plant March–June. Alano is best suited to zones 10–11 but performs in protected zone 9b microclimates where winter lows rarely drop below 28°F. Young trees need frost protection their first two winters; established trees tolerate brief dips into the upper 20s°F with only leaf damage. Fruiting is year-round once mature, with the heaviest flush in late spring through summer.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor, alkaline-tolerant soil — Alano is one of the few high-quality sapodilla cultivars that sets fruit reliably on South Florida's rocky, calcareous soils. The round to oval fruits have smooth, thin skin and fine-grained, low-grit tan flesh with a rich, malty, brown-sugar sweetness that Florida growers rank among the best-flavored sapodilla selections available, distinct from and often preferred over 'Brown Sugar' for its smoother texture. Trees are self-fertile, wind-tolerant, and extremely drought-hardy once established, needing supplemental water mainly during establishment and dry fruit-set periods. Harvest fruit when it develops a dull, scurfy skin and yields slightly to gentle pressure, then ripen off the tree for several days at room temperature before eating.

common_name: Albariño Wine Grape (Crisp Coastal Spanish White)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Albariño's notably thick skin gives it above-average resistance to the fungal disease pressure common in humid coastal growing regions.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Albariño is the signature white grape of Galicia in northwestern Spain, known there as Albariño and just across the border in Portugal as Alvarinho, producing crisp, aromatic wines with bright citrus and stone fruit character and a distinctive faint salinity often attributed to the vineyards' proximity to the Atlantic coast. The grape's notably thick skin gives it real practical resistance to the rot and fungal pressure common in the humid, maritime climate of its home region, a useful trait that also helps it perform well in other humid growing areas where thinner-skinned white varieties struggle. Train to a permanent trellis, prioritize good airflow through the canopy, and harvest to preserve the variety's signature bright acidity, since Albariño loses its refreshing character if left to hang too long.

plant_note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun. Albemarle is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine.
directions: Albemarle is a self-fertile, black-skinned muscadine named for the Albemarle Sound region of northeastern North Carolina, where it has long been prized as a dependable dooryard and small-vineyard selection. Berries are medium-sized with unusually high sugar content and a dry stem scar that lets fruit be pulled cleanly for fresh eating, juice, or preserves without tearing. It ripens early to midseason and holds up reliably through the humid Carolina and Gulf South growing season. Train vines on a two-wire trellis or arbor and prune hard each winter to keep fruiting wood renewed and productive.

common_name: Alexandrian Laurel (Tamanu, Beauty Leaf, Beautyleaf, Kamani)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil; Alexandrian Laurel is extremely salt-tolerant and is one of the best large trees for coastal zone 10-11 landscapes. It is frost-sensitive but very fast-growing — young trees damaged by cold recover rapidly. The round fruits contain 'tamanu oil' (foraha oil), a golden-green, nutty-fragrant oil with significant value in cosmetics and traditional medicine throughout Polynesia and Southeast Asia.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or rocky coastal soils — Alexandrian Laurel is one of the most salt-tolerant large trees available for tropical coastal gardens and is an outstanding choice for beachfront and coastal landscapes in zone 10-11. Calophyllum inophyllum is a large, slow-to-moderately growing evergreen tree native to coastal environments from East Africa through South and Southeast Asia to Australia and the Pacific Islands — one of the few tree species with a genuinely pan-tropical coastal distribution, adapted to sandy, saline soils and salt-laden coastal winds. The tree produces a broad, spreading, dense canopy of large (4–8 inch), glossy, dark-green, oval leaves with distinctive parallel lateral veins that converge at both the midrib and leaf edge — a leaf venation pattern so distinctive that it is diagnostic for the genus Calophyllum. In spring and summer, the tree produces small clusters of intensely fragrant, white, 4-petaled flowers with prominent yellow stamens — the fragrance is sweet, fresh, and carries on the breeze. The round, green fruits (1–1.5 inches) contain a nut that is pressed to yield tamanu oil — a thick, nutty, golden-green fixed oil traditionally used throughout Polynesia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific Islands for wound healing, skin care, and as a muscle pain remedy, and now widely used as a premium ingredient in natural cosmetics. The wood has been used for traditional outrigger canoes and structural timber throughout the Pacific.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in full sun, well-drained soil; because bloom is very early in the season, site trees away from low-lying frost pockets to protect the flowers that set the nut crop.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, since almonds are highly intolerant of wet feet and poorly drained sites lead to root rot. All-in-One is a genetic dwarf almond selected in California for reliable self-fertility, so unlike most almond varieties it does not need a separate pollinizer tree to set a crop, making it a practical choice for smaller home gardens with room for only one tree. The compact, naturally semi-dwarf habit stays smaller than standard almond trees while still producing a full-size, sweet, flavorful kernel. Very early spring bloom is both a strength and a risk: it allows an early start to the growing season but also exposes flowers to occasional late frost damage, so avoid planting in frost pockets. Harvest in late summer to early fall once the outer hulls split open, then dry nuts thoroughly before storing.

plant_note: Plant in early spring; fresh seed should be cold-moist stratified for 60–90 days and planted immediately — viability drops quickly on drying; a single plant is self-fertile, unlike many hybrid chestnuts.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; the Allegheny chinkapin is the smaller native cousin of the American chestnut and is fully resistant to chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) — making it an irreplaceable food plant in regions where the American chestnut was eliminated. It produces small but richly flavored sweet nuts enclosed in a spiny bur, just one nut per bur (unlike 2–3 per bur in true chestnuts); they are superb eaten raw or roasted. Forms a thicket-like shrub to small tree via root-sprouting and is heavily used by deer, turkeys, and squirrels as mast. Best performance is on well-drained, acidic upland soils; heavy or wet soils cause decline.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Allegheny is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars and sets its best crops when planted with Susquehanna, Shenandoah, or another genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to more sun as the tree matures; Allegheny is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars selected by pawpaw breeder Neal Peterson from decades of evaluation work aimed at identifying the largest, best-flavored, and most productive pawpaw seedlings for named release. It produces good-sized fruit with the rich, complex banana-mango-custard flavor pawpaw enthusiasts prize, on a vigorous, dependable tree. As with all pawpaws, Allegheny is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar such as Susquehanna or Shenandoah planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and fruit set — pawpaw flowers are pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, so hand-pollinating with a small brush between two open flowers of different cultivars can meaningfully improve yield in a home planting. In zone 9, site trees where they get afternoon shade in the hottest years and expect best performance toward the cooler end of the zone.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in fall or spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Allegheny plum spreads by root suckers and forms thickets over time, useful for naturalizing on a slope or bank.
directions: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in fall or spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Allegheny plum spreads by root suckers and forms thickets over time, useful for naturalizing on a slope or bank. Clouds of white flowers cover the thicket-forming branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, followed by small, dark purple, tart plums historically gathered by Appalachian settlers for jams and preserves, ripening in late summer on a small, suckering native tree found on dry ridges and rocky slopes of the central Appalachian region. Its suckering, thicket-forming habit makes it useful for stabilizing an eroding bank or naturalizing a difficult dry slope where its dense thicket provides wildlife cover as well as fruit. Water during establishment, then rely on natural rainfall, and allow it to sucker and spread if a naturalized thicket is the goal, or remove suckers to maintain a single specimen.

plant_note: Divide root suckers in early spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; Allegheny serviceberry tolerates wetter and shadier conditions than most fruiting trees and is one of the best choices for a productive edible understory tree under tall oaks and maples.
directions: Divide root suckers or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade; Allegheny serviceberry is a native eastern North American multi-stemmed small tree of exceptional four-season ornamental value — in early spring (March–April), before the leaves emerge, the smooth gray-barked stems become covered with clusters of delicate, drooping, pure-white, star-shaped flowers that are among the first tree flowers of the year; the bronze-red emerging leaves turn green in summer; round, sweet, dark-purple, blueberry-like fruits ripen in June (hence an alternative common name 'Juneberry') and are edible, sweet, and excellent fresh, in pies, jams, and for drying like raisins; and the foliage turns vivid orange-red to burgundy in autumn. As a native understory tree that grows naturally at forest edges and in open woodlands, Allegheny serviceberry is one of the most shade-tolerant fruiting trees available and will produce a useful fruit crop in partial shade conditions where no other small fruit tree would bear productively. The ripe berries are eagerly sought by at least 35 species of birds. Excellent combined with witch hazels and native azaleas in a naturalistic woodland edible garden.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Allred is a dual-purpose plum grown for both its dramatic red-purple foliage and its sweet-tart, red-skinned fruit, and benefits from a second compatible plum nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second compatible plum cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set. Allred is a hybrid plum valued as much for its landscape impact as its harvest, holding rich red-purple foliage color through the growing season that rivals purpleleaf ornamental plums, while still producing sweet-tart, red-skinned, yellow-fleshed fruit good for fresh eating and preserves. Its dual-purpose nature makes it a good choice for a home orchard that also wants ornamental structure in the landscape. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy that improves airflow and fruit quality.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees after last frost risk; in zone 9 plant February–April for full establishment before summer heat. Alma is primarily a second-crop (main crop) variety, producing one large crop in late summer through fall. Site in a warm, south-facing location with well-drained soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Alma is a Texas-bred fig developed by Texas A&M University and released in 1974, bred specifically for the alkaline, calcareous soils and hot, humid summers of Texas. It is the most widely planted fig variety in Texas home gardens because of its exceptional adaptability to Texas soils, heat, and moderate drought tolerance. The fruit is small to medium, golden-tan to amber when ripe, with very sweet, rich, amber-colored flesh and a distinctive honey flavor superior to most brown-skinned varieties. Alma produces a very heavy main crop in August–October in zone 9. Skin is thin and the fruits are best eaten fresh or for preserves; they do not ship well, which is why Alma remains primarily a home and farmers' market variety. The tree produces few to no Breba (first-crop) figs but compensates with tremendous main-crop productivity. Trees are slightly cold-sensitive below 10°F; in zone 8, protect with mulch around the base in winter.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter before bud break; almonds bloom very early and need a frost-free spring.
directions: Almonds bloom earlier than almost any other tree fruit and are severely damaged by late spring frosts, which is why commercial production is limited to Mediterranean-type climates. Most varieties require a cross-pollinator — plant at least two compatible cultivars (Non-Pareil with Carmel or Price, for example). Trees thrive in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soils and are drought-tolerant once established. Harvest when the hulls split open and the shells dry and harden, typically in late summer; spread nuts to dry for two weeks before storing.

common_name: Alstonville Finger Lime (Commercial Australian Caviar Lime Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; Alstonville tolerates brief frosts to about 25°F once established but grows best where winters stay mild, similar to other finger lime selections.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Alstonville is the leading commercial finger lime cultivar in Australia, selected for vigorous upright growth, heavier yields, and consistent production of glossy green, cylindrical fruit filled with pale green caviar-like pulp vesicles. It is self-fertile and bears at a younger age than most finger lime seedlings when grown on grafted rootstock. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the tangy pulp fresh as a garnish since it does not store well once opened.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Amazon grape is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Amazon grape is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the western Amazon basin, this fast-growing relative of cecropia trees bears grape-like clusters of purple, thin-skinned fruit with sweet, translucent, juicy pulp eaten fresh, unusual among tropical fruit trees for reaching bearing age within just a few years of planting rather than a decade or more. Its palmate, cecropia-like leaves and relatively quick growth to fruiting make it an appealing option for a tropical fruit collector wanting faster results than many slower Amazonian species, though it still needs consistent warmth and humidity to thrive. Water regularly, especially during establishment, and expect the first fruit clusters within three to five years under good growing conditions.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 9b–12) in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ambarella (Golden Apple, June Plum) is a fast-growing tropical fruit tree native to the Society Islands of the South Pacific, widely cultivated throughout tropical Asia, the Caribbean, and tropical Americas for its oval, golden-yellow fruits with crisp, tart, pineapple-mango-flavored flesh eaten green as a condiment or ripe as a sweet fruit.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Spondias cytherea is fast-growing and drought tolerant once established — water deeply and infrequently in subtropical conditions; excellent performance in South Florida's calcareous soils and in Gulf Coast sandy soils. Spondias cytherea (Ambarella, Golden Apple, or June Plum) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous tropical tree native to the Society Islands of French Polynesia, spread throughout tropical Polynesia by Polynesian voyagers and later widely planted across tropical Asia, the Caribbean, Central and South America, and tropical West Africa. The oval, 2–3 inch, golden-yellow fruits have crisp, fibrous, firm, juicy, tart-sweet, aromatic flesh with flavors of unripe mango, pineapple, and apple — remarkably refreshing as a fresh fruit when ripe (golden-yellow), and extensively used green (firm, crunchy, very tart) as a condiment, relish, chutney base, and snack with salt, fish sauce, and chili across South and Southeast Asia. In the Caribbean (Jamaica) it is 'June Plum,' in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia 'Ambarella.' Trees are fast-growing — fruiting in 3–4 years from cuttings — and highly productive, dropping fruit that must be gathered regularly. One of the easiest tropical fruit trees to establish in zone 9b–12; an outstanding choice for South Florida, the Gulf Coast, and similar warm subtropical climates where it naturalizes readily.

common_name: Ambarella (June Plum, Golden Apple, Otaheite Apple)
plant_note: Plant air-layered or grafted trees in spring in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; ambarella grows quickly and requires protection from frost — only suited for frost-free zone 10–11 gardens or large containers moved indoors in winter.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; ambarella is a fast-growing tropical fruit tree native to Melanesia and widely cultivated throughout the Pacific islands, Caribbean, and Southeast Asia for its versatile fruit. The oval, golden-yellow to orange fruits are eaten at all stages: the crisp, acidic green fruit is popular in Southeast Asian salads, slaws, and pickles with a tart mango-apple flavor, while fully ripe fruits are sweeter and eaten fresh. The fibrous pit germinates reliably in a few weeks. Ambarella is one of the faster-fruiting tropical trees, often bearing within 2–3 years from air-layers. It drops leaves briefly in dry season. In zone 9a it grows in a large container (25+ gallon) and must be moved indoors or into a greenhouse before the first frost; in zone 10+ it is an outstanding productive landscape tree.

common_name: Ambersweet Orange (Cold-Hardy Early Hybrid Sweet Orange)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Released by the USDA in 1989 after breeding work in Orlando, Florida, Ambersweet is a complex hybrid combining Clementine mandarin, Orlando tangelo, and sweet orange parentage, developed specifically to withstand occasional hard freezes better than standard sweet oranges while still tasting like a true orange. Fruit ripens unusually early for a sweet orange, often ready by October, with a deep orange rind, easy peeling for an orange type, and rich, low-acid sweetness. The tree's improved cold tolerance has made it a useful option for growers along the cooler margins of the citrus-growing Gulf Coast.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun; Ambersweet tolerates more cold than most sweet oranges and ripens very early, from October, extending the citrus season in areas at the cooler edge of the Gulf Coast citrus belt.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ambrosia requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ambrosia requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. Discovered as a chance seedling in a British Columbia orchard in the 1980s, likely a natural cross of Golden Delicious and Jonagold, it produces large, blushed pink-and-gold fruit with exceptionally low acidity, a honeyed sweetness, and fine, crisp, low-tannin flesh that resists browning better than many apples once cut. The tree is precocious and productive, often bearing at a young age, and the fruit's mild, sweet flavor and attractive coloring have made it a fast-growing favorite in both commercial orchards and home gardens since its introduction. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator, and harvest when the background skin color shifts from green to yellow beneath the pink blush.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Dragon fruit is an epiphytic cactus that needs a sturdy support structure — a wooden post 6–8 feet tall is typical for commercial production; in home gardens it can also be grown on a fence or trellis. The plant blooms at night (flowers open around 8 PM and close by dawn), requiring night-time hand pollination to guarantee fruit set — gently transfer pollen with a brush or cotton swab between flowers of the same plant (self-fertile variety) or between plants. In zone 9 protect from any frost — even brief exposure to freezing temperatures can damage the succulent stems. In the warmest zone 9 locations, established plants may survive mild winters with heavy mulching of the root zone.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil — dragon fruit is an epiphytic cactus requiring extremely well-drained soil and excellent air circulation; American Beauty is one of the most popular self-fertile dragon fruit cultivars, producing large (0.5–2 pound), oval fruits with vivid pink-red skin, prominent green-tipped scales, and brilliant magenta-red flesh with small, soft black seeds — one of the most visually stunning and nutritionally distinctive tropical fruits available. The intense magenta-red color of the flesh is caused by betacyanin pigments (similar to those in beets) that transfer vivid color to smoothies, drinks, yogurt, and desserts that incorporate the fruit, creating a dramatically colored culinary presentation that has made dragon fruit one of the most popular colorful ingredients in contemporary food photography and high-end food service. As an epiphytic cactus, dragon fruit requires a different cultural approach from conventional fruit trees — treating it more like a succulent with periodic deep watering rather than regular irrigation, and providing structural support for the long, three-ribbed, succulent stems that climb by aerial roots. Zone 9 gardeners in the warmest, most frost-free locations can grow dragon fruit successfully in the ground; others should use large containers that can be moved to frost-free locations during cold spells.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in early spring in rich, moist, well-drained, acidic soil.
directions: American beech is monoecious and wind-pollinated, but nut production is highly variable and irregular — large mast crops occur every 2–5 years, driven by weather patterns; at least two trees (ideally a grove) dramatically improves mast yield in any given year. The triangular beechnuts are sweet and nutritious, high in fat and protein, and valued by both wildlife and people; they are best eaten raw or lightly roasted and are traditionally used for oil extraction. Beech is extremely sensitive to soil compaction and grade changes around the root zone — construction damage is the primary killer of mature trees in urban settings. Plant in deep, moist, well-drained, acidic soil away from construction zones and plan for very long-term production: significant nut crops typically begin 10+ years after planting.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; American black currant is one of the most shade-tolerant fruiting shrubs available and will produce fruit even in substantial shade — a valuable quality for woodland edible gardens. It requires moist soil conditions and tolerates wet soils better than most fruiting shrubs.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to full shade; American black currant is a native fruiting shrub found in moist woodlands and streambanks from Nova Scotia to Virginia and west to the Rockies, producing clusters of small, round, black-purple currants in July–August that are excellent for jams, jellies, juice, and wine. The fruit flavor is similar to European black currant but milder, without the strong 'cassis' musk of Ribes nigrum, making it more palatable to those who find European black currant too strong. Most importantly, it is one of very few fruiting shrubs that produces in deep shade, making it irreplaceable for woodland edible gardens where blueberries and most other fruit shrubs fail.
