The fragrant, small, white to yellowish tubular flowers in spring are attractive to hummingbirds and native bees. The foliage is attractively lobed and resinous-scented when brushed. American black currant is alternate host for white pine blister rust and should not be planted within 900 feet of white pines in susceptible regions — check with local extension before planting.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts or container-grown seedlings in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy, deep soil in full sun; American chestnut requires two or more trees for cross-pollination to set nuts. Consider blight-resistant hybrid trees from the American Chestnut Foundation for greater long-term survival.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy, deep soil in full sun — the American chestnut was once the dominant tree of the eastern forest, comprising 25% of all trees from New England to the Deep South and providing the primary mast crop sustaining deer, turkeys, bears, and passenger pigeons across millions of acres. The introduction of chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) from Asia in the early 1900s killed an estimated 4 billion trees within 50 years in the most catastrophic ecological disaster in American history. The root system of most trees survives and sends up shoots that grow to 10–20 feet before dying of blight — these sprouts can produce a small crop of nuts. The American Chestnut Foundation has developed blight-tolerant hybrid trees (about 94% American chestnut genetics) and restoration planting is actively underway. Planting American chestnut seedlings or blight-resistant hybrids is a meaningful conservation act; the trees grow fast, produce sweet nuts, and support 125 species of caterpillars.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; American hazelnut tolerates a wide range of soil conditions but produces the most nuts in full sun; it spreads by root suckers and should be allowed to form thickets for best wildlife habitat value.
directions: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; American hazelnut tolerates a wide range of soil conditions but produces the most nuts in full sun; it spreads by root suckers and should be allowed to form thickets for best wildlife habitat value. Corylus americana is a vigorous, multi-stemmed native shrub of eastern North American woodlands and thickets, producing small, round hazelnuts similar in flavor to European hazelnuts (C. avellana) enclosed in distinctive, toothed, leaf-like husks from August through October; the nuts are eagerly consumed by squirrels, blue jays, turkeys, and other wildlife. Long yellow-green male catkins appear very early in spring (February–March), providing one of the first pollen sources for emerging native bees, and the rounded, hairy leaves turn bright orange-yellow in fall. It is native, low-maintenance, and excellent for naturalizing into wildlife hedgerows and edible landscaping.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall to allow natural warm-then-cold stratification over winter; seeds require both phases to break dormancy and will sprout the following spring.
directions: Collect seeds in autumn as soon as the berries ripen and sow immediately in a prepared bed or seed flat at a depth of about 1/4 inch, then allow winter temperatures to provide the necessary stratification sequence. Seeds will germinate in spring once soil warms; transplant seedlings to a permanent site in their second year when they have developed a robust root system. Choose a cool, moist site with well-drained, acidic soil and full sun to partial shade, reflecting this tree's preference for northern forests and high-elevation ridges. Consistent moisture during establishment is critical, as young trees are drought-sensitive; once established, they are exceptionally cold-hardy and low-maintenance.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring; American persimmon has a deep taproot and transplants poorly — use young container-grown trees and minimize root disturbance. Most trees are dioecious (separate male and female plants); plant one male per 8–12 female trees for reliable fruiting.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained to average soil in full sun to partial shade; American persimmon is a tough native tree with striking blocky, alligator-hide bark and excellent fall color that produces small, intensely sweet, apricot-flavored fruits after the first hard frost when they become fully ripe and astringency disappears. The fruits are outstanding for puddings, breads, and fresh eating and are highly attractive to deer, foxes, opossums, and birds. Trees are quite drought-tolerant once established and will grow in poor, rocky, or clay soil where few fruit trees survive. Named female cultivars (Meader, Szukis, Yates, Pieper) with improved fruit size are grafted onto seedling rootstock — grow these for reliable, large-fruited production. Allow fruits to fall naturally after frost and collect from the ground before wildlife does.

plant_note: Plant bare-root stock in early spring before bud break in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; American plum is one of the most adaptable native fruit trees, thriving from the Great Plains to the Atlantic Coast in well-drained to dry soils.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; American plum is drought-tolerant once established and naturalizes readily in hedgerows and woodland edges. Prunus americana (American wild plum) is a native small tree or large shrub found across much of the eastern and central United States, producing clusters of fragrant white flowers in March–April before leaf emergence (a spectacular early-spring display that attracts native bees, especially mining bees and andrenid bees) followed by abundant 3/4-inch, red to orange-yellow plums in July–August. The fruits are quite tart when fully ripe but develop excellent plum flavor when fully ripe and dead-ripe, and are highly prized for jams, jellies, wines, and preserves; they were a staple food of many Native American peoples and European settlers. American plum spreads by root suckers to form thickets valuable for wildlife (providing dense nesting cover for songbirds and food for over 70 bird species), and has been extensively used as rootstock for grafting hybrid plum cultivars. It is among the most cold-hardy, drought-tolerant, and disease-resistant of all plums.

plant_note: Plant bare-root stock in late winter or early spring while dormant; direct sow stratified seed (90 days cold) in fall or early spring. Plant multiple individuals to ensure cross-pollination and maximum fruit set.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; American wild plum is a rugged native shrub or small thicket-forming tree that produces fragrant white flower clusters in early spring before the leaves emerge, then bright red or yellow-orange tart plums 3/4–1 inch in diameter in July through August. The thickets provide excellent wildlife cover and nesting sites. Wild plum suckers heavily and can naturalize into large hedgerows — a valuable feature in permaculture designs. The tart fruits are excellent for jams, jellies, sauces, and fruit leathers; deer, foxes, raccoons, and dozens of bird species rely on them. Tolerates drought, clay, alkaline soils, and extreme cold once established.

common_name: Amethyst Passionflower (Deep Purple Fringed Flower Vigorous Vine)
plant_note: Plant container vines after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Amethyst bears deep, saturated purple flowers with a fine, fringed filament corona on a vigorous, fast-growing vine.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils. Amethyst bears deep, rich purple flowers with a fine, densely fringed filament corona, an intensely colored bloom that has made it a popular hybrid for gardeners seeking a bolder purple than the paler blue-lavender of the straight species. It flowers heavily through summer and draws pollinators readily. In zones at the cooler edge of its range it dies back to the ground in winter and regrows strongly from deep roots in spring; mulch the crown heavily where marginal.

common_name: Amfissa Olive (Greek Dual-Purpose Table and Oil Olive)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun. Amfissa, also known as Conservolia, is grown around the Greek town of Amfissa near Delphi and is one of Greece's most important dual-purpose olive varieties, producing large, round, mild-flavored fruit used both as a popular table olive, typically cured black and glossy, and pressed for good-quality oil when the crop or market calls for it. The tree is reliably productive and well adapted to traditional Greek Mediterranean growing conditions, and the fruit's large size and mild flavor have made it a familiar sight in Greek markets and export products. As with all olives, harvested fruit must be properly cured before eating, since fresh olives straight off the tree are intensely, unpalatably bitter regardless of variety.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; amla needs a long frost-free season and full sun to fruit well. Grafted cultivars fruit years sooner than seedlings and preserve known fruit quality; seedling trees vary widely in fruit size, sourness, and precocity.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; amla is a deciduous small tree native to South and Southeast Asia, grown for its round, pale green, translucent fruits that are extremely high in vitamin C and intensely sour and astringent when fresh. The tree tolerates poor, rocky soils and considerable drought once established, and produces feathery, fine-textured foliage that drops in the dry season. Fruits ripen in fall to early winter and are typically pickled, candied, dried, or processed into juice, chutney, and the Ayurvedic preserve chyawanprash rather than eaten out of hand. Trees are usually grafted onto seedling rootstock for faster, more reliable bearing and are sensitive to hard freezes, restricting outdoor culture to the warmest parts of zones 9-11 or container growing elsewhere.

plant_note: Plant a dormant bare-root or container-grown grafted tree in late fall through winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Amling is a Type I (protandrous) pollinator, so plant it alongside a Type II cultivar such as Elliott or Sumner for reliable cross-pollination and a full nut set.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving it plenty of room to reach its mature size and pairing it with a Type II pollinator cultivar for a good nut set. Amling is a Gulf South pecan cultivar valued for strong resistance to pecan scab, the humid-climate fungal disease that is the single biggest challenge to growing pecans without a heavy fungicide spray program in the Southeast, making it a lower-maintenance choice than older scab-susceptible standards. It bears a good crop of medium-sized, well-filled nuts with good kernel quality on a vigorous, productive tree. Young trees take several years to bear their first nuts and reach full production only after ten years or more; water deeply and regularly during establishment and through nut fill in late summer, since drought stress during fill reduces kernel quality. Provide deep, infrequent irrigation rather than frequent shallow watering to encourage a deep root system.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds in spring or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; anacua is a Texas native of the Rio Grande Plains and Gulf Coast that is semi-evergreen and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and coastal conditions well.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; anacua is a native south Texas and Mexico tree of the Rio Grande Plains and Gulf Coast, valued for its multi-season ornamental interest: fragrant white flowers in spring, followed by clusters of small orange-yellow fruits (edible, slightly sweet) in late spring and early summer that attract numerous birds. The rough, sandpaper-textured leaves give the tree its secondary common name. The fruit is eaten by numerous bird species, particularly golden-fronted woodpeckers, white-tipped doves, and mockingbirds. Semi-evergreen in mild winters in zone 9a; may lose some leaves in hard freezes but re-leafs readily from the base or branch tips. An excellent, underused native tree for south and central Texas gardens providing year-round interest, wildlife value, and adapting well to the alkaline soils of the Edwards Plateau and lower Rio Grande valley.

plant_note: Plant on a sturdy trellis in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun, siting a male Actinidia arguta vine nearby since Ananasnaja is a female cultivar and will not set fruit alone.
directions: Ananasnaja (sometimes sold as Ananasnaya) is a heavy-bearing Russian-bred hardy kiwiberry selection valued for grape-sized, smooth-skinned fruit with a distinctive pineapple-tinged sweetness. Vines are extremely vigorous twining climbers that require a strong permanent trellis or arbor and yearly winter pruning to control growth and encourage fruiting wood renewal. As a female clone it must be planted within about 30 to 50 feet of a compatible male arguta vine for pollination and fruit set. Fruit ripens in early to mid fall and is typically harvested by taste-testing a few berries, since the smooth green skin gives little visual ripeness cue.

common_name: Angel Red Pomegranate (Soft-Seeded Sweet Red Fresh-Eating Pomegranate)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in late winter to spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral to slightly alkaline (pH 5.5–7.5) soil in full sun; Angel Red's soft seeds make fresh eating far more practical than hard-seeded varieties — the entire aril including the seed can be eaten without the tough, crunchy seed of standard pomegranates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Angel Red is a soft-seeded pomegranate variety — one of the most important distinctions in pomegranate selection for fresh eating. Standard pomegranate varieties (including Wonderful) contain hard, woody seeds at the center of each aril that some people find unpleasant to eat; soft-seeded varieties like Angel Red have soft, barely-noticeable seeds that allow the entire aril to be eaten without extraction, fundamentally changing the fresh-eating experience. Angel Red produces large, bright-red fruits with deep-red, juicy arils and rich pomegranate flavor — somewhat sweeter and less astringent than Wonderful at peak ripeness. The soft-seeded quality makes Angel Red excellent for fresh eating out of hand (where hard seeds are an obstacle), salads (where whole arils are used as a garnish), and for fresh juice where the softer seeds blend or press more easily. Like all pomegranates, Angel Red is self-fruitful, drought-tolerant, heat-adapted, and ornamentally attractive with showy orange-red flowers in summer and richly colored fall fruit. In zone 9, Angel Red ripens in October–November at essentially the same time as Wonderful — the harvest timing is similar but the eating experience is distinctly more accessible for fresh consumption.

common_name: Angelique Fig (Early Yellow French Heirloom Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Angelique is a centuries-old French heirloom valued for ripening earlier than most fig cultivars, giving Gulf Coast growers a crop before peak-summer humidity promotes splitting in later varieties.
directions: Angelique is a centuries-old French heirloom fig, historically grown around Paris and known there as Angelique or Melette, that Thomas Jefferson brought to Monticello after seeing it cultivated abroad. It bears medium to large fruit with pale greenish-yellow, subtly striped skin and sweet, cream-colored flesh, ripening notably early in the season and extending the fig harvest before later-season cultivars come in. As a common-type fig it is self-fertile and produces without pollination, and its long history of wide cultivation across France attests to its adaptability across a range of soils and climates. In the Gulf South, Angelique's early ripening window helps growers bring in a crop ahead of the peak summer humidity that promotes fruit souring and splitting in later-maturing varieties.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter (December–February in zone 9) or container trees spring through fall; Anna requires only 200–400 chill hours and is the most widely recommended apple for zone 9. Plant with Dorsett Golden or Ein Shemer for cross-pollination — Anna is not fully self-fertile.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5) in full sun; Anna is a low-chill apple cultivar developed in Israel and introduced to the United States in the 1960s, requiring only 200–400 chill hours (hours below 45°F). This low chill requirement makes it the most successful apple in Florida, south Texas, and the Gulf Coast South where winter temperatures rarely accumulate the 800+ hours needed by most apple varieties. The medium-large fruits are greenish-yellow with a red blush, similar in appearance to Golden Delicious, with crisp, juicy flesh and a pleasant sweet-tart flavor. Anna is an early-season apple ripening in May–June in zone 9 — remarkably early, making fresh Gulf Coast apples available in late spring when no other apple is in season. Cross-pollination with Dorsett Golden or Ein Shemer significantly improves yields; plant them within 50 feet. For the finest flavor, allow fruit to ripen fully on the tree until it lifts easily from the branch. Anna is susceptible to apple scab and fire blight — maintain good air circulation and remove infected wood promptly.

plant_note: Plant male and female vines in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade on a strong trellis; Anna is a productive female cultivar that needs a male Actinidia arguta pollinator planted nearby for fruit set.
directions: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator (one male per 6-8 females) on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Anna is a widely grown, reliably productive hardy kiwiberry cultivar valued for good vigor and heavy fruit set once a compatible male is nearby. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet, bright green flesh and classic kiwi flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. As with all kiwiberry vines, plants take a few years to reach full bearing size but then produce heavily and reliably for decades. Prune hard each winter on a permanent framework of cordons to control the very vigorous twining growth and keep the fruiting wood renewed and productive, and install a sturdy trellis or pergola from the start, since mature vines and their fruit load become quite heavy.

plant_note: Plant bare-root seedlings in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Antonovka is grown chiefly as an extremely cold-hardy rootstock or grafting understock rather than for its own fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root seedlings in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Antonovka is grown chiefly as an extremely cold-hardy rootstock or grafting understock rather than for its own fruit. A historic Russian apple selection prized above nearly all other apple rootstocks for exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating winter temperatures that kill or severely damage most other apple rootstocks, making it the standard understock for grafting desired apple varieties in the coldest northern growing regions of North America. Trees grown from Antonovka seed produce full-sized, vigorous trees rather than the dwarfing habit of modern clonal rootstocks, and the fruit itself, while edible, is tart and primarily used for cooking and processing rather than fresh eating. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young Antonovka seedlings in late winter or early spring for a cold-hardy, long-lived, full-sized tree well suited to harsh northern climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Apollo is partially self-fertile and can produce some fruit without a cross-pollinator, but planting with Nazemetz, Coolidge, or Mammoth significantly increases crop size. Apollo has good cold tolerance to approximately 15–18°F when established, making it reliable in zone 8 and zone 9. Harvest fruits as they fall naturally from the plant in October–December.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Apollo is a New Zealand-selected feijoa (pineapple guava) cultivar prized for producing very large, oval fruits with exceptionally smooth skin and outstanding flavor — rated by New Zealand feijoa growers as one of the best-flavored cultivars, with a rich, complex tropical aroma combining pineapple, guava, strawberry, and mint notes. The thick-skinned, moderately large fruits (3–6 ounces) have a balance of sweetness and acidity that appeals to a wide range of palates. Apollo is among the earlier-ripening feijoa varieties, beginning to drop fruit in October in zone 9 — ahead of the main feijoa season — and providing a longer total harvest window when planted alongside mid-to-late ripening varieties. Like all feijoa, Apollo's spring flowers with white petals and edible bright red stamens are ornamental and can be eaten fresh as a sweet-tart floral treat. The silvery-green evergreen foliage and attractive compact shrub form make Apollo an excellent edible landscape plant for year-round interest.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring while still dormant, before buds break.
directions: Plant bare-root stock in well-drained soil, spreading roots carefully; stake dwarf trees for the first two seasons. Most varieties require a second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination — check chill-hour requirements to match your climate (600–1200 hours for standard types, under 400 for low-chill selections). Prune annually in late dormancy to an open-center or central-leader form to improve light penetration and air flow. Harvest when fruit separates with a gentle upward twist and seeds have turned brown, 2–5 years after planting.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in spring or fall; apple serviceberry is extremely adaptable to a wide range of soils and moisture levels and is one of the most reliable multi-season small trees for temperate gardens. 'Autumn Brilliance' is the most popular cultivar for its consistent orange-red fall color and larger, sweeter fruit.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; apple serviceberry is the most widely planted Amelanchier hybrid — a cross between A. arborea and A. laevis producing larger flowers and larger, juicier berries than either parent. In early to mid-spring, before or just as the leaves emerge, it produces a spectacular display of pure-white flowers in drooping clusters that are among the first flowers of the season for early native bees, mining bees, and other spring pollinators that emerge before many plants are flowering. The blueberry-like fruits that ripen in June are sweet, purple-black, and edible fresh, in pies, jams, and wine — they are exceptionally rich in antioxidants and have a pleasant flavor combining blueberry and mild almond notes. The fruits are intensely attractive to birds. In fall, the foliage turns brilliant shades of orange, red, and occasionally yellow, providing a final season of interest. Multi-season value: spring flowers, summer edible fruit, fall color, ornamental winter silhouette. Tolerates part shade and is among the most wildlife-valuable small trees available.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter, as early as the soil can be worked, to allow root establishment before bloom.
directions: Most apricot varieties are self-fertile, which simplifies home-orchard planting, but two trees will increase yields. The key limiting factor in temperate climates is the tree's early bloom time — a hard frost after bud break will eliminate the crop, so choose a sheltered north-facing or slightly elevated site to delay bloom, or select late-blooming cultivars. Prune in early summer rather than winter to reduce risk of cytospora canker infection. Harvest when the fruit is fully orange, fragrant, and gives slightly to the touch.

plant_note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring.
directions: An aprium is an apricot-dominant hybrid with the sweetness of apricot and a hint of plum, often bearing a faint fuzz. Plant in full sun on light, well-drained soil in a frost-protected spot, since apricot-type blooms open very early. Many apriums are self-fruitful but crop more heavily with an apricot pollinator nearby. Prune in dry summer weather to limit disease and thin the fruit for good size.

common_name: Arbequina Olive (World's Most Popular Home Garden Olive, Compact Spanish Oil Olive)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Arbequina is self-fertile and produces a good crop without a companion tree; it requires approximately 300–400 chill hours — one of the lowest requirements of any olive variety, making it well-suited to mild coastal California and Gulf South gardens; Arbequina is the most compact named olive variety, growing 10–15 feet compared to the 20–30 feet of Mission and Frantoio, making it practical for home landscapes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Arbequina is extremely drought-tolerant once established and actually produces better oil quality under moderate stress — do not over-fertilize or over-water; harvest olives in November–December when shifting from green to purple-black for oil; for table olives, harvest green in October–November and cure in brine for 6–12 months. Arbequina olive is the most widely planted olive variety in the world and by a large margin the most popular olive for home garden use globally — a small Spanish variety from the town of Arbeca in Catalonia that was historically confined to a small region of northeastern Spain before becoming a worldwide standard through its adoption in super-high-density olive plantations in California, Australia, Chile, and Argentina. The variety's global success derives from a combination of characteristics ideally suited to modern olive production: extremely compact habit (10–15 feet versus the 25–30 feet of traditional olive varieties), heavy and precocious bearing (producing significant crops in year 3–4 rather than the 7–10 years of traditional varieties on standard spacing), self-fertility (producing good crops as a single tree), low chill requirement (300–400 hours, allowing successful growing in zones 7–10), and excellent high-quality oil — mild, fruity, golden-colored oil with low acidity that is considered among the finest olive oils. For home gardeners, Arbequina's compact size makes it suitable for large containers, small gardens, and courtyard plantings where standard olive trees would be too large. The small, round olives (1–2g each) can also be table-cured in brine though the size is small by table olive standards.

common_name: Arbosana Olive (Compact Cold-Hardy High-Density Oil Olive)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Arbosana is largely self-fertile though yields improve with a compatible pollinizer such as Arbequina nearby, and it tolerates somewhat colder winters than many other olive cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; avoid over-fertilizing or over-watering, since moderate stress improves oil quality. Arbosana is another small Spanish olive variety, alongside Arbequina, widely adopted in modern super-high-density olive orchards for its compact habit, precocious and heavy bearing, and good cold hardiness relative to larger traditional olive cultivars. The small fruit yields a well-regarded, balanced, mildly fruity oil, and the tree's naturally smaller size makes it practical for large containers and compact home landscapes, similar in scale to Arbequina but noted for handling occasional colder winter dips slightly better. Harvest olives as they shift from green to purple-black for oil production in late fall to early winter, or pick green and cure in brine for table olives. Established trees are drought-tolerant and need minimal fertilization.

plant_note: Plant male and female vines in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; Arctic beauty kiwi is the hardiest of all kiwi species, surviving to -40°F (zone 3), and produces smooth-skinned, grape-sized kiwi fruits — the male plants are also ornamental, developing spectacular pink, white, and green variegated foliage.
directions: Plant male and female vines (one male per 6-8 females) on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; prune heavily each winter to manage size. Actinidia kolomikta (Arctic beauty kiwi or kolomikta kiwi) is an East Asian kiwi vine native to the cold, humid forests of Siberia, northern China, Korea, and Japan — the hardiest of all Actinidia species, surviving temperatures to -40°F (USDA zone 3) with no winter protection. It produces abundant, smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruits (no need to peel) with green flesh, a flavor similar to full-sized kiwi fruit, and a slightly sweeter, more complex character — excellent fresh or in fruit salads, smoothies, and preserves. The vine is dioecious — plant at least one male per 6-8 female vines for pollination and fruit set. What makes Arctic beauty kiwi especially garden-worthy is the extraordinary variegated foliage of the male plants: in late spring and early summer, the new leaves emerge with spectacular patches and splashes of bright pink, cream-white, and green — rivaling any ornamental vine in beauty. Female vines are solid green but highly productive. A superb ornamental-edible vine for cold-climate gardens where fuzzy kiwi (A. deliciosa) cannot survive.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Arctic Frost was bred for exceptional cold hardiness among satsuma mandarins, allowing gardeners in the cooler parts of zone 8 to grow sweet, seedless, easy-peel citrus that would otherwise require zone 9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, siting in the warmest available microclimate for the first few winters. Arctic Frost is a satsuma mandarin selection bred for improved cold hardiness beyond standard satsuma cultivars, allowing mature trees to tolerate brief drops into the low 20s or upper teens Fahrenheit with only minor wood damage, when standard citrus of similar fruit quality would be killed to the ground. Fruit is sweet, low-acid, essentially seedless, and easy to peel, with the loose, glossy rind typical of satsumas, ripening in fall to early winter. Young trees need cold protection for the first two to three winters until established, but mature wood is notably tougher than most edible citrus. Like other satsumas, it is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, and it tends to bear well even as a young tree. Protect the trunk and graft union with mulch or wrap in the coldest years, and avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization in late summer, which can push tender new growth that is more vulnerable to an early freeze.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or young container specimens in spring; Arizona walnut has a deep taproot and should be planted small; it is resistant to juglone toxicity concerns of eastern black walnut, producing juglone but in smaller quantities than Juglans nigra.
directions: Plant young trees in full sun in deep, well-drained, rocky to sandy soil in spring; Arizona walnut (Juglans major) is a native walnut of the Desert Southwest, growing along canyon bottoms and mountain slopes in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and northern Mexico. The small, round, thick-shelled nuts are labor-intensive to crack but have excellent, rich flavor comparable to eastern black walnut — and have been a valued food of indigenous peoples of the Southwest (Apache, Navajo, Pueblo peoples) for centuries. More heat and drought tolerant than eastern walnuts, the tree is the dominant native walnut of the semi-arid West and an outstanding choice for dry-climate food-forest systems. It is also an important wildlife tree and rootstock for grafting cultivated walnuts in desert climates.

common_name: Arkansas Black Apple (Ozark Heirloom Dark-Skinned Keeper Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Arkansas Black has a fairly high chill requirement (800+ hours) and needs a pollinator such as Winesap or Stayman.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator variety. This late-1800s Ozark heirloom is famous for skin that darkens from deep red to nearly black in full sun, and for fruit that is rock-hard and tart at harvest but mellows into a dense, sweet, aromatic apple after two to three months in storage. Because of this, growers pick it in October and cellar it rather than eating it fresh off the tree. The thick skin and firm flesh make it an outstanding long-keeping cider and baking apple that was once a major shipping variety before modern refrigeration existed.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Carambola trees are frost-sensitive — young trees are damaged below 30°F and established trees can be killed at 25°F. In zone 9a, plant in the most frost-protected microclimate available (south-facing walls, under taller trees, or in containers that can be moved indoors). Zone 9b provides better conditions; zone 10 is ideal. Arkin fruits primarily in August–November and again in March–June, providing two annual harvest periods.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Arkin is the leading commercial carambola cultivar in Florida, selected by the University of Florida for its combination of large fruit size, sweet flavor, and attractive appearance — the five-lobed, waxy, golden-yellow fruits are the classic star-fruit appearance when sliced crosswise, producing the familiar star-shaped cross-sections used to garnish drinks, fruit platters, and Asian dishes. Unlike the sour Malaysian varieties (planted for processing), Arkin is a sweet variety with a balanced sweet-tart flavor suitable for fresh eating, juicing, and garnishing. The self-fertile tree is moderately productive even as a single plant, producing 200–400 pounds annually in good conditions. Carambola is high in vitamin C and very low in sugar compared to most tropical fruits, making it popular in health-conscious cuisines. In zone 9 the tree requires careful siting to avoid frost damage — plant against south-facing structures for maximum cold protection.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; needs roughly 500-600 chill hours, so it performs best in the cooler-winter parts of zone 8-9 Gulf South rather than immediate mild-winter coastline.
directions: A California-bred medium-chill nectarine long grown across the Deep South for its large, semi-freestone fruit with olive-green skin blushed deep red and richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening in early-to-mid June. It sets fruit heavily and shows good tolerance to bacterial spot, but nectarines as a group are more prone to brown rot than peaches in humid Gulf climates, so maintain a preventive fungicide program through ripening. Choose an inland or upland Gulf South planting site over the immediate coast to ensure it receives adequate winter chilling for consistent bloom and fruit set.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, raised or mounded soil in full sun with cold-air drainage; Armstrong satsuma is among the more cold-hardy satsuma selections and is a Gulf South dooryard favorite from Louisiana to coastal Texas.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, raised or mounded soil in full sun with cold-air drainage; Armstrong satsuma is among the more cold-hardy satsuma selections and is a Gulf South dooryard favorite from Louisiana to coastal Texas. A bud-sport selection of Owari satsuma found in the Gulf South, it produces the same sweet, easy-peeling, nearly seedless fruit but ripens two to three weeks earlier, letting growers harvest ahead of the season's first hard freeze in marginal citrus climates. The compact, glossy-leaved, thornless tree is heavily productive and, like other satsumas, hardier to cold than most other mandarins, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s Fahrenheit once mature. Mulch the root zone and wrap or cover young trees during hard freezes, and pick fruit as soon as it colors since satsumas hold poorly on the tree once ripe.

common_name: Aromatnaya Quince (Russian Quince Edible Fresh Without Cooking)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and begins bearing within a few years of planting, producing hard, aromatic fruit that is typically cooked rather than eaten raw.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Aromatnaya is a Russian quince cultivar notable among quince types for fruit that is mild and pleasant enough to eat fresh, unlike most quince varieties that require cooking to be palatable due to their hard, astringent flesh. The pineapple-yellow fruit is intensely fragrant and still excellent for cooking into preserves and quince paste, but its unusually mild, less astringent flavor when fully ripe has made it popular with gardeners who want a more versatile quince. The tree is self-fertile, cold-hardy, and otherwise managed like other quince cultivars, benefiting from good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk.

common_name: Ascolano Olive (Large Mild Table and Oil Olive)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Ascolano bears more reliably with a second olive cultivar such as Manzanillo or Mission nearby for cross-pollination, and has thinner skin than most table olives, so handle fruit gently at harvest.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Ascolano is an Italian-origin olive cultivar long grown in California for its large, thin-skinned, mild-flavored fruit — one of the highest-quality table olives available, with less bitterness before curing than most cultivars and flesh that separates easily from the pit. Its thin skin bruises more readily than firmer-skinned table olives such as Manzanillo or Sevillano, so fruit is best hand-harvested carefully rather than shaken or mechanically picked. Ascolano can be cured green or ripe black and also produces good-quality oil, though its lower oil content and thinner skin make it less common in commercial oil orchards. Trees are moderately vigorous and only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second, compatible olive cultivar nearby improves fruit set and overall yield. As with other olives, established Ascolano trees are notably drought-tolerant and adapt well to the alkaline, low-fertility soils common across much of the Gulf Coast and Texas.

common_name: Ashmead's Kernel Apple (English Heirloom Sharp-Flavored Russet Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Ashmead's Kernel is a light, biennial-prone bearer, so thin fruit in heavy years to encourage more even annual cropping.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Raised from seed around 1700 by Dr. William Ashmead of Gloucester, England, this is one of the oldest russet apples still grown and is treasured by cider makers and flavor enthusiasts for its intense, sharp, pear-drop sweetness balanced against high acidity. The medium, dull green-gold fruit is entirely covered in rough russet skin and looks unassuming, but the dense, dry, richly flavored flesh has made it a favorite of English apple connoisseurs for centuries. It ripens in mid-fall and its flavor improves somewhat with a few weeks of storage.

plant_note: Direct sow nuts in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification, or cold-moist stratify for 90-120 days and sow in early spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, allowing the shrub to form its natural dense, multi-stemmed thicket. Asian hazel is native to Siberia, Korea, northern China, and Japan and is exceptionally cold hardy compared with the European hazelnut, tolerating harsh continental winters that would damage most commercial filbert cultivars. It produces small nuts in short, bristly husks and is widely used by breeders working to develop cold-hardy, blight-resistant hazelnut cultivars for the northern United States and Canada by crossing it with European hazelnut.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring; in mild-winter zones plant in fall.
directions: Asian pears ripen on the tree — unlike European pears they do not need post-harvest ripening — so taste-test for sweetness before picking. Most varieties are self-unfruitful and yield best with a second Asian pear or even a compatible European variety nearby. Chill requirements are moderate (450–700 hours), making many selections suitable for zones 5–9. Annual thinning of fruit clusters to one per spur prevents limb breakage and encourages larger, better-flavored fruit.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger has passed; fall planting is fine in zones 8–10.
directions: Asian persimmons come in astringent types (such as Hachiya, best eaten when jelly-soft) and non-astringent types (such as Fuyu, eaten firm like an apple). Most cultivars are self-fertile and produce well as single trees. Trees need very little pruning — maintain a central leader and remove inward-growing branches to open the canopy. In cooler parts of zone 7, choose hardier varieties and site against a south-facing wall; in zones 9–10, low-chill cultivars perform best.

plant_note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; atemoya requires hand pollination for reliable fruit set as natural pollinators (nitidulid beetles native to South America) are absent in most US gardens. Hardy to about 28°F when established.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 9–11; atemoya is a hybrid between the cherimoya (Annona cherimola) and the sugar apple (Annona squamosa), combining the better qualities of both parents — the large size and richly flavored flesh of cherimoya with the tropical heat tolerance of sugar apple. Atemoya is widely considered one of the finest-flavored fruits in the world, with a rich, creamy white flesh tasting of vanilla custard with notes of pineapple and coconut. It requires hand pollination in most US gardens — transfer pollen from flowers in the male stage to flowers in the female stage in the morning using a small brush. Plant grafted trees for faster fruiting (typically 2–3 years) rather than seedlings. Popular cultivars include 'Gefner' (nearly self-fruitful) and 'African Pride'. An outstanding subtropical fruit for South Florida and Gulf Coast gardens where winter temperatures stay above 28°F.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seeds for 4 to 6 weeks before sowing, then plant in deep containers to avoid disturbing the taproot at transplanting time.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds in damp sand in the refrigerator for four to six weeks before sowing in spring into deep pots to encourage taproot development before transplanting. Move seedlings to their permanent site while still young and small, choosing a spot in full sun with rocky, sandy, or otherwise fast-draining soil. Once established this tree is exceptionally drought-tolerant and long-lived, requiring no supplemental irrigation in Mediterranean or dry climates. Plant at least one male and one female tree to ensure fruit production, as this species is dioecious.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; expect a light breba crop in early summer followed by the main crop in late summer.
directions: Atreano is a Portuguese fig notable for its pale yellow-green skin that stays light even when the fruit is fully ripe, which makes judging harvest timing by color alone unreliable; instead check for softening and a slight neck droop. The amber flesh is mild, honeyed, and low in seediness, making it a favorite for fresh eating among growers who find darker figs too intensely flavored. It is a vigorous, heavy-bearing tree well suited to warm Mediterranean-type and humid subtropical climates alike. Give it full sun, good drainage, and room to spread, since it can become a large, dense specimen if left unpruned.

common_name: Au Amber Plum (Auburn University Amber-Skinned Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Au Amber requires a cross-pollinator for good fruit set — plant with Au Rosa, Methley, or another Japanese or Japanese-American plum within 50 feet. Requires approximately 400–500 chilling hours, placing it reliably in the productive range for most zone 8 and the cooler parts of zone 9 in north Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. In the warmest zone 9b locations, chill accumulation may be marginal in mild winters; zone 8 locations typically produce reliably. Ripens June in zone 9. Plant in full sun in very well-drained soil — like all Prunus species, Au Amber is highly susceptible to root rot in poorly drained conditions. The Auburn University Au-series plums were bred specifically for the disease pressure, humidity, and modest chill of the Gulf South, giving them practical advantages over Japanese plums bred for Pacific Coast or California conditions.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; requires cross-pollinator within 50 feet. Thin fruit clusters to 3–4 inches. Harvest when amber-yellow skin has fully developed and flesh gives slightly. Au Amber Plum is one of the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station's series of Japanese-American plum hybrids bearing the 'Au' prefix — a family of Gulf South-adapted plum varieties developed by crossing Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) with American plum (Prunus americana) to combine quality fruit with regional disease and humidity tolerance. The 'Amber' designation refers to the fruit's distinctive amber-yellow to golden skin, which sets it apart from the red and rose-colored Au-series varieties (Au Rosa, Au Rubrum) within the same breeding program and from the predominantly red-skinned Japanese plum varieties available in American nurseries. The amber-yellow coloring of the ripe fruit is unusual among commonly available plums — most market plums are red, purple, or dark-skinned — making Au Amber visually distinctive both in the garden and at market or farmers markets where consumers are accustomed to seeing darker plum colors. The flesh is yellow-amber, juicy, and sweet with mild plum flavor appropriate for fresh eating, jams, and jellies. The relatively high chilling requirement within the Au-series makes Au Amber better suited to zone 8 and the cooler parts of zone 9 than the lower-chill Au Rosa, providing a range of options across the Gulf South's varied climate zones. Auburn University developed the Au series specifically based on performance trials in Alabama, and the varieties' continued presence in extension service recommendations decades after their introduction reflects their practical suitability to the region.

common_name: Au Producer Plum (Auburn University High-Yielding Japanese-American Hybrid Plum for the Upper Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Au Producer requires a cross-pollinator, such as another Auburn 'Au' series plum or Methley, within about 50 feet. Its chill requirement of roughly 650-700 hours is higher than most Gulf series plums, making it best suited to zone 8 and the cooler parts of zone 9 rather than the warmest coastal microclimates.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun in well-drained soil, since Prunus species decline quickly with wet feet. Au Producer was released by the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station in 1977 as a high-yielding early-season plum, part of the Auburn 'Au' series of Japanese-American hybrids bred to combine the disease tolerance of native American plum with the fruit quality of Japanese plum for the humid Southeast. The clingstone fruit has purple skin and sweet, juicy red flesh good for fresh eating and canning, and the tree carries strong resistance to bacterial spot, bacterial leaf spot, and bacterial canker, diseases that trouble many plum varieties in Gulf South humidity. Because its moderate chill requirement is higher than the ultra-low-chill 'Gulf' series plums, Au Producer performs most reliably in zone 8 gardens and should be evaluated cautiously in the warmest parts of zone 9.

common_name: Au Rosa Plum (Auburn University Low-Chill Japanese-American Plum for Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Au Rosa requires a cross-pollinator for best fruit set — plant with another Japanese or Japanese-American plum variety (Methley, Bruce, or another Auburn University release such as Au Producer or Au Amber) within 50 feet. Requires approximately 350–450 chilling hours — more reliable than very low-chill varieties in years with limited winter cold, and still appropriate for zone 9 in most years. Ripens May–June in zone 9. Plant in full sun with very well-drained soil; all Prunus species are extremely sensitive to root rot in waterlogged conditions. The Auburn University (Auburn, Alabama) releases were specifically developed for the Gulf South's humidity, disease pressure, and modest winter chill, making them among the most zone-specific plum options for the region.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit clusters when marble-sized. Harvest when skin shows full rose color and fruit gives slightly. Au Rosa Plum is one of the Auburn University Agricultural Experiment Station's series of Japanese-American plum hybrids developed specifically for the Gulf South — an ongoing breeding program at Auburn that produced a family of plum varieties (the 'Au' prefix indicating Auburn University origin) adapted to the unique challenges of plum production in the humid southeastern coastal plain. The Au series hybrids combine genetics from Japanese plum (Prunus salicina, a high-quality fruiting species requiring adequate cross-pollination and moderate chill) with American plum (Prunus americana, a native North American species with significant humidity and disease tolerance) to produce varieties that retain good fruit quality while performing more reliably in the humid, relatively mild-winter conditions of the Gulf South than either parent species performs alone. Au Rosa produces medium-sized fruits with rose-pink to dark red skin and yellow flesh — the distinctive pinkish-red blush of the 'rosa' name. The flesh has good sweetness and plum flavor, appropriate for fresh eating, jams, and jellies. Au Rosa was one of the earlier Auburn releases and established the pattern of named, region-specific plum varieties that Gulf South extension services could recommend with confidence based on local trial performance rather than relying on variety data from California or Pacific Northwest conditions that may not translate to Gulf Coast performance.

plant_note: Plant grafted or own-root stock in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; this thorny shrubby citrus handles both Gulf Coast heat and brief hard freezes far better than typical lime cultivars.
directions: Native to the semi-arid interior of Australia, this small-fruited citrus relative is among the most cold-hardy true citrus species available, tolerating brief dips into the high teens Fahrenheit once established, which makes it a worthwhile dooryard planting for zone 9a gardeners where standard limes struggle. The pea-to-marble-sized round fruits have a tart, intensely aromatic lime flavor and are used in marmalades, cordials, and as a lime substitute; the species is also valued by citrus breeders as rootstock and hybrid parent material for cold tolerance. Give it excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water once established, since it is adapted to low-rainfall conditions and resents wet feet more than most citrus.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted or potted tree; move outdoors after frost.
directions: The Australian finger lime bears elongated fruit packed with juicy, caviar-like vesicles that burst with tart citrus flavor, making it a chef's favorite. Native to rugged coastal Australia, this compact, thorny citrus is tough and adapts well to container culture. Grow from a potted tree in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and protect it from frost by moving it indoors in cold climates. Feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season and water steadily without letting roots sit wet.

common_name: Autumn Beauty Jujube (Qiyuexian, Early-Ripening Crisp Fresh-Eating Jujube)
plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established. Autumn Beauty, also sold as Qiyuexian, needs only about 400 chill hours and stays compact at 8 to 10 feet tall, with attractive zigzag branching and glossy foliage that turns yellow in fall. The apple-crisp, subtly spicy fruit is prized for fresh eating when harvested at the crunchy green-to-tan stage, ripening earlier than many other Chinese jujube selections. Its low chill requirement and tolerance for hot, humid summers make it a good complement to Gulf Coast-adapted jujube selections like Li and Sherwood.

plant_note: Plant in spring when all frost risk is past and soil is warm; avoid planting in summer heat.
directions: Avocados bear Type A flowers (open as female in the morning) and Type B flowers (open as female in the afternoon); planting one of each type near each other ensures pollen is available throughout the day and greatly increases fruit set. Grafted trees begin fruiting in 3–5 years; seedlings may take 8–10 years. Avocados are sensitive to root rot in heavy or poorly drained soils — plant on a mound or raised bed and irrigate deeply but infrequently. Fruit does not ripen on the tree; pick when full-sized and let ripen at room temperature for 3–8 days.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter; Ayers requires 600 chill hours and is better suited to zone 7–8b than coastal zone 9. In inland zone 9a areas with colder winters, it performs well. Plant with Kieffer or Orient for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Ayers is a mid-to-late season pear developed at the Tennessee Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1939. It is valued in the mid-South and upper Gulf Coast (zone 7–8b) for producing excellent-quality, Bartlett-like pears with moderate fire blight resistance in climates where Bartlett itself succumbs to disease. The medium-large, yellow, bell-shaped fruits have sweet, juicy, white flesh with a smooth texture and excellent Bartlett-like aroma and flavor — considerably better quality than Kieffer for fresh eating. Ayers is widely considered the best-flavored Southern pear for zones 7–8b and is recommended by extension services across Tennessee, Alabama, and Georgia for home orchards. Harvest when green-yellow color appears and the fruit begins to soften at the neck; ripen at room temperature for 3–5 days for best flavor. Fire blight susceptibility requires vigilant pruning and copper spray during bloom in wet springs. Not recommended for zone 9a where insufficient chill accumulation is likely.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees or bare-root saplings in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; azarole is a Mediterranean hawthorn with unusually large, sweet, edible fruits used fresh and in preserves throughout southern Europe and the Middle East.
directions: Plant grafted trees or container-grown saplings in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; azarole is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the dry, hot summers of the Mediterranean basin and similar climates in the American South and West. Crataegus azarolus is a large shrub or small tree native to southern Europe and western Asia cultivated for millennia for its edible fruits — unusually large for a hawthorn (up to 3/4 inch across), round to oblong, and ripening yellow, orange, or red depending on selection, with sweet to slightly tart, apple-like flesh used fresh, in jams, jellies, liqueurs, and preserves throughout Italy, Spain, and the Middle East. The profuse white spring flowers and ornamental fruits make it as attractive as it is useful; it is well adapted to alkaline, dry, rocky soils. The Arabic name for this species, "za'rour" or "azaroul," is the origin of the English name.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted plants in spring after frost danger passes; in zone 9 plant March–May. B-17 acerola is a fast-fruiting shrub that can flower and set fruit within its first year under warm conditions. Established plants tolerate light frost and resprout from the base after a hard freeze, but repeated hard freezes will prevent fruiting. Plants flower and fruit in flushes throughout the warm season, roughly every six to eight weeks.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; B-17 is a selected acerola cultivar developed in Puerto Rico for larger fruit size and heavier yields than seedling acerola, while retaining the species' famously high vitamin C content, among the highest of any fruit. The small, bright-red, cherry-like fruits are thin-skinned, juicy, and tart, best used fresh in juice, syrups, and preserves rather than fresh eating alone since the flavor is quite acidic. The dense, rounded shrub can be maintained as a hedge or specimen and bears repeatedly through the warm months, making it one of the most productive fruiting shrubs for Gulf Coast home gardens. Fruit is highly perishable once ripe and should be harvested promptly and processed or refrigerated within a day or two.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; babaco is self-pollinating (parthenocarpic) and does not require a separate male plant. Protect from frost below 28°F.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 9–11; babaco is a naturally occurring hybrid of two Andean Vasconcellea species, selected and cultivated in Ecuador for its large, distinctively five-angled, torpedo-shaped fruits that are entirely seedless — a parthenocarpic trait that makes it the only papaya relative that does not require cross-pollination for fruit set. The flavor is refreshing and tropical, combining papaya with pineapple and strawberry notes, with lower enzyme activity than mountain papaya so the fruit can be eaten fresh. The tree stays compact at 6–10 feet and fruits prolifically in zone 9. In zone 9a, provide frost protection below 28°F or grow in large containers moved indoors in winter. A novelty fruit tree that produces a steady supply of unusual, edible fruit without the gender complications of other Vasconcellea species.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Babcock has a low chill requirement (around 250-300 hours), making it well suited to mild-winter zones like the Gulf South where higher-chill peaches fail to fruit reliably.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Babcock is a heritage California peach dating to the late 1800s, valued for its low chill requirement and its white, sweet, low-acid, freestone flesh, quite different in character from the more common yellow-fleshed commercial peaches. The medium-sized fruit has a red-blushed, creamy-white skin and delicate, aromatic, honey-sweet flavor that is prized for fresh eating, though the tender white flesh bruises more easily than firmer yellow peaches and is less suited to shipping. Its low chill requirement makes it one of the more reliable white peaches for warm, mild-winter climates where standard high-chill peach varieties struggle to break dormancy properly. Thin fruit early to improve size and prevent limb breakage, and pick at full ripeness for the best flavor, since white peaches do not ripen further once picked.

common_name: Bacon Avocado (Cold-Hardy Mild Avocado, Type B Winter Avocado, Zone 8b Avocado)
plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after frost danger; Bacon is one of the most cold-hardy avocado varieties (damaged at approximately 26°F, killed below 22–24°F), making it suitable for zone 8b–9 gardens with frost protection; Bacon is a Type B avocado and produces best when planted alongside a Type A variety (Hass, Mexicola); the mild flavor and thin skin make Bacon a good choice for Gulf Coast and warm-winter zones where Hass is marginally hardy.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with frost protection on the coldest nights; Bacon benefits from a Type A companion for maximum fruit set; harvest November through March when fruit is fully sized and softens slightly when gently squeezed; Bacon's mild flavor makes it versatile for cooking, guacamole, and fresh eating for those who prefer less rich avocado. Bacon avocado was developed by James Bacon in Buena Park, California, and introduced in 1954 — it became valued primarily for its cold-hardiness among avocado varieties, with documented survival at temperatures below 26°F that would damage Hass and below 22°F in some trials, making it one of the most cold-tolerant commercial avocado varieties available and the most commonly recommended cold-hardy variety for zone 8b home orchards. The variety's cold-hardiness derives from its pure Mexican race genetics (Persea americana var. drymifolia lineage), which evolved in the highlands of Mexico at elevations where frost occurs regularly — an origin that also confers anise-scented leaves and a distinctive flavor to the fruit. Bacon produces medium-sized, oval to pear-shaped avocados with smooth, thin, deep green skin that does not change color appreciably as it ripens; the flesh is pale yellow-green, creamy, and mild in flavor — significantly less rich in oil content than Hass or Fuerte, giving it a lighter taste that some consumers prefer. Bacon ripens winter to early spring (November–March in California). A good choice for zone 8b–9 gardens in the Gulf South, Texas, and similar climates where the extra cold-hardiness margin matters.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in part shade to full sun; bacupari is a slow-growing, understory-adapted tropical fruit tree related to mangosteen that thrives in the shade of larger trees in tropical gardens and fruiting landscapes.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; bacupari is slow-growing and may take 8–10 years to fruit from seed. Garcinia madruno (bacupari or madruno) is a Colombian and South American tropical fruit tree in the mangosteen family (Clusiaceae/Guttiferae) — related to the famous mangosteen (G. mangostana) and native to the cloud forests and tropical lowlands of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela. It produces small (1–2 inch), oval, bright-yellow to orange fruits when ripe, with thin, slightly resinous skin and white, juicy pulp with 1–3 seeds — the flavor is sweet-tart with floral-citrus notes similar to mangosteen but somewhat less complex. The tree is adapted to partial shade as an understory species in its native cloud forest habitat, making it one of the few tropical fruit trees that can be grown productively in partial shade. Bacupari/madruno is virtually unknown outside of Colombia and the Andean region where it is grown as a local specialty fruit. For zone 11–12 tropical gardeners seeking the most unusual and rare edible collectors' plants. Extremely rare in commercial availability.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bacuri is a frost-tender Amazonian tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bacuri is a frost-tender Amazonian tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the Amazon and Brazilian cerrado regions, this large forest tree produces a thick-shelled, yellow fruit containing creamy, tangy-sweet white pulp considered one of the finest-flavored fruits of the Amazon, used fresh and in ice creams, juices, and preserves across northern Brazil, though the tree is notoriously slow to reach fruiting age. A relative of mangosteen in the same plant family, it shares that group's exacting climate requirements and very long juvenile period, often a decade or more before first fruiting, making it a specialty tree for dedicated tropical fruit collectors and botanical gardens rather than a quick home orchard planting. Water regularly during the long establishment period, and provide the warm, humid, consistently frost-free conditions the tree requires to eventually bear fruit.

plant_note: Plant in spring after cold weather passes; bael tolerates light frost once established but does best in warm subtropical to tropical climates.
directions: Bael is a spiny citrus relative (family Rutaceae) highly revered in South Asian horticulture and medicine that tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and brief frosts to about 25°F once the trunk is mature — among the hardiest of the true tropical fruit trees. Trees are self-fertile and pollinated by insects; a single specimen fruits reliably. The hard-shelled, woody fruit takes 9–12 months to ripen on the tree; harvest when the skin turns from green to yellowish-green and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. The sticky, aromatic flesh is scooped out and eaten fresh with sugar, blended into a popular cooling drink (bael sherbet), or dried; dried slices brew into a medicinal tisane with mild anti-diarrheal properties.

common_name: Balaton Cherry (Hungarian Sour Cherry, Dark Sour Cherry, Sweet-Tart Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Balaton is self-fertile and requires no cross-pollinator; it is a Hungarian sour cherry variety introduced to North American production by Michigan State University in the 1980s–90s and is the most significant alternative to Montmorency for commercial and home sour cherry production, with superior fresh-eating quality due to its darker, less tart, higher-sugar flesh.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Balaton is self-fertile; it ripens 7–10 days after Montmorency (late June to mid-July in Michigan and the northeastern states), producing large, dark red to mahogany-red fruits with dark red flesh and juice — unlike Montmorency's lighter flesh — with a distinctly sweeter and milder flavor that can be enjoyed fresh as well as used for processing. Balaton sour cherry is a Hungarian variety (from the Balaton region of Hungary, named for Lake Balaton) introduced to North American production through Michigan State University's cherry breeding and evaluation program in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming the most important new sour cherry variety introduced to the American market since Montmorency dominated the category throughout the 20th century. The primary distinction of Balaton from Montmorency is the fruit character: Balaton produces large (slightly larger than Montmorency), very dark red to nearly black fruits with dark red flesh and intensely colored juice, in contrast to Montmorency's lighter pink-red skin and clear to pale yellow flesh. This dark flesh and sweet-tart balance gives Balaton a distinct advantage for certain uses: the fruit can be eaten fresh (it is significantly sweeter and less acidic than Montmorency, approaching the level of fresh-eating quality), the juice is intensely pigmented for concentrated cherry products, and the fruit makes darker, richer-colored preserves and pies. MSU Extension has actively promoted Balaton as an alternative to Montmorency for Michigan commercial producers and home orchardists, particularly for growers wanting a second variety to extend the harvest window and access specialty markets.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Baldwin requires a compatible pollinizer variety, needs substantial winter chill, and is best adapted to zones 4-7.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Baldwin originated in Massachusetts in the late 1700s and went on to become the single dominant commercial apple across New England through most of the 1800s and into the early 1900s, prized for large, firm, red-blushed fruit with crisp, juicy, slightly tart flesh that stores exceptionally well and holds up beautifully for baking, sauce, and hard cider alike. Baldwin's commercial dominance ended abruptly after the catastrophic winter of 1933-34, when extreme cold killed a huge share of New England's Baldwin trees, prompting growers to replant with hardier varieties like McIntosh; the apple never fully regained its former commercial standing, though it remains treasured by heirloom orchardists and cider makers. Harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and expect flavor to improve somewhat with a few weeks of cold storage, a classic trait of many old New England keeper apples.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Baldwin is a University of Florida-bred fig selected for good resistance to fruit souring in humid, rainy climates where many other fig varieties spoil on the tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor soils better than most fruit trees and do well in raised beds or large containers where restricted roots encourage fruiting over rampant growth. Baldwin was developed at a University of Florida research station and selected specifically for resistance to souring, a common problem in the Gulf South and Florida where warm, humid weather during ripening lets yeasts and bacteria enter the open eye of the fruit and spoil it before harvest. The medium, brown-skinned fruit has sweet, pink-amber flesh and a closed eye that helps keep out rain and insects, giving Baldwin an edge over open-eyed varieties in humid climates. It produces a reliable main crop in late summer without needing a pollinator, and benefits from a thick mulch layer and occasional deep watering during dry spells.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Baldwin, a Louisiana-origin pear, was selected for adaptability and fire blight resistance in Gulf South growing conditions.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Baldwin is a Louisiana-origin pear valued by Gulf South growers for its adaptability to the region's heat, humidity, and disease pressure, showing good resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that limits many higher-chill European pear cultivars in the Deep South. Like other regionally adapted low-chill pears it produces reliably even after a mild winter and pairs well with a second locally adapted pear cultivar for improved pollination and fruit set. Prune to an open, airy framework to reduce disease pressure, and remove any fire blight-infected shoots promptly, cutting well below visible damage into clean wood.

plant_note: Plant offshoots ('pups') with attached roots in rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; each stem fruits once then dies, but the clump produces a continuous succession of pups. Plant in a protected spot sheltered from strong winds, which shred the large leaves.
directions: Plant pups in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; banana is the most-consumed fruit on earth and one of the most productive food plants for Gulf Coast zone 8–11 gardens, where established clumps produce a nearly continuous succession of hands. Each pseudostem flowers once and fruits once, then should be cut to the ground after harvest, allowing the pups already pushing up around it to take over. In zone 8–9 the top growth dies back in hard freezes but established root mats resprout reliably in spring; heavy mulching protects the rhizomes. Popular zone-8-hardy varieties include 'Orinoco,' 'Lady Finger,' 'Dwarf Cavendish,' and the ultra-cold-hardy ornamental/edible 'Basjoo' hybrid. The large, exotic leaves make banana a spectacular tropical accent plant even in years when the winter prevents fruiting.

plant_note: Listed as an invasive species in Hawaii and New Zealand — check local regulations before planting; plant in mild coastal or mountain climates; tolerates light frost better than most passion fruits.
directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with trellis or fence support; banana passion fruit produces elongated pale yellow-green fruits 2–4 inches long with a strong passion fruit flavor and abundant aromatic juice used in drinks and ice cream throughout the Colombian highlands, where it is called curuba. The soft-hairy three-lobed leaves and pendant pink tubular flowers attract hummingbirds and are highly ornamental; the vine tolerates light frost better than most passion fruits and grows best in mild, humid conditions rather than the hot lowland tropics. It has escaped cultivation in Hawaii and New Zealand where it is invasive — deadhead spent fruits to prevent self-seeding when grown in mild climates.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; banana passionflower is more cold-hardy than most passionflowers and can survive light frost once established — it is considered invasive in Hawaii and some Pacific Islands, check local regulations.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; banana passionflower is more cold-tolerant than most passionflowers, surviving brief frosts to about 27°F when established, and has been successfully grown in sheltered spots in zone 8b and even zone 8a. Passiflora mollissima is an Andean native cultivated throughout the Andes from Colombia to Bolivia for its edible, banana-shaped, yellow, oblong fruits (curuba) 3–5 inches long with juicy, bright-orange, passion-fruit-flavored pulp used in juices, ice cream, and desserts; it is one of the most commercially important passionfruit species in South America. The flowers are beautiful — long-tubed, rose-pink to coral-pink, with a reduced corona — and are pollinated by hummingbirds. It grows vigorously and is considered invasive in warm, humid climates outside its native range (especially Hawaii, New Zealand, and South Africa); confirm it is legal to grow in your area.

plant_note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun; banana yucca stays low and largely stemless, unlike its tree-forming relatives, spreading into a dense clump of offsets over time.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; banana yucca forms a dense, largely stemless or low-trunked clump of thick, rigid, blue-green leaves and is notable among yuccas for producing a large, fleshy, banana-shaped fruit rather than the typical dry, papery capsule of most yucca species. A stout flower stalk of creamy white to purple-tinged bell-shaped blooms appears in late spring, followed by heavy green fruit that ripens to brown by late summer and was a significant traditional food source for Native American peoples of the Southwest, eaten fresh, dried, or baked once fully ripe and soft. It spreads slowly into a substantial multi-headed clump over the years and is exceptionally drought and cold tolerant, thriving in the same lean, rocky soils used by mountain mahogany and other tough Southwestern natives. Harvest fruit once it softens and begins to turn brown, and wear gloves when working near the sharp, rigid leaf tips.

common_name: Banyan Tree (Bengal Fig, Indian Banyan, Strangler Fig)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with well-drained, fertile soil; Banyan Tree is frost-sensitive and only suitable for outdoor planting in zone 10-11. In zone 9, it can be grown as a large indoor container specimen or seasonal patio tree — it tolerates pot culture better than many large figs, growing slowly in containers. Never plant near foundations, pipes, or pavement — the spreading roots and canopy are powerful and have lifted concrete across broad areas. The milky sap is a skin irritant.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in deep, well-drained soil with ample space — Banyan Tree is one of the largest living organisms on Earth and requires consideration before planting in any developed landscape. Ficus benghalensis is a massive evergreen fig tree native to the Indian subcontinent (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal), sacred in Hinduism and one of the national trees of India. The Banyan Tree has produced the largest tree canopy of any living plant species: the famous Great Banyan Tree in the Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden near Kolkata, India covers more than 4 acres with approximately 3,500 aerial prop roots and a canopy circumference of more than 1,500 feet.
