The tree's extraordinary growth mechanism — aerial roots that descend from the branches, root in the soil, and gradually thicken into secondary trunks capable of supporting additional branches — allows an individual tree to expand laterally without limit, progressively creating a multi-trunked 'forest' from a single genetic individual. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and Florida, Banyan Trees are major landscape and street trees. Small specimens are excellent as container bonsai or large indoor specimens in zone 9. The milky sap is irritating to skin. The small figs are eaten by birds but are not palatable to humans.

subcategory: African iconic ancient dryland multi-use tree
plant_note: Sow seeds (scarified with sandpaper or soaked 24 hours in warm water) in spring in full sun in deep, very well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in zone 10–12; Baobab is the most iconic tree of sub-Saharan Africa — a massive, long-lived deciduous tree with a distinctive swollen, water-storing trunk reaching immense girth — producing large, hard-shelled fruits containing a dry, white, powder-coated pulp extremely rich in Vitamin C and calcium, used as a food and commercial superfood ingredient across Africa.
directions: Plant Baobab in deep, freely draining, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; they are highly drought-tolerant once established and dislike any root waterlogging — excellent drainage is non-negotiable; water moderately during summer active growth and reduce or stop watering in winter when deciduous; container-grown Baobabs make striking bonsai or patio specimens for decades before size becomes an issue. Baobab is one of the most extraordinary trees on Earth — capable of living 2,000–5,000+ years (and possibly far longer), storing thousands of liters of water in its massive, spongy, swollen trunk, and providing food, medicine, fiber, and shelter for both people and wildlife across its native sub-Saharan Africa range. The large, white, bat-pollinated flowers open at night and are strongly fragrant; they are followed by the football-sized, hard, hanging fruits — known commercially as 'baobab fruit' or 'monkey bread' — containing dry, chalky-white pulp naturally rich in Vitamin C (6x more than oranges per weight), calcium, potassium, and antioxidants. The pulp, leaves, seeds, bark, and roots all have documented food and medicinal uses across Africa; commercial baobab fruit powder has grown into a global superfood industry. In zone 10–12, it makes a spectacular, extraordinarily long-lived specimen tree; young plants grow slowly but rewards patient gardeners with one of the planet's most remarkable organisms.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; barbados cherry is drought-tolerant once established but fruits most heavily with regular irrigation during the three to four annual fruiting cycles; protect from frost in zone 9a.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; barbados cherry (acerola, West Indian cherry) is a subtropical shrub or small tree that produces cherry-sized, three-lobed, bright red to orange-red fruits containing the highest natural concentration of Vitamin C of any food crop — approximately 65 times the Vitamin C of orange juice by weight. In south Florida, Texas Gulf Coast, and zone 9–11 climates, established plants produce three to four fruiting cycles annually, yielding heavy crops of sweet-tart, highly perishable fruits that must be processed immediately (fresh eating, juice, smoothies, frozen puree) as they deteriorate within hours of harvest. The plant is an attractive, dense, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub with small, pink, orchid-like flowers and is often grown as a fruiting hedge or informal screen. Productive and relatively pest-free in tropical and subtropical climates. 'B-17', 'Manoa Sweet', and 'Florida Sweet' are improved selections with larger, sweeter fruit.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Barbados gooseberry is a primitive (leafy) cactus that grows as a woody climbing vine and can be trained on a fence or trellis. It is frost tender and suited to zone 9b–12 in the ground, or grown as a container plant.
directions: Root cuttings in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Barbados gooseberry is one of the most botanically fascinating of all edible plants — a primitive cactus (family Cactaceae) that retains true persistent leaves unlike all other cacti, making it a living link between leafy plants and the succulent cacti. The woody, thorny scrambling vine can reach 30 feet when climbing, with oval, slightly succulent leaves and masses of fragrant white to pale pink flowers in fall. The yellow to orange fruits ripen to 0.75 inches with multiple seeds embedded in pulp with a pleasant acid-sweet, citrus-like flavor — used fresh, in jams, and as a vegetable cooked with rice in the Caribbean. The young leaves are edible as a potherb. In South America the leaves are consumed as 'ora-pro-nobis,' valued for their exceptionally high protein content (25% dry weight). An unusual and productive edible vine for frost-free gardens.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Barbera is a vigorous, adaptable, productive vine that performs reliably across a fairly wide range of climates.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Barbera is a red wine grape native to the Piedmont region of northern Italy, historically the everyday table wine of the region before a wave of quality-focused winemaking in the late 20th century elevated it to serious status, prized for naturally high acidity paired with relatively low tannin, producing fresh, juicy, food-friendly red wines with bright cherry and berry flavors. The vine is notably vigorous and productive, more forgiving and adaptable to a range of growing conditions than many of the finicky, low-yielding grapes used for premium wine, which has made it a popular choice both in its native Italy and increasingly in New World regions including California. Train to a permanent trellis, manage vigor and crop load through canopy work and thinning to avoid diluted flavor from overcropping, and harvest once sugars are adequate, since Barbera's naturally high acidity gives some flexibility in exact picking date.

common_name: Barcelona Hazelnut (Barcelona Filbert, Pacific Northwest Commercial Filbert Standard)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container hazelnuts in late winter or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Barcelona is self-incompatible and requires a cross-pollinating companion variety — plant with Ennis, Daviana, or the newer OSU releases (Yamhill, Jefferson) for reliable nut set; IMPORTANT: Barcelona is highly susceptible to Eastern Filbert Blight (EFB), a devastating fungal disease that is endemic throughout the eastern United States — Barcelona is NOT recommended for gardens east of the Mississippi; in the Pacific Northwest it produces reliably without EFB pressure.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Barcelona requires a companion pollenizer variety; the catkins (male flowers) shed pollen in late winter before the tiny female flowers emerge; nuts ripen in September–October and fall naturally when ripe — sweep them from the ground daily for best quality before mold develops. Barcelona hazelnut is the dominant commercial hazelnut (filbert) variety in the Willamette Valley of Oregon, which produces approximately 99% of the American commercial hazelnut crop and is the third-largest hazelnut production region in the world after Turkey and Italy. The variety was introduced from Spain (where it was a standard filbert cultivar) to the Oregon hazelnut industry in the late 1800s and quickly became the commercial standard because of its productive, consistent cropping, large nut size for the era, and good kernel quality. For over a century, Barcelona dominated Oregon hazelnut production so completely that the Oregon hazelnut industry and Barcelona hazelnut were essentially synonymous. The primary limitation of Barcelona — and the reason it has begun to be replaced by newer OSU-released varieties — is its extreme susceptibility to Eastern Filbert Blight (EFB), a canker disease caused by the native American fungus Anisogramma anomala that is devastating in the eastern United States where it is endemic but historically absent from Pacific Coast orchards. EFB reached Oregon in the 1990s, and its spread has prompted the Oregon hazelnut industry to shift toward the new EFB-resistant OSU varieties (Jefferson, Yamhill, others).

plant_note: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Barhi needs a long, hot, dry summer to properly ripen its fruit and is best suited to low-humidity desert climates.
directions: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Barhi needs a long, hot, dry summer to properly ripen its fruit and is best suited to low-humidity desert climates. An Iraqi soft date variety highly prized for being one of the very few dates good to eat fresh at the crisp, yellow, apple-like khalal stage rather than only after fully drying to the traditional wrinkled brown tamr stage, giving it a uniquely refreshing, crunchy-sweet quality unlike most commercial dried dates. Once fully ripened to the soft, caramel-brown stage it becomes exceptionally sweet and soft with a rich, almost butterscotch flavor, making it a favorite among date connoisseurs for both fresh and fully cured eating. Like all date palms it demands a long, hot, dry growing season to ripen properly, needs a male pollinator tree or hand pollination for fruit set, and requires many years of growth before reaching bearing maturity.

plant_note: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Barland is an exceptionally slow tree to reach bearing age, sometimes taking well over a decade.
directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Barland is an exceptionally slow tree to reach bearing age, sometimes taking well over a decade. A classic Herefordshire perry pear long prized for producing exceptionally high-tannin, astringent juice that gives finished perry real structure and aging potential, it is considered one of the finest true perry pears despite, or because of, fruit far too harsh and bitter for fresh eating. Its notoriously slow growth to first bearing has always made it a tree planted for a future generation rather than quick reward, a tradition reflected in the old West Country saying about planting pears for one's heirs. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften and mellow, then mill and press for perry.

common_name: Bartlett Pear (Williams' Bon Chrétien Pear, Williams Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Bartlett requires 600–800 chill hours and benefits from a pollinizer (Bosc, Anjou) for maximum production in most situations.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Bartlett (Williams' Bon Chrétien in Europe) is the most widely grown pear in North America and the world's most commercially important pear cultivar — the classic yellow, buttery, bell-shaped fruit that defines the word 'pear' in popular culture. The large, sweet, aromatic fruit with fine-grained, melting flesh ripens from late summer to early fall and is excellent fresh, canned, dried, and used in pies and preserves. Trees are moderately susceptible to fire blight (Erwinia amylovora), which can cause significant damage in warm, humid climates; planting on well-drained sites and applying copper during bloom reduces risk. Bartlett needs 600–800 chill hours and is best suited to zones 5–7 where winters reliably provide sufficient cold. For warmer zones 8–9, low-chill pears like 'Hood', 'Flordahome', and 'Orient' are more appropriate than Bartlett. Trees bear at 3–5 years and live for decades.

plant_note: Sow fresh seeds in fall immediately after harvest; cold winter temperatures provide the natural stratification required for germination the following spring.
directions: Collect ripe blue-black berries in midsummer and sow seeds fresh in fall, pressing them lightly into moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered outdoor bed or cold frame. Unlike most serviceberries that bear fruits in long clusters, Bartram's Serviceberry ripens single fruits or small groups of 2–4, making hand-harvest easy. This cold-hardy species thrives in cool, moist conditions resembling its native boreal and subalpine habitat; avoid planting in heavy clay or hot, dry sites. Established shrubs are trouble-free and begin producing their first meaningful berry crops within 2–5 years of transplanting.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; bay starvine grows naturally in moist, rich, shaded woodland understory conditions in the southern Appalachians and adjacent areas and is dioecious — male and female plants are required for fruit set.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade at forest edges and woodland understory positions; bay starvine is the native North American member of the Schisandraceae — the same family as the famous five-flavor berry (S. chinensis) of Chinese medicine. It grows in the moist, shaded ravines, stream bottoms, and rich forest understory of the southern Appalachians and adjacent lowlands, producing small red flowers in spring that require cross-pollination between male and female plants. The fruits, clustered like a miniature bunch of grapes on an elongated stalk, ripen red in late summer. The plant tolerates deep shade better than most fruiting vines, filling a valuable niche in shaded woodland garden designs. Though less medicinally celebrated than the Asian species, the native bay starvine has similar phytochemical constituents. A rare and beautiful native vine deserving wider use in woodland shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in fall or early spring; seeds need 2–3 months of cold stratification and should be sown outdoors in fall or cold-stratified in the refrigerator before spring sowing.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; beaked hazelnut is distinguished from American hazelnut (Corylus americana) by the long, tubular, beak-like husk that encloses each nut — the 'beak' can be twice the length of the nut itself. The nuts ripen in late summer and are enthusiastically gathered by squirrels, chipmunks, turkeys, woodpeckers, and grouse; you must act quickly to harvest any for yourself. Plant two or more seedlings for reliable cross-pollination since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and often self-infertile. The catkins that appear in late winter before the leaves are an early source of pollen for native bees.

common_name: Beall Fig (Heirloom Gulf South Bronze Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; figs are self-fertile and need no pollinator. Beall is an old Gulf South heirloom fig, passed down and shared among home growers for generations rather than commercially released.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; figs tolerate a wide range of soils but produce their best fruit with consistent moisture during ripening. Beall is a long-passed-down heirloom fig from the Gulf South, maintained by home orchardists and fig collectors rather than through commercial nursery release, producing medium bronze-brown fruit with sweet, richly flavored, pink-to-amber flesh. Like most Gulf Coast heirloom figs, it is valued for its vigor and reliability under regional heat and humidity, ripening over an extended midsummer-to-fall season. Prune in late winter to control size and remove winter dieback, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system; established Beall trees tolerate the occasional hard freeze common to zone 8-9 winters, resprouting from the base if top growth is killed back.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Beaumont macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, but bears at a younger age than many macadamia cultivars.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Beaumont macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, but bears at a younger age than many macadamia cultivars. A hybrid between the two main macadamia species, this Australian-bred cultivar is widely planted for home gardens and smaller orchards because it begins bearing noticeably earlier than many other macadamia selections, often within three to four years, and produces large clusters of good-quality nuts on a moderately vigorous tree. Its relatively quick time to first bearing makes it a popular choice for home growers wanting a faster return than the decade-plus wait typical of some macadamia cultivars, though like all macadamias it needs consistent warmth and is easily damaged by frost. Water regularly, especially during nut development, and harvest nuts as they fall naturally from the tree when fully mature, since immature nuts do not ripen further once picked.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Beauty is the earliest-ripening Japanese plum and pollinates well with Santa Rosa and Methley. It requires approximately 250–400 chill hours, suitable for zone 7–9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Beauty is one of the earliest-ripening Japanese plum cultivars, producing medium-sized, bright scarlet-red to crimson fruit with red-streaked yellow flesh in late spring — often the first plum available from the orchard in a given season. The flesh is sweet and juicy with good flavor for fresh eating, canning, and jam production. Beauty is partially self-fertile but produces best crops with a pollinizer nearby (Santa Rosa, Methley, or other Japanese plums). Its low chill requirement (approximately 250–400 hours) makes it well-adapted to zone 7–9, where it performs more reliably than higher-chill European plum cultivars. Trees are moderately vigorous and somewhat susceptible to brown rot, which can be managed with timely fungicide applications and prompt removal of infected fruit. Beauty ripens over an extended period of 2–3 weeks, reducing harvest pressure compared to plums that ripen all at once.

common_name: Belle de Boskoop Apple (Large Tart Dutch Heirloom Cooking Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby, since Belle de Boskoop has poor pollen and needs a strong pollinizer partner.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a strong compatible pollinizer variety nearby, since this apple's own pollen is of poor quality and it benefits from a robust partner variety. Belle de Boskoop was discovered in the Dutch town of Boskoop in 1856 and became one of the most important cooking and baking apples in continental Europe, prized for large, rough-skinned, red-and-russet fruit with dense, notably tart, aromatic flesh that holds its shape beautifully under heat, making it outstanding for pies, tarte tatin, and applesauce. The tree is vigorous and long-lived, and the fruit stores exceptionally well, often keeping well into winter and even improving somewhat in flavor with a few weeks of storage. Its sharp, assertive tartness sets it apart from milder modern eating apples, making it a favorite specifically among European-style baking enthusiasts.

common_name: Belle of Georgia Peach (Classic White Freestone Heirloom Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Belle of Georgia requires approximately 850 chill hours (temperatures below 45°F) and is reliably productive in zones 5–9 where adequate winter chilling accumulates; plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), deep fertile soil in full sun; space 15–20 feet apart.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Belle of Georgia is a self-fruitful peach requiring no cross-pollinator; thin fruit to 6–8 inches after petal fall; harvest when fruit is fully colored and gives slightly to pressure — white-fleshed peaches like Belle of Georgia lose the green background and develop a creamy-white blush at full ripeness. Belle of Georgia is one of the great classic American peach varieties, an heirloom white-fleshed freestone that has been grown in Southern home orchards for over 150 years, originating in Georgia before 1870 from a cross believed to involve Chinese Cling and other Southern peach stock. The variety demonstrates a characteristic that distinguishes white-fleshed peaches from the more common yellow-fleshed types: the flesh is pure white to blush-pink, with a flavor that is typically sweeter and less acidic than yellow peaches, with floral aromatic notes that many peach connoisseurs consider more complex and refined than yellow varieties. The flavor at peak ripeness — juicy, very sweet, almost honeyed, with a delicate fragrance — is exceptional for fresh eating and traditional Southern preserves. The skin is creamy white to pale pink with a bright red blush over much of the surface, making the ripened fruit visually distinctive. Belle of Georgia is a mid-season variety that ripens in late June to mid-July in most of the South, producing large, fully freestone fruits that separate cleanly from the pit at full ripeness. The trees are vigorous and consistent producers with reasonable disease tolerance under good management. A genuine heirloom variety that has earned its continuous popularity over more than a century of Southern home orchard growing.

common_name: Ben Davis Apple (Mortgage Lifter Apple, New York Pippin)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant; moderate chill requirement of about 600-700 hours and notable tolerance of heat, drought, and poor soils made it a favorite pioneer-era orchard apple across a wide range of climates.
directions: Ben Davis tolerates less-than-ideal soil and irregular watering better than most apples, making it forgiving for beginning orchardists or marginal sites. Introduced in the early 1800s and possibly of Kentucky or Tennessee origin, it became one of the most widely planted commercial apples in 19th-century America, prized for its precocious, heavy, reliable annual crops and its exceptional storage life rather than for outstanding fresh flavor, which is mild and somewhat bland compared to dessert apples. It remains of interest to homesteaders and heirloom growers today mainly for its toughness, productivity, and long keeping quality in cold storage.

common_name: Beni Shogun Fuji Apple (Low-Chill Early-Ripening Pink-Blushed Fuji Sport)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring; not self-fruitful, plant with another low-chill apple such as Anna or Dorsett Golden for pollination. Beni Shogun Fuji needs only about 500 chill hours, well below the 550-600 hours standard Fuji requires.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Beni Shogun Fuji, a pink-blushed sport of standard Fuji, needs roughly 500 chill hours rather than the 550 to 600 hours true Fuji requires, letting it flower and fruit more reliably in gardens at the warmer edge of apple-growing range where standard Fuji sets an uneven crop. It ripens about a month earlier than standard Fuji, with the same sweet, crisp, juicy flesh but a slightly deeper pink blush over the yellow skin. Thin fruit to one per cluster in late spring to improve size, and pick when fully colored for the best sweetness.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bergamot orange requires a subtropical climate similar to coastal Calabria in southern Italy where the commercial crop is grown. In zones below 9, grow as a container plant and bring indoors during frost.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in a frost-free location; bergamot orange is a small citrus tree grown almost exclusively in Calabria, Italy, for the essential oil extracted from the peel — the aromatic compound that gives Earl Grey tea its distinctive floral-citrus character. The fruit is yellow-green when ripe, roughly lemon-sized, and inedible raw due to intense bitterness. The peel oil is also used extensively in high-end perfumery, providing the top notes to Chanel No. 5 and countless other classic fragrances. In the garden it is an ornamental conversation piece; harvest peels from ripe fruit and dry them, or make a simple extract by steeping fresh peel in vodka. A reliable performer in zone 9–11 with minimal maintenance beyond regular citrus feeding.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Beurre Hardy is a vigorous, reliable tree well suited to a home orchard.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Beurre Hardy is a vigorous, reliable tree well suited to a home orchard. A classic French dessert pear introduced in the early nineteenth century, its name meaning roughly buttery and hardy, it bears attractive bronze-russeted, greenish fruit with exceptionally juicy, melting, sweet flesh carrying a distinctive light rosewater aroma prized by pear connoisseurs, on a notably vigorous, reliably productive, and disease-tolerant tree. Its combination of rich flavor, vigorous growth, and good disease resistance compared to some other classic European pears has kept it in cultivation as a favorite home orchard variety for two centuries. Harvest while still firm and green in late summer to early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for a few days until the flesh yields slightly to gentle pressure near the stem.

common_name: Beurré Giffard Pear (Early-Ripening French Summer Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Beurré Giffard is a French heirloom from the 1820s prized for ripening remarkably early, among the very first quality European pears of the summer, well ahead of the classic fall and winter storage pears most gardeners grow. The medium, greenish-yellow fruit blushed with red has soft, juicy, melting, richly flavored flesh in the classic 'buttery' (beurré) style, but the tradeoff for its buttery texture and early ripening is a very short window of peak quality — the fruit must be picked at just the right moment and eaten promptly, since it goes from underripe to overripe quickly with little margin. For gardeners willing to watch the crop closely, it rewards with some of the season's first fresh pears.

common_name: Beverly Hills Apple (Very Low-Chill California-Bred Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Beverly Hills needs only about 300 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any apple, making it one of the few apples that can fruit reliably in zone 9 Gulf South winters.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible low-chill pollinator such as Anna, Dorsett Golden, or Ein Shemer. Beverly Hills was discovered as a chance seedling in Beverly Hills, California and remains valued today as one of the lowest-chill apples available, needing only around 300 chill hours, which lets it set fruit reliably even after the mild winters typical of the Gulf South where most standard apple varieties bloom poorly or not at all. Fruit is medium-sized, red-striped, with tart, crisp flesh good for fresh eating and cooking, ripening in mid to late summer. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good airflow and fruit quality in humid conditions.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; needs about 750 chill hours, so it is best matched to the cooler-winter, upper Gulf South (inland zone 8) rather than the immediate mild coastline.
directions: An early-season Southern peach named for the 1976 US bicentennial, producing attractive medium-to-large freestone fruit with yellow flesh streaked red and good eating quality for an early ripener. It is a solid choice for growers in the cooler, higher-chill pockets of the Deep South who still want an early harvest, complementing very-low-chill coastal types on properties that span a range of microclimates. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, prune annually to an open-center form, and thin fruit in spring to improve size and reduce limb breakage from heavy crop loads.

common_name: Big Jim Loquat (Large-Fruited Orange Loquat, Jim's Loquat)
plant_note: Plant grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Big Jim is one of the largest-fruited loquat varieties available, producing fruits that can reach 2–3 inches in length with a correspondingly smaller seed-to-flesh ratio than smaller-fruited varieties — ideal for home gardens where fruit quality and ease of eating are prioritized over heavy production per tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil; thin fruit clusters heavily (3–4 per cluster) to achieve the maximum individual fruit size that Big Jim is capable of; harvest when fruit is fully golden-orange and gives slightly to pressure; consume quickly as loquats have short shelf life (2–3 days at room temperature, 2 weeks refrigerated). Big Jim is a large-fruited loquat variety selected for the home garden market for its impressive individual fruit size — one of the largest-fruited loquat varieties available to home gardeners in the United States. The fruits are elongated, pear-shaped to oblong, with a warm orange skin and deep orange flesh that is sweet-tart and richly flavored — the classic loquat flavor in a package that provides more edible flesh per fruit than smaller varieties. Because loquats have large central seeds relative to their flesh, fruit size matters considerably in terms of eating efficiency: a large loquat like Big Jim offers a much better flesh-to-seed ratio than a small-fruited variety. The tree is moderately vigorous with an upright to spreading habit reaching 15–20 feet at maturity, blooming in fall (October–December in the Gulf South) with fragrant white flower clusters and ripening fruits from late winter through spring. Big Jim performs well in zones 8–10 and has been popular in Gulf Coast and California home gardens for generations. Heavy fruit thinning (to 3–4 fruits per cluster) is particularly important with Big Jim to achieve the maximum individual fruit size.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Big Red mayhaw fruits in May (hence the name 'May-haw') — harvest the small, red fruits from the ground or by shaking branches over tarps when the berries begin dropping naturally. Trees begin fruiting in 3–5 years from planting and become increasingly productive for decades. Mayhaw prefers wet, poorly drained, acidic soils — a wetland native that grows naturally in swamps, bayou edges, and bottomlands of the Gulf South. Excellent cross-pollinator: plant two or more varieties for maximum production.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil — mayhaw is a wetland native that actually thrives in poorly drained areas where most fruit trees would fail; Big Red is an improved cultivar of native mayhaw (Crataegus aestivalis), the regional fruit of the Gulf South that has been gathered wild for generations and more recently cultivated for commercial jelly production. The small (grape to crabapple sized), round, bright red berries are borne in clusters and ripen in May — giving the tree its common name — with a tart, mildly astringent, aromatic flavor that makes exceptional jelly and is used in sauces, wines, and sweet preparations throughout southern Louisiana, Mississippi, and east Texas where mayhaw culture is a regional food tradition. Mayhaw jelly is the Gulf South equivalent of beach plum jelly in New England — a hyperlocal, regionally specific preserve made from a native fruit with no close cultural equivalent elsewhere in the United States. Big Red was selected for larger-than-average fruit size and high productivity compared to wild-collected mayhaw. The tree's unusual preference for wet, acidic, swampy conditions makes it one of the few commercially valuable fruit trees suitable for low-lying zone 9 sites that would be unsuitable for conventional orchards.

common_name: Big V Mayhaw (Selected Western Mayhaw Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Big V is a named western mayhaw selection that fruits best with a second mayhaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a native wetland tree that thrives in the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most fruit trees fail. Big V is a named selection of western mayhaw grown by Gulf South orchardists for its good fruit size and productive habit, bearing clusters of small, tart, aromatic red fruit that ripen in May and are gathered for the region's traditional mayhaw jelly. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar nearby to ensure strong cross-pollination and fruit set, and expect the young tree to begin bearing within three to five years, with production increasing steadily as it matures over the following decade. Mayhaw needs little care once established beyond occasional pruning to remove crossing or damaged limbs.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; bigflower pawpaw is adapted to Florida scrub and sandhill habitat and requires sharp drainage, performing poorly in heavy or poorly drained soils.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; bigflower pawpaw is adapted to Florida scrub and sandhill habitat and requires sharp drainage, performing poorly in heavy or poorly drained soils. Asimina obovata is a Florida-endemic shrub or small tree grown for its large, showy, creamy-white, three-petaled flowers with a sweet fragrance in spring, followed by yellow-green, custard-fleshed fruit smaller than the common pawpaw but edible fresh. Its thick, leathery, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen leaves and drought tolerance make it a distinctive addition to a sandy-soil food forest or native pollinator garden in the Deep South, where it serves as a larval host plant for zebra swallowtail butterflies just as its northern relative does. It needs excellent drainage and full sun to partial shade, tolerates poor, infertile sand, and should never be irrigated on a schedule suited to typical garden shrubs.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; bignay is dioecious — both male and female trees are needed for fruit; female trees produce large, pendulous clusters of berries. Hardy to about 28°F in zone 9b–12.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — bignay is a medium-sized tropical tree of Southeast Asia and the Pacific, producing spectacular long (12–18 inch) pendulous clusters of small (pea-sized) berries that ripen from green through red to deep purple-black in sequence on the same cluster, creating a striking multi-colored effect. The berries have a pleasant tart-sweet flavor with some astringency and are eaten fresh, made into wine, juice, and jam; in the Philippines bignay wine is a traditional fermented beverage. The tree is dioecious and shade-tolerant, growing naturally as an understory tree in mixed tropical forests. The polished, reddish-brown seeds (resembling small nutmegs) are made into decorative necklaces in the Philippines. An outstanding ornamental fruiting tree for zone 9b–12 gardens offering shade tolerance and dramatic fruiting clusters.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, sandy to gritty, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; bilberry cactus is native to dry, rocky hillsides of central Mexico and requires essentially no supplemental irrigation once established in appropriate soil — overwatering is the primary cause of failure.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy to gritty soil in full sun; water sparingly — once every 2–3 weeks in summer, almost none in winter. Myrtillocactus geometrizans (bilberry cactus or garambulla) is a striking Mexican columnar cactus forming a large, candelabra-like tree cactus with multiple blue-green columnar branches — the blue-grey waxy coating on the branches gives it an extraordinary, almost artificial blue-steel color that makes it one of the most ornamentally distinctive columnar cacti for full-sun landscaping in warm, dry climates. The columns have 6 prominent ribs with clusters of short spines. The plant produces abundant small, grape-sized, dark-purple to blue-black fruits called garambullos in Mexico — they are sweet, mildly flavored, and eaten fresh or made into aguas frescas; they are among the most economically important wild cactus fruits in Mexico. The flowers are small, white, and produced in spring. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant and cold-hardy to about 25°F. An outstanding specimen or hedge cactus for dry, alkaline, sunny gardens in zone 9–12.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or air-layered plants in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; bilimbi is more shade-tolerant than carambola and is a smaller, more compact tree excellent for home orchards in zone 10+.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or air-layered trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bilimbi is more shade-tolerant than its close relative starfruit and is a good choice for partially shaded spots in tropical gardens, though it fruits best in full sun. Averrhoa bilimbi is a relative of carambola producing clusters of small (2–4 inch), cucumber-shaped, intensely sour, pale-green to yellow fruits that grow directly from the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) in a bizarre but highly productive display; the extremely tart fruit is rarely eaten fresh but is valued in Southeast Asian and Caribbean cuisine for its acidity in curries, preserves, pickles, and beverages, substituting for tamarind or lime. Trees fruit heavily multiple times per year in frost-free climates (zones 10–12) and can be grown in large containers moved indoors in zone 9; the pinnate leaves and clustered trunk fruits make it an ornamental specimen even when not fruiting.

common_name: Bing Cherry (Dark Sweet Cherry, American Commercial Cherry Standard)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Bing requires 700–1000 chill hours and a cross-pollinating sweet cherry — Rainier, Lapins, or Black Tartarian — that is bloom-time compatible; Bing cannot pollinate Stella or Lambert; zones 5–7 are ideal.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Bing must be paired with a compatible pollinizer (Rainier, Lapins, or Black Tartarian) — Bing cannot cross-pollinate Stella, Lambert, or Napoleon; protect ripening fruit from birds using netting; avoid planting in poorly drained sites or low spots where frost collects; Bing ripens in late June to early July in the Pacific Northwest, the timing that has made it the dominant commercial cherry. Bing cherry is the most widely grown commercial sweet cherry variety in the United States — the cherry that defines what most Americans mean when they say 'sweet cherry' — a dark mahogany-red to nearly black, large, firm, heart-shaped variety with exceptionally sweet, complex flavor developed in Oregon in 1875 by Seth Lewelling on his fruit farm near Milwaukie, Oregon. Lewelling named the variety after his Chinese foreman, Ah Bing, in recognition of his contributions to the orchard — an unusual act of recognition for a Chinese immigrant worker in that era. The variety quickly spread from Oregon throughout the Pacific Coast commercial cherry-growing regions (the Columbia Basin of Oregon and Washington State, the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys of California) because its combination of large size, dark color, firm flesh, excellent sweetness, and good shipping characteristics made it ideal for the developing rail-shipped fresh fruit trade. Today, Bing accounts for more than 90% of the sweet cherry production in the Pacific Northwest and a major share of all American commercial sweet cherries. The characteristic Bing appearance — large, round to heart-shaped, very dark mahogany-red to black — is so iconic that 'a bag of Bings' has become synonymous with sweet cherries in American culture, and fresh Bing cherries in early summer represent one of the quintessential seasonal fruits of the American marketplace.

common_name: Bingo Mandarin (Early-Season Seedless Easy-Peel HLB-Tolerant Florida Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Bingo, a University of Florida release, is an early-season (October-November) seedless, easy-peel mandarin bred primarily for tolerance to citrus greening (HLB) rather than cold hardiness.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and bring container-grown trees under cover or protect in place during hard freezes, since Bingo is a true mandarin without the added cold tolerance of trifoliate-hybrid citrus. Bingo, released by the University of Florida, was bred primarily for improved field tolerance to huanglongbing (citrus greening), the bacterial disease that has devastated citrus groves across Florida and the Gulf South, while still delivering good fresh-market quality: an easy-peel, essentially seedless mandarin with sweet, richly flavored flesh ripening early in the season, from October into November, ahead of many other mandarin selections. It suits the milder, more coastal parts of the Gulf South citrus range where standard mandarins are already grown, rather than the colder inland areas where cold-hardy hybrids are needed. Fertilize according to standard citrus nutrition programs and monitor for greening symptoms even on resistant selections, since tolerance reduces but does not eliminate disease impact.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall immediately after cleaning to allow natural warm-then-cold stratification; the two-phase dormancy requires both a warm period and a cold period before germination will occur.
directions: Clean seeds from ripe black fruits in late summer and sow immediately to take advantage of the warm-soil period before winter cold sets in; this two-phase stratification requirement is essential and skipping either phase will delay germination by a full year. Plant in moist, fertile soil near a stream bank or in a woodland clearing, reflecting its natural preference for riparian and marginal woodland habitats throughout northern Eurasia. Bird cherry grows vigorously once established and will naturalize readily, so site it where suckering can be managed or is welcome as a thicket for wildlife. Expect the first flower racemes by year four to six, filling the garden with a heavy almond-like fragrance in mid to late spring before the leaves fully expand.

plant_note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a sturdy arbor or fence in well-drained sandy soil in full sun; this small, thin-barked native grape of Florida and the Gulf Coast is far more heat- and drought-tolerant than most cultivated bunch grapes.
directions: Plant dormant cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a sturdy arbor, fence, or large shrub in well-drained sandy soil in full sun. Bird grape is a slender, thin-barked native vine of Florida hammocks, pinelands, and Gulf Coast scrub, distinguished from the related muscadine by its smaller leaves and less shaggy bark, and it climbs readily by tendrils once given support. Its small, sweet black grapes ripen over a long season and are eaten avidly by songbirds, making it a valuable addition to a wildlife hedge or fence line rather than a fruit crop for the table. It tolerates the heat, humidity, sandy soils, and periodic drought of the Gulf Coast better than most grape species, needing only occasional pruning to keep it in bounds.

common_name: Biriba (Wild Sweetsop, Rollinia, Lemon Meringue Fruit)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in late spring when soil is warm; Rollinia is frost-tender and should be protected from temperatures below 32°F — it is strictly a zone 10–11 outdoor tree but can be grown as a large container specimen moved indoors during frost events in zone 9. It grows rapidly from seed and can fruit in 2–4 years. Plant in partial shade to full sun with well-drained, fertile, moist soil. The fruits must be harvested before they fall and consumed immediately as they deteriorate extremely rapidly — the flesh bruises and ferments within hours of harvest or impact.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil; Biriba grows rapidly in zone 10–11 humid conditions and benefits from regular irrigation and fertilization to produce its heavy crops of large, distinctive fruits. Rollinia deliciosa (often treated as a synonym within the soursop genus: Annona mucosa) is a tropical fruit tree from the Amazon basin of Brazil, Colombia, and Peru, prized by tropical fruit enthusiasts for producing one of the most extraordinarily flavored and unusual-looking fruits in the Annona family. The fruits are large (4–8 inches), covered in soft, flexible, yellowish-green to golden spines or fingerlike projections that soften completely when ripe, and contain white, extremely juicy, sweet-tart flesh described as tasting like a combination of lemon meringue, vanilla custard, and banana — some connoisseurs consider it the finest-flavored of all the Annona relatives, surpassing cherimoya and soursop. The fruits ripen very rapidly (within 1–2 days of picking) and bruise at the slightest touch, making commercial distribution virtually impossible and confining the fruit almost entirely to home gardens and local markets in tropical growing regions. In zone 10–11 South Florida, Biriba is increasingly grown by rare-fruit enthusiasts and community gardens as a fast-growing, productive tree that rewards the patient gardener with extraordinary fruits unavailable in any market.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; bitter kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; bitter kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the humid rainforests of West and Central Africa, this understory to mid-canopy tree bears a fruit whose bitter, astringent seeds are widely chewed fresh across West Africa, valued both as a traditional stimulant, similar in cultural role to true kola nut, and as an important item in traditional hospitality and ceremony. Trees take many years to reach bearing age and require the warm, humid, shaded forest conditions of their native range to thrive, making this a specialty planting for tropical botanical collections, ethnobotanical gardens, or large frost-free properties rather than a typical home garden tree. Water regularly, especially while young, and protect from any exposure to direct hot afternoon sun, which the shade-adapted seedlings do not tolerate well.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall at 1-2 inches depth in moist, well-drained to wet soil; bitternut hickory naturally grows in moist bottomlands and slopes and is one of the fastest-growing and most adaptable hickories. Seeds require natural cold stratification over winter.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, fertile, loamy or clay soil in full sun; bitternut hickory is the most widely distributed hickory in eastern North America and one of the fastest growing, making it valuable as a canopy tree where time to a large shade tree is a priority. The nuts are notably bitter and unpalatable to humans (hence the common name), being too high in tannins for human consumption even after shelling — unlike the sweet-nutted shagbark and shellbark hickories. However, they are consumed by squirrels, deer, and wood ducks after additional caching and processing. The distinctive butter-yellow winter buds are an important winter identification trait. The golden-yellow fall color is attractive, and the tree provides superb canopy for native plant understories. One of the most moisture-tolerant hickories.

common_name: Black Beauty Mulberry (Large Sweet Black Mulberry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Black Beauty is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator, and it fruits at a young age.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant. Black Beauty is a black mulberry selection prized for producing unusually large, elongated berries with the rich, intensely sweet-tart, wine-like flavor characteristic of true black mulberry (Morus nigra), widely regarded among mulberry enthusiasts as having the finest flavor of any mulberry species — deeper, more complex, and more balanced between sweet and tart than the milder white or red mulberries. The large fruit size makes hand harvest more efficient than picking the smaller berries of many other mulberry types. Because ripe mulberries drop as they mature and stain heavily, plant away from patios, walkways, and parking areas, or spread a sheet beneath the canopy at harvest time to catch fruit. Trees need only light annual pruning to maintain shape and size.

common_name: Black Beauty Plum (Dark-Skinned Amber-Fleshed Japanese Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in early spring or in fall in mild climates in well-drained soil in full sun; provide a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer such as Santa Rosa nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer nearby. Black Beauty is a Japanese-type plum grown for its striking dark purple-black skin, which encloses firm, amber-yellow flesh with a sweet, well-balanced flavor and good, meaty texture that holds up well to handling and eating fresh out of hand. The vigorous tree is a reliable commercial and home-orchard producer in California-style plum growing regions, valued for combining attractive dark color with genuinely good flavor rather than color alone. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest once fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and has developed full dark color, since plums ripen further off the tree but develop the best flavor with some vine-ripening first.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, rocky or sandy tropical soil in partial shade to full sun; black calabash grows naturally in tropical coastal hammocks and forest edges of Central America, the Caribbean, and southernmost Florida, tolerating shade and coastal conditions well.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average tropical soil in partial shade to full sun in zone 10–12; black calabash is a tropical tree of the Bignoniaceae family (the same family as trumpet creeper and catalpa) native to Central American and Caribbean coastal forests, producing unusual, large, round-to-oblong, gourd-like fruits with extremely hard, black shells when mature. The hard shells are used throughout Central America and the Caribbean to make maracas, rattles, cups, bowls, and other traditional crafts and musical instruments — the same traditional use as the unrelated calabash gourd (Lagenaria). The fleshy inner pulp is eaten by bats and birds, which disperse the seeds. The flowers, which appear directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory), are interesting botanical curiosities. Adapted to partial shade of tropical forest edges and hammocks. A rare conversation piece for south Florida collectors and native plant enthusiasts.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil; plant two or more trees for better fruit set. Seeds require cold stratification for 90 days.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; black cherry is arguably the most ecologically important fruiting tree in eastern North America, supporting the larvae of over 400 species of moths and butterflies (more than almost any other tree genus), providing early-spring nectar in its white flower racemes, and producing thousands of small black cherries in summer that are consumed by over 70 species of birds — robins, waxwings, thrushes, catbirds, woodpeckers — as well as bears, foxes, and raccoons. The small black cherries are edible and intensely flavorful, traditionally used for cherry wine, jelly, and syrups. The wilted leaves and seeds contain prussic acid and are toxic to livestock. The bark has traditional medicinal use as a cough suppressant. A fast-growing native tree (2–3 feet per year) that can seed prolifically.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted-cutting stock in spring in full sun; it reliably sets both a breba and a main crop in warm climates, giving two harvest windows.
directions: Black Genoa is a widely grown Italian heirloom producing purplish-black skinned fruit with deep amber-pink flesh and a rich, sweet flavor that many growers rank among the best dark-skinned figs for fresh eating. It is a reliably heavy producer of both an early breba crop on overwintered wood and a larger main crop on new growth, giving an extended summer-into-fall harvest in warm climates. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and prune in winter to control size, since trees can become quite large and dense without management. Long popular in California and Australian home orchards, it performs well in Mediterranean and humid subtropical climates alike.

common_name: Black Gilliflower Apple (Elongated Deep Purple-Red New England Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Black Gilliflower, also historically known as Sheepnose for its distinctive elongated, conical shape said to resemble a sheep's nose, is a New England heirloom dating to the 1700s prized for skin that darkens to a deep, dusky purple-red so intense it appears nearly black, one of the most visually striking older American apple varieties. The dry, mildly sweet, somewhat coarse flesh is not as juicy as many modern apples but was historically valued for baking whole and for its distinctive appearance in mixed heirloom displays. The tree is a dependable, long-lived bearer typical of old New England farmstead varieties; harvest in fall once fruit fully darkens, and expect moderate storage life typical of the era's cooking apples.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Jackfruit is frost-sensitive — temperatures below 32°F can damage foliage and temperatures below 28°F can kill established trees. In zone 9a plant only in the most frost-protected microclimate (south or west wall exposure) and protect young trees with frost cloth during the first 3–5 winters until the trunk thickens. Black Gold is a dwarf or semi-dwarf jackfruit selection producing smaller trees (15–20 feet vs 40–60 feet for the standard species) with earlier bearing (3–4 years from transplant) and sweet, aromatic, yellow-fleshed fruits weighing 10–20 pounds — manageable for home production versus the massive 30–60 pound fruits of some species seedlings. Trees require deep, well-drained soil — jackfruit is very intolerant of standing water or waterlogged roots.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — jackfruit is intolerant of waterlogged soil and will decline rapidly if the root zone remains saturated; Black Gold Jackfruit is a named, semi-dwarf cultivar of Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus), the world's largest tree-borne fruit, selected for compact tree size and superior fruit quality — sweet, aromatic, deep yellow flesh with lower latex content than seedling trees, making the fruit more pleasant to prepare and eat. Jackfruit is one of the most nutritionally complete and calorie-dense tropical fruits: the ripe, sweet arils (seed pods) are eaten fresh and have a flavor combining banana, pineapple, and mango; the unripe green fruit, with its fibrous, neutral, meat-like texture, has become internationally popular as a plant-based meat substitute in pulled pork, tacos, curries, and other savory dishes. The combination of edible ripe fruit and valuable unripe culinary use gives jackfruit two entirely different roles in the kitchen — one as a sweet tropical fruit and one as a versatile vegetable protein. In the warmest zone 9 microclimates and zone 10 the semi-dwarf Black Gold produces a manageable ornamental and productive fruit tree that brings one of the most unique and globally significant tropical fruits into the home garden.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; seeds require double dormancy of 18+ months and are best obtained from a specialist nursery. The plant typically begins fruiting in 4-6 years from transplant.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; black hawthorn is a widespread native of western North America from Alaska to California and east to the Rocky Mountains, producing distinctive shiny black fruits (rather than the red of most hawthorns) that ripen in late summer. The blackish-purple haws are sweet and flavorful, traditionally eaten fresh and dried by Pacific Northwest Native peoples including the Klallam, Nlaka'pamux, and many others. The thorny thickets provide exceptional nesting habitat for songbirds. White spring flowers attract numerous pollinators. The fruit is also made into jam, jelly, and wine. More tolerant of wet soils than most hawthorns and common along stream banks in its native range.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall at 1-2 inches depth in well-drained soil; hickory nuts need natural cold stratification over winter to germinate in spring. Black hickory develops a long taproot quickly, so transplant only small seedlings before the taproot becomes difficult to move.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, rocky, or red clay soils in full sun; black hickory is the most drought-tolerant hickory native to Texas and the Coastal Plain, naturally inhabiting dry sandy uplands, rocky ridges, and sandstone hills where other hickories fail. The nuts are small and have thick shells relative to their edible kernel, but are consumed by squirrels, deer, wild turkeys, and other wildlife that provide the ecological services of seed dispersal. The dark, rough, blocky bark becomes increasingly distinctive with age. Like all hickories, black hickory is very slow to establish (most growth goes underground in early years as the taproot develops) but eventually becomes a long-lived, tough, low-maintenance tree well-suited to the challenging dry sandy soils of east Texas and Oklahoma. Important wildlife food tree for dry upland woodland habitats.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or set out container plants in spring after frost danger passes; give it full sun and good drainage.
directions: Black Ischia is a small-to-medium fig with near-black, purple-black skin that lacks a pronounced neck, opening to reveal strawberry-pink to red flesh with a rich, sweet flavor. Long grown on the Mediterranean island of Ischia and popularized in American gardens through heirloom fruit exchanges, it typically bears both a light early breba crop and a heavier main crop in warm climates. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and prune lightly in winter to maintain an open, easily harvested framework, since the thin skin bruises readily. It is valued by home growers for its rich flavor rather than shipping quality, making it best suited to dooryard planting rather than commercial production.

common_name: Black Jack Fig (Compact Semi-Dwarf Dark-Fruited Container Fig)
plant_note: Plant cuttings or nursery plants in spring in full sun; Black Jack is semi-dwarf (8–12 feet) and can be maintained smaller with annual pruning, making it well-suited to containers (15-25 gallon) and small spaces. In zone 9, Black Jack typically produces two crops: a small breba (early) crop on old wood in June and a larger main crop on new wood in August–October. Protect from frost below 20°F when young; established trees tolerate brief periods to 15–18°F.
directions: Plant nursery trees or rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; prune in late winter to maintain size and shape. Black Jack is a compact, semi-dwarf fig tree — a sport or selection from the Brown Turkey class producing somewhat smaller stature (8–12 feet rather than the 15–25 feet of standard fig trees) while bearing large, richly flavored dark purple-black fruits. The moderate compact habit makes Black Jack one of the most practical fig varieties for residential gardens and particularly well-suited to large containers (20–25 gallon) for small spaces, patios, and areas where a standard-sized fig would be too large. The fruits are medium to large, elongated, with dark purple-black to near-black skin and deep strawberry-red flesh — a visually dramatic appearance that makes the fruits ornamentally attractive at the harvest stage. The flavor is rich, very sweet, and fig-like with deep, complex, sweet notes that improve when fruits are allowed to fully ripen on the tree (they should feel soft and droop slightly at the neck before harvest). Black Jack produces reliably in zone 7–11 with proper cold protection when young. In zone 9, the long, warm growing season allows excellent main crop development and often a bonus early-season breba crop.

common_name: Black Madeira Fig (Prized Dark-Skinned Strawberry-Red Fleshed Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; moderate vigor and best adapted to warmer zones with a long growing season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Black Madeira, of Portuguese origin, is prized among serious fig growers as one of the finest-flavored dark fig varieties available, producing deep purple-black skinned fruit that opens to reveal dense, richly colored strawberry-red flesh with an intensely sweet, complex flavor that has earned it a devoted following among fig collectors and specialty growers. The tree has moderate vigor compared to some more rampant fig varieties and performs best with a long, warm growing season to fully ripen its crop and develop peak flavor. Given its more particular growing requirements and somewhat lower yields than workhorse varieties, it is often grown as a specialty or connoisseur's fig alongside more prolific everyday varieties rather than as a primary production tree.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees; Black Mission is the standard commercial California fig and performs best in hot, dry summer climates with low humidity.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Black Mission fig is the most widely grown commercial fig in California, introduced by Spanish Franciscan missionaries in the 1700s and now the cornerstone of the California fig industry. It produces two crops yearly in favorable climates — a breba crop on last year's wood in early summer, and a main crop in late summer to fall. The large, purplish-black figs have pink to reddish flesh with an intensely rich, complex, sweet-jammy flavor that is among the finest of all fig varieties. Excellent fresh, dried, or made into preserves. It thrives in hot, dry conditions and is relatively drought-tolerant once established. In humid climates, fruit splitting and souring can be problematic; select LSU Purple or Celeste for the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger passes in a warm, sheltered position.
directions: The black mulberry is a slow-growing, long-lived tree bearing intensely flavored dark fruit far superior to that of white or red mulberries. Plant in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in a spot sheltered from cold winds. It is self-fertile, so one tree crops well, though the staining fruit is best sited away from paving. Prune only lightly in winter, as mulberries bleed heavily from large cuts.

common_name: Black Oxford Apple (Maine Heirloom Long-Keeping Purple-Black Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy and best adapted to zones 3-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Black Oxford originated in Paris, Maine in the 1790s and takes its name from its remarkably dark skin — deep purple, nearly black, and covered with a dusty blue-gray bloom — one of the most visually striking apples in American horticulture. Fresh off the tree in fall the dense, firm flesh is sharply tart, but Black Oxford is famous for its extraordinary keeping ability, mellowing and sweetening in cold storage over months and often holding excellent quality clear into spring, longer than almost any other apple variety. This long storage life made it historically valuable in northern New England before mechanical refrigeration, and it remains prized today by cider makers and heirloom orchardists both for its keeping quality and its distinctive appearance. Harvest in mid to late fall and store cool for the best results, tasting periodically since the flavor genuinely improves with age.

subcategory: West African edible black plum ornamental shade tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, deep, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in zone 10–12; Black Plum (West African Plum, Loko, Donno) is a large, spreading shade tree native to the Sahel, savanna, and Sudan zones of West and Central Africa — highly valued across sub-Saharan Africa for its sweet, purple-black, date-sized plum-like fruits eaten fresh and for jam, its leaves consumed as a cooked vegetable, and its exceptionally dense, hard, golden-yellow wood — one of the most economically important multi-use agroforestry trees in West Africa.
directions: Plant Vitex doniana in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; highly drought-tolerant once established; prune young trees to develop good branching structure; the tree grows slowly at first then more vigorously once the root system is established. Black Plum is one of the most important multi-purpose trees of the African sahel and Sudan savanna zone — spread across a vast belt from Senegal and Gambia through Mali, Burkina Faso, Nigeria, and east to Sudan, Uganda, and Kenya. The sweet, date-like, purple-black fruits are eaten fresh throughout the region, made into local beverages, and dried for storage; the nutritional profile includes iron, calcium, and vitamins. Young leaves are cooked and eaten as a vegetable (especially important during the 'hungry season' before the harvest) and the leaves are also used medicinally for fever and rheumatism. The dense, golden-yellow heartwood is highly prized for furniture, carvings, drums, and mortars; a single tree can be worth significant sums in local markets. In the Sahel agroforestry system, Black Plum is a valued component of parkland farming systems (farmer-managed natural regeneration) where it provides food, shade for crops, fodder, and materials. An outstanding drought-tolerant shade tree for zone 10–12 dry tropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost risk has passed; young trees are cold-sensitive and need protection until the trunk is at least 2 inches in diameter.
directions: Black sapote is a relative of the Asian persimmon; when ripe its flesh turns chocolate-brown and has a rich, pudding-like flavor often described as chocolate mousse. Trees are dioecious or polygamous — plant at least two seedlings or a grafted female with a male nearby for reliable fruiting. They prefer well-drained, fertile soils with a pH near 6.5 and are sensitive to frost, waterlogging, and salt winds. Harvest when the skin turns from bright olive-green to olive-yellow-green and the fruit gives to very gentle pressure; leave at room temperature 5–7 days until the inside is completely dark and custardy.

plant_note: Plant in frost-free conditions with well-drained soil; black sapote is more drought-tolerant than many tropical fruits once established and tolerates mild neglect in zone 10 conditions.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in frost-free conditions; black sapote produces tomato-sized fruits with thin green skin that turns olive-yellow at full ripeness, concealing soft black pulp with a rich, sweet, chocolate-like flavor that famously resembles chocolate pudding — often eaten directly from the skin with a spoon. A relative of persimmons, it must be completely soft before eating; hard fruits are extremely astringent. Excellent used in smoothies, ice cream, mousses, and as a low-fat substitute for chocolate in baked goods. Trees are moderately fast-growing and begin bearing 3–5 years from transplant; an outstanding conversation piece and genuinely delicious tropical fruit for zone 10–12 gardens.

common_name: Black Spanish Grape (Lenoir Grape, Jacques Grape, Historic Gulf Coast Red Grape)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Black Spanish (Lenoir) is one of the oldest cultivated grapes in Texas and the Gulf South — a Vitis aestivalis hybrid of ambiguous parentage that has been grown in Louisiana and Texas since at least the 1800s and demonstrates exceptional Pierce's disease resistance combined with heat tolerance, making it the most historically important red wine grape of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — Black Spanish is notably drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the thin, rocky soils of the Texas Hill Country; train on cordon system; prune in late winter; fruit ripens in July–August in the Gulf South; the small, dark blue-black berries are very juicy with moderate tannins and produce a robust, full-bodied red wine and excellent red grape juice. Black Spanish (also called Lenoir, after a French viticulturalist named Lenoir who promoted it, or 'Jacques' after a French settler who may have introduced it) is a historic American hybrid grape variety that has been cultivated in Louisiana, Texas, and the broader Gulf South since before the Civil War — one of the earliest wine grapes to be grown commercially in Texas. Its precise parentage is disputed (likely a complex hybrid of Vitis aestivalis or Vitis berlandieri with other American species, possibly with some vinifera ancestry from early French colonial plantings), but its performance characteristics are well-established: Black Spanish is exceptionally tolerant of Pierce's disease, heat, and drought. In the 19th century, when European settlers attempted to establish vineyards in the South with vinifera varieties, virtually all of these plantings failed within a few years due to Pierce's disease — but varieties like Black Spanish, which incorporated native American species with natural resistance, survived and produced fruit year after year. This made Black Spanish the cornerstone of the early Texas and Louisiana wine industries, and it remained the dominant red grape in Texas through much of the early 20th century. The wine produced is dark, deeply colored, with robust tannins and an earthy, slightly rustic character that is quite different from European reds but has its own distinctive appeal. Modern Gulf Coast winemakers continue to work with Black Spanish as a component of blended wines.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Black Tartarian is self-unfruitful and requires a pollinizer; it is itself an excellent pollinizer for Bing and Rainier and is often planted as a pollinizer companion.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Black Tartarian is one of the oldest and most reliable sweet cherry cultivars in cultivation — an early-season cherry with large, dark mahogany-red to nearly black, heart-shaped fruit with sweet, rich, dark-red flesh. It ripens 1–2 weeks before Bing and is one of the first sweet cherries to mature in a given location. The fruit is softer than Bing or Rainier and does not store or ship as well, making it particularly suited to home garden production and immediate fresh consumption. Black Tartarian also serves as an excellent pollinizer for most other sweet cherry varieties. It was imported from Russia in the early 1800s and is one of the oldest sweet cherry cultivars still in commercial and home garden production. Trees are vigorous, relatively disease-resistant, and productive. Require 900+ chill hours; best suited to zones 5–8 in areas with reliable cold winters.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring; site carefully as the tree grows very large and produces juglone.
directions: Black walnut is a native North American species grown primarily for its richly flavored nuts and valuable timber. It produces high concentrations of juglone in its roots, leaves, and hulls, which is toxic to many garden plants including tomatoes, peppers, apples, and blueberries; maintain a 50–80 foot buffer from sensitive plants. Trees are monoecious and partially self-fertile but cross well with a second tree. Hulls stain skin and clothing an indelible dark brown; wear gloves when husking. Nuts are ready when hulls are yellow-green to black and dent when pressed; cure for 2–3 weeks after husking.

plant_note: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Blakeney Red is a vigorous, self-fertile perry pear, but still crops more heavily with a second variety for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Blakeney Red is a vigorous, self-fertile perry pear, but still crops more heavily with a second variety for cross-pollination. One of the most widely planted traditional English perry pears, originating in the Forest of Dean area of Gloucestershire, it produces a heavy, reliable crop of small, red-blushed pears on a large, vigorous, long-lived tree, valued by perry makers for moderate tannin and good juice yield that blends well in traditional West Country perry production. Unlike many perry pears, it is self-fertile, making it a more forgiving choice for an orchard with limited space for a dedicated pollinator tree, though a second variety still improves cropping. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, and let it sweat in a pile for a few days before milling and pressing.

common_name: Blanc du Bois Grape (Gulf Coast Pierce's-Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown vines in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Blanc du Bois is the most important white wine grape variety developed specifically for the Gulf Coast and Southeast — bred by Dr. John Mortensen at the University of Florida for resistance to Pierce's disease (the bacterial disease spread by the glassy-winged sharpshooter that kills European vinifera grapes throughout the South) while producing high-quality white wine in the warm, humid Gulf South climate.
directions: Train on a cordon trellis system in full sun; prune in late winter; Blanc du Bois ripens in June–July in the Gulf South, much earlier than northern grapes; the fruit is white-green to golden at maturity and produces crisp, fruity white wine with notes of melon, citrus, and tropical fruit; fruit can also be eaten fresh or made into juice. Blanc du Bois is the most important Gulf Coast white wine grape variety, bred by Dr. John Mortensen at the University of Florida's Levin College of Law agricultural breeding program (USDA-ARS Fort Pierce) specifically for the hot, humid climate of the American Southeast and Gulf South where European vinifera varieties cannot survive. The critical factor in Gulf Coast viticulture is Pierce's disease — a bacterial infection caused by Xylella fastidiosa spread by the glassy-winged sharpshooter leafhopper (Homalodisca vitripennis) — which kills European vinifera varieties (Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, etc.) within 1–5 years throughout the Gulf South. Blanc du Bois was developed as a complex hybrid incorporating Vitis champinii (heat-tolerant wild Texas grape) and other native American species to provide Pierce's disease resistance, while retaining enough vinifera quality characteristics to produce high-quality white wine comparable to European-style dry whites. The resulting wine is crisp, fruity, and aromatic with Muscat-like floral notes and good acidity — genuinely world-class for a Pierce's disease-resistant variety and the backbone of the emerging Gulf Coast wine industry. Blanc du Bois grapes ripen unusually early — in June to early July in zone 9a, compared to September ripening in northern vineyards — which allows harvest before the peak summer heat and humidity.
