Several Texas and Florida wineries produce award-winning Blanc du Bois wines that have helped establish the variety's reputation nationally.

common_name: Blenheim Apricot (Royal Blenheim, California Standard Apricot, Santa Clara Valley Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Blenheim is self-fertile and requires no cross-pollinator; it has a low chill requirement (approximately 400–600 hours, among the lowest of any standard apricot) making it particularly well-adapted to the mild winters of coastal California, the Sacramento Valley, and similar zone 7–9 climates where other apricots with higher chill requirements perform unreliably.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Blenheim is self-fertile and drought-tolerant once established; thin to 3–4 inches after June drop; harvest when fruits are deep golden-orange and begin to soften — Blenheim must be harvested and eaten within days of peak ripeness, as the aromatic, intensely flavored flesh does not hold. Blenheim (sold commercially as 'Royal Blenheim' to distinguish it from Moorpark, with which it shares British origins) was the commercial apricot standard of California for over a century, dominating the Santa Clara Valley apricot industry that made California's 'Apricot Capital' from the 1880s through the mid-20th century before urban development replaced the orchards. The variety's characteristics — low chill requirement, self-fertility, reliable production in California's mild winters, and exceptional flavor — made it ideal for the Central Valley and Bay Area climates where it had no commercial equal. The fruits are medium-sized, golden-orange with a red blush, with rich, highly aromatic, intensely flavored flesh that is considered by many apricot enthusiasts to be the most complex-flavored of any commercial apricot variety — a concentrated sweetness with floral, honeyed notes and classic apricot fragrance at peak ripeness that far surpasses the flavor of supermarket apricots harvested underripe for shipping. Blenheim's low chill requirement (400–600 hours) makes it a good choice for zone 7–9 gardeners where higher-chill varieties like Moorpark and Harcot may not receive adequate winter cold.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Blenheim Orange is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it cannot pollinate other apples and needs two different diploid varieties nearby.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Blenheim Orange is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it cannot pollinate other apples and needs two different diploid varieties nearby. An old English variety dating to the eighteenth century, it bears large, handsome, orange-red-flushed apples with dry, nutty, richly flavored flesh good for both fresh eating once fully ripe and for cooking, one of the classic dual-purpose apples that bridges the line between dessert and culinary use. As a triploid, it produces sterile pollen and requires two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination of itself and each other, a detail worth planning for before planting, and it makes a large, vigorous, long-lived tree. Harvest in mid-fall and let the fruit mellow in storage for a few weeks before eating fresh, since the flesh is at its best after a short period off the tree.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk has passed; blood oranges require cool winters for anthocyanin color development — they color best in climates with cold nights during ripening.
directions: Blood orange cultivars (Moro, Tarocco, Sanguinello) develop their signature ruby-red flesh and juice through the accumulation of anthocyanins, a pigment triggered by cool nights during fruit development — temperatures between 40 and 50°F for several weeks from late autumn through midwinter produce the deepest coloring. In frost-free tropical climates the flesh remains orange with little anthocyanin. Trees are self-fertile, medium-sized, and managed identically to other sweet oranges: plant in well-drained soil, fertilize with a citrus blend three times per year, and irrigate deeply but infrequently. Harvest from late winter through early spring when the flesh has developed full color and the fruit is sweet.

plant_note: Plant grafted stock in spring in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; blood oranges require a cool autumn to develop their characteristic red pigmentation (anthocyanins) — in zone 9, fall night temperatures below 60°F trigger the color development; without cool nights, the flesh remains orange.
directions: Plant grafted stock in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; fertilize with citrus formula in late winter, late spring, and early fall. Citrus × sinensis 'Moro' (Moro blood orange) is the most intensely red-fleshed blood orange variety — a Sicilian mutation of sweet orange in which the flesh, juice, and sometimes the rind develop stunning deep-red to near-purple color from anthocyanin pigments produced in response to cool autumn nights. The 'Moro' cultivar produces the deepest, most intensely colored blood-red flesh and dramatic dark-red juice of any blood orange, with a distinctive flavor that combines sweet orange with a raspberry-berry overtone from the anthocyanins. In zone 9, the cool fall and winter nights (below 60°F) trigger the red pigment development; in warmer climates the color development is minimal. Blood orange juice makes extraordinary cocktails, salad dressings, and sauces. The 'Tarocco' variety (less cold-hardy, zone 10) produces the best flavor; 'Sanguinelli' is another reliable variety. Blood oranges ripen December through March in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Bloomsweet is noticeably more cold-tolerant than true grapefruit, making it a better fit for zone 8b-9 gardens where standard grapefruit struggles.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Bloomsweet is a grapefruit-like hybrid selected for cold hardiness beyond that of standard grapefruit cultivars, producing pale yellow, thin-skinned, juicy fruit with a mild, less bitter flavor than classic grapefruit and only a light blush of the typical grapefruit tang. The tree's improved cold tolerance, credited to its mixed parentage, has made it a popular choice for gardeners in the cooler parts of the Gulf Coast citrus belt who want grapefruit-style fruit without the cold sensitivity of true Citrus x paradisi selections. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree, sweetening further if left to hang after coloring fully. Give young trees winter protection for their first several years in zone 8, since even improved hardiness has limits; mature trees tolerate brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s F with minimal damage.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in deep, moist, humus-rich soil beneath high canopy or on a woodland edge; fresh seed needs several months of cold stratification and germinates unevenly, so nursery-grown plants are the more reliable start.
directions: Give this large, coarse-leaved shrub a sheltered spot with dappled or half-day shade and consistently moist, rich soil, mimicking the Himalayan and Chinese forest margins it comes from. By autumn, established plants hang thick with startling metallic-blue, finger-like seed pods several inches long; split one open to reach the sweet, translucent, gelatinous pulp inside, which tastes something like watermelon or lychee, though the numerous black seeds must be spit out. It needs a male and female plant, or a self-fertile seedling, to set the curious pods reliably. Few other fruiting shrubs offer both genuine shade tolerance and such a conversation-starting harvest.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; blue bean shrub needs a second, genetically distinct plant nearby for reliable pod set and benefits from a sheltered site out of harsh drying wind.
directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; blue bean shrub needs a second, genetically distinct plant nearby for reliable pod set and benefits from a sheltered site out of harsh drying wind. Decaisnea insignis is a striking, large, multi-stemmed shrub from the Himalaya and western China with big, compound, tropical-looking leaves and drooping clusters of small yellow-green flowers in late spring, followed by the plant's signature feature — dangling, metallic blue, sausage-shaped seed pods in fall that give rise to its unsettling common name. The pods split open to reveal a translucent, gelatinous, mildly sweet pulp around black seeds that can be eaten fresh, similar in texture and flavor to a mild melon, though it is grown mostly as a conversation-piece ornamental rather than a serious food crop. It prefers a woodland-edge setting with shelter from wind and consistent moisture, and its architectural form and unusual fruit make it a standout specimen in a shaded border.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or pups in well-prepared soil after last frost; Blue Java is more cold-tolerant than most bananas and can handle brief dips to 22°F with some protection. In zone 8, established rhizomes often survive winters even when tops freeze.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Java banana is a cold-hardy hybrid distinguished by its striking silvery-blue unripe fruit that turns pale yellow when ripe and by the remarkably creamy, vanilla-like flavor of the flesh — so reminiscent of vanilla ice cream that it is commonly called the ice cream banana. The silver-blue color of the unripe fruit is caused by a natural wax coating on the skin. It is one of the hardiest bananas available, tolerating temperatures to 22°F without damage when established, which expands its range significantly compared to Cavendish and plantain types. The fruits are eaten fresh (with a scoopable ice cream-like texture) or frozen for a natural one-ingredient ice cream. A single pup planted in spring will produce a full bunch within 18 months in zone 9+.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; alternately, sow fresh ripe seed directly in late summer — blue passionflower germinates most reliably from very fresh seed; established plants die back to roots in zones 7–8 and resprout vigorously in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils; blue passionflower is the most cold-hardy of the fruiting passion vines, tolerating brief dips to 10–15°F when established roots are protected by mulch. The intricate blue, white, and purple flowers with their alien-looking filament corona rank among the most striking summer blooms of any garden vine, followed by oval orange-yellow fruits that are edible but bland compared to commercial passion fruit — grow it primarily for the spectacular flowers and cold hardiness. Dies to the ground in zones 7–8 but regrows strongly from deep roots; do not remove dormant crowns too early in spring.

plant_note: Train young plants onto a wall, pergola, or fence in part shade in spring, in fertile soil with reliable drainage; grow two plants together for markedly better fruiting.
directions: Train young plants onto a wall, pergola, or fence in part shade in spring, in fertile soil with reliable drainage, since this evergreen twiner from central China resents waterlogging even though it tolerates low light well. Small, fragrant purple-and-white flowers open in spring and are followed in a good year by sausage-shaped purple fruits with sweet, translucent pulp, though fruiting improves markedly when two plants are grown together. Its leathery, trifoliate evergreen leaves make it a valuable year-round screen for shaded boundaries where deciduous vines would leave a winter gap. Prune after flowering to control its vigorous twining growth.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; plant at least two different highbush blueberry cultivars for cross-pollination to maximize fruit set; Bluecrop requires 800–1000 chill hours, which limits its suitability in zone 9 compared to southern highbush cultivars.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Bluecrop is the gold-standard northern highbush blueberry cultivar — developed by the USDA at Beltsville, Maryland, and introduced in 1952, it remains the most widely planted highbush blueberry in commercial production worldwide and the benchmark against which other northern highbush cultivars are measured. The very large, firm, light-blue, mildly flavored berries are produced in long, loose clusters in mid-season (July in zone 6–7) and hold exceptionally well on the bush without dropping or softening. The fruit quality combines large berry size, excellent flavor, distinctive whitish bloom, and good resistance to cracking in rain that makes Bluecrop outstanding for both fresh eating and freezing. The vigorous, upright shrub grows 4–6 feet tall with attractive white urn-shaped flowers in spring, bright-blue fruit in summer, and outstanding red-orange to crimson fall color. Bluecrop requires 800–1000 chill hours and is best suited to zone 4–7; in zone 8 and warmer, southern highbush cultivars (Vaccinium corymbosum hybrids with V. darrowi) requiring only 200–400 chill hours are more appropriate. Plant with another mid-season highbush cultivar such as Blueray or Legacy for cross-pollination. Maintain strict soil pH below 5.5 using elemental sulfur and acidic fertilizers — pH above 6.0 causes severe iron chlorosis.

common_name: Bob Gordon Elderberry (Kansas State University Very Large Fruit Elderberry)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; plant at least two different elderberry cultivars for cross-pollination — Bob Gordon is self-fertile but produces significantly larger crops with a pollinator cultivar planted nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Bob Gordon was selected by James Millican from a wild elderberry population in Kansas and released through Kansas State University — it produces some of the largest individual berries of any American elderberry cultivar, with berry diameter significantly exceeding the standard wild-type, and heavy, pendant clusters of dark purple-black berries that ripen in late summer. American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) is a vigorously suckering native shrub producing flat-topped, white flower clusters (cymes) in June–July — large, fragrant, and excellent for elderflower cordials, vinegars, and baked goods — followed by heavy clusters of dark purple-black berries in August–September used for elderberry syrup, wine, jelly, and juice. 'Bob Gordon' performs well in the humid heat of Gulf South zone 8-9 conditions, though elderberries prefer the slightly cooler and more reliably moist soils of zone 7-8 for maximum production. In zone 9, provide consistent moisture and afternoon shade protection to maintain health through summer. The very large berry size and heavy production make Bob Gordon one of the top choices for home and commercial elderberry production in the eastern US. Plants spread by suckers to form colonies — remove suckers regularly to maintain a well-defined shrub form.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Bonanza is a genetic dwarf that stays compact enough for a large container or small patio bed, though its early bloom means it should be sited where late frosts are less likely to damage the flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Bonanza is a genetic dwarf apricot that naturally stays under six feet tall while still producing normal-sized, sweet, orange-fleshed fruit, making it one of the few apricots practical for a large container or a very small yard. Like most apricots it blooms quite early in spring, so a sheltered site away from low-lying frost pockets improves the odds of a good fruit set. The dense, compact form needs little pruning to maintain shape beyond removing crossing branches, and the tree is self-fruitful, requiring no separate pollinator variety.

plant_note: Plant the dormant or potted dwarf tree in spring; grown from a grafted tree, not seed.
directions: Bonanza is a genetic dwarf peach that fits easily on a patio yet produces full-size, sweet, rosy fruit. Its naturally compact habit and showy pink spring blossoms make it as ornamental as it is productive, ideal for containers and small yards. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and provide a large pot or a spot with room for the roots. Thin the young fruit for better size, prune in late winter to shape, and water consistently while fruit is developing.

plant_note: Plant the dwarf ornamental peach in spring; grown from a grafted tree.
directions: Bonfire is a compact ornamental peach grown chiefly for its striking deep-crimson foliage and pink spring flowers, though it can set small edible fruit. Its fiery color and dwarf size make it a dramatic focal point for patios and small gardens. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil in a large container or bed. Prune after flowering to maintain its tidy form, water regularly during the growing season, and expect the best leaf color in full sun.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs under 400 chill hours, performing well in zone 8-9 winters too mild for standard high-chill peaches.
directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. A California-bred freestone needing under 400 chill hours, Bonita performs well in zone 8-9 winters too mild for standard high-chill peaches. Fruit is medium to large, yellow-fleshed with a red blush, and has repeatedly scored among the top varieties in formal taste trials for its sweet, subacid flavor. It ripens in mid to late summer, later than most low-chill Gulf selections, which helps extend the home orchard's peach season. Self-fruitful and vigorous, a single tree sets a full crop without a pollinizer.

common_name: Bonnie Brae Lemon (California Heirloom Slender Lemon)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed, in a warm, well-drained, sunny site.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed, in a warm, well-drained, sunny site, giving this vigorous, somewhat thorny tree room to spread. Water consistently during establishment and avoid waterlogged soil, which quickly stresses lemon roots. Bonnie Brae produces distinctively long, slender, thin-skinned lemons with abundant tart juice and few seeds, and it can flower and fruit nearly year-round in mild climates. Once grown commercially in Southern California, it remains a sought-after heirloom for home growers who prize its exceptionally juicy fruit over its irregular, less market-friendly shape.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Booth is a Florida-selected cultivar suited to zones 10-12 and sheltered zone 9b microclimates. Hand-pollination with a small brush is strongly recommended for reliable fruit set.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in zones 10-12; Booth is a long-established Florida cherimoya selection prized for reliable production and good-sized, conical, mildly ribbed fruit with rich, sweet, custardy white flesh and the classic tropical flavor blend of pineapple, banana, and vanilla. It has a reputation as one of the more dependable croppers among named cherimoya cultivars in Florida's warm, humid subtropical conditions, which can otherwise be a challenging environment for a species that prefers the cooler, drier climate of its Andean homeland. As with all cherimoya, hand-pollinate by transferring pollen from freshly opened male-phase flowers to receptive female-phase flowers with a small brush in the morning hours, since the flowers' protogynous timing makes natural self-pollination unreliable. Grafted trees bear within two to four years; protect young trees from frost and give them consistent moisture during fruit development.

plant_note: Move container plants outdoors only once nights stay above 55°F, and bring them under cover well before the first fall cold front.
directions: Grow this understory shrub from the Colombian Chocó rainforest in a large pot of rich, moisture-retentive potting mix, since it wants filtered light and constant humidity rather than harsh full sun. It produces large, dense, brown fruits packed with a thick, tart pulp that is almost always processed into juice or preserves rather than eaten fresh. Because it is one of the most cold-sensitive fruiting plants grown by tropical fruit collectors, Gulf Coast and Florida growers keep it strictly as a greenhouse or sunroom container specimen and never leave it outside once temperatures dip toward 50°F. Consistent watering and high humidity are more important to fruit set than any particular soil type.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break, or container-grown trees in spring or fall; Bosc pear requires 600–900 chill hours (cool nights below 45°F) and performs best in zones 5–8; a cross-pollinator (Bartlett, Anjou, or Comice) must be planted within 100 feet for reliable fruiting, as Bosc is not self-fruitful.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5) soil; amend with compost before planting; Bosc pear requires a cross-pollinator within 100 feet — plant with Bartlett, Anjou, or Comice for best fruit set. Bosc pear (Beurré Bosc, also marketed as Kaiser in Europe) is a Belgian heirloom originating in the early 1800s and named for Louis Bosc, a French diplomat and naturalist; it is immediately distinguished from other pears by its elongated shape, long graceful neck tapering to a slender stem, and russeted skin ranging from golden-yellow to russet-brown — unlike the smooth, green or yellow skin of Bartlett and Anjou types. The flesh is white to cream, dense, crisp and aromatic when just harvested but quickly transitions to the typical soft, buttery, juicy pear texture; the flavor is spicy-sweet with hints of vanilla, cinnamon, and honey — considered by many pear enthusiasts among the most complex and interesting flavors of the major commercial pear varieties. Bosc ripens mid to late season (September–November depending on location), later than Bartlett; it is the superior pear for cooking, baking, and poaching because it holds its shape under heat better than soft-fleshed types, while also excellent for fresh eating at peak ripeness. Requires 600–900 chill hours; zones 5–8.

common_name: Bouche de Betizac Chestnut (Large-Nutted Blight-Resistant Hybrid Chestnut)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Bouche de Betizac benefits from a compatible pollinator chestnut nearby for the best nut set, though it shows some self-fertility.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator chestnut within range for the best nut production, since yields improve substantially with cross-pollination even in partially self-fertile cultivars. Bouche de Betizac is a French-bred hybrid between European and Japanese chestnut species, combining the large, sweet, high-quality nuts prized in European chestnut cookery with meaningful resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that devastated native American chestnut populations and continues to threaten susceptible European chestnut plantings. It bears precociously, often producing a first crop within just a few years of planting, and continues with heavy, reliable yields of large, easy-to-peel nuts on a vigorous, productive tree. Its blight resistance and large nut size have made it a popular choice for both commercial and home chestnut orchards seeking a reliable, disease-tolerant alternative to susceptible pure European chestnut cultivars. Harvest nuts as burs split and drop in fall, collecting promptly to avoid rodent and insect loss.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Bourbon coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Bourbon coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Named for the former French colonial name of Réunion Island, where it was first cultivated after being introduced from Yemen, this historic Arabica coffee variety is one of the parent lines behind many modern specialty coffee cultivars and is still prized by growers and roasters for producing sweet, well-balanced, complex cups, though its lower yield compared to newer hybrid varieties has made it less common in large-scale commercial production. Like other Arabica coffees it grows best in the dappled shade of taller companion trees, mimicking its native highland forest understory habitat, and needs consistent warmth and moisture without ever standing in wet, waterlogged soil. Water regularly but ensure good drainage, provide filtered shade, and expect the first coffee cherry harvest after three to four years of growth.

plant_note: Plant cutting-grown stock in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; it ripens its main crop mid-to-late season, so it suits regions with a long, warm growing season.
directions: A classic fig of Provence, Bourjassotte Grise bears medium-sized fruit with a distinctive grayish-brown to violet-tinted skin covering deep strawberry-red flesh with a rich, sweet, complex flavor long prized in French markets. The tree is moderately vigorous and reliably productive once established, generally favoring a single strong main crop over a heavy breba crop. Plant in full sun with good air circulation, since the thin skin is prone to splitting after heavy rain near harvest. It is best suited to long, warm-summer climates where the late-season fruit has time to fully ripen before cool weather arrives.

plant_note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; atemoya generally needs hand pollination for reliable fruit set in US gardens, since its natural beetle pollinators are absent.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bradley is a Florida-developed atemoya cultivar valued for ripening later in the season than Gefner, extending the atemoya harvest window into late fall and helping spread out the crop for home growers with more than one tree. Like other atemoya cultivars it produces rich, custardy, sweet flesh with tropical vanilla and pineapple notes, and benefits from hand pollination for the most reliable and largest fruit set. Harvest when fruit begins to soften slightly and the skin color lightens, then finish ripening at room temperature before eating.

common_name: Braeburn Apple (Crisp Aromatic New Zealand Sweet-Tart Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Braeburn needs roughly 700–800 chill hours and a compatible pollinator such as Gala or Golden Delicious flowering at the same time.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and provide a cross-pollinator, since Braeburn is not reliably self-fruitful. Discovered as a chance seedling near Motueka, New Zealand in 1952, it quickly became one of the most widely exported dessert apples of the late 20th century for its dense, crisp flesh and layered sweet-tart flavor with a faint spice note. Fruit ripens late in the season and colors in streaky red over a green-gold background; it keeps exceptionally well in cold storage, often holding good eating quality for months. Thin heavy fruit sets in early summer to improve size and prevent biennial bearing.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Bramley's Seedling is a vigorous, triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby and ample permanent space.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Bramley's Seedling is a vigorous, triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby and ample permanent space. Grown from a pip planted in Nottinghamshire, England around 1809, this is the definitive British culinary apple, producing very large, bright green, sharply tart fruit that cooks down into a smooth, fluffy puree prized above nearly all other apples for pies, sauces, and traditional English cooking, though it is far too acidic and firm-fleshed for most people's taste eaten fresh off the tree. As a triploid it produces sterile pollen and needs two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for cross-pollination, and it makes a notably large, vigorous, long-lived tree that benefits from ample permanent space and a sturdy semi-standard or standard rootstock. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fully ripe, and the acidic fruit stores exceptionally well through winter when kept cool, making it a valued keeper for a home cook's cooking apple supply.

subcategory: Amazonian iconic edible nut canopy tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic tropical soil in zone 10–12; Brazil Nut is an enormous Amazonian canopy tree — one of the largest trees in the Amazon rainforest — bearing hard, cannonball-sized woody seed capsules (each containing 8–25 edible seeds) that require orchid pollinators and large mammals like agoutis for reproduction, and one of the most commercially important non-timber forest products in the Amazon.
directions: Plant Brazil Nut trees in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with adequate space for their ultimate enormous size; they require mycorrhizal fungi associations established in forest soil for optimal growth; fruiting does not begin until trees are 10–15 years old and requires the presence of orchid bees (Eulaema spp.) for pollination of their complex flowers — making commercial fruiting difficult outside the Amazon Basin. Brazil Nut trees are among the most ecologically important trees in the Amazon — their hard, 4-inch woody seed pods (cocos) fall from the canopy with enough force to be fatal, making harvesting genuinely dangerous; they are collected by harvesters who enter the forest after the natural fall season. The seeds (nuts) are extraordinarily rich in selenium — a single Brazil nut provides the recommended daily allowance — and are one of the world's most nutritionally dense foods. Brazil Nut is also an indicator of primary forest health: the trees only reproduce successfully in intact, undisturbed Amazonian rainforest where their Euglossine bee pollinators (attracted exclusively by certain orchid species) and agouti seed dispersers are both present. This extraordinary ecological dependency makes Brazil Nuts one of the best arguments for conservation of intact Amazonian forest, as deforestation eliminates both the trees and their irreplaceable ecosystem partners.

common_name: Brazil Nut Tree (Para Nut, Castanheiro do Para)
plant_note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring; brazil nut trees require deep, fertile, well-drained tropical soil and high humidity — they are strictly zone 11-12 trees that rarely fruit outside their native Amazonian habitat; grown in the US primarily in south Florida and Hawaii as specimen trees.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, moist to wet tropical soil; Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) is one of the largest trees of the Amazon rainforest, reaching 150 feet tall, and requires 10–20 years from seed to first fruiting in optimal conditions. The pods (actually large, woody capsules weighing up to 5 lbs) each contain 8–24 seeds (the 'nuts') and fall from height, posing a safety hazard — harvest sites require protective gear. The Brazil nut ecosystem depends entirely on the orchid bee (Eulaema sp.) for pollination and the agouti (a large rodent) for seed dispersal, making it nearly impossible to grow commercially outside its native ecosystem. Trees in south Florida and Hawaii produce limited fruit but are grown primarily as impressive specimen trees; the heavy, dense, rot-resistant wood is also extremely valuable.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Brazilian guava is more cold-tolerant than common guava (Psidium guajava) and can survive brief frosts in the warmer parts of zone 9. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and is notably resistant to guava wilt disease, making it valuable in areas where common guava struggles.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in zones 9–11; Brazilian guava (also called cas in Costa Rica) is a small to medium-sized tree native to tropical America that produces heavy crops of small, round fruits with white, aromatic, pleasantly sour flesh — highly prized throughout Latin America for fresh-squeezed juice, fruit nectars, jellies, fermented beverages, and agua fresca. Unlike common guava, it shows considerable resistance to the devastating guava wilt fungus (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. psidii) and is more tolerant of occasional frosts, making it a practical choice for gardeners at the cool edge of the tropical fruit range in zones 9–10. Trees begin producing in 3–6 years from transplant and fruit prolifically once established, often producing two crops per year in warm climates. Fruits drop quickly when ripe and should be harvested promptly or they will be taken by wildlife.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; breadfruit is one of the most productive food plants in the tropics and is propagated from root cuttings or air layers rather than seed, as most cultivated varieties are seedless. Give each tree ample space — at least 25–40 feet — as the canopy spreads broadly and the tree grows rapidly to 40–85 feet tall.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis) is a Polynesian staple food tree that has been cultivated throughout the Pacific and Caribbean for centuries, prized for its large, starchy fruit that can be roasted, boiled, fried, or dried into flour — providing a remarkably complete carbohydrate staple that sustained entire island civilizations. A single mature tree can produce 50–200 or more large fruits per year, yielding hundreds of pounds of nutritious food with minimal inputs. Most improved varieties are seedless triploids propagated from root suckers or cuttings; plant these for the fastest fruiting and best productivity. Trees are highly sensitive to frost and cold winds, but once established in a frost-free tropical location they are vigorous, long-lived, and capable of producing fruit within 3–5 years of planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or root cuttings in spring in rich, deep, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; breadnut thrives in warm tropical and subtropical conditions and is best suited to zones 10–12 in the continental US, though protected specimens may survive in zone 9b.
directions: Plant in rich, deep, well-drained, moist, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free tropical conditions; in south Florida, protect young trees from the rare hard freeze. Artocarpus camansi (breadnut) is the seeded ancestor of the seedless breadfruit (A. altilis) and produces large, spiny, oblong to round fruits 8–12 inches long containing 20–50 large, protein-rich seeds embedded in creamy, starchy, edible flesh; both the seeds and flesh are eaten. The seeds (when boiled, roasted, or ground into flour) are the primary food value of breadnut, tasting somewhat like chestnuts or macadamia nuts — they are a traditional protein-rich staple in the Pacific Islands and Philippines (where the tree is called 'kulo'). The flesh (ripe) is sweet and may be eaten similarly to breadfruit. The large, deeply lobed, tropical leaves and rapid growth rate make breadnut an impressive specimen tree in tropical gardens. Breadnut is native to New Guinea and the Philippines and widely naturalized in tropical America; it is closely related to jackfruit, durian, and the edible fig within the family Moraceae.

plant_note: Plant grafted, bare-root or container trees in early spring or fall while dormant; Breda Giant is self-fertile and needs no pollinator. Choose a sheltered, sunny site, as the large white spring flowers can be damaged by hard late frosts.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Breda Giant is a classic Dutch medlar selection prized for producing unusually large, russeted brown fruit on a small, gnarled, ornamental tree with showy white spring flowers and good fall color. Fruit is rock-hard and inedible at harvest in late fall and must be 'bletted' — stored in a cool place for several weeks after the first frosts until it softens and browns internally to a soft, spiced, wine-like custard texture before eating fresh or making jelly and butter. The tree is very cold-hardy, tolerates poor soils, and is largely pest- and disease-free, making it an easy, low-maintenance addition to a home orchard once its unusual harvest-and-ripen routine is understood.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted or air-layered tree; move outdoors after frost.
directions: The Brewster lychee is a classic favorite bearing sweet, juicy fruit encased in a glossy red shell over fragrant white flesh. This subtropical evergreen prefers hot, humid summers and needs a brief cool period to trigger flowering. Grow a grafted or air-layered tree in full sun with acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and shelter it fully from frost. Keep the root zone consistently moist, mulch heavily, and protect young trees from wind while they establish.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost risk; in zone 9 plant March–May. Brogdon is one of the most cold-tolerant named avocado cultivars, surviving temperatures as low as 22–24°F — making it viable in zone 9a and the warmer parts of zone 8b with microclimate protection. The dark purple-black skin color that develops at full ripeness is not present in all stages of maturity; harvest based on days from flowering rather than color alone.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — root rot in heavy wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable; Brogdon is a Florida-developed avocado cultivar prized as one of the most cold-hardy named avocado varieties, making it the top choice for gardeners in zone 9a and the warmer parts of zone 8b who want to grow avocados at the northern edge of their hardiness range. The medium-to-large fruits develop deep purple-black skin when ripe — the color change from green to dark purple indicates increasing maturity, but fruits may be harvested slightly early and ripened indoors. The flesh is creamy, rich, and flavorful with excellent avocado oil content. Brogdon has Guatemalan race genetics that contribute its cold hardiness — Guatemalan race avocados are considerably more cold-tolerant than West Indian race types and can survive light frosts. In zone 9 Brogdon is one of the few avocado varieties that can survive the occasional subfreezing nights that occur during cold winters, making it the recommended variety for the most frost-challenged avocado planting sites.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a frost-free or nearly frost-free location.
directions: The bronze loquat is grown both for its striking coppery new foliage and small, tart edible fruit. Plant in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered position, as the flowers and young growth are frost-sensitive. Water regularly while establishing, then only during dry spells once mature. Prune after fruiting to shape the canopy and remove any frost-damaged tips.

common_name: Brown Select Satsuma (Premier Gulf Coast Satsuma Mandarin, Louisiana Commercial Standard)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in spring after frost risk passes; Brown Select Satsuma is one of the most important and widely grown satsuma mandarin selections for the Gulf Coast region, particularly in Louisiana, Mississippi, and southern Alabama where it was selected and evaluated for superior performance under Gulf Coast conditions. It ripens earlier than Owari (the other leading Gulf Coast satsuma) and produces exceptionally sweet, rich juice with the characteristic easy-peel, seedless Satsuma profile. The trees are moderately cold-hardy (tolerating temperatures to around 28°F briefly without major damage) and perform best in zone 8b–9b. Brown Select is named for L.H. Brown, the Louisiana citrus enthusiast who selected it. In zone 9, the fruit typically ripens October–November, making it one of the earliest fresh-tree-ripened citrus available in the season. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil with full sun. Protect from frost below 28°F by covering young trees. Harvest October–November when fully orange. Brown Select Satsuma is a mandarin orange selection developed and popularized in Louisiana, where Satsuma mandarins have been grown commercially and in home gardens along the Gulf Coast since Japanese immigrants introduced the variety to Louisiana in the late 19th century. Satsuma mandarins (Citrus reticulata, specifically the 'Unshiu' or 'Satsuma' group) became an integral part of Gulf Coast culture — Louisiana's St. Bernard Parish and adjacent areas were once a significant commercial Satsuma production center, and Satsuma season (October–December) remains a beloved Gulf South annual event with home trees producing for family and community distribution. The name Satsuma comes from the Satsuma Province of Japan, where the variety was cultivated for centuries before reaching the United States. Brown Select's primary distinction from the more widely distributed Owari Satsuma is earlier ripening (Brown Select ripens 2–3 weeks earlier, in October rather than November) and what many Gulf Coast growers consider superior juice quality — slightly richer, sweeter, and with more complex flavor than Owari in typical Gulf Coast growing conditions. The tree is vigorous and productive under good culture, reliably producing heavy crops of 2-inch flattened-round fruits with loose, easy-peel skin, seedless flesh (typically zero to few seeds per fruit), and intensely sweet, juicy mandarin character. For zone 9 gardeners seeking a productive citrus tree, Brown Select Satsuma is often the first recommendation — earlier than most other mandarins, reliably productive, cold-tolerant enough for zone 9, and producing fruit of exceptional quality.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Brown Select is among the earliest-ripening of all satsuma mandarins — ripening in late September to October, 3–4 weeks earlier than Owari Satsuma. This earliness is its key distinguishing advantage, providing fresh homegrown citrus before any other commonly grown mandarin ripens. Cold hardiness is comparable to Owari (to approximately 15°F when fully dormant). Trees begin producing their first significant crop in the third or fourth year and reach full production in 6–8 years. Protect young trees with frost cloth during the first 2–3 winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — satsuma mandarins require excellent drainage and regular deep watering during the growing season; Brown Select is a distinctly early-ripening Satsuma mandarin developed and selected in Louisiana as an improvement on Owari Satsuma in terms of harvest timing — the trees produce ripe, full-flavored, easy-peeling mandarins in late September to October, making Brown Select the first commonly grown citrus to ripen in the Gulf South citrus season. The flavor at peak ripeness is comparable to Owari — sweet, aromatic, with the characteristic Satsuma complexity — but the earlier timing extends the homegrown citrus season by 3–4 weeks before Owari becomes ready. Brown Select carries the same exceptional cold hardiness as Owari (among the hardiest of all citrus to freezing temperatures) and the same practical advantage of loose, easily peeled skin and nearly seedless, juicy flesh. The combination of extreme cold hardiness, high productivity, and early ripening makes Brown Select specifically important to Gulf South citrus culture in the zones where winter cold is a genuine risk factor for citrus growing, and where starting the fresh fruit season as early as possible is valuable.

common_name: Brown Snout Apple (Herefordshire Bittersweet Cider Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Brown Snout is a late-ripening, reliably productive variety valued in traditional Herefordshire cider blends.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Brown Snout is a late-ripening, reliably productive variety valued in traditional Herefordshire cider blends. A traditional Herefordshire, England cider apple named for the distinctive russeted, elongated end of its small, dull orange-brown fruit, it is a well-regarded bittersweet variety contributing good tannin structure and moderate sugar to a blended cider, and it remains a component of some well-known commercial English cider blends. It ripens late in the season, later than many other classic cider varieties, and stores reasonably well after harvest before milling, giving cider makers some flexibility in scheduling the press. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press once fully ripe, since the astringent fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

plant_note: Plant grafted or air-layered trees in spring; in zone 10 plant March–June. Sapodilla is best suited to zones 10–11 but can be grown in protected zone 9b microclimates. Established trees tolerate brief temperatures to 27–28°F; young trees are damaged below 32°F. Brown Sugar is the preferred cultivar in South Florida for home orchards due to its superior flavor and consistent production. Trees fruit throughout the year with peaks in spring and fall.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil — sapodilla is one of the few tropical fruits that tolerates the alkaline, rocky soils of South Florida; Brown Sugar is a Florida-selected sapodilla cultivar named for its extraordinary sweetness and distinctive brown-sugar-molasses flavor that sets it apart from standard sapodilla varieties. The medium-sized, round to slightly oval, brown-skinned fruits have grainy, sandy-textured, translucent tan flesh that is so sweet it rivals candy — one of the sweetest fruits grown in North America, with a caramel-brown-sugar-molasses flavor that is universally appreciated even by people unfamiliar with the species. Sapodilla latex in the flesh (chicle, historically the base of chewing gum) gives the texture a slightly sticky, granular quality that is distinctive. Brown Sugar is considered the finest-flavored sapodilla cultivar for fresh eating and is the recommended variety for home orchards in zone 10 South Florida. The evergreen, windproof tree is also extremely drought-tolerant once established.

plant_note: Plant after the last hard frost; in colder zones grow in a container that can be moved to shelter.
directions: This cold-hardy fig tolerates temperatures near 10 degrees F, making it a good choice for cooler regions where most figs struggle. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and provide consistent moisture while fruit is developing for deep burgundy fruit with a pink center. In borderline zones, mulch heavily around the base or grow in a pot to overwinter in a protected spot. Prune in late winter to keep the tree at a manageable height and encourage a strong branching structure.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile loam in full sun; Bruce is partially self-fertile but bears more heavily when cross-pollinated by Methley or another low-chill Japanese plum variety; requires 250–400 chill hours.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Bruce is a classic Gulf Coast Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) developed by B.W. Stone at the Texas A&M Experiment Station in the early twentieth century and released in 1952 — one of the first specifically developed low-chill plum varieties adapted to the warm winters of the Gulf South. Bruce requires only 250–400 chill hours and ripens in late May to early June in zone 9, producing heavy crops of medium to large, red-skinned, yellow-fleshed plums with sweet, juicy, pleasant flavor that makes it excellent for fresh eating, jams, and preserves. The tree is vigorous, productive, and fairly disease-resistant under Gulf South conditions — it handles the humid climate better than many other plum varieties. Bruce is partially self-fertile but benefits significantly from cross-pollination: planting with Methley or another low-chill Japanese plum reliably doubles production. Prune annually in late winter to maintain open-center structure at 10–12 feet; thinning fruit to 3–4 inches after June drop produces full-sized, high-quality plums. Brown rot is the primary disease challenge for plums in humid climates; preventive fungicide applications during bloom and as fruit develops reduce losses significantly.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Brunswick has been grown in the southeastern United States for generations under the name 'Magnolia fig' and is one of the most widely distributed Southern heirloom figs, well-adapted to humid Gulf Coast conditions and reliable in zones 7–10.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Brunswick is a common fig type requiring no pollinator and one of the most widely grown figs in the American South under various regional names. Brunswick (known throughout the southeastern United States as 'Magnolia fig' and occasionally as 'Madonna fig') is an old European fig variety that has been grown in Southern gardens for at least 150 years, widely distributed through cuttings exchanged between generations of gardeners in the Gulf Coast states; the very large (3–5 oz), pear-shaped to oblong fruits have thin, pale yellowish-green to bronze-green skin, prominent ribs, and dark amber to brownish-strawberry interior flesh with moderately sweet flavor and good quality. A vigorous, large-growing tree that tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers better than many European fig varieties. Excellent for preserves, fresh eating, and drying. Because of widespread cutting-sharing over generations, plants sold or shared under the name 'Magnolia fig' may vary somewhat; most are similar to or identical with Brunswick.

common_name: Brush Cherry (Magenta Brush Cherry, Australian Cherry)
subcategory: tropical evergreen hedge and fruit shrub
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Brush cherry is an Australian native Syzygium grown in zone 9–12 primarily as an ornamental hedge and specimen tree, but producing abundant small, bright magenta-pink, edible fruits with a mild, slightly astringent, rose-water-like flavor.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; shape with hedge shears for formal use or allow to grow naturally as a specimen. Syzygium paniculatum (brush cherry or magenta brush cherry) is an Australian native tree or large shrub in the rose apple family (Myrtaceae) — closely related to rose apple (S. jambos) and other Syzygium fruit trees — that has become one of the most widely planted evergreen hedge, screen, and topiary plants in zone 9–12 landscapes in Florida, California, and the Gulf Coast. The plant produces glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green new growth that flushes copper-red to bronze-red as it emerges — making it attractive year-round — and responds well to shearing into formal hedge shapes. It produces abundant, 1/2-inch, bright magenta-pink fruits in summer that are edible but primarily astringent and mild, with a rose-water and mild apple flavor; they are eaten fresh in small quantities, made into jams, or used in drinks. The flowers are fluffy, cream-white, and produced in clusters; they attract bees and butterflies. As a hedge plant, brush cherry is outstanding: it maintains dense, dark-green foliage, responds well to clipping, and is salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant once established. More widely available in the nursery trade in Florida and California than most other Syzygium species.

common_name: Bryan Apricot (Texas Heat-Tolerant Home Orchard Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Bryan is self-fruitful and does not require a second apricot for pollination, and is among the more reliable apricot choices for Texas home orchards.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Bryan is self-fertile so a single tree can produce fruit without a pollinizer. A found seedling selection promoted by Texas A&M for its ability to bear fruit in the state's difficult apricot climate, Bryan is considered one of the more dependable apricots for Texas gardeners even though, like all apricots grown there, it does not crop every single year because of erratic late-winter warm spells followed by hard freezes. Fruit is medium-sized with the classic sweet-tart apricot flavor, good for fresh eating, preserves, and drying. Choose a site on a slope or high ground with good air drainage to reduce frost damage to the early spring blooms.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall for natural stratification, or cold-moist stratify for 90-120 days and plant grafted or seedling trees in spring, in deep, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, siting two or more trees for reliable pollination. Buartnut is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between butternut (Juglans cinerea) and Japanese walnut or heartnut (Juglans ailantifolia), combining some of butternut's rich, oily flavor with heartnut's heavier and more reliable nut production. Because true butternut has been decimated across its range by butternut canker disease, buartnut is grown by nut enthusiasts in colder climates as a hardier, often more disease-tolerant alternative that still carries much of the butternut flavor profile.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring; pair with another Japanese or American plum for cross-pollination.
directions: This cold-hardy hybrid plum produces juicy reddish-purple fruit with a distinctive sweet, spicy flavor often compared to bubblegum. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and include a compatible pollinizer nearby since Toka also serves as an excellent pollinator for other plums. Water consistently during fruit set and thin heavy fruit clusters to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Prune in late winter to an open-center form for good light penetration and air flow.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Buckingham, also historically known as Byers, is a large Southern heirloom apple with red-striped skin over a yellow-green background, carrying juicy, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh that made it a favorite for fresh eating, cooking, and cider across the mid-Atlantic and upper South for generations. The tree is well adapted to warmer Southern growing conditions than many Northern-bred heirlooms tolerate comfortably, making it a good option for gardeners in the middle latitudes of apple-growing range wanting a genuine historic Southern variety. Harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and expect reasonably good, though not exceptional, storage life in cool conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; buckthorn bumelia grows naturally in moist to mesic forests, forest edges, and bottomland woodlands across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in woodland garden settings; buckthorn bumelia is a native thorny shrub of the eastern Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, growing naturally in moist, mixed woodlands and forest edges from Virginia to Texas. Unlike the more drought-adapted gum bumelia, this species prefers moist woodland soils and grows in shade-adapted situations at woodland margins and in the forest understory. The small, black fruits in fall are eaten by numerous species of birds and the thorny branches provide valuable nesting habitat. A useful shrub for creating dense, bird-friendly hedgerows at the edge of native woodland garden designs in zones 6–9. The small white flowers in summer attract pollinators.

plant_note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; Bud 9 is grown as a fully dwarfing understock, not for its own fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; Bud 9 is grown as a fully dwarfing understock, not for its own fruit. Bred in Russia and among the most cold-hardy of the fully dwarfing apple rootstocks available, it produces a small, highly precocious tree roughly a quarter to a third the size of a full seedling tree, bearing fruit remarkably early, often within two to three years of grafting. Its combination of extreme size control and superior winter hardiness compared to similarly dwarfing rootstocks like M9 has made it a favorite for high-density home and commercial orchards in cold-winter regions. Provide permanent staking or trellising, since its small root system anchors poorly without support, and expect a compact, easy-to-harvest and easy-to-spray tree well suited to a small home orchard.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk passes; Buddha's hand is very cold-sensitive and ideal for container culture.
directions: Buddha's hand is a citron variety bearing distinctive finger-like lobes that contain only aromatic peel with no juice or pulp; it is valued entirely for its intensely fragrant zest used in baking, cocktails, and as a natural air freshener. Trees are self-fertile and small enough to grow in 15–20 gallon containers, making them suitable for patios and sunrooms in colder climates; bring indoors before temperatures fall below 32°F. Fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer three times per year and maintain consistent moisture to prevent fruit drop. Harvest when the fingers have turned fully yellow and the fragrance is intense; fruit can be stored at room temperature for 1–2 weeks.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Bulida is a rustic Spanish heirloom apricot with roughly 500 chill hours, adaptable and reliable where winter chilling is marginal.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Bulida, a long-cultivated Spanish heirloom apricot, bears large, golden-orange, sweet and juicy fruit on a rustic, adaptable tree with a history of reliable performance across variable climates. Its chill requirement, while not the lowest among apricots, is manageable in much of zone 8, and its tough, forgiving nature has kept it in cultivation for generations. As with other apricots, early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap, so good air drainage at the planting site helps protect the flowers.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed (which loses viability quickly) directly from a fallen cone into a deep pot, since the large seed and long taproot resist transplanting once established; move seedlings to their permanent frost-free site after the first year, protecting young trees through their first several winters.
directions: Sow fresh seed straight from a fallen cone into a deep container, since the large nut and long taproot make this towering Australian conifer resent transplanting once it is well rooted. Bunya pine takes many years to reach flowering and cone-bearing size but rewards patient growers with basketball-sized cones containing dozens of large, chestnut-flavored nuts that are traditionally roasted or boiled. Give it a wide, open site well away from structures, parking, and foot traffic, because mature cones can weigh more than twenty pounds and drop from a great height without warning. Young trees tolerate a light frost but need full protection for their first several winters in the coolest parts of their growable range.

common_name: Burbank Plum (Luther Burbank's Japanese Plum, Red Plum Classic)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Burbank requires cross-pollination from another Japanese plum such as Santa Rosa, Beauty, or Methley for reliable fruit set — it is not reliably self-fruitful; requires approximately 600–700 chill hours, making it adaptable to zones 5–9 with adequate winter cold; in zone 9a, a nearby companion is essential.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; thin fruit in spring to 4–6 inches apart; plant with a companion Japanese plum for reliable fruiting; Burbank produces medium to large round, dark red to mahogany-red fruits in mid-July to early August with amber-yellow flesh; the flavor is very sweet with tropical-fruity notes and low acidity — one of the best fresh-eating Japanese plums. Burbank plum is Luther Burbank's most famous and historically significant Japanese plum variety, released by the legendary plant breeder in the 1880s from his Santa Rosa, California plant breeding operations where he created an extraordinary number of new fruit varieties through deliberate hybridization and selection from germplasm imported from Japan. Burbank introduced Japanese plums (Prunus salicina) to American horticulture, obtaining seeds directly from Japan through the USDA and developing multiple varieties — but 'Burbank' became the most widely planted and commercially important of these, establishing the Japanese plum as a standard American backyard fruit and farm market crop throughout zones 5–9. The fruits are medium to large, round, with a distinctive deep red to mahogany skin and amber-yellow flesh that is firm, juicy, and very sweet with characteristic Japanese plum flavor — a somewhat tropical, stone-fruit sweetness with lower acidity than European plums. The combination of low chill requirement (approximately 600–700 hours), broad adaptability from zone 5 to zone 9, and excellent fresh-eating quality makes Burbank one of the most successful home garden stone fruits of the 20th century. Santa Rosa plum (also by Luther Burbank) is considered the superior variety by many modern tasters, but Burbank predates it and remains widely planted and recommended.

plant_note: Plant rooted pad cuttings in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; Burbank Spineless is propagated only from pads, never seed, and pads root readily after callusing for a week or two in a dry, shaded spot before planting.
directions: Plant rooted pad cuttings in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; Burbank Spineless is propagated only from pads, never seed, and pads root readily after callusing for a week or two in a dry, shaded spot before planting. Bred by Luther Burbank in the early twentieth century, this classic selection produces broad, paddle-shaped pads that are nearly free of the large spines typical of prickly pear, though fine, easily irritating glochids remain and gloves are still recommended when harvesting. Both the tender young pads (nopales) and the sweet, magenta-fleshed fruit (tunas) are edible, giving the plant dual value as a low-water vegetable and fruit crop for hot, dry gardens. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and needs little more than occasional pad thinning to control its spreading, architectural form.

common_name: Burgundy Plum (Small Dark-Red Japanese Plum for Zone 9, Very Low Chill Requirement)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Burgundy requires approximately 200–250 chilling hours — among the lowest chill requirements of any plum variety — making it one of the most reliable Japanese plum choices for zone 9 conditions where many standard plums (requiring 500–800 chill hours) fail to bloom and produce reliably. Plant with a cross-pollinator (Santa Rosa, Methley, or Beauty plum) within 50 feet for best fruit set, as Burgundy benefits significantly from cross-pollination. Burgundy ripens June–July in zone 9, producing small to medium fruits with deep red-burgundy skin. The compact tree size (smaller than most Japanese plum types) makes Burgundy practical for smaller home gardens where a standard-sized plum would be impractically large. Excellent for Gulf Coast gardens where low-chill performance is essential.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit clusters to 3–4 inches when marble-sized. Harvest when deep burgundy-red and slightly soft. Burgundy Plum is a Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) variety originating in California that has become one of the most valued low-chill plum varieties for gardeners in zones 8–10 where the winter chilling hours required by standard plum varieties are inconsistently accumulated. The variety takes its name from the fruit's distinctive deep red to burgundy-purple skin color — one of the darkest red Japanese plum varieties — which covers a sweet, amber-yellow flesh with good sweetness and mild plum flavor. The fruit is smaller than most Japanese plum types (typically 1.5–2 inches) but produced prolifically in good crop years, and the deep color makes Burgundy one of the most visually attractive plums when displayed at market or in fresh fruit arrangements. California agriculture recognized the low-chill potential of Burgundy and similar varieties in the warm Central Valley and southern coastal regions, leading to its adoption as a commercial variety in some California districts and its recommendation by cooperative extension services in low-chill regions nationwide. For Gulf Coast and Gulf South gardeners in zone 9, Burgundy represents one of the few plum varieties that can be grown reliably without the risk of insufficient chilling — a real advantage in an area where most stone fruit production is challenging.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently wet soil at a pond or wetland margin in full sun; buriti palm is a frost-tender wetland species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11 and grows naturally standing in shallow water.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently wet soil at a pond or wetland margin in full sun; buriti palm is a frost-tender wetland species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11 and grows naturally standing in shallow water. One of the most iconic palms of the Amazon basin and Venezuelan and Colombian llanos wetlands, it forms dense stands, called buritizais, in permanently waterlogged swamp forest, its tall, solitary trunk topped with a crown of large fan-shaped fronds and heavy clusters of reddish-brown, scaly-skinned fruit prized fresh or processed into juice, oil, and traditional foods across the Amazon region. It is an exceptionally slow-growing, long-lived palm that needs many years, often a decade or more, before reaching fruiting maturity, and its dependence on permanently wet or flooded soil makes it unsuitable for anything but a wetland or pond-margin planting. Provide constant moisture or standing water at the roots and full sun, and be prepared for a very long wait before any fruit harvest.

common_name: Burkett Pecan (Large-Nutted West Texas Commercial Pecan)
plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter while dormant in deep soil in full sun with reliable irrigation; Burkett is best suited to drier, low-humidity growing regions and needs a compatible pollinator, since it is notably more scab-prone than modern releases in humid climates.
directions: Discovered around 1912 as a chance seedling near San Saba, Texas, Burkett became one of the signature commercial pecan cultivars of the arid irrigated orchards of West Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. It produces a large, attractive, well-filled nut with excellent cracking quality that made it a favorite for retail and gift-pack sales under the Texas pecan label. Burkett performs best where humidity stays low, since it is notably more susceptible to pecan scab than modern disease-resistant cultivars and struggles in the humid Gulf South without an aggressive fungicide program. Give it full sun, deep soil, and reliable irrigation through nut fill, along with a compatible pollinator, for consistent large-nut production.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Burmese Grape (Latka, Mafai) is a medium-sized tropical tree native to Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, and Southeast Asia that produces its clustered grape-like fruits directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) — round, yellow to pinkish-red, thin-skinned fruits with juicy, sweet-sour white pulp surrounding large seeds.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Baccaurea ramiflora benefits from consistent moisture, high humidity, and protection from strong drying winds — mulch heavily and water regularly throughout the growing season. Baccaurea ramiflora (Burmese Grape, Latka, or Mafai) is an evergreen to semi-deciduous tree of the Phyllanthaceae family native to Bangladesh, Myanmar, Bhutan, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and south into the Malay Peninsula, where it is cultivated and semi-wild in forest edges, village gardens, and homestead agroforestry systems. The tree exhibits cauliflory — fruiting directly on the trunk and large branches in dense, pendulous racemes — producing small (1–2 inch), round to slightly oval, yellow-to-pinkish-red, thin-skinned fruits with translucent, white, sweet-sour, mucilaginous pulp around large seeds. The fruits are eaten fresh when ripe, made into jams, pickles, and fermented drinks, and are an important local market fruit in Bangladesh (where it is called Lotkon), Thailand (Mafai thet), and Myanmar. The tree is dioecious — male and female trees are separate — so plant at least one male with every 4–6 female trees. Baccaurea ramiflora is related to rambai (B. motleyana) and shares the genus's characteristic trunk-borne fruiting and acid-sweet flavor profile popular across Southeast Asian tropical fruit markets.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Burro is suited to zones 9b–12 and does not tolerate hard freezes well, though the rhizome may survive brief dips to 28–30°F with heavy mulching and a warm microclimate.
directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Burro banana (also called 'Chunky Banana', 'Horse Banana', or 'Bluggoe') is a distinctive ABB genome banana producing uniquely short, thick, blocky fruits (4–6 inches long but very broad and nearly square in cross-section with squared-off ridges) that stand out visually from the typical elongated banana shape. The fruits ripen from green to yellow and develop a characteristic tangy, lemon-tinged sweetness with a slightly chewy texture when fully ripe (skin may be greenish-yellow outside but flesh is cream-colored and sweet); when eaten green-ripe or cooked, the starchy texture is similar to plantain, making Burro a dual-purpose banana suited to both fresh eating when ripe and cooking applications when green. The trees are medium-large (10–14 feet) and vigorous in tropical to subtropical conditions, producing large bunches with up to 8 hands. Burro is well adapted to Gulf Coast humidity and heat in zones 9b–11 and is particularly popular in Mexican and Central American households for its unique dual-use character.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky calcareous or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; bustic grows naturally in tropical hammocks and rockland habitats of south Florida and the Keys, tolerating thin, rocky, alkaline oolitic limestone soils well.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; bustic (false mastic) is a medium to large evergreen tree native to the tropical hammocks and rockland forests of south Florida and the Caribbean, producing a dense, spreading canopy of large, glossy, leathery leaves. The small, white, fragrant flowers are produced throughout the year in clusters, followed by small, yellow to orange edible fruits with a sweet, apricot-mango-like flavor. The fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons, gray catbirds, and numerous other birds as a critical food source in the south Florida hammock ecosystem. The wood is extremely hard and durable — historically used for railroad ties and boat building. A superb shade tree for south Florida native landscapes, providing an evergreen canopy, wildlife food, and attractive flowers. One of the characteristic dominant trees of the endangered Miami rock ridge hammock ecosystem.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; a compatible pollenizer variety is required nearby.
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer variety planted nearby, since Butte is not self-fertile. Butte is a mid-to-late blooming California commercial almond noted for its heavy, consistent bearing, semi-hard shell, and small, plump kernel, and it is frequently interplanted with Nonpareil as a reliable cross-pollinating partner. Its later bloom compared with Nonpareil reduces exposure to early spring frost damage in many California growing regions.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring; choose disease-resistant hybrid selections due to butternut canker pressure on the native species.
directions: Butternut, or white walnut, produces rich, oily nuts with a milder, sweeter flavor than black walnut and is native to eastern North America. The species is severely threatened by Sirococcus clavigignenti-juglandacearum (butternut canker), so seek out canker-resistant cultivars or hybrids (butternut x heartnut crosses, or selections from university breeding programs) rather than straight-species seedlings. Like other walnuts, butternut is monoecious and partially self-fertile but benefits from a second tree nearby; it also produces juglone that can inhibit nearby sensitive plants. Harvest when the sticky, hairy green hulls begin to soften and turn yellow-brown in early to mid-fall; hull promptly and dry nuts for 2–3 weeks before cracking or storing.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Byrongold, released in 1985 by the USDA research station in Byron, Georgia, was bred for improved disease tolerance under the heavy fungal and bacterial pressure of the humid Southeast.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second compatible Japanese plum nearby for cross-pollination and best fruit set. Byrongold was released in 1985 by the USDA-ARS research station in Byron, Georgia, from Ozark Premier breeding lines, selected specifically to hold up better against the disease pressure common in humid Southeastern orchards while producing round, yellow-fleshed fruit with good eating quality. Its Southeastern breeding background makes it a solid choice for Gulf South home orchards facing the fungal and bacterial diseases that trouble many plum cultivars developed for drier climates. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy that promotes airflow and reduces disease pressure.

subcategory: Brazilian Atlantic Forest myrtaceous berry tree
plant_note: Plant in spring in partial shade to full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 9–11; Cabeludinha (Hairy Jaboticaba, Peluda) is a small to medium fruiting tree in the Myrtaceae family from the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil (Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, São Paulo) — closely related to the jaboticaba complex — producing clusters of small, round, yellowish-orange to golden fruits covered in short, fine hairs, with sweet-tart, grape-like translucent pulp used for fresh eating, juices, and liqueurs in the region.
directions: Plant Cabeludinha in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water consistently; maintain high organic matter; protect from hard frost below 28°F; harvest fruits when fully colored and give slightly to gentle pressure. Myrciaria glazioviana is one of the lesser-known but highly regarded wild fruits of Brazil's endangered Atlantic Forest — a small to medium-sized tree whose golden, hairy fruits are prized locally though almost unknown internationally. The fruits (roughly 0.5–1 inch diameter) are covered in short, fine hairs that give them a distinctly fuzzy appearance, unlike the smooth skin of the closely related jaboticaba (Myrciaria cauliflora).
