plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Conference sets a reasonable crop on its own but yields much better with a compatible pollinizer such as Comice or Bartlett.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Conference sets a reasonable crop on its own but yields much better with a compatible pollinizer such as Comice or Bartlett. The single most widely grown pear in the United Kingdom and one of the most recognizable European pears, it bears reliable, heavy crops of long, tapered, bronze-russeted fruit with sweet, juicy, fine-textured flesh that stores and ships notably well compared to more delicate dessert pear varieties. Its partial self-fertility, reliable heavy cropping, and good disease tolerance compared to some other European pears have made it a standard, forgiving choice for a home orchard, though a second variety nearby still meaningfully boosts yield. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the characteristic sweet, juicy texture, since pears ripen from the inside out and are best picked underripe from the tree.

common_name: Constance Eliott Passionflower (Fragrant Pure White Hardy Passion Vine)
plant_note: Plant container vines after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Constance Eliott is a fragrant, pure white-flowered selection of the cold-hardy blue passionflower.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils; Constance Eliott shares the exceptional cold hardiness of its parent species, blue passionflower, tolerating brief dips to 10 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit when established roots are protected by mulch. It bears creamy pure-white flowers with a soft, sweet fragrance, a cleaner, more subtle color than the blue-and-purple typical of the species, followed by oval orange-yellow fruits that are edible but mild-flavored. Dies to the ground in zones 7-8 but regrows strongly from deep roots; do not remove dormant crowns too early in spring.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in a sunny, well-drained site.
directions: Contender is a disease-resistant, cold-hardy, self-pollinating peach that produces abundant medium-to-large juicy freestone fruit across many climates. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water consistently during fruit development. Thin young fruit to about 6 inches apart to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Prune annually in late winter to an open-center shape for light penetration, and apply dormant sprays as needed to manage common peach diseases.

plant_note: Plant in spring in mild-winter regions.
directions: Coolidge is a self-fertile pineapple guava selection, useful where only one plant can be grown. Set it in full sun on well-drained soil and water consistently through the fruiting season for the best crop. It tolerates coastal conditions and light frost once established, and can be grown as a shrub or clipped hedge. Fruit is ripe when it drops naturally, so gather it daily from the ground beneath the plant.

common_name: Coratina Olive (High-Polyphenol Southern Italian Oil Olive)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Coratina is largely self-fruitful but produces a heavier crop with a second cultivar such as Frantoio or Leccino nearby, and is a vigorous grower that tolerates heat well.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Coratina is a Southern Italian olive cultivar from Puglia prized for producing intensely robust, bitter, peppery oil with exceptionally high polyphenol content — among the highest of any commonly grown olive cultivar — making it a favorite for growers and consumers seeking a bold, health-forward oil rather than a mild table experience. The tree is vigorous, heat-tolerant, and productive, and has performed well in warm-climate US oil-olive trials outside its native Mediterranean range, including in parts of the Southeast. Harvest early, while fruit is still green to just turning color, for the most intensely peppery, high-polyphenol oil; later harvest mellows the flavor but reduces polyphenol content. Coratina is largely self-fruitful, though yields improve with a second compatible cultivar nearby. Established trees are drought-tolerant and, like most olives, thrive on benign neglect once past the first two establishment years, needing supplemental water mainly during prolonged dry spells at fruit set.

plant_note: Plant acorns in fall in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; cork oak is native to the western Mediterranean and requires excellent drainage, moderate to low fertility, and dry summer conditions. It tolerates moderate drought and salt spray but not wet, heavy clay soil.
directions: Plant acorns in fall in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; cork oak is the source of virtually all wine and champagne cork in the world — the extraordinarily thick, spongy, deeply furrowed outer bark is harvested every 9–12 years from mature trees (a process called 'cork stripping') that does not harm the tree, as the bark regenerates completely. Portugal and Spain produce about 80% of the world's cork. The tree is an evergreen with a broad, spreading canopy and small, evergreen, slightly holly-like leaves. First cork harvest is typically at age 25 years; subsequent harvests every 9–12 years for the remaining 150–200 years of the tree's life. In California, cork oaks have been grown for over a century as ornamentals and heritage trees, thriving in the Mediterranean climate. An interesting tree with historical and economic significance for home gardeners in zones 7–10.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in late winter to early spring before bud break; fall planting also works in zones 5–7.
directions: Cornelian cherry is one of the earliest-blooming woody plants — small yellow flowers appear in late winter before the leaves — and the small, olive-shaped drupes ripen in late summer to a rich ruby red. Plant at least two seedlings or cultivars for best fruit set, as it is partially self-fertile but cross-pollination greatly improves yields. The tree is extremely cold-hardy and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and urban pollution once established. Harvest when fruit is fully dark red and slightly soft; it is too tart to eat out of hand but makes outstanding preserves, syrups, and fruit leather.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; cornelian cherry is exceptionally cold-hardy and adaptable, tolerating a wide range of soil conditions and even modest drought once established.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; cornelian cherry tolerates a wide range of soil conditions. Cornus mas (cornelian cherry dogwood) is a large, multi-stemmed European and Asian shrub or small tree producing one of the very earliest spring flower displays of any hardy plant — tiny, bright-yellow flowers clustered in small, button-like heads that cover the bare branches in February–March (often while snow still falls) before any other spring-blooming shrub. The flowers are followed by oval, cherry-like fruits that ripen to deep scarlet-red in August, tasting like a tart-sweet cranberry crossed with a sour cherry — used in jams, jellies, liqueurs (the Georgian chacha), and sauces throughout Eastern Europe and the Caucasus, where the sour flavor is prized in cooking much like tamarind. The tree is also fall-ornamental with excellent red-pink fall foliage and attractive peeling bark. 'Golden Glory' and 'Redstone' are widely grown cultivars. At the warm edge of its range (zone 8), it grows best with afternoon shade and consistent moisture; it is marginal in zone 9 and does best in the cooler northern parts of zone 8.

common_name: Cortland Apple (McIntosh × Ben Davis Cross, Non-Browning Salad Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Cortland requires approximately 1000 chill hours and is well-adapted to zones 4–7; it is an excellent cross-pollinator for McIntosh and other varieties — Cortland pollen is compatible with a very wide range of apple varieties.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cortland is an excellent cross-pollinator for many other apple varieties including McIntosh; ripens mid-season (September–October); the non-browning flesh makes it uniquely valuable for salads, charcuterie boards, and fresh-cut preparations where apples must remain attractive for hours without discoloring. Cortland apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1915 from a cross of McIntosh and Ben Davis — two of the most important apple varieties of the early 20th century. Cortland inherits McIntosh's aromatic, sweet-tart flavor character in a larger, firmer fruit with significantly better keeping quality than McIntosh. However, Cortland's most famous and unique characteristic is the slow-browning tendency of its flesh when cut: while most apple varieties brown rapidly after cutting due to enzymatic oxidation, Cortland flesh is notably slower to brown, making cut pieces remain white and attractive for much longer than most varieties. This property makes Cortland uniquely valuable for fresh preparations where apple slices need to remain appealing: fresh fruit platters, salads, charcuterie boards, and school lunch boxes where the apples won't be eaten immediately after cutting. The fruit is large, round, red over greenish-yellow skin with very white, juicy, tender flesh and the characteristic McIntosh aromatic quality. It is an excellent cross-pollinator for most other apple varieties due to its abundant, viable pollen. A classic in northeastern U.S. home orchards.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cosmic Crisp requires a substantial chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cosmic Crisp requires a substantial chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A cross between Honeycrisp and Enterprise developed by Washington State University and released commercially in 2019 after two decades of breeding and testing, it combines Honeycrisp's exceptionally crisp, juicy texture with dramatically better storage life, keeping fresh in refrigeration for up to a year without the bruising and softening problems that plague its Honeycrisp parent. Large, deep red fruit with a name inspired by the pale lenticel dots scattered across the skin like stars against a dark sky, it has rapidly become one of the most sought-after new apple varieties for both commercial orchards and home growers wanting Honeycrisp's texture without its notorious storage and growing difficulties. Thin fruit in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator variety within range, and harvest based on color and taste rather than a fixed date, since ripening time varies by climate.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Costa Rican Guava (Cas Guava, Cas, Guayaba Agria) is a small to medium fruit tree native to Costa Rica, Panama, and adjacent Central America — highly important in Costa Rican national cuisine and culture — bearing abundant small, tart, white-fleshed fruits with a refreshing, lemon-bright guava flavor that is more acidic than common guava, prized for fresh juice, agua de cas, and in cooking.
directions: Plant Psidium friedrichsthalianum in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment and fruit development; tolerates some frost once established but best in zone 10–12; harvest fruits when they turn fully yellow and give slightly under gentle pressure. Costa Rican Guava ('cas' in local parlance — a word so fundamental it has no direct English translation outside of the botanical name) occupies a unique place in Costa Rican culture — the guava-sized, white-fleshed, intensely tart fruits are the basis of agua fresca de cas (the most popular fresh juice in the country), used in refresco mixtures, ice creams, jams, and as a souring agent in cooking. The flavor is bracingly tart and intensely guava-fragrant, with significantly more acidity than the common tropical guava (Psidium guajava) — more similar to a tart lemon guava in flavor profile. The tree is somewhat smaller and more cold-tolerant than the common guava, performing well in humid subtropical conditions. In zone 10–12 Gulf Coast gardens and Florida, it fruits reliably and heavily with minimal care. The fruit's high pectin content makes it excellent for jams and jellies without needing commercial pectin. For Costa Rican immigrants and lovers of Central American cuisine, this tree represents home in a way that the common guava cannot replicate.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Cot-N-Candy is a Zaiger Genetics aprium, an interspecific apricot-plum hybrid weighted mostly toward its apricot parent, with fuzzy orange skin and sweet, aromatic flesh, and needs a compatible pollinator such as an early plum or another aprium/pluot nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible pollinator flowering at the same time, since Cot-N-Candy sets fruit poorly on its own. This Zaiger Genetics aprium, an apricot-plum interspecific hybrid weighted mostly toward apricot, looks much like a fuzzy-skinned apricot but carries noticeably sweeter, richer, more aromatic flesh thanks to its plum parentage. It ripens early in the stone fruit season, giving a jump on the summer harvest, and is generally grown and pruned like a standard apricot, with an open-center form and moderate annual pruning to renew fruiting wood. Because apricots and apriums bloom very early, plant in a site protected from the latest spring frosts, which can damage the flowers before fruit ever sets.

common_name: Court Pendu Gris Apple (Ancient Late-Blooming Frost-Avoidant Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; blooms notably late, giving it strong resistance to spring frost damage that threatens many earlier-flowering varieties, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Court Pendu Gris is one of the oldest apple varieties still in cultivation, with a history some trace back to Roman times and documented in France and England for centuries, prized above all for blooming remarkably late in spring, well after most other apple varieties, which gives it outstanding natural resistance to the late frosts that damage or destroy the crop of earlier-flowering trees. The small, flattened, gray-russeted fruit has firm, dense, sharply flavored flesh that mellows and sweetens with storage, and the variety is an exceptional keeper, often holding good quality into late winter or even spring. Its low, spreading, naturally compact growth habit and remarkable frost avoidance have kept it valued by heirloom orchardists for centuries despite its modest fruit size.

common_name: Cox's Orange Pippin Apple (World's Finest Eating Apple, English Dessert Apple Standard)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun in a sheltered location with good air circulation; Cox's Orange Pippin requires approximately 800–900 chill hours and cross-pollination from a compatible variety (Bramley's Seedling, Worcester Pearmain, or Egremont Russet); it is challenging to grow in the humid eastern United States (susceptible to apple scab, mildew, and fire blight) but flourishes in the Pacific Northwest and UK maritime climate.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with good air movement; Cox's Orange Pippin is highly susceptible to apple scab and powdery mildew in humid climates — a preventive spray program or planting in the dry Pacific Northwest is strongly recommended; it requires a cross-pollinator; harvest in October when fully colored and giving slightly to pressure, then store 4–6 weeks to allow flavor to fully develop. Cox's Orange Pippin is the variety most consistently named by apple connoisseurs worldwide as the finest-flavored dessert apple in existence — a small to medium English heirloom discovered as a seedling by retired brewer Richard Cox in his garden at Colnbrook Lawn in Slough, Berkshire, England around 1825, and distributed commercially from 1850 onward. The flavor at peak ripeness is extraordinarily complex and rich by apple standards: intense, spicy-sweet, aromatic, with distinct notes of pear, mango, honey, and fresh nuts that no other apple variety precisely replicates — and which Cox's defenders argue no modern commercial variety (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) can equal in flavor depth and complexity. Cox's became the dominant apple of British gardens and orchards for 150 years and remains the benchmark of the English fresh-eating apple tradition. In the United States, Cox's is most successfully grown in the maritime Pacific Northwest (Oregon and Washington's western valleys, similar in climate to England) where the cool, moist summers allow the apple to develop its characteristic complex flavor without disease pressure overwhelming the susceptible trees. In the humid eastern states, disease resistance is a significant challenge that requires diligent management.

plant_note: Plant dormant trees in early spring or fall in mild areas.
directions: Crabapples bear small, tart fruit excellent for jelly and serve as reliable pollinizers for dessert apples. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, choosing disease-resistant selections to limit scab and rust. They are extremely cold-hardy and adaptable, tolerating a wide range of soils. Prune in late winter to maintain an open canopy, and harvest the high-pectin fruit after the first firm color develops.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Creek Plum tolerates a range of soil types from sandy loam to clay. It spreads by root sprouts to form thickets — a valuable quality for erosion control but plan for the eventual colony footprint. Seeds require 90–120 days of cold stratification.
directions: Creek Plum is a native shrubby plum of stream banks, creek margins, woodland edges, and disturbed open lands across Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and adjacent states, producing clusters of small, bright red to yellow plums in mid-summer that are sweet, tart, and excellent fresh or for jams, jellies, and preserves. The profuse clusters of white flowers that cover the branches in early spring before leaf emergence are as ornamentally striking as any cultivated ornamental plum, making Creek Plum a multi-season landscape value as well as an edible landscape plant for zone 6–9 gardens. Spreads readily by root sprouts to form dense, multi-stemmed thickets that provide valuable wildlife habitat — nesting cover for mockingbirds and other birds, and the plums are consumed by mockingbirds, thrashers, raccoons, and white-tailed deer. Plant in full sun in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil; Creek Plum tolerates heat, periodic drought, and moderate clay once established.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very moist, highly acidic, peaty or sphagnum soil in full shade; creeping snowberry requires extremely specific conditions — cool, wet, acidic, shaded bogs or mossy, acid conifer forest floors in the boreal zone. It does not tolerate heat, dryness, or neutral to alkaline soils.
directions: Plant in very moist, highly acidic, peaty or sphagnum-based, humus-rich soil in full shade in cool, humid climates zones 2–6; creeping snowberry is a delicate, thread-like native evergreen groundcover of boreal bogs, mossy conifer forests, and cool, acid swamps across Canada and the northern United States. The tiny, rounded, glossy evergreen leaves form a fine mat just 1–3 inches tall, and the tiny white berries that form in late summer are pure white, edible, and have the characteristic wintergreen flavor of the Gaultheria genus. They were collected and eaten by indigenous peoples and early settlers as a minor food source. Like all Gaultheria, the leaves contain methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) and have been used as a flavoring. This species requires very specific, cool and perpetually moist conditions and is not appropriate for most garden settings, but excellent for recreating boreal bog gardens in the northern states and Canada.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cresthaven needs roughly 800 chill hours to break dormancy properly and performs best in zone 5-8, making it marginal for the mild winters of zone 9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart after petal fall to size fruit properly. Cresthaven was released by Michigan State University in the 1960s and became one of the standard late-midseason freestone peaches across the Midwest and Northeast, valued for firm, richly flavored, yellow flesh that holds up exceptionally well to canning, freezing, and other preservation, in addition to excellent fresh eating quality. The tree is notably cold-hardy for a peach, tolerating harsher winters than many Southern-bred varieties, but that same trait means it needs a real winter chill to fruit well and is not well suited to the mild winters of the Deep South. Prune annually to an open-vase form for good light penetration and fruit quality, and maintain a regular fungicide and dormant-oil spray program, since brown rot and peach leaf curl affect Cresthaven as they do most peach cultivars.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring next to a sturdy arbor, pergola, or large fence, since this is an extremely vigorous climber grown mainly for its dramatic foliage and fall color rather than for fruit quality.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun on a strong, large-scale support, since this East Asian ornamental grape climbs vigorously by tendrils and can quickly cover an arbor, pergola, or old tree. It is grown chiefly for its huge, heart-shaped, deeply veined leaves, which can reach 10 inches or more across and turn spectacular shades of crimson, scarlet, and purple in autumn, rivaling any deciduous tree for fall color. Small, fragrant flowers in late spring are followed by clusters of small, dark purple grapes that are edible but seedy, tart, and generally considered better for jelly or wildlife forage than fresh eating. Because of its exceptional vigor, Crimson Glory Vine needs a sturdy, generously sized structure and room to run, and benefits from hard annual pruning in late winter to control size and encourage the largest, most colorful leaves the following season.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; CrimsonCrisp is from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program and, like its stablemates GoldRush and Enterprise, needs little or no fungicide spraying in most home gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. CrimsonCrisp comes from the same Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois breeding program that produced GoldRush and Enterprise, carrying genetic immunity to apple scab along with resistance to cedar-apple rust and fire blight, making it a strong low-spray choice for home orchards in humid climates where scab is a constant pressure on susceptible varieties. The medium-size fruit has deep crimson-red skin over crisp, dense, juicy flesh with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor, ripening in early-to-mid fall — earlier than the late-season GoldRush and Enterprise, giving a staggered harvest when planted alongside them. It stores reasonably well under cool conditions, though not as long as the latest-ripening disease-resistant selections. Thin fruit clusters to one apple per cluster in late spring to improve size and reduce limb breakage.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Criollo cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Criollo cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Considered the finest-flavored and rarest of the three main cacao varieties, Criollo (Spanish for 'native' or 'creole') produces pale, thin-shelled pods with mild, complex, low-bitterness flavor prized by fine chocolate makers, but the tree is notably more susceptible to disease and lower-yielding than the hardier Forastero variety that dominates most commercial cacao production worldwide. It requires the warm, humid, sheltered understory conditions of a tropical rainforest, ideally grown beneath taller shade trees, and demands more careful disease management than more robust cacao types, making it a specialty planting for dedicated chocolate enthusiasts and tropical fruit collectors rather than an easy home crop. Provide consistent shade, humidity, and warmth, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity.

common_name: Cripps Pink Apple (Pink Lady, Late-Season Low-Chill Sweet-Tart Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Cripps Pink has a comparatively low chill requirement (around 400–500 hours) and needs a very long, warm growing season to ripen fully, so it is best suited to areas with mild winters and hot, extended autumns.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator, since this cultivar is not self-fertile. Bred by John Cripps in Western Australia from a cross of Golden Delicious and Lady Williams, it is marketed commercially as Pink Lady and is among the latest-ripening apples grown, often left on the tree into late autumn to fully develop its rosy-pink blush and dense, crisp, sweet-tart flesh. Its lower chill requirement compared to classic northern apples makes it one of the more workable dessert apples for warmer growing regions. Fruit stores exceptionally well and resists browning better than many varieties once cut.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Croisic is primarily valued for its breba crop (early summer figs on previous season's wood); in zone 9 the first breba figs ripen in late May–June, providing some of the earliest figs of the season. The main crop matures August–September.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Croisic is a French fig variety named for the coastal commune of Le Croisic in Brittany, notable primarily for its prolific breba crop — the early-season figs produced on previous year's wood that ripen in late May to early June in zone 9, weeks ahead of the main crop figs on most other varieties. The early-ripening breba figs are medium to large, with a yellow-green to yellow skin and amber to orange-tinged flesh with a mild, honey-sweet flavor. In zone 9 the Croisic fig provides the earliest fresh fig harvest of the season and is particularly valued by gardeners who want to extend the fig-eating season by starting early. The main crop figs on new wood ripen in August–September and are similar in quality to the breba crop. In zone 9 the mild winters and long growing season allow Croisic to produce heavy breba crops — the consistently warm temperatures maintain the tree's vigor for prolific breba production.

plant_note: Transplant grafted or rooted trees into full sun once nights stay reliably above 50°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving this compact-growing selection room to branch out into a small, rounded tree. Unlike typical seedy sugar apples, this cultivar sets fruit that are largely seedless or nearly so, with the same custardy, sweet, segmented flesh that makes the species popular across south Florida dooryards. It defoliates in cool weather and is killed back by hard frost, so Gulf Coast growers favor sheltered south-facing walls or grow young trees in containers that can be moved into a garage during freezes. Hand pollination with a small brush in the early morning often improves fruit set, since natural pollinators can be scarce in home gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; cupuassu is an understory tree native to the Amazon rainforest that produces its remarkable cauliflorous fruits (borne directly on trunk and main branches) in dappled shade — do not plant in full sun, which causes leaf scorch.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part to full shade; cupuassu requires consistent moisture and high humidity and will not tolerate any frost or prolonged dry periods. Theobroma grandiflorum (cupuassu) is a Brazilian Amazon rainforest relative of cacao (T. cacao) producing large, 8-to-12-inch, oblong, woody fruits borne directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflorous), each containing 20–50 seeds surrounded by a thick, creamy-white, intensely fragrant pulp with a flavor combining chocolate, pineapple, banana, and guava — considered by many food scientists to be one of the most complex and delicious tropical flavors in the world. The pulp is used to make juices, ice creams, yogurts, and confectioneries throughout Brazil, where it is the second most important Amazonian fruit after açaí. The seeds can be fermented and processed into a chocolate-like product ('cupuaçu butter') and are the basis of a proprietary chocolate-substitute trademarked as 'cupulate.' Growing cupuassu outside zones 11–12 requires a greenhouse; at the frontier of zone 10b, protected microclimates may support growth. A rare and extraordinary specialty fruit for true tropical enthusiasts.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9); Curtis is a Type II pollinator and needs a Type I cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination and full nut set.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Curtis is an old, Florida Panhandle-origin pecan cultivar valued for its outstanding resistance to pecan scab and other humid-climate fungal diseases, making it one of the most reliable low-spray options for Deep South home orchards. The nuts are smaller than many modern commercial cultivars but well filled, with good flavor, and the tree bears consistently and precociously once established. Because of its disease tolerance and long track record along the Gulf Coast, Curtis is frequently recommended as a dependable, low-maintenance pollinator and production tree for home growers who do not want to run a fungicide spray program. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in full sun after soil has warmed; custard apple prefers well-drained soil and does not tolerate waterlogging. Grafted trees begin fruiting in 3–5 years, while seed-grown trees take 5–7 years.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; custard apple is a deciduous to semi-evergreen Annona tree producing round to heart-shaped yellow-green to brownish fruits 3–4 inches in diameter with a reticulated (net-patterned) skin. The creamy white flesh inside is sweeter and softer than sugar apple, with a custard-like texture and a mild, slightly musky flavor. It is the Annona most widely grown across tropical Latin America, the Caribbean, and South Asia, where it is known variously as bull's heart, corazon, nona, and anon. Hand-pollinate flowers using a small brush in the morning to transfer pollen between flowers on the same tree; like other Annona species, the stigma and anther are not receptive at the same time.

plant_note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Czar is self-fertile, reliably productive, and one of the earliest-ripening European plums.
directions: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Czar is self-fertile, reliably productive, and one of the earliest-ripening European plums. An English culinary plum introduced in the 1870s, it bears heavy, reliable crops of dark purple-black, medium-sized fruit ripening notably earlier in the season than most other European plums, with tart, firm flesh that holds together well for cooking, canning, and jam-making even though it is somewhat less sweet than a fresh-eating dessert plum. Its self-fertility, reliable heavy cropping, and early ripening have made it a longstanding favorite for a productive, low-maintenance home orchard plum, particularly where an early culinary crop is wanted ahead of the main plum season. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit for better size, since it often sets a very heavy crop.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring with a compatible pear nearby for pollination.
directions: D'Anjou is a vigorous, productive European pear yielding sweet, juicy fruit excellent for fresh eating, baking, and canning. Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and include a different pear variety nearby for cross-pollination. Water consistently during fruit development and prune in late winter to a central-leader form. Harvest the fruit while still firm and ripen it off the tree in cool storage for the best texture.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site with well-drained soil and a compatible pollinator; D'Arcy Spice needs a warm season to develop its distinctive flavor and can be a shy, unreliable bearer.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site with well-drained soil and a compatible pollinator; D'Arcy Spice needs a warm season to develop its distinctive flavor and can be a shy, unreliable bearer. A rare old English apple originating in Essex in the late eighteenth century, it bears small, dull green-brown, unassuming-looking russeted apples that belie a uniquely rich, warm, nutmeg-and-spice-like flavor unlike any other apple, prized by heirloom enthusiasts and considered one of the most distinctively flavored traditional English dessert apples. It is a late-ripening, long-keeping variety that develops its best spiced flavor only after a period of storage, but the tree can be an unreliable, biennial bearer and needs a warm, sheltered site to ripen and flavor the fruit well, making it better suited to a favorable microclimate than an exposed site. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for a month or more before eating, since the distinctive spiced flavor develops and intensifies in storage.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Dabinett is reliably productive and a good choice for a first cider-apple planting.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Dabinett is reliably productive and a good choice for a first cider-apple planting. Originating in Somerset, England, this small, red-flushed apple is one of the most widely planted bittersweet cider apples in both traditional English cider and the modern American craft cider industry, valued for contributing soft, rounded tannin and moderate sugar that blends smoothly with sharper or more acidic varieties. Unlike the temperamental Kingston Black, it is a reliable, consistent, heavy-bearing tree that ripens late in the season and tolerates a range of growing conditions reasonably well, making it a popular starting point for home cider orchardists. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the small, tannic fruit is grown exclusively for cider rather than fresh eating.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring; tolerates cooler, wetter sites than dessert plums.
directions: The damson is a hardy, self-fertile culinary plum whose tart, astringent fruit shines in jams, gins, and preserves. It thrives even on heavier soils and in exposed positions where dessert plums struggle. Plant in full sun to partial shade and keep young trees weed-free and mulched. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in summer; expect reliable heavy crops after three to four years.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring before bud break in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Damson plum is an ancient European plum type with smaller, more astringent, intensely flavored oval fruits that are outstanding for preserves, jams, gin, and damson cheese — it requires less winter chill than Japanese plums and is one of the hardiest and most disease-resistant plum types.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; prune to open center form after harvest. Prunus domestica 'Damson' (Damson plum or Blue Damson) is an ancient, small-fruited European plum type — distinct from both Japanese plums (P. salicina) and common European plums in being smaller, more astringent, and more intensely flavored when raw, but superb when cooked or preserved. The small (1-inch), oval, blue-purple to nearly black fruits ripen in late summer through fall with a rich, complex, winelike, slightly tannic flavor that becomes sweet and luscious when cooked with sugar. Damson plum is the traditional fruit of English damson jam, damson cheese (a firm fruit paste), damson gin (sloe-gin equivalent made with damsons rather than sloes), and damson wine. The Shropshire Damson is the most celebrated English variety; Merryweather is the largest-fruited commercial type. Damson trees are notably hardy, long-lived, disease-resistant, and productive — often naturalizing at hedgerow edges across England — and require less winter chill than Japanese plums. Generally self-fertile or partially self-fertile; a pollination partner improves yields.

plant_note: Plant grafted or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; damson plum is more tolerant of thin, alkaline, and dry soils than most plums and produces astringent, aromatic, dark-purple fruit exceptional for preserves.
directions: Plant grafted or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; damson is more self-fertile than most plums and often sets good crops without a pollinator, though cropping improves with cross-pollination from another plum. Prunus instititia is the wild source of the cultivated damson, a small tree or large shrub producing small, oval, blue-black to purple plums in late summer with dense, richly flavored, astringent flesh quite distinct in character from the sweet, fresh-eating Japanese plums; damsons are the traditional plum for cooking, being too astringent to eat in quantity raw but transforming into superb jam (damson jam is one of Britain's most prized traditional preserves), jelly, cheese, wine, and gin. The tree is extremely long-lived, hardy, and productive even in cold, exposed, and acid soils where other plums fail.

common_name: Dana's Hovey Pear (Small Exceptionally Rich-Flavored Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Dana's Hovey was raised by Francis Dana of Massachusetts in 1854 and is prized for exceptional flavor in a small fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Raised by Francis Dana of Massachusetts in 1854, this heirloom bears small, yellow, lightly russeted pears that are widely considered among the richest and most refined-flavored of all American-bred pears, with dense, buttery, aromatic flesh that rewards patient ripening despite the fruit's unassuming size. Its late-season timing extends the home orchard's pear harvest well into the cooler months. Harvest while still firm in fall and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure; the fruit stores and keeps notably well for a dessert pear.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk; Dancy tangerine requires well-drained soil — standing water even briefly can cause root rot. In zone 9, Dancy ripens December through January, making it a classic Christmas citrus fruit. Protect from frost below 27°F with frost cloth or row cover when young; established trees tolerate brief exposure to 25–26°F. Space trees 12–15 feet apart, or prune to maintain compact 6–8 foot size for easy harvest.
directions: Plant grafted nursery trees in full sun, well-drained soil; fertilize with a citrus fertilizer 3 times per year (February, May, September). Dancy is the original American tangerine — named for Col. George L. Dancy of Orange Mills, Florida, who cultivated this variety beginning around 1867, making it one of the oldest named tangerine cultivars in the United States. For over a century, 'Dancy tangerine' was synonymous with 'tangerine' for most Americans — it was the predominant commercial tangerine grown in Florida and the citrus most commonly associated with Christmas stocking traditions, the holiday season timing of its December–January ripening. The fruits are medium-small, oblate, and deep orange-red at maturity with a distinctively loose, easily peeled 'zipper-skin' — the loose skin peels away from the flesh with minimal effort, releasing the fruit in clean, separate segments. The flavor is the classic tangerine profile: tart, sweet, aromatic, and intensely citrus with the characteristic spicy-sweet note that distinguishes tangerines from oranges. Dancy has substantial seeds (8–15 per fruit), which reduces its appeal compared to modern seedless mandarin hybrids; however, the intense traditional tangerine flavor is considered by many to be unmatched by the sweeter but blander modern seedless types. Trees are productive and long-lived in zone 9–11.

common_name: Danube Cherry (Hungarian Duke-Type Sweet-Tart Cherry for Zone 9)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Danube is a Hungarian duke-type cherry (a natural sweet-sour hybrid) needing roughly 450 chill hours, among the very few named cherries explicitly marketed as workable in zone 9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, choosing a site with good air drainage to reduce spring frost risk to the early flowers. Danube, a Hungarian duke-type cherry combining sweet and sour cherry parentage, was introduced to American growers by cherry breeder Amy Iezzoni and needs only about 450 chill hours, unusually low for a cherry, making it one of the very few named cherry cultivars explicitly marketed as workable at the northern edge of zone 9. It is partially self-fertile and ripens in early July, with balanced sweet-tart flavor typical of duke cherries. As with other low-chill stone fruit at the edge of their range, true performance under Gulf Coast humidity and disease pressure is less proven than in drier low-desert climates, so treat as a promising trial selection.

common_name: Dapple Dandy Pluot (Dinosaur Egg Red-Fleshed Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Dapple Dandy, nicknamed the Dinosaur Egg, is a Zaiger Genetics pluot (a plum-apricot interspecific hybrid predominantly plum) needing a second plum or pluot pollinator nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible plum or pluot pollinator such as Santa Rosa or Flavor Supreme, since Dapple Dandy is not reliably self-fruitful. Bred by Floyd Zaiger, this pluot, an interspecific plum-apricot hybrid weighted mostly toward its plum parentage, is instantly recognizable by its greenish-yellow skin dappled with maroon-red splotches, which gave rise to its Dinosaur Egg nickname, and by the vivid magenta-red flesh inside that is exceptionally sweet with a rich, complex flavor many tasters rate among the best of the pluot varieties. Fruit ripens over a fairly long midsummer window, giving a spread-out harvest rather than one concentrated picking, and the tree is otherwise managed much like a standard plum, with dormant pruning to an open center and thinning of heavy fruit sets to improve size. Its moderate chill requirement fits mild-winter Southern gardens better than many traditional European plums.

common_name: Dapple Fire Pluot (Dramatic Dappled Red-Green Skin, Red-Fleshed)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; needs a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer such as Santa Rosa nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer nearby. Dapple Fire is a Zaiger Genetics pluot notable for its striking appearance, with dark green skin splashed and streaked with fiery red dapples that intensify as the fruit ripens, opening to reveal firm, deep red flesh with a rich, sweet-tart flavor and good, dense texture. The visual drama of the skin pattern makes it a favorite at farmers markets and among home orchardists who enjoy growing something visually distinctive alongside more conventionally colored stone fruit. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure, since the dappled skin can make judging ripeness by color alone trickier than with solid-colored varieties.

plant_note: Collect and plant acorns immediately after they fall in autumn; press 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained to moist soil. Darlington oak is native to upland dry sandy soils of the Coastal Plain, distinct from the closely related Q. laurifolia which grows in moist lowlands.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; Darlington oak is a medium-sized semi-evergreen oak of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, often confused with the closely related laurel oak (Q. laurifolia) that grows in moister soils. The elliptical leaves are semi-evergreen to evergreen in the deep South, making this an excellent year-round shade and wildlife tree for zone 8–10 landscapes. Like most oaks, it produces abundant small acorns that provide essential food for wild turkeys, wood ducks, blue jays, and white-tailed deer. It is one of the most commonly encountered oaks in dry upland portions of the Florida peninsula and the Gulf Coastal Plain, thriving in the kind of deep, dry, infertile white sand that challenges most trees. An excellent canopy tree for naturalistic landscapes in the coastal Southeast where heat, drought, and sandy soils limit tree choices.

plant_note: Plant offshoots or container stock in spring when the soil is warm; dates require the specific combination of desert heat and dry air to ripen properly.
directions: Dates are dioecious — you need a male tree to pollinate female trees, with one male sufficient for up to 50 females; commercial growers hand-pollinate by shaking male flower strands over female inflorescences in spring. Ripe dates require extremely hot, dry summers (110°F daytime heat preferred) with very low humidity during the ripening period — this limits quality fruit production in the continental U.S. almost entirely to the Coachella Valley and low desert Arizona. Offshoots from the base of female palms are the preferred planting material as they preserve the sex and fruit type of the parent; seed-grown palms yield 50% males and highly variable fruit. Harvest in fall when fruit reaches the desired stage: khalal (crisp, astringent), rutab (partly soft, sweet), or tamr (fully dried).

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in moist, well-drained soil in spring or fall; date plum is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and is notably more cold-hardy than Asian persimmon. Female trees require a male pollinator for reliable fruit set. It is commonly used as a rootstock for grafting Diospyros kaki.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; date plum is a medium to large tree native from the Caucasus and Mediterranean to eastern Asia, producing small (1/2–1 inch) yellow to blue-black persimmon fruits in October–November that resemble tiny plums and have a sweet, date-like flavor — hence 'date plum.' The fruit contains high tannin levels when unripe (astringent like American persimmon) but becomes sweet after frost or extended hanging on the tree. Historical records suggest the fruit may be the legendary 'lotus fruit' of Homer's Odyssey that made Odysseus's sailors forget their homes. The tree is highly ornamental with glossy, dark-green leaves that turn yellow and red in fall, interesting orange bark on mature specimens, and small, attractive cream-colored flowers. More cold-hardy than Asian persimmon and easier to establish in temperate gardens, it is used as a rootstock for kaki persimmons.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; dattock or sweet detar is a large West African forest tree producing small, round, date-like fruits with sweet-acid, edible brown flesh that is exceptionally rich in vitamin C — one of the sweetest and most pleasant wild fruits of the West African coastal forests, eaten fresh throughout Senegal, Guinea, and Sierra Leone.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; dattock is a forest tree that benefits from some shade protection when young. Detarium senegalense (dattock or sweet detar) is a tall leguminous tree from the coastal forests, gallery forests, and moist woodland savannas of West Africa — native across Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Ivory Coast, Ghana, and Nigeria. The tree produces round to slightly flattened, 1–1.5 inch, thin-shelled fruits containing large, flat, hard seeds embedded in sweet, brown, fibrous, edible mesocarp with a distinctive sweet-acid, almost tamarind-like flavor. The fruits are exceptionally rich in vitamin C (up to 100 mg per 100g — roughly twice that of orange juice), and are eaten fresh as a pleasant sweet-sour snack across rural West Africa. The hard seeds contain a starchy meal used in traditional foods. The tree yields a useful timber and a resin used in traditional medicine. In Senegal, the sweet detar fruits are particularly popular and are sold in local markets. Sweet detar (D. senegalense) is the sweet-fruited species, distinguished from bitter detar (D. microcarpum), which has similar fruits but with an unpleasantly bitter taste — an important distinction for edibility. A largely unknown and underexplored fruit tree outside West Africa.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Dauphine is a main-crop variety producing its heaviest harvest in August–September in zone 9. The vigorous, large tree requires generous spacing. It is known for exceptional productivity and large fruit size.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Dauphine is a French fig variety named for the Dauphiné region of southeastern France, producing large, round to flattened fruits with violet to brown-purple skin and pink to reddish-amber flesh with a rich, sweet, mild flavor. The large fruit size (2–3 inches) is among the biggest in the fig world and makes Dauphine figs particularly impressive for fresh eating and market presentation. The vigorous, productive tree performs well in zone 9 heat and provides abundant harvests of the large, handsome fruits from August through September. Dauphine figs are best eaten fresh at peak ripeness; the large size can lead to cracking if late-season rains arrive during ripening. The French Dauphiné region has a tradition of fig cultivation in its milder southern valleys, and Dauphine represents the large-fruited table fig tradition of this region. In zone 9 the Gulf Coast conditions closely approximate the warm, humid conditions of the Dauphiné valleys.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Davidson's plum is a rainforest understory tree from tropical and subtropical Queensland, producing large, dark-purple to almost-black, very tart, sour plums on the trunk and branches (cauliflorous) — the primary fruit of the Australian native food industry for jams, sauces, cheeses, desserts, and gin liqueurs — and remarkably rich in antioxidants and vitamin C.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Davidson's plum grows naturally as a rainforest understory tree and requires protection from direct hot afternoon sun. Davidsonia pruriens (Davidson's plum or ooray) is a rainforest understory tree native to the tropical and subtropical rainforests of Queensland, Australia — one of the most commercially important fruits in the Australian native food industry. The tree is notable for its highly unusual growth habit: the large (1.5–2.5 inch), dark-purple to burgundy-black, plum-like fruits grow directly from the trunk and main branches in dense clusters (cauliflory), similar to cacao and jaboticaba. The fruits are intensely, mouth-puckeringly tart — far too sour to eat fresh in quantity without processing — but with extraordinary depth of flavor that has made them the darling of Australian native food chefs and product makers. Davidson's plum jam, Davidson's plum sauce (excellent with game, lamb, and dark meats), Davidson's plum sorbet, Davidson's plum wine and gin, and Davidson's plum dried food products are among the most celebrated products of the native food movement. The fruits are extremely rich in antioxidants — anthocyanins, ellagic acid, vitamin C — with a deep, complex, sour-fruity character that processing and sweetening reveals as intensely flavorful. Hardy to light frost in zone 9, Davidson's plum is increasingly available from Australian specialty nurseries.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Davis is an American elderberry cultivar grown alongside Adams, York, and Nova as a cross-pollination partner, with a second cultivar nearby giving a substantially heavier crop than a single variety planted alone.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant at least one other named elderberry cultivar nearby, since elderberries set a far heavier crop with cross-pollination than they do alone. Davis is a selected American elderberry cultivar grown for its broad, flat clusters of small white flowers in early summer, useful for elderflower cordial and fritters, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer that are cooked into syrup, jelly, and wine rather than eaten raw. Like other American elderberry cultivars it spreads by root suckers to form a multi-stemmed thicket if left unmanaged, so remove unwanted suckers each season to keep the planting to a defined shrub. Elderberry prefers consistently moist soil and performs best in a low spot or near a downspout where it won't dry out during summer heat; prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the shrub vigorous and productive.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Davis needs a second, genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Davis is one of the oldest widely propagated named pawpaw cultivars, selected by Michigan pawpaw breeder Corwin Davis in the mid-20th century from wild seedling trees and long valued for its consistent, reliable production and good flavor. Fruits are medium-sized with smooth, pale yellow, fiber-free flesh and a rich, sweet, banana-custard flavor, though the seeds are somewhat larger in proportion to flesh than in some newer cultivars. Davis ripens in the early-to-mid part of the pawpaw season and, alongside cultivars like Sunflower and Taytwo, played a foundational role in the mid-20th-century revival of interest in pawpaw as a cultivated fruit. Hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief flowering window to improve fruit set, since pawpaw's natural pollinators (flies and beetles, drawn to the maroon flowers' faint carrion scent) are often scarce in home gardens.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with excellent drainage; Day is one of the most cold-hardy avocado cultivars available, an important trait for Gulf South growers pushing avocado culture north of the traditional Florida and California ranges.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with excellent drainage; Day is one of the most cold-hardy avocado cultivars available, an important trait for Gulf South growers pushing avocado culture north of the traditional Florida and California ranges. A Mexican-race avocado selected in the mid-Atlantic for cold tolerance, it bears small, thin-skinned, rich, high-oil fruit with the anise-scented foliage typical of Mexican-race avocados, ripening in late summer to early fall on a tree reported to tolerate brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit once well established. Like all avocados it demands sharp drainage and will not tolerate wet feet, so plant on a mound or raised bed in heavy Gulf Coast soils, and protect young trees with frost cloth during their first several winters. Its cold hardiness makes it one of the more realistic avocado choices for gardeners in zone 8b who want to attempt the crop outside the classic Florida-Texas-California avocado belt.

common_name: Deer Magnet American Persimmon (Heavy Annual Fruit-Drop Native Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding root disturbance to the long taproot; Deer Magnet was selected specifically for exceptionally heavy, reliable annual fruit drop, valued for both eating and wildlife food plots.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding root disturbance to the long taproot native persimmons develop early in life. Deer Magnet is a named American persimmon selection prized above all for the sheer volume and reliability of its annual fruit drop, a trait that made it a favorite among wildlife food-plot growers before its excellent eating qualities also drew fresh-eating enthusiasts, producing abundant deep-orange, soft, honey-sweet fruit through fall once fully ripened. Like other native persimmons, the fruit is harshly astringent while firm and must be allowed to soften fully, or be picked up once it drops, before eating. The tree develops a deep taproot and tolerates heat, drought, and marginal soils far better than typical orchard fruit trees once established, and as a native species it is right at home in the Gulf South's heat and humidity. Plant a second, genetically distinct persimmon cultivar nearby for pollination and heavier fruit set.

plant_note: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Deglet Noor needs a long, hot, dry summer to properly ripen its fruit and is best suited to low-humidity desert climates.
directions: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Deglet Noor needs a long, hot, dry summer to properly ripen its fruit and is best suited to low-humidity desert climates. Known as the 'light of the date' for its translucent amber color when held to the light, this semi-dry cultivar is the most widely grown commercial date variety in the United States, historically the backbone of California's Coachella Valley date industry after being introduced from Algeria in the early twentieth century, prized for a firm, chewy texture and balanced, not-too-sweet flavor that holds up well in baking and storage. Like all date palms it requires an extremely long, hot, arid growing season to properly cure and sweeten its fruit on the tree, making it poorly suited to humid climates where fruit is prone to souring or fermenting before it fully ripens. Female trees need a nearby male date palm or hand-pollination to produce fruit, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity.

common_name: Del Rio Avocado (Cold-Hardy Texas Mexican-Type Avocado)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost risk; Del Rio is a cold-hardy Texas Mexican-race avocado cultivar named for the border city where it originated or was extensively trialed.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; root rot in heavy, wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable once established. Del Rio is a Mexican-race avocado cultivar selected for cold hardiness in South and West Texas, where hard freezes regularly test the limits of what avocado trees can survive, bearing medium fruit with rich, high-oil flesh and the anise-tinged flavor typical of Mexican-race types. It represents the ongoing regional effort among Texas home orchardists to identify and propagate avocado selections tough enough for zone 8b-9a gardens. Harvest based on typical days from flowering for the cultivar rather than skin color alone, and ripen indoors at room temperature after picking.

common_name: Delaware Grape (Historic Small-Berried American Pink Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Delaware, a historic mid-1800s American grape, bears small, sweet, pink-red berries long valued for high-quality wine as well as fresh eating; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.
directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Delaware is a historic American grape dating to the mid-1800s, producing small, tightly clustered, pink-red berries with notably high sugar content and a delicate, sweet, wine-quality flavor considered superior to many other Labrusca-type grapes of its era, and it remains valued today for both fresh eating and wine and juice production. It is self-fruitful and matures in midseason. As a high-chill Labrusca type it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Delbarestivale was bred by the Delbard nursery in France and released for ripening notably early in the season, giving gardeners fresh apples well ahead of the main fall harvest window most varieties occupy. The medium, bright red-striped fruit over a yellow-green background has crisp, juicy, sweet flesh with good, well-balanced flavor for such an early-season apple, since many early apples sacrifice flavor complexity for speed. The tree is productive and reliable; harvest in mid to late summer once fruit fully colors, and use fairly promptly, since early-season apples typically do not store as long as fall and winter varieties.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun. Delicious is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine.
directions: Delicious is a self-fertile, black-fruited muscadine bred at the University of Florida from a cross between a bronze parent and a large-fruited self-fertile black selection, released in the late 2000s. The oval berries color to a deep purple-black at full ripeness and the vine ripens its crop earlier than many older black cultivars, making it a useful bridge between early and midseason harvest. Vines are vigorous, disease-resistant, and heavy-bearing, holding up well to the fungal pressure typical of humid Gulf Coast summers. Grow on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun and well-drained soil, pruning hard each winter to renew fruiting wood.

common_name: Denniston's Superb Plum (Cold-Hardy American Gage-Type Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, and is well adapted to zones 4-8.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, though a nearby pollinizer can improve yields. Denniston's Superb is an early 1800s American gage-type plum bred for cold hardiness and reliable self-fertility, two practical advantages over many European gage selections that need cross-pollination and struggle in harsher climates. The medium, round, greenish-yellow fruit has dense, sweet, richly flavored flesh in the classic gage tradition, good for both fresh eating and preserves. The vigorous, hardy tree bears reliably once established, making it a solid choice for northern home orchardists who want good gage-type flavor without the fussier pollination and hardiness requirements of some European varieties. Harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and has fully colored.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy, dryland soil in full sun; desert date is an extremely drought-tolerant, thorny, small tree of the African and Middle Eastern drylands — producing oval, olive-sized, yellow-brown fruits with sweet-bitter, date-like flesh around a hard seed — one of the most drought-resistant multi-use trees in the Sahel, used across the semi-arid belt of Africa from Senegal to Ethiopia and into the Middle East.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy dryland soil in full sun; one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available — tolerates 3–6 months of complete drought once established. Balanites aegyptiaca (desert date, heglig, or soap berry tree) is a thorny, slow-growing tree native to the arid and semi-arid regions of sub-Saharan Africa, the Sahel, and the Middle East — one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important trees of the African drylands, found from Senegal and Mauritania east through Sudan and Ethiopia and into the Arabian Peninsula. The tree produces oval, olive-sized, yellow-brown to dark-brown fruits (drupes) with fleshy, oily mesocarp that is sweet-bitter with a date-like character; the fruits are eaten fresh, used to flavor traditional porridges, fermented into beer, and pressed for oil. The seed kernel yields an edible oil used in cooking and as a skin preparation. The bark, leaves, and fruit rind contain saponins traditionally used as soap — hence 'soap berry tree' — and in traditional fish stunning for fishing (the saponins narcotize fish). The tree has extensive traditional medicinal applications across Africa (treatment of malaria, diabetes, skin conditions) and is increasingly studied for bioactive compounds. One of the premier trees for the dryland agroforestry systems of the Sahel, where it withstands extreme drought, poor soils, and degraded conditions that defeat most other trees.

common_name: Desert Gold Peach (Early Low-Chill Semi-Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs about 250 chill hours and blooms early, so site it sheltered from late cold snaps.
directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Introduced from Fresno, California in 1969 for about 250 chill hours, Desert Gold opens peach growing to the mildest winters of zone 8-9 where standard varieties will not set fruit. It is among the earliest peaches to ripen, often by late April to May, with medium semi-freestone fruit, yellow flesh, red-blushed skin, and a sweet, slightly tart flavor. Because it blooms early, a site sheltered from late cold snaps helps protect the blossoms from frost damage. Self-fruitful and heat-tolerant, it remains a long-standing standard recommendation for warm-winter home orchards.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Desert King is the most widely grown and most reliably productive fig for the Pacific Northwest and similar cool-summer climates, where it produces an abundant breba crop that ripens reliably even in cool, short summers that defeat most other fig varieties.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun against a south-facing wall in cooler climates to maximize heat accumulation; Desert King is a San Pedro type that requires no pollinator for its reliable breba crop but benefits from caprification for main crop development in warm climates. Desert King is the dominant fig cultivar in Pacific Northwest gardens (Oregon, Washington, British Columbia) where it excels for its large, spectacular breba crop (early summer, June–July) that ripens reliably without the extended heat required by most other figs; the very large (3–6 oz), flattened-turbinate fruits have thick, green to greenish-yellow ribbed skin and dark strawberry to amber-red interior flesh with rich, sweet flavor. In warm climates (California, Gulf Coast) it also produces a substantial main crop in August–October. Among the most cold-hardy of all quality fig varieties, surviving to about 10–12°F when established and dormant. A vigorous, large tree that requires space; well-suited to training as an espalier against south-facing masonry walls.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January–February in zone 9); Desirable requires a cross-pollinator such as Stuart, Elliott, or Caddo for reliable nut production since it is a Type II pollinator (pistillate flowers receptive before pollen shed). Space 50–60 feet apart for full-sized trees, or 30–35 feet for orchard plantings.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil (pH 6.0–7.0) in full sun; Desirable is the most widely planted named pecan cultivar in the United States and the benchmark against which other commercial varieties are measured. Developed by the USDA and released in 1940, it produces large, well-filled nuts (50–55 per pound) with an excellent kernel percentage (58–62%) and superb flavor — considered by many pecan growers to be the highest-quality commercial pecan available. It is a consistent, reliable producer in zone 7–9 and well-adapted to the Gulf Coast South from Texas to Georgia. The principal challenge is susceptibility to pecan scab disease (Fusicladium effusum) in humid climates — in very humid areas like coastal Louisiana and Mississippi, it may require fungicide protection in wet years. Space trees widely: pecans ultimately become very large trees (60–80 feet tall, 40–60 feet wide) that shade out everything below. Supplement with zinc spray in spring; pecan is notorious for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils.

common_name: Diamond Grape (Moore's Diamond, Historic White American Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Diamond, also called Moore's Diamond, is an 1880s American white grape valued for its mild, sweet flavor and good disease resistance for a Labrusca-type grape; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.
directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Diamond, also known as Moore's Diamond, is a white American grape introduced in the 1880s, producing greenish-yellow berries in compact clusters with a mild, sweet flavor much less pronounced in the musky 'foxy' Labrusca character than many other American grapes, making it a pleasant fresh-eating and juice grape as well as a wine grape valued for delicate white wines. It is self-fruitful and ripens in early to midseason with good vigor and disease resistance for its type. As a high-chill Labrusca-derived grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

plant_note: Plant air-layered or grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Diamond River is noted among longan cultivars for superior cold hardiness, with mature wood surviving brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s°F that would kill standard longan cultivars to the ground — this makes it the preferred selection for Central and North Florida and coastal zone 9 Gulf plantings. Like other longans it benefits from a brief cool, dry winter rest to trigger flowering, which occurs naturally in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Diamond River is a Florida-selected longan valued for combining good fruit quality with markedly better cold tolerance than 'Kohala' and other tropical longan selections, allowing it to be grown successfully in zone 9 areas of the Gulf South where longan was historically considered too tender to fruit reliably. Clusters of thin-shelled, tan-brown fruit ripen in mid-to-late summer, with sweet, juicy, translucent flesh similar in flavor to lychee but more floral and less acidic. Prune young trees to an open, low-branched form for wind resistance and ease of frost-cloth coverage during establishment; mature trees need protection only in unusually severe freezes.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Discovery is one of the earliest apples of the season and does not store for long once picked.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Discovery is one of the earliest apples of the season and does not store for long once picked. Bred in Essex, England in the mid-twentieth century, this bright red, crisp early-season apple is prized for being one of the first dessert apples ready to eat each year, typically harvested in late summer well ahead of most other varieties, with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart white flesh that occasionally shows an attractive pink-tinged blush just under the skin. Its early ripening and reliable, moderate cropping have made it a popular home garden choice for gardeners eager for the first fresh apple of the season, though the fruit is best eaten within a few weeks of picking rather than stored long-term. Harvest in mid-to-late summer as soon as fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat promptly for the best crisp texture and flavor.

plant_note: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; Dogridge is a highly vigorous, nematode-resistant understock bred for sandy Southern soils.
directions: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; Dogridge is a highly vigorous, nematode-resistant understock bred for sandy Southern soils. Selected from a wild Texas grape species adapted to the sandy, nematode-prone soils of the Gulf South and Southern Plains, it is among the most vigorous grape rootstocks available, imparting strong nematode and Pierce's disease tolerance along with drought resistance once established, making it a favored choice for vineyards planted on marginal, sandy, or previously grape-planted soils in the warm-summer South. Its exceptional vigor can be excessive on rich soils, where it tends to promote overly vegetative growth at the expense of fruit quality unless managed with appropriate canopy and irrigation control. Graft a desired named wine or table grape variety onto young rootstock, and reserve it for sandy, low-fertility, or nematode-prone sites where its vigor and resistance traits are most valuable rather than a liability.

plant_note: Plant the dormant or potted grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Named for the noted Arnold Arboretum horticulturist, Donald Wyman produces a heavy spring flush of white flowers from pink buds, followed by small, bright red fruit that persists on the branches well into winter, often until the following spring, providing months of ornamental interest and emergency food for birds during lean winter weeks. It is a vigorous, wide-spreading, disease-resistant crabapple with good resistance to apple scab, making it a dependable, low-maintenance flowering shade tree. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches, giving it room to reach its considerable mature spread.

common_name: Dorset Golden Apple (Ultra-Low-Chill Gulf Coast Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile loam in full sun; Dorset Golden requires only 100–200 chill hours — it is one of very few apple cultivars that reliably produces fruit in zone 9a where chill hours frequently fall below 500 hours in warm winters.
