The popular double-flowered cultivar 'Paul's Scarlet' (Crimson Cloud in North America) produces vivid deep pink to red double flowers that smother the thorny branches before the leaves fully emerge. The small red fruits (haws) ripen in fall and are consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and numerous other birds. The thorny dense habit makes it one of the most effective wildlife-friendly hedging plants for gardens. More susceptible to leaf blight diseases than native American hawthorns in humid summer climates.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring; in mild-winter zones fall planting works well.
directions: English walnuts are monoecious — male (catkins) and female flowers occur on the same tree — and most cultivars are partially self-fertile, though a second tree improves yields. The tree produces juglone, a chemical that inhibits growth of many plants beneath its canopy; avoid planting near vegetables, berries, or sensitive ornamentals. Grafted Carpathian-strain trees are more cold-hardy and begin fruiting in 4–7 years; seedling trees may take 10+ years. Harvest in fall when hulls begin to crack and turn dark; remove husks promptly and cure nuts for 2–3 weeks before storing.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby; Ennis is susceptible to eastern filbert blight and best suited to the drier Pacific Northwest growing region.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby; Ennis is susceptible to eastern filbert blight and best suited to the drier Pacific Northwest growing region. A classic Oregon hazelnut cultivar prized for producing exceptionally large, high-quality kernels favored by the fresh-eating and confectionery trade, it has long been a benchmark large-nut variety even as newer blight-resistant cultivars have gained ground in commercial orchards. Like older Pacific Northwest hazelnut cultivars bred before eastern filbert blight resistance was a priority, it is quite susceptible to that serious fungal disease and performs best in the relatively dry summer climate of western Oregon, struggling with disease pressure in humid eastern growing regions. Plant a compatible pollinator variety within range for good nut set, and monitor closely for filbert blight cankers, pruning out infected wood promptly if the disease appears.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Enterprise ripens in October, later than most main-season apples, and its disease-resistant genetics mean it needs little or no fungicide spraying in most home gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program and released in the early 1990s, Enterprise is immune to apple scab and resists fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it a strong choice for low-spray or organic orchards. The medium-large, dark red fruit is crisp, firm, and sweet-tart with flavor that holds up well and even improves somewhat in storage. It ripens late in the season and keeps for several months under cool conditions.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Envy requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Envy requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A New Zealand-bred cross between Braeburn and Royal Gala, it produces large, brilliantly two-toned red-and-pink fruit with dense, sweet, exceptionally slow-to-brown flesh that stays fresh-looking far longer than most apples once cut, making it a favorite for lunchboxes, fruit trays, and salads. The tree is vigorous and productive with good disease resistance for a modern apple, and the fruit's slow browning and long storage life have made it an increasingly popular commercial and home-orchard variety since its introduction. Thin fruit clusters in early summer to improve size and annual bearing, provide a compatible pollinator, and harvest when the background color shifts from green to yellow-green beneath the red blush.

common_name: Esopus Spitzenburg Apple (Thomas Jefferson's Favorite Rich-Flavored Heirloom Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Esopus Spitzenburg is a light, somewhat biennial bearer and benefits from thinning and a vigorous rootstock to encourage more consistent annual crops.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating in Esopus, New York in the 1700s, this heirloom became famous as the reported favorite eating apple of Thomas Jefferson, who planted it at Monticello. The bright red-orange fruit, dotted with pale russet, has firm, yellow, intensely rich and spicy-sweet flesh that many consider among the finest-flavored of all apples, though the tree can be a shy, uneven bearer compared to modern commercial varieties. It ripens in mid-to-late fall and keeps reasonably well in cold storage, developing more complexity over several weeks.

plant_note: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; etrog citron is among the most cold-sensitive of all citrus and requires a frost-free microclimate in zone 9b or container culture that can be moved indoors in zone 9a and below.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in the warmest available microclimate; Etrog citron (Citrus medica 'Etrog', also spelled 'Esrog') is the specific cultivar of citron used for the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles), where it serves as one of the Four Species (arba minim) central to the religious observance — a use with over 2,000 years of continuous documented history, making it one of the oldest cultivated citrus varieties still grown for a specific purpose. The fruits are very large (4–8 inches long), yellow, highly aromatic, with a very thick, white-fleshed rind and very little juice; the entire fruit, including the extraordinarily thick, sweet, resinous peel, is the primary edible product, commonly candied, used in liqueurs and confections, or made into jam. The strongly ribbed, warty, irregular shape and intense, complex citrus-resin fragrance make etrog citron immediately distinctive. Ritual-quality etrogs (used for Sukkot) must meet specific halachic requirements — fully yellow, unblemished, with the pitam (style/stigma) intact at the blossom end — and command very high prices. Etrog trees are quite ornamental, with large leaves and dramatic fruit, but are tender and need winter protection in most of zone 9.

common_name: Eureka Lemon (Standard Lemon Tree, Four-Season Lemon)
plant_note: Plant container trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Eureka lemon is among the most cold-sensitive of commonly grown citrus — protect from temperatures below 28°F, which can cause significant damage to the tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Eureka is the standard lemon cultivar in American commercial production and one of the most widely grown home-orchard lemons in zone 9–11 — a vigorous, nearly thornless tree that is truly everbearing, producing lemons year-round with peak crops in winter and spring. The classic medium-to-large, yellow lemons have thin, smooth skin, high juice content, classic lemon acidity, and excellent fragrance — the gold standard of lemon flavor for culinary use. The everbearing production habit means there is nearly always some fruit on the tree in zone 9, even if the heaviest crops come in winter and early spring. The tree reaches 8–15 feet with glossy, aromatic leaves and fragrant white flowers that bloom repeatedly throughout the year. Eureka is slightly more cold-sensitive than Lisbon lemon and significantly more cold-sensitive than mandarins or kumquats; temperatures below 28°F for more than 4 hours can cause fruit and leaf damage. In cooler parts of zone 9, Lisbon lemon (more cold-tolerant) or Meyer lemon (much more cold-tolerant) may be better choices. Fertilize with a citrus-specific balanced fertilizer three times annually; iron and zinc deficiencies are common in alkaline soils and should be corrected with chelated micronutrient sprays.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Eureka is astringent until fully soft-ripe, so let fruit color deep orange-red and soften completely on the tree or after picking before eating.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Eureka is a long-established Southern astringent persimmon valued for its reliable heavy production and good cold tolerance compared to many Asian cultivars. The medium, flattened, deep orange-red fruit must fully soften after ripening before eating, since the tannins in unripe flesh are strongly puckering, but once jelly-soft it turns richly sweet and custardy, excellent fresh or baked into puddings and breads. Trees are self-fruitful, precocious, and tend to bear reliably once established, with fruit typically ripening from October into November after color develops fully.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Eureka is an old American pomegranate cultivar noted for compact size and reliable production of small, deep-red, tart-sweet fruit. Self-fertile; no cross-pollination needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Eureka is a long-cultivated American pomegranate valued for its compact, more shrubby growth habit compared to larger cultivars, making it a good fit for smaller yards or container culture, and for producing small to medium, bright red fruit with tender, tart-sweet, deep-red arils over a long harvest season. Its attractive orange-red spring flowers also make it useful as a flowering ornamental in addition to fruit production. Trees are drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; European hazel is wind-pollinated and requires at least two genetically different plants (or two named cultivars) for reliable nut production — one plant alone may produce few or no nuts.
directions: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; European hazel is wind-pollinated and requires at least two genetically different plants (or two named cultivars) for reliable nut production — one plant alone may produce few or no nuts. Corylus avellana is the hazel of European woodlands and hedgerows, grown for millennia for its nutritious hazelnuts (cobnuts and filberts in commerce); flexible, coppiced stems have been used for furniture, wattling, and charcoal production since prehistoric times; and the soft, round catkins that dangle from every bare stem in February and March are one of the earliest and most important pollen sources of spring for emerging native bees, including queen bumblebees and early Andrena mining bees. The large, rounded leaves turn golden-yellow in fall; the twisted cultivar 'Contorta' (Harry Lauder's Walking Stick) is a popular ornamental selection. Plant two different cultivars for best nut yield.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Eustis is the original and most widely grown limequat, a cross of Key lime and kumquat developed in Florida in 1909, combining true lime flavor with cold hardiness well beyond that of any true lime.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a lime-flavored citrus, tolerating temperatures that would kill true Key lime and Persian lime trees outright. Eustis limequat was developed in Eustis, Florida, in 1909 by USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle as a cross between Key lime and kumquat, aiming to combine the tart, aromatic lime flavor with the cold hardiness of kumquat, one of the toughest edible citrus species. The resulting small, oval, yellow-gold fruit has a genuinely lime-like tart flavor along with an edible, sweet-tart rind in the kumquat tradition, making the whole fruit usable — sliced fresh, juiced, or preserved in marmalade — without peeling. The compact tree bears prolifically and tolerates cold that would damage or kill a true lime, making it one of the few practical ways to grow lime-flavored citrus in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 outside the true lime-growing range. Protect young trees through their first few winters; mature wood handles cold considerably better. Harvest fruit once it colors up gold, and use promptly, as limequats do not store as long as some other citrus.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Evelyn ripens ahead of most native persimmon selections, useful where hard fall frosts arrive early.
directions: Evelyn is a named native persimmon selection prized chiefly for ripening its crop earlier than most American persimmon cultivars, letting growers in shorter-season areas harvest a full crop of soft, sweet fruit before hard frost cuts the season short. Fruit is medium-sized and richly sweet once fully soft-ripe, but like all American persimmons is intensely astringent while firm and must be left to ripen fully on the tree or after dropping. The tree shares the species' deep taproot, drought tolerance, and adaptability to poor or marginal soils, asking little beyond routine watering while young and occasional sucker removal. Pair Evelyn with a second, genetically distinct persimmon selection nearby to improve pollination and fruit set.

plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Eversweet is a unique pomegranate variety with clear, non-staining juice — unlike all other common pomegranates whose deep red juice stains hands and clothing permanently, Eversweet has very soft pink arils that produce a light pink juice that does not permanently stain — a practical advantage for families with children or for fresh eating over white fabric or clothing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil; Eversweet is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant once established, requiring little irrigation in most Gulf Coast settings after the first year; harvest when fruits are fully colored (rosy-orange to red skin) and sound hollow when tapped; fruits are sweet enough to be eaten with minimal mess. Eversweet is a distinctive pomegranate variety unlike any other in its combination of extreme sweetness, very soft (almost absent) seeds, and clear non-staining juice. Most pomegranates have deep red to crimson arils producing intensely colored red juice — the juice stains are notorious and pomegranate processing indoors is typically done over the kitchen sink with care to avoid contact with clothing. Eversweet breaks this rule: the arils are a soft rose-pink rather than deep red, and the juice they produce is clear to very light pink rather than the deep crimson of standard pomegranates, and crucially, it does not stain permanently. This characteristic makes Eversweet a more family-friendly choice for fresh eating, especially with children, and allows pomegranate eating and juicing without the usual mess concerns. The flavor is very sweet with low acidity — milder and less complex than Parfianka or Wonderful, but consistently rated among the sweetest pomegranates available. The seeds are extremely soft and virtually undetectable when eating the arils fresh. The exterior of the fruit is more orange-pink than red, making it visually distinct from other varieties at harvest.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cutting transplants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Excel figs begin producing in their second year and become increasingly productive as trees establish. In zone 9 figs typically produce two crops: a small breba (early) crop on the previous season's wood in June–July, and the main crop on new wood in August–October. Excel is well-adapted to the Gulf South climate and produces good crops even in partial shade. Prune lightly in late winter to shape the tree and remove dead wood; heavy pruning reduces fruit production.
directions: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — figs are adaptable to a wide range of soils but require good drainage; Excel is an LSU (Louisiana State University) AgCenter-developed fig cultivar released specifically for Gulf South production, selected for its large, distinctively yellow-skinned fruit with rich amber flesh and the high resistance to fruit souring that is a serious problem for figs in the humid Gulf Coast climate. While traditional Southern figs like Celeste and Brown Turkey are prone to splitting and souring in rainy, humid conditions at harvest time, Excel was specifically bred for improved resistance to these problems — producing firmer skin that resists splitting and reduces the entry of yeasts that cause souring. The large, sweet fruits have an extremely rich, complex, honey-fig flavor that is the archetypal fresh fig experience — one of the most sophisticated and complex flavors of any temperate fruit. Figs are the quintessential Gulf South home fruit tree: tolerant of heat, humidity, and occasional drought once established, self-fruitful (no cross-pollination required), highly productive, and producing fruit of exceptional quality that cannot be found in stores (fresh figs ship and store very poorly, making the homegrown experience irreplaceable).

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9); Excel is a Type I pollinator (sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive) and needs a Type II cultivar such as Elliott or Desirable nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Excel is a modern Louisiana-bred pecan cultivar selected for strong resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum), the humid-climate fungal disease that plagues many older commercial cultivars along the Gulf Coast, reducing or eliminating the need for fungicide sprays in home plantings. It produces large, well-filled nuts with good kernel quality and ripens relatively early, helping it escape late-season disease and weather pressure. Because of its disease tolerance, Excel is increasingly recommended for Gulf South home orchards where spray programs are impractical. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and watch for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils, correcting with a foliar zinc spray in spring.

common_name: Excelsior Plum (Heirloom Low-Chill Japanese-American Hybrid Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Excelsior needs a compatible plum cultivar such as Methley or Bruce nearby for cross-pollination, and its low chill requirement suits Gulf Coast and lower Southern gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and site a compatible plum cultivar such as Methley or Bruce within pollinating distance, since Excelsior needs a partner to set fruit reliably. Introduced from Florida nurseries over a century ago as one of the early hybrids between the Japanese plum and native American plum species, Excelsior has persisted as a heirloom home-orchard favorite in the Deep South thanks to a modest chill requirement of roughly 400 hours that suits mild Gulf Coast winters. Fruit ripens mid-season with deep wine-red skin and juicy yellow flesh, offering a good balance of sweetness and tartness for fresh eating. Give the upright tree room to spread and thin the crop if it sets heavily, since Excelsior can overbear on young trees.

plant_note: Plant divisions or pups after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sheltered from wind.
directions: FHIA-03 is a tetraploid hybrid banana bred by the Honduran Foundation for Agricultural Research for resistance to Black Sigatoka leaf spot and Panama disease, the pathogens that most limit backyard banana growing in the humid Gulf South. Unlike its sibling Goldfinger (FHIA-01), FHIA-03 produces a starchier, dual-purpose fruit that can be eaten cooked when green or sweet when fully ripe, giving gardeners flexibility similar to a plantain. The plant regrows readily from the rhizome after a freeze knocks back the pseudostem, making it a practical choice where winter dieback is expected most years. Give it heavy summer feeding and constant soil moisture to reach fruiting size within a single warm season.

plant_note: Plant grafted or seedling-grown trees in spring; in zone 9b–10 plant March–May. Canistel is more cold-tolerant than most egg-fruit relatives, with established Fairchild trees recovering from brief dips into the upper 20s°F. Young trees need frost protection for their first two winters. Fruit ripens over a long season from late summer into winter.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to sandy soil; Fairchild is a long-established Florida canistel selection known for smooth-textured, deep golden-orange flesh with the dense, dry, custard-like texture that gives the fruit its common name, 'egg fruit.' The flavor is sweet and mealy, often likened to a baked sweet potato or boiled egg yolk sweetened with brown sugar, and the flesh is popular blended into shakes, flans, and baked desserts throughout South Florida and the Caribbean. Trees are attractive, glossy-leaved evergreens that tolerate a range of soils and are relatively wind-firm. Pick fruit when the skin turns fully glossy orange-yellow and let it finish softening at room temperature for several days before eating, as canistel is only palatable when fully ripe and soft.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Fairchild's small, dense, dwarf-tending habit makes it one of the easiest mangoes to keep manageable in a container in zone 9.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Fairchild is a Panama-origin mango named for plant explorer David Fairchild and grown widely in South Florida dooryards for its small, dense, naturally dwarf-tending habit that suits small yards and container culture better than most mango cultivars. Fruit is small to medium with mild, sweet, fiberless flesh and a gentle flavor that is a good introduction to mango for those used to only supermarket varieties. The tree's compact growth and tolerance for hedging or pruning make it especially practical for zone 9 gardeners who want to keep a container specimen small enough to move indoors or into a greenhouse before winter cold arrives. Reduce irrigation as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor and protect the tree from any frost, since mango wood is damaged even by brief cold exposure.

plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Fairchild tangerine requires cross-pollination from a compatible citrus variety (such as Dancy tangerine, Orlando tangelo, or other mandarins) for adequate fruit set — plant a pollinizer within 50 feet.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fairchild tangerine is a Clementine x Orlando tangelo hybrid developed by USDA breeders in 1964, producing deep reddish-orange, medium-sized (2.5–3 inch) fruits with rich, sweet-tart, spicy-aromatic tangerine flavor — one of the most intensely flavored mandarins available. The skin is thin, slightly rough, and adheres somewhat to the flesh (tighter than most loose-skinned mandarins but peels relatively easily by hand); fruits typically contain 6–12 seeds, which is a trade-off for the exceptional flavor. Fairchild is one of the earlier-ripening mandarins in the California/Gulf South season, ripening November through December, and is an excellent choice for gardeners who want full-size mandarin flavor earlier in the season than the late-ripening Honey or Murcott types. The tree is medium-sized (8–14 feet), well-branched, and productive under good conditions with a cross-pollinator present. Trees in zone 9 should be sited in the warmest available microclimate as Fairchild is somewhat cold-sensitive; it tolerates brief temperatures to about 26–28°F when established but young trees need frost protection in the first 2–3 years.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Fallglo ripens notably early, often ready by early fall, giving its name.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures. Fallglo was bred by USDA researchers in Florida from a cross involving Bower citrus and Temple orange, producing large, deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with rich, sweet flavor that ripens notably early in the citrus season, often ready to harvest by early fall well ahead of most other mandarins — the trait that gives the variety its name. The tree is vigorous and productive, and the early ripening window makes Fallglo a good choice for growers wanting to open their mandarin harvest as soon as possible each year. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit size and quality.

common_name: Fameuse Apple (Snow Apple, French-Canadian Heirloom with Pure White Flesh)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; very cold-hardy and best adapted to zones 3-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Fameuse, commonly called the Snow Apple for its strikingly pure white flesh, traces back to French settlers in what is now Quebec in the 1600s, making it one of the oldest apple varieties associated with North American cultivation, and it is widely believed to be a parent of the famous McIntosh. The small to medium fruit has deep red, sometimes nearly crimson skin over snow-white flesh that is tender, juicy, and aromatic with a mild, sweet-tart flavor, best enjoyed fresh rather than cooked, since the delicate flesh breaks down quickly with heat. The tree is exceptionally cold-hardy, reflecting its origins in the harsh climate of early Quebec, and fruit ripens in fall but does not keep especially long, so it is best used within a couple of months of harvest.

common_name: Fantasia Nectarine (Large-Fruited California Standard Nectarine, Freestone Commercial Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep fertile soil in full sun; Fantasia requires approximately 400–500 chill hours and is self-fertile; best adapted to the warm interior valleys of California, the Pacific Northwest, and zones 6–9 where summer heat ripens fruit fully; in the humid Southeast, standard fungicide spray programs for brown rot are required as nectarines' smooth skin (unlike peach fuzz) allows brown rot spores to penetrate more readily.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Fantasia is self-fertile; thin to 5–6 inches in spring for maximum fruit size; Fantasia ripens mid-to-late season (late July to mid-August in California) producing very large, red to yellow-red blushed freestone nectarines with firm, yellow flesh and excellent sweet-tart flavor; outstanding for fresh eating and fruit stands. Fantasia nectarine is one of the most widely planted mid-season nectarine varieties for commercial and home production in California and the warmer western states, developed by Zaiger Genetics and released in the 1970s as part of the wave of nectarine variety improvement that transformed nectarine from a specialty fruit to a mainstream commercial crop in California's San Joaquin Valley. The variety's primary attributes — very large fruit size (among the largest freestone nectarines available), excellent red skin color with bright yellow background, firm flesh for shipping and handling, and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor — made it ideal for the fresh market where visual appeal and size command premium prices. Fantasia consistently produces one of the largest individual fruits of any nectarine variety, with well-colored red-over-yellow skin that is visually very attractive, and the freestone flesh separates cleanly from the pit at full maturity — a practical advantage for home eating and cooking. The variety's moderate chill requirement (400–500 hours) makes it reliable in zone 7–9 climates beyond California, including the Pacific Northwest and some parts of the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters.
directions: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and protect young trees through their first few winters with frost cloth or temporary cover. Fantastic is a Mexican-race avocado selected for cold hardiness and dependable fruiting, grown by Gulf Coast and Texas dooryard orchardists alongside sister selections like Joey and Lila as part of the small pool of avocado cultivars that can be planted in-ground north of the traditional Florida and California avocado belt. Fruit is small to medium with thin, edible-adjacent skin typical of Mexican-race avocados and rich, high-oil-content flesh with a pronounced anise note in the foliage and fruit. Fruit set improves with a complementary Type A or Type B flowering cultivar planted nearby. Mature, well-established trees can shrug off brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit, though reliable fruiting still depends on avoiding a hard freeze during bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; feijoa is one of the hardiest subtropical fruit plants, tolerating temperatures to about 12–15°F when established, making it viable in zones 8–11 and an outstanding dual-purpose ornamental and fruiting shrub for Gulf Coast and Southeast gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; established feijoas tolerate drought but produce better fruit with regular moisture during flowering and fruit development. Acca sellowiana (feijoa or pineapple guava) is a South American evergreen shrub native to southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, and northern Argentina, producing exceptionally ornamental flowers in May — petals of white and crimson with red stamens that are edible and sweet, often harvested from the ground — and unique oval fruits in fall that have an intensely aromatic, tropical, pineapple-guava flavor unlike any other temperate-climate fruit. The silvery-green leaves with white undersides are attractive year-round; the plant is exceptionally cold-hardy for a subtropical fruiting plant, tolerating 12–15°F and making it viable throughout the Gulf Coast, the Southeast, and mild West Coast gardens. Most selections require two plants for cross-pollination, though self-fertile cultivars like 'Coolidge' and 'Pineapple Gem' are available.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root figs after the last frost date when soil has warmed; in mild climates, fall planting works well.
directions: Common figs (the type grown in most gardens) are parthenocarpic and self-fertile — no pollinator or fig wasp is needed. In zones 6–7 protect the trunk and lower branches over winter by wrapping with burlap or mounding mulch; established roots often resprout even after top-kill. Figs bear two crops on some cultivars: a small breba crop on old wood in early summer and a main crop on new growth in late summer. Harvest when the neck droops, the skin splits slightly, and the fruit is soft and fragrant; a drop of syrup at the eye signals perfect ripeness.

plant_note: Plant after frost danger; grow in a pot to overwinter indoors in cold zones.
directions: Fignomenal is a true dwarf fig reaching only 2 to 3 feet, making it ideal for containers and small patios while still producing full-sized sweet fruit. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil and water consistently, easing off as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor. Its compact size makes it easy to move indoors to a cool bright space for winter in colder regions. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove weak wood. Feed during the growing season for steady production of its self-fertile crop.

plant_note: Plant bare-root stock in early spring while dormant, or container-grown plants any time in the growing season; plant at least two different varieties or seedlings for cross-pollination, as filberts are largely self-infertile.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing at least 10–15 feet from other plants to allow for the naturally wide-spreading form; filbert (Corylus maxima) is the large-fruited European hazelnut, distinguished from Corylus avellana by its longer tubular husk that completely encloses the nut, and is the parent of many named cultivars including 'Butler', 'Ennis', and 'Tonda di Giffoni'. A multi-stemmed deciduous shrub that bears pollen-heavy catkins in late winter while fully dormant — one of the earliest signs of spring — with small red pistillate flowers that require wind cross-pollination from a second genetically distinct plant to set nuts. Harvest when husks begin to brown and nuts release easily; dry in a single layer before storage to prevent mold.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; finger lime tolerates brief frosts to about 22–25°F once established.
directions: Finger lime is an Australian rainforest citrus producing cylindrical finger-length fruits filled with spherical pulp vesicles that burst on the palate like caviar — highly prized in fine dining as a garnish. Grafted trees are strongly preferred over seedlings, which are slow to fruit and thorny; grafted plants begin fruiting in 2–3 years and are more manageable in size. The tree is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator; it performs well in containers and espalier forms. Fruit ripens in late autumn through winter; harvest when the skin (green, yellow, red, or black depending on variety) is fully colored and the fruit releases easily with gentle pressure — avoid overripening, as the vesicles lose their pop.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Fire Cherry is a fast-growing pioneer species that thrives in disturbed, open, forest-gap conditions; it grows too fast to compete well in established forest understory. Seeds require 90–150 days of cold stratification before spring germination.
directions: Fire Cherry — also called Pin Cherry — is a fast-growing native pioneer tree of disturbed forest openings, clear-cuts, burned areas, and roadsides across the northern United States and Canada, where it is usually the first woody species to colonize forest gaps and recently disturbed sites, earning the name 'fire cherry' for its rapid colonization of burned forest. The clusters of bright red, pea-sized cherries ripen in summer and are among the most important late-season wildlife fruits in northern forest ecosystems, heavily consumed by American robins, cedar waxwings, grosbeaks, ruffed grouse, bears, and deer during the late summer fattening period before winter. Short-lived by nature — typically 15–30 years in the wild — Fire Cherry grows extremely fast for a native cherry, reaching 20 feet in just a few years and serving as a pioneer nurse species that modifies the site for longer-lived forest trees to follow. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Fire Cherry thrives in open, disturbed conditions and makes an excellent fast-growing wildlife planting for northern gardens, fields, and woodland restoration projects.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Flame is a seedless red grapefruit selected in the Texas Rio Grande Valley and ripens over a long winter window, developing its deepest red flesh color with cool nights.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected and released by Texas A&M's citrus breeding program in 1987 from the Rio Red lineage, Flame produces medium-large, seedless fruit with intensely red-pigmented flesh and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. It is one of the reddest-fleshed grapefruit cultivars commercially grown and holds its color reliably even in warmer winters that can wash out the blush in older red grapefruit types. Fruit matures from late fall through winter and holds well on the tree, allowing a long, flexible harvest window.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun.
directions: Flame Red Seedless is a vigorous grape producing sweet, juicy, ruby-red seedless berries in large clusters. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil and provide a strong trellis or arbor to support the heavy vining growth. Train a permanent trunk and cordons the first years, then prune hard every dormant season to a few productive spurs or canes, as grapes fruit on the current year's growth. Water steadily while fruit swells but reduce moisture as harvest approaches for sweeter grapes. Good air circulation helps prevent mildew.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; Flanders is notably more cold-hardy than most fig cultivars, tolerating winter dieback and regrowing reliably from the crown even after a hard freeze, making it a good choice at the cooler edge of fig-growing range.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the more cold-hardy fig cultivars available, reliably resprouting from the roots after winters that kill back the top growth of less hardy varieties. Flanders is an old Belgian fig cultivar long grown in home gardens and small orchards for its dependable production of medium, brown-skinned figs with sweet, amber flesh and good flavor, and for its resilience in marginal fig-growing climates where winter cold is a limiting factor. It typically produces a modest breba (early summer) crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, and the fruit holds reasonably well against splitting in humid weather. Its cold tolerance makes it a valuable choice for gardeners at the northern edge of the fig range, or in a Gulf South garden where an occasional hard freeze is a risk, zone 6–10.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container specimens in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; flatwoods plum grows naturally in the sandy, acidic, dry soils of pine flatwoods and woodland edges throughout the Gulf Coast and adapts well to similar garden conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — flatwoods plum is a spectacular native small tree of the southeastern coastal plain and Gulf Coast pine flatwoods, producing masses of pure white five-petaled flowers on bare branches in February–March, among the earliest and most profuse of all native spring-blooming trees and a critical early nectar source for native bees before other flowers open. The small round fruits (3/4 inch) ripen in July to purple-black with a blue bloom; they are tart to sweet depending on the tree, used for preserves, jellies, wine, and as wildlife food for deer, foxes, and dozens of bird species. An excellent candidate for wildlife food plots and naturalistic plantings in the pine flatwoods region. Many individual trees have superior fruit; select superior-fruiting trees to propagate for orchard use. Drought tolerant once established in adapted sandy soils.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Flavor Delight is one of the original Zaiger Genetics aprium introductions, ripening very early with sweet, aromatic, apricot-like fruit, and needs a compatible pollinator nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and site it away from the latest spring frost pockets, since aprium flowers open very early and are vulnerable to late cold snaps. Flavor Delight was among the first apriums released by Zaiger Genetics, and it remains valued for ripening earlier than almost any other stone fruit hybrid, giving gardeners a fresh, sweet, apricot-flavored fruit well ahead of the main summer harvest. The reddish-blushed, apricot-like skin covers dense, aromatic, low-acid flesh, and a compatible pollinator, such as an early-flowering plum, pluot, or aprium, is needed nearby since it is not reliably self-fruitful. Prune and thin as for a standard apricot, removing crossing interior branches in the dormant season and thinning heavy fruit sets in spring to improve final size.

common_name: Flavor Grenade Pluot (Firm Late-Season Green Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Flavor Grenade is a Zaiger Genetics pluot bred for exceptionally firm flesh and a long shelf life, and needs a second plum or pluot pollinator nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a second plum or pluot variety nearby for pollination, since Flavor Grenade sets fruit poorly on its own. Another of the Zaiger Genetics pluot introductions, Flavor Grenade keeps its green skin even at full ripeness, which can make judging harvest timing tricky for gardeners used to color-based cues, but the crisp, exceptionally firm, deep red-streaked flesh holds its sugary, tangy-sweet flavor for days after picking better than most stone fruit, making it a favorite for gardeners who want fruit that doesn't turn to mush a day after ripening. It ripens later in the season than most pluots, extending stone fruit harvest into late summer, and the moderately vigorous tree is managed and pruned much like a standard plum. Thin heavy fruit sets in late spring to improve final fruit size.

common_name: Flavor Heart Pluot (Heart-Shaped Dark Red Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; needs a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer such as Santa Rosa nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer nearby. Flavor Heart is a Zaiger Genetics pluot notable for its distinctive elongated, heart-like fruit shape, with dark red to nearly maroon skin covering rich, sweet, deeply flavored red-tinged flesh characteristic of the best pluot varieties. The unusual fruit shape sets it apart visually from the more typically round or oval pluots, making it a conversation piece as well as a good-eating specialty stone fruit for home orchards. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and has fully colored, since pluots generally do not continue to ripen significantly after picking.

common_name: Flavor King Pluot (Reddish-Purple Sweet Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Flavor King is a Zaiger Genetics pluot with reddish-purple skin and deep red, exceptionally sweet flesh, and needs a compatible plum or pluot pollinator such as Santa Rosa nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible pollinator, since Flavor King is not self-fruitful. This Zaiger Genetics pluot ripens to a deep reddish-purple skin over intensely sweet, dark red flesh with very little tartness, making it one of the sweeter pluot selections and a favorite for fresh eating out of hand. It ripens in mid-to-late summer, after earlier pluots like Flavor Supreme have finished, extending the harvest window for gardeners growing more than one pluot variety. As with other pluots, thin heavy fruit sets in late spring to improve final size and quality, and prune in the dormant season to an open center to let light into the canopy.

common_name: Flavor Queen Pluot (Sweet Yellow-Skinned Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; needs a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer such as Santa Rosa nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer nearby. Flavor Queen is a Zaiger Genetics pluot, an interspecific hybrid combining plum and apricot parentage weighted toward plum, producing golden-yellow skinned fruit with sweet, richly flavored, apricot-tinged yellow flesh that ripens in mid to late summer. Like other pluot varieties, it delivers intensely concentrated, complex sweetness that many growers find surpasses either parent species on its own, a hallmark of the entire pluot breeding program. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and reaches full color, since pluots do not continue ripening much once picked, unlike some other stone fruit.

common_name: Flavor Supreme Pluot (Original Red-Fleshed Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Flavor Supreme was one of the first Zaiger Genetics pluots introduced and remains one of the highest-flavored, with mottled maroon-and-green skin over vivid magenta-red flesh, and needs a second plum or pluot pollinator nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a compatible plum or pluot pollinator nearby, since Flavor Supreme does not set a reliable crop on its own. Bred by Floyd Zaiger and one of the earliest pluot introductions, Flavor Supreme is still considered by many fruit growers to have the finest flavor of the whole pluot group, with mottled dark red-and-green skin over intensely sweet, richly flavored, deep red flesh that drips juice when fully ripe. It ripens early in the pluot season, and fruit left to color fully on the tree develops noticeably better flavor than fruit picked while still firm and greenish. Thin the heavy early fruit set to improve final size, and manage the tree with the same dormant pruning to an open center used for standard plums.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring in full sun.
directions: Flavortop is a fast-growing nectarine producing large, juicy, well-balanced freestone fruit that ripens in mid to late summer. Plant it in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, avoiding low frost pockets that harm early bloom. It is self-fruitful, so one tree will bear without a partner. Prune yearly in late winter to an open-center form for light and airflow, and thin developing fruit to boost size and prevent limb breakage. Provide steady water while fruit develops, and manage peach leaf curl with dormant sprays if needed.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; very cold-hardy and best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Flemish Beauty originated in Belgium around 1810 and became historically important in North American pear growing for its outstanding cold hardiness, allowing pear cultivation in regions too harsh for many other European varieties. The large, golden-yellow fruit blushed with russet has sweet, aromatic, juicy flesh with real depth of flavor when picked and ripened properly. The tree's biggest weakness is susceptibility to fire blight and pear scab, which can be a real challenge in humid, disease-prone climates, so it benefits from good air circulation and, where scab pressure is high, a basic fungicide program. Pick while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature for the best texture.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fleshy hawthorn tolerates a range of soils and is thorny, so site away from foot traffic.
directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fleshy hawthorn tolerates a range of soils and is thorny, so site away from foot traffic. Clusters of white spring flowers cover this thorny native small tree, followed by unusually large, juicy, bright red fruit for a hawthorn, historically gathered and eaten fresh or made into preserves by Indigenous peoples and early settlers across its native range in the northern and central United States and Canada. Like other hawthorns it provides valuable dense, thorny cover for nesting birds and small wildlife, along with fall fruit that persists into winter as a food source when little else remains available. Water during establishment, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and prune to remove crossing or damaged branches while avoiding the sharp thorns.

common_name: Floragold Apricot (Early-Ripening Reliable Low-Chill Backyard Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Floragold needs about 400 chill hours or less and was bred as a reliable low-chill backyard producer, ripening two to three weeks before Blenheim.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Floragold was bred specifically as a dependable low-chill backyard apricot, needing roughly 400 chill hours or less and ripening two to three weeks ahead of the classic Blenheim, with all-purpose freestone fruit good for fresh eating and preserving. As with other low-chill apricots, its early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well.

common_name: FlordaGrande Peach (Ultra-Low-Chill University of Florida Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; requires fewer than 100 chill hours, among the lowest of any named peach, so it sets fruit reliably even where winters barely dip below 60°F.
directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. FlordaGrande requires fewer than 100 chill hours, among the lowest of any named peach, so it sets fruit reliably even where winters barely dip below 60°F. It ripens very early, typically late April into May, on medium to large freestone fruit with orange-red skin and sweet, melting yellow flesh. Self-fertile and vigorous, it benefits from a hard summer prune to keep growth compact and from fruit thinning to prevent limb breakage under a heavy set. This is the standard recommendation for growers at the extreme low-chill end of zone 9-11 where even other Florida-bred peaches may fall short.

common_name: Flordabest Peach (Early Large-Fruited University of Florida Low-Chill Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; developed for about 250 chill units, well matched to zone 8-9 winters across the Gulf South.
directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Developed by the University of Florida for about 250 chill units, Flordabest is well matched to zone 8-9 winters across the Gulf South and peninsular Florida. It ripens very early, about a week to ten days ahead of TropicBeauty, with large, firm yellow melting flesh under 90-100 percent bright red skin. Trees are self-fertile, moderately vigorous, and semi-upright, setting heavy annual crops that need early thinning to size the fruit well. A strong pick for gardeners who want an early low-chill peach with above-average fruit size.

common_name: Flordacrest Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant, in full sun with excellent drainage; Flordacrest needs roughly 300 chilling hours, low enough for reliable bloom and fruit set across most of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, since peach roots are quickly damaged by standing water. Flordacrest is a low-chill freestone peach from the University of Florida breeding program, bred to extend the low-chill peach harvest window with medium to large fruit, attractive red-blushed yellow skin, and firm, good-flavored yellow flesh that holds up well for fresh eating. It is self-fertile and does not require a second tree for pollination, though planting a second early-blooming low-chill peach nearby can improve fruit set in a light bloom year. Thin fruit clusters to 6-8 inches apart when fruit reaches marble size to improve final size, and expect ripening in late spring to early summer, consistent with other low-chill Florida-bred peaches.

common_name: Flordadawn Peach (Early University of Florida Low-Chill Peach for North Florida)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; bred for roughly 350 chill hours, suiting the milder end of zone 8 through 9.
directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bred by the University of Florida for roughly 350 chill hours, Flordadawn suits the milder end of zone 8 through 9 where standard peaches often set little or no fruit. It ripens in the early season with melting, semi-clingstone flesh and the mild sweet flavor typical of Florida's low-chill breeding lines. Like most Gulf South peaches it benefits from a dormant fungicide application and open-center pruning to manage the fungal pressure that comes with humid winters and springs.

common_name: Flordaglo Nectarine (University of Florida Very Low-Chill Yellow Nectarine for Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Flordaglo requires only 150–200 chilling hours — among the absolute lowest chill requirements of any nectarine variety, making it one of the only nectarines reliably producible in zone 9b-10 where mild winters rarely accumulate the 500–700 hours needed by standard nectarines. In zone 9 on the Gulf Coast, Flordaglo ripens in late May to early June — very early for a nectarine. The tree is self-fertile and does not require a cross-pollinator, though yield may improve with nearby compatible stone fruit. As with all nectarines in humid climates, bacterial spot and brown rot can be significant; preventive copper and fungicide sprays during bloom and leaf-out help maintain plant health and fruit quality in the Gulf South's humid conditions.
directions: Plant bare-root tree in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart. Harvest when fully yellow-orange and gives slightly to pressure. Flordaglo Nectarine was released by the University of Florida IFAS as part of the same low-chill stone fruit breeding program that produced Flordaking, Flordaprince, and other Gulf South-adapted peach and nectarine varieties. Nectarines (smooth-skinned peaches, genetically a single-gene variant of the standard fuzzy peach) are typically even more demanding in their chill hour requirements than their peach counterparts, making the development of a reliable very low-chill nectarine a significant achievement. With approximately 150–200 chilling hours required, Flordaglo can be grown in most of Florida and the Gulf Coast — conditions under which virtually all standard nectarine varieties fail to bloom and set properly. The fruit is medium-sized, with a yellow-red skin and yellow freestone flesh — the smooth nectarine skin distinguishing it visually from the closely related fuzzy peaches. The flavor is typically sweeter and slightly more aromatic than many standard low-chill peaches, with the characteristic nectarine quality that growers in cool climates take for granted but that gardeners in zone 9 rarely get to experience from home-grown fruit. For zone 9 home orchardists who want to grow nectarines — generally considered nearly impossible in the Gulf South — Flordaglo is one of the very few varieties with a realistic chance of success.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in January-February while dormant; Flordaguard requires only about 150 chill hours, a University of Florida release grown both as a very-low-chill fruiting peach and widely used as a root-knot nematode-resistant rootstock.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Flordaguard is a University of Florida release with an exceptionally low chill requirement of roughly 150 hours, making it one of the few peaches that reliably flowers and fruits in the mildest winters of the Gulf South and peninsular Florida, and it is separately valued in the nursery trade as a root-knot nematode-resistant rootstock for grafting less-hardy peach cultivars. Its own fruit is small to medium, clingstone, and mainly ornamental to fair-eating quality, with showy pink spring flowers that make it attractive even where fruit quality is secondary. Thin fruit if a heavier crop sets than the tree can properly size, and prune to an open-center vase shape after leaf drop.

common_name: Flordahome Peach (Early University of Florida Low-Chill Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Flordahome needs roughly 400-450 chill hours, one of the earlier University of Florida low-chill releases bred to fruit reliably through the state's mild winters.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun on well-drained soil, and prune to an open-vase shape in the first year or two to establish a strong, light-filled framework. Flordahome is one of the University of Florida's early low-chill peach releases, bred alongside Flordaking to give Gulf Coast and Florida growers a dependable option where standard high-chill peaches bloom erratically or fail to set fruit after mild winters. It bears medium, yellow-fleshed freestone fruit with a red-blushed skin and pleasant, mild flavor for a low-chill selection, ripening in late spring before the worst of the summer heat. The tree is self-fertile and productive, though a late-season freeze after unusually early bloom can still reduce a crop, so avoid planting in frost-prone low spots. Thin developing fruit to 6-8 inches apart and fertilize lightly each spring to sustain consistent annual production.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile loam in full sun; Flordahome requires only 150–200 chill hours and is the best pear choice for zone 9b–10 and the warmest portions of zone 9a where other pear varieties fail to produce consistently.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Flordahome is a University of Florida-developed pear cultivar requiring only 150–200 chill hours — the lowest chill requirement of any commonly available pear cultivar, making it the primary choice for zone 9b, zone 10, and any warm-winter location where standard pear varieties (which require 600–1000+ chill hours) consistently fail to bloom and fruit adequately. Flordahome produces medium-sized, yellow-green, round fruits with mild, sweet flesh that ripens in early summer — often in June in zone 9 — earlier than most other pear varieties. The fruit quality is pleasant but not as buttery or complex as high-chill European pears; it is best enjoyed fresh at peak ripeness or processed into preserves and sauces. Plant with Hood or Orient pear for cross-pollination — Flordahome is not self-fertile and requires a pollinizer. Fire blight resistance is moderate; preventive copper sprays at bloom reduce fire blight incidence in humid Gulf South climates. Flordahome trees grow vigorously in zone 9 and may need pruning to maintain manageable size — prune annually during dormancy to develop and maintain an open-center structure.

common_name: Flordaking Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Early Freestone Peach for Zone 9)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Flordaking requires only 250–350 chilling hours (hours below 45°F), making it one of the lowest-chill peach varieties adaptable to zone 9 conditions where winters are mild. In zone 9 (Gulf Coast region), the standard 400–500 chill hours required by most standard peach varieties are often not accumulated, leading to poor bloom and production; Flordaking's low chill requirement allows reliable production in zone 9. The fruit ripens in May–June — relatively early in the peach season — before summer heat becomes intense. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; peach trees are susceptible to root rot in poorly drained soils. Flordaking is self-fertile and does not require a cross-pollinator, though cross-pollination with another early-blooming peach may increase fruit set.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; prune to an open-vase shape in year 1. Thin fruit clusters to 6–8 inches between fruits when marble-sized. Flordaking Peach was released by the University of Florida Tropical Research and Education Center (then Florida Agricultural Experiment Station) in 1957 as one of the pioneering low-chill peach varieties specifically bred for Florida and Gulf Coast conditions. The development of low-chill peach varieties began in earnest at the University of Florida under the leadership of George Lyrene and others who recognized that the warm-winter climate of Florida and the Gulf Coast made it impossible to grow standard peach varieties requiring 600–800+ chilling hours. Flordaking became one of the landmark early low-chill releases: a freestone variety (the pit separates easily from the flesh at full ripeness) with medium-large fruit, yellow skin blushed with red, and yellow flesh of good eating quality for a low-chill variety. The variety's reputation for reliability in low-chill conditions — producing consistent crops when other peach varieties bloom prematurely or fail to set properly in zone 9's mild winters — established Flordaking as a foundation variety in Gulf Coast peach production, and it remains planted and recommended decades after its introduction. For zone 9 gardeners, Flordaking represents one of the most accessible routes to growing tree-ripe peaches at home in a climate where most stone fruits are impractical.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in January–February in zone 9, containerized trees through early spring; Flordaprince requires only 150–200 chill hours (hours below 45°F), making it one of the very few peach varieties that fruits reliably in zone 9a–9b and coastal zone 8. Requires a cross-pollinator or self-fruitfulness depends on climate — plant with Tropic Beauty for best yields.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5) in full sun; Flordaprince is a very-low-chill peach released by the University of Florida's fruit breeding program in 1982, bred specifically for the Gulf Coast and central Florida where most standard peach varieties fail to fruit because winters are too mild to accumulate sufficient chill hours. With only 150–200 chill hours required, Flordaprince blooms and sets fruit consistently across zone 9. The fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, semi-freestone, with a pleasant mild peach flavor ripening in mid-April to early May — remarkably early compared to northern varieties. Trees grow vigorously and require annual pruning to an open-center form to maintain size and fruit quality. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart in April for large fruit size. Protect blooms from late cold snaps in zone 8b; blooms appear in January–February and can be damaged by freezes below 28°F. Fire blight can be a problem — remove affected wood promptly.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in January-February; needs about 150 chill hours, well suited to north and central Florida, coastal Alabama, and other mild-winter Gulf Coast sites.
directions: An early University of Florida low-chill introduction bearing firm, juicy yellow-fleshed fruit with an attractive light red blush and a fairly long shelf life for a low-chill peach. It ripens earlier than most standard peaches, giving Gulf Coast gardeners fresh fruit well ahead of the general peach season. Grow in full sun with well-drained, slightly acidic soil, thin heavy fruit set for larger peaches, and monitor for bacterial spot, which can be more troublesome on early-blooming, low-chill types in wet springs.

common_name: Floriana Muscadine Grape (Self-Fertile Pierce's-Disease-Resistant Red Wine Muscadine)
plant_note: Plant rooted vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun; Floriana, bred by Florida A&M University, is a self-fertile red-fruited muscadine developed specifically for Pierce's-disease-resistant red wine production, ripening August-September.
directions: Plant self-fertile vines in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy two-wire trellis, since muscadines are vigorous, long-lived vines that need substantial permanent support. Floriana, bred by Florida A&M University, was developed specifically to fill a gap in muscadine wine production: while most muscadine wine cultivars produce white or bronze fruit, Floriana bears deep red berries suited to producing genuine red muscadine wine, combined with strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease spread by sharpshooter insects that devastates traditional bunch grapes across the Gulf South and much of Florida. Being self-fertile, a single vine sets a full crop without a pollinator. Fruit ripens in August and September. Prune annually in winter to renewal spurs along the permanent cordons to maintain productivity and vine health.

common_name: Florida Beauty Strawberry (Day-Neutral Gulf Coast Strawberry)
plant_note: Transplant plugs or bare-root plants in fall (October–November in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile, sandy loam in full sun; Florida Beauty is a day-neutral variety developed for Gulf South production — it does not require the long cold periods needed by June-bearing northern varieties.
directions: Transplant plugs or bare-root plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, sandy loam in full sun; Florida Beauty is a University of Florida IFAS strawberry introduction developed specifically for Gulf Coast production — a day-neutral cultivar adapted to the warm winters and mild springs of zone 8–10 where standard June-bearing northern varieties (Chandler, Camarosa) perform unreliably in recent warmer winters. Day-neutral strawberries are not dependent on day length for flower initiation — they flower and fruit based on temperature rather than photoperiod, making them more reliably productive across a range of winter weather patterns in the Gulf South. Florida Beauty produces attractive, large (medium-to-large), bright red, excellent-flavored fruits with firm texture and good fresh-eating quality. In zone 9, transplant in October–November for a production window from January through April — the peak of Gulf South strawberry season when temperatures are ideal for fruit development and quality. The plants are treated as annuals in commercial production (removed after the spring harvest) but can be maintained as short-lived perennials in home garden beds. Florida Beauty represents the most recent generation of Gulf South strawberry breeding that addresses the challenges of warm-winter climate change on traditional day-length-sensitive cultivar performance.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized trees in midwinter; this University of Florida release needs under 100 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any peach, so it sets fruit reliably even in mild coastal zone 9a-9b winters.
directions: Bred by the University of Florida stone fruit program for the state's subtropical climate, this very-low-chill freestone peach produces medium red-skinned fruit with soft, melting yellow flesh and good flavor for such an early-ripening variety. Because it blooms extremely early, protect flowers from occasional cold snaps and avoid planting in low-lying frost pockets. Keep trees pruned to an open, low-vase form for easy harvest and better airflow, which helps limit fungal disease in humid Gulf Coast springs.

common_name: Florida King Peach (Large Low-Chill Yellow Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile soil in full sun; Florida King requires approximately 450–500 chill hours (hours below 45°F) for adequate dormancy break — it is suited for zone 8–9a where chill hours are sufficient but temperatures are mild enough for low-chill fruit production.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Florida King is one of the premier low-chill peach cultivars for the Gulf South — a large-fruited, yellow-fleshed, freestone peach that produces high-quality fruit with approximately 450–500 chill hours of cold requirement, making it adapted to the winter climate of zone 8–9a where higher-chill northern peach varieties fail to break dormancy properly. The large fruits (2.5–3 inches diameter) have golden-yellow skin with an attractive red blush, yellow-orange flesh, small pit (freestone type), and excellent sweet peach flavor. Florida King ripens in May in zone 9 — one of the earliest major peach harvests, ahead of the intense summer heat that can reduce quality in later-ripening cultivars. Like all peaches, Florida King must be thinned aggressively after set: thin to one fruit every 6–8 inches on each branch to allow the remaining fruits to develop to full size — unthinned trees produce large numbers of small, inferior fruits. Prune annually in late winter (February in zone 9) to maintain tree size at 10–12 feet, promote new wood development on which next season's crop will form, and open the canopy to air circulation that reduces disease pressure. Peach leaf curl and brown rot are the primary disease challenges in the humid Gulf South — preventive dormant sprays with copper fungicide are standard practice.

common_name: Florida Onyx Muscadine Grape (Large-Cluster Black Fresh-Market Muscadine)
plant_note: Plant rooted vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun; Florida Onyx, a Florida A&M fresh-market release, bears unusually large, deep black-red berries in dense 8-15-berry clusters with extended shelf life, ripening August-September.
directions: Plant vines in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy two-wire trellis, since muscadines are vigorous, long-lived vines that need substantial permanent support. Florida Onyx, released by Florida A&M University's muscadine breeding program for the fresh market, is notable for forming unusually dense, tight clusters of 8 to 15 large, deep black-red berries, far more than the loose groups of three to five berries typical of most muscadine cultivars, giving it a bunch-grape-like cluster appearance while retaining the thick skin, disease resistance, and heat tolerance of true muscadine. The berries also hold their quality unusually well after harvest, extending shelf life for fresh sales or home storage. It shows good resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease that limits bunch grape production across the Gulf South. Prune annually in winter to renewal spurs along the permanent cordons to maintain productivity.

common_name: Florida Prince Peach (Low-Chill Gulf South Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in January–February in zone 9 in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), deep, fertile soil in full sun; Florida Prince is a true low-chill peach requiring only 150 chill hours, making it appropriate for the warmest parts of zone 9 and zone 10 where standard peaches fail.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), deep, fertile soil in full sun; Florida Prince is the standard low-chill peach cultivar for Gulf Coast zone 9–10 production — requiring only approximately 150 chill hours (hours below 45°F), compared to 800–1000 hours required by standard northern peach cultivars. This dramatically low chill requirement allows reliable peach production in coastal Louisiana, southern Texas, central Florida, and other warm winter areas where standard peach cultivars receive inadequate chilling to bloom and set fruit properly. Florida Prince produces medium-sized, round, yellow-fleshed, semi-freestone to clingstone fruit with a red blush on the sunny side — quality is good for fresh eating and suitable for canning and preserves, though not equal to the finest high-chill peach cultivars in flavor complexity. Fruit ripens in late April through May in zone 9 — very early in the season — which helps avoid much of the summer disease pressure that affects later cultivars. The tree is vigorous, productive, and well-adapted to the clay and sandy loam soils of the Gulf Coastal Plain. Thin fruit heavily (6–8 inches between remaining fruits) after natural June drop to develop full-sized fruits. Annual pruning to maintain an open-vase form is essential for air circulation and disease management in humid Gulf Coast conditions.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after removing the fleshy seed coat in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or well-drained soil in full sun; Florida soapberry grows naturally in upland sandy forests and sandhills of the Florida Peninsula and is adapted to poor, sandy, well-drained soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Florida soapberry is a native tree of the Florida Peninsula, growing naturally in upland sandy forests, sandhills, and dry flatwoods. Like its relative western soapberry (S. drummondii), it produces fleshy, translucent, amber fruits high in saponins that lather in water and have been used as natural soap. The pinnately compound leaves turn yellow in fall. Florida soapberry tends to be smaller and more restricted in distribution than western soapberry, naturally adapted to the sandy, acid, well-drained soils of Florida's uplands rather than the calcareous plains soils of the central US. The fruits are eaten by mockingbirds and robins. An underused drought-tolerant native for sandy, dry garden conditions in Florida and adjacent Gulf States where its multiple seasons of interest — spring flowers, fall color, and persistent amber fruits — make it a useful ornamental native.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida strangler fig is native to subtropical hammocks and rockland habitats of south Florida and the Florida Keys. It typically starts as an epiphyte but can also be planted as a free-standing tree from container stock.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida strangler fig is the only native fig species of the continental United States (excluding Hawaii), naturally occurring in the subtropical hammocks and rockland of south Florida and the Keys. In nature it begins as an epiphyte — a seed dropped by a bird into a tree crotch germinates and sends aerial roots down to the soil that eventually engulf and 'strangle' the host tree. As a free-standing garden tree it simply grows as a magnificent, large-canopy evergreen. The small yellow-orange figs are eaten by an extraordinary variety of wildlife — dozens of bird species, Florida panthers, and raccoons — making the strangler fig one of the most ecologically productive trees in south Florida. The dense canopy provides important nesting habitat for raptors. A keystone species of the south Florida hammock ecosystem.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late autumn or plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; flowering quince is extremely adaptable, tolerating clay, sandy, poor, and alkaline soils once established. It blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering, never in late summer or fall, or next year's flowers will be removed.
directions: Plant in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; flowering quince is one of the earliest-blooming ornamental shrubs of the temperate garden — producing brilliant flowers in red, scarlet, orange, salmon, pink, or white directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter and very early spring (February–March in the mid-South), often through snow. The dense, interlocking thorny growth makes it an impenetrable barrier hedge as well as an ornamental specimen. After the flowers, the shrub produces hard, green to yellow-green quincelike fruits 2–3 inches across that are not particularly palatable raw but make excellent jelly, preserves, and liqueurs — a quality long exploited in Japanese and Chinese cuisine. The fruits are high in pectin, which makes them particularly valuable for preserving, and have an intense quince fragrance when ripe. Extremely cold-hardy, drought-tolerant once established, and adaptable to a wide range of soils. The many named cultivars span the full color range from pure white ('Jet Trail') to deepest blood-red ('Crimson and Gold').

plant_note: Plant in spring; a dwarf, contorted form of the hardy orange.
directions: Flying Dragon is a dwarf, contorted selection of trifoliate orange with curved thorns and twisting stems, valued both ornamentally and as a size-controlling rootstock. It bears the same small, aromatic fruit and shares the species' extreme cold hardiness. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, where its sculptural winter silhouette is a feature. Prune minimally to preserve the natural twisting form, and use the tart autumn fruit for preserves.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Forastero cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.
