American hazelnut (C. americana) is hardier and more disease-resistant than European types; many gardeners grow hybrid selections for both traits. Eastern filbert blight (Anisogramma anomala) is a serious fungal disease in the eastern United States — choose blight-resistant cultivars such as Jefferson or York for eastern plantings. Harvest in late summer when nuts begin to fall from the husks on their own.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring; heartnut adapts to a wide range of soils and is one of the most productive walnuts for northern growers.
directions: Heartnut is a variety of Japanese walnut bearing distinctively heart-shaped nuts that crack open cleanly along a suture to release a whole kernel — unlike black walnut, which requires significant effort to extract meat. Trees are monoecious and partially self-fertile but yield better with a second tree; they begin bearing in 4–7 years from grafted stock. Heartnut is notably less allelopathic than black walnut, making it more garden-friendly as a specimen tree. Nuts fall in clusters in late summer to early fall; hull and dry for 2–3 weeks before cracking and storing.

plant_note: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Hendre Huffcap is one of the more precocious perry pears, bearing somewhat sooner than many other traditional varieties.
directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Hendre Huffcap is one of the more precocious perry pears, bearing somewhat sooner than many other traditional varieties. A well-regarded Herefordshire perry pear producing large, elongated, aromatic fruit for the type, it yields fragrant, medium-tannin juice that makes for a softer, more approachable perry than the harshest bittersharp varieties, contributing floral aromatics valued by perry makers seeking a more delicate finished blend. Its comparatively earlier bearing age and good, consistent yields have made it one of the more commercially popular traditional perry pears for new plantings. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften and develop aroma, then mill and press for perry.

common_name: Hewes Virginia Crab Apple (Colonial-Era Cider Crabapple)
plant_note: Plant in full sun; the tough, disease-tolerant tree needs little pampering once its roots are established.
directions: Grown at Monticello and documented by Thomas Jefferson himself, this small, hard, tannic crabapple was a workhorse of colonial Virginia cider production, adding astringency and complexity when blended with sweeter apples at the press. The tree is markedly tougher and more disease-resistant than standard dessert apples, tolerating poorer soil and less spray attention. Fruit is far too tannic and small to eat out of hand, so it is grown specifically as a blending variety for traditional heritage ciders. Choose it to recreate historically accurate colonial-style cider or to add backbone to a home cider blend.

plant_note: Plant grafted named varieties in spring in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained soil; hicans require a cross-pollinator from either pecan or shagbark hickory for reliable crop; named hican varieties include 'McCallister', 'Pleas', and 'Burton'.
directions: Plant grafted named-variety trees in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained bottomland soil in full sun; hicans are natural and intentionally bred hybrids between pecan (Carya illinoinensis) and various hickory species (most commonly shagbark or bitternut), combining traits of both parents — the nuts are usually larger and easier to crack than hickory but with a richer, more complex flavor than straight pecan, with less oil and a firmer, drier kernel. Trees are typically very vigorous and disease-resistant, combining pecan's productivity tendency with hickory's cold hardiness and adaptability. Suitable for zones 5–9 where pecan may be too tender or unreliable; an excellent choice for nut tree diversification in humid eastern forests. Requires cross-pollination from pecan or a compatible hickory nearby.

common_name: Himrod Grape (Cornell-Bred White Seedless Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Himrod, bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York station, is a widely grown early-ripening white seedless table grape; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.
directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Himrod was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and remains one of the most widely planted seedless table grapes for home gardens in cooler climates, producing loose clusters of amber-green, honey-sweet, crisp berries that ripen early in the season. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning to improve berry size. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

common_name: Hog Plum (Wild Olive, Seaside Plum, Tallow Wood)
plant_note: Plant in well-drained coastal or dry tropical soils; hog plum is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in thin sandy or rocky soils where little else grows.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil — tolerates poor, rocky, and alkaline soils exceptionally well once established; hog plum is a pantropical shrub or small tree with strongly fragrant white flowers and small oval fruits that ripen from green to yellow-orange then red, with thin skin, juicy sour-sweet flesh, and a large oily seed. The fruit is eaten fresh when fully ripe but is very sour; it makes excellent jellies, juices, and fermented drinks popular across sub-Saharan Africa, the Caribbean, and coastal Brazil. The seeds contain a high-quality oil used for cooking and cosmetics in West Africa. A superb drought- and salt-spray-tolerant fruiting hedge plant for coastal gardens.

common_name: Hojiblanca Olive (Dual-Purpose Spanish Oil and Table Olive)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; provide a compatible pollinizer variety for the best fruit set, since Hojiblanca benefits from cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer nearby. Hojiblanca, meaning 'white leaf' in Spanish for the strikingly silvery undersides of its foliage, is one of the most important olive varieties of Andalusia in southern Spain, valued for genuine dual-purpose flexibility, producing both good quality mild oil and firm, attractive table olives from the same tree depending on how the crop is used and harvested. The tree is vigorous, productive, and reasonably disease-tolerant, contributing to its widespread commercial planting across southern Spain. Harvest earlier and greener for table olive curing, or later for oil pressing, and remember that all olives require proper curing before eating fresh off the tree, since raw fruit is intensely bitter.

plant_note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring after frost risk passes, in full sun with well-drained soil; protect young trees their first two winters, since the root system is hardier than the top growth and will often resprout after a hard freeze.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes; Homestead is a South Florida dooryard guava selected for reliable production and good fruit quality in a home-garden setting, bearing medium-sized fruit with yellow skin and pink-tinged, sweet-tart flesh that is popular for fresh eating and for guava paste and juice alike. Like other guavas it fruits on new wood, so an annual late-winter prune keeps the shrub-form tree productive and manageable in size rather than letting it grow into an unwieldy small tree. Guava roots generally tolerate brief dips into the upper 20s Fahrenheit even when the canopy is killed back, so zone 9 gardeners should mulch the root zone heavily going into winter and expect to prune out and regrow frozen top growth in a hard year. In a favorable year with a long warm season, established plants can produce two overlapping flushes of fruit.

common_name: Honey Jar Jujube (Small Sweet Early Chinese Jujube)
plant_note: Plant grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Honey Jar is an early-maturing jujube variety producing small, very round fruits that ripen weeks ahead of Li and Lang — it is considered by many tasters to be the sweetest-flavored jujube available, with a flavor that lives up to its name of a fruit as sweet as concentrated honey.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Honey Jar is among the earliest jujubes to ripen (mid-August in many areas, 3–4 weeks before Li and Lang); the small fruits are best consumed fresh at peak ripeness rather than dried; trees are moderately compact compared to other jujube varieties. Honey Jar is widely regarded as the sweetest-tasting jujube variety available in American nurseries — the fruits are small (about 3/4 to 1 inch), round, and at perfect ripeness have a flavor described as pure concentrated honey with very little acidity and no bitterness, earning the variety its descriptive name. The small size, while meaning less fruit per piece, is actually an advantage in fresh eating situations where you want to pop a whole fruit in your mouth without cutting — Honey Jar is the jujube equivalent of a cherry tomato or Champagne grape, perfectly sized for snacking directly from the tree. The early ripening season (mid-August in zones 6–8, somewhat earlier in zone 9a) makes Honey Jar valuable for extending the fresh jujube harvest over the longest possible season when planted alongside the mid-season Li and the late-season Lang — a three-variety planting can provide fresh jujubes from late July through October. The trees are somewhat more compact than Li and Lang, making Honey Jar a good choice when space is limited. Cross-pollination with Lang or Li improves fruit set on Honey Jar trees significantly.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring in dry, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; honey mesquite has an extraordinarily deep taproot that allows it to reach permanent water tables — do not transplant seedlings once established, and plant only in permanent locations.
directions: Honey mesquite is the defining native tree of Texas plains and prairies, a thorny, nitrogen-fixing legume of unmatched drought resilience that has sustained both wildlife and indigenous cultures of the semi-arid Southwest for thousands of years — its sweet, nutritious seed pods were ground into mesquite meal (pinole) by many Southwestern and Gulf Coast tribes and are the source of distinctively flavored mesquite honey produced by Texas beekeepers from the abundant, fragrant yellow catkin flowers in spring and summer. The hard, dense wood is the premier smoking wood for Texas barbecue and is also used in flooring, furniture, and decorative woodworking; charcoal from honey mesquite burns hotter and longer than most other hardwoods. Honey mesquite is an important wildlife tree: the pods are consumed by deer, javelinas, coyotes, and dozens of bird species; the canopy provides nesting habitat for doves, mockingbirds, and scissor-tailed flycatchers across Texas ranchlands. Long-paired spines on the branches can be hazardous — site away from foot traffic, but within wildlife habitat and native plantings it is invaluable.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; needs a compatible plum, pluot, or nectaplum pollinizer nearby with overlapping bloom time.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer nearby with overlapping bloom time. Honey Punch is a Zaiger Genetics 'nectaplum,' an interspecific hybrid combining nectarine and plum genetics, producing smooth-skinned, deep red fruit with dense, richly flavored red-tinged flesh that carries the smooth skin and juiciness of nectarine along with the depth of flavor plum breeding contributes. As with other Zaiger interspecific stone fruit hybrids, the combination produces a genuinely distinctive eating experience different from either parent species grown alone, with concentrated sweetness and complex flavor prized by specialty fruit growers. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and fully colors for the best flavor.

plant_note: Plant grafted container trees in spring after cold risk; in zone 9 plant February–April in full sun with southern exposure protection. Honey tangerines are tender and more cold-sensitive than navel oranges — require protection below 28°F. Late-season (January–March) ripening makes them the last mandarin of the season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in the warmest available location in full sun; Honey tangerine (also called Murcott or Murcott honey mandarin) is one of the most intensely flavored and sweetest commercial citrus varieties — the name 'Honey' reflects its extraordinary sugar content (Brix up to 14–16) and rich, honeyed, complex flavor that combines mandarin aromatics with tangerine sweetness and a characteristic mild tartness. The fruit is medium-sized, deep orange, with thin, peelable skin and tender, very juicy flesh. Ripening in January–March, Honey tangerines extend the citrus season into late winter and early spring when other citrus is winding down. They have seeded flesh (unlike some modern mandarins) but flavor more than compensates. Trees are productive and attractive landscape specimens; they can have alternate-bearing tendencies (heavy crop one year, lighter the next) that are managed by thinning in the on-year. Feed with citrus fertilizer; protect from temperatures below 28°F. Florida produces commercial quantities in Polk and Highlands counties.

plant_note: Plant dormant in early spring; requires a second apple variety nearby for pollination.
directions: Honeycrisp is beloved for its explosively crisp texture and balanced sweet-tart flavor, and it is notably cold-hardy. It needs a compatible pollinating apple variety and thrives in cooler northern climates. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and water steadily through the season. Thin fruit clusters and prune in late winter to promote large, well-colored apples and reduce disease pressure.

subcategory: East Asian small-fruiting Garcinia ornamental tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–11; Hong Kong Garcinia is a small to medium ornamental and fruiting tree native to southern China, Hong Kong, and Vietnam — bearing small clusters of bright-orange to red fruits with sweet-sour, translucent flesh above attractive, glossy, oblong leaves — relatively cold-tolerant compared to tropical Garcinias and adaptable to humid subtropical conditions.
directions: Plant Garcinia oblongifolia in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to dappled sun; maintain consistent soil moisture and avoid prolonged drought; protect young plants from temperatures below 32°F; established trees tolerate light frost. Hong Kong Garcinia is one of the more cold-hardy Garcinia species — adapted to the subtropical climate of South China and Hong Kong where winters can be cool with occasional brief frost — making it more tractable in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens than strictly tropical Garcinias. The ornamental value is high: the tree has a neat, dense, compact form with attractive, glossy, oblong, dark-green leaves and produces small clusters of bright orange-red fruits that are decorative on the tree. The fruits have a sweet-sour, juicy, translucent-white pulp somewhat resembling a small mangosteen in flavor — less rich than Purple Mangosteen but pleasant and refreshing. The tree is appreciated in Hong Kong and southern Chinese traditional culture both as an ornamental and for the edible fruits; it also has traditional medicinal uses in Chinese herbal medicine, particularly the dried rind of the fruit (similar to Garcinia cambogia). Relatively uncommon in Western cultivation but deserves wider planting in humid subtropical gardens as a hardy, attractive alternative to more tropical Garcinias.

common_name: Hong Kong Kumquat (Hong Kong Wild Kumquat)
plant_note: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a container to shelter indoors in winter; Hong Kong kumquat tolerates light frost once established but is best treated as tender outside zones 9-11.
directions: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a container to shelter indoors in winter; Hong Kong kumquat tolerates light frost once established but is best treated as tender outside zones 9-11. This dense, twiggy, thorny shrub from the rocky hillsides of southern China and Hong Kong bears masses of tiny, pea- to marble-sized round fruit with thin, sweet, edible rind wrapped around intensely tart, seedy pulp, best nibbled whole rather than juiced. It flowers and fruits abundantly even as a small potted specimen, making it a popular choice for bonsai and container citrus collections as much as for the fruit itself, and its fine, small-leaved habit distinguishes it from the larger-leaved kumquats grown for eating fresh. Feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season, water deeply but infrequently, and prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in winter dormancy (December–February in zone 9); Hood requires only 100–150 chill hours, making it one of the lowest-chill pear cultivars available and successful in zone 9b–10a where most pears cannot fruit. Plant with Pineapple or Floridahome for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hood is a low-chill European pear cultivar developed by the University of Florida's fruit research program, requiring only 100–150 hours of chilling — one of the lowest chill requirements of any successful pear. This makes Hood exceptional for zone 9 and even zone 9b–10a, where most European pear varieties fail to produce consistent crops. The fruit is large, greenish-yellow to yellow at maturity, with sweet, white, juicy flesh ripening in June–July in zone 9 — much earlier than conventional pear season. Flavor is mild and pleasant, suitable for fresh eating and canning. Fire blight can be a problem in humid conditions; prune out infected wood promptly and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization. Cross-pollination with Pineapple pear or Floridahome significantly improves yields. Hood is one of the three low-chill pears (with Orient and LeConte) most reliably recommended for Gulf Coast zone 9 home orchards where conventional Bartlett and Bosc fail to fruit.

common_name: Horse Apple (Large Southern Heirloom Cooking Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Horse Apple has one of the lowest chill requirements of the old Southern apples and sets fruit reliably in warmer zone 8–9 winters where many Northern apple cultivars fail to break dormancy properly.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and plant a second apple cultivar nearby for pollination, since Horse Apple is not reliably self-fruitful. A large, old Southern heirloom of uncertain origin, Horse Apple produces big, greenish-yellow fruit with a coarse, tart flesh best suited to cooking, drying, and cider rather than fresh eating out of hand — its name reflects both its large size and its traditional use as livestock and orchard fruit as much as table fruit. Its low chill requirement and long history of successful cultivation across the Deep South make it one of the more reliable heirloom apples for Gulf Coast gardens, where many higher-chill Northern cultivars struggle to fruit consistently. Fruit ripens in mid to late summer and does not store especially well, so plan to process it into sauce, butter, or cider soon after harvest.

common_name: Hosui Asian Pear (Japanese Golden-Russet Round Asian Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Hosui requires approximately 400–450 chilling hours (hours below 45°F) — achievable in most of zone 7–9 in most years. Asian pears are not self-fertile — plant at least two different Asian pear varieties (Shinsei, Twentieth Century, Olympic, or another Pyrus pyrifolia) within 50 feet for pollination; European pears (Pyrus communis) are generally not compatible pollinators. Hosui fruit ripens in August in zone 9 — earlier than most Asian pears — and should be harvested when still firm on the tree (unlike European pears, Asian pears do not improve in storage and should be harvested at full ripeness). Fruits do not ripen after harvest the way European pears do.
directions: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil; thin fruit clusters to one fruit per cluster when fruits are marble-sized for maximum size. Asian pears need no post-harvest ripening period. Hosui is a Japanese-bred Asian pear (nashi pear, Pyrus pyrifolia) — one of the finest Asian pear varieties available in North America for both flavor quality and adaptability to warmer zones (zone 5–9 with adequate chill). The fruit is large (8–12 oz), round to slightly oblate, with distinctive golden-brown russeted skin — the russet texture of Hosui's skin is one of its defining aesthetic characteristics, giving it a warm, autumn-toned appearance that differs from the smooth green or yellow skin of other Asian pear varieties. The flesh is the extraordinary feature: extremely crisp, almost crunchy — quite unlike the soft, butter-like texture of ripe European pears — with very high juice content and a sweet, aromatic, complex flavor with notes of honey and vanilla. Asian pears are eaten fresh at harvest, when crisp and juicy at peak quality; they do not improve with storage and are not used for cooking or canning the way European pears are. Hosui is among the most popular and widely planted Asian pear varieties in Japan and California, where its early ripening, excellent flavor, and moderate chill requirement make it adaptable to a wider range of climates than many Asian pear types.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them to accommodate the tree's naturally compact, spreading form. Howard is a widely planted California commercial English walnut variety valued for its lateral bearing habit, which sets nuts along the length of each branch rather than only at the tips, boosting yields per acre. It produces a light-colored, high-quality kernel and buds out later than older varieties such as Hartley, reducing the risk of spring frost damage to the crop.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Howell was introduced from Connecticut in 1806 and long valued for dependable, heavy annual crops.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Introduced from Connecticut in 1806, Howell bears medium to large, yellow, red-blushed pears with sweet, juicy, fine-grained flesh, and the tree became a widely planted commercial and home orchard variety through the 19th century thanks to its dependable, heavy annual bearing and relatively early start to production compared to many other pears of its era. It remains a solid, low-fuss choice for a home orchard wanting reliable fall pears without fussy care. Harvest while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; bred in Texas for good disease and nematode resistance, making it a strong choice for Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Hunt was developed in Texas and selected for genuinely good resistance to root-knot nematodes and several fig diseases that trouble other varieties in the warm, humid soils of the Gulf South, making it a particularly reliable, low-maintenance choice for Texas, Louisiana, and neighboring Gulf Coast gardens. The medium, brown-skinned fruit has sweet, richly flavored pink-amber flesh, good for fresh eating and preserves, and the productive tree bears a heavy main crop in late summer. Its combination of regional disease resistance and dependable production has made it a long-standing favorite among Gulf Coast home orchardists specifically dealing with the nematode-prone sandy soils common across the region.

common_name: Hyakume Persimmon (Gosho, Nearly Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hyakume is self-fruitful, but pollination and seed formation encourage its flesh to develop the brown sugar-flecked pattern that lets it be eaten while still firm.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hyakume, also sold as Gosho, is a large, flattish Japanese kaki persimmon cultivar notable among astringent-type persimmons for a distinctive trait — when the flowers are pollinated and seeds form, the flesh develops streaks and flecks of brown, sugary tissue, and fruit with enough of this coloring can be eaten firm and crisp like a non-astringent type rather than requiring full softening. Unpollinated fruit without seeds remains fully astringent until soft-ripe, so planting near another kaki cultivar for pollination noticeably improves the eating experience. The fruit is large, pale orange, and mild-flavored with a pleasant, slightly spiced sweetness once the brown sugar-flecking develops. Trees are vigorous, productive, and, like most Asian persimmons, largely trouble-free once established, tolerating heat and a range of soils well. Harvest in fall as fruit colors fully; taste-test a fruit or two to judge whether the crop has enough pollination-driven flecking to eat crisp, or whether it needs to soften fully before eating.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups/suckers) after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Ice Cream banana is one of the more cold-tolerant banana varieties — the rhizomes survive frost to about 22°F if heavily mulched, and the plant resprouts vigorously from the rhizome in spring even when the above-ground pseudostem is killed. In zone 9 a plant that survives multiple seasons as a ratoon crop (resprouting from the surviving rhizome) will bloom and produce fruit within 9–12 months of the spring resprouting. Allow suckers to develop as replacement ratoon plants when the main pseudostem flowers, since banana plants fruit only once per pseudostem.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil with consistent moisture — banana requires abundant water, nutrients, and heat to produce fruit; Ice Cream banana (also called Blue Java) is a cold-tolerant banana cultivar notable for its distinctive blue-green to silvery-blue coloring on unripe fruits and the unusually rich, creamy flavor of ripe fruit described as reminiscent of vanilla ice cream — a flavor and texture quality that sets this cultivar apart from the standard Cavendish banana flavor most North Americans are accustomed to. The ripe fruits develop a pale yellow to creamy-white flesh with a particularly soft, smooth, melting texture and vanilla-banana flavor that is among the finest of all banana varieties for fresh eating. Ice Cream's relative cold tolerance compared to Cavendish and other commercial varieties (the rhizome surviving to approximately 22°F with mulching) makes it one of the most practical banana varieties for zone 9 Gulf South gardens where winter freezes regularly kill the above-ground pseudostem. In zone 9 the combination of the summer heat, humidity, and rain that banana requires, combined with the cold-hardiness that allows ratoon production from surviving rhizomes, makes Ice Cream banana one of the most rewarding tropical fruit plants available.

common_name: Ice Cream Banana (Blue Java Cold-Hardy Vanilla-Flavored Banana)
plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Java tolerates frost to approximately 20°F (-7°C) — the pseudostem may be killed but the rhizome survives most zone 9 winters and regenerates new shoots in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Blue Java (Ice Cream banana) is one of the most cold-hardy banana cultivars available for Gulf South gardens — tolerating frost temperatures to approximately 20°F, allowing the rhizome to survive most zone 9 winters even when the pseudostem is frozen to the ground and regenerate productive new shoots in spring. The variety name 'Blue Java' refers to the distinctive blue-green color of the unripe fruit bunches; the 'Ice Cream' name describes the rich, creamy, vanilla-like flavor of the ripe fruit — a flavor profile distinctly different from the standard Cavendish banana of commerce and more complex, with smooth, creamy, slightly vanilla-custard characteristics that justify the evocative name. The medium-length (6–8 inch), pale-yellow ripe fruits have a soft, creamy texture that reinforces the ice cream comparison. In zone 9, Blue Java typically requires the full warm season (May–October) for pseudostem development, and established plants with multiple offsets may fruit in warm years with protection through mild winters. Even when pseudostems are killed by frost, the vigorous rhizome system regenerates multiple new shoots in spring, making Blue Java a reliable ornamental tropical even in years when fruit production is not achieved. Heavy mulching around the base protects the rhizome during cold snaps.

plant_note: Plant the pup after frost; grow in a large pot to shelter indoors in cold climates.
directions: Also called Blue Java, this banana yields creamy, vanilla-flavored fruit and tolerates more cold and wind than most bananas. Give it full sun, rich soil, and abundant water plus regular feeding to fuel its fast growth. The bluish fruit ripens to pale yellow and is best eaten fresh. In marginal climates grow it in a large container and overwinter the plant in a bright, frost-free spot.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; ice cream bean grows rapidly and begins fruiting in 2–3 years from seed. Hardy to about 29°F; zone 9b–12 in the ground, containers in zone 9a.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — ice cream bean is a fast-growing Central and South American legume tree producing enormous pods (12–30 inches long) filled with white, cottony, sweet pulp that wraps the seeds and tastes unmistakably of vanilla ice cream. The white pulp is eaten fresh directly from the pod; it melts on the tongue with a sweet, mild, creamy vanilla flavor that surprises everyone who encounters it for the first time. Beyond the extraordinary fruit, ice cream bean is a nitrogen-fixing legume that improves soil fertility, an excellent shade and windbreak tree (growing 30–40 feet), and a valuable component of agroforestry systems throughout the tropics. The fragrant white flower pompoms attract hummingbirds and native bees. It grows rapidly in the frost-free tropics and sub-tropics, beginning to fruit in 2–3 years from seed.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Ichang lemon is one of the most cold-hardy citrus species, with mature wood tolerating temperatures down to around 0°F, and is often grown as much for its hardiness and rootstock value as for its tart fruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the hardiest citrus species available, surviving winter conditions that kill standard lemons and limes outright. Citrus ichangensis (Ichang lemon, or Ichang papeda) is a wild citrus species native to the mountainous borderlands of China, prized by cold-hardy citrus breeders and enthusiasts as one of the parents behind many of today's cold-tolerant citrus hybrids, thanks to its unusual combination of true citrus flavor and genuine winter hardiness. The rough-skinned, lemon-like fruit is highly acidic and aromatic with a distinct floral note, used much like a true lemon for juice, zest, and flavoring rather than fresh eating out of hand. Its glossy, deep green, notably large-winged leaves and modest thorns give it strong ornamental value even apart from fruiting. A rewarding choice for gardeners in the Gulf South and Southeast who want to grow citrus outside the usual protected range, and a useful parent plant for anyone interested in breeding hardier citrus hybrids, zone 7–10.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Ichang Papeda is among the most cold-hardy citrus species, tolerating temperatures to about 0–5°F when established — making it suitable for zone 7 and a nearly indestructible rootstock or ornamental in zone 9. It is primarily grown as an ornamental, rootstock, or specimen tree for its exceptional cold hardiness; the fruits are used for juice and flavoring but are not eating citrus. Ichang Papeda has contributed cold hardiness to many citrus breeding programs.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Ichang Papeda (Citrus ichangensis, Ichang lemon) is a wild citrus species from the mountains of central China near Yichang on the Yangtze River — the hardiest true citrus species, capable of surviving brief temperatures near 0°F and making it valuable for cold-climate citrus experimentation far beyond the normal range. The large, fragrant, lemon-yellow fruits are highly aromatic but extremely acidic and seedy, used for juice, fragrance, and culinary flavoring rather than fresh eating. The distinctive winged petioles on the leaves identify the plant and give it an interesting ornamental appearance with an almost tropical look. In zone 9 Ichang Papeda grows vigorously and produces abundant, highly aromatic fruit with a distinctive floral-citrus fragrance used in Chinese cooking and perfumery. Ichang Papeda is a parent of the Yuzu lemon hybrid and has contributed cold hardiness to many important citrus breeding programs; it thrives in zone 9 as an ornamental citrus tree with exceptional cold insurance.

common_name: Ichi Ki Kei Jiro Persimmon (Self-Fertile Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Ichi Ki Kei Jiro is a self-fertile, non-astringent Asian persimmon that can be eaten crisp like an apple as soon as it colors, without needing to soften first.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, and stake young trees until well established. Ichi Ki Kei Jiro is a compact, heavy-bearing Japanese persimmon cultivar belonging to the non-astringent group, meaning the fruit can be harvested and eaten crisp and sweet as soon as it reaches full orange color, unlike astringent Asian and American persimmons that must fully soften before they are palatable. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will produce a full crop without a pollinator, and its naturally smaller stature suits home orchards with limited space. Thin fruit if the tree sets an especially heavy crop to improve size, and harvest by clipping fruit from the branch rather than pulling, since the stem can tear the skin.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Idared requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 4-8.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Idared was bred at the University of Idaho and released in 1942 from a cross of Jonathan and Wagener, developed specifically to combine good eating quality with truly outstanding long-term storage life, and it remains one of the best-keeping apples widely available, often holding good quality for six months or more in cold storage. The bright, uniform red fruit has firm, crisp, white flesh that starts out notably tart and mellows into a pleasant, mild tartness in storage, making it a favorite for pies, sauce, and baking, since it holds its shape well under heat. The tree is vigorous, productive, and reliable, and the fruit's long shelf life makes it an especially practical choice for home orchardists wanting apples that last well into winter without special storage facilities.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a frost-free setting with a distinct dry season to stimulate bloom.
directions: Ilama is a semi-deciduous Annona from Mexico and Central America that tolerates drier conditions than most of its relatives, preferring a pronounced dry season to trigger leaf drop and subsequent flowering. Like other Annonaceae, flowers are protogynous and benefit strongly from hand-pollination — collect pollen in the afternoon from half-closed male-stage flowers and dab onto receptive stigmas of newly opened female-stage flowers in the morning. Fruit comes in pink-fleshed and white-fleshed strains; the pink-fleshed type has a slightly acidic flavor while the white is sweeter and more custard-like. Harvest when the skin has slightly separated at the segment lines and the fruit gives to gentle pressure; shelf life at room temperature is only 1–2 days.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Illinois Everbearing is one of the most cold-hardy mulberry cultivars and produces fruit over an exceptionally long season (6–8 weeks vs 2–3 weeks for single-crop varieties). Trees are fast-growing, reaching significant size (30–35 feet) quickly — allow ample permanent space. The fruit stains everything it contacts — plant away from walkways, patios, and vehicles. In zone 9 mulberries produce prolifically in April–May and may fruit again in fall.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — mulberry is adaptable to a wide range of soil types and conditions; Illinois Everbearing is a hybrid mulberry (Morus alba x Morus rubra) that produces the longest fruit season of any widely available mulberry cultivar — harvesting over 6–8 weeks from late spring into early summer compared to the brief 2–3 week window of standard mulberry varieties. The large, cylindrical, 1–1.5 inch fruits ripen from red through dark purple-black over the extended season, with the sweet, mild, slightly bland flavor characteristic of mulberries — less complex than blackberries, softer-textured, and milder-tasting, primarily valued for fresh eating, smoothies, and baked goods where the abundant, easily harvested fruit compensates for the relatively mild flavor. The practical appeal of Illinois Everbearing is unambiguous: a single established tree produces quantities of fruit (hundreds of pounds in a mature tree) over an extended period with essentially zero cultivation requirements beyond harvesting. As a wildlife plant, mulberry is unparalleled — the fruit is consumed by more than 60 species of birds and dozens of mammal species — making it the single most productive wildlife-supporting tree available for home landscapes.

common_name: Illinois Everbearing Mulberry (Long-Season Red Mulberry Hybrid, Eastern Standard Mulberry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring; Illinois Everbearing is self-fertile and produces without a pollinator; it is a hybrid between white mulberry (Morus alba) and red mulberry (Morus rubra) with the cold-hardiness of the white parent (zones 4–8) and the superior fruit flavor of the red parent; it is the most widely recommended mulberry variety for home orchards in the eastern United States by most university cooperative extension services.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Illinois Everbearing is self-fertile; the trees are fast-growing and begin bearing in year 2–3; fruit ripens over an extended 4–6 week season (June–July in zones 5–7) rather than dropping all at once; the long harvesting period makes it practical to collect ripe fruit repeatedly from the ground or by shaking branches. Illinois Everbearing mulberry is a naturally occurring or deliberately selected hybrid of Morus alba (white mulberry) and Morus rubra (red mulberry) that was selected and propagated in Illinois in the mid-20th century and subsequently became the standard recommended mulberry variety for home orchards in the eastern and midwestern United States. The variety combines the key qualities of both parent species: from Morus rubra, it inherits superior fruit flavor — significantly more complex and berry-like than the often bland white mulberry — along with better fresh-eating quality; from Morus alba, it inherits cold-hardiness to zone 4 and adaptability to a wide range of soils and climates. The most practically important feature reflected in its name is the extended ripening season — berries mature gradually and drop over a period of 4–6 weeks rather than all ripening within 1–2 weeks as many mulberry seedlings do. This extended season makes it much more manageable for home fruit harvesting and wildlife feeding, and reduces the dramatic mess that concentrated mulberry drop can create on driveways, paths, and patios. The fruit quality is good: long (1–1.5 inch), dark red to black-purple berries with sweet, mild, pleasant mulberry flavor — not as intensely sweet as Pakistan Mulberry but far superior to most seedling trees.

subcategory: Brazilian Caatinga native dryland fruit tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to stony, poor to average soil in zone 9–11; Imbu (Umbuzeiro) is a remarkable drought-adapted fruit tree endemic to the Brazilian Caatinga semi-arid scrubland — one of the most important wild food trees of the Brazilian Northeast — that stores water in massive, starchy, underground tubers and produces small, round, yellow-green, sweet-sour fruits vital to subsistence food security in one of the world's driest inhabited regions.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to stony, poor to average soil; Spondias tuberosa is exceptionally drought tolerant — the underground water-storage tubers allow the tree to survive months of total drought; overwatering or waterlogged soil is fatal. Spondias tuberosa (Imbu, Umbú, or Umbuzeiro) is a drought-deciduous, small to medium tree endemic to the Brazilian Caatinga (semi-arid thorny scrubland) of the northeastern states of Pernambuco, Bahia, Sergipe, Piauí, and Ceará — one of the most important and beloved wild fruit trees of the Brazilian Northeast. The tree's defining ecological adaptation is remarkable: a system of massive, water-filled, carrot-to-sweet-potato-sized underground storage tubers (technically water-storing roots) that can accumulate hundreds of kilograms of water, allowing the tree to survive the brutal, multi-month droughts of the Caatinga and burst into fruit production with the first rains — typically January through March. The small (1–1.5 inch), round, pale-yellow to yellow-green fruits have juicy, sweet-sour, tropical, mango-lychee-like pulp eaten fresh, made into the beloved Brazilian drink umbuzada (fruit pulp boiled with milk and sugar), jams, and fermented into Caatinga wine. The tree has become a symbol of northeastern Brazilian cultural identity and food resilience. Spondias tuberosa is well adapted to dryland gardens in zone 9–11 where excellent drainage and full sun are provided; it is one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available.

common_name: Improved Brown Turkey Fig (Larger-Fruited Brown Turkey Selection)
plant_note: Plant after the last hard frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Improved Brown Turkey is a selection valued for producing somewhat larger fruit than standard Brown Turkey while retaining the same reliable cold hardiness and heavy production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Improved Brown Turkey is a selection of the classic Brown Turkey fig valued for producing somewhat larger, bronze-brown fruit with sweet, amber-pink flesh compared to standard Brown Turkey, while keeping the same dependable cold hardiness and heavy, reliable production that has made Brown Turkey one of the most widely planted figs in home gardens. Like other figs it bears on both old and new wood, giving an early breba crop in late spring followed by the main crop in late summer, and it needs minimal care beyond routine mulching and occasional pruning to control size. In colder zones, grow in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; like standard Celeste, Improved Celeste fruits on second-year wood and on new growth late in the season, so avoid heavy winter pruning that removes developing fruit buds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun, and mulch around the root zone to help protect against winter root injury in the northern part of its range. Improved Celeste is a selection of the classic Celeste fig chosen by growers for producing noticeably larger fruit than the standard cultivar while retaining Celeste's honey-sweet, rose-pink flesh and thin, violet-brown skin, along with its reputation for exceptional cold hardiness and dependable, heavy production in Deep South gardens. It ripens over the same mid-July through August window as standard Celeste and requires the same minimal care — established trees rarely need fertilizer and produce well without spraying. As with all Celeste-type figs, the small, closed eye at the base of the fruit helps deter souring insects and fruit spoilage common in open-eyed fig varieties in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. The 'Improved' designation refers to the virus-indexed, certified clean version released by UC Davis following the discovery that the original Meyer lemon carried citrus tristeza virus — all nursery-sold Meyer lemons are now this certified clean selection. Meyer lemon is the most cold-hardy of all true lemons, tolerating temperatures to about 22–24°F — borderline zone 8b/9a. In zone 9 it produces fruit through winter (harvest November–March), providing fresh lemons when the tree is at peak ornamental interest with simultaneous flowers and fruit. Grow in containers in colder zones to move indoors when freezes threaten.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — Meyer lemon requires excellent drainage, regular deep watering during the growing season, and full sun for maximum fruit production; Improved Meyer Lemon is the most widely grown home lemon tree in the United States — a hybrid between a true lemon (Citrus limon) and a mandarin or sweet orange (possibly Citrus sinensis) that produces fruit with significantly less acidity and more sweetness than commercial lemons, combined with a distinctively rich, complex, floral lemon fragrance that makes it the preferred fresh lemon for culinary applications requiring the full flavor profile rather than pure acidity. The thin, smooth, deep yellow to orange-yellow skin is edible and aromatic, zesting beautifully for baking applications where the combination of lemon oil and zest from a Meyer produces a more complex, rounded result than commercial Eureka or Lisbon lemons. The combination of cold hardiness (extending the range further north than most citrus), compact tree size (6–10 feet), heavy and recurrent fruit production, beautiful flowers, and superior culinary quality has made Meyer lemon the definitive home citrus tree across zones 8–11.

plant_note: Set out after frost; ideal as a container plant to overwinter indoors.
directions: A younger, bushier form of the classic Improved Meyer, this lemon-orange hybrid produces sweet-tart, thin-skinned fruit on a compact plant well suited to pots. Grow in full sun with fast-draining, slightly acidic soil and feed with citrus fertilizer during active growth. Let the top inch of soil dry between deep waterings to prevent root rot. Bring it indoors to a bright window before frost in cooler zones.

plant_note: Set out after frost; grow in a container to overwinter indoors in cold climates.
directions: Improved Meyer is a low-maintenance lemon-orange hybrid that bears masses of fragrant, sweetly tart fruit, and it is nearly thornless and disease-resistant. It fruits reliably even for beginners and works beautifully as a container specimen. Provide full sun, fast-draining acidic soil, and regular citrus feeding through the growing season. In cold-winter areas keep it potted and move it indoors near bright light before the first frost.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; a single tree can set a crop without a separate pollenizer.
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike most almond cultivars, Independence is self-fertile and can produce a good crop as a solid block planting without a separate pollenizer variety or heavy reliance on pollinator bees during bloom. It produces a semi-hard shell nut comparable in size and quality to Nonpareil, blooms later than many traditional varieties, and has become popular with growers seeking to reduce pollination costs and frost risk.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile and needs no pollinizer; best adapted to zones 5-9.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Independence is a widely grown California nectarine prized for its brilliant, nearly solid red skin and firm, richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening in midsummer on a vigorous, productive tree. The freestone pit and firm texture make it easy to prepare fresh or for preserving, and the fruit's excellent eating quality has kept it a standard commercial and home-orchard variety for decades. Like all nectarines, it shares peach genetics closely enough to suffer the same pest and disease pressures — particularly brown rot and peach leaf curl — so a routine dormant-season spray program is important for a clean crop. Thin fruit to four to six inches apart after natural drop for the best size and flavor.

common_name: Indian Almond (Tropical Almond, Beach Almond, Sea Almond)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Terminalia catappa is extremely salt-tolerant and thrives in sandy coastal soils. It is frost-sensitive in zone 9 but recovers rapidly from cold damage. The tree is briefly deciduous in late fall — leaves turn brilliant red, orange, and yellow before falling, a striking display unusual in tropical trees. The leaves and bark are widely used in aquaculture for their tannins and antimicrobial properties; Indian almond leaves are added to aquariums to lower pH and release beneficial compounds. The edible nuts are encased in a fibrous husk that requires processing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil — Indian Almond is extremely drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established, making it one of the best trees for exposed coastal sites in zone 10-11. Terminalia catappa is a large, deciduous to briefly deciduous tropical tree of uncertain original native range (possibly the Malay Archipelago and Indian Ocean Islands) that has been transported and naturalized throughout tropical coastlines worldwide by human action over millennia, now found on virtually every tropical coast from South and Southeast Asia through the Pacific Islands, tropical Africa, the Caribbean, Central America, and South Florida. The tree has a distinctive tiered, horizontal branching pattern that creates a naturally formal, layered silhouette. Large, glossy, oval leaves (8–12 inches) turn spectacular shades of red, orange, and crimson before dropping twice per year (briefly deciduous in dry or cool periods), a display of fall color unusual in the tropics. The fruits are oval drupes (1.5–2 inches) containing a hard inner kernel that, when extracted and dried, has an almond-like flavor and is eaten throughout Asia and the Pacific — though the extraction requires significant processing. The large leaves are prized in aquarium and aquaculture for their tannins, which lower pH, release antimicrobial compounds, and replicate conditions of tropical black-water streams favored by certain fish.

common_name: Indian Free Peach (Red-Fleshed Heirloom Blood Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Indian Free is a late-ripening, low-chill heirloom peach with striking red-streaked flesh, valued as much for its unusual appearance and flavor as for fresh eating.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Indian Free is a distinctive American heirloom peach, likely of Native American cultivation origin, prized for its dramatic dark red, almost blood-colored flesh streaked through pale background flesh, and a rich, tangy-sweet, wine-like flavor unlike typical commercial peaches. It is a late-season variety, ripening well after most other peaches have finished, and shows notable resistance to peach leaf curl, a fungal disease that troubles many other peach cultivars in humid climates. The freestone fruit is best used fresh, in preserves, or in baking where its vivid color makes a striking presentation. Because it is an older, less commercially refined variety, fruit size and uniformity are more variable than modern hybrid peaches, but its unusual flavor and disease resistance have kept it popular among heirloom fruit collectors and home orchardists.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Indian jujube is more heat- and drought-tolerant but less cold-hardy than Chinese jujube (Ziziphus jujuba). Grafted plants bear fruit much earlier than seedlings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun in zones 9–12; Indian jujube is one of the most widely cultivated fruits of the tropical and subtropical world, producing abundant crops of round to oval fruits that ripen from green to yellow, red, or purplish-black depending on cultivar — eaten fresh when crisp and apple-like, or dried when they become wrinkled and date-like in flavor. It is more heat-adapted and tolerant of alkaline soils than Chinese jujube, making it suited to south Texas, the Rio Grande Valley, and Gulf Coast zone 9–10 gardens. The fruit is one of the most important traditional fruits of South Asia, the Middle East, and West Africa, and is now gaining attention in the US as a dual-season crop that produces prolifically even under drought stress. Named cultivars such as 'Umran', 'Gola', and 'Seb' are selected for large fruit size and superior flavor.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to average soil in zone 8–11; Indian Plum (Paniala) is a multipurpose South and Southeast Asian Flacourtia shrub or small tree bearing clusters of small, round to oval, red-to-dark-purple berries with juicy, sweet-tart, plum-like flesh that are eaten fresh, preserved, and made into jams across South Asia — more palatable than the related Governor's Plum (F. indica) when fully ripe.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to poor soil; Flacourtia jangomas is drought tolerant once established and adaptable to a wide range of soils including lateritic, sandy, and slightly calcareous soils — water regularly only in establishment. Flacourtia jangomas (Indian Plum, Paniala, or Paniyala) is a thorny shrub or small tree native to South Asia from India and Sri Lanka east through Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, and Malesia, cultivated and semi-wild in village gardens and homestead agroforestry systems across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia for its clusters of small (0.5–1 inch), round, red-to-deep-purple, juicy fruits. The fruits are sweeter and less astringent than F. indica when fully ripe — tasting of a mild plum with slight tartness — and are eaten fresh, made into jams, chutneys, pickles, and preserves. Ripe fruits stain dark purple-red and can be fermented into a mild wine. The plant is dioecious (male and female on separate plants); at least one male tree is required among a group of female plants for fruit set. Flacourtia jangomas is very similar in growth habit and care to F. indica and makes a productive, low-maintenance fruiting shrub or edible hedge plant for zone 8–11 gardens in warm, sunny, well-drained conditions.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; like other kumquat types, Indio Mandarinquat tolerates brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F once established.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; like other kumquat types, Indio Mandarinquat tolerates brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F once established, better than most true mandarins or oranges. It arose as an open-pollinated seedling beneath a Nagami kumquat tree and was later selected and named at a USDA date and citrus research station in Indio, California, for its unusually large, elongated, bell-shaped fruit. The thin, sweet, edible peel and tart, juicy flesh are eaten together like a kumquat, but the fruit is markedly bigger and juicier than standard Nagami or Meiwa types. Its kumquat parentage gives it cold hardiness comparable to the kumquats already grown successfully along the Gulf Coast, making it a novel option for gardeners who already grow Nagami or Meiwa.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; seeds require cold stratification and germinate in spring — clumps can also be expanded by transplanting rooted suckers in early spring before bud break.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade on dry, rocky upland slopes or brushy hillsides across the northern Great Plains and Great Lakes region; interior serviceberry is a cold-hardy, drought-tolerant clump-former that slowly spreads by root suckers to create a dense thicket of arching stems. White flowers in early spring emerge before the leaves and provide critical nectar for early native bees and overwintered butterflies when few other sources are available. The blue-black berries that ripen in early summer are sweet, flavorful, and high in antioxidants — excellent for fresh eating, jams, and pies, and consumed eagerly by fruit-eating birds before most gardeners can harvest them. It is one of the hardiest serviceberries available, making it a top choice for prairie-edge and windbreak plantings in zones 2–4 where other fruiting shrubs cannot survive.

common_name: Interlaken Grape (Cornell-Bred Early White Seedless Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Interlaken, bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York station, is one of the earliest-ripening white seedless table grapes, a parent of Himrod; best in zones 5-8 where its chill requirement is reliably met.
directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Interlaken was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station as one of the earliest-ripening seedless table grapes available, producing sweet, crisp, pale green-gold berries in compact clusters well ahead of most other seedless varieties, an advantage for gardeners in shorter-season climates wanting a head start on the grape harvest. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning to improve berry size. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade on a strong trellis or pergola; Issai is unusual among kiwiberries for being self-fertile, so a single vine can fruit without a separate male pollinator.
directions: Plant on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Issai is a self-fertile hardy kiwiberry cultivar, a rare trait among Actinidia arguta selections that are normally dioecious and need a separate male vine for pollination. This makes Issai a practical choice for a small garden with room for only one vine, though yields still improve somewhat with a male pollinator nearby if space allows. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten skin and all, with sweet green flesh and classic kiwi flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. Issai also tends to fruit at a younger age than many hardy kiwi selections, often within two to three years of planting rather than the longer wait typical of the species. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous, twining growth and keep fruiting wood renewed, and provide a sturdy support structure from the start, since mature vines become heavy.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown plants in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Issai is self-fertile, precocious, and compact, often fruiting the first year after planting and staying small enough for a large container.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container where its compact, naturally dwarf habit is a real advantage. Issai is a Japanese-bred mulberry selection prized for its exceptional precocity — plants commonly bear their first crop within a year of planting, far faster than seedling or standard-sized mulberry cultivars — combined with a compact, easily managed size well suited to small yards, espalier training, and container culture. The sweet, juicy, dark purple-black berries ripen over an extended season, and the plant is self-fertile, needing no second tree for pollination. Because of its smaller stature, Issai is easier to net against birds and to harvest by hand than full-sized mulberry trees, while still producing a generous crop relative to its size. Prune to control height and encourage branching if a bushier form is desired.

common_name: Italian Prune Plum (Fellenberg Plum, Pacific Northwest Prune Plum, Dried Prune Standard)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun; Italian Prune is largely self-fruitful and will produce without a cross-pollinator, though yields improve with a companion European plum nearby; it requires approximately 700–800 chill hours and is best adapted to zones 5–8 with reliable winter cold.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; Italian Prune is self-fruitful but benefits from cross-pollination; the oval blue-black fruits ripen in September in the Pacific Northwest; allow fruits to fully soften and develop their sweet flavor before fresh eating; for prune production, pick slightly underripe and dry at low heat (135–145°F) for 18–24 hours in a dehydrator. Italian Prune plum (also known as Fellenberg after a German horticulturist, and as 'Prune' or 'Italian' in the Pacific Northwest) is the foundational prune variety of the Pacific Northwest commercial prune and dried fruit industry — the variety responsible for making the Willamette Valley of Oregon the center of American prune production and the source of most of the dried prunes consumed in the United States. The tree was brought to the Pacific Northwest in the mid-1800s by European immigrants (primarily German and Italian settlers) for whom dried prunes were a staple preserved food, and the variety proved ideally suited to the mild, moderately humid climate of the Willamette Valley where warm, dry summers during ripening allowed on-tree drying and hand-harvest at low cost. The fruits are medium-sized, oblong, classic 'prune-shaped' with deep blue-purple to nearly black skin and amber-yellow to golden flesh that is firm, moderately dry (essential for making quality prunes), and freestone at full ripeness — all characteristics essential for the drying process. At fresh-eating maturity, Italian Prune is sweet, richly flavored, and excellent for preserves, tarts, and plum butter as well as fresh consumption. A traditional home garden plum throughout the Pacific Coast states and the Northeast.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Izu is a compact, early-bearing non-astringent persimmon well suited to smaller home gardens and containers.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Izu is a compact, early-bearing non-astringent persimmon well suited to smaller home gardens and containers. A Japanese non-astringent cultivar related to Fuyu, it bears small to medium, flattened, sweet fruit that can be eaten crisp like an apple straight off the tree, ripening earlier in the season than most other non-astringent types. The naturally small, dense, spreading tree bears at a young age and stays compact even without heavy pruning, making it one of the better persimmon choices for a limited-space garden or large container. Persimmons need little spraying or care once established; thin heavy fruit set in early summer to prevent limb breakage and improve fruit size.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring after all frost risk passes; jaboticaba is extremely slow-growing and may take 8–15 years from seed to first fruit.
directions: Jaboticaba produces grape-like berries directly on its trunk and main branches (cauliflory) in dramatic clusters; the fruit ripens just 20–25 days after flowering and can bear several times per year in frost-free climates. It is self-fertile and requires well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5); chlorosis is common in alkaline soils and can be corrected with chelated iron and sulfur. Trees are slow-growing, making them well-suited to container culture where they can be overwintered in zone 8 or moved under frost protection. Harvest berries when they are entirely deep purple-black, soft, and sweet-tart — they ferment within 3–4 days at room temperature, so refrigerate or process promptly.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–October. Jabotilla tolerates light frosts to about 28°F when established, making it marginally cold-hardy for zone 9. In zone 9b–10 it grows as an evergreen specimen and produces fruit seasonally; in zone 9a protect from hard freezes. The tree grows slowly and produces small annual crops of berries on the trunk and branches in the characteristic Myrciaria style.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, acidic, organically rich soil; Jabotilla (also called Guavaberry or Rumberry in the Caribbean) is a medium to large Myrciaria species producing small, round, dark-purple to black berries directly on the trunk and main branches in the same cauliflorous pattern as Jaboticaba — but the fruit is smaller, more tart, and has a distinctive spiced, aromatic quality with notes of cloves, vanilla, and exotic spice that make it highly prized in Caribbean culinary traditions. In the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico, jabotilla berries are the foundation of 'guavaberry rum' — a traditional Christmas liqueur in which the berries macerate in rum to produce a spiced, aromatic, deeply colored drink of cultural significance. The fresh berries are also eaten raw, made into jams and jellies, and used as a flavoring for drinks and sauces. The tree is ornamental year-round with attractive bark, shiny leaves, and the unusual cauliflorous fruiting pattern. In zone 9 it is a specimen fruit tree for collectors and enthusiasts.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost danger passes in a sheltered, frost-free site with rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil; jabuticaba is extremely slow-growing but rewards patience with a spectacular fruiting habit — the grape-sized fruits emerge directly from the trunk and main branches rather than on new shoots.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in deep, fertile, consistently moist, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), well-drained soil; jabuticaba is one of the most spectacular food plants in the world, producing dark purple to black grape-like fruits that burst directly from the bark of the trunk and major branches in a phenomenon called cauliflory, which causes the whole tree to turn dark with fruit clusters several times per year in its native Brazil. The fruits are eaten fresh within a day or two of harvest (they ferment rapidly on the tree), pressed into wine, or made into jelly and liqueur. The skin is thick and slightly astringent while the white flesh is sweet, gelatinous, and fragrant with a flavor suggesting muscadine grape. In zone 9 the tree benefits from a sheltered position and protection when temperatures dip below 26°F. Though extremely slow to fruit from seed — sometimes 5–10 years — air-layered or grafted plants can bear in 2–3 years.

plant_note: Plant in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; jackfruit is frost-sensitive and suited only to zones 10–12, though established trees briefly tolerate temperatures down to about 28–30°F. Trees grow rapidly once established and require substantial spacing to accommodate their large canopy and the world's largest tree-borne fruit, which can weigh up to 80 pounds.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) is a fast-growing tropical tree from India and Bangladesh that produces the world's largest tree-borne fruit — massive, spiky green-to-yellow pods weighing 10–80 pounds that hang directly from the trunk and main branches in a spectacular display of cauliflory. The flesh (arils) surrounding each seed is sweet, fragrant, and fiber-rich, eaten fresh when ripe or cooked as a meat substitute when unripe — a use that has made jackfruit globally popular as a plant-based protein source. Trees grafted from superior selections begin fruiting in 3–4 years and can produce 100–200 fruits per year on mature specimens. Plant in well-drained soil, as jackfruit is highly susceptible to root rot in waterlogged conditions; once established, trees are moderately drought-tolerant and grow vigorously in the humid tropics.

plant_note: Set out container-grown trees only after nighttime lows are reliably above 50°F and give young trees a sheltered, warm microclimate.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil enriched with compost, choosing the warmest and most wind-protected spot available since this tree resents any chill below the mid-40s. Keep the root zone consistently moist during establishment and expect a large, glossy-leaved tree that eventually bears heavy, applesauce-scented fruit with a pale, custard-like pulp. On the Gulf Coast it is realistically grown only in the warmest coastal pockets of south Florida or in a large container that can be moved into a greenhouse for winter. Young trees should be protected from any frost, as even brief freezes can kill wood back to the ground.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, sandy, or thin soil in full sun to partial shade; Jamaican caper grows naturally in tropical hardwood hammocks, coastal scrub, and coastal strand of south Florida and the Keys, tolerating salt spray and rocky, thin alkaline soils well.
directions: Plant in well-drained, thin, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Jamaican caper (formerly Capparis cynophallophora) is a native Florida and Caribbean shrub or small tree related to the Mediterranean caper (Capparis spinosa), sharing the family's distinctive flowers — large, white, nocturnally fragrant blooms with numerous long, showy purple stamens that create a shaving-brush or firework appearance. The flowers open at night and are gone by mid-morning, attracting moths and long-tongued bees. The fruit, which resembles an elongated sausage, splits to reveal brilliant orange-red flesh containing the seeds — an attractive food source for white-crowned pigeons and other subtropical birds. A salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant native for coastal and hammock-edge gardens in south Florida. The young flower buds could theoretically be pickled like Mediterranean capers but this use is not traditionally practiced.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; James Grieve is a reliable, heavy-blooming pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; James Grieve is a reliable, heavy-blooming pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties. Bred in Edinburgh, Scotland in the late nineteenth century, it bears medium, yellow-green apples flushed with red stripes and juicy, tender, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, ripening in late summer to early fall as one of the more reliable early-to-mid-season dual-purpose apples for a cooler climate. Its good cold hardiness, heavy and reliable annual bearing, and value as a strong cross-pollinator for many other apple varieties have kept it a widely planted favorite in home orchards across the British Isles and other cool-summer regions for well over a century. Harvest in late summer once fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat within a few weeks, since the tender flesh does not store especially long.

subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree
plant_note: Plant grafted specimens in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 6–9; Japanese Apricot (Chinese Plum, Mei, Ume) is a small to medium flowering stone-fruit tree — among the earliest spring bloomers, flowering January–March before leaf emergence — native to China and widely cultivated in East Asia for ornamental value and for the sour, aromatic green fruits used to produce umeboshi (pickled plums), ume liqueur (umeshu), and traditional medicines.
directions: Plant grafted Japanese Apricot in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; prune to open vase shape after fruiting; harvest fruits green-yellow when firm for pickling (umeboshi), or wait for full yellow ripeness for eating fresh or making ume liqueur. Prunus mume is revered in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean culture as the herald of spring — its fragrant, five-petaled flowers in shades of white through deep rose appear January–March, often while snow still falls, making it one of the most poetically celebrated trees in East Asian art and literature. The fruits, called ume (Japanese) or mei (Chinese), resemble apricots but are sharply sour when ripe due to high citric acid content; they are almost always processed rather than eaten raw. Traditional umeboshi preparation involves salt-pickling the green fruits with red shiso leaves to produce a strongly sour, salty Japanese condiment used in rice balls, with noodles, and as a digestive aid — extraordinarily long-lasting, with some umeboshi aged decades or more. Umeshu (ume liqueur, often called plum wine) is made by steeping whole green fruits in shochu spirits with sugar. Many named ornamental cultivars exist with double flowers and deep pink to red color; fruiting varieties for culinary use include 'Nanko' and 'Kairyou Ouseibai'.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall at 2 inches depth in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy soil; Japanese chestnut naturally cold-stratifies over winter and germinates in spring. Plant two or more seedlings for cross-pollination and heavier nut production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; Japanese chestnut is critically important in chestnut breeding programs as a source of resistance to chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica), the fungal disease that virtually eliminated the American chestnut from eastern North American forests in the early 20th century. While Japanese chestnut is not immune to the blight, it carries resistance genes that allow infected trees to survive and produce nuts despite infection — a trait intensively incorporated into breeding lines for blight-resistant American chestnut restoration. The nuts are large (often larger than American chestnut), sweet, and excellent roasted or boiled in Japanese cuisine. Japanese chestnut has been cultivated in Japan for over 2000 years and is the source of many cultivated varieties. Requires cross-pollination; plant two or more trees.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall to begin the warm-stratification phase naturally; seeds require a full warm period followed by a cold period, meaning germination typically occurs in the second spring after sowing.
directions: Sow cleaned seeds in fall and be patient, as double dormancy means most seeds will not sprout until the second spring; mark the bed clearly and keep it weeded during the waiting period. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are adaptable to a range of soil types and tolerate summer heat better than its European relative Cornus mas. The clusters of tiny yellow flowers that stud the bare branches in late winter are among the earliest blooms of the year, providing a vital nectar source for early pollinators; the cherry-like fruits that follow ripen to bright red by midsummer and are edible fresh or made into jams and wines. With age, the exfoliating bark develops an ornamental patchwork of grey, brown, and orange, making this a genuinely four-season specimen plant for gardens across a wide range of climates.
