plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun; Japanese flowering quince is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay, drought, and pollution once established — excellent for slopes, hedges, and difficult urban sites.
directions: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun; Japanese flowering quince is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay, drought, and pollution once established — excellent for slopes, hedges, and difficult urban sites. Chaenomeles japonica is a compact, thorny, deciduous shrub that blooms in early spring before the leaves expand (often in February–March in mild climates), producing a spectacular display of vivid orange to scarlet-red, five-petaled flowers on bare stems — some of the earliest and most vivid spring color in the garden; the flowers provide critical early nectar for overwintered and emerging queen bumblebees. The hard, fragrant, yellow-green, apple-like fruits that follow in autumn are too astringent to eat raw but make outstanding jelly, quince paste (membrillo), and homemade quince wine with excellent flavor and natural pectin content. More compact and cold-hardy than the larger C. speciosa.

plant_note: Plant after frost; this evergreen blooms in fall and ripens fruit in spring.
directions: The evergreen Japanese loquat offers handsome, bold foliage and clusters of sweet-tart, apricot-like fruit that ripen in spring. It flowers in autumn, so late frosts can damage the developing crop in colder zones. Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil and water regularly while young. Thin fruit clusters for larger loquats and prune lightly after harvest to shape the canopy.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Japanese quince is one of the earliest spring-flowering shrubs, blooming before its leaves emerge — a spectacular sight in late winter. Tolerates poor, rocky, clay, or sandy soils once established.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained to moderately moist soil; Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica) is a compact, thorny, deciduous shrub native to Japan, producing masses of brilliant red-orange to scarlet flowers on bare winter-spring branches — one of the most vivid early spring-flowering shrubs available. The small, apple-scented, greenish-yellow fruits that follow are too astringent to eat raw but make excellent jelly, jam, and cordial with a flavor combining quince, lemon, and apple; very high in pectin and requiring no added pectin when making preserves. The thorny habit makes it an effective barrier hedge. Extremely adaptable and long-lived, thriving in a wide range of soils and tolerating air pollution, drought, and neglect; a reliable garden shrub with multiple seasons of interest.

plant_note: Scarify seeds or soak in warm water for 24 hours before sowing indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Trees can also be started from softwood cuttings in early summer.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the Japanese raisin tree is an unusual and little-known deciduous tree from East Asia cultivated for its fleshy, branched fruiting stalks (peduncles) that swell and become sweet, raisin-like, and edible in fall when the actual seeds have dropped. It is the peduncles — not the small, round seeds — that are consumed; they have a mild, sweet flavor resembling dried figs or raisins and have been used in Japan, China, and Korea both as a food and as a traditional remedy for alcohol intoxication and liver protection. The tree is an attractive ornamental with large, tropical-looking leaves and fragrant white flowers in summer. In zone 9, it may bloom and fruit erratically due to insufficient winter chilling; it performs best in zones 6–8 where winter cold is reliable. An excellent and unusual fruit tree for the adventurous edible landscape.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall (cold stratification over winter) or transplant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile, loamy soil in full sun; Japanese walnut is allelopathic like other walnuts — its roots produce juglone, which inhibits growth of many plants beneath the canopy. Give adequate space (40–60 feet from other susceptible plants).
directions: Plant fresh nuts in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile, loamy soil in full sun; Japanese walnut is an impressive large nut tree from the mountains of Japan, Hokkaido, Honshu, and Sakhalin — closely related to Persian walnut (Juglans regia) but growing in colder climates and producing rounder, harder-shelled nuts. The trees are immediately distinguished by their enormous compound leaves (the largest of any walnut — up to 4 feet long with 11–17 leaflets) and by the sticky glandular hairs covering young growth and fruit husks. The nuts are round to slightly oval, with a very hard, thick shell and rich, oily kernel. The variety 'cordiformis' (heartnut) produces a distinctively heart-shaped nut that cracks more easily than the round-nutted species. Used in Japanese cuisine and for nut oil. Like all walnuts, releases juglone from its roots that can inhibit many nearby plants. The closely related Manchurian walnut (J. mandshurica) is even hardier. An excellent, ornamental, large-canopy nut tree for cooler northern gardens.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. As the name indicates, Jaune de Deux Saisons produces two crops: a breba crop on old wood in June–July and a main crop on new wood in September–October. The two-crop habit extends the fresh fig season significantly. In zone 9 both crops ripen reliably.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Jaune de Deux Saisons (Yellow of Two Seasons) is a French two-crop fig producing yellow-green to golden-yellow fruits in both the breba (early summer) and main crop (fall) seasons — one of the most productive two-crop fig varieties for home gardens because both crops are of comparable quality and size. The medium-sized, round to slightly pear-shaped fruits have golden-yellow skin and pale amber to pink-tinged flesh with a mild, honeyed sweetness and delicate flavor. The yellow color is distinctive and immediately identifiable among darker-skinned varieties. Two-crop figs like Jaune de Deux Saisons are particularly valuable in zone 9 where the long warm season allows both crops to mature fully — the breba crop in June provides early-season figs while the main crop extends harvest into October. The golden color makes this fig outstanding for fresh presentations and pale fig jam.

common_name: Java Olive (Tropical Chestnut, Bastard Poon Tree)
plant_note: Plant container stock or seeds in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Java olive is a large tropical tree of the Old World tropics producing distinctive, star-shaped, woody, red seed pods that split open to reveal black, edible, oily seeds — one of the most dramatic ornamental seed displays of any tropical tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; a fast-growing tree that requires ample space. Sterculia foetida (Java olive or poon tree) is a large, fast-growing tropical tree native from East Africa and India through Southeast Asia to northern Australia, producing an impressive display of distinctive, star-shaped, woody, bright-red seed pods 4–6 inches across that split open dramatically to reveal 5–18 shiny black seeds with a high (55%) oil content. The common name 'Java olive' refers to the traditional use of the seeds as cooking oil and food in Java and other Indonesian islands — the seeds have a mild, slightly bitter, nutty flavor when roasted and can be pressed for a high-quality edible oil similar to olive oil in fatty acid composition. CAUTION: Raw seeds contain cyclopropene fatty acids that are mildly toxic; seeds should be roasted or heated before consumption. The tree has striking large, palmate leaves and produces flowers with a distinctive unpleasant odor ('foetida' = stinking) that attracts pollinating flies. An unusual specimen tree for large tropical landscapes where few food trees provide such dramatic seed pod displays.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Java plum is a fast-growing large tree suited to zones 10–12 that can reach 30–60 feet at maturity and should be sited with ample space away from structures, pavement, and other trees. Fruit-staining from the dark purple berries can be significant, so avoid planting directly over patios or walkways.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; Java plum (Syzygium cumini), also called jambolan or jamun, is a large, fast-growing evergreen tree from India and Southeast Asia in the Myrtaceae family that produces dense clusters of small, oblong, deep purple to nearly black fruits with a distinctive flavor that is simultaneously sweet, tart, and astringent — with a tongue-staining purple juice widely used in wines, vinegars, syrups, and preserves across South and Southeast Asia. The astringency is due to tannins that diminish when the fruit is fully ripe; fruits are also eaten fresh with a pinch of salt, which tempers the bitterness and heightens the sweetness. Java plum has a long history in Ayurvedic medicine, with seeds, bark, and fruit used in preparations for diabetes management, digestive complaints, and other conditions. Trees are vigorous, moderately drought-tolerant once established, and remarkably adaptable — growing in a range of soil types — but produce the best fruit quality with regular moisture and full sun.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Jazz requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Jazz requires a moderate chill period and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A New Zealand-bred cross between Gala and Braeburn, it produces medium-sized, densely crisp, juicy fruit with a distinctive sweet-tart flavor balance and a pear-drop aroma that sets it apart from its sweeter Gala parent, marketed commercially since the early 2000s as a premium eating apple. The tree bears reliably and the fruit stores exceptionally well in refrigeration, holding its crisp texture and flavor for months, which has helped make it a popular choice for both commercial orchards and home growers wanting a long-keeping late-season apple. Thin fruit clusters in early summer, provide a compatible pollinator variety, and harvest once the background color turns from green to yellow beneath the red blush for the best flavor balance.

common_name: Jefferson Hazelnut (OSU Premium Large-Nut EFB-Resistant Filbert, OSU 2009 Release)
plant_note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Jefferson is self-incompatible and requires a cross-pollinating companion variety — plant with Yamhill, Wepster, or another EFB-resistant OSU release; Jefferson is the OSU hazelnut release most comparable to Barcelona in nut size and quality while adding Eastern Filbert Blight resistance, making it the premium home and commercial selection for both Pacific Northwest and eastern US hazelnut production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Jefferson hazelnut requires a companion variety for cross-pollination; nuts ripen in September–October and drop naturally; harvest promptly from ground and dry immediately at low heat to cure and extend shelf life; Jefferson's large, well-filled nuts are suitable for roasting, confectionery, and fresh consumption. Jefferson hazelnut was released by Oregon State University in 2009 — named after Thomas Jefferson, who was an enthusiastic hazelnut grower at Monticello — and represents the flagship of OSU's first generation of EFB-resistant hazelnut varieties. Among the OSU 2009 releases, Jefferson stands out as the variety with the largest nut size and highest kernel quality comparable to the longtime commercial standard Barcelona, while adding the critical Eastern Filbert Blight resistance that Barcelona lacks. In Oregon and Washington State hazelnut orchards, Jefferson is being planted as a replacement for Barcelona both in existing orchards where EFB has arrived and in new plantings where EFB resistance is now considered standard. In the eastern United States, Jefferson has opened hazelnut production to a region that was essentially unable to grow commercial European hazelnuts due to the endemic EFB — Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern university variety trials show Jefferson performing strongly under heavy EFB pressure that devastates Barcelona in just 2–3 seasons. The nuts are large, round to oval, with a clean, thin shell and excellent sweet hazelnut flavor — considered among the best-tasting of any named variety, justifying the Jefferson name's association with culinary excellence.

common_name: Jefferson Plum (Fine-Flavored American Golden Gage-Type Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; partially self-fertile but sets heavier crops with a nearby European plum pollinizer, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Jefferson was raised in New York in the 1820s and became one of the most highly regarded American plums of the 19th century, producing large, golden-yellow fruit blushed with red and carrying rich, sweet, aromatic flesh often compared favorably to the classic European gage plums it descends from. The vigorous tree crops reliably and the large fruit size, combined with outstanding flavor, made it a standard for fine dessert plums in American orchards for generations. Thin fruit if a heavy crop sets to maintain good size, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and has fully colored for the best flavor, since Jefferson plums picked too early lack the full richness the variety is known for.

plant_note: Plant container-grown palms in spring after frost; avoid disturbing the root ball during transplanting.
directions: Jelly palm is one of the hardiest fruiting palms, surviving temperatures down to 12–15°F, and is well-suited to zones 8–11 in well-drained soils ranging from sandy to clay. The tree is monoecious, with male and female flowers on the same large branched inflorescence, so a single specimen fruits reliably without a pollinator. It produces abundant clusters of small orange-yellow drupes in summer; the sweet-tart pulp is rich in pectin and classically used for jelly, wine, and preserves. Allow fruit to fall naturally or gently shake clusters when most fruit has colored; process quickly as the thin-skinned fruit ferments rapidly after harvest.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring after last frost in well-drained soil with full sun; avoid disturbing the root system during planting as butia is sensitive to root damage.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; the jelly palm is one of the hardiest feather palms in cultivation, tolerating temperatures to about 12°F (-11°C) with minimal damage, making it reliable across zone 8b-10. The silvery-blue arching fronds give a dramatic tropical appearance while the plant chugs through drought and poor soils with little supplemental care once established. Clusters of small orange-yellow fruits ripen in summer and have a sweet-tart apricot-pineapple flavor prized for jellies, wine, and juice — harvest when the entire cluster begins to drop. Water deeply but infrequently during the first two years to encourage deep root development, then reduce irrigation significantly.

common_name: Jewel Blueberry (UF Very-Early Southern Highbush Low-Chill Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root plants in late fall to early spring in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Jewel's very early ripening season makes it particularly valuable for commercial operations and home gardeners who want the season's first fresh blueberries — it ripens 1–2 weeks ahead of most other southern highbush varieties.
directions: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Jewel is a University of Florida IFAS very-early-ripening southern highbush blueberry that starts production 1–2 weeks ahead of Emerald and most other Gulf South varieties — providing the season's first fresh blueberries in February to March in zone 9, making Jewel particularly valuable for extending the blueberry harvest season when planted with later-ripening varieties. The medium-large, blue berries have good flavor and firm texture with a small dry scar — the fresh-eating quality is good for a very early variety, though some tasters find the peak flavor of mid-season varieties like Emerald and O'Neal slightly superior. Jewel's very low chill hour requirement (approximately 150–200 hours) makes it one of the best-adapted blueberries for the warmest zone 9 locations where winters are mild and chill accumulation is uncertain. Jewel is upright and moderately vigorous, reaching 4–5 feet with regular management. As with all southern highbush blueberries, very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) is the fundamental requirement — plant in raised beds or containers with acidic media (50% pine bark plus peat) if native soil pH cannot be sufficiently lowered. Plant with Emerald, Southmoon, or O'Neal for cross-pollination that significantly increases berry size and total yield.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Jiro is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, though production typically improves with a nearby pollinizer variety; requires 200–400 chill hours.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Jiro is the most widely grown non-astringent Japanese persimmon cultivar in California, Asia, and the Gulf South — producing large, slightly flattened, bright orange-red fruits that can be eaten crisp, firm, and crunchy directly from the tree without waiting for softening, making them much more approachable than astringent persimmons (like Hachiya) that must be fully soft before eating. The non-astringent quality means Jiro persimmons are eaten like apples — sliced, eaten fresh, added to salads, or simply eaten out of hand with no waiting for ripeness. The sweet, mild, honey-like flavor is pleasant and distinctive. In zone 9, Jiro ripens in October–November, adding late-season ornamental color when the bright orange fruits hang on the increasingly bare branches after leaf drop — a striking autumn display that has made ornamental persimmons popular landscape trees. The tree is naturally well-shaped and attractive with excellent fall foliage color. Jiro requires very little care once established — it is drought-tolerant, highly pest-resistant, and adapts to clay soils that challenge many fruit trees. One of the most productive and reliable fruit trees for Gulf South landscapes.

common_name: Joey Avocado (Extreme Cold-Hardy Texas Mexican-Type Avocado)
plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters.
directions: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters. Joey was discovered as a chance seedling near Uvalde, Texas, and stands out among avocado varieties for its cold tolerance, with mature trees reported to survive brief drops into the teens Fahrenheit that would kill most avocados. It is a Type B, Mexican-race avocado producing medium, egg-shaped fruit with thin purple-black skin and rich, creamy, nutty-flavored flesh that ripens in late summer through fall. Joey's combination of cold hardiness and dependable production makes it one of the better avocado choices for in-ground planting along the warmer parts of the Gulf Coast and coastal Texas.

common_name: John Rick American Persimmon (Large Sweet Indiana Persimmon Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained to average soil; John Rick is a female cultivar and produces seeded fruit when a male American persimmon or compatible pollinator is within range — pair with a known male seedling or another cultivar for reliable seed-set and fruiting. Cold-hardy to about -15°F, adapted to zones 5–9.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun, ideally with a male American persimmon seedling or another pollinator cultivar nearby to ensure reliable fruit set; drought-tolerant once established. John Rick is a long-cultivated named American persimmon selection out of the Midwest, valued among heirloom fruit-tree collectors and permaculture growers for its large, richly flavored fruit and dependable productivity once a pollinator is present. The fruit ripens in fall and, as with all American persimmons, needs a hard frost or full ripening on the tree to shed its astringency, after which the deep orange flesh turns intensely sweet, custardy, and rich with notes of caramel and dried fruit. It is commonly grafted onto native persimmon rootstock and grown alongside other named cultivars in mixed persimmon plantings to guarantee cross-pollination and a heavier crop. A good choice for zone 5–9 growers assembling a diverse American persimmon collection.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; John's is not self-fertile and should be planted alongside Adams, Nova, or another distinct elderberry cultivar for reliable pollination and a full crop.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; pair with a second, genetically distinct elderberry cultivar within cross-pollinating range for a full crop, since John's does not set well on its own. John's is one of the oldest named Canadian elderberry selections, long grown as a classic pollinator and companion cultivar for Adams in commercial and home elderberry plantings — the two cultivars were historically recommended together as a standard cross-pollinating pair for decades before more recent university releases like Bob Gordon and Wyldewood became available. The tall, vigorous shrub produces large, flat-topped flower clusters in early summer, valued for elderflower tea, cordial, and fritters, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer used for jams, syrups, wine, and traditional elderberry preparations. Its long track record and reliable vigor make it a solid, time-tested choice for a home elderberry planting, especially paired with Adams for cross-pollination, zone 3–8.

plant_note: Plant male and female plants for seed production; approximately one male per five females suffices for cross-pollination by wind; jojoba grows best in hot, dry desert conditions and resents overwatering.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy desert soil; jojoba is a remarkable desert shrub native to the Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California, and Mexico whose seeds produce a liquid wax (not technically an oil) used extensively in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and lubricants as a spermaceti whale-oil substitute. The seeds are edible but contain a waxy compound (simmondsin) that causes nausea if eaten in quantity; indigenous peoples roasted or ground them into a paste. The shrub is among the most drought-tolerant woody plants in North America, surviving on 10 inches of rainfall annually, and provides important cover and food for desert wildlife. Excellent for erosion control and dryland restoration in zone 8–11.

common_name: Jolico Cornelian Cherry (Large-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown Jolico in early spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade, giving it room to grow into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown Jolico in early spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade, giving it room to grow into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Jolico is an Austrian selection prized for its unusually large, pear-shaped, bright red fruit, up to twice the size of the wild species, produced on a plant that still tolerates the dappled light of a woodland edge better than most fruiting shrubs. The tart-sweet, cranberry-like fruit ripens in late summer and is traditionally cooked into jams, syrups, and sauces, though fully ripe fruit can also be eaten fresh. A part-shade planting slows ripening slightly but the shrub remains healthy and productive, making Jolico a good fit for the partly shaded fringe of an edible landscape.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Jonafree is a Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) breeding program release bred to bring classic Jonathan flavor into a scab-resistant, low-spray apple, also resisting powdery mildew, fire blight, and cedar apple rust.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Jonafree was bred by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative program to capture the classic tangy-sweet flavor of the old Jonathan apple in a tree resistant to apple scab, powdery mildew, fire blight, and cedar apple rust, sparing home growers the heavy fungicide schedule that susceptible heirloom apples like Jonathan itself require. The medium-sized, bright red fruit has crisp, juicy flesh with the familiar sprightly Jonathan flavor, good for fresh eating, sauce, and baking. Because it combines classic flavor with broad disease resistance, Jonafree is a good choice for gardeners who love old-fashioned apple flavor but want a low-spray, low-maintenance tree. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and harvest once fruit has developed full color and separates easily from the spur.

common_name: Jonagold Apple (Jonathan × Golden Delicious, Best-Flavor Commercial Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jonagold requires approximately 800 chill hours and performs best in zones 5–8; IMPORTANT: Jonagold is triploid — its pollen is not viable and it cannot serve as a cross-pollinator for other apple varieties; plant with two other diploid pollinizers (Honeycrisp + Cortland, or Gala + McIntosh) for good fruit production on all three trees.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; because Jonagold is triploid, plant it with two compatible diploid pollinator varieties — it needs two compatible pollinators and cannot pollinate other trees itself; thin fruit clusters in late spring for maximum size; Jonagold ripens mid-to-late season (October) producing very large fruit with outstanding sweet-tart flavor. Jonagold is widely considered one of the best-tasting apple varieties in the world — a cross of Jonathan and Golden Delicious developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1943 and released in 1968. The variety combines the aromatic, spicy sweet-tart character of Jonathan with the sweetness and crispness of Golden Delicious, resulting in very large, yellow-orange to red-blushed apples with exceptional, complex flavor that many apple connoisseurs consider among the finest eating apples available. Jonagold has become particularly important in European apple markets — it is one of the most widely planted apple varieties in Belgium and the Netherlands, and is highly regarded throughout European specialty apple production — in part because its substantial size and richly complex flavor profile make it stand out at specialty and farmers' market venues. In the United States, Jonagold is less prominent commercially than varieties with better storability (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) but widely recognized among apple enthusiasts as a flavor benchmark. An important practical consideration: Jonagold is a triploid variety (three sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two) — its pollen is sterile, meaning it cannot pollinate other apple trees and requires two compatible diploid varieties for its own fruit production.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Jonathan requires roughly 700-800 chill hours and cross-pollination from a compatible variety such as Golden Delicious or Winesap, and is best adapted to zones 4-8.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Jonathan was discovered as a chance seedling in Woodstock, New York in 1826 and went on to become one of the most widely planted apple varieties in American history, remaining a dominant commercial and home-orchard apple for over a century. The medium-sized fruit ripens to a bright red over a yellow background, with crisp, juicy, aromatic white flesh balancing bright tartness with real sweetness, excellent for fresh eating, sauce, and pie alike. Jonathan is also historically significant as a parent variety, having been crossed with Golden Delicious to produce the modern Jonagold. Harvest when fruit colors fully and separates easily from the spur with a gentle twist, and note that Jonathan is somewhat more prone to bitter pit and early softening in storage than some modern keeper varieties, so plan to use it within a few months of harvest.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the last frost date; jujubes establish quickly in warm soil.
directions: Jujube is exceptionally drought-tolerant and thrives in hot, dry climates where other fruits struggle; it prefers well-drained, even sandy soils and performs poorly with excessive moisture. Most cultivars are self-fertile, though a second variety increases yields. Li and Lang are the most widely planted in North America; Li produces large, round, date-like fruit while Lang is more elongated. Fruit is eaten fresh when crisp and apple-flavored or dried to a sweet, wrinkled date; harvest when skin turns from yellow-green to mahogany-red.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Julie's dwarf, compact habit and Caribbean popularity make it a favorite dooryard mango where space and winter protection are both limited.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Julie is a small, dwarf-habit mango of Caribbean origin, especially beloved in Jamaican and Trinidadian dooryard gardens for its compact size, precocious bearing, and intensely sweet, fiberless, deep orange flesh with a distinctive rich flavor that fans consider among the best of any mango. Because it stays notably smaller than most mango cultivars, Julie is one of the better choices for zone 9 gardeners growing mango in a large container that can be sheltered through winter rather than risking an in-ground planting. Reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars and flavor, and protect trees from any frost, since even brief freezing temperatures can damage or kill mango wood.

common_name: Jumbo Muscadine (Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine Grape)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root vines in late winter or spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Jumbo is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator, making it practical for single-vine plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Jumbo is one of the largest-berried muscadine grape cultivars available — producing extra-large, 1–1.5 inch diameter, dark black to purplish-black berries that are significantly larger than standard muscadines and create a dramatic visual impression both on the vine and at harvest. The large size makes Jumbo berries outstanding for fresh eating, where the large, sweet, musky flesh provides a more substantial bite than smaller cultivars. The flavor is rich, sweet, and distinctly muscadine with the characteristic musky, fruity flavor that distinguishes muscadine grapes from bunch grapes. Jumbo ripens in mid to late season (September in zone 9) and is self-fertile — producing good crops without a pollinator. The vine is vigorous, productive, and well-adapted to Gulf South conditions including clay soil, heat, humidity, and the fungal disease pressure that affects European grapes in the Southeast. Muscadines are the most naturally disease-resistant grapes for the Gulf South — they have evolved in the region and require far fewer pesticide applications than bunch grapes in the humid Southeast. Jumbo is perfect for fresh eating, home juice, wine, and preserves. Train on a 5–6 foot high wire trellis and prune hard in winter, leaving only 2–4 lateral spurs per cane.

common_name: June Gold Peach (Early Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun; June Gold requires approximately 650 chill hours and is well-suited to zone 8–9 conditions with consistent chill hour accumulation.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; June Gold is an early-season freestone peach cultivar that ripens in late May to early June in zone 9 — one of the earliest-ripening freestone peach selections available for Gulf Coast production. The medium-large, round fruit has yellow flesh with red coloring and a rich, full peach flavor with good sweetness. The early ripening season avoids the peak summer disease pressure (brown rot, oriental fruit moth) that damages later-ripening cultivars, and it extends the Gulf South peach season earlier. June Gold requires approximately 650 chill hours — reliably accumulated in zone 9a and most zone 9 climates during typical winters, and less frequently limiting than the 800–1000 hours required by standard northern peach cultivars like Elberta and Redhaven. The tree is vigorous and productive with proper annual pruning to an open-vase form. In zone 9, peaches are planted in January–February for the spring growing season, and the orchard management cycle includes dormant oil and copper sprays at bud swell, thinning to 6–8 inches between fruits after natural drop, and a preventive brown rot spray program as harvest approaches.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or large cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; june plum is very fast-growing and can begin fruiting from cuttings in 2–3 years. Hardy to about 30°F; best in zone 9b–12.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; june plum (ambarella) is a fast-growing tropical fruit tree of the Pacific Islands and Southeast Asia, producing clusters of oval green-to-yellow fruits 2–3 inches long that are consumed at all stages of ripeness. Unripe fruits are prized throughout Asia and the Caribbean for their crisp, tart flesh, used in fresh salads, pickled condiments, and green mango-style preparations; ripe fruits are sweet-tart with a fibrous spiny seed and are eaten fresh or juiced. The tree is extremely fast-growing (10–15 feet in the first 2 years), the leaves are edible as salad greens when young, and the tree propagates easily from large hardwood cuttings that fruit in 2–3 years. It thrives in zone 9b–12 as a reliable, low-maintenance, highly productive tropical fruit tree and is one of the best 'beginner' tropical fruits for warm-climate gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; KSU-Atwood needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar such as Sunflower or Susquehanna nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.
directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before they can handle full sun. KSU-Atwood is a Kentucky State University research program release bred from Atwood x Overleese parentage, chosen for consistently large, well-filled fruit with rich, sweet flesh and a relatively low seed count for the species. Trees are vigorous and productive once established, ripening their crop in the midseason window and holding fruit quality well compared to many wild seedling trees. Because pawpaws are not self-fertile, interplant with a second unrelated cultivar within about 50 feet and consider hand-pollinating with a small paintbrush during the brief, unpleasant-smelling maroon bloom, since the flies and beetles that pollinate pawpaw in the wild are often scarce in home gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; KSU-Benson needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.
directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before they can tolerate full sun. KSU-Benson is a Kentucky State University pawpaw research program release, selected alongside sibling cultivars like KSU-Atwood for good fruit size and flavor from the university's decades-long regional germplasm evaluation program. Trees are vigorous and productive once established, bearing medium-to-large fruit with smooth, rich, custardy flesh in the late-summer harvest window typical of named pawpaw selections. Because pawpaws are not self-fertile, interplant with a second, genetically distinct cultivar within about 50 feet, and consider hand-pollinating with a small paintbrush during the brief, faintly unpleasant-smelling maroon bloom, since the flies and beetles that pollinate pawpaw in the wild are often scarce around home gardens.

common_name: Kadota Fig (Italian Honey Fig, Dottato Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Kadota produces a good Breba (first) crop in June on old wood, followed by a heavy main crop in August–October. Self-fertile — no pollinizer needed. Best in full sun with well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Kadota is one of the oldest known fig cultivars, documented in Italian records since at least the 16th century and known as Dottato or Dottato Bianco in Italy, where it has been cultivated around Naples and in Calabria for over 400 years. The American name 'Kadota' is an Anglicized corruption of 'Dottato.' The fruits are small to medium, rounded, pale green to yellowish-white at maturity (not turning brown like most figs) with amber to violet interior flesh that is seedless (no viable seeds) and extraordinarily sweet — among the highest sugar content of any fig. The nearly seed-free flesh is ideal for fig preserves, dried figs, and fresh eating. Kadota is self-fertile, drought-tolerant, and among the most productive figs per tree. It is the most widely used commercial fig in California's Central Valley canning and drying industry. The pale, golden-green skin requires learning when it is ripe — pick when it bends at the stem and yields gently to pressure, the skin turns a barely perceptible yellowish hue, and the neck softens. Excellent for the Gulf Coast Zone 9 garden.

plant_note: Plant air-layered or grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Kaimana requires a cool-dry period in winter to initiate flower buds — temperatures below 59°F for several weeks trigger flowering. Zone 9 winters typically provide this naturally, making it one of the better lychee climates. Do not overwater in winter; controlled mild stress during cool season promotes flower initiation. Young trees are frost-sensitive and should be protected below 28°F.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Kaimana is a lychee cultivar developed at the University of Hawaii for its exceptional combination of large fruit size, outstanding flavor, and reliable production in subtropical conditions. The name means 'diamond' in Hawaiian and reflects the premium quality of the fruit. The large, dark red fruits have a very small ('chicken tongue') seed — a highly valued characteristic that means more of the edible white aril is present relative to seed volume. The translucent, white, juicy flesh has a complex, floral, honey-lychee fragrance and flavor. Kaimana ripens in June–July in zone 9, providing fresh lychee in a season when few other tropical fruits are available. As a relatively cold-tolerant lychee, Kaimana has gained popularity in zone 9 gardens from Florida's Gulf Coast to California's coastal areas, where the mild winters provide flower-inducing chilling without the destructive hard freezes that damage lychee trees.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy, seasonal-dry tropical soil in full sun; Kakadu plum is a Northern Territory and Western Australia native tree producing small, round, pale-green fruits with the highest naturally occurring vitamin C concentration of any fruit in the world — approximately 1,000–5,300 mg per 100g (20–50 times more vitamin C than oranges by weight) — and now a globally sought-after ingredient in the native food, cosmetics, and nutraceutical industries.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Kakadu plum requires excellent drainage and tolerates seasonal drought — water only in establishment first year, then rely on rainfall in tropical monsoonal climate. Terminalia ferdinandiana (Kakadu plum, gubinge, or billygoat plum) is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree native to the open woodland and savanna regions of the Northern Territory and northwestern Western Australia — and the producer of what is recognized as the single richest natural source of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in the world. The small (1/2–1 inch), round, pale-green to olive-colored fruits contain an extraordinary 1,000–5,300 mg of ascorbic acid per 100g fresh weight — 20 to 80 times more vitamin C than oranges and roughly 100 times more than most commercial fruits. Aboriginal Australians across the Top End and Kimberley have eaten Kakadu plums as a traditional food and medicine for at least 65,000 years. The fruits are also remarkably high in ellagic acid and other polyphenol antioxidants. In contemporary Australian native food and cosmetics industries, Kakadu plum extract has become one of the most sought-after botanical ingredients for antioxidant skincare products, functional foods, and vitamin C supplements — and Kakadu plum jam, sauce, and fruit purée are premium native food products sold across Australia and internationally. The tree adapts well to tropical and subtropical low-humidity conditions with good drainage.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Kalamata olive needs a Mediterranean-type climate with dry summers and tolerates only brief light frost.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Kalamata olive needs a Mediterranean-type climate with dry summers and tolerates only brief light frost. Native to and named for the region around Kalamata, Greece, this classic dual-purpose olive cultivar produces large, almond-shaped, deep purple-black fruit famous worldwide when brine-cured for eating, along with good-quality oil, making it one of the most recognizable named table olive varieties globally. Like other olives it thrives on neglect once established, tolerating poor, rocky, alkaline soil and long dry summers far better than regular watering and rich soil, and needs a genuinely Mediterranean-type climate with wet winters and hot, dry summers to fruit and ripen well. Raw olives straight from the tree are intensely bitter and inedible; fruit must be cured through brining, salt-curing, or lye processing before eating, a process requiring several weeks depending on the method used.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Kampong Mauve is a distinctive pink-blushed sugar apple suited to zones 10-11 and warm, sheltered zone 9b sites, with no cold tolerance to speak of.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in a warm, frost-free site; Kampong Mauve is a striking sugar apple selection with a distinctive dusty pink-to-mauve blush over its bumpy, segmented skin, standing out visually from the typical pale green sugar apple, while the sweet, creamy, custard-textured white flesh inside is classic sugar apple in flavor and texture. It is more cold-sensitive than cherimoya or atemoya and needs consistently warm, essentially tropical conditions to thrive, making it best suited to south Florida, south Texas, and similarly frost-free zones, or container culture that can be moved under cover in cooler areas. Hand-pollination with a small brush, transferring pollen between flowers in the evening or early morning when they are receptive, significantly improves fruit set in home garden settings where the tree's natural beetle pollinators may be scarce. Harvest when the segments on the fruit begin to separate slightly and the fruit softens, and eat promptly since ripe sugar apples do not store well.

common_name: Kanza Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Mid-Season Pecan, Excellent for the Midsouth)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter while dormant; Kanza is a Type I (protandrous) pecan that releases pollen before the pistillate flowers are receptive on the same tree, requiring a Type II pecan pollinator within 150 feet for reliable fertilization and full crop. Pair Kanza with Pawnee, Oconee, or Desirable (all Type II) for best results. In zone 9, pecan trees require deep, well-drained, fertile soil with adequate zinc availability — zinc deficiency is common in Gulf South pecan trees and causes rosette symptoms; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays as recommended by extension guidelines. Trees begin significant production 5–8 years after planting and remain productive for 50–100+ years. Annual pruning to maintain open canopy structure improves light penetration and air circulation — critical for scab management even in a resistant variety.
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually. Pair with a Type II pollinator within 150 feet. Kanza Pecan was released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service (ARS) Pecan Breeding Program in 1984 as part of the Northern Pecan Testing Program — a cooperative breeding effort between the USDA and several state agricultural experiment stations to develop superior pecan varieties adapted to a wide range of conditions from the Gulf Coast northward through Oklahoma, Kansas, and Missouri. Kanza is notable for its excellent resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum), the most economically damaging disease of pecans in the humid Gulf South region, where high summer humidity and rainfall create ideal conditions for scab development on susceptible varieties. Standard commercial varieties like Desirable and Stuart have significant scab susceptibility and require intensive fungicide programs in humid regions; Kanza's improved scab resistance significantly reduces the fungicide inputs required for commercial-quality nut production. The nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality and relatively thin shells, and they mature in mid-season — earlier than some standard varieties — allowing harvest before fall rains that can cause nut deterioration. For Gulf South pecan growers (backyard and small-scale), Kanza's disease resistance reduces management burden substantially compared to growing standard susceptible varieties.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost, in a sheltered, sunny spot.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost, in a sheltered, sunny spot, since this cultivar can be shy-bearing in cooler coastal fog belts and benefits from reflected heat. Keep soil evenly moist and feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season to support its dense, spreading canopy. Kara fruit ripens late, often improving in flavor if left on the tree into late winter, developing a rich, aromatic sweetness with a soft, slightly fragile peel. It is a favorite among California backyard growers for its dessert-quality flavor, though it ships poorly and is rarely found in stores.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; karanda is drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established, growing naturally in dry scrub forests and coastal areas of India and Southeast Asia. More cold-tolerant than natal plum, surviving brief dips to 24°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; karanda is a thorny, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree from India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia — widely used throughout South Asia as an impenetrable security hedge and as a productive fruit shrub. The small, oval fruits (1/2 to 1 inch) ripen from green through white to pink and finally red-purple or black, with the white stage being particularly popular for pickling (used extensively in Indian pickles, chutneys, and preserves) while the ripe red-black fruits are eaten fresh or used for jams. The fruits have a mild, slightly tart flavor when ripe. Extremely drought and heat tolerant — one of the tougher fruiting shrubs for hot, dry gardens in zones 8–11. More cold-tolerant than natal plum (Carissa macrocarpa), making it useful in the warmer parts of zone 8 where natal plum would be damaged. Exudes a milky latex sap when cut — wear gloves when pruning. Forms an excellent thorny security hedge.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Karla Rose needs only about 300 chill hours, suiting it to mild-winter coastal and Southern California gardens as well as similar warm zone 7-9 climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and thin developing fruit to a few inches apart to encourage larger, sweeter fruit. Karla Rose is prized for white, low-acid, semi-freestone flesh with an intensely sweet, aromatic flavor that stands apart from typical yellow-fleshed nectarines. It is self-fertile and blooms attractively with showy pink flowers in early spring. Because it sets a heavy crop, an annual dormant-season prune helps maintain an open canopy and manageable size for home orchards.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, staking young trees until established.
directions: Karp's Sweet is a cold-hardy quince selection notable for fruit mild enough to eat fresh out of hand, unlike most quince cultivars that require cooking to be palatable. Trees are compact, self-fertile, and produce fragrant, pear-shaped golden fruit in fall after a single showy spring bloom. Its hardiness makes it a good choice for northern growers where standard Smyrna-type quinces struggle with winter dieback. Site in full sun with good air circulation to reduce fire blight and leaf spot pressure, and thin fruit if branches appear overloaded.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Starfruit is frost-sensitive — temperatures below 32°F can damage foliage and young fruit, and temperatures below 27°F can kill established trees, though mature trees may resprout from the roots after moderate freezes. In zone 9a plant in the warmest, most frost-protected microclimate. Kary is a sweet starfruit cultivar (low oxalic acid content, higher sugar) selected for superior eating quality over tart, sour commercial varieties. Trees can produce fruit year-round in south Florida; in zone 9 expect one to two main fruiting seasons, typically late summer–fall and winter–spring. Starfruit is self-fertile.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent moisture during the growing season — starfruit requires full sun and adequate water for consistent fruit production; Kary Starfruit is a superior sweet cultivar of Carambola (Averrhoa carambola), a tropical fruit tree originally from Southeast Asia that produces the distinctive 5-ribbed, translucent yellow-orange fruits that create the characteristic star cross-section when sliced. Unlike commercial starfruit varieties selected for high acidity and sour flavor, Kary was selected specifically for sweet eating quality — lower oxalic acid content, higher sugar content — producing fruits that are genuinely enjoyable eaten fresh without the puckering tartness that characterizes inferior varieties. The crisp, juicy flesh with a mild, sweet, tropical flavor combined with the visually stunning star-shaped cross section makes Kary starfruit both an eating and a culinary presentation fruit of first quality. In the warmest, most frost-protected zone 9 microclimates, starfruit can be grown successfully as a landscape tree with both ornamental value (pretty pink flower clusters, handsome tropical foliage) and substantial fresh-fruit production — providing a tropical fruit experience that very few other fruit trees can offer in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Katy (also sold as Katja), a Swedish cultivar, needs roughly 500 chill hours, moderate enough to perform in some Southern low-chill apple lists alongside Anna and Dorsett Golden.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Katy, bred in Sweden and also sold as Katja, produces attractive, bright red, crisp apples with a pleasant, slightly tart, sweet flavor, ripening in mid to late summer, well ahead of most main-season apples. Its moderate chill requirement makes it one of the apple cultivars sometimes recommended for the milder end of Southern apple-growing country, though it needs somewhat more winter chill than the very lowest-chill Florida-bred selections. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to keep the canopy open for good air circulation.

common_name: Katy Apricot (Low-Chill Gulf South and Texas Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Katy has a low chill requirement of around 300 hours, making it one of the few apricots that can fruit reliably in zone 8-9, though its very early bloom means late frosts can still damage the crop in some years.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Bred by Zaiger Genetics in California and selected specifically for regions with mild winters, Katy is one of the more dependable apricots for Texas and the Gulf South, where most northern apricot cultivars fail to set fruit due to insufficient winter chilling. It blooms quite early, so late cold snaps remain the main risk to the crop even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well. Fruit is medium, orange-blushed, and sweet-tart, ripening in late spring to early summer, and the tree is self-fruitful, needing no separate pollinator.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Kazake is a cold-hardy Central Asian pomegranate cultivar noted for tolerating colder winter temperatures than many fruiting pomegranates. Self-fertile; no cross-pollination needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Kazake, originating from the cold-winter regions of Central Asia, is grown chiefly for its exceptional cold hardiness among fruiting pomegranate cultivars, tolerating winter temperatures that would damage or kill less hardy selections, which gives extra insurance against rare hard freezes in zone 8b-9a gardens. Fruit is medium-sized with dark red skin and tart-sweet, deep-red arils, ripening in fall for fresh eating and juicing. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and long-lived; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring after last frost; Kei Apple is dioecious — separate male and female plants are required for fruit production. Plant at least one male per 5–8 females for good pollination. Female plants are identified by their flowers (pistillate, without stamens). Grafted female selections on male rootstocks are available from specialty nurseries and remove the uncertainty of seedling-grown plants.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — Kei Apple tolerates poor, sandy, alkaline, and mildly saline soils and is extremely drought-tolerant once established. Dovyalis caffra is a large thorny shrub or small tree native to the coastal thornveld and thicket of South Africa's Eastern Cape province, named for the Kei River region where it grows wild. The formidable 2-inch spines make it one of the most impenetrable barrier plants available for zone 9 — a mature hedge is impassable to deer, livestock, and intruders. The small, round fruits (3/4 to 1 inch diameter) ripen in summer (July–September in zone 9) to a bright golden-yellow or amber color with paper-thin skin and juicy, very acidic pulp that is rarely eaten fresh but makes extraordinary jams, jellies, chutney, and preserves with a distinctive bright, tart flavor combining notes of apricot, plum, and citrus. The glossy, willow-like evergreen foliage is ornamentally attractive year-round. Kei Apple can be grown as a specimen tree (2–4 trunks) or planted 4–6 feet apart and clipped into a dense, absolutely impenetrable hedge. Drought tolerance, extreme heat resistance, and salt spray tolerance make it valuable for coastal Gulf South gardens.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Kelsey is one of the earliest Japanese plums introduced to North America, brought from Japan in 1870 by John Kelsey of Berkeley, California and valued for its very large, dramatically shaped, green-yellow fruits and excellent heat tolerance that suits Gulf Coast and Southern California gardens well.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Kelsey cross-pollinates with Santa Rosa, Shiro, Satsuma, and most other Japanese plums. Kelsey is historically significant as one of the first Japanese plums introduced to North America, brought from Japan in 1870 by John Kelsey of Berkeley, California and widely distributed through the California nursery trade in the late 19th century, where it contributed to Luther Burbank's subsequent Japanese plum breeding work. The very large (3–5 oz), heart-shaped to irregular, somewhat flattened fruits have distinctive mottled green and yellow skin with a red blush on the sun-exposed cheek, ripening to golden-yellow with a sweet, mild, honeyed yellow flesh. Kelsey is a late-season variety (August–September) with lower chill requirements than many Japanese plums (approximately 300–400 hours), making it well-suited to Gulf Coast zone 8 and mild California gardens; the flesh firms up during ripening, giving the fruit good keeping quality and making it one of the better shipping and storage plums for home orchardists.

plant_note: Plant female vines with a compatible male Actinidia arguta pollinator in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade on a strong trellis; Ken's Red is a New Zealand-bred selection known for its distinctive red-blushed skin.
directions: Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Ken's Red is a New Zealand-bred hardy kiwiberry cultivar notable for its smooth skin blushed red-purple over green, distinguishing it visually from the plain green skin of most kiwiberry cultivars, with sweet green flesh and rich kiwi flavor inside. Fruit ripens in late summer to early fall and is eaten whole without peeling, like other kiwiberries. As with all Actinidia arguta selections, plants need a few years to reach full bearing size but then crop heavily and reliably for many years once established. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous twining growth, train onto a permanent trellis or pergola from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within range for consistent pollination and fruit set.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kepayang is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Raw seeds and unprocessed plant parts contain cyanogenic compounds and must be properly fermented and processed before eating.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kepayang is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Raw seeds and unprocessed plant parts contain cyanogenic compounds and must be properly fermented and processed before eating. This large Southeast Asian rainforest tree produces football-sized fruit containing large seeds that, after a traditional fermentation and boiling process to remove naturally occurring toxic compounds, become the famous kluwak or keluak used to flavor the dark, earthy Indonesian dish rawon and Peranakan ayam buah keluak. The raw seeds, bark, and leaves are toxic and must never be eaten without proper traditional processing, which involves burying, boiling, and fermenting the seeds over an extended period to render them safe. Grow only as a specialty tree for a large tropical property or botanical collection, and never attempt to process or consume the fruit without expert traditional knowledge of the detoxification method.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; kepel fruit is a rare and legendary Javanese fruit tree associated with the royal court of the Yogyakarta Sultanate — the deep-brown, plum-sized cauliflorous fruits have the unusual property of making the sweat, breath, and urine of those who eat them smell like violets — and were traditionally reserved for the exclusive use of Javanese royalty.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; kepel fruit is slow-growing and best suited to zone 11–12 humid tropical conditions with consistent moisture. Stelechocarpus burahol (kepel fruit or burahol) is one of the world's most unusual and historically remarkable fruit trees — a medium-sized tropical tree in the custard apple family (Annonaceae) native to Java, Indonesia, where it has been deeply associated with the royal courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta for centuries. The rounded, deep-brown, plum-sized fruits emerge cauliflourously in dense clusters on the trunk and main branches, and have a pleasant, sweet, melon-custard apple flavor. What makes kepel fruit uniquely extraordinary, however, is its documented effect on body chemistry: eating the fruits causes the sweat, breath, and urine of the consumer to take on a floral fragrance — reportedly reminiscent of violets or jasmine — for several hours. This effect was so prized in Javanese royal culture that kepel trees were traditionally planted exclusively in the gardens of the Kraton (royal palace), and common people were reportedly forbidden to grow or eat the fruit. The active compounds are thought to be terpenoids that are metabolized into aromatic volatiles excreted through the skin and kidneys. Kepel is extremely rare in cultivation outside Java; it is categorized as a vulnerable species due to limited habitat and restricted cultivation history.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost; Kerman is a female cultivar and needs a male pollinator such as Peters planted within wind-pollination range (one male per 8-10 females is typical) to set nuts.
directions: Kerman is the standard commercial female pistachio cultivar grown across California's Central Valley, chosen for its large nut size and heavy production once mature, though trees can take 7-10 years to bear a full crop. It needs the same demanding climate as the species overall: 700-1000 hours of winter chill combined with long, blisteringly hot, low-humidity summers to fill and split the shells properly, which makes it a poor fit for humid Gulf Coast gardens even where winter cold is adequate. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil and expect strong biennial bearing, with a heavy crop one year followed by a lighter one the next. A male pollinator such as Peters must bloom at the same time and be planted nearby, since pistachio is wind-pollinated and entirely dioecious. Harvest when hulls loosen and nuts show the characteristic natural shell split, typically in early autumn.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; ketembilla is frost-sensitive but tolerates brief dips to 28°F when established. Dioecious — both male and female plants are needed for fruit production; plant at least one of each.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; ketembilla (Ceylon gooseberry) is a thorny, multi-stemmed shrub from Sri Lanka producing small (1/2 to 1 inch diameter), round, reddish-purple to deep purple fruits with a tart, acidic, gooseberry-like flavor that makes them outstanding for jams, jellies, preserves, and syrups — not particularly pleasant raw due to their sharp acidity, but among the best tropical fruits for processing. The plant is heavily thorned and makes an impenetrable hedge — widely used in Sri Lanka and tropical gardens for security hedging. Requires both male and female plants for fruit (dioecious). Grows quickly in warm, humid, well-drained conditions. The tart fruits are exceptionally high in vitamin C. In Florida it is occasionally grown as a specialty fruit and hedge plant. Underutilized as a jam fruit in the US — the intense, tart purple jam from ketembilla rivals the finest domestic berry jams.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost risk has passed; key lime is the most cold-sensitive common citrus and is suitable only for zones 10–11 in the ground.
directions: Key lime is a small, thorny tree distinct from the larger Persian lime (Citrus latifolia) — its fruit is smaller, more aromatic, more acidic, and nearly seedless at full yellow ripeness. It is self-fertile and bears prolifically in truly tropical conditions; the tree is damaged by any frost and requires zone 10–11 for outdoor culture, though it adapts well to large containers for zone 9 growers who can move it inside. Harvest fruit while still light green to yellow-green, before it turns fully yellow; yellow fruit is riper and less acid but also more perishable. Apply citrus fertilizer three times per year and ensure excellent drainage to prevent root rot.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted tree; move outdoors after frost.
directions: Key lime, also called Mexican lime, produces small, intensely aromatic and juicy fruit beloved for pie, drinks, and marinades. This tender, somewhat thorny citrus stays compact and grows readily in a container that can shelter indoors in cold weather. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with excellent drainage and feed it a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply, letting the top of the soil dry between waterings, and protect it from any frost.

plant_note: Set out after frost; well-suited to containers moved indoors for winter.
directions: A younger, compact form of the Key lime, this semi-tropical evergreen produces small, juicy green limes nearly year-round, famous for Key lime pie. Grow in full sun with fast-draining acidic soil and feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply, letting the surface dry between soakings to avoid soggy roots. Its small size makes it perfect for patio pots that can be sheltered indoors in cold weather.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring while dormant; in zone 9 plant December–February. Kieffer pear is partially self-fertile but bears more heavily with a cross-pollinator such as Orient, Moonglow, or another pear variety planted within 50 feet. In zone 9 Kieffer requires only 150–200 chill hours (temperatures below 45°F) to break dormancy — one of the lowest-chill requirements of any commercial pear, making it specifically well-suited to Gulf Coast and warm-winter gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Kieffer is an 1863 American pear hybrid (Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia) with extraordinary disease resistance and low chill hour requirements that make it the most reliably productive pear for hot-summer, mild-winter climates in the Southeast and Gulf South — regions where most European pear varieties fail from fire blight disease or insufficient winter chilling. The yellow-green to russet fruits with white, gritty, aromatic flesh are at their best when harvested slightly firm and allowed to ripen at room temperature for several days — the fresh eating quality improves dramatically with proper ripening off the tree. Kieffer pear is primarily a cooking and canning pear in American tradition: the firm, gritty flesh holds its shape beautifully in cooked preparations, and canned Kieffer pear preserves, spiced pears, and pear butter have been produced from this variety for over 150 years in Southern home kitchens. Exceptionally vigorous and productive once established, bearing full crops even in zone 9 conditions that exclude most pear varieties.

plant_note: Plant dormant in early spring; partly self-fertile but a second pear improves yields.
directions: Kieffer is a tough, adaptable pear valued for its heavy crops of crisp, gritty fruit that is excellent for canning, cooking, and preserves. It shows strong resistance to fire blight and tolerates a wide range of climates. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and water regularly while establishing. Prune in late winter to build a strong scaffold and allow light into the canopy for even ripening.

plant_note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in full sun in moist to well-drained soil; Killen is self-fruitful, so a single tree can set a crop without a separate pollinator nearby.
directions: Killen is a named native persimmon selection valued for its exceptionally sweet, blemish-free orange fruit and its self-fruitful habit, meaning a single tree can set a crop without a separate pollinator planted nearby. It is a somewhat smaller-statured American persimmon, typically maturing around 25 feet, which makes it easier to fit and harvest in a home orchard than many seedling-grown native persimmons. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, Killen fruit remains firm and astringent until fully ripened and softened by autumn frosts, after which it turns rich, sweet, and custard-like. The tree is drought-tolerant once established, adaptable to a wide range of soil types, and well suited to the long, humid growing season of the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile soil in full sun; Kimbrough Satsuma is among the most cold-hardy satsuma selections, surviving temperatures as low as 14–18°F with some canopy damage but root survival — a critical advantage in zone 8a–8b where winter freezes periodically occur.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Kimbrough is a cold-hardy satsuma mandarin selection developed and evaluated by the Louisiana State University AgCenter — selected specifically for superior cold hardiness compared to standard Owari satsuma, making it the recommended satsuma cultivar for zone 8a–8b gardens where occasional hard freezes occur. Satsuma mandarins are the most cold-hardy commonly grown citrus — Kimbrough extends the cold hardiness envelope even further, surviving brief exposure to 14–18°F without permanent damage when grown in well-drained soil (saturated roots dramatically reduce cold tolerance). The fruit is easy-peeling, seedless, and has the classic sweet-tart satsuma mandarin flavor that ripens early (October–November) — delivering fresh citrus fruit months before oranges and before the most demanding winter cold arrives in the Gulf South. In zone 9, Kimbrough satsumas perform reliably with minimal cold protection. Satsumas are fast to bearing — often producing some fruit in the second or third year — and are moderate-sized trees that fit comfortably in residential landscapes. Plant in the warmest, most protected microclimate (south-facing, near a wall or fence) for zone 8 plantings.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; King David is an 1893 Arkansas heirloom apple, likely a chance seedling of Jonathan and Winesap, known for a rich, wine-like flavor and better disease resistance than many of its high-chill Northern contemporaries.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. King David originated as a chance seedling discovered on an Arkansas farm in 1893, believed to be a natural cross of Jonathan and Winesap, and quickly gained a following for its rich, aromatic, distinctly wine-like flavor that many heirloom apple enthusiasts still rank among the best-tasting of the old Southern apples. Fruit is medium-sized, deep red over a yellow background, with firm, crisp, juicy flesh that holds up well for fresh eating, baking, and cider. Trees show good vigor and better resistance to common apple diseases than many high-chill Northern varieties of the same era, though it still needs a moderate winter chill and performs best in zone 5-8, becoming marginal in the mildest parts of zone 9. Plant with another apple variety for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open, well-ventilated canopy that reduces disease pressure in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; King of the Pippins is a strong, reliable pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties, though it can bear biennially if not thinned.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; King of the Pippins is a strong, reliable pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties, though it can bear biennially if not thinned. An old variety of uncertain French or English origin dating to at least the eighteenth century, it bears attractive orange-red-striped apples over a golden ground, with crisp, aromatic, sweet-sharp flesh that made it a widely planted commercial dessert apple across Europe for generations before more modern varieties took over the market. Its strong, abundant bloom makes it a valuable cross-pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties in a mixed home orchard, though the tree has a tendency toward biennial bearing, alternating heavy and light crop years unless fruit is thinned in a heavy year. Harvest in mid-fall and eat within a couple of months, since it does not keep quite as long as some other classic dessert varieties.

common_name: Kingston Black Apple (Classic English Bittersharp Cider Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Kingston Black is notoriously shy-bearing and susceptible to scab, so site it in an open spot with good air circulation.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Kingston Black is notoriously shy-bearing and susceptible to scab, so site it in an open spot with good air circulation. Originating in Somerset, England, this small, dark red-purple apple is the most celebrated of the true single-variety, or vintage, cider apples, prized as a rare bittersharp carrying both the tannin and acid balance needed to produce a complex, well-structured cider entirely on its own without blending. Its fruit is far too astringent and acidic for fresh eating, but its combination of tannin, sugar, and acid in a single apple has made it the benchmark variety against which other cider apples are measured. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and expect a light, sometimes biennial crop, since Kingston Black is well known among cider makers for being a difficult, temperamental tree to grow well.

common_name: Kinnard's Choice Apple (Tennessee Heirloom Dessert Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant; needs roughly 600-700 chill hours, well suited to the upper and middle South.
directions: Grow as a standard tree in deep, well-drained soil and thin fruit clusters to improve size and reduce limb breakage in heavy years. Kinnard's Choice originated in Tennessee in the 19th century and has long been prized by Southern heirloom apple collectors for its rich, aromatic, exceptionally sweet flesh, considered by many old-timers to be among the best-flavored dessert apples of the region. It ripens in late summer to early fall and is primarily grown today by small orchardists and heritage-fruit enthusiasts rather than commercial producers.

common_name: Kinnow Mandarin (King x Willowleaf Hybrid Tangerine)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost danger has passed, once soil has warmed.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost danger has passed, choosing a well-drained site with at least eight hours of direct sun and protection from cold winds.
