For decades, Loring was the dominant commercial peach in Tennessee, Missouri, Arkansas, and adjacent southeastern states, praised for its reliable high yields, large fruit size, excellent flavor, and shelf life compared to other varieties of its era. The fruits are large to very large, round to slightly oblate, with a predominantly red skin over a yellow-orange background — very attractive at roadside markets and farm stands. The flesh is yellow, firm, and fully freestone at full maturity, with a well-balanced rich peach flavor that compares favorably with Elberta while generally producing larger, better-colored fruit under mid-South conditions. Loring's moderate chill requirement (approximately 750 hours) fits the climate of the mid-South better than Elberta (which needs 800–1000 hours) in years with insufficient winter cold. It has been partially replaced by newer varieties with improved disease resistance in commercial production, but remains a standard recommendation for home orchardists throughout the Southeast.

common_name: Louise Bonne Pear (Louise Bonne of Jersey, Reliable French Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Louise Bonne, widely known in England as Louise Bonne of Jersey, is a French heirloom dating to the 1780s that became one of the most reliably productive and widely planted pears of the 19th century, valued for its dependable, heavy annual bearing as much as its fruit quality. The medium, greenish-yellow pear blushed with brownish-red has juicy, sweet, melting flesh with a good, well-balanced flavor, excellent for fresh eating and reasonably good for canning as well. The vigorous, precocious tree tends to bear young and heavily, sometimes needing fruit thinning to avoid limb breakage or biennial bearing. Pick while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature for the best eating quality.

common_name: Louisiana Sweet Satsuma (Gulf South Cold-Hardy Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring after frost danger has passed; Louisiana Sweet is a satsuma selection promoted for Gulf Coast dooryard growing for its reliable sweetness and cold tolerance close to that of Owari.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and give young trees frost cloth protection on the coldest nights until they are several years established. Louisiana Sweet is a satsuma mandarin selection grown and promoted along the Gulf Coast for combining good cold hardiness with consistently sweet, low-acid flavor even in years when cooler, cloudier falls can leave other citrus tart. Fruit is medium-sized, nearly seedless, and easy to peel, ripening in the standard satsuma window from October into December ahead of most other citrus. As with all satsumas, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization late in the season, which delays the hardening off trees need to withstand winter cold, and mulch well to protect the root zone.

plant_note: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach or nectarine variety onto the young rootstock.
directions: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach or nectarine variety onto the young rootstock. A long-standing standard peach seedling rootstock widely used across commercial and home orchards for its reliable vigor, good compatibility with a broad range of peach and nectarine varieties, and adaptability to a range of well-drained soil types. It produces a full-sized, vigorous tree without the size control offered by modern clonal dwarfing rootstocks, making it best suited to a home orchard with ample space for a standard-sized peach tree. Graft a desired named peach or nectarine variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and provide well-drained soil, since peach rootstocks in general are notably intolerant of wet, poorly drained conditions.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall into well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; the shrub's natural habitat preference makes it well suited to difficult sites where improved soils are unavailable.
directions: Sow fresh seeds in fall directly into sandy, well-drained soil, as Low Serviceberry is adapted to dry, rocky ground and performs poorly in rich or consistently moist conditions. Winter cold provides the stratification seeds need, and seedlings emerge in spring when soil temperatures warm to 40–55 degrees Fahrenheit. This spreading, colony-forming shrub is excellent for naturalizing slopes, stabilizing sandy soils, and providing wildlife habitat; allow adequate space for root-sprouting colonies to develop. Expect the first berry crop 2–5 years after transplanting; the sweet, dark blue fruits ripen in midsummer and are relished by birds and mammals.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free to near-frost-free conditions; lucuma is damaged below 28–30°F but tolerates brief cool temperatures better than most tropical fruit trees. Grafted trees begin fruiting in 3–5 years versus 7–10 years for seedlings. Good drainage is essential — it does not tolerate waterlogged soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun in a frost-free location; lucuma is a Peruvian fruit tree native to the Andean valleys, where it has been cultivated since ancient times and was called the 'Gold of the Incas.' The large, oval fruits (3–4 inches) have a dry, starchy, bright orange-yellow flesh with an extraordinary flavor — intensely sweet with a rich, complex caramel-maple-sweet potato quality that is completely unlike any familiar fruit. The taste is so distinctive and rich that lucuma powder (dried, ground lucuma flesh) is used as a natural sweetener and flavoring for ice cream, smoothies, pastries, and confections in Peru, where lucuma ice cream outsells chocolate and vanilla in many surveys. The flavor is particularly popular as a low-glycemic sweetener alternative. Fresh lucuma is eaten locally in Peru and Chile but ships poorly, so it is rarely found fresh outside its home region. An exceptional specialty fruit tree for collectors in frost-free zones.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost risk; in zone 9 plant March–May. Lula is a hybrid avocado with West Indian and Guatemalan ancestry that provides moderate cold tolerance — surviving temperatures down to approximately 24–26°F when established. Plant in the warmest, most frost-protected microclimate available: south-facing walls, raised beds, and sheltered positions increase cold tolerance significantly. Young trees under 3 years are more frost-sensitive than established trees.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — avocados are extremely sensitive to root rot in poorly drained or clay soils; Lula is a historic Florida avocado cultivar developed by George Lula in Homestead, Florida in the 1920s and valued for its combination of good cold hardiness, large fruit size, and excellent fresh-eating quality. The large fruits (often 12–18 ounces) have smooth green skin that remains green when ripe — ripeness is determined by giving the fruit a gentle squeeze, not by color change. The flesh is pale yellow-green, creamy, and mild-flavored with good avocado oil content. Lula is classified as a hybrid between West Indian and Guatemalan race avocados, inheriting moderate cold tolerance from its Guatemalan genetics and fruiting reliability from its West Indian parentage. In zone 9 Lula is one of the more reliable cultivars for home production; the long, warm growing season develops the oil content that gives mature fruits their buttery richness. Cross-pollinate with a Type A avocado such as Bacon for best fruit set.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Luscious requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is exceptionally cold-hardy, well adapted to zones 3-7.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Luscious was bred by South Dakota State University specifically for the harsh northern Great Plains climate, combining excellent cold hardiness and good fire blight resistance with genuinely good eating quality, living up to its name with sweet, juicy, melting flesh comparable to much less hardy European dessert pears. The medium-sized, greenish-yellow fruit ripens in early to mid fall and should be picked while still firm, then ripened at room temperature indoors for the best texture, as with most European-type pears. Its combination of hardiness and flavor has made it a favorite recommendation for northern home orchardists who want a genuinely good fresh-eating pear without relying on tender varieties bred for milder climates.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost risk has passed; in zones 10–11, fall planting after summer heat breaks is preferred.
directions: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) in a site sheltered from salt spray and drying winter wind; lychee cannot tolerate waterlogged roots at any age. Trees require a cool-dry stress period of 4–6 weeks in late autumn — nights reliably below 59°F — to trigger flower bud development, so hold irrigation during that window rather than watering on a regular schedule. Fruit clusters develop rapidly after bloom and benefit from thinning to 3–5 fruits per panicle when marble-sized to improve final fruit size and reduce limb stress. Harvest clusters when the rough, bumpy skin has turned fully red to pinkish-red and the aroma is distinctly floral and sweet, typically 90–112 days after bloom.

plant_note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M111 is grown as a semi-dwarfing to semi-standard understock, not for its own fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M111 is grown as a semi-dwarfing to semi-standard understock, not for its own fruit. One of the classic Malling-Merton series rootstocks developed in England, it produces a vigorous, semi-standard-sized tree that develops a large, sturdy, self-supporting root system needing no permanent staking, along with good drought tolerance and adaptability to a wide range of soil types compared to the smaller, more demanding fully dwarfing rootstocks. Its self-supporting, low-maintenance root system and tolerance of poor or dry soil have made it a traditional standard for larger home orchard trees and for growers unwilling or unable to install permanent trellising for dwarf trees. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and give the eventual tree ample room, since it grows nearly as large as a full seedling tree.

plant_note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M26 is a semi-dwarfing understock that benefits from staking in its early years.
directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M26 is a semi-dwarfing understock that benefits from staking in its early years. Another classic East Malling selection, it produces a semi-dwarf tree roughly 40-50 percent the size of a standard seedling tree, notably hardier and more cold-tolerant than M9 while still offering meaningful size control and precocious early fruiting, making it a popular choice for colder-climate home orchards wanting a manageable tree size. Its root system is sturdier than M9 but still benefits from staking for the first several years until the tree is well established, and it performs best in fertile, well-drained soil, showing some susceptibility to fire blight and collar rot in poorly drained sites. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, stake for the first few years, and expect a compact, productive tree well suited to a small home orchard in a colder climate.

plant_note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M7 is a semi-dwarfing understock that is largely self-supporting once established.
directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M7 is a semi-dwarfing understock that is largely self-supporting once established. A long-standing East Malling selection producing a semi-dwarf tree roughly 50-60 percent the size of a standard seedling tree, it develops a sturdier, more self-supporting root system than the more fully dwarfing M9 and M26 rootstocks, generally needing staking only while young rather than for the tree's entire life. It has a tendency to produce root suckers that should be removed periodically, and it shows good tolerance of a range of soil types along with reasonably good cold hardiness, making it a reliable choice for a home orchard tree of moderate, easy-to-manage size. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, remove root suckers as they appear, and expect a productive tree that needs only temporary staking while establishing.

plant_note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M9 is a fully dwarfing understock requiring permanent staking or trellising.
directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M9 is a fully dwarfing understock requiring permanent staking or trellising. Selected at England's East Malling Research Station in the early twentieth century, it remains the benchmark fully dwarfing apple rootstock against which most modern rootstocks are compared, producing a small tree roughly 25-30 percent the size of a standard seedling tree that bears fruit remarkably early and heavily for its size. Its brittle, shallow root system anchors poorly and requires permanent staking or trellising for the life of the tree, and it demands consistently fertile, well-drained soil and regular irrigation to perform well, making it best suited to intensively managed high-density plantings rather than a low-maintenance home orchard. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, provide permanent support, and expect an extremely compact, easy-to-harvest tree bearing within two to three years.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring; needs about 450 chill hours, well matched to Gulf Coast winters.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Maayan was bred by Chanan Oppenheimer at the Rehovot experiment station in Israel specifically for hot, low-chill growing regions, and needs about 450 hours of winter chilling — well matched to Gulf Coast Texas and Louisiana winters. It ripens mid-season, later than Anna, with round-oblong fruit that is yellow with more than half its surface flushed red. The flesh is notably crisp and highly juicy, making it a good fresh-eating choice among the Israeli low-chill introductions. It keeps reasonably well in storage compared to some of its lower-chill counterparts.

plant_note: Plant grafted, self-fertile tree in spring in full to partial sun in compost-rich, well-drained soil; MacBeth is a late-season loquat noted for exceptionally large, richly flavored fruit and is well suited to zones 8-10, including the Gulf Coast, given a sheltered site protected from hard freezes during bloom.
directions: Plant in compost-rich, well-drained loam in full to partial sun; MacBeth is self-fertile and does not require a second loquat for fruit set, though nearby trees can improve yield. The tree has a handsome, symmetrical growth habit and can reach around 20-30 feet at full maturity if left untrained, so prune annually to keep fruit within easy reach in a home orchard. MacBeth ripens later than early cultivars like Gold Nugget and produces exceptionally large, orange-skinned fruit with creamy flesh that balances sweetness and acidity, often compared to notes of plum; the size and flavor have made it one of the most sought-after loquat cultivars among backyard growers and collectors. Like other loquats, MacBeth blooms in fall and ripens fruit in late winter to spring, and open flowers and young fruit are more cold-tender than the mature tree, so a warm, sheltered planting site near a south-facing wall improves crop reliability at the cooler edge of its range.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost; macadamias grow best in frost-free zones with well-distributed rainfall.
directions: Macadamias are self-fertile but cross-pollination between two or more varieties meaningfully increases yields; grafted trees start bearing at 3–5 years, while seedlings can take 10–15 years. The tree prefers well-drained, slightly acid soil (pH 5.5–6.5) and is sensitive to root disturbance — plant without disturbing the root ball. Trees produce racemes of cream-white flowers that fall and create a slippery surface; harvesting is done by collecting nuts that have dropped naturally as the green husk splits and the nut falls. Shell and dry nuts for 3–4 weeks before cracking; the shells require a commercial or heavy-duty nut cracker as they are among the hardest of any food nut.

plant_note: Plant grafted container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; grafted trees produce in 4–6 years vs. 8–12 from seed; macadamia is native to the subtropical rainforests of southeast Queensland and northeast New South Wales — the only major commercial nut crop to originate from Australia — producing the world's most expensive commercial nut, with creamy, buttery, sweet, incomparably rich flavor.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; protect from frost below 26°F until established; plant 2+ varieties for cross-pollination and better yields. Macadamia integrifolia (smooth-shell macadamia) is one of the world's most celebrated nut trees and the only major food crop originating in Australia — native to the subtropical rainforests of southeast Queensland. The macadamia nut is universally recognized as one of the finest-flavored nuts in the world: round, ivory-white, buttery-smooth, with an extraordinarily rich, creamy, sweet flavor unlike any other nut. The fat content (75%) is predominantly monounsaturated, making macadamia oil one of the most desirable culinary and cosmetic plant oils. The smooth-shell species (M. integrifolia) is the primary commercial macadamia — most Hawaiian, Australian, South African, and Kenyan commercial orchards are primarily or entirely M. integrifolia or its hybrids. Trees are evergreen, grow slowly to 25–35 feet, produce dark-green, glossy, leathery leaves, and begin bearing in 5–7 years from grafted stock. The extremely hard shell (requiring 300+ psi to crack) requires a specialized macadamia cracker. Zone 9b–11, damaged below 26°F. Hawaii, California, and South Florida can grow macadamia commercially; zone 9a gardens can succeed with protected sites.

common_name: Macoun Apple (Beloved Northeast Eating Apple, McIntosh-Type Geneva Station Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Macoun requires approximately 1000 chill hours and cross-pollination — plant with Cortland, Empire, or McIntosh; Macoun is a mid-to-late-season variety (ripening October in most of New York and New England) with a high chill requirement that limits it to zones 4–7; the trees are moderately biennial-bearing, often producing a heavy crop one year followed by a lighter crop the next.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic fertile soil in full sun; requires cross-pollinator; thin biennial crops by hand-removing half the fruit clusters in early summer to encourage annual bearing; Macoun ripens October and must be harvested at peak ripeness — slightly soft at the stem end, fully red, and with characteristic spicy aroma — as it deteriorates quickly after peak. Macoun apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva from a cross involving McIntosh, and named for W.T. Macoun, Dominion Horticulturalist of Canada who made significant contributions to fruit breeding and evaluation — released in 1923, making it roughly contemporary with McIntosh's commercial rise. Among apple connoisseurs of the northeastern United States, Macoun occupies a unique status: it is considered by many the finest-eating apple of any variety available in New York and New England, with a complex, spicy-sweet, intensely aromatic flavor at peak ripeness that exceeds even McIntosh in intensity and depth. The fruit is medium-sized, dark red (often nearly all-red with a purple-red hue at full maturity), with pure white, tender, very juicy flesh and the characteristic McIntosh floral fragrance amplified. Macoun's intense flavor comes with a significant limitation: the variety has a very short window of peak eating quality — typically 1–2 weeks at the height of ripeness in October — after which the flesh softens rapidly and flavor diminishes. This poor keeping quality has limited Macoun's commercial viability but made it a cult variety among farmers' market customers who know to seek it out during its brief peak season.

common_name: Madison Peach (Cold-Hardy Virginia Heirloom Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, fertile soil; Madison requires approximately 850 chill hours and is one of the most cold-hardy named peach varieties, with flower buds tolerating temperatures down to 0°F or below — significantly more cold-resistant than Elberta and other standard varieties, making it the premier choice for orchards in zones 4–6 where late spring frosts or severe winter cold reduce peach production reliability.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Madison is self-fruitful; thin fruit in spring to 6–8 inches; this variety is particularly valuable where late spring frosts endanger developing blossoms — its cold-hardy flower buds and frost resistance make it among the most reliable peach varieties in colder zones. Madison peach was developed at the Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (released 1963) as part of a program to develop peach varieties combining high fruit quality with improved cold-hardiness of the flower buds — addressing the primary limitation on peach production in the colder parts of the South and the lower Midwest where late spring frosts can destroy the blossoms of standard varieties like Elberta even in years when winter temperatures are adequate for the trees to survive. The key innovation of Madison is its extraordinary flower bud cold-hardiness: Madison buds have been documented surviving temperatures of -5°F to 0°F with minimal damage in some trials, making it significantly more frost-resilient than Elberta (whose buds are damaged at 28–30°F during bloom). This characteristic translates to reliable cropping in zones 4–6 where other varieties fail every few years due to late frost blossom kill. The fruits are medium to large, red-blushed over golden-yellow skin, with firm, yellow, fully freestone flesh and a well-flavored, balanced sweet-tart peach quality. Madison ripens in mid-season (late July to mid-August in its Virginia homeland, somewhat earlier in warmer zones). It remains one of the most important variety recommendations for cold-region home orchardists in the Mid-Atlantic, Appalachian, and upper Midwest states.

plant_note: Set out grafted trees in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has passed and soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Grow this Cuban-origin, grafted mamey sapote cultivar in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing plenty of room for a large, long-lived tree. It is valued by south Florida growers for reliably producing smooth-skinned fruit with dense, sweet, salmon-pink flesh often compared to sweet potato or pumpkin custard. Young trees are noticeably cold-tender and can lose leaves or twigs at temperatures in the mid-30s, so Gulf Coast growers stick to the warmest coastal locations or grow smaller trees in large containers that come indoors for winter. Mature trees take several years to bear their first crop, and fruit is harvested firm and then ripened off the tree at room temperature.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Magness is a USDA release famous for outstanding dessert flavor and strong fire blight resistance, but its pollen is sterile so it needs two other pear cultivars nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting it near two other pear cultivars since Magness produces sterile pollen and cannot pollinate itself or other pears, though other pears can pollinate it. Magness is a USDA-released pear celebrated among fruit growers for its outstanding dessert quality, with smooth, buttery, exceptionally sweet flesh often ranked among the best-tasting of all pear cultivars, paired with strong resistance to fire blight that makes it a dependable choice for humid Southern growing conditions. Because of its sterile pollen, plant it alongside two compatible, fertile pear cultivars to ensure good fruit set on all three trees. Prune to an open framework for good air circulation, and remove any fire blight-infected shoots promptly, cutting well into clean wood below the damage.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mahan produces some of the largest pecan nuts of any cultivar but has a lower kernel percentage and is more prone to alternate bearing than modern selections.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. One of the earliest widely planted named pecan cultivars, dating to the early 1900s, Mahan is known for producing exceptionally large nuts, among the biggest of any pecan cultivar, though the kernel fill and disease resistance lag behind modern breeding selections. It remains of historical interest and is still grown in some older orchards and by collectors of heirloom pecan varieties for its striking nut size, even though it has largely been superseded commercially by higher-yielding, more scab-resistant cultivars.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 9b–10 plant March–June. Maher is best suited to zones 10–11, though it can succeed in warm, protected zone 9b microclimates near the coast. Young trees need frost protection; established trees tolerate brief dips to near 27°F but suffer significant dieback below that. Fruit ripens in fall and early winter, later than most other Gulf Coast tree fruits.
directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Maher is a Florida-selected black sapote valued for its large, round, apple-green fruit that ripens to a dull olive-brown and reveals dark, chocolate-brown, custard-smooth flesh once fully soft — hence the common name 'chocolate pudding fruit.' Unlike astringent persimmons, black sapote is only palatable when completely soft-ripe, at which point the mild, sweet flesh is eaten fresh with a spoon or blended into puddings, smoothies, and baked goods. Trees are attractive, glossy-leaved evergreens that tolerate light shade better than most fruit trees, making them useful in mixed edible plantings. Harvest fruit while still firm and green and allow it to fully soften indoors over one to two weeks, as tree-ripened fruit is quickly taken by wildlife.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mahlab is grown primarily for the aromatic kernel inside its cherry pits, and is also widely used as an understock for grafting other Prunus species because of its adaptability and drought tolerance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mahlab, or mahaleb cherry, is a small ornamental cherry species native to the Mediterranean and Middle East, grown far more for the fragrant kernel inside its small, bitter cherry pits than for the fruit's thin, tart flesh, which is not typically eaten fresh. The dried, ground kernels — called mahlab or mahleb — have a distinctive bitter-almond, floral, faintly cherry aroma used to flavor Middle Eastern, Greek, and Mediterranean pastries and breads, including Greek tsoureki, Cypriot flaounes, and Middle Eastern ka'ak. To harvest the spice, collect ripe pits, crack them to remove the kernel inside, and grind the kernels just before use, since their aroma fades quickly once ground. The tree itself is small, fragrant-flowered in spring, and notably drought- and alkaline-soil-tolerant, which is also why it is widely used as a rootstock for grafting sweet and sour cherries in regions with dry, calcareous soils unsuited to standard cherry rootstocks. It tolerates heat and poor soil well once established.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained to moderately well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Mahua is a large tropical tree of paramount economic and cultural importance in India — the fleshy, sweet, edible flowers are used to distill a traditional fermented spirit (mahua liquor), the seeds yield a high-quality edible and industrial fat (mahua butter), and the tree is sacred to numerous Indian tribal communities.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun; mahua is drought-tolerant once established and thrives on poor soils. Madhuca longifolia (mahua or Indian butter tree) is a large, slow-growing tropical tree native to the forests of central and southern India, deeply woven into the culture and economy of indigenous tribal communities across Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Madhya Pradesh. The tree provides multiple distinct food, economic, and cultural products: the fleshy, sweet, cream-colored flowers (corollas) that drop prolifically in spring are edible and extremely sweet — they are eaten fresh (tasting like a mild honey-flower combination), sun-dried and used as a sweetener, fermented into mahua wine, and distilled into mahua liquor, one of India's most important traditional tribal spirits and an important livelihood product. The seeds contain 30–40% mahua butter (a semi-solid vegetable fat) with a composition similar to cocoa butter, used in traditional cuisine, soap-making, and cosmetics. The leaves provide fodder; the bark and flowers have Ayurvedic uses. Mahua is considered a 'tree of life' by many Indian adivasi (tribal) communities — the flowers are economically critical, often constituting a significant fraction of tribal household income in forest villages. A remarkable tree with enormous cultural depth and genuine multiple-use value.

common_name: Maiden Blush Apple (Early American Heirloom Dual-Purpose Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Maiden Blush is a New Jersey heirloom dating to the late 1700s, grown for its pale, translucent yellow skin blushed with red and its dual use fresh and in cooking.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator, since Maiden Blush is not reliably self-fruitful. First noted in New Jersey in the late eighteenth century, Maiden Blush became one of the most widely planted American heirloom apples of the nineteenth century for its striking pale lemon-yellow skin marked with a rosy pink blush on the sun-exposed side, a color pattern early writers likened to a blushing cheek. The crisp, tart-leaning flesh cooks down into a pale, delicately flavored sauce and dries well, while a fully ripe apple mellows enough for pleasant fresh eating, making it a genuinely dual-purpose variety by the standards of its era. It ripens over a fairly early late-summer window and does not keep as long in storage as later-season heirlooms, so plan to use or process the crop within a few weeks of picking. Thin heavy fruit set in early summer to improve size and reduce biennial bearing.

common_name: Malabar Chestnut (Money Tree, Guiana Chestnut, Saba Nut)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; in zone 9a protect from frost — young trees are killed by hard freezes, though established trees may resprout from the base after a light freeze. Full sun to partial shade; tolerates wet or seasonally flooded soils well, which makes it valuable near ponds or in low spots where other trees struggle.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained to seasonally wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Malabar chestnut is best known to most people as the ornamental 'money tree' with braided trunks sold as a houseplant across the world, but it is also a genuine food plant producing 12-inch oval pods filled with 20–25 large, edible seeds that taste remarkably like chestnuts or roasted peanuts when cooked — the seeds can be roasted, boiled, or ground into flour, and the young leaves and flowers are edible as vegetables. As a landscape tree in zone 9b–12 it can reach 30–40 feet in the ground with a spreading tropical canopy, but is easy to keep pruned to 10–15 feet. The large, palmate leaves and buttressed trunk give it outstanding ornamental character. Native to the seasonally flooded forests of Central and South America, it tolerates both dry periods and extended flooding — a rare combination that makes it valuable for challenging low-lying sites.

common_name: Malay Apple (Mountain Apple, Jambu Bol, Rose Apple Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with consistently moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Malay Apple is frost-sensitive and suitable for zone 10-11 outdoor planting or zone 9 container culture. The tree exhibits cauliflory — flowers and fruits emerge directly from the trunk and major branches, not the growing tips. Fruiting begins within 3–5 years of planting. The fruits mature in spring to early summer and must be harvested promptly as they do not store well.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Malay Apple grows most rapidly with regular watering and fertilization in the warm humid conditions of zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and South Florida. Syzygium malaccense is a large, fast-growing, evergreen fruit tree native to Malaysia and the Indonesian islands, now cultivated throughout the tropics from the Pacific Islands to Central America, Africa, and the Caribbean. The tree is doubly ornamental: in spring, it produces spectacular displays of crimson-red to deep rose-purple flowers that emerge directly from the bark of the trunk and major branches (cauliflory), creating an extraordinary effect of flowers growing from the wood — dozens to hundreds of 1-inch flowers with brush-like clusters of bright crimson stamens covering the trunk in a fiery display. These flowers are followed by the fruits: dark red to magenta, pear-shaped, 2–3 inch fruits with white, spongy, mildly sweet flesh and a faint floral flavor — eaten fresh throughout Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands and used in jams and beverages. The tree is an important crop and dooryard fruit tree throughout tropical Oceania and Southeast Asia. The Hawaiian name 'Ohia Ai' (mountain apple) reflects its long cultivation history in the Hawaiian Islands. In zone 10-11 South Florida landscapes, it serves as both an ornamental shade tree and a productive home fruit tree.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Malbec prefers warm, sunny conditions and is somewhat more cold-sensitive than many other red wine grapes.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Malbec prefers warm, sunny conditions and is somewhat more cold-sensitive than many other red wine grapes. Originally a minor Bordeaux blending grape in France, this deeply colored red variety found its true expression in the high-altitude vineyards of Mendoza, Argentina, where abundant sunshine and cool nights produce the rich, plush, dark-fruited wines with soft tannins that have made Malbec Argentina's signature grape and an internationally beloved red wine style. It is somewhat prone to coulure (poor fruit set in cool, wet spring weather) and benefits from a warm, sheltered site with reliable sunshine through flowering and fruit set. Provide full sun and a warm site sheltered from late spring cold snaps, prune to a moderate crop load for the best concentration, and harvest when tannins are ripe alongside sugar development.

common_name: Malta Fig (Small Sweet Early-Ripening Mediterranean Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; ripens notably early, giving a reliable crop even in shorter growing seasons.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Malta is a small, dark purple-brown Mediterranean heirloom fig grown for ripening notably early in the season, giving gardeners a reliable, dependable crop of sweet, richly flavored fruit even where the growing season isn't long enough for later-ripening varieties to fully mature a full crop. The compact, manageable tree size makes it a practical choice for container culture or smaller garden spaces, and the fruit's small size and thin skin make it excellent for fresh eating straight from the tree, though it does not ship or store as well as firmer, larger fig varieties. As with all figs, protect the roots with heavy mulch in winter in the colder parts of its range, since the top can die back in hard freezes but typically regrows from the root system.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; mamey apple is killed by any frost and requires a truly tropical or subtropical climate. It is slow-growing but extremely long-lived — trees in the Caribbean are known to exceed 100 years in age. Grafted trees bear fruit earlier than seedlings.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; mamey apple is a large, stately fruit tree native to the Caribbean, Mexico, and northern South America, producing round to oval fruits 3–8 inches across with a thick, rough, bitter brown-russet skin enclosing firm, apricot-orange to yellow flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavor suggesting apricot, vanilla, and almond — quite unlike most other tropical fruits. The flavor is complex and distinctive: the outer flesh directly under the skin can be slightly bitter, while the inner flesh is sweet and aromatic. The tree is magnificent as a landscape specimen — densely leafy, with thick, glossy, oval leaves and a formal, dome-shaped crown. Small, white, fragrant flowers appear on the branches directly. The timber is dense and valuable. Not to be confused with Mamey Sapote (Pouteria sapota), an entirely different fruit despite the similar name. Mamey apple was a staple food of the Taino people of the Caribbean before European contact and was described by Columbus's men. It is now primarily grown in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mamey sapote is a Central American tropical tree suited to zones 10–12, with mature established trees tolerating brief drops to 28–30°F in protected zone 9b microclimates. Named grafted varieties such as 'Magaña' and 'Pantin' begin producing the distinctive brown-skinned, salmon-fleshed fruits within 3–5 years of planting.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; mamey sapote (Pouteria sapota) is a majestic Central American tree in the Sapotaceae family that produces one of the most beloved tropical fruits in Caribbean and Latin American cuisine — a large, russet-brown, football-shaped fruit with vivid salmon-to-brick-red flesh of exceptional richness, sweetness, and smooth texture, often compared to a pumpkin-sweet potato-almond fusion. The fruit is eaten fresh, blended into milkshakes and batidos (a staple across Miami's Cuban community and throughout the Caribbean), made into ice cream, and used in desserts. Only grafted trees of named selections should be planted, as seedling trees can take 10–15 years to fruit and produce variable quality; grafted trees begin bearing in 3–5 years. Mamey sapote is moderately drought-tolerant once established but produces larger, higher-quality fruit with consistent irrigation and regular fertilization with a balanced citrus-type fertilizer.

common_name: Mammoth Black Twig Apple (Paragon, Arkansas Black Twig)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in a sunny, well-drained site; needs about 700-800 chill hours and benefits from a nearby pollinator such as Winesap or Grimes Golden.
directions: Give this vigorous tree plenty of room and prune annually to keep the spreading, upright canopy open to light and air. Originating in Arkansas in the 1830s as a Winesap seedling, Mammoth Black Twig became a popular commercial apple across the South and lower Midwest for its large size, dark red color, and firm, tart-sweet flesh that stores well into winter. It is a distinct cultivar from the unrelated Arkansas Black and is grown today mainly by heirloom orchardists and collectors seeking a taste of 19th-century Southern apple culture.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Mammoth is largely self-infertile and needs a genetically distinct cultivar such as Apollo, Coolidge, or Unique planted nearby for good fruit set. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9. Harvest fruit as it falls naturally October-December.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Mammoth is an older New Zealand-selected feijoa cultivar named for its unusually large, elongated fruit, which can weigh well over 4 ounces and sometimes tops the size chart among common home-garden feijoa varieties. The flesh is aromatic and juicy with the classic pineapple-guava-mint flavor, though quality is somewhat more seed-heavy toward the fruit's center than in top dessert cultivars like Apollo. Mammoth ripens mid-to-late season, extending harvest when planted with earlier cultivars, and its vigorous, upright growth habit makes it useful as an informal evergreen screening hedge as well as a fruiting shrub. Because Mammoth sets fruit poorly on its own pollen, interplanting with a second cultivar is essential for a worthwhile crop; the showy white-and-crimson spring flowers and edible sweet petals are ornamental bonuses either way.

plant_note: Plant grafted or air-layered trees in warm, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed; mamoncillo is strictly tropical and is damaged below 28°F. Grafted trees may begin fruiting in 5–8 years versus 10–15 years for seedlings. A single tree may produce fruit but two trees of different seedling origin improves fruiting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free climates; mamoncillo (Spanish lime, quenepa, genip) is a large tropical tree native to Central America and the Caribbean that produces clusters of golf-ball-sized green fruits with a brittle outer skin concealing a translucent, salmon-colored pulp clinging tightly to a large seed. The flavor is a unique combination — simultaneously sweet-tart, tropical, and faintly lime-like with a passionfruit quality — that is utterly distinctive among tropical fruits. Fruits are eaten by biting through the skin and sucking the pulp off the seed, which is the traditional way to consume them across the Caribbean. They are also made into juice, fermented into wine, and processed into candy. Mamoncillo is an important street-food fruit in Puerto Rico, Colombia, Cuba, and throughout the Caribbean, where it is eaten fresh out of hand in large quantities. The tree is drought-tolerant once established and very long-lived.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost; mandarins are among the hardiest citrus, tolerating brief dips to 24°F.
directions: Mandarins (including tangerines, clementines, and satsumas) are the most cold-hardy of the common sweet citrus, with satsumas surviving to about 15°F and thriving in zone 8. Most are self-fertile, though some varieties set more fruit with a compatible pollinator nearby. Fruit tends to ripen earlier in the season than oranges — from October through January depending on variety — and the loose peel and sweet-tart flavor make them popular for fresh eating. Avoid overwatering, as mandarins are somewhat drought-tolerant and susceptible to root rot in wet soils.

plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; mandarins are generally more cold-hardy than sweet oranges and many are self-fruitful, though cross-pollination from other citrus usually improves fruit set and fruit size.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Citrus reticulata is the species encompassing all mandarins, tangerines, satsumas, clementines, and most mandarin-type hybrids — a diverse group of loose-skinned, easily peeled, aromatic citrus originating in Southeast Asia and southern China that includes hundreds of named varieties ranging from tiny, seedless clementines to large, deeply flavored Ponkans. As a group, mandarins are the most cold-hardy common citrus (Satsuma types tolerating temperatures to 18–22°F when established) and one of the most adaptable to Gulf South conditions, performing well in zones 8b–11 where sweet oranges or grapefruit might struggle with cold or humidity-related issues. Key mandarin varieties for Gulf South gardens include Satsuma (most cold-hardy), Owari Satsuma, Owens Navel, Clementine, Ponkan, Murcott (Honey mandarin), and Dancy tangerine. Most mandarins ripen November through February, and the loose skin that peels easily by hand makes them the most user-friendly fresh citrus. The species is very adaptable to container culture, making it practical for zone 8 gardeners who want moveable citrus.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after all frost risk has passed; in zones 10b–11 the rainy-season break in early spring is the optimal planting window.
directions: Plant grafted trees of named cultivars (Kent, Tommy Atkins, Haden, Keitt) rather than seedlings; grafted trees fruit in 3–5 years and produce fruit true to type. Mangoes require a cool-dry period of 4–6 weeks during winter — nights below 60°F without frost — to trigger uniform flowering; excess rainfall during bloom causes anthracnose and poor fruit set. Prune after harvest each year by removing one-quarter to one-third of the outer canopy to keep the tree at a manageable height and promote fresh fruiting wood. Fruit is ripe when the shoulders near the stem fill out, color develops according to the cultivar, and the flesh yields slightly to pressure; the stem end is often the last to color.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break; in zone 9 plant February–March. Mango is a named cultivar from the USDA breeding program at Beltsville that produces distinctly mango-like fruit flavor. Requires a second pawpaw variety for cross-pollination; use another named cultivar within 50 feet. Avoid disturbing the fragile taproot at transplanting.
directions: Plant in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; Mango Pawpaw is a named USDA-selected cultivar known for producing fruits with a distinctly tropical, mango-like flavor quality that is more pronounced than in typical seedling pawpaws — a richer, more aromatic, tropical sweetness beyond the standard banana-vanilla pawpaw flavor. The medium to large fruits weigh 6–12 ounces with bright yellow flesh and a creamy, custard-like texture. Mango is considered one of the finest-flavored named pawpaw cultivars in the Corwin Davis breeding tradition and is widely used in taste trials as a benchmark for outstanding pawpaw flavor. Like all pawpaw cultivars, Mango requires cross-pollination from a different named cultivar — plant alongside Overleese, Wells, or NC-1 for reliable fruit set. Ripe fruits fall from the tree in September–October and must be refrigerated or eaten within a few days; the short shelf life is inherent to the species.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a site with reliably warm temperatures year-round; mangosteen is extremely sensitive to cold and drought stress.
directions: Mangosteen is one of the slowest-growing and most demanding tropical fruit trees, requiring deep, rich, well-drained, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5), humidity above 80%, and temperatures that never fall below 40°F or rise above 100°F. It is apomictic — seed-grown trees are genetically identical to the mother, eliminating the need for pollinators, though fruit set is parthenocarpic in cultivation. Young trees require shade for the first several years; gradually transition to full sun as the canopy develops. Harvest when the thick purple rind has deepened to a dark maroon-purple and yields slightly to thumb pressure, typically 5–6 months after fruit set.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Manila Tamarind is more cold-hardy than most tropical fruits — established trees survive light frosts to approximately 24–26°F and quickly resprout from the roots if frozen back. In zone 9 the tree is semi-deciduous in cold winters. The twisted, ornamental seed pods ripen from December through May. Trees may naturalize in zone 9 conditions and should be sited where fruit drop is not a nuisance.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-fertile soil — Manila Tamarind is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, sandy, even compacted soils where most fruit trees fail; Manila Tamarind (also known as guamúchil, Madras thorn, or camachile) is a thorny, tropical legume tree from Mexico and Central America that produces coiled, bright red-and-white seed pods containing sweet, fibrous white pulp surrounding shiny black seeds. The sweet-tart, cotton-candy-like flavor of the fresh white aril (the edible fleshy layer around the seeds) is popular in Mexican street food markets and throughout tropical Asia where the tree has naturalized. Despite the common name, Manila Tamarind is not related to true tamarind (Tamarindus indica) but belongs to the legume family with nitrogen-fixing roots. The tree is highly productive and drought-tolerant, making it valuable for edible landscape use in hot, dry zone 9 conditions. Pods are harvested when the husks split open to reveal the red-pink exterior and white interior with sweet pulp.

common_name: Manzanilla Olive (Spanish Table Olive Standard, Green Martini Olive, Seville Table Olive)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Manzanilla is self-fertile and produces well as a single tree though cross-pollination with Sevillano, Frantoio, or another olive variety increases yields; it requires approximately 300–400 chill hours, well-suited to California, the Gulf South, and similar zones 8–10 climates; Manzanilla blooms somewhat earlier than some other varieties, extending the effective pollen window.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Manzanilla is extremely drought-tolerant once established; harvest for green table olives in October when fully sized but still green; harvest for black table olives in November–December when fully ripe; home-cured Manzanilla olives require brine treatment for 6–12 months to remove bitter oleuropein before eating. Manzanilla (meaning 'little apple' in Spanish, for the round fruit shape) is the dominant commercial table olive variety in the world — the variety behind the iconic green olives stuffed with pimentos found in cocktail jars and martini glasses throughout the Western world, and a major component of Spanish, American, and Mexican table olive production. Its origin is in the Seville region of Spain (particularly the province of Huelva), where it has been the foundation of the Spanish table olive trade since the 1800s, and it was introduced to California (where it is called 'Manzanillo') in the 19th century with California's Spanish-mission heritage, becoming established in the central California olive-growing regions (Fresno, Madera counties) and eventually as the dominant commercial table olive variety in the United States. The olives are medium-sized, round to slightly oblate, with firm, meaty flesh and a relatively small pit that makes them ideal for stuffing — the characteristic American 'green olive' of commercial production is almost always a Manzanilla cured at the green stage. The trees are medium-sized (15–25 feet), productive, and adapted to a wide range of California and Gulf South conditions with adequate drainage and minimal rainfall during the ripening period.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Manzanillo is largely self-fertile though a compatible pollinizer such as Mission improves fruit set, and it grows into a larger, traditional-sized tree than compact modern cultivars like Arbequina.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Manzanillo is a classic Spanish olive cultivar and the most widely grown table olive variety in the world, valued for its large, plump, meaty fruit with a favorable flesh-to-pit ratio that makes it the standard choice for brine-cured green and black table olives found in grocery stores worldwide. The tree bears heavily and reliably, and while it can also be pressed for oil, its primary use and reputation is as a table olive. Harvest green in fall for green-cured olives, or let fruit ripen to black for black-cured olives, then cure in brine or lye solution for several weeks to months to remove natural bitterness before eating; olives are inedible straight off the tree. The tree grows to a more traditional, larger size than modern compact cultivars, so allow ample space.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Manzano is less cold-hardy than Cavendish or Orinoco types and is best suited to zone 9b–11 or container culture in cooler climates where it can be overwintered indoors.
directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Manzano banana (also called Apple Banana, Finger Banana, or 'Bocadillo' in Colombia) is a widely grown short-fruited banana popular throughout Latin America and the Caribbean, producing plump, stubby fruits (3–5 inches long, broader in proportion than Cavendish) with a distinctive, complex flavor reminiscent of strawberry and apple when fully ripe — a significantly more aromatic and interesting eating experience than a standard Cavendish. The fruits turn bright yellow and then develop black skin patches as they ripen, and the flesh remains firm even when sweet and fully ripe, giving them better shelf life than many banana types. Manzano banana plants are more compact than Cavendish (8–12 feet versus 12–20 feet) making them practical for smaller yards. Manzano is moderately susceptible to Black Sigatoka and should be grown in well-drained, well-fertilized conditions with regular irrigation; it thrives in Gulf Coast conditions (zones 9b–11) but pseudostems are killed by even brief freezes.

plant_note: Sow 3 seeds per planting spot 1/2 inch deep after frost danger passes, thin to strongest plant; or start transplants 6 weeks early and transplant after frost; 'Maradol' plants include males and females — plant 2–3 plants to ensure a bisexual or female plant is included, and remove male plants (identified by long-stalked tubular flowers) after sex is determined, keeping one male per 8–10 females if needed.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Maradol is the dominant commercial papaya of Mexico and the variety most commonly sold in American supermarkets, producing very large, oblong fruits (3–8 pounds, sometimes to 10 pounds) with distinctive salmon-red to deep orange flesh, moderate to high sweetness, and a mild, pleasant, non-musky flavor that appeals to consumers who find tropical Solo papayas too strongly flavored. The skin turns from green to yellow-orange at ripeness, with clear indicator spots appearing near the stem. 'Maradol' plants are dioecious (separate male and female plants) which means planting multiple trees is necessary to ensure fruiting; approximately one-third of seedlings are male. The tall plants (10–18 feet under optimal conditions) bear heavily from the main trunk, with fruits maturing in dense clusters below the umbrella of large leaves. Originally developed in Cuba, 'Maradol' is now the main papaya in Mexico's Veracruz and Tabasco production regions and thrives in Gulf Coast conditions — hot humid summers, mild winters, and fertile lowland soils of zone 9b–11.

plant_note: Plant seedlings or air-layered cuttings in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained tropical soil; marang requires genuine tropical conditions (zone 11-12) and high humidity; it is cultivated in southern Mindanao (Philippines), Borneo, and throughout Southeast Asia as a valued fruit tree.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, rich, consistently moist, well-drained tropical soil; marang (Artocarpus odoratissimus) is a close relative of breadfruit and jackfruit, native to Borneo and Mindanao, producing rounded, yellow-green fruits about the size of a small jackfruit with an extremely sweet, creamy white flesh surrounding large, edible seeds — many who have tasted it rank it among the finest tropical fruits, with a rich, sweet, almost vanilla-custard flavor with a fragrant aroma. The seeds are also edible when cooked (roasted, boiled, or ground) and have a pleasant chestnut-like flavor. Strictly tropical and not tolerant of any frost; best suited for south Florida and Hawaii collections and food-forest enthusiasts in zone 11+. Less well-known outside Southeast Asia but increasingly available from specialty nurseries.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in well-drained soil; Marbrite is an Italian fig variety valued for its pale green skin and sweet, amber-white flesh, offering a distinct fresh-eating alternative to the pink- and red-fleshed figs most common in Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun. Marbrite is an Italian fig cultivar bearing medium-sized figs with pale green to yellow-green skin and sweet, translucent amber to white flesh, a lighter-colored departure from the deep pink and red interiors of Gulf Coast standards like Celeste and Brown Turkey. It typically produces two crops in warm climates: a smaller breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer, followed by a larger main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Figs fruit on both second-year wood and current-season growth, so avoid heavy winter pruning, which removes the breba crop; light shaping after the main harvest is sufficient. Trees are vigorous and productive once established and rarely need fertilizer, though a layer of mulch over the root zone helps in zone 7-8 where occasional hard freezes can damage unprotected roots. Harvest when fruit softens and the neck bends over, since figs do not ripen further once picked.

common_name: Marcona Almond (Spanish Queen of Almonds, Round Blanched Premium Almond)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun in a Mediterranean or dry-summer climate; Marcona is self-incompatible and requires a companion almond variety for pollination; requires approximately 200–300 chill hours, making it suitable for warmer zones 8–10 with mild winters; it is specifically adapted to the dry, calcareous soils and Mediterranean climate of coastal Spain.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile soil (calcareous or sandy loam preferred) in full sun; Marcona requires a companion pollenizer variety; harvest in late summer when hulls begin to split; the round, flat kernels are best roasted in olive oil and sea salt in the traditional Spanish preparation — the rich, buttery texture of roasted Marcona is distinctly different from any California variety. Marcona is a Spanish almond variety traditionally grown along the eastern Mediterranean coast of Spain (the Valencian Community and Murcia region) that has become known internationally as the 'queen of almonds' for its extraordinarily rich, buttery flavor and distinctive round, flat shape that makes it immediately recognizable on a charcuterie board or tapas spread. The flavor difference between Marcona and California varieties (Nonpareil, Mission, Carmel) is significant and immediately apparent to tasters: Marcona has a much higher fat content and a softer, more buttery texture with a sweeter, more intensely almond-flavored profile — often described as having hints of marzipan and fresh sweetness that California varieties cannot replicate. The traditional preparation — blanched (skin removed), roasted in olive oil, and salted — is the standard presentation in Spanish tapas and increasingly common in American specialty food and charcuterie culture. Marcona's very low chill requirement (200–300 hours) makes it the almond most adapted to warm-winter zones 8–10 where standard California varieties may also grow, but Marcona's flavor sets it apart for culinary use. Not as productive as California commercial varieties in California growing conditions.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Marigoule bears young and reliably and benefits from a second chestnut cultivar nearby for best pollination.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. Bred in France from a cross of European and Japanese chestnut, Marigoule combines good resistance to chestnut blight and ink disease with large, easy-to-peel nuts and a precocious habit, often bearing within a few years of planting. It has become a popular choice in North American chestnut orchards specifically because its hybrid vigor and disease tolerance let it thrive where the straight American chestnut has been devastated by blight. The tree is moderately vigorous and more compact than a full-sized American chestnut, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or food forest planting.

common_name: Mars Grape (Disease-Resistant Southern Seedless Blue Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; bred at the University of Arkansas for disease resistance and good performance in warm, humid Southern climates, well adapted to zones 5-8.
directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Mars was bred at the University of Arkansas specifically for good disease resistance and reliable performance in the warm, humid Southern climates where many other seedless table grapes struggle with fungal disease pressure, combining that practical resilience with sweet, blue-black, seedless berries carrying a mild, classic grape flavor. The compact, manageable vine is well suited to home garden trellises and arbors, and its combination of hardiness and disease tolerance has made it one of the more dependable seedless grape choices for Southern home gardeners. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter to control vigor, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size.

common_name: Marsh Grapefruit (Seedless White Grapefruit, Marsh Seedless)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; grapefruit trees are large and require adequate space (20–25 feet diameter at maturity), so site carefully; Marsh is self-fruitful and productive without a pollinator.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Marsh grapefruit (introduced commercially around 1860 from a seedling found in Florida) is the foundational white grapefruit of the citrus industry — virtually all seedless white grapefruits sold commercially today are Marsh or descended from it. The large, round, pale-yellow fruits (4–5 inches diameter) are nearly or completely seedless (a major practical advantage over older seedy varieties like Duncan), with pale-cream to light-yellow flesh, balanced sweet-tart grapefruit flavor, and abundant juice. The flavor is the benchmark classic grapefruit flavor — moderately tart with characteristic bitterness from naringin — excellent eaten fresh (halved and sectioned with a serrated spoon), juiced, or used in salads and cocktails. The large tree (15–20 feet when mature, larger on vigorous rootstocks) is cold-hardier than many citrus and can tolerate brief temperatures to about 26–28°F when established. Marsh grapefruit is the parent of most modern grapefruit varieties, including Ruby Red (a bud sport of Marsh) and Thompson Pink. Ripens November through May in Florida; the fruits hold on the tree exceptionally well, improving in flavor through winter.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Maru is a pollination-variant astringent (PVA) persimmon — when unpollinated, the fruit remains astringent until fully soft; when cross-pollinated, the seeds stimulate the flesh to develop dark-colored, non-astringent regions (jelly-like, very sweet spots) even before the fruit softens. Plant with a male persimmon or another D. kaki cultivar within 50 feet for full PVA expression.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Maru is a Japanese persimmon cultivar that exemplifies the PVA (pollination-variant astringent) type — uniquely, the flavor and texture of its fruit changes dramatically based on whether the flower was pollinated. Unpollinated Maru fruits are uniformly orange-colored and astringent until fully ripe-soft; pollinated fruits develop dark brown or black spots and streaks in the flesh (called 'chocolate flesh') around the seeds, and these dark regions are sweet, jelly-like, and completely non-astringent while still firm — a prized texture and flavor combination. Fully pollinated Maru fruits may have most of the flesh dark-colored and sweet, making them among the most interesting persimmon-eating experiences available. In zone 9 Maru produces reliable crops of medium-sized, round to slightly oblate fruits ripening in October–November. The dark flesh and sweet, pudding-like texture of cross-pollinated fruits makes Maru an outstanding garden and fresh-market variety.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in late spring in full sun with very well-drained, deep soil; Marula is highly drought-tolerant once established but intolerant of waterlogged soils. Marula is dioecious — separate male and female trees are required for fruit production; purchase sexed (grafted) stock from specialty nurseries or plant 2–3 seedlings and hope for mixed sexes. Established trees in zone 9b have survived brief dips to 26–28°F. Young trees require frost protection for the first 2–3 winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil of any type — Marula is remarkably adaptable to poor, sandy, or rocky soils and intensely drought-tolerant, thriving in conditions that challenge most fruit trees. Sclerocarya birrea subsp. caffra (Marula) is a large, spreading, deciduous African fruit tree native to the woodlands and savannas from Ethiopia and Nigeria south to South Africa, famous throughout sub-Saharan Africa as one of the most important traditional food and beverage trees of the continent. The plum-sized fruits (1–1.5 inches diameter) ripen in December–March in South Africa; in zone 9 they ripen in late summer–fall. When ripe, the thin, pale yellow skin covers soft, extremely juicy, intensely aromatic flesh with a rich, complex flavor combining tropical fruit notes reminiscent of mango, pineapple, and lychee — prized fresh, fermented into a traditional beer, and distilled into the popular Amarula Cream liqueur (produced commercially in South Africa). The large, brown, extremely hard seeds inside each fruit contain edible kernels with a rich, nutty flavor and high oil content used in traditional African cosmetics. Elephants travel great distances to feed on fallen marula fruits, giving rise to the folklore that they become inebriated — a myth, though the fruits do ferment rapidly when fallen. Marula is increasingly grown as an edible landscape tree in zone 9b–11.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Marumi is among the most cold-hardy kumquats and, like other kumquats, is eaten whole, skin and all, since the sweet rind contrasts with tart flesh.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Marumi is one of the oldest kumquat cultivars grown, producing small, round fruit with thin, sweet, edible skin surrounding a tarter, seedier pulp, eaten whole rather than peeled. It is among the more cold-hardy kumquats and, being a naturally small, dense shrub, adapts well to container culture and can be moved under cover during hard freezes in the cooler parts of its range. Fruit ripens in winter and holds on the tree for weeks without dropping, giving a long, flexible harvest window; established plants are otherwise low-maintenance and require only routine citrus fertilizing.

common_name: Mary Foos Johnson Pawpaw (Historic Vigorous Named Pawpaw Selection)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Mary Foos Johnson needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Set out a grafted tree in spring in rich, well-drained soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before letting them mature into full sun. One of the earliest widely propagated named pawpaw selections, Mary Foos Johnson is valued for its vigorous, heavy-cropping habit and medium-to-large fruit with smooth, well-flavored yellow flesh. Gardeners choose it as a reliable, historically proven pollinator partner and producer alongside newer cultivars like Sunflower or Susquehanna, giving an extended pawpaw harvest window in late summer and early fall.

common_name: Matsumoto Wase Satsuma (Extra-Early Cold-Hardy Satsuma Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring after frost danger passes, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; as a bud-sport selection of Miyagawa, Matsumoto Wase ripens even earlier, letting Gulf Coast growers harvest well ahead of the first hard freeze.
directions: Site Matsumoto Wase in full sun with excellent drainage and mulch the root zone to buffer soil temperature swings through winter. This compact, precocious satsuma strain is prized for ripening its seedless, easy-peel fruit several weeks ahead of standard Owari trees, which lets home growers in marginal zone 8b-9a areas get a full crop in before the first significant cold snap. The small, glossy-leaved tree bears young and stays manageable in size, making it a popular choice for espalier or large containers as well as open-ground planting.

plant_note: Plant only where winters stay above freezing; young trees are very frost-sensitive and benefit from wind protection.
directions: Mauritius is a productive lychee bearing rough-skinned red fruit with sweet, fragrant, translucent flesh. It needs a frost-free subtropical or tropical climate with a brief cool, dry period to trigger flowering. Plant in full sun in deep, acidic, well-drained soil and protect young trees from wind and cold. Water generously during flowering and fruit development but ease off during the winter rest period. Mulch heavily to keep the shallow roots moist and feed with a balanced fertilizer through the growing season.

common_name: Maxine Pear (Starking Delicious Fire Blight-Resistant Southern Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Maxine, also sold as Starking Delicious, is a large-fruited fire blight-resistant pear developed for Southern growing conditions, similar in use and reliability to Moonglow and Orient.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Maxine cross-pollinates well with Moonglow, Orient, Kieffer, and most other fire blight-resistant Southern pear varieties. Maxine, also marketed as Starking Delicious, was developed for good disease resistance and reliable production in the humid Southeast, where fire blight quickly kills susceptible European pear varieties like Bartlett. It produces large, smooth, yellow-green fruit with sweet, juicy, only lightly gritty flesh, notably larger than many of its fire-blight-resistant peers, ripening in late summer. Like most Southern-adapted pears, it should be picked while still firm and green and ripened off the tree in a cool spot for the best texture and flavor, since fruit left to ripen on the tree tends to soften unevenly from the core outward. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the strong disease resistance means Maxine needs little to no fungicide spraying to produce a reliable crop in Gulf South conditions. Plant with another European pear variety for best cross-pollination and yield.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained, limestone-tolerant soil in full sun; Maya nut is a large canopy tree of Mesoamerican tropical forests that grows in zones 10–12 and can tolerate brief cold to about 32°F in protected zone 9b microclimates. The seeds must be planted fresh, as viability drops rapidly; sow immediately after extraction from ripe fruit.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil — including rocky, limestone-based soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; Maya nut (Brosimum alicastrum) is a towering canopy tree in the Moraceae family that the ancient Maya and other Mesoamerican peoples relied upon as a critical famine food for thousands of years, with seeds that are extraordinarily nutritious — high in protein, calcium, potassium, iron, zinc, and B vitamins — and can be boiled, roasted, dried, and ground into flour. The ripe purple-skinned fruits are also edible fresh, with a sweet, fig-like flavor, and the abundant leaves serve as high-quality livestock fodder. Trees are long-lived, moderately drought-tolerant once established, and grow naturally in limestone-rich soils where other fruit trees may struggle. Though primarily a large timber and food tree rather than an orchard crop, Maya nut is gaining recognition as an exceptionally valuable multipurpose agroforestry species, with first seed harvests typically beginning 5–10 years after planting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in late winter to early spring in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich, occasionally flooded soil in full sun to part shade; mayhaw is native to bottomlands, pond margins, and stream banks in the Gulf South and requires moist to seasonally wet acidic soils for best production.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to occasionally flooded soil in full sun; mayhaw thrives in the heavy, wet, acidic soils of the Gulf Coast plain that frustrate most fruit trees. Crataegus aestivalis (mayhaw) is the iconic native fruit tree of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, producing small (1/2-to-3/4-inch), bright-red to orange-red, apple-like fruits in April–May (hence 'may haw' — haw is an old name for hawthorn fruit) that are traditionally harvested by spreading sheets under the tree or raking from the water's surface when the tree grows over ponds and bayous. Mayhaw jelly is a Southern culinary tradition — the vivid, translucent, coral-red jelly with a unique tart-sweet, apple-berry flavor is considered a regional treasure and a gift-worthy specialty product throughout Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi. The tree is also highly ornamental — producing masses of white flowers in February–March (often among the first spring blossoms), followed by the distinctive April berry crop, then good fall foliage color. Named cultivars for improved fruit production include 'Big Red,' 'Crimson,' 'Super Berry,' and 'Texas Star.' Mayhaw grows naturally in wet bottomland forests, bayou margins, and pond edges throughout the Gulf Coastal Plain.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in late winter or spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; mayhaw is native to the river bottomlands and swampy depressions of the Gulf Coastal Plain from east Texas to the Carolinas — it thrives in seasonally wet soils and is the source of the most beloved traditional preserve of the Deep South, mayhaw jelly.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; mayhaw naturally grows in wet bottomlands and tolerates seasonal flooding. Crataegus opaca (Western mayhaw or May haw) is a native hawthorn of the Gulf Coastal Plain — a small to medium deciduous tree growing in the wet, seasonally flooded bottomlands, bayous, and boggy depressions of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia.
