plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Nova is a good pollinator for Bob Gordon and Adams cultivars — planting two or more different cultivars consistently increases fruit production.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Nova is a Canadian elderberry cultivar developed by Agriculture Canada that produces large, dense, heavy berry clusters ripening one of the earliest in the American elderberry season — typically 7–10 days earlier than Adams and other mid-season cultivars. The large, heavy clusters of very dark purple-black berries — dense and pendant when fully ripe — combine good fresh eating quality with excellent processing characteristics for elderberry syrup, juice, wine, and jelly production. Nova produces abundant flat-topped flower clusters in June–July, providing one of the most productive native pollinator resources in the early summer garden — elder flowers are visited by extraordinary numbers of native bees, small native bees, and beneficial insects that use the pollen and nectar. The compact cyme structure of Nova clusters makes harvesting somewhat easier than looser-clustered varieties. Nova's combination of early ripening, high production, and compact plant habit (slightly smaller than some other cultivars at 5–10 feet) makes it a practical choice for home gardens. As with all American elderberry, Nova spreads by root suckers to form colonies — plan for the suckering habit and remove suckers regularly to maintain the desired planting footprint.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring once the danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring once the danger of frost has passed, siting them in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and room for a moderately vigorous canopy. Provide steady irrigation through bloom and fruit set, and fertilize with a balanced citrus formula during the growing season. Nova produces deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with a rich, honeyed flavor that ripens early in the mandarin season, though a pollinator variety nearby improves fruit set and reduces seediness. It suits home orchards across Florida, the Gulf Coast, and coastal California where winters stay above the low 20s F.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall at 2–3 inch depth in moist, deep, slightly acidic, loamy bottomland soil in full sun; cold stratification of 90–120 days over winter is required before spring germination. Nutmeg Hickory develops a deep taproot early and transplants poorly once established — direct seeding or very young container stock is strongly preferred.
directions: Nutmeg Hickory is the rarest of the true hickories native to North America, found scattered in moist to wet bottomlands, alluvial flats, and river swamps of the southeastern coastal plain from South Carolina west to southeastern Texas, where it reaches its greatest abundance in Louisiana and Mississippi. The round, dark nuts — resembling nutmegs in shape and borne in thick, 4-parted husks — are smaller than those of most hickories but are relished by squirrels, white-tailed deer, and wild turkeys, and were historically gathered and eaten by Native Americans. Plant fresh nuts directly in fall in deep, moist, slightly acidic loamy soil in full sun, allowing 90–120 days of cold stratification over winter before spring germination; the deep taproot that forms in the first growing season makes older trees virtually impossible to transplant. Trees grow steadily in bottomland soils and develop spectacular golden-yellow fall color and deeply furrowed gray bark that make them outstanding additions to naturalized floodplain or riparian plantings.

common_name: O'Neal Southern Highbush Blueberry (Low-Chill Highbush Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in late winter in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; O'Neal requires only 200–400 chill hours, making it one of the best highbush blueberries for zone 9; plant with another low-chill southern highbush cultivar like Legacy or Sunshine Blue for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; O'Neal is widely considered the finest-tasting southern highbush blueberry cultivar — a North Carolina State University release with remarkably low chill requirements (200–400 hours) that makes it appropriate for zone 9 and even warmer parts of zone 8, where northern highbush cultivars receive insufficient chilling. The large, medium-blue berries have exceptionally complex, aromatic, rich blueberry flavor — consistently rated among the best-tasting of all blueberry cultivars in taste trials by the North Carolina breeding program. The flavor profile is described as rich, aromatic, and complex with a good balance of sweetness and acidity. O'Neal is an early-season cultivar, ripening in April–May in zone 9, which helps avoid peak summer heat and provides early-season fruit at a premium time. The bush grows vigorously to 5–7 feet with attractive white urn-shaped flowers in late winter and outstanding fall color (orange to red) that makes it an ornamental landscape plant as well as a fruiting shrub. Plant with at least one other southern highbush cultivar (Legacy or Sunshine Blue) for cross-pollination, which dramatically increases berry size and total yield. Maintain strict soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5 — blueberries fail in soils above pH 6.0.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings after last frost; in zone 9 plant February–April. O'Rourke is a biennial bearer, producing a Breba crop in June and a main crop in August–October. Well-suited to humid Gulf Coast conditions where many fig varieties suffer from souring (internal fermentation) caused by rainfall splitting ripe fruit — O'Rourke's closed eye greatly reduces this problem.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; O'Rourke is a fig developed by the LSU AgCenter and named for Dr. Ed O'Rourke, the Louisiana fruit breeder who led decades of fig research at LSU. Released in the late 20th century, it was bred specifically for Louisiana and Gulf Coast conditions, where the challenges of summer rain, humidity, and insect pressure at the eye (ostiole) cause fruit souring and internal pest damage in many standard varieties. O'Rourke has a distinctively tight, nearly closed eye that greatly reduces fruit souring caused by rain entering the ostiole and internal splitting — making it one of the best varieties for humid Gulf Coast gardens. Fruit is medium-sized, greenish-yellow to tan at maturity with amber-pink flesh, very sweet with complex fig flavor. The breba crop on old wood in June is modest; the main crop in August–October is abundant. Trees are vigorous and well-adapted to heavy clay soils when drainage is adequate.

common_name: OHxF 97 Pear Rootstock (Old Home x Farmingdale 97)
plant_note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired pear variety onto the young rootstock; OHxF 97 is a semi-dwarfing, fire blight-resistant understock, not grown for its own fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired pear variety onto the young rootstock; OHxF 97 is a semi-dwarfing, fire blight-resistant understock, not grown for its own fruit. Bred from a cross of the fire blight-resistant Old Home pear and Farmingdale pear at what is now Oregon State University, this rootstock in the widely used OHxF series produces a semi-dwarf to semi-standard tree around 75-85 percent the size of a standard seedling pear tree, valued above all for outstanding resistance to fire blight, one of the most destructive diseases of pear in humid growing regions. Its combination of moderate size control, strong anchorage that needs no permanent staking, and disease resistance has made the OHxF series the standard modern choice for pear rootstocks in North America, largely displacing the fire blight-susceptible quince rootstocks used in parts of Europe. Graft a desired named pear variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect a sturdy, disease-resistant, moderately sized tree well suited to humid-climate pear growing.

common_name: Oconee Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Southeastern Pecan, Type I Mid-Season Pecan)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Oconee is a Type I pollinator (sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive) — plant with Type II varieties including Stuart, Elliott, Caddo, or Wichita for reliable cross-pollination; Oconee is one of the premier recommendations from University of Georgia Extension for home and commercial pecan production in the southeastern states, specifically selected for performance under southeastern humidity and scab pressure.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained to moderately moist fertile soil; Oconee is a mid-season variety (ripening October in the Gulf South) with large nuts and good kernel fill; its scab resistance makes it particularly valuable in the humid southeastern states from Virginia through the Gulf Coast; trees are moderately vigorous and productive. Oconee pecan is a University of Georgia-developed variety (released in the 1990s) that has become one of the most highly recommended pecan cultivars for the southeastern United States, specifically bred and selected for performance under the humid conditions, disease pressure, and climate of the southeastern coastal plain and Gulf South. The breeding program at the University of Georgia's Tifton Campus has focused on developing pecan varieties with significantly improved scab resistance compared to the older standard commercial varieties (Desirable, Stuart, Schley) while maintaining nut quality comparable to those benchmarks — and Oconee represents one of the successful outcomes of this program. The nuts are large (40–48 per pound), well-filled, with good kernel percentage (58–62%), and produce a clean, sweet, buttery pecan flavor that compares favorably with the best commercial varieties. Oconee's most important attribute is its considerably better scab resistance than Desirable or Schley in the humid conditions of Georgia, Alabama, and the Gulf South — in UGA variety trials under disease pressure, Oconee consistently shows significantly lower scab infection rates on leaves and shucks, resulting in cleaner nuts and more consistent yields without the intensive fungicide programs that scab-susceptible varieties require. A premier choice for home orchard planting throughout the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Okitsu ripens earlier than standard satsuma and its seedless, easy-peel fruit develops full sweetness ahead of most other citrus in the garden.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected at Japan's Okitsu horticultural research station as an early-ripening sport of common satsuma, this cultivar produces small, flattened, deep-orange fruit that colors and sweetens several weeks before standard satsuma, often ready by October. The seedless, loose-skinned segments are tender and richly sweet with low acidity, and the compact tree bears reliably from a young age. Its early ripening window makes it especially useful in areas where an early hard freeze can threaten later-maturing citrus.

common_name: Old Home Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant European Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in fall or late winter; needs roughly 600-700 chill hours and is especially valuable where humid summers bring heavy fire blight pressure.
directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation, and prune lightly since vigorous new growth is the most blight-susceptible tissue on a pear tree. Old Home was released by USDA breeders in Oregon in the early 20th century and is famous chiefly for its outstanding resistance to fire blight, the disease that devastates most European pears in the humid Southeast, and it is widely used as a parent of blight-resistant rootstocks as well as a scion cultivar in its own right. The medium-sized, yellow-green fruit is firm and good for canning and baking, and a second pear cultivar such as Bartlett or Moonglow should be planted nearby for reliable pollination.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the last frost; in Mediterranean-climate zones fall planting is also suitable.
directions: Olives thrive in the classic Mediterranean climate — hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters — and are extremely drought-tolerant once established, but they require 200–400 chill hours to set fruit reliably. Most cultivars are self-fertile, but cross-pollination with a second variety improves yields significantly. Trees are long-lived and slow-growing; minimal pruning is needed beyond thinning for light penetration. For table olives, harvest when fruit is still green-to-straw colored; for oil, pick when about half the fruit has turned black.

plant_note: Plant after frost; grow in a container in zones colder than 8 so it can shelter indoors over winter.
directions: The olive is a slow-growing Mediterranean evergreen with silvery foliage, gnarled character, and small fruit ripening from green to black. It thrives in hot, dry conditions and needs a stretch of winter chill to set fruit well. Plant in full sun in fast-draining, even rocky soil and water deeply but infrequently once established. In zones below 8, grow it in a large pot and move it to a cool, bright indoor space during hard freezes. Prune in late winter to open the canopy and cure the fruit before eating, as fresh olives are bitter.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Olosapo (Zapotillo, Cacaito, Olosapo de Playa) is a medium-sized tropical fruit tree from the Pacific coast lowland forests of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica — bearing oval to pear-shaped, russet-brown, thin-skinned fruits with rich, creamy, yellow flesh of exceptional flavor combining avocado, sweet potato, and almond — a prized traditional food of coastal Mesoamerica.
directions: Plant Couepia polyandra in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; trees begin fruiting at 5–8 years and can produce heavy crops of excellent-quality fruit once mature. Olosapo is a member of the Chrysobalanaceae family (relatives of coco plum) native to the Pacific coastal lowlands of Mesoamerica, where it is a traditional food tree in local communities in Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Costa Rica. The russet-brown to olive-green, oval fruits (resembling a small russet potato externally) contain very rich, creamy, yellow-orange flesh surrounding a single large seed; the texture is smooth and buttery, not unlike a ripe avocado, and the flavor is sweet and complex — combining notes of sweet potato, almond, and a mild tropical richness. The fruit is eaten fresh out of hand (removing the thin skin) or processed into beverages. The tree produces attractive, large, oval, glossy leaves and clusters of small white flowers followed by the distinctive fruits. Rarely seen outside its native range but considered by those who know it to be one of the finest-flavored Pacific coast Mesoamerican fruits; deserving wider cultivation in zone 10–12 tropical gardens in Florida, Hawaii, and southern California.

common_name: Olympian Fig (Exceptionally Cold-Hardy Brown-Skinned Productive Fig)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Olympian is one of the most cold-hardy fig cultivars — suitable for zone 6-7 gardens where most other figs are marginal, and exceptionally reliable in the Gulf South where cold hardiness is rarely a limiting factor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Olympian is a fig cultivar noted for exceptional cold-hardiness and reliable productivity — it is one of the hardiest named figs commercially available, surviving temperatures well below those that damage other cultivars, making it the preferred choice for gardeners at the northern edge of fig culture (zone 6-7) and an extremely reliable fruiting tree throughout zone 8-10. The medium to large fruits have brown to brown-violet skin, amber flesh with reddish tones, and a pleasant sweetness — not as dramatically flavored as Violette de Bordeaux but consistently good and productive. Olympian typically produces a breba (early summer) crop on previous year's wood in addition to the main crop on current year's wood, extending the harvest season. The cold-hardiness advantage of Olympian is most significant in zone 9a and northward, where occasional cold snaps below 20°F would damage less-hardy cultivars; in zone 9b-10, it provides a comfortable margin of cold tolerance safety. Self-fertile, like all common figs, and a vigorous, productive tree that begins bearing in its second or third year from planting. The large, distinctive lobed leaves of all figs provide attractive tropical-looking foliage through the growing season. Figs produce two crops in warm climates: the early breba crop in June and the main crop in late summer through fall.

common_name: Onondaga Pear (Swan's Orange, New York Fall Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Onondaga, also known as Swan's Orange, is a large New York heirloom fall pear.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Also known historically as Swan's Orange, Onondaga is a New York heirloom bearing large, yellow, lightly russeted pears with juicy, sweet, aromatic flesh that ripens in fall, filling the gap between summer pears and the long-keeping winter varieties. The vigorous, productive tree was a staple of upstate New York orchards through much of the 19th century. Harvest while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Opal requires a moderate chill period, good disease resistance for a modern apple, and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Opal requires a moderate chill period, good disease resistance for a modern apple, and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. A Czech-bred cross between Golden Delicious and the scab-resistant Topaz, it produces smooth, bright golden-yellow fruit with dense, crisp, exceptionally slow-browning flesh and a sweet, mild flavor, marketed since the 2010s as a naturally non-browning apple achieved through conventional breeding rather than genetic modification. The tree carries good genetic resistance to apple scab, a significant fungal disease that plagues many apple varieties, reducing the need for fungicide spraying in a home orchard setting. Thin fruit clusters in early summer, provide a compatible pollinator variety, and harvest once fruit reaches full golden-yellow color for the best sweetness and texture.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters.
directions: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and protect young trees through their first few winters with frost cloth or temporary cover. Opal is a Mexican-race cold-hardy avocado cultivar grown by Gulf Coast and Texas dooryard orchardists as part of the small group of named selections that make in-ground avocado growing possible north of the traditional Florida and California avocado belt. Fruit is small to medium, thin-skinned, and richly flavored, with the anise-scented foliage characteristic of Mexican-race avocados, ripening through late summer and fall. Cross-pollination with a complementary Type A or Type B flowering cultivar planted nearby generally improves fruit set over a single isolated tree. Established trees tolerate brief cold snaps into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit with minimal damage, though young trees remain frost-tender and need winter protection for their first two or three years.

plant_note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Opal is self-fertile, precocious, and among the earliest dessert plums to ripen.
directions: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Opal is self-fertile, precocious, and among the earliest dessert plums to ripen. A Swedish-bred dessert plum from a Victoria and Oullins Golden Gage cross, it bears reliably heavy crops of medium, reddish-purple fruit with sweet, juicy, richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening notably early in the plum season, well ahead of Victoria, which makes it a valued choice for extending the home orchard's fresh plum harvest earlier into summer. Its good cold hardiness relative to many English and French plum varieties, combined with reliable self-fertile heavy cropping and precocious young bearing, has made it a popular choice for colder-climate home orchards across northern Europe and the northern United States. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit clusters to improve size in a heavy-cropping year.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk passes; in frost-free zones, spring or early fall planting is ideal.
directions: Sweet oranges (Citrus sinensis) are self-fertile; navel oranges and many blood oranges are seedless because they are parthenocarpic. Most oranges need warm nights to develop sweetness and cannot be grown outdoors north of zone 9; the Hamlin and Navel types are slightly more cold-tolerant. Fruit can stay on the tree for weeks to months after ripening, extending harvest, but may re-green in warm weather without losing quality. Apply a balanced citrus fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and midsummer for best production.

common_name: Orange Frost Satsuma (Cold-Hardy Changsha-Satsuma Hybrid Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, ideally against a south-facing wall for extra winter protection; Orange Frost is a Texas Superstar cold-hardy citrus selection, a Changsha tangerine x satsuma hybrid bred to extend in-ground citrus growing further into zone 8.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, ideally in a sheltered, south-facing spot near a wall or structure for extra winter warmth; Orange Frost is a Texas Superstar-designated cold-hardy mandarin, a hybrid between Changsha tangerine and satsuma bred to survive colder winters than standard satsuma varieties can tolerate, extending reliable in-ground citrus growing into zone 8 with proper siting and young-tree protection. It produces small, sweet, easy-peel orange fruit with the classic satsuma-type flavor in fall and early winter. Young trees still need frost protection — cover or use string lights on hard-freeze nights for the first several winters — but a well-established, mature tree in a good microclimate can survive cold snaps that would kill less hardy citrus outright. Water deeply and regularly during establishment and fruit development, and avoid heavy fertilizing late in the season, which can push tender new growth vulnerable to frost.

common_name: Orange Quince (Classic Round Golden American Heirloom Quince)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and begins bearing within a few years of planting, producing hard, aromatic fruit that is typically cooked rather than eaten raw.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Orange Quince is a long-established American heirloom cultivar producing large, round, golden-orange fruit with a strong, sweet fragrance, among the most widely planted quince cultivars in home orchards for its reliable production and good flavor when cooked into preserves, jelly, and paste. Like other quince it is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, blooming with attractive pale pink flowers in spring before the hard, aromatic fruit develops and ripens in fall. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and needs only routine pruning to maintain an open form that allows good air circulation, which helps reduce fire blight, the main disease concern for quince in humid regions.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors in spring in very well-drained, sandy, neutral to alkaline cactus mix; transplant into the garden when several inches tall. In zone 8-9, site in the warmest, most frost-protected microclimate available. Organ pipe cactus is slowest to mature from seed; cuttings root more readily.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil in full sun in zones 9–12; organ pipe cactus is a multi-stemmed columnar cactus native to the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, Mexico — the signature species of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. The dark green, 20+ ribbed columns eventually reach 15–20 feet in height in a candelabra form. The night-blooming, pale lavender to pink-white flowers are pollinated by long-nosed bats, which migrate northward from Mexico specifically to feed on cactus blooms. The reddish-purple, spiny fruits — the pitaya dulce (sweet pitaya) — are among the most important traditional foods of the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert, eaten fresh or dried into fruit leather. A freeze-sensitive cactus (damaged below 26°F) best suited to the warmest, driest areas of zone 9 and the true desert Southwest.

common_name: Orient Nanking Cherry (Historic Self-Fertile Large-Fruited Bush Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Orient is a 1925 University of Minnesota self-fertile Nanking cherry selection with large oval fruit, a heat-tolerant bush cherry substitute for true cherries in the Deep South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Orient, a self-fertile Nanking cherry selection released by the University of Minnesota in 1925, bears unusually large, oval, sweet-tart red fruit on a vigorous, dense, multi-stemmed shrub, offering a genuinely heat-tolerant bush-cherry alternative to true sweet and sour cherries, which generally fail in the Deep South's mild winters and humid summers. Ripening in early summer, the fruit is excellent fresh, for jam, or for wine, though birds compete heavily for the crop. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain an open, productive form, since Nanking cherry blooms and fruits on one-year-old wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees January–February in zone 9; Orient is partially self-fertile but benefits from cross-pollination with LeConte, Kieffer, or Garber. Low chill requirement (100–150 hours) makes it one of the best pears for zone 9. Ripens July–August in zone 8–9 — earlier than most European pears.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Orient is a hybrid between European and Asian pear species released by the USDA in 1945 and one of the most recommended pears for zone 7–9 because of its exceptionally low chill requirement (100–150 hours), outstanding fire blight resistance, and reliable productivity in the humid South. The large, yellow-brown, russeted fruits are sweet and juicy with a slightly gritty, Asian pear texture — firm enough to eat fresh immediately after harvest (unlike European varieties that must ripen off the tree) and excellent for canning, preserves, and cooking. Orient trees are vigorous, productive, and relatively easy to grow in zone 9. The early ripening (July–August in most of the Gulf South) makes fresh pears available in midsummer — a time when pear production from the northern states is still weeks away. Orient is considered slightly more fire blight resistant than Kieffer and a better fresh-eating pear. One of the most reliably productive pear choices for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 home orchards.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; in zone 9 plant December–February. Orient pear is partially self-fertile and will produce some fruit without a cross-pollinator, but production increases substantially when planted with Kieffer, Moonglow, or another pear variety within 50 feet. Chill hour requirement is approximately 350–450 hours below 45°F, making it one of the more widely adapted pears for zone 9 inland gardens. Fruits ripen in August–September in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil — like the Kieffer, Orient pear tolerates the heavier clay soils common in the Gulf South better than most fruit trees; Orient is a Southern-bred pear hybrid (Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia) released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1945, developed specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the American Southeast. The large, golden-yellow, round to bell-shaped fruits are among the largest of any pear variety commonly grown in the South, with smooth, butter-textured, mildly sweet flesh that ripens earlier than Kieffer (August rather than September-October). Orient's exceptional resistance to fire blight — the bacterial disease that devastates pears in humid southern climates — was the primary breeding objective that made it a success in the Southeast. The combination of large fruit size, fire blight resistance, adequate flavor, and low chill hour requirement makes Orient one of the most reliably productive pears for zone 9 conditions in the inland South.

common_name: Orinoco Banana (Very Cold-Hardy Cooking and Eating Gulf South Banana)
plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Orinoco is one of the most cold-tolerant banana cultivars — the rhizome survives temperatures into the high teens (°F) and regenerates reliably from the roots in spring in zone 8b–9.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Orinoco is among the most cold-hardy banana cultivars for Gulf South gardens — a large, vigorous variety with remarkable rhizome hardiness that allows reliable regrowth from the roots even after severe freezes that kill the pseudostem entirely. The cold hardiness is Orinoco's primary practical advantage over most other banana cultivars in zone 8b–9: while the aboveground pseudostem is typically killed in hard freezes below 25–28°F, the underground rhizome system survives temperatures into the upper teens (°F), regenerating aggressively in spring and frequently reaching full pseudostem height again within a single growing season. Orinoco produces medium-large, thick-skinned, angular-ribbed fruits that are excellent for cooking when green (plantain-like, with a slightly starchy, mild flavor that takes on seasonings well in frying, baking, and sautéing) and sweet for fresh eating when fully ripe and yellow to black. The thick skin provides good shelf life and handling resistance. The very large, bold tropical foliage (8–12 foot pseudostems with 4–6 foot leaves in Gulf South conditions) creates dramatic tropical landscape impact even in years when fruit production is not the priority. Orinoco has been grown in Gulf South gardens for generations and is particularly favored in coastal Louisiana where its heat and humidity tolerance are well-matched to the climate.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Orlando tangelo is largely self-incompatible and needs a compatible pollinizer such as a Dancy tangerine or Temple orange planted nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and site a compatible pollinizer citrus within about 50 feet since Orlando sets poorly on its own. This USDA-bred hybrid of Duncan grapefruit and Dancy tangerine, developed in Orlando, Florida, produces medium-sized, deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with juicy, mildly sweet flesh that ripens in midseason, generally ahead of its offspring cultivar Minneola. The tree is vigorous, moderately cold-hardy for a tangelo, and productive once established. It is one of the parent cultivars behind several modern tangelo hybrids but is less commonly planted itself today, making it a good candidate for home orchards seeking classic mid-century Florida citrus.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Orleans Reinette is a classic French dessert apple that stores well and develops fuller flavor after a few weeks off the tree.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Orleans Reinette is a classic French dessert apple that stores well and develops fuller flavor after a few weeks off the tree. An old French variety documented since the eighteenth century, it bears medium-to-large, golden-orange, russet-dappled apples with dense, rich, nutty-sweet flesh long considered among the finest-flavored dessert apples grown in continental Europe, comparable in reputation to Cox's Orange Pippin in Britain. Its excellent, complex flavor and good keeping qualities have kept it a favorite of European apple connoisseurs and heirloom orchardists for centuries, even as it remains less widely known in North America than its English counterparts. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for several weeks to a couple of months, during which the rich, nutty flavor continues to deepen.

scientific_name: Citrus grandis x C. paradisi 'Oro Blanco'
plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Oro Blanco is self-fruitful and sets good crops without a cross-pollinator, though bee activity always improves fruit set.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Oro Blanco ('White Gold' in Spanish) is a remarkable hybrid of pomelo (Citrus grandis) and white grapefruit (Citrus paradisi) developed by University of California breeders in the 1950s and released in 1980, producing pale greenish-yellow to yellow fruits that appear externally unripe but are actually fully ripe and extraordinarily sweet — completely lacking the bitter notes of standard grapefruit due to the absence of the flavanone naringin, the compound responsible for grapefruit's characteristic bitterness. The result is a large citrus (slightly larger than grapefruit) with thick, spongy peel, white, juicy flesh, and a flavor that is pure sweet citrus without any bitterness — outstanding for people who love grapefruit flavor but dislike the bitterness, and for those who take medications contraindicated with grapefruit. Fruits ripen October through February (one of the earliest-ripening grapefruits) and hold on the tree for months; the thick peel insulates the flesh and extends storage life. The large tree (12–18 feet) is handsome in the landscape and produces heavily. A superb and under-known citrus for Gulf South zone 9 gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Oroblanco is a grapefruit-pomelo hybrid developed by UC Riverside, released in 1981 — less cold-hardy than grapefruit or satsuma, tolerating temperatures only to about 27–28°F. In zone 9a plant in the most protected microclimate (south or west wall exposure) and protect young trees with frost cloth during the first 3–4 winters. Harvest in winter (December–February) when the thick, pale yellow-green rind begins to yellow — the fruit does not need to fully color for the flesh to develop full sweetness. The flesh is notably sweeter than standard grapefruit, with lower acidity and bitterness.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil with consistent deep watering during the growing season — Oroblanco citrus requires full sun, good drainage, and regular irrigation for fruit production; Oroblanco is a grapefruit-pomelo hybrid (Citrus x paradisi) developed at UC Riverside specifically to combine the large, sweet, low-acid flesh of pomelo with the familiar grapefruit flavor profile — producing a fruit that is distinctly sweeter and less bitter than standard white or pink grapefruit while retaining the clean, refreshing citrus character that makes grapefruit family fruits distinctive. The large, pale yellow-green to yellow fruit (5–6 inches in diameter) has a thick rind and abundant, juicy, very pale yellow-white flesh with the reduced bitterness that makes Oroblanco accessible to consumers who find standard grapefruit too bitter without sugar. Oroblanco is one of the most productive and consistent hybrid citrus varieties for zone 9 — the combination of large fruit size, high juice content, and notably superior eating quality compared to bitter grapefruit types makes it a practical and rewarding home citrus tree in the warm, protected microclimates of zone 9 where adequate winter temperatures allow year-round outdoor culture.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seeds for 30–60 days, or wash seeds from the large fruits and plant in spring; seeds germinate readily in warm soil. For hedgerow use, plant small potted plants 3–4 feet apart in a row and trim annually to form a dense, impenetrable barrier.
directions: Plant in virtually any well-drained soil in full sun — osage orange is extraordinarily tough and tolerates drought, flooding, extreme heat, alkaline soils, heavy clay, and compaction better than almost any other large deciduous tree; it was originally native to a small area of Texas and Oklahoma but was spread across much of North America in the 19th century for use as a living fence (a hedge of osage orange is literally 'horse-high, bull-strong, and hog-tight'). The dense, thorny branches form impenetrable barriers; the orange-colored heartwood is one of the most rot-resistant and hardest of any American wood, traditionally used for fence posts, bows (the tree's French name 'bois d'arc' means 'bow wood'), and railroad ties. The large, lumpy yellow-green fruits (osage oranges or hedge apples) are not edible for humans but are consumed by squirrels and, historically, by mammoths and ground sloths — the tree is a relic of the Pleistocene megafauna era.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter; Osage is part of the USDA pecan breeding program's series of cultivars named for Native American nations, alongside Kanza, Lakota, Choctaw, Sioux, and Oconee, and is grown for reliable production on a moderately vigorous tree.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and pair with a compatible pollinator of the opposite pollen type for full production, since pecans do not reliably self-pollinate. Osage belongs to the USDA pecan breeding program's family of cultivars named for Native American nations, developed to give growers better disease resistance and more consistent bearing than many older heirloom pecans, particularly in humid regions where pecan scab is a persistent problem. It produces medium-sized, good-quality nuts with a solid kernel percentage on a tree that begins bearing at a relatively young age for a pecan. As with other pecans, deep, well-drained soil and a large amount of room to grow are essential, since mature trees can eventually reach well over sixty feet with a comparably wide canopy. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, since drought stress at that stage is the most common cause of poor kernel fill.

common_name: Osborne Prolific Fig (San Francisco Bay Fig, Cool-Climate California Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring after frost danger; Osborne Prolific is particularly well-adapted to the cool maritime climates of the San Francisco Bay Area, coastal Oregon, and Washington State, where it ripens well even in cool foggy summers that prevent many other fig varieties from fully maturing — it is the most recommended fig for Pacific Coast cool-summer gardens and bears two crops: a breba crop in early summer on old wood and a main crop in late summer.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Osborne Prolific is drought-tolerant once established and requires minimal fertilization; prune in late winter to maintain desired size; fruits ripen brownish-purple to dark reddish-purple and should be harvested when completely soft and sweet — they do not store or ship well and are best eaten immediately. Osborne Prolific is an heirloom California fig variety of unknown but apparently pre-1900 California origin, named for and associated with the nursery trade of the San Francisco Bay Area region where it became the standard recommended fig for maritime and cool-summer Pacific Coast gardens. Its primary distinguishing attribute is its ability to ripen fruit adequately in the cool, foggy summers of the Pacific Coast, where the heat units accumulated from May through October are significantly lower than in the Sacramento Valley or Central Valley fig-growing regions — conditions under which varieties like Calimyrna, Kadota, and Brown Turkey may fail to fully sweeten or ripen the main crop before autumn. Osborne Prolific's adaptation to cool conditions appears to involve both earlier ripening of the main crop and a reliable breba (first) crop in early summer that provides fruit even if the main crop is delayed by a cool summer. The fruits are medium-sized, brownish-red to dark reddish-purple, with amber to strawberry-pink flesh and an excellent rich, sweet, honey-fig flavor that is considered one of the finest of any California fig variety. Very productive and reliable — living up to the 'Prolific' in its name — it is also a good choice for mild-winter coastal gardens in the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full to partial sun on well-drained soil; Oscar is self-fertile, vigorous, and benefits from annual pruning to keep it at a manageable home-orchard size.
directions: Oscar is a red-white mulberry hybrid named for naturalist Oscar Clark, prized for early-ripening fruit that can be picked at the red stage for a tart, raspberry-like flavor or left to fully darken for a rich, blackberry-like taste. It is a fast-growing, easy-care tree that responds well to pruning and training, making it practical to keep at a manageable home-orchard height despite naturally vigorous growth. Ripening runs through mid-to-late summer, and the tree tolerates cold well into USDA zone 5.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun to part shade; Otaheite gooseberry is a Southeast Asian tropical tree producing dense clusters of small, ribbed, waxy, pale-yellow fruits with intensely sour, vitamin-C-rich flesh — they grow directly on the branches and main trunk (cauliflory) and are used throughout Southeast Asia as a sour flavoring in curries, pickles, and relishes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; tolerates short dry periods once established. Phyllanthus acidus (Otaheite gooseberry or star gooseberry) is a pantropical small tree native to Madagascar and widely grown throughout Southeast Asia, India, and the Caribbean, producing dense clusters of tiny (1/2-inch), deeply ribbed, 6–8 angled, pale cream to yellow fruits that grow directly from the branches and main trunk in a striking display of cauliflory. The fruits are extremely sour and high in vitamin C — almost inedibly tart fresh — but excellent when cooked with sugar to make preserves, pickles, chutney, and a distinctive sour relish used in Filipino and Southeast Asian cooking as a souring agent (similar to tamarind) in soups, stews, and curries. In India, the fruits are pickled in salt and used in rice dishes. The tree is ornamental in its own right — the delicate, deciduous, compound-leafed branches resembling fine fern fronds contrast with the heavy clusters of waxy fruits on the bare branches. In zone 9, the tree may be damaged by hard freezes but usually recovers from the roots. A neglected tropical food tree that produces abundantly with minimal care in warm climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break; in zone 9 plant February–March. Pawpaws have a fleshy, easily-damaged taproot that makes transplanting difficult — purchase container-grown trees and disturb the root ball as little as possible at planting. A second variety is required for pollination; use hand-pollination with a small brush between different pawpaw varieties for best fruit set. Trees need 2–3 years of establishment before significant fruiting begins.
directions: Plant in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; Overleese is a named pawpaw cultivar selected by Charles Zimmerman from southern Indiana, producing very large, high-quality fruits — among the largest of any named pawpaw variety at 6–16 ounces per fruit, with a distinctive elongated shape. The creamy, custard-like yellow flesh has a rich tropical flavor combining notes of banana, vanilla, and mango with a dense, smooth texture and relatively few, large seeds. Overleese is regarded as one of the premier flavor varieties in the Corwin Davis and Neal Peterson selection programs and produces heavy crops on mature trees. Pawpaws are the largest edible fruit native to North America and require cross-pollination from a different named variety — plant two or more cultivars within 50 feet, or hand-pollinate using a brush to transfer pollen between flowers on different trees. Ripe fruits fall from the tree in September–October and must be eaten or refrigerated within a week; they do not ship well, which is why pawpaws remain a local specialty.

plant_note: One of the more cold-tolerant citrus; grown from a grafted tree.
directions: The Owari satsuma is the early bird of citrus, ripening juicy, seedless, easy-peel mandarins in early winter. It is among the most cold-tolerant citrus, making it a good choice for growers in warm-temperate regions or in containers that overwinter indoors. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply but allow the surface to dry between waterings, and give some frost protection during hard cold snaps.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–October. Owari Satsuma is the most cold-hardy mandarin and one of the most cold-hardy of all citrus — tolerating temperatures down to about 15°F for brief periods when fully dormant and acclimated, significantly hardier than navel oranges or other citrus. Trees produce their first significant harvest 3–4 years after planting and reach full production in 5–7 years. Fruit ripens October–December, earlier than most citrus, providing fresh citrus before other varieties are ready. Protect young trees with frost cloth for the first 2–3 winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, sandy loam soil — satsuma mandarins require excellent drainage and regular deep watering during the growing season; Owari Satsuma is the most widely grown mandarin in the Gulf Coast region and one of the best-adapted citrus for zones 8–9 where its exceptional cold hardiness (among the hardiest of all edible citrus) allows reliable production in climates that would damage other mandarin varieties. The medium-sized, flattened-globe fruits with loose, easily peeled orange skin and nearly seedless, exceptionally sweet, aromatic flesh begin ripening in October — well before navel oranges and most other citrus — providing fresh homegrown citrus through December from a single, low-maintenance tree. The loose peel (puffy skin that separates easily from the fruit segments) makes Satsumas the easiest-to-eat citrus variety for fresh consumption, requiring no knife and no mess — a significant practical advantage over oranges and grapefruits. Owari Satsuma's cold hardiness has made it the standard citrus for the Gulf South, where it is grown commercially in Louisiana and Texas as well as throughout zone 9 home gardens.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Own Choice macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued for its naturally compact, easy-care habit.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Own Choice macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued for its naturally compact, easy-care habit. This Australian-bred cultivar is prized for a naturally more compact, self-shaping growth habit that needs little pruning to maintain a manageable size compared to larger, more sprawling macadamia varieties, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or smaller property with limited space. It produces reliable crops of good-quality, high-oil-content nuts and, like other named macadamia cultivars, benefits from cross-pollination with a second variety planted nearby to maximize nut set. Water regularly, especially during nut development, and allow nuts to fall naturally from the tree at full maturity before collecting and drying them for storage or cracking.

common_name: Ozark Beauty Strawberry (Reliable Everbearing Strawberry for Home Garden Production)
plant_note: Plant bare-root crowns in late winter to early spring (January–February in zone 9) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; in zone 9, fall planting (October–November) is often preferred as it allows plants to establish during the cool season and produce a heavy spring crop before summer heat declines production.
directions: Plant bare-root crowns in late winter–early spring (or fall in zone 9) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Ozark Beauty is one of the most widely grown and long-proven everbearing strawberry varieties for home gardens — producing two to three crops annually (spring, summer, and fall in cooler regions; spring and fall in the Gulf South) versus the single annual spring crop of June-bearing types. The everbearing fruiting habit provides strawberries across a much longer season than June-bearers, making Ozark Beauty the preferred choice for home gardeners who want a sustained harvest rather than the concentrated single-season production of June-bearing varieties. The medium-to-large fruits are bright red, firm, and sweet — not quite the exceptional fresh flavor of the best June-bearing varieties (like Chandler) but reliably good across all crop flushes. The everbearing habit is maintained by growing the plant without harvesting runners during the first year, allowing energy to concentrate in fruit production rather than vegetative spread. In zone 9, Ozark Beauty performs best when planted in fall (October–November) to allow establishment during the cool season — spring transplants in zone 9 have limited time to establish before summer heat reduces productivity. Mulching with straw or pine straw conserves soil moisture, maintains even soil temperature, and keeps fruit clean. Remove runners from plants dedicated to fruit production to maintain fruiting energy.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall at 2 inches depth in well-drained, acidic, rocky to loamy soil; Ozark chinkapin grows in dry, rocky, ridge-top conditions and requires good drainage. Plant two trees for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; Ozark chinkapin is a native chestnut relative endemic to the Ozark Highlands of Arkansas and Missouri, historically less severely impacted by chestnut blight than the eastern American chestnut and still producing viable nuts in remnant populations. The tree occupies a niche on dry, rocky, acidic Ozark ridges where it was a valuable food resource for both wildlife and people — the sweet, thin-shelled nuts were gathered and eaten raw, roasted, and dried for winter storage. Like other American Castanea species, it is threatened by chestnut blight, though some individual trees show variable resistance. Conservation organizations actively collect seeds from resistant individuals for propagation and restoration. The nuts are smaller than Japanese chestnut but excellent in flavor, with a rich, sweet taste.

common_name: Ozark Gold Apple (Early-Season Golden Delicious-Type Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late fall or late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; Ozark Gold ripens several weeks ahead of Golden Delicious and needs a compatible early- to mid-season pollinator.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Released by the University of Missouri as an early-ripening improvement on Golden Delicious, Ozark Gold produces medium to large, smooth, yellow-gold fruit with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flesh, ready for picking in mid to late summer well ahead of its parent. Its early ripening and heat tolerance have made it a long-standing favorite for southern and midwestern home orchards where summer heat can push standard Golden Delicious to ripen unevenly. Like other Golden Delicious types, the thin skin bruises easily, so handle fruit gently at harvest, and thin clusters to one apple each in late spring to improve size and reduce biennial bearing.

common_name: Ozark Premier Plum (Large Red Japanese-Type Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Ozark Premier requires roughly 800 chill hours and, although partially self-fruitful, produces a heavier crop with a compatible Japanese plum pollinator such as Methley or Morris planted nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and thin developing fruit to about 4–6 inches apart along the branch to encourage larger size and prevent limb breakage from a heavy crop. Developed in Arkansas and long a favorite in Southern orchards, Ozark Premier is a vigorous Japanese-type plum producing very large, round, red-skinned fruit with firm, juicy, amber-yellow flesh and a rich, sweet-tart flavor that holds up well for fresh eating, canning, and preserves. It ripens in mid to late summer and is partially self-fruitful, though yields improve significantly with a second compatible plum variety nearby for cross-pollination. The tree is vigorous and productive with moderate disease resistance for the region, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South home orchards where lower-chill plum selection is important. Prune annually in late winter to maintain an open center for good light penetration and fruit quality.

common_name: PA Golden Pawpaw (Pennsylvania Selection with Rich Golden Flesh)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; PA Golden needs a second, genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; PA Golden is a Pennsylvania-origin pawpaw selection prized for its rich, deep golden-yellow flesh, smooth fiber-free texture, and intensely sweet, tropical flavor that many growers rank among the best-tasting named cultivars available. The medium-to-large fruits ripen over a relatively long window in the mid-to-late season, and the tree is a consistent, productive bearer once established. Because of its outstanding flavor and reliability, PA Golden is one of the more widely recommended cultivars for new home pawpaw plantings. Hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief flowering window to improve fruit set, and plant with a second distinct cultivar such as Sunflower, Shenandoah, or Susquehanna for cross-pollination.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Packham's Triumph is a vigorous, productive tree valued for reliable cropping.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Packham's Triumph is a vigorous, productive tree valued for reliable cropping. Bred in New South Wales, Australia in the nineteenth century from a Bartlett seedling, it has become one of the most important commercial pear varieties in the Southern Hemisphere and a significant global export pear, bearing knobbly, irregular, pale green fruit that ripens to yellow-green with sweet, juicy, Bartlett-like flavor and notably good storage and shipping qualities. Its productive, reliable bearing and adaptability to a somewhat wider climate range than more cold-demanding European pears have made it a valued choice for warmer-winter home orchards seeking a Bartlett-type dessert pear. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the best sweet, juicy dessert texture.

plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; self-unfruitful and requires a compatible pollinizer such as Nonpareil with overlapping late bloom time.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety such as Nonpareil is planted nearby with overlapping bloom time. Padre is a California almond variety notable for blooming later than most, which gives it valuable protection against the late-winter and early-spring frosts that can devastate the crop of earlier-flowering varieties, and it is widely used specifically as a pollinizer partner for Nonpareil orchards for this reason. The medium, hard-shell nut has good flavor and the tree is a consistent, productive bearer, valued in commercial orchards as much for its reliable pollination role as for its own direct nut production. Water deeply through the growing season, especially during summer kernel fill, and harvest once hulls split open in late summer to early fall.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Page is a compact hybrid mandarin that ripens in winter and performs well in containers, making it a good choice for gardeners with limited in-ground space.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Developed by USDA researchers in Orlando, Florida in 1963 from a cross of Minneola tangelo and Clementine mandarin, Page produces small, deep reddish-orange fruit with very sweet, richly flavored, easy-peeling segments. The compact, dense growth habit makes it well suited to smaller yards and large containers that can be moved to shelter during hard freezes. Fruit ripens from December into February, and the tree benefits from thinning in years of especially heavy fruit set to maintain size.

common_name: Pakistan Mulberry (Giant Mulberry, Long Mulberry, Sweet Giant Mulberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger; Pakistan Mulberry is self-fertile and produces without a pollinator; it thrives in zones 7–10 with warm summers and mild winters, performing particularly well in the Gulf South, California, and similar climates; the extraordinarily long fruit (up to 3 inches) is the defining characteristic that distinguishes Pakistan Mulberry from all other mulberry varieties — no other named mulberry produces fruit even close to this size.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pakistan Mulberry is drought-tolerant once established; trees bear in year 2–3 from transplant; fruit ripens May–June, producing very long (2–3 inch), deep red to black-purple mulberries with extraordinary sweetness — far more intensely sweet than red or white mulberry; spread a sheet under the canopy and shake branches to harvest ripe fruit. Pakistan Mulberry is a named selection of Morus macroura (the long mulberry of South Asia and Central Asia) introduced and popularized in American home orchards in the late 20th century, valued almost entirely for its exceptional fruit size — the berries of Pakistan Mulberry are dramatically longer than any other mulberry variety, with ripe fruits reaching 2–3 inches in length, nearly twice the length of the longest standard mulberries. This extreme length gives Pakistan Mulberry a visual impact unlike any other berry and a practical advantage in harvesting and fresh eating — the long, cylindrical berries are easy to pick individually and contain more juice and sweetness per fruit than shorter mulberries. The flavor of ripe Pakistan Mulberry is exceptional: intensely sweet, deeply fruity, and far richer than the wild red or white mulberry, with a complex sweetness that improves significantly on the flavor of seedling-grown mulberry trees. The trees are large and vigorous (30–40 feet on standard, smaller with pruning), adapting well to the hot summers of the Gulf South, central California, and the lower Midwest. In zone 9a, Pakistan Mulberry performs very well and has become one of the most-sought specialty fruit trees at Gulf Coast nurseries.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; pale pawpaw is a Florida/Georgia endemic of dry, sandy soils and sandhills — unlike common pawpaw (Asimina triloba), which prefers moist, rich bottomland, this species is adapted to xeric, nutrient-poor, sandy habitats in the lower South.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, slightly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; pale pawpaw is a shrubby member of the custard apple family endemic to dry sandhills, sandhill scrub, and dry oak-pine woodland of northern and central Florida and southern Georgia — a very different habitat than the moist bottomlands of common pawpaw (A. triloba). The white flowers with pale cream to white petals are produced before leaf emergence, showy against the bare stems in late winter to early spring. The small, oval fruits are edible and custard-flavored like common pawpaw but smaller. The larvae of the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Protographium marcellus) feed exclusively on Asimina species, making all pawpaws critically important for this distinctive butterfly. A rare and threatened species in its native Florida sandhill habitat, valuable for ecological restoration of dry, sandy, native ecosystems.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; palillo is a South American tropical fruit tree in the guava family producing small (1-inch), round to oval, yellow-orange fruits with creamy, sweet-aromatic flesh resembling a cross between guava and mango custard — an important native fruit tree of the Andean and Amazon foothills of Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; palillo prefers consistent moisture and excellent drainage. Campomanesia lineatifolia (palillo or yellow guabiroba) is a Colombian, Peruvian, and Ecuadoran tropical fruit tree in the myrtle family (Myrtaceae) — the same plant family as guava, feijoa, and jaboticaba — producing small, round to oval, bright-yellow-orange fruits with smooth, thin, aromatic skin and a small quantity of cream to golden, very fragrant, sweet-rich flesh surrounding a few small seeds. The flavor is described as combining guava, mango, and custard in one fruit — aromatic, sweet, with pronounced tropical fragrance. The fruit is eaten fresh or made into juice, ice cream, and preserves; it is an important traditional food of indigenous Andean communities in Colombia and Peru. The genus Campomanesia encompasses many species of native Brazilian and South American myrtle-family trees — some famous (like guabiroba, C. xanthocarpa), most virtually unknown outside their native regions. Palillo is the Colombian and Peruvian name for C. lineatifolia; the tree is an important ornamental in Bogotá urban parks. Extremely rare in cultivation outside South America.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; Palmyra palm is one of the most economically important and versatile palms in all of Asia and Africa — documented to yield more than 800 distinct products from its sap, fruit, leaves, and timber — it is the national tree of Cambodia (Kingdom of Cambodge) and the state tree of Tamil Nadu, India.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; Palmyra palm is remarkably drought-tolerant once established. Borassus flabellifer (Palmyra palm or toddy palm) is one of the oldest cultivated plants in Asia — documented in Tamil literature for over 2,000 years — and one of the most economically important multi-use palms in the tropics. The tree is the national tree of Cambodia and the state tree of Tamil Nadu (India), reflecting its profound cultural and economic significance. The sap (toddy) tapped from the immature flower stalks is an extremely important product: fresh, it is a sweet, mildly alcoholic fermented drink; boiled down, it produces palm jaggery (tan-neera sugar), one of the most traditional sweeteners of South and Southeast Asia; left to ferment fully, it produces palm wine. The young, firm, jelly-textured fruit segments inside the unripe fruit are 'ice apples' (nungu) — refreshing, mildly sweet, hydrating; eaten as a summer cooling food throughout South India. The ripe orange-yellow outer flesh is edible; seeds are cooked and eaten when young. The leaves are used for traditional palm-leaf manuscripts (the medium of Southeast Asian scripture and literature for millennia), baskets, mats, and roof thatching. A truly remarkable plant of civilization.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Palora is a self-fertile yellow dragon fruit selection from Ecuador prized for its exceptionally sweet flavor compared to red-skinned types.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Palora is a yellow-skinned dragon fruit selection originally from Ecuador, grown for fruit that is generally sweeter and more intensely flavored than red-skinned Selenicereus undatus types, with crisp white flesh and small edible black seeds. Unlike many dragon fruit cultivars, Palora is self-fertile and does not require hand pollination or a second plant to set fruit, which simplifies home cultivation, though the spiny, ridged yellow skin needs more careful handling at harvest than smooth-skinned red types. As an epiphytic cactus, give it a sturdy post or trellis to climb and cactus-like watering rather than the frequent irrigation a conventional fruit tree would need. Palora is generally slower-growing and somewhat more cold-sensitive than red dragon fruit types, so zone 9 gardeners should plan on container culture with winter shelter rather than in-ground planting except in the very warmest, most protected microclimates.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis. Pam is a female-flowered cultivar and needs a nearby self-fertile or male muscadine to pollinate it and produce a crop.
directions: Pam is a heavy-bearing bronze muscadine known for very large, loose clusters that can carry a dozen or more berries, among the biggest cluster counts of the female-flowered bronze varieties. Fruit runs sweet with notably high sugar content and pulls free with a dry stem scar, which helps individual berries keep their shape and quality for several days after harvest. Vines are vigorous, disease-tolerant, and productive once established, making Pam a good choice for a pick-your-own row or a home arbor with plenty of room to spread. Because it bears only female flowers, plant it near a self-fertile variety such as Carlos or Nesbitt to ensure reliable pollination and fruit set.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Panache needs long, hot summers to ripen its main crop fully and is best sited against a warm, sheltered wall in marginal areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally sheltered from strong wind; Panache, also sold as Tiger Fig for its striking green-and-yellow striped skin, is a French heirloom fig grown as much for its ornamental fruit as for eating, with each ripe fig displaying bold longitudinal stripes over deep red, strawberry-jam-colored flesh. The breba (first) crop on old wood tends to be the more strongly striped and ornamental of the two annual crops, while the main crop on new wood ripens later in the season with slightly less pronounced striping. Fruit is sweet but not among the richest-flavored figs, so it is often grown as a conversation piece and fresh-eating novelty alongside more productive workhorse varieties like Celeste or Brown Turkey. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and control size, and protect young plants from hard freezes their first few winters, since Panache is somewhat less cold-hardy than common Gulf South fig standards.

common_name: Panache Tiger Fig (Ornamental Yellow-Green Striped Fig with Strawberry-Like Flavor)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Panache requires maximum sun to develop the best striped skin coloring and fruit sweetness — shaded fruits tend to be less sweet and less distinctively striped.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Panache (Tiger Fig, Strawberry Fig) is one of the most visually distinctive and ornamentally beautiful fig cultivars — producing medium-sized fruits with unmistakable yellow-to-green and darker-green vertical striping on the skin that resembles the pattern of a tiger or the appearance of a watermelon rind, creating an arresting visual display unlike any other commonly grown fig. The striped skin pattern is formed by differential ripening of the fruit skin, with the yellow portions ripening ahead of the green stripes and both shifting gradually toward gold-and-green as the fruit matures. The interior flesh is light strawberry-red to pale rose — the flesh color and an unusually sweet, almost strawberry-like flavor that gives 'Strawberry Fig' its other common name. The ornamental quality of Panache at all stages of fruit development makes it an outstanding specimen tree for edible landscape use — the striped fruits hanging in clusters from late summer through fall are genuinely decorative. Production is somewhat lower than some other cultivars — Panache prioritizes flavor quality over quantity. In zone 9, Panache is grown successfully as a standard landscape fig tree; it is somewhat less cold-hardy than varieties like Celeste and may need frost protection below 20°F.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in full sun well after the soil has warmed past last frost; in zone 9a treat as a large container specimen that can be moved under cover, since mature wood is damaged by hard freezes.
directions: This extremely fast-growing pioneer tree bears small, soft, cotton-candy-sweet red berries almost continuously in warm weather, often fruiting within its first year or two from seed. It tolerates poor soil and drought once established but is reliably hardy only in zone 10-11, so Gulf Coast growers farther north typically grow it in a large pot that can be sheltered indoors during freeze events. Fruit is eaten fresh, dropping by the handful onto the ground when ripe, and it draws strong bird and wildlife interest, making it a useful fast-establishing pollinator and wildlife planting in warm-climate food forests.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Panama Red is a large-fruited purple-red passionfruit selection popular for fresh eating and juice.
directions: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Panama Red is a purple-red-skinned passionfruit selection valued for producing larger fruit than many standard purple passionfruit types, with rich, aromatic, tart-sweet pulp well suited to both fresh eating and juicing. The vigorous vine climbs quickly and begins bearing within its first year from a rooted cutting, dropping ripe fruit naturally from the vine when ready to harvest. Provide sturdy support and pinch new growth periodically to keep the vine directing energy into fruiting wood rather than unchecked vegetative sprawl. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily each winter, since this cultivar shares the cold sensitivity typical of purple passionfruit and can be damaged or killed by a hard freeze.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Panamint has a low chill requirement well suited to zone 8-9 and produces reliably where standard nectarines struggle to break dormancy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Panamint is a low-chill freestone nectarine developed for mild-winter growing regions, producing medium-to-large, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit with a sweet-tart balance typical of good dessert nectarines. Its comparatively low chilling requirement lets it flower and fruit reliably in areas like the Gulf South and lower South where standard high-chill nectarines fail to leaf out and bloom evenly. The tree is self-fruitful and ripens in early-to-mid summer; thin fruit to four to six inches apart along the branch in years of heavy set to improve size and reduce limb strain.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and provide young trees with cold protection for their first few winters.
directions: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and well-drained soil, and shield young trees through their first few winters with frost cloth or a temporary structure. Pancho is a Mexican-race avocado bred for cold hardiness, part of the small group of dooryard cultivars (alongside Joey, Lila, and Fantastic) that Gulf Coast and Texas growers rely on for in-ground avocado production outside the traditional Florida and California growing regions. Fruit is small to medium, thin-skinned, and rich in flavor with the anise-scented foliage typical of the Mexican race. Because avocados bear more reliably with cross-pollination between a Type A and Type B flowering cultivar, plant Pancho alongside a complementary flowering-type variety where space allows. Established trees tolerate brief dips into the low 20s Fahrenheit with only minor damage, though young trees need protection their first two or three winters before developing full cold tolerance.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted tree; more frost-tolerant than most avocados.
directions: Pancho is a cold-hardy Mexican-type avocado that shrugs off chills that would damage tender varieties, extending avocado growing into cooler regions. It is low-maintenance and rewards patient growers with creamy, homegrown fruit. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with deep, fast-draining soil, since avocados are extremely sensitive to soggy roots and root rot. Water regularly but never let the tree stand in water, mulch well, and protect young trees during their first few winters.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 10 plant March–June. Mamey sapote is a true tropical suited to zones 10–11 and is not reliable in zone 9; young trees are damaged by any frost and mature trees are injured below about 29°F. Give it the warmest, most wind-sheltered spot available in coastal South Florida or South Texas plantings. Pantin fruits mainly in summer, with fruit taking well over a year to mature from flower to harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil with room for a large canopy; Pantin is one of the oldest and most widely planted named mamey sapote cultivars in South Florida, tracing to early Cuban plantings in Miami-Dade County, and remains a benchmark for commercial-quality fruit. The large, football-shaped fruit has rough, russet-brown skin and dense, salmon-pink to brick-red flesh with a rich, sweet flavor often described as a cross between pumpkin, sweet potato, and almond. Trees are vigorous, long-lived, and eventually very large, so site them well away from structures and power lines. Harvest by scratching the skin lightly — ready fruit shows green beneath the russet surface — then ripen at room temperature for several days to a week until it yields to gentle pressure.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all cold risk has passed; even a light frost kills papaya plants.
directions: Papaya is one of the fastest-bearing fruit plants — grafted or transplanted seedlings can fruit within 6–12 months of planting. It is highly sensitive to frost, waterlogged soil, and root disturbance; plant in well-raised, excellently drained beds and never let roots sit in water even briefly. Most commercial papaya is hermaphroditic (self-fertile), allowing a single tree to produce fruit; dioecious types require a male plant within 20 feet. Cut the growing tip back at 3–4 ft to encourage a compact, easily harvested form. Harvest when at least one-quarter of the skin has turned yellow; ripen fully at room temperature and refrigerate only after fully ripe.

common_name: Paradise Nut (Zabucajo, Monkey Pot, Sapucaia Nut)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in partial shade to full sun with consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Lecythis zabucajo is frost-sensitive and suitable only for zone 10-11 outdoor planting. The tree is related to the Brazil Nut (Bertholletia excelsa) and requires similar conditions — warm, humid, and fertile. The famous 'monkey pot' fruits open with a lid (operculum) to release the seeds — the narrow pot opening allows monkeys to reach in for the nuts but traps their closed fist. The seeds (Paradise Nuts) are considered superior in flavor to Brazil Nuts.
