directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Pinotage was created in South Africa in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsaut (then locally known as Hermitage), combining the two into a distinctive grape now considered South Africa's signature red wine variety, producing deeply colored wines with bold red and dark fruit character often accompanied by a distinctive smoky, earthy, sometimes rubbery note that divides wine drinkers but has become part of the grape's identity. The vine is considerably more vigorous and heat-tolerant than pure Pinot Noir, adapting well to warmer growing regions where its more finicky parent would struggle, and it produces reliably heavy crops if not deliberately restricted. Train to a permanent trellis, thin crop for concentrated flavor if quality wine is the goal, and manage canopy carefully, since overcropped Pinotage can accentuate unwanted rubbery, volatile aromas.

common_name: Pinova Apple (Crisp Sweet-Tart German Modern Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Pinova was bred in Germany in the 1980s from crosses tracing back to Golden Delicious and Clivia, released for its crisp, dense, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh and attractive red-striped skin over a yellow background, quickly gaining popularity across Europe as a quality dessert apple with genuinely good storage life. The vigorous, productive tree bears reliably, and fruit holds its crisp texture and flavor well in cold storage for months, making it a satisfying choice for home orchardists wanting fresh apples well past the immediate harvest season. Harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for the longest keeping quality.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; pinyon pine is highly drought tolerant once established — an essential xeriscape tree for the Southwest. Does not tolerate waterlogging, heavy clay, or excessive fertilization.
directions: Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; pinyon pine is the most ecologically and culturally important small tree of the American Southwest — the source of the highly prized and commercially valuable piñon nuts (pine nuts) that are a cornerstone of both Native American foodways and southwestern cuisine. A two-needle pine (two needles per bundle) forming dense, round-crowned, picturesque small trees in the classic piñon-juniper woodland that dominates millions of acres of the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin at 4,500–8,000 feet elevation. Pinyon nut harvests are a major economic and cultural event across the Southwest — harvested by Native peoples and marketed commercially for centuries. The large, wingless nuts are rich in protein, fat, and calories. Drought tolerant to an extraordinary degree — essentially requiring no supplemental irrigation once established in appropriate Southwest climates. Trees live 200–1,000 years. Pinyon jays are entirely dependent on pinyon nuts as their primary food source. An excellent, slow-growing, low-water landscape tree for hot, dry, rocky gardens in zone 4–8.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root grafted trees in early spring while dormant; Pioneer was selected for larger, sweeter fruit than the wild species and benefits from a second cornelian cherry cultivar nearby for heavier fruit set, though it will set some fruit alone.
directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; Pioneer is a fruit-selected cultivar of Cornus mas, a small multi-stemmed tree that opens clusters of tiny yellow flowers on bare branches in very early spring, weeks before forsythia. Its oblong, cherry-red fruits ripen in midsummer and drop as they soften, so most growers harvest by shaking the tree onto a tarp or gathering fallen fruit daily; the tart, plum-like flesh is used for syrup, jam, liqueur, and traditional Eastern European preserves. The tree is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerates urban conditions and a range of soils, and is largely untroubled by pests or diseases that plague other stone fruit. Pioneer bears earlier and more heavily than unselected seedlings, typically fruiting within three to four years of planting.

common_name: Pisang Raja Banana (Southeast Asian Dessert Banana)
plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pisang Raja is a true tropical banana with little cold tolerance, so in zone 9 grow it in the warmest, most protected microclimate available and expect it to freeze back most winters.
directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, feeding heavily through the growing season since bananas are gross feeders. Pisang Raja, meaning 'king banana' in Malay and Indonesian, is one of the most widely grown and highly regarded dessert bananas in Southeast Asia, prized for its dense, creamy, richly aromatic flesh with a distinctive honeyed flavor that many consider superior to Cavendish-type bananas for fresh eating. The moderately sized fruits have thick yellow skin with characteristic black spotting when fully ripe. In zone 9a, where winter freezes routinely kill the pseudostem to the ground, treat it as a root-hardy perennial: mulch heavily over winter and expect regrowth from the rhizome in spring, though a freeze-free run of 12-15 months is typically needed to reach fruiting size, so a large container that can be moved to shelter improves the odds of a crop.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost; pistachios need hot, dry summers and cold winters — a very specific climate.
directions: Pistachio is dioecious — you must plant at least one male tree (typically Peters variety) for every 8–10 female trees; pollen is wind-carried. The tree requires 700–1000 chill hours in winter and blisteringly hot, dry summers (100°F+ is ideal) to ripen nuts properly, making it poorly suited to humid or mild-summer climates. Trees are extremely drought-tolerant and actually prefer alkaline, well-drained soils. Nuts are ready when hulls turn from green to red-pink and slip off easily; harvest by shaking limbs and collect nuts off tarps laid below.

common_name: Pitmaston Pineapple Apple (Small Pineapple-Flavored English Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Pitmaston Pineapple is an English heirloom dating to 1785, named for a genuinely distinctive tropical, pineapple-like flavor and aroma that sets it apart from every other common apple variety, a quality that has kept it a beloved curiosity among heirloom apple collectors for well over two centuries. The small, golden-yellow, lightly russeted fruit is far smaller than a typical dessert apple, more the size of a large crabapple, but the intensity of its unusual flavor more than compensates for its modest size, making it a favorite for fresh eating in small quantities and an interesting addition to hard cider blends. The compact tree bears reliably; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and expect a short storage life typical of many aromatic heirloom dessert apples.

plant_note: Plant in frost-free, humid tropical conditions; pitomba is slow-growing but long-lived — choose a permanent position with well-drained but consistently moist soil.
directions: Plant in full sun in rich, moist but well-drained, slightly acidic soil in frost-free conditions; pitomba is a small to medium Brazilian Eugenia producing clusters of golden-orange round to ovoid fruits about cherry-sized with smooth thin skin and juicy sweet-acidic orange flesh surrounding a single large seed — the flavor blends apricot, mango, and peach with a pleasant tartness. Trees are slow to mature but once established bear heavy crops excellent eaten fresh, juiced, or preserved as jams. Slightly more cold-tolerant than many tropical Eugenias, tolerating brief dips near 30°F on established trees. A rewarding and unusual addition to the zone 10–12 food garden.

common_name: Pix-Zee Genetic Dwarf Peach (True Dwarf Container Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees any time in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Pix-Zee is a genetic dwarf — its compact size comes from the tree's own genetics rather than a dwarfing rootstock — and is self-fertile, so a single tree fruits without a pollinator.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container; Pix-Zee is a true genetic dwarf peach, meaning its compact 5–8 foot mature size is controlled by the tree's own genes rather than achieved through a dwarfing rootstock or heavy pruning — a genuinely different growth mechanism from popular container peaches like Bonanza or Bonfire that are simply naturally shorter standard-type trees. This makes Pix-Zee well suited to a large patio pot, small urban yard, or anywhere a full-sized peach tree would be impractical, while still producing normal, full-sized, freestone yellow-fleshed fruit with good sweet peach flavor. It is self-fertile, so a single tree sets fruit without a second pollinator variety nearby. Thin fruit to about 4–6 inches apart once set to improve size and prevent limb breakage, since the compact branches can be overwhelmed by a heavy crop. Provide full sun and consistent moisture, especially for container-grown trees, which dry out faster than trees planted in the ground.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Pixie Crunch is from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program and has a naturally more compact tree habit than most of its scab-resistant stablemates, making it easier to fit into a smaller home orchard.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Pixie Crunch, also released as Co-op 33 from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program, combines genetic immunity to apple scab with a naturally denser, more compact growth habit than most other apple varieties, making it a good fit for smaller home orchards or higher-density plantings where a full-size tree would be too much. The fruit is medium-size, crisp, and juicy with a lively sweet-tart flavor and good storage quality, ripening in the fall alongside other mid-season scab-resistant varieties. Because the tree naturally stays more compact, it requires somewhat less aggressive pruning to control size than typical apple varieties, though annual pruning to maintain an open canopy and good light penetration is still recommended for fruit quality and disease control in humid climates.

common_name: Pixie Mandarin (California Heirloom Seedless Late-Season Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Pixie is a California heirloom mandarin prized for staying seedless and ripening notably late, into spring and early summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Pixie is a longstanding California heirloom mandarin valued for small, easy-peel, essentially seedless fruit with rich, sweet flavor, and for an unusually late ripening window that stretches into spring and even early summer, well past when most other mandarins have finished, giving a long tail to the citrus season. The tree tends to be moderately vigorous with a somewhat spreading habit. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality.

plant_note: Plant corm divisions (pups/suckers) in spring after last frost in full sun in rich, deeply cultivated, well-drained, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil; in zone 9, plantains fruit reliably as perennials and should be mulched heavily in winter to protect corms from the occasional hard freeze.
directions: Plant suckers in deeply cultivated, rich, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; keep consistently moist, feed heavily with high-potassium fertilizer, and mulch the root zone heavily in winter in zones 8–9. Musa paradisiaca (plantain banana) is the starchy, cooking banana — botanically a giant herbaceous perennial growing from a massive underground corm, producing a 10–20 foot pseudostem (not a true trunk, but a compressed stem made of overlapping leaf sheaths) topped with enormous, paddle-shaped leaves up to 9 feet long; fruiting occurs 10–18 months after planting when the plant produces a pendant inflorescence that develops into a bunch containing 5–12 hands of 10–20 plantain fruits each. Unlike dessert bananas, plantains are harvested and consumed at all ripeness stages: green plantains are starchy and firm, used for tostones, chips, and savory dishes; yellow plantains are semi-sweet; and fully ripe, black-skinned plantains are sweet enough for desserts. In zone 9, established corms reliably resprout each spring after winter dieback and fruit every 12–18 months from established stools. Plantains are a dietary staple across the Caribbean, West Africa, and Latin America.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring; fall planting suits zones 7 and warmer.
directions: European plums (Prunus domestica) are often self-fertile, but Japanese plums (P. salicina) generally need a compatible pollinator planted nearby within 50 feet. Prune European types to a central leader and Japanese types to an open center; remove crossing branches each dormant season. Thin fruit clusters to 3–4 inches apart after natural fruit drop to encourage larger size. Pick when fruit achieves full color and yields gently to pressure — overripe plums are soft and ferment quickly.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–11; Plum Pine (Illawarra Plum, Brown Pine) is a large, handsome Australian rainforest tree — endemic to the rainforests of coastal New South Wales — prized for its small, dark purple to black, edible receptacles (the swollen fruit stalk that surrounds the actual seed) with a rich, complex, slightly piney, sweet-tart flavor increasingly popular in Australian native food cuisine and with commercial potential as a specialty fruit crop.
directions: Plant Podocarpus elatus in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; mature trees are fairly drought-tolerant; female plants bear the edible receptacles only when a male tree is planted nearby for pollination. Plum Pine is one of the most ecologically and gastronomically interesting of all Australian rainforest trees — a conifer (in the Podocarpaceae family, relatives of pines) whose 'fruit' is technically the swollen, fleshy, purple-black stem (receptacle) that develops beneath the actual seed. The edible receptacles are about 1–2 cm across with dark purple-black skin and rich, soft, slightly jammy flesh with a distinctive, complex flavor that combines sweetness, tartness, and a subtle piney, resinous note unlike any other fruit. Aboriginal Australians used the receptacles as a food source; today Plum Pine is a celebrated ingredient in Australian native food (bush tucker) cuisine — used in jams, sauces, cocktails, and gourmet desserts. Commercial cultivation is expanding in subtropical Australia. In the garden, it is a handsome, slow-growing evergreen tree with dense, narrow, yew-like foliage; it tolerates urban conditions well and makes an excellent shade tree or screen. Dioecious — both male and female trees needed for fruit production.

plant_note: Plant bare-root in early spring while dormant.
directions: The pluot is a complex plum-apricot hybrid skewed toward plum, prized for intensely sweet, richly flavored fruit. Plant in full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and provide a suitable Japanese plum or another pluot for cross-pollination. Train to an open vase form and thin fruit to 4-6 inches apart to prevent overbearing. In cold regions protect the early blooms from frost, as flowering can precede that of many plums.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the last frost; in zones 9–11 fall planting is also suitable.
directions: Pomegranates are self-fertile and thrive in hot, dry conditions with well-drained soil; they tolerate drought but produce sweeter, larger fruit with regular deep watering from bloom through harvest. In zone 7, mulch the root zone heavily and site against a south-facing wall to protect against winter kill. Allow plants to develop as a multi-stemmed shrub or train to a single trunk by removing suckers. Fruit is ready in fall when it turns deep red, sounds hollow when tapped, and the crown (calyx) is prominent.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed; pomelo requires a long, hot growing season and performs best in zones 9b–11.
directions: Pomelo is the largest citrus fruit — often the size of a large cantaloupe — and the ancestor of the grapefruit. It is less bitter than grapefruit, with a sweeter, milder flavor, and a very thick pith that insulates the segments. Trees are self-fertile but cross-pollination with another variety increases fruit set. Pomelos require heat to develop sweetness and need a longer season than most citrus — fruit set in spring is ready from October through February of the following year. Apply citrus fertilizer three times annually and maintain consistent moisture during fruit development; drought stress during sizing causes dry, pithy fruit.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost risk; Poncho is a cold-hardy Texas-selected Mexican-race avocado cultivar.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; root rot in heavy, wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable once established. Poncho is one of several Texas-selected Mexican-race avocado cultivars bred and trialed for cold hardiness at the northern limit of where avocados can survive outdoors, bearing medium fruit with rich, high-oil flesh and the anise-tinged flavor typical of Mexican-race types. Its selection reflects decades of Texas home-gardener efforts to identify avocado seedlings that survive occasional hard freezes with only minor damage. Harvest based on typical days from flowering for the cultivar rather than skin color alone, and ripen indoors at room temperature after picking.

plant_note: Plant in spring in moist to wet, fertile, acidic soil in full sun; pond apple is a native Florida Annona uniquely adapted to flooded, swampy, and low-lying soils where most other fruit trees would fail. It is suited to zones 10–12 and grows naturally in freshwater marshes, pond edges, and Everglades hammock margins; it tolerates seasonal flooding and salt-tolerant enough for brackish conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 10–12; pond apple (Annona glabra) is a native Florida Annona that holds the distinction of being the only member of its genus adapted to flooded, swampy, and periodically inundated soils — growing naturally along the edges of ponds, marshes, and Everglades sloughs where it often forms dense thickets. The round to oval, apple-sized fruits are bland compared to other Annonaceae relatives, with a pale yellow to cream custard-like flesh that is edible but not widely prized for fresh eating; they are consumed by wildlife and occasionally used in preserves or as rootstock for grafting more flavorful Annona species such as cherimoya and soursop. Trees reach 20–40 feet at maturity and produce dense, evergreen canopies well suited to wildlife habitat, riparian buffers, and edible landscape plantings in consistently wet, low-lying sites. Pond apple requires no irrigation once established in suitable wet conditions and is tolerant of brackish water and poor, waterlogged soils.

plant_note: Plant after frost; ideal as a container tree that overwinters indoors in cold climates.
directions: Ponderosa is a lemon-citron hybrid famous for enormous, grapefruit-sized, thick-skinned fruit with tart, seedy flesh. It is compact and free-fruiting, making it a rewarding container tree for patios and sunrooms. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and keep the graft union above the soil surface. Water deeply, letting the surface dry between waterings, and feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In zones colder than 9, bring the pot indoors to a bright spot before frost arrives.

common_name: Ponkan Mandarin (Chinese Honey Orange, Taiwanese Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Ponkan is self-fruitful and typically produces good crops without a pollinator, though it is alternate-bearing (heavy crop one year, lighter the next) and benefits from fruit thinning in heavy crop years to prevent limb breakage and encourage more even annual bearing.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ponkan (also called 'Chinese Honey Orange', 'Warnurco', or 'Batangas' in the Philippines) is one of the most widely grown mandarin varieties in the world, dominant in China, Taiwan, Brazil, Japan, and throughout Southeast Asia — though less well known in North America than Satsuma or Clementine types. It produces large (3–4 inch diameter), round to slightly flattened, loose-skinned fruits (the skin slips off in large intact pieces much more easily than tighter-skinned mandarins) with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid juice and deeply orange, highly fragrant flesh divided into 10–13 segments with typically few seeds. The flavor profile emphasizes sweetness and intense mandarin aroma more than tartness, making Ponkan distinctively different from the more acid Clementine and Satsuma — excellent for people who prefer very sweet citrus. Ripens November through January in subtropical climates. The tree is medium-large and productive under good subtropical conditions in zone 9–11; it is moderately cold-hardy (tolerates brief temperatures to 26–28°F when established). An outstanding landscape and edible tree for Gulf South gardens.

common_name: Portugal Quince (Large Highly Aromatic Heirloom Quince)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, though Portugal is a shier bearer than some other quince cultivars and benefits from a warm, sheltered site.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ideally in a warm, sheltered spot; Portugal is an old European heirloom quince long grown in American heritage orchards, prized above most other quince cultivars for its very large, intensely aromatic fruit and, uniquely among quinces, flesh that cooks down to a rosy-red color with a smoother, less gritty texture than most quince varieties — traditionally considered the finest quince for jelly and paste making. It is a somewhat shier, slower bearer than heavier-cropping cultivars like Meech's Prolific or Orange, and performs best with a warm site and attentive care in its early years, but the exceptional fruit quality has kept it in cultivation for centuries despite more productive alternatives. As with all quince, fruit is hard and astringent raw and must be cooked to develop its rich, honeyed, floral flavor. Prune to an open form for good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk, and harvest in fall once fruit turns golden-yellow and is strongly fragrant.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost.
directions: Train this vigorous, purple-fruited passion vine onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, watering deeply during dry spells to keep production steady. It is grown for its noticeably better cold tolerance than typical yellow passion fruit selections, often resprouting from the root crown after the top growth is cut back by a freeze. On the Gulf Coast growers mulch the root zone heavily going into winter and treat the vine as a root-hardy perennial that regrows each spring even where hard freezes are common. Ripe fruit, which drops naturally from the vine, has an intensely aromatic, tart-sweet pulp used fresh or for juice.

plant_note: Plant two or more different selections together for better berry production through cross-pollination. Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; excellent for wet areas and rain gardens.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; possumhaw viburnum (also called smooth witherod) is a native shrub of swamp margins, streambanks, and wet coastal plain forests that provides one of the most remarkable fall berry displays of any native shrub. The berry clusters ripen in stages through August–November, with individual berries changing from apple-green to blush-pink to rose to blue-black on the same cluster simultaneously — creating a stunning multi-colored mosaic of color that extends for weeks. The berries provide essential fall nutrition for migrating and resident birds. The glossy, deep green leaves turn burgundy-red in fall. The cultivar 'Winterthur' is particularly floriferous and berry-laden. Plant in rain gardens, bog borders, or any consistently moist location.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Potomac is a named Peterson Pawpaw cultivar valued for consistent productivity and sets its best crops when planted with Susquehanna, Shenandoah, or another genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun at fruiting age; Potomac is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars, selected by breeder Neal Peterson for dependable, heavy production alongside good flavor and size — a combination that has made it a popular choice for growers who prioritize consistent yield in a home or small-orchard planting. The rich, custardy flesh has the classic pawpaw flavor profile reminiscent of banana, mango, and vanilla custard, best eaten fresh once the fruit yields to gentle thumb pressure and has developed full aroma. As with all pawpaws, Potomac is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and full fruit set. Pawpaws thrive as an understory tree when young, so give newly planted trees light shade for the first year or two before they adjust to more direct sun, and provide steady moisture through establishment.

common_name: Pound Sweet Apple (Pumpkin Sweet, Giant New England Baking Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; very cold-hardy and best adapted to zones 3-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Pound Sweet, also called Pumpkin Sweet for its large, rounded, greenish-yellow fruit, is an old New England heirloom grown for exceptionally large, mild, sweet apples with dense, coarse flesh that holds its shape and flavor beautifully when baked whole, a traditional preparation that takes full advantage of both the apple's size and its low acidity. Unlike sharper cooking apples that need added sugar, Pound Sweet's natural sweetness makes it a classic choice for simple baked apple desserts and old-fashioned New England apple dishes calling for a mild, sugary apple rather than a tart one. The tree is notably cold-hardy, reflecting its New England origins, and reliably productive; harvest in fall once fruit reaches full size and color.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root plants in late fall to spring in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Powderblue rabbit-eye blueberries require cross-pollination from another rabbit-eye variety (Brightwell, Tifblue, Climax) for adequate fruit set — plant at least two different rabbit-eye varieties within 50 feet.
directions: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Powderblue is one of the most widely planted and highly regarded rabbit-eye blueberry varieties — producing large, light-blue to sky-blue, firm berries with excellent flavor and good fresh-eating and processing quality on a vigorously productive, heat-adapted bush that is among the most reliable blueberry types for zone 9 conditions. Rabbit-eye blueberries (Vaccinium virgatum, also classified as V. ashei) are the blueberry type most naturally adapted to the Gulf South — native to the coastal plain and Piedmont of the southeastern US, rabbit-eye varieties tolerate heat, drought, clay soils, and the region's soil conditions better than northern highbush types and are generally more productive and longer-lived in zone 9 landscapes. Powderblue is mid-season to mid-late season (June in zone 9), ripening after the early southern highbush varieties (Emerald, Jewel) and extending the blueberry harvest season. The vigorous, upright to spreading bushes reach 6–10 feet at maturity — larger than southern highbush varieties but very productive and long-lived, with established Powderblue bushes commonly producing for 30–50+ years. As with all blueberries, very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) is essential — rabbit-eye varieties may tolerate slightly higher pH than southern highbush but still require highly acidic conditions for nutrient availability and healthy growth.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Prague tolerates colder winters than standard mandarins thanks to its trifoliate orange parentage.
directions: Prague is one of a small group of citrandarins USDA breeders produced by crossing cold-hardy trifoliate orange with mandarin to push edible citrus further north than pure mandarins can survive. The small, tart, seedy fruit is more useful for juice, ade, or marmalade than fresh peeling, and the tree carries the trifoliate parent's semi-deciduous habit and light thorns. Grow it as a curiosity for pushing the cold edge of dooryard citrus in the Gulf South, siting it in a warm microclimate and protecting young trees for their first few winters. Established trees tolerate hard freezes that would kill a standard orange or mandarin outright.

plant_note: Plant the dormant or potted tree in spring; grown from a grafted tree.
directions: Prairie Fire is an ornamental crabapple that puts on a spectacular show of magenta spring blossoms followed by fiery fall foliage and small persistent fruit that feeds birds. Disease-resistant and adaptable, it makes a durable landscape tree for cold and temperate gardens. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches, and enjoy the tiny fruit as wildlife forage or for jelly.

common_name: Prairie Flameleaf Sumac (Texas Sumac, Limestone Sumac)
plant_note: Plant in spring in alkaline, rocky, well-drained soil; prairie flameleaf sumac is native to Texas Hill Country limestone soils and thrives in the alkaline conditions of the Edwards Plateau and Gulf Coast — one of the best native fruiting shrubs for Texas and the Gulf Coast region.
directions: Plant in full sun in alkaline, rocky, well-drained limestone or caliche soil; prairie flameleaf sumac (Rhus lanceolata) is the primary sumac of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau, a large shrub to small tree with narrow, willow-like leaflets that turn brilliant flame-red in fall — one of the best fall color plants native to Texas and the Gulf Coast. The small, densely clustered red berries can be used to make a tart sumac lemonade or dried and ground as a spice, and are a critical winter food source for birds across the Gulf Coast. Exceptionally heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant, and adapted to the shallow, alkaline limestone soils of central and south Texas where other plants struggle. Provides dense thicket habitat for wildlife and butterfly larval host for several species.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Praying Hands is grown for its unusual fused fruit as much as for eating, and performs best treated as a container plant in zone 9 given its limited cold tolerance.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Praying Hands is a novelty banana whose individual fingers fuse together in pairs along most of their length, opening only at the tips, so each fused pair resembles a pair of hands pressed together in prayer. The fruit itself is sweet and fully edible, similar in flavor to a standard dessert banana, but it is grown chiefly as a talking-point specimen for its unusual form rather than for volume production. Plants have the typical bold, tropical Musa acuminata habit and need the same rich, moist soil, full sun, and heavy feeding as other dessert bananas to fruit well. Cold tolerance is limited, so in zone 9 grow it in a large container that can be sheltered over winter, or provide substantial protection to the rhizome if planting in the ground, since a hard freeze can kill the below-ground growing point outright rather than allowing simple resprouting.

common_name: Premier Loquat (Florida Premier Loquat, Gulf Coast Orange Loquat)
plant_note: Plant grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Premier is the most widely planted commercial loquat variety in Florida and one of the best-adapted varieties for the humid Gulf Coast — selected for its reliable cropping under Florida and Gulf South conditions, good fruit quality, and consistent performance in the hot, humid subtropical climate of zones 9–10.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil, avoiding heavy clay or areas where water stands; Premier loquat blooms in October–November and ripens fruit in February–April in zone 9–10; thin fruit clusters to 4–6 per cluster for better-sized fruit; harvest when skin is fully golden-orange and slightly soft; store refrigerated for up to 2 weeks. Premier is the principal commercial loquat variety of Florida and one of the most reliable fruiting loquats for the Gulf Coast region, selected by the University of Florida extension system for its consistent performance in Florida's hot, humid, subtropical climate. The fruits are medium to medium-large, rounded to slightly pear-shaped, with warm orange to golden skin and orange flesh that is sweet, mildly acidic, and typically richer-flavored than Champagne (which is milder and more delicate). The variety bears consistently and prolifically in the Florida and Gulf Coast climate — more reliably than many California selections that may be adapted to a drier summer climate — and is the standard recommendation from UF IFAS Extension for home and commercial loquat production in Florida. Premier trees are moderately vigorous, reaching 15–20 feet at maturity, and are considered one of the best-adapted loquats for the humid subtropical conditions of zones 9–10 including the Gulf South, Louisiana, and coastal Texas.

plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; President is self-fertile but benefits from a nearby European plum pollinator, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. President is a classic English European plum valued for ripening notably late in the season, well after most other plums have finished, which extends the fresh plum harvest into early fall for home orchards growing several varieties. The large, deep purple-blue fruit has firm, greenish-yellow flesh with a good sweet-tart balance, holding its texture and quality well both for fresh eating and for cooking and preserves. The tree is reliably productive and the firm-fleshed fruit keeps and handles better than many earlier, softer-fleshed plum varieties, making President a practical choice for gardeners who want to stretch the plum season and have fruit that travels well from tree to kitchen.

plant_note: Root cuttings indoors in late winter or plant out container stock in spring; site against a warm, sheltered wall in marginal climates to boost heat accumulation.
directions: An English heirloom selected for reliability in cool, short-season climates, Preston's Prolific produces medium-sized, brown-purple fruit with sweet amber flesh and is prized for setting a dependable breba crop even where summer heat is limited. Plant in full sun against a south-facing wall or in a warm microclimate to maximize ripening in marginal areas, and mulch the root zone well for winter protection. It fruits readily on both old and new wood, so light annual pruning to remove crossing branches is usually all that's needed. This cultivar is a good choice for gardeners in cooler temperate regions who want fruit without a heated greenhouse.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Priam carries genetic scab immunity, making it a strong choice for low-spray or organic orchards in humid climates.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Priam is a French-bred apple carrying genetic immunity to apple scab, one of the most damaging and widespread apple diseases, particularly troublesome in humid climates where standard varieties require regular fungicide applications to produce clean fruit. The medium-sized, red-blushed fruit has crisp, juicy, well-balanced flesh suitable for both fresh eating and cooking, and while it may not match the absolute peak flavor of the finest dessert apples, its dramatically reduced spray requirements make it an attractive option for organic growers and home gardeners wanting to minimize chemical inputs. As with other scab-immune apples, some resistance can erode with new scab races over time, so continued monitoring is worthwhile even on a genetically resistant tree.

plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; self-unfruitful and requires a compatible pollinizer with overlapping bloom time.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety with overlapping bloom time is planted nearby. Price is a California almond selected in the Ne Plus Ultra lineage, producing a similar long, slender, soft-shell kernel with good sweet flavor, and it has historically been planted as a reliable pollinizer partner for other soft-shell varieties in mixed orchard plantings. The tree is a consistent producer, and its soft shell makes for easy hand-cracking, a practical advantage for home orchardists processing a home harvest without commercial equipment. Water deeply through the growing season, especially during summer kernel fill, and harvest once hulls split open in late summer to early fall, drying nuts thoroughly before storage.

common_name: Prilop Pecan (Historic Scab-Resistant Texas Native Pecan)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9) in deep, well-drained soil; Prilop is a native-type Texas selection valued mainly for its strong scab resistance in humid regions, and benefits from a second, genetically distinct pecan cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar nearby. Prilop originated as a native pecan seedling growing along the Lavaca River south of Halletsville in Lavaca County, Texas, and was propagated and preserved by grafters after the original tree was destroyed in a 1940 flood; it is sometimes also found under the names Steffek or Kallus after growers who helped keep the selection in circulation before wood was sent to the USDA-ARS pecan collection. Like many Texas native-type selections, Prilop produces a smaller nut than large modern commercial cultivars but is notably scab-resistant, an important trait for low-spray home orchards in the humid Gulf South, and it was recognized as a Texas Pecan Show state champion native selection. It remains a solid, low-maintenance choice for East Texas and similar Gulf Coast growing conditions, though it is generally considered less productive overall than higher-yielding modern releases like Caddo or Oconee. Correct zinc deficiency with a spring foliar zinc spray and water deeply during nut fill in late summer for the best kernel development.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Prima 1216 needs a second, unrelated pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and dependable fruit set.
directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, shading young trees for their first couple of seasons before exposing them to full sun. Prima 1216 is one of the oldest named pawpaw selections still in commerce, originally chosen from wild Michigan trees by pawpaw breeder Corwin Davis decades before the modern named-cultivar boom, and it remains valued for early, reliable ripening and consistent, medium-sized fruit with mild, smooth-textured flesh. It tends to bear at a younger age than many other named selections, making it a good anchor tree for a new pawpaw patch. Interplant with a genetically distinct cultivar such as Sunflower or Wabash for cross-pollination, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during bloom if fruit set seems light in early years.

plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 7–9; Princess Persimmon is a small, multi-stemmed deciduous tree or large shrub from coastal woodlands of eastern China (Zhejiang, Fujian, Jiangsu) — grown primarily as an ornamental for its spectacular autumn display of tiny, bright orange-red persimmon fruits massed on bare or nearly bare branches, with excellent container and bonsai potential, and foliage that turns vivid red-orange in autumn.
directions: Plant Princess Persimmon in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; minimal pruning needed — mainly to shape; the tiny fruits persist through winter and are best left for ornamental effect and wildlife. Diospyros rhombifolia is a gem of the East Asian ornamental plant palette — a compact, slow-growing tree or large multi-stemmed shrub that transforms dramatically in autumn. The tiny round persimmon fruits (barely 0.5 inch across) ripen to vivid orange-red and are produced in such abundance that entire branches become festooned with bright baubles, creating one of the most spectacular ornamental displays of any small tree in the autumn and early winter garden. The fruits are technically edible once fully ripe and soft — very sweet, but seedy and small — though most gardeners leave them for wildlife and ornamental effect. Autumn foliage also turns attractive shades of red-orange before leaf drop, leaving the brilliant fruit display on bare branches well into winter. An excellent subject for container growing, bonsai, and small garden spaces where a larger persimmon tree would be impractical. Dioecious (male and female plants separate) — fruiting plants are female; ensure at least one male plant is within pollination range for reliable fruit set.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Priscilla was one of the earliest releases from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program, rated very resistant to apple scab and also resistant to fire blight and cedar apple rust.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Priscilla was introduced in 1972 by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative breeding program and rates very resistant to apple scab while also resisting fire blight and cedar apple rust, letting a home orchard get by with little or no fungicide spraying. The medium-sized, red-striped fruit has crisp, juicy, mildly tart flesh good for fresh eating and cooking, ripening in late summer to early fall. As one of the earlier disease-resistant apple releases, Priscilla helped establish the case that good disease resistance and good eating quality did not have to be a trade-off. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and harvest once fruit has developed full color and separates easily from the spur with a gentle twist.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Pristine ripens in midsummer, among the earliest disease-resistant apples available, well ahead of Enterprise and GoldRush from the same breeding program.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Released from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois program, Pristine is immune to apple scab and shows good resistance to fire blight and powdery mildew, making it a dependable low-spray choice for an early crop. The clear yellow, medium-sized fruit has crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh best enjoyed fresh soon after picking, since it does not store as long as the program's later-season siblings. Its early ripening extends the home orchard's harvest window well before fall apples come in.

common_name: Prok American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Cold-Hardy Native Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Prok is a self-fertile American persimmon selection that sets seedless fruit without a pollinator, though it tolerates a very wide range of soils and some drought once established.
directions: Plant a bare-root or container-grown tree in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; American persimmon develops a long taproot, so set young trees carefully and avoid transplanting older ones. Prok is a well-known named selection of the native American persimmon valued for its unusually large fruit for the species, along with reliable, heavy, self-fertile production that does not require a second tree for pollination. Orange fruit ripens in fall and is intensely sweet and rich once fully soft-ripe, but astringent and unpalatable if eaten before that point, so wait until fruit is soft to the touch or has dropped naturally. The tree tolerates heat, drought, and a wide range of soils once established, needing little care beyond occasional watering during establishment and removal of root suckers that can form a thicket if left unchecked.

plant_note: Plant in spring on a sturdy trellis; this self-fertile variety fruits without a male vine.
directions: Prolific is a self-fertile, cold-hardy hardy kiwi bearing sweet, grape-size fruit with smooth green skin you can eat whole, no peeling required. Train the vigorous vine onto a strong trellis or arbor in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Water consistently during the growing season and prune in winter to control its rampant growth and encourage fruiting spurs. Fruit typically arrives two to three years after planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break; Prolific is one of the older named pawpaw cultivars, selected and propagated by grafting for its unusually heavy, consistent bearing rather than for the largest possible fruit size.
directions: Plant in partial shade while young, since pawpaw seedlings and young trees are naturally understory plants that scorch in full sun, and transition the tree to more sun as it matures and begins bearing. Prolific is one of the longer-established named pawpaw cultivars grown for grafted orchards, valued less for exceptional fruit size than for its dependable, heavy annual crops of medium fruit with good flavor, making it a useful workhorse variety in a mixed planting. Like all pawpaws it needs cross-pollination from a genetically distinct cultivar to set a full crop, since a pawpaw's own pollen rarely fertilizes its own flowers well, so plant it alongside a different named variety or seedling tree flowering at the same time. The maroon, unpleasant-smelling flowers are pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, and hand pollination with a small brush can improve fruit set in a planting with poor natural pollinator visits.

common_name: Puget Gold Apricot (Pacific Northwest Maritime Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained soil in the sunniest available spot; Puget Gold needs about 600-700 chill hours and was specifically bred at WSU Puyallup to bloom later and set fruit reliably in the cool, wet spring conditions of the maritime Pacific Northwest.
directions: Site trees against a south-facing wall or in the warmest microclimate available to maximize summer heat and ripening in cool coastal climates. Puget Gold is self-fertile and was developed at Washington State University's Puyallup research station specifically to succeed where most apricots fail in the region's damp, late springs, thanks to a later bloom period that dodges frost and better tolerance of humid growing conditions. Fruit is medium-large, golden-orange, and freestone with good flavor for a cool-summer climate. Thin fruit after the natural June drop to improve size and reduce limb stress.

plant_note: Plant in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained tropical soil in full sun; pulasan requires warm tropical conditions with high humidity and no frost; it is strictly a zone 11-12 tree in the United States, found in south Florida and Hawaii botanical gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained tropical soil; pulasan (Nephelium ramboutan-ake) is a close relative of rambutan (Nephelium lappaceum) native to the Malaysian peninsula, producing clusters of oval, red fruits with short, thick, blunt protuberances (versus rambutan's long, flexible hairs) — distinguishing it from rambutan at a glance. The white, translucent, sweet, juicy flesh is widely considered sweeter and better-flavored than rambutan, and the seed of pulasan is also edible (unlike rambutan's bitter seed) — roasted or boiled with a flavor similar to cocoa or almond. A premium tropical fruit rarely available commercially outside Southeast Asia; highly prized by tropical fruit collectors. Requires high humidity, consistent moisture, and no frost.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root specimens in spring in any moist to wet, acidic soil; purple chokeberry adapts to a wider range of conditions than either black or red chokeberry, including full shade, wet soils, and dry periods once established. Spreads slowly by suckering.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil; purple chokeberry (Aronia prunifolia) is a naturally occurring hybrid between black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) and red chokeberry (Aronia arbutifolia), often found growing where the two parent species overlap. The dark purple to purple-black berries are intermediate in size and flavor between the parent species, with very high anthocyanin content (among the highest of any berry), strong tart-bitter flavor excellent for juices, jams, and wine, and exceptional antioxidant properties that have driven significant commercial interest. The shrub offers year-round interest: white flowers in spring, dark glossy leaves in summer, brilliant red to purple fall color, and persistent berries attractive to birds through winter.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Dragon fruit is an epiphytic cactus that needs a sturdy support structure and, for most cultivars, night-time hand pollination to guarantee fruit set.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Purple Haze is a dragon fruit cultivar grown for its deep magenta-purple flesh, one of the most intensely colored selections available, with a sweeter, more aromatic flavor profile than the classic white-fleshed types. As an epiphytic cactus it needs a sturdy post or trellis to climb and support its long, three-ribbed, succulent stems, along with excellent drainage rather than the regular watering a conventional fruit tree would need. Flowers open at night and close by dawn, so for best fruit set hand-pollinate after dark by transferring pollen with a small brush between open flowers, since many dragon fruit selections are only partially self-fertile. Zone 9 gardeners in the warmest, most frost-protected locations can attempt in-ground planting, but most should grow Purple Haze in a large container that can be moved to a sheltered spot whenever a freeze threatens, since even brief cold exposure damages the succulent stems.

common_name: Purple Heart Pomegranate (Deep Purple-Red Aril Pomegranate)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted trees in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate drought, alkaline soils, and heat, making them well suited to zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate drought, alkaline soils, and heat, harvesting when the skin deepens to full color and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. Purple Heart bears fruit with a deep purple-red skin blush and arils that run notably darker than the bright ruby-red of most pomegranate cultivars, with rich, sweet-tart flavor and juice that stains a deep, saturated purple-red. Its striking dark coloring makes it a distinctive choice among pomegranate cultivars both for fresh eating and for juice with an unusually deep color. Prune to an open, vase-shaped form in the early years and remove root suckers regularly, since pomegranates sucker readily from the base; established trees are long-lived and require little routine care.

plant_note: Root cuttings or plant container-grown vines after all frost danger has passed; in zones 9–11 plant year-round in frost-free periods. Provide a sturdy trellis or fence to support the vigorous climbing vine.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a strong trellis or chain-link fence; the purple passion fruit vine grows rapidly and requires physical support for the tendrils. Unlike the cold-hardy native maypop (P. incarnata), this is a true tropical vine that produces the familiar large, purple, wrinkled fruits of commerce, intensely aromatic with sweet-tart yellow pulp. Fruits ripen and fall to the ground when ready — simply collect them from the ground. In zones 9b–11 plants produce heavily twice yearly, in spring and fall. The spectacular 3-inch flowers with purple, white, and yellow corona filaments are among the most intricate in the plant world and are visited by bumblebees, which are the most effective pollinators.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; purple passionflower spreads by root suckers and is very drought-tolerant once established — do not plant in rich, wet soil, which promotes rank vegetative growth over flowering and fruiting.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a fence, trellis, or wire support; allow some room for root sucker spread. Passiflora incarnata (purple passionflower or maypop) is the cold-hardy native passionflower of the eastern United States, producing the most extraordinarily ornate flowers in temperate horticulture — each 3-inch flower displays five white petals and five sepals framed by a crown of lavender to purple, fringed, radiating filaments arranged in concentric rings, the whole structure appearing more like an alien artifact than a flower. Flowers bloom from June through September and are followed by edible, golf-ball-sized, yellow-green to orange fruits (maypops) with a sweet-tart, guava-like flavor used for jams, jellies, and drinks. The vine is the obligate host plant for Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterfly larvae — caterpillars consume the leaves, making it exceptional for butterfly gardens. Passiflora incarnata is cold-hardy to zone 5 (dying to the ground in winter but resprouting vigorously from roots), and in zones 7–10 it is virtually indestructible once established, spreading from root suckers.

common_name: Purple Pershore Plum (Classic English Cooking and Jam Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Purple Pershore takes its name from the English town of Pershore in Worcestershire, historically the center of a major English plum-growing and jam-making industry built substantially around this variety, prized for consistently heavy crops of small to medium, deep purple, tart-fleshed fruit that cooks down into excellent jam, chutney, and stewed plum preparations. The fruit is generally considered too tart and firm for fresh eating out of hand but excels once cooked with sugar, developing rich, deep plum flavor that made it a commercial jam standard for generations in England. The tree is notably reliable and productive, an important trait for a variety grown primarily for volume processing rather than fresh market appeal; harvest once fruit fully colors and yields slightly to pressure.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple-leaf plum blooms very early in spring — often in February — before the leaves emerge. The species is the parent of numerous purple-foliage cultivars widely used in landscaping.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple-leaf plum (cherry plum) is a small Asian ornamental tree and one of the most widely planted landscape trees in North America for its combination of very early white to pale pink spring flowers — often blooming in February in zones 7–9 — and the dramatic burgundy-purple foliage retained through the summer. The species itself has green leaves, but the purple-leaved cultivars 'Atropurpurea', 'Thundercloud', 'Krauter Vesuvius', and 'Newport' are among the most common ornamental trees in American residential landscaping. Small, round, yellow to red plums are produced in summer and are edible, making acceptable jam and jelly. Self-sows readily and some cultivars can become invasive outside gardens in mild climates. Short-lived compared to other ornamental trees (15–25 years) but very fast-growing and reliably floriferous.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring; Qing is a Chinese chestnut selection that bears precociously (often within 2-4 years) and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set. Space wide to accommodate a broad, spreading mature canopy and good air circulation in humid Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut trees for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Qing is a widely planted Chinese chestnut cultivar selected for strong resistance to chestnut blight, dependable annual production, and a manageable, relatively compact tree form compared with seedling Chinese chestnuts; nuts are medium-large, glossy mahogany-brown, and sweet, dropping free of the burr for easy harvest in September-October. It is a mainstay of southern nut-orchard and food-forest plantings because it tolerates heat and humidity far better than American or European chestnut, sets a heavy crop at a young age, and shows good resistance to the ambrosia beetle and gall wasp pressure that troubles many other chestnut selections in the Gulf South.

common_name: Queen Ann Plum (Large Sweet Dark Purple California Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in early spring or in fall in mild climates in well-drained soil in full sun; provide a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer such as Santa Rosa nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible Japanese plum pollinizer nearby. Queen Ann is a California Japanese plum producing large, dark purple-black fruit with sweet, juicy, amber flesh, prized for its substantial size and dependable, heavy production in commercial and home orchard settings. The tree is vigorous and well suited to standard Japanese plum growing conditions, delivering fruit with good flavor balance and firm enough texture to handle well from harvest to table. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop to maintain good size, and harvest once fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and reaches full dark color for the sweetest, best-developed flavor.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings in very well-drained, sandy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun after last frost; this species is faster-growing than most columnar cacti and will begin producing flowers and fruit within 3–5 years from cuttings.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil in full sun in zones 9–12; the 'Queen of the Night' name is shared with several night-blooming cacti, but this species — the monstrose cereus sold commonly in garden centers and grocery stores as 'peruvian apple cactus' (now distinguished from C. repandus) — is a large, multi-ribbed columnar cactus from South America that becomes a substantial, multi-stemmed specimen in frost-free conditions. The large, white, intensely fragrant flowers open at night for a single evening in summer — a dramatic event attracting moths and night-pollinators. The fruits that develop are round, red to yellow, with white, sweet, refreshing flesh surrounding black seeds, eaten raw in South America where they are called 'pitaya' or 'tuna.' More cold-tolerant than most tropical cacti, this species survives brief temperatures down to about 25°F in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring before bud break.
directions: Quince is self-fertile and one of the easier tree fruits to grow, tolerating heavier and wetter soils than apples or pears. It needs 300–500 chill hours, which suits zones 5–9 broadly. The fruit is astringent and almost always cooked rather than eaten raw; it turns pink when heated with sugar and is prized for marmalade, paste (membrillo), and jelly. Harvest in late autumn when the fruit turns fully golden-yellow and fragrant, before the first hard freeze.

plant_note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a compatible desired pear variety onto the young rootstock, using an interstem for varieties incompatible with quince; BA29 is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a compatible desired pear variety onto the young rootstock, using an interstem for varieties incompatible with quince; BA29 is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit. A French quince selection long used as a dwarfing pear rootstock in European orchards, it produces a smaller, more precocious tree than seedling pear rootstocks, roughly 50-65 percent of standard size, though it is somewhat less cold-hardy and more prone to iron chlorosis on high-pH soils than the seedling and OHxF pear rootstocks more commonly used in North America. Because many pear varieties are graft-incompatible with quince, an interstem of a compatible pear variety such as Old Home is often bench-grafted between the quince rootstock and the desired scion variety. Graft or double-work a desired named pear variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and reserve this rootstock for milder climates and growers specifically wanting a smaller, earlier-bearing pear tree.

plant_note: Plant clonally propagated rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired English walnut variety onto the young rootstock; RX1 is a disease-resistant clonal understock, not grown for its own nuts.
directions: Plant clonally propagated rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired English walnut variety onto the young rootstock; RX1 is a disease-resistant clonal understock, not grown for its own nuts. Developed by the University of California walnut breeding program as a clonally propagated hybrid rootstock, it was bred specifically for strong resistance to Phytophthora root and crown rot and to lesion nematode, two of the most damaging soil-borne problems limiting walnut orchard longevity on the traditional seedling Paradox rootstock, while offering the genetic uniformity that open-pollinated seedling Paradox lacks. Its combination of disease resistance and vigor comparable to Paradox has made it an increasingly popular modern choice for new commercial walnut plantings on disease-prone or replant sites. Graft a desired named English walnut variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect vigorous, disease-resistant growth well suited to sites with a history of walnut root disease.

plant_note: Plant container-grown bushes in fall or late winter in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, highly organic soil in full sun to part shade; rabbiteye blueberry is the heat- and low-chill-tolerant species specifically adapted to the Gulf Coast region from Texas to Florida. Plant two or more different cultivars to ensure cross-pollination and maximum yield. Recommended cultivars for zone 9: 'Climax,' 'Premier,' 'Tifblue,' 'Brightwell.'
directions: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun with at least two different cultivars for cross-pollination; rabbiteye blueberry is the blueberry of the Gulf Coast South — native to the coastal plain from Texas to Florida and naturally adapted to hot summers, mild winters, and the low-chill conditions (below 45°F hours) that prevent highbush blueberries from fruiting reliably in zone 8–9. The name 'rabbiteye' refers to the pale, pinkish color of the unripe berries before they turn deep blue-purple at maturity. Plants are large, vigorous, and long-lived — potentially producing for 40–50 years — with spring flowers that attract early native bees, summer berries that ripen over an extended period from May through August depending on cultivar, and attractive red-orange fall foliage. A fundamental food plant for Gulf Coast edible gardens that produces abundantly with minimal care in appropriate acidic soil conditions. The primary challenge in the Gulf Coast is achieving and maintaining the necessary soil acidity; soil acidification with sulfur or planting in raised beds filled with peat, pine bark, and acidic compost is often necessary.

common_name: Rainier Cherry (Blushing Cherry, Yellow Sweet Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Rainier requires 700–800 chill hours and a pollinizer (Bing, Black Tartarian, or Lapins) for good fruit production in most situations.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Rainier is considered the premium sweet cherry cultivar — producing large, blush-yellow to golden-red fruit with creamy yellow flesh that is exceptionally sweet, almost honeylike, with delicate flavor considered superior to the firmer, darker varieties. It was developed at Washington State University in 1954 and named for Mount Rainier. The firm, thick skin makes Rainier more resistant to cracking than some sweet cherries, but the pale color means bird damage can be severe — netting is often necessary. Rainier requires 700–800 winter chill hours (hours below 45°F) to fruit reliably, limiting it to zones 5–8; in warmer climates, performance is inconsistent. A pollinizer (Bing, Black Tartarian, or Lapins cherry) planted within 50 feet is necessary for full crop production. Prune during dormancy to maintain an open-center or modified central-leader form. Bears fruit on spurs that persist for many years — avoid pruning productive spur wood.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Raja Puri's short, dwarf stature is what lets it fruit within a single warm season even where winter freezes kill the pseudostem back to the ground each year.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Raja Puri is a dwarf, fast-fruiting banana cultivar especially popular with Gulf Coast and Florida home growers because its short 4–7 foot pseudostem reaches flowering size and produces a bunch within one warm growing season — a critical advantage over taller bananas that need more than a year of frost-free growth to reach fruiting size, since a hard freeze that kills the pseudostem each winter resets a tall variety's clock but barely slows a fast, compact grower like Raja Puri. Fruit is medium-small, sweet, and good for fresh eating, borne in bunches lower to the ground than most bananas, which also makes bunches easier to bag and protect from wind damage. Provide consistent moisture and heavy monthly feeding through the growing season, since bananas are fast, heavy feeders. In zone 8b–9, mulch the root zone deeply in fall to protect the rhizome through winter, and expect the pseudostem to die back with hard freezes and resprout from the root system in spring.

common_name: Rajapuri Banana (Compact Indian Dessert Banana, Cold-Tolerant Edible for Zone 9)
plant_note: Plant pups (suckers) or divisions after frost risk has passed in spring; Rajapuri is a compact Indian banana cultivar reaching only 8–12 feet tall (compared to 15–20 feet for tall types), making it more manageable in Gulf South home landscapes while still producing genuine, full-flavored dessert bananas. In zone 9, Rajapuri pseudostems may die to the ground after frost, but the rhizome survives and regrows vigorously in spring — planting in a protected, south-facing location against a wall or fence significantly improves survival. The bananas produced are shorter and chubbier than Cavendish but very sweet, with rich flavor and a smooth, creamy texture. Rajapuri is traditional in Indian subcontinent banana culture and has been grown in South Asia for centuries. It is one of the more cold-tolerant edible banana cultivars, making it practical for zone 9 in most years. Plant in full sun with consistently moist, rich, well-drained soil.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in full sun, rich soil. Maintain moisture and fertilize regularly. Cut fruited pseudostems to ground after harvest; allow pups to develop for next year's crop. Rajapuri Banana is a traditional cultivar from the Indian subcontinent where it is one of the most popular dessert bananas — cultivated in home gardens and small plantations throughout India, particularly in Maharashtra and other banana-growing states, for its excellent flavor and manageable plant size. In the Gulf South context, Rajapuri offers several practical advantages over the more common edible bananas: its compact height (8–12 feet) is more appropriate for most home landscapes than the 15–20 foot height of tall cultivars, making management of the pseudostems easier; its cold tolerance is better than most Cavendish types, improving survival in zone 9's occasional freezes; and its fruit quality — shorter, chubby fingers with extremely sweet, rich, creamy flesh — is considered superior to supermarket Cavendish bananas by most fresh-tasting evaluations. The fruit is typically ready to pick when the skin is still green-yellow (watch for the ridges to round out and the skin to lighten) and ripened indoors to full yellow with a pronounced aroma. For zone 9 Gulf Coast home gardeners with full sun and space for 8×10 feet of planting, Rajapuri is one of the most rewarding fruiting plants that can be grown — producing large bunches of genuinely excellent bananas within 12–18 months of planting a good-sized pup.

common_name: Ralls Janet Apple (Late-Season Virginia Heirloom, Parent of Red Delicious and Fuji)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring while still dormant, in well-drained soil away from late-spring frost pockets.
directions: Ralls Janet dates to 18th-century Virginia and became famous in 20th-century Missouri and Illinois orchards for its ability to shrug off harsh winters and heat waves alike. Very late bloom time helps the flowers dodge spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering apples, and the small, firm, tart-sweet fruit stores in a root cellar into late winter. It is one of the two parents of Red Delicious and, through a Japanese breeding program, a grandparent of Fuji, making it an interesting living link for gardeners who grow both modern and heirloom apples. Choose it for its toughness and storability rather than fresh-eating size, since the fruit is on the small side compared to modern dessert apples.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; rambai is a lowland Southeast Asian rainforest tree that thrives in the consistently warm, humid conditions of zones 10–11. Plant only in frost-free locations, as the tree has little cold tolerance and is killed by temperatures below freezing.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–11; rambai is a medium-sized Southeast Asian fruit tree in the Phyllanthaceae family that produces large, pendulous clusters of small, grape-like fruits — ranging in color from pale yellow to deep pink or red — borne on the branches and trunk in the cauliflorous habit shared by many tropical rainforest species. The translucent, sweet-tart flesh surrounds relatively large seeds and is eaten fresh or made into juices, wines, and pickles across Myanmar, Bangladesh, Thailand, and Malaysia, where the fruit is a beloved seasonal treat sold in local markets. Trees are dioecious, meaning separate male and female trees are required for fruit production, so plant at least two seedlings or obtain a confirmed female tree grafted onto a rootstock. Maintain high humidity and consistent moisture for best growth, and apply a thick layer of organic mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist throughout the year.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; rambai is a Southeast Asian cauliflorous fruit tree — the fruits hang in long pendant clusters directly from the trunk and main branches — dioecious (separate male and female trees required for fruit), best suited to zone 11–12 humid tropics.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; plant at least one male and one female tree for fruit production — rambai is dioecious. Baccaurea motleyana (rambai or rambeh) is a tropical Southeast Asian fruit tree native to the humid lowland forests of the Malay Peninsula, Thailand, and Borneo — closely related to langsat (Lansium domesticum) in lifestyle and fruit appearance, though in a different botanical family (Phyllanthaceae). The tree produces long, pendulous clusters of small (1–1.5 inch), thin-skinned, yellow to pale-orange fruits directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory), similar in habit to cacao and jackfruit. The sweet-acid, translucent-white, jelly-like flesh has a pleasant, mild, tropical flavor — somewhat sweet, gently tart, with a slight astringency when slightly underripe. Rambai is eaten fresh in Malaysia and southern Thailand, and is also used in traditional cooking and beverages. The tree requires genuinely hot, humid, tropical conditions without frost — suitable only for zone 11–12 in the continental US (extreme South Florida, Hawaii). It is dioecious, requiring both a male and female tree for fruit production; grafted female trees are occasionally available from specialty tropical nurseries. Almost entirely unknown outside Southeast Asia in cultivation; an exceptional and very rare find for the dedicated tropical fruit collector.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after all cold risk has passed; young trees are extremely frost-sensitive.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) in a frost-free location; rambutan is damaged at any temperature below 40°F and is one of the most cold-sensitive common fruit trees. Most cultivars bear both male and hermaphrodite flowers on separate trees, so plant at least one male tree alongside female or hermaphrodite fruiting trees to ensure pollination. Trees require consistent rainfall or irrigation — roughly 60–150 inches of annual precipitation equivalent — especially during fruit development, with a short dry period to stimulate flowering. Harvest clusters when the leathery spines (soft spinterns) have turned fully red or yellow depending on variety and the flesh is translucent, sweet, and separates cleanly from the seed.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Ranch is self-fertile but produces best when planted with a second elderberry cultivar for cross-pollination and higher yield.
directions: Ranch is an American elderberry selection developed through the University of Missouri's elderberry improvement program alongside better-known releases like Bob Gordon and Wyldewood, chosen for productive, well-formed clusters and reliable performance in commercial-scale plantings. Plant in full sun in moist, fertile soil, and keep well watered during establishment since elderberries are shallow-rooted and drought-sensitive. Large, flat-topped white flower clusters appear in early summer and can be harvested for elderflower cordial, followed by heavy clusters of dark purple-black berries in late summer used for syrup, jam, and wine after cooking.
