Prune out the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the shrub vigorous and productive.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; Rangpur lime is hardier than true limes and withstands brief frosts to about 25°F.
directions: Rangpur lime is actually a mandarin-lime hybrid (not a true lime) prized for its mandarin orange appearance, intensely sour juice, and significantly greater cold-hardiness than Key or Persian limes, making it a practical choice for zone 8 citrus gardens and container culture. It is self-fertile, productive as a single tree, and bears fruit nearly year-round in warm climates; fruit ripens to a deep orange-red color similar to a tangerine. Use the juice as a direct substitute for regular lime juice in cocktails, marinades, and curries — it is slightly more complex and aromatic. Harvest when the fruit has turned fully orange-red and yields to gentle pressure; fruit can be held on the tree for several weeks after ripening without significant quality loss.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun. RazzMatazz is self-fertile (perfect-flowered) and does not require a separate pollinator vine.
directions: RazzMatazz is a patented hybrid between muscadine grape and European wine/table grape (Vitis vinifera), bred to combine muscadine-type disease resistance with the seedless berries and thin skin of a bunch grape. Fruit is deep red with crisp flesh and a sweet flavor, and unlike most muscadines the self-fertile vines flower and ripen berries continuously from midsummer until frost rather than in a single concentrated harvest window. It ripens earlier than most straight muscadine cultivars and has shown strong resistance to the fungal diseases that trouble bunch grapes in humid Southern climates, allowing it to be grown with minimal spraying. Train on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun and well-drained soil, and expect a more compact, less sprawling vine than typical full-size muscadine cultivars.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Rebecca's Gold predates the modern Peterson Pawpaw releases and sets its best crops when planted with a second, genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun as the tree matures; Rebecca's Gold is one of the older named pawpaw selections, predating the modern Peterson Pawpaw cultivars and long maintained in pawpaw germplasm collections for its rich, deep-golden flesh and excellent sweet flavor. It is a productive, reliable tree that has stood the test of decades of cultivation among pawpaw enthusiasts and collectors, valued alongside historic selections like Overleese and Sunflower as part of the foundation on which today's larger-fruited cultivars were bred. As with all pawpaws, Rebecca's Gold is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and fruit set; hand-pollinating between two open flowers of different cultivars with a small brush can improve yield where natural fly and beetle pollinators are scarce. Provide consistent moisture through the first two seasons while the shallow root system establishes, and expect the tree to fruit within four to eight years from a grafted start.

common_name: Red Anjou Pear (Red-Skinned Firm Winter Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Red Anjou requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 4-8.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Red Anjou is a red-skinned bud sport of the classic D'Anjou pear, carrying the same dense, firm, sweet, low-fiber flesh and outstanding storage life as the parent variety, wrapped in a deep burgundy-red skin that adds visual appeal without altering flavor or texture. Like other Anjou-type pears, the fruit does not change color noticeably as it ripens, which makes checking for ripeness by color unreliable — instead, press gently near the stem end and harvest or eat once that area yields slightly to pressure. Anjou-type pears are prized for exceptionally good long-term cold storage, often holding good quality for months, making Red Anjou a satisfying choice for home orchardists who want fresh pears well into winter.

common_name: Red Bartlett Pear (Red-Skinned Sport of Classic Bartlett)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Red Bartlett requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 5-8.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Red Bartlett is a naturally occurring red-skinned sport of the classic green Bartlett pear, discovered as a bud mutation and propagated for its striking burgundy-red skin, while retaining the same sweet, juicy, melting flesh and classic pear flavor that made Bartlett the standard American pear for over a century. Because the tree and fruit share Bartlett's genetics apart from skin color, growers get the familiar reliable flavor with added ornamental interest in the orchard and a more eye-catching fruit for fresh eating, gift baskets, and market sales. Harvest while still firm and green-tinged with a hint of red blush, then finish ripening at room temperature indoors, since pears ripen from the inside out and develop the best texture and flavor off the tree rather than fully ripened on the branch.

plant_note: Plant pups or tissue-culture plants in spring after frost; in zone 9 plant March–May. Red Dacca is ornamentally striking — the dark red-maroon pseudostem, leaf undersides, and unripe fruit color make it one of the most visually distinctive edible bananas. In zone 9 protect from hard freezes; mulch heavily at the base in late fall to insulate the rhizome.
directions: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moisture-retentive, fertile soil; Red Dacca (also called Red Banana, Claret Banana, or Pisang Raja Udang in Southeast Asia) is a distinctive red-skinned banana cultivar producing medium-sized fruits with deep maroon to reddish-purple skin when unripe that turns dark yellow-orange when fully ripe. The flesh is creamy white with a slightly firmer, sweeter, and more aromatic flavor than standard Cavendish bananas — often described as having hints of raspberry or tropical fruit notes beyond the typical banana flavor. The entire plant is ornamentally striking, with dark red-purple pseudostems, contrasting green leaf tops and red-purple leaf undersides, and the colorful fruit clusters adding exceptional visual interest. Red Dacca is widely grown as a dual-purpose ornamental and edible banana in zone 9-11 gardens and is popular in Southeast Asian and Caribbean cuisine both fresh and cooked. The fruits are ready to harvest when the skin color begins to lighten from deep red toward orange-red.

common_name: Red Delicious Apple (Hawkeye Apple, Most-Planted American Apple, Classic Red Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Red Delicious requires approximately 700–900 chill hours and cross-pollination from a compatible variety such as Gala, Fuji, Honeycrisp, or Golden Delicious; standard strains can reach 20+ feet while spur-type strains on dwarfing rootstock are more practical for home orchards.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Red Delicious requires cross-pollination from a compatible diploid apple variety; harvest when the background color turns fully yellow-green under the red and the calyx basin softens slightly — Red Delicious harvested too late becomes mealy, while picked at proper maturity it is firm and pleasantly mild. Red Delicious is the most historically planted apple variety in the United States, dominating American commercial apple production for most of the 20th century and serving as the iconic image of an apple in American culture — the deep red, elongated, five-pointed shape was for decades what millions of Americans pictured when they thought 'apple.' The variety originated as a chance seedling discovered by farmer Jesse Hiatt on his farm near Peru, Iowa around 1872; Hiatt named it 'Hawkeye' and sent samples to a Stark Brothers Nurseries competition in 1893, where it won first prize and was renamed 'Delicious' (later 'Red Delicious' to distinguish it from Golden Delicious). Over the following century, commercial selection pressure for maximum red color and long shelf life produced the modern market strains with deep, all-red skin and elongated shape — but these selections simultaneously reduced the flavor quality that made the original Hawkeye notable. By the early 2000s, Red Delicious had become widely criticized for waxy skin, mealy texture, and mild flavor — a cautionary example of how breeding for appearance at the expense of eating quality can undermine a variety's standing. However, heritage strains and home-grown Red Delicious harvested at correct maturity are noticeably better than commercial examples. Highly productive and disease-tolerant in its home range of zones 5–8.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings (preferred) or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Red dragon fruit requires a sturdy trellis, fence, or concrete post for its climbing stem — provide a flat-topped support (old telephone pole, concrete post, or T-post with a flat wooden disc) for the sprawling crown of cladodes. In zone 9 protect from temperatures below 28°F; the thick cladodes survive brief cold snaps but repeated freezes will damage the vine. Fruiting begins 1–2 years from cuttings.
directions: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, sandy, gritty, low-fertility soil — red dragon fruit is a cactus and will rot rapidly in rich, wet, or clay soils; Red Dragon Fruit (Selenicereus costaricensis, formerly Hylocereus costaricensis) is the red-fleshed species of dragon fruit, producing large, oval, deep red-skinned fruits with vivid magenta-red flesh flecked with tiny black seeds. The deep crimson flesh color comes from betacyanin pigments (the same class as beet pigments) that turn smoothies, yogurt, and beverages a dramatic pink-red color. The flavor is mild and sweet with a watermelon-like freshness that is more subtle than the appearance suggests. Red dragon fruit typically ripens 30–35 days after the large, white nocturnal flowers open — the flowers must be pollinated on the night they open (by hand or by nocturnal pollinators) for fruit to set. In zone 9 the long warm season provides ideal conditions for multiple fruiting cycles per year, typically producing 4–6 fruit-set periods from May through November.

plant_note: Plant cuttings 12–18 inches long in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after last frost; red dragon fruit requires a trellis or support structure for its vining habit. In zone 9, provide frost protection below 32°F.
directions: Plant cuttings in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12, with trellis support; red-fleshed dragon fruit differs from the common white-fleshed variety (S. undatus) in producing fruits with vivid deep magenta to crimson flesh — dramatically more colorful and considered by many to have superior flavor with sweeter, slightly more complex notes. The spectacular, white, night-blooming flowers up to 12 inches across are among the largest of any cactus, pollinated by moths and bats. Like all pitayas, this species vines with aerial roots along support structures and requires staking when young. The red-pigmented flesh contains high levels of betacyanins — potent antioxidants responsible for the vivid color. Multiple self-fertile clones exist; 'American Beauty' and 'Physical Graffiti' are popular red-flesh varieties. Needs at least 2 years from cuttings to first fruit; grafted plants begin producing sooner.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container seedlings in early spring; red hickory develops a deep taproot and resists transplanting once established, so site it carefully.
directions: Plant seedlings in deep, well-drained upland soil in full sun, allowing room for a tall, straight-trunked tree. Red hickory is a native eastern North American species closely related to pignut hickory, distinguished by its reddish twigs and a husk that splits more readily and completely from the nut at maturity. Its kernels are notably sweeter and less bitter than those of true pignut hickory, and the tree is a valuable wildlife mast producer as well as a source of dense, strong wood.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil in full sun to part shade; red jaboticaba (Plinia trunciflora) is a smaller, thinner-skinned, and slightly sweeter jaboticaba species than the commonly grown P. cauliflora, bearing red to deep-red-purple fruits directly on the trunk in the characteristic jaboticaba fashion; slightly more cold-tolerant than some jaboticaba species.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; jaboticabas are slow-growing and may take 5–8 years to first fruit but eventually produce multiple crops per year. Plinia trunciflora (red jaboticaba or jaboticaba vermelha) is one of several species in the jaboticaba group of Brazilian native fruit trees — distinct from the commonly cultivated Plinia cauliflora (the dark-purple or black jaboticaba) by producing smaller fruits that ripen red to deep ruby-red rather than purple-black, with thinner skin, slightly sweeter flavor, and a somewhat shorter delay before first flowering after planting in good conditions. Like all jaboticabas, P. trunciflora produces its fruits cauliflourously — directly on the bark of the trunk and main branches, covering the tree's lower structure with dense clusters of round, grape-like fruits that appear to erupt directly from the wood, creating one of the most visually spectacular fruiting displays in subtropical horticulture. The fruits are eaten fresh or made into wine, liqueur, and jam in Brazil; they are thin-skinned enough that the entire fruit (including the somewhat tannic skin) can be popped into the mouth. Jaboticabas produce multiple crops per year in warm, humid conditions. P. trunciflora is noted as marginally more cold-tolerant than some jaboticaba relatives, making it a candidate for protected zone 9 microclimates.

common_name: Red Jewel Crabapple (Upright White-Flowered Red-Fruited Crabapple)
plant_note: Plant the dormant or potted grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Red Jewel produces pure white spring flowers from pale pink buds, followed by an abundant crop of bright, glossy red, jewel-like fruit that holds on the branches into winter, providing striking color against bare branches and snow long after most ornamental trees have finished their season of interest. Its narrower, more upright-oval form than many crabapple cultivars fits smaller landscapes and tighter planting spots where a wide-spreading crabapple would not fit. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; shows good resistance to common crabapple diseases.

plant_note: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before last frost date and transplant after danger of frost passes into moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; 'Red Lady' is a bisexual (hermaphrodite) F1 hybrid that produces fruits when planted individually — no separate male pollinator is needed, simplifying home garden production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow in warm soil in full sun after frost passes; 'Red Lady' is a commercially successful Taiwanese F1 hybrid papaya developed by Known-You Seed, widely sold in tropical and subtropical regions around the world and favored for its tolerance of Papaya Ring Spot Virus (PRSV), the most devastating papaya disease, which allows it to maintain productivity in areas where most other papayas fail. The bisexual (hermaphrodite) flower type means a single plant can self-pollinate and fruit without needing a separate male, a practical advantage for home gardens with space for only one or two trees. Fruits are medium-large (2–4 pounds), round to slightly oblong, with thin yellow skin blushed with orange-red at maturity and deep, salmon-red flesh with exceptional sweetness and fragrance. 'Red Lady' is an earlier-bearing variety than most papayas, producing fruits within 7–10 months from seed under good growing conditions, and is particularly productive in hot-summer climates like Gulf Coast zone 9. An excellent choice for any zone 9b–12 food garden seeking a reliable, disease-tolerant, self-fruitful papaya.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Red Malaysian Guava has moderate cold tolerance to about 28°F for brief periods when established. The deeply red fruit color is most intense in slightly cooler temperatures — fall and winter fruits in zone 9 often color more deeply than summer fruits. Protect young trees from freezes in zone 9a with frost cloth.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Red Malaysian Guava is a striking cultivar producing fruits with a red-blushed skin and deep salmon-pink to red flesh — the most colorful of the common guava cultivars, with a vibrant internal color that is dramatically vivid when the fruit is sliced. The flavor is rich, aromatic, and sweet with the characteristic guava fragrance, perhaps slightly less musky than standard pink guava types. The red flesh color is due to lycopene, the same antioxidant pigment as in tomatoes, and red-fleshed guavas contain significantly more lycopene than pink-fleshed varieties. Red Malaysian guava is visually impressive at the market and on the table — the vivid red cross-section makes it one of the most photographed fresh tropical fruits. In zone 9 the trees produce multiple crops annually and fruit most heavily in late summer–fall and late winter–spring. Fruits ripen from green to a yellow-red skin color and should be eaten when fully soft.

plant_note: Plant large hardwood cuttings directly in full sun in any well-drained soil; red mombin roots and establishes extremely easily from 1–2 foot branch cuttings inserted directly into the ground. Established trees tolerate brief freezes to 28°F; best in zone 9b–12.
directions: Plant large hardwood cuttings directly in well-drained soil in full sun — red mombin is a small tropical plum tree of Central America and the Caribbean notable for two things: the flavor of its egg-shaped, wine-red to dark purple fruits (a thin skin over sweet-tart orange flesh with an enormous seed, eaten fresh or in agua fresca throughout Mexico and Central America where it is called 'jocote') and its ability to propagate from large cuttings stuck directly in the ground — even fenceposts made from the wood can sprout. The deciduous tree drops its leaves in the dry season, then blooms and leafs out simultaneously in the rainy season. It is remarkably drought tolerant and is grown in poor, dry soils throughout the tropics. The small reddish fruits ripen over a long season and are consumed by birds and wildlife. An excellent low-water, easy-care tropical fruit tree for zone 9b–12.

plant_note: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip after the last frost in fast-draining soil in full sun, or grow in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter; Red Spanish is an older heirloom pineapple valued for its tough skin and good shipping and storage qualities.
directions: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Red Spanish is an heirloom pineapple cultivar with a squat, barrel-shaped fruit and tough reddish-orange skin that historically made it a favorite for shipping and fresh market sale before modern refrigerated transport, since the thick rind resists bruising and handling damage. Flesh is pale yellow, firm, and tangy-sweet with good flavor for fresh eating and preserving alike. Like other pineapples, the low rosette of stiff, often spiny leaves takes about 18-24 months to mature a single fruit at its center, after which offset suckers can be detached and replanted. Pineapple has virtually no cold tolerance, so zone 9 gardeners should grow Red Spanish in a large container that can be moved indoors or to a greenhouse before the first freeze and returned outside once nights stay reliably above 50F.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; red-fleshed durian (Durio kutejensis) is a wild durian species from the lowland dipterocarp forests of Borneo — producing smaller, less intensely odorous fruits than common durian (D. zibethinus) with bright red-orange to yellow flesh considered by many connoisseurs to be sweeter and more nuanced in flavor, without the overwhelming sulfurous aroma of commercial durian.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; requires genuinely tropical, humid, frost-free conditions; a collectors' tree for dedicated tropical fruit enthusiasts. Durio kutejensis (red-fleshed durian, durian merah, or kuning) is one of approximately 30 Durio species native to the forests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula — and considered by many tropical fruit connoisseurs to produce superior-quality fruit to the common commercial durian (D. zibethinus). The fruits of D. kutejensis are smaller than commercial durian (typically 2–4 lbs) and covered with shorter, broader spines; the flesh is distinctively bright red-orange to golden-yellow — dramatically different from the pale cream-yellow flesh of common durian. The flavor is often described as richer, sweeter, more complex, and less sulfurous than D. zibethinus — with strong caramel, butterscotch, and tropical fruit notes without the overwhelming, polarizing odor that makes commercial durian controversial. The relative mildness of the aroma compared to D. zibethinus is one of the key reasons D. kutejensis is considered by Southeast Asian fruit lovers to be among the finest of all wild durian species. Wild animals in Borneo (orangutans, civets, bearded pigs) are major consumers and dispersers of durian fruits; D. kutejensis provides critical nutrition to Borneo wildlife. Extremely rare in cultivation outside Borneo.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown plants in moist to dry, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; red-flowering currant is drought-tolerant once established and native to the dry coastal chaparral and mixed forest of the Pacific Northwest. The cultivar 'King Edward VII' produces the deepest crimson flowers; 'White Icicle' is a white-flowered form.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; red-flowering currant is a Pacific Northwest native shrub and one of the most spectacular early-spring-blooming shrubs for Pacific Coast gardens, producing pendulous clusters of deep rose-red to carmine-pink flowers in March and April before the leaves emerge. It is the first major nectar source for returning rufous hummingbirds on their northward spring migration, and hummingbirds converge on flowering specimens in large numbers. The timing of its bloom — earliest of any showy ornamental shrub in coastal Pacific Northwest gardens — combined with its value to hummingbirds and other early pollinators makes it ecologically as well as ornamentally outstanding. The flowers are followed by small, blue-black, bloom-covered berries attractive to birds. The maple-like, aromatic leaves are attractive through summer and the shrub develops an open, graceful form. Highly drought-tolerant once established and naturally adapted to the summer-dry Pacific Coast climate. The cultivar range includes colors from white through all shades of pink to deep crimson.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Redfree is a Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) breeding program release, field-immune to apple scab and resistant to the other major apple diseases, and ripens earlier than most disease-resistant apples.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Redfree was released by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative breeding program in 1981 and is field-immune to apple scab while also resisting the other major fungal and bacterial apple diseases, making it one of the most reliably low-spray apples available. It ripens earlier than most disease-resistant varieties, giving a mid-to-late-summer crop of medium-sized, bright red, crisp, juicy fruit with a mild, sweet flavor good for fresh eating. Because it is one of the earliest scab-immune apples to ripen, Redfree is a good choice for gardeners who want disease resistance without waiting until fall for the harvest. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and pick fruit once it has developed full color and separates easily from the spur.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Redhaven requires approximately 950 hours of chilling — this is toward the upper end of reliable accumulation in zone 9 and may occasionally result in poor bloom set in mild winters.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Redhaven is one of the most widely grown and consistently performing freestone peach cultivars in American horticulture — an early-season variety ripening in late May through mid-June in zone 9, which is 2–3 weeks ahead of the main-season peach crop. The medium-large, round fruit has attractive red-blushed skin over yellow background color, with yellow, firm, freestone flesh of excellent quality and rich, aromatic flavor. The early ripening is a significant advantage — early fruit escapes the worst of the summer disease pressure from brown rot and oriental fruit moth that builds through the season. The vigorous tree produces reliably heavy crops with good thinning practices. Redhaven requires approximately 950 chill hours, which is well-suited to zone 7–8 and marginal in zone 9 — growers in lower zone 9 or inland zone 9a should evaluate local chill hour accumulation data (available from county extension offices) before planting. In borderline chill-hour years, Redhaven may set a reduced or irregular bloom. Annual pruning to an open-vase form and consistent summer disease management are necessary for reliable production.

plant_note: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in spring after frost danger, in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil.
directions: Redlands Tropic Star was released by University of Florida breeders working near the Redland agricultural district south of Miami and combines the fragrant, deep-purple fruit of common passion fruit with improved tolerance of the fungal diseases that plague vines in Florida's humid growing season. It is a vigorous, self-fertile climber that needs a strong trellis or arbor, since a single plant can cover a large structure within its first year. Fruit ripens over a long summer-to-fall season and drops when fully ripe, signaling harvest time without guesswork. Choose this cultivar over unnamed seedling passion fruit when disease pressure has been a recurring problem in the garden.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Redskin needs roughly 750 chill hours and is best suited to zone 5-8, marginal for zone 9's mild winters.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart once fruit set is confirmed. Redskin was released by the USDA in the mid-1940s and went on to become a widely planted mid-20th-century commercial and home orchard peach, valued for firm, yellow, freestone flesh under an attractive skin heavily blushed with red, holding up well to handling and processing while still delivering good, classic peach flavor fresh off the tree. The reliable, productive tree set the standard for decades before being gradually supplanted by newer disease-resistant cultivars, but it remains a solid, dependable choice for home orchards wanting an old-fashioned, well-proven variety. Prune to an open-vase form and follow a routine dormant-season spray program for peach leaf curl and brown rot, which affect Redskin as they do most peach cultivars.

common_name: Reliance Grape (Cold-Hardy Pink Seedless Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Reliance is exceptionally cold-hardy for a seedless grape, tolerating winters well beyond what most seedless table grapes survive, but still needs a real winter chill and is not suited to the Deep South.
directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Reliance was bred at the University of Arkansas and is prized for its outstanding cold hardiness among seedless grapes, along with medium-sized pink-red berries that are sweet, tender-skinned, and easy to eat fresh off the cluster. It ripens in midseason and is self-fruitful, though thinning clusters improves berry size and vine longevity. Because it needs sustained winter chill to perform well, it is best suited to northern and mid-South gardens rather than the humid, mild-winter Gulf Coast, where muscadines and Pierce's-tolerant hybrids are more reliable.

common_name: Reliance Peach (Ultra-Cold-Hardy Northern Peach, New Hampshire Freestone)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil; Reliance requires approximately 850 chill hours and is one of the most cold-hardy peach varieties available, with dormant wood hardy to -25°F and flower buds among the most cold-tolerant of any named variety — the premier peach for zones 4–6 where winter hardiness and late-frost resilience are paramount; self-fruitful.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; thin to 6–8 inches in spring; Reliance is self-fruitful and requires no cross-pollinator; the trees are vigorous and productive, delivering reliable crops in zones where other peach varieties fail due to winter cold; fruit ripens early-mid season (late July to mid-August in zones 4–6). Reliance peach is the most cold-hardy named peach variety in widespread cultivation in North America, developed by F.H. Emerson at the University of New Hampshire (released 1964) specifically for the challenging peach-growing conditions of New England and the northern United States where standard peach varieties like Elberta, Loring, and Madison lose their flower buds to winter cold or late spring frosts too frequently to be reliable crops. The extraordinary cold-hardiness of Reliance is its defining characteristic: dormant wood has survived -25°F in New Hampshire orchard trials, and the flower buds show significantly better cold-tolerance than most other varieties. In comparative cold-hardiness tests, Reliance consistently outperforms all other widely-available named peach varieties, giving it a unique market niche as 'the peach you can actually grow in the North.' Fruit quality is good but not exceptional compared to premium mid-South varieties — the fruits are medium-sized, round to oval, with a red blush over yellow background, and a pleasant yellow-fleshed, sweet, fully freestone flavor. The flavor is somewhat mild compared to full-sun, high-quality southern peaches, reflecting the shorter, cooler northern growing season. However, for gardeners in zones 4–6 where reliable peach production from standard varieties is difficult or impossible, Reliance delivers consistent, acceptable-quality fresh peaches from a tree that simply survives winters that would kill other varieties.

common_name: Reliance Seedless Grape (Red Seedless Home Garden Grape, Hardy Seedless)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines or container plants in early spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Reliance is the most widely planted seedless red table grape for home gardens in the northern and central United States, bred by James Moore at the University of Arkansas for its combination of seedlessness, cold-hardiness (to -15°F), excellent fresh-eating quality, and reliable production in zones 4–8 — filling the niche for an easy-to-eat, sweet, seedless home grape in climates where the Thompson Seedless (a warm-climate variety) is not reliably productive.
directions: Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun; spur-prune in late winter to 2 buds per spur; Reliance is self-fruitful; fruit ripens mid-August in most zones; the medium-sized, rose-red to red berries are seedless, tender-skinned, and sweet with a mild, pleasant flavor more subtle than Concord; excellent for fresh eating, fruit salads, and home winemaking. Reliance seedless grape is a University of Arkansas-bred red seedless table grape (released 1982, bred by James Moore) that became the most widely planted cold-hardy seedless home garden grape in the United States, filling a genuine need for a sweet, seedless fresh-eating grape that could be grown reliably in zones 4–8 where the California-bred Thompson Seedless and Flame Red Seedless (developed for California's mild winters and low humidity) perform poorly or inconsistently. The breeding background of Reliance includes multiple American Labrusca and hybrid species crosses selected for cold-hardiness, which gives the variety a very cold-tolerant profile — mature canes are hardy to -15°F and the variety tolerates late spring frosts reasonably well. The berries are medium-sized, red-rose to medium red (lighter than dark blue varieties like Mars), round to slightly oval, and truly seedless with a tender, non-slip skin (unlike the slip-skin character of Concord and Niagara). The flavor is sweet, mild, and pleasantly fruity without the strong Labrusca 'foxiness' of slip-skin varieties — closer to the flavor profile of commercial seedless grapes but with its own mild aromatic quality. Reliance is a productive, reliable variety that earns its place as the standard seedless home garden grape for most of the northern and central United States.

common_name: Republic of Texas Fig (Cold-Hardy Brown Sugar Fig)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings after last frost; Republic of Texas is an exceptionally cold-hardy, drought-tolerant Texas heirloom fig that reliably resprouts from the roots even after a hard freeze kills the top growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Republic of Texas is among the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant fig cultivars grown in Texas home orchards, tolerating both harder winter freezes and drier soil than many other figs. Fruit is medium-sized with brownish-purple skin and sweet, deep amber-pink flesh with a rich, honeyed flavor, ripening over a long harvest window from summer into fall. Even where winter cold kills the top growth to the ground, the vigorous root system reliably resprouts and fruits again the following year, making it a forgiving choice for the cooler edge of fig-growing range. Prune to control size and remove winter-killed wood in spring once new growth reveals what survived.

common_name: Republic of Texas Lime (Cold-Hardy Thornless Lime)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Republic of Texas is grown widely as a large patio container plant in zone 8b–9 so it can be moved under cover on the coldest nights, and planted in the ground only in zone 9b–11 or the most protected zone 9a microclimates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a large container that can be sheltered during hard freezes; Republic of Texas is a nearly thornless lime of uncertain hybrid parentage that has become a favorite dooryard and patio citrus across the Gulf South because it is noticeably more cold-tolerant and heat-tolerant than true Key lime, while still delivering a strongly aromatic, classic lime flavor. Trees are vigorous, heavy-bearing, and begin fruiting young, producing abundant small to medium, thin-skinned, seedy fruit that ripens from pale green to yellow — harvest while still green for the brightest acidity, since fully yellow fruit turns sweeter and less lime-like. It is self-fertile and does not need a pollinizer. In zone 9a, site trees against a south-facing wall for extra winter protection and wrap or cover young trees during freeze events; established in-ground trees recover from light freeze damage by resprouting from the trunk. Fertilize with a citrus-specific blend three times during the growing season and keep the root zone mulched but not piled against the trunk.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring; Revival is a blight-resistant American-Chinese hybrid chestnut bred for precocious bearing and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set.
directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut trees for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Revival is an American-Chinese hybrid chestnut developed as part of the blight-resistant breeding lineage that also produced the well-known Dunstan chestnut, combining some of the American chestnut's tree form and nut quality with the Chinese chestnut's resistance to chestnut blight. Trees bear precociously, often within a few years of planting, and produce medium to large, sweet nuts that drop free of the burr for easy harvest in fall. Because it carries genuine blight resistance rather than simply avoidance, Revival can be planted with more confidence in areas with a history of chestnut blight pressure than pure American chestnut. Good heat tolerance makes it a reasonable choice for Gulf South food-forest and small-orchard plantings, though as with all chestnuts, well-drained soil and good air circulation help minimize disease pressure in humid summers.

common_name: Rhode Island Greening Apple (Classic Colonial-Era Tart Pie Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Rhode Island Greening dates to around 1650, one of the oldest apple varieties native to New England, and it became one of the most celebrated American cooking apples of the 18th and 19th centuries, prized for large, green to yellow-green fruit with firm, tart, aromatic flesh widely considered among the very best for pie-making, since it holds its shape and delivers bright, well-balanced flavor when baked. The vigorous, spreading tree bears heavily once established, and the fruit keeps reasonably well in cool storage through much of the winter. While less commonly planted commercially today than in its heyday, Rhode Island Greening remains a favorite among heirloom orchardists and bakers who specifically seek out its superior pie-apple qualities.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; riberry is an Australian native rainforest tree producing abundant, small (1/2-inch), vivid crimson, pear-shaped fruits with a sour-sweet, spicy flavor combining apple and clove-cinnamon notes — widely used in Australian native food products and highly regarded as a bushfood ingredient.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; riberry can be pruned as a formal hedge or left to grow as a specimen small tree. Syzygium luehmannii (riberry or small-leaf lillypilly) is an Australian native rainforest tree from the subtropical and warm-temperate rainforests of New South Wales and Queensland — one of the most commercially important of the Australian lilly pilly (Syzygium) species in the native food industry. The tree produces abundant clusters of small (1/2-inch), teardrop-shaped, vivid magenta-crimson fruits, and is one of the most prolific and reliable fruiting lilly pillies in the genus. The riberry flavor is unique and highly prized: sour, fruity, and sweet with distinctive warm cinnamon-clove spice notes from the high eugenol content — a flavor combination with no equivalent in European or American fruits. In Australian native food (bushfood) cuisine, riberries are used in jams, sauces, wines, ice creams, vinegars, and as a garnish for savory dishes — particularly with game, lamb, and cheese. As a landscape plant, riberry is compact, attractive, and responds very well to formal clipping into hedge shapes; the coppery-red new growth flushes make it ornamentally outstanding. Its combination of ornamental and food value makes it one of the best lilly pillies for zone 9–12 edible landscapes.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Ribston Pippin is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Ribston Pippin is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby. Raised in Yorkshire, England around 1707 and one of the two parent varieties of the famous Cox's Orange Pippin, it bears medium, orange-red-flushed, lightly russeted apples with rich, aromatic, sharp-sweet flesh that made it one of the most celebrated English dessert apples of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries before its own offspring largely eclipsed its popularity. As a triploid it produces sterile pollen and needs two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination, and it can be a somewhat biennial, uneven bearer from year to year. Harvest in mid-fall and store for a few weeks, during which the rich, sharp flavor continues to develop and mellow slightly.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Riesling is one of the more cold-hardy classic wine grapes and performs well in cooler climates unsuited to many other vinifera varieties.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Riesling is one of the more cold-hardy classic wine grapes and performs well in cooler climates unsuited to many other vinifera varieties. Late-ripening, aromatic, and capable of producing wines ranging from bone-dry to intensely sweet depending on when the grapes are picked, it retains bright, food-friendly acidity even at high sugar levels, a hallmark that has made it one of the most versatile and food-pairing-friendly white wine grapes grown worldwide. Its relatively high tolerance for winter cold makes it a realistic choice for home vineyards in cooler regions where more tender vinifera varieties struggle to survive, though it still needs a long growing season to fully ripen. Prune for an open canopy to promote airflow and reduce disease pressure, and consider harvest timing carefully, since flavor and sweetness profile change significantly the longer fruit hangs on the vine.

common_name: Rio Grande Peach (Texas-Bred Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; bred for roughly 400-500 chill hours, a dependable mid-season choice for the warmer half of zone 8 into zone 9.
directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bred in Texas for roughly 400-500 chill hours, Rio Grande is a dependable mid-season choice for the warmer half of zone 8 into zone 9 where many standard peaches underperform. It produces large yellow freestone fruit with a red blush, ripening in June with rich, classic peach flavor. Self-fertile and heat-tolerant, it needs hot, sunny summers to size its fruit properly and can disappoint in cooler, cloudier growing seasons. A good mid-season companion to earlier ultra-low-chill selections for a longer harvest window.

plant_note: Plant grafted container trees in spring after last cold risk; in zone 9 plant February–April in the warmest location with excellent drainage. Grapefruit requires more accumulated heat units than oranges to develop full sweetness — site in the hottest spot available. Rio Red ripens October through March in Texas and Florida.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, the warmest available location; Rio Red is a grapefruit cultivar developed at Texas A&M University through irradiation mutagenesis of Ruby Red stock and released in 1984 — and has since become the dominant commercial grapefruit variety in Texas, replacing both Ruby Red and Star Ruby on most commercial acreage. The fruit is the gold standard for Texas red grapefruit: large, with yellow skin blushed deep red-pink, and flesh that is deep crimson-red, very sweet (low acidity), with complex flavor and very few seeds. Rio Red's flesh has the deepest, most consistent red color of any commercially significant grapefruit variety, a characteristic valued by both fresh market buyers and for appearance when halved. The trees are vigorous and productive. Feed with citrus fertilizer 3–4 times annually and supplement with zinc and manganese chelate if leaves show deficiency symptoms on alkaline soils. Protect below 28°F. In zone 9 the long hot summers develop excellent sweetness and color in the fall crop.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil; riverbank grape is one of the most cold-hardy native grapes and has been used extensively in cold-climate wine grape breeding programs. It prefers moist, fertile bottomland soils but adapts to upland conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, fertile, loamy soil in full sun along riverbanks, fences, and arbors; riverbank grape is native to streambanks and forest edges across most of North America, from Quebec to Texas, and is one of the most cold-hardy wild grapes — surviving to zone 2. The small, highly fragrant flowers in spring are intensely honey-scented and attract numerous pollinators. The small, blue-black, tart grapes ripen after the first fall frost (hence 'frost grape'), becoming slightly sweeter and less astringent with cold exposure. This species has been critically important in wine breeding — it is a parent of numerous cold-hardy wine grape cultivars including 'Marquette', 'Frontenac', and 'Frontenac Gris' developed for cold northern climates. Also an important source of phylloxera-resistant rootstock for European wine grapes.

plant_note: Plant nursery trees in spring after frost risk passes, in a sunny, sheltered location.
directions: Plant nursery trees in spring after frost risk passes, in a sunny, sheltered location with well-drained soil enriched with organic matter. Keep the root zone evenly moist during establishment and reduce watering slightly as fruit begins to color to concentrate sugars. Robinson bears loose-skinned, richly flavored orange fruit that ripens earlier than most mandarins, often by early fall, but it tends toward seediness unless grown in isolation from other citrus. It is popular with Florida and Gulf Coast home growers for its dependable early harvest and moderate cold tolerance.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in part shade; robusta coffee (C. canephora) is the second most important commercial coffee species after arabica (C. arabica) — more disease-resistant, more drought-tolerant, and higher in caffeine than arabica, but with a harsher, more bitter, earthier flavor; widely grown for espresso blends and instant coffee production; the natural understory habitat of the species makes it well-suited to part-shade garden positions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in part shade; robusta coffee grows naturally as an understory shrub and performs best with afternoon shade in hot climates. Coffea canephora (robusta coffee or Congo coffee) is the second major commercial coffee species, accounting for approximately 40% of world coffee production — ranking second only to arabica (C. arabica) but distinctly different in origin, physiology, flavor, and agricultural use. C. canephora is native to the humid tropical forests of central and West Africa (particularly the Congo Basin region — hence 'Congo coffee'), where it grows as a spreading, multi-stemmed understory shrub. Robusta coffee has several significant differences from arabica: it is more disease-resistant (particularly to coffee leaf rust — Hemileia vastatrix — the devastating fungal disease that has devastated arabica crops worldwide); it is more drought-tolerant; it contains approximately twice the caffeine content of arabica (2–4% vs. 1.2–1.5%); and it can be grown at lower elevations and in hotter, more humid climates than arabica. These traits make robusta the preferred crop for hot, humid, lower-elevation tropical regions including Vietnam (the world's largest robusta producer), India, Ivory Coast, Uganda, and Indonesia. The flavor profile of robusta — stronger, more bitter, earthier, with woody and chocolate-cocoa notes — suits espresso blends (where it adds body and crema), instant coffee, and cold brew. In zone 10–12 gardens, both coffee species can be grown for home production and as ornamental shade-tolerant specimens.

plant_note: Plant in spring in extremely well-drained or rocky soil in full sun; avoid any soil that holds moisture as this palm of dry limestone mountains is prone to root rot in poorly drained sites.
directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining, lean soil — this native of dry Mexican limestone mountains thrives on neglect and is one of the most drought-tolerant palms available for zone 8-9 gardens. The silvery-blue fan leaves are similar to other Brahea species and provide striking year-round color; the palm is slow-growing but extremely long-lived. Small, dark, date-like fruits are produced in pendant clusters and are sweet and edible, though they are used mainly by local communities in Mexico for food, wine, and traditional crafts. Once established, reduce irrigation to near zero; overwatering is the most common cause of failure with this species.

plant_note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in a frost-free tropical site; biriba is among the faster-fruiting Annona relatives.
directions: Rollinia / biriba is an Annona relative from Amazonia that prefers deep, fertile, consistently moist soil and produces fruit faster than cherimoya or soursop under hot, humid conditions. Like other Annonaceae, the flowers exhibit protogynous dichogamy — the female stage opens first, closes, then reopens in the male stage — so hand-pollination at the correct time greatly increases fruit set: collect pollen from half-open flowers in the afternoon and apply to fully open receptive stigmas the following morning. The soft, custard-flavored fruit is covered in soft yellow spines and must be handled very gently — it bruises and ferments within hours of reaching peak ripeness. Harvest when the spines have softened and yellowed and the fruit gives noticeably to pressure; consume immediately or refrigerate for no more than 24 hours.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rollinia is damaged below 30°F and should be protected from frost. It grows faster and bears fruit at a younger age than cherimoya — typically fruiting within 3–4 years from seed. It tolerates wet soils better than most Annonaceae and thrives in high humidity.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; rollinia (biribá) is a South American tropical tree in the custard apple family, native to the Amazon basin and considered by fruit connoisseurs one of the finest fruits in the Annonaceae family — potentially superior to cherimoya and sugar apple in flavor. The fruits are large (often 4–6 inches across) and round to heart-shaped with distinctive, pointed tubercles (bumps) on the yellow-green exterior that turn golden-yellow at maturity. The interior is snow-white, sweet, translucent, and juicy — much moister and more refreshing than cherimoya — with a flavor combining banana, pineapple, and caramel with a sweet lemon-custard quality. The texture is extremely delicate, almost like thick cream, and it must be eaten immediately after harvest as it deteriorates within 1–2 days of ripening. Rollinia is faster-growing and more prolific than most Annonaceae and is better adapted to humid tropical conditions. It tolerates wet soils and high humidity better than cherimoya or atemoya. An important and growing orchard crop in tropical South America.

common_name: Rome Beauty Apple (The Baking Apple, Ohio Heirloom Baker, Rome)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep fertile soil in full sun; Rome Beauty is partially self-fruitful and will produce some crop without a pollenizer, though yields improve significantly with a companion variety; requires approximately 800 chill hours; well-adapted to zones 5–8, where late ripening (October–November) in the open orchard is feasible before killing frost; blooms late, reducing frost risk.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Rome Beauty is the classic baking apple and benefits from being cooked rather than eaten fresh — its firm, low-acid flesh holds structure beautifully under heat; harvest in October when fully colored deep red, typically after McIntosh and Empire are finished; baked whole apples with butter and brown sugar are the signature preparation. Rome Beauty (often sold simply as 'Rome') is an Ohio heirloom apple discovered as a branch sport on a seedling tree near Rome, Ohio (Lawrence County) by Joel Gillett around 1816, propagated by his neighbor Alanson Gillett, and introduced to the nursery trade in the 1840s where it rapidly became one of the most important American commercial apples of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The variety has an unusual characteristic that defines its culinary use: the flesh is relatively low in acid and somewhat dry in texture compared to most eating apples, which means it is not the most interesting variety for fresh consumption but becomes exceptional when baked — the firm flesh holds its shape without collapsing, the mild, sweet flavor concentrates under heat, and the large round shape makes it the ideal vessel for a whole baked apple filled with butter, sugar, and spices. For a century, 'Rome' and 'baking apple' were nearly synonymous in American cookery. The round, symmetrical, deep red to all-red appearance also made Rome Beauty particularly popular with retailers when unblemished fruit mattered; a barrel of large, perfectly round, uniformly deep-red Romes was among the most visually impressive of any apple variety.

plant_note: Plant dormant trees in early spring once the soil is workable.
directions: Romeo and Juliet are a pair of compact, extremely cold-hardy bush cherries that produce sweet, robust fruit good for snacking and baking. Plant both varieties near each other in full sun with well-drained soil to improve cross-pollination and yields. Space plants 5-8 feet apart and water consistently while young to establish strong roots. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain an open, productive shape. These dwarf trees stay small enough for backyard gardens and fruit reliably even in harsh winter regions.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Ronde de Bordeaux is a compact-to-medium fig tree well-suited to container growing and small gardens. In zone 9 it produces a breba crop in June–July and a main crop in August–October. The compact habit makes it one of the better figs for container growing in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Ronde de Bordeaux (Round Bordeaux) is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region producing small, round, dark-purple to nearly black-skinned fruits with brilliant deep red to garnet-colored flesh — one of the most richly colored of all fig varieties. The dark skin and brilliant interior make Ronde de Bordeaux a spectacular fresh eating fig and an equally attractive fig for jam and preserves where the deep color produces richly-hued products. The flavor is very sweet, rich, and slightly winey with the complexity associated with dark-skinned fig varieties. The compact tree habit makes Ronde de Bordeaux one of the most practical figs for home gardens and container growing — it produces prolifically despite its modest size. It is an early-maturing variety with the main crop ripening in late July–August in zone 9, among the earliest of the dark-skinned European fig types. This fig has become very popular among fig enthusiasts in zone 9 and zone 10 for its combination of early ripening, outstanding flavor, and manageable tree size.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rose apple is a medium-sized Myrtaceae tree suited to zones 10–12 that is prized for its ornamental showy white to pale yellow pompom flowers as much as for its fruit. Trees naturalize readily in humid tropical climates and are considered invasive in parts of Hawaii and other Pacific Islands — check local invasive species regulations before planting.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; rose apple (Syzygium jambos) is a medium-sized evergreen tree in the Myrtaceae family native to Southeast Asia that produces waxy, pale yellow to cream or blush-pink, oval fruits with a uniquely crisp, crunchy texture and a delicate, unmistakable flavor of rose water — floral, lightly sweet, and aromatic in a way unlike any other fruit. The fruits are primarily eaten fresh out of hand, and their distinctive rose fragrance also makes them popular for flavoring drinks, syrups, and desserts across Southeast Asia and the Caribbean. The tree produces spectacular ornamental flower clusters of long, creamy-white stamens resembling shaving brushes before fruit development, making it a dual-purpose landscape tree. Rose apple is adaptable, moderately fast-growing, and performs well with consistent moisture and regular balanced fertilization.

common_name: Rosseyanka Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Non-Astringent American-Asian Hybrid Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Rosseyanka is a cold-hardy hybrid of American and Asian persimmon developed in Ukraine, combining strong hardiness with fruit that becomes non-astringent when firm-ripe.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, staking young trees until established. Rosseyanka is a hybrid between the native American persimmon and Asian persimmon, developed in Ukraine to combine the cold hardiness of the American species with fruit quality closer to Asian persimmons, notably becoming non-astringent and pleasant to eat while still firm rather than requiring the full softening American persimmons need. It is a productive, vigorous tree well suited to a wider hardiness range than most pure Asian persimmon cultivars while still offering good fruit size and flavor. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest by clipping the fruit from the branch to avoid tearing the skin at the stem.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root grafted trees in spring; Rossiyanka is a cross between the American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) and the Oriental persimmon (Diospyros kaki) bred in Russia for extreme cold hardiness, tolerating winter lows to roughly -25 to -30°F once dormant while retaining the larger, less astringent fruit of its Asian parent.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; established trees are drought-tolerant and need little supplemental fertilization beyond a light annual feeding. Rossiyanka is a Russian-bred hybrid between the native American persimmon and the Asian kaki persimmon, developed to combine the extreme winter hardiness of the American parent with fruit size and eating quality closer to Asian types. The medium-large orange fruits are strongly astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point they turn sweet and jammy with a rich, honeyed flavor; frost or a period of cold storage speeds the softening. Self-fruitful and reliably productive once established, it is a good choice for growers who want Asian-persimmon-quality fruit in a climate too cold, or on a rootstock too marginal, for standard kaki cultivars, and it also performs well in the milder Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown vines in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Roucaneuf is a French-American hybrid grape (Seyve-Villard lineage) documented by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension as resistant to Pierce's disease and well suited to hot, dry Gulf South and Texas conditions.
directions: Train on a cordon trellis system in full sun in well-drained soil; prune in late winter. Roucaneuf is a complex French-American hybrid grape carrying genes from several wild American Vitis species alongside European vinifera, giving it real resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European wine grapes across the humid Gulf South within a few seasons. It is one of a small group of Pierce's-disease-resistant varieties recommended by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for gardeners and small growers in the region who want to make wine or juice without the constant disease losses that come with standard vinifera grapes. Harvest clusters once berries have colored and developed good sugar content, and expect the vigorous vines to need regular summer pruning to manage growth in a warm, humid climate.

plant_note: Plant grafted container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; rough-shell macadamia (M. tetraphylla) is marginally more cold-hardy than smooth-shell M. integrifolia, tolerating brief dips to about 24–26°F in established trees — slightly extending the zone range into protected zone 8b–9a sites; the prickly-edged leaves (unlike the smooth-edged M. integrifolia) distinguish the species.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; M. tetraphylla is slightly more cold-tolerant than M. integrifolia and may succeed in protected zone 8b sites. Macadamia tetraphylla (rough-shell macadamia or prickly-leaf macadamia) is the second of the two commercially important macadamia species — closely related to the smooth-shell macadamia (M. integrifolia) but distinguishable by its prickly-edged leaves arranged in whorls of four (the species name 'tetraphylla' means 'four-leaved'), and by the rough, ridged texture of its nut shell. Both species produce equally delicious, buttery, rich macadamia nuts with the same world-class flavor, and in commercial macadamia production, the two species and their hybrids are grown side by side with little practical flavor difference noted by consumers. The practical distinction for home growers is cold tolerance: M. tetraphylla is marginally more cold-hardy than M. integrifolia, typically tolerating temperatures of 24–26°F in established trees — potentially extending the range to protected zone 8b–9a microclimates in warm-wall or frost-pocket-free sites. M. tetraphylla is also slightly smaller in tree size. Both species benefit from cross-pollination, and planting one of each species is commonly recommended to ensure good nut set.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall on rocky or sandy, well-drained soil; this species naturally colonizes exposed outcrops and barrens where soil is thin and lean.
directions: Harvest berries when fully dark blue-black and extract seeds by mashing and rinsing before sowing in fall into lean, well-drained soil in a sunny outdoor bed. The round, coarsely toothed leaves that give this species its name are a useful identification feature as seedlings mature through their first growing seasons. Roundleaf Serviceberry tolerates shallow, rocky soils and gravelly barrens far better than most shrubs, making it a strong candidate for challenging landscape sites. Plants begin bearing their sweet, dark berries within 2–5 years of transplanting and attract a wide variety of frugivorous birds during the midsummer ripening period.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Roxburgh fig is a large-leafed fig native to the foothills of the Himalayas and Southeast Asia, producing enormous, rounded, elephant-ear leaves 12–24 inches across and clusters of large, brownish-red, edible figs that form directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory), similar to jackfruit.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Roxburgh fig grows rapidly and produces large clusters of edible figs. Ficus auriculata (Roxburgh fig or timla fig) is one of the most ornamentally dramatic and useful fruiting figs in tropical horticulture — a large, fast-growing tree from the Himalayan foothills and Southeast Asia producing the largest leaves of any commonly cultivated Ficus: enormous (12–24 inch), rounded, dark-green, slightly hairy leaves with a bold, tropical texture that gives the plant a genuinely dramatic visual presence, resembling a cross between a giant philodendron and an elephant ear. The figs are equally remarkable: large (1.5–2.5 inch), distinctly ribbed, brownish-red when ripe, produced in pendant clusters directly on the trunk and older branches (cauliflory) — the same unusual fruiting pattern as jackfruit. The figs are sweet, moist, seedy, and pleasant to eat fresh when ripe, with a mild, sweet flavor; they are also eaten as a cooked vegetable when unripe in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking (stewed, pickled, or curried). In Himalayan and hill-station gardens in India, Roxburgh fig is grown as a major multi-use tree; in zone 9–12 Gulf Coast gardens, it is an outstanding bold-textured ornamental that also produces an edible crop.

common_name: Roxbury Russet Apple (Oldest Documented American Apple Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Roxbury Russet is vigorous and productive, and its thick russeted skin gives the fruit outstanding storage life compared to smooth-skinned apples.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. First recorded in Roxbury, Massachusetts in the 1630s, this is the oldest apple cultivar documented as having originated in North America, predating the country itself by well over a century. The medium, dull yellow-green fruit is almost entirely covered in rough golden-brown russet, with firm, crisp, sweet-tart flesh well suited to fresh eating, cider, and long winter storage, since the thick skin sheds moisture slowly and resists shriveling. It ripens in mid-fall and was historically prized precisely because it kept so well through the winter months before refrigeration existed.

common_name: Royal Ann Cherry (Napoleon Cherry, Classic Light Sweet Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Royal Ann is self-unfruitful and requires a compatible pollinizer such as Black Tartarian or Van, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety is planted nearby. Royal Ann, known in Europe by its original name Napoleon, is a historic light-colored sweet cherry with pale yellow skin blushed with red and firm, sweet, translucent flesh, and it holds particular commercial significance as the primary variety historically used for maraschino cherries, since its light color takes dye and processing well. Beyond processing, Royal Ann is an excellent fresh-eating cherry, with a classic sweet flavor and firm texture that also makes it good for canning. The vigorous tree requires cross-pollination from another sweet cherry variety and grows quite large without size-controlling rootstock, so plan orchard spacing accordingly; harvest when fruit reaches full color and sweetness, since light-skinned cherries like Royal Ann do not continue ripening once picked.

common_name: Royal Crimson Cherry (Self-Fruitful Low-Chill Sweet Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Royal Crimson is self-fruitful and does not require a second cherry tree, though planting near Minnie Royal or Royal Lee will improve fruit set.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; unlike most sweet cherries, Royal Crimson is self-fruitful, so a single tree can produce a crop without a separate pollinizer, though a nearby second tree improves yields. Bred from the same low-chill program that produced Minnie Royal and Royal Lee, Royal Crimson needs only about 200 to 300 chill hours, allowing it to fruit reliably in warm-winter Southern gardens where classic sweet cherries fail to break dormancy properly. The tree bears large, crimson-red, sweet fruit in early to mid-spring, ahead of most other sweet cherries. Because the crop ripens and blooms so early, choose a well-drained site with good air movement to protect flowers from late frost.

common_name: Royal Lee Cherry (Low-Chill Southern-Adapted Sweet Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Royal Lee requires cross-pollination with its companion cultivar Minnie Royal, which blooms at the same time, and the pair is planted together as interlocking pollinizers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and always pair with Minnie Royal for pollination, since Royal Lee will not set a usable crop alone. Like its companion, Royal Lee needs only around 200 to 400 chill hours, making it one of the few sweet cherries genuinely worth trying south of the traditional cherry belt, including parts of the Gulf Coast and lower South with mild winters. Fruit is firm, dark red, and ripens early in the season, roughly two weeks ahead of Bing, giving Southern growers a short but real cherry harvest window. Select a sunny, frost-protected planting site, since the trees' early bloom leaves flowers exposed to any late cold snaps.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun to part shade on well-drained soil, staking young trees until they establish.
directions: Royal is a traditional English medlar cultivar grown for centuries for its russet-brown, apple-shaped fruit that must be bletted, or softened by frost and storage, before eating, developing a soft, spiced, wine-like flavor. Trees are small, gnarled, and self-fertile, producing single white blossoms in late spring followed by fruit that ripens hard on the tree into autumn. Harvest fruit after the first hard frost and store in a cool, dark spot for two to three weeks until the flesh softens and darkens before use in preserves or eaten fresh. The species tolerates a range of soils and needs little pruning beyond removing crossing or damaged branches.

plant_note: Plant the dormant or potted grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, watering regularly until established.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Royal Raindrops is a distinctive ornamental crabapple with deeply cut, purple-red, finely serrated foliage unlike the broad, rounded leaves of most crabapple cultivars, opening with a heavy flush of magenta-pink spring flowers followed by small, persistent red fruit that hangs on into winter as forage for birds. It shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases — apple scab, fire blight, cedar-apple rust — that plague many older crabapple cultivars, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a small flowering shade tree. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; the small, hard fruit persists well into winter, providing months of ornamental and wildlife value beyond the spring bloom.

common_name: Royal Rosa Apricot (Zaiger White-Fleshed Low-Chill Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Royal Rosa has a low chill requirement of roughly 300 hours, making it one of the few apricots reliable in mild-winter Southern California and similar warm zone 8-9 gardens.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid frost pockets, since early bloom makes flowers vulnerable to late cold snaps. Royal Rosa is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, and thinning developing fruit to a few inches apart improves size and prevents limb breakage. It is prized for pale creamy-white to blush-pink skin and sweet, low-acid, aromatic white flesh that distinguishes it from standard orange-fleshed apricots. Its unusually low chill requirement makes it a go-to choice for gardeners in mild-winter regions where Blenheim and Moorpark can bloom unevenly.

common_name: Rubinette Apple (Intensely Aromatic Swiss Dessert Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 5-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Rubinette is a Swiss apple with parentage tracing through both Golden Delicious and Cox's Orange Pippin, and it is widely regarded by connoisseurs as one of the most intensely aromatic and best-flavored modern apples available, delivering a complex, richly perfumed sweet-tart flavor reminiscent of its Cox heritage in a smaller, russet-blushed, red-striped fruit. The tree is only moderately productive compared with high-yield commercial varieties, a common tradeoff with exceptionally flavorful apples, but home orchardists focused on eating quality over sheer yield consider it well worth growing. Harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and enjoy fresh, since the fruit's aromatic complexity is best appreciated soon after harvest.

common_name: Ruby Red Grapefruit (Original Texas Pink Grapefruit, First US Plant Patent Recipient)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in spring; Ruby Red grapefruit is most successfully grown in the Rio Grande Valley of south Texas (zone 9b-10) and the Gulf Coast where the combination of warm summers and cooler winters produces the best red pigmentation development — the pink-red color intensifies with cooler temperatures and the fruit may remain pale in very mild winters. In zone 9 (Louisiana, Mississippi), grapefruit trees are near the northern cold limit and require frost protection when young and during severe cold events; mature trees can tolerate brief temperatures to 26–28°F. The fruit matures late (November–June), with peak quality typically in January–April. Ruby Red grapefruit should hang on the tree until fully mature — the bright pink flesh and sweet-tart flavor develop fully only at ripening and do not improve if picked early.
directions: Plant grafted tree in full sun, deep well-drained soil; mulch for moisture retention. Protect from frost in zone 9. Ruby Red is the original pink/red-fleshed grapefruit variety and one of the most historically significant citrus varieties in American horticulture: it holds the distinction of being the first variety to receive a US plant patent, issued February 4, 1930 (US Plant Patent 1), when Bonnie Nance's discovery of a pink bud sport on a Thompson grapefruit tree in Weslaco, Texas in 1929 was submitted by Stark Brothers Nursery. The story of Ruby Red begins in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas — one of the finest grapefruit-producing regions in the world — where the combination of warm days, cool nights, and alkaline soil produces grapefruit of exceptional sweetness and flavor. Ruby Red's pink flesh coloration comes from lycopene (the same pigment in tomatoes and watermelons) — a pigment that accumulates in the fruit's flesh during the cool nights of the growing season. The variety has less red pigmentation than its descendants (Rio Red and Star Ruby, which were developed specifically for deeper coloration), but it was the original breakthrough that made pink grapefruit a distinct commercial category. The fruit is large (3–5 inches), mildly fragrant, with blushed pink skin and sweet, mildly acidic, aromatic flesh that made pink grapefruit the preferred fresh-eating grapefruit variety in American markets through the mid-20th century.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted or potted tree; move outdoors after frost.
directions: Ruby Supreme is a tropical guava that bears fragrant fruit with sweet, pink-red flesh rich in flavor and nutrition. This fast-growing evergreen fruits young and adapts well to containers, making it accessible even where winters are cold. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and feed regularly during the warm season for the heaviest crops. Keep the soil evenly moist, prune to maintain a manageable size, and bring potted trees indoors before frost.

plant_note: Plant bare-root shrubs in late winter or early spring; rugosa rose establishes quickly and begins producing hips in its second or third year.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil including poor sandy or salty soils where few shrubs survive; rugosa rose is extraordinarily tough and requires almost no maintenance once established. The intensely fragrant single or semi-double flowers in magenta, pink, or white bloom repeatedly from late spring to fall, followed by the largest and most nutritious rose hips of any commonly grown species — orange-red to scarlet tomato-shaped hips up to 1 inch in diameter that are exceptionally rich in vitamin C. Hips are harvested after the first frost when fully soft and red for rosehip tea, syrup, jam, and wine. The dense, thorny habit makes an excellent barrier hedge. Remove only dead wood; avoid hard pruning, which disrupts repeat flowering.
