plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Shinseiki is one of the most widely grown Asian pears, producing medium-large yellow fruits that are juicy, crisp, and mild-flavored, excellent for Gulf Coast and mild-climate orchards where low-chill Asian pears perform better than European pears.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; requires a pollinator — plant with Nijisseiki, Hosui, or another compatible Asian pear variety for good fruit set. Shinseiki (Japanese for 'New Century') is one of the most important commercial and home-garden Asian pear cultivars worldwide, bred in Japan in 1945 and widely grown in California, Oregon, and southern states; it produces medium-large (6–10 oz), round, smooth-skinned, pale yellow to cream-yellow fruits in August with crisp, white, juicy flesh and mild, refreshing, lightly sweet flavor. Low-chill requirement (approximately 300 chill hours) makes it excellent for Gulf Coast, Texas, and California gardens where traditional European pears fail. Fruits store well for 2–3 months refrigerated; highly productive and relatively disease-resistant compared to European pears. Cross-pollinate with Nijisseiki, Hosui, or another Asian pear for best yields.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Shiro is a Luther Burbank introduction from 1899 and remains one of the most widely grown Japanese plums in American home orchards — a vigorous, very productive yellow-fruited variety with a reliably sweet, mild flavor and early ripening that makes it one of the first summer stone fruits to harvest.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; requires a pollinator — plant with Santa Rosa, Methley, Beauty, or another Japanese plum for best fruit set. Shiro plum was introduced in 1899 by Luther Burbank, America's preeminent fruit breeder, as part of his extensive Japanese plum improvement program; it remains one of the most popular and widely grown Japanese plums more than 125 years after its introduction, prized for very early ripening (late June to July), consistent heavy production, and large, round, golden-yellow fruits with thin, transparent yellow skin and sweet, mild, honey-flavored yellow flesh. Chill requirement is approximately 400–500 hours, making it suitable for zones 5–9 but less reliable in the lowest-chill Gulf Coast areas. The large crops ripen quickly and have short shelf life; fruit should be harvested when skin turns fully yellow and fruit gives to gentle pressure. An excellent pollinator for other Japanese plum varieties.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring; needs only about 375 chill hours, the lowest of the Israeli low-chill group.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Also bred by Chanan Oppenheimer at Rehovot in Israel, Shlomit has the lowest chill requirement of the Israeli low-chill group at roughly 375 hours, blooming as early as March in warm climates. It ripens from late June through mid-July, ahead of Michal, Elah, and Maayan but slightly behind Anna. Fruit is large and round with light-to-medium yellow skin brushed with a rusty red blush over about a quarter of its surface, and the crisp, highly juicy flesh makes it a solid fresh-market choice for Gulf South backyard orchards. It shares bloom timing closely enough with Anna and Dorsett Golden to serve as a useful cross-pollinator.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; Shockley is a small-fruited Georgia heirloom apple from the early 1800s celebrated for extraordinarily long storage life, historically keeping in a root cellar into the following spring without refrigeration.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Shockley is a Georgia heirloom apple dating to the early 1800s, once one of the most widely planted commercial apples in the South before refrigerated shipping and storage made its greatest strength less essential: fruit stored in a cool root cellar could reportedly keep in good eating condition into the following spring, an almost unmatched keeping quality among apples of any era. Fruit is small, yellow with a red blush, firm and crisp with a mildly sweet, slightly tart flavor that some describe as unremarkable fresh off the tree but that mellows and improves markedly in storage, developing a richer, more complex flavor over weeks and months. Trees are vigorous, productive, and relatively disease-resistant for an older Southern heirloom, ripening late in the season. Plant with another apple variety nearby for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation and disease prevention in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or cuttings in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; shortleaf fig grows naturally in tropical hardwood hammocks and coastal strand of south Florida and the Keys, often germinating in the crevices of strangler fig fashion — growing down aerial roots to eventually envelope host trees.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; shortleaf fig is the native banyan tree of south Florida and the Florida Keys — a hemiepiphytic strangler fig in the Moraceae family that begins life as an epiphyte in the crevices of trees or walls before sending down aerial roots that fuse around the host, eventually forming a trunk that can outlive the original host. Related to and similar in growth habit to the more commonly planted Florida strangler fig (Ficus aurea), shortleaf fig is distinguished by its somewhat smaller, more oval-rounded leaves with a distinctive drip tip. The small, rounded figs produced on short stalks are consumed by white-crowned pigeons, mockingbirds, and other subtropical birds. A critically important food source for south Florida's native bird community. More cold-sensitive than strangler fig, and restricted to zone 10–12. Used in native-plant gardening in Dade and Monroe Counties for habitat restoration.

common_name: Siam Ruby Banana (Striking Red-and-Green Striped Ornamental Banana)
plant_note: Plant container or divided pups after all frost danger has passed in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Siam Ruby is grown chiefly as a dramatic ornamental foliage banana for its vivid red-and-green striped leaves rather than for reliable fruit production outside true tropical climates.
directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, watering generously and feeding regularly through the growing season to support the fast, lush growth typical of ornamental bananas. Siam Ruby is prized above all for its spectacular foliage, with broad leaves striped and mottled in deep wine-red over green in an ever-shifting pattern that makes it one of the showiest tropical-look foliage plants for a Gulf South summer landscape, whether in a large container or planted directly in a bed. While it can produce small bananas in long, warm growing seasons, it is grown primarily as an ornamental rather than for reliable fruit in most of its hardiness range. In zone 8-9 gardens the top growth is usually killed by winter frost but the underground rhizome often survives with heavy mulching, resprouting in spring; in colder areas, dig and overwinter indoors or grow in a large movable container.

plant_note: Fall-sow stratified seed outdoors, or plant bare-root or container nursery stock in early spring; Sierra plum is largely self-incompatible, so plant two or more seedlings or a second Prunus subcordata clone nearby to ensure good fruit set.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Sierra plum is a thicket-forming small tree or large shrub native to the mountains of California and southern Oregon, valued by home orchardists and native plant gardeners for its drought tolerance, fragrant white spring flowers, and small, tart-sweet red-to-purple plums that ripen in late summer. Fruit quality is variable from seed, so growers who want reliable, larger fruit often select and propagate superior wild clones by cuttings or grafting. The species is tough and adaptable to rocky, thin mountain soils and needs little supplemental water once established, but it suckers readily and can form dense thickets if not managed. Fruit is traditionally used fresh, for jam and jelly, and was an important food source for indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest and California.

common_name: Sihong Jujube (Dense Crisp Caramel-Flavored Fresh-Eating Jujube)
plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; Sihong is a widely acclaimed Chinese jujube cultivar rated by American growers among the best-tasting available, with dense, crisp, caramel-flavored flesh, ripening September.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than nearly any other fruit tree once established. Sihong is one of the most highly regarded jujube cultivars grown in the United States, consistently rated by fruit collectors and evaluation trials among the best-tasting available, prized for its dense, exceptionally crisp texture and rich, caramel-like sweetness that develops fully as the fruit ripens to a mahogany-brown color in September. It bears within its first few years and, like other jujubes, tolerates Gulf South heat, humidity, and periodic drought with minimal input once established. Harvest at the fully colored, slightly wrinkled stage for peak sweetness, and expect vigorous root suckering, which can be managed by mowing or used to propagate additional trees.

common_name: Silk Hope Mulberry (Southern Heirloom Black Mulberry)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; Silk Hope is a Southern heirloom black mulberry passed down through generations of home orchards for its rich, wine-dark fruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Silk Hope is a Southern heirloom black mulberry, named for the small North Carolina community where it was long cultivated and passed down among home orchardists for its rich, deep-purple-black fruit and dependable production. The elongated berries are intensely sweet with a wine-like depth of flavor considered by many mulberry enthusiasts to surpass the milder white and red mulberry types more commonly sold. Like other black mulberries it is somewhat slower-growing and less cold-hardy than white mulberry hybrids, but well suited to Gulf South heat and long growing seasons once established. Trees tolerate poor soil and drought once established, needing little more than occasional deep watering during extended dry spells. Site female-fruiting trees well away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the ripe, juicy berries drop over an extended summer harvest window and stain hard surfaces.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in zone 8–11; Silver Date Palm is the most widely distributed wild date palm of the Indian subcontinent — native to India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka — producing edible, small, orange-to-dark-brown dates and a fermented sap (toddy) of cultural and economic importance, while also being one of the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant ornamental date palms available.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, alkaline-tolerant soil; Phoenix sylvestris is drought tolerant once established and adapts well to alkaline, calcareous, and slightly saline soils — water regularly only in establishment; excellent for hot, dry, alkaline landscape positions in zone 8–11. Phoenix sylvestris (Silver Date Palm, Indian Date Palm, or Wild Date Palm) is a large, majestic, single-trunked feather palm native to the plains and hills of the Indian subcontinent — India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Sri Lanka — where it is one of the most culturally and economically important wild palms. The silvery-gray crown of long, recurving, pinnate fronds gives the palm a distinctively glaucous, blue-silver appearance that differs from the common date palm (P. dactylifera). The fruits are small (1 inch), orange-to-brown dates — edible but less sweet and more fibrous than commercial dates. The primary economic use is 'toddy' production: tapping the crown to collect sweet sap, which is fermented into palm wine, distilled into arrack, or boiled into jaggery (palm sugar). Phoenix sylvestris is substantially more cold-hardy than many date palms — tolerating temperatures to 18–22°F when established — making it excellent for zone 8b–9 date-palm landscapes. Outstanding ornamental and shade palm for Gulf Coast, Southwest, and Mediterranean-climate gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring next to a sturdy arbor, fence, or trellis; silver vine is dioecious, so a male and female plant are both needed for fruit, though many gardeners grow it strictly for its cat-attracting foliage and stems rather than for the fruit.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun on a sturdy support, since this is a vigorous twining vine related to kiwifruit; silver vine is best known in the West as a potent feline attractant, with dried leaves, wood, and galls used in cat toys because most cats respond to its nepetalactol compounds even more strongly than to catnip. Left to grow, it produces heart-shaped leaves that often develop a distinctive silvery-white blaze in summer, small white fragrant flowers, and yellow-orange fruit on female vines pollinated by a male plant; the normal fruit is edible though mild and rarely prized, while galled fruit caused by a gall wasp has a long history of use in traditional Japanese medicine. Because the vine is very vigorous and twining, give it a sturdy arbor or fence well away from smaller plants it could overwhelm, and expect enthusiastic garden cats to rub, chew, and roll on any part of the plant they can reach, which can slow young vines' establishment.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Silverhill, named for the jujube-growing community of Silverhill, Alabama, is a heat- and humidity-adapted selection well suited to Gulf South conditions.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Silverhill, named for the jujube-growing community of Silverhill, Alabama, is a heat- and humidity-adapted selection well suited to Gulf South conditions. This historic American jujube selection traces to the early twentieth-century Gulf Coast jujube plantings around Silverhill and Fairhope, Alabama, where USDA plant introductions from China were trialed and locally adapted decades before jujube saw its recent surge in popularity. It bears medium, round to oval fruit with crisp, sweet, apple-like flesh at the green-mature stage, sweetening further and wrinkling like a date as it ripens to mahogany-brown, and the tree is notably tolerant of the humid, disease-prone summers that can trouble jujube varieties bred for drier climates. Once established the tree is extremely drought-tolerant, largely pest-free, and requires only light pruning to maintain an open shape; harvest fruit in stages from crisp-green through fully wrinkled-brown depending on preferred texture.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Silverhill is an old, cold-hardy satsuma selection long grown along the central Gulf Coast and is a good choice where winter lows occasionally dip lower than a typical satsuma can tolerate.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting it in a warm microclimate such as near a south-facing wall in the cooler parts of its range. This satsuma selection takes its name from the historic citrus-growing community of Silverhill in Baldwin County, Alabama, once a center of satsuma production shipped north by rail in the early 20th century. Like other satsumas, the small, deep-orange fruit is essentially seedless with loose, easy-to-peel skin and sweet, mild flesh, ripening from October into December. The tree is notably cold-hardy for a satsuma, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s°F once mature, which made it a mainstay of small Gulf Coast dooryard orchards.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; simpson stopper is native to the coastal hammocks and pinelands of South Florida and the Keys and is one of the most wildlife-valuable native shrubs for zone 9b–11 gardens. Tolerates salt spray and brief flooding; very drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; simpson stopper is a Florida-native small tree or large shrub with flaking cinnamon-colored bark, glossy dark green oval leaves, and small white flowers with prominent stamens that have a pleasant spicy fragrance — the flowers are followed by small, orange to red, berry-like fruits that are edible and have a pleasantly spicy, aromatic flavor used for wildlife food, flavoring, and nibbling fresh. The peeling bark is one of the most distinctive features, revealing warm salmon-cinnamon tones beneath. Native to the coastal hammocks, pine rocklands, and tropical hardwood hammocks of South Florida and the Florida Keys, it is exceptionally well-adapted to the calcareous, well-drained soils of peninsular Florida and tolerates salt spray, drought, and partial shade. An important nectar source for butterflies and the berries are eaten by many species of birds and wildlife, making it an outstanding Florida native wildlife plant for landscapes in zone 9b–11.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to very dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; singleleaf pinyon is the most drought-tolerant of the pinyons, native to the driest Great Basin and Mojave desert transition habitats at 3,500–9,500 feet elevation.
directions: Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to very dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; singleleaf pinyon pine is the botanical oddity of the pine family — the only pine in the world with one needle per fascicle (bundle) rather than the 2–5 needles typical of all other pines. The stout, curved, single needle is one of the most distinctive identification features in the western flora. The dominant tree of the Great Basin at mid-elevations — forming the classic Nevada and Utah basin-and-range piñon-juniper woodland with Utah juniper (Juniperus osteosperma) across millions of acres of the intermountain West. Produces large, wingless, edible pine nuts (piñon nuts) comparable in size and quality to the two-needle pinyon's nuts — both species' nuts are harvested commercially and by Native peoples. The nuts are an essential fall food for many Great Basin birds and mammals, including pinyon jays, Clark's nutcrackers, and mule deer. An exceptional xeriscape tree for hot, dry, rocky Great Basin and Mojave-edge gardens.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sinton is among the most cold-hardy of the historic citrangequats, tolerating winters that would kill standard citrus.
directions: Sinton was bred alongside the better-known Thomasville and Telfair citrangequats in the early 1900s by USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle, crossing cold-hardy citrange (trifoliate orange x sweet orange) with kumquat to create an edible-skinned, tart-sweet novelty citrus for the coldest edge of the citrus range. Small, rounded, orange fruit has an aromatic marmalade-type flavor best suited to preserves and candying rather than fresh eating. The tree is a compact, thorny large shrub well suited to Gulf Coast hobbyist plantings where standard citrus struggles to survive hard freezes. Give it full sun, good drainage, and winter protection for young trees to get established.

common_name: Sioux Pecan (High Kernel-Percentage Type I Pecan)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Sioux is a Type I pollen shedder, so pair it with a Type II variety such as Choctaw, Caddo, or Elliott for cross-pollination. Its more compact growth habit than most pecans suits smaller home orchard spacing at the tighter end of the range.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sioux, released from the USDA breeding program in Texas, produces small to medium nuts but is valued for an exceptionally high kernel percentage and rich, sweet flavor that makes it a favorite among home growers for eating fresh out of hand. Its smaller, more manageable tree size compared to old-line pecans like Stuart makes it a good fit for home orchards with limited space. It is a Type I pollinator and needs a Type II variety nearby for good nut set. Scab susceptibility is a real concern in humid Gulf Coast conditions, so Sioux performs best in drier inland areas or with a fungicide spray program during wet springs; irrigate deeply during nut fill for the best kernel quality.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; slimleaf pawpaw is adapted to dry, sandy pinelands and needs sharper drainage than the common pawpaw of the eastern woodlands.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; slimleaf pawpaw is adapted to dry, sandy pinelands and needs sharper drainage than the common pawpaw of the eastern woodlands. Narrow, willow-like leaves and creamy white to pale yellow, nodding flowers set this small shrubby tree apart from the common pawpaw, and it bears small, fragrant, yellow-green fruit with the characteristic custardy pawpaw flavor, though smaller and less commonly harvested than named common pawpaw cultivars. Native to the fire-maintained sandhill and scrub habitats of Florida, Georgia, and the western Gulf coastal plain, it is well adapted to the region's characteristic dry, sandy, nutrient-poor soils and periodic natural fire, resprouting readily from its root system after top damage. It serves the same role as other pawpaws as a larval host plant for zebra swallowtail butterflies and needs little supplemental water once its extensive root system is established in sandy soil.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or bare-root plants in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; blackthorn is an extremely tough, thorny, wildlife shrub excellent as a stock-proof hedge and for its small, tart, blue-black fruits used in sloe gin and preserves.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs or bare-root plants in spring in any well-drained soil — poor, thin, alkaline, or rocky — in full sun to partial shade; blackthorn is one of the most adaptable and tough woody plants available, tolerating exposure, drought, poor soil, and neglect. Prunus spinosa is a very thorny, dense, suckering European native shrub that flowers brilliantly in early spring with masses of small, white blossoms on bare black stems before the leaves appear, creating a spectacular display; the flowers are followed by small (1/3–1/2 inch), round, blue-black fruits (sloes) with a white bloom, astringent flesh, and complex flavor that is unpalatable raw but transforms with frost and sugar into excellent jams, jellies, wine, and the essential ingredient of sloe gin. The dense, thorny thickets provide superb nesting habitat for birds and small mammals. Harvest sloes after the first frost for best flavor.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; small viburnum is native to moist streambanks and wet flatwoods of the Southeast and tolerates periodic flooding better than most viburnums.
directions: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; small viburnum is an underused evergreen to semi-evergreen native of Florida and the Gulf Coastal Plain, valued for its small, glossy, spoon-shaped leaves, masses of tiny white flower clusters in early spring before most plants awaken, and the bright red to dark purple-black drupes that provide exceptional wildlife food in summer and fall. Unlike many large viburnums, small viburnum stays naturally compact, to 6–8 feet in cultivation, and responds well to pruning — it can be maintained as a low hedge or specimen shrub. Very drought tolerant once established despite its riparian origins. The cultivar 'Mrs. Schiller's Delight' stays under 3 feet with particularly glossy foliage. An excellent choice for shaded understory positions and moist areas in zone 8–10 landscapes.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Smokehouse originated in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania in the early 1800s, reportedly discovered as a seedling growing near a farm smokehouse, and it became a widely planted, dependable all-purpose apple across the Mid-Atlantic for over a century. The medium to large fruit has yellow skin streaked and blushed with red, and the crisp, firm, juicy flesh carries a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that performs equally well fresh, baked, and pressed for cider, a genuine multipurpose apple in the old farmstead tradition. The vigorous, productive tree bears reliably and holds fruit reasonably well in storage, making it a solid choice for home orchardists who want a historic variety without the finicky habits of some rarer heirlooms.

plant_note: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip after the last frost in fast-draining soil in full sun, or grow in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter; Smooth Cayenne is the classic commercial pineapple, needing about 18-24 months from planting to fruit.
directions: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Smooth Cayenne is the classic commercial pineapple cultivar grown throughout the tropics for its large, cylindrical, juicy, sweet-tart fruit with relatively smooth, spineless leaf margins that make handling far easier than older spiny pineapple types. Plants form a low rosette of stiff, strap-like leaves and take 18-24 months from planting to produce a single fruit at the center of the rosette, after which side suckers can be removed and replanted to start new plants. Because pineapple has essentially no frost tolerance, zone 9 gardeners should grow it in a large container that can be moved to a greenhouse, garage, or bright indoor spot before the first freeze, bringing it back outside once nights stay reliably above 50F. Full sun, warmth, and free-draining soil or potting mix are the main requirements for good fruit size and flavor.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or root divisions in spring in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; smooth sumac spreads aggressively by root suckers to form large colonies and should be sited where this spreading habit is acceptable or where it can be managed by periodic mowing at the colony perimeter.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; smooth sumac is the most cold-hardy North American sumac, naturally colonizing roadsides, old fields, and dry slopes throughout most of the continent. It is distinguished from staghorn sumac (R. typhina) by its smooth stems — staghorn has velvety, fuzzy new growth resembling a stag's antler in velvet. The brilliant, fire-engine-red fall color of smooth sumac is among the most spectacular of any native shrub, often turning color before most other plants. The large, upright, cone-shaped clusters of fuzzy, dark red berries persist through winter and are critically important food for numerous birds including robins, catbirds, mockingbirds, and cedar waxwings. Spreads by root suckers to form thicket colonies — an excellent native for erosion control on dry slopes but needs containment near formal gardens.

common_name: Smyrna Quince (Classic Large Fragrant Turkish Quince)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and begins bearing within a few years of planting, producing hard, aromatic fruit that is typically cooked rather than eaten raw.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Smyrna is one of the classic Old World quince cultivars, originating in Turkey and long grown commercially in the eastern Mediterranean, producing large, golden-yellow, intensely fragrant fruit prized for preserves, quince paste (membrillo), and poaching, since the hard, tart flesh is rarely eaten raw. The tree is self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator, and blooms with attractive pale pink spring flowers before setting fruit that ripens in fall. Quince trees are generally low-maintenance once established, tolerating a range of soil types, though good air circulation helps reduce fire blight risk in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after removing the fleshy seed coat in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; soap tree grows naturally in coastal hammocks and scrub of south Florida and the Caribbean and is drought and salt tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; soap tree is a small evergreen to semi-evergreen tree of the Caribbean and south Florida with pinnately compound leaves and clusters of small white flowers followed by translucent, fleshy, amber fruits containing high concentrations of saponins — natural soap compounds. The crushed or moistened fruits lather readily in water and have been used throughout the Caribbean for centuries as soap for washing clothes and hair. Unlike the more common western soapberry (S. drummondii) of the southern plains, soap tree is a subtropical to tropical species better adapted to the hot, humid conditions of south Florida. The fruits are also used in some ayurvedic traditions and in natural cleaning products. A drought-tolerant, low-maintenance native tree providing both ornamental interest and functional soap production for eco-conscious gardeners in zone 9–11.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; wingleaf soapberry is native to rocky limestone soils, coastal chaparral, and sandy plains of southern Texas through Mexico and is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; soapberry is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in poor, alkaline soils. Sapindus saponaria (wingleaf soapberry or wild China tree) is a native Texas, Caribbean, and tropical American tree producing clusters of small, round, translucent, amber-gold berries in fall that contain saponins — the natural soap compounds that give the genus its Latin name (Sapo = soap, Indus = Indian, originally referring to 'soap nut from the New World'). When the berry flesh is worked with water, it creates a genuine, biodegradable, soap-like lather that has been used by indigenous peoples and settlers for washing clothes, hair, and skin for centuries; the berries are the same 'soapnuts' sold in natural products stores as a biodegradable laundry detergent. The tree is a handsome, medium-sized shade tree with pinnately compound leaves, small white flowers, and attractive amber berries that persist into winter. The hard, black seeds inside the berries have traditionally been used as beads. Outstanding for low-maintenance, drought-tolerant landscaping in the Gulf South, especially on alkaline soils.

plant_note: Sow seeds 3–4 per location, thin to best plant, or start transplants 6–8 weeks before transplanting after frost danger passes in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; 'Solo' papayas are bisexual (hermaphrodite) or female — plant two plants together and cull males (identified by long-stalked clusters of tubular flowers) to ensure cross-pollination.
directions: Sow seeds directly or start transplants in warm soil in full sun after frost danger passes; 'Solo' papaya is the classic Hawaiian commercial papaya developed at the University of Hawaii, the standard against which most commercial papayas are measured — a compact tree producing pear-shaped to round fruits averaging 0.5–2 pounds with deep orange-yellow flesh, exceptional sweetness, and a very small seed cavity. The 'Solo' name refers to being a manageable single-serving size (as opposed to the enormous Mexican papayas). 'Solo' plants may be hermaphrodite (bisexual, which set cylindrical fruits and are preferred for fruit quality), female (which require a male pollinator and produce more spherical fruits), or occasionally male (identified by long dangling chains of tubular flowers and producing no fruit). Plant 2–3 plants and remove males unless one is needed for pollination; bisexual plants are preferred and produce the finest fruit shape. In zone 9, 'Solo' papaya grows as a productive short-lived perennial but needs frost protection; it fruits within 6–10 months from seed, producing continuously in warm weather. The University of Hawaii's 'Rainbow' Solo is the transgenic PRSV-resistant variant widely grown commercially in Hawaii.

common_name: Somerset Redstreak Apple (Historic Bittersweet Cider Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Somerset Redstreak is a vigorous, spreading tree that benefits from a wide planting spacing.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Somerset Redstreak is a vigorous, spreading tree that benefits from a wide planting spacing. A traditional West Country English cider apple distinct from the unrelated old Redstreak variety once famous in Herefordshire, it produces a reliable crop of medium, red-streaked bittersweet fruit valued by cider makers for good, well-balanced tannin and juice yield in a full-flavored traditional English-style cider blend. Its vigorous, spreading growth habit and reliable annual bearing have kept it in cultivation in traditional Somerset cider orchards for generations, even as many other historic regional varieties have become rare. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

common_name: Somerset Seedless Grape (Extremely Cold-Hardy Spicy-Sweet Red Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; exceptionally cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 3-7.
directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Somerset Seedless was bred by pioneering grape breeder Elmer Swenson in Wisconsin, developed for extreme cold hardiness that lets it survive winters far too harsh for most table grapes, while still producing small, red, seedless berries with a sweet flavor carrying a distinctive light spiciness reminiscent of some native American grape species in its parentage. This combination of genuine cold hardiness and good eating quality has made it one of the standard recommendations for far-northern home gardeners wanting a real seedless grape harvest. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Soncoya (Cabeza de Negro, Sincuya) is a large tropical fruit tree native to the dry Pacific coast forests of Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Costa Rica — bearing very large, spiny, round to oval fruits with a distinctively sweet, dense, orange-yellow custard flesh and a strong, complex aroma — an underappreciated relative of the more widely grown cherimoya and sugar apple.
directions: Plant Annona purpurea in full sun in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; water regularly during establishment and during fruiting; the tree is more drought-tolerant than Cherimoya or Sugar Apple once established; hand-pollinate flowers with a small brush during the female phase (when petals are slightly opening) to ensure fruit set, as natural pollinators may be absent outside the native range. Soncoya is the largest of the commercially relevant Annona fruits — with individual fruits commonly weighing 2–5 kg and occasionally much more — distinguished from the better-known custard apples by its dark-green, spiny surface (resembling a chestnut or sea urchin) and very dense, deep-orange to apricot-yellow flesh. The aroma is powerful and characteristic: sweet, musky, and fruity, sometimes described as a combination of mango, pineapple, and vanilla custard. The flesh is eaten fresh with a spoon scooped from the halved fruit; the flavor is very sweet and rich, though the large brown seeds must be removed. Soncoya is native to tropical dry forests of the Pacific coast of Central America and Mexico, making it better adapted to a pronounced dry season than most other Annonas; it performs well in zones with a dry winter season (zone 10–12 in Florida, Hawaii, and South Texas). Rarely seen in cultivation outside its native range but occasionally available from rare fruit nurseries.

plant_note: Sow fresh seeds in spring as soon as possible after extracting from ripe fruit; viability drops quickly with dry storage. Plant in deep containers or in situ at final spacing, as the taproot is sensitive to transplant disturbance.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with consistent moisture during the growing season; Soncoya is intolerant of frost and prolonged waterlogging but handles the heat and humidity of tropical climates better than its relative cherimoya. The large, spiny, orange-brown fruits weigh up to several pounds each and develop on the branches and trunk; they are ready to harvest when the skin begins to soften and the segments start to separate. The orange, fibrous interior pulp is most commonly processed into drinks, sorbets, and frozen desserts rather than eaten fresh due to its strong flavor. Hand pollination with a small brush, transferring pollen between flowers on different trees, can significantly improve fruit set.

plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sonora is self-unfruitful and requires a compatible pollinizer with overlapping early bloom time.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible early-blooming pollinizer variety is planted nearby. Sonora is a California almond variety valued for large, attractive, very soft-shell kernels that crack open easily by hand, along with sweet, well-flavored nutmeat that makes it popular for home orchards and specialty markets alike. The tree blooms early, which gives it a head start on the growing season but also increases exposure to spring frost risk during flowering, so site selection matters for reliable annual crops. Water deeply and regularly through the growing season, especially during kernel development, and harvest once hulls split open in late summer, allowing the nuts to dry thoroughly before storage to prevent mold.

common_name: Sops of Wine Apple (Ancient English Red-Fleshed Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Sops of Wine is an English heirloom dating back before the 1600s, one of the oldest named apple varieties still in cultivation, taking its evocative name from the old English custom of soaking bread ('sops') in cider or wine, since the flesh of this apple is streaked with a distinctive pink-red color reminiscent of wine-soaked bread when cut. The medium-sized, red-skinned fruit ripens early in the season, well ahead of most storage apples, with tart, aromatic flesh well suited to cooking and cider blending, and it has historically been valued for both its early ripening and its striking, unusual flesh color. As a variety carried by some of the earliest American colonists, it also has genuine historical significance for orchardists interested in colonial-era American fruit growing.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring before bud break.
directions: Sour (tart) cherries such as Montmorency are self-fertile, reliably productive, and significantly hardier than sweet cherries, making them the better choice for zones 4–6. They require 1000–1200 chill hours and tolerate heavier soils than sweet cherries do. Thin lightly to maintain canopy airflow and prune in early summer to manage brown rot pressure in humid climates. Harvest when fruit is fully red and slightly soft — tart cherries rarely sweeten on the tree and are best for cooking, preserving, or juice.

plant_note: Plant in spring in frost-free regions.
directions: The sour or Seville orange yields bitter, aromatic fruit that is the classic base for marmalade and its fragrant blossoms for perfume. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, protecting it from frost, and note that it is also widely used as a hardy, disease-resistant rootstock. Water deeply and feed during the growing season for steady growth. Harvest the deeply colored fruit in winter and use the tart juice and peel rather than eating it fresh.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost risk has passed; soursop requires truly tropical conditions and is limited to zone 11 and the most sheltered frost-free pockets of zone 10b.
directions: Soursop is a rapid-growing small tree bearing the largest fruit of the Annona genus — sometimes exceeding 10 pounds — with spiny dark-green skin and white, fibrous, intensely aromatic pulp that is used primarily in beverages and desserts. Like its relatives (cherimoya, sugar-apple), soursop flowers have a specialized pollination mechanism that benefits greatly from hand-pollination using a small brush or cotton swab in late afternoon. The tree prefers deep, well-drained loam and is sensitive to standing water, drought stress, and cold below 32°F. Harvest when the skin has darkened from bright green to dull olive-green, the spines soften, and the fruit yields to gentle pressing; ripen at room temperature for 1–2 days.

subcategory: Colombian tropical sapote Malvaceae fruit tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 10–12; South American Sapote (Chupa-chupa, Sapote Costeño) is a fast-growing tropical fruit tree from the lowland forests of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Brazil — bearing large, oval, salmon-orange fruits with very sweet, creamy, rich, apricot-orange flesh with a flavor combining apricot, peach, mango, and cream — among the finest-flavored of all Amazonian fruits and an important commercial fruit in Colombia.
directions: Plant Quararibea cordata in fertile, moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; water consistently throughout the year, maintaining soil moisture without waterlogging; the tree grows rapidly under good conditions and can begin fruiting in 3–5 years from a good-sized transplant. South American Sapote (chupa-chupa in Amazonian Colombia, where the name likely derives from the act of sucking the sweet flesh off the large seed) is one of the truly outstanding tropical fruits — combining the rich creaminess of mamey sapote with the bright tropical flavor of ripe apricot and mango in a way that is entirely its own. The orange-fleshed, salmon-skinned, football-sized fruits produced in large quantities on mature trees are eaten fresh out of hand or blended into juices, shakes, and ice creams. The tree is in the Malvaceae family (related to chocolate and kapok) and shares the fast growth and large size of its relatives. Fruiting is precocious for a tropical tree — beginning at 3–5 years from a good-quality transplant — and production can be heavy, with large trees bearing hundreds of fruits per season. Currently little-known outside Colombia and adjacent Amazonian countries but considered by tropical fruit enthusiasts as one of the best-tasting of all Neotropical fruits; wider cultivation in zone 10–12 tropical gardens is warranted.

common_name: Southern Bartlett Pear (Low-Chill Gulf Coast Bartlett Sport)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with a second pear cultivar (such as Warren, Hood, or Kieffer) for cross-pollination. Southern Bartlett is a chance sport of Bartlett found on an old Louisiana homestead, selected for its low chilling requirement of roughly 350-400 hours, letting it fruit reliably in Gulf Coast winters too mild for standard Bartlett.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Southern Bartlett is a chance sport of the classic Bartlett pear discovered on an old Louisiana homestead and selected specifically for its low chilling requirement, letting it set fruit reliably in the mild Gulf Coast winters that leave standard Bartlett trees short on the cold hours they need to flower well. It bears the same classic bell-shaped, buttery, sweet pear fruit familiar from Bartlett, ripening in mid to late summer. Like most European pears grown in the humid South, it remains more vulnerable to fire blight along the immediate Gulf Coast than truly blight-resistant Southern selections such as Warren or Ayers, so prune out and destroy any blighted shoots promptly and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth blight favors. Harvest while still firm and green-yellow, then ripen off the tree at room temperature for the best buttery texture and flavor.

common_name: Southern Belle Nectarine (Deep South Very-Low-Chill Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Southern Belle needs only about 150-200 chill hours, making it suitable for the mild winters of the Deep South and Gulf Coast where standard nectarines fail to bloom reliably.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Southern Belle is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer. Bred for the Gulf South, it produces yellow-fleshed fruit early in the season, giving warm-climate gardeners a nectarine option where most standard cultivars cannot accumulate enough winter chill to fruit well. Thin fruit after natural drop to improve size, and watch for brown rot and plum curculio, both common challenges for stone fruit in the humid Deep South. It performs best with a regular fungicide program suited to warm, humid summers.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained to moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; southern blackhaw is a tough, drought-tolerant native shrub or small tree of the southeastern US, producing clusters of dark blue-black, edible berries with a sweet, raisin-date flavor in fall — excellent wildlife food and an underused native food plant for zone 5–9 landscapes.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; very drought-tolerant once established — one of the most adaptable native shrubs for difficult sites. Viburnum rufidulum (southern blackhaw or rusty blackhaw) is a native deciduous shrub or small tree of the southeastern United States — found naturally in dry rocky woods, cedar glades, roadsides, and forest edges from Virginia south to Florida and west to Texas — and one of the most ecologically important and underused native fruiting shrubs for Gulf Coast wildlife gardens. The plant is distinguished from blackhaw (V. prunifolium) by its larger size, glossy dark-green leaves, and the distinctive rusty-red to reddish-brown fuzz (rufidulum = rusty) that covers the buds, new twigs, and leaf undersides. It produces large, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in spring, followed by large clusters of 1/3-inch, dark blue-black drupes (berries) in fall. The berries have a remarkable, sweet, prune-raisin-like flavor when fully ripe after frost — uniquely pleasant among native berries, and used by indigenous southeastern peoples for food. Birds (especially mockingbirds, bluebirds, and cedar waxwings) consume the fruit enthusiastically. The plant provides outstanding fall color (glossy burgundy-red), excellent winter bark interest, and remarkable drought tolerance — among the most xeric-adapted native shrubs for alkaline, rocky, and dry sites in the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; a single tree is self-fertile and will produce fruit without a pollinizer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; southern crabapple is the native crabapple of the southeastern United States, producing a spectacular display of intensely fragrant pink flowers in early spring and small (1/2–1 inch) yellow-green to red crabapples in late summer and fall. The crabapples are too tart to eat fresh but make outstanding jelly, cider, and preserved fruit with excellent pectin content. The flowers are superb for native bees; cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and deer consume the fruit through fall and winter. It tolerates the heat and humidity of zone 8–9 better than most crabapple cultivars and produces cleaner foliage with fewer disease problems in the warm South. A self-fertile tree, so only one is needed for fruit.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun. Southern Jewel is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine.
directions: Southern Jewel is a self-fertile black to deep-purple muscadine bred at the University of Florida from a cross of the bronze cultivar Granny Val and a large black selection. Its most distinctive trait is fruiting habit: berries form in tight bunches of roughly six to twelve that cling firmly to the stem rather than dropping individually, so whole clusters can be picked and handled like bunch grapes instead of gathering loose berries off the ground. The thin, tender skin and crisp, crunchy flesh make it especially well suited to fresh eating, with good disease resistance and heavy yields under humid Southern conditions. Grow on a sturdy arbor or trellis in full sun, and expect this warm-climate selection to perform best in the Gulf Coast and peninsular Florida heat it was bred for.

common_name: Southern King Pear (Low-Chill Self-Fruitful Gulf Coast Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Southern King needs only about 400 chill hours and is self-fruitful, making it a popular choice for home orchards around Houston and the Texas Gulf Coast.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Southern King is a low-chill Asian-European pear hybrid popular around Houston and the Gulf Coast of Texas, valued for reliable fruiting even after mild winters that leave higher-chill pears short on bloom, along with strong resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that devastates many European pear cultivars in humid Southern climates. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree will set fruit, though planting a second low-chill pear nearby can improve yields. Fruit is medium-sized with the sweet, mild flavor typical of Asian-pear influenced hybrids. Prune to an open, well-spaced framework to improve air circulation and further reduce fire blight risk, removing any blighted shoots promptly by cutting well below visible damage.

common_name: Southern Queen Pear (Low-Chill Fire-Blight-Resistant Mississippi Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Southern Queen, selected in south Mississippi, needs a low chill requirement and is grown across the Gulf South for its excellent fire blight resistance.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Southern Queen, a low-chill pear selected in south Mississippi, is grown throughout the Gulf South for its large, bell-shaped fruit with russet-bronze skin and its excellent resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that limits many European pear cultivars in the region's warm, humid conditions. It ripens with the mild, sweet flavor typical of Southern low-chill pear selections and pairs well with a second low-chill pear nearby for improved cross-pollination and yield. Prune to an open, well-spaced framework to maximize air circulation, and cut out any fire blight-infected shoots promptly well below the visible damage to prevent the disease from spreading into older wood.

plant_note: Collect and plant acorns immediately after falling in autumn — southern red oak acorns are biennial, meaning they require two growing seasons to mature on the tree. Press acorns 1 inch deep in well-drained, dry, acidic, sandy or loamy soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; southern red oak is a dominant canopy tree of the southeastern US Coastal Plain and Piedmont, thriving in the dry, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy soils that characterize much of the region. The distinctive leaves have a broadly lobed base with a narrow middle and a multi-lobed apex — sometimes described as bell-shaped — turning dark red in fall. The tree is a significant mast producer with small, round, bitter acorns consumed by deer, wild turkeys, squirrels, and many other wildlife species. It is more drought-tolerant and better adapted to dry sandy soils than northern red oak (Q. rubra), making it a preferred choice for tough Coastal Plain sites. Historically valuable as a timber tree and important in the ecology of southeastern pine-oak communities.

common_name: Southern Sensation Seedless Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun; Southern Sensation is a joint Texas A&M / University of Arkansas release, a Texas Superstar seedless table grape with proven long-term resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease that limits standard table grapes across the humid South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Southern Sensation is a Texas Superstar-designated table grape, a joint release from Texas A&M and University of Arkansas breeding programs, bred to combine yellow, thin-skinned, seedless fruit with strong flavor and years of demonstrated resistance to Pierce's disease — the bacterial disease spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European-type table grape varieties within a few years across the humid South and has long limited backyard grape growing in Texas and the Gulf region. It has outperformed standard seedless varieties like Flame Seedless in regional trials specifically for disease survival and fruit quality in southern conditions. Prune to a permanent cordon system in late winter, and thin crowded fruit clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation, which helps reduce fungal disease pressure in humid weather.

common_name: Southmoon Blueberry (UF Mid-Season Large-Berry Southern Highbush Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root plants in late fall to early spring in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Southmoon can tolerate higher pH (up to 6.0) compared to other highbush blueberries — a practical advantage in Gulf South soils where achieving pH below 5.0 can be challenging.
directions: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Southmoon is a University of Florida IFAS southern highbush blueberry introduction valued for its large berry size, excellent flavor, higher-pH tolerance than most highbush varieties, and vigorous upright growth habit that makes it one of the most productive and commercially successful southern highbush varieties. The large, light-blue to sky-blue berries are firm with a small, dry picking scar — the combination of large size, good flavor, and excellent firmness makes Southmoon outstanding for both fresh market and home garden production. Southmoon's relative tolerance for soil pH up to 6.0 (compared to the strict 4.5–5.5 requirement of most blueberries) is practically significant for Gulf South gardeners who have difficulty reducing clay soil pH — Southmoon performs in slightly less-acidic conditions where other varieties would show severe nutrient deficiency. Southmoon is mid-season (April–May in zone 9), producing its main crop after the early varieties (Jewel, Emerald) and before the latest-ripening types, making it valuable for extending the blueberry season as part of a multiple-variety planting. The vigorous, upright habit reaches 6–7 feet and benefits from annual post-harvest pruning to maintain productive, manageable size. A primary recommendation from University of Florida extension for Gulf South blueberry production.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with a second pear cultivar such as Hood or Flordahome for cross-pollination. Spalding is recommended by LSU AgCenter for southern Louisiana, ripening mid-September and useful for extending the Hood/Flordahome harvest window.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Spalding is explicitly recommended by the LSU AgCenter for southern Louisiana home orchards, prized for its fire-blight tolerance in the humid Gulf South and for ripening in mid-September, later than early-season selections like Hood and Flordahome, which extends the fresh pear harvest into fall. Fruit is used both fresh and for canning, with the firm, gritty texture typical of Southern-adapted pear selections bred more for reliability than the buttery texture of European dessert pears. Prune out and destroy any blighted shoots promptly and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth fire blight favors. Harvest while still firm, then ripen off the tree at room temperature.

common_name: Spanish Cherry (Bakul, Bullet Wood, Tanjong Tree)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy soil in full sun; Spanish cherry (bakul) is a slow-growing, long-lived tropical evergreen tree producing exceptionally fragrant, small white flowers used in Indian garlands and hair oil — the intensely sweet, jasmine-like fragrance of the dried flowers intensifies as they dry; the olive-sized, orange-red fruits are sweet-acid and edible.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy soil in full sun; Spanish cherry is slow-growing but long-lived and very low-maintenance once established. Mimusops elengi (Spanish cherry, bakul, or tanjong tree) is a slow-growing, long-lived tropical evergreen tree native to India, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, and the Pacific Islands — one of the most beloved ornamental and fragrance trees of the Indian subcontinent. The tree produces small (1/2-inch), white, star-shaped flowers with deeply fringed petals that emit an extraordinarily intense, sweet, jasmine-like fragrance — particularly at night. Remarkably, the fragrance of the flowers intensifies dramatically as they dry: fallen bakul flowers can perfume an entire courtyard for days after dropping, and dried bakul flowers are strung into garlands, threaded into women's hair (a classic Indian tradition), used in temple offerings, and dried for pot-pourri and perfume production. The sweet-acid, olive-sized, orange-red to orange fruits (the 'Spanish cherry') are edible — sweet, slightly astringent, with a pleasant, mild flavor — eaten fresh or used in preserves across the plant's native range. The hard, dense wood (bullet wood) is extremely durable. In zone 10–12 tropical gardens, bakul is an outstanding shade tree and long-term ornamental investment valued as much for its fragrance as its appearance.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; Spanish Lime (Genip, Mamoncillo, Quenepa) is a large, handsome, long-lived tropical evergreen tree native to the Caribbean and northern South America producing clusters of small, round, lime-green, thin-shelled fruits with a sweet-sour, salmon-to-orange, firm, jelly-like pulp clinging tightly to the seed — eaten by sucking or scooping the translucent pulp, a beloved street food of the Caribbean.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil; Melicoccus bijugatus is drought tolerant and adapted to calcareous, rocky, and coastal soils typical of the Caribbean — water regularly only in establishment and during flowering and fruit set. Melicoccus bijugatus (Spanish Lime, Genip, Mamoncillo, Quenepa, or Limoncillo) is a large, stately, long-lived evergreen tree native to Colombia, Venezuela, and the Lesser Antilles, now widely naturalized and cultivated throughout the Caribbean, Central America, and parts of Florida and Hawaii. The common name 'Spanish Lime' describes the fruit's appearance — small (1–1.5 inch), perfectly round, lime-green, thin-shelled, resembling a small lime — but the flavor is a sweet-sour, tropical, guava-lychee combination with firm, translucent salmon-to-orange jelly-like pulp clinging tightly to the large seed. Fruits are sold in street markets in enormous clusters of hundreds — eaten by cracking the thin shell between the teeth and sucking or scraping the juicy pulp from the seed. Spanish lime is one of the most beloved street foods and market fruits of the Caribbean, Puerto Rico, Cuba, and Colombia. The ripe fruits are also made into juice, jams, wine, and fermented beverages. Trees are dioecious (separate male and female plants), so plant at least one male per several females for fruiting. Very long-lived — specimens 100+ years old still fruit productively. Well adapted to South Florida's alkaline limestone soils where many tropical fruits perform poorly.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in acidic, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; avoid clay. Do not over-fertilize — sparkleberry grows naturally in very poor, acidic, sandy soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), poor to average sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; sparkleberry is the largest native blueberry relative in the Southeast, growing to 25 feet as a gnarly, multi-trunked small tree with distinctive exfoliating gray-brown bark that reveals warm cinnamon-red underbark — one of the most ornamental native bark patterns in southern woodland plants. The white bell-shaped flowers in spring are followed by small, persistent dark black berries that, while dry and astringent compared to commercial blueberries, are eagerly consumed by wood thrushes, mockingbirds, foxes, and other wildlife throughout fall and winter. It grows naturally in dry, sandy upland forests and longleaf pine savannas. An outstanding specimen tree for dry, sunny or partly shaded naturalistic landscapes.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with full sun exposure and ample room to mature.
directions: Sparrow is a long-cultivated named black walnut selection recognized among nut growers for producing unusually large nuts with good kernel fill for the species. Like other grafted black walnut cultivars, it bears years earlier than seedling trees and produces more uniform crops. Deep taproots make bare-root or containerized grafted stock the practical planting choice, and trees should be sited well clear of gardens sensitive to juglone.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Spartan is a cold-hardy, reliably productive apple well suited to northern climates.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Spartan is a cold-hardy, reliably productive apple well suited to northern climates. Bred in British Columbia, Canada in the 1920s from a McIntosh and Yellow Newtown Pippin cross, it bears medium, deep purple-red apples with crisp, snow-white, juicy flesh and a sweet flavor with the light, distinctive tang inherited from its McIntosh parent, ripening in early-to-mid fall as a reliable, attractive dessert apple. Its excellent cold hardiness, reliable annual bearing, and good disease resistance compared to many other apples have made it a longstanding favorite for northern and Canadian home orchards where more tender varieties struggle. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once fruit colors up deeply and pulls easily from the spur, and expect good storage life of a couple of months under cool conditions.

common_name: Spice Zee Nectaplum (Genetic Dwarf Nectarine-Plum Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Spice Zee is a Zaiger Genetics genetic dwarf nectaplum (nectarine-plum hybrid) that stays small enough for a large container, with striking reddish-purple spring foliage and self-fertile fruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred by Floyd Zaiger, Spice Zee is a genetic dwarf nectaplum, a nectarine-plum interspecific hybrid, that naturally stays compact enough for a large patio container or small-yard planting while still bearing full-sized, sweet, richly flavored fruit with a flavor many describe as somewhere between a nectarine and a plum. The reddish-purple young foliage in spring, aging to bronze-green, makes it an attractive small ornamental tree even outside of fruiting season, and its self-fertile flowers mean a single tree can set a full crop without a second pollinator. Fruit ripens in early summer, and the naturally dense, rounded canopy benefits from light annual thinning to keep light reaching the interior and to manage fruit size.

common_name: Spigold Apple (Cornell Red Spy x Golden Delicious Cross)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Spigold requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 4-8.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Spigold was bred at the Cornell University research station in Geneva, New York, from a cross of Red Spy and Golden Delicious, combining Red Spy's large size and crisp texture with Golden Delicious's sweetness in one of the largest apples commonly grown, with fruit that can rival a softball in size. The skin is yellow-green heavily striped and blushed with red, and the crisp, juicy flesh carries a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up well in storage. The tree tends toward biennial bearing (heavy crops every other year) if not thinned properly, so thin fruit in heavy-set years to encourage more consistent annual production, and stake young trees, since the very large fruit puts real strain on branches.

subcategory: Spineless edible prickly pear cactus cultivar
plant_note: Root a dried, calloused pad cutting in dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun in zone 8–11; Spineless Prickly Pear is a cultivated, spineless form of Opuntia ficus-indica — selected and grown without the stinging glochid hairs (and with reduced or absent spines) for easier harvesting and handling of both the young pads (nopales) and ripe fruits (tunas/prickly pears) — widely grown for food production across Mexico, the Mediterranean, South Africa, and increasingly in Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Root a calloused Opuntia pad cutting in dry, coarse, sandy soil in full sun; allow the cut end to dry for 1–2 weeks before planting to prevent rot; plant only 2–3 inches deep; water sparingly until established (3–4 months), then infrequently; harvest young pads in spring and ripe fruits in late summer/fall. Spineless Prickly Pear cultivars lack the dangerous glochid clusters that make wild and spiny Opuntia so irritating to work with, making the harvest of both young pads and ripe fruits safe and practical with only minimal care (lightweight gloves recommended). Young pads (nopales), harvested in spring when 4–6 inches long, are a major vegetable in Mexican cuisine — grilled, diced into salsa, cooked into soups, or scrambled with eggs; they have a mild, slightly mucilaginous, tart-green flavor. The ripe fruits (tunas) in late summer and fall range from yellow to red to deep purple depending on variety; the sweet, melon-like flesh makes excellent juice, sorbet, jam, and candy. The spineless form was famously promoted by Luther Burbank in the early 1900s as a drought-resistant livestock fodder crop for arid lands — though that particular venture was not entirely successful commercially, his selections remain the basis of modern spineless cultivar lines. An outstanding plant for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens where heat, drought, and alkaline soils challenge most edibles.

common_name: Splash Pluot (Yellow Skin with Red Splash Pattern)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; needs a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer such as Santa Rosa nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible plum or pluot pollinizer nearby. Splash is a Zaiger Genetics pluot with pale yellow skin marked by irregular red splashes and streaks, giving each fruit a slightly different, hand-painted appearance, and it produces sweet, juicy, richly flavored flesh typical of the best pluot selections. The tree is a reliable producer within the pluot family, and the fruit's bright, cheerful coloring along with its excellent eating quality has made it a popular choice among specialty fruit growers and farmers market vendors. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to concentrate flavor and size, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and the splash pattern has fully developed.

plant_note: Plant the dormant or potted grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Spring Snow is prized for producing essentially no fruit at all, a genetic trait that makes it a popular choice where the messy fruit drop of ornamental crabapples is unwelcome — around patios, walkways, and driveways — while still delivering the classic crabapple spring show of dense, fragrant, pure white flowers covering the tree before the leaves fully emerge. Its clean, tidy habit and lack of fruit litter have made it one of the most widely planted flowering crabapples for urban and residential landscapes. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; watch for occasional fire blight and apple scab in humid climates.

common_name: Squibnocket Beach Plum (Named Cape Cod Beach Plum Selection)
plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun on well-drained, sandy soil, including seaside sites, with a genetically distinct beach plum nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Squibnocket is a named beach plum selection identified from wild coastal populations for its reliable cropping and better-than-average fruit size, part of a group of named clones evaluated for improving on typical unselected seedling beach plum. Shrubs produce abundant white blossom in mid-spring followed by tart-to-sweet purple-red plums in late summer, prized for jams and jellies. Beach plum is naturally adapted to sandy, salt-sprayed, wind-exposed coastal soils and needs excellent drainage rather than rich garden soil to thrive. Because most beach plum is only partially self-fertile, planting more than one genetically distinct shrub greatly improves fruit set.

common_name: St. Edmund's Pippin Apple (Aromatic English Russet Dessert Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. St. Edmund's Pippin originated in Bury St Edmunds, England, in the 1870s, prized as one of the finest early russet dessert apples, with golden-yellow, rough-textured russeted skin covering crisp, aromatic, richly flavored flesh with a distinctive nutty sweetness characteristic of the best russet apples. It ripens earlier than most other russets, extending the season for gardeners who enjoy this distinctive style of apple beyond the typical late-fall russet harvest. The tree bears reliably and the fruit, while not a long keeper, offers exceptional eating quality fresh off the tree, making it a favorite among heirloom apple enthusiasts and collectors of English dessert apple varieties.

plant_note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired plum or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; St. Julien A is a semi-vigorous understock, not grown for its own fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired plum or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; St. Julien A is a semi-vigorous understock, not grown for its own fruit. A selection of the wild bullace or damson-type plum long used as the traditional English standard rootstock for grafted plums, gages, and apricots, it produces a semi-vigorous tree roughly two-thirds to three-quarters the size of a full seedling tree, with good compatibility across most plum and apricot varieties and reasonable tolerance of heavier soils compared to some other stone fruit rootstocks. Its long track record of reliable size control and broad graft compatibility has kept it in wide use for both commercial and home orchard plum and apricot production. Graft a desired named plum or apricot variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect earlier bearing and a more manageable tree size than on a vigorous seedling rootstock.

common_name: Stanley Plum (European Prune Plum, American Standard Freestone Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun; Stanley is partially self-fruitful but produces heavier crops with a nearby European plum pollinator such as Italian Prune, Damson, or Greengage; it is the most widely planted European prune plum in the eastern United States and the commercial standard for fresh and dried prune production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prune annually to an open-center form; thin heavy fruit crops to 3–4 inches apart after natural fruit drop; Stanley ripens in late August to September in most of the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic; harvest for fresh eating when fully ripe and soft, or pick slightly firm for drying into prunes; self-fruitful but plant with a companion European plum for best yields. Stanley plum is the most important and widely planted European prune plum (Prunus domestica) in the eastern United States, developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1926 and released in the 1930s. For decades, Stanley was synonymous with 'prune plum' throughout the eastern states — the word 'Stanley' and 'prune' were used interchangeably by many orchardists and home growers, reflecting its dominance as the only widely-grown European-type freestone plum in the region. The fruits are large to very large (for prune-type plums), oval to oblong, with deep blue-purple to nearly black skin and golden-yellow, firm, freestone flesh with a rich, sweet, slightly winey plum flavor. They are excellent for fresh eating at peak ripeness, cooking in preserves and tarts, and the definitive prune-type plum for drying — the firm, dry flesh and freestone characteristic make them ideal for dehydrating into prunes. Stanley requires approximately 800 chill hours and is reliably productive in zones 4–7, with reliable but sometimes marginal performance in zone 8 in mild-winter years. It is partially self-fruitful, producing some crop when grown alone but yielding significantly more when cross-pollinated with other European plum varieties. The trees are moderately vigorous and productive, with moderate disease susceptibility under humid conditions.

plant_note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; star apple is damaged by temperatures below 30°F and is best suited to zone 10–12 in the ground, or containers in zone 9 moved to frost protection when needed.
directions: Plant grafted trees in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; star apple is a highly ornamental tropical fruit tree native to the West Indies, producing beautiful round fruits 2–4 inches across in purple or green skin with a distinctive star pattern in the cross-section of the white, gelatinous, sweet, milk-filled flesh — the 'star' that gives the fruit its name. The leaves are distinctively two-toned: dark glossy green above, silky golden-bronze beneath, creating a shimmering display when the breeze moves through the canopy. The fruit is eaten fresh by cutting in half and scooping the sweet, creamy flesh; the latex in the skin and rind is astringent and should not be consumed. Grafted trees begin producing in 3–5 years. The sweet, mild flavor is a favorite in the Caribbean and South Florida. An outstanding ornamental and fruiting tree for zone 10–12 gardens.
