plant_note: Plant container trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; star gooseberry is a fast-growing tropical that performs as an evergreen shrub-tree in zone 9–11 and begins bearing fruit within 2–3 years of planting.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; star gooseberry is a productive tropical fruit tree widely grown throughout Southeast Asia and the Caribbean, bearing clusters of ribbed, waxy, pale yellow to white drupes — each resembling a miniature star when cut cross-section — directly on the trunk and older branches in a distinctive cauliflorous pattern. The tart, acidic fruit has a crisp, translucent flesh somewhat reminiscent of a sour apple or green gooseberry and is consumed fresh (with salt and chili in Southeast Asia), pickled, candied, or made into jams and juices. Trees reach 10–30 feet in frost-free conditions but are easily maintained smaller through pruning. In zone 9 they may be damaged by frost below 28°F but typically recover from light frost damage at the root. Prolific bearers that fruit twice yearly in good conditions. The unusual trunk-fruiting habit and fine-textured, pinnate foliage are ornamental assets in the tropical garden. A worthwhile and underused edible tree for zone 9–11 gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April in the warmest, most sheltered location. Grapefruit requires more heat to develop full sweetness than oranges — perform best in the warmest zone 9b locations and in zone 10. Star Ruby ripens October–January in Texas and Florida.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in the warmest location with maximum sun exposure; Star Ruby is a red-fleshed grapefruit variety developed by Texas A&M University through irradiation mutagenesis and released in 1970 — the variety that set the standard for deep-red, sweet, low-acid grapefruit. Texas Rio Grande Valley grapefruit production is dominated by Star Ruby and its offspring Rio Red (1984), both producing the deep ruby-red flesh and low-acid, sweet flavor that made Texas red grapefruit internationally famous. The fruits are large, with thin, yellow-blushed skin and deep crimson flesh that is sweeter and less bitter than white grapefruit — so sweet they are often eaten without added sugar. Star Ruby requires a long, hot growing season to develop maximum sweetness and color: in zone 9, summer heat is critical. Trees are vigorous, productive once established, and moderately cold-tolerant to about 26°F. Feed with citrus fertilizer (especially nitrogen and zinc) 3–4 times per year. An excellent landscape tree in warm zone 9 that provides both ornamental value and substantial food production.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after all danger of frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; starfruit is frost-tender and should be grown in containers in zones 8–9 or planted in frost-protected microclimates.
directions: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; purchase grafted trees for earlier bearing — seedling trees may take 5–7 years to fruit while grafted trees can bear in 1–2 years after planting. Averrhoa carambola is a tropical Southeast Asian fruit tree producing the unique, deeply 5-ridged, golden-yellow, translucent fruit known as starfruit or carambola that when sliced crosswise yields the distinctive five-pointed star shape; the fruit ranges from very tart to sweet depending on cultivar and is excellent fresh, in fruit salads, as a garnish, and in tropical beverages. Trees bloom and fruit multiple times per year in tropical climates, producing an almost continuous harvest in zones 10–11; in zone 9 they need frost protection and may lose leaves in cold winters but often recover. Sweet cultivars 'Arkin', 'Kari', and 'Fwang Tung' are the most popular for home orchards.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring against a shaded wall, fence, or understory trellis in rich, well-drained soil; semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer root more reliably than seed for this evergreen climber.
directions: This evergreen woody vine is unusual among fruiting plants for genuinely preferring shade to partial shade, making it one of the few climbers suited to a north-facing wall or the dim understory of a garden pergola. Train the twining stems onto a trellis or fence and be patient, since named or grafted plants fruit far sooner than seedlings, which can take years to bear. In autumn the vine produces oblong purple fruit similar to its relative akebia, splitting to reveal a sweet, milky-white pulp studded with small black seeds that is eaten fresh by hand in Japan. Plant two vines for best pollination and fruit set, since a single plant fruits sparsely on its own.

common_name: Stayman Apple (Stayman Winesap, Rich Wine-Flavored Keeper Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Stayman produces little viable pollen and needs a separate pollinator variety such as Golden Delicious or Jonathan.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Discovered in Kansas in 1866 by Dr. J. Stayman as a seedling of the older Winesap apple, this cultivar keeps the tangy, wine-like flavor of its parent in a larger, more productive fruit. The dark red skin covers dense, juicy flesh that holds up well in storage and in cooking, and the tree has long been a Mid-Atlantic and Southern favorite for cider and pie making. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once the background color turns from green to yellow-green.

common_name: Stella Cherry (First Self-Fertile Sweet Cherry, Canadian Self-Fertile Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Stella requires approximately 700–800 chill hours and is self-fertile — the critical advantage that made it famous — eliminating the need for a cross-pollinating companion variety; Stella will also pollinate most other sweet cherry varieties including Bing, Rainier, and others, making it a useful pollenizer in mixed orchards.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Stella is self-fertile and will set a crop without a pollenizer — it will also cross-pollinate many other sweet cherry varieties as a companion tree; protect ripening fruit from birds with netting; Stella ripens mid-season (late June to early July) producing large, dark red to nearly black fruits with good sweet flavor. Stella sweet cherry was bred by Dr. Karl Lapins at the Summerland Research Station in British Columbia, Canada, and released in 1968 — it became historically significant as the first widely available self-fertile sweet cherry variety, a characteristic that transformed home garden cherry growing by eliminating the requirement for two compatible cherry trees with overlapping bloom times. Before Stella, growing sweet cherries required careful selection of compatible pollinating pairs (cherry pollination compatibility is complex and variety-specific), which limited practical cherry growing to gardeners with space for at least two trees and the knowledge to select compatible varieties. Stella's self-fertility made sweet cherries accessible for single-tree planting in small gardens throughout its zone range. The fruits are large (similar to Bing in size), dark red to nearly black at full ripeness, with firm, juicy, sweet flesh and excellent flavor — somewhat less complex than Bing by some evaluations, but reliably good and productive. Stella also serves as a pollinizer for most other sweet cherry varieties, making it a valuable companion in mixed plantings where Bing or other varieties need cross-pollination.

common_name: Steuben Grape (Cornell-Bred Spicy Blue Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Steuben, bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York station, needs a real winter chill and is best suited to zones 5-8 rather than the Gulf South.
directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil, pruning heavily each winter with a cane-pruning system. Steuben was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and is grown for its blue-black, slip-skin berries with a rich, spicy-sweet, almost wine-like flavor that many growers consider superior to Concord for fresh eating, though it also makes excellent juice and jelly. It is a reliable, productive vine that ripens in midseason and stores unusually well for a labrusca-type grape. As a high-chill northern grape, it is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters favor muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; sticky groundcherry spreads by underground rhizomes through beach dunes, sandy prairies, and disturbed sandy ground across the southeastern and Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Direct sow or plant divisions into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun. Sticky groundcherry is a low, spreading native perennial of coastal dunes, sandy prairies, and disturbed sandy soils across the southeastern and Gulf Coastal Plain, its finely hairy, gently sticky foliage and stems giving the plant its common name. Small, nodding, pale yellow flowers with a darker throat appear from spring through fall, followed by round yellow fruit enclosed in a papery, lantern-like husk typical of the groundcherry group; the ripe fruit is edible once the husk dries and browns, with a mild, slightly tart flavor. It spreads steadily by underground rhizomes in loose, well-drained sandy soil, making it useful for stabilizing a sunny sandy bank or naturalized dune-edge planting, and it tolerates drought, heat, and poor soil with ease once established.

subcategory: Central American Lecythidaceae tropical ornamental fruit
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade in fertile, moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 10–12; Stinkwood Plum (Membrillo, Sachamango) is a magnificent ornamental small to medium tree from lowland rainforests of Colombia, Panama, Costa Rica, and Ecuador — producing enormous (up to 12 inches across), dramatically beautiful flower clusters of white to pink petals with hundreds of pink stamens, followed by large, ornamental, brown, pumpkin-shaped fruits with edible orange-yellow, mango-flavored flesh surrounding large seeds.
directions: Plant Gustavia superba in partial shade in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil; maintain consistent moisture and protect from temperatures below 40°F; the tree is a good candidate for large containers in warm greenhouses in cooler climates. Gustavia superba is in the Lecythidaceae family — the same family as the Brazil nut and Cannonball Tree — and shares the family trait of producing extraordinarily ornamental, large, spectacular flowers; in Gustavia superba, the flowers can reach 10–12 inches across, with broad white to pink petals and a dramatic ring of hundreds of pink stamens forming a flower of breathtaking beauty. The common name 'Stinkwood' refers to the strong, pungent scent of the cut wood; the fruit name 'membrillo' (Spanish for quince) describes the pumpkin-shaped, brownish fruits. The orange-yellow, fibrous, mango-flavored flesh surrounding the large seeds is eaten locally in Colombia and Panama by both people and wildlife; it is not widely commercialized. The tree is exceptionally ornamental at every stage and stage-of-growth — its unusual, club-shaped leaves, spectacular flowers, and ornate fruits make it one of the most showstopping specimens for tropical garden collections. Rarely seen in cultivation outside botanical gardens and specialist collectors in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; stone pine develops a deep taproot early — avoid disturbing roots.
directions: Stone pine is the classic Mediterranean umbrella-form pine grown for the large, richly flavored pine nuts (pignoli) used in pesto, pastries, and Middle Eastern cuisine; it is monoecious, self-fertile, and pollen-heavy — individual trees produce both male and female cones. Cones take three years to mature from pollination to seed release, so a productive tree has three overlapping cone crops at any given time. Harvest brown, closed cones by hand or after they fall naturally in late autumn, then sun-dry or gently heat them until the scales open and release the papery-shelled nuts inside. The tree thrives in sandy, well-drained, alkaline to acidic soil and is extremely drought-tolerant once the taproot is established.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost danger passes; Strawberry Ground Cherry is a compact, dwarf annual groundcherry — smaller than common Cape Gooseberry (Physalis peruviana) — native to eastern North America and the West Indies, producing abundant small, papery-husked fruits with sweet, tropical-strawberry-vanilla flavor, excellent for fresh eating, jam, and baked goods.
directions: Start Strawberry Ground Cherry seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun after frost; water regularly; fruits are ready when husks turn tan and papery and fruits drop to the ground — collect daily. Physalis pruinosa is the dwarf cousin of the taller Cape Gooseberry and common Ground Cherry (P. peruviana, P. heterophylla), distinguished by its compact, sprawling habit and intensely sweet, strawberry-vanilla flavored fruits inside papery husks. The plant is more compact than other groundcherries, topping out at 1–2 feet, making it easier to manage in small gardens and containers. Like all groundcherries, the ripe fruits naturally drop from the plant when fully ripe — the papery husk keeps them clean and extends shelf life for weeks at room temperature. The flavor is distinctly different from tomato or tomatillo: sweet, fruity, and aromatic, reminiscent of strawberry jam with vanilla undertones. Used fresh in fruit salads, made into preserves and pie filling, or dried like raisins. Extremely productive and easy to grow, self-seeding reliably in warm gardens once established.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry guava is remarkably adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and tolerates periodic drought, clay, sand, salt spray, and partial shade — one of the most site-tolerant small fruit trees for the Gulf Coast region.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry guava (cattley guava, cherry guava, purple guava) is a Brazilian evergreen small tree or large shrub that produces small, round, dark-red to burgundy-purple fruits about 1 inch in diameter with a distinctive strawberry-guava flavor — sweet, aromatic, and mildly acidic — that are excellent eaten fresh, made into jams, jellies, juice, and desserts, or dried. The fruits ripen from late summer through fall and fall when fully ripe, making harvest simple. The plant is one of the most attractive year-round fruiting shrubs for zone 9–11, with smooth, mottled, tan and brown peeling bark, glossy, thick, oval, dark-green leaves, and small, white, fragrant guava flowers that precede the fruit. Hardy to approximately 22°F, it is more cold-tolerant than tropical guava (Psidium guajava). However, strawberry guava is listed as a highly invasive species in Hawaii and parts of Florida, where it spreads rapidly in natural areas, and should not be planted near natural habitats in those regions. In drier Gulf Coast areas it is better behaved and is a productive, attractive, low-maintenance small fruit tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or young trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry guava is extremely adaptable to poor, acidic, and sandy soils. Note: it is considered invasive in Hawaii and subtropical areas with high rainfall — do not plant near natural areas in Hawaii, Florida, or other humid subtropical regions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry guava is a highly productive and flavorful small fruit tree or large shrub that produces abundant crops of 1-inch round fruits in red (the classic form) or yellow (Psidium cattleyanum var. lucidum, lemon guava) with an intensely sweet, slightly strawberry-like flavor — arguably the finest-flavored guava species, often preferred over the larger common guava by people who taste it. The glossy, dark-green evergreen leaves and smooth, mottled reddish-brown bark provide year-round ornamental value. In zone 9 it may suffer light frost damage but typically recovers well. It is extremely drought, heat, and poor-soil tolerant once established and produces fruit with minimal care. Important note: strawberry guava is listed as one of the world's 100 worst invasive species in subtropical humid regions — do not plant where it can escape to natural areas in Hawaii, Florida, and similar climates. In drier Gulf Coast locations it is less problematic.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or plant rooted offsets in spring into sharply drained, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; Texas pitaya forms large sprawling mounds and is grown both as an ornamental and for its sweet, strawberry-flavored fruit.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; Texas pitaya is a robust, clump-forming hedgehog cactus native to the Chihuahuan Desert and South Texas brushlands, forming large sprawling mounds of thick, blue-green stems that can eventually spread several feet across. Large magenta-purple flowers open in mid-spring, followed by egg-sized, spiny red fruit that ripens in early summer and, once the spines are removed, has a sweet flavor reminiscent of strawberries — long harvested by regional residents as a wild treat, giving rise to the Spanish common name pitaya. It is more cold-hardy than many South Texas cacti and tolerates the milder winters of zones 7 through 10 as long as drainage is excellent, making it a good dual-purpose ornamental and fruiting choice for a xeriscape or rock garden planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall in extremely well-drained, acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry tree is highly drought tolerant once established and actually performs better in poor, infertile soil — rich, fertile soil promotes lush growth that is more susceptible to diseases.
directions: Plant in poor, very well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the strawberry tree is a beautiful, slow-growing Mediterranean evergreen that produces clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers in fall and winter simultaneously with the ripening of the previous year's strawberry-like red and orange fruits — a unique garden spectacle of flowers and ripe fruit coexisting on the tree. The rough-textured red fruits are edible but taste nothing like a strawberry: they are mealy, mildly sweet, with a somewhat gritty texture, best used for jams, jellies, and wine rather than eating fresh (the name refers only to their appearance). The bark is a beautiful cinnamon red and exfoliating. The dwarf cultivar 'Compacta' stays 5–6 feet; 'Elfin King' is an ultra-compact form. Excellent drought-tolerant, deer-resistant evergreen for zone 7–10.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9); Stuart is a Type II pollinator that pairs well with Desirable (Type I) for cross-pollination. Established in the landscape before 1874, Stuart is one of the oldest named pecan varieties still in commercial production.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stuart is an old heirloom pecan variety originating in the Gulf South before the Civil War and one of the most historically important named pecans — it was among the first varieties to be systematically propagated by grafting and was widely planted throughout the Southeast from the 1880s through mid-20th century. Nuts are very large (45–50 per pound) with an excellent kernel percentage, rich flavor, and attractive appearance that made Stuart the standard commercial variety for much of the 20th century. Though partially supplanted by more scab-resistant modern varieties in humid commercial orchards, Stuart remains extremely popular for home planting in zone 7–9 because of its large, beautiful nuts, adaptability to a wide range of soils, and long productive lifespan — well-established Stuart trees may continue producing heavily for 100+ years. The principal weakness is moderate scab susceptibility in very wet years; in most zone 9 home orchards, this is manageable without spraying. An excellent choice for the Gulf Coast gardener who wants large, flavorful nuts from a landscape tree.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Sturmer Pippin needs a long, warm growing season to ripen and store well, and performs best where autumns stay mild.
directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Sturmer Pippin needs a long, warm growing season to ripen and store well, and performs best where autumns stay mild. Bred in Suffolk, England in the early nineteenth century from a Ribston Pippin and Nonpareil cross, it bears firm, greenish-yellow apples with dense, crisp, sharply flavored flesh that ripens very late in the season and keeps exceptionally well, sometimes into late winter or early spring under good storage conditions, making it one of the longest-keeping traditional apples grown. Its late ripening and long storage life made it especially popular in Southern Hemisphere growing regions like Australia and New Zealand, where the extended warm autumn allows the fruit to mature fully; in cooler, shorter-season climates it can struggle to ripen well before frost. Harvest as late in fall as the season allows, letting the fruit hang as long as possible, and store cool for a remarkably long keeping period.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Success is an older cultivar that is more disease-prone than modern selections and benefits from a fungicide program in humid regions.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Introduced in the early 1900s, Success was among the important early named pecan cultivars that helped establish the commercial pecan industry in the South, valued in its day for good nut size and quality. It has largely been replaced in modern commercial orchards by more disease-resistant, higher-yielding cultivars, since it is fairly susceptible to pecan scab and other diseases common in humid climates, but it remains of historical interest and is still found in older plantings and heirloom nut collections.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sudachi is the signature souring citrus of Tokushima Prefecture, Japan — smaller than yuzu, used exclusively as a juice and zest ingredient, and one of the most aromatic and distinctively flavored of all Japanese citrus with an intense, complex fragrance unlike any other.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sudachi is self-fruitful and produces tiny, green fruits that are harvested before they ripen to yellow for the most aromatic juice. Sudachi (Citrus sudachi) is a small, intensely aromatic souring citrus virtually unknown outside Japan but recently gaining attention in American culinary circles for its exceptional flavor; native and endemic to Tokushima Prefecture on Shikoku island (which produces approximately 98% of Japan's sudachi), the small (1–1.5 inch diameter), round, green fruits are always used before they ripen to yellow when their intense, fragrant juice and zest are at peak. The flavor is tart, fragrant, and floral with a complexity and intensity that surpasses lime or lemon — used by Japanese chefs exclusively for its aromatic quality as a garnish squeeze over grilled fish, mushrooms, soba noodles, and in ponzu sauce alternatives. Virtually unavailable commercially outside Japan; growing your own is the only way to access fresh sudachi in the US.

common_name: Suebelle White Sapote (Self-Fruitful Compact White Sapote)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm, wind-sheltered spot since young trees are more cold-sensitive than mature specimens.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm, wind-sheltered spot since young trees are more cold-sensitive than mature specimens. Suebelle stays more compact than seedling white sapote trees, generally topping out around 15 to 20 feet, and it is self-fruitful so a single tree can set a full crop without a pollinator. The smooth green-to-yellow fruit has a custardy, banana-and-pear flavor prized by growers from the warmer parts of the Gulf Coast into Central Florida, and established trees tolerate brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s°F that would seriously injure many other subtropical fruits.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; sugar apple requires a long, hot, humid growing season and is limited to frost-free zones.
directions: Sugar apple is a semi-deciduous small tree that drops leaves during the dry season — a natural dormancy that can be encouraged in cultivation by reducing water in late autumn to trigger uniform bloom flush in spring. Like other Annona species, the flowers are bisexual but dichogamous; hand-pollinate using a soft brush to transfer pollen from male-stage flowers (petals separating but pollen not yet shed) to female-stage flowers (stigma sticky and receptive). Fruit is composed of loosely packed segments that separate when ripe; harvest when skin segments begin to separate and the fruit yields to light pressure. Trees are fast-growing and benefit from annual pruning after fruit set to maintain canopy density and manageable size.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes; Sugar Belle is a modern University of Florida release (a cross of Clementine and Minneola tangelo) bred for a combination of cold-hardiness, disease tolerance, and heavy production that has made it an increasingly popular recommendation for Gulf Coast and Southeastern home orchards.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season; Sugar Belle is a University of Florida-bred mandarin cross prized for its distinctive bell-like shape, deep orange rind, and rich, intensely sweet, honeybell-style flavor, combined with better cold tolerance and canker resistance than many older mandarin varieties. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree without becoming puffy or losing flavor, giving a longer harvest window than many mandarins. Water deeply but let the soil surface dry between waterings, mulch to protect the root zone, and provide frost protection for young trees during their first couple of winters until they gain size and hardiness.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sugar bush is an evergreen California native of chaparral and dry, rocky slopes and is fully drought-tolerant once established in appropriate dry, well-drained conditions. Summer irrigation is harmful — water only to establish.
directions: Plant in dry, well-drained, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sugar bush is an evergreen sumac native to chaparral and dry, rocky slopes of the California Coast Ranges and Baja California, one of the most reliable and ornamental drought-tolerant shrubs for California-climate gardens. The large, bold, leathery, ovate leaves are folded lengthwise like a taco shell — a distinctive feature that sheds rain and reduces water loss. The small, red, waxy-coated berries produced in summer are coated with a tart, malic-acid-rich white sugar that was mixed with water by indigenous peoples to make a refreshing, lemonade-like drink — hence the common name 'sugar bush.' A cornerstone shrub for California native and Mediterranean-climate gardens, providing year-round evergreen screening, early spring flowers for native bees, summer berries for birds, and outstanding drought tolerance. Never irrigate in summer once established — it prefers natural summer drought.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the soil has warmed; Sugar Cane jujube tolerates heat and drought well and is valued for exceptionally high sugar content and crisp, apple-like texture when eaten fresh.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most fruit trees once established. Sugar Cane is a jujube cultivar valued for its exceptionally high sugar content and crisp, refreshing texture, similar to biting into a small, sweet apple, best enjoyed fresh at the green-to-mahogany transitional stage when both sweetness and crunch are at their peak. Fruit can also be left to fully ripen and wrinkle on the tree for a chewy, date-like texture and flavor if a different eating quality is preferred. The tree is largely self-fertile, extremely low-maintenance, and one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available, making it a good fit for the hot, dry margins of a Gulf South orchard.

common_name: Sugar Palm (Black Fibre Palm, Aren Palm)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun to part shade; sugar palm is one of Southeast Asia's most economically important palms, tapped for sweet sap that produces palm sugar (aren sugar, gula aren), the distinctly flavored dark-brown sweetener used throughout Indonesian and Filipino cooking — the tapped sap also ferments to produce palm wine (tuak).
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun to part shade; sugar palm tolerates some shade when young. Arenga pinnata (sugar palm or aren palm) is one of Southeast Asia's most culturally and economically important palms, native to tropical Asia from India through Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines, and the primary source of aren sugar (gula aren or gula jawa) — a distinctive, rich, deeply caramel-flavored, dark-brown palm sugar that is the traditional sweetener of Indonesian, Filipino, and Malay cooking. The palm produces sweet sap (neera) by cutting the flower stalks; the fresh sap is collected daily, boiled down to produce palm sugar, or allowed to naturally ferment to produce palm wine (tuak) and then palm vinegar. Beyond sugar, the tree produces fibrous black leaf-base material (ijuk fiber) used for centuries in Indonesia as a natural roofing thatch and rope material — renowned for durability and water resistance. The starchy pith of the trunk trunk is processed into a primitive palm starch (aren starch). The fruits contain three seeds each surrounded by a thick, starchy gel coating that is caustic when raw (irritating calcium oxalate) but edible when processed; young seed gel is used in Southeast Asian desserts (kolang-kaling). A monocarpic palm — it flowers once, over many years, then dies after seed set.

plant_note: Plant seeds after cold stratification in spring or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; sugar pine grows naturally in mixed conifer forests of the Sierra Nevada and Cascades at 2,000–10,000 feet elevation. Plant in a permanent site as transplanting established trees is very difficult.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; sugar pine is the largest and longest-coned pine in the world — individual trees reach 200–270 feet in height, and the cones (hanging from branch tips on stalks) measure 10–26 inches long, the longest cones of any conifer. John Muir called it 'the king of the conifers.' The species has the largest seed (pine nut) of any western pine, and the seeds were an important food source for Sierra Nevada Native peoples. The common name comes from the sweet, sugary sap or resin that exudes from wounds, tasting like brown sugar and used as a sweetener by indigenous peoples. Native to the Sierra Nevada and Cascade Range from Oregon through central California, the species is unfortunately threatened by white pine blister rust (Cronartium ribicola) — plant blister-rust-resistant selections when available. The five-needle bundles, massive trunk, and extraordinary long cones make it one of the most impressive trees in North America.

common_name: Sugar Tyme Crabapple (Fragrant Pink-Bud White-Flowered Crabapple)
plant_note: Plant the dormant or potted grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Sugar Tyme is a heavy, reliable bloomer, its deep pink buds opening to abundant, fragrant white flowers each spring, followed by a persistent crop of small, bright red fruit that holds through winter and draws birds when other food sources are scarce. It is one of the most disease-resistant crabapple cultivars available, showing strong resistance to apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew, which has made it a widely recommended low-maintenance choice by extension services across many regions. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil; summer grape is very adaptable to soil type and pH and requires only pruning to maintain fruit production. Train on a strong trellis, arbor, or fence.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil of any pH in full sun; summer grape is one of the most widespread wild grape species in eastern North America, climbing high into the forest canopy from New England to Florida and west to Nebraska. The large, deeply lobed leaves resemble European wine grape leaves and provide dense, ornamental screening on arbors and fences. Clusters of small, blue-black, seedy but sweet-tart grapes ripen in late summer to fall and are consumed by over 90 species of birds and mammals. The grapes are edible for humans and have been used to make juice, jelly, and wine — they are tart when underripe but improve after frost. Summer grape is a host plant for multiple moth and butterfly species including the grapeleaf skeletonizer. Prune back in late winter to a few buds on the main stems to encourage fruiting shoots.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Summer Rambo, also known by its original French name Rambour, dates to at least the 1500s in France, making it one of the oldest apple varieties still in cultivation today and a variety that traveled to North America with some of the earliest European settlers. The large, somewhat flattened fruit has pale greenish-yellow skin streaked with red, and the crisp, juicy, notably tart flesh cooks down quickly into excellent sauce and is well suited to pies and other baked goods, though it can also be eaten fresh by those who favor a sharper apple. True to its ancient origins as a working farm variety, the tree is vigorous, disease-tolerant, and reliably productive; fruit ripens in mid to late summer, well ahead of most fall storage apples, and should be used within a few weeks since it does not keep long.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Summercrisp requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is exceptionally cold-hardy, well adapted to zones 3-7.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Summercrisp was bred by the University of Minnesota for extreme cold hardiness and good resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that devastates many European pears, making it a reliable choice for northern growers who struggle with more tender pear varieties. Unlike most European pears, which must be picked hard and ripened off the tree, Summercrisp is meant to be eaten while still firm and crisp, straight off the tree or shortly after picking, with sweet, juicy flesh and a flavor reminiscent of a crisp Asian pear crossed with a European one. Fruit ripens early, in mid to late summer well ahead of most storage pears, giving northern growers a reliable pear harvest even in regions where longer-season varieties may not fully mature.

common_name: Summit Muscadine (Large Bronze Self-Fertile Muscadine Grape)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root vines in late winter or spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Summit is self-fertile and particularly well-suited for fresh eating due to its large berry size and mild, sweet flavor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Summit is a bronze (amber-green) muscadine grape cultivar released by the University of Georgia — selected for its combination of large berry size, excellent fresh-eating quality, self-fertility, and late-season ripening. Bronze muscadines are generally milder and sweeter in flavor than black muscadines, making Summit particularly outstanding for fresh table use, wine production (bronze muscadines produce white/rosé wines), and juice. The large, uniform berries ripen in mid-to-late season (September in zone 9) in loose clusters that fall into collection bags or tarps for easy harvesting — a distinct muscadine characteristic compared to bunch grapes. Summit's self-fertility makes it an excellent standalone vine for gardeners with limited space, though yields are typically improved with a male or other self-fertile pollinizer within 50 feet. Muscadines are the native grapes of the southeastern United States — naturally adapted to Gulf South heat, humidity, and disease pressure that make European (Vitis vinifera) grapes impractical without intensive spray programs. Summit is disease-resistant, long-lived, and productive — established vines 20–30 years old commonly produce 30–50 pounds of fruit per year. The vine becomes a significant landscape feature as it ages, with thick, gnarled main canes and attractive fall foliage.

common_name: Sumner Pecan (UGA Release Large-Nut Type II Southeastern Commercial Pecan)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter while dormant; Sumner is a Type II (protogynous) pecan — the pistillate flowers become receptive before the pollen is shed from the same tree's catkins, requiring a Type I pecan pollinator within 150 feet for reliable fertilization. Pair Sumner with Stuart, Desirable, Pawnee, or another Type I pollinator for full crops. In zone 9, pecan trees require deep, fertile soil with good internal drainage; shallow or waterlogged soils dramatically reduce production and tree longevity. Apply zinc sulfate foliar applications each spring before leaf-out to prevent zinc deficiency, which is extremely common in Gulf South pecans and causes rosette (distorted small leaves clustered at branch tips). Trees produce significant crops beginning 6–8 years after planting and are long-lived (50–100+ years in suitable conditions).
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep well-drained soil; pair with Type I pollinator. Apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually. Harvest when husks split and nuts fall. Sumner Pecan was released by the Georgia Agricultural Experiment Station (now part of the University of Georgia) as a named cultivar selected for the southeastern United States — a region that represents one of the traditional heartlands of US pecan production, with Georgia consistently among the top pecan-producing states nationally. Sumner is classified as Type II (protogynous) in the pecan flowering system that categorizes varieties by the relative timing of pistillate and staminate flower emergence: Type II varieties have pistillate (female) flowers ready to receive pollen before the same tree's catkins shed pollen, creating a natural cross-pollination requirement and making mixed-type plantings more productive than single-variety blocks. The nuts are large to very large for a southeastern pecan variety, with a good shell thickness-to-kernel ratio and above-average kernel quality — the kernel is plump, well-filled, and has good flavor. Sumner's relatively good resistance to pecan scab (compared to varieties like Desirable and Curtis, which have significant susceptibility) has made it a practical choice for home orchards and small commercial operations in humid areas where fungicide application is difficult to maintain consistently. The variety is widely available from Gulf South and southeastern nurseries and has remained in commercial production for decades despite the introduction of newer scab-resistant varieties.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sumo mandarin requires more careful management than standard mandarins and trees benefit from removal of excess fruit (thinning) to prevent biennial bearing and maintain large fruit size, which is a hallmark of the variety.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sumo mandarin — sold under the trademarked name 'Sumo Citrus' in North America and known as 'Dekopon' in Japan and 'Shiranui' by its cultivar name — is a premium mandarin hybrid (Kiyomi tangor x Ponkan mandarin) developed in Japan and widely considered one of the finest fresh mandarin fruits in the world: extraordinarily sweet (very high Brix), completely seedless, easily peeled with thick, bumpy, loose skin, and so large (typically 3–4 inches in diameter) that a single fruit is a generous one-person serving. The characteristic topknot bump at the stem end and enormous size make Sumo instantly recognizable in markets, where it commands premium prices ($3–5 per fruit or more). The flavor is intensely sweet with very low acid and a honey-like aromatic quality unlike any other mandarin, and the peel comes off in large easy-to-remove sections. Sumo/Dekopon trees are slow to come into full production (4–5 years from grafted trees to reliable crops), somewhat demanding in their cultural requirements, and require fruit thinning to produce the signature large fruits — but the result is exceptional. A wonderful specialty tree for zone 9–11 home orchards and edible landscapes.

common_name: Sunbest Nectarine (Early Low-Chill University of Florida Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs only about 225 chill hours, one of the few reliable nectarines for zone 8-9 winters.
directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Released by the University of Florida in 2001, Sunbest needs only about 225 chill hours, making it one of the few reliable nectarines for zone 8-9 winters across the Gulf South and north-central Florida. It ripens very early, typically by early May, several days ahead of the widely grown Sunraycer, with yellow melting semi-freestone flesh under 90-100 percent red-blushed skin. Trees are self-fertile and heavy-bearing, though like most low-chill nectarines they need close monitoring for bacterial and fungal leaf spot in humid climates.

common_name: Sunburst Tangerine (Deep Orange-Red Florida Hybrid Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Sunburst ripens from November into January and is a heavy, reliable bearer, though fruit should be thinned in on years to avoid excessive limb breakage from heavy crop loads.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Released by the USDA in 1979 from a cross of Robinson and Osceola mandarins, Sunburst produces medium-sized fruit with a strikingly deep orange-red rind and sweet, juicy, richly flavored flesh with relatively few seeds. It is one of the more widely planted modern mandarin cultivars in Florida and the Gulf South because of its dependable, heavy annual production and attractive fruit color. The tree bears young and can overbear, so removing some fruit in spring helps maintain fruit size and reduce alternate-year bearing.

common_name: Suncoast Nectarine (University of Florida Low-Chill Nectarine for the Gulf Coast)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in full sun with excellent drainage; Suncoast was released by the University of Florida in 1995 with a chill requirement of roughly 250-300 hours, suiting it to north Florida, south Alabama, and nearby Gulf Coast gardens. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with sharp drainage, siting them where good air movement helps foliage dry quickly after Gulf Coast humidity and rain. Suncoast is a University of Florida low-chill release with yellow, semi-clingstone flesh, a red blush covering most of the fruit, and notably better resistance to bacterial spot on leaves and fruit than many older nectarine varieties, an important trait in humid growing conditions where bacterial spot is a persistent problem. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set, and expect harvest in late April to early May, among the earliest tree fruit of the season in a Gulf Coast garden.

common_name: Suncrest Peach (California Freestone Prized for Exceptional Flavor)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Suncrest has a moderate chill requirement of roughly 500-600 hours, giving it reasonably good adaptability to zone 9 winters.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and thin fruit to six to eight inches apart once fruit set is confirmed. Suncrest was bred in California by peach breeder Fred Anderson in the 1950s and became famous, decades later, through farmer-author David 'Mas' Masumoto's writing about the variety's near disappearance from commercial markets despite exceptional flavor, because its relatively short shelf life made it unsuited to long-distance commercial shipping in the era of firm, durable supermarket peaches. The yellow, freestone flesh is richly aromatic, intensely sweet, and complex, widely considered among home orchardists and flavor-focused growers to rank with the best-tasting peaches available, even if it will never win a shipping-durability contest. Grow it as a backyard or local-market tree where fruit can be picked and eaten at full ripeness rather than shipped hard and green, and maintain routine peach leaf curl and brown rot management with dormant-season spraying.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Sunflower is self-fertile to a degree but performs much better when cross-pollinated by another cultivar such as Shenandoah, Wells, or Susquehanna.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, full sun at maturity; Sunflower is a named pawpaw cultivar selected in Ohio from wild seedlings notable for its large, somewhat self-fertile nature (better fruit set when grown alone than most pawpaw cultivars), medium-large fruit size, and rich, sweet, yellow-gold flesh with excellent banana-custard flavor. The 'sunflower' name refers to both the yellow-gold flesh color and the cultivar's tendency to produce better solo fruit set than most pawpaws, though production is still significantly improved with a cross-pollinator. Sunflower's partial self-fertility is its most important practical attribute for gardeners who have space for only one tree — it will produce some fruit without a pollinator while most other pawpaw cultivars produce little or none. The medium-to-large fruits (4–6 oz average) have green to yellowish-green skin that softens slightly and turns more yellow-toned when fully ripe; the rich, sweet, banana-custard flesh is among the most popular of named pawpaw selections. Harvest by feel rather than appearance — ripe pawpaws yield to gentle pressure like a ripe peach. As with all pawpaws, the very short post-harvest shelf life (2–5 days at room temperature) makes them a specialty fruit for home gardeners and local direct-sale; they cannot be commercially distributed through standard grocery supply chains.

common_name: Sungold Apricot (Cold-Hardy Minnesota Apricot, Moongold Pollinizer Pair)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Sungold is self-unfruitful and must be planted with Moongold apricot nearby for pollination, since the two were bred as a matched pair.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, always alongside a Moongold apricot, since Sungold cannot pollinate itself and the two varieties were released together by the University of Minnesota specifically to pollinate one another in cold climates. The medium, golden-yellow fruit has sweet, tender flesh good for fresh eating and preserving, and the tree carries the same excellent cold hardiness as its pollination partner, allowing apricot production in regions well north of where most other varieties can survive winter. Because spring frost during the tree's early bloom is a greater practical risk than winter cold itself, site the pair away from low frost pockets and, where possible, in a slightly elevated or air-draining location to reduce frost damage to the flowers that determine the year's crop.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunki is among the most cold-hardy true mandarins available and is also widely used as a cold-hardy rootstock, including in Flying Dragon trifoliate crosses bred for the Gulf South and Southeast.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunki is an exceptionally cold-hardy sour mandarin, tolerating brief dips into the low teens F once well established, well beyond what a standard satsuma or sweet orange survives. The small, seedy fruit is too tart and sour for most people to eat fresh, but it makes excellent marmalade, ade, and juice for cooking, and the tree's extreme hardiness has made it one of the parents behind many of the cold-hardy citrus hybrids bred for the Southeast. Sunki is also planted specifically as a dwarfing, cold-tolerant rootstock for grafting less-hardy scion varieties, which is how many home gardeners in zone 7-8 encounter it even without seeking out the fruit itself. Give young trees winter protection for their first few years; mature, well-established wood is considerably tougher. Harvest fruit once fully colored, and expect to use it in the kitchen rather than eating it fresh off the tree.

common_name: Sunraycer Nectarine (Low-Chill Nectarine for Warm Winters)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunraycer needs only about 250-300 chill hours, letting it set fruit reliably through mild Gulf Coast winters. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with deep, well-drained soil; nectarines share peach culture but their smooth skin makes them more prone to fruit-scarring insects and bacterial spot, so a warm-humid Gulf Coast planting benefits from an open, breezy site. Sunraycer sets a heavy early crop of medium-to-large fruit with bright red skin and sweet-tart yellow flesh, typically ripening ahead of most peaches in the same yard. Thin fruit clusters to one nectarine every 4-6 inches once they reach marble size to prevent limb breakage and improve final fruit size, and prune annually to an open, low vase shape after harvest to renew the one-year wood nectarines fruit on.

common_name: Sunred Nectarine (Ultra-Low-Chill Gulf South Nectarine, Florida-Texas Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep fertile soil in full sun; Sunred has an extraordinarily low chill requirement of approximately 150–200 hours below 45°F — the lowest of any widely available named nectarine — making it the standard recommended nectarine for the Gulf South, central and south Texas, and the southern half of Florida where winter temperatures are too mild for standard nectarines; self-fertile, no cross-pollinator needed.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sunred is self-fertile; thin fruits to 6 inches after natural drop; Sunred ripens early (May in zone 8–9, one of the earliest nectarines available), producing medium-sized, bright red, freestone fruits with yellow flesh and good sweet-tart flavor — the first fresh nectarines of the season in Gulf Coast markets. Sunred nectarine is the primary low-chill nectarine for Gulf South and Florida gardening, selected for its exceptionally low chill hour requirement (approximately 150–200 hours) that allows it to bloom and fruit reliably in the mild winters of Houston, New Orleans, Tampa, and similar Gulf Coast cities where the 400–600 chill hours required by standard California nectarines are rarely accumulated in a typical year. The variety was developed through University of Florida and related southern breeding programs specifically to fill the gap in the Gulf South stone fruit palette, where peaches had low-chill options (Flordaking, Florida Crest) but the nectarine category was essentially absent for warm-climate gardeners. Sunred ripens in May in zone 8–9 — among the very earliest of any nectarine — providing a fresh stone fruit harvest at a time when nothing else is ripe, giving it a clear market window at Gulf Coast farmers' markets and specialty farm stands. The fruits are medium-sized, bright red, with yellow freestone flesh and a pleasant sweet-tart nectarine flavor that, while not matching the complex richness of premium California nectarines in cool growing conditions, is excellent for the region.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Superior is a University of Minnesota 1957 release combining Japanese and American plum genetics for outstanding cold hardiness and excellent fruit quality — one of the best plum varieties for zones 4–6 where most Japanese plums winter-kill or fail to fruit reliably.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Superior is partially self-fruitful but produces heavier crops cross-pollinated with Toka, Pipestone, or another Minnesota plum hybrid. Superior plum was released in 1957 by the University of Minnesota fruit breeding program, which developed a series of plum hybrids combining Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) quality and fruit size with the extreme cold hardiness of native American plum species (Prunus americana); these hybrids fill an important niche for gardeners in zones 4–6 where winters regularly kill Japanese plums or prevent adequate chill hours for European varieties. Superior produces large (2–3 inch), dark red-maroon, round fruits with yellow flesh and excellent sweet-tart flavor — one of the largest and best-flavored of the Minnesota hybrids and clearly superior in fruit quality to earlier hybrid selections. Very cold-hardy (surviving to –40°F) and blooms late enough to avoid most late spring frosts. A large, vigorous, productive tree suited to the Upper Midwest and Northern Plains where most stone fruits struggle.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Superspur was selected for its heavily spurred fruiting wood, which sets an unusually dense crop, and benefits from a second mayhaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since mayhaw is a wetland native that tolerates the poorly drained, low-lying ground where most other fruit trees decline. Superspur is a named western mayhaw selection valued by Gulf South growers for the unusually dense, short fruiting spurs that line its branches, packing on a heavier crop of small, tart, aromatic red berries than many seedling or older cultivars produce. Fruit ripens in May, giving the tree its common name, and is harvested from the ground or by shaking branches over tarps for the classic mayhaw jelly of Louisiana, Mississippi, and east Texas. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar for best cross-pollination and yield, and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years and to keep improving in production for decades.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Surinam cherry is a frost-sensitive tropical fruiting shrub native to Brazil and Paraguay that has naturalized extensively in South Florida, Gulf Coast, and tropical regions worldwide as both an ornamental hedge and food plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are drought-tolerant but produce best fruit with consistent moisture during the fruiting period. Eugenia uniflora is a glossy-leaved evergreen shrub or small tree native to tropical South America, widely naturalized in Florida, the Gulf Coast, Hawaii, and subtropical regions worldwide; the deeply ribbed, round, eight-segmented fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, and finally to deep red or nearly black, with a distinctive sharp-sweet, resinous flavor that is immediately distinctive — excellent fresh when fully ripe (dark red to black stage), in juices, jellies, ice cream, and fermented beverages. The foliage is beautifully aromatic when crushed. It is commonly planted as a fast-growing hedge or screening shrub in zone 9–12 and has become naturalized (and invasive in some areas of Florida). Hardy to about 28°F; protect from frost in zone 9a.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Suruga is a Japanese astringent persimmon that must be fully soft (bletted) before eating, unlike non-astringent types like Fuyu. Trees are partially self-fertile but produce more heavily with cross-pollination from another Japanese persimmon variety. In zone 9 Suruga ripens October–November; the orange fruits color up dramatically and can be harvested for drying while still firm.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile soil; Suruga is a large-fruited astringent persimmon from Japan, producing brilliant deep-orange fruits of 8–14 ounces with smooth, thin skin and exceptionally rich, complex, honey-sweet flavor when fully bletted (softened to near-liquid jelly consistency). Astringent persimmons like Suruga contain high tannin levels when unripe that create an intensely mouth-puckering sensation; the astringency disappears completely when fruits are allowed to ripen and soften fully on or off the tree. Suruga is specifically valued in Japan for hoshigaki — traditional Japanese dried persimmon — where peeled fruits are hung on strings and massaged daily over 4–6 weeks to produce a sweet, concentrated dried fruit with a crystalline sugar bloom on the surface. In zone 9 Suruga trees are productive and long-lived, with spectacular fall foliage adding ornamental value. The large fruits are less susceptible to fruit fly damage than non-astringent types because they are harvested firm and ripened off the tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0) soil in partial shade when young; Susquehanna pairs effectively with Shenandoah or Wells for cross-pollination, as the Peterson pawpaws were selected to maximize cross-productivity with one another.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Susquehanna is one of the flagship 'Peterson Pawpaws' — the group of named cultivars selected and introduced by Neal Peterson from decades of pawpaw breeding aimed at developing the largest, sweetest, and most productive cultivars available. Susquehanna produces some of the largest individual pawpaw fruits of any named cultivar, with exceptional fruits reaching 12–16 ounces — two to three times the average size of a good seedling-grown pawpaw — on a productive, healthy tree. The extraordinarily large fruit size, excellent sweet flavor with rich banana-custard-vanilla character, and low seed-to-flesh ratio (maximum edible flesh per fruit) make Susquehanna the top choice among pawpaw enthusiasts seeking maximum yield from a home orchard planting. Cross-pollination from Shenandoah, Wells, or another unrelated cultivar is required for reliable production — plant two or more different named cultivars within 50 feet. Because pawpaw flowers have an unusual pollination mechanism (receptive to pollen only briefly, with fly/beetle pollinators), hand-pollination using a small brush to transfer pollen between flowers at different stages significantly improves fruit set. In zone 9, pawpaws perform in the northern portions of the zone; deep South heat and insufficient winter chilling can limit production in zones 9b and warmer.

common_name: Swaar Apple (Dense Spicy-Sweet Hudson Valley Dutch Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Swaar traces to the Dutch settlers of New York's Hudson Valley in the colonial era, taking its name from the Dutch word for 'heavy,' a direct reference to the unusually dense, weighty flesh of the fruit for its size. The large, dull yellow-green apple has rich, aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh considered by heirloom apple enthusiasts to be among the finest-flavored of the old Dutch-American varieties, and it stores exceptionally well, holding quality for months in proper cold storage. The tree is moderately vigorous and hardy, reflecting its long history of cultivation in the cold winters of the Hudson Valley; harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for the best keeping.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall directly in a sheltered seedbed; the cold of winter provides the stratification needed for spring germination.
directions: Harvest berries in early autumn and mash to separate seeds from pulp, then rinse seeds thoroughly before sowing to remove germination inhibitors in the flesh. Sow in a prepared seedbed or deep containers left outdoors to experience natural winter cold, which substitutes for manual stratification. Swedish Whitebeam is exceptionally adaptable and tolerates coastal winds, compacted urban soils, and exposed hillsides better than most ornamental trees. Move seedlings to their permanent site by the second year, choosing a location with full sun and good drainage where the tree can develop its distinctive white-backed foliage.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late fall or late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; SweeTango needs a compatible pollinator such as another mid-season apple and full sun for best fruit quality.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby, since apples are not reliably self-fertile. Developed by the University of Minnesota from a cross of Honeycrisp and the earlier-ripening Zestar!, SweeTango combines Honeycrisp's signature explosive crunch and juiciness with a sweeter, more complex, slightly spicy flavor and a harvest window about three weeks ahead of its famous parent. The tree bears at a younger age and more heavily than Honeycrisp, though the fruit is prone to bitter pit and benefits from consistent watering and calcium availability during fruit development. Because it is a managed variety, most trees are sold under license through Next Big Thing Growers, but home gardeners can still plant and grow it for personal use; thin fruit to one per cluster for the best size and to reduce biennial bearing.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Sweet Alice needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.
directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving them toward full sun as they mature. Sweet Alice is a historic Indiana-origin pawpaw prized for exceptionally large, sweet fruit with a mild, low-astringency flavor that many tasters rank among the best of the older named selections, though it can bear somewhat irregularly compared to more modern, heavier-cropping cultivars. Trees are vigorous with the typical pyramidal pawpaw habit and glossy drooping foliage, and they tolerate the wet-but-drained bottomland soils pawpaw favors in the wild. Because pawpaws require cross-pollination, plant Sweet Alice with a genetically unrelated cultivar such as Shenandoah or Wabash, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during bloom to improve fruit set in home settings where natural pollinators are scarce.

common_name: Sweet Calabash (Sweet Granadilla, Hard-Shell Passion Fruit)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or seedlings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; sweet calabash is a Caribbean and northern South American passionflower that produces round, hard-shelled, brownish-yellow fruits with intensely sweet, aromatic, orange-yellow juice — considered by many Caribbean islanders to be the best-flavored of all wild passionfruits, far sweeter than common purple passionfruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide very strong trellis or arbor support. Passiflora maliformis (sweet calabash or sweet granadilla) is a passionflower native to the Caribbean islands and northern South America that produces one of the sweetest and most intensely aromatic of all passionfruits. The fruits are rounded to slightly apple-shaped, roughly 2–3 inches across, with a hard, woody, yellow-brown to dark-brown shell when ripe (much harder than purple or yellow passionfruit shells), protecting an extremely sweet, aromatic, orange-yellow pulp with a flavor that combines passion fruit, apricot, and guava with a honeyed sweetness rarely found in cultivated passionfruits. The hard shell makes it less susceptible to insect damage than thin-shelled species, and the fruits can be stored for weeks at room temperature. To eat, crack the hard shell and scoop out the aromatic pulp with seeds; the juice is excellent mixed with water as a tropical drink. Sweet calabash is prized in Caribbean home gardens and is occasionally grown in tropical botanical gardens worldwide; it remains very little known in commercial cultivation despite its outstanding fruit quality. The attractive, divided leaves and intricate blue-and-white flowers are typical of the genus. In zone 10–12, the vine is vigorous and productive in full sun.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring before buds swell.
directions: Sweet cherries require 700–1100 chill hours and are among the least self-fertile of the stone fruits — always plant at least two compatible varieties, choosing cultivars from the same incompatibility group (or self-fertile types such as Stella and Lapins). They prefer well-drained, slightly alkaline soil and dislike wet feet, which promotes root rot and crown rot. Protect ripening fruit with bird netting. Harvest when fruit is deeply colored, fully sweet, and the stem parts cleanly from the spur.

common_name: Sweet Frost Mandarin (Cold-Hardy Seedless Changsha-Type Tangerine)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm microclimate for extra protection during the coldest nights.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm microclimate for extra protection during the coldest nights. Sweet Frost is a University of Georgia release bred from Changsha tangerine specifically to make a hardier, more dependable citrus for gardeners as far north as zone 8b, well beyond where most mandarins survive outdoors. The small to medium fruit is easy-peeling and notably sweeter and less seedy than standard Changsha, ripening in fall into early winter. Mature trees have shown better cold tolerance in trials than satsuma, making Sweet Frost a strong option for pushing citrus culture into the cooler fringes of the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Thrives in cool tropical highland conditions at 60–75°F; not suited to hot, humid lowland tropics where flavor and sugar content diminish — plant at elevation where temperatures are mild.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun with wire or trellis support; sweet granadilla is widely considered the sweetest and most delicately flavored of all passion fruits, with a brittle hard shell that rattles when ripe and a translucent sweet-gelatinous interior pulp eaten with a spoon — the dominant commercial species in Colombia, Peru, and Venezuela. It differs from P. flavicarpa in preferring cool highland conditions (3,000–8,000 feet elevation in the tropics, or mild Mediterranean climates); excessive heat reduces sugar content significantly. Harvest when the shell becomes brittle and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. A single established vine on a strong trellis can yield 100 or more fruits per season.

plant_note: Plant in spring in frost-free areas or grow in a container to overwinter indoors.
directions: Sweet lime yields mild, low-acid fruit prized in South Asia and the Mediterranean for fresh juice. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, protecting it from any frost, or keep it in a large pot to shelter indoors in cold climates. Feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season and water deeply but infrequently. Harvest when the rind turns pale yellow-green and the fruit yields slightly to pressure.

subcategory: tropical Southeast Asian cauliflorous fruit tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; sweet rambai (Baccaurea dulcis) is a small tropical fruit tree from the lowland forests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula, producing clusters of small, round, yellowish to orange-red, sweet, jelly-fleshed berries — cauliflorous, forming on the trunk and branches — the sweetest of the Baccaurea fruit species, with mild, sweet, pleasant flavor; dioecious (male and female plants needed for fruiting).
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; plant at least one male and one female tree for fruiting — Baccaurea dulcis is dioecious. Baccaurea dulcis (sweet rambai or jentik-jentik) is a small tropical fruit tree from the humid lowland forests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula — one of the sweetest and most pleasant of the Baccaurea fruit species (the species name 'dulcis' means sweet in Latin). The tree is a compact size compared to other Baccaurea relatives, making it somewhat more suitable for home tropical gardens. Like other Baccaurea species, the fruits are cauliflorous — forming in pendant clusters directly on the trunk and main branches in the distinctive pattern shared with cacao, jackfruit, and related tropical trees. The small (1/2-inch), round to oval fruits ripen to yellowish to orange-red with thin skin and translucent, white, jelly-like flesh; the flavor is genuinely sweet and mild, with less of the tartness characteristic of other rambai relatives (B. motleyana). The tree is dioecious, requiring both male and female plants for fruit production. Sweet rambai is largely unknown in cultivation outside its native Borneo and Malaysian range; a rare collectors' fruit tree for dedicated tropical fruit enthusiasts in zone 11–12.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sweetheart is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, though yields improve with a compatible sweet cherry nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; protect ripening fruit from birds with netting and avoid low, frost-prone planting sites. Sweetheart is a Canadian-bred sweet cherry from the Summerland research station in British Columbia, valued for being self-fertile — unlike Bing and many other sweet cherries, it sets a reliable crop without a separate pollinizer tree, making it a practical choice where space allows for only one cherry tree. It ripens notably late in the sweet cherry season, extending fresh harvest well after earlier cultivars like Bing and Rainier have finished, with medium-large, bright red, firm, sweet fruit of good flavor. The tree is vigorous and productive, and its self-fertility combined with late ripening has made it a popular choice for home orchards and small commercial plantings alike. Provide consistent moisture during fruit development to avoid cracking, especially if rain falls as fruit nears full ripeness.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree only where winters stay frost-free or nearly so; Sweetheart is self-fertile and bears reliably without a pollenizer tree, which makes it a more forgiving choice than Brewster for growers at the marginal, subtropical edge of lychee range.
directions: Sweetheart is a widely recommended Florida and Gulf Coast lychee cultivar prized because it is self-fertile and sets a reliable crop even in climates too marginal to trigger consistent flowering and fruit set in less adaptable cultivars such as Brewster. It bears clusters of medium-sized, bumpy-skinned red fruit with sweet, juicy, aromatic flesh and a comparatively small seed. Plant in full sun in deep, acidic, well-drained soil, sheltered from strong wind, and protect young trees from any frost since even brief freezes can kill unestablished plants. Lychee needs a brief, cool, relatively dry period in winter to initiate flower buds, so avoid heavy fertilizing or irrigation in late fall and winter; once flowering begins, water and feed generously through fruit development.

common_name: Swenson Red Grape (Cold-Hardy Northern Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; very cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 4-7.
directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Swenson Red is another cold-hardy northern grape developed by breeder Elmer Swenson in Wisconsin, producing medium, pinkish-red table grapes with sweet, richly flavored flesh and a tender skin, considered by many Northern growers to be one of the best-tasting hardy grapes available, even though it retains seeds unlike some of Swenson's later seedless introductions. The vigorous vine is a reliable producer in climates too cold for most vinifera or Southern-bred hybrid grapes, extending quality fresh grape growing well into regions with harsh winters. Train to a permanent trellis, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if the vine sets a heavy crop for the best berry size and flavor.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Swingle citrumelo is grown almost exclusively as a rootstock onto which a desired orange, grapefruit, or mandarin scion is grafted, rather than for its own fruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Swingle citrumelo is a grapefruit x trifoliate orange hybrid that became the standard commercial citrus rootstock across much of Florida and the Gulf South after older rootstocks succumbed to citrus blight and tristeza virus, valued for disease resistance, cold hardiness well beyond standard sweet orange, and good compatibility with most common scion varieties. Its own fruit is bitter, seedy, and essentially inedible, so it is used as understock for grafting a named orange, grapefruit, mandarin, or lemon variety rather than being grown for fruit. Trees show trifoliate-influenced foliage with small, three-part leaves and light thorns, especially on young wood. Home gardeners most often encounter Swingle citrumelo already grafted beneath a named citrus at the nursery rather than planting it directly, but it can also be grown from seed to produce rootstock trees for home grafting projects.

common_name: Sylvester Date Palm (Silver Date Palm, Wild Date Palm)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring when soil is warm (70°F+); Sylvester Date Palm establishes best in warm soil. Purchase the largest container size affordable — palms cannot branch to compensate for a frozen or damaged growing tip, so a wider, established trunk is more cold-resilient in zone 8b. Space 15–20 feet from structures. Plant with the root ball slightly above grade in clay soils to prevent crown rot.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — clay, sand, alkaline, or loam — Sylvester Date Palm is broadly adaptable and extremely drought-tolerant once established; avoid waterlogged soils. Phoenix sylvestris (Wild Date Palm or Silver Date Palm) is native to Pakistan, India, and Sri Lanka, where it is heavily tapped for the sweet sap used to produce date palm jaggery, a prized molasses-like sweetener throughout South Asia. In Gulf Coast zone 9 landscapes it is one of the most dramatic and widely-planted feather palms, prized for its striking silvery blue-green fronds — significantly more silver-blue than the commercial Date Palm (P. dactylifera) — and its distinctive diamond-patterned trunk that becomes increasingly textured and photogenic with age. Unlike P. dactylifera, Sylvester Date Palm tolerates more cold (zone 8b, to about 20–22°F with brief exposure), adapts to the high humidity and rainfall of the Gulf South, and resists the root and crown rots that plague commercial date palms in wet climates. The palm produces clusters of small, yellow to orange-red date-like fruits that ripen in fall and are edible fresh or used for making jaggery syrup.
