It became a cornerstone rootstock during California's mid-20th-century tristeza virus crisis, when UC Riverside's Bill Bitters screened hundreds of rootstock-scion combinations and found Troyer, along with its sister selection Carrizo from the same navel orange x trifoliate parentage, resistant to the disease that was devastating sour-orange-rooted groves. Troyer imparts strong cold tolerance, good tristeza resistance, and vigorous, well-anchored growth to whatever citrus variety is grafted onto it, though it is more sensitive than Carrizo to certain heavy or poorly drained soils. Home growers wanting a hardy, disease-resistant understock for grafting favorite citrus in a Gulf Coast dooryard planting can use Troyer much as they would Carrizo, providing full sun and good drainage for best results.

plant_note: Grown from a pup or potted plant, not seed; move outdoors after frost.
directions: Truly Tiny is a miniature Dwarf Cavendish banana that stays compact enough for a container or a bright corner indoors while still producing edible fruit. Its bold tropical leaves make it an ornamental standout, and its small size suits patios and sunrooms. Grow from a potted plant or pup in full sun with rich, moisture-retentive soil, feeding heavily during active growth. Keep the soil consistently moist since bananas are thirsty, shelter it from wind, and move it indoors before frost.

plant_note: Propagate by detaching and allowing pads to callus for 2 weeks before planting in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tulip prickly pear requires excellent drainage and establishes in almost any well-drained, dry condition. Handle with extreme care using thick gloves and tongs — the tiny glochids (hairlike spines) embed in skin and are difficult to remove.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tulip prickly pear is one of the most widely distributed native cacti of the American Southwest and southern Plains, producing large, satiny, lemon-yellow flowers with orange centers in May and June that are among the most beautiful cactus flowers — 2–3 inches across, silky-textured, and glowing in full sun. The pads are flat, blue-green, and covered with clusters of spines. The fruits (tunas) ripen from green to deep red-purple in late summer and fall and are edible fresh or cooked into juice, jelly, candy, and syrup, having a sweet, watermelon-like flavor. The young pads (nopales) are also edible as a vegetable when the spines are removed. This species is one of the most cold-hardy prickly pears, surviving to zone 4 in well-drained conditions. It naturalizes across the Southwest and Texas and is an important wildlife plant — the fruit feeds desert tortoises, coyotes, javelinas, and birds. CAUTION: the tiny glochid spines embed invisibly in skin and cause intense, persistent irritation.

common_name: Tung Oil Tree (China Wood Oil Tree)
plant_note: Plant seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist soil in full sun; tung oil tree was extensively planted in the Gulf South from the 1930s–1950s as a commercial oil crop. It tolerates mild frosts but is killed back to the ground by hard freezes in zone 8, often resprouting from roots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; tung oil tree is a Chinese tree cultivated throughout zone 8–11 for its seeds, which yield tung oil — a fast-drying, water-resistant drying oil used extensively in paints, varnishes, wood preservatives, and wood finishing products. The spring flower display is spectacular — large clusters of white flowers with red or pink veining cover the bare branches before leaf emergence, followed by bold, large, heart-shaped leaves. The golf-ball-sized fruits contain 3–7 seeds with 50–60% oil content. The entire plant is poisonous if consumed — the seeds, leaves, and oil are toxic. The Gulf South has abandoned remnant tung orchards from a failed commercial industry of the mid-20th century. Now a naturalized, occasionally invasive ornamental/landscape tree notable for its spring flower show. Caution: all plant parts are toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow nuts in fall for spring germination after cold stratification; or cold-stratify nuts for 90-120 days in the refrigerator and sow in early spring. Turkish hazel is one of the best hazelnut trees for challenging urban conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, even dry or compacted soil in full sun; Turkish hazel is the most drought-tolerant and urban-adaptable of all hazelnuts, renowned in the horticultural trade as one of the few large nut trees that tolerates dry, alkaline soils, compacted city conditions, and air pollution — a remarkable feat for any tree. It is used as a rootstock for grafting cultivated filbert and hazelnut varieties, and the straight species produces small edible nuts enclosed in deeply fringed husks. The distinctive corky, deeply ridged bark and broadly pyramidal form make it an ornamental specimen tree even when not in nut. Long-lived and very low-maintenance; used extensively in European forestry and urban planting programs.

common_name: Twenty Ounce Apple (Massive American Heirloom Cooking Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Twenty Ounce is a 19th-century American heirloom named quite literally for its enormous fruit size, with individual apples commonly reaching well over a pound, making it one of the largest apples in common cultivation and a genuine novelty at the dinner table. The green-yellow skin, heavily striped and blushed with red, covers coarse, tart, juicy flesh best suited to cooking, baking, and sauce rather than fresh eating out of hand, since the sharp acidity and large size make it primarily a kitchen apple. A single Twenty Ounce apple can fill a whole pie shell on its own, a practical advantage that kept it popular in home orchards for generations of American cooking. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, since branches can be genuinely strained by fruit of this size.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Typica coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Typica coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Considered the original Arabica coffee variety from which nearly all other Arabica cultivars ultimately descend, having spread from Yemen through European colonial cultivation to become the ancestral genetic base of the world's coffee industry, it is still valued today for its classically sweet, clean, well-balanced cup quality despite its taller, more open growth habit and lower yield and disease resistance compared to modern hybrids. Its lanky, open branching habit and susceptibility to coffee leaf rust and other diseases have led most commercial growers to switch to higher-yielding, more disease-resistant hybrid varieties, but heirloom Typica plantings remain prized by specialty coffee producers for their traditional flavor profile. Provide the same dappled shade, consistent moisture, and good drainage other Arabica coffees need, and expect the first harvest after three to four years of growth.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Tyson is a self-sown seedling discovered in Pennsylvania in 1794 and grown ever since for its honeyed flavor.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Discovered as a chance seedling on Jacob Tyson's Pennsylvania farm in 1794, Tyson bears small to medium yellow pears with a distinctive honeyed sweetness and fine, melting texture that made it a favored dessert pear among American orchardists for generations, even though its modest size kept it from ever becoming a major commercial variety. The tree is notably vigorous, productive, and disease-resistant compared to many European pears of its era, qualities that helped it persist in old homestead orchards long after flashier varieties fell out of favor. Harvest while still firm in late summer and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure.

common_name: UFBeauty Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in full sun with excellent drainage; UFBeauty requires only about 250–300 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any peach cultivar, making it well suited to the mild winters of zone 9 and coastal Gulf gardens.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with excellent drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape in the first year to establish good light penetration and easy harvest access. UFBeauty is a University of Florida release from the same low-chill peach breeding program that produced Flordaking and TropicBeauty, bred specifically to bloom and fruit reliably where standard peach varieties fail to accumulate enough winter chill, ripening medium-large, attractive red-blushed yellow freestone fruit of good quality in late spring. Its very low chill requirement makes it one of the most dependable peach choices for the warmest parts of zone 9, where many older peach cultivars bloom too early, too late, or too erratically to set a reliable crop. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart when marble-sized to improve size and quality, and provide full sun and sharp drainage, since peach roots are highly susceptible to rot in wet soil.

common_name: UFBest Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in December-January while dormant; UFBest is a University of Florida IFAS release bred alongside UFSun and UFGold for an extremely low chill requirement, letting it fruit reliably through the warm winters of central and south Florida. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, siting trees away from low frost pockets since bloom can begin in December during mild winters. UFBest is one of the University of Florida's ultra-low-chill peach releases, developed to give growers south of the traditional Gulf Coast peach belt a dependable home-orchard option despite winters too warm for standard varieties. Fruit is medium to large, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with good sugar and a bright red blush, ripening in mid-to-late April. Because such a low chill requirement makes bloom erratic and extended in unusually warm years, watch closely through late winter and be ready to cover young trees if a hard freeze threatens; otherwise care follows standard peach practice — thin fruit to about 6 inches apart and prune annually to an open, low vase shape to keep the tree productive and easy to harvest.

common_name: UFGem Peach (Low-Chill Yellow Clingstone Florida Peach)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; UFGem, bred at the University of Florida for subtropical winters, bears firm yellow clingstone, non-melting flesh, ripening around May and suited to central-to-south Gulf Coast plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. UFGem, bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville alongside UFGlo and other low-chill selections, requires only a small number of chill hours, allowing it to break dormancy and bloom reliably even after a mild Gulf Coast or Florida winter. It bears firm, yellow, non-melting clingstone flesh with good sweetness and mild acidity, ripening in early May and holding up well for fresh eating or short-distance transport. As with other very-low-chill peaches, expect a somewhat shorter productive tree life and smaller fruit size than higher-chill Northern cultivars, and maintain a preventive fungicide program for brown rot and bacterial spot, both of which are aggressive in humid Gulf Coast summers.

common_name: UFGlo Peach (Low-Chill White Non-Melting-Flesh Florida Peach)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; UFGlo, bred at the University of Florida for subtropical winters, needs fewer than 150 chill hours and bears white, non-melting flesh, ripening around May.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; because UFGlo needs so few chill hours, it is one of the few peach cultivars reliable in the immediate Gulf Coast and Florida climate where winters may not deliver enough cold for standard peach varieties to bloom and fruit properly. Bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville, UFGlo requires fewer than 150 chill hours below 45°F, allowing it to break dormancy and bloom reliably even after mild subtropical winters, then ripens by early May, well ahead of most Southern-adapted peaches. The white flesh is firm and non-melting, holding its texture well for fresh eating, canning, or short transport, with a mild, sweet flavor. As with other very-low-chill peaches, expect a shorter productive lifespan and somewhat smaller fruit than higher-chill Northern cultivars, and maintain a preventive fungicide program, since brown rot and bacterial spot pressure is high in humid Gulf Coast summers.

common_name: UFGold Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Non-Melting-Flesh Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in full sun with excellent drainage; UFGold needs only about 200 chill hours, released by the University of Florida IFAS breeding program in 1997 for growers south of the traditional peach belt.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with sharp drainage, and prune to an open-vase shape in the first couple of years to keep light reaching the interior wood. UFGold is a low-chill University of Florida release with firm, non-melting yellow flesh, a texture that holds up well for canning and preserving in addition to fresh eating, unlike the soft melting flesh of most low-chill dessert peaches. Its roughly 200-hour chill requirement lets it set a reliable crop through the mild winters typical of the Gulf Coast, where bloom on high-chill peach varieties is often erratic. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set to improve size, and watch for a hard late freeze during an unusually warm bloom period, since low-chill peaches can flower earlier than the local last-frost date in some years.

common_name: UFOne Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in winter while dormant; UFOne is a University of Florida release with an ultra-low chilling requirement of roughly 100-150 hours, allowing peaches to be grown successfully as far south as central and southern Florida, well beyond the range of standard peach varieties. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; UFOne is part of the University of Florida's ultra-low-chill peach breeding program, developed to extend peach growing well south of where the fruit was traditionally thought possible, into areas that see only 100-150 hours of winter chill each year — far too little for standard or even most other Gulf South low-chill varieties. Fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with good flavor for such an early-ripening, low-chill selection, typically ready in early spring. Because it flowers so early, a late cold snap can occasionally damage blooms even in mild climates, so a somewhat sheltered planting site helps protect the crop. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart once set, and prune to an open-center vase shape after harvest to maintain airflow and light penetration through the humid growing season.

common_name: UFRoyal Nectarine (Vivid Red-Skinned Very Low-Chill Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; UFRoyal, bred at the University of Florida, needs only about 250 chill hours and bears near-100%-red-skinned fruit over firm, non-melting yellow flesh, ripening roughly 85 days from bloom in early May.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. UFRoyal, bred at the University of Florida in Gainesville for the subtropical Deep South, needs only about 250 chill hours to break dormancy reliably, making it well suited to zone 8b-10 winters too mild for most standard nectarines. Its skin colors an especially striking, nearly solid deep red over firm, non-melting yellow flesh, giving it strong fresh-market eye appeal, and the fruit ripens quickly, roughly 85 days from bloom, in early May. As with other nectarines, it is more susceptible to brown rot than fuzzy-skinned peaches in humid Gulf Coast conditions, so maintain a preventive fungicide program through fruit development and ripening. Expect a somewhat shorter productive tree life than higher-chill Northern cultivars, typical of very-low-chill stone fruit breeding.

common_name: UFSharp Peach (Firm Non-Melting-Flesh Low-Chill Clingstone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; released in 2006 with an estimated 325 chill unit requirement, suited to zone 8-9 gardens.
directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Released by the University of Florida in 2006 with an estimated 325 chill unit requirement, UFSharp suits zone 8-9 gardens wanting a mid-to-late-season low-chill peach. Unusual among low-chill types, its flesh is firm and non-melting rather than melting, holding up well to handling, with 50-70 percent red blush over yellow-orange skin. Trees are vigorous, self-fertile, semi-spreading, and productive, ripening in late May in north-central Florida trials. The firmer texture makes it a useful option for growers who want a low-chill peach suited to fresh market handling or preserving.

common_name: UFSun Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in December-January while dormant; UFSun was released by the University of Florida IFAS stone fruit breeding program with a chill requirement of only about 100 hours, letting it fruit reliably in central and even south Florida where standard 'Gulf' series peaches (about 400 hours) can bloom erratically. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, choosing a site without a low-lying frost pocket since bloom can begin as early as December in warm winters. UFSun is one of the University of Florida's ultra-low-chill releases, bred to extend backyard and commercial peach production into areas of central and south Florida too warm for even the Texas 'Gulf' series. Fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with a mild, sweet flavor and an attractive red blush, ripening in April, well ahead of most other peach varieties. Because bloom happens so early, protect trees from a late hard freeze with row cover if a cold snap threatens, and thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set to improve size. Prune annually to an open-center vase shape after harvest to keep the canopy low and to renew the one-year-old wood that peaches fruit on.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes; US Early Pride is a USDA-bred navel selection valued for ripening notably earlier than the classic Washington navel, extending the home harvest season into early fall.
directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season; US Early Pride is a modern navel orange selection bred for an early ripening window, often ready for harvest well ahead of standard Washington navels, and produces sweet, low-seed, easy-to-peel fruit with the classic navel form. Water deeply but allow the soil surface to dry between waterings, and mulch to protect the shallow root zone from summer heat. Give young trees frost protection through their first winters, and expect a light first crop within a few years of planting a grafted tree, building to full production as the tree matures.

scientific_name: Citrus paradisi x Poncirus trifoliata x Citrus sinensis 'US-119'
plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; US-119 is a USDA hybrid combining citrumelo (grapefruit x trifoliate orange) and sweet orange parentage, and mature wood has reportedly tolerated brief dips to around 15°F with limited damage, considerably colder than a standard sweet orange survives.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a protected spot such as a south-facing wall for extra winter buffering in zone 8-9 gardens. US-119 was developed by USDA breeders from a cross of citrumelo and sweet orange, giving it roughly one-quarter trifoliate orange parentage and correspondingly greater cold tolerance than a true sweet orange, while retaining a genuinely sweet, orange-like flavor rather than the sharp bitterness typical of many trifoliate hybrids. Fruit has a smooth, attractive orange peel, relatively few seeds, and juicy flesh with just a hint of the trifoliate parent's distinctive aftertaste. Because of its unusual hardiness for citrus with real dessert-orange flavor, it has become popular among cold-climate citrus hobbyists pushing sweet citrus north of the traditional growing range; protect young trees through their first few winters, since mature specimens are considerably tougher.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; US-852 tolerates winter cold to around 0 degrees F once dormant, among the hardiest citrandarins available to home growers.
directions: US-852 was bred in 1965 by USDA researcher Joe Furr at the Indio, California field station, crossing Changsha mandarin with a large-flowered trifoliate orange selection to combine mandarin flavor with trifoliate orange's exceptional cold hardiness. Among the citrandarin group of USDA cold-hardy citrus hybrids, US-852 is regarded as one of the better-flavored for fresh eating, with a sweeter, less bitter profile than many trifoliate crosses, though fruit remains seedy and more tart than a standard mandarin. The tree shows the trifoliate parent's light thorns and part-deciduous winter habit and tolerates temperatures near 0 degrees F once wood is fully dormant and hardened off, well beyond what any true mandarin survives. Give it full sun and good drainage, and protect young trees through their first winters before relying on their cold tolerance in a Gulf Coast dooryard planting.

common_name: US-897 Citrandarin (Semi-Dwarfing Cold-Hardy HLB-Tolerant Rootstock Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, protecting young wood the first winter or two; US-897, a 2007 USDA-ARS citrandarin (Cleopatra mandarin x trifoliate orange), is a semi-dwarfing, cold-hardy hybrid with some tolerance to citrus greening (HLB).
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and protect young trees during their first winter or two while cold hardiness develops. US-897, released by the USDA-ARS citrus breeding program in 2007 from a cross of Cleopatra mandarin and trifoliate orange, was developed primarily as a semi-dwarfing rootstock but has also drawn interest for direct planting because of its combination of good cold hardiness, inherited from its trifoliate parent, and documented tolerance to huanglongbing (citrus greening), the disease that has devastated citrus production across Florida and the Gulf South. Fruit is tart and seedy, more useful for juice or marmalade than fresh eating, similar to other citrandarin hybrids. As with other trifoliate-derived hybrids, expect a semi-deciduous habit and light thorns in colder winters. Established trees tolerate significantly colder temperatures than standard mandarin or sweet orange.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Unique is self-fertile and can crop well on its own, though fruit set and size improve further with a second cultivar such as Apollo or Mammoth nearby. Established plants tolerate brief dips to around 15-18F, making them reliable in zone 8 and zone 9. Harvest fruit as it falls naturally October-December.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Unique is a self-fertile New Zealand feijoa cultivar that reliably sets a good crop as a single plant, making it the best choice for gardeners with room for only one bush. Fruits are medium-large, pear-shaped, and smooth-skinned with sweet, aromatic, low-seed flesh and a good balance of pineapple-guava flavor, ripening across a fairly long mid-to-late season window rather than all at once. Because it does not depend on a pollinator partner, Unique is a popular choice for small urban gardens, patios, and hedgerows where only one feijoa can be fit in, though a second cultivar nearby will still increase yield and fruit size. The compact, dense, evergreen habit takes well to hedging or espalier, and the edible spring flowers are a bonus harvest in their own right.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Unryu is grown primarily as an ornamental specimen for its dramatically twisted, contorted branch structure, which is especially striking in winter when leafless.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Unryu, meaning 'dragon's claw' in Japanese, is an ornamental white mulberry selection grown chiefly for its strikingly twisted, corkscrew-contorted branches, a dramatic sculptural feature that is most visible and prized in winter after leaf drop, and which also makes the cut branches valued by florists and flower arrangers. It produces small, sweet, mild-flavored white-to-pinkish mulberries in season, a secondary bonus to its main ornamental appeal. Because the twisted branch character can be lost in overly vigorous growth, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization, and prune minimally, removing only dead or crossing wood, to preserve the natural contorted form. Like other mulberries, ripe fruit drops and stains, so site it away from paved areas.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ussurian pear is the most cold-hardy of all pear species and is widely used as a rootstock and breeding parent for ultra-cold-hardy hybrid pears in Canada and northern US.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ussurian pear tolerates temperatures to -40°F and is the hardiest pear species available, making it the only viable pear for zones 2–3 where European pears cannot survive. Pyrus ussuriensis is a large, ornamental, extremely cold-hardy pear species from northeastern China and Siberia; it bears masses of white flowers in early spring before the leaves, followed in fall by small (1–2 inch), round, green to yellow-green, gritty-fleshed fruits with a rough texture that are best cooked or used for preserves rather than fresh eating. Its primary agricultural value is as a rootstock for grafted pear varieties and as a breeding parent for cold-hardy pear cultivars (e.g., 'Ure', 'Rescue', 'David', 'Nova') developed by Canadian and university breeders for the northern Great Plains. The glossy, dark-green leaves turn brilliant red in fall, making it an outstanding ornamental even where fruit quality is secondary.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or bare-root plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Utah serviceberry is the most drought-tolerant of the native serviceberries and is excellent for arid western landscapes and wildlife gardens.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun to light shade; Utah serviceberry thrives in dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the West and Great Basin where other serviceberries would fail. Amelanchier utahensis is a native shrub of dry foothills, rocky slopes, and canyon walls from the Great Basin west, producing white spring flowers, small (1/3 inch) dark-blue berries with a sweet, mild, blueberry-like flavor in early summer (ripe very early, often by late May-June), and outstanding fall color in shades of orange and red. The berries are an extremely important wildlife food — essentially every frugivorous bird and mammal in the arid West relies on serviceberries during the brief ripening window. Extremely drought- and cold-hardy, this is the recommended serviceberry for xeric and high-altitude western gardens. Use for wildlife plantings, erosion control, and native landscaping.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in late winter to spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Utah Sweet is grown for arils that are notably sweeter and less tart than Wonderful, with softer, more tender seeds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; pomegranate is highly drought-tolerant once established and performs well on minimal irrigation in well-drained Gulf South soils. Utah Sweet is valued for pink-tinged skin and pulp with a notably sweeter, less tart flavor than the widely grown Wonderful pomegranate, along with softer, more tender seeds that make the arils easier to eat fresh without the firmer crunch typical of many other pomegranate cultivars. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will fruit, though yields can improve with cross-pollination from a second cultivar. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit is developing, then ease back as fruit nears ripeness to help prevent splitting, and harvest when the fruit gives a dull, metallic sound when tapped.

plant_note: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; uvaia prefers subtropical to tropical conditions and can tolerate brief light frosts once established — suited to zone 9b-12 in the US.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; uvaia (Eugenia pyriformis) is a beautiful Brazilian Myrtaceae tree closely related to Surinam cherry and pitanga, producing pear-shaped to round yellow fruits about 1 inch in diameter with a juicy, aromatic, sweet-acidic flesh — the flavor is often described as a complex blend of passion fruit, citrus, and Eugenia aromatics with a pleasant acidity that makes the fruit excellent fresh, as juice, in ice cream, and as jams. The tree has attractive bronze-red new growth and small white flowers. Increasingly popular among Brazilian native fruit enthusiasts and tropical fruit collectors in south Florida and Hawaii; one of the finest of the genus Eugenia for flavor. Fruits appear in clusters along the branches and trunk.

plant_note: Plant clonally propagated rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired English walnut variety onto the young rootstock; VX211 is a vigorous clonal understock with improved crown gall tolerance, not grown for its own nuts.
directions: Plant clonally propagated rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired English walnut variety onto the young rootstock; VX211 is a vigorous clonal understock with improved crown gall tolerance, not grown for its own nuts. Another clonally propagated hybrid rootstock selection from the University of California walnut breeding program, it combines strong vigor and good tolerance of a range of soil conditions with improved resistance to crown gall compared to traditional seedling Paradox rootstock, while offering the propagation uniformity that clonal selections provide over genetically variable seedling stock. It has become a favored alternative to RX1 on sites where crown gall rather than Phytophthora or nematode pressure is the primary soil-borne concern. Graft a desired named English walnut variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect vigorous, uniform growth with improved resilience against crown gall infection.

plant_note: Plant container citrus in spring after cold risk passes; in zone 9 plant February–April. Valencia oranges require 3–5 years from grafted transplant to first significant crop. Site in the warmest, most frost-protected location available — south or southeast exposure near a masonry wall is ideal in zone 9a.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–7.0) in full sun in the warmest available location; Valencia is the world's most important juice orange and the benchmark orange of Florida's commercial citrus industry. The medium-large, thin-skinned, deep-orange fruits mature in March–June — uniquely late for citrus, which is why Valencia becomes the dominant fresh-market and juice orange in late spring when all other oranges have finished. The juice is abundant, sweet-tart, and intensely flavored. Valencia is known for re-greening: mature ripe fruit turns orange during cool weather, then re-greens as temperatures warm in spring — this does not affect juice quality but can confuse growers expecting a uniformly orange skin. In zone 9, Valencia is one of the most cold-tolerant sweet oranges and often survives temperatures to 25°F with minimal damage; below 20°F the tree may be severely damaged. Feed with citrus fertilizer (including zinc, iron, and manganese) three times per year and maintain a 3–4 inch citrus mulch ring. Excellent fresh or for juice.

plant_note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost risk has passed; give this vigorous, upright cultivar generous room to reach full size, and stake young trees against wind until well established.
directions: Bred in Delray Beach, Florida, this cultivar bears very large, elongated fruit with orange-yellow skin blushed red and rich, fiberless, sweet flesh with a relatively small seed. It shows notably better field tolerance to anthracnose than many older cultivars, making it a dependable choice for humid Gulf Coast summers. Fruit typically ripens early to midsummer; harvest when the shoulders swell and a few fruits begin to color, then allow the rest of the crop to finish ripening at room temperature indoors.

common_name: Van Cherry (Canadian Firm Dark Sweet Cherry and Pollinizer)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Van is self-unfruitful and requires a compatible pollinizer, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ensuring a compatible pollinizer variety is planted nearby. Van was bred at the Summerland research station in British Columbia, Canada, and remains a widely grown dark sweet cherry valued for firm, glossy, deep red-black fruit with rich flavor and good resistance to cracking, along with a bloom period that overlaps well with many other sweet cherry varieties, making it a dependable pollinizer choice throughout the industry. The tree is vigorous, cold-hardy, and productive, bearing reliably once established, and the firm fruit texture holds up well to handling for both fresh eating and processing. Net trees against birds as fruit begins to color, and harvest once cherries reach full dark color and firmness, since sweet cherries do not continue ripening after picking.

common_name: Van Deman Quince (Historic USDA-Named Heirloom Quince)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, and Van Deman is a productive, well-documented older American heirloom cultivar.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Van Deman is a historic American quince cultivar named for USDA pomologist Henry E. Van Deman, documented in older state and federal pomology references among the notable named quince selections grown in American orchards in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It produces large, aromatic, golden-yellow fruit with the classic hard, tart flesh that transforms into a fragrant, rosy-pink preserve or paste once cooked with sugar. Like other quince, it is self-fertile, needs no separate pollinator, and begins bearing within a few years of planting on a young tree. Prune to an open vase form for good air circulation, which is the primary defense against fire blight, the main disease risk for quince in humid climates. Harvest fruit in fall once it has turned fully golden and developed its strong, characteristic perfume, and store in a cool, dry spot, where quince keeps considerably longer than most tree fruit.

common_name: Vanessa Grape (Cold-Hardy Canadian Seedless Red Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, on a sturdy trellis in full sun, well-drained soil; very cold-hardy and well adapted to zones 4-8.
directions: Plant bare-root vines on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Vanessa was bred in Ontario, Canada, for cold hardiness and reliable production of seedless red table grapes even in shorter, cooler growing seasons than many seedless varieties tolerate. The medium-sized, crisp, firm berries carry a bright, sweet, well-balanced flavor and hold well on the vine without splitting, making them good for fresh eating straight off the vine as well as for juice. The vigorous, productive vine is a solid choice for northern home gardens wanting a genuinely good-tasting seedless grape without relying on less cold-hardy varieties bred for milder climates. Train to a permanent trellis system, prune annually in late winter, and thin clusters if overcropping occurs for the best berry size and flavor.

common_name: Variegated Pink Lemon (Pink Eureka Lemon, Eureka Variegated Pink)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Variegated Pink Lemon performs best in full sun but is slightly more shade-tolerant than standard lemon trees; the variegated foliage is attractive enough for use as a decorative container specimen or landscape accent.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Variegated Pink Lemon (sold as 'Pink Eureka Lemon' or 'Eureka Variegated Pink') is a striking sports mutation of the standard Eureka lemon, valued both as a productive lemon and as a highly ornamental landscape or container specimen. The foliage is distinctively variegated in green and cream-white patterns that remain attractive year-round; the unripe fruits are dramatically striped in green and yellow (somewhat like a watermelon in miniature), and the flesh is pale pink when cut — a surprise and visual delight that makes this lemon memorable and photogenic. As the fruit ripens to full yellow, the pink-flesh color fades but remains just slightly pink in fully ripe fruit; the flavor is standard Eureka lemon — tart, aromatic, excellent for culinary use in anything requiring fresh lemon juice, zest, or slices. Production is good but somewhat lighter than standard Eureka. An outstanding choice for container culture, ornamental edible gardens, and any setting where visual interest in the plant matters as much as production.

common_name: Velvet Apple (Mabolo, Butter Fruit, Kamagong Fruit Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Velvet Apple is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 10-11 outdoor planting. In zone 9, container culture is practical for young trees. Trees are dioecious — plant male and female trees for fruit production. Fruits have a peculiar strong cheese-like or onion-like odor when just picked that dissipates as the flesh ripens fully; the mature flesh itself has a sweet, mild, mango-banana flavor. Considered a luxury fruit in Filipino markets.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Velvet Apple grows most vigorously in full sun but tolerates and often benefits from afternoon shade protection in the intense heat of zone 9-10 summers. Diospyros blancoi is an evergreen fruit tree from the Philippines in the family Ebenaceae (the ebony and persimmon family), producing one of the most striking and unusual fruits in the tropical fruit world. The ripe fruits are perfectly round (3–4 inches in diameter), covered in a dense coat of fine reddish-brown to coppery velvet-soft hairs — like an incredibly large, round, red-brown cherry with velvet skin — from which the common name 'Velvet Apple' derives. Beneath the velvety skin is a firm, creamy-white to pink flesh with a sweet, mild flavor combining banana, cream, and mango notes and a dry, slightly astringent texture similar to some persimmons. The fruits have a striking, pungent odor when freshly harvested that many people find unpleasant (sometimes compared to ripe cheese or onion), but this odor dissipates with ventilation and does not affect the pleasant flavor of the flesh. In the Philippines, the tree is doubly valued: for its edible fruit and for its heartwood (called 'kamagong' — Philippine ebony), one of the hardest and heaviest woods in Southeast Asia, used for fine furniture and tool handles. The tree is also an ornamental specimen with glossy, dark-green foliage.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds in spring (soak in boiling water and cool overnight before planting) in well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep soil in full sun; velvet mesquite grows naturally in desert grasslands, dry washes, and desert scrub of southern Arizona and Sonora, Mexico.
directions: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep, well-aerated soil in full sun; velvet mesquite is the dominant mesquite of Arizona desert grasslands and saguaro cactus country, nearly identical to honey mesquite (P. glandulosa) but more densely hairy (velutinous) on the leaves and pods, tolerating the extreme heat and seasonal drought of the Sonoran Desert. The long, flat, tan seed pods mature in late summer and are very high in sugar and protein — edible by humans (ground into mesquite flour), consumed by coyotes, javelinas, deer, and dozens of bird species. The fragrant, cream-colored flower spikes in spring attract swarms of native bees. Deep taproots (up to 60 feet) access groundwater far below the surface. An important nitrogen-fixing tree that improves soil fertility. The aromatic wood produces some of the finest barbecue smoke in the world — prized for smoked meats throughout the Southwest.

common_name: Ventura Strawberry Fig (Adriatic-Type Red-Fleshed California Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; this Adriatic-type California selection is grown for its deep red, berry-flavored flesh and performs well in hot, sunny Gulf Coast conditions.
directions: Ventura Strawberry is a California selection within the Adriatic group of fig cultivars, named for the deep red, berry-like color and flavor of its flesh rather than for any trait of its skin. Fruits are medium-sized with dark purple-black skin and a thick, juicy, red interior that carries a distinct strawberry-like sweetness; as with other Adriatic types it sets a dependable main crop without needing pollination. The tree performs well in hot, sunny conditions and has become a sought-after specialty selection among Southern fig collectors for its rich flavor and productivity. Grow it as you would other common-type figs, in full sun with excellent drainage, and expect the first fruit within two to three years of planting a rooted cutting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Vermentino is notably heat- and drought-tolerant once established, well suited to warm growing regions.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Vermentino is a Mediterranean white grape most closely associated with Sardinia, Liguria, and Corsica, prized for producing crisp, refreshing wines with bright citrus and herbal notes and a characteristic faint saline minerality, made in a style well suited to warm-climate coastal cuisine. The vine is naturally heat- and drought-tolerant, retaining useful acidity even in hot growing conditions better than many other white varieties, which has made it an increasingly popular choice for warm-climate plantings outside its traditional Mediterranean range. Train to a permanent trellis, manage vigor through canopy work since the variety can be quite vigorous, and pick based on acid retention rather than sugar alone, since Vermentino's appeal rests heavily on preserving its signature freshness.

common_name: Vermont Beauty Pear (Small Richly Flavored New England Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Vermont Beauty was introduced in the 1890s and prized for exceptional flavor packed into a small fruit.
directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Introduced from Vermont in the 1890s, this heirloom bears small, yellow, red-blushed pears that punch well above their size in flavor, with rich, sweet, aromatic flesh that made it a favorite dessert pear in New England home orchards despite never achieving wide commercial distribution. The compact fruit size and hardy constitution suited it well to the shorter growing seasons and colder winters of its home region. Harvest while still firm in early fall and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Vernon is among the more cold-tolerant white sapote cultivars, with mature trees withstanding brief lows in the mid-20s°F with only minor twig damage, making it a workable choice for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree will set fruit without a pollinator. Fruit ripens over an extended window from fall into winter depending on climate.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil sheltered from strong wind; Vernon is a California-bred white sapote selection prized for consistent, heavy production and self-fertility, removing the need to plant a second tree for pollination as some white sapote cultivars require. The medium-sized, thin-skinned, green-to-yellow fruit has smooth, custard-textured flesh with a sweet flavor often compared to a blend of banana, peach, and vanilla pudding. Trees grow fast and can reach substantial size, so plan for eventual shade and root spread; prune after harvest to maintain a manageable height and encourage branching for next season's crop. Fruit is ready to pick when it softens slightly and yields to gentle pressure, then finishes ripening at room temperature over several days.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Verte de Bordeaux is a productive, compact-to-medium fig tree well-suited to zone 9 conditions. It produces two crops in zone 9: a breba crop on old wood in June–July and a main crop on new wood in August–September. Prune lightly after harvest to maintain size and encourage productive new wood.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — figs produce best in lean conditions and can become overly vegetative in rich, heavily fertilized soil; Verte de Bordeaux is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region of southwestern France, producing small to medium, pear-shaped fruits with green to greenish-yellow skin that remains green even when fully ripe — a distinctive appearance that surprises consumers expecting a ripe fig to be darker. The deep burgundy-red interior flesh has an intensely rich, wine-like, complex sweetness that fig connoisseurs often rate among the finest flavors in the Ficus carica species. The petite size (1–2 inches) and striking green skin with deeply colored interior make it a specialty market favorite. In zone 9 Verte de Bordeaux produces consistently and handles the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers well. The green skin can be confusing to novice growers who may pick the fruit too early — harvest when the neck of the fig bends and the fruit softens.

plant_note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Victoria is self-fertile and does not require a second variety for pollination, though a pollinator improves yield.
directions: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Victoria is self-fertile and does not require a second variety for pollination, though a pollinator improves yield. The single most widely grown plum in England and one of the best-known European dessert plums in the world, it bears heavy crops of large, oval, red-blushed yellow fruit with juicy, sweet flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, and its reliable, self-fertile heavy bearing has made it a standard first-choice plum for a home orchard with room for only one tree. Its very heavy crops often require significant hand thinning of young fruit to prevent limb breakage and to improve the size and quality of the remaining plums. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, thin crowded fruit clusters, and support heavily laden branches in a good fruiting year.

common_name: Victoria Red Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown vines in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Victoria Red is a jointly released University of Arkansas / Texas A&M AgriLife table grape named a 2017 Texas Superstar for its sustained tolerance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease that kills most table and wine grapes throughout the humid Gulf South within a few years.
directions: Train on a trellis system in full sun in well-drained soil; prune in late winter. Victoria Red is a seeded red table grape that has survived over 25 years of extreme Pierce's disease pressure at the Tarkington Vineyards test site near Victoria, Texas, making it one of the few table grapes with genuinely sustained tolerance to the disease that otherwise makes grape growing across the Gulf Coast so difficult. It produces large, sweet clusters with sugar levels reaching up to 25 brix, eaten fresh, dried into raisins, or made into juice. Because it was bred specifically for hot, humid Texas and Gulf Coast conditions, it needs none of the intensive spray programs required to keep Pierce's-disease-susceptible European grapes alive in the region. Harvest clusters once berries have colored fully and taste sweet, since grapes do not continue ripening after picking.

common_name: Vidal Blanc Grape (Vidal 256, Cold-Hardy French-American White Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring in full sun on a well-drained site; Vidal Blanc is a heavy-cropping, cold-hardy French-American hybrid that ripens late in the season and often needs cluster thinning to keep wine quality high.
directions: Vidal Blanc, officially Vidal 256, is a French-American hybrid bred from Ugni Blanc and Seibel 4986 that has become one of the most widely planted white wine grapes in the eastern and southern United States for its combination of productivity, cold hardiness, and good fungal-disease tolerance. It produces heavy clusters of thick-skinned, golden berries late in the season, valued both for crisp dry table wines and for late-harvest or ice-wine-style dessert wines where hard freezes concentrate the sugars. Train it on a high-wire cordon or Geneva double-curtain system in full sun, and prune to manage its vigorous, fruitful growth, which can overcrop and require cluster thinning for best wine quality. Like most French-American hybrids, Vidal Blanc carries only moderate Pierce's disease tolerance, so southern extension programs generally recommend it for the upper and middle South rather than the most Pierce's-disease-prone Gulf Coast counties.

plant_note: Plant nursery trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil.
directions: Plant nursery trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil, allowing space for a nearly thornless, densely foliaged canopy. Provide even moisture throughout the year and protect young trees from hard freezes with covers or trunk wraps. Villafranca bears Eureka-type lemons that are medium-sized, juicy, and nearly seedless, produced almost continuously in warm climates with a heavier main crop in winter. Long grown in Florida and the Gulf Coast as a dooryard favorite, it is valued for producing well even under humid, subtropical conditions that can trouble other lemon cultivars.

common_name: Villard Blanc Grape (Seyve-Villard 12-375, French-American Hybrid White Wine Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring in full sun on a well-drained site; Villard Blanc is a vigorous French-American hybrid bred for resistance to the fungal diseases that plague vinifera grapes in humid climates and performs best trained on a cordon or high-wire system with attentive canopy management.
directions: Villard Blanc, registered as Seyve-Villard 12-375, is one of the classic French-American hybrid wine grapes bred in the early 20th century by Bertille Seyve and Victor Villard to combine vinifera-quality fruit with the fungal-disease resistance of American parentage. It produces large clusters of greenish-white berries that ripen into a crisp, aromatic dry white wine and has historically been planted across the humid eastern and southern United States, where straight vinifera varieties struggle with black rot, downy mildew, and powdery mildew. Train vines on a cordon or high-wire trellis in full sun with good air movement, and prune hard each winter, since Villard Blanc is a vigorous grower that needs canopy management to ripen fruit well and avoid disease pressure in wet years. It carries only moderate Pierce's disease tolerance compared with purpose-bred Gulf Coast hybrids, so it performs best in the upper and middle South rather than the most humid Gulf Coast counties.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Viognier is a moderately vigorous variety that can struggle with poor, uneven fruit set in unfavorable spring weather.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Viognier is a white wine grape native to the Rhône Valley of France, historically centered on the tiny appellation of Condrieu, where it came perilously close to disappearing entirely in the mid-20th century before a revival brought it back to prominence in France, California, and beyond. The grape produces full-bodied, richly aromatic white wines with pronounced notes of peach, apricot, and honeysuckle, a distinctive perfumed character that sets it apart from crisper, more neutral white varieties. The vine can be inconsistent in fruit set, sometimes producing loose, uneven clusters in cool or wet spring weather, so site selection and bloom-time weather matter more for Viognier than for many other varieties. Train to a permanent trellis, thin fruit if clusters set unevenly, and pick based on aromatic ripeness, since Viognier can lose its signature perfume if left to hang too long.

common_name: Violette de Bordeaux Fig (Negronne Fig, Petite Negri Fig)
plant_note: Plant in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Violette de Bordeaux is a small-statured fig tree (6–8 feet) highly suited to container growing and small urban gardens. It produces predominantly on the main crop (August–October in zone 9) with a modest Breba crop in June.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Violette de Bordeaux (called Negronne in California and known as Petite Negri in some American nurseries) is a small-statured French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region of France — one of the most beloved fig varieties among connoisseurs because of its extraordinary flavor. The small (1.5–2 inch), deep purple-violet to nearly black berries have blood-red interior flesh with a rich, complex, intense sweetness with strawberry-raspberry undertones — a flavor profile significantly deeper and more complex than larger, milder figs. The tree's compact size (6–8 feet tall and wide) makes it an ideal container specimen for patios, balconies, and small urban gardens where a standard fig would overwhelm the space. Violette de Bordeaux is the go-to container fig recommended by specialty nurseries. The skin is quite thin and fruits bruise easily, limiting its commercial shipping potential but making it perfect for eating fresh off the tree. In zone 9, it fruits reliably August–October and can be moved into protected areas during cold snaps in zone 9a.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Violette de Sollies is primarily a fall-ripening fig; in zone 9 the main crop ripens September–October, later than most other varieties. The late ripening extends the fresh fig season into fall. It produces minimal breba fruit and is primarily valued for its exceptional main crop quality.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Violette de Sollies has Protected Designation of Origin (AOP) status as the primary fig of Sollies-Pont commune in Var, Provence — the most commercially important fig production area in France. It accounts for approximately 80% of French commercial fig production and is the fig you encounter in French supermarkets and on French cheese boards. The large, round to pear-shaped fruits have dark violet to nearly black skin and deep red to garnet flesh with an exceptionally creamy, melt-in-the-mouth texture and rich, complex sweetness. The PDO designation reflects the specific microclimate of the Var region and the care taken to produce the variety at optimal quality. Violette de Sollies is a fall-ripening variety, producing its main crop in September–October in zone 9 — later than most other figs and extending the fresh fig season into autumn. The exceptional flavor quality and French culinary prestige make it a premium choice for zone 9 gardens where the warm fall provides ideal ripening conditions.

common_name: Virginia Beauty Apple (Spicy Russeted Virginia Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in a sunny, well-drained site; requires roughly 700 chill hours, so it is best suited to the upper and middle South rather than low-chill Gulf Coast areas.
directions: Plant in a sheltered but sunny site and prune to an open canopy to help the fruit color and to control the tree's tendency toward biennial bearing. Virginia Beauty is a late-19th-century Virginia heirloom noted for its striped red skin, patches of russet, and distinctively spicy, aromatic flesh that improves in flavor during a few weeks of storage. It has long been a favorite among Southern heritage orchardists for fresh eating and cider, prized as much for its complex flavor as for its keeping ability into winter.

plant_note: Plant grafted tree in spring in full to partial sun in well-drained soil; Vista White is prized for its unusually sweet, pale, sherbet-like flesh, distinct from the more common orange-fleshed loquat cultivars, and performs well in zones 8-10, though a run of hard freezes below the upper 20s F during bloom or fruit set can reduce or eliminate the crop for the year.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; loquats tolerate poor soils and short dry spells once established but size and flavor improve with regular moisture during fruit development; thin heavy clusters for larger fruit and harvest when fully colored and slightly soft, since loquats do not continue ripening after picking. Vista White is a California-selected loquat grown mainly by home orchardists and specialty growers for its distinctive creamy white to pale-yellow flesh, a marked contrast to the orange flesh of widely grown cultivars like Premier and Big Jim. The round, light-yellow fruits hang in grape-like clusters of fifteen to twenty and have a delicate, very sweet, almost sherbet-like flavor with mild tang, making them popular for fresh eating. Trees bloom in fall and ripen fruit in late winter to spring, ahead of most other tree fruit, and tolerate periods of drought and a range of soil types once established as long as drainage is good and soil salinity is low. As with all loquats, the open flowers and developing fruit are more cold-sensitive than the tree itself, so a sheltered, south-facing planting site improves crop reliability in zone 8-9 gardens near the cooler edge of the loquat's range.

plant_note: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Volkamer lemon is a vigorous, cold-hardy understock widely used in Gulf Coast home citrus production.
directions: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Volkamer lemon is a vigorous, cold-hardy understock widely used in Gulf Coast home citrus production. A vigorous, cold-hardy lemon relative of uncertain hybrid origin, its own fruit is coarse and of little culinary value, but it is highly valued as a rootstock for producing large, fast-growing, precocious, and productive trees with notably better cold tolerance than many other citrus rootstocks, making it a common choice for home citrus trees in the marginal-climate Gulf South. Its vigor and cold hardiness have made it especially popular for backyard citrus in Texas, Louisiana, and coastal areas of the Gulf Coast where winter cold snaps threaten less hardy rootstocks. Graft a desired named citrus variety onto young rootstock, and expect a large, fast-growing, heavily-bearing tree that will need ample permanent space.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings and transplant to a sturdy support once nighttime lows are reliably above 50°F.
directions: Grow from cuttings taken from a healthy mother plant and support the vining stems on a post or arbor in full sun with fast-draining, cactus-style soil. This deep magenta-red-fleshed selection is grown by home collectors specifically for its intensely colored, richly flavored fruit, which stands out from the milder white-fleshed types. Because the succulent stems are damaged by hard freezes, Gulf Coast growers generally keep it container-grown so it can be moved to a garage or greenhouse whenever a freeze warning is issued. Fruit set improves with hand pollination shortly after the night-blooming flowers open, since many dragon fruit types are only partially self-fertile.

common_name: W. Murcott Afourer Mandarin (Late-Season Seedy Parent of Tango Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; fruit stays seedless only if no other citrus blooms nearby, since Afourer readily cross-pollinates.
directions: Afourer, marketed in the US as W. Murcott, is a late-winter Moroccan-origin mandarin valued for deep orange color, intensely sweet flavor, and easy-peel skin, ripening after most other mandarins have finished. Unlike its seedless sport Tango, Afourer readily develops seeds when planted near other citrus, so growers wanting guaranteed seedless fruit should isolate it or choose Tango instead; those without nearby citrus can grow Afourer itself for a slightly richer, more complex flavor some tasters prefer. It is a vigorous, productive tree that bears heavily once established and benefits from fruit thinning in on years. Water deeply but infrequently and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for best fruit quality.

common_name: Wabash American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Cold-Hardy Native Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, setting young trees carefully to avoid disturbing the long taproot.
directions: Wabash is a historic Midwestern selection of native American persimmon valued for its large fruit size relative to wild trees and its vigorous, dependable growth. Orange-fleshed fruit ripens in fall and turns intensely sweet, custardy, and rich once fully soft, but stays mouth-puckeringly astringent if eaten too early, so wait until fruit yields to gentle pressure or drops naturally. The tree tolerates heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established, and its deep taproot makes it a long-lived, low-maintenance choice for food-forest or wildlife plantings. Provide a second genetically distinct native persimmon nearby for best fruit set unless a known self-fertile selection is planted, and remove root suckers regularly to keep it from forming a thicket.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Wabash is a vigorous named Peterson Pawpaw cultivar and sets its best crops when planted with Susquehanna, Shenandoah, or another genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun as the tree matures; Wabash is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars, selected from Neal Peterson's long-running breeding program for its combination of large fruit size and notably vigorous, healthy tree growth. Fruit has the classic rich, tropical pawpaw flavor — often described as a cross between banana, mango, and custard — with good flesh-to-seed ratio. As with all pawpaws, Wabash is self-incompatible and requires a second, unrelated named cultivar planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination; hand-pollinating between two different cultivars' open flowers with a small brush improves fruit set in home gardens where natural fly and beetle pollinators may be scarce. Mulch young trees well and keep soil consistently moist through the first two seasons, since pawpaw's shallow, fleshy root system is intolerant of drought while establishing; mature trees are considerably more drought-tolerant.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-8, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Wagener originated in New York State in 1791 and became a widely respected 19th-century American apple, valued for its crisp, juicy, well-balanced tart-sweet flesh and, notably, its long storage life, holding good eating quality well into winter under proper cold storage conditions long before mechanical refrigeration was common. The medium, red-striped fruit is a genuine dual-purpose apple, good for fresh eating as well as cooking, and it holds a place in apple breeding history as a parent of the modern cold-hardy Idared. The precocious, productive tree bears young and reliably; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for the longest keeping quality.

plant_note: Transplant seedlings in spring once soil and air are reliably warm, in full sun and well-drained soil in a frost-free spot.
directions: Waimanalo was developed by the University of Hawaii as a low-branching, compact papaya bred to resist mechanical damage and reduce losses from fruit fly infestation compared to older Hawaiian selections. The medium-large, round-to-oval fruit has thick orange flesh with good sugar content, and the short, sturdy trunk starts fruiting closer to the ground than many other papaya types, easing harvest. It performs best in a warm, sheltered spot with fast-draining soil, since papayas are highly susceptible to root rot in wet ground. Gulf Coast growers usually treat it as a fast-fruiting annual or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter.

plant_note: Plant a container-grown grafted tree in spring after all danger of frost, in full sun and well-drained soil away from low-lying frost pockets.
directions: Waldin is one of the oldest named Florida dooryard avocados still commonly planted, valued for its early-to-midseason harvest and reliable heavy bearing on a vigorous, wind-tolerant tree. Fruit is medium to large, smooth-skinned, and pear-shaped with pale green, watery-textured flesh typical of the West Indian race, which lends good tolerance of Florida's hot, humid lowland conditions but less cold tolerance than Mexican-race cultivars. As a Type A flowering cultivar it benefits from a nearby Type B pollinator for heavier fruit set. Choose Waldin where summer heat and salt-air exposure near the coast are bigger concerns than winter cold, since it lacks the frost hardiness of Mexican-race selections.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; wampee is sensitive to cold and is best protected from any frost. It is smaller and more compact than most tropical fruit trees, reaching 10–20 feet, and can be grown in large containers in cooler climates and moved indoors in winter.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-protected conditions; wampee (wampi) is a Chinese subtropical fruit tree in the citrus family (Rutaceae) producing large drooping clusters of small, round, yellowish-white to golden fruits about the size of a large grape, with a thin, slightly oily skin and aromatic, translucent flesh that ranges from sweet to pleasantly acid-sweet, with a distinctive, complex, resinous-floral fragrance from essential oils in the skin. The flavor profile has notes of citrus, lychee, and a slight bitterness that makes it uniquely refreshing. Native to South China and widely grown in southern China, Vietnam, and Thailand, it has been cultivated for over 2,000 years and is a significant regional fruit crop in Guangdong. The fruits are eaten fresh, made into preserves and wine, and the essential oil from the rind is used in Chinese medicine and as a fragrance. It grows well in the humid subtropics of zones 9–11 and is more compact and manageable than many tropical fruit trees.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Wani or Binjai mango is a Borneo and Sumatra native Mangifera species producing large, pale-green to whitish-green, very heavy fruits with sweet-tart, somewhat turpentine-flavored white to pale-yellow flesh — one of the most important traditional fruit trees of Malaysian Borneo.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; requires consistent rainfall or irrigation during fruit development. Mangifera caesia (wani mango or binjai) is a large Mangifera species native to the humid lowland rainforests of Borneo, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula — one of the most important traditional fruit trees of Sarawak and Sabah (Malaysian Borneo), where it is planted around villages and sometimes bears enormous quantities of fruits. The fruits are remarkable: large (4–6 inches long), elongated-oblong to kidney-shaped, pale green to yellowish-white when ripe — larger on average than common mangoes — with white to pale-yellow flesh. The flavor is more distinctly turpentine-acidic than common mango, with a sweetness that varies considerably by seedling; selected clones can be mild and pleasant. The flesh is rather fibrous and the skin is not eaten. In Sarawak, wani fruits are sold fresh in markets and eaten as a fresh fruit, in rujak (spicy fruit salads), and processed into pickles. The bark and young leaves have traditional medicinal uses in Malaysian herbal medicine. Wani requires a genuinely tropical, hot, humid, low-frost-risk climate and is suitable only for zone 11–12 in the continental United States (extreme South Florida, Hawaii). A collectors' fruit tree for the most dedicated tropical fruit enthusiast.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile loam in full sun; plant two different pear cultivars for cross-pollination (Hood, Kieffer, Ayers); Warren pear requires only moderate chill hours (600–800) and excels in zone 7–9.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Warren is an outstanding southern heirloom pear discovered in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, by T.O. Warren around 1960 — a chance seedling that produces buttery, very sweet, nearly grit-free fruit with the silky texture of a fine European dessert pear. This exceptional fruit quality, combined with good fire blight resistance (the most devastating pear disease in humid southern climates), has made Warren one of the most highly regarded pear varieties for the Gulf South in recent decades. Most European pears are highly susceptible to fire blight (Erwinia amylovora), the bacterial disease that kills branches and causes heavy losses in hot, humid climates — Warren's relative resistance makes it a practical choice where standard European pears like Bartlett routinely fail. The medium-to-large, greenish-yellow fruits ripen in August in zone 9 and require off-tree ripening (store at room temperature after harvest) to reach their full, buttery sweetness. Plant with Hood or Kieffer for cross-pollination. Warren is not always easy to find at nurseries but is available from regional southern specialty nurseries and bare-root mail-order sources.

common_name: Washington Navel Orange (Classic Seedless Navel Orange)
plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the last frost in full sun with sharp drainage; Washington Navel is one of the least cold-hardy sweet oranges and needs a warm, sheltered site or container culture with winter protection outside zones 9b-10.
directions: Plant grafted trees in full sun in well-drained soil, keeping the graft union above the soil line, and water deeply and regularly while the tree establishes its root system. Washington Navel traces to a bud sport discovered in Bahia, Brazil in the early 1800s and became the foundation of the California citrus industry after Eliza Tibbets planted budwood from it in Riverside in 1873; it remains the standard by which other navel oranges are judged, prized for its large, easy-peeling, essentially seedless fruit with sweet, richly flavored flesh and the small secondary "navel" fruit embedded at the blossom end. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree for weeks without losing quality, but the tree itself is notably more cold-sensitive than many other sweet oranges, so gulf coast growers outside the mildest coastal pockets should plant it in a warm microclimate or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover during hard freezes. Fertilize lightly but regularly through the growing season and thin out crossing or dead wood in late winter to keep the canopy open.

common_name: Water Apple (Watery Rose Apple, Bell Fruit)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to periodically waterlogged, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; water apple is a Southeast Asian tropical fruit tree that tolerates wet soils and periodic flooding and produces crisp, bell-shaped, mildly sweet, extremely watery fruits — very distinct from the rose apple (Syzygium jambos) in fruit size, texture, and tree form.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; water apple tolerates periodic waterlogging and is well-suited to wet, low-lying areas. Syzygium aqueum (water apple or watery rose apple) is a Southeast Asian tropical fruit tree native to the Malay Peninsula and Indonesia that produces the most 'watery' of all the rose apple relatives — distinctive, bell-shaped to pear-shaped fruits (1.5–2 inches long) in white, pale pink, or red, with an extremely high water content (as the name suggests), a thin, glossy skin, crisp texture, and a very mild, barely-sweet, cucumber-like flavor. The fruit is refreshing rather than richly flavored — in tropical heat, the high water content makes water apple a thirst-quenching fruit eaten fresh as a hydrating snack, cut into slices and served with salt and chili, or made into a light agua fresca. The tree is notably tolerant of wet soils and periodic flooding compared to other Syzygium species — it grows naturally along stream banks and in seasonal swamps in its native habitat. It is distinctly different from the rose apple (S. jambos) in its smaller, lighter, more watery fruit, smaller tree size, and tolerance of wet conditions. Widely grown in home gardens throughout Southeast Asia and the Philippines.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic, deep alluvial soil in full sun. Water Hickory is adapted to the seasonally flooded bottomlands and swamp edges of the Gulf Coast and should be sited in low-lying areas that experience periodic flooding.
directions: Water Hickory is the hickory of the riverine swamps, bottomland hardwood forests, and floodplain edges of the southeastern coastal plain, native from Virginia to Florida and west to Illinois and Texas, where it grows alongside bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp chestnut oak in the seasonally flooded alluvial soils of river terraces and floodplain edges. Its small, thin-shelled nuts are very bitter and not generally eaten by people, but they are an important food for wood ducks, squirrels, and wild turkeys in bottomland habitat — waterfowl consume large quantities of the nuts that fall into flooded bottomland pools in fall. Like all hickories, Water Hickory is slow-growing but extremely long-lived, with the deep taproot making transplanting nearly impossible after the first year of growth; direct-seed into the permanent planting site in fall for best results. Grow in moist to periodically flooded, rich, slightly acidic alluvial soil in full sun — the only hickory species reliably tolerant of extended seasonal flooding.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds indoors in warm, moist, fertile soil; water rose apple is frost-tender and suited only for zones 10–12 outdoors or container culture in zone 9 brought indoors before frost. Plant in fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun.
