plant_note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall in sandy, dry, acidic soil in full sun; as with most hawthorns, seeds require double dormancy and will germinate in their second spring — sow on-site whenever possible, as transplanting established plants is difficult.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy or rocky, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun along the Coastal Plain; yellow haw is a rare and botanically distinctive native hawthorn prized for its fall display of attractive yellow to greenish-yellow, pear-shaped to rounded haws that are notably sweeter and more palatable than those of most other hawthorns. Its spring flowers provide nectar for early native bees, and the fruit is consumed by mockingbirds, brown thrashers, and other birds that frequent the dry, sandy-woods habitats where this species thrives. It performs best in lean, well-drained soils and is intolerant of heavy clay, standing water, or overly enriched garden beds. Yellow haw's rarity in the wild makes cultivating it from locally sourced seed a valuable contribution to the conservation of Coastal Plain plant diversity.

common_name: Yellow Long Neck Fig (Distinctive Elongated Bottleneck-Shaped Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Yellow Long Neck is a heirloom fig grown as much for its unmistakable, unusual shape as for eating quality, producing fruit with a dramatically elongated, narrow neck tapering to a rounded body, a form so distinctive that a single glance identifies the variety among any collection of figs. Beneath the pale yellow-green skin, the amber-honey flesh is sweet and richly flavored, good for fresh eating, drying, and preserves once the tree is established and producing reliably. The vigorous tree performs well in fig-collector gardens seeking novelty forms alongside more standard varieties, and general fig culture practices — full sun, well-drained soil, and winter root protection in colder zones — apply equally here.

common_name: Yellow Mangosteen (Mysore Gamboge, Yellow Gamboge, Egg Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Garcinia xanthochymus is frost-sensitive but somewhat more cold-tolerant than the Purple Mangosteen (G. mangostana), surviving brief temperatures to 32°F if the soil drains well. In zone 9b-10, it can be tried as a large container or borderline landscape tree in sheltered spots. The yellow fruits ripen summer–fall; the sweet-sour flesh is eaten fresh or used in preserves and beverages. Trees are self-fertile — a single tree produces fruit.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Yellow Mangosteen grows best in the filtered light and moist, rich conditions of its native South Asian forest habitat and benefits from shade protection during establishment. Garcinia xanthochymus is an attractive, medium-sized, evergreen tree native to the Western Ghats and Mysore region of India and adjacent Burma (Myanmar) in the family Clusiaceae — the same family as the famous Purple Mangosteen (G. mangostana). The tree has a naturally elegant form: a pyramidal to columnar crown of large, glossy, deep-green, lance-shaped leaves that hang in graceful, slightly pendant arrays from the branches. In summer, the tree produces smooth, round to slightly oval fruits 2–4 inches in diameter with bright golden-yellow skin when ripe, containing 1–4 large seeds surrounded by soft, translucent, sweet-sour, juicy pulp. The flavor is distinctive — a complex sweet-sour combination reminiscent of both apricot and tamarind, refreshing as a fresh fruit and excellent in juices, jams, and chutneys. Yellow Mangosteen is considered by tropical fruit enthusiasts to be more adaptable to cultivation outside the tropics than the famously difficult Purple Mangosteen — it tolerates a somewhat wider range of soil conditions and performs in zone 10 where G. mangostana struggles. Also grown as an ornamental specimen tree for its attractive form and handsome foliage.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; yellow mombin is damaged below 30°F. Large stem cuttings (hardwood) root readily and are a common propagation method in tropical countries. The tree drops its leaves briefly in dry season and fruits shortly after.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; yellow mombin (hog plum) is a large deciduous tropical tree of Central and South America and the Caribbean producing clusters of small, oval, golden-yellow fruits, 1–2 inches long, with a distinctive sweet-tart, highly aromatic tropical flavor that combines elements of mango, plum, and passionfruit with a resinous, citrus-like quality. The thick, waxy skin encloses a small amount of translucent yellow flesh surrounding a large seed. In the Caribbean, Central America, and tropical Brazil, the fruit is eaten fresh, made into juice, agua fresca, ice cream, wine, and vinegar — Spondias mombin juice is a major street beverage in countries like Colombia, Costa Rica, and Brazil. The tree is fast-growing, highly drought-tolerant once established, and tolerates a range of soil conditions from light sandy to heavy clay. It is distinct from the ambarella (S. dulcis) and red mombin/jocote (S. purpurea).

common_name: Yellow Passion Fruit (Golden Passion Fruit, Maracujá Amarelo)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before planting out; transplant only after all frost risk has passed and soil is warm above 65°F; in frost-free zones, direct sow after the wet season begins.
directions: Sow seed just below the surface in warm starting mix and maintain 75–85°F for germination; yellow passion fruit is the world's most commercially cultivated passion fruit, producing golf-ball- to lemon-sized yellow-skinned fruits with intensely fragrant, tart orange-yellow pulp that is the basis of most commercial passion fruit juice. A rampant perennial vine to 30 feet, it needs a very sturdy trellis or fence and frost-free conditions; train two or three main canes horizontally along wires and allow laterals to cascade. Flowers require cross-pollination between two genetically distinct plants, or hand-pollination outside the tropics where native bee pollinators are absent. Harvest when fruit begins to show yellow color and drops easily from the vine.

subcategory: Southeast Asian ornamental small-fruit persimmon tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in zone 10–12; Yellow Persimmon (Madan, Ten-stamen Persimmon, Burmese Persimmon) is an attractive ornamental and fruiting tree from Indochina, Thailand, and the Malay Peninsula — bearing round to oval, small, bright-yellow fruits with very sweet, yellow flesh and no astringency, prized as a fresh-eating persimmon across Southeast Asia and grown as both an ornamental and edible tree in tropical gardens.
directions: Plant Diospyros decandra in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly throughout the year; protect from temperatures below 40°F; harvest fruits when they reach full yellow color and have a slight give to finger pressure — they should be non-astringent even when firm, unlike temperate persimmons. Yellow Persimmon is an underappreciated tropical fruit tree that deserves far wider cultivation than it currently receives outside Southeast Asia. Unlike the more widely known Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki) which is astringent when underripe, Yellow Persimmon (madan in Thai, 'ten stamen' in English — referring to its ten stamens vs. 16 in D. kaki) produces small, round, bright-yellow fruits that are sweet and non-astringent even when firm, and have a honey-sweet, mildly vanilla-flavored flesh. The fruits are eaten fresh in Thailand and throughout Indochina as a dessert fruit, and the tree is planted as both an ornamental (handsome, glossy-leaved, with fragrant, cream-white flowers) and a fruit tree in village gardens. The tree grows as a medium-sized, evergreen shade tree in the tropics, producing fruits that ripen over an extended season from late summer through winter. An excellent rare fruit tree for zone 10–12 tropical and subtropical gardens seeking both ornamental beauty and unusual fresh fruit.

common_name: Yellow Transparent Apple (Very Early Translucent-Skinned Russian Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Transparent ripens extremely early, often by late June to early July, and fruit should be used quickly since it bruises easily and does not keep.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Introduced from Russia in the 1870s, Yellow Transparent is one of the earliest-ripening apples grown in North America, producing pale, almost translucent yellow-green skin over soft, tart, juicy flesh that cooks down quickly into a smooth sauce. Because the thin skin bruises easily and the fruit does not store, it is best picked directly for immediate use in pies, sauce, and fresh eating rather than for the fruit bowl. The tree is notably cold-hardy and productive, and its extremely early ripening has long made it a favorite for the first homemade applesauce of the year.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or stratify seed in a moist medium in the refrigerator for 8–10 weeks before spring sowing; yellowhorn strongly prefers excellent drainage and a drier continental-type climate, so it is best suited to zone 8 in drier margins of the Gulf region rather than humid, heavy-clay coastal ground.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, fast-draining, even poor or rocky soil; yellowhorn is a small deciduous tree native to northern China where it grows on dry hillsides, and it is notably drought tolerant once established but intolerant of wet feet or heavy, poorly drained clay. In spring it puts on a striking floral display of white, horse-chestnut-like flower panicles marked with red-to-yellow throats, followed in late summer by leathery green seed capsules that split open to release large, dark, chestnut-flavored seeds edible raw or roasted. Trees need several years of establishment before producing a meaningful nut crop, and while broadly self-fertile, planting more than one seedling improves pollination and yield. Give it a full-sun, well-drained site away from irrigation runoff or low spots where water collects.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; shagbark hickory develops a long taproot and transplants best while young and dormant, with minimal root disturbance.
directions: Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; shagbark hickory develops a long taproot and transplants best while young and dormant, with minimal root disturbance. A named selection prized among nut tree enthusiasts for producing thinner-shelled, easier-to-crack nuts with excellent sweet flavor compared to typical wild shagbark hickory seedlings, which often have very thick, difficult shells that discourage home processing despite the excellent nut quality. Like all shagbark hickories it is a large, long-lived forest tree distinguished by its shaggy, peeling bark and needs considerable time, often a decade or more, before reaching significant nut-bearing maturity, making it a true multi-generational planting. Provide deep, well-drained soil and full sun, protect the young tree's long taproot from damage during transplanting, and be prepared for a long wait before the improved, easier-cracking nuts this selection is known for become available in quantity.

common_name: York Elderberry (Largest-Cluster American Elderberry, New York Station Release)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; York is a late-ripening American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) released by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, and it is the recommended companion pollenizer for Adams elderberry — plant York alongside Adams (or any early-season American elderberry) for reliable cross-pollination and maximum yield on both plants; York can also be planted as a single specimen but produces better with a companion.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun; York elderberry is drought-tolerant once established but produces better with consistent moisture; prune back to 6–12 inch stubs in late winter every 2–3 years to rejuvenate; harvest berry clusters in August–September when fully ripe and deep purple-black; process or cook berries within days of harvest as raw elderberries contain cyanogenic compounds and must be cooked for safe consumption. York elderberry was released by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in the mid-20th century as part of an American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) improvement program aimed at developing varieties with larger, more consistently sized berries and heavier individual clusters compared to wild-harvested elderberries. York is noted for producing some of the largest individual berry clusters of any named American elderberry variety — the flat-topped cymes (berry clusters) of York regularly reach 10–12 inches across and bear very heavy loads of ripe berries at the dark purple-black ripening stage. The individual berries are also somewhat larger than those of Adams and many other named varieties. This large cluster size and individual berry size make York an excellent choice for home elderberry production where maximum yield per plant and ease of harvest (larger clusters are faster to pick) are priorities. York ripens approximately 2 weeks after Adams, making the York + Adams combination the standard planting recommendation for home elderberry operations wanting to extend the harvest window and ensure reliable cross-pollination between the two varieties. All elderberry processing requires cooking — raw elderberries contain sambunigrin, a cyanogenic glycoside that is destroyed by heat; cooked elderberries are used for syrup, juice, jam, jelly, and elderberry wine.

common_name: York Imperial Apple (Pennsylvania Heirloom Keeping and Cider Apple)
plant_note: Plant a compatible pollinizer nearby, since York Imperial is not reliably self-fertile and blooms mid-season.
directions: Discovered near York, Pennsylvania in the early 1800s, this apple built the Mid-Atlantic processing and cider industry for over a century thanks to its exceptional storage life and steady yields. The fruit has a distinctive lopsided, flattened shape and firm yellow flesh with a red blush, making it easy to pick out among other apples in the bin. Flavor is mild and sweet-tart, better suited to pies, cider blends, and long winter storage than fresh eating off the tree. Choose York Imperial where a long-keeping, reliable dual-purpose apple with real regional history matters more than dessert-apple looks.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; yuzu is among the most cold-hardy citrus species, tolerating temperatures to about 14–17°F when established and making it viable in zone 8 and some protected zone 7 sites where most citrus would be killed.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; yuzu is self-fruitful and produces better with cross-pollination, though single-tree production is adequate. Yuzu (Citrus junos) is a Japanese and Chinese citrus species of great antiquity, prized throughout East Asian cuisine — particularly in Japanese cuisine — for its extraordinary aromatic zest and juice that has a flavor profile unlike any other citrus: intensely fragrant, complex, floral-tart with notes of grapefruit, mandarin, and pine. The rough, bumpy, medium-sized (2–3 inch diameter) yellow fruits are rarely eaten whole but their zest and juice are foundational in ponzu sauce, yuzu kosho, miso soup, hot pots (nabe), cakes, and flavoring sake. Yuzu trees are extremely thorny (the thorns can be 3–4 inches long) and slow to begin fruiting (5–8 years from seed; 3–5 years from grafted trees) but among the most cold-hardy of all citrus, surviving to 14–17°F. Now widely available as grafted plants and grown by American chefs and home gardeners.

plant_note: Establish this Chilean rainforest vine in part shade against a sheltered wall or trellis in spring, in fertile, humus-rich soil; both a male and female plant are needed to set fruit.
directions: Establish this Chilean rainforest vine in part shade against a sheltered wall or trellis in spring, in fertile, humus-rich soil, since it is less cold-hardy than its Asian Lardizabalaceae relatives and appreciates protection from harsh winter wind. Deep maroon-purple flowers appear in winter, and because plants are typically dioecious, both a male and female specimen are needed to set the dark purple, sausage-shaped fruits filled with sweet white pulp. Its thick, glossy, evergreen trifoliate leaves make an unusual dense screen for shaded courtyards in mild coastal climates. Water regularly during establishment, then allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings once mature.

plant_note: Plant in full sun with a pollinizer nearby, and pick promptly once ripe since fruit does not hold long in storage.
directions: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1999 out of the same breeding program that later produced Honeycrisp, Zestar! ripens in late summer, weeks ahead of most main-season apples, filling a gap for gardeners wanting a crisp fresh apple early in the season. The flavor pairs bright tartness with a distinctive brown-sugar sweetness and a notably crunchy texture for such an early apple. Winter hardiness is excellent, letting it succeed in cold northern gardens where many early apples struggle. Grow it for the first crisp, flavorful apple of the year, but plan to eat or process the crop quickly since it does not store as long as later-season cultivars.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Zimmerman needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.
directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving toward full sun once established. Zimmerman is an Ohio-origin pawpaw selection known for very sweet, richly flavored flesh with a notably low seed count for the species, making the fruit easier to eat fresh than many wild seedlings. It ripens in the midseason window and produces medium to large fruit on a vigorous, cold-hardy tree with the classic pyramidal pawpaw form and large, tropical-looking drooping leaves. Because pawpaws will not set fruit from their own pollen, interplant Zimmerman with an unrelated cultivar such as Susquehanna or Taytwo, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief spring bloom to improve fruit set in home orchard settings.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Zinfandel thrives in warm climates and is prone to uneven ripening within a single cluster, requiring careful harvest timing.
directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Zinfandel thrives in warm climates and is prone to uneven ripening within a single cluster, requiring careful harvest timing. Genetically identical to the Croatian variety Crljenak Kaštelanski and Italy's Primitivo, this vigorous red wine grape produces loose clusters of thin-skinned, sweet grapes that ripen unevenly on the same bunch, with green, pink, and fully ripe purple-black berries sometimes present simultaneously, a quirk growers must manage carefully to avoid overripe, raisined fruit alongside underripe berries at harvest. Vigorous and productive in warm, sunny climates, it also produces the pink blush wine known as White Zinfandel when pressed with minimal skin contact, making a single variety the source of two very different wine styles. Manage canopy density to promote even ripening, monitor clusters closely as harvest approaches given the variety's uneven ripening tendency, and provide full sun and heat for the best sugar development.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Zinner is a Type-2 (protogynous) pecan noted for scab resistance and a thin, easy-cracking shell, and pairs well with a Type-1 cultivar like Gafford for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, siting a compatible Type-1 pollinator such as Gafford nearby, since pecans are wind-pollinated and cross-pollination between a Type-1 and Type-2 cultivar produces much better nut set than a single cultivar alone. Zinner is a Type-2 pecan valued for combining good resistance to pecan scab with a notably thin, easy-cracking shell that yields plump, high-quality kernels, making it appealing for home growers who want good disease resistance without sacrificing nut quality. As with other scab-resistant cultivars, it is a lower-maintenance choice for Gulf South home orchards without a regular commercial fungicide program. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches consistent bearing age.

common_name: Zutano Avocado (Low-Chill Type B Avocado, Early Season Pale Green Avocado)
plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after all frost danger; Zutano is a Type B avocado (flowers open female in the afternoon, shed pollen the following morning) and cross-pollinates effectively with Type A varieties including Hass and Mexicola; Zutano has an early ripening season (September–November), making it valuable for extending fresh avocado harvest before the main Hass season; requires approximately 300 chill hours, among the lowest requirements of any commercial avocado variety.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Zutano performs best with a Type A companion (Hass, Mexicola) for cross-pollination; harvest September through November when fruits are full-sized and soften slightly over 5–7 days after picking; Zutano fruits stay green at ripeness and have a watery, mild flavor — better for cooking than fresh eating but valuable for early-season harvest timing. Zutano avocado is a California-developed variety from the Mexican race lineage with one of the lowest chill requirements of any commercial avocado, performing well in the warmest avocado-growing regions and ripening its crop earlier in the season (September–November) than the dominant Hass variety (January–June harvest). The variety was developed by R.J. Hazzard in Fallbrook, California in the 1920s and entered the California nursery trade where it became valued primarily as a cross-pollinator for Hass and other Type A varieties due to its abundant, reliable Type B pollen production and good overlap with Hass bloom times. Zutano's fruit quality is frankly mild and somewhat watery compared to Hass, Fuerte, or Reed — the flesh is pale yellow-green, less rich in oil, and more watery in texture — making it less valued for fresh eating than the richer varieties. However, Zutano provides practical value as: (1) the best early-season fresh avocado available from your own tree in September when Hass season hasn't started; (2) a reliable Type B pollinator that ensures good fruit set on Hass and other Type A trees in the same garden; and (3) a lower-chill, cold-somewhat-tolerant variety for zone 9 margins where Hass reliability is borderline.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist soil; African basil grows as a woody perennial shrub in zones 9–11 and can reach 3–6 feet tall. In colder climates it can be wintered indoors as a container plant and brought outside in summer.
directions: Root cuttings in warm conditions and transplant to rich, well-drained soil in full sun; African basil is a large, woody, heat-tolerant basil relative native to tropical Africa and widely grown across West Africa, East Africa, and South Asia as a culinary and medicinal herb. The flavor differs substantially from European sweet basil — it has a strong clove-like note, more eucalyptus, and a camphor-like medicinal quality rather than the sweet anise of Italian basil. Used in soups, stews, and pepper sauces across Nigeria, Ghana, and Ethiopia; the dried leaves are an ingredient in berbere spice blend. In hot, humid Gulf Coast gardens it thrives and produces prolifically where annual basil struggles with disease. Small white flowers attract pollinators profusely.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings after last frost; this sterile hybrid does not set viable seed and must be propagated vegetatively.
directions: Take 4–6 in stem cuttings, remove lower leaves, and root in moist perlite or water; transplant once a vigorous root system develops. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; in zones below 10, treat as a long-season annual or overwinter rooted cuttings indoors under grow lights. Because this sterile hybrid never sets seed, it flowers continuously throughout the season — a great benefit for pollinators — without the bolting problem common to culinary basil. Harvest stem tips freely; the camphor-scented, dark-veined foliage is used in cooked dishes and infused oils.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in zone 8–10; African Cherry is a slow-growing, large montane forest tree native to the afromontane forests of sub-Saharan Africa, grown for its anti-inflammatory phytosterol-rich bark — one of the most widely prescribed botanical medicines in Europe for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — and critically threatened by over-harvesting; sustainable cultivation from nursery-grown trees is the responsible sourcing option.
directions: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade or full sun in cooler climates; Prunus africana requires the cool, moist conditions of montane forest environments — it performs poorly in hot, humid tropical lowlands and is best suited to highland subtropical and warm-temperate climates. Prunus africana (African Cherry, Pygeum, or African Plum) is a large, slow-growing, evergreen tree native to the montane forests of sub-Saharan Africa — occurring on nearly every major mountain range from Mt. Cameroon and the Ruwenzori to the Ethiopian Highlands, Drakensberg, and Kilimanjaro above 1,500m elevation — and listed on CITES Appendix II due to severe overharvesting of its medicinal bark. The bark contains a rich complex of phytosterols (beta-sitosterol, beta-sitostenone), ferulic acid esters, and n-docosanol with well-documented anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects on prostate tissue — making standardized Pygeum bark extract one of the most widely prescribed botanical medicines in France, Germany, and Italy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) symptoms. The annual global trade in Prunus africana bark exceeds 4,000 metric tons, putting wild populations under severe pressure across its range. Cultivating nursery-grown trees (which require 8–15 years to produce harvestable bark) is a sustainable alternative to wild collection. The small, cherry-like, red-to-black fruits are edible but very bitter; primarily a timber and medicinal tree.

plant_note: Transplant container-grown seedlings into deep, rich, well-drained soil in a sunny to lightly shaded, wind-sheltered site; expect 5-9 years before the tree flowers and sets its first large fruit.
directions: Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, humid, wind-protected location; African nutmeg is a mid-sized rainforest tree of West and Central Africa closely related to custard apple, notable for its unusual pendulous, ribbon-like, spiraling flowers followed by large round woody fruits the size of a grapefruit. Inside each fruit, numerous seeds embedded in aromatic pulp are dried and grated much like true nutmeg, imparting a similar warm, slightly bitter, musky-spicy flavor used in West African soups, rice dishes, and traditional remedies. Because seedlings take many years to reach bearing size, it is best suited to permanent agroforestry plantings or large tropical gardens rather than short-term cultivation, and young trees should be shaded and kept consistently moist during establishment.

subcategory: South African traditional medicinal aromatic shrub
plant_note: Root stem cuttings or sow seed in spring in full sun in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in zone 8–11; African Wormwood (Lengana, Umhlonyane in Zulu, Wilde Als in Afrikaans) is the most important traditional medicinal herb in southern Africa — a strongly aromatic, silver-green shrubby perennial native to the Afromontane grasslands, rocky slopes, and forest margins of sub-Saharan Africa — used for treating colds, flu, malaria, coughs, and stomach disorders by Zulu, Xhosa, Sotho, and Cape Malay traditional practitioners for centuries.
directions: Plant Artemisia afra in well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; avoid rich, wet soils which produce lush but less aromatic and medicinally active foliage; prune back hard each spring to maintain compact, bushy form; propagate easily from cuttings in late spring. African Wormwood is the cornerstone of South African traditional herbal medicine — a deeply aromatic, silver-grey-green shrub with finely divided leaves and a characteristic powerful, camphor-dominated fragrance that is instantly recognized across southern Africa. Traditional use includes steaming the crushed leaves in a bowl of hot water for inhalation to relieve cold and flu symptoms; drinking infusions (umhlonyane tea) for fever, malaria, coughs, and stomach complaints; and rubbing the leaves on the body as an insect repellent. The plant is used by practitioners of all major South African healing traditions — Zulu izinyanga, Xhosa izangoma, Cape Malay bonesmiths — and is sold in enormous quantities at traditional medicine markets (muthi shops) throughout the country. Research has confirmed antibacterial, antifungal, and antiparasitic activity of various leaf extracts. The plant is hardy, attractive, and easy to grow in any warm, dry garden position; it makes an excellent border shrub for drought-tolerant Mediterranean-style gardens in zone 8–11. Related to the Northern Hemisphere wormwoods (Artemisia absinthium, A. annua) but distinct and more cold-hardy than expected for an African species.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall for natural cold stratification over winter, or stratify seeds in moist sand in the refrigerator for 4–6 weeks before spring sowing; agrimony establishes best when seeds receive a cold stratification period to break dormancy — it is a classic hedgerow and woodland-edge herb of dry, calcareous, or neutral soils.
directions: Agrimonia eupatoria is a slender, upright, rosette-forming perennial herb native to dry grasslands, hedgerows, and woodland edges throughout Europe and western Asia, producing pinnate, strongly aromatic, slightly rough-hairy leaves and long, slender spikes of small, five-petaled, bright-yellow flowers from early to mid summer, followed by small, hooked bur-fruits that cling to clothing and animal fur for seed dispersal. Direct-sow seeds in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline or calcareous soil in a sunny to partly shaded position; seeds require cold stratification for reliable germination and will germinate in spring after a natural winter cold period. In traditional Western herbalism, the whole above-ground plant is harvested in flower and used as a gentle astringent, anti-inflammatory, and tonic herb with a long history of use for wound healing, sore throats, digestive complaints, and urinary tract support — it was a primary wound herb of medieval European medicine. Plants are drought-tolerant once established and perform best in lean, well-drained soil; avoid rich, wet conditions. The dried herb makes a pleasant, mildly apricot-scented tea.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aidan fruit tree is a frost-tender West African tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aidan fruit tree is a frost-tender West African tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to West African forests, this legume tree bears distinctive long, dark brown, four-winged (tetrapterous) pods filled with an intensely aromatic pulp used as a seasoning in soups and stews across Ghana and Nigeria, known as prekese, and long valued in traditional medicine for its aromatic properties. A member of the pea family, it fixes nitrogen in the soil like many of its legume relatives, and its distinctive winged seed pods make it an interesting specimen tree for a tropical botanical or ethnobotanical planting in frost-free climates. Water regularly while young, and expect pods to be harvested for seasoning once the tree reaches bearing maturity after several years.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; ajwain is a cool-season annual native to the Near East and South Asia that performs best in warm-dry spring conditions — in zone 9, fall to winter planting produces the best spring seed crop.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 8–12 inches. Trachyspermum ammi (ajwain or carom seed) is an annual herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae) native to Egypt and the Near East, cultivated extensively in India, Pakistan, and Iran for its small, ribbed seeds with an intensely pungent thyme-like but more piercing aroma and flavor — the dominant compound is thymol, which is also found in thyme, but present in much higher concentrations in ajwain seeds. In Indian cooking, ajwain is used in breads (naan, paratha), lentil dishes (dal), fritters (pakoras), pickles, and dry spice blends where its strong, distinctive flavor contributes essential character that cannot be substituted. The seeds are used whole (dry-roasted to release their oil before adding) or ground; they also have significant traditional medicinal use in South Asian medicine for digestive complaints. The plant resembles a small, upright dill or caraway with feathery, blue-green leaves and compound white flower umbels in spring; harvest when seed heads dry and turn brown.

plant_note: Transplant after the last frost into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this form behaves exactly like common culinary sage in the garden.
directions: Albiflora is ordinary common sage in every respect except flower color: instead of the usual violet-blue spikes, it blooms in pure white in early summer, making it a useful choice for a white or moon garden where the typical purple sage flower would clash. The grey-green pebbled leaves are fully flavored and can be harvested and used in the kitchen exactly like standard culinary sage. It shares the same drought tolerance, sprawling woody habit, and need for excellent drainage as the species, and old plants benefit from a hard spring pruning to keep them from becoming leggy. Choose it when you want the culinary reliability of common sage without the purple flower color competing with nearby plantings.

plant_note: Direct-sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; like most members of the carrot family with large seeds, alexanders germinates best after a cold period — sow in moist, fertile soil near the coast or in mild, maritime gardens where it naturally thrives.
directions: Smyrnium olusatrum, known as alexanders, is one of the oldest cultivated European pot herbs, widely grown by the Romans throughout their empire as a celery substitute and still naturalized along coastal cliffs, roadsides, and hedgebanks in mild, maritime regions of Europe from the Azores to the British Isles; it is a robust, biennial or short-lived perennial with bright, glossy, three-lobed leaves, hollow celery-scented stems, and distinctive rounded heads of small, greenish-yellow flowers followed by large, ridged, black seeds. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade, particularly in mild coastal gardens where it performs best; it is frost-hardy but prefers mild, maritime climates and does not thrive in hot, continental summers. All parts of the plant were used in Roman and medieval cooking as a celery substitute before celery (Apium graveolens) was cultivated: the young shoots and leaves are eaten as a potherb, the blanched stems as a vegetable, the flower buds in salads, and the roots and seeds as flavoring — the flavor is a distinctive, aromatic blend of celery and black pepper. Alexanders largely fell from culinary use after the widespread adoption of cultivated celery in the 17th century but is undergoing a revival among foragers, chefs interested in historical European cuisines, and those growing heritage kitchen garden crops.

plant_note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before starting indoors 6-8 weeks ahead of the last frost, then transplant into full sun and sandy, fast-draining soil once nights stay warm.
directions: CAUTION: for short-term use only, contraindicated in pregnancy and intestinal obstruction; can cause cramping or electrolyte imbalance with overuse. Nick or soak the hard seed coat before starting indoors 6-8 weeks ahead of the last frost, then transplant into full sun and sandy, fast-draining soil once nights stay warm. Leaves and pods contain sennosides and are dried for the classic short-term stimulant laxative used in traditional and modern medicine alike.

plant_note: Grown indoors year-round on trays; sow densely and harvest as young shoots.
directions: Sow the small seed densely across a moist tray or shallow container of medium, indoors year-round. Keep evenly moist and provide bright, indirect light once the shoots emerge and green up. Harvest the tender, nutty micro shoots with scissors in about a week when the first leaves appear. Rinse and eat fresh in salads and sandwiches; no thinning or spacing is needed for this quick indoor crop.

common_name: All Gold Lemon Balm (Bright Golden-Yellow Foliage Lemon Balm)
plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; All Gold bears bright golden-yellow foliage that holds its color best out of the hottest afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; some morning sun deepens the golden foliage color while afternoon shade prevents scorch and leaf burn in hot climates. All Gold bears strikingly bright, uniform golden-yellow leaves rather than the plain green of the species, carrying the same fresh, lemony scent and flavor prized for teas, sachets, and culinary use, and its bright color makes it a strong foliage accent in a partly shaded herb bed even when not being harvested. Cut back hard after flowering to encourage fresh, brightly colored new growth and to reduce self-seeding, since Melissa officinalis can spread aggressively from seed. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

common_name: Alleppey Turmeric (High-Curcumin Kerala Turmeric for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Plant rhizome pieces (2–3 inches with at least one bud) 2–4 inches deep after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; harvest rhizomes in November–December after the leaves die back naturally — the die-back signals the completion of rhizome development.
directions: Plant rhizome pieces 2–4 inches deep after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Alleppey turmeric is a high-curcumin selection named for the Alleppey (Alappuzha) region of Kerala, India — one of the primary commercial turmeric production areas — where this variety is selected for the deep orange-yellow color and high curcumin content that make it particularly valuable for culinary and medicinal uses. Curcumin is the bioactive compound responsible for turmeric's anti-inflammatory properties and vivid yellow-orange color; Alleppey selections typically contain 5–7% curcumin by dry weight versus 2–3% in ordinary turmeric. The turmeric plant itself is ornamentally beautiful in Gulf South tropical gardens: broad, paddle-shaped leaves (similar to canna) on upright stems reaching 3–4 feet, with occasional cream-and-pale-purple flower spikes that emerge from the leaf bases in summer. In zone 9, turmeric grows as a perennial if mulched heavily during winter, or the rhizomes can be stored frost-free and replanted each spring. Harvest fresh turmeric rhizomes in fall for immediate use — the fresh rhizome flavor is brighter and more complex than dried powder — or cure, dry, and powder for long-term storage. The plant grows best in the same conditions as its ginger relatives: warm, humid, partially shaded, with consistent moisture.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring in tropical conditions; closely related to grains of paradise and ginger in the Zingiberaceae family — grows best in humid tropical conditions similar to ginger.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in tropical conditions; alligator pepper is a West African spice plant in the ginger family producing large ridged pods (resembling a small alligator's head, hence the name) packed with numerous seeds that have a complex, resinous, cardamom-like flavor with black pepper heat and citrus overtones. An important ceremonial and culinary spice in Nigeria, Cameroon, and other West African nations, used to season soups, stews, and meat dishes, and traditionally presented to guests as a mark of respect. Related to and used similarly to grains of paradise (Aframomum melegueta) but with a more complex flavor profile. Rare in Western cultivation but rewarding for adventurous tropical gardeners.

common_name: Alligator Root (Renealmia, Vanilla-Leaf Ginger, Wild Ginger Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in late spring in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Renealmia alpinia grows naturally as a forest understory plant and performs best in the filtered light beneath large trees. In zone 10-11, it is a dependable, spreading perennial; in zone 9, treat as a container plant. The plant produces stems with large, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves with a vanilla-like fragrance when crushed. The showy inflorescences bear red-orange flowers followed by bright red to orange-scarlet berries. Propagate by rhizome division.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Renealmia alpinia thrives in the shaded, moist conditions of a tropical understory garden and wilts and declines in exposed, dry, or overly sunny positions. Renealmia alpinia is a clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to the Caribbean Islands, Mexico, Central America, and northern South America in the family Zingiberaceae (the ginger family), related to Alpinia and Zingiber. The plant produces tall (4–8 foot), cane-like, leafy stems clothed in large, lance-shaped to oblong, dark-green leaves that, when crushed, release a pleasant fragrance combining vanilla, ginger, and green herbs — a quality that has led to the plant's use in traditional folk medicine and cooking throughout its native range, where the aromatic leaves, rhizomes, and berries flavor foods and beverages. The inflorescences emerge near the base of the plant on short separate stems — a basal inflorescence style common in Renealmia — bearing showy clusters of orange-red to red flowers followed by decorative, bright red to scarlet berries (capsules) that are genuinely ornamental. The berries are used medicinally and as a condiment in parts of Colombia and Venezuela. An unusual and attractive shade-garden ginger relative for zone 10-11 tropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; allspice is dioecious — both male and female trees are needed for fruit production. In zone 10–12 only outdoors; can be grown in a large container and overwintered indoors in zone 9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — allspice is a tropical Caribbean tree native to Jamaica and Central America, the source of the spice whose dried unripe berries combine the flavors of cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg in a single berry (hence 'allspice'). The large, glossy, aromatic leaves also contain significant allspice flavor (used to wrap jerk meats in Jamaica). The tree is medium-sized (30–40 feet at maturity) with attractive smooth, exfoliating bark and fragrant white flowers. Allspice is a dioecious tree — both male and female plants are needed for fruit production, though the leaves of either sex can be harvested for culinary use. In South Florida it grows well outdoors in zone 10–11; in zone 9 it requires a container that can be moved to frost protection. An extraordinary ornamental, aromatic, and culinary tree for warm gardens.

plant_note: Plant offsets (pups) in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; aloe vera tolerates light frost to about 28°F but is killed by prolonged hard freezes — in zone 8 and colder, grow in containers that can be moved indoors or provide heavy mulch and frost protection.
directions: Plant offsets in very well-drained, dry, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade — aloe vera is one of the oldest cultivated plants in human history, grown for millennia in tropical and subtropical climates as the premier first-aid plant for minor burns, sunburns, cuts, insect bites, and skin irritation; the clear gel inside the thick, fleshy leaves contains anti-inflammatory and wound-healing compounds including polysaccharides, vitamins, and amino acids. Break off a lower leaf and apply the clear gel directly to burns for immediate cooling relief. In zone 9–12 it grows as an outdoor landscape succulent, tolerating drought, poor soil, reflected heat, and neglect with remarkable resilience; it produces dramatic yellow to orange tubular flower spikes in late winter on established plants. It spreads prolifically by offsets (pups) that form around the base — remove and replant pups to create new plants. Every household and kitchen garden should have one within reach.

plant_note: Direct-sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a cool site with some shade; germination is slow and often spread over the following spring.
directions: Alpine lovage is a true high-mountain relative of garden lovage native to the Alps, Pyrenees, and other European mountain ranges, forming a much smaller clump of finely divided, aromatic leaves that carry a milder, more herbaceous version of lovage's celery flavor. Unlike garden lovage, it thrives in cool, humus-rich, well-drained mountain soils and struggles in hot, humid lowland summers, making it best suited to alpine troughs, rock gardens, and cool-summer climates. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall so it experiences natural winter chilling, since seed loses viability quickly and often germinates unevenly the following spring. Young leaves can be used fresh as a celery-like potherb or dried for tea, and the whole plant has a long history of traditional culinary and medicinal use in Alpine farming communities.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall so they undergo natural cold stratification over winter; press seeds onto the soil surface and cover lightly, as they benefit from a period of cold before germinating in spring.
directions: Sow seeds directly in fall onto the surface of prepared soil in a lightly shaded, calcareous or neutral spot, covering them with a thin layer of fine grit or soil; the cold of winter breaks dormancy and promotes reliable germination the following spring. Plants establish slowly in their first season, focusing energy on root development, so expect the tall, woolly-leafed stems and whorled purple flower spikes in the second year. Choose a site with good drainage and moderate moisture — Alpine Woundwort tolerates partial shade under open tree canopy where it would naturally occur in mountain scrub and woodland edges. Leave spent flower stems standing through winter to provide structure and overwintering habitat for beneficial insects, then cut back to the base in early spring before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Amarillo is a trademarked hop variety with proprietary status limiting commercial rhizome availability.
directions: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Amarillo is a trademarked hop variety with proprietary status limiting commercial rhizome availability. Discovered as a chance seedling in Washington's Yakima Valley in the 1990s and named for its bright golden-orange color, this widely used American aroma hop delivers pronounced orange citrus and floral notes that became a defining character of American pale ale and IPA styles through the 2000s and remains a brewer favorite for its distinctive, bright citrus aromatics. Its exact genetic parentage was kept proprietary for years, and while cuttings are now more widely available to home growers, tracking down true, correctly identified Amarillo rhizomes can still be more difficult than sourcing more common commercial hop varieties. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery, and provide full sun and consistent moisture through the growing season.

plant_note: Amazel is a sterile hybrid basil bred for strong resistance to downy mildew, a disease that devastates sweet basil in humid climates; because it does not flower or set seed, all energy goes into vigorous, extended leaf production.
directions: Transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun only after all frost danger passes. Amazel was bred specifically to resist downy mildew, a fungal disease that can wipe out a planting of traditional Genovese basil in a single humid season, and because the plant is sterile it never flowers or goes to seed, channeling all of its energy into continuous, vigorous leaf growth all season long. The flavor is classic sweet basil, well suited to pesto and general cooking, and the plant's disease resistance and non-flowering habit make it especially valuable for humid Gulf South gardens where downy mildew is a persistent problem. Because it is propagated from cuttings rather than seed, plants are typically purchased as starts.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in full sun after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; American basil (Ocimum americanum) is a distinct basil species from Africa and Asia — despite the misleading common name — with a flavor profile somewhat different from sweet basil (O. basilicum), featuring lighter, more lemony-herbal, slightly more resinous notes; used in West African, East African, and South Asian cooking; more drought-tolerant and heat-resistant than sweet basil.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after soil warms in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; pinch regularly to prevent bolting and encourage bushy growth; more heat and drought tolerant than sweet basil. Ocimum americanum (American basil, spice basil, or hoary basil) is a distinct basil species with a somewhat confusing common name — it originated in Africa and Asia, not the Americas, though it has become naturalized in tropical regions worldwide including the Americas. It differs from sweet basil (O. basilicum) in several ways: the leaves are smaller and lighter green, often with a slightly hairy (hoary) surface texture; the flavor is lighter, more lemony-citrus, with less of the clove-richness of sweet basil and a more herbal, slightly resinous character. O. americanum is widely used in West African cooking (particularly in Nigeria, Ghana, and Cameroon, where it is known as 'efirin' and is a common soup herb), East African cuisine, and in parts of South and Southeast Asia where it grows wild. It is significantly more drought-tolerant and heat-resistant than cultivated sweet basil, making it a good choice for hot, dry gardens where O. basilicum struggles. Several cultivated basil varieties are hybrids between O. americanum and O. basilicum, including lemon basil cultivars. The plant produces attractive white flower spikes and is a good pollinator plant.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; American bugleweed grows naturally along stream banks, wet meadow edges, and pond margins throughout North America. The plant spreads by rhizomes to form colonies in appropriate wet conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile to average soil in partial shade to full sun at pond edges, stream banks, and wet meadow margins; American bugleweed is a native mint-family herb of North American riparian habitats, closely related to European gypsywort (Lycopus europaeus). The plant has a long history of use in American herbal medicine, particularly for reducing elevated thyroid function (hyperthyroidism) — a traditional application supported by modern research showing that lycopus extracts inhibit thyroid hormone activity. The small, white tubular flowers are inconspicuous but attract numerous small native bees and hoverflies. The plant is valuable in rain gardens, bioswales, and wet garden edges where its preference for saturated soil makes it naturally suited. Note: persons with thyroid conditions should consult a healthcare provider before using medicinally.

plant_note: Plant divisions or transplants in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; American germander spreads by stolons in ideal conditions — it is most appropriate for naturalistic or wildlife plantings where spreading is welcome.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — American germander is a native perennial of moist woodland edges, wet meadows, roadsides, and stream margins throughout eastern North America, producing spikes of rose-pink to lavender tubular flowers with exserted stamens in summer that are excellent for native bees, bumble bees, and hummingbirds. The aromatic foliage has a sage-like scent when crushed (giving rise to the common name 'wood sage') and was used medicinally by indigenous peoples and early American herbalists. It spreads by stolons to form colonies in moist, shaded conditions — excellent for naturalizing along shaded stream banks, wet meadow edges, and the shaded margins of rain gardens. A relative of culinary germander (T. chamaedrys) and a historically used bitter herb for digestive complaints. Very adaptable and requires essentially no care once established in appropriate moist-to-moderate-moisture soil.

plant_note: Sow stratified seed in autumn in a woodland bed; seeds require 18–24 months of warm-then-cold stratification before germinating.
directions: Purchase properly stratified seed and sow 1–2 in deep in a shaded, forested bed with well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; do not expect germination until the following spring at the earliest. Ginseng requires 60–75% canopy shade and the deep, crumbly forest soil of its native Appalachian habitat — it will not thrive in open garden conditions. Plants must grow for a minimum of 5–7 years before roots reach marketable size, making patience the primary gardening virtue here. Harvest roots in autumn by carefully digging to preserve the branched root shape; roots are dried slowly at low heat and used in adaptogenic teas, tinctures, and traditional Chinese medicine preparations.

plant_note: Plant root divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy, deep soil in full sun to partial shade; American licorice spreads by deep, extensive root systems and can be difficult to remove once established — site it where expansion is acceptable.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy, deep soil in full sun to partial shade; American licorice is the native North American relative of the commercial licorice plant (Glycyrrhiza glabra), native to the Great Plains and western prairies where it grows along stream banks, roadsides, and moist prairie edges. The thick, deep roots have a genuine licorice flavor from glycyrrhizin compounds (the same compound as commercial licorice) and were used extensively by Native American nations as a food and medicine — chewed fresh, dried as candy, brewed as tea, and used to treat sore throats, toothaches, and stomach complaints. The pinnate compound leaves and small white to pale violet flowers are attractive; the bur-like bristly seed pods cling to fur and clothing. A nitrogen-fixing prairie legume, it improves soil fertility. Spreads by rhizome; contain in smaller gardens.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in a shaded, moist woodland bed; seeds benefit from cold stratification over winter and germinate in spring. American lovage is a tall, celery-scented native herb of rich, moist eastern woodlands whose white umbel flowers attract native bees, flies, and wasps from late spring through summer.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade; cold stratification over winter improves germination rates significantly, and established plants will self-sow once the colony matures. Ligusticum canadense is a robust native carrot-family herb of rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests across the central and southern Appalachians and adjacent piedmont, growing 2 to 4 feet tall with large, finely divided, celery-scented leaves and broad, flat-topped white umbel flowers in late spring and early summer that are among the most effective native plants for attracting small native bees, parasitoid wasps, and syrphid flies. The aromatic roots and foliage were used extensively in food and medicine by many Indigenous peoples throughout the plant's range, and the plant serves as a larval host for the black swallowtail butterfly. It is an excellent structural plant for the back of shaded borders and native woodland gardens where height and late-season structure are needed.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in dry, sandy, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; American pennyroyal is a native annual of dry, open, sandy or rocky soils that self-sows freely in appropriate conditions. It was widely used by Native Americans and colonial settlers as an insect repellent and medicinal herb.
directions: Direct sow in lean, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; American pennyroyal is a small, aromatic native annual in the mint family, distinct from the European pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium) but similarly pungently mint-scented with a sharp, camphor-like quality. Indigenous peoples throughout eastern North America used the plant extensively as an insect repellent (rubbing the leaves on skin to repel mosquitoes and flies), a medicinal herb for colds and fevers, and a culinary flavoring. The plant self-sows freely in dry, lean, open, sandy conditions and can be left to naturalize in appropriate sandy garden areas. Caution: do not use medicinally in large amounts, especially during pregnancy, as concentrated pulegone-containing plants can be toxic in excess. For fragrance and insect-repellent purposes, moderate use is traditional and appropriate.

plant_note: Plant divisions carefully in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, undisturbed forest soil in partial to deep shade; like most pyrolas, American wintergreen depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi and resists transplanting and cultivation in standard garden conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained, undisturbed forest soil in deep to partial shade; American wintergreen is a native evergreen herb of cool, moist, acidic woodland floors in the northern hardwood and mixed conifer forests of eastern North America. The rounded, leathery, glossy dark-green leaves form attractive low rosettes that persist through winter. The raceme of nodding, waxy white flowers in summer resembles a miniature lily-of-the-valley flower stalk. Like its relatives in the family Pyrolaceae (now Ericaceae), it depends on mycorrhizal fungi and resists conventional cultivation — it is best appreciated in its natural habitat or in undisturbed, established woodland gardens with intact acidic duff. The plant has a long history of herbal use in traditional medicine, with the leaves containing substances similar to aspirin. Collect only nursery-propagated stock; do not disturb wild populations.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Amethyst is an All-America Selections winner bred for uniform, deep purple color and improved bolt resistance on a compact plant.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun for the deepest, most uniform purple leaf color. Amethyst is an All-America Selections winner bred for consistent, richly saturated purple foliage from seedling stage onward, along with improved resistance to premature bolting compared with older purple basil types, keeping the compact plant productive and attractive for a longer stretch of the growing season. Its uniform color and tidy habit make it useful as an ornamental edible in containers and border plantings as well as a culinary and vinegar-infusing basil. Pinch growing tips regularly to delay flowering and encourage bushier growth, and harvest leaves often to keep new growth coming.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in autumn just before first frost; seed loses viability quickly and requires cold stratification through winter to germinate reliably in spring.
directions: Sow fresh seed immediately after harvest or purchase in autumn, pressing 1/4 in deep into moist soil; stored or old seed germinates poorly. Angelica is a short-lived perennial or biennial that requires deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil and partial shade — its ideal habitat is moist woodland edge. Removing the flower head in the second year prolongs the plant's life, while allowing it to set seed means the plant dies after seeding but self-sown seedlings will follow. Harvest young leaf stems and petioles in spring for candying; collect seeds when ripe for use in gin and liqueur flavoring.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost; anise dislikes transplanting and needs a long, warm season.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in their final location in rich, well-drained soil; anise develops a taproot that transplants poorly. Thin to 6–12 in apart once seedlings are established, and stake plants in exposed sites as they can be top-heavy when in flower. Anise needs a long, frost-free season to set seed—at least 120 days—so start as early as possible in cool climates. Harvest umbels when seeds begin to turn gray-green, cutting whole heads into paper bags to catch seeds as they ripen.

common_name: Anise Basil (Licorice Basil, Thai Anise Basil)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil has warmed, or direct sow after frost danger has passed; Anise Basil is an old heirloom basil type with purple-tinged stems and flower spikes and a pronounced anise-licorice flavor distinct from sweet basil.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost danger has passed, since basil is quickly killed by cold. Anise Basil, sometimes called licorice basil, is a classic heirloom type with dark purple stems, purple-flushed leaf veins, and tall spikes of pinkish-purple flowers that make it as ornamental as it is useful in the kitchen, where its bold anise-licorice flavor is prized in Vietnamese and Persian cooking and pairs well with fruit, fish, and Asian-style dishes that sweet basil can't match. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and productive through the season, though leaving a few spikes to bloom brings in a steady stream of pollinators. It tolerates the heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer as well as most basils and will grow in a large container with the same care as sweet basil.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; anise hyssop self-sows reliably and can be used as a short-lived perennial that renews itself annually from seed in suitable conditions.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; anise hyssop is a native prairie perennial with strongly anise-scented leaves and stems that produces upright spikes of densely packed lavender-blue flowers from midsummer through fall — arguably the single most attractive plant for native bumblebees in the temperate garden, hosting extraordinary numbers of pollinators at peak bloom. The leaves make an excellent herbal tea with a pleasant, sweet anise flavor and can be used fresh in salads and fruit dishes. Plants are short-lived perennials or biennials that self-sow reliably to maintain a colony. Deadhead half the spent spikes to extend bloom; leave the rest for self-seeding and winter finch food. Very drought-tolerant. 'Blue Fortune' (robust, long-blooming hybrid) is the most widely grown cultivar.

plant_note: Direct sow ripe seeds in fall as they require cold stratification to germinate — do not store seeds; harvest and sow fresh; anise root thrives in moist, rich, shaded woodland soil and self-seeds freely once established.
directions: Anise root is a native woodland perennial of moist, rich, shaded forests across the eastern United States and Canada — every part of the plant, from root to leaf to seed, is intensely fragrant with a sweet, anise-licorice scent that is among the most pleasant of any native wildflower. The thick, fleshy, white taproots are edible raw or cooked and taste strongly of anise; the seeds are used as a spice similar to caraway or anise; and the leaves are used fresh as an anise-flavored garnish and in teas. It is one of the finest shade-garden herbs available, thriving in deep, moist woodland conditions under hardwood canopy where most culinary herbs fail, and it attracts a wide variety of native pollinators to its small white flower umbels in late spring. Sow seeds immediately after ripening in fall — seeds lose viability rapidly if dried and stored; once established, it spreads by self-seeding to form a pleasant aromatic colony in the woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in compost-enriched, consistently moist, well-drained soil, sited with protection from cold wind and, ideally, afternoon shade in hotter climates; young plants need frost protection until well established.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in compost-enriched, consistently moist, well-drained soil, sited with protection from cold wind and, ideally, afternoon shade in hotter climates. Native to subtropical rainforest gullies of coastal New South Wales and southeast Queensland, this glossy-leaved tree contains one of the highest natural concentrations of anethole of any plant, giving the dried, ground leaf an intensely sweet licorice-anise flavor. Use the dried leaf in baking, fruit desserts, herbal tea blends, and as a striking substitute anywhere star anise or fennel seed is called for; it can be clipped and kept as a large shrub in gardens where space is limited.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown plants in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; annatto is drought tolerant once established and grows quickly in warm, humid conditions. It is frost-sensitive and suited to outdoor culture only in frost-free zone 10–12.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; annatto (achiote) is a tropical American shrub known worldwide as the natural source of the orange-red pigment used to color cheese, butter, smoked fish, and countless processed foods — the intensely colored seeds inside the spiny red seed pods are ground or infused in oil to make the widely used Latin American spice paste. The seeds color and flavor rice, tamales, soups, and sauces in Latin American and Filipino cuisine. The attractive plant also produces large pink-lavender flowers similar to single roses followed by striking, bristly bright-red seed pods in clusters. A striking ornamental and useful spice shrub for zone 10–12 gardens; in zone 9a it may be grown in a large container and protected from frost.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Appalachian mountain mint is a vigorous, spreading perennial with intensely minty foliage and exceptional pollinator value.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Appalachian mountain mint is a spreading native perennial of the eastern US with narrowly linear, intensely minty-scented leaves and flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers with purple spots from July through September that are exceptional pollinator magnets — research has found that mountain mint species attract more species of native bees per plant than virtually any other wildflower, making this one of the highest-value pollinator plants for the eastern garden. It spreads by rhizomes to form colonies but is not aggressively invasive and can be controlled by edging; cut plants to the ground in fall. The crushed foliage repels insects and can be used as a natural mint flavoring. A workhorse plant for native meadows, rain gardens, and sunny to lightly shaded borders.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade to partial shade; Appalachian wild ginger is an evergreen shade groundcover of mountain and Piedmont forest understories of the central Appalachians, slowly spreading by rhizomes to form dense, low patches.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; Appalachian wild ginger is a variable-leaved native evergreen groundcover of the central and southern Appalachians, one of several closely related Hexastylis species with overlapping ranges in the mountain and foothill forests of the Southeast. The heterophylla species name (variable-leaved) refers to the tendency to produce leaves of varying shapes on the same plant or population. Like all Hexastylis, it produces the characteristic leathery, heart-shaped, dark evergreen leaves and the odd, urn-shaped, brownish-maroon flowers at ground level in spring, pollinated by ground beetles. A low, slow-spreading, extremely shade-tolerant groundcover that is virtually maintenance-free once established in appropriate forest conditions. Best combined with other evergreen groundcovers like wild ginger, green-and-gold (Chrysogonum), and Christmas fern for a natural mountain forest floor planting.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–11; Apple Geranium is a low-growing, trailing South African pelargonium — one of the most pleasantly scented of all scented geraniums — with distinctively round, soft, velvety, bright-green leaves that release an intensely fresh, sweet apple scent when touched, and small clusters of tiny white flowers with red markings throughout the warm season.
directions: Root Apple Geranium cuttings in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; water moderately and allow to dry between waterings — it is susceptible to root rot in wet conditions; pinch stems to encourage compact growth; bring indoors as a houseplant in winter in zone 8 and colder. Apple Geranium is the most apple-scented of all the scented pelargoniums — the round, soft, velvety leaves have a pure, sweet, green apple scent with a slight minty freshness that is immediately recognizable and universally appealing. The plant has a low, spreading, trailing habit quite different from the upright rose geranium, making it excellent for container edges, hanging baskets, ground cover in sunny borders, and spilling over walls. In the kitchen, the apple-scented leaves are used to flavor jellies and jams, infused in cream or sugar for desserts, floated in cocktails and lemonade, and used to scent and flavor herbal teas. The small white flowers with pink-purple veining are charming though the plant is grown primarily for the scented foliage. Native to the southwestern Cape of South Africa in sandy, rocky, fynbos-adjacent soils, it is adapted to lean, well-drained, slightly dry conditions — performing best without heavy fertilization or overwatering. One of the most useful and fragrant herbs for the container herb garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; apple mint is more drought-tolerant and more vigorous than most mints and adapts to a wider range of soil conditions.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; apple mint is more drought-tolerant and adaptable than peppermint or spearmint and tolerates poorer, drier soils. Mentha suaveolens is a densely woolly-leaved European mint producing large, round, velvety, gray-green leaves with a pleasant, fruity mint flavor with mild apple overtones; it is especially valued for making mint jelly, apple-mint sorbet, fruit salads, and flavored vinegars, and is an attractive, textural contrast to smooth-leaved herbs in the garden. The variegated cultivar 'Variegata' (pineapple mint) has cream-edged leaves and is one of the most ornamental of all mints, excellent in containers. Apple mint is more heat-tolerant than most mints and performs well in the Gulf South if given afternoon shade and consistent moisture.

common_name: Archer's Gold Thyme (Golden Creeping Groundcover Thyme)
plant_note: Root cuttings or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Archer's Gold produces bright golden-yellow foliage year-round, most vivid in full sun, over a low, spreading, groundcover habit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Archer's Gold is a low, spreading thyme selection valued as much for its bright, glowing golden-yellow foliage, which holds its color through the growing season, as for its mild, lemon-tinged thyme flavor and fragrance. It forms a dense, low mat well suited to edging a path, filling gaps between paving stones, or spilling over a rock garden wall, and small lavender-pink flowers appear in summer, drawing bees. Like other thymes it needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, quickly declining in heavy, wet soil, and a light shearing after flowering keeps the mat dense and encourages fresh new growth.

common_name: Aristotle Basil (Compact Downy Mildew-Resistant Genovese-Type Basil)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay above 50°F; bred for resistance to downy mildew, a disease that thrives in the Gulf Coast's humid summers.
directions: Transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, spacing plants to keep air moving through the dense, compact canopy. Aristotle is a modern Genovese-type basil bred specifically for resistance to downy mildew, the fungal disease that turns older sweet basil varieties yellow and defoliated within weeks in hot, humid climates, making it a far more reliable choice for Gulf Coast summers than heirloom Genovese types. The tight, uniform, mounding habit produces an abundance of medium-sized, classic sweet-basil-flavored leaves that hold quality well in containers and small beds. Harvest by pinching stem tips regularly, which delays flowering and keeps the compact plant producing tender new leaves through the entire growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow shallowly at or just after the last frost once soil has warmed; this German-bred strain is grown exactly like ordinary summer savory but is selected for a bushier habit and higher essential-oil content.
directions: Aromata is a German (Erfurt-bred) seed strain of summer savory selected for a bushier, more branched habit and a notably higher essential-oil content in the leaf than common summer savory, giving a more concentrated peppery bite from the same amount of fresh or dried herb. It is grown exactly like ordinary summer savory, direct-sown after the last frost into full sun and lean, well-drained soil, then thinned and pinched to encourage branching. Because the oil content is higher, cooks can generally use it more sparingly than standard summer savory in the bean, lentil, and sausage dishes where the herb is traditional. Cut whole stems for drying just as the first flower buds appear, when oil concentration peaks.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, or direct sow once soil has warmed.
directions: Transplant into full sun after the last frost and pinch flower spikes regularly to prolong leaf production through summer. Aromatto is an All-America Selections winner bred to combine deep, glossy purple foliage with the robust, spicy-sweet flavor of a true Genovese-type basil, filling a gap left by most purple basils, which tend toward milder, clove-like flavor. Its vigorous upright habit and strong aroma make it useful both as a culinary basil for pesto and vinegars and as an ornamental accent in the herb bed.
