plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun, well-drained soil; Arp is the most cold-hardy commonly available rosemary cultivar, surviving temperatures to 0°F or below in protected locations — making it a viable perennial in zones 6–7 where standard rosemary frequently winter-kills; it was discovered in Arp, Texas, and introduced by Madalene Hill, the Texas herb expert, in the 1970s.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; rosemary prefers alkaline to neutral soil (pH 6.5–8.0) and tolerates poor, rocky, sandy soils far better than rich garden soil which promotes lush but frost-tender growth; prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape; Arp's cold hardiness makes it worth trying in zone 6 with winter protection in sheltered spots. Arp rosemary is one of the most important named rosemary cultivars for American gardens, selected for its exceptional cold hardiness compared to standard rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis), which is reliably perennial only to zone 7 or 8 depending on drainage and shelter. The variety was discovered by Madalene Hill, the pioneering Texas herb expert and founder of the Festival Hill herb garden in Round Top, Texas, growing in the East Texas town of Arp — a small town in Smith County where a rosemary plant had survived an unusually cold winter that killed most other rosemaries in the area. Hill propagated the surviving plant and introduced it to the herb gardening world, where its superior cold hardiness was documented and confirmed in trials at locations as far north as zone 5 in sheltered exposures. The cold hardiness of Arp is thought to come from a slightly different chemical composition of its essential oils that provides better antifreeze protection at cellular level. The culinary quality and fragrance are equivalent to any standard rosemary variety — piney, resinous, intensely aromatic — and the upright habit and light blue flowers are identical in garden appearance to standard rosemary. A significant contribution to herb garden culture, introduced by one of the most important figures in the American herb movement.

plant_note: Sow in fall for spring germination in a deep, well-drained location; asafoetida is a Central Asian steppe plant requiring deep, dry, alkaline to neutral soil and is not suited to humid Gulf Coast climates — it is most reliably grown in arid Western gardens; in humid climates, grow in raised beds with excellent drainage.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall in deep, perfectly drained, alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun; asafoetida is a tall, carrot-family perennial (Ferula assa-foetida) native to the dry steppes and mountains of Iran and Afghanistan, grown for the pungent resinous sap (hing) tapped from the roots of mature 4–5 year old plants — used as a cooking spice in South Asian, Middle Eastern, and ancient Roman cuisine that imparts an onion-garlic flavor when cooked in oil despite its famously unpleasant raw odor. The plant requires full sun, perfectly dry, well-drained alkaline soil and is very intolerant of summer humidity and wet conditions, making it challenging to grow outside arid regions. Primarily of interest to specialty herb growers; commercial hing is tapped from plants growing wild in Central Asia.

common_name: Ashanti Pepper (West African Black Pepper, Uziza)
plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in rich, well-drained soil at the base of a sturdy support after the last frost; this woody pepper-family vine climbs by clinging roots much like true black pepper and needs several years to reach fruiting size.
directions: Train cuttings up a post, tree trunk, or trellis in fertile, well-drained soil with light shade, especially while young; Ashanti pepper is a woody perennial climber native to the West and Central African rainforest that is prized for two distinct products from the same plant. The young, peppery-aromatic leaves, known as uziza leaf in Nigeria, are chopped fresh into pepper soups and stews, while the dried unripe fruit, uziza seed, is ground as a pungent, more intensely hot substitute for true black pepper. Harvest leaves lightly and repeatedly once the vine is established; fruit clusters ripen from green to red over several years as the plant matures. Mulch well and water during dry spells, since the species comes from consistently humid forest conditions.

common_name: Ashitaba (Tomorrow's Leaf, Japanese Angelica, Longevity Herb)
plant_note: In zones 8–11, surface sow fresh seed in early fall for germination in the cool season; in zones 3–7, sow in early spring as soon as soil is workable; ashitaba seed must be used fresh (it loses viability rapidly) and requires light to germinate — do not cover the seed with soil; the plant is named for its remarkable regrowth rate: cut a leaf today and tomorrow ('ashita') another leaf ('ba') has already emerged.
directions: Surface sow fresh seed in a partially shaded, moist, humus-rich location; ashitaba prefers morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates — in zone 9a it is best grown in a site with dappled shade or east-facing exposure to protect from summer afternoon heat; harvest young stems and leaves regularly to promote continuous new growth; the yellow sap of the cut stems is edible but bitter. Ashitaba (Angelica keiskei, meaning 'Angel Herb of Keiske') is a remarkable culinary and medicinal herb native to the Izu Islands of Japan — a subtropical island chain stretching south from the Izu Peninsula, where the inhabitants are noted for their exceptional longevity and good health, which traditional Japanese culture attributes in part to regular consumption of ashitaba. The plant is a tall, hollow-stemmed member of the carrot family (Apiaceae) with large, glossy, deeply divided leaves and the characteristic umbellate flower clusters of the family; unlike most Apiaceae herbs which are harvested for seeds or roots, ashitaba is grown for its young leaves and tender stems. The common name 'Tomorrow's Leaf' (ashita = tomorrow, ba = leaf) reflects the plant's extraordinary regrowth rate — young leaves emerge with such speed that a stem cut today is visibly growing another leaf by the following morning, an exceptional characteristic even among fast-growing herbs. The leaves are somewhat bitter, celery-like in flavor, and rich in flavonoids — particularly chalcones and xanthoangelol — that are the subject of extensive research in Japan for potential health benefits. The stems and leaves are used in Japanese cooking in tempura, salads, juices, and tea. The distinctive yellow sap that oozes from cut stems is a characteristic feature of the species.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; ashwagandha grows rapidly in hot, dry conditions and can be grown as a long-lived perennial in zone 9 or as an annual in cooler climates — roots are harvested after 150–180 days when dried-out looking berries are present.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 24 inches; harvest roots when berries form on the plant and begin to dry. Withania somnifera (ashwagandha or Indian ginseng) is one of the most important medicinal plants in Ayurvedic medicine — a short-lived perennial shrub native to the dry regions of India, North Africa, and the Mediterranean, producing an extensive root system with thick, fleshy, woody roots that are the primary medicinal product. The roots contain withanolides, a class of steroidal lactones that are the subject of extensive clinical research showing adaptogenic, stress-reducing, anti-inflammatory, and potential cognitive-protective effects. Ashwagandha root powder and extracts are among the most widely sold herbal supplements globally, used for stress management, anxiety reduction, athletic performance enhancement, and cognitive support. The plant itself is an attractive, somewhat felty-leaved, branching shrub with small, inconspicuous flowers and small, tomato-like red berries enclosed in paper lantern-like calyces. Harvest roots 5–6 months after transplanting. The plant is in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) — the berries are mildly toxic.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes into a sunny, warm location.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix and keep consistently warm at 70–80°F until germination; transplant after last frost into sandy or loamy, well-drained soil. Ashwagandha thrives in hot, dry conditions similar to its native Indian range — avoid overwatering and boggy soil. The fleshy taproot is the primary medicinal part and is harvested after the plant's first autumn, when the small lantern-like berries begin to turn red. Wash, slice, and dry the roots for use in adaptogenic powders and decoctions; yields improve substantially if plants are grown through a full growing season.

plant_note: Sow stratified seeds in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; ginseng requires 2 years of stratification for reliable germination and is typically grown from pre-stratified seed or 2-year rootlets; roots are not harvested until the plant is 5–7 years old.
directions: Plant pre-stratified seeds or 2-year rootlets in fall in moist, deeply humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil under 70–80% shade from deciduous trees; ginseng is extremely slow and demanding, needing years of careful growing before harvest. Asian ginseng is one of the most prized medicinal herbs in East Asian traditional medicine, used for thousands of years as a general tonic and adaptogen; commercially grown in Korea and China where demand far exceeds supply from wild populations. Home cultivation requires patience — seeds need 18 months of stratification, plants take 5–7 years to produce marketable roots, and they are highly susceptible to damping-off, voles, and deer. Excellent drainage is critical; plant in raised woodland beds with 50% shade cloth or under deciduous trees on a north-facing slope. Consult a qualified herbalist before medicinal use of the root.

common_name: Assam Indigo (Indigo Bush, Japanese Indigo Strobilanthes)
plant_note: Plant in spring in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Strobilanthes cusia prefers cool, shaded conditions and will perform poorly in full sun in zone 9. In zone 9a, it may die back to the roots in hard winters but resproutes vigorously in spring. Harvest leaves in summer (June-August) when indigo content is highest for natural dyeing. The blue-purple fall flowers appear September-December.
directions: Plant in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Strobilanthes cusia performs best in dappled shade and will wilt or scorch in full afternoon sun in zone 9. Strobilanthes cusia (Assam Indigo or Indigo Strobilanthes) is a subtropical shrub native to the hill country of Assam (India) and southern China that has been cultivated for centuries as the primary source of natural indigo dye in Japan, where it is called 'Ryukyu-ai' and used to produce the distinctive deep blue of traditional Japanese katazome (paste-resist dyeing) and aizome (indigo dyeing). The leaves contain the indigo precursor indican, which when fermented produces indigotin — the same deep blue pigment as in Indigofera tinctoria (true indigo), though the two plants are from different families. In zone 8–10 Gulf Coast and Southeast gardens, Strobilanthes cusia is a striking shade plant: large, dark-green, quilted leaves form a bold textural mass in shaded beds, and in fall (September–December) the plant produces compact clusters of small, violet-blue, snapdragon-like flowers. An excellent shade shrub with historical textile craft significance. The leaves can be processed into a paste indigo vat for natural dyeing wool, silk, and cotton.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Assam tea is the broad-leaved tropical botanical variety of the tea plant, less cold-tolerant than the small-leaved China variety but well suited to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun; Assam tea is the large-leaved, tropical botanical variety of the tea plant, native to the hot, humid Assam region of northeastern India, and is the source of the malty, full-bodied character prized in classic Assam and many English breakfast-style black teas. Compared to the small-leaved China variety (Camellia sinensis var. sinensis) more commonly grown in cooler climates, Assam tea grows faster, produces larger leaves, and tolerates heat and humidity better, but it is noticeably less cold-hardy, making it a better fit for the warm, humid Gulf South than for northern tea gardens. Begin harvesting the tender top two leaves and a bud once plants are three to four years old and well established; frequent light plucking encourages a dense, bushy, more productive shape. Provide consistent moisture, since tea plants are sensitive to drought stress, and mulch well to keep roots cool and the acidic soil moist.

plant_note: Nick or soak seed to soften the hard coat, then direct-sow or start in deep pots in spring in loose, deep, well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun; the long taproot resents transplanting and disturbance, so deep containers or direct seeding give the best results.
directions: Astragalus is a long-lived perennial legume grown for its pale, fibrous taproot, dried and sliced into the flat, tongue-depressor-shaped root known in traditional Chinese herbalism as huang qi, one of the most widely used tonic herbs in that tradition. The plant itself is an airy, pea-family perennial with ferny, pinnately compound leaves and small pale-yellow flowers in early summer, useful as a low-key border filler and pollinator plant as it slowly builds root mass over three or more growing seasons before harvest. It prefers lean, deep, well-drained soil and full sun and, like most deep-rooted legumes, is very drought-tolerant once established but does poorly in heavy, poorly drained clay. Roots are traditionally harvested in fall after the third or fourth year of growth, once they have reached pencil-to-finger thickness.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before sowing in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; astragalus develops a deep taproot from which the medicinal dried root is harvested — roots are typically dug in the fall of the 3rd or 4th year, when the root is at maximum potency. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves poor soils. Avoid heavy, wet soils which cause root rot.
directions: Sow scarified seeds in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; astragalus (huang qi, huang qi root) is one of the most important medicinal plants in Chinese medicine — used for over 2,000 years as a primary tonic herb for immune system support, energy, and longevity. The dried, sliced root (huang qi) appears in countless traditional Chinese medicine formulas and is increasingly studied in Western medicine for its immunomodulatory, adaptogenic, and antioxidant properties, including possible effects on telomerase activation. The plant itself is an attractive legume producing pinnate leaves on erect stems and small, pale-yellow pea flowers in spring. The root (used medicinally) is harvested in year 3–4 and dried into the characteristic yellow sticks sold in Chinese herb shops. As a legume, it fixes nitrogen and tolerates poor, dry soils. Now increasingly grown as a medicinal garden plant in North America as interest in traditional Chinese herbs grows.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Australian rosemary is very drought-tolerant once established and sensitive to waterlogged soils. It tolerates coastal salt spray and alkaline conditions. Lightly shear after each flowering flush to keep plants compact and bushy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Australian rosemary is a coastal Australian native shrub from the mint family that closely resembles culinary rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis) in appearance — with narrow, whorled, needle-like leaves, a similar upright to spreading habit, and small tubular flowers — but is not used as a culinary herb and is generally more drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and adaptable than true rosemary. The flowers are white to pale lavender, produced nearly continuously through the year in mild coastal climates, providing a steady nectar source. It is one of the most reliable evergreen flowering shrubs for hot, dry, coastal zones 8–11, tolerating conditions of salt spray, poor soil, and extended drought that defeat most ornamentals. Widely planted in California coastal landscaping as a rosemary substitute where salt exposure makes true rosemary struggle. The cultivar 'Wynyabbie Gem' has more consistent lavender-mauve flowers; 'Morning Light' has cream-variegated foliage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species resents winter wet more than most creeping thymes.
directions: Native to the Azores, Madeira, and the northwest Iberian coast, this diminutive species forms a very low, dense tuft of narrow, spatula-shaped leaves that carry a resinous, almost pine-like fragrance distinct from the thymol scent of common thyme. In early summer it disappears under a haze of small bright-pink flowers that draw bees heavily. The tiny leaves can substitute for lemon thyme in the kitchen, but most gardeners grow it as a choice rock-garden or trough plant, where its compact tufted habit and unusual scent set it apart from sprawling creeping thyme cultivars. Give it gritty, fast-draining soil and avoid rich or consistently damp ground, which quickly rots the crown.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; aztec sweet herb spreads by rooting stolons and can be used as a low groundcover in tropical gardens — trim periodically to maintain compact growth.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; aztec sweet herb (hierba dulce, Mexican candy herb, honeyherb) is a Mexican native tropical herb that contains hernandulcin, a natural sesquiterpene sweetener approximately 1,000 times sweeter than sucrose by weight — placing a single small leaf on the tongue immediately produces an intensely sweet, slightly anise-flavored sweetness that lasts for several minutes. The plant has been used in traditional Mexican medicine and as a sweetening herb since pre-Columbian times. It grows as a low, spreading, stoloniferous herb with small, oval, hairy, wrinkled leaves and small white flower clusters, and functions as a low groundcover in tropical garden settings. Current medical interest focuses on hernandulcin's potential as a natural low-calorie sweetener. Tea made from the fresh or dried leaves is pleasantly and intensely sweet with subtle herbal notes. In zones 9–12 it grows as a perennial groundcover; in cooler climates it is grown in containers brought indoors in autumn.

plant_note: Start indoors early; slow to germinate and frost tender when young.
directions: Start the fine seed indoors well before the last frost, surface-sowing it into a well-drained mix and keeping it warm, as germination is slow and uneven. Grow this florist's silver dollar eucalyptus in full sun with lean, well-drained soil once transplanted; it is frost tender and grown as an annual in cold regions. Harvest the long stems of rounded, dusty blue-green leaves for fresh or dried arrangements, where they hold up well and carry a menthol-like fragrance.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; bacopa grows naturally in wet, marshy conditions and can even grow in standing water up to 2 inches deep. It makes excellent ground cover for the margins of ponds, rain gardens, and wet areas where it spreads by creeping stems.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; brahmi (bacopa) is a small, creeping, succulent-looking wetland herb native to tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, widely used in Ayurvedic medicine for over 3,000 years as a brain tonic and cognitive enhancer — modern clinical research has substantiated its traditional use for improving memory, reducing anxiety, and supporting neurological function. The small, rounded, fleshy leaves have a mild, slightly bitter flavor and are eaten fresh in salads or cooked in the coastal cuisines of India and Southeast Asia. In the garden it forms a low mat in consistently wet or boggy conditions, producing tiny white five-petaled flowers nearly continuously in warm weather that attract small native bees. It is one of the few edible herbs that thrives in the partially shaded margins of water gardens and boggy low spots. In zone 8–9 it may die back after hard freezes but regrows from the roots; in zone 10–11 it is evergreen year-round.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile soil in zone 10–12; Baheda (Beleric Myrobalan, Vibhitaki) is a large deciduous tree from the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, and Sri Lanka — one of the three foundational herbs in Triphala (along with Amla and Haritaki), the most important classical formula in Ayurvedic medicine — bearing round to elliptical, grey-green fruits rich in astringent tannins used medicinally for thousands of years in Ayurvedic, Siddha, and traditional Southeast Asian healing systems.
directions: Plant Terminalia bellirica in deep, well-drained, fertile, moderately moist soil in full sun; the tree grows large and needs space to develop its wide-spreading crown; water during establishment and in dry periods, though mature trees are somewhat drought-tolerant. Baheda (vibhitaki in Sanskrit — meaning 'that which removes disease') is one of the three foundational plants in Triphala (Sanskrit: 'three fruits'), the cornerstone polyherbal formula of Ayurvedic medicine used for thousands of years across India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. Triphala — consisting of equal parts Amla (Phyllanthus emblica), Haritaki (Terminalia chebula), and Baheda (Terminalia bellirica) — is the most widely used compound herb in Ayurveda, prescribed as a rejuvenating tonic, digestive aid, gentle laxative, and general health formula. The dried rind of Baheda fruits is particularly high in tannins (gallic acid, ellagic acid, chebulagic acid) with demonstrated antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and hepatoprotective activity in research studies. Baheda's traditional Ayurvedic indications include respiratory conditions (bronchitis, asthma, cough), hair loss, eye diseases, and digestive disorders. The tree is also valuable for its hard, durable timber and as a shade and avenue tree in India; it produces inconspicuous cream-white flower spikes and later the characteristic ridged, oval grey-green fruits. An important tree for gardens serving South Asian communities in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant into rich, well-drained soil after frost; roots are typically dug for use in autumn of the second growing year.
directions: Sow in a loose, humus-rich, well-drained bed in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun, as this thistle-like aster relative resents soggy or heavy clay soil. Foliage is coarse and somewhat ornamental with purplish thistle-type flower heads in late summer, but the plant is grown almost entirely for its aromatic, camphor-scented rhizome, dug in fall of the second or third year for traditional use in Chinese herbal preparations. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer, and divide or replant offsets in early spring to keep a patch productive. Because it is slow to establish from seed, many gardeners start with purchased rhizome divisions instead.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring (or fresh in fall) in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile mountain-type soil in full sun to part shade; baldmoney is a Scottish and Alpine European mountain herb of the carrot family with feathery, intensely aromatic foliage combining anise, caraway, and lovage flavors — it requires cool growing conditions and does not perform in hot lowland climates.
directions: Direct sow fresh seed in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, cool, moderately fertile soil; fresh seed germinates best — old seed has very poor germination. Meum athamanticum (baldmoney or meu) is a rare and unusual European mountain herb of the carrot family (Apiaceae), native to the highlands of Scotland, Wales, and the Alps, where it grows on moist, acidic mountain meadows and rocky slopes at high elevations. The intensely aromatic, finely cut, ferny, bright-green foliage has a distinctive, complex fragrance and flavor combining anise, caraway, dill, celery, and lovage — more aromatic and complex than any of those herbs individually. The roots (called 'bear root' — bears reportedly seek out and dig the roots in spring) are also aromatic and have been used in alpine herbal medicine and liqueur production. In Scottish Gaelic folk medicine and cooking, the leaves were used to flavor soups and stews in the Highlands where few other herbs grew. The plant produces white umbel flowers in early summer, resembling a small cow parsley. As a garden plant, baldmoney requires cool, moist, acidic conditions found in zone 4–7 mountain and cool-temperate climates — it does not tolerate summer heat and is genuinely rare in cultivation, making it a prized collector's plant for cool-climate herb enthusiasts.

common_name: Balsamic Blooms Basil (Texas Superstar Edible-Flower Basil)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Balsamic Blooms is a Texas Superstar basil bred to keep producing tender, mild-flavored leaves and edible purple flowers together all season without the bitterness that normally develops in flowering basil.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Balsamic Blooms is a Texas Superstar-designated basil bred to solve a problem common to every other basil variety — once basil flowers, the leaves typically turn bitter and the plant's culinary usefulness declines — by keeping leaf flavor mild and pleasant even as it flowers continuously, so the whole plant, showy purple flower spikes included, stays harvestable and edible all season. This lets it double as both a productive culinary herb and an ornamental, pollinator-friendly bedding plant without the usual tradeoff of pinching off every flower to preserve leaf quality. Harvest leaves and flower spikes together for salads, garnishes, and infused vinegars. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage a fuller, bushier plant, though unlike most basil, letting it flower freely does not ruin its usefulness in the kitchen.

plant_note: Propagate by division; spreads fast.
directions: Start banana mint from divisions or cuttings, as it will not reproduce true from seed. Its soft fuzzy leaves carry a sweet fruity aroma prized for desserts and beverages. Grow in consistently moist, fertile soil in dappled sun, keeping roots contained to stop rampant spreading. Water generously in hot weather and cut plants back hard mid-season to renew tender foliage. Lift and divide crowded clumps every couple of years.

common_name: Barbecue Rosemary (Stiff Upright-Stemmed Culinary Rosemary Grown for Skewers)
plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Barbecue's extra-stiff, straight stems are grown specifically to be cut, stripped of leaves, and used as fragrant skewers for grilling.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil, and avoid overwatering since rosemary is far more likely to fail from soggy roots than from drought. Barbecue is an upright culinary rosemary selected for unusually long, straight, rigid stems that hold together well enough to thread meat and vegetables directly onto for grilling, imparting a subtle piney rosemary flavor as the skewer chars. Its needle-like leaves have the same robust, resinous culinary flavor as other upright rosemary types and are equally good stripped fresh for roasting and seasoning. Established plants are drought-tolerant and long-lived in the Gulf South once past their first season, though in zones below 8 they should be grown as a container plant and brought in over winter, since rosemary's hardiness varies considerably by selection.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun, well-drained soil; Barbeque is an upright rosemary cultivar selected for long, strong, straight woody stems well suited to stripping and using as flavorful skewers for grilling, in addition to standard culinary use.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; rosemary tolerates poor, rocky, sandy soils far better than rich garden soil, which promotes lush but frost-tender growth. Barbeque is an upright, vigorous rosemary cultivar selected specifically for producing long, strong, straight woody stems, prized by cooks for stripping the needles and using the stem itself as an aromatic skewer for grilling meat, seafood, or vegetables, infusing the food with rosemary flavor as it cooks. Beyond its skewer use, it is a fully capable culinary rosemary with the classic piney, resinous fragrance and flavor, and its upright, well-branched habit also makes an attractive hedge or specimen shrub. Like other rosemary cultivars, it thrives on relative neglect once established, needing little water or fertilizer, and is more prone to root rot from overwatering than from drought. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a tidy shape and to harvest a fresh supply of long, straight stems for skewers.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant only after nights stay reliably above 50°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in a warm, moist seed-starting mix and keep soil above 65°F for reliable sprouting. Pinch out flower buds as soon as they appear to encourage bushy leaf production and delay bolting. Water at the base to avoid fungal spots, and feed lightly with a balanced fertilizer mid-season. Harvest by snipping stems just above a leaf node once plants have at least six true leaves.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this understory ginger relative needs the warm, humid, sheltered conditions of a tropical forest floor and is not frost-tolerant.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this understory ginger relative needs the warm, humid, sheltered conditions of a tropical forest floor and is not frost-tolerant. A clumping, cane-forming member of the ginger family native to the forest understories of southern China and Southeast Asia, it produces small flowers low on the rhizomes near the soil surface, followed by reddish-brown, spiny-husked seed capsules that are dried and used as a substitute for true cardamom in traditional Chinese medicine and cooking, with a similar but more camphorous, less refined aroma. Its broad, glossy, tropical foliage and shade tolerance make it a useful textural understory plant in a warm, humid shade garden even where the spice itself is not harvested. Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and maintain vigor, and protect from any temperature below the mid-40s Fahrenheit.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or established transplants after last frost in spring.
directions: Take semi-ripe stem cuttings in summer, dip in rooting hormone, and insert into gritty propagating mix; expect rooting in 6–9 weeks. Plant in well-drained soil in a sheltered, sunny site; in zones 7 and colder, grow in containers that can be moved indoors before hard frost. Clip the canopy to shape annually and remove any reverted plain shoots from variegated forms. Harvest individual leaves as needed once the plant is established; leaves are most pungent when dried for 1–2 weeks.

common_name: Bay Rum Tree (West Indian Bay, Bay Laurel of the Caribbean)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; bay rum tree is a Caribbean native in the allspice family (Myrtaceae) — the aromatic, glossy leaves yield bay rum oil, the basis of the classic West Indian bay rum aftershave and hair tonic used throughout the Caribbean since the 19th century; the leaves can also be used as a culinary spice similar to bay laurel but with warmer, more complex, eugenol-clove notes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; the leaves can be harvested year-round for culinary and aromatic use. Pimenta racemosa (bay rum tree or West Indian bay) is a small to medium-sized aromatic evergreen tree native to the Caribbean islands — particularly Puerto Rico, the Lesser Antilles, and the Virgin Islands — in the myrtle family (Myrtaceae), closely related to allspice (P. dioica). The glossy, elliptic, leathery leaves of P. racemosa are extraordinarily aromatic when crushed or steam-distilled — yielding 'bay oil' or 'bay rum oil,' a complex essential oil rich in eugenol (clove-scented), myrcene, and chavicol, with warm, spicy, clove-bay character. Bay rum oil is the defining ingredient in traditional West Indian bay rum — a classic men's aftershave, hair tonic, and skin care product used throughout the Caribbean since the mid-19th century and still produced in the Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico today. The same leaves can be used as a culinary herb: dried or fresh leaves add a warmer, more complex, clove-tinged bay flavor to Caribbean stews, soups, and marinades compared to Mediterranean bay laurel. Small, white, fragrant flowers are produced in panicles, followed by small, black, spice-flavored berries. An outstanding aromatic tree for zone 10–12 gardens that combines culinary, aromatic, and cultural heritage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space 18–24 inches apart as bee balm spreads vigorously by underground runners and needs room. Improve air circulation by avoiding overcrowding to reduce powdery mildew.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart; bee balm is an eastern North American native herb with shaggy, whorled, scarlet or pink flower heads from midsummer through early fall that are the preferred nectar source of ruby-throated hummingbirds in eastern gardens. The leaves and flowers have a bergamot-orange flavor and aroma, making them valuable for brewing Oswego tea (historically used by the Oswego nation and early American colonists), garnishing salads, and flavoring jellies. Powdery mildew is a persistent issue in humid climates — choose resistant cultivars like 'Jacob Cline', 'Raspberry Wine', or 'Gardenview Scarlet'. Divide overcrowded clumps every 2–3 years in spring; replant vigorous outer portions and discard the worn-out center.

common_name: Benenden Blue Rosemary (Narrow-Leaf Vivid Deep-Blue-Flowered Rosemary)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Benenden Blue is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit rosemary with narrow dark-green leaves and especially vivid deep-blue flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Benenden Blue, a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit holder, bears narrow, dark green needle-like leaves and an especially vivid, saturated deep-blue flower display in spring, among the showiest flowering of any commonly grown rosemary cultivar. It needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, performing well in a container, raised bed, or rock garden, and its fragrant, flavorful foliage is fully usable in the kitchen in addition to its strong ornamental value. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 65°F; benne thrives in the long, hot, humid Gulf Coast summer that many other crops struggle with, and is notably drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Sow seed a quarter-inch deep in warm, well-drained soil once the danger of frost has passed and soil has thoroughly warmed. Benne is the historic name for sesame brought to the South Carolina Lowcountry by enslaved West Africans, who carried both the seed and the West African Bantu word 'benne' for it, and who used it in traditional dishes and confections that remain part of Lowcountry foodways today, most famously benne wafers and benne brittle. The tall, branching plants produce small tubular flowers followed by seed pods that split open when fully dry, releasing the small, flavorful seeds prized both toasted for cooking and pressed for oil. Benne is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving in conditions that stress many other summer crops, and needs relatively little care beyond weeding while young. Harvest whole seed stalks once the lower pods begin to split, and finish drying upside down in a paper bag to catch seed as pods open.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall, or root stem cuttings in water; plant in moist, fertile soil in part shade to full sun. Like all mints, bergamot mint spreads vigorously by runners and is best grown in containers or with a root barrier to prevent it from taking over the garden. The distinctive bergamot-citrus fragrance is strongest from midsummer leaves.
directions: Divide runners and plant in moist, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; bergamot mint is a peppermint relative with a distinctive, complex fragrance of bergamot orange, lavender, and lemon — caused by the predominance of linalool and linalool acetate rather than the menthol characteristic of peppermint. The scent is sometimes described as eau de cologne, hence the alternate name. The flavor is equally distinctive and less sharply mentholous than peppermint, making it preferred for herb teas, lemonade, cocktails, and delicate desserts where a floral-citrus mint quality is desired. The leaves are rounded, dark-green to slightly bronze-tinged, and the plant produces small, pale-lavender flower spikes in summer that attract pollinators. Several named cultivars exist including Chocolate Mint (with a chocolate-menthol scent), Orange Mint (with a stronger orange character), and Grapefruit Mint (grapefruit-citrus overtones) — all are selections of this same botanical grouping. Grows identically to spearmint or peppermint in its need for consistent moisture and tendency to spread.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants after last frost; this non-blooming cultivar is propagated vegetatively.
directions: Root 3–4 in semi-ripe cuttings in moist perlite in late summer; Berggarten sage rarely flowers and is almost exclusively vegetatively propagated. Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; the exceptionally large, rounded, gray-green leaves make it one of the most productive and ornamental culinary sages. Because it does not bolt to flower, the plant concentrates energy into leaf production and remains more compact and tidy than the species. Harvest large leaves throughout the season, cutting back the plant by one-third in spring to remove any winter-killed wood and encourage fresh basal growth.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; like other lemon thyme cultivars it is prone to crown rot in humid, poorly drained conditions and appreciates a raised bed or container in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Bertram Anderson is a golden-leaved lemon thyme cultivar prized as much for its bright chartreuse-yellow foliage, which deepens toward green in summer heat, as for its citrus-scented culinary use, making it a useful low, spreading edger that lights up a sunny herb bed or path edge. The lemon-thyme flavor and fragrance are shared with green-leaved lemon thyme and work well in the same fish, poultry, and tea preparations. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the low mat tidy and encourage fresh, brightly colored new growth, and ensure sharp drainage year-round, since wet feet in humid climates are the most common cause of failure.

common_name: Betel Pepper (Betel Vine, Paan Leaf, Sirih)
plant_note: Plant stem cuttings in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with support for climbing; Piper betle is a shade-loving, moisture-preferring vine that grows naturally in the understory of tropical forests and performs best in humid, partially shaded conditions with regular watering. The glossy, heart-shaped leaves are harvested for traditional use throughout South and Southeast Asia — fresh betel leaves are used as a digestive herb, as a wrapper for the traditional 'paan' preparation, and in various medicinal applications across Indian, Sri Lankan, Indonesian, Malaysian, Thai, and Vietnamese traditions. In zone 9, protect from frost; in zone 10-12, grows as a perennial climbing vine. Non-toxic in moderate culinary/herbal amounts.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with a support for climbing — Betel Pepper grows most luxuriantly in the warm, moist, shaded understory conditions similar to its native habitat and will languish in full sun or dry soil. Piper betle is a perennial, climbing vine in the Piperaceae family native to South and Southeast Asia — the same genus as black pepper (P. nigrum) — and one of the most culturally and economically significant plants in the traditional medicine and daily life of South and Southeast Asia. The plant produces heart-shaped, glossy, smooth, dark-green leaves on a climbing, node-rooting vine that ascends trees and structures by adhesive root pads. The leaves are the harvest product: fresh betel leaves (called 'paan' in South Asian tradition) are harvested and used in the preparation of the traditional South Asian chewing combination of areca nut (from Areca catechu), slaked lime, and betel leaf — a preparation with mild stimulant effects consumed by hundreds of millions of people across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia. Beyond this traditional use, fresh betel leaves are used as a cooking wrapper, an herbal digestive, and in various ethnobotanical and Ayurvedic applications throughout the Asian traditional medicine systems. The leaves contain chavicol, eugenol, and other phenolic compounds that contribute their distinctive flavor and mild bioactivity. Grown in zone 10-12 as a permanent perennial shade vine, or as an annual-treated container plant in zone 9. Non-toxic in culinary amounts.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; cold stratification for 4 weeks improves germination.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds for 4 weeks in the refrigerator before sowing 1/4 in deep in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Betony (Betonica officinalis, synonym Stachys betonica) has a long history in European herbal medicine as a nervine tonic and digestive herb; the leaves are dried for tea. Grow in partial shade with moisture-retentive soil; plants are long-lived once established and require little attention beyond dividing crowded clumps every 3–4 years. Harvest leaves and flowering tops in early summer when the rosy-pink flower spikes are just opening, then dry thoroughly in a well-ventilated space.

subcategory: West African culinary medicinal bitter shrub
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zone 9–12; Bitter Leaf is a large, fast-growing African shrub (formerly Vernonia amygdalina) — one of the most important culinary and medicinal plants in West and Central Africa — with large, soft, dark-green leaves that are processed by washing and kneading to reduce bitterness before use in classic West African soups including Ofe Onugbu and Bitter Leaf Soup, and used widely as a medicinal herb across the continent.
directions: Root Gymnanthemum amygdalinum (Bitter Leaf) stem cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; plants establish quickly and grow vigorously in warm climates — prune regularly to maintain a compact, shrubby form and encourage dense, tender leaf production; older stems become woody and less productive. Bitter Leaf (formerly Vernonia amygdalina) is arguably the most important vegetable shrub in West and Central African cuisine — a fast-growing, multi-purpose plant grown in every kitchen garden from Nigeria to the DRC, valued equally as a culinary ingredient, medicinal herb, and forage plant. The leaves contain bitter sesquiterpene lactones (vernodalin, vernomygdin) that give the plant its distinctive medicinal and flavor properties; for culinary use, fresh leaves are washed thoroughly, squeezed and kneaded repeatedly in water, and the liquid pressed out to reduce bitterness to a palatable level before adding to soups, stews, and sauces. The squeezed leaves add a distinctive savory, slightly bitter depth to Ofe Onugbu (Igbo bitter leaf soup with cocoyam and assorted meats) and other traditional dishes. In tropical Africa, the plant is also used to treat malaria, diabetes, fever, and intestinal parasites; research has identified antihelminthic and hypoglycemic compounds. In zone 9–12, Bitter Leaf grows as a perennial shrub reaching 4–8 feet; in cooler areas it can be grown as an annual in a large container.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring and plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in deep shade to partial shade in zone 8–10; Black Cardamom is a large, clumping, ginger-family perennial native to the cool, moist, shaded mountain forests of the Sikkim Himalayas, Nepal, and Bhutan, where the large, dark-brown, wrinkled, smoke-dried seed pods are harvested as a distinctive warming spice with a camphor-menthol-smoke flavor characteristic of North Indian cuisine.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained but consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in deep to partial shade; Black Cardamom thrives in cool, moist conditions resembling its native Himalayan forest understory — mulch heavily, maintain consistent moisture, and protect from hot afternoon sun and frost. Amomum subulatum (Black Cardamom, Large Cardamom, or Nepal Cardamom) is a large, clumping, ginger-family rhizomatous perennial native to the cool, misty, shaded montane forests of Sikkim (India), Nepal, Bhutan, and adjacent mountain regions, where it grows wild at elevations of 3,000–5,000 feet in dense forest understory along streams and in humid ravines. The plant is cultivated extensively under Alnus nepalensis alder trees in the traditional 'Sikkim Cardamom' agroforestry system, which provides the required dense shade, consistent moisture, and forest microclimate. The seed pods — harvested and kiln-dried or traditionally fire-dried over bamboo smoke — are large (1–1.5 inch), dark brown, wrinkled, and distinctively smoky-camphor-menthol in aroma and flavor, completely different from green cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum). Black cardamom is a fundamental spice in North Indian biryani, dal makhani, garam masala blends, and many Nepali and Tibetan dishes; it is also used medicinally in Ayurvedic, Tibetan, and Chinese traditional medicine. A superb shade-garden spice plant for warm, humid zone 8–10 climates; the large, banana-like foliage is ornamentally attractive even when not in pod.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in a sheltered, partially shaded location with deep, moisture-retentive soil, setting the crown just at the soil surface and watering in well.
directions: Choose a partially shaded site with deep, rich, constantly moist soil and plant divisions at least 3-5 feet apart, as established clumps spread broadly through underground rhizomes. Water frequently and generously throughout the growing season, as Black Cardamom requires high moisture levels to produce its characteristic large, aromatic pods. Feed with a balanced organic fertilizer in spring and a potassium-rich fertilizer in summer to encourage flower and pod formation, which typically begins in the second or third year. Harvest the mature seed pods at the base of the plant by hand when they turn deep reddish-brown, traditionally before smoke-drying to develop their distinctive camphor-like flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost; it self-sows readily once established.
directions: Black cumin is an easy, drought-tolerant annual with delicate blue flowers followed by seed pods full of pungent black seeds used in cooking and traditional wellness. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun, as it dislikes root disturbance. The ornamental flowers attract pollinators before giving way to inflated seed capsules. Let pods dry on the plant, then crush them to release the peppery, aromatic seeds.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, loamy soil in full sun; black cumin (kala jeera or shahi jeera) is the genuine Kashmiri and Persian 'royal cumin' — an Apiaceae plant from Central Asian mountain meadows with dramatically different flavor from common cumin, black seed, and nigella, used as the defining spice in Kashmiri rice dishes, korma, and Persian breads.
directions: Direct sow in early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 6 inches; harvest seed heads when fully mature and dry. Bunium persicum (black cumin, kala jeera, or shahi jeera — literally 'royal cumin' in Urdu) is a wild carrot family (Apiaceae) plant from the mountain steppes and alpine meadows of Central Asia — particularly Kashmir, Iran, Afghanistan, and the Hindu Kush range — and represents the genuine botanical source of the highly aromatic spice sold in Indian specialty markets as 'kala jeera' or 'shahi jeera.' It is frequently confused with two other spices sharing the common name 'black cumin': Nigella sativa (black seed or black caraway, an entirely different plant) and regular cumin (Cuminum cyminum). Bunium persicum has a uniquely complex, intense, earthy-herbal-thyme-like aroma with bitter-sweet warmth — dramatically different in character from common cumin, more aromatic and complex, with additional notes reminiscent of dried thyme and warm spice. In Kashmiri cooking, kala jeera is the defining spice of pulao rice (the famous Kashmiri mutton pulao), yakhni lamb broth, and korma dishes. In Persian cuisine, it flavors traditional breads, rice dishes, and pickles. The plant grows as a delicate, feathery-leaved annual resembling miniature Queen Anne's lace, producing small umbel flowers followed by the narrow, ridged, black-brown aromatic seeds.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once soil temperatures are above 70 degrees F, barely covering the rhizomes with 1-2 inches of loose, fertile soil in a partially shaded bed.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in a partially shaded spot with loose, well-draining, humus-rich soil, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart. Keep the soil consistently moist throughout the active growing season, then reduce watering as the foliage dies back in autumn to allow the rhizomes to cure. Harvest rhizomes in late fall once the tops have yellowed, or leave them in the ground in frost-free climates to naturalize over time. For the best development of the characteristic dark purple flesh, ensure plants receive warm temperatures (above 65 degrees F) through the entire growing season.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 1–2 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in zone 8–11; Black Ginger (Krachai Dam, Thai Ginseng) is a compact, deciduous ginger-family perennial from Thailand and Laos grown for its dark-purple-to-black, aromatic rhizomes — one of Thailand's most important medicinal plants used for energy, vitality, and adaptation, and now internationally recognized for compounds supporting exercise performance and male health.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions just 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled light; Kaempferia parviflora is compact and low-growing — dies completely back to dormant rhizomes in winter and re-emerges in spring; mulch in zone 8–9 to protect rhizomes from hard frost. Kaempferia parviflora (Black Ginger, Krachai Dam, or Thai Ginseng) is a compact, deciduous, rhizomatous perennial native to Laos and northern Thailand, traditionally cultivated at altitude in the Chiang Mai and Mae Hong Son highlands, and one of the most important medicinal plants in Thai and Lao traditional herbal medicine. The small, dark-purple to nearly black rhizomes (distinctive in color compared to all other Kaempferia species) contain a unique array of methoxyflavones — particularly 5,7-dimethoxyflavone and 3,5,7,3',4'-pentamethoxyflavone — that have been extensively researched for anti-fatigue, adaptogenic, vasodilatory, and exercise-performance properties. Black Ginger is now marketed internationally as a sports supplement and traditional herbal tonic. Small, pale-purple, orchid-like flowers are held just above the ground among attractive, broad, ground-level leaves from spring through summer. An excellent partial-shade novelty herb for zone 8–11 gardens; the compact size makes it ideal for container growing in cooler climates.

plant_note: Direct-sow around the last frost into average, well-drained soil; naturalizes easily and self-seeds once established.
directions: Avoid during pregnancy, as this herb has a traditional history of use as a uterine stimulant. Direct-sow around the last frost into average, well-drained soil; this coarse, strong-smelling mint-family perennial naturalizes easily and self-seeds once established. Traditionally the flowering tops are dried for tea used to settle nausea and mild anxiety, distinct from white horehound (Marrubium vulgare), which is used mainly for coughs.

plant_note: Set rooted divisions or cuttings into moist, fertile soil after the last frost; mint cultivars do not come true from seed, so propagation is always vegetative.
directions: Black Mitcham is the historic English-origin peppermint strain that became the backbone of American commercial peppermint oil production in the Pacific Northwest, prized for its exceptionally high menthol content and clean, intense peppermint flavor. Stems and leaf undersides carry a distinctive dark bronze-red flush that darkens further in cool weather, making the plant easy to distinguish from ordinary green peppermint at a glance. Grow it in a contained bed or sunken pot in consistently moist, rich soil, since like all mints it spreads aggressively by rhizome and will overrun neighboring plants if left unchecked. Choose this cultivar over generic peppermint when you want the strongest, most classic peppermint flavor for tea, extracts, or candy-making.

plant_note: Direct sow 4 weeks before last frost, or in early fall in mild-winter climates, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; black mustard bolts and sets seed quickly once summer heat arrives, so aim for a full life cycle in cool weather.
directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in early fall where winters are mild; black mustard grows quickly into a tall, branching plant with small, bright yellow, four-petaled flowers in loose clusters, followed by slender seed pods that shatter readily when fully ripe. It produces the pungent, sharply flavored small brown-black seeds traditionally used to make true Dijon-style prepared mustard and are also used whole in Indian and other South Asian tempering and pickling, delivering more heat and complexity than the milder white mustard seed. Because ripe pods shatter and drop seed the moment they dry, harvest whole seed heads into a paper bag as soon as pods begin to turn from green to brown, then finish drying and threshing indoors to avoid losing the crop to shattering in the field. Rotate away from other brassica family crops each season to reduce pest and disease buildup, and expect volunteer seedlings the following year from any seed that drops before harvest.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with a support structure; black pepper requires warmth above 60°F year-round and high humidity. Zone 10–12 outdoors; excellent as a container specimen in zone 8–9 moved indoors in winter.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with a support structure or trellis — black pepper is the world's most traded spice and a shade-tolerant climbing vine native to India's Malabar Coast, where it grows as a climbing epiphyte in the forest understory. In tropical gardens (zone 10–12) the vine climbs 10–30 feet up a tree or post, producing clusters of peppercorns that start green, turn red when fully ripe, and are picked at different stages to produce green pepper (fresh), black pepper (dried unripe), red pepper (ripe), and white pepper (ripe, hull removed). The vine requires warmth, humidity, and consistent moisture. As a container plant in zone 8–9 gardens, it makes an attractive tropical accent vine moved indoors for winter. A genuinely rewarding home-grown spice for warm-climate gardeners.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings after last frost in contained beds or pots — black peppermint spreads by vigorous underground runners and becomes invasive in open garden beds; contain with buried barriers or grow in submerged pots.
directions: Plant divisions in moderately moist, fertile soil in partial to full sun and contain spreading runners with buried barriers or grow in submerged pots; black peppermint (Mentha x piperita f. piperita) is distinguished from white peppermint by its dark purple-tinged stems and leaf margins, deeper green leaves, and significantly higher menthol content — the form prized for peppermint tea, essential oil production, and confections where strong clean menthol flavor is essential. Harvest stems just before flowering for maximum oil content, cutting back to 2–3 inches above ground to promote bushy regrowth; a second flush will come before frost. Divide every 2–3 years as older plants lose vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or plant container-grown plants in fall or spring in very well-drained, dry, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; black sage is native to coastal sage scrub and chaparral of the California Coast Ranges and Channel Islands, adapted to the Mediterranean climate of California. Summer drought is essential — avoid irrigation in summer.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; black sage is one of the dominant shrubs of California coastal sage scrub — a white-flowered, strongly aromatic native sage with dark green, wrinkled, very fragrant leaves that produce a characteristic camphor-sage scent that perfumes the California coastal air on warm days. The clusters of small, white to pale lavender flowers in spring are exceptionally attractive to native bees — black sage is one of the most important native bee plants in California, producing abundant nectar and pollen particularly for bumble bees, carpenter bees, and many solitary native bees. The dried seed capsules (nutlets) are eaten by seed-eating birds and small mammals. Completely drought-tolerant once established, requiring no summer irrigation in coastal California gardens. The aromatic leaves can be used as a culinary sage substitute, with a flavor described as a blend of culinary sage and camphor. An essential native for California habitat gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring, 2–4 weeks before last frost; black seed is a cool-season annual that bolts in summer heat and is harvested in late spring to early summer. In zones 8–11, sow in fall for a winter to spring crop.
directions: Broadcast or direct sow in well-drained soil in full sun; black seed (Nigella sativa) is the source of one of the oldest and most significant medicinal spices in the world, used continuously for 3,000 years in Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African medicine. It is entirely distinct from love-in-a-mist (Nigella damascena), though both share the same feathery foliage and ornamental seed capsules. The peppery, slightly bitter, toasted seeds are used to top breads in Egypt and Turkey, are a key component of Indian panch phoron spice blend, and flavored Ethiopian berbere. Allow seed capsules to fully ripen and dry on the plant before harvesting, then shake seeds into a bag. Plants self-sow reliably in suitable climates.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sections 2–3 inches deep after last frost when soil is warm; black turmeric goes dormant in winter — dig and store rhizomes above freezing in zones below 8.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in enriched, loose, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade once soil temperatures reach 65°F; black turmeric is a rare curcuma species from northeastern India with striking blue-gray to nearly black interior flesh in contrast to the familiar orange of common turmeric — the color derives from anthocyanins rather than curcuminoids. Prized primarily in Ayurvedic medicine and traditional tribal use in Odisha and Bengal as an anti-inflammatory and pain reliever; it is less a culinary spice than an important medicinal plant. The attractive large leaves with a dark maroon central midrib stripe make it highly ornamental as a shade garden subject. Lift rhizomes after foliage dies back in fall; store dry above 50°F.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; as a cool-season annual, it can also be sown in late summer for an autumn harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in well-drained, poor to moderately fertile soil in full sun; blessed thistle thrives in lean conditions and declines in rich, moist soil. As a cool-season annual it bolts in summer heat, so early spring or late summer sowing provides the best leaf harvest. Harvest the young leaves and leafy stems before the spiny flower heads fully open, wearing gloves to protect against the prickles. Dried aerial parts are used in traditional bitter digestive tinctures, teas for stimulating appetite, and historical preparations reputed to support lactation.

plant_note: Direct-sow shallowly after frost danger passes into hot, dry, well-drained soil, since this low rosette-forming annual is prone to rot in humid or overwatered conditions.
directions: Psyllium must always be taken with plenty of water, since swallowing it dry can cause choking or intestinal blockage. Direct-sow shallowly after frost danger passes into hot, dry, well-drained soil, since this low rosette-forming annual is prone to rot in humid or overwatered conditions. The mature seed husks, threshed and cleaned once seed heads dry, are the source of psyllium fiber, traditionally and medically used as a bulk-forming laxative and to support healthy cholesterol levels.

plant_note: Cool-season perennial green.
directions: Direct-sow in early spring in cool, moist soil, covering seed lightly and thinning to a hand's width. The striking red-veined leaves add tangy lemon flavor and ornamental color to salads. Grow in partial shade with steady moisture to keep leaves tender and slow bolting. Remove flower stalks to prolong leaf harvest and prevent aggressive self-seeding. Cut leaves young for the best texture and divide crowns every few years.

plant_note: Root cuttings in late spring or early fall; in zone 9 plant September–November or February–April. Blue Boy is the standard dwarf compact rosemary for container growing, topiary, and small herb gardens. Its compact size allows it to be grown in a 6-inch to 1-gallon container indefinitely with regular trimming. It flowers more prolifically than many upright rosemary types, covering the mound in small blue flowers in late winter to early spring.
directions: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil; Blue Boy is a dwarf, compact, mounding rosemary that forms a tight hemisphere of small, fine-textured, intensely aromatic needlelike leaves — the most compact of the named rosemary cultivars and the best choice for container growing, small herb gardens, edging, and topiary. Unlike the large, sprawling upright rosemary types that reach 3–6 feet, Blue Boy stays under 18–24 inches with a mounding, naturally rounded habit that requires little pruning to maintain its shape. The flavor and fragrance are identical to full-sized rosemary — strongly resinous, piney, and aromatic — and the fine leaves are actually preferred for delicate uses where coarser standard rosemary leaves are too large. Blue Boy blooms prolifically in late winter and early spring, covering the mound in tiny blue flowers that are excellent for bees. In zone 9 the compact habit and lean soil requirements make it ideal for containers on patios and decks, where the intensely aromatic foliage is accessible for kitchen harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, loamy soil in full sun; blue fenugreek is a distinct Mediterranean and Central Asian annual herb — the seeds are the essential flavoring ingredient of Schabziger (Swiss green cheese) and various Austrian Alpine cheeses, imparting a warm, herbaceous, hay-like, fenugreek-coumarin aroma different from and milder than common fenugreek (T. foenum-graecum).
directions: Direct sow seeds in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; harvest seed heads when yellow-brown and dry seeds thoroughly. Trigonella caerulea (blue fenugreek or sweet trefoil) is a Mediterranean and Central Asian annual herb in the legume family — the specific herb used to flavor Schabziger, a distinctive small, green, very hard Swiss cheese also known as 'green cheese' or 'sap sago.' The ground seeds of T. caerulea are the source of the unique flavor of Schabziger — a warm, herbaceous, slightly fenugreek-coumarin aroma with hay-like notes, distinctly milder and less bitter than common fenugreek (T. foenum-graecum). The seeds contain coumarin and are also used to flavor breads, crackers, and Alpine herb mixtures in Austria, Switzerland, and Germany. The plant produces distinctive blue-purple flower heads somewhat resembling clover (hence 'blue fenugreek') and trifoliate clover-like leaves. The dried, ground seeds are available in specialty stores as 'Trigonella' or under the name 'blue fenugreek powder.' The fresh leaves are also edible — mildly herb-scented, usable as a green in salads and cooked dishes. Rarely grown in North American gardens but easily cultivated as a spring annual where fenugreek grows.

plant_note: Sow seed or plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade.
directions: Sow seed or plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, since this Siberian steppe native colors up best when protected from the harshest midday heat. Flower buds nod distinctively as they emerge before straightening into dense, rounded pink-purple umbels in mid to late summer, well after most other alliums have finished. Both the blue-green strap leaves and the flowers are edible with a clean onion flavor, and the clumps are useful for filling gaps in partly shaded herb borders. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant but perform best with even moisture during active growth.

common_name: Blue Spice Basil (Compact Mild Anise-Flavored Basil with Lavender Flower Bracts)
plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting or direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Blue Spice Basil is compact (12–16 inches) and well-suited to container growing. In zone 9, plant March–May for spring-summer production and August–September for fall production. Blue Spice has better heat tolerance than standard Genovese basil, making it a more practical choice for Gulf Coast zone 9 where midsummer heat stresses large-leafed Italian types. The name 'Blue Spice' refers to the distinctly lavender-blue flower bracts that develop as the plant matures — technically the plant is flowering at this stage, which reduces leaf production, but the blue flower clusters are ornamental and edible, with the same mild anise-sweet flavor as the leaves. Pinch out flower buds frequently to extend leaf production.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F or direct sow after last frost. Pinch growing tips frequently to encourage bushy growth. Harvest leaves before flowers fully open. Blue Spice Basil is a compact sweet basil variety selected for its distinctive lavender-blue flower bracts and mild anise-sweet flavor profile, which is lighter and less intensely clove-like than standard Genovese basil. The variety produces small, bright green oval leaves on compact bushy plants with a tidy, mounding habit that makes it well-suited to container and edging use, as well as herb gardens where a more compact, ornamental basil is preferred over the large-leafed Italian varieties. The 'Blue Spice' name reflects the plant's most distinctive feature: the flower spikes develop conspicuously blue-lavender bracts (the small leaves associated with each flower) that give the blooming plant a distinctly blue-tinted appearance unusual in the basil family. This blue coloration makes Blue Spice one of the most ornamental of the sweet basil group, bridging the gap between standard culinary basil and the more intensely colored Thai basils. The flavor is in the mild, sweet end of the basil spectrum — less intense than Genovese, with a gentle anise note and sweet basil fragrance — making it appropriate for fresh use in salads, as a garnish, and in preparations where a subtle basil flavor is preferred over the intensity of full-strength Italian types. The flowers and bracts are edible with the same flavor as the leaves and make an attractive edible garnish.

common_name: Bocking 14 Comfrey (Sterile Russian Comfrey for Permaculture Green Mulch and Fertilizer)
plant_note: Plant root cuttings (sections of the thick taproot, 2–4 inches long) or crown divisions 2–4 inches deep in spring; Bocking 14 is sterile and produces no viable seed — it can only be propagated vegetatively from root or crown cuttings. Plant in a permanent location as comfrey is difficult to remove once established — the deep taproot regenerates from any root fragment left in the soil. In zone 9, plant fall through spring; established plants are cut back 3–5 times per year for mulch harvests. Bocking 14 is more compact than most comfrey types (3–4 feet vs. 5+ feet for common comfrey) and has higher potassium content in leaves — ideal for tomatoes, potatoes, and fruiting crops.
directions: Plant root cuttings 2–4 inches deep, 24–36 inches apart; the cutting can be placed horizontally. Cut leaves to the ground 3–4 times per season when the plant reaches 2 feet and use as mulch. Bocking 14 is a sterile cultivar of Russian comfrey (Symphytum × uplandicum, the hybrid between S. asperum and S. officinale) selected by Lawrence D. Hills at the Bocking research station in Essex, UK during the 1950s-60s under the auspices of the Henry Doubleday Research Association (now Garden Organic) — the British organic horticulture organization Hills founded and named for the Victorian market gardener who first championed comfrey's agricultural value. Hills's systematic variety trials of Russian comfrey selected Bocking 14 as the best cultivar for productive leaf yield, high mineral content (particularly potassium, which is 2–3× higher than in most organic mulch materials), and sterility — ensuring that once planted, Bocking 14 would not become an invasive weed spreading by seed across the garden. The sterility that makes Bocking 14 the preferred permaculture comfrey is also the reason it must be purchased as root cuttings rather than seed: no viable seed is produced. The deep taproot (reaching 6+ feet in established plants) functions as a dynamic accumulator — mining calcium, phosphorus, and especially potassium from deep in the soil and concentrating these nutrients in the rapidly-growing leaves. These nutrient-rich leaves, laid around fruiting plants as mulch, break down quickly to release plant-available nutrition, making Bocking 14 a valued fertility tool in organic and low-input garden systems.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface (seeds need light to germinate) 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow October–January for winter-spring harvest. Do not cover seeds with soil — press lightly into the surface and keep moist. Bodegold self-sows abundantly; allow some seedlings to naturalize for a self-perpetuating chamomile patch. Harvest flowers just as the petals begin to reflex downward for highest essential oil content.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-moderate soil — chamomile prefers lean soil and self-seeds most productively when not over-fertilized; Bodegold is a German-selected high-yield commercial chamomile cultivar developed for maximum essential oil production — the flowers contain 2–3 times the essential oil of wild-type chamomile plants, with particularly high chamazulene (the anti-inflammatory blue compound responsible for chamomile oil's characteristic deep blue color when steam-distilled). This variety is widely grown in Germany, Hungary, and Eastern Europe for pharmaceutical and cosmetic chamomile production where standardized high-oil content is required. For home herbal use, Bodegold provides substantially stronger tea and extract from the same weight of dried flowers compared to ordinary chamomile. The apple-scented white flowers with yellow centers are used fresh or dried for chamomile tea, herbal baths, hair rinses, and digestive tinctures.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions in spring or fall in moist to wet, peaty, slightly acidic to neutral, poor, boggy soil in full sun to part shade; bog myrtle is a native aromatic shrub of peat bogs, wet heathlands, and lakeshores of North America and northern Europe — the strongly fragrant, resinous leaves were the primary bittering and flavoring agent in European ale before hops became dominant (medieval gruit ale), and are still used to flavor gin, whisky, and craft beers.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, peaty, slightly acidic to neutral, poor, boggy soil in full sun to part shade; bog myrtle requires consistently moist to wet conditions and does not tolerate drought; fixes nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis. Myrica gale (bog myrtle or sweet gale) is a deciduous aromatic shrub native to the peat bogs, wet heathlands, and lakeshores of northern North America, northern Europe, and northern Asia — found from Labrador and Maine across Canada to Alaska, and from Ireland and Scotland east through Scandinavia and Russia. The small, lance-shaped, blue-green leaves are intensely aromatic when crushed — a warm, sweet, resinous, herbal fragrance combining elements of bay, eucalyptus, and spice — that has been exploited for culinary and brewing purposes for thousands of years. Before hops (Humulus lupulus) became the universal bittering agent in European beer in the late Middle Ages, bog myrtle (along with other herbs in the 'gruit' mixture) was the primary flavoring of European ale — recorded in historical documents as far back as the 5th century CE. Gruit ale is currently experiencing a major revival in craft brewing, with bog myrtle used in traditional Scottish, Scandinavian, and craft brewery gruit beers. The leaves are also used to flavor Scandinavian aquavit, Scottish whisky cocktails, and gin botanicals. The plant naturally spreads by rhizomes in wet soils and fixes nitrogen through Frankia bacterial symbiosis. A unique and historically significant herb plant for pond edges and bog gardens in zone 1–6.

plant_note: Root semi-ripe cuttings taken in late summer and set young plants out in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, sheltered from hard freezes.
directions: Boldo is a slow-growing, aromatic evergreen shrub native to the Mediterranean-climate scrublands of central Chile, where its thick, leathery, sandpapery leaves release a strong camphor-eucalyptus fragrance when crushed. Propagate from semi-ripe cuttings taken in late summer, since seed is slow and erratic to germinate, and set young plants in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade with protection from hard freezes. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well but need winter protection or container culture outside zone 9, and in the ground it takes several years to reach a size worth harvesting. The dried leaves, rich in the alkaloid boldine, are steeped as a traditional after-meal digestive tea throughout Chile and are also used to flavor some South American liqueurs.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Bolivian coriander is a fast-growing, strongly scented South American herb with an aroma and flavor combining cilantro, rue, and black pepper — it is used fresh as a cilantro substitute in Bolivian, Peruvian, and southern Mexican cuisine, especially in salsas and ceviches.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest tender young leaves frequently. Porophyllum ruderale (Bolivian coriander or quilquiña) is a fast-growing, erect annual herb from South America in the daisy family (Asteraceae) — notable for the distinctive oil glands visible as dark dots on the leaves when held to light. The leaves have an intensely aromatic flavor that is often described as combining cilantro (coriander) with rue and black pepper — pungent, citrus-herbal, with a slightly sharp, medicinal undertone. In Bolivia, the herb is called 'quilquiña' and is used fresh (never cooked — heat destroys the volatile oils) as a condiment for salteñas, silpancho, and sauces; in Peru and Colombia it is called 'papalo quelite' and used in ceviches, guacamole, and fresh salsas.
