The herb is especially valued in regions where cilantro bolts rapidly in summer heat — Porophyllum is more heat-tolerant and continues producing leaves through summer when cilantro fails. A closely related species, P. macrocephalum (also called papalo), is grown in Mexico and the southwestern US. The leaves must be used fresh and sparingly — the flavor is roughly 4-5 times more intense than cilantro.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date; borage dislikes root disturbance and self-seeds freely.
directions: Sow seeds 1/2 in deep directly in their permanent position; borage has a taproot that is easily damaged and transplants poorly. Grow in full sun in any well-drained soil—even poor, dry soil suits it. Once established it self-seeds readily, so remove unwanted seedlings while they are small. The star-shaped blue flowers are edible with a cool cucumber flavor; harvest them when newly opened for garnishing salads and drinks.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring into sandy, well-drained, slightly saline-tolerant soil in partial shade to full sun; boufu grows naturally on Japanese and Okinawan coastal dunes and bluffs and tolerates poor, sandy soil and salt spray better than most culinary herbs.
directions: Direct sow into sandy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; boufu is a coastal Japanese and Okinawan perennial in the carrot family, grown for its tender young shoots and finely divided, aromatic leaves, which are harvested in spring and used in Okinawan cooking much like a cross between celery and parsley — lightly blanched, added to tempura, or used fresh in salads. It forms a low mound of blue-green, feathery foliage and produces flat clusters of small white flowers on taller stalks if allowed to bolt in its second year. In its native coastal habitat it tolerates sandy soil, salt spray, and part shade from adjacent dune vegetation, making it a good choice for a lean, well-drained herb bed that doesn't stay wet. Harvest young leaves and shoots regularly to keep the plant productive and delay flowering, which coarsens the texture.

plant_note: Direct sow where it is to grow, since dill resents transplanting.
directions: Direct sow seed where the plants are to grow, since dill has a taproot and resents being transplanted; make succession sowings for a steady supply. This variety is especially good for pickling thanks to its early, abundant seed heads, while the aromatic foliage is delicious on potatoes, fish, and vegetables. Let some plants flower to attract pollinators and support swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, for which dill is an important host plant.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Boxwood basil forms a dense, rounded, globe-shaped mound reminiscent of a small clipped boxwood shrub, useful as an edible edging or container plant.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Boxwood basil forms an unusually dense, tightly rounded mound of small, aromatic leaves that closely mimics the look of a miniature clipped boxwood shrub, making it a favorite for formal-looking edible edging, knot gardens, and containers where a tidy, structural basil is wanted alongside its classic sweet basil flavor. Its slow-to-bolt, compact habit needs little shaping beyond occasional light trimming to keep the globe form neat, and regular harvesting for the kitchen doubles as maintenance pruning. Keep soil evenly moist and pick leaves regularly through the season to encourage continued dense, bushy growth.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, or propagate by division or cuttings. Broad-leaf thyme is more cold-hardy and more tolerant of clay soils than common thyme (T. vulgaris). Shear lightly after flowering to keep plants compact and promote fresh growth.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; broad-leaf thyme is a more robust and cold-hardy thyme species than the common culinary thyme (Thymus vulgaris), producing larger, broader, oval leaves with a strong, sweet thyme fragrance and flavor used interchangeably with common thyme in cooking. Native to limestone hills and rocky grasslands of central and western Europe, it forms a semi-shrubby, spreading mound of woody stems with soft, gray-green to dark-green, aromatic leaves and clusters of pink-purple flowers in summer that are magnets for bees — particularly bumblebees and honeybees. The culinary quality of the leaves is excellent and often considered superior to common thyme in flavor intensity. It is more tolerant of heavier soils and colder winters than Thymus vulgaris, making it a better choice for gardens in zones 4–5 where common thyme may winterkill. Several cultivars exist including 'Foxley' (silver-variegated), 'Kurt' (very compact), and 'Oregano-Scented' (with marjoram-like notes).

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; broad-leaved bulbine is more cold-tolerant and larger than the commonly grown orange-flowered B. frutescens. The gel from the fresh leaves is used in South African traditional medicine similarly to aloe vera — for burns, skin irritation, and minor wounds. The leaves are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; broad-leaved bulbine is a larger South African species than the orange-flowered B. frutescens — producing broader, more succulent, aloe-like strap leaves in rosettes and in spring through summer, tall, branching scapes of small, yellow, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers with distinctive, fluffy, bearded yellow stamens that give each individual flower a charming, hairy-bearded appearance. The multiple scapes on an established clump produce a fine, airy cloud of small yellow flowers over the striking succulent foliage for an extended period. In South African traditional medicine, the clear, viscous gel from the leaves is used topically for burns, itching, and skin irritations, similarly to aloe vera but with a more watery, less viscous consistency. As a garden plant it is a low-maintenance, drought-tolerant succulent perennial for hot, dry, sunny positions, combining well with other South African succulent plants — kniphofia, bulbinella, agapanthus, and ornamental grasses — in water-wise subtropical plantings.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost or plant nursery transplants in spring; broad-leaved thyme is the most aromatic of the European thymes, with larger leaves than common thyme that hold their flavor better when dried, and a sprawling habit that makes it excellent for paths and edges.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after last frost in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; thyme is intolerant of wet, heavy soils and will rot quickly in poorly drained ground. Thymus pulegioides is the broad-leaved thyme of European meadows and hedgerows, producing larger, broader leaves than common thyme (T. vulgaris) with a pungent, highly aromatic thymol fragrance that is considered by many herb growers to be the most intensely flavored thyme species for cooking; the broader leaves also dry and crumble more easily than narrow-leaved types. The sprawling, somewhat woody stems root where they touch the soil, making it an effective aromatic path-side groundcover, and the pink to lilac flowers in summer are heavily visited by bees. Harvest before full bloom for the most concentrated flavor; cut stems back by half after flowering to keep plants compact.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out; a hardy perennial in most zones.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant seedlings into full sun and well-drained soil, spacing them 18 to 24 inches apart. This drought-tolerant, hardy perennial has bold, assertive, savory flavor valued for seasoning rich foods like pork, poultry, and cheese, plus stuffing, soups, and stews. It also bears edible purple-blue flowers that draw pollinators; cut plants back in spring to keep them bushy and productive year after year.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date; fennel dislikes transplanting.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in their final position; bronze fennel resents root disturbance and transplants poorly. Grow in full sun with well-drained, fertile soil and deadhead spent flower heads to limit self-seeding, which can become excessive. Plant away from dill, coriander, and most vegetables as fennel is allelopathic to many garden neighbors. Harvest the feathery bronze fronds as needed; flavor is best before flowering.

common_name: Browne's Savory (Swamp Savory, Florida Pennyroyal, Creeping Savory)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, well-drained to seasonally flooded soil; Clinopodium brownei is a native wetland and moist-habitat herb that thrives at pond margins, in rain gardens, and in moist Florida/Gulf Coast garden beds where many other herbs would drown. In zone 9, it grows as a reliable perennial in moist areas, spreading by stolons. The aromatic foliage has a pleasant pennyroyal/savory fragrance when crushed. Excellent groundcover for consistently moist to seasonally wet areas. Attractive to bees and pollinators. Native plant of high ecological value.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist to wet soil — Browne's Savory is uniquely among aromatic herbs in tolerating and preferring consistently moist, even seasonally wet, conditions that would rot most culinary herbs. Clinopodium brownei is a low-growing, mat-forming, rhizomatous aromatic herb native to the coastal plain of the southeastern United States (peninsular Florida north through coastal Georgia), the Caribbean islands, Mexico, and Central and South America in the Lamiaceae (mint family). The plant grows as a trailing, spreading groundcover with small, oval to round, bright-green, somewhat succulent leaves that, when brushed or crushed, release a pleasant, distinctly pennyroyal-like to savory-like aroma — a clean, slightly minty, herbal fragrance that makes Browne's Savory attractive as a groundcover in garden areas where foot traffic will release the scent. Tiny, pale lavender to white, two-lipped flowers are produced in clusters throughout the warm months, attractive to native bees and small pollinators. The plant spreads by stolons (horizontal runners) to form a low, dense, aromatic groundcover over moist soil areas. Browne's Savory is a native Florida plant of high ecological value — it serves as a larval host plant for the Florida-native hairy-footed flower bee and supports numerous native pollinator species. Excellent for rain gardens, pond margins, and consistently moist landscape areas in zone 8-11 where a fragrant, low-growing native groundcover is needed.

common_name: Brussels Winter Chervil (Cold-Hardy Heirloom Anise Herb)
plant_note: Direct-sow Brussels Winter chervil seed shallowly into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in late summer or early fall, since this old cold-hardy strain thrives on a fall-to-spring schedule and resents the heat that makes most chervil bolt.
directions: Direct-sow Brussels Winter chervil seed shallowly into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in late summer or early fall, since this old cold-hardy strain thrives on a fall-to-spring schedule and resents the heat that makes most chervil bolt. Give it a partly shaded spot with dappled light, where its fern-like foliage stays tender and productive right through cold snaps that would finish off less hardy sowings. The leaves carry chervil's signature mild anise-parsley flavor, best used fresh and added at the end of cooking to season eggs, soups, and delicate sauces. Because it holds quality in cold, shaded conditions better than standard chervil, Brussels Winter is a reliable way to keep a fresh culinary herb coming from a shady bed through the off-season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; buchu requires excellent drainage and lean conditions — it is native to the sandy, peaty fynbos soils of the Western Cape mountains. Avoid heavy clay or overly rich soils. The strongly aromatic leaves (dried and fresh) have been used in South African traditional medicine for centuries and are the source of a commercial herbal supplement with urinary and anti-inflammatory properties.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; buchu is one of the most important medicinal plants of the South African Cape fynbos and one of the few Cape plants to have achieved significant international commercial significance as a herbal supplement. The small, oval, dark-green leaves are powerfully aromatic — the fresh or dried leaf releasing a strong, distinctive, somewhat blackcurrant-minty-spicy scent from oil glands visible as transparent dots in the leaf surface. In traditional San and Khoikhoi medicine, and later in European colonial medicine, buchu was used primarily for urinary tract and kidney complaints, and dried buchu leaf extract is still sold today as a supplement for urinary health and anti-inflammatory purposes. As a garden plant it is a neat, bushy, heather-textured small shrub of the fynbos type — small, oval, aromatic leaves on fine stems — that produces in spring small, white, five-petaled flowers in moderate quantity. The aromatic foliage is the primary ornamental and practical value. Excellent for a dedicated medicinal herb garden or Cape fynbos planting in zones 8–11 where its drainage and lean-soil requirements are met.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; buckler-leaf sorrel is one of the first perennial herbs to produce harvestable leaves in spring.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained soil with moderate fertility; thin to 12 in apart once seedlings reach 2 in. Buckler-leaf sorrel has small, shield-shaped silvery-green leaves with a clean, bright lemon-acid flavor that is preferred over common sorrel in French cuisine for sorrel soup and sauces. Remove flowering stalks as they appear to redirect energy into leaf production; divide clumps every 2–3 years to maintain vigor. Harvest the small leaves regularly while they are fresh and tender, as flavor intensifies in older foliage to the point of bitterness.

plant_note: Cold-stratify or scarify seed and direct sow in early spring into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; germination is slow and uneven, so sow generously.
directions: Bupleurum chinense is an upright, clump-forming perennial in the carrot family grown in traditional Chinese medicine gardens for its slender taproot, known as chai hu, one of the most frequently prescribed herbs in Chinese herbal formulas. Direct sow scarified or cold-stratified seed in early spring into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; germination is slow and uneven, so overseed generously and be patient. The narrow, willow-like leaves and small yellow umbel flowers resemble a fine-textured fennel or dill and make an attractive, airy addition to an herb border while the root develops below ground. Roots are traditionally left undisturbed for two to three growing seasons before being dug in autumn, cleaned, and dried for use in tea and decoction.

plant_note: Direct sow into deep, loose soil after the last frost; the long taproot resists transplanting.
directions: Burdock, also called gobo, is a vigorous biennial grown for its long, slender edible roots and traditional herbal uses. Sow directly in deep, loose, stone-free soil so the roots can grow straight and long. Harvest the tender first-year roots in fall before they turn woody in the second year. Keep the bed weeded and evenly watered to encourage crisp, mild-flavored roots.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown stock in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; bush tea establishes slowly and benefits from grassland-edge conditions with good air movement.
directions: Athrixia phylicoides is a wiry, heath-like shrub of South African grassland margins and forest fringes, long harvested by Zulu and other southern African communities for its narrow, resinous, silver-backed leaves, which are dried and steeped into a mild, reddish, slightly astringent herbal tea traditionally valued for soothing coughs and settling digestion. Clusters of small, daisy-like, mauve-pink flowers with yellow centers appear from late summer into autumn, giving the plant ornamental interest beyond its use as a tea herb. It responds well to light, regular tipping to keep growth dense and to encourage the fine new leaf growth preferred for harvest. Give it open, airy placement rather than dense shade, since crowding encourages dieback in humid climates.

common_name: Bushy Lippia (White Lippia, Lemon Verbena Relative)
plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; Lippia alba is a South American and Caribbean aromatic shrub with lemon-mint to spearmint scented leaves — it is one of the most widely used medicinal herbs in Brazil (cidreira) and throughout Latin America, used as a calming tea for anxiety, insomnia, and digestive upset.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established. Lippia alba (bushy lippia or cidreira in Brazil) is a sprawling, aromatic, semi-woody perennial shrub from South America and the Caribbean, native from Mexico south to Argentina, that has become one of the most widely used and important medicinal herb teas throughout Latin America. The leaves have a pleasant, complex aroma ranging from lemon-mint to spearmint-citrus to slightly camphor-herbaceous depending on the chemotype (several distinct essential oil chemotypes exist: carvone-type, linalool-type, and citral-type, each with different scent profiles). In Brazil, where it is called 'erva-cidreira' or 'falsa melissa,' it is the most popular folk remedy for anxiety, nervous tension, insomnia, and digestive upset — sold fresh in markets and as a prepared tea in pharmacies. Throughout South and Central America, the leaves are used as a flavoring herb for desserts, drinks, and savory dishes. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, Lippia alba is ornamental, drought-tolerant, and virtually pest-free. The small, pale-lavender to white flowers attract pollinators. It is distinct from lemon verbena (Aloysia citrodora, formerly Lippia citriodora) but closely related and in the same family (Verbenaceae).

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or divide established plants in spring; transplant after frost danger has passed.
directions: Surface-sow seeds on well-drained seed-starting mix and lightly press in; germination is steady within two to three weeks in warm conditions. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; calamint thrives in rocky or gravelly sites and is highly drought-tolerant once established. The small, aromatic leaves have a flavor that blends pennyroyal-mint with oregano, making it a traditional Italian seasoning for mushrooms and bean dishes. Cut back by half after the first flush of lavender flowers in midsummer to encourage a second bloom and fresh, tender growth for harvesting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; calamint is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and thrives in conditions that challenge most herbs.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; calamint (nepitella) is a Mediterranean and European herb with small, rounded, intensely minty-oregano-scented leaves and a sustained cloud of tiny, lavender-blue to white tubular flowers from midsummer through frost that attract bees in extraordinary numbers — few plants are visited more intensely or continuously by native bees at peak bloom. The plant forms a neat, mounding, drought-resistant groundcover that is virtually pest-free. Used in Italian cooking as a substitute for mint in pasta and bean dishes (the leaves are more savory and less sweet than true mint). Self-sows moderately in suitable conditions. Excellent for edging, rock gardens, and sunny herb borders. 'Blue Cloud' (compact, intense blue) is a widely grown cultivar.

plant_note: Resents transplanting; sow in place.
directions: Direct-sow in early spring onto lean, sandy soil, as the taproot dislikes disturbance and transplanting. The whole plant is used in traditional herbalism as a mild sedative and sleep aid. Give it full sun and minimal water, since rich, moist ground produces weak, floppy growth. Thin seedlings to prevent crowding and let some flowers set seed for reliable self-sowing. Harvest the aerial parts when in bloom and dry them for tea or tincture.

common_name: Calypso Cilantro (F1 Hybrid Bolt-Resistant Cilantro with Extended Leaf Production Season)
plant_note: Direct sow only; cilantro does not transplant well. Calypso is the most bolt-resistant of the modern F1 hybrid cilantro varieties, extending leaf production significantly beyond what open-pollinated slow-bolt varieties can achieve. In zone 9, plant October–November for fall-winter production or February–March for spring. Calypso's extended bolt resistance means it can continue producing harvestable leaves even as temperatures climb into the 70s and low 80s°F — conditions that trigger bolting in standard varieties within days to weeks. For zone 9 spring production, Calypso provides the longest productive harvest window of any commonly available cilantro variety. The trade-off of F1 hybrid status is that saved seed will not reproduce Calypso's characteristics reliably — gardeners must purchase fresh seed each season. Calypso was developed by Johnny's Selected Seeds.
directions: Direct sow in cool soil; thin to 6 inches. Harvest outer leaves continuously; Calypso's extended bolt resistance allows repeated harvests well into warming spring weather. Calypso is an F1 hybrid cilantro variety developed and released by Johnny's Selected Seeds, the Maine-based seed company known for developing and trialing specialty vegetable varieties for commercial and home garden use. The variety represents the current apex of bolt-resistance breeding in cilantro — the characteristic that most limits cilantro's usefulness in spring and fall gardens, where temperatures inevitably warm and trigger the plant's transition from vegetative leaf production to reproductive flowering and seed set. In university and industry trials comparing cilantro varieties for bolt resistance, Calypso consistently produces the most leaf material and maintains quality leaf production the longest under warming conditions. The mechanism of Calypso's extended bolt resistance involves both the genetic selection for delayed photoperiod and temperature sensitivity in triggering the flowering response, and the F1 hybrid vigor that produces more robust vegetative growth generally. Calypso plants are somewhat taller and more vigorous than many open-pollinated varieties, producing more leaf material per plant in addition to bolting more slowly. The flavor is standard cilantro — the same characteristic aromatic profile from the volatile oils common to all Coriandrum sativum — with no meaningful flavor difference from other cilantro varieties. For zone 9 spring gardens where the cilantro harvest window is compressed by rapid warming, Calypso is the most productive choice among commonly available varieties; in the fall-winter planting season (October–March in zone 9), when temperatures are consistently cool, the bolt-resistance advantage is less important and open-pollinated varieties perform nearly as well.

common_name: Camphor Basil (African Basil, East African Basil)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; camphor basil is a fast-growing, shrubby tropical basil that becomes woody at the base in warm climates. In zone 9–10 it may perennialize, but most gardeners treat it as an annual.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; camphor basil is a species from East Africa (particularly the slopes of Kilimanjaro, as the name suggests) with a strong, sharp, camphor-eucalyptus fragrance unlike any other basil. The essential oil is composed primarily of camphor and 1,8-cineole rather than the linalool or estragole that characterize most familiar culinary basils. In East Africa, the plant is used medicinally for respiratory conditions (inhaling the vapors), as an insect repellent, and as a flavoring ingredient in certain traditional foods. It has been used as a parent in breeding disease-resistant basil hybrids, contributing resistance to Fusarium wilt. A larger, woodier, more shrubby plant than culinary sweet basil, it makes an impressive ornamental with a strong fragrance when brushed. Bees and butterflies are attracted to the white flower spikes.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds or container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; camphor tree is an extremely vigorous, large evergreen tree that can reach 50–100 feet. Consider size carefully before planting — it becomes a major landscape tree. It is invasive in Florida.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; camphor tree is a majestic, aromatic evergreen tree from China and Japan, the source of natural camphor extracted from the wood and leaves. Every part of the tree contains camphor and 1,8-cineole, giving the foliage a powerful medicinal scent when crushed. It is an important timber, medicinal, and aromatic tree in traditional Asian culture. In the American South (particularly Texas and California), it is a common large shade tree planted for its ornamental value and fragrant foliage. NOTE: Camphor tree is classified as invasive in Florida and should not be planted there; it is suitable for other Gulf Coast states. The berries are consumed by birds but the plant as a whole is toxic to humans. Provides exceptional shade and is remarkably drought tolerant once established.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring, surface-sown since seed needs light to germinate, in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Canada wild lettuce self-sows readily, so allow it room to naturalize or deadhead before seed matures if volunteers are unwanted.
directions: Direct sow in spring, surface-sown since seed needs light to germinate, in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Canada wild lettuce self-sows readily, so allow it room to naturalize or deadhead before seed matures if volunteers are unwanted. Lactuca canadensis is a tall, biennial-to-short-lived-perennial North American native related to cultivated lettuce, forming a basal rosette of deeply lobed leaves the first year and a towering flowering stalk topped with numerous small, pale yellow, dandelion-like flowers in late summer that draw bees, small butterflies, and seed-eating songbirds. Young spring leaves are edible and were traditionally eaten like garden lettuce, though they turn increasingly bitter as the plant matures and bolts toward flowering. It tolerates partial shade and a wide range of soils, making it a low-maintenance native for a woodland edge, pollinator meadow, or informal naturalized planting, though its height and reseeding habit suit an informal setting better than a tidy border.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after cold stratification; or cold stratify seeds 60 days and sow indoors in late winter. Canadian burnet prefers moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade or at moist meadow edges.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Canadian burnet is a magnificent tall native of wet meadows and moist openings, producing elegant, pinnate compound leaves and distinctive bottlebrush flower heads — pure white 'poker' shapes on tall, airy stems — in late summer and fall. The flowers are among the most important late-season pollen sources for native bees, attracting sweat bees, bumblebees, and specialist pollen foragers to their elongated catkin-like heads. In the garden, Canadian burnet provides distinctive architectural interest when paired with tall ornamental grasses and late asters in moist borders or rain gardens. Unlike European sanguisorbas often found in nurseries, this native species naturally colonizes moist, shaded bottomlands and moist meadow edges throughout eastern North America.

plant_note: Scarify hard seed coat and soak overnight before sowing into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; cancer bush germinates readily once scarified and grows quickly into a flowering shrub in its first season.
directions: Lessertia frutescens (long known as Sutherlandia frutescens) is a fast-growing, silver-grey-leaved legume shrub from the dry interior of South Africa, prized in Khoisan and Cape traditional medicine as a general tonic and immune-supporting herb; the dried leaf is still sold today as a popular southern African herbal supplement. Showy, brilliant orange-red, pea-shaped flowers appear over a long season and are followed by distinctive, inflated, papery, balloon-like seed pods that give the plant strong ornamental appeal beyond its medicinal use. It is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the same lean, sharply drained conditions favored by most Cape fynbos and Karoo herbs. Prune lightly after flowering to keep growth compact, and expect a relatively short-lived shrub of three to five years that is easily renewed from fresh seed.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds after last frost in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in zone 9–12, or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier; Candle Bush (Ringworm Cassia) is a large, fast-growing, pantropical medicinal shrub bearing spectacular, upright, candle-like flower buds of tightly enclosed golden-yellow blooms arranged in bold spikes — the individual flowers remaining wrapped in copper-toned bracts that peel back from the base upward as the plant blooms, creating a glowing effect — and widely used in traditional medicine across the tropics for treating skin fungal infections.
directions: Direct sow Senna alata seeds (scarify or nick seed coat before sowing to improve germination) in full sun in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; plants grow very rapidly in warm conditions and can reach 4–8 feet in a single season; deadhead spent spikes to prolong blooming and cut back hard in late winter to prevent woodiness. Candle Bush is one of the most dramatic flowering shrubs of the tropics and subtropics — its upright, glowing flower spikes are truly candle-like before the bright-yellow, butterfly-shaped individual flowers open, giving the plant an almost magical quality in the garden. It is a pan-tropical species now naturalized throughout the tropics worldwide, spread from its likely South American origin. In traditional medicine across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, a leaf paste or extract is applied topically to treat ringworm, athlete's foot, and other fungal skin infections — giving rise to the common name 'Ringworm Bush'; the antifungal compound chrysophanol has been isolated from the leaves. The plant is also an important butterfly host plant, particularly for sulphur butterflies (Catopsilia spp.) whose caterpillars feed on the leaves. In zone 9, it self-sows readily and may re-establish from seed each year after frost kills the tops; in zone 10–12, it grows as a woody perennial shrub.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth; transplant out after frost as a tender plant.
directions: Start seed indoors with warmth and transplant the bushy plants out only after the danger of frost has passed. Stevia, also called sweetleaf, produces leaves up to 300 times sweeter than sugar, giving a calorie-free, low-glycemic sweetener with a faint anise aftertaste. Grow it in full sun and pinch the tips to encourage branching; harvest leaves before flowering for peak sweetness and dry them for storage, or overwinter potted plants indoors in cold climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Cape aloe develops a single, upright trunk over many years and is slower-growing than aloe arborescens. It is more cold-tolerant than most trunk-forming aloes and tolerates brief dips to 25°F. It is a major commercial crop in South Africa for the cosmetics and natural medicine industries.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Cape aloe is a magnificent large aloe from South Africa that develops a single upright trunk over time, crowned by a rosette of large, glaucous, spiny-toothed leaves that may develop reddish or copper tints in strong sun. It produces tall (4–5 foot) candelabra-like flower spikes in winter and spring bearing dense clusters of orange-red to orange tubular flowers that attract sunbirds in South Africa and hummingbirds in cultivation. The plant is one of the primary sources of commercial aloe latex (used in laxative preparations and cosmetics) — distinct from aloe gel — produced as a dark, bitter exudate from the cut leaves. The botanical name 'ferox' (meaning fierce) refers to the prominent spines on the leaf margins and surfaces, which are more numerous than in aloe vera. As a landscape plant it is outstanding for large, bold, architectural effect in zone 8–11 gardens, developing impressive specimens over decades. The commercial production of Aloe ferox bitter is centered in the Eastern Cape of South Africa.

common_name: Cape Snow Bush (African Rosemary, Wild Rosemary)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; Cape snow bush is a South African fynbos shrub with needle-like, intensely aromatic leaves used as a rosemary substitute in cooking and as a traditional Cape Malay spice — it is more drought and heat-tolerant than European rosemary and thrives in hot, dry, calcareous soils.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; prune after flowering to maintain compact shape. Eriocephalus africanus (Cape snow bush or African rosemary) is a native South African fynbos shrub with needle-like, silver-grey, intensely aromatic leaves — the leaves have a fresh, camphor-pine aroma similar to rosemary but with distinctly South African floral-herbal notes. The plant is used in Cape Malay traditional cooking and South African herbal medicine as a seasoning and medicinal herb: the dried leaves flavor lamb stews, braai (barbecue) marinades, and herbal teas; the essential oil is used in aromatherapy for respiratory conditions. Common name 'Cape snow bush' derives from the small, fluffy, white seed heads that cover the plant in late summer, giving a snow-dusted appearance. As a landscape plant, Eriocephalus africanus is outstanding for hot, dry, lean, well-drained soils where European rosemary often struggles with root rot — it has superior drought tolerance and performance in alkaline coastal soils. The cultivar 'Silver Beads' is grown as an ornamental for its exceptionally silvery foliage. An excellent substitute for rosemary in challenging dry garden conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to sandy, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; caper bush is a Mediterranean cliff-dwelling plant that rots in rich, moist, or poorly drained soil and thrives on neglect once established.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to sandy, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; caper bush is a Mediterranean cliff-dwelling plant that rots in rich, moist, or poorly drained soil and thrives on neglect once established. Sprawling, spiny stems carry rounded, fleshy, blue-green leaves and large, showy, white-to-pink flowers with a prominent burst of long purple stamens, opening for just a single day each but produced continuously through the hot summer months. The edible product is the unopened flower bud, hand-picked daily at pea size and brine- or salt-cured into the tangy, briny capers used in Mediterranean cooking; unpicked buds open into flowers and later develop into a caper-berry fruit that can also be pickled. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established, it is well suited to a rock wall, dry slope, or container where poor soil and reflected heat are assets rather than liabilities, and it dies back to the root in hard freezes, resprouting the following spring in marginal zones.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (August–September in zone 9) for overwintering as a small rosette and bolting and seeding the following spring; caraway is a biennial (or winter annual in mild climates) that requires cool temperatures to flower and set seed — in zone 9, it can be grown as a cool-season annual by fall-sowing for early spring seed harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; caraway does not transplant well — sow in place. Carum carvi (caraway) is a biennial or short-lived annual herb producing the anise-flavored, ribbed, crescent-shaped seeds indispensable in German and Central European rye bread, sauerkraut, cheese (Havarti caraway), and liqueurs (aquavit, Kümmel); the seeds are also a traditional flavoring for sausages, pickles, and roasted vegetables across northern and eastern European cuisines. The fresh leaves and roots are also edible (roots somewhat parsnip-like) and used in Scandinavian and German cooking. In the first year, caraway forms a low rosette of finely divided, feathery, carrot-like leaves; in the second year (or the same spring after fall sowing in mild climates), it sends up 1.5-to-2-foot stems topped with compound white flower umbels, setting seed in May–June. Harvest seed heads when they turn brown and before they shatter; thresh out seeds and dry fully before storing. In zone 9, treat as a fall-sown winter annual for best results.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions and cuttings in spring; caraway thyme spreads by layering where stems contact soil, forming a dense weed-suppressing mat in time.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean soil — excellent in rock gardens, paving cracks, and dry stone walls where other thymes excel; caraway thyme gets its distinctive name from the strong caraway-like aroma of its leaves, which contain carvone (the same compound that gives caraway seed its character), producing an anise-caraway fragrance quite unlike common thyme. This low-growing prostrate thyme from the mountains of Sardinia and Corsica forms a tight mat of tiny dark green leaves covered in small pink to pale lavender flowers in summer that are excellent for bees and other pollinators. Use fresh or dried in the same applications as caraway seed: potato dishes, sauerkraut, braised meats, and bread.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial to full shade; cardamom requires consistently moist soil and high humidity — it is not suited to dry climates or exposed windy sites. In zone 10–11 only.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade — cardamom naturally grows as an understory plant in the humid rainforests of southern India and is one of the world's most valuable spices after vanilla and saffron. The large, aromatic leaves are beautiful throughout the growing season; fragrant flowers are produced on separate ground-level stems and develop into the prized seed pods. Cardamom is only reliably hardy in zone 10–12 but makes an outstanding container plant in zone 8–9 that overwinters indoors. It requires high humidity, consistent moisture, and shade from afternoon sun — an excellent fit for the shaded, humid conditions of South Florida and the Gulf Coast. Harvest pods when they are pale green before they open.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out after frost, or direct sow in warm soil.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant out after all danger of frost, or direct sow once the soil is warm, spacing plants about a foot apart. This dual-purpose basil combines robust culinary flavor with large, richly colored maroon flower heads that make it a striking accent in mixed containers and bouquets. Pinch the plants often to keep them bushy; its strong aroma means a little goes a long way in cooking, and it can be grown indoors on a sunny sill.

common_name: Cascade Hops (Iconic Citrus-Floral American Aroma Hop)
plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cascade climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Cascade, released by Oregon State University in 1972, is the single most influential American hop cultivar, prized for its distinctive grapefruit-citrus and floral aroma that came to define the American craft beer movement and remains the signature hop of classic West Coast pale ales and IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; soft green cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and slightly sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Performs best in cool-summer climates with long day length; struggles with the persistent heat and humidity of zone 8-9 Gulf South summers, so give it the coolest, best-ventilated site available and expect reduced cone yield compared with Pacific Northwest production.

plant_note: Transplant dormant bare-root or potted stock in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in the dappled shade of an understory site.
directions: WARNING: bark must be harvested only from mature (8+ year old) trees and aged at least a year before use — fresh, unaged bark causes severe cramping and should never be used directly off the tree, and long-term laxative use is discouraged due to dependency and electrolyte loss risk. Transplant dormant bare-root or potted stock in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in the dappled shade of an understory site, mimicking its native Pacific Northwest forest habitat. This slow-growing native tree is the traditional source of cascara bark, a classic stimulant laxative once aged properly.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes in spring around the last frost date in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a tall trellis or pole for the vigorous bines to climb; Cashmere is a Washington State University release descended from Cascade, bred for a similar aroma profile with higher yields.
directions: Plant rhizomes in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy 12-20 foot trellis, pole, or string for the twining bines to climb; Cashmere was released by Washington State University's hop breeding program as a descendant of Cascade, developed to offer a similar mild, floral-citrus aroma profile with improved yield and a more manageable, less vigorous growth habit than its parent. Cones are used mainly for aroma and flavor additions in craft brewing, contributing notes of citrus, melon, and mild spice. Hops are perennial bines that die back to the crown each winter and regrow vigorously each spring, needing several years to reach full production. Water consistently during the growing season, especially as cones develop in mid-to-late summer, and harvest when cones feel dry and papery and release a strong aromatic, slightly sticky lupulin scent when rubbed. Hops generally prefer a period of winter chill and struggle with the mild winters and intense summer humidity of the Deep South, performing best in cooler, drier climates.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade in zone 8–11; Cassumunar Ginger (Plai) is a medium-sized ginger-family perennial native to Thailand, India, and Southeast Asia grown for its aromatic rhizomes with an intense green-pine-turpentine aroma — the source of plai essential oil widely used in Thai traditional massage therapy, pain-relief liniments, and deep-tissue anti-inflammatory preparations.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Zingiber montanum dies back in winter in zone 8–9 — mulch the root zone heavily after frost and the plant will re-emerge reliably from the persistent rhizome in late spring. Zingiber montanum (Cassumunar Ginger, Plai, or Bengal Root) is a medium-sized rhizomatous ginger-family perennial native to South Asia (India, Bangladesh) and Southeast Asia (Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Vietnam, Indonesia), where its aromatic, yellow-fleshed rhizomes are the source of one of the most important herbal medicines in Thai traditional medicine — 'Plai' or 'Phlai.' The essential oil distilled from the rhizomes is rich in terpinen-4-ol and sabinene, giving it strong anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antispasmodic properties extensively documented in Thai traditional medicine for joint pain, sprains, bruises, and postpartum care. Plai oil is a standard ingredient in Thai massage therapy liniments and is now internationally distributed as a sports and pain-relief product. The plant is ornamentally neat — compact, clumping, with attractive narrow lanceolate leaves — and the aromatic rhizomes are easy to harvest by simply digging, taking what is needed, and replanting the remainder. An outstanding and under-grown medicinal spice for warm-climate herb gardens in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Root cuttings in spring or start from seed; prefers dry, alkaline, rocky, poor soil with excellent drainage — perfect drainage is essential as cat thyme rots quickly in wet conditions; a classic Mediterranean rock garden plant.
directions: Propagate from stem cuttings or sow seeds in well-drained, poor, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cat thyme is a compact, woody Mediterranean subshrub (despite the name, not a true thyme) with small, oval, intensely aromatic leaves and small pink-purple flowers that attract bees; the plants have a strong, pungent, resinous, slightly camphor-like scent distinct from culinary thyme. As its common name suggests, it attracts cats intensely, similar to catnip but stronger in effect — cats will roll on the plants and sometimes destroy them, so caging or placing them in pots on high shelves is advisable in gardens with cats. Used in traditional herbal medicine and as a garden plant for rocky banks, walls, and Mediterranean-themed plantings. Excellent drainage is non-negotiable.

common_name: Cat's Whiskers (Java Tea, Kidney Tea Plant)
plant_note: Plant cuttings or transplants after all frost danger passes in warm (65°F+) soil in partial shade; in zone 9–11 cat's whiskers is a perennial that thrives in the humid summer conditions and partial shade where many herbs struggle. Easily propagated from tip cuttings rooted in moist potting mix.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; cat's whiskers is one of the most striking tropical herbs for zone 9–11 shade gardens, producing distinctive white or lavender flower spikes with extraordinarily long stamens that project like cat's whiskers beyond the petals — an unusual, eye-catching floral structure that attracts bees and butterflies. The plant is widely cultivated throughout Southeast Asia as a medicinal herb — Orthosiphon leaves are dried to make Java tea, a traditional remedy for kidney and urinary tract conditions. In the Gulf Coast garden it is an outstanding tender perennial for partial shade where it blooms almost continuously from late spring through frost in frost-free climates. The fresh or dried leaves make a mild, pleasant-tasting herbal infusion. Harvest leaves and young stems by pinching before they flower to encourage bushy growth and maximize leaf yield. Propagate easily from tip cuttings placed in moist soil in a warm, humid location. In zone 9 it dies back to the roots in frost but recovers vigorously in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; catnip is very easy from seed and will self-sow prolifically unless deadheaded, naturalizing readily in garden edges and roadsides.
directions: Nepeta cataria is a bushy, square-stemmed perennial in the mint family with distinctive soft, gray-green, heart-shaped to triangular leaves with a strong, distinctive musky-minty scent, and dense spikes of small, white to pale lavender, purple-spotted flowers from June through September that are excellent bee plants; the nepetalactone compound in the foliage produces the well-known euphoric response in domestic cats, and the plant is used to stuff cat toys and promote play. As an herbal tea, catnip has mild sedative and digestive properties; it has a long history of use for insomnia, anxiety, and infant colic. Cut back hard after the first bloom flush to promote fresh growth and a second flowering.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade with strong climbing support; Cat's Claw is a large, woody tropical liana native to the Amazon and Orinoco rainforests of Peru, Brazil, and Bolivia — one of the most widely sold medicinal herbs of the Americas — whose thorned bark and root contain alkaloids with well-documented anti-inflammatory and immune-modulating properties used across the Amazon Basin for centuries.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with a large, strong support structure — trellis, pergola, or tree — for the vine to ascend; Uncaria tomentosa is a vigorous grower in tropical conditions and requires annual pruning to manage size and direct growth. Uncaria tomentosa (Cat's Claw or Uña de Gato) is a large, woody liana in the Rubiaceae (coffee) family native to the humid tropical rainforests of the Amazon Basin, particularly Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, and Ecuador, where it climbs to the forest canopy using distinctive, recurved, claw-like thorns at the leaf nodes — the feature giving it its common name. The thorned inner bark and root bark are the primary medicinal parts, containing a unique array of pentacyclic oxindole alkaloids (mitraphylline, isomitraphylline, rhynchophylline) with well-documented anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immune-modulating activities. Cat's Claw has been used for centuries by Peruvian Asháninka and other Amazonian peoples to treat arthritis, gastrointestinal inflammation, infections, and cancer — and is now one of the top-selling botanical supplements in the United States and Europe for arthritis and joint pain. Bark is harvested sustainably by removing sections of outer bark without felling the vine. In the garden, it is an ornamental, fast-growing tropical vine with attractive, paired opposite leaves and small, tubular, white flowers.

common_name: Centennial Hops (Super Cascade, Balanced Citrus-Floral Hop)
plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Centennial climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Centennial is a Washington State-bred hop, often nicknamed 'Super Cascade' for its higher alpha acid content and similar but more intense citrus and floral aroma compared with Cascade, making it a versatile dual-purpose hop used for both bittering and aroma in American pale ales and IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin resin, then dried promptly. Like other Humulus lupulus cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect a smaller harvest than in traditional hop-growing regions.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet soil in partial to full shade, ideally inside a buried barrier or large container; Chameleon plant spreads aggressively by rhizome and can quickly overrun a bed if planted directly in the ground without containment.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet soil in partial to full shade, ideally inside a buried barrier or large container; Chameleon plant spreads aggressively by rhizome and can quickly overrun a bed if planted directly in the ground without containment. Houttuynia cordata 'Chameleon' is a colorful variegated sport of the East Asian herb prized in Vietnamese and Chinese cooking for its citrus-and-fish-scented leaves, with heart-shaped foliage splashed in red, cream, yellow, and green and small white flower bracts in summer. The leaves are edible with the same distinctive pungent, coriander-and-citrus flavor as the plain green species and are used fresh in salads and wraps, but the cultivar is grown mainly as a striking, tough groundcover for wet shade, pond margins, and rain gardens where its color and vigor are assets rather than liabilities. Because it spreads so readily by rhizome and is difficult to fully eradicate once established, confine it firmly to containers or barrier-lined beds away from more delicate neighbors.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; light frost will not harm established seedlings.
directions: Surface-sow the tiny seeds by pressing them onto moist soil without covering; they require light to germinate. Thin seedlings to 6–9 in apart in well-drained, moderately poor soil—rich soil encourages lush stems that flop easily. German chamomile self-seeds reliably and will naturalize in a sunny spot with minimal care. Harvest flower heads just as the white petals begin to reflex downward, which indicates peak essential oil content for tea.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or allow to self-seed in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; chanca piedra is a Pantropical annual that volunteers readily in zone 9 gardens and is used throughout South America, Asia, and Africa as a traditional remedy for kidney stones and liver conditions.
directions: Direct sow in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; thin to 12 inches; harvest whole aerial plant before seeding for herbal use. Phyllanthus niruri (chanca piedra or stone breaker) is a small, unassuming tropical annual from the spurge family — widely distributed across the humid tropics of South America, Asia, and Africa — that has become one of the most studied herbal remedies for kidney stones, liver health, and hepatitis B. The common name 'chanca piedra' (Spanish: 'stone breaker') and 'shatterstone' reflect the plant's traditional Amazonian use for dissolving kidney and gallstones, a use with some clinical support in published research. The plant contains phyllanthin, hypophyllanthin, and other compounds with documented effects on calcium oxalate crystal formation (the primary component of kidney stones). As a garden plant, it is a neat, small annual with tiny, oval, alternate leaves arranged on graceful, feathery branches resembling a miniature fern — it volunteers readily in warm, moist gardens and self-seeds prolifically once established. Harvest the entire aerial plant when it begins to flower; dry for use in tea or tincture.

plant_note: Plant in fall in very well-drained, dry, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; chaparral sage grows naturally on dry slopes and chaparral edges of the southern California Coast Ranges and Santa Barbara area. Completely summer drought tolerant — do not water in summer once established; overwatering causes rapid decline.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; chaparral sage (purple sage) is a large, aromatic California native shrub of the southern Coast Ranges, producing distinctive white-woolly (leucophylla = white-leaved) leaves that reflect harsh summer sunlight and reduce water loss — an adaptation to the extreme summer heat and drought of California chaparral. The lavender-purple flowers in late spring to early summer are striking and produce abundant nectar for native bees and hummingbirds. One of the 'allelopathic' California sages — the plant releases volatile chemicals that inhibit the germination of competing plants around it, creating a distinctive bare zone between the sage canopy and the surrounding grassland. The famous 'elfin forest' scent of California chaparral comes largely from this species and coast sage (S. apiana). Essential for authentic California coastal sage scrub plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in a shaded spot; again in late summer for a fall harvest.
directions: Scatter seeds on the soil surface and press them in lightly, or cover with 1/8 in of fine soil; chervil prefers cool, partly shaded conditions and bolts quickly in heat. Direct sow rather than transplanting, as the taproot is sensitive to disturbance. Keep the soil consistently moist during germination and throughout the cool season. Harvest delicate, fern-like leaves when plants are 6–8 in tall, before any flower stalks emerge, to capture the mild anise flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; for root harvest, sow by early summer so roots mature by autumn.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in deep, well-drained soil; chicory develops a long taproot that makes it drought-tolerant once established but resists transplanting. Young leaves provide a pleasantly bitter addition to salads and are most palatable before the plant flowers; blanching the developing crown under an upturned pot for 2–3 weeks produces creamy, milder forced leaves in late winter. The thick taproot is roasted and ground as a coffee substitute or additive, harvested in the plant's second autumn. Bright blue flowers open and close with the sun daily, attracting bees through summer.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese cinnamon is hardy to about 25°F and can be grown outdoors year-round in zone 9–11. It may defoliate after hard freezes but re-sprouts from the roots.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 8b–11; Chinese cinnamon is the source of most commercial cinnamon sold in the United States — the cassia bark sold in grocery stores as 'cinnamon' is typically the bark of this or related Cinnamomum species rather than true Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum). The inner bark is harvested by stripping the outer bark from young shoots and allowing it to dry into the familiar quills. Chinese cassia has a stronger, more pungent flavor with higher coumarin content than the mild, sweet Ceylon cinnamon — a trait that limits consumption quantities but makes it the preferred spice for strongly-flavored applications. In zone 9 gardens, this attractive evergreen tree or large shrub provides handsome, dark green, three-veined leaves and an aromatic quality throughout the year. Harvest bark from branches 2–3 years old for optimal flavor concentration.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once the soil has warmed above 65 degrees F, setting them just 1-2 inches below the soil surface in a partially shaded bed or large container.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in moist, well-draining soil enriched with compost, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart in a partially shaded bed or in a large container with excellent drainage. Water regularly to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and feed monthly with a balanced liquid fertilizer during the active growing season to support lush foliage and rhizome development. The distinctive clusters of finger-like yellow rhizomes are ready to harvest when the foliage begins to yellow and die back in autumn, typically 6-10 months after planting. In cooler climates (zone 8-9), dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter in slightly damp peat or coconut coir at 55-65 degrees F, replanting the following spring.

plant_note: Grown for edible flower stems.
directions: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost, sowing in clusters and keeping soil around 65F. This garlic chive selection is grown especially for its tender edible flower stalks used in stir-fries. Transplant clumps to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly watered. Harvest the round flower buds and stems just before they open for the mildest flavor. Divide the perennial clumps every few years and cut back foliage after frost.

plant_note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before direct sowing in spring into deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun.
directions: Chinese licorice is a rhizomatous perennial legume native to the steppes of northern China, Mongolia, and Siberia, cultivated for its sweet, fibrous root, known as gan cao, one of the most frequently used herbs in traditional Chinese medicine formulas, prized for harmonizing other herbs in a blend. Nick or soak the hard seed coat before direct sowing in spring into deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; as a nitrogen-fixing legume it tolerates poor, sandy soils but struggles in heavy, waterlogged clay. The plant spreads steadily by underground rhizomes and can become assertive in loose soil over time, so give it room or a root barrier in smaller gardens. Roots are traditionally left in the ground for three to four years to bulk up before being dug in autumn, then sliced and dried; this species is distinct from the Mediterranean licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra) more commonly grown in Western herb gardens.

plant_note: Direct-sow after the last frost into full sun and average garden soil; grows quickly and self-seeds much like its Western relative, common motherwort.
directions: Its uterine-stimulant action means it should be avoided in pregnancy except under professional postpartum guidance. Direct-sow after the last frost into full sun and average garden soil, where this tall, bitter mint-family plant grows quickly and self-seeds much like its Western relative, common motherwort. The flowering tops are dried for TCM decoctions traditionally used to invigorate blood flow, ease menstrual discomfort, and support postpartum recovery.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun; established clumps spread by rhizome and are most reliably increased by division rather than seed.
directions: Artemisia argyi is the specific mugwort species (known in Chinese as ai ye) that supplies the compressed floss burned in moxibustion, a cornerstone practice of traditional Chinese medicine distinct from the more general culinary and craft uses of European mugwort or Japanese yomogi. The deeply lobed leaves have a dense, silvery-white wooly underside that is processed and aged before being rolled into moxa sticks or cones. Cut foliage in mid-summer just before flowering, when the aromatic oil content is highest, and dry bundled stems in a shaded, airy location. The plant spreads vigorously by rhizome and self-sows in favorable sites, so confine it with a root barrier or grow it in a dedicated bed away from cultivated borders.

common_name: Chinese Prickly Ash (Flatspine Prickly Ash, Sichuan Pepper Relative)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to rocky soil in full sun; Chinese prickly ash (Zanthoxylum simulans) is a thorny deciduous shrub from eastern China — one of the Zanthoxylum species used as a source of Chinese Sichuan pepper-type spice, producing small, red, split seed husks with the characteristic numbing, floral-citrus, electric-tingling spice compound hydroxy-alpha-sanshool — used as a Sichuan pepper substitute and in traditional Chinese medicine.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; wear thick gloves when harvesting or pruning due to sharp thorns. Zanthoxylum simulans (Chinese prickly ash or flatspine prickly ash) is a thorny deciduous shrub from eastern and central China — one of several Zanthoxylum species used as sources of the Sichuan pepper-type spice in Chinese cooking, alongside the more commonly cultivated Z. bungeanum (Sichuan pepper) and Z. piperitum (Japanese sansho). Like its famous relatives, Z. simulans produces small, red, split-open seed husks (pericarps) after the black seed falls out; these husks contain hydroxy-alpha-sanshool and related sanshool compounds that cause the unique 'ma' (numbing-tingling) sensation of Sichuan cooking — a distinctive electric, oscillating numbness of the tongue and lips, combined with floral, citrus, and spicy aromatic notes. Z. simulans is more cold-hardy than the primary Sichuan pepper (Z. bungeanum) and is one of the species sometimes sold as 'Sichuan pepper' in the US market. The fresh husks, dried husks, and sometimes the young leaves are all used as aromatic seasonings. As a garden plant, it is an attractive, fast-growing thorny shrub with fragrant compound leaves that provides hedging function while producing a useful spice crop.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost; cold stratification aids germination of this hardy perennial.
directions: Chinese skullcap, or Huang Qin, is a hardy perennial with violet-blue tubular flowers, long valued in traditional East Asian herbalism. Sow seed after a period of cold stratification into well-drained soil in full sun. Roots are typically harvested from plants three or more years old, after the tops die back. Keep soil moderately moist and avoid waterlogging, which can rot the crown.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Chinook climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Chinook, released by the USDA in 1985, is a high-alpha dual-purpose hop valued for strong bittering power paired with a distinctive piney, spicy, slightly grapefruit aroma, widely used in American IPAs and pale ales that call for assertive hop character. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet on a trellis; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, aromatic, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect reduced yield compared with traditional hop-growing regions.

plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; chives tolerate light frost.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in groups of 4–6 and thin clumps to 6–9 in apart once established; thinnings are edible. Water regularly and divide crowded clumps every 2–3 years in spring or fall to maintain vigor. Remove spent flower heads to prevent excessive self-seeding, or leave a few for their edible, mildly onion-flavored blooms. Harvest by snipping leaves to about 1 in above the soil; plants regrow quickly.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings around the last frost date; this cultivar is a sterile peppermint hybrid and must be propagated vegetatively to maintain its chocolate-mint character.
directions: Plant divisions in rich, consistently moist soil and confine the roots with a buried barrier or container, as this mint spreads aggressively like all peppermint cultivars. Provide consistent moisture and partial shade in hot climates to prevent the dark-stemmed foliage from scorching. Harvest stems just before flowers open for the most pronounced menthol-and-chocolate aroma; the leaves are prized for their distinctive scent in desserts, hot chocolate, and after-dinner teas. Cut plants back to 2–3 in above ground after each main harvest to stimulate a flush of fragrant new growth.

common_name: Christine's Choice Tea (Cold-Hardy Southeast Tea Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Christine's Choice was selected in North Carolina specifically for reliable performance in the humid Southeast, including the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal, especially in hot Gulf South summers; Christine's Choice is a tea cultivar selected and named by Camellia Forest Nursery in North Carolina from Southeast-grown seedling stock, chosen specifically for vigorous, reliable growth and good leaf quality in the humid, hot-summer conditions of the American Southeast rather than for the extreme cold tolerance bred into Sochi-type selections. It is a popular choice for home tea growers from the Carolinas through the Gulf Coast who want a productive plant adapted to regional humidity and disease pressure rather than one optimized for northern cold snaps. Leaves and growth habit are typical of small-leaved China-type tea, suitable for green, oolong, or black tea processing depending on how the harvested leaf is handled. Begin light harvesting of the top two leaves and a bud once plants are well established at three to four years old, and mulch well to protect the acid-loving root system.

common_name: Christmas Basil (Compact Heat-Tolerant Clove-Scented Hybrid Basil for Extended Season)
plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting or direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Christmas Basil is a hybrid between sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum) and Thai/Asian basil types, combining the leaf size and general appearance of sweet basil with the more intense, clove-like fragrance of Thai basil and improved heat tolerance. In zone 9, plant March–May and August–September. Christmas Basil is significantly more heat and disease tolerant than standard Genovese basil — it is better able to withstand the Gulf Coast's summer heat without declining and shows good resistance to Fusarium wilt and downy mildew, the two most damaging pathogens affecting basil production in warm-humid climates. The name 'Christmas' refers not to the holiday but to the compact, rounded, mounded growth habit that some gardeners liken to a Christmas tree shape.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after last frost in warm soil. Pinch flower buds to extend leaf production. Harvest continuously. Christmas Basil is a hybrid basil variety that represents a key development in warm-climate basil breeding: the combining of sweet basil's mild, widely-appealing flavor with the improved heat tolerance and disease resistance of Asian basil species, particularly Thai basil (Ocimum × citriodorum). Standard Genovese-type sweet basil, while ideal for Italian cooking and widely preferred for pesto, has two significant limitations in zone 9 and other hot-humid climates: it is susceptible to Fusarium wilt (a soilborne fungal disease that wilts and kills plants) and downy mildew (an airborne pathogen that devastates basil foliage in warm-humid conditions), and it performs poorly in sustained heat, often bolting and declining during the Gulf Coast summer. Christmas Basil's hybrid origin provides significantly better tolerance to both heat and these pathogens — plants remain productive and healthy through conditions that would collapse standard Genovese types. The flavor of Christmas Basil occupies an intermediate position between sweet basil and Thai basil: more complex and spicy than plain Genovese, with distinct clove and anise notes from the Thai parentage, but milder than full-strength Thai basil. This flavor profile is versatile — appropriate for Italian applications (especially where some aromatic complexity is desired), for Southeast Asian-inspired dishes, and as a general culinary herb where the assertive clove character of straight Thai basil would be too dominant. The compact, mounding growth habit (12–20 inches) keeps plants tidy and manageable in containers and herb beds.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chuan Xiong is a cool-climate herb traditionally grown at higher elevation in Sichuan and prefers cooler summer conditions than the Gulf South provides.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chuan Xiong is a cool-climate herb traditionally grown at higher elevation in Sichuan and prefers cooler summer conditions than the Gulf South provides. Finely divided, celery-like aromatic foliage and small umbels of white flowers grow from a knobby, strongly aromatic rhizome that is the part harvested and dried for use in traditional Chinese medicine, where it has long been valued for supporting healthy circulation. Historically cultivated at elevation in Sichuan province, it performs best where summers stay relatively mild and struggles with prolonged heat and humidity, making it a better fit for a cooler mountain or northern garden than a hot, humid Gulf Coast bed. Harvest and dry the rhizomes in fall after the foliage dies back, typically after one to two seasons of growth.

plant_note: Grown indoors in trays year-round; harvested at the seedling stage.
directions: A fragrant basil blend grown as microgreens for a milder, nutrient-rich basil flavor any time of year. Sow seed densely on the surface of a shallow tray of moist growing mix and keep warm and evenly moist. Provide bright light once the seedlings emerge, since basil microgreens grow best warm. Harvest with scissors at the first true leaf stage, about two to three weeks after sowing, and use fresh.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather and make successive sowings, since it bolts in summer heat.
directions: This open-pollinated cilantro produces lush leafy greens and, when it bolts, aromatic coriander seed. Sow directly in cool weather since it bolts quickly once temperatures climb. Make small successive sowings every two to three weeks for a steady leaf harvest. Allow a few plants to flower and set seed to collect coriander or let them self-sow for the next round.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; succession-sow every 3 weeks through spring and again in early fall.
directions: Lightly crush the husks before sowing, then press seeds 1/4 in into the soil and keep evenly moist until germination. Thin seedlings to 6 in apart so plants don't compete for moisture, which slows bolting. Avoid transplanting; cilantro's taproot resents disturbance. Begin harvesting outer leaves once plants reach 4–6 in, and harvest seed heads (coriander) when they turn tan and dry on the stem.

plant_note: Slower microgreen; cracking or presoaking the split seed speeds germination.
directions: Cilantro is one of the slower microgreens, so gently crack or presoak the split coriander seed to encourage faster, more even sprouting. Sow densely on a moist tray and keep it covered and warm for up to a week while germination gets underway. Once shoots appear, move to bright light and water carefully to avoid mold on the extended growing surface. Harvest the aromatic, citrus-scented greens after two to three weeks when the first true leaves emerge.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant only after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in fertile, moist seed-starting mix held above 65°F, and transplant outdoors once night temperatures stay above 50°F. Cinnamon basil has reddish stems and pink-purple flowers; it contains methyl cinnamate, which gives the foliage a distinct warm spice note alongside the usual basil flavor. Pinch out flower stalks as they appear to maintain leaf production, and harvest by cutting stems back to a set of lower leaves. Use fresh or dried in fruit dishes, desserts, teas, and anywhere a subtle cinnamon note complements the basil flavor.

plant_note: Grow outdoors only in tropical zones; elsewhere keep as a container plant moved indoors for winter.
directions: This tropical evergreen yields true cinnamon, harvested from the fragrant inner bark of young stems. Grow in full sun to part shade in rich, well-drained soil kept consistently moist but never soggy. Outside frost-free regions, keep it potted and bring it into a warm, bright room before temperatures drop, since it is very frost-sensitive. Coppice mature stems to encourage the tender shoots that produce the best bark for harvesting.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Citra is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation.
directions: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Citra is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in 2007 and quickly becoming one of the most sought-after and widely used hop varieties in modern craft brewing, this vigorous climbing bine produces resinous, aromatic cones with a distinctive tropical fruit, citrus, and gooseberry character that helped define the juicy, hazy IPA styles that have dominated craft beer for over a decade. Like other hops it is a perennial vine that dies back to the ground each winter and regrows vigorously each spring, needing a sturdy tall support and full sun to reach its full trellis height and cone production.
