Train young bines up the support as they grow, harvest cones in late summer when they feel dry and papery and spring back after being squeezed, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season for the best cone development.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring and plant after all frost danger has passed in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; citronella grass is damaged at 32 degrees F and killed below 28 degrees F. In zone 9-10 it grows as a perennial; in cooler zones it can be grown as an annual or overwintered in containers indoors. It is distinct from lemon grass (Cymbopogon citratus) in its scent profile — citronella oil contains citronellol and geraniol rather than the citral-dominant scent of lemon grass.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free or frost-protected conditions; citronella grass is a large, clumping, tropical grass native to Sri Lanka that is the primary commercial source of Ceylon citronella oil — the essential oil used in mosquito-repellent candles, torches, sprays, and lotions worldwide. The essential oil from the leaves and stems contains citronellol, geraniol, and related terpenes that mosquitoes find repellent. The plant itself, when its leaves are crushed or bruised, releases a strong, complex citrus-rose fragrance. Growing it in the garden is an attractive proposition — the blue-green, arching grass clumps are handsome and the repellent effect is modest when the plant is growing undisturbed, but crushing a few leaves releases the fragrance. It is completely distinct from lemon grass (C. citratus), which is grown for cooking rather than insect repellency and has a different chemical profile dominated by citral rather than citronellol. In zones 10-12 it is a reliable perennial ornamental grass; in zones 9 it often overwinters with protection.

plant_note: Set out after frost; grow in containers to overwinter indoors in cold climates.
directions: This fast-growing scented geranium has citrus-fragrant foliage and pretty pink blooms, thriving in hot, sunny gardens and patio pots. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and let the top of the soil dry slightly between waterings. Pinch stems to keep it bushy and take cuttings easily to make more plants. It is frost-tender, so bring containers indoors to a bright window before the first freeze.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun; clary sage is a biennial that grows vegetatively in its first year, then blooms spectacularly in its second year, after which it typically dies but self-seeds freely to maintain the colony.
directions: Salvia sclarea is a majestic biennial sage with large, wrinkled, woolly, gray-green leaves and tall (4-5 foot), airy panicles of pale lavender-blue and white flowers with large, colorful bracts in early summer of the second year that are spectacular in the garden and highly attractive to bumblebees; it is one of the most valuable aromatic plants for the perfume industry (used in Eau Sauvage and Chanel No. 19), for aromatherapy (clary sage essential oil), and as a culinary herb for flavoring wines and beers. The large leaves can be dipped in batter and fried as a traditional Italian dish; the essential oil is considered antispasmodic and is used in herbal medicine.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed immediately after harvest in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds have complex dormancy requirements (double dormancy requiring one warm then one cold period) and germinate in the second spring after sowing — purchasing nursery transplants is faster.
directions: Direct sow fresh seed immediately after harvest in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds have complex dormancy requirements (double dormancy requiring one warm then one cold period) and germinate in the second spring after sowing — purchasing nursery transplants is faster. Clayton's sweet cicely is a native woodland herb of eastern North American deciduous forests that is nearly identical in appearance and use to Osmorhiza longistylis and O. berteroi; it produces large, feathery, compound leaves with a strong, sweet anise-licorice fragrance when crushed, and small, white, flat-topped flower clusters (umbels) in spring that are excellent for native bees and beneficial insects. The roots and leaves are edible with a mild anise flavor, historically used by Native Americans; it is an excellent, fragrant, deep-shade groundcover that naturalizes quietly under deciduous trees.

plant_note: Cleavers self-sow freely and are primarily harvested as a foraged weed appearing in early spring; if growing intentionally, sow in fall or very early spring in moist, shaded or partly shaded garden soil.
directions: Harvest young plants in early spring from moist, shaded garden beds and hedgerow edges before they become too large and stringy; cleavers are primarily encountered as a scrambling annual weed notable for the tiny hook-covered stems and leaves that cling to clothing and pet fur. In herbal medicine traditions across Europe and North America, the fresh plant has been used as a lymphatic tonic, diuretic, and spring cleansing herb — the young shoots are the most active medicinally and are harvested in early spring. The young tips can be eaten as a pot herb or juiced; the roasted seeds have been used as a coffee substitute. Note that cleavers is different from sweet woodruff (Galium odoratum), which is grown as a shade groundcover. As a medicinal herb, cleavers is best used fresh rather than dried.

plant_note: Warmth-loving; frost kills it.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, surface-pressing it and keeping flats near 78F. This African and Asian shrubby basil carries a warm clove-like scent used medicinally and in cooking. Transplant to warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost, giving each plant ample room to bush out. Pinch flowering tips to prolong leaf production and improve branching. In cool climates grow it as a container plant that can overwinter indoors.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy soil in zone 11–12; Clove Tree is a medium-sized tropical tree native to the North Maluku Islands of Indonesia — the original source of one of the world's most valuable spices — bearing aromatic, red-tinged young leaves and flower buds that are harvested dried (cloves) for use as the whole or ground spice in cooking, baking, dentistry, and traditional medicine worldwide; the most commercially important tree in its native range for centuries.
directions: Plant Syzygium aromaticum (Clove Tree) in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic, deep loamy soil in full sun; requires consistent moisture year-round and high humidity; protect from all frost and cold winds; harvest flower buds (cloves) when they turn from green to light pink but before they open — dried immediately after harvest to the familiar dark-brown clove. Clove is one of the most historically significant spice plants on Earth — the dried, unopened flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum, native exclusively to the North Maluku (Spice Islands) of Indonesia, were so extraordinarily valuable in the medieval spice trade that they were literally worth their weight in gold in European markets. The trade in cloves drove European exploration and colonialism throughout the 15th–17th centuries; the Banda Sea spice islands' control by the Dutch VOC was among the most economically significant monopolies in history. Today, Zanzibar (Tanzania), Indonesia, and Madagascar are the primary producers. The essential oil eugenol (80–90% of clove bud oil) is the source of clove's characteristic powerful aroma; it is used in dentistry as a topical analgesic, in perfumery, and as a food flavoring. The whole spice is used in biryani, mulled wine, pumpkin spice blends, pickling, and traditional medicine worldwide. A large, handsome, aromatic evergreen tree with attractive red-flushed young growth and cream-white flower clusters when not harvested.

common_name: Clove Vine (Cipo Cravo, Cipó Cravo, Panama Clove Vine)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in late spring on a strong trellis, tree, or arbor in full sun to partial shade; Tynanthus panurensis is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 10-11 outdoor culture. The vine climbs vigorously and its bark, when scraped or cut, releases an immediate, powerful clove fragrance — the same eugenol compound found in true cloves (Syzygium aromaticum). In traditional Amazonian herbal medicine, the bark is macerated in rum or cachaça to create a tonic ('licor de cipó cravo'). Grows in zone 9 as a container plant moved indoors in winter. Propagate from cuttings.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with strong climbing support — Clove Vine grows vigorously and its stems will clothe a fence, trellis, or tree in dense, attractive foliage once established. Tynanthus panurensis is a woody, liana-climbing vine native to the Amazonian regions of Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, and Ecuador in the Bignoniaceae family, known not primarily for its flowers (small, tubular, cream to white, produced in axillary clusters) but for one of the most remarkable aromatic properties of any tropical climbing plant: the bark, stems, and wood of the vine smell powerfully, precisely, and unmistakably of cloves — the familiar spice from Syzygium aromaticum — when cut, scraped, or bruised. The fragrant compound responsible is eugenol, the same aromatic phenol that gives true cloves their characteristic fragrance, occurring in Tynanthus panurensis as a convergent natural chemistry that produces an olfactory experience nearly identical to the spice. Throughout the Amazon Basin, the bark of T. panurensis is harvested and macerated in spirits (rum, cachaça, or aguardiente) to create 'licor de cipó cravo' (clove vine liqueur) — a traditional tonic drink used medicinally and consumed recreationally with an unmistakable clove-spice flavor. A genuinely unique aromatic plant for zone 10-12 tropical garden enthusiasts interested in useful and ethnobotanically significant plants.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cluster climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Cluster is the oldest surviving American hop cultivar, an heirloom variety of unclear original parentage that dominated US hop production for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries before newer aroma hops took over, and it remains valued today for its clean, mild, slightly spicy and floral character and reliable, disease-resistant vigor. The vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; harvest the soft green cones in late summer when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin resin, then dry promptly for brewing or storage. Like other hops, Cluster performs best in cool-summer climates with long day length, and struggles with the sustained heat and humidity of zone 8-9 Gulf South summers, so give it the coolest, best-ventilated site available and expect a lighter cone yield than in traditional hop-growing regions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring in full sun, sharply drained, lean soil; like other creeping thymes it needs excellent drainage and struggles in heavy, wet, or humid conditions.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since this low, mat-forming thyme is intolerant of wet or heavy soil and thrives on genuine neglect once established. Coconut Thyme is grown primarily as an ornamental ground cover for its dense, glossy, dark green foliage and — true to its name — a distinctly sweet, coconut-like fragrance released when leaves are brushed or crushed, an unusual scent profile among thymes that are more typically savory or lemony. Small pink flowers appear in early summer and are attractive to bees, and the tight, trailing mat is well suited to cascading over rock walls, edging pathways, or filling gaps between pavers. Avoid overhead watering and rich, moisture-retentive soil, both of which encourage root and crown rot in this drought-adapted plant.

plant_note: Plant root cuttings or crown divisions in early spring; even small root fragments will regenerate into new plants so choose the planting site carefully.
directions: Propagate from 2–4 in root cuttings planted horizontally 2–3 in deep; plants grow vigorously and are nearly impossible to eradicate once established, so site them permanently. Mulch heavily around plants and cut back to the ground two or three times per growing season to harvest the biomass-rich leaves as a liquid fertilizer or compost activator. Leaves can also be processed into poultice form for topical soothing use on bruises and minor sprains. Note that internal use is not recommended due to pyrrolizidine alkaloid content.

plant_note: Surface-sow the dust-fine seed directly in early spring, since it germinates best with light exposure and resents root disturbance from transplanting.
directions: Should be avoided by anyone with active peptic ulcers given its intense bitterness. Surface-sow the dust-fine seed directly in early spring, since it germinates best with light exposure and resents root disturbance from transplanting. The whole flowering plant is cut and dried at bloom time to make a classic bitter tea, taken in small amounts before meals in traditional European herbalism to stimulate appetite and digestion.

common_name: Common Chervil (Classic French Fines Herbes Anise Herb)
plant_note: Direct sow chervil in place and do not transplant — the taproot is extremely sensitive to disturbance. Sow fresh seed immediately; old seed has poor germination. In zone 9, sow August–October for fall and winter harvest when chervil performs best; spring planting is possible (January–February) but the plants bolt quickly in warming weather. Chervil grows well in partial shade and actually benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9 — use it under taller plants or in a partially shaded bed.
directions: Direct sow fresh seed on or near the soil surface in cool weather; do not cover deeply — chervil needs some light. Do not transplant. Chervil (Anthriscus cerefolium) is one of the four classic herbs of the French fines herbes blend (with parsley, chives, and French tarragon) — a cool-season, shade-tolerant herb with delicate, lacy, bright green leaves resembling a more refined parsley, and a distinctive flavor that combines mild parsley with a clean anise note. The anise quality distinguishes chervil from all other common culinary herbs — it is present but not dominant, providing a refined freshness that enhances eggs, fish, chicken, and light cream sauces without overwhelming the primary ingredients. Chervil is the most perishable of the major culinary herbs: the delicate flavor dissipates rapidly when dried (dried chervil has almost no culinary value), when cooked at high heat (add at the end of cooking), or when refrigerated for more than 2–3 days. These perishability characteristics mean chervil is essentially only available to gardeners — it is rarely found fresh in American markets. Chervil bolt rapidly (runs to seed) in heat, making it strictly a cool-season herb for zone 8–9 gardeners, but the fall-through-spring window in zone 9 provides several months of harvest from a fall planting.

plant_note: Sow in early spring around the last frost; clumps return reliably each year.
directions: Common chives are a hardy perennial allium forming grassy clumps with a mild onion flavor and edible lavender-pink flowers. Sow seed in clusters and thin lightly, since chives grow happily in tight bunches. Snip leaves from the outside of the clump throughout the season and they will regrow. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep them vigorous and productive.

plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow; a hardy perennial that returns each year.
directions: Sow seed indoors or direct sow in clusters, since chives grow best planted in small clumps rather than single plants. This easy, low-maintenance perennial tolerates drought and returns year after year, offering hollow foliage with a mild onion flavor for salads, potatoes, and eggs. The edible lavender flowers attract bees, make a flavorful chive vinegar, and dry well for arrangements; snip the leaves regularly to keep fresh growth coming.

plant_note: Direct sow and press into the surface; a hardy perennial with edible leaves, flowers, and roots.
directions: Scatter seed on the surface and press it in lightly, as dandelion needs light to germinate. This tough perennial thrives in a wide range of soils and will naturalize if flowers are allowed to set their puffball seed heads. Harvest young leaves before flowering for the mildest greens, use the blooms fresh, and dig the taproots in fall for roasting.

plant_note: Direct sow outdoors in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; or cold stratify seeds 4–6 weeks and sow indoors in late winter. Lady's mantle self-sows readily once established and typically perpetuates itself without attention.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; common lady's mantle is one of the most beloved cottage garden perennials, treasured for the exquisite way its rounded, softly pleated, velvety leaves catch and hold water droplets and dew in perfect spherical beads that roll around the leaf surface. The frothy sprays of tiny, chartreuse-yellow flowers in early summer are superb as a foil for pink and lavender flowers and effective cut fresh or dried. In traditional European herbal medicine, Alchemilla was used as a wound herb and for women's health conditions — the genus name references medieval alchemists who collected the dew from the leaves. Self-sows reliably to naturalize in cool, moist, shaded garden areas. Best in cool-summer climates; in the South, plant in shade and ensure consistent moisture.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in cool spring or fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; common mallow self-seeds freely and will establish self-maintaining colonies in suitable conditions — one spring sowing typically ensures perpetual renewal.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in cool spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; common mallow is a biennial or short-lived perennial edible herb of European origin that has been used as food and medicine for thousands of years — the young leaves, fresh or cooked, have a mild, slightly mucilaginous, pleasantly neutral flavor and can be used in salads, cooked as a pot herb (substitute for spinach), or simmered in soups and stews. The leaves, stems, seeds (called 'cheeses' for their round shape), and flowers are all edible. The plant has long been valued in herbal medicine for its mucilaginous properties, which soothe irritated tissues of the throat, digestive tract, and urinary system. The attractive, pale to deep-pink or purple flowers with darker veining are produced throughout the growing season and are excellent in salads. The ornamental cultivar 'Zebrina' with striped purple-and-white flowers and 'Brave Heart' are grown primarily for their striking flowers. Tolerates partial shade, poor soil, and drought once established. Self-seeds freely to maintain persistent garden colonies.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant; a vigorous perennial best contained in pots.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant seedlings out, ideally into a buried pot or contained bed, since mint spreads aggressively by runners. Grow it in moist soil and partial to full sun; the aromatic leaves enhance iced tea, mixed drinks, and savory dishes like meats, stews, and vegetable fritters. Cut plants back regularly to encourage tender new growth, and let some tiny flowers bloom to feed the bees.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in average, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mugwort spreads aggressively by rhizomes and self-sowing and can become invasive — it is listed as a noxious weed in some states, so check local regulations before planting and use root barriers or plant in wild areas away from manicured gardens.
directions: Artemisia vulgaris is one of the most widespread and ancient medicinal herbs in the world, used across Europe, Asia, and the Americas for digestive complaints, menstrual regulation, and as a flavoring in traditional European and Korean cuisine; the leaves have a distinctive aromatic, slightly bitter flavor and are traditionally used to stuff roast goose or used in moxibustion in traditional Chinese medicine. The silver-backed, deeply dissected foliage is attractive, and the plant is highly drought-tolerant once established; however, it is potentially invasive and should be managed carefully.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or summer; biennial plants form a rosette the first year and flower the second year.
directions: Scatter tiny seeds on bare, disturbed soil and do not cover — they need light to germinate; thin to 18–24 in apart once seedlings are established. As a biennial, mullein forms a large, velvety rosette of leaves in the first year before sending up a tall flower spike in its second season. First-year leaves are harvested and dried for use in respiratory-support teas and smoking blends; flowers are gathered as they open along the stalk, often infused into olive oil for ear-drop preparations. Allow the towering flower spike to set seed for reliable self-sowing in subsequent years.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; common myrtle is drought-tolerant once established and native to the dry Mediterranean basin. It performs well in zone 8–10 gardens with dry summers, is sensitive to prolonged hard freezes below 10°F, and does best in sheltered positions in zone 8.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; common myrtle is one of the oldest cultivated plants in human history — sacred to Aphrodite, woven into Roman bridal wreaths, and mentioned in the Old Testament — a Mediterranean evergreen shrub with small, intensely aromatic leaves (releasing a fresh, clean, camphor-like fragrance when brushed), white flowers with prominent yellow stamens in summer, and small, round, blue-black berries in autumn. All parts of the plant are aromatic and culinary: the leaves are used to flavor meats and poultry in Sardinian and Corsican cuisine (similar to bay leaves), the berries are edible with a resinous, slightly gin-like flavor and are used to flavor liqueurs and as a spice in traditional Mediterranean cooking. The plant is compact and shapeable into hedges, topiary, and formal geometric shapes. Both leaves and berries are used in myrtle liqueur, particularly the Sardinian Mirto. It grows well in zone 8–10 with dry summers and is an excellent plant for Gulf Coast and California gardens with mild winters.

plant_note: Start indoors; surface sow since seed needs light, and transplant out.
directions: Start the tiny seed indoors, pressing it onto the surface since it needs light to germinate, then transplant into full sun and well-drained soil. This common oregano, also called wild marjoram, has a milder flavor than the pungent Greek type and is the traditional variety for medicinal use. It is a hardy perennial with pretty pink to lavender flowers that draw pollinators; harvest leaves before flowering for the strongest flavor, fresh or dried.

plant_note: Surface sow; a hardy broadleaf perennial used medicinally and to improve compacted soil.
directions: Press seed onto the soil surface without covering, since it germinates best with light. This resilient broadleaf perennial establishes even in compacted or disturbed ground where little else grows. Harvest the young leaves for fresh or dried herbal use, and let a few plants set seed to maintain the patch year after year.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost, or plant container stock in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; rue demands excellent drainage and low soil fertility — in rich, moist soil it grows lush but has reduced aromatic oil concentration and shorter lifespan.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; avoid wet or highly fertile soils. CAUTION: Handle with gloves — rue contains furanocoumarins that cause photodermatitis (severe skin blisters on contact followed by sun exposure). Ruta graveolens (rue or herb-of-grace) is one of the oldest cultivated herbs in Western horticulture, used since antiquity as a culinary, medicinal, and ritual plant; in the kitchen it is used very sparingly as a seasoning in Mediterranean cuisines (especially in Southern Italian and Ethiopian cooking), where a few leaves are added to salads, cheeses, grappa, and meat dishes for its intensely bitter, aromatic, slightly citrusy, and resinous flavor — the bitterness is powerful, and it should be used in very small quantities by those not accustomed to it. The attractive blue-green, finely divided foliage and small yellow flowers make rue an ornamental herb-garden plant; it is also reputed to repel many insects including aphids, Japanese beetles, and cats, making it useful as a companion plant. It is the larval host plant for Giant Swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, adding wildlife value.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed as young plants are more cold-sensitive than mature ones.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix; germination is reliable at 65–70°F. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and prune plants hard in spring to remove winter-killed tips and promote bushy growth from the base. Harvest leafy stems before flowering for culinary and medicinal use; the volatile oils are most concentrated on sunny mornings before flowering. Dried sage leaves and bundles are used in cooking, traditional salubrious teas, and as smudge sticks in ceremonial contexts.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant; a hardy perennial that returns each spring.
directions: A hardy perennial green whose lemony, tangy leaves brighten salads, soups, and sauces in the French tradition. Sow seed directly a quarter inch deep and thin plants to eight to twelve inches apart. Harvest young spring leaves for the mildest flavor, cutting outer leaves so the plant keeps producing. Remove flower stalks to prolong leaf production, and divide clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

plant_note: Direct sow shallowly in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in spring after last frost; tansy spreads aggressively by rhizomes and self-seeding and is best confined by root barriers in garden borders or planted in naturalistic areas where spreading is acceptable.
directions: Tanacetum vulgare is a vigorous, aromatic perennial producing deeply divided, fern-like, dark-green leaves with an intensely camphor-like scent and flat-topped clusters of bright, button-yellow flower heads in late summer that were historically planted near doorways to repel flies, ants, and fleas; the dried flowers hold their color well and are valuable for dried arrangements. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested in significant quantities; it contains thujone, a neurotoxic compound, and should not be consumed internally. Do not grow near vegetables or edible crops as the allelopathic compounds can inhibit germination.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow or barely cover seed as light aids germination.
directions: Surface-sow seeds or cover to 1/8 in in warm, well-drained starting mix; seedlings are small and slow to establish so start early indoors. Plant in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun — like other Mediterranean herbs, thyme deteriorates in fertile, moist conditions. Trim plants lightly after each harvest to prevent woodiness; replace plants every 3–4 years when the center becomes unproductive. Harvest leafy stem tips before or during flowering for the highest thymol content, using fresh or dried in culinary preparations and traditional antiseptic and cough-relief remedies.

plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost in dry, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun; common thyme must have excellent drainage to survive humid summers — in the deep South, grow it as a cool-season perennial (fall through spring), as it tends to die out in zone 9 summer heat and humidity.
directions: Thymus vulgaris is the primary culinary thyme of European and world cuisine — a low, bushy, semi-woody perennial with tiny, aromatic, gray-green leaves containing thymol and carvacrol, the essential oil compounds responsible for its powerful, distinctive fragrance. It is the definitive herb of French, Italian, Spanish, and Middle Eastern cooking; an essential component of bouquet garni and herbes de Provence; and one of the most important medicinal herbs in Western herbalism, used for respiratory infections, coughs, and as an antimicrobial. The tiny, pale-lavender flowers in late spring are outstanding for honeybees and are the source of highly prized thyme honey.

plant_note: Direct-sow on or just before the last frost date; seeds benefit from light cold stratification and can be surface-sown or barely covered with fine soil in a sunny, well-drained position. Common vervain self-sows readily once established and naturalizes well in dry, open, disturbed ground.
directions: Verbena officinalis is an ancient medicinal herb with one of the longest recorded histories of use in European and Near Eastern herbal tradition, valued from classical antiquity through the Middle Ages as a nervine tonic, digestive bitter, and sacred ritual plant; it is a slender, upright perennial with deeply lobed, rough-textured gray-green leaves and long, wiry spikes of tiny, pale lilac to white flowers throughout summer that are visited enthusiastically by small native bees and hoverflies. Direct-sow seeds in a dry, sunny, well-drained position — common vervain is a plant of waste ground, roadsides, dry grasslands, and disturbed soils and thrives in lean, free-draining, neutral to alkaline conditions where more vigorous herbs might be out-competed; it will decline in rich, moist, or shaded sites. Harvest the leafy, flowering tops during full bloom for use fresh or dried in traditional herbal preparations; the bitter iridoid glycosides (particularly verbenalin) give the plant its characteristic medicinal properties valued by herbalists for supporting the nervous system and digestion. Common vervain self-sows reliably and naturalizes easily in gravel gardens, dry banks, and cottage herb gardens, where it adds an airy, wild-flower quality while maintaining its important role as a medicinal herb and pollinator plant.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost; the taproot dislikes transplanting.
directions: This dwarf dill stays short and bushy, making it ideal for containers, raised beds, and small gardens while delivering classic dill flavor. Sow directly where it will grow, as dill resents root disturbance. Harvest the ferny foliage as needed and let some plants flower for pickling heads and seed. Make successive sowings for a continuous supply of fresh leaves through the season.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; its low, dense habit suits border edges and container growing as well as the herb bed.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where the plant develops its strongest flavor. Compactum is a dwarf oregano selection that stays low and dense, only 4–8 inches tall, forming a tidy mound rather than the looser, more upright growth of standard oregano, making it useful as a fragrant edging plant or rock garden filler in addition to a culinary herb. It carries the same bold, aromatic flavor as standard oregano in a more compact package suited to smaller herb gardens and containers. Harvest sprigs regularly and shear plants back after flowering to keep growth dense and productive for years.

common_name: Compactum Thyme (Dense Non-Flowering Culinary Edging Thyme)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; Compactum forms a dense, low, mostly non-flowering mound of culinary thyme well suited to edging beds and paths.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; thyme performs poorly and can rot in heavy, wet, or overly rich soil. Compactum is a dense, mounding form of common culinary thyme that stays low and tidy without the sprawling, woody growth typical of standard thyme, and flowers only sparingly, keeping its energy focused on producing tender, flavorful leaves rather than seed. Its neat habit makes it a popular choice for edging garden beds and paths, filling gaps between stepping stones, or growing in containers. Trim lightly after any bloom and shear back by about a third in early spring to keep the mound dense and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody over time.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; conehead thyme (Thymbra capitata, sometimes sold as Thymus capitatus) is a strong-flavored Mediterranean subshrub from dry hillsides of Spain, Portugal, and the Eastern Mediterranean — sold commercially in some markets as 'Spanish oregano' due to its intense oregano-thyme flavor, and one of the traditional za'atar herbs of the region.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant; the most flavorful and intense of all thyme-related herbs. Thymbra capitata (conehead thyme, also known as Coridothymus capitatus or sold as Thymus capitatus) is a compact, thorny-based, perennial aromatic subshrub from the dry Mediterranean hillsides of Spain, Portugal, the Balearic Islands, and extending east through the Mediterranean basin. It is one of the most intensely aromatic herbs in the Mediterranean flora — the small, crowded, stiff leaves and pink flower heads (arranged in the characteristic rounded 'cone' clusters that give the plant its name) contain very high concentrations of carvacrol and thymol, the same aromatic compounds found in both thyme and oregano, but at higher concentrations than either cultivated thyme or Greek oregano. The flavor is powerfully savory, hot, and intensely aromatic — making it highly valued as a culinary herb (used as a substitute for oregano in Spanish cooking), as one of the traditional components of Mediterranean za'atar blends, and as a source of essential oil. In Israel and the Levant, dried conehead thyme is an important za'atar component. The plant requires perfectly drained, lean, alkaline, sun-baked conditions — overwatering or clay soil will kill it. In zone 8–10 Mediterranean-climate gardens, it is long-lived, decorative, and worth growing as a specimen culinary herb.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings after last frost; prefers rocky or gravelly soil with excellent drainage.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; this subshrub suffers in heavy clay or waterlogged ground and thrives on neglect. Shear lightly after the distinctive cone-shaped flowers fade to maintain a compact mound and encourage fresh aromatic growth. Avoid overhead watering and do not fertilize heavily, as rich soil dulls the intensely oregano-like fragrance that makes this herb prized in Greek and Middle Eastern cuisines. In zones 7–8, mulch the crown lightly before hard freezes; in zones 9–10 it grows virtually year-round with minimal care.

plant_note: Direct sow only, cilantro resents transplanting; sow in early spring or, in mild-winter climates, in fall for a longer cool-season harvest window.
directions: Sow seed directly into well-drained soil a quarter inch deep and thin to a few inches apart, since cilantro's taproot makes it a poor candidate for transplanting. Confetti is a fine-cut ornamental-leaf selection producing lacy, thread-like foliage instead of the broad lower leaves of standard cilantro, while keeping the same citrusy coriander flavor. Its dissected leaves make it a favorite for garnishing and for gardeners who want a distinct texture from a typical cilantro planting. Succession sow every few weeks in cool weather since, like all cilantro, it bolts quickly once temperatures climb into the 80s.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or stem cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; contain in pots or bottomless containers sunk into the ground to prevent the aggressive rhizomatous spread typical of all mints.
directions: Plant rooted divisions in moist soil in partial shade to full sun, containing the plant in a buried pot or raised bed to limit rhizome spread; corn mint is the most widely distributed of all mints and the primary commercial source of natural menthol, producing a strong, clean, true peppermint-like fragrance and flavor that makes it excellent for tea, beverages, cooking, and distillation. Harvest stems for fresh use throughout the growing season, cutting plants back by half monthly to promote fresh, tender growth and delay flowering. The plant tolerates wetter, shadier, and more challenging conditions than many other mints. Dry harvested stems in bundles for winter use.

plant_note: Divide or transplant rooted mats around the last frost date; Corsican mint is the smallest mint and prefers cool, moist conditions.
directions: Plant small divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded spot; Corsican mint forms a moss-like carpet of tiny peppermint-scented leaves just 1–3 in tall and is ideal between stepping stones or at the edge of a cool, moist path. Unlike most mints, it dislikes hot, dry conditions and should never be allowed to dry out completely. The plant releases a powerful peppermint fragrance when lightly stepped on, making it a sensory ground cover. In zones 6–7 it may die back in hard winters but typically returns from the root; mulch lightly in late autumn to protect the shallow root system.

common_name: Costa Rican Mint Bush (Jamaican Mint Bush, Minty Savory)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Costa Rican mint bush is a tropical perennial shrub from Central America and the Caribbean — with one of the most intensely minty, clean, peppermint-like fragrances of any plant in the Lamiaceae family — used as a culinary herb, a mint tea, and as an ornamental aromatic shrub in tropical and subtropical gardens of zone 9–11.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pinch regularly to maintain bushy form and encourage leaf production; propagate by stem cuttings. Satureja viminea (Costa Rican mint bush or Jamaican mint bush, also known as Clinopodium vimineum) is a tropical perennial shrubby herb from the mountainous regions of Jamaica, Costa Rica, and Central America — notable for producing one of the most intensely and cleanly 'minty' fragrances of any plant in the Lamiaceae (mint) family, far exceeding true peppermint (Mentha x piperita) in the purity and strength of the mint-eucalyptus aroma. The aromatic compound profile is dominated by pulegone and other menthane-family compounds that create the characteristic cool, clean mint sensation. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, Costa Rican mint bush grows as an upright, multi-branched, woody-based shrub with small, oval, intensely aromatic leaves and small white to lavender flowers attractive to bees and butterflies. The leaves are used as a fresh mint substitute for teas, cocktails (authentic mojito-style drinks in parts of Central America), and culinary uses wherever fresh mint flavor is desired. The plant tolerates light shade and thrives with regular trimming in tropical and subtropical gardens. Hardy to about 28–30°F; useful in containers in zone 8.

plant_note: Divide established root clumps in early spring around the last frost date; seed germination is slow and unreliable so division is the standard propagation method.
directions: Divide the clumping rhizome in early spring, replanting sections 2–3 in deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; costmary tolerates partial shade but becomes straggly and produces fewer of the large, minty-balsamic leaves. The broad, silver-green leaves were historically placed in Bibles and hymnals as bookmarks because the pleasant fragrance helped keep the reader awake during long services — hence the common name. Harvest large, mature leaves at any point during the growing season for use as a herb in ales and meat dishes, for sachets in linen, or as a flavoring in salads and teas. Cut plants back hard after flowering to rejuvenate the foliage and prevent excessive spread.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cotton lavender is a classic herb garden and knot garden plant excellent for low hedging and edging.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cotton lavender requires superb drainage — it will rot in wet or waterlogged soil and performs poorly in humid climates without excellent drainage. Santolina chamaecyparissus is a low, aromatic, silvery-gray, evergreen Mediterranean subshrub with dense, coral-like, deeply cut foliage that emits a strong, somewhat pungent, herbal scent when brushed; it produces small, button-like, bright-yellow flower heads on long, slender stems in mid-summer. In the traditional European herb garden, it was used as a low hedging plant in knot gardens and formal herb borders (the silver foliage contrasting beautifully with the green of boxwood and rosemary), and the dried leaves were used as a moth repellent for linen closets. Shear after flowering to maintain a neat, compact shape and prevent woodiness; takes well to clipping.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; coyote mint is a California chaparral and woodland-edge native with a strong minty-oregano fragrance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; coyote mint is a low, mounding California native with soft, gray-green, strongly aromatic foliage carrying a fragrance somewhere between mint and oregano, released readily when the leaves are brushed. Dense, rounded clusters of pale lavender-pink flowers cover the plant from summer into fall, drawing large numbers of native bees and butterflies, including numerous specialist pollinators adapted to the mint family. It is well suited to dry, sunny slopes, rock gardens, and low-water borders once established, needing little more than good drainage and occasional deep watering during the longest dry spells. Shear lightly after the main flowering flush to keep growth compact and encourage a second, lighter bloom later in the season.

plant_note: Plant root divisions in spring or fall in any reasonably moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; creeping comfrey spreads vigorously by underground stolons in favorable conditions but is far less invasive than common comfrey. The smallest piece of root will grow into a new plant.
directions: Plant in moist to average, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; creeping comfrey is the most refined and garden-worthy of the comfreys for shade groundcover use, forming a low, dense mat of hairy, elliptical leaves with pale cream to yellow tubular flowers in spring that attract bumblebees. Unlike the vigorous and sometimes invasive S. x uplandicum (Russian comfrey) and S. officinale, creeping comfrey stays low to 12-14 inches and spreads at a moderate pace rather than becoming aggressively weedy. The leaves are mineral-rich and can be cut repeatedly and used as mulch or compost accelerator, as with other comfreys, but this species is primarily grown as an ornamental shade groundcover. Excellent for suppressing weeds under trees and shrubs where little else grows. The semi-evergreen foliage provides year-round weed suppression in mild winters.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun; Creeping Red Thyme forms a dense, low mat covered in vivid magenta-crimson flowers in late spring and early summer, among the most colorful of the low groundcover thymes.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun. Creeping Red Thyme forms a very low, dense mat of tiny, dark green leaves that disappears almost entirely beneath a vivid carpet of magenta-crimson flowers in late spring and early summer, among the showiest bloom displays of any low-growing groundcover thyme and a strong draw for bees. It tolerates light foot traffic once established, making it useful between stepping stones, along the edges of dry paths, and cascading over rock walls, and it spreads steadily to fill gaps without becoming aggressive or weedy. Like other creeping thymes, it is grown primarily for ornamental groundcover use and pollinator value rather than culinary purposes, and it thrives in the same lean, sharply drained, sun-baked conditions that stress most other groundcovers, making it valuable for hot, dry sites such as gravel gardens and rock gardens. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and encourage fresh new growth.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; creeping savory is a low-growing, prostrate perennial savory from the Caucasus region with more intense, persistent flavor than summer savory (S. hortensis) — spreading to form a low aromatic mat excellent for rock gardens, herb path edging, and gaps in stone paving.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, gravelly or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; creeping savory spreads by runners to form a low aromatic mat — excellent for stone paths and rock gardens. Satureja spicigera (creeping savory or Caucasian savory) is a low-growing, spreading perennial from the dry hillsides, steppe meadows, and rocky outcrops of the Caucasus region (Turkey, Georgia, Armenia) — one of the most useful and underplanted creeping herbs for Mediterranean-style gardens. The plant spreads by prostrate stems to form a dense, aromatic mat (2–4 inches tall, 18–36 inches wide) of tiny, needle-like, intensely aromatic leaves with a flavor more persistently savory-peppery than summer savory (S. hortensis), containing high concentrations of carvacrol and thymol. As a culinary herb, creeping savory is used like summer and winter savory — for beans, lamb, poultry, marinades, and herb vinegars. It produces abundant small white-to-pale-lilac flowers in late summer that attract bees and beneficial insects. The mat-forming habit makes creeping savory outstanding for ground-cover use between stepping stones, in herb spirals, and in rock garden crevices where no other herbs would thrive. More cold-hardy than winter savory (S. montana) and consistently more flavorful than annual summer savory.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or divide established plants in spring; transplant after frost danger has passed.
directions: Surface-sow tiny seeds on well-drained seed-starting mix and press in without covering; germination is slow and irregular over 2–4 weeks. Plant in dry, gritty soil in full sun; creeping thyme thrives in rock gardens, between stepping stones, and on sunny slopes where it forms a fragrant, flowering mat. Avoid heavy clay and excessive moisture, which rot the shallow roots quickly. Harvest sprigs as needed for cooking — the flavor is milder than upright thyme but usable; the primary garden value is as a low, aromatic, bee-friendly ground cover.

plant_note: Surface sow around the last frost; seed is tiny and needs light to germinate.
directions: Creeping thyme forms a low, fragrant evergreen mat covered in purple-lavender blooms that draw bees and butterflies. Surface sow the tiny seed and press it into the soil without covering, since it needs light to germinate. It thrives in lean, well-drained soil and tolerates foot traffic, making it excellent between pavers and in rock gardens. Trim after flowering to keep the mat dense and tidy.

plant_note: Plant bulbs or bulbils in fall 2 inches deep in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; crow garlic is naturalized throughout North America and spreads aggressively — site with care as it can become invasive in lawns and gardens.
directions: Plant small bulbs or bulbils 2 inches deep in fall in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; crow garlic is extremely adaptable and cold-hardy, naturalizing in lawns, roadsides, and disturbed ground throughout much of North America — control by harvesting the bulbils before they disperse if you want to limit its spread. Allium vineale is a European native now widely naturalized in North America, producing slender, hollow, cylindrical, dark-green leaves in late fall through spring and tall scapes bearing umbels of bulbils (and sometimes pinkish flowers) in early summer; it is the "wild garlic" most commonly encountered as a lawn weed in the eastern US. All parts are strongly garlic-flavored and fully edible; the leaves can be harvested in fall through spring and used like garlic chives, and the small bulbs are edible as a substitute for garlic. It is best harvested as a forage plant rather than deliberately cultivated due to its weedy nature.

common_name: Cuban Mint (Mojito Mint, Large-Leaf Heat-Tolerant Gulf South Spearmint)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Cuban Mint spreads by underground runners like other mints — plant in containers or with a physical root barrier to prevent spreading beyond intended areas.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Cuban Mint (also called Mojito Mint or Apple Mint hybrid) is Mentha x villosa — a hybrid mint between spearmint (M. spicata) and apple mint (M. suaveolens) that produces the distinctive large, crinkled, soft-textured, heavily aromatic leaves most closely associated with the traditional Cuban mojito cocktail. The broad, deeply textured leaves have a strong, clean spearmint fragrance with a sweeter, fruitier quality than standard spearmint — a flavor complexity that is particularly well-suited to the classic mojito (fresh Cuban Mint + lime + rum + sugar + soda) and makes excellent fresh herb tea. Cuban Mint's practical advantage over standard spearmint and peppermint for Gulf South gardeners is substantially better heat and humidity tolerance — where peppermint and even spearmint often melt out in the intense summer heat of zone 9, Cuban Mint produces reliably through Gulf South summers with consistent moisture and partial shade protection from afternoon sun. The large, broad leaves are easy to pick and produce abundantly. Spreads by vigorous underground runners in the mint family manner — grow in containers or with buried root barriers to keep contained. In zone 9, Cuban Mint may be semi-evergreen through mild winters or die back and return vigorously in spring. An indispensable herb for Gulf South gardeners who want fresh mint for mojitos, tea, and culinary use during the summer months.

plant_note: Root cuttings in water or moist mix and transplant after frost; in zone 9–11 plants overwinter but may die back to roots in zone 9 hard freezes.
directions: Propagate from stem cuttings 4–6 in long; cuttings root in 1–2 weeks in moist perlite or a glass of water and are far more reliable than seed. Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun to bright partial shade; Cuban oregano tolerates heat, humidity, and dry spells far better than Mediterranean oregano. The thick, succulent leaves have a pungent, oregano-like aroma intensified by thyme — use fresh in Caribbean, Indian, and Southeast Asian cooking. Remove flower spikes to keep the plant in vigorous vegetative growth; take a few cuttings before the first frost if growing as an annual.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings in tropical conditions; grow in high humidity with consistent warmth above 60°F; does well in containers brought indoors in cooler climates.
directions: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and grow in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade in tropical or subtropical gardens; cubeb is a spice pepper from Indonesia (primarily Java), its dried unripe fruits distinguished by a distinct 'tail' (the dried stalk) that gives it the alternative name 'tailed pepper.' The flavor is complex — peppery, slightly bitter, with eucalyptus, camphor, and allspice overtones distinctly different from black pepper. A major spice in medieval European and Arab cuisines and still used in Moroccan ras el hanout and in Indonesian, East African, and West African cooking. The unique flavor profile is winning new culinary attention as chefs explore historical spice traditions.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in a warm, partially shaded site; culantro prefers high heat and humidity.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface and press in lightly; germination can be slow and erratic, so sow generously and keep soil consistently moist and warm. Culantro thrives in partial shade and high humidity, performing well in spots too hot and bright for cilantro; its strap-like, serrated leaves have a much more intense cilantro flavor and hold up better in cooking. Thin seedlings to 9–12 in apart and keep soil moderately moist; the plant bolts to flower in dry or cool conditions. Harvest individual outer leaves at any time; one or two leaves substitute for a much larger amount of cilantro in sofrito, chutneys, and Caribbean stews.

subcategory: classic culinary and medicinal spice rhizome
plant_note: Plant fresh, plump ginger rhizome sections (each with at least one eye/bud) in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; culinary ginger is not fully sun-tolerant in hot climates — it performs best in morning sun with afternoon shade or dappled filtered light. Plant rhizome sections 2–4 inches deep and 8–12 inches apart. Harvest young ('green') ginger 4–5 months after planting or mature ginger after leaves die back (8–10 months). In zone 9 it may remain in the ground year-round as a perennial. Use supermarket ginger or specialist growers for seed rhizomes.
directions: Plant fresh, plump rhizome sections with viable buds in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade, keeping the rhizome section just below soil surface level; culinary ginger is the universal spice plant — one of humanity's most ancient, most widely used, and most globally traded spice and medicinal plants, native to tropical Asia (probably India or coastal southern China) but cultivated throughout the tropics for at least 3,000 years and now grown in tropical and subtropical regions of every continent. The rhizome (underground stem) is the harvested, used portion: the knobby, multi-branched, pale-tan to buff-tan fresh rhizome with its characteristic pungent-hot, warm-spicy, aromatic flavor and scent comes from the volatile oil compounds (primarily gingerol, shogaol, and zingerone) that also provide the medicinal properties (anti-nausea, anti-inflammatory, digestive). In the garden, it is a handsome, substantial plant reaching 3–4 feet — erect, reed-like stems with alternating, glossy, lance-shaped, aromatic leaves of deep green — with an attractively tropical, lush appearance. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it grows as a reliable perennial, the aerial stems dying back in winter and rhizomes resprouting each spring. Young (green) ginger can be harvested after 4–5 months (mild, juicy, less fiber); mature ginger after the leaves die back naturally (8–10 months, full pungency). One of the most rewarding home-garden edibles for partial-shade plots in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost; plants establish over the first season and overwinter as woody perennials.
directions: Culinary sage is a woody perennial with dusty gray-green leaves and a savory, aromatic flavor essential in the kitchen. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil, watering sparingly once established since it dislikes wet feet. Harvest leaves lightly the first year and more freely in following seasons. Prune in spring to remove dead wood and keep the plant compact and productive.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, even poor soil; culinary sumac is extremely drought-tolerant once established and does not need irrigation or fertilizing in most climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun; culinary sumac (Rhus coriaria) is the source of the brilliant deep-red, intensely tart spice used throughout Middle Eastern cooking as the primary acidifying agent before lemons became available. The dried, ground berries coat kebabs, top hummus, season fattoush salad, and form the backbone of za'atar spice blend. Harvest berry clusters (drupes) in late summer when fully red and dark but before rain softens them; dry completely before grinding. This species is distinct from the ornamental staghorn sumac (Rhus typhina) of North American gardens — culinary sumac is a Mediterranean species grown specifically for its tart, lemony fruit. The shrub is extremely drought-adapted and well-suited to zone 7–10 gardens.

plant_note: Surface-sow; needs cold and light.
directions: Surface-sow the dust-fine seed in fall, leaving it uncovered so cold and light can trigger germination. This tall native perennial was used by Indigenous peoples and early settlers as a liver remedy. Grow it in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade where the white flower spires shine in summer. Keep the roots evenly moist, as dry soil causes lower leaves to scorch. Harvest roots from established plants in autumn and dry for at least a year before use.

plant_note: Transplant rooted cuttings in spring into dry, lean, sandy, slightly acidic, very well-drained soil; avoid clay and enriched soils.
directions: Propagate from stem cuttings taken in late spring or summer rather than from seed, as germination is erratic and slow; root cuttings in clean sand and transplant rooted starts in spring into dry, lean, sandy, slightly acidic, very well-drained soil in full sun. Avoid clay, enriched, or moisture-retentive soils, as the species is endemic to sandy and gravelly river bars along the Big South Fork and upper Cumberland River system in Tennessee and Kentucky, where it is federally listed as threatened. Dense mats of wiry, upright stems bear tiny, needle-like, intensely rosemary-scented leaves and masses of small, pale pink to lavender, 2-lipped mint flowers in spring; the entire plant releases a strong fragrance when brushed. An outstanding native aromatic subshrub for rock gardens and sandy borders in zones 5-8 where its narrow habitat requirements of sharp drainage, lean soil, and full sun can be met.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–October in zone 9) or very early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; cumin is an annual that matures its seed crop in warm, dry weather (not humid) — zone 9 spring growing conditions are ideal, with the crop seeded and harvested before the humid summer arrives.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in fall or early spring; thin to 6 inches. Cuminum cyminum (cumin) is the annual herb whose seeds are the third most-consumed spice in the world after salt and black pepper — the warm, earthy, aromatic, slightly bitter cumin flavor is foundational to the spice profiles of Indian, Mexican, Middle Eastern, North African, and Turkish cuisines, appearing in curry powders, garam masala, chili powder, taco seasoning, hummus, and countless spice blends. The small (6–18 inch), slender, feathery-leaved annual herb native to Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean is rarely grown in North American home gardens, yet it is straightforward to grow in well-drained, dry, infertile soil in full sun in climates with warm, dry summers or cool, dry springs. In zone 9, fall planting produces spring harvest before summer humidity arrives. Harvest when seed heads turn brown and dry; cut stalks and hang to dry in paper bags, then thresh out seeds. Growing your own cumin produces seeds with fresher, more intense aroma than store-bought.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather; it bolts quickly in heat, so grow in spring and fall.
directions: Curled chervil, sometimes called French parsley, is a delicate cool-season herb with lacy leaves and a subtle anise flavor. Sow directly in cool weather and part shade, as it bolts rapidly in summer heat. Make successive sowings in spring and again in late summer for fall harvests. Snip the tender leaves young and use them fresh, since their flavor fades when dried or cooked long.

plant_note: Mucilaginous seed; do not presoak, sow dry on moist medium indoors.
directions: Sow curled cress seed dry and densely on a moist tray, since it forms a gel coat that makes presoaking impractical. It germinates almost overnight, so uncover early and give it bright light to keep growth compact. Mist frequently to keep the fine seedlings hydrated without drowning them. Snip the fast-growing, peppery peppergrass greens within a week to ten days for a bold, spicy garnish.

plant_note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; Curly Mint bears tightly ruffled, crinkled leaves with a milder flavor than plain spearmint.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Curly Mint bears distinctively tightly ruffled, crinkled leaves that give it strong ornamental and textural interest in an herb garden beyond its milder, softer spearmint flavor compared to plain spearmint, useful for garnishing where a decorative leaf shape is wanted. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage.

plant_note: Sow in early spring; soaking seed overnight speeds notoriously slow germination.
directions: Curly parsley is a hardy biennial grown as an annual for its bright green, frilled leaves used as garnish and seasoning. Germination is slow, so soak seed overnight and keep the soil consistently moist. Harvest outer stems first and the plant will keep producing from the center. In milder zones it overwinters and flowers the second year, at which point flavor declines.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock after last frost; in zone 9 protect with frost cloth during freezes — the woody stems can survive brief dips to 28°F once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; curry leaf shrubs grow slowly at first but accelerate once established in a warm zone 9–11 site. Fresh leaves are essential to South Indian cooking and release their aroma only when heated in oil — dried leaves are a poor substitute, so growing your own is worthwhile. Harvest by snipping young branch tips regularly, which encourages dense new growth; remove flower clusters as they appear if you prefer to maximize leaf production. Mulch heavily through zone 9 winters and wrap the trunk if temperatures below 28°F are expected for more than a night or two.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost; easier to propagate from cuttings than from slow and variable seed.
directions: Take 3–4 in softwood cuttings in late spring, strip lower leaves, and insert into sharp-draining propagating mix; roots develop in 3–4 weeks. The silver-needle foliage has a striking curry-like aroma but this herb is primarily used for its fragrance rather than as a true culinary spice — a leaf or two can be added to braises or soups but should be removed before serving. Plant in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; it is native to Mediterranean coastal cliffs and thrives under hot, dry conditions. Trim lightly after the yellow button flowers fade to keep the plant tidy; in zone 7 mulch over winter or take cuttings as insurance against hard freezes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification over winter; press seeds onto the surface of short-mown or lightly raked soil and leave uncovered, as seeds need light and moisture contact to germinate well in spring.
directions: Broadcast seeds onto short, closely mown grass or lightly raked bare soil in fall, pressing them into good contact without covering; winter cold stratifies the seed naturally so that germination occurs reliably the following spring. Cut-leaved Selfheal thrives in dry, calcareous grassland conditions — once established it is drought-tolerant and competes well among low meadow plants, making it an excellent candidate for wildflower turf or lawn alternatives. Allow flower heads to mature and set seed before mowing so the colony can spread and self-sow; mow no lower than three inches to protect the low rosettes. Where it co-occurs with common selfheal (Prunella vulgaris), expect natural hybridization producing intermediate flower colors ranging from white to pale lilac.

plant_note: Grown for leaves, not stalks.
directions: Surface-sow indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, keeping the fine seed moist and lightly covered. This leafy celery is grown for its strongly flavored foliage rather than thick stalks. Transplant to rich, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade and never let it dry out. Harvest outer stems and leaves as needed, and the plant will keep producing all season. In mild winters it survives to provide an early spring cut, and it stores well dried.

plant_note: Root cuttings in late spring and transplant after all frost danger has passed; damiana is a subtropical shrub that needs consistent warmth to establish.
directions: Take 3–4 in stem cuttings in spring or summer and root in gritty, barely moist medium; damiana is easier and faster from cuttings than from the slow-germinating seed. Plant in sharply drained, sandy or rocky, poor soil in full sun — damiana is native to the dry shrublands of Mexico and the Caribbean and rots in moist, fertile conditions. In zones below 9, grow in containers and overwinter in a frost-free, bright location, watering sparingly. Harvest leafy stems and the small yellow flowers throughout the growing season, drying them for use in traditional Mexican tonic teas and liqueur preparations.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and set out in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Dan Shen is grown chiefly for its distinctive brick-red roots, harvested after the plant has grown for at least one full season.
directions: Start transplants indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and set out in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Dan Shen is grown chiefly for its distinctive brick-red roots, harvested after the plant has grown for at least one full season. Soft, hairy, deeply veined leaves and spikes of violet-blue, two-lipped flowers typical of the sage family top a clumping perennial whose real value lies underground, in thick, branching roots with a distinctive brick-red exterior that is a cornerstone herb of traditional Chinese medicine, long used to support healthy circulation. It is easy to grow in ordinary garden conditions much like culinary sage relatives, tolerating a range of soils, and the showy flowers are an added bonus for pollinators even where the roots are not harvested. Dig roots for use in fall after two or more years of growth, when they have reached a useful size, and cut back spent flower stalks after bloom to keep the clump tidy.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil is workable; also sow in late summer for autumn and early spring harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in deep, loose, well-drained soil; cultivated broad-leafed varieties produce larger, more tender leaves than typical lawn weeds. Blanch developing rosettes under a cover for 1–2 weeks in spring to produce milder, less bitter leaves for salads. All plant parts are useful: young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, flowers are made into wine or fritters, and the taproot is roasted as a coffee substitute or used fresh in bitter-tonic preparations. Harvest roots in autumn of the second year when they are largest and most concentrated in the liver-supportive compound taraxacin.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost in well-drained, humus-rich starting mix; transplant to a shaded position with trellis support after last frost. The plant needs 3-5 years from seed to produce roots large enough for medicinal harvest.
directions: Plant in moist, deep, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade with a trellis or fence to climb; dang shen is one of the most important tonic herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine, used as an energy-building adaptogen and substitute for the more expensive Panax ginseng. The twining, climbing vine produces pale greenish-yellow bell-shaped flowers with purple-veined interiors in summer. The thick, fleshy taproot is harvested after 3-5 years and used in soups, teas, and tonic preparations throughout China, Korea, and Japan. Modern research confirms adaptogenic compounds in the root that support energy and immune function. The plant dies back in winter and re-emerges from the root in spring. Grow in a position where the deep taproot will not be disturbed.

plant_note: Purple foliage; ornamental and edible.
directions: Sow indoors 4-6 weeks ahead of the last frost and keep flats warm and bright to preserve rich color. This deep-purple basil adds dramatic color to vinegars, salads, and garnishes. Transplant after frost into full sun, where strong light intensifies the burgundy pigment. Pinch regularly to build a dense plant and prevent early flowering. Harvest young leaves for the most vivid color and infuse them into oils or vinegars.

common_name: Delfino Cilantro (Feathery Fernlike-Leaf Cilantro Variety for Ornamental and Culinary Use)
plant_note: Direct sow only — cilantro does not transplant successfully; sow in early spring several weeks before last frost or in fall in zone 9. In zone 9, the best planting window is October–November for fall-winter leaf production (the optimal season), with a short spring crop sown February–March before bolting from summer heat. Delfino Cilantro is a named variety selected for its distinctively different leaf form: rather than the typical broad, flat lobed cilantro leaves, Delfino produces very finely divided, feathery, fernlike foliage similar in appearance to dill. The flavor is classic cilantro with the same citrus-soapy aromatic profile of standard varieties; the texture and appearance are quite different and make Delfino particularly attractive for garnishing, edible landscaping, and situations where visual distinction from standard flat-leaf cilantro is desired. Delfino also shows reasonably good slow-to-bolt characteristics.
directions: Direct sow thinly in cool soil; thin to 6 inches. Harvest young leaves before bolting for best flavor; allow some plants to flower for seed production. Delfino Cilantro is a named selection of Coriandrum sativum distinguished by its unusual leaf morphology: while standard cilantro produces broad, somewhat lobed leaves resembling flat-leaf parsley at the base, Delfino produces very finely divided, thread-like foliage that resembles dill or fennel fronds far more than it resembles conventional cilantro. This leaf form is caused by a genetic trait affecting leaf development — Delfino consistently produces only the finely dissected leaf form throughout its growth, never the broad lower leaves typical of standard cilantro. The flavor and aroma are identical to standard cilantro: the same distinctive volatile compounds (primarily linalool and various aldehydes) that give cilantro its characteristic citrusy, herbaceous, and for some people soap-like quality are present in the same proportion in Delfino as in standard types. The feathery foliage has several culinary advantages: the very fine texture integrates easily into salads and garnishes, the delicate fronds are visually striking on finished dishes, and the fine cut of the leaves releases aromatic compounds easily when torn or chopped. For zone 9 gardeners growing cilantro in fall and early spring gardens, Delfino provides a visually distinctive alternative to standard varieties with the same flavor and culture requirements. Like all cilantro, Delfino is a host plant for black swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, which feed on cilantro, dill, fennel, and related Apiaceae plants.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost in well-drained, humus-rich starting mix; transplant to a shaded position with a trellis or fence to climb after last frost. Roots take 3-4 years to size up for harvest.
directions: Plant in moist, deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with a trellis, fence, or shrub to climb; deodeok, known as sha shen in Chinese medicine, is a twining East Asian vine grown for its thick, aromatic, ginseng-scented taproot, which is a well-known ingredient in Korean cuisine, roasted, grilled, or pounded and seasoned as a savory side dish (deodeok-gui and related preparations) and also used in traditional herbal tonics. The vine climbs by twining stems clothed in soft blue-green leaves and produces distinctive bell-shaped flowers, greenish outside and dramatically mottled maroon-purple within, that hang facing downward through mid to late summer. Unlike its close relative dang shen (Codonopsis pilosula), deodeok's root has a stronger, more resinous, distinctly aromatic flavor that intensifies with the plant's age, and roots are traditionally harvested at three years or older for the best culinary and medicinal quality. Grow it where the deep root can develop undisturbed, and provide support for the twining vine to climb.

plant_note: Transplant bare-root divisions or rooted stem sections into moist, humus-rich soil beneath a dense forest canopy in fall or early spring.
directions: Site in deep, consistently moist shade beneath conifers, mimicking its native Pacific Northwest old-growth understory habitat. Wear gloves when handling, as stems and leaf undersides bear dense sharp spines. Bark and root bark are traditionally harvested from mature stems in fall for medicinal preparations, similar in use to Panax ginseng. Grows slowly and spreads by layering sprawling stems that root where they touch moist duff; leave leaf litter in place as mulch rather than clearing it away.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost in very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, low-fertility soil in full sun in zone 8–11; Devil's Claw is a low-growing, trailing perennial native to the Kalahari Desert and Namib-Karoo dryland of southern Africa, grown for its secondary storage tubers — one of the most widely sold botanical medicines in Europe for osteoarthritis, lower back pain, and inflammation — and characterized by spectacular claw-shaped, woody seed pods evolved for dispersal by large mammals.
directions: Direct sow in very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, low-fertility soil in full sun; Harpagophytum procumbens is a dryland plant that requires excellent drainage and tolerates severe drought — overwatering or clay soils cause root rot; grow in raised beds or sandy garden beds with no supplemental fertilizer. Harpagophytum procumbens (Devil's Claw, Grapple Plant, or Duiwelsklauw) is a low-growing, trailing, tender perennial in the Pedaliaceae family native to the Kalahari Desert, Namibian desert, and Karoo drylands of Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa — an extraordinarily specialized dryland plant adapted to survival in some of the harshest desert soils in the world. The plant is named for its grotesque, claw-covered, woody seed pods — each pod festooned with multiple long, hooked claws designed to attach to the hooves and legs of large mammals (springbok, wildebeest, zebra) for long-distance dispersal across the desert. The secondary storage tubers (secondary roots) are the medicinal part — harvested commercially in Namibia and Botswana — containing harpagoside, 8-p-coumaroylharpagide, and related iridoid glycosides with well-documented anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties. Devil's Claw root extract is one of the top three best-selling botanical medicines in Germany and France, prescribed for osteoarthritis, lower back pain, and musculoskeletal inflammation. Wild harvesting is regulated; cultivated production increasingly supplies European pharmaceutical markets.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Devotion is a Rutgers-bred Genovese-type basil selected for strong tolerance of downy mildew, the fungal disease that quickly ruins basil plantings in the humid Gulf South.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Devotion is one of the Rutgers University downy-mildew-tolerant Genovese basil releases, bred specifically to resist Peronospora belbahrii, the airborne fungal pathogen that causes basil downy mildew and can wipe out an entire planting of standard Genovese basil within days during warm, humid, or rainy weather — a near-annual problem for basil grown along the Gulf Coast. It retains the classic large, glossy, sweetly aromatic Genovese leaf and flavor prized for pesto and Italian cooking, without sacrificing disease resistance for flavor. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and productive all season; harvest leaves anytime once the plant is established, picking in the morning for the best essential oil content.
