plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant into rich, well-worked soil once nights stay above 45°F; roots are dug in fall for processing.
directions: Grow in loose, deeply worked, fertile soil so the thick tuberous roots can expand without obstruction, and site in full sun to light afternoon shade in hotter climates. The plant forms a low rosette of hairy, wrinkled leaves and sends up spikes of tubular reddish-purple flowers reminiscent of foxglove, its distant relative. Fresh root or steamed, dried root is the part used in traditional Chinese herbalism, and mature roots are typically harvested in autumn after two full growing seasons. Keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged, and mulch in colder zones since the crown can be marginally hardy where winters are severe.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; succession-sow every 2–3 weeks for a continuous leaf harvest.
directions: Broadcast seeds thinly over a weed-free bed and cover with 1/8 in of soil, firming gently; dill needs light to germinate well. Avoid transplanting—the long taproot is easily damaged. Stake tall plants if the site is windy, and keep irrigation steady to delay the rush to flower. Snip feathery fronds once the plant has at least five leaf sets; for seed, allow umbels to go fully brown before cutting.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer, or start from seed indoors; dittany of Crete requires sharply drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. It is sensitive to overwatering and wet winter conditions. In zones 8–10 it is perennial; in colder climates, grow as a container plant brought indoors before frost or overwinter cuttings.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; dittany of Crete is one of the most distinctive and ornamental of all Mediterranean herbs — a native of the rocky hillsides of Crete and the eastern Aegean producing small, rounded, densely woolly, silver-gray leaves so thickly covered with white hairs that the plant appears to be made of pale velvet or silver felt, with a warm, spicy aromatic scent when brushed. In summer it produces nodding clusters of small pink to purple flowers surrounded by overlapping, hop-like, purple-green bracts in elegant dangling clusters — both the foliage and flowers being remarkably ornamental. It has been valued since antiquity: Aristotle described wild goats eating it to remove arrows from wounds; it appears in Virgil and Pliny as a wound herb; and it is still used in Cretan herbal tea and liqueur (Cretan digestif). Outstanding as a trailing container plant where the woolly, nodding flower clusters can cascade over the pot edge. Related to culinary oregano but much more ornamental than culinary.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into very well-drained, lean, gritty, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Doerfler's thyme forms a dense, low, silvery mat prized as much for its felted foliage as for its flowers.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; Doerfler's thyme forms a dense, mat-forming carpet of small, gray-green, softly hairy leaves that give the foliage a silvery, felted appearance distinct from smoother-leaved culinary thymes. Clusters of small, rich pink to rose-lilac flowers cover the mat in late spring to early summer, drawing bees heavily and creating a striking two-toned effect against the silvery foliage. Like other creeping thymes, it tolerates light foot traffic and is well suited to planting between stepping stones, along path edges, or cascading over a low rock wall, releasing a mild aromatic scent when brushed or stepped on. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which shortens its life.

common_name: Dolce Fresca Basil (AAS-Winning Compact Genovese Basil)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Dolce Fresca is a compact, slow-to-bolt Genovese-type basil bred to hold a tidy, dense mounded shape through the season in beds or containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a container on a sunny patio. Dolce Fresca is an AAS-winning Genovese-type basil bred for a naturally compact, dense, dome-shaped habit and slower bolting than standard Genovese basil, so it holds its productive shape and classic sweet, clove-and-anise basil flavor for a longer stretch of the season without becoming leggy or rushing to flower. Its tidy size makes it especially well suited to containers, window boxes, and small kitchen gardens where a full-size Genovese plant would sprawl. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove any flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and delay bolting further; harvest leaves anytime once the plant is established, picking in the morning for the best flavor.

plant_note: Use fresh seeds — angelica seeds lose viability quickly. Cold-stratify for 2-4 weeks before sowing indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Transplant to deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade. Roots are harvested in fall of the 3rd year.
directions: Plant in deep, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; dong quai is one of the most important herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine and ranks among the top-selling botanical supplements globally. The fleshy taproot, harvested in the fall of the third year of growth, has been used for over 2000 years in Chinese medicine primarily for women's reproductive health — regulating menstruation, easing menopausal symptoms, and treating anemia — earning the common name 'female ginseng.' Modern research confirms phytoestrogenic and blood-moving compounds in the root. Use only under guidance of a healthcare professional as it interacts with blood-thinning medications. The plant is a biennial to short-lived perennial that dies after flowering; remove flower stalks as they appear to extend the life of the root. Partial shade and consistent moisture are essential.

common_name: Doone Valley Thyme (Gold-Variegated Lemon-Scented Creeping Thyme)
plant_note: Plant divisions or small plugs in spring in well-drained soil; Doone Valley is a low, spreading lemon thyme selection with gold-flecked foliage that takes on deeper bronze-red tones in cool weather.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Doone Valley thyme is a low, mounding, spreading lemon thyme cultivar with dark green leaves speckled and edged in gold that flush deep bronze-red in cool fall and winter weather, giving it strong multi-season ornamental interest beyond its culinary use. The foliage carries a distinct lemony fragrance and flavor, milder and more citrusy than common thyme, and is good for teas, poultry and fish dishes, and infused oils and vinegars. Small pale lilac flowers appear in early summer and attract bees. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and encourage fresh new growth, and avoid heavy, wet soils, which lead to crown rot.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or start indoors in spring, into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; dotted horsemint is native to coastal dunes and sandy prairies and thrives in poor, dry, sandy soil, declining in rich, moist garden beds.
directions: Plant in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established and one of the best late-summer nectar plants for a huge diversity of native bees and wasps. Monarda punctata (dotted horsemint, or spotted beebalm) is a striking native mint-family perennial with an unusual bloom structure quite different from typical bee balm: pale creamy-yellow flowers marked with fine purple spots are packed into tight whorls stacked in tiers up the stem, each whorl subtended by showy, pale pink to lavender bracts that provide much of the plant's ornamental color and persist attractively after the small flowers fade. The strongly aromatic, thymol-scented foliage was traditionally used by Indigenous peoples and early American settlers as a source of thyme-like oil and as a folk remedy. In late summer, the plant becomes a genuine pollinator magnet, attracting an exceptional diversity of native bees, wasps, and other beneficial insects, more so than almost any other native perennial. An outstanding, easy-care choice for a dry, sunny pollinator garden or sandy coastal planting, zone 4–9.

plant_note: Set out rooted divisions or nursery plugs in spring, since 'Flore Pleno' rarely sets viable seed and is propagated vegetatively to keep its fully double flowers true; plant into well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.
directions: Plant divisions into well-drained soil and water them in well, then let the low, apple-scented foliage knit into a dense mat over the season. Unlike the single-flowered species, 'Flore Pleno' produces fully double, button-like white blooms that are especially prized for drying into chamomile tea and for scenting chamomile lawns and garden seats. It tolerates light foot traffic and releases a sweet, fruity fragrance when brushed or mown, but it flowers less heavily in deep shade or overly rich soil. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in well-drained, dry to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or average soil in partial shade; downy wood mint is more drought-tolerant than hairy wood mint and grows in drier woodland conditions on rocky slopes, limestone outcrops, and dry open woodland throughout the eastern US.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, average to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; downy wood mint is a drought-tolerant native mint relative of dry, rocky, open woodlands, slopes, and wood margins across the eastern US, more tolerant of dry conditions than hairy wood mint and naturally at home on thin, rocky soils over limestone or sandstone. The whorled clusters of small, lavender to pale purple flowers with purple spotting are produced in midsummer and attract numerous small native bees, bumblebees, and clearwing sphinx moths. The leaves are fragrant with an oregano-mint scent and can be used as a culinary herb or brewed as tea. Spreads modestly by self-sowing in appropriate dry, rocky, shaded conditions. A refined, low-maintenance native herb for dry shade gardens, rocky woodland edges, and naturalistic settings in zones 4–8.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 2 to 4 weeks before the last expected frost date into well-drained, alkaline or neutral soil; barely cover seeds and thin seedlings to 18 to 24 inches once established.
directions: Sow seeds directly into their final position in early spring, 2 to 4 weeks before the last expected frost, in a sunny site with well-drained, lean, preferably alkaline or neutral soil; cover seeds very lightly and thin seedlings to 18 to 24 inches apart once they are large enough to handle. Downy Woundwort demands excellent drainage and suffers in heavy, wet soils — raised beds, gravel gardens, and south-facing slopes suit it well and show off the intensely felted, silver-white foliage to its best advantage. Plants flower in their second year, sending up stems of pale pink, whorled flowers that attract bees; leave a portion of the flower heads to ripen for self-sowing. Cut back dead stems in late winter and apply a grit mulch rather than organic material to keep the base dry and prevent crown rot during wet winters.

plant_note: Direct sow where it is to grow, since fennel resents transplanting.
directions: Direct sow seed where it is to grow, since fennel forms a taproot and dislikes being transplanted; keep the soil evenly moist. This bulbing fennel is easy to grow and slow to bolt, producing big, sweet, succulent bulbs that are excellent raw, added to soups and pasta, or charred on the grill. Hill soil around the swelling bases to keep them tender and white, and let the feathery fronds attract pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Drummond's false pennyroyal is a small, short-lived native mint of dry Texas and Southwest prairies and rocky slopes.
directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; Drummond's false pennyroyal is a small, wiry, intensely aromatic native mint relative found on dry limestone slopes and prairies from Texas through the Southwest, releasing a strong, minty-camphor scent when the foliage is brushed or crushed. Tiny, tubular, pale lavender to pink flowers appear in the leaf axils from spring through fall, adding subtle color to a dry rock garden or xeriscape planting rather than serving as a showy bedding flower. Historically used in folk medicine as a tea and traditional remedy, it is grown today mostly for its fragrance, drought tolerance, and value as a low, textural filler among rocks and gravel mulch. It is short-lived but self-sows readily in loose, undisturbed soil, so allow some plants to set seed each year to maintain a self-renewing population.

common_name: Dukat Dill (High-Oil European Dill Variety with Superior Foliage Flavor)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring several weeks before last frost; dill germinates in cool soil and does not transplant well (direct sow only). In zone 9, plant October–November for fall-winter production and February–March for a short spring crop before heat triggers bolting. Dukat has somewhat better slow-to-bolt characteristics than standard dill varieties, giving it slightly longer leaf production before it rushes to flower. However, all dill in zone 9 will bolt in summer heat — treat as a cool-season crop. For successive harvest, sow every 3–4 weeks. Dukat dill is valued for its exceptionally high essential oil content in the leaves (dill weed) compared to standard varieties, which translates to stronger, more aromatic flavor per unit of leaf material.
directions: Direct sow thinly in early spring or fall; thin to 6–9 inches. Harvest leaves before flowering for best flavor. Dukat Dill is a Danish dill variety (Dukat is a Danish word for a coin or ducat) developed and selected for high essential oil content in the leaves — the characteristic that translates to superior flavor intensity in dill weed, the fresh or dried feathery leaf material used in cooking rather than the seeds. All dill contains aromatic volatile oils (primarily carvone and limonene), but the proportion and intensity of these oils varies substantially among varieties, with Dukat consistently showing higher leaf oil content than standard American dill varieties in comparative trials. This difference is directly perceptible in the kitchen: Dukat dill weed has a stronger, more clearly identifiable dill aroma and flavor than standard varieties harvested at the same stage, making it preferable for recipes where dill flavor should be distinct without using large quantities of herb. The plants are tall (3–4 feet) with the characteristic ferny, blue-green dill foliage and produce yellow flower umbels at maturity. Dukat has also been noted for slightly more vigorous early leaf growth than standard varieties, giving it a head start on production. Like all dill, it is a favorite host plant for black swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, which feed on dill, fennel, parsley, and related Apiaceae members — planting dill in zone 9 gardens supports local butterfly populations while providing a culinary herb.

plant_note: Plant tubers or divisions in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, cool, humus-rich, loamy woodland soil in full to partial shade; dwarf ginseng grows naturally in moist, cool eastern deciduous forests and requires consistently moist, shaded, acidic, humus-rich conditions. Very slow to establish from seed — division of the small tuber-like root is more practical.
directions: Plant tubers or divisions in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, cool, humus-rich, loamy woodland soil in full to partial shade; dwarf ginseng is the smallest and least-known member of the ginseng family (Araliaceae) — a tiny, ephemeral woodland wildflower of cool, moist eastern deciduous forests from Nova Scotia and Quebec south to the Appalachians. Unlike its much larger relative American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius), dwarf ginseng produces a small, round, tuber-like root (rather than the large, spindle-shaped ginseng root). The small plant emerges early in spring, produces a tiny umbel of white flowers, sets seed, and dies back to the ground by midsummer — a spring ephemeral that completes its entire above-ground life cycle in just a few weeks. The small, peppery-tasting root was eaten raw by Cherokee, Iroquois, and other Indigenous peoples. An excellent, highly ephemeral native wildflower for naturalizing in deeply shaded, moist, acidic woodland gardens where it grows with hepatica, bloodroot, trout lily, and spring beauty.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings or divisions after the last frost into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this dwarf selection is propagated vegetatively rather than from seed to keep its compact, mat-forming habit true.
directions: This naturally compact sport of common winter savory forms a dense, low mat of narrow, glossy dark-green leaves rather than the upright woody shrublet of the species, making it well suited to edging paths, tumbling over container rims, and filling gaps between paving stones. The flavor is slightly milder and less resinous than standard winter savory but is used the same way, especially with beans, lentils, and slow-cooked meats. Shear lightly after the small white-to-lilac summer flowers fade to keep the mat tight and prevent bare, woody centers from developing. Because true dwarf plants must be propagated from cuttings or divisions to hold their compact form, start new plants vegetatively rather than from seed.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring into lean, sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; germination is often slow and uneven, and roots are dug for dye only after plants are well established in their second year.
directions: Dyer's alkanet is a low, bristly-leaved Mediterranean perennial in the borage family, distinct from the common bugloss and borage grown for their edible flowers, valued instead for its thick, dark-skinned taproot. The root bark contains alkannin, a red-purple pigment historically used to color wax, wood stains, cosmetic rouges, and oils, and still sought by natural-dye and soap-making hobbyists today. Small blue, forget-me-not-like flowers appear over a low rosette of hairy gray-green leaves in late spring. Roots are traditionally lifted in autumn of the second year, when pigment concentration peaks, then cleaned and dried whole for later dye extraction. Give it the leanest, driest, sunniest spot available; rich or damp soil produces lush foliage but weak, thin, poorly colored roots.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in early spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; dyer's chamomile thrives in poor, dry, sunny conditions and performs best in lean soil — rich, moist soil produces lush growth but fewer flowers and shorter plant life.
directions: Anthemis tinctoria is an upright, bushy perennial or biennial native to Europe and western Asia, producing deeply divided, fernlike, aromatic foliage and an exceptionally long succession of bright, golden-yellow, 1.5-inch daisy flowers from early summer through early fall; it is one of the most prolific and long-blooming of all yellow-flowered perennial herbs. Direct-sow seeds in early spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in a warm, sunny position; it performs best in poor, gritty, or stony soil and will decline in rich, moist conditions — lean soil extends plant longevity and promotes maximum flowering. The whole plant, especially the flowers, yields a clear, warm, golden-yellow dye when used with an alum mordant; it has been used as a natural textile dye throughout Europe and the Middle East for centuries and was a primary source of yellow for wool dyeing. Deadhead or shear plants after the first main flush of bloom to stimulate continued flowering; short-lived plants are easily renewed from self-sown seedlings.

plant_note: Nick or soak the hard-coated seed before sowing directly into lean, well-drained soil in full sun in spring; as a legume it resents root disturbance, so avoid transplanting older seedlings.
directions: Dyer's greenweed is a low, mounding, nitrogen-fixing legume shrub of European heaths and dry meadows, covered in bright golden pea-like flowers along its wiry stems from early to mid-summer. For centuries the flowering tops were cut and boiled to yield a strong yellow dye for wool and linen, which was traditionally over-dyed with woad or indigo to produce the deep green historically known as Kendal Green. The plant thrives on neglect in poor, lean, unamended soil and sulks or sprawls loosely if given rich ground or extra water. Cut back lightly after flowering to keep the low mound dense and to collect flowering tops at their peak dye potency; established plants are long-lived and need no routine feeding thanks to their own nitrogen fixation.

common_name: East Indian Lemon Grass (Tall Aromatic Culinary Lemon Grass for Tea and Cooking)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; East Indian Lemon Grass is more cold-sensitive than West Indian Lemon Grass (C. citratus) and less commonly available in nurseries — propagate from seed or divisions from existing clumps; in zone 9, mulch heavily in winter to protect the crown from brief freezes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; East Indian Lemon Grass (Cymbopogon flexuosus) is a tall, strongly aromatic grass from India and Sri Lanka — the primary source of lemongrass essential oil in commercial production worldwide and an excellent culinary and medicinal herb for Gulf South gardens where it grows as a warm-season perennial. The flavor and aroma are distinctly similar to but slightly different from West Indian Lemon Grass (C. citratus): both produce the characteristic bright, clean, citrus-lemon fragrance from the essential oil citral, but East Indian Lemon Grass is considered more intensely aromatic and is the preferred species for essential oil distillation. For culinary use, both species are suitable for Thai cooking, Vietnamese soups, herbal teas, and marinades — the inner stalks harvested and used the same way as standard lemongrass. East Indian Lemon Grass grows taller and more slenderly than C. citratus, reaching 4–6 feet with a more open, arching habit rather than the dense clumping habit of West Indian Lemon Grass — the differences in habit and aroma make it worth growing alongside the common species for comparison. In Gulf South zone 9, it grows as a warm-season perennial, potentially surviving mild winters with mulch protection but requiring replanting if hard freezes kill the crown. Fresh lemongrass harvested from the garden has a brighter, more vivid flavor than dried or frozen commercial lemongrass — a strong argument for growing your own in the Gulf South kitchen garden.

plant_note: Set out only after nights stay above 50F.
directions: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost in warm, moist flats and keep soil at 75-85F for reliable sprouting. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil once nights stay above 50F, spacing clumps well apart to allow fanning growth. Water consistently through the season and feed monthly with a nitrogen-rich fertilizer for lush stalks. In zones colder than 9, dig and pot up a division to overwinter indoors in a bright window. Harvest by twisting off outer stalks at the base once they reach pencil thickness.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Sow seed on the surface or just 1/8 in deep; cold stratification for 4–8 weeks significantly improves germination rates, especially for fresh seed. Plant in well-drained soil and avoid overwatering once established, as echinacea tolerates drought well. Roots are the primary medicinal part and are harvested in fall of the third or fourth year; flowers and leaves can be harvested earlier for teas and tinctures. Allow some seed heads to remain for self-seeding and to feed overwintering birds.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a brief cold stratification of 2–3 weeks can improve germination.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep indoors after a brief cold stratification period; plants grow into impressive clumps by their second year, eventually reaching 6–8 feet tall. Plant in moist, deep, fertile soil as this large plant develops an extensive root system that benefits from ample space. Harvest the thick, inulin-rich roots in autumn of the second or third year, washing and slicing them before drying for respiratory-supportive preparations. The yellow daisy-like flowers appear in midsummer of the second year and are attractive to pollinators.

plant_note: Plant root divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; eleuthero is a hardy adaptogenic medicinal shrub of eastern Asian forests used for centuries in Chinese and Russian herbal medicine, with well-documented studies on its stress-adaptogenic properties.
directions: Plant root divisions or hardwood cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; eleuthero is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and tolerates drought once established. Eleutherococcus senticosus (commonly marketed as Siberian Ginseng, though not a true Panax ginseng) is a thorny, deciduous shrub of northeastern Asia that is one of the most studied adaptogenic medicinal plants; its root bark is used in clinical herbalism as a tonic to improve stress resilience, physical endurance, and immune function, with hundreds of published studies supporting its use in Russian and Chinese traditional medicine. The dried root bark is made into tea or tincture; harvest bark from roots of 3–5 year old plants in autumn. The plant is fully hardy, grows readily in cool northern climates, and is far easier to cultivate than true ginseng. Note: consult a qualified herbalist before medicinal use.

plant_note: Plant divisions or small plugs in spring in well-drained soil; Elfin Thyme forms an extremely dense, low mat and is often used between stepping stones or as a lawn substitute in small areas, tolerating light foot traffic once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Elfin Thyme is one of the smallest and slowest-growing creeping thyme cultivars, forming an extremely dense, tight, mossy-textured mat only an inch or two tall that is prized for planting between stepping stones, in rock garden crevices, and as a miniature lawn substitute in small, well-drained areas. Tiny pink flowers appear in early summer, drawing bees, and the foliage releases a mild thyme fragrance when brushed or lightly stepped on. Because it is slower and more compact than most creeping thymes, it is best used in smaller, well-defined spaces rather than as a large-scale groundcover, where faster-spreading thyme cultivars are more practical. Established plantings are drought-tolerant and need very little care beyond an occasional light shearing after flowering to keep the mat tidy.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has fully passed into well-drained, alkaline soil.
directions: Surface-sow seeds and keep barely moist; germination is slow and uneven, so starting from cuttings or divisions is often more reliable. Plant in fast-draining, lean soil — rich or wet conditions promote rot and weak growth. Prune plants back by about one-third after the first flush of blooms to keep growth compact and encourage a second flowering. Harvest flower spikes just as the buds begin to open, bundling and hanging upside down in a warm, airy space to dry for sachets, culinary use, and aromatherapy.

plant_note: Seed needs light and cold stratification for best germination; set out after frost danger passes.
directions: This tall, old-fashioned English lavender is intensely fragrant and prized for sachets, potpourri, and cut or dried arrangements. Start seed indoors in a light, well-drained mix, as germination is slow and benefits from a few weeks of cold stratification before sowing. Give plants full sun and sharp drainage; lavender resents wet feet and thrives in lean, alkaline soil. Space transplants well for air circulation and shear lightly after bloom to keep plants compact and productive.

plant_note: Surface-sow tiny seed and keep evenly moist until seedlings establish.
directions: English thyme offers a subtle, woodsy flavor that suits a wide range of dishes and is a key component of bouquet garni. Start seed indoors and barely cover, since the seed is fine and needs some light to sprout; transplant to a sunny, well-drained bed after frost. This drought-tolerant perennial forms a low, spreading mat with small leaves and edible flowers that draw pollinators. Harvest sprigs regularly to encourage bushy growth and avoid overwatering, which can rot the crown.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost once soil has warmed; epazote self-seeds prolifically once established.
directions: Surface-sow the tiny seeds by pressing them gently into soil without covering, as they require light for germination; thin to 12–18 in. Epazote is remarkably drought-tolerant once established and thrives in lean, well-drained soil; rich, moist conditions encourage excessive growth. Deadhead regularly to control self-seeding, which can be invasive in warm climates. Harvest young stem tips throughout the season; the pungent, resinous flavor mellows somewhat with cooking.

plant_note: Warmth-loving; do not set out until nights stay above 50 F.
directions: This columnar basil grows into an upright herbal tower of deep, glossy emerald leaves, making it as ornamental as it is useful. It delays flowering up to twelve weeks longer than standard types, so plants keep producing tender leaves without the flavor decline that comes with bolting. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant only after the soil has thoroughly warmed. Its compact, non-branching habit suits patio pots and small beds; harvest leaves often and provide steady moisture and full sun.

common_name: Everleaf Thai Basil (Non-Flowering Extended-Harvest Thai Basil)
plant_note: Everleaf Thai is a non-flowering hybrid selected to hold classic anise-clove Thai basil flavor and columnar growth without bolting to seed, extending the usable harvest window compared to standard Thai basil.
directions: Start seed indoors or transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes. Part of the Everleaf breeding series that also produced Everleaf Emerald Towers, this Thai-type basil carries the classic anise-clove flavor and purple-tinged stems and flower bracts of traditional Thai basil, but its non-flowering habit means the plant keeps producing fresh, flavorful leaves for weeks longer than seed-setting types before quality declines. The upright, columnar growth habit also makes it a good choice for narrow spaces and containers. Harvest by cutting whole stem tips, which encourages continued branching and leaf production through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Extrakta was bred for an unusually high essential oil content, giving it a more concentrated, robust oregano flavor than typical culinary oregano.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; oregano flavor intensity is strongest when grown a bit lean rather than heavily fertilized. Extrakta was selected for an unusually high concentration of essential oils in its leaves, giving a bolder, more pungent, more robustly flavored oregano than many ordinary culinary strains, prized by cooks who want maximum flavor impact from a smaller amount of fresh or dried herb. The compact, mounding perennial forms a tidy clump well suited to an herb garden border or container. Harvest leaves and stems regularly through the growing season, and for the most concentrated flavor for drying, cut just before the plant flowers, when essential oil content peaks.

subcategory: culinary herb bred for essential-oil content
plant_note: Transplant seedlings or rooted cuttings after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; avoid rich, wet ground, which shortens the plant's life and dilutes flavor.
directions: Extrakta was selected as a commercial oil strain and carries a noticeably higher essential-oil content in its leaves than ordinary garden sage, translating into a bolder, more pungent flavor from the same amount of fresh or dried leaf. The narrow, upright green leaves are less broad than common culinary sage, and the plant sends up generous spikes of lilac-purple flowers in early to midsummer that draw bees well before most other kitchen herbs bloom. Because the flavor is more concentrated, cooks can use noticeably less of it per dish than standard sage, making it a good choice for drying and storage. Harvest leaves anytime through the season but cut for drying just before flowering, when oil content peaks.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth emerges; replant divisions at the same depth in well-drained soil and water in well to establish.
directions: Because Faassen's Catmint is a sterile hybrid, propagate it by dividing established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, or take stem cuttings in late spring; replant divisions promptly in well-drained soil in full sun. Site in average to lean, dry soil — fertile or overly moist conditions produce floppy, open growth rather than the neat mounding habit this plant is prized for. Shear the entire plant back by half immediately after the first heavy flush of bloom in late spring to promote a dense second flush of lavender-blue flower spikes through summer and into fall. Divide clumps every three to four years to keep them vigorous, as the center of older plants can die out over time.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; false daisy germinates readily in warm, damp soil and self-seeds freely once established, so it is best confined to a pot or a bed where its spread is welcome.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, near a pond edge, rain garden, or regularly irrigated bed; false daisy, known as bhringraj in Ayurvedic and Southeast Asian herbal traditions, is a sprawling, low-growing annual with small white daisy-like flowers, traditionally harvested for its leaves and juice, which are infused into hair oils and used in folk remedies for hair and scalp health, liver support, and minor wound care. It grows as an opportunistic weed of damp ditches, rice paddy margins, and pond edges throughout the warm regions of the world, which translates in the garden to a plant that thrives with regular moisture and spreads readily by both trailing stems that root at the nodes and abundant self-seeding. Harvest leaves and stems as needed through the growing season; the plant regrows quickly after cutting. Because it seeds around freely in consistently damp soil, site it where volunteer seedlings are easy to manage or grow it in a container to keep it contained.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in dry, sandy or rocky, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; false pennyroyal is an annual of dry, sandy, and rocky prairies and open disturbed areas of the central US. It self-sows freely where conditions are appropriate and can establish a self-maintaining colony.
directions: Direct sow in dry, sandy or rocky, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; false pennyroyal is a small, hairy (hispid — reflecting the species name) annual of dry, sandy, and rocky prairies and open areas across the central US, closely related to American pennyroyal (H. pulegioides). The plant has a similar pungent, camphor-mint aroma when crushed and has been used in similar ways as a mild insect repellent and flavoring herb. The small, lavender-blue, tubular flowers are produced throughout summer and are visited by small native bees. Like American pennyroyal, the plant self-sows freely in appropriate dry, lean, sandy conditions and can be left to naturalize in a dry wildflower or prairie garden. More common in the Great Plains and Midwest than eastern pennyroyal, occupying similar dry, disturbed, sandy-soil habitats.

plant_note: Propagate from softwood cuttings taken in spring, as seeds are slow and germination is erratic. Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy, acidic soil; false rosemary will not survive in poorly drained or heavy clay soils even for a short period.
directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained, dry, acidic soil in full sun; false rosemary is a stunning native shrublet of the Florida Panhandle and Gulf Coastal Plain that looks remarkably like culinary rosemary but is a separate genus in the mint family. The needle-like foliage has a pleasant resinous-minty fragrance when crushed, and the plant produces masses of lavender-pink flowers in spring. In its native Florida scrub habitat, it grows on the most droughty, infertile white sand where almost nothing else survives. It is a critically rare and threatened species in the wild due to habitat loss from development. Growing false rosemary in Gulf Coast gardens both provides an ornamental plant suited to the region's sandy soils and supports the conservation of a plant under severe pressure in the wild. Needs excellent drainage above all else — no standing water ever.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall before the ground freezes, or in very early spring, into loose, deep, sandy loam that encourages a long, straight taproot.
directions: Fang Feng is a cold-hardy, drought-tolerant Apiaceae grown in northern China for its aromatic taproot, a staple ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries. It produces finely divided, carrot-like foliage and flat umbels of small white flowers typical of the carrot family, followed by ribbed seed that loses viability quickly and should be sown fresh. Deep, loose, unobstructed soil is essential for straight root development, and the plant resents heavy clay, waterlogging, or salty soils. Roots are traditionally dug in the second year of growth after the foliage has died back, then dried for storage.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring (direct seeding preferred — fennel taproot does not transplant well) in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, full-sun soil; fennel is a Mediterranean perennial herb that produces aromatic, feathery anise-flavored foliage, edible yellow flower heads, and flavorful seeds — the fronds, seeds, and (in Florence fennel var. azoricum) the bulb are all culinary staples used across European, Indian, and Middle Eastern cuisines; avoid planting near tomatoes, kohlrabi, or peppers, which are allelopathically suppressed by fennel root exudates.
directions: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, lean, full-sun soil; does not transplant well due to taproot — sow in place; in zone 7+, often self-sows prolifically. Foeniculum vulgare (fennel or sweet fennel) is one of the most versatile and widely used culinary herbs in the world — a perennial (often treated as a biennial) Mediterranean herb producing delicate, feathery, bright-green to bronze-purple fronds, hollow stems, and golden-yellow flat-topped flower umbels followed by aromatic oval seeds. The distinctive, sweet-anise, warm-licorice flavor of fennel fronds, seeds, flowers, and the swollen stem base pervades cuisines worldwide: Italian sausage, Provençal bouillabaisse, Indian chai spice, Bengali panch phoron (five-spice), Indian paan, Middle Eastern bread, German sauerkraut, and Scandinavian aquavit all rely on fennel. Florence fennel (var. azoricum) produces the fat, crisp, sweet, anise-flavored stem base eaten as a vegetable across Mediterranean Europe. The dried seeds are one of the most important spices in Italian cuisine and make a classic digestive tea. COMPANION PLANTING CAUTION: Fennel produces allelopathic compounds from its roots that stunt the growth of tomatoes, peppers, kohlrabi, and many other vegetables — plant it in a separate herb bed away from the vegetable garden or at the garden perimeter.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; can also sow in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Soak seeds overnight to speed germination, then sow 1/2 in deep in rows and thin to 6 in apart; fenugreek prefers cool conditions and will bolt quickly in summer heat. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Days to maturity listed is for young leaf harvest; allow 3–5 months for seed pods to develop and dry if growing for seed spice. Harvest leaves at any time for use as a slightly bitter herb, and collect seed pods once they turn tan and feel firm.

plant_note: Sprout indoors year-round in a jar or tray; no garden bed needed.
directions: Fenugreek sprouts are easy to grow indoors and rich in vitamins A, B6, and C along with iron and potassium. Rinse seeds and soak overnight, then drain and rinse two to three times daily in a sprouting jar or tray. Keep them at room temperature out of direct sun and harvest in about four to seven days when small shoots appear. Enjoy the mildly bitter, nutty sprouts fresh in salads and sandwiches. Refrigerate after harvest to keep them crisp.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow October–February for fall and winter harvest. Fernleaf dill is a compact, bolt-resistant variety that stays in the leafy foliage stage 2–3 weeks longer than standard dill before bolting to flower. Ideal for container growing and small gardens.
directions: Scatter seeds thinly and press in lightly on the soil surface in full sun; Fernleaf is an All-America Selections winner dwarf dill variety that grows to only 18–24 inches (versus 4–5 feet for standard dill) with fine, feathery, dark blue-green foliage. The compact size makes it ideal for container growing, small herb gardens, and raised beds where standard dill would overwhelm its neighbors. It is also notably slower to bolt than standard varieties — where standard dill races to flower within 6 weeks, Fernleaf holds its leafy form for 8–10 weeks before setting flower heads. For zone 9 gardeners, this bolt resistance is particularly valuable since the cool season is short and every extra week of foliage harvest matters. Harvest the feathery leaves ('dill weed') regularly — cutting the tips encourages branching and delays bolting. Dill weed is used fresh in tzatziki, salmon dishes, deviled eggs, potato salad, and dressings; dried dill weed loses much of its fresh flavor. A second sowing in September provides fall dill.

common_name: Fernleaf Lavender (Egyptian Lavender, Cut-Leaf Lavender, Warm-Climate Lavender Species)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or take cuttings in spring; Fernleaf Lavender is much more heat-tolerant than English lavender (L. angustifolia) but significantly less cold-hardy — it is rated hardy to approximately 20–25°F, making it reliably perennial in zone 9 but marginally hardy in zone 8 and not recommended in zone 7 or colder without winter protection. In zone 9, Fernleaf Lavender behaves as a short-lived perennial, typically living 3–5 years, and may self-seed in favorable conditions. Unlike English lavender, which prefers the cool summers and moderate humidity of the Pacific Northwest or high-elevation mountains, Fernleaf Lavender tolerates warm, somewhat humid conditions better, making it a more practical lavender species for Gulf Coast gardens where English lavender often declines in the summer heat and humidity.
directions: Start seeds indoors or take cuttings; transplant to full sun, very well-drained soil. Cut back lightly after flowering. Fernleaf Lavender (Lavandula multifida), also known as Egyptian Lavender or Cut-Leaf Lavender, is a Mediterranean lavender species native to North Africa and southern Europe that differs from the familiar English lavender (L. angustifolia) in both appearance and adaptability. The most distinctive visual characteristic is the foliage: instead of the narrow, smooth gray-green leaves of English lavender, Fernleaf Lavender has deeply cut, ferny, bipinnate leaves that create a lacy, delicate appearance quite unlike other lavender species. The leaf texture is more reminiscent of carrot foliage than conventional lavender, and the overall plant has a lighter, airier appearance that makes it attractive as a foliage plant even when not in bloom. The flowers are produced on branched spikes (unlike the simple single spikes of English lavender) in the characteristic lavender-purple color, and the plant blooms repeatedly through the warm season when deadheaded regularly. The fragrance is lighter and less intense than English lavender — closer to rosemary than the heavy camphor-lavender scent of L. angustifolia — which some gardeners prefer as a more delicate aromatic quality. For zone 9 gardeners, Fernleaf Lavender fills an important niche: it provides the lavender aesthetic (gray-green aromatic foliage, purple flowers, bee attraction) in a form that tolerates warm summers and mild winters better than the standard English lavender types that often decline in zone 9's summer heat and humidity.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; press seeds onto the surface of the mix as they need light to germinate.
directions: Seeds are tiny and require light for germination — press them gently onto moist starting mix without covering. Once established, plants are quite drought-tolerant and spread readily by self-seeding. Shear plants back by half after flowering to maintain a tidy mound and encourage fresh foliage. The leaves are the medicinal part; harvest fresh leaves for tea or tincture — wear gloves as some people experience skin irritation from the foliage.

common_name: Field Horsetail (Common Horsetail, Scouring Rush Cousin)
plant_note: Divide rhizome sections in spring and plant in moist to wet, sandy to gravelly, poor soil; field horsetail spreads aggressively by rhizomes and is very difficult to eradicate once established — plant in contained beds, pots, or where naturalizing is acceptable. It thrives in moist disturbed soils.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, sandy, poor to moderately fertile soil in full sun; field horsetail (Equisetum arvense) is an ancient, primitive, spore-bearing plant (a living fossil) in the same lineage as 300-million-year-old coal forest horsetails, identifiable by its distinctive jointed, whorled, branched stems. The dried sterile stems are used medicinally as one of the highest-silica herbal remedies available — traditional use includes strengthening nails, hair, and connective tissue; teas made from dried stems are used for urinary tract support and bone health. Young fertile fronds (the brown, non-branched spring shoots) were historically eaten by Native American peoples. Caution: horsetail contains thiaminase and can cause thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency in livestock and humans if consumed in large quantities; use medicinally in moderate amounts only.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings or divisions after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; fiery costus is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.
directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings or divisions after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; fiery costus is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Fleshy, spirally arranged leaves wind distinctively up thick, jointed stems in the characteristic 'spiral ginger' habit, with small yellow-orange flowers emerging from cone-like bracts at the stem tips through the warm season. Native to Mexico and Central America, its fresh leaves are chewed or brewed as a folk remedy for blood sugar management in traditional Latin American and South Asian herbal medicine, earning it the common name insulin plant, though this use has not been established by rigorous clinical evidence and it should not replace medical treatment. Grown primarily for its striking spiraled foliage in a humid, shaded container or greenhouse setting, it propagates readily from stem cuttings rooted in water or moist soil.

plant_note: Sow or divide established clumps into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring, since this woodland-edge perennial prefers damp ground similar to a stream bank or ditch.
directions: Because related Scrophularia species contain cardioactive compounds, internal use should be approached cautiously and avoided by anyone with heart conditions without professional guidance. Sow or divide established clumps into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring, since this woodland-edge perennial prefers damp ground similar to a stream bank or ditch. The whole flowering plant, despite its strong odor, is traditionally made into a poultice or wash applied topically for minor skin irritations and historically taken to support lymphatic health.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 1–2 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; fingerroot grows naturally on the shaded forest floor and is one of the most shade-tolerant culinary gingers — it can be harvested as a root crop beginning approximately 4–6 months after planting when the leaves begin to die back.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fingerroot (Chinese ginger, Chinese keys, krachai) is a Southeast Asian tropical ginger widely used in Thai, Cambodian, and Indonesian cuisine, where the elongated, finger-like rhizomes (resembling a bunch of small, yellowish fingers, hence the common name) have a distinctive, slightly bitter-pungent, gingery-citrus flavor and aroma used to season curries, seafood dishes, stir-fries, and medicinal preparations. The rhizomes are harvested 4–6 months after planting, with a cluster of 6–12 finger-like secondary rhizomes branching from the central rhizome. The above-ground plant produces a compact rosette of attractive, oval, dark-green leaves with ornamental silver and green feathering similar to Kaempferia, and periodically produces small, pale-pink to white, orchid-like flowers at the leaf base. Fingerroot is medicinally important in traditional Southeast Asian medicine and is the subject of modern pharmaceutical research for its antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties. More shade-tolerant than most culinary gingers. In zone 10–12 it is a year-round perennial; elsewhere lift and store the rhizomes in winter.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start February–March and transplant March–April. Fino Verde tolerates more heat than large-leafed basil types and can continue producing through early summer in zone 9 before heat finally causes bolting. In zone 9 start a second planting in July–August for fall production. Pinch flower buds regularly to extend the productive leaf season.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Fino Verde is the classic Italian Greek-style dwarf basil used throughout southern Italy as a border herb, pot herb, and fresh seasoning for Caprese and Neapolitan-style dishes — producing a dense, compact mound of tiny, intensely fragrant leaves with a strong, clove-spicy basil aroma more concentrated than large-leafed sweet basil varieties. The extremely small, oval leaves (roughly the size of a fingernail) are traditionally used whole, directly stripped from the stem, and scattered over sliced tomatoes and mozzarella, into pasta, or onto pizza immediately before serving — the tiny leaf size means no chopping is needed. Fino Verde is the correct basil for traditional Neapolitan pizza making, where the small leaves are placed on the cooked pizza whole. The naturally compact, self-branching mound habit needs minimal pinching and forms a tidy, ornamental rounded shape in containers or along garden borders. The flavor intensity is noticeably higher per leaf than in large-leafed sweet basil.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 weeks early or direct sow after last frost; in zone 9 sow February–March and August for fall. Fino Verde's compact habit makes it ideal for containers, window boxes, and tight spaces in raised beds. Pinch stem tips regularly to maintain compact, bushy form and delay bolting.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Fino Verde is the classic compact Ligurian basil from the Italian Riviera, where the small, dark green, rounded leaves are the traditional variety used in authentic Genovese pesto. The tiny leaves (less than 1 inch) are more aromatic per unit area than large-leafed varieties — the essential oil concentration is higher in the smaller leaves — and the resulting pesto has a brighter, more complex flavor than pesto made with Genovese or large-leaf types. The compact, tidy, 12–18 inch plants are ideal for container growing and rarely need staking. Regular pinching maintains bushiness and dramatically delays bolting in summer heat. In zone 9 the small leaf size also makes it more heat-tolerant than large-leafed types in peak summer.

plant_note: Cold-sensitive; wait for warm soil.
directions: Sow indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, barely covering the seed and keeping flats around 75F. This tiny-leaved Italian basil naturally forms a dense round bush without much pinching. Transplant after all danger of frost into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Water evenly and harvest by clipping whole stems just above a leaf pair to keep growth bushy. Remove flower buds promptly to extend the productive leafy season.

plant_note: Also called Florence fennel; direct sow for the bulb, avoid transplant shock that triggers bolting.
directions: Florence fennel forms a swollen, anise-flavored bulb that can be eaten raw, sauteed, or added to soups and pasta, while its feathery leaves garnish fish. Direct sow into rich, moist soil since transplanting can stress plants and cause premature bolting. Keep the bed evenly watered and blanch the bulb by mounding soil around its base as it swells. Grow it as a cool-season crop, timing plantings for spring or fall to avoid the summer heat that pushes it to seed.

plant_note: Vigorous spreader; contain in beds or pots.
directions: Plant rooted divisions in moist to boggy soil in spring, ideally in a sunken container to curb its aggressive rhizomes. This Southeast Asian herb carries a distinctive tangy, fishy-citrus aroma used raw in Vietnamese and Chinese cooking. It thrives in partial shade with constant moisture and even tolerates shallow standing water. Cut back runaway runners to keep it from overtaking a bed. Harvest young leaves and tender shoots through the growing season, and mulch crowns in colder zones.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds or plant tubers in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Florida Betony spreads very aggressively by underground tubers and can become difficult to control in lawn and garden settings — intentional cultivation in a contained bed or pot is strongly recommended.
directions: Florida Betony is a native perennial herb of moist, disturbed habitats, roadsides, and open areas across Florida and the southeastern coastal plain, best known for its white, segmented, rattlesnake-rattle-shaped underground tubers — earning it the folk name 'rattlesnake weed' — that are crisp, sweet, and edible raw or cooked with a flavor reminiscent of water chestnuts. The small pink flowers produced in spring attract native bees and are mildly ornamental, though the plant is primarily known as a prolific lawn weed throughout the Southeast due to its ability to spread rapidly from fragments of its segmented tubers. As a cultivated edible herb, the tubers are harvested in late fall through early spring when the plant is dormant or growing slowly, cleaned, and eaten raw in salads, pickled, or stir-fried. Plant in contained beds to prevent uncontrolled spreading — once established in a garden, Florida Betony is virtually impossible to eradicate without repeated effort.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic, lean to average soil in full sun; Florida mountain mint grows naturally in moist pine flatwoods, flatwood pond margins, and open, moist sandy areas in Florida and adjacent Gulf Coast states.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic, lean to average soil in full sun; Florida mountain mint is an endemic species of Florida and the Gulf Coastal Plain, adapted to the subtropical growing conditions of zone 8–10 where more northern mountain mints fail in summer heat and humidity. Like all Pycnanthemum species, it produces small white flowers with purple speckling in dense, flat-topped clusters in summer — an absolute magnet for native bees, especially small sweat bees and Halictid bees that are specialist mountain mint pollinators. The crushed foliage is intensely minty-aromatic, similar to wild mint but more pungent. Mountain mints are among the top-ranked native plants for native bee diversity in scientific studies. This Gulf-adapted species fills the role of mountain mint in zones 8–10 where slender mountain mint (P. tenuifolium) is the most common alternative.

plant_note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions/nursery starts after frost danger passes; give it a sturdy trellis or arbor since the twining vine can reach 20+ feet once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil against a strong trellis, fence, or arbor, since this vigorous twining vine can climb 20 feet or more in a season once mature. The tuberous roots, harvested at three to four years or older, are the part traditionally processed and used in Chinese herbalism, most often after steaming with black beans; fresh raw root is generally considered unsuitable for casual use. Grown ornamentally for its glossy heart-shaped leaves and airy sprays of small white flowers in late summer, it tolerates a range of soils but appreciates consistent moisture while establishing. Cut back hard in late winter to control size, as unmanaged vines can become congested and woody at the base.

plant_note: Soak seed overnight and direct sow or transplant after last frost; parsley germinates slowly so keep the seedbed consistently moist.
directions: Forest Green is a tightly curled parsley selected for its dark, glossy foliage and dense, upright habit that holds its color and vigor later into the season than older curly strains. The deeply ruffled leaves are excellent for garnish work while still offering good fresh-eating flavor, milder than flat-leaf types. It performs well in containers and edging plantings thanks to its compact, uniform growth. Gardeners pick Forest Green when they want a curly parsley with richer color and better heat tolerance than standard moss-curled selections.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; forskohlii is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11.
directions: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; forskohlii is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. A relative of ornamental coleus and culinary sage, this fleshy-rooted perennial produces soft, aromatic, gray-green leaves and small blue-purple flowers, but is grown chiefly for its thick, tuberous roots, the source of the compound forskolin studied in traditional Ayurvedic medicine and modern dietary supplements. It tolerates poor, dry, sandy soil and drought better than ornamental coleus relatives, reflecting its native habitat on dry, rocky hillsides in India, and is easy to propagate from stem cuttings or root divisions. Harvest roots for use after the plant has grown for at least one full season, and protect from any frost, since both foliage and roots are damaged by freezing temperatures.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Foxtail bears unusually dense, congested, bottlebrush-like foliage giving each stem a distinctive fox-tail silhouette.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Foxtail bears unusually dense, tightly congested foliage packed along each stem, giving it a distinctive bottlebrush or fox-tail silhouette unlike the more open, spreading branch habit of most rosemary cultivars, making it a novelty specimen for collectors and a striking textural accent in the landscape. It needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, performing well in a container or raised bed where its unusual form can be appreciated up close. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape and encourage dense new growth.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring or fall in full sun with excellent drainage; Fred Boutin forms a large, dense, rounded mound and is often grown as an informal low hedge or border edge in California and Southern gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, in lean soil amended with coarse grit if the site tends to hold moisture; Fred Boutin is a lavandin hybrid, originally selected in California, prized for its exceptionally broad, dense, silvery-gray foliage mound and reliable production of long, richly fragrant purple-blue flower spikes in early summer. It is one of the more heat- and humidity-tolerant lavandins, making it a workable choice for Gulf South gardeners who have struggled with English lavender, and its large, uniform habit suits mass plantings and low hedges as well as single specimens. Shear the plant back by about a third right after flowering to keep growth compact and prevent the woody, sparse center that develops in unpruned lavenders over time.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; French lavender is less cold-hardy than English lavender and is damaged below 25 degrees F, making it suitable for zones 8-11 or as an annual in colder climates. In mild climates it blooms nearly year-round. Trim after each flush of bloom to keep compact and prevent legginess.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; French lavender is a distinctly different lavender species from English lavender, immediately recognizable by its linear, gray-green leaves with serrated, tooth-like margins along their length — the dentata name refers directly to these toothed leaf edges. The oblong flower spikes are topped with small, pale-purple, feathery bracts and produce a strong, somewhat medicinal-aromatic scent. In zones 8-11, it blooms nearly year-round — producing flowers in almost every month — making it by far the longest-blooming lavender species and an invaluable year-round pollinator plant in mild climates. Native to rocky Mediterranean hillsides and the Canary Islands, it thrives in the heat, drought, and alkaline soils of Gulf Coast and California gardens where English lavender can struggle with summer humidity. An excellent choice for low hedges, herb gardens, and companion planting in drought-tolerant borders where a near-perpetual lavender bloom is desired.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings or divisions in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; French tarragon does not produce viable seed and must be propagated vegetatively — purchase only plants labeled Artemisia dracunculus var. sativa to ensure the true French culinary variety.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; French tarragon is one of the defining herbs of classical French cuisine, with long, narrow, glossy dark-green leaves that carry an intense, distinctive anise-like flavor irreplaceable in béarnaise sauce, fines herbes blends, tarragon vinegar, and chicken dishes. It does not produce viable seed and must be propagated vegetatively — any plant sold as 'tarragon' from seed is the inferior Russian tarragon (A. dracunculus) with little flavor. Harvest by snipping stem tips regularly from spring through fall; the plant dies back to the ground in winter and re-emerges from the roots in spring. Divide established clumps every 2–3 years in spring, replanting vigorous outer portions to maintain flavor intensity.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring in well-drained soil; French Thyme is a narrow-leaved, milder-flavored culinary thyme selection favored by cooks for its delicate, refined flavor compared with broader-leaved common thyme.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which shortens the plant's life and dilutes flavor. French Thyme is a narrow, gray-green-leaved culinary thyme selection, distinguished from broader-leaved common thyme by its more delicate texture and milder, sweeter flavor, making it a favorite of classically trained cooks for bouquet garni, herbes de Provence blends, and dishes where a subtler thyme flavor is desired. The small, upright, woody-based subshrub bears tiny pale lavender-pink flowers in early summer that attract bees, and the foliage can be harvested year-round in mild climates, though flavor is best just before flowering. Shear lightly after flowering and again in late summer to keep the plant compact and prevent it from becoming leggy and woody; replace plants every 3-4 years, as thyme naturally declines with age.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Fuggle climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Fuggle is a classic English hop cultivar dating to the late 19th century, long the backbone of traditional English bitters and other cask ales, prized for its mild, earthy, woody, and slightly minty aroma that defines the classic English hop character as distinctly as Cascade defines American craft brewing. The vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring, climbing 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; cones ripen in late summer and should be picked when papery, aromatic, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for use. Fuggle prefers a cool, temperate, long-day growing season and struggles with the intense heat and humidity of Gulf South summers, so site it in the coolest, most open-air spot available and expect reduced yield and cone quality compared to traditional English or Pacific Northwest production.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes horizontally 1–2 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; kaempferia galanga is a ground-hugging, no-stem species with leaves that lie nearly flat on the soil and is one of the most shade-tolerant of all culinary gingers. It can be grown in containers and brought indoors in zones below 9.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally 1–2 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; kaempferia galanga is a small, ground-hugging tropical herb with flat, round, beautifully marked leaves and white flowers with a violet center that bloom at soil level; the aromatic rhizomes are a key flavoring ingredient in Indonesian, Thai, and Malaysian cuisine (known as kencur, cekur, or pro hom) and have a distinctive, camphor-pine-earthy aroma quite unlike other galangals. It can be grown in containers and brought indoors in zones below 9; in zone 9–10 it thrives in partial to deep shade under tropical canopy and goes dormant in winter.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions after last frost once soil has thoroughly warmed to at least 70°F; galangal needs extended warm conditions.
directions: Plant rhizome sections with at least one growing bud 2–4 in deep in rich, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade; galangal needs consistent moisture and high humidity to thrive. Unlike ginger, galangal has a distinctly peppery, piney, medicinal flavor with less sweetness, and is a foundational ingredient in Thai, Indonesian, and Malay cuisines. In zones below 9, grow in large containers that can be moved indoors before frost; the rhizomes are frost-sensitive but the plant can be stored dormant above 50°F in winter. Harvest rhizomes after 10–12 months when the foliage begins to yellow in fall, digging with care to take only what is needed while leaving part of the clump to regrow.

plant_note: Sow fresh seeds in late summer or fall (seeds require cold stratification and lose viability rapidly — sow within weeks of harvest); plant in moist, humus-rich, deep, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; angelica is a biennial or monocarpic perennial native to cool, moist northern European riverbanks and requires shade and moisture in southern gardens.
directions: Sow fresh seeds in late summer or fall in moist, humus-rich, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; seeds lose viability quickly — sow immediately after harvest. Angelica archangelica (garden angelica) is a magnificent biennial herb of Scandinavian origin — one of the most architecturally impressive herbs in cultivation, reaching 5–8 feet in its flowering year with hollow, bright-green, purple-tinged stems as thick as a wrist and enormous, compound umbrella-flower heads (3–6 inches across) of tiny yellow-green flowers beloved by beneficial insects, especially predatory wasps and hoverflies. The stems, leaves, roots, and seeds are all used in European cuisine and confectionery: the young stems are candied (crystallized angelica) as a traditional cake and pastry decoration; the leaves and seeds flavor aquavit, vermouth, Chartreuse, Bénédictine, and Cointreau liqueurs; the roots have been used medicinally for centuries in Scandinavian and central European folk medicine. The plant prefers cool, moist, shaded conditions and struggles in hot, humid southern summers — in zone 9, a shaded, moist spot with afternoon protection is essential. CAUTION: sap can cause phototoxic skin reactions.

plant_note: Fast; succession-sow every two weeks.
directions: Direct-sow thickly in cool weather, barely covering the seed, which sprouts within days. This peppery quick crop is harvested young as a spicy microgreen or baby salad green. Sow in succession every couple of weeks and keep the soil evenly moist to slow bolting. Provide partial shade in warm spells to extend the harvest window. Snip seedlings with scissors just above the soil once they reach a few inches tall.

plant_note: Sow in early spring; clumps return each year and produce edible white flowers.
directions: Garlic chives are a hardy perennial allium with flat, grass-like leaves that carry a mild garlic flavor, plus fragrant edible white flowers late in the season. Sow seed in clumps and harvest leaves by snipping from the outside as needed. The star-shaped blooms attract pollinators but self-sow prolifically, so deadhead if you want to limit spread. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

plant_note: Sow directly 4–6 weeks before last frost or transplant established divisions in spring.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep and keep soil moist; germination is similar to common chives but the flat, grass-like leaves have a distinct mild garlic flavor. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil and divide clumps every 2–3 years to prevent overcrowding and maintain productivity. Deadhead flowers promptly, as garlic chives self-seed prolifically and can become weedy. Harvest flat leaves at any height; older leaves become slightly tough but remain useful cooked.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in early spring around the last frost date in well-drained, fertile, moist soil in full sun; thin seedlings to 6-8 inches apart within clumps. Garlic chives self-seed prolifically — deadhead spent flower heads promptly to prevent unwanted spread throughout the garden.
directions: Allium tuberosum, commonly known as garlic chives or Chinese chives, is a vigorous, clump-forming perennial allium native to eastern Asia and widely cultivated throughout China, Japan, and Southeast Asia as both a culinary herb and a vegetable; unlike common chives, its flat, strap-like leaves carry a mild but distinct garlic flavor, and its star-shaped white flowers borne on upright scapes in late summer are both ornamental and edible. Direct-sow seeds in early spring in moderately fertile, consistently moist but well-drained soil in full sun; plants are more drought-tolerant than common chives once established but produce the most flavorful and abundant foliage with consistent moisture. Harvest leaves by cutting to within 1-2 inches of the ground, repeating every few weeks throughout the season; garlic chives are also commonly grown in the dark to produce blanched, yellow-etiolated leaves (jiu huang) prized in Chinese cooking for their tenderer texture and milder flavor. Deadhead the attractive white flower clusters before seeds ripen, as garlic chives self-sow prolifically and can become invasive in favorable garden conditions; established clumps benefit from division every 3-4 years in early spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Geisha Garlic Chives (AAS-Winning Late-Flowering Garlic Chives)
plant_note: Sow directly 4-6 weeks before last frost or transplant established divisions in spring; Geisha is an AAS-winning garlic chive bred with wider, more vigorous leaves and a later flowering time than standard garlic chives, which reduces the unwanted self-seeding that can make common garlic chives weedy.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and keep soil moist; germination is similar to common chives, but Geisha produces noticeably wider, more vigorous, flat, grass-like leaves with the same mild garlic flavor as standard garlic chives. Its key improvement, and the reason for its AAS award, is delayed flowering — by blooming later in the season than common garlic chives, it produces far fewer of the seed heads responsible for the prolific, sometimes weedy self-seeding that gives standard garlic chives a reputation for spreading where unwanted. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and divide clumps every 2-3 years to prevent overcrowding and keep production vigorous. Harvest the flat leaves at any height for kitchen use; older leaves become slightly tough but remain useful cooked into dishes.

plant_note: Classic pesto basil.
directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, covering lightly and keeping soil near 75F. This large-leaved Italian classic is the standard for pesto and Mediterranean cooking. Transplant into warm, rich soil in full sun only after all frost danger passes. Pinch out the growing tips at six leaves to force a bushy, high-yielding plant. Harvest whole stems above a leaf node and remove flower buds promptly to keep leaves tender and sweet.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost once soil and nights are warm.
directions: Genovese basil is the classic Italian pesto basil, prized for its large, tender, deeply fragrant green leaves. Sow once soil is warm and keep plants well watered in full sun. Pinch the growing tips regularly and remove flower buds to encourage bushy growth and prevent the leaves from turning bitter. Harvest often, as frequent picking keeps the plant producing until frost.

plant_note: Sow seeds in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Georgia basil is a naturally drought-tolerant native of the southeastern piedmont and coastal plain. It grows in the thin soils of pine flatwoods, open roadsides, and dry woodland edges and does not require supplemental fertilization. Self-sows in appropriate conditions to maintain a colony.
directions: Sow seeds in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Georgia basil is a small, aromatic, mint-family native wildflower of the southeastern Piedmont and coastal plain, native to Georgia, Alabama, South Carolina, and northern Florida, growing in pine flatwoods, open roadsides, and dry woodland edges. It produces slender stems with small, oval, hairy, basil-scented leaves and bears clouds of small, two-lipped, pink to lavender-pink flowers throughout summer into fall that attract small native bees, bumblebees, and butterflies. As a genuine southeastern native, it is superbly adapted to the hot, humid summers, periodic drought, and acid sandy soils of the Deep South where non-native mints often struggle. The strong basil-like fragrance from the crushed leaves is pleasant and distinctive. An excellent plant for native gardens, pollinator borders, and naturalized areas in zones 6-9 where it provides season-long bloom with minimal care once established.

plant_note: Surface sow; seed needs light to germinate and self-sows readily.
directions: German chamomile bears masses of small, daisy-like flowers whose apple-scented petals make a soothing tea and lend themselves to dried arrangements and crafts. Sow seed on the soil surface and press in lightly, since it needs light to germinate; it establishes easily and often self-sows for future seasons. Grow in full sun with average, well-drained soil and modest water. Harvest the open flower heads regularly to keep the plant blooming and to build up a supply for drying.

plant_note: Direct sow or set divisions in average, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed in spring; divide congested clumps every three to four years.
directions: Direct sow or set divisions in average, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed in spring, spacing clumps to allow the twisting, chive-like foliage room to fan outward. It tolerates light woodland-edge shade far better than most culinary onions and forms a tidy, long-lived edging clump rather than spreading aggressively. Leaves and the late-summer lilac-pink flower heads are both edible with a mild, chive-like bite, making it useful as both a garnish plant and a low border feature. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep vigor up.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–April for best establishment.
