In zones 10–12 it grows as a short-lived perennial; everywhere else it is grown as an annual. Seed is produced prolifically if a few flower stalks are allowed to mature.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; do not transplant until nights are reliably above 55°F as cold soil stunts growth.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix at 75–85°F; germination is swift when soil is adequately warm. Transplant after night temperatures stay above 55°F and pinch growing tips immediately to promote bushy growth. Regular pinching and removal of flower spikes prolongs the leaf harvest and delays bitterness; harvest leaves in the morning after dew has dried for the most aromatic result. Fresh or dried leaves are used in adaptogenic teas, Ayurvedic preparations, and as a sacred plant in Hindu tradition.

plant_note: Plant container stock or root divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in zone 7–11; Honduran Sarsaparilla is a thorny, woody, climbing vine native to the humid forests of Central America — Honduras, Mexico, Jamaica, and Guatemala — whose aromatic, starchy rhizomes are the authentic source of the flavoring used in traditional root beer and the original sarsaparilla beverages, and a valued traditional medicine for joint pain and skin conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with trellis or other support for climbing; Smilax ornata is adaptable to a range of conditions including full sun with consistent moisture and deep shade — mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and supply organic matter to the root zone. Smilax ornata (Honduran Sarsaparilla, Zarzaparilla) is a thorny, woody, perennial climbing vine in the Smilacaceae family native to humid tropical forests, forest edges, and riparian corridors of Central America — particularly Honduras, Guatemala, Mexico (Veracruz and Chiapas), Cuba, and Jamaica — where it climbs through the understorey using tendrils. The long, aromatic, reddish-brown rhizomes are the authentic source of 'true' sarsaparilla flavoring — the complex, vanilla-anise-wintergreen root flavor historically used in 19th-century American sarsaparilla beverages and root beer before artificial flavors displaced it. Medicinally, sarsaparilla root was a major export from Central America and the Caribbean to European pharmaceutical markets in the 16th–19th centuries for treatment of syphilis, psoriasis, rheumatism, and as a blood-purifying tonic. Modern phytochemical research confirms anti-inflammatory steroidal saponins (sarsasaponin, smilasaponin) in the rhizomes. The rhizomes are harvested by carefully digging, removing a portion, and replanting the crown; the vine regenerates. Excellent shade-tolerant medicinal vine for forest-garden and woodland-garden settings in zones 7–11.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; honewort self-sows freely and can naturalize in the shade garden. A perennial herb that dies back in winter and re-emerges in early spring from a taproot.
directions: Honewort is a shade-loving native edible herb, native to moist, rich woodlands and forest edges throughout eastern North America from Quebec to Florida and west to Kansas, producing tender, edible leaves and stems in spring and early summer that taste mildly of parsley and celery — used raw in salads or cooked as a pot herb. It is closely related to Japanese mitsuba (Cryptotaenia japonica) and can substitute for it in East Asian cooking; the young leaves are particularly flavorful in early spring. A self-seeding perennial that naturalizes freely in the shade garden, it fills in the difficult deep-shade spaces where most vegetables fail, providing a continuous harvest of tender greens from early spring to summer heat. Harvest outer leaves regularly to maintain plant vigor; allow some plants to set seed for natural self-renewal.

plant_note: Start from cuttings or transplants; in zone 9 plant March–May. Honey Stevia flowers profusely in September–October when days shorten — harvest leaves for drying before flowering begins, as the sweetness is highest in pre-flower leaves. In zone 9 the plant is a short-lived perennial, often surviving 2–3 years before requiring replacement. Provide light shade during the hottest summer weeks to prevent leaf scorch and premature bolting.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Honey Stevia is a named cultivar of stevia (Stevia rebaudiana) selected for a smoother, more honey-like sweetness compared to the standard species, which can have a distinct licorice-menthol aftertaste that some people find unpleasant in large quantities. The sweetening compounds in stevia (steviosides and rebaudiosides) are 200–350 times sweeter than sugar by weight, so only small amounts of fresh or dried leaf are needed to sweeten foods and beverages. The Honey cultivar has been selected to emphasize the rebaudioside-A fraction (which provides the cleaner, honey-like sweetness) relative to the stevioside fraction (associated with the bitter aftertaste) — making it the preferred variety for fresh leaf use in teas, lemonades, and fresh preparations where subtle sweetener differences are most noticeable. Leaves are used fresh in drinks and food, or dried and powdered for longer storage.

plant_note: Nick or hot-water scarify seed before sowing into lean, acidic, very well-drained fynbos-type soil in full sun; honeybush is slow to establish and is usually grown from nursery-raised seedlings rather than direct field sowing outside its native range.
directions: Cyclopia subternata is a wiry, yellow-flowered legume shrub of the Cape fynbos, one of several Cyclopia species harvested for honeybush tea, a naturally sweet, caffeine-free herbal infusion made by fermenting the cut, needle-like leaves and stems until they darken and develop the tea's characteristic honey-like aroma. Bright yellow, sweetly scented, pea-like flowers appear in spring and give the plant its common name as much as the finished tea does. As with rooibos and other fynbos legumes, deep, nutrient-poor, acidic sandy soil and excellent drainage are essential; rich garden soil or wet feet quickly kill it. Established plants are cut back periodically to encourage the fine new growth used for tea production. Best suited to a dedicated fynbos or Mediterranean-climate herb bed rather than a conventional border.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings ('rhizomes') horizontally 2–3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hops climbs vigorously (up to 20 feet in a single season) — provide a very strong trellis or support. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; hops is the perennial vine whose dried female flower cones ('hops') are the essential bittering and preserving agent in virtually all beer styles. Native to temperate North America and Europe, it is a vigorous, tendriled vine that dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15–20 feet on strings, trellises, or arbors. The soft green hop cones (strobiles) ripen in late summer; harvest when papery and fragrant, then dry immediately for use in home brewing. The young spring shoots emerging from the ground are edible as a vegetable, cooked like asparagus. The dried seed cones have traditional medicinal use as a mild sedative. Ornamental cultivars like 'Aureus' (golden-yellow foliage) are widely grown for their dramatic summer screening effect. Performs best in cool-summer climates (zones 3–7); struggles in the persistent heat of zone 8+.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow as seeds are small and benefit from light for germination.
directions: Surface-sow onto moist mix 6–8 weeks before transplanting; horehound germinates readily in warm soil but can be slow and erratic. Plant in dry, well-drained, even rocky or sandy soil where most plants would struggle — fertile, moist conditions cause leggy, weak growth. Harvest stems and leaves before flowering for the most potent bitterness, bundling for drying or infusing fresh into candy and cough syrups. Shear plants back in late summer to keep growth compact and prevent excessive self-seeding.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings or root division in spring; horse mint spreads vigorously by underground runners like all mints and is best contained in a pot or a bed with root barriers. Plant in moist soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, contained in pots or with root barriers to limit spreading; horse mint is a European native mint with long, lance-shaped, silver-green leaves that are more strongly and sharply aromatic than spearmint, with a mentholated, camphor-like fragrance. The dense, elongated spikes of small lavender flowers in late summer are exceptionally attractive to bumblebees, honey bees, and numerous other pollinators. The leaves can be used as a tea, culinary seasoning, or insect repellent — the intense menthol content makes it more suited to teas and infusions than to fresh eating. In South Africa it is widely used as a traditional medicine and culinary herb (called 'ballerja'); it naturalizes in moist streamside habitats across North Africa, Europe, and western Asia. Contrast with 'horse mint' used in the US (Monarda punctata), which is an entirely unrelated native wildflower.

common_name: Hot and Spicy Oregano (Compact High-Oil Pungent Culinary Oregano)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Hot and Spicy oregano is a compact (12–15 inch) shrubby perennial in zones 5–9 that grows well year-round in zone 9 with some protection from extended hard freezes. Can also be direct sown outdoors in spring. In zone 9, plant in well-drained, somewhat poor soil in full sun — rich, moist soils reduce the concentration of aromatic oils that give the variety its name. Harvest stems before or during early bloom for maximum essential oil content and flavor intensity.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct sow in spring; transplant to full sun, well-drained soil. Harvest stems for drying just as flower buds begin to open. Hot and Spicy Oregano is a compact cultivar of common oregano (Origanum vulgare) selected for higher essential oil content and more pronounced, pungent flavor compared to the bland, low-oil common oregano that grows widely in American gardens. Standard common oregano (Origanum vulgare) grown in the United States often has relatively low essential oil content and mild flavor — the reason that most dried commercial 'oregano' products in American grocery stores are a blend of Origanum vulgare with Greek oregano (O. heracleoticum) or marjoram. Hot and Spicy represents a more flavorful selection of the common oregano type, with significantly more essential oil and a more robust, peppery, slightly camphoraceous character approaching that of true Greek or Italian cooking oregano. The compact habit (10–15 inches), fine texture, and purple-tinged flowers make Hot and Spicy also ornamentally attractive in herb gardens and Mediterranean-style plantings. The variety is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in containers where watering can be controlled.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; can also be started indoors 4 weeks early for a longer season.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained soil after last frost; thin to 18–24 in apart as huacatay grows into a tall, upright plant. This Andean herb — essential in Peruvian cuisine for dishes like ocopa sauce and anticuchos marinades — has a complex flavor combining mint, tarragon, and citrus. Plants are day-length sensitive and flower in late summer to fall; harvest leaves and stem tips throughout the vegetative season before flowering commences. Grow in full sun with moderate fertility; the plant is drought-tolerant once established and spreads by self-seeding in warm climates.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential — this plant rots in heavy, moist clay. Excellent in gravel gardens and rock gardens.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; hummingbird mint is a native sage relative of the Texas-New Mexico border region with the most extraordinary foliage fragrance in the genus — a pure, sweet bubblegum-spearmint scent that fills the air when brushed. The deep rose-pink tubular flowers from summer through frost are consumed almost exclusively by hummingbirds, which are so attracted to the flowers that the plant earns its common name. It is genuinely drought tolerant and thrives in hot, dry conditions where it has excellent drainage. The plant self-sows modestly and is short-lived as a perennial (3–5 years); take cuttings in summer to maintain the garden. Deer resistant. An excellent choice for zone 8–9 pollinator gardens in full sun with excellent drainage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or loamy soil in partial shade; hummingbird sage spreads by underground rhizomes to form dense, weed-suppressing groundcover colonies under oaks and in dappled shade, making it an excellent low-maintenance native California groundcover.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in partial shade; hummingbird sage is one of the most useful native California salvias for gardens, tolerating more shade than most salvias while producing large, striking, rose-magenta flower spikes on tall stems — among the largest flowers of any native California sage, strongly attractive to Anna's hummingbirds and rufous hummingbirds throughout the blooming season from late winter through spring. The large, crinkled, gray-green aromatic leaves smell strongly of fresh pineapple and sage when crushed. Spreads by rhizomes to form gradually expanding colonies that provide excellent, drought-tolerant groundcover under California oaks and in dappled shade. One of the best California natives for replacing invasive English ivy under trees while maintaining shade coverage and providing outstanding wildlife value for hummingbirds and native bees.

common_name: Huntington Carpet Rosemary (Extremely Prostrate Groundcover Rosemary)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Huntington Carpet is one of the most prostrate rosemary selections available, hugging the ground closely and spreading widely, making it a strong choice as a large-scale groundcover on a sunny slope.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Huntington Carpet is among the most flat-growing, ground-hugging rosemary cultivars available, spreading widely while staying only a few inches tall, making it an excellent choice for covering a sunny bank or slope, cascading over a wall, or filling a large container where a true groundcover habit is wanted rather than an upright shrub form. It shares the same fragrant, culinary-quality foliage as other rosemary cultivars and produces small blue flowers in season. Excellent drainage is essential, since rosemary is highly prone to root rot in heavy or poorly drained soil, and it needs very little pruning to maintain its naturally flat, spreading form.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow or cover lightly with 1/8 in of fine mix.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep indoors in warm starting mix; germination is fast and reliable at 65–70°F. Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil — hyssop is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in conditions similar to lavender. Prune plants back by about one-third after flowering to keep them from becoming woody and to promote a compact, bushy habit. Harvest leafy stems and flowers in the morning just as the blossoms begin to open, drying them for use in expectorant teas, culinary herb blends, and potpourri.

plant_note: Root tip cuttings in moist potting mix in spring, since Icterina does not come true from seed. Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun after last frost.
directions: Root tip cuttings in moist potting mix in spring or summer and plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Icterina is a variegated culinary sage with soft gray-green leaves broadly edged in gold, giving a brighter, more luminous look to an herb garden or mixed border than plain green sage while carrying the same savory, slightly peppery flavor used in stuffings, poultry dishes, and herb butters. It stays a bit more compact than green garden sage, making it useful for edging or container plantings. Cut back hard in early spring to remove winter-worn growth and encourage fresh, well-colored new leaves.

plant_note: Surface-sow fine seed into lean, well-drained soil in full sun and keep evenly moist until germination; impepho self-sows readily once established and needs little further care.
directions: Helichrysum odoratissimum is a strongly aromatic, woolly-grey-leaved perennial of South African grasslands, widely known as impepho and burned as dried bundled foliage in Zulu, Xhosa, and other southern African traditions to honor ancestors and cleanse a space, one of the most culturally significant smudging herbs of the region, comparable in role to white sage or sweetgrass elsewhere. The felted, silver-green leaves release a warm, honey-curry-like scent when brushed or dried, and clusters of small, papery, everlasting, golden-yellow flowers appear in summer and hold their color well after drying, making the plant useful for dried arrangements as well as ceremonial bundles. It thrives in poor, gritty soil and full sun, tolerating drought far better than excess moisture, and benefits from an annual cutback to keep growth dense and prevent legginess.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost, or divide established clumps in spring, and set out after frost danger passes into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade.
directions: Set out divisions or transplants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, spacing plants 12–18 inches apart, and pinch stems through early summer to build bushy, floriferous plants. Chrysanthemum indicum is the wild East Asian species behind centuries of chrysanthemum tea (ju hua cha) and one of the parents of the modern florist mum, bearing masses of small, single, bright yellow daisy flowers on wiry stems from late summer into fall. Harvest flowers just as they open and air- or oven-dry them for tea, or leave them standing for pollinators — hoverflies and late-season bees depend on the nectar when little else is blooming. Divide congested clumps every 2–3 years in spring to keep plants vigorous and floriferous.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Indian coleus is related to ornamental coleus (Plectranthus scutellarioides) and is an easy-to-grow perennial herb in warm climates, roots are harvested for the compound forskolin.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; root cuttings readily in moist soil or water. Plectranthus barbatus (Indian coleus or forskohlii) is a fragrant-leaved tropical herb closely related to ornamental coleus, native to East Africa and tropical Asia and used extensively in Ayurvedic medicine under the name 'makandi' or 'coleus.' The roots of P. barbatus contain the diterpene compound forskolin, which has been extensively studied for its ability to activate the enzyme adenylate cyclase, increasing cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels in cells — a mechanism that has been researched for effects on weight management, glaucoma, and thyroid conditions. Forskohlii supplements (standardized root extracts) are widely sold in the herbal supplement market. As a garden plant, Indian coleus is an attractive, square-stemmed, aromatic, soft-leaved herb with pale-blue flower spikes in late summer — resembling a coarser-leaved version of its ornamental coleus relatives. It roots readily from stem cuttings and grows vigorously in humid, subtropical conditions. CAUTION: May interact with anticoagulants and medications metabolized by the CYP system; consult healthcare provider before medicinal use.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds where plants are to grow permanently in spring (or fall in mild climates) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Indian dill does not transplant well due to its taproot. It can be sown more thickly than European dill and the young plants thinned for fresh leaf use while remaining plants mature for seed harvest. The seeds are larger than common dill and more pungently aromatic.
directions: Direct sow seeds in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Indian dill is a distinct species from the common European dill (Anethum graveolens), native to South Asia and widely used throughout Indian, Sri Lankan, and Iranian cuisines where it occupies a culinary role analogous to but distinct from European dill — the seeds are larger, more flattened, with a stronger, earthier, more camphoraceous aroma than common dill, and the fresh leaves have a more pungent, slightly different flavor profile that is essential to certain South Asian fish curries, lentil dishes, and the Persian herb-rice dishes that are among the oldest continuously prepared foods in culinary history. The whole plant is taller and somewhat coarser than common dill. The seeds are used both whole in tempering (bloom in hot oil to release aromatics) and ground in spice blends. The essential oil chemistry differs meaningfully from A. graveolens, containing higher carvone concentrations that give the seeds their more assertive character. It is used medicinally throughout South Asia as a carminative and digestive herb. Excellent for South Asian herb gardens and cross-cultural culinary herb collections.

plant_note: Plant seedlings or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, extremely well-drained, rocky soil in full sun; Indian frankincense is a dryland tree that needs sharp drainage above all else and is realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.
directions: Plant seedlings or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, extremely well-drained, rocky soil in full sun; Indian frankincense is a dryland tree that needs sharp drainage above all else and is realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Native to dry, rocky hills across India, it is tapped for its fragrant resin, which hardens into aromatic amber 'tears' burned as incense and used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine, closely related to the African and Arabian frankincense trees that supply the resin of biblical and ancient trade fame. The papery, peeling bark and sparse, compound leaves give the tree an open, drought-adapted silhouette suited to a xeriscape or succulent-collection planting in frost-free climates, where it can be grown as much for its unusual form as for eventual resin tapping. Water sparingly, provide maximum sun and heat, and avoid any risk of standing water at the roots, which quickly kills this dryland species.

common_name: Indian Mulberry Root (Bai Ji Tian, Morinda Root)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in part shade; Morinda officinalis (Bai Ji Tian) is one of the 50 fundamental herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine, used for over 2,000 years to tonify Kidney Yang, treat impotence, lower back pain, and bone weakness — the starchy, medicinal roots are harvested after 3–5 years of growth.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; harvest roots after 3–5 years. Morinda officinalis (bai ji tian or Indian mulberry root) is a trailing and climbing vine from southern China and Southeast Asia in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) — one of the 50 fundamental herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and a plant used continuously in Chinese medical practice for over 2,000 years. The medicinal part is the dried root (bai ji tian in Chinese, meaning 'a hundred joints stretching to the sky') — starchy, slightly sweet, mildly warming — used in TCM specifically to tonify (strengthen) Kidney Yang energy, treating impotence, infertility, lower back and knee pain and weakness, fatigue, and osteoporosis from a TCM perspective. It is one of the principal herbs in many male reproductive tonifying formulas (like the classic Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan). The root contains anthraquinones, polysaccharides, and flavonoids with studied effects on testosterone levels, bone density, and adaptogenic activity. As a garden plant in zone 8–12, it is an attractive, semi-woody vine with glossy, ovate leaves and small white flowers in rounded clusters, followed by compound, white, aggregate fruits similar to noni (M. citrifolia) but smaller. Quite different from commercial noni in use and chemistry despite being in the same genus.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining stems; Indian sarsaparilla is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11.
directions: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining stems; Indian sarsaparilla is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Slender, twining stems carry narrow, leathery leaves with a whitish midrib and small, purplish-brown flowers, but the plant is grown chiefly for its long, aromatic, cinnamon-scented roots, traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine and as a flavoring agent similar to true sarsaparilla, to which it is not closely related botanically. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and light levels once established, scrambling over low supports or trailing from a container, and roots are typically harvested for use after at least a year or two of growth. Water moderately, allowing soil to dry somewhat between waterings, and protect from any frost, which damages both foliage and roots.

plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Indian snakeroot is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Wild populations are heavily overharvested and vulnerable across much of its native range, so source only nursery-propagated plants.
directions: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Indian snakeroot is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Wild populations are heavily overharvested and vulnerable across much of its native range, so source only nursery-propagated plants. Glossy, whorled leaves and small clusters of white flowers followed by small purple-black fruit grow on a compact forest-understory shrub native to South and Southeast Asian shade, historically significant as the original plant source of reserpine, one of the first modern drugs used to treat high blood pressure, and long used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine before that. Because unsustainable wild collection has made the species vulnerable across parts of its range, cultivated plantings from nursery-propagated stock, whether in a botanical collection or a home shade garden in a frost-free climate, help take pressure off remaining wild populations. Provide consistent warmth, humidity, and shade, and never attempt to self-medicate with plant material, since reserpine and related alkaloids have a narrow margin of safety and require professional medical guidance.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the surface of moist soil in partial shade after last frost; do not cover seeds with soil as they require light to germinate. Indian tobacco self-sows freely once established in a woodland garden.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface (do not cover) in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost; Indian tobacco is a native annual wildflower of eastern North American woodland clearings and disturbed areas, recognized by its inflated, balloon-like seed capsules after the small, pale lavender-blue flowers fade. It is an important plant in the history of American botanical medicine — the leaves and seeds contain lobeline and related piperidine alkaloids that act as respiratory stimulants and were traditionally used by Indigenous peoples and 19th-century physicians for asthma, croup, and as an emetic. IMPORTANT CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic in quantity; it should be used medicinally only under professional guidance. Do not confuse with garden lobelia cultivars (L. erinus) which are ornamentals. Indian tobacco is primarily of botanical and ethnobotanical interest rather than general garden use.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Irene is a vigorous, low, trailing rosemary well suited to cascading over a wall, raised bed edge, or large container.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Irene is a vigorous, low-growing, trailing rosemary selection that spreads and cascades rather than growing upright, making it an excellent choice for spilling over a retaining wall, raised bed, or large container edge. It carries the same fragrant, needle-like foliage and culinary use as upright rosemary types, along with small blue flowers in spring, and it tolerates heat and drought exceptionally well once established. Good drainage is essential, since rosemary quickly develops root rot in heavy, wet soil, and only minimal pruning is needed to keep the trailing habit tidy.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Irish lace marigold forms a low, dense mound of finely divided, thread-like foliage and needs no staking.
directions: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Irish lace marigold forms a low, dense mound of finely divided, thread-like foliage and needs no staking. Extremely fine, feathery, fern-like foliage carries a strong anise or licorice fragrance and flavor when crushed, used in parts of Mexico and Central America as a culinary herb and traditional flavoring, quite different from the coarser leaves and stronger, more medicinal scent of common marigold species. Tiny, inconspicuous white flowers appear over a long season, but this species is grown chiefly for its ornamental, lacy foliage texture and edible, licorice-scented leaves rather than a showy floral display. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it makes a fine edging plant or herb-garden filler, and harvested leaves can be used fresh or dried as a licorice-flavored seasoning.

plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; tolerates light frost.
directions: This heirloom flat-leaf parsley produces broad, dark green leaves with a clean, robust flavor prized in Mediterranean cooking. Soak seed overnight to speed the naturally slow germination, then sow shallowly and keep the soil consistently moist for the two to four weeks it takes to sprout. Thin seedlings to about eight inches apart in rich, well-drained soil and full sun. Harvest outer stems first so the plant keeps producing tender new growth through the season.

plant_note: Set out only after nights stay reliably above 50 F.
directions: Genovese is the classic Italian basil, offering the traditional fragrance and flavor that make it the top choice for pesto and countless summer dishes. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant after the soil is warm and settled weather has arrived, as cold stunts young plants. Give it full sun, rich soil, and even moisture for lush growth. Pinch out flower buds and harvest from the top to keep plants leafy, tender, and productive all season.

common_name: Italian Large Leaf Basil (Oversized Smooth-Leaf Classic Pesto Basil)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Italian Large Leaf basil bolts quickly in Gulf South summer heat — pinch flower stalks immediately and repeatedly to extend leaf production; succession sowings every 3 weeks from April through August ensure continuous fresh basil.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Italian Large Leaf basil produces very large (3–4 inch), smooth, flat, slightly cupped, glossy leaves with the classic sweet, aromatic, clove-and-anise basil flavor of traditional Italian cooking — the preferred basil for pesto, where the large leaf size dramatically reduces the time and effort required to harvest sufficient leaf mass for a batch. The large, smooth leaves with their flat, relatively unwrinkled surface represent a distinctly different basil character from small-leaf and ruffled types — they are easier to clean, process, and stack, and produce a cleaner pesto with less stem fiber. The vigorous plants reach 2–2.5 feet with regular harvesting that removes flower buds and promotes continued vegetative growth. In zone 9, Italian Large Leaf basil grows throughout the warm season (April–October) and succession planting every 3 weeks maintains continuous fresh supply despite the tendency of summer heat to promote bolting in individual plants. For maximum leaf harvest, remove flower stalks immediately when they appear — flowering redirects plant energy from leaf production and quickly reduces the quality and flavor of remaining leaves. A single-season basil capable of producing many pounds of leaves from a short row under good management.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Italian oregano is a natural hybrid and does not come true from seed — propagate from cuttings or purchase plants. It is cold hardier than sweet marjoram and more flavorful than common oregano, making it the most versatile culinary oregano for most American gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Italian oregano (Origanum x majoricum) is a naturally occurring hybrid between sweet marjoram (O. majorana) and Greek oregano (O. vulgare subsp. hirtum) that combines the complex, warm sweetness of marjoram with the earthy intensity of oregano to produce the characteristically mild, aromatic flavor used in Italian cuisine — the flavor profile preferred for pizza, pasta sauces, and Italian-American cooking. It is more cold-hardy than sweet marjoram, more flavorful and complex than ordinary wild oregano, and easier to grow with consistent harvest quality. The small, oval, gray-green leaves are harvested before flowering for maximum essential oil content; dried Italian oregano is far more intensely flavored than the thin, often stale commercial product and vastly superior for cooking. Excellent for container growing and performs well in zone 9 heat if given good drainage and lean soil.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for zone 9's main cilantro season, or 2-4 weeks before the last spring frost; Jantar bolts noticeably later than older standard cilantro strains, giving roughly an extra week to ten days of usable leaf in university trial comparisons.
directions: Jantar is a Central European coriander cultivar bred for a longer productive leaf stage before bolting, developed for both fresh cilantro leaf and coriander seed production. In side-by-side trials it has held its leafy stage notably longer than common cilantro strains, giving growers extra harvest time from the same planting before plants run to flower. Its aromatic seed also has a good oil yield, so gardeners who let a planting go to seed get a worthwhile coriander spice harvest in addition to the fresh leaf crop. Grow it exactly as you would other cilantro: direct-sown, in full sun, kept evenly moist, and sown in fall or very early spring to avoid the heat that triggers bolting in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in spring after the last frost; established clumps expand steadily and are divided every 3–4 years. In zone 7–9 myoga grows as a fully perennial ground cover in part shade to full shade, dying back to the ground each winter and re-emerging reliably in spring. The harvest season for the edible flower buds is August–September in zone 9.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in rich, moist, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade; Japanese ginger (myoga) is a shade-thriving edible perennial rarely seen in American gardens despite being widely grown in Japan for its prized flower buds. The plant's ginger-scented strap leaves reach 24–36 inches in shade conditions, forming a handsome ground cover through the growing season. The harvest is the unopened flower buds, which emerge at soil level in August–September — these small, pink-tipped buds are sliced thin and used as a pungent, mildly spicy garnish in miso soup, sashimi, noodle dishes, and pickled in vinegar. Young spring shoots are also edible with a more delicate flavor. The flavor is distinctly gingery but milder and more aromatic than culinary ginger root. Plants naturalize slowly and are nearly care-free once established in a shaded spot with consistent moisture.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 start February–March and transplant March–April. Japanese Indigo is a warm-season annual harvested before flowering for the highest leaf indican content; harvest the first flush of leaves when plants are 12–18 inches tall, then allow regrowth for a second harvest. In zone 9 the long warm season allows 2–3 harvests before fall. The plants self-sow readily in zone 9 conditions and may naturalize in moist garden areas.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Japanese Indigo (Ai, Tade Ai) is the traditional indigo dye plant of Japan, used for over 1,500 years to produce the brilliant blue textile dye that colors traditional Japanese fabrics including indigo-dyed cotton, shibori tie-dye, and katazome stencil-printed cloth. The blue dye precursor indican is stored in the fresh leaves and requires a fermentation vat (sukumo) or direct fresh-leaf dyeing process to produce the indigo pigment that bonds to fiber. Unlike the tropical indigo plant (Indigofera), Japanese Indigo thrives in temperate garden conditions and is accessible to North American home growers. Fresh leaves yield blue dye directly when crushed and applied to cotton in the sun — a simple process known as 'leaf printing' that produces soft blue marks without a dye vat. The ornamental plants with reddish stems and oval, deep green leaves and pink flower spikes in fall are attractive in the garden and valuable to craft dyers, fiber artists, and natural dye enthusiasts.

common_name: Japanese Pepper Vine (Fuji Kadsura, Asian Pepper Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full shade; Japanese pepper vine is a tropical Asian climbing vine related to black pepper that grows as an understory climber in humid, shaded forest conditions — it can be used as a shade-tolerant ornamental and culinary herb in warm gardens.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; provide trellis or tree trunk support. Piper kadsura (Japanese pepper vine) is a Japanese and East Asian climbing vine in the pepper family (Piperaceae) — related to true black pepper (P. nigrum) but native to the humid, shaded forests of Japan, China, and Korea. The plant produces attractive, heart-shaped, deeply veined, dark-green leaves with conspicuous venation and a mildly spicy pepper aroma when crushed. Small, string-like flower spikes produce tiny, red to dark-purple peppercorns-like berries in fall that are mildly peppery-spicy and have been used as a seasoning and traditional medicine ingredient in East Asian cuisine and herbal practice. The vine climbs by adhesive stem roots similar to Virginia creeper and can attach to rough stone, brick, and wood surfaces. As a shade-tolerant ornamental vine for zone 9–12, it provides year-round interest with its attractive foliage and subtle fruiting display. Used in Japanese herbal medicine (kampo) for joint pain and circulation. Extremely rare in Western horticulture.

common_name: Japanese Sweet Flag (Dwarf Sweet Flag, Grassy-Leaved Sweet Flag)
plant_note: Plant clump divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or in containers submerged up to 2–3 inches of water in shade to part shade; Japanese sweet flag is a small, grass-like aquatic-marginal perennial from East Asia — the mildly anise-scented leaves are used in traditional Japanese ikebana arrangements, as a marginal water feature plant, and in various ornamental cultivars with variegated gold-and-green foliage.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or in containers in shallow water (up to 3 inches deep) in shade to part shade. Acorus gramineus (Japanese sweet flag or dwarf sweet flag) is a small, compact, grass-like aquatic-marginal perennial from Japan and China — a diminutive relative of the larger sweet flag (A. calamus) — producing dense tufts of narrow, grass-like, slightly arching, aromatic leaves in solid green or with variegated golden-yellow striping. The leaves, when crushed, release a mild, pleasant anise-cinnamon fragrance similar to (but softer than) the larger A. calamus. Several ornamental cultivars are widely grown: 'Ogon' (yellow-green striped leaves), 'Variegatus' (white-striped leaves), and the miniature 'Pusillus' (just 3–4 inches tall). Japanese sweet flag naturally grows along stream margins and in wet meadows in Japan and Korea, tolerating conditions from moist soil to shallow water up to 3 inches deep; it is an ideal marginal plant for water garden pots, pond edges, and shade rain gardens. In Japanese flower arranging (ikebana), the upright leaves provide linear structure. In Chinese and Japanese traditional medicine, the root and leaves are used as a mildly stimulating tonic and insect repellent herb. A wonderfully versatile plant for moist shade situations.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; Java citronella is the primary commercial source of citronella essential oil worldwide — a large, clumping aromatic grass closely related to lemongrass, grown in Java, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, and Central America for its leaves, which distill to produce the citronella oil used in insect repellents, candles, and soaps.
directions: Plant clump divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; harvest leaves after 4–6 months and steam-distill or use fresh as repellent. Cymbopogon winterianus (Java citronella) is a large, clumping tropical aromatic grass that is the world's primary commercial source of citronella essential oil — one of the most commercially important aromatic crop plants globally, with the highest geraniol and citronellal content of any Cymbopogon species. Java citronella oil (named for its origin in Indonesian cultivation on Java) is the primary active ingredient in citronella candles, insect repellent products, and many natural insect-deterrent sprays worldwide. The plant is named for Cornelius de Winter, a Dutch botanist. Java citronella (C. winterianus) is distinct from Ceylon citronella (C. nardus) — Java citronella has significantly higher citronellal and geraniol content and produces a superior, more commercially valuable oil. The plant resembles lemongrass but has a more pronounced citrus-floral-rose fragrance (from geraniol content) rather than purely lemon. As a garden plant in zone 10–12, Java citronella forms an attractive, 4–6 foot clump of narrow, arching, blue-green leaves with a strong pleasant scent when crushed. Fresh stems placed around outdoor seating areas provide some mosquito deterrence, though less than the concentrated essential oil.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed as young plants are cold-sensitive.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm, moist starting mix and provide a trellis or support on which the vigorous twining vine can climb; jiaogulan grows 10–20 ft if given the right conditions. Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates; consistent moisture promotes the most lush and harvestable leaf growth. In zones 7–8 the plant dies to the ground in winter but regrows from the root; in zone 9 and above it may be evergreen. Harvest the five-lobed leaflets throughout the growing season for fresh or dried tea; known as southern ginseng, the leaves contain saponins similar to those in Panax ginseng and are used in adaptogenic preparations.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; in zones 9–10 it can remain outdoors year-round. In zones 7–8 grow in containers and overwinter indoors above 50°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; makrut lime is grown primarily for its distinctive double-lobed leaves, which are the indispensable aromatic herb of Thai and Cambodian cooking, used in curries, soups, and stir-fries to impart an intensely floral, citrusy perfume that no other herb can substitute. The bumpy, knobbly green fruit has very little juice but extremely aromatic zest used in marinades and Thai curry pastes. Leaves can be harvested whenever new growth appears; young leaves have the strongest flavor. In containers (the most practical approach north of zone 9), use a quality potting mix, fertilize monthly with citrus fertilizer spring through fall, and overwinter indoors in a bright window above 50°F.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or transplant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; kalmegh thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast summer and is one of the most important medicinal herbs in Indian Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, used for immune support and respiratory infections.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; harvest aerial parts when plants begin to flower for maximum andrographolide content. Andrographis paniculata (kalmegh, green chiretta, or king of bitters) is one of the most important and widely researched medicinal plants in Asian traditional medicine systems — a tropical Asian annual herb producing intensely bitter leaves (among the bitterest of any plant) containing the bioactive diterpene compound andrographolide. Clinical research has documented significant efficacy for andrographolide in reducing the severity and duration of upper respiratory infections (common cold and flu) — it is one of the better-supported herbal remedies for viral respiratory illness. The plant is used extensively in Ayurvedic medicine (as kalmegh), traditional Chinese medicine, and Southeast Asian folk medicine for fever, liver conditions, and infections. Despite its extreme bitterness, the plant is consumed as an herbal tea, tincture, and tablet supplement throughout South and Southeast Asia. The plant grows as an upright, branching annual with lance-shaped leaves and small, white, pink-speckled flowers; it is well-adapted to hot, humid conditions and grows vigorously through Gulf Coast summers.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; kalonji prefers cool spring conditions and dislikes heat.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly where they are to grow; kalonji has fine, thread-like foliage similar to its ornamental cousin love-in-a-mist and dislikes transplanting. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; the plant bolts quickly in summer heat, so time sowing for a cool-season harvest. Harvest the swollen seed pods when they begin to turn tan and paper-like, cutting whole stems into bags before the pods split and release the seeds. The intensely aromatic black seeds are used in South Asian cooking on naan breads and in spice blends, and have a long history of medicinal use; they are not to be confused with black cumin (Bunium persicum).

plant_note: Sow surface-sown seed indoors in a lean, gritty, fast-draining mix at warm temperature, or set out nursery plants after frost into lean, sandy, alkaline soil in full sun; kanna is a low, sprawling succulent from the semi-arid Karoo and needs excellent drainage above all else.
directions: Sceletium tortuosum is a mat-forming, jointed-stemmed succulent of the fig-marigold family, native to the dry Karoo and Namaqualand regions of South Africa, where the fermented leaf and stem material (traditionally called kougoed, or chew-stuff) has long been chewed, smoked, or brewed as a mood-lifting and appetite-suppressing traditional remedy. Small, star-shaped, pale yellow to white flowers open in sunny weather over succulent, fleshy, sometimes purple-tinged leaves. Grow it exactly as you would a hardy mesemb or ice plant: bone-dry, mineral soil, full sun, and minimal winter water, since rot rather than cold is the main threat in cultivation. Established plants tolerate long dry spells and light frost once mature. Container culture with a cactus-style mix is the most reliable approach outside its native climate.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 weeks early or direct sow after last frost; in zone 9 sow February–March for spring and August for fall. Kapoor is heat-tolerant and well-adapted to Indian-subtropical growing conditions that resemble the Gulf Coast climate, making it one of the better basil varieties for sustained summer production in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Kapoor is a compact Indian sweet basil cultivar selected for high essential oil content and strong clove-camphor aroma with a distinctive spicy note absent from European Genovese varieties. The small-to-medium dark green leaves have a more robust, pungent flavor than Genovese basil and are used extensively in Indian cooking — in chutneys, raitas, and as a fresh herb added to dals and curries. Kapoor's compact habit and heat tolerance make it particularly suitable for year-round indoor container growing and for outdoor herb gardens in subtropical zone 9 where it often survives mild winters as a short-lived perennial. The slightly camphoraceous aroma also has medicinal uses in Ayurvedic tradition, closely related to but distinct from true holy basil (tulsi).

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Kapoor tulsi is a compact (12–18 inch) holy basil that thrives in zone 9's warm, humid summers and often self-seeds to create a self-perpetuating colony. In Ayurvedic tradition the plant should not be harvested after dark or on certain days; for culinary and medicinal use, harvest fresh leaves continuously to prevent bolting. In zone 9 the plant can overwinter in frost-free spots as a short-lived perennial, but is best treated as an annual that self-seeds.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Kapoor Tulsi is a named variety of holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum) selected for compact habit and exceptionally high eugenol content — the volatile oil component that gives tulsi its characteristic warm, clove-like fragrance is highest in the Kapoor selection, making it the preferred variety for medicinal use in Ayurvedic preparations where eugenol concentration matters. In Hindu tradition, Tulsi (also called Vrinda or the Holy Basil) is the most sacred plant in the home, representing Lakshmi and kept in a tulsi pot on the veranda of traditional Indian homes where it is tended daily. Beyond its religious significance, Kapoor Tulsi is used medicinally for digestive support, as an adaptogen for stress, in tea blends for respiratory health, and as an aromatic in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking where the clove-camphor notes are distinctly different from sweet basil. The compact Kapoor selection fits easily in container or herb garden cultivation and grows robustly in the warm conditions of the Gulf South.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September for a fall harvest. Kaprao holy basil thrives in zone 9's heat and humidity — unlike sweet basil which may decline in extreme summer heat, holy basil actively thrives in tropical-humid conditions. In zone 9 Kaprao can be grown as a perennial in frost-free microclimates, returning from roots or self-seeding abundantly. The plants flower quickly in long summer days — pinch frequently to maintain vegetative growth if leaf production is the goal.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Kaprao (กะเพรา in Thai, pronounced 'kra-pao') is the specific holy basil type used in Thai cooking — its clove-and-pepper-forward flavor with a faint anise note and spicy heat is the defining herb of pad kra pao (stir-fried basil), Thailand's most popular everyday dish. While all holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum) has the characteristic clove-spice aroma from eugenol, the Kaprao type selected for Thai cooking has a particularly pungent, peppery quality and narrow, slightly serrated leaves that are used exclusively in their cooked form — unlike Italian sweet basil or Vietnamese basil, Kaprao is wilted into hot wok dishes where the heat activates and transforms the volatile oils. The fresh leaves cannot be substituted by Italian sweet basil in pad kra pao, as the clove-pepper flavor profile is essential to the dish. In zone 9 Kaprao thrives in the hot, humid summers that are close to its native tropical Thai climate, performing far better than sweet basil in the season's peak heat.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; kava is a Pacific Island understory plant that is sterile and propagated only from cuttings, and it needs warmth, humidity, and shelter from direct sun and wind.
directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; kava is a Pacific Island understory plant that is sterile and propagated only from cuttings, and it needs warmth, humidity, and shelter from direct sun and wind. This large, heart-leaved shrub has been cultivated for centuries across Polynesia, Melanesia, and Micronesia, where its thick roots are pounded and mixed with water to produce a traditional ceremonial and social beverage valued for its mild relaxant effect. It requires consistently warm, humid, frost-free conditions and rich, well-drained soil in filtered light, essentially replicating the sheltered forest-garden conditions of its native Pacific islands, and struggles badly with cold, dry air or direct hot sun. Roots are typically harvested for use after three to five years of growth; further north than zone 10, it must be grown as a protected container plant moved indoors well before any cold weather.

common_name: Kent Beauty Oregano (Ornamental Hop-Flowered Trailing Oregano)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants after the last hard frost in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Kent Beauty is grown almost entirely for its ornamental flower bracts rather than for culinary use and is best sited where its trailing stems can spill over a wall, rock, or container edge.
directions: Kent Beauty is an ornamental oregano hybrid grown for its unusual dangling flower clusters, in which large, papery, chartreuse-to-rose-pink bracts overlap like tiny hops and gradually flush pink as they age, held above rounded, blue-gray, aromatic leaves on trailing stems. Unlike culinary oregano, it is grown chiefly for this striking flower display rather than for the kitchen, and it performs best trailing from a raised bed, rock garden pocket, or hanging container where the pendant flower clusters can be seen and admired at eye level. Give it lean, very well-drained soil in full sun, since it is prone to rot in humid, poorly drained conditions, and expect it to be shorter-lived than standard oregano, particularly where summer humidity is high.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings after the last frost in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Kentucky Colonel is a large-leaved spearmint selection traditionally used for mint juleps and grows best confined to a container or bed with a root barrier, since mint spreads aggressively.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally in a container or a bed edged with a root barrier, since mint spreads aggressively by rhizome and can quickly overrun a garden bed. Kentucky Colonel is a spearmint selection with unusually large, crinkled, dark green leaves and a smooth, sweet, mild mint flavor without the sharper bite of peppermint, making it the traditional choice among Southern bartenders and home mixologists for mint juleps and other cocktails where a clean, refined mint character matters. It is also excellent for iced tea, fresh garnishes, and simple syrups. Keep soil consistently moist, since mint wilts quickly in dry conditions, and cut back hard in mid-summer if growth becomes leggy to encourage a fresh flush of tender new leaves. In light shade the leaves stay more tender and less prone to leaf spot than in full, hot Gulf South sun.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant year-round except in peak summer heat. Kentucky Colonel spreads aggressively by underground runners — plant in a buried container or with root barriers to prevent takeover of surrounding beds. In zone 9 partial shade reduces aggressive spread while maintaining large, high-quality leaves; harvest frequently to prevent flowering, which diminishes leaf flavor. Cut to the ground after flowering and the plant will regenerate with fresh, flavorful new growth.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil — mint thrives with consistent moisture and morning sun with afternoon shade protection; Kentucky Colonel is widely considered the finest spearmint cultivar for culinary use, producing very large, broad, slightly crinkled, bright green leaves with a smooth, intensely sweet, clean spearmint fragrance and flavor that is more refined and less harsh than standard commercial spearmint. The large leaf size makes Kentucky Colonel practical for fresh cocktail garnishes (mint juleps, mojitos), cold drinks, and herb preparations where leaf presentation matters — the substantial leaves are picked individually for floating in glasses or bruising for infusions, rather than stripped from stems. The Kentucky Colonel name connects this variety to the classic bourbon-and-mint culture of Kentucky where spearmint was historically associated with the mint julep tradition — the sweet spearmint character complements bourbon's caramel and vanilla notes without the sharp mentholated edge of peppermint. Kentucky Colonel is also excellent in iced tea, fruit salads, desserts, and fresh herb sauces where a classic spearmint flavor is desired.

plant_note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, and keep soil consistently moist through the tree's slow multi-year establishment; both male and female trees are needed for fruit.
directions: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, and keep soil consistently moist through the tree's slow multi-year establishment. Kokum is dioecious, so both male and female trees are needed for fruit, and it is native to the moist forests of India's Western Ghats. The purple-rind fruit is sun-dried into the deep reddish-black souring spice used throughout Goan and Konkani cooking, such as kokum curry and solkadhi, and pressed into kokum butter; fresh pulp is also boiled into a tart, cooling summer syrup.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown rhizomes after all frost danger passes in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; korarima needs consistent warmth and humidity year-round and is best grown as a container plant that can be moved under cover outside of zone 10–11.
directions: Plant in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; korarima, or Ethiopian cardamom, is a ginger-family relative whose aromatic seed pods are a key spice in Ethiopian cooking, most notably in berbere spice blend and in the traditional Ethiopian coffee ceremony, where whole pods are sometimes added to the roasting coffee. It is a distinct species from both true cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum) and the West African spice grains of paradise (Aframomum melegueta), with its own warm, slightly citrusy-peppery, resinous flavor. The plant grows as a clumping, ginger-like perennial with broad leaves and produces its aromatic seed pods near the base of the plant close to the soil. It needs consistent warmth, humidity, and moisture year-round and is intolerant of any frost, so outside of zone 10–11 it is best grown in a large container that can be moved to a warm, bright indoor spot for winter. Harvest pods once they mature and dry to a deep reddish-brown, then dry further and store whole, grinding just before use to preserve aroma.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4–6 weeks early in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean mint self-sows freely and often maintains a persistent colony by self-seeding in suitable conditions.
directions: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean mint (Korean hyssop) is an East Asian culinary and medicinal herb with large, anise-mint-scented leaves used fresh in Korean, Vietnamese, and Chinese cooking — particularly in ssam (lettuce wrap), salads, and teas — and dense spikes of lavender-purple to pink flowers from midsummer through fall that attract extraordinary numbers of bees and swallowtail butterflies. Distinctly different from the North American native A. foeniculum (anise hyssop) in flavor and growing conditions, though botanically similar. More heat-tolerant and easier in southern gardens. Self-sows freely once established; leave some spent flower stalks for seed to maintain the colony.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil or transplant seedlings; Korean perilla (kkaennip) is distinct from Japanese shiso in having larger, thicker, rounder, more strongly aromatic leaves with a more complex anise-mint-basil fragrance used extensively in Korean cuisine as a ssam wrap leaf, banchan pickle, and seasoning — one of the most important herbs in Korean cooking.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface (they need light to germinate) or barely cover; Korean perilla self-seeds prolifically and will return each year once established — deadhead if you want to control spread. Perilla frutescens var. japonica (Korean perilla, kkaennip, also called Korean sesame leaf or Korean mint) is distinct from the Japanese shiso (var. crispa) in its larger size, rounder leaf shape, flat rather than crinkled leaf margin, thicker leaf texture, and stronger, more complex fragrance — a blend of anise, mint, basil, and sesame that is deeply characteristic of Korean cuisine. The large (3–5 inch), round-oval, bright green leaves (occasionally flushed with purple on the underside) are used in Korean cooking in numerous ways: as ssam wraps for grilled meats (samgyeopsal, bulgogi), as perilla kimchi (kkaennip kimchi), marinated in soy and sesame as a banchan side dish, fried in batter as pajeon ingredients, and as a culinary herb in soups and stews. Distinguished from Japanese shiso by larger leaf size and the more potent, less floral fragrance. Excellent for hot, humid Gulf Coast gardens where it thrives in summer heat; tolerates partial shade.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Korintje cinnamon is slightly more cold-tolerant than Ceylon cinnamon and may survive light frosts to 28°F in protected locations in zone 8b.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 9–12; Korintje cinnamon is an Indonesian species from Sumatra that is actually the most commonly sold type of cinnamon in the United States under the generic label 'cinnamon' — accounting for the majority of commercial cinnamon imports. Named for Kota Kerinci in Sumatra, it produces thick, dark-brown bark quills with a strong, mildly sweet flavor intermediate between Ceylon and Chinese cassia cinnamons. The bark is harvested from trees 3–4 years after planting by stripping young branches; coppicing the trees stimulates new shoot production for repeated harvests. Like all commercial cinnamon, the attractive, broad, three-veined leaves are also aromatic when crushed. In zone 9–11, it grows well outdoors as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree; regular harvesting of branches maintains a bushy, productive form suitable for the home garden.

plant_note: Transplant after all frost danger has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; koseret is a tender perennial in frost-free climates but is typically grown as a warm-season annual or overwintered in a container further north.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade after frost danger passes; koseret is an aromatic Ethiopian shrub whose dried, crumbled leaves are a foundational seasoning in Ethiopian and Eritrean cooking, most notably in kitfo (spiced raw or lightly cooked minced beef) and gomen (collard-style greens), lending a pungent, herbal, faintly citrusy-minty aroma unlike common Western culinary herbs. Leaves are typically harvested, dried in the shade, and crumbled into a fine seasoning rather than used fresh, concentrating their aromatic oils. The plant grows as a soft-wooded perennial shrub in frost-free tropical and subtropical climates and can be grown as a warm-season annual or container plant that overwinters indoors farther north. Harvest leafy stems regularly through the growing season to encourage bushy new growth, and dry the harvest in a warm, shaded, well-ventilated spot before storing in an airtight container for use throughout the year.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil has warmed to at least 65°F; seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep the plant bushy and productive. Krishna is the deep purple-leaved, purple-stemmed form of holy basil (tulsi), named for the Hindu deity traditionally depicted with dark blue-purple skin, and valued both for its striking ornamental coloring and its more intensely spicy, peppery, clove-forward flavor compared to the milder green Rama type. The rich purple foliage and purple-tinged flower spikes make it as much an ornamental accent for a sunny herb bed as a culinary and tea herb, and its stronger flavor makes it a favorite for those who prefer a more assertive tulsi tea. Like other holy basil types, it is considered sacred in Hindu tradition and is easy to grow in a warm, sunny herb garden through the summer. Zone 10–12 or as a warm-season annual elsewhere.

plant_note: Scarify and soak the hard legume seed before starting indoors in early spring, then transplant out after frost into deep, well-drained soil.
directions: Concentrated extracts of this root are not intended for prolonged internal use without professional guidance due to potential liver-related concerns. Scarify and soak the hard legume seed before starting indoors in early spring, then transplant out after frost into deep, well-drained soil, since the developing taproot resents later disturbance. Roots are harvested from plants three to four years old and traditionally decocted or used in topical washes in TCM to relieve itching and eczema-type skin conditions and as a folk antiparasitic.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall for cold stratification over winter, or sow in spring in well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline, calcareous soil in full sun to light partial shade; lady's bedstraw is a plant of dry grasslands, hedgerows, and coastal dunes — it spreads by slender rhizomes to form loose, scrambling mats and naturalizes readily in dry, sunny, wild garden settings.
directions: Galium verum is a slender, scrambling, rhizomatous perennial herb of dry grasslands and hedgerows throughout Europe and temperate Asia, producing whorls of very fine, needle-like, dark-green leaves along square stems and masses of tiny, four-petaled, honey-scented, bright-yellow flowers in dense, frothy panicles from early to mid summer; the whole plant when dried emits a pleasant, sweet, coumarin-like (new-mown hay) fragrance. Direct-sow seeds in fall in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline, calcareous soil in a sunny or lightly shaded position; seeds benefit from cold stratification and germinate most reliably after a natural winter cold period — established plants spread by shallow rhizomes to form loose, weed-suppressing mats. Lady's bedstraw has a rich history of traditional use: the flowering tops were used to curdle milk in cheese-making (especially for Cheshire and Gloucester cheeses, as a vegetable rennet substitute), and the roots yield a warm red to orange dye with an alum mordant, while the stems and flowers produce yellow; the dried plant was historically stuffed into mattresses and strewn underfoot for its pleasant scent and supposed flea-repelling properties. Tolerant of drought and coastal conditions once established; excellent for naturalizing in wild or meadow gardens with other dry-grassland species.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant only after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: This sweet Italian basil is grown for its unusually large, aromatic leaves and slow-bolting habit that stretches the harvest for pesto and fresh cooking. Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost and keep it warm, since basil resents cold soil. Transplant into rich, well-drained ground in full sun once nights stay reliably above fifty degrees. Pinch flowering tips regularly to keep the plant bushy and encourage a steady supply of tender leaves.

plant_note: Plant container plants or start from seed (seeds are tiny; surface-sow in spring on moist medium and do not cover) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; calamint prefers a position sheltered from drying winds and produces the most flowers with a few hours of afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Calamintha grandiflora is the showiest of the calamlints, producing soft, aromatic, mint-scented foliage and large (for the genus), vivid pink, tubular, two-lipped flowers in whorled clusters from late spring through early fall that are extraordinarily attractive to bumblebees and are among the most bumblebee-visited ornamental herbs in British and European garden trials. The leaves and young shoots have a strong, pleasant, minty-oregano flavor and can be used fresh or dried as a seasoning and herbal tea; the flavor is similar to but more delicate than wild mountain oregano.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; lavandin does not come true from seed and must be propagated vegetatively. It is more vigorous and faster-growing than English lavender. Grosso is the most widely planted cultivar for oil production and dried bundles; Provence and Fred Boutin are also excellent landscape cultivars.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; lavandin is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) and spike lavender (L. latifolia) that has become the dominant commercial lavender worldwide — over 90 percent of the lavender essential oil sold globally comes from lavandin rather than true English lavender. It is larger, more vigorous, and more heat- and drought-tolerant than English lavender, with longer, more branched flower spikes and a stronger scent that is higher in camphor and has a slightly sharper, more penetrating quality than the pure English lavender fragrance. As a sterile hybrid, it produces no viable seed but blooms heavily and reliably. The cultivar Grosso produces the most oil and the largest, most dramatic dried bundles; Provence is the classic lavender-field cultivar of the Provence region of France. Excellent for mass planting, dried flower production, cut flowers, and herb gardens. Slightly less cold-hardy than English lavender but more heat-tolerant in zones 7-8.

plant_note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; Lavender Mint combines peppermint's cooling menthol with floral lavender notes.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Lavender Mint layers soft, floral lavender notes over the classic cooling menthol scent of peppermint, an unusual fragrance combination that makes it a favorite for potpourri, herbal sachets, and fragrant tea blends beyond straightforward culinary use. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun, ideally at the top of a wall or in a hanging container; Lebanese oregano is grown almost entirely for its cascading habit and ornamental flowers rather than for culinary use.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun, ideally where its trailing stems can cascade over the edge of a raised bed, wall, or hanging basket; Lebanese oregano is grown chiefly as an ornamental rather than a culinary herb, producing long, wiry stems draped with rounded, blue-green leaves and dangling clusters of papery, chartreuse-pink, hop-like bracts that persist attractively for weeks in mid- to late summer. The trailing habit and long-lasting bracted flower clusters make it a favorite for dry, sunny container plantings and rock wall crevices where its cascade can be fully appreciated. It is somewhat more tender than common culinary oregano, so provide winter protection or grow it as a container plant that can be moved to shelter in climates colder than its hardiness range. Trim lightly after the main flowering display fades to keep growth tidy, and avoid rich soil or excess water, both of which produce leggy, less floriferous growth.

common_name: Leisure Cilantro (Classic Open-Pollinated Slow-Bolt Cilantro for Leaf Production)
plant_note: Direct sow only in cool soil; does not transplant well. In zone 9, plant October–November for fall-winter production or February–March for a brief spring crop. Leisure is one of the classic open-pollinated slow-bolt cilantro varieties — selected specifically for delayed bolting (the rush to flower and seed that ends leaf production) compared to standard varieties. The 'slow-bolt' trait means Leisure stays in leaf-producing mode for a longer period under warming conditions than standard cilantro varieties, extending the productive harvest window in spring gardens. This is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the spring temperature rise is rapid and cilantro planted in late February may have only a short window before bolting; Leisure's extended slow-bolt characteristic can add 2–3 weeks of productive leaf harvest in spring conditions. The leaves are typical broad, flat cilantro foliage with the standard cilantro flavor.
directions: Direct sow thinly in cool soil; thin to 6–9 inches. Harvest outer leaves successively before bolting. Leisure Cilantro is one of the most widely recommended open-pollinated cilantro varieties for home gardeners specifically wanting maximum leaf production before the plant bolts to seed. All cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) is genetically programmed to flower — it is an annual that must complete its seed cycle — but the timing and speed of this transition from vegetative (leaf-producing) growth to reproductive (flower/seed) growth varies considerably among cultivated varieties, and selecting for delayed bolting has been a primary breeding objective in cilantro improvement since leaf herb production became the primary commercial use of the crop in North America. Leisure was selected from open-pollinated cilantro populations for its consistent tendency to remain in vegetative leaf production mode longer than standard unselected populations, particularly as temperatures increase in spring. This character is not the same as the more dramatically extended bolt resistance of F1 hybrid varieties like Calypso, but it is meaningfully better than generic cilantro seed and substantially better than truly fast-bolting varieties. For zone 9 gardeners, the distinction matters: in the rapid spring temperature rise of the Gulf Coast (February through April), even 2–3 extra weeks of leaf production before bolting is a meaningful difference in total harvest. Leisure's open-pollinated status means seed can be saved from selected late-bolting individual plants to potentially improve the variety further for local conditions over successive generations.

plant_note: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost or start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; lemon balm germinates readily in cool soil and grows vigorously in full sun to partial shade, tolerating more shade than most herbs.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; lemon balm tolerates more shade than most herbs and is one of the few culinary herbs that produces acceptable quality even in partially shaded sites.
