The flavor is uniquely delicate: more complex than parsley, less anise-forward than chervil, with a clean, fresh quality that bridges East Asian and Western herb traditions. Unlike most herbs that demand full sun, Mitsuba thrives in the deep shade of a woodland garden or the north side of a building — making it one of the most valuable herbs for shaded kitchen gardens. In zone 7 and warmer it can be semi-evergreen; in zone 4–6 it dies back to the root in winter but regrows reliably in spring. The plant self-sows freely in suitable conditions and can naturalize under trees or along shaded borders. Etiolated (blanched) stems grown in darkness are particularly prized for their milder, more delicate flavor.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant year-round except in the hottest summer weeks. Like all mints, Mojito Mint spreads aggressively by underground runners — plant in containers or in beds with buried barriers to prevent it from overtaking other plants. In zone 9 Mojito Mint grows robustly in partial shade, which slows its spread slightly while maintaining leaf quality. Harvest frequently to prevent flowering; once mint flowers the leaf flavor diminishes.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil — mint tolerates a wide range of conditions but is most productive with consistent moisture and morning sun with afternoon shade protection; Mojito Mint (also called Cuban Mint or Hierba Buena) is the specific mint variety traditionally used in Cuban mojito cocktails and throughout Latin American cuisine where the common name 'hierba buena' (good herb) refers to this distinctive spearmint type. The large, soft, round, slightly fuzzy leaves have a distinctive mint character that is milder and fruitier than standard peppermint — less cool and piercing, with sweet spearmint notes and a smooth, rounded flavor that makes it the preferred mint for beverages where a harsh mint punch would overpower the other ingredients. The mojito's balance of rum, lime, sugar, and mint depends on this softer mint character to support rather than dominate. Mojito Mint also works excellently in fresh summer drinks, desserts, herb sauces, and anywhere a gentle, approachable mint flavor is desired over the assertive cool of peppermint.

plant_note: Transplant young trees in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; check local regulations before planting, since molle is classified as invasive or restricted in parts of California and the desert Southwest.
directions: Transplant young trees in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this fast-growing, drought-tolerant evergreen from the Peruvian Andes develops graceful, weeping, willow-like branches and clusters of small berries that ripen from green to bright rose-pink. The dried berries are sold commercially as pink peppercorns and add a fruity, mildly resinous heat to pepper blends, sauces, and infused oils, though botanically the tree is unrelated to true pepper (Piper nigrum). Handle fresh fruit and sap with care, as some people develop mild skin or respiratory irritation, and check local regulations before planting, since molle is classified as invasive or restricted in parts of California and the desert Southwest.

plant_note: Direct sow; grown mainly for its abundant coriander seed.
directions: Moroccan coriander is a fast-growing, four-in-one herb, giving a quick flush of leaves, edible white flowers for beneficial insects, and, above all, large aromatic seeds. It is especially valued for its heavy yield of round coriander seed used in baking and spice blends. Direct sow into cool soil since the taproot resists transplanting, and let plants flower and set seed for harvest. Provide full sun and even moisture, then cut seed heads once they turn tan and dry them fully before storing.

common_name: Moroccan Mint (Classic Culinary Spearmint for Tea)
plant_note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; plant in partial shade in consistently moist, fertile soil and contain the roots to stop rampant spread.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Moroccan Mint is the classic spearmint selection traditionally used for Moroccan mint tea, prized for its clean, sweet, true spearmint flavor without the sharper menthol bite of peppermint, making it the standard choice for hot mint tea sweetened with sugar as well as for cocktails like mojitos and juleps. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather to prevent wilting, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut the planting back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage for the rest of the growing season.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Mosaic is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation.
directions: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Mosaic is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in 2012, this vigorous, high-yielding American hop produces cones with an unusually complex aroma profile combining tropical fruit, citrus, pine, and berry notes all at once, living up to its name by contributing a shifting mosaic of different flavor impressions depending on how it is used in a beer recipe. Its complexity and versatility across both bittering and late-addition aromatic brewing uses have made it one of the most in-demand hop varieties among craft brewers since its release, commanding premium prices and frequently being in short supply. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery and spring back when squeezed, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season.

plant_note: Slow to germinate; soaking seed overnight speeds sprouting.
directions: This curled parsley forms dense, ruffled rosettes of deep green that garnish plates beautifully and pack in vitamins A, B, and C. Cold-tolerant, it can be grown as an annual that carries on through fall and into mild winters. Parsley seed is famously slow to sprout, so soak it overnight and be patient, keeping the soil consistently moist. Grow in full sun to part shade with steady water and harvest outer stems first to keep the plant producing.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mother of thyme forms a tighter, denser mat than T. serpyllum and is the preferred species for most lawn-substitute and stepping stone plantings.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential — plants will rot in waterlogged soil. Thymus praecox is a low, mat-forming thyme of central and southern European rocky terrain, producing very flat carpets of tiny, dark-green, aromatic leaves 1–4 inches tall that bear a profusion of bright magenta-pink to lilac flowers in early summer smothered with honeybees; it forms a tighter, denser mat than wild thyme (T. serpyllum) and is the preferred species for most ground-cover, stepping-stone, and lawn-substitute plantings. The aromatic leaves are fully culinary-quality; the plant tolerates foot traffic and shearing well. Subsp. arcticus (with cultivars 'Coccineus', 'Purple Creeping') offers deep red-purple flowers for ornamental use.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as the seed benefits from natural cold stratification or a brief refrigerator stratification period of 2–4 weeks.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late autumn and allow natural freeze-thaw cycles to stratify the seed over winter for strong spring germination. Motherwort thrives in partial shade and moderately fertile, well-drained soil, often naturalizing along hedgerows and woodland margins. Harvest the upper third of flowering stems just as the lower flowers begin to open, using aerial parts fresh or tinctured in alcohol. Wear gloves when harvesting as the prickly calyces are sharp; avoid use during pregnancy due to its uterine-stimulating properties.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun in spring; mountain mint spreads aggressively by rhizomes and is best contained or given space to naturalize in a pollinator garden or meadow planting.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 18–24 inches apart; mountain mint is a native Eastern North American herb whose square stems and small white flowers appear in mid-to-late summer and are among the most powerful pollinator attractors in the native plant palette, drawing dozens of bee, wasp, and butterfly species simultaneously. The foliage has an intense peppermint-spearmint fragrance when brushed and can be dried for tea, used fresh in beverages, or as a culinary mint substitute. Plants spread vigorously by underground rhizomes — contain in raised beds or mow surrounding areas annually to limit spread. Fresh or dried leaves repel insects effectively.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring into sharp-draining, lean soil in full sun.
directions: Propagate from softwood cuttings taken in early summer and root them in a gritty, fast-draining mix before setting plants out in spring in their permanent location of full sun and extremely well-drained, lean soil. This exceptionally fragrant mounding subshrub is native to rocky slopes and mountain meadows of the American West, where it produces dense heads of pinkish-purple flowers in summer that are avidly worked by native bees and hummingbirds. Once established it is highly drought-tolerant and demands little supplemental water, making it an outstanding choice for xeric rock gardens and dry slopes in western gardens. Avoid overwatering or clay soils, which quickly cause root rot; treat it as a Mediterranean herb by cutting back lightly in early spring to remove winter-killed tips and encourage fresh growth.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; mountain pepper (Litsea cubeba) is a small laurel-family tree from subtropical China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia — the small, pepper-like fruits have an intensely lemon-floral, citrus-pepper aroma and are used as a spice and as one of the world's most important natural sources of citral, the primary compound in lemongrass oil, used in perfumery, flavoring, and as an antimicrobial.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; litsea grows naturally as an understory tree in subtropical forest and tolerates partial shade well. Litsea cubeba (mountain pepper, fragrant litsea, or maychangberry) is a small to medium-sized deciduous to semi-evergreen tree in the laurel family (Lauraceae) native to the subtropical mountain forests of central and southern China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. The tree produces small (1/4-inch), round, pepper-like black fruits (cubeba = resembling cubeb pepper) with an extraordinarily intense, clean, lemon-floral-citrus aroma — one of the most concentrated natural sources of citral (60–80% of essential oil content), the same aromatic compound found in lemongrass (Cymbopogon), melissa, and other citrus-scented plants. The essential oil of L. cubeba (may chang oil or litsea oil) is extracted commercially and used extensively in high-end perfumery, soap, and cosmetic formulations, and as a natural food flavoring. The dried fruits can be used as a spice — adding a bright, lemony, floral-pepper note to dishes — in a culinary style similar to Sichuan pepper or pink peppercorn. In Taiwan and southern China, the fruits, leaves, and bark are used in traditional mountain tribal cuisine as a distinctive aromatic spice. The tree also has documented antimicrobial activity from citral. It performs well in zone 8–11 subtropical gardens as an aromatic specimen or food forest understory tree.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; mountain pepper is an Australian native highland shrub from Tasmania and the alpine regions of southeast Australia — the berries and dried leaves are used as an intensely hot, aromatic, native Australian spice and are one of the signature ingredients of modern Australian native cuisine.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist. Tasmannia lanceolata (mountain pepper or Tasmanian pepperberry) is a native Australian alpine shrub from the cold, moist rainforests and alpine heathlands of Tasmania, Victoria, and New South Wales — the most important native Australian spice plant and a signature ingredient of contemporary Australian native cuisine. Both the black, ripe berries and the dried, ground leaves are intensely peppery-hot, with a heat that is initially sharp and then evolves into a prolonged, warming burn distinct from black pepper's heat — the primary pungent compounds (polygodial and drimanyl acetate) belong to a different chemical class from piperine (black pepper's heat compound) and interact differently with the tongue. The dried leaves have a complex, eucalyptus-clove-pepper aroma and are used in Australia as a seasoning rub for lamb, game, and seafood; the berries are used whole or crushed as a distinctive peppercorn substitute. Mountain pepper has become a centerpiece of the Australian 'bush tucker' (native food) movement and is increasingly available in gourmet food markets internationally. The plant is dioecious — plant male and female shrubs for berry production. In cultivation outside Australia, it requires cool, moist, acidic, shaded conditions.

common_name: Mrs. Burns' Lemon Basil (New Mexico Heirloom Lemon Basil)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mrs. Burns' Lemon is a New Mexico heirloom lemon basil selected for unusually intense lemon fragrance and strong vigor in heat.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Mrs. Burns' Lemon is a New Mexico heirloom lemon basil long saved and passed along by seed keepers for its unusually intense, true lemon fragrance and flavor, stronger and cleaner than many other lemon basil selections, on plants that grow taller and more vigorously than typical lemon basils even through Gulf South summer heat. The bright citrus flavor makes it outstanding in teas, fish and seafood dishes, fruit salads, and infused vinegars or oils. Pinch growing tips regularly to delay flowering and keep the plant bushy and productive, and harvest leaves often since frequent picking encourages fuller, more branched growth through the season.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or plant root divisions around the last frost date; mugwort also self-seeds freely if flower stalks are allowed to mature.
directions: Plant root divisions in any well-drained soil; mugwort is extremely vigorous and can become invasive via rhizomes, so consider installing a root barrier or growing in a contained bed. The deeply lobed, silver-backed leaves are strongly aromatic with a bitter, sage-like scent used in traditional European and East Asian medicine. Harvest leafy stems just before flowering in midsummer for use in moxibustion, digestive bitters, dream pillows, and traditional holiday flavoring of fatty meats. Cut plants back hard in late summer to control spread and prevent self-seeding.

plant_note: Surface sow; a biennial that flowers in its second year.
directions: Mullein is a striking hardy biennial that forms a rosette of soft, silver-green leaves the first year and sends up a tall yellow-flowered spike the second. Surface sow the dust-fine seed onto disturbed soil and leave it uncovered, as it needs light to germinate. It thrives in poor, well-drained ground and full sun with minimal water, making it ideal for lean sites. Allow a few plants to set seed and it will naturalize, returning on its own from year to year.

plant_note: Cold stratify seed, then surface sow indoors under light.
directions: Munstead is a compact, early-blooming English lavender prized for its sweet fragrance and tidy habit that suits containers and small gardens. Chill the seed for a few weeks, then surface sow indoors under light and be patient, as germination is slow and uneven. Transplant into sharply drained, even gritty soil in full sun, since lavender rots in wet ground. Prune lightly after flowering to keep plants dense and harvest the fragrant flower spikes for culinary or craft use.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seed for a few weeks before sowing to improve germination.
directions: Introduced in 1916 and named for Gertrude Jekyll's garden at Munstead Woods, this compact English lavender blooms earlier than most and stays neatly mounded. Its sweet flowers are among the best for culinary use as well as sachets and dried bouquets. Cold-stratify seed before sowing, then start indoors and transplant to full sun with sharp drainage. Keep water low once established, trim after flowering to maintain a tidy shape, and avoid rich or soggy soil.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; musk mallow grows as an annual in most of North America but perennializes in frost-free zones 10–12. In zone 9a it regrows from the base if frost kills the top in mild winters.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; musk mallow is a tropical Asian relative of okra and hibiscus grown primarily for the musky-aromatic seeds used in perfumery, liqueurs, and traditional medicine across South and Southeast Asia. The seeds contain ambrette seed oil, which has a rich, nutty-musky fragrance closely resembling animal musk — used as a natural, ethical alternative to animal musk in fine perfumery and as a fixative in high-end fragrance. The seeds are also used medicinally in Ayurveda and are added to the Egyptian spice blend 'beharat'. The large, showy, hibiscus-like flowers in yellow to red are highly ornamental. The entire plant — seeds, leaves, and roots — is edible, with the young leaves used as a cooked green. In zone 9, it behaves as a warm-season annual that may overwinter in protected spots.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade, replicating the rocky Andean slopes of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador where muña grows wild.
directions: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade, replicating the rocky Andean slopes of Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador where muña grows wild at elevation. This shrubby mint relative has hairy, serrated, intensely camphor-mint-scented leaves traditionally added to cooking beans and potatoes to reduce flatulence and brewed as a digestive tea. Harvest leafy stems just before flowering for the strongest aroma, and use fresh or air-dried in place of huacatay or regular mint in Peruvian stews and ceviche marinades.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; myoga is one of the few edible gingers that actively prefers shade and performs poorly in full sun in hot climates.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; myoga is the only ginger species that genuinely prefers shade, making it one of the most valuable edible plants for the shaded food garden. The edible parts are the flower buds and young shoots that emerge directly from the ground in late summer and fall — they are sliced and used as a fresh garnish in Japanese cuisine with a mild ginger-citrus flavor. The tall, arching reed-like stems make attractive foliage throughout summer. In zone 7–11 the roots are winter-hardy and re-emerge each spring, slowly spreading to form a clump; divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. An outstanding shade-garden edible for Gulf Coast gardens where deep shade under trees is otherwise difficult to plant productively.

common_name: Napoletano Basil (Italian Large-Leaf Lettuce-Leaf Neapolitan Basil)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Napoletano's very large leaves (sometimes 4–6 inches across) require slightly more space than smaller-leafed basil types. In zone 9, transplant March–April; a second planting in August–September provides fall production before the first frost. Napoletano is the traditional basil of Neapolitan pizza — large leaves torn and placed on pizza just before serving, where the heat wilts them without cooking, preserving the aromatic character.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil after last frost. Pinch flower buds as they appear to maintain leaf production. Napoletano (also called Italian Large-Leaf or Lettuce Leaf Basil) is the traditional basil of Neapolitan cuisine — a variety with exceptionally large, broadly oval, slightly crinkled, aromatic leaves that can reach 4–6 inches across in good growing conditions, two to three times the size of standard Genovese basil leaves. The very large leaf size makes Napoletano particularly well-suited to certain traditional Italian preparations: the leaves are large enough to use whole as a pizza topping without chopping, attractive as a garnish or salad base, and produce impressive yields of leaf area per harvest. The flavor is rich, sweet, and classically basil — virtually identical to Genovese in fragrance and taste, as the large leaf size is a morphological rather than a chemical difference between the varieties. Napoletano performs well in zone 9's warm summers and is one of the basil varieties that handles Gulf South heat and humidity acceptably, though like all basil it bolts in response to day length and hot temperatures — regular pinching extends productive life.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in warm, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; neem is very frost-sensitive and is killed at 32°F. It grows extremely fast in ideal tropical conditions — up to 10 feet per year — and is remarkably drought-tolerant once established. Seeds lose viability within weeks of ripening and should be planted fresh.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to fertile soil in full sun in a frost-free location; neem is one of the most multipurpose trees in tropical horticulture, revered for thousands of years in India where virtually every part of the tree is used: the seeds yield neem oil, widely used as an organic pesticide and insect repellent containing azadirachtin, a potent botanical insecticide; the leaves are used medicinally for their antibacterial, antifungal, and antiparasitic properties; young shoots and leaves are eaten as a bitter vegetable in some South and Southeast Asian cuisines; and the twigs are traditionally used as disposable toothbrushes (chew sticks). The tree itself is a spectacular ornamental — fast-growing with a broad, spreading crown of dense, pinnate leaves and clusters of fragrant white flowers beloved by bees. It is one of the most drought-tolerant trees available and tolerates alkaline, poor soils that support little else. The organic pesticide market for neem oil products has created significant commercial cultivation in Florida and Hawaii.

common_name: Negro Pepper (Grains of Selim, Ethiopian Pepper, Hwentia)
plant_note: Set out container-grown seedlings in spring into deep, moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; trees typically need 5-8 years before producing a useful pod harvest.
directions: Plant seedlings in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with full sun to partial shade, giving the tree ample room since it eventually reaches a slender, tall canopy form. Negro pepper is an aromatic evergreen tree native to the humid lowland forests and savanna transition zones of West and Central Africa, grown for its finger-like, slightly twisted seed pods that are sun-dried and often smoked before use. The dried pods and their small seeds carry a warm, smoky, camphor-and-pepper flavor used whole or ground in West African soups, stews, and spice blends, and are also valued in traditional medicine and smoked-fish preparation. Because it is slow to bear, most growers outside Africa treat it as a long-term agroforestry or specimen tree rather than a quick spice crop; young trees benefit from light shade and should be protected from strong wind while establishing.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; New Zealand tea tree requires excellent drainage and will not survive in heavy, poorly drained soil. Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings in summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean to average soil in full sun; New Zealand tea tree is one of the most important plants of Maori tradition and modern apiculture — the intensely antibacterial nectar from manuka flowers produces the famous manuka honey, scientifically documented for its exceptional wound-healing and antibacterial properties. The leaves were used by Maori as a medicinal tea. In the garden, manuka is a handsome small to medium shrub covered in masses of small, open flowers — white in the species, pink to deep crimson in many cultivars — in late winter through spring. The tiny, heather-like aromatic leaves are evergreen. Many ornamental double-flowered cultivars are available ('Martini', 'Red Damask', 'Crimson Glory') that are showy but produce less nectar for bees. Full drainage is essential — root rot in wet soil is the primary cause of failure.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; nodding onion tolerates poor, dry soils and is excellent in rock gardens and dry prairie plantings.
directions: Plant bulbs 2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; nodding onion is exceptionally adaptable and tolerates poor, dry, rocky soils where most alliums would struggle. Allium cernuum is a native wildflower of dry prairies, rocky slopes, and open woodlands across much of North America, named for its distinctive drooping, nodding flowerhead — the flower stalk curves or bends at the top so the umbel of small, pink to white, bell-shaped flowers faces downward in a charming, pendant cluster in mid-summer. All parts are edible with a mild onion flavor, and the plant was an important food source for many Native American peoples; it is also an excellent pollinator plant, attracting native bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects. Outstanding in rock gardens, dry meadows, and native prairie restorations; it self-seeds freely without being invasive.

plant_note: Transplant only after soil warms and nights stay above 50 F.
directions: Noga basil balances heavy yields with classic Genovese flavor, producing tall, uniform plants that grow fast and stand up to repeated cutting. Its large, glossy, dark green leaves perform well in the field, greenhouse, or a patio container. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant only after the soil has warmed thoroughly. Provide full sun, steady moisture, and frequent harvests, pinching out flower buds to keep leaf production high.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun to partial shade; northern bedstraw grows naturally in open prairies, meadow edges, rocky stream banks, and open woodlands across northern North America and Eurasia. Seeds benefit from cold stratification.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; northern bedstraw is an attractive native perennial of prairies, open rocky meadows, and woodland edges across northern North America and Eurasia, producing whorled leaves in groups of four and dense clusters of tiny, bright white, fragrant flowers in early to midsummer — among the most floriferous of the native Galium species. Unlike the scrambling, sticky-stemmed cleavers (G. aparine), northern bedstraw is upright and well-mannered, forming attractive clumps that spread slowly by rhizomes. The dried plant was historically used to stuff mattresses (giving the genus its common name 'bedstraw'), and the seeds can be roasted as a coffee substitute — the genus Galium is closely related to coffee (Coffea). The small white flowers are heavily visited by small native bees, flower flies, and beneficial wasps. A good, underused native for dry to average, rocky meadow gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; spicebush is dioecious — plant both male and female shrubs for berry production. One male plant is sufficient to pollinate 4–5 female plants within 50 feet.
directions: Plant in moist, average to rich soil in partial to full shade; northern spicebush is one of the few large shrubs truly native to the forest understory, making it invaluable for shaded landscapes. The tiny yellow flowers in early spring appear before the leaves and provide early nectar for native bees; the brilliantly yellow fall foliage is outstanding. Bright red, oil-rich berries on female plants in fall are devoured by migratory thrushes and are the primary larval host plant for the spicebush swallowtail butterfly. The dried berries are edible with a complex allspice-bay-pepper flavor once used as a colonial-era spice — they can replace allspice in recipes. All parts are intensely aromatic when crushed.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors under warmth and light a month or so before the last frost, then transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed, or direct sow once the garden has thoroughly warmed. Nufar was bred specifically to combine the classic large, glossy, sweet-scented leaves of Genovese basil with resistance to fusarium wilt, a soilborne disease that can devastate basil plantings, especially in beds where basil has been grown repeatedly. Its robust, upright plants hold up well through a full season of repeated pinching and harvesting for pesto and other Italian cooking. Regularly removing flower spikes keeps the plant leafier and extends its productive life into fall.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nugget climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Nugget, released by the USDA in 1982, is a reliable high-alpha American hop grown chiefly for its strong bittering power and productive, vigorous growth, with a robust herbal, slightly piney aroma that makes it a workhorse bittering hop in many American beer styles. It is valued by home growers in part for being an especially heavy yielder and easy to grow compared with some finicky aroma cultivars. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, aromatic, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring or late summer in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; nutmeg geranium is perennial in zones 9–11 and can be overwintered indoors as a houseplant in colder zones. It is compact enough for windowsill culture and is one of the most commonly grown and shared scented-leaf geraniums in cottage and herb gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; nutmeg geranium is a compact hybrid scented-leaf pelargonium with small, roundish, slightly gray-green, softly hairy leaves that release an unmistakable warm, spicy nutmeg-and-pine fragrance when touched or rubbed — quite different from the rosy fragrance of P. capitatum or the lemony notes of P. crispum. The fragrance is immediately recognizable as nutmeg with a fresh, slightly turpentine-woody undertone. Small, white, pink-veined pelargonium flowers appear in spring and early summer. A traditional cottage and kitchen garden herb grown for centuries for the use of its fragrant leaves in cooking (particularly in pound cakes, custards, and sugar syrups where a leaf placed in the bottom of the pan imparts its fragrance), for herbal sachets, and as a fragrant window-sill plant. Very easy to grow from cuttings, which root readily and were traditionally passed between neighbors and friends — the most common mode of propagation for all scented geraniums, which are grown almost exclusively as cutting-propagated plants rather than from seed.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring or late summer in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; oak-leaf geranium grows into a large, woody shrub in zones 9–11, reaching 4–5 feet or more in warm climates. Prune back hard each spring to maintain compact, vigorous growth and fresh aromatic foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; oak-leaf geranium is a boldly distinctive scented-leaf pelargonium species prized for two features — its unusually large, deeply lobed, oak-leaf-shaped leaves (which give the plant its species name quercifolium, Latin for 'oak-leaved') and the strong, pungent, bitter-almond to balsamic fragrance released when the sticky, glandular leaves are handled, distinctly different from the rose or citrus notes of other scented pelargoniums. The leaves are large and rough-textured compared to most pelargoniums, sticky to the touch, and the plant becomes a large, somewhat gawky but aromatic shrub in warm climates. Small rose-pink to magenta flowers appear in spring and summer. Used in the fragrance industry and in potpourri for its balsamic notes. In zones 9–11 it can grow into an impressive specimen shrub with an overwhelming presence when the foliage is disturbed in the breeze. 'Fair Ellen' is a widely available cultivar with particularly deep-cut, decorative leaves. A plant grown more for fragrant-foliage effect than ornamental flowers — one of the most botanically interesting of the diverse scented pelargonium group.

plant_note: Start indoors in warmth; transplant after frost has passed.
directions: Opal basil is an ornamental sweet basil with glossy, deep violet leaves and delicate pink blooms that make it as decorative as it is flavorful. Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm to trigger quick germination. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun once nights are reliably warm, spacing plants about a foot apart. Pinch flower buds to prolong leaf production and preserve the vivid purple color for garnishes and infused vinegars.

plant_note: Citrus-scented; propagate vegetatively.
directions: Propagate from cuttings to preserve the distinct orange-balsam fragrance of this thyme. The narrow grey-green leaves lend a citrusy note to poultry, fish, and marinades. Set plants in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun and keep water to a minimum. Shear lightly after bloom to maintain a tidy mound and prevent the base from going woody. Harvest sprigs throughout the season and protect crowns with gravel mulch over winter.

plant_note: Best grown from cuttings; contain roots.
directions: Propagate from stem cuttings or divisions, since named mints do not come true from seed. This citrusy peppermint variety perfumes teas, desserts, and cocktails with orange-bergamot notes. Plant in moist, rich soil in partial shade and confine roots to a buried pot or bottomless container. Water frequently and shear plants back after flowering to renew fresh leafy growth. Divide clumps every two or three years to keep the patch vigorous.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors; tiny seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Oregano is a hardy Mediterranean perennial with bold, aromatic leaves that are a cornerstone of Italian and Greek cooking. Surface sow the fine seed indoors and leave it uncovered under light, keeping it barely moist until sprouts appear. Transplant into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where the plant develops its strongest flavor. Harvest sprigs regularly and shear plants back after flowering to keep them compact and productive for years.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings, leaf cuttings, or divide clumps in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; orpine is extremely drought-tolerant once established and declines in rich, moist, poorly drained soil — lean, dry conditions produce compact, floriferous plants.
directions: Root cuttings or divide clumps in well-drained, average to poor, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; orpine (live-forever, stonecrop) is a European edible succulent perennial and one of the oldest known medicinal plants, used for wound healing throughout northern Europe since ancient times. Now correctly classified as Hylotelephium telephium, it produces attractive fleshy, blue-green, oval, toothed succulent leaves (edible raw in salads with a mild, slightly acidic flavor, or cooked) on upright stems, topped in late summer and fall by large, flat-headed clusters of star-shaped flowers in shades of deep-rose-pink, crimson-red, or white. The late-summer flowering season (August–October) makes it particularly valuable as a late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies, bumblebees, and migrating painted ladies. Extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived. It is the parent of the Hylotelephium 'Herbstfreude' (Autumn Joy) hybrid — one of the most widely planted autumn-flowering perennials in temperate gardens. 'Matrona' (purple-flushed foliage, dark stems, rose-pink flowers) and 'Purple Emperor' (deep-purple foliage) are outstanding cultivars.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall (require cold stratification) in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; osha is native to moist mountain meadows and open forests of the Rocky Mountains at 6,000–11,000 feet elevation and prefers cool summers — it may struggle in hot, humid lowland climates. The deep, dark-brown, hairy roots with a distinctive celery-like fragrance are the part used medicinally.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun (in cool climates); osha is one of the most important medicinal plants of the Southwest and Rocky Mountain Native American healing traditions — the pungent, dark-brown, shaggy-coated roots with their distinctive, strong, celery-fennel fragrance were used for centuries by Pueblo, Navajo, and other western peoples for respiratory conditions, immune support, and as bear medicine (bears seek out and roll in the roots emerging from hibernation, and the plant is sometimes called bear root). The large, finely divided, carrot-family foliage is attractive in the garden, and in summer the plants produce typical flat-topped umbel flowers in white. It grows naturally in cool, moist, mountain meadows of the Rocky Mountains from New Mexico to Wyoming at high elevations where cool summer temperatures persist. In lowland gardens it requires the coolest, most protected, shadiest positions available and adequate moisture. A plant of great ethnobotanical significance and unique aromatic character.

common_name: Osmin Basil (Compact Dark Purple Basil, Ornamental and Culinary Dwarf Purple Variety)
plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting or direct sow after last frost; Osmin is a compact, uniformly purple basil that stays significantly smaller (12–14 inches) than Dark Opal or other large-leafed purple basil types, making it better suited to containers, borders, and formal herb gardens where a tidy, predictable size is wanted. In zone 9, plant March–May and August–September. The deep purple coloration of Osmin is consistent and stable throughout the plant's life — unlike some purple basil varieties that may revert to green in high heat, Osmin maintains good color through warm summer conditions. Pinch out flower buds to extend the productive leaf stage; the pink to lavender flowers of Osmin are also ornamental and edible.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F or direct sow after last frost. Pinch growing tips frequently to maintain compact form. Harvest leaves as needed. Osmin Purple Basil is a compact, dark-purple ornamental-culinary basil variety selected specifically for consistent, uniform deep-purple coloration and a dwarf, tidy growth habit smaller than the standard Dark Opal and other large purple basil varieties. The name Osmin may reference Ottoman or Turkish naming conventions, reflecting the Central Asian and Middle Eastern origins of purple basil cultivar development. Purple basil varieties derive their color from anthocyanin pigments — the same class of compounds responsible for purple coloration in red cabbage, blueberries, and eggplant skin — and have been cultivated for centuries both for their visual distinction and for the herb's culinary uses. In the ornamental garden context, Osmin's uniformly purple foliage and compact size make it one of the most useful purple basil varieties for edging, formal herb garden designs, and container arrangements, where the consistent dark color provides a reliable foil for green herbs and bright flowers. The culinary value of purple basil is in the distinctive peppery, slightly clove-flavored fragrance (same family as green sweet basil but somewhat less intensely sweet) combined with the visual effect of purple-tinted vinegars (one of the most popular uses of purple basil), herbed oils, and fresh presentations where the purple leaf color adds visual interest. Osmin's smaller leaf size compared to Dark Opal means individual leaves are more delicate in presentations and salads. The flavor and fragrance are typical of the purple basil group: spicy, mildly clove-like, and sweet with less of the intense Italian character of Genovese.

common_name: Otto Quast Spanish Lavender (Compact Rabbit-Ear Lavender)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in fall in extremely well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; perfect drainage matters more than any other factor for this cultivar.
directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; like other Spanish lavenders, Otto Quast tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity far better than English lavender, but it still fails quickly in wet or heavy clay. This compact, free-flowering selection produces an unusually heavy show of purple flower spikes topped with prominent lavender-pink rabbit-ear bracts, blooming earlier in spring and repeating through the season more reliably than the straight species. Its tidy, rounded habit suits containers, border edges, and rock gardens where taller lavenders would flop. Shear back by about a third after each bloom flush to keep growth dense, and avoid heavy mulch or fertilizer, both of which encourage the rot that kills most garden lavenders.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in full sun; in zone 9 plant March–June. PKM-1 grows explosively fast in warm weather — seedlings can reach 8–10 feet in a single season. Moringa is killed to the ground by frost but the roots survive in zone 9 to resprout vigorously in spring. For continuous leaf harvest, cut plants back to 3–4 feet when they reach 6–8 feet to stimulate dense, bushy branching with easily reachable leaves. Seeds germinate without treatment but soaking overnight speeds germination. PKM-1 was developed by Periyakulam Horticultural College and Research Institute in Tamil Nadu and is one of the most productive pod-bearing selections available.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — moringa is extremely drought tolerant once established and is one of the few productive food trees that thrives in poor, dry, neglected sites; PKM-1 is an improved selection of Moringa (Moringa oleifera, the 'miracle tree') developed specifically for high pod yield and early production — bearing its first edible pods within 6–8 months of sowing from seed compared to the 12–18 months typical of seedling-grown moringa. The leaves, young pods (drumsticks), and flowers of moringa are all edible and among the most nutritionally dense plant foods available — the leaves contain protein, vitamin C, calcium, iron, and a range of antioxidants at concentrations that have made moringa a focus of nutritional research and a widely promoted food security crop. In zone 9 moringa grows as a rapidly resprouting tender perennial — killed to the ground by frost but regenerating vigorously from the root in spring and often reaching 10–15 feet before the next frost. The soft, ferny, compound leaves are harvested continuously throughout the growing season by cutting branch tips, and the long, angular seed pods (the 'drumsticks' of Indian cuisine) are harvested when young and tender for cooking in curries, soups, and stir-fries.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Padang cassia is the cinnamon most commonly sold in North American grocery stores and is more cold-hardy than true Ceylon cinnamon.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) in full sun; Padang cassia grows vigorously once established in frost-free conditions and begins producing harvestable bark on young shoots within 2–3 years after planting. Cinnamomum burmannii is an Indonesian native and the species that provides the majority of "cinnamon" sold in North American grocery stores and spice jars; it is harvested by stripping the bark from young branches and allowing it to dry into the familiar quills, and has a strong, sweet-spicy, slightly more pungent flavor and higher coumarin content than true Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum). The tree is an attractive, medium-sized, evergreen with oval, three-veined, cinnamon-scented leaves and can be grown as a landscape ornamental in zone 9–10; harvest bark from young shoots 1–2 years old and re-coppice to regenerate the plant cyclically for ongoing production.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall onto dry, rocky, well-drained soil; winter cold provides natural stratification and supports reliable spring germination.
directions: Direct sow in fall onto dry, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral, very well-drained soil in full sun, allowing winter temperatures to cold-stratify seed naturally before spring germination. Once established, thin plants to 18-24 inches and provide no supplemental irrigation, as this species is adapted to the parched mountain slopes and canyon edges of New Mexico, Arizona, and adjacent Mexico where it is native. Dense, upright spikes of pale pink to lavender-pink, anise-scented tubular flowers appear from summer through fall and draw hummingbirds, monarch butterflies, and native bumblebees in great numbers. The broad, aromatic leaves carry a pleasant anise-mint flavor and can be dried and brewed as herbal tea; this species is far more drought-tolerant than Agastache foeniculum and thrives where other hyssops fail.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; palmarosa is a tropical Indian aromatic grass in the same genus as lemongrass, grown for the essential oil distilled from its fresh leaves — one of the world's most important fragrance grass crops.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in warm soil in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; palmarosa is drought-tolerant once established. Cymbopogon martinii (palmarosa or gingergrass) is a tall, tropical Indian aromatic grass closely related to lemongrass (C. citratus), citronella (C. nardus), and vetiver (Chrysopogon zizanioides) — grown commercially as one of the world's most important perfumery and aromatherapy raw material crops. The leaves and stems distill to a pale-yellow essential oil with a soft, sweet, floral-rose fragrance with undertones of geranium — the compound geraniol (up to 90% of the oil) is responsible for the characteristic rose-like smell. Palmarosa oil is used extensively in perfumery as a low-cost rose substitute or adulterant, in cosmetics, soaps, and aromatherapy (antibacterial, skin-conditioning properties), and as a flavoring in some food products. The plant itself resembles a coarser, more upright lemongrass with narrower leaves and a somewhat less pronounced citrus scent — though the leaves are pleasantly fragrant when crushed. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, palmarosa is ornamental and easy to grow; fresh leaves can be used to scent soaps, sachets, and infused oils at home.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; palmarosa grass grows in tropical and subtropical conditions and is killed by frost. In zone 9, it may be grown as a warm-season annual or perennial in frost-free microclimates.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; palmarosa grass is an Indian aromatic grass in the same genus as lemongrass and citronella, cultivated throughout tropical Asia and Madagascar for its essential oil — one of the most widely used in perfumery. The essential oil, distilled from the leaves and tops, is dominated by geraniol (70–85%), giving it a sweet, rose-like fragrance with floral and earthy undertones. It is used extensively in cosmetics, soaps, food flavorings, and aromatherapy and is one of the most popular natural geraniol sources in the fragrance industry. The grass has traditionally been used to adulterate or substitute for expensive attar of roses in Indian perfumery — a use reflected in the common name. In the home garden, it provides an attractive clumping grass that can be harvested by cutting back and steam-distilling the biomass for aromatic purposes.

plant_note: Plant rooted suckers or stem cuttings after last frost in a warm, sheltered position; requires consistently warm temperatures above 60°F.
directions: Propagate by removing rooted basal suckers from an established plant and potting into rich, moist, well-drained potting mix; cuttings without roots should be allowed to callous before planting. Pandan is a tropical Southeast Asian herb that rarely sets seed in cultivation and must be grown vegetatively; the long, strap-like leaves impart a distinctive vanilla-like, grassy fragrance used throughout Southeast Asian sweets, rice dishes, and drinks. Grow in bright indirect light or dappled shade with consistent moisture and high humidity; in temperate climates it makes an excellent houseplant or conservatory specimen. Harvest mature outer leaves by cutting at the base; knot or tie leaves before use in cooking to release their fragrance, or blend with water to make an extract.

subcategory: Southeast Asian fragrant culinary leaf herb
plant_note: Root stem cuttings or offshoots in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12, or grow as a container plant in zone 8–9; Pandan Leaf (Pandan, Screwpine Leaf, Daun Pandan) is the most important flavoring herb in Southeast Asian cuisine — the intensely aromatic, long, bright-green, strappy leaves provide a distinctive vanilla-coconut-like fragrance and vivid green color to rice, cakes, drinks, desserts, and savory dishes across Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam.
directions: Root Pandanus amaryllifolius offshoots or stem cuttings in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; keep evenly moist at all times; in zone 10–12 grow in the ground in a sheltered, partially shaded position; in cooler zones grow in a large container brought inside in winter. Pandan Leaf is the vanilla of Southeast Asia — the green, aromatic leaves of this compact pandanus screwpine are as fundamental to Southeast Asian cooking as vanilla is to Western baking, providing an intensely fragrant, green, vanilla-coconut aroma and flavor to an extraordinary range of foods. The long, stiff, bright-green leaves (tied in knots and simmered in dishes, or juiced and blended into batters) flavor coconut rice (nasi lemak), ketan (sticky rice cakes), chiffon cakes, kaya jam, onde-onde, and countless other Southeast Asian sweets and desserts. Pandan juice (squeezed from crushed leaves) provides a vivid natural green color and strong flavor to pandan chiffon cake and kueh (traditional sweets). The active flavor compound is 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline — the same compound found in basmati rice and jasmine flowers — explaining its distinctive, reminiscent aroma. Unlike most Pandanus, this species is known only from cultivation (never found in the wild) and reproduces entirely vegetatively by offshoots; it is believed to be a sterile cultigen developed in ancient Southeast Asian agriculture. Indispensable for any garden serving Southeast Asian cuisine.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost once soil has warmed to 65°F; papalo thrives in hot summers when cilantro fails.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in the garden once soil is warm and all frost danger has passed; papalo does not transplant well due to its taproot. This Mexican culinary herb is used raw, added at the table rather than during cooking — heat destroys its unique flavor, which blends notes of cilantro, rue, and citrus. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates heat and moderate drought admirably, making it valuable as a summer substitute for cilantro. Harvest young leaves and stem tips regularly while the plant is in vegetative growth; use very sparingly as the flavor is more intense than cilantro.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil; papaloquelite self-seeds readily in zone 9–11 and may naturalize in warm gardens. In Mexico it is often grown with corn, beans, and squash in traditional milpa gardens, tolerating the partial shade of taller corn plants.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; papaloquelite is a traditional Mesoamerican culinary herb used throughout Mexico, Central America, and Bolivia with a distinctive aroma that combines cilantro, rue, and a strong, almost petroleum-like note that is at once exotic and intensely savory — the flavor used extensively in Mexican salsas, pozole, tacos de canasta, and Oaxacan cooking as a bolder, heat-stable alternative to cilantro. Unlike cilantro, which wilts when heated, papaloquelite retains flavor when briefly cooked and is used as a fresh herb added at the end of cooking or stirred into hot soups tableside. The oval, glandular-dotted leaves on the blue-green stems are harvested by pinching stem tips regularly. In zone 9 it grows as a warm-season annual that self-seeds freely in favorable sites; drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in the heat that limits cilantro production in Gulf Coast summers, making it a superb cilantro substitute for tropical-climate gardeners.

plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; parsley tolerates light spring frosts once established.
directions: Soak seeds overnight to soften the hull, then sow 1/4 in deep; germination is notoriously slow—up to four weeks. Thin to 6–9 in and keep soil consistently moist, as parsley bolts quickly under drought stress. Apply a light nitrogen feed at mid-season to sustain lush leaf production. Harvest outer stems at the base, leaving the inner crown intact to keep the plant productive.

plant_note: Sow early; soaking seed overnight speeds notoriously slow germination.
directions: Italian Giant is a robust flat-leaved parsley prized by cooks for its strong, fresh flavor and easy-to-chop leaves. Grown as an annual, it produces large, dark green leaves ideal for soups, stews, and garnishes. Sow seed directly or start indoors, keeping the soil consistently moist since germination is slow and can take up to three weeks. Give it full sun to part shade and harvest outer stems first so the plant keeps producing. It tolerates light frost and can be grown in containers on a sunny windowsill.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in moist perlite at 75°F indoors; plant outside after last frost in a sheltered spot. In frost-free zones 10–11 it persists as a woody perennial subshrub.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite at 75°F and provide high humidity during rooting; commercial patchouli rarely sets viable seed and is almost universally propagated vegetatively. Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. The broad, irregularly toothed leaves release the characteristic heavy, earthy patchouli fragrance when touched or bruised, a scent that intensifies as leaves dry and ferment. Harvest branches before flowering for maximum essential oil content by cutting stems back to a node; the plant re-sprouts vigorously. Essential oil is steam-distilled from dried leaves and used widely in perfumery and aromatherapy.

plant_note: Plant after all danger of frost has passed in zone 9; in frost-free areas it can be planted any time. This Honduran native thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers and will return reliably from the roots in mild winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and water consistently through the establishment period, then maintain moderate irrigation as the plant is sensitive to prolonged drought but equally intolerant of waterlogged roots. The enormous, velvety leaves emit a sweet peach fragrance when brushed, and tall spikes of bright magenta-pink flowers appear in late fall and winter, drawing hummingbirds throughout the cool season. Pinch stem tips during the growing season to promote bushy, compact growth and delay flowering until the plant is well branched. In zone 9, cut back frost-damaged stems to the ground in late winter and the plant will resprout vigorously from established roots.

plant_note: Direct-sow into sharply drained, gritty soil after the last frost; in colder zones grow as an annual or overwinter potted specimens under cover.
directions: Anacyclus pyrethrum forms a low, feathery-leaved mat of finely divided foliage topped with chamomile-like daisy flowers whose petals are white above and deep maroon-red beneath. It is not the same plant as insecticidal pyrethrum (Tanacetum cinerariifolium) despite the shared common name; the pungency here comes from the root, which contains a numbing, saliva-stimulating compound that has made it a classic Mediterranean and North African remedy chewed fresh or dried to relieve toothache and dry mouth. Plant in gritty, low-fertility, sharply drained soil in full sun; standing winter wet is the most common cause of failure. Harvest roots from established two-year-old plants in autumn for drying.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow as seeds need light and keep soil consistently moist.
directions: Surface-sow seeds onto moist starting mix as they need light to germinate, keeping the medium evenly moist throughout germination. Pennyroyal spreads by creeping stems and works well as a fragrant ground cover in moist, partially shaded spots; it spreads less aggressively than other mints. The intensely peppermint-scented leaves are used fresh or dried as a traditional flea-repelling herb for pet bedding and as a strewing herb. Caution: pennyroyal oil is highly toxic and internal use carries serious risk — use the dried herb only in small quantities for tea and keep away from pregnant women and pets.

plant_note: Surface sow; seed needs light and warmth to germinate.
directions: Peppermint is a vigorous, cool-flavored perennial beloved for teas, desserts, and savory dishes. Press the fine seed onto the surface without covering, as it needs light to germinate, and keep it warm and evenly moist. It thrives in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun to part shade and spreads aggressively by runners, so grow it in a container or a contained bed. Harvest sprigs anytime and cut plants back before flowering to keep the foliage flavorful.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; contain in pots or with underground root barriers as peppermint spreads aggressively by stolons.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; contain in buried pots or with root barriers sunk 12 inches into the soil as peppermint spreads aggressively by underground stolons and will colonize a large area if uncontained. Mentha × piperita is a sterile hybrid between water mint (M. aquatica) and spearmint (M. spicata) that is propagated vegetatively; it is the mint whose essential oil (menthol) is used in toothpaste, confections, medicine, cosmetics, and a vast range of products, and whose leaves are used for peppermint tea, juleps, mojitos, and as a culinary flavoring. Black peppermint (var. piperita) has purple-tinged stems and the strongest menthol flavor; white peppermint (var. officinalis) has greener stems and is slightly milder. Both types prefer moist, fertile soil and appreciate afternoon shade in hot climates.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade; peppermint geranium is the most shade-tolerant of the scented pelargoniums and performs acceptably in quite bright indirect light — avoid hot, intense afternoon sun which causes the velvety leaves to scorch.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade; peppermint geranium is the most shade-tolerant and large-leaved of the scented pelargoniums — its enormous, densely hairy, velvety, gray-green, rounded leaves give the plant a soft, textural, spreading quality unlike any other herb, and crush the leaves to release an intensely fresh, clear peppermint-eucalyptus fragrance that is one of the most pleasant and cooling herb scents available. The velvety, felt-like texture of the large leaves is as much a tactile as a visual pleasure. It spreads by lax, trailing stems to cover considerable ground in partial shade, making it useful as a low, scented groundcover in shaded containers, window boxes, and garden edges. Small, white, purple-spotted flowers appear at intervals. Leaves are used to flavor sachets, tea, and baked goods. It is more water-tolerant than most scented pelargoniums. The most commonly grown cultivar for ground coverage and shade tolerance is the straight species; 'Chocolate Mint' (dark-spotted center) is an attractive variant.

plant_note: Plant in spring or autumn; pepperwort spreads aggressively by rhizomes and can become invasive in moist, disturbed soils — contain in raised beds or large containers, or plant where spread is acceptable. It has been cultivated as a horseradish substitute since the Middle Ages.
directions: Plant rooted divisions in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; pepperwort (Lepidium latifolium) is a vigorous, spreading, perennial cress with large, thick leaves that have a strong, peppery to horseradish-like flavor much more intense than common garden cress — used as a horseradish substitute in medieval European cooking and still used traditionally in parts of Britain and Scandinavia. Young leaves can be eaten raw in small amounts as a condiment or added sparingly to salads and sandwiches; older leaves and the roots are used cooked as a flavoring. Caution: the plant is listed as an invasive weed in parts of the western United States where it colonizes riparian areas and wetlands; plant only in contained situations in those regions. Produces masses of small white flowers attractive to bees.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; perennial basil benefits from regular tip-harvesting to prevent flowering, which prolongs the productive leafy growth stage.
directions: Root stem cuttings in water or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; perennial basil (African basil, East Indian basil, spice basil) is a tropical perennial species grown in Gulf Coast and subtropical gardens for its superior performance in the heat and humidity that causes standard sweet basil (O. basilicum) to bolt and decline rapidly in midsummer — perennial basil withstands zone 9–12 summer heat, continues producing through the hottest months, and in frost-free climates grows as a large, multi-stemmed perennial shrub to 3–4 feet that persists for several years. The flavor is similar to sweet basil but carries an additional spicy, clove-like note that distinguishes it in cooking. Like all basils, the culinary quality is best before flowering; tip-prune regularly to delay bolting. It roots readily from stem cuttings placed in water, making it easy to propagate and share. Excellent in containers and mixed herb borders as a large, bushy accent. In zones below 9, grow as a long-season annual or bring cuttings indoors in fall to overwinter.

common_name: Perennial Basil (East African Basil, Tree Basil)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or root cuttings; grows as a large perennial shrub in frost-free zones 9–12; bring containers indoors before first frost in cooler climates.
directions: Start from seed or cuttings and plant in full sun after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; perennial basil (Ocimum gratissimum, also called East African or tree basil) is a large woody-based perennial subshrub native to tropical Africa and Asia that grows year-round in frost-free gardens, eventually reaching 4–6 feet tall and requiring no replanting. The flavor is more pungent and medicinal than sweet basil — strongly clove-like with hints of eucalyptus and camphor — and is the basil of choice in West African, Southeast Asian, and South American cooking rather than Italian cuisine. Used fresh or dried in stews, soups, bean dishes, and rice preparations. An excellent container plant for northern gardeners overwintered indoors on a sunny sill.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface after last frost when soil is warm; shiso seed requires light to germinate — do not cover. Cold-stratification improves germination rate: chill seed at 40°F for 2 weeks before sowing.
directions: Surface sow on moist soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; perilla (shiso) is the essential Japanese herb with large, ruffled leaves in green or deep purple-red that have a distinctive flavor combining cinnamon, anise, cloves, and mint — unique in the herbal palette. Green shiso (ao-jiso) wraps sushi, flavors salads, and garnishes sashimi; red/purple shiso (aka-jiso) colors umeboshi pickled plums and makes the vivid magenta shiso juice (yukari). Both forms are ornamentally striking, especially the 'Britton' frilly-leafed type. Plants self-seed extremely prolifically — thin seedlings carefully and pull unwanted volunteers before they go to seed, as it can naturalize aggressively in favorable climates.

plant_note: Press seed onto the surface of moist starting mix without covering — the fine seed needs light to germinate — 6-8 weeks before last frost, and transplant seedlings out after frost danger has passed; historically grown in the rich alluvial soils of St. James Parish, Louisiana.
directions: Transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Nicotiana rustica is a shorter, broader-leaved, much more potent species than common tobacco, historically grown by the Choctaw and later by Acadian farmers along the Mississippi River in St. James Parish, Louisiana, where its cured leaf became the base for Perique, a uniquely fermented tobacco with a distinctive dark, fruity, spicy character produced by packing the cured leaf under heavy pressure in wooden barrels for months, a traditional process protected as a geographic specialty of the region. The broad, crinkled, yellow-green leaves are harvested and air-cured much like common tobacco before undergoing the distinctive pressure-fermentation that sets Perique apart from other tobaccos. This species is also of historical significance as one of the tobaccos originally cultivated and traded by Indigenous peoples of North America prior to European contact. All parts of the plant contain nicotine at notably higher concentrations than common tobacco and are toxic if ingested, so keep well away from pets, livestock, and children, and wear long sleeves when handling mature plants to avoid skin absorption.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into full sun once soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Persian Basil, a 2015 All-America Selections winner, produces large, soft silvery-green leaves with an assertive spicy flavor combining clove, anise, and a hint of lemon that sets it apart from sweeter Genovese-type basils. The sturdy, upright plants are notably slow to bolt, holding good flavor and tender texture well into summer while many other basils turn bitter once they flower. It is the traditional basil of Persian cuisine, eaten fresh as part of sabzi khordan herb platters and stirred into stews, rice dishes, and grilled meats. Give it full sun and steady moisture, and harvest by pinching stem tips regularly to keep the plant bushy and delay flowering even longer.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Persian catmint is a low, mounding, sterile hybrid-like species excellent for border edging and as a groundcover in dry, sunny situations.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Persian catmint blooms most freely with good drainage and lean, somewhat dry soil — avoid rich, moist soil which produces lush but less floriferous plants. Nepeta mussinii is a low, aromatic, mounding European catmint with soft, gray-green, scalloped, strongly fragrant leaves and prolific spikes of small, lavender-blue flowers from late spring through early summer; shear plants by half after the first flush of bloom to stimulate a second flowering period in mid- to late summer. Unlike the commonly grown N. × faassenii (a sterile hybrid), N. mussinii is the true species from the Caucasus; it is slightly smaller than faassenii and sets viable seed. Attractive to bees, butterflies, and cats; resistant to deer and rabbits. Use as a low, billowing border edger or path-side planting.

common_name: Pesto Perpetuo Basil (Variegated Non-Flowering Columnar Basil)
plant_note: Plant cuttings or purchased starts after last frost in full sun to partial shade; Pesto Perpetuo is a sterile hybrid (will not set seed) and must be propagated vegetatively from cuttings. Root 4-inch stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix at 70–80°F for 2–3 weeks. In zone 9, Pesto Perpetuo can be grown as a semi-perennial — it may survive mild winters if protected from frost. The columnar form (18–30 inches tall, only 8–12 inches wide) fits neatly into tight spaces and container arrangements.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun after last frost; pinch occasionally to maintain compact form — unlike most basil, Pesto Perpetuo never flowers and never needs pinching for flower removal. Root 4-inch stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix. Pesto Perpetuo is a unique sterile basil hybrid — a cross between Ocimum basilicum and Ocimum citriodorum — that distinguishes itself from all other basil varieties by never flowering and never setting seed. Standard basil becomes progressively less productive, more bitter, and eventually dies after flowering and setting seed; the entire management practice of regular pinching (removing flower buds before they open) is devoted to delaying this flowering. Pesto Perpetuo's sterility eliminates this entirely: it produces leaves continuously throughout the entire growing season without any flower development, making it the most consistently productive basil for a full-season harvest without intervention. The leaves are small to medium, oval, with a distinctive cream-white to ivory variegated margin around a green center — an ornamental quality unlike any other basil type. The flavor is lemon-basil in character — aromatic, mildly sweet, with distinct citrus notes alongside the standard basil character — very pleasant fresh but somewhat different from classic Genovese pesto basil. The columnar habit (upright, narrow, 18–30 inches) makes it ideal for containers, herb pots, and edible ornamental arrangements.

common_name: Phenomenal Lavender (Heat-Humidity Tolerant Lavandin for Southern Gardens)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring or fall in full sun with excellent drainage; Phenomenal is a lavandin hybrid selected for superior performance in hot, humid climates where standard English lavenders rot or fail — it is the most widely recommended lavender for the Southeastern US, Texas, and other regions with hot, humid summers that are particularly hard on lavender; significantly more disease-resistant than any English lavender variety.
directions: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; in humid climates amend clay soil with coarse sand or gravel; excellent air circulation is essential; in zones 7–9 with humid summers, plant in fall for establishment; Phenomenal resists the root rots and fungal diseases that kill standard lavenders in humid heat, making it essentially the only lavender that can be grown reliably as a long-lived perennial in the humid South. Phenomenal is a lavandin hybrid (Lavandula × intermedia) that was selected specifically for exceptional performance in hot, humid climates — a characteristic set that very few lavender varieties possess, since most lavenders originate from the Mediterranean region and are adapted to hot, dry summers rather than the humid heat of the American Southeast. The selection and introduction of Phenomenal represented a significant advance for Southern gardeners who had long struggled to grow lavender as a lasting perennial in zones 7–9 with high summer humidity — the conditions that cause root rot and crown fungal diseases in English lavenders within 1–3 years. Phenomenal's superior disease resistance in humid conditions comes from a combination of its thicker, more robust stems, greater inherent resistance to Botrytis and Phytophthora, and possibly greater ability to shed moisture from the crown. The plants are large, vigorous, and productive, with long silver-gray spikes and a strongly fragrant, slightly camphor-accented scent. For zone 9a Texas and Gulf Coast gardens, Phenomenal is the practical choice when other lavenders have repeatedly failed.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or divisions in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; the variegated form grows more slowly than plain mints and performs best with some afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant stem cuttings or divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, containing in a buried pot to limit spread; pineapple mint is a variegated form of apple mint with cream-edged, textured, rounded leaves that carry a fruity, tropical fragrance somewhere between pineapple and mint that makes it popular in fruit salads, cocktails, mojitos, and desserts. The plants are striking enough to use as ornamental container plants, with the white-edged leaves providing bright contrast in shade gardens. Not as aggressively invasive as spearmint or peppermint, but still spreads by rhizome and benefits from containment. Harvest regularly to keep growth compact and fresh.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix at 65–75°F in spring and plant after all frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil in zone 8–11; in colder climates grow as a container plant and bring indoors before frost.
directions: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix in spring and plant after all frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; pineapple sage is a large-leaved Mexican native with a striking, true pineapple fragrance that makes it one of the most popular ornamental-culinary herbs for Gulf Coast and zone 8–11 gardens. The soft, bright-green leaves are used fresh in fruit salads, herbal teas, cocktails, and desserts where the pineapple-mint flavor adds an unexpected tropical note; the long stems are also attractive in floral arrangements. Brilliant scarlet tubular flowers appear in late fall and winter in warm climates, making pineapple sage one of the best late-season hummingbird plants for southern gardens. In zone 8 it may freeze to the ground but re-emerges from the roots in spring; take cuttings before first frost in colder climates to overwinter indoors.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall in compacted, poor, lean, disturbed soil in full sun to partial shade; pineapple weed is a pioneer annual that naturally colonizes path edges, gravel, and disturbed ground. It self-sows freely and typically requires no deliberate sowing once established in appropriate conditions.
directions: Scatter seeds on compacted, lean, disturbed, sunny to partly shaded soil and allow to naturalize; pineapple weed is a small annual of the chamomile tribe, native to northeastern Asia but widely naturalized as a weed of paths, roadsides, and disturbed ground throughout North America. Unlike true chamomile, the tiny dome-shaped flower heads lack white ray petals — only the central yellow-green disc flowers are present, giving the plant a distinctive button-like appearance.
