When crushed, the entire plant releases an intense, sweet pineapple-chamomile fragrance that is unmistakable and charming. The flower heads can be brewed into a pleasant, mild, pineapple-scented herbal tea similar to chamomile tea but with a tropical twist. The plant typically colonizes compacted, poor soils where it often grows in path edges, gravel driveways, and worn turf without any encouragement. Gather the button-like heads for tea when fully yellow-green and fragrant.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; pinecone ginger thrives in the warm, humid conditions of the Gulf Coast and produces its most spectacular inflorescences in the heat of summer and fall. In zone 9 it goes dormant in winter and regrows reliably in spring.
directions: Plant rhizomes in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; pinecone ginger (shampoo ginger, wild ginger) is a spectacular tropical ginger grown for its unusual inflorescences — tight, compact, cone-shaped flower heads that look exactly like green pinecones on thick stems, which mature from green to brilliant red as the season progresses. The small, yellow flowers emerge briefly from between the bracts. The ripe, red cones produce a fragrant, slightly slimy liquid when squeezed that has been used as a hair conditioner and shampoo in Pacific Island and Asian cultures for centuries — the liquid has a pleasant, gingery fragrance and actually conditions hair effectively. The rhizomes are edible with a slightly bitter, medicinal ginger flavor and are used in Southeast Asian cooking. In zone 9 the tall, bamboo-like stems die back completely in winter and regrow from rhizomes in spring, providing both edible, fragrant, and ornamental value throughout the warm season.

common_name: Pink Chintz Thyme (Fuzzy Gray-Green Creeping Thyme)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring or fall in very well-drained, sandy or gritty, lean soil in full sun; thyme rots readily in wet, heavy soil.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy or gritty, lean soil; thyme rots quickly in wet or heavy ground. Pink Chintz is a low, mat-forming creeping thyme with soft, fuzzy, gray-green leaves that give the foliage a distinctive downy texture, covered in a heavy flush of small salmon-pink flowers in late spring to early summer that draw bees in large numbers. Its dense, mat-forming habit makes it a favorite for planting between stepping stones and pavers, where light foot traffic releases its herbal fragrance, as well as for draping over rock walls and border edges. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tidy and encourage dense new growth.

plant_note: Sow seeds after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; pipicha is a warm-season annual herb grown for the fresh culinary use of its pungent, narrow leaves. In zones 9-11 it can be grown as a short-lived perennial. Harvest leaves frequently to delay flowering and extend the harvest season. The leaves are most aromatic when harvested young.
directions: Sow seeds after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pipicha is a strongly aromatic Mexican herb native to the dry, mountainous regions of Oaxaca, Puebla, and Guerrero, used in Oaxacan cuisine as one of the distinctive flavoring herbs — recognizable by its very narrow, linear leaves dotted with visible oil glands (the 'porophyllum' = pore-leaf name refers to these), which release a pungent, complex aroma combining elements of rue, cilantro, and anise when bruised or used in cooking. It is used in tlayudas, quesillo dishes, soups, black beans, and as a fresh herb scattered over completed dishes. Pipicha is closely related to papalo (Porophyllum ruderale) which is already more widely known in US markets, but has narrower, more pungent leaves and a slightly different flavor profile preferred by cooks from the Oaxacan Valleys. In regions with good Mexican grocery supply, both pipicha and papalo can sometimes be found fresh. Grow as a warm-season annual in most of North America.

plant_note: Plant small rooted divisions in spring in very well-drained, dry to moist, highly acidic, humus-rich, needle-duff soil in full shade; pipsissewa grows symbiotically with mycorrhizal fungi in conifer forest duff and is notoriously difficult to transplant successfully — disturb the roots as little as possible and never use garden soil.
directions: Plant in dry to moist, highly acidic, humus-rich, conifer-needle duff soil in full shade beneath pines or oaks; pipsissewa is a small, semi-woody, evergreen native of dry conifer and mixed forests across the Northern Hemisphere, recognized by its whorled, dark green, glossy, toothed leaves with pale midribs and its nodding clusters of waxy, pink-white, fragrant flowers in summer. Like spotted wintergreen (C. maculata) and other Pyrola relatives, it is mycoheterotrophic — partially dependent on mycorrhizal fungi for nutrition and extremely difficult to establish in garden conditions without intact fungal partners. The plant has a long history of use in traditional Native American medicine and was an ingredient in the original commercial root beer formulas. Do not collect from wild populations. Best appreciated as a feature of intact native forest rather than a cultivated garden plant.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start February–March and transplant March–April. Pistou can also be direct-sown in warm soil in April. A second planting in July provides fall production. The naturally compact, globe-forming habit needs minimal maintenance — pinch flower buds as they appear to extend the leaf harvest.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Pistou Basil is a French compact dwarf basil named for the Provençal paste pistou — the French equivalent of Italian pesto made with fresh basil, garlic, olive oil, and sometimes cheese and tomatoes. The plant forms a naturally round, globe-shaped mound of small to medium-sized aromatic leaves with a rich, clove-spicy basil flavor slightly sweeter and less anise-forward than Italian sweet basil. The compact habit (8–16 inches, self-branching) makes Pistou ideal for container growing, window boxes, and herb gardens where space is limited. Unlike Fino Verde with its tiny, fingernail-sized leaves, Pistou produces slightly larger leaves that are easier to harvest individually and better-suited to chopping for pistou paste, compound butter, and herb-infused oils. The two cultivars — Pistou and Fino Verde — are distinctly different: Pistou is more upright and globe-forming, Fino Verde is a lower spreading mound with smaller leaves. In zone 9 both provide an excellent warm-season herb harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; plains bee balm is an annual or short-lived perennial that self-seeds reliably in dry, open conditions — sow in masses on poor, sandy soil where it can naturalize without competition from taller plants.
directions: Plains bee balm is the drought-tolerant Monarda of the southern Great Plains, growing naturally on dry, sandy, rocky soils of the short-grass and mixed-grass prairies of Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Colorado where rainfall is too scarce and the climate too extreme for other bee balms to survive. The plant is intensely aromatic — a strong, pleasant oregano-like scent rises from the leaves when brushed — and it has been used by indigenous peoples and settlers as a culinary herb and tea plant; it makes an excellent substitute for Mexican oregano in southwestern cooking. Small, pink to lavender whorled flowers appear on branching stems in summer and are heavily visited by native bees and small butterflies for nectar; the aromatic oils deter deer and most mammalian herbivores. In dry, sunny native garden situations and xeriscape designs, plains bee balm provides both ornamental interest and aromatic culinary value with essentially no irrigation required once established in sandy, well-drained soil.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratification improves germination.
directions: Sow in fall or cold-stratify seed for four weeks before spring sowing to break dormancy. This drought-tough native milkweed has a deep taproot historically used for respiratory ailments. Plant in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid moving it once established. The brilliant orange flowers are a magnet for butterflies and native bees. Water only during severe drought and harvest roots from mature plants in autumn.

common_name: Portuguese Pink Rosemary (Upright Pink-Flowered Culinary Rosemary)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container starts in spring in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; propagate this cultivar vegetatively, since seed-grown rosemary does not come true to flower color.
directions: Portuguese Pink is an upright culinary rosemary similar in size and habit to Tuscan Blue, but distinguished by soft pink flowers marked with darker pink veining instead of the usual blue-violet. The glossy deep-green foliage is fully aromatic and flavorful, making it as useful in the kitchen as any standard rosemary while adding a less common flower color to the herb border. Its tall, dense growth habit lends itself to hedging, topiary, and use as a specimen shrub, much like other large upright rosemary cultivars. Grow it in full sun with sharp drainage, and prune after flowering to maintain a tight form.

plant_note: Start from cuttings or divisions in spring; Origanum onites (pot marjoram or Turkish oregano) is the oregano of eastern Mediterranean and Turkish cuisine, with stronger, more resinous, pungent flavor than sweet marjoram and milder, sweeter flavor than Greek or Italian oregano — used as a bridge herb between the two in Middle Eastern and Turkish cooking.
directions: Propagate from stem cuttings or divisions in spring; plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — pot marjoram is a Mediterranean native that dislikes heavy, moist soils and grows best in conditions similar to its native rocky hillside habitats. Origanum onites is distinct from both sweet marjoram (O. majorana) and common Greek oregano (O. vulgare subsp. hirtum), occupying a middle flavor ground between the two: it is more aromatic and peppery than sweet marjoram but less aggressively pungent than the intense Greek species used on pizza. In Turkish and eastern Mediterranean cooking it is the standard 'kekik' (thyme/oregano) used on meat, in köfte, on lahmacun, and in herb blends; the white to pale pink flowers in summer are smaller than many oregano species. Hardy only to about 5–10°F (zone 7); treat as an annual or pot plant in cooler climates.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring around the last frost date; Profusion is sterile and produces no viable seed, so it must be propagated by root division.
directions: Profusion is a naturally occurring sterile selection of garden sorrel that never bolts to flower or set seed, so all of the plant's energy stays in leaf production and it can only be increased by dividing an established clump. Plant divisions in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in early spring, spacing them roughly a foot apart in a permanent bed since the plants are long-lived perennials. Because it never diverts energy into flowering, Profusion keeps producing tender, fleshy, mildly tart leaves later into summer heat than seed-grown sorrel, which typically turns tough and bitter once it sets flower stalks. Harvest outer leaves continually through the growing season and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

plant_note: Prospera is a downy-mildew-resistant series bred to keep the classic Genovese basil flavor and growth habit while resisting the fungal disease that devastates sweet basil in humid climates.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes. Bred through conventional breeding to carry strong resistance to downy mildew, Prospera keeps the familiar large-leaved, classic sweet flavor and growth habit of Genovese basil while standing up far better to the humid conditions that favor mildew outbreaks in traditional pesto basil. Pinch growing tips to encourage bushy growth and harvest whole stems above a leaf node, removing flower buds promptly to keep the leaves tender. Its disease resistance makes it a strong choice for humid Gulf South gardens where standard Genovese basil often declines by midsummer.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; prostrate rosemary is less cold-hardy than upright rosemary and is best suited to zones 8-11. It is an excellent groundcover on sunny slopes and tolerates salt spray, making it particularly valuable in coastal California and Gulf Coast gardens where it grows as a reliable evergreen groundcover.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; prostrate rosemary is the trailing, spreading form of rosemary that grows horizontally rather than upright, producing long, cascading stems that hug the ground or spill dramatically over walls, retaining walls, raised beds, and the lips of containers. The culinary use, flavor, and aromatic quality are identical to upright rosemary, but the growth habit is fundamentally different — prostrate rosemary reaches 1-2 feet tall and spreads 3-6 feet wide in a flowing groundcover form, making it an outstanding choice for erosion control on sunny slopes, as a cascading element in large containers, or as a low-water groundcover between stepping stones. Flowers are typically a deeper blue-violet than many upright forms and are produced freely from fall through spring in mild climates, providing nectar for honeybees and native bees during the cooler months. The salt tolerance makes it particularly valuable in coastal landscapes where few other herbs thrive.

plant_note: Set rooted cuttings or nursery starts out around the last frost in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this cultivar does not come reliably true from seed and is propagated vegetatively.
directions: Provence is a selected culinary thyme grown for its high proportion of thujanol in the essential oil, giving a rounder, fruitier, less medicinal flavor than ordinary common thyme, which is why it is prized specifically for herbes de Provence blends. It grows into a broader, more sprawling woody mound than upright French thyme, with wiry intertwining stems and small grey-green leaves. Shear back hard after the spring flowering flush and again in late summer to prevent the center from opening up and going woody, and replace plants every three to four years as vigor declines. Because it forms a wider mat than most culinary thymes, it also works well cascading over a raised bed edge or low wall.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; punarnava is a wide-ranging tropical weed and Ayurvedic medicinal plant of India and the tropics whose edible leaves, roots, and seeds have been used for centuries as a liver tonic, diuretic, and kidney-support herb.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; punarnava spreads readily by seed and can naturalize in warm climates. Boerhavia diffusa (punarnava or red spiderling) is a tropical prostrate or spreading perennial herb found throughout the tropics and subtropics of India, Africa, Asia, and the Americas — simultaneously one of the most widespread tropical 'weeds' and one of the most important medicinal plants in Ayurvedic medicine. In Ayurveda, punarnava ('the one that renews the body') is one of the top-ranked diuretic, liver-protective, and kidney-supporting herbs, with documented clinical studies supporting its hepatoprotective (liver-protective) and anti-inflammatory effects. The leaves are also eaten as a pot herb in India and West Africa — boiled like spinach, with a mildly mucilaginous texture and bland-earthy flavor. The plant produces tiny, attractive, magenta-pink flowers throughout the warm season, followed by small, glandular, sticky seeds. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, punarnava is a low, spreading, self-seeding herb that naturalizes readily in disturbed areas and lean soils. It tolerates drought and poor soils that few other herbs can survive. The red-stemmed spreading growth creates a soft, groundcover-like effect in dry garden areas. An important herb for those interested in Ayurvedic herbal practice.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or start indoors in late winter in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in partial shade to full sun; purple bergamot is a naturally occurring hybrid between scarlet beebalm (M. didyma) and wild bergamot (M. fistulosa), combining traits of both parents.
directions: Plant in moist to average, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; purple bergamot is a natural hybrid monarda occurring where the ranges of scarlet beebalm (M. didyma) and wild bergamot (M. fistulosa) overlap, producing intermediate flowers in rich purple-lavender tones. The plant is more vigorous and mildew-resistant than pure M. didyma in many gardens and produces large, showy whorled flower heads that are exceptionally attractive to bumblebees, ruby-throated hummingbirds, and fritillary butterflies. The bergamot fragrance of the crushed leaves is distinctive and pleasant. Spreads by rhizomes to form substantial colonies in moist, fertile conditions — divide every 2–3 years to maintain vigor and control spread. An outstanding native pollinator plant that bridges the gap between the red and lavender monarda color spectrum in native plant gardens.

plant_note: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; purple giant hyssop is one of the largest native agastaches, growing to 4–6 feet tall in moist, fertile soils.
directions: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; purple giant hyssop tolerates partial shade better than most agastaches and adapts to the moist, fertile soils of woodland edges and naturalized meadow gardens. Agastache scrophulariifolia is an impressive, tall (4–6 feet) native perennial of eastern North American open woodlands and forest edges producing large, mint-scented, heart-shaped leaves and tall, dense spikes of violet-purple flowers in mid- to late summer that are outstanding for native bees (especially bumblebees), butterflies, and hummingbirds. The plant is one of the most prolific native pollinator plants available for the North American garden; it self-seeds moderately to naturalize in favorable spots and is excellent at the back of native plant borders, along fence lines, and in naturalized meadow plantings. The leaves and flowers are edible and were used medicinally by several Native American peoples.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; purple mitsuba self-sows readily in a shaded herb bed once established and naturalizes as a woodland-edge perennial herb.
directions: Direct sow in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; purple mitsuba self-sows readily in a shaded herb bed once established and naturalizes as a woodland-edge perennial herb. This ornamental purple-leaved form of Japanese wild parsley (mitsuba) carries deep burgundy-purple, three-lobed leaves on slender stems, combining the same mild parsley-celery-anise flavor prized in Japanese cooking with striking, season-long foliage color for a shaded herb or ornamental border. Unlike most culinary herbs, it thrives in full shade and actually prefers it to hot sun, making it a useful flavor and color addition to the deep-shade parts of a garden where few edible herbs perform well. Harvest young leaves and stems continuously for soups, salads, and garnishes, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Warmth-loving; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Purple Petra offers a mild, sweet basil flavor without the peppery bite of some varieties, making it a favorite for those who prefer gentle herbal notes. Its deep purple foliage doubles as an ornamental accent and tints vinegars and oils a lovely pink. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant after frost, giving plants full sun and rich, moist soil. Pinch tips regularly to encourage bushy growth and keep the vivid leaf color coming.

common_name: Purple Ruffles Basil (AAS-Winning Ornamental Deep-Purple Frilled Basil)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; purple basil colors are most intense in full sun — partial shade produces greenish-purple foliage with less dramatic color.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Purple Ruffles is an All-America Selections gold medal-winning basil combining exceptional ornamental quality with full culinary utility — producing large, deeply ruffled, deeply frilled leaves in rich dark-purple to reddish-purple coloration that is immediately striking in the herb garden or as an ornamental annual. The large, heavily ruffled leaf margins — with deeply incised, wavy, almost lace-like edges — distinguish Purple Ruffles from other purple basils whose leaves are smooth or only slightly ruffled. The ornamental quality is outstanding: the combination of the vivid dark-purple color and elaborate leaf texture creates a decorative impact far beyond most culinary herbs. The basil flavor is good — a full, classic basil flavor with a slight spicy-anise character and a pleasant mild bitterness from the purple anthocyanins — suitable for pesto, salads, and infused oils where the purple color creates a striking visual effect (purple basil vinegar is particularly beautiful). In zone 9, purple basil grows through the warm season from April–October but often bolts (flowers) quickly in summer heat; pinch flower buds promptly and repeatedly to extend the harvest season. The purple leaf color makes excellent contrast with silver herbs (artemisia, horehound) and chartreuse-leaved companions in herb garden designs.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–October. Purple Sage performs as a perennial in zones 5–8 but may decline after 2–3 years in zone 9 heat and humidity — treat as a short-lived perennial or replant every few years from cuttings. Cut plants back by one-third in early spring and again after the main flush of spring bloom to maintain compact shape and prevent woodiness. Excellent drainage is essential in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — culinary sage rots in heavy, wet soils; Purple Sage is a cultivar of common culinary sage (Salvia officinalis) selected for its ornamental foliage — the leaves are a soft, velvety purple-gray rather than the standard gray-green, creating a striking two-tone ornamental effect when the plant is in growth. The culinary flavor and fragrance are identical to standard sage — the same warm, resinous, camphor-and-pine aroma and savory flavor used in Thanksgiving stuffing, sage butter for pasta, sausage seasoning, and Italian cooking — making Purple Sage a practical dual-use plant where ornamental value complements culinary function. The lavender-blue flowers in spring (April–May) add a third color to the already-attractive plant, and both the flowers and the purple-gray foliage are used in dried wreaths, herbal sachets, and potpourri. Purple Sage retains the same beneficial compounds as common sage (ursolic acid, rosmarinic acid, thujone) used medicinally for generations.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer; purple sage is the same species as common garden sage but with ornamental purple-toned leaves. Grow from cuttings as the cultivar does not come true from seed.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; purple sage is a handsome ornamental-culinary cultivar of common garden sage whose young leaves emerge in rich purple tones that soften to purple-green as they mature. The flavor is fully equivalent to common sage — warm, peppery, slightly bitter, and intensely aromatic with notes of camphor and eucalyptus — and it can be used as a complete substitute in all sage-seasoned dishes. The purple foliage provides attractive contrast in herb gardens where it pairs visually with silver thyme and golden oregano. It requires the same excellent drainage and full sun as common sage and is equally deer-resistant. Trim lightly in spring to prevent woodiness and promote compact, leafy new growth.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall (the preferred planting time for California native plants) in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; purple sage is a California coastal sage scrub native adapted to summer drought — water only until established (first winter), then rely on rainfall in zone 8–10; excessive irrigation is the primary cause of death for established plants.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; water sparingly — established plants need summer dry conditions to thrive. Salvia leucophylla (purple sage or coastal sage) is a California native aromatic shrub from the coastal sage scrub and chaparral communities of coastal and inland California. The plant produces aromatic, wrinkled, silver-gray to white-felted leaves with a strong, distinctive fragrance — more complex and resinous than common garden sage (S. officinalis), with additional notes of camphor, eucalyptus, and warm spice. The soft, gray foliage creates a beautiful silvery landscape effect, especially dramatic when paired with purple lavender and other Mediterranean-climate plants. In late spring through early summer, it produces whorled clusters of pink to light-purple flowers on white-felted stems — both fragrant and attractive to hummingbirds and bumblebees. Purple sage is a classic plant of the California chaparral and is notable for producing volatile allelopathic compounds (camphor, 1,8-cineole) from its leaves that inhibit the germination and growth of competing plants beneath its canopy — a natural herbicide effect. The leaves are traditionally used by California indigenous peoples for ceremonial smudging, and can be used as a culinary sage substitute (though stronger). Drought tolerance once established is extreme.

plant_note: Press seed onto surface without covering — light aids germination; requires fresh seed as viability drops sharply after one season; self-sows freely once established.
directions: Press seed onto the soil surface without covering (light aids germination) after last frost in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; purple shiso is the red-leafed cultivar group of perilla, with deep burgundy leaves essential in Japanese pickling — umeboshi (pickled plum) gets its characteristic pink-red color and complex flavor from red shiso leaves layered with the salted plums. The entire plant is strongly aromatic, blending mint, anise, and basil; in Korean cuisine the leaves (kkaennip) are used to wrap grilled meats or pickled in soy sauce. Allowed to flower and set seed, it self-sows freely and returns each summer; use leaves whole or finely chiffonaded.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; press seeds onto the surface of the mix since they need light to germinate, then transplant out after frost danger has passed into lean, well-drained soil in full sun. Flowering, and therefore pyrethrin content, builds up over the plant's second and third seasons.
directions: Start seed indoors under light, since it needs light to germinate, then transplant into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; pyrethrum forms a low mound of finely cut, silvery-gray, aromatic foliage similar in texture to feverfew, and from late spring into summer sends up wiry stems topped with cheerful white, daisy-form flowers with yellow centers. This is the source plant of natural pyrethrin insecticide, which is concentrated in the still-closed flower heads and traditionally harvested just as the outer ring of petals opens, then dried quickly out of direct sun to preserve potency before grinding into powder. As an ornamental it needs only average care: good drainage is the one non-negotiable requirement, since wet winter soil is far more likely to kill it than cold. Plants are relatively short-lived, usually productive and vigorous for three to four years before they benefit from division or replacement. Deadhead spent flowers not being harvested to keep the plant tidy and encourage further bloom.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start February–March and transplant March–April. Queen of Siam is more bolt-resistant than many sweet basil varieties and performs well through zone 9 summer heat. A second planting in July–August provides fall production. Pinch flower buds as they form to extend the leaf harvest.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Queen of Siam basil is an ornamental and culinary hybrid producing striking dark purple-stemmed plants with large, green leaves and purple-flushed undersides, topped by spectacular spikes of deep purple to magenta flower bracts — one of the most ornamentally dramatic of all basil types. The flavor combines the clove-sweet base of sweet basil with a distinct anise and licorice note similar to Thai basil, making it suitable for both Italian and Southeast Asian cooking. The bolt-resistant, continuously flowering habit produces an extended season of ornamental bloom that makes this basil equally valuable in the flower garden as in the herb garden. The deep purple flower spikes are excellent as cut flowers. In zone 9 the heat tolerance and continuous flower production through summer make Queen of Siam the most reliably ornamental basil for summer landscapes, where it continues flowering attractively even after the flavor of the leaves has declined with heat.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil has warmed to at least 65°F; seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep the plant productive and bushy through the season. Rama is the classic green-leaved, green-stemmed form of holy basil (tulsi), considered by many Ayurvedic practitioners to be the mildest and sweetest-flavored of the traditional tulsi types, with a fragrant, clove-and-pepper aroma softer than the more pungent purple Krishna form. It is the variety most commonly dried for tulsi tea, prized for its balanced, adaptogenic-reputed flavor, and is also used fresh in Thai and Indian cooking. The vigorous, upright plants produce abundant foliage over a long warm season and, like other tulsi, are considered sacred in Hindu tradition and often grown near the home for both culinary and spiritual purposes. A rewarding, productive warm-season herb for tea and cooking, zone 10–12 or as a warm-season annual elsewhere.

plant_note: Plant root divisions or crowns in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zone 7–11; Ramie is a large, rhizomatous perennial nettle-family plant native to subtropical China, grown since ancient times as the primary source of one of the world's longest, strongest, and most lustrous bast fibers — used for thousands of years in Chinese textiles, mummies' wrapping cloth, and now blended with linen and cotton for high-quality natural fabric.
directions: Plant root divisions 2–3 inches deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Boehmeria nivea spreads aggressively by rhizome — contain with deep edging or grow in a dedicated plot; harvest stems when 36–50 inches tall by cutting at ground level, typically 2–4 harvests per year in warm climates. Boehmeria nivea (Ramie, China Grass, or White Ramie) is a robust, rhizomatous, herbaceous perennial in the Urticaceae (nettle) family native to subtropical to tropical East Asia — China, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and the Indo-Chinese peninsula — where it has been cultivated for textile fiber for at least 6,000 years, making it one of the oldest cultivated fiber crops on earth. The bast fiber extracted from the long, upright stems is among the strongest, longest (individual fibers can reach 4–6 inches), and most lustrous of all natural textile fibers — stronger than flax (linen) and comparable to cotton in softness but with a silky sheen — and is used for high-quality clothing, table linens, lace, canvas, industrial fiber, and blended with cotton and silk. Processing ramie for spinning is labor-intensive (requiring degumming), which limited commercial adoption in the West, but in China, Korea, Japan, and the Philippines, Ramie clothing production is substantial. Leaves of Boehmeria nivea are also nutritious (20–27% crude protein) and fed to livestock and fish (particularly carp) in China as a high-protein fodder. An ornamental value in the large, white-undersided leaves.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial to full shade; seeds require cold stratification and germinate in early spring — bulb offsets may be planted in fall for faster establishment.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade, or plant bulb offsets 2–3 inches deep in fall; ramsons naturalizes readily by seed and offsets to form dense colonies under deciduous trees, though the foliage dies back completely by early summer and must be located carefully to avoid disturbing the dormant bulbs. Allium ursinum is a European native wild garlic with broad, glossy, bright-green, strap-shaped leaves (resembling lily of the valley) that carpet the woodland floor in spring and bear strong garlic flavor and aroma; the leaves, bulbs, and the attractive white, star-shaped umbel flowers in late spring are all edible and highly prized in European culinary traditions — the fresh leaves can be used exactly like garlic in pestos, soups, salads, and compound butters. It naturalizes to form spectacular carpets under deciduous trees and is one of the finest and most useful edible groundcovers for partial to full shade; plant away from lily of the valley (Convallaria) which is toxic and has similar foliage.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade to full sun; red bay grows naturally in moist, sandy, coastal soils and bottomlands. Note: red bay is devastated by laurel wilt disease caused by the redbay ambrosia beetle (Xyleborus glabratus) throughout much of its native range — check local extension for current recommendations.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; red bay is the native American aromatic bay of the coastal Southeast and Gulf Coast, producing glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves with the same aromatic oils and culinary bay-laurel fragrance as the Mediterranean bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) — the leaves are used identically in Southern cooking for seasoning gumbos, soups, stews, and bean dishes. In fact, red bay has traditionally been used in Gulf Coast cuisine (particularly in Louisiana) for generations as the local bay leaf. It is a fast-growing native tree of coastal hammocks and stream margins that provides excellent wildlife value — the blue-black fruits are important food for migrating songbirds, and the palamedes swallowtail butterfly uses red bay as its exclusive larval host plant. Tragically, laurel wilt disease (spread by an invasive ambrosia beetle) has killed the vast majority of red bay trees throughout the Southeast — consult local extension services before planting.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in any well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; red deadnettle is a winter annual that germinates in fall, overwinters as a rosette, and flowers in early spring before dying back. Self-sows prolifically once established.
directions: Sow in any garden soil in fall or early spring in partial shade to full sun; red deadnettle is a common European winter annual now naturalized worldwide, growing as a charming winter and early spring wildflower in lawns, gardens, and disturbed areas. The small, purple-hooded flowers, which appear from late winter through spring, are one of the earliest nectar sources for queen bumblebees emerging from winter dormancy — a service of significant ecological value. The purplish-tinged young leaves are edible raw in salads or cooked as a pot herb, high in vitamins and minerals. The plant germinates in fall and overwinters as a low rosette, making it valuable as a living mulch and green cover during winter months. It does not compete with summer crops and dies naturally as temperatures rise. Embrace this plant as a beneficial winter ground cover rather than treating it as a weed.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in frost-free conditions; red passionflower is an outstanding hummingbird plant in tropical and subtropical gardens.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in frost-free zones (10–12) or grow in containers that can be protected from frost in zones 9 and below. Passiflora coccinea is a Brazilian tropical passionflower vine with large, heart-shaped to deeply lobed, oblong leaves and brilliant scarlet, orange-red, or vermilion flowers with a prominent corona of white-banded filaments from late spring through fall in tropical climates; it is one of the finest plants for attracting hummingbirds in tropical gardens. The small, edible fruits are yellow-green when ripe with soft, sweet, aromatic pulp. Related to P. vitifolia but with somewhat different leaf shape and flower proportions; both are outstanding for tropical garden collections and large container culture. Excellent on arbors, fences, and trellises in frost-free climates.

common_name: Red Rubin Basil (Purple Basil, Red Basil)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Rubin holds its deep purple color best in full sun — in shade the leaves may become more greenish-purple; pinch flowering stems to maintain full-leaf production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Rubin is the finest and most consistent deep-purple basil cultivar — an improved selection of 'Dark Opal' basil that produces more uniformly dark, deep burgundy-purple leaves across the entire plant with a richer, more saturated color than older purple basil selections. The deep crimson-purple foliage provides striking ornamental value in the herb garden and the edible landscape — the dark leaves contrast beautifully with green herbs, chartreuse foliage, and brightly colored flowers. Red Rubin basil has the same classic sweet basil fragrance and flavor as green Genovese-type basils and can be used interchangeably in cooking, where its purple color creates dramatic purple-tinted basil oil, purple pesto, and deep-toned herb vinegars that standard green basil cannot produce. The purple color also migrates to other ingredients when the fresh herb is used — providing a subtle tinting effect in salads. In zone 9, Red Rubin grows vigorously through the warm season. Regular harvest by pinching the upper leaves and flower buds maintains the bushy habit and delays flowering. Once the plant bolts and sets seed, leaf production diminishes — cut back hard or compost the plant and start fresh.

common_name: Red Rubin Holy Basil (Deep Purple-Red Sacred Tulsi Basil for Tea and Ritual Use)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Red Rubin' produces the most intense deep-purple foliage color in full sun — partial shade produces more greenish-purple leaves with less dramatic color, though the plants still grow well.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Red Rubin Holy Basil is a deeply colored cultivar of tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum, holy basil) — the sacred plant of Hinduism, considered the most important of the sacred plants (tulsi) present in virtually every Hindu household as a revered manifestation of the goddess Lakshmi. The deep purple-red to burgundy-red foliage of 'Red Rubin' is substantially more ornamental than standard green tulsi, combining the sacred herb's distinctive aromatic qualities with a plant form visually comparable to red basil varieties used in Western herb gardening. The aroma of holy basil is distinctly different from sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum) — a complex, spicy-clove-mint-camphor fragrance with earthy, slightly medicinal undertones rather than the purely sweet-anise of Italian basil. This aroma makes tulsi specifically suited for herbal teas (tulsi tea is a traditional Ayurvedic beverage), aromatherapy, and as a basil flavor component distinct from sweet basil in fusion cooking. In zone 9, Red Rubin Holy Basil grows as a vigorous warm-season annual from spring through fall, potentially self-seeding in sheltered positions. Regular harvest of stem tips prevents bolting and maintains vegetative growth. The ornamental purple foliage and small lavender-pink flowers make it equally valuable as a garden ornamental and as an herb with the distinctive tulsi fragrance.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–June. Red Shiso self-seeds prolifically — one or two plants in the first year will result in dozens of volunteers in subsequent years from dropped seeds. Allow a few plants to go to seed in desirable locations; otherwise harvest all flowering stalks before seeds form to prevent unwanted spread. In zone 9 red shiso grows rapidly in summer heat and thrives in conditions that would stress most cool-season herbs. Partial shade is tolerated and may produce larger, more tender leaves.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Shiso (Perilla frutescens var. purpurea) is the red-purple-leaved form of Japanese shiso — a herb central to Japanese and Korean cuisine with a distinctive flavor combining anise, mint, basil, and cinnamon in a complex, aromatic profile unlike any other commonly grown herb. The deep red-purple to burgundy leaves are used fresh in Japanese food preparations: wrapping nigiri sushi and maki rolls, as a garnish for sashimi, mixed into rice, and used in the traditional preparation of umeboshi (Japanese pickled plums) where red shiso provides the characteristic color and flavor of the classic pink umeboshi. Red shiso produces the vivid red pigment (anthocyanin perillins) that colors umeboshi and red shiso juice — the brilliant magenta-red natural dye is water-soluble and stable enough for food and beverage coloring. Beyond Japanese and Korean applications, red shiso's ornamental burgundy foliage makes it valuable in kitchen garden designs where its striking color provides contrast against green vegetables, and the self-seeding habit provides a reliable annual return once established.

common_name: Red Shiso (Japanese Purple-Leaf Culinary and Pickling Herb)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; shiso self-seeds prolifically — allow a few plants to flower and set seed at season end for a naturalized patch that returns reliably without replanting in subsequent years.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; red shiso (Aka Shiso) is the purple-red-leafed variety of the Japanese culinary herb perilla — one of the foundational herbs of Japanese cuisine, used fresh in sushi (wrapped around rice and fish), as a garnish and flavoring for sashimi, in Japanese pickles (umeboshi ume plums pickled with red shiso leaves which provide both color and flavor), and as a tempura vegetable. The deeply colored, crinkled, rounded leaves in vivid burgundy-purple to dark-red-purple create striking ornamental foliage as well as excellent culinary value — red shiso is one of the most ornamentally attractive culinary herbs for the garden. The flavor is uniquely complex: simultaneously minty, anise-like, citrusy, and herbaceous with a spicy undertone that has no direct Western equivalent and is immediately recognizable as distinctly Japanese in character. Red shiso produces its most intense color and flavor in full sun; partial shade lightens the leaf color to red-green but maintains culinary quality. In zone 9, red shiso grows as a warm-season annual (April–October), tolerating Gulf South heat and humidity well. Allow plants to set seed at season end — shiso self-seeds prolifically, establishing a self-renewing naturalized patch that provides leaves season after season without replanting. Fresh young leaves are the primary harvest; flowers are also edible.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in spring or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade; red valerian self-seeds prolifically and thrives in poor, dry, alkaline conditions — rich, fertile, or wet soil produces rank, floppy growth and reduces flowering.
directions: Direct-sow or plant container specimens in well-drained to dry, poor to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; red valerian (Jupiter's beard, fox's brush, kiss-me-quick) is a Mediterranean perennial that has naturalized on rocky coastal cliffs, stone walls, and dry limestone outcrops throughout Europe and warm-climate North America — its ability to root into the smallest crevices of dry stone walls and cliff faces, producing clouds of intensely fragrant, deep coral-red, rosy-pink, or white flower clusters from late spring through summer, makes it a classic companion to stone walls, gravel gardens, and dry, chalky slopes. The young leaves and roots are edible (leaves used in salads in France and Italy as a raw herb with a mild, slightly bitter flavor), and the large, fluffy seed heads provide excellent cut material for dried arrangements. It self-seeds freely into any available dry, alkaline crack or gravel area, naturalizing remarkably quickly. Excellent in dry stone wall gardens, Mediterranean-style plantings, and hot, dry coastal gardens. 'Albus' (white), 'Coccineus' (deep crimson-red), and 'Rosenrot' (rose-pink) are named cultivars.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; red-veined sorrel tolerates light spring frosts and can also be sown in early fall.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in moist, well-drained soil and thin to 9–12 in apart; red-veined sorrel germinates readily in cool soil. The lance-shaped leaves with vivid crimson veins are ornamentally striking and have a mild lemony-tart flavor suitable for salads, garnishes, and light sautés. Remove flower stalks promptly to prevent self-seeding and to keep the plant producing tender new foliage throughout the season. Harvest outer leaves when they are young and vibrant; flavor and texture deteriorate in the largest, oldest leaves.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost or in fall; in zone 9 sow October–February for winter-spring bloom. Resina calendula is best grown as a cool-season annual in zone 9 — it flowers prolifically in cooler months (November–April) and declines in summer heat. The sticky, resinous flowers should be harvested with gloves as the resin stains hands and fabric. Harvest flowers in the morning when fully open.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Resina is a calendula cultivar specifically selected by the Heritage Seed Program for maximum resin content rather than ornamental appeal — the flower heads are visibly more resinous and sticky than standard ornamental calendula varieties, with a higher concentration of the triterpenoid saponins and flavonoids that make calendula one of the most important herbs in traditional and contemporary herbal medicine. The high-resin flowers are the preferred type for making calendula-infused oil (used in salves, lip balms, and skin care products), tinctures, and medicinal teas where the active compound concentration per flower is significantly higher than in standard varieties. Resina flowers are single to semi-double in pale to deep orange and yellow, with the characteristic sticky feel of the bracts when harvested. In zone 9 the cool-season planting from October through February produces the most productive and resinous flower crop.

plant_note: Cover seed well, as calendula germinates best in darkness.
directions: Resina calendula was bred for exceptionally resin-rich petals, making it the go-to variety for herbalists preparing salves and infused oils. Its bright yellow, daisy-like blooms shine in the garden and are so frost tolerant they may keep flowering into the snow. Direct sow and cover the seed well, since darkness aids germination, in a sunny spot with average soil. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering and harvest fully open flower heads on a dry morning for the best medicinal quality.

plant_note: Nick or soak the hard-coated seed before sowing directly into lean, well-drained soil; plants form a dense root system in year one and flower from the second year onward.
directions: Ononis spinosa is a wiry, spine-tipped European legume subshrub of dry chalk grassland and roadside verges, named for its tenacious, tough taproots that were said to catch and stop a horse-drawn harrow. Small pink pea flowers appear along the spiny stems in mid to late summer, followed by small pods, and the plant fixes its own nitrogen, thriving in poor, lean, unamended ground. The dried root bark has a long folk history as a mild diuretic used for gravel and minor urinary complaints. Grow in full sun on sharply drained, even gravelly, low-fertility soil; rich or damp ground produces lank, floppy growth and shortens the plant's lifespan.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or plant in boggy, consistently wet soil after all frost danger; rice paddy herb performs best in wet to aquatic conditions — it thrives planted at the edge of ponds, in water gardens, in consistently wet raised beds, or in containers sitting in trays of water. In zone 9–10 it is a true perennial; in colder zones grow as an annual in a sunny spot with moist soil.
directions: Root stem cuttings in water or wet soil in partial shade to full sun; rice paddy herb is the fresh herb most responsible for the distinctive, complex aroma of Vietnamese pho and many other Southeast Asian soups — the crushed leaves have a remarkably layered fragrance combining cumin, rice, lemon, and a unique floral quality that is difficult to describe but instantly recognizable in a bowl of authentic pho. It is used fresh as a tableside herb for hot soups and spring rolls in Vietnamese cuisine, where it is called rau om. The plant grows naturally in rice paddies and flooded fields throughout tropical Asia, requiring consistently wet to aquatic conditions — it will not thrive in typical garden soil that dries between waterings. Plant at pond margins, in water gardens, or in containers kept sitting in 1–2 inches of water for reliable production. In zone 9–10 it persists as a perennial through mild winters; harvest regularly by pinching stems to keep plants bushy and productive.

plant_note: Sow seeds fresh (they lose viability quickly) in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; rock samphire is native to sea cliffs and coastal rocks and requires extremely well-drained, lean, slightly saline soil to thrive. It does not transplant well — direct sow in permanent position. In zones 8–10 it is perennial and quite long-lived in appropriate conditions. Use seeds as soon as possible after harvest — they lose germination viability within a year.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; rock samphire is a historical edible coastal herb that was once widely gathered and pickled throughout coastal Europe — Shakespeare referenced its dangerous collection by cliff-hangers in King Lear ('half-way down hangs one that gathers samphire; dreadful trade!') and it was a common market vegetable in London through the 18th century. The finely divided, succulent, gray-green, carrot-family foliage has a strong, distinctive, aromatic flavour combining fennel, anise, and iodine — intensely herbal and marine. It produces flattened umbel flowers in summer followed by seeds. The young shoots are used fresh in salads, cooked as a vegetable, or pickled in vinegar. It grows naturally on sea cliffs, rock crevices, and shingle beaches of the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, clinging to completely vertical cliff faces and experiencing salt spray, full sun, and total drought. In the garden it requires similarly lean, well-drained, open conditions. Excellent in rock gardens, coastal gardens, and as a maritime-flavored culinary herb for adventurous cooks.

common_name: Roman Beauty Rosemary (Chef's Choice Compact Culinary Rosemary)
plant_note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; Roman Beauty is propagated from cuttings and is sold under the patented trade name Chef's Choice.
directions: Roman Beauty, marketed under the trademark Chef's Choice, is a compact, slow-growing culinary rosemary selected for a noticeably higher essential-oil content than standard rosemary, giving a spicier, more concentrated flavor from the same amount of leaf. Its dense, finely textured gray-green foliage and pale blue flowers hold a tidy, upright habit that stays under 3 feet, making it a good choice for containers, herb-garden borders, and small kitchen beds where sprawling rosemary cultivars would outgrow the space. Like other culinary rosemaries it thrives on neglect, wanting lean soil, full sun, and minimal supplemental water once established. Harvest sprigs throughout the growing season; the concentrated flavor means a little goes further in cooking than with milder rosemary types.

plant_note: Surface-sow seeds in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; do not cover seeds as they need light to germinate — Roman chamomile is a low, mat-forming perennial ideal for path edging, lawn substitutes (especially the non-flowering 'Treneague' cultivar), and herb garden borders.
directions: Chamaemelum nobile is a low-growing, apple-scented perennial chamomile native to western Europe, producing fine, feathery, bright-green foliage and small white daisy flowers with yellow centers from early summer through early fall; the crushed foliage releases a distinctive sweet, fruity, apple-like scent that distinguishes it from the taller German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla). Surface-sow seeds in early spring directly in well-drained, poor to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun or light partial shade; seeds require light to germinate and should not be covered — press them lightly onto the soil surface and keep evenly moist until germination occurs in 7–14 days. The non-flowering cultivar 'Treneague' is propagated vegetatively and used as a fragrant, low-maintenance lawn substitute that releases its apple scent when walked upon; it requires no mowing but does best in well-drained, sunny sites. Harvest flowers by hand when fully open for use in herbal tea; flowers and foliage have traditional uses for soothing teas, topical rinses, and as a mild sleep aid.

plant_note: Transplant rooted cuttings after last frost into sharply draining soil; this Levantine subshrub demands full sun and resents any standing moisture at the roots.
directions: Establish plants in the sunniest, driest spot in the garden, as this Eastern Mediterranean subshrub is evolved for calcareous, rocky soils and intense summer heat; poor drainage is the primary cause of failure. Harvest leafy stem tips before or just as the whorled pink-purple flowers open, when the essential oil content peaks, then dry in bunches to use in homemade za'atar spice blends. Trim lightly after each harvest and cut back by a third following the main flowering period to maintain a bushy form and prevent the base from becoming too woody. In zone 7, provide a light mulch around the crown in winter and site plants against a south-facing wall for additional warmth.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or softwood cuttings after last frost; Roman wormwood spreads by shallow rhizomes and is almost always propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.
directions: Native to southeastern Europe, Artemisia pontica forms a low, finely cut, silver-gray colony of aromatic foliage that is markedly less bitter than common wormwood, making it prized historically as a gentler flavoring herb in the production of vermouth and certain herbal bitters and cordials. Its old English name Roman wormwood distinguishes it from both true wormwood and mugwort. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it spreads slowly by rhizome to form an attractive weed-suppressing patch; rich, damp soil causes floppy, sprawling growth. Shear plants back hard in early spring to keep the silvery foliage dense and prevent the clump from thinning at the center.

plant_note: Soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to soften its hard coat, sow into acidic, sandy, low-fertility soil, and grow seedlings on for about two months before transplanting into their permanent full-sun position.
directions: Soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to soften its hard coat, sow into acidic, sandy, low-fertility soil, and grow seedlings on for about two months before transplanting into their permanent full-sun position. Rooibos is a fine-needled legume shrub found only in South Africa's Cederberg mountains, where hot dry summers and cool wet winters shape its narrow native range. Harvested stems are cut, bruised, and left to oxidize before drying, turning the leaves the deep red-brown that gives the naturally caffeine-free, sweetly earthy tea its color and name.

subcategory: South African rose-scented aromatic culinary pelargonium
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in zone 9–11; Rose Geranium is a South African shrubby pelargonium — the primary commercial source of geranium essential oil (used extensively in perfumery, aromatherapy, and skin care) — with deeply lobed, velvety, fragrant leaves that smell intensely of fresh roses, used to flavor jellies, cakes, lemonade, and tea, and producing small pink flowers with darker veining throughout the warm season.
directions: Root Rose Geranium stem cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; avoid overwatering — the plant prefers to dry out between waterings and is highly susceptible to root rot in wet conditions; prune regularly to maintain compact, bushy shape and encourage continuous fresh, fragrant foliage; fertilize lightly. Rose Geranium is the primary commercial source of geranium essential oil — steam-distilled from the leaves and stems — and is one of the most important fragrance crops in the world, with major production in Egypt, China, South Africa, and Réunion Island. The oil is used extensively in fine perfumery (often blending as a rose substitute or modifier), aromatherapy, and high-end skin care products. In the culinary garden, the intensely rose-fragrant leaves are used fresh: layered in sugar (rose geranium sugar) to transfer their scent; pressed into the bottom of cake tins before baking (rose geranium pound cake); infused in cream for ice cream; floated in lemonade and iced tea; and used to scent herb vinegars and syrups. The flavor is a delicate rose with a slight leafy, green note — distinctive and sophisticated. A well-drained, hot, sunny position suits Rose Geranium perfectly in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens; it grows vigorously in the long warm season and tolerates light frost with some protection.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring or late summer in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; rose-scented geranium is perennial in zones 9–11 and grows as a sprawling, scented shrub in mild climates. In colder zones bring indoors in winter. The leaves and stems are the commercial source of geranium essential oil (often labeled rose geranium oil) used in perfumery, cosmetics, and aromatherapy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; rose-scented geranium is a South African coastal dune native and the primary commercial source of geranium essential oil — one of the most important fragrance materials in perfumery, used to round out and fix rose notes in countless fine fragrances. The deeply lobed, velvety, gray-green leaves release an immediately recognizable, rich, rosy-citrusy fragrance when touched — often described as a green rose or rose combined with mint — that is more complex and interesting than an actual rose. The small, pink, pelargonium-type flowers appear in clusters through the growing season but are secondary to the extraordinary aromatic foliage. In zones 9–11 it grows as a substantial, spreading sub-shrub. The oil is extracted by steam distillation of the green stems and leaves; commercial production centers on the island of Réunion and South Africa. Excellent as a container herb for patios where the fragrant foliage can be brushed when passing. Dried leaves retain fragrance well for sachets and potpourri.

plant_note: Start indoors early; germination is slow and erratic.
directions: Rosemary is an aromatic Mediterranean perennial with needle-like leaves that bring a warm, piney flavor to roasts, breads, and herb blends. Start seed indoors ten or more weeks early and be patient, as germination is slow and often spotty. Transplant into sharply drained soil in full sun, since rosemary dislikes wet feet, and water only when the soil dries. In colder climates grow it in a pot and bring it indoors before hard frost, as it is only reliably hardy in mild zones.

plant_note: Divide thick rhizomes in spring or fall, or direct-sow seeds in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, poor to average, gritty or rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; roseroot thrives in alpine and coastal conditions with cool summers and requires excellent drainage — it fails and rots in hot, humid, poorly drained soil common in zone 7 and below.
directions: Divide rhizomes or direct-sow in well-drained, poor to average, rocky or gritty soil in full sun to partial shade; roseroot (golden root, Arctic rose) is a circumpolar arctic and alpine succulent perennial of the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae) that is one of the most extensively studied adaptogenic herbs in modern phytotherapy — the thick, fragrant rhizome (smelling of roses when cut, hence the name) contains rosavins and salidroside, compounds that have been demonstrated in clinical trials to reduce fatigue, improve physical and mental performance under stress, and support mood in states of mild anxiety and depression. It has been used in Scandinavian, Siberian, and Tibetan traditional medicine for at least 3,000 years as a stamina- and stress-resistance herb, and modern Scandinavian military and sports research has documented its adaptogenic effects. The plant itself is an attractive dwarf succulent with fleshy, toothed, blue-green leaves and clusters of small, bright-yellow to yellow-green, star-shaped flowers in late spring. It is extremely cold-hardy (surviving to zone 1) but requires cool summers and excellent drainage; it fails in warm, humid, poorly drained conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil has warmed.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 in deep indoors in a warm spot; rue germinates best at around 68°F. Plant in poor, well-drained, alkaline soil and avoid overhead watering to prevent fungal issues in the bluish-green foliage. Always wear gloves and long sleeves when handling rue, as the sap can cause severe phototoxic skin burns when exposed to sunlight. Harvest small sprigs of foliage before flowering for traditional uses as a strewing herb or insect deterrent; internal use requires professional guidance due to toxicity at high doses.

plant_note: Plant root cuttings (4–6 inch sections of root, placed horizontally 3–4 inches deep) in spring; Russian comfrey 'Bocking 14' is the preferred sterile (non-seeding) cultivar for garden use — it spreads only by root division, so it cannot become invasive the way self-seeding common comfrey can. Once established, it is virtually impossible to eradicate, so site carefully.
directions: Plant root cuttings 3–4 inches deep in moist, fertile soil in sun to part shade; Russian comfrey (Symphytum x uplandicum) is a hybrid between common comfrey and tuberous comfrey, producing a much more vigorous and productive plant than either parent — it is the preferred comfrey for permaculture systems and organic gardening as a dynamic accumulator, deep-rooting perennial that mines subsoil minerals (particularly potassium, phosphorus, calcium, and nitrogen) and concentrates them in its large, hairy leaves that can be cut 3–5 times per year and used as a mulch, liquid fertilizer (composted in water to make comfrey tea), or composted directly. The leaves decompose rapidly and are an outstanding activator for compost piles. The purple-blue flowers are beloved by bumblebees. Unlike common comfrey, 'Bocking 14' does not set viable seed and is non-spreading except through root division, making it the gardener's preferred choice for a controlled, productive stand.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors; light aids germination.
directions: Unlike French tarragon, Russian tarragon grows readily from seed and forms a vigorous perennial with a milder, anise-like flavor. Surface sow the seed indoors and leave it uncovered under light, then transplant into well-drained soil in full sun. It is hardy, drought tolerant, and grows larger than its French cousin, so give it space at the back of an herb bed. Harvest young leaves for the best flavor and cut plants back to keep them from becoming leggy.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Saaz is a lower-yielding traditional variety compared to modern high-alpha hops.
directions: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Saaz is a lower-yielding traditional variety compared to modern high-alpha hops. One of the original four European 'noble hop' varieties, grown for centuries in the Žatec region of Bohemia (now the Czech Republic), it imparts the mild, spicy, earthy, floral bitterness that defines classic Czech and German pilsner beer styles, a subtle character quite different from the bold citrus and tropical fruit notes of modern American hop varieties. It is a lower-yielding, more disease-susceptible variety than many modern hybrid hops, reflecting its long, unimproved heritage, and rewards patient, attentive growing rather than the vigorous, high-output performance of newer cultivars. Train young bines up a sturdy support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery, and expect a lighter yield than modern high-alpha varieties in exchange for its classic, historic flavor profile.

plant_note: Plant corms 6–8 weeks before the first autumn frost so they establish before winter; flowers appear in the first autumn after planting.
directions: Plant corms (not seeds) 3–4 in deep in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun during late summer to early autumn; good drainage is critical as corms rot quickly in waterlogged soil. Each corm produces lilac-purple flowers in autumn of the first year; within each flower are three vivid red stigmas — these are saffron. Harvest the flowers as soon as they open in the morning and carefully pluck the three red stigmas from each blossom, drying immediately on a warm screen or in a low oven. Corms multiply each year; lift and divide every 3–4 years to prevent overcrowding and maintain flowering vigor.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost has passed and soil is warm.
directions: Press seeds 1/8 in into well-drained seed mix and keep at 60–70°F; germination is steady but takes two to three weeks. Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; wet, poorly drained soil is the leading cause of sage death. Prune hard in early spring once new growth shows at the base to prevent the plant from becoming too woody. Harvest young leaves throughout the season, cutting stems back by no more than one-third at a time.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; can also be sown in autumn for spring germination.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in well-drained, alkaline or neutral soil; salad burnet tolerates poor, thin soils and performs well on chalky or limestone ground. As an evergreen perennial, it provides fresh cucumber-flavored leaves through mild winters when little else is harvestable. Remove flower stems as they appear to keep the plant producing the most tender, flavorful leaves rather than diverting energy into seed production. Harvest the youngest leaves at the tips of each stem for the freshest cucumber taste in salads, cool drinks, and herb butters.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun with excellent drainage; Salem is a semi-upright to cascading cold-hardy rosemary cultivar considered nearly as cold-hardy as Arp (surviving to -5°F in some reports) with particularly good culinary flavor and a graceful, slightly arching habit that makes it attractive as both an herb plant and an ornamental garden shrub.
directions: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; rosemary is particularly sensitive to wet winter soils which cause crown rot; Salem's semi-cascading habit makes it attractive planted at the edge of raised beds, retaining walls, or terraces where the arching stems can spill gracefully downward; harvest sprigs as needed throughout the growing season. Salem is a cold-hardy named rosemary cultivar that combines the primary traits that herb gardeners seek in a rosemary plant: excellent cold hardiness comparable to Arp, superior culinary flavor and fragrance, and attractive garden presence with a graceful semi-upright to slightly arching habit that is more ornamental than the sometimes rigid upright form of standard culinary rosemary. The variety is considered by many herb specialists to have slightly better culinary quality than Arp — the fragrance and flavor is more intensely resinous and sweet-piney with less medicinal sharpness. Salem is named for Salem, Oregon (not Salem, Massachusetts), reflecting its introduction and testing in the Pacific Northwest where it demonstrated exceptional cold hardiness. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Salem rosemary is one of the most reliable long-lived perennial rosemary cultivars alongside Arp and Tuscan Blue — the combination of good cold hardiness and heat tolerance makes it adaptable across a very wide geographic range. The blue to pale blue-violet flowers in winter and spring are an important early nectar source for bees before most other garden plants have begun to bloom.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring alongside a compatible host plant (sandalwood is a partial root parasite and needs a nearby host tree or shrub to thrive) in well-drained soil in full sun; realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.
directions: Plant seedlings in spring alongside a compatible host plant (sandalwood is a partial root parasite and needs a nearby host tree or shrub to thrive) in well-drained soil in full sun; realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. This slow-growing tropical tree produces the fragrant, dense, oil-rich heartwood prized for centuries in incense, perfumery, and religious ceremonies across South and Southeast Asia, but the tree must be interplanted with a suitable host species from an early age, since its roots form haustoria that tap into a neighboring plant's roots for water and nutrients even as it also photosynthesizes on its own. Decades of growth (typically fifteen years or more) are needed before the valuable, densely aromatic heartwood develops in commercially useful quantity, making it a long-term, multi-generational planting rather than a quick garden project, and wild populations have historically been overharvested, making legally sourced plantation-grown seedlings the responsible choice. Water young trees regularly during establishment, choose a nitrogen-fixing or otherwise compatible host species to plant alongside it, and be prepared for a very long wait before any wood harvest.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a sheltered position; seed requires cold stratification for 90 days; container-grown plants establish more readily than bare-root transplants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in a sheltered position; sansho is the Japanese pepper of Japanese cuisine, an aromatic shrubby tree of the citrus family unrelated to black pepper but producing a similar numbing, tingling 'hot' sensation on the tongue from compounds called hydroxyl-alpha-sanshool — the same effect as Sichuan pepper from the related Zanthoxylum bungeanum. The ground green unripe berries are sprinkled on broiled eel (unagi), miso soup, and grilled dishes; the fresh aromatic young leaves (kinome) are used to garnish spring dishes. Both male and female plants are needed for berry production. A unique and rewarding specialty crop for culinary enthusiasts.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; scented geraniums are more heat tolerant than zonal geraniums and can be maintained through Gulf Coast summers with afternoon shade and adequate water.
directions: Root cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; scented geraniums are a diverse group of Pelargonium species grown primarily for their extraordinary aromatic foliage rather than their flowers. The rose-scented P. graveolens is the classic, with deeply lobed leaves smelling of rose-lemon; other varieties offer scents of peppermint, cinnamon, nutmeg, coconut, apple, apricot, pine, and many other aromas, achieved by rubbing or crushing the leaves. The dried leaves are used to flavor sugar, pound cake, jams, and teas; fresh leaves infuse a subtle rose flavor into cream, sorbet, and pound cake. They are more heat-tolerant than zonal geraniums and can survive Gulf Coast summers in partial shade with adequate water. All scented geraniums root easily from cuttings taken in late summer to bring indoors for the winter in zone 8a.

plant_note: Direct-sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, gritty or sandy, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial sun; Scotch lovage is a plant of coastal clifftops, rocky shorelines, and seaside meadows and performs best in exposed, well-drained, cool, northerly sites with good air circulation.
directions: Ligusticum scoticum, known as Scotch lovage or sea lovage, is a compact, hardy, aromatic perennial of the carrot family (Apiaceae) native to coastal cliff tops, rocky shores, and seaside grasslands of Scotland, northern England, Iceland, Scandinavia, and northeastern North America, where it grows in some of the most exposed and salt-swept maritime habitats imaginable; the glossy, dark-green, divided leaves have a strong, pleasant aroma and flavor closely resembling lovage (Levisticum officinale) and celery, and were eaten by coastal peoples as a potherb and flavoring herb long before cultivated celery was available. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall in well-drained, gritty or stony, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in a cool, sunny to partly shaded position; it is a cool-climate coastal plant that prefers excellent drainage and good air circulation and is not well-suited to hot, humid summers. Young leaves and stems can be harvested in spring and used as a celery-flavored potherb in soups and stews; historically important to the diet of remote coastal and island communities in Scotland and Scandinavia, where it was one of few flavoring herbs available and was also used as a green vegetable. Scotch lovage is rarely offered commercially but is a unique and culturally significant culinary herb for northern gardens and maritime heritage plantings.

common_name: Scotch Spearmint (Smooth Sweet Commercial Oil-Production Mint)
plant_note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; Scotch Spearmint is a commercial oil-production cultivar with a smoother, sweeter spearmint flavor than native spearmint.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Scotch Spearmint, a hybrid cultivar long grown for commercial mint oil production, offers a smoother, sweeter spearmint flavor with less of the sharper bite found in native spearmint, making it a favorite for candy, gum, and toothpaste flavoring as well as home culinary use. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage.

plant_note: Italian foraged green; self-sows.
directions: Direct-sow in early spring in well-drained soil, covering seed lightly and thinning young plants. This Italian wild green, also called bladder campion, has a mild sweet-grassy flavor for risottos and omelets. Grow in full sun with moderate water where it forms tender leafy rosettes.
