Harvest young shoots and leaves before flowering for the best texture and taste. Let a few plants flower to self-sow for a continuing patch.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring into lean, gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun; sea wormwood tolerates salt spray and saline ground and declines quickly in heavy, wet, or overly rich soil.
directions: Native to salt marshes, shingle beaches, and estuary flats of coastal Europe and the steppes of Central Asia, sea wormwood is a low, mounding subshrub with finely cut, silver-gray foliage and a sharper, more resinous scent than common wormwood. Central Asian populations were historically the commercial source of santonin, an anthelmintic compound extracted from the dried, unopened flower heads before synthetic alternatives replaced it. In the garden its salt tolerance and compact silver mass make it a useful edging plant for coastal gravel gardens, and it has also been used in small quantities to flavor regional bitters. Shear lightly after flowering to keep growth dense and prevent the base from becoming woody and open.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; cold stratification for 2–3 weeks improves germination rates for this low-growing native plant.
directions: Surface-sow seeds onto moist soil in early spring; a 2–3 week cold stratification in the fridge before sowing can improve germination rates. Self-heal spreads by stolons and will naturalize into a dense mat in moist, partly shaded spots; it tolerates light foot traffic and can work as a lawn substitute. Harvest aerial parts — leaves, stems, and flowers — when plants are in full bloom throughout summer, using them in poultices, teas, and infused preparations traditionally associated with wound healing. The purple flower spikes are also attractive and pollinator-friendly, making self-heal a useful dual-purpose ground cover.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; Sensational! grows unusually large for a lavandin and should be given extra spacing to show off its full mounded habit and long flower spikes.
directions: Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, amending heavy soil with coarse sand or gravel; Sensational! is a robust lavandin hybrid bred for exceptionally large size, with vigorous silvery foliage and some of the longest, most strongly fragrant flower spikes available in a garden lavender, held well above the foliage on tall, sturdy stems. Its bigger stature and heavier bloom make it a strong choice as a specimen plant, low hedge, or cut-flower and dried-lavender crop where scale and bloom quantity matter. Like other lavandins it is more tolerant of humidity than pure English lavender, though good air circulation and lean, fast-draining soil remain essential to prevent crown rot. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to maintain a tidy mound and encourage a second, lighter bloom later in the season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Severn Sea has an arching, semi-trailing habit intermediate between fully upright and fully prostrate rosemary types, with deep blue flowers that are showier than many rosemary cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Severn Sea is a compact, semi-trailing rosemary cultivar with gracefully arching branches, striking a middle ground between the tall, upright habit of culinary types like Tuscan Blue and the fully flat, prostrate groundcover forms. It produces an especially heavy show of deep violet-blue flowers in spring, showier than many other rosemary cultivars, in addition to fragrant, flavorful foliage suitable for cooking. It performs well in a container, raised bed, or rock garden where its arching form can spill attractively over an edge, and like all rosemary it needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; shankhpushpi is a low, spreading groundcover that tolerates poor, dry soil and needs minimal supplemental water once established.
directions: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; shankhpushpi is a low, spreading groundcover that tolerates poor, dry soil and needs minimal supplemental water once established. Small, hairy, gray-green leaves and delicate, pale blue to white, funnel-shaped morning-glory-like flowers cover a low, sprawling groundcover native to dry open ground across India, harvested whole (leaves, stems, and flowers together) for use in traditional Ayurvedic preparations valued for their calming properties. Its low, spreading habit and drought tolerance make it a workable, unfussy groundcover for a warm-climate medicinal or ethnobotanical garden bed, tolerating heat and poor soil with little care once established. Harvest above-ground growth as needed through the growing season, and expect the plant to die back in any significant cold, behaving as a tender perennial in the warmest zones or an annual further north.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant into a sunny, well-drained bed or large container once soil has warmed; in cold-winter regions grow it as a container plant brought indoors for winter or replanted annually.
directions: Plant in loose, sandy, well-drained soil and provide a trellis or nearby shrub for the scrambling, thorny stems to climb, as this relative of garden asparagus can sprawl or vine several feet. Fine feathery foliage and small white flowers give way to red berries, but the plant is grown primarily for its clustered tuberous roots, traditionally harvested at one to two years and used in Ayurvedic tonics. It is frost-tender and best treated as a container specimen or annual outside zones 9-11, overwintered indoors in a bright spot where winters are cold. Keep soil evenly moist during the growing season and reduce watering once roots go dormant in cooler months.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; She Chuang Zi is grown as a cool-season annual and is harvested for its seed once the flat seed umbels turn brown and dry.
directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; She Chuang Zi is grown as a cool-season annual and is harvested for its seed once the flat seed umbels turn brown and dry. Finely divided, carrot-like foliage and flat-topped clusters of small white flowers, typical of the carrot family, are followed by small, ribbed, aromatic seeds that are the part collected and dried for use in traditional Chinese medicine, historically applied topically for skin conditions. An easy, weedy annual related to Queen Anne's lace and wild carrot, it grows quickly from seed in ordinary garden soil with minimal care and self-sows readily if seed heads are left standing. Harvest seed umbels once they have dried and turned brown on the plant, and thresh the small seeds free before storing in a cool, dry place.

plant_note: Direct-sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring or again in fall; self-seeds readily and often persists as a low-maintenance garden edge herb.
directions: Because of its traditional use to stimulate uterine contractions, it should be avoided in pregnancy except under professional supervision. Direct-sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring or again in fall; this fast-growing, cold-tolerant mustard-family plant self-seeds readily and often persists as a low-maintenance garden edge herb. The flowering aerial parts are traditionally dried and used as a styptic tea or tincture to help slow minor bleeding and to support postpartum recovery.

plant_note: Mount on bark or rock, or pot in coarse orchid bark mix, in bright, indirect light in a warm, humid location; Shi Hu is frost-tender and grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as a greenhouse or indoor orchid.
directions: Mount on bark or rock, or pot in coarse orchid bark mix, in bright, indirect light in a warm, humid location; Shi Hu is frost-tender and grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as a greenhouse or indoor orchid. Slender, jointed, cane-like stems bear narrow leaves and small, fragrant, pale yellow-green to white flowers, but the plant is prized chiefly for its thick, mucilage-rich fresh or dried stems, one of the most highly valued tonic herbs in traditional Chinese medicine and historically among the most expensive due to its slow growth and vulnerability to overharvesting in the wild. Cultivated commercially on rock faces or tree bark in parts of China to relieve pressure on rapidly declining wild populations, it can be grown similarly in a home setting mounted on bark or grown in an orchid-appropriate bark mix with good humidity and air movement. Water regularly during active growth, allow the mount or mix to dry somewhat between waterings, and maintain high humidity and warmth year-round for the best growth.

plant_note: Direct sow or allow to self-seed in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade; shiny bush is a tiny, succulent-stemmed, heart-leaved tropical herb that grows in moist, shaded conditions and is entirely edible — the mild, slightly peppery, watercress-like leaves and stems are used fresh in salads and as a cooked vegetable throughout Southeast Asia, the Philippines, and tropical Latin America.
directions: Direct sow or transplant seedlings in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in shade to part shade; allow to self-seed for a continuous supply. Peperomia pellucida (shiny bush or clearweed) is a tiny, semi-succulent tropical annual or short-lived perennial herb — a member of the pepper family (Piperaceae) related to black pepper — native to tropical South and Central America but naturalized throughout the tropical world in shaded, moist, disturbed areas, including the floors of tropical markets, along walls, and in garden beds. The plant produces translucent-stemmed, bright-green, heart-shaped, succulent leaves just 1–2 inches across with a mild, slightly peppery, watercress-like flavor and juicy, tender texture when fresh. The entire plant — leaves, stems, and all — is edible raw in salads or lightly cooked as a pot herb; in the Philippines (where it is called 'pansit-pansitan'), it is eaten fresh as a salad green and cooked in soups; in Brazil (where it is called 'erva-de-vidro') and throughout Latin America, it is used as a mild culinary herb and folk remedy for arthritis and skin conditions. Peperomia pellucida is one of the easiest and most useful shade herbs for warm, humid gardens: it self-seeds abundantly, grows in deep shade under trees where little else will grow, and provides a continuous harvest of mild salad greens from a minimal footprint.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part shade; shiso (Japanese basil) is an indispensable herb in Japanese and Korean cuisine — the fringed, aromatic leaves come in green (ao-shiso) and red/purple (aka-shiso) forms, each with a distinctive flavor combining basil, mint, anise, and cinnamon; red shiso is also used to color umeboshi (pickled plums) and to make perilla vinegar.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface (needs light to germinate) in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; shiso self-seeds prolifically once established. Perilla frutescens var. crispa (shiso or Japanese basil) is an East Asian annual herb — one of the most important culinary herbs in Japanese cuisine — with large, ruffled, deeply crenate (toothy-edged), intensely aromatic leaves in green (ao-shiso) or red-purple (aka-shiso) forms, each with a distinctive, complex flavor combining basil, mint, anise, cinnamon, and fresh herbal notes unlike any other culinary herb. In Japanese cooking, green shiso leaves are used fresh and whole to wrap sashimi and sushi (providing a fresh, aromatic counterpoint to raw fish), cut into chiffonade as a garnish for cold noodles and soups, and fried whole in tempura batter. Red/purple shiso leaves are used to color and flavor umeboshi (salt-pickled sour plums) a bright magenta-pink, to make perilla vinegar, and in Korean cuisine to make kkaennip kimchi (perilla leaf kimchi). The seeds are also edible and are used in Japanese cooking as a condiment. Shiso tolerates partial shade better than most herbs and thrives in the heat and humidity of Southern summers; it self-seeds abundantly in warm climates, effectively naturalizing in the garden once established. The plant is nutritionally rich in vitamins A and C, rosmarinic acid, and luteolin.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost; shiso needs warm soil and will self-seed freely.
directions: Refrigerate seeds for a few days before sowing to break dormancy, then surface-sow or cover with 1/8 in of soil after the last frost. Grow in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; shiso tolerates partial shade but growth is less vigorous. Pinch flower spikes promptly to extend leaf production, or allow a few to go to seed for next year's volunteer plants. Harvest the large, ruffled leaves at any stage; young leaves are most tender and aromatic for fresh use.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in early spring or fall in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average soil in full sun to partial shade; short-toothed mountain mint tolerates damp conditions and is one of the most adaptable of the mountain mints to average garden soils.
directions: Sow seed in early spring or fall in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — short-toothed mountain mint is widely regarded as one of the single most valuable native plants for pollinators in the eastern US, producing dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny white to pale pink flowers whose nectar is irresistible to a remarkable diversity of native bees, wasps, beetles, flies, and butterflies. The silvery-white leaf bracts surrounding each flower cluster give the plant a striking frosted appearance at bloom time. Strongly mint-scented throughout, it repels deer and rabbits. Unlike most mountain mints, it tolerates partial shade and moist soils well, making it more adaptable than the narrow-leaved species. Spreads by rhizome to form a colony; divides easily to share. An outstanding native herb for mixed borders, rain gardens, and any setting where maximum pollinator support is the primary goal.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, lean, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; shrubby blue sage is a woody, somewhat sprawling shrub native to the Rio Grande Plain and Trans-Pecos Texas, tolerating alkaline limestone soils, extreme heat, and extended drought.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in zones 8–11; shrubby blue sage is a woody native salvia of southern Texas and northern Mexico, producing bright lavender-blue flowers in loose terminal spikes over a very long season — from early spring to hard frost in warm climates — making it one of the most persistently flowering native sages in the South Texas garden. The strongly aromatic, gray-green, woolly-felted leaves have a distinctive strong fragrance and have been used traditionally in Mexico as a tea herb (mejorana is a traditional name in northern Mexico). The shrubby, semi-evergreen habit and extreme drought tolerance make it valuable as a foundation plant or informal hedge in alkaline, dry landscape conditions where few shrubs thrive. Consistently attractive to migrating hummingbirds, monarch butterflies, and native bees throughout its long blooming season.

common_name: Siam Queen Basil (Thai Basil, Clove Basil)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9, Siam Queen can be started any time from February through August and will produce through the growing season, cutting back after flowering to stimulate fresh growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Siam Queen is the 1997 All-America Selections Herb Award winner — the premier Thai basil cultivar for American gardens, producing a compact, well-branched plant with deeply fragrant, dark-green, slightly crinkled leaves and a distinctive spicy-clove fragrance that is sharply different from sweet Italian basil. The clove-anise-pepper flavor profile of Siam Queen is essential to authentic Thai, Vietnamese, and other Southeast Asian cuisines — it is the correct basil for Thai basil chicken (gai pad krapao), pho, green papaya salad, and spring rolls. Unlike sweet basil cultivars, Siam Queen's flavor and fragrance remain strong even after the plant flowers, giving it a longer useful harvest window. The ornamental purple flower spikes and purple stems add visual interest beyond the herb's culinary value. In zone 9, Siam Queen grows vigorously through the long warm season and handles the summer heat better than many sweet basil cultivars — pinching the flowering stems back regularly prolongs the harvest but the herb remains usable even when flowering. The compact plant is well-suited to container growing where it can be positioned conveniently near the kitchen for ready harvesting. Excellent in containers and raised beds.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring as soon as growth resumes, or in early fall; replant divisions 8-12 inches apart in well-drained, fertile, moist soil in full sun. Division every 3-4 years maintains plant vigor and prevents clumps from becoming congested.
directions: Allium schoenoprasum var. sibiricum, commonly called Siberian chives or giant chives, is a robust, cold-hardy variety of common chives native to the harsh continental climates of Siberia, northern China, and Alaska, distinguished by its noticeably broader, thicker, hollow leaves and larger, showier lavender-pink flowerheads that make it both a more productive culinary herb and a bolder ornamental plant than standard chives. Propagate by dividing established clumps in early spring or fall, replanting divisions at the same depth in moderately fertile, consistently moist but well-drained soil in full sun; Siberian chives are more tolerant of cold, wind, and dry conditions than common chives and are an excellent choice for exposed northern gardens. Harvest leaves by cutting 1-2 inches above soil level, repeating every 3-4 weeks throughout the growing season; the flavor is essentially identical to common chives — mild onion — with the advantage that the broader leaves are easier to harvest in quantity. The large, globe-shaped flowerheads in late spring are highly attractive to native bees and can be used fresh as a garnish or steeped in vinegar; deadhead after flowering to maintain leaf production and prevent excessive self-seeding.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in a sheltered, sunny position; Sichuan pepper shrubs have sharp spines and should be sited away from foot traffic. Wear gloves when harvesting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sichuan pepper (not related to black pepper or chili peppers) is the dried husk of the fruit of Zanthoxylum shrubs, whose defining characteristic is a numbing, buzzing sensation on the tongue caused by the compound hydroxy-alpha-sanshool — a sensation called ma (tingling/numbing) that is the foundation of the ma-la (numbing-spicy) flavor profile of Sichuan Chinese cuisine. Harvest the small red fruits in fall when fully ripe, then dry and separate the husks from the black seeds — only the husks are used, as the seeds are bitter and gritty. The shrub is spiny and produces attractive clusters of small red fruits on female plants. Plant at least one male for pollination.

common_name: Silver Lace Society Garlic (Variegated Society Garlic)
plant_note: Plant rhizome clumps in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 7 provide heavy mulch for winter protection, as plants can be damaged below 20°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this South African native is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in zone 9–10 gardens. Silver Lace is a variegated society garlic selection, its strap-like leaves crisply edged in creamy white, adding season-long foliage interest to the near-year-round clusters of lavender, garlic-scented flowers typical of the species. Like the plain green form, leaves and flowers carry a mild garlic flavor without lingering breath and make a useful, ornamental garlic substitute in the kitchen, while the flowers reliably draw bees and small pollinators. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor and clean variegation.

plant_note: Variegated; propagate from cuttings.
directions: Grow this variegated thyme from cuttings or division to keep the silver-edged leaf pattern true. It offers standard culinary thyme flavor along with attractive frosty foliage. Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun and water sparingly once established. Trim after flowering to prevent woodiness and encourage fresh compact growth. Harvest sprigs any time and mulch the crown in cold-winter regions.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Simcoe is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation.
directions: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Simcoe is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in the early 2000s, this high-alpha dual-purpose hop delivers a distinctive combination of passionfruit and pine aromas alongside earthy, dank undertones that became a signature flavor of the West Coast IPA style, and its high alpha acid content also makes it effective as a clean bittering hop. Its unique aroma profile and versatility for both bittering and late-addition dry-hopping uses have made it a foundational variety in modern American craft brewing since its introduction, prized enough that supply is often constrained relative to brewer demand. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery and spring back when squeezed, and provide consistent moisture and full sun through the growing season.

plant_note: A blend of basil types; all are warmth-loving and set out after frost.
directions: This blend gathers six basils, including Genovese and large-leaf types for pesto, Dark Opal for colorful vinegars, plus lime and lemon basils for oils, sauces, and sorbets. Because every type in the mix is a form of Ocimum basilicum, they share the same warm-weather culture and can be grown together for a diverse harvest. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant after frost into full sun with rich, moist soil. Pinch flower buds and harvest often to keep the range of scents and flavors at their peak.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; cold-moist stratification for 4 weeks before sowing greatly improves germination of this native wildflower.
directions: Cold-stratify seed in moist peat in the refrigerator for 4 weeks before surface-sowing onto a warm starting mix; germination is slow and erratic. Plant in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil that mimics its woodland-edge native habitat. Harvest aerial parts — stems, leaves, and small flowers — in full bloom during summer, using them fresh or dried for tinctures and teas valued for their calming properties. Divide established clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow; bred to stay leafy longer before flowering.
directions: Direct sow seed where plants are to grow, as cilantro has a taproot and dislikes transplanting. This beginner-friendly variety is bred to stay leafy longer before bolting to seed, extending the harvest of flat, flavorful leaves. Plants reach about twelve to twenty-four inches and respond well to successive sowings every few weeks. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage fresh growth and delay flowering. If plants do bolt, let them go to seed to collect coriander.

plant_note: Direct sow or set out small starts in spring into loose, sandy or shelly soil in full sun; this low mint-family herb self-sows readily on disturbed sandy ground and short-lived plants are usually replaced by their own seedlings within a season or two.
directions: Sow directly into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; small coastal germander is a diminutive, aromatic mint-family annual to short-lived perennial found on coastal sands and shell middens from Texas and Louisiana to Florida. Its lobed gray-green leaves and tiny white to pale blue speckled flowers stay low and inconspicuous, making it best suited to a sunny gravel path, dune restoration planting, or the gaps between coastal paving stones rather than a formal bed. It tolerates the long, humid Gulf Coast growing season without irrigation once established and self-sows into bare sandy patches, filling niches too dry and infertile for most other groundcovers.

subcategory: North American native anise-flavored shade herb
plant_note: Sow seeds in fall (they require cold stratification — naturally satisfied by winter cold) in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral forest soil in zone 3–8; Smooth Sweet Cicely is a graceful native woodland herb of North America — closely related to the European Sweet Cicely (Myrrhis odorata) — with a distinctive, pervasive anise-licorice fragrance throughout the plant and edible roots, young shoots, and seeds used by Native Americans for centuries as food, flavoring, and medicine.
directions: Sow Osmorhiza longistylis seeds in fall directly in the garden — seeds are slow to germinate and require cold stratification; alternatively cold-stratify in damp paper towels in the refrigerator for 60–90 days before spring sowing; plants self-sow freely once established and can naturalize into a fragrant woodland groundcover. Smooth Sweet Cicely is an elegant, airy, native woodland herb that fills the shaded understory with its finely divided, carrot-family foliage and pervasive anise fragrance throughout the growing season — the roots especially smell strongly of sweet anise when bruised. All parts are edible: young spring leaves used as a mild anise flavoring in salads, fish dishes, and desserts; the thick, carrot-like taproot grated or eaten raw for its strong anise flavor; the immature green seeds used as a spice. Multiple Indigenous nations used Osmorhiza roots as food and medicine — the Cheyenne as a cold remedy, the Ojibwe as an eye wash, and the Iroquois as a root vegetable cooked with meat. The white, flat-topped flower clusters attract numerous small native bees, wasps, and flies. An excellent companion for ferns, wild ginger, and trilliums in naturalistic woodland gardens; once established, it requires no care beyond controlling spread if self-sowing becomes excessive.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once the soil has warmed above 65 degrees F, setting them 2-3 inches deep in compost-enriched soil in a partially shaded to shaded bed.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 2-3 inches deep in moist, organically rich, well-draining soil in partial to full shade, spacing clumps 24-36 inches apart to allow the lance-shaped, aromatic foliage to fill in naturally. Water consistently throughout the growing season to maintain even soil moisture, and apply a balanced slow-release fertilizer in spring to fuel vigorous growth. In zone 8 gardens, mulch the root zone heavily after the first frost to protect the rhizomes through winter, as the tops will die back but the roots typically survive. Harvest young leaves and rhizomes as needed for culinary use in Sri Lankan and South Asian cooking, where both impart a mild cardamom-like fragrance to curries and rice dishes.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; soapwort can also be started indoors or divided from established clumps in spring or autumn.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil; soapwort is extremely adaptable and tolerates poor, dry soils once established, spreading by both seed and rhizome. The entire plant — especially the roots — contains saponins that create a soapy lather when bruised and agitated in water, making it historically valuable for washing delicate textiles and woolens. Harvest roots in autumn and foliage before flowering for use in gentle natural soap preparations; the lather cleans without the harshness of detergents. Deadhead spent flowers to limit self-seeding, or allow a few to naturalize for a low-maintenance informal planting of clove-scented pink blooms.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Sochi is among the most cold-hardy named tea cultivars available, originally selected for cultivation on Russia's Black Sea coast, and is the standard recommendation for growers pushing tea cultivation into cooler zones than the species typically tolerates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; Sochi is a cold-hardy tea cultivar originally developed for the Black Sea coastal tea-growing region of Russia, the northernmost commercial tea-producing area in the world, and is widely sold in the US specifically because it tolerates significantly colder winters than typical tea plants, with reports of surviving briefly into the single digits °F once well established. This makes it the go-to choice for tea growers in cooler zones than the Gulf South, such as the mid-South and lower Appalachians, though it also performs well in the milder winters of zone 8–9. Leaves and growth habit are similar to standard small-leaved China-type tea, suitable for the same green, oolong, or black tea processing depending on how the harvested leaf is handled. Begin light harvesting of the top two leaves and a bud once plants are well established at three to four years old, and mulch heavily to protect the acid-loving root system through winter in the colder end of its range.

plant_note: Divide clumps or plant container starts in spring; establishes quickly and begins blooming within the first season. In zone 8, mulch heavily for winter protection.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; society garlic is a South African native perfectly adapted to Gulf Coast heat and drought, producing strappy blue-green foliage and clusters of lavender-pink flowers almost continuously from spring through fall. Despite the name, it lacks the offensive breath component of garlic while retaining a mild garlic flavor — the leaves, flowers, and bulbs are all edible and used in salads, stir-fries, and as a cooked vegetable in South African cuisine. It is a superb low-maintenance edging plant for sunny borders, extremely tolerant of heat, reflected heat, poor soil, and dry conditions once established. Deer and rabbits avoid it completely. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring.

plant_note: Sow in early spring; this hardy perennial returns each year and is among the first greens up.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in spring and thin plants to about a foot apart in a permanent bed, since sorrel is a long-lived perennial. It is one of the first greens to emerge in spring, offering a bright, tart, lemony flavor to salads and soups. Harvest outer leaves regularly and remove flower stalks to keep the plant producing tender new growth. In hot weather the leaves can turn tougher and more sour, so pick young for the best flavor.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; South African geranium grows from a stout, woody, tuberous root system that survives moderate drought. In zone 9 it can remain in the ground as a perennial. The velvety, silver-gray to blue-gray leaves and dark red-maroon flowers are distinctive. The roots are the source of the commercially significant herbal supplement EPs 7630 / Umcka, widely sold for upper respiratory support.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; South African geranium is a low-growing pelargonium from the semi-arid grasslands and rocky hillsides of South Africa that has achieved global commercial significance as a medicinal herb: the dried, powdered root extract — sold under the names Umcka, Umckaloabo, and EPs 7630 — is one of the best-studied herbal supplements for upper respiratory tract infections, with multiple clinical trials supporting its efficacy for reducing the duration and severity of acute bronchitis and the common cold. As a garden plant, independent of its medicinal significance, it is quietly attractive: the velvety, rounded, silver-gray to blue-gray leaves with deeply scalloped edges form a soft, spreading, woolly-textured mound, and above this cloud of silver foliage appear, in late spring through summer, clusters of small, dark, wine-red to almost-black maroon, five-petaled flowers — one of the most unusually dark-colored flowers of any pelargonium. The combination of silver foliage and very dark maroon-purple flowers is sophisticated and distinctive. It grows from a thick, tuberous, carrot-like root that survives significant drought and moderate frost. An interesting, medicinally significant herb for the zone 9 herb garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, dry, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; southern agastache grows naturally on dry, rocky, calcareous slopes and canyon walls of the Chihuahuan Desert and the Trans-Pecos of Texas and is adapted to extreme heat and drought.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; southern agastache is a compact hyssop-mint native to dry, rocky, calcareous slopes of the Chihuahuan Desert region in west Texas and adjacent New Mexico and Mexico. The small but attractive rosy-pink to salmon-red flower spikes are produced from midsummer through fall and are magnets for hummingbirds and large bumblebees throughout the blooming period. More drought-tolerant than most agastaches and adapted to the thin, rocky, alkaline soils of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos, making it an excellent choice for dry, rocky, calcareous gardens in zone 9. Unlike many agastaches that decline in the summer heat and humidity of the Gulf South, southern agastache thrives in the hot, dry conditions of west Texas and is more durable in drier zone 9 gardens than humid-adapted species.

plant_note: Plant tuberous root divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; southern stoneroot is a tuberous-rooted mint-family herb of the southeastern coastal plain closely related to the better-known C. canadensis.
directions: Plant tuberous root divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade in zones 7–10; southern stoneroot is a mint-family perennial of the Gulf and South Atlantic coastal plain — found naturally in moist, shaded bottomlands and rich upland forests of Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, and adjacent states — that produces large, coarsely toothed, opposite leaves with a distinctive lemon-horse-balm fragrance and branching panicles of small, pale yellow flowers in late summer and fall. The large, knotty, tuberous root system gives the plant its common name and was used in traditional herbal medicine for digestive complaints, as with the related C. canadensis. It tolerates the heat and humidity of zone 8–10 better than its northern relative and is a useful large-leafed foliage plant for shaded southern gardens where few fragrant herbs thrive. Pair with native gingers, beautyberry, and spicebush for a fragrant native shade border.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants after last frost; southernwood rarely sets viable seed and is almost always propagated vegetatively.
directions: Root 4–6 in semi-ripe cuttings in late summer in gritty, moist propagating mix; cuttings root readily without hormone treatment. Southernwood is a woody, feathery-leaved Artemisia with a sharp lemon-camphor fragrance historically used as a moth repellent and insect deterrent in drawers and linen presses. Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; like most artemisias it suffers in wet or rich conditions and prefers slightly alkaline soil. Cut back hard to within 6 in of the ground in early spring to prevent excessive woodiness and stimulate a fresh flush of aromatic silver-green growth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in fall in extremely well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; lavender fails quickly in fertile, moist, or clay soils — the single most important factor is perfect drainage. In zone 9a fall planting allows roots to establish before summer heat.
directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Spanish lavender (L. stoechas) is the most heat- and humidity-tolerant of the lavenders, making it the best choice for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens where English lavender (L. angustifolia) typically fails from summer humidity. It produces distinctive flowers topped with long, rabbit-ear-like purple bracts in spring, with a repeat bloom in fall. Like all lavenders it requires perfect drainage — root rot in wet or heavy soil is the most common cause of death. Plant in a raised bed or on a slope in amended sandy soil. Harvest stems when flowers are half-open; dry hanging upside down for wreaths and sachets. Shear by one-third after each bloom flush to maintain compact growth.

plant_note: Take semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in spring in sharply drained, poor to average soil in full sun; Spanish sage is drought-tolerant and resents wet winter soils.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in spring in sharply drained, poor to average soil in full sun; Spanish sage is a Mediterranean subshrub with narrow gray-green, lavender-scented leaves that are interchangeable with garden sage in the kitchen and are considered superior for making herbal extracts and infusions. It is more drought-tolerant, more compact, and harder to kill than Salvia officinalis, performing well in dry gardens, rock gardens, and gravel paths where the soil drains quickly even in winter. Trim lightly after each flush of small blue-purple flowers to maintain shape and prevent woodiness. Avoid heavy clay soils — perfect drainage is essential to year-round survival.

common_name: Spanish Thyme (Jamaican Oregano, Puerto Rican Oregano)
plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Spanish thyme is a small Caribbean shrub with intensely thyme-oregano scented leaves — it is the traditional dry-climate oregano and thyme substitute of Jamaica and the Caribbean islands, far more drought-tolerant than either European thyme or oregano.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; harvest stems frequently to maintain compact, bushy growth. Lippia micromera (Spanish thyme or Jamaican oregano) is a small, woody, aromatic shrub native to the dry limestone hills of Jamaica and other Caribbean islands, producing small, densely crowded, grey-green, strongly thyme-oregano scented leaves. The plant occupies the culinary niche of thyme and oregano in Caribbean cooking — the dried or fresh leaves are used in jerk seasoning blends, seasoning rubs for meats and fish, and traditional Caribbean herbal teas (sooshal, orosul). It is notably more drought- and heat-tolerant than either European thyme (Thymus vulgaris) or Mediterranean oregano (Origanum vulgare), making it well-suited to hot, dry, tropical and subtropical gardens where those herbs struggle. Lippia micromera belongs to the verbena family (Verbenaceae) and is distinct from Plectranthus amboinicus (Cuban oregano, also sometimes called 'Spanish thyme') — both are Caribbean oregano substitutes but from unrelated plant families. The essential oil is rich in thymol and carvacrol, the same primary compounds responsible for thyme and oregano's characteristic aroma. Excellent in containers in subtropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring once soil has warmed; space generously to promote air circulation around the mounding gray-green foliage.
directions: Establish rooted cuttings in fast-draining, alkaline to neutral soil in a location with maximum sun exposure, mirroring its native Spanish hillside habitat. Water sparingly once established; the camphor-rosemary-marjoram scent is most concentrated in dry conditions and will diminish if the plant is overwatered or grown in shade. Trim back by one-third after the white fluffy flower heads fade to keep the plant bushy and to prevent it from becoming overly woody at the base. Protect from prolonged hard freezes with a cloche or cold frame, as it is less cold-hardy than common thyme.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; contain with root barriers as spearmint is vigorously stoloniferous — container planting is the most reliable method for small gardens.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; spearmint tolerates light shade better than most culinary herbs and is one of the better mints for partially shaded kitchen gardens. Mentha spicata is the garden mint of European tradition with smooth, bright-green, wrinkled leaves and a sweet, relatively cool, characteristic mint flavor (from carvone rather than menthol) used in mint sauce with lamb, jelly, juleps, mojitos, tabbouleh, and Middle Eastern cuisine. Unlike peppermint (M. × piperita) which is a sterile hybrid, spearmint sets viable seed and can be started from seed (though vegetative propagation produces more reliable, uniform plants). It is generally considered a milder, sweeter mint than peppermint and is the preferred choice in savory cooking and cocktails; cultivars 'Kentucky Colonel' and 'Moroccan' are popular selections with especially fine flavor.

common_name: Spice Islands Rosemary (Classic Strongly Flavored Culinary Rosemary)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun, well-drained soil; Spice Islands is a classic, widely grown culinary rosemary cultivar valued for strong, pungent, traditional rosemary flavor and consistent, easy-to-maintain upright growth.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil. Spice Islands is a long-established culinary rosemary cultivar bred for strong, classic, pungently resinous rosemary flavor and fragrance, considered one of the most reliably flavorful rosemary cultivars for everyday cooking use. It grows into a dense, upright, well-branched shrub with the typical narrow, needle-like, dark green leaves and pale blue flowers of standard rosemary, making it equally useful as a culinary herb, an evergreen landscape shrub, or a low informal hedge. Like other rosemary, it thrives in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil and full sun, and is far more likely to suffer from overwatering and poor drainage than from drought or neglect. Harvest sprigs anytime for fresh use, or cut and dry larger quantities for winter storage. Prune lightly after flowering, or anytime during the growing season when harvesting, to maintain a full, bushy shape and encourage continued tender new growth.

common_name: Spicy Globe Basil (Globe Basil, Bush Basil)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. Spicy Globe naturally forms a mounded, spherical shape without pinching — simply harvest regularly and it maintains its globe form. Excellent container herb.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Spicy Globe is a compact, naturally mounded basil variety that forms a near-perfect sphere shape 10–14 inches in diameter without any pruning or training. The tiny, fine-textured leaves are intensely fragrant and spicy — more intensely basil-flavored than large-leaf Genovese types — with a sweet, warm, clove-like spice note that makes Spicy Globe excellent for herbes de Provence blends, compound butters, and infused oils. The self-regulating globe shape and compact 10–12 inch height make it an ideal container plant, a neat edging for herb beds, and a productive houseplant in a sunny window. In zone 9's warm season it thrives April–October; the tiny leaves wilt at the first frost. Harvest by snipping 1/3 of the plant at a time to maintain the globe shape; never remove more than 1/3 at once. The dense, tight growth resists bolting slightly better than Genovese types, giving a longer leaf-harvest window before flowers appear.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or divide established plants in spring or fall; spiked speedwell transplants easily and blooms reliably in its first or second year from seed. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage reblooming.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; spiked speedwell is one of the most reliably beautiful summer perennials in the European tradition, producing dense, tapering spikes of tiny flowers in intense shades of violet-blue, lilac, or white (depending on cultivar) that bloom from midsummer into fall. The plant is extremely tough and drought tolerant once established, thriving in lean, well-drained soil where it is long-lived, but declining in rich, moist conditions where it becomes floppy and short-lived. Popular cultivars include 'Royal Candles' (deep violet, compact), 'Icicle' (white), 'Red Fox' (deep pink), and 'Heidekind' (rose-pink). An excellent front-of-border perennial that combines beautifully with ornamental grasses, sedums, and rudbeckia in late-season gardens. Attracts numerous small butterflies and bumblebees.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in warm, moist seed-starting mix at 75°F; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture. Spilanthes is notable for spilanthol, a compound in the flowers and leaves that causes an intense, numbing tingle on the tongue — hence the common name toothache plant; it has uses in local anesthetic preparations and salivation-stimulating tinctures. The distinctive red and yellow, cone-shaped flower heads are harvested fresh or dried for tinctures and topical preparations; even a small piece of flower head produces a pronounced oral sensation. Grow in full sun with moderate moisture; deadhead regularly to encourage continuous flowering throughout the warm season.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall (or spring) in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; spiny chicory grows naturally on sea cliffs and rocky coastal slopes exposed to wind and salt spray. It is notably salt-tolerant and wind-resistant. Harvest young shoots and leaves for cooking before the plant becomes too spiny in late season; older growth is unpleasantly prickly.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; spiny chicory is a Cretan and eastern Mediterranean coastal plant — native to the rocky, wind-exposed, salt-spray-drenched sea cliffs of Crete and other Greek islands — that is one of the most important traditional wild food plants of Cretan cuisine. The young shoots and basal leaves are collected in late winter and spring, before the plant develops its characteristic spiny character, and prepared as horta — the classic Greek-Cretan tradition of boiling or sautéing wild greens in olive oil with lemon. The flavor is pleasantly bitter in the chicory family tradition. In the garden it forms a low, spiny, somewhat cushion-like perennial with small, pale-blue chicory flowers in summer. Extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and wind-resistant — qualities that make it outstanding for coastal and exposed Mediterranean-climate gardens where the combination of salt spray, wind, and lean, rocky soil defeats most ornamentals. An authentic plant for a Greek or Mediterranean-themed herb garden.

common_name: St. John Wort (Common St. John Wort)
plant_note: Direct sow on surface (seeds need light to germinate) in early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; St. John's wort is adaptable and easy to establish, self-seeding readily once established — site carefully as it can spread aggressively.
directions: Surface sow seeds in early spring (press lightly into soil but do not cover — seeds require light for germination) in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; thin or transplant to 18 inches. Hypericum perforatum (St. John's wort) is the most important medicinal herb in the Western world after echinacea — a Eurasian perennial producing cheerful, 5-petaled, bright-yellow flowers with numerous golden stamens from June through August, on upright, two-winged, branching stems with small, oval, opposite leaves dotted with translucent oil glands (the characteristic 'perforations' visible when the leaf is held to light). Standardized Hypericum extracts are among the best-documented herbal treatments for mild to moderate depression, with multiple clinical trials showing efficacy comparable to conventional antidepressants. The flowers and upper leaves are harvested at peak bloom and tinctured or dried for medicinal use. The plant is easy to grow in lean, well-drained soils and self-seeds prolifically — it has naturalized across North America and is considered an invasive weed in some western states; grow responsibly. CAUTION: St. John's wort causes photosensitivity in fair-skinned people and may interact with numerous prescription medications including birth control, antidepressants, and anti-rejection drugs.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow as seeds need light, and a 2–3 week cold-moist stratification period can improve germination rates.
directions: Surface-sow seeds onto moist mix; cold stratification for 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator prior to sowing can improve germination, especially with older seed. Plants thrive in poor, well-drained soil and become weedy in fertile conditions — resist the urge to fertilize. Harvest flower buds and newly opened blossoms around the summer solstice, when hypericin content peaks; rub a bud between your fingers and look for a red-purple stain confirming good potency. Dry flowers quickly on screens to preserve the active compounds.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in permanently moist to wet, organically rich soil at pond margins, swales, or floodplain edges; Lycopus rubellus naturalizes by stolons and is best suited to rain gardens, constructed wetlands, or streambank restoration plantings.
directions: Lycopus rubellus thrives in saturated or inundated soils and is an excellent choice for rain gardens, constructed wetlands, and streambank stabilization plantings where standing water is common in spring. The small white flowers appearing in summer attract native bees and are characteristic of the mint family; the plant is strongly aromatic when the leaves are crushed. Historically, the starchy tubers were eaten by indigenous peoples of the Southeast, and the plant remains an important habitat species supporting wetland food webs. Plant in partial shade with consistently wet roots, and divide every two to three years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Set out container-grown nursery stock in spring into humid, acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil sheltered from wind, ideally with morning sun and afternoon shade.
directions: Set out container-grown nursery stock in spring into humid, acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil sheltered from wind, ideally with morning sun and afternoon shade. True star anise is a slow, long-lived subtropical evergreen native to southern China and northern Vietnam that needs six to eight years of consistent warmth and humidity before it forms its first harvestable star-shaped seed pods. Pods are picked while still green, then sun-dried until they turn the familiar deep reddish-brown, and are essential to Chinese five-spice powder, pho broth, and mulled wine. Do not confuse it with the toxic ornamental anise relatives (Illicium floridanum, I. anisatum) sold for landscaping — only I. verum pods are safe to eat.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, just pressing them into moist seed-starting mix, as light aids germination; note that germination rates for stevia seed can be inconsistent. Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil after temperatures are reliably warm, and water consistently—stevia is sensitive to both drought and waterlogging. Pinch growing tips early to encourage a bushy form with more harvestable leaf area. Harvest leaves before the plant flowers, when glycoside content (sweetness) is at its peak; dry or use fresh.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; seeds are tiny and require light to germinate — surface-sow and do not cover. Transplant outdoors after all frost danger has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. In zones 9-11, stevia is a true perennial; in zones 7-8, treat as a tender annual or overwinter cuttings indoors.
directions: Stevia rebaudiana is a tender perennial herb native to the subtropical highland borderlands of Paraguay and Brazil, where indigenous Guarani peoples have used its intensely sweet leaves for centuries as a sweetener and medicinal plant; the steviol glycosides in its leaves are 30-300 times sweeter than sucrose, making even a few fresh leaves a potent, calorie-free sweetening agent for teas, lemonades, and desserts. Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date by surface-sowing onto moist, sterile seed-starting mix — seeds need light to germinate and must not be covered; germination is often erratic, and cuttings from established plants root readily and produce more uniform plants than seed-grown specimens. Transplant hardened seedlings into well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; stevia dislikes waterlogged conditions but benefits from consistent moisture and regular feeding during the growing season. Harvest leaves throughout summer by pinching branch tips to encourage bushiness; dry harvested leaves completely before crumbling them for storage as a concentrated sweetener, or use fresh leaves directly in beverages.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; sticky sage is one of very few salvias that genuinely thrives in shade — most salvias require full sun, making this species uniquely valuable for shaded situations. The sticky stems and leaves can be irritating to sensitive skin; handle with care or wear gloves.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; sticky sage is a woodland native of mountain forests across central and southern Europe and Asia Minor — one of the very few salvias genuinely adapted to shade, making it uniquely valuable as a large, flowering herb for shaded sites where virtually all other sages would fail. The large, hairy, somewhat sticky (glandular) leaves are strongly aromatic when rubbed, with an odor somewhat like oregano mixed with damp vegetation. In summer the tall stems produce whorled clusters of pale lemon-yellow to soft yellow flowers with a darker reddish-brown spot in the throat — smaller than many cultivated salvias but distinctive in their soft yellow color (unusual among salvias, which are most commonly blue, purple, or red). The sticky-hairy texture of the plant is responsible for the common name 'sticky sage' and makes the leaves adhesive to the touch. It self-sows modestly in appropriate shaded conditions to maintain small colonies. A rare example of a shade-adapted Salvia, outstanding combined with hostas, ferns, and woodland wildflowers in moist, cool, semi-shaded positions.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil is workable; surface-sow as seeds need light and cool temperatures to germinate.
directions: Surface-sow onto moist, nitrogen-rich soil in a dedicated bed with underground barriers if possible, as nettles spread aggressively by rhizome. Always wear thick gloves and long sleeves when handling plants, as the hollow stinging hairs inject formic acid on contact. Harvest young growing tips in early spring before plants reach knee height, using them in soups, teas, and nutritive infusions — cooking or drying neutralizes the sting completely. Cut plants back to the ground two or three times per season to encourage fresh new growth throughout the year.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into moist, rich forest soil in a shaded location; cold stratification over winter improves germination, and seedlings emerge in spring.
directions: Sow seed in fall into deeply amended, humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees where the site remains consistently moist but not waterlogged. Cover seed lightly with sifted leaf mold and allow the winter chill to stratify the seed naturally before spring germination. Stoneroot grows large with age and benefits from generous spacing so that its broad, lemon-scented leaves can spread without crowding neighboring plants. Once established, it is a long-lived woodland fixture that needs little care beyond maintaining soil moisture and a mulch of decomposing leaves.

plant_note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; Strawberry Mint bears small leaves with a fruity strawberry-mint aroma, popular for garnishing desserts and drinks.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Strawberry Mint bears small, fine-textured leaves with a distinctly fruity strawberry aroma layered over a mild mint base, a fun, kid-friendly fragrance that makes it a popular garnish for desserts, fruit salads, and summer drinks. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in warm, humid conditions and transplant outside once nights stay above 60F, giving the scrambling vine a trellis or host shrub to climb.
directions: Suma is a vigorous, climbing perennial from the Amazon basin grown for its deep, sweet-tasting root, prized in traditional medicine as a general tonic and adaptogen thanks to its saponin and ecdysteroid content. It thrives in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil under the dappled light of a humid tropical or subtropical garden, scrambling over neighboring shrubs or a trellis as it matures. Roots are left undisturbed for several growing seasons to bulk up before harvest, similar in patience required to true ginseng. Protect from any frost and mulch heavily to keep the root zone consistently warm and moist through the growing season.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds on the surface of prepared soil after last frost date in full sun in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; summer savory germinates readily in warm soil and can also be started indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost.
directions: Sow seeds directly on the surface of well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun after last frost; summer savory germinates quickly in warm conditions and thins to 12–15 inches apart for best branching. It has a peppery, thyme-like flavor with slightly more intensity than its perennial relative winter savory, and it is the classic herb for seasoning fresh or dried beans (in German it is called Bohnenkraut, bean herb), as well as poultry, sausages, stuffings, and herb vinegars. Harvest regularly by cutting stem tips to keep plants bushy and delay flowering, as flavor declines after bloom; leaves are most aromatic just before the small pink or white flowers open. Dry whole sprigs tied in small bundles in a warm, well-ventilated place — summer savory dries well and retains excellent flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has fully passed.
directions: Superbo is an Italian-bred Genovese-type basil selected specifically for plant-to-plant uniformity, giving growers a medium-compact, evenly sized crop that is easier to manage than open-pollinated Genovese strains. The broad, spoon-shaped leaves are a brilliant deep green and hold their glossy sheen and flavor well after cutting, which is why this cultivar became a standard for commercial bunching and pesto processing in Italy. Pinch flower spikes as they appear to extend the harvest window and prevent the leaves from turning bitter. Grow it side by side with a standard Genovese basil if you want to compare uniformity and leaf shape, since the two share nearly identical flavor profiles.

plant_note: Direct sow just before or at last frost; seeds are tiny and need light for germination — do not cover.
directions: Broadcast the dust-like seeds onto a weed-free seedbed and press in without covering; they require light to germinate and will not sprout if buried. Sweet Annie grows rapidly into a large, feathery-leaved annual with an intensely sweet, camphor-like fragrance widely used in wreath-making and dried floral arrangements. The plant is the natural source of artemisinin, a compound researched extensively for anti-malarial properties; harvest aerial parts when the plant begins to flower for the highest artemisinin content. Self-seeds prolifically in warm climates, so deadhead spent plants before seeds fully ripen if reseeding in the garden is not desired.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 55F; in zone 9 sweet broom grows year-round in a sheltered, partly shaded bed but should be protected or brought into a container for winter if a hard freeze threatens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to partial sun; sweet broom is a low, spreading tropical American herb long used across the Caribbean and South America as a folk remedy for coughs, colds, and respiratory complaints, brewed as a sweet, vanilla-and-hay-scented tea from the fresh or dried leaves, which contain coumarin, the aromatic compound also found in sweet woodruff and tonka bean. The small, narrow, bright-green leaves release their characteristic sweet fragrance most strongly once cut and dried, making it a plant grown as much for scent and tea as for garden appearance. It thrives in the dappled shade of a tropical understory planting and tolerates the humidity of a Gulf South summer well, though it has no frost tolerance and needs to overwinter indoors or under cover outside of zone 10-11. Harvest stems as needed for fresh tea, or cut and hang-dry bundles for longer storage; regular light harvesting encourages bushier regrowth.

plant_note: Direct-sow fresh, ripe seed immediately in fall — sweet cicely requires a prolonged cold stratification period of at least 8–12 weeks to break dormancy and will not germinate reliably without it; seeds sown in fall will germinate the following spring, while seed stored over winter quickly becomes non-viable, so fall sowing of fresh seed is strongly preferred.
directions: Myrrhis odorata is one of the finest shade-tolerant culinary herbs available to the northern-hemisphere gardener, thriving in the dappled shade of woodland edges, hedgerows, and north-facing borders where few aromatic herbs will grow; the large, finely divided, fern-like, bright-green leaves emit a strong, sweet anise-licorice scent and flavor when crushed, making them prized in the kitchen for flavoring fruit desserts, salads, and herbal liqueurs. Sow fresh seed immediately in fall directly in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moisture-retentive, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; the seed has a hard coat and requires a prolonged cold period (at minimum 8–12 weeks) to germinate — stored seed rapidly loses viability, so fresh fall sowing is essential. Plants grow 2–4 feet tall and spread to form attractive, long-lived clumps with flat-topped, white umbel flowers in late spring followed by large, ridged, glossy-brown seeds; they will self-sow freely in suitable conditions once established. All parts are edible and anise-flavored: the leaves, young seeds (excellent chopped into salads), and sweet, parsnip-like roots; the sweetness of the leaves means they can be used to reduce sugar needed in recipes for rhubarb and tart fruits.

common_name: Sweet Dani Lemon Basil (AAS-Winning Strongly Lemon-Scented Large Basil)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sweet Dani is an excellent cut-and-come-again herb — regular harvest of stem tips prevents bolting and maintains vigorous leaf production through the growing season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sweet Dani is an All-America Selections award-winning lemon basil (Ocimum x citriodorum) recognized for its exceptional lemon fragrance, large plant size, and outstanding performance as both a culinary herb and ornamental annual. The intense lemon scent — produced by the citral compounds that distinguish lemon basil from sweet basil — is significantly stronger in Sweet Dani than in standard lemon basil varieties, filling a small garden area with citrus fragrance when brushed or harvested. The large, medium-green, slightly textured leaves have a complex flavor combining sweet basil aromatics with a bright, clean lemon note that is outstanding for lemon pasta sauces, fish preparations, lemon-herb vinaigrettes, herb teas, and potpourri. Sweet Dani is substantially larger than older lemon basil varieties — reaching 24–30 inches versus the compact 12–15 inches of some lemon basil selections — producing more harvestable leaf mass per plant. The plants bolt to flower in late summer in zone 9 heat but regular pinching of the growing tips delays this and extends the harvest season. The white flowers attract numerous bee species when allowed to bloom. Lemon basil provides a valuable flavor dimension distinct from standard sweet basil in herb garden collections and culinary applications where citrus brightness is desired.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; in zone 9 sow February–March for spring or September–October for fall. Sweet Fennel does not transplant well — always direct sow in place. Unlike Florence fennel (finocchio) which is grown for a swollen bulb base, Dulce Sweet Fennel is grown for seeds and leaf — the characteristic Italian feathery herb. Fennel is allelopathic (inhibits growth of many neighboring plants); site it away from tomatoes, peppers, and dill.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun — do not transplant; Dulce (Sweet) fennel is the culinary fennel grown for its fine, feathery, anise-flavored fronds and seeds — the herb fennel of Italian and Mediterranean cooking used in fish preparations, sausages, salads, and as a garnish, distinct from Florence fennel (finocchio) which forms the swollen bulb base. The tall, graceful, blue-green fronds have an intensely sweet anise-licorice flavor and fragrance; both fresh and dried fronds are used throughout Italian and Provençal cooking. The seeds (technically a double achene) are the primary flavoring in Italian sausage, Tuscan salumi, the spice mixes of southern French cooking, and liqueurs including pastis and absinthe. Dulce fennel is perennial in zone 9 and zone 10, returning from roots each spring; in colder zones it is grown as an annual. Site carefully as fennel inhibits the growth of many neighboring vegetables through allelopathic root exudates — keep it at least 3 feet from tomatoes, peppers, and beans.

plant_note: Surface sow seed in early spring or fall in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; sweet goldenrod self-sows and naturalizes readily in well-drained areas and is not aggressive in ordinary garden conditions.
directions: Sow seed on the surface of dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in early spring; sweet goldenrod is unique among goldenrods for its exceptionally strong anise-licorice fragrance in the leaves and stems — when the foliage is crushed or brushed, the pure, clean anise scent is released. This fragrance comes from trans-anethole, the same compound that flavors anise seed, licorice, and tarragon. Historically, sweet goldenrod was used as an anise tea substitute known as 'Blue Mountain Tea,' and the leaves are still used to make an herbal tea with a pleasant anise flavor. Like all goldenrods, the flowers are an exceptional late-season nectar source for monarchs, native bees, and butterflies. It tolerates partial shade and dry, poor soils — performing in conditions where many goldenrods fail. The only goldenrod with significant culinary and herbal value.

plant_note: Also called Mexican mint marigold.
directions: Sow seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost, barely covering it and keeping flats warm. This anise-scented marigold serves as a tarragon substitute and yields golden fall flowers for tea. Transplant to full sun in well-drained soil once the weather settles and nights warm. It tolerates heat and drought better than French tarragon, thriving where that herb fails. Pinch stems for bushier growth and harvest leaves through the season, drying flowers for winter tea.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; sweet marjoram is frost-tender and should only be transplanted outdoors after all danger of frost has passed — seeds are tiny and germinate erratically indoors at 65–70°F.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost date in well-drained, slightly alkaline seed mix; seeds are tiny and slow to germinate — do not cover deeply. Transplant outdoors after all frost risk has passed in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, spacing 9–12 inches apart; sweet marjoram is frost-tender and is grown as an annual in all but the mildest climates. Origanum majorana is the sweeter, more delicate culinary counterpart to wild oregano, with a complex, warm, floral-herbal flavor that is the defining ingredient in many European sausage and stuffing recipes, and is used extensively in French and German cooking where oregano would be too pungent; the flavor diminishes sharply after cooking, so add at the end. Harvest branch tips frequently before flowering to keep plants producing fresh foliage through summer; in zones 9–11 it persists as a perennial shrublet.

plant_note: Grown as annual outside zone 9.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and press it onto the surface without burying, since light triggers germination. This improved culinary strain offers sweeter, milder flavor than wild oregano relatives. Transplant to a sunny, well-drained bed once frost danger passes, spacing plants closely. Pinch tips regularly to promote branching and harvest just as flower buds form for peak aroma. Bring a potted plant indoors over winter in colder climates.

plant_note: Warmth-loving; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Thai basil is a cornerstone of Southeast Asian cooking, prized as the aromatic garnish served alongside Vietnamese pho and stirred into curries and stir-fries. Its anise-scented leaves hold their flavor and texture better through cooking than sweet basils, and its purple stems and flower spikes add ornamental appeal. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant only after the soil warms. Grow in full sun with even moisture, pinching flower spikes to prolong tender leaf production.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface (seeds require light to germinate) after last frost in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sweet wormwood grows extremely fast and will reach 6–8 feet in a single season — allow adequate space.
directions: Artemisia annua is a strongly camphor-scented annual from China that has become globally important as the source of artemisinin, the active compound in the most effective modern antimalarial drugs; the plant is now grown at large scale throughout Africa and Asia for pharmaceutical production. In gardens it is grown as an intensely fragrant ornamental annual with feathery, bright-green foliage and masses of tiny yellow flower heads in late summer; the dried branches retain their sweet, camphorous scent for months and are used in dried arrangements, herbal sachets, and potpourri. It self-seeds prolifically in mild climates.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or plugs in spring into consistently moist to wet soil, since seed germination is slow and unreliable and most growers establish new plantings vegetatively.
directions: Plant divisions into damp, low-lying soil near a pond edge, ditch, or consistently irrigated bed, since this native grass naturally grows in moist meadows and spreads by shallow rhizomes to form a loose colony. It tolerates full sun in reliably wet ground but appreciates part shade where soil dries out more. The blades carry a sweet vanilla-like fragrance, especially when cut and dried, and have long been braided and burned in Indigenous North American ceremonies, woven into baskets, and steeped as a fragrant herbal tea or used to flavor bison-grass-style spirits. Divide and replant crowded clumps every few years to keep the planting vigorous.

plant_note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; Swiss Mint has very high menthol content and an intensely cooling flavor used in confectionery and lozenge production.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Swiss Mint carries an unusually high menthol content and an intensely cooling flavor, historically favored for confectionery and lozenge production where a strong, sharp mint punch is wanted rather than the softer flavor of culinary spearmint types. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; in zones below 8 grow as an annual or overwinter rooted cuttings indoors.
directions: Surface-sow seeds on moist, gritty seed-starting mix and keep at 68–72°F; tiny seeds need light so do not cover. Syrian oregano is the primary botanical ingredient in the Middle Eastern spice blend called za'atar; its flavor is strongly oregano-thyme with a hint of marjoram. Grow in very well-drained, poor to moderate soil in full sun — it is native to rocky limestone slopes and rewards lean conditions with the most aromatic foliage. Harvest young stems and leaves throughout the growing season, drying them for use in the za'atar spice blend or using fresh in flatbreads, salads, and dips.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, fast-draining, slightly acidic to neutral, organic-rich growing medium in part shade; Tahitian vanilla (V. tahitensis) is a distinct species from Mexican vanilla (V. planifolia, already well-known) — producing plumper, thicker, more aromatic beans with a distinctly different, more floral, anise-like, cherry-heliotropin flavor profile preferred by many gourmet pastry chefs; requires hand-pollination and a tree, trellis, or post to climb.
directions: Root stem cuttings containing 3–4 nodes in moist, organic, fast-draining medium in part shade; hand-pollinate the flowers as they open; harvest beans after 9 months on vine when tips turn yellow. Vanilla tahitensis (Tahitian vanilla) is a separate species from the dominant commercial vanilla (Vanilla planifolia) — distinguished botanically and aromatically by several key differences: the beans are shorter, plumper, and contain more moisture; the primary aromatic compound is heliotropin (piperonal) — a floral, anise-cherry compound — rather than the vanillin-dominated aroma of V. planifolia; and the overall scent profile of Tahitian vanilla beans is more complex, fruity, and intensely floral, with distinctive cherry, anise, and licorice notes absent from Mexican or Madagascar vanilla. These aromatic differences have made Tahitian vanilla the preferred choice of French pastry chefs and many gourmet bakers for delicate preparations where the distinctive floral complexity can shine — French vanilla ice cream, pastry creams, and fine chocolates. Tahitian vanilla is grown primarily in Tahiti and French Polynesia, with smaller production in Papua New Guinea. Like V. planifolia, V. tahitensis requires hand-pollination in cultivation outside its native range, as the natural pollinators (specific bees and hummingbirds) are absent. The vine climbs strongly on trees or supports in humid tropical conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, average to humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; tall hairy agrimony grows naturally at woodland edges, along fence rows, roadsides, and in open, brushy habitats throughout eastern North America. Division in spring is the most reliable propagation method.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; tall hairy agrimony is the most common of the native North American agrimonies — a tall, erect perennial with pinnately compound leaves and slender, tapering spikes of small yellow flowers throughout summer.
