The entire plant is covered in soft, spreading hairs (glandular on the stems), giving it a pleasantly tactile, soft-textured appearance. The distinctive burr-like fruits with hooked hooks cling readily to clothing and animal fur — a classic hitchhiker in the summer garden. Like European agrimony (A. eupatoria), the native species has a long history in traditional American herbal medicine as an astringent herb used for throat conditions, wounds, and digestive complaints. The dried herbage makes a pleasant, slightly astringent, aromatic tea. An excellent low-maintenance native for naturalized, semi-wild garden areas and hedgerow plantings.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or plant nursery divisions around the last frost date; tansy self-seeds freely and can also be direct-sown.
directions: Plant divisions in any well-drained soil in full sun; tansy is a vigorous, drought-tolerant perennial that spreads by rhizome and can become invasive — site it where its spread can be managed or grow it in a contained bed. The finely cut, strongly aromatic foliage contains thujone, which is toxic in large doses, so tansy should not be consumed internally and should be handled with care. Harvest leafy stems and flat-topped clusters of button-like yellow flowers throughout summer for use as a traditional insect-repelling strewing herb, moth-deterring sachets, and companion-planting aromatic barriers. Deadhead promptly to reduce the copious self-seeding that can make tansy weedy in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Camellia sinensis is the source of all true teas — green, white, oolong, and black — and grows best in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil similar to its native subtropical mountain forest habitat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; water regularly as tea plants are sensitive to drought but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Camellia sinensis is the plant species from which all true tea is made; the young leaves and leaf buds ('flush') are harvested and processed differently to produce green tea (unoxidized), oolong (partially oxidized), or black tea (fully oxidized) — the same plant, processed differently. Home tea gardens are feasible in zones 7–10 where the plant grows as a reliable evergreen shrub; in the Gulf Coast and Southeast United States (zone 8–10) it performs particularly well in the moist, acidic conditions similar to its natural subtropical mountain habitat in China and Southeast Asia. Begin harvesting the tender top two leaves and a bud once the plant is 3–4 years old and 2–3 feet tall; regular harvesting keeps the plant productive and bushy. Small white flowers in fall are fragrant.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in zone 8–11; Tea Tree (Melaleuca alternifolia) is a small Australian tree or large shrub native to the coastal swamps and creek margins of northeastern New South Wales — the source of tea tree essential oil, one of the most widely used natural antimicrobial and antiseptic agents in the world — bearing narrow, needle-like leaves rich in terpinen-4-ol and producing creamy-white bottlebrush flowers beloved by pollinators.
directions: Plant Melaleuca alternifolia in full sun to light shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to occasionally wet soil; it tolerates periodic waterlogging and moderate drought once established; prune after flowering to maintain shape and encourage dense growth; harvest leaves in late summer to early fall when terpinen-4-ol content is highest. Tea Tree is the world's most commercially important medicinal Melaleuca — grown on a large scale in the coastal plains of northeastern New South Wales, Australia, where its essential oil is steam-distilled from the leaves and young stems. Tea tree oil is one of the most thoroughly researched of all plant essential oils, with well-documented antibacterial (effective against MRSA and other resistant strains), antifungal, and antiviral properties; it is used in skin care products, toothpastes, wound antiseptics, and household cleaning products worldwide. In the garden, it is an attractive small tree or large shrub with papery, peeling whitish bark, fine needle-like leaves, and showy cream-white bottlebrush flower spikes that are excellent for native bees and other pollinators. Tolerates poorly drained and seasonally wet soils better than most ornamentals, making it useful in low-lying areas of Gulf Coast gardens; it performs best in zone 9–10 in the United States. Caution: tea tree oil is toxic if ingested and should not be used internally.

plant_note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into loamy, well-drained soil with a near-neutral pH, in full sun to partial shade; established trees tolerate brief light frost better than true tropical cinnamon relatives.
directions: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into loamy, well-drained soil with a near-neutral pH, in full sun to partial shade; established trees tolerate brief light frost better than true tropical cinnamon relatives. The glossy, distinctly three-veined leaves carry a warm cassia-cinnamon-clove aroma entirely different from true bay laurel and are picked and sun-dried once the tree is a few years established. Tejpat is essential to North Indian garam masala, biryani, and dal tadka, and should not be substituted with Mediterranean bay leaf, which lacks its cinnamon character.

plant_note: Direct sow; the taproot resents transplanting.
directions: Tetra is a bushy, late-flowering dill bred for heavy leaf production, so it stays leafy longer before running to seed. Its heat tolerance makes it slow to bolt, letting you pick fresh, aromatic foliage through the warmer months. Direct sow in full sun where plants will grow, since the taproot dislikes being disturbed, and sow in succession for a steady supply. Harvest leaves before flowering for peak flavor, and leave a few plants to bloom for pollinators and seed.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil and night temperatures are reliably warm.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix and transplant after the last frost when soil has warmed; Thai basil withstands heat slightly better than sweet basil. The glossy, dark-green leaves with purple stems carry a spicy anise-clove flavor that holds up better during cooking than sweet basil, making it ideal for stir-fries, curries, and pho. Pinch out purple flower spikes as they emerge to maintain vigorous leaf production, though the flowers are edible and attractive to pollinators. Harvest stems above a leaf node; plants branch densely and remain productive throughout the warm season.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors; tiny seed needs light and warmth.
directions: Thyme is a hardy, low perennial with tiny fragrant leaves that season soups, roasts, and sauces and also make an aromatic groundcover. Surface sow the very fine seed indoors and leave it uncovered under light, keeping it just barely moist until it sprouts. Transplant into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it develops the best flavor and resists rot. Trim plants after flowering to keep them tidy, and harvest sprigs anytime through the growing season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this thorny, deciduous, high-elevation Himalayan relative of Sichuan pepper is markedly more cold-hardy than its lowland cousins.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this thorny, deciduous, high-elevation Himalayan relative of Sichuan pepper is markedly more cold-hardy than its lowland cousins, tolerating winters at elevation across Nepal and northern India. The dried, husked berries deliver an intense citrus-grapefruit aroma alongside the characteristic tongue-tingling numbness of the genus, and are ground fresh for Nepali achar, momo dipping sauces, and spice blends. Harvest ripe berry clusters in autumn and dry them whole before grinding just before use to preserve the volatile citrus notes.

plant_note: Press seed onto the surface of moist starting mix without covering — tobacco seed needs light to germinate — 6-8 weeks before last frost, and transplant seedlings out after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; tobacco is a fast-growing annual grown for its large, broad leaves, which are harvested, cured, and fermented into the leaf used in cigars, cigarettes, and pipe tobacco. As flower buds form, most growers 'top' the plant by removing the flowering tip, which redirects energy into leaf size and thickness, and then remove the side shoots ('suckers') that sprout below the cut, though some plants can be left to flower for their tall spikes of pink, trumpet-shaped blooms if seed saving or ornamental effect is the goal. Harvest leaves progressively from the bottom of the stalk upward as they mature and turn pale yellow-green, then cure them by hanging in a warm, well-ventilated, shaded space for several weeks before further fermentation. All parts of the plant contain nicotine and are toxic if ingested by pets, livestock, or children, and the sticky leaf hairs can cause skin irritation (green tobacco sickness) in sensitive individuals during handling, so wear long sleeves when working with mature plants.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Tongkat Ali is a slow-growing, small to medium understory tree native to the primary and secondary rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines, whose long taproots are one of the most commercially important medicinal herbs of Southeast Asia — the long, bitter, orange-red roots are used as a traditional adaptogen and tonic for energy, stress resistance, and male health.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic, forest-type soil in partial shade to deep shade; Eurycoma longifolia requires the warmth, humidity, and consistent moisture of a tropical rainforest environment — avoid cold, drought, or standing water, and provide forest-floor-type organic mulch to mimic its natural habitat. Eurycoma longifolia (Tongkat Ali, Longjack, or Malaysian Ginseng) is a slender, dioecious, understory tree native to the lowland and hill dipterocarp rainforests of Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo, Vietnam, and the Philippines, recognized as the most commercially important and widely exported medicinal plant of Southeast Asia by trade value. The long, slender, deeply penetrating taproots — sometimes over 6 feet long and difficult to harvest — are the medicinal part, dried, powdered, and used in traditional Malay, Indonesian, and Vietnamese medicine as a bitter tonic for fatigue, stress, fever, and debility. Modern phytochemical research has identified quassinoids (eurycomanone) and other bioactive compounds with adaptogenic, testosterone-supporting, anti-fatigue, and antimalarial properties, driving a large international dietary supplement industry. Tongkat Ali is now one of the most over-harvested wild medicinal plants in Southeast Asia — Malaysia has established cultivation standards and sustainable harvesting programs to prevent wild population collapse. Cultivation from seed is slow; plant in deep, organically rich, moist, shaded conditions similar to rainforest understory.

plant_note: Frost-tender; needs warm season.
directions: Surface-sow seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost and keep warm and bright until sprouts appear. The gold-and-red buds contain spilanthol, which produces a numbing, tingling sensation when chewed. Transplant into rich, moist soil in full sun after frost, spacing plants for their sprawling habit. Deadhead spent buds to keep new ones coming and pinch stems to encourage bushiness. Harvest flower buds fresh for medicinal use or to add a buzzing zing to salads.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in acidic, peaty or lean, well-drained soil in partial shade; tormentil grows naturally on heathlands, acidic meadows, and open woodland edges throughout Europe and grows slowly from seed. Division of established clumps in spring or fall is more reliable for propagation.
directions: Plant in lean, acidic, well-drained to dry soil in partial shade to full sun; tormentil is a creeping, low-growing European perennial of heathlands and acidic meadows, recognized by its distinctive four-petaled yellow flowers (most Potentilla have five petals) and deeply divided leaves with 3–5 leaflets. The roots are exceptionally rich in tannins and astringent compounds — among the highest tannin content of any European herb — and have been used for centuries in traditional medicine as an anti-diarrheal remedy, wound herb, and tea substitute. The root was also historically used in leather tanning and as a red dye. In the garden, tormentil makes a charming low groundcover for dry, acidic, heather-garden conditions where few ornamental plants thrive. The yellow flowers bloom profusely from early summer through fall.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–May or September–October. Trailing Rosemary is less cold-hardy than upright varieties — tolerating temperatures to about 10°F compared to 0°F or below for the hardiest upright types — but in zone 9 this is rarely relevant. The trailing, spreading habit creates an excellent ground cover for slopes, walls, and sunny dry areas. Prune lightly after bloom to maintain shape and prevent woodiness. In zone 9 rosemary is an evergreen perennial shrub that may live for decades in well-drained locations.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil — rosemary rots in heavy, wet soil and thrives in conditions that would kill most other herbs; Prostratus is the trailing, prostrate form of rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) that cascades naturally over walls, slopes, and raised planters rather than growing upright — a different growth habit from the shrubby upright rosemary but with identical culinary flavor and fragrance. The woody, spreading stems reach 4–6 feet across while remaining only 1–2 feet high, creating an extensive ground cover with the characteristic needle-like, intensely aromatic rosemary leaves and lavender-blue flowers that appear in late winter and spring. Trailing Rosemary is particularly useful in zone 9 landscapes for covering slopes and dry, sunny, hard-to-maintain areas where conventional ground covers fail — the combination of extreme drought tolerance, deer resistance, salt tolerance, and attractive year-round appearance makes it one of the most practical landscape plants for these challenging conditions. The culinary quality is identical to upright rosemary: harvest sprigs of the strong, resinous, pine-and-camphor-scented leaves for roasting meats, flavoring breads, making herb oils, and the full range of Mediterranean herb applications.

plant_note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; do not cover deeply as germination is fastest near the surface.
directions: Tribulus is a low, trailing warm-season plant native to dry, sandy, disturbed ground across Africa, southern Europe, and Asia, grown commercially for its spiny, star-shaped fruit capsules (gokshura in Ayurveda, bai ji li in Chinese medicine) rather than its foliage. Direct sow after the soil has warmed into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; small yellow flowers appear within weeks and are quickly followed by the hard, thorny seed capsules that give the plant its common name puncture vine. Harvest capsules as they dry and turn tan, before they fully harden and disperse, since mature spines are sharp enough to puncture bicycle tires and bare feet — contain plantings to a dedicated bed, as the species self-sows aggressively and is classified as a noxious weed in parts of the western United States. Grow as a warm-season annual in most gardens; it persists as a short-lived perennial only in essentially frost-free zones.

plant_note: Root tip cuttings in moist potting mix in spring or take semi-ripe cuttings in summer; tricolor sage does not come true from seed and must be propagated by cuttings. Plant in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil in full sun after last frost.
directions: Root tip cuttings in moist potting mix in spring or take semi-ripe cuttings in summer and plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun after last frost; tricolor sage is an ornamental-culinary variety of common sage whose leaves are splashed with irregular cream, pink, and green variegation that makes it one of the most striking foliage herbs for the ornamental kitchen garden. The flavor and fragrance are the same as common sage — used for the same culinary purposes in poultry, stuffings, bean dishes, and herb butters — but the striking leaf coloration adds decorative value that green sage cannot match. Less cold-hardy than the plain-leaf species and may die back in zone 6 winters; take cuttings each fall as insurance. Prune lightly in spring to remove winter-damaged stems and encourage bushy growth.

common_name: Triple Curled Parsley (Dense Dark-Green Garnish Parsley)
plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; parsley seed germinates very slowly (14–28 days) and benefits from soaking in warm water overnight before planting. In zone 9, direct sow September–February for fall through spring production; parsley is a biennial that survives zone 9 winters and produces best in cool weather. Germination is notoriously slow — keep soil consistently moist for up to 4 weeks waiting for seedlings.
directions: Soak seeds overnight before sowing 0.25 inch deep; thin to 8–12 inches. Triple Curled parsley (also called Extra Curled or Triple Moss Curled) is the standard garnish parsley of American restaurant and commercial use — a Petroselinum crispum variety selected for the densest, most tightly packed curling of the leaves, creating a compact, almost moss-like texture in the leaf heads that makes neat, visually attractive garnishes. The triple curling (each leaf curled multiple times rather than the single curl of standard curly parsley) creates a denser, darker green head with more surface area and a more formal, decorative appearance than less-curled types. The flavor of curly parsley types is milder and slightly less complex than flat-leaf Italian parsley — less aromatic oils, less intense flavor — which is why many serious cooks prefer flat-leaf for cooking while curly types dominate in garnish applications where appearance is primary. Triple Curled produces compact, upright plants with excellent visual appeal in both ornamental and kitchen herb gardens. As a biennial, parsley lives through its first winter (when harvested from), sets seed in the second year, and dies — a growth cycle that supports fall planting in zone 9 for winter and spring harvest.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after last frost in fertile, well-drained, sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; true cinnamon is frost-tender and suitable for zones 10–12 outdoors. In zone 9, grow in a large container and bring indoors in winter.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; true cinnamon (Ceylon cinnamon) from Sri Lanka is considered the 'real' cinnamon of culinary tradition — lighter, sweeter, and more delicate than the cassia cinnamon (Cinnamomum cassia) sold in most North American supermarkets. True cinnamon has very low coumarin content compared to cassia, making it safer for regular consumption. The cinnamon spice is harvested from the inner bark of shoots cut from coppiced trees — the thin bark curls into the familiar quills as it dries. In the home garden, the tree provides an ornamental, fragrant, tropical presence; the young leaves can be used as a bay leaf substitute. In zones 9 and below, grow in a large container and harvest leaves and small stems for culinary use. Coppice regularly to keep the plant at a manageable size.

plant_note: Surface sow tiny seed, which needs light to germinate.
directions: True Greek oregano is the genuine culinary type prized by Italian and Greek cooks for its intense, pungent aroma and flavor. It elevates tomato sauces, marinated vegetables, meats, fish, and poultry, and grows compactly enough for containers. Surface-sow the fine seed indoors since it needs light, then transplant to full sun with lean, well-drained soil. Keep water on the low side to concentrate the essential oils, and shear plants after flowering to maintain dense, flavorful growth.

plant_note: First-year flowering perennial; start indoors for earliest bloom.
directions: True hyssop is an easy-care perennial that flowers in its first year and lights up the late-summer garden with spikes that draw bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects. This ancient herb has long been valued for culinary and medicinal use as well as its ornamental blue blooms. Start seed indoors and transplant to full sun with well-drained soil, where it tolerates dry conditions once established. Trim after flowering to keep plants tidy, and grow it near vegetables to attract pollinators.

plant_note: Direct-sow after last frost in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun; true indigo grows as a perennial in zones 9–11 and as an annual grown for dye in cooler climates. Leaves are harvested when the plant is in flower for maximum dye concentration. The extraction process involves fermenting the leaves in water, oxidizing the liquid, and drying the precipitate to yield indigo pigment.
directions: Sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; true indigo is the historical source of indigo blue dye — one of the oldest and most important natural pigments in human history, used for 6,000 years to dye textiles from ancient Egypt and India to colonial America, where indigo was South Carolina's most valuable colonial export crop. The blue compound (indigotin) is extracted from the leaves through a multi-step fermentation and oxidation process. The plant itself is a tropical shrub or subshrub with small, pinnate leaves and inconspicuous small pink-mauve pea flowers. It is nitrogen-fixing and improves soil fertility. Indigo dye has experienced a revival among natural dye artists and sustainable textile producers. In zone 9–11, the plant grows as a perennial shrub and can be harvested multiple times per season; in cooler climates it is grown as an annual specifically for dye production. Woad (Isatis tinctoria) provides the same dye compound but from a European temperate plant. The pure, rich blue of indigo dye is not achievable from any other widely cultivated plant.

plant_note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; nutmeg is a true tropical rainforest tree that needs consistent warmth, humidity, and shelter from wind and is only realistic outdoors in frost-free zone 11 or as a large container specimen kept above 60°F year-round elsewhere.
directions: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; nutmeg is a true tropical rainforest tree that needs consistent warmth, humidity, and shelter from wind and is only realistic outdoors in frost-free zone 11 or as a large container specimen kept above 60°F year-round elsewhere. Native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia, this evergreen tree bears apricot-like fruit that splits open to reveal a hard seed wrapped in a bright red, lacy covering; the seed itself is dried and ground into nutmeg, while the red aril is separately dried and ground into mace, making a single fruit the source of two distinct spices. Trees are dioecious, so both a male pollinator and a female fruiting tree (or a grafted tree combining both) are needed for fruit production, and trees typically take seven to nine years to begin bearing and up to twenty years to reach full production. Grow in the dappled shade of taller trees as it would experience in its native rainforest understory, keep humidity high, and protect from any cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk passes and nights stay above 50°F. In zone 9 direct sow is also possible from March through July. Tulsi is a short-day plant and will bolt faster in longer days; successive sowings every 4–6 weeks extend leaf harvest.
directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; tulsi is more heat and humidity tolerant than sweet basil but equally frost-sensitive. Pinch flower buds as they form to prolong leaf harvest and maintain essential oil concentration in the foliage; once plants flower the leaves become more pungent and may turn slightly bitter. The clove-scented leaves are used in Indian cooking (especially in Hindu religious rituals), Ayurvedic medicine, and increasingly in Western herbal teas. In zone 9 tulsi often self-seeds, and seedlings can persist from year to year as tender perennials if protected from the rare hard frost.

plant_note: Surface sow; seed needs light and warmth to germinate.
directions: Known as the Queen of Herbs in India, tulsi or holy basil is treasured for its sacred status and prized for tea and wellness uses. This kapoor or temperate type is fast-growing with a distinctive bubble-gum fragrance and better cold tolerance than most basils. Surface-sow seed indoors in warmth since it needs light to germinate, then transplant to full sun after frost. Pinch flower spikes to prolong leaf harvest, though many growers let it bloom to attract pollinators and gather leaves and flowers for tea.

subcategory: golden-rhizomed anti-inflammatory spice and dye plant
plant_note: Plant fresh turmeric rhizome sections (each with at least one growing point) 2 inches deep and 12 inches apart in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; turmeric grows and produces best with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot zone 9 climates — harsh midday sun in summer heat can stress the foliage. Harvest after leaves die back in fall (8–10 months from planting). The bright orange-yellow flesh of the rhizome stains skin, clothing, and surfaces permanently — handle with care. In zone 9 rhizomes may overwinter in the ground.
directions: Plant fresh rhizome sections with viable growing points 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; turmeric is the ancient golden spice of South Asian cooking and traditional medicine — the underground rhizome that when harvested, dried, and ground yields the vivid, saturated, warm-golden-yellow powder that gives curry its characteristic color, imparts a mild, earthy-peppery-slightly-bitter flavor, and delivers the curcumin compound that has become one of the most researched natural anti-inflammatory substances in modern phytomedicine. Native to tropical South Asia (most likely India or Southeast Asia), it has been cultivated throughout the tropical world for at least 4,000 years as both spice and dye (it provided the yellow color in Asian textiles long before synthetic dyes). The garden plant itself is a handsome, lush, tropical-looking Zingiberaceae (ginger family) member with large, paddle-shaped, bright-green, distinctly ribbed and veined leaves similar to those of cannas or gingers, reaching 3–4 feet in height and providing excellent tropical effect in the part-shade garden throughout the growing season. The rhizomes are internally a vivid, saturated orange-yellow (the curcumin pigment) and stain anything they contact that same bright orange-yellow. Harvest the fresh rhizomes in fall after the aerial stems die back; they can be used fresh (milder, more aromatic), dried and ground (the familiar powder), or replanted for next season. A highly rewarding dual-purpose ornamental and culinary/medicinal herb for zone 8–11 shade gardens.

plant_note: Usually grown from a live plant or cutting; set out after frost.
directions: Tuscan Blue is a robust, upright rosemary that grows into an aromatic evergreen shrub prized for both cooking and Mediterranean-style landscaping. Its stiff, fragrant stems are ideal for skewers and roasting, while blue flowers draw pollinators. Because rosemary is slow and erratic from seed, it is best established from a live plant or cutting set out after frost. Give it full sun and fast-draining soil, water sparingly once established, and shelter or overwinter indoors in cold-winter zones.

common_name: Tuscan Blue Rosemary (Tall Upright Culinary Rosemary with Deep Blue-Violet Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tuscan Blue is one of the most cold-sensitive rosemary cultivars among the upright types — it is rated to zone 7 but may be marginal in zone 7b and the colder portions of zone 8; in zone 9, it is reliably perennial.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean soil in full sun; Tuscan Blue is the classic tall, strongly upright rosemary cultivar — one of the most commonly grown culinary rosemaries in Gulf South herb gardens, selected for its vigorous, columnar-upright habit, robust culinary fragrance and flavor, and particularly vivid deep blue-violet flowers that are more intensely colored than many other rosemary cultivars. The tall, strictly upright habit (4–6 feet) makes Tuscan Blue distinctly different from spreading and prostrate rosemary forms, functioning as a narrow, evergreen vertical accent in herb and kitchen garden designs rather than a low-spreading groundcover. The strongly aromatic, narrow, needle-like leaves are the standard culinary rosemary used in Mediterranean cooking — with the same powerful resinous rosemary scent and flavor as the straight species. In Gulf South zone 9, Tuscan Blue grows as a long-lived evergreen perennial that thrives in the heat and dry conditions that characterize Mediterranean-climate herbs. Well-drained soil is the critical requirement: rosemary in heavy clay or poorly drained soil declines rapidly. The fragrant blue flowers in late winter (February–March in zone 9) provide important early nectar for honeybees and native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Tuscan Blue can be trained as a formal herb garden accent, clipped as a low hedge, or grown as a specimen shrub. Prune after flowering to maintain a compact habit; avoid cutting into old, woody, leafless stems.

common_name: Twickel Purple Lavender (Dutch Heirloom English Lavender)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring or fall in full sun with excellent drainage; Twickel Purple is a true English lavender and, like other Lavandula angustifolia types, is less tolerant of humid summers than lavandin hybrids, so give it maximum air circulation and sharp drainage in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun with sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil; amend heavy or clay soil with coarse sand or gravel, and avoid overhead watering or mulch touching the crown. Twickel Purple is a long-cultivated Dutch heirloom English lavender, named for the historic Twickel estate in the Netherlands, valued for its compact, tidy, rounded habit and deep violet-purple flower spikes with the classic sweet, floral fragrance and flavor of true English lavender, prized for culinary use, sachets, and potpourri. Because true English lavenders are more prone to root and crown rot in hot, humid conditions than lavandin hybrids, plant Twickel Purple in the driest, sunniest, best-draining spot available and consider it a shorter-lived perennial in the Gulf South compared with more heat-tolerant lavandins like Phenomenal or Grosso. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain shape and prevent the plant from becoming woody and open in the center.

common_name: Ulam Raja (King's Salad, Cosmos Herb, Wild Cosmos, Purple Cosmos Herb)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Ulam Raja grows rapidly and begins producing edible young leaves and shoots within 6–8 weeks. It self-seeds prolifically and can naturalize as a beneficial weed in zone 9-11 gardens. Young leaves, stems, and flower buds are eaten raw in salads or as a vegetable throughout Southeast Asia — particularly popular in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand as 'ulam' (raw herb eaten with meals). The leaves have a pleasantly sour, slightly bitter, herbal flavor and are high in antioxidants and nutrients. Pull plants when they become woody and reseed continuously.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Ulam Raja is a fast-growing, easy-care tropical annual that germinates rapidly and begins producing harvestable young leaves and shoot tips within 6–8 weeks of seeding. Cosmos caudatus is a tropical annual herb native to Mexico and Central America in the Asteraceae family that has become widely naturalized and deeply embedded in the food cultures of Southeast Asia — particularly Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and the Philippines — where it is consumed daily as an 'ulam,' the term for raw herbs and vegetables eaten fresh alongside cooked rice meals. The young leaves, tender shoots, and flower buds are eaten raw in salads, combined with other 'ulam' herbs, or used as a garnish and vegetable in cooking — the flavor is pleasantly sour, slightly bitter, and distinctly herbal, reminiscent of a more complex watercress. Research by Malaysian institutions has documented exceptionally high levels of antioxidants, phenolic compounds, and nutrients in the young foliage, and traditional Malay medicine credits the plant with anti-aging properties that are reflected in its honorific common name 'Ulam Raja' — 'the king's herb/salad.' The plant also produces the characteristic fine-petaled pink to magenta flowers of the Cosmos genus throughout the warm months. Self-seeds abundantly and naturalizes in zone 9-11 gardens as a continuously productive edible green.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; seed viability drops quickly so use fresh seed and surface-sow as light aids germination.
directions: Use the freshest seed available, as viability declines within a year; surface-sow and keep cool and moist for best germination. Plants grow very tall in their second year and may need staking in windy locations; keep soil consistently moist and add compost annually. Remove flower heads in the first year to direct energy into root development. Harvest roots in the second autumn after the tops die back, washing and slicing them for drying; the characteristic musky odor intensifies as the root dries.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all danger of frost has passed and soil is warm.
directions: Surface-sow or press seeds 1/8 in into warm seed-starting mix; maintain 70–80°F for best germination. Vana tulsi (forest holy basil) is the most clove-like and pungent of the tulsi varieties, with green leaves and a more open, branching habit than Rama tulsi; it is revered in Ayurvedic practice and used widely in adaptogenic herbal teas. Pinch growing tips early to encourage branching, and remove flower spikes as they emerge to extend vegetative leaf production throughout the season. Harvest by cutting stem tips; dry leaves at low temperature to preserve the volatile eugenol-rich essential oils.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings with at least 3 nodes in moist, well-drained, organic, slightly acidic bark or orchid mix in heavy shade; vanilla requires aerial root attachment to a support structure, consistent warmth above 55°F, and high humidity. Zone 10–12 outdoors; excellent in a warm greenhouse or conservatory in zone 9.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in coarse, well-drained, slightly acidic organic bark mix in heavy shade with a support structure for aerial roots to climb — vanilla is the only edible-fruiting orchid and the world's second most expensive spice (after saffron), native to the tropical forest understory of Mexico and Central America where it climbs into the forest canopy in deep shade. The pale yellow-green flowers open one at a time for only a few hours and in most cultivated gardens must be hand-pollinated (the natural pollinators, stingless bees of the genus Melipona, are restricted to Mexico). Successfully pollinated flowers develop into the familiar vanilla bean pods (technically seed capsules) over 9–10 months. After harvest, the pods undergo a complex curing process (blanching, sweating, drying) to develop the characteristic vanilla flavor from the compound vanillin. An extraordinary container or greenhouse specimen for warm-climate gardeners who want to grow their own vanilla extract.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in warm water or moist propagating mix; cuttings root readily in 2–3 weeks. In zone 9 plant outdoors March–May; the plant is perennial in zone 9b–11 and root-hardy with mulching in zone 9a. Variegated Cuban Oregano grows well in containers, where the cream-and-green foliage and trailing habit are particularly attractive. Overwinter indoors in zone 8 and below.
directions: Grow from cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Variegated Cuban Oregano ('Variegatus') is a cream-and-green variegated selection of Plectranthus amboinicus with the identical strong oregano-thyme aroma and flavor of the plain green type, but with striking ornamental foliage — the irregular cream margins on each thick, succulent leaf give the plant a luminous quality in shaded garden spots that plain Cuban oregano lacks. It is one of the more useful dual-purpose (culinary and ornamental) plants for zone 9 gardens and container plantings. The thick, succulent leaves retain the distinctive pungent aroma that Caribbean, Indian, and Cuban cooks use in sofrito, black beans, marinades, and rice dishes. The partially succulent nature of the leaves makes the plant somewhat drought-tolerant once established, and the trailing habit makes it excellent for hanging baskets and container combinations. Flavor intensity decreases if plants are too heavily shaded — partial sun gives the best balance of ornamental appearance and aromatic leaf quality.

plant_note: Plant root divisions (sets) in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 plant January–March. Variegated Horseradish spreads aggressively from root pieces — site carefully, as even small root fragments left in soil will resprout. The variegated foliage shows the most distinct white and green patterning when grown in partial shade; full sun may cause some bleaching. Harvest roots in fall after the first frost, which improves flavor and pungency. The entire plant is edible, including the young leaves.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — deep, loose soil produces the straightest, most harvestable roots; Variegated Horseradish is an ornamental form of standard horseradish (Armoracia rusticana) with leaves that are boldly splashed and streaked with irregular cream-white markings against green, creating a dramatically two-tone foliage effect throughout the growing season. The ornamental value is high — the large, wavy, cream-splashed leaves are attractive in herb borders and edible landscape designs where standard all-green horseradish might seem too utilitarian. The roots have the same intensely pungent, sinus-clearing horseradish flavor and heat as the standard species — the variegation is purely a foliar characteristic with no effect on root quality. Horseradish root is freshly grated or processed with vinegar to make prepared horseradish sauce; the pungency from allyl isothiocyanate is highest immediately after grating and dissipates over time, which is why freshly grated horseradish is dramatically more powerful than commercial prepared products.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegated Society Garlic is an outstanding evergreen edible-ornamental for zone 8–10 gardens — the cream and green striped foliage and long-blooming pink flowers provide year-round ornamental interest while the edible leaves offer mild garlic-chive flavor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegated Society Garlic is the ornamentally superior form of Tulbaghia violacea — a South African bulbous perennial producing narrow, strap-like leaves with a striking cream to cream-white longitudinal stripe along the center or edge of each leaf. The two-tone cream-and-green variegated foliage has significantly higher ornamental value than the solid-green species and creates a bright, light-catching effect particularly valuable in partial shade. The long bloom season (May through October in zone 9, often year-round in frost-free winters) produces clusters of small, tubular, lilac-pink to rose-violet flowers on slender scapes 12–18 inches tall — the pink flowers above the cream-variegated foliage create an outstanding three-season color combination. The leaves, stems, and flowers are all edible with a mild garlic-chive flavor — milder than either garlic or chives individually — appropriate for salads, garnishes, and any dish where a delicate garlic note is desired. The common name 'society garlic' reflects this mild, socially acceptable garlic flavor (lacking the persistent breath odor of true garlic). Variegated Society Garlic is drought-tolerant, deer-resistant (due to the garlic scent), and virtually pest-free. In zone 9, it is evergreen year-round in mild winters and recovers quickly from any frost damage. An outstanding dual-purpose plant for the Gulf South garden.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost into well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; propagate only by cuttings, as the cream-and-green leaf pattern does not come true from seed.
directions: This sport of sweet marjoram carries an irregular cream-to-white margin on each small oval leaf, giving mounded plants a frosted, two-tone look that reads more ornamental than the golden form while retaining the same delicate sweet-marjoram flavor in the green portion of the leaf. Some afternoon shade helps prevent the pale leaf margins from scorching in hot climates, unlike plain sweet marjoram, which tolerates full sun more readily. It is grown as a tender perennial in mild climates and as a container or annual herb elsewhere, and can be brought indoors over winter where space allows. Propagate only from stem cuttings, since seedlings do not reliably retain the variegated pattern.

common_name: Variegated Thyme (Silver Posie Thyme, Gold Thyme)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun; Variegated thyme provides the same culinary uses as common English thyme but with striking ornamental appeal — silvery-white-edged leaves ('Silver Posie' type) or golden-yellow-edged leaves ('Gold' type) that brighten herb gardens, rock gardens, and container plantings while still providing fully flavored thyme for the kitchen.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun; clip lightly after flowering to maintain compact mound shape. Thymus vulgaris 'Variegatus' (variegated thyme) encompasses several cultivated varieties of common garden thyme selected for ornamental variegated foliage rather than just culinary use. The two primary types are: silver-variegated ('Silver Posie,' 'Silver Queen') with small, dark-green leaves edged in silver-white, creating a soft, frosted effect; and gold-variegated ('Gold,' 'Aureus') with leaves edged in yellow-gold, brightening the herb garden considerably. Both retain the characteristic thyme fragrance and flavor of common thyme (Thymus vulgaris) and can be used identically in cooking — the variegated leaves look beautiful in cooking and as garnishes. Variegated thyme cultivars tend to be slightly less vigorous than solid-green common thyme but grow readily under the same cultural conditions: excellent drainage, lean soil, hot sun, and minimal water. They are especially effective in herb garden borders, rock gardens, and as edging plants where the contrast between the dark green leaf centers and the cream, silver, or gold margins can be appreciated at close range. Also excellent in containers or topiaries. In hot, humid zone 9 climates, variegated thyme benefits from excellent air circulation to prevent fungal problems.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; Veldt grape is an African and Asian tropical succulent vine with square, segmented, succulent green stems and small deciduous leaves — it is one of the most important plants in Ayurvedic medicine for bone and joint conditions, used for centuries to treat fractures, osteoporosis, and joint pain.
directions: Plant stem section cuttings in well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to part shade; water sparingly — Cissus quadrangularis is drought-tolerant and susceptible to root rot in wet soils. Cissus quadrangularis (veldt grape or harjora) is a tropical African and Asian succulent vine that looks unlike any typical grape-family plant (Vitaceae) — it produces thick, fleshy, distinctly four-winged-square (quadrangular = four-cornered) green stems segmented at intervals like bamboo nodes, with small, deciduous, kidney-shaped leaves and tiny clusters of red berries at the nodes. The plant is primarily known not as a food or ornamental but as one of the most important plants in Ayurvedic medicine — it is called 'harjora' in Sanskrit (literally 'bone-joiner') and is used for more than 2,000 years to accelerate fracture healing, treat osteoporosis, joint pain, and as a bone-strengthening tonic. Scientific studies have confirmed that extracts of C. quadrangularis stimulate osteoblast (bone cell) activity and accelerate bone mineralization. It is widely sold as a supplement in India and, increasingly, in Western natural health markets. In the garden in zone 9–12, Veldt grape is an ornamental curiosity — the square, succulent, bright-green stems and climbing or trailing habit make it an unusual specimen for a succulent or tropical garden.

plant_note: Direct sow shallowly, barely covering the seed, in late summer to early fall for a fall-through-spring harvest in zone 9, or in very early spring for a quick cool-season crop before heat causes bolting.
directions: Vertissimo is a dense, clump-forming chervil selected for vigor and slow bolting, producing more leaf over a longer harvest window than older curled types before running up to flower. Its dark green, tightly curled foliage regrows quickly after cutting, making it well suited to repeated harvests from the same planting rather than a single cut-and-done crop. Like all chervil it carries a mild anise-parsley flavor best used fresh, since drying or prolonged cooking destroys the delicate flavor. Give it partial shade and consistently moist soil in zone 9, where the cool months from fall through spring are its only realistic growing window.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted slips in spring after last frost; in zone 9 plant March–May. Vetiver establishes slowly in the first year but develops a deep, extensive root system (reaching 10–15 feet deep) that provides exceptional erosion control on slopes by year 2–3. Plant in rows across slopes for contour erosion barriers.
directions: Plant divisions 6–12 inches apart in well-drained or heavy clay soil in full sun; Vetiver is one of the most useful multipurpose plants for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens. Its roots grow extraordinarily deep (10–15 feet), anchoring slopes and roadsides against severe erosion even in the heavy subtropical rains of the Gulf South — making it the preferred bioengineering plant for slope stabilization in zone 9–12. The roots contain vetiverol and vetivone compounds that are among the most valuable fixatives in high-end perfumery (Chanel No. 5 uses vetiver root) and aromatherapy — dried roots can be used in sachets, potpourri, and natural insect repellents. The tall, upright, blue-green clumps are ornamentally attractive and exceptionally drought-tolerant once established. Vetiver is non-invasive — unlike many ornamental grasses, it does not self-seed prolifically and spreads only by clump expansion. The Vetiver Network International promotes its use for sustainable soil and water conservation throughout tropical and subtropical regions. Harvest roots after 2–3 years for fragrance; divide clumps every 3 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring in moist potting mix; established plants can go into the garden in zone 9b–11 after all frost risk has passed, or grow year-round in containers that can be brought indoors in winter in zones 9a and below.
directions: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix in spring; established plants prefer well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun and are drought-tolerant once established. Vicks Plant is a succulent, aromatic tropical Plectranthus with rounded, thick, velvety, grey-green leaves that release a strong, unmistakable mentholated camphor scent when touched or bruised — the exact aroma of Vicks VapoRub, from which it takes its common name. It is grown primarily as an aromatic novelty and sensory herb for children's gardens, therapy gardens, and container collections, but has traditional use as a steam inhalant for colds and congestion in South African folk medicine. The stems are succulent and snap easily in frost; treat as a houseplant or tender annual north of zone 10, or grow in containers that overwinter indoors. Propagates extremely easily from stem cuttings placed in water or moist soil.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors; light aids germination.
directions: Victoria Blue, or mealycup sage, is a drought-tolerant salvia grown for its deep blue-purple flower spikes dusted with a powdery texture. Surface sow the seed indoors under light about eight weeks before the last frost, since it needs light and warmth to germinate. Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, spacing plants about a foot apart. Deadhead spent spikes to prolong the long bloom season, which supports bees and makes excellent cut and dried flowers.

plant_note: Scarify the hard seed coat and soak before sowing to improve germination, then transplant near a trellis or host shrub once temperatures are reliably warm and frost-free.
directions: Vidanga is a sprawling, woody, scandent shrub native to the forest margins of India's Western Ghats, valued in Ayurvedic tradition for its small peppercorn-like berries. Its hard seed coat is dormant and benefits from mechanical scarification before sowing to achieve reliable germination. In cultivation it needs a host tree, fence, or trellis to scramble over as it matures, along with dappled light and consistently moist, well-drained soil typical of a humid subtropical or tropical understory. Berries are harvested once fully ripe and dried for use in traditional preparations, though overharvesting from the wild has made cultivated sources increasingly important.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September-November in zone 9) or very early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Vierling's thick stems and slow-bolting habit let it stand longer before flowering than most dill, extending the fresh-leaf harvest window.
directions: Vierling is a European heirloom dill grown for its steel-blue, finely cut foliage and thick, sturdy stems that hold up well in cut-flower arrangements once the chartreuse seed umbels open. It is notably slow to bolt compared with older dill strains, keeping tender leaf production going longer into warm weather before the plant switches over to flowering and seed. In zone 9, fall sowing lets plants establish through the cool months and reach their full 3-to-5-foot height by spring, when the wide seed heads attract beneficial insects and pollinators. Harvest leaves continuously for fresh dill weed, and let a few plants flower and seed to collect dill seed for pickling or to let the planting self-sow.

plant_note: Direct sow seed after the last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vietnamese balm self-sows readily in mild climates and returns year after year in zone 8–9. It grows quickly and reaches harvest size within 60 days of germination.
directions: Direct sow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after the last frost; Vietnamese balm (kinh gioi) is one of the most important and distinctive aromatic herbs in Vietnamese cuisine, with a complex flavor profile that combines lemon, mint, and slightly pungent herbal notes in a fresh, cooling combination that is essential in classic Vietnamese dishes. The leaves are used fresh as a raw herb garnish in pho, spring rolls, banh mi, and grilled meat dishes, added at the last moment so the volatile aromatics are preserved. It looks similar to lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) but has a completely different and more complex fragrance. In Vietnam it is used both as a culinary herb and medicinally for digestive and respiratory complaints. It grows rapidly in warm weather and is highly productive with regular harvesting from the growing tips, which also keeps the plant compact and delays flowering. Self-sows freely in warm climates; treat as an annual in zones 7 and colder.

common_name: Vietnamese Cilantro (Rau Ram Heat-Tolerant Cilantro Substitute)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in partial shade to full sun after last frost; Vietnamese cilantro is a tropical perennial that will survive mild zone 9 winters with some frost protection, making it a semi-permanent herb planting in the Gulf South. In zone 9, established plants often survive to grow back in spring unless temperatures drop below 28°F. Stem cuttings root readily in water or moist potting mix. Vietnamese cilantro is one of the few heat-tolerant herbs with a cilantro-like flavor profile, making it valuable in Gulf South summers when true cilantro bolts.
directions: Root 4-inch stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix; transplant to partial shade after last frost. Vietnamese Cilantro (Persicaria odorata, Rau Răm in Vietnamese) is a Southeast Asian tropical herb that produces an aroma remarkably similar to cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) combined with a slightly peppery, more complex note — making it the primary heat-tolerant substitute for cilantro in Gulf South gardens, where true cilantro bolts and becomes bitter in temperatures above 75°F. Vietnamese cilantro is a creeping, semi-aquatic perennial that grows vigorously in warm, moist conditions — it is widely grown in Vietnam and Southeast Asia where it is used fresh in spring rolls (gỏi cuốn), rice paper wraps, laksa (the spicy Southeast Asian noodle soup that uses rau răm as a key garnish), and various dipping sauce accompaniments. The narrow, pointed leaves with distinctive dark V-shaped markings are the visual identifier. In the Gulf South, Vietnamese cilantro solves the common problem of wanting fresh cilantro-flavored herbs in July through September when true cilantro is impossible to grow — it grows vigorously in the summer heat and provides a suitable (though not identical) flavor substitute.

common_name: Vietnamese Coriander (Rau Ram, Hot Mint, Laksa Leaf)
plant_note: Propagate by stem cuttings in warm water (roots in 5–7 days) and transplant after last frost in zone 9 (February–March); Vietnamese coriander is a tropical herb that performs exceptionally well in Gulf Coast gardens, thriving in heat and humidity where true cilantro bolts — grow in partial shade to moderate the intense summer heat and extend the harvest.
directions: Root stem cuttings in water and transplant to moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; in zone 9, partial shade is strongly preferred to prevent leaf scorch in summer heat. Persicaria odorata (Vietnamese coriander or rau ram) is the tropical herb that resolves the gardener's dilemma of having fresh coriander flavor through the heat of summer — it produces pointed, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves with distinctive chocolate-brown chevron markings that taste intensely of fresh cilantro with a spicy, peppery undertone; the flavor is actually considered more complex and intense than true coriander by many Southeast Asian cooks. Rau ram is indispensable in Vietnamese cuisine — it is the canonical garnish for pho, rice noodle salads, and laksa soups and is used extensively in Cambodian and Malaysian cooking. In zone 9, it thrives year-round (dying back in rare hard freezes but resprouting from roots), making it far more practical than annual cilantro for consistent harvest. Plants root from stem cuttings placed in water within days — the easiest possible propagation; overwintered plants in pots can be brought indoors when frost threatens.

plant_note: Direct sow in garden after last frost; in zone 9 sow February–March for spring and August for fall. Vietnamese perilla self-seeds prolifically once established and may naturalize in warm-climate gardens. Barely cover seed with soil or press onto the surface, as seeds require light for germination. In zone 9 it functions as a warm-season annual that reseeds itself year after year.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Vietnamese perilla (rau tia to) is the large-leafed, flat-surfaced green strain of perilla used extensively in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cooking, distinctly different in appearance and flavor from the ruffled Japanese shiso cultivars. The broad, flat, dark green leaves with a slightly purple reverse are used as a table herb in pho, bún bò Huế, spring rolls, and salad plates — leaves are torn and added raw at the table rather than cooked. The flavor is more robust and less refined than Japanese shiso, with strong anise, mint, and basil notes that pair well with the bold flavors of Vietnamese broths. In zone 9 the plant performs best in the cool seasons of spring and fall; it tends to bolt and become bitter in peak summer. It tolerates partial shade and is ideal for the edge of a vegetable garden or under taller plants where it can capture filtered light.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 1–2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; violet wood sorrel is one of the most charming native spring wildflowers of eastern open woodlands.
directions: Plant small bulbs 1–2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; violet wood sorrel tolerates drier soil and more sun than O. acetosella and is better suited to most eastern US garden conditions, naturalizing in open woodlands, dry meadows, and thin lawns. Oxalis violacea is a native eastern North American spring wildflower producing small clusters of violet to rose-pink, 5-petaled flowers with a yellow throat above clover-like, trifoliate, green to purple-tinged leaves in mid-spring, and often reblooming again in fall; the bulbs multiply slowly to form colonies in well-drained soils. The leaves and flowers are edible with the characteristic sour, lemony oxalis flavor and can be used as a garnish or in salads; consume in moderation due to oxalic acid content. It is a charming, low-growing native for rock gardens, shaded borders, and naturalizing under deciduous trees.

common_name: Virginia Mountain Mint (Native Perennial Aromatic Pollinator Mint)
plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and plant 12–18 inches apart; Virginia Mountain Mint is a rhizomatous native perennial that spreads steadily by underground rhizomes once established, eventually forming a substantial colony. It can also be started from seed (surface sow; needs cold stratification or fall sowing), but division is far faster for garden establishment. In zone 9, plant fall or early spring in a moist to well-drained site in full sun or light shade. Blooms July–September. One of the top-rated native plants for pollinator attraction — documented as highly attractive to 200+ native bee species in eastern North American studies.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil; thin rhizome spread by division every 2–3 years if needed. Harvest fresh stems for herbal use any time before flowering. Virginia Mountain Mint (Pycnanthemum virginianum) is a native perennial herb of the mint family (Lamiaceae) native to eastern and central North America from the Atlantic coast west to the Great Plains — one of approximately 20 native Pycnanthemum species in North America, all of which share the common characteristic of intense, spearmint-like aroma from leaves and stems. Pycnanthemum species are among the most scientifically documented pollinator plants in eastern North American native plant research: the dense flat-topped clusters of small, two-lipped white flowers with purple markings attract an extraordinary diversity of native bees, with studies recording 200+ native bee species visiting Pycnanthemum in bloom. This extraordinary pollinator attraction makes Virginia Mountain Mint one of the highest-value native plants for residential pollinator gardens and meadow plantings. The aromatic leaves have culinary and traditional medicinal uses — dried leaves make a spearmint-character tea, fresh leaves can be used as a mint herb substitute, and the strong fragrance deters deer browsing. Virginia Mountain Mint is a robust, reliable native for moist meadow and garden borders where the spreading habit can be accommodated.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Virginia mountain mint is the most heat-tolerant mountain mint species, thriving in zone 8–9 where its northern relatives decline, and is an exceptional pollinator plant for the Gulf South.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Virginia mountain mint is the most heat-tolerant and southeastern species of the mountain mints, thriving through the summer of zone 8–9 where its more northerly relatives like P. virginianum begin to decline. Pycnanthemum pycnanthemoides produces erect, branching stems with lance-shaped, strongly mint-scented leaves and the flat-topped clusters of tiny, white, purple-dotted flowers that are the genus hallmark, blooming July through September and attracting an astonishing diversity of native bees, wasps, beetles, butterflies, and skippers. Mountain mints are among the most comprehensively documented native pollinator plants in eastern North America, with studies recording over 100 insect species on a single planting. The plant spreads by rhizomes into a colony but is not aggressive; divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and share with other gardeners. Excellent in naturalistic meadow plantings, rain gardens, and native border plantings from Virginia through the Gulf Coast.

common_name: Virginia Wild Ginger (Little Brown Jug Ginger)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; Virginia wild ginger is an evergreen woodland groundcover of Appalachian and Piedmont deciduous forests that slowly spreads by rhizomes to form low-growing patches.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; Virginia wild ginger is a native evergreen groundcover of Appalachian and Piedmont forests, closely related to the little-brown-jug (Hexastylis arifolia) and sometimes confused with it. The heart-shaped to arrowhead-shaped, leathery, dark evergreen leaves are ornamental year-round, providing low, dense coverage under deciduous trees. The odd, reddish-brown, jug-shaped flowers are hidden under the leaves at ground level, pollinated by ground beetles and ants. Like all Hexastylis species, it spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeds modestly to naturalize in appropriate shade conditions. Distinguished from H. arifolia by its broader distribution extending into Virginia and Maryland and subtle leaf differences. More cold-hardy than H. arifolia. An excellent, low-maintenance evergreen groundcover for Appalachian native woodland gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or propagate from cuttings; transplant after frost danger has passed.
directions: Surface-sow seeds or take 3 in softwood cuttings in late spring; cuttings are generally more reliable as germination can be slow. Wall germander is an ancient medicinal herb used historically as a bitter digestive tonic; it has glossy, dark-green, oak-like leaves and rosy-pink summer flowers that attract bees. Plant in lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; it is extremely drought-tolerant once established and makes an excellent low edging or clipped knot-garden hedge. Trim after flowering to maintain a tidy, compact form; harvest small quantities of fresh foliage for occasional medicinal use.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or seedlings in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade; wasabi requires cool, constantly moving, mineral-rich water (streams or regular irrigation with mineral-rich water) and temperatures between 46–68°F — hot summers above 80°F will kill or severely stress it. In hotter climates deep shade, consistent watering, and a cool microclimate are essential. The edible part is the thick rhizome, which takes 18–24 months to reach usable size.
directions: Plant in constantly moist, cool, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade; wasabi is among the most challenging and most coveted of culinary herbs — the genuine pungent root condiment used in Japanese cuisine is irreplaceable by the horseradish-and-green-dye substitute sold widely as 'wasabi paste.' It grows naturally along cool, shaded mountain stream banks in Japan, where it is cultivated in channels of continuously flowing, mineral-rich spring water under dense forest canopy. The combination of strict cool-temperature requirements (above 68°F it declines, above 80°F it may die), full shade, and consistently high, reliable moisture makes it one of the most exacting herbs to grow in most American gardens. It produces handsome, heart-shaped, glossy leaves on long petioles that are attractive in a shaded, moist position, and after 18–24 months the thick, knobby, pale-green rhizome is ready to harvest and freshly grate — releasing the volatile, sinus-clearing, horseradish-like compounds far more nuanced and complex than anything in a tube. In zones 8–10 it can succeed in deeply shaded, constantly moist, cool microclimates such as the north-facing side of a house or under dense tree canopy near water.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist to aquatic conditions in partial shade to full sun in spring; water celery grows most vigorously in shallow water (1–3 inches deep) at pond margins, in rain gardens, and in wet soil beside streams — it requires consistently wet soil and will not thrive in normal garden conditions.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently wet soil, shallow water, or at pond margins in partial shade to full sun; water celery (water parsley, minari, Japanese parsley) is an East Asian aquatic edible herb widely consumed in Korean, Japanese, and Chinese cuisines — fresh young stems and leaves have a crisp texture and fresh, parsley-celery flavor that makes them excellent in Korean naengmyeon (cold noodles), doenjang-jjigae (soybean paste soup), japchae, salads, and as a garnish. It grows naturally in shallow streams, rice paddies, and wet meadows, making it an excellent functional plant for rain gardens, constructed wetlands, and ornamental pond margins where few edible plants thrive. The lacy, finely divided, bright-green foliage creates an ornamental effect at the water's edge, and the plant spreads steadily by stolons in ideal wet conditions to create dense, productive colonies. A variegated cultivar ('Flamingo') with pink, white, and green foliage is grown as an ornamental. Harvest the young stem tips continuously for kitchen use. Avoid consuming the related O. crocata (hemlock water dropwort), which is highly toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in saturated to moist, acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; water hyssop thrives in shallow water (1–4 inches), at pond margins, in rain garden depressions, and in consistently moist to wet garden beds — it requires consistently moist to wet conditions.
directions: Plant in saturated to moist, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; water hyssop is an aquatic or semi-aquatic plant that thrives in shallow water, at pond margins, and in consistently wet garden beds — it will not thrive in dry or even moderately dry conditions. Bacopa monnieri (water hyssop or brahmi) is a creeping, aquatic to semi-aquatic herb native to wetlands across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, including the southeastern United States; in Ayurvedic medicine, brahmi is one of the most revered medicinal herbs, used for centuries as a cognitive enhancer and adaptogen to support memory, concentration, and anxiety reduction — modern pharmacological research has partially supported these traditional uses, identifying bacosides as the active compounds. The fleshy, succulent, oblong leaves and small, white to pale-blue 4-petaled flowers identify the plant in the wild; in cultivation it is grown in water gardens, at pond margins, and in constantly moist beds. In zone 9 gardens it grows as a year-round perennial in moist areas and may naturalize. The botanical Bacopa monnieri is completely different from the ornamental Sutera cordata (also marketed as 'Bacopa' — see separate entry).

plant_note: Plant divisions or pot cuttings in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; water mint thrives in the boggy margins of ponds, streams, and rain gardens in partial shade. It can grow in standing water up to 4 inches deep. Contain in buried pots to control the spreading stolons where spread is unwanted.
directions: Plant in moist to wet soil or at the margin of a pond or stream in partial shade; water mint is the wild European native mint from which the widely planted peppermint (Mentha x piperita) was bred as a hybrid with spearmint, and it retains a strong, cool menthol fragrance in its leaves and stems. It is one of the most shade- and moisture-tolerant of all mints, making it uniquely valuable for the shaded bog garden, rain garden, or pond margin where other herbs struggle. The strongly scented leaves are used exactly like other culinary mints — in teas, as a culinary herb, in drinks, and for fragrance. Dense clusters of lilac-mauve flowers in summer and fall attract an outstanding variety of pollinators, particularly hoverflies, bumblebees, and small native bees. Like all mints, it spreads by underground stolons and should be contained with buried barriers or grown in sunken pots where spread is unwanted.

common_name: Water Pepper (Smartweed, Tade, Marsh Pepper Knotweed)
plant_note: Direct sow into consistently moist to boggy soil after frost danger passes; it thrives at pond margins, in rain gardens, or in a container standing in a saucer of water, and self-sows freely once established.
directions: Sow seed shallowly into wet, rich soil or shallow standing water in full sun, thinning seedlings once established; the plant self-sows readily, so many gardeners simply let a small patch persist year to year. Young leaves and sprouts carry a sharp, peppery bite from a compound related to capsaicin and are used fresh in Japanese cuisine, most famously as benitade, the tiny red-leaved sprouts served with sashimi, and historically as a pungent seasoning across Europe before black pepper became widely available. Harvest leaves continually through summer for the strongest heat and pinch flower spikes to keep foliage production going. Because it spreads by seed in wet ground, site it where naturalizing is welcome rather than near sensitive wetlands.

plant_note: Nick or soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to break the hard seed coat, then direct-sow shallowly into well-drained sandy or gravelly soil in full sun once the site is frost-free.
directions: Nick or soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to break the hard seed coat, then direct-sow shallowly into well-drained sandy or gravelly soil in full sun once the site is frost-free; this arid-zone Australian shrub tolerates drought, poor soil, and salinity once established. The ripe, dried seed pods are harvested, roasted, and ground into wattleseed, an Aboriginal bushfood staple with a nutty, roasted-coffee, caramel flavor used to season breads, ice cream, and native spice blends. Prune lightly after seed harvest to maintain a manageable shrub form and encourage a fuller next season's pod set.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; southern wax myrtle is one of the most versatile and useful native shrubs of the Gulf South — salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant once established, adaptable to wet or dry soils, fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing, and productive of waxy berries used for bayberry candles and incense.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; minimal care once established. Morella cerifera (southern wax myrtle or bayberry) is one of the most ecologically important and garden-useful native shrubs of the Gulf Coastal Plain, native from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Texas and Oklahoma. The aromatic, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves (crushed, they release a distinctive bayberry-bay-spice fragrance) are used dried in wreaths, sachets, and as a flavoring herb similar to bay laurel in coastal Southern cooking. The small, silvery-waxy, blue-gray berries produced on female plants are the basis of bayberry candle wax — melted from the berries and cast into candles with the distinctive bayberry fragrance beloved in New England and Colonial American tradition. Wax myrtle is among the most adaptable native plants for Gulf Coast gardens: it tolerates salt spray, wet conditions, drought, poor soils, and coastal conditions equally well, making it outstanding for beach landscapes, rain gardens, wet corners, and dry banks alike. The plant fixes nitrogen through root symbiosis with Frankia bacteria (actinorrhizal nitrogen fixation), improving soil fertility. As a screening shrub, hedge, or small tree, it grows rapidly (2–3 feet per year when young) to 10–15 feet. Native birds eat the waxy berries and nest in the dense foliage.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or layer low branches, then plant out in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or layer low branches, then plant out in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Distinct from the common ornamental hybrid forsythia, this species is grown for its fruit capsules, harvested green or ripe and used in traditional Chinese medicine formulas said to clear heat and support the body during colds and sore throats. Prune right after spring flowering so next year's fruiting wood has time to develop.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in spring (do not cover — needs light to germinate) in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; weld is biennial to short-lived perennial, forming a rosette in the first year and flowering in the second. It self-sows freely in lean, disturbed soils. The entire above-ground plant is harvested for dye at full flower for the deepest, most lasting yellow.
directions: Surface sow seeds in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; weld is a Mediterranean native biennial that was, for two millennia before the development of synthetic dyes, the primary source of the most important yellow dye in European textile history — yielding from the whole plant at flower a brilliant, pure, fast, golden-yellow color from the flavonoid luteolin (the plant's specific epithet) that was far more color-fast than the yellow of many competing dye plants and combined with blue woad or indigo to produce the green used in many historical tapestries and textiles. Archaeological evidence of weld cultivation dates to Neolithic Europe. As a garden plant it is ornamental in a quiet way — producing tall, narrow, spike-like racemes of small, four-petaled, pale-yellow-green flowers in summer. The self-sowing habit maintains naturalized colonies in disturbed, lean, sunny situations. A meaningful plant for natural dyers, herb gardens, and historical plant collections, and an important species for the sustainable textile and craft revival of plant-based natural dyeing.

plant_note: Set out only after nights stay reliably above 50 degrees F in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; West Indian lemongrass is the classic culinary type used in Southeast Asian and Caribbean cooking, forming a large, dense clump of aromatic, citrus-scented leaves.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay warm. West Indian lemongrass is the standard culinary lemongrass of Southeast Asian and Caribbean cooking, forming a large, dense, fountain-like clump of long, narrow, intensely citrus-scented leaves surrounding thickened, tender stalk bases that are harvested, crushed, and used to flavor soups, curries, teas, and marinades. Unlike East Indian lemongrass, which is grown mainly for essential oil production and has a somewhat harsher aroma, West Indian lemongrass has the milder, sweeter citrus fragrance preferred for cooking. In zone 9 the clump usually dies back after a hard freeze but often regrows from the roots in spring if mulched heavily; in colder zones it is best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter or replanted annually.

common_name: West Indian Vanilla (Pompona Vanilla, Vanillón, Big-Leaved Vanilla)
plant_note: Plant stem cuttings (3–5 nodes, leafless, air-dried 1–2 days) in late spring in partial shade on a rough-textured wooden trellis, tree, or vertical support with moist, well-drained orchid bark or organic medium; Vanilla pompona is a hemi-epiphytic vine that climbs by aerial roots and produces the best results when growing up a natural surface. Hand-pollinate the short-lived flowers with a toothpick (pollen must be transferred to the stigma within the flower's single-day lifespan).
