The pods are shorter and thicker than V. planifolia but contain good vanilla flavor compounds. Frost-sensitive, zone 10-12 outdoors.
directions: Plant in partial shade to bright indirect light in moist, well-drained, organic-rich medium — West Indian Vanilla climbs most vigorously on rough-textured supports in conditions that approximate its native tropical forest habitat: bright, filtered light, consistent warmth, and humid air with good drainage at the roots. Vanilla pompona is a hemi-epiphytic climbing orchid vine native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean islands, and northern South America in the Orchidaceae family, closely related to the commercially dominant Vanilla planifolia but producing shorter, thicker, more barrel-shaped vanilla pods with a distinctly different, somewhat sweeter aromatic profile. As with all Vanilla species, the vine climbs by clasping aerial roots to tree bark or other rough surfaces, can reach impressive lengths (30+ feet), and produces axillary clusters of the characteristic large (2-inch), greenish-yellow to pale yellow vanilla orchid flowers — each lasting only a single day, requiring prompt hand pollination in cultivation to set the pods. The pods (the 'vanilla beans' of commerce) take 9–12 months to mature after pollination, then must be cured through a weeks-long process of sweating, drying, and conditioning to develop the characteristic vanilla aroma. Vanilla pompona has been used as an alternative and supplement to V. planifolia in commercial vanilla production, particularly in the Caribbean, and is more resistant to the Fusarium root rot disease that threatens V. planifolia plantations. An interesting food plant for zone 10-12 tropical gardens with appropriate climbing structures.

common_name: Western Wild Ginger (British Columbia Wild Ginger)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; western wild ginger forms slowly expanding mats by horizontal rhizomes under conifers, oaks, and maples in moist Pacific Northwest forests. Spreads more aggressively than eastern wild ginger (A. canadense).
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; western wild ginger is the native groundcover wild ginger of Pacific Northwest moist forests, producing large, glossy, dark evergreen, heart-shaped leaves and the characteristic small, brownish-maroon, three-pointed, urn-shaped flowers hidden at the base of the plant and pollinated by ground beetles and ants. The leaves have a pleasant ginger scent when crushed. Western wild ginger spreads more vigorously than eastern wild ginger by horizontal rhizomes, eventually forming dense, weed-suppressing mats under conifers and deciduous trees. An exceptional shade groundcover for the Pacific Northwest, competing effectively with English ivy and other invasives while providing excellent, low-maintenance native coverage. The rhizomes have been used as a ginger substitute by Pacific Northwest indigenous peoples, though in small quantities only — large amounts of Asarum species may be toxic. Evergreen foliage persists through Pacific Northwest winters.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in moist to average, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; white bee balm is more shade-tolerant than other Monarda species and thrives in the dappled shade of a woodland edge or shrub border.
directions: White bee balm is the most shade-tolerant of all native bee balms — the only species that thrives in partial shade under deciduous trees rather than requiring full sun — and produces whorls of pure white to pale lavender flowers on upright stems from June through August, providing a critical nectar source for native bumble bees, hummingbird moths, and butterflies in shaded garden areas where most pollinator plants fail. Its strong basil-like fragrance (the 'clinopodia' means 'resembling basil') makes it useful as a culinary herb and potpourri ingredient; leaves dried at peak bloom make an aromatic tea with a floral, oregano-like character. Unlike red bee balm (Monarda didyma) and wild bergamot (M. fistulosa), white bee balm is less aggressive and more restrained in its spread, forming tidy clumps rather than rampaging colonies; it is also more resistant to the powdery mildew that plagues its relatives in humid conditions. An excellent choice for native shade gardens under mature hardwoods where its white flowers provide elegant, fragrant bloom from early to midsummer.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination or sow indoors in late winter; white deadnettle grows in moist to moderately dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun, and self-sows to naturalize in appropriate conditions. Plant in shade where it provides spring ground cover.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; white deadnettle is a European mint-family herb with nettlecreeper-shaped leaves (which it resembles but it does not sting — hence 'deadnettle') and conspicuous white hooded flowers throughout spring and early summer. The white flowers, with their distinctive hood and nectar guides, are exclusively pollinated by long-tongued bumblebees that can reach the nectar at the base of the long corolla tube — shorter-tongued bees cannot access it. The plant has a long history of use in European herbal medicine, with the flowers and leaves used as an anti-inflammatory herb, wound herb, and menstrual regulator. Young leaves and flowers are edible in salads. Spreads moderately by rhizomes and self-sows to form a semi-wild presence in the shade garden.

plant_note: Surface sow; benefits from cool conditions to germinate.
directions: White horehound is a hardy, wooly-leaved perennial in the mint family, long used for herbal candies and traditional remedies. Surface sow the seed on well-drained soil and keep it cool and lightly moist, as germination can be slow and uneven. It thrives in full sun and lean, dry ground, tolerating drought once established, and its bitter foliage tends to be deer resistant. Harvest leaves as flowering begins and cut plants back to prevent excessive self-seeding.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; white micromeria (zuta levanit in Hebrew, meaning 'white za'atar') is an Eastern Mediterranean native subshrub with white-hairy oval leaves and a gentle thyme-mint tea flavor — used in Israel and the Levant both as a traditional herbal tea and as a component of za'atar spice blends.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, rocky or gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; trim lightly after flowering to maintain compact form. Micromeria fruticosa (white micromeria, white za'atar, or zuta levanit) is a small aromatic subshrub native to the dry rocky hillsides, terra rossa soils, and limestone outcrops of the Eastern Mediterranean — particularly Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, and the Palestinian territories. The plant has distinctive small, oval, white-hairy (tomentose) leaves with a soft, felted texture, giving the plant an overall white-gray appearance; hence 'white' za'atar or zuta levanit. The fragrance and flavor are unique: a gentle, warm, herbal-thyme character with a subtle mint and tea-like undertone — softer and more delicate than either thyme or savory. In Israel and the Levant, M. fruticosa is one of the most beloved traditional herbal teas, prepared by infusing fresh or dried leaves in hot water; it is believed to be calming, digestive, and to relieve cold symptoms. It is also one of the plants historically used in za'atar spice blends in the Levant, where different communities have distinct formulations using various combinations of Origanum syriacum, Thymbra spicata, Satureja thymbra, and M. fruticosa. A delightful low-growing groundcover for sunny, dry, Mediterranean-climate gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; mature plants tolerate brief light frost but establish best in warm, dry conditions.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in lean, fast-draining mix; refrigerate seeds for 2 weeks before sowing to improve germination rates. Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun — white sage is a California chaparral native that is highly drought-tolerant once established but will rot quickly in wet, heavy soil. Avoid supplemental irrigation once plants are established in their second season; overwatering is the most common cause of death. Harvest mature leaves and small branches by cutting, and dry in bundles in a warm, well-ventilated space for aromatic and ceremonial use.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in spring after soil warms; goes fully dormant in winter and regrows reliably from stored rhizomes in zones 8–12.
directions: Plant in loose, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; white turmeric (zedoary) has white to pale yellow flesh with a complex camphoraceous, ginger-mango-like aroma and a peppery-bitter flavor quite different from yellow turmeric. An ancient spice from India and Southeast Asia, it was an important medieval European import and remains in use in Indonesian, Sri Lankan, and Japanese cuisines as well as Ayurvedic and Traditional Chinese medicine. Fresh rhizomes are sliced thin and eaten in salads, pickled, or used to flavor rice and curries; the dried powder gives a pale cream-yellow color to foods. The showy cone-like flower bracts are also used in tropical landscaping.

plant_note: Direct-sow fresh seed immediately after harvest in fall — angelica seed is short-lived and loses viability rapidly in storage; sow in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil at the edges of woodland, in damp borders, or beside water features in partial shade, and allow to self-sow freely as the parent plant is monocarpic and dies after setting seed.
directions: Angelica sylvestris is a tall, statuesque biennial or short-lived monocarpic perennial native to moist woodland margins, riverbanks, and damp meadows throughout Europe and temperate Asia, closely related to garden angelica (A. archangelica) but more tolerant of shade and with a wilder, more ornamental character; it produces large, pinnate, bright-green leaves, hollow, purplish-tinged stems, and showy, rounded umbels of white to pink-flushed flowers in summer that are exceptionally attractive to a wide range of pollinators including native bees, hoverflies, and butterflies. Sow fresh seed in fall in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained to moisture-retentive, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade of a woodland edge, damp border, or streamside planting; seed viability is very short-lived and must be sown as fresh as possible — refrigerator storage can extend viability for a few weeks. The plant dies after flowering and setting seed (monocarpic) but self-sows prolifically in suitable moist, partially shaded conditions, maintaining a garden colony once established; remove spent flower heads promptly if self-sowing is not desired. The ornamental purple-dark cultivar 'Purpurea' ('Vicar's Mead') has become popular in naturalistic garden design for its striking, deep-purple stems and foliage, particularly effective in damp, partly shaded wild gardens.

plant_note: Direct-sow in fall for cold stratification, or surface-sow in early spring.
directions: Surface-sow seed in fall directly in the garden, or press it lightly into a moist seedbed in early spring, as the fine seed needs light and cool temperatures to germinate well. This minty-aromatic native of Europe and western Asia thrives in lean, well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade, where it forms upright clumps bearing dense whorls of small purplish-pink flowers from June through September that are magnets for bumblebees and butterflies. The leaves can be used fresh or dried as a thyme-like culinary herb in soups, stuffings, and savory dishes. Cut plants back by half after the main flush of bloom to encourage a second flush and keep growth compact.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow as seeds are tiny and need light for good germination.
directions: Surface-sow seeds onto moist starting mix and keep at 65–70°F; wild bergamot germinates in 10–21 days and is more drought-tolerant than the cultivated red bee balm. Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun for the most aromatic foliage and best disease resistance. Harvest leaves and flowers throughout summer for oregano-scented teas with a mild thymol character, used traditionally by many Indigenous nations for cold and fever support. Divide established clumps every 2–3 years as the center tends to die out.

common_name: Wild Betel Leaf (La Lot, Cha Plu)
plant_note: Root 4–6 inch stem cuttings in moist potting mix or set divisions out after all danger of frost, into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in shade to deep partial shade; this low, spreading Southeast Asian groundcover scorches and stalls in direct sun or dry soil.
directions: Set rooted cuttings or rhizome divisions in humus-rich, constantly moist soil in full to partial shade; a thin bark or leaf mulch keeps the shallow, creeping stems from drying out between waterings. Piper sarmentosum spreads as a low groundcover of heart-shaped, glossy, peppery-aromatic leaves used fresh as a wrap for Thai miang kham and grilled in Vietnamese cha la lot, so keep harvesting young leaves to encourage bushy new growth rather than flowering spikes. It dies back hard below about 40°F, so gardeners outside zone 9–11 grow it in containers that overwinter indoors near a bright, humid window. Divide congested clumps every year or two in spring to renew vigor and generate new plants for sharing.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wild chervil self-seeds prolifically and can become invasive in disturbed sites — thin seedlings to prevent overcrowding.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wild chervil self-seeds prolifically and can become invasive in disturbed sites — thin seedlings to prevent overcrowding. NOTE: Anthriscus sylvestris closely resembles Conium maculatum (poison hemlock) and Oenanthe crocata (hemlock water dropwort), both deadly poisonous; always positively identify by the red-flushed hollow stems and distinctive aroma before handling. Anthriscus sylvestris is a widespread European biennial or short-lived perennial that produces large, finely cut, fern-like, bright-green leaves from spring through early summer and frothy, flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers on tall stems that are spectacular bee and hoverfly forage in May and June; the ornamental dark-leafed cultivar 'Ravenswing' has deep, chocolate-burgundy foliage that is one of the most striking dark-leaved plants for partial shade in cool-climate gardens. The young leaves and stems have a mild anise-parsley flavor and are edible as a salad herb before flowering, though positive plant ID is essential.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 1–2 inches deep in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; wild ginger spreads slowly to form a dense, deer-resistant groundcover under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 1–2 inches deep in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in deep shade to partial shade; wild ginger is one of the finest native groundcovers for dense shade, forming a low, tight carpet of large, velvety, heart-shaped leaves that suppresses weeds effectively under mature trees where even grass fails. The small, maroon-brown, jug-shaped flowers bloom at soil level in early spring, hidden beneath the foliage and pollinated by early ground beetles. The rhizomes have a spicy, ginger-like fragrance and have been used as a ginger substitute in traditional cooking, though they are not botanically related to culinary ginger (Zingiber officinale). An outstanding native groundcover for moist, deeply shaded sites under deciduous canopy.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; wild mint spreads vigorously by rhizome and should be contained in a pot or planting bed edged with a barrier, or allowed to naturalize in a wet, shaded area where spreading is welcome.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; wild mint is North America's only native mint species and has the widest natural range of any mint in the world — native from the Atlantic Coast to Asia across the boreal zone. It grows naturally at stream banks, pond margins, moist meadows, and woodland edges, forming spreading mats of intensely aromatic leaves with a clean mint-spearmint fragrance used exactly like cultivated spearmint for teas, cooking, and flavoring. The small lavender-purple flower whorls in summer attract numerous native bees including specialized pollen bees in the genus Cleptes. Unlike garden mints, it is fully native and supports native insects while providing the same culinary utility. It tolerates partial shade and moist soil conditions that are inhospitable to most culinary herbs. Contain with underground barriers or allow to naturalize in appropriate wet areas.

plant_note: Direct sow in autumn; seeds require cool temperatures (below 65°F) and light to germinate reliably, so surface-sow without covering and allow cold winter temperatures to break any dormancy.
directions: Lactuca virosa is a tall, coarse European biennial that has naturalized widely in North America; it produces a milky latex called lactucarium that was historically used as a mild sedative and opium substitute, though its effects are weak and its safety profile is poorly established. Surface-sow the light-dependent seeds in autumn or early spring into open, disturbed soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to 12–18 inches apart; plants form a basal rosette in the first year before bolting to flower in the second. This plant is NOT recommended for eating raw — the sap is intensely bitter, and the plant's medicinal alkaloids should be treated with caution; consult qualified herbalists and current literature before any medicinal use. Grow primarily as a botanical curiosity or living link to historical apothecary gardens, where it was once a staple of the physician's herb patch.

plant_note: Sow direct or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; oregano requires excellent drainage and lean, infertile soil for the strongest flavor — rich soil produces rank growth with weak aroma.
directions: Sow direct after last frost or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; avoid rich, fertile soil which produces lush but relatively flavorless plants — oregano's essential oils are most concentrated when the plant is slightly stressed by poor soil and minimal water. Origanum vulgare is the common wild oregano of Europe and the source of dried Italian-style oregano; the species varies enormously in flavor intensity depending on climate and selection, with Mediterranean-climate plants (especially Greek 'Hirtum') being the most pungent, while cool-climate plants can be nearly flavorless. The species naturalizes easily in dry, sunny banks and rock gardens and produces masses of tiny, pink to white flowers in summer that are excellent nectar sources for bees and butterflies. Subsp. hirtum (Greek oregano) is the pungent, strongly flavored selection recommended for culinary use.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings after all frost danger has passed; this heat-loving shrub establishes fastest when nighttime temperatures remain above 55°F.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun and well-drained soil after the last frost date; this tropical shrub grows vigorously in heat and humidity that would stress common oregano, making it an excellent substitute in warm-climate gardens. Water deeply but infrequently once established, allowing the soil to dry out between sessions, as the plant is highly drought-adapted and prone to root rot in soggy ground. Harvest stem tips regularly throughout the warm season, as frequent cutting promotes dense branching and keeps the intensely oregano-scented leaves at peak potency for culinary use. In zone 8, mulch heavily around the base before the first frost and cut plants back to a few inches in late winter; they will resprout vigorously from the woody base as temperatures climb.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring, burying them 3–4 inches deep; they spread slowly by rhizome to form colonies in favorable woodland conditions.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; this low-growing woodland native has a single compound leaf rising on an upright stem from the underground rhizome, giving it a distinctive appearance among shade plants. The fragrant root has long been used as a flavoring agent and sarsaparilla-like tonic, and the small dark berries are edible though not particularly flavorful. It spreads slowly by horizontal rhizome to form colonies and is excellent for naturalizing a dry shade area under conifers. Division is necessary for propagation as seed requires a double dormancy period of warm-then-cold stratification.

plant_note: Set out cuttings after last frost in lean, well-drained soil; avoid amended beds that encourage lush but less flavorful growth.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun and gritty, low-fertility soil to replicate the rocky Iberian slopes where this thyme naturally carpets the landscape. Harvest small-leaved stems frequently throughout the growing season to encourage branching and to capture the delicate, slightly floral thyme flavor before the plant flowers. After blooming, shear plants back by about half to prevent woodiness and to stimulate a flush of fresh growth for late-season harvesting. This species forms a tidy, low mat suitable for edging herb beds or tucking into gaps in stone walls.

plant_note: Sow seed direct in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, or plant divisions or cuttings in spring or fall; wild thyme is excellent as a lawn substitute, ground cover between stepping stones, and in rock gardens.
directions: Sow seed in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; wild thyme is variable from seed — for specific flower color or mat habit, use vegetatively propagated plants. Thymus serpyllum is the low, mat-forming wild thyme of European heaths and rocky hillsides, spreading to form dense, fragrant carpets 2–6 inches tall bearing tiny, deep rose-pink to purple flowers in early summer that are covered with honeybees and butterflies; it is equally valuable as a culinary herb (leaves have a pleasant, mild thyme flavor) and as a ground cover, lawn substitute, and rock garden plant. It tolerates light foot traffic, making it excellent for planting between stepping stones and in paths; it is more cold-hardy and mat-forming than common thyme (T. vulgaris) and significantly more ornamental in flower. Shear lightly after blooming to keep compact.

subcategory: South Asian cosmetic and medicinal rhizome
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 3–4 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in zone 8–11; Wild Turmeric is a showy ornamental and cosmetic/medicinal Curcuma native to the eastern Himalayas and South Asia, grown for deeply yellow rhizomes with a rose-camphor-turmeric aroma used in skin-lightening and cosmetic preparations across South Asia — less culinary than common turmeric and famous for producing some of the most spectacular pink flower spikes of the genus.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Curcuma aromatica is dormant in winter and emerges in spring — mulch heavily to protect rhizomes from frost below zone 9, lift and store indoors in colder climates. Curcuma aromatica (Wild Turmeric, Kasturi Manjal, or Cochin Haldi) is a clumping rhizomatous ginger-family perennial native to the subtropical forests of northeast India, Bhutan, and Myanmar, now cultivated across South Asia, Southeast Asia, and China. The rhizomes are bright orange-yellow internally — richly aromatic with a floral rose-camphor-turmeric scent — and are the primary ingredient in traditional South Asian skin-care and cosmetic preparations: traditional face packs (ubtan), skin-brightening pastes, and bath scrubs used in Hindu ritual bathing ceremonies, wedding preparations, and daily skin care, particularly in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal. The curcumin content is lower than common turmeric (C. longa) so it is rarely used as a food spice. The ornamental value is exceptional: stunning pink to rose-purple, cone-shaped flower spikes emerge directly from the ground on separate stems before the large paddle-shaped leaves in spring — among the most beautiful of all Curcuma flowers. Excellent partial-shade ornamental spice plant for zone 8–11 gardens.

common_name: Wild Yam (American Wild Yam, Colic Root)
plant_note: Plant root divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Wild Yam is a twining, herbaceous vine that dies back to its rhizome each winter and re-emerges in spring, slowly forming a spreading colony under trees and along woodland edges.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to dappled shade, giving the twining vine a fence, shrub, or trellis to climb. Wild Yam is a native North American woodland vine long used in traditional herbal medicine, historically valued for its knotty rhizome, which contains diosgenin, a plant steroid compound that served as an early industrial source for synthesizing progesterone and other steroid hormones; despite folk claims, the raw rhizome is not directly hormonally active when eaten and is not a food crop like true cultivated yams. In the garden it is grown chiefly as a native woodland vine for naturalized shade plantings, valued for its heart-shaped leaves, twining habit, and small, inconspicuous summer flowers followed by distinctive three-winged seed capsules in fall. It spreads slowly by rhizome once established and tolerates a range of shaded conditions, making it a good choice for a low-maintenance native groundcover vine at a woodland edge.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Willamette climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Willamette, named for Oregon's Willamette Valley where it is extensively grown, is a widely planted English-type aroma hop bred as a Fuggle-derivative, valued for its mild, pleasant, slightly floral and spicy character well suited to English-style ales, brown ales, and other beer styles calling for a gentler hop presence than the assertive citrus hops popular in American IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect a lighter harvest than in the Pacific Northwest.

plant_note: Windowbox is a dwarf, mounding basil bred specifically for small containers and windowsill growing, staying compact without becoming leggy.
directions: Start seed indoors or direct sow after the last frost, and grow in a container or small bed in full sun. This compact, naturally mounding basil was selected specifically for small spaces, staying dense and tidy in a windowsill pot or patio container rather than stretching tall and leggy like standard Genovese basil. The small, aromatic leaves have classic sweet basil flavor and are well suited to snipping a few at a time for garnish and light cooking use. Regular light pinching keeps the plant full and encourages continuous new growth through the season.

plant_note: Sow direct around last frost date in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; winter savory requires perfect drainage and is excellent in herb gardens, rock gardens, and container plantings.
directions: Sow direct around last frost date in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; winter savory requires excellent drainage and performs poorly in heavy clay or moist soil. Satureja montana is a woody-based, semi-evergreen perennial herb with narrow, glossy, dark-green, very aromatic leaves and masses of tiny, lilac-white flowers in late summer; it has a more robust, resinous, slightly bitter-peppery flavor compared to the more delicate annual summer savory (S. hortensis) and is the traditional seasoning for beans and lentils in many European countries, particularly in the south of France (where it is called poivre d'âne — donkey pepper). The semi-evergreen foliage can be harvested year-round in mild climates; it is an attractive, low, mounded, shrubby herb for the front of sunny borders and herb gardens.

plant_note: Heat-tolerant tarragon alternative.
directions: Start seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost, covering lightly and keeping flats warm. This anise-flavored marigold thrives in heat and humidity where true tarragon struggles. Transplant into full sun in well-drained soil once nights stay warm, and pinch to encourage branching. Harvest leaves through the season for culinary use in place of French tarragon. In frost-free zones it behaves as a perennial, blooming golden flowers in fall.

plant_note: Plant nursery divisions or transplants in early spring around the last frost date; wintergreen establishes slowly and is best sourced as a division rather than grown from seed.
directions: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil under deciduous or evergreen shade; wintergreen is a native North American woodland plant that thrives in conditions hostile to most herbs, particularly under conifers or in acidic woodland gardens. Established plants slowly spread into a glossy evergreen mat bearing small white flowers in summer and bright red berries through winter. Harvest the thick, aromatic leaves at any season for wintergreen tea; crush a leaf to confirm the characteristic methyl salicylate fragrance before using. Both berries and leaves are edible and safe in culinary quantities; the essential oil is very concentrated and should not be used internally.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall or early spring in partial shade to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil under trees or shrubs; wood avens colonizes shaded woodland edges and naturalizes freely once established.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall or early spring in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil under trees or shrubs; wood avens is a versatile woodland herb long used in traditional European herbal medicine and as a flavoring, with roots that carry a mild clove-like fragrance and were historically used to flavor ale and preserve linens. The small, five-petaled yellow flowers appear from late spring through summer and are followed by burr-like seedheads that cling to clothing and fur, dispersing the plant throughout the woodland garden. Both the young leaves and roots are edible — add young leaves to salads and use the dried roots as a mild clove substitute in cooking or herbal infusions. Establishes readily under deciduous canopy and self-seeds to form a low, naturalistic groundcover that tolerates root competition.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost after a brief cold stratification; transplant to a partially shaded site after frost danger passes.
directions: Cold-stratify seed for 2–4 weeks in the refrigerator, then surface-sow onto moist, peat-based starting mix in a warm location; germination can be slow and erratic. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade or dappled light, where wood betony colonizes the herbaceous layer of meadow and woodland edge. The square stems bear whorls of rosy-purple flowers in early to midsummer and are ornamental as well as useful. Harvest aerial parts — stems, leaves, and flowers — in full bloom, drying for use in traditional headache and digestive bitters teas, where the herb is valued for its mild nervine and astringent properties.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; wood betony is long-lived and undemanding once established. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor. The plant was one of the most highly regarded medicinal herbs of medieval Europe and was grown in virtually every monastery physic garden.
directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; wood betony is a European native wildflower of woodland edges, meadows, and hedgerow banks that was for centuries one of the most widely used and highly valued medicinal herbs of the Western herbal tradition — credited with such broad healing powers in medieval Europe that the Saxon physicians listed 29 distinct ailments it was believed to cure, and the advice 'sell your coat and buy betony' circulated as a proverb for its all-encompassing virtue. As a garden ornamental it forms neat rosettes of deeply veined, scallop-edged, dark-green, softly hairy leaves and in early summer produces upright, square-stemmed spikes of densely clustered, bright rose-pink to magenta-purple tubular flowers that are magnets for bumblebees and other long-tongued pollinators. The rich flower color is clear and cheerful in the summer border, and the plant is undemanding in well-drained to average soils. Excellent for the cottage herb garden, medicinal garden, or wildlife border. White ('Alba') and pink cultivars are available alongside the species.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; Wood calamint is a European woodland herb of the mint family with leaves that smell and taste like a combination of basil and thyme — the 'basil thyme' common name is apt — it is used in Italian cooking, particularly in Umbria and Lazio (where it is known as 'nepitella'), as a seasoning for artichokes, mushrooms, and tripe.
directions: Sow seeds or plant divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; harvest leaves as needed before flowering for best flavor. Calamintha sylvatica (wood calamint or basil thyme) is a European woodland herb in the mint family (Lamiaceae), native to the forests, hedgerows, and shaded rocky slopes of southern and central Europe — with a particularly close association with Italian cuisine. The leaves have a distinctive aroma and flavor that has been aptly described as a synthesis of fresh basil and thyme with additional minty notes — more complex and interesting than either herb alone. In Italian cooking, this herb is known as 'nepitella' (or 'mentuccia' in Lazio) — an important and distinctly Italian culinary herb with a long tradition in Roman and Umbrian cooking. It is a classic pairing for artichokes (in Roman-style carciofi alla romana), porcini mushrooms, tripe (trippa alla Romana), and game dishes; the herb adds a fresh, aromatic complexity that is genuinely distinct from standard basil or thyme. Wood calamint is notably more shade-tolerant than most herbs — it grows well at the edge of light shade under trees, making it useful for herb gardens with limited full-sun space. The small, white to pale-lavender flowers attract bees prolifically and the plant is excellent for pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or autumn; wood sage naturalizes readily under trees and at woodland edges, self-seeding gently in suitable conditions; prefers well-drained, slightly acidic, poor to moderate soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant divisions or transplants in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, poor to moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; wood sage (Teucrium scorodonia) is a European woodland perennial with wrinkled, sage-like leaves with a distinctive garlicky-sage aroma, producing graceful spikes of small yellow-green flowers in summer that are excellent for bees and hoverflies. Despite the name it is a germander (Teucrium genus), not a true sage, and has been used historically as a bittering agent in ale before hops became standard and as a medicinal herb in European folk medicine. Naturalizes beautifully under oak trees and at woodland edges, spreading slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding; tolerates dry shade well once established. A valuable shade-tolerant herb for the woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; wood sorrel is a classic woodland groundcover of cool, moist, conifer and hardwood forest floors.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly to moderately acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) in partial to full shade; wood sorrel requires cool, consistently moist conditions and performs poorly in heat and drought, making it a plant for zones 3–7 and cool, moist microclimates. Oxalis acetosella is a delicate, low-growing European and Asian native found in cool, moist woodland floors; it has characteristic shamrock-like, trifoliate, bright-green leaves that fold down at night and in bright light, and bears small, white flowers with pink veins in spring. The leaves have a distinctive, sharp, lemony-sour taste from oxalic acid and are used as a garnish, in salads, and to make refreshing cold drinks in Scandinavian and European folk traditions; the flavor is best when the plant is growing in cool shade. Consume in moderation as oxalic acid can be problematic in large quantities, especially for those prone to kidney stones.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in fast-draining soil; avoid clay and do not irrigate once established.
directions: Trichostema lanatum is a stunning California native evergreen shrub in the mint family, prized for its intensely aromatic narrow leaves and dramatic spikes of electric-blue flowers wrapped in showy woolly purple-violet calyxes that bloom from spring through summer and draw hummingbirds and native bumblebees in abundance. Propagate by softwood cuttings rather than seed, and plant out in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun — this plant will not tolerate clay, wet soils, or summer irrigation once it is established. It is native to the dry chaparral and coastal sage scrub of southern California and performs best in California-style dry gardens in zones 8-10. Excellent drainage is the single most important factor for long-term success; plants sited correctly are long-lived and largely care-free.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in well-drained perlite or plant container-grown specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun; woolly thyme tolerates foot traffic and drought exceptionally well once established and is ideal for filling gaps between paving stones.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun; woolly thyme forms one of the lowest, densest, most carpet-like groundcovers available, producing a silvery-gray, velvet-textured mat of tiny, densely woolly leaves only 1–3 inches tall that spreads steadily without becoming aggressive. Pale pink flowers cover the mat in early summer, attracting bees. The plant is one of very few groundcovers that tolerates moderate foot traffic and thrives between flagstones, along dry stone paths, and in gravel gardens. It is primarily ornamental — the woolly leaves are not as flavorful for cooking as other thymes — and is grown for its exceptional textural effect. Excellent in rock gardens, as an alternative to lawn in dry, sunny spots, and in Mediterranean-style plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface (seeds need light) in dry, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, poor to average soil in full sun; wormwood thrives in lean conditions and will become rank and floppy in fertile, moist soil.
directions: Artemisia absinthium is a silver-white, intensely aromatic shrubby perennial with silky, deeply dissected, ghostly pale foliage that makes it one of the most striking foliage plants in the dry garden; the bitter compounds (including thujone) were historically used medicinally as an anthelmintic (worm expeller), digestive bitter, and febrifuge, and are the source of the bitterness in vermouth and historically in absinthe. The foliage is strongly allelopathic — plant away from edible crops. The silver-gray foliage is an outstanding foil for purple-flowered companions like salvias and catmints.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yabukita tea is a cold-hardy cultivar bred in Japan and tolerates more winter cold than many other tea cultivars.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yabukita tea is a cold-hardy cultivar bred in Japan and tolerates more winter cold than many other tea cultivars. Developed in Shizuoka Prefecture in the early twentieth century and released commercially in 1953, this cultivar became so dominant in Japanese tea production that it now accounts for the large majority of all tea grown in Japan, prized for its balanced, clean, slightly sweet flavor well suited to sencha and other steamed green tea styles. Its relatively good cold hardiness compared to many tea cultivars, combined with reliable yields and disease resistance, made it the standard choice for Japanese tea farmers for decades and a natural benchmark against which newer Japanese tea cultivars are still compared. Harvest the youngest leaves and unopened buds by hand in spring for the highest-quality tea, and prune the shrub into a rounded hedge form typical of commercial tea cultivation to encourage dense, flush new growth.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers in fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil, ideally under deciduous trees, since this spring ephemeral emerges before the canopy leafs out.
directions: Should be avoided during pregnancy. Plant dormant tubers in fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil, ideally under deciduous trees, since this spring ephemeral emerges and flowers before the canopy leafs out, then dies back and stays dormant through summer heat. The tuber is a well-known TCM analgesic, traditionally decocted to invigorate blood circulation and relieve menstrual, abdominal, and musculoskeletal pain, and is distinct from ornamental Corydalis grown for foliage.

common_name: Yaw Weed (Wild Indian Mulberry, Cheese Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy coastal soil in full sun to part shade; yaw weed is a native Florida, Caribbean, and Gulf Coast coastal shrub related to noni (Morinda citrifolia) that grows on sandy beaches, shell middens, and disturbed coastal areas — it is an important native host plant for several butterfly species and produces unusual, compound white fruits similar in structure to noni.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; drought and salt-spray tolerant once established. Morinda royoc (yaw weed or wild Indian mulberry) is a native North American coastal shrub in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) — related to noni (Morinda citrifolia) and producing very similar compound, syncarpous white fruits (multiple small flowers fuse into a single fleshy structure), though much smaller and with a less objectionable odor than commercial noni. It is native to the coastal hammocks, shell middens, sandy beaches, and disturbed coastal areas of South Florida, the Florida Keys, the Caribbean islands, and the coastal Gulf of Mexico. The plant has a distinctly scrambling or climbing growth habit, with the stems leaning on and scrambling through other shrubs. The roots yield a traditional reddish-orange dye used by Caribbean indigenous peoples; the leaves and bark have traditional medicinal uses in Caribbean herbal medicine for skin conditions and fevers — the 'yaw weed' name refers to use for yaws (a tropical bacterial infection). As a native coastal landscape plant, yaw weed is exceptionally salt, drought, and wind tolerant — suitable for difficult coastal conditions where little else grows. The fruits are edible but not palatable fresh; birds eat them readily, providing wildlife habitat value.

plant_note: Seed needs a cold stratification period before it will germinate reliably, so sow in containers and chill for 4-6 weeks or start outdoors in fall; plants take several years to reach flowering and harvestable root size.
directions: Sow stratified seed in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil, since this long-lived alpine meadow perennial forms a substantial taproot and resents being moved once established. Broad ribbed leaves form a large basal clump for the first several years before the plant sends up tall stalks of striking whorled yellow flowers, usually not before its third or fourth season. The intensely bitter root, harvested only after many years of growth, is a classic European digestive bitter used in traditional tonics and liqueurs; commercial harvest generally waits until plants are at least four to ten years old. Give it cool summers, good winter drainage, and full sun to light shade, as it struggles in hot, humid climates.

plant_note: Self-sows freely throughout gardens — typically not intentionally cultivated but harvested as a wild edible; yellow wood sorrel naturalizes in disturbed soil, lawn edges, and garden beds across the eastern US and makes a refreshing wild salad herb when leaves are young and tender.
directions: Yellow wood sorrel is a native perennial that self-sows throughout gardens and lawns without cultivation; it is included here as a wild edible and forager's herb rather than a planted crop. Oxalis stricta produces the classic shamrock-shaped, clover-like trifoliate leaves and tiny yellow five-petaled flowers that are familiar to any gardener as a common weed; the young leaves and stems have a pleasant, sour, lemon-like flavor from oxalic acid that is refreshing in small quantities in salads, garnishes, and herb butters. Children particularly enjoy the tangy flavor of the raw leaves. Foragers note: consume in moderation as large quantities of oxalic acid can irritate the kidneys; avoid if prone to kidney stones. The small seed pods explode when ripe, launching seeds several feet — the primary reason it spreads so freely.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in shade.
directions: Propagate from stem-tip cuttings or layered runners, as nursery plants are more reliable than seed-grown starts, and set into cool, shaded beds in spring with consistent moisture. This low, mat-forming evergreen herb of Pacific Coast forests produces an intensely sweet mintlike fragrance that made it the aromatic plant of choice for tea among Indigenous peoples of California and the Pacific Northwest. Plant it beneath conifers or deciduous trees where it can sprawl freely as a fragrant groundcover in dappled shade with moderate, even moisture. Harvest young stems and leaves throughout the growing season to steep as a refreshing herbal tea, and divide established mats every few years to keep growth vigorous.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yerba buena is a California and Pacific Northwest woodland native that spreads as a low, trailing groundcover under trees.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yerba buena is a trailing California and Pacific Coast native mint relative that forms a loose, low groundcover of small, rounded, glossy leaves with a refreshing, minty fragrance released when brushed or crushed. Historically brewed as a mild, pleasant herbal tea by Native Californians and early Spanish settlers (the plant lent its name to the original Spanish name for the settlement that became San Francisco), it remains valued today mostly as a fragrant, shade-tolerant groundcover rather than a major culinary herb. Small, inconspicuous white to pale lavender flowers appear in the leaf axils in summer, largely incidental to the plant's soft-textured foliage display. It spreads gently by trailing, rooting stems under open tree canopy, tolerating dry shade better than many groundcovers once established, making it a good low-maintenance choice for woodland garden paths and understory plantings.

plant_note: Best established from root divisions or nursery plugs set into permanently damp, mineral-rich soil; it spreads by thick aromatic rhizomes and colonizes wet seeps, ditch banks, and pond edges.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions into saturated, mineral-rich soil in full sun to light shade near a pond edge, rain garden low point, or irrigated bed that never fully dries out. The thick, spicy-scented roots have long been used by Southwestern Indigenous peoples and traditional herbalists as an antimicrobial wash and poultice, and the plant is equally valued as a striking wetland groundcover with white, cone-centered spring flowers reminiscent of anemones. It spreads steadily by rhizome once established, so give it room or a contained wet bed. Divide congested clumps in early spring to renew vigor and share starts.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–November or February–April. Yerba mate is best established from container stock as germination from seed is slow and irregular. In zone 9 it grows as a large evergreen shrub or small tree and tolerates light frosts to about 20°F when established. The plant requires moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and benefits from partial shade in zone 9 to prevent leaf scorch during peak summer heat.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Yerba Mate is the holly-family tree whose dried, roasted leaves produce the traditional caffeinated infusion consumed throughout South America — Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Brazil — where it is estimated that hundreds of millions of people drink it daily. The dried leaf contains caffeine, theobromine, and theophylline at levels between tea and coffee, producing an alert, focused energy without the jitteriness of coffee. The flavor is distinctly grassy, herbaceous, slightly bitter, and smoky from the traditional drying process, though home-dried leaf from fresh garden plants is milder and greener. In zone 9 the plant grows as a large, handsome evergreen shrub or small tree with glossy, dark green, oval leaves. Harvest young leaves in spring for the most delicate flavor; leaves harvested throughout the growing season become progressively stronger. The plant tolerates the moist, acidic, sandy loam soils of the Gulf Coast better than many ornamentals, thriving where high rainfall and humidity prevail.

plant_note: Set rooted stem cuttings or rhizome divisions in spring into fast-draining, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; seed germination is notoriously unreliable without fire cues.
directions: Yerba santa is a drought-adapted evergreen shrub native to the dry chaparral and foothill slopes of California and southern Oregon, where it forms colonies from spreading underground rhizomes. Establish new plantings from rooted stem cuttings or transplanted rhizome divisions set into fast-draining, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun, since the resinous, sticky, lance-shaped leaves and seed have a notoriously low, fire-cued germination rate in cultivation. Once established, the deep root system needs little to no summer irrigation and resents heavy clay or regular watering, which promotes root rot. Harvest mature leaves any time after the second year; it has a long history of use brewed into a bittersweet tea for coughs and colds, and the dried leaf was historically used to mask the bitterness of other medicines.

plant_note: Divide clumps or plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in zone 8–11; Yi Zhi (Sharpleaf Galangal) is a clumping ginger-family perennial native to Hainan Island and southeastern China, commercially cultivated on Hainan for its aromatic, peppery, warmly spiced seed pods — among the most highly valued medicinal herbs in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) for treating cold conditions of the spleen and kidney.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alpinia oxyphylla prefers high humidity and consistent moisture — mulch deeply, water regularly during the growing season, and cut back dead stems after dormancy; mulch root zone in zone 8 to protect from hard freezes. Alpinia oxyphylla (Yi Zhi or Sharpleaf Galangal) is a large, clumping, rhizomatous ginger-family perennial native to the tropical forest understory of Hainan Island, Guangdong, and Guangxi provinces in southern China. It is one of the 'Four Southern Chinese Herbs' (Nan Yao Sì Hua) — Hainan-native plants of highest importance in Traditional Chinese Medicine — commercially cultivated at scale on Hainan as one of the most economically significant medicinal crops of the island. The aromatic, cone-shaped seed pods (harvested before full ripeness and dried) are used in TCM preparations for digestive complaints, frequent urination, and cold-deficiency conditions of the spleen and kidney. The spicy, warming, aromatic seeds taste of a combination of cardamom, pepper, and ginger. The plant is also ornamentally beautiful — tall, graceful, lanceolate leaves and elegant, arching inflorescences bearing white flowers with bright-pink suffused lips. Excellent partial-shade specimen for Southern gardens (zone 8–11) where the tall, tropical-looking foliage provides substantial presence even when not in bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or seedlings in spring into ordinary, moisture-retentive garden soil at a woodland edge or under high shade; established clumps spread by rhizome and are easiest to propagate by dividing an existing patch rather than starting from seed.
directions: Grow yomogi in loose, humus-rich soil in the light shade beneath deciduous trees, where its silvery-backed leaves stay tender and less coarse than plants grown in full sun. Cut the youngest leaf tips repeatedly through spring and early summer before flowering begins, since older leaves turn tough and bitter. The finely chopped, blanched leaves give kusa mochi and other Japanese rice sweets their deep green color and a distinctive herbal, slightly resinous flavor, and the dried leaf is also steeped as tea. It spreads by rhizome, so give it a bounded bed or a large container if you want to keep its cheerful colonizing habit in check.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in a sandy, gritty mix and transplant into lean, well-drained soil once the ground can be worked; resents wet, heavy conditions.
directions: May interact with sedative medications and is not a substitute for treating depression or cognitive decline. Start seed indoors in a sandy, gritty mix and transplant into lean, well-drained soil once the ground can be worked, since this steppe native resents wet, heavy conditions and is slow and seldom available outside specialty herb nurseries in the US. The pencil-thin roots are dried and aged for three to four years before use in TCM formulas traditionally taken to calm the mind, ease coughs with phlegm, and support memory.

plant_note: Start from cuttings or established plants 4–6 weeks before last frost; Origanum syriacum is the plant known as za'atar in Middle Eastern cooking and as Biblical hyssop (aizov) in Hebrew, the foundational herb of the Middle Eastern za'atar spice blend and one of the most widely used herbs in Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian, and Israeli cuisine.
directions: Propagate from stem cuttings (seeds are slow and variable) and plant in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky soil in full sun; Origanum syriacum is native to rocky limestone hills of the eastern Mediterranean and requires excellent drainage — it declines in heavy or wet soil. Origanum syriacum is the 'true za'atar' plant of the Middle East — the primary ingredient in the za'atar spice blend that is ubiquitous in Levantine cuisine (the blend also includes sesame seeds, sumac, and salt). It is sometimes called Biblical hyssop because many scholars believe it is the ezov/aizov of the Hebrew Bible. The flavor is more intense, pungent, and earthy than Italian oregano with a distinctive mineral-herb complexity that makes it unique among Mediterranean herbs; harvest by cutting stems before full flowering for maximum flavor. Hardy only to zone 7; treat as an annual or pot plant in colder climates. In warm zones 8–11 it can be grown as a perennial hedge-shrub.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or gravelly soil in full sun; za'atar savory is a drought-tolerant subshrubby perennial from the Eastern Mediterranean dry hillsides — one of the specific plants contributing to za'atar spice blends, with a warm, thyme-oregano-savory flavor — requiring excellent drainage above all else.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, rocky or gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; avoid overwatering — this plant demands dry conditions. Satureja thymbra (za'atar savory, pink savory, or thyme-leaved savory) is a compact, woody-based perennial from the dry limestone hillsides, macchia scrub, and garrigue of the Eastern Mediterranean — native to Greece, Turkey, Cyprus, Lebanon, and Israel. It is one of several specific plants that go into the za'atar herb blend of the Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean — alongside Origanum syriacum, Thymbra spicata, and Micromeria fruticosa — and is also used independently as a culinary and medicinal herb. The flavor of S. thymbra is warm, complex, and intense: more resinous and thyme-like than common summer savory (S. hortensis), with oregano notes and a subtle bitterness that adds depth to za'atar blends, grilled meats, and herb breads. The plant forms a neat, mounding, evergreen (in mild winters) subshrub with small, deep-green, aromatic leaves and pink to light-purple flowers that attract bees abundantly in early summer. It performs well in Mediterranean-climate gardens (zone 8–10) with excellent drainage and lean soil — exactly the conditions found on Greek island hillsides.

plant_note: Needs sharp drainage to survive winter wet.
directions: Surface-sow the tiny seed and press in without covering, as light aids germination. Grow in lean, gritty soil in full sun where it forms a low aromatic mound prized in Middle Eastern spice blends. Water sparingly once established, since the plant resents soggy roots and rots in wet clay. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the habit compact and encourage fresh flavorful leaves. In cold zones, mulch the crown or overwinter a potted plant under cover.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost, or plant container stock in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, alkaline to neutral, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Thymbra spicata is native to rocky limestone slopes in Turkey, Cyprus, and the Levant and demands excellent drainage and low soil fertility.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry, lean, alkaline to neutral, sandy or stony soil in full sun; never plant in heavy, wet, or fertile soil, which causes rot and premature death. Thymbra spicata (zahter) is a small, woody, drought-tolerant perennial herb native to rocky limestone hillsides in Turkey, Cyprus, Syria, Lebanon, and Israel — a close relative of thyme (Thymus) with a similar but distinctly more savory, spicy-bitter, oregano-like aroma and flavor profile. It is one of the traditional species used to make the Middle Eastern spice blend 'za'atar' (which includes multiple wild herb species depending on region), and the fresh or dried leaves and flowering tops are used to season meats, breads, cheese, and olive oil throughout Turkey and the Levant. In Turkish cuisine, zahter (za'atar in Arabic/Hebrew) is a primary herb for the spice blend used with olive oil and flatbread. The plant produces dense, spike-like inflorescences of pink to purple flowers in summer that are excellent for pollinators. In zone 9, it thrives in dry, alkaline, well-drained conditions and is highly drought-resistant once established.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun in zone 8–11; Zedoary is a large, clumping tropical ginger native to northeast India and the Indo-Malayan rainforest zone, grown for its camphor-pepper-bitter aromatic rhizomes used in Southeast Asian and South Asian cuisine, traditional medicine, and perfumery — historically traded on the medieval European spice routes.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Curcuma zedoaria is dormant in winter — cut back dead stems after frost and mulch heavily in zone 8–9, then lift and store rhizomes in colder climates. Curcuma zedoaria (Zedoary or White Turmeric) is a large, ornamental, clumping ginger-family perennial native to northeast India (Assam), Bangladesh, and the Malay Archipelago, cultivated throughout South and Southeast Asia for its fat, fleshy, grayish-white rhizomes with a distinctive camphor-lemon-pepper-bitter aroma and flavor profile entirely different from common turmeric (C. longa). The rhizomes are used fresh, dried and ground, or steam-distilled for essential oil in Indonesian, Thai, and Indian cuisines for curries, pickles, and medicinal preparations; zedoary was also an important European medieval spice — traded under the name 'zedoary' in Arab and European commerce as early as the 6th century CE. Medicinally, the rhizomes are used in Ayurvedic and Unani medicine as a digestive tonic, carminative, and anti-inflammatory. The plant is also ornamentally attractive — large, paddle-shaped leaves with a distinctive purple midrib stripe, and showy, cone-shaped pink-and-white flower spikes emerge from the ground before the main foliage in spring. Excellent food garden spice for partial-shade positions in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Zeus climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Zeus (also sold as Columbus/Tomahawk/Zeus, or CTZ) is a high-alpha-acid American bittering hop developed for efficient, potent bitterness in a wide range of beer styles, with a pungent, slightly herbal and resinous aroma alongside its primary role as a bittering rather than aroma hop. The vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges vigorously each spring, climbing 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; because its high alpha-acid content delivers strong bitterness from a relatively small harvest, even a modest home planting can supply a meaningful amount of bittering hops for brewing. Harvest cones in late summer when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin resin, then dry promptly. Like other hops, Zeus prefers a cool, long-day growing season and performs poorly through the sustained heat and humidity of Gulf South summers, so give it the coolest, most open site available and expect a lighter yield than in traditional hop-growing regions.

plant_note: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, as this Trinidad strain is slow to establish and needs a long warm season.
directions: 7 Pot Barrackpore takes its name from the Barrackpore district of Trinidad and is prized among superhot growers for pods that are less bumpy and wrinkled than most other 7 Pot strains, ripening from green to a glossy orange-red. Its heat arrives with a noticeably smoky, savory edge that Trinidad cooks favor for pepper sauces rather than fresh eating. Provide rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, since irregular watering causes blossom drop and stunted pod set on this variety. Because plants are tall and heavily branched once mature, stake or cage them early to keep the fruit-laden limbs from snapping in wind.

common_name: 7 Pot Brain Strain Pepper (Yellow Brain Strain)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, as this superhot needs a long warm season to size up and ripen.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, keeping the medium warm to encourage the slow-to-sprout chinense seed, then transplant once the soil has warmed well past frost danger. Stake heavily loaded plants and keep watering even to prevent blossom end rot on the convoluted pods. Brain Strain is a 7 Pot type selected for its intensely wrinkled, brain-like fruit surface and sits among the hottest strains within the already fierce 7 Pot family. It is grown in both yellow and red-fruited forms, both intensely pungent.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, giving this slow-maturing superhot a long head start.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since chinense seed can take several weeks to germinate, and pot up seedlings before moving them to the garden once nights are reliably warm. Support the branching stems as fruit accumulates, and reduce watering slightly as pods mature to concentrate flavor. Douglah is a Trinidad 7 Pot strain that ripens to a distinctive dull brown 'chocolate' color rather than red, and it is regarded as one of the hottest of the 7 Pot varieties with a smoky, earthy flavor. Always wear gloves when handling ripe fruit.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost with steady bottom heat near 85°F, since superhot Capsicum chinense types germinate slowly and unevenly; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 60°F.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; handle ripe fruit with gloves and avoid touching eyes or skin, since the extreme capsaicin content can cause burns even from brief contact. 7 Pot Pepper is a legendary superhot pepper from Trinidad, named for the traditional claim that a single pod is potent enough to season seven pots of stew — a nod to its extreme heat, which commonly measures in the range of 800,000 to over 1,000,000 Scoville heat units, placing it among the hottest peppers ever recorded alongside its close relatives Trinidad Scorpion and Trinidad Moruga Scorpion. The gnarled, bumpy, lantern-shaped pods ripen from green to a deep, glossy red and carry a fruity, floral Capsicum chinense aroma beneath the ferocious heat, making it prized by hot sauce makers who want maximum intensity along with genuine habanero-family flavor complexity. A serious specialty pepper for heat enthusiasts only, best grown where its extended season can be accommodated, zone 8–11.

plant_note: Start on a heat mat 10–12 weeks before last frost; 7 Pot Primo is a Louisiana-developed superhot cross between a Naga Morich and a Trinidad 7 Pot pepper, measuring 1.0–1.5 million Scoville units, with a distinctive elongated tail; handle with gloves and treat as an extreme culinary novelty — a single pod flavors a large batch of hot sauce.
directions: Germinate at 85°F on a heat mat for 2–4 weeks; grow under strong lights before transplanting outdoors after all frost risk has passed. 7 Pot Primo was developed by Louisiana hot pepper grower Troy Primeaux (the 'Primo' in the name) as a cross between a Naga Morich and a Trinidad 7 Pot variety; the name '7 Pot' refers to the traditional Trinidadian claim that one pod is hot enough to season 7 pots of food. At 1.0–1.5 million SHU it is among the most intensely hot peppers available to home growers, with a distinctive gnarled, elongated 'tail' that distinguishes it from the rounder Trinidad 7 Pot types. The flavor beneath the heat is described as fruity, earthy, and robust; used in extremely small quantities in hot sauces, fermented hot pepper mash, and as a smoking or drying chile for superhot spice blends.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Sow two or three seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil once frost danger has passed, thinning to the strongest seedling per hill. These white-skinned fruits reach 12 to 15 pounds and hold their clean color well after harvest, so give vines plenty of room to sprawl. The strong, sturdy handle makes them ideal for carving and display. Intermediate powdery mildew resistance helps vines stay productive, but water at the base and space plants for airflow to further reduce disease pressure.

common_name: Abraham Lincoln Tomato (Classic 1923 Red Beefsteak Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost risk has passed; this vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from sturdy staking or caging.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, fertile soil in full sun. Abraham Lincoln is an American heirloom tomato dating to 1923, prized for large, deep-red, meaty beefsteak fruit with rich, well-balanced flavor and good disease tolerance for a variety of its age, which helped it remain popular with home gardeners for decades after its introduction. The vigorous indeterminate vines are strong producers over a long season and benefit from sturdy staking or caging to support the heavy fruit. Water evenly to reduce cracking and blossom end rot, and harvest once fruit is fully colored and yields slightly to gentle pressure for the best flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for cool-season production, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Acadia carries resistance to an unusually wide range of downy mildew races, a valuable trait for the damp, disease-prone conditions of a Gulf South winter spinach planting.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2-4 inch spacing and use thinnings in salads. Acadia is a semi-savoy spinach hybrid, with leaves that carry moderate crinkle for good texture while staying easier to wash clean than fully savoy types, bred with resistance to an unusually wide range of downy mildew races that helps it stay healthy through the damp, humid conditions common in a Gulf South fall or winter garden. It is well suited to both field and high-tunnel production for a spring or fall crop. Harvest by cutting outer leaves for continued production or cutting the whole plant at the base once it has filled out, and use promptly since fresh spinach quality declines quickly after harvest.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before your last frost, keeping the mix at 70 to 85 degrees for quick germination. This 1950s heirloom is a determinate type, so most of its 6 to 8 ounce, low-acid fruits ripen over a concentrated window, making it excellent for canning. Transplant seedlings deeply once nights stay warm, and stake or cage the compact bushes to keep fruit off the ground. Harvest tomatoes when fully colored and slightly soft for the best fresh flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors, transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Ace 55-VF is a determinate heirloom bearing round, low-acid red fruits of 5-6 inches with thick, juicy flesh, and it carries resistance to verticillium and fusarium wilt. Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before your last frost, then harden off and transplant once nights stay above 50F. Give plants a sturdy cage even though the compact vines are self-limiting, and mulch to keep soil moisture even and prevent blossom-end rot. Because it sets much of its crop at once, this variety is well suited to canning and batch preserving.

common_name: Ace Pepper (AAS-Winning Early Green Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed; Ace, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is an early-maturing bell pepper on a compact, productive plant.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Ace, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is prized for reaching harvestable size unusually early compared with other bell peppers, producing blocky, thick-walled, mild green fruit that ripens to red if left on the plant longer, all on a compact, sturdy plant that sets fruit reliably even in less-than-ideal conditions. Its early maturity makes it a good choice for gardeners wanting a head start on the pepper harvest or a reliable crop in shorter growing seasons. Harvest at green stage for classic bell pepper use or let fruit ripen to sweeter red for a different flavor, and pick regularly to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date; in zone 9 start in September and transplant October for fall through winter harvest. Savoy cabbage is more cold-hardy than smooth green cabbage types and can withstand harder freezes without head damage. In zone 9 the distinctive crinkled leaves provide more air circulation than smooth-headed types, which may help with the humidity-related disease issues common in Gulf South winters. Harvest when heads are firm; savoy holds in the garden longer than smooth cabbage after reaching maturity.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ace Savoy is a compact, early-maturing savoy cabbage producing small to medium (3–4 pound), round heads with the distinctively crinkled, blistered, dark blue-green leaves that define the savoy type — quite different from the smooth, pale heads of standard green cabbage. Savoy cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. sabauda) has a more complex, refined flavor than standard smooth cabbage: milder, sweeter, more tender, and less pungent, making it the preferred cabbage for fresh preparations where the subtle flavor can be appreciated rather than cooked down to blandness. The crinkled texture and tender leaves hold sauces and dressings differently than smooth cabbage — savoy is the cabbage preferred for upscale coleslaws, stuffed cabbage leaves (the larger, more pliable leaves wrap easily), and any preparation where delicate texture matters. Ace's compact size and rapid maturity (72–82 days) make it practical for fall planting in zone 9 where the cool growing window is relatively short.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep after the last frost once soil has warmed; in zone 8 and south, rhizomes can overwinter in the ground with heavy mulch — harvest the largest rhizomes for food and replant the smaller ones each spring.
directions: Achira is the oldest cultivated plant in South America, grown for thousands of years by Andean civilizations for its large, starchy rhizomes that produce a superior arrowroot starch used in gluten-free cooking and baking — distinct from ornamental cannas (Canna indica and hybrids) because the rhizomes are the primary crop, though the tall plants also produce showy flowers. Rhizomes are harvested 8–10 months after planting when plants begin to die back; they can be cooked like a starchy root vegetable, peeled and steamed, or dried and ground into a fine white starch known as 'canna starch' or 'Queensland arrowroot' that is an excellent thickener for sauces and soups. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, achira grows vigorously as a warm-season perennial that fills in quickly from spring through fall, providing both edible harvest and tropical visual interest; the leaves are also traditionally used to wrap foods for cooking like corn husks. Divide and replant small side rhizomes each spring to maintain a productive colony.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–October in zone 9) or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; achocha is a fast-growing Andean cucurbit that prefers cooler growing conditions than regular cucumbers — it thrives in zone 9's mild fall–spring season and produces prolifically before summer heat sets in.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide strong trellis — achocha is a vigorous climber. Cyclanthera pedata (achocha, wild cucumber, or stuffing cucumber) is an underappreciated Peruvian and Andean cucurbit vine producing distinctive, hollow, pale-green, cucumber-like fruits 3–4 inches long with a pointed beak and soft, edible seeds inside — the hollow interior makes them naturally adapted for stuffing with meat, rice, and cheese (a traditional Andean dish). The flavor of the raw fruit is mild, slightly bitter, and reminiscent of a blend of cucumber and green pepper; they can be eaten raw in salads, stir-fried, or stuffed and baked. The vine is extremely productive and easy to grow, climbing rapidly with coiled tendrils and producing prolific fruits over a long season in cool to warm conditions. In Andean markets, achocha is a common and affordable everyday vegetable; it is essentially unknown in North American supermarkets but straightforward to grow from seed as a specialty home garden vegetable. In zone 9, the fall-to-spring season is ideal; direct sow in September for a fall-through-spring harvest.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant March–April. In zone 9 Aci Sivri will persist as a perennial through mild winters — cut back hard in late winter and the plant will regrow from the woody base, producing earlier and more heavily than first-year plants. Individual plants can grow to 3–4 feet tall over multiple seasons.
