directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Aci Sivri (pronounced ah-juh SIV-ree, meaning 'hot sharp' in Turkish) is a Turkish heirloom cayenne-type pepper producing long (4–6 inch), thin, slightly wrinkled, pointed fruits that turn from pale green to deep red when ripe. The heat level ranges from mild when young and green to genuinely hot (15,000–30,000+ Scoville) when fully red-ripe, with the heat increasing significantly as the fruit matures and dries. The thin-walled, aromatic fruits dry quickly and are widely used in Turkish cuisine as a dried spice pepper, ground into flakes or paprika-style powder. Fresh green Aci Sivri is used in Turkish salads and grilled vegetable dishes where its mild-to-medium heat adds flavor without overwhelming. The prolific, heavily-bearing plants are extremely popular in Turkish home gardens and have been grown continuously for centuries. In zone 9 the long warm season allows multiple harvests and the plants often overwinter as perennials, returning larger each year.

common_name: Aconcagua Pepper (Argentine Giant Sweet Frying Pepper, 12-Inch Fruits with Mild Flavor)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Aconcagua is a large, late-season frying pepper requiring 75–90 days from transplant to reach full development — the largest fruits take the most time. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production; the variety's heat tolerance allows continued production through Gulf Coast summers, and the late season ripening means peak harvests often come in July–August. Provide large containers (5-gallon minimum) if growing in pots — the tall (3–4 foot) plants and large fruit weight require good stability. Stake or cage plants to support the fruit load. Aconcagua is named for the highest peak in the Andes Mountains in Argentina, referencing the variety's South American origin. Harvest green for mild use or fully ripened to salmon-red for sweetest flavor and full carotenoid development.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake plants; harvest green or fully ripe to salmon-red. Aconcagua is an Argentine heirloom sweet frying pepper that produces some of the largest sweet pepper fruits of any variety in home garden cultivation — individual fruits typically measuring 8–12 inches in length and 2–3 inches wide, with a conical to slightly flattened form that tapers to a point. The variety takes its name from Aconcagua, Argentina's (and the Americas') highest mountain, a reference to the pepper's origin in the Andean region of South America where diverse pepper varieties have been cultivated for millennia. The fruit size is genuinely dramatic: Aconcagua peppers dwarf most other sweet peppers in the garden and attract immediate attention at farmers markets and in garden displays where their unusual scale distinguishes them from any standard frying or bell pepper. Despite the imposing size, the walls are moderately thin (thinner than bell peppers, in the frying pepper tradition) and the flavor is mild, sweet, and fruity — the flesh has the pleasant, slightly aromatic quality characteristic of good heirloom frying peppers. The ripening progression of Aconcagua goes from green through light yellow-green to a distinctive salmon-pink to pale red-orange, a color not typical of most peppers and part of the variety's visual distinction. The large individual fruit size makes Aconcagua exceptionally practical for stuffing (the hollow interior accommodates substantial filling) and for roasting whole, where the large peppers yield significant amounts of sweet roasted flesh per fruit. The variety is open-pollinated and seed-saving is straightforward from fully ripe fruits.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in compost-enriched hills after soil reaches 65°F, planting 3–4 seeds per hill and thinning to 2. Allow vines to spread freely or train onto a sturdy trellis. Leave fruits on the vine until the rind is hard and resists a thumbnail; the stem will also begin to dry and cork over. Cure harvested squash at room temperature for 1–2 weeks to harden the skin before storage.

common_name: Adirondack Blue Potato (Cornell High-Anthocyanin Blue Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; Adirondack Blue was released in 2003 by Cornell University's potato breeding program, specifically developed as a distinct improvement over older All Blue-type varieties with higher anthocyanin content, better yield, improved disease resistance, and more consistent blue-purple flesh coloration throughout the tuber without white streaking.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30–36 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost in cool weather; hill soil over emerging plants twice as they grow to increase yield and prevent tubers from greening. Adirondack Blue was developed by Dr. Walter De Jong and colleagues at Cornell University's potato breeding program and released in 2003, representing a significant improvement over older blue-flesh potato varieties; it was specifically bred for the uniformly intense blue-purple flesh coloration (without the white marbling or streaking common in older blue varieties), higher anthocyanin content (the pigment responsible for blue and purple coloration and associated health benefits), and better agronomic performance than heirloom blue types. The tubers have blue-purple skin and uniformly vibrant blue-purple flesh that holds its color remarkably well when boiled or steamed; the texture is waxy and the flavor is rich and earthy — similar to high-quality waxy potatoes with an additional visual dimension. The blue color is striking in potato salads, mashed potatoes (turns lavender-blue), and roasted presentations. Mid-season maturity of 70–90 days from planting; produces reliably in most US climates.

common_name: Adirondack Red Potato (Cornell Red-Flesh Specialty Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; Adirondack Red was released in 2004 by Cornell University's potato breeding program as a companion to Adirondack Blue, producing uniformly red-pink flesh from peel to center with high anthocyanin content and excellent flavor — the color holds well through cooking and provides nutritional and visual value comparable to the blue version.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; hill twice as plants grow. Adirondack Red was released in 2004 by Dr. Walter De Jong's Cornell University potato breeding program, one year after Adirondack Blue, specifically developed to provide a red-fleshed complement to the blue-fleshed Adirondack Blue; both share the goal of combining high anthocyanin content, superior visual appeal, and reliable agronomic performance in a named, certified-disease-free variety. The medium-sized, round to oblong tubers have rose-red skin and uniformly pink to red flesh throughout — significantly more uniformly red than older red-flesh varieties like 'Red Gold' which tend to develop red only near the skin. The flavor is excellent — rich, waxy, earthy, and slightly nutty — with flesh that holds its color when boiled or steamed, making it excellent for colorful potato salads, roasted potato platters, and any presentation where the red color adds visual value. Disease resistance, yield, and overall agronomic performance are significantly improved compared to heirloom red-flesh types.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant only after nights stay reliably above 60°F.
directions: Adjuma is a traditional pepper of Guadeloupe and Martinique, prized in Antillean kitchens for a strikingly fruity, floral aroma alongside solid habanero-level heat. Its squat, deeply wrinkled orange-yellow pods form in clusters and are typically used fresh, muddled into vinegar-based hot sauces rather than dried, so plan for repeated light harvests through the season instead of one large drying batch. Like other chinense types it thrives in consistent warmth and humidity, so mulch heavily and water deeply but infrequently to avoid the stress that triggers blossom drop. Choose Adjuma over a standard habanero when the goal is a more perfumed, less sharply citrusy aroma to complement Caribbean-style marinades and condiments.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Adriana is a Little Gem-type miniature romaine bred for fast maturity and heat tolerance, producing dense, sweet, crunchy heads well suited to close spacing and succession planting.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Adriana is a miniature romaine lettuce in the Little Gem tradition, producing small, dense, upright heads with crisp outer leaves and a sweet, tender heart, but bred for notably faster maturity and better heat tolerance than older Little Gem strains, letting gardeners push both the early spring and late fall ends of the lettuce season a bit further. Its compact size makes it well suited to intensive spacing and container growing, and the whole small heads work perfectly as individual salad or Caesar-salad portions without needing to be cut down for a mixed bowl. Harvest the whole head once it feels firm and dense at the base, or begin picking outer leaves earlier for a cut-and-come-again approach. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings in zone 9 to delay bolting as temperatures rise.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–3 weeks after last frost when soil is warm; adzuki beans need a full warm season to produce dried beans.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained soil; adzuki beans are relatively drought-tolerant once established and prefer soil that is not overly rich in nitrogen. Plants produce clusters of small, dark red beans in slender pods; harvest fresh pods at 60–70 days for green shelling beans, or leave pods until they dry and turn tan for the classic small red dried bean. Watch pods closely at maturity as they shatter easily — harvest when most pods are tan but before they split open. The small, sweet beans are famous in East Asian cuisine, particularly for red bean paste in confections.

plant_note: Seedless triploid; start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm, and plant alongside a seeded pollenizer watermelon for fruit set. Affirmed is part of a modern seedless watermelon series bred for reliable yields in warm Southern production regions.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Affirmed is a seedless triploid watermelon hybrid bred as part of a modern commercial series developed for consistent, high-count yields under Southern growing conditions. Because triploid seedless varieties produce little viable pollen, plant a seeded pollenizer variety nearby to ensure good fruit set on the vines. It produces medium to large, crisp, sweet, deep red-fleshed fruit with the classic dark green striping. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned, and handle seedless melons gently since their rinds tend to be slightly thinner than seeded types.

common_name: African Birdseye Pepper (Tiny Very Hot Piri-Piri Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; African Birdseye is the tiny, extremely hot pepper traditionally used to make piri-piri sauce in southern and East Africa.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, since germination is slower and less even than most peppers; transplant only after nights stay warm. African Birdseye produces tiny, upright, intensely hot red pods on a compact, heavily branching bush, the traditional source pepper for piri-piri (peri-peri) sauce across southern and East Africa, later carried by Portuguese traders to become a staple flavoring in Mozambican and Angolan cuisine as well. In frost-free gardens the plant persists as a short-lived shrubby perennial; elsewhere grow it as a warm-season annual and pick continuously to keep new flowers setting.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil reaches 70°F and nights are reliably above 55°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix at 80°F and provide consistent warmth until transplanting. This West African species produces small, rounded fruits in white, green, yellow, or red and is more heat and drought tolerant than common eggplant; it is widely grown as a staple vegetable across sub-Saharan Africa. Harvest fruits while skin is still glossy and firm — they are best eaten cooked in stews, soups, and sauces where their slightly bitter flavor mellows and complements. Plants are perennial in frost-free climates and can be cut back hard after the main season to produce a second flush of fruiting growth.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; transplant when soil temperature reaches 70F. In warm climates (zones 9-11) direct sow in flooded beds after last frost.
directions: Start seeds in shallow flats of moist potting mix at 70-80F, then transplant 6-9-inch seedlings to flooded paddies, water gardens, or large containers filled with heavy garden soil and submerged under 2-4 inches of standing water; African rice tolerates upland, non-flooded cultivation somewhat better than Asian rice, but still performs best with consistent moisture or shallow flooding. Domesticated independently in the Niger River delta region of West Africa thousands of years ago, entirely separately from Asian rice (Oryza sativa), African rice was brought to the Americas by enslaved West Africans and became foundational to the historic Carolina and Gulf Coast lowcountry rice culture, carrying deep agricultural and culinary heritage. It is generally more tolerant of heat, drought, poor soil, and weed competition than Asian rice, though yields tend to run lower and the grain shatters (drops from the panicle) more readily at maturity, so harvest promptly once panicles droop and grains turn golden. Drain standing water three to four weeks before harvest and allow the plant to dry on the stalk before cutting; hand threshing is practical for small home plots.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 2–4 weeks before last frost or direct sow after soil warms in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; cranberry hibiscus is an exceptionally fast-growing tropical shrub used for both edible leaves and ornamental foliage — the deep burgundy-red leaves are among the most striking of any edible plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct sow after frost; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; cranberry hibiscus grows rapidly in warm conditions and begins producing harvestable leaves within 6–8 weeks of planting. Hibiscus acetosella (cranberry hibiscus or African rosemallow) is a tropical West African edible shrub producing dramatically beautiful, deeply lobed, maple-leaf-shaped, deep burgundy-red to maroon foliage on rapidly growing plants that reach 4–6 feet by summer's end — among the most ornamental of all edible plants. The young leaves are harvested and eaten raw in salads (slightly tart, like sorrel, with a bright red-purple color that bleeds into dressings) or cooked as greens in the same manner as its close relative roselle (H. sabdariffa); the tart, cranberry-like flavor comes from hibiscus acids and anthocyanins. Small, lavender-pink flowers bloom in late summer and are also edible. In zone 9, it grows as an annual (or short-lived perennial) from March through November; in zones 10–12, it persists year-round. The rich leaf color and tropical texture make it as ornamental as it is edible — outstanding as a focal point or screening plant in the vegetable garden.

common_name: African Runner Peanut (Historic Small-Seeded Heirloom Peanut)
plant_note: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into loose, sandy, calcium-rich soil that lets the pegs push down easily to form pods.
directions: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into loose, sandy, calcium-rich soil that lets the pegs push down easily to form pods. This small-seeded heirloom peanut traces to peanuts brought to the American South through the transatlantic slave trade and was documented growing at Monticello in Jefferson's own garden notes, making it one of the oldest peanut lines still in American cultivation. Its bushy, low-spreading habit and heavy yield of small, sweet, easy-shelling pods make it well suited to home-scale roasting and boiling, and the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season matches its full maturity window better than most northern gardens can offer.

common_name: African Spiderflower (Spiderwisp, Cat's Whiskers Vegetable, Mchicha wa Pori)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun in any well-drained garden soil; Gynandropsis gynandra grows quickly and can be harvested for greens beginning 4–6 weeks after seeding. The young leaves, tender shoot tips, and flower buds are all edible — boil or steam briefly (the raw leaves can be bitter) and serve with oil or sauce as a nutritious cooked leafy green. It is one of the most nutritious leafy greens available in hot-season gardens, rich in protein, iron, calcium, and vitamins. Self-seeds freely. Closely related to Cleome but now classified in a separate genus. Widely grown as a vegetable throughout sub-Saharan Africa.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — African Spiderflower germinates rapidly in warm soil and begins producing harvestable leaves within 4–6 weeks. Gynandropsis gynandra (formerly Cleome gynandra) is a fast-growing, warm-season annual native throughout tropical Africa, South and Southeast Asia in the Cleomaceae family, one of the most nutritionally important leafy vegetables in the diets of millions of people throughout sub-Saharan Africa, where it is known by many names including 'mchicha wa pori' (Swahili), 'mbikira' (Uganda), and 'nyanya' (parts of West Africa). The plant produces compound leaves of 3–5 leaflets on upright, slightly sticky, aromatic stems, terminating in elongated clusters of small white to pale purple flowers with prominent, long, spider-like stamens — the spider-flower appearance is characteristic of the Cleomaceae family. The young leaves and shoot tips, harvested before the plant flowers, are boiled or stir-fried as a nutritious cooked vegetable — the flavor is slightly bitter and cabbage-like when raw, becoming mildly pleasant when cooked. Nutritional analyses document exceptionally high protein content (the highest of commonly grown leafy vegetables), high iron, calcium, and riboflavin levels — properties that have made G. gynandra the subject of food security research as a nutrient-dense leafy green for hot climates where cool-season greens cannot be grown. Self-seeds prolifically in zone 9-12 gardens once established.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a sturdy trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; African wild calabash produces small, bitter, non-culinary fruit grown mainly for its ornamental or utilitarian gourd rather than eating fresh.
directions: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a sturdy trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; African wild calabash produces small, bitter, non-culinary fruit grown mainly for its ornamental or utilitarian gourd rather than eating fresh. A wild relative of the cultivated bottle gourd, this vigorous, fast-climbing African vine bears small, round, hard-shelled fruit that, unlike the sweeter cultivated bottle gourd, is intensely bitter and not eaten fresh, but the dried, hollowed shell is used traditionally as a small container, rattle, or utensil much like other calabash gourds. Its vigorous growth and attractive white, evening-opening flowers make it a fast-covering vine for a trellis or fence in a frost-free warm-season garden, valued more for ornamental screening and traditional craft use of the dried gourds than as a food crop. Harvest fruit once the shell hardens and the vine begins to die back, then dry thoroughly before hollowing and using the shell.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; African yam bean is a long-day adapted tropical legume that fixes nitrogen and tolerates infertile, slightly acidic, sandy soils typical of West African savannas. Sow 2–3 inches deep.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun after danger of frost has passed; African yam bean is a twining annual legume from West Africa producing seeds with an extremely high protein content (23–29%) — one of the richest protein sources among African grain legumes. The seeds are a major staple and market commodity in Nigeria, Ghana, and surrounding countries, used in a variety of traditional dishes including moi-moi (steamed bean pudding), bean stew, and roasted bean snacks. A notable cooking challenge is the trypsin inhibitors in the raw beans, which require extended cooking or fermentation to neutralize — the seeds cook much more slowly than common beans. The vine is ornamental when trained on a fence or trellis. In zone 9a it grows as a warm-season annual from late spring through fall, producing a reasonable harvest in the long Texas growing season.

common_name: Agati (Hummingbird Tree, Vegetable Hummingbird, August Tree)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in zone 9; Agati is an extremely fast-growing tropical tree — seedlings can reach 15 feet in their first year in zone 9-10. Sow seeds 1 inch deep; nick or scarify the seed coat or soak overnight in warm water before planting. In zone 9, treat as a warm-season annual or short-lived perennial that regrows from the base if frozen. Harvest leaves and flowers continuously from 2-3 months after germination.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil after temperatures warm above 70°F; Agati grows equally well in poor, sandy, or clay soils and fixes atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility. Sesbania grandiflora is one of the most useful edible trees in tropical and subtropical agroforestry — a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing legume tree native to South and Southeast Asia where its white or red flowers (2–4 inches long, the largest flowers in the Fabaceae), young leaves, and tender seed pods are prized vegetables in Thai, Filipino, Indonesian, and Indian cuisines. The flowers are eaten raw in salads, battered and fried, or cooked in curries and soups; the young leaves are used like spinach or kale; the long, flat seed pods are cooked as a vegetable. The tree is also an important fodder and green manure crop. In zone 9, Sesbania grandiflora grows spectacularly fast — often reaching 20+ feet in a single growing season — and produces beautiful pendant flowers continuously. It is killed to the ground by hard frost but may resprout from the crown in zone 9b. Harvest foliage and flowers regularly to stimulate continuous production and prevent the plant from becoming leggy. The large white or red flowers are highly attractive to hummingbirds and native bees.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; fresh seed is critical as viability drops sharply after 6 months — sow generously.
directions: Sow very fresh seed 1/4 inch deep thickly in cool, well-drained soil, as germination rates drop dramatically when seed is more than a few months old — plan to sow thickly and use thinnings. Agretti is an Italian coastal plant related to glasswort, and it thrives in sandy, saline, or alkaline soils where most vegetables struggle; it is very intolerant of waterlogged conditions. Harvest young shoot tips and the grass-like, succulent leaves when 6–8 inches tall by snipping with scissors 1–2 inches above the soil, allowing the plant to regrow once or twice before it goes to seed. The slender, fleshy, bright-green leaves have a mildly salty, slightly mineral flavor outstanding blanched with lemon or served alongside fish and seafood in the Italian spring tradition.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after the last frost once soil is thoroughly warm; unlike jicama, ahipa is not photoperiod-sensitive and will size up its roots reliably during long temperate summer days, so it does not need a tropical short-day season to bulk up.
directions: A domesticated relative of jicama from the eastern Andean valleys of Bolivia and northern Argentina, ahipa grows as a compact, bushy, semi-erect legume rather than jicama's rampant climbing vine, so it needs no trellis and fits closer garden spacing. Pinch off flower buds as they form throughout the season to keep the plant's energy directed into the turnip-shaped storage roots instead of seed production. As with jicama, only the root is edible; the foliage, pods, and seeds contain rotenone and should not be eaten. Harvest once foliage begins to yellow in fall, typically 5–6 months after sowing.

plant_note: Long-day onion; start early indoors for northern gardens.
directions: Ailsa Craig is a long-day heirloom producing very large, globe-shaped golden bulbs with a mild, sweet flavor, best grown in northern latitudes. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and set out seedlings as soon as the soil is workable, spacing 4-6 inches apart. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly watered through bulbing, then taper off water as tops begin to fall. These sweet onions store only a few months, so use the largest bulbs first.

common_name: Ailsa Craig Tomato (Classic Scottish Heirloom Slicer)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Ailsa Craig is a compact-vined indeterminate variety long favored in Scottish and English glasshouses and outdoor gardens alike, so it appreciates staking and consistent moisture through fruit set.
directions: Sow seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees F, staking or caging the vines as they grow. Ailsa Craig was bred in Girvan, Scotland in the early 1900s and quickly became one of the most widely grown tomatoes in British gardens and allotments, prized for producing heavy clusters of medium, smooth, bright red fruit with a well-balanced, classic tomato flavor. It remains a benchmark variety in the UK for home growers wanting a dependable, flavorful, mid-sized slicer.

plant_note: Plant aerial bulbils or underground tubers after last frost in well-drained, sandy to loamy, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; air potato is an extremely vigorous tropical vine that can grow 20–30 feet in a single season — site with care to avoid the plant overwhelming support structures or neighboring plants. Note: Dioscorea bulbifera is a USDA Federal Noxious Weed listed as invasive in Florida — check local regulations before planting.
directions: Plant aerial bulbils (the small, potato-like structures that form along the stems) or underground tubers after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with a sturdy trellis, fence, or tree for support; air potato grows extremely rapidly in warm conditions. IMPORTANT: In Florida and other warm states, Dioscorea bulbifera is listed as invasive and its cultivation is regulated or prohibited — consult USDA and state Department of Agriculture guidelines before planting. Dioscorea bulbifera is a tropical Asian vine grown widely in Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and the Pacific Islands as a minor food crop — the aerial bulbils (small, edible tubers that develop at the leaf axils) and the underground tubers are both edible after cooking, though many wild or feral populations contain potentially toxic compounds that require thorough boiling in multiple changes of water to render safe; cultivated varieties are generally milder. In markets across West Africa and Asia, edible cultivars are distinguished from bitter, toxic ones by appearance and flavor; seek out named edible cultivars from specialty tropical plant sources. The vine is a remarkably productive food plant in tropical gardens but must be managed aggressively to prevent escape.

common_name: Aji Amarillo Pepper (Fruity Orange-Yellow Peruvian Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Aji Amarillo has a long season to maturity (90–120 days from transplant) — in zone 9, the long warm season supports full production from spring transplants.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aji Amarillo is the foundational hot pepper of Peruvian cuisine — considered one of the essential 'holy trinity' ingredients of Peruvian cooking (with garlic and onion) and the basis for Peru's iconic yellow sauces. The 3–5 inch, elongated-conical, thin-walled fruits ripen from green through orange-yellow to bright yellow-orange, with a distinctive fruity, tropical flavor and significant heat (30,000–50,000 Scoville units) that is entirely different from the neutral burn of jalapeños. The fruity, complex flavor — often described as combining apricot, mango, and passion fruit with a persistent, building heat — makes Aji Amarillo irreplaceable in Peruvian cooking and increasingly prized by chefs worldwide for its unique flavor profile. As a Capsicum baccatum species (the Andean species group distinct from C. annuum and C. chinense), Aji Amarillo requires somewhat warmer germination temperatures and a longer season than standard bell peppers. In zone 9, the long growing season is ideal for the 90–120 day maturity period, and the plants may become quite large (3–4 feet) and productive by mid-summer. Fresh fruits, paste, and dried/powdered form all have distinct culinary applications. The dried, rehydrated paste is the standard form used in traditional Peruvian cooking.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum chinense requires warm soil (80–90°F) and is slow to germinate — use a heat mat. In zone 9 start in December–January and transplant in March–April. Aji Charapita is a short-day plant from equatorial Peru and may produce more freely with supplemental lighting in northern areas. In zone 9 the plant can be maintained as a perennial, returning to larger size each year from a woody base.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Aji Charapita is a wild-type Capsicum chinense pepper from the Peruvian Amazon, producing an extraordinary abundance of tiny pea-sized (3–5 mm) round yellow fruits on a prolific, heavily branching plant. The fruits are one of the most expensive peppers by weight in the world — sold as a specialty ingredient in high-end Peruvian and international cuisine for their unique combination of intense heat (30,000–50,000 Scoville), exceptional fruity citrus-tropical fragrance, and concentrated flavor. Because each fruit is pea-sized, a single productive plant can bear hundreds of fruits simultaneously, covering the plant in an impressive display of tiny yellow peppers. The flavor is described as intensely fruity with citrus, mango, and passion fruit notes beneath the heat — the signature Capsicum chinense fruity aromatic character concentrated into a miniature fruit. In Peru, Aji Charapita is used in ceviche, sauces, and as a table condiment in vinegar brine.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since this Bolivian-Peruvian baccatum type needs a long warm season to fully ripen its pendant pods.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since this Bolivian-Peruvian baccatum type needs a long warm season to fully ripen its pendant, 3-5 inch pods. Fruit matures from green through orange to a deep brick-red, carrying a fast-hitting heat (roughly 20,000-30,000 Scoville units) that fades quickly and leaves a sweet, fruity aftertaste. Thin walls make it well suited to drying or blending into fresh aji sauces once red-ripe; harvest continuously to extend production into fall.

common_name: Aji Crystal Pepper (Chilean Mild Yellow Baccatum Sweet Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Aji Crystal is a Capsicum baccatum species pepper, which requires slightly higher germination temperatures than C. annuum types and benefits from longer indoor growing time before transplanting. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer harvest. The pale, translucent-looking fruits develop their characteristic crystal-clear quality when harvested at the green-yellow stage; harvesting when pale yellow-cream rather than waiting for orange-red gives the mildest, most crisp results.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest pale yellow to cream-white fruits for mildest flavor; allow to ripen orange-red for sweeter, more developed flavor. Aji Crystal is a Chilean baccatum pepper from the Capsicum baccatum species — a pepper species distinct from the common C. annuum and characterized by the spotted calyx markings at the base of the flower, a more complex flavor profile, and a heat level that can range from mild to medium-hot. Aji Crystal is at the mild end of the baccatum spectrum, with very low heat (typically under 500 SHU) that makes it essentially a sweet pepper with baccatum's distinctive flavor complexity. The fruits are elongated (4–5 inches), thin-walled, and pale yellow to near-white at the harvest stage — almost translucent in appearance, suggesting the crystal-clear quality for which the variety is named. The flavor is crisp, bright, slightly sweet and tangy with a fruity, aromatic quality distinctive of baccatum peppers — difficult to describe but clearly different from C. annuum sweet peppers and very pleasant raw in salads, stuffed, or used fresh in Peruvian-style preparations where baccatum peppers are traditional. Aji Crystal is popular among pepper enthusiasts and chefs interested in flavors beyond the standard C. annuum palette.

common_name: Aji Dulce Pepper (Sweet Habanero, Cachucha Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes. Aji dulce is heat-loving and thrives in the Gulf Coast and tropical gardens — in zone 9 it often returns as a perennial from the base after mild winters. The flavor is essential in Caribbean cooking, particularly in Puerto Rican sofrito and Cuban recao sauce.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger; aji dulce is the sweet-fruited strain of the habanero pepper species (Capsicum chinense) — it looks exactly like a miniature habanero with thin, wrinkled skin in green ripening to yellow-orange or red, and has all the distinctive floral, fruity, intensely aromatic habanero fragrance without any heat whatsoever (Scoville 0–500, vs 100,000–350,000 for regular habanero). The aroma and flavor are extraordinary — simultaneously citrusy, floral, fruity, and deeply savory — making aji dulce irreplaceable in Puerto Rican, Dominican, Venezuelan, and Cuban cooking, where it is the backbone of sofrito, the aromatic base paste for countless dishes. In zone 9–12 gardens it often becomes a short-lived perennial shrub. An outstanding unique pepper for gardeners who love the habanero aroma but want zero capsaicin heat.

common_name: Aji Fantasy Pepper (Finnish-Bred Translucent Yellow Baccatum)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost; this compact, high-yielding baccatum variety matures faster than most aji types.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost; this compact, high-yielding baccatum variety was developed in Finland and matures faster than most aji types, making it a good option for shorter growing seasons. The roughly 2 inch, bonnet-shaped pods ripen to a translucent yellow and deliver a mild-to-medium heat (about 5,000-10,000 Scoville units) with pronounced tropical sweetness. Stake plants as they load up with fruit, and pick continuously to keep the heavily branching bushes producing.

plant_note: Start on a heat mat 8–10 weeks before last frost; Aji Panca is one of Peru's most important culinary peppers, a large, deep red to dark chocolate-red chile with mild heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) and an exceptional smoky, fruity, berry-like flavor used as the base of many traditional Peruvian sauces, marinades, and stews including aji de gallina.
directions: Start seeds on a heat mat at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost when soil is warm. Aji Panca is one of the most important and distinctive chiles in Peruvian cuisine, a large (3–4 inch), elongated, deep brownish-red pepper belonging to Capsicum chinense but with very mild heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) and an extraordinary flavor profile: smoky, deeply fruity, berry-like, and slightly sweet with almost no raw pungency — it is more like a richly flavored dried fruit than a typical hot pepper. In Peru it is primarily used dried and pureed as a chile paste (pasta de aji panca) that forms the flavor base of marinades, braises, anticuchos (grilled beef hearts), and the classic preparation aji de gallina. Rarely found outside Latin American grocery stores in the US; growing your own from seed is the only way to access this unique pepper fresh in most American gardens.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March for spring production. Support the large, indeterminate vines with cages or stakes. In zone 9 the fall planting in August–September often produces the highest-quality fruits as temperatures moderate; spring crops should be harvested before peak summer heat reduces fruit quality.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy stake or cage support; Akers West Virginia is an heirloom tomato preserved in the Appalachian tradition of West Virginia seed saving, producing large, meaty, deep red beefsteak-type fruits with a classic, complex, sweet-acidic flavor typical of the best Old World tomato varieties maintained by Appalachian farm families for generations. The large (often 12–24 ounce) fruits have thick, meaty walls with small seed cavities and outstanding fresh-eating flavor — the balanced combination of sweetness and bright acidity makes Akers West Virginia one of the most satisfying large heirloom varieties for fresh slicing. The fruit shows good resistance to cracking despite its size. Like most Appalachian heirlooms, Akers West Virginia developed in a region with variable, challenging weather and has proven adaptability to different growing conditions. In zone 9 the fall crop (planted in August, harvested October–November) often produces exceptionally flavored fruits as cooler temperatures concentrate sugars and acid.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Alabama Blue is a cold-hardy heirloom collard whose flavor sweetens noticeably after frost.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or transplant to final spacing once seedlings have several true leaves. Alabama Blue is a Deep South heirloom collard grown for generations for its striking blue-green, slightly savoyed leaves and excellent cold hardiness, surviving hard freezes that damage less hardy greens and developing sweeter, milder flavor after exposure to frost. The tall, upright plants produce abundant leaves over a long harvest window when picked cut-and-come-again style, taking outer leaves as needed while the center continues producing. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season for the best leaf production, and watch for cabbage worms and aphids, which can be managed with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide.

common_name: Alabama Blue Collards (Southern Heirloom Blue-Green Collard)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Alabama Blue is a traditional open-pollinated Deep South collard passed down through generations of home gardeners.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alabama Blue is a traditional open-pollinated Deep South collard with broad, slightly savoyed, distinctly blue-green leaves, maintained and passed down through generations of Southern home gardeners rather than developed by a commercial breeding program. The flavor is rich and full-bodied even before frost, and like other collards sweetens further after the first light freezes of fall. Plants are tall and vigorous, tolerating both Gulf South summer heat and winter cold well, and the open-pollinated nature means seed can be saved from the best plants each year to maintain the strain in a home garden. Harvest the lower and outer leaves as needed, leaving the growing tip intact so the plant keeps producing fresh leaves from the top over a long cool-season harvest window.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Alabama Red is a tall, productive Deep South heirloom okra with dark red pods developed and maintained in Alabama home gardens, one of several distinct regional red okra heirloom strains and generally taller and more vigorous than shorter red okra types.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 18–24 inches in rows 3 feet apart; soak seeds overnight before planting. Alabama Red is a regional heirloom okra from Alabama home gardens, one of the distinct Deep South red-podded okra strains that differs from Red Velvet in being taller, more vigorous, and producing somewhat more slender pods with an intensely dark red to mahogany coloring; the flavor is excellent, with a slightly richer taste than some green varieties, and the pods are harvested at 3–4 inches for peak tenderness. Like other red okras, the pigment is water-soluble and leaches from the pods during cooking unless they are quickly roasted or fried. The tall plants (5–8 feet) with deeply lobed leaves and large yellow-centered flowers make Alabama Red an outstanding ornamental-edible for the Southern food garden. Maintained by seed savers in Alabama and nearby states and representative of the regional diversity in Southern okra cultivation.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or late winter in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alamo is a hybrid turnip greens variety bred for moderate bolt resistance and tolerance of aphids and mosaic virus, with vigorous regrowth for repeated cut-and-come-again harvest starting as early as 33 days.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alamo is a modern hybrid turnip grown for its greens rather than its roots, producing up to 50% higher yield than standard turnip greens varieties along with excellent regrowth after cutting, letting a single planting support several harvests through the cool season. It shows moderate resistance to bolting and tolerates aphids and mosaic virus better than many older turnip greens varieties, useful for stretching a spring planting later into warming weather. Harvest young leaves at 6-10 inches for the most tender greens, cutting to about 4 inches above the crown and allowing regrowth for the next cutting. Because it establishes and regrows quickly, Alamo suits both a fall planting for winter greens and a spring planting for an early crop.

plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; because Albina Vereduna's roots are pure white, they never stain cutting boards or bleed color into other foods the way red beets do.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to 3–4 inches once true leaves appear. Albina Vereduna is an old Dutch heirloom beet that produces round, creamy-white roots with a sweet, mild flavor generally regarded as less earthy than red beets, and because it contains no betalain pigment it can be roasted, pickled, or grated into salads without staining hands, cutting boards, or other ingredients pink. The glossy green tops are also excellent cooked as greens and, lacking red pigment, cook up a cleaner green than the tops of red beet varieties. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, tender roots and harvest at 2–3 inches across for the best texture, since oversized roots can turn woody.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 the prime window is October–February for a fall/winter/spring crop. White beet seed is a cluster like all beets — one 'seed' germinates multiple seedlings that must be thinned to 4 inches apart for full-sized roots.
directions: Sow seed clusters 1/2 inch deep in loose, deep, well-amended soil; thin to 4 inches after seedlings reach 2 inches tall. Albino White Beet is a German heirloom producing smooth, round, pure white-fleshed roots that completely lack the red pigment (betalain) of standard beets. The absence of betalains means Albino White beets do not bleed red — they do not stain cutting boards, hands, clothing, or dishes, solving the primary practical complaint about cooking with beets. Flavor is milder, sweeter, and less earthy than red beets — some tasters describe the flavor as more like a very sweet parsnip than a classic beet. Excellent raw in salads where they won't discolor other ingredients, roasted until caramelized and sweet, or pickled in the traditional manner (they turn slightly golden-pink when pickled in wine vinegar). The greens are pale green and mild, also excellent cooked. White beets are often grown alongside red and golden beets for a colorful root vegetable display. In zone 9, fall-planted white beets mature beautifully through mild winters.

plant_note: Start indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost and set transplants out as soon as soil is workable, or start a second round in midsummer for a fall crop.
directions: Alcosa forms dense, medium-sized heads wrapped in deeply blistered, blue-green savoyed leaves that hold their crinkled texture well into cold weather. Its compact frame allows tighter in-row spacing than standard round cabbages, making it a good fit for smaller beds or intensive succession planting. The heavily textured leaves are notably tender for a savoy type and hold up in the garden without splitting for an extended harvest window. Choose Alcosa when you want the classic savoy crinkle and cold tolerance in a shorter-season, space-efficient package.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter to early spring; in zone 9 sow January–February for a March–April harvest before heat ends the season. Alderman is a tall vine (4–5 feet) requiring a sturdy trellis or fence. In zone 9 the spring pea season is brief — 6–10 weeks from planting to heat shutdown. A fall sowing in October can extend the season, but fall peas in zone 9 often produce a lighter crop than spring.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; provide a trellis or fence for the tall vines; Alderman (also known as Tall Telephone) is a large-vine heirloom shelling pea producing very large, dark green pods of 4–5 inches, each containing 7–9 fat, sweet, dark green peas — the largest peas of any standard shelling type. It has been grown in American gardens since the 1880s and remains a benchmark for flavor and production among home garden peas. The large, starchy-sweet peas are particularly good for freezing because their size and firm texture hold up better than smaller-seeded varieties. The tall vines (4–5 feet) require stout support but reward with heavy production when trellised properly. Alderman is specifically adapted to the heavy production that makes the short cool-season window economically worthwhile for home gardeners and market growers — the high pod count and large pod size maximize yield from the brief growing window in zone 9. Do not fertilize heavily with nitrogen; peas fix their own and excess nitrogen promotes foliage over fruit.

common_name: Aleppo Pepper (Halaby Pepper, Syrian Dried Spice Chile with Fruity Mild Heat)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Aleppo pepper is grown primarily as a drying pepper — the fruits are harvested when fully red and ripe, then halved and dried before being crushed into the characteristic coarse flakes with their distinctive oily texture and dark red color. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production. The variety is adapted to hot, dry Mediterranean conditions and performs well in zone 9's summer heat with moderate irrigation. A single productive plant can yield enough peppers for a year's supply of home-ground Aleppo pepper flakes. The drying process is critical to developing the characteristic flavor: Aleppo peppers are traditionally partially dried, then crushed while retaining some moisture and oil content — producing the characteristic slightly moist, aromatic flakes rather than the bone-dry texture of paprika or cayenne.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest when fully red; dry and crush for spice. Aleppo Pepper (also known as Halaby pepper, from Halab, the Arabic name for Aleppo) is a Capsicum annuum variety from Aleppo, Syria — a historic spice and trading city in northern Syria that gave its name to the region's most important spice pepper. Aleppo pepper occupies a unique position in global spice use: with a Scoville rating of approximately 10,000 units, it provides mild to moderate heat (significantly less than cayenne at 30,000–50,000 SHU) combined with a complex, distinctive flavor profile — fruity and slightly sweet, with undertones of cumin and salt, and a characteristic oiliness and depth unlike any other commonly used dried pepper spice. The pepper's distinctive quality comes from the drying and processing method: fruits are split, seeds are removed (seeds are slightly bitter), and the halved peppers are dried partially before being crushed into coarse, slightly moist flakes with a characteristic dark red color and shiny surface from the natural oils retained through partial drying. This traditional processing is quite different from completely desiccated paprika or cayenne, producing a spice with a unique fresh-dried quality. The Syrian civil war that began in 2011 severely disrupted Aleppo pepper production, causing supply shortages and price spikes in global markets; production has since been supplemented by Turkish-grown peppers of similar varieties and by growers in North America who have adopted the variety.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is at least 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–April. Ali Baba is an Iraqi/Middle Eastern landrace watermelon specifically adapted to intense heat and dry conditions — an excellent choice for zone 9 where summer heat can stress ordinary watermelons.
directions: Plant in hills spaced 6–8 feet apart in full sun, well-drained, fertile soil; Ali Baba is an heirloom watermelon landrace from Iraq, where it has been cultivated for centuries in the intense heat and aridity of the Tigris-Euphrates region. The large (20–30 pound), pale green, blocky-oval fruits have vibrant red, exceptionally sweet and flavorful flesh with small seeds. What sets Ali Baba apart for Gulf Coast and zone 9 gardeners is its remarkable adaptation to heat: it continues setting fruit and maintains its characteristic sweetness through temperatures that stress modern commercial varieties, making it one of the best heirlooms for hot, dry or hot-humid summer conditions. It is also notably drought-tolerant compared to most watermelons once established. Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds introduced it to American growers and it has gained a devoted following among gardeners who prize heat tolerance and excellent flavor. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit dries and the skin lightens; the yellow ground spot also intensifies as fruit ripens.

common_name: Alicante Tomato (British Garden and Greenhouse Slicer)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Alicante sets fruit reliably in cooler summers and short seasons, making it a mainstay of British allotments and greenhouses.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once temperatures are reliably warm, providing a stake or cage for the indeterminate vines. Alicante is a long-established open-pollinated British variety known for consistent early cropping and smooth, medium-sized, deep red fruit with a well-rounded, sweet-tart flavor that holds up in cooler, shorter growing seasons. It has been a staple recommendation of UK seed catalogs and gardening programs for decades as a reliable outdoor and unheated-greenhouse tomato.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring once soil is workable; parsnips need a long season.
directions: Sow fresh seed 1/2 inch deep directly in loose, stone-free soil, since parsnips do not transplant well and seed is short-lived. Germination is slow, often two to four weeks, so keep the bed evenly moist and mark the row. This variety thickens early, maturing in as little as 95 days, producing tender white roots with a sweet, distinctive flavor. Flavor sweetens further after a fall frost, so leave roots in the ground and harvest as needed through cold weather.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces January–February in zone 9; All Blue is a mid-season variety (75–90 days) that maintains its striking blue-purple flesh color throughout cooking. Plan for May harvest before summer heat arrives in zone 9.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in rich, loose, well-drained soil; All Blue (also called All Purple) is a heritage variety with Andean ancestry, producing medium-sized, oblong tubers with deep blue-purple skin and intensely blue-purple flesh throughout — the color does not fade with cooking, making brilliant blue-purple mashed potatoes, blue potato salad, and striking roasted wedges. The color is produced by anthocyanins — the same pigments in blueberries — that are potent antioxidants. Flavor is earthy and slightly nutty, pleasant but not as rich as Yukon Gold or fingerlings. All Blue has relatively firm, waxy flesh that holds its shape when boiled or roasted. The plants are vigorous and productive. In zone 9, the unusual color makes them a conversation-starting crop at the farmers' market or dinner table; they are consistently one of the most visually dramatic vegetables in the garden when cut open. Plant alongside Red LaSoda for a striking red, white, and blue potato planting.

plant_note: Succession sow spring through fall; heat-tolerant and slow to bolt.
directions: This adaptable heirloom lettuce forms crisp, mild green heads and resists bolting better than most, letting you harvest across spring, summer, and fall. Sow seed shallowly, barely covering it, since light aids germination, and thin plants to 8-12 inches for full heads. Succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply, and provide afternoon shade during hot spells to keep leaves sweet. It also performs well in containers and hydroponic setups.

common_name: Alliance Bell Pepper (Multi-Virus and Bacterial Spot-Resistant Hybrid)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Alliance combines resistance to several races of bacterial leaf spot with tolerance to multiple viruses (potato virus Y, potato yellow mosaic virus, tobacco mosaic virus, and cucumber mosaic virus), an especially broad virus-resistance package for aphid-prone Gulf South gardens.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Alliance is a bell pepper hybrid bred for resistance to several races of bacterial leaf spot along with tolerance to an unusually wide range of viruses, giving it strong protection against both the bacterial and viral diseases that spread readily through humid Gulf South gardens via rain splash and aphid activity. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good flavor if left on the plant. Because viral diseases have no cure once a plant is infected, Alliance's broad tolerance package helps prevent the stunting, mottled foliage, and reduced yield that viruses cause in more susceptible varieties. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued fruit set.

common_name: Allsweet Watermelon (Striped Oblong Southern Heirloom Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is 70°F or warmer; Allsweet is a large-fruited heirloom watermelon producing classic oblong fruits with dark green skin and bold pale green stripes weighing 25–35 pounds — one of the traditional 'picnic watermelons' prized for its high sugar content, bright red flesh, and excellent keeping quality after harvest; one of the defining watermelon varieties of Southern U.S. home gardens.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds (thin to 2 plants) or individual transplants after soil warms; provide ample space (6–10 feet in all directions) for vigorous vines; stop irrigation when fruits are nearly ripe to concentrate sugars; test ripeness by thumping (dull thud), checking the ground spot (turning yellow), or pressing on the vine end of the fruit. Allsweet is a large, oblong, open-pollinated watermelon developed and marketed by Dessert Seed Company that became one of the most widely grown home garden and commercial watermelons in the Southern states during the latter decades of the 20th century. The classic appearance — elongated oval fruits averaging 25–35 pounds with dark green skin boldly marked by lighter green stripes, bright red flesh, and black seeds in the traditional style — made Allsweet the archetypical 'picnic watermelon' of the American South. The flavor lives up to the name: exceptionally sweet (Brix 12–14), with the characteristic deep red color and firm, crisp texture that distinguished traditional open-pollinated watermelons from modern seedless varieties. Allsweet produces fruits with good keeping quality after harvest — they hold well in cool storage for 2–3 weeks — and the vines are productive and disease-tolerant under Gulf Coast and Deep South summer conditions. A standard comparison point against which other traditional watermelons are measured in Southern gardens, and an important landmark in the history of American watermelon breeding.

plant_note: Direct sow thickly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alltop was bred purely for greens production and does not bulb, so plant closer than a root-crop turnip and cut leaves repeatedly rather than thinning for roots.
directions: Direct sow thickly in fertile, well-drained soil, in full sun for the fastest growth or partial shade in warmer weather; Alltop is a Southern-bred turnip selected purely for its tops and produces no usable bulb at all, channeling its energy instead into a heavy, upright flush of smooth, dark, mild-flavored leaves. It is markedly more heat- and bolt-tolerant than dual-purpose turnip varieties, which lets it be sown earlier in late summer and later into spring than most turnip greens, and it regrows vigorously after cutting for repeated cut-and-come-again harvests through fall and winter. Because there is no root to size up, plants can be spaced tightly and simply mowed or sheared back by a third to a half whenever leaves reach eating size, making it an efficient, high-yield choice for gardeners who grow turnips strictly for potlikker and greens rather than roots.

common_name: Alma Paprika Pepper (Hungarian Round Paprika for Drying and Grinding)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Alma Paprika is a Hungarian heirloom producing small round fruits (1.5–2 inches diameter) that ripen from creamy white through yellow to vivid red. The round shape and thick but not waxy flesh make it ideal for drying and grinding into genuine sweet Hungarian paprika. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the compact plant habit (18–24 inches) makes it suitable for containers. Fruits are very mild (500–1,500 SHU) with a rich, sweet paprika flavor that develops fully when dried. Unlike many commercially produced paprika peppers that are harvested by machine and dried at high temperatures, home-dried Alma Paprika can be slow-dried at low heat to preserve volatile aromatics.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost and harvest when fully red for drying. Alma Paprika Pepper is a Hungarian heirloom variety prized by home paprika makers for its compact, round fruits that dry easily and produce an aromatic, sweet paprika powder with far more complexity than commercially available dried paprika. The variety belongs to the traditional Hungarian paprika pepper classifications — distinguished from the longer 'szegedi' or 'kalocsal' types by its apple-like round shape — and is named 'Alma' (Hungarian for 'apple') in direct reference to this distinctive fruit form. The flavor progression through ripening stages is one of this variety's most interesting characteristics: at the creamy-white stage the fruit is mildly sweet and slightly starchy, similar to a mild Italian frying pepper; at yellow it develops a fruitier, slightly citrusy edge; at full red ripeness the paprika sweetness is fully expressed with a rich, slightly smoky underlying note. Gardeners can use Alma Paprika at any ripe stage for fresh eating — it performs well in salads, stuffed preparations, and light sautés — but its primary use is drying. Halved and laid cut-side-down on screens in warm sun or placed in a food dehydrator at 120–130°F, the fruits dry thoroughly within 3–5 days and grind to a vivid orange-red powder. Compact plant size makes Alma Paprika one of the most productive paprika types per square foot of garden space.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes; the long maturity period is intended to bring heads to harvest just before hard fall frost for winter storage.
directions: Amager is a Danish heirloom bred for the cold, damp climate of its namesake island, producing extremely dense, round heads that keep in a root cellar longer than most cabbage varieties. The tight internal packing that makes it a slow, late-season grower is the same trait that gives it exceptional storage life, often into late winter under proper conditions. Its heavy cold tolerance lets it stay in the field later into fall than earlier-maturing cabbages, concentrating sugars and improving flavor after frost. Plant Amager specifically for long-haul winter storage rather than fresh summer eating.

common_name: Amana Orange Tomato (Very Large Sweet Low-Acid Orange Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Amana Orange originated in the Amana Colonies of Iowa, an historic German communal settlement that maintained distinctive traditional varieties; the tomato was preserved by colony members for generations before entering the American heirloom seed trade.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Amana Orange is one of the finest very-large orange beefsteak heirloom tomatoes — producing massive (1–2 lb), irregularly shaped, deeply orange-colored fruits with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid flesh that creates the most mild, sweet, non-acidic fresh tomato experience available from any heirloom type. The very large fruit size and characteristic sweet, almost candy-like low-acid flavor make Amana Orange one of the most distinctive eating experiences among heirloom tomatoes. The brilliant, uniform deep-orange color — consistent across the exterior and interior flesh without the bicolor patterns of Pineapple or Big Rainbow — provides a vivid single-color presentation that is striking in its own right. The meaty, dense orange flesh has relatively few seeds and an exceptionally high flesh-to-gel ratio that maximizes the edible portion. As an open-pollinated heirloom from the Amana Colonies of Iowa, the variety carries cultural significance alongside its outstanding eating quality. Amana Orange plants are large, vigorous indeterminate vines requiring sturdy 6-foot support. The long growing season (80–95 days) means zone 9 gardeners should start seeds as early as possible to ensure fruit development before summer heat. An outstanding choice for anyone who finds standard tomatoes too acid.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before the last frost, or later in summer for a fall crop; leaves can be cut young or left to mature.
directions: Direct sow shallowly into fertile soil and thin seedlings as they grow, cutting outer leaves for continuous harvest or letting plants reach full size. This traditional Ethiopian selection produces large, smooth, paddle-shaped blue-green leaves with a sharper, more pungent bite than common mustard greens, and it is a staple ingredient in Ethiopian gomen dishes. It tolerates both heat and cool weather better than many mustards, giving it a longer harvest window through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–3 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65°F; seeds are tiny and benefit from surface sowing.
directions: Scatter tiny seeds on the soil surface or press in no deeper than 1/8 inch, and keep moist until germination; thin to 6–12 inches once seedlings are established. Vegetable amaranth thrives in heat and is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established, making it a reliable summer green when spinach has bolted. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips continuously from 30 days onward; regular harvesting delays flowering and extends the harvest window. Leaves are best cooked briefly — sautéed, steamed, or simmered in soups — and are rich in iron and calcium.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 8-9 gardens transplant in August-September, adding roughly two extra weeks beyond the stated maturity to account for slower fall growth as light and temperatures decline.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart with 24-36 inches between rows, and feed generously since Amazing needs vigorous leaf growth to protect its curd. This variety is valued for its self-blanching habit: large, upright wrapper leaves naturally curl in over the developing curd, shielding it from sun and weather so it stays creamy white without the hand-tying required by older cauliflower varieties. Amazing's extended, somewhat uneven maturity window is actually an asset for home gardeners, since plants in the same bed don't all come ready at once, spreading a single planting's harvest out over several weeks instead of demanding it all be used or preserved immediately. It is widely regarded as one of the more forgiving fall cauliflowers for gardeners still learning to time brassica plantings against the first frost.

common_name: Amazonian Yam Bean (Chuin, Jicáma de Árbol)
plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil well after all frost danger has passed; this species needs a long, humid tropical-to-subtropical growing season of eight months or more to fully size its roots, so outside true tropical climates it is best attempted in a large container or greenhouse border.
directions: Native to the Amazon basin and cultivated across lowland tropical South America, this vigorous twining vine produces the largest storage roots of the cultivated yam beans, sometimes exceeding several pounds under good conditions, with flesh that is starchier and less sweet than jicama's. Provide a sturdy trellis or fence, since the vine climbs aggressively and can smother nearby plants if left unsupported. Remove flower buds as they appear to keep the plant's energy focused on root bulking rather than seed set. As with its relatives, only the cooked or raw root is edible; the leaves, pods, and seeds contain rotenone and are toxic.

common_name: Ambercup Squash (Golden Orange Compact Kabocha-Style Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Ambercup is a kabocha-type winter squash with golden-amber to deep orange skin and intensely rich, sweet, dry flesh — one of the best-flavored compact winter squashes for home gardens, producing 5–7 lb fruits with firm, dense flesh that stores well through winter; similar to Red Kuri in texture and sweetness but with a distinctive golden-orange skin.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil; vines are moderate in length (6–8 feet), more manageable than butternut or hubbard types; harvest when the skin is a uniform deep golden-amber and resists fingernail denting; cure for 2–3 weeks after harvest to maximize sweetness and storage life. Ambercup is an heirloom-type open-pollinated winter squash of the Cucurbita maxima species — the same species as kabocha, Red Kuri, Blue Hubbard, and Buttercup — that produces compact, round to slightly flattened fruits with smooth, glossy, deep golden-orange skin and a very small indented cavity at the blossom end. The flesh is the dry, dense, intensely orange, and very sweet type characteristic of the best maxima squashes, making Ambercup one of the most flavorful winter squashes for baking, roasting, and soup-making. The golden-amber skin is distinctive and attractive — warmer in color than the grey-green of standard kabocha, lighter than Buttercup's dark green, and different from Red Kuri's red-orange — making it visually distinctive in the garden and at market. Ambercup performs reliably across a wide range of climates from zone 3 to zone 9 and stores exceptionally well under cool, dry conditions — quality often improves with 1–2 months of storage as the starches convert to sugars. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Ambercup should be direct-sown in late March or early April to allow the full season before summer heat arrives.

plant_note: Plant shallot sets 4–8 weeks before last frost in spring, or in fall in zones 7–10 for a June harvest; Ambition is a widely grown European F1 shallot producing uniform, oval, red-violet to copper-skinned bulbs in clusters of 5–10 per set with the classic shallot flavor — mild, sweet, and slightly garlicky — in a reliable, high-yielding variety preferred in professional kitchens throughout Europe.
directions: Plant shallot sets 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart, with the tip just at soil level; each set multiplies into a cluster of 5–10 bulbs; keep consistently moist during establishment and in spring; reduce watering as leaves begin to yellow and fall over; harvest when tops fall and bulb skins are dry and papery, then cure for 2–3 weeks before storage. Ambition is a European F1 hybrid shallot produced by commercial seed companies primarily in the Netherlands, where the commercial shallot industry has been refined over centuries into highly productive, uniform varieties for both professional kitchen use and home garden production. The Ambition variety produces medium-sized, uniformly shaped, oval to pear-shaped bulbs with red-violet to copper-mahogany skin and purplish-pink inner flesh; each planted set multiplies into a cluster of 5–10 distinct bulbs, the characteristic growth habit that distinguishes shallots from onions (which produce a single bulb from a set). The flavor is the classic shallot character — more subtle, sweet, and complex than onions, with a slightly garlicky undertone that distinguishes shallots as the preferred allium in French haute cuisine for vinaigrettes, pan sauces, and dishes where onion flavor would be too harsh. Storage life is excellent — 6–9 months under proper conditions (cool, dry, dark). The F1 hybrid nature of Ambition means it does not come true from saved seed, but sets (bulbs) from the previous year's crop can be replanted successfully.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Ambrosia is an open-pollinated variety requiring the full 84–90 days; succession is not practical but a single well-timed planting in zone 9 produces abundantly through summer. Ripe Ambrosia melons slip easily from the vine with a gentle tug — full-slip is the traditional ripeness indicator for cantaloupe. Reduce watering in the final 2 weeks before harvest to intensify sweetness and flavor. The powdery mildew resistance makes Ambrosia particularly reliable in zone 9's humid summer conditions.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil — melons require warm soil, abundant sun, and good air circulation; Ambrosia is an All-America Selections award-winning cantaloupe (muskmelon) that earned recognition for its exceptionally sweet, deeply aromatic, thick-fleshed, orange interior — with sugar content and fragrance significantly exceeding most commercial cantaloupe varieties bred for shipping durability. The medium-sized, rounded fruits with heavily netted tan rind and the unmistakable, intensely musky-sweet fragrance that announces ripeness from several feet away represent the classic cantaloupe eating experience at its best. Most commercial cantaloupes are harvested before full-slip (when they still cling to the vine) to withstand shipping without bruising — the result is fruit that is often underripe, bland, and lacking the musky sweetness that a vine-ripened cantaloupe develops. A homegrown Ambrosia harvested at true full-slip ripeness is fundamentally different from any commercial cantaloupe — genuinely aromatic, extremely sweet, and with a perfumed complexity that makes tasting it for the first time a revelation about what cantaloupe actually tastes like. Powdery mildew resistance makes Ambrosia reliable in the humid conditions of zone 9 summer.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September for a fall harvest. Plant in solid blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate wind pollination. Ambrosia is a sugary-enhanced (SE) bicolor variety — isolate from field corn and popcorn by at least 250 feet or 2 weeks of tasseling time to prevent starch dilution by cross-pollination. The sugary-enhanced trait gives better flavor retention after harvest than standard sweet corn.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ambrosia is an All-America Selections award-winning bicolor sweet corn recognized in 1982 for its outstanding combination of sweetness, tenderness, and one of the best flavor profiles of any bicolor sweet corn variety. The sugary-enhanced (SE) genetics give Ambrosia a higher sugar content and better post-harvest sugar retention than traditional open-pollinated sweet corn — the ears remain sweet and tender for several days after harvest rather than converting sugars to starch rapidly as standard sweet corn does. The bicolor ears with alternating white and yellow kernels have been the classic American sweet corn appearance for backyard gardens since the 1980s, and Ambrosia set the standard for bicolor flavor that later varieties aimed to match. The slender, well-filled ears (7–8 inches) have a fine kernel texture, tender pericarp (no toughness in the kernel skin), and outstanding raw flavor for eating directly off the cob without cooking. Ambrosia remains one of the most widely grown and recommended bicolor sweet corn varieties for home gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches at least 65 degrees.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of at least four short rows rather than a single long row to ensure good pollination. This bicolor sugar-enhanced hybrid produces 8-inch ears of tender, creamy kernels and offers early vigor plus strong disease resistance. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill. Harvest when silks brown and kernels release a milky juice when punctured, and refrigerate quickly to preserve sweetness.

common_name: Amelia Tomato (Disease-Resistant Hybrid Slicing Tomato with Broad Southeast-Adapted Resistance Package)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Amelia is a vigorous indeterminate slicing tomato with a comprehensive VFFNTAs disease resistance package: Verticillium wilt (V), two races of Fusarium wilt (F, FF), nematodes (N), tobacco mosaic virus (T), and Alternaria stem canker (As). The Alternaria stem canker resistance in Amelia is a notable differentiator — Alternaria is a fungal pathogen (Alternaria alternata f. sp. lycopersici) that causes stem canker and early fruit death in susceptible varieties and is particularly prevalent in warm, humid conditions. Amelia was developed to address the full suite of southeastern disease pressures in a single variety, making it particularly appropriate for zone 9's warm, humid climate where multiple diseases commonly limit tomato production. Transplant March–April in zone 9. Fruits are medium-large (8–12 oz), round to slightly flat, and ripen to a deep, uniform red.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake to 6 feet. Harvest when uniformly deep red. Amelia Tomato is a commercially developed F1 hybrid slicing tomato specifically designed for production in the humid southeastern United States, where the combination of warm temperatures, high humidity, and disease inoculum in garden soils creates challenging conditions for standard tomato varieties. The variety's VFFNTAs resistance code represents one of the most comprehensive disease resistance packages available in a single tomato variety: resistance to Verticillium wilt (a soilborne fungal disease that colonizes the xylem and causes progressive wilting), two races of Fusarium wilt (a related soilborne pathogen with multiple strains that can overcome single-race resistance), root-knot nematodes (a serious pest in the warm, sandy soils of the Gulf Coast), tobacco mosaic virus (a seed- and contact-transmitted virus), and Alternaria stem canker (a foliar and stem fungal pathogen that can cause significant early-season damage in humid conditions). This combination of resistances directly addresses the primary disease challenges in zone 9 tomato production: nematode pressure is extremely common in the sandy soils of the Gulf Coast plain; Fusarium and Verticillium are endemic in soils with previous tomato production history; Alternaria stem canker increases in severity during warm, wet weather. For gardeners who have experienced repeated tomato crop failures in zone 9 from disease without knowing the specific cause, Amelia's broad resistance package provides protection across the most likely disease scenarios.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil is workable, or again in late summer.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep in cool soil in early spring or late summer, thinning seedlings to give each plant room.
