This 1952 All-America Selections winner has thick, savoyed leaves and unusual tolerance to both heat and drought, extending the harvest window. It performs well in the ground or in containers, so it suits small gardens. Harvest outer leaves as needed, or cut the whole plant before it bolts in warm weather.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed into moist, disturbed or garden soil in partial shade to full sun; seeds require warm soil and light to germinate well.
directions: Direct sow onto the soil surface after last frost in partial shade to full sun; seeds need light and warmth to germinate and will often self-sow where established. This widely distributed native annual bears small white star-shaped flowers followed by clusters of small berries that turn fully black when ripe in late summer and fall. CAUTION: green and unripe berries and all other plant parts are toxic and must never be consumed; only correctly identified, fully black, ripe berries have a history of use cooked (never raw) in certain African, Southeast Asian, and indigenous North American culinary traditions. Plants naturalize readily in gardens and disturbed open ground, requiring little care once established.

plant_note: Start indoors early; extremely cold-hardy for fall and winter harvest.
directions: American Flag is a cold-hardy heirloom leek with long white shanks, blue-green leaves, and a mild, sweet onion flavor that holds in the garden through fall and into winter. Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into holes 6 inches deep to blanch the stems white. Hill soil up around the shanks as they grow to lengthen the tender white portion. Harvest as needed once shanks reach an inch across; the plants tolerate hard frost and can be dug even after snow.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; provide a trellis or other structure for the vining stems to climb. As a legume it fixes atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility while producing food. Thrives in moist, partially shaded woodland edges, streambanks, and open forest understories.
directions: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; provide a trellis or other structure for the vining stems to climb. Apios americana is a native North American twining vine in the legume family that produces chains of small, starchy, potato-like tubers in the soil that were a major food staple for dozens of indigenous tribes throughout eastern North America and reportedly sustained the Pilgrims through their first harsh New England winter; the tubers can be boiled, roasted, or mashed like potatoes with a sweeter, nuttier flavor. As a legume, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility while producing food. The vine also produces attractive, fragrant, dark-rose to reddish-brown flower clusters in late summer that are excellent for native bees; it thrives in moist, partially shaded woodland edges, streambanks, and open forest understories.

plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally in a container of heavy clay soil and submerge in a pond or water garden after the water reaches 65°F; the curved tip of the tuber should point upward.
directions: Plant tubers in heavy clay-loam soil (not potting mix, which will float) in containers placed in 12–24 inches of water in full sun; the massive circular leaves and huge pale-yellow flowers up to 10 inches across are among the most spectacular sights in water gardening. All parts of this native aquatic plant are edible — the starchy rhizomes are eaten like potatoes, the seeds like nuts, and the young leaves and flower petals as vegetables. The large, sculptural seed heads remain on the plant through winter and are popular in dried floral arrangements. In a natural pond, the rhizomes can spread aggressively; use containers to control spread in small water features.

plant_note: Divide rooted stem sections in spring and press into consistently saturated or wet soil at the edge of a stream, seep, or rain garden; keep divisions moist until new growth is established.
directions: American Pennywort is a native semi-aquatic groundcover of eastern North American forest seeps, springheads, and streambanks, forming a low carpet of small, round, glossy leaves on slender creeping stems. Plant in constantly moist to saturated, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; it will not tolerate drought or dry conditions even briefly. The leaves are edible in small quantities, with a mild, slightly peppery flavor similar to other pennyworts, and have a long history of use as a trail nibble or minor salad green. Use it as a living mulch beneath moisture-loving ferns and native wildflowers in rain gardens or along shaded pond margins.

plant_note: Direct sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest after frost sweetens roots.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep in loose, fertile soil about three months before your first fall frost, thinning to 6 inches apart. Roots grow 4 to 6 inches long with sweet, mellow yellow flesh that mashes like potatoes or adds body to soups and stews. The tender tops are also edible as sauteed greens. Rutabagas develop the best flavor in cool weather, so leave them in the ground until after a light frost before harvesting.

plant_note: Direct sow into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun near the coast; sea rocket is adapted to shifting dune sand, salt spray, and periodic sand burial, so avoid rich garden soil and heavy mulch, which encourage rot.
directions: Direct sow into loose, well-drained beach or dune-type sand in full sun; American sea rocket is a fleshy-leaved, mustard-family annual that colonizes the upper beach and foredune along both Atlantic and Pacific coasts, tolerating salt spray, sand burial, and drought that would kill nearly any conventional vegetable. The succulent, deeply lobed leaves and young seed pods have a sharp, peppery, radish-like bite and are eaten fresh in salads or as a pungent garnish, much like a wild, salt-tolerant arugula. Small four-petaled pale lavender to white flowers appear over a long season, followed by distinctive two-segmented, corky seed pods that float and disperse on tides and currents. It self-sows readily in loose sand and is best grown in a sandy raised bed or true beach-adjacent garden rather than ordinary rich soil, where it becomes leggy and short-lived.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost for spring, or midsummer for fall.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before transplanting, then set out sturdy seedlings in rich, evenly moist soil. This variety forms striking purple, domed heads that mature early and reliably in spring or fall and hold color best with steady moisture. Vigorous plants tolerate a range of climates and perform especially well in the Eastern US. Harvest heads while the curds are still tight, and enjoy the tender, flavorful florets steamed or roasted.

common_name: Amethyst Radish (Bright Purple Uniform Spring Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; Amethyst is a spring radish with smooth, bright purple skin and crisp white flesh, bred for uniform round shape and reliable color.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Amethyst is a modern spring radish bred for uniform, smooth, round roots with bright, consistent purple skin and crisp white interior, offering reliable color and shape for gardeners and market growers who want a purple radish that performs predictably. Flavor is mild and clean, similar to other fast-maturing spring radish types, without the excess pepperiness that develops in some varieties left too long in the ground. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, and succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks well after last frost and isolate from other corn types by distance or timing to keep popping quality true.
directions: Maintained for generations among Pennsylvania Dutch growers, Amish Butter is a pre-1885 heirloom popcorn that produces tall, dark-green stalks topped with two conical ears carrying a mix of rice- and pearl-shaped ivory-white kernels. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, or finish drying them indoors on their husks, until kernels rattle loosely in the cob before shelling and storing in a breathable container. Because the kernels are soft enough to also grind for flour, hominy, or polenta, gardeners get a genuinely dual-purpose corn from a single planting rather than a popcorn-only crop. The fluffy white pop and rich, naturally buttery flavor are the main reasons collectors keep this variety in circulation.

common_name: Amish Deer Tongue Lettuce (Heirloom Pointed-Leaf Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; more heat-tolerant and slower to bolt than many loose-leaf lettuces.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. Amish Deer Tongue is a longtime Pennsylvania Dutch heirloom named for its distinctive triangular, pointed leaves that resemble a deer's tongue, forming loose, upright rosettes of thick, crisp, richly flavored green leaves. It is notably more heat-tolerant and slower to bolt than many other loose-leaf lettuces, making it a dependable choice for extending the lettuce harvest into warmer weather in Gulf South spring gardens. Harvest outer leaves individually as a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole rosette at the base once it fills out.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger passes and soil has warmed thoroughly; give vines full sun and room to sprawl or a sturdy trellis with fruit slings.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to the strongest seedlings once established. Amish Melon is an open-pollinated heirloom muskmelon preserved and passed down through generations of Amish farming families, producing medium to large, netted, orange-fleshed cantaloupe-type fruit with a rich, sweet, aromatic flavor typical of well-grown heirloom melons. The vigorous, productive vines are known for reliable fruit set and good flavor even in less-than-ideal seasons, a hallmark of many Amish-preserved garden varieties bred for dependable performance in working farm gardens rather than showy uniformity. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the netted rind color has turned from green to tan, and reduce watering in the final week before harvest to concentrate sweetness.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, keeping the mix warm for even germination. This indeterminate heirloom produces meaty, acorn-shaped red fruits of 8 to 12 ounces with few seeds, excellent for rich sauce and paste but also good for slicing. Provide a tall stake or trellis and prune suckers to manage the vigorous vines. Water consistently at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot, and pick fruit as it colors fully.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; the large fruit size requires staking even as a paste tomato; prolific producer that benefits from a long growing season.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes; Amish Paste is an heirloom paste tomato from Wisconsin Amish communities, producing large (6–8 ounce) ox-heart to plum-shaped fruits with very few seeds, thick meaty flesh, low water content, and rich concentrated flavor that makes it outstanding for sauces, pastes, and canning. It far outperforms Roma for sauce production due to its greater size while retaining the low acidity and meatiness needed for good paste. Also excellent sliced fresh. An indeterminate vine with a long season; in short-summer climates, start early and use season-extension techniques.

plant_note: Start indoors, transplant after all frost danger.
directions: Amish Paste is a vigorous indeterminate heirloom yielding large, plum-to-oxheart-shaped fruits of 8-12 ounces with dense, richly flavored flesh ideal for sauce and canning. Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights are reliably warm. Provide tall stakes or a strong trellis and prune suckers to improve air flow, since the sprawling vines produce all season. Keep watering even and mulch well to reduce cracking and blossom-end rot on the heavy fruit.

common_name: Amish Pie Pumpkin (Heirloom Sweet Baking Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Amish Pie is a Plain-community heirloom pumpkin grown for its dense, sweet, fine-grained flesh, prized above the watery flesh of jack-o'-lantern types for baking.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills of warm, fertile soil and give the sprawling vines plenty of room to run, or trellis smaller fruit for a large vertical crop. Amish Pie is a heritage pumpkin passed down through Plain communities for its large, ribbed, deep-orange fruit and thick, dense, notably sweet flesh, considered by many bakers superior to jack-o'-lantern pumpkins, which tend to be stringy and watery by comparison. Fruits commonly run 10-20 pounds and store well into winter in a cool, dry spot, making it practical to bake from a single pumpkin over several months. Keep vines well watered as fruit sizes up and reduce watering as the rind hardens and colors fully in fall, then cure harvested pumpkins for a week or two before storage to concentrate sweetness and toughen the skin.

plant_note: Plant cloves pointed end up in fall, about 4-6 weeks ahead of hard frost, so root systems form before winter.
directions: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in well-drained, compost-enriched soil and mulch for winter insulation in cold regions. Snap off the coiling scape as it appears to send more energy into the developing bulb, and cure bulbs in a shaded, breezy spot before trimming roots and tops for storage. Amish Rocambole is a long-grown American heirloom hardneck strain passed down through Pennsylvania Dutch farming communities, admired for its rich, robust garlic flavor, easy-peeling cloves, and classic rocambole scapes once used fresh in early-summer cooking.

plant_note: Sow directly in cool soil as early as it can be worked, and give vines a tall trellis or fence to climb, since this heirloom grows considerably taller than most modern snap peas.
directions: Amish Snap is a tall heirloom snap pea passed down through Amish and Mennonite farm families in Pennsylvania and the Midwest and preserved by seed savers rather than commercial breeding programs. Vigorous vines climb readily on a trellis and set heavy quantities of sweet, plump, stringless pods that hold their quality well in variable spring weather. Because the vines are unusually tall, plan on netting or a fence at least five to six feet high and harvest every couple of days once pods fill out to keep the plants productive. The pods are good eaten fresh off the vine, lightly steamed, or stir-fried.

common_name: Amsterdam Forcing Carrot (Fast Early Dutch Baby Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow in loose, stone-free soil as soon as the ground can be worked; Amsterdam Forcing is bred for very fast, uniform early growth and is a classic choice for the first carrot sowing of spring or for tight succession plantings.
directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in loose, well-worked soil in full sun, keeping the surface evenly damp until the slow-to-emerge seedlings appear, then thin to about 2 inches apart. Amsterdam Forcing is a classic Dutch heirloom bred specifically for speed, producing slender, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots with a fine, sweet flavor and almost no core, ready to pull well before slower main-crop carrots. Its small size and rapid growth make it an excellent choice for containers, cold frames, and tight succession sowings every few weeks through the cool season. Harvest young, at finger to baby-carrot size, for the best texture and sweetness, since roots left in the ground too long lose the tenderness that defines the type.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth; transplant well after frost.
directions: Anaheim, also called New Mexico chile, is a mild heirloom pepper producing long, tapered fruits with a smoky flavor prized for roasting, stuffing, and grilling. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost using bottom heat, since the seeds need warm soil to sprout. Transplant only after nights stay above 55F, spacing plants about 18-24 inches apart in full sun. Harvest green for chiles rellenos or leave fruit to ripen red for a sweeter, deeper flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 1–2 weeks after frost danger passes when soil is warm.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm mix at 80°F and provide bright light once germinated to prevent leggy growth; transplant after frost danger has completely passed. Anaheim peppers are mildly hot (500–2,500 Scoville units), long and tapered, and the classic pepper for green chile and chiles rellenos. Harvest green at 75 days for mild flavor, or allow pods to ripen to red for a sweeter, slightly hotter pepper that can be dried and ground into pure chile powder. Consistent watering and a light fertilizer application when flowers begin to set helps prevent blossom drop in heat.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, deeply amended soil; Ananas (French for 'pineapple') melon is a Middle Eastern and Mediterranean heirloom producing large (3–5 lb), netted, oval fruits with intensely aromatic, spicy-sweet orange or white flesh that many consider among the finest-flavored of all melons — widely grown from Israel to France.
directions: Sow in hills or rows after last frost in deeply enriched, well-drained soil; Ananas is a large-fruited type needing 6–8 feet of row space or a very strong trellis with hammock-style fruit supports. Ananas melon (ananas is French and many Mediterranean languages for pineapple) is a widely grown Middle Eastern, Israeli, and Mediterranean heirloom producing large, oval to round, netted fruits (3–7 lb) with a sweet, spicy, intensely aromatic fragrance when ripe that has been compared to pineapple, vanilla, and spiced honey. The flesh can be white (in the traditional Israeli 'Ananas Yokneam' type) or orange, always with a distinctive rich, complex fragrance that perfumes a room when a ripe fruit is present. Several regional strains exist: French Ananas (yellow netted, orange flesh), Israeli Yokneam (white smooth skin, white flesh), and American strains. Generally large-fruited and somewhat heat-sensitive; best grown in dry conditions as wet weather can dilute flavor. Considered by some the finest-flavored muskmelon type in existence.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil reaches 60°F; Anasazi beans are bush varieties that need no staking and mature relatively quickly for a dry bean type.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, thinning to 4–6 inches apart; Anasazi beans are an ancient Southwest Native American dry bean with distinctive burgundy-and-white speckled seeds that cook faster than most dry beans due to thinner seed coats and produce a sweet, rich, mealy flavor. Unlike many heirloom dry beans, they are reputed to cause less flatulence because their lower oligosaccharide levels. Harvest pods when they are fully dry and yellow-brown before rainfall can cause mold. In humid climates, pull whole plants and hang to finish drying in a sheltered location. Seeds remain viable for 3–5 years when stored in cool, dry conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 to 8 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay warm.
directions: Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the mix at 75 to 90 degrees since peppers germinate slowly in cool soil. Transplant into warm, well-drained soil after nights are reliably above 55 degrees. The 3 to 6 inch green poblano is excellent stuffed for chiles rellenos, while the dried, reddish-brown ancho anchors sauces like mole poblano, with mild heat around 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units. Harvest green for fresh use or leave fruit to ripen red for drying.

plant_note: Direct sow into loose, deeply worked soil once it is workable in spring, since roots fork in heavy or rocky ground.
directions: Andovy is a Hamburg-type root parsley grown for its smooth, parsnip-like white taproot rather than its foliage, with a mild, earthy, parsley-scented flavor that works well roasted, mashed, or added to stocks. It produces uniform, straight, slow-to-fork roots when grown in loose soil, along with edible flat leaves that can be harvested lightly through the season without harming root development. As a hardy biennial root, it can be left in the ground and harvested through fall and into early winter after light frosts, which sweetens the flavor. Gardeners grow Andovy as a dual-purpose crop, choosing it over standard leaf parsley when a storable root vegetable is the goal.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, spacing hills to give vines room to run. Prolific plants yield up to fifteen uniform fruits weighing 1.5 to 2 pounds each, sized perfectly for serving on the half-shell. When cooked, the flesh forks away in tender spaghetti-like strands. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, dry spot for a week or two to improve storage life, and keep on the vine until the rind hardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 weeks before last frost or direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; in zone 9 angled luffa can be planted March through May for a summer harvest. Unlike smooth luffa, angled luffa is harvested primarily as a tender vegetable at 6–10 inches long, not allowed to mature into a sponge.
directions: Grow on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; angled luffa (turiya in Gujarati, turai in Hindi) is a staple vegetable in South Asian cuisine, prized for its delicate, slightly bitter flavor and ability to hold up in cooked dishes. Unlike the smooth luffa used for sponges, the angled luffa has prominent longitudinal ridges and must be harvested young at 6–10 inches while the flesh is tender and the ridges peel off easily; older fruits become fibrous and bitter. The plant grows vigorously in summer heat and humidity, producing heavily if given consistent moisture and regular fertilization. Harvest every 2–3 days to prevent fruits from maturing on the vine.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; one of the earliest-maturing large heirloom tomatoes, making it excellent for short-season gardens and for getting a jump on the harvest before summer heat sets in at southern latitudes.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to well-prepared, deeply amended soil after all frost risk has passed and stake or cage firmly to support the heart-shaped fruits. Anna Russian is a Ukrainian/Russian oxheart-type heirloom with distinctive heart-shaped, pink-red fruits up to 12 ounces that are extremely fleshy, nearly seedless, and have a rich, sweet, mild flavor making them outstanding for eating fresh; it is one of the earlier-maturing large heirloom types at 68–80 days, which makes it especially valuable for growers who want to harvest ahead of the worst summer heat. The indeterminate vines set fruit in loose clusters of 2–3 and continue producing through the season if heat stress does not prevent fruit set; in the South, plant early for spring harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant April–June for main crop, or March under row cover. Annie Oakley II is among the earliest okra varieties to produce, making it valuable for gardeners in northern zones. In zone 9 the earlier production means pods are setting before peak summer heat reduces pod quality; plant a fall crop in August for continued production into November.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Annie Oakley II is a hybrid, spineless, compact okra developed as an improved successor to the original Annie Oakley hybrid — the 1988 AAS Award-winning variety that introduced the compact, spineless, early-maturing concept that transformed home garden okra production. Annie Oakley II improves on the original with earlier maturity (48 versus 56 days), heavier production, improved disease resistance, and better heat tolerance for extended season production. The compact, 3–5 foot plant produces straight, uniform, deep green, 5-ribbed pods with excellent tenderness when harvested at 3–4 inches. The thornless, compact habit makes Annie Oakley II the best choice for gardeners with limited space, raised beds, and those who find full-size okra plants too large to manage easily. In zone 9 the compact habit is advantageous because plants fit more naturally into intensive garden beds without overwhelming neighboring crops.

plant_note: Soak seeds overnight before planting to speed germination; direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F. In zone 9 plant March–July; Annie Oakley is earlier than most okra varieties and begins producing within 52 days of sowing, valuable for a longer harvest window.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms to 65°F in full sun; Annie Oakley is a spineless, compact hybrid okra that produces early (52 days) and prolifically on plants 3–4 feet tall — smaller than most standard okra and suitable for smaller gardens or containers. The smooth, straight, dark-green pods are 5-ridged and should be harvested at 3–4 inches for maximum tenderness; pods become fibrous and woody if left beyond 5–6 inches. The spineless habit makes harvest comfortable without gloves; hand-pick every 2–3 days in summer heat. An AAS Award winner, Annie Oakley has proven reliable across the South and performs especially well in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans resent transplanting and rot in cold ground. This vigorous variety produces 5 to 5.5 inch pods that stay tender and crisp even as the season heats up. Sturdy, upright plants hold pods off the soil for clean, easy picking and do well in containers. Harvest frequently while pods are young and snap crisply to keep plants producing over a long window.

subcategory: Italian-type hybrid eggplant bred for productivity
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seed indoors under warm conditions and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay above 55F, since this hybrid performs best with steady heat. Provide even moisture and support for the upright plants as fruit clusters develop. Antigua is a modern Italian-type hybrid bred for a compact plant habit and heavy early set of glossy, dark purple, oval fruit, making it a reliable choice for market growers and small gardens alike. Its relatively quick maturity suits gardeners in cooler regions who want classic eggplant flavor without a long growing season.

common_name: Antiquorum Taro (Imperial Taro, Small Taro, Dasheen)
plant_note: Plant corms 2–4 inches deep in partial shade to full sun in moist to wet, fertile soil; Colocasia antiquorum is an older botanical name for a group of small-corm taro types distinct from the large-corm Colocasia esculenta forms. In historical and botanical literature it denotes the classic 'small taro' with golf-ball to tennis-ball sized corms and a characteristic purple marking at the center of the corm. Corms are edible when thoroughly cooked. In zone 9, the plants die back in frost but the corms survive in the ground and resprout in spring. CAUTION: all raw Colocasia parts contain calcium oxalate and cause intense mouth irritation — always cook thoroughly.
directions: Plant corms in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained to wet soil — Antiquorum Taro grows vigorously in the warm, moist conditions of Gulf Coast zone 8b-12 and produces harvestable corms through a long growing season. Colocasia antiquorum is a tuberous, rhizomatous perennial aroid in the Araceae family — botanically, the name C. antiquorum has been applied to the smaller-corm types of taro grown throughout Asia, the Pacific, and the Caribbean that differ from the larger-corm 'dasheen' forms of C. esculenta in corm size, corm flesh color (often with a distinct purple center), and the number of cormels (small side corms). The plant is a core food staple throughout the Pacific Islands, the Caribbean, West Africa, and parts of Asia where taro is a traditional staple crop — the corms are peeled and cooked (boiled, steamed, baked, or fried) to neutralize the calcium oxalate crystals present in all raw Colocasia, and the cooked flesh has a distinctive mildly sweet, somewhat starchy, earthy flavor similar to potato. The large, distinctly peltate (shield-shaped, with the petiole attached in the center of the blade rather than at the edge), arrow-shaped leaves are ornamentally attractive and can reach 24–36 inches. In zone 8b-12, the plants grow through the warm months, die back to the corms in cold winters, and resprout in spring. The corms are harvested in fall before frost. Multiple smaller cormels form around the central corm and can be replanted. CAUTION: cook thoroughly before eating.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Antohi Romanian is a distinctly early, mild, sweet frying pepper introduced to North American gardeners by Romanian dissident Silviu Antohi, who brought seeds from Romania to Canada in the 1980s — producing pale yellow to orange, blocky to elongated, thin-walled fruits with exceptional sweetness and very early production for a sweet pepper.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Antohi Romanian is notably earlier than most sweet peppers and can be productive even in short-season gardens. Antohi Romanian pepper arrived in North American heirloom seed circles through Romanian dissident Silviu Antohi, who escaped Romania during the Communist period and brought pepper seeds with him that he shared with gardeners and seed savers in Canada; the variety entered the Seed Savers Exchange network in the 1990s and has since become widely appreciated for its exceptional earliness and high quality. The medium-sized (3–4 inch), blocky to elongated-oval, pale yellow to orange fruits have thin walls and an exceptionally sweet, fruity flavor with virtually no bitterness; they are among the earliest sweet peppers to begin producing, with plants in production 60–72 days from transplant — significantly earlier than most sweet bell types. Outstanding fresh, roasted, or pickled; the thin walls cook down quickly and the fruits need no peeling when roasted. A highly productive plant for short-season gardens and an outstanding choice for Gulf Coast early-season plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow from early spring into late spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; unlike most lettuce, Anuenue seed germinates readily even at soil temperatures above 80°F, which lets Gulf Coast gardeners sow it later into warming weather than typical lettuce varieties.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning to 8-12 inches, and harvest as a full head once the center fills in. Anuenue was released by the University of Hawaii in 1987 specifically for tropical and subtropical climates, forming a small, crisp, iceberg-type head with bright green outer leaves and a well-packed pale heart, but with seed and heat tolerance far beyond typical crisphead lettuce. It is one of the few lettuce varieties whose seed will germinate reliably in hot soil rather than going dormant, and the plant resists developing the bitterness that ruins most lettuce as summer heat builds. For Gulf Coast gardeners this makes Anuenue a valuable bridge variety, extending fresh salad lettuce production later into late spring and earlier into late summer than standard cool-season types allow.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Appaloosa bean is a distinctive bush dry bean with dramatic black and white spotted coloring reminiscent of an Appaloosa horse — a visually striking heirloom that produces excellent-flavored, creamy-textured beans for baking, soups, and slow-cooking.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; direct seeding is preferred as beans do not transplant well. Appaloosa bean is an heirloom dry bean named for its dramatic black and white spotted coloring that closely resembles the distinctive coat pattern of the Appaloosa horse breed; the irregular black speckles and splashes on creamy white background make each bean unique and the dried beans are among the most visually striking of all heirloom bean varieties, remaining attractive even after cooking. The flavor is rich and earthy with a creamy texture similar to pinto beans but with more character; they are excellent for baked beans, bean soups, and slow-cooked dishes. Can be eaten as a snap bean when pods are young and tender; most commonly grown for dry use at 85–100 days to full maturity. Drought-tolerant once established; performs well in Gulf Coast spring planting with harvest before summer heat peaks.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost, or grow indoors year-round for baby greens.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep and thin lightly, or broadcast densely for a cut-and-come-again baby-greens crop. This chard blend produces colorful young leaves ideal in salads or steamed, stir-fried, and added to soups, omelets, and lasagna. It can be grown indoors any time of year for a fresh winter harvest. Snip outer leaves when a few inches tall and the plants will regrow for repeated cuttings.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Applegreen is a compact, high-yielding plant that performs well in containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Applegreen is an All-America Selections winner grown for its smooth, round, apple-sized fruit with pale to medium green skin, mild flavor, and tender, virtually seedless flesh that resists browning better than many purple eggplants once cut. Plants are compact and heavily productive, setting fruit steadily over a long season and performing well in raised beds or large containers where space is limited. Harvest fruit while still glossy and firm, roughly the size of a baseball, since overripe fruit dulls in color and develops tougher skin and more seeds. Its mild flavor and quick cooking time make it a versatile choice for grilling, roasting, and stir-fries.

plant_note: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into deeply worked, stone-free soil, thinning to a wide final spacing so the roots can size up without forking; also sowable in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into deeply worked, stone-free soil, thinning to a wide final spacing so the smooth white Minowase-type roots can size up without forking. April Cross is prized among daikon growers for its unusually strong resistance to bolting, which lets it be sown earlier in spring than most daikon types without running to seed. Roots stay tender, mild, and non-pithy even when left in the ground to reach full size, making them well suited to fresh eating, pickling, and simmered dishes.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or very early spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop.
directions: Sow seeds 1.5 to 2 inches deep directly in the garden while soil is still cool, spacing plants closely in blocks so they can support each other or provide staking for tall stems. This classic English heirloom is prized for its exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating hard frosts that would kill other legumes, making it a favorite for autumn sowing in mild climates or the earliest possible spring planting elsewhere. Pods grow long and fleshy, typically holding six to eight large, buttery-flavored beans that are excellent shelled fresh, dried for storage, or used in traditional Mediterranean and British dishes. Pinch out the growing tips once the first pods set to discourage aphids and encourage the plant to channel energy into pod development.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Arcadia is specifically valued for its exceptional cold tolerance — the variety holds its heads in quality through heavy frosts and cool temperatures that would damage most broccoli. In zone 9, transplant August–September for November–January harvest. Arcadia's ability to hold heads without yellowing or loosening during cold weather provides a wider harvest window than cold-sensitive varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil with pH 6.0–7.0. Arcadia is an F1 hybrid broccoli that has become a benchmark variety for fall and overwintering broccoli production in zones 6–8 — valued specifically for the combination of excellent cold tolerance, uniformly dark blue-green head color, and disease resistance. Most broccoli varieties produce their best heads in the narrow temperature range of 60–65°F and deteriorate rapidly when exposed to hard frosts — heads yellow, open up, or develop loose, poor-quality florets. Arcadia was selected specifically for the ability to hold tight, well-formed heads through significantly colder temperatures, allowing gardeners and growers in the mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest to harvest marketable broccoli after hard frosts in October and November that would compromise most other varieties. The deep blue-green color of Arcadia heads is exceptionally attractive — darker and more uniform than many broccoli varieties — and holds through the cold exposure. Disease resistance includes downy mildew, black rot, and clubroot, which are important fall disease concerns in humid climates. Arcadia is a top recommendation from Johnny's Selected Seeds for fall production and has a loyal following among market gardeners who rely on fall broccoli as a key late-season crop.

common_name: Argentata Swiss Chard (Silver Ribbed Italian Heirloom Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date, or a bit earlier under cover, spacing seed clusters several inches apart.
directions: Sow seed clusters directly into fertile soil, thinning to one seedling per cluster once plants have a couple of true leaves, and keep beds evenly watered through summer heat. This old Italian type produces broad, dull green savoyed leaves atop wide, flat, silvery-white ribs that many cooks prize for braising separately from the greens. It is notably heat tolerant and slow to bolt, allowing continuous cut-and-come-again harvest well into the warm months.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant crowns to a permanent bed.
directions: Argenteuil is an award-winning French heirloom asparagus with tender, sweet purple-and-green spears tipped in pink, valued for early, heavy yields. Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, soaking seed first to speed the slow germination, then transplant seedlings to a deeply prepared permanent bed. Wait until the third spring to begin cutting spears so the crowns can build strong roots, and let ferns grow all summer to feed the plants. A well-tended bed remains productive for 15 to 20 years.

common_name: Arikara Yellow Bean (Ree Bean, Northern Plains Native American Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Arikara Yellow is an heirloom bush bean from the Arikara people of the Missouri River basin in present-day North Dakota, adapted to the short growing season and continental extremes of the northern Great Plains — exceptionally quick to mature for a dry bean (80–95 days) and tolerant of cool temperatures at both ends of the season.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Arikara Yellow is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in poor to moderately fertile soils without supplemental irrigation in all but the driest conditions; harvest dry pods before fall rains can induce mold on the dried pods. Arikara Yellow Bean is a traditional heirloom dry bean of the Arikara people (also called the Ree), a Caddoan-speaking people who lived in permanent earth-lodge villages along the Missouri River in present-day North Dakota and South Dakota, where they practiced intensive agriculture including cultivation of corn, squash, sunflowers, and beans for centuries before European contact. The Arikara were important traders in the Missouri River trade network, and their agricultural products — including seeds — were traded widely, distributing their bean varieties to neighboring peoples and eventually to European and American settlers and traders. Arikara Yellow is characterized by small to medium-sized, oval, pale yellow to light tan seeds with a mild, earthy, somewhat buttery flavor that is excellent in soups, stews, and as a baked bean. The variety's most distinctive horticultural characteristic is its extremely short maturity for a dry bean — 80–95 days — which allows it to be grown and harvested in the short frost-free season of zones 3–4 where most dry beans cannot ripen before fall frost. This same short-season adaptation makes Arikara Yellow valuable for gardeners in any region who want a reliable dry bean with insurance against early fall frosts or a compressed summer schedule.

common_name: Aristocrat Hybrid Zucchini (AAS-Winning Compact Green Zucchini)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil; compact size suits raised beds and small plots.
directions: Aristocrat won an AAS award in 1973 for combining a compact, space-saving bush habit with the kind of dark green fruit color and shape consistency that open-pollinated zucchini of the era could not match. Plants stay under two feet tall, making this a practical choice for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast garden plots where vining winter squash would take over. Water deeply every few days rather than a light daily sprinkle to keep production steady through hot spells, and harvest fruit at 6-7 inches before the skin toughens. Decades after its release it remains available from mainstream seed catalogs, a testament to its enduring garden performance.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Aristotle carries resistance to three races of bacterial leaf spot (X3R), a disease that spreads rapidly in the humid, rain-splashed conditions typical of Gulf South summers and can defoliate less resistant bell pepper varieties.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aristotle is a widely grown commercial and home-garden bell pepper hybrid bred specifically for resistance to three races of bacterial leaf spot, a disease that thrives in the warm, humid, rain-prone conditions common across the Gulf South and can otherwise strip a pepper plant of foliage and ruin fruit quality. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red if left on the plant, on a compact, well-branched plant that holds up well to heat. Because it keeps its leaf canopy healthier than more disease-susceptible varieties, Aristotle tends to shade and protect its own developing fruit from sunscald better through the peak of summer. Harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes. In zone 9 this is an outstanding choice for both spring and fall seasons; plant a second crop in late July or August for fall harvest. Arkansas Traveler is notably heat-tolerant and continues setting fruit at temperatures where most tomatoes drop blossoms.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in warm (70–85°F) starting mix; transplant to full sun after frost risk passes; Arkansas Traveler is the quintessential heat-tolerant Southern heirloom, developed at the University of Arkansas and introduced around 1939 as a reliable producer through the oppressive midsummer heat of the South and Gulf Coast that causes most other tomatoes to drop blossoms and go dormant. The indeterminate vines produce medium to large (6–8 oz) pink, globe-shaped fruits with mild, low-acid flavor, thin skin, and very good crack resistance — exactly the qualities that make it a top recommendation for zone 8–10 gardeners frustrated by summer tomato failure. The meaty, juicy flesh has classic sweet tomato flavor without sharp acidity. A dependable heirloom for hot climates: one of the best-adapted tomatoes for gardens where summer heat is the limiting factor.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Armenian cucumber is botanically a muskmelon (Cucumis melo) but used as a cucumber — it produces extraordinary long, pale green, lightly ridged fruits that can reach 3 feet, are almost completely seedless with a very thin skin and mild, delicate melon-cucumber flavor, and are extremely heat-tolerant and productive in hot Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile, moist soil in full sun; provide trellis for best fruit shape; harvest at 12–18 inches for best texture. Cucumis melo var. flexuosus (Armenian cucumber or snake cucumber) is one of the most unusual cucurbits in cultivation — despite being called a 'cucumber,' it is botanically a muskmelon, not a true cucumber. The distinction matters in practice: Armenian cucumber is significantly more heat-tolerant and better-adapted to Gulf Coast summers than true cucumbers (Cucumis sativus), continuing to produce prolifically in summer heat that stresses and collapses standard cucumber vines. The extraordinarily long fruits (reaching 12–36 inches) are pale sage-green, lightly ridged, with a very thin, edible skin and white flesh that has a mild, slightly melon-scented cucumber flavor without bitterness. The seeds are nearly absent in young fruits, only becoming prominent in overripe specimens. Armenian cucumber does not need peeling, has no bitterness (the cucurbitacins that cause cucumber bitterness are absent), and is excellent fresh, in Middle Eastern salads (fattoush, tabbouleh), and in tzatziki. A standard fixture in Middle Eastern, Armenian, and Persian home gardens, it deserves much wider use in Southern gardens where true cucumbers struggle in summer.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms; heat-loving vine.
directions: Armenian Pale Green is actually a heat-tolerant melon grown like a cucumber, producing long, ribbed, pale-skinned fruits that stay crisp and mild without bitterness. Direct-sow after the soil warms to at least 70F, planting seeds about an inch deep, and thin or transplant to 12-18 inches apart. Grow on a trellis to keep the long fruits straight and clean, harvesting at 12-18 inches while the skin is still tender. Because the thin skin needs no peeling, these are excellent for fresh salads and quick pickles.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings (side shoots from the crown) in spring in well-drained, deeply cultivated, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; arracacha requires 9–12 months from planting to harvest and performs best where temperatures range 57–75°F — it struggles in heat above 85°F and is best suited to mild coastal or highland climates in zones 8–10.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in spring in deeply cultivated, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; arracacha is one of the most important root crops of the South American Andes and is gaining attention among adventurous food gardeners in mild climates for its exceptional flavor — the white to cream-colored roots have a starchy texture and a flavor that combines the best qualities of celery, carrot, and parsnip with a slightly sweet, buttery richness. The roots are boiled, roasted, fried, or used in soups; they do not store well after harvest and are best consumed within a few days. The plant resembles a flat-leafed parsley or celery relative with compound leaves and naturally produces multiple offsets from the crown that can be replanted as cuttings to propagate. It thrives in the cool, humid conditions of zones 8–10 coastal areas and mild highlands where temperatures remain moderate — it is not well suited to the extreme summer heat of the Gulf Coast interior but performs in coastal areas and in partial shade.

plant_note: Plant tubers or potted divisions in shallow water (1–6 inches deep) or at the margin of a pond or rain garden in full sun to partial shade once water temperature reaches 60°F.
directions: Plant tubers or divisions in shallow water (1–6 inches deep) or in saturated soil at a pond or stream margin in full to partial sun; arrowhead is a native aquatic perennial with distinctive arrow-shaped leaves, three-petaled white flowers in midsummer, and underwater starchy tubers (called wapato or katniss) that were a critically important food source for many Native American peoples across North America, harvested by wading and loosening the tubers with the feet in fall when starches are concentrated. The tubers are nutritious and delicious when boiled or roasted like small potatoes. The plant also provides outstanding wetland habitat — frogs shelter in the leaves, diving ducks (especially mallards and teals) eat the tubers, and shorebirds and herons hunt at its margins. In favorable conditions it spreads aggressively; contain in submerged containers if space is limited.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sections 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil after last frost; in zone 8 and south, rhizomes can overwinter in the ground under mulch — harvest mature rhizomes in fall when foliage begins to die back.
directions: True arrowroot is a tropical perennial native to the Caribbean and northern South America, cultivated for its slender, white rhizomes that produce the purest, most digestible starch of any root crop — genuine arrowroot starch is almost flavorless, dissolves crystal-clear in cooking (unlike cornstarch which turns cloudy), and is prized in gluten-free baking and as a thickener for delicate sauces, jellies, and gravies. In Gulf Coast gardens, it grows vigorously as a shade-tolerant understory crop under fruit trees and along the edges of covered patios — one of the few starchy root vegetables that thrives in partial shade, making it ideal for interplanting beneath taller tropical crops. Harvest slender, finger-like rhizomes 10–12 months after planting when the leafy tops begin to yellow; the rhizomes can be eaten boiled or baked, or processed into starch by grinding, washing, and drying. Start rhizome sections each spring; in frost-free areas it grows as a true perennial, expanding into spreading clumps.

plant_note: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in October–November in zone 9; Artichoke types are adaptable softneck garlics that perform in a wide range of climates from cold zone 4 to warm zone 9. They are the garlic most commonly sold in grocery stores and braided in kitchens. Named varieties include California Early, California Late, Inchelium Red, and Red Toch.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Artichoke garlic (named for its overlapping layers of cloves resembling an artichoke) is the most widely grown garlic group in the world and the standard garlic of commercial production. The large, white to purple-streaked bulbs contain multiple layers of cloves (10–20 per head) with a mild to moderately pungent flavor that is the familiar 'standard' garlic taste of commerce. Artichoke types are softneck garlics (no central flower stalk), making them the type used for braiding and one of the longer-storing types. In zone 9, Artichoke types perform better than most Hardneck varieties (Rocambole, Porcelain, Purple Stripe) because they require somewhat less cold vernalization. Named Artichoke varieties recommended for the South include 'Inchelium Red' (already in the dataset), 'California Early,' 'Red Toch,' and 'Lorz Italian.' Plant in fall, fertilize in late winter with high-nitrogen fertilizer, and harvest in April–May when lower leaves are dry but 4–5 green leaves remain. Cure in a shaded, well-ventilated area for 3–4 weeks.

common_name: Artisan Bumble Bee Blend Pole Cherry Tomato
plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This blend combines Pink, Purple, and Sunrise Bumble Bee cherry tomatoes, each striped and no two alike, sweet and tangy right off the vine. The indeterminate plants grow large and yield heavily, so provide sturdy support and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly to reduce cracking, and harvest fruit as it colors fully throughout the season.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in mid- to late summer for a fall crop; Artwork is a stem-type (broccolini-style) broccoli that yields a small central head followed by a long, extended harvest of tender side shoots rather than one large main head.
directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or midsummer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Artwork is an AAS-winning stem broccoli, closer in style to broccolini than a traditional single-head broccoli, forming a modest central head that is quickly followed by a long, heavy, extended flush of slender, tender side shoots that can be harvested continuously for weeks — total yield per plant far exceeds a standard main-head variety. It is notably more heat tolerant than most broccoli, holding quality and continuing to produce shoots even as warm weather sets in, which makes it a good choice for stretching the harvest later into a Gulf South spring than most broccoli allows. Harvest shoots with 4-6 inches of stem while the small flower buds are still tight; regular picking encourages more side shoots to form. Keep soil consistently moist and side-dress with compost partway through the harvest period to sustain the long production window.

plant_note: Succession sow spring and fall; bolts quickly in heat.
directions: Arugula is a fast-growing, cool-season green with a bold, peppery bite that is delicious in salads, on pizza, and lightly wilted. Direct-sow shallowly every two to three weeks from early spring through fall for a steady supply of tender leaves. Harvest young outer leaves cut-and-come-again, and cut the whole plant before hot weather triggers bolting and a sharper flavor. In warm regions grow it in partial shade or indoors to extend the harvest window.

plant_note: Scatter seeds thinly over moist, prepared, well-drained soil and press without covering — arugula germinates in cool soil almost immediately; succession-sow every 2–3 weeks from early spring through fall for continuous harvests. Fall crops are sweeter and slower to bolt than spring crops.
directions: Scatter seeds on the surface of moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil and press lightly without covering; arugula is one of the fastest-maturing and easiest-to-grow leafy vegetables, germinating within 5–7 days in cool conditions and ready to harvest as baby greens in 3 weeks or full-size leaves in 4–6 weeks. The peppery, nutty, mustardy flavor is most mild and complex in cool weather; leaves become intensely bitter and peppery in hot weather. Succession-sow every 2–3 weeks from early spring through fall for a continuous supply; cut-and-come-again harvesting (cutting 1 inch above soil) extends each planting significantly. Both flowers and leaves are edible; the white flowers with purple veins are excellent salad garnishes. Fall-planted arugula has superior flavor to spring plantings in most climates.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer, or grow indoors year-round.
directions: Broadcast seed thickly about 1/4 inch deep for a dense baby-greens crop, sowing every couple of weeks for a steady supply. Peppery leaves are rich in vitamin C and potassium and taste great with balsamic and Parmesan. This crop grows quickly in cool weather and can be raised indoors year-round for fresh winter greens. Cut leaves when 2 to 3 inches tall and the bed will often regrow for a second harvest.

plant_note: Grown indoors year-round; sow densely on a shallow tray of moist medium.
directions: Broadcast the tiny seeds thickly and evenly across a moist tray of soil or a microgreen mat, then keep covered for the first two days to speed germination. Sprouts appear within a few days and grow best in bright indirect light at room temperature. Mist gently to keep the surface moist without waterlogging, and harvest with scissors once the first true leaves show, usually around a week to ten days. The peppery, mustard-like bite is at its best when cut young and eaten fresh.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for fall harvest.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool weather and thin for full-size plants, or leave dense for baby greens ready in about 20 days. The peppery, mustardy leaves brighten salads and are also good steamed or on pizza. Grow in full sun to part shade and keep soil moist to slow bolting, which turns leaves bitter and hot in heat. Succession sow every two to three weeks in spring and fall for a continuous harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; this perennial-type arugula grows slowly.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool soil; wild rocket grows more slowly than common arugula but offers a stronger, more complex peppery flavor. Harvest as baby greens or let plants reach full size for salads, pizza, or pesto. It grows well in containers and tolerates part shade, and the deeply lobed leaves regrow after cutting. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest regularly to keep leaves tender and slow flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65°F; a second sowing in mid-to-late summer keeps slicers coming once spring vines decline in Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Ashley was released in 1956 by the Clemson Agricultural Experiment Station's Truck Experiment Station in Charleston, bred to hold up under the humidity and downy mildew pressure typical of Lowcountry and Gulf Coast summers. Vines are vigorous and medium-length, producing dark green, slightly tapered slicers 7-9 inches long with a mild, sweet flavor. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year, making it a practical choice for gardeners wanting a self-sufficient summer slicer rather than a hybrid. Provide a trellis or let vines sprawl, and pick regularly to keep production going through peak heat.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost for spring, or midsummer for fall.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before setting out sturdy transplants into rich, evenly moist soil. This hybrid combines the mild, sweet flavor of broccoli with tender, asparagus-like stems and matures quickly. After the first central shoots, plants keep producing slender side shoots for multiple harvests. Cut stems when buds are still tight and harvest often to encourage continued production; steam or stir-fry the whole tender stem.

plant_note: Plant one-year-old crowns as soon as soil is workable in spring; dig 8-in-deep trenches and set crowns 18 in apart.
directions: Set one-year crowns in 8-in-deep trenches with roots spread over a ridge of compost, then gradually backfill as growth emerges. Do not harvest any spears in the first year and harvest lightly in year two to let the root system build strength. Beginning in year three, cut or snap spears at soil level when they are 6–8 in tall and before the tips begin to feather open. Stop harvesting after 4–6 weeks to allow ferns to grow and replenish the crown for the next season.

plant_note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; asparagus pea germinates best at cool temperatures and bolts quickly in summer heat — in zone 9 treat as a late-fall to early-spring crop, sowing in October through February.
directions: Sow 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; the asparagus pea is a Mediterranean annual legume with attractive brick-red flowers and uniquely four-winged seed pods. Pods must be harvested when they are tiny — no more than 1 inch long — because they become woody and inedible extremely quickly. At the correct size they have a mild flavor reminiscent of asparagus, delicious lightly steamed, stir-fried, or pickled. The plant fixes atmospheric nitrogen and improves soil for subsequent crops. It is low-growing and sprawling rather than climbing, often used as a flowering groundcover in cool-season borders in addition to its edible value. The deep red flowers attract pollinators. In mild-winter climates sow in fall and harvest through winter.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is thoroughly warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant April–July. Yard-long beans are a twining vine requiring a trellis, fence, or support of at least 6 feet tall — they are not self-supporting and will sprawl without structure. Harvest pods when 14–18 inches long and still tender and pliable; longer pods become tough and stringy. Harvest every 2–3 days during peak production — pods develop very rapidly in hot weather. In zone 9 these beans thrive in the summer heat that stresses or stops production of common snap beans.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with sturdy trellis support; Asparagus Yard-Long Bean is a traditional variety of the Chinese long bean (Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis), producing impressively long (18–24 inch), slender, pale green to light-colored pods that hang in pairs from the vines, resembling bundles of very long, thin asparagus spears in their pendant arrangement. The flavor of Asparagus yard-long beans is distinctly different from common snap beans — denser, less watery, slightly nutty, with a pleasant asparagus-like quality that explains the variety name. The texture holds up well to stir-frying and high-heat cooking that would make common snap beans too soft, making yard-long beans the preferred bean for stir-fries, curries, and Asian vegetable preparations where snap beans would become unpleasantly mushy. As a heat-adapted legume related to black-eyed peas rather than to common beans (Phaseolus), yard-long beans genuinely thrive in zone 9's summer conditions — producing abundantly in temperatures that stop snap bean production — making them one of the most practical fresh-bean crops for the Gulf South summer garden.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm; loves heat.
directions: This heat-loving Asian cowpea is a vigorous pole bean that produces slender pods up to a meter long, best picked young at 12-18 inches for tender eating. Direct-sow after the soil has thoroughly warmed to 70F or more, planting an inch deep at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis. The climbing vines thrive in hot, humid weather where common beans struggle and keep producing with regular harvest. Pick pods frequently while still smooth and firm to encourage continued set.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is warm; a thick, sturdy stem and solid flesh give this pumpkin good field-storage life through a hot, humid harvest season.
directions: Direct sow in hills after frost danger has passed, spacing hills three to four feet apart to suit the semi-bush growth habit, which takes up markedly less room than sprawling field-pumpkin types. Aspen finishes quickly at around 95 days, producing large, solidly fleshed fruit with a rich orange rind, a thick stem, and handles that hold up well through harvest handling and shipping. Its dense flesh and sturdy rind translate into good post-harvest storage and shipping quality, useful for growers who need fruit to hold up in warm regional markets. Cut fruit with several inches of stem once fully colored and firm, cure in a warm, airy spot, then move to cool, dry storage.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost; well suited to large containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Astia is a French-bred bush zucchini selected specifically for container growing and tight garden spaces, with silvery, deeply lobed foliage that makes the compact plant almost as ornamental as it is productive. Fruit sets close to the base of the plant, which keeps harvest easy even in a large pot on a patio, and the smooth, glossy green zucchini are best cut at about 5 inches for peak tenderness. Because it stays under 30 inches across, Astia suits Gulf Coast gardeners who want fresh zucchini without dedicating a full bed to a sprawling vine, and frequent picking keeps the early, prolific plants setting new fruit.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a long, cool-season harvest.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool soil and thin for full plants or leave dense for baby greens ready in about a month. This variety has wider leaves and is slower to bolt than other arugulas, giving more leaf per harvest and a milder, peppery flavor. Keep soil moist and grow in part shade during warm spells to delay bolting. Cut outer leaves regularly, and succession sow for a steady supply through spring and fall.

subcategory: small round black-purple Middle Eastern heirloom eggplant
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date, providing consistent bottom heat, then transplant into hot, sunny beds after frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seed indoors with steady warmth and transplant into full sun after the soil has warmed, since this heirloom thrives in hot climates and resents cool, wet soil. Keep watering consistent to avoid stress that can toughen the skin. Aswad, whose name means "black" in Arabic, is an Iraqi heirloom prized for its small, round, near-black fruit and dense, creamy flesh that holds up well in stews and grilling. It is a favorite among growers seeking heat-tolerant regional varieties adapted to arid conditions.

common_name: Athena Cantaloupe (Eastern US Commercial Standard, AAS-Winning Disease-Resistant Hybrid Melon)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Athena is widely adapted and performs well across the eastern US including the Gulf South's humid, warm conditions. In zone 9, plant April–May for June–July harvest. Athena has powdery mildew resistance — an important advantage in zone 9's humid late-spring and summer conditions where mildew often terminates melon plantings prematurely. The fruit is large (5–8 lbs), round, with heavy netting and excellent shelf life after harvest — the flesh remains firm and sweet for several days post-harvest, making it practical for gardeners who harvest and store melons rather than eating immediately. Athena requires two plants or more for cross-pollination by insects; plant in groups and maintain good pollinator habitat nearby.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil; thin to 2 plants per hill, 3–4 feet between hills. Harvest when skin shows cream-yellow color under netting and fruit is fragrant. Athena Cantaloupe is an F1 hybrid melon developed by Seminis Vegetable Seeds for commercial production in the humid, warm conditions of the eastern United States — particularly the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast commercial melon-producing regions. Athena received All-America Selections recognition for its outstanding disease resistance, productivity, and flavor in eastern growing conditions, and became one of the dominant commercial cantaloupe varieties in the eastern US melon industry after its release. The eastern US commercial melon market has distinct requirements from California production: the combination of high summer humidity, heavy disease pressure (particularly powdery mildew, downy mildew, and Alternaria leaf blight), and earlier harvest requirements create conditions where California-bred varieties with limited disease resistance often underperform. Athena's development specifically addressed the eastern market's disease challenges, with strong powdery mildew resistance and tolerance to the other major eastern melon pathogens. The fruit quality is excellent for a hybrid: large, round melons with thick, deeply netted tan skin, firm orange flesh with good Brix (10–12 typical) and genuine cantaloupe flavor, and a shelf life after harvest of 10–14 days — significantly better than most heirloom types. For zone 9 Gulf Coast gardeners, Athena's disease resistance is particularly valuable: the Gulf South's combination of warm temperatures and high humidity creates ideal conditions for foliar diseases that terminate melon plantings before maximum fruit production.

common_name: Athens Cantaloupe (University of Georgia Heat-Tolerant Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Athens cantaloupe was selected specifically for the hot, humid Southeast and performs reliably under conditions that reduce quality in Western cantaloupe varieties. In zone 9, plant March–April for June harvest. Reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity to concentrate sugar content. Athens cantaloupe benefits from black plastic mulch to maintain soil warmth and reduce soil moisture contact with developing fruits.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; maintain consistent moisture during vine development and fruit set, then reduce irrigation as fruits approach full size to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip (fruit pulls free from vine with light pressure). Athens is a cantaloupe variety developed by the University of Georgia (named for the city of Athens, Georgia, home of the university) specifically for performance in the hot, humid Southeast — a regional adaptation that addresses the specific challenges of cantaloupe production in the Gulf South and mid-Atlantic coastal plain where high humidity, heat, and disease pressure reduce quality and yield in the Western-adapted muskmelon types that dominate commercial production in California and Arizona. Athens produces medium-sized (4–5 lb), round, well-netted fruits with the orange flesh, small seed cavity, and aromatic sweetness that define quality cantaloupe; it has good disease resistance to Fusarium wilt and Alternaria leaf blight. The flavor is consistently excellent even under the humid, warm conditions that cause quality to drop in less-adapted varieties. Athens is the most commonly recommended cantaloupe for home gardens in the southeastern states, where the combination of heat tolerance, disease resistance, and consistent eating quality under Gulf South growing conditions makes it the appropriate regional choice over the Western-adapted varieties that dominate seed catalogs.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; very long season, start indoors in short-season areas.
directions: Atlantic Giant is the classic record-breaking pumpkin, capable of producing fruits weighing hundreds of pounds under ideal care. Sow seed after all frost danger in deeply amended, compost-rich soil, giving each plant sprawling room of 10 feet or more. For the largest fruit, allow only one or two pumpkins per vine and remove the rest, then feed and water generously all season. Support the growing fruit on sand or a board to prevent rot, and protect the tender vines from any late frost.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall-through-spring harvest. Atomic Red's red color deepens significantly after cooking — the lycopene pigment that makes the carrot red is more bioavailable from cooked carrots, and the color is more vivid in roasted or steamed preparations than in raw. For maximum color development, grow Atomic Red in cool weather — heat reduces the intensity of the red pigmentation. Thin to 2–3 inches apart after germination.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil free of rocks and compaction; Atomic Red is a red-exterior, red-interior carrot variety producing the color from lycopene — the same antioxidant carotenoid that makes tomatoes and watermelon red — rather than the beta-carotene that makes standard orange carrots orange. This makes Atomic Red carrots a rare lycopene-containing vegetable that is not a tomato, with research suggesting that lycopene from carrots has similar bioavailability to tomato lycopene. The flavor of Atomic Red is less sweet than orange carrots and has a slightly more complex, herbal quality — different from, not inferior to, standard orange. The intense red color makes Atomic Red striking in mixed-carrot salads and vegetable platters alongside yellow, white, purple, and orange carrots. Like all colored carrots, the unique color is the primary appeal for market gardeners and home cooks interested in visual diversity in vegetable cooking.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring once soil is workable, with successions every three weeks.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the bed evenly moist until the slow seedlings emerge. This imperator-type carrot grows 8 to 10 inches long with a brilliant deep-red exterior and orange core, and roasting or steaming intensifies the color contrast. Thin seedlings to 2 to 3 inches so roots size up well. Sow successive crops every three weeks for a continuous supply of these colorful, sweet, crisp carrots.

plant_note: Direct sow at the base of a trellis or pole after last frost; pick at about 3 inches, when the outline of the beans just bulges the pod, for the best snap-bean stage.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep and provide a tall pole or trellis, since this vigorous climber produces over a long season. Aunt Ada's Italian is a family heirloom pole bean brought from Italy to Colorado around the turn of the twentieth century, prized for its dual usefulness: the flat, tender pods make excellent snap beans when picked young, while pods left to mature and dry yield a flavorful soup bean. Its productivity and reliability across a long harvest window made it a treasured keeper variety passed down within one family for generations before wider seed-saver distribution. Pick regularly for fresh eating to keep vines producing, or let the last flush dry fully on the vine for winter storage beans.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Aunt Gertie's Gold is a large, golden-orange heirloom of Southern Appalachian origin with exceptionally sweet, low-acid, deeply flavored fruits that are among the finest of any golden tomato and particularly well-suited to hot, humid Southern summer conditions.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost has passed and provide staking or caging for the tall, indeterminate vines. Aunt Gertie's Gold is a Virginia heirloom reportedly traced to a Virginia woman named Aunt Gertie; it produces very large, golden-orange, oblate to slightly irregular fruits that can weigh 1–2 pounds, with sweet, rich, complex flavor that is noticeably lower in acid than red tomatoes — making it a preferred choice for people who find red tomatoes too acidic. The color is beautiful ranging from deep gold to orange-gold, and the fruits are meaty with dense flesh and few seeds. An outstanding fresh-eating tomato; the low-acid flesh is also excellent for sauces and drying. Grow as a standard indeterminate in full sun with consistent moisture and fertility.

plant_note: Start indoors, transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Aunt Ruby's German Green is an indeterminate heirloom beefsteak that ripens to a green-and-amber blush and offers a sweet, slightly spicy, well-balanced flavor. Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once the weather is settled and warm. Cage or stake the tall vines and prune suckers for airflow, since the large fruits can reach a pound each. Judge ripeness by a slight softening and yellow-green color rather than by red, harvesting before the fruit becomes overly soft.

common_name: Aunt Ruby's German Green Tomato (Large Sweet Green-When-Ripe Heirloom)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Aunt Ruby's German Green stays green when ripe — tell ripeness by slight softening to pressure, subtle yellowing of the shoulder, and an internal color check revealing amber-green flesh rather than pure green.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aunt Ruby's German Green is one of the most famous and beloved green-when-ripe heirloom tomatoes — a large (10–16 oz), irregularly shaped beefsteak type that retains a bright, chartreuse-green to apple-green exterior color even at full ripeness, producing green flesh with amber-yellow internal marbling that makes it unique among ripe tomatoes. The flavor is exceptional: sweet, rich, spicy, and complex with a distinctive quality often described as 'herbal' or 'spicy-sweet' — quite different from the fruity sweetness of yellow types or the savory depth of purple/dark varieties. This variety is named for Ruby Arnold of Greeneville, Tennessee, who saved the seed from German origins and preserved it for decades. The green color at full ripeness challenges harvest timing: rather than using color change as a ripeness indicator, judge by gentle pressure (ripe fruits yield slightly, like a ripe peach), by the subtle yellowing of the blossom-end shoulder, and by cutting a sample fruit to check for amber-green flesh and developed seeds. Aunt Ruby's German Green is outstanding in fresh preparations where the unusual green color and spicy-sweet flavor create memorable flavor combinations with standard red and yellow tomatoes.

plant_note: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring harvest, and again in late summer for a fall and winter crop; resow every 7-10 days for continuous baby-leaf harvest.
directions: Direct sow into cool, fertile soil and keep consistently moist; Auroch produces large, oval, smooth, dark green leaves on an upright plant with long, sturdy stems, a habit that resists leaf damage and soil-splash from heavy rain better than more sprawling spinach types. It can be picked at any stage from baby leaf through full bunching size, giving flexibility for both quick salad greens and larger cooking leaves, and it shows strong resistance to multiple downy mildew races.
