It performs best as a fall, winter, or early spring crop and tolerates moderate winter cold with light protection. Cut whole plants at the base or harvest outer leaves individually to extend the picking window.

plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for fall.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. This easy variety forms bright green leaves dusted with iridescent bronze tips and combines the buttery texture of a butterhead with the upright habit of a mini romaine. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade in warm weather to delay bolting. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head once it fills out.

plant_note: Start seed indoors in late winter and set out transplants about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost date.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant hardened-off seedlings into loose, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, spacing plants to give bulbs room to expand. Water consistently during bulb development, then withhold water once tops begin to yellow and fall, curing bulbs in a warm, airy spot before storage. Australian Brown is an old open-pollinated storage onion prized for its exceptionally firm, small-to-medium copper-brown bulbs and pungent flavor that mellows in cooking, and it has a long-standing reputation among heirloom growers for keeping longer in storage than many modern hybrids.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills of compost-enriched soil after all danger of frost, spacing hills widely for the vigorous vines.
directions: Australian Butter is an uncommon heirloom maxima squash producing large, pale peach-orange fruit with a hard rind and dry, deep-orange flesh that bakes up dense and sweet. It needs a long, warm season and generous spacing since a single vine can cover significant ground while setting several 15-pound fruits. Harvest once the rind hardens fully and the vine begins to die back, then cure in a warm, airy location for one to two weeks before storing. It appeals to gardeners hunting for lesser-known maxima types with outstanding dessert-quality flesh and long winter storage life.

plant_note: Sow directly in early spring, and again in late summer where summers are mild, harvesting outer leaves as they size up.
directions: Sow directly in early spring, and again in late summer where summers are mild, harvesting outer leaves as they size up for extended cut-and-come-again production. An Australian heirloom loose-leaf lettuce with tall, crinkled, chartreuse-yellow leaves and notable heat tolerance, it is a reliable performer where many lettuces bolt or turn bitter in warm weather. It has been preserved largely through heirloom seed exchanges as a distinct warm-climate alternative to common green and red leaf types.

common_name: Austrian Crescent Potato (Nutty Yellow-Fleshed Heirloom Fingerling)
plant_note: Plant seed potato pieces with 2-3 eyes per piece in cool soil; Austrian Crescent is a late-season heirloom fingerling. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling as vines grow; harvest when vines begin to die back. Austrian Crescent is a classic heirloom fingerling potato with tan-gold skin and yellow, waxy flesh, prized for its rich, buttery, nutty flavor that many consider among the best-tasting of the fingerling types. Tubers grow in a distinctive curved, crescent shape, and the plant is a reliable, moderately high-yielding producer. As with other fingerlings, the low-starch, waxy texture holds its shape well through boiling, roasting, and potato salad preparations rather than becoming mealy or falling apart. Because it is a later-maturing variety, allow it a longer season than early potatoes; harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or wait for full maturity and vine dieback for larger tubers with better storage life.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 3 weeks early in short-season climates and transplant out once soil has warmed.
directions: Autumn Crown is a modern interspecific F1 hybrid bred by crossing a Crown Prince-type maxima with a butternut moschata to combine butternut's sweet, dense flesh with earlier ripening and better cool-weather set. Its more compact vines and shorter days to maturity make it a good option for gardeners in cooler or shorter-season regions where standard butternuts often fail to fully ripen. Fruit develops a classic buff-tan skin and a small seed cavity, giving high usable flesh yield per squash. Grow it as you would any butternut, but expect a slightly earlier harvest window and more reliable ripening under marginal heat conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Autumn Giant is a traditional European leek bred for very large shaft size — producing enormous, thick, long white shanks weighing up to 1–1.5 lbs per plant — and timed for autumn harvest from October through December before the hardest winter weather arrives.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; sow 1/4 inch deep in trays at 65–70°F; transplant when seedlings are pencil-thick, 6–8 inches tall, in late spring. Autumn Giant (sometimes listed as 'Autumn Giant Carentan' in older European catalogs) is a traditional European heirloom leek developed specifically for the production of very large, thick-shafted leeks harvested in autumn — it consistently produces some of the most substantial, heavy-yielding individual leek plants of any variety, with shanks that can exceed 2–3 inches in diameter and 8–10 inches of usable white shank. The name refers to both the size (genuinely giant compared to most leek varieties) and the harvest timing: Autumn Giant is best harvested from September through December, before the coldest winter weather arrives, as it does not have the extreme winter hardiness of specifically bred winter leeks like Bleu de Solaise or Musselburgh. Plant deeply in a trench or use a dibble to create 6-inch planting holes to encourage long, blanched shanks; the rich, mild, sweet flavor is excellent for any leek preparation.

common_name: Autumn Gold Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Early-Turning Orange Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Autumn Gold's most important attribute is that it turns orange on the vine before most other pumpkins, allowing harvest of fully colored orange pumpkins 2–3 weeks earlier in the fall season — critical for growers who want to offer orange pumpkins at farm stands in early-to-mid September before standard varieties are ready. In zone 9, plant May–June for a September harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after last frost in full sun, well-drained, fertile soil; fertilize generously and maintain consistent moisture. Autumn Gold is a 1987 All-America Selections-winning pumpkin that earned recognition for addressing one of the most practically important challenges in pumpkin production: the timing gap between Halloween (when orange pumpkins are in peak demand) and most pumpkin varieties' natural maturity schedule. Standard pumpkin varieties like Connecticut Field and Jack-O-Lantern reach their mature orange color in late September to October — sometimes too close to Halloween to allow adequate display time and recovery from any early-season shortfalls. Autumn Gold was bred to turn orange earlier than standard varieties while still maintaining an acceptable carving-type form, giving growers 2–3 extra weeks of salable orange pumpkins in the critical mid-September to early October market window. The fruits are medium-large (10–15 lbs), round to slightly flat, with bright orange skin and a good handle-stem; the flesh is moderately thick and adequate for cooking in addition to decorative use. Autumn Gold's earlier orange color development is driven by genetics that accelerate chlorophyll breakdown in the skin — the fruits reach full orange color when they are still in the immature stage compared to standard varieties. A consistently valuable variety for pumpkin patch operators and farm stand growers who want to extend the salable orange pumpkin window into early fall.

common_name: Autumn King Carrot (Berlikum-Type Large Storage Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow in deeply tilled, loose soil in late summer for fall and winter harvest; Autumn King is a large-rooted type that needs deep, unobstructed soil to develop its full potential (roots commonly reach 10–12 inches). In zone 9, sow August–October for harvest November–February; roots left in the ground over winter become sweeter after light frosts. Requires more soil depth than other carrot types and more growing time but produces substantially larger, longer-storing roots.
directions: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in very deep, loose, stone-free soil enriched with compost; thin to 3–4 inches when seedlings reach 2 inches. Autumn King (also sold as 'Autumn King 2') is a Berlikum/Flakkee-type heirloom carrot that represents the large-rooted tradition of European storage carrot breeding — producing very large, long (10–12 inch), broad-shouldered, tapered roots with dark orange skin and rich orange flesh that are built for cold storage and extended winter use. The Berlikum/Flakkee type was developed in the Netherlands for large-scale commercial storage carrot production and is characterized by the widest shoulders and largest root volume of any carrot type, with correspondingly excellent storage characteristics: properly cured Autumn King roots keep 4–6 months in cold storage (32–38°F, high humidity) without significant quality loss. The flavor is rich, sweet, and distinctly carrot-forward — more concentrated and traditional in character than some modern sweet hybrids, with a satisfying density and substance that makes these carrots outstanding for soups, stews, roasting, and winter cooking generally. Autumn King is the standard large storage carrot in British gardens (where it has been grown since the 1950s) and is valued throughout northern Europe for its combination of large yield per plant, excellent storage, and authentic robust carrot flavor. An excellent choice for home gardeners who want to store carrots through winter.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; Avalanche is an AAS-winning pure-white beet that does not bleed or stain, with sweet flavor and none of the earthy, bitter aftertaste some gardeners dislike in red beets.
directions: Direct sow seed clusters 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun, thinning to one seedling per cluster once plants have their first true leaves. Avalanche is an AAS-winning beet with pure-white roots and a sweet, clean flavor without the earthy or bitter aftertaste that some gardeners and children dislike in standard red beets. Because it produces no red pigment, it does not stain hands, cutting boards, or other ingredients when cooked or pickled — a genuine kitchen convenience, particularly useful for gardeners who want to combine beets with other vegetables without turning everything pink. The greens are tender and edible as well, cooked the same way as other beet tops. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, evenly sized roots, and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the best texture; oversized roots can become woody.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost at the base of a tall trellis or pole tepee, as this Mesoamerican runner bean climbs vigorously and rewards a sturdy support.
directions: Direct sow around last frost at the base of a tall trellis or pole tepee, as this Mesoamerican runner bean climbs vigorously and rewards a sturdy support with a long season of striking scarlet-purple flowers that draw hummingbirds. Ayocote beans have been cultivated in the highlands of central and southern Mexico since long before European contact, and the deep purple-black seeds of this particular landrace are prized in Oaxacan and other regional cuisines for their dense, meaty texture and earthy flavor once cooked. Like other runner beans, it sets pods best when nights stay cool, so growers in hot-summer regions may see reduced yields in high summer. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine before shelling for the best storage-quality dry bean.

common_name: Ayocote Negro Bean (Black Mexican Runner Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy trellis; Ayocote Negro is a large-seeded black Mexican runner bean, a staple of central Mexican cooking.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous vines to climb. Ayocote Negro bears large, glossy black seeds inside long runner bean pods, a traditional Mexican dry bean valued for its meaty texture and rich, earthy flavor in stews and slow-cooked dishes, distinct from the smaller common bean species most Americans grow. As a runner bean it produces attractive clusters of flowers that also draw hummingbirds before setting pods, making it ornamental as well as productive. Allow pods to dry fully on the vine before shelling for storage.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Azoychka is a rare Russian heirloom yellow-orange tomato of uncertain origin brought to the Seed Savers Exchange from Moscow in the early 1990s, producing medium-sized, flattened, lemon-yellow to pale orange fruits with an exceptionally bright, tangy, citrus-touched flavor unlike most yellow heirloom tomatoes, which tend toward the sweet and bland.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained, deeply prepared soil; provide staking or caging as plants grow 4–6 feet tall. Azoychka is a Russian heirloom yellow tomato brought to American seed preservation networks from Moscow in the early 1990s and distributed through the Seed Savers Exchange; its exact origins are unclear, but it is believed to be a traditional Russian variety grown in home gardens for generations before reaching Western gardeners. The medium-sized (4–8 oz), flattened to slightly oblate, lemon-yellow to pale golden-orange fruits are distinguished from other yellow heirloom tomatoes by their flavor profile — Azoychka has a bright, tangy, citrusy complexity rarely found in yellow tomatoes, which typically run sweet and mild; the flavor has been compared to a lemon-spiked yellow tomato with good acid balance for a yellow-fruited type. The combination of mild sweetness and tanginess makes Azoychka outstanding for fresh slicing, tomato salads where both color and flavor stand out, and gazpacho. An indeterminate variety of moderate size and good productivity; excellent for any region with a long warm season.

plant_note: Transplant after all danger of frost once soil has warmed, spacing plants generously for good airflow around the semi-determinate vines.
directions: BHN 589 is a widely grown Southeastern hybrid valued by market growers and home gardeners for combining excellent flavor with a strong resistance package to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, Verticillium wilt, and tobacco mosaic virus. Semi-determinate vines set heavy clusters of crack-resistant 8-10 ounce fruit that hold shelf life well after picking. Stake or cage for support and maintain even soil moisture to minimize splitting during the humid summer fruit set. Choose this variety where disease pressure is high but you still want dependable, large-fruited flavor rather than a purely commercial round tomato.

common_name: BHN 602 Tomato (Heat-Set Disease-Resistant Gulf South Hybrid)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and set out transplants once soil has warmed; BHN 602 was bred in Florida specifically to keep setting fruit through the high heat and humidity that stall many other slicing tomatoes.
directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, staking or caging to support the compact determinate vines. BHN 602 is a Florida-bred hybrid slicing tomato carrying a strong disease package — resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, and tomato spotted wilt virus — that holds up well against the soilborne and thrips-vectored diseases common in humid Gulf South gardens. The plants produce large, firm, deep-red, globe-shaped fruit averaging 10-12 ounces with good flavor for a hybrid of its size. It is widely recommended by Gulf South extension services as a reliable heat-set variety for both spring and fall planting windows, continuing to set fruit at temperatures that cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in less heat-adapted tomatoes.

common_name: BHN 968 Tomato (Heat-Tolerant Disease-Resistant Hybrid Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed; BHN 968 is rated among the most heat-tolerant cherry tomatoes in university trials, continuing to set fruit through the hottest stretch of a Gulf South summer.
directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the compact determinate plants to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. BHN 968 produces abundant clusters of small, shiny, deep-red cherry tomatoes prized for being notably sweeter and better textured than most determinate cherry types, backed by broad resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, tobacco mosaic virus, tomato spotted wilt virus, and root-knot nematodes. Its combination of compact habit, disease resistance, and standout heat tolerance makes it a dependable producer through the peak of Gulf Coast summer, when many indeterminate cherry varieties slow down or drop blossoms. Harvest continuously as fruit ripens to encourage ongoing production through the warm season.

plant_note: Plant bulbils (tiny bulbs produced in the flower head) or transplants in spring or fall; Babington's leek is best propagated from bulbils, planting them 1 inch deep and 6–8 inches apart. It takes a full season to establish but then persists indefinitely, spreading slowly by underground bulblets and overhead bulbils.
directions: Plant bulbils or transplants in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Babington's leek is a wild, perennial form of the cultivated leek native to the Atlantic coasts of western Europe, where it naturalizes on cliffs and hedgerows. Unlike annual leeks, it forms a persistent clump that produces new leaves each season, dies back in summer heat, then regrows vigorously in fall — making it particularly well-adapted to Mediterranean-climate and zone 9 gardens where annual leeks struggle in summer. Harvest leaves, stems, and green tops throughout the cool season much like walking onions. In late summer it produces a tall umbel of flowers plus abundant aerial bulbils — collect these and replant to expand your patch. The flavor is mild and leek-like, less pungent than multiplying onions. A classic cottage garden perennial allium valued in permaculture systems for its low maintenance once established.

common_name: Baby Bear Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Small Hull-Less-Seed Pie Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Baby Bear is an AAS-winning small pie pumpkin prized both for sweet baking flesh and for its hull-less, easy-to-roast seeds.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Baby Bear is an AAS-winning small pie pumpkin, producing round, deep-orange fruit around 1.5 pounds each with sweet, fine-grained, good-baking flesh well suited to pies, soups, and purees, and small enough to make an attractive miniature carving or decorative pumpkin as well. Its standout feature is hull-less (naked) seeds — unlike most pumpkins, the seeds lack the tough outer hull, so they can be roasted and eaten whole with no shelling required, making Baby Bear a favorite for gardeners who want a dual-purpose crop of both good-eating flesh and easy snacking seeds from the same fruit. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and color deepens, cutting the stem with a few inches attached, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before use or storage.

common_name: Baby Blue Hubbard Squash (Little Gem Hubbard, Compact Blue Hubbard)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Baby Blue Hubbard is a compact, appropriately sized version of the giant Blue Hubbard squash, producing 4–8 lb teardrop-shaped, slate-blue fruits with the same exceptional sweet, dry, richly flavored flesh of the full-sized type — but in a manageable size that a typical household can consume in 2–3 sittings and a vine that requires much less space.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Baby Blue Hubbard produces compact vines of 4–6 feet, more manageable in home gardens than full-sized Hubbard; harvest when the teardrop-shaped fruits are fully blue-gray and the skin resists fingernail penetration; cure for 2–3 weeks and store up to 6 months in a cool, dry location. Baby Blue Hubbard is a compact selection from the classic Blue Hubbard squash (Cucurbita maxima 'Hubbard') — one of the premier American heirloom winter squash varieties, famous for its distinctive blue-gray, bumpy, teardrop-shaped fruits and its extraordinarily sweet, dry, richly flavored flesh. The standard Blue Hubbard can produce fruits of 15–25 lbs or more — too large for most modern households to use in one or even several meals, requiring the awkward step of cutting up a huge squash and storing the remainder. Baby Blue Hubbard addresses this practical limitation by producing fruits of 4–8 lbs with the same culinary qualities as the full-sized type: the thick, deeply orange, dry, intensely sweet flesh that has made Hubbard squash the gold standard of American winter squash for over a century. The skin is the same distinctive blue-gray, somewhat bumpy, teardrop-shaped form of the parent variety, recognizable at a glance, and equally hard to cut open (a mallet or drop from a height is the traditional method). The flavor after curing is superb — often described as the richest, most complex flavor of any winter squash, combining sweetness with an earthy, slightly nutty character. Stores exceptionally well for 4–6 months.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Baby Boo pumpkins pair well with Jack Be Little (orange mini pumpkin) for two-color autumn arrangements from a single planting space. Allow fruits to cure on the vine until stem shrivels and skin is hard. The pure white skin of Baby Boo makes it a striking element in mixed ornamental displays — it retains its white color for months after harvest when kept in a cool, dry location.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Baby Boo is a white-skinned miniature pumpkin producing small (2–3 inch), perfectly round, deeply ribbed fruits of pure creamy white — the white color makes it the natural complement to the orange Jack Be Little in autumn decorating, where the two varieties together provide the classic orange-and-white color combination of fall décor. The white skin remains crisp and ornamental for 3–4 months after harvest, making Baby Boo extremely long-lasting in decorative arrangements compared to fresh-cut flowers. Like all miniature pumpkins, Baby Boo is edible — the small amounts of sweet, dense flesh inside the tiny fruits can be scooped out after roasting in the oven. The pure white skin is unusual among Cucurbita pepo varieties and results from absence of the carotenoid pigments that give most pumpkins their orange color. Baby Boo plants are productive, often generating 8–15 fruits per plant from compact vines.

common_name: Baby Bubba Okra (AAS-Winning Dwarf Compact Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65 degrees F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Baby Bubba is a compact, dwarf okra cultivar bred specifically for smaller gardens and container growing, staying considerably shorter than standard okra varieties while still producing a good crop of tender, dark green, ribbed pods over a long summer season. Its shorter stature also makes harvesting easier, without needing a ladder or long reach for pods higher up on a tall plant. As with all okra, pick pods young, at two to four inches, and harvest every day or two during peak production to keep the compact plant setting new pods rather than diverting energy into maturing tough, oversized ones.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring and again in late summer; heat can trigger bolting.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool, fertile soil and thin to about 5 inches apart, or grow in containers. This Asian green, also called pak choi, is ready in about 35 days when harvested at 5 to 6 inches tall for tender baby choi. It resists bolting and makes an attractive addition to mixed containers. Keep soil evenly moist to prevent bolting, and harvest whole heads or outer stalks for stir-fries and marinated salads.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer; cold improves flavor.
directions: Sow this blend of curly, flat-leaf, and oak-leaf kales thickly in a band for baby-leaf harvests, or thin to 6 inches for full-size plants. Direct-seed 1/4 inch deep as soon as soil can be worked in spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop. Cut outer leaves at 3-4 inches for tender salad greens, harvesting cut-and-come-again over several weeks. Cold weather and light frost sweeten the leaves, so this mix carries well into winter in mild zones.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; make a second planting 6–8 weeks before first fall frost for a fall crop. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches; baby pak choi matures much faster than full-size bok choy and is harvested as a complete, tender plant rather than by removing individual leaves. The entire head — including the thick, juicy white or light green stems and soft jade leaves — is cut at soil level when 4–6 inches tall. Mild, sweet, and slightly mustardy in flavor, it needs only a very brief stir-fry or a quick blanch. Baby pak choi is excellent for cut-and-come-again growing: cut above the growing crown and plants will resprout several times before bolting. Consistent moisture is essential; drought stress causes premature bolting.

common_name: Baby Pam Pumpkin (Small Sweet Pie Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; give the vines room to run, and expect several small, uniform fruits per plant.
directions: Direct sow seed in warm, rich soil in full sun after the last frost, planting in hills with ample space for the vines to spread. Baby Pam is a widely grown pie pumpkin hybrid producing small, uniformly round, deep-orange fruit around 4 to 6 pounds, prized for dense, sweet, fine-grained flesh with less watery fiber than large carving pumpkins, making it excellent for pies, purees, and soups. It sets fruit reliably and uniformly across the vine, giving a more consistent harvest than many open-pollinated pie pumpkin varieties, and its handsome, deeply ribbed miniature form also works well for small-scale fall decorating. Harvest once the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry, then cure in a warm, airy spot for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage.

common_name: Bahamian Goat Pepper (Small Elongated Very Hot Bahamian Pepper)
plant_note: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Bahamian Goat is the traditional small, very hot pepper used to make Bahamian goat pepper sauce.
directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Bahamian Goat bears small, elongated, tapering pods that ripen from green to yellow-orange, carrying intense habanero-relative heat and a bright, fruity aroma, and is the traditional pepper behind Bahamian goat pepper sauce, a fiery condiment served throughout the islands with seafood and conch dishes. The compact, productive plants bear heavily over a long warm-season harvest. Handle ripe pods with gloves and harvest regularly to keep new flowers setting.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun; balsam apple is closely related to but distinct from bitter melon (Momordica charantia). It requires a trellis and warm, humid conditions. Native to tropical Africa and naturalized across many tropical regions.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun; balsam apple is the African species of the bitter gourd group — a climbing vine with deeply lobed, attractive leaves and small, oval, prominently warty orange-yellow fruits (smaller and rounder than bitter melon) that split dramatically when ripe to reveal bright scarlet-coated seeds in a striking display. Native to tropical and subtropical Africa and widely naturalized across Africa, South Asia, and northern Australia. The leaves, young shoots, and unripe fruits are eaten as cooked vegetables across Africa, where it is an important pot herb and relish ingredient in many regional cuisines. The ripe fruit is ornamental and was traditionally used medicinally as a topical treatment for skin conditions (the name 'balsam' refers to the resinous, aromatic properties historically attributed to the fruit). More compact and less bitter than bitter melon (M. charantia). The red-seeded, splitting fruit display is striking and ornamental in the garden.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil temperature exceeds 65°F; like peanuts, the flowers bend downward and developing pods push underground to mature — grow in loose, easily penetrated, well-drained soil.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after last frost in loose, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in full sun; bambara groundnut is a West African staple legume that forms its nutritious pods underground after pollination — a fascinating growth habit that requires loose, easily penetrated soil for the gynophore (pod peg) to bury itself. The seeds contain 19–21% protein and 40–65% carbohydrate with a nutty, slightly sweet flavor; they are boiled fresh or dried for storage, ground into flour, or fermented into condiments. Among the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant legumes in cultivation, outperforming cowpeas and soybeans on poor dry soils where other legumes fail while fixing nitrogen and improving soil structure.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, and again in late summer for a fall crop; can be grown at tight spacing in containers because of its small mature size.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer, thinning or transplanting to close spacing since mature heads stay compact. Bambi is an All-America Selections winner bred as a true miniature romaine, forming dense, upright 6-inch heads with sweet, crisp leaves in about half the space and time of standard romaine, and it holds quality and resists bolting notably longer as temperatures rise. Its small size also makes it well suited to container growing and to serving as an individual single-portion salad head.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. Banana Legs is indeterminate and benefits from staking or caging. The golden-yellow paste tomatoes are sweet enough for fresh eating — useful as a dual-purpose paste/fresh tomato. In zone 9 fall planting in August extends the productive season well into December.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with stake or cage support; Banana Legs is a yellow paste tomato producing clusters of elongated, banana-shaped fruits (4–5 inches long, 1–1.5 inches across) with pale golden-yellow skin that deepens to a richer yellow at full ripeness. The low-acid, sweet, mild flavor of yellow paste tomatoes like Banana Legs fills a different culinary niche than standard red paste tomatoes — the mildness and sweetness make Banana Legs outstanding for golden tomato sauces, sun-dried yellow tomatoes, and fresh eating as a snack tomato, where the sweet, non-acidic character appeals to people who find standard red tomatoes too sharp. The thick walls and small seed cavities are characteristic of paste tomatoes, making Banana Legs efficient to process for sauce and giving it a meaty, dense texture when eaten fresh. Unlike many paste tomatoes that are primarily functional, Banana Legs produces well-flavored fruits suitable for both cooking and fresh eating.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills or rows; needs a long, hot growing season to fully sweeten.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart, or in rows 6 feet apart, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Banana Melon is a 19th-century American heirloom named for its distinctive shape — long, cylindrical fruit up to 20 inches that closely resembles an oversized banana — with smooth yellow skin and pale salmon-pink flesh that is sweet and aromatic when fully ripe. As a winter (inodorus) melon type, the fruit has little external fragrance even when ripe, so gardeners should judge readiness by the skin turning fully yellow and the blossom end softening slightly to the touch. Its long, heat-loving growing season makes it well suited to Gulf South summers with a long, warm stretch to fully mature and sweeten.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and keep at 75–80°F until sprouts appear. Transplant to the garden after last frost and water evenly to maintain steady growth and prevent fruit splitting. Banana peppers are mild and productive; pick fruits at 4–6 inches long when pale yellow for the mildest flavor. Leaving fruits to mature to orange or red increases both sweetness and slight heat.

plant_note: Plant sets pointed tip up with the neck just above soil.
directions: A large elongated shallot combining the size of an onion with a shallot's refined flavor. Plant individual sets in early spring with the tip barely showing, spacing them 6 inches apart. Unlike clustering shallots, banana shallots often size up as a single large bulb, so give each room. Keep weeded and evenly watered until tops begin to yellow in midsummer. Lift, cure thoroughly, and store the papery bulbs in a cool dry place for months.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; Banana squash is one of the largest commonly grown winter squash varieties, producing enormously long (18–36+ inches), cylindrical, banana-shaped fruits in pale pink-orange-salmon skin with dense, sweet, golden-orange flesh — a Western US market and home-garden staple sold in cut wedges because the fruits are too large for whole-fruit sale.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows; Banana squash requires a long season (105–120 days) and is best suited to zones 5–11 with warm summers; in short-season areas, start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting. Banana squash is a Cucurbita maxima type producing some of the longest and heaviest fruits of any winter squash, with cylindrical, slightly curved, banana-shaped fruits typically 18–36 inches long and weighing 10–35 lbs; the distinctive pale pink-salmon to peachy-orange skin makes it instantly recognizable and it is commonly sold in cut wedges at Western US grocery stores and farmers' markets where the whole fruit would be too large for most households. The flesh is dense, smooth-textured, golden-orange with excellent sweetness and a rich, slightly nutty flavor excellent for roasting, soups, and pies. A vigorous, sprawling vine requiring considerable space (at least 8 feet in each direction); store harvested fruits in a cool, dry location where they keep for 3–6 months.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost and transplant pencil-thick seedlings out for a late-season crop that will stand through winter.
directions: Bandit is an open-pollinated late-season leek bred for standing through hard freezes without splitting or losing quality, making it a favorite for gardeners who want fresh leeks well into winter rather than a single fall harvest. Trench or hill soil around the dark blue-green shanks as they grow to lengthen and blanch the edible white portion, since this variety produces very little natural bulbing and stays uniformly thick and straight. Keep plants weeded and evenly watered through summer so the stalks bulk up before cold weather triggers the hardiness that lets Bandit sit in the garden, unharvested, through repeated freezes. Choose Bandit over early-season leeks when the goal is a reliable, cold-tolerant crop to pull as needed from November through late winter.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights remain above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a productive spring through fall season. Barker's Hot is one of the hottest New Mexico type varieties, producing 10,000–15,000 SHU, and thrives in the heat and low humidity of zone 8–9.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Barker's Hot is a New Mexico State University-developed hot New Mexico-type chile with significantly higher heat (10,000–15,000 SHU) than standard Hatch and New Mexico No. 9 varieties, making it the choice for gardeners who want traditional New Mexico flavor with serious heat. The long, 7–8 inch fruits are produced in abundance on large, productive plants and are harvested green for roasting or left to ripen and dry red for red chile powder and ristras. Roasting mellows the heat while concentrating the flavor; roasted Barker's Hot chiles freeze well for year-round use. This variety is particularly well-suited to hot, dry climates but also performs in the humidity of zone 9 Gulf Coast with good air circulation.

common_name: Barossa Fest Tomato (Bicolor Red-and-Black Australian Dwarf Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Barossa Fest is an Australian-bred Dwarf Tomato Project release with bicolor red-and-black fruit, named for the Barossa Valley wine region.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Barossa Fest bears medium fruit blending red and dusky purple-black tones in a distinctive bicolor pattern, combining the rich, complex flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomatoes with the compact habit of a Dwarf Tomato Project plant, developed through the program's Australian breeding collaboration and named for the country's famous Barossa Valley wine region. Its manageable size suits raised beds and containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

common_name: Basket of Fire Pepper (Texas Superstar Hanging-Basket Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Basket of Fire is a Texas Superstar pepper bred specifically for hanging baskets and containers, with a naturally cascading habit and strong heat tolerance for Texas summers.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into a hanging basket, large container, or garden bed in full sun. Basket of Fire is a Texas Superstar-designated ornamental-edible pepper bred for a compact, naturally trailing habit that shows off its abundant small, upright-then-cascading fruit especially well in a hanging basket, unlike most hot peppers, which grow upright. The fruit carries substantial heat, around 80,000 Scoville units, well into cayenne-and-above territory, ripening from green through yellow and orange to red, so a single plant often displays several fruit colors at once. It thrives in the heat and lower humidity of a Texas summer and continues producing heavily through the hottest months when many other peppers slow down. Harvest continuously to keep new fruit setting, and water container plantings regularly, since pots dry out faster than garden soil.

plant_note: Sow direct in fertile, stone-free soil; harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots and tops.
directions: An Italian heirloom documented in 19th-century European seed catalogs, grown for its flattened roots with distinctive pink-and-white concentric rings when sliced, milder and less earthy than solid red beets. It matures quickly, making it well suited to early spring sowings ahead of summer heat or a late-summer succession crop. Sow direct in fertile, stone-free soil and harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots and tops, which can also be cooked as greens.

common_name: Bates Cereal Rye (Early-Maturing Winter-Hardy Grazing and Cover Crop Rye)
plant_note: Direct sow 1-1.5 inches deep in fall (September-November in zone 9) in well-drained soil in full sun; Bates is an early-maturing, winter-hardy cereal rye selection bred with good grazing tolerance and vigorous fall establishment.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed in fall into well-drained, average soil in full sun; cereal rye tolerates poor, sandy, or compacted ground better than almost any other cover crop grain. Bates is an early-maturing cereal rye selection noted for rapid, vigorous fall establishment and good tolerance to grazing or repeated mowing, making it a practical dual-purpose choice for gardeners or small farms wanting both winter forage and spring soil-building biomass. Its dense, fibrous root system scavenges leftover soil nitrogen, prevents winter erosion, and suppresses weeds, while the extensive root mass and above-ground residue break up compacted soil and add substantial organic matter when terminated by mowing, rolling, or tillage in spring, generally two to three weeks before the following crop is planted to allow allelopathic residues to break down. Cereal rye is among the most cold-hardy of all cover crop grains and will continue growing through cold snaps that stop other winter cover crops.

plant_note: Small stature suits close spacing and cold-frame culture.
directions: Sow directly in cool soil; one of the oldest documented cos lettuces, dating to eighteenth-century England and named for the city of Bath, it produces compact, upright, small-to-medium heads with sweet, buttery, self-blanching hearts. Its small stature suits close spacing and cold-frame culture, and it was historically valued for delivering a fine cos lettuce in a smaller garden footprint than larger romaines. Heirloom seed savers maintain it as a variety predating most commercial romaine breeding.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost for a spring crop; Bauer is a green oakleaf-type lettuce bred for slow bolting and good performance as days warm, extending the spring harvest window further than older oakleaf strains.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently, or start transplants indoors for an earlier crop; germinate at 50-70F. Bauer is an AAS-winning oakleaf lettuce recognized for outstanding heat tolerance and slow bolting compared to older oakleaf varieties, producing a loose, deeply lobed rosette of tender, mild green leaves that hold their quality and texture well into warmer weather. It is well suited to both cut-and-come-again harvesting of outer leaves and a single whole-head cut. In zone 9, use it as an early-spring or fall crop and provide afternoon shade during any unseasonably warm stretch to delay bitterness. Keep soil consistently moist for the sweetest, most tender leaves.

plant_note: Plant certified slips after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65F in well-drained, loamy soil in full sun; Bayou Belle is an LSU AgCenter release selected for improved resistance to soil rot compared to older Louisiana sweet potato varieties.
directions: Plant certified sweet potato slips after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Bayou Belle is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release bred to combine the deep-orange, sweet flesh Gulf South consumers expect with improved resistance to soil rot and other soil-borne diseases that build up in continuously cropped sweet potato ground. Roots are smooth-skinned, uniform, and size up reliably in Louisiana's long warm season. As with all sweet potatoes, cure freshly dug roots at 85-90F and high humidity for about a week to heal skin wounds and convert starches to sugars before storing or eating; uncured roots taste starchy rather than sweet. Start with certified, virus-indexed slips rather than sprouting grocery-store roots, since accumulated viral disease is the main long-term yield killer in home sweet potato patches. Rotate planting beds year to year to keep soil-borne disease pressure low.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date. Beam's is a distinct, seed-saver-maintained strain of Yellow Pear kept true-to-type through generations of hand selection.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Beam's Yellow Pear is a named heirloom strain of the classic yellow pear cherry tomato, kept distinct from the generic commercial Yellow Pear seed line by seed savers who selected it over many generations for productivity and reliable pear-shaped fruit. The small, teardrop-shaped fruits ripen to a bright, glossy yellow and carry the same mild, low-acid, sweet flavor the type is known for, making them a favorite for salads and snacking as well as for gardeners sensitive to more acidic tomatoes. The indeterminate vine is vigorous and needs sturdy staking or caging, setting fruit in long, heavy clusters over a long season. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom strain, seed can be saved true-to-type from the healthiest, most productive plants for future seasons.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and set out transplants once the soil is warm and nights are frost-free.
directions: Sow indoors with warm soil temperatures and transplant into full sun after frost danger has passed, keeping plants evenly watered so the tender skin does not toughen. Mulching helps retain the consistent moisture this heirloom prefers. Beatrice is an Italian heirloom similar in type to Rosa Bianca, producing rounded to oval fruit blushed rose-pink over creamy white, with dense, mild, and notably low-bitterness flesh. It is often grown for its striking market appearance as well as its tender texture when roasted or grilled.

common_name: Beauregard Sweet Potato (Louisiana-Developed Leading Commercial Orange Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified slips after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, sandy loam to loamy, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Beauregard produces best in loose, deep soil — heavy clay limits tuber expansion and produces misshapen roots; raised beds with amended soil are ideal in clay-heavy Gulf South soils.
directions: Plant certified sweet potato slips (rooted cuttings) after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Beauregard is the dominant commercial sweet potato variety in the United States — developed by Louisiana State University AgCenter and released in 1987 to address both production efficiency and consumer preference for the deep-orange-fleshed sweet potato that now defines the American market standard. The deep orange-copper skin over vivid orange flesh, consistently uniform tuber shape, and high sugar content that develops fully after curing represent the qualities LSU breeders targeted: a variety that performs reliably in the humid Gulf South climate while producing the attractive, sweet, deeply colored roots that American consumers prefer. Beauregard matures in 90–110 days from slip transplanting, making it one of the faster-maturing sweet potato varieties and allowing good production within the Gulf South warm season. Sweet potatoes require curing to develop their characteristic sweetness — newly harvested tubers are starchy and less sweet than properly cured ones. Cure at 85–90°F with high humidity (85–90%) for 5–7 days to heal skin wounds and convert starches to sugars. Plant certified virus-indexed slips rather than home-grown slips from grocery store sweet potatoes to avoid introducing sweet potato virus diseases that reduce yield. As a Gulf South native crop commercially centered in Louisiana, Beauregard performs with particular reliability in zone 8-10 humid conditions.

common_name: Beaver Dam Pepper (Wisconsin Hungarian Heirloom Mild Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil warms; a Hungarian family heirloom brought to Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, in 1912 and listed in the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant outdoors once nighttime temperatures stay above 55F, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Beaver Dam is a Hungarian-American heirloom brought to Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, by immigrant Joe Hussli in 1912 and is still celebrated there with an annual pepper festival; it is also listed in the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste. Fruits are large, horn-shaped, and mildly hot, roughly comparable to a pimento in heat, ripening from lime green to a deep reddish-orange and reaching 6-9 inches long on tall, vigorous plants. Harvest green for milder flavor or let fruits ripen fully red for sweeter, more intense flavor; plants are heavy yielding and adapt well to a range of climates.

common_name: Beck's Big Buck Okra (Texas Heirloom Giant-Pod Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed once soil has warmed to at least 65°F; Beck's Big Buck is a Texas heirloom bred to hold size without turning woody, so it forgives gardeners who cannot harvest every single day.
directions: Soak seed overnight and direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun; Beck's Big Buck is a Texas heirloom prized for pods that stay tender and stringless even when allowed to grow well past the 4-inch mark where most okra varieties turn fibrous, making it far more forgiving for gardeners who cannot check the patch daily during peak summer production. Plants are tall and vigorous, often topping 6 feet by late summer, and keep setting pods heavily through the worst of the Gulf South's heat once regular blackeyed-pea-type production varieties have slowed. Harvest pods at 4–8 inches for the best balance of size and tenderness, and keep picking to encourage continued flowering; a single well-fed row easily supplies a household through the summer for gumbo, frying, and pickling.

common_name: Beedy's Camden Kale (Maine Heirloom Overwintering Curly Kale)
plant_note: Direct sow in spring, or sow in late summer for a fall crop and overwintering in mild climates; Beedy's Camden is unusually tender for such a cold-hardy kale and tends to self-sow readily where left to flower.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or space plants 12-18 inches apart and harvest outer leaves as needed. Beedy's Camden traces to a single kale plant that gardener Beedy Parker noticed overwintering in her Camden, Maine garden in the 1980s; she saved and shared its seed for years before Fedco Seeds arranged commercial production, introducing it more widely in 2009. The semi-savoyed, ruffled, medium-green leaves are notably more tender than the true Siberian types it resembles, staying pleasant through summer heat while also surviving hard New England winters, and the flavor turns markedly sweeter after several fall frosts. Its ready self-seeding habit and strong regional pedigree have made it a favorite among Northeast market growers and seed savers looking for a genuinely open-pollinated, locally adapted alternative to hybrid curly kales.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Beefmaster requires a very sturdy support system — heavy cages or strong staking — due to the extreme weight of mature fruit clusters.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Beefmaster is one of the most popular extra-large slicing tomato hybrids in American home gardens — an indeterminate hybrid producing truly giant fruits averaging 16–32 ounces (1–2 pounds) or more per fruit, with the classic beefsteak form: large, meaty, low-seed, deep-red flesh with rich, balanced tomato flavor that makes it the premier choice for thick-sliced tomatoes for sandwiches and BLTs. The extremely heavy fruit size requires robust support — the vines need strong cages or stakes and should have the heaviest fruit clusters supported or tied as they develop to prevent stem breakage. Beefmaster was developed to combine maximum fruit size with disease resistance (V, F, N, T, A resistance package) that most older beefsteak heirlooms lack, making it significantly more reliable in warm, humid Gulf South climates. In zone 9, Beefmaster performs best in the spring window (February–May transplanting) when temperatures allow the large fruits to develop without excessive heat during fruit set — temperatures above 95°F can cause blossom drop and inhibit fruit development on large-fruited varieties. Consistent, deep watering reduces blossom-end rot, which can affect the large-fruited types more than small-fruited varieties.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and keep the mix warm for even sprouting. This century-old indeterminate heirloom produces thick, meaty slices prized for sandwiches and any dish wanting rich tomato flavor. Vines are extremely vigorous, reaching 6 feet or more, so provide a sturdy cage or wire support and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot, and harvest fruit fully colored.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–85°F; transplant in full sun in very fertile, deeply prepared, well-drained soil and provide heavy-duty caging or staking as beefsteak plants grow large and carry heavy fruit that requires strong support.
directions: Start seeds 1/4 inch deep indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–85°F and transplant in full sun in deeply cultivated, very fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; beefsteak tomatoes produce the largest fruits of any tomato type, with individual fruits commonly weighing 1–2 pounds and sometimes exceeding 3 pounds in favored varieties. They are indeterminate and long-season (78–95 days to first harvest), requiring heavy-duty caging or staking and consistent, deep watering throughout the season. Prune to one or two main stems for the largest individual fruits; allowing multiple stems produces more but smaller fruits. The unrivaled flavor and meaty, low-seed flesh make beefsteaks the top choice for fresh slicing, caprese salads, and sandwiches. Popular heirloom varieties include 'Brandywine' (pink), 'Cherokee Purple', and 'German Johnson'.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This determinate type delivers a rich, umami-packed flavor that finishes with smoky, fire-roasted notes, ripening most of its crop over a concentrated window. Stake or cage the compact bushes to keep fruit clean and support the yield. Water consistently at the base to avoid cracking, and harvest tomatoes when fully colored and slightly soft.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after last frost; soybeans are sensitive to cold, wet soil and germinate poorly if sown too early.
directions: A popular Japanese edamame cultivar named for its traditional role as a beer-hall snack, Beer Friend produces sturdy, upright plants that concentrate their pod set for an unusually uniform, once-over harvest. Pods are plump, hold 3 to 4 large light-green beans each, and mature earlier than many edamame types, making this a good choice for shorter-season gardens. Harvest whole plants or individual clusters when pods are fully filled but still bright green, then blanch briefly and serve pods lightly salted for snacking straight from the pod. Because the crop ripens together rather than trickling in over weeks, it is well suited to a single big harvest for freezing or serving fresh.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost; make a second sowing in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow beet clusters (each is a multi-seeded fruit) 1/2 in deep in rows 12 in apart. Because each corky seed can produce 2–3 seedlings, thin early to 3–4 in to avoid crowding, and use the thinnings as salad greens. Maintain even soil moisture to prevent woody, cracked roots. Harvest globe roots at 1.5–3 in diameter; larger roots become pithy and lose sweetness.

plant_note: Grown indoors on trays; soak the corky seed clusters before sowing to improve germination.
directions: Presoak the multigerm seed balls for several hours so they sprout more evenly, then sow them densely across a moist tray. Beet microgreens germinate a little slower than brassicas, so keep them covered and warm until shoots emerge, then move to bright light to develop their deep red stems. Water carefully from below or with a fine mist to avoid crushing the delicate seedlings. Harvest the striking crimson-stemmed greens at the cotyledon or first-true-leaf stage for their mild, earthy sweetness.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms; can start indoors 3 weeks early.
directions: Beit Alpha is a burpless, thin-skinned heirloom cucumber that is parthenocarpic, setting smooth, mild fruit without pollination and free of bitterness. Direct-sow after the soil warms to 70F, or start indoors three weeks early, and grow up a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Harvest at 4-6 inches while the skin is deep green and tender, picking often to keep the vines producing. Because no peeling is needed, these cucumbers are ideal for fresh salads and snacking.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Beit Alpha is heat-tolerant and parthenocarpic (sets fruit without pollination), making it excellent for hot, enclosed or pest-challenged gardens.
directions: Trellis for best results; sow 3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep, thinning to the strongest when 3 inches tall. Beit Alpha is the classic Middle Eastern cucumber type — short (4–6 inches), thin-skinned, virtually seedless, and extremely crisp and sweet, with no bitterness even at room temperature. It is parthenocarpic, meaning it sets fruit without pollinator visits, and gynoecious (predominantly female flowers), resulting in extremely heavy production from compact vines. The thin skin requires no peeling and wilts less in high summer heat than standard American slicing cucumbers. Harvest frequently — the fruits reach ideal eating size within 24–48 hours in zone 9's summer heat and become puffy if left too long.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in moist soil or water; bele grows as a perennial shrub in zones 9–11 and cuttings establish quickly. It thrives in hot, humid conditions and tolerates partial shade — often growing more productively in light shade in the hottest months, which reduces leaf toughening and extends the harvest season.
directions: Root cuttings and plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; bele (aibika) is a large-leafed tropical relative of okra grown widely across Papua New Guinea, the Pacific Islands, and Southeast Asia as one of the most important leafy vegetables — the large, soft, mucilaginous leaves are harvested young and eaten as a cooked green vegetable, used to thicken soups and stews, or wrapped around other foods before cooking, exactly as collard or banana leaves are used. The mucilage thickens soups in the same way okra does. The large, showy yellow hibiscus flowers with dark centers are ornamental and also edible. Bele is heat-tolerant, productive, and thrive in Gulf Coast zone 9 summers when other leafy greens bolt and fail. It grows as a perennial shrub in frost-free conditions and can be harvested continuously. Rich in protein relative to most leafy vegetables.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring for summer root production, then force roots in fall or winter indoors; in mild climates, sow in late summer for fall root harvest followed by winter forcing. Do not direct sow too early — chicory bolts in the long days of late spring if sown too early.
directions: Sow seeds thinly in rows 12–18 in apart in late spring; thin to 8–10 in spacing when seedlings reach 2–3 in tall. Grow the plants through summer, then in fall dig the roots (which resemble fat parsnips), trim tops to 1 in, and store in a cool, dark, humid place. To force the distinctive tight pale chicons (the white-leaved heads sold in stores), pack roots vertically in a box of moist sand, cover to exclude all light, and keep at 50–60°F for 3–4 weeks — the blanched white chicons emerge from the root tops. The bitter, tender chicons are excellent braised, roasted, or eaten raw. Never allow light to reach the forcing roots or the chicons will turn green and bitter.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; keep the seedbed consistently moist since carrot seed germinates slowly.
directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in loose, stone-free soil, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once true leaves appear so roots have room to size up. Belgian White is a long, tapered, white-skinned and white-fleshed heirloom carrot historically grown across Europe as a large, productive dual-purpose root for both the table and livestock feed. The roots often push up out of the soil as they mature, developing a green shoulder where exposed to light, and can grow considerably larger than typical orange table carrots while staying reasonably tender. Its mild, less sweet flavor compared to orange carrots and unusual coloring make it a distinctive choice for gardeners wanting to diversify beyond the standard Nantes and Danvers types already common in home gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 2 weeks after frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix; peppers germinate best when soil stays above 75°F. Harden off transplants over 7–10 days before planting, and wait until soil temperature reaches at least 65°F. Keep moisture consistent to prevent fruit drop, and apply a balanced fertilizer once flowering begins. Pick green for mild flavor or leave on the plant to ripen to red, yellow, or orange for maximum sweetness.

common_name: Bella Rosa Tomato (Disease-Resistant Gulf South Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting to harvest in May–June. Bella Rosa is a determinate hybrid recommended specifically for Southern gardens where diseases and heat are primary challenges.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Bella Rosa is a determinate hybrid tomato developed for disease resistance and heat adaptation in humid Southern gardens, an AAS (All-America Selections) winner that earned recognition for reliable production in difficult growing conditions. The medium-large (8–12 oz), round, firm, bright red fruits have excellent flavor — more complex and acidic than purely mild hybrids but not harsh — with thick walls and small seed cavity that make them suitable for slicing, sandwiches, and fresh preparations. The broad disease resistance package (Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and gray leaf spot) addresses the main failure modes of standard tomatoes in humid Gulf South gardens where disease pressure is severe. The determinate compact plants (3–4 feet) produce a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for gardeners who want a concentrated harvest for preserving, sauce-making, or sharing with neighbors. An excellent choice for zone 9 spring and fall tomato seasons where disease resistance is more important than variety novelty.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost for spring, or midsummer for fall.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist soil. Selected for heat tolerance, this variety suits both spring and late-summer sowings and forms large, 6 to 8 inch, tightly packed blue-green heads. After the main head is cut, many smaller side shoots follow for continued harvests, and it grows well through winter in mild climates. Cut the central head while buds are tight, then keep harvesting side shoots.

common_name: Benning's Green Tint Scallop Squash (Pale Silvery-Green Heirloom Pattypan)
plant_note: Direct sow once soil has warmed in spring; pick the scalloped fruit young and small for the finest-grained, most tender texture.
directions: Direct sow after soil has warmed in spring, spacing plants about 3 feet apart in full sun; this early-20th-century heirloom produces flattened, scalloped fruit in a pale, silvery-green that sets it apart from the more common yellow and white pattypan types. It was popular in home gardens well before many modern hybrid scallop squash were developed, valued for its fine-grained, nutty flavor when picked young. Harvest the scallop-shaped fruit at 3-4 inches across for the best texture, since older fruit becomes seedy and less tender.

common_name: Berkeley Tie Dye Tomato (Multicolor Striped Modern Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; the vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from strong staking and even watering to support its heavy clusters of colorful fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Berkeley Tie Dye is a modern specialty tomato bred for its vividly striped fruit, splashed with purple, green, red, and orange in a swirled, painterly pattern that makes it one of the most visually striking tomatoes a gardener can grow, with rich, complex, sweet-tart flesh to match its looks. It is a strong, productive indeterminate vine that sets clusters of medium-to-large fruit over a long season. Stake or cage plants securely for the heavy fruit load, water evenly to reduce cracking, and pick once the stripes have fully developed and fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure.

common_name: Berrettina Piacentina Squash (Italian Heirloom Turban Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil once frost has passed, giving sprawling vines ample room, and water deeply during fruit development to build dense flesh.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil once frost has passed, giving sprawling vines ample room, and water deeply during fruit development to build the dense flesh this variety is known for. Named for its distinctive tan, beret-like elongated turban shape, this traditional squash from the Piacenza province of Emilia-Romagna has long been grown for the region's celebrated tortelli di zucca, a pumpkin-filled pasta requiring dry, intensely sweet flesh. Its knobby, ridged rind and rich orange interior set it apart from rounder turban types, and it stores well through winter when cured properly. Regional seed houses in northern Italy have kept the variety in circulation for home and market gardeners alike.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring crop, or start in late July for transplant mid-August for fall. Better Boy is an indeterminate that benefits from sturdy staking or caging to support 4–5 foot plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–75°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after last frost; Better Boy is a Petoseed Company introduction from the 1960s that became one of the best-selling tomato varieties in US history, consistently appearing in Guinness World Records lists for the heaviest yields from a single plant — a Better Boy at the Chattanooga Times Free Press Demo Garden reportedly produced 342 pounds of fruit from a single plant. The large (8–16 oz), smooth, deep-red fruits are meaty with thick walls, excellent rich-sweet tomato flavor, and few seeds — the archetype of what many American gardeners consider an ideal home garden tomato. Indeterminate vines continue growing and producing until frost, requiring substantial staking or a heavy-duty cage. Disease resistance covers Fusarium wilt (race 1) and Verticillium wilt. Better Boy's long production season, large fruit size, and excellent flavor have kept it among the top five best-selling tomato varieties in the US for over 50 years. In zone 9, it thrives as a spring crop and can resume production in fall after summer heat subsides.

common_name: Better Bush Tomato (Compact Semi-Determinate Container Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Better Bush is outstanding in containers (at least 15-gallon) — its compact habit and sturdy self-supporting stems are ideally suited to patio, deck, and balcony growing.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Better Bush is one of the finest compact tomatoes for container gardening and small-space production — a semi-determinate hybrid that naturally stays 3–4 feet tall with sturdy, stocky stems that are largely self-supporting (minimal or no staking required), compact enough for large containers, and productive enough to provide a meaningful harvest without the sprawling, aggressive growth of indeterminate types. The medium-sized (8–10 oz), round, globe-shaped, bright-red fruits have good flavor and firm texture appropriate for fresh eating and all standard culinary uses. Better Bush carries disease resistance to V, F, and N — a standard Gulf South disease package. The compact size, self-supporting habit, and container suitability make Better Bush the first recommendation for zone 9 gardeners growing tomatoes on patios, balconies, or in raised beds where space is limited. For best container production, use containers of at least 15 gallons with premium potting mix and consistent watering and fertilization — container-grown tomatoes require more frequent irrigation and feeding than in-ground plants. Two plants per patio can provide significant summer tomato production with only 30–40 square feet of container space.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest. Bianca Riccia is the standard Italian fine-cut white endive for winter production, producing a naturally pale center without tying. In zone 9 the cooler temperatures from October through December provide ideal growing conditions.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bianca Riccia (White Curly) is an Italian fine-cut curly endive producing a loose, open rosette of very finely divided, heavily frizzy white-to-cream leaves — naturally self-blanching at the center without the tying required by some other frisee types. The fine cutting and natural pale color of the interior make Bianca Riccia one of the most elegant frisee types for Italian insalata recipes and for the French frisee au lardons preparation where the delicate pale center is the centerpiece. The outer leaves, being more exposed, are darker green and more bitter; the pale interior heart is the culinary prize with its mild, slightly bitter, elegant flavor. Unlike darker-centered frisee varieties, Bianca Riccia requires little or no artificial blanching because the dense, overlapping outer leaves naturally shade the center as the head matures. In zone 9 fall planting produces heads of excellent quality through November and December.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring; Bibb lettuce is a Kentucky heirloom developed by Jack Bibb of Frankfort around 1865, a butterhead type producing small, loose, cupped heads of buttery, sweet, tender leaves — the definitive American butterhead lettuce and considered by many the most flavorful lettuce for salads.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring in fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil; thin to 9–12 inches and harvest the whole head when the center begins to feel firm. Bibb lettuce was developed by amateur horticulturist Jack Bibb of Frankfort, Kentucky around 1865 and was distributed to neighbors and friends for decades before entering commercial seed trade; it is a butterhead-type lettuce producing small, loose, semi-cupped heads of exceptionally tender, silky, buttery leaves with a mild, sweet, distinctive flavor that many consider the finest of any lettuce for raw salads. The original Limestone Bibb (named for the limestone water of Kentucky) is more delicate and refined than commercial butterhead varieties but slightly slower and less uniform; it is the 'real' Bibb for flavor purists. Modern hybrid butterhead varieties ('Boston,' 'Summer Bibb,' etc.) are improvements in yield and bolt-resistance but lack some of the exceptional flavor of the true heritage Bibb.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Big Beef is an All-America Selections winner hybrid that combines the large, meaty fruit of a beefsteak with broad disease resistance and consistent productivity — one of the most widely grown large-fruited tomatoes in American home gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and provide sturdy caging or staking for the vigorous indeterminate vines, which can reach 6 feet or more. Big Beef was introduced by Seminis Vegetable Seeds and won the All-America Selections award in 1994 — it has since become one of the best-selling tomato varieties in the United States, valued for combining the large size and exceptional flavor of old-fashioned beefsteak types with outstanding disease resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt, nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus) that makes it more reliable across a wide range of climates and conditions. Fruits are large (8–12 oz or more), round to slightly oblate, meaty with few seeds and small blossom scars, and richly flavored — among the best-tasting large hybrid tomatoes available. Widely adaptable from cool northern gardens to Gulf Coast conditions.

common_name: Big Bertha Bell Pepper (Giant Extra-Large Sweet Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Big Bertha's exceptional fruit size benefits from consistent fertility — apply balanced fertilizer at transplanting and again when fruits begin to size up for maximum development.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Big Bertha is one of the largest bell pepper varieties in general cultivation — producing extra-large, four-lobed fruits 7 inches long and 3.5–4 inches wide with very thick, crunchy walls and excellent sweet flavor. The enormous fruit size makes Big Bertha outstanding for stuffed pepper preparations where the cavity size determines how much filling can be used, and for slicing use where individual slices are large, substantial, and visually impressive. Big Bertha is a hybrid variety with disease resistance that includes tolerance to tobacco mosaic virus — an important practical quality in zone 9 gardens where virus pressure is a consistent challenge for sweet peppers. Fruits ripen from green to red, with the sweet flavor deepening and vitamin C content increasing significantly as the pepper fully ripens red. However, the thick-walled green stage is also excellent for fresh use. Big Bertha plants are vigorous and produce prolifically through the long Gulf South pepper growing season. The combination of extra-large fruit, good disease tolerance, and excellent fresh-eating quality makes Big Bertha one of the most popular large-fruited bell pepper varieties in American home gardening. Support plants with a stake or cage as the heavy fruits can cause branches to break.

common_name: Big Boy Tomato (Classic Large Beefsteak Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after the last frost date; in zone 9 (Houston/New Orleans area), transplant in mid-February for spring production before summer heat ends fruit set.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after last frost; Big Boy is one of the most historically important and widely grown large-fruited tomato cultivars in American home gardens — introduced by Burpee in 1949 and still one of the most recognizable tomato names in American horticulture. The large beefsteak-type fruits typically weigh 1–1.5 pounds with deep red, meaty, flavorful flesh and the classic balanced tomato flavor — rich, full, and aromatic without the extreme acidity of some heirloom beefsteaks. Big Boy is an indeterminate, vining cultivar that continues to grow, flower, and fruit until killed by frost — it requires a strong cage or staking support to manage its vigorous 4–7 foot growth. The large fruit production and classic flavor made Big Boy the standard large-fruited tomato in American garden catalogs for decades. In zone 9, tomatoes should be transplanted in mid-February for the spring window, with the goal of harvesting as much as possible before temperatures consistently exceed 95°F (at which point pollen viability fails and fruit set stops). A second planting in late August captures the fall window. Prevent blossom end rot with consistent irrigation and calcium-balanced fertilization. Better Boy is the improved hybrid successor with added disease resistance — both are widely grown.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and keep the mix warm for even germination. This hybrid crosses Big Dwarf with Brandywine to yield dark pink, ribbed fruits of 12 to 15 ounces with rich flavor and productive, nearly blemish-free yields. Provide a tall stake or trellis for the indeterminate vines and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly at the base to prevent cracking, and harvest tomatoes when fully colored.

common_name: Big Girl Tomato (Classic Large Red Hybrid Slicer)
