The Mignonette name (French for 'small and delicate') describes both the size and the tender, buttery character of these compact heads, which provide the soft, sweet, melt-in-the-mouth texture of butterhead lettuce in a size perfectly proportioned for a single-person salad. Unlike large butterhead varieties where a single head may be too much for one meal, Bronze Mignonette heads can be harvested and eaten in one serving — a practical advantage for small households and container growers who want variety without waste. The bronze outer leaves and buttery-sweet interior flavor make Bronze Mignonette one of the most attractive and best-tasting small lettuces for kitchen garden edging, window boxes, and mixed salad plantings.

common_name: Brown Crowder Southern Pea (Heirloom Drying Crowder Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Brown Crowder is a vigorous, heat-loving heirloom that thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South growing season.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in warm, well-drained soil, allowing extra room for the semi-vining growth habit to sprawl. Brown Crowder is a traditional Southern heirloom named for the way its brown-hulled peas pack tightly, or 'crowd,' against one another inside the pod, developing the rich, earthy flavor and quick-cooking texture prized in old-fashioned Southern pea dishes. Vigorous vines produce heavily even in the poor, sandy soils and intense heat that stall many other legumes, and the plants show good general tolerance to common cowpea pests and diseases. Like other cowpeas, Brown Crowder fixes nitrogen through its root nodules, leaving the soil enriched for a following crop. Pick pods green for fresh shelling once well filled, or let them dry fully on the vine for classic dried crowder peas.

plant_note: Sow in late summer or early fall for a winter and early-spring harvest, or in early spring for a standard-season crop.
directions: Sow in late summer or early fall for a winter and early-spring harvest, or in early spring for a standard-season crop, since it is also reasonably slow to bolt. This French heirloom butterhead, whose name translates to brown of winter, forms compact rosettes of bronze-tinged green leaves and ranks among the most cold-hardy lettuces in cultivation, often overwintering under row cover or in a cold frame. Its history traces to at least the nineteenth century in France, where it kept kitchen gardens supplied with greens through the cold months.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out; a cold-hardy drumhead cabbage for fall and winter harvest.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in summer for a fall crop. This heirloom forms dense, flattened drumhead heads that tolerate hard frosts and store well. Keep the soil evenly moist and feed with nitrogen to build large heads, and harvest after cool weather sweetens the leaves.

plant_note: Start indoors 14–18 weeks before first fall frost so plants mature in cool autumn weather.
directions: Sow 1/4 in deep indoors under bright lights; transplant into deeply prepared soil and stake tall plants against wind. When sprouts at the base reach marble size, remove the growing tip (topping) to concentrate energy and speed maturation of the remaining sprouts. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward once they are 1–2 in across and tight. Flavor peaks after exposure to a hard frost.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; buckler sorrel (Rumex scutatus) is a distinct species from common garden sorrel (Rumex acetosa) with smaller, shield-shaped leaves, a lemony-tart but notably milder flavor than common sorrel, and better tolerance for light shade and dry conditions — the preferred sorrel of French cuisine for cream of sorrel soup, chiffonade in salads, and fish sauces.
directions: Sow directly in spring or fall in any well-drained soil; buckler sorrel is drought-tolerant when established and tolerates light shade, making it useful under taller plants; harvest young leaves by cutting 2–3 inches above the crown; remove flowering stalks to encourage continued leaf production; plants are perennial and will regrow from the crown each spring. Buckler sorrel (Rumex scutatus) is a European perennial herb closely related to but distinct from common garden sorrel (Rumex acetosa) — the differences are important for culinary use: where common sorrel has large, elongated arrow-shaped leaves with a strong, pungent, distinctly acidic flavor, buckler sorrel has small, rounded, shield-shaped (scutate — hence 'scutatus') leaves with a more delicate, lemony-tart flavor that is fresh and citrusy without the harsh tang of the larger-leaved species. The name 'buckler' refers to the small round medieval shield (a buckler) that the leaf shape resembles. Buckler sorrel is considered the superior culinary sorrel in French cooking: it is used in the classic potage à l'oseille (cream of sorrel soup), as a chiffonade in salads where the milder flavor is more versatile, in sauce oseille served with fish and eggs, and as an herbal flavoring in vinaigrettes where lemon-acid flavors are desired without citrus. The leaves are high in oxalic acid (as is common sorrel), so large quantities should not be eaten regularly, but culinary use in normal amounts is entirely safe. Once established, buckler sorrel is a tough, long-lived perennial that self-sows readily and can spread if not managed.

plant_note: Use unhulled seed and soak overnight; grown indoors on trays year-round.
directions: Soak the unhulled buckwheat seed overnight and rinse it before spreading it densely on a moist tray. Cover for a few days while the heart-shaped cotyledons push up, then expose to bright light and mist as needed. Keep an eye out for seed hulls clinging to the leaves and mist them off before harvest. Cut the tender, lightly nutty greens once the cotyledons have fully opened, generally around a week to ten days.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; an African-American heirloom pepper from Philadelphia with striking color changes through the ripening cycle — highly ornamental as well as edible.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Buena Mulata is a treasured African-American heirloom pepper with roots in Philadelphia's Black community, saved for generations and brought to wider attention through Seed Savers Exchange; it produces thin, cayenne-shaped pods 4–5 inches long that pass through a remarkable spectrum of colors as they ripen — pale cream to lavender-purple to orange to red — making the plant highly ornamental at every stage. The flavor is moderately hot (about 30,000 SHU) with a distinctive spicy, slightly fruity complexity; use fresh at any stage or dry to a rich red powder. This is a historically significant cultivar that deserves preservation and wider growing.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost in any well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; buffalo gourd has a massive perennial taproot that can reach 100+ pounds and regrows aggressively after frost or cutting — it is best suited to large-scale naturalistic plantings where the extensive spread (15–30 feet) is acceptable.
directions: Direct sow in spring after last frost in any well-drained, dry to moderately moist, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — buffalo gourd is one of the most extraordinarily drought-tolerant plants native to North America, a perennial-rooted annual vine of dry prairies, roadsides, and desert washes from Nebraska to California, extending its large, rough-textured, gray-green leaves on trailing stems up to 30 feet in a single season. The plant has a distinctly unpleasant, musky-fetid odor when handled (hence the species name 'foetidissima' — most stinking). Round, striped, baseball-sized gourds develop in summer that are toxic and extremely bitter when raw (cucurbitacins); these were used by indigenous peoples after processing to remove bitterness, and the seeds are oil-rich and nutritious. The massive taproot (potentially hundreds of pounds on mature plants) stores enormous water reserves. Most appropriate for large-scale wildlife habitat plantings, erosion control on dry slopes, and arid restoration projects rather than conventional garden settings.

common_name: Bugle Butternut Squash (Compact Powdery Mildew-Resistant Butternut)
plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; Bugle is a Cornell-bred butternut selected for strong powdery mildew resistance on a more compact vine than older butternut varieties, letting the foliage stay productive later into a humid Gulf South summer.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the vines room to spread; Bugle is a butternut squash bred at Cornell University with strong resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that typically coats squash foliage in a white film and shuts down photosynthesis well before fruit has finished sizing and curing in humid Southern gardens. Because the leaf canopy stays healthier longer, Bugle tends to fill out a fuller crop of the classic tan, elongated-neck fruit with dense, sweet orange flesh than mildew-susceptible butternut varieties planted in the same conditions. Let the squash mature fully to a hard rind before harvest, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks; properly cured fruit stores for several months and is excellent roasted, baked, or pureed into soup.

plant_note: Plant sets or transplants 2–4 weeks before last frost; onions from sets mature faster and are simpler for home gardeners.
directions: Press sets or transplants 1 in deep with the pointed tip facing up in rich, well-drained, loose soil. Onion bulb size is determined by the number of leaves at the time of bulbing: each leaf corresponds to a ring, so healthy top growth is essential throughout spring. Reduce watering once the necks begin to soften and tops start to fall over naturally. Cure harvested bulbs in a warm, airy spot for 2–3 weeks before moving to dry, cool storage.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk passes and soil has warmed; this Bulgarian heirloom produces carrot-shaped, brilliant orange fruits that are thin-walled but very prolific.
directions: Start seed at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost in a moist starting mix and pot up once the first true leaves appear; transplant after frost danger passes and begin fertilizing with a low-nitrogen, high-phosphorus fertilizer to encourage fruit set. Bulgarian Carrot is an eastern European heirloom producing vivid orange, carrot-shaped fruits 3–4 inches long with thin, crispy walls and a surprising fruity, almost apricot-like sweetness that precedes a sharp, clean, medium heat (5,000 SHU). It is exceptionally productive, with dozens of fruits per plant, and is highly ornamental as fruits turn from yellow to brilliant orange at maturity. Use fresh in salsas and relishes where the fruity flavor is showcased, or pickle whole for a pantry staple.

common_name: Bulgarian Triumph Tomato (Meaty Bulgarian Heirloom Paste Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Bulgarian Triumph is a traditional Bulgarian heirloom bred for meaty, low-seed paste fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Bulgarian Triumph is a traditional heirloom from Bulgaria, bearing medium-sized red fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh well suited to sauce and paste, a style of tomato long favored in Eastern European home gardens for preserving. Its productive, reliable vines yield a heavy crop over the growing season in gardens with a long, warm summer. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor and texture in cooked preparations.

common_name: Bull Nose Pepper (Historic Jefferson-Era American Sweet Pepper)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed; Bull Nose is one of the oldest documented American sweet peppers, grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello in the early 1800s.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Bull Nose is one of the oldest documented sweet pepper varieties in American gardens, grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and preserved by seed savers as a living link to early American kitchen gardens, producing blocky, mild, thick-walled fruit that matures from green to red. It performs reliably through the long, hot Gulf South growing season on compact, productive plants well suited to garden beds or large containers. Harvest fruit green for a milder flavor or let it ripen fully to red for peak sweetness, and pick regularly to encourage continued fruit set through summer.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer for fall harvest; Bull's Blood is a Victorian-era heirloom beet grown as much for its strikingly deep burgundy-red, ornamental foliage as for the edible roots, making it one of the most beautiful of all vegetable garden plants and an outstanding edging or salad green.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden 2–4 weeks before last frost in fertile, deeply worked, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil; soak seeds overnight to improve germination and thin to 3–4 inches when plants are 3 inches tall. Bull's Blood is a Victorian-era heirloom beet first listed in Burpee's catalog in the 1840s, grown for 175+ years for its spectacular deep burgundy-red to near-purple foliage that is among the most vivid of any vegetable; the young leaves and stems are intensely colored and are prized as a microgreen, baby salad leaf, and ornamental edging plant. The roots are also deep red, sweet, and excellent at any size from marble (35–40 days) to mature golf ball (55–60 days). The dramatic foliage remains strongly colored through the season and is highly heat-tolerant for a beet. An outstanding dual-purpose ornamental-vegetable for edible landscaping, container growing, and intensive salad gardens.

common_name: Bulltongue Arrowhead (Lanceleaf Arrowhead, Duck Potato, Wapato)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown plants in spring in shallow water (0–6 inches deep) or consistently saturated soil at the pond, rain garden, or stream edge; Bulltongue Arrowhead is a native emergent aquatic plant that thrives in the shallow margins of freshwater ponds, marshes, ditches, and slow streams throughout zone 7–11. It spreads by runners to form dense colonies and tolerates both fresh and mildly brackish water. The small, starchy tubers (corms) produced at the ends of the underground runners are the edible portion — harvest in fall when the above-ground foliage begins to die back.
directions: Plant in shallow water, saturated soil, or the wet margins of ponds and rain gardens in full sun to partial shade; Bulltongue Arrowhead is a native Gulf Coast emergent aquatic plant that provides outstanding wildlife habitat, water quality improvement, and ornamental interest in naturalistic water features. Sagittaria lancifolia is one of the most common native aquatic plants of the Gulf Coast from Texas through Florida, growing in freshwater marshes, ditches, bayous, pond edges, and slow-moving streams where it forms dense, productive stands of bold, lance-shaped, upright leaves. The three-petaled white flowers with yellow centers appear throughout summer on tall stalks above the foliage and attract native pollinators including specialist bees that rely on aquatic pollen sources. The small, acorn-sized, starchy tubers or corms produced at the tips of underground runners ('duck potatoes') are an important food source for ducks, geese, muskrats, and other waterbirds — and are edible for humans when cooked like a potato or roasted in coals: mild, slightly nutty, and starchy, they were a staple food for southeastern indigenous peoples. In water gardens and rain garden plantings, Bulltongue Arrowhead is a native alternative to non-native aquatic plants, providing the same bold vertical accent while supporting native wildlife.

plant_note: Plant corms or divisions in spring when soil has warmed to 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Bun Long taro is a wetland-adapted variety that thrives in consistently moist or periodically flooded conditions — ideal for poorly drained garden spots, pond margins, and bog gardens. It can also be grown in well-watered containers. The corms are harvested 7–12 months after planting when the large leaves begin to yellow.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in rich, moist to wet soil — Bun Long thrives at pond margins and in consistently waterlogged conditions that would kill most vegetables; Bun Long is a Hawaiian-adapted wetland taro cultivar used as the primary taro for poi production in Hawaii, producing large starchy corms with a distinctive pale lavender-purple flesh that turns light gray-purple when cooked and pounded. The large corms (often 2–5 pounds each) are a primary poi taro precisely because of their excellent starch content and texture when cooked and pounded or processed. The leaves and stems are also edible when thoroughly cooked — the tender young leaves (luau leaves in Hawaiian cuisine) are used in laulau, stew, and other dishes. In zone 9 Bun Long taro is an outstanding productive crop for the long, hot, humid growing season and thrives in the wet spots and poorly drained areas of Gulf Coast gardens where other vegetables struggle. The handsome large leaves with their distinctive pale purple veins provide ornamental value as well.

common_name: Bunch Porto Rico Sweet Potato (Compact Vintage Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant rooted slips 2–4 weeks after last frost in well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; the compact, semi-bush vine habit takes noticeably less room to sprawl than most heirloom sweet potatoes, making it a better fit for smaller garden beds.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil formed into ridges in full sun; Bunch Porto Rico is an early-20th-century American selection from the old Porto Rico sweet potato line, valued for a more compact, semi-bush vining habit that spreads far less aggressively than standard long-vine heirlooms, making it practical for gardeners short on space. It produces copper-skinned tubers with moist, deep-orange, sweet flesh similar in eating quality to its Porto Rico parent, and its shorter vines are easier to manage, hill, and keep out of walkways through the growing season. Dig tubers once the vines begin to yellow and before frost threatens, then cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to heal cuts and concentrate sweetness before storage.

plant_note: In zone 9 direct sow in fall (September–November) for a winter through spring harvest, or in late winter (February–March) for a spring crop. Bunching onions do not form bulbs; they are harvested as green onions at any stage and regrow continuously from the base if the roots are left in place.
directions: Direct sow thinly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in fall or late winter; thin to 3–4 inches as seedlings grow, using thinnings as your first scallion harvest. Unlike common onions, bunching onions never form a bulb — the entire plant from leaf tip to root is used, and cutting stems back to 1–2 inches above soil level promotes regrowth for a cut-and-come-again harvest cycle. Clumps can be divided every year or two to rejuvenate growth; older clumps become crowded and produce thinner stalks. In zone 9 they overwinter reliably and often survive light freezes, making them a year-round perennial green-onion source.

plant_note: Sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in deep, raised beds or containers; roots can reach 3 feet and demand well-prepared deep soil.
directions: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in soil loosened to at least 18 inches; raised beds filled with light, compost-rich mix make harvest far easier than attempting to dig clay or compacted soil. Thin to 4–6 inches once seedlings are established. Gobo roots are harvested at 18–24 inches long and about 3/4 inch in diameter, typically 120 days after sowing; use a spading fork to loosen the soil alongside the root before pulling to prevent breakage. Scrub roots and slice thinly for kinpira and stir-fries; soaking cut pieces in acidulated water prevents browning.

common_name: Burgess Buttercup Squash (1932 Heirloom Dark Green Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Burgess Buttercup requires a full season (100–110 days) and benefits from the long, warm summers of zone 7–10. In zone 9, plant March–April for September–October harvest. Harvest before hard frost when the gray-green button (the distinctive flattened cap on the blossom end) is visible and the stem is dry and corky; cure for 10 days at 80°F. Burgess Buttercup stores 3–4 months in cool, dry conditions.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants. Cure harvested fruits at warm temperature for 10 days to harden skin. Burgess Buttercup is an heirloom winter squash introduced by the Burgess Seed and Plant Company in 1932 — the original 'buttercup' type squash from which the entire buttercup squash class takes its name. The distinctive physical characteristic of Burgess Buttercup is the prominent gray-green button or cup on the blossom end — a flat, circular, gray-green protrusion that sits like a cap on the bottom of the round, turbaned, dark green-and-striped fruit. The fruits are medium-sized (3–5 lbs), round and flattened, with dark forest green skin and narrow lighter stripes. The flesh is very deep orange-yellow, extremely dry and dense with a fine, smooth grain — a floury, potato-like texture (similar to kabocha, to which it is related) rather than the moist, stringy texture of acorn or some other winter squash types. The flavor is intensely sweet and rich, widely considered among the finest-flavored of all winter squashes — sweeter than butternut, drier and more concentrated than acorn. Burgess Buttercup improved on by the sweet, slightly dry, concentrated squash flavor that has made the buttercup/kabocha class the most highly-rated squash type in culinary comparison.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant; also excellent as a fall crop timed to mature in cool weather.
directions: This purple sprouting type forms a modest central head, then rewards patient growers with abundant tender side shoots. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before the last frost and set transplants eighteen to twenty-four inches apart in rich, consistently moist soil. Purple broccolis can be finicky, so keep them well fed and cool for the best flavor and antioxidant-rich color. Harvest the main head first to encourage a long flush of flavorful, tender side shoots.

common_name: Burgundy Okra (Ornamental AAS-Winning Deep-Red Pod and Stem Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost when soil is warm (70°F+) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; soak seeds overnight before planting to improve germination; harvest Burgundy pods at 2–3 inches for best tenderness — they toughen rapidly after 3–4 inches.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Burgundy is an All-America Selections award-winning okra cultivar with outstanding dual ornamental and culinary value — producing deep burgundy-red to crimson-red pods, stems, leaf veins, and flowers that make it one of the most visually spectacular edible garden plants available. The crimson coloration extends through virtually every part of the plant: the pods are deep red-burgundy rather than the standard green, the main stems carry the same red coloring, leaf veins are crimson, and the large (3–4 inch), yellow hibiscus-like flowers have a red center. The dramatic color creates an outstanding ornamental display in the summer garden that standard okra varieties cannot approach. The pods are edible and flavorful when harvested young (2–3 inches) — tender and mild, with the typical okra character. A critical practical note: the dramatic burgundy pod color disappears when cooked — the pods turn green when heated, which surprises first-time Burgundy okra growers. For the best ornamental and culinary effect, harvest pods at 2–3 inches (they toughen very quickly after 3–4 inches on this variety). In zone 9, Burgundy okra thrives through the brutal Gulf South summer when most other vegetables struggle, and produces prolifically from May through October with regular harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65 degrees F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Burmese is a vigorous heirloom okra producing long, tender, ribbed green pods on tall, productive plants that continue bearing heavily through the hottest part of summer, a season when many other vegetables slow down. It has a reputation among heirloom seed savers for strong yields and reliable performance across a range of Southern growing conditions. Harvest pods every day or two once production begins, picking at three to four inches for the most tender texture, since pods left too long on the plant quickly become tough and fibrous.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Burpee Butterbush is a compact, non-vining bush-type butternut squash bred to produce full-sized butternut fruit on a plant small enough for raised beds and container culture, unlike standard sprawling butternut vines that need 50-100 square feet.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills spaced 2-3 feet apart, or start indoors and transplant after the danger of frost has passed. Burpee Butterbush was bred to solve the space problem that keeps many gardeners from growing butternut squash — standard butternut vines sprawl 10-15 feet and can overrun a small garden — by combining a compact, bush-type growth habit that stays within a 3-4 foot footprint with fruit that is essentially identical in size, shape, and sweet, nutty flavor to full-sized vining butternut varieties. This makes it one of the few butternut options practical for raised beds, small gardens, and even large containers. Vines still produce a running habit to a modest degree as the season progresses, but nowhere near the sprawl of standard butternut, and yield per plant is comparable to vining types when given full sun and consistent water. Harvest when the tan rind is hard enough to resist a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry and corky, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storage to concentrate sugars and toughen the skin for long keeping.

common_name: Burpee Hybrid Cantaloupe (Classic Reliable American Muskmelon)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Burpee Hybrid is a long-standing American cantaloupe standard, producing medium-large, heavily netted, orange-fleshed melons with sweet, aromatic flavor and reliable, heavy production that made it a home garden mainstay for decades. The vigorous vines set fruit dependably under a wide range of growing conditions, and the variety's decades-long track record reflects genuinely good, consistent performance rather than novelty. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the netted rind has turned from green to golden-tan, and reduce watering in the final week before harvest to concentrate sweetness.

common_name: Burpless Beauty Cucumber (Mild Non-Bitter Slicing Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Burpless Beauty is a classic slicing cucumber selected for thin, dark-green skin and a mild flavor with little of the bitterness or gas-causing compounds found in older slicing types.
directions: Direct sow seeds an inch deep into warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a trellis to keep fruit straight and reduce disease pressure. Burpless Beauty produces long, slender, dark-green fruit with thin, tender skin that can be eaten unpeeled, and it was bred specifically to be milder and easier to digest than standard slicing cucumbers, a trait long marketed as burpless. Vines are vigorous and productive over a long summer harvest window when picked regularly. Harvest fruit at 8-10 inches while still glossy and firm; letting cucumbers oversize on the vine slows further production and can make the skin tougher and more bitter.

common_name: Burr Gherkin (West Indian Gherkin, Maroon Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; burr gherkin is extremely heat-tolerant and one of the few cucumbers that performs reliably through Gulf Coast summers without collapsing from heat or disease.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; burr gherkin is a West Indian species distinct from common cucumber (Cucumis sativus), producing 2–3 inch oval fruits densely covered with short spines or warts — it has been grown in the Caribbean and Gulf South for centuries and is extremely heat and drought tolerant compared to regular cucumbers. The fruits are harvested young for pickling or sliced fresh with a flavor somewhere between cucumber and zucchini; mature fruits become bitter and dry. Excellent for hot-summer gardens in zones 8–12 where standard cucumbers decline in midsummer heat; the vines are vigorous, prolific, and resistant to cucumber mosaic virus and most diseases that afflict common cucumbers.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after the last frost when soil is reliably warm; succession sow every 2–3 weeks for a continuous harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1 in deep in well-drained soil once nighttime temperatures stay above 50°F. Avoid overhead watering once flowers appear to reduce bean rust and fungal issues. Pick pods when they snap cleanly and the seeds inside are still small; regular harvesting extends production. Inoculating seed with rhizobium before planting boosts nitrogen fixation and yield.

common_name: Bush Delicata Squash (Compact Vine Delicata for Small Beds)
plant_note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Bush Delicata forms a compact, short-vined plant that fits raised beds and small gardens where a standard sprawling delicata vine would take up far too much room.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 2 to 3 feet apart since the compact bush habit needs far less room than a standard vining delicata. Bush Delicata produces the same sweet, creamy, striped-skinned fruit prized in classic delicata squash, but on a tidy, short-vined plant that stays contained rather than rambling 6 to 10 feet like the traditional vining type, making it a good fit for raised beds, small gardens, or anywhere space is at a premium. Provide steady, even moisture through flowering and fruit set, and mulch around the base to conserve water and suppress weeds. Harvest once the rind hardens and the cream-and-green stripes deepen in color, then cure fruits in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to concentrate their sweetness and extend keeping quality.

common_name: Bush Early Girl Tomato (Compact Container Slicer)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into full sun after danger of frost has passed; this compact determinate selection needs no staking beyond a small cage.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 50F, or grow directly in an 18-24 inch container. Bush Early Girl is an All-America Selections winner bred as a true determinate, space-saving counterpart to the classic indeterminate Early Girl, staying under 30 inches tall while still producing full-flavored, 6-8 ounce red slicing tomatoes only a few days later than its parent. Its short, sturdy frame makes it a favorite for patios, raised beds, and small gardens where staking a full-size vine is impractical, and it carries verticillium and fusarium wilt resistance for reliable production.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; broadcast thickly for a dense leaf-harvest stand or row-sow for repeated cut-and-come-again picking.
directions: Sow seed directly into warm, fertile soil after the last frost and keep evenly moist until germination, which is fast in hot weather. Bush okra is a fast-growing annual jute relative widely eaten across West Africa and Sudan, where the young leaves and shoots, known locally as krin krin, kraan kraan, or bush okra, are chopped and simmered into a slippery, okra-like soup base rich in vitamins and minerals. It is closely related to tossa jute (Corchorus olitorius) but tends to be more low-growing and branching, tolerating poorer soils and shorter, drier growing seasons. Harvest by pinching tender shoot tips every couple of weeks, which encourages continued branching and delays the onset of tough, fibrous stems and flowering.

common_name: Bush Pickle Cucumber (Compact Pickling Cucumber for Small Gardens)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Bush Pickle is a compact, determinate pickling cucumber that grows as a bush (18–24 inch spread) rather than a long vine, making it ideal for raised beds, containers, and small gardens where standard pickling cucumber vines (4–6 feet) would be unmanageable; it produces a concentrated set of uniform pickling cucumbers and then declines — plant a second succession for extended harvest.
directions: Sow directly 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; no trellis required for the compact bush plants; harvest pickling cucumbers at 3–4 inches for small gherkin-style pickles or 4–5 inches for standard dill pickle size; pick every 2–3 days to maintain production. Bush Pickle is a compact, determinate (bush-habit) pickling cucumber developed specifically for small-space gardening — raised beds, containers, urban gardens, and patios where growing the standard trailing pickling cucumber vines (Boston Pickling, National Pickling, Calypso) is impractical due to their 4–6 foot spread. The compact plants (18–24 inches wide) produce a dense cluster of uniform, blocky, 3–5 inch pickling cucumbers with the classic pickling cucumber characteristics: firm, crisp flesh; thin skin; minimal hollow seeds; and a blocky, multi-bumped exterior that is traditional for dill pickles. Production is somewhat concentrated in a shorter harvest window compared to vining types — Bush Pickle tends to set most of its fruit within 2–3 weeks of first harvest, then declines, making succession planting (a second sowing 3–4 weeks after the first) useful for extended pickle production. Still holds well under warm summer conditions for Gulf Coast gardeners growing in small raised beds.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil; a giant hard-shelled gourd needing a long season and strong support.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and sow an inch deep once frost danger is well past, giving this long-season gourd every warm day it can get. Provide a very sturdy trellis or let vines run on the ground with straw beneath the developing fruit. The enormous round gourds can reach three to five feet in circumference and dry into durable containers and craft shells.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum chinense requires warm temperatures (80–90°F) for germination and is slow to germinate. In zone 9 start in January and transplant in March–April. Butch T thrives as a perennial in zone 9 and 10 — the woody plants return from the roots after light winter die-back and produce extremely heavily in their second and subsequent years. Wear gloves when handling fruits; the extremely high capsaicin content can cause skin burns and eye damage.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and handle fruits with protective gloves; Butch T Trinidad Scorpion was recognized as the world's hottest pepper by the Guinness World Records in 2011 (since surpassed by the Carolina Reaper), measuring over 1.4 million Scoville Heat Units in official testing — placing it among the most intensely hot peppers ever documented. The variety was developed by Troy Primeaux ('Butch T') in Louisiana from Trinidad Moruga Scorpion genetics. The small to medium, wrinkled, deeply colored red-orange fruits have the distinctive scorpion tail-like protrusion at the tip that gives the Trinidad Scorpion type its name. The extreme heat is accompanied by a pronounced fruity, tropical Capsicum chinense flavor beneath the intense burn. Used in tiny quantities in hot sauce production, powders, and as a daring culinary challenge. In zone 9 the long warm season and perennial habit allow Butch T plants to develop into large, extremely productive multi-year shrubs.

common_name: Butch T Trinidad Scorpion Pepper (Former World's Hottest Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Butch T Trinidad Scorpion once held the Guinness World Record for the hottest pepper in the world, with extreme heat well over one million Scoville Heat Units, requiring careful handling with gloves.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Butch T Trinidad Scorpion, a selection developed by grower Butch Taylor, held the Guinness World Record for the world's hottest pepper in 2011, testing over 1.4 million Scoville Heat Units, among the most extreme heat levels achievable in a pepper. The small, wrinkled, scorpion-tail-shaped fruits ripen from green to a deep red and carry the fruity, slightly sweet undertone typical of superhot Capsicum chinense peppers beneath the overwhelming heat. Always wear gloves when handling fresh or dried fruit and avoid touching the face, since the capsaicin can cause serious skin and eye irritation; use in tiny quantities, typically a single pepper diluted into a large batch of hot sauce or infused oil. Plants are moderately productive and benefit from a long, warm growing season and consistent moisture. This is a specialty pepper for heat enthusiasts and hot sauce makers, not general culinary use.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, in blocks of at least four short rows for reliable pollination.
directions: This long-popular bicolor normal-sugary (SU) hybrid produces two ears per stalk with kernels randomly mixed between golden yellow and creamy white, giving each cob a distinctive speckled look on the plate. Because it is a standard SU type rather than a supersweet, it does not need to be isolated from other sugary corns and holds its eating quality on the stalk for several days past peak, giving gardeners a wider harvest window. Keep plants well watered from tasseling through ear fill, since drought stress at that stage is the most common cause of poorly filled tips. It remains a favorite roadside-stand and home-garden choice for gardeners who want classic old-fashioned corn flavor rather than the extra crunch of newer sh2 hybrids.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a semi-restricted vine that can be grown in-ground or trellised, producing single-serving butternuts ideal for small households and space-limited gardens.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; Butterbaby's semi-compact vines can be left to sprawl or trained up a trellis to save garden space. Butterbaby is a hybrid mini butternut bred for uniform, single-portion fruits weighing about a half to one and a half pounds, with the same tan skin and rich, nutty-sweet, deep orange flesh as full-size butternuts but scaled down for one or two servings. Plants set fruit heavily and consistently, making them well suited to succession harvests through the fall. Harvest when the rind has hardened and turned fully tan, cure for a week or two, and store in a cool, dry spot for several months.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, since seedlings are sensitive to cold, wet ground.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in rows or wide bands, inoculating with rhizobia bacteria if soybeans have not been grown in that bed before to boost nitrogen fixation and yields. Harvest whole pods while still bright green and plump but before the beans inside turn hard and yellow, usually indicated by pods filling out fully along the stem. This variety produces unusually large, sweet-flavored beans on tall, productive plants, making it a favorite among home gardeners who want bigger portions per pod than typical edamame types. Blanch or steam the harvested pods briefly and pop the beans free of the fuzzy pod before eating as a snack or adding to salads and stir-fries.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant; succession sow every two to three weeks and grow in cool weather to avoid bolting.
directions: A vigorous butterhead beloved since 1963 for its buttery flavor and melt-in-your-mouth texture around a creamy yellow heart. Sow seed shallowly, barely covering it, since lettuce needs light to germinate well. Its compact heads are ideal for containers and single-serve salads, and tolerate a bit more heat than most butterheads. Keep soil evenly moist and provide afternoon shade in warm weather to delay bolting and bitterness.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather; an AAS-winning Bibb lettuce with good heat tolerance.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them, and keep the surface moist during cool spring or fall weather. This Bibb-style butterhead forms loose rosettes with a tender, sweet yellow heart and holds up better to heat than most lettuces. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head, and succession sow every few weeks for a steady supply.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, enriched soil; Buttercup is a classic Cucurbita maxima winter squash with a distinctive button-like cap on the blossom end, dark green to grey-green skin, and dense, dry, sweet orange flesh — for decades the standard of flavor comparison for all winter squash and still considered one of the finest for table use.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost when soil is above 65°F; thin to 2 plants per hill and allow 5–8 feet between hills. Buttercup squash was introduced by Harris Seeds of Rochester, New York in 1932 and became the gold standard for winter squash flavor for much of the twentieth century; a Cucurbita maxima type with a distinctive flattened-round shape, dark green skin with grayish-green stripes, a small, warty 'button' (the remnant of the blossom end), and dense, dry, sweet, deep-orange flesh that is exceptionally dry and rich — much less watery than kabocha or acorn types. The sweet, nutty, slightly dry flesh is outstanding for mashing, baking, and pies; it stores for 2–3 months. The modern 'kabocha' squash type is very similar in form and is often confused with Buttercup; true Buttercup is larger and has the distinctive button. Cure for 10 days at room temperature before storage.

plant_note: Scatter seeds on the surface of moist, well-drained, fertile soil — lettuce seeds need light, so do not cover — and thin to 8–12 inches apart; direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring, or for fall crops, 6–8 weeks before first frost.
directions: Scatter seeds on the surface of moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun and thin to 8–12 inches apart; butterhead (Boston/Bibb) lettuce forms a loose, soft, irregular head with velvety-tender, mild-flavored leaves that are more delicate and buttery-textured than the crisp crunchiness of romaine or crisphead types. It is more heat-sensitive than loose-leaf types and should be grown as a spring or fall crop in most climates — high heat causes rapid bolting and bitterness. Harvest the entire head when formed and compact, or harvest outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again approach. Excellent in simple green salads dressed with vinaigrette; the cupped leaves are also ideal for individual salad presentations. 'Bibb', 'Tom Thumb', 'Buttercrunch', and 'Boston' are classic varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost; count back from first fall frost to ensure enough days to maturity.
directions: Sow 2–3 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to the strongest vine. Butternut is a long-season crop, so calculate the days to maturity against your first fall frost date before planting. The vines spread widely; allow 8–10 feet of run per plant. Harvest when the skin has turned uniformly tan and the stem dries out fully; cure for 10–14 days in a warm location before storing.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Butterscotch is an AAS-winning personal-size butternut squash on compact semi-bush vines, bred for notably sweet flavor and a manageable single-serving fruit size.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Butterscotch is an AAS-winning butternut-type squash bred for a compact, semi-bush vine and small, personal-size fruit — about a pound each, roughly half the size of standard butternut squash — making it easy to fit multiple plants into a smaller garden and giving perfectly portioned single-serving squash for roasting or stuffing without leftovers. The tan-skinned, elongated fruit has dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh with the classic butternut flavor, and its smaller size means faster cooking too. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens fully and turns a deep tan color; cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two after harvest to improve flavor and storage life. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common problems on all winter squash in the Gulf South.

common_name: Butterstick Hybrid Squash (Golden-Yellow Straightneck Summer Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost into warm, fertile soil; single-stem habit needs less room than sprawling squash types.
directions: Butterstick is a straightneck-type hybrid that carries the zucchini plant's productive, single-stem habit but sets bright golden-yellow, straight-necked fruit instead of green cylinders. Its smooth skin and creamy flesh stay tender at a generous 7-8 inches, giving a bit more forgiveness than crookneck types if a fruit is missed during a hot Gulf Coast picking cycle. Plants bear over a long season with a steady, single-stem habit rather than sprawling widely, so regular spacing in a sunny bed keeps air moving through the foliage. Consistent moisture and twice-weekly harvest keep the plant setting new fruit rather than bottlenecking on a few oversized squash.

plant_note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. CP 65-357 is a Canal Point-bred commercial sugarcane variety that was a mainstay of the Louisiana sugar industry for decades.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. CP 65-357 (the CP designation stands for Canal Point, Florida, the site of the joint USDA-University of Florida sugarcane breeding program) was one of the standard commercial sugarcane varieties grown across the Louisiana sugar belt for many years, valued for reliable tonnage and sugar content under Gulf South growing conditions. While it was developed for large-scale sugar production rather than dooryard syrup-making, home growers can use it the same way as heirloom syrup canes: harvest in late fall after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, strip the leaves, crush the stalks, and cook the juice down into syrup, or simply chew the sweet stalks fresh. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows from the root each spring.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant 4 weeks before last frost for spring crop, or start midsummer for fall harvest.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors and harden seedlings off gradually before setting out into cool soil. Feed transplants with a balanced fertilizer at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when heads begin to size. Keep soil moisture consistent, as uneven watering causes heads to split. Harvest when the head feels firm and solid when squeezed; a light frost sweetens the flavor.

common_name: Cabernet Eggplant (AAS-Winning Glossy Purple-Black Hybrid Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed well past frost danger; Cabernet is a 2006 All-America Selections winner hybrid eggplant bred for vigor, high yield, and classic glossy purple-black fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60°F. Cabernet, a 2006 All-America Selections winner, produces glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit on a vigorous, high-yielding hybrid plant that holds up well to the heat and disease pressure of a long Gulf South growing season. Its strong vigor and heavy fruit set make it a reliable choice compared with some older open-pollinated eggplant varieties that struggle in extended summer heat. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and taut, before seeds inside begin to harden, and pick regularly to keep the plant setting new fruit through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil, or start indoors 3–4 weeks early; provide a trellis or fence immediately as caigua climbs rapidly by tendrils and produces heavily in hot weather.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and provide a trellis; caigua is an Andean climbing cucurbit that produces hollow, oblong fruits 3–4 inches long with a soft interior cavity perfect for stuffing — the hollow fruits are filled with meat, cheese, or vegetable mixtures and baked in Peruvian cuisine. The flavor is mild and crisp, similar to cucumber or chayote. Fruits are harvested when young and still tender; if left on the vine they develop soft, black seeds. The plant climbs vigorously and produces prolifically in hot summer conditions in zones 8–11. In traditional Andean medicine the plant has a long history of use for managing blood sugar and cholesterol. An unusual and conversation-starting vegetable for adventurous gardens.

common_name: Cajun Belle Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Sweet Pepper for Hot-Humid Gardens)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Cajun Belle is a compact, productive sweet pepper variety developed specifically for garden performance in hot, humid conditions — the type of climate where standard large bell peppers often struggle to set fruit. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The plant stays compact (18–24 inches tall) and produces small blocky bell-shaped fruits that ripen from green through red. The Cajun Belle name emphasizes its adaptation to Gulf Coast conditions where Creole and Cajun culinary traditions use sweet peppers heavily in the Holy Trinity (onions, celery, bell pepper) base of most dishes. This is an appropriate name for a variety that performs well where those culinary traditions are strongest: Louisiana, Mississippi, and the Gulf Coast region.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or fully red. Cajun Belle is an All-America Selections (AAS) winning pepper variety recognized for its consistent performance across diverse North American growing conditions, including the hot-humid southeastern United States where standard large bell pepper varieties often underperform due to blossom drop during heat peaks. The variety produces compact plants (18–24 inches) bearing abundantly on the small, blocky 3-inch bell-shaped fruits — smaller than the standard 4-lobed market bell but produced in much greater abundance per plant, especially in conditions that cause larger-fruited varieties to set poorly. The fruit profile of Cajun Belle differs from standard market bell peppers not only in size but in flavor: the smaller, thinner-walled fruits ripen fully and develop sweetness more quickly in the garden than large bells, which can take additional weeks to reach full red-ripe stage in the garden. Cajun Belle can be harvested green (mild, slightly sweet, similar to grocery-store green bell peppers) or allowed to ripen to red (sweeter, more complex, with the characteristic sweetness of fully ripe sweet peppers). The flavor is genuinely sweet — comparable to the best large red bell peppers — with none of the bitterness associated with unripe green bell peppers. The variety's most important attribute for zone 9 gardeners is heat tolerance: Cajun Belle continues setting fruit during warm periods that cause standard bells to drop their blossoms, providing reliable production through more of the Gulf Coast growing season.

common_name: Cajun Delight Okra (AAS-Winning Compact Early Hybrid Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Cajun Delight is an early hybrid that begins production 55–60 days from seed — about 2 weeks earlier than standard okra types. In zone 9, sow March–May for summer production; the compact habit (4–5 feet) is manageable without staking and fits smaller garden spaces better than tall heirloom types.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Cajun Delight is a 1997 All-America Selections-winning compact hybrid okra developed for Southern garden production — selected specifically for early production (55–60 days, versus the 65–80+ days typical of older varieties), compact plant habit (4–5 feet vs. the 6–8 feet of full-size types), and exceptional pod quality. The dark green, straight, smooth-ridged, spineless pods are harvested at 2–4 inches for best tenderness and flavor; at this size they are non-fibrous, mild-flavored, and have the classic okra texture that makes them outstanding for gumbo, fried okra, and all Southern okra preparations. The compact habit makes Cajun Delight ideal for smaller plots, raised beds, and gardens where the full-height traditional types would be difficult to manage, and the early production date extends the productive season at both ends. Recognized as one of the best commercial and home-garden okra varieties for the Gulf South, where early establishment before peak summer heat is advantageous.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost when soil is warm above 65°F; soak seeds 12–24 hours before planting to improve germination. Cajun Jewel was developed at the Louisiana State University AgCenter specifically for the humid, disease-pressure conditions of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Cajun Jewel was developed by LSU AgCenter plant breeders as a compact, dwarf-type okra specifically adapted to Gulf Coast conditions, producing spineless, dark-green, tender pods on 4–5 foot plants that are more manageable in home garden beds than the 6–8 foot giants of traditional varieties. The pods are ready to harvest at 2–4 inches long and have excellent flavor and tenderness; harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants producing — pods left too long become fibrous and woody in days in Gulf Coast heat. The compact size makes it easier to pick, the spineless pods reduce irritation from the fine hairs on standard varieties, and the improved disease package helps the plants maintain production through the summer. Outstanding for zone 7–10 gulf coast gardens.

common_name: Cal Sweet Bush Watermelon (Compact Bush-Habit AAS Winner)
plant_note: Start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; Cal Sweet Bush is a 2019 All-America Selections winner with a true short-internode bush habit, growing on vines only 14-18 inches long rather than sprawling 8-10 feet like standard watermelon, making it ideal for small Gulf Coast raised beds and containers.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Cal Sweet Bush is a genuine dwarf-vine watermelon, growing on compact 14-18 inch vines instead of the sprawling 8-10 foot vines of standard varieties, so it fits in a small raised bed or even a large container without taking over the garden. It still produces good-sized, 8-10 pound, round melons with sweet red flesh and the classic striped rind. Because the compact vines carry fewer leaves to shade developing fruit, keep an eye on ripening melons in intense heat to prevent sunscald. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in large hills with 3–4 seeds per hill, thinning to 2 plants per hill; calabaza requires more space than butternut squash and performs best in warm, humid climates from Florida through the Gulf Coast and Caribbean.
directions: Direct sow 3–4 seeds per hill 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-amended, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning each hill to the 2 strongest plants; calabaza (also called West Indian pumpkin or Cuban squash) is the quintessential winter squash of the Caribbean and Gulf South, producing large, round to pear-shaped fruits with mottled green-to-tan skin and deep-orange, sweet, dry flesh that rivals butternut squash in flavor. Plants are notably more heat-tolerant and disease-resistant than other Cucurbita species and produce well through hot, humid Gulf Coast summers. Harvest when the skin is hard and the stem corky-dry; fruits store for 2–5 months in a cool, dry location. Excellent for soup, stews, and tamales.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Calabrian peperoncino is the foundational hot chile of southern Italian cuisine, particularly from Calabria (the 'toe' of Italy's boot) — small, round to slightly elongated, intensely red, moderately hot (25,000–40,000 SHU) fruits used dried, in olive oil, as chili flakes, and as the spicy heat element in Calabrian cuisine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Calabrian peperoncino benefits from a long, hot growing season and thrives in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens where it often behaves as a perennial in zone 9–11. Calabrian peperoncino (piccante calabrese, diavolicchio) is the defining hot chile of Calabria in southern Italy, where it has been grown for centuries as the primary heat element of the local cuisine; the small (1–2 inch), round to conical, bright red fruits (at 25,000–40,000 Scoville) are moderately hot with a fruity, complex flavor that distinguishes them from the clean heat of cayenne or the fruity intensity of habanero. Calabrian peperoncino is most commonly used dried — strung in traditional pepper braids (sporte di peperoncini) to air-dry in the Mediterranean sun — and is used throughout Italian cuisine as 'nduja filling (the spreadable Calabrian salumi), peperoncino in olio (chiles preserved in olive oil), as crushed dried flakes on pizza, pasta, and grilled meats, and as chili paste. The plants are highly productive and the small fruits dry readily on the vine or indoors.

common_name: Calhoun Crowder Pea (Wilt- and Nematode-Resistant Louisiana Heirloom Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65F and all frost danger has passed; Calhoun Crowder was developed at the Calhoun Research Station in Louisiana in 1949 and bred for resistance to fusarium wilt and nematodes.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Calhoun Crowder, developed in 1949 at the Calhoun Research Station in Louisiana, bears speckled crowder-type peas packed tightly in the pod, bred specifically for resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematodes, two pressures that limit cowpea production in the heavy, humid soils of the Deep South. Its disease resistance makes it a dependable choice for gardens where cowpeas have struggled in the past, without sacrificing the rich, hearty crowder-pea flavor Southern cooks favor. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed past 70°F; space hills generously since vines are vigorous and disease-tolerant enough to be grown in humid climates without heavy spray programs.
directions: Released in 1965 from the LSU AgCenter's Calhoun Research Station as a cross involving Calhoun Sweet and Charleston Gray, this variety was bred specifically to bring stronger disease resistance to the classic gray-rind Southern watermelon type. It produces 25-30 pound oblong fruits with light gray-green rind and sweet red flesh, and it holds up better against fungal wilts than its Charleston Gray parent, letting it succeed as far north as Massachusetts with proper season length. Give it full sun, warm fertile soil, and steady moisture through fruit development, then withhold water as fruits near maturity. It's a solid choice for gardeners who want old-style picnic-watermelon size and flavor with fewer disease headaches than older heirlooms.

common_name: Calico Crowder Pea (Heirloom Multi-Color Seed Crowder Southern Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Calico Crowder is a vining type — provide a trellis or fence for support, or allow plants to sprawl on the ground in traditional field-pea planting style.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Calico Crowder is an heirloom Southern pea producing the characteristic multi-colored seeds that give it its calico name — tan, brown, black, and cream mottled seeds with a distinctive pattern that creates a beautiful, rustic visual when dried and stored, distinguishing this traditional variety from the uniform-colored modern selections. Crowder peas are named for their growing habit: the seeds are so tightly packed in the pod that they are 'crowded' and develop flattened sides where they press against each other — this crowding is a defining type characteristic that distinguishes them from black-eyed peas and cream peas. The crowder texture — denser, starchier, and more potato-like than cream peas — produces a hearty, substantial broth when slow-cooked, which is the traditional cooking method for old-field varieties like Calico. As a vining-type crowder, Calico produces well on a trellis or fence and can be managed in a smaller space than sprawling bush types. The heirloom seeds can be saved year after year from the dried pods. In zone 9, Calico Crowder can be planted from April through August for multiple successive crops through the long warm season — Southern peas are uniquely suited to Gulf South heat that stops most other legumes.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring and July–August for fall. Lima beans require warm, settled weather to germinate and thrive — cold or wet soil at planting causes rot. Calico is a pole type requiring support; provide a trellis or bean poles at least 6 feet tall. In zone 9 the vines may overwinter as short-lived perennials in mild winters.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Calico lima bean is a large, pole-type heirloom producing spectacular seeds splashed with deep red-purple and cream in an irregular speckled pattern — each seed is uniquely marked, no two alike, and the visual drama makes them among the most beautiful beans in the garden and at harvest. The large seeds are best used as fresh-shell or dry beans; the meaty, starchy texture and rich, buttery lima flavor are excellent. Fresh-shell calico limas cook faster than dried and have a creamier texture. Despite the striking appearance of the dried seeds, the calico pattern largely disappears when cooked as the pigments are water-soluble. The vigorous pole vines need substantial support and are highly productive through the long Gulf Coast growing season. Heat tolerance is excellent, and the plants continue to set pods when green beans have long since quit in summer heat.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil is thoroughly warm; California Blackeye 5 was bred at UC Davis from a California Blackeye x Iron cross and carries resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea (Fusarium) wilt, valuable traits for the sandy, nematode-prone soils common along the Gulf Coast.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; California Blackeye 5 is an improved release from the University of California, Davis, bred from a cross of California Blackeye and the nematode-resistant Iron cowpea to combine the classic black-eyed pea's mild, earthy flavor with real genetic resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea (Fusarium) wilt, two soil-borne problems that persist for years in garden soil and are especially common in sandy Gulf Coast ground. The semi-bush plants are more compact and manageable than old-fashioned vining types and need no staking. Harvest the fresh green pods as snap beans, pick the shelled green peas for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully on the vine for the classic dried black-eyed peas of Southern cooking. Like other Southern peas, it fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility as it grows.

common_name: California Blackeye Cowpea (Classic Commercial Black-Eyed Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; in zone 9, plant from late spring through midsummer for successive harvests, since California Blackeye thrives in peak summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after the soil has warmed, and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which promotes foliage at the expense of pod set. California Blackeye is an upright, semi-bush cowpea developed by University of California breeding programs and grown extensively as the standard commercial black-eyed pea, valued for its concentrated pod set that ripens fairly uniformly for efficient once-over harvest, along with good disease resistance and dependable yields. The classic cream-colored pea with its signature black eye has excellent flavor whether cooked fresh, dried for storage, or prepared in the traditional Southern black-eyed pea dishes served for New Year's luck. Like all cowpeas it fixes nitrogen in the soil and thrives in hot summer weather that stalls cooler-season legumes, making it a reliable, low-input crop for Gulf South vegetable gardens.

common_name: California Blackeye Pea (California Blackeye Southern Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil is thoroughly warm (minimum 65°F); in zone 9, sow April through July for summer production — the long warm season allows 2–3 successive plantings for continuous harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; California Blackeye is the most commercially significant blackeye pea cultivar — the variety responsible for most of the blackeye peas sold in American grocery stores. The distinctive black-eyed, cream-colored dry beans cook quickly, have a mild, earthy, slightly sweet flavor, and a mealy texture that makes them a staple of Southern cooking — particularly the iconic Southern New Year's Day dish of hoppin' john (black-eyed peas and rice), eaten for good luck. California Blackeye is a semi-bush type that is more compact and less sprawling than old-fashioned vine types, making it manageable in typical garden beds without staking. The fresh green pods are eaten as snap beans or the fresh shelled green peas are eaten before the seeds dry; the dried seeds are the standard black-eyed peas of commerce. In zone 9, California Blackeye thrives in the long hot season, producing crops from June through September with successive plantings. Southern peas fix nitrogen in the soil through symbiotic bacteria and actually improve soil fertility — one of the few warm-season vegetables that enriches rather than depletes garden soil.

common_name: California Early Garlic (Classic Commercial Silverskin Softneck)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall; California Early has one of the lowest chilling requirements of any garlic type and is the softneck silverskin grown commercially through California's mild-winter Central Valley, making it one of the more dependable garlics for zone 8-10 gardens where hardneck types divide poorly.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil; in mild-winter zones like the Gulf Coast, planting in October-November gives roots time to establish before the brief winter chill. California Early is the classic commercial silverskin softneck grown across California's Central Valley and is prized for its adaptability to warm-winter regions, low chilling requirement, and tight, easy-to-braid skins. Bulbs are medium-sized with 12-16 cloves in white to faintly purple-blushed wrappers and a flavor that is strong raw but mellows well when cooked. As the name suggests, it matures earlier than most other varieties, often ready for harvest by late spring, which helps it dodge the fungal pressure that builds in humid Gulf Coast soil as summer heat arrives. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store; well-cured bulbs keep 6-8 months.

common_name: California Late Garlic (Long-Storing Commercial Silverskin Softneck)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall; like its sister strain California Early, California Late has a very low chilling requirement and grows reliably in mild-winter zone 8-10 gardens, but needs several extra weeks in the ground to size up its larger bulbs.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost. California Late is the other pillar of California's commercial silverskin garlic industry alongside California Early, grown for its higher yield, larger bulb size, and notably long storage life of up to 10-12 months when well cured — among the best of any garlic type. Bulbs typically hold 16-20 cloves in tight white wrappers arranged in the overlapping layers characteristic of true silverskins, with a flavor that is sharp raw and mellow when roasted. Its low chilling requirement makes it as well suited to warm-winter Gulf Coast gardens as California Early, though it needs several additional weeks in the ground to fully size before harvest. Harvest once the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed and browned, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, airy location for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store somewhere cool and dry.

plant_note: Start indoors early and transplant after the soil warms; a blocky heirloom sweet bell.
directions: Start seeds indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and keep them warm for even germination. Transplant out only after nights stay reliably warm, spacing plants so air moves freely between them. The thick-walled, blocky fruits ripen from green to sweet deep red; harvest at either stage and support heavily laden plants if needed.

common_name: California Wonder Bell Pepper (Classic Red/Green Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost date; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date; in zone 9, transplant in mid-February for spring production — peppers require consistent warmth and will stall in cool spring weather below 55°F.
directions: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; California Wonder is the standard classic bell pepper — introduced in 1928 and for most of the twentieth century THE bell pepper grown in American home gardens and produced commercially. The large, blocky, thick-walled, four-lobed fruits are harvested green when mature (70–80 days after transplant) or allowed to ripen to deep red for sweeter, fully ripe peppers. The thick, crisp walls and mild, sweet, distinctly 'bell pepper' flavor are the benchmarks against which other bell peppers are measured. California Wonder is a vigorous, productive plant well-suited to Gulf Coast growing conditions — tolerant of heat and humidity better than some northern-bred bell peppers. In zone 9, bell peppers can produce from February transplants through June and then resume production in September–October after the worst summer heat passes — temperatures above 90°F during flowering cause blossom drop. Apply calcium-containing fertilizer (or side-dress with gypsum) to prevent blossom end rot, which is common in bell peppers during irregular watering. The plants are technically short-lived perennials in frost-free zone 9 and can be carried over winter for a second year of production in protected locations.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant only after soil warms and all frost danger passes.
directions: A classic bell pepper since 1928, valued for its large, blocky, uniform fruits that are perfect for stuffing. Start seed indoors eight weeks before the last frost and keep soil warm for reliable germination. Transplant after nights stay above 55 degrees, spacing plants eighteen to twenty-four inches apart. Green peppers left on the plant ripen to sweet red with even higher vitamin C, so harvest at whatever stage you prefer.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–August. Callaloo is extremely heat-tolerant and productive during the Gulf Coast summer when cool-season greens have long bolted; harvest young leaves and shoot tips continuously to maintain production. Plants self-sow prolifically and naturalize easily.
directions: Direct sow on the soil surface in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; callaloo is the name given in the Caribbean to green amaranth (Amaranthus viridis), a self-sowing annual leafy green that thrives in tropical heat and humidity and is one of the most important summer vegetables in the Caribbean and West Africa. The young leaves, shoot tips, and tender stems are harvested continuously and cooked like spinach — the most famous preparation is callaloo soup, a velvety Caribbean dish made with coconut milk, crab or salt fish, and okra. The plant tolerates poor soil, drought, and intense heat, and is one of the few summer greens that genuinely thrives in zone 9's most challenging months. Flavor is mild and slightly earthy; texture softens quickly when cooked. Plants self-sow freely and will return each summer without replanting once established.

common_name: Calliope Eggplant (Compact Globe Magenta-White Striped Italian Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Calliope is a compact F1 hybrid eggplant producing small globe-shaped fruits with distinctive magenta-purple and white striping. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the plant's compact size (18–24 inches) and heavy production habit make it excellent for containers, raised beds, and small gardens where a standard large eggplant would be impractically large. Harvest fruits when 2–3 inches in diameter while still firm and glossy — at this stage the flesh is tender, the seed cavity is minimal, and the flavor is sweet without bitterness. Like all eggplants, Calliope thrives in the heat of zone 9 summers and can produce through the entire warm season with irrigation and occasional fertilization.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 2–3 inches diameter when firm and glossy. Calliope is a compact F1 hybrid eggplant bred for small-fruit production with an Italian-type rounded form and striking bicolor fruit appearance. The fruits are globe to slightly pear-shaped, 2–3 inches in diameter, with a distinctive pattern of deep magenta-purple on the upper half and creamy white on the lower half — a color distribution that differs from the vertical striping of varieties like Fairy Tale or Listada de Gandia. The bicolor magenta-white pattern makes Calliope one of the most visually distinctive eggplants in garden displays and farmers market presentations. As a culinary variety, Calliope's small globe form is practical for preparations requiring the whole fruit: the 2–3 inch fruits are ideal for stuffing (halved or hollowed), for roasting whole, for grilling cut in half, or for slicing into rounds for layered preparations. The flesh is tender and sweet at harvest size, with minimal seed development and no bitterness — a consistent characteristic of modern F1 hybrid eggplant varieties. The compact plant habit and prolific fruiting make Calliope one of the best eggplant choices for container gardens where standard varieties would be impractically large and less productive per square foot.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Caloro is a yellow wax hot pepper in the Hungarian Wax style developed in California, with conical yellow fruits that ripen to red and carry moderate heat of 5,000–10,000 Scoville units — excellent for pickling, roasting, and fresh use in California-Mexican cuisine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost when nighttime temperatures are consistently above 55°F into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Caloro is a yellow wax-type hot pepper developed in California in the mid-twentieth century and widely grown in commercial agriculture as the standard pickled yellow hot pepper of California; the conical, medium-sized fruits (3–4 inches long) emerge green, ripen to bright yellow (the commercial harvest stage for pickling), and eventually turn orange-red at full maturity. Heat level is moderate at 5,000–10,000 SHU — noticeably hot but not extreme — with a waxy, crisp texture ideal for pickled pepper rings, banana pepper-style pickles, roasting, and fresh eating. Highly productive and disease-resistant; particularly well-suited to warm California, Gulf Coast, and Southwestern climates.

common_name: Calypso Bean (Yin Yang Bean, Oreo Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; a bush bean requiring no support — excellent for market gardeners and home canners.
