directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Calypso is a bush dry bean with a striking black and white two-toned pattern — each seed is precisely half black, half white — that has earned it nicknames such as 'yin yang bean' and 'oreo bean' for the dramatic visual contrast. The pattern fades somewhat on cooking but the bean retains excellent earthy, full-bodied flavor with a smooth creamy texture when fully cooked. Among the fastest dry beans to reach maturity, making it suitable for short-season gardens; the compact bush habit produces a concentrated flush excellent for preserving. Color fades on drying — store in a dark, cool location to preserve seed appearance.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Calypso is a gynoecious (all-female) pickling cucumber that produces an extremely concentrated set of fruits — a male pollenizer (typically a small percentage of open-pollinated seed included in the packet) is required for fruit set. Harvest frequently, every 1–2 days, to maximize production; fruits left on the vine signal the plant to stop producing.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a trellis for straighter fruits and improved air circulation. Calypso is a 2009 All-America Selections-winning pickling cucumber that earned recognition for its exceptional disease resistance package and concentrated production — bred to perform reliably in a wide range of climates and conditions where fungal and viral diseases limit cucumber yields. Calypso carries resistance to angular leaf spot, cucumber scab, cucumber mosaic virus, papaya ringspot virus, watermelon mosaic virus, and zucchini yellow mosaic virus, plus tolerance to powdery mildew — one of the most comprehensive disease resistance packages available in a pickling cucumber. The dark green, warted, blocky fruits (3–4 inches for fresh pickle use, 1.5–2 inches for whole baby pickles) have thick, crisp walls and excellent pickle texture that holds up to both quick-process and long-fermented pickle methods. The gynoecious (all-female) breeding concentrates fruit set into a shorter, more predictable harvest window — convenient for processing large pickle batches. An outstanding choice for home pickle-makers, zone 9 summer gardens where disease pressure is high, and any gardener wanting maximum yields with minimum disease management input.

common_name: Camaro PMR Pumpkin (Powdery Mildew Resistant Hybrid Jack-O-Lantern)
plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after the last frost; built-in powdery mildew resistance is especially valuable in the humid Gulf Coast growing season, when foliar disease usually cuts vines down before fruit finishes sizing.
directions: Direct sow in hills after danger of frost has passed, giving the reduced-vine plants a bit less room than sprawling heirloom types but still allowing air circulation between hills. Camaro PMR carries genetic resistance to powdery mildew, keeping foliage photosynthesizing later into the season so that fruit reaches its full 20-22 pound, near-round, lightly ribbed potential even under heavy disease pressure. The strong handles and deep orange rind make it a reliable choice for growers selling carving pumpkins, and the shorter vine habit suits smaller Gulf Coast garden plots better than old-line field pumpkin types. Watch soil moisture during fruit set, since consistent watering paired with the plant's disease tolerance produces the most uniform, market-ready fruit.

plant_note: Sow as early as the ground can be worked in spring; tolerates light frost and thin, dry soils where most oilseeds fail.
directions: Surface-sow tiny seed at 5–8 lb/acre and tamp firmly; camelina requires light for good germination and should not be buried more than 1/4 in deep. It matures in under 100 days and tolerates drought and cold better than any other oilseed crop, making it a fine spring or overwintered autumn oilseed in short-season gardens. Harvest when 80% of the pods are golden and dry — thresh by beating bundled stalks into a bucket, then winnow. The oil is exceptionally high in omega-3 fatty acids and has a pleasant nutty flavor for culinary use.

plant_note: Plant slips after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–June. Camouflage produces attractive vines with lobed leaves and is vigorous enough to suppress weeds when given room to ramble. Harvest carefully with a digging fork to avoid puncturing the skin; purple-white streaked flesh appearance is best when roots are not damaged.
directions: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil amended with sand or compost in full sun; Camouflage is an ornamental-edible sweet potato selected for striking purple-and-cream streaked or mottled flesh that creates a dramatic presentation when sliced — the irregular pattern of cream and purple pigmentation resembles military camouflage when cut crosswise. The flavor is mild and moderately sweet, suitable for roasting, baking, and mashing where the color pattern is partially preserved; water-boiling dulls the visual effect. The exterior skin has a similar mottled purple-green or purple-tan coloring that makes the roots attractive at harvest and at market. Flavor quality is secondary to the ornamental value of the flesh pattern — for pure eating quality, standard colored varieties outperform Camouflage, but for presentations and table drama it is unmatched among commonly grown sweet potatoes. Cure harvested roots at 85°F and high humidity for 7–10 days to develop sweetness.

common_name: Camus de Bretagne Artichoke (Large Round Breton Artichoke)
scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Camus de Bretagne'
plant_note: Transplant after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Camus de Bretagne is the classic large, rounded artichoke of Brittany, France, holding Protected Geographical Indication status there.
directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, working in plenty of compost before planting. Camus de Bretagne produces very large, rounded, tightly closed globe artichokes with a pale green color and tender, meaty heart, the classic variety grown in Brittany, France, where it holds Protected Geographical Indication status and accounts for the majority of French artichoke production. Like other globe artichokes it is a true perennial in mild-winter climates, though it can be grown as an annual from an early start in colder zones. Harvest buds while still tightly closed, before the scales begin to loosen, for the best eating quality.

common_name: Canada Red Rhubarb (Cold-Hardy Sweet Red Rhubarb)
plant_note: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while dormant; Canada Red performs best in zones with reliable cold winters that provide the extended chilling rhubarb needs for vigorous dormancy break and growth, and it is milder and sweeter than many green-stalked rhubarb varieties.
directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Canada Red is a cold-hardy rhubarb cultivar prized for its uniformly deep red stalks that stay red all the way through the flesh, not just the skin, along with a sweeter, milder flavor than many tart green-stalked rhubarb varieties, meaning less sugar is needed when cooking. It performs best in climates with cold winters that satisfy its chilling requirement for strong spring growth, making it less reliable in the mild winters of the Deep South. Harvest by pulling individual stalks from the outside of the crown rather than cutting, and always discard the leaves, which are toxic and should never be eaten.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Canary melons require warm to hot weather for full sugar development and are at their best in the extended heat of zone 9 summers. Unlike cantaloupe, canary melons do not slip from the vine when ripe — gauge ripeness by skin color turning from lime-green to brilliant chrome-yellow, slight softening at the blossom end, and the characteristic mild sweet fragrance. Cut from the vine when fully yellow and allow to rest at room temperature for 1–2 days for best flavor. The long shelf life (10–14 days at room temperature) compared to cantaloupes makes canary melons practical for home garden production.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-amended soil with consistent moisture during fruit development; Canary Melon (also called Spanish Melon or Yellow Melon) is an Inodorus-group muskmelon producing large (5–7 pound), oval to oblong fruits with a distinctive, intense, brilliant chrome-yellow skin at full ripeness — one of the most visually striking melons available, with the vivid yellow color making ripe fruits immediately identifiable in the garden and market. The flesh is white to pale ivory, very sweet, very juicy, with a mild, clean, faintly musky flavor that differs from cantaloupe's complex aromatic sweetness — canary melon's flavor is cleaner, lighter, and more delicate, making it the preferred melon for many people who find cantaloupe flavor too intense. The Inodorus (winter melon) classification means canary melons have firmer flesh and longer shelf life than cantaloupes — they don't 'slip' from the vine at ripeness, can be kept at room temperature for up to two weeks, and ship better than soft-fleshed types. Zone 9's extended warm season and summer heat are ideal for canary melon production, providing the long, hot growing period these melons need for full sugar development.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Canary Melon is ripe when the skin turns from yellow-green to vivid canary yellow and the fruit gives slightly under thumb pressure at the blossom end. Unlike netted muskmelons, Canary does not separate from the vine easily when ripe — check for color, firmness, and fragrance rather than slip. The thick rind allows extended storage (several weeks at room temperature) compared to most melons.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Canary Melon (also called Juan Canary or amarillo melon) is an oblong to football-shaped melon with dramatically vivid, glossy, bright canary-yellow skin that makes it one of the most visually striking melons in the market or garden — the name describes the intense yellow of a canary bird's plumage. The creamy white to very pale green flesh is smooth, firm-crisp rather than soft, mildly sweet, and extremely mild-flavored with a delicate freshness completely different from the musky richness of cantaloupe — the flavor is subtle and refreshing, with a light sweetness and almost no aroma. This delicate flavor profile is characteristic of Spanish-type melons (inodorus group), which are also notable for their thick rind and long post-harvest shelf life. Canary Melon is widely grown in Spain and is a standard melon type in Spanish and Latin American markets. In zone 9 the long, warm summer produces the full sweetness that Canary Melon develops best in extended heat.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills or rows; Canary melon (Juan Canario, Yellow Canary) is a popular commercial and home-garden melon throughout the Mediterranean and Latin America, known for its brilliant canary-yellow skin and very sweet, pale white-to-green flesh with a mild, honey-like sweetness distinct from other melon types.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart or in rows 6 feet apart; Canary melon is an inodorus type that stores well on the vine and post-harvest — harvest when skin turns deep canary yellow and the blossom end yields to gentle pressure. Cucumis melo var. inodorus 'Canary' (Juan Canario, Yellow Canary melon) is a winter melon type grown extensively in Spain, Latin America, and the Middle East and sold widely in American Hispanic grocery markets; the medium to large (5–10 lb), elongated oval fruits have a striking, smooth, bright canary-yellow skin and white to pale green flesh with a delicate, honey-sweet flavor that is milder and less aromatic than muskmelon or cantaloupe types but refreshingly sweet and very appealing. The inodorus type means the ripe fruit has little fragrance from the exterior — you must taste to judge ripeness; the flesh is crisp at the center and creamy near the rind. An excellent heat-tolerant melon for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens that maintains flavor even in high temperatures; stores well at room temperature for 2–4 weeks after harvest.

common_name: Candle Fire Okra (AAS-Winning Red Round-Podded Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; soak seed overnight to speed germination. Candle Fire is a red, round-podded okra bred to stay tender even at a larger pod size, giving a wider harvest window than most okra before pods turn woody.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost into warm soil in full sun; thin to 18-24 inches apart. Candle Fire is an AAS-winning okra selected for round (not sharply ribbed), deep-red pods that resist the rapid fiber buildup common in older red okra varieties, so pods stay tender for harvest over a longer size range and a more forgiving picking schedule — useful in the Gulf South's fast summer growth, when okra can go from tender to woody within a day or two. The tall, upright plants are heavy producers with attractive maroon-tinted foliage and pale yellow, red-throated flowers that make the whole plant a good-looking addition to the summer vegetable garden. Like other red okra, the color is water-soluble and fades during cooking unless pods are quickly grilled, roasted, or fried rather than boiled. Harvest every day or two once pods start forming to keep the plant productive.

common_name: Candy Cane Chocolate Cherry Sweet Pepper
plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; excellent in patio containers.
directions: An ornamental edible with variegated foliage and striped fruit that ripens from green-and-white to chocolate-red and cream. Start seed indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and keep warm to encourage germination. Its compact, showy habit makes it a standout in patio containers and balcony gardens. Harvest peppers green for a crisp bite or let them fully stripe and color up for sweeter flavor.

common_name: Candy Corn Pepper (Multicolor Ornamental Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Candy Corn is an ornamental-edible pepper bred to produce upright, tapered, yellow-to-orange-to-red fruit that resembles the classic autumn candy, providing striking multicolor display alongside genuine culinary use.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Candy Corn is compact enough for containers and makes an eye-catching patio or border plant. Bred for its ornamental-edible dual purpose, Candy Corn produces upright clusters of small, tapered fruit that ripen through a sequence from pale yellow at the base through orange to a bright red tip while still on the plant, closely mimicking the look of the classic Halloween candy for which it is named. Fruits carry moderate heat, milder than a typical cayenne but with real chile flavor, and are fully usable fresh, dried, or in hot sauce at any color stage, though flavor and heat both increase slightly as fruit ripens toward red. The compact, well-branched plant holds its colorful fruit upright above the foliage for maximum visual display, making it as valuable in a mixed ornamental border or container planting as in a dedicated vegetable bed. Harvest fruit continuously through the season to encourage more flowering and fruit set.

common_name: Candy Onion (AAS Winner Intermediate-Day Sweet Onion)
plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Candy is an All-America Selections award-winning intermediate-day (12–13 hour) hybrid onion that fills the gap between long-day northern onions and short-day southern onions — it performs across a wider geographic range than most onion types and produces large, round, flat-topped bulbs with white skin and exceptionally sweet, mild flesh that can be eaten like an apple.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost (onion transplants tolerate light frost); set 4–6 inches apart with the bulb base at soil level; keep consistently moist through bulb formation; reduce watering as tops begin to yellow and fall over; harvest and cure 2–3 weeks before storage. Candy is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning hybrid onion developed specifically for its exceptional sweetness and adaptability as an intermediate-day variety capable of producing high-quality bulbs across a wider latitudinal range than either long-day or short-day types. Intermediate-day onions (requiring 12–13 hours of daylight to trigger bulbing) are particularly valuable in zones 5–8 — the mid-latitude transition zone where long-day varieties (14+ hours required) often form small bulbs in the shorter days of the mid-latitudes and short-day varieties (10–12 hours) often bolt prematurely in the longer summer days further north. The result is that Candy succeeds in climates from Maine to Georgia where the 'wrong type' onion is a common gardening mistake. The large, round to slightly flattened, white-skinned bulbs have extraordinarily sweet, mild flesh with low pyruvate content — the same characteristic that makes Vidalia and other famous sweet onions nearly non-pungent; Candy onions can be eaten raw like a mild apple, used in salads without overwhelming other flavors, or caramelized into an intensely sweet onion jam. Yields are excellent for a sweet onion type.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; this Southern Appalachian heirloom has been grown in the mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee for generations and is one of the best-flavored large winter squashes for warm-climate gardeners.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in a prepared hill of well-composted soil after last frost, planting 3 seeds and thinning to the strongest; Candy Roaster needs a long season of 90–110 days, so in zone 9–11 plant in late winter for a spring harvest or late summer for fall. Candy Roaster is a Southern Appalachian heirloom producing large, elongated, banana-shaped fruits 12–20 inches long with pinkish-tan to salmon-orange skin often tipped with blue-green at the stem end, and sweet, orange, dry-textured flesh that roasts to a concentrated, candy-like sweetness the name describes perfectly. Fruits can reach 15–30 pounds; cure for 2 weeks in warm, dry conditions and store for 3–5 months. An essential heirloom for gardeners who want an authentic piece of Appalachian foodway heritage.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Candyland Red is a 2020 All-America Selections winner currant tomato bred for a prolific, intensely sweet harvest of tiny fruit on a tall indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine for support. Candyland Red, a 2020 All-America Selections winner, is a currant-type tomato producing an enormous quantity of tiny, intensely sweet, deep red fruit in loose clusters continuously from midsummer until frost, offering some of the highest sugar content of any tomato type for snacking straight off the vine. The vigorous vine benefits from regular watering and feeding to sustain its heavy, continuous fruit set through the Gulf South growing season. Harvest clusters as fruit ripens to full red color, and expect the plant to keep producing right up until cold weather ends the season.

common_name: Cannellini Bean (White Kidney Bean, Fazolia Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil 2–3 inches deep; cannellini is a cool-to-warm season crop — in zone 9 plant in early spring (February–March) for a late spring harvest, or again in fall (September–October) for a winter harvest when temperatures are cooler. Avoid planting in summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; cannellini is the classic Italian white kidney bean — an heirloom variety of the white kidney bean with large, plump, white seeds and a distinctly creamy, mild, earthy flavor that absorbs olive oil, garlic, rosemary, and sage beautifully. It is the essential bean of Tuscany: the foundation of ribollita and pasta e fagioli, the bean that defines Florentine cuisine, and arguably the finest-flavored dry bean for Italian cooking. The seeds are harvested dry for storage or 'semi-dried' (fresh-shelled and briefly cured) for a fresh-eating texture that is superior to fully dried beans. Bush-type plants produce pods that are allowed to dry on the vine before harvest; the dry seeds store indefinitely in cool, dry conditions.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in groups of 2–3 after last frost when soil is above 70°F; alternatively start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost in individual pots to avoid root disturbance. Melons need at least 90–100 frost-free days and warm nights for sweetest fruit development.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy-loam soil in full sun after last frost when soil exceeds 70°F; cantaloupe requires consistently warm temperatures (over 70°F days and over 60°F nights) for fruit to develop maximum sugar content — cool, cloudy summers produce watery, bland melons. Reduce watering significantly about 1 week before harvest to concentrate the sugars; overwatering near maturity is the most common cause of bland, watery flavor. Harvest when the stem slips easily from the vine ('full slip') and the blossom end gives slightly to pressure with a sweet, musky fragrance; these indicators are more reliable than days-to-maturity. The cultivar 'Hales Best Jumbo', 'Ambrosia', and 'Athena' are standard slippage-type cantaloupes.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil reaches 65°F; can start indoors 2–3 weeks early.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile hills after all frost danger has passed, planting 4–5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2. Reduce watering as fruits near maturity to concentrate sugars in the flesh. Ripe cantaloupes emit a sweet fragrance at the blossom end and slip easily from the vine with gentle pressure; this is called full-slip harvest. Avoid overwatering late in the season, which dilutes flavor and can cause splitting.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil warms; succession sow for a long harvest.
directions: A high-yielding French filet-style bush bean producing dark green, stringless pods five to six inches long with excellent flavor. Sow seed directly one inch deep after the soil warms, since beans resent cold, wet ground. Its strong disease resistance and productivity make it a reliable succession crop for a long harvest window. Pick pods regularly while young and slender to keep the plants producing.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather; a fast white-stemmed bok choy prone to bolting in heat.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in cool spring or late summer weather, as heat and stress push this brassica to bolt. Thin plants to give each room to form crisp white stems and tender green leaves. Keep the soil consistently moist for fast, mild growth and harvest whole heads when they reach full size, ideal for stir-fries and soups.

plant_note: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in fall; in zone 9 cape sorrel grows through winter and spring, blooming in March–April, then going dormant in summer heat. It naturalized across the Gulf Coast as an edible winter weed. Harvest leaves and flowers from December through April before dormancy.
directions: Plant small bulbils in fall in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, sandy soil; cape sorrel is a Mediterranean import that has naturalized across California, the Gulf Coast, and many mild-winter regions as a winter-growing edible. The clover-like leaves and bright yellow flowers are both edible — the leaves have a pleasantly tart, lemony flavor from oxalic acid and can be used in salads, stir-fries, or as a garnish in the same way as garden sorrel. The bright yellow flowers are also edible and attractive as a garnish. Note that like all oxalis, cape sorrel should be consumed in moderation as oxalic acid can interfere with calcium absorption in large quantities. Plants die down completely in summer heat and re-emerge from dormant corms in fall.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant; also grows well as a fall crop.
directions: A compact, pointed cabbage weighing just one and a half to two pounds, ideal for small households and small gardens. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before the last frost and transplant twelve to eighteen inches apart. Its tightly wrapped, ornamental conical heads shrug off weather and pests while protecting the tender interior. Keep evenly watered and harvest when heads feel firm and full for the sweetest flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; provide sturdy support for this indeterminate vine.
directions: An award-winning heirloom slicer with ten to twelve ounce fruits that are purplish-brown outside and brick-red within. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant after nights warm. As an indeterminate vine it needs a tall stake or cage and regular pruning of suckers for airflow. Water deeply and evenly to prevent cracking, and let the fruit fully color for its rich, complex flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a November–February harvest. Cardinale is a mid-season radicchio that heads reliably in zone 9 fall conditions without requiring excessively cold temperatures to form tight heads. The color deepens and bitterness mellows after exposure to several light frosts.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinale is an Italian radicchio variety producing medium-sized, round to slightly elongated heads with deep garnet-red to cardinal-red leaves and white midribs — the color is consistently deeper and more saturated than many other radicchio varieties, which gives it its name. The bitter-sweet, complex radicchio flavor is characteristic of the Cichorium intybus species, with the bitterness mellowing appropriately after cold exposure. Cardinale is valued by market growers for its reliable head formation in variable fall weather and its consistent deep color that holds through the harvest and storage period. In Italian cooking, Cardinale works in all standard radicchio preparations — grilled, braised, in risotto, in pasta, or raw in salads where its deep color provides dramatic visual contrast. In zone 9 the fall-winter-early spring season produces the most deeply colored and best-flavored heads, with improvement after the first frosts.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed into deep, rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — cardoon is a dramatic architectural plant reaching 4–6 feet in its first year.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deep, rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun after all frost risk has passed, spacing 3–5 feet apart as cardoon is a very large plant. Cynara cardunculus is the wild ancestor of the globe artichoke and a spectacular ornamental-cum-culinary plant; unlike artichoke (grown for flower buds), cardoon is grown for its thick, silvery-gray, thistle-like leaf stalks (blanched in fall by wrapping plants in burlap or paper for 3–4 weeks to remove bitterness), which are then braised, gratinéed, or served in the Italian-French Christmas tradition. The plant reaches 4–7 feet tall with dramatic, silver-arching, deeply cut leaves and produces purple, artichoke-like flower heads in its second year that are exceptionally attractive to bees and beautiful as cut or dried flowers.

common_name: Caribbean Red Habanero (Extremely Hot Red Habanero Type with Fruity Heat)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Capsicum chinense species require warmer germination temperatures (80–90°F) and longer germination times than C. annuum — use a heat mat for reliable, fast germination.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Caribbean Red is a habanero-type pepper (Capsicum chinense) producing wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits that ripen from green to bright scarlet-red — one of the hottest commercially available habanero types, typically measuring 400,000–500,000 Scoville heat units compared to the 100,000–350,000 SHU of standard orange habaneros, making it roughly 2–4 times hotter than standard habanero by Scoville measurement. The heat is the intense, building, lingering habanero burn style — not the immediate sharp heat of cayenne — accompanied by the same characteristic fruity, tropical, citrus-floral aroma that makes habanero-type peppers uniquely valuable in hot sauces, salsas, Caribbean jerk seasonings, and mango-habanero condiments. The red color produces a visually different (and often considered more attractive) hot sauce than the orange of standard habanero, making Caribbean Red popular with home hot sauce makers. The large, productive plants grow well in zone 9's long warm season, often continuing to fruit into November after a spring transplant. In zone 9b and warmer, the plants may overwinter and become large perennial pepper shrubs producing for multiple seasons.

plant_note: Direct sow as early as the ground can be worked in late winter, several weeks ahead of the last frost, since this small brown-seeded field pea shrugs off cold snaps.
directions: Direct sow as early as the ground can be worked in late winter, several weeks ahead of the last frost, since this small brown-seeded field pea shrugs off cold snaps. Carlin Pea is a survivor of a once-widespread English tradition of eating dried, soaked, and pan-fried peas on Carlin Sunday in the weeks before Easter, and it remained a staple crop in northern England long after most gardeners moved on to modern shelling peas. Give the vining plants light twiggy brush or netting for support, and either pick pods young for shelling green or let them dry fully on the vine for the traditional parched preparation. The plants tolerate poor soil and are notably resilient compared with modern pea cultivars.

common_name: Carmen Pepper (AAS-Winning Italian Frying Pepper, Early-Producing and Heat-Tolerant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Carmen is an F1 hybrid Italian frying pepper developed for superior earliness and productivity compared to heirloom Italian frying pepper types like Corno di Toro. In zone 9, transplant March–April; Carmen performs well through the Gulf Coast summer and fall. As an Italian frying pepper type, Carmen produces elongated (4–6 inches), slightly blocky-to-tapered fruits that ripen from green to bright red. The fruits are meaty, sweet, and thin-walled — more uniform in shape and earlier to ripen than heirloom Italian types. Carmen received All-America Selections (AAS) recognition in 2006, confirmed as performing well across diverse North American growing conditions. The early maturity of Carmen compared to heirloom frying types makes it practical for zone 9's spring production window before summer heat limits continued fruit set.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or fully red for best flavor. Carmen pepper is an F1 hybrid Italian frying pepper that received the All-America Selections recognition in 2006 for its consistent performance across varied North American growing conditions — specifically for its combination of earliness (reaching harvest stage significantly sooner than traditional Corno di Toro types), productivity (high fruit set per plant), and fruit quality. The All-America Selections program evaluates new vegetable and flower varieties across multiple trial locations nationwide, and a 2006 AAS designation reflects verified performance advantages over competing varieties at the time of release. Carmen's fruits are medium-large (4–6 inches long, 2 inches wide), with a form intermediate between a large Cubanelle and a Corno di Toro: longer and more pointed than a Cubanelle, but somewhat less dramatically curved and elongated than a classic Corno di Toro. The flesh is thick enough to provide substance for roasting and stuffing but still thinner-walled and more flavorful at full ripeness than standard bell peppers. The ripening process in Carmen goes through green to light orange to fully red — a complete color change that signals maximum sweetness and vitamin C content. Carmen's Italian frying pepper lineage gives it the characteristic sweetness and frying quality that makes this pepper type so valued in Mediterranean cooking: roasted Carmen peppers develop a silky, caramelized richness that is genuinely different from roasted bell peppers. For zone 9 gardeners, the early-producing quality of Carmen means productive harvests before midsummer heat stress limits continued flower and fruit production.

common_name: Carmen Sweet Pepper (AAS Winner Italian Frying Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes; Carmen is one of the fastest-maturing sweet peppers available, particularly valued in short-season northern gardens and in hot Southern gardens where the season window for maturing peppers before fall temperatures drop can be compressed; an All-America Selections 2006 winner recognized for early maturity, high yield, and exceptional sweet flavor.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Carmen peppers ripen from green to vivid red about 2 weeks earlier than most bell peppers, making them excellent for northern gardens; harvest at any stage from green (mild, slightly tangy) to full red (sweet, rich, complex flavor). Carmen is a top-performing Italian-style sweet frying pepper that won the All-America Selections award in 2006 — one of the most widely grown sweet pepper varieties to emerge from recent AAS trials, valued for combining the Italian frying pepper form (long, tapered, thin-walled, easy to peel) with exceptional earliness and garden productivity. The peppers are long (5–7 inches), tapered, and horn-shaped in the classic Italian style, maturing from pale green through deep red in about 70–80 days from transplant — significantly earlier than standard bell peppers (85–95 days) and most sweet Italian types. The flavor at full red maturity is distinctively sweet, rich, and complex in a way that sets Italian frying peppers apart from bell peppers: the thin walls cook faster and more evenly, caramelize beautifully in a hot pan, and develop a sweeter, more concentrated flavor than the thick-walled bell. Carmen is the go-to recommendation from most seed companies and extension services for gardeners who want a reliable sweet Italian frying pepper that performs consistently across a wide range of climates from zones 3 to 11. Excellent raw in salads, roasted, sautéed, or used for Italian-American pepper-and-egg preparations.

plant_note: Direct sow only; carrots do not transplant well. Keep soil surface moist until germination.
directions: A colorful mix of red, purple, yellow, and orange carrots, each carrying its own nutrients and sweet flavor. Sow seed directly a quarter inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the surface consistently moist during the slow germination. Thin seedlings to two to three inches so roots can size up evenly. Harvest young for baby carrots or at full size, and note that colors sweeten with a light frost.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Carnival is a compact acorn-type squash on a semi-bush vine well suited to smaller gardens. No two fruits look identical — the cream, orange, and green patterning varies on every squash, making Carnival ornamentally striking for fall displays as well as edible. Cure harvested fruits for 2 weeks at room temperature before eating to improve sweetness; storage improves flavor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Carnival is an All-America Selections award-winning acorn-type winter squash that produces medium-sized (1–2 lb), acorn-shaped fruits in an extraordinarily variable pattern of cream, orange, yellow, and green — no two Carnival squash are identical in coloration, with each fruit displaying a unique combination of the variety's characteristic colors in an irregular patterned display. The diversity of color on each individual squash and across the harvest makes Carnival as ornamental as it is edible, used for autumn fall displays, Thanksgiving centerpieces, and decorative arrangements alongside pumpkins. The flesh is orange, mildly sweet, and nutty — essentially the same eating quality as high-quality acorn squash, with a dry, dense texture that accepts butter, brown sugar, or maple syrup preparations well. Carnival is extremely productive and compact for an acorn-type, making it practical for backyard gardens with limited space.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 2–3 seeds after last frost; thin to one plant per hill. In zone 9 plant in late February for a spring-summer harvest or in late July for a fall harvest — the cooler fall season often produces better-flavored, more colorful fruits.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with ample compost; carnival squash is a hybrid acorn-type winter squash with uniquely multicolored skin — a striking mosaic of orange, yellow, cream, and green that deepens and brightens as the season cools. The compact, semi-bush vines fit smaller gardens better than most winter squash. Individual fruits weigh 1–2 pounds and have sweet, dense, orange-yellow flesh with good nutty flavor for roasting, baking, or steaming in halves. Fruits that have been exposed to light frost tend to develop richer color and sweeter flavor. Cure for 7–10 days at room temperature and store up to 3 months in a cool, dry location. The colorful fruits make excellent decorative gourds through autumn and into winter.

common_name: Carola Potato (German Waxy Yellow All-Purpose Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January-February for harvest before summer heat sets in. Cut seed pieces to egg size with 1-2 eyes each and let cut surfaces cure a day or two before planting.
directions: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. Carola is a German-bred potato valued for its smooth, thin, light tan skin and dense, waxy, deep yellow flesh with rich, buttery flavor, performing well boiled, roasted, and in potato salads where a firm texture that holds together is wanted. It is a reliable, heavy-yielding variety with good resistance to common potato diseases and stores reasonably well after curing. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge, and harvest for storage after the vines have died back naturally.

common_name: Carolina Bunch Sweet Potato (Compact Bush-Type for Small Gardens)
plant_note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is reliably warm; the short, compact vines make this a good candidate for raised beds or large containers.
directions: Carolina Bunch was developed at North Carolina State University specifically for small-space growers, with a tight, semi-bush habit that stays under 3 feet of spread instead of sprawling 6-8 feet like standard vining sweet potatoes. Despite the compact vines, it is a solid producer of light copper-skinned, dark orange-fleshed roots that store and bake well. Because the plants don't sprawl and cover ground the way most sweet potatoes do, keep the bed mulched to suppress weeds and maintain even soil moisture. This is a practical choice for raised beds or anywhere a gardener wants sweet potatoes without letting vines take over the whole plot.

common_name: Carolina Cayenne Pepper (AAS-Winning Early Compact Cayenne)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Carolina Cayenne is an All-America Selections winning cayenne bred for earlier maturity and a more compact, uniform plant than traditional cayenne varieties, with classic thin, curved, hot red fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Carolina Cayenne was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining classic cayenne heat and flavor with notably earlier maturity and a more compact, well-branched plant habit than older cayenne varieties, making it a reliable choice for gardeners with a shorter growing season or limited space. Fruits are thin, curved, and about 5-6 inches long, ripening from green to bright red with the sharp, straightforward heat cayenne is known for, well suited to drying, grinding into cayenne powder, or using fresh in cooking. The compact plants are heavily productive relative to their size, and the early maturity allows for a longer overall harvest window within the growing season. Harvest regularly, or let a portion of the crop ripen fully red and dry on or off the plant for storage as dried cayenne.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed, giving each vine a generous hill with heavily amended soil since this hybrid is bred purely for enormous fruit size, routinely exceeding 100 lbs and holding several giant-watermelon world records.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in a heavily amended hill after last frost, allowing at least 8-10 feet in every direction per vine since this variety produces exceptionally long, vigorous runners. Carolina Cross #183 is an oblong striped hybrid bred specifically for maximum fruit size rather than eating quality, and it has been the variety of choice for generations of giant-watermelon growers at county fairs and record competitions, with individual fruits commonly reaching 100-200 lbs and record specimens well over 200 lbs. To grow oversized fruit, limit each vine to one or two developing melons, feed heavily throughout the season, and water deeply and consistently since the huge fruit places large demands on the root system. Flesh is red and reasonably sweet, but the plant's primary appeal is spectacle and competition rather than refined flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant April–May for an August–October harvest. Carolina Gold can be grown in standard garden beds kept consistently moist rather than flooded, though paddy conditions give the highest yields. Expect 2–4 pounds of rough rice per 100 square feet in garden conditions.
directions: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Carolina Gold is America's most historically significant rice variety, the first variety commercially grown in colonial South Carolina and Georgia during the 18th century, and the foundation of lowcountry cuisine including pilau, perloo, and hoppin' john. It is a long-grained, gold-hulled, aromatic variety with exceptional flavor — nutty, fragrant, and creamy when cooked — that is the standard against which all Southern rice is measured. The variety nearly disappeared after the Civil War but was revived by dedicated seed savers and is now grown by specialty mills in the Carolinas. Home gardeners can grow it in consistently moist beds without true paddies; simply keep soil saturated throughout the growing season. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain has turned golden, then thresh and process as whole-grain brown rice or hull fully.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost at 85°F with bottom heat; Carolina Reaper is slow to germinate and slow to reach transplant size. In zone 9, start in November–December for February transplant. Plants are perennial in zone 9b–11 and can be kept as multi-year producers with frost protection.
directions: Start seeds at 85–90°F soil temperature with bottom heat — germination is erratic and may take 3–4 weeks; transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay above 60°F. Carolina Reaper was certified by Guinness World Records as the world's hottest pepper in 2013, averaging 1.57 million Scoville Heat Units (SHU) with peak measurements above 2.2 million SHU — roughly 200 times hotter than a jalapeño and significantly more potent than habaneros. It was bred by Ed Curlin (PuckerButt Pepper Company) in Rock Hill, South Carolina, by crossing a Pakistani Naga with a Red Habanero. The distinctive wrinkled, red-orange fruits are small (1–2 inches) with a characteristic scorpion-tail sting at the tip and a fruity, complex flavor underneath the extreme heat. Handle with nitrile gloves and eye protection — touching eyes or face after handling can cause serious irritation. Used in hot sauces, salsas, and challenge eating. The plants are attractive and productive in warm climates. In zone 9, treat as a long-season annual or overwinter as a perennial in zone 9b.

common_name: Carolina Ruby Sweet Potato (Early Deep-Red-Skin Orange Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F; ridge rows to keep the developing roots loose and well-drained.
directions: Carolina Ruby was bred at North Carolina State University and released in the late 1990s as an earlier-maturing companion to Beauregard, with striking deep red-purple skin and moist orange flesh. It bulks up quickly and can be dug a couple of weeks ahead of most other orange sweet potatoes, which is a real advantage for beating fall's first frost in a home garden. Vines are thin and trailing rather than bushy, so give them room to ramble or trellis them along a fence. Roots can develop pronounced lenticels if soil stays wet close to harvest, so time digging for a dry stretch and avoid heavy irrigation in the final weeks.

common_name: Carolina Wonder Sweet Pepper (NCSU Disease-Resistant Sweet Bell)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Carolina Wonder was developed by North Carolina State University as a disease-resistant sweet bell pepper with resistance to Phytophthora blight, bacterial leaf spot, and tobacco etch virus — disease complex that significantly limits sweet bell pepper production in humid Southeastern climates — making it one of the most reliable sweet bells for home gardeners across the Atlantic and Gulf Coast states.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after last frost; Carolina Wonder's disease resistance package makes it superior to susceptible commercial bell varieties in humid climates where Phytophthora blight and bacterial leaf spot cause mid-season collapse of unprotected plants. Carolina Wonder was developed at North Carolina State University's pepper breeding program to address the specific disease challenges of Southeastern sweet bell pepper production — the combination of summer heat, humidity, rainfall, and the disease complex it creates (Phytophthora capsici root and crown rot, bacterial leaf spot caused by Xanthomonas, tobacco etch virus) creates extremely difficult conditions for standard sweet bell varieties that lack specific resistance genes. Carolina Wonder combines resistance to multiple diseases with excellent sweet bell quality: the large (4-lobed, blocky, 3.5–4 inch), thick-walled fruits are green-to-red with crisp, sweet flesh typical of the best sweet bells. The disease resistance package — particularly the Phytophthora crown and root rot resistance — gives Carolina Wonder dramatically better survival in wet years and poorly drained soils compared to susceptible varieties. Carolina Wonder is sometimes paired with Charleston Belle (which adds nematode resistance not included in Carolina Wonder) in gardens where both nematodes and Phytophthora are concerns; together they address the full disease complex of Gulf South pepper production.

common_name: Carouby de Maussane Snow Pea (French Provence Heirloom Large Flat Edible-Pod Pea)
scientific_name: Pisum sativum var. saccharatum 'Carouby de Maussane'
plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked; Carouby de Maussane is a tall (4–5 foot) snow pea requiring trellis support. In zone 9, direct sow November–February for spring harvest (March–April); fall planting is preferred in zone 9 where the mild winter allows establishment and early spring production before summer heat arrives. The distinctive large flat pods (3–5 inches) are harvested when still flat and before seeds develop — the snow pea stage. The purple flowers and bicolor pods make this one of the most ornamental of edible pod pea varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep along a trellis or fence; thin to 3–4 inches. Provide 4–5 foot support. Harvest pods flat before seeds bulge. Carouby de Maussane is a French Provençal heirloom snow pea — a mangetout (French for 'eat all,' referring to the edible pod) variety from the village of Maussane-les-Alpilles in the Alpilles region of Provence that has been grown continuously in the gardens and small farms of that region for generations. The variety is distinguished by unusually large flat pods (3–5 inches long) that are visually unlike standard snow peas: broader, larger, and often tinged with purple at the shoulders when young — and by the ornamental beauty of the plant itself, which produces the bi-colored purple-and-white flowers of the original pea species (most modern pea varieties have been selected for white-only flowers) against dark green foliage on 4–5 foot vines. The pods have the flat, wide, meaty snow pea character at optimal harvest — tender, crisp, and sweetly flavored without the starchy density of fully-podded shelling peas. Carouby de Maussane is a cold-hardy, vigorous variety well-suited to fall planting in zone 8–9 where it can grow through the mild winter and produce the spring snap-pod harvest before summer heat arrives. The variety is maintained by seed savers and heirloom seed companies as an example of the genetic and culinary diversity that existed in traditional European peasant food gardens.

plant_note: Plant cloves pointed end up in fall, roughly 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes solid, allowing roots to establish before dormancy.
directions: Set cloves 2 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil and mulch heavily through winter, especially in northern climates, removing mulch gradually in spring. Cut the scape once it curls to direct the plant's energy into bulb formation, then cure bulbs for several weeks in a dry, shaded, well-ventilated space. Carpathian is a cold-hardy porcelain-type hardneck originating in the Carpathian Mountains of Eastern Europe, grown for its large white bulbs, thick papery wrappers, and strong, long-lasting garlic flavor well suited to harsh winter climates.

subcategory: wild edible shoots / native climbing vine
plant_note: Plant root divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures.
directions: Plant root divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures. Unlike its thorny greenbrier relatives, this species is unarmed and herbaceous, dying back to its tuberous rootstock each winter and resprouting reliably each spring. Young emerging shoots are harvested and cooked like asparagus in early spring before the tendrils toughen, while the small, unshowy flowers give off a carrion-like scent that draws fly pollinators later in the season. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is best left undisturbed once established.

plant_note: Direct sow 3 weeks before to 2 weeks after last frost; succession sow every 3 weeks.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the surface consistently moist until sprouting, which is slow. Thin seedlings to 2–3 in so roots can size up. Harvest when shoulders reach desired diameter; flavor sweetens after a light frost.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Casaba is the longest-season common American melon (105–120 days), requiring the extended heat of Gulf Coast and Western summers for reliable ripening, but rewarding patient gardeners with large, golden-yellow, wrinkled-skinned fruits that store for months and have a distinctive mild, sweet, creamy-white flesh.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Casaba needs dry conditions at harvest to prevent splitting and rind cracking — reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity. Casaba melon takes its name from Kasaba (now called Turgutlu), a city in western Turkey from which seeds were brought to the United States in the late 19th century; it is an inodorus winter-type melon with no surface netting and little external fragrance when ripe, unusual among American melons. The large (8–14 lb), round to slightly pointed-at-one-end fruits have deeply furrowed, wrinkled, golden-yellow skin and creamy-white to pale yellow flesh with mild, sweet, cucumber-like flavor that is less intensely aromatic than cantaloupe but refreshing and distinct. Casaba's extraordinary keeping quality (3–5 months at cool room temperature without refrigeration) made it historically important as a late-season melon available well after other varieties were finished; harvested in October it could remain in good condition through December. Excellent for dry summer climates (California, Arizona, Gulf Coast with good drainage); susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; a traditional Mexican dried chile harvested red and used primarily dried — do not harvest green. Zone 8–11 gardeners can grow this easily as a spring crop in the ground.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to the garden in warm soil after all frost risk has passed. Cascabel — named for the rattle the seeds make inside the dried pod — is a round, 1.5-inch, deep red-brown dried Mexican chile with mild to moderate heat (1,500–2,500 Scoville), a uniquely nutty, slightly smoky, woody flavor with an earthy depth that is used in traditional Mexican moles, salsas, and braised meats; it is harvested fully red on the plant and dried for 2–3 weeks in a warm, airy location. Plants are compact and bushy, producing round pods in clusters; the fully dried pods have a distinctive rattling sound from the loose seeds inside, making them easy to identify in a pantry. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture to maximize fruit set.

common_name: Cascade Glaze Collard (Oregon Re-Selection of Heirloom Green Glaze)
plant_note: Direct sow or set transplants 10-12 weeks before the first fall frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cascade Glaze is a modern re-selection of the 1820s Southern heirloom Green Glaze, sharing its glossy, waxy, insect-resistant leaves.
directions: Set transplants or thin direct-sown seedlings to 24-30 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cascade Glaze was bred as a careful re-selection of the classic 1820s Southern heirloom Green Glaze collard, retaining the same smooth, glossy, waxy leaf surface that sheds cabbage worm eggs and deters other leaf-eating pests better than fuzzier-leaved collard varieties, while offering improved uniformity from the breeding work. The open, non-heading rosette produces tender, mild-flavored leaves that hold up well to both heat and light frost, making it productive across a long Gulf South growing season. Harvest outer leaves continuously as the plant grows, and expect sweeter flavor after the first light frosts convert starches to sugars.

common_name: Cascadia Snap Pea (Disease-Resistant Oregon State-Bred Snap Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Cascadia is an Oregon State University-bred snap pea noted for disease resistance and reliable production on compact vines.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked, providing light support such as netting or twiggy brush for the vines. Cascadia was bred at Oregon State University and is valued for good resistance to powdery mildew and other common pea diseases, along with sweet, crisp, edible pods on compact, easy-to-support vines that produce reliably even in less-than-ideal spring weather. Its snap-pea type pods are eaten whole, pod and all, once they fill out but before the peas inside become starchy. Harvest regularly once pods reach full size to encourage continued production through the relatively short Gulf South pea season.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 65°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide an 8-foot pole or trellis, since this vigorous semi-runner climbs readily and produces best when given full support.
directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick young for snap beans, at the shelly stage for a creamy fresh bean, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage beans. Case Knife is an old Southern heirloom pole bean named for its long, flat, slightly curved pods, which resemble the folding blade of a case knife (a traditional pocketknife). The vigorous vines climb readily to 6–8 feet and bear heavily over a long summer season, producing broad, tender pods best picked young for snap use before the beans inside swell; left to mature, the pods yield plump, cream-white beans that shell out easily and cook to a smooth, buttery texture, or can be dried fully for winter storage. Valued in old Southern gardens for its dependable heat tolerance and heavy yield from a small footprint of trellis space, making it a practical choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens where many bush beans falter in midsummer heat.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Caserta is one of the most heat-tolerant open-pollinated zucchini varieties, typically yielding well into summer heat that causes hybrid types to stall. The AAS-winning bush habit is compact and manageable in small gardens.
directions: Direct sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to the strongest plant; Caserta is an All-America Selections award-winning heirloom Italian zucchini with distinctive gray-green striped skin and creamy interior, different in appearance and texture from the solid dark-green standard zucchini. The cylindrical, 6–8 inch fruits have firmer, denser, less watery flesh than most hybrid zucchini — excellent for grilling, sautéing, and stuffing where a firmer texture is preferred. The compact, AAS-winning bush plant produces abundantly in both spring and fall crops in zone 9; summer production may slow during peak heat. Harvest at 6–8 inches for best flavor and texture — oversized fruits become seedy and pithy. The attractive, striped fruits are ornamental as well as useful.

common_name: Cash Flow Hybrid Zucchini (High-Yield Market Zucchini)
plant_note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for a jump on the season.
directions: Cash Flow was bred as a market-grower's zucchini, prized for setting an unusually high number of straight, uniform dark-green fruit in quick succession from an open, easy-to-harvest plant. Pick fruit small, at 6-8 inches, for the best texture and to keep the vigorous plant cranking out more; a single well-fed plant can produce for weeks with regular harvest. The open habit makes fruit easy to spot under the leaves, cutting down on the oversized zucchini that hide until harvest day. A dependable choice for gardeners who want a steady, heavy zucchini harvest without much fuss.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Harvest fruit when glossy and firm, before the skin dulls and yellows, which signals overripeness and increasing bitterness.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick fruit young and glossy for the mildest, sweetest flavor and fewest seeds. Casper is a classic heirloom eggplant producing smooth, pure ivory-white, oblong fruit with tender skin that needs no peeling, and notably mild, sweet, non-bitter flesh that browns less than purple varieties once cut — a practical advantage for dishes where appearance matters, like gratins or stuffed preparations. The productive, well-branched plants set fruit reliably over a long summer season and are less prone to the bitterness that can develop in some eggplant varieties under stress. Its striking white color and mild flavor make it a favorite for gardeners wanting a visually distinctive eggplant with excellent kitchen versatility, zone 4–12.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; an heirloom white-skinned pumpkin for decor and baking.
directions: Plant seeds an inch deep in warm soil in hills, thinning to the two best vines each. Give the plants space and steady moisture to develop the smooth, ghostly white rinds and sweet orange flesh. Harvest when the stems harden and cure in the sun to firm the skin for both fall displays and baking.

common_name: Casper White Eggplant (Italian Ivory White Heirloom Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Casper white eggplant shows good heat tolerance and performs well in zone 9. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer and fall production. Harvest when fruits are 5–7 inches long and creamy white — white eggplants turn slightly yellowish as they over-ripen, which is the signal to harvest before quality declines. Do not allow to over-ripen on the plant; harvest slightly early compared to purple types.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun. Harvest when fruits are 5–7 inches and solid creamy white before yellowing. Casper is an Italian-style white eggplant — a medium-sized, oval-to-elongated variety producing distinctive ivory-white to cream-white fruits in the 4–7 inch range. White eggplant varieties have a long tradition in Italian cooking, where they are considered particularly well-suited to oven-roasted preparations and eggplant parmesan, as the white skin and flesh remain visually lighter during cooking compared to the purple-flesh types that can discolor. The flavor of Casper white eggplant is noticeably different from standard purple varieties: consistently milder, creamier, with significantly less bitterness — white-skinned eggplants in general tend toward less bitterness than dark-skinned types, though the reason may be as much cultural (bred and selected for mild flavor in the white-eggplant tradition) as biological. The flesh is very creamy and smooth-textured, making Casper an excellent choice for dips, spreads, baba ganoush-style preparations, and dishes where a mild, creamy eggplant flavor is desired without the assertiveness of purple types. The ivory-white skin also makes Casper a visually interesting garden plant and conversation piece at farmers markets.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, or start indoors a few weeks early in short-season areas.
directions: A petite ornamental pumpkin producing pure-white fruits four to four and a half inches across, perfect for painting and displays. Sow seed directly one inch deep once the soil is warm, or start indoors briefly in short-season climates. Give the vines room to run and keep soil evenly moist while fruit sizes up. Harvest when the skin is hard and the stem corks, leaving a length of stem attached for longer storage.

common_name: Caspian Pink Tomato (Russian Heirloom Low-Acid Beefsteak Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Caspian Pink is an indeterminate beefsteak that produces large, heavy fruits (8–14 oz) and benefits from strong stake or sturdy cage support. In zone 9, transplant March–April for July–August harvest. Like many large beefsteak types, Caspian Pink requires warm nights to set fruit well — the Gulf South's warm summer nights are typically favorable for fruit set in this variety.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun in fertile, deeply prepared soil. Stake securely — the large, heavy fruits can pull down unsupported vines. Caspian Pink is a Ukrainian-Russian heirloom beefsteak tomato introduced to the United States by Marianna Kezenberger, an immigrant from the Caspian Sea region of the former Soviet Union — the name references both the geographic origin and the distinctive color. The variety is a large-fruited, low-acid pink-skinned beefsteak type: fruits weigh 8–14 oz or more, with the flattened, slightly irregular, shouldered shape characteristic of traditional beefsteaks. The skin is thin, smooth, and a clear rose-pink rather than true red, indicating the absence of the yellow skin gene — a characteristic associated with lower perceived acidity and sweeter flavor in tomatoes. The flavor profile is rich, complex, and less sharp than red-skinned beefsteaks — noticeably sweeter at the same sugar content because lower acid allows sweetness to predominate. Caspian Pink is consistently rated among the best-tasting pink heirloom beefsteaks in comparative tastings, often mentioned in the same conversation as Brandywine and Cherokee Purple as a top-tier beefsteak for eating quality.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost date to give this long-season vine enough time to mature. Transplant to a permanent, frost-free location with a sturdy trellis or fence once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Start seeds indoors in warm, moist potting mix at least 4–6 weeks before the last expected frost, as cassabanana needs a very long growing season to produce its large, fragrant fruits. Provide a strong trellis, arbor, or fence — this vigorous vine can easily reach 20–30 feet in a single season. Water consistently and fertilize every few weeks with a balanced fertilizer; reduce watering once fruits begin to color and fill out. In frost-free zones (USDA 10–11) the vine is perennial and will produce fruit year after year from the same root system.

plant_note: Plant 8–10 inch stem cuttings (stakes) horizontally 4–6 inches deep or at a 45-degree angle after soil warms to 65°F; upright planting produces fewest tubers while horizontal planting maximizes yield.
directions: Plant stem cuttings (stakes) horizontally 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; cassava is drought tolerant once established and produces in poor soils where other root crops fail, making it one of the world's most important calorie crops. All varieties contain some cyanogenic glycosides — sweet varieties are low enough for safe eating after cooking, while bitter varieties require extensive washing and fermentation to detoxify. Never eat raw cassava. Harvest tubers when 8–18 months old by digging carefully to avoid breaking the fragile roots; they must be used within a few days of harvest or frozen, as they deteriorate rapidly. In zone 9, the above-ground plant freezes back but roots may survive with heavy mulch.

plant_note: Sow in midsummer (late July to August in most climates) for fall and winter harvest; this Italian heirloom requires cool temperatures to develop its distinctive markings and mild flavor, so timing is critical — too-early sowing leads to bolting, too-late means insufficient size before hard freezes.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in summer, thinning to 12–14 inches apart; Castelfranco is sometimes called the 'Flower of the Veneto' for its extraordinarily beautiful, loosely ruffled heads that open like a rose, with creamy white or pale yellow leaves splashed and spotted with deep wine-red markings — no two heads are alike. The flavor is distinctly milder and more buttery than the sharply bitter Chioggia or Treviso types, making it accessible to diners who find radicchio too harsh. Cool autumn temperatures intensify the color development — heads grown in warm weather are primarily green. Use individual leaves as edible cups for salads or hors d'oeuvres; the visual presentation is stunning. In the South, this is an ideal late-fall and winter salad green for gardens in zones 8–9.

common_name: Catalina Spinach (Heat-Tolerant Flat-Leaf Fall Spinach Hybrid)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or early fall for fall and winter harvest; Catalina is particularly valued for fall sowing in zone 8–10 where it establishes quickly in warm soil and then grows through winter. In zone 9, sow September–November for November–February harvest. Spring planting is possible (sow February–March) but Catalina shows its best performance in the cooler temperatures of fall and winter production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2–4 inch spacing for full-sized leaves or leave more densely sown for baby spinach harvest. Catalina is a flat-leaf hybrid spinach from Johnny's Selected Seeds selected specifically for fall and winter production in a wide range of climates — a smooth, flat-leaved type (as opposed to the crinkled savoy and semi-savoy types) that is preferred for salad mixes, commercial baby spinach production, and any application where the spinach will be eaten raw rather than cooked. The flat-leaf type is easier to wash than savoy types because soil and debris don't get trapped in the leaf crevices, making Catalina a practical choice for cut-and-wash baby greens. Catalina carries good resistance to multiple races of downy mildew, extending its productive life in humid fall conditions. The leaves are medium-large, oval to lance-shaped, dark green, and have the clean, mild spinach flavor that works well in all raw applications. Its performance in fall and winter production makes Catalina particularly valuable for the Gulf South zone 8–10 garden where fall and winter are the primary growing seasons for spinach — direct-seeding in September and October establishes plants that grow slowly through winter and provide steady leaf harvests.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–October for harvest November through February. Catalogna can also be sown in spring (January–February) for a shorter harvest before summer heat causes bolting. The dandelion-like leaves are most tender and mild when harvested young at 60–70 days; older plants become progressively more bitter. Harvest the whole rosette or strip outer leaves for continuous production.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Catalogna Chicory (Cicoria di Catalogna, also called Asparagus Chicory or Puntarelle in its bolted form) is the traditional Italian cut-leaf chicory of Lazio and Apulia, producing elongated, deeply toothed, dandelion-shaped leaves with a pleasantly bitter, refreshing flavor that is considerably milder than radicchio. In Italy the outer leaves are eaten braised or in soups, while the inner pale stems are prized as the luxury green 'puntarelle' — the hollow, pale, crunchy stem shoots that emerge when the plant begins to bolt, traditionally served raw in Rome with an anchovy-garlic-lemon dressing. Catalogna is one of the most widely eaten cooking greens in southern Italy and is slowly gaining recognition in North American specialty markets. In zone 9 it provides a productive cut-and-come-again winter green harvest from fall sowings, and the mild temperatures allow it to slowly develop the inner stem shoots (puntarelle) that make it exceptional. Harvest outer leaves throughout winter and allow the center to develop stem shoots in late winter for puntarelle.

plant_note: Plant topset bulbils in early fall so they root before winter; spring planting also works but establishes more slowly. Catawissa is a 19th-century American heirloom walking onion selection, distinct from the common Egyptian walking onion in its looser, more open topset clusters and occasional true flowers mixed among the bulbils.
directions: Plant topset bulbils 1-2 inches deep in well-drained soil in fall or early spring; established clumps are extremely low-maintenance and benefit from dividing every few years to maintain vigor. Catawissa is a historic American heirloom perennial onion, first documented in Pennsylvania in the 1800s, that produces clusters of small aerial bulbils atop tall seed stalks; as the topsets mature and become heavy, the stalk arches over and the bulbils root wherever they touch soil, letting the planting slowly spread, or 'walk', across the bed on its own. Compared with the more commonly sold Egyptian walking onion, Catawissa's topset clusters are looser and sometimes mixed with small true flowers, and some gardeners find its flavor slightly milder. Harvest green tops through the season like scallions, or dig the underground bulbs once foliage begins to die back; the aerial bulbils themselves can be pickled or used as new planting stock.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant for a fall crop; sprouts sweeten after frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors and set out sturdy transplants so the long season finishes as cool fall weather arrives. This 1940s heirloom forms compact, dwarf stalks packed with large, tightly wrapped sprouts. Keep the plants well fed and watered, and wait to harvest until a few frosts have sweetened the sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 50–65°F; cold-stratify seeds for 2–4 weeks in the refrigerator to improve germination. Transplant to a shaded, moist wall or fence where the climbing stems have support.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade against a wall, fence, or trellis; Caucasian spinach is a remarkable perennial climbing green from the Caucasus mountains and one of the very few shade-tolerant vining vegetables, making it invaluable in north-facing or deeply shaded spots. The young leaves and shoot tips are harvested throughout spring and summer exactly like spinach — steamed, sautéed, or eaten fresh — with a mild, pleasant flavor similar to New Zealand spinach. The plant dies back to the ground in winter and re-emerges reliably from its rootstock in spring, climbing vigorously to 6–12 feet when given support. In zone 9, provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture to prevent summer decline; the plant often goes partially dormant in peak heat and recovers for fall harvests.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant about 4 weeks before last frost.
directions: Sow 1/4 in deep in well-drained starter mix 6–8 weeks before transplanting; cauliflower is sensitive to temperature swings and nutrient deficiencies. When the developing curd is about the size of a golf ball, gather outer leaves over it and secure with a rubber band to blanch for white varieties. Harvest when the head is firm, tight, and 6–8 in across before the curds begin to separate. Consistent soil moisture and boron-sufficient soil prevent hollow stem and poor curd formation.

plant_note: Flavor sweetens after frost; also spring-sow for summer harvest.
directions: Also known as Tuscan or lacinato kale, this Italian heirloom bears puckered blue-black strap leaves used in soups and braises. Start indoors and transplant, or direct sow, spacing plants 15 inches apart in fertile soil. Harvest lower leaves first, working upward and leaving the growing crown intact for continuous production. Cold weather concentrates sugars, so the best-flavored leaves come after the first hard frosts. Watch for cabbage worms in warm spells and cover with row fabric if needed.

plant_note: Start indoors early and transplant after all frost danger passes.
directions: A prolific blend of pencil-thin cayenne peppers used fresh, dried, ground, or strung into a decorative ristra. Start seed indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and keep warm for good germination. Transplant after nights stay above 55 degrees and support heavily laden plants if needed. Let fruits ripen to red for full heat, and dry them whole or grind for homemade red pepper flakes.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix, maintaining soil temperature above 75°F for prompt sprouting. Set transplants out once the garden is fully warm and side-dress with a balanced fertilizer once plants begin flowering. Thin-walled cayenne fruits dry exceptionally well; allow them to redden fully on the plant before harvesting for drying. String harvested peppers in a warm, airy location or use a dehydrator to preserve them.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Cayennetta is a compact cayenne-type pepper bred with sturdy branches that hold the fruit upright without staking, and with milder heat than a traditional cayenne.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cayennetta is an AAS-winning cayenne-type pepper bred for a compact, sturdy, well-branched plant that holds its heavy load of slender, upward-pointing red fruit without staking, unlike tall traditional cayenne varieties that tend to flop under the fruit's weight. The heat is noticeably milder than classic cayenne — moderate rather than fiery — making it more versatile for cooks who want cayenne flavor and color without maximum heat. Fruits can be picked green or left to ripen to full red for the best flavor and heat development, and the tidy plant size suits containers as well as garden beds. Harvest continuously to keep the plant setting new fruit through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant; tolerates heat better than most greens for a long season.
directions: A rainbow-stemmed chard in red, magenta, orange, pink, yellow, and white beneath glossy dark green leaves. Sow the seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to six to twelve inches apart. It tolerates both light frost and summer heat, making it productive from spring through fall. Harvest outer leaves regularly and the plant keeps generating new growth from the center all season.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January and transplant in March. Celebrity is an early-to-mid-season determinate that sets fruit reliably under hot conditions — well-suited for both spring and fall tomato seasons in zone 9.
