directions: Start seeds at 70–80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F; Celebrity is the most widely sold tomato variety in the United States, an All-America Selections winner from 1984 that became ubiquitous in home gardens because of its extraordinary disease resistance, consistent production, and reliable flavor across a wide range of climates. The medium-large (7–8 oz), red, globe-shaped fruits ripen uniformly and have classic tomato flavor — not exceptional, but reliably good and much better than supermarket tomatoes. The determinate, semi-bushy plants (3–4 feet tall) resist nearly every major tomato disease: Fusarium wilt (races 1 and 2), Verticillium wilt, nematodes, Alternaria, tobacco mosaic virus, and gray leaf spot — the VFFNTASt on the label. This combination of compact size, disease resistance, and reliability makes Celebrity the recommended first tomato for new gardeners and the backup choice for experienced growers in difficult disease environments. In zone 9, it performs well in the spring window (transplanted February–March for May–June harvest) and in fall (transplanted late August for October–November harvest).

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed when plants are 3–4 in tall.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist starting mix — they need light to germinate — and barely cover with vermiculite; seedling growth is extremely slow for the first 6 weeks. Transplant into rich, consistently moist soil and remove the lower side shoots throughout summer to encourage bulb development. Celeriac bulbs are at their best after light autumn frosts, which deepen the nutty flavor. Harvest before the ground freezes hard; trim roots and leaves and store in slightly moist sand in a cold root cellar.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil has warmed slightly.
directions: Surface-sow or barely cover tiny seed with 1/8 in of moist mix; celery germinates slowly and needs consistent warmth and bright light from the start. Transplant into deeply prepared, rich soil and provide consistent, abundant moisture throughout the season, as drought quickly causes tough, stringy stalks. Hill soil around the base or use collars to blanch stalks to a paler color and milder flavor if desired. Harvest entire plants by cutting at soil level when stalks are 12–18 in tall and firm.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring; can also be started indoors 4 weeks early and transplanted out.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep or start indoors and transplant at 4–5 weeks; celtuce is grown primarily for its swollen, asparagus-like central stalk rather than its leaves, though young leaves are also edible. The stalk is ready when it is 1–1.5 inches in diameter and 12–15 inches tall; peel away the outer layer to reveal the crisp, mild interior. Keep soil consistently moist and rich in nitrogen for the fastest stalk development. Harvest before the plant bolts, as heat causes bitterness and pithy texture in the stalk.

common_name: Centennial Sweet Potato (LSU 1966 Orange Gulf Coast Standard)
plant_note: Plant slips after last frost when soil warms above 65°F; Centennial was released in 1966 by Louisiana State University Agricultural Center and was the dominant Southern sweet potato for 20+ years before Beauregard's introduction, noted for its excellent disease resistance, consistent yields, and reliable performance specifically in Gulf Coast growing conditions.
directions: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in rows 3–4 feet apart in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost; avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes excessive vining and reduces root yield. Centennial was developed and released in 1966 by the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center, named to commemorate the 100th anniversary of LSU's establishment, and rapidly became the standard commercial sweet potato in Louisiana and throughout the Gulf South; it held that position for nearly two decades before Beauregard displaced it commercially in the late 1980s. Centennial produces medium to large, elongated, smooth, red-orange-skinned roots with deep orange, moist, sweet flesh of excellent quality; it was specifically selected for resistance to Fusarium wilt and other soilborne diseases persistent in Gulf Coast sweet potato production. Now maintained by seed savers and specialty nurseries as an important historical variety of Louisiana and Gulf South agriculture; excellent for home garden use with low inputs.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4 weeks before transplanting in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; soak seeds 24 hours before planting to improve germination. Provide a trellis or other support for climbing.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade with a support to climb; Ceylon spinach is the red-stemmed form of Malabar spinach, producing striking bright-red vining stems, dark green to purplish leaves, and decorative dark reddish-purple berries. Like green Malabar spinach (B. alba), the leaves are thick, succulent, and mild-flavored when young, used fresh in salads or cooked as a spinach substitute in stir-fries, soups, and curries throughout tropical Asia. The red-stemmed form is highly ornamental — it can be used as a colorful edible trellis plant or allowed to cascade over a fence. It thrives in heat that wilts true spinach and is particularly productive in Gulf Coast summer gardens. In zone 9–11 it overwinters as a short-lived perennial. Tolerates partial shade better than most summer leafy greens.

common_name: Cha-Cha Kabocha Squash (Sweet Dry-Fleshed Japanese Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; give the compact vines room to run and cure fruit for one to two weeks after harvest to fully develop sweetness.
directions: Direct sow seed in warm, fertile soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, planting in hills with room for the moderately compact vines. Cha-Cha is a Japanese-bred kabocha-type squash that won recognition as an All-America Selections winner for its exceptionally sweet, dry, dense orange flesh and reliable, early, high-yielding production compared to older kabocha types. The dark green, lightly ribbed rind covers flesh that develops a rich, nutty-sweet flavor similar to roasted chestnut once cured, making it a favorite for soups, roasting, and tempura in Japanese cooking. Harvest when the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before moving to cool storage to concentrate sugars.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; stake or cage this indeterminate vine.
directions: An heirloom indeterminate cherry tomato named for horticulturist Alan Chadwick, bearing heavy trusses of sweet, crack-resistant one to two ounce fruits. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. Provide a tall trellis or cage and prune suckers to keep the vigorous vines manageable. Water evenly and pick the glossy red fruits regularly to encourage continued production.

common_name: Chadwick Cherry Tomato (Vigorous Heirloom Red Cherry)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Chadwick Cherry is an extremely vigorous, sprawling indeterminate vine that needs sturdy, tall staking and ample space.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, providing tall, sturdy support for the exceptionally vigorous vines. Chadwick Cherry is a heirloom cherry tomato associated with biodynamic gardening pioneer Alan Chadwick, grown for its large, sprawling vines and heavy production of medium-sized, deep red, richly flavored cherry fruit with classic old-fashioned tomato taste. The plants are notably larger and more vigorous than many cherry tomato varieties, often reaching well over 8 feet if left unpruned, so give them generous space and a tall cage or trellis system. Harvest regularly once fruit turns fully red for the best flavor, and prune selectively to improve air circulation, since the dense vine growth can encourage fungal disease in humid climates.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Champion was developed as an improved Southern collard with resistance to downy mildew — a significant disease concern in the humid Gulf Coast climate where other collard varieties may develop foliar disease in warm, wet conditions. In zone 9 Champion's disease resistance makes it particularly well-suited to the humid fall growing season; frost improves the flavor significantly as it does with all collards. Harvest outer leaves as needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Champion is an open-pollinated Southern collard variety developed as a disease-resistant improvement over traditional Georgia Southern — the same large-leafed, upright, non-heading collard type of traditional Southern cuisine but with improved resistance to downy mildew (Peronospora brassicae) that affects other varieties in warm, humid growing conditions typical of the Gulf South. The large, smooth, dark green to blue-green leaves with a prominent pale midrib are slightly more uniform in size and more upright in growth habit than Georgia Southern, making Champion a preferred choice for growers seeking both culinary quality and consistent appearance. The classic slow-simmered Southern preparation — cooking collard leaves for hours with smoked pork until deeply tender — works identically with Champion; the mild, rich flavor and large leaf size produce the same deeply satisfying braised greens associated with Southern food culture. Disease resistance makes Champion the practical choice for fall production in the Gulf South where humidity and warmth encourage fungal disease in more susceptible varieties.

common_name: Champion Collards (Upright Heat-Adapted Medium-Leaf Gulf South Collard)
plant_note: Direct sow 10–12 weeks before the first frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun; in zone 9, Champion Collards can also be sown in late January–February for a spring harvest, though the fall/winter crop produces the sweetest, most tender greens.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Champion is a widely recommended collard variety for Gulf South home gardens — producing upright plants with medium to large, waxy, blue-green leaves that are somewhat more compact and manageable than old-fashioned large-leaf types. Champion is valued for its combination of good heat tolerance in the planting period (August–September establishment in zone 9 requires tolerance of remaining summer heat), productive fall and winter yields, and excellent flavor quality that improves after frost exposure — the cold sweetens collard leaves by converting starches to sugars, a phenomenon well-known to Gulf South gardeners who prefer the post-frost harvest for their finest-flavored greens. The waxy leaf surface of Champion reduces water loss and contributes to the heat-establishment tolerance. In zone 9, collards are grown as a cool-season crop planted in August–September and harvested through November–February; the mild Gulf South winter allows continuous harvest from established plants without the repeated freeze damage that ends collard production in northern climates. Harvest outer leaves progressively (leaving the growing tip intact) for extended production from each plant. Champion has been recommended by southern cooperative extension services for decades as a reliable, productive, good-quality collard for both home garden and small-farm production.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather; a fast heirloom round red radish for spring and fall.
directions: Sow seeds a half inch deep directly in the garden and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots. These fast radishes are ready in under a month, producing round, cherry-red roots with crisp, mild white flesh. Keep the soil evenly moist to avoid pithiness and pungency, and sow in succession during the cool ends of the season.

plant_note: Sow directly in cool soil several weeks before the last frost; set stakes, netting, or brush at planting time, as the tall vines will topple without sturdy support.
directions: Sow directly in cool soil several weeks before the last frost, since this tall Victorian heirloom needs a long, cool season to reach its full six-foot height. Introduced in England in 1843, Champion of England quickly became renowned among market gardeners and exhibitors for the exceptionally sweet flavor of its plump pods, a reputation that has kept it in cultivation among heirloom growers ever since. Set stakes, netting, or brush at planting time, as the tall vines will topple without sturdy support. Pick pods regularly once they fill out to keep the vines productive and to catch the peas at their sweetest before starches develop.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; Chantenay is the best carrot for heavy clay soils or stony ground where long varieties would fork or fail — the short, broad shape reaches full size in difficult soil conditions.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Chantenay is the ideal carrot for difficult clay or stony soils where standard longer varieties fork and struggle — the squat, broad-shouldered, 4–6 inch roots with wide tops and tapered tips develop fully in heavy or shallow soils that prevent the growth of Nantes or Imperator types. Despite being originally bred for difficult soils, Chantenay has excellent rich flavor and high sugar content, with crisp orange flesh and a traditional carrot taste. Perfect for canning, juicing, and storage; the broad shoulders and high shoulder content also make it efficient to harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow; a stocky heirloom carrot that performs well in heavy soils and stores long.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in loose soil and keep the surface consistently moist through the slow germination period. This stocky, tapered variety about four to five inches long tolerates heavier and clay soils better than long carrots. Thin seedlings to prevent crowding and harvest as needed, storing the sweet, red-cored roots in a cool place for winter use.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; Chaotian, meaning 'facing heaven,' is a small, very hot Chinese chili named for its pods pointing upward as they ripen.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Chaotian bears clusters of small, conical, very hot red chilis that point upward toward the sky as they ripen, giving the pepper its Chinese name, and is a staple in Sichuan and Guizhou cooking, used both fresh and dried in chili oil, hot pots, and spice blends. The compact, heavily fruiting plants produce abundant small pods over a long summer harvest. Harvest continuously to encourage more flowering, or leave pods to dry on the plant for storage.

common_name: Chapalote Corn (Ancient Mexican Popcorn-Type Flint Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; Chapalote is among the oldest surviving Mexican corn varieties, a popcorn-textured flint type grown for centuries in Sinaloa.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Chapalote is one of the oldest documented corn varieties still cultivated in the Americas, a tall, dark-kerneled flint corn from the coastal state of Sinaloa in northwestern Mexico with a distinctive popcorn-like kernel texture that connects it to some of the earliest domesticated maize lineages. It is used both for pinole (roasted, ground corn) and as a genuinely popping corn, reflecting its ancient, less fully domesticated kernel structure. Harvest and dry ears fully before shelling and storing kernels.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost at 80–85°F; charapita peppers germinate slowly and benefit from bottom heat and patience. Transplant after all cold risk passes. In zone 9, transplant March–April; plants may overwinter as tender perennials in zone 9b–11 if protected from frost.
directions: Start seeds at 80–85°F with bottom heat and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after nights are reliably above 60°F; charapita is a tiny wild Capsicum chinense from the Peruvian Amazon, producing hundreds of pea-sized (4–5mm), perfectly round yellow to orange fruits on sprawling, branchy plants. Despite their diminutive size, charapita peppers are among the hottest available (50,000–100,000 Scoville) with an extraordinary fruity, citrusy, aromatic complexity that has made them the world's most expensive pepper by weight in specialty markets — a single small jar of charapita paste can command premium prices in European cuisine. The flavor is uniquely fruity and intensely floral, unlike the purely sharp heat of most hot peppers. Plants are prolific producers if given warmth and consistent moisture, loaded with dozens of tiny fruits that ripen from green to yellow to orange over several months. In zone 9, treat as an annual or overwinter indoors; in zone 10–12, plants can become productive multi-year shrubs.

plant_note: Start indoors two to three weeks early or direct sow in warm soil; melons dislike root disturbance.
directions: A true French cantaloupe too fragile to ship commercially, with smooth skin, light green stripes, and intensely fragrant creamy-orange flesh. Start seed indoors in peat pots two to three weeks before setting out, or direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm. Give vines full sun, warmth, and steady moisture while fruit develops. Harvest at full slip when the fruit detaches easily from the stem and the aroma turns rich and sweet.

plant_note: Needs consistent heat; use black mulch in cooler climates.
directions: This intensely fragrant French melon has smooth gray-green skin and deep orange, aromatic flesh. Start seed indoors three weeks before transplanting to gain a head start in short-season areas, handling the sensitive roots gently. Grow on black plastic mulch with row cover early to trap warmth, removing cover at flowering for pollinators. Reduce watering as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the fruit turns yellowish, smells sweet, and slips easily from the vine.

common_name: Charisma PMR Pumpkin (Cornell-Bred Powdery Mildew Resistant Jack-O-Lantern)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is reliably warm; intermediate powdery mildew resistance from Cornell breeding helps this later-maturing pumpkin hold healthy foliage through humid Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Sow directly in hills after the soil has warmed, spacing hills three to four and a half feet apart to give the reduced-length vines room to develop without crowding. Charisma PMR emerged from a joint Cornell University and Johnny's Selected Seeds breeding program and matures a bit later and lighter orange than earlier types like Racer, filling out to 14-18 pounds with a blocky, slightly russeted rind and a slender but sturdy handle. Its intermediate resistance to powdery mildew keeps leaves functional longer into the season, which matters most in regions where warm, humid nights favor the disease. Let fruit color fully and the rind harden before cutting from the vine, leaving several inches of stem attached to prolong storage life.

common_name: Charleston Belle Sweet Pepper (USDA Nematode-Resistant Sweet Bell)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Charleston Belle was developed by the USDA-ARS Vegetable Research at Charleston, South Carolina specifically to provide root-knot nematode resistance combined with excellent sweet bell pepper quality — making it one of the most important sweet bell pepper varieties for gardeners in the Gulf South and Southeast where root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita) routinely devastate standard pepper varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Charleston Belle is particularly important for Gulf South gardeners with heavy, sandy soils where root-knot nematodes are endemic — standard sweet bell varieties often show severe stunting and yield loss in nematode-infested soils where Charleston Belle performs normally. Charleston Belle was developed by USDA-ARS researchers at the U.S. Vegetable Laboratory in Charleston, South Carolina specifically to address one of the most significant problems in Southern pepper production: root-knot nematodes (primarily Meloidogyne incognita and M. arenaria), soil-dwelling parasites that infest the roots of peppers and virtually every other vegetable grown in the sandy soils of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, causing severe root galling, stunted growth, and dramatically reduced yields. Most commercial sweet bell pepper varieties are highly susceptible to these nematodes; Charleston Belle incorporates strong resistance derived from Capsicum chinense sources, allowing normal growth and fruit production in soils that would cripple susceptible varieties. The bell-shaped fruits are medium to large (3–4 lobes, 3–4 inches in diameter) and ripen from pale cream-yellow to red; they are crisp, sweet, and of excellent quality comparable to standard commercial bell varieties. Charleston Belle is an invaluable vegetable for Gulf South gardeners (zones 8–10) gardening in sandy or loamy soils where nematodes are a documented problem.

plant_note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; Charleston Gold ripens noticeably earlier than its Carolina Gold parent, an advantage in shorter growing seasons.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; keep the bed consistently saturated through the growing season, whether in a true flooded paddy or a well-watered garden bed. Charleston Gold was bred at Clemson University by crossing historic Carolina Gold rice with a semi-dwarf Southeast Asian variety to combine Carolina Gold's prized nutty, aromatic flavor with sturdier, shorter stalks that resist lodging and a shorter season to maturity. The gold-hulled, long grain cooks up fragrant and tender, much like its Carolina Gold parent, but the more compact plants stand up better to wind and rain and free up the bed several weeks earlier. Harvest when seed heads droop and the grain has turned golden-brown, then thresh and dry before hulling.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Charleston Gray is one of the largest home garden watermelons — fruits typically reach 25–35 pounds and the large vine needs generous space. Thump for a hollow sound and check the ground spot (which turns from white to creamy-yellow when ripe) to determine harvest. In zone 9 the long, hot summer is ideal for this variety, which thrives in heat and high-light conditions.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, fertile soil — watermelons are especially productive in sandy soils common to the Gulf South and Southeast; Charleston Gray is a 1954 All-America Selections award winner developed by the USDA in Charleston, South Carolina, and for several decades it was the dominant commercial and home-garden watermelon variety in the American South. The large, oblong fruits with distinctive pale gray-green skin and bright red, sweet, crisp flesh are resistant to anthracnose and fusarium wilt — the two most destructive watermelon diseases in the humid Southeast — which made Charleston Gray vastly superior to earlier varieties in southern garden conditions. The extra-thick rind (up to 1 inch) also gave exceptional shipping durability, which drove its commercial adoption. The sweetness and texture of Charleston Gray flesh represent the classic Southern watermelon flavor profile: intensely sweet, very juicy, with a fine-grained, melting texture that differs from modern seedless types. In zone 9 the heat and long growing season bring out the best flavor and maximum size.

plant_note: Start indoors two to three weeks early or direct sow in warm soil; needs a long, hot season.
directions: A classic oblong watermelon with greenish-gray rind and sweet red flesh, bred by the USDA for disease resistance to Fusarium wilt and anthracnose. Start seed indoors in peat pots or direct sow once soil is warm, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room. Water consistently while fruit sizes up, then ease off as melons approach ripeness to concentrate sweetness. Harvest when the ground spot turns creamy yellow and the tendril nearest the fruit dries.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Charleston Hot is a Southern cayenne-type that was bred for the humid, hot conditions of the Carolinas and Gulf Coast and has strong resistance to tobacco etch virus and tobacco mosaic virus — significant disease pressure in zone 8–9 pepper production.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Charleston Hot is a Clemson University-developed cayenne-type hot pepper (70,000–100,000 SHU) bred specifically for production in the hot, humid South. An All-America Selections winner, it produces abundantly on compact, upright plants and carries strong disease resistance to tobacco etch virus and tobacco mosaic virus, which is valuable in zone 8–9 where solanaceous virus pressure is high. The slim, tapered, 3–4 inch fruits ripen from yellow-green through yellow-orange to red; they are used fresh, dried, or ground into hot sauce and cayenne powder. The heavy yield of small-fruited plants makes this variety excellent for hot sauce production — a single mature plant can yield hundreds of pods per season. Dry fully ripe red fruits in a dehydrator or oven for ground cayenne.

plant_note: Direct sow an inch deep once soil has warmed well past 70°F, since this vigorous climbing sieva-type lima rots readily in cool, damp spring ground.
directions: Set a sturdy 6- to 8-foot trellis or pole at planting time, since this old South Carolina Lowcountry heirloom is a rampant climber that will not perform as a bush type. The small, flattened seeds are handsomely mottled brown-on-tan, giving the variety its name, and cook down tender with the rich, mild, buttery flavor Charleston cooks prize in a proper pot of butterbeans and rice. It sets pods steadily through the hottest, most humid weeks of a Gulf Coast summer when many snap beans have stalled, and because it flowers over a long season, regular picking at the green-shell stage keeps vines productive into fall. Save seed by letting some pods dry fully on the vine, since this open-pollinated heirloom breeds true.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 2–3 weeks before the last frost; in the Gulf South, Charleston Wakefield is also a reliable fall-through-winter crop from a late-summer sowing, taking mild freezes without damage.
directions: Set transplants 15–18 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; keep evenly watered as heads size up to avoid splitting. Charleston Wakefield was selected in South Carolina from Early Jersey Wakefield stock as a slightly larger, slightly later-maturing improvement, retaining the same distinctive pointed, conical head shape while producing bigger 3–4 pound heads with a bit more heat tolerance for Southern spring gardens. It became a standard commercial and home-garden variety across the South in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, valued for uniform heads, good tip-burn resistance, and dependable performance under the variable spring weather of the Gulf Coast and Southeast. The sweet, tender, finely textured heads are excellent fresh, in slaw, or braised. A dependable regional heirloom for zone 4–10 gardens.

common_name: Charlotte Swiss Chard (AAS-Winning Compact Red Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost date, or start indoors and transplant a couple weeks after; also suitable for fall sowing in mild climates.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into rich soil and keep evenly watered, since this compact hybrid rewards close, container-friendly spacing. Named an All-America Selections winner, it produces bright cherry-red stalks and veins beneath glossy, deeply savoyed dark green leaves on a notably uniform, tidy plant. Its shorter stature and vigorous regrowth after cutting make it well suited to raised beds and pots as well as open garden rows.

plant_note: Propagate by 12–18 inch stem cuttings stuck directly into moist soil in spring; unlike most cuttings, chaya cuttings establish easily even without rooting hormone. Plant in a site with full sun and well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in well-drained to sandy soil in full sun; chaya is a vigorous, heat-tolerant tropical shrub native to the Yucatan that produces enormous crops of large, spinach-like leaves year-round in frost-free climates. The leaves are exceptionally nutritious — very high in protein, calcium, iron, and carotenoids — but must be cooked for at least 5 minutes before eating, as raw leaves contain hydrocyanic glycosides that dissipate completely with cooking. Once cooked, leaves taste like a mild, slightly earthy spinach and can substitute in any cooked greens recipe. Chaya is extraordinarily productive: a single mature bush can yield over 10 pounds of leaves per week in warm weather. It tolerates drought, poor soil, and neglect better than almost any other vegetable.

plant_note: Propagate exclusively from stem cuttings (6–12 inch hardwood cuttings root readily in moist soil at 70°F+); true seeds are uncommon in cultivation. Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in full sun to partial shade. In zone 9, Chaya freezes to the ground in hard winters but resprouts vigorously from the root crown in spring. Mulch heavily. The stinging hairs on young leaves and stems cause skin irritation — wear gloves when harvesting. IMPORTANT: all parts of the plant are toxic if eaten raw — cooking for at least 5 minutes destroys the hydrocyanic glycosides and makes the leaves safe and nutritious.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Chaya is extremely drought-tolerant once established and adapts to poor, sandy, or clay soils with minimal fertilizer. Cnidoscolus chayamansa is a spinach tree native to the Yucatan Peninsula and Central America where it has been cultivated as a staple cooked green by the Maya civilization for over a millennium. The leaves are exceptionally nutritious — with higher concentrations of protein, calcium, iron, vitamin C, and beta-carotene than most leafy vegetables including kale and spinach — and Chaya has become a widely promoted food security crop in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. The plant is an incredibly productive cut-and-come-again perennial: harvest the top 6–10 inches of stem tips continuously through the warm season and the plant regrows rapidly. The large, dark-green, deeply-lobed, maple-like leaves are strikingly ornamental. CRITICAL SAFETY NOTE: Never eat Chaya raw — the fresh leaves contain hydrocyanic glycosides that can cause poisoning. Cook for a minimum of 5 minutes (boiling, steaming, or sautéing) to neutralize the toxins. Once cooked, the greens are safe and delicious, tasting like a mild spinach-collard cross. In zone 9, Chaya is one of the most productive warm-season leafy greens available, producing from May through November even in summer heat that wilts conventional spinach.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings 12–18 inches long in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost in zone 8–12; Chaya (Tree Spinach) is one of the most productive and nutritious leafy green vegetables available for warm-climate gardens — a Mesoamerican semi-succulent shrub producing abundant, bright-green, large, nutritious leaves year-round in tropical and subtropical climates — but MUST be cooked for 20 minutes before eating as raw leaves contain toxic hydrocyanic glycosides.
directions: IMPORTANT: Cook leaves for 20 minutes before eating — raw chaya contains toxic hydrocyanic acid glycosides; also do not cook in aluminum cookware as the reaction can cause illness. Plant cuttings in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained, fertile soil; Cnidoscolus chayamansa grows vigorously in warm climates, producing abundant leaves for harvest within 90 days of planting. Cnidoscolus chayamansa (Chaya, Tree Spinach, or Mayan Spinach) is a vigorous, semi-succulent, fast-growing shrub in the Euphorbiaceae family native to the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico and cultivated throughout Mesoamerica, the Caribbean, and increasingly in warm-climate gardens worldwide as one of the most productive and nutritious perennial leafy greens available for subtropical and tropical climates. The Maya civilization used chaya as a primary vegetable crop for thousands of years — and modern nutritional analysis confirms it is extraordinarily nutrient-dense: the leaves contain 2–3 times more protein, iron, calcium, and vitamin C than spinach (Spinacia oleracea), and are among the highest vitamin-K-containing vegetables known. Chaya is propagated exclusively from stem cuttings (it rarely sets seed in cultivation) and grows into a large, productive bush that can be harvested continuously throughout the year in warm climates — making it potentially the most productive perennial leafy green per square foot available for Gulf Coast, Florida, and subtropical gardens. CRITICAL WARNING: raw chaya leaves contain hydrocyanic acid glycosides that cause serious illness if eaten raw or undercooked — leaves must be boiled (not steamed or microwaved) for a minimum of 20 minutes and the cooking water discarded before eating.

plant_note: Start indoors 2–4 weeks before last frost by placing an entire fruit on its side in a pot of moist mix; transplant after all frost danger is past.
directions: Plant the whole fruit (it is the seed) on its side with the broad end slightly angled down, barely covered with moist soil; sprouting begins from the narrow end. Provide a very strong trellis as a single mature vine can reach 30 feet and produce dozens to hundreds of fruits per season. Harvest fruits when they are 3–6 inches long and the skin is still smooth and light green; older fruits become pithy and hard. In Zones 9–11, chayote is perennial and will produce an edible tuberous root as well as fruits; in cooler zones, grow as an annual by starting fresh each spring.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or in midsummer for a fall crop (most reliable season in the South); Cheddar is a yellow-orange cauliflower with dramatically higher beta-carotene content than white varieties — the orange color intensifies when cooked rather than fading, and the flavor is slightly sweeter and nuttier than standard white cauliflower, making it visually distinctive and nutritionally superior.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; set out transplants in rich, moist, well-drained soil 18–24 inches apart; keep consistently moist; in warm climates (zones 7–10) plant for fall harvest from summer transplants for best head development; harvest when heads are tight and before the curds begin to separate. Cheddar is a yellow-orange cauliflower that gets its remarkable color from high concentrations of beta-carotene — the same orange pigment found in carrots, sweet potatoes, and winter squash — resulting in orange cauliflower heads that retain and even intensify their color when cooked (unlike red cabbage, which loses color to cooking liquid). The orange coloring signals significantly higher nutritional value than white cauliflower: approximately 25 times more beta-carotene per serving, providing provitamin A activity that white cauliflower lacks. The flavor is slightly sweeter and nuttier than standard white varieties, and the heads hold their color well through roasting, steaming, and cauliflower 'steaks' — making Cheddar cauliflower one of the most visually dramatic and nutritionally enriched brassicas for the home garden. The AAS award-winning orange/yellow Cheddar type was developed by Cornell University researchers and initially commercialized by Bejo Seeds; it performs best as a fall crop in warm climates where summer transplants mature into cooler fall temperatures that favor head development.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Cheers carries high resistance to Fusarium yellows and intermediate resistance to black rot, and is notably resistant to head-splitting even in high heat, giving it flexibility across the Gulf South's spring and fall cabbage windows.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Cheers is a cabbage hybrid bred with high resistance to Fusarium yellows and intermediate resistance to black rot, two diseases that can persist in garden soil and spread through wet conditions. It is especially valued for resisting head-splitting even when hit by high heat or a sudden heavy rain after a dry spell, a common cause of wasted cabbage crops in changeable Gulf South weather. The round, dense, blue-green heads have good storage quality once harvested. Cut heads once firm and fully sized, and keep soil evenly moist through head formation for the best flavor and texture.

common_name: Chef's Choice Bicolor Tomato (AAS-Winning Gold-and-Pink Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Chef's Choice Bicolor is a vigorous indeterminate beefsteak tomato in the Chef's Choice series, bred for streaked golden-yellow-and-pink fruit with sweet, low-acid heirloom flavor, and needs sturdy staking or caging for the large fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Bicolor is an AAS-winning beefsteak tomato producing large fruit with a striking golden-yellow background streaked and blushed with rose-pink, giving each slice a marbled, sunset-like appearance on the plate as well as sweet, low-acid, heirloom-style flavor with far less of the tanginess of standard red tomatoes. It shares the reliable size, productivity, and disease resistance of the wider Chef's Choice series. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture.

common_name: Chef's Choice Black Tomato (AAS-Winning Dark Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Chef's Choice Black is a vigorous indeterminate beefsteak tomato in the Chef's Choice series, bred for dark, mahogany-colored fruit with rich, smoky-sweet flavor, and needs sturdy staking or caging for the large fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Black is an AAS-winning beefsteak tomato bringing the dense, complex, almost smoky-sweet flavor associated with heirloom black tomatoes into a modern hybrid, with large, dusky mahogany-red-brown fruit and a meaty, low-seed interior well suited to slicing. It joins the wider Chef's Choice color series — the fruit color changes but the reliable size, disease resistance, and productivity of the line carry through. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture.

common_name: Chef's Choice Orange Tomato (AAS-Winning Orange Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Chef's Choice Orange is a vigorous indeterminate beefsteak tomato bred from the heirloom Amana Orange with improved disease resistance, and needs sturdy staking or caging for the large fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Chef's Choice Orange is an AAS National Winner bred from the beloved heirloom Amana Orange, keeping its rich, sweet, low-acid flavor and bright orange beefsteak-size fruit while adding the disease resistance and productivity of a modern hybrid. Fruits regularly reach a pound or more, with a meaty, low-seed interior well suited to slicing, and the vivid orange color makes a striking addition to a mixed tomato platter or salad. Prune suckers lightly on the lower third of the plant to improve airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture even, since large-fruited beefsteaks are more prone to blossom-end rot and cracking under fluctuating moisture.

common_name: Chef's Choice Pink Tomato (AAS-Winning Large Pink Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50°F; in zone 9, set out in March for a spring crop and again in July for a fall crop that runs until frost.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile soil after all danger of frost, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vines and pruning to a few main leaders for the largest fruit. Chef's Choice Pink is an AAS-winning member of the Chef's Choice series of large-fruited, richly colored heirloom-type beefsteaks bred for exceptional flavor alongside modern disease resistance, producing smooth, deep rosy-pink 10–12 ounce fruit with the low-acid, sweet, complex flavor prized in classic pink heirlooms like Brandywine but on sturdier, more productive plants. Consistent watering and monthly feeding through the season support the heavy fruit load these large-fruited types carry, and mulching helps prevent blossom end rot during dry spells. The rich pink color and superior flavor make it a favorite for fresh eating and slicing, holding up well in Gulf South heat better than many thin-skinned pink heirlooms.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed; give plants extra room since the vines spread more than compact bush hybrids.
directions: Chefini was bred by Petoseed and released in 1965 as one of the first hybrid zucchinis to win an AAS award, valued for fruit so deeply dark green it reads almost black under garden light. The vigorous vines spread more than many modern compact hybrids, so give plants extra room or plan on a wider bed than typical bush-type zucchini. Harvest young at 6-8 inches for the most tender skin and flavor, and keep picking every couple of days since the sprawling growth habit hides fruit under the foliage. In Gulf Coast gardens, its early maturity lets gardeners get a harvest in before summer heat and squash vine borer pressure peak.

plant_note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65F; in zone 9 plant April-May for harvest August-September. Cheniere is an early-maturing LSU AgCenter long-grain release, useful where a shorter Gulf South growing window is a concern.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Cheniere is a very early-maturing, semi-dwarf long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter and named for the wooded ridges (cheniers) of coastal Louisiana, bred to reach harvest several days sooner than standard varieties like Cocodrie while keeping good milling quality and yield. The early maturity is useful for a second (ratoon) crop from the same plants after the first harvest, a practice common in the Gulf South where the long warm season allows regrowth from cut stubble to produce a smaller second harvest in fall. Keep the bed continuously saturated through the growing season for best results, and harvest the first crop when seed heads droop and turn golden-tan. After cutting the first crop high (leaving several inches of stubble), keep the field flooded and fertilized lightly to encourage ratoon regrowth for gardeners who want to try the extended Gulf South rice-growing technique.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 0-2 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed.
directions: Cultivate in full sun with consistent watering, staking taller plants once heavily laden with fruit. Bred in South Korea in the early 1980s as a cross between a Thai chile and a Korean landrace pepper, Cheongyang delivers notably more heat than standard Korean green chiles while keeping their thin walls and grassy flavor. Slice fresh into stews like jjigae, dip raw into ssamjang, or dry and grind for a fiery version of gochugaru.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; stake or cage this indeterminate vine.
directions: A cross of the heirlooms Cherokee Purple and Carbon that delivers rich purple-beefsteak flavor earlier, with more fruit and fewer cracks. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. The indeterminate vines need a tall cage or stake and periodic pruning for airflow. Water deeply and evenly, and harvest the ten to twelve ounce fruits when fully colored and slightly soft for peak flavor.

common_name: Cherokee Carbon Tomato (Deep-Dark Rich-Flavored Hybrid of Cherokee Purple)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Cherokee Carbon combines the heirloom flavor profile of Cherokee Purple with improved productivity and disease resistance from the Carbon parent — a practical advantage for gardeners who want deep dark tomato flavor with better reliability than pure heirlooms.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Cherokee Carbon is a hybrid cross between two celebrated dark tomatoes — Cherokee Purple and Carbon — that combines the outstanding flavor profile of Cherokee Purple (one of the most beloved dark heirloom tomatoes) with improved productivity, crack resistance, and disease resistance contributed by the Carbon parent. The result is a medium-large (8–12 oz), deep mahogany-to-near-black-brown tomato with characteristic green shoulders and the dense, complex, rich, earthy-sweet flavor that makes dark tomatoes so compelling — a flavor often described as having depth, smokiness, and wine-like complexity quite unlike standard red tomatoes. Cherokee Carbon achieves the flavor combination of its heirloom parent varieties while outperforming both in garden productivity: the plants set more fruit, crack less in wet weather, and show better resistance to soilborne diseases than the pure-heirloom parents. For Gulf South gardeners who have been frustrated by the relatively low productivity and disease susceptibility of pure heirloom dark varieties in the hot, humid zone 9 climate, Cherokee Carbon provides the dark tomato flavor experience with practical garden performance. The deep color results from anthocyanin accumulation in the skin enhanced by sun exposure. In zone 9, grow as a spring crop (February–June) for best fruit development before summer heat.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a true black/brown-type beefsteak related to Cherokee Purple, with darker, more chocolatey skin and flesh coloration; stake or cage firmly to support large fruits.
directions: Start seed indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, rich soil after all frost risk has passed; bury the stem deeply to develop a robust root system. Cherokee Chocolate is a sport or selection from Cherokee Purple with even darker, mahogany-brown skin and deep chocolate-red flesh, yielding large 10–16 ounce beefsteak fruits with an outstandingly rich, complex, slightly smoky flavor prized by growers who love the dark-fruited heirlooms. Harvest when fruit softens slightly at the blossom end since the unusual dark coloring makes it difficult to judge ripeness by color alone; shoulder color transitions from green to brownish rather than the typical red flush. Excellent raw or in salads where the dramatic interior color makes a striking visual impact.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Cherokee is a cold-hardy heirloom collard whose leaves take on a deeper purple tinge and sweeter flavor after frost.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning or transplanting seedlings to final spacing once they have a few true leaves. Cherokee is a Southeastern heirloom collard carried for generations by seed savers, notable for its blue-green leaves brushed with a purple tinge that deepens with cool weather, along with excellent cold hardiness and a mild, sweet flavor that improves further after frost. Harvest cut-and-come-again by picking the lower, outer leaves while the growing point continues to produce new leaves through fall and winter. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer to sustain steady leaf production, and monitor for cabbage worms and aphids, controlling with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide as needed.

common_name: Cherokee Gold Tomato (Golden-Orange Beefsteak, Cherokee Series)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Cherokee Gold belongs to the celebrated Cherokee family of heirloom beefsteaks alongside Cherokee Purple and Cherokee Chocolate, distinguished by large, smooth, golden-orange fruit with the same rich, complex, low-acid flavor and meaty texture that made the original Cherokee Purple a modern heirloom classic. The bright, sunny color makes it a favorite for mixed heirloom tomato platters and salads alongside its darker-fruited siblings, and the indeterminate vine produces reliably over a long season. Water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking on the smooth skin, and harvest once color deepens to full gold for the sweetest, most complex flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; an indeterminate green beefsteak from the Cherokee Purple line.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once the soil warms. This indeterminate heirloom, bred from the Cherokee Purple lineage, produces large fruits that ripen green with an amber blush and firm, juicy flesh. Stake or cage the tall vines, water evenly to prevent cracking, and judge ripeness by a slight softening since the color stays green.

common_name: Cherokee Long Ear Small Popcorn (Heirloom Native Popcorn)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 60°F in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; plant in blocks of at least four short rows rather than a single long row to ensure reliable wind pollination, and isolate from other corn varieties by at least several hundred feet to keep the strain true.
directions: Plant in blocks in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cherokee Long Ear Small is a slender-eared heirloom popcorn preserved through Cherokee seed-saving tradition and maintained today by heritage seed savers, notable for its small stature and small, narrow ears carrying rows of hard, glossy kernels in mixed colors from white through red and blue. Plants are shorter and the ears smaller than modern hybrid popcorn, but the strain is valued for its resilience, drought tolerance, and the deep cultural history tied to Southeastern Native American foodways. Allow ears to dry fully on the stalk until husks are papery and kernels are hard before harvesting; cure further indoors for several weeks in a well-ventilated spot before shelling and storing. Kernels pop reliably once fully cured, with a notably tender hull compared to many commercial popcorn hybrids. Save the best ears for the following year's seed to keep the strain vigorous and true.

common_name: Cherokee Long Greasy Bean (Shiny-Podded Appalachian Heirloom Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 60°F; greasy beans get their name from smooth, glossy pods that lack the fuzzy texture of most snap beans.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6-9 inches apart along a trellis or corn stalks. Cherokee Long Greasy is one of many named greasy bean varieties preserved within Cherokee communities of the Southern Appalachians, its pods smooth and shiny rather than fuzzy, a trait that gives the whole greasy bean class its name, with tender, flavorful pods good for snapping and flavorful seeds that also dry well for winter storage. It reflects a long tradition of bean cultivation and seed saving among Cherokee gardeners in the mountains of western North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia. Harvest young for snap beans or let pods dry fully on the vine for a dry bean crop.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; stake or cage this indeterminate heirloom.
directions: A century-old heirloom said to trace to the Cherokee people, prized for dusky purple-red fruits balancing sweetness with a hint of smoke. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil warms. This indeterminate vine needs sturdy support and regular pruning to keep it productive from summer to fall. Water consistently to reduce cracking and harvest when the shoulders stay dusky and the fruit yields slightly.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; stake or cage firmly as an indeterminate variety; the dusky coloring makes ripeness harder to judge — harvest when the shoulders soften and the fruit yields to gentle pressure.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant after all frost risk has passed into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun; Cherokee Purple is a large beefsteak heirloom tomato with a striking dusky rose to purple-maroon skin, deep reddish flesh with purple-green shoulders, and a rich, complex, smoky-sweet flavor that makes it a standout at the table and at farmers' markets. Harvest when fruits soften slightly at the blossom end and shoulders lose their green tinge, as the unusual coloring can make standard ripeness indicators unreliable. An outstanding variety for cooler summers; in zone 9 plant early for spring harvest.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; an indeterminate dusky-rose heirloom beefsteak.
directions: Start seeds indoors roughly six weeks before the last frost and set transplants deeply once nights are warm. This indeterminate heirloom yields large, dusky rose-purple beefsteaks with dense, meaty flesh and a rich, smoky-sweet flavor. Provide strong support and even watering, and harvest when the shoulders take on their characteristic dusky hue and the fruit yields to gentle pressure.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after all frost danger is past and soil is warm; give vines a full summer since this long-season moschata needs 100+ frost-free days to fully cure.
directions: This Cherokee heirloom from the North Carolina and North Georgia mountains produces medium-sized, buff-tan skinned fruit with dense, deep orange, sweet-nutty flesh well suited to pies, soups, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata, it carries the family's excellent resistance to squash vine borer and better tolerance of humid, disease-pressured Southern summers than most Cucurbita pepo pumpkins. Let vines sprawl generously, since a single plant can cover a large area and set several fruit; harvest once the rind resists a thumbnail and stems have begun to dry and corky. Cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot, making it a reliable keeper crop for fall and winter kitchens.

common_name: Cherokee Trail of Tears Bean (Black Snap Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis or poles 6–8 feet tall; Cherokee Trail of Tears bean is a black-seeded pole bean variety historically carried by the Cherokee people during their forced removal to Oklahoma in 1838–1839 — one of the most culturally significant American heirloom beans, maintained for nearly two centuries as a living connection to Cherokee agricultural heritage and the tragedy of the Trail of Tears.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost at the base of poles, trellis, or fence 6–8 feet tall; provide support immediately as vines grow rapidly; thin to 4–6 inches apart in rows 24–30 inches apart. Cherokee Trail of Tears bean is one of the most historically significant heirloom varieties in American cultivation — a pole bean carried as seeds by members of the Cherokee Nation during the forced removal from their homelands in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama to what is now Oklahoma in 1838–1839, the journey now known as the Trail of Tears in which more than 4,000 Cherokee people died. The black-seeded, purple-streaked pod variety was maintained by Cherokee families after their arrival in Indian Territory and has been preserved as a living memorial to this history, entering mainstream heirloom seed preservation networks through the Seed Savers Exchange in the 20th century. The vigorous vines produce long, slender pods with deep purple to black markings at the snap bean stage; fully mature dry seeds are glossy black and excellent for cooking as a dry bean. The dual snap-and-dry utility, vigorous productivity, and deep cultural history make Cherokee Trail of Tears one of the most important heirloom beans available.

common_name: Cherokee Wax Bush Bean (Heirloom Yellow Wax Snap Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Cherokee Wax is an open-pollinated heirloom that has been maintained for generations as a reliable yellow wax bean for home garden production. In zone 9, plant March–May and again in late August–September for fall production. The open-pollinated nature allows seed-saving from year to year — select the straightest, most productive plants for the best maintained seed stock.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart after last frost; harvest when pods are 5–6 inches long and bright golden-yellow before pods begin to become stringy. Cherokee Wax is a traditional open-pollinated yellow wax bush bean that has been grown in American gardens since at least the early 20th century — one of the oldest continuously maintained wax bean varieties in American seed commerce. Unlike modern hybrid wax beans selected for mechanical harvest uniformity, Cherokee Wax represents the traditional wax bean type: productive, reliable, with good flavor, and completely open-pollinated so seed can be saved from season to season. The pods are bright golden-yellow, fairly straight, moderately thick-podded, with the characteristic waxy skin that gives the wax bean type its name. The eating quality is excellent — the thick walls provide a satisfying snap and the mild, slightly sweet wax bean flavor is cleaner and lighter than green bean types. Cherokee Wax has a loyal following among seed-saving gardeners and those who prefer open-pollinated varieties for independence from commercial seed sources.

common_name: Cherokee White Eagle Corn (Native American Flint-Dent White Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; Cherokee White Eagle is a Cherokee Nation heirloom corn maintained by members of the Cherokee people across the original homelands of the southern Appalachians and Ozarks — it is a white flour/dent-type corn notable for occasional dark kernels in the cob that create an eagle-wing pattern, a characteristic considered sacred in Cherokee tradition.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks for pollination; allow ears to fully dry on the stalk before harvest for the best grain quality; Cherokee White Eagle makes excellent hominy (nixtamalized corn), grits, and cornbread; select seed from ears showing the traditional dark-kernel eagle pattern to maintain the variety's distinctive characteristic. Cherokee White Eagle is a corn variety maintained and revered by the Cherokee people, one of the Five Civilized Tribes of the American Southeast (originally from the mountains of North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia), who grew multiple varieties of corn as a primary food staple for centuries before European contact. The corn takes its name from the visual pattern that occasionally appears on a cob: most kernels are white, but scattered dark blue-black or red-black kernels create a pattern that, when viewed on the ear, suggests the spread wings of an eagle — a symbol of great importance in Cherokee culture. The proportion and distribution of dark kernels varies among individual ears, and Cherokee tradition holds that cobs with the most pronounced eagle pattern should be selected for seed saving to perpetuate both the variety and its spiritual significance. As a grain, Cherokee White Eagle is a flour/dent-type corn producing large, soft, white kernels that grind into fine, flavorful cornmeal and are excellent for making hominy (the traditional Indigenous preparation where corn is nixtamalized with alkali — wood ash or lime — to improve nutritional availability). The variety adapts well to the heat and humidity of the southeastern United States where it was developed.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again every 10-14 days for a continuous harvest through cool weather.
directions: Cherriette is an F1 hybrid improvement on the classic Cherry Belle type, bred for extra uniformity and unusual resistance to pithiness even if roots are left in the ground past ideal size. Sow seed shallowly in loose, stone-free soil and thin early so roots have room to size up into smooth, bright cherry-red globes with dense, crisp white flesh. Its speed and evenness make it a favorite for market growers who need a reliable, uniform crop, while home gardeners appreciate that a missed harvest window rarely ruins the eating quality.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather; succession sow every one to two weeks for continuous harvest.
directions: A fast, easy Holland heirloom producing round, bright-red radishes with mild, crisp white flesh in about a month. Sow seed directly half an inch deep and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots. Keep soil evenly moist and grow in cool weather to avoid pithy, overly pungent roots. Harvest promptly when roots reach about an inch across, since they turn woody if left in the ground too long.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Cherry Bomb is an All-America Selections winner with round, cherry-like fruits ripening to red, moderate heat of 2,500–5,000 SHU, and thick walls ideal for fresh eating, pickling, and stuffing — one of the most versatile and productive hot-pepper garden standards.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cherry Bomb is an All-America Selections winning pepper producing compact, globe-shaped, 1.5–2 inch fruits that resemble large cherries; at 2,500–5,000 SHU (mild-to-medium heat) it is significantly hotter than banana peppers but much milder than jalapeños, with thick, juicy, crunchy walls and excellent sweet pepper flavor with a moderate bite. Fruits ripen from green to brilliant red and are prized for stuffing whole (the round shape makes perfect stuffed cherry peppers), pickling in oil and vinegar in the Italian style, and fresh slicing. Compact, bush-type plants are highly productive and perform well in containers. Widely available in the Italian-American food tradition as pickled cherry peppers in antipasto.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; ideal for hanging baskets and containers.
directions: A compact, cascading cherry tomato bred for containers and hanging baskets, spilling clusters of bright red one-and-a-half-inch fruits. Start seed indoors six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights warm. Its trailing habit is ornamental and needs little staking, making it ideal for balconies and patios. Keep container soil evenly moist and harvest the abundant fruit throughout the season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–85°F; transplant after nights consistently stay above 50°F in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.2–6.8) soil with a cage or tall stake for support.
directions: Start seeds 1/4 inch deep indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–85°F and transplant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil after nights consistently stay above 50°F; cherry tomatoes are the most prolific and carefree of all tomato types, producing hundreds of small, intensely sweet fruits per plant from midsummer through frost with minimal attention. Most cherry types are indeterminate (continue growing and fruiting all season) and need a tall cage or stake; compact determinate cherry types like 'Tumbling Tom' and 'Tumbler' are ideal for containers. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and fruit cracking; irregular watering causes cherry tomatoes to split their skins. Harvest when fruits are fully colored and come off the vine easily with gentle pressure. Outstanding for container growing, children's gardens, and fresh snacking.

common_name: Cherry Vanilla Quinoa (Deep Cherry-Red and Cream Bicolor Quinoa)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cherry Vanilla quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather.
directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; quinoa performs best in cool weather and can struggle through extended hot, humid summers. Cherry Vanilla bears striking bicolor seed heads combining deep cherry-red and creamy vanilla-white tones on the same plant, one of the most visually dramatic quinoa selections available and prized as much for its ornamental cut-flower value as for its edible seed. The tall, colorful seed-head spikes make an eye-catching addition to a cutting garden as well as a productive grain crop. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before rinsing to remove the bitter saponin coating and cooking or storing.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes; harvest the following summer.
directions: A hardneck heirloom from the Republic of Georgia with purple-streaked bulbs and nine to ten easy-to-peel cloves of rich, mellow flavor. Plant individual cloves pointed end up about two inches deep in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, and mulch for winter protection. Snap off the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into bulb formation. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place before storage.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Cheyenne is a classic All-America Selections winning cayenne cultivar bred for a compact, upright habit with fruit held above the foliage, making harvest easy and keeping pods off the ground.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Cheyenne is a long-established All-America Selections winning cayenne cultivar bred for a compact, upright plant that holds its thin, curved, hot red pods well above the foliage rather than letting them dangle near the soil, keeping fruit cleaner and easier to spot and harvest. The classic sharp cayenne heat and flavor make it well suited to drying and grinding into cayenne powder, pickling, or fresh use in cooking. Its compact size makes it a good choice for containers and smaller garden beds where a sprawling pepper plant would be impractical. Harvest regularly for fresh use, or let a portion of the crop ripen fully red and dry on the plant for storage as dried cayenne.

plant_note: Sow after last frost; chia is a short-day plant that flowers in fall, so it is best suited to climates with a long frost-free autumn.
directions: Surface-sow seed on a firm, moist seedbed and barely press in, as chia seed is mucilaginous and will stick to the surface when wet; thin plants to 18–24 in once seedlings emerge. Chia does not respond well to transplanting and should be direct-sown where it will grow. The plant flowers in autumn as day length shortens and produces whorled spikes of small purple flowers followed by seed-filled calyces; harvest stalks when the calyces begin to dry and before birds consume the seed. Place harvested stalks head-first into paper bags to finish drying, then shake out seed and screen away debris; seeds are rich in omega-3 fatty acids, calcium, and fiber.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; a compact bushy edamame with large green beans.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep directly in warm soil after frost, as soybeans dislike transplanting. The compact, bushy plants set clusters of plump pods that fill with large, sweet green beans. Harvest the whole plant when most pods are full but still bright green, then boil the pods briefly and pop out the tender edamame.

common_name: Chicago Pickling Cucumber (1888 Heirloom Pickling Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Chicago Pickling is a productive 19th-century heirloom bred specifically for commercial and home pickle production, still favored for its high yields of blocky, uniform fruit.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after the soil has warmed, and provide a trellis or ample vine room. Chicago Pickling dates to the late 1880s and was long a mainstay of Midwestern commercial pickle production, producing an abundant crop of medium-green, black-spined fruit that holds its blocky shape well through brining and fermentation. Pick fruit small, at around 2-4 inches, for classic dill and bread-and-butter pickles, and harvest frequently to keep the vigorous vines setting new fruit. Because it is open-pollinated, gardeners can save seed season to season, continuing a variety with over a century of documented use in American home and commercial pickling.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost date; chickpeas prefer a cool start but need warm, dry weather to mature properly.
directions: Sow chickpeas 2 in deep in light, well-drained soil with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH; they perform poorly in heavy, waterlogged ground. The plants produce distinctive sticky, glandular hairs on stems and pods that can cause a mild skin reaction in sensitive individuals, so harvest with gloves. Pick pods when they are green and plump for fresh eating, or leave plants to dry fully in place and harvest entire plants when 90% of pods have turned tan. Shell and sun-dry for a day before long-term storage.

plant_note: Scatter seed on the surface of moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade or full sun; chickweed requires cool temperatures (35–60°F) and fades quickly when weather warms above 65–70°F. In zone 9a it is a useful winter green from November through March, self-sowing to establish as a permanent winter groundcover in suitable spots.
directions: Scatter seed on the surface of moist, fertile soil in partial shade in fall; chickweed is one of the most nutritious and widely available wild edibles in the world — a cool-season annual that appears in gardens, lawns, and disturbed areas throughout winter, producing mats of small, oval-leaved stems with tiny, deeply notched white petals that look like stars (the genus name Stellaria means 'star'). The tender shoots and leaves are rich in vitamins C, B-complex, iron, and calcium, used fresh in salads, smoothies, and as a potherb (briefly cooked like spinach). The flavor is mild and pleasant, reminiscent of corn silk. In zone 9a it grows vigorously from November through March and self-sows prolifically, providing free winter salad greens in any garden patch where temperatures stay below 70°F. A traditional forage food eaten across Europe and Asia for centuries and by many indigenous North American peoples.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this mid-season red round variety is well suited to northern-tier growing regions.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Chieftain is a red-skinned, white-fleshed round potato released from a USDA and North Dakota State University breeding program in the 1960s for the Upper Midwest fresh market. The smooth, deep red skin holds its color well in storage, and the moist, moderately waxy flesh boils cleanly without excessive breakdown, making it a dependable variety for potato salad and general table use. It has a strong reputation among northern growers for consistent yields and good storage quality compared to older red cultivars of its era. Choose it over Red Norland or Red Pontiac when a slightly later, higher-yielding red round is wanted for storage rather than earliest harvest.

common_name: Chieftain Savoy Cabbage (1938 AAS-Winning Heirloom Savoy)
plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or sow in early-to-midsummer for a fall crop, since Chieftain reaches full size only in cool weather and improves in flavor after light frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost, or in early-to-midsummer for a fall crop, since Chieftain reaches full size only in cool weather and its flavor improves markedly after light frost. Chieftain Savoy is a 1938 All-America Selections winner bred by Ferry-Morse, producing large, nearly round, densely savoyed dark green heads averaging four to six pounds with a tender, sweet crunch that distinguishes savoy types from smooth-leaved cabbage. It is notably cold hardy and holds well in the garden into late fall and early winter, making it a dependable choice for extending the cabbage harvest well past the first frosts. Space plants generously to allow the broad, crinkled outer leaves to develop fully, and side-dress with nitrogen midseason to support the long growing period to a full-sized head.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; squash resents root disturbance.
directions: An early, heavy-yielding summer squash on upright, compact two-foot bushes with moderate powdery mildew resistance. Sow seed directly one inch deep once the soil is warm and settled. The open, upright habit makes harvesting easy and improves airflow around the plants. Pick fruit young and tender, checking daily at peak season since squash size up quickly.

plant_note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed near a trellis or open ground where its vigorous, fig-shaped-leaved vines can climb or sprawl, watering regularly during establishment.
directions: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed near a trellis or open ground where its vigorous, fig-shaped-leaved vines can climb or sprawl, watering regularly during establishment. Distinct from other Cucurbita species, this cool-tolerant Andean and Mesoamerican heirloom produces watermelon-striped fruit with black seeds and stringy white flesh traditionally candied into the Mexican sweet cabello de ángel or brewed into a folk remedy. Its unusual cold hardiness for a squash and ability to fruit at higher elevations made it a long-season staple crop from Mexico through the Andes. Fruit stores exceptionally well, often lasting a year or more in cool, dry conditions.

common_name: Chile Puya (Mexican Dried Chile, Guajillo's Fiery Cousin)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost and set plants out after danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Grow as a standard warm-season pepper in full sun with well-drained soil, watering deeply but infrequently once established. Chile Puya produces slender pods closely resembling guajillo but shorter, narrower, and notably hotter, typically left on the plant to ripen fully to deep red before drying. Dried pods are toasted and rehydrated for robust red salsas, adobos, and marinades across central and western Mexico, often blended alongside guajillo and ancho for layered heat and flavor.

common_name: Chile de Agua (Fresh Oaxacan Valley Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Chile de Agua is a fresh green pepper of Oaxaca's central valleys, used widely for rajas and stuffed chile dishes.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Chile de Agua produces medium-to-large, tapered, pale to medium green pods with mild-to-moderate heat, a defining fresh chile of Oaxaca's central valleys used widely for roasted rajas (strips) and stuffed chile dishes in Oaxacan cuisine. The productive plants perform well over a long warm season, and pods are typically harvested and used green rather than allowed to ripen to red. Harvest regularly to encourage continued production through the summer.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil has warmed; chile de arbol thrives in hot conditions and produces heavily in Gulf Coast gardens throughout summer.
directions: Start indoors and transplant to warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; chile de arbol (tree chili) is a tall, upright-growing Mexican pepper variety that produces prolific clusters of slender, 2–3 inch pointed red fruits that ripen from green through red and are both the primary flavor base of traditional Mexican table salsas and one of the most frequently used chilis in Mexican restaurant kitchens. The heat level is substantial (15,000–30,000 SHU) with a clean, slightly smoky, grassy flavor. They are dried and toasted whole for use in salsas de chile de arbol or ground into powder. The plant's name comes from its tree-like growth habit — stems become woody and the plant can produce prolifically for years in frost-free zones 9–11.

common_name: Chilhuacle Negro Pepper (Black Chilhuacle, Oaxacan Black Mole Chile)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in a warm location (80–85°F); transplant after all frost danger passes; chilhuacle negro is a large-fruited Mexican landrace chile that takes 110–130 days from transplant to reach its distinctive dark reddish-black mature color — the key stage for authentic Oaxacan mole negro and mole coloradito sauces.
directions: Start indoors in a warm seedling tray 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after all frost danger passes; chilhuacle plants are large and productive but slow-maturing — plan the long growing season carefully; harvest when fruits turn fully dark reddish-black to black and the skin begins to feel slightly leathery; dry thoroughly on screens in a single layer.
